title: Robust Path Planning and Execution for Multi-Agent Systems
abs: In many real-world applications such as automated warehouses and aircraft-towing, agents including robots and automated guided vehicles move around concurrently to carry out tasks. To avoid collisions and deadlocks, we need to carefully plan the paths and coordinate the execution of the plans for agents. However, existing research work suffers from two major deficiencies. First, while path planning has been extensively studied, designing robust and effective execution policies of the path plans has received less attention. Robust plan execution is not only crucial but also challenging because agents may suffer from unforeseen failures and anomalies during the execution. Second, classical path planning usually assumes that time is discretized into timesteps and an agent either waits at its current location or moves to an adjacent location in each timestep. Nevertheless, in practical applications, time flows continuously and move actions are tightly coupled with trajectories and do not always take uniform times to complete. In this project, we will study robust path planning and execution for multi-agent systems to address these deficiencies. The main objective of this project is to develop a path planning and execution framework to deal with delays arising from unforeseen circumstances in the operation of multi-agent systems. We shall consider a general model of multi-agent systems characterized by continuous time notions, non-uniform action

title:
Enhancing the Foundation of Relative Smooth Optimization: 
New Non-Euclidean Lipschitz Toolkit and Better Optimality Measure
abs: Over the past decades, the optimization community has witnessed a wave of breakthroughs in the global convergence and complexity theory of first-order methods (FOMs), in which the exploitation of the gradient global Lipschitz continuity (GGLC) assumption plays a key role. However, despite the wide adoption of GGLC, many problems do not satisfy this condition. Examples include regularized quadratic or Poisson inverse problems, D-optimal design, generalized volumetric optimization, etc. For stochastic composite optimization (SCO) topic, it is even generally observed that a paper’s theoretical analysis relies on GGLC while the proposed applications violate GGLC, leading to gaps between the practice and theory of FOMs. Due to these gaps, there have been significant efforts to derive new convergence and complexity analysis framework without relying on GGLC. In this proposal, we shall study the FOMs under the relative smoothness condition, which is a popular new concept proposed around 2017 that attempts to relax the GGLC assumption. Many leading researchers in optimization community contributed to the initial establishment of this concept, and a relative smooth mirror descent (RSMD) method has been proposed. Despite the numerous follow-ups in the recent years, the convergence behavior and complexity of RSMD is still not well-understood for nonconvex problems. Several gaps still need to be cleared. First, we observe that if not additionally assuming strong conditions that makes the problem essentially GGLC, all the existing convergence and complexity analysis of RSMD typically studies some algorithmic residual optimality measures and hence provide an O(ϵ^(-2)) iteration complexity. Such result seems to convey the message that nonconvex optimization under relative smoothness is as easy as that under GGLC, as both of them share the same O(ϵ^(-2)) complexity. However, is this true? In this proposal we would like to provide a negative answer. The relative smooth problems have its inherent difficulties. The above misleading message is because the widely adopted algorithmic residual type optimality measures are only well-behaved under GGLC, but they tend to overstate the quality of a solution under relative smooth setting, indicating the existence of solutions with small algorithmic residual, but badly-behaved under standard optimality measure like minimal limiting Fréchet subdifferential. Due to this phenomenon, to find a solution with O(ϵ) minimal limiting Fréchet subdifferential for nonconvex relatively smooth problems, the actual complexity of RSMD can be much higher than O(ϵ^(-2)). Such a misuse of optimality measure widely invalidates the global convergence and complexity analysis of RSMD. title: Scalable Mixed Integer Programming Computation for Interpretable Decision Making
abs: The rise of modern applications for Decision-Making Problems (DMPs) has dramatically increased the number of decision variables in their Mixed Integer Programming (MIP) formulations. This surge is prevalent across various fields, including operations management, transportation, logistics, supply chain, power systems, signal processing, and data analytics. Such an increase in decision variables significantly impedes the computational scalability of finding optimal solutions and diminishes the interpretability of these decisions by decision-makers. This proposal addresses the above challenges through Interpretable DMPs (IDMPs), which incorporate an additional cardinality constraint to enhance interpretability. To further improve scalability, this proposal seeks to explore variable reduction methods designed to reduce or pre-identify/tighten decision variables in given MIPs, regardless of the solving methods employed. Unlike existing methods, this proposal argues that a great deal of information and structures inherent in IDMPs should be leveraged when developing variable reduction methods. Specifically, this proposal will focus on the following two paradigms: P1: Variable reduction via low-dimensional embedding. This paradigm focuses on improving variable reduction methods for High-dimensional-Output IDMPs (HO-IDMPs) via embedding techniques. Recently, the Principal Investigator (PI) and his Ph.D. student developed a computationally scalable framework for a special case of HO-IDMPs. They demonstrated that the framework preserves the same order of training and prediction loss before and after compression (a low-dimensional embedding method), even under arbitrary or relatively weak sample set conditions. This work can be regarded as a first step towards designing novel & better variable reduction methods for proposed HO-IDMPs, and the PI intends to investigate the answer to the proposed open questions. P2: Variable reduction via screening & probing. This paradigm focuses on identifying and certifying the quality of subsets of decision variables based on solutions from convex relaxations. Existing screening methods mainly utilize convex perspective relaxation of standard sparsity constraints and employ closed-form Fenchel duals on component-wise decomposable elements of their objective functions. A preliminary ongoing project by the PI and his collaborators generalizes existing results on three key aspects: (i) the tightness of the provided convex perspective relaxation, (ii) the component-wise decomposability of the objective function, and (iii) algorithms for generating cutting planes that partition the feasible set for screening. Moreover, this proposal's findings are anticipated to foster related research directions, including the design and analysis of dimensionality reduction methods for samples in data science, a computation framework for the Smart "Predict-then-Optimize" (SPO) scheme, and the development of novel branch-and-bound or column/row

title: Automated Single Cell Impedance Bioanalysis and Predictive Metabolic Modeling for Culture Media Development in Cell Therapy Manufacturing (SIMBA)
abs: Background In cell-based biomanufacturing, bioreactor is an efficient way to scale up cell production for stem cell cultures (e.g. 3D stem cell aggregates) and culture media optimization plays a vital role in bioprocess development. There is an unmet need to develop novel process analytical tools (PATs) for automatic direct sampling/cell analysis and new innovations to accelerate media formulation or culture process. Specific aims In this proposal, we aim to develop an innovative platform solution that integrates novel microfluidics PAT (µPAT) for single cell/aggregate impedance bioanalysis, spent media metabolite profiling and genome-scale metabolic modelling to guide culture media development. We will demonstrate proof-of-feasibility by manufacturing multipotent cardiovascular progenitors (CVPs) using a laminin-based differentiation protocol. Hypothesis Label-free µPAT offer direct bioanalysis of single cells/aggregates to resolve 3D stem cell aggregates heterogeneity in size and viability. Automated µPAT for closed sampling methodologies (cells and spent media) and advanced modelling approaches can accelerate culture media optimization to produce CVPs of defined sizes. Methodology Aim 1: Microfluidic PAT (µPAT) for on-line impedance bioanalysis of single cells and spent media metabolite profiling. We will design and fabricate an integrated “sample in-answer out” microfluidic PAT (µPAT) platform for automated on-line sampling of 3D adipose-derived mesenchymal stem cells (ADSC) aggregates (model cell line). Cell aggregates will undergo a novel “vortex-assisted” buffer exchange for sample washing, spent media collection and enzymatic cell dissociation for multi-frequency impedance bioanalysis to quantify viable cell density (VCD) at single cell resolution. Spent media will be processed on-chip for real-time metabolite profiling of glucose, ammonia and lactate using electrochemical enzymatic biosensors. Aim 2: Predictive metabolic modeling and impedance validation for culture media formulation. We will apply genome-scale metabolic model (GEM) of stem cells, a network-based tool that incorporate metabolic information of a cell through associated gene-protein-reaction (GPR) rules and metabolites to characterise intracellular metabolic state. VCD and metabolites data obtained from Aim 1 will be fed into the GEM to identify metabolic bottleneck and predict optimal culture formulation through in-silico in-house DoE algorithm for maximal biomass production of stem cells (ADSC, human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) and CVP). Predicted media formulation will be validated experimentally. Aim 3: Multiplexed µPAT impedance sorter for cardiovascular progenitors (CVP) size-based sorting and biological characterisation. title: Integrated photonic source for entanglement generation with subwavelength 2D materials
abs: The main goal of the project is to develop a universal and broadband source of entangled-photon pairs integrated on a photonic platform. The compactness and portability of the source will ensure it is adapted to the most technologically relevant quantum communication and quantum computing schemes, including entanglement distribution and quantum teleportation. The new integrated quantum source will be based on van der Waals NbOX2 (X=Cl, Br, I) and 3R transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) materials with subwavelength thickness. The reduced thickness of the nonlinear material, smaller than its coherence length, will ensure spectrally broadband nonlinear optical response and high angular tunability, overcoming at a stroke the limitations of standard bulk nonlinear materials. These advantages come at the expense of a reduction in the nonlinear emission intensity, which scales down as the square of the thickness. To overcome this practical drawback we will couple the subwavelength quantum sources with dielectric/metal stacks and dielectric photonic resonators in two configurations, compatible with vertical extraction of the entangled-photon pairs and with integrated photonics, respectively. Therein, enhanced light-matter coupling will increase the emission rate of photon pairs. Our preliminary results show that the second order nonlinear response of van der Waals materials can be indeed enhanced by at least two orders of magnitude. In view of exploiting these new sources of entangled-photon pairs in photonic quantum computing platforms, we propose to integrate these subwavelength sources in a SiN photonic chip, as SiN displays a much larger transparency than SOI across a broad wavelength range. This integration will be achieved thanks to the versatility and resilience of van der Waals materials, which can be mechanically transferred onto foreign materials without sacrificing their intrinsic physical properties, in particular their second order susceptibility. Once integrated onto a basic photonic circuit, comprising of a waveguide and two out-couplers, we will demonstrate the generation of entangled-photon pairs by parametric down conversion and their efficient coupling into guided modes for the first time, proving thereby the compatibility and the enhanced generation rate enabled by the dielectric/metal cavities. Overall, our project aims to provide a universal source of entangled-photon pairs closing the gap between applied quantum technologies and fundamental physics, which is at the heart of momentum-conservation breaking in subwavelength materials.
kw: Entangled photon; photonic chip; subwavelength; nonlinear photonics; quantum photonics; van der Waals

title: Epitaxial organic-inorganic halide perovskites (ECHO)
abs: The ECHO project aims to transform the synthesis of metal halide perovskite (MHP) thin films through epitaxial growth techniques on industrially compatible substrates. By eliminating grain boundaries, the project addresses key limitations of conventional polycrystalline perovskites, including material degradation, restricted carrier diffusion, and ion migration. Using a scalable thermal evaporation epitaxial deposition method, ECHO will develop high-quality MHP films with enhanced charge carrier mobility, reduced defects, and improved phase stability, making them ideal for integration into optoelectronic devices. The project is structured into three main phases. First, it will establish vacuum-based epitaxial growth of MHP films on substrates like sapphire and GaN-on-sapphire, examining the impact of crystal symmetry, lattice mismatch, and interface chemistry on film quality. Second, it will benchmark optoelectronic properties against polycrystalline films, focusing on carrier mobility, diffusion length, and defect density using advanced spectroscopic techniques. The project will also explore strain engineering and develop Pb-Sn alloyed epitaxial MHP for tunable infrared applications. Third, epitaxial MHP films will be integrated into light-emitting diodes (LEDs) to evaluate their efficiency, operational stability, and interface engineering strategies. Supported by NTU’s world-class facilities and the team’s expertise in perovskite epitaxy, ECHO builds on successful preliminary growth of highly oriented PbI₂ films. By addressing long-standing stability challenges, the project will unlock high-efficiency, durable optoelectronic devices for infrared applications, bridging the gap between perovskites and traditional semiconductors to drive next-generation photonic innovations

title: A Multi-source Data Fusion and Learning Framework to Forecast Travel Demand with Social Networks
abs: Traditional travel demand forecasting models rely on infrequent household travel surveys, which capture a limited sample and fail to reflect sudden behavioral shifts caused by factors such as emerging mobility trends and system disruptions like pandemics. As a result, transportation planning decisions often lack the precision needed to respond to dynamic urban mobility patterns. To address these limitations, this study develops a data-driven, end-to-end travel demand forecasting framework that fuses household survey data with real-time travel records from mobile devices and transit smart cards. This integration provides a more comprehensive and frequently updated representation of travel behavior, allowing for more accurate demand forecasts. Another key innovation is the consideration of social network effects, recognizing that many travel decisions—especially for leisure activities, carpooling, and shared mobility—are interdependent. To model these interactions, the study introduces a space-time coincidence matching approach, which reconstructs population-wide social networks and integrates them into travel demand models. This approach has two key applications. First, it ensures that transport planners can forecast mobility patterns with social network considerations without relying on costly and infrequent surveys, making travel demand prediction more responsive and cost-effective. The model will be validated in Singapore by leveraging pre- and post-pandemic data. Second, beyond improving the resilience of transportation planning, this research has significant implications for epidemiology and public health. By leveraging mobility and social network data, this study will enable the creation of dynamic, high-resolution contact matrices, improving the accuracy of epidemiological models. These enhanced models will provide more precise predictions of disease transmission, aiding policymakers in designing better containment strategies, public health interventions, and resource allocation plans during outbreaks. The proposed framework will be tested using COVID-19 data from Singapore, demonstrating its ability to inform real-time decision-making for future pandemics.
kw: Passively collected mobility data; Data fusion; Social network effects; Travel demand forecasting; epidemiological models

title: Advanced Photonic AI Chips for Robust Predictions of Stochastic Process Using Photonic Bayesian Neural Networks
abs: This proposal aims to develop a Photonic Bayesian Neural Network (PBNN) that leverages photonic randomness, hybrid thermo-optic (TO) and electro-optic (EO) tuning, and dual-layer photonic platforms to enhance probabilistic computing. Traditional electronic neural networks, including Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) based on transistors and memristors, face scalability and power-efficiency challenges. Photonic Neural Networks (PNNs) offer superior speed and energy efficiency but suffer from deterministic weight constraints and noise susceptibility. This project overcomes these limitations by developing a tunable Photonic Random Number Generator (PRNG) as a key building block for PBNNs, enabling independent control of mean (μ) and standard deviation (σ) in probabilistic weight distributions. The research is structured into three key tasks: Task A: Design and implementation of PRNGs using photonic noise sources, with different architectures (single-device and cascaded configurations) to ensure tunability and scalability. Task B: Construction of PBNNs on single-layer platforms using PRNGs, comparing TO-based Si/SiN implementations and EO-based AlN platforms to assess speed, power efficiency, and tunability. Task C: Development of dual-layer photonic platforms, integrating hybrid TO/EO tuning to decouple μ and σ tuning, ensuring flexibility, energy efficiency, and scalability for large-scale PBNN applications. The feasibility of this project is supported by prior research in photonic computing, photonic modulators, and neural networks, as well as collaborations with A*STAR IME for AlN-on-Si monolithic integration. Experimental validation will be performed on uncertainty-aware tasks, including MNIST image classification, financial forecasting, and medical diagnostics, demonstrating the advantages of probabilistic inference in photonic AI. This research paves the way for next-generation uncertainty-aware photonic computing, with applications in real-time decision-making, edge AI, and AIoT.
kw: Photonic Neural Networks, Bayesian Neural Networks, Stochastic Processes, Photonic Integrated Circuits, Photonic Random Number Generators, Uncertainty Quantification

title: Metaxins: the link between mitochondria, iron metabolism and aging
abs: Iron is an essential element involved in many biological processes inside the body, including oxygen transport, DNA synthesis and ATP generation. Iron dysregulation causes significant health issues such as anemia, liver damage and cardiovascular disease. Iron stores generally increase with age, although the causal relationship between iron and aging is not clear. In the cell, mitochondria act as central hubs for iron metabolism, by storing excess iron and utilizing iron in the synthesis of co-factors of proteins such as heme and iron-sulfur clusters. A deeper understanding of how the mitochondria regulate iron metabolism could therefore help in designing treatments for iron-related disorders. Metaxins are outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM) proteins which are involved in sorting and inserting B-barrel proteins in the OMM. A recent study has found that loss of Metaxin 2 (MTX2) causes a severe premature aging disorder known as Mandibuloacral Dysplasia Associated to MTX2. However it is unclear how loss of MTX2 leads to reduced mitochondrial activity or to the bone resorption and severe hypertension phenotypes observed in patients. To dissect the role of MTX2 function in mitochondrial and organismal health, we generated an mtx2 knockout zebrafish model. Our preliminary studies uncovered a strong dysregulation of iron metabolism and increased ferroptosis in the mtx2-/- fish. Using patient cells, we further confirmed that the iron dysregulation is also conserved in humans. As mitochondria are key sites of iron regulation, we hypothesize that MTX2 directly or indirectly regulates iron metabolism in the mitochondria. In this proposal, we aim to elucidate the role of metaxins in iron metabolism in the mitochondria and their connection to disease, potentially uncovering new pathways and therapeutic targets in iron metabolism and aging. Using transgenic zebrafish lines, we first aim to characterize the effect of Mtx2 loss in liver, bone and vasculature, tissues that are affected in patients. Then at a cellular level, we will examine the role of metaxins in regulating mitochondrial structure and function. Finally we will elucidate the biochemical role of metaxins in iron metabolism. While the mitochondria play important roles in iron regulation, metaxins are not known to be involved. Our research can therefore uncover novel players and pathways in iron metabolism. Our research using a premature aging disease aims to draw a stronger link between the mitochondria, iron metabolism and biological aging. As there are pharmaceutical compounds that chelate iron, our study could serve as the foundation of future studies on the use of iron chelators for age-related disorders.
kw: mitochondria; iron; ferroptosis; aging; zebrafish

title: From fundamental physics to next generation magnetic memories based on altermagnets
abs: With the advent of the Big Data era, the demand for computational power and information storage capabilities has surged, driving the need for innovative memory devices. Magnetic random access memory (MRAM) stands out as a promising next-generation non-volatile information storage technology. Non-volatile MRAM technologies are built on magnetic tunnel junctions (MTJ) comprised of two ferromagnetic (FM) layers separated by a thin insulator. One of the FM layers, known as the free layer (FL), stores information, while the other, the pinned layer (PL), provides a stable reference for reading the FL information. Bilayer information can be stored in the FL and the on/off ratio of these binary states is represented as the tunneling magnetoresistance (TMR) ratio. Two main technologies relying on electrically generated spin-currents have emerged to control the FL magnetization: spin transfer torque (STT) and spin orbit torque (SOT). Currently, commercialized STT-MRAM faces significant challenges of limited storage density and relatively high power consumption, which hinder its large-scale industrial applications, and SOT-MRAM is under intense research efforts. The primary limitation arises from the recording layers. For the in-plane ferromagnets, weak magnetic anisotropy limits the miniaturization of the device. Although perpendicular ferromagnets overcome this problem, the external field is required for electrically driven spin-orbit torque switching, which is not desirable for integrated applications. Altermagnets can generate spin splitting torques with the out-of-plane spin polarization, enabling field-free switching of perpendicular magnetization. It paves the way to construct high density MRAM. Besides, the stray field induced by ferromagnetic (FM) functional layers is another critical limitation for MRAM integration. A potential solution to this issue is to replace FM layers with antiferromagnets (AFM). However, the Kramers spin degeneracy, which states that the energy states of systems with an odd number of electrons remain at least doubly degenerate, in AFM makes it difficult to achieve a significant TMR effect. Fortunately, altermagnets have recently been proposed to combine the advantages of FMs and AFMs, offering a giant TMR ratio, no stray field, and high frequency operation. However, experimental research of this material is still in its early stages. Developing tunnel junctions with altermagnetic functional layers will greatly enhance the storage density and operation speed of MRAM. The high power consumption in MRAM primarily arises during information writing, where Joule heating caused by electric currents leads to significant energy waste. Employing magnons as carriers of spin angular momentum can address this problem, as the magnon torque provides a Joule heat-free method for information writing. title: New tools for understanding extracellular matrix-based mechanisms of cardiac aging dysfunction
abs: During healthy ageing, intra- and extracellular molecular alterations lead to a gradual deterioration in biological function of our tissues. The extracellular matrix (ECM) undergoes drastic biochemical, architectural, and mechanical changes with age that directly impact cellular behaviour. In the heart, tissue stiffens up to four-fold throughout a lifespan, which has important implications in the numerous mechanobiological signalling events that cardiac cells integrate to perform their specific tasks, e.g., the beating of cardiomyocytes within their surrounding matrix. Indeed, recent studies have revealed that substrate stiffness influences the behaviour of ageing cardiomyocytes. Specifically, elevated stiffness that is seen in aged tissues is associated with a decline in cardiomyocyte function, while the transfer of cardiomyocytes from a rigid to soft substrate can partially reverse this stiffness-induced dysfunction. Furthermore, the composition and architecture of tissues has been shown to play dominant roles in determining the age state of cells: aged ECM drives young cells toward senescence while young ECM elicits rejuvenation effects in aged cells. These findings underscore the fact that cardiomyocytes are mechanosensitive and exhibit stiffness- and ECM-dependent plasticity. Therefore, we hypothesize that ECM remodelling in the aging heart causes cardiac dysfunction via mechanosensitive mechanisms. By understanding how this reorganization occurs, we can build better models for cardiac aging in the lab. Further, we propose that restoring specific aspects of aged ECM to a more youthful state can reverse age-related cardiac dysfunction. This project aims to uncover new mechanistic insights into matrix-based regulation of cardiac aging, as well as to develop tools that enable our understanding of ECM-specific contributions to the cellular aging state. To do this, we will employ correlative spatial omics and nanoindentation mapping to link transcriptional states to mechanical states across a lifespan in mouse hearts. We will systematically design new dynamic biomaterials that recapitulate ECM reorganization to undergo in vitro 'ageing,' leading to better models that can ultimately replace costly, time-intensive, and limiting animal model systems. Using our identified aging regulators, we aim to explore the therapeutic potential of ‘tissue normalisation’ via restoration of aged ECM properties to that of a young state by employing interdisciplinary and multiscale in vitro and ex vivo strategies. To achieve our project goals, we will employ interdisciplinary approaches in biomaterials design (dynamic, phototunable), living cardiac tissue slice models (versatile, functional), live tissue imaging (ECM labelling), targeted biochemical ECM modification (enzymatic targeting), mechanical testing (nanoindentation), and robust omics (genomics and proteomics) that can ultimately inform translational applications. title: Elucidating the molecular mechanisms of Plasmodium vivax invasion: implications for vaccine development
abs: Malaria caused by Plasmodium vivax poses a significant global health threat, particularly in South and Southeast Asia. The absence of a continuous culture system and the parasite's unique preference for invading reticulocytes have hampered research progress. Recent studies have identified additional parasite ligands (RBP2b, RBP2a, and EBP) and their corresponding reticulocyte receptors (CD71, CD98, and CD35), expanding beyond the initially believed Duffy antigen/receptor interaction. However, antibodies against these ligands haven't completely blocked invasion, suggesting parasite ligand polymorphism or alternative invasion pathways. Preliminary data also shows that EBP and RBP2b can bind to CD98, underscoring its potential importance in invasion. This proposal aims to comprehensively characterize these ligand/receptor interactions, focusing on CD98, to advance the development of effective vaccines against P. vivax.

title: Development of Highly Electron-rich Metal Complexes Supported by Multidentate Aluminyl Ligands
abs: This project aims to develop novel complexes involving extremely electron-rich metal centres driven by strong sigma-donating anionic aluminyl ligands. The ultimate goal is to establish the challenging catalyses that are not attainable by the conventional catalysts. Transition metal (TM) complexes play a pivotal role as the catalysts in diverse laboratory syntheses and industrial processes. While a variety of catalysts are available nowadays, there are still many challenging transformation reactions that cannot be accomplished by the conventional catalysts. Our preliminary results have demonstrated that aluminyl anions can significantly increase the negative charge of the metal centre of TM complexes, rendering them extremely reactive. In this project, we will for the first time design a new type of multidentate ligands based on aluminyl anions and develop the extremely reactive TM reactive catalysts. We will challenge to establish the following hitherto unachievable catalyses to produce industrially important chemicals: (a) Palladium-catalyzed diboration of alkenes/alkynes (b) Gold-catalyzed Buchwald-Hartwig amination (c) Titanium-catalyzed Tebbe-Petasis olefination This project involves the fundamental study (ligand design) and applied research (new catalyses), representing the academic significance as well as potential applications.
kw: Ligand design; Aluminum; Transition metals; Catalysis; Organic Synthesis

title: Development of Efficient Spinel Catalysts for High-Energy Lithium-Sulfur Batteries
abs: Lithium-sulfur (Li-S) batteries are a promising next-generation energy storage technology due to their abundant sulfur resources and high specific capacity. However, their practical application is hindered by the dissolution of intermediate lithium polysulfides (LiPS) and slow conversion kinetics. Recent research has focused on improving battery performance by integrating catalysts into the sulfur cathode. Despite extensive exploration of transition metal compounds, trial-and-error methods have not consistently produced highly active catalysts, particularly under high sulfur loading. The PI’s team has focused on optimizing the catalytic activity of transition metal compounds, investigating the atomic-level interactions of each compound and the catalytic mechanisms in Li-S batteries. Spinel compounds, with their abundant reactive sites, have the potential for catalyzing the transformation of LiPS. This proposal intends to analyze the electronic structures of various spinel compounds, focusing on tetrahedral, octahedral, and anionic sites. Spinel compounds will be synthesized using hydrothermal methods and thermal treatment. X-ray diffraction (XRD) will be used to verify their crystal structures, while scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) will assess their morphology and size. Additional characterization will involve X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES), extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS), and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) to provide detailed structural and surface information. The study will assess the catalysts' ability to adsorb LiPS and their electrocatalytic performance using symmetrical cells and rotating disk electrodes. Electrochemical techniques, including cyclic voltammetry (CV) and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), will be employed to analyze their activity and kinetics. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations will summarize the electronic structures of various catalysts and their corresponding electrocatalytic performances, aiming to extract descriptors that reflect catalytic activity. Based on these descriptors, new spinel catalysts with enhanced catalytic activity will be designed, synthesized, and characterized. Further tuning of the spinel catalysts will involve ion doping or introducing vacancy defects. To achieve practical Li-S batteries with high sulfur loading and low electrolyte volume, additional optimization of host materials (including catalysts and conductive agents) will be required to ensure sufficient reaction sites and good electrical conductivity. Pouch cells will be assembled and tested for charge-discharge performance, with key metrics including specific capacity, rate performance, and cycling stability. title: Modification of Polyethylene Glycols (PEGs) via Organic Catalytic C-H Functionalizations
abs: Polyethylene glycols (PEGs) are widely used in pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, and material sciences due to their biocompatibility, low toxicity, and chemical versatility. Despite their importance, introducing structural diversity into PEGs remains challenging. Current approaches rely either on functionalized epoxide monomers, which are constrained by polymerization conditions, or on transition metal-catalyzed post-polymerization modifications, which pose issues related to metal toxicity and limited functional group tolerance. This study aims to address these challenges by developing a metal-free organocatalytic strategy for the functionalization of PEGs via N-heterocyclic carbene (NHC)-catalyzed sp3 C-H acylation. The central objective of this work is to establish a broadly applicable, transition metal-free method for modifying PEG backbones under mild conditions. Our hypothesis is that NHC catalysis enables direct acylation of PEG sp³ C-H bonds, affording structurally enriched polymers with improved functional versatility. Furthermore, the polymeric nature of PEGs, with its oxygen-rich backbone, may influence reaction behavior in ways distinct from small-molecule analogs, necessitating a detailed mechanistic investigation. To achieve these goals, the study is organized into three specific aims. First, reaction development will focus on optimizing NHC catalysts and reaction conditions to achieve selective PEG acylation. Second, mechanistic studies will compare PEG’s reactivity to small-molecule systems, shedding light on how polymeric environments influence NHC-catalyzed transformations. Third, application-oriented studies will explore the functionalized PEGs in key domains: (i) biomedical applications, where acylated PEGs can enhance drug conjugation and pharmacokinetic performance; (ii) materials science, where PEG modifications can improve the properties of water treatment membranes; and (iii) agrochemicals, where tailored PEG derivatives can optimize pesticide formulations. The feasibility of this approach is strongly supported by the established principles of NHC catalysis and the increasing interest in metal-free polymer functionalization. By circumventing the drawbacks of metal-catalyzed approaches, this work will enable PEG modifications that are more chemoselective, scalable, and biocompatible. Beyond its methodological advancements, this study is expected to have broad scientific and industrial impacts. The integration of NHC catalysis with polymer functionalization represents a fundamentally new strategy for modifying PEGs, expanding their utility in drug delivery, biomaterials, and beyond. By providing a direct and efficient platform for PEG functionalization, this work has the potential to unlock previously inaccessible PEG architectures and drive new developments in both academic and industrial settings.
kw: Polyethylene Glycols (PEG); C-H Functionalization; NHC Organocatalysis; Drug Delivery; Agrochemical binding; Membrane application

title: Nonsolvating Diluents in Localized Water-in-Salt Electrolytes for High-Voltage, Low-Temperature Energy Storage Devices
abs: This study is dedicated to the development of localized water-in-salt (LWIS) electrolytes, enriched with nonsolvating diluents, to achieve high-voltage operation and excellent low-temperature performance in aqueous energy storage systems. The project investigates the fundamental solvation chemistry of zinc ion batteries (ZIBs) and zinc-ion hybrid capacitors (ZICs), aiming to identify the mechanisms by which diluents influence ionic conductivity, solvation structures, and electrochemical stability. A key area of investigation is the role of nonsolvating diluents in facilitating the formation of a stable solid electrolyte interface (SEI) on the zinc anode, which is critical for mitigating dendrite growth and ensuring uniform zinc deposition. A suite of advanced characterizations and simulation techniques, including in-situ Raman spectroscopy, X-ray diffraction, X-ray absorption near-edge spectroscopy, and molecular dynamics simulations, will be utilized to provide insights into the solvation structure, SEI formation, and solvation structural stability within LWIS electrolytes. The optimized electrolyte formulations will be applied to zinc-based energy devices, achieving efficient operation even at temperatures as low as –50°C. This research aims to significantly expand the electrochemical stability window, reduce electrolyte viscosity, and enhance charge transport, thereby addressing critical challenges in energy storage under extreme conditions. The outcomes of this study have the potential to transform the performance and reliability of energy storage systems in wide-temperature environments, advancing the development of next-generation energy storage technologies for a wide range of applications, from grid-scale storage to portable electronics and beyond.
kw: Localized Water-in-Salt Electrolytes, Low-Temperature Performance, Ehanced Zinc Ion Storage

title: High-responsivity deep ultraviolet (DUV) photodetectors on ultra-wide bandgap semiconductors
abs: DUV (Deep Ultraviolet) light, with a wavelength of less than 280 nm, serves as an essential component for a multitude of critical health and industrial applications, among these are air-water purification and germicidal systems, bio-medical imaging sensing, UV secure communication, and semiconductor manufacturing. These applications hold paramount significance in medical and industrial domains, playing a pivotal role in enhancing the quality of life. In these applications, the DUV dose will need to be precisely manipulated. A high responsivity DUV photodetector is thus essential to meet such a precision function in the integrated DUV systems. Current DUV photodetectors all have low sensitivity and are mainly from three categories: (a) photo-multiplier tubes (PMT), (b) silicon photomultiplier or silicon avalanche photodiodes, and (c) diodes of ultra-wide bandgap materials. The PMT has a best measured quantum efficiency of 22.5% @ 122 nm and anode sensitivity of 5.2×10^5 A/W @ 254 nm, which provides a sensitive DUV photo-response. However, it requires a typical bias voltage of 1000V applied at the anode. For the silicon avalanche photodiode, it has 40% top quantum efficiency under operation voltage of 40V to 100V for avalanche multiplication. In addition, its operation is highly influenced by temperature and bias condition. For the ultra-wide bandgap photodetectors, materials of Ga2O3, AlN, Al2O3, h-BN and C are currently used. These materials have the wide bandgap for DUV photo-carrier generation. However, due to the high resistivity and limited quantum efficiency, their photo-responsivities are typically very low with values less than 1 A/W, which is not significant enough in sensing the precise dose of DUV irradiation. In this proposal, a novel approach will be implemented to integrate both the GaOX(N1-X) and AlOX(N1-X) compounds through the selective oxidation approach on the AlGaN/GaN epitaxy to interact with the polarized 2-dimensional electron gas channel (2DEG). The innovative approach provides both the ultra-wide bandgap photocarrier generation as well as the application of AlGaN/GaN 2DEG internal current gain to boost up the photo-responsivity to a high value. From our prior works done on UV(A) photodetectors, such an internal gain was able to boost up the responsivity (from less than 1 A/W) by several orders, i.e. 104 or higher to allow ultra-high detectivity for extreme precision in UV photodetection. It is also possible to further integrate MgO of bandgap 7.7 eV to cater the detection of 160 nm in the FUV (Far Ultraviolet) band. It is believed that this innovation of using selective oxidation approach to produce GaO_X(N_1-X) and AlO_X(N_1-X) wide bandgap DUV compounds on the AlGaN/GaN epitaxy platform has not been done by anyone before and it has great potential to improve the DUV/FUV photodetection by a huge advancement. The physics of this innovation sits on the AlGaN/GaN polarisation platform where 2DEG high-mobility conductive laye

title: MEMS enabled adaptive p-bits for annealing-enhanced large-scale probabilistic computing
abs: Digital bits are the basic building blocks of computers. Although modern computers are very sophisticated machines with hundreds of billions of transistors, they still struggle with efficiently solving certain complex NP-hard problems, such as combinatorial optimization. Additionally, the continued downscaling of transistors faces physical limitations, including current leakage, heat generation, and bandwidth constraints of on-chip interconnects, prompting interest in alternative computing architectures. While quantum computers offer a potential solution by using qubits that can represent the superposition of quantum states, they face significant challenges, such as short coherence time and the need for cryogenic temperatures. Probabilistic computing, on the other hand, leverages principles like quantum computing but operates within the realm of classical physics, thus avoiding the limitations of quantum systems. This type of computing serves as an intermediate solution between conventional deterministic digital computers and emerging quantum computers. Probabilistic bit (p-bit), first demonstrated with stochastic magnetic tunnel junctions (MTJ), has shown significant promise in solving combinatorial optimization problems, including logic operations, integer factorization, traveling salesman problem, etc. However, current MTJ p-bit implementations in probabilistic computing usually have a fixed potential well depth hence a fixed inherent fluctuation rate that cannot be adjusted after fabrication. This is different from the natural thermal annealing process, where the fluctuation rate can be gradually controlled by adjusting the temperature. Microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) technology, on the other hand, presents a solution to this challenge by enabling dynamic adjustment of the fluctuation rate, thereby enabling adaptive p-bit and improving system flexibility and performance. MEMS is also advantageous due to its compact size, scalability, and low power consumption. This makes it a promising technology for annealing-enhanced large-scale probabilistic computing, which has wide-ranging practical applications in fields such as logistics, cryptography, nuclear physics, etc. This project hence aims to provide a solution for annealing-enhanced probabilistic computing based on our innovative MEMS adaptive p-bits through a series of technological developments. These include (1) The development of annealing-enhanced probabilistic computing theory and architecture based on the MEMS adaptive p-bits, which is inspired by physical annealing process and optimized for finding global minimum. The project involves theoretical development, mathematical modelling, and numerical simulation/demonstration using MATLAB SIMULINK. (2) Experimental demonstration of the small/medium-scale annealing-enhanced probabilistic computing with adaptive MEMS p-bits integrated with both ultra-low power electrostatic actuators and high-precision piezoresistive displacement sensor

title: Development of high-entropy perovskite-supported high-entropy alloy catalysts for efficient oxygen evolution
abs: Green hydrogen production via water electrolysis in alkaline electrolytes using renewable electricity has shown great promise to realize a sustainable energy landscape, which, however, is hindered by the notorious sluggish kinetics of oxygen evolution reaction (OER). Currently, the commercial catalysts for industrial OER are Ir/Ru-based catalysts, characterized by a high material cost and scarcity. Recently, non-precious metal-based oxide, hydroxide, and chalcogenides emerge as a promising alternative and can even show comparable performance for alkaline OER compared to the precious-metal catalysts. Despite the progress, the activity and durability of non-precious metal-based nanocatalysts are still unsatisfactory to meet the rigorous requirements of industrial applications. In this project, we propose to address the activity and durability challenges by developing a new class of non-precious catalysts, i.e., high-entropy perovskite-supported high-entropy alloy (HEP-HEA) catalysts, for durable OER in alkaline electrolytes. The proposed HEP-HEA catalyst is (LaSr)1(FeNiCoCuMnTi)1O3/FeNiCoCuMn and can be synthesized by a two-step protocol: formation of high-entropy perovskites (LaSr)0.95(FeNiCoCuMnTi)1O3 and generation of FeNiCoCuMn HEA nanoparticles via in situ metal exsolution from perovskites. We envision the HEP-HEA catalysts will show promising OER activity and durability because (1) Fe, Ni, Co, Mn, and Cu-based nanoparticles have demonstrated their potential to display OER performance comparable to those of Ru/Ir-based catalysts in alkaline electrolytes; (2) the synergistic effect of multiple elements in both the HEA nanoparticles and high-entropy perovskites can boost the OER activity; (3) the lattice distortion and hysteresis diffusion effect of an HEA structure can remarkably reinforce the durability of catalysts; (4) the strong perovskite-HEA particle interactions could greatly prevent the HEA particle sintering and thus improve the catalyst durability; (5) transition-metal doped perovskites also show outstanding OER performance in alkaline electrolytes. To rationalize the reaction mechanisms during OER, we propose to develop a super-resolution fluorescence imaging platform to investigate the adsorption behaviours of key reaction intermediates, i.e., reactive oxygen species, at the single-particle level. Moreover, the degradation mechanisms of HEP-HEA catalysts will be examined by in situ monitoring the leaching of various metals throughout OER via in situ spectroscopy. The diverse HEP-HEA catalysts will then be tested in water electrolysers to evaluate their potential for industrial applications. In our preliminary results, we successfully synthesized HEP catalysts and proved the feasibility of metal exsolution via thermal heating. The proposed research will not only innovate a new class of cost-effective and durable OER catalysts for advancing green H2 production via water electrolysis, but also enhance the fundamental knowledge of mater
kw: oxygen evolution, high-entropy nanomaterials, perovskites, chemical imaging, in situ tests

title:
Holocene Beach Ridge Evolution and Modern Sediment Dynamics: Palaeoenvironmental Insights
from the Riau Islands, Indonesia
abs: This proposal outlines a three-year study to examine sediment dynamics and palaeoenvironmental records within the beach ridge systems of the Riau Islands, Indonesia. The project has four objectives: (1) reconstruct past sea level variations and their impact on coastal morphology over the last 5000 years; (2) quantify sediment sources and volumes contributing to beach ridge formation, assess reef systems' role in sediment supply, and model sediment transport dynamics; (3) identify, characterise, and date washover sand deposits from storms and tsunamis in swale environments; and (4) trial new geochemical, pollen, diatom, and ancient DNA (aDNA) proxies to detect volcanic tephra layers and assess past tropical droughts. Methods include Ground Penetrating Radar (GPR), sediment cores, and Optically Stimulated Luminescence (OSL) and Radiocarbon Dating. This study will advance understanding of beach ridge responses to sea level changes, sedimentation, and extreme events, improving models of coastal dynamics and aiding in future climate adaptation strategies in the Riau Islands and Singapore. It will provide training for a PhD student, 2 MSc students, 7 Undergraduate students and benefit Singapore and local communities by informing coastal management practices in the Riau Islands.
kw: Beach Ridges, coral reefs sediment transport modeling, field-based measurements, artificial intelligence, machine learning, interdisciplinary research geomorphology OSL dating

title: Tracing Nurse Trajectories: Multinational Migration Amid Global Competition
abs: As global migration patterns become increasingly complex, social scientists face growing pressures to make sense of migrants’ long-term trajectories. Research has shown how people can move to multiple countries throughout their lives, challenging a long-held belief that migration involves only a single origin and destination. Yet, scholars have also been limited to framing multinational trajectories as an individual experience – a result of the resources, aspirations, and circumstances of migrants themselves. Largely missing is the question of how other actors and institutions can shape migrants’ multinational pathways. This project shifts scholarly attention to how different actors move people across multiple borders, channelling migrants toward some places and drawing them away from others. We aim to examine how global competition over migrant skills defines people’s multinational trajectories. Specifically, we seek to determine how governments, recruitment agencies, and employers compete to direct migrants to and from specific destinations, reshaping their trajectories across time. We focus on the case of migrant nurses, a healthcare profession projected to face severe labour shortages in the coming decade (WHO 2023). We also centre our study on the movement of Filipinos, the largest nationality group among migrant nurses. We ask: How have nurse migration trajectories diversified over time amid a growing competition for healthcare labour? How have state institutions, commercial agencies, and employers sought to influence nurses’ migration trajectories? How might nurses alter their migration trajectories in relation to changing state policies, workplace incentives, and recruitment strategies? The project brings together an interdisciplinary team of scholars from sociology, geography, nursing and implementation science. With over a decade of experience in studying healthcare workers and health systems, the research team has built strong connections in major source countries like the Philippines and established destinations like Singapore. We will implement a mixed-method research design that includes a survey of nurses’ international trajectories, in-depth interviews with different actors competing for nurses’ labour, and a digital story completion method that determines how nurses respond to changing state policies, employer incentives, and recruitment strategies. This project is original because it examines what scholars have called the “middle space” of international migration, where different actors compete to direct migrants toward specific destinations, often at the expense of other nations in need of such labour. This middle space has been relatively understudied in research on migrant trajectories, despite their key role in shaping people’s international pathways. title: Exploring “Electrode-philicity” to tune electrolyte-electrode interactions towards high performance aqueous Zinc-Sulfur batteries
abs: The escalating global demand for batteries, driven by the need to mitigate climate change, underscores the urgency for advancements in energy storage technologies. Zinc-sulfur (Zn-S) batteries are emerging as a promising alternative to lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) due to their lower cost, environmental benefits, and the abundance of their materials. Zn-S batteries are versatile, suitable for applications ranging from grid storage to portable electronics. However, they face several significant challenges: 1. Narrow Electrochemical Stability Window (ESW): This limitation restricts the voltage output and prevents the use of certain high-capacity redox reactions, impacting overall performance. 2. Insufficient Kinetics: Sulfur’s insulating properties and the formation of poorly conducting compounds lead to reduced efficiency and capacity of the battery. 3. Volumetric Electrode Expansion: Significant volume changes during cycling affect the electrical contact and reversibility of the battery, complicating its operation. 4. Inadequate Understanding of Cathode-Electrolyte Interactions: There is a lack of detailed analysis of these interactions in quasi- or solid-state Zn-S batteries, which hinders optimization and understanding of sulfur’s complex electrochemistry. This proposal seeks to address these challenges by developing a fully optimized Zn-S battery through refined electrode and electrolyte materials. The project aims to enhance electrochemical properties by deeply investigating the physicochemical characteristics of various electrolytes and the interaction mechanisms at the electrode-electrolyte interface. Approaches will involve a multidisciplinary effort, integrating chemistry, materials science, and engineering expertise. Key aspects of the proposed research include: • Optimizing Sulfur Cathodes and Zinc Anodes: The project will focus on combining conversion-type sulfur cathodes with zinc anodes to improve capacity and energy density. This involves modifying sulfur cathodes to enhance their interaction with electrolytes and manage volumetric expansion. Potential strategies include: o Using Metal-Organic Framework (MOF)-Derived Oxides or Conductive Carbon containing Metal Catalysts: These materials will be used as hosts for active sulfur, chosen for their porosity and ability to accommodate large volume changes during cycling. •Advanced Electrolyte Design: The research will explore new polymer electrolyte formulations and compatibilization with selected cathode binders. The use of hydratable polymer electrolytes and amphiphilic co-polymer electrolytes will be selected the choices to address issues related to hydrophobic sulfur-cathode interfaces. • Characterizing Electrolyte and Electrode Interactions: Advanced characterization methods will be employed to gain a comprehensive understanding of the interactions between electrodes and electrolytes, aiming to resolve interface challenges and improve overall battery performance. title: Genome evolution of plant volatile signaling under symbiosis: ant-plant interactions in genus Macaranga
abs: In plant-ant associations, ants protect their hosts from herbivores, pathogens and competing plants. These myrmecophytic associations represent an untapped resource for biological control because they provide protection from a wider array of pests than previous approaches, such as ladybirds. Here, we will analyse the evolution of ant associations in the genus Macaranga. The system is particularly useful for identifying genome evolution associated with myrmecophytism, as the trait has either evolved independently several times, or then has been lost several times, among Southeast Asian species. Because of this reason, the genus contains several recently diverged myrmecophytic – non-myrmecophytic species pairs, allowing us to look at small scale genome evolution that leads to the losses or gains of these traits. To understand these interactions, we will first generate reference-quality genome assemblies for nine Macaranga species exhibiting varying degrees of ant association and carry out comparative genomics analyses to identify candidate genes involved in these interactions. Concurrently, we will conduct a controlled experiment to determine the changes in transcriptomic, metabolomic and volatile signal spectrum emitted by the plants when the plant calls the ants for colonization and for its defence. Specifically, we will examine how (i) the volatile and -omics spectra differ between colonized and non-colonized plants, and (ii) what kinds of volatile and -omics profiles are emitted in response to wounding. The experiment will include three phylogenetically related ant-plant vs. non-ant-plant species pairs to detect convergent gene family gains, losses, and expression patterns. Altogether, we generate transcriptomic, metabolomic, and volatile spectra data from over 500 samples, enabling both detailed species-specific analyses as well as an integrative approach that incorporates also evolutionary modelling. This project will advance understanding of genome evolution under symbiotic interactions by providing a novel system for answering the long-standing fundamental question of whether these interactions accelerate or hinder genome evolution. It also develops methodologies for integrating multi-omics data, with volatile spectrum as a new component, and finally, it identifies the specific volatile compounds involved in plant-ant interactions, paving way for novel methods of biocontrol.
kw: ant-plants, genomics, evolution, plant volatiles

title: Theranostic Dressing with Integrated Multiplexed Biomarker Profiling and Controlled Electrochemical Generation of Nitric Oxide for Diabetic Wound Management
abs: Diabetes mellitus is a chronic metabolic disorder that profoundly affects wound healing, leading to a high incidence of chronic wounds, particularly diabetic foot ulcers. As diabetic wounds are slow to heal and easily infected due to prolonged inflammation and lack of growth factors, current treatment modalities often fall short, necessitating innovative approaches that can effectively address the complexities of diabetic wound healing. This proposal aims at developing theranostic dressings with integrated functions of continuous drainage of wound exudate, real-time multiplexed biomarker profiling, and controlled release of therapeutic NO to provide personalized diabetic wound management for individual patient. Different phases in wound healing are characteristic of distinct signaling events, cell types, and biomolecule levels, making it essential to reveal disease progression for precise intervention. Nitric oxide (NO), an endogenous gasotransmitter, shows concentration-dependent physiological activities: At pM–nM levels, NO regulates cytokines that initiate inflammation and recruit keratinocytes, supporting anti-inflammatory activities and wound healing; At nM–µM levels, NO acts as an antimicrobial agent within the innate immune response. Smart wound dressings with built-in sensing and therapeutic mechanisms can go beyond wound protection and moisture maintenance to monitor wound conditions in real-time and offer the possibility of integrating precision medicine into routine clinical care. Our design of smart theranostic wound dressings is built upon strong preliminary development of Janus membranes with two sides of distinct hydrophobicity, ultrasensitive multiplexed immunosensors enabled by surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) probes, and metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) that lead to precisely controlled release of NO locally in response to electrical stimulation. We will develop Janus membranes of a conductive hydrophobic layer and an antibody-conjugated hydrophilic layer for unidirectional transport of wound exudate from the wound-contacting hydrophobic side to the hydrophilic side. SERS probes based on tailored metal nanoparticles with internally encoded Raman tags that generate highly amplified signals will be used for multiplexed detection of inflammatory biomarkers, which provides critical feedback for tailoring treatment strategies to the dynamic needs of the wound environment. We will load MOF-919 electrocatalysts that we developed into the hydrophobic layer of Janus membranes to promote selective electrochemical reduction of NaNO2, giving rise to precisely controlled release of NO locally for desired anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and antibacterial effects. This dual-action approach addresses two primary barriers to effective wound healing: infection and inflammation, which are particularly pronounced in diabetic patients. We envision that our strategy not only personalizes wound treatments but also allows for ongoing assessment

title: Investigating Adipose Tissue derived Beta Amyloid aggregates’ role in Alzheimer’s Disease
abs: Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) is a major neurodegenerative disease that is sweeping through the aging population in many countries. Patients often spend their last decade of life suffering through a progressive downhill journey in their cognitive and physical faculties. Currently there is no cure for AD despite billions of investment dollars have been poured into the field in search of solutions. AD is a complex disease such that The current paradigm of the cause of AD revolves around Amyloid Beta (Aβ) in the brain. It is believed that Aβ is first formed by neurons and due to certain residues in the peptide, they can grow in sizes from subnanometers to micrometers dimensions in a process known as amyloid cascade. It is believed that it is the larger sized Aβ aggregates that causes toxicity in the brain. The brain attempts to expel these toxic Aβ aggregates through the cerebral vasculature from the brain side but their toxicity damages the cerebral vasculature which can result in microbleeding events. These vascular events further deteriorated the brain’s condition. There are attempts to use antibody-based drugs to arrest the growth of the Aβ aggregates but these drugs are administered to patients who have already developed AD symptoms which further limited their clinical efficacy. Based on the above, we have two research questions: 1) Would it be possible that there are also non-brain sources of Aβ (like the adipose tissue) that could induce cerebral vasculature leakiness before the onset of AD? 2) Could the adipose derived Aβ induce cerebral vasculature leakiness through the formation of Aβ nanoaggregates from the blood side? In this proposal, we found that the adipose tissue may be a new non-brain source of Aβ (preliminary data). Epidemiological studies of aging population suggests that AD is a complication of obesity. Our own preliminary studies on patients’ blood samples showed a good positive correlation of increased plasma Aβ with higher BMI. Our in vitro data using mouse adipose tissue lysates showed elevated levels of Aβ are of even higher levels than in the brain and in blood. Exposing the adipose tissue lysates that contains Aβ to confluent monolayer of endothelial cells induces endothelial leakiness. Adipocytes cell lines secrete high levels of Aβ into the media and using just the conditioned media induced endothelial leakiness. Earlier, we published that in vitro size evolved Aβ aggregates indicated that those aggregates in the size ranges of nanometers were able to induce in vitro endothelial leakiness. Injecting Aβ nanoaggregates into general circulation in a mouse model also increases the brain vascular leakiness and the Aβ could enter into the brain interstitial through this path. title: Learning from evolution: investigating pancreatic adaptations in nectarivorous bats to advance therapeutic strategies for Type 2 diabetes
abs: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) is a global epidemic, characterized by peripheral insulin resistance and a progressive decline in pancreatic β-cell mass and function. The cave nectar bat Eonycteris spelaea is a rare specialist nectarivore adapted to a nectar diet rich in simple sugars (10-50% by weight), yet shows no signs of metabolic dysfunction and excellent glycaemic control. Preliminary data reveal that E. spelaea exhibits a striking tenfold higher pancreatic islet density compared to mice. We hypothesize that studying developmental and nutritional adaptations in the endocrine pancreas of E. spelaea will provide novel mechanistic insights into β-cell development, regeneration, and survival pathways, which would open new therapeutic avenues for T2D treatment. Specific Aim 1 will investigate the developmental ontogeny driving enhanced islet density in E. spelaea. We will generate single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) datasets from fetal, weaning, juvenile, and adult pancreas tissue, generating a high-resolution map of pancreatic cellular heterogeneity across developmental stages. We will establish the transcriptional identity of E. spelaea endocrine progenitors and delineate their developmental trajectory, determine whether marked islet hyperplasia is pre-natally programmed or induced by high-sugar feeding after weaning stage, and characterize how prolonged sugar exposure affects pancreatic cell populations post weaning through adulthood. Specific Aim 2 will establish an organoid model to elucidate β-cell fate determinants in E. spelaea. We will systematically evaluate growth factors and small molecules for optimal expansion and endocrine differentiation in vitro. Using single-cell multiome profiling (ATAC-seq coupled with RNA-seq), we will identify key regulatory elements governing β-cell differentiation. We will then use dCas9-based perturbations to validate identified regulatory regions, testing whether their activation or suppression influences β-cell development and function in E. spelaea organoids. Collectively, this study will generate a unique knowledge base and critical resources to understand evolutionary adaptations of a nectarivorous mammal to a natural, chronic high sugar diet.
kw: Type 2 diabetes; β-cells; pancreas; nectarivory; comparative biology; metabolic syndrome

title: Physics and Computational Screening of Topological Semimetals for Solid-State Terahertz Device Technology
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: Terahertz (THz) technology holds immense potential for applications in material diagnostics, healthcare, and security, yet its progress is hindered by inefficient THz sources and modulators. Topological semimetals (TSMs), characterized by topologically protected band crossings, offer a promising avenue for high-performance THz devices due to their high carrier mobility and strong nonlinear optical responses. However, the lack of predictive models, integrated simulation frameworks, and systematic material screening methods limits the development of TSM-based solid-state THz devices. This project aims to establish a novel “material-to-device” multiphysics simulation platform that combines first-principles material simulations, high-throughput screening, and computational electromagnetics to identify optimal TSMs for THz applications. By bridging condensed matter physics with device-level performance predictions, this research will provide key insights into the interaction between band topology and THz waves, accelerating the discovery of high-efficiency THz materials. The outcomes of this project will drive advancements in THz technology with far-reaching implications for telecommunications (6G and beyond), healthcare, and advanced manufacturing, thus positioning Singapore at the forefront of THz science and innovation.
kw: Topological semimetal; Terahertz waves; Material screening; Light-matter interaction physics; Density functional theory simulation

title: Analyzing the influence of CD137 ligand on the immune synapse and its potential therapeutic applications for treatment of immune-mediated pathologies
abs: CD137 is a costimulatory molecule expressed on activated T cells. CD137 agonists induce potent T cell responses and are being evaluated for tumor immunotherapy. The ligand for CD137 (CD137L), is expressed on antigen presenting cells (APC). Our current data reveal an entirely novel and unexpected function of CD137L. We find that CD137L influences the composition of the immune synapse. Coimmunoprecipitation (co-IP) revealed that CD137L associates with molecules of the immune synapse, including Fyn, Lck, Rac1, CD11a, CD18, GRIP-1, CD45 and NCKAP1L. Further, CD137L increases the cell surface expression of CD80, CD86, CD83, TLR4, CD14, CD16/CD32 and PD-L1 on APC, several of which are part of the immune synapse. Expression levels of CD137L and of these molecules correlate with the readiness and vigor of monocytes to respond to activation by the pattern recognition receptor ligand lipopolysaccharide, as shown by increased secretion of inflammatory cytokines, e.g. IL-6, IL-8 and IL-1β. This property of CD137L is conserved between human and mouse. Since the costimulatory signal by CD137 into T cells is very potent, a negative feed-back mechanism exists that prevents overstimulation and autoimmune damage. This inhibitory mechanism consists in CD137 being transferred from T cells to APC by trogocytosis during their interaction, upon which CD137 and CD137L form a complex that is internalized and degraded by the proteasome. We have isolated an anti-CD137L antibody, clone P4A4, that mimics this negative feed-back mechanism and induces the internalization of CD137L and the immune synapse via endocytosis. Thereby P4A4 inhibits activation, proliferation and differentiation of T cells of healthy donors and of patients suffering from systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) in vitro, as evidenced by reduced expression of activation markers and master transcription factors, diminished secretion of cytokines and lower T cell numbers. In this proposed project, we want to build on these data by confirming and extending them. In addition, we will investigate whether P4A4 has the potential of a novel drug candidate for treatment of immune-mediated pathologies such as autoimmune disease or graft versus host disease (GvHD). Aim 1 will investigate the influence of CD137L on the immune synapse. Previously, we did co-IP of CD137L in the monocytic THP-1 cell line. Now we will perform it in peripheral human monocytes, and verify CD137L-associated molecules with a range of different assays (Western blot, proximity ligation assay, reverse co-IP). Further, since our current data show that CD137L reduces the activation threshold of monocytes in response to bacterial pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs), we will analyse whether it also reduces the activation threshold of monocytes in response to fungal (zymosam) and viral (CpG oligonucleotides) PAMPs. title: A biodiversity accounting framework integrating fundamental ecological and economic principles
abs: The ongoing global biodiversity crisis has motivated interest in measuring impacts of economic activities on biodiversity. Notably, the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, adopted in 2022 by 195 countries including Singapore, is the main global policy framework for biodiversity conservation until 2030 and encourages companies, for the first time, to measure and report their impacts on biodiversity. Rigorous biodiversity accounting frameworks are thus becoming essential, yet there is currently no universally accepted framework. The intellectual merit of our project is that we are tackling this globally important problem by assembling a world-class interdisciplinary team, comprising a theoretical ecologist, an ecological economist, and an expert in green finance. The novelty and innovation of our proposal is that our biodiversity accounting framework will be grounded in fundamental ecological and economic principles, thus giving valuations that more accurately reflect reality than do existing accounting methods. Although biodiversity accounting can draw some inspiration from well-established methods for carbon accounting, it is uniquely beset by thorny conceptual and technical problems, mainly arising from non-additivity of biodiversity value across species and land units, lower certainty of permanence of biodiversity (due to extinction risk), and lack of clarity on how to conduct intertemporal comparisons. Building from mechanistic principles will allow us to create a framework whose emergent properties solve these problems parsimoniously. The broader impact of our work will be to facilitate biodiversity impact disclosure and footprint estimation, and the development of financial markets for biodiversity credits. Biodiversity valuation is a growing multi-billion dollar industry, in which Singapore can be a key actor.
kw: biodiversity accounting; biodiversity credits; biodiversity markets; biodiversity footprints; ecological economics; ecological modelling

title: A Multi-Modal Foundation Model for Unified Structural Modelling of Proteins, RNAs and Small Molecules and Their Interactions
abs: Proteins and RNAs are fundamental biomolecules that drive essential biological functions within human cells. Accurate three-dimensional (3D) structure modeling of these molecules, along with small ligands, is critical for understanding their biological roles and designing therapeutics to modulate their functions. While recent advances in AI-driven single-chain tertiary protein structure prediction have shown promise, current approaches fall short for quaternary structure modeling of protein-protein and protein-RNA complexes, which is crucial for biological function annotation and drug discovery. This proposal is based on the hypothesis that different biomolecular structures are governed by similar atomic-level interaction principles. To address the limitations of current methods, we aim to develop a novel multi-modal foundational model (MMFM) capable of accurately and uniformly predicting the 3D structures and interactions of proteins, RNAs, and small molecules (ligands). In particular, improving the modeling of protein/RNA-ligand interactions will significantly enhance virtual screening and de novo drug design. The project is structured around four Specific Aims: (1) Development of MMFM for unified modeling of proteins, RNAs, and small molecules, by incorporating a novel unified diffusion language model to leverage abundant sequence datasets and complement limited structural data through representation learning. (2) Atomic-level tertiary structure prediction for individual proteins and RNAs, extending MMFM’s modeling capability beyond existing AI-based approaches. (3) Quaternary structure prediction for protein-protein and protein-RNA complexes, improving our ability to model biomolecular assemblies. (4) Protein/RNA-ligand interaction modeling and drug discovery applications, by integrating MMFM with structure-based drug design pipelines. The proposed methods will be rigorously evaluated through large-scale benchmarking and community-wide validation experiments against state-of-the-art approaches. To maximize the scientific impact, all AI models and datasets developed in this project will be made freely available to the biomedicine community. The successful execution of this project is expected to drive a paradigm shift in molecular computational biology, significantly advancing the accuracy and applicability of biomolecular modeling and AI-driven drug discovery.
kw: Deep learning; large language model; multi-modal foundation model; protein structure prediction; RNA structure prediction; drug discovery

title: Exploiting Tumor-specific RNA-editing for Antigen-based Cancer Therapy (ExTRACT)
abs: Adenosine deaminases acting on RNA (ADARs) can catalyse the co- or post-transcriptional deamination of adenosines to inosines. Since inosine is recognized as guanosine by cellular machineries, this A-to-I editing can change the amino acid translated independent of the genetic code, to generate noncanonical neoantigens. RNA editing can also regulate RNA splicing and thereby fuel the further generation of alternative transcripts and protein products that could give rise to spliced antigens. Moreover, ADAR1 activity is elevated in almost all cancer types, including colon, lung and nasopharyngeal, and ADAR1 editing follows a recognisable sequence motif. Collectively, these suggest that similar editing and shared edited products may exist across multiple cancer types, and be exploitable for therapy even in cancers of low mutational burden. In this project, we aim to study the impact of RNA editing on the generation of edited cancer antigen peptides, and to identify an Asian repertoire of reactive CD4 and CD8 TCRs as starting points to generate off-the-shelf therapeutics for population-level cancer therapy against ADAR1-edited neo-epitopes.
