title: Development of the next-generation live attenuated tetravalent dengue vaccine using a novel orthoflavivirus genome recoding approach
abs: The current live attenuated tetravalent dengue vaccines cannot provide complete protection against all four dengue virus serotypes (DENV1-4) and may even increase the risk of severe dengue by inducing antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE). This limitation arises from their use of chimeric vaccine strains that fail to induce complete T-cell immunity. It is now understood that protection against DENV infection and ADE requires both antibody and T-cell immunity. To overcome these challenges, this proposal aims to develop a non-chimeric live attenuated tetravalent dengue vaccine that induces comprehensive antibody and T-cell immunity against DENV1-4. We will achieve this by developing vaccine strains for DENV1-4 using a novel approach called orthoflavivirus genome recoding, which confers genetically stable attenuation using only silent mutations. This method preserves all the original antibody and T-cell epitopes of DENV1-4. Additionally, we have identified immunogenic mutations to further enhance the immunogenicity of recoded DENV strains, ensuring the vaccine induces robust B-cell and T-cell responses. Our previous and preliminary studies confirm that recoded DENV2 is attenuated in both mouse and mosquito models. Moreover, vaccinating AG129 mice with recoded DENV2 induces neutralising antibodies and provides protection against lethal DENV2 challenge, confirming that our genome recoding approach preserves immunogenicity. We also observed that recoded DENV4 is attenuated in mice, demonstrating that our genome recoding approach is applicable across the other DENV serotypes. We will validate the vaccine strains for DENV1-4 both individually and as a combined tetravalent formulation in mosquito, immunocompetent mouse, and non-human primate models to assess attenuation, short-term efficacy, and long-term vaccine efficacy. For the tetravalent formulation, we will prioritise confirming serotype-specific antibody responses through antibody depletion techniques and serotype-specific T-cell responses using epitope mapping and adoptive transfer studies. This comprehensive strategy ensures that our dengue vaccine can provide long-term, complete protective immunity against DENV infection and ADE.

title: Autonomizing Environmental Governance in Asian Cities: AI, Climate Change, and Frictional Urbanisms
abs: This project aims to investigate the interactions between two rapidly evolving and critical areas of AI implementation and urban climate governance in cities across South and Southeast Asia. The project will examine the complexities of autonomizing urban governance at the intersection of AI and climate change and will focus on the challenges that emerge when integrating AI into environmental governance in cities. The focus is not on the technicalities of AI technologies or climate change crises, but rather the governance and management of the impacts in AI-driven cities. By ‘autonomizing’ we refer to the deployment of AI-driven autonomous systems to manage various climate change-related challenges, that does not only involve analyzing historical data to automate processes but also engage in independent decision-making. In doing so we will introduce and develop the concept of ‘frictional urbanism’ to help understand the conflicts and frictions that arise between the digital and material urban realms while integrating AI to the city. The specific aims are organized based on the conceptual framework that considers three themes: i) the politics of smart vs. sustainable cities i) AI-nature frictions iii) glitches in the autonomous city. Throughout these themes, the broader concept of frictional urbanism will provide the guiding lens for understanding the tensions at the intersection of technology, governance and the environment. The conceptual framework is explained in more detail below. title: SynapSee: Multi-Light Probing for Event-Based Pupil Sensing in Neuro-Ocular Health Applications
abs: Eye tracking, encompassing pupil kinematics (both micro and macro movements) and pupillometry, is revolutionizing healthcare by providing non-invasive, objective biomarkers for neurological and systemic health conditions. Macro movements, such as saccades and fixations, provide critical insights into high-level neural or ocular motor issues, including mental fatigue and low-vision conditions. Meanwhile, micro anomalies—including nystagmus, tremors, micro saccades, and drifts—offer valuable information about neural control, attention, and motor coordination, serving as early indicators for neurodegenerative conditions such as Parkinson’s disease, Alzheimer’s disease, and multiple sclerosis. Pupillometry further enriches these capabilities by assessing pupil size and reactivity, providing a window into autonomic nervous system function, cognitive load, emotional states, and affect. Recognizing the deep interconnection between these ocular motor features and neuro-ocular health, this proposal focuses on the continuous and dynamic tracking of both macro and micro movements in real time. To realize the vision of a wearable device with a convenient form factor for continuous, real-time, personalized, and unobtrusive monitoring of pupil kinematics, we propose the development of a comprehensive end-to-end system. This system integrates two core components: (a) high-fidelity, high-resolution eye-tracking hardware capable of capturing both macro and micro-scale movements with precision, and (b) computationally optimized algorithms and machine learning models that are both memory- and power-efficient, enabling seamless operation on resource-constrained wearable devices. To address these twin goals, we propose leveraging neuromorphic vision cameras and a novel multi-light active probing hardware setup. Specifically, we utilize the "dark pupil" effect to manipulate the event camera, enabling it to generate events exclusively related to pupil movements, significantly reducing data volume and processing overhead. Additionally, we develop power-efficient algorithms that exploit the structured nature of both large-scale and minute-level pupil displacements, ensuring accurate tracking while minimizing computational and energy demands. Together, these innovations form the foundation for a transformative solution to neuro-ocular health monitoring. In our preliminary results we demonstrate the following: (a) Development of a Novel Event Camera-Based Multilight System: We successfully designed a rudimentary, dual-NIR light source-based event camera system embedded in a pair of wearable eyeglasses. This setup demonstrates our ability to capture events exclusively generated by the pupil without incurring preprocessing overhead or requiring firmware modifications to the event camera. title: Self-Adaptive Planning with Environmental Awareness for Embodied Agents
abs: Embodied AI is a domain within artificial intelligence that focuses on developing intelligent agents capable of interacting with the physical world in ways that mimic human or animal behavior. These agents—such as robots or autonomous vehicles—are equipped with physical bodies that allow them to sense, act, and learn within their environments. This integration bridges the critical gap between perception, decision-making, and physical interaction, allowing agents to perform complex tasks in real-world settings. Significant advancements in embodied agents have been made, encompassing both hardware (e.g., robot arms, sensors, and grippers) and software systems for tasks like visual navigation, manipulation, embodied question answering, instruction following and foundation models. While hardware innovations provide the physical capabilities for interaction, our focus is on addressing key limitations in the software frameworks that enable adaptive and environment-aware task planning. Current embodied AI planning approaches face three critical limitations that restrict their applicability in dynamic, real-world settings. First, embodied agent planning approaches often rely solely on large language models (LLMs) with pre-trained general world knowledge. This can lead to hallucinated or impractical plans that are not grounded in task-specific contexts or external knowledge, resulting in failures when executing complex tasks. Second, these systems lack the capability to perceive and track fine-grained environmental changes, such as object state transformations during tasks (e.g., a potato being peeled and sliced). Without this awareness, agents struggle to monitor and adapt to task progression effectively. Third, even when plans are generated, they remain static and struggle to adapt to accommodate unexpected changes during task execution, such as interacting with objects that are hidden or not initially visible. This inflexibility often leads to task execution failures. Although recent robotic foundation models like RT‑2 and OpenVLA demonstrate impressive performance by leveraging large‑scale vision‑language pretraining fine‑tuned on robotic data, they typically predict robot actions directly from observations without an explicit planning stage. As a result, they lack mechanisms for effective task decomposition, dynamic state tracking, and adaptive plan refinement, limiting their adaptability in evolving environments. These limitations are significant as they hinder the ability of embodied agents to perform effectively in dynamic environments, such as homes, workplaces, or assistive scenarios. To address these limitations, this project proposes the development of self-adaptive embodied agents that can dynamically refine their plans and adapt to their environment through a deep understanding of interaction contexts. title: Electrically assisted heat transfer enhancement and temperature stabilisation of pool boiling for cooling of high-performance computing devices
abs: Boiling heat transfer is essential in many industrial and technological applications, including chemical processing, desalination, advanced manufacturing, and electronic device cooling, where increasing heat emission density poses significant challenges. Achieving maximum critical heat flux, stabilising temperatures, and preventing film boiling are key objectives in these systems. While passive cooling techniques are limited by their inability to adapt to varying heat flux, active cooling methods, which use external fields to control liquid behaviour, offer greater potential. However, the lack of a fundamental understanding of how electric fields affect boiling at the microscopic scale has hindered progress. This proposal aims to enhance boiling heat transfer and temperature stabilisation, while preventing film boiling, through a mechanistic investigation of how spatially and temporally modulated electric fields influence boiling on superheated surfaces. By combining theory, simulations, and experiments, we will explore the effects of electric fields on liquid-vapour-solid interactions, focusing on the three-phase contact line. Preliminary results show that interdigital electrodes (IDEs) generating periodic electric fields can enhance liquid spreading, rupture vapour films, and significantly improve heat transfer (by over 50%) while suppressing film boiling. This interdisciplinary project will leverage the expertise of investigators in thermal engineering and micro/nano fabrication. The research will generate new insights into electric field-assisted boiling, with implications for high-performance cooling systems. It will contribute to developing scalable, reliable solutions for thermal management in modern electronic devices, and train students in heat transfer, fluid mechanics, and material science.

title:
Implantable Wireless Optogenetic Brain Encoder for Advanced Cognitive and Behavioural
Studies
abs: Developing brain-machine interfaces (BMIs) that establish communications between the brain and the external world has been consistently fuelling the passion of the science community as these technologies provide researchers exciting opportunities to study the underlying neural dynamics behind consciousness, intelligence, senses, and behaviours. This proposal aims to develop a wireless optogenetic brain encoder that propels these pursuits by providing cellular-scale and cell-specific neural modulation to rodents or non-human primates without restricting their movement. Unlike traditional electrical BMIs, optogenetic encoder fundamentally resolves the issue of uncontrolled spread of electricity, offering theoretically more precise control of neural dynamics. This device will utilize inductive charging with paired antennas to deliver continuous wireless power, eliminating the need for batteries or tethered connections. The optogenetic stimulations utilize densely packed μ-OLEDs-on-CMOS arrays with real-time individual addressability. Furthermore, a mechanically guided compressive buckling method will form arrayed penetration probes with distribute μ-OLEDs-on-CMOS units at arbitrary depths. Implantation of this device will not disrupt animals' natural behaviours, thus broadening the scope of cognitive neuroscience research. Moreover, the technology's fabrication process can be standardized for commercialization, benefiting the neuroscience community and generating economic value for Singapore, as it meets the needs of researchers worldwide.

title: LuminAI: Accelerating Ternary Organic Solar Cell Innovation with Self-Driving Labs
abs: This research proposal outlines the development of a self-driving lab (SDL) aimed at optimizing ternary organic photovoltaic devices fabricated in ambient conditions. The core objective is to achieve power conversion efficiencies (PCE) exceeding 11%, pushing beyond the current ambient-fabrication benchmark of 10.2%. The research is built on the hypothesis that a digital twin-enabled fabrication process can outperform traditional optimization methods through rapid parameter exploration, particularly in managing ambient condition variations. The team proposes that incorporating a ternary component to SDL-optimized binary blends will enhance exciton generation, thereby boosting current density while maintaining environmental stability. The project is structured around three specific aims: first, to develop an SDL that integrates high-throughput experimentation using Opentrons Flex Robot and automated fabrication via custom Jubilee3D slot-die coating robots; second, to implement an AWS-based RAG chatbot and Bayesian Optimization framework for enhanced process control; and third, to optimize and characterize ternary NFA combinations targeting consistent PCE above 11%. The methodology is organized into three work packages. WP1 focuses on SDL development, integrating both ambient and glovebox fabrication capabilities with comprehensive environmental monitoring. WP2 involves developing the RAG chatbot and Bayesian optimization framework for cross-environment experimentation. WP3 encompasses the systematic optimization of ternary blends through high-throughput screening and process window mapping. The feasibility of the proposal is well-supported by several factors. The team has already achieved preliminary results of 9.31% PCE in ambient conditions using a D-18Cl:L8-BO:Y7 system. The research team brings established expertise in PVs, digital twinning, and RAG chatbots, with access to necessary facilities and equipment. They have implemented clear risk management strategies including multi-layered monitoring systems and have demonstrated previous success with similar digital twin systems in binary OPV optimization.
kw: Photovoltaics, Self-Driving Labs, Machine Learning

title: Theoretical and Algorithmic Fundamental Performance Limits of Symbolic Regression
abs: Symbolic Regression (SR) is a machine learning method that discovers mathematical equations from data, providing a transparent alternative to black-box artificial intelligence models. Despite its growing adoption in fields such as medicine, physics and material sciences, the fundamental performance limits of SR remain unknown. This research aims to establish both theoretical and algorithmic performance limits for SR and apply these insights to real-world applications. By uncovering these limits, the study will provide a deeper understanding of SR’s capabilities and enable the development of more effective and interpretable machine learning models. Our study focuses on three research questions, as described below. The first research question is: What are the theoretical performance limits of SR? To answer this question, our specific aims are to: 1). Develop theoretical bounds for performance of SR algorithms to increase the understanding of SR and even spark new theoretical results for SR and 2). Verify the obtained theoretical bounds empirically on existing SR benchmark datasets to build intuition on how to design and improve SR algorithms. Our hypothesis is that generalization of SR algorithms is bounded by measures of stability. The methodology involves deriving theoretical bounds for SR’s performance using generalization theory and stability analysis. This will require developing new mathematical techniques to quantify how SR algorithms respond to small changes in the data. These theoretical results will then be tested against real-world benchmark datasets to determine their practical applicability. The second research question is: What are the algorithmic performance limits of SR? To answer this question, our specific aims are to: 1). Perform large-scale exhaustive search of models in SR on real-world benchmark datasets, in which data of all equations searched and optimized will be stored as an `optimized equation' repository hosted online for reuse by other SR researchers and 2). Compare the obtained algorithmic performance limits against state-of-the-art SR algorithms and SR benchmarks, and draw meaningful insights in terms of the efficiency of existing SR algorithms and whether there is sufficient room for improvement. Our hypothesis is that current SR algorithms do not sufficiently explore the search space of short, explainable equations. The methodology involves conducting large-scale exhaustive searches using high-performance computing resources. This process will systematically explore the space of possible equations, optimizing their parameters using multiple numerical optimization methods. This search will provide an absolute reference point for assessing SR’s algorithmic performance limits, allowing researchers to measure how close current SR algorithms are to the best possible solutions. title: Physics-informed sheaf neural network for chemical data analysis
abs: Chemistry is essential to not only our everyday life of food, clothing, shelter, and health, but also fundamental solutions to global crisis in energy, environment, and climate. With the establishment of large-sized chemical databanks, including PubChem, ChEMBL, ZINC, ChemSpider, Materials project, and others, AI is beginning to revolutionize various areas in chemical research and industries, including computational chemistry, chemical informatics, analytical chemistry, chemical synthesis, chemical reaction, chemical engineering, chemical design and discovery, drug discovery and material. Since all chemical systems are controlled or governed by physical laws and principles, failure to incorporate physical principles into the representations and learning architectures of AI models will result in unrealistic results. To design physics-informed AI models is a major challenge not only in AI for chemistry and AI for sciences, but also in Large Language Models (LLMs), of which hallucinations and weakness in reasoning significantly hinder their applications. In this project, we propose, for the first time, the sheaf-theory-based mathematical foundation for normal mode analysis (NMA). As a powerful tool for molecular dynamics analysis, NMA is widely used in the study of the vibrational properties of molecules. By analyzing how atoms within a molecule move in response to small perturbations, NMA offers valuable insights into the flexibility, dynamics, and function of molecules. We will establish the intrinsic connections between sheaf theory and NMA. In particular, we will develop an anisotropic sheaf model, in which the corresponding sheaf Laplacian matrix will be equivalent to the Hessian matrix from NMA, and its eigenvectors represent intrinsic global molecular motions. Sheaf theory-based cohomology, global section, and Hodge theory will be used in the characterization of the deeper insights of molecular intrinsic dynamics from NMA. Further, we will develop physics-informed geometric deep learning models, including sheaf spectral networks and sheaf attention networks. With the proper restriction map based on molecular normal mode analysis, molecular sheaf representations will be developed, and sheaf Laplacian matrices will be constructed accordingly. Similar to spectral network models, sheaf spectral networks can be constructed by using different polynomial filters on sheaf Laplacian matrices. More importantly, the sheaf Laplacian matrices can be regarded as a special weighting mechanism and further incorporated into sheaf attention models. Moreover, we will develop higher-order sheaf models and higher-order sheaf neural networks. Based on higher-order topological representations, including simplicial complexes and cellular complexes, higher-order molecular sheaf models will be proposed and used to systematically analyze the influence of higher-order terms on NMA, offering a more sophisticated framework to explore molecular dynamics. title: Cost-efficient hydrolysates for cultivated meat using proteases from edible fungi strains
inst: SIFBI - Singapore Institute of Food and Biotechnology Innovation
abs: The objective of this project is to establish a protease-producing fungi platform that will allow for the hydrolysis of agricultural raw materials into low-cost hydrolysates which can be used to replace Fetal Bovine Serum (FBS) and growth factors in Cultivated Meat (CM) production. In traditional cell culture, FBS and growth factors often contributes to the majority of the production costs. The high cost of cell culture media presents a significant barrier to make CM available for the masses. Furthermore, FBS composition varies from batch to batch, and FBS from certain countries may contain viral, microbial and prions risks. In addition, different cell lines have different growth factors requirement, further adding on to the cost of production. To replace the use of FBS and growth factors, some groups have already shown the effectiveness of plant-based hydrolysates in supporting mammalian cell growth. However, their approach of generating hydrolysates typically relies on using commercial enzymes such as viscozyme, alcalase and flavourzymes. These commercial enzymes are highly purified and expensive and continual addition of these commercial enzymes will eventually drive up the cost of hydrolysates production. In our approach we will harness the proteolytic activity of the edible fungi available from A*STAR Natural Product Library (NPL) to hydrolyze affordable raw materials such as soybean meal, peanut meal and okara. The generated hydrolysates will be assess for cell-growth promoting activity and positive hydrolysates will be subjected to bioassay-guided mass spectrometric analysis in order to identify possible bioactive components. By optimizing the degree of hydrolysis, we will be able to obtain hydrolysates with different cell growth promoting profiles. Characterisation of the fungal proteases that yielded active hydrolysates will be performed to identify the types of proteases... The final hydrolysates candidates will be fractionated into different sizes and be used to upscale our porcine cell lines to 1.5 billion cells as a proof of concept.

title: Maritime Continent Atmospheric Regional Reanalysis (MCARR)
inst: IHPC - Institute of High Performance Computing
abs: This project aims to produce a high-resolution weather reanalysis dataset for Singapore and the surrounding Southeast Asian region from 1990 to 2025. The reanalysis will assimilate ground-based measurements and satellite observations using advanced ensemble data assimilation and a km-scale regional climate model to improve spatial and temporal resolution compared to currently available global reanalyses (e.g. ERA5). The dataset will support the National AI Strategy by providing high-quality historical weather data essential for training AI-driven weather models. These models will enhance (1) real-time operational decision-making in the aviation and maritime sectors and (2) long-term planning capabilities for government agencies. Key challenges to the endeavour include (1) the limited availability of high- quality historical weather data, (2) biases and inconsistencies in different observational datasets, and (3) the need for robust data assimilation methods to merge multiple sources while maintaining physical consistency. Additionally, regional climate variability and urban influences pose challenges for high-resolution reanalysis. We hypothesize that integrating multi-source weather data with advanced assimilation techniques will significantly improve regional weather reanalysis accuracy. We also propose that machine learning-based bias correction and downscaling will enhance the dataset’s quality, making it more suitable for AI applications in operational forecasting and policy planning. The project will adopt a multi-step approach: (1) building on global reanalysis observation datastores to compile a comprehensive regional historical observation database; (2) applying advanced data assimilation techniques and a tuned regional climate model to accurately represent historical local weather; (3) using machine learning to correct biases and inconsistencies; and (4) validating the reanalysis dataset against independent observations. By developing the most comprehensive high-resolution weather reanalysis dataset for Southeast Asia, this project will provide the foundation for AI-driven predictive capabilities, supporting Singapore’s leadership in climate resilience and intelligent weather forecasting.

title: Novel neural network models and architectures for the post-silicon era
abs: This research proposal addresses the imminent limitations of silicon chip technology as predicted by the approaching end of Moore's Law, which has historically guided the semiconductor industry by predicting the doubling of transistors on a chip approximately every year. As silicon transistors reach their physical and energy efficiency limits—manifested in challenges like dark silicon, where power delivery and heat dissipation issues prevent the full utilization of chips—the need for alternative materials and technologies has become urgent. This proposal seeks to explore and develop post-silicon technologies, particularly focusing on materials such as carbon nanotubes, graphene and other 2D material, as potential successors to silicon. Graphene, in particular, is recognized for its exceptional properties, including high electron mobility and excellent thermal conductivity, making it an ideal candidate for high-performance, energy-efficient devices. Recent breakthroughs have enabled the creation of graphene-based transistors, overcoming previous limitations related to its lack of a band gap, which is critical for logic applications. The proposed research will focus on characterizing the performance and error profiles of these post-silicon materials and leveraging them in the context of deep learning. Devices built using these material are inherent susceptible to noise and errors, especially at small scales. Deep learning models are well known to tolerate error. Hence, the research will investigate how neural network models can be adapted to work effectively with them. Specifically, the proposal will explore novel models such as spiking neural networks, hyperdimensional computing, stochastic computing, and Kolmogorov-Arnold networks, which may be particularly suited to the unique characteristics of these materials. The primary research goals are as follows: 1. Develop a model framework: We will create a framework that abstracts the key features, characteristics, and constraints of post-silicon materials used in computing, with a focus on understanding and mitigating the error rates associated with these technologies. Carbon nanotubes and graphene will be the primary focus, though other materials such as gallium nitride (GaN) and resistive RAM (RRAM) will also be considered, particularly in processing-in-memory architectures. 2. Explore deep learning models: Using insights from the material modeling, we will investigate how novel neural network models can be optimized for use with these post-silicon devices. The goal is to identify which models are best suited to the idiosyncrasies of specific post-silicon materials and the devices that can be created from them. 3. Innovate training and inference algorithms: We will develop new training and inference algorithms tailored to the unique properties of these emerging materials, addressing their relatively unexplored computational potential, as well as work out the limitations, and hence find the conditio

title: Fundamental Computational Aspects of Neuro-symbolic AI
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: In this proposal, the over-arching theme is the utilization of algebraic computations to enhance the performance of neuro-symbolic AI systems, with an emphasis on the fundamental computational aspects of symbolic methods, and their synergy with neural-based methods. First, we tackle what is arguably one of the biggest technical challenges for incorporating symbolic methods: scalability. State-of-the-art symbolic solvers predominantly rely on an efficient implementation of a satisfiability (SAT) solver as their core computational engine, which could be invoked iteratively, to solve diverse computational tasks. Hence, it is not surprising that there has been intense effort from the SAT community in recent years, focused on speeding up SAT-solving, primarily via optimizing the management of a portfolio of search heuristics and meta-heuristics. Crucially, all existing approaches are inherently based on search optimization, possibly guided by supervised learning. In our first work package (WP), we propose a completely new non-search-based approach for SAT-solving. Our key technical insight relies on a strong parallelism between the conjunctive normal form-disjunctive normal form (CNF-DNF) duality, and the algebraic Alexander duality; this parallelism has thus far been unnoticed by both logicians and algebraists. As part of our preliminary work, we have proven a precise formulation of this parallelism. Using algebraic algorithms for computing Alexander duals, we thus get a new paradigm for SAT-solving: Rather than search through the space of candidate assignments and check one-by-one until a first valid assignment is discovered, we can *directly compute* the analog of Alexander dual for the input CNF formula, to get *all possible* valid assignments at once. We shall study how this new algebraic paradigm can be used to significantly speed up the solving of various SAT-related tasks, as well as to improve the efficiency of SMT solvers, which are the latest state-of-the-art constraint solvers that allow arbitrary non-Boolean constraints (e.g. numerical inequalities). Second, we tackle the challenge of symbolic representations. This challenge is particularly pertinent in the context of neuro-symbolic programming. From logical expressions to algorithms/programs written in some domain specific language (DSL), such symbolic data are inherently discrete, so they do not gel well with gradient descent and other continuous optimization techniques commonly used in neural-based methods. However, for generative tasks (e.g. inductive program synthesis), where the desired output is a program (e.g. Python code) that must be consistent with user-provided specifications and/or exemplars, any neuro-symbolic learning approach would intrinsically require a suitable representation of the space of candidate programs. title: Photonic Time Crystals Interacting With Free Electrons
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: This project explores the interactions between free electrons and spatiotemporal photonic crystals (also known as photonic time crystals), a class of optical media with periodic variations in both space and time. Unlike conventional photonic crystals, which are spatially periodic, the spatiotemporal modulation introduces rich physics, including energy gaps, momentum gaps, and mixed energy-momentum gaps. A key feature of temporal modulation is the exponential energy growth within the momentum gap, enabling potential light amplification. We focus on electron-induced light emission processes such as Cherenkov radiation, transition radiation, Smith-Purcell radiation, and surface wave phenomena like surface plasmons. Our research methodology includes: (1) developing universal theoretical models for spatiotemporal electron-induced radiations to highlight differences from conventional spatial systems; (2) performing numerical simulations with simple spatiotemporal structures, such as time gratings, to isolate fundamental physics; and (3) conducting in-silico experiments to design practical spatiotemporal photonic crystals and free-electron sources as a step toward experimental validation. The goal is to provide a mechanistic understanding and quantitative designs for light sources in photonic time crystals interacting with electrons, paving the way for future experimental demonstrations. This project advances the field of optoelectronics by transitioning from spatial to spatiotemporal systems and moving from passive to active free-electron radiation sources.

title: Elucidating the Nanoscale Origin of Unconventional Hall Effects in Anisotropic Chiral Magnets
abs: The anomalous Hall effect (AHE) has been imperative to understanding and exploring magnetism for over a century. Its proportionality to magnetization, rooted in spin-orbit physics, enables detection of magnetic phases with broken symmetry and topological properties. These notably include noncollinear magnets hosting chiral spin-textures (e.g. skyrmions), whose emergent electrodynamics have profound scientific and practical implications. Beyond AHE, chiral spin-textures should also produce a topological Hall effect (THE), firmly established in isotropic helimagnets. Since 2016, numerous anisotropic chiral magnets have shown beyond-AHE “residual” Hall effects (RHEs), e.g. metallic multilayers, complex oxides, and 2D chalcogenides, topological materials, alloys etc., that can host aperiodic spin-textures. While widely attributed to THE, these signals are up to 10,000 times larger than theoretically expected from imaged spin textures. The origin of these RHEs remains highly controversial. The absence of a conclusive experimental and theoretical understanding is a longstanding bottleneck in condensed matter, spanning ~4,000 papers. Resolving this controversy requires a fundamentally distinct strategy. We will elucidate the nanoscale magnetic phenomena underlying RHE via (a) concurrent magnetic-electrical studies; (b) quantitative magnetic imaging; (c) tunable material parameters, and (d) spatio-temporal evolution. Our custom-built system combines magnetometry and electrical transport with unprecedented resolution (100 ppm). Together with multi-modal nanoscale imaging and 3 well-established magnetic thin film platforms, we are uniquely positioned to uncover the physics of RHEs in anisotropic magnets. Our project comprises four tasks to systematically examine different facets of anisotropic magnets and their role in Hall effects. Task-1 on metallic multilayers will investigate the relationship of RHEs with spin-texture morphology and chirality. Task-2 on oxide superlattices will explore the influence of spatial morphology on emergent magnetism, spin-textures and Hall effects. Task-3 on 2D chalcogenides will examine the effect of magnetic intercalation and exchange frustration on competing phases and Hall signatures. Finally, Task-4 on spatio-temporal dynamics will explore unconventional Hall effect signatures of magnetization nucleation and dynamics. The project leverages the PI (A.S.)'s expertise in materials growth, electrical, magnetic, and magneto-microscopic characterization – demonstrated through several high-visibility publica-tions[Nature ’16, Nat Mtrls ’17, Nat Comm ’19, Nat Comm ’21, Nature ’24]. This is complemented by established collaborations with Ariando (oxide heterostructures), Okada (2D chalcogenides[PR Mtrls ’20, Adv Mtrls ’23]), and Atatüre (nitrogen-vacancy magnetometry[PR Mtrls ‘21]). title: Photoreforming of Plastic Waste Enabled by Chiral Ferroelectric Perovskite/Semiconductor Heterostructured Photocatalysts
abs: Plastic waste in the environment has led to significant white pollution, however, its rich carbon content offers the potential for conversion into valuable chemicals, presenting a promising solution to energy and environmental challenges. Compared to traditional pyrolysis, photoreforming of plastic waste offers the potential for plastic upcycling under mild conditions, yet its advancement is hindered by the development of efficient photocatalysts. In this context, the proposed project aims at (a) developing chiral ferroelectric perovskite/semiconductor heterostructures (i.e., Type II and Z-scheme heterostructures) with optimized charge separation efficiency, (b) unravelling the influences of chirality, piezoelectric field, and heterostructure on charge carrier dynamics, (c) scrutinizing the photocatalytic activities of plastic waste photoreforming under visible light irradiation and piezoelectric field, and (d) exploring the yields and generation mechanisms of plastic upcycling products. Intellectual Merit: The intellectual merit of the proposed project lies in developing a robust plastic photoreforming strategy that not only degrades plastic waste but also converts it into valuable chemicals under mild conditions by capitalizing on rationally designed chiral ferroelectric perovskite/semiconductor heterostructured photocatalysts. Notably, the chirality and ferroelectric property can be readily tuned and optimized by varying the chiral organic A site in halide perovskites with the general formula ABX3. Moreover, the chiral ferroelectric perovskite/semiconductor heterostructures with desirable energy band alignment between them can be conveniently constructed. Such judicious design and integration of chirality, ferroelectricity, and heterostructure to yield a set of perovskite/semiconductor photocatalysts provides unique opportunities to markedly improve charge separation, thereby enhancing the photoreforming of plastic waste. Furthermore, the generation mechanisms of plastic upcycling products will be elucidated, aiding in the development of robust multifunctional photocatalysts to enable the increased yield of value-added products. Broader Impact: Knowledge generated by this project will significantly impact the development of next-generation chiral ferroelectric perovskite-derived heterostructured photocatalysts. Noticeably, a variety of chiral ferroelectric halide perovskites ABX3 can be produced by tailoring chiral and ferroelectric organic A site, inorganic B site, and halide C site. Moreover, a diversity of semiconductors with the proper band structures for pairing with chiral ferroelectric ABX3 can be easily accessed to yield ABX3/semiconductor heterostructures with desirable band energy alignment. They can be regarded as hybrid nanomaterials. title: Nonlinear Twistronics: Twisted Two-Dimensional Nanomaterials for High-Efficiency, Functional and Ultrathin Nonlinear Optics
abs: This project is inspired by the emerging field of twistronics[1], which aims to regulate electron transport and localization via twisted stackings of two-dimensional (2D) materials for many-body physics and unusual applications such as superconductivity[2,3] and others. Extending this scientific frontier, we will explore how the twist in multilayer quantum materials can regulate the nonlinear harmonic generations and their practical applications. Our approach starts from rigorous analysis of nonlinear harmonic generation processes, where the pumping depletion, material dispersion due to interband transitions, damping, strong anisotropy, interfacial nonlinear effect, and arbitrary twisted geometry are all considered in first-principle calculation from Maxwell equations. This will end up with the world’s first numerical open-source nonlinear solver as the enabler of our proposed scientific frontier--nonlinear twistronics. We will experimentally verify it with twisted transition-metal dichalcogenides (TMD) multilayers and twisted van der Waals (vdW) materials. These know-hows will enable a few unique applications in this project such as atomically thin interfacial nonlinear effect, strong backward nonlinear generation, configurable nonlinear vortex generation and others with ultrathin footprint and high efficiency, while future and global efforts could benefit from this project to develop other disruptive nonlinear optical technologies. Our synergetic team combines the comprehensive expertise of physics, materials science, and optics. The lead PI oversees the theory and experimental measurements with collaborators on materials synthesis (Prof. Zheng Liu) and optical characterizations (Prof. Qijie Wang). We believe our scientific efforts here have the broad impact in highly efficient nonlinear integrated nanodevices and the functional structured nonlinear generation with simultaneous multidimensional manipulations, important for high-capacity communication, advanced imaging, ultrathin quantum light source and information processing, and other technologies. This proposal is re-submitted with an invitation from the Ministry of Education. Compared to the previous one, the current version has: (i) a new project summary highlighting the novelty and broad impact; (ii) the discussion highlighting the uniqueness (Session 1 and 2); (iii) added discussions of the risk and mitigation plan (Session 4); (iv) added the pathway towards impact on science, technology, and society (Session 6); and (v) more preliminary results on nonlinear models agreeing with experiments and experimental results of vortex generation that supports our hypothesis (Session 4).

title: OMNICON: Towards Task-Agnostic Representations for Long-Term Multi-Human Motion-with-Context Generation
abs: Introduction This proposal presents OMNICON, a comprehensive framework for generating realistic long-term multi-human motions with environmental context. By designing novel motion representations with generative solutions, OMNICON addresses critical challenges in long-term motion generation, multi-human interactions, and motion-with-context synthesis. Designed to advance applications across animation, gaming, virtual reality, and robotics, OMNICON leverages principles from physics and spatial reasoning to produce temporally consistent, contextually adaptive, and socially coherent motion sequences. Academic Significance OMNICON introduces a transformative approach to 3D human motion generation. Current methods often rely on task-specific models and isolated datasets, resulting in limited adaptability and performance. OMNICON’s generalizable representations seamlessly integrate into diverse frameworks, addressing key limitations such as error accumulation in long-term sequences, insufficient modeling of multi-human interactions, and disjointed scene-motion synthesis. By unifying spatial reasoning, physical plausibility, and generative AI techniques, OMNICON redefines motion generation and expands the scope of its applications. The research findings will significantly contribute to the fields of generative AI, motion synthesis, and spatial modeling. Research Questions This project seeks to address the following research questions: 1. How can long-term multi-human motion be represented to minimize error accumulation while maintaining physical coherence? 2. How can spatial relationships between human motions and the environment be jointly modeled with the same representation for seamless motion-with-context synthesis? 3. How can multi-human interactions be effectively represented and synthesized to ensure spatial coherence, temporal coordination, and realistic group dynamics? Existing Gaps Current motion generation techniques face several critical limitations. Frame-by-frame generation accumulates errors, degrading long-term motion consistency. Multi-human modeling often focuses on pairwise interactions, failing to capture complex group dynamics. Motion and scene synthesis are typically treated as separate tasks, leading to inconsistencies between generated motions and environmental context. Additionally, existing datasets primarily feature short-duration sequences, limited environmental diversity, and either single or dual-person interactions, lacking the comprehensive data necessary to model long-term, multi-human motions in rich contextual environments. These gaps highlight the need for a unified framework and dataset capable of addressing long-term, context-aware, and multi-human motion generation holistically. title: Online Optimization with Egalitarian and Fairness Constraints
abs: In online decision-making problems, one selects actions that maximize rewards based on previously selected actions and observed rewards. However, scant attention is paid to egalitarian and fairness constraints. In this project, we design algorithms that shed light on the tradeoff between reward maximization and these new constraints by studying the multi-armed bandits (MABs) model, which is a canonical statistical model that exemplifies the exploration-exploitation tradeoff. Take, for instance, a job assignment problem depicted in which there are U users with recurring jobs of equal load (e.g., hourly database updates) and K computing resources with fluctuating computational power (e.g., due to hardware degradation and thermal throttling). The agent’s objective is to distribute these jobs fairly among the available resources such that over T time steps, the user who must wait the longest across all their jobs (i.e., receives the least cumulative reward) is not significantly worse off compared to other users. Another example involves ride-hailing services which present another scenario where fair assignment is desirable. In this scenario, there are U passengers and K drivers who offer varying degrees of experience to passengers (e.g., due to vehicle condition and driver behavior). The agent’s objective is to allocate users fairly to vehicles such that over T trips, no passenger faces a significantly worse overall experience than others. Additionally, we consider the Nash social welfare (NSW) objective, which corresponds to equating the performance of the algorithm to the geometric mean. There are four specific aims in this project. Aim 1: Achieving Egalitarian Fairness: We wish to design algorithms to achieve egalitarian fairness in the combinatorial multi-armed bandits problem. Specifically, we ask how one can design an agent’s assignment policy that optimizes overall utility for individual users while also ensuring that no user within a group consistently encounters substantially suboptimal outcomes? Aim 2: Fairness of Exposure with Profitability Considerations We also consider another framework in which one arm (instead of U > 1) is played at each round and the number of times each arm is played is (in some way) proportional to its merit, the mean of the arm. This differs from most existing work in fairness in exposure, where the goal is to ensure that the policy π at timestep T plays each arm with a probability proportional to its merit. In other words, it does not matter how many times each arm is played in the T timesteps. However, linear regret—an undesirable outcome—ensues, if this is strictly enforced. Thus, we want to ensure that the decision maker’s policy π has the flexibility to optimize for profit. title: Learning Vision-language-action Models for Robotic Mobile Manipulation
abs: The Problem Mobile manipulation plays an important role in diverse robotic tasks such as household service, industrial assembly and logistics, especially in large working areas. Vision-language-action (VLA) models acquired high generalization ability across tasks and environments for manipulation, while three challenges remain unsolved in their deployment for mobile manipulation applications. First, the working range is limited due to the fixed base. Second, existing VLA models cannot understand complex high-level instructions of mobile manipulation tasks. Third, collecting tremendous mobile manipulation expert trajectories for VLA model training leads to heavy human labor cost in data collection. Our Proposal We propose to learn a VLA model for general robotic mobile manipulation. Compared with existing VLA models, our framework (a) enables mobility in large working range for manipulation policies; and (b) understands complex high-level instructions with long manipulation sequences; and (c) requires only 10% data collection cost. Specific Aims Training a VLA model should align commonsense knowledge in multimodal large language models (MLLM) with the realistic physical world to generate feasible robot actions, which consists of three key components including target, model architecture and training recipe of the alignment. Our fundamental research focuses on designing above three components. Fundamental Research #1: Representing visual clues of the large working environment Fundamental Research #2: Designing VLA model architecture for whole-body trajectory generation Fundamental Research #3: Sample-efficient training of VLA models for mobile manipulation Methodology Our overall system consists of three components including the online scene map for environment representation, hierarchical VLA model architecture for mobile manipulation policy generation and the world model for efficient VLA agent training. The online scene map represents semantic and geometric information of the entire environment. The hierarchical VLA agents include the high-level task planner, the mid-level navigation controller and the low-level manipulation controller. The world model simulates the interactive physical environment to provide feedback in VLA training. Expected Outcomes and Impacts We propose the framework for next-generation robotic foundation model learning with higher flexibility in open working environments, stronger ability in solving real-world tasks with complex hierarchies, and higher sample-efficiency in large-scale robot learning. Due to acquired benefits, an industry standard is potentially built for robot-assisted manufacturing and service. Patents and impactful papers are expected.

title: Electrochemical low-grade heat harvesting using deep eutectic solvents
abs: This proposal outlines an innovative approach to develop an electrochemical system designed for the efficient harvesting of low-grade heat energy, leveraging the capabilities of a thermally regenerative electrochemical cycle (TREC) coupled with advanced electrode materials and novel electrolytes characterized by an enhanced temperature coefficient. The primary goal is to significantly boost the efficiency of converting low-grade heat energy from diverse sources, such as power plant coolants, into usable electricity. A key focus of the research will be to examine the impact of temperature fluctuations on the temperature coefficient of electrode materials, facilitated by phase separation and solvation dynamics within specialized concentrated and deep eutectic electrolytes. The project will: 1) Explore the effects of temperature-induced phase separation in deep eutectic solvents on electrochemical performance; 2) Develop and evaluate concentrated and deep eutectic electrolytes aimed at maximizing the temperature coefficient; 3) Aim to achieve an electrochemical cell with a temperature coefficient exceeding 2.5 mV/K; 4) Construct a prototype TREC system to demonstrate and validate its efficiency in laboratory settings. This research is expected to significantly advance our understanding of the underlying mechanisms of electrochemical reactions influenced by thermal variations, crucial for the design of more effective low-grade heat harvesting systems.

title: Mapping the Daily Mobility of Older Adults: A GPS-Based Study of Mobility and Built Environment Interaction in Singapore's Public Housing Neighbourhoods
abs: Daily mobility is a crucial indicator of environmental exposure and access to resources, as it reflects when, where, and how individuals interact with their surroundings. In recent years, research has increasingly focused on the daily mobility of community-dwelling older adults to understand its relationship with lifestyle, health, and the effectiveness of neighbourhood environments in supporting their mobility needs. However, the connection between daily mobility and neighbourhood environments among older adults, particularly in high-rise, high-density cities like Singapore, remains underexplored. This study aims to address this gap by using GPS tracking technology to empirically explore the daily mobility patterns and activity radii of older adults with varying physical abilities, as measured by their Activities of Daily Living (ADL) levels, across public housing neighbourhoods developed in different periods in Singapore. By analysing activity locations, movement patterns, and the shapes of these patterns (including walking distances and activity ranges) in three dimensions—point, line, and plane—this research seeks to challenge the generalised assumptions often used in urban planning (e.g., movement radii of 400m or 500m. Examples include standardized movement radii of 400m or 500m, distinctions between void decks and environmental decks, and the relationship between public space design and the presence of services or shops. These assumptions typically overlook the specific urban context of high-rise, high-density environments and the unique mobility needs of older populations. The study will leverage GPS data from 300 participants living in public housing neighbourhoods developed across three different stages of urban planning, complemented by field observations and in-depth interviews. The GPS data will provide an accurate depiction of the movement patterns and activity radii of older adults, offering a quantitative foundation to analyse their interactions with the built environment. Field observations and interviews will complement the GPS data to uncover the contextual and experiential factors that shape how the built environment influences these mobility behaviours. Grounded in the competence-environmental press model, this study is expected to contribute to both ecological theories of ageing and to practical urban planning applications. Specifically, the research will demonstrate how variations in personal competence interact diverse neighbourhood typologies to shape daily mobility patterns of older adults. The findings are expected to inform future neighbourhood planning and renewal programmes, with the goal of enhancing accessibility, promoting independent living, and creating age-friendly environments that support older adults at different ADL levels in ageing in place.

title: Robust Visual Perception for Video Question-Answering
abs: Video Question-Answering (VideoQA) is the task of answering natural language questions about videos. It is a multimodal challenge that tests both the visual perception and natural language reasoning capabilities of AI systems. State-of-the-art performance has improved significantly on benchmark datasets by incorporating large language models (LLMs). However, recent studies, including our preliminary studies, have revealed that these models are ``right for the wrong reasons'' -- models tend to ignore the visual inputs and rely on language biases in the datasets and common sense hallucinations of the LLMs to predict the answers. This project aims to put the ``video'' back into VideoQA, by improving VideoQA models' conditioning and understanding of videos. We tackle the problem from a data, modeling, and learning perspective. From the data perspective, we propose to curate a new VideoQA dataset. Through model- and human-in-the-loop strategies, we aim to limit dataset bias while simultaneously promoting visually-grounded question-answers. From a model perspective, we aim to develop more effective video representations that capture fine-grained spatial information and temporal dynamics. From a learning perspective, we will explore visual-language alignment strategies within visually grounded and evidence-based learning paradigms to discourage models from LLM-inherited shortcuts. The outcome of this project will advance the robustness and trustworthiness of VideoQA and vision-language models as a whole and bring us closer to comprehensive multimodal perception and reasoning.
kw: video understanding, video question-answering, multi-modal learning, vision-language models

title: Evaluating Public Sector Governance in Asia
abs: Nearly all economic and social programmes are ultimately implemented at scale by government bureaucrats. Fostering a capable, clean bureaucracy is therefore critical for good governance – and a cornerstone of Singapore’s political and economic success. To build an effective bureaucracy, governments must (i) attract talented citizens to public service, (ii) motivate them effectively, and (iii) leverage information and data systems to enhance their performance. We examine each of these dimensions by conducting three research projects in collaboration with governments in three Asian countries – Singapore, India, and Bangladesh. Our three sub-projects employ quasi experimental methods such as difference-in-differences and randomized controlled trials to estimate the causal effects of different policies aimed at improving each of these three dimensions. Project 1 examines Singapore’s bureaucracy and exploits administrative and survey data to analyze how recruitment policies shape the composition and effectiveness of the civil service. We assess how remuneration structures and leadership programs influence who joins and remains in public service. Project 2 studies the impact of a 91% salary increase for village secretaries in Telangana, India. This natural experiment allows us to measure how pay influences bureaucrat performance, effort on the job, and retention. Our project is one of the first to evaluate the causal effect of public sector pay. Project 3 investigates whether better monitoring systems can improve environmental regulation in Bangladesh. We implement an information dashboard that prioritizes enforcement efforts against the brick kilns causing the largest public health harms. By linking satellite data with air quality models, we provide frequently updated and actionable insights to regulators, and assess whether better information improves enforcement and ultimately public health.
kw: Governance, Bureaucracy, Meritocracy, Political Economy, Climate

title: The mechanism of PIH1D1 in co-translational, cytoplasmic preassembly of the flagellar outer dynein arm complex
abs: A protein often functions together with other proteins in the form of a multimeric complex. While different protein subunits are synthesized, likely in different parts of a cell and under different regulations, the cell needs to orchestrate their encounter, stoichiometry and interactions. In recent years, co-translational protein folding and interaction is emerging as a common principle in eukaryotic systems, governing both homomeric and heteromeric protein complex formation [1]. However, the factors regulating this process and their mechanistic details are largely unknown. In this study, we will focus on the outer dynein arm (ODA) complex, a highly conserved structure found in motile cilia (or flagella) in eukaryotic cells. Each ODA complex is composed of two or three heavy chains, two intermediate chains (IC1 and IC2) and a number of light chains (LCs). All subunits are synthesized and pre-assembled into a full ODA complex in the cytoplasm (Fig. 1). The full, pre-assembled complexes are then transported into the ciliary compartment and incorporated into specific sites along the microtubule axoneme [2,3]. Several cytoplasmic proteins known as dynein axonemal assembly factors (DNAAFs) are required to assist the formation of the ODA complex [4]. Mutations in the ODA subunits or DNAAFs lead to defects in ODA assembly and have been implicated in motile ciliopathies such as primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD) [5]. The mechanisms of the DNAAFs and how they facilitate ODA cytoplasmic preassembly, are not fully understood. Using Trypanosoma brucei as a model for motile cilia, we identified an essential role of PIH1D1 (aka DNAAF14) in ODA pre-assembly (Fig. 2). In the absence of PIH1D1, formation of full ODA complex was inhibited, and the protein levels of ODA heavy chains were reduced. ICs and most LCs however, were enriched in an intermediate IC-LC complex (Fig. 3). Using a custom-produced, anti-PIH1D1 polyclonal antibody, PIH1D1 was localized to cytoplasmic foci containing translating ODA heavy chains (Fig. 4A). The number of PIH1D1 foci in each cell was correlated with the cell cycle, being most abundant in cells that were constructing a new flagellum (Fig. 4E). Based on our preliminary results, known ODA structure and subunit interactions as well as the widely-accepted function of PIH1D1 in the R2TP co-chaperone complex [6–9], we hypothesize that PIH1D1 functions in full ODA complex preassembly that is coupled to the translation of the ODA heavy chains, facilitating efficient expression of the ODA heavy chains and their sequential interactions with other ODA subunits (Fig. 5). In this proposal, we aim to map the precise point-of-function of PIH1D1 in ODA heavy chain co-translational assembly (Aim 1). We will also investigate the biochemical composition and function of the PIH1D1 foci, which may act as cell-cycle regulated, translation/assembly factories for the ODA complex (Aim 2). title: A global modelling framework for frugivory and seed dispersal interactions to understand ecosystem functioning in the human-modified tropics
abs: Seed dispersal is a crucial ecological process underpinning the diversity and long-term sustainability of ecosystems globally, but quantifying the impact that human activities has had on this ecosystem function remains a massive challenge. The vast majority of potential seed dispersal interactions have never been observed, owing to the difficulty of collecting such data and the rarity of most species. Furthermore, many existing studies are often unconsolidated, and a comprehensive, harmonised and curated database at the global scale does not exist, hampering richer comparative studies that span tropical realms. Most studies are typically site-based or taxon-specific observations that are limited in both space and time, hampering quantitative predictions of the seed dispersal function of a given species from empirical observations alone and extending them into novel ecological settings. Thus, a comprehensive framework to quantify human impacts on seed dispersal functioning, will not only require the data infrastructure but also new analytical tools to model ecological interactions. Here, we aim to provide an unprecedented global-scale analysis of human effects on seed dispersal functioning in tropical ecosystems. We will do this by first developing a pantropical database of frugivory and seed dispersal interactions and characterise the taxonomic, geographic and functional gaps in our understanding of these interactions. Using this data infrastructure, we will then develop novel trait-based interaction models, which will allow us to leverage information on species attributes to predict the likelihood of certain interactions and fill the gaps in interaction information. By integrating such models with counterfactual models of biodiversity change, we will then quantify how seed dispersal function is being affected by human activities as well as identify areas and species that are most vulnerable to these impacts. Overall, our work will pave the way for future research avenues on the role of ecosystem functioning in nature-based climate policy, conservation prioritization, sustainable ecosystem management and restoration and biodiversity protection of tropical forests, at a crucial time when the effects of biodiversity loss and climate change are intensifying worldwide. title: Architectures and circuits for pervasive 5G silicon chip connectivity with end-to-end system millimeter scale and 1,000X reduction in radio power consumption
abs: The exponential diffusion of connected devices and distributed sensing for Internet of Things (IoT) is requiring fundamental scientific innovation to enable aggressive miniaturization (unobtrusiveness, pervasiveness) and power consumption reduction (battery life) in short-range communications (~10 m). Circuit advances have reduced silicon system size to mm scale (excluding the antenna) [3] and power to sub-µW [1], as commonly supported by mm-scale micro-batteries with 10-year lifespan and < 100 µW power delivery [2]. Unfortunately, the antenna cannot currently achieve the same level of miniaturization, as its size is constrained to a significant fraction of the wireless carrier wavelength lambda (e.g., lambda/2), for example 10-cm scale in existing 2.4-GHz infrastructures (e.g., WiFi, Bluetooth). Miniaturizing the antenna while keeping transmitter power well below 100 µW is currently unfeasible as fundamental barrier impeding true system miniaturization at mm scale. As up-and-coming wireless technologies, mm-wave 5G wireless communications (e.g., 28 GHz) enable connectivity of more pervasive (10-100X) connected devices thanks to its large number of supported links via spatial diversity (beamforming, shorter range), high data rate for minimal temporal channel occupation/collisions, and mm-scale antenna size [12]. Unfortunately, expanding the use of 5G transmitters from smartphones to mm-scale silicon systems is currently unfeasible due to high power > >100 mW [4], [5], which vastly exceeds power delivery limitations of mm-scale energy sources. In an attempt to reduce power by reflecting an incident power rather than emitting it, 5G mm-wave backscattered communications were recently proposed in simulations [6], [7], [8], uncompetitive off-the-shelf [11], preliminary silicon demonstrations of connected device [9], or relay [10] containing few selected parts of the physical layer. [10] is restricted to operate at an impractical 20 cm from an RF power source. Also, power (unsuitable for mm-scale systems) does not include the dominant contribution of the necessary digital modulation [4], [5], [9]-[11]. In other words, miniaturization is not an antenna research challenge, but instead requires fundamental advances in silicon chip design methodologies and techniques. title: Demonstrating efficient multi-parameter quantum metrology using stationary two-mode squeezed vacuum states
abs: The ability to perform precise measurements is a crucial element in both scientific and technological pursuits, as it is through the measurement outcomes that we gain information about the system under investigation and make educated decisions regarding further explorations and optimisation efforts. In the quantum world, we face a unique challenge in realising high-precision measurements due to the fundamental constraint imposed by the Heisenberg uncertainty relation, which states that we cannot obtain precise knowledge of two non-commuting quantities associated with a single physical system, such as its position and momentum, simultaneously. One can measure any quantity with arbitrary precision by “squeezing” the state of the meter along that direction, but at the cost of losing precision (anti-squeezing) in the complementary quantity. Remarkably, this fundamental constraint can be circumvented using another purely quantum feature, namely entanglement. In this proposal, we present a scheme that harnesses the unique features of a two-mode squeezed vacuum (TMSV) state to achieve quantum-enhanced measurement precision of a pair of non-commuting quantities concurrently. We propose to demonstrate these features in a bosonic circuit quantum electrodynamics (cQED) platform, which is one of the most promising physical systems to explore continuous-variable (CV) quantum science and technology, thanks to its robustness and versatility. In this project, we take advantage of these features to create high-quality TMSV in the stationary modes of the superconducting cavities through three specific experimental aims. First, we propose a new cQED device that can be programmed to produce high-quality stationary TMSV as a resource state on-demand, via the parametric driving of an engineered non-linear coupler between two superconducting cavities. Next, we formulate a simple yet efficient measurement technique to directly probe the quadrature information of the stationary TMSV states by applying tailored numerical optimisation. Finally, we present the protocol for jointly probing a pair of non-commuting quantities and demonstrate efficient multi-parameter quantum metrology. Conceptually, this project serves as a stepping stone towards understanding the fundamental connections between nonlocality and uncertainty relations. Technically, the experimental capabilities on multi- parameter quantum metrology will pave the way for a wide range of applications, such as quantum dense coding, imaging, and continuous-variable quantum teleportation. Although the set of goals envisioned in this project is rich and ambitious, it is fully attainable thanks to the rigorous preliminary verifications as well as the comprehensive set of existing expertise developed by PI Yvonne Gao’s team.
