title: Elucidating molecular mechanisms of lipid transport for maintenance of bacterial membrane asymmetry
abs: Gram-negative bacteria depend for their survival on having an intact outer membrane (OM), which functions as a permeability barrier against toxic molecules including antibiotics. The OM is an asymmetric lipid bilayer in which the outer leaflet is comprised of lipopolysaccharides (LPS) and the inner leaflet of phospholipids (PLs). Lipid asymmetry in the OM is required for its barrier function, but building and maintaining this asymmetric bilayer is a challenge. Maintenance of lipid asymmetry is believed to be mediated by the OmpC-Mla system. This system removes PLs that are mislocalized in the outer leaflet of the OM, and transports them back to the inner membrane (IM). The OmpC-Mla system is the first PL trafficking system reported in Gram-negative bacteria, and uses a lipid binding protein that shuttles between the two membranes. While biochemical and structural characterization of the sub-complexes of the OmpC-Mla system have led to important insights thus far, critical information for the molecular bases of PL transport is still lacking. Furthermore, some Gram-negative bacteria express homologs of the Mla system that feature trans-envelope bridge complexes, presumably also required for PL transport; however, nothing is known about how these bridge systems move lipids. This proposal outlines experiments to characterize the protein complexes of the OmpC-Mla system, as well as bridge-like Mla complexes, to elucidate the molecular mechanisms of PL transport across the Gram-negative bacterial cell envelope. We will apply molecular genetics, chemical biology, biochemical reconstitution, and structural biology to reveal (1) how the OmpC-MlaA complex spontaneously transfers PLs from the outer leaflet of the OM to MlaC, (2) how the MlaFEDB complex couples ATP hydrolysis to drive the transfer of PLs from MlaC into the IM, and finally (3) how MlaFED-bridge complexes transport PLs through their hydrophobic tunnels that connects the IM and the OM. Given the role of OM lipid asymmetry in intrinsic Gram-negative antibiotic resistance, this proposal will provide a key foundation for future studies into small molecule inhibitors against these systems that may function as novel antibiotics or as adjuvants to existing antibiotics.
kw: Gram-negative bacteria; outer membrane lipid asymmetry; phospholipid transport; cryo-EM

title: BIOSYNTHESIS AND APPLICATIONS FOR CYCLOPHANE-CONTAINING PEPTIDES
abs: Peptide macrocycles are crucial in drug discovery due to their unique ability to combine the binding specificity of biologics with the cell permeability and oral bioavailability of small molecules. Their constrained structure enhances target affinity and stability against proteolytic degradation. Notable examples include cyclosporine, an immunosuppressant used in organ transplantation, and vancomycin, a glycopeptide antibiotic effective against bacterial infections. These macrocycles can target challenging protein-protein interactions, expanding the therapeutic possibilities for diseases traditionally considered undruggable. Cyclophane-containing peptides are a new modality for drug discovery and a growing class of peptide natural products. They are found in bacteria, fungi, and plants and contain diverse bioactivities, including anticancer, antiviral, and antibacterial activities. These natural products form a new class of ribosomally-synthesized and post-translationally modified peptides (RiPPs) termed cyclophane RiPPs. Cyclophane RiPPs are encoded in biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) containing a precursor peptide, cyclophane synthase, protease, and transporter. Our group identified a subfamily of cyclophane RiPPs termed triceptides. Triceptide BGCs are found in >4000 bacterial genomes of diverse phyla, representing a significant RiPP family and a new source for antimicrobial peptides. Since triceptides are a new peptide modality for drug discovery their biosynthesis, bioactivities, drug properties, and therapeutic potential are largely unknown. This project is original and innovative because triceptides represent a new and unexplored modality for peptide-based drug discovery. The objective of this proposal is to broaden our understanding of the biosynthesis and therapeutic potential of triceptides. First, we are interested in producing additional natural products that can target bacterial pathogens that cause clinical infections. Second, we are interested in understanding the interactions between the substrate precursor peptide and modifying enzymes (triceptide synthases and other tailoring enzymes) that will ultimately allow us to engineer enzymes for greater chemical diversity. Third, to identify new-to-nature triceptides with activity against a target relevant to cancer. Since triceptides represent a new modality, all the molecules we produce are unique and would represent new chemical entities for drug discovery, which would be valuable and patentable IP. Our long-term goal is to create a structurally diverse range of natural and new-to-nature triceptides and apply them to chemical screening platforms against infectious diseases or molecular targets of interest.
kw: natural products, peptides, biosynthesis, biocatalysis, antimicrobial, enzymes

title: Reversing Brain Aging Through Individualized fMRI-Based Thought Manipulations
abs: Specific aims: We aim to reverse (functional) brain aging. We can assess a person’s brain health by comparing the apparent age of their brain's functional connections (i.e., functional brain age) with their chronological age. Older functional brain ages relative to chronological ages were found to be generally associated with worse cognitive and brain health. We propose a novel and individualized approach to reverse brain aging— to rewire the brain to make it look younger. This individualized approach is of paramount importance since the vast majority of cognitive training and lifestyle interventions, which are designed in a one-size-fits-all manner, have led to weak gains in brain health. Hypotheses: Participants will exhibit a significant decrease in their brain ages relative to their baseline brain age, when they are presented with personalized psychological stimuli. Methodology: 62 community-dwelling seniors (60 ≤ age ≤ 90; not diagnosed with dementia) will complete three sessions of data collection, which includes two rounds of MRI scans. They will be guided to recreate ‘youthful’ thoughts, using personalized sets of AI-generated images, to engender brain age reversals. The selection of these images will be personalized according to the subject’s neural response (i.e., fMRI-based functional connectivity) to movie stimuli. Brain ages will be estimated using a machine-learning model trained from a comparable population. The brain ages associated with viewing these images will then be compared to the subjects’ baseline brain ages using a dependent samples t-test. Importance to science or medicine: The proposed research is the first of its kind to attempt to reverse brain aging in a systematic and individualized manner. If successful, our approach represents a novel angle we can work on to enhance brain health. Our study will inspire a series of psychological treatment strategies, personalized using the individual’s objective neural responses to naturalistic stimuli.
kw: brain aging; fMRI; functional connectivity; precision medicine

title: A single-arm, open-label study to examine the effectiveness of an accelerated theta burst stimulation to enhance cognitive function among patients with amnesia mild cognitive impairment
abs: Emerging evidence suggests that repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) enhances cognition in patients with mild cognitive impairment (MCI). Accelerated intermittent theta burst stimulation (iTBS), the subtype of rTMS protocols, is promising to treat MCI as it substantially reduces disease burden by shortening the treatment course, but the effectiveness, safety, feasibility, and acceptability of iTBS have not been established. A total of 30 adults with amnestic MCI due to possible Alzheimer's disease will be enrolled in a phase I trial of a single-arm, open-label study of an accelerated iTBS targeting the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (five stimulation sessions of 1800 pulses of iTBS/day for five working days). Enrolled participants will complete a neuropsychiatric evaluation toolbox, which includes several memories, mood conditions, daily functional activities, subjective quality of life and other cognitive function tests before and after treatment and being followed up for three months. The primary outcome is the change in the Montreal Cognitive Assessment score immediately after treatment. Participants will also rate possible common side effects during and after treatment. Patients’ one-year MCI-to-dementia conversion rate will be exploratorily tracked from patients’ electronic health records. The findings of this trial will help to examine the treatment effectiveness, feasibility, and safety profile of a novel accelerated iTBS treatment regime among the local aged population to improve cognitive function as well as mood conditions. This intervention might also delay the conversion rate of MCI to dementia and provide preliminary data for a larger scale study with longer-term follow-up to assess the clinical utility of precision and personalized iTBS as a preventive tool for dementia disease.
kw: mild cognitive impairment, dementia, neurostimulation, accelerated treatment, cognition improvement; augmentation therapy

title: Harnessing Metaplasticity Through Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation: A Novel Approach to Combat Age-Related Cognitive Decline
abs: Age-related cognitive decline significantly impacts the health and independence of aging populations, driven by impairments in neural plasticity and memory mechanisms. This project investigates the potential of transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) to fine-tune metaplasticity—an adaptive mechanism regulating synaptic plasticity thresholds—to preserve memory and enhance cognitive function in aging brains. We hypothesize that tDCS can restore aberrant metaplasticity in aged neural networks, improving synaptic plasticity and associative memory mechanisms. Using an optimized Animal Transcranial Electrical Stimulation (tES) System, we will apply precisely controlled tDCS protocols in aged (22–24 months) and young control (2–3 months) rodents. Behavioral tests will evaluate cognitive improvements, while electrophysiological studies will assess synaptic plasticity, including mechanisms like synaptic tagging and capture (STC). Outcomes will be measured at one day, one week, and one month post-stimulation to validate efficacy. This study is supported by existing laboratory resources and collaboration with clinician-scientists specializing in transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) to standardize metaplasticity time windows, facilitating translational applications. Findings will establish the basis for non-invasive interventions to combat cognitive decline, offering insights into scalable therapies for aging populations. This project will generate foundational data for larger collaborative grants, including clinical trials, to bridge preclinical results with real-world healthcare solutions.
kw: Aging, Healthy longevity, memory, tDCS, plasticity

title: In silico discovery of natural NNMT inhibitors as Alzheimer’s disease therapeutics
abs: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common form of dementia, affecting approximately 8.8% of Singaporeans aged 60 and above. Currently, no effective therapies exist for AD, and drug development programs have failed to achieve consistent clinical improvement. Recent research has highlighted the importance of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) metabolism in the context of AD and brain health. NAD+ is crucial for energy metabolism and DNA repair, and its depletion is implicated in pathophysiological processes associated with AD. Another critical alteration observed in AD is epigenetic changes of the brain. These have been linked to risk and progression of AD, likely contributing to the dysregulation of AD-related gene expression. In mammals, the primary methyl donor involved in DNA methylation events is S-adenosylmethionine (SAM), whose modulation has also been linked to AD. Importantly, the cross-talk between NAD+ metabolism and SAM-mediated methylation processes is controlled by the enzyme nicotinamide N-methyltransferase (NNMT). In fact, NNMT utilizes SAM to methylate and therefore reduce levels of the NAD+ metabolite nicotinamide (NAM), which is critical for NAD+ synthesis. As NNMT expression has been shown to increase in AD and its activity regulates NAD+ metabolism and epigenetics, both altered in AD, inhibition of NNMT could be a new therapeutic strategy for slowing or halting AD progression by optimizing NAD+ and SAM levels in the brain. In particular, this proposal aims to identify and validate the first natural inhibitors of NNMT for ameliorating AD pathology. The project will leverage in silico compound library screenings and NNMT structure prediction, validate potential NNMT inhibitors in neuronal cells, and explore their mechanisms in AD rodents in 3 specific aims. Identifying first-in-class natural NNMT inhibitors for brain health applications holds potential for rapid clinical development of supplements or novel pharmaceuticals, offering an alternative approach to managing AD and related conditions.
kw: Alzheimer's disease, NNMT inhibition, In silico compound screening, natural compounds

title: High-throughput screening to identify drugs that reverse aging clocks in vitro and could mitigate progeroid phenotypes
abs: Our long-term goal is to find drugs that can slow the process of aging, thereby improve neurocognitive outcomes in the elderly, and substantially boosting healthy lifespans. Towards this goal, we aim to develop a new in vitro epigenetic clock (“CellPopAgeV2”) and use it screen for drugs that reverse epigenetic aging clocks. The CellPopAgeV2 clock will be a dual-purpose clock optimized for high-throughput screening which captures aspects of in vitro cell aging, while maintaining the ability of predicting mortality from blood. Furthermore, we will combine the screening hits with data from internal screens and published databases to identify candidates most likely to improve aging, progeroid and neurodegenerative phenotypes. The internal screens include a large screen for lifespan extending drugs in yeast and another screen for activators of the TFEB/autophagy pathway. Published databases include DrugAge to identify hits that extend lifespan, earlier published data from studies that used the LOPAC library and Cmap to identify candidates most likely involved in neurodegeneration pathways. As a proof of principle, we will test whether the identified candidates improve progeroid phenotypes in vitro at the end of the grant period. Finally, these candidates will be tested in mouse models, invertebrates and human studies using internal funding or future Catalyst funding.
kw: aging, longevity, epigenetics, high-throughput screening, aging clocks, rejuvenation

title: Clinical and biological relevance of clonally-related B cells and pre-plasma cells in multiple myeloma
abs: Multiple Myeloma (MM) remains incurable despite advanced therapies targeting plasma cell antigens like CD38 and BCMA. This study proposes to elucidate the role of clonally related B-cells and pre-plasma cells in MM, focusing on their contribution to treatment resistance and relapse. The specific aims are: (1) to identify VDJ rearrangements associated with MM clones and assess the clinical relevance of clonally related B-cells and pre-plasma cells at baseline, hypothesizing these correlate with early relapse risk; (2) to compare VDJ rearrangements of these cells at baseline and relapse, hypothesizing their persistence post-treatment and prominence at relapse; and (3) to characterize the distinct gene and protein expressions of these cells and the immune microenvironment in early versus late relapse patients. Methodologically, the study will use single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq) and single-cell B-cell receptor sequencing (scBCRseq) to analyze bone marrow samples at diagnosis, post-treatment, and relapse stages, along with spatial proteomics to evaluate the immune microenvironment. The feasibility of this research is supported by the availability of archived samples and a strategic recruitment framework. This investigation is poised to advance our understanding of MM pathogenesis by identifying novel biomarkers and therapeutic targets, offering significant implications for developing strategies that mitigate relapse and improve patient outcomes in MM.
kw: myeloma, B cell, relapse, single cell sequencing, spatial omics, plasma cell

title: Mechanistic understanding of a programmable RNA-sensing ribozyme to develop a platform for cell context-specific release of non-coding RNA therapeutics
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Non-coding RNA modalities like antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) and small interfering RNA (siRNA) have recently entered the clinic, with hundreds more in clinical development. However, like other therapeutic modalities, RNA therapeutics can have off-target effects that cause poor outcomes, due to unwanted effects of the drug in non-diseased cells. For example, in the case of siRNA therapeutics for cancer, if the target gene has important roles in normal cells, it would be critical to be able to target the therapy only to diseased cells, to avoid killing of healthy cells. Similarly, for mRNA gene therapy, there may be less toxicity if the RNA therapy is only active in cells that normally express the mutant gene, and not non-diseased cells. Hence, the next generation of RNA medicines will have better controllability and targeting at the cell-specific level. Ribozymes are RNA molecules with catalytic activity. We have developed a synthetic ribozyme, which we propose can form the basis of a generalisable strategy for cell context-specific release of a range of non-coding RNA modalities. Our programmable, trigger-activated ribozyme comprises one trigger-binding domain and two cleavage sites, between which is embedded a releasable RNA cleavage product (e.g. a non-coding RNA). Upon trigger-binding, ribozyme self-cleavage is activated, leading to release of the embedded product. We have optimised the ribozyme for maximum signal-to-noise activity through iterative engineering (Lim et. al., in preparation; TD-1 (2024), TD-2 (2024), PCT/SG2020/050226 (2020), PCT/SG2023/050318 (2023)). This activity is fully encoded within a compact strand of RNA (~200-300 nt), and no protein co-factors are required. UNBAR ribozymes can encode and release CRISPR-Cas guide RNA, short hairpin RNA (shRNA), aptamer, and fully chemically modified ASOs in an RNA-trigger-dependent manner in cell-free assays. Here, we propose to characterise and optimize the ribozyme as a modular platform for cell-context-specific, trigger-activated release of non-coding therapeutic RNA modalities.
kw: ribozyme; catalytic RNA; RNA therapeutics; RNA biology; neurological diseases; cancer

title: Foundational Building Blocks for Next-Generation Magnetic Memories
abs: MRAM Market. The advent of the internet of things (IoT) era has created a vast interconnected network of electronic devices, used for multi-modal monitoring, control, and decision-making. Advancements in artificial intelligence (AI), including generative AI, have fuelled exponential growth in consumer and commercial infor-mation-processing needs. This has in turn driven a surge in computing and memory demands – both for “edge” devices, and for “cloud” data centres. To achieve a sustainable future with AI, it is imperative for future computing technolo-gies to employ efficient, high-performance memory platforms. Unsurprisingly, re-cent years have witnessed a surge in investment across a broad spectrum of emerging memory technologies. Prominent among these is magnetoresistive ran-dom access memory (MRAM), now commercially manufactured by all major found-ries. Currently, MRAM is deployed in industrial and automotive applications, with market size of over $1 billion. Technology Gap. MRAM has vast growth opportunities across several new market sectors, driven by increasing market demands for high-performance solutions. However, broader MRAM adoption is limited predominantly by four fundamental constraints in current commercial device characteristics. Its core component is the magnetic tunnel junction (MTJ), where data is stored within the magnetic orientation of the free layer (FL). Conventional MTJs have a key vulnerability: the FL is sensitive to external magnetic fields, which undermines their immunity in noisy environments. Additionally, their switching speed and efficiency are constrained by the precessional dynamics of its mechanical-torque-based switching mechanism. Finally the scalability of MRAM to smaller nodes is limited by reduction in volumetric stability. New Functionalities. The timely emergence of several new spintronic functionali-ties provides lucrative opportunities for future MRAM technologies. One key ad-vancement is the development of myriad types of antiferromagnets (AFs), which are inherently immune to external fields and switch at faster speeds. Another break-through involves the engineering of symmetry breaking at the interfaces of layered materials, which enables interfacial switching mechanisms with vastly higher speeds and efficiencies. Additionally, “spin wave” excitations, or magnons, can ro-bustly propagate interfacial effects with substantially reduced dissipation. Finally, nanoscale topological spin textures can be generated and electrically manipulat-ed in such systems, providing an efficient path for scalability and multi-bit function-ality. Work Plan. title: Broad-spectrum antibody therapeutics and vaccine development via precision targeting of hypervirulent and multi-drug resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae
abs: Antimicrobial drug resistance is a significant global health threat worldwide and multidrug-resistance and carbapenem-resistance Klebsiella pneumoniae is on the rise. The 2024 World Health Organisation Bacterial Priority Pathogens List underscores the serious threat of carbapenem-resistant (CR) Klebsiella pneumoniae (Kp) due to their high mortality rates and limited treatment options. The convergence of the hypervirulent lineage of Kp and CR Kp leads to creation of superbugs that can cause disease in healthy individuals and are almost impossible to treat. There is a significant gap in the development of alternative therapeutics such as vaccines or monoclonal antibodies against Kp. Most vaccine development target the capsule or LPS of the bacteria, but these approaches are limited in the number of strains they can target due to the diversity of capsular types and LPS types. We propose to target the conserved protein antigens lying below the capsule either as vaccine candidates or targets for monoclonal therapeutics. Furthermore, we examine when and where the protein antigens and virulence factors are expressed and exposed to the immune system to achieve precision targeting at each infection niche. The proposal is divided into 3 themes or aims. Theme 1 (Aim 1): Identification of niche-specific mechanisms of colonization & pathogenesis for hypervirulent and MDR Kp Theme 2 (Aim 2): Integrated antibody discovery and vaccine target identification against Kp surface antigens Theme 3 (Aim 3): Characterization of antibody correlates in hvKp cohort for infection outcomes and validation of targets against clinically relevant Kp isolates in preclinical models. The final outcome we envision is to deliver a small library of monoclonal antibodies against conserved protein antigens and protein vaccine candidates that are effective against multiple lineages of Kp that can go into phase 1 development.

title: Novel Biopolymers to Manage the Electrochemical CO2 Conversion Microenvironment: Replacing Nafion to Improve Selectivity to C2 Products at Current Densities    >2 A/cm2
abs: Carbon-based fuels and chemicals are essential for the global economy, but they also cause CO2 emissions, which drive climate change. To limit climate change to < 1.5°C, scalable CO2 conversion approaches must be developed to convert CO2 back to valuable chemicals and fuels. The electrocatalytic CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) converts CO2 into valuable chemicals like ethylene and ethanol, but CO2RR is not yet economically viable. CO2RR faces challenges and fundamental knowledge gaps that include: (1) competition with unwanted co-production of H2, (2) low selectivity between CO2RR products, (3) poor stability, and (4) unavoidable use of toxic and high-priced fluorinated ionomer catalyst ink materials, such as Nafion. These super-hydrophobic perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) repel water from reaction sites to limit H2 formation. However, toxic PFAS materials draw grave concerns about health and environmental effects, only magnified by the gigaton scale of CO2 conversion needed to mitigate climate change. To address these 4 challenges, this program develops breakthrough biopolymers that improve CO2RR performance by limiting unwanted H2 production while replacing Nafion and similar PFAS materials with sustainable and green biomass-derived polysaccharide biopolymers. Regarding novelty and innovation, these polysaccharide biopolymers demonstrate exciting new chemical principles for designing local CO2RR (micro)environments. Unlike PFAS materials, polysaccharide biopolymers optimize CO2RR performance through 3 synergistic effects: (1) high CO2/CO affinity, (2) reduced water activity to suppress H2, and (3) efficient ion transport, enabling state-of-the-art C2+ selectivity (FEC2+=83% at 2.2 A/cm2). Regarding scientific merit, we explore exciting specific aims: (1) modify biopolymer functional groups to optimize the microenvironment, (2) tune *CO coverage to adjust selectivity, (3) maximize ethylene yield, (4) analyze impacts on commercialization potential via life cycle analysis (LCA) and technoeconomic analysis (TEA), and (5) maximize stability. Regarding broader impacts, this program customizes the reaction (micro)environment to enable stable, high-performance CO2RR by replacing PFAS-based catalyst inks, opening exciting new directions to improve the viability of CO2RR to counteract climate change while providing new insights toward universal design rules for electrocatalysis chemical environments. Overall, this program aligns with Singapore’s priority to remain a chemical and fuel production hub while obtaining net-zero carbon emissions by 2050.
kw: electrochemical CO2 conversion; CO2RR; electrocatalysis; CCUS; PFAS; catalysis

title: The evolution of novel complex traits from preexisting traits: Identifying shared and unique cellular identities across traits
abs: Novel complex traits are likely to evolve from the activation of pre-existent gene regulatory networks (GRNs) in different cell types in the body. We have recently found evidence for this process when examining the differentiation of eyespot color patterns on the wings of butterflies. Messenger RNA extracted from a pool of cells dissected from the eyespot region of a developing wing was closest in profile to mRNA extracted from pools of cells from whole antennae and whole legs, rather than to mRNA from other dissected bits of the wing. Furthermore, when individual cis-regulatory elements (CREs) of genes expressed in eyespots, antennae and legs were disrupted, all traits were disrupted. These experiments indicate that the same genes and the same regulatory regions are being used to control very different traits in different parts of the body of a butterfly. However, since eyespots, antennae, and legs are distinct entities, there must be differences between the GRNs being read in these tissues. In this proposal we will examine similarities and differences between these trait’s GRNs at the single-cell level to understand how common GRNs produce distinct outputs in different regions of the body. We hypothesize that either 1) co-option of only parts of a pre-existent gene network to a novel location in a body, 2) the presence of a distinct chromatin landscape in cells at the novel location, or 3) the presence of unique activators/repressors at that novel location, might create distinct complex traits in the process, instead of just repeated traits or serial homologs. To test these hypotheses we will 1) conduct RNA sequencing and chromatin profile analysis at the single-cell level across embryos, when appendages develop, and larval wings, when eyespots develop, to identify cell types with similar gene expression and chromatin profiles across these different tissues; 2) Focusing only on those cells, identify the list of genes and list of open chromatin peaks that are shared across wings and embryos; those that are wing-specific, and those that are embryo-specific; 3) visualize the position of these cells across whole tissue mounts using shared (and unique) transcripts as probes; 4) characterize the role of pioneer or other transcription factors uniquely expressed in eyespot cells in regulating eyespot-specific chromatin landscapes and trait-specific development using CRISPR-Cas9; 5) characterize the role of eyespot-specific chromatin landscapes in eyespot-specific development using CRISPR-Cas9; 6) localize the interactions between these transcription factors and open chromatin regions directly in specific cells of the tissues involved. This work provides a novel approach to the field of evolution of novel complex traits by dissecting complex traits into their constituent cell types and exploring how gene network co-option affects the identities of cells and their chromatin profiles at novel locations in a body.
kw: gene-regulatory networks, evolution, novel traits, genetics, multiomics

title: The discovery and characterization of a natural sterol that resolves inflammaging
abs: The regulation of cellular senescence is critical in both aging and in cancer. Our team recently identified a Wnt- and cancer-regulated enzyme (FAXDC2) that is rate-limiting in cancer senescence and controls the accumulation of a poorly characterized signaling sterol, lophenol. Lophenol is a natural product also present in aloe vera gels but its biological effects have not been previously elucidated. Our preliminary data indicates that lophenol, which we have shown regulates receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) and MAPK signaling also regulates macrophage senescence associated with metabolic decline during aging, and we have identified a potential mechanism. With our team’s singular ability to chemically synthesize lophenol in pharmacologic quantities, this allows us to perform unique and novel in vivo studies in Drosophila and mice and mechanistic studies in primary macrophages during aging. We will (i) identify the molecular link between lophenol and a specific senescence pathway (RTK/MAPK) in macrophages, (ii) characterize how lophenol treatment impacts macrophage senescence and polarization in vitro and in vivo, and (iii) investigate the effect of lophenol on healthspan and lifespan in model organisms. This multidisciplinary proposal offers a unique opportunity for understanding how sterol metabolism can regulate macrophage senescence and aging - a topical and timely question for Singapore and the world.
kw: Inflammaging; Sterol; Cholesterol; MAPK, Macrophages; Senescence

title: Large-Language-Model–Integrated Multimodal Dynamic Model for Analyzing Patients’ Differential Treatment Responses
abs: Human individuals are heterogeneous, and their responses to treatment can vary considerably. Accurately estimating individual patient responses to different treatments enables more precise and personalized disease management. Over the past decade, machine learning methods have been used to estimate treatment responses. More recently, generative machine learning models have been employed to produce multiple data types simultaneously, offering a comprehensive view of patients before and after treatment and thereby supporting clinical decision-making. Among the various multimodal generative models available, transformer-based methods are currently the most widely adopted. However, the unique properties of medical data often render existing transformer-based generative models unsuitable. Two critical aspects illustrate this mismatch. First, although real-world medical data for a single patient may be massive and span multiple data types, only a very small subset of medical data is critical for clinical decision-making. For instance, in the eye images of an early-stage diabetic patient, fewer than 1% of the pixels may contain signs of disease. Second, there is substantial heterogeneity among individuals, leading to high variance in medical data that poses significant challenges for machine learning models attempting to capture underlying patterns. This proposed research program aims to address the critical challenges outlined above, with the goal of enhancing the use of generative models for estimating patient treatment effects. Specifically, it will focus on four key objectives: 1) Developing a Learnable Dynamic Discrete Tokenizer: We will design a learnable tokenizer that allocates more tokens and larger vocabulary sizes to clinically important data types, ensuring robust support for diverse data. 2) Establishing Hierarchical Uncertainty Estimation: We will implement probabilistic machine learning techniques to refine uncertainty estimates for model-generated content at multiple levels—an essential component of reliable decision-making in heterogeneous patient populations. 3) Integrating with Language Models for Versatile Use: To broaden applicability and improve human-AI interaction, we will integrate the generative model with a large language model, thereby making it accessible to a wide range of users. 4) Applying to Real-World Medical Data in Singapore: Finally, we will adapt these approaches to clinical practice by developing models that predict personalized, differential treatment responses for eye and other diseases, utilizing real-world datasets from NUHS in Singapore.
kw: tokenizer, generative model, uncertainty, patient treatment

title: Harnessing Ion-Pairing for Asymmetric DNA Catalysis and Elucidating the Process Through Integrative Experimental and Computational Approaches
abs: Negatively charged phosphates are essential for life, serving as the backbone of DNA and RNA and playing a crucial role in electrostatic interactions with positively charged amino acid residues in proteins. These interactions, remarkably stable even in aqueous environments, are likely protected by the hydrophobic interface that prevents ion solvation and separation. While ion-pairing interactions are vital in biological systems, their application in asymmetric catalysis has been largely confined to non-polar or low-polarity organic solvents, where solvation effects are less disruptive. Chiral phosphoric acids, particularly those with the BINOL backbone, have emerged as privileged organocatalysts for asymmetric ion-pairing catalysis, effectively producing chiral products via ion-pairing with prochiral cations since 2006. However, achieving ion-pairing catalysis in water, despite its economic, sustainable, and eco-friendly advantages, remains challenging due to the solvation effects. Nature’s prevalent ion-pairing interactions suggest that a hydrophobic microenvironment is essential for such catalysis in aqueous media. While enzyme active sites could theoretically facilitate asymmetric ion-pairing catalysis, site-specific installation of phosphate groups on proteins remains technically challenging. Despite phosphates being key post-translational modifications in cell signaling, their catalytic potential through ion-pairing remains unknown. In contrast, DNA phosphates are well understood, particularly their ion-pairing interactions with lysine, arginine, and other positively charged molecules in water. This raises the possibility of utilizing the inherently chiral and conformationally rigid (in duplex form) phosphates in DNA for asymmetric ion-pairing catalysis in water. DNA’s grooves may provide a hydrophobic environment for ion-pairing interactions, shielded from aqueous disruption. However, the heterogeneity of chiral environments presented by DNA phosphates could compromise stereoinduction if all phosphates were involved in the stereodetermining step. To mitigate this, we propose site-specific anchoring of substrate to DNA and activation by a Lewis acid, using our chemoenzymatic conjugation method. This approach ensures that only spatially proximal phosphates interact directly with cationic reactants, synergistically with the Lewis acid catalyst, to exert a stereoinductive effect on the transition state. The remaining phosphates may act as reservoirs, sequestering cationic electrophiles and delivering them to the reaction site as needed, potentially accelerating the reaction by increasing local electrophile concentrations. Given that Selectfluor® and iminium ions are established cations in asymmetric ion-pairing catalysis with chiral phosphates, we aim to explore the potential of DNA phosphates in facilitating stereoselective transformations in aqueous environments in Aim 1. title: CELL2VIRUS: AI-Driven Mapping of Virus-Host Interactions at Single-Cell and Spatial Resolution
abs: Viral infections remain a major global health challenge, requiring innovative approaches to study virus-host interactions and disease progression. This project integrates single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), spatial transcriptomics, and artificial intelligence (AI) to systematically investigate viral cellular tropism, virus-induced transcriptomic reprogramming, and virus-disease associations at an unprecedented scale. We will develop CELL2VIRUS, a bioinformatics pipeline to detect and quantify viral transcripts within large-scale single-cell datasets, addressing key challenges such as false negatives and misalignments. By integrating CELL2VIRUS with the DISCO database—comprising over 19,000 human samples—we will construct a comprehensive virus-host interaction atlas, mapping viruses to their target cell types and associated diseases. To enhance predictive capabilities, we will develop AI-driven “virtual” cells, trained on CELL2VIRUS data, to model infection dynamics and predict cellular responses based on viral strain, load, and time post-infection. This will enable the rapid identification of unknown viruses through distinct gene expression signatures, improving disease surveillance and preparedness for emerging pathogens. Furthermore, we will apply single-cell spatial transcriptomics to explore virus-infected and bystander cell interactions at the tissue level, focusing on Zika virus (ZIKV) infection in the fetal brain. Our preliminary data suggest that bystander cells play a key role in disease pathology, contributing to neuroinflammation and neural progenitor cell (NPC) depletion, a hallmark of Congenital Zika Syndrome (CZS). We will also incorporate spatial AI models to simulate virus-host and cell-cell interactions across tissues, enabling more precise predictions of infection-driven cellular responses. By combining large-scale data integration, AI-driven modeling, and spatial analysis, this project will advance our understanding of viral pathogenesis, facilitate early detection of novel pathogens, and provide a scalable framework for studying virus-induced diseases.
kw: virus; AI; virus-host interaction; single-cell omics; spatial omics

title: Determine gain-of-toxic mechanisms caused by disease-linked mutations in TDP-43 in motor neuron degeneration and their application in RNA-based therapy
abs: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is the most common adult motor neuron disease, characterized by progressive motor neuron degeneration, muscle atrophy, and loss of voluntary movement, leading to death within an average of three years. While ~90% of ALS cases are sporadic (sALS) with no clear cause, ~10% are familial (fALS) with inherited mutations. Despite different origins, both forms share indistinguishable symptoms and pathologies, making fALS mutations useful for disease modeling and therapeutic development. A key protein in understanding ALS disease mechanism is TDP-43: (i) TDP-43 aggregation is the defining pathological hallmark for ALS, and (ii) mutations in TARDBP (which encodes TDP-43) cause ALS. The gene-pathology relationship of TDP-43 to ALS indicate that (1) dysfunctions in TDP-43 is able to trigger disease cascade as mutations in TARDBP gene are causal for ALS, and (2) regardless of causes, the pathogenic process converges on TDP-43 as pathological TDP-43 aggregations are present in the majority (~97%) of ALS patients. Thus, Our study aims to elucidate the mechanisms by which TDP-43 dysfunction contributes to ALS and develop potential therapeutic strategies based on the identified mechanisms. TDP-43, an RNA-binding protein with a low-complexity domain, regulates RNA metabolism and trafficking. Based on TDP-43 pathologies, the disease mechanisms could be driven by gain of toxic properties (due to TDP-43 aggregates), or loss of nuclear TDP-43 function, or both, in neurons and/or glia in the affected brain regions. Our lab and others have shown that deleting TDP-43 in specific cell types causes damage in a manner dependent on cell type and developmental stage, affecting RNA splicing, such as the inclusion of cryptic exons. However, no TDP-43 deletion models, including motor neuron-specific knockouts, fully recapitulate human ALS pathology, suggesting additional toxic mechanisms are at play. Indeed, TDP-43 can undergo liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), forming dynamic liquid-like condensates. Under pathological conditions, prolonged cytoplasmic mislocalization of TDP-43 leads to the transition from liquid to solid aggregates, initiating various pathways leading to motor neuron degeneration. Preventing this transition presents a viable therapeutic strategy to halt disease progression. Given that (i) TDP-43 regulates biogenesis and process for coding and noncoding RNAs, (ii) RNA influence TDP-43 solubility via LLPS, and (iii) TDP-43’s role in long-noncoding RNA (lncRNA) metabolism remain unexplored, we hypothesize that ALS-causal mutations in TDP-43 may cause gain-of-function changes in lncRNA metabolism that triggers cytoplasmic TDP-43 aggregates and neuronal damages leading to motor neuron degeneration. To investigate this, we used ALS patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) motor neurons with a familial TDP-43-M337V mutation and isogenic corrected controls. title: Structure and function of NleA, a critical virulence factor of pathogenic E coli
abs: Structure and function of NleA, a critical virulence factor of pathogenic E. coli Background: Bacteria use a Type III secretion system (T3SS) to inject host cells with dozens of proteins, known as virulence factors (effectors), to initiate infection. With rising antibiotic resistance, targeting the T3SS offers a promising strategy, as it is specific to bacteria and absent in human cells. Attaching and effacing (AE) pathogens, such as Enterohemorrhagic and Enteropathogenic E. coli (EHEC and EPEC), cause severe illnesses, including diarrhea and kidney failure, often through contaminated food. NleA is an indispensable effector for the virulence of AE pathogens. Understanding NleA's function is crucial for developing treatments and vaccines against these infections. Injected via the T3SS, NleA targets the host Golgi, where it is glycosylated. It has been reported to disrupt host processes via interactions with host NHERF2, NLRP3, and Sec24 proteins. However, how NleA impacts these potential targets remains elusive. Significance: Structural and functional studies are crucial for understanding the mechanism of action of NleA. Specific Aims: 1) Determine NleA structure and post-translational modifications, 2) Study NleA quaternary structure’s impact on localization, 3) Investigate binding partner complexes, 4) Understand oligomerization control during infection stages. Novelty and Hypothesis: Our preliminary structural study reveals that NleA oligomerizes, forming unexpected and fascinating filaments. These findings provide a novel foundation for our project. We hypothesize that NleA transitions from a monomer to an oligomer after being injected into host cells, which aids its function and modification. In other words, this novel structural feature contributes to bacterial virulence. Preliminary Studies: Preliminary studies support NleA oligomerization, observed as filaments in vitro. We purified NleA, determined its cryo-EM structure at 3.15Å, and generated mutations to disrupt oligomerization and found that this mutant demonstrated perturbed interaction with infected host cells.
kw: Secretion Systems, Effectors, Infection, Complex, Oligomerization

title: Verifiable Large Language Models via Scalable Zero-Knowledge Proofs
abs: Recent strides in machine learning (ML), particularly with large language models (LLMs) like GPT-4, have revolutionized a wide array of industries. These models are now central to functions ranging from chatbot dialogues to complex web searches and coding assistance. However, as these models become more widespread, they also introduce significant challenges concerning the accuracy, security, and transparency of ML processes. As LLMs grow increasingly sophisticated, verifying that they operate correctly and as intended becomes more challenging. Users frequently lack insight into how these models generate outputs, making it difficult to confirm whether they are utilizing full-fledged, legitimate models or simplified, cost-saving versions. This situation is further complicated by the potential for service providers to deploy less capable models while charging for comprehensive services, ultimately compromising the quality users expect. Ensuring the security and privacy of these ML models is also a critical issue. Given that these models are often proprietary and represent valuable intellectual property, users need to be confident that their data is being processed correctly without exposing sensitive information or the model's internal parameters. Traditional approaches to verifying computational integrity fall short, particularly with the complexity inherent in LLMs. Zero-knowledge proofs (ZKP) offer a promising solution, enabling a prover to validate the correctness of a computation without divulging any details about the underlying secret model. In the context of LLMs, ZKPs can help ensure that users receive the expected level of service without risking exposure of sensitive model details. Additionally, ZKPs can be a powerful tool for regulatory bodies to enforce compliance and maintain standards in AI services, thereby protecting consumer rights with minimal impact on existing service structures. In 2020, the Principal Investigator (PI) of this proposal, Jiaheng Zhang, pioneered the field of zero-knowledge machine learning (ZKML) by developing the first tailored ZKP system for decision tree inference. This foundational work laid the groundwork for subsequent advancements, extending ZKP techniques to modern neural networks. Despite these advancements, existing ZKP methods either do not support LLM architectures or are hampered by inefficiencies and high communication overhead. For instance, current solutions may take over an hour to generate a single proof for models like GPT-2, rendering them impractical for real-world applications. The core challenge lies in efficiently proving different layers within LLMs, such as matrix multiplication, attention mechanisms, GeLU activation functions, and normalization layers, which are essential for their functionality. title: The Local Consequences of Global Capital Flows: Evidence from Historical Data
abs: This project proposes to investigate global capital flows, boom-bust cycles, and financial crises using several novel historical datasets in three sub-projects. I aim to address the following research questions: • How do shocks to the availability of funding for global banks in financial centers spill over to other countries? When faced with an increase in funding, which countries—and which types of borrowers within these countries—tend to be the major recipients of the resulting extension of credit? • Is there a causal relationship between an increase in banks’ funding availability in financial centers and boom-bust cycles abroad, especially in small open economies? • Are cross-border lending flows predominantly accounted for by syndicated loans, i.e. loan contracts with multiple lenders? Has the share of non-bank financial institutions in cross-border transactions increased over time, and if yes, in which markets? How has the borrower composition of cross-border loans changed over time in terms of sector or industry, firm size, credit risk, and so on? • Historically speaking, is there a change in the composition of cross-border borrowing around banking crises, currency crises, and “sudden stop” episodes? How do this compare to the composition of domestic credit, and what are the reasons for any potential differences? Can these patterns be explained by existing economic theories? Relative to the existing literature, two key contributions will be made: 1. The creation and dissemination of two entirely new datasets on (a) newly digitized international loan-level data covering the period 1971-1989, and (b) measures of cross-border debt by sector, firm size, and risk for most countries.. 2. Using granular data, the first project will show that an increase in funding of banks in a financial center (in this case, London) can lead to a boom-bust cycle, economic downturns, and financial crises in other, faraway countries. The second project will show that such crises tend to be preceded by an inflow of cross-border loans to the tradable sector (e.g., manufacturing) rather than non-tradable sector (e.g., construction), rejecting what would be predicted from a large class of models in international macroeconomics. The methodologies underlying these studies are relatively straightforward, given that the main contributions come from the use of innovative historical datasets. Project 1 will use a first-difference and difference-in-differences methodology to relate changes in loan terms on the bank or loan-level to whether a bank is exposed to an increase in funding availability arising from inflows of so-called petrodollars into the market for international currency borrowing (“Eurodollar” market). This analysis is made possible thanks to a new dataset covering the time period 1971 to 1989. title: Investigating In-Context Representation Learning and Hypernetworks for Projection in Large Language Models for Efficient Domain-Specific Knowledge Augmentation
abs: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities, yet they are not inherently trained on specialized data such as protein sequences or chemical structures. This research aims to develop novel in-context representation learning and hypernetwork frameworks to enhance LLM adaptability in specialized domains. By integrating knowledge from domain-specific Foundation Models (FMs), our approach enables efficient adaptation without extensive retraining. Specifically, we propose: (1) Unsupervised projection layers to incorporate high-dimensional FM representations into LLMs, reducing dependence on labeled data; (2) Hypernetworks to dynamically generate parameters for these projection layers, minimizing redundant training; and (3) Validation in RNA therapeutics development, demonstrating real-world applicability through in-silico screening and wet-lab experiments. The intellectual merit of this work lies in its novel integration of in-context learning, unsupervised learning, and hypernetworks to extend LLMs' capacity for specialized tasks. By leveraging external foundation models, our approach broadens predictive accuracy and generalizability in domains such as drug discovery. The introduction of unsupervised projection layers and hypernetwork-based parameter generation significantly reduces computational overhead compared to traditional fine-tuning, making LLM adaptation more scalable. Beyond deep learning innovations, the broader impact of this research is its potential to democratize AI-driven scientific discovery, accelerating breakthroughs in drug development and biomedicine.
kw: Artificial Intelligence; Deep Learning; Large Language Model; In-context learning; drug discovery

title: Mitigating Hallucinations in Large Vision Language Models
abs: Hallucinations in large vision language models (LVLMs) refers to the phenomenon where LVLMs are prone to generate textual responses that are not factually aligned with image inputs. It has direct implications to the integrity, reliability, and broad applicability of LVLMs, leading to misinformation, misinterpretation, and even erroneous decision-making if not addressed properly. In this project, we will investigate how to deal with hallucinations in LVLMs from two perspectives. The first is on hallucination benchmarks. Though several hallucination benchmarks have been created, they largely focus on object hallucinations with brief text queries and simple yes-or-no answers. We will create two new hallucination benchmarks that focus on long-context hallucination data (including object-level descriptions, scene-level descriptions, and multi-round conversations, all in a form of multiple-choice-questions) and inter-object relations (including spatial, action, and comparative relations) which are better aligned with real-life data and tasks. The second is on hallucination mitigation methods. Leveraging our prior study on visual contrastive decoding that introduces augmented visual uncertainty to mitigate the statistical bias and unimodal priors in LVLMs, we will design a novel hallucination mitigation method that introduces query-relevant local attention to compensate the deficiency of global attention which often predominantly attends to salient and high-frequency objects or object pairs in images (ignoring query-related image information) and leads to hallucinations. The two created benchmark will empower the research community with valuable suites for evaluating the hallucination levels of existing and future LVLMs. The mitigation method will dig deep into the root causes of hallucinations in LVLMs and address them by introducing local and query-relevant attention.
kw: large vision language models, hallucination benchmarks, hallucination mitigation, inter-object relation understanding

title: Federated Learning for Foundation Models
abs: Foundation Models (FMs) have revolutionized machine learning, but fine-tuning them across decentralized and privacy-sensitive data sources remains a challenge. Traditional Federated Learning (FL) methods struggle with the scale, heterogeneity, and evolving nature of real-world data, as well as the increasing reliance on closed-box FMs accessible only via APIs. This project aims to develop approaches to enable efficient, privacy-preserving federated fine-tuning of FMs. First, to address the domain heterogeneity challenge, we propose a prototype-based FL framework that allows clients to share compact representations instead of their raw data or model parameters, improving domain adaptation while maintaining privacy. A continual learning mechanism further detects and addresses distribution shifts while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Second, to address the challenges brought about by the inherent multi-task nature of FMs, we propose an aggregation strategy that prioritizes high-impact client updates and dynamically schedules client participation, significantly reducing communication overhead while improving model performance. Third, in response to the growing trend of closed-source FMs, we propose a black-box federated optimization method that introduces textual gradient aggregation across federated clients, enabling prompt-based fine-tuning of closed-source FMs without direct access to model parameters. By addressing these challenges, our research advances FL for FMs, paving the way for practical applications in sensitive domains like healthcare and finance, where collaborative model improvement is essential but data sharing is restricted.
kw: Federated Learning; Foundation Models; Collaborative AI; Distributed Machine Learning

title: Enhancing adolescent mental well-being in Singapore: The Youth Connect programme
abs: Background/Objectives: The mental health of young people is an increasingly significant public health challenge globally and in Singapore, where approximately 1 in 3 adolescents report significant symptoms of depression and anxiety. Despite increased recognition of youth mental health challenges, significant gaps remain in meeting the mental health needs of our young people. Effective scalable interventions are urgently needed to address the youth mental health problems confronting Singapore. The extent to which low-intensity early interventions administered by school counsellors and community mental health practitioners can help to address these gaps remains unknown. The objectives of this pilot study are to evaluate the effectiveness and potential for implementation of Youth Connect, a locally-developed process-based early intervention package aimed at enhancing psychological resilience and emotional well-being among community-dwelling Singaporean adolescents aged 10-19 years. Methods: We will conduct a type 1 pilot hybrid effectiveness-implementation trial to explore the following specific aims: 1) to evaluate the effectiveness of Youth Connect for building psychological resilience, enhancing mental well-being, and improving psychosocial functioning among adolescents in the community using an interrupted time series design (n=50), and 2) to assess barriers and facilitators to implementation of the Youth Connect programme from the perspectives of key stakeholders using a mixed methods design (n=30). Participants will be recruited from social service agencies such as SHINE Children & Youth Services, Singapore Children’s Society, and Limitless, as well as schools under the Youth Area Local Network (West). Significance: Results from this pilot study will enable understanding of the effectiveness and implementation potential of process-based interventions locally and globally, setting the stage for a larger definitive intervention trial. Insights regarding successes and areas for improvement will be used to propose scalable early intervention strategies for adolescents in schools and the community. Perhaps even more importantly, delivering effective process-based interventions for young people early in the course of illness has the potential to avert the intangible costs of lost academic, social, and occupational opportunities and help youth to maximize their potential in the long-term.
kw: process-based therapy, brief psychological interventions, adolescent mental health

title: Language, Learning, and Living Well in Middle Adulthood and Beyond (L3MA)
abs: Growing evidence supports that bilingualism, the use of more than one language, confers general cognitive benefits across the lifespan. The magnitude of these benefits, referred to as bilingual effects, is positively associated with a person’s degree of bilingualism, most notably proficiency. Singapore, a linguistically diverse country with a bilingual education policy, is uniquely positioned to enjoy the impact of these benefits across many sectors of society. However, in English-Mandarin bilinguals, the largest proportion of Singapore’s population, levels of English and Mother Tongue (MT) proficiency begin declining in early adulthood, and continue to decline throughout the remainder of the working years. Beyond limiting fluid communication, lower proficiency levels may be associated with reduced cognitive control, potentially impacting on a range of critical outcomes including learning, vocational success, and cognitive aging. As a consequence of global aging trends, there is a crucial need to better understand lifestyle factors that can modulate the potential for aging Singaporeans to remain active, productive, and healthy throughout adulthood. The Language, Learning, and Living Well in Middle Adulthood and Beyond (L3MA) project aims to address Challenge Statement 4 by leveraging research in the Science of Learning (SoL) to investigate lifestyle factors that can enhance learning and vocational success during middle adulthood in light of cognitive decline associated with healthy aging. This project will investigate the relationship between patterns of bilingualism, cognitive control, and learning among middle-aged, English-Mandarin bilingual Singaporeans. The L3MA project aims to accomplish three key objectives: Objective 1: Synthesize existing research on bilingual effects on cognitive control in healthy adults. An exhaustive systematic review will provide an updated and comprehensive understanding of the relationship between bilingual language experience and cognitive control in the broader population of interest from which the behavioral project’s sample will be recruited. Findings from this review will directly inform the design of empirical aspects of this project and will allow for easier interpretation of findings within the broader literature. Additionally, it will address a significant gap in the extant literature for researchers and policy makers in Singapore and beyond. Objective 2: Characterize the relationships between bilingual language experience, cognitive control, and learning-related behaviors. An empirical investigation will be carried out in a large sample of middle-aged English-Mandarin bilingual Singaporeans (n = 1000). Extensively validated language experience assessments and both conventional and updated cognitive control tasks will be administered through the Internet to increase participation rates. Background information, measures of vocational success, and learning agility and efficacy will also be collected. Analys

title: Quality of Care for Seriously Ill Nursing Home Residents
abs: Integrating palliative care (PC) within nursing homes (NHs) is a key focus for the 2023 National Strategy for Palliative Care (NSPC). This, however, presents a challenge for some NHs, resulting in a wide variation in the quality of NH care provided to seriously ill residents. Assessing this variation in quality of NH care for seriously ill residents is imperative to monitor progress towards PC integration within NHs, and requires comprehensive, validated and salient measures of NH quality of care. We therefore aim to conduct a mixed-methods study to develop and validate measures to assess quality of care within NHs. This includes development of a NH PC checklist comprising a list of indicators to assess PC infrastructure considered necessary for high-quality NH PC; and refining and validating the Quality of Care for Patients with Advanced Illness (QCPAI) scale to assess seriously ill resident/proxy experience with NH care among 200 seriously ill NH residents (those cognitively intact) and 400 proxies to assess its construct validity and reliability. Lastly, we will establish the predictive criterion validity of the NH PC checklist and QCPAI-NH by assessing their association with NH resident healthcare use and resident outcomes. The study will advance NSPC goals by acting on its key focus areas related to improving PC infrastructure and processes within NHs. It will also advance the Singapore Ministry of Health’s goals for reducing hospitalizations and hospital deaths among seriously ill residents and improving NH care in line with the Enhanced NH Standards. Thus, findings from this study will have direct policy and clinical applications.
kw: nursing homes; palliative care; quality; person-centered care; end-of-life care

title: A Randomized Controlled Trial for Very Low Nicotine Cigarettes in Singapore
abs: Nicotine is the principal driver of sustained tobacco use. A very low nicotine cigarettes (VLNC) policy, which restricts nicotine in cigarettes from regular levels (15-17 mg/g) to a non-addicting level (1 mg/g), could drastically reduce tobacco-related disease burdens in Singapore. Prior randomized controlled trials, which modelled a VLNC policy by switching daily smokers not interested in quitting to VLNCs, reported improved quit related outcomes with no prolonged withdrawal or compensatory smoking. Other studies suggest that providing free nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) could further improve quit outcomes. As no study has assessed the potential impact of a VLNC policy in an Asian population, this project aims to measure the effects of switching Singaporean daily smokers with no quit intention to VLNCs, with or without NRT compared to continuing the use of cigarettes with regular nicotine levels. Hypothesis 1: Compared to those who continue using cigarettes with a regular nicotine level, those who switch to VLNCs report fewer cigarettes smoked per day and more smokefree days. Hypothesis 2: After switching from regular cigarettes to VLNCs, any increases in compensatory smoking and nicotine withdrawal symptoms subside within 7 days. Hypothesis 3: Compared to switching to VNLCs with no free NRT, switching to VLNCs with free NRT results in fewer cigarettes smoked per day and more smokefree days. We will conduct a 12-week randomized controlled trial with three parallel conditions: (1) regular nicotine content cigarettes (control), (2) VLNCs, and (3) VLNCs with free NRT. We will recruit 270 adult daily smokers with no 30-day quit intention from our existing cohorts and switch them in a single step to either control cigarettes (15.8 mg/g nicotine) or VLNCs (1.4 mg/g nicotine). Participants in condition 3 will also receive free NRT. We will use bogus pipeline verification and financial incentives to increase trial adherence.
kw: Addiction; Chronic Disease Prevention; Smoking Cessation; Tobacco Control

title: Unravelling the Mechanobiology of Cardiovascular Aging
abs: The broad objective of this research proposal is to understand, predict, and control tissue mechanoresponses driving cardiovascular diseases. It has become increasingly evident that mechanical forces from the microenvironment continually alter cell and tissue functioning to maintain health. Any disruptions in this force sensing or adaptation results in an imbalance that drives disease progression. Despite early evidence of this, integrating biochemical signalling and physical adaptation in tissues leading to disease remains a grand challenge in mechanobiology. We will tackle this long-standing problem by unravelling spatiotemporal molecular mechanisms underlying multi-scale force adaptation (from subcellular, cellular to tissue-scales) in healthy and diseased tissues. In this context, we will define a novel concept of a “mechanostat” model (similar to a thermostat for temperature control), wherein tuning specific mechanoresponsive proteins and signalling will allow us to engineer tissues to reset their mechanical state, that is, regain normal tissue health to control or reverse disease progression. Leveraging our expertise in biochemical and physical approaches, advanced transcriptomic profiling, and powerful machine learning modelling, this proposal is organised into three specific aims: 1) Determine mechanosensitive genes responsible for cardiovascular aging, 2) Elucidate the mechanochemical feedback loops underlying tissue-scale force responses driving cardiovascular aging, and 3) Domain-tailored machine learning modelling of mechanoresponses in aging. These three interconnected and not mutually dependent thrusts will revolve around a common theme of providing crucial mechanistic insight into how defects in the cytoskeleton, cell-cell interactions, and force adaptation across tissues drive aging-related diseases. We will work closely with an interdisciplinary team of biophysicists, clinicians, and bioengineers and integrate with our unique domain knowledge of mechanotransduction to predict and control tissue functions. The feasibility of this research is supported by solid preliminary data, extensive domain expertise and training, the strength of our interdisciplinary approaches and established collaborations from MBI, Singapore and other parts of the world. This comprehensive research strategy will have broad implications in identifying targets for therapies, and engineering of adaptive tissues to tune physiology and mitigate disease progression. This work will open exciting avenues for basic as well as clinical and translational research in the Singapore research landscape.
kw: mechanotransduction; cardiovascular; cytoskeleton; transcription; machine learning

title: High-performance and Sustainable Coastal Protection Materials: Lightweight Aggregates Produced from Singapore’s Solid Wastes
abs: Singapore requires a substantial amount of construction materials for coastal protection infrastructure, while simultaneously facing the challenge of managing the large amount of waste being disposed of at its only landfill. Transforming waste into valuable resources is indispensable for extending the landfill's lifespan and promotes sustainability by reducing the use of nonrenewable natural resources. This proposal is built upon the achievements of ZA’s previous research projects that produce lightweight aggregates (LWA) from industrial wastes for non-structural concrete and gardening application. In this project, the same approach will be adopted to produce and utilize waste-derived LWA as coarse aggregates in structural marine concrete. Various types of local wastes will be explored for LWA production, including incineration bottom ash and fly ash from waste-to-energy facilities, ash from biomass combustion and oil sludge incineration, waste concrete slurry from ready-mixed concrete plant, and retired solar photovoltaic panels. The wastes will be pretreated, milled, mixed, pelletized, and sintered to produce LWAs with unique properties, such as high porosity, low density, and low water absorption. The mix formulation and process will be optimized for better engineering performance and lower pollutant leaching. The waste-derived LWA will partially or entirely replace coarse aggregates in marine concrete to provide lightweight properties while maintaining sufficient concrete strength. The lightweight concrete (LWC) will be tested for compressive strength, durability, and chemical resistance to evaluate its engineering performance. Additionally, environmental risk assessment of the LWA and LWC will be conducted through leaching tests. To evaluate the product’s performance and environmental risks under marine conditions, customized accelerated durability tests and seawater leaching test will be performed, respectively. Furthermore, a field trial, including pilot production of waste-derived LWA and LWC, as well as product application and monitoring, will be conducted. Finally, the economic viability and carbon footprint of this technology will be assessed based on a commercial-scale model.
kw: coastal protection; lightweight aggregates; lightweight concrete; waste-to-resource; sustainable construction materials

title: Enhancing Next-Generation Numerical Weather Prediction Over Singapore with Radar Data Assimilation in the Joint Effort for Data Assimilation Integration (JEDI)
abs: Extreme rainfall events (EREs) are becoming more frequent globally, particularly in Asia, driven by regional and large-scale climatic factors. These events pose significant risks to agriculture, infrastructure, and human health. Climate modelling studies indicate that the frequency of EREs is expected to increase due to changing weather and climatic patterns caused by climate change. In Southeast Asia, the intensity and occurrence of EREs have risen, highlighting the need for improved forecasting to mitigate their impacts. However, accurately predicting these events remains challenging due to the rapid variation in precipitation intensity and location, especially in convective rainfall, which Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) systems often struggle to capture. A key dependency of NWP systems is their reliance on precise initial conditions, requiring high-resolution input data at fine spatial and temporal scales. This research focuses on enhancing ERE prediction over Singapore, a tropical region highly susceptible to EREs. The study explores the integration of Doppler Weather Radar (DWR) data into Singapore’s Next-Generation (SINGV_NG) modelling system using the Joint Effort for Data Assimilation Integration (JEDI) framework. DWR provides critical high spatial and temporal resolution data on mesoscale convective systems, which can improve forecast accuracy by refining mesoscale dynamics and rainfall predictions, particularly for short-
