title: Unraveling Nanoscale Chirality: Chiral Cation-Based Synthesis of Chiral Nanoparticles, Enantioselective Catalysis and Biomolecular Recognition
abs: Chirality, a fundamental property evident in the realms of chemistry, biology, and physics, becomes discernible through use of circularly polarized electromagnetic fields. Crafting chiral objects strategically at the nanoscale serves as a versatile platform, allowing customization of their chemical, biological, and physical attributes for diverse applications in catalysis, medicine, photonics, and sensing. While chiral metal nanoparticles are predominantly synthesized using chiral thiol compounds derived from natural sources, leading to the successful preparation of specific chiral gold nanoparticles, the limited availability of these chiral thiol molecules curtails the chemical and structural diversity of the resulting nanoparticles. We are known for our work in chiral cation chemistry and have spearheaded the development of two innovative classes of chiral cation catalysts: pentanidium (PN) and bisguanidiums (BG). We have noticed that the use of capping agents such as cetyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB) is crucial in nanoparticle synthesis. Through serendipitous discovery, we have found that chiral cations, such as chiral guanidiniums, can be leveraged to tailor the preparation of chiral nanoparticles. Hence, 1) we propose a comprehensive exploration of the chiral cation strategy to expand the chemical and structural diversity of chiral nanoparticles. Enantioselective catalysis can be achieved by using a chiral feature that favors the formation of one enantiomer over another through interactions at the transition state. Current methods for achieving enantioselective catalysis predominantly rely on molecular-level chiral features. Localized Surface Plasmon Resonance (LSPR) is a phenomenon that results in the collective oscillations of electrons at the surface of metal nanoparticles upon excitation by incident light. This leads us to pose the following question: 2) Can chiral metal nanoparticles at the nanoscale catalyze and modulate chiral outcomes at the molecular level through plasmonic resonance? We would also like to delve into the origins of this enantioselectivity, determining whether it arises from spatial orientation or from spin selectivity of the electrons influenced by surface plasmon resonance. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are single-stranded, non-coding RNA molecules comprising 19 to 25 nucleotides. Owing to their stability in bodily fluids, miRNAs are promising biomarkers for various conditions, notably viral infections. However, current identification methods, like quantitative realtime PCR and Northern blotting, often lack the speed and sensitivity needed in clinical settings. Thus, we ask: 3) Can chiral nanoparticles selectively interact with biomolecules, presenting opportunities for the rapid identification of biomarkers such as miRNAs? title: Mechanistic dissection of brain-intrinsic immunity against viral encephalitis
abs: There is immense inter-individual clinical variability upon arboviral infections, ranging from asymptomatic to life-threatening disease. However, the molecular and cellular mechanisms governing arboviral diseases are unclear. We hypothesize that monogenic inborn errors of immunity, along with their phenocopying autoantibodies (autoAbs), and autoantibodies to type-I interferons, are major determinants of hitherto unexplained severe viral hemorrhagic fever, shock syndrome or neurological complications arising from arbovirus infections. We will systematically search for monogenic lesions that can predispose an individual to severe arboviral disease, by analyzing Whole Exome Sequencing (WES) or Whole Genome Sequencing (WGS) data collected from existing cohorts available in A*STAR or Singapore public hospitals, or from newly recruited arboviral infected patients with severe hemorrhagic fever, systemic shock syndrome or encephalitis. Using an optimized computational variant filtering strategy and in silico predictive tools, along with subsequent comprehensive in vitro characterization, we will identify monogenic lesions or phenocopying autoAbs that are causal to their severe disease presentation. We will then decipher the underlying mechanisms of cell-intrinsic or immune system-conferred protection of individuals from developing severe disease in tissue-specific human pluripotent stem cell (hPSC)-derived cellular, organ-on-a-chip or organoid models. This proposed research program on the investigation of genetic determinants to severe arboviral infections will dissect mechanistically the cell-intrinsic or organ-specific immunity against life-threatening diseases. It will also facilitate precision medicine globally, in terms of diagnosis, counselling, prevention, and treatment.
kw: Host genetics; Inborn Errors of Immunity; Autoantibodies; brain-intrinsic immunity; viral encephalitis; arboviruses

title: Accelerating the discovery of molecular glues for next-generation small-molecule therapeutics
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Molecular glues represent a promising class of small molecules capable of targeting the 'undruggable' proteome. Despite their clear-cut therapeutic advantages, there is a lack of systematic and rapid methods to discover molecular glues. I propose the use of DNA-encoded library (DEL) screening for the high-throughput discovery of molecular glues. The optimal DEL screening methodology for molecular glues, particularly using monovalent and unbiased DEL, remains largely unexplored. Leveraging my prior pioneering expertise in using bifunctional DEL to identify molecular glue-like compounds, I aim to address this technical gap. I will then use the optimized screening conditions to address two therapeutic gaps that have been inadequately tackled by conventional small molecules. Firstly, I will develop molecular glue degraders to target drug-resistant proteins, particularly the most commonly mutated metabolic enzymes IDH1/2, to treat glioma. Secondly, I aim to use molecular glues to disrupt protein-protein interactions in signalling pathways, specifically targeting TEAD-YAP in the Hippo pathway, which is implicated in many cancers. I aim to identify molecular glues both as therapeutic solutions and as chemical tools to further elucidate the disease mechanisms associated with IDH and TEAD-YAP. The screening and characterization data generated from these efforts will also allow me to transform the screening approach into a rational design strategy. Combining screening approach and rational design strategy will accelerate the discovery of molecular glues, thereby facilitating the development of next-generation small-molecule therapeutics.

title: From Pixels to Physics: Integrating Physical Properties in 3D Virtual World Creation
abs: Generative AI has shown remarkable success in generating images and views. However, there is a notable gap for 3D content creation, as well as the physical-aware generation. The broad objective of the proposed research is to create a realistic 3D virtual world adhering to physical principles, rather than dealing with only the realistic pixels as in traditional novel view synthesis. Physics-based 3D world creation is challenging because it requires a holistic interpretation of scenes and objects within it, including but not limited to geometry, materials, support, occlusion, shadow, depth, mess, gravity, velocity, motion, and interaction. The project aims to make "casual capture" of physics-based 3D content creation possible, allowing casual users to capture and virtualise real-life physical scenes into a 3D virtual world through cheap and accessible sensors, like phone cameras, with no requirement for specialized expertise, elaborate equipment, or excessive effort. In general, such a few images from casual users do not contain sufficient information for compressive physical 3D creation. However, our scientific hypothesis is that the physics-based 3D creation from a minimal set of views is still possible by learning, from billions of images and videos, the geometry and physics capability of Generative AI to hallucinate unobserved 3D content, and reason and replicate the underlying physics within in it reasonably. To achieve this, this project is committed to ushering in the new era, with pioneering theories, algorithms, systems, and datasets. Particularly, the project will i) pioneer foundational theory for physical properties definition and estimation in vision modality; ii) build a unified 3D reconstruction and generation system that creates plausible 3D contents from a minimal set of views using a probabilistic generator; iii) introduce object-centric technology to reason and decompose a whole scene into individual 3D assets, or even parts, enabling physical interaction in 3D virtual world; iv) and collect datasets with physical annotations, which will serve as invaluable resources for benchmarking physics in vision community. The project’s outcomes, delivered as open-source software, promise to make waves in academia and industry alike. In line with Singapore’s priorities of being “AI Singapore” and building “Smart Nation and Digital Economy”.
kw: 3D Reconstruction and Generation; Physical properties; Generative AI

title: One Size Does Not Fit All: Personalized Machine Learning in Psychiatry
abs: Psychiatric disorders are highly heterogeneous with large variability among individuals with the same diagnosis. The holy grail of psychiatry is to replace one-size-fits-all treatments with personalized treatments, but few precision treatments exist. A breakthrough arrived in Sep 2022, when the United States FDA approved SAINT, a new personalized treatment for treatment-resistant depression. SAINT uses resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) to select personalized targets for transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). SAINT greatly outperforms one-size-fits-all TMS and is comparable to electroconvulsive therapy, a treatment of last resort involving seizure inducement under general anesthesia. Despite SAINT’s promise, several challenges hinder the full realization of MRI-based precision psychiatry. First, while rs-fMRI can create personalized brain network maps for treatment, most network mapping algorithms requires 30-40 minutes of imaging, which is impractical for clinical use. Furthermore, most brain network mapping models are developed from data of young Western adults and specific MRI scanners, limiting their generalizability to diverse populations and different scanner types. Second, current psychiatric treatments rely heavily on trial and error based on symptoms, lacking objective neurobiological markers. This often leads to poor responses, requiring multiple treatment attempts to achieve remission. Therefore, there is significant interest in using brain imaging and other measures (e.g., symptom profiles) to predict how well treatments will work and how the disease will progress. However, the largest relevant datasets only involve 200-300 patients, limiting prediction accuracy and generalizability. This proposal aims to overcome these challenges by leveraging my group’s influential contributions in machine learning of brain MRI data. The first two aims will build machine learning models from large-scale datasets, which can then be used to predict new phenotypes (e.g., disease progression, treatment outcomes) and delineate personalized brain networks from limited data. The third aim utilizes models developed in the previous aims to deeply phenotype individuals with treatment-resistant depression in Singapore.
kw: MRI; Brain Imaging; Machine Learning; Precision Psychiatry; Depression; Brain stimulation

title: Designer carbon-based quantum spin architectures for quantum computing
abs: Individual electron spins in solids are promising contender for quantum bits (qubits), fundamental building block for quantum computing1. Quantum computation is dedicated to developing qubits, establishing their interconnections for quantum logic gate operations, and integrating them into scalable architectures for quantum information storage and processing2. Over the past decade, significant strides have been made in experimental pursuits, exploring various materials as potential qubits, including defects in solids, superconducting systems, trapped ions, and semiconductor quantum dots3-6. Despite this progress, several obstacles persist for many of these candidates, primarily revolving around the trade-offs between versatility, size, variability, and robustness4-6. At the smallest scale, such as atoms, uniformity among units is assured, but their electronic properties are challenging to engineer. Conversely, in systems like superconducting circuits and quantum dots, energy spectra can be tuned in situ, yet achieving identical mesoscopic circuits remains arduous, with effective energy scales that govern their interactions smaller than those of atoms and small molecules. Moreover, significant sources of spin decoherence have been identified in existing materials systems, particularly those involving heavy metals, including the spin-orbit interaction linking spin to lattice vibrations, and the hyperfine interaction of electron spin with neighboring nuclear spins4-6. Carbon-based quantum nanomagnets (CQMs), hosting designer quantum spin architectures, emerge as prime candidates for next-generation qubits7-9. Unlike the d-or f-orbitals derived magnetism in conventional materials with heavy metals10-12, the π-electrons of carbon assume a distinctive role in fostering robust and precisely engineered π-spin centers with long coherence times, thanks to their weak spin-orbit (low atomic weight) and hyperfine couplings (zero-nuclear spin isotope 12C) that helps prevent spin decoherence9,11-14. Moreover, in comparison to other solid-state candidates, CQMs possess the potential to strike a delicate balance between reproducibility, robustness, and chemical versatility in design, along with scalability in production, rendering them highly promising contenders to build robust and scalable qubits platform for quantum computing.To tackle such challenges outlined in the technology roadmap, our objective is to pioneer a novel material platform for designing carbon-based quantum spin architectures and to develop a new technology platform for accurately constructing, controlling, and reading out these CQM-based qubits. This endeavor lays the groundwork for practical qubit applications in quantum computing.
kw: Quantum spin architectures, carbon-based Qubits, on-surface synthesis, STM

title: Investigating Cognitive Flexibility in Complex Real-World Problem-Solving Contexts
abs: Cognitive flexibility (CF), the ability to swiftly shift between and adapt mental strategies in facing novel situations, is recognized as pivotal in adapting to and navigating the fast-paced world (Sahakian, Langley & Leong, 2021). Such an ability is susceptible to environmental influence and training and thus, it can be enhanced through interventions especially in adolescence. Evidence suggesting a relationship between CF and learning outcomes (Johann & Karbach, 2021; Titz & Karbach, 2014; Yeniad et al., 2013) has yet to be investigated from an educational perspective to be useful in classroom pedagogy and practice. One reason for the dearth of research on CF in educational settings and applications is that traditional lab-based measures used to assess CF often lack ecological validity to be used in academic settings such as in the classroom. These lab-based CF tasks are supervised and the settings in which CF is exercised are narrow, predictable and often guided externally through instructional paradigms with little translational value to real-world contexts. This fails to capture CF's multifaceted nature for findings to be utilized in educational settings. These are major drawbacks in understanding the educational implications of CF, as situations requiring CF in everyday naturalistic settings are typically unguided and unpredictable. The remit of the present proposal is to, therefore, develop CF paradigms that assess the spontaneous, natural use of CF observed in complex settings such as in the classroom, which, to date, has scarcely been investigated. Addressing this gap requires a review of the nexus of practice research and the complex interdisciplinary interface between mainstream neurocognitive and educational research. We propose a systematic approach to developing tasks that will generate data to model the spontaneous use of CF in real-world settings, including classrooms. This study will especially focus on the CF mechanisms adolescents use to navigate uncertainties and challenges in learning, creating theory-driven, evidence-based education practices. In a nutshell, this proposal aims to investigate the measurement and development of cognitive flexibility in increasingly complex real-world contexts through: Developing game-based measures to inform an integrated model of CF in complex real-world contexts, Investigating individual factors (e.g. prior knowledge, personality traits) that mediate the relationship between learning and CF in such naturalistic contexts, Developing techniques for studying CF in the classroom through game-based activities involving collaboration and socializing.
kw: Cognitive flexibility, problem solving, creativity, game-based tasks, pedagogy

title: Digital InteRvention to promotE Adolescent sleep, learning and Mental well-being (DREAM)
inst: IHDP - Institute for Human Development and Potential
abs: Background: Sleep is crucial in maintaining and optimizing adolescents' health and emotional well-being. A high prevalence of sleep deprivation and insomnia is presented in this population, associated with poor decision-making, memory, risk-taking, mood disruptions, and lower academic performance. Furthermore, it is a risk factor for anxiety, depression, and suicidal ideation. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia (CBT-I) is considered a gold standard intervention, with several studies supporting its effectiveness in adults. Few studies have been conducted on adolescents. Digital CBT-I dCBT-I offers a scalable, affordable, cost-effective, evidence-based, and accessible alternative for this age group. Aim: to develop and test the initial efficacy and technical feasibility of a culturally relevant dCBT-I to promote sleep, learning, and mental well-being among adolescents in Singapore. Method: A mixed-method approach utilizing quantitative and qualitative approaches will be conducted to assist in designing and tailoring the intervention to the target population in Singapore by identifying cultural and local aspects. The proposal is founded on Persuasive System Design (PSD), based on the idea that technology can also act as a catalyst to promote and support specific behaviors, emotions, and mental states. Also, the multiphase Optimization Strategy (MOST) underpins the digital intervention developmental approach. Conceptually rooted in engineering, MOST provides a methodological framework for building, optimizing, and evaluating multicomponent digital interventions. The methodology is divided into 3 phases: Phase 1 involves App prototype designing a conceptual model based on stakeholder and end-user engagement (co-design intervention). This involves gathering initial insights from adolescents, parents, teachers, and mental health professionals through focus group discussions (FGDs) and interviews. Phase 2 consists of a feasibility study, which assesses the technical feasibility, user satisfaction with the intervention, and the preliminary effects of the intervention on outcomes. Phase 3 comprises an optimization phase, which measures improvements in clinical outcomes using a micro-randomized trial (MRT)design. MRT will involve recruiting 201 adolescents to test various intervention components. Sixty-seven participants in each group will be randomly assigned to (1) M= automatic text messages delivering CBT-I, (2) MH=automatic text messages + human support, and (3)T= time at which messages will be sent. Participants: The study will recruit adolescents between 12 and 17 years old who have short sleep duration (less than 7 hours of sleep per day in a given week) or insomnia, as measured by the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) and quantitative electroencephalography (QEEG). title: Synthetic Carbon Allotropes and Topological Molecular Carbons
abs: This research proposal aims to address the formidable challenge of synthesizing new carbon allotropes and topological molecular carbons (TMCs), pushing the boundaries of Organic Chemistry and Materials Science. Our objectives are threefold: (1) explore the synthesis of new carbon allotropes with diverse topological structures; (2) investigate the synthesis of TMCs with intricate topological properties; and (3) examine the unique physical properties and potential applications of these novel materials in photonics, electronics, and spintronics. Leveraging recent advancements and our team’s extensive expertise, this 5-year program will employ innovative synthetic strategies such as metal-mediated on-surface synthesis, liquid-liquid interface synthesis, and dynamic covalent chemistry. Targets include non-benzenoid 2D carbon networks, sp- and sp2-hybridized carbon-based 2D networks, and sp3-hybridized 3D networks, alongside sophisticated TMCs like Vögtle’s belt, Schlüter’s belt, and helical graphene nanoribbons. A multidisciplinary team of experts in organic synthesis, surface chemistry, computational chemistry, condensed matter physics, quantum physics, and photonic device engineering will collaborate to achieve these goals. Through this program, we aim to develop efficient synthetic methods, uncover new insights into carbon-based materials' physics, and create novel devices for various technological applications. Additionally, the program will train over 15 PhD students and postdocs, publish over 40 high-quality papers, and file at least 2 patents, positioning Singapore as a global leader in advanced materials research.

title: Understand the Relationship between Visual Decline and Age-related Muscle Mass Loss (assessed using D3Cr technique) in Elderly Singaporeans
abs: Age-related visual impairment (VI) has been postulated as a key pathogenic mechanism associated with sarcopenia, a condition of progressive decline in muscle mass (MM) and function. Sarcopenia can lead to significant adverse health outcomes, such as poor functioning, frailty, falls and hospitalization. Despite VI being a potential modifiable correlate of sarcopenia, the VI-sarcopenia relationship is understudied. One of the key reasons contributing to the limited published literature is the difficulty in assessing MM accurately and in a resource-effective manner. Recently, the deuterated creatine (D3Cr) dilution technique has been proposed as an innovative and accurate assessment of whole-body MM using a simple and clinically feasible procedure; however, validation data of this novel technique against the current gold standard i.e., MRI in humans, are scant worldwide. Importantly, normative data for D3Cr-MM in healthy young adults are currently unavailable but much needed because it is usually used as a reference to estimate cut-off thresholds for low D3Cr-MM in older adults. In this proposal, I will address these gaps. First, I will determine the agreement between MM values measured by D3Cr, DXA-assessed appendicular lean mass (ALM; the most used proxy measure to assess whole-body MM), and MRI in a healthy population of young multi-ethnic Singaporeans aged 21-39 years. Second, I will compare the agreement between MM values measured by D3Cr, DXA-ALM, and MRI in this younger sample with multi-ethnic Singaporeans aged ≥60 years. Third, using data from young multi-ethnic Singaporeans, I will establish gender- and ethnic-specific normative data for D3Cr-MM, adjusted for body weight and height. Finally, I will evaluate the relationship of clinically measured bilateral VI with D3Cr-MM and DXA-ALM in multi-ethnic older Singaporeans. Ultimately, my research findings will contribute to the future establishment of precise age-related MM and vision as a strongly predictive and modifiable risk factor for age-related MM loss.
kw: Age-Related Visual Impairment; Deuterated Creatine; Muscle mass/Sarcopenia; Dual energy x-ray absorptiometry; Aging; Magnetic Resonance Impression (MRI)

title: Combating Sarcopenia in Surgical Patients from Bench-to-bedside – a translational approach to improving the current understanding of sarcopenia in colorectal cancer patients.
abs: Sarcopenia represents a major risk factor for adverse events associated with frailty. Several lines of evidence have further linked sarcopenia with delayed recovery from illnesses, increased surgical morbidity and reduction in survivability. To date, there are no effective pharmaceutical intervention, further underscoring the importance and need for better understanding of its underlying molecular mechanisms. In our earlier work, we have established the a sarcopenia-phenotyped muscle-serum biorepository, starting with colorectal cancer patients going for curative surgery, and have promising results from the use of ß-hydroxy-ß-methylbutyrate (HMB) in the prehabilitation of these patients. In this proposal, we aim to leverage on our existing work by adding proteomics to our transcriptomics and epigenetics molecular taxonomy and further investigate the effect of HMB on sarcopenia in the colorectal cancer patient cohort: Specific Aim 1: To compare the serum proteomic profiles of colorectal cancer patients to existing transcriptomic and epigenetic characteristics of muscle tissue samples, elucidating pathways and biomarkers associated with sarcopenia. Hypothesis 1: The integration of overlapping dysregulated pathways identified through previous transcriptomic and epigenetic analyses, with the proposed proteomic analysis in serum, will assist the identification of regulatory cascades implicated in sarcopenia among colorectal cancer patients. Specific Aims 2a: Evaluate the impact of supplemental HMB-enriched ONS for patients going for curative colorectal surgery on their functional outcomes and muscle quality. Hypothesis 2a: Patients who have had supplemental HMB had improved muscle quality (15% better Intramuscular Adipose Tissue (IMAT) and 15% better functional outcomes at 1-month post-surgery than those who did not. Specific Aim 2b: Evaluate the mechanistic impact of HMB on older (≥65-years-old) compared to younger (< 65-years-old) skeletal muscle. Hypothesis 2b: The supplementation of HMB resulted in downregulation of inflammatory pathways, which result in improve lipogenic pathways in older skeletal muscles and improved myogenic pathways in younger skeletal muscles.
kw: Sarcopenia; Branched Chain Amino Acid; Multi-omic Analysis; Colorectal Cancer; Ageing
