title: Co-Developing a Culturally Adapted Digital Intervention to Improve Cancer Screening Uptake
abs: Background: Malay women in Singapore have significantly lower cancer screening uptake rates compared to other ethnic groups, contributing to higher cancer mortality. Barriers such as low perceived susceptibility, modesty concerns, and misconceptions about screening exacerbate these disparities. Additionally, Malay women face a higher genetic predisposition to breast cancer, further compounding their risk. Addressing these barriers through culturally adapted interventions is critical to improving screening participation and promoting early detection. This study aims to co-develop a culturally tailored WhatsApp chatbot intervention with the Malay community to increase participation in breast, colorectal, and cervical cancer screenings. Methods: This study follows the UK Medical Research Council (MRC) framework for complex interventions. The intervention will be co-developed in Phase 1 through participatory focus groups with Malay women. Key components include personalized cancer risk assessments, culturally adapted messaging to address socio-cultural barriers, patient reminders and navigation for booking screening appointments. These components are designed to target constructs of the Health Belief Model (HBM), such as perceived susceptibility, perceived severity, perceived benefits, perceived barriers and cues to action. Phase 2 involves a pilot randomized controlled trial (RCT) with 80 participants to evaluate the feasibility, acceptability, and preliminary effectiveness of the intervention through a mixed-methods approach. Discussion: This study underscores the importance of community involvement in designing culturally tailored interventions to ensure relevance and acceptance. By integrating personalized cancer risk assessments and culturally sensitive strategies into a familiar digital platform, the WhatsApp chatbot aims to address key barriers to screening participation. If successful, it could significantly improve cancer screening uptake among Malay women, serve as a model for addressing health disparities, and inform national policies to enhance equitable access to preventive healthcare.
kw: Early detection of cancer, Digital Health

title: Novel 3D-Printed variable modulus Titanium Rods: Advancing Surgical Treatment for Osteoporosis and Metastatic Spine Disease
abs: The increasing demand for spine surgeries, driven by an aging population and medical advancements, has highlighted challenges with current spinal implants, particularly titanium rods used in Osteoporosis Spine Surgery (OSS) and Metastatic Spine Tumour Surgery (MSTS). These titanium rods, while effective, fail to accommodate the biomechanical needs of osteoporotic or tumour-afflicted bones, leading to complications such as adjacent segment fractures, disc degeneration, implant loosening/pull-out, and kyphosis. To address these issues, we aimed to develop and test 3D-printed titanium spine rods that offer improved mechanical properties, better integration with bone, and superior imaging compatibility compared to traditional titanium rods. Our hypothesis is that by varying the modulus elasticity along the rod’s length, thereby better matching the elasticity of the surrounding bone. It will enhance the ability of the implant for post-operative realignment in the spinal construct, reducing implant related complications. This would promote better osseointegration, reduce stress shielding, and prevent complications like adjacent segment fractures, implant loosening, and junctional kyphosis. Our proposed designs with core-shell structures will be produced at a standard diameter of 5.5 mm and length of 150 mm using 3D printing technology. 3D printed rods will be tested for mechanical properties according to ASTM standard, alongside human cadaveric specimens as well as imaging, radiotherapy and biological compatibility. The safety profile will be established via toxicity testing in large animal model implantation studies. All these tests will be carried out in comparison with commercially available 5.5 mm titanium rods. These novel 3D-printed rods will not only improve patient outcomes but also offer significant advantages in healthcare cost, industry efficiency, and the potential for personalized surgical treatment. They will offer significant advantages in diagnosis, prevention, and treatment of post-operative problems. In addition, they will open new avenues for scientific research, interdisciplinary collaboration, and the development of advanced, personalized implant standards.
kw: metastatic spine disease; osteoporosis; titanium rods; implant; 3D printing; surgery

title: Chewing Function Estimation for Partially Edentulous Patients using Intra-oral 3D Scan Data and Machine Learning Models
abs: Chewing function plays a critical role in overall health by facilitating proper nutrition intake and digestion. Dental conditions such as teeth loss significantly impact chewing function, particularly among older individuals. Dentists currently lack effective tools to assess compromised chewing function, relying primarily on subjective assessments. This study aims to develop an objective and quantitative evaluation method for chewing function based on individual teeth patterns and various prosthodontic options using intra-oral 3D scan data and machine learning models. The research proposes the utilization of machine learning algorithms to extract tooth features from intra-oral scan data and estimate personalized assessments of chewing function based on individual dental anatomy. The algorithms will assess chewing efficiency (CE-Status) and predict post-treatment chewing enhancement (CE-Predict) following diverse restoration treatments. These algorithms will be trained using patient ground truth data and then validated. Lastly, the plan involves piloting an implementation trial in a prosthodontic clinic to gather user feedback from patients and dentists regarding the two algorithms. The successful development and validation of these algorithms will provide clinicians with precise assessment tools for evaluating chewing status and predicting chewing enhancement following diverse restoration treatments, thereby facilitating personalized treatment plans and informed decision-making in dental care.
kw: Chewing Function, 3D scan, partial edentulous, Machine Learning

title: Understanding Asian-prevalent Rare Cancers Beyond Genomics
abs: Rare cancers collectively account for 25% of all malignancies and represent a major healthcare problem worldwide. Currently, their immuno-molecular landscape and pathobiology remain largely unknown, presenting an opportunity for scientific discovery and clinical translation. We propose to investigate Asian-centric rare cancers – focusing on angiosarcomas and phyllodes tumors of the breast, both aggressive cancers with dismal prognosis. Our preliminary data supports the hypothesis that epigenetic dysregulation may be responsible for perturbed gene transcription networks in both angiosarcoma and phyllodes tumor. Early data also supports an immunomodulatory mechanism through metagenomic stimuli in angiosarcoma. Based on these findings, we propose a detailed investigation of the epigenomic, metagenomic and immune landscapes of these rare cancers. There are three independent yet complementary study aims in this proposal. We will 1) investigate the epigenetic landscape of angiosarcoma and phyllodes tumors; 2) investigate viral-immune crosstalk and explore the metagenomic landscape in angiosarcoma; 3) establish a biobank of patient-derived models of these tumors for drug discovery and mechanistic studies. We will focus on technologies for DNA methylation profiling and chromatin immunoprecipitation, as well as tumor-immune microenvironmental studies using spatial transcriptomics and single-cell sequencing. Target validation and mechanism studies will be conducted using ex vivo models. Through Aim 1, we will derive novel insights from a more complete understanding of the multi-omic landscape of these rare cancers, and identify new drugs for therapeutic evaluation. Aim 2 will examine mechanisms of virally-induced angiosarcoma, including potential host-immune interactions, and facilitate development of immunotherapeutics. Aim 3 will provide live material to be used for biological modeling and drug screening. In addition, molecular information analyzed in relation to real-world treatment response and survival data may identify potential predictive and prognostic biomarkers. This study will redefine the value of rare cancer research as a unique model for discovery at the forefront of precision medicine.
kw: precision oncology, sarcoma, rare cancers, biomarkers

title: Single Cell Perturbation Landscapes of Phenotypic Plasticity in Gastric Cancer
abs: Cancer metastases and therapy resistance are pivotal end-stage drivers of global cancer mortality. Recent evidence suggests that epigenomic and transcriptomic alterations are vital in establishing these deadly phenotypes by promoting phenotypic plasticity, where cancer cells adopt a spectrum of functionally distinct and fluid cell states. Gastric cancer (GC) is a leading cause of global cancer mortality and highly prevalent in Asia, with tumors often exhibiting treatment resistance and multifocality. Here, we propose to dissect the epigenomic basis of GC phenotypic plasticity and how plasticity contributes to clinically relevant cellular state transitions and malignant phenotypes. As plasticity is highly dynamic, we will study plasticity in pre-clinical models leveraging on a unique set of molecularly annotated GC PDOs (patient-derived organoids) from the Singapore Gastric Cancer Consortium (SGCC). Our Specific Aims are: 1) Define the boundaries of GC PDO phenotypic plasticity at the single-cell epigenomic level. Using single-nucleus RNA and Assay for Transposase-Accessible Chromatin sequencing (ATAC-seq) (single-cell Multiome profiling), we will define cell-state associated expression programs and quantify how these states shift between primary and metastatic lesions and in response to therapeutic challenge. 2) Dissect the epigenomic regulatory circuity controlling GC phenotypic plasticity. We will perform computational analyses linking chromatin landscapes (scATAC-seq) to the Aim 1 cell states and expression programs, identifying master regulatory cis-regulatory factors and signaling pathways underpinning clinically relevant expression modules. 3) Functionally intercept targets controlling phenotypic plasticity at scale. Using CRISPR droplet sequencing (dcPerturb-seq), we will disrupt candidate targets (Aims 1 and 2) to pinpoint functional regulators of plasticity and their mechanisms. Importantly, in vitro findings from PDOs will be validated in the in vivo patient setting through SGCC databases of primary GCs. Our findings will provide critical insights into GC plasticity and reveal novel therapeutic strategies targeting these dynamic processes,that likely underpin many features of refractory malignancy.
kw: Gastric Cancer; Organoids; Epigenomics; Phenotypic Plasticity; Cellular States transition; Malignant Phenotypes

title: Using AS01 adjuvant to improve immune response in older adults through trained immunity
abs: The innate immune system defends against pathogens through specialized myeloid cells that trigger rapid, non-specific immunity. However, this defense declines with age, increasing infection vulnerability and reducing vaccine responses in older adults – a growing public health concern with aging population and increasing global outbreaks. In recent years, AS01-adjuvanted vaccines have shown remarkable efficacy in zoster (RZV) and respiratory syncytial virus vaccines. Initially known to activate innate immunity, AS01 has now been discovered to possibly exert broader immunological effects by inducing trained immunity (TI) through epigenetic reprogramming of myeloid cells, leading to enhanced and sustained immune responses that extend beyond its conventional adjuvant role. We have recently found that in older adults who received RZV, first dose was needed to restore cellular immune responses to the second dose by modulating the expression of genes that correlate with robust T cell response. Furthermore, our humanized mouse model studies revealed that AS01 alone induced epigenetic reprogramming of myeloid cells, with peak effects at one month. When challenged with Mycobacterium tuberculosis at one-month, AS01-treated mice showed protection against disease, suggesting AS01 alone has the potential to enhance innate immune defenses through TI. Nonetheless, the effects of AS01 alone on the human ageing immune system has yet to be examined. We will investigate the molecular mechanisms and durability of AS01-alone induced TI response at one- and three-months post AS01 administration in healthy older adults. To evaluate its potential for broad protection, we will employ a viral challenge study at month 1 and 3, using the live-attenuated yellow fever vaccine strain (YF17D) that can induce detectable viremia safely. We will compare the YF17D viral levels between AS01 and placebo groups. If successful, our findings could enable development of novel vaccination strategies through TI to enhance immune response and elicit broadly cross protective immunity.
kw: AS01; trained immunity; older adults; YF17D; innate immune response

title: Molecular engineering and drug development of the humanized TRPM4 antibody for therapy
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: TRPM4 channel has been identified to play a crucial role in the pathophysiology of stroke. With various limitations of current TRPM4 blockers, we have developed a novel approach to block TRPM4 channel with antibodies. A series of antibodies were produced including a polyclonal antibody M4P for rodent TRPM4, a mouse monoclonal antibody M4M for human TRPM4, and most recently, a humanized monoclonal antibody M4H for human TRPM4. These antibodies demonstrate very high specificity. M4P is specific for rodent TRPM4, while M4M and M4H only recognize human TRPM4. Importantly, the therapeutic potential of these antibodies has been validated in animal models of stroke. Potential protective mechanisms include attenuation of oncotic cell death of vascular endothelial cells and neurons after cerebral hypoxia. In the previous application, we proposed to perform Fc engineering on M4H to reduce potential side effects. While preparing this resubmission, we completed the Fc modification and generated three new clones. Among them, M4H_IgG4 demonstrated the least toxic effect assessed by assays for antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity, complement-dependent cytotoxicity, and antibody-dependent cellular phagocytosis. In this resubmit proposal, we will perform study the electrophysiological properties of M4H_IgG4. We will also examine the in vivo toxicity of this antibody. Following reviewer’s recommendation, we will focus on the characterization of M4H_IgG4 on ischemic stroke models. Both early and delayed reperfusion models will be used to examine the efficacy of the M4H_IgG4. Currently, M4H was found to achieve therapeutic effect at a dose of 1mg/kg body weight in animal model of stroke reperfusion. This dose is within the lower range of the therapeutic antibodies on the market. After Fc engineering, it is expected that the dosage will be further reduced, and the side effects will be minimized. This study marks an important step towards translation of the antibody for stroke therapy.
kw: therapeutic antibody, TRPM4 channel, neurological disorders

title: Singapore Primary Angle Closure Glaucoma Evaluation and Progression Initiative (SPACE-PRO)
abs: Glaucoma remains the leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide, with primary angle closure glaucoma (PACG) a predominant form of glaucoma in Singapore and Asia. PACG is a complex heterogeneous disease, influenced by genetic, biological and anatomical factors. Current methods for assessing PACG progression risk are subjective and rely primarily on clinical features and anterior segment parameters, which have proven to be poor predictors of disease progression. This highlights the need for objective predictive tests and novel ocular biomarkers to improve disease management and enable personalized care. Advances in imaging and computational technologies have facilitated detailed investigation of the optic nerve heard (ONH), providing insights into the biomechanical processes underlying glaucomatous optic neuropathy. However, its role in PACG remain largely unexplored, representing a critical knowledge gap. Notably, some angle closure eyes progress despite interventions such as laser iridotomy or cataract extraction, highlighting the need to identify additional risk factors beyond anterior segment changes. We hypothesize that ONH susceptibility and impaired functional aqueous outflow facility – key factors in elevated intraocular pressure and primary open angle glaucoma – are also associated with PACG progression and can help identify high-risk eyes. To address our hypothesis, we will apply advanced AI algorithms for detailed 3D structural and biomechanical ONH analysis. Aqueous outflow facility will also be evaluated using tonography and the water drinking test (WDT), a provocative surrogate marker for outflow reserve. We will also perform clustering analysis to identify disease subtypes based on shared clinical, imaging and genetic characteristics. Finally, by building a well characterized longitudinal PACG cohort (currently lacking), we aim to develop disease progression prediction models that integrate multi-dimensional data to accommodate for disease heterogeneity and improve risk stratification and facilitate personalized, targeted treatment and preventive strategies for individuals at highest risk of vision loss from PACG.
kw: Primary angle closure glaucoma, progression, outflow facility, optic nerve head, biomechanics, machine learning

title: Clinical integration of whole genome sequencing and molecular epidemiology for infection control targeting carbapenem-resistance transmission
abs: Background: Carbapenem-producing Enterobacterales (CPE), which are extensively resistant to multiple classes of antimicrobial agents, has been ranked as one of the top four “critical priority” pathogens by the World Health Organization. In Singapore, despite strict hospital infection control measures, CPE cases are rising, mainly due to the spread of antibiotic resistance genes through mobile genetic elements such as plasmids. These plasmids can move between bacteria, making conventional tracking methods ineffective. Aims: Our study aims to improve hospital infection control by using advanced genetic sequencing to track and stop the spread of CRE. We will focus on two key areas: (1) identifying hospital environments where CRE bacteria persist and spread, and (2) studying how resistance genes evolve and spread under antibiotic pressure. CRE infections lead to longer hospital stays, higher medical costs, and a greater risk of death. In contrast to other drug-resistant bacteria that have declined in Singapore, CRE remains a growing problem. Our research will help hospitals take targeted actions to reduce CRE infections, improve patient safety, and inform national policies. The results will contribute to the global fight against antibiotic resistance, leading to better healthcare practices and outcomes.
kw: Antimicrobial Resistance; Carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales; Whole Genome Sequencing; Molecular Epidemiology; Plasmids; Horizontal Gene Transfer

title: Implementing ICOPE in the COmmunity: A Mixed-Methods Evaluation of Feasibility, Fidelity, and Sustainability iN Singapore (ICONS)
abs: Background: The global aging population necessitates innovative models of community-based integrated care to maintain functional ability and intrinsic capacity in older adults. The WHO’s Integrated Care for Older People (ICOPE) framework emphasizes early detection and management of declines in intrinsic capacity, but its full real-world implementation remains underexplored, particularly in Asian, multi-ethnic settings. Objective: This study aims to evaluate healthcare providers’ perspectives and experiences in implementing the ICOPE framework within a multi-ethnic, community-dwelling population in Singapore. Specific objectives are to assess feasibility, adoption fidelity, and sustainability; identify barriers and facilitators using RE-AIM, Diffusion of Innovations, Normalization Process Theory, and the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research; and generate scalable strategies for broader ICOPE integration. Methods This is a 12-month, longitudinal, mixed-methods implementation study conducted in Boon Lay, Singapore. Healthcare providers and community partners will be purposively sampled. Quantitative data (surveys, structured observations, EHRs) and qualitative data (interviews, focus groups) will be collected at baseline, 3, 6, and 12 months. Analysis will focus on implementation outcomes across stages of early adoption, fidelity, and sustainability. Impact: Findings will inform scalable, sustainable models for ICOPE adoption under Healthier SG, providing evidence-based recommendations for policy and practice. This study also aims to contribute to implementation science by validating theory-driven frameworks in real-world Asian contexts and supporting clinician-investigator career development.
kw: intrinsic capacity; implementation science; healthy ageing;

title: The ENHANCE Study - Can a daily supplement improve egg quality? The effects of NR (Nicotinamide riboside) supplementation on the egg quality of women of advanced age undergoing IVF: a randomised placebo-controlled double-blind proof of concept clinical trial
abs: The ENHANCE study is a proof-of-concept study involving randomisation of women 35 years of age or above, undergoing in vitro fertilisation (IVF) prior to egg collection treatment with either of two doses of nicotinamide riboside (NR) - a form of Vitamin B3 - that is widely commercially available without prescription via the internet. These doses of NR are already commonly used by infertile women trying to conceive. The adverse effects of age on oocyte quality are believed to be irreversible. However, recent research in aged mice has suggested the use of NAD(P)H might improve oocyte quality, embryo development, and functional fertility (Bertoldo et al. 2020). Research has shown that oral NR gave a dosedependent increase of NAD+ from 250-1000mg/day plateauing at a 2 fold increase (Airhart et al. 2017). The medication is well tolerated, with no serious adverse effects or dose-dependent events. The main adverse effect described is hot flushes. It has been demonstrated that oral NR is safe and well tolerated up to 1000mg/day for 8 weeks (Conze et al. 2019).
kw: Reproductive; cell biology; oocyte aging; fertility preservation; male fertility; embryology

title: The Impact of Cochlear Implantation on Cognitive Function in Older Adults with Advanced Hearing Loss
abs: Specific Aims Hearing loss (HL) has been linked to various negative health indicators, including cognitive decline. Recent studies suggest that the negative health implications of HL appear to be mitigated by hearing intervention with hearing aid fitting. However, there remains a group of patients with such advanced HL that hearing aids are no longer able to provide any significant audiological benefit. In this group of patients, cochlear implantation (CI) is an established treatment modality. The aim of this study is to investigate the short term (12-18 months) impact of CI on cognitive function in older Singaporean adults. We will also investigate which cognitive domains, such as immediate memory, visuospatial/constructional, language, attention, and delayed memory, are most impacted by CI. Hypothesis We hypothesize that the dramatic improvement in hearing provided by CI may translate into significant cognitive benefits for older adults, potentially mitigating the negative effects of HL. Methodology This is a prospective, longitudinal case controlled study. Potential CI patients meeting inclusion and exclusion criteria will be recruited from the ENT clinics. Assessments will be performed at baseline and every 6 months for 18 months. Primary outcome measures will be the change in Montreal Cognitive Assessment for Hearing Impaired individuals (MoCA-H) and Repeatable Battery for the Assessment of Neuropsychological Status for Hearing Impaired individuals (RBANS-H). Feasibility and Importance This study is feasible, and can be completed with the resources from this grant and with the expertise of the study team. This work has significant importance especially in the context of Singapore’s aging population, where HL is a prevalent condition and mitigating its negative effects is an important public health concern. There is a paucity of data on how hearing intervention with CI can mitigate cognitive decline and this study can fill that gap.
kw: Hearing loss; cognitive decline; cochlear implantation

title: The development and feasibility testing of a caregiver-mediated, technology-facilitated, home-based frailty prevention program (FITWISE) for pre-frail and frail community-dwelling older adults: a three-arm pilot randomised controlled trial
abs: We aim to develop a 24-week caregiver-mediated, technology-facilitated, home-based exercise and psychosocial support intervention entitled Frailty Improvement through Technology With Informal Caregiver Supported Exercise (FITWISE) for pre-frail and frail community-dwelling older adults and evaluate its feasibility and potential effectiveness in improving physical performance, frailty status, cognitive function, perceived social support, quality of life, health-related outcomes and reducing unplanned health services used among pre-frail and frail community-dwelling older adults. A stratified three-arm pilot randomised controlled trial will be conducted. Community-dwelling older adults aged 60 years and older who are prefrail or frail, assessed and scored 3-5 on the Clinical Frailty Scale, and their adult informal caregivers of age 21 and above will be recruited from Lion Befrienders. They will be randomly allocated to the Intervention Group A, Intervention Group B or the Control Group. Older adult participants in all groups will continue their usual activities at active ageing centres and existing befriending services as they wish. Participants in the Intervention Group A will receive caregiver-mediated multicomponent exercise intervention, including exergaming and on-site intervention support, every two weeks for the first 12 weeks (active intervention). Afterward, they will continue with caregiver-mediated exercise intervention, but with monthly home visits by the research nurse to monitor their progress for the next 12 weeks (maintenance phase). Participants in Intervention Group B will receive the same intervention as those in Intervention Group A, additionally caregivers in this group will receive training on communication skills and behavioral modification techniques based on theories. Participants in the control group will receive bi-weekly home visits by the research nurse, who will provide general health education (Sham intervention). Feasibility outcomes, including recruitment and eligibility rates, intervention engagement, and safety will be evaluated. Potential effectiveness outcomes will be measured at baseline and immediately after the intervention (24 weeks from baseline).
kw: caregiver-mediated, frailty prevention, technology-facilitated, exergaming, feasibility study, pilot RCT

title: Evaluation of Breath Analysis for Monitoring Pulmonary Tuberculosis Treatment [TB-Breath Study 2]
abs: Tuberculosis (TB) is a global health emergency, infecting millions every year and requires a prolonged six-to-nine-month multi-drug therapy for cure. This research proposal aims to investigate the longitudinal changes in volatile organic compound (VOC) profiles in the exhaled breath of patients with pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) throughout the standard six-to-nine-month treatment course. The primary hypothesis is that the VOC profiles will progressively change with treatment, correlating with bacterial clearance and treatment response. Secondary aims include determining the time point at which VOC profiles normalize compared to healthy controls and assessing the feasibility of VOC analysis as a non-invasive biomarker for monitoring treatment adequacy. This will be a prospective observational cohort study, recruiting treatment naïve pulmonary TB patients from the outpatient TB clinic of National Tuberculosis Care Centre (NTBCC) at Tan Tock Seng Hospital and following them up over the standard six-to-nine-month treatment course. The VOC profiles will be evaluated longitudinally throughout the TB treatment and compared against a cohort of healthy controls. Breath samples for TB patients will be collected at multiple time points during treatment, and VOC analysis will be conducted by mass spectrometry using a proprietary breath analyser produced by the National University of Singapore. The anticipated outcomes include the development of a reliable biomarker for monitoring TB treatment, leading to personalized TB treatment, which could significantly improve patient outcomes and contribute to global TB control efforts.
kw: Tuberculosis; Breath analysis; Monitoring; Biomarker

title: Neutrophil-mediated host response in viral pneumonia and its association with disease severity
abs: Background: Viral pneumonias are common and can cause severe disease. Neutrophils are integral components of the innate immune system, and are increasingly recognised as pivotal contributors to the immunopathogenesis of severe disease. Specific aims: (i) To delineate specific neutrophil pathways that are dysregulated in severe viral pneumonias; (ii) To investigate differences in three common etiologies of viral pneumonias (influenza, respiratory syncytial virus and rhinovirus); (iii) To compare transcriptomics profile between respiratory and blood compartments; and (iv) To explore changes in neutrophil-mediated response from the acute to convalescence phase and their association with post-infectious sequelae. Hypothesis: (i) Dysregulated pathways include neutrophils differentiation, migration, degranulation and neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) formation; (ii) Profiling of different etiologies of viral pneumonia can reveal specific host responses and gene signatures; (iii) Differences in airway and blood transcriptomic profiles may offer novel insights into tissue-specific host responses that drive immunopathology in severe viral pneumonia; and (iv) Persistent dysregulated neutrophil-mediated host response is associated with long-term post-infectious sequelae. Methodology: Transcriptomics study will be performed on respiratory and whole blood samples from viral pneumonia patients in the acute and convalescence phase from the Respiratory Infectious Research and Outcome (RESPIRO) study. This will be validated using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) or multiplex assays (e.g., Luminex) to quantify key cytokines/chemokines and neutrophil granule proteins. Clinical significance: Delineating the contribution of the various neutrophil mediators to disease severity across various etiologies of viral pneumonia, within both the respiratory and blood compartments and over different time points, will allow rational development of adjunctive therapies to attenuate the dysfunctional responses.
kw: neutrophil, phenotyping, community acquired pneumonia, pneumonia severity, post-infectious sequalae

title: Defining the role of immunosenescence in innate and adaptive immune responses in latent tuberculosis
abs: Tuberculosis (TB) is a global infectious disease killer, particularly in older adults. Latent TB infection (TBI) is the biggest risk factor for TB disease in older adults. A crucial underlying phenomenon contributing to this susceptibility is immunosenescence, the age-related decline in immune efficacy and inflammaging. However, its role is understudied in TBI. From our data on COVID-19 vaccination response, we found that older adults have higher levels of polyfunctional T-cells which contracts over time upon exposure to antigens, and a relative CD4+ interferon-gamma (IFNγ) and Th17 deficiency. These findings have implications on TBI, a predominant T-cell driven infection. Additionally, age-related deficiencies in T-cell subsets like Th17 have potential downstream effects on other immune cells such as neutrophils, which is pivotal in TB granuloma formation and maintenance. Importantly for TB, a respiratory infection which classically has been diagnosed with the Mantoux skin reaction, investigation into the tissue-resident cells of the nasal mucosa and skin in tandem with the peripheral innate and adaptive immune system will provide key insights to how the aged immune system functions holistically. Hence, we aim to characterise the age-differentiated innate immunophenotypes in tissue-resident cells in the nasal mucosa and skin, as well as peripheral innate and adaptive age-differentiated immune responses in TBI with high-dimensional flow cytometry for neutrophil and T-cell immunophenotyping and functional immune assays. Finally, we will investigate mechanisms of these age-differentiated immune responses in TBI with single-cell RNA sequencing across peripheral and tissue-resident immune cells. Our results will identify underlying mechanisms that predispose the older adult to TB disease, with potential for translation to other infections that commonly affect older adults. As human immunosenescence is a universal syndrome across infection and geriatric syndromes, results from my study will form basis for in-depth investigation into therapeutic avenues for human healthspan expansion.
kw: immunosenescence; elderly; latent tuberculosis; innate; adaptive; tissue resident

title: Mapping the trajectory and prognosis of patients with mild-moderate traumatic brain injury – The NEurodegeneration & Understanding of Risk Overlay in Neuroimaging Study (NEURON) 3
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Brain injury can profoundly alter the way the brain works. It is caused by acute (e.g. traumatic brain injury (TBI) or intracerebral haemorrhage (ICH)) or chronic (cumulative damage from neurodegeneration or post-infection/ inflammation) incidents. Post-acute brain injury (ABI), structural remodeling of brain architecture may be favourable or unfavourable. Predisposition to poorer late outcomes may be due to harmful host reactions to injury, chronic inflammation and imbalances of immune mediators. We termed this “Chronic Brain Injury” (CBI). Characterizing CBI was the focus of our work in NEURON 2; we interrogated genotypic, blood/ fluid and imaging markers, host physiological responses and neurocognitive reserve/ resilience to gain knowledge towards a personalized approach to treat TBI. There is a paucity of markers documenting the neuroanatomical/ microstructural capacity of the brain to adapt and/or recover. To address this gap, we pioneered a novel imaging marker classification scheme, a Periodic Table of DTI Elements. We organized distinct diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) profiles into a unifying framework to document different brain tissue signatures from neurological cohorts with varying pathophysiological mechanisms. We developed a hierarchical algorithm to map such cohorts to “Orders”, indicative of their degree of microstructural/ tissue capacity for reversibility-to-irreversibility of brain injury. Next, to evolve the Periodic Table into a true translational taxonomy, we will validate it against clinical outcomes of CBI trajectories. Our aims are to: i) classify patterns of unique brain tissue signatures based on the Periodic Table of DTI Elements, associate them with brain injury outcomes across the breadth of neurological diseases (ABI-to-CBI subtypes), and build a road map of imaging markers representing differing CBI trajectories, then ii) correlate reversibility-to-irreversibility of DTI signatures, predicted by the Periodic Table at injury, with clinical outcomes of CBI trajectories in a 90% subsample of cohorts and validate the classification over 1-3 years prospectively.
kw: Brain Injury; diffusion tensor imaging; normal pressure hydrocephalus; dementia; neurodegenerative disease

title: iPSC-derived vasculature and microglia-competent human brain organoids as a platform for modeling Alzheimer's disease
abs: We aim to develop a preclinical human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-based syngeneic brain organoid model incorporating vascular endothelial cells and immune cells (microglia) to investigate the pathogenic mechanisms associated with Alzheimer's disease (AD. AD is a prevalent neurodegenerative disorder and the primary cause of dementia on a global scale. In Singapore, around 82000 elderly suffer from dementia which is mainly attributed to AD and vascular dementia. Worldwide, over 44 million individuals currently suffer from AD, a number projected to escalate with the aging population. Despite advancements in iPSC technologies that facilitate the creation of patient-specific brain organoids, existing models often lack the endothelial and immune cell populations that play critical roles in the progression of AD. This research seeks to address this major shortcoming by generating iPSC-derived Vascularized Brain Immune Organoids (VBIO) through the integration of iPSC-derived endothelial vessels (iEV) and microglia (iMicro). The primary objectives of this investigation include: establishing a reproducible in vitro platform for AD modeling, elucidating the interactions between microglia and vascularization, and enhancing the fidelity of AD modeling. This will involve utilizing iPSC lines harboring AD-specific genetic mutations, including TREM2-R47H and the ApoE ε4 allele, alongside their respective isogeneic controls. These mutations are highly associated with AD and pose a very high genetic risk factor. The study's aims are as follows: 1. To model AD utilizing the syngeneic hiPSC-derived VBIO model harboring AD-specific mutations with their isogeneic controls. 2. To elucidate the impact of microglial and vascular integration on neurodevelopment in both control and AD brain organoids. 3. To identify the key molecular pathways that underlie AD pathology through effective and robust modeling employing the VBIO system.
kw: Brain Organoid; microglia; Alzheimer's Disease; vascular; iPSC

title: Defining the extent cross-reactive T cells protect against secondary heterologous dengue virus infection: Filling a major gap in knowledge of dengue immunity
abs: Dengue, an acute mosquito-borne viral disease, remains a significant threat to human health. Effective and sustainable dengue control must include vaccination to boost population immunity. Current dengue vaccines, however, are “imperfect” and do not fully protect against symptomatic infection from all four dengue (DENV) serotypes. It remains unclear however, whether vaccination can still reliably prevent severe disease, even in cases of breakthrough infection. The risk of severe disease in breakthrough infection could indeed be mitigated by components of adaptive immunity such as T cells, although the degree to which this is possible remains unknown. Our overarching goal is thus to quantitatively and clinically define the extent to which DENV-specific T cells can control secondary heterologous DENV infection, and thus reduce the risk of severe disease. Herein, we will conduct a controlled human infection challenge study of secondary heterologous DENV infection using PDK-53, an attenuated strain of DENV-2 that has a well-established safety profile in humans. Our specific aims are as follows: 1) To quantitatively define the extent pre-existing cross-reactive T cell responses reduce viremia and reduce the pro-inflammatory host response in secondary heterologous DENV-2 infection, 2) To demonstrate that the response kinetics of different T cell phenotypic subsets influences viral control during secondary heterologous DENV-2 infection, and 3) To identify host determinants that modulate the anamnestic cross-reactive T cell response during secondary heterologous DENV-infection. The knowledge gleaned from this study will contribute to establishing T cells as a correlate of protection against severe dengue, and guide the safe integration of “imperfect” vaccines as part of countermeasures for sustainable dengue prevention.
kw: dengue; cellular immunity; T cells

title: Strategies for Kidney Outcomes Prevention Evaluation (SKOPE)-MIND for Preservation of Cognitive Function- an embedded proof-of-concept RCT.
abs: Cognitive impairment (CI) and chronic kidney disease (CKD) are major public health threats, particularly among the elderly, affecting thousands of Singaporeans. Both conditions, are linked to frailty, reduced quality of life, and tremendous sufferings. Despite effective therapies for these conditions, their translation into practice remains grossly inadequate. We recently implemented our NMRC-funded Strategies for Kidney Outcomes Prevention and Evaluation (SKOPE) trial of a multicomponent intervention (MCI) versus usual care on kidney function in patients with CKD over 3 years. The SKOPE MCI includes the following components: 1) nurses trained as health coaches in motivational conversation and lifestyle counselling on diet and exercise; 2) physicians trained in CKD management; 3) subsidy on sodium-glucose transport protein-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i); and 4) CKD case review meetings. Currently 717 participants have been enrolled in SKOPE and completed excellent follow-up ( >90%) at one year- representing the largest cohort of its kind. We now propose the SKOPE-MIND trial- a proof-of-concept embedded RCT to evaluate the effectiveness of SKOPE MCI on cognitive function (primary outcome) and frailty in 717 patients with CKD at 36 months post randomization. The Specific Aims are to assess: 1. the effectiveness of MCI in preserving cognitive function (neuropsychological battery test) and reducing frailty compared to usual care. 2. how lifestyle, clinical risk factors, biomarkers, and pharmacologic therapy mediate the intervention's effects. 3. the facilitators, barriers, and acceptability of interventions among patients, caregivers, and providers. 4. the relationship between kidney function, cognitive performance, and related lifestyle/clinical factors. 5. An ancillary aim is to analyze genotype-based associations with response to treatment on kidney and cognitive function in patients with CKD beyond the horizon of the trial. If proven effective and acceptable, the findings of our hypothesis-driven SKOPE-MIND trial could serve as a pioneering proof-of-care model for addressing CI in patients with CKD.
kw: Multicomponent intervention; chronic kidney disease; cognition; frailty; health systems; randomized clinical trial

title: Breast Cancer RISk Prediction (BCRisP)
abs: We aim to develop, validate and calibrate a multi-ethnic breast cancer risk prediction tool for Southeast Asia. We hypothesize re-estimation of Gail model with body mass index will produce a model calibrated for Singapore’s population. Case-control study design with a 1:1 ratio will be applied, with Singapore Breast Cancer Cohort as cases and BREAst cancer screening Tailored for HEr and/or Singapore Population Health Study Multi-Ethnic Cohort as controls. Data of female aged 35 to 80 years will be used to enable generalizability to at-risk population of Singapore. Model will be validated internally using 20% of the datasets and externally using an independent validation dataset from Malaysia. Successful validation results in a risk prediction tool to inform mammogram starting age. We aim to determine the association between breast density changes and cancer score changes, with breast cancer risk changes. We hypothesize that changes in mammographic density and cancer scores over time can identify individuals at higher risk of breast cancer. We will use EMory BrEast imaging Dataset and Lifepool datasets, specifically data from females aged 35 to 80 years with at least two mammograms, whereby the first is breast cancer free. We will use AI-powered tool by FathomX to derive mammographic density and compute cancer score. Our outcomes of interest are subsequent diagnosis of breast cancer after first mammogram for the study on mammographic density and cancer occurrence for the study on cancer scorer. Determining association between breast density and/or cancer score with changes in breast cancer risk and stratification of individuals by risk may inform optimal mammogram screening frequency. These tools may enable earlier detection of breast cancer and lower breast cancer mortality when implemented. Our access to existing cohort data, track record in developing risk prediction tools and AI-powered tool expertise ensure feasibility of these projects.
kw: Prediction tool; Artificial Intelligence; Breast Cancer; Mammogram

title: Optimizing cell therapies for scalable and effective regenerative treatment of corneal stromal and endothelial disorders
abs: Corneal transplantation is the most common tissue/organ transplant, with over 185,000 procedures performed annually. However, the severe global shortage of donor grafts leaves more than 12.7 million patients awaiting surgery. To address this gap, we propose two scalable, minimally invasive cell-based therapies for corneal stromal opacities and endothelial dysfunctions. Theme 1 focuses on keratocyte therapy to treat corneal stromal opacities with specific aims that include: (1) elucidating the mechanisms of stromal matrix reconstruction by cultivated corneal stromal keratocytes (CSKs) using single-cell transcriptomics; (2) optimizing therapeutic strategies such as multiple injections to enhance outcomes in chronic opacities; (3) evaluating efficacy in Pseudomonas and Fusarium keratitis models; and (4) validating safety in rabbits and non-human primates using Good Manufacturing Practice-compliant CSKs. These efforts build on our previous grant that demonstrated the ability of CSKs to restore native collagen organization and proteoglycan structures, with superior outcomes compared to mesenchymal stem cell therapies. Theme 2 expands on our ongoing studies on corneal endothelial regenerative therapy using cultured and non-cultured primary corneal endothelial cells (CEnCs) for the treatment of corneal endothelial dysfunction through innovative cell injection approaches. Here, our specific aims include: (1) determining the minimal therapeutic dose using cultured CEnCs for corneal endothelial cell injection (CEC-I) therapy required to achieve functionality within two animal models; (2) developing a regulatory-compliant corneal endothelial cell injection kit that will be streamlined towards clinical use; and (3) enhancing the Descemet Membrane Transplantation (DMT) model with CEC-I to address the challenges posed by Fuchs’ endothelial dystrophy. Preliminary studies have demonstrated the feasibility of both cultured and non-cultured endothelial cell therapies in restoring corneal transparency. By advancing cell-based therapies as an alternative to keratoplasty, our research program has the potential to transform clinical practice, reduce dependency on donor tissue, and improve accessibility, thereby alleviating the global burden of corneal blindness.
kw: cornea: endothelial cells: keratocytes: cell therapy: fibrosis: animal model

title: Induced Pluripotent Stem Cell (iPSC)-Derived Erythroblasts as Models of Fetal Nucleated Red Blood Cells: A Novel Approach to Enhancing Cell Isolation and Whole Genome Sequencing for Noninvasive Prenatal Diagnosis
abs: Approximately 1 in 17 births globally are affected by significant genetic birth defects, half lacking identified genetic causes. In 2012, the economic burden of pediatric diseases accounted for nearly half of the national pediatic costs (USD 14-15 billion). This significant expense was due to these conditions being undetected during prenatal screening or at the time of delivery. Current non-invasive prenatal screening/testing methods, implemented from 9-10 weeks of gestation, include serum screening, nuchal translucency, ultrasound, and cell-free fetal DNA (cffDNA) screening. These tests serve as initial screenings for genetic disorders and sex chromosomal aneuploidies but are not considered diagnostic. Positive, inconclusive results or abnormalities detected on ultrasound, often lead to invasive diagnostic procedures such as chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis, which carry risks of infection and miscarriage in otherwise healthy fetuses. Fetal nucleated red blood cells (fnRBCs) for non-invasive prenatal diagnosis (NIPD) is a promising alternative to cffDNA due to their intact fetal genome, early presence in maternal circulation and short life-span (limited to index pregnancy). However, clinical application is limited by their low abundance and isolation challenges, which risk maternal contamination and DNA damage as the cells undergo terminal differentiation and enucleation. Our approach involves optimizing cell culture conditions to enhance proliferation and yield, delaying enucleation, and reversing chromatin condensation. These strategies aim to reduce DNA damage during cell isolation and more importantly, improve genome accessibility for whole genome amplification or digital Polymerase Chain Reaction (dPCR). The short-term objective is to refine these methods using induced Pluripotent Stem Cell (iPSC)-derived erythroblasts to facilitate fnRBC processing and sequencing. The long-term goal is to enhance NIPD methods, offering safer, more comprehensive diagnostics from maternal blood. This strategy intends to decrease reliance on invasive procedures, mitigating associated risks while improving genetic anomaly detection.
kw: noninvasive prenatal diagnosis; induced pluripotent stem cell; reprogramming; next-generation sequencing; fetal erythroblast

title: Microbiome Profiling in Uveitis: A Roadmap to Precision Therapies and Immune Modulation
abs: Uveitis is a complex inflammatory eye disease that presents significant diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. Emerging evidence suggests that the microbiome plays a critical role in modulating immune responses and influencing disease progression. This study aims to comprehensively profile the gut, oral, and ocular microbiomes in patients with uveitis and matched healthy controls using advanced metagenomic sequencing. Our objectives are to identify distinct microbial signatures associated with uveitis, discern differences between infectious and non-infectious subtypes, and evaluate the dynamic changes in microbiome composition throughout treatment. Furthermore, we will explore the interactions between microbial composition, dietary patterns, and immunological markers to establish potential correlations with disease severity and therapeutic response. Leveraging a multidisciplinary approach, our study integrates expertise in ophthalmology, metagenomics, and bioinformatics to provide a comprehensive understanding of the microbiome's role in uveitis pathogenesis. Advanced analytic techniques, including mathematical modeling, will be employed to decode complex interactions between the microbiome and host immune responses, offering novel insights into inflammatory pathways. The findings from this study are expected to pave the way for microbiome-targeted therapies, such as probiotics and dietary interventions, aimed at restoring immune homeostasis and mitigating uveitis severity. This research has significant implications for precision medicine by enabling personalized diagnostic and therapeutic strategies based on microbiome profiling. By uncovering the intricate relationships between the microbiome and immune system, our study could revolutionize the clinical management of uveitis, providing a foundation for more targeted, effective, and individualized treatment approaches. Ultimately, this project represents a critical step toward integrating microbiome science into ophthalmology, potentially improving patient outcomes and quality of life.
kw: Uveitis; Precision Medicine; Microbiome: Salutogenesis

title: Sensors In-home for Elder Well-being: Integrating explainable artificial intelligence, biomarkers and digital phenotypes for early detection and intervention of cognitive decline (SINEW+)
abs: Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) serves as a critical window for intervention to delay dementia onset, especially with recent advancements in monoclonal antibody treatments for Alzheimer’s disease. However, many individuals with MCI are diagnosed late, missing the ideal intervention window. To address this, our study proposes a comprehensive, real-world approach to monitoring and predicting cognitive decline in older adults using advanced artificial intelligence (AI) models and multi-modal data collected from in-home sensors and wearable devices. Building on our ongoing projects, Sensors In-home for Elder Wellbeing (SINEW) and Activities of Daily Living (ADL) Monitoring and Wellness Analysis (AMWA), we have demonstrated proof of concept by accurately classifying MCI with an F1 score greater than 0.9. In this study, we aim to refine and validate these predictive models, incorporating well-established and emerging biomarkers such as structural 3T MRI brain scans, plasma p-Tau 181, p-Tau 217, amyloid β proteins, and Apolipoprotein E4. Our specific aims are threefold: (1) to enhance our AI models by integrating multi-modal data from biomarkers and sensors to predict MCI and dementia progression with high sensitivity and specificity; (2) to develop fine-grained Activities of Daily Living (ADL) models that provide qualitative insights into cognitive health; and (3) to demonstrate the proof-of-value of digital biomarker-driven AI models for effective case finding and early intervention in a community setting, using the RE-AIM framework to evaluate effectiveness, sustainability, and cost-effectiveness. We hypothesize that early detection of MCI through digital biomarker AI models will lead to timely interventions, improving health outcomes and quality of life, while proving to be cost-effective and scalable within community-based eldercare settings. This research will lay the foundation for more proactive, AI-driven approaches to managing cognitive decline in older adults.
kw: Cognition; Early Detection; Community Prevention; Explainable Artificial Intelligence; Sensors

title: Retina-Enhanced Cognitive-impairment Opportunistic and Generative Neural Intelligent Screening Evaluation (RECOGNISE)
abs: Dementia is a growing public health concern with profound impacts on the quality-of-life, mental health, and socio-economic well-being of individuals and their families. While interventions are available to slow cognitive decline, many cases go undiagnosed until advanced stages, limiting their effectiveness. One major issue is the difficulty in detecting early cognitive decline outside specialized clinics, where diagnosis often involves costly, sometimes invasive, and time-consuming neuropsychological and neuroimaging tests. Therefore, the overall objective of our proposal is to co-create and test-bed a stakeholder-centric screening pathway, involving the Quick Dementia Rating System (QDRS) questionnaire, and a novel fundus-based vision-language generative AI model to enhance early detection and diagnosis of MCI and dementia in primary care and community settings. We will first develop our vision language generative AI model, which includes development of a robust modality-specific visual foundation model for image analysis, multi-modal biomarker learning through contrastive learning, and a vision language model for diagnostic reporting. Concurrently, we will engage our stakeholders from participating polyclinics and St Luke’s community clinic and Eldercare to co-create a screening pathway to integrate the QDRS and our generative AI model in screening for MCI and dementia at the community level. Next, we will implement and validate the diagnostic performance of QDRS and our generative AI model in detecting MCI diagnosed with gold-standard neuropsychological tests and brain MRI imaging in adults ≥60 years old presenting to participating polyclinics and St Luke’s community clinic. We will repeat the co-creation process with our stakeholders after implementation to elucidate the feasibility and elucidate best practice to drive adoption. We will further conduct health economic evaluations to assess the cost-effectiveness, cost-saving, and net monetary benefits of adapting the QDRS and our generative AI model in screening for MCI in the community to inform decision making.
kw: Cognitive Impairment; Dementia; Retinal Images; MRI Images; Population Screening; Vision Language Foundation Models

title: Innovative Methods for Proactive Risk Optimization and adVancEment in Cognitive Health (IMPROVE-COG)
abs: Current dementia surveillance methods often fall short in terms of reliability and accuracy and capture dementia only after significant neurodegenerative changes have occurred, making it challenging to intervene effectively and mitigate cognitive decline. This highlights the pressing need for more proactive and precise surveillance techniques. To overcome these limitations, it is essential to develop a surveillance method that integrates modifiable risk factors for dementia, focusing on early identification and monitoring to transition from reactive to proactive care. This research aims to establish a robust surveillance system for cognitive health that incorporates modifiable risk factors and introduces a scalable population health intervention in transforming the approach to cognitive health and potentially mitigating the onset of dementia. 1. To develop and evaluate an AI-driven large language model (LLM) to improve diagnosis of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and dementia. The LLM will be trained on comprehensive patient data from clinically diagnosed cases across 3 hospitals. Key metrics like sensitivity and specificity will be used to evaluate diagnostic performance against clinician diagnoses. 2. Spatial analysis will identify environmental/social factors associated with cognitive outcomes by correlating dementia prevalence maps with proximity to highways, green spaces, markets etc using GIS and statistics. 3. The Brain Care Score (BCS), a 21-point tool predicting dementia/stroke, will be implemented via chatbot to assess individual risk profiles in the cohort. BCS scores will be correlated with cognitive outcomes to evaluate utility in Asian populations. 4. Personalized AI coaching will provide tailored recommendations to improve adherence to brain health interventions in collaboration with community partners. Pre- and post- analysis will assess impact on behavior change. This infrastructure will enable surveillance, predictive modeling and timely interventions. Enhanced data collection will create a comprehensive database to understand risk factors and cognition.
kw: brain health; cognition; screening; behavioural nudges; spatial epidemiology

title: RESTORES trial: RESToration of Rehabilitative function with Epidural spinal Stimulation (Phase 2)
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: RESTORES trial: RESToration Of Rehabilitative function with Epidural spinal Stimulation (Phase 2) Background/ hypothesis Spinal cord injury (SCI) severely impacts functional independence and quality of life. In a Phase 1 trial, our multidisciplinary team from NNI Neurosurgery, TTSH Neurorehabilitation, and A*STAR demonstrated that combining spinal cord stimulation (SCS) with advanced robotic neuro-rehabilitation restored functional movements and enabled independent overground walking in three participants with chronic motor-complete thoracic SCI. Building on these promising results, we aim to expand this innovative approach in a Phase 2 trial with a larger patient cohort. Aims/Methods This study evaluates the efficacy of SCS combined with personalized neuro-rehabilitation in improving neurological function in individuals with chronic motor-complete cervical or thoracic SCI. Primary outcomes: Improvement in AIS motor scores and/or achieving independent overground walking. Secondary objectives: Assess SCS safety, enhance functional and autonomic outcomes (e.g., bladder and bowel control), improve quality of life, and explore brain-spine neuroplasticity using resting-state functional MRI (rsFMRI). The trial will recruit 15 participants nationwide for surgical SCS electrode implantation, followed by a tailored perioperative rehabilitation program utilizing robotic technology. Non-invasive assessments like surface electromyography (sEMG) and computer vision tools will optimize stimulation parameters and track neuronal recovery. Computational analysis of sEMG and rsFMRI will support advanced SCS algorithm development. Comprehensive evaluations of neurological, autonomic, cognitive, and quality-of-life outcomes will be conducted at predefined intervals. Significance SCS presents exciting potential in a field lacking disease-modifying therapies. This Phase 2 trial could provide compelling evidence that human spinal networks can be reactivated and transformed post-chronic injury through an integrated approach combining targeted neurotechnology, advanced personalized neuro-rehabilitation, and computational innovations. Success could establish a groundbreaking therapeutic strategy for SCI.
kw: Spinal cord injury; Neuromodulation; Epidural stimulation; Neurorehabilitation; Robotic technology

title: A Multicentre phase II clinical trial of ex-vivo testing guided combination therapy in relapsed/refractory T-cell lymphoma.
abs: Background Peripheral T-cell lymphomas (PTCL ) are a heterogeneous group of tumours with a poor prognosis. Combination chemotherapy is the current standard of care for relapsed PTCL, however overall response rates (ORR) are poor at less than 20%.We propose evaluating ex vivo drug sensitivity guided combination therapy using the quadratic phenotypic optimisation platform (QPOP) for personalised therapy of relapsed PTCL. Hypothesis We hypothesize that QPOP based therapy will result in an improvement in the primary end point of ORR by 20% above the published ORR. Proposed Study Design and Methods We propose a multi-centre phase 2, single arm clinical trial focusing on patients with relapsed or refractory PTCL aged above 21 years. Patients will undergo a biopsy of the lymphoma which will undergo QPOP drug sensitivity testing. A drug sensitivity report will be generated and reviewed by the clinical trial team. QPOP guided drug combinations will be derived from a pre-planned drug set. Patients will receive 6 cycles of QPOP guided treatment, and all patients will undergo a PET-CT scan after their second and sixth cycles. Patients in CR/PR maybe taken to transplant if eligible, non-transplant eligible patients in partial response or stable disease will receive up to 6 months of maintenance therapy with the same doublet regimen. Based on a Simon 2-stage minimax design, assuming an 80% power and a one-sided alpha of 0.05, a sample size of 33 patients is required. Accounting for a 10% attrition rate, a total of 36 patients will be enrolled. Feasibility The feasibility of applying QPOP analysis on lymphoma samples and its potential clinical efficacy has been demonstrated in a prospective study in patients with relapsed lymphoma (Goh J, de Mel S et al Sci Trans Med 2022) published by our group.
kw: peripheral T cell lymphoma; personalised therapy; clinical trial; ex vivo drug sensitivity testing

title: Structural Variation Imputation in Asian Populations: A Path to Better Disease Association Studies
abs: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) are typically carried out to identify associations between genetic variations and traits of interest. Typically, these studies utilises genotyping arrays to interrogate the genomes of samples. Although genotyping arrays are relatively cost-effective, they often do not encompass a significant portion of the genome. As a result, genomic imputation is frequently employed to infer unobserved genotypes on the genotyping arrays. Structural variations (SVs) are large genetic alterations of at least 50 base pairs and they are recognised as key contributors to many human diseases. However, SVs are often overlooked in GWAS due to their exclusion from the data. In recent years, several groups have highlighted the importance of using an imputation panel with SVs in GWAS. Their findings indicate that integrating SVs into imputation reference panel improves the resolution of GWAS and facilitates the identification of SVs that are associated with various diseases. Our research aims to develop a multi-ethnic reference panels that incorporate SVs, using the PRECISE-SG100K dataset. To demonstrate the effectiveness of the imputation local panel with SVs, we will apply it to two studies: (1) investigating the genetic basis of ageing within the Singaporean population, using the Singapore Chinese Health Study cohort and (2) exploring the role of SVs in schizophrenia risk.
kw: Bioinformatics; population genetics; structural variation; Imputation; Schizophrenia; ageing

title: Building Resilience Across Socioeconomic Contexts: A Multi-Site Study on Self-Administered Mindfulness (SAM) Interventions.
inst: IHDP - Institute for Human Development and Potential
abs: This pre-registered multi-site study aims to evaluate the efficacy of self-administered mindfulness (SAM) interventions in reducing stress and enhancing resilience, with a focus on underserved populations in Singapore and globally. Specifically, the study hypothesizes that SAM interventions will result in significant reductions in self-reported stress levels and improvements in heart rate variability (HRV) as a physiological marker of resilience, compared to a rigorously designed sham meditation control. Using a multi-site, randomized controlled trial with a decentralized and adaptive Bayesian sequential design, the study will assess both psychological and physiological outcomes across 21 international sites, with at least 33% of participants recruited from low socioeconomic status (SES) backgrounds. The methodology includes a one-month intervention with three experimental mindfulness conditions varying in the ratio of formal to informal practices, compared against a structurally equivalent sham control. Assessments will measure self-reported stress and resilience (measured via HRV), leveraging digital tools for data collection in remote settings. The study's feasibility is supported by strong preliminary data, including results from a high-powered multi-site investigation on the topic (n = 2239), and a well-established international research network. This research addresses critical gaps in scalable mental health interventions, offering a scientifically rigorous and equitable approach to reducing stress and building resilience. Its findings have significant implications for public health by advancing digital mental health solutions that are accessible, cost-effective, and applicable across diverse populations.

title: Sweet Spot: Unravelling the role of N-linked Glycans in Dengue Virus Immune Evasion and Crafting the Next-Gen Live Attenuated Vaccines
abs: Viruses depend on their host cell for post-translational modifications of their viral proteins. Glycosylation in particular, has been shown to play a critical role in the fitness and virulence of many viruses. However, the role of protein glycosylation during dengue virus (DENV) infection has remained elusive with in vitro observations mainly, a gap that is likely due to limited availability of relevant symptomatic animal models. Work performed under the previous award has led us to uncover two novel immune evasion strategies that involve two highly conserved N-glycosylation sites on DENV Envelope (E) and non-structural 1 (NS1) protein respectively. Leveraging on a unique symptomatic mouse model of dengue, we demonstrated that glycans at position N153 on E protein protected DENV2 from premature IgM-mediated viral clearance early during infection according to a non-neutralizing mechanism. In addition, we demonstrated that N153-linked glycans on E protein also protected DENV2 from IgG-mediated neutralization. Furthermore, we discovered that glycans at N207 on NS1 of DENV2 played a critical role in T cell apoptosis, by limiting T-cell mediated killing of infected cells. We demonstrated that the PD-L1/PD-1 axis was involved in this process, and we identified PD-1 blockade as a potential intervention strategy. In this renewal application, we propose to i) continue deciphering the molecular mechanisms involved in N153- and N207-linked glycans mediated viral evasion strategies; ii) extend our findings to the four serotypes of DENV and another important member of the Flaviviridae family, namely Zika virus (ZIKV); and iii) translate these fundamental discoveries into potential novel therapeutic approaches by characterizing the protective immune responses induced by de-glycosylated DENV and ZIKV strains. This groundbreaking preclinical investigation fills a crucial void in understanding the pathogenesis of dengue and Zika, laying a robust foundation for the development of innovative treatment approaches for combating both viral infections.
kw: Dengue; N-glycosylation; immune evasion; antibody shielding; PDL1-PD1

title: Investigating and Mitigating Structural and Functional Alterations in Rodent Brains Caused by Juvenile Stress
abs: Stress during childhood can pose potent risk factors for learning and memory, leading to altered cognitive biases and decision-making later in adulthood. Since memories are constructed through biochemical and synaptic plasticity changes that occur over time after the learning process, we aim to investigate how the interference of stress during juvenility, even long after the elimination of actual stressors, continues to have a lasting impact on adulthood. This impact is facilitated by an inhibitory metaplastic state that influences synaptic transmission regulation, patterns of gene expression, structural modifications, and consequently, behavior. To achieve this, we will employ a combined approach involving electrophysiological, behavioral, chemogenetic, and transcranial direct current stimulation techniques. Our goal is to target and restore defective neural networks in the rodent brain, thereby enhancing long-term plasticity, functional connectivity, and long-term memory in animal models that have experienced juvenile stress.
kw: Juvenile Stress; Long-Term Poetntiation; Memory; Synaptic Tagging; Metaplasticity; Social memory

title: Converting the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment of solid cancers to an immunostimulatory milieu
abs: Immunotherapy can be very effective for hematological cancers but its therapeutic efficacy for solid cancers is generally low. Reasons are the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) and the inaccessibility of solid cancers. This application addresses both hurdles. A novel immune escape mechanism, which we recently identified, is the ectopic expression of CD137 within the TME. This finding was initially very puzzling since CD137 is one of the most potent T cell costimulatory molecules. But regulatory T cells (Treg) in virtually all (21/21) solid cancers, and malignant cells in nasopharyngeal carcinoma and some other cancers, express high levels of CD137, which allows them to utilize/hijack a negative feedback mechanism that downregulates the immunostimulatory CD137 ligand (CD137L) on antigen presenting cells, and facilitates escape of the cancer from immune surveillance. Our hypothesis is that depleting CD137-expressing cells, and/or increasing the levels of CD137L within a tumour, will result in a stronger anti-cancer immune response and a reduced progression or even a regression of the tumor. In Aim 1, we will use molecules to deplete CD137+ cells within the tumor, while in Aim 2, we will develop switch receptors that convert immunoinhibitory signals (e.g. PD-L1) to the immunostimulatory CD137L. In Aim 3, we will enhance CD137L expression within the tumor, and evaluate different methods for efficient delivery of these treatments. This includes in vivo electroporation that can overcome the physical barriers of solid cancers. In Aim 4, we will test the most potent treatments and delivery methods in human organoids and PDX in humanized mice. This highly translational project brings together basic and clinical scientists with strong complementary expertise in cancer immunotherapy. This proposal will develop effective methods to convert an immunosuppressive to an immunostimulatory TME, and lay the groundwork for a novel therapeutic approach to be evaluated in a phase I clinical trial.
kw: tumor immunotherapy, tumor microenvironment, nasopharyngeal carcinoma

title: Combating cancer-induced muscle wasting through mTORC1 signaling
abs: The mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) complex 1 (mTORC1) integrates nutrient and growth factor signals to regulate cell growth and proliferation. While mTORC1 hyperactivation is well-documented in tumorigenesis, its role in cancer-associated syndromes remains poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that oncogenic mTORC1 in tumors not only promotes cancer growth but also drives muscle wasting, a condition known as cancer cachexia. Our preliminary findings reveal that mTORC1 regulates the biogenesis of extracellular vesicles (EVs) in tumors, and these cachectic EVs suppress muscle regeneration, leading to progressive muscle wasting. To further investigate mTORC1's role in cancer cachexia, we aim to: (1) characterize the regulation of cachectic EVs by mTORC1 in cancer, (2) identify the molecular cargos within these EVs, and (3) modulate LC3 EV cargos to reverse muscle and cardiac wasting associated with cachexia. This study will uncover novel mechanisms by which mTORC1 signaling in tumors disrupts muscle homeostasis, offering a foundation for developing therapies to inhibit cancer progression and mitigate muscle wasting, ultimately improving the quality of life for cancer patients.
kw: mTORC1; LC3 EV; muscle; cancer

title: Pan-Merbecovirus and Pan-Henipavirus vaccines and therapeutic monoclonal antibodies
abs: The impact of a pandemic is devastating. It not only claimed millions of lives but also disrupted livelihoods and shuttered economies in an unprecedented manner. Since the COVID-19 pandemic, public health agencies and non-profit organizations such as CEPI and WHO have urged the need for vaccine candidates against priority emerging viral threats such as the Ebola virus, MERS-CoV, and Nipah virus. However, the key question is whether virus-specific vaccine candidates are sufficient to prevent future related zoonotic virus outbreaks. Since the SARS outbreaks in 2003, no similar virus was detected in humans until an antigenic unrelated SARS-CoV-2 emerged in Wuhan, China, 17 years later. A specific MERS-CoV or Nipah virus (NiV) vaccine might be useful to prevent current MERS-CoV or NiV infections. Still, it might not be effective against antigenic unrelated future MERS-CoV-2 or NiV-2 that potentially cause the next pandemic(s). This highlights the need for vaccine candidates that are capable of inducing broad-spectrum neutralizing antibodies. This proposal aims to develop pan-merbecovirus and pan-henipavirus vaccine candidates and therapeutic monoclonal antibodies that are agnostic to future pre-emerged related viruses. We applied the cross-clade prime-and-boost strategy that we learned from COVID-19-vaccinated SARS survivors to induce broadly neutralizing antibodies in animal models. Together with bioinformatic modeling, we designed vaccine candidates that induced pan-sarbecovirus immunity in mouse models. We applied this pipeline to the design of the merbecovirus and henipavirus vaccines, and the neutralizing breadth induced by these candidates will be validated using our sophisticated high-resolution neutralization assay and in vivo challenge studies. Vaccine candidates that induced potent neutralizing antibodies will be used to immunize human Ig-transgenic mice for therapeutic monoclonal antibody discovery. We aim to identify broadly neutralizing antibodies (or cocktail of monoclonal antibodies) that can be administrated intranasally as prophylaxis to prevent infection or reduce disease transmission.
kw: Vaccine, Monoclonal antibody, Emerging Infectious Diseases, Pandemic preparedness

title: Investigating the mechanisms and therapeutic potential of modulating homeostatic pathways to treat exfoliation glaucoma
abs: Exfoliation syndrome (XFS) is a blinding disease that highly prevalent worldwide but still not well understood. XFS manifests as build-up of exfoliative deposits (ED) in the eye, impeding aqueous outflow and raising intra-ocular pressure. This eventually leads to glaucoma and blindness. By studying the risk genes LOXL1 and CYP39A1, we have developed a cell model that recapitulates ED. Expressed LOXL1 expressed is secreted extracellularly and a proportion manifests as insoluble aggregates, which nucleates follow-up aggregation leading to ED. We also found a) there is increased abundance of LOXL1 protein in aqueous humor (AH), from XFS patients and b) LOXL1 variants that protect against XFS have decreased extracellular secretion and extracellular aggregation. LOXL1 aggregation is c) also exacerbated by endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, an important hallmark in aged cells. These data supports the hypothesis that LOXL1 aggregation causes exfoliative deposition and accounts for the late age-of- onset of ED. We previously discovered that functionally deficient variants of CYP39A1 was strongly associated with XFS. Following up, we found that accumulation of its substrate 24-hydroxycholesterol (24-OHC) is a a consequence of XFS-associated CY39A1 decrease in expression that activates the nuclear receptor LXR, leading to metabolic remodeling events with two consequences: 1) increased release of aggregated LOXL1 to the extracellular media, and 2) excessive efflux of cholesterol and sphingomyelin from epithelial cells. These metabolites are key in maintenance of the blood ocular barrier (BOB) that is essential for proper functioning of the eye while loss of BOB is an defining feature of XFS and is thought to exacerbate LOXL1 aggregation. Here we propose to use leverage this cell model to investigate LOXL1 aggregation mechanisms driven by aging/ER stress and loss of BOB integrity, and then at the same time, develop a LOXL1-driven pre-clinical XFS mouse model to assess therapeutic approaches to modulate ED.
kw: exfoliation glaucoma, homeostasis, protein aggregation

title: The function of mammalian ADP-ribosylation factor 1 (Arf1) GTPase in brain development and neurodevelopmental disorders
abs: Neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs), encompassing conditions such as microcephaly, affect approximately 5% of the paediatric population in Singapore, contributing significantly to intellectual disability, epilepsy and developmental delays. Our prior research underscored crucial roles of the Drosophila ADP-ribosylation factor 1 (Arf1) GTPase in Golgi integrity, secretory pathway, and microtubule assembly in postmitotic sensory neurons and quiescent neural stem cells (NSCs).
