However, the roles of mammalian Arf1 during brain development and NDD remain unexplored. This study aims to address this gap by unravelling the novel role and mechanism of rodent and human Arf1 in brain development, with a specific focus on neural stem cell proliferation and neuronal migration. Recently, missense heterozygous variants in human ARF1 gene were identified in human patients with microcephaly and periventricular nodular heterotopia, NDDs characterized by smaller brain formation and neuronal migration defects. We propose to model ARF1 variants-associated microcephaly and neuronal migration defects in human cerebral organoids. Our central hypothesis is that mammalian ARF1 plays a crucial role in NSC proliferation and neuronal migration by regulating microtubule growth during brain development; moreover, ARF1-dependent microtubule growth is mediated by its physical interaction with the microtubule polymerase ChTOG. To address this hypothesis, we propose the following specific aims: Specific Aim 1. Investigate the function of mouse Arf1 GTPase in brain development. Specific Aim 2. Determine the function of human ARF1 in brain development and neurodevelopmental disorders. Specific Aim 3. Investigate the function of human ARF1 in microtubule growth and underlying mechanisms The feasibilities of this study are strongly supported by our preliminary studies. The outcomes of this project are anticipated to provide significant and unprecedented novel insights into the functions of the human ARF1 and its disease-related variants during brain development, shedding light on the mechanisms underlying ARF1-associated neurodevelopmental disorders.
kw: Neurodevelopmental disorders, microcephaly, periventricular nodular heterotopia (PNH), ADP-ribosylation factor 1, ARF1, neural stem cell proliferation, neuronal migration

title: Elucidation and therapeutic targeting of NDRG1 to mitigate inflammation, fibrosis, and enhance epithelial repair in influenza and COVID-19
abs: Despite vaccines for influenza A viruses (IAVs) and SARS-CoV-2, frequent viral mutations and the resulting vaccine mismatches, and the emergence of novel viruses remain major public health challenges. No effective treatments currently exist for the severe pathology and post-acute sequelae of these infections, including chronic inflammation, impaired epithelial repair, and fibrosis. Virus-targeting therapeutics often lose efficacy due to rapid viral mutations, underscoring the urgent need to identify host factors that can be targeted to mitigate severe complications. Preliminary studies by our team reveal that IAV infection reduces NDRG1 expression, disrupting iron homeostasis and promoting inflammation, fibrosis, and impaired epithelial repair in human primary nasal epithelial cells cultured at the air-liquid interface. NDRG1 knockdown exacerbates these pathological features, shared by IAV and SARS-CoV-2. People with asthma suffer more severe infection and diseases and we find that asthmatic bronchial epithelial cells exhibit baseline NDRG1 reduction and dysregulated iron homeostasis, both of which are further diminished upon IAV infection, correlating with more severe disease. Importantly, recombinant epithelial repair factor BPIFA1 preserves epithelial integrity following IAV infection, highlighting its therapeutic potential. Building on these exciting findings, this study will elucidate the roles of NDRG1 in inflammation, fibrosis, and epithelial repair during IAV and SARS-CoV-2 infections. We will explore its links with iron dyshomeostasis and assess therapeutic strategies targeting NDRG1, iron homeostatic and epithelial repair factors to mitigate severe immunopathology and promote repair. This work could transform the management of IAV- and SARS-CoV-2-mediated diseases, long-COVID, long-Flu, and other chronic conditions such as asthma and pulmonary fibrosis.
kw: Influenza; COVID19; innate immunity; fibrosis: epithelial repair

title: Unraveling the molecular mechanisms of ARID1A loss in bile duct carcinogenesis to identify therapeutic vulnerabilities
abs: Cholangiocarcinoma (CCA, aggressive bile duct cancer) presents significant clinical challenges due to poor prognosis, limited treatment options, and increasing global incidence. The etiology of CCA varies geographically: liver fluke infection is a major cause in endemic regions like Thailand (fluke-positive CCA), while primary sclerosing cholangitis is a key risk factor in Western countries (fluke-negative CCA). We have identified prevalent mutations in the tumor suppressor ARID1A, a component of the SWI/SNF complex involved in chromatin remodeling, in CCA (Chan-On et al. 2013, Nature Genetics; Jusakul et al. 2017, Cancer Discovery). These mutations are associated with distinct epigenomic changes (Hong and Yong et al. 2024, GUT) and impact on CCA biology (preliminary data), with effects that vary depending on etiology. There are currently no effective therapeutic strategies for ARID1A-deficient CCA, underscoring an urgent clinical need to better understand its role in CCA initiation and progression, and to identify potential etiology-specific therapeutic targets. To address this, we will first develop etiology-specific preclinical models for ARID1A-deficient CCA, including patient-derived cell lines, organoids, xenografts, and transgenic mice (Aim1). Next, we will explore the mechanisms behind ARID1A loss in CCA initiation and progression by analyzing its impact on the SWI/SNF complex, protein interactome, chromatin structure, and transcriptomic landscape. This will be done using mass spectrometry, chromatin sequencing, single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, and molecular genetics techniques, on both established preclinical models and primary tissues (Aim2). Finally, we will identify cancer dependencies in ARID1A-deficient CCA through high-throughput CRISPR/Cas9 screening, correlating these dependencies with the mechanisms uncovered in Aim2 (Aim3). This comprehensive study will advance our understanding of the complex biological mechanisms driving CCA initiation and progression, not only due to ARID1A loss but also other SWI/SNF complex alterations. Our findings will reveal therapeutic vulnerabilities and inform development of targeted treatments for ARID1A-deficient CCA patients of diverse etiologies.
kw: Cancer dependencies; mechanisms; bile duct cancer

title: Leveraging on AS01-induced immune cell reprogramming to improve vaccine responsiveness in older adults
abs: Life expectancy is increasing in many parts of the world. While the longer lifespan is desirable, aging results in weakened immunity, which causes older adults to be more susceptible to infections. At the same time, it also limits the potency of vaccines. Recently, our team and others have shown that the AS01 adjuvant, besides contributing to remarkable efficacies of the shingles and respiratory syncytial virus subunit vaccines, could also reprogram immune cells. Furthermore, our recent transcriptomic pathway analyses revealed that Shingrix modulates the overactive basal innate immune pathways, specifically neutrophil, monocyte and toll-like receptor inflammatory signaling pathways. At the gene level, PADI4 was identified as a compelling immunomodulatory candidate, where Shingrix-induced reprogramming resulted in significant reduction in PADI4 expression. These findings support that the AS01 adjuvant in Shingrix not only restores T cell responses, but may also induce durable gene expression changes that can confer broader immunomodulatory benefits in older adults. Indeed, emerging studies are showing that AS01-adjuvanted vaccines can reduce incidence and severity of COVID-19 and dementia onset in older adults compared to non-AS01 adjuvanted vaccines. As high PADI4 expression is associated with increased risk of rheumatoid arthritis, and with our recent preliminary data demonstrating that PADI4 expression is significantly reduced after Shingrix vaccination in healthy older adults, the goal of the study is thus to demonstrate that Shingrix vaccination can reduce PADI4 levels in rheumatoid arthritis patients, thereby modulating key immune pathways that alleviate the symptoms and disease activity in rheumatoid arthritis patients. To achieve this objective, we will determine the extent of PADI4 downregulation in rheumatoid arthritis patients after Shingrix vaccination. We will also determine the spectrum of immune cells, along with the genes and the biological pathways that are altered following PADI4 downregulation. Finally, we will determine the changes in rheumatoid arthritis activity in these patients after Shingrix vaccination. If successful, this study will provide an opportunity to explore using Shingrix vaccination to reduce the burden of rheumatoid arthritis patients.
kw: vaccine; adjuvant; AS01; T cell response; immune cell reprogramming

title: Microbial Tryptophan Metabolites as Potential Targets for HCC Surveillance
abs: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a global concern, attributed to lack of appropriate biomarkers and poor prognosis. Abnormal tryptophan (Trp) catabolism by host enzymes has been associated with HCC. Gut bacteria can also metabolize Trp into specific indole derivatives (here we refer them as “microbial-TrpMet”). In preliminary studies, we detected increased accumulation of microbial-TrpMet in HCC patients’ tumor tissues compared to their adjacent normal liver tissues. Cultured liver/HCC cells showed increased growth while T-cells exhibited refractoriness to Th17 differentiation in the presence of microbial-TrpMet. We therefore hypothesize a crucial role for microbial-TrpMet in HCC development and immune regulation. To analyze microbial-TrpMet in HCC and comprehensively characterize their roles in HCC pathology and immune function, we propose three specific aims. In Aim 1, we will perform targeted metabolomic assessments to measure microbial-TrpMet levels in tumors (multiple sites within a tumor) versus non-tumor liver tissues from about 150 HCC patients (representing TNM stages 1A/B, II & IIIA/B; ~50 each) and also in patients’ blood and stool samples compared to non-HCC healthy donors. In Aim 2, we will examine presence of bacterial genes encoding specific enzymes that produce microbial-TrpMet in the stool samples collected under aim 1 (~50×3 HCC patients) and matching non-HCC healthy controls. We will validate increased expression/activity of Trp metabolizing bacteria/bacterial enzymes in HCC patients’ fecal microbiota (n=10) using 13C-Trp-based orthogonal assays and mass-spectrometry. In Aim 3, we will elucidate the mechanism of microbial-TrpMet involvement in HCC development/progression and immune regulation using various in vitro cell culture, spheroid & co-culture models and cellular, molecular, and immunological assays. We will examine overall effects of “Fecal Microbiota Transplant” mediated HCC development in humanized mouse models. The project will enhance our comprehension of HCC genesis and development, presenting microbial-TrpMet as potential targets for improved diagnostic accuracy, innovative surveillance strategies and personalized treatment planning.
kw: Liver cancer; HCC; Microbiome; Antitumour immunity; Tryptophan

title: Wearable Garment for Non-invasive AI-assisted Blood Pressure Monitoring
abs: Hypertension is an urgent global health challenge affecting more than one billion people worldwide, significantly contributing to the burden of cardiovascular diseases including stroke, acute myocardial infarction, heart failure, and renal complications (WHO, 2021). Current blood pressure monitoring methods often rely on episodic clinic visits, which may miss crucial fluctuations throughout the day, leading to underdiagnosis and inadequate management of hypertension (World Heart Federation, 2020). This intermittent approach fails to capture the dynamic nature of blood pressure changes and contributes to increased healthcare costs associated with hypertension-related complications due to inadequately controlled blood pressure. Our research proposal addresses these critical gaps by developing a wearable garment for non-invasive, tetherless, AI-assisted blood pressure monitoring. This innovative solution integrates novel fiber pneumatics, fiber-based sensors, AI algorithms for decision support, and wearable computing to enable real-time measurement and monitoring of blood pressure levels. By seamlessly embedding these technologies into everyday clothing through traditional weaving and knitting approaches, the wearable garment offers a convenient and unobtrusive method for measuring and monitoring blood pressure over prolonged periods in suspected and established hypertensive patients.
kw: blood pressure monitoring, hypertension management,  ambulatory blood pressure, cardiovascular diseases, remote health monitoring, diagnostic wearables

title: Repurposing Pathogenicity Islands as Antibacterial Agents Indifferent to Antibiotic Resistance for Precision Therapy
abs: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a critical global public health threat, limiting our ability to treat infections and perform essential medical procedures. Bacteriophage therapy, or the use of viruses to target and eradicate bacteria, has emerged as a promising alternative to antibiotics. Phages are inherently effective against antibiotic-resistant bacteria as they bypass traditional resistance mechanisms. However, two major challenges hinder its therapeutic potential: (1) most pathogenic bacteria harbour multiple dormant prophages that protect their host against invading phages, and (2) extensive screening is often required to match candidate phages to bacterial isolates. To address these challenges, we propose the development of Antimicrobial Prophage Activators (APAs): engineered genetic elements delivered via phage particles to activate resident prophages and induce bacterial cell lysis. This approach builds upon our recent discovery that Staphylococcus aureus Pathogenicity Islands (SaPIs) express a small protein, Sam (SaPI activator of MGEs), that inactivates phage repressors and triggers prophage induction independently of the bacterial SOS response. The SaPIs then propagate and exploit the activated phages for dissemination, spreading to neighbouring cells as bacteria lyse. Therefore, we hypothesise that SaPIs can be engineered into APAs capable of infecting, replicating, and lysing bacterial cells while exploiting resident prophages for dissemination. The objectives of this study are to: (1) identify diverse phage repressor binding partners for a range of Sam proteins, (2) engineer a delivery system with customised sam gene panels to create a versatile APA toolkit, and (3) evaluate APA efficacy against S. aureus clinical isolates from Singapore. APAs represent the first therapeutic strategy that targets resident prophages, and the catalogue of Sam-repressor interactions will enable APA-host matching for precision medicine. In conclusion, this proposal aims to develop a novel antimicrobial therapy with significant potential to address the AMR crisis and improve global public health.
kw: antimicrobial, resistance, bacteriophage, therapy, pathogenicity island, precision

title: A point of care medical device for fast and accurate screening of peripheral artery disease
abs: Peripheral artery disease (PAD) is a common and severe complication of diabetes mellitus (DM), significantly increasing the risk of lower-limb amputations and cardiovascular events. However, diagnosing PAD in DM patients remains challenging due to limitations in existing methods such as the ankle-brachial index (ABI), toe-brachial index (TBI), and transcutaneous oxygen pressure (TcPO2), which are either unreliable, inaccessible, or time-intensive in primary care settings. This project aims to address this critical gap by developing a first-in-class, cost-effective, multi-wavelength optical device capable of simultaneously measuring blood flow, blood volume, and tissue oxygen saturation. These parameters provide a comprehensive assessment of tissue metabolism and viability, enabling accurate and rapid PAD diagnosis in primary care. Building on our patented diffuse speckle pulsatile flowmetry (DSPF) technology, we will design and integrate a multi-wavelength system featuring real-time data processing and machine learning algorithms for PAD risk assessment. The proposed clinical study will recruit 150 subjects, including healthy individuals and DM patients with varying PAD severity, to train and validate the system. The feature extraction algorithms will process 30 seconds of measurement data from three wavelengths to derive key physiological parameters, which will be analyzed using a locally deployed machine learning model to calculate PAD risk. The proposed system combines advanced optical design, signal processing, and artificial intelligence to overcome the limitations of existing methods. With a compact and user-friendly design, the device is well-suited for primary care settings and has significant potential to improve early PAD detection, reduce healthcare costs, and enhance patient outcomes. This research aligns with Singapore's healthcare priorities and positions the country as a leader in MedTech innovation, addressing the pressing need for scalable and accessible PAD diagnostics in the region and globally.
kw: peripheral artery disease; biophotonics; disease screening; point of care; medical device

title: Unravelling the origin and functional role of the bone marrow-like niche in hepatocellular carcinoma
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the most common type of primary liver cancer and a major global health burden. Despite advances in early detection and treatment modalities, including surgical resection and liver transplantation, HCC remains challenging to manage due to high recurrence rates and limited treatment options in advanced stages. Understanding the molecular mechanisms driving HCC progression is crucial for developing more effective therapeutic strategies. We have observed an enriched subset of endothelial cells in mouse and human HCCs that highly express the progenitor marker, CD34. Preliminary characterization of these CD34+ endothelial cells reveal close similarities with fetal liver and adult bone marrow endothelial cells, which are known to promote immune exclusion. Origin and functional relevance of these cells to HCC pathogenesis remain elusive. We hypothesize that CD34+ endothelial cells in HCC are derived from bone marrow during tumourigenesis, and promote immunosuppressive microenvironments to potentiate HCC development. In this proposal, we aim to spatially define the bone marrow-like niche in mouse and human HCCs, determine the origins of the CD34+ endothelial cells using lineage tracing methodologies, and investigate the functional role of CD34+ endothelial cells in HCC pathogenesis using a combination of genetic and orthotopic HCC mouse models. We apply multiplex immunohistochemistry, 3D volumetric light sheet microscopy, single cell transcriptomics and immune profiling by flow cytometry to understand the immunomodulatory function of these cells and their importance to HCC progression.
kw: Hepatocellular carcinoma; endothelial cell; oncofetal; immunosuppression; bone marrow

title: Explosive centriole amplification and differentiation of multiciliated cells: links to airway disease
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Inhaled air is laden with pathogens and pollutants that impact the health of our respiratory system. Multiciliated cells (MCCs) function as janitors to drive mucus clearance that traps inhaled pathogens and pollutants. Post-mitotic MCC precursors amplify large numbers of centrioles that mature into basal bodies for multiciliation. Genetic defects in MCC development and cilia motility cause diseases such as primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD). In addition, secondary insults to MCCs by pollutants and pathogens also lead to airway diseases like chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and pneumonia. We have used model vertebrates like zebrafish, Xenopus and mice to study mechanisms of MCC formation and ciliary motility. We have identified important regulatory proteins, Gmnc and its paralogue Mcidas, as central drivers of MCC specification and differentiation. More recently, use of human embryonic stem cell (hESC) derived MCCs in culture has allowed us to establish mutant hESCs for several MCC regulatory genes and the identification of a coupled transcriptional and centriole biogenesis program, organized by the nuclear-cytoplasmic shuttling of MCIDAS. We have also assembled a comprehensive list of MCIDAS targets that contains many genes not associated with MCCs previously. In this proposal, we describe experiments that will allow us to address a number of key outstanding issues regarding human MCC biology. A) First, we will use CRISPR/Cas9 mediated gene editing to generate transgenic hESCs that will allow us to efficiently generate MCCs through conditional induction of MCIDAS expression. B) Secondly, we aim to decipher the molecular details of how cytoplasmic MCIDAS organizes massive centriole biogenesis during MCC differentiation. C) Finally, we have selected a set of novel MCIDAS target genes to functionally interrogate for their roles in MCC differentiation and function. We believe our research findings will expand our knowledge of MCC biology and will have clinical ramifications for airway diseases like PCD.
kw: multiciliated cells; cilia; centrioles; MCIDAS; leucine-rich repeat; respiratory disease

title: Improving the Accuracy of Ultra Long Read Sequencing Technology to Facilitate Assembly and Phasing of Cancer Genomes
abs: This research proposal aims to develop an AI-driven methodology for improving the accuracy of ultra-long nanopore reads to enable the reconstruction and phasing of complex cancer genomes. The project focuses on achieving telomere-to-telomere reconstruction for most of the chromosomes of several primary and metastatic cancer genomes. Specifically, it seeks to create an AI-based method for precise error correction of ultra-long reads by leveraging DNA methylation pattern differences across haplotypes and clones. The study will reconstruct genomes from five pairs of primary and metastatic head and neck squamous carcinoma (HNSCC) cell lines, two gastric cancer cell lines, and two pancreatic cancer cell lines as part of the Cancer Genome in a Bottle initiative. A key aspect of the research is the analysis and reconstruction of extrachromosomal DNA and breakage-fusion-bridge cycles. The project will include sample and data preparation, AI model development, genome assembly, model fine-tuning, and the analysis of structural variants and methylation patterns between primary and metastatic tumours. The outcomes are expected to offer new insights into cancer genome heterogeneity and pave the way for personalized medicine and therapeutic strategies across diverse cancer types.
kw: cancer genome, assembly, structural variations, extra chromosomal DNA (ecDNA), Breakage-Fusion-Bridge (BFB) cycle, DNA modification

title: Development of therapeutic phages for the treatment of Mycobacterium abscessus complex strains.
abs: A century after bacteriophages were first identified and proposed as therapeutic agents for bacterial infections, phage therapy targeting multidrug resistant and recalcitrant infection has finally gained momentum with a series of well publicized clinical successes. Noteworthy are the success of recombinant mycobacteriophages for the treatment of Mycobacterium abscessus complex strains. In these leading examples phage strain specificity and phage resistance emerged as leading stumbling blocks. Another report has underlined the critical aspect of the turn-around time from the time of request to administration of the selected phage cocktail for treatment, in some instances lasting 363 days. Here we aim to (1) isolate and characterize phenotypically and genotypically mycobacteriophages targeting M. abscessus of the smooth and rough morphotypes with broad range properties, (2) determine phage-bacterial interactions regarding host adhesion, ligand-receptor interactions, and receptor-mediated phage resistance mechanisms, and (3) select appropriate therapeutic phage cocktail combinations via a layered approach to avoid overlapping phage resistance mechanisms and the emergence of escape M. abscessus mutations. Our goal is to have at least one phage-cocktail pre-approved and certified for clinical use in Singapore. We will use the established clinical approval system from Sciensano, the Belgian Department of Health, as a starting point given their established guidelines for phage therapy and use this approval for discussions with the Health Sciences Authority in Singapore.
kw: Mycobacterium abscessus; phage; phage therapy

title: Liquid biopsy micro-sampling for scalable and high-resolution cancer surveillance
abs: Liquid biopsies have revolutionized clinical oncology by offering a less invasive method for early cancer detection, diagnostics, and real-time monitoring of treatment responses. The integration of cell-free DNA (cfDNA) assays into clinical practice has been accelerated by advancements in molecular profiling technologies and sophisticated data analytics. Early detection of disease relapse and treatment response using circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) in blood has the potential to improve survival rates and generate significant cost savings in healthcare systems. Additionally, tracking tumor growth via ctDNA levels in blood provides a novel clinical tool for monitoring disease progression during therapy and clinical trials. In this proposed project, we aim to develop a scalable approach for cancer liquid biopsies (Fig. 1). By optimizing an experimental-computational method for cfDNA micro-sampling, using a finger-prick capillary Dried Blood Plasma Spot (DPS) technique, we seek to accurately detect and characterize ctDNA in blood droplets from cancer patients. Our preliminary data demonstrate that the DPS sampling approach yields results comparable to standard phlebotomy blood samples. The first aim focuses on developing and validating a ctDNA DPS assay, optimizing assay accuracy and minimizing reagent/sequencing costs. The second aim involves developing a new DPS-compatible multi-modal machine learning model for joint prediction of both ctDNA levels and tumor tissue-of-origin (TOO) from a DPS sample. In the third aim, we will apply these methodologies to study ctDNA dynamics with unprecedented temporal resolution in lung cancer patients undergoing a 6-week chemo-radiation therapy (CRT). By correlating ctDNA dynamics with treatment outcomes, these data could provide novel insights into radiation-induced cell death, ctDNA biology, and potentially guide the rational use of dose-escalation or de-escalation during CRT.
kw: Cancer Biomarkers Oncology Bioinformatics

title: A metabolomics-driven approach to manufacture patient-derived human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-specific Chimeric Antigen Receptor Regulatory-T cells (CAR-Tregs) to prevent rejection of transplanted islets in diabetes
abs: Diabetes mellitus (DM) and its associated comorbidities are growing in Singapore with an increasing healthcare burden. DM patients exhibit immune dysfunction, which can result in a loss of tolerance towards pancreatic islet β-cells. Hence, efforts to replace islets through transplantation have been hampered by host immune cells rejecting donor islets, necessitating the use of immunosuppressants. Regulatory T cells (Tregs) specialize in mediating immunological tolerance in the body, making them a promising candidate for the treatment of autoimmune diseases and preventing transplant rejection. While Tregs are known to utilize distinct metabolic pathways for synthesis and energy usage compared to CD4 Teffs, many of the reagents to activate and expand them in current investigator and industry-led clinical trials are borrowed from reagents designed for expanding CD4 Teff cells. Using published literature as well as in-house transcriptomics and metabolomics analyses, we aim to tailor reagents that can improve Treg expansion and fitness. This metabolomics-guided approach to promote Treg expansion will be validated through the manufacture of human leukocyte antigen (HLA) A2-specific Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR) Tregs that prevent immune cell activation against transplanted A2+ hiPSC-derived pancreatic islets. This approach redirects the activity of Tregs specifically towards donor islets to obviate the need for post-transplant immunosuppression, potentially leading to a cure for patients with diabetes.
kw: Islet transplantation; induced pluripotent stem cell; Regulatory T cell; Chimeric Antigen Receptor; Immune Tolerance; Diabetes

title: Improving Advance Care Planning processes and outcomes for patients with advanced cancer
abs: Advance care planning (ACP) is essential for patients with advanced cancer, but its implementation faces two significant challenges. First, ACP’s success is often measured by goal-concordant care, which is not a feasible outcome given the evolving nature of patients' goals. Second, ACP is frequently implemented as a one-time process, rather than an ongoing exploration of patients' values and goals. Our proposal aims to address these issues through two complementary objectives. The first objective is to establish a global consensus through an International Delphi Study on the outcomes that are both relevant and feasible for evaluating the success of ACP interventions in cancer care. The second objective is to adapt and evaluate My Voice – Cancer, a web-based ACP tool for patients and their informal care partners, through a Hybrid Type 1 two-arm randomized controlled trial with 120 participants per arm. My Voice – Cancer will be based on prior tools developed for patients with Heart and Renal failure, incorporating education, artificial intelligence-driven value clarification, coaching on goal-sharing, and regular reminders for patients and informal care partners to revisit their values and goals. By pursuing these dual objectives concurrently, we ensure that the outcomes identified through the Delphi will directly inform the evaluation of My Voice – Cancer. The proposal builds on the PI’s previous work in rethinking ACP outcomes and developing disease-specific, web-based ACP tools. Ultimately, it seeks to promote a patient-centred approach to ACP, enhancing communication, decision-making, and care experiences for both patients and their informal care partners.
kw: advance care planning, digital health; advanced cancer; Delphi; artificial intelligence

title: Progression of Right Ventricular MOrphology, Physiology, Anatomy and Exercise Capacity – LonGitudinal Assessment with Trial Expansion (PROPAGATE)
abs: Assessing right ventricular (RV) function is crucial for treatment guidance and outcome prediction, yet challenging due to factors like complex anatomy and hemodynamic interplay. Leveraging insights from the INITIATE study (2017-2022), including 200 controls and 200 patients with pulmonary artery hypertension (PAH) or repaired tetralogy of Fallot (rTOF) with significant pulmonary regurgitation (PR), using cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) and cardiopulmonary exercise tests (CPET), we aim to define RV progression trajectories and correlate them with outcomes. Specific Aim #1: define trajectories in serial progression of RV structure, function and hemodynamics as well as CPET-assessed exercise capacity in RV pressure or volume overload states exemplified by PAH and rTOF, respectively, in association with the primary composite clinical outcome of time to first occurrence of all-cause death, hospitalization for right ventricular failure or ventricular tachyarrhythmia, or pulmonary valve intervention. Hypothesis 1: While some have relatively stable RV structure, function, and hemodynamics over time, others may show more rapid deterioration in rates of RV progression based on RV imaging phenotypes (adverse RV remodeling, dysfunction, and failure). Specific Aim #2: quantify intra-blood RV kinetic energy and RV-PA coupling using artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled analysis of 4D flow CMR measurements; and investigate their utility for predicting progression of RV remodeling, exercise function and clinical outcomes. Hypothesis 2: RV 4D flow hemodynamic parameters can classify the patients into RV adapted, RV adapted–remodeled, and RV adverse–remodeled. Specific Aim #3: characterize metabolomic profiling in RV pressure- and volume-overloaded patients, in relation to RV morphological, functional, and hemodynamic alterations, specifically, RV failure and RV-PA coupling dysfunction. Hypothesis 3: Antecedent markers are associated with subsequent (i) development and progression of RV remodeling and dysfunction and (ii) cardiopulmonary functional capacity. This comprehensive approach aims to identify determinants of RV remodeling and functional capacity, aiding in prognostication, surveillance, and therapeutic development.
kw: Right ventricle, structure-function relationship, congenital heart disease, ventricular mechanics and stiffness, hemodynamics, computational fluid dynamics

title: Elucidating Comprehensive Molecular Mechanisms in Cardiomyocyte Dedifferentiation for Novel Therapeutic Approaches to Heart Failure
abs: Heart failure (HF) remains a leading cause of mortality globally, with limited therapeutic options due to the adult mammalian heart's poor regenerative capacity. Cardiomyocyte dedifferentiation (CMDD) represents a potential regenerative strategy by enabling mature cardiomyocytes (CMs) to revert to a more primitive phenotype, which may promote cardiac repair. Our proposed study focuses on asparagine synthetase (Asns), a novel marker and functional player in CMDD, previously identified as upregulated during CM regeneration pathways. This project aims to delineate the roles and mechanisms of Asns in HF using two specific aims: (1) to evaluate the therapeutic effects of transient Asns overexpression in mouse models of acute and chronic HF via an inducible adeno-associated virus (AAV) delivery system, and (2) to explore the molecular drivers of CMDD, focusing on the Hippo-Yap and mTORC1/Asns pathways. Our hypothesis, supported by preliminary data, suggests that Asns not only participates in the enzymatic processes essential for CMDD but may also engage in non-enzymatic functions crucial for cardiac repair. This study will employ advanced genetic tools, including CRISPR screening and transcriptomic analyses, to identify and validate new molecular targets within the CMDD pathway. By elucidating the comprehensive molecular mechanisms mediated by Asns, our research could uncover novel therapeutic strategies for HF, thereby addressing a significant unmet medical need and potentially reducing the global HF burden.
kw: heart failure; cardiomyocyte; regeneration; therapy; cell cycle

title: Enhancing Macrophage Phagocytosis through Dual Inhibition of CD73 and SIRPα Combined with Oxaliplatin for Treating Advanced Microsatellite Stable Colorectal Cancer
abs: Microsatellite stable (MSS) colorectal cancer (CRC), the most prevalent subtype of CRC, is characterised by poor CD8+ T cell infiltration and resistance to T cell immune checkpoint blockade therapy. In recent years, macrophages have emerged as a promising target for cancer treatment. As key player in innate immunity, macrophages play a vital role in tumor surveillance and bridging innate and adaptive immunity. Tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) are the most abundant infiltrating immune cells in MSS CRC. Leveraging macrophage phagocytosis for MSS CRC treatment holds significant potential. However, TAMs in MSS CRC predominantly exhibit an immunosuppressive M2-like phenotype with reduced phagocytic activity and impaired antigen presentation. Overexpression of phagocytosis checkpoints further suppress macrophage phagocytosis. Restoring macrophage functionality and blocking phagocytic checkpoints could enhance macrophage-medicated tumor clearance. The adenosine-CD73-A2AR axis is a key driver of TAM polarization toward the M2-like phenotype, while the CD47-SIRPα axis functions as the primary phagocytosis checkpoint in MSS CRC, protecting tumor cells from unwanted killing. Dual inhibition of these pathways have the potential to significantly enhance macrophage phagocytic activity. Moreover, surface-exposed calreticulin (CALR), a hallmark of immunogenic cell death (ICD), could further enhance macrophage phagocytosis. In this study, we hypothesize that co-inhibition of CD73 and SIRPa, in combination with oxaliplatin, a well-established chemotherapeutic ICD inducer, will synergistically enhance macrophage phagocytosis, activate adaptive immunity, and improve treatment responses in advanced MSS CRC. To test this hypothesis, we will evaluate macrophage reprogramming and phagocytic capacity using an in vitro co-coculture model comprising monocyte-derived macrophages and MSS CRC cells engineered to overexpress and knock out CD73. The therapeutic efficacy of this combination therapy will also be assessed using patient-derived organoids.
kw: Microsatellite stable colorectal cancer; macrophages; CD47-SIRPa; CD73;  immunogenic cell death

title: Genotypic-phenotypic characterisation of KCNA2 drug-resistant epilepsy and novel treatment strategies
abs: Epilepsy accounts for approximately 1% of the global burden of disease. It affects more than 65 million people worldwide, occurs at all ages in all regions of the world and has a high impact on disability-adjusted life years and psychosocial quality of life. Medical management of this immensely burdensome disorder remains remarkably inadequate. We rely only on symptomatic anti-seizure medications that are empirically prescribed, on a trial-and-error basis. 1 in 3 individuals do not respond to the current treatments we have available and continue having refractory seizures along with worsening co-morbidities. There is an urgent unmet need to deepen our understanding of disease mechanisms underlying epilepsy and develop treatment strategies that target root causes. Approximately half of all paediatric epilepsy has been attributed to a monogenic cause. Distilling the functional effects of causative gene variants advances our understanding of epilepsy disease mechanisms and facilitates development of targeted therapy. This research aims to advance our understanding of epilepsy related to KCNA2 gene mutations. We have identified two, previously unreported, de novo KCNA2 mutations [c.1220C >G, (p.Pro407Arg) and c.1208C >T (p.Ala403Val)], in two patients with refractory epilepsy and severe psychomotor co-morbidities. In this study, we will: (i) refine KCNA2 genotype-phenotype correlation by in-depth clinical review of affected patients, and by exploring the behavioural phenotype of the Drosophila fly model; (ii) evaluate the functional effects of these mutations on protein function via electrophysiological studies performed on patient derived induced pluripotent stem cells differentiated to cortical neurons; and (iii) explore the efficacy of a novel anti-sense oligonucleotide therapy designed to target each of these specific mutations. Beyond KCNA2, the knowledge and experience gained from this project, along with the collaborations, it establishes, can be extended to future projects to investigate other genes, their contributions to mechanisms underlying epilepsy and the further design/evaluation of novel treatment strategies.
kw: KCNA2; paediatric; epilepsy; genetics; precision therapy

title: The Cardiovascular-Cognitive Health Initiative
abs: Background: Recent evidence suggests complex bidirectional interplay between cognitive health and cardiovascular disease (CVD) that has synergistic effects on the adverse progression of each other. Furthermore, impairments in one domain ( e.g.., cognitive impairment) will affect treatment strategies targeting other domains (e.g., CVD management). Therefore, early screening and intervention of at-risk individuals (CVD patients with mild cognitive impairment) whilst incorporating cognitive health management into clinical CVD care pathways may address (via early prevention) the tsunami of dementia in CVD patients. This will be a four-year multi-site initiative between hospitals and community that addresses the current absence of cognitive care among cardiovascular patients. Methods: Using a multi-site study design, the main study will involve i) screening for cognitive impairment in (n=3500) CVD patients, scaled by technology, providing prevalence estimates for case-finding and development of diagnosis protocols; ii) incorporating cognitive assessment protocols into targeted CV disease phenotypes where cognitive impairment challenges current clinical care paradigms, with proper implementation frameworks; iii) provide a range of tools and community programs to patients, where patients receive appropriate cognitive care bidirectionally from hospital and community, whilst assessing patient and caregiver uptake and feedback. In a randomized clinical trial sub-study, CVD patients (n=440) will be randomized to receive multi-component intervention versus usual care. Over 24 weeks, the intervention will comprise of cardiac rehabilitation instruction, including a digital cardiac rehabilitation education package, cognitive stimulation therapy, mental health programs, and sleep coaching, delivered via a hybrid hospital and home-based telehealth platform. We will compare the proportion of patients in the Intervention group versus the Usual care group who demonstrate an improvement in cognitive tests scores at 24 weeks. Significance: This proposal will embed cognitive screening, detection, and implementation of strategies into routine CVD management. Our focus is to develop real-world clinical platforms to manage cognitive health of cardiac patients.
kw: cognition; cardiovascular disease; prevention; technology; digital health; ageing

title: Transition from HBsAg abundance to functional cure and virological cure
abs: Chronic Hepatitis B (CHB) affects 257 million persons and is responsible for 780,000 deaths annually which can largely be prevented by functional cure (loss of HBsAg and negative HBV DNA 6months off therapy). The difficulty in achieving this with current therapies are due to a number of factors. One of the key issues is the excessive levels of HBsAg produced by the virus as subviral non-infectious particles which may lead to immune exhaustion and inability to remove the virus. The peculiar excess of HBsAg may occur epigenetically but our preliminary studies have shown that Hepatitis B transcript stoichiometry may play an important role as well as degradation pathways. Investigation of mechanisms behind this may yield insights that may be used therapeutically. This will be complemented by new technology using spatial transcriptomics that can provide spatial relationships between infected versus non-infected hepatocytes as well as immune cells in proximity that are related to HBsAg loss. However, in order to achieve HBsAg loss, not only must cccDNA be silenced or eliminated but integrated HBV needs to be removed as this is the most common transcript in HBeAg negative CHB. Our preliminary data shows that there is considerably heterogeneity of viral integration in CHB but a dramatic reduction of integrants after HBsAg loss. Mechanisms by which integrated HBV are secreted will also be investigated using cell lines. Finally , functional cure may not be as durable as we found 47.5% of our patients with HBsAg loss have detectable HBV DNA while HBsAg negative, fulfilling criteria for occult HBV. More sensitive HBsAg assays may determine a lower threshold for virological cure defined as absence of cccDNA in liver. Overall the study proposes to study the pathway from abudance of HBsAg to functional cure and virological cure.
kw: functional cure; cccDNA; quantitative HBsAg; spatial transcriptomics; HBV RNA; occult HBV infection

title: Mapping high-resolution lifespan normative charts of brain structure to uncover diagnostic and prognostic imaging biomarkers of Alzheimer’s disease dementia
abs: Growth charts for tracking age-related changes have long been a cornerstone of pediatric care, focusing on early-life trajectories of simple phenotypes such as weight and height. Recent efforts extended this concept to brain phenotypes like gray matter thickness and volume, though at low spatial resolution. Building on these advances, we developed novel methods to create high-resolution normative brain charts spanning the human lifespan. This increased spatial precision holds significant promise for advancing diagnostic and prognostic tools in precision medicine. This proposal aims to estimate population-informed lifespan trajectories for brain imaging phenotypes and to develop predictors of Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) dementia progression. Healthy brains follow normative trajectories governed by biological processes shaping cortical thickness, area, volume, and microstructure. These trajectories provide critical insights into typical brain development and aging, while deviations are linked to neurological and psychiatric disorders. AD, in particular, is characterized by neurodegenerative mechanisms—including Aβ plaque accumulation, tau protein tangles, and glial responses—that result in widespread neuronal loss. These pathological changes manifest as deviations from normative trajectories, gradually evolving as individuals progress from healthy to mild cognitive impairment and ultimately to AD dementia. Our recently developed framework enables the detection of fine-grained deviations in brain phenotypes, allowing earlier identification of subtle abnormalities compared to traditional low-resolution methods. This approach offers a crucial window for early diagnosis and intervention, providing personalized imaging biomarkers of AD-associated atrophy. Leveraging this framework, we aim to track individual-level neurodegeneration, enabling early detection and targeted interventions to slow disease progression, delay severe cognitive impairments, and improve long-term patient outcomes. Using a diverse imaging dataset of over 100,000 participants across the human lifespan, this proposal will (1) map high-resolution normative brain charts, (2) cross-sectionally investigate deviations in AD dementia, and (3) longitudinally explore prognostic insights to advance precision medicine in neurodegenerative diseases.
kw: Imaging Biomarkers; Imaging Neuroscience; Brain Charts; Normative Models; Alzheimer's Disease Dementia; Perecision Medicine

title: The chicken or egg in Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD): mucus dysfunction or microbial dysbiosis?
abs: Each day, we breath 22,000 times inhaling 11,000 litres of air, an actuality taken for granted without lung disease. Four percent of the world lives with Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD), a persistent, progressive airways disease with no curative treatment. Despite smoking cessation, COPD advances and currently no pharmacological intervention slows progression. Current therapy is limited to symptomatic control and exacerbation prevention and although smoking is a risk, only 15-20% of smokers develop COPD with one-third non-smokers. While significant data exists in established disease, no work assesses early COPD. By the time COPD is symptomatic, significant lung function is lost and therapy limited. A ‘chicken or egg’ phenomenon exists in COPD: which comes first, infection or inflammation? Mucus dysfunction is an inflammation surrogate and can be infection independent. Whether infection leads to or is a consequence of COPD is unknown, and whether airway inflammation and mucus dysfunction drive COPD, independent of infection is unclear. To inform COPD prevention, distinguishing ‘chicken’ from ‘egg’ is essential. Here, we address this using novel, prospective and integrative approaches. Current evidence suggests that mucus composition and microbiomes play independent but significant roles in COPD pathogenesis, progression and clinical outcomes. Our central hypothesis is that differences in mucus dysfunction and microbial dysbiosis occur in early COPD, preceding symptoms and loss of lung function, offering opportunities to identify biomarkers and therapeutic targets. Through mucus biology, metagenomics and integrative analytics and based on strong preliminary findings, we build on our published work linking mucus-microbiome signatures to lung function decline in established COPD. We will assess biochemical and biophysical mucus properties (Aim 1), microbiomes (Aim 2) and perform integrative analyses (Aim 3) in early COPD, leveraging two international cohorts. Addressing early disease offers insight into origins of COPD and facilitates disease prevention, a key feature of Healthier SG.
kw: Respiratory; COPD; mucus; microbiome; metagenomics

title: The Role of Stress Granule-Lysosome Interactions in Microglial Function
abs: Recent advances indicate that RNA metabolism plays a critical role in the pathophysiology of neurodegenerative diseases. RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) regulate mRNA utilization under stress, partly through the formation of membraneless organelles, namely stress granules (SGs). A growing body of evidence suggests that the initial formation of SGs may serve as a protective response to cellular stress. However, prolonged or aberrant SG formation, driven by mutant proteins, can contribute to neurodegenerative pathology. While much of this research has focused on neuronal cells, the role of SGs in microglia, which are the largest population of brain macrophages, remains unknown. We have recently identified a role for SGs in macrophages, where they form after lysosomal damage to stabilize membranes and restore lysosomal function—a mechanism that may also be relevant in neurodegeneration, where lysosomal damage is linked to amyloid-β (Aβ) and other amyloid aggregations and spreading. Notably, recent studies suggest that amyloid aggregation can occur in microglial lysosomes in a process influenced by microglial lipid metabolism. Together, these findings suggest a promising link between amyloid aggregation, lysosomal damage, and SG function in microglia. We hypothesize that lysosomal damage in microglia triggers an SG-dependent response that modulates lysosomal function and dictates microglial activity. This hypothesis posits that the SG-lysosome axis is a critical regulatory node in microglial homeostasis, and its dysregulation is a key contributor to neurodegenerative processes. We will leverage human iPSC-derived microglia models and cutting-edge techniques, including super-resolution live-cell imaging, sequencing, and proteomics, to 1. Identify specific SG composition and SG-lysosome dynamics in microglia; 2. Investigate the impact of SGs on microglial functions, such as phagocytosis, cytokine production, and lysosomal activity; and 3. Identify molecular mechanisms linking SGs to neurodegeneration. Building on this, my project breaks new ground by investigating SGs in microglia, potentially unlocking new therapeutic targets for these debilitating diseases.
kw: microglia; lysosome; condensates; neurodegeneration

title: A Dimensional Approach to Mental Health Disorders in Children
inst: IHDP - Institute for Human Development and Potential
abs: Traditional clinical diagnosis of mental health disorders is confounded by heterogeneity of the patient population. Specifically, different patients are diagnosed with the same mental health disorder and assigned the same treatments despite having few, or even no, overlapping symptoms. We propose to adopt a dimensional approach to mental health disorders in children, translating and adapting the NIH RDoC framework developed for adult psychiatric patients. Specifically, we propose to derive latent transdiagnostic dimensions based on deviations from typical neural and behavioral functioning. We hypothesize that these dimensions will underlie and span different mental health disorders in children and have unique distinct associations with exposure factors and brain circuitry. We will use a combination of parent-reported, self-reported questionnaires and behavioral tasks to generate dimensions of mental health. We will then test for the association between early life exposures, neural circuitry profiles and these dimensions of mental health. Lastly, we will use Structural Equation Modelling to establish the pathways between early life exposures and our dimensions of mental health. We postulate that our dimensions of mental health will uncover novel correlations and pathways and improve our understanding of the neurobiology underlying mental health disorders. Our key focus will be on the identification of modifiable exposure, moderating and mediating factors that are directly associated with the dimensions of mental health. These modifiable factors can act as future targets for policy-based interventions and markers for early detection of mental health disorders. Potential factors include screen time exposure, maternal mental health, nutrition and parent-child interaction time. Our research will provide concrete evidence to support governmental guidelines and advisories on this topic. Furthermore, our dimensional approach allows researchers to focus on the crux of the issue - addressing the aetiology of mental health disorders to improve and complement current symptom-based treatments.
kw: Children Mental Health; Neuroimaging; Childhood Depression; Children Anxiety

title: Ambient Intelligent Monitoring Systems for Health in Hospitals and Homes (AmI H3): User Perceptions and Their Amenability
abs: Ambient intelligence refers to a group of sensors embedded in physical spaces. In hospitals, they help to relieve the workload of healthcare professionals. At home, they support care for people with disability and enable aging-in-place for older adults, reducing incidences that lead up to (re)hospitalizations. This study aims to maximize the impact of ambient intelligence for health by bridging the gap between development and implementation, ultimately improving patient outcomes and quality of life. First, we seek to uncover end-user perceptions and to identify the determinants associated with these perceptions. We posit that people with weaker health will be more accepting of ambient intelligence technologies, contingent on their social capital and intention to age in place. In addition, healthcare professionals and caregivers would generally welcome the technology, apart from when they feel that their role may be undermined. Second, we aim to test different frames of messaging for driving acceptability and for promoting adoption. We posit that messaging frames will drive acceptability, with the risk frame being more effective than the benefit frame, contingent on people’s social capital and intention to age in place. We plan to recruit 2000 participants, including 500 medical officers, nurses, and allied health professionals ≥21 years old; 1000 older adults ≥60 years old and adults 21–59 years old with physical disability; and 500 formal and informal caregivers. We will apply quota sampling within each group to get a nationally representative sample. Participants will answer a baseline questionnaire before being randomly assigned to a framing condition, where they will watch a video presenting ambient intelligence with a benefit or loss frame, or a control condition. Thereafter, they will complete a post-intervention questionnaire. Multivariate analyses will be applied to identify the drivers of perceptions, and between-group analyses to test the effectiveness of different messaging frames.
kw: smart environments; health technology; aging-in-place; health monitoring; user perception; framing

title: Understanding the interplay between mitochondriopathy and synucleinopathy using human midbrain organoids
abs: Parkinson’s disease (PD) is an ageing-associated neurodegenerative disease afflicting millions of people worldwide, including our Singapore society. PD causes severe motoric disorders due to progressive demise of dopaminergic (DA) neurons in the substantia nigra in the midbrain. PD is incurable and present treatment options only relieve some of disease symptoms. This is largely due to our incomplete understanding of PD pathogenesis, owing to lack of experimental models that can recapitulate the complex cytoarchitecture of the human brain. In this study, we aim to explore how mitochondria and the synaptic protein α-Synuclein interact, both of which show consistent abnormalities in PD brain tissues. We hypothesize that mitochondrial dysfunctions and abnormal α-Synuclein dynamics synergistically promote neurodegeneration in PD. We will employ the human stem cell-derived midbrain-like organoid (hMLO) with PD-associated mutations in mitochondrial protein CHCHD2 and synucleinopathy induced by α-Synuclein pre-formed fibrils (PFF). A combination of fluorescence microscopy, biochemical study, and flow cytometry analyses will be performed to determine the impacts of these PD models on mitochondria functions and DA neurons viability. Furthermore, we will develop a microfluidic-based platform to determine the impact of CHCHD2-associated mitochondriopathy on α-Synuclein seeding and propagation between different hMLOs, which simulates clinical α-Synuclein prion-like transmission seen in PD brain tissues. We anticipate that this study will provide valuable insights into PD pathogenesis as well as identifying novel molecular players, which can be therapeutically targeted at the early stage of disease progression prior to neurodegeneration. In the long run, this knowledge could be utilized to develop an effective disease-modifying treatment against PD and other synucleinopathies, such as Lewy Body dementia and multiple system atrophy.
kw: Parkinson's disease; synuclein; mitochondria; brain organoid; neurodegeneration; CHCHD2

title: Dissolving microneedle-mediated delivery of AIEgens-conjugated phages for combating wound infections caused by antimicrobial resistance bacteria
abs: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) poses a significant global health threat, particularly in wound infections caused by resistant pathogens such as Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. These infections challenge existing therapies and increase healthcare burdens. This proposal aims to develop an innovative therapeutic platform integrating bacteriophage therapy, aggregation-induced emission luminogens (AIEgens), and dissolving microneedles (MNs) to effectively combat AMR wound infections. The project includes three specific aims: (1) Isolate and characterize phages targeting wound pathogens, emphasizing their host range, stability, and inhibitory efficacy. Phage cocktails will be developed to enhance therapeutic outcomes and reduce resistance development. (2) Conjugate phages with AIEgens to facilitate photodynamic therapy and enable real-time visualization of phage-pathogen interactions. This dual-functional approach is designed to improve bacterial clearance and inhibit resistance evolution. (3) Incorporate engineered phages into dissolving MNs for precise and localized delivery to wound sites. Optimized MNs will ensure high phage viability, controlled release, and effective penetration of biofilms. This multidisciplinary research combines phage biology, chemical synthesis, and biomedical engineering. Phages will be isolated from diverse environmental sources and screened for optimal therapeutic properties. AIEgens, such as TPEPy and TTPy, will be synthesized and conjugated with selected phages to create multifunctional antimicrobial agents. These conjugates will be loaded into dissolving MNs fabricated from biocompatible polymers. In vitro assays will test antimicrobial efficacy, while in vivo wound infection models will evaluate therapeutic performance. Leveraging access to advanced facilities and the team’s expertise, this innovative approach addresses the AMR crisis by offering a targeted, sustainable solution for chronic wound infections. The proposed strategy has significant potential to improve patient outcomes, reduce resistance risks, and alleviate the healthcare burden associated with AMR.
kw: Bacteriophage therapy; Antimicrobial resistance; Dissolving microneedles; Aggregation-induced emission luminogens; Wound infection treatment; Biofilm penetration

title: Novel bacteriophages treatment for Multi-drug or Carbapenem-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa eye infections
abs: In recent years, the emergence of pan-drug and multi-drug resistant bacterial pathogens that are resistant to last resorted antibiotics poses a substantial threat to the global healthcare systems. The World Health Organization (WHO) has listed antimicrobial resistance as one of the ten biggest threats to humanity. Bacteriophages are viruses that are considered as a natural antibiotic, that can infect and replicate in bacteria with no or very few reported side effects to humans. Bacteriophage resurgence has been hailed as one of the possible and effective treatment options to overcome AMR infections in this post-antibiotic era. The presence of an asymmetric bilayer outer membrane (OM) in Gram-negative bacteria, Pseudomonas aeruginosa (PA) confers greater protection from toxic agents than Gram-positive bacteria. We hypothesize that the presence of ionic liquids may dissipate the outer membrane permeability of the bacteria and the topical formulation of bacteriophages in the ionic liquid salt buffer is safe and effective for treating multi-drug resistant (MDR) PA keratitis. As shown in the preliminary results, bacteriophage is synergistic with aquatic normal salt buffer to enhance bacteriophage’s antibacterial effect, and we hypothesize that combination of bacteriophages and ionic liquid salt buffer may improve adsorption, permeabilization, bioavailability, and antibacterial effects by encapping the hydrophobic lipid bilayer of PA. Specific aim-1 is to screen a library of cationic ionic liquids that will interfere with bacterial outer membrane permeability. Specific aim-2 is to characterize bacteriophages and its efficacy in selected ionic liquid salt buffers (Bacteriophages isolation, characterization, infectivity, sequencing, optimization in ionic liquid salt buffer, investigation of the best combinations of bacteriophages and ionic liquid salt buffer, and evaluation of its mechanism of synergistic action. Specific aim-3 is to assess the safety and efficacy in in vitro and in vivo animal models.
kw: Bacteriophages; Ophthalmology; novel antimicrobial treatment; Pseudomonas aeruginosa

title: Investigating heart-brain-cognition relationships and the effects of lifestyle modifications in hypertensive heart disease
abs: Hypertensive heart disease (HHD) is related to increased risk of cardiovascular mortality, however how HHD relates to cognitive decline and brain changes remain poorly elucidated. Further, how lifestyle modifications improve brain and cognitive outcomes in individuals with HHD remain unknown. Leveraging a larger randomized controlled trial (RESET RCT) assessing the effectiveness of a 12-month digital lifestyle intervention programme on cardiac outcomes in 200 HHD individuals with left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH), this proposed study aims to examine how features of HHD relate to disruptions in brain structure/function and cognition cross-sectionally in these individuals, as well as how a lifestyle modification programme aimed at reversing HHD-related cardiac damage influences brain structure/function and cognition. Further, we aim to investigate individual differences in responsiveness to the lifestyle intervention based on the baseline characteristics of participants. To achieve this, we propose to perform and analyze brain MRI scans and cognitive assessments pre- and post-intervention. This study will specifically test the following hypotheses: 1) HHD features, including LVH and myocardial fibrosis, would be associated with disruptions in brain structure/function and cognitive performance cross-sectionally, with brain measures mediating the associations between HHD features and cognitive performance; 2) compared to participants in the control arm, participants in the intervention arm would show less disruptions in brain structure/function and improved cognitive performance following intervention; and 3) participants would show individual differences in responsiveness to the lifestyle intervention, whereby participants with greater brain and cardiac structural/functional disruptions as well as more cardiovascular risk factors at baseline would show greater responsiveness to lifestyle interventions. This research is expected to advance scientific understanding on the heart-brain-cognition connection and guide the development of future policies and interventions that improve both brain and cardiovascular health, particularly in the context of HHD.
kw: Neuroimaging; Cardiac imaging; lifestyle intervention; cognition

title: From placenta to skin: Exploring in-utero influences on the risk of atopic dermatitis.
inst: IHDP - Institute for Human Development and Potential
abs: Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a common chronic inflammatory skin condition affecting approximately 10% of Singaporean children. AD can significantly diminish one’s quality of life and impose a considerable strain on the healthcare system. It often manifests early in life and is caused by an imbalance in the immune system, due to a predominant Th2 immune response. The placenta, a vital interface between the mother and fetus, shapes the offspring's immune system and is influenced by maternal factors such as diet and environmental exposures. As an essential amino acid, tryptophan is important in immune regulation and may affect AD risk, although its specific role in early development remains unclear. We hypothesize that maternal environmental exposures may disrupt tryptophan-associated immune regulation in the fetoplacental unit, altering in utero programming and increasing AD risk. We aim to identify placental tryptophan metabolites and immune markers associated with AD risk and explore the interplay between maternal diet, exposure to ‘forever chemicals’ and placental tryptophan signatures in the development of AD. We will analyze placental biopsies collected at delivery from two Singaporean mother-child cohorts Growing Up in Singapore Towards healthy Outcome (GUSTO) and Singapore PREconception Study of Long-Term Maternal and Child Outcomes (S-PRESTO). We will also screen inflammatory signatures using Olink® multiplex protein arrays in 176 samples (AD and controls) and validate candidate proteins via ELISA kits across the cohorts. Placental expression of AD-related genes will be assessed using qPCR, with protein-level validation through immunoblotting. Associations between placental signatures and AD status up to 18 months will be evaluated using Bayesian Multiple Index Models. This study could uncover novel biomarkers and insights into the early origins of AD, enabling potential clinical interventions to prevent and/or modify its progression. Future potential collaborations with biotech companies may facilitate the development of precision biomarker panels for prenatal care.
kw: atopic dermatitis; placenta; PFAS; maternal nutrition; tryptophan; childhood

title: Rational design of specific allosteric modulators targeting serotonin GPCR 5-HT2A for HCC immunotherapy
abs: Orthosteric drugs targeting the conserved ligand-binding site of G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) typically cause off-target toxicity due to a lack of selectivity for targeted receptors. Allosteric drugs bind outside of conserved orthosteric sites, allowing to achieve desired and specific functional effects by modulating the protein structural dynamics. The goal here is to develop a combined high-throughput in silico and in vitro framework for rational design of high-confidence drug leads targeting GPCRs. We hypothesize that highly selective modulator drugs designed by our framework could circumvent the issue of off-target toxicity. Here, the primary target is the serotonin receptor 5-HT2A, inhibition of which was recently found to reinvigorate cytotoxic phenotype of T cells for immunotherapy in immunosuppressive microenvironment in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Specific aims: (i) development of a new sequence-dependent model of allostery for prediction of allosteric sites; (ii) development of a generative model for de novo design of allosteric modulator drug; (iii) rational design of modulator drugs targeting 5-HT2A to inhibit its functional activity and (iv) experimental validation of predicted leads by evaluating specific effects on functional phenotype of activated CD8 T cells and molecular signaling. For Aim 1, all-atom molecular simulation will be used in the new model for exact description of allosteric communication on per-residue resolution. We will develop a generative model for design of modulators using a variational autoencoder architecture for Aim 2. Using our established directed design protocol, the predicted allosteric site and modulators will be further optimized in Aim 3 for target selectivity, allosteric modulation and affinity. For Aim 4, high-throughput multiparameter flow cytometry will be performed on co-culture assays of CD8 T cells. The proposed research would lead to selective allosteric drug leads targeting 5-HT2A to complement immunotherapy for HCC. The framework could also be extended to target other GPCRs with unmet clinical needs.
kw: Drug design; Allostery; GPCR; Liver cancer; Immunotherapy; T cells

title: Mechanistic dissection of adrenergic brain-gonad interactions that shape intra- and intergenerational behaviors and health.
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Parentally-experienced stresses can profoundly affect progeny physiology and health, however, the molecular and cellular processes that underlie the transmission of parental experiences to their offspring are generally unknown. Hence, my overall goal is to mechanistically understand and control adrenergic brain-gonad interactions that shape offspring physiology and health. I hypothesize that sympathetic neural innervation, in particular adrenergic inputs, to the gonads play a physiological role in ensuring both parental reproductive and progeny health. I expect that modulating these adrenergic connections in a molecularly-informed manner will eventually enable us to guide and improve parental reproductive physiology and offspring health outcomes. I will carry out our studies of brain-gonad interactions in the vertebrate zebrafish, Danio rerio, which combines access to vertebrate physiology (circulatory system, adaptive immunity etc.) with the ease of high-throughput, high-resolution imaging and precise molecular dissection at a whole-animal scale. Aim 1: Characterize intergenerational behaviors in progeny (F1) generations that are elicited by (P0) parental adrenergic system activation. Aim 2: Generate functionally annotated anatomical maps of adrenergic inputs onto gonadal tissues that control intergenerational behaviors Aim 3: Define novel molecular pathways that interface with adrenergic brain-gonad connections using integrated unbiased multi-omic approaches.
kw: Brain-body interaction; Reproductive health; Intergenerational health; Adrenergic

title: PREcision MApping and NEuromodulation after thalamic hemorrhage: The PREMANE Trial
abs: Spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) is increasingly affecting younger adults in the working population, leading to significant motor and cognitive impairments. Recent advancements suggest that precision functional mapping combined with precision neuromodulation may improve recovery outcomes after ICH. This study aims to explore the role of precision brain mapping and neuromodulation in improving long-term motor and cognitive function after thalamic hematomas. Our central hypothesis is that thalamic ICH induces acute neurological injury, leading to long-term functional dysconnectivity in cortical networks. We propose that this dysconnectivity varies across individuals and contributes to diverse motor and cognitive outcomes. Furthermore, precision neuromodulation using navigated transcranial magnetic stimulation (nTMS) can modulate these networks, potentially improving functional outcomes after ICH. The study consists of two primary aims. Aim 1 is to estimate individual-specific cortical networks of functional connectivity following thalamic ICH. Six patients with thalamic ICH will undergo more than 10 functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) scans over six-months. Using an established pipeline, we will identify differences in spatial topography of functional networks, correlating these with motor and cognitive outcomes at three months post-ICH. Aim 2 is to conduct a pilot trial of precision neuromodulation using nTMS for neurorehabilitation. This double-blind randomized cross-over trial will include two arms: motor first nTMS and cognition first nTMS. Each patient will receive targeted stimulation over the individual-specific ipsilesional motor cortex or dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, with motor and cognitive outcomes assessed at six months and one year. This study aims to demonstrate that precision functional mapping and neuromodulation can improve recovery after thalamic ICH, offering a novel therapeutic approach to mitigate long-term impairments in stroke.
kw: spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage; precision functional mapping; precision neuromodulation; functional magnetic resonance imaging; transcranial magnetic stimulation; stroke rehabilitation

title: Blood biomarkers associated with cognitive impairment among adult patients with epilepsy
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Background Epilepsy is a common neurological disorder affecting more than 65 million people worldwide. Almost 50% of adults patients with epilepsy (PWE) have cognitive impairment at diagnosis. It is postulated that neurodegeneration and neuroinflammation are causes of cognitive impairment among adults with epilepsy. Hypothesis Blood biomarkers such as serum neurofilament light chain (NFL) and inter-leukin 6 (IL-6) are associated with cognitive impairment among adult PWE Aims This study aims to evaluate the association of NFL and IL-6 with cognitive impairment among adult PWE Methods 50 non-demented adults with epilepsy aged > 21 years old will be recruited across two tertiary hospitals in Singapore. Participants will undergo baseline cognitive assessments and questionnaires to characterize their cognitive profiles, epilepsy control and lifestyle habits. Blood will be collected to evaluate the serum NFL and IL-6 levels. The association of blood biomarkers with cognitive scores will be evaluated via regression models. Significance This study will help to evaluate the blood biomarkers associated with cognitive impairment among adult patients with epilepsy. This will enable clarification of the pathophysiology of cognitive impairment among these patients.
kw: Epilepsy, cognitive impairment

title: Understanding mechanisms and developing new therapies for MASH effects on the heart
abs: Metabolic dysfunction-associated liver disease (MASLD) is a spectrum of progressive liver conditions comprising hepatic steatosis, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), and cirrhosis that affects 30% of adults worldwide. It is linked to metabolic diseases such as obesity and diabetes, and associated with extrahepatic manifestations, particularly cardiovascular disease (CVD), the major cause of mortality in MASH patients. Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is the most common form of CVD in MASH. Currently, little is known about the contribution and mechanisms of MASH effects on HFpEF. Accordingly, we hypothesize: MASH has distinct effects on HFpEF apart from concurrent obesity/diabetes. MASH mediates these effects by direct signaling to the heart and/or via effects on the immune system. Thus, we propose: Specific Aim 1. Understand the role(s) of MASH vs. obesity/diabetes on cardiometabolic heart disease. We will compare liver-specific Tgfbr2 knockout (L-Tgfbr KO) mice that are resistant to MASH with control mice that develop MASH when fed a specific diet. We will examine the effects of homocysteine, hepatokines, age, and endocrine status on HFpEF in mice with MASH vs. mice with primarily obesity/diabetes yet protected against MASH. Specific Aim 2. Investigate monocyte/macrophage recruitment in the liver and heart during MASH. We will examine the effects of MASH on monocyte/macrophage recruitment and subpopulations in the liver and heart using single-cell sequencing and state-of-the-art bioinformatics. Specific Aim 3. Evaluate the efficacies of novel therapies for MASH on the heart. We will examine the effects of vitamin B12/fol, T2, and estradiol in preventing and/or treating MASH and HFpEF. Determining the relative contributions of MASH, obesity, and diabetes on HFpEF; understanding hepatic signaling to the heart and immune system during MASH; and identifying potential treatments for HFpEF will help prolong lifespan and improve clinical outcomes in patients with MASH and HFpEF in Singapore.
kw: NAFLD; MAFLD; NASH; HFpEF; liver;  heart failure; immune; fibrosis

title: Biomedical Data Hub Phase 1
abs: The Biomedical Data Hub would combine, enhance, and scale biomedical repositories, developed across multiple A*STAR Research Institutes into an enhanced national research data node for data management operations of strategic de-identified research datasets; to complement TRUST and NCO as key enablers of research.
