title: Urban Meteorology Nowcasting: Building Climate Health Resilience for the General Public in the Immediate Living Environment
abs: Climate change presents significant challenges to cities, especially in densely urbanised tropical climates like Singapore. Heat stress resulting from increased temperatures is a critical risk factor for vulnerable groups, requiring urgent mitigation and management measures. However, addressing this challenge is complex due to large uncertainties in the microclimate of the immediate living environment, varying individual risks, and delays in taking timely actions. To address these issues and enhance climate resilience, this research proposes an innovative approach that integrates urban meteorology nowcasting with considerations of demographics and socioeconomic factors. Compared with traditional downscaling methods, the research aims to reduce climate modelling uncertainties by employing a ground-based Doppler LiDAR and IoT sensing network, multiscale numerical simulations, and machine learning. The proposed nowcasting system will be developed by combining high-resolution mapping of heat risk with demographics and socioeconomic distributions. This system will be applied to evaluate heat risks at the individual level, complementing existing nowcasting information. The nowcasting system will facilitate timely decision-making and provide customised advisories on heat-related climate hazards at the individual level, promoting the development of a climate-resilient society. The proposed research will deliver an urban boundary layer observation network, perform high-fidelity numerical simulations, train a high-performance machine learning model, map demographics and socioeconomic distributions, and develop an urban nowcasting system. The findings will assist government agencies in implementing effective mitigation and adaptation strategies while fostering public acceptance of these measures. The research outputs and model itself will be openly accessible for application in other cities and countries.
kw: 1) Climate Health Resilience; 2) Urban Meteorology Nowcasting; 3) Immediate Living Environment; 4) Doppler Lidar; 5) High-Fidelity Numerical Simulation; 6) Machine Learning

title: Towards Large Scientific Learning Models with In-Context Operator Networks
abs: We aim to develop algorithms, theories, and software to promote the development of large-scale models for scientific machine learning. Such large scientific learning models could serve as "foundation models" that can be used directly for a variety of scientific learning tasks, or be fine-tuned to enhance their proficiency in dealing with a specific set of tasks. In particular, we will conduct research under our proposed in-context operator learning paradigm. A distinguishing feature of an in-context operator network (ICON) is its ability to learn physical knowledge from "data prompts" and solve the corresponding scientific problems, during the forward pass of the model without the need for weight adjustments. This is in parallel with large language models, where a single model can learn the knowledge from textual prompts and solve a variety of natural language processing tasks.
kw: Artificial Intelligence; Scientific Machine Learning; Large Models; In-Context Learning; Operator Learning

title: Ultra-high-throughput enzymology with ensembles of single molecules
abs: An integrated platform to interrogate post-translational modification (PTM) enzymes will be established. The platform features an interdisciplinary fusion between ultra-high-throughput wet lab techniques (mRNA display and next-generation sequencing), and deep learning/AI, with the ultimate goal of dissecting the inner workings of PTM enzymes. The resulting AI models will enable accurate analysis of catalytic mechanisms and the dynamics of substrate engagement by PTM enzymes at an unprecedented scale. The methods will be expanded in two directions: i) to analyze and engineer the biosynthesis of natural products belonging to the ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptide (RiPPs) family, and ii) to better understand the effects of PTM crosstalk phenomena in human cell biology by profiling key PTM writer/eraser enzymes such as kinases, E3 ligases, lysine deacetylases, etc. With respect to RiPP engineering, the platform should facilitate both the fundamental study of RiPP enzymes, and also enable translational applications in early drug discovery and natural product engineering.
kw: Enzymes, peptides, mRNA display, deep learning

title: Unified Semiparametric Likelihood-based Hypothesis Tests with Boundary Constraints
abs: As a foundation of statistical inference, hypothesis testing is essential in assessing the validity of our discovery and making informed decisions about the population based on sample data. This project considers hypothesis testing in a semiparametric model indexed by a finite-dimensional Euclidean parameter θ and an infinite-dimensional nuisance parameter. We are interested in testing H_0: θ=θ_0 versus H_1:θ≠θ_0. Compared with parametric models, semiparametric models can greatly mitigate the risk of model misspecification. Our objective is to construct an efficient and easy-to-compute test statistic for the above hypothesis based on a random sample of size n. Unlike parametric models where exact likelihood inference is usually viable, semiparametric hypothesis testing presents unique challenges because the presence of the infinite-dimensional nuisance parameter necessitates variants of likelihood inference, such as a pseudo-likelihood that substitutes a consistent estimator for in the semiparametric likelihood, or profiling the semiparametric likelihood the composite likelihood, or a working model likelihood (an illustration is given in Examples 4 and 5 in the proposal). In addition, statistical error from the estimated infinite-dimensional nuisance parameters can compromise statistical efficiency of the test. To improve efficiency, domain knowledge on the Euclidean parameters of interest is usually available from domain experts, and they can be incorporated into the model. This usually transfers to constraints on the Euclidean parameter (e.g., non-negativity, or ordering relation), leading to a smaller parameter space for θ and the possibility for θ_0 to be at the boundary of the space. In the proposal, we provide five motivating examples with different variants of the semiparametric likelihood methods to support this claim. In these semiparametric likelihood-based inferences, we usually obtain an estimator θ_n for θ_0 by maximizing a random criterion function obtained from the likelihood variant (e.g., through profiling or substituting an estimator for the nuisance parameter), and compare the random criterion function evaluated at θ_n and θ_0 to define a test statistic that mimics the likelihood ratio test. We call the resulting statistic as a likelihood-based test statistic. When the random criterion is the profile semiparametric likelihood or the profile semiparametric composite likelihood, it is well-established that the likelihood-based test statistics asymptotically follow (possibly generalized) a chi-squared distribution when θ_0 is an interior point of the parameter space under mild regularity conditions, while other likelihood methods such as the working-model likelihood remains unexplored. If the null parameter value θ_0 lies on the boundary of the parameter space, the likelihood-based test statistic no longer converges to a chi-squared distribution. This project aims to develop a unified likelihood-based semiparametric inference fram

title: Data-Driven Visual Analytics Platform: Exploring RCEP’s Impacts on ASEAN’s Trade in the Wake of the COVID-19 Pandemic and Amidst Economic and Political Tensions
abs: The Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP), being the world’s largest free trade agreement (FTA), was introduced during an unprecedented period marked by the COVID-19 pandemic, rising economic protectionism, geopolitical tensions, and the intensifying US-China technological rivalry. This proposal aims to study the intricate interactions between RCEP and these global events from a comprehensive perspective using a multi-disciplinary approach to build a real-time data-driven visual analytics framework. This near real-time surveillance system will be the first of its kind to support decision-making in this critical period for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). Existing theories and explanations on FTAs may be insufficient to inform any predictions made in the context of RCEP given the unparalleled nature of shocks and challenges that have emerged in the current global context. This project will employ a human-centric approach to allow for the integration of human intuition and domain knowledge with computational analysis. Robust monitoring of RCEP’s impacts is of paramount significance to research, policy, and strategy. The project will answer three key questions: (1) How does RCEP impact ASEAN’s trade patterns and dynamics in terms of globalization and regionalization? (2) How do rising economic and political tensions, including the US-China trade war and the Russian-Ukraine War, impact ASEAN’s trade including value-added patterns in terms of the footprint of trade barriers and sanctions and the position of Chinese suppliers in trade networks? (3) How does RCEP promote economic recovery and growth in the post-pandemic era? This project also takes into account existing research on RCEP and using those findings as motivation, we will also test hypotheses: (1) RCEP implementation leads to increased intra-regional trade in intermediate goods and value-added within ASEAN amidst rising protectionism. (2) RCEP enhances ASEAN countries’ participation in global value chains across sectors. (3) Instead of providing substitutes for China within the global trade framework, ASEAN nations are more likely to integrate further into value chains anchored around Chinese suppliers. The research will employ a multi-disciplinary approach by incorporating various social science and computer science research methods across the fields of economic geography and international economics. Machine learning with graphs will be used to study the interdependent structure of economic interactions among RCEP member nations and between RCEP nations and the rest of the world, and to map out the production and trade network as well as supply chain linkages. The gravity model of trade will be used to predict bilateral trade flows from RCEP and the rest of the world, using economy size, geographical distance, bilateral trade agreement, cultural and political similarity, and global institutional connections. Event-study models will be used to analyze the impa

title: Traversing the BBB: cellular and biochemical mechanisms of phospholipid uptake into the brain
abs: Brain development requires a large supply of phospholipids and essential fatty acids and neuronal membranes are particularly enriched in the omega-3 fatty acid docosahexaenoic acid (DHA). The brain acquires a large complement of its phospholipid and DHA through the transport of lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC) mediated by the transporter Major Facilitator Superfamily Domain-containing 2a (MFSD2A) that is expressed by endothelial cells and astrocytes, two key cell types in addition to pericytes that constitute the blood-brain barrier (BBB). MFSD2A functions as a Na+-dependent LPC transporter. Humans with inactivating mutations in MFSD2A present with severe microcephaly and hypomyelinated brains, a disease designated as Primary Autosomal Recessive Microcephaly 15, underscoring the essentiality of the Mfsd2a/LPC transport pathway in human brain development. The cellular and biochemical mechanism for LPC transport from the BBB endothelium into the brain parenchyma remains poorly understood. In this grant application, we present a dataset that strongly supports feasibility of this program that utilizes unique endothelial and astrocyte-specific Mfsd2a inducible knockout mouse models. We found that early postnatal deficiency of Mfsd2a specifically in astrocytes resulted in the downregulation of Mfsd2a in the BBB endothelium, ultimately resulting in microcephaly and brain DHA deficiency, but no effect on survival. In contrast, deletion of Mfsd2a specifically in astrocytes in the adult brain did not downregulate Mfsd2a in the BBB endothelium but resulted in catastrophic breakdown of the BBB, leading to brain infiltration of neutrophils. These combined findings suggest that coordinated expression of Mfsd2a in both endothelial cells and astrocytes is required for LPC uptake into the brain and maintenance of the BBB tight junctions. Moreover, these findings indicate that during early postnatal brain development, the expression of Mfsd2a in astrocytes is co-ordinately regulated with Mfsd2a expression in the BBB endothelium, without which the BBB will be disrupted. The central hypothesis of this grant proposal is that LPC uptake into the brain involves a two-cell system composed of endothelial cells and astrocytes that require coordinated expression of Mfsd2a in both cell types to uptake and transport LPC into the brain. Furthermore, we hypothesize that Mfsd2a expression in endothelial cells without Mfsd2a expression in astrocytes results in toxic build-up of LPCs in endothelial cells leading to breakdown of the BBB. This hypothesis will be tested by two specific aims: 1) To determine the mechanism by which Mfsd2a expressing astrocytes regulates the integrity of the BBB; 2) To determine the mechanism by which Mfsd2a expression in astrocytes during postnatal brain development regulates the expression of Mfsd2a in the BBB endothelium. This research will test a conceptually new cellular and biochemical model for how essential LPCs traverse the BBB and will fill a ma

title: SMCHD1: a new regulator of genome architecture
abs: In addition to transcription factors and histone modifications, recent studies have discovered an important role of DNA 3D conformation in controlling gene expression. However the mechanisms by which DNA is moved in a regulated fashion are just beginning to be elucidated. Our preliminary work has identified SMCHD1 as a novel regulator of genome organisation. SMCHD1 is an epigenetic repressor that plays a vital role in X chromosome inactivation and the silencing of specific autosomal genes. Furthermore, mutations in SMCHD1 cause two distinct human diseases, facioscapulohumeral dystrophy (FSHD) and Bosma arhinia microphthalmia syndrome (BAMS). Neither disease currently has a cure. Despite its importance in gene regulation, the precise mechanism of SMCHD1 remains unclear. Our preliminary data has shown that SMCHD1 can directly compact DNA into tight protein-DNA clusters, in a new mechanism that resembles bridging-induced phase separation. In this project, we aim to further investigate how SMCHD1 regulates DNA 3D conformation and explore its impact on gene expression. Specifically we will characterize SMCHD1’s ability to directly move and compact DNA in vitro through bulk binding assays and single molecule assays using atomic force microscopy imaging. We will then investigate the properties of the SMCHD1-DNA clusters to determine if they are truly phase-separated droplets and whether they exhibit phase-separation properties, such as the exclusion of other proteins. Finally we will examine the functional relevance of SMCHD1-induced DNA clustering in cells. Using FSHD patient-derived myoblasts which lack SMCHD1 function, we will overexpress various SMCHD1 constructs to determine if they can cause target gene repression, protein exclusion or long-range DNA interactions. The feasibility of our research plan is supported by the strong preliminary data already obtained using the proposed techniques, including atomic force microscopy and the use of patient-derived myoblasts. Our comprehensive study will not only shed light on a novel DNA compaction mechanism exhibited by SMCHD1 but may also reveal a broader mechanism that could be employed by other proteins involved in DNA organization.
kw: epigenetics; single molecule; biophysics; muscular dystrophy; genome architecture

title: Deciphering the ecology of climate-driven microbial pathogens in the equatorial coastal waters of Singapore
abs: Vibrios, the most important human pathogens found in coastal waters, are deeply influenced by climate, so much so that they have been deemed “the microbial barometers of climate change”. Recently, these bacteria’s overall abundance has been increasing worldwide, being directly correlated with water temperature, causing a rising number of infections in both humans and marine animals. They have also been found associated with increasingly frequent algal blooms. Despite decades of study in the laboratory and the environment, their ecological niche is still elusive, with no unique vector identified, making it difficult to predict risks associated with these bacterial species. Furthermore, the vast majority of studies have been conducted in temperate climates and there is much less information on dynamics of these pathogens in equatorial waters. We have recently found that rates of human infections from vibrios (vibriosis) are three times as high in Singapore than temperate/subtropical countries such as the USA. Furthermore, infections are not increasing here, despite a rise of >10% per year in the USA over the last five years. Finally, the main vibrio pathogens of humans in temperate climates (V. parahaemolyticus, V. cholerae, V. alginolyticus and V. vulnificus), termed the “Big Four”, are not all the same species as those dominating infections in Singapore, leading us to coin the term the “Equatorial Four”. There is therefore an urgent need to better understand the relationship between biotic (e.g. plankton) and abiotic (e.g temperature, salinity) environmental parameters in equatorial coastal waters and the occurrence of different species of pathogenic vibrios. The presence of large gaps in our understanding of vibrio ecology is due to several factors. First, most previous attempts at describing the niche of various Vibrio species used culture-based approaches, and a large proportion of vibrios often exists in a viable but non-culturable (VBNC) state in the environment. Secondly, vibrios usually represent a small fraction of aquatic bacterial communities, but can experience rapid blooms when attached to nutrient rich organisms or particles, holding the record for growth rates among all bacteria. Third, they are also fast-evolving, displaying large phenotypic variability even inside a single species. Last, molecular microbial ecology markers, such as 16 rDNA metabarcoding, lack resolutions at the species (or subspecies) level required for ecological studies. We have developed high-throughput low-cost techniques for the metabarcoding of vibrios using protein-coding marker genes at the species level, and specifically for V. cholerae at the subspecies level, which allows us to overcome these obstacles. Just like the 16S rRNA gene revolutionized microbial ecology, these protein-coding markers finally make possible the determination of statistically significant associations of environmental factors with particular Vibrio species and V. cholerae subspecie
kw: vibrio, pathogen, coastal water, ecology, climate, infection

title: Elucidate the coordination between capsule, lipid, and peptidoglycan syntheses in Streptococcus pneumoniae.
abs: Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus) is a human respiratory pathogen that claims ≈900,000 people annually. To establish an infection, pneumococcus evades complement deposition and opsonophagocytosis by covering the bacterial cell with capsular polysaccharide (CPS). The layer determines the serotype of pneumococcus. CPS is also the exclusive target of all pneumococcal vaccines. Capsule synthesis must be coordinated with the synthesis of other cell envelope layers. Otherwise, the daughter cells will have vulnerabilities at the division septa because they may not be completely encapsulated. Our laboratory showed that the tyrosine kinase system CpsCD controls the length of the CPS polymers by CpsD phosphorylation. Additionally, CpsCD organizes the capsule synthesis complex and recruits it to the division septum. The CPS complex interacts with a yet-to-be-identified cell division protein in the divisome but not the factors required for cell elongation. Aim 1 of the proposal will fill this knowledge gap through immunoprecipitation and bacterial two-hybrid experiments to find the exact protein interacting partner that bridges the divisome and the CPS complex. We will also identify the signal that modulates CpsD phosphorylation status. The regulation by CpsCD does not apply to serotypes that employ the synthase-dependent pathway for CPS synthesis. Our preliminary data illustrate that the capsule synthase Cps3S is also localized to the division septum but by a different mechanism. It does not require the divisome or the elongasome. Instead, recruitment of Cps3S is dependent on active capsule synthesis and the cardiolipin synthase Cls. In Aim 2, we will elucidate the recruitment pathway of Cps3S and determine whether cardiolipin and Cls are needed to target capsule proteins to the appropriate sites. Building on the findings of Aim 1 and 2, we will investigate the importance of capsule polymer length and location on pathogenesis in Aim 3. A collection of mutants that generate the same CPS polymer but different sizes will be used to study the influence of chain length on pneumococcal colonization and CPS antigenicity. The results will inform vaccine development by improving our understanding of the immunobiology of glycans. Furthermore, the findings of this aim will explain the selective advantage of controlling CPS polymer lengths. This proposed study is based on a solid body of published work and preliminary results. If the aims are achieved, we will address fundamental questions about a conserved regulatory mechanism that controls glycan polymer length in prokaryotes. It will also likely uncover potential drug targets that inhibit two widespread glycan synthesis pathways.
kw: Streptococcus pneumoniae; Capsule synthesis; Peptidoglycan synthesis; Cardiolipin

title: Developing Systemic Small Circular mRNA Cancer Nanovaccines
abs: The effectiveness of cancer immunotherapy, including immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) and adoptive T cell transfer, relies on optimizing the magnitude, quality, breadth and ability of T cells to infiltrate tumours. While cancer vaccines hold promise for inducing tumour-specific T cell immune responses, their ability to achieve therapeutic efficacy is often limited. To address this, we propose an innovative systemic vaccination strategy using a nanoplatform to deliver small circular mRNA (circRNA) antigens to dendritic cells (DCs) in secondary lymphoid organs (SLOs), aiming to stimulate a high magnitude of stem cell-like CD8+ T cells for robust and durable antitumor responses. Our preliminary data demonstrate that NIR-920 nanoparticles effectively deliver antigens to SLOs, inducing DC maturation and antigen presentation in both spleen and lymph nodes, generating high-quality stem-like TCF1+CD8+ T cells and remodelling the tumour microenvironment (TME). CircRNA’s enhanced stability and prolonged half-life surpass linear mRNA and protein vaccines in eliciting robust adaptive immune responses. Furthermore, mannose-functionalized circRNA nanovaccines improve DC targeting and antitumor efficacy. Therefore, this project aims to develop IV-circVax, a systemic nanovaccine composed of circRNA-loaded mannose-modified NIR-920 nanoparticles. We hypothesize that administration of IV-circVax will efficiently deliver circRNA to SLO-resident DCs, generating high-magnitude, stem-like CD8+ T cells and inducing durable antitumor immunity, particularly against poorly immunogenic tumours. Our specific aims are: Aim 1, Optimize and characterize IV-circVax nanoformulations. Aim 2, Investigate the immunomodulation mechanisms and efficacy of IV-circVax. Aim 3, Evaluate the prophylactic and therapeutic efficacy of IV-circVax in both "hot" and "cold" tumour models, alone or in combination with ICB. The interdisciplinary research team brings together expertise in drug and gene delivery, nanovaccines, chemical analysis and synthesis, cancer biology, and immunotherapy. The successful completion of this project will advance our understanding of vaccine design and immune modulation, and facilitate the translation of circRNA nanovaccines into clinical applications.
kw: mRNA vaccines; circular mRNA; systemic vaccination; nanovaccines; cancer immunotherapy; Immune checkpoint blockade

title: Rapid identification of immunogenic epitopes and antigen specific T cells with high throughput microfluidic platform for vaccine development and personalized immunotherapy
abs: Immunotherapy, including vaccines and adoptive cell therapy, has demonstrated remarkable success in treating patients with infectious disease and various cancers. As these treatments make use of our own immune system machinery, they are in principle applicable to any disease as long as the immunogenic epitope (e,g, reactive viral protein fragment or cancer neoantigen) can be identified. However, current approaches to finding immunogenic epitopes are very costly and time-consuming, as they involve synthesizing and testing individual peptides. In view of the need for rapid vaccine development for evolving viral threats and affordable personalized immunotherapy for cancer patients, there is pressing need for a rapid and scalable platform to screen for immunogenic epitopes. We propose to combine microfluidics engineering, novel molecular biology reactions and next generation sequencing to create a universal platform for T cell epitope screening. Firstly, we will use microfluidics to enables massively parallel reactions in picoliter scales to simultaneously test multiple peptides. Secondly, we will perform in vitro transcription translation to enzymatically synthesize peptides from DNA library overcome the challenges of conventional peptide production. Lastly, a novel strategy of barcoding peptide with DNA will enable global interrogation of peptide immunogenicity landscape with next generation sequencing. We envision that this highly interdisciplinary project, involving collaborations in the space of biomedical engineering and immunotherapy, would be a scientific breakthrough in transforming the current practice of antigen epitope and T cell screening. In Aim 1: Develop an integrated microfluidic platform for high-throughput preparation of DNA-barcoded antigen-presenting cell (APC) library, we will establish the technological platform for creating a large library of cells expressing specific peptides in optimal conformation. Importantly, these cells are labeled with unique DNA barcodes that allow their tracking by next-generation sequencing. This microfluidic strategy for producing APC library will vastly surpass the scale that is feasible in current methodologies. In Aim 2: T-cell epitope screening of virus using DNA-barcoded APC library, we will perform epitope profiling of the Cytomegalovirus (CMV). CMV is the most common cause of complications post transplantation (solid-organ and hematopoietic stem cells transplant). Our work will contribute to the understanding of the immunogenicity of this virus and serve as a framework for vaccine candidate screening in other diseases. In Aim 3: Develop an integrated microfluidic platform for high-throughput preparation of DNA-barcoded library, we will adapt the microfluidic platform developed in Aim 1 to create a large library of DNA-barcoded MHC-peptide complex. The barcoded MHC-peptide complex can bind to specific T cells, allowing us to not only identify the immunogenic peptides, but also the correspondin

title: Sustainable biomass-derived absorbents: unravelling the impacts of feedstock characteristics on hydrogel fabrication and application
abs: Biomass utilization currently is limited to pyrolysis and anaerobic digestion for biochar production and/or energy recovery. Wider applications, i.e., high-value materials and chemicals in particular, are greatly limited by the diverse compositions of biomass, which vary with the plant species, sourcing locations, and upstream processing. As such, it remains challenging to standardize the large-scale operation of biomass transformation into specialty products and to secure a stable supply of compliant feedstocks. This project aims to unleash the potential of biomass by addressing how the compositional variation impacts the end-product quality and formulating solutions to quality control. Hydrogel, which possesses 3D networks of polymer chains, is chosen as the versatile material of interest in this project. Making hydrogels from biomass is a nature-centric technology, leveraging the naturally occurring polymeric structure of biomass components (cellulose, lignin, hemicellulose, etc.). The literature has demonstrated the great potential of hydrogels in absorption applications for enhanced agriculture, using spent coffee grounds, okara, etc. as the raw biomass materials. The use of hydrogel as nutrient carriers is more sustainable than the conventional practice, where chemical fertilizer loss to the environment is significant (through run-off or volatilization), not only embedding enormous carbon footprint but also incurring high material cost in agriculture. Despite the broad interest in literature, there is insufficient understanding about the decisive characteristics of biomass feedstock that determine the hydrogel structure and hence performance. Moreover, the reported hydrogel materials were often prepared from a single waste stream or commercial compounds as starting materials. Synthetic, fossil-based modifying agents and crosslinkers are often used in the hydrogel making process. To promote wider application, more fundamental understanding of both the biomass matrix and hydrogel design should be revealed for green tech development in the future. This project aspires to tackle biomass as a highly complex, heterogenous matrix, which contains cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin, etc. The research question revolves around the nature of the effects of different biomass components on hydrogel formation and performance. This will inform strategies to streamline biomass treatment and potentially broaden the spectrum of viable biomass feedstocks for high-end applications. Three work packages (WP) are proposed in this project. WP1 will collect the locally produced biomass waste (e.g., spent coffee grounds, spent tea leaves, and horticultural waste). They represent lignocellulose-rich as well as protein- and lipid-containing biomass categories. The collected biomass will be chemically treated under rapid and energy-efficient microwave heating, to tune the biopolymer composition and properties. title: Simulating frontier many-body physics on noisy-intermediate scale quantum processors
abs: Nature, in all its complexity, is often most intriguing at the intersection of multiple frontier phenomena. Departing from the decade-old paradigm of deriving robustness from topological band structures, interacting non-equilibrium many-body systems exhibit novel forms of robustness such as time crystals and quantum scars. They are characterized by strongly recurrent protected state evolution that defies common intuition – they do not naturally thermalize into randomness in the presence of heat. Furthermore, many-body interactions can impose energy penalties that compel the ground (lowest energy) state to enter special configurations where excitations behave like de-facto “quasi”-particles obeying special interference rules. Unlike bosons or fermions, they are “anyons” that can only evolve along certain topological spacetime trajectories, an attractive property that has been touted for fault-tolerant quantum computation. Partially fueled by these exciting conceptual developments, the recent years have seen rapid developments in quantum simulators such as ultracold atomic platforms and universal quantum computers. The latter are particularly promising, leveraging on quantum superposition and entanglement to process information in ways impossible for current classical computers. They are extremely versatile and programmable, and can simulate any desired model in principle. Companies such as IBM, Google and Rigetti have invested great efforts in developing scalable quantum computers, with flagship quantum processors now containing over 100 qubits with single qubit gate error rates below 0.1%, ushering a new Moore’s law era where quantum computing capabilities are improving exponentially. These new developments beg the natural question of quantum advantage – that is, when can quantum computers outperform their classical counterparts in tackling specific computational challenges? While exponentially more efficient quantum algorithms such as Shor factorization for quantum encryption have been the holy grail for quantum advantage, they require millions of quantum gates and qubits operating at almost perfect fidelity, and are thus too large-scale for current quantum devices. In the current "Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum" (NISQ) era, non-negligible gate errors and quantum decoherence limit quantum circuits to dozens of layers deep, with typically less than a hundred qubits. Despite these limitations, we have identified classes of fundamental condensed matter physics problems which are not just at the scientific frontiers, but also feasible for computation on NISQ-era devices, with likely quantum advantage in the next 3-5 years, as predicted by the eminent Prof. John Preskill and earlier by Richard Feynman. Specifically, we shall use quantum computers to investigate new robust phenomena in many-body non-equilibrium systems, such as to uncover emergent phases of matter and quasi-particles in concrete physical platforms. title: Unravelling the impact of sea-water intrusion on carbon loss from coastal peatland plantations in Southeast Asia
abs: Southeast Asia's coastal peatlands are vital for carbon sequestration, biodiversity, and ecosystem services. However, they face significant threats from sea-level rise and agricultural conversion, notably to oil palm and acacia, resulting in major carbon (C) losses. Nearly half of these peatlands have been deforested and drained, increasing emissions and making them vulnerable to coastal erosion and sea-water intrusion. Seawater intrusion threatens agricultural yields, potentially affecting 30-69% of these lands in the next fifty years. This disruption impacts biogeochemical cycles and microbial communities, increasing carbon release. The detailed effects of seawater intrusion on these cycles remain largely unexplored, highlighting a critical research gap in predicting C loss due to sea-level rise. Our research aims to investigate seawater intrusion's impact on C cycling in Southeast Asia’s coastal peatlands, focusing on two areas. The Terrestrial Emissions and Microbial Dynamics package (WP1) will examine CO2 and CH4 emissions and microbial community shifts, hypothesizing that seawater intrusion increases CO2 and decreases CH4 emissions by shifting microbial respiration from methanogenesis to sulphate reduction. The Aquatic Carbon Loss and Microbial Dynamics (WP2) will study how seawater intrusion affects C loss into water and microbial responses to salinity changes, tracking peat-derived dissolved organic carbon (DOC) movement and assessing microbiome alterations along the salinity gradient. The hypothesis suggests seawater intrusion shifts DOC fate towards the marine C cycle rather than atmospheric emission. To deliver our WPs, we chose Pontianak, Kalimantan, Indonesia, and Maludam, Sarawak, Malaysia, to account for differences in seawater intrusion and spatial variability between tropical peatlands. We will study seawater intrusion gradients by establishing transects from the coast inland, measuring biogeochemical parameters including Ecosystem Respiration (ER) and CH4 fluxes. Comparisons will be made between impacted and control sites to assess variables such as organic carbon, nitrogen, and salinity using surface water conductivity measurements. We will also explore microbiome shifts due to seawater intrusion by collecting peat samples for genomic DNA extraction and sequencing, aiming to understand how microbial community structures adapt to changing environmental conditions. This analysis will provide insights into microbial ecology and its impact on C cycling. Additionally, aquatic carbon loss will be quantified by analyzing DOC, particulate organic carbon (POC), and dissolved gases in canal waters to calculate the C budget for plantation sites and assess their contribution to marine carbon pools. Remote sensing will complement ground observations to analyze land cover change, primary productivity, elevation change, and DOC loss at a landscape level. title: Unlocking the Synergy of Multiple External Fields for Enhanced Oxygen Evolution Reaction
abs: The hurdle to achieve efficient hydrogen production lies in the sluggish kinetics of oxygen evolution reaction (OER) in water electrolysis. Such sluggishness in OER kinetics is ascribed to the intricate multiple electron transfer process during the formation of oxygen molecules (O2). Tremendous challenge remains in designing efficient and durable non-precious-metal OER catalysis, which necessitates an abundance of active sites meticulously optimized for performance. In this context, external fields (e.g., photothermal and magnetic field) may stand out as an alternative and robust means of enhancing OER. This, however, has yet to be largely explored. The objectives of this proposal are to (a) craft a series of electrocatalysts (i.e., high-entropy metal alloys) responsive to both photothermal and magnetic fields via laser ablation, followed by coating on chiral molecules-decorated electrodes, to accelerate electron transfer during the course of OER under near-infrared light illumination and magnetic field applied, and (b) unlock the synergy of photothermal effect, magnetic enhancement, and CISS effect (i.e., mechanistic pathways) for enhanced OER of high-entropy metal alloys in water electrolysis. Intellectual Merit: The intellectual merit of the proposed research is manifested in (i) the ability to create a host of electrocatalysts with tunable electronic structures and compositions, which are external fields-responsive (i.e., photothermal and magnetic fields), (ii) deepening the understanding of how multiple external fields interact synergistically to enhance the OER, a crucial process in energy conversion and storage, and (iii) developing a paradigm-shift strategy to markedly boost the sluggish kinetics of OER. The central hypothesis of this research is that electrocatalysts with judiciously designed dimensions and compositions could enable (a) the concerted effect between two different external fields (i.e., photothermal/magnetic field, photothermal/CISS, and magnetic field/CISS) and (b) the orchestrated interplay among photothermal, magnetic enhancement, and CISS effects in enhancing OER kinetics. The fundamental knowledge derived from the success of the proposed project will render the appealing utilities of this new class of electrocatalysts in external-field-assisted, high-efficiency overall water splitting for hydrogen production via leveraging external fields that are environmentally friendly, and by extension, apply to other energy-related fields. Broader Impact: Knowledge generated by this project will lead to the development of robust strategies by judiciously leveraging a set of robust external fields and process for crafting a variety of electrocatalysts with tunable electronic structure and surface electrochemistry. title: Multiscale data disaggregation with application to climate studies
abs: Data disaggregation aims at estimating the distribution of a sequence of data given its aggregated values, instead of modeling data at low time scales and then performing higher scale predictions by aggregating low scale measurements. This project proposes a new approach to data disaggregation at different space-time scales with application to the study of extreme value distributions, for example in the design of hydrological models for the space-time flood and rainfall forecasting. Rather than relying on classical quantile estimation, which may fail to anticipate the risk of extreme events, we will use the peaks-over-threshold (POT) method from extreme value theory, which performs much better for extreme values. However, the application of the POT method requires to find a reliable estimate of an optimal threshold u, which represents a major practical challenge. This projects aims at overcoming those difficulties via recent developments in probability approximation by Stein’s method, by the derivation of new distance bounds between a target distribution and the conditional distribution of the aggregated values given extreme events. Those distance bounds will then be used as decision tools to determine whether the conditional target distribution of aggregated values is closer to normal or Pareto distribution, by comparison of the scale parameter d with the threshold u. In particular, they will be applied to determine optimal thresholds u, depending explicitly on a chosen time scale via simple and rigorous heuristics. We will then explore high-dimensional extensions, in which case justifying rigorously the choice of an optimal threshold u is much more difficult, due to the fact that the multidimensional Pareto distribution case is more complex than in the one-dimensional setting. In addition, we plan to extend a number of techniques useful in e.g. geostatistics such as kriging, via the use of generalized Pareto distributions, which to the best of our knowledge, has not been attempted so far. Our theoretical results will be tested on real data originating from the Climate and Environment Sciences Laboratory (LSCE), a French research institute with expertise in climate change, and from the Asian School of the Environment (ASE) at NTU. We also plan to explore applications of disaggregation techniques to other fields such as quantitative finance and insurance, where the tails of the data can be heavier, in which case aggregated data should converge to non-Gaussian distributions.

title: Towards Scalable Machine-Assisted Reasoning of Entropic Inequalities with Applications to Information Theory and Learning
abs: The trend of "Machine-Assisted Proof," championed by mathematicians like Fields Medalist Terence Tao, highlights the collaborative use of AI and computational tools to advance mathematical theorem proving. Tao’s work with entropic inequalities in additive combinatorics exemplifies the potential of these methods for discovering new theorems. This proposal aligns with the current trend of AI-assisted proving by exploring the application of machine-assisted proof and automated reasoning to tackle complex entropic inequalities. In information theory—a vital field for communications and causal inference—precise proof methods are crucial, especially for entropy inequalities that are fundamental to understanding data transmission limits and algorithmic efficiency. Our research aims to integrate computational proof assistants with formal methods and optimization techniques to address the inherent challenges in proving these inequalities. We will collaborate with leading experts to advance this field: Prof. Raymond Yeung from the Chinese University of Hong Kong, a Shannon Award laureate recognized for his contributions to entropic inequalities, and Prof. Wen Zaiwen from Peking University, who is focused on formalizing algorithmic convergence for first-order methods in optimization theory. By combining their expertise with machine-assisted proof and automated reasoning, our approach seeks to develop new design principles for information systems, uncover novel insights, and transform communication and information processing in the AI era. This research aims to enhance the reliability of mathematical proofs and advance the field of information theory and its applications.
kw: Information theory, Artificial intelligence, Optimization, Algorithms

title: Macroeconomy Without FIRE: Full Information Rational Expectation
abs: The mainstream macroeconomic models typically assume firms operate with full information rational expectation (FIRE) and make policy recommendations based on this assumption. With FIRE, firms are assumed to know everything about the world, including the reaction function of each individual firm, the unobserved shocks that trigger other firms’ actions, and the entire list of shocks that occur in the complex world. Moreover, the super-rational FIRE assumption is considered true for all firms: both a large publicly listed company like Apple Inc. and a small bakery store are assumed to share the same degree of rationality and information processing ability. These assumptions do not hold in reality. The existing literature has made progress in relaxing some of these assumptions. For example, the information frictions literature (Woodford 2001, Lorenzoni 2009, 2010, Angeletos and Lian 2018, Zhang 2022a,b, Ou et al. 2021, 2023 and Ou et al. 2022) relaxes the assumption that firms observe all shocks driving economic fluctuations, which practitioners and policymakers struggle to estimate in reality. Instead, they assume that firms observe noisy signals about unobserved shocks. The rational inattention literature takes this a step further by assuming that firms actively learn about the unobserved stochastic aggregate economic conditions, subject to an information processing constraint modeled as rational inattention (Sims 2003 and Mackowiak and Wiederholt 2009). Clearly, different departures from the FIRE assumption have different implications for the macroeconomy and policy. The proposed project relaxes the FIRE assumption and studies the policy and welfare implications in models without FIRE firms. Specifically, building on the previous literature, we relax the FIRE assumption along the following lines: First, firms might not fully understand the structural relationship between key variables in the model. As a result, the perceived model might differ from the actual model. Second, firms might not be aware of the existence of all shocks in the economy – a condition we term limited awareness. Third, we introduce firm heterogeneities in a setting where firms are subject to information frictions. Notably, we allow heterogeneous firms to determine the heterogeneous extent of the information they acquire. Broadly speaking, this project addresses a common question: What are the policy and welfare implications of the proposed deviations from FIRE? Due to the complexity of the proposed features, we will tackle the proposed deviations in two interrelated parts. Overall, the project builds on recent advances in theoretical, quantitative, and empirical economic research to provide answers. The answers to this question are relevant within the academic community and important for policymakers. Part I: Macroeconomic Expectations and Limited Awareness The first part aims to depart from the FIRE assumption by introducing limited awareness to the macroeconomic literature.
kw: Macroeconomics; Policy ; Limited Awareness; Information Frictions; Heterogeneous Firms

title: Chiral Surface Engineering: Advancing Biomolecular Detection Through Engineered Interfaces and Advanced Electron Microscopy
abs: Current biomolecular detection methods are often complex and inefficient, hindering advancements in fields such as medicine and environmental science. Additionally, there are limitations in controlling chirality at the nanoscale, limiting their application in sensing technologies. This research proposes to simplify biomolecular detection by developing chiral substrates using advanced TEM and optical spectroscopy. By arranging biomolecules on these substrates, the chiral-optical response can be amplified, streamlining detection processes. The study aims to understand the influence of chirality on material properties and create dielectric chiral structures through bottom-up colloidal approaches. Characterization methods sensitive to electron beams will be developed to map chirality at atomic and nano scales. Scientifically, this research will expand the scope of chiral materials by introducing chirality to traditionally non-chiral materials like semiconductors, metals, and dielectrics. Nanoscale control over chirality will facilitate the design of optically active materials by 100x enhancement with g-factors close to 1 across various length scales, enabling applications in holography, optical storage, encryption, and machine vision. Technologically, the study will develop strategies for coupling dielectric interfaces with biomolecules, improving detection sensitivity and specificity of biomarkers. This advancement will aid in RNA-based drug design and enhance understanding of biomolecular interactions with polymers, potentially mitigating adverse effects of microplastics in the human body.
kw: Chirality; Microscopy; Synthesis; Characterization; Metamaterials

title: Leveraging Molecular Design for Sustainable Catalysis by Earth Abundant Metals
abs: The overall objective of the proposal is to develop a new generation of Earth abundant metal catalysts based on Fe, Co, Ni and Ta for asymmetric C-H functionalization and molecular editing chemistry. Aim1 focuses on developing Fe-catalyzed asymmetric C-H amination enabled by chiral ligand design. Aim2 harnesses electrophilic C-H activation for asymmetric allylic functionalization by Fe and Co catalysis. Aim3 aims to develop a toolkit of organometallics based on Co, Ni and Ta for molecular editing from an organometallic perspective. To achieve these aims, a combination of organometallic synthesis of well-defined metal precatalysts, spectroscopic and crystallographic characterization of relevant metal intermediates, elucidation of correlation between catalytic activity and metal spin states, reaction optimizations, mechanistic studies including kinetics and kinetic isotope effect as well as DFT computation will be applied. The key hypothesis, based on prior literature findings, is that the metal spin states of first-row catalysts such as Fe, plays a decisive role in the reaction rate and selectivity for C-H oxidation and amination chemistry, yet its full demonstration remains elusive. The proposal aims to systematically investigate this important question by sampling a family of synthetic Fe catalysts and benchmarking their spin state-reactivity relationship. The proposed work is high-risk and high-significance, while solid theoretical proof and literature precedence based on the precious metal Rh supports its feasibility and my expertise in organometallic chemistry and catalysis support the executability of the aims. The research holds strong significance in advancing fundamental organometallic knowledge of Earth abundant metals, which is of very high interest to the organometallic and catalysis research community in Singapore and globally. Applications of the research in late-stage C-H functionalization and molecular editing are also of high importance in pharmaceutical science.
kw: Catalysis; Organometallic chemistry; Organic synthesis; Enantioselective; C-H activation

title:
Earth-Abundant Catalysis: New Opportunities to Redefine Chemical Logic for
Sustainable Production of Functional Molecules
abs: Chemical manufacturing has been a key pillar of Singapore’s economy for decades, and this field heavily relies on organic chemistry and catalysis R&D. Given that the world’s energy and resources are finite, there is now a global push towards more concise, economical and sustainable ways of producing functional heterocyclic molecules for wide-ranging applications such as medicine, food, cosmetics and energy. Unfortunately, this initiative has had limited success due to the lack of reliable modern transformations that streamline chemical synthesis, as well as the lack of cheap, efficient and selective catalysts derived from earth-abundant materials for mediating chemical reactions. Current processes for constructing functional heterocycles mainly rely on traditional chemical transformations, which were developed based on the conventional logic of organic synthesis. This approach restricts disconnection approaches, increases synthetic steps (more energy consumption, more waste) and limits molecular shapes and functions. To address the above challenges and trigger a paradigm shift from the traditional logic of synthesis, my proposal aims to redefine the norms of organic chemistry by inventing unprecedented “structural editing” transformations that (i) simplify the synthesis of functional molecules and (ii) access previously unexplored areas of the chemical space to create unknown structures with new exciting functions. I envision to achieve this by designing novel catalysts derived from cheap and earth-abundant elements, such as base metals (for instance, iron, boron) and main group elements (for instance, aluminium, boron). The proposal’s scope is divided into three work packages, namely (1) 2-component structural editing transformations, (2) 3-component structural editing transformations and (3) reaction mechanism studies. My group’s previous studies have shown that earth-abundant elements can be combined with tunable ligands to afford catalysts that possess fascinating reactivity and selectivity profiles. This will lay the foundation for the proposed work of investigating earth-abundant catalysis that mediate unprecedented chemical transformations to create new opportunities in the sustainable production of functional molecules. Success of the proposal will make a significant impact on organic chemistry and chemical production by reducing environmental footprint and promoting sustainable development in Singapore.
kw: earth-abundant; catalysis; organic chemistry; sustainability; functional molecules; chemical manufacturing

title: SINGLE-PHOTON-EMITTING DIODES OF COLLOIDAL QUANTUM WELLS: UNRAVELING ELECTRICALLY-DRIVEN SINGLE PHOTON EMISSION FROM HIGHLY STABLE AND PURE QUANTUM COLLOIDS
abs: Quantum technologies, encompassing quantum communications, imaging, and computation, demand single-photon sources (SPS) that are efficient, pure, indistinguishable, and stable. Current platforms such as self-assembled III-V quantum dots (QDs) encounter limitations due to the complexities of molecular beam epitaxy and the necessity for cryogenic temperatures. Conversely, traditional II-VI colloidal QDs suffer from poor single-photon indistinguishability caused by homogeneous and inhomogeneous broadening of their emission spectra. This proposal introduces a novel electrically-driven SPS material system and device platform, leveraging quasi-2-dimensional colloidal quantum wells (CQWs) with a doubly-gradient (DG) architecture. The DG-CQWs combine three-dimensional soft spatial carrier confinement with two-dimensional strong and uniform quantum confinement, resulting in the simultaneous emission of highly pure, indistinguishable, and stable single photons. We aim to enhance the SPS attributes of DG-CQWs by integrating them into optical cavities and pioneering the development of electrically-driven single-photon devices within a colloidal diode architecture. This approach promises to improve the Purcell factor and outcoupling efficiency in both optical and electrical regimes, owing to the orientation-controllable assembly of the CQWs. Our innovative colloidal material platform offers significant potential for realizing high-purity, Fourier-transform-limited emission from colloidal single-photon diodes, thereby addressing critical challenges in the field and advancing the state-of-the-art in quantum technology applications.
kw: Colloidal quantum wells (CQWs); Semiconductor nanocrystals; Wavefunction engineering; Electrically-driven single-photon emission; Single-photon sources (SPS); Quantum technologies

title: Predicting Annoyance Responses: Mapping the Influence of Green Infrastructure in High-Rise Residential Estates
abs: Urban noise has become a significant environmental concern impacting public health and well-being. The ultimate objective of this proposal is to understand and predict the physical and psychological effects of greenery on noise reduction. The proposed research aims to provide valuable insights into the 3D noise mapping technique, psychological effects of greenery, and noise annoyance prediction, thereby contributing to greenery-corrected noise mapping for the management and policy-making of healthy cities. The proposed project aims to achieve the following objectives: 1. Establish a 3D noise mapping approach based on traffic noise modelling for high-rise, high-density urban areas with green spaces in Singapore. - Validate the source and propagation models of noise mapping in Singapore. - Investigate the noise mitigation effects of existing greenery and topography. - Develop a new propagation model incorporating greenery mitigation. 2. Develop an AI/ML model to predict subjective annoyance responses using large-scale internet surveys and GIS technology. - Create a prediction model linking greenery-corrected noise map data and annoyance responses. - Identify potential landscape and planning features that may significantly influence subjective responses. 3. Investigate the causal relationship between greenery and noise annoyance through small-scale, well-controlled Virtual Reality (VR) and Extended Reality (XR) studies. - Validate the VR and XR experiments for noise annoyance studies. - Explore optimal landscape and planning features (vegetation height, tree spacing distances, vegetation density) to maximize psychoacoustical traffic noise mitigation. Three corresponding research thrusts will address the specific aims. This proposed study will apply a rigorous and local-based development plan for noise mapping. Two research paradigms, large-scale survey and small-scale in-situ/laboratory studies, will be established for investigation. The PI's research involved analyzing landscape features and traffic conditions, revealing a negative correlation between roadway visibility and auditory pleasantness (Tan, Hasegawa, Lau, et al., 2022). The study emphasizes the potential benefits of incorporating green canopies at higher residential levels. While the psychoacoustic advantages of greenery are well-documented, the optimal design of greenery in high-rise residential areas, particularly in varying traffic noise conditions, remains undefined. The proposal aims to develop a three-dimensional noise mapping technique in Singapore, integrating both greenery and visual context, to inform landscape planning aimed at mitigating traffic noise annoyance. The objective is to identify which landscape features effectively reduce noise and annoyance in high-rise residential areas by optimizing the psychoacoustic and physical effects of greenery and drawing on insights from Singaporean practices. title: Dimensionality Reduction in Novel Superconductors: A Pathway from Quantum Sensors to Probabilistic Computing
abs: Since its discovery, superconductivity has significantly impacted science and technology, giving rise to numerous practical applications. Historically, superconductivity was thought to be unable to persist upon dimensionality reduction, observable only in bulky, three-dimensional metals. However, recent discoveries have challenged this perspective with the advent of new material platforms. The unexpected and sometimes counterintuitive interplay among reduced dimensionality, low charge carrier density, quantum geometry, magnetism, and ferroelectricity in novel superconductors has opened promising avenues for further fundamental exploration and the development of future applications. Our proposal aims to investigate whether the superconductivity hosted by such novel material platforms can survive under strong confinement, thus facilitating applications in optoelectronics and probabilistic computing. Addressing this question experimentally presents significant challenges due to limitations inherent in modern material processing techniques that are inapplicable to new superconducting materials sensitive to air and heat. We aim to reveal the fundamental and technological limits of dimensionality reduction in novel superconducting materials using non-standard nanofabrication protocols, including helium ion beam exposure, electrode-free lithography enabled by atomic force microscopy, and electrostatic confinement in low-electron density superconductors. We will then investigate the interaction between light and matter in low-dimensional nanowires produced from these novel superconducting materials to gain a comprehensive understanding of the mechanisms responsible for generating photovoltage in response to incident radiation, covering a spectrum from mid- to far-infrared photon energies. We will test the feasibility of mid- and far-infrared (IR) single-photon detection using produced quasi-1D nanowires, which has proven challenging to realize using conventional superconductors. Lastly, we will explore the viability of practical applications for the produced superconducting nanowires targeting probabilistic computing. We will investigate the interplay between reduced dimensionality, gate-tunability, and ferroelectricity with superconducting properties and examine the implications of this interplay for probabilistic logic. The proposed topics will advance our understanding of complex superconducting systems and their applications in optoelectronics and probabilistic computing, potentially enabling breakthroughs in mid- and far-IR sensing for night vision, security, observational astronomy, gas detection, and green computing.
kw: optoelectronics, superconductivity, probabilistic computing

title: Tokenizing Everything: A Truly Multimodal GPT
abs: In the realm of artificial intelligence, the development of Large Language Models (LLM) like GPT-4 has marked a significant advancement, but their applicability is confined to a single text modality. While multimodal-inference models such as GPT-4v have expanded capabilities by allowing multimodal inputs, their training requires restrictive image-text pairwise data, and their models are limited by only being able to generate text outputs. Similarly, multimodal-generation models like DALL-E also rely on pairwise data for training and lack the capacity for inference about the images they produce (e.g., classification). Addressing these limitations, we propose an unprecedented unification---a truly multimodal model---Multimodal GPT (MGPT). We use a novel tokenizer to convert multimodal data into semantically meaningful tokens, enabling both inference and generation capabilities. This also gives our MGPT the flexibility to directly train on multimodal data without pairwise training restrictions. This innovative approach ensures that both the input queries and the outputs of our model can be seamlessly multimodal, fostering a more integrated and flexible AI system.
kw: Generative AI; Multimodality; Tokenization; GPT

title: Global traditions, local allegiances: How lived religion shapes morality in Singapore and across Southeast Asia
abs: Anthropologists and historians of religion have long debated whether religion tends to make humans more cooperative, encouraging prosocial behaviour, or by contrast, whether it tends more to drive believers toward intergroup competition and outgroup prejudice. Recent work in the cognitive science of religion has shed new light on this debate, showing that religious affiliation in general drives so-called ‘parochial altruism’, in which individuals are more likely to help members of their own religion, to the detriment of other groups (Reddish & Tong, 2023). However, this work has yet to be combined with a parallel line of inquiry in cognitive science and anthropology, which has argued that religious affiliation is not a monolithic category. Individuals participate in religions at multiple levels, bonding not only to the imagined community of their religion, but to local groups of coreligionists. But if multiple forms of affiliation can coexist within a single religion, it is crucial to address the question of how each form of religious affiliation affects prosociality distinctly. title: Breaking the Octet Rule: From Octet-Defying Carbon Species to Transition Metal Surrogates
abs: Carbon, an element quintessential to life, typically possess 8e−, therefore is said to obey the octet rule. However, there are some notable exceptions. In 1900, Gomberg made the ground-breaking discovery of a stable carbon species with 7e− − namely a carbon radical (R3C•). Almost a century later in 1988, Bertrand reported the seminal discovery of a stable carbene (R2C:) with only 6e−. Recently, such octet-defying molecules were found to exhibit transition metal-like abilities, elevating them to be among the most powerful organic tools in the chemical, material, and biological sciences. Inspired by these pioneering work, Bertrand and I discovered in 2023 that the carbene can be further undressed by 2e− to afford a stable, doubly oxidized carbene (R2C2+) − a new carbon species with formally 4e−. In fact, many families of octet-defying species have yet been isolated due to their extreme instability. The aim of this research proposal is to challenge the octet rule, discover new stable carbon species with less than 8e−, and use them as surrogates for transition metals. To embark on this quest, a new platform − namely a carbene-substituted carbene − is proposed, which features a novel design that leverages the ancillary carbene (for which a broad library is available) for precise control over the properties at the carbene center. This strategy can impart stability to new families of carbenes previously believed to be unattainable due to the absence of heteroatom-stabilization. Hitherto unknown 5e− carbene radical cation (R2C•+) and 7e− carbene radical anion (R2C:•−) might also be accessible via 1e− redox chemistry, pushing the boundaries of the octet rule. This proposal concludes by illuminating the potential of these organic molecules as transition metal surrogates, to advance the areas of sustainability, catalysis, and materials science − key areas in Singapore’s research landscape.

title: Information theory at the quantum frontier
abs: Progress in quantum information theory often goes hand in hand with a more thorough understanding of the mathematical framework underlying the theory, in particular the study of quantum measures of correlation, entanglement and uncertainty. On the one hand such measures have operational significance both for quantum information processing and quantum cryptography and thus can help us analysing problems in these application areas. On the other hand many arguments in information theory can be formulated in terms of such information measures, and often this formulation is most amenable to a generalisation to the quantum setting. This proposal aims at push forward our understanding of quantum information measures in several directions, which are detailed in the full proposal.
kw: theory of quantum information

title: Boosting the palatability and nutritional value of Alternative Proteins via discovery of natural flavour enhancers
inst: SIFBI - Singapore Institute of Food and Biotechnology Innovation
abs: Alternative Proteins (AP) have fared poorly in the market due to their unsatisfactory taste. We aim to discover novel kokumi compounds that can boost the flavour and nutritional value of AP. Although kokumi compounds are tasteless on their own, they amplify the intensity of flavours like umami, saltiness, and sweetness. They work by potentiating the activity of Calcium-Sensing Receptor (CaSR), a class C G-Protein Coupled Receptor (GPCR). Kokumi compounds identified thus far are mainly γ-glutamyl peptides isolated from sources such as yeast, beans, garlic, onions, fish and meat. However, a vast fraction of food systems remains unexplored for the presence of kokumi compounds. Moreover, γ-glutamyl peptides and aromatic amino acids bind competitively to the same site in CaSR’s Venus Fly Trap (VFT) domain potentially diminishing the kokumi effect. We propose the notion of deploying non-peptide allosteric modulators of CaSR for flavour enhancement. Use of non-peptide modulators along with γ-glutamyl peptides might synergistically activate CaSR and hugely enhance flavour. In our first approach, we will screen for CaSR modulators (peptide & non-peptide) from untested Asian food sources using an established high-throughput assay. In our second approach, we will use bioinformatic tools to predict natural non-peptide allosteric modulators of CaSR and experimentally test their activity. Finally, we will shortlist the hit compounds based on their stability, nutritional benefits, e-tongue taste profile and lack of cytotoxicity/bitter flavour for human sensory trials in follow-up studies. Our research can boost the acceptability of AP, reduce excessive consumption of sugar, salt and fat and improve food intake in the elderly population.
kw: kokumi compounds, Calcium-sensing receptor, alternative proteins, flavour enhancers

title: AudioScribe: Enhancing Audio Transcription with Acoustic Scene and Event Analysis through Large Language Models
abs: Automatic audio captioning has historically grappled with the challenge of accurately delineating the intricate temporal aspects of complex acoustic environments and events, especially over extended audio segments. In response to this challenge, this study introduces "AudioScribe," a proposed system that harnesses the power of large language models (LLMs) in tandem with a novel hybrid token-semantic contrastive learning framework. We put forward a refined pre-trained, hierarchical, token-semantic Audio Transformer by infusing it with a contrastive learning mechanism that interlinks diverse acoustic representations. Utilizing LLMs, AudioScribe adeptly generates concise, descriptive logs that capture the essence of auditory scenes. We propose to evaluate AudioScribe on datasets annotated with both acoustic scenes and sound events on its effectiveness across both tasks. The system has the potential to outperform previous methods in acoustic scene classification and sound event detection. Further, the prompts designed for LLMs empower AudioScript to effectively encapsulate extensive audio narratives, an endeavour unprecedented to our knowledge. This proposed approach marks a significant stride in the realm of audio sequence summarization and opens up many new applications in smart hearables with an assistant that tells you what’s happening; smart urban sensors that can be used to design a more harmonious space for people to live and work; and a doctor for machinery detect anomalous sound.
kw: audio transcription, audio scene analysis, sound event detection and localization, large language models, smart devices, real-time processing, summarization

title: Estimation and Inference with Many Weak Instruments and Controls
abs: Weak instruments, numerous instruments and/or control variables, and clustered observations are common features in empirical research involving instrumental variable (IV) regressions. For example, Andrews, Stock & Sun (2019) survey 230 IV regressions from 17 papers published in the American Economic Review (AER) and find that many first-stage F-statistics (and non-homoskedastic generalizations) are in a range that raises concerns, with nearly all papers reporting at least one first-stage F-statistic below 10. Similarly, Lee, McCrary, Moreira & Porter (2022) survey 123 AER articles involving IV regressions and find that 105 out of 847 specifications have first-stage F-statistics below 10. Many IV applications involve many IVs and/or controls. For instance, in their seminal paper, Angrist & Krueger (1991) study the effect of schooling on wages using 180 instruments derived from interacting three base instruments (dummies for the quarter of birth) with state and year of birth. Hansen, Hausman & Newey (2008) show that these 180 instruments give tighter confidence intervals than using the base instruments, even after adjusting for the effect of many instruments. Empirical papers employing the “judge design” (e.g., Maestas, Mullen & Strand (2013), Sampat & Williams (2019), and Dobbie, Goldin & Yang (2018) typically have the number of instruments (judges) proportional to the sample size. The famous Fama-MacBeth two-pass regression in empirical asset pricing (e.g., Fama & MacBeth (1973), Shanken (1992), and Anatolyev & Mikusheva (2022) is equivalent to IV estimation with the number of instruments proportional to the number of assets. Additionally, as pointed out by Goldsmith-Pinkham, Sorkin & Swift (2020), the shift-share or Bartik instrument (e.g., Bartik (1991) and Blanchard, Katz, Hall & Eichengreen (1992)), widely applied in fields such as labor, public, development, macroeconomics, international trade, and finance, can be seen as a way of combining many instruments. It is also common to have many control variables when fixed effects are included in the regression. Lastly, clustered data is often present in applied research. For example, Young (2021) analyzes 1,359 IV regressions in 31 papers published by the American Economic Association (AEA), with 24 of these papers accounting for clustering of observations. The well-known dataset of Autor, Dorn, and Hanson (2013) in the estimation of the effects of Chinese imports on local labor markets in US Census Bureau-designated regions with clusters at the state level. For the “judge” fixed-effects instrumental variables strategy, researchers usually cluster data at the judge shift level. The research in this proposal aims to provide theoretically sound estimation and inference methods for linear IV regression when some or all of the three data features mentioned above are present. While existing research explores IV regressions with high-dimensional data, it often assumes strong and few relevant instrument
