title: Towards Generalist Visual Perception Platform for Cost-effective and Precise Clinical Decision-making Support in Surgery
abs: Computer-assisted interventions (CAI) are revolutionizing surgical procedures for better patient outcomes. The next generation of CAI systems, powered by artificial intelligence (AI), is crucial and in high demand. These systems, which effectively interpret surgical videos captured by digital cameras, can support surgeons with context-aware decision-making, reduce adverse events by providing early warnings, facilitate remote surgical proctoring and team communication, and enhance surgical education. Consequently, these systems can improve patient safety, enhance operative quality, and reduce recovery times. However, there are still challenges: 1) most existing AI methods for understanding surgical video are tailored specifically for a single type of surgery at one clinical institution, struggling to adapt to other surgical scenarios due to domain gaps; 2) these methods depend heavily on sufficient training data and annotations from each new surgical scenario for model training; 3) methods for 4D visualization require retraining the reconstruction model even for each video, under a static camera pose, which further limits their generalization. These algorithms are far from being cost-effective and do not yet suffice for usability in real-world clinical practice. In this project, we aim to develop a novel AI-enabled generalist visual perception platform, named AI-SURG, for improving decision-making support with high resource efficiency. To accomplish this goal, we propose to innovate a set of advanced AI techniques to address challenges in analyzing dynamic and complex surgical videos, and exploit the models for different safety-critical applications. Specifically, five major contributions are made: 1) To achieve a real-time, universal model for generic surgical workflow recognition, we will design novel techniques that harness large vision-language pre-trained models, efficiently incorporating bimodal information including textual descriptions and long-range temporal dynamics. 2) To segment multiple critical anatomical regions in different surgical scenes with limited training data, we will develop a medical video foundation model with a series of prompt-based adaptive mechanisms to effectively transfer knowledge from large pre-trained models to the target task. 3) To precisely track critical structures throughout the surgical procedure with only the first frame labeled, we will design novel one-click promotable models for tracking without retraining. 4) To achieve fast and generalizable 4D reconstruction of surgical scene, we will propose to learn generalizable Gaussian with adaptable attributes and jointly train the model with pose estimation task. 5) We will integrate all these algorithms into a modularized and scalable platform. We will construct the new databases on two essential surgeries in Singapore for eye and brain care, and perform user experiments with our clinical teams to validate the feasibility and additional benefits of our develo
kw: Surgical data science; Surgical safety; Surgical AI; Medical video foundation model; Resource-efficient medical AI; Temporal information modeling

title: Engineering of reductive aminases and cascade reactions for enantioselective synthesis of chiral secondary and tertiary amines towards green pharmaceutical manufacturing
abs: The green and efficient synthesis of chiral amines represents a major target for pharmaceutical manufacturing but remains as a key challenge with classic chemistry: chemical synthesis usually requires toxic reagents and harsh conditions and suffers from unsatisfactory enantioselectivity. In contrast, enzymes can catalyse chiral amine formation in a much greener and enantioselective manner. Reductive aminase (RedAm) is a promising and unique enzyme to produce chiral secondary or tertiary amine via reductive amination of ketone with a primary or secondary amine. Despite of great recent achievement in discovery and application of RedAms, there are only a limited number of known RedAms which also often show narrow substrate scope and/or unsatisfied activity/enantioselectivity/stability. Directed evolution is a powerful tool for enzyme engineering, which can improve the catalytic performance of RedAms. Nevertheless, the low-throughput of the current microplate-based enzyme screening technologies has limited the rapid evolution to engineer desirable RedAms. In this project, we aim to 1) engineer new RedAms via fast directed evolution for the target synthesis of (i) secondary amines and (ii) tertiary amines, with enhanced catalytic performance (activity, enantioselectivity, and/or stability) and expand substrate scope; 2) develop RedAms toolbox for general synthesis of chiral secondary and tertiary amines; 3) develop efficient RedAm-catalysed reductive aminations of ketones for high-yielding and enantioselective synthesis of selected chiral amines (APIs and their intermediates); and 4) engineer new cascades reactions involving RedAms to produce chiral amines from easily available substrates (eg: alkenes and epoxides) in an efficient and sustainable manner (one-pot, no isolation of intermediates, minimised waste generation, etc). The goals are achieved by following approaches: 1) directed evolution with a novel screening strategy consisting of growth-based selection and microfluidic enzyme screening to rapidly develop desirable RedAms for target reductive aminations ( >98% product ee, >90% conversion); 2) investigation of new RedAms for reductive aminations regarding substrate septicity, activity, selectivity, kinetics, and structure-function relationship; 3) engineering of RedAm-catalysed reactions to optimize conditions for high-yielding synthesis of targeted chiral amines, with scaling-up (1-2 L); and 4) establishment of new types of cascade biotransformations involving RedAms and other enzymes via cell-free or whole-cell system to synthesize selected chiral amines from cheap alkenes and epoxides, with high-yielding and gram-scale demonstration. This project will deliver new technology for fast enzyme evolution, new RedAms toolbox for the synthesis of chiral secondary and tertiary amines; efficient RedAm-catalysed aminations of ketones for high-yielding synthesis of target amines; and new cascade reactions for efficient and sustainable synthesis of se
kw: Enzyme engineering; reductive aminase; chiral amine synthesis; cascade reactions; microfluidic enzyme screening; green pharmaceutical manufacturing

title: In depth molecular analysis of the interaction between BRCA2 and DSS1 and the effect of pathogenic missense mutations
abs: Missense mutations in BRCA2 predispose to hereditary breast and ovarian cancers. They cluster primarily within the ~340 residue DSS1/DNA binding domain (DBD), at an interface mediated by interaction with the ~70 residue DSS1 accessory protein. DSS1 stabilizes BRCA2 and facilitates its nuclear localization, essential for homology directed repair (HDR) of DNA breaks. Defective HDR due to pathogenic BRCA2 mutations leads to genomic instability and cancer progression. We have shown that DSS1 over-expression can rescue phenotypic abnormalities associated with certain pathogenic BRCA2 missense mutations, highlighting the therapeutic potential of stabilizing the BRCA2-DSS1 interaction. In preliminary work, we isolated monomeric wildtype (WT) and mutant DBDs and directly measured DSS1 binding for the first time. The DBD/DSS1 complex forms through coupled folding and binding mechanisms, and our initial data suggest that pathogenic missense mutations (W2626C and G2748D) perturb the dynamics of this process. Pilot Hydrogen-Deuterium exchange mass spectrometry comparing WT and G2748D DBDs exemplify this mechanism, indicating differences in the stability and folding of interface regions. Interestingly, these data also suggest allosteric co-operativity between DSS1 and DNA binding sites in the WT DBD that is perturbed in the G2748D mutant. In further preliminary experiments measuring the interaction of DSS1 fragments with WT and mutant DBDs we have identified short regions of DSS1 that bind with high affinity, suggesting the possibility of developing peptidomimetics to stabilize the interaction. Overall, our data reveal exciting opportunities to uncover important mechanistic details of the interplay between BRCA2 and DSS1 function and how this is perturbed by pathogenic missense mutations, guiding potential therapeutic strategies to counteract their deleterious effects. Exploiting these preliminary results, the proposed work will complete an in-depth biochemical study of a panel of pathogenic mutations, optimize methods to isolate and characterize mutants, build benchmark tests of BRCA2 DBD function and identify therapeutic precursor moieties.
kw: BRCA2; DSS1; missense mutations; protein-protein interactions; HDR (Homology Directed Repair); HDX-MS (Hydrogen-Deuterium Exchange Mass Spectrometry)

title: Organization, trafficking, and dynamics of the mitotic Golgi
abs: The Golgi apparatus is pivotal in membrane trafficking and glycosylation processes of secretory proteins and lipids. Despite its significance, the molecular and cellular function and organization of the Golgi remain poorly understood. During interphase, the Golgi forms a characteristic stacked ribbon structure consisting of multiple Golgi stacks, each comprising 4 – 7 cisternae. However, during mitosis, it was conventionally believed to disassemble into structures known as mitotic Golgi clusters and small vesicles, with a prevailing notion that all these structures are unstacked. Contrary to this view, utilizing a numerical super-resolution imaging tool developed in our lab, we have compelling evidence suggesting that mitotic Golgi clusters consist of small, stacked Golgi units, termed mitotic Golgi ministacks, mirroring the organization seen during interphase. This groundbreaking revelation challenges longstanding assumptions and prompts a re-evaluation of our understanding of trafficking and the dynamics of mitotic Golgi. Leveraging state-of-the-art imaging technologies, we propose three aims: (1) to validate the organization of mitotic Golgi ministacks using light and electron microscopy, (2) to investigate membrane trafficking pathways at the mitotic Golgi ministacks, including ER-Golgi and endosome-Golgi cycling pathways, and (3) to explore the dynamics of mitotic Golgi ministacks and vesicles. Our comprehensive investigations aim to rectify misconceptions surrounding the mitotic Golgi, providing crucial insights into its molecular organization and trafficking mechanism. Ultimately, our work holds the potential to open new avenues of research and reignite interest in the mitotic Golgi field.
kw: Golgi; mitosis; Golgi stack; cisternal organization; membrane trafficking; organelle dynamics

title: Investigating age-dependent metabolic reprogramming in alveolar macrophages to understand immune responses to respiratory infections in early life
abs: Acute respiratory infections are the leading cause of hospitalization in children, and are associated with significant morbidity and mortality even in previously healthy children with no comorbidities. This fact clearly highlights that the pulmonary immune system of children is in a distinct state from that in adults; however, the developmental trajectory of the immune system in children and its interaction with the maturing lung environment, as well as its functional specialization in response to the unique challenges of early life, remain poorly understood. Alveolar macrophages (AMs) are the most abundant innate immune cells present in the lungs, and they are the first line of defense against inhaled pathogens, demonstrating remarkable plasticity to adapt to the ever-changing needs of the lung microenvironment. As such, we hypothesize that in early life, AMs are programmed to adapt to the energy demands of growth and development, and differences in the metabolic programming of AMs between children and adults contribute to their different disease outcomes upon respiratory infections. Our preliminary data supports this notion, showing that there is one AM subset in children and two in adults, and the second subset in adults results from metabolic reprograming of AMs by microbiome-derived factors during host development. The current proposal will examine the age-dependent differences in the metabolic and functional capabilities of AMs in response to several classes of respiratory pathogens, at the cellular and molecular level. We will use mouse models and combine powerful single-cell and spatial approaches with state-of-the-art flow cytometry and metabolomics technologies. Overall, our proposed research will provide a foundation for understanding the developmental trajectory of AMs and elucidate the microbiome-derived factors governing AM reprogramming in early life. This work is innovative and significant as it is based on a newly identified subset of AMs, and the knowledge yielded could aid in the development of broadly enhancing immunomodulatory therapies and vaccines to protect children against respiratory infections.
kw: macrophages; innate immunity; respiratory infections; immune development; early life

title: Towards Scalable and Powerful Similarity Search on High-dimensional Vector Data
abs: Nowadays, large-scale high-dimensional vector data has become pivotal. Notably, various forms of unstructured data, including images, videos, texts, and speeches, are routinely converted into vectors through the application of deep learning techniques like word2vec, node2vec, item2vec, and others. These resulting vectors are subsequently harnessed in various downstream analytical tasks. One of the fundamental challenges in this domain is the nearest neighbor (NN) search within high-dimensional vector spaces. This problem holds immense significance, finding applications in fields such as databases, information retrieval, recommendations, and retrieval-based large language models. However, exact NN queries often lead to unacceptable response times due to the curse of dimensionality. To strike a balance between response time and accuracy, researchers have increasingly explored the realm of approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search. Nevertheless, existing ANN algorithms still suffer from costly time consumption for vectors generated by deep neural network models such as GPT since their dimensionality is high. In addition, most of them predominantly revolve around vector data and may encounter limitations in real-world scenarios involving data types beyond mere vectors. This project aims to develop new algorithms to achieve better time-accuracy trade-off for the conventional ANN problem as well as to support more powerful ANN queries namely attribute-filtering ANN and multi-vector ANN. Through these novel approaches, we seek to further improve the scalability of ANN queries and bridge the gap between ANN solutions and real-world applications featuring diverse data types.
kw: High-dimensional vector; similarity search; attribute-filtering; multi-vector search

title: Designing Scalable and Robust Storage Systems – From New Theories to Real Systems
abs: In Singapore, “the digital economy contributed to more than 17% of its gross domestic product in 2022 — higher than the 13% logged in 2017”. The digital world fosters the surge in data volume and this trend is further accelerated by the proliferation of generative AI tools. Today, more than 300 million terabytes of data are created each day. In such a big data era, the solution to managing data efficiently is of utter importance. Effective big data storage solutions, capable of handling storage, retrieval, and updates, are vital for empowering data science applications across numerous sectors such as healthcare, finance, education, and e-commerce. This underscores the critical need for scalable and robust data storage infrastructure at the heart of the big data economy. NoSQL or NewSQL data systems capable of handling various data formats have become the industry standard for big data storage solutions. Most real-world data can be processed to be {\it data value} items indexed by corresponding keys, and hence, many modern systems rely on key-value storage systems that manage a collection of key-value data, exemplified by RocksDB in Meta, LevelDB in Google, Voldemort in LinkedIn, Apache Cassandra, and MongoDB WiredTiger. These industrial systems rely on Log-Structured Merge Trees (LSM-trees) to serve as the foundational data engine, and improving LSM-trees has been a core topic in big data systems. The proposal discusses the existing limitations of key-value storage systems in terms of {\it robustness} and scalability, aiming to design a new generation of key-value storage system that desirably balances three crucial system operator costs and space cost. The project outcome will have the potential to attract global industrial attention due to the wide adoption of the key-value storage systems. This project will also significantly contribute to the theoretical study and system developments, thus having both academic and industrial impact.
kw: Big data systems; Data structures

title: Project Honesty: Investigating the Long-term Impact of Parenting by Lying and Promoting Honesty in Families
abs: Project Honesty is a multi-method research project aimed at unravelling the intricate dynamics of parenting by lying and promoting honesty in parents and children. Project Honesty is the world’s first longitudinal study of the impact of parental lying and dishonesty. The primary objective is to investigate the mechanisms and long-term outcomes of parental lying and dishonesty to deliver tailored interventions using quantitative and qualitative methodologies. Our expert consortium leverages on the Principal Investigator Associate Professor Setoh’s established collaboration with Singapore’s largest birth cohort study (GUSTO), uniting the world’s foremost researchers on this topic from Singapore, Toronto, and the Netherlands to examine the role of lying behaviour in shaping children’s developmental outcomes, and to identify effective strategies to promote honesty in parents and children. Project Honesty aims to address significant research gaps by answering the three research questions below: Study 1: What are the motivations behind parenting by lying, and how do children perceive their parents’ lying? Study 2: How does parenting by lying impact children’s psychosocial adjustment outcomes and parent-child relationships in the short and long term? Study 3: How do we promote children and parents’ honesty? By achieving these aims, the research will not only provide valuable theoretical insights into the antecedents and consequences of parenting by lying, but also offer practical implications through interventions which aim to promote honesty within families in Singapore. In Study 1, we conduct a quantitative investigation of how parents’ intentions, beliefs and values about parents’ lying, as well as how perceived normativity and moral evaluations of parenting by lying are related to their use of parental lies. In addition, we examine how their children experience and understand parenting by lying. Next, Study 2 uses a longitudinal study design to investigate the short- and long-term effects of parenting by lying on children’s psychosocial outcomes (i.e., internalising problems, externalising problems, prosociality), parent-child relationship quality, and children’s lying behaviours. Building on our previous research (Low et al., 2023), we examine parent-child relationship quality and children’s lying as intermediary mechanisms between parenting by lying and children’s outcomes. Finally, Study 3 aims to promote honesty in parents and children through two separate interventions. First, we investigate the utility of a naturalistic intervention in reducing parenting by lying in Study 3i. Specifically, we examine the motivations and rationale driving parents’ use of lies, through conducting reflective interviews. We will adopt a mixed-methods approach combining qualitative interviews with quantitative measures, to comprehensively evaluate the short-term outcomes of the intervention. title: The Pseudomonas aeruginosa T6SS antibacterial gun: Identification, characterization and loading of toxin bullets
abs: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a leading cause of antibiotic-resistant, hospital-acquired infections, and placed on the WHO and CDC critical threat lists. When colonizing a host this organism can use the type VI secretion system (T6SS) to outcompete resident mircrobiota and other invading pathogens. P. aeruginosa uses the T6SS to deliver plethora of T6SS toxins directly into prey bacteria. We and other have characterized several T6SS toxins which have targets that are already used by the available antibiotics (e.g. cell wall, membrane, nucleic acids). The concept here is to hypothesize that the number of new toxins to be discovered is huge, and more importantly that the target of these toxins may have not been explored for antimicrobials development. P. aeruginosa is a potent T6SS killer and has three distinct systems. We published preliminary evidence in Nature Microbiology and mBio that we can identify, by using unbiased approaches, novel toxins such as the anti-transamidosome Tse8. Here we will use P. aeruginosa as model organism and exploit several concepts. One is that all toxins are encoded with an immunity to prevent self-intoxication. The other is that some toxins interact directly with a T6SS element called Hcp before being fired and delivered in prey cells. We will thus use a TraDIS approach to identify randomly on the P. aeruginosa genome all toxin/immunity gene pairs by comparing efficiency of Tn insertion in different background (i.e T6SS active vs inactive). The other will use a systematic pull-down approach with either one of the three P. aeruginosa Hcps. All selected hits will then be taken through a pipeline of toxin characterization (secretion, activity, target, etc…) for which my laboratory has demonstrated ample expertise through numerous publications in high impact journal. Finally, some of the selected hits will be taken in a pipeline to resolve their structure, namely in interaction with Hcp. This will provide insightful information on the loading mechanism so that the number and diversity of toxins delivered at each T6SS firing event could be determined. The expected outcome is to harness the huge reservoir of yet uncharacterized T6SS toxins, by exploiting the dark matter of the genome thanks to our unbiased genetic approach. Our findings should then lead the development and design of novel antimicrobials.
kw: Pseudomonas aeruginosa; type VI secretion system; bacterial toxins; antimicrobial resistance; microbial communities

title: Real-Time Scheduling of Deep Neural Network Workloads with Performance and Data Dependency
abs: There has been an increasing deployment of deep-neural networks (DNNs) in real-time cyber-physical systems. However, end-to-end DNNs that take sensory input and determine a control action are not popular for safety-critical tasks; rather, pipelines of DNN models that provide greater explainability and a modular component-based architecture are commonly preferred. Furthermore, motivated by the timing and accuracy requirements of applications with the necessity of respecting the memory limit of resource-constrained systems, anytime neural networks and model variants are two widely employed techniques that allow exploiting the time-memory-accuracy trade-offs. However, existing works have ignored the necessity to adapt the schedule at runtime to take into account the performance dependency of one component on the other. Firstly, the problem of confidence-aware real-time scheduling of anytime neural networks with performance dependency on a heterogeneous computing system is considered in this project. The goal is to find a dynamic schedule that yields optimal utility while respecting confidence thresholds and timing constraints. Afterward, the problem of model variant selection and confidence-aware scheduling of real-time DNN tasks with performance dependency is studied. As the next contribution, we consider the problem of co-scheduling a set of pairs of performance dependent DNN workloads. The proposed comprehensive scheduling framework also considers both performance and data dependencies. Furthermore, to embrace the uncertainty, we will also perform sensitivity analysis of the proposed algorithms. Finally, we evaluate the proposed algorithms for an autonomous vehicle prototype. Specifically, we plan to develop a robotic testbed to evaluate our algorithms. Furthermore, for an extensive evaluation, we also plan to evaluate our algorithms in a simulation environment, such as based on the CARLA simulator.
kw: Real-Time Scheduling, Anytime Deep Neural Networks, Multi-resource co-Scheduling, Confidence-aware Scheduling

title: Investigation of Second Order Nonlinearity in Thin Film Barium Titanate – Physics and Devices
abs: The second order nonlinearity in nonlinear optical crystals forms the physical mechanism underpinning important optoelectronic processes such as laser frequency conversion, frequency comb generation, ultrafast electro-optical modulation, pure light-light scattering, and quantum optics. The functionality of the internet (fast optical modulators), optical metrology (gravitational wave detection using squeezed light, for instance), and the entire field of photonic quantum cryptography/computing are all based on a very limited number (single digits) of usable nonlinear optical materials. We know that better materials exist; if they could be grown in a way that retains their useful bulk properties while enabling dense integration, improvements in many downstream fields can subsequently become possible. In this proposal, we target a particularly good but tricky material, barium titanate, for exploitation. In other more common materials (especially lithium niobate), recent progress has been made to integrate light sources, amplifiers, modulators, and detectors all together on a single chip for better speed, functionality, stability, available complexity, and efficiency. The ideal form of a nonlinear crystal is a thin optical single crystal film, and this type of crystal can lead to subtle differences in properties from the bulk form while providing more degrees of freedom in terms of interplay between strain, crystallinity, crystal domains, polarization state in each domain, as well as doping. These factors can affect not only the linear dielectric functions but also the nonlinearities, as the crystal symmetry can become more complicated by the application of voltage, strain, etc. In this proposal, we aim to elucidate these fundamental properties for an important nonlinear crystal (barium titanate) which we are able to grow in thin film form at NUS, and which has intrinsic nonlinear optical benefits over existing alternative materials (lithium niobate, AlN, silicon, etc.) useful for a wide range of potential applications, but which very few researchers have explored in other institutions due to crystal growth challenges. Barium titanate (BTO) is an experimental material with particularly strong bulk electro-optic coefficient (EOC), an order of magnitude stronger than that in lithium niobate which is in commercial use. When BTO is typically grown, it can wind up with different types of crystallinity (polycrystalline, multidomain structures, or single crystal), with different resultant electro-optic properties. However, an ideally large EOC has not yet been achieved in thin film BTO as compared to that in its bulk, and there is a current lack of understanding of how the crystal properties are related to the EOC within the crystal. The EOC can be affected by crystallinity, crystal orientations, domains, strain states, stoichiometry, phase transition temperature, defects and dislocations, poling, which we are able to control, while no systematic studies of

title: Artificial Symmetry Breaking of Mid-Infrared Hyperbolic Polaritons in Mixed-Dimensional Heterostructures and Their Device Applications
abs: Middle-infrared (MIR) frequency is important for defence, sensing, molecular vibrational spectroscopy, thermal radiation control, and other applications. In the era of nanotechnology, main fundamental challenges of MIR nanophotonics are: (1) the intrinsic size disparity of MIR photons (wavelength λ0~10 µm) and dimensions of nanodevices (λ0/100); (2) the manipulation of carrier excitations in MIR-active natural materials given their available crystallographic symmetries. Scientifically, these are related to dispersion manipulations, requiring both high momentum (high-k) of MIR eigenmodes and on-demand configurability. Our approach encompasses both theoretical and experimental study of mix-dimensional (mD) heterostructures comprising layered two-dimensional (2D) van der Waals (vdW) solids, and three-dimensional (3D) optical crystals. These crystals host MIR active optical phonon resonances and extreme optical anisotropy, known as hyperbolic phonon polaritonic response for strong confinement of MIR photons. Via twisted stacking of the 2D+2D and 2D+3D heterostructures in our system, we aim to realize: (1) comprehensive full-wave analysis and dispersion control of MIR polaritons; (2) extreme broken mirror symmetry of propagation characteristics of MIR polariton; (3) practical device applications such as interconnect devices, near-field thermal radiation management, and controllable waveguide-free long-range coupling of quantum emitters. The choice of mD heterostructure can break intrinsic limits of crystals regarding both the fixed crystal symmetry and dimensionality. This can also combine advantages of both 2D crystals with the flexibility to control the symmetry and 3D crystals with long-range polariton propagation, thus unlocking new frontiers of MIR nanophotonics through the artificial mirror symmetry breaking in our heterogeneously integrated structures. Our work is at the interface of MIR optics, nanophotonics, crystal optics, material science, metamaterials, and thermal photonics, which will be an important milestone for long-wavelength nanophotonics. This includes MIR nanotechnologies including radiative energy harvesting, MIR nanoscale interconnection and sensing and will also inspire THz nanotechnologies for communications and others in the long term. Our proposal is also aligned with RIE 2025 to explore fundamental research knowledge to innovate novel technologies for sustainable growth and competitiveness of Singapore’s engineering sectors.
kw: Mid-Infrared Nanophotonics; Polaritonics; van der Waals materials; Dispersion Engineering; Optic Crystals; Scanning Near-Field Microscopy

title: Innovating multiscale 3D printing technology for advanced composites with bio-inspired hierarchical structures
abs: The hierarchical structure is an amazingly common phenomenon encountered in natural materials, combining two-dimensional mineral materials as basic building blocks with the bonding of soft tissues, to break the trade-off between stiffness and toughness in material properties. Coincidentally, two-dimensional materials are found to be aligned regularly under the shear forces of the flow field in extrusion-based printing process, resulting in concentric structures after extrusion and then hierarchical structures after printing-on-bed, which opens up possibilities for manufacturing biomimetic microstructures. Yet, it is still a puzzling phenomenon with many unexplained features, including the influence of material selection and printing parameters, the evolution of alignment during the printing process, and the relationship between two-dimensional material reinforced microstructure and mechanical properties. Thus, by investigating two typical extrusion-based 3D printing technologies, Direct Ink Writing (DIW) and Fused Deposition Modelling (FDM), this project aims to progress towards a deep understanding of the evolution of 2D nanosheet alignment through the combination of experiments, X-ray microtomography characterization, and through-process simulation. It also seeks to comprehend the relationship between printed microstructure and mechanical properties through progressive Representative Volume Element (RVE) models. Finally, by integrating the manufacturing freedom of 3D printing, gradient and optimized designs at the mesoscale are achieved, thereby creating multiscale biomimetic structures to produce advanced materials that are lightweight, high-strength, and high-toughness. This project, at the borderline of advanced manufacturing, offers a unique integration of approaches, competences and resources in of materials science, mechanics, physics, and technological developments of observation techniques. For advanced material and manufacturing, the versatility of the process and its control could yield potential breakthroughs in numerous key applications of tremendous human, technological, environmental and economic importance such as aerospace, biomaterials or green energy production, and open a whole new field of research. Far-reaching implications are expected, both from the developments in mechanics for the RVE models and physics for the fluid–structure interaction simulation, and from the implications of extrusion-based printing and two-dimensional materials in many situations and fields of research.
kw: 3D printing, Direct Ink Writing, Ceramics, Composites, Mechanical Property, Bio-inspiration

title:
Enabling Extremely-Low Power AI Hardware 
using Novel Ferroelectric Capacitive Synapse and Arrays
abs: The increasing amount of data and demands for data-centric computing call for the emerging non-volatile memories (eNVMs) with high data storage density, fast speed, low power consumption, and decent reliability. So far, major research activities in eNVMs have been focused on resistive memory devices, e.g., RRAM, PCM, MRAM, FTJ, and FeFET, which modulate the device conductance by various approaches to store the data. However, the read current of the devices leads to static power consumption, limiting the power efficiency of the storage or in-memory computing system. In this proposal, we will explore a new concept and solution using capacitive memory based on doped-HfO2 ferroelectric material which has the following key features and advantages: (1) Different from the conventional resistive memories, the novel ferroelectric capacitive memory (FCM) modulates the capacitance to store data, enabling the further reduction of power consumption with near-zero static power in principle. (2) With the ultra-high resistance, the IR drop problem faced by the resistive memories can be circumvented. Negligible read disturbance is possible as the large readout signal for sensing the memory states can be maintained even at zero DC bias with charge-based readout scheme. (3) Write power can also be optimized by reducing the leakage current which is irrelevant to both the reading and the field-driven ferroelectric switching. (4) Such concept and device enable computations to be executed by injecting and accumulating the charges in the capacitors, circumventing the need for DC signals. The charge domain operation is able to achieve zero static power in the array, further making the FCM promising as the technology enabler for the ultra-low-power computing-in-memory (CiM) edge computing system. We will focus on the development of a high-performance, low-power, and scalable ferroelectric capacitive memory device as the artificial synapse for AI applications, leveraging the unique properties of HfO2-based ferroelectric materials and the capacitive storage mechanism. The project consists of hardware and software development and can be divided into four sub-programs, involving the studies at material, device, and array levels. The studies at each level are highly correlated, which will be conducted through experiments, as well as the assistance of modeling and simulation. Details of the sub-programs are: Sub-Program 1: Optimizing HfO2-Based Ferroelectric Materials Sub-Program 2: Developing High-Performance Ferroelectric Capacitive Memory Device Sub-Program 3: Modeling of Ferroelectric Capacitive Synapse for Device Optimization and High-Level Evaluation Sub-Program 4: Integrating the Ferroelectric Capacitive Synapse into Crossbar Array The proposed project will provide comprehensive development guideline, understanding, and evaluation of FCM as a promising synapse device for ultra-low power AI applications, which would revolutionize eNVM-based CiM, particularly for resource-

title: Novel High Performance Piezoelectric Thin Film Composite (TFC) Nanofiltration/Reverse Osmosis (NF/RO) Membrane for Industrial Separation and Purification Application
abs: Ultra-permeable membrane (UPM), requiring lower energy consumption and smaller footprint, is attractive for industrial separation and purification applications such as seawater desalination, water reclamation, toxic liquid waste treatment, resource recovery, etc. However, bottlenecks such as low mass transfer and severe membrane fouling often impede the practical application of UPM. Common methods for membrane fouling control such as bubbling and module vibration are energy intensive. In addition, nanofiltration/reverse osmosis (NF/RO) UPM is typically fabricated by incorporating nanomaterials such carbon nanotube (CNT), graphene, aquaporin biomolecules and metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), etc. that are expensive, and may have issues such as non-compatibility with process solutions and long-term stability due to leaching. In this proposal, a piezoelectric NF/RO membrane with superior permeability and possesses an “active” vibrating mechanism under an electric field to improve mass transfer and to disturb concentration polarization (CP) layer for reduced fouling will be developed. It shall be noted that the energy requirement for vibrating the membrane is much lower than that of vibrating the module. In general, the piezoelectric NF/RO membrane has a thin film composite (TFC) structure with a piezoelectric porous substrate (i.e., bottom layer, ~200 microns in thickness, that provides the active vibration as well as mechanical support) and a non-porous selective layer (i.e., top layer, < 200 nm in thickness, responsible for permeability and selectivity). A two-step fabrication process will be employed to achieve the TFC structure. First, the piezoelectric porous substrate will be prepared by ultrasound assisted nonsolvent induced phase separation (NIPS) method. High-power ultrasound would assist in controlling the thermodynamic-kinetic NIPS process to favour the formation of β-phase (i.e., crystalline phase that shows piezoelectric properties) as well as in alignment of ferroelectric domains through thermal and/or cavitation effects to enhance the piezoelectric properties. Then, a novel ultrasound assisted interfacial polymerization (IP) method will be applied to prepare the polyamide (PA) selective layer onto the piezoelectric porous support. Low-intensity pulsed ultrasound would activate the piezoelectric porous support, which creates instability at the interface to control the reaction-diffusion IP process and led to formation of a PA layer with homogenous Turing pattern that improve the permeability and selectivity. The piezoelectric porous substrate and NF/RO membrane will be characterized, and their performance will be assessed to identify the best fabrication method and parameters. The filtration performance and energy consumption of the piezoelectric NF/RO membrane will be evaluated. title: Role of Firm-to-Firm Input-Output Linkages in Transmitting Aggregate Shocks: Impacts on Firm-Level Productivity, Labor Demand, and Innovation
abs: The proposed research program seeks to establish datasets on firm-to-firm input-output (IO) linkages for the Singapore economy, and to identify the mechanisms via which external and internal shocks transmit via these IO linkages to affect the firm-level performances, such as productivity, labor demand, and innovation activities. By proposing the use of the Singapore GovTech’s enTRUST platform (where datasets from multiple sources can be merged, using privacy-preserving technologies built on an AWS cloud-based platform), the current research program has obtained support from the Singapore Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) to facilitate the request of administrative data from various source government agencies, including: (i) firm-level financial statement data; (ii) firm-level trade data; and (iii) employer-employee matched data. In parallel, the research program has obtained agreement in-principle from DBS, the largest local bank, to share data (using the same enTRUST platform) on the banking flows of its account holders. Because there exists no infrastructure in the Singapore public sector that systematically digitizes business-to-business value-added tax (VAT) data, the banking flow data of DBS (with a 70% market share in the local banking industry) constitute a best available option to take a first look into the firm-to-firm linkages of the Singapore economy. Given the fused firm-to-firm dataset with firm-level financial / trade / employment data, the research program will embark on several important and interrelated research projects organized under three themes. First, by combining the local firm-to-firm supply linkages, firm-level trade flows, and the global inter-country input-output (ICIO) tables, the research project aims to develop global value chain (GVC) measures at the firm level, by building on the gross-exports decomposition framework of Koopman, Wang, and Wei (2014) and Borin and Mancini (2019), who have provided accounting methods to track value-added flows across borders using ICIO tables at the country-sector level. A few recent studies (Kee and Tang, 2016; Bems and Kikkawa, 2021; Boehm et al., 2023; Flaaen et al., 2023) have used firm-level data to highlight potential heterogeneities across firms and potential aggregation bias when measuring GVC participation based on sectoral-level data. These recent studies, however, do not utilize the global ICIO tables and hence focus only on the backward linkage of a firm in trade (using the share of imported contents in a firm’s production of gross exports), and except Bems and Kikkawa (2021), capture only the direct imported contents, ignoring upstream imported contents by a firm’s domestic suppliers. title: I-AGE: Interactive & multimodal AI, Gaming and continuous Engagement (I-AGE) platform to enhance cognitive impairment detection and management
abs: There is a pressing need for solutions that enable the early detection of cognitive decline in seniors, allowing for timely interventions that can slow progression. Additionally, there is a demand for interactive, portable, and digital therapy platforms that are easy for seniors to use. Such platforms should engage them with compelling interactions, motivating them to consistently participate in the therapy program. Motivated by these unmet needs, our study aims to develop and implement the Interactive & multimodal AI, Gaming, and continuous Engagement (I-AGE) platform to enhance the early detection and management of cognitive impairment. The proposed integrated solution capitalizes on the strengths of a gamified interactive system and a multimodal AI agent capable of extracting and combining information from multiple sensors. We plan to develop sensors that continuously monitor gait signals, finger tapping, physical activity levels, heart rate variability (HRV), and speech capabilities, both during our elderly participants’ daily routines and their interactions with our games. For this initiative, we will collaborate with Active Ageing Centres (AACs) in Boon Lay and Queenstown. Our goal is to recruit a total of 300 elderly participants. To assess the efficacy of our proposed solution, we will monitor these individuals for at least one year, starting from their initial week-long cognitive impairment risk assessment or during a three-month period of continuous engagement and training intervention, to clinically survey their cognitive functions and related secondary outcomes.
