title: Determining Human Leukocyte Antigen Allele Frequencies at High-Resolution and its Impact on Eplet Mismatches to Personalize Immune Risk Evaluation in a Multi-Ethnic Kidney Transplant Cohort in Singapore
abs: Donor-recipient human leukocyte antigen (HLA) mismatch is the main driver of alloimmune injury in transplantation. Previous methods of HLA genotyping at low- to intermediate-resolution enabled assessment of immunological risk at antigen and allele levels but are unable to address the relative immunogenicity of specific mismatches at the molecular level, nor the potential for cross-reactivity of donor-specific anti-HLA antibodies (DSAs) that develop post-transplant. Quantifying molecular mismatch has been shown to correlate with de novo DSA development, rejection, and allograft survival. Advances in immunogenetics have enabled molecular, or eplet, mismatch analyses with high-resolution HLA genotyping. Studies that imputed high-resolution typing using registry data revealed several limitations. South-East Asian (SEA) ethnicities, especially Malays and SEA Indians, are not well-represented; imputation inaccuracies have been identified, particularly for non-Caucasians, and many cohorts did not have all 11 HLA loci typed. Describing high-resolution typing for all 11 HLA loci remains a critical unmet need for precision medicine and immune evaluation for Singapore and Asian kidney transplantation (KT). We hypothesize that in our multi-ethnic cohort, there will only be modest prediction accuracy using imputation. The resultant characterization of anti-HLA antibodies and eplet mismatches will result in a re-classification of immunological risk in a proportion of KT recipients. This will be a single-center, retrospective cohort, exploratory study. We aim to recruit 300-350 recipients and donors of Chinese, Malay, and Indian ethnicities who have not had high-resolution HLA typing performed at all 11 HLA loci. DNA will be obtained for high-resolution typing with next-generation sequencing (NGS). We will correlate pre-transplant anti-HLA antibodies and post-transplant alloimmune outcomes using eplet mismatch and alloimmune risk categories using high-resolution typing compared to that obtained by imputation from low-resolution typing. Precision in immune risk assessment will be key to personalizing immunosuppressive therapy and monitoring in our population with unique HLA diversity.
kw: Kidney Transplantation; Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA); Immunogenetics; Eplets; Precision Medicine; Personalized Medicine,

title: Proteomic and transcriptomic analysis of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid and whole blood in immunocompromised patients with undiagnosed pulmonary infiltrates
abs: Background Interstitial lung diseases (ILD) encompass a heterogeneous group of disorders of the lung parenchyma. Drug-induced interstitial lung diseases (DI-ILD) have emerged as notable entities due to development of novel therapeutic agents for treatment of hemato-oncologic diseases. Clinical and radiographic features of DI-ILD are non-specific. Bronchoscopy aids diagnosis by excluding infective causes. However, there remain no gold-standard diagnostic tests for DI-ILD. Positive microbiological yield from bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) in immunocompromised hosts (ICH) including hemato-oncology patients ranges 44-68% based on historical cohorts. Our local prospective registry (CIRB 2021-2148) showed that DI-ILD was the eventual diagnosis in 11.3% of patients. At the same time, underlying mechanisms of DI-ILD remain poorly understood. We propose that advancements in bioinformatics will allow for a comprehensive examination of molecular-level changes in ICH with both infective and non-infective pulmonary complications. Methods An exploratory single-centre, prospective observational study is proposed. ICH being evaluated for new pulmonary infiltrates detected on computed tomography (CT) imaging and planned for bronchoscopy would be recruited with informed consent. 6 mls of whole blood will be obtained via routine venipuncture for proteomic analysis using Olink target 96 cytokine panel and transcriptomic analysis via bulk RNA sequencing. During bronchoscopy, an additional 10 mls of BAL fluid would be collected and processed using the omics assays. Deidentified patient data will be entered into a prospective registry and outcomes including final diagnosis, mortality and functional status would be monitored from the electronic medical record. Aims The study aims are: Aim 1: Establish a robust protocol for proteomic analysis of BAL fluid. Aim 2: Determine the concordance in immune signatures between whole blood and BAL fluid in ICH with undifferentiated lung infiltrates. Aim 3: Correlate transcriptomic and proteomic signatures in BAL fluid and blood with the eventual clinical diagnosis of DI-ILD or infective causes of pneumonitis.
kw: Interstitial lung diseases; precision medicine; cancer treatment; drug-induced pneumonitis; immunocompromised hosts

title: Adaptive NK cell-based combination therapies for head and neck cancer
abs: Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) ranks as the third most prevalent cancer globally, significantly impacting survival rates, particularly in Southeast Asia. Conventional treatment strategies offer limited success in recurrent or metastatic stages, necessitating innovative approaches. Recent advances in targeted therapies, particularly those combining chemotherapy with EGFR- or PD-1-targeting antibodies, have demonstrated improved overall survival rates, showcasing the potential of immune system-based interventions. Notably, natural killer (NK) cell-based therapies emerge as a promising alternative due to their lower risk of graft-versus-host disease and feasibility as allogeneic “off-the-shelf” therapies. However, challenges such as donor variability and short in vivo half-lives persist. We have developed a technology that effectively expands naturally-occurring adaptive NK (aNK) cells from Singaporean donors, enhancing their cytolytic capabilities. We would like to evaluate aNK cells as a modular platform that can be combined with other existing or novel treatments, to enhance their efficacy against HNSCC. Accordingly, our preclinical studies will assess the performance of expanded aNK cells, both independently and in synergistic combinations with EGFR- and PD-1-targeting antibodies, alongside novel trispecific killer engagers (TriKEs) targeting the B7H3 antigen, which is overexpressed in HNSCC. Additionally, we will genetically engineer aNK cells to express B7H3-targeting CAR alongside optimized IL-2 and PDL1 single-chain variable fragments. Our specific aims are: (1) To refine a patented platform for aNK cell expansion, focusing on mechanistic dissection and small molecule enhancements; (2) To evaluate rational combinations of current HNSCC therapies with aNK cells; (3) To explore aNK applications with next-generation B7H3-targeting therapeutics against advanced HNSCCs. Achieving these aims will yield essential preclinical data, guiding optimal therapy combinations for Phase I/II trials and potentially transforming advanced HNSCC treatment.
kw: Adaptive NK cell; Head and neck cancer; Immunotherapy; TriKe;  Humanized mice; CAR-NK

title: Harnessing the Regenerative Capacity of the Bat Heart
abs: Heart failure (HF) following acute myocardial infarction (AMI) is one of the leading causes of death and disability in Singapore and worldwide. The objective of this study is to elucidate the myocardial regenerative capacity of the bat heart in order to gain insights and identify new treatment targets for inducing myocardial regeneration post-infarction to replace cardiomyocyte loss and prevent HF following AMI. We hypothesise that adult bat cardiomyocytes remain proliferation-competent and are capable of orchestrating spontaneous myocardial regeneration in response to injury. Aim 1: To demonstrate that the adult bat heart can undergo myocardial regeneration following apical resection or acute myocardial infarction We hypothesise that apical resection and acute myocardial infarction will promote cardiomyocyte proliferation to replace lost cardiomyocytes with minimal fibrotic scarring in the adult bat heart. Aim 2: To elucidate the mechanisms through which the bat heart preserves its regenerative capacity beyond the postnatal period We hypothesise that unlike other mammalian hearts, where increased mitochondrial ROS production, oxidative DNA damage, and activation of the DNA damage response induce cardiomyocyte cell cycle arrest in the postnatal period, bat hearts maintain regenerative capacity due to enhanced ROS scavenging, resulting in reduced oxidative DNA damage and an attenuated DNA damage response. Aim 3: To identify novel mediators of myocardial regeneration in the adult bat heart and validate them in human cell models We hypothesise that the bat heart contains unique targets for inducing cell cycle re-entry in cardiomyocytes leading to efficient myocardial regeneration after injury which can be validated in human cell models of injury. The expected outcomes of this proposal is to discover novel treatment targets for inducing cardiomyocyte proliferation which can be targeted using either small molecules of RNA therapeutics to promote cardiac regeneration to replace injured cardiomyocytes and prevent HF following AMI.
kw: Regeneration; Bat; Heart Failure; Stem cells; Proliferation

title: Investigating the function and interaction partners of heterotrimeric Gα12 in regulating tumor microenvironment, cancer progression and response to therapy
abs: Heterotrimeric guanine nucleotide-binding regulatory proteins (G-proteins) transmit a wide array of extracellular signals from cell surface G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) to intracellular effector molecules. Many GPCRs are upregulated in different cancers, and several of these GPCRs signal through the G12 family of G-proteins. The G12 family, which is comprised of two members as defined by their α-subunits, Gα12 and Gα13, has well-established roles in tumorigenesis and metastasis in solid tumors. Recently, we made the exciting discovery that Gα12 in particular controls the expression of IL-6 and CXCL5 cytokines, which are recognized for their roles in promoting an immune-suppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) and resistance to immune-checkpoint-inhibitors (ICIs). There exist, however, gaps in understanding the mechanism of Gα12 regulation of cytokine production and its role in TME and immune evasion. These gaps in knowledge limit the clinical translation of the findings. In this application, we propose plans to study how Gα12 regulates cytokine production, and how the Gα12-cytokine axis of signaling controls TME, and subsequently tumor growth, invasion, and response to immunotherapy. Specifically, we aim to: (1) confirm the role of IL-6 and CXCL5 in GNA12-regulated tumorigenesis and metastasis, (2) examine the role of G12-cytokine signaling in regulating TME and tumor growth, and as a novel mechanism of immune evasion and poor response to ICIs, and (3) identify GNA12 interacting proteins that mediate G12-regulated cytokine production and cancer properties. Further, we will identify potential routes to development novel cancer therapies and immunotherapy adjuvants, leveraging on the new findings of Gα12 and its interaction partners in shaping the immunosuppressive TME.
kw: G12; cytokine secretion; tumor microenvironment; BioID of interaction proteins; tumor growth and invasion; immune modulation therapy

title: Novel Diagnostics and Therapeutics for Endemic Asian Cancers
abs: There is an unmet clinical need for novel diagnostics and therapeutics for Asian-endemic cancers, often linked to pathogens and carcinogens. This renewed Singapore Translational Research Award (STaR) builds on prior genomic and epigenomic research, particularly in cholangiocarcinoma (CCA) associated with liver fluke and aristolochic acid (AA)-related cancers. Key advancements include the Tissue 500™ diagnostic panel and start-ups Lepidyne and Auristone. This proposal focuses on (1) developing non-invasive early cancer detection, (2) developing novel therapeutic targets, and (3) expanding AI-driven drug discovery. Our proposed diagnostics will leverage collaborations with Lepidyne, Lucence and DXD Hub to refine liquid biopsy techniques using DNA methylation analysis. We aim to develop CCA diagnostics in high-risk populations and expand predictive models integrating multi-omics data. Therapeutic efforts build on our prior discoveries, including targeting PBRM1 and BAP1 in CCA and RCC. Besides planning for their clinical trials such as the use of bortezomib and combined PARP! And LSD1 inhibitors, our current research focuses on establishing our recently discovered ZNF395 as the master regulator of Glutamine Shunt in cancer metabolism. A collaboration with XtalPi (a prominent quantum physics-AI drug discovery company), aims to develop peptide inhibitors for ZNF395, translating research into clinical applications. Additionally, we contribute to the national AI-Drug Discovery Program by integrating in-silico screening through our AI-pipeline called i-DEEP, optimizing drug-target interactions for candidates like MAT2A, and CDK9 to expedite clinical translation. Through this STaR award, we will continue driving biomedical innovation, translating discoveries into impactful healthcare solutions regionally and globally.
kw: Endemic Asian Cancers; Diagnostics; Therapeutics; Translation

title: Evaluating immune pathways in patients with myositis and implications on treatment
abs: Background Idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (IIM) are a group of autoimmune conditions characterized by inflammation of muscles with possible extra-muscular manifestations which can include skin and lung involvement. Particular subtypes of IIM carry different prognosis specifically with regards to interstitial lung disease (ILD) which can lead to high mortality. IIM are currently divided based on clinical, histopathological and serological factors. Myositis-specific and myositis-associated autoantibodies have been identified and are linked to different subtypes of IIM though their role in pathogenesis of the disease have not been fully elucidated. The mainstay of treatment for IIM involves immunosuppression though there is significant variability in treatment regimes. Since the underlying immune mechanisms leading to disease and progression remain unclear, this contributes to the differences in practices. Aim The overall goal is to evaluate the underlying immune pathways driving IIM, particularly to elucidate the differences in the various subtypes of IIM. The objective of this study is to identify how these differences in immune pathways impact clinical outcomes including response to treatment. We hypothesize that different subtypes of IIM are driven by different immune pathways, leading to different responses in treatment. Methods Our approach involves a prospective cohort study of patients diagnosed with IIM and analysis of their immune profile before and after treatment. Clinical data will be analyzed as they undergo treatment, with analysis of their blood samples prior to treatment and at 6 and 12 months post treatment. Significance If successful, this study could contribute significantly to improving clinical outcomes for patient with IIM through increased understanding of underlying pathogenesis of the disease, allowing for identification of specific targets for therapy.
kw: Myositis; Rheumatology; Immunology

title: An artificial intelligence (AI)-driven predictive tool to identify high-risk individuals for lung cancer screening in Singapore (LungAI-Screen)
abs: This proposal aims to address critical gaps in lung cancer through the following specific aims. Firstly, we seek to pioneer the development and validation of an innovative artificial intelligence (AI)-driven predictive model for lung cancer risk stratification to identify high-risk individuals based on individualized risk profiles, particularly females and non-smokers in Singapore. This model will revolutionize early detection efforts by accurately identifying high-risk individuals based on comprehensive demographic, lifestyle and clinical data. The prediction model will be validated across multiple epidemiological cohorts in Singapore. Secondly, we aim to translate these advancements into clinical practice by implementing the validated AI model in a local pilot screening program, evaluating its feasibility and impact on improving patient outcomes. Lastly, we aim to quantify and project population-level historical and future trends in hospitalization utilization and associated healthcare costs related to lung cancer with and without the AI model as a risk assessment tool for screening, providing essential insights into the evolving burden of this disease. This research is crucial for advancing precision medicine in lung cancer by leveraging AI technology to improve risk assessment and early detection. By elucidating trends in healthcare utilization and introducing innovative predictive tools, this study aims to empower clinicians, policymakers, and patients in their fight against lung cancer, ultimately reducing its societal burden, economic costs and improving long-term health outcomes.
kw: AI, lung cancer, risk prediction, screening

title: Cost-effectively implementing an Artificial intelligence Clinical Decision Support for individualized holistic care of chronic RESpiratory patients: The AiRES-CDS project.
abs: Background: The aging Singapore faces significant healthcare burdens from chronic diseases and multimorbidity, but Her phased implementation of a harmonized electronic health records (EHR) system offers an opportunity for artificial intelligence (AI) to solve this problem. The potential lies in the integration of AI-empowered Clinical Decision Support (CDS) program into health systems to automate risk prediction and enable preventive holistic care at the point of care. Chronic respiratory conditions, with their high multimorbidity burden, are ideal for developing such a system. Objectives: To develop a robust AiRES (AI for chronic RESpiratory conditions) CDS alert system that optimizes risk surveillance and individualizes prevention strategies for acute hospitalization in patients with chronic respiratory conditions, and calibrates its usability and cost-effectiveness for swift integration into the Singapore health system . Methods: First, using national health administrative data, we will develop and validate an AI-based tool to predict 6-month risks of both index-disease and all-cause hospitalizations in chronic respiratory patients, considering multimorbidity. Second, we will use Bayesian network analysis to decode the causal prediction pathways underlying hospitalization risks, and develop a rule-based algorithm to automate CDS alerts, recommending the most relevant clinical decisions for healthcare providers. Third, we will perform an early-stage economic evaluation to define target product profiles of the AiRES-CDS alert and quantify system uncertainties, calibrating its economic viability for integration into the EHR system. Finally, we will implement the AiRES-CDS alert program as a proof-of-concept web application, and conduct workshops and a qualitative pilot study to refine the program and examine real-world health outcomes. Feasibility: The study team has obtained all the necessary data and has a strong track-record in building risk prediction models, Bayesian network analysis, cost-effectiveness analysis. Importance: This proposed work is a critical step towards precision medicine and digital health in the context of multimorbidity and population aging.
kw: Artificial Intelligence, Clinical Decision Support, Precision Medicine, Cost Effectiveness, Chronic Respiratory Conditions, Multimorbidity

title: Targeting cancer-secreted extracellular vesicles in cancer cachexia
abs: Cancer-induced cachexia is a muscle-wasting disease that affects up to 80% of the late-stage cancer patients. This disease not only diminishes patients' quality of life but also reduces their responsiveness to chemotherapy, leading to increased mortality rates. Despite ongoing research efforts to unravel the mechanisms of cancer cachexia, persistent knowledge gaps contribute to the current lack of effective treatments. We have identified cancer-derived Extracellular Vesicles (EV) as the crucial mediator of cancer cachexia through a genetic screen in Drosophila. The functions of EVs secreted by cachectic cancers are also conserved in mammals. To further explore the roles of EVs in cancer-induced muscle wasting, we will first investigate the oncogenic signaling pathways that regulates EV formation. Additionally, we will identify and modulate the cargo contents within EV responsible for inducing muscle wasting. Using cross-species approaches involving Drosophila, primary cells, mice and human models, this study aims to uncover new insights into tumor-to-muscle signaling and establish a mechanistic basis for cachexia. The success of this project will accelerate the development of effective treatments for cachectic patients.
kw: Extracellular vesicles; cancer cachexia; mTOR-TFEB; LC3

title: Orally Administrable Hydrogel Therapeutics for Ulcerative Colitis
abs: This proposal aims to develop an orally administrable hydrogel platform for ulcerative colitis (UC) treatment. Specific aims include designing biodegradable hydrogels for mucosal protection, integrating probiotics to restore microbiome balance, and evaluating therapeutic efficacy with in-vivo models. The hypothesis is that a hydrogel platform combining biocompatible materials and probiotics can achieve synergistic effects in alleviating UC symptoms by enhancing mucosal integrity, reducing inflammation, and correcting dysbiosis. The methodology involves engineering hydrogels with tailored biomechanical properties for gastrointestinal compatibility, integrating probiotics for controlled release, and conducting preclinical testing to assess inflammation reduction, mucosal healing, and microbiome modulation. This research addresses critical gaps in UC therapy, offering a non-invasive, targeted solution with significant potential for translational impact in gastrointestinal medicine.
kw: Orally Administrable Hydrogels, Ulcerative Coliti, Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD), Mucosal Protection

title: Immune-Stimulating Anti-Cancer RNA Lipid Nanoparticle Design with Deep Learning
abs: Cancer immunotherapy has revolutionized oncology by harnessing the immune system to target tumors. Effective activation of dendritic cells and T cells is essential for robust anti-tumor responses. However, current mRNA-based immunotherapy delivery systems often fail to achieve optimal immune stimulation, highlighting the need for improved lipid nanoparticle (LNP) formulations that enhance both mRNA delivery and immune activation. To address this challenge, we propose an integrated approach combining high-throughput experimental screening with deep learning to optimize LNP design. Our central hypothesis is that systematic screening of LNP formulations can identify compositions that maximize immune activation, and that deep learning models can predict these properties based on chemical characteristics, enabling rapid in silico screening of extensive LNP libraries. Aim 1: We will screen a diverse LNP library to establish a dataset linking lipid composition to immune activation and mRNA delivery efficiency. Cytokine profiling and luciferase reporter assays will be used to assess immune stimulation and delivery efficacy, respectively, identifying lead LNP candidates. Aim 2: Using the dataset from Aim 1, we will develop a deep learning model, COMET-I, to predict the immunogenicity and delivery efficiency of LNPs. In silico-identified candidates will undergo in vitro validation to accelerate the discovery of immune-stimulating formulations. Aim 3: Optimized LNP formulations delivering IL-15 mRNA will be tested in colorectal cancer mouse models to evaluate their therapeutic efficacy and safety. MC38 tumor models will be used to assess tumor suppression, establishing a foundation for improved LNP-based cancer therapies. This study integrates experimental and AI-driven approaches to revolutionize the design of immune-stimulating LNPs. By advancing cancer immunotherapy through safer, more effective treatments, this work will pave the way for precision LNP-based therapies applicable to a wide range of cancers.
kw: cancer; vaccines; RNA therapeutics; deep learning

title: Genome-Wide Antibody-Antigen Interaction Prediction Through Large Language Models
abs: Antibody-antigen interactions are fundamental to the development of antibody-based therapeutics and vaccines. However, accurately predicting these complex interactions remains a challenge. This proposal presents a novel computational strategy, leveraging advanced artificial intelligence (AI) to achieve precise and efficient antibody-antigen interaction predictions. Central to this approach is the development of a specialized protein language model, AbAgLM, specifically designed for antibody-antigen interactions. Unlike conventional models trained on individual protein datasets, AbAgLM is pre-trained on large-scale protein-protein interaction data and fine-tuned using antibody-antigen-specific datasets, enabling it to capture critical interaction details often missed by traditional methods. This research proposes two AI-driven models based on AbAgLM: one for rapid identification of antibody-antigen interactions and another for assessing interaction strength. This dual-model framework bridges the limitations of current methods, which either focus solely on interaction probabilities or depend heavily on structural prediction tools. Additionally, the project will construct a comprehensive human genome-wide antibody-antigen interaction network, offering unprecedented insights into the design of antibody-based therapeutics and vaccines. Preliminary studies demonstrate the promise of this approach. The pre-trained language model has already outperformed state-of-the-art methods, such as ESM2 and AlphaFold-Multimer, in predicting protein-protein interactions and interface contacts. These results validate the model’s ability to capture essential features of molecular interactions with higher accuracy. By integrating AI-driven predictions with large-scale interaction network construction, this research has the potential to revolutionize antibody-based drug development. The outcomes promise to improve therapeutic precision, accelerate vaccine design, and provide new tools for addressing complex diseases.
kw: Antibody-antigen; interaction prediction; protein-protein contact; large language models; human genome

title: Glycine supplementation as a novel treatment for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease
abs: Background: Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (MASLD) is the most common chronic liver disease, ranging from simple hepatic steatosis to Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatohepatitis (MASH). Individuals with MASH and advanced fibrosis (“fibrotic MASH”) risk developing liver cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma and death. Hence, MASLD needs to be treated early and aggressively. There is only one approved pharmacologic agent with limited effect, and novel therapies are urgently needed. Glycine is deficient in MASLD, and in rodents, this led to impaired glycine-dependent metabolic reactions and MASLD. Further, dietary glycine supplementation in rodents and non-human primates improved hepatic steatosis, inflammation, and fibrosis. However, in humans with MASLD, the dysregulated glycine-dependent pathways have not been identified, nor has the effectiveness of glycine supplementation been examined. Aims and hypothesis: Hypothesis: Patients with fibrotic MASH have impaired glycine-dependent metabolic pathways, which can be corrected using dietary glycine supplementation. In addition, glycine supplementation reduces the severity of MASLD by decreasing hepatic steatosis. Aim 1: To identify the defect(s) in the glycine-dependent metabolic pathways in patients with fibrotic MASH by comparing the differences in glycine conjugation detoxification reactions, GSH synthesis, redox balance, and 1-carbon cycle metabolites levels between patients with fibrotic MASH and healthy controls. Aim 2: To determine the effect of dietary glycine supplementation on hepatic steatosis and glycine-dependent metabolic pathways compared to placebo at 26 weeks in patients with fibrotic MASH. Methods: This project has two parts. Study 1 compares glycine-dependent metabolic pathway measures in 30 individuals with fibrotic MASH and 30 healthy controls. Study 2 will be a randomized placebo-controlled trial to evaluate the effect of 26-week dietary glycine supplementation on hepatic steatosis and glycine-dependent metabolic pathways versus 26-week placebo in patients with fibrotic MASH. Impact: This proposal continues my earlier research and may lead to a novel, effective, safe, and affordable treatment for MASLD.
kw: Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver ; Fatty Liver; Glycine Supplements; Glycine Conjugation Detoxification Reaction; Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatohepatitis; Randomized Controll Trial

title: Towards Healthy Ageing: Decoding Cognitive Frailty through Multimodal Markers
abs: Aims and hypothesis: Cognitive frailty, a condition marked by the coexistence of physical frailty and cognitive decline, represents a major challenge to healthy ageing leading to poorer health outcomes, reduced quality of life, and increased healthcare costs. Unlike prior studies that often focus on late-life cognitive frailty, this proposal aims to advance our understanding of cognitive frailty by investigating the role of environmental, lifestyle, and sociocultural factors in its development and progression among middle-aged and older adults utilising both subjective assessments and real-time data capture via a mobile-based app, MRI markers, and machine learning approaches. We hypothesise that adverse conditions, i.e. poor-nutrition, sedentary behaviours, air pollution, low socioeconomic status, and weak social networks, will accelerate the progression of cognitive frailty. Additionally, we propose that structural and functional brain alterations mediate and moderate the relationship between these factors and cognitive frailty. Finally, the development of a machine-learning prediction algorithm leveraging environmental, lifestyle, and MRI data predicts cognitive frailty. Methods: This research is nested within the ongoing Neurological biomarkers of Blood, MRI, and Cognition study, which follows a cohort of 600 participants aged 45–85. We will recontact 300 participants who have completed atleast three years of follow-up. A comprehensive collection of self-reported data, real-time monitoring through mobile-apps, 3Tbrain MRI, physical frailty, and cognitive assessments will be collected at baseline and follow-ups. The machine learning algorithm will consist of an ensemble model (logistic regression, support vector classifier, and gradient boosting). Significance: These findings will contribute to developing personalised interventions aimed at preventing or mitigating cognitive frailty, with potential implications for public health policies and clinical practices. By identifying early predictors and underlying mechanisms, this research will help create effective strategies for maintaining cognitive and physical resilience, promoting healthy ageing, and reducing the burden of cognitive frailty in Singapore and beyond.
kw: Midlife; Cognitive frailty; MRI, Multimodal biomarkers; Machine learning

title: Deciphering the functional role of the menin-RelA/p65 complex in suppressing NF-κB driven tumorigenesis in pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours (PNETs)
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (PNETs) are a group of rare tumours arising from the endocrine pancreas. Despite the increasing global incidence of PNETs, surgical intervention remains to be the only curative solution. Whole genome and exome sequencing of human PNET tissues unanimously identified the tumour suppressor gene, MEN1, to be the most frequently mutated gene. Importantly, approximately 60% of patients with MEN1 mutated PNETs are ineligible for surgery, the only curative treatment available, highlighting an unmet clinical need for treatment options available to these patients. However, to formulate a therapeutic strategy effective for treating MEN1-mutated PNETs, a clear understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying how the MEN1 gene suppresses PNET tumorigenesis is pivotal. The MEN1 gene encodes for a nuclear scaffold protein known as menin, which interacts with a variety of protein partners and epigenetic modulators. However, the identity of the specific partners of menin crucial for menin’s protective role remains understudied. In our preliminary data, we have identified that hyperactive NF-κB is a characteristic feature of human PNETs and confirmed that the NF-κB subunit, RelA, is an important driver of PNET tumorigenesis. Importantly, we have also demonstrated that menin 1) forms a complex with RelA to repress selected NF-κB target genes and 2) antagonizes against NF-κB driven proliferation. As both menin and RelA are known to interact with a plethora of epigenetic modulators, I thus hypothesize that the menin-RelA complex recruits epigenetic modulators to form a hitherto protein complex to epigenetically silence functionally relevant genes and suppress PNET development. In my proposal, I seek to 1) identify functional targets repressed by the menin-RelA complex and 2) the epigenetic modulators present in the menin-RelA complex. Doing so would unravel mechanistic insights into the protective function of the menin-RelA complex and also identify potential therapeutic targets for MEN1-mutated PNETs.
kw: pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours; MEN1; menin; p65; RelA; NF-κB

title: Reducing uncertainty in the estimation of mediated causal effects for randomised trials and observational studies.
abs: # Background Mediated causal effects are causal effects where a variable influences an outcome via a mediator. Mediators can form a chain and the longer the chain of mediators, the larger the sample size needed to detect the mediated causal effect. My proposal seeks to reduce sample size needed by reducing the uncertainty in the estimation of mediated causal effects. My proposal builds on work done as part of my PhD and applies two strategies to reduce the uncertainty. The first is to use the James-Stein estimator to aggregate results of the simulations used to estimate the mediated causal effects and the second uses a method known as prediction powered inference (PPI) to model prediction errors and use it to rectify predictions for outcomes that were not observed. Both strategies can be combined into a single method for estimating mediated causal effects. # Methods The proposed research will be carried out in five phases. The first and second phase is to develop and validate the James-Stein and PPI estimators for estimating mediated causal effects respectively. The third phase is to combine both strategies into a single method. The fourth phase is to apply the methods to a real world dataset to demonstrate utility and the last is to package the software so that it is easily accessible. # Feasibility The proposed plan is feasible and given my prior experience in estimating mediated causal effects and programming in R, I am confident of carrying out the work needed to complete this research. # Importance to science Medical science strives to understand both if and how treatments work, and this understanding needs mediated causal models which can be challenging to estimate. The proposed work aims make these methods more practical for researchers investigating treatment mechanisms.
kw: causal inference, mediation

title: CAR-ing 4ALL: Improving outcomes of CAR T therapy for Acute Lymphoblastic Leukaemia and Lymphomas
abs: Lymphoid cancer is the 4th most common cancer in Singapore and despite chemo-immunotherapy and BMT, 40% relapse and die. Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has revolutionized treatment of previously incurable lymphoid cancers. In NUHS, after CAR T-cell infusion, 97% of 66 relapsed/refractory lymphoid cancer patients went into deep molecular remission and ~70% are cured. This study aims to define which subgroups of patients with lymphoid cancers who will benefit from early CAR T therapy and develop actionable laboratory tests to identify these patients. This study has 3 aims: Aim 1. To define high-risk patients who do not benefit from high dose chemotherapy and BMT and give CAR T therapy early to cure them in first remission. There are 3 trials: • CAR-T-ALL for T-ALL using fratricide-resistant CD7 CAR, a novel CAR from NUS. • ALaCART for B-ALL using CD19 with or without CD22 or CD123 CAR depending on antigen expression. • CARPool for large B-cell lymphoma with Epo-Rm CD19 CAR that harnesses erythropoietin signalling to improve CAR T persistence (starting April 2025). Aim 2. Using NGS, we will study how target antigens (CD19, CD22, CD7 and CD123) are lost. We will BH3 profile blasts and determine their sensitivity to venetoclax. Aim 3. We will purify long-term persisting CAR T-cells from patients and determine their molecular profile and the clinical and biological features that predict CAR T persistence. I have 1. Strong track record of successful innovative trials in ALL (MS2003, MS2010). 2. MOH licensed laboratory tests for acute leukaemia and CART. 3. GMP and infused >66 patients with CART. 4. QoL study (Growing QoLas) This grant is innovative and feasible. If successful, we will transform care of relapsed/refractory lymphoid cancers and establish CAR T therapy as a clinical service, bringing economic returns to Singapore.
kw: CAR T; immunotherapy; lymphoma; acute lymphoblastic leukaemia; precision medicine

title: In Vivo Base and Prime Editing of Haemopoietic Stem Cells expressing Common Beta-Globin Mutations in Humanized Mouse Models derived from Transfusion-dependent Thalassaemia Patients using Non-Integrating Vectors: A Scalable Model for Screening and Prediction of Molecular Effects of Gene Modification Therapies
abs: >300 pathological mutations that cause β-thalassaemia benefit from a genome editing approach which causes less genotoxicity than transgene integration. Global accessibility of ex-vivo gene modification therapies (GMT) using CRISPR/Cas or integrated transgenes to treat transfusion-dependent β-thalassaemia (TDT) is restricted by prohibitive costs and myeloablation-related morbidities, and it is typically not available in populations with high TDT prevalence. This burden can be partially addressed by adopting an in-vivo strategy. In-vivo GMT is avoided due to potential integration mutagenesis. Biosafety can be enhanced with non-integrating vectors which can package large editors, and base/prime editing which causes less genomic injury than CRISPR/Cas but presents challenges with the vast array of pathogenic mutations in TDT. To increase its clincial applicability, in-vivo GMT requires a library of editors designed for the commonest mutations, packaged in ready-to-use vectors efficient in transducing haemopoietic stem cells (HSC), with minimal off-target effects. This requires extensive, scalable and cost-effective editor and vector screening. We have identified four recurrent, pathogenic β-globin mutations amenable to base/prime editing in our TDT patients, from whom we have derived induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSC). Our goal is to produce a scalable in-vitro system to screen vectors, predict editing effects on HSC function and test in-vivo effectiveness. Our specific aims are to (1A) Design and screen base/prime editors and non-integrating vectors for the target mutations using patient-derived iPSC; (1B) Investigate vector transduction molecular effects on haemopoietic function using induced HSC and humanized mice; (2) Interrogate in-vivo editing with promising vectors in patient-derived humanized mice. These will test the overarching hypothesis that in-vivo HSC-directed GMT can efficiently and safely correct pathogenic β-globin mutations. Advantages of this research include personalized in-vitro systems to predict molecular consequences of editing on a scale not possible with animal models, and a library of editing tools applicable to common Asian mutations.
kw: haemopoietic stem cell, induced pluripotent stem cell, thalassaemia major, non-integrating lentiviral vectors, lipid nanoparticles, humanized mouse model

title: Optimising Cardiovascular Risk Prediction Strategies for people with Familial Hypercholesterolemia
inst: Khoo Teck Puat Hospital Pte Ltd
abs: Background: Cardiovascular risk among people with Familial Hypercholesterolemia (FH) is heterogenous. Risk stratification is important to personalise intensity of therapy and guide family screening approaches. Current risk stratification in FH has limitations. Clinical criteria has limited accuracy in predicting a genetic variant, and traditional cardiometabolic risk factors do not completely account for the heterogeneity in risk. Additional strategies are needed to enhance the clinical utility and accuracy of clinical risk stratification. Aims: Our aim is to derive risk stratification strategies for FH by improving clinical prediction of a genetic variant and investigating the influence of cardiometabolic factors, Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS) and lipid metabolites on cardiovascular outcomes. Methods: Prospective cohort within SG100K with either the FH phenotype (LDL-C >4.9 mmol/l) or a genetic variant in causative genes. Participants will be grouped into clinical categories: Definite, Probable, Possible, Unlikely FH. Primary Outcome is any cardiovascular event during follow up while Secondary outcome will be increase ( >5%) in carotid artery intima media thickness (CIMT) in the follow up measurement, compared to baseline. Baseline clinical data collection for all participants. Whole genome sequencing performed and PRS calculated. Cardiovascular outcomes will be determined through national registries (TRUST). Follow up carotid ultrasonography for CIMT will be performed for variant-positive participants and matched variant-negative controls. Untargeted metabolomic analysis will be performed. We will investigate the clinical predictors of variant positivity and develop a new criteria for clinical implementation. Study differences, between genetic and non-genetic FH, in the influence of cardiometabolic risk factors and PRS on cardiovascular outcomes, according to the number of cardiovascular risk factors present and PRS score. Identify metabolites that may influence cardiovascular risk. Clinical Translation. Develop a care strategy based on the derived risk stratification approaches to guide intensity of therapy and right-siting of care for patients with FH in Singapore.
kw: Familial Hypercholesterolemia; Precision Medicine; Risk stratification

title: Investigating Cardiometabolic Risk Factors and Cognitive Decline: A Longitudinal Study Using AI-Driven Predictive Models
inst: Khoo Teck Puat Hospital Pte Ltd
abs: Cognitive impairment is increasingly recognized as a significant complication associated with metabolic and cardiovascular risk factors, including diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and obesity. Despite the growing prevalence of these conditions, the mechanisms linking cardiometabolic health to cognitive decline remain poorly understood. This study aims to elucidate these pathways and develop predictive models to identify individuals at risk of cognitive impairment early. Utilizing data from the longitudinal Biomarkers and Cognition Study, Singapore (BIOCIS), which follows 1,500 participants aged 30 to 95, we will analyze cognitive trajectories and their key predictors. These predictors include traditional cardiometabolic risk factors, neuroimaging markers, blood-based biomarkers of neurodegeneration and neuroinflammation, and retinal imaging measures. Advanced machine learning techniques will be employed to construct predictive models. These models will be rigorously validated using cross-validation techniques and assessed based on performance metrics such as the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC). To ensure clinical utility, explainability strategies will be incorporated, enhancing model interpretability and applicability in real-world healthcare settings. A primary outcome of this research is the creation of a risk prediction calculator tailored to the Asian population. This tool will integrate clinically relevant cardiometabolic and vascular factors to enable the early detection of cognitive impairment, supporting timely interventions. By providing a practical and accurate predictive tool for clinicians, this study seeks to improve patient outcomes and advance understanding of the mechanistic links between cardiovascular health and cognitive decline. The findings will also guide the development of preventive strategies to mitigate cognitive impairment in at-risk populations, contributing to the broader goal of addressing the burden of cognitive decline in aging societies.
kw: dementia, cognition, cardiometabolic, artificial intelligence

title:
Local Formal Research Training - Master of Clinical Investigation (MCI)
- Project title: "3D Printed Foot Insoles - Sole Much Better"
abs: Diabetes, affecting global healthcare systems significantly, incurs over $1 billion annually in Singapore. The two main types, Type 1 and Type 2, can lead to complications like peripheral neuropathy, particularly in the feet, heightening the risk of foot ulcers due to impaired sensation. Those with diabetic neuropathy are 1.7 times more likely to develop foot ulcers, which precede 84% of non-traumatic amputations in diabetes patients. Managing diabetic foot ulcers is costly, with over 50% recurring within three years. Currently, foot screenings are infrequent, typically conducted once a year, delaying necessary interventions. Therapeutic footwear, especially custom-made insoles, effectively relieves plantar pressure and prevents wounds but requires time-consuming manual production and multiple podiatrist visits. This study explores the potential of 3D printing as a solution, offering rapid, customized insoles that precisely address pressure points and reduce waste. A randomized control trial with 50 participants will compare the effectiveness of 3D-printed insoles to traditional CAD-CAM insoles in reducing plantar pressure and promoting healing. Outcomes will be assessed through plantar pressure data and patient satisfaction, providing insights into the feasibility of 3D-printed insoles as a cost-effective, patient-centered diabetic foot care option.
kw: diabetes; diabetic foot ulcer; 3D-printing; custom insoles; podiatry

title: Evaluating the Carbon Footprint of Acute Care Pathways and Strategies for Mitigation
abs: The healthcare sector contributes 4-5% of global greenhouse gas emissions; however data on the carbon footprint (associated direct or indirect greenhouse gas emissions) of medical drugs, devices, and clinical services is limited, preventing clinicians from identifying major emission sources and implementing mitigation strategies. Although inpatient care is a significant contributor, a gap exists in research employing process-based life cycle assessments (LCA) to evaluate acute care pathways. This study aims to estimate the carbon footprint of five acute care pathways—stroke, acute myocardial infarction, hip fracture, asthma, and dengue—in a Singapore hospital, from emergency admission to discharge, and to model mitigation strategies targeting hotspots (largest sources of greenhouse gas emissions). Primary activity data will be collected at Changi General Hospital. The functional unit will be the clinical pathway for one patient and for each pathway, five patients will be analyzed. The environmental impact of each item within set boundaries will be assessed using a process-based LCA of the greenhouse gas emissions, or extracting data from existing literature and adjusting the data for local use. In the event no existing data is available or relevant characterisation factors are absent, a top down Environmentally Extended Input-Output approach will be used. The process-based LCA will be conducted following ISO 14044 guidelines and modelled using the OpenLCA platform and Ecoinvent database, with the greenhouse gas emissions associated with each pathway expressed as carbon dioxide equivalents (CO2e). Hotspots within pathways will be identified, and mitigation strategies will be modelled through literature review and clinician engagement. The findings will empower clinicians with actionable data on the carbon footprint of their daily practices, contribute to a global open-access platform led by the National University of Singapore Centre for Sustainable Medicine and provide insights into delivering high-quality patient care while transitioning to low-carbon care pathways.
kw: Carbon Footprint; Healthcare Sustainability; Care Pathways; Life Cycle Assessment;

title: Upfront biopsy in suspected malignant pleural effusions
abs: Introduction Malignant pleural effusions (MPEs) account for more than 125,000 hospital admissions per year in the United States and estimated inpatient charges of greater than $5 billion per year. MPEs are also associated with significant morbidity and an average survival of 4 - 7 months. The goals of care are therefore to achieve early diagnosis and symptom control, whilst minimising healthcare utilisation. Because of the poor yield (approximately 32%) of pleural aspiration, upfront pleural biopsy with diagnostic yields of 95% are an attractive approach. However, this approach has never been evaluated prospectively or compared with usual practice of performing pleural aspiration as a first step. We therefore aim to perform a feasibility study comparing upfront biopsy versus standard of care, which will inform a larger definitive study. Aims We sought to determine the acceptability of randomisation and an achievable recruitment rate in a feasibility randomised controlled trial (RCT) comparing an upfront biopsy approach versus standard of care in suspected MPEs. A secondary aim is to compare the time required and number of procedures performed, to achieve a diagnosis. Methodology This single centre trial will aim to recruit 40 participants over an 8-month period. Patients aged ≥ 18 years with suspected MPE will be invited to participate. Participants will be randomised to an upfront biopsy strategy, with either thoracoscopic or image guided pleural biopsy in the intervention group, versus standard of care in the control group. At baseline and at the 12th week follow up, patient demographics, symptom and quality of life scores will be recorded. The primary outcome of interest is the acceptability rate for participation and randomisation. Secondary outcomes are the time and number of pleural procedures to achieve full histological diagnosis, time to treatment decision made, number of hospitalisation days, procedural complications, quality of life and dyspnea scores.
kw: pleural effusion; cancer

title: Pioneering locoregional therapy clinical decision support system for patients with hepatocellular carcinoma
abs: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), the most prevalent form of primary liver cancer, is the third leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide. Treatment options include locoregional therapy, surgery and chemotherapy. Up to 60% of HCC patients undergo locoregional therapies, which comprise transarterial chemoembolization, ablation, and transarterial radioembolization. Treatment recommendations usually follow the latest 2022 Barcelona-Clinic Liver Cancer (BCLC) Guidelines which have inherent limitations, these are recognized by the authors who advocate tailored treatment approach following discussion in a multidisciplinary tumor board. BCLC guidelines incorporate selected clinical and radiological parameters, excluding radiomic data. Although prior research has explored development of clinical decision support system (CDSS) treatment recommendation models for HCC patients to improve patient outcomes, such studies are limited, and exclude transarterial radioembolization. This study seeks to utilise artificial intelligence to evaluate clinic-radiological data for the provision of individualized locoregional treatment recommendations for HCC patients. We propose to develop a CDSS focusing on locoregional therapies for HCC patients deemed unsuitable for surgical resection, liver transplant, and systemic therapy. We hypothesize that integrating clinical parameters and radiomic features can enhance treatment recommendations, improving patient outcomes such as post-treatment survival and tumor recurrence. By leveraging novel clinical and radiomic parameters not currently utilized in BCLC guidelines, our CDSS aims to adopt a precision medicine approach to improve clinical decision making. The research is structured into three phases. Phase 1 involves creating a comprehensive registry from existing electronic health records featuring clinic-radiological data of HCC patients treated with locoregional therapy at our institution. Phase 2 focuses on optimizing data for analysis by organizing clinical datasets. Additionally, image data is prepared for radiomic analysis through image segmentation, feature extraction, and feature selection. In Phase 3, we will develop a CDSS model that incorporates clinical and radiomics data, facilitating locoregional treatment modality recommendations to improve patient survival outcomes.
kw: Interventional Radiology; Radiomics; Hepatocellular Carcinoma; Deep Learning

title: Automated Surgical Planning in Chinese Orthognathic Surgery Patients
abs: Background: Orthognathic surgery (OGS) planning is a complex and time-consuming process requiring collaboration from multiple specialists. The subjective nature of esthetics and consideration of multiple factors further complicate the process, leading to significant variations in plans between surgeons. Despite the potential benefits of artificial intelligence (AI) in automated OGS planning, current research is limited by small sample sizes and neglect of a critical factor: the patient's occlusion or bite. Aims: This study aims to develop an algorithm for automated planning of Skeletal III patients undergoing OGS, integrating occlusion into the AI training model. Hypothesis: The null hypothesis is that there is no significant difference in the accuracy of orthognathic surgical outcomes predicted by an automated planning algorithm versus planning by expert specialists. Methods: A sample of approximately 500 patients will be retrieved from the centre's database. Data will be anonymized, and patient information, intra-oral scans, cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) scans, and virtual surgical plans will be retrieved. A geometric deep learning model will be developed to predict transformation parameters, taking into account the occlusion. The model will be trained using a multi-layer perceptron, and the network will learn to minimize losses between predicted and ground truth surgical plans. Significance & feasibility: This study breaks new ground by incorporating occlusion as a crucial factor in its prediction model, with the largest sample size of any previous study. It does not require extensive data annotation, representing significant time savings. Additionally, the input data is non-sensitive, eliminating the need for hospital intranet integration. As a result, implementation is expected to be seamless, enhancing existing systems and workflows.
kw: Artificial Intelligence; Advanced Digital Technology; Orthognathic Surgery; Virtual Surgical Planning

title: Effectiveness of Whole Body Vibration Therapy and Usual care compared to Usual care in improving muscle mass, strength and function in Older Adults
abs: Background: The prevalence of Frailty and Sarcopenia is increasing with increasing proportion of older adults in the population. While screening for frailty and sarcopenia has become more common, frailty interventions are still developing. Effective interventions include resistance exercise programs that are progressive and sustained. However, take up rate and adherence to these programs are low due to many barriers like time, cost and convenience to the older adult. Many older adults who are frail may be unable to adhere to exercise programs due to cognitive impairment and tolerability. An alternative modality, Whole Body Vibration Training (WBVT), has emerged with evidence in improving muscle strength and function which may be easier to complete and a safe alternative. Aim: Our study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of a novel progressive 4-week, thrice-weekly WBVT intervention and usual care compared to usual care in improving muscle mass, strength and function in the pre-frail and mildly frail older adult. Methods: 20 participants would be randomly allocated to each arm. Data on participants’ demographics, medical history, quality of life (EQ-5D-5L), physical activity level using the Physical Activity Scale for the Elderly (PASE), Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS) score, Malnutrition Universal Screening Test (MUST) and Modified Barthel’s Index (100-point) scores would be collected. Physical measurements including body composition analysis for Appendicular Skeletal Mass Index (ASMI), hand grip strength (HGS), isometric knee extensor strength, gait speed (GS) and 5 timed chair stands would be performed. The measurements would be done at 3 points, namely pre-intervention (baseline), post-intervention and at 6 months. Qualitative data on participants’ user experience would be recorded in the form of a survey and post intervention quality of life (EQ-5D-5L) and PASE scores would be repeated. Secondary outcomes would include falls rate during the study, 1-year unplanned emergency department visits, hospitalizations as well as all-cause mortality. (300 words)
kw: Ageing; Frailty; Sarcopenia; Exercise; Older Adults

title: Blinatumomab Integration in Frontline Therapy for B-Cell Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia: Harnessing T-Cell Dynamics to Improve Outcomes in Ma-Spore ALL Trials
abs: This research aims to optimize the integration of blinatumomab, an anti-CD3/CD19 bispecific T-cell engager, into frontline therapy for B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL) within the Ma-Spore ALL trials. While blinatumomab has shown remarkable efficacy in relapsed/refractory B-ALL, its potential to improve frontline treatment outcomes remains underexplored. The study hypothesizes that the optimal timing for blinatumomab administration coincides with peak T-cell activity, characterized by elevated effector memory T cells, reduced regulatory T cells (Tregs), and minimal T-cell exhaustion. To address this, the research will employ a dual approach: Retrospective Analysis: Peripheral absolute lymphocyte counts (ALC) from patients treated under Ma-Spore protocols will be analyzed to identify time points with peak lymphocyte activity during chemotherapy cycles. Prospective Analysis: Flow cytometry will be used to characterize T-cell subsets, including cytotoxic T cells (CD3+/CD8+), Tregs (CD4+/CD25high/FOXP3+), and markers of T-cell exhaustion (PD-1, Tim-3, TIGIT). These findings will be correlated with blinatumomab timing to refine its integration into treatment regimens. The feasibility of the study is supported by the availability of Ma-Spore trial data, established treatment protocols, and access to advanced immunophenotyping tools. The study’s importance lies in its potential to significantly improve B-ALL outcomes by reducing relapse rates, enhancing long-term survival, and minimizing treatment-related toxicities. It also contributes to a deeper understanding of T-cell dynamics in cancer therapy, with broader implications for immunotherapy development.
kw: leukemia, pediatric, oncology, blinatumomab, targeted

title: “You sure or not?” Examining the Trust, Acceptance and Adoption of Falls risk – Artificial Intelligence Recommender (FAIR) system by nurses
abs: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) has the power to transform healthcare, analysing electronic health record data and recommending clinicians on appropriate care. However, its adoption in clinical practice remains limited, as highlighted by systematic reviews. A critical facilitator for the integration of AI into clinical decision-making has been identified to be clinician trust and acceptance of these tools as reliable decision partners. Falls risk-Artificial Intelligence Recommender (FAIR) is a prototype AI tool intended to help nurses more effectively identify and manage patients at high risk of falls. However, its success depends on nurses’ trust and acceptance, ensuring it is seen as a valuable tool and not a burden. This requires effective design and implementation strategies that align FAIR with nursing needs and care. . Hypothesis A programme theory guiding FAIR and its implementation will result in (1) Improved nurse trust and acceptance (2) Improved integration of FAIR recommendations into falls risk assessment, (3) Improved identification of falls-risk patients and (4) Reduced nursing time for falls risk assessments Methods An Implementation Science approach will be applied to build and test a programme theory on how FAIR should function and support nurses, with 5 components: 1. A rapid realist review on the application of AI risk models in acute care 2. Focus group interviews with nurses to understand their perceptions on fall risk assessments and AI application. 3. Co-creation workshops with nurses to build a working programme theory of ‘how FAIR should help nurses’ 4. Multimethod feasibility testing of FAIR in a simulated ward 5. Multimethod feasibility testing of FAIR in a general ward Implications This study will provide insights on effective integration of AI into nursing care as demonstrated by FAIR, helping better identify at-risk patients and save time. This provides a blueprint for the integration of AI tools into healthcare.
kw: Implementation Science; Realist Evaluation; Artificial Intelligence; Trust

title: Genetic polymorphisms in drug-resistant epilepsy (GPE)
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Background Despite the increasing availability of pharmacogenomic testing and its potential to guide medication choices, knowledge gaps have hindered its application to the management of epilepsy. Previous studies have reported that certain P450 genotypes such as CYP2C9 and CYP2C19 slow metabolizers are associated with better response to anti-seizure medications (ASMs). However, there has not been any analysis by specific ASM, even though different ASMs have different metabolism pathways. Methodology and approach The proposed study has three phases. Phase A is a cross-sectional study to determine the prevalence of drug-resistant epilepsy amongst epilepsy patients who are CYP2C9 or CYP2C19 slow metabolizers. The majority of patients who are recruited in Phase A can be segued into Phase B of the study. Phase B is a prospective observational study of drug-responsive epilepsy patients to determine the 3-year incidence of drug-resistant epilepsy, categorized by CYP2C9 or CYP2C19 metabolizer genotype and analysed by each ASM (both P450-metabolized ASMs and non-P450-metabolized ASMs). Phase B of the study will identify the P450 genotype and the ASM combination that has the largest impact on the incidence of drug-resistant epilepsy. Phase C of the study is a randomized controlled trial investigating the utility of P450 genotype testing before ASM selection, amongst patients with newly diagnosed epilepsy. Importance of proposed research Identification of the specific combinations of P450 genotypes and ASMs that have the largest impact on seizure control can help to shorten the time taken to find the right ASM for a given patient, reduce the patient’s frequency of seizures, reduce the incidence of drug-resistant epilepsy, save multiple visits to the clinic, save multiple blood draws to check serum ASM concentration, and reduce both morbidity and healthcare costs.
kw: Pharmacogenomics; epilepsy; seizure; refractory; resistant; drug

title: Investigating the potential of chimeric antigen receptor T cells as a desensitization strategy in patients with kidney failure
abs: Transplantation is the best modality of kidney replacement therapy for patients with kidney failure. However, many patients are unable to receive a transplant due to the potential for irreversible rejection mediated by pre-formed donor-specific anti-HLA antibodies. Desensitization strategies to reduce these antibodies durably remain a critical unmet need in transplantation. Considering the role of B-cells in generating anti-HLA antibodies, we hypothesize that chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cells may hold the potential to eliminate allospecific B-cells and achieve sustained suppression of anti-HLA antibody production. Our aims include investigating the following in kidney failure patients: (1) A comprehensive characterization of the quality and function of T- and B-lymphocytes to determine the feasibility of CAR-T production and identify targets for CAR-T construct, (2) Investigation of the quality of CAR-T transduction, and (3) Investigation of the safety and efficacy of the novel mutant erythropoietin receptor (Epo-RM) CAR construct, which may abrogate the need for lymphodepletion due to the ability for these CAR-T cells to tap additional Epo signaling in these patients with supraphysiological levels of Epo. We aim to recruit sensitized and unsensitized patients on hemodialysis, sensitized KTRs, and healthy controls to isolate peripheral blood mononuclear cells and measure plasma cytokines and erythropoietin levels. A comprehensive investigation of cellular immunobiology will include immunophenotyping by flow cytometry and surface-marker analyses, functional analyses, cytokine secretion assays, and alloreactive cellular responses. CAR manufacture and transduction will be attempted with the conventional CD19 and Epo-RM CAR, and the functional potency of CAR-T cells will be studied in vitro and in vivo. Finally, CAR-T cells will be administered in selected sensitized patients with kidney failure, and the efficacy and safety will be studied. CAR-T cell therapies represent a potential novel frontier of transplantation medicine to provide sensitized patients with kidney failure an opportunity at transplantation while avoiding antibody-mediated rejection.
kw: Kidney Failure; Immunobiology; Alloimmunity; CAR-T; Kidney Transplant; Desensitization

title: Evaluating the clinical and imaging determinants for decision making in the biopsy of PI-RADS 3 lesions in detecting clinically significant prostate cancer
abs: Multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) has been established as a first line investigation for men with clinical suspicion of prostate cancer. The Prostate Imaging-Reporting and Data System (PI-RADS) is a structured reporting scheme which aims to stratify the probability of clinically-significant prostate cancer (csPCa) on mpMRI a scale of 1 to 5, to guide targeted biopsy. Despite 2 revisions, with the latest PI-RADS v2.1 being implemented in 2019, csPCa detection rates in PI-RADS 3 lesions (intermediate probability of clinically significant disease) remains low, with reviews citing 11-20% pooled cancer detection rate. This has led to unnecessary intervention for patients and increased discomfort, while placing greater strain on the healthcare system. This project aims to risk stratify all PI-RADS 3 lesions in both transition and peripheral zones into ‘higher-risk’ and ‘lower-risk’ subgroups. We aim to combine pertinent clinical parameters (prostate specific antigen (PSA), PSA density and prostatic health index), mpMRI features (lesion size, location, diffusion weighted imaging score, presence of enhancement) and radiomics-based techniques to guide decision making for targeted biopsy in PI-RADS 3 lesions, in the identification of csPCa. As the use of radiomics is an emerging and promising tool which allows a quantitative tumour evaluation from mpMRI images via conversion of digital images into mineable high-dimensional data, this can help enhance imaging features available to detect csPCa. The results of our project will allow for risk stratification of PI-RADS 3 lesions in the clinical setting, so that we can prioritize biopsies for ‘higher-risk’ lesions to be performed more urgently in a shorter time frame, thereby reducing the likelihood and risk of transformation of these potentially curative lesions into locally advanced or metastatic disease. Similarly, this will reduce unnecessary biopsies for the patients with ‘lower-risk’ lesions which can be observed on imaging instead, and reduce overall strain on the healthcare system.
kw: clinically significant, prostate cancer, clinical determinants, imaging determinants, decision making, biopsy, PI-RADS 3, transition zone, peripheral zone

title: Assessment of the Diagnostic Accuracy of Artificial Intelligence Solution in the Detection of Pneumonia using Pediatric Chest X-Rays in the Emergency Department
abs: Chest x-ray (CXR) report turnaround times in KK Women’s and Children’s Hospital Children’s Emergency Department (ED) is 24hours due to manpower constraints. The lack of timely and accurate CXR reports may negatively impact the prevalence of antibiotic use, recall rate, and ED revisits. In current standard clinical practice, ED physicians make empirical CXR diagnoses to guide decision for antibiotics. The radiology department worked with the Institute of High Performance Computing and developed a paediatric CXR artificial intelligence (AI) model to detect pneumonia with good pilot results. We propose a pilot study to assess the diagnostic accuracy and prevalence of antibiotic use in treatment of paediatric patients with suspected pneumonia using AI in CXR compared to standard clinical practice. Primary aim is to assess the diagnostic accuracy of AI in CXR for radiological pneumonia detection compared to standard clinical practice. Secondary aim is to assess prevalence of antibiotic use in the treatment of paediatric patients with suspected pneumonia using AI in CXR compared to standard clinical practice. We will perform a study that collates CXRs and clinical information for patients in ED who attended for respiratory symptoms to assess the diagnostic accuracy. CXRs will be read by consultant paediatric radiologist (gold standard). We will compare the gold standard with AI model (intervention) and ED physicians (control), and obtain the physicians’ decision on antibiotics based on empirical reading. Primary outcome measure would be the receiver operating characteristics of AI in CXR and standard clinical practice in the radiological diagnosis of pneumonia. Secondary outcome measure would be the prevalence of antibiotic use for treatment of suspected pneumonia with and without the aid of AI in CXR pneumonia detection. With the results of this pilot data, we will design a future study to assess the cost-effectiveness of deploying this AI solution into clinical practice.
kw: Paediatric, Chest X-ray, Pneumonia, Artificial intelligence, Diagnostic accuracy

title: Centre for Advancing Regulatory Science Research in Next-Generation Therapeutics (ASCENT)
abs: The vision of ASCENT is to enable Singapore to be a leading hub for regulatory science and: a. Phase 1 will address scientific gaps in priority areas, focusing on the development of new tools and methods for robust evaluation and surveillance of new biotherapeutic modalities, and refining regulatory guidelines using science-based evidence.

title: Research Training Fellowship to Support Singapore Biodesign Fellowship 2025
abs: The Singapore Biodesign Innovation Fellowship is an intensive 6 months hands-on multidisciplinary team-based training on the entire biodesign process of health technology innovation, focused on developing new health technologies for unmet clinical needs in Asia. Following are the components/structure of the programme that the fellows will embark on: 1) Workshops – Bootcamp (5 days), Intro to product development & QMS workshop (1 day), Business Model Innovation workshop (3days) & Business Implementation (2 days) 2) Relevant conferences and events such as APAC Medtech Forum (2 days) 3) Pitch Training with a pitch coach 4) IP consultations with local and international Patent attorneys and officers 5) Local Immersion for 3 weeks typically in a hospital 6) Regional Immersion for 2 weeks typically in a country like China to understand the ecosystem variances from local practices 7) US Immersion for 3 weeks at Stanford and Forgarty Innovation to meet with experts, network, attend workshops and also present top need and concepts for that need, to obtain feedback In addition, the fellows will also have weekly or bi-weekly sessions with various mentors and innovation head to guide them along in the fellowship.

title: Stochastic subgradient methods for nonsmooth nonconvex optimization
abs: We study the design and convergence of efficient algorithms for solving nonsmooth nonconvex (NSNC) optimization problems, possibly with constraints. These optimization problems have great importance in deep learning as they include the training of the loss function of a deep neural network with nonsmooth activation functions (e.g., ReLU) which typically lacks certain regularity property (known as Clarke regularity, a property that is assumed to hold in many conventional problems). In the training of deep neural networks, stochastic subgradient based methods, including the stochastic subgradient descent method (SGD) and ADAM, have become the default optimization methods to use. Despite extensive study over the past decades, most existing works assumed Clarke regularity in the objective functions when analysing the convergence of various algorithms, thus leading to a gap between theoretical analysis and real-world applications. To handle the nonsmoothness of the objective functions, some recent works employ ordinary differential equation (ODE) approaches to establish the convergence properties for stochastic subgradient methods in minimizing NSNC functions. However, their results are primarily restricted to unconstrained cases. On the other hand, when establishing the convergence properties of a given subgradient method, it is important to guarantee its global stability (i.e., uniform boundedness of its iterates), which is required in existing ODE approaches. Despite this, most existing works assumed that global stability holds without providing any explicit guarantee. Although several pioneering works have conducted global stability for stochastic subgradient methods, their analysis is restricted to only SGD and momentum SGD, but not the recent advanced variants such as ADAM, AdamW, signSGD, etc. In this project, we aim to overcome some of the stated inadequacies and advance the state-of-the-art NSNC optimization, especially those arising from deep neural networks. We consider developing stochastic subgradient methods for nonsmooth nonconvex unconstrained, as well as constrained, optimization problems and establish the corresponding mathematical foundations for our developed methods. We first focus on the stability of stochastic subgradient methods in unconstrained NSNC optimization where the objective functions may not be Clarke regular. We aim to develop a general framework to establish the global stability for a wide range of stochastic subgradient methods that admit coercive Lyapunov functions. Subsequently, we will demonstrate that a wide range of stochastic subgradient type methods, including SGD, momentum SGD, SignSGD, and ADAM, fit into our proposed framework and thus inherit the established convergence guarantees in the training of nonsmooth neural networks. Notably, we will develop some novel stochastic subgradient methods based on our proposed framework, and evaluate their efficiency in training neural networks and generalization perfor
