title: Reverse engineering of reinforced composites with multiphysics couplings
abs: The aim of this project is to reverse engineer 3D printed reinforced composites with self-morphing capabilities and Multiphysics couplings for new intelligent complex materials. The project will make use of recent 3D printing methods developed by the PI, finite element modelling, machine learning, and high throughput screening algorithms. By employing specific microstructures based on microplatelet specific orientations, as well as specific chemical nature of these microplatelets, Multiphysics couplings will be realized where the morphing will be associated with a change in functional properties due to the local strain developed in the composite. Physical samples will be 3D printed to demonstrate potential application to robotics, energy harvesting, precision machining, and others. Contrary to existing morphing systems, the key novelty here is that the composites also exhibit strong mechanical properties (not soft robotics) and that the mechanical and functional elements are all embedded together within the composite composition. The resulting materials are expected to be robust, resilient against delamination and able to operate in more stringent environments that existing soft materials.
kw: Microstructured materials; morphing; multiphysics couplings; machine learning; reverse engineering; applications;

title: Innovative integration of bipolar membrane electrodialysis (BMED) into seawater desalination plants for decarbonization, resource recovery, and low-energy, low-chemical desalination
abs: Seawater desalination is an energy-intensive process, contributing significantly to carbon emissions. On the other hand, seawater can act as a large carbon sink to absorb CO2 for storage. In this project we propose to develop an innovative system via integrate bipolar membrane electrodialysis (BMED) into seawater reverse osmosis (SWRO) desalination plants to valorize waste SWRO brine for producing chemicals (i.e., acid and base) that can be strategically used for decarbonization and simultaneously reducing both energy and chemical consumptions during desalination. While NaOH is used to alkalize seawater to either immobilize dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC), HCO3-, in terms of calcite (CaCO3) or enhance absorption of CO2 from atmosphere, HCl is used to acidify seawater to convert DIC into H2CO3 or CO2 where highly purified and concentrated CO2 can be captured and utilized for other purposes. When feed seawater is alkalized to remove DIC, its pH is elevated to above 9, which enhances boron removal at the 1st pass SWRO, thereby eliminating the 2nd pass RO from conventional desalination plants, leading to ~0.5 kWh/m3 energy saving and significant CAPEX reduction. When alkalizing SWRO brine, high-value Mg associated materials with high purities can be recovered such as Mg(OH)2, cement additive MgCO3 and reactive cement MgO, at a lower energy consumption and carbon emissions compared with Portland cement production, suggesting a significant amount of carbon abatement. Moreover, an innovative electrochemically assisted ultrafiltration (EAUF) coupled with high performance SiC ceramic membranes is also proposed which can simultaneously realize pretreating seawater and carbon sequestration. Both laboratory and pilot-scale studies will be performed to optimize and demonstrate the proposed BMED-integrated system. It is expected that that the proposed system and method can decarbonize >2.5 million tonnes of CO2 capture per year for all the SWRO desalination plants in Singapore. The success of this project will help Singapore significantly reduce its carbon emissions.
kw: seawater desalination; decarbonization; resource recovery; bipolar membrane electrodialysis (BMED); electrochemically assisted ultrafiltration (EAUF)

title: MedicaTwin: A Collaborative Digital Twin for Accessible Digitalization of HealthCare Environments
abs: The MedicaTwin project aims to develop and validate an innovative digital twin authoring system tailored for non-technical healthcare staff and patients. The specific objectives are to implement MedicaTwin, enabling hospital staff to collaboratively create and maintain interactive 3D environments for various medical operations, and to validate the system through a user study involving medical personnel and patients in a controlled hospital environment. The project posits that MedicaTwin will significantly improve the ease and efficiency with which healthcare staff can create and manage digital twins for medical applications. Additionally, it is anticipated that the use of MedicaTwin will enhance operational efficiency, patient care, and satisfaction in a hospital setting. To achieve these goals, the project adopts a Research-through-Design (RtD) approach to iteratively develop and refine MedicaTwin. In the initial phase, the system will be built upon the SIT's existing demoConstruct framework, incorporating enhanced functionalities such as 3D reconstruction, scenario simulation, and user interfaces tailored for medical settings. In the subsequent phase, the system's effectiveness will be validated through a user study involving healthcare professionals and patients at Tan Tock Seng Hospital (TTSH). Participants will engage in simulated realistic scenarios to provide qualitative and quantitative feedback on system usability, effectiveness, and impact. The feasibility of MedicaTwin is underpinned by the strong foundational technology of demoConstruct, which has been validated through prior peer-reviewed publications. The collaboration with TTSH ensures the system’s real-world applicability and leverages expert insights, enhancing the project's credibility and potential impact. This study is poised to significantly advance the field by democratizing the use of sophisticated digital twin technologies among non-technical staff, thereby leading to substantial improvements in patient care, operational efficiency, and cost-effectiveness. The anticipated success of this project could catalyze further research and development in the domain of digital twin technologies within the healthcare sector.
kw: Digital Twins, Metaverse, 3D Authoring, 3D Reconstruction, Healthcare, Rehabilitation, Virtual Reality

title: PROJECT VICTORIA: Versatile Incorporation of C-V2X To Others Relying on Artificial Intelligence
abs: Specific Aims: 1. Develop a system to determine precise locations of construction vehicles and workers using AI and a network of Software Defined Radios (SDRs). 2. Enhance position accuracy to sub-meter levels by integrating Machine Learning (ML) techniques with Time Difference of Arrival (TDOA) localization. 3. Improve collision prediction alerts through ML analysis of Basic Safety Messages (BSM) and enhanced positional data. Hypotheses: 1. AI and SDR networks can provide highly accurate real-time positioning of construction vehicles and workers. 2. ML algorithms can leverage TDOA, pseudo-range, RSSI, and CSI data to enhance positional accuracy beyond conventional methods. 3. ML-based analysis of BSM messages can predict collisions more effectively than traditional trajectory-based methods. Methodology & Approach: - Position Determination: Deploy SDRs with precise timing capabilities across the construction site. Vehicles will be equipped with C-V2X On-board Units (OBUs), and workers will carry wireless devices. By measuring the time differences of signals reaching the SDRs, the system will use TDOA methods for initial position estimates. - Position Enhancement: Integrate ML algorithms to refine TDOA-based estimates using additional data (pseudo-range, RSSI, and CSI). The system will learn the unique propagation characteristics of the RF environment to achieve sub-meter accuracy. - Collision Prediction: Develop ML models to analyze BSM messages in conjunction with enhanced positional data. These models will identify patterns indicative of potential collisions and generate timely alerts. - Data Processing and Communication: Utilize a robust communication infrastructure to process data from SDRs and relay enhanced position data to OBUs via C-V2X Road Side Units (RSUs). title: GAIA: Rethinking Data Center Computation and Communication Design for Green AI
abs: We present an ambitious programme aimed at tackling the significant challenge of energy consumption in Artificial Intelligence (AI) inference, especially in the context of the growing complexity and scale of deep learning models like large language models (LLM). We seek to pioneer a new computing system architecture in data centers, emphasizing energy efficiency and sustainability. The need for this project is underscored by the current energy demands of AI inference – the process of applying pre-trained models to new data to make predictions or decisions, often in real-time. SemiAnalysis estimates that OpenAI operates ~3,617 A100 GPUs to serve roughly 195 million queries per day, consuming 260 MWh energy, comparable to the daily energy usage of 200,000 Singapore households. As AI becomes increasingly integral in various sectors, including healthcare and finance, the associated cumulative energy consumption is a growing concern, necessitating innovative solutions for green AI. Our proposal introduces a forward-thinking approach that revolves around redesigning computing system architecture for data centers to prioritize energy efficiency and sustainability. We will leverage distributed AI inference, where a model is partitioned across multiple devices, to manage the increasing computational demands of complex models. Central to our approach is the integration of energy-efficient computing technologies and the optimization of computer system infrastructure for distributed AI inference. This involves minimizing compute, storage, and networking resource usage through algorithmic advancements and architectural innovations. Our strategy adheres to the reduce, reuse, recycle paradigm: reduce energy consumption through systemic optimizations; reuse by adapting models to existing compute resources and creating a versatile reconfigurable AI accelerator for use across multiple models and tasks; and recycle by repurposing and pooling together older hardware for less demanding AI tasks. To achieve our goal, we propose transitioning to heterogeneous computing in data centers to support dense and sparse tensor operations, fundamental in AI workloads. Our system will integrate GPU, FPGA, and specialized accelerators (Google TPU, AMD AI Engine etc.), addressing the inefficiencies of current homogeneous GPU-based systems. As FPGAs excel in quantized sparse operations and GPUs are ideal for dense operations, we will develop optimized sparse inference acceleration on FPGA and align diverse models to the most efficient hardware for their workloads. With the advent of the new MX data-format as an example, the changing landscape for new data types demonstrates how FPGAs can adapt quickly to play an important role in modern system design. We will shift from a traditional CPU-centric system design to a network-coordinated approach, where the smart network interface will play a crucial role in distributing workloads and facilitating data transmission across heterogeneous

title: Exploring the Functional Insights and Mechanisms of CRISPR-Associated Toxin Systems (CATs)
abs: The CRISPR-Cas system is a versatile adaptive immune mechanism in bacteria, traditionally recognized for its role in targeting and degrading phage DNA/RNA. Recent studies have revealed additional functionalities, such as RNA-guided transport and protease activities, highlighting its potential for novel applications in gene-editing technologies. Our research uncovers a novel CRISPR-associated Toxin (CAT) system within the type I-C CRISPR-Cas3 framework. This system comprises two key proteins, Cat1 and Cat2, which synergistically enhance bacterial defense. Cat2, while inherently toxic, exhibits significantly increased toxicity when interacting with Cat1. This interaction also augments the Cascade complex's R-loop formation, boosting the efficiency of the CRISPR-Cas3 system. Moreover, we have identified a CRISPR-like motif, Cascade-CreA, which regulates Cat2 expression and can sense anti-CRISPR (Acr) proteins, leading to a controlled cell death response to prevent phage propagation. Our research aims to validate two key hypotheses: that the CAT system enhances DNA-targeting efficiency and serves as an anti-anti-CRISPR mechanism, offering a robust bacterial defense against Acr proteins. We will employ advanced biochemical, microbiological, and cryo-electron microscopy techniques to explore these mechanisms and develop new applications for CRISPR technologies. This study has the potential to significantly advance our understanding of bacterial immunity and pave the way for innovative biotechnological tools.
kw: CRISPR-Cas; Adaptive immune system; Toxin-anti toxin; Gene editing; Phage therapy.

title: Voxel-like Integration of Bioprinting and Engineered Spheroids (VIBES) for the Fabrication of Pancreatic Islet Model
abs: The transplantation of pancreatic islets or β cells is highly attractive for the treatment of diabetes. However, this cell replacement therapy suffers from low cell survival rate and requires immediate vascularisation upon transplantation. To address these limitations, this proposal presents a novel 3D bioprinting concept, Voxel-like Integration of Bioprinting and Engineered Spheroids (VIBES), to enable the fabrication of a highly vascularised pancreatic islet model for the future treatment of diabetes. Transplantation of pancreatic islets or beta (β) cells is highly attractive for the treatment of diabetes. However, cell replacement therapy suffers from low cell survival rate and requires immediate vascularisation upon transplantation. To address these limitations, the first aim of this project is to 3D bioprint pre-vascularised spheroids consisting of human pluripotent stem cell (hPSC)-derived β cells and human pancreatic microvascular endothelial cells (HPMECs), leveraging upon the high cellular density, diverse genotypes and phenotypes of spheroids. The second aim is to cooperatively bioprint a perfusable 3D vascular network using co-axial bioprinting, to be integrated with the pre-vascularised spheroids. The third aim is to assemble the spheroids into a geometric 3D pancreatic hPSC-derived β cell model. The results of this project will address the β cell apoptosis due to the lack of vascularisation. Furthermore, the development of a novel concept of 3D spheroid bioprinting provides an engineering solution for vascularising complex soft tissue models and for the fabrication of disease models and drug screening platforms.
kw: 3D Bioprinting; Beta cell; Diabetes; Pancreas; Spheroids; Tissue Engineering

title: Haldane Twistronics: Engineering Novel Topological and Non-Hermitian Moiré Physics via Bilayer Stacking
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: The discovery of chiral edge states in 2D honeycomb lattices by F. Duncan Haldane in 1988 has profoundly impacted condensed matter physics. In this proposal, we propose the novel concept of Haldane hybrid bilayer in which Haldane physics, non-Hermtiain physics, bilayer stacking and moiré superlattice engineering are synergized. By engineering the interplay between Haldane, non-Hermtian and interlayer coupling as well as twisting, we aim to discover new topological and non-Hermitian phenomena unique to bilayer twistroncis with no monolayer counterparts. This proposal aims to address the following specific aims: (1) To establish a comprehensive catalogue of Haldane hybrid bilayers, especially those composed of monolayers with contrasting lattice symmetry classes, and those with small twisted angle forming moiré patterns. (2) To discover novel phase transitions and percolation in Haldane hybrid bilayers in the presence of non-Hermtian effect, so to uncover unusual skin, topological, and topological-skin modes not present in monolayer forms. (3) To simulate and to experimentally realized novel Haldane physics and moiré interference in bilayer heterostructures using electrical circuits. The project is expected to significantly enrich the physics of Haldane and non-Hermtiain system in a bilayer platform. The concept of Haldane hybrid bilayers and their non-Hermitian counterparts introduces an innovative platform to engineer topological phases and skin effects beyond monolayer systems. The use of electrical circuits provides a versatile method to study complex interplays that are challenging to realize in traditional materials and metamaterials. The outcomes of this project are expected to significantly enrich the phenomenology of Haldane systems, paving a way towards not only the fundamental breakthroughs in condensed matter physics, but also towards novel topological and non-Hermitian device applications.
kw: Moiré heterostructures; Haldane model; topological phases; non-Hermitian physics; skin effect

title: Towards Sustainable, Error-Resilient Graph Data Acceleration with Graph Convolutional Neural Networks and Approximate Processing-In-Memory
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) are inherently suited for approximate computing. For instance, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) can tolerate Bit Error Rates (BERs) on a scale of 10^–4, orders of magnitude higher than non-ANNs CPU workloads (e.g., 10–15) due to algorithmic resilience such as Winner-Take-All mechanism and non-linear activations. However, CNNs primarily operate on Euclidean data, such as 2D images and 1D texts. To process geometric data and their dependencies, GCNs have been proposed to extend the concept of convolutions for graph data, achieving state-of-the-art performance with fault tolerance capabilities. Previous studies have revealed that the fault tolerance of CNNs varies depending on the model, layer type (e.g., fully connected layers, convolutional layers), and structure. When extended to graph, how to exploit the intrinsic fault resilience of GCNs in hardware acceleration, particularly with PIM for improved compute efficiency (i.e., Tera Floating Point Operations Per Second/Watt) and ultimately contribute to sustainability is still not well understood. This project will provide an innovation solution via hardware-software co-design to expedite on-chip GCN-based graph processing with approximate computing by answering (a) how to optimize PIM-centric architecture with well-suited dataflow and kernel mapping for SpDeGEMM to enhance the compute efficiency; (b) how to forgo deterministic output accuracy in favor of compute efficiency by applying approximate computing technique in PIM macros and recover the performance loss when the errors are significant; (c) how to leverage PIM circuitry and tailor it for temporal data locality in graph partitioning to suppress frequent data access to off-chip memory for efficient and scalable GCNs processing.
kw: Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNs), Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNs), Processing-In-Memory (PIM), Mapping, Approximate Computing, Content-Addressable Memory

title: Deterministic mega-electron volt ion implantation with high spatial precision
abs: Ion implantation is a key technology that has driven the semiconductor industry since the 1960-70s and is used for multiple fabrication steps in the CMOS process. Commercial implanters are optimized to deliver relatively large ion fluences to wafers for doping. New and emerging applications of ion implantation, such as quantum technologies and photonics, require unprecedented 3-dimensional control over the implantation process and the positioning of the implanted ion. A new class of implanter that can deliver a pre-determined number of ions for doping or defect generation with nanometre spatial precision will be required. In this proposal, a deterministic single ion implanter for mega-electron volt beam energies will be developed. The implantation system is comprised of an Akiyama tip AFM system mounted on several vacuum stages for sample manipulation and beam alignment. Akiyama probes are self-oscillating and do not require optical feedback for measurement of deflection making them well suited to vacuum systems. The AFM tip will be modified with the fabrication of a nano aperture that acts as an implantation mask and can be positioned with nanometre precision on a sample or device. The in-situ vacuum AFM system will enable both positioning and imaging of the device or sample to be implanted so that incident ions can be precisely delivered to the active regions of the device. An example is the positioning of an ion implant forming a colour centre in a prefabricated optical resonator. The new system will be retrofitted to an existing beamline and target chamber at the Centre for Ion Beam Applications (CIBA), Department of Physics NUS. This beamline has a proven track record for routine delivery of beam spot sizes down to 20 nm. This will be crucial for beam alignment in the new system. In addition, a new fast beam deflection system will be implemented so that an accurate number of ions can be delivered to the sample or device. Coupled with a single ion detection system and low noise in-vacuum front-end electronics, deterministic ion implantation will be made possible. There are numerous potential applications of an implantation system that is capable of nanometre spatial precision, full control of penetration distance through beam energy, and the ability to deliver a predetermined number of ions through fast deflection and detection. The new implantation system will be used to study two main material systems. The first material that will be studied is diamond. Diamond has more than 500 documented colour centres and in recent times several of these have emerged as strong candidates for quantum technologies such as temperature and magnetic sensing. Two optical centres that are of interest are the negatively charged nitrogen vacancy centre NV-and the negatively charged silicon vacancy centre (SiV-). title: Surface Enhanced Random Raman Lasing
abs: One of the major objectives is the fundamental research on Surface Enhanced Random Raman Lasing (SERRL), a currently unexplored research domain, with the goal of developing an intense, spectrally stable, narrow-linewidth (< 0.5 nm) and spatially incoherent laser with potential bio-medical applications. Disordered structures offer potential platforms for enhanced light-matter interaction, uncovering fascinating physics and promising possibilities for light harvesting, sensing, and bio-medical imaging. In the presence of an appropriate gain medium, the disorder in a material can leads to scattering-induced light localization, which acts as a cavity for feedback to generate spatially incoherent lasing emission called random lasing. Though random lasing has got many interesting features, its applications are limited majorly due to the mode instability and larger bandwidth in comparison to conventional lasers. Random Raman lasing, using Raman active gain materials, has been proposed to overcome these limitations. However, fundamental studies in the linear and nonlinear interactions of Raman light transport in turbid media is lacking and it still remains a challenge to develop an efficient laser source using Raman emission in 3D systems. The project aims to develop an intense, spectrally stable, narrow linewidth (< 0.5 nm), and spatially incoherent laser through fundamental research on Surface Enhanced Random Raman Lasing (SERRL), a novel, unexplored research domain. The project will address theoretical simulations and experimental investigations to establish the correlation between the disorder strength of turbid media and Raman light propagation and aims to enhance localization and manipulate nonlinear dynamics using micro and nanoscale plasmonic concepts. An SERRL device with optimized parameters will be fabricated and characterized, followed by exploring its potential for imaging and sensing applications. The project's intellectual merit lies in introducing the concept of SERRL for enhancing and tuning Raman lasing emission from turbid media using micro and nanoscale plasmonics. The project has the potential to lead to the development of a one-of-a-kind laser source that is highly stable, spatially incoherent, chemically specific, and tuneable for use in biomedical applications such as wide-field speckle-free fluorescence imaging and multianalyte sensing. The proposed project aligns with RIE 2025, Singapore's strategic thrust areas in White Space for new research areas, Health and Biomedical Sciences, and Additive Manufacturing. It is envisaged to achieve the potential to drive and contribute to the economic development upon successful completion.
kw: Random lasing; Raman lasing; Surface Plasmon Resonance; Sensing; Turbid media; Imaging.

title: Intelligent Single Pixel Opto-Spintronic Terahertz Imaging (iSPOT)
abs: The proposed research represents a significant advancement in the field of terahertz (THz) imaging, which has historically been underexplored despite its immense potential. By harnessing the unique characteristics of THz frequencies, such as their high penetration depth in semiconductor materials and low photon energy, this research aims to unlock a plethora of applications that have thus far remained elusive. The key breakthrough of this research is driven by the first introduction of spintronic THz emission and exploiting its ability to push the boundaries of THz imaging beyond the conventional limits. Overall aim: of our project is to achieve intelligent single-pixel-based THz imaging with image resolutions < 20 µm (~λ/15) using spatially configurable patterned THz radiation obtained using an emerging concept of spintronic THz source activated selectively in an arbitrary spatial pattern using spatial light modulators. Specific aims: The key target of the project is to achieve intelligent single-pixel-based terahertz imaging with the aims to (i) Surmount the current limitations in imaging capabilities and develop solutions by harnessing the unique capabilities of emerging spintronic THz emitters, a cutting-edge technology for generating scalable and spatially patterned THz waves. (ii) Investigate and unveil the potential of THz waves for unprecedented surface and sub-surface imaging, promising to revolutionize the field through exhibiting image resolutions < 20 µm (~λ/15). (iii) A critical aspect of this advancement lies in realizing an enhanced signal-to-noise ratio, achieved by recording transient pulse intensity rather than relying on large-area bolometers. The strategy involves developing improved and patterned emitters for refining single-pixel imaging, obviating the need for multipixel cameras, reducing costs, and enhancing durability. (iv) In addition to conventional imaging, our research also aims to explore the imaging of metamaterials. These metamaterials often exhibit sensitivity to the polarization state of incident THz radiation, making them ideal candidates for advanced imaging techniques. In principle, the external electric fields, magnetic fields, and incident fluence on the spintronic heterostructures can be used to manipulate the polarization of the emitted THz waves. Thus, the external stimuli will allow us to dynamically control the polarization state of the emitted THz radiation, opening up new avenues for intelligent imaging. The computational algorithms developed for conventional objects will be modified to account for the polarization sensitivity of the THz imaging process and provide enhanced insights into the microstructure and properties of the metamaterials. title: De novo anti-cancer therapeutic agent design in equivariant 3D space with conditional diffusion models
abs: Motivation: Cancer remains one of the leading causes of morbidity and mortality worldwide. Drug development for cancer has been a time-consuming endeavour since mechanisms of most existing drugs remain obscure and we can hardly bridge chemical structures and desired biological properties. Small molecule drugs have achieved tremendous success in the therapeutic history due to their low production cost. However, small molecules sometimes can bind with unexpected targets and thus readily cause sides effects. Biologics such as peptides and antibodies, on the other hand, have more sophisticated structures and only react with specific targets in most cases. Traditional biologics design approaches such as rational design and phase display rely on high-throughput searching for candidates with the desired amino acid sequence in a vast chemical library. Extensive efforts must be made to optimize the candidate structures with regard to stability, immunogenicity, membrane permeability, etc. Without understanding the structure-action relationship, this process could be expensive and time-consuming, resulting in a high attrition rate. Methods: The blossom of deep learning has brought us an unprecedented opportunity to disclose the underlying pattern of cancer drug mechanism and to design de novo structures that likely induce desired biological activities in a targeted manner. In this project, we first propose to develop equivariant geometric learning models to predict peptide and antibody efficacy and leverage on eXplainable AI (XAI) approaches to interpret the prediction model. By identifying salient chemical and biological features such as protein binding pocket structures by XAI, we intend to identify features underpinning the mechanism of action of the drugs. Thereafter, we plan to develop constrained deep generative models, namely constrained diffusion models, to discover novel drug candidates under the constraints of salient features that are identified by interpreting the predictive model. We will further validate the druggability of the generated molecules by using various computational measures and molecular dynamic simulations. Anticipated results: Our preliminary work for small molecule drug generation has achieved promising results. Our graph diffusion model is able to generate hit candidates that achieve high binding affinity with potential protein targets while maintaining decent synthetic accessibility and quantitative estimate of drug-likeness. In this project, we intend to adapt our approach based on 2D graphs to generate 3D structures of potential anticancer peptides or antibodies. Existing approaches mostly rely on generation of sequence representations, which still requires daunting endeavor of chemical synthesis and modifications afterwards. By generating 3D structures under the constraints of salient features of targeted protein, our aim is to obtain hit anticancer candidates in one shot.
kw: cancer; diffusion models; explainable AI; generative AI; peptide-based drug design

title: AI-Oriented Software Configurable Network-on-Chip
abs: The increasing core count in modern many-core systems necessitates efficient on-chip communication. Network-on-Chip (NoC) has emerged as a promising solution, but traditional NoCs face challenges in power dissipation and latency due to complex arbitration and buffering mechanisms, hindering their scalability and performance. Furthermore, the fixed nature of existing NoC architectures limits their adaptability to diverse application requirements, particularly in the context of AI workloads with dynamic communication patterns. This proposal introduces a novel AI-oriented software-configurable NoC architecture to address these challenges. The proposed architecture enables dynamic reconfiguration of the communication topology, minimizing contention and maximizing the utilization of single-cycle multi-hop express bypasses. This flexibility allows the NoC to adapt to varying traffic patterns and application demands, leading to improved communication efficiency and overall system performance. To further optimize performance, we will develop algorithms for the co-optimization of task mapping and routing, considering both computation and communication aspects. The NoC will also feature parallel multipath data transmission to enhance throughput and reduce latency. Additionally, we will design dataflow-specific communication backbones tailored to the unique traffic patterns of deep neural networks (DNNs), enabling efficient execution of various DNN dataflows and other data-intensive applications. Through rigorous evaluation using the GEM5 simulator and exploration of hardware implementation pathways, this project aims to demonstrate the superior performance and adaptability of the proposed NoC architecture. The research outcomes will contribute to the advancement of NoC technology and its application in future many-core systems, particularly those targeting AI workloads.
kw: Network-on-Chip; Software Configurability; Hardware-Software Co-design; Task Mapping; Routing; AI Acceleration

title: High-Performance Ionic Thermoelectric Materials for Waste Heat Harvesting
abs: We aim at developing high-performance ionic thermoelectric materials for waste heat harvesting in this project. The ionic thermoelectric materials will have high ionic conductivity and high thermopower. They can be used to directly harvest waste heat into electricity. There is abundant waste heat on earth. Heat has been the primary energy for human society. However, the heat utilization efficiency is only about 30-40%. Plentiful heat is generated in natural process such as geothermal and photothermal processes as well. In addition, fossil fuels are usually burned to generate heat. CO2 is emitted during the combustion of fossil fuels, and CO2 can trap heat and cause the global warming. Harvesting waste heat can reduce the consumption of fossil fuels and the CO2 emission. Thus, this project can be of great significance for sustainable development. Recently, ionic thermoelectric materials particularly ionogels, hydrogels and organogels emerged as the next-generation thermoelectric materials mainly due to their high thermopower of several to tens mV/K, higher than that of the electronic counterparts by 2-3 orders in magnitude. Their thermoelectric performance can be evaluated by the ionic figure of merit (ZTi). The ionic figure of merit depends on the ionic thermopower or ionic Seebeck coefficient, the ionic conductivity, the absolute temperature, and the thermal conductivity. An ionic thermoelectric material with higher ZTi value can give rise to high thermoelectric conversion efficiency. Because ionic thermoelectric materials usually have very low thermal conductivity, we plan to develop ionic thermoelectric ionogels with high ionic conductivity and/or high thermopower. Ionogels are in quasi-solid state, since the ionic liquids are immobilized by gelator that can be a polymer, nanoparticle, or molecule. They can have better thermal stability and high ion concentration than other ionic thermoelectric materials like organogels and hydrogels, because ionic liquids are non-volatile and do not require any solvent. We have carried out preliminary studies on thermoelectric ionogels and observed interesting results. For example, we reported the world-record ionic thermopowers (38 mV/K in 2020 and 44 mV/K in 2022) and ZTi values (1.5 in 2020, 1.8 in 2021 and 6.1 in 2022) at room temperature. In this project, we propose novel methods to greatly improve the ionic conductivity and ionic thermopower of both p-type and n-type ionogels. (1) Ionogels with high ionic conductivity A high ionic conductivity is required for both p-type and n-type ionic thermoelectric materials. The ionic conductivity depends on the concentrations, mobilities, and valences of cations and anions. We will develop ionogels with high ionic conductivity by rationally choosing materials and controlling the microstructure of the ionogels. In addition, we propose to adopt oxidized nanomaterials, such as TiO2 nanoparticles or oxidized carbon nanotubes (CNTs) that can provide ion transport chann

title: Efficient Asymmetric Dual-Atom Catalysts for High Performance Lithium-sulfur Batteries
abs: In comparison with the Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs), Lithium-sulfur batteries (LiSBs), leveraging the multi-electron redox reactions of sulfur (16 electrons), offer a theoretical energy density of up to 2567 Wh/kg. There are also characterized by the very low materials cost and abundant availability of sulfur for long-term sustainability, presenting an attractive power solution for new generation energy storage, long-range electric vehicles and aero-transports at low cost, and showcasing an immense market potential. However, the scale-up and commercialization of LiSBs are facing significant challenges, where a primary bottleneck obstacle is the slow and complex sulfur reduction reactions (SRR), involving multi-step "solid-liquid-solid" transformations between S8 and Li2S in the cathode. Moreover, the “shuttle effect” caused by soluble LiPSs intermediates leads to severe sulfur loss and corrosion of the lithium metal anode, resulting in rapid decay in lifespan and very poor cycling ability. In this project, we take the novel dual-atom catalysts (DACs) approach to address this bottleneck issue. In particular, we first investigate the heteronuclear dual-atoms with asymmetric coordination, which feature two different adjacent metal atoms as the active centers. The Fe and Co combination, assembled on porous carbon-based materials, will be first studied for DACs, before extending to other combinations of transition metals and dual-atom coordination structures. By proper tuning and optimization of the interactions between two different metal atoms, and their bond environments, heteronuclear dual-atom catalysts with asymmetric configuration can game-change the scaling relation limit (SRL). For LiSBs, they can break the localization of metal d-orbital electrons, accelerate electron transfer, and optimize polysulfide adsorptions, thus disruptively raise the electrocatalytic kinetics. By efficiently catalyzing the transformation species into insoluble Li2S2 and Li2S, they can significantly reduce polysulfide shuttling. Upon successful completion of this project, a new class of LiSBs with disruptively improved electrochemical performance will be delivered, including a capacity of >1000 mA h g-1 and cycling ability of >1000 charging cycles. This will pave the way for LiSBs to be ready for scale up and being commercialized. DACs have not been properly studied for LISBs before, where the bottleneck issues for poor electrochemical performance and very poor cycling ability is due to the sluggish and complex sulfur reduction reactions (SRR), which take place in multi-steps in cathode, as well as the “shuttle effect” arising. By taking the holistic approach of experimental work and computational study combination, we will establish the key scientific principles governing the complicated process, and the catalysis of DACs to catalyze them.
kw: Dual-atom Catalysts, Lithium-sulfur Battery, Energy Storage

title: Design and Analysis of Robust Computational Methods for Complex PDEs: Singularity and Oscillation
abs: The solutions of many complex PDEs arisen from emerging applications can easily develop singular structures (such as sharp interfaces, chaotic transition layers, Delta-function type peaks and even blowups) and/or highly oscillatory patterns that are computationally challenging to resolve, as one needs both to store a great deal of information and to have efficient, robust, high-precision algorithms. Mathematical theory can possibly predict the existence and some quantitative characterization of the solution behaviors, which certainly can shed light on computation. However, the theory oftentimes finds itself difficult to provide more concrete information and precise conclusions. This project is to develop fast, robust, and mathematically grounded computational methods for several classes of complex PDEs with singular or highly oscillatory solutions. More precisely, we aim to propose (i) new analysis framework and tools for a class of nonlinear dispersive PDEs with non-differentiable nonlinearity and low-regularity solutions; (ii) robust space-time spectral methods significantly improving current approaches to resolve nonlinear dispersive waves in highly oscillatory regimes and in rich transition dynamics in dispersionless limit; (iii) novel perfectly matched layer technique termed as real compressed layer for accurate domain truncation of wave scattering problems disproving the common claim on failure of real coordinate transformation; and (iv) new local and global coordinate systems for complex geometries formulating PDEs and underlying singularity study, substantially boosting the capability of spectral methods for singular problems. The innovative findings will substantially advance the computational methodologies for complex simulations and computer-assisted techniques for exploring new theories.
kw: Nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs), Singularity, Oscillation, Radial perfectly matched layer (PML), Spectral and spectral-element methods, Complex geometries, Topological insulator

title: Smart System Development for High Performance Pre-engineered Steel-Concrete Composite Beams (HPCB)
abs: In Singapore, multi-storey industrial buildings are predominantly reinforced concrete (RC) structures designed for heavy loadings (15 to 20 kN/m2) and long-spans (≥12 m). While RC structural systems have served the industry well as a technically viable and economical solution, the deployment of large amount of low strength-to-weight ratio materials result in structural members of huge sizes as well as high CO2e per gross floor area (GFA). To address the material utilization and structural efficiency issues in industrial buildings, the team has materialised the new concept of high-performance pre-engineered steel concrete composite beam (HPCB). The HPCB combines a high-performance green concrete slab in grade C55/67 or C60/75 and an asymmetrical steel section in grade S460M that is designed according to the bending moment and shear force diagrams. At technology readiness level of TRL 6 (prototype demonstration), the remaining gaps between the prototype and industry application have been identified: (1) design method for partial shear connection to improve productivity and cost-effectiveness, (2) Castellating the web for integration with mechanical, electric and plumbing (MEP) services to reduce floor height, and (3) validation of performance under the serviceability limit state (SLS) including deflection and vibration which are often governing the design in local industrial buildings. This project aims to close these gaps and bridge the last mile towards industry application for HPCB. The objectives are to (a) Develop an automated optimisation tool for the web castellation taking into account the input variables (loading, span, floor conditions), constraints (height, thickness, spacing, joint conditions, MEP duct specifications) and the global performance requirements (ULS and SLS); (b) Calibrate the design equations for partial shear connection through mass finite element analysis (FEA) and small number of full-scale testing; and (c) Validate the serviceability performance of a fully integrated HPCB system incorporating partial shear connection and castellated web through experimental and numerical studies. Significance of this innovation is mainly on the improvement of productivity, sustainability and safety in construction of long-span industrial and commercial buildings. It is expected that this system is able to increase productivity by 20% and reduce embodied carbon by 30% and cost by 5%. Foreground IP on the optimization design tool will be created and licensed out to consulting firms and construction companies to grant them greater flexibility and efficiency in designing sustainable and high-performance composite flooring systems. This tool shall be useful in relieving many common pain points the industry is facing, such as design of composite beam with varying steel section geometry, partial shear connection with asymmetrical beams, and deflection and vibration response. To achieve greater impact, the team also aims to publish the researc

title: Advanced Reactor Development for CO2 Utilization and Energy-efficient Lithium Extraction and Recycling
abs: The market for lithium-ion batteries is growing rapidly, leading to a significant increase in the demand for lithium in the form of lithium carbonate (Li2CO3), the most common form of lithium mineralization. Traditionally, lithium is extracted as Li2CO3 using sodium carbonate (Na2CO3) to precipitate lithium ions from an aqueous solution. However, Na2CO3 can be replaced by CO2, presenting a sustainable and economically viable alternative. Based on our preliminary results and background IP, we propose to develop a high-efficiency gas/liquid reactor to enhance the reaction efficiency between CO2 and a lithium-ion solution. Our reactor design would create a mist from the LiOH solution, increasing the specific surface area of the reaction surface to enhance CO2 gas utilization and produce micro-sized Li2CO3 particles. We envision this cost-effective approach could also be extended to future CO2 capture applications.

title: Location-aware Underwater 3D Imaging With Digital Twin Technology(DTT)  For  Proactive Sustainable Underwater Inspection

title: Low pressure membrane system for low energy water filtration and pre-treatment
abs: Ensuring the accessibility of sustainable water resources stands as a pivotal objective within the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). As raw water quality deteriorates due to climate change and increased pollution, water treatment processes must be upgraded to handle increased contamination load. Membranes have been proven to be an advanced technology for large scale water production but have been hampered by its high cost. Innovative technology in enabling low cost, affordable water treatment that can be scaled up is the key to tackling water scarcity, as highlighted by President Tharman at Lee Kuan Yew Water Price 2024. To bridge this gap, two challenges must be overcome. The first is reduce the capital costs of deploying the membranes A patented technology has been developed (by Atera Water Pte Ltd) that uses commodity polymers to manufacture membranes for the low-pressure operation that is up to 50% more affordable, allowing it to be widely adopted. The second is to develop an operating protocol that takes advantage of unique characteristics of the affordable membrane. This project aims to overcome this second challenge. This project proposes the use of a low-pressure membrane system (LPMS) to address this technology gap. This project focuses on developing effective anti-fouling strategies that can significantly increase the output flux of LPMS without incurring high energy costs. There are four specific aims to this project. First, the project aims to develop a validated numerical model that can be used to optimize anti-fouling system designs for LPMS. This will eliminate the need to run expensive and time-consuming experimental measurements for different system configuration. Second, a 100 m3 LPMS system setup will be installed at a PUB test-bedding site to allow controlled monitoring and precise experimentations and data collection and analysis involving LPMS. This living lab like setup is expected to operate 24/7, and will provide the required validation datapoints for our numerical model. Third, with the numerical and experimental model, the project aims to develop a LPMS anti-fouling strategy that is capable of increasing the stable flux of the system by 20%. Lastly, the project will demonstrate large-scale (100 m3/day) low-cost water production for water treatment in 3 focus areas: surface water filtration, pre-treatment for desalination, rainwater harvesting. This project aims to achieve the specific aims described in two parallel approaches. First, with the experience gained from our lab-scale setup with SIT Ignition Grant (from Mar 2023 to Jul 2024), a living-lab like setup that can house a proper demonstration-sized membrane module will be installed at a PUB test bedding site. With the experiences learnt from our Ignition Grant project, the team have identified key areas that are required to be addressed to scale up anti-fouling strategies for LPMS. title: Advancing Health and Taste with Allulose as a Sugar Substitute: Novel Formulation and Processing
abs:
The increasing rates of obesity and type-2 diabetes are linked to high sucrose intake, prompting a need to reduce added sucrose in foods.

D-Allulose, a rare natural sugar, shows promise as a sugar substitute due to its low calories, similar taste to sucrose, and minimal impact on blood glucose levels. title: Biodegradable Unpowered Temperature-Controlled Cold Box for Cold Chain/Logistics
abs: The development of biodegradable unpowered temperature-controlled cold boxes represents a significant innovation in cold chain logistics, addressing the pressing need for sustainable, efficient, and reliable solutions for transporting temperature-sensitive goods. This project focuses on creating an advanced cold box design that integrates cost-effective, biodegradable Cornstarch Foam Panels (CFP) and a proprietary Phase Change Material (PCM) to enhance temperature control and energy efficiency. Unpowered frozen shippers, such as the 'Standard Dry Ice Shipper' and 'PCM Frozen Shipper,' are commonly used in cold chain logistics. These shippers comply with IATA Packing Instructions PI 650 and PI 620, withstanding temperatures up to 40°C and maintaining controlled temperatures for 24 to 120 hours. While effective, these traditional solutions often rely on non-biodegradable materials and can have significant environmental impacts. The cold box design incorporates thin biodegradable films and specialized coatings on internal and external surfaces, along with an insulating coat on six eutectic plates. These materials significantly reduce heat transfer, resulting in a controlled internal environment and reduced energy consumption. Laboratory tests have shown that CFPs used in the cold box have an insulating efficiency comparable to traditional materials, achieving a thermal conductivity of 0.025 W/m·K. CFPs are made from renewable cornstarch, which is biodegradable and free from harmful substances, contributing to reduced environmental impact. A lifecycle assessment indicated that using these materials could decrease the overall carbon footprint of cold chain logistics by 30%. Additionally, the cold box's collapsible nature minimizes space and resources required for transportation when not in use, further enhancing sustainability. The new cold box design aims to be both environmentally friendly and cost-effective. A detailed cost analysis showed a potential 14% reduction in expenses compared to existing solutions, achieved through optimized material selection and manufacturing processes. Furthermore, the weight of the new cold box is reduced by 30%, making it easier to handle and lowering transportation costs. Extensive testing, including long-term performance evaluations and real-world application scenarios, has been conducted to assess the cold box’s reliability. Results demonstrated that the cold boxes maintained the required temperature range for over 120 hours under varying environmental conditions. Tests involving the transportation of pharmaceutical products and fresh produce confirmed the effectiveness of the cold boxes in preserving product integrity and extending shelf life. Addressing current cold box challenges involves innovative solutions such as reducing the carbon footprint, using collapsible and reusable components, employing biodegradable materials, and implementing sustainable insulation techniques. title: Advanced Graph Neural Network for neural mechanisms and fNIRS Based Depression Diagnosis
abs: Understanding how the brain works is vital for improving our knowledge of human behaviour and thinking. This understanding may lead to better diagnosis and treatments for mental health problems such as dementia and major depressive disorder (MDD). As an advanced imaging modality, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) holds more valuable information than we currently understand, including complex brain organization. However, there lack a comprehensive mathematical framework and clear deep-learning methods for explaining brain processes and predicting cognitive abilities. This project has a dual mission -- to uncover intricate neural mechanisms explaining cognition and to leverage predictive and forecasting capabilities to explore optical biomarkers for depression. We introduce a novel algebraic topology approach to neuroscience by treating fMRI data as a simplicial complex, allowing for the versatile definition of graph-structured data on any k-dimensional simplex. We will develop a Simplicial Attention Network (SAN), leveraging Hodge-Laplacian (HL) operators and attention mechanisms. SAN excels at learning heterogeneous signal representations across k-dimensional simplices, such as functional time series on brain regions (nodes), and functional connectivity between two brain regions (edges) and among multiple brain regions (triangles, etc). Its innovation lies in three core components: simplicial convolutional filters (SC-filters), simplicial projection (SP), and simplicial attention pooling (SAP) operators, all operating on this complex data structure. The innovative mathematical framework of SAN has the capability to predict and forecast cognitive functions, whether they are related to a single domain or multiple domains. It can also distinguish between neural mechanisms that are shared across different functions and those that are specific to each function. We will conduct a rigorous evaluation using a longitudinal brain image dataset (n=11,875) to measure SAN prediction accuracy and robustness in forecasting cognition. We validate the contribution of the brain regions from SAN to cognition via meta-analysis of existing cognition-brain studies. This framework is versatile and can be applied to various types of data structured like graphs, such as functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) data. fNIRS is an emerging optical imaging technique for non-invasive imaging of the human brain. It uses near-infrared (NIR) light in the optical window (700-900 nm) to probe physiological structures and functions deep inside human tissues. fNIRS can measure hemoglobin concentrations in the cerebral cortex, which is linked to brain activity via neurovascular coupling. Compared with established medical imaging modalities such as MRI and PET, fNIRS is more suitable for longitudinal studies and research projects involving children and elderly people as well as in-field applications such as cognitive performance monitoring and enhancement. title: Data-Centric High-Level Synthesis for FPGA Accelerator Design
abs: Specific Aims: The research aims to address inefficiencies in High-Level Synthesis (HLS) tools for FPGA-based accelerators, specifically targeting data-centric applications characterized by irregular memory access and runtime data dependencies. The project proposes a novel HLS framework that enhances FPGA performance through a non-blocking programming model, efficient task decomposition, and an automated benchmarking suite tailored to data-centric applications. Hypotheses: - A non-blocking programming model designed for FPGAs can significantly reduce pipeline stalls and optimize the performance of data-centric applications with irregular memory access. - A novel task decomposition method can align better with FPGA architectures, improving resource allocation and operational frequency. - An automated benchmarking framework can streamline the design and validation of FPGA-based accelerators, leading to more efficient and scalable solutions for data-centric applications. Methodology & Approach: - Non-blocking Programming Model: Develop a programming model tailored for non-blocking execution on FPGAs to efficiently manage irregular memory access and data dependencies. This model will enable asynchronous execution and concurrent processing of multiple queries. - Task Decomposition and Resource Allocation: Implement a systematic method for task decomposition and hardware resource allocation using a functional programming front-end, focusing on modern multi-SLR FPGA platforms. - Automated Evaluation: Create a benchmarking framework to assess FPGA performance on data-centric applications, integrating automated unit testing for low-level operators. Feasibility and Importance: The research leverages the inherent parallelism of FPGAs, proposing a paradigm shift in how data-centric applications are executed and optimized on these platforms. The expected outcomes include significant latency reduction and throughput improvement for data-centric applications compared to current HLS tools. This project is crucial for advancing FPGA-based acceleration in fields such as machine learning, graph processing, and real-time analytics, with potential applications in industries like finance and healthcare. This study is feasible given the team’s extensive experience in FPGA design and HLS, supported by access to advanced FPGA hardware resources through collaboration with AMD. The research holds significant potential to influence both academic and industrial practices in FPGA accelerator design, particularly for complex data-centric applications.
kw: FPGA Accelerator Design;  High-Level Synthesis (HLS); Asynchronous Programming Model; Data-Centric Applications; Graph Learning; Graph Processing

title: Rational design of high-performance polymer solid-state electrolyte towards stable lithium metal batteries
abs: Lithium metal batteries (LMBs) integrated with solid-state electrolytes (SSEs) can deliver high energy densities to meet the stringent requirement to power long-distance driving vehicles, and at the same time, possess intrinsic safe battery operation. However, the introduction of the solid-solid electrolyte/electrode interface brings significant challenges, including poor interfacial contact (i.e., high interfacial impendence > 500 ohm cm-2), even exacerbated lithium dendrite growth and so on. Compared with inorganic SSEs, polymer SSEs display a better intimate interfacial contact with the electrode. However, the low ionic conductivity and unstable interfaces restrict their application. Recently, optimizing the micromolecular structure of polymer SSEs has been adopted to fundamentally enhance the Li+ migration environment. For instance, polymer SSEs with altered side chain sequences have been synthesized, resulting in uniform Li+ distribution and improved site-to-site ion transport, thereby enhancing electrochemical performance at ambient temperatures. Despite the versatility of side chains in tailoring polymer SSEs properties, the criteria for side chain selection, the correlation between side-chain structure and properties, and the amalgamation of all functions into a unified system still represent huge challenges in the design of polymer SSEs. Hence, the structure-property relationship between the polymer SSEs and the ionic conductivities is of great necessity to be built up for designing highly ionic conductive polymer SSE. Moreover, the electrolyte/electrode interface evolution during charge/discharge process determines the compatibility between the polymer SSEs and electrode. The ultimate goal of this proposal is to design nonflammable and highly elastic polymer solid-state electrolytes (SSEs) possessing good compatibility with electrodes (i.e., anode and cathode), to provide design principles for constructing dendrite-free electrolyte/electrode interface, to establish the direct correlation between interface engineering approaches and the performance of lithium metal batteries (LMBs), and finally to fabricate LMBs with long cycle lifetime over 500 cycles, high energy density larger than 350 Wh Kg-1 based on the interface engineered polymer SSEs. To achieve this, the project is organized into three interlinked subprojects, namely: (1) Design highly elastic fluorinated nonflammable polymer solid-state electrolyte with high ionic conductivities ( >1 mS cm-1 at room temperature) (2) Characterize the interface evolution between the Li metal anode and the polymer solid-state electrolyte (3) Fabricate high performance solid-state lithium metal batteries with good interface stability (interfacial impedances below 200 Ω cm-2 after 1000 cycles) Our proposal aligns with the objectives of the Singapore Green Plan 2030, concentrating on designing a fluorinated nonflammable polymer solid-state electrolyte with exceptional elasticity and high ionic condu

title: Elucidate the gating mechanism of pentameric ligand-gated ion channels (pLGICs) by cryo-EM using a new in-house data processing pipeline
abs: Pentameric ligand-gated ion channels (pLGICs) are crucial for synaptic transmission and are implicated in neurological disorders. Understanding their gating mechanism and modulation by lipids is essential for therapeutic development. Prokaryotic pLGICs like GLIC have been instrumental in advancing our understanding of pLGICs due to their structural and pharmacological similarities to their mammalian counterparts. Our recent cryo-EM research on GLIC has revealed insights into symmetric channel gating. However, previous MD simulations hinted at asymmetric channel opening. Therefore, a new cryo-EM data processing pipeline has been developed in our laboratory to isolate asymmetric protein particles, yielding additional insights into asymmetric channel opening. Furthermore, we found that lipidic modulators which alter the rate of desensitization also influence asymmetric channel gating. This indicates the potential link between structural asymmetry and channel desensitization. This work has been extended in studying human 5-HT3AR, a eukaryotic channel with similar gating mechanisms. Initial small-scale purification revealed the presence of monodispersed protein particles on negative staining grids, critical for subsequent cryo-EM experiments. Therefore, upon completion of this project, we anticipate not only gaining insights into the asymmetric channel opening and lipid modulation mechanisms of GLIC but also illuminating the gating mechanism and lipid modulation of human 5-HT3AR.
kw: Membrane proteins; Ion channels; Lipidic modulators; cryo-EM; MD simulations; Electrophysiology

title: Investigating a transcriptional role of primary cilia in striatal neural computation mediating cognitive flexibility
abs: Cognitive rigidity, or a lack of flexible thinking, is a transdiagnostic endophenotype commonly presented in neurodevelopmental disorders such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD). In ASD, one core symptom is an insistence on sameness behavior that entails difficulties with changes in the environment and reflects dysfunction in cognitive flexibility regulated by the basal ganglia circuitry. Within this neurocircuitry, the dorsomedial striatum (DMS) plays a principal role in associating cortical inputs with motor outputs to flexibly adapt our actions based on current sensory information, previous memories, expectations and motivational state. This type of associative learning is goal-directed and essential for us to learn and update contingencies between our actions and outcomes (A-O). While human genetic studies have identified over a thousand ASD-linked genes, whether these genes function in DMS, how they are regulated during learning and how they contribute to cognitive flexibility are largely not understood. Interestingly, recent literature underscores a potential link between ASD and primary cilia. An increasing number of cilia-related genes have been implicated in ASD and mutations of ASD-linked genes are demonstrated to either affect ciliary structure or gene expression. Further, behavioral rigidity has been reported in ciliopathies e.g. Bardet-Biedl syndrome and Joubert syndrome. The primary cilium is an ubiquitous organelle present on mammalian cells and it has been proposed to functions as a “nuclear antenna” that senses extracellular signals, transduces them into the nucleus and induce changes in gene expression. In the DMS, each differentiated neuron possesses a solitary primary cilium that is approximately 10μm long. Primary cilia of DMS neurons are enriched with G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs) that interpret neuromodulators including dopamine and serotonin. These neuromodulators are known to regulate neuronal plasticity through a variety of molecular mechanisms including gene transcription and modulate brain activity mediating learning rate and cognitive flexibility. Collectively, these pieces of evidence prompted us to hypothesize a novel transcriptional role of primary cilia in regulating gene expression that shape DMS neural computation underlying goal-directed learning. This hypothesis is supported by our recent findings that cilia loss induced by AAV-CRISPRko in adult DMS alters A-O learning in mice. Here, we plan to take on a quantitative approach to unravel the cells and genes in the DMS neurons that contribute to A-O associative computation and how they influence learning flexibility. In Specific Aim 1, we will first elucidate the genes regulated by goal-directed learning in molecularly defined cell types in DMS and understand how cilia dysfunction regulates cell-type specific gene regulatory networks to influence learning. Accordingly, we have determined learning-induced gene candidates in the DMS and defined a GPCR-based a
