title: Upgrading formate into aromatic amino acid using engineered microbes
abs: This 3-year project focuses on engineering of Escherichia coli to improve its growth on formate. Captured CO2 can be reduced into formate using green hydrogen through thermo-catalysis. However, upgrading formate into a wide spectrum of value-added chemicals is challenging, especially when the product molecules have multiple functional groups and chiral center. E. coli is the best studied bacterium and has been engineered to produce this class of molecules, but it cannot naturally utilize formate. Despite that E. coli has been engineered to utilize formate, the growth rate is still low. In the past few years, the PI of this proposed project (Zhou Kang) has concentrated his research efforts on utilizing non-conventional substrates derived from waste streams, including glycine, ethanol, ethylene glycol, and 1,3-propanediol. Seven research articles on this topic are listed in his CV. These research efforts have allowed the PI to accumulate important strains and expertise for tackling the “formate challenge” in this proposed project, where his team plans to engineer a glycine-utilizing strain they previously developed to grow on formate at a much higher rate (100% higher than the record in the literature) and to produce L-tyrosine at the gram per liter concentration using formate (only simple product [lactate] had been made at 0.1 g/L at the time of preparing this proposal). To achieve these goals, they will systematically optimize the “building block formation” module and “energy” module, using state-of-the-art technologies and novel pathway engineering strategies. For example, a cost-effective nanopore RNA sequencing method they recently developed in the lab will be employed to discover new variants of the rate-limiting enzymes and to identify genetic parts that could enable effective dynamic pathway control; formate dehydrogenase will also be co-localized with cellular machineries that consume NADH and CO2 to kinetically push the flux towards the desired pathway. This project will deliver a critical strain to developing commercial formate-utilizing fermentation, and will also provide valuable tools to many other metabolic engineering applications.
kw: Biomanufacturing, Formate utilization, Fermentation, Metabolic Engineering, Escherichia coli

title: Unravelling the molecular basis for viral translation takeover in β-coronaviruses
abs: With a large reservoir of coronaviruses in wild animals such as bats, coronaviruses pose a constant threat to human health due to the potential risk of zoonotic spillover. While vaccines and antiviral drugs have been developed for Covid-19, they are susceptible to viral mutations and less effective towards other coronaviruses, highlighting the pressing need for effective broad-spectrum anti-coronaviruses strategies. Host-virus interactions are critically important for various stages of the viral replication cycle. Therefore, rationally targeting the host-virus interactions required for a viral survival mechanism is an attractive antiviral strategy. This host-directed therapeutic approach is also less likely to have therapeutic resistance, because resistance would require the virus to use an alternative host factor for replication. One survival mechanism, commonly employed by the β-coronaviruses (β-CoVs), is to selectively degrade the host mRNA in order to prevent translation of host mRNAs and delay production of type-I interferon (IFN) required for host immune responses. This viral translation takeover is mediated by the conserved β-CoVs virulence factor, Nsp1 protein, via a two-pronged strategy: blocking of the mRNA entry tunnel and selective degradation of the host mRNA. Together, Nsp1 inhibits the translation of host factors to delay immune responses and hijack the translation machinery for viral replication. Thus, the Nsp1-mediated translation takeover represents a conserved viral survival mechanism that can be targeted for development of broad-spectrum antivirals for β-CoVs. In this proposal, we focus on the molecular interactions required for the Nsp1-mediated translation takeover in β-CoVs. Our unpublished results demonstrated that the viral translation takeover relies on a key interaction between the nuclease domain of Nsp1 and a ribosomal subunit. As the Nsp1 proteins of β-CoVs shared a conserved function in suppression of host gene expression and translation shutoff, we hypothesise that the identified Nsp1-host interactions can be targeted as a novel anti-β-CoVs strategy. Herein, we will use a combination of biochemical, structural and cell biology approaches to study the following aims. Aim 1. Define the molecular interactions required for Nsp1-mediated viral translation takeover Aim 2. Investigate the conservation and functional significance of the Nsp1-host interactions Aim 3. Understand the mechanism of inhibition for identified Nsp1-inhibitors
kw: viral translation takeover, Host-virus interaction

title: Functional and genomic profiling for precision medicine in childhood T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia
abs: T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) is an aggressive blood cancer. Relapsed T-ALL is currently incurable. Despite stark biological differences, most protocols still treat B-ALL and T-ALL similarly, which may account for their disparate outcomes. The paradigm of risk stratification to guide therapy in T-ALL now includes only clinical features and treatment response, and the utility of functional profiling and comprehensive somatic genomic tumor profiling remains unknown. Our overarching hypothesis is that a multi-prong, orthogonal profiling approach in T-ALL through somatic genomic sequencing, ex vivo pharmacotyping, and measuring anti-apoptotic dependencies, will provide a comprehensive evaluation of leukemia characteristics. This, in turn, will more accurately inform on the patient’s overall risk stratification and also better predict response to chemotherapy. Therefore here, we aim here to: 1) Determine the drug sensitivity profile (through ex vivo pharmacotyping) of newly diagnosed T-ALL treated on our frontline trial, and 2) Identify the anti-apoptotic dependencies of T-ALL lymphoblasts using BH3 profiling assays and their correlations with treatment response and survival outcomes. To address these aims, we plan to systematically characterize the above across a cohort of newly diagnosed pediatric and young-adult T-ALL. This will be a prospective, observational, non-interventional study to assess baseline genomic, BH3-profile, and ex vivo drug sensitivity characteristics, and determine their clinico-genomic correlates and associations with treatment response and outcomes. We surmise that these findings will provide valuable added dimensions of tumor and host profiling, beyond the current paradigm of clinical features and MRD, for improved risk stratification and to potentially enhance individualized treatment in T-ALL. We will leverage on our already ongoing current multicentre clinical trial for childhood T-ALL across 4 centres in the existing Malaysia-Singapore (Ma-Spore) collaborative study group network. This study would lay the foundation for innovative and novel shifts towards future biomarker-driven, precision-medicine therapy trials in T-ALL.
kw: leukemia; acute lymphoblastic leukemia; childhood; precision medicine; pharmacotyping; BH3 profiling

title: Mechanistic Investigation and Clinical Innovation for Sarcopenia Diagnosis and Therapy (MAGNET)
abs: Sarcopenia is a common clinical symptom characterized by muscle waste and weakness, which affect 25-30% of hospitalized patients and more than 25% of community-dwelling and functionally independent individuals in Singapore. It is associated with ageing and a frequent complication of chronic illnesses such as cancer, heart failure and metabolic disorders. Given the accelerated ageing in Singapore, sarcopenia is emerging to be a significant threat to quality of life and health span across Singapore populations. However, clinical diagnosis of sarcopenia remains descriptive, and the current management largely focuses on symptomatic mitigation while an effective treatment for sarcopenia remains elusive. We propose here a national program entitled “Mechanistic Investigation and Clinical Innovation for Sarcopenia Diagnosis and Therapy (MAGNET)” to fundamentally improve the current detection and stratification, and therapeutic intervention for sarcopenia by better understanding the mechanistic basis of its pathogenesis. This program is developed from ongoing collaborations of a multidisciplinary team of physicians/scientists and their exciting milestones and findings, including the establishment of sarcopenia clinic and programs, sarcopenia biobank, sarcopenia pre-clinic models and promising biological insights based on molecular and metabolomic profiling. It will focus on four related themes, (i) Define the molecular and metabolic signature to stratify sarcopenia subtypes; (ii) Investigate key molecular and metabolic networks mediating the onset and progression of sarcopenia; (iii) Develop metabolic, immunologica and imaging based strategy for quantification of sarcopenia onset and progression and (iv) Mechanism based clinical intervention for sarcopenia prevention and treatment. The outcomes will address an important unmet clinical need by providing novel, innovative and cost-effective management schemes (from early and accurate detection, prevention to treatment) for a highly prevalent health problem in our fast-aging population and put Singapore on the map as a global leader in the field.
kw: Sarcopenia; diagnosis; therapy; transcriptome; metabolome

title: Advancing precision medicine for cardiovascular disease and diabetes in Asian populations
abs: Improving prevention and control of diabetes, cardiovascular disease (CVD) and other age-related conditions is a national and global public health priority. To address this need, we have created a globally outstanding, longitudinal population study comprising >100,000 Singaporeans (“SG100K”). Study participants have comprehensive phenotypic characterisation, high-quality biological samples, whole-genome sequence and other molecular data, and linkage to electronic health records. In our renewal, we will use SG100K to reveal the behavioural, environmental, and molecular factors that underpin diabetes, CVD and other age-related diseases in Singapore, and translate the findings into tools and scalable interventions, that support healthy aging and maintain human potential. We propose 4 interlinked themes. Theme 1 will follow SG100K participants to quantify progression of key disease endophenotypes, and ascertain incident disease endpoints. We will use the comprehensive clinical and molecular data collected at baseline and follow-up, to unravel genetic and non-genetic exposures that impact health and wellbeing in Singapore, and to reveal the biological pathways involved. Theme 2 will use baseline dietary data, health outcomes and controlled feeding studies, to determine how Asian dietary habits shape metabolic diversity and health outcomes in Singapore, and to develop metabolite profiles that provide objective assessment of diet quality in research and clinical settings. Theme 3 will leverage our unique retinal images, to identify retinal biomarkers that predict incident diabetes and CVD, and then translate the findings into clinical application. Theme 4 integrates observational data from Themes 1 to 3, to inform the design and evaluation of digitally delivered ecological momentary interventions aimed at promoting healthy behaviours, in real world settings. Our interlinked translational research actions will thus advance population and precision health for diabetes, CVD, and other age-related diseases in Singapore, and demonstrate the unique value of SG100K for advanced epidemiological, translational and precision medicine research relevant to multi-ethnic Asian populations.
kw: Precision; Cardiovascular; Diabetes; Diet; Bio-imaging; Behavioural

title: Singapore Gastric Cancer Consortium – Therapeutic Interception of Gastric Cancer
abs: Gastric cancer (GC) is a major cause of global cancer burden, ranking 5th in both incidence and mortality worldwide. The Singapore Gastric Cancer Consortium (SGCC) has achieved noteworthy outcomes in academia, innovation, and commercial fronts through sustained multi-institutional collaborative research since 2007. Besides a scientific footprint of a Field-Weighted Citation Impact of 2.41 and h-index of 81, the SGCC has made substantial contributions to clinical practice, exemplified by incorporation of the Gastric Cancer Epidemiology Program (GCEP)'s findings on gastric intestinal metaplasia risk features into local clinical practice guidelines since 2022. Through industry-supported projects, we launched a serum miRNA panel for screening of GC, GASTROClear, which is now clinically applied and registered in Singapore, and designated Breakthrough Device by the US FDA. We have also established world-class resources of invaluable clinically annotated biological materials, molecularly annotated in-house databanks, and a strong network of partners and know-how. In this renewal, we aim to move from descriptions to interception with the aim to bring tangible benefits for patients. First, we pioneer a clinical trial utilizing pyrvinium, a MEK/ERK and STAT3 inhibitor, to mitigate GC risk by reversing gastric intestinal metaplasia alongside developing a novel endoscopic tool and diagnostic kit. We will continue our quest on peritoneal metastasis (PM), by developing humanized antibodies targeting PAI-1 and a clinical trial on fibroblast-activation protein (FAP)-targeted radiopharmaceutical 177Lu-EB-FAPI in FAP-positive GC with PM. Third, we seek to characterise longitudinal changes in the microbiome across the GC carcinogenesis cascade and identify novel microbiome-based biomarkers and predictive models. Fourth, to unleash the GC non-coding regulatory genome for immunotherapy, we will apply a novel single-cell 5’CAGE-based platform to evaluate its epigenetic landscape. These concerted efforts will consolidate Singapore as a global leader in GC research as we strive to advance early detection strategies, therapeutic interventions, and predictive biomarkers of GC.
kw: Gastric cancer; Carcinogenesis; Clinical Trial; Intestinal metaplasia; Therapeutics; Peritoneal Metastasis

title: Singapore Parkinson’s Disease Programme (SPARKLE)
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Background: Parkinson’s disease (PD) is a common neurodegenerative disease and >25% of our elderly population has mild parkinsonian signs. Objectives: 1. We will conduct screening in healthy subjects to identify risk and prodromic markers of Parkinson’s disease (PD) and identify and cross validate authentic clinical biomarkers of disease progression and prognosis in those who have PD. 2. We will test interventional neurotechnology and develop cutting edge autologous stem cell resources and advanced novel therapeutics with disease modifying capability for clinical trials. Methodology Population screen: We will conduct population health screening to identify and validate Asian specific and prodromal factors associated with the development of PD. The findings will be cross validated in different Asian centres. Biomarker Discovery: We will conduct an international multicentre longitudinal study in PD cohorts to identify diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers that are associated with PD progression and develop an interpretable risk scoring model to predict the loss of function. Neurotech intervention: We will conduct a randomized controlled clinical trial in PD patients to compare the effectiveness of an interventional digital platform and physical activity for motor and cognitive functions using a novel home wireless monitoring system, to current standard of care. Neurotransplantation: We will develop preclinical strategies for cell production and packaging from patient derived induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) lines and to conduct consistency studies on GMP-grade iPSC lines from PD patients to fulfil USA FDA requirements and to subsequently conduct a clinical trial in PD. Advanced Therapeutics: We will test the safety and efficacy of the lead therapeutics and one new cell source that we have recently identified in non-human primate models of PD for subsequent first-in-man trials. Conclusions: We will improve early disease detection, identify biomarkers that can better detect progression and develop new therapies for PD.
kw: Parkinson’s disease; Clinical studies; Biomarkers; Animal models; Therapeutics

title: Conquering Lung cancer Across all stages with Research and InnovatiON (CLARION)
abs: Lung cancer is the highest cause of cancer-related mortality globally. In contrast to patients with European descent, approximately 60% of lung cancers occur in never smokers in Singapore, with EGFR mutations being the predominant oncogenic driver. Although targeted therapies have led to high response rates, treatment resistance often emerges after 12-18 months. Moreover, only a fraction of patients haboring oncogenic drivers benefit from immune checkpoint inhibitors (PD1/CTLA4), underscoring a major unmet need in the clinic. Our five-theme multidisciplinary proposal aims to reduce lung cancer mortality across all stages in Singapore. Theme 1 centres around translational clinical trials as well as broad molecular profiling with exome/ RNA-seq to supplement panel-based sequencing. The goal will be to build a unique and comprehensive body of clinical data and serial biospecimens that can provide clinical insights to the other themes. REVERSO, is an EGFR TKI resistance platform study that evaluates novel therapeutic approaches through a series of phase II studies to examine the biomarker-drug relationship. Theme 2 will utilise cutting edge single-cell and spatial tools to unravel immunobiology and novel immune targets for Asian lung cancers. Theme 3 will focus on computational genomics and data analytics to develop predictive models for lung cancer precision oncology. The models will be integrated into the clinical decision-support system in our existing molecular tumour board (MTB). Theme 4 will address disease relapse and therapy resistance through in vitro and in vivo disease modelling of cellular plasticity and tumour microenvironment. Theme 5 will evaluate feasibility, cost-effectiveness, and psychological burden of screening at risk individuals who have never smoked, and by studying environmental exposures in our population. Overall, these collaborative efforts are underpinned by a shared clinico-genomic knowledge base to facilitate data sharing across institutions for our goal of significantly improving the survival outcome of lung cancer patients in Singapore.
kw: Lung cancer; Early detection; Multimodal AI; Immunogenomics; Clinical Trials; Lung Cancer Screening

title: A Randomized Trial and Impact Evaluation of Singapore's New Beverage Label on Freshly-Prepared Beverage Purchases and Diet Quality
abs: Based on Singapore’s country profile, non-communicable diseases (NCDs) are the largest contributors to premature death and disability, with primary drivers being rising rates of obesity caused, in large part, by poor dietary intake. The Singapore government has recognized this challenge and responded on multiple fronts. One recent policy change was implementation of a new front-of-pack nutritional label, Nutri-Grade, focusing on freshly-prepared beverages from most retailers. This application, conducted in collaboration with colleagues at the Health Promotion Board (HPB), aims to quantify the effectiveness of this new label in the freshly-prepared beverage establishment environment overall and for select population subsets via two complementary studies: Aim 1) to test the effectiveness of Nutri-Grade on actual freshly-prepared purchases at the individual level by conducting a randomized controlled trial via an intercept survey at local retail establishments; and Aim 2) to assess the impact of Nutri-Grade at the retailer level using actual purchase data from retailers before and after Nutri-Grade implementation and including a sample of retailers subject to and not subject to the new policy (i.e., a difference-in-differences analysis). In Aim 1, we hypothesize that the percentage of sugar purchased from beverages will be lower among those exposed to Nutri-Grade; and Nutri-Grade will be less effective in hawker centers (vs. other established retail chains), and more effective among young and middle-aged adults, those with BMIs in the normal range and those with higher education attainment. In Aim 2, we hypothesize that the percentage of sugar purchased from beverages will be lower among retailers exposed to Nutri-Grade, but that effectiveness will wane over time. Given rising rates of obesity, diabetes, and other chronic diseases, this research is both timely and has high potential to have a significant public health impact in Singapore.
kw: Nutri-Grade, front-of-pack beverage labelling, sugar, diet quality

title: Evaluate the feasibility and effectiveness of a community-based care bundle in managing and preventing pressure injuries.
abs: The care of pressure injuries (PIs) is complex, requiring a coordinated multidisciplinary approach. Care bundles for PI prevention and management are standard practice in hospitals, but a community-based PI care model is lacking in Singapore. This study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of the PI care bundle in improving PI staging among the intervention group compared to the waitlist-control group, six weeks post-randomisation. We hypothesise that after six weeks, a higher proportion of patients in the PI care bundle group will achieve at least a one-stage reduction in PI compared to the waitlist-control group. This pragmatic, parallel, two-group randomised waitlist-control trial will enrol 156 patients discharged with PI and their caregivers (paid/unpaid). Using a randomisation app, participants will be randomly allocated to either the intervention or waitlist-control group. The intervention group will receive routine PI care plus the PI care bundle immediately upon discharge. The PI care bundle follows the aSSKINg model and includes home assessments, skincare, nutrition and hydration and PI preventive measures that are tailored to the individual needs. The waitlist-control group will receive routine PI care initially but will receive the PI care bundle after six weeks. Both groups will undergo weekly remote monitoring of the PI wound using the eKare inSight app. The study's significance lies in its potential to provide the first evidence of the effectiveness and feasibility of a community-based PI care bundle in Singapore. By offering comprehensive and individualised care, the project aims to significantly support and empower patients and caregivers in managing PIs more effectively at home, thereby enhancing overall care quality and reducing the burden on healthcare systems.
kw: pressure injury; older adults; skin care; community health; care bundle; multidisciplinary care

title: Advancing precision neuromodulation through individualised brain maps using functional connectivity and in-vivo electrophysiology
abs: The overarching goal of this NMRC Research Training Fellowship is to enable the PI to develop expertise for translating state-of-the-art techniques in resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI), stereo-electroencephalography (SEEG), and electrocorticography (ECoG) for the development of individualised brain maps of functional connectivity in patients with drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE) in order to investigate human cognition and develop precision neuromodulation techniques. These techniques are transferable to other neurological and psychiatric diseases and will enable the PI to advance scientific understanding of human cognition and functional dysconnectivity in these diseases, as well as to implement precision neuromodulation using non-invasive and invasive techniques in Singapore. The specific aims are to (1) characterise the spatiotemporal dynamics of coupled hippocampo-cortical ripples within individualised functional parcellations of the default mode network (DMN) in patients with DRE; (2) to investigate the role of coupled hippocampo-cortical ripples in the DMN on the retrieval of human episodic memory; and (3) to develop precision neuromodulation techniques using individualised brain maps of functional connectivity for memory enhancement. We hypothesise that replay (represented by ripples) propagates down a connectivity gradient from the hippocampus to DMN nodes, and subsequently from DMN nodes to primary sensory cortices such as the visual and auditory cortices, which are important in encoding information for episodic memory. To investigate the above, individualised parcellations of functional connectivity using rs-fMRI in DRE patients undergoing surgical evaluation will be conducted. Implanted SEEG and ECoG electrodes within individualised DMN nodes will be identified using individualised brain maps of functional connectivity that are developed for each patient. The spatiotemporal dynamics of hippocampo-cortical ripples will be characterised using raster plots of whole-brain ripples grouped by individualised functional parcellations. Real-time monitoring of DRE patients undergoing subthreshold precision neuromodulation using electrical stimulation at individualised functional parcellations of DMN nodes will be conducted.
kw: neuromodulation; functional connectivity; electrophysiology; epilepsy; memory; cognition

title:
Integrated bioprocess to recycle culture media proteins for cultivated meat
production
abs: To meet the rising demands of food production, global agricultural output must increase by 70% by 2050. Additionally, worldwide meat consumption is anticipated to rise by at least 10% by 2032 compared to 2023 levels. Cultivated meat emerges as a promising, and environmentally more sustainable alternative protein source. However, a significant challenge lies in the high operational costs associated with cultivated meat production, where cell culture media accounts for at least 50% of these costs. This expense is primarily attributed to the growth factors (GFs) and recombinant proteins (RPs) supplemented into the media for higher biomass production. To mitigate this cost, we propose to recycle the proteins in the used cell culture media, including the supplemented GFs and RPs, and cell-secreted autocrine factors. Our preliminary results show that recovered GFs/RPs not only retained their biological activities, but the cell-secreted autocrine factors also helped to promote higher cell growth. By reusing the GFs and RPs present in the spent media, we aim to substantially reduce the media costs required for achieving high biomass production by up to 88% depending on the scale and type of the bioreactor run. Notably, this approach not only addresses cost concerns but also contributes to environmental sustainability by minimizing waste. To enable the recycling of proteins, we will (1) design a bioprocess for the recovery and recycling of supplemented GFs, RPs, and cell-secreted autocrine factors; (2) evaluate cell growth rates and determine the optimal ratio of recycled to protein-free basal media required to achieve high biomass production. Ultimately, our research aims to identify critical process parameters for media recycling in bioreactor setups. By successfully implementing this approach, we anticipate a significant reduction in the overall cost of culture media for cultivated meat production and contributes to environmental sustainability through minimizing waste.
kw: Cultivated Meat; Alternative Proteins; Biomanufacturing; Bioreactor Process Development; Process Analytical Technologies; Proteomics

title: Cellular Gyms: Regulation of Energy Metabolism for Organoleptic Enhancement in Cellular Agriculture
inst: SIFBI - Singapore Institute of Food and Biotechnology Innovation
abs: Cultivated meat (CM) promises to be a sustainable alternative to traditional meat production without substantial resources for animal husbandry. However, animal muscle cells grown in vitro encounter a starkly different environment from their in vivo counterparts. In particular, unlike muscle cells in vivo which undergo regular exercise activity characterized by contraction and relaxation cycles, muscle cells cultured in vitro are not subjected to the same activity. We hypothesize the lack of physiological activity and associated energy metabolism will significantly impact the overall taste quality of in vitro cultivated compared with in situ muscle cells. Lack of muscle stimulation in vitro results in lower levels of intracellular purine nucleotide monophosphates. Excess adenosine monophosphate (AMP) produced during muscle contraction is converted to inosine monophosphate (IMP) through AMP deaminase, which is then recycled when required. Crucially, these purine nucleotides combine synergistically with acidic amino acids, glutamate and aspartate, to umami taste intensity. Hence, we propose to stimulate muscle cells in vitro and analyze these cells for an increase in purine nucleotide content and umami taste intensity. Through this project, we aim to demonstrate as proof-of-concept that interventions to appropriately activate energy metabolism will improve the overall organoleptic properties of CM. Collectively, our findings will lead to a paradigm shift in CM production in which intracellular energy regulation becomes an important consideration for promoting not only cell proliferation but also flavour.
kw: cultivated meat; umami; flavour; myospheres; nucleotides; magnetic pulse stimulation

title: Engineering cultivated meat cells to produce growth factors to eliminate factor supplementation in culture media
abs: Cell culture media is a major cost driver to cultivated meat, accounting for as much as 99% of current production cost. This is primarily due to the use of prohibitively expensive, highly purified growth factors and other recombinant proteins essential for supporting cell growth. To address this, we propose to engineer cultivated meat and seafood cells to endogenously produce growth factors that will stimulate autocrine signalling and eliminate the need for exogenous supplementation of factors, ultimately lowering media cost. We will adopt bioinformatics to identify promoter elements and growth factor genes in the genomes of species from which the cells are derived. The rationale is to allay potential safety concerns arising from introducing foreign DNA such as viral promoters or cross-species growth factors. We will then validate species-specific growth factors, and screen for promoters that drive high and sustained gene expression, using cell-based reporter and viability assays prior to their integration into target cells of given species such as Anguilla japonica (unagi). To demonstrate proof-of-concept, we will deliver constructs bearing these optimised promoters and growth factor genes to target cells in a way that negligibly alters their genome yet enables stable production of growth factors and evaluate their capacity to proliferate autonomously in the absence of exogenous factors. We envisage that the creation of a catalogue of species-specific promoters and library of growth factor genes will serve as an invaluable resource to cultivated meat researchers and manufacturers aiming to develop high-performing animal cell lines for cost-effective production of cultivated meat.
kw: cisgenic engineering of cell lines; species-specific promoters; scarless genome integration; autocrine growth factors; reduced culture media cost; cultivated meat manufacturing

title: Van Der Waals Niobium Oxide Dihalide-Based Ferroelectric Photovoltaic Synapses for Neuromorphic Computing
abs: Human brain-inspired neuromorphic computing demands the creation of a massively parallel and energy-efficient computing system to replicate functions of human intelligence. It has been suggested that these demands can be met by artificial synapses, which emulate biological synapses. Artificial synapses based on ferroelectric (FE) memristors demonstrate significant application potential, due to their non-volatility, ultra-high write/read speeds and ultra-low power consumption. However, classical FE materials have some intrinsic problems, such as large band gap, poor photo response in visible light spectrum and thickness limit, restraining their functionality and hindering device miniaturisation. In contrast, van der Waals (vdW) FE materials have smaller band gaps and offer stronger spontaneous electrical polarization (Ps) at atomic-level thickness. In particular, the recently discovered family of niobium oxide dihalides (NbOX2, where X is chlorine (Cl), bromine (Br), or iodine (I)) are promising vdW FE materials for the advancement of artificial synapses in neuromorphic computing. Unlike other vdW FE materials, NbOX2 generate higher ferroelectricity from stronger Ps. Moreover, NbOX2 have band gaps about 1.7~1.9 eV, suitable for switchable bulk photovoltaic (PV) response in visible light spectrum. Such properties make NbOX2 potential building blocks of artificial synapses with new working paradigm for neuromorphic computing. However, the fundamental properties of NbOX2 and high-performance FE memristors based on NbOX2 remain largely unexplored, particularly in the context of their application in neuromorphic computing. In this project, we will study the basic FE and PV properties of NbOX2, explore the polarisation switching mechanism of NbOX2, optimize the performance of NbOX2 based memristors, and demonstrate novel FE-PV synapses for neuromorphic computing. This proposed project will generate deep insights into NbOX2, especially in terms of their polarisation mechanisms and PV effects and clarify the correlation between these fundamental properties. The knowledge generated in this project will open new avenues for the evolution of neuromorphic computing characterised by high speeds, low power consumption and multifunctionality.
kw: Niobium oxide dihalides; van der Waals materials; Ferroelectrics; Photovoltaic; Artificial Synapse; Neuromorphic Computing

title: Developing Lead-Free Single-Crystals for Improved X-ray Detection Using Chiral Ligands
abs: I. The Academic Significance of the Research Metal halide perovskites are rapidly emerging as the forefront materials in semiconductor technology, thanks to their impressive long carrier lifetimes, high carrier mobility, and cost-efficient synthesis. These properties position them as ideal candidates for a wide array of applications, including photovoltaics, light-emitting diodes (LEDs), and photon detection. Unlike their polycrystalline or nanocrystal counterparts, perovskite single crystals showcase superior optoelectronic performance attributed to their long-range, periodic lattice structures. These structures are free from grain boundaries and have fewer defects, resulting in enhanced environmental stability and reduced energy loss. Despite significant advances in the synthesis of high-quality perovskite single crystals, current methodologies remain constrained by their specificity to certain perovskite types. Techniques such as additive/ligand-assisted growth, strain engineering, and temperature-controlled synthesis have been successful for organic-inorganic hybrid and all-inorganic Pb-based single crystals but fall short for Sn-based perovskites. Sn perovskites, recognized for their eco-friendly profile and remarkable carrier mobility, are seen as the superior alternative to Pb perovskites. Yet, the synthesis of large, high-quality Sn perovskite single crystals remains elusive, hindered by challenges in controlling nucleation, growth, and the introduction of defects through foreign seed-assisted crystallization. Our research proposal aims at developing a novel chiral ligand-mediated growth methodology for synthesizing large perovskite single crystals. Leveraging the unique properties of chiral ligands to control nucleation and crystal growth, this project seeks to overcome existing limitations in perovskite crystal synthesis, such as rapid nucleation and irregular crystallization, which have hindered the production of high-quality, large-scale Sn-based perovskite crystals. The successful execution of this project promises to yield perovskite single crystals with unprecedented dimensions, enhanced optoelectronic properties, and improved chemical stability, paving the way for the next generation of Pb-free X-ray detectors with record-high sensitivity. II. Research Questions to Be Addressed: • To develop a simple, universal crystallization strategy that enables the growth of large-size, high-quality Sn and Pb perovskite single crystals in aqueous solutions. • To overcome the rapid nucleation and irregular crystallization challenges particularly prevalent in Sn-based perovskite synthesis. • To leverage the enhanced optoelectronic properties of Sn perovskite single crystals for the development of high-sensitivity, eco-friendly X-ray detectors. • To decrease the dose rates used in direct X-ray imaging by the high sensitivity of Sn perovskite-based X-ray detector. III. Approach • Selection of Chiral Ligands: Identify and synthesize chiral ligands
kw: Chiral ligands, Single crystals, Lead-free perovskites, X-ray imaging

title: Development of a Living Biobank of Cancer Organoids Incorporating Cancer-Associated Fibroblast Heterogeneity for Drug Testing
abs: In solid tumors such as head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), it is now increasingly understood that the abundant cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) in the tumor microenvironment (TME) exist as distinct subsets which likely display unique functions, with some subsets having anti-tumoral properties, while others contribute to immunosuppression and resistance to immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) through effects on immune cell recruitment, infiltration, and cytotoxic function. However, clinical success of CAF-targeting strategies has not been achieved as the precise role of specific CAF subsets in contributing to cancer progression and drug resistance is still unclear. This is largely because robust in vivo and in vitro preclinical models which controllably recapitulate CAF heterogeneity and the immune-suppressive tumor microenvironment of human tumors do not yet exist. Research into CAF-immune biology is currently based on genetically-modified murine models which harbor relevant oncogenic driver pathways and amongst which, only those which contain large amounts of murine stroma are selected for use. These murine models may not recapitulate the biology of human CAFs and their interaction with human immune cells. Accordingly, while there are now several clinical trials investigating the co-targeting of CAFs in combination with ICB to augment the efficacy of ICB in patients, most of these CAF targets being evaluated are still broad strokes that target all CAFs in general, with very few CAF subset-specific targets. To address this problem, we envision the development of a living biobank that represents the next generation of scalable, in vitro patient-derived organoid (PDO) models incorporating CAF heterogeneity and tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs); these models can be used to understand the role of CAF subsets in the TME and to identify and test potential CAF subset-targets that augment the efficacy of ICB. The aim of this project is to develop novel in vitro tumor models that recapitulate the impact of CAF heterogeneity on immunotherapy resistance. Focusing on HNSCC, we hypothesize that PDO models with incorporated CAF heterogeneity and TILs will better reflect in vivo response to ICB (and combinations) as compared to PDO and TILs alone. As one of the first demonstrations, we recently reported how tunable hydrogels enable the generation of different CAF subsets from the same pool of 2D-expanded CAFs but in separate matrices (Ho et al. Advanced Science 2024). Given that different CAF subsets exist in the same TME, in Aim 1, we hypothesize that photo-crosslinkable GelMA hydrogels will enable the derivation of different CAF subsets all within the same matrix by controlling hydrogel stiffness. The resulting CAF subset cultures will be validated transcriptomically and functionally. title: Ageing Effect on Neuromodulatory Circuits and Their Interplay with The Prefrontal Cortex Underpinning Cognitive Learning
abs: Cognitive learning is fundamental to human intelligence, nurturing creativity, innovation, and the continual acquisition of new knowledge throughout life. The prefrontal cortex (PFC) plays a pivotal role in cognitive functions such as working memory, attention, decision-making, and cognitive flexibility. Neuromodulatory systems, particularly catecholamines like norepinephrine (NE) and dopamine (DA), provide essential inputs to the PFC, regulating its activity, connectivity, and plasticity. However, ageing brings substantial disruptions to NE and DA systems, which are closely linked to cognitive ageing processes and age-related pathologies like Alzheimer's disease. We hypothesize that age-associated imbalances or dysfunctions in NE and DA catecholamine systems lead to diminished cognitive learning abilities, impairing processes such as working memory, attention, and decision-making. However, the precise mechanisms by which NE and DA modulate PFC function and cognitive learning, particularly in the context of ageing, remain incompletely understood. This proposal aims to address this gap by investigating the synergistic yet distinct roles of NE and DA in modulating PFC function and cognitive learning, with a focus on ageing influences. Advanced techniques such as dual-color imaging, neurotransmitter-selective sensors, and optogenetics will be employed to achieve the following aims. In Aim 1, we will measure extracellular NE and DA concentrations in the PFC of actively learning mice across different age groups to track changes in these catecholamine dynamics during cognitive learning. In Aim 2, we will elucidate the interplay between catecholamine systems and PFC neurons during learning by concurrently measuring NE or DA signals alongside PFC neuronal activity across different age cohorts, aiming to understand how ageing influences these learning-associated alterations. In Aim 3, we will assess the causal influence of catecholaminergic pathways on cognitive learning in the PFC by selectively inhibiting key projections using optogenetic techniques while monitoring PFC neuron activity, enabling a precise examination of the causal influences of these pathways on cognitive learning processes. This research not only fills a critical gap in understanding the interplay between catecholamine systems and PFC function but also carries implications for education in late adulthood and potential breakthroughs in treating neuropsychiatric disorders associated with cognitive dysfunction.
kw: Learning; Catecholamines; Norepinephrine; Dopamine; Prefrontal Cortex; Neuroplasticity

title: Structural determinants of the pathophysiology of corneal amyloids
abs: TGFBI-related corneal dystrophy (CD) is characterized by the buildup of insoluble protein deposits in the corneal tissues, ultimately leading to progressive corneal opacity. Interestingly, like the pathophysiology of Alzheimer's disease, the severity and type of corneal amyloidosis in patients are not solely determined by their genetic background. This suggests that environmental factors and the patient's history play a role in the structural variability of amyloids, thereby influencing the manifestation of corneal dystrophy (CD) and its response to treatment. Our goal is to demonstrate that corneal amyloids can be disassembled both in laboratory settings (in vitro), in surgically removed corneas from patients (ex vivo), and in rat and mouse models (in vivo), using the ATP-independent amyloid-beta chaperone L-PGDS abundant in the brain but absent in cornea. Previously using cryo-electron microscopy and NMR, we reconstructed atomic models of the amyloids self-assembled from TGFBIp-derived peptides and their complex with L-PGDS. We found that L-PGDS specifically identifies structurally frustrated regions in the amyloids and breaks them in vitro and ex vivo. We plan to utilize corneal samples from human patients with different genotypes and pathophysiology to initiate and cultivate TGFBI-derived peptide amyloids. We will then analyse how their atomic-resolution structures correlate with the patients' disease manifestation. We propose that the ability of physiologically relevant amyloids to resist disassembly by the chaperone is a crucial factor in understanding the pathophysiology of corneal dystrophy (CD). We believe that the L-PGDS chaperone can serve as a probe to evaluate the structural resilience of amyloids, aiding in the development of a detailed, quantitative, and predictive physicochemical model of CD amyloidosis. These predictions will be tested in our rat and mouse models, which can develop visible amyloids in their corneas, thereby facilitating the development of treatments. Through the investigation of various types of seeded amyloids in animal models and the assessment of in vivo amyloid disaggregation by the amyloid chaperone, we aim to establish a foundation for utilizing L-PGDS as an innovative therapy for the previously untreatable condition of corneal dystrophy.

title: The mechanism and impact of seizure induced nuclear SUMOylation and transcriptional repression in epileptogenesis
abs: Epilepsy is one of the most common chronic neurological disorders that impacts millions globally. Patients with epilepsy suffer from prolong seizures that are characterized by waves of hypersynchronous electrical activity that originate from epileptic foci in the brain. While epilepsy can be inherited or acquired, one of the more interesting hallmarks of epilepsy – and perhaps the least understood - is the increased risk of spontaneous recurrent seizures after the initial seizing event. The onset of these recurrent seizures are hard to detect and can be triggered years after the initial bout of pathological activity. Studies show that the process of developing these recurrent seizures are rooted in progressive changes within the brain that lower the threshold for future seizures. These events such as the reorganization of neural circuits is often the consequence of cumulative changes in cell molecular cascade that regulate neuroplastic properties of individual neurons. In many cases, these persistent changes are encoded within the nucleus of impacted neurons, and involves changes in the genome, epigenome or nuclear signaling pathways that regulate gene expression. In our lab, we have employed a transgenic mouse model to affinity purify neuronal nuclei from mock and pilocarpine-induced seizure mice to characterize the nuclear proteome and transcriptome during acute seizures. Quantitative analysis of the protein dataset indicates a robust enrichment of protein SUMOylation machinery along with cellular pathways regulated by SUMOylation. We have experimentally verified elevated SUMOylation in animals as well as in stimulated neuronal cultures. In addition, transcriptome data revealed a striking downregulation of KRAB domain zinc finger gene expression, an event that we hypothesized is linked to enhanced protein SUMOylation. Both seizure-induced changes in neuronal nuclei are novel observations with potential implications on epileptogenesis. In this proposal, we outline three major aims to understand the nature of enhanced protein SUMOylation during acute seizures and its impact toward epileptogenesis. We will use an epitope-tagged SUMO mouse to identify the nuclear proteins that are targeted for SUMOylation during seizures and explore their role in different nuclear pathways during seizures. We also study the impact of protein SUMOylation on transcriptional repression of KRAB domain genes and establish a link with SUMOylation-mediated silencing of gene expression. Finally, we want to extend our methodology to profile changes in nuclear processes across other phases (latent and spontaneous recurrent seizure) of epilepsy, with the ultimate goal of monitoring the persistence of these acute changes during progression of the disorder.
kw: nucleus; seizures; epilepsy; epileptogenesis; pilocarpine; SUMOylation; transcription; proteome

title: Cancer eradication with mechanical reprogramming of chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-macrophages
abs: Globally, one in every five people is expected to receive a cancer diagnosis during their lifetimes, and 90% of adult cancer are solid tumours. Within solid tumours, there is abundant tumour-associated macrophages (TAMs) and clinical evidence has shown that TAMs promote cancer growth and metastasis. TAMs also suppress the healthy functions of cytotoxic T cells, and their presence is correlated to poorer clinical prognosis. As macrophages can preferentially traffic and are abundant in solid tumours, they are being actively developed into chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-macrophages as an alternative form of cell-based cancer immunotherapy. Despite the significant academic and commercial interest to exploit CAR-macrophages for cancer eradication, there are at least two hurdles that need to be resolved urgently to realise this treatment: (1) It is challenging to genetically engineer CAR-macrophages directly from monocytes or macrophages. (2) As the tumour microenvironment is immunosuppressive, intratumoral CAR-macrophages may be reprogrammed into an immuno-suppressive M2-like state which limits their efficacy as macrophages are a highly plastic cell type. When solid tumours were subject to dynamic mechanical stimulations (DMS) using 3D magnetic hydrogels (PCT/SG2024/050124), there was a reduction in the number of immunosuppressive M2-like macrophages and an increase in the numbers of immunostimulatory M1-like macrophages. This further led to an increase in the numbers of cytotoxic CD8+ T cells and decrease in the numbers of immunosuppressive CD4+Foxp3+ T regulatory cells and Gr1+CD11b+ myeloid-derived suppressor cells in the solid tumours, resulting in remissions of primary orthotopic pancreatic tumours in immunocompetent mice, and subcutaneous pancreatic tumours in humanised mice. To generate CAR-macrophages, we have optimised the nano-electro-injection (NEI) method (WIPO: WO2019018415A1) to deliver CAR plasmids efficiently into M1-like macrophages. In this proposal, we aim to investigate the molecular mechanisms underlying mechanical polarisation of macrophages from different cancer origins from an M2 to M1 state. Additionally, we aim to integrate mechanical macrophage reprogramming with NEI-transfected CAR-macrophages for synergistic therapy against solid cancer. We hypothesise that DMS could induce M2 to M1 polarisation by altering the transcriptomic profiles of macrophages through mechanotransduction pathways. The degree of polarisation is hypothesised to be influenced by force magnitudes, durations and (cancer) tissue origins. Additionally, we hypothesise that NEI is an efficient method to generate highly functional CAR-macrophages. Finally, we hypothesise that mechanical immunoengineering strategy could enhance the anti-tumour activities of CAR-macrophages even in an immunosuppressive tumour microenvironment. title: Cellular Pathophysiology of Na+/K+-ATPase dysfunction in Parkinson’s disease.
abs: Parkinson's disease (PD) represents a substantial global socioeconomic burden, yet disease-modifying therapies remain elusive due to a limited understanding of the mechanisms behind the specific loss of nigral midbrain dopaminergic (mDA) neurons. Our laboratory is addressing this knowledge gap using human pluripotent stem cell-derived midbrain-like organoids (hMLOs) and cultured mDA neurons, with a focus on alpha-synuclein (α-syn), a protein associated with synucleinopathies. Our preliminary results suggest that α-syn overexpression increases intrinsic neuronal excitability, possibly related to dysfunction in the neuronal Na+/K+-ATPase pump. We hypothesize that α-syn oligomers, induced by secreted dopamine, trigger Na+/K+-ATPase dysfunction, leading to impaired ion homeostasis, increased neuronal excitability, and selective vulnerability of A9 mDA neurons in PD. Our study aims to investigate the impact of dopamine α-syn oligomers on neuronal hyperexcitability, to study endogenous α-syn release and dopamine oligomer formation, and to explore in vivo functional consequences. Successful completion of these studies has the potential to uncover a novel pathogenic mechanism of PD and provide valuable insights for the development of therapeutic strategies targeting mDA neuronal dysfunction and loss.

title: Augmented Serendipity in Photocatalysis for Reaction Discovery Assisted by High Throughput Experimentations
abs: The pursuit of novel organic transformations is pivotal for advancing scientific knowledge and addressing pressing global challenges. However, traditional approaches often overlook serendipitous reactivity, hindering the exploration of uncharted reaction pathways. Moreover, the linear "one mechanism at a time" exploration further impedes the rate of new discovery. Conversely, relying solely on serendipity in scientific research is unsustainable. Thus, our proposal seeks to address the critical problem of inefficient reaction discovery methodologies. In response to these limitations, our proposal introduces an innovative approach called 'Augmented Serendipity', aiming to revolutionize synthetic chemistry by leveraging high-throughput experiments (HTEs) and strategic planning to expedite the discovery process. 'Augmented Serendipity' represents a departure from conventional methodologies, deliberately embracing unexpected results and actively seeking serendipitous discoveries. Unlike pure serendipity, this approach involves intentional experimentation guided by existing knowledge and literature to enhance the likelihood of uncovering new transformative reactions. By adopting a systematic yet flexible approach, ' Augmented Serendipity' offers the potential to overcome the limitations of traditional hypothesis-driven methods and unlock new avenues for exploration, especially with systems exhibiting dynamic chameleon-like reactivities. Within the realm of organic transformations, photocatalysis emerges as a promising research field due to its ability to drive chemical reactions using light energy, offering cleaner and more sustainable alternatives to conventional methods. Photocatalytic reactions exhibit diverse modes of action, and reagents demonstrate dynamic chameleon-like reactivity, making them ideal candidates for exploration within the 'Augmented Serendipity' framework. This inherent complexity presents both challenges and opportunities for serendipitous discovery, highlighting the need for innovative methodologies to navigate this dynamic landscape. The primary objective of this research is to develop a standardized protocol for 'Augmented Serendipity' assisted by HTEs, specifically tailored for diverse photocatalytic systems. The utilization of HTEs significantly expedites the discovery rate by executing numerous experiments in parallel. However, they also present challenges, notably the resource-intensive and time-consuming analysis of vast amounts of generated data. Thus, a key component of our research involves designing an automated analysis tool to streamline this process (WP1), ensuring efficient utilization of resources and timely data interpretation. To assess the efficacy of the 'Augmented Serendipity' protocol, we will commence with a proof-of-concept study centered on elemental sulfur as a model system, leveraging our prior expertise (WP2). title: The Nature of Human-AI Interactions in Multimodal Academic Lecture Assessment: A Generative AI and Sensor Technology Investigation
abs: Recent breakthroughs in text-to-video AI, empowered by deep fusion models and transformers, present unique opportunities to advance educational material development in general and listening assessment in particular. Researchers have shifted their attention to the affordances of AI in language assessment development. For example, the incorporation of AI for language assessment purposes in high-stakes tests is a significant development, as it can directly impact the lives of many stakeholders involved. Despite this rapid uptake of generative AI, it is unknown to what extent users’ responses to AI-generated materials, specifically video lectures under listening assessment conditions, resemble engagement with lectures delivered by humans. The perceived authenticity, accuracy, and attributes of AI videos may significantly impact listeners’ neurocognitive processing, emotional reactions, and overall behavior (see Liu & Siau, 2023). For example, human-computer interaction research reveals that people tend to have a negative bias against AI-created artworks compared to those created by humans (Bellaiche et al., 2023) for various reasons like the degree of AI avatars’ anthropomorphism (de Visser et al., 2016), trustworthiness (Choung et al., 2022), willingness to engage with the system (Ling et al., 2021), or appearance (Little, 2014). This within-subject design study, thus, builds upon the PI’s award-winning work on listening assessment method effects (Aryadoust et al., 2022), using eye-tracking, galvanic skin response, electroencephalogram (EEG), and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS). It specifically aims to investigate the impact of presentation mode (videos vs. audios) and presenter type (recorded human speakers vs. AI characters) on listeners’ neurocognitive, affective, and behavioral responses in academic lecture (listening) situations (n=200). It will also examine how the perceived features of AI characters and human speakers, as well as their visual presentation, influence listener comprehension and engagement. The study will develop lectures representing academic domains, featuring both AI-generated human characters and human lecturers in a half-body view with a distinct facial depiction. Advanced sensor technologies, including eye-tracking, neuroimaging, and galvanic skin response, will be employed to collect neurophysiological, affective, and behavioral evidence under different conditions. Questionnaires will also be employed to gather evidence from self-appraisals of anxiety and perceptions of the AI avatars. Subsequent data analysis will include Rasch measurement for psychometric validation of the data, linear mixed effect model and MANOVA to examine the effect of presentation mode and presenter type on the above-mentioned measures. title: Has the Inflection Point Come? Economic Analysis for the Impact of AI on Jobs Across Sectors
abs: The development of generative AI technologies, such as ChatGPT, has sparked widespread reactions ranging from admiration to concerns about potential job disruption. This uncertainty complicates strategic decision-making for businesses considering AI adoption and stirs concern among workers about their future career paths. To help address this, the proposed research aims to investigate the relationship between AI and jobs, examining whether an inflection point has been reached and to what extent AI is replacing jobs across various sectors. We propose a conceptual framework grounded in the statistical properties of AI and jobs. When discussing AI performance in implementing human tasks, we need to compare to what extent the intelligence of AI technologies has caught up with human intelligence in implementing various tasks. Our proposed framework will visualize this comparison through the lens of four factors, namely (1) task learnability, which is an inherent property of each task and can be decomposed into statistical complexity and computational complexity, (2) statistical and (3) computational resources which are necessary to tackle the two aspects of task learnability, and (4) learning techniques which utilize these resources to learn the task. Visualizing a task plane and representing a job as a task set, we are then able to compare the current intelligence of AI with the minimal intelligence required by implementing the tasks in a job, which leads to three phases of AI-jobs relation: decoupled, honeymoon, and substitution. With a stylized analytical model, we propose “inflection point conjecture” - before AI crosses the performance inflection point for an occupation, improvements benefit human workers; after crossing it, further AI improvements make human workers worse off. Therefore, our research is specifically formulated as, What’s the impact of AI on human labor market? Has the inflection point come and to what extent does AI replace jobs in various sectors? Our theoretical framework and analytical model provide a foundation to conceptually understand the impact of AI on human labor jobs. The intelligence of AI techniques in reality determines how AI techniques in practice affect various business sectors. When new advancements, such as the introduction of LLMs like ChatGPT, emerge, they elevate the overall intelligence of AI. This shift in AI capabilities leads to diverse effects across different job categories, including potential job substitution or enhancement. To empirically test our inflection point conjecture derived through the analytical model, we plan to use the launch of ChatGPT as an external shock to assess its impact on various business sectors. Our initial focus will be on the online freelance markets, which are particularly vulnerable to the influence of LLMs. Unlike regular employees who have contractual protections, freelancers are at higher risk of losing jobs if LLMs can perform their tasks efficiently. title: Synthesizing Complex Data under Differential Privacy
abs: The research proposal aims to develop novel methodologies for generating synthetic datasets that retain the statistical properties of real-world data while ensuring strong privacy protections under the framework of differential privacy (DP). This research focuses on three complex and widely used data types: relational data with foreign keys, social networks with rich attribute information, and vehicle/pedestrian trajectory data. The research seeks to address the limitations of existing DP-based synthetic data generation techniques, which predominantly handle simpler, homogeneous data structures and often fail to preserve the nuanced correlations present in more complex datasets. Specific Aims: 1. Algorithm Development: The project aims to devise new DP-based algorithms tailored to synthesize relational data with foreign keys, social networks, and trajectory data. These algorithms will be designed to capture and preserve complex correlations within and between datasets while maintaining strict privacy guarantees. 2. Evaluation Metrics: The research will establish comprehensive performance evaluation metrics to rigorously assess the statistical similarity and utility of the synthetic data compared to the original datasets. These metrics will be used to validate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithms through extensive experimentation on real-world data. 3. Foundational Contributions: The project aims to develop general algorithmic components that can be utilized beyond the scope of this research, serving as building blocks for future work in the privacy research community. Hypotheses: The central hypothesis is that the effective synthesis of complex data types under differential privacy will enable more advanced data analysis and increase the utility of protected data without compromising privacy. This research posits that the synthesis of relational data, social networks, and trajectory data, when handled with appropriately designed DP mechanisms, can achieve a balance between data utility and privacy protection that is currently unattainable with existing methods. Methodology and Approach: The research will adopt a systematic approach, beginning with the development of DP algorithms for each of the three targeted data types. For relational data with foreign keys, the research will explore methods for preserving inter-attribute, intra-group, and inter-relational correlations. In the case of social networks, the research will leverage attributed network embeddings to retain both topological features and attribute information in the synthetic data. For trajectory data, the approach will involve modeling source-destination pairs and waypoint distributions to generate realistic, privacy-preserving trajectories. The research will employ a combination of mathematical analysis, algorithm design, and empirical testing. This will include the use of real-world datasets to evaluate the performance of the proposed methods and to refine the algorithms bas

title: FoCo: Fast, Communication- and Memory-Efficient Optimizers for Training Large AI Models
abs: Large artificial intelligent (AI) models like the GPT and LLaMA series have become prominent recently, with successful applications in natural language processing, multi-modal domain, and more. Despite their achievements, large AI models, typically comprising hundreds of millions of parameters or more, necessitate an optimizer (training algorithm) for parallel training on extensive GPUs, and often incur extremely high training costs. For instance, a single training session of LLaMA 75B cost millions of dollars, consumed 43,000 GPU training days, and emitted 142 tons of CO2. Moreover, the rapid growth in AI model size and training datasets compounds these challenges, raising energy crisis concerns. Thus, developing advanced optimizers for efficient AI model training is more pressing than ever. Such optimization efforts promise to reduce training costs and carbon emissions while expediting AI model development, benefiting academia, industry, and society. By scrutinizing current optimizers like Adam and AdamW used in training large AI models, we have identified three significant issues contributing to high training costs and prolonged training times: 1) slow convergence due to inaccurate stochastic gradients; 2) high communication costs among GPUs for gradient synchronization; and 3) substantial GPU memory costs for maintaining optimization states like first- and second-order moments in Adam. Addressing these issues is crucial for achieving fast, efficient, and sustainable training of large AI models. This also aligns well with Singapore’s visions, including the Smart Nation vision which requires extensive AI model training, and the Green Plan 2030 for sustainable, resource-efficient, and climate-resilient development. To this end, our proposed project, FoCo, aims to develop Fast, cOmmunication-, and memory-effiCient Optimizers, specifically targeting these three issues. Firstly, FoCo aims to develop fast convergent optimizers to reduce the costs of large AI models. The large GPU memory cost of large AI models allows only a small minibatch of data to be processed per training iteration, e.g., four samples on an A100 40G GPU when training InstructBLIP 13B. Consequently, stochastic gradients estimated on small minibatches significantly deviate from the full gradient, causing training oscillation, instability, and slow convergence in conventional optimizers like Adam and AdamW. To address this, FoCo designs two complementary solutions: a Lookahead-Corrected optimizer (LoCo) for stable and fast convergence and a Primal-dual aLternative acceleration framework (PaLa) to accelerate LoCo. LoCo decomposes the parameter update of Adam per iteration into two sub-updates: the first sub-update from the previous iteration and the second one involving current gradient. title: Robust and Adaptive Multiperiod Stochastic Optimization
abs: Data-driven optimization is concerned with making decisions with imperfect models calibrated on limited historical data that perform well out-of-sample. Applications include supply chain management, risk management, finance and healthcare. The objective of the proposed research is to develop theory, insights and algorithms for solving multi-period data driven stochastic optimization problems. A central concern in all multi-period data-driven optimization problems is the tradeoff between optimizing the current estimate of the model (exploitation), being appropriately conservative so that out-of-sample performance is not too sensitive to model errors (robustness), and making decisions that generate data which improves parameter estimates and the quality of future decisions (exploration). These objectives can complement or conflict: actions that are good for learning (exploration) may be costly in the short-term and undermine robustness by increasing the sensitivity of the out-of-sample reward to errors in the model, while data generated under conservative (robust) actions might not be beneficial for learning. There is, however, little understanding how exploration, exploitation and robustness should be integrated, or the structure of decisions that efficiently trade-off between these objectives. We propose two projects to explore fundamental elements of multi-period data-driven optimization. Project 1 concerns the exploration-exploitation-robustness tradeoff which we introduce using a robust optimal stopping problem with learning that is inspired by an insurance application. We also introduce the notion of ``hedging for robustness" as a way for a DM to be robust without having to be conservative on exploration or exploitation. Project 2 proposes a novel method for extracting the exploration component from the optimal solution of a Bayesian control problem which we introduce using the problem of ``Optimal trade execution with learning". This leads to a new method for solving difficult control problems with active learning and a way to gain insight into the structure of the optimal exploration policy that will be useful in algorithm design. The methods introduced in Project 2 will enable us to compute and analyze optimal exploration policies and extend the ideas from Project 1 to more general problems.
kw: Exploration, robustness to model uncertainty, exploitation, stochastic control, online decision making, perturbation methods

title: Meta-Learning of Robust State Estimation for Agile Mobile Robots
abs: Agile mobile robots, such as unmanned aerial vehicles, wheeled robots, humanoids, etc., are rapidly gaining traction in various industries and everyday scenarios. Compounded with the fast-developing artificial intelligence, these agile robots are expected to achieve greater autonomy to continuously and reliably undertake various tasks that are traditionally performed by humans across diverse environments. Such advanced capabilities are critically underpinned by robot state estimation techniques, which integrate onboard sensor measurements (such as cameras and inertial measurement units) to provide precise robot pose estimates and environment modeling. As a prominent example, they include the visual-inertial odometry (VIO) that enables robots to navigate autonomously in GPS-denied unknown environments without relying on external sensors. However, conventional control-theoretic estimation algorithms rely heavily on manually tuning a fixed set of hyperparameters, which lacks adaptation to different environments. On the other hand, the emerging pure learning methods based on deep neural networks (DNN) generalize poorly to different hardware specifications and configurations. Moreover, disturbances encountered during agile robot operations and sparse sensor measurements all challenge existing estimators’ performance. This project proposes to combine traditional control-theoretic estimator and deep learning techniques to achieve robust and fast adaptive state estimation. We draw inspiration from the emerging field of meta-learning and aim to learn DNN-modeled hyperparameters that can dynamically adjust to different environments to facilitate robust and agile robot operations. There are three specific and progressive aims pursued in this proposal in a meta-learning framework. They set out to achieve respectively fast hyperparameter adaptation, simultaneous disturbance estimation, and sparse measurements adaptation. These aims represent the cutting-edge challenges of robot state estimation research and meet the urgent requirement of rapid growth and wide applications of agile mobile robots. Our first aim is to develop a fast-adaptive neural visual-inertial odometry (Neural VIO) for agile mobile robots. The goal is to achieve automated hyperparameter tuning using deep meta-learning techniques and to improve adaptability to different environments. Existing VIO typically neglects robot dynamical models and cannot sense external forces disturbances, which causes inaccurate state estimation. Hence, our second aim is to incorporate robot control dynamics to enable simultaneous disturbance estimation with neural adaptive hyperparameters. This will significantly improve both the state estimation accuracy and control robustness. The last aim is to further improve Neural VIO by addressing the practical challenge of sparse, unsynchronous, and misaligned sensor measurements.
