title: Autonomous generic nano-robotic platform with bottom-up driven translation-rotation bi-motility, record-breaking force output, and high directional fidelity for task encoding
abs: A promising route towards advanced nano-robotics is nanomechanical systems based on submicroscale DNA origami platforms of many different shapes, which are folded structures of a long circular DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) strand by short inter-binding ‘staple’ strands. Thanks to DNA origami’s rich design and functionalization, the DNA origami-based nanomechanical systems already demonstrate a wide variety of nano-robotic applications. However, the driving mechanisms for these origami-based nano-robotic applications are still limited to unrepeatable ‘bridge-burnt’ driving, tedious manual operation, or even intrusive driving. This proposal aims to develop DNA origami-based nano-robotic systems with autonomous, non-intrusive, and truly sustainable driving from advanced DNA molecular motors. Specifically, we will exploit a recent breakthrough in PI’s lab to develop two high-performing nano-robotic platforms. One is a single-motor platform potentially with a record-high speed; the other is a multi-motor rotor-plate platform with translation-rotation bi-motility outputs and likely a record-breaking force plus amplified directional fidelity for accurate task encoding. The two new nano-robotic platforms may automate and scale up many previously reported nano-robotic applications, especially those proximity-based applications like nanoscale assembly lines, sub-diffraction control for nano-photonics, chemical synthesis, and computing. New applications are possible too, e.g., in high-throughput mechanochemical sensing for cancer biomarkers by capitalizing on the multi-motor platform’s high force, small size and full bio-compatibility. These applied areas are in line with Singapore's vision of future high-tech industries, especially in manufacturing and health care. From a larger scientific perspective, the two nano-robotic systems from this project are the first batch of a new category of nano-robots that start to unleash the great potential of ‘marrying’ DNA molecular motors and DNA origami for advanced nano-robotics, with the former for nanometres-resolved complex motion and the latter as an ideal platform to host the motors and diverse robotic functions. This project thus will have lasting impact to future nano-robotics.
kw: nano-robotics, nanomechanical systems, DNA origami, artificial molecular motors, DNA nanotechnology

title: Active regulation of cell motion in epithelial tissues: adhesion vs contact inhibition of locomotion
abs: The accurate regulation of tissue motion is vital during embryonic development and in adult organisms, where tissues must remain stationary for protection but move for healing and repair. Dysfunctions in these regulatory mechanisms can lead to pathologies, such as the invasiveness of cancer cells. This proposal aims to understand how cells regulate epithelial tissue motion by adjusting their adhesive interactions and triggering an active response leading to an effective repulsive interaction and contact inhibition of locomotion (CIL). CIL occurs when a cell senses a contact and turns away from it. The interaction between adhesion and CIL is complex, as these regulating mechanisms partly rely on the same internal regulatory pathway. Thus far, it has been challenging to manipulate one without affecting the other experimentally. To address this, we will utilize an innovative computational model allowing us to connect the subcellular to the macroscopic scale, which we have recently developed. The model accounts for cell deformability, interaction, motile properties and sensing capabilities, which is essential to accurately describe tissue properties and CIL. Our proposal focuses on the interplay between adhesion and CIL in the biological processes of wound healing and malignant cell invasion. We propose a combined numerical and experimental approach to understand how CIL leads to irreversible cell dynamics and acts as an entropy generation mechanism. Elucidating the mechanisms underlying cell regulatory motion is critical for advancing our knowledge of biological systems and developing treatments for diseases caused by their dysfunctions. Furthermore, by viewing tissue behaviour as that of a responsive, living, out-of-equilibrium system, we can inspire the development of materials with living-like properties such as self-healing, and push the boundary of nonequilibrium statistical physics.
kw: Epithelial tissue; Active Matter; Mechanosensing; Nonequilibrium

title: Deterministic integration of electrically-driven 2D single-photon emitters into photonic integrated circuits for quantum processing
abs: We will aim to explore the potential of electrically-driven quantum emitters using 2D materials and their deterministic integration with SiN photonics. The specific objectives are as below,1) Fabricate the electrically-driven 2D single-photon emitters (ED-2D-SPEs) using emergent 2D materials and 2D van der Waals (vdW) heterostructures: This objective will focus on the electrical control of light emitting devices using p-n junction of WSe2, the electrical generation of SPEs using quantum-engineered confinement effect, and the measurement of their purity. Technical trials will be conducted to adjust the emission wavelength of the SPE, which will encompass factors such as selection of 2D materials, Stark shift, and photonic filtering effect. 2) Fabricate the high-precision, low-loss and phase-stable photonic waveguides consisted by silicon nitride (SiN): This part will involve the design and fabrication of essential functionalities of SiN photonics, followed by measurement of insertion loss (designed as < 0.5 dB/cm). For fabrication, specially optimized CMOS technology is used, and essential photonic components such as photonic crystals (PhC) and grating mirrors are also fabricated with waveguides. 3) Optimize the deterministic integration of ED-2D-SPEs into SiN waveguide: The objective will improve the coupling efficiency by optimizing the integration progress of ED-2D-SPE devices into SiN waveguides. With the precise positioning for deterministic integration, PhCs designed to increase coupling with the waveguide at 790 nm, the emission wavelength of WSe2 SPEs, and grating mirrors that reflect single-photon heading in an undesired direction increase the quantum coupling efficiency. 4) The objective will measure the function of waveguide coupled SPEs to process and confirm their performance of Brightness, Purity and Indistinguishability. The photon correlation of SPEs is performed in the Hanbury-Brown Twiss (HBT) setup, and the indistinguishability, which indicates the degree of interference of two SPEs is measured in the Hong-Ou-Mandel (HOM) setup. Our innovative approach allows for deterministic integration of chosen sources in complex photonic structures on a single chip. The potential outcome would inspire future scientists and engineers to pursue quantum research and development for chip-scale quantum hardware. The success of our project will address (i) the intellectual merit of being the first development of a robust and scalable method for on-chip quantum computing using electrically-driven 2D quantum light sources and SiN waveguides; (ii) the broader impact in translating research into potential practical applications in optical quantum computing, cryptography, and sensing, with breakthroughs in fields like medicine and finance. Our proposed project will bring together the strengths of electrically-driven SPEs and their integration into high-precision SiN photonics, resulting in on-chip, controllable, and deterministic quantum sources. title: Fundamental investigation of the mechanics of a multicomponent physical-bond-based gel (MPG)
abs: In this project, we aim at proposing a three-pronged approach to unveil the mechanism of an unprecedented multicomponent physical-bond-based gel (MPG), made from a biopolymer and four other organic components. MPG is a new class of gel material recently discovered by our group. It exhibits superior toughness when compared to other biopolymers enhanced using traditional strengthening methods by at least an order of magnitude. This is of high academic significance as our study introduces a new approach to toughening biopolymers without the need to add synthetic components. The proposed material investigation involves experimental approaches, and the results will be validated against fundamental constitutive gel models and computational simulations. We are confident that this project is feasible given that similar methodologies have been demonstrated on hydrogels and ionogels. Moreover, our project team also has vast expertise in the realm of material fabrication, solid mechanics, and computational modelling.

title: Bubble management for transfer-resistance-free gas production electrocatalysis
abs: Green-energy gases, such as hydrogen, produced via electrocatalytic water-splitting in proton-exchange membrane (PEM) electrolyzers, are crucial for a sustainable energy future due to their high energy density and ease of transport and storage. However, the scalability of these technologies is often hampered by gas bubbles that form on the electrode surfaces during electrolysis, blocking mass transfer and decreasing device efficiency, potentially leading to operational failures. Overcoming the challenges posed by these gas bubbles, especially at the nanoscale, remains a critical hurdle due to the absence of operando imaging techniques that combine high spatiotemporal resolution with precise material definitions. In this proposal, our objective is to elucidate the dynamics and effects of gas bubbles at both the nano and (sub)millimeter scale on electrocatalytic efficiency, using advanced operando imaging techniques. We plan to develop a micro-cell-based super-resolution inverted imaging platform (μ-TIRF) to visualize nanobubble behavior and larger bubble dynamics directly at the catalytic interface. This approach will allow us to link bubble behavior with electrochemical reactions, uncovering their impact on energy efficiency and guiding the development of strategies to mitigate their negative effects while leveraging their potential benefits. Our research will pioneer techniques for managing gas phases in PEM electrolyzers, aiming to enhance the performance and reliability of gas production, thus supporting the transition towards a low-cost, reliable, and green hydrogen economy globally.
kw: gas transport; hydrogen; electrolysis; mass transfer blockage; clean energy

title: Deciphering nanoconfined ion intercalation with higher energy, power, and stability
abs: Metal ion batteries (MIBs) are the dominating electrochemical energy storage (EES) devices nowadays both in practical applications and scientific research. Ion intercalation and solid diffusion are the two limiting steps for MIBs’ energy, power, and stability. Currently, strategies towards high energy and power MIBs, like nanomaterial and electrolyte designs, are driven mainly by untying active channels and/or ion solvation, with an intuition that looser channel and weaker solvation make more intercalation and faster diffusion. However, nanostructured interfaces and complex solvation bring varying ion confinement, which leads to anomalous behaviors like solvated/multilayer intercalation with unpredictable or even contradictive energy, power, and stability performances (Scheme 1). Confinement engineering therefore opens new avenues for advanced MIBs, which requires urgent attention and atomistic understandings. Herein, we aim to decode the confinement effect on ion intercalation and diffusion, to achieve simultaneous high energy, power, and stability MIBs. As a resubmission of T2EP10223-0016, we learned from the comment and refocused our attention to V2O5, MnO2 and VOPO4 materials, for their wide/emerging MIB applications. We paid additional attention to the volume expansion with confinement engineering. We also strengthened our capability and team towards material design and battery fabrication to complement the characterization and modelling. In the revised project, widely studied layered materials like MnO2, V2O5, and emerging candidates like VOPO4 will be engineered on the interlayer space as intercalation platforms. Sodium/zinc-ion batteries will be fabricated with solvation-engineered electrolytes for their widespread applications and good spectroscopic compatibility. Specific capacity, ion diffusivity, and volume expansion will be evaluated and linked to the confined intercalation. Synchrotron XAS and XRD, which capture the local structure and long-range periodicity quickly, will be measured. Theoretical calculation will be used for foundational confinement model and experimental validation. Our preliminary result has shown simultaneous higher capacity, rate, and stability in V2O5-PANI electrodes with varying interlayers, and in H2O-ACN dual-solvent electrolytes with engineered solvation. The migration of Zn2+ intercalation from desolvated Faradic to solvated electrostatic to partially solvated pseudocapacitive is captured with expanding WO3 interlayer. The results suggest less desolvation and charge transfer with less confinement. However, it migrates stagewisely than continuously, considering the quantumly modulated intercalation and solvation. Further studies on MnO2/V2O5/VOPO4 layered materials and tailored electrolytes should be conducted to define the physics of confinement, uncover further intercalation electrochemistry, and establish their correlation. This project will uncover quantitatively the confinement effect on intercalation

title: Security and Fairness Co-Design of Decentralized Applications
abs: Decentralized Applications (DApps) refer to computer programs that operate on blockchain plat- forms and are designed to handle significant amounts of money, facilitate transactions involving valuable assets, and oversee the transfer of digital rights among numerous parties. DApps provide a trustless environment for autonomous, transparent, and fully traceable exchange of value. As a result, there has been notable progress in utilizing them to support various activities. The implementation of DApps is expected to revolutionize traditional industries such as finance, supply chain, energy, legal and medical services. However, in reality, DApps have often been developed in an undisciplined manner, despite the significant stakes involved. Consequently, the reliability of DApps is constantly at risk, resulting in costly repercussions worth millions of dollars. The decentralized nature of the blockchain environment has made it extremely challenging to establish trust among multiple anonymous parties with almost always conflicting interests. In this project, we propose to address the issue by adopting a co-design approach in order to harden the trustworthiness of DApps from both the security and fairness perspectives. In particular, insecure DApps are vulnerable to malicious attacks, where security bugs may be exploited to steal the funds locked; unfair DApps may be used to lure innocent users, resulting in the victims’ financial losses. Both types of problems are rooted in the mismanaged interests among contending parties interacting through decentralized applications, and as such, they should be analyzed and solved under a unified lens. In the proposed project, we will first develop automated analysis techniques to effectively identify security and fairness issues in DApps. The initial analysis results can then be used to recommend appropriate fixes that mitigate the discovered issues in the new releases. The proposed techniques will bring a holistic solution to the table, which is fundamental to solving the trustworthiness problem: the existing approaches mostly focus on the security aspect, and when fairness is considered, it is only studied in isolation. With guarantees from both sides, DApps can truly become reliable value channels and serve as solid foundations to many important applications in the future.
kw: Blockchain, decentrailzed applications, smart contract, program verification, program repair and synthesis

title: Generative Fine-Grained Visual Perception with MLLMs
abs: The notable rise of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) has been the evolving frontier in Artificial Intelligence (AI) research and development, demonstrating groundbreaking abilities for human-AI interactions across various vision-language tasks, e.g. visual captioning, understanding, and question answering. One typical MLLM framework involves three essential components. 1) It utilizes a visual encoder to transform visual inputs into a set of visual representations (or embeddings). 2) An alignment mechanism is used for mapping visual embeddings into a language space. 3) A large language model plays a key role in generating relevant, task-specific text responses for given aligned visual embeddings and text instructions in an autoregressively generative way. Such a generative visual perception paradigm not only enhances the way machines understand and interact with the visual world but also allows more intuitive and meaningful human-computer interactions. Though impressive results have been achieved, existing MLLMs mainly conduct general visual perception tasks, facing challenges in performing well on fine-grained perception tasks, due to the following reasons. First, recent MLLMs often struggle with capturing the fine-grained details required for detailed visual understanding. These models excel at understanding general concepts and broader contexts but may miss subtle visual cues and nuances that are crucial for tasks like distinguishing between very similar objects or recognizing specific attributes within an image. Second, aligning visual and language modalities at a fine-grained level is complex. Ensuring that the model accurately matches highly detailed visual information with precise linguistic expressions remains a challenge, which can hinder performance on tasks requiring detailed visual descriptions. Third, the training datasets for MLLMs might not always include sufficient examples of fine-grained visual perception tasks, leading to a lack of specialized domain knowledge. Fourth, many fine-grained visual perception tasks require a deep understanding of context or common sense reasoning, which can be difficult for AI models to replicate. While MLLMs can learn patterns and associations from data, they might not fully grasp the subtleties of context that humans use to interpret fine details in visual inputs. To enable AI models with the abilities of fine-grained visual perception, in this project, we would like to investigate: ’Can MLLMs directly understand visual concepts at any granularity in the real world?’ The question is now one of the most emphasized topics in the community of artificial intelligence. The main objective of this project is to develop effective and efficient approaches that enable MLLMs to perceive and understand visual information with fine-grained details and nuances as humans. title: Pilot-scale investigation of semi-closed reverse osmosis (SCRO) for low-energy, low-fouling, and highly adaptive seawater desalination
abs: Seawater desalination is an energy-intensive treatment process. Although reverse osmosis (RO) membrane process for seawater desalination has achieved a significantly reduced energy consumption, the existing seawater RO (SWRO) desalination plants based on conventional single stage RO (SSRO) design still consumes much higher than thermodynamic minimum energy consumption primarily due to the inevitable over-pressurization of the feed seawater during operation. In this project, we propose to demonstrate the low-energy consumption of a novel desalination process, namely, semi-closed reverse osmosis (SCRO) which was invented in our recent research, via pilot-scale testing. The ultimate goal is to push the lower bond of energy need for seawater desalination. The project aim is to be achieved systematical investigation and optimization of various factors affecting SCRO performance such as number of elements per pressure vessel, number of cycles, operating flux, and system water recovery during pilot testing. Facilitated by the incorporation of tanks for intermediate concentrate storage, the multi-cycle operation with the various-pressure mode realizes the significant mitigation of issue of over-pressurization in the conventional single-stage RO (SSRO) configuration without adding extra membrane and pumping stages. Moreover, as the feed and intermediate concentrate in each cycle are stored in separate tanks, energy losses due to entropy generation can be avoided. It is projected that the innovative SCRO based desalination plant can achieve the lowest specific energy consumption of < 2.0 kWh/m3, which is superior to conventional SSRO and other state-of-the-art RO processes, such as batch RO (BRO) and closed-circuit RO (CCRO). The success of the pilot testing can lay a solid foundation for the future validation of SCRO at demonstrate scales, and eventually it.

title: Novel Yeast Platform for Purification-free Production of animal cell culture media Components
abs: Cell-based meat (CBM) offers a promising eco-friendly solution for food and nutrition supply, especially in densely populated urban regions like Singapore. Despite recent advances in cell culturing techniques, the usage of expensive serum and serum-derived ingredients in cell culture media (CCM) limits the scale-up ability and its industrial application. Thus, formulation of cost-effective serum-free CCM is vital to unlocking the full potential of CBM in urban agriculture. So far, various platform technologies that produce recombinant serum proteins by microbes, plant hosts or cell-free systems have been established. Though tremendous efforts have been made to improve protein yield and functionality for cost reduction, the high purification costs remain a challenge. This proposal aims to produce ready-to-use serum components in inexpensive CCM by bypassing protein purification. We will integrate advanced synthetic biology strategies, including precision genetic engineering, colorimetry-based directed laboratory evolution, and microfluidics-based ultrahigh-throughput screening platform, to generate cytotoxicity-free yeast strains with augmented secretion levels of serum ingredients. We will also establish strains co-secreting multiple serum proteins in appropriate ratios to formulate cocktail recipes for CCM, by testing on relevant cell lines used for CBM production. The platform technologies established in this proposal will be applied to select optimal strain variants suited for fed-batch fermentation and scale-up culture conditions. We will also conduct genome-wide association studies (GWAS) to obtain valuable genomic traits favouring secretion and scalable fermentation. This proposal will focus on two essential growth factors - fibroblast growth factor (FGF2) and transforming growth factor (TGF)-β used in CCM. Our preliminary studies have laid a solid groundwork and have gotten promising data in cell growth tests using crude fermentates and lysates. In summary, this practical proposal will not only create yeast strains tailored for CBM but also contribute to the establishment of cost-competitive serum substitutes for developing sustainable CBM production in Singapore.

title: Strongly Enhanced Nonlinear Interaction using Optical Resonators (SENIOR)
abs: Activity in processing quantum information has seen an explosive growth in recent years. The original promise to implement highly efficient algorithms (for certain problems) using the new paradigm of controlled superposition of information is starting to find tangible implementation in early quantum computing devices. These early quantum computers are still too small for meaningful use, but have reached a sufficient maturity in terms of stable operation that some of them are available for testing via internet access, or may be procured for on-premise experimentation. A necessity for quantum computing schemes is the implementation of a set of universal gates between physical quantum information carriers (typically qubits) that form the basis for actual quantum algorithms. These gates and the carriers of quantum information have to be implemented as physical systems that are governed by quantum physics. These universal gates (like CNOT, C-phase or equivalent) require a physical nonlinearity in the fields transporting quantum information between processing nodes. A physical nonlinearity is the only way to change the state of one photon (or phonon) in the presence of another. Universal quantum gates are found in the emerging quantum computers based on superconducting systems, ion traps or detector-based photonic networks, each using specific types of light-matter interaction to implement an effective nonlinearity. This programme proposes a complementary approach, which is to explore direct optical nonlinearities between optical qubits, enabling interaction between photons. If the programme were successful, this would result in an alternative method for implementing photonic quantum computing by replacing detector-based nonlinearity with direct optical nonlinearities. The specific elements to be investigated in this programme are strong direct optical nonlinearities at the single photon level in two different physical platforms. The first platform is based on an emerging integrated photonics material known as thin-film lithium niobate. This approach uses second-order optical nonlinearities accessible in specially engineered microresonators made in thin-film lithium niobate. The second-order nonlinearities in lithium niobate are well understood, but it is only recently that high quality micro-resonators could be fabricated in this platform. By keeping photons in the micro-resonators for a long time, the overall nonlinear interaction is enhanced. This programme will support work on pushing the quality of fabricated micro-resonators and to understand the limits of such a platform for photon-photon interaction. The second platform is not based on integrated photonics, but on a more traditional atomic physics arrangement using a free-space cavity that traps Rubidium atoms. title: Ammonium-fuelled carbon dioxide fixation for innovative water reclamation with reduced carbon footprint
abs: Energy-efficient and resource-recovery-focused technologies are needed for the next generation of water reclamation plants to pave the way for a more sustainable and economically viable future. Innovative approaches that minimize the physical and environmental footprint of wastewater treatment and facilitate the reclamation of energy from organic materials in wastewater are integral to achieving net-zero emissions from wastewater treatment. During water reclamation, methane capture from anaerobic digestion can mitigate the energy and carbon footprints of wastewater treatment and is considered a necessary feature of sustainable energy economies. While hydrogen and formate are known to act as carriers for interspecies electron transfer in methanogenic microbial communities, recent evidence suggests that direct interspecies electron transfer (DIET) among methanogenic and autotrophic bacteria is an important contributor to the overall metabolic resilience of methane-producing microbial communities. Similarly, fixed nitrogen removal by ammonium-utilizing bacteria supported by extracellular electron acceptors has been shown under specific cultivation conditions. A wastewater treatment system that couples the biological removal of fixed nitrogen, such as ammonium, with the conversion of carbon dioxide to methane via direct electron transfer would dramatically reduce the need for anaerobic digestion of sludge and mitigate many of the negative environmental impacts of municipal wastewater treatment plants. This project will develop and demonstrate a biogas-producing biological nutrients removal system that exploits DIET among methanogens and anammox bacteria within a defined microbial consortium. Requiring significantly fewer resources and producing less sludge than conventional nitrification-denitrification and anaerobic digestion systems, the microbial consortium developed in this project could significantly reduce the environmental footprint (e.g., the greenhouse gases CO2 and N2O) of water reclamation processes and contribute meaningfully to low-carbon energy production goals, showcasing the potential for simultaneous nitrogen removal, carbon dioxide fixation, and biogas production from wastewater.

title: Developments of 8-inch bioprogrammable reverse osmosis spiral wound module for seawater desalination
abs: Our prior studies at NTU about biomolecule assisted interfacial polymerization (IP) showed that this approach could form a polyamide rejection layer with increased membrane water permeance as compared with the conventional fabrication method. Unlike other nanoparticle or new materials-assist IP, our approach can be easily scaled-up with minimal alteration made to the current coating machine (with only one step of vesicle spray added after aqueous monomer soaking). The aim of this proposed project is to further scale-up the membrane fabrication method from 2.5-inch to 4-inch and 8-inch commercial scale, and to demonstrate the first Singapore-made seawater reverse osmosis (SWRO) spiral wound module in PUB demo plant at single-pass RO configuration. Based on our current 2.5-inch spiral wound module (SWM) performance, it is expected that the 8-inch membrane module will have a permeate flow of approximately 52 m3/day (with a membrane effective surface area of 37 m2) at an operating pressure of 55 bar, which is equivalent to pure water permeability of ≥3 Lm-2h-1bar-1 (for ultrapure water feed) and salt water permeability (seawater feed) of ~2 Lm-2h-1bar-1, with specific energy consumption (SEC) reduced by 3-15% as compared to the state-of-the-art commercially available SWRO modules. At the same time, the single-pass RO product water will have a boron concentration of less than 1 ppm.

title: An Integrated Multimodal Quantification Method to Designing Landscapes for Well-being
abs: A large and growing body of literature has emerged over the past two decades in support of the health-promoting benefits associated with urban green spaces (UGS). For instance, there are 70 empirical studies conducted in 40 cities, which collectively point to the benefits of UGS in reducing mortality and morbidity and improving physical and mental health (Zhang et al., 2017). This health-promoting aspect of UGS is important for two key reasons. First, public healthcare costs, especially in an ageing society like Singapore, have been rising and will continue to increase due to increased healthcare demand, sedentary urban lifestyles, and paradoxically, the longevity of urban dwellers. According to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), public expenditure on health and long-term care across OECD countries will increase to 8.2% of GDP in 2030, up from 6% in 2015. In Singapore, government health expenditure is projected to be $18.84 billion in FY2021, which is $2.19 billion or 13.2% higher than the FY2020 total expenditure. Second, the urban population is expected to grow, especially in Asia, further adding to the health care burden in cities. It is therefore not surprising that there is growing focus by city planners to create urban environments using a salutogenic (defined as being able to support human health and well-being) approach to health management and to promote non-pharmacological, nature-based and cost-effective interventions. Additionally, the role of UGS in strengthening mental well-being during a pandemic has been highlighted by a large volume of published studies. It is stated in the WHO report that “a deeper understanding of the beneficial and restorative impacts of various types and characteristics of green and blue spaces can help guide policy-makers in designing cities that not only support mental health, but also reduce costs to the health-care system” (WHO, 2021). Although there is an overall positive relationship between green spaces and mental health, there is no strong objective study of which aspect of urban green spaces can improve mental health. To bridge this gap, the research team seeks to bring together two different areas of research to reveal a more definitive answer to the question of what combination of landscape elements and in what quantities are required to achieve landscapes that promote restorativeness. The first stems from a landscape ecological idea of measuring the spatial quality of landscapes through landscape metrics. However, this has thus far been limited to 2D and 2.5D metrics that record the visual impressions of landscape through photographs and videos or extract 2.5D topography attributes via digital elevation model (DEM). title: Development of an integrated operational tool for Risk Assessment of Container Stackings at terminal yards under extreme gust conditions (RACS)
inst: IHPC - Institute of High Performance Computing
abs: This project is motivated by a critical safety incident on December 1st, 2022, where fifteen empty containers toppled into the water at Keppel Terminal during a sudden high-wind event. Initial assessments attributed the cause to a downburst—a type of intense, localized thunderstorm wind that is common in Singapore’s tropical climate. Preliminary computational fluid dynamics (CFD) analysis confirmed that aerodynamic forces on the containers exceeded stability limits, highlighting vulnerabilities in container stacking under extreme wind conditions. However, limitations in the current modelling approach—such as reliance on steady wind profiles, lack of real-time environmental inputs, and absence of transient downburst modeling—necessitate a more robust and operationally viable solution. In response, this project proposes the development of an integrated risk assessment and decision support tool to improve the resilience of container stacking at terminal yards. The tool will couple real-time environmental sensing with a hybrid physics-informed and machine learning model for wind gust prediction, and use CFD simulations to evaluate aerodynamic loads on stacked containers under dynamic conditions. Key deliverables include a gust forecasting system, a CFD-based stacking risk engine, an intuitive user interface for planners and terminal operators, and system integration with existing port infrastructure. While the primary use case is container yard safety, the system is designed for future extension to other port terminals, land depots, and environmental risk applications such as plume dispersion and wind energy optimization.
kw: risk assessment, extreme weather condition, operational resilience, weather prediction, aerodynamic force

title: Achieving a sustainable aquaculture environment with innovative biological processes
abs: A sustainable aquaculture industry providing a high seafood yield is a critical component of food security in Singapore. Recirculating aquaculture systems (RAS) are more compact, productive and sustainable than traditional net-pen or raceway systems. The environmental and economic benefits of RAS rely upon efficient recycling of water, which requires effective wastewater treatment. Coupled with the need for low HRT, the elevated total nitrogen and low COD of RAS wastewater can adversely impact the efficiency of nutrients removal by conventional biological wastewater treatment processes. In particular, accumulation of nitrogenous compounds in RAS water is detrimental to animals in rearing tanks and potentially increases the environmental impact of RAS operations. Building on previous work, this project will leverage the metabolic activity of proprietary denitrifying and ammonium-oxidising microbial populations that are uniquely suited to RAS wastewater to achieve improved nutrients removal efficiency and reduce sludge production. The project will focus on development and on-site test-bedding of a demonstration-scale biofilm bioreactor seeded with a novel microbial consortium. A quantitative comparison of nutrients removal by this bioreactor with existing systems will inform optimisation of reactor operation and guide further scaling. Optimisation will focus on reducing HRT and evaluating potential downstream effects of introducing our novel microbial consortium into the RAS.
kw: recirculating aquaculture system (RAS); wastewater treatment; enhanced nutrients removal; sustainable aquaculture; denitrification

title: Carbon Capture from Biogas Using Framework Materials
abs: Treatment of wastewater for reusable resources has evolved into a challenging task, given that a substantial portion of untreated industrial wastewater is discharged into open drains, lakes, and rivers, thereby contributing to environmental pollution and posing threats to human health and aquatic life. Within the domain of wastewater treatment, anaerobic digestion (AD) stands out as the most widely adopted sustainable technology, transforming organic solid wastes into more valuable organics while generating biogas as a renewable energy source for heat, electricity, and biofuel production. However, biogas, primarily composed of methane (CH4) and carbon dioxide (CO2), requires purification (mainly CO2 removal) before direct use. Traditional purification methods, such as biofiltration, refrigeration, pressurized water scrubbing, and membrane separation, suffer from low efficiency and high costs. In contrast, pressure/temperature swing adsorption emerges as a promising approach for CO2 separation from CH4, involving the adsorption/desorption of CO2 on adsorbents at alternating pressure/temperature levels. Frequently employed adsorbents like zeolite, carbon molecular sieve, silica gel, and activated carbon have limitations that require frequent replacement or possess a finite regenerative capacity, resulting in heightened operational costs. This proposal seeks to address these challenges through the design and synthesis of a series of framework materials, specifically metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) and covalent organic frameworks (COFs). Initial efforts involve the creation and screening of functional MOFs/COFs. For example, NUS-MOF-3, a hybrid metal ion-based microporous sorbent exhibiting superior CO2 capture efficiency over CH4, will be the promising candidate. Additionally, NUS-MOF-3 demonstrates exceptional chemical stability in the presence of water and other gases, allowing for straightforward large-scale preparation at relatively low temperatures. Subsequently, simulated biogas purification experiments will be conducted using breakthrough equipment to comprehensively investigate purification performance, stability, and reactivation conditions. Finally, demo-scale tests in operational environments will be executed, and techno-economic analysis will be performed to evaluate technology deployment.
kw: Wastewater Treatment; Anaerobic Digestion; Biogas Upgrading; Carbon Capture; Metal-Organic Frameworks; Covalent Organic Frameworks

title: Singapore Aquaculture Solution Center (SAS-C)
inst: CREATE - Singapore HUJ Alliance for Research and Enterprise (CREATE-SHARE)
abs: The main challenge in Singapore's food production and security is maximizing productivity while conserving energy. Expanding marine fish aquaculture is critical, given Singapore's ocean access. Singapore aims to lead the "blue revolution" by enhancing mariculture to address this. Despite a growing population and seafood consumption, local fish production remains low. This proposal targets key challenges in marine fish aquaculture, aiming to increase productivity and efficiency. It focuses on developing novel farming practices and optimizing technologies for the key species Asian seabass and for underdeveloped, yet the desirable species Red snapper, which are essential species for Singapore's mariculture. The research will focus on improving health and survival of early life stages, alleviating stress and improving reproduction and hatchery practices towards sustainable production. Improving hatchery production and farm practices can enhance the food chain and export potential. A consortium of experts from Singapore and Israel collaborates closely with local aquaculture enterprises and government agencies to ensure practical solutions. With expertise in life history, reproduction, and genetics, the consortium aims to effectively address Singapore's marine aquaculture challenges. Our work will focus on the most important species in Singapore aquaculture: Asian seabass (Lates calcarifer) and Red snapper (Lutjanus spp.).Once methodologies are established, they can be extended to other species in the future. Additionally, a key outcome of this project will be a Training and Engagement Platform. It will involve engaging various stakeholders, including farmers, Institutions of Higher Learning (IHLs), and government agencies, through workshops, conferences, and other outreach efforts. This platform will also contribute to nurturing a new generation of aquaculture researchers through structured degree programs and educational initiatives. While integral to the proposal, funding for this platform will be sought externally.

title: Intelligent online heavy metals analyzer using ions imprinted polymers for rivers, catchments, & sewers
abs: In our previously granted project (PUB-1804-0076), we have successfully developed an online heavy metals sensor using molecularly imprinted polymers for rivers, catchments, and sewers, and are commercializing it under a start-up company， MIPS Innovations Pte Ltd. In this proposal, we are going to develop it further with artificial intelligence, multi-channels, and database. Furthermore, we also plan to get the new smart analyzer certified and commercialized after completion of the further development. Proper sample pretreatment (such as filtration, dilution, pH adjustment, interference removal) and calibration for online sensors are challenging with requirements of fastness, accuracy, stability, low amount of waste discharge, and so on. Artificial intelligence would enable the sensor to self-adjust data analysis process to provide more accurate results, higher confidence and better interpretation. Inclusion of artificial intelligence may also make the sensor to be smart, self-tuning pretreatment and analyzing processes for quicker pretreatment, better stability, lower amount of waste discharge and greater thruput. Our current sensor has one channel only, measuring one type of metal ions with one sensor. However, in many scenarios, users would like to monitor multiple toxic metals. The current proposal would integrate multiple sensors into one sensor with multi-channels monitoring multiple metal ions simultaneously. There are also more and more users requiring a trend of historical analysis data in the same factory, data comparison among the different factories in the same company, and data comparison of their own companies against the belonged industry sector. This proposal would also establish database & its management system for AI and the trend of historical analysis data, data comparison, etc.

title: GROW Meats: Generating Resource-Optimized Workflows for cultivated Meats manufacturing
abs: Cultivated Meat (CM) is explored globally as alternative meats, since it can potentially replace meats from slaughtered animals to mitigate issues such as animal cruelty, greenhouse gas emissions, high land requirements, fishery depletion and loss of biodiversity. Currently CM products have not achieved commercial viability with key bottlenecks in high costs of culture media and manufacturing, due to the use of expensive recombinant proteins and pharmaceutical grade nutrients in culture media, lack of cost-effective scalable cell production and harvest methods to produce cells with required quality, lack of well-defined processes and scale-up limits to model manufacturing set-up costs, operation costs and sustainability. We hypothesize that solutions to these challenges will enable cost-effective CM cell mass manufacturing. To achieve this, we will (1) develop low-protein/protein-free media and characterize cheaper food-grade components to reduce CM culture media costs to less than $2/L, (2) develop cost-effective production processes by increasing cell yield, developing cell harvest and quality control solutions, (3) determine cell mass scale up limit, develop in silico facility and process models to investigate sustainability and cost-effectiveness of CM cell mass manufacturing. Overall, we aim to develop cost-effective manufacturing technologies to anchor CM as a sustainable and viable meat alternative in land-scarce Singapore to contribute to the nation’s 30-by-30 vision.

title: multi-puRposE modular FlOaters for integRated mangrovE & Seagrass planTer (REFOREST)
abs: Background: Numerous research conducted locally and globally has revealed the significance of mangroves and seagrasses to our ecosystems as natural habitats, coastal defence, carbon sinks. This unique mangrove ecosystem, although has the capability to sequestrate three to five times more carbon per hectare than other forest types, only covers less than six per cent of the forest area in Singapore. Seagrasses, on the other hand, also has the additional capability to filter and trap sediment and thus act as an excess nutrient buffer. While urbanisation is needed to propel the growth of the nation, a more effective means for natural coastal habitats to co-exist with urban development infrastructure has to be sought by means of eco-engineering. This proposal thus proposed a modular floating planter unit to house mangroves and seagrasses, with the aim to achieve habitat restoration, carbon sequestration and bioremediation. As opposed to the conventional bottom-founded structure, the utilisation of floating solution has numerous benefits because the former is environmentally friendly as it does not disrupt the current flow and damage the seabed, is easily deployable/dismantled/expandable and cost-effective. However, when such floating units are assembled to form a structure with a larger waterplane area, i.e., a floating platform, the structure will be deformed when subjected to wave action, a term known as hydroelastic responses due to the large structural length to depth ratio. As a result, the stress results due to the structural deformation has to be taken into consideration in addition to stresses due to the deadweight (weight of mangroves and seagrasses). In view of this, the development of a floating modular unit for seagrass and mangroves requires a substantial engineering design, rigorous simulation, as well as experimental and on-site testing. Research Questions: The proposal aims to address the following research questions: (a) How can the proposed modular floating planter house a suitable living condition for mangroves and seagrasses and be integrated into existing coastal infrastructure? (b) How effective is the modular floating planter towards habitat restoration, bioremediation and biodiversity and at the same time create additional space for recreational and eco-tourism? (c) How effective is the modular floating solution in withstanding the adverse wave climate, adapting to climate change and attenuating wave force? Methodology and Approach: To address the aforementioned research questions, three work packages (WP) are proposed, i.e. WP1 Design and numerical simulation WP2 Prototyping and Experimental Test WP3 Test-bedding. The project team involves academia (SIT), research institute (TCOMS), industry partner (Worldbizz WB) and overseas collaborators from University Malaya and University Science Malaysia who will contribute their expertise in the aforementioned WPs. title: Overcoming Boltzmann’s Tyranny with Quantum Tunnelling Transistors for Sustainable Nanoelectronics
abs: The humble transistor lies at the heart of all modern electronics. This semiconductor device which regulates electrical signals remains key today as the world grapples with the existential threat of climate change. Forecasts suggest information and communications technology (ICT) energy demand will rise to ~20% of total energy demand by 2030. Sustainable electronics innovation must prioritize both performance and energy efficiency. The key to improving performance is to minimize the subthreshold swing (SS), the speed at which transistors switch between 'off' and 'on' states. However, metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor (MOSFET) design is fundamentally limited by the Boltzmann distribution. Room temperature SS cannot be reduced below 60 mV/dec (Boltzmann’s Tyranny). Voltage scaling is thus impossible unless we can address this limitation. As transistor sizes shrink to the nanometre scale, quantum mechanics introduces a new problem: quantum tunnelling. Quantum tunnelling causes energy inefficiency and errors as currents ‘leak’ even when the transistor is ‘off.’ But what if we could harness quantum mechanics instead of being restricted by it? Unlike the fundamentally limited MOSFET, a quantum tunnel field-effect transistor (TFET) offers superior switching (SS < 60 mV/dec) and energy efficiency (low leakage current). However, few TFETs have been experimentally realized, and none have achieved the necessary performance due to material and device engineering challenges. Two-dimensional (2D) quantum materials are an exciting material choice offering unique properties ideal for TFETs. The extensive family of 2D van der Waals (vdW) materials offers a wide range of band structures for optimal band alignment through ‘Lego-like’ vertical assembly. Their atomically thin 2D bodies and dangling bond-free surfaces ensure excellent electrostatics and interface quality. A 2D tunneling transistor represents the ultimate scaling limit to break Boltzmann’s tyranny. We aim to build TFETs with exceptional performance and energy efficiency using 2D quantum materials.
kw: Quantum Materials; 2D Semiconductors; Electronics; Contact; Dielectric; Transistor

title: Novel approaches for nano-microplastics (NMPs) characterization in water systems in Singapore -NMPWaterSG
abs: Water pollution caused by nano-microplastics (NMPs) is a paramount environmental concern garnering global attention. Reports from around the world highlight their ubiquitous presence in various water sources, spanning from wastewater and marine environments to freshwater and even drinking water. The persistence of NMPs, along with their adverse impacts on ecosystems and human health, underscores the urgent challenges faced by water systems. While extensive research has been conducted on microplastics, the analysis of NMPs in water faces significant inconsistencies among methodologies, data processing, and result reporting, leading to variations of several orders of magnitude and making it challenging to discern trends. Furthermore, there is a scarcity of studies focusing on the extraction and characterization of nanoplastics to low-level microplastics. This research proposal prioritizes the development of novel and standardized methods for extracting and characterizing NMPs in Singapore's water systems. The outcome of the study will provide methodologies for sample preparation, quantification, qualification, and size distribution of NMPs. Additionally, an investigation of Singapore's water supply systems, encompassing tap water, water treatment processes, surface water, and seawater, will be conducted.
kw: Nanoplastics; Microplastics; Water pollution; Extraction of plastics; Characterisation method; Quantitative analysis

title: Shifting tipping point of Singapore’s seagrasses meadows: using microbiome to build seagrass resilience to anthropogenic and climate change impacts
abs: This project aims to identify environmental factors that push seagrass ecosystems towards their tipping point and to investigate the role of microbiome in promoting the health and resilience of seagrass meadows along Singapore's coastline. By identifying such ‘tipping point’ factors that threaten seagrass ecosystems and how microbes extend seagrasses tolerance to such factors, the goal is to use microbiome transplantation to improve and extend meadows along the Singapore coastline. By integrating macro and micro-ecology, environmental genomics, plant ecology and ecosystem function (e.g., nutrient and biogeochemistry cycling), the expected outcomes are new knowledge to enhance seagrass resilience, which could be integrated in restoration, management, and policy.

title: Singapore Indoor Farm System (SingFarm)
abs: Sustainable and efficient food production is the most prominent global challenge including Singapore, in particular in view of the increasing food supply chain disruptions due to climate change, the COVID-19 pandemic, and the war in Ukraine. To enhance food resilience and sustainability, scientific and technological innovations in food production from crops need to be integrated into the industry-centric food production system. Our CREATE initiative, SingFarm, aims to provide comprehensive scientific knowledge, strategies, and technologies for the indoor farming food systems and value chain, covering production, nutrition, damage control, and energy optimization. We plan to integrate synergistic, complementary, and innovative agriculture technologies with zero-waste and energy-optimized cultivation conditions. Synthetic- and bio-engineering-based agriculture technologies will be developed and deployed to enhance plant yield, nutrition, and resilience to biotic and abiotic stresses. Due to their very promising value for food security and familiarity and use for Singapore's indoor farming system, we chose Choy sum (Chinese flowering cabbage) and Kai Lan (Chinese broccoli) as the initial focus crops. Our agri-food technologies to be developed are platform based and thus expected to be applicable and transferable to other indoor farming leafy vegetables. To enhance plant nutrient profiles with a cost-saving strategy, we will integrate bioengineering-enabled plant performance enhancers and biofertilisers with zero-food waste engineering to provide nutrient ingredients from upcycling of food processing side-stream waste, reduce the energy costs of indoor farming, and enhance plant performance and energy efficiency. To enable rapid monitoring and timely loss management and prevention of growing agri-food, comprehensive plant surveillance systems will be developed and deployed. They will provide a wide array of real-time analysis and monitoring of plant traits and nutrient status of different edible indoor vegetables. Our excellent scientific partners drive this highly interdisciplinary project within Singapore and Netherlands, the world leader in agri-food technologies, industry-centric translational competence, and agri-food production. The research consortium comprises NTU, WUR, NUS, TLL, and RP to ensure the discovery of new science for indoor farming and the development of innovative agri-food technologies to solve our most urgent challenges in food sustainability and indoor farming.
kw: Efficient Indoor Farming

title: Establishing the SINgapore Carbohydrate Engineering and Research Enterprise (SINCERE)
abs: Glycans play a multifaceted role in the cell. Despite their importance, tools for studying glycans are limited compared to those for proteins and nucleic acids. This project aims to exploit our recent breakthroughs in genetic glycoengineering to revisit the biology of carbohydrates, focusing on the interface between the pathogen and the host. Objective 1 aims to understand how the host recognizes and responds to foreign glycans and identify the receptors responsible for capturing bacteria. We will also study the impact of pre-existing antibodies on vaccination outcomes. Next, we will utilize genetic glycoengineering to define the responsible glycan motifs at an unprecedented structural resolution. The results will inform vaccination strategies against pathogens and cancer epitopes. Objective 2 focuses on expanding the capabilities of the genetic glycoengineering platform to produce medically relevant glycans. We will modify the specificity of flippases and glycosyltransferases to overcome the constraints of our current system. The engineered glycans will be harnessed for therapeutic or prebiotic purposes. As these glycans are structurally related, they will facilitate the mechanistic studies in Objective 1. Lastly, we will investigate the immunomodulatory effects of glycans in mouse models and study how glycans influence the gut microbiome. The two main objectives are built on a solid foundation of preliminary data that support the hypotheses, which include enabling tools like a large collection of isogenic capsule-switch mutants, a glycan array platform for detecting antibody responses, and various in vivo models. This program will be led by a team of experts in glycobiology, genetics, molecular biology, biochemistry, immunology, and microbiome studies, with support from international colleagues specializing in clinical studies and immunology. The outcomes of this program have the potential to revolutionize glycobiology and immunobiology, leading to the development of new vaccines, therapeutics, and diagnostic tools.
kw: Microbiology; Genetics; Glycobiology; Bacteriology; Molecular biology

title: Understanding and tackling cooperative cancer chemoresistance with comprehensive single-cell transcriptomic profiling
abs: This research proposal aims to develop and apply a novel single-cell RNA profiling technology, scComplete-seq, to investigate and combat cooperative cancer chemoresistance. The central hypotheses of this work are that miRNAs act as regulatory hubs influencing complex cellular behaviors and that reducing cellular heterogeneity or disrupting cellular interactions can mitigate cooperative chemoresistance. This study has four specific aims: First, to create scComplete-seq, a platform capable of comprehensive single-cell transcriptome profiling by analyzing both polyadenylated and non-polyadenylated RNAs. Second, to utilize this technology to study the role of miR-125b in breast cancer chemoresistance, identifying its gene targets and mediators of cell-cell interactions. Third, to apply the workflow to various other cancer models, including prostate cancer, Ewing’s sarcoma, and head and neck cancers, to explore the generality of miRNA-driven social dynamics. Lastly, to validate therapeutic strategies that disrupt cooperative chemoresistance by targeting miRNA heterogeneity and cell-cell interaction mediators. Our methodology involves implementing in-vitro enzymatic polyadenylation within scComplete-seq for high-throughput single-cell RNA analysis, followed by comprehensive transcriptome analysis in breast cancer cells to elucidate miR-125b’s role in drug resistance. Further, this approach will be extended to other cancer types and patient-derived cultures. Therapeutic interventions targeting miRNA heterogeneity and cell-cell interactions will be tested in vitro to disrupt resistance mechanisms. The feasibility of this study is supported by existing expertise in single-cell transcriptomics and miRNA research, along with preliminary data validating miR-125b’s role in chemoresistance. The scalable technology ensures high-throughput capability, making the study practical and achievable. This research is significant as it addresses the critical issue of cancer chemoresistance by exploring cancer cell cooperation, with the potential to uncover new therapeutic targets and strategies. Successful outcomes could revolutionize cancer treatment, improving patient survival by preventing cooperative drug resistance.
kw: single-cell analysis; micro RNA; cancer; cooperation; altruism; drug resistance

title: Polaritonic Hybrid Optomechanics
abs: Optomechanical systems are a class of experimental devices in which a microscopic mechanical resonator is coupled to a photonic degree of freedom. Nowadays, this coupling can be engineered to be very large, and allow ultra-sensitive control and measurement of mechanical motion. To achieve this, several strategies have been explored so far, often involving an intermediate electronic system. In Pho we propose a new strategy in which an extended state of electron-hole pairs (excitons) is involved, which is designed to be maximally coupled to both photons and motion, and that also provides a strongly nonlinear optical response to the photonic part of the system, that can be exploited to amplify even further the coupling. We will design prototypes of this system that we call a polariton drum, and its full optomechanical response will be assessed quantitatively using the external application of radiation pressure onto the mechanical resonator, using both classical light, and quantum light to explore the most sensitive regime.
kw: Optomechanics; Quantum Sensing; Nonlinear photonics; Quantum optics; advanced semiconudctor nanofabrication

title: From LLMs to LGMs: LLM-empowered Sub-Graph Learning for Large Graph Models
abs: Inspired by the vast success of Large Language Models (LLMs), there is a recent trend of developing Large Graph Models (a.k.a., Graph Foundational Models) aimed at creating unified models trained on extensive graph-structured data. These models seek to adapt effectively to diverse graph downstream tasks spanning various application domains and task categories. LGM in the graph domain entails the same spirit of LLMs, aiming to bring in the generality and expressiveness of handling a wide spectrum of graph tasks, the latter being widely applied in all sectors including transportation, biology, chemistry, computer vision, and social media. This proposal aims to push an important step towards achieving a versatile Large Graph Model (LGM) by further enhancing the graph model expressiveness, scalability and generality in graph learning, by employing a new set of techniques. Our main idea to architect scalable and effective LGM is to orchestrate various learning models over sub-graphs. We consider a sub-graph as a neighbourhood context of a node, e.g., the 2-hop sub-graph centered at the node. In our framework, a range of graph models can be applied at the granularity of sub-graphs, and these choices can be further optimized for specific online graph analytical tasks using hybrid sub-graph encoding techniques and Mixture-of-Expert (MoE) strategies. This approach allows for highly configurable model expressiveness, especially concerning various graph-related tasks, by increasing the model’s parameters, thereby empowering large-scale models. In summary, our project represents the pioneering effort to harness the potential of sub-graph-based learning, scalable sub-graph storage, MoE learning over sub-graphs, graph prompt learning techniques, and LLMs to realize a versatile LGM with robust expressiveness across various graph tasks and domains. Scientifically, the success of this project will serve as direct evidence of applying the scaling law to graphs, giving a significant breakthrough in the field of graph research.
kw: Large Graph Model; Large Language Model; Graph Learning

title: CMOS Photonics Platform for Next Generation Photonics AI Engines
abs: To reduce power consumption and increase the operation bandwidth of AI processing chips, we propose photonic neural network (PNN) chips based on a CMOS electro-optic (EO) photonic platform as a disruptive technology to overcome the limitations of electronic processors. Currently, most photonic AI chips primarily utilize thermal processes, such as thermo-optic and phase change materials, for weight adjustments. However, these methods have significant drawbacks, including high power consumption, noise issues, stability concerns, and considerable delays during weight modifications. Additionally, existing photonic computing architectures rely on devices like Mach-Zehnder Interferometers (MZIs) and Microring Resonators (MRRs) to realize photonic neurons. These devices, with sizes ranging from several to tens of micrometers, hinder the scalability of photonic processors. For photonic in-memory computing, phase-change materials (PCM) are effective but require high temperatures and lack CMOS compatibility, presenting further challenges. Our proposed Work Package 1 will focus on developing a CMOS-compatible EO photonic platform to address these issues. This platform will explore the feasibility of employing EO properties for photonic AI computations and demonstrate enhanced computational efficacy by utilizing materials such as aluminum nitride (AlN), scandium aluminum nitride (ScAlN), and lithium niobate (LN). Work Package 2 will explore new photonic computing architectures and functionalities using subwavelength diffractive metadevices, EO tuning mechanisms, and photonic EO memory. These innovations aim to achieve high-efficiency, in-memory photonic computing, eliminating the need for data transfer with electronic memory and enabling operations in ultra-high-frequency ranges. By simultaneously exploring these two work packages, we aim to develop a novel CMOS-compatible photonic platform that combines EO tuning mechanisms with photonic memory. This platform is expected to support the burgeoning AI industry in Singapore by providing robust hardware foundations for next-generation photonic AI engines, including photonic interposers/interconnects, accelerators, and neural networks.
kw: Photonic AI Computing; Photonic Neural Networks; Photonic Integrated Circuits; CMOS Photonics; Electro-optic Photonics; Photonic Memory

title: Building a Herpes Simplex Virus based gene delivery platform for ocular gene therapy
abs: As gene therapy moves from debilitating conditions to common ailments like glaucoma, the cost-benefit equation necessitates increased safety. A natural approach is to use gene circuits to constrain genetic payloads delivered by a viral vector capable of carrying large therapeutic cassettes. State-of-art AAV vectors have limited capacity (~4kb) and thus cannot be used for monogenic diseases that require augmentation of larger genes, nor can it deliver multifunctional genetic circuits for polygenic complex diseases requiring carefully tuned gene expression. These include, but are not limited, to cell-type specific expression and tunability of output via exogenous agonists or antagonists. A Herpes Simplex virus based vector system overcomes these limitations. It has a large cargo capacity (15-130 kb) and the innate ability to infect human cells persistently while evading the host immune system. However, current iterations of replication-defective HSV vectors retain viral genes and require live helper virus to manufacture. Here we propose to develop a new producer cell line carrying integrated HSV replication genes that can package payloads that are free of HSV viral sequences without helper viruses. Virus production will be triggered upon transfection of a trigger plasmid and amplicon cargo. As proof of principle, we will use the producer line to generate HSV vectors carrying larger, more complicated genetic circuits that are responsive to both endogenous disease relevant metabolites and exogenous small molecule modulators, enabling cell-specific, self-tuning gene expression. These will then be used to restore gene function in mouse models of Stargardt’s disease (ABCA4) and exfoliation glaucoma (CYP39A1), which respectively affects the retina and anterior chamber of the eye. Success in our aims will showcase HSV as an ideal alternative to AAV as vector-of-choice for next-generation genetic circuits and confer a disruptive advantage over gene-therapy startups using current HSV packaging technology.
kw: viral gene therapy; glaucoma ; retinal dystrophy

title: A Quantum Catalyst Leap: Shaping the New Paradigm in Water Oxidation
abs: The advancement of electrochemical methodologies for key chemical synthesis, CO2 and nitrogen reduction, and metal-air battery systems is hindered by inefficient and costly oxygen evolution reaction (OER) catalysts. Traditional catalyst discovery is slow and resource-intensive. Our research aims to transform this field by leveraging quantum electrochemistry to redefine electrocatalysis through quantum-derived descriptors. By engineering quantum states of catalysts and reagents—using single-site/atom manipulation, electronic state modulations, charge transport, and spin injection—we aim to overcome scaling relationship limitations and enhance catalytic efficiency and selectivity. Our project focuses on the complexities of OER catalysis with three strategic aims: developing a library of quantum-based catalysts with advanced in-situ characterization techniques, creating a simulation framework integrating quantum principles with OER dynamics, and investigating atomic-scale electronic behaviors at the catalyst-electrolyte interface to design high-efficiency electrolyzers. Leveraging advances in supercomputers, high-purity chemicals, and state-of-the-art equipment, this project aims to reignite interest in quantum electrochemistry. Supported by our recent breakthroughs such as the spin pinning effect, we aim to develop high-efficiency water electrolyzers and extend these innovations to reactions like ammonia oxidation, CO2 reduction, and methanol oxidation. This research could revolutionize catalyst design, enhance industrial processes, and advance materials science, offering efficient and sustainable solutions for various electrochemical applications.
kw: Energy; electrochemistry; electrocatalysis; water oxidation; quantum catalyst

title: Extreme Bose-Einstein Condensates for On-chip Ising Machines
inst: IMRE - Institute of Materials Research and Engineering
abs: This project proposes a unique approach for scalable all-optical on-chip Ising machines by leveraging advancements in designing, fabricating, and characterizing exciton-polariton condensates in photonic structures. The implementation of Ising machines involves solving the Ising model, which is equivalent to searching for the ground state spin configuration of the general Ising Hamiltonian. Our Ising machines proposal revolves around harnessing a photonic supercavity (i.e., a photonic structure that can efficiently confine light) coupled with excitonic materials with high binding energies at room temperature. To engineer the supercavity operating at the material's emission wavelength, we rely on the foundational principles of Mietronics. By applying new cavity concept such as bound state in the continuum (BIC), we can efficiently localize light within unconventional meta-structures and manipulate the transport of polariton condensates at will. We will be able to facilitate the realization of exciton-polariton condensates under extreme conditions, including at room temperature and within tightly confined spaces which is not achievable by conventional microcavities. Consequently, this advancement paves the way for scaling up the network of Ising spins to realize all-optical on-chip Ising machines.
kw: Ising machine; metasurface; Bose Einstein Condensation; Bound state in continuum; nanophotonics

title: Engineering Spin-Triplet Zero-Energy Quasiparticles in Ferromagnet-Superconductor Heterostructures
inst: IMRE - Institute of Materials Research and Engineering
abs: The advent of quantum computing has forged a lucrative avenue to address complex computational problems facing modern society. Quantum bits (aka. “qubits”) encode information using the superposition of quantum states, typically in superconducting (SC) devices. Indispensable to scale quantum computing for complex problems is the need for coherent interactions between thousands of qubits. However, state-of-the-art qubits are highly sensitive to local fluctuations and disorder, which introduce propagating errors and decoherence, and inhibit scaling. This decoherence bottleneck can be circumvented by employing intrinsically protected “topological” qubits – immune to local perturbations. But unlike conventional qubits, topological qubits need spin-triplet zero-energy quasi-particles (TZQs), with p-wave pairing symmetry. Despite exhaustive studies of several candidates, TZQs with qubit-like attributes remain elusive. Material platforms to stabilize, engineer, and detect TZQs are a critical need for quantum technologies. Our team has established world-leading capabilities in ferromagnetic (FM) heterostructures and devices, which, when interfaced with SCs, promise robust, scalable TZQ platforms. First, we have used chiral FMs to develop designer topological spin textures, or “skyrmions”. When coupled to a SC, they can form skyrmion-vortex pairs – promising TZQ candidates. Our recent, world-first achievement of all-electrical skyrmion control can exclusively enable SVP readout and manipulation. On the other hand, we have developed spin-resolved 2D van der Waals heterostructures. Upon dilute magnetic doping, some 2D materials exhibit unconventional SC, which can also generate TZQs. This project aims to engineer FM/SC heterostructures to (1) create tunable, device-compatible TZQs by leveraging both chiral multilayer and 2D material platforms, and (2) investigate the potential of such TZQs towards fault-tolerant qubits. It exploits the unique characteristics of FM/SCs designed by each PI to develop tunnel junction and Josephson junction devices for detecting, characterizing, and controlling TZQs. It leverages the complementarity of materials and synergy of imaging and transport capabilities of the 2 PIs, as well as the experimental and theoretical expertise of the 3 collaborators. It is expected to set the stage for a larger effort on scalable topological qubits centered in Singapore.
kw: magnetism, superconductivity, topology, spintronics, 2D materials, thin films, tunnel junctions

title: Enabling Self-Stabilized Optical Levitation based on Metasurfaces
inst: IMRE - Institute of Materials Research and Engineering
abs: Standard approaches manipulate matter using focused optical or electromagnetic fields. These face fundamental limits to precision based on the ability of bulk elements to localise electromagnetic fields. These also require bulky optics, magnets, or coils. Only some materials can be trapped in this manner, which often suffer from stochastic, imprecise fabrication. Metasurfaces structure the reflected light using engineered subwavelength features. This provides exquisite, local manipulation of the optical field with extremely thin and lightweight devices. Since the optical manipulation is performed by the metasurface layer, much simpler setups are required, and a wider range of materials and geometries are enabled. This frontier CRP project will develop an entirely new class of levitated systems, leveraging metasurfaces to exhibit self-stabilised levitation. The sub- wavelength features will scatter light so as to apply a restoring force which stabilises the levitated system against lateral motions or tilts. This will introduce a new paradigm to optical manipulation, enabling the field to leverage structured light for unprecedented control, and entirely new regimes of operation, with vast applications in sensing and metrology, micro and nano-robotics and even space exploration.
kw: Nano-optics, Optical levitation, metasurfaces, sensors

title: Altermagnets: A new avenue to emerging spintronics
abs: Magnetism plays an important role in the field of data storage and memory technologies. Magnetic recording helps to store 80% of the data that we generate. Magnetic memory has entered into conventional semiconductor technology to replace e-Flash. These applications are possible due to ferromagnetic materials (FM). However, the data stored in FM are susceptible to stray magnetic fields and the time required to switch is a few ns, which limit the speed of operation. In contrast, antiferromagnetic (AFM) materials overcome these problems and there is a surge in research activity. More recently, a new class of materials called altermagnets were discovered, which combine the benefit of AFM and FM materials. This is an emerging area and there are a lot of unexplored academic and technological significance in altermagnets. The lead PI and team will work on these altermagnets to achieve the following objectives: 1. To grow new altermagnet materials using sputtering, pulsed-laser deposition (PLD), and molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) and to study their effectiveness in magnetization switching for spintronics applications. 2. Probing the fundamentals of altermagnet materials, such as antiferromagnetic order, lifting of degeneracy etc., using spin-polarized scanning tunnelling microscopy (SP-STM) and complementing techniques. 3. Fabrication of devices using altermagnets and investigation of multifunctional materials combining altermagnets with ferroelectric materials. In order to achieve the three major objectives, we have divided the project into three work packages (WP1-WP3). WP1 on growth and basics of altermagnet materials will be led by the lead-PI (S.N. Piramanayagam), where growth of new materials and field-free magnetization switching will be the main focus. WP2 will be led by team-PI (Bent Weber) and will focus on the fundamental investigations of altermagnets, where insights will be developed from spin-polarized tunnelling microscopy and quasiparticle interference. WP3 will be led by team-PI (Wang Xiao Renshaw) and will focus on developing novel multifunctional materials and devices based on altermagnets. These three work packages are closed tied to achieve the objectives mentioned above. In the first two years, the team will focus on (a) growing at least 2 new altermagnet materials and the study of magnetization switching (b) development of SP-STP and investigations of 1 or 2 altermagnet material and (c) the growth of various multifunctional materials and characterization. After the mid-term evaluation, the team will focus on (a) field-free magnetization switching, (b) quasiparticle interference mapping and visualization of magnetic order (c) fabrication of tunnel junction devices and (d) altermagnet/superconductor heterostructures. Technologically significant innovations will be filed as patents. Attempts will be made for technological translation with GlobalFoundries and/or other semiconductor companies.
