Through interdisciplinary collaboration spanning EUV generation, nanophotonics, and materials science, our research aims to lay the groundwork for the development of next-generation EUV light sources and pave the way for their widespread adoption in various industrial and scientific domains.
kw: extreme ultraviolet (EUV); light-matter interactions; quantum electrodynamics; metastructures; quantum materials; Purcell effect

title: Molecular mapping of genomic factors in host-microbiome interplay during MASH onset
abs: The disruption of microbial commensals in the gastrointestinal tract, also known as gut dysbiosis, is a main driver of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). Thus far, no single gut bacterium has been definitively identified as a pathobiont. Given the heterogeneity in MASLD progression, we hypothesize that host multiomic factors are key modulators of host-microbiome interplay during the transition of milder condition of MASLD (metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver; MASL) to a more severe form (metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis; MASH). Leveraging a unique humanized mouse model with MASH-associated microbiome and the Hybrid Mouse Diversity Panel (HMDP) which is optimized for mouse genome-wide association study, the research explores host genetic-microbiome interactions during MASH development. Adopting a systems biology approach, the study pursues two specific aims: first, unraveling host genetic factors linked to susceptibility to gut dysbiosis-induced MASH, and second, investigating the molecular mechanisms underpinning the host-microbiome interaction. By using a subset of genetically diverse HMDP, we can tap into the rich publicly accessible genetic and traits resources to unveil precise host gene-pathobiont pairs dictating susceptibility and exacerbation of MASH. We will integrate the GWAS findings from PRECISE-SG100K cohort to ensure clinical significance and translatability of the mouse data to the local and Asian MASH patients. Validation of the host gene-pathobiont pairs in MASH pathogenesis will be conducted via interrogation of dynamic changes in transcriptomic and metabolomic profiles as the disease deteriorates. Coupled with integrative data analysis, we will systematically map out the reciprocal host-microbiome crosstalk driving MASH. The identification of distinctive molecular features and their correlation with gut pathobionts contributes to a comprehensive understanding of MASLD heterogeneity, presenting translational significance in the development of enhanced screening methods and personalized therapeutics in MASLD. These efforts have broader implications in alleviating healthcare burdens, economic implications, and well-being loss linked to the chronic disease.
kw: gut dysbiosis; metabolic-associated fatty liver disease; systems biology; precision medicine; host-pathogen interaction; gut-liver axis

title: Reprogramming a behavioural setpoint for neurodevelopmental disorder
abs: Risk factors like genetic predispositions and environmental teratogens can derail neurodevelopment leading to lifelong conditions; autism spectrum disorder (ASD) being one of such conditions. We observed that a single application of psilocybin can rescue social deficits in well-established mouse models of ASD. This rescue effect is sustained for weeks and can be blocked by DNA methyltransferase inhibition, pointing towards a yet unexplored epigenetic route of action. Our data also indicated that psilocybin may manipulate critical period timing to facilitate behavioural re-adjustments. Building on these observations, this YIRG aims to 1) uncover in mechanistic detail the epigenetic route of psilocybin action; 2) identify and deduce the fundamental neuronal circuit rescuing mechanisms common to genetic and environmental neurodevelopmental risk factors; 3) examine the potential of reversing social deficits in ASD model mice through reprogramming during an experimentally induced or extended critical period. Collectively, the YIRG will test the central hypothesis that the sustained effects of psilocybin is mediated via epigenetic mechanisms independent of its currently known action through serotonergic signalling, and that this contributes to a pharmacological manipulation of critical period. To test this, we will conduct a multi-level investigation using epigenetic profiling, histological analysis, electrophysiology, and behavioural pharmacology using both genetic and non-genetic ASD mouse models. Psilocybin’s therapeutic potential has already been recognised by US FDA as “Breakthrough Therapy” status and entered clinical controlled use in Australia starting July 2023. Its ability to lastingly alleviate mental health issues in humans following a single treatment is particularly striking but the enigmatic mechanistic basis of this mode of action cannot be studied in humans. This YIRG work will 1) better inform its clinical application and usage; 2) mechanistically inform further drug development efforts; 3) open new research directions for enhancing our brain’s potential via rejuvenation of critical period-associated brain plasticity.
kw: Neurodevelopment; epigenetics; synaptic plasticity; sociability; reprogramme; critical period

title: Precise functional measurements of synthetic lethal nodes in treatment-resistant non-small-cell lung cancer
abs: Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) are used as first-line therapy for non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients with actionable driver mutations. However, patients eventually progressed on therapy. Although immuno-checkpoint inhibitions have given a new angle in NSCLC treatment, this again did not prevent subsequent progression. Thus, more research is warranted into finding alternate therapy to address such resistant or progression cases. TKI-resistant cells often undergo metabolic reprogramming with increased dependence on oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and production of reactive oxygen species (ROS). Nonetheless, how mitochondrial functions affect survival in the context of TKI resistance is still unclear. Deregulated kinase activity and apoptotic signaling are some of the key pathways that drive drug resistance. As ROS is a key regulator of kinases, it is possible that increased OXPHOS may promote survival and drug resistance by changing the redox milieu, thus reprogramming the kinome enzymatic landscape to affect apoptotic signaling. Ascertaining these complex interactive signals would help to identify novel actionable targets and drug combinations to eliminate TKI-resistant NSCLC cells. Here, we propose an orthogonal approach, incorporating functional precision medicine techniques to profile the mitochondrial OXPHOS, ROS, kinome enzymatic levels in treatment-resistant NSCLC cells and select for drugs against these functional nodes. Given that OXPHOS, ROS and kinases are potential upstream regulators of apoptotic proteins, targeting these nodes may increase priming of resistant cells for apoptosis. As such, we will further utilize the functional precision medicine technique BH3 profiling to measure the ability of drugs-of-interest to prime cells for apoptosis and to identify survival dependences on specific anti-apoptotic proteins for combinatorial inhibition. Collectively, our study uses specific functional profiles to identify drugs-of-interest, capable of inducing an Achilles’ heel at the apoptotic protein level, thus permitting subsequent combination with specific anti-apoptotic protein inhibitors, BH3 mimetics, to induce synthetic lethality on treatment-resistant NSCLC cells.
kw: Tyrosine kinase inhibitor resistance; lung cancer; Mitochondrial metabolism; BCL-2 family proteins; Cell death; Functional precision medicine

title: Dissecting the importance of cholesterol transport machineries for brain health
abs: Demographic shift in aging societies, including Singapore, is increasing the burden of neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s diseases. Despite decades of research, there is currently no cure for any neurodegenerative disorders. Cholesterol is the most abundant lipid in the brain. In adults, cholesterol is synthesized in astrocytes and delivered to neurons, oligodendrocytes, and microglia for their proper functions. In neurons, cholesterol is enriched in the primary cilium, an antenna like structure protruding from cell surface, and contributing to the regulation of signaling events. Dysregulation of cholesterol in the brain has been linked to neurodegenerative diseases; however, little is known about how cholesterol distribution is regulated in these different brain cell types to maintain brain health. Growing evidence indicates the importance of non-vesicular transport facilitated by evolutionarily conserved family of lipid transfer proteins (LTPs), including GRAMD1s (GRAMD1a/1b/1c), OSBP and ORPs, for cellular cholesterol homeostasis. Importantly, mutations in LTPs are associated with neurological diseases, indicating potential roles of LTPs in neuronal health. I hypothesize that the dysregulation of LTPs, including GRAMD1s, OSBP and ORPs, leads to the disruption of cholesterol homeostasis in various brain cell types, ultimately impacting brain health. In this project, I will elucidate 1) the importance of LTPs in various brain cell types (focusing on neurons and astrocytes) differentiated from human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) for their cellular functions; 2) how cholesterol is delivered to the primary cilium, where cholesterol plays a critical role in regulating neuronal signaling events. This project will reveal the importance of cholesterol homeostasis maintained by LTPs in various brain cell types and the molecular mechanisms that are responsible for critical signaling events for brain health.
kw: cholesterol; primary cilia; lipid transfer protein; membrane contact sites; neurodegenerative diseases; glia cells

title: Targeting serotonin signalling to boost HCC immunotherapy
abs: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a major global disease burden with East and Southeast Asia having the highest incidence rates. Despite recent clinical advances in treating HCC with combination immunotherapy, around two-thirds of patients do not respond to any treatment. Because the strongly immunosuppressive liver microenvironment dampens any tumour-specific immune reactions, there is a critical need to identify dominant immunosuppressive mechanisms restraining anti-tumour immune responses within the liver and HCC microenvironments to rationally design effective (combination) immunotherapies. We recently identified 5-HT2A and 5-HT7, two serotonin (5-HT) receptors, as potential targets for HCC immunotherapy using complementary functional in vitro small molecule screening and in vivo CRISPR screening approaches, respectively. In addition, a 5-HT-associated gene signature is enriched in HCC patient tumours that do not respond to combination immunotherapy. We therefore hypothesise that serotonin signalling suppresses the anti-tumour immune response within the HCC tumour microenvironment. We will validate 5-HT7 as a candidate for HCC immunotherapy by evaluating the in vivo efficacy of disrupting 5-HT7 signalling using drug inhibitors (systemic blockade) or by CRISPR knockout of Htr7 in HCC tumour-specific CD8 T cells (Aim 1). In parallel, we will identify key cellular and molecular responses to serotonin signalling in HCC tumours by transcriptional profiling of the tumour microenvironment following systemic blockade of peripheral 5-HT signalling (Aim 2). We will also determine the source of immunologically active 5-HT within livers with HCC tumours to facilitate designing of therapeutic approaches to precisely ablate 5-HT signalling (Aim 3). We envision that our proposed research will shed light on a relatively unexplored area of liver and HCC immunology to open up new avenues for HCC therapeutics development.
kw: Immunotherapy; HCC; Serotonin; T cells; Liver cancer

title: Insights into Newborn Immune Response Signatures Conferring Susceptibility to Atopic Dermatitis using Cord Blood Single Cell RNA Sequencing
abs: Atopic dermatitis (AD) or eczema is the commonest chronic inflammatory skin disease in children and is usually the first manifestation of the atopic phenotype which begins in early infancy. Although genetic factor plays an important role, environmental risk factors interacting with host genes contribute significantly to the development of allergy. The influence of potentially modifiable environmental risk factors begin as early as the pregnancy period, and maternal health influences this outcome. Using cord blood mononuclear cells (CBMCs), researchers have shown a distinctive signature of phenotype of cells in response to toll-like receptors (TLR) stimulation in infants who subsequently developed allergic disorders. We hypothesize that immune programming commences in the prenatal period and extends as a continuum through to the postnatal period into infancy. Infants born with a pro-inflammatory immune phenotype(s) sets the stage towards aberrant postnatal immune responses and increase the susceptibility to allergic disease. We aim to leverage on maternal-infant dyads of the Singapore's PREconception study of long-Term maternal and child Outcomes (SPRESTO) cohort to deep phenotype human umbilical CBMCs of infants with/without AD by using an array of in vitro stimuli that could mimic/represent postnatal immune responses to microbials and their products, and to delineate immunological patterns that may influence the development AD using the approach of single cell RNA (scRNA) sequencing. This will help guide the development and monitoring of prenatal preventive intervention strategies to reduce the susceptibility to allergic disorders.
kw: atopic dermatitis, cord blood, single cell RNA sequencing

title: Regulation of Cav1.2 channel by deubiquitinases USP13 and USP5: Implications in vascular and neuronal dysfunction
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Cav1.2 calcium channel plays crucial roles in numerous physiological functions, such as learning and memory. Altered Cav1.2 channel functions are associated with neurodegenerative disorders. Cav1.2 channels have been reported to be ubiquitinated by E3 ligase RFP2 and degraded via proteasome. However, the modulation of Cav1.2 channel by deubiquitinases, particularly in neurodegenerative diseases, remains unknown. Here, we propose a completely novel mechanism about the regulation of Cav1.2 channel by deubiquitinases (DUBs), USP5 and USP13. Contrary to our expectation, an inverse correlation between Cav1.2 and USP13(5) expressions was identified in rat brains with vascular dementia. Our hypothesis: By suppressing CaVβ, the deubiquitinases USP5 and USP13 downregulate Cav1.2 expression and function by binding to the proximal C-terminus of Cav1.2 channel, which may lead to the pathophysiology of vascular dementia with cerebral chronic hypoxia. Three specific aims are proposed to test the hypothesis: Aim #1: To characterize the mechanism and functional outcome of the Cav1.2-USP13(5) interactions (Molecular cloning, co-IP, Western blotting, surface protein biotinylation, calcium imaging, patch-clamp electrophysiological recordings and immunostaining will be performed) Aim #2: To investigate roles of Cav1.2-USP13(5) interactions under chronic hypoxia and in animal model of vascular dementia (Primary microglia and neuron culture and USP13(5) knockout mice will be used and vascular dementia animal models will be generated) Aim #3: To test a peptide blocking Cav1.2-USP13(5) interaction in vascular dementia animal models (Luxol fast blue/cresyl violet staining and behaviour tests will be performed to evaluate the blocking peptide’s effects in vascular dementia animals) Feasibility: We have acquired substantial preliminary data to support our hypothesis that USP13(5) binds to the proximal region of Cav1.2 C-terminus and down-regulates Cav1.2 by suppressing Cavβ, which reveals a novel mechanism involved in the pathogenesis of vascular dementia and provide a potential way to intervene in the progression of vascular dementia by developing a blocking peptide.
kw: Cav1.2 channel; deubiquitinase; USP13; USP5; hypoxia; vascular dementia

title: Mitigating Colorectal Cancer Development by investigating the role of Helios in anti-tumor intestinal tissue-resident Vg7 Gamma Delta intraepithelial lymphocytes
abs: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the 3rd most common cancer globally and the most prevalent cancer type in Singapore, affecting 48.9 per 100,000. One of the critical challenges of CRC is identifying the early immunological events before the metastatic stage, and the risk factors associated with CRC development include dysregulated gut microenvironment and dysfunctional mucosal immune response. Intestinal intraepithelial lymphocytes expressing the gd T cell receptor (gd IEL) are sentinel immune cells along the intestinal epithelium that provide the first line of defense against tumors and are predominantly Vg7. Helios, a transcription factor, limits T cells’ effector functions and is associated with immunosuppressive functions. Our preliminary data indicates increased expression of Helios in Vg7 IEL after the 1st and 2nd rounds of AOM/DSS, with polyps developing after the 2nd round. Thus, we hypothesize that Vg7 IEL anti-tumor effector functions become increasingly impaired with increased Helios expression during successive AOM/DSS treatment in C57BL/6 Wild-type mice model of CRC. However, the role of Helios in Vg7 IEL and its mode of modulation, molecular mechanisms, and impacts on effector functions of Vg7 IEL have not been investigated. Thus, this proposed study aims to characterize the kinetics of Helios expression in Vg7 IELs during CRC development, as well as elucidate its role and molecular mechanisms in determining Vg7 IEL anti-tumor effector functions. Using high-dimensional flow cytometry, multiplex proteomics, pharmacological degraders, functional assays, antibody depletion of Vg7 IEL, and scRNA-seq, we aim to elucidate the role and molecular mechanism of Helios on Vg7 IEL both in-vitro and in-vivo. Findings obtained from this study will enable us to identify novel targets and biomarkers, develop potential cell therapies, and design new prophylactics associated with Helios and Vg7 IELs against CRC.
kw: colorectal cancer; gamma delta T cells; helios; gut immunity; intestinal intraepithelial lymphocytes

title: Deciphering invasion factors involved in zoonotic malaria.
abs: Malaria is a vector borne disease that affects millions mainly in developing countries. Four different Plasmodium species are known to infect human – P. falciparum, P. vivax, P. ovale and P. malariae. In addition, in the last two decades two simian malaria species, P. knowlesi and P. cynomolgi prevalent in Southeast Asian region have been reported as zoonotic malarias. Zoonoses refers to infectious diseases which can cross species barriers from their natural animal host to humans and include viruses, bacteria, fungi, or parasites. Examples include SARS-CoV-2, and salmonellosis, while extensive research and literature exist on viral zoonotic diseases, zoonotic malaria remains largely understudied. Zoonotic malaria is a growing global problem associated with increasing deforestation and urbanization and is predicted to increase with global warming and global travel, particularly in Southeast Asia. The parasite has a complex life cycle, with a pre-erythrocytic and an erythrocytic stage in its mammalian hosts. Studies have indicated that the barrier to infection is at the level of the blood stage but not the at pre-erythrocytic stages. The objective of this study is to identify the molecular mechanisms of zoonotic malaria parasites that allow them to invade red blood cells. Specifically, we will focus on understanding the role of parasite invasion ligands and host cell receptors required for zoonotic malaria infections through the specific aims below: Aim 1: Characterization of P. knowlesi invasion ligands Aim 2: Identification of receptors present on the surface of red blood cells responsible for P. knowlesi invasion Aim 3: Biochemical validation of human receptor-ligand interactions
kw: Malaria, Zoonosis, Plasmodium knowlesi, Host-switch, Invasion, Vaccine

title: Unveiling genetic, epigenetic and environmental risk factors in early onset colorectal cancers through computational approaches leveraging on long read sequencing
abs: Early onset colorectal cancer (EO-CRC) affects patients younger than the age of 50 years compared to late onset CRC (LO-CRC) patients. EO-CRC is rising in incidence worldwide and in Singapore, despite the trend of LO-CRC decreasing due to screening programs. EO-CRC have been shown to have substantial differences in clinical and molecular phenotypes, such as higher prevalence of germline variants in DNA repair pathways including the mismatch repair (MMR) and polymerase epsilon. EO-CRC without defects in DNA repair pathways can have changes in epigenetic profiles, prior exposures to carcinogens from pathogenic E.coli species and presence of an inflammatory microenvironment as potential risk factors. However, it is difficult to detect all these risk factors in a single assay and a comprehensive comparison of these risk factors are lacking. Furthermore, there are no tools that can determine if these risk factors can increase the fitness of a sub-population of clones. We aim to discover genetic and non-genetic risk factors in a cohort of 200 EO-CRC and LO-CRC patients and develop a computational tool to detect mutational signatures in real-time using Oxford Nanopore long read sequencing data. Long read sequencing can detect both genetic and non-genetic alterations by spanning complex rearrangements and deconvoluting immune profiles based on methylation on the same reads. Using the long read CRC and publicly available data, we aim to develop new computational methods and build a real-time point-of-care mutational signatures diagnostic tool that runs on consumer-grade laptops. Lastly, we will model EO-CRC risk factors by exposing patient-derived organoids to the mutagen colibactin. We will sequence the organoid, at timepoints and single cell resolution, to observe clonal dynamics, track clone populations and determine the effects of the exposure in clonal populations. The effects on clonal fitness can be quantified and inform on cancer risks of patients with prior exposure.
kw: Early onset colorectal cancer; cancer genomics; long read sequencing; real-time genetic testing; Mutational Signatures; Patient derived organoids

title: Evaluating Lgr5/6-Expressing Cells as Prognostic Markers and Therapeutic Targets in Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma (ESCC)
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Esophageal cancer ranks as the 7th most prevalent cancer globally and the 6th leading cause of cancer-related deaths, with a low five-year overall survival rate. Pathologically, esophageal cancer is commonly classified into two types: esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) and esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC), with ESCC being the predominant form, accounting for more than 80% of cases. The Asian population exhibits exceptionally high rates of esophageal cancer frequency, accounting for 80% of cases detected globally. ESCC diagnosis is often associated with poor prognosis due to late detection, disease complexity, and high relapse rates. In Singapore (2020), 94% of reported cases were fatal, emphasizing the urgent need for innovative approaches enabling early detection and a comprehensive understanding of esophageal cancer molecular features and cell dynamics. Our study aims to address this gap by focusing on deciphering the role of Lgr5/6-expressing cells in ESCC development. Elevated Lgr5 and Lgr6 expression, together with their ligands RSPO1-4, are often associated with dysregulated Wnt signalling in disease settings, including cancer. We aim to evaluate Lgr5+/6+cell presence and roles at pre-tumour, early, and advanced tumour stages using a validated mouse model for ESCC induction. We will identify potential biomarkers or therapeutic targets associated with these cells using advanced sequencing technologies and exploring available databases, followed by q-PCR, ISH, and IHC/IF validations on mouse samples and human biopsies. Functional validation of Lgr5+/6+ cells will be done in organoid culture to assess their effect on ESCC organoid initiation, survival, and growth potential. Combining mouse models, in vitro culture, and human samples, our study aims to gain a comprehensive understanding of ESCC onset and progression and offers insights that could significantly advance clinical research and improve outcomes for ESCC patients.
kw: ESCC; Esophagus; Cancer; Biomarkers; Stem Cells

title: Towards rationale vaccine design: Elucidating the transcriptional regulation of memory B cells and plasma cells differentiation
abs: Long-lived antibody responses are essential for durable vaccine protection. Memory B cells (MBC) and plasma cells (PC) are key B cell subsets in mediating this response. However, there is incomplete understanding of the molecular determinants of MBC and PC development during germinal centre (GC) responses. Using mouse models with B-cell specific deletion of core binding factors (CBFs) and a T cell-dependent immunisation protocol, we propose to interrogate the requirements of these transcription factors in the differentiation and maintenance of MBC and PC. We also aim to understand the role of these proteins in regulating the quantity and quality of antibody responses during immunisation and infection. Since MBC express high levels of CBFs, we hypothesize that these transcription factors are necessary to regulate the differentiation of MBC and that the magnitude and quality of antibody response will be negatively impacted in mice with deficiency in CBFs. Upon completion of this project, our work will lead to discovery of novel transcriptional circuitry underlying B cell fate decision during GC responses. A better understanding of the factors that control the differentiation and maintenance of MBC and PC is crucial for designing novel therapeutics for the enhancement of long-lived antibody responses against infectious diseases as in the case of rationale vaccine design. In addition, this work can uncover novel drug targets that can eliminate pathogenic MBCs and PCs in B cell-mediated malignancies such as cancer or autoimmunity.
kw: Memory B cells, Plasma cells, Antibodies

title: Inducible CHO Display Expression System for Accelerated Development of Bispecific Antibody Producing Cell Lines
abs: Bispecific antibodies (bsAbs) are powerful therapeutic agents, but producing them in CHO cells is challenging due to the need to express three or more chains. The relative expression of these chains affects bsAb pairing, yield, and aggregation. Current cell line development technologies cannot control gene expression at optimal ratios. Companies design vectors with different copy numbers and gene arrangements, testing them in transient transfection. However, results from transient transfection do not translate well to stable cell lines due to integration site variability, requiring extensive screening. We propose developing a targeted integration-based inducible CHO display system for high-throughput screening of cell lines producing high titer and correctly paired bsAbs. This system includes two key components: 1) a CHO master cell line with two landing pads in active genomic sites for site-specific integration, and 2) vectors with different chain arrangements capable of switchable display and secretion of antibodies. After transfection, an inducer traps bsAbs on the cell surface, followed by antigen staining and FACS sorting for optimal gene expression. Identified cells are then grown in medium without inducers to allow bsAb secretion. This platform aims to significantly reduce the timeline and effort for developing bsAb-producing cell lines compared to current technologies.
kw: bispecific antibodies; cell line development; antibodies; vector

title: Enhancing the efficacy of chemotherapy for colorectal cancer through butyrate producing bacteria consortia
abs: Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains a major health burden, with chemoresistance posing significant challenges. Emerging evidence suggests that gut microbiota, particularly butyrate-producing bacteria, may enhance chemotherapy responsiveness. This study hypothesizes that butyrate-producing bacteria can act as bio-therapeutics to improve the efficacy of CRC chemotherapy, either through direct interactions with cancer cells or by modulating the gut microbiome. Specific Aim 1 evaluates the efficacy of butyrate-producing bacteria in enhancing CRC chemotherapy response by assessing their impact on chemoresistant CRC cell lines, patient-derived organoids, and gut-on-chip systems, and testing their therapeutic effects in xenograft and spontaneous CRC mouse models. Specific Aim 2 investigates the mechanisms by which butyrate-producing bacteria influence chemotherapy efficacy through RNA sequencing and pathway analysis on treated cells and tissues to identify key genes and pathways, and validates hub-gene expression and receptor activation via western blot and qPCR. Specific Aim 3 evaluates the impact of butyrate-producing bacteria on human microbiome composition by analyzing changes in microbial communities using stool-derived in vitro communities (SIC) and humanized microbiome models, and assessing colonization efficacy and microbial modifications via metagenomics sequencing and strain-specific qPCR. The study uses advanced in vitro systems, in vivo mouse models, multi-omics techniques, and humanized microbiome models to systematically explore the therapeutic potential and mechanisms of action of butyrate-producing bacteria. This research leverages cutting-edge methodologies and robust experimental designs to ensure reliable results. The findings could significantly enhance current CRC treatment strategies by providing a novel microbiome-based therapeutic approach, potentially leading to improved patient outcomes.
kw: colorectal cancer; chemotherapy; microbiome

title: Identifying early determinants of childhood obesity mediated through host-microbiome interactions
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: The gut microbiome plays a crucial role in host energy homeostasis by regulating eating behaviour and energy expenditure. Gut microbiome dysbiosis has been associated with many diseases including gastrointestinal diseases, metabolic disorders, cognitive development and mental health. Understanding the complex interplay between the gut and the host can help to develop early interventions and deter poor health outcomes. Existing studies have investigated biomarkers and risk factors associated with obesity and obesity-related diseases. However, the relationship between microbiome and health outcomes remains elusive. The microbiome during the first 10 years of early life is highly dynamic and maternal factors such as breastfeeding, maternal obesity and mode of delivery contributes towards the diversity of the child’s microbiome and future health outcomes. It remains unclear to what extent maternal factors during pregnancy and extrinsic factors during developmental ages can shape the child’s microbiome to affect later life. We hypothesized that maternal factors only affect the child’s microbiome during early childhood and extrinsic factors play a more important role in shaping the child’s health from middle childhood onwards. Dysbiosis of the gut microbiota during early age will affect child’s health in the future and there are distinct host-microbiome interactions that can predict these changes. It is crucial to adopt a holo-omics approach to study the possible interactions between the environment, host and the gut microbiome. We aim to investigate the factors influencing gut microbiome composition and identify novel host-microbiome interactions that are associated with childhood obesity and health outcomes. At the same time, we will develop a tool to combine microbiome data with host molecular information to derive host-microbiome signatures characterizing future health outcomes. Leveraging on data collected from the GUSTO study combined with cross-cohort and preclinical validation, we will investigate how the future childhood obesity can be mediated through host-microbiome interactions.
kw: Multi-omics; Network approach; Gut microbiome; host-microbiome interactions; Metabolic health; Early childhood

title: Diabetic Corneal Neuropathy: A Potential Window into Diabetic Microvascular Complications
abs: Diabetes presents significant microvascular complications, including neuropathy, nephropathy and retinopathy. The unmet clinical needs are there are no sensitive functional evaluation and direct imaging tools for diabetic peripheral neuropathy (DPN), leading to late and underdiagnosis. Additionally, the relationship between these diabetic microvascular complications remains unclear, although they are interlinked. Diabetic corneal neuropathy (DCN) is a form of DPN. Studies have demonstrated that DCN precedes DPN and diabetic retinopathy (DR), and corneal nerve status is significantly correlated with the severity of diabetic microvascular complications. Given this positive evidence, we hypothesize that DCN can serve as a window into diabetic microvascular complications as these microvascular complications share common pathogeneses, and neuronal degeneration precedes microangiographic alterations. With the incorporation of multimodal data, artificial intelligence (AI) techniques and novel imaging modalities, such as large-area nerve scanning, the relationship between DCN and diabetic microvascular complications can be established, and predictive algorithms can be developed. We will recruit 600 patients with diabetes in this longitudinal study. We will develop AI-based prediction models for the progression of DPN and diabetic nephropathy, using corneal nerve images, corneal clinical features and clinical risk factors (Aim 1). We will investigate the relationship between DCN and DR using multimodal corneal neural and retinal imaging, corneal and retinal data, and tear molecular profiles (Aim 2). Additionally, we will construct a deep learning model for automated evaluation of large-area corneal nerve images, and validate its performance in the assessment of DCN (Aim 3). Our study will early identify patients at risk, allowing timely and stratified management. It will unravel the relationships between diabetic microvascular complications, providing the basis for exploring new imaging or molecular biomarkers, as well as strengthening the multidisciplinary approach for diabetes management. The development of quantitative software for large-area corneal nerve scanning is innovative and tremendously addresses unmet clinical needs.
kw: Cornea; corneal nerves; corneal neuropathy

title: SUREFIND-NDD: Singapore Undiagnosed Disease Research Endeavour For Identification of Novel genetic Discoveries in NeuroDevelopmental Disorders
abs: Background: Neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) are a socially debilitating disorder affecting ~5% of the paediatric population in Singapore, and have considerable overlap with adult neurological disorders. Although there is a strong genetic component to NDD, due to extreme genetic heterogeneity, a cause cannot be identified in majority of the individuals by traditional genetic tests, signifying a critical unmet medical need. Through the current CSA, we have used complementary genetic tools such as whole genome sequencing (WGS), transcriptome sequencing and long-read WGS to increase our diagnostic yield by 20%. However, >50% of the patients still remain undiagnosed. Objective: The overarching goal of this research is to integrate the information through a multi-modal platform that combines cutting-edge AI and cellular models to identify and prioritise variants most likely to be clinically relevant. Methods: Over the past 10 years, the applicant and team have recruited over 240 families with NDD, referred to our clinics at KKH and NUHS, achieving a diagnostic yield of 49.0%. In SA1, we will apply standardized phenotyping and advanced bioinformatic analysis on the multi-omics data from our cohort of patients with undiagnosed neurodevelopmental disorders (n=100) to identify causal variants. In SA2, we will perform functional characterisation of selected variants in human neural stem cells and establish disease models in human cerebral organoids. Clinical Significance: Use of these advanced computational tools and functional characterisation will allow us to identify the underlying aetiology for NDDs. Elucidating the genetic causes will allow us to understand molecular pathways and provide insights into potential biomarkers and therapeutic targets. Given the overlap with adult neurological disorders, understanding from these rare disorders can be applied to the commoner adult disorders.
kw: Neurodevelopmental disorders; Genetics; organoids; iPSCs; bioinformatics

title: Elucidating disease-relevant ligand-receptor interactions in early Multiple Sclerosis cortical pathology
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Progressive Multiple Sclerosis (MS) pathology is characterized by prominent meningeal inflammation overlying regions of cortical pathology. The precise mechanisms underlying the development of meningeal inflammation and its role in inducing cortical pathology as well as the cellular substrates and interactions contributing to cortical tissue injury remained unresolved. These knowledge gaps represent the greatest barrier to the development of therapies to arrest accumulating pathology underlying progressive MS. While recent spatial transcriptomics work (Kaufmann 2022) on progressive MS post-mortem tissues have identified potential pathogenic mechanisms, this represents only a snapshot of accumulated injurious mechanisms, thus, biologically-relevant animal models are required to understand the true temporal nature of these pathomechanistic processes. Recently, a novel rat model of MS cortical pathology was developed (James 2022) utilizing lentiviral transfer vectors (LV) packaged with human lymphotoxin-alpha (LTα) transgene stereotaxically injected into the sagittal sulcus. This produced profound meningeal inflammation with adjacent cortical tissue injury, recapitulating the morphological features of MS cortical pathology. The overarching hypothesis of this project is that the principal molecular targets in MS cortical pathology (from Kaufmann 2022) are present in the LV-LTα model, recapitulating key disease processes. The overarching aim of this project is to validate and establish this rat model as a biologically-relevant animal model of MS cortical pathology, and by applying spatial transcriptomics, understand the spatiotemporal characteristics of injurious molecular changes at single-cell resolution. Specifically, we aim to identify disease-associated cell types/cell states and decipher relevant cell-cell interactions (particularly between meningeal immune cells and cortical glial/neuronal cells) from which relevant ligand-receptor pairs can be identified at the earliest stages of cortical pathology. These candidate ligand-receptor pairs will be ‘back-validated’ in post-mortem MS tissues and in the cerebrospinal fluid of MS patients to elucidate druggable targets to stop cortical tissue injury early and to uncover novel biomarkers of early cortical pathology.
kw: multiple sclerosis; cortical pathology; spatial transcriptomics; ligand receptor; demyelination, progressive

title: Effect of Light on Atropine response in Myopic children.
abs: Myopia is a common problem in Singapore affecting 80% of our children by their 18th year. The challenge is to delay myopia onset and slow myopia progression so as to decrease the socio-economic burden of high myopia in the future. Fortunately, there are now pharmacological and optical treatments which can slow myopia by 50-70%. However, 20-30% of children continue to progress despite intervention. This may be due to poor compliance, genetic or life-style factors (especially light exposure). Time spend outdoors has been shown to protect children against myopia. Indeed, during COVID shutdowns, myopia progression spiked in many countries globally. We currently advocate that children spend at least 2 hours per day, but many parents and children find this challenging. In this study, we hope to determine if life-style behaviour (ie. light exposure) is linked to atropine treatment response, and whether modification is possible. To do this, we plan to identify children (n200) in our clinic with good-poor responses to atropine and determine if there are differences in their light exposure with a questionnaire, and a wearable device which will collect light exposure over a 3-week period. Concurrently, we will look to see if, by providing real-time feedback to parents and child (n150) through an app linked to their wearable devices, we could help them modify behaviour to introduce more light into their life-styles. We will also assess use of questionnaire, wearable linked app, and tear dopamine levels to see which would provide the most useful measure of light exposure. We hope that through this study, we address the questions of whether outdoor activity (or light exposure) is important for treatment outcome; how we could measure light exposure accurately, and if modifying life-style is possible. Results from this study could influence the way we counsel and treat children with myopia
kw: light atropine myopia

title: The Effects of Ripasudil in patients with Fuchs Endothelial Corneal Dystrophy undergoing Femtosecond Laser Assisted Cataract Surgery
abs: Cataract surgery is one of the most frequently performed surgical procedures worldwide. There is an inevitable corneal endothelial cell (CEC) loss up to 23.6-30.9% from surgical trauma in routine cataract surgeries, greater in high-risk conditions like Fuchs Endothelial Corneal Dystrophy (FECD). CECs maintain corneal clarity by regulating hydration through pump and barrier functions. Corneal transplantation remains the only way to restore corneal clarity after CEC loss, an intervention limited by a global scarcity of donor corneas. Topical Rho kinase inhibitors (ROCK-I) could increase cell proliferation rate, cellular adhesion, and reduce apoptosis of CECs, with promotion of peripheral CECs migration. To date, few randomized clinical trials examine the role of ROCK-I in maintaining CECs post-cataract surgery. Moreover, current standard imaging methods only image < 1% of the central endothelium. I have demonstrated the utility of novel widefield (WF) endothelial imaging to provide a more comprehensive peripheral to paracentral endothelial map (Transition Award). Thus, my current CSA proposal is a double-masked randomized clinical trial to study the effects of ROCK-I treatment (Ripasudil 0.4%) on corneal clarity and CEC loss in FECD eyes undergoing cataract surgery, using our WF endothelial imaging with DL-enabled analyses. We aim to demonstrate that ROCK-I treatment (Ripasudil 0.4%) in FECD eyes undergoing cataract surgery will: (a) promote post-operative corneal clarity; (b) maintain central CECs through centripetal migration of the peripheral CECs; and (c) reduce visual symptoms and minimize impact on vision-related quality of life (VRQoL) associated with post-operative corneal edema over 3-months post-surgery. Future studies will enable the development of a DL-enabled model to predict CEC loss and cornea edema, using a larger cohort with other conditions at risk of CEC loss. Ultimately, this research effort could lead to the development of a key clinical solution that could reduce corneal blindness following cataract surgery in Singapore, and worldwide.
kw: Fuchs Endothelial Corneal Dystrophy, Rho kinase Inhibitors, Corneal endothelial cells, Corneal Imaging, Artificial Intelligence

title: ExTrACT - Establishing an eX vivo Tumor infiltrating lymphocyte program for Adoptive Cell Therapy
abs: Cell therapy in solid tumors such as head and neck squamous cell cancers (HNSCC) are limited by a lack of consistent tumor antigens. One approach to circumvent this and achieve tumor-antigen targeting is to exploit tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) which contain small sub-populations of tumor-specific cytotoxic lymphocytes (CTLs): to harvest, stimulate and expand ex vivo, and autologously reinfuse to specifically kill cancer cells. This approach has shown significant promise in melanoma treatment. The major issues with this approach are the need for robust, point-of-care manufacturing capabilities for TIL-expansion and better protocols focused on expanding tumor-specific CTLs. Our hypothesis expands on the notion that tumor-specific CTLs exist in most solid tumors and requires specific or personalized protocols to expand these for adoptive cell therapy. Here, we aim to conduct a Phase 1b/2 clinical trial using our existing TIL-expansion protocol on 20 patients (10 HNSCC and 10 basket). This will be coupled with biomarker discovery and ex vivo co-clinical trials, that are purpose-designed to identify markers of therapy response, efficacy, and adverse events including cytokine release syndrome. We will simultaneously conduct a range of experiments to optimize TIL-expansion protocols with an aim to specifically expand tumor-targeting CTLs, improve efficacy, reduce time for expansion and increase in vivo longevity. General approaches include modification of cytokine cocktails and the used of unique immune-cytokine reagents designed for subpopulation activation. Apart from patient-agnostic stimulation, we will also employ a personalized neo-antigen prediction/peptide-activation strategy to stimulate tumor-specific CTLs. These conditions can be rapidly tested using autologous ex vivo TIL-primary tumor culture pairs that we have been developing over the years. Effective methods will continually be incorporated into TIL-manufacturing protocols for future trials. The long-term objective of this grant is to establish a robust TIL-manufacturing system that can continue to deliver effective cell therapy through a national resource.
kw: Cytotoxic T cells; TIL; cell therapy; tumor targeting T cells; neoantigen; peptide vaccine

title: Role of Glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonist (GLP1 RA) Dulaglutide on cerebral hemodynamics in patients with severe and symptomatic stenosis of intracranial internal carotid artery or middle cerebral artery with impaired cerebral vasodilatory reserve- an open-label randomized clinical trial
abs: Background & aims- Intracranial large artery atherosclerotic disease (ICAD), widely prevalent among Asians, carries high-risk of cerebral ischemia despite standard medical therapy. Recent trials, performed on newer glucose lowering agents, suggested that glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP1 RA) reduced major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), including stroke. In this proposed trial we aim to evaluate- a. whether GLP-1 agonist (Dulaglutide) therapy would improve cerebral vasodilatory reserve (CVR) in patients with recently symptomatic and severe stenosis of intracranial internal carotid (ICA) or middle cerebral artery (MCA). b. the impact of Dulaglutide therapy on reducing recurrence of cerebral ischemic event in patients with recently symptomatic and severe stenosis of ICA or MCA. c. whether Dulaglutide therapy would reduce MACE. Hypothesis- we hypothesize that addition of Dulaglutide to the standard medical therapy would improve cerebral hemodynamics in patients with severe ICAD. Methods- This single-center randomized, open-label trial will evaluate the role of once weekly injection of Dulaglutide in patients with recently symptomatic severe ICAD. 130 eligible patients (with or without diabetes mellitus) would be randomized (1:1) to receive standard medical therapy or Dulaglutide plus standard medical therapy for 1-year. Collected data would include demographic characteristics, underlying risk factors, neurological deficits and functional status at baseline. Cerebrovascular hemodynamic parameters would be evaluated by transcranial Doppler, acetazolamide-challenged HMPAO-SPECT and magnetic resonance imaging. Patients will be followed up for changes in cerebral vasodilatory reserve on SPECT and clinical events for 1-year and 2-years, respectively. Feasibility- We treat about 1200 new ischemic stroke/TIA patients yearly, of which at least 20% would satisfy our inclusion criteria. Our team is quite experienced in performing all the clinical and cerebral hemodynamic assessments. Importance- Anticipated successful results of this study would change the treatment paradigm of stroke prevention as well as prevent downstream suffering of a life-long aftermath of major stroke.
kw: stroke; transient ischemic attack; intracranial cerebral atherosclerotic disease (ICAD); GLP1 receptor agonists; Dulaglutide; cerebral vasodilatory reserve (CVR)

title: Arthralgia, Muscle Strength and Menopausal Origins of Health and Disease (MOHaD).
abs: Joint pains and muscle aches (menopausal arthralgia) are the most common symptoms of menopause in Singapore women and globally. Aim #1: We hypothesize that the steep decline in estrogen levels during the menopause transition causes symptoms such as arthralgia reduces physical activity to result in visceral adiposity and poor muscle strength. These conditions in turn lead to higher incidence and persistence of urinary incontinence, depression, insulin resistance, diabetes, hypertension, osteoporosis, preclinical cardiovascular disease and cognitive decline. To this end, we will perform comprehensive phenotyping of mid-life Singapore women on their third 12-year follow-up (mean age: 70 years) visit, adding to and greatly enhancing the value of the already completed baseline (n=1201, mean age: 56 years) and 6-year follow-up (n=998, mean age: 63 years) visits of the richly phenotyped Integrated Women's Health Program (IWHP) cohort started in 2014. Aim #2. We will study whether targeted interventions for menopausal arthralgia and associated symptoms, such as judicious estrogen replacement therapy and curated exercises, can arrest trajectories of ill-health, in a pilot feasibility 12-week randomized controlled trial to examine the effects of MUscle Strengthening exercises and Estrogen replacement therapy (the MUSE-RCT) to alleviate menopausal arthralgia and associated symptoms. Aim #3. To support Aims #1 and #2 above, our lab will the pioneer innovative technologies below: A) Urinary D3-creatine dilution assay to measure skeletal muscle mass using Liquid chromatography and tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS). B) Serum Creatinine/Cystatin C ratios: a simple method to assess skeletal muscle mass C) Measurement and establishment of cut-offs for estrogens and androgens (using LC-MS/MS) that predict trajectories of poor health D) Exploratory study: Unbiased Protein and cell-free RNA signatures of presymptomatic cognitive decline and vascular disease. Achievement of our aims will secure an improvement in the health and longevity of Singaporean women.
kw: menopause, arthralgia, health disease, muscle, phenotype

title: Deep phenotyping and multi-omics in a large prospective Asian type 2 diabetes cohort to understand diabesity associated cardiorenal failure
inst: Khoo Teck Puat Hospital Pte Ltd
abs: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) or diabesity (diabetes & obesity), partly driven by unhealthy lifestyle (dietary practice & physical activity (PA)), is a major cause of cardiorenal failure. We reported that a metabolomic signature, which suggested lipid-oversupply associated mitochondrial dysfunction, was strongly predictive of diabetic kidney disease (DKD) progression. This pro-inflammatory metabolomic signature was also observed in obese insulin resistant T2D, who are high risk for cardiorenal failure. However, the contribution of lifestyle factors (which are culturally sensitive & modifiable) towards similar differential metabolomic signature, is unknown. We hypothesize that lifestyle patterns (e.g. healthy vs. unhealthy) (i) are associated with differential metabolomics & proteomics signatures (which may further reveal biological insights) (ii) predict cardiorenal failure. From our large prospective diabetic cohorts (SMART2D & DORIS), in a subset of ~3,000 individuals with comprehensive lifestyle data & biobanked samples, we will study: Aim 1: the association (with replication) between lifestyle patterns & omics-biomarkers: untargeted proteomics & targeted metabolomics (including but not limited to plasma amino acid, acylcarnitine, lipids & urine Krebs cycle organic acid), both by mass-spectrometry. Subsequently, to elucidate the biology by advanced approaches such as genomic co-localization, pathway & tissue enrichment analyses. Aim 2: the association between lifestyle patterns & cardiorenal failure prospectively over ~10 years. PA has been objectively assessed by tri-axial accelerometery (AX3). Dietary practice has been assessed by web-based tools employed by the Singapore GUSTO (Growing Up towards Healthy Outcomes) cohort. Subsequently, to study the relationship between lifestyle-differential (from aim1) proteome & metabolome biomarkers (endophenotypes) & cardiorenal outcome, for biological insights. Aim 3: potential causality of these biomarkers by advanced genetics (Mendelian Randomization (MR)). Our study may shed-light on the relationship (& potential causal pathobiology, revealed by OMICS biomarkers) between modifiable lifestyle factors & long-term cardiorenal failure. This may inform therapeutic targets for Asians with T2D.
kw: Type 2 Diabetes; Obesity; Metabolomics; Lifestyle; Cardiorenal; Proteomics

title: Development, Validation, and Testing of DR-GPT - A Multi-modal Generative AI Agent for Diabetes Eye Care in Primary and Tertiary Eye Care Settings
abs: Diabetes mellitus (DM) is a rapidly growing global health issue, projected to affect 780 million people by 2045, up from 171 million in 2000. In Singapore, the Singapore Integrated Diabetic Retinopathy Program (SiDRP) screens around 100,000 patients annually for diabetic retinopathy (DR). Advances in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models (LLMs), offer promising applications in medicine, including note summarization, translation, and clinical decision support. Our team developed SELENA+ and DR-PREDICT to detect DR and DR incidence and progression. We propose DR-GPT, a generative AI-based system for comprehensive diabetes eye management, leveraging electronic medical records (EMR) and imaging data to triage patients, diagnose vision-threatening DR, and provide educational support in multiple languages. DR-GPT aims to achieve >90% accuracy in triaging diabetes patients with visual complaints for urgent, semi-urgent, elective referrals, or no referral needed, tested using SNEC records in Singapore and international cohorts. Additionally, the IMAGE DR-GPT model will detect vision-threatening DR (DME, severe NPDR, PDR) with >90% accuracy, tested in tertiary eye care clinics and international cohorts. A multi-modal vision language model, VLM DR-GPT, will provide diabetes eye care information in multiple languages (English, Chinese, Malay, Tamil, Cantonese, Austrian, Thai), aiming for >90% accuracy in educational responses, tested in international sites. This initiative aligns with Singapore's Smart Nation 2.0 strategy and seeks to address the global burden of diabetic eye disease. The AI algorithms have strong potential for commercialization and implementation beyond Singapore, offering a comprehensive solution to the rising burden of diabetes-related eye complications. The National Research and Medical Council (NRMC) envisions leveraging cutting-edge technology to enhance healthcare outcomes and patient experiences worldwide. Its mission is to foster innovation and interdisciplinary collaboration, ensuring the translation of research into practical, effective healthcare solutions. This project exemplifies NRMC's commitment to advancing medical research and improving global health through technological innovation.
kw: Artificial Intelligence; Digital Health; Diabetes Eye Diseases; Population Health

title: Heart Failure Screening In Primary Care Using Digital Tools
abs: Despite advances in heart failure (HF) therapies, challenges in early detection and accurate diagnosis have hindered the reduction of morbidity and mortality. This issue is particularly critical in primary care, where most patients with early HF are first seen, yet misdiagnosis is more likely compared to hospital settings, and resources for systematic screening are often inadequate. Emerging digital health tools offer a promising solution to enhance HF screening and detection in the community, potentially preventing severe decompensation, hospitalization, and death. The proposed study aims to develop and validate a novel HF screening pathway, supported by digital health tools, suitable for use in primary care and community settings. Specific Aims: 1. WHO TO SCREEN: To determine the best risk stratification approach to screen individuals in the community who are at elevated risk for HF or in the early stages of HF. The hypothesis is that combining clinical risk scoring with selected cardiac biomarker testing will effectively identify high-risk adults who could benefit from preventive therapies. A machine learning-based clinical risk score for HF will be derived using diverse real-world datasets. 2. HOW TO SCREEN: To develop a novel HF screening pathway in a Singapore outpatient non-cardiology setting using AI-enabled mobile diagnostic tools. The hypothesis is that recent advancements in point-of-care testing, including natriuretic peptides and echocardiography enhanced by AI, will facilitate appropriate HF diagnostic testing in outpatient settings. This will be tested in a prospective observational study at Singapore General Hospital. 3. EXTERNAL VALIDATION: To externally validate the AI-enabled HF screening pathway in various primary care and community-based settings worldwide. The hypothesis is that the pathway will be applicable globally, enabling early HF detection and the application of therapies. This will be tested in a multinational randomized study comparing AI-assisted mobile testing to usual care in general practice and community settings.
kw: Heart Failure, Digital Tools, Artificial Intelligence

title: Clinical and Biological Significance of Oncogenic Co-expression in DLBCL
abs: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) remains a formidable clinical challenge due to its aggressive nature and high relapse rates. Our recent publication showed that a particular subpopulation of DLBCL cells, overexpressing MYC and BCL2 but lacking BCL6 (M+2+6−), is correlated with poorer patient outcomes. This proposed research aims to: 1) elucidate the evolutionary origin and trajectory of M+2+6− cells, 2) evaluate the impact of their spatial distribution on survival outcomes, and 3) validate the M+2+6− metric in clinical settings. To accomplish these aims, we will utilise advanced methodologies, such as computational reconstruction of the oncogenic amplified regions and fluorescent in situ hybridisation (FISH) to dissect the genetic underpinnings of the M+2+6− subpopulation, with a focus on the role of extrachromosomal DNA (ecDNA) in driving MYC and BCL2 amplifications. We will use spatial point pattern analyses to evaluate how the spatial organisation of M+2+6− cells influences clinical outcomes. Additionally, single-cell spatial multiomics will enable us to determine the biological significance of this subpopulation within the tumour microenvironment. Multiplex fluorescent immunohistochemistry (mIHC) will be used to visualise and quantify oncogenic co-expressions at the single-cell level in DLBCL biopsies, facilitated by our automated pipeline for image analysis developed in this study. Ultimately, we will validate the M+2+6− metric across DLBCL cohorts with various therapeutic approaches, to ensure its applicability for patient stratification. This research promises to revolutionise DLBCL prognostication by demonstrating the clinical and biological significance of the M+2+6− subpopulation in diverse cohorts. The findings could lead to personalised treatment approaches and improved survival rates. By integrating AI and deep learning approaches for automated image analysis, the project ensures that this diagnostic tool is accessible and practical for clinical use. Essentially, this study will deliver a transformative impact on lymphoma diagnosis and treatment, improving patient outcomes and quality of life.
kw: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma; Prognostic biomarker; Oncogenes; Spatial biology; Tumour microenvironment; Artificial intelligence

title: Immune signatures of psoriatic arthritis defining treatment response and relapse
abs: Background. Psoriatic arthritis (PsA) is an autoimmune disease affecting working-age adults, causes joint damage and disability. 40% of patients are not having adequate response despite advanced treatments. There is huge need to develop predictive biomarkers for treatment response and relapses. Aims. Aim 1 To discover and validate PsA pathogenic immunome signatures in the peripheral blood using system biology approach that 1) predict treatment response to tumor necrosis factor inhibitor (TNFi), and 2) Predict successful withdrawal of TNFi. Aim 2. To explore the pathogenic mechanisms involving interactions between the local tissue microenvironment and infiltrating systemic immune cells from the circulation using the following paired tissues: 1) synovial fluid and blood cells, and 2) skin tissue and blood cells. Methods. We will build prospective cohorts of PsA, who have 1) active disease and starting TNFi; and 2) inactive disease and stopping TNFi; and followed-up for treatment response/ relapse. We will use single cell proteomics and a systemic biology approach to discover subsets of immune cells that correspond to 1) treatment response, and 2) relapse. We will validate the immune cell subsets with clinical variables using predictive models. To study the communication between tissue and systemic inflammation, we will explore 1) the spatial transcriptomic profile of psoriasis skin comparing with the immunomes in paired blood; and 2) compare the immunome in paired synovial fluid and peripheral blood This proposal is feasible with existing biological samples, experiments conducting on validated and operational platforms, and the team has pre-existing track records for similar discoveries. Significance. It will be a game changer to guide treatment for the best care for PsA using biomarkers, providing means to stratify patients to receive therapies with best predicted response; and facilitate tapering of therapies, saving cost and minimizing side effects. The understanding of pathogenesis will provide insights to innovative therapeutics.
kw: Psoriatic arthritis, immunology, treatment responses

title: Recombinant Singapore Mistletoe Lectin (rSML): An Anti-Tumor Protein Agent Rendered by a Sialoglycan-Targeting Chitosan Scaffold
abs: Cancer is a major global health concern, with significant mortality rates, contributing to over 23% of total deaths in Singapore in 2022. Sialic acids, commonly overexpressed on cancer cell surfaces, has been shown to interact with glycoimmune checkpoints, sialic acid-binding immunoglobulin lectin (Siglec) on immune cells. This interaction facilitates cancer cells to evade from the immune system, leading to increased resistance to immune therapies, including currently populated immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapies. The situation underscores the need for innovative treatment targeting hypersialylated cancer cells to effectively eradicate tumors and achieve long-term survival. Singapore Mistletoe Lectin (SML), a ribosome-inactivating protein with potential anti-cancer properties. Due to its low-concentration natural occurrence, we have produced and isolated a recombinant SML-A chain (rSML-A) from bioengineered E. coli. We then developed a sialoglycan-targeting nanosystem combining rSML-A, a boronic acid (BA) ligand specifically binding to sialic acids, and the endosome escape peptide Aurein with a chitosan scaffold (GC). This BA-GC/Aurein@rSML-A nanocomplex is designed to target hypersialyated cancer cells, facilitate cell entry, and evade endolysosomal degradation, allowing rSML-A to selectively inactivate ribosomes in cancer cells, leading to cell death. Preliminary results demonstrated that this system selectively targets and effectively eliminates HeLa cervical cancer cells, and significantly inhibites the tumor growth in A549 xenografted mice. Our project aims to further optimize the BA-GC/Aurein@rSML-A nanosystem to improve its anti-tumor efficacy and minimize its impacts on healthy tissues. This will involve toxicity assays, labeled systems for imaging, and cancer mouse models to evaluate delivery efficiency, anti-tumor potency, sialoglycan-targeting mechanisms, biosafety, and therapeutic potential. The successful development of this nanosystem promises a novel and effective approach for treating a wide range of cancers with significant clinical relevance.
kw: Recombinant Singapore Mistletoe Lectin (rSML); Anti-Tumor Protein; Chitosan Nanocomplex; In Vitro and In Vivo Studies

title: Harnessing the power of p53 for cancer prophylaxis
abs: Cancer is a major disease that is on the rise and the incidence is expected to double by 2040. Novel treatment modalities, though having transformed cancer treatment, are insufficient to counter the disease burden. Revolutionary measures are therefore necessary to delay or even prevent the onset of cancers to keep the population cancer-free. The tumor-suppressor p53 is the most mutated gene in cancers. Germ-line mutations in p53 lead to cancer predisposition, as noted in the Li-Fraumeni syndrome (LFS) carriers, and there are currently no options available to delay or prevent cancer development in this population. Conversely, animals which are relatively resistant to cancer development, such as the elephants, carry multiple copies of p53, indicating that controlled overexpression of p53 might be nature’s strategy against cancer predisposition. Inspired by nature, we propose here a molecular prevention approach to obviate cancer development, by enhancing our body’s tumor-suppressive mechanisms. Our preliminary data suggest that expression of a third p53 copy in mice, either constitutively or in an inducible manner, can significantly delay tumor development and mice live longer, in both the E-myc lymphoma model, and the LFS model, without any observable side-effects. Our data provide genetic evidence that harnessing the power of p53 can be a prophylactic strategy against development. Based on these data, we hypothesize that novel compounds that can activate p53 systemically and subtly can be developed for use in humans. As such, we propose here to evaluate our recently generated tool compounds, and will also identify diet-based factors, both which are cell-permeable and/or capable of activating p53, for their prophylactic activities. Moreover, we will investigate the mechanistic basis of cancer prophylaxis afforded by 3 p53 copies. The results will establish the concept of molecular cancer prophylaxis, with a focus on p53 activation, and provide opportunities for cancer-prophylactic regimens in future.
kw: p53; cancer; prophylaxis; Li Fraumeni syndrome; familial cancers

title: Polymeric Nanogel Delivering mRNA to Lesional Macrophages for Synergistic Anti-oxidative and Anti-inflammatory Treatment of Atherosclerosis
abs: Atherosclerosis (AS) is the major feature of cardiovascular diseases, which are the leading causes of morbidity and mortality worldwide and in Singapore. AS is characterized by excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) production and unresolved inflammation, which promotes each other in a vicious cycle and drive the AS plaque progression. Lesional macrophages are promising therapeutic targets in AS treatment and promoting efferocytosis of apoptotic cells by macrophages mediated via MER proto-oncogene tyrosine kinase (MerTK) can enhance anti-inflammation responses and benefit plaque stability. To this end, developing nanotherapeutics to target macrophages and concurrently suppress ROS production and resolve inflammation is a hopeful therapeutic strategy for AS therapy. mRNA therapy is a potent and safe therapeutic method, but facing several challenges including short in vivo circulation time, non-specific mRNA release, and difficulty in simultaneously achieving anti-oxidative and anti-inflammation effects with a single nanotherapeutics. In this proposal, we will develop a reversible-crosslinking polymeric nanogel (PNG) for delivering MerTK mRNA to macrophages for AS treatment. We hypothesize that PNG/mMerTK nanotherapeutics can prolong circulation time, realize ROS-responsive mRNA release, and simultaneously achieve anti-oxidative and anti-inflammatory responses, thus decreasing plaque area and enhancing plaque stability in atherosclerotic-plaque-bearing Apoe−/− mice without eliciting adverse effects after long-term treatment. Our specific aims can be summarized as follows: Specific Aim 1: Library screening of polymeric nanogel to achieve effective mRNA delivery with a prolonged circulation time and ROS-responsive mRNA release behavior. Specific Aim 2: In vitro validation of anti-oxidative and anti-inflammatory efficacy of PNG/mMerTK to delay atherosclerosis progression. Specific Aim 3: In vivo assessment of the pharmacokinetics, therapeutic efficacy, therapeutic mechanism, and safety of PNG/mMerTK in atherosclerosis Apoe−/− mouse models.
kw: mRNA therapy; polymeric nanogel; macrophage regulation; anti-oxidation; anti-inflammation; atherosclerosis treatment

title: Mouse and non-human primate model evaluation of a single dose live attenuated Zika virus vaccine developed using a novel genome recoding approach
abs: Zika virus (ZIKV) is a mosquito-borne virus that has emerged as a significant threat to human health. ZIKV infection can lead to long-term complications such as Guillain-Barré syndrome and congenital anomalies such as microcephaly. There are currently no approved antivirals or vaccines against ZIKV. A ZIKV vaccine that can induce long-term immunity against ZIKV with a single dose would be the most cost-effective approach for preventing ZIKV infection. Only a non-chimeric live attenuated vaccine that can induce complete antibody and T-cell immunity against ZIKV can fulfil this requirement, but no such vaccine designs have progressed to clinical trials. To address this need, we have developed a non-chimeric live attenuated ZIKV vaccine called VacZen. VacZen was developed using a combination of attenuating and immunogenic vaccine technologies. VacZen utilises a novel attenuation approach called genome recoding. Genome recoding confers genetically stable attenuation, whilst preserving 100% of antibody and T-cell epitopes, ensuring that VacZen retains the ability to induce complete antibody and T-cell immunity against ZIKV. VacZen also incorporates genetically stable mutations that enhance the immunogenicity of VacZen. These immunogenic mutations help VacZen to induce an effective innate immune response, which in turn helps to recruit and activate antibody and T-cell adaptive immunity. Our preliminary studies in mice demonstrates that VacZen is attenuated in vivo. Our preliminiary studies also demonstrates that VacZen can induce protection against ZIKV infection, which includes protection against ZIKV pathogenicity and protection against maternal-fetal transmission of ZIKV. Therefore, the aim of this proposed study is to further validate VacZen by demonstrating that the protective immunity induced by VacZen includes both antibody and T-cell immunity. We will demonstrate that VacZen can induce protective antibody and T-cell immunity in both mouse and non-human primate models. This will demonstrate that VacZen is a safe and effective vaccine against ZIKV.
kw: Zika virus; Vaccine; live attenuated vaccine; genome recoding; non-human primate model;

title: Deep learning-based neurodegeneration and cerebrovascular-related brain age to predict long-term outcomes of a multidomain lifestyle intervention in community-dwelling seniors - the SINGER study
abs: Given the increasing prevalence of dementia in Singapore and worldwide, primarily due to Alzheimer’s disease and cerebrovascular disorder, preventive strategies targeting multiple risk factors at the population level are crucial. However, few studies have longer-term follow-up. Understanding the factors influencing the long-term health outcomes of lifestyle interventions is essential. Brain age is a surrogate marker of brain health and has been associated with Alzheimer’s disease and dementia. Deep learning models of brain age have gained popularity due to their minimal processing requirements and adaptability to diverse domains. Nevertheless, important gaps remain. Most brain age models are trained on cross-sectional data from Caucasian participants, making it unclear how well these models capture longitudinal changes in brain aging (i.e., brain pace) and generalize to Asian populations. Most studies focus on T1-structural MRI, which only accounts for neurodegeneration-related brain age, with no established models for cerebrovascular brain age. Our group has demonstrated the potential of brain pace, brain microstructural, and functional measures in predicting cognitive decline, though their additional value over readily available assays remains to be tested. Here, we aim to develop deep-learning models for brain age and leverage the existing two-year randomized control trial - SINgapore GERiatric intervention study to reduce cognitive decline and physical frailty (SINGER) cohort and its planned long-term follow-up. We will test the following hypotheses: 1. Determine if neurodegeneration & cerebrovascular-related longitudinal brain pace will outperform cross-sectional brain age in predicting long-term outcomes of the SINGER intervention. 2. Evaluate whether cerebrovascular-related microstructure and functional network phenotypes provide additional value over brain age. 3. Investigate the relationship between longitudinal multimodal brain measures and blood markers. If successful, this proposal will yield new insights into factors contributing to long-term intervention outcomes and facilitate the development of effective strategies to delay the onset and progression of dementia.
kw: Brain age, deep learning, neurodegeneration, cerebrovascular disease, long-term outcome, multidomain lifestyle intervention

title: Designer natriuretic peptides as precision therapeutics against heart failure
abs: Heart failure (HF) affects 64.3 million people worldwide and is a leading cause of hospitalization in people older than 65. Despite advances in HF therapies, HF prevalence is expected to rise due to increasing risk factors like hypertension, obesity, physical inactivity, diabetes, and smoking, particularly in aging societies like Singapore. Natriuretic peptides (NPs) and their receptors offer multiple benefits to HF patients including vasodilation, diuresis, natriuresis, inhibition of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, anti-fibrosis, anti-apoptosis, anti-hypertrophy, lipolytic, increased lipid mobilization, and enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis and metabolism. Therefore, targeting NPs is becoming a significant focus in HF drug development. Previously, we reported two novel analogues of atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) designed based on a snake venom toxin, which decouples the tightly-associated diuretic/natriuretic and vasodilatory activities. One of the novel peptides, DGD-ANP, exhibits exclusively diuretic/natriuretic function without a hypotensive effect; the other, DRD-ANP, is exclusively vasodilatory, inducing a drop in peripheral blood pressure without affecting urine output. Given the complexity of HF symptoms, we aim to develop these novel ANP analogues as precision therapies for specific subgroups of HF patients. DGD-ANP targets ‘cold and wet’ acute decompensated HF (ADHF) and HFrEF/HFpEF with low/normal blood pressure, providing cardiorenal- and cardiometabolic-protection without excessive hypotension. Conversely, DRD-ANP targets ‘warm and wet’ ADHF and HFrEF/HFpEF with resistant hypertension, offering vasodilation, RAAS inhibition, and cardiometabolic-protection without affecting renal balance. Our project aims to advance these ANP analogues through the drug development pipeline. We will elucidate the cardiorenal and cardiometabolic benefits of the peptides through transcriptomic and phosphoproteomic analyses. We plan to develop a thermo-sensitive hydrogel for subcutaneous delivery of the peptides, improving their pharmacokinetic profiles for once-weekly treatments. Lastly, we will validate the efficacy of these formulations in murine HFrEF and HFpEF models. Successful development will lead to innovative precision medicine therapies for HF patients.
kw: Natriuretic peptide; heart failure; cardiovascular; drug development; precision medicine; animal model

title: A new reticulocyte population: unravelling its origin and role in malaria infection and erythropoietic stress responses
abs: Malaria, a global health threat, disrupts red blood cell (RBC) function, leading to severe complications like anemia. We previously identified CD98 as a receptor for the malaria parasite Plasmodium vivax in young RBCs. Further research unexpectedly revealed a unique CD98+CD71- RBC population in both rodent and human malaria infections, absent in healthy individuals. This suggests an altered RBC maturation process during infection. We hypothesize that this unique RBC subset plays a role in parasite survival, proliferation, and anemia development. We aim to further characterize these cells, investigate their presence in erythropoietic stress responses, and identify the mechanisms behind their generation. Our study will involve: i) characterizing the CD98+CD71- RBCs using flow cytometry, microscopy, and hemoglobin quantification in both mouse and human malaria models.; ii) investigating the presence of CD98+CD71- RBCs in various anemia/erythropoietic stress response models and assessing the impact of erythropoietin treatment; iii) identifying the mechanisms leading to CD98+CD71- RBC generation by transferring cells between mice, investigating serum factors, and exploring the role of the spleen and immune cells; and iv) assessing the susceptibility of CD98+CD71- RBCs to invasion by different malaria parasite species in both rodent and human models. This research will enhance our understanding of malaria pathogenesis, potentially leading to novel therapeutic targets and interventions for malaria-induced anemia. Additionally, it may contribute to a broader understanding of erythropoiesis and erythropoietic stress responses, potentially benefiting patients with various blood disorders.
kw: hematology; infection; Reticulocytes; erythropoiesis; malaria; erythropoietic stress response

title: Addressing barriers to data in ophthalmology with generative artificial intelligence
abs: The development of artificial intelligence (AI) requires large and representative datasets.
