In healthcare, privacy concerns, data compatibility and distribution bias can limit the quantity and quality available data. Generative AI (GAI) is a type of deep learning approach which is able to synthesize data without containing specific identifiers that can be matched to an individual, while retaining characteristics of the input data. The objective of this proposal is to develop GAI approaches towards addressing barriers to data sharing and improving data availability in ophthalmology for collaborative data-driven research between institutions and across national boundaries. Our central hypothesis is that synthetically generated data, which embodies the anatomical and pathological characteristics of real data without personal identifiers, can be used to address privacy, compatibility, and bias challenges in the development of AI models. In Specific Aim 1, we will set out to develop generative approaches to synthesize privacy-agnostic ocular imaging data and adjust their distributions to train AI models for glaucoma and neurodegenerative disorders. In Specific Aim 2, we will develop generative approaches to adapt data from different imaging platforms to improve inter-platform compatibility. In Specific Aim 3, we will assess AI models trained with synthetic image generation strategies in external overseas datasets. We will evaluate our hypotheses with multi-site and multi-ethnicity imaging data of 27,316 participants, consisting of healthy participants, glaucoma patients, and patients with neurodegenerative disorders (mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer’s disease) from local and overseas studies. Improving data availability with the findings of this study has the potential to reduce barriers to collaborative data-sharing, enabling improved data availability to facilitate the development and validation of AI models on large and better datasets, without risk to patient privacy. Beyond ophthalmology, the insights and approaches obtained from this grant can also benefit the development of AI models in other medical fields.
kw: privacy, ophthalmology, generative artificial intelligence

title: Senescent cell depletion to improve outcomes of chimeric antigen receptor immune cell manufacturing and therapies
abs: Globally, cancer has claimed over 10 million lives annually since 2020. In Singapore, cancer affects one in every four people over their lifetime. Chimeric Antigen Receptor T cell (CAR-T) therapy has successfully cured patients with leukaemia and lymphoma, with six approved products containing patient-derived CD4+ and CD8+ T cells. Owing to the limitations of autologous CAR-T therapy, there is rising interest to develop allogenic CAR-immune cell (IC) products using Natural Killer (NK) cells and Gamma-Delta (GD) T cells. In both autologous and allogenic therapy, clinicians and manufacturers are shifting away from simply the total number of infused cells, to consider cell quality which is critical in influencing therapeutic efficacy. Immune cell quality is strongly affected by senescence, arising due to old age, cancer, chemotherapy, and rapid ex vivo stimulation of cell receptors and expansion. In our preliminary data, we found that older donors (autologous) had a greater proportion of senescent CD8+ T cells and after a standard two-week CAR-T expansion with cells from young allogenic donors. Senescent cells had poorer transfection efficacy, proliferation rate and cytotoxicity than non-senescent cells. After depleting senescent cells, we observed increased CAR-T persistence and proliferation. This suggests that reducing the % of senescent immune cells may be promising to improve manufacturing and clinical outcomes for both autologous and allogenic CAR-IC products. Here, we aim to deplete senescent cells to enhance the outcomes of CAR immune cell manufacturing and therapy. We will also develop a label-free microfluidic cell sorting platform and compare it to flow cytometry technique in terms of efficiency and cell quality after depleting senescent immune cells. Finally, we will optimise our nano-scale electroporation system for non-viral genetic engineering of CAR-immune cells. This project is highly aligned with Singapore’s ambition to be a leader in the regional cell therapy market.
kw: Cancer; immunotherapy; microfluidics; nanotechnology

title: Exploring host innate immune system during human Plasmodium blood stage infection
abs: The innate immune system plays a critical role in preventing or containing an infection and provides critical signals that enable the adaptive immune system to mount a specific response. Pathogens therefore have developed a range of mechanisms to either manipulate or escape the innate immune response thereby enhancing their ability to colonize a host. A wide range of studies in both human and rodents have shown that NK cells as well as macrophages play an important role in the initial control of malaria parasites. The secretion of pro- as well as anti-inflammatory cytokines in response to parasites by immune effector cells is tightly regulated and critical for an efficient immune response. Disruption of this response can result in severe clinical pathology and even death. The human malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum has developed a range of so far a wide range and poorly understood mechanisms that enable it to manipulate the immune response and enhance immune evasion. We have obtained preliminary data that have indicated the role of different parasite multigene families in modulating both macrophages and NK cells. In this proposal, we aim to obtain a more complete understanding of the recognition of parasite-infected RBCs by macrophages and the different parasite factors that modulate the innate immune system. Particularly, we aim to determine the role of the parasite in monocyte maturation and evaluate the role of macrophage polarization in response to parasite and whether the parasite is able to directly modulate polarization during an infection. The data obtained from this study will not only be important for obtaining a better understanding of host and parasite interactions that shape immune response but also could identify potential host and parasite targets for therapeutic development.
kw: malaria; innate immunity; NK cells; macrophages; parasite ligands

title: Compact and Cost-effective Optoretinography for High-throughput Assessment of Outer Retinal Dysfunctions
abs: Retinal degenerative diseases caused by the dysfunctions of photoreceptors and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), such as age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and inherited retinal dystrophies, are among the leading causes of blindness. Until now, there has been a lack of rapid, non-invasive, objective, and cell-specific imaging tools for assessing photoreceptor and RPE dysfunctions, whether in preclinical studies or clinical diagnosis. Recently, researchers, including our team, discovered that these cells also undergo mechanical deformations on the order of tens to hundreds of nanometers in response to light stimuli. Such deformations can be measured in a new fashion termed optoretinography (ORG) primarily through phase-resolved optical coherence tomography (OCT). In this proposal, we hypothesize that abnormal patterns in these light-evoked ORG signals can enable rapid mapping of photoreceptor and RPE dysfunctions across the retina, thereby accelerating disease diagnosis, therapy development, and treatment monitoring by providing both structural and functional retinal imaging within a single OCT machine. We propose to bridge the gap between the current scientific understanding of ORG and clinical practice, by conducting cross-sectional and longitudinal studies in animal models and developing a novel, compact, and cost-effective ORG system for applications in clinical settings. If successful, such technology may enable early diagnosis of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and inherited retinal dystrophies, allowing proactive screening of retinal degeneration before irreversible functional damage occurs. It can also significantly accelerate the development of new therapeutic approaches, where ORG can serve as a critical lead measure for functional recovery.
kw: Optoretinography; Retinal degeneration; Functional imaging; Optical coherence tomography; Ocular imaging

title: Elucidating the detrimental roles of astrocytic lipid dysregulation in Alzheimer’s disease pathogenesis
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is the most common neurodegenerative disease worldwide. Due to the complexity of the brain and the disease and limitations with animal models, the understanding of AD pathophysiology is still rudimentary. Increasing evidence has indicated that the neurodegeneration in AD is not solely neuron autonomous, and the involvement of astrocytes in the pathogenesis of AD is considered important but less studied. Here, we differentiated cerebral organoids (COs) from dementia patient PBMC-derived iPSCs that harbours PS1 mutation (MT) and its isogenic mutant-corrected controls (Ctrl). We conducted various molecular and cellular studies on PS1 MT and Ctrl astrocyte and found that multiple functions of astrocyte, especially lipid metabolism, were dysregulated in PS1 MT astrocytes. Hypothesis: PS1 mutation induces dysregulated lipid metabolism of astrocytes which in turn exhibits detrimental effect on their neuron counterparts, that contribute to AD pathogenesis. Objective: To decipher the detrimental effect of the astrocytes exhibit on neurons, and identify the toxic lipids produced by AD astrocytes that mediate the neurodegeneration. Eventually, we aim to evaluate the targeted intervention of astrocyte lipid dysregulation as novel therapeutic strategies. Methodology: We will apply astrocyte-neuron co-culture system to elucidate the detrimental effect that astrocytes exhibit on neuron. Lipidomic screen/profiling will be utilized to identify the toxic lipid species which mediated the detrimental effect. Lastly, using both in vitro co-culture and in vivo AD transgenic mouse model will evaluate the therapeutic potential by targeting toxic lipid species in astrocyte for AD. Scientific/Clinical Impact: Elucidating the pathogenic role of lipid dysregulation in astrocyte would allow us to identify novel druggable targets to prevent AD progression.
kw: Alzheimer's disease.  PS1. cerebral organoid, astrocyte, lipidomic

title: Investigating XAGE1B as a novel LLPS and transcriptional regulator in lung cancer
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: In this proposal, we aim to comprehensively study XAGE1B, a poorly characterized cancer-testis antigen (CTA) that we discovered in a transcriptomic screen for genes with cancer-specific expression. Our preliminary investigations revealed a novel role of XAGE1B in regulating co-transcriptional processes, mediated through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), which in turn promotes lung cancer oncogenesis. As there is limited prior biochemical information about XAGE1B, our first goal is to gain a better understanding of the mechanisms by which XAGE1B influences co-transcriptional processes. We will employ genomics approaches such as POINT-seq and MERFISH, to gain insights into how XAGE1B regulates transcriptional processes (Aim 1). Second, we will determine how XAGE1B harnesses its LLPS ability to promote lung cancer, by performing CUT&Tag and qPLEX-RIME on WT XAGE1B and its corresponding LLPS-deficient mutants to assess the differences in their genomic occupancies and interactomes respectively. We will further address the degree by which these mutants can functionally rescue key features of cancer progression when over-expressed in XAGE1B-depleted cells (Aim 2). Third, our preliminary findings have revealed a partnership between XAGE1B and the splicing regulators SRRM2 and ARGLU1, suggesting a role of XAGE1B in RNA binding and splicing. To explore this further, we will conduct seCLIP-seq and long read sequencing respectively. The latter technique will also be applied to XAGE1B, SRRM2 and ARGLU1-knockdown cells to better understand the partnership between the trio, and how they impact alternative splicing events that promote tumorigenesis (Aim 3). XAGE1B holds therapeutic potential due to its selective expression in tumors but not in healthy cells, raising its prospect as a viable targeted therapeutic with minimal toxicity. Importantly, our study of XAGE1B will serve as a primer to better understand CTA-induced condensate behaviors in diverse human cancers, and contribute to the burgeoning field of LLPS-based therapeutics.
kw: transcription; chromatin; gene regulation; epigenetics; cell biology; cancer

title: Targeting Vascular Dysfunction in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer (NSCLC): Unraveling the Pivotal Role of Endothelial STARD8 in Tumor Progression and Therapeutic Prospects
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), the most prevalent cancer in Asia, has a poor prognosis linked to dysfunctional blood vessels formed by tumor endothelial cells (TECs). Current treatments targeting tumor vascularization have limited success and significant side effects. This proposal investigates TECs in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), the most common and lethal form of NSCLC, focusing on genetic and molecular dysfunction linked to mutations such as EGFR, P53, and KRAS, using innovative in-vitro approaches, gold-standard mouse xenograft assays, advanced zebrafish imaging, and human LUAD sample analysis. Preliminary findings link TEC dysfunctions to changes in Rho GTPase signaling, notably the downregulation of STARD8, a RhoGAP essential for endothelial cell (EC) functions in LUAD tumors. This disrupts cell motility, network formation, and affects proteins involved in the cytoskeleton, angiogenesis, and the interferon alpha-STAT1 pathway in ECs. In NSG mouse models, xenografts with ECs downregulating STARD8 show rapid tumor growth. We hypothesize that manipulating endothelial STARD8 offers a specific strategy for (a) uncovering genetic mechanisms behind vascular dysfunction in LUAD; (b) understanding interactions between vascular irregularities and key LUAD driver mutations (EGFR, P53, and KRAS); and (c) exploring the bidirectional relationship between vascular dysfunction and LUAD progression. We propose the following aims: (i) Deciphering the EC-STARD8 interactome and key regulators of STARD8-Mediated immunovascular dysfunction: Using proteomic-approaches, we will map STARD8's interactors regulating endothelial signaling, behavior, and immune regulation. (ii) Elucidating cancer-immune-endothelial crosstalk mediated by endothelial STARD8: We will characterize EC STARD8's effect on tumor growth and progression using in-vitro coculture systems, transcriptomic analysis, and mouse models. (iii) Decoding the molecular relationship and clinical significance between endothelial STARD8 downregulation and specific driver mutations (EGFR, P53, or KRAS) in LUAD: We will investigate the link between STARD8-induced vascular dysfunctions and LUAD driver mutations using mouse models, coculture systems, and human LUAD samples.
kw: NSCLC; LUAD; Tumor endothelial cells; immunovascular dysfunction; STARD8;

title: Biomanufacturing an allogeneic-hMSCs-derived Cartilage membrane and Investigating using Transcriptomic and Proteomic Approaches and Validating via Clinically Relevant Animal Models
abs: Countries with aging populations, like Singapore, are experiencing a rise in cartilage diseases such as osteoarthritis, which primarily affect the elderly, reducing quality of life and increasing the socioeconomic burden. These diseases often progress to cartilage degeneration, necessitating cartilage repair surgery to preserve the joint function. The current gold-standard treatment is an advanced cell therapy known as autologous chondrocyte implantation (ACI). However, ACI requires two surgeries, prolonged hospitalisation, is expensive, and inapplicable for older patients due to the lack of healthy cartilage for harvesting. To address this critical medical need, we propose developing an allogenic cartilage tissue membrane, named ChondroMesh, that can be applied in a single surgery to repair cartilage defects. This will be achieved using donor mesenchymal stem cells cultured in vitro utilising our proprietary membrane technology to stimulate the stem cells to differentiate into a thin cartilage tissue membrane. Our technology involves assembling hMSC cell spheroids between biodegradable mesh scaffolds, supported by a membrane holding device (patent pending), and applying biological and mechanical stimulation to develop a robust and biomimetic cartilage membrane. We will comprehensively characterise ChondroMesh using both conventional and advanced transcriptomics and proteomics methods and validate the membrane in relevant animal models for cartilage repair. Specific aims: 1. Optimise in vitro production of ChondroMesh through testing different biological and mechanical stimulations. 2. Characterise the ChondroMesh prototypes using both traditional and multi-omics approaches. 3. Evaluate the ChondroMesh in vivo using clinically relevant animal models (rat and pig models). Hypothesis: ChondroMesh, produced using our proprietary technology that incorporates optimised biological and mechanical stimulation, can outperform ACI in treating cartilage defects of the knee. Our key innovation is the method of making tissue membranes from cell spheroids. This is a platform technology that can also be applied for other tissues such as bones, tendons, ligaments, skin, and muscles.
kw: Biomanufacturing, hMSCs, Cartilage Regeneration, Tissue Engineering, Regenerative Medicine

title: Phase I/Ib, open label, dose-escalation study of CD5-directed CAR  γδT-cells (COGADE-C5) in patients with relapsed/refractory CD5+ haematological malignancies
abs: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has revolutionized the treatment for B-cell malignancies. However, the same success has yet been achieved for T-cell malignancies. We have developed COGADE-C5 – a cord-blood derived, allogeneic CD5-directed CAR γδT-cell (CB-γδT) therapy for the treatment of relapsed and/or refractory (R/R) CD5+ haematological malignancies including T-cell malignancies. The low cell surface expression of CD5 in CB-γδTs differentiates it from conventional αβT cells enabling COGADE-C5 to circumvent issues of fratricide and requirements for additional CD5 or T-cell receptor knock-out with its incumbent manufacturing complexities. CB-γδTs also avert tumour contamination and offers an off-the-shelf, polyclonal and potentially less exhausted product setting it apart from autologous αβT-cell and peripheral blood derived γδT-cell products. We propose a first-in-human (FIH) study, using a 3+3 dose escalation approach, to identify a safe and tolerable dose of COGADE-C5 and assess preliminary anti-tumour activity of COGADE-C5 following a single administration on study Day 1 and to evaluate the feasibility of the CAR CB-γδT manufacturing process. A preparatory lymphodepleting regimen with fludarabine and cyclophosphamide will occur prior to COGADE-C5 administration. We hypothesize that: 1. COGADE-C5 is safe and efficacious in CD5+ haematological malignancies The aims of this FIH study are to: 1. To assess safety and tolerability of COGADE-C5 in subjects with R/R CD5+ haematological malignancies and to provide single-agent dose recommendation for future studies 2. To evaluate feasibility of the manufacturing process 3. To evaluate the preliminary anti-tumour activity of COGADE-D5 in R/R CD5+ haematological malignancies Clinical Significance: Outcomes for patients with R/R T-cell malignancies are guarded and there is an unmet need for therapeutic developments to treat these patients. The establishment of the CB-γδT manufacturing process will also allow for rapid and scalable production of other CAR CB-γδT products to address unmet needs in R/R solid tumors and beyond.
kw: γδT-cell therapy; CAR T-cell therapy; T-ALL; PTCL; CD5+ haematological malignancies;

title: A Randomized Controlled Clinical Trial to Assess the Effect of Dapagliflozin on Renal and Cardiovascular Outcomes in Patients with Severe Chronic Kidney Disease (Renal Life Cycle Trial)
abs: Sodium glucose co transporter 2 inhibitor (SGLT2-i) drug class significantly improves kidney-cardiovascular outcomes in subjects with chronic kidney disease (CKD) with or without type 2 diabetes and heart failure and is now guidelines-directed medical therapies for patients with these conditions. Remarkably, the trials performed thus far have excluded patients with eGFR < 20mL/min/1.73m2, dialysis and kidney transplanted patients. We propose this multinational, multi-center prospective randomized double-blind placebo-controlled investigator-initiated trial with the primary aim to evaluate the cardiovascular-kidney protective effects of SGLT2-i, dapagliflozin in patients with severe CKD (defined as those with eGFR ≤ 25ml/min per 1.73m2, those with kidney failure receiving dialysis or kidney transplanted subjects with eGFR ≤ 45 mL/min/1.73m2). We hypothesized that dapagliflozin reduces the incidence of all-cause mortality, hospitalization for heart failure and kidney failure in the overall group of patients with severe CKD compared to placebo. As secondary hypothesis, we test whether dapagliflozin is superior to placebo in reducing each component of the primary composite in the overall population, and in reducing the primary composite endpoint in each of the 3 subgroups. We will test whether dapagliflozin improves quality of life measures and cardiac functional status compared to placebo. Eligible and consented subjects will be stratified by the 3 subgroups and then randomized to receive either oral Dapagliflozin 10mg daily or matching placebo and followed up prospectively. The trial is event-driven and will terminate when 468 primary composite events are captured. Safety and cost- effectiveness analysis will be done. The trial aims to bring a new treatment pillar to optimize kidney and cardiovascular outcomes of this high-risk population and initiate a paradigm shift in managing cardiovascular-kidney complications in patients with severe CKD. The research outcomes, if positive, will provide strong evidence for translation into clinical implementation, incorporation into global clinical practice guidelines and healthcare policy.
kw: Sodium Glucose Co-Transporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors, clinical trial, kidney and cardiovascular outcomes, advanced chronic kidney disease, dialysis, kidney transplant, cost effectiveness, patient centered outcomes

title: Investigating the Underlying Disease Mechanism of PURA Syndrome: Modelling Cortical Dysfunction for Therapeutic Target Discovery
abs: Background: Neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) are socially debilitating disorders affecting ~5% of the paediatric population in Singapore. NDDs also affect the adult population, due to considerable overlap with adult neurological disorders. However, currently, there is little or no treatment available for NDDs. One of NDDs is PURA syndrome, first reported in 2014. However, the disease mechanisms underlying PURA syndrome, such as cortical dysfunction, are not established. Objective: This proposal aims to establish the causal link between PURA variants and cortical dysfunction (aim 1), and identify downstream targets of PURA for potential therapeutic target discovery (aim 2). Methods: Through our Undiagnosed Disease Programme, we have identified two novel PURA variants (p.Gly47ArgfsTer155 and p.Arg199Pro) in two Singaporean patients with developmental delay. Our preliminary data suggest that neural stem cell proliferation is decreased in patient-derived cerebral organoids. In aim 1, we plan to investigate the novel role of PURA in brain development in human cerebral organoids and establish the causal link between two PURA variants and cortical dysfunction. In aim 2, we will use scRNA-seq to identify the alterations of gene expression networks in PURA patient-derived human cerebral organoids and establish the novel link between PURA and its downstream targets, which allows for identification of potential novel therapeutic targets. Clinical Significance: This project is anticipated to be the first to establish the functional characterization of PURA variants in human brain organoid models, leading to better understanding of pathophysiological mechanisms underlying PURA syndrome. Given that PURA is also involved in neurodegenerative disorders, such as FXTAS and ALS/FTD, our study not only contributes to the development of potential treatment strategies for NDDs, but also may provide novel insight into neurodegenerative diseases.
kw: PURA syndrome, neurodevelopmental disorder

title: Impact of a personalized, multidimensional & adaptive exercise intervention on endothelial function in type 2 diabetes mellitus
abs: Background and aims: Physical inactivity contributes to excess mortality and increases the risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) in type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). More than two-third of T2DM patients in Singapore do not reach the recommended exercise targets. Our preliminary data showed that the main barriers to exercise in T2DM patients point toward an overall lack of personalization in the exercise regime. Based on these results, we developed a personalized, multidimensional and adaptive exercise intervention to deliver individualized exercise prescriptions, and assess the impact of this exercise model on endothelial function, which is a key early marker of CVD. We piloted our intervention in 5 sedentary T2DM patients for 12 weeks. All participants showed improvement in endothelial function and exercise participation. In this proposal, we aim to expand to a larger scale and longer

title: Cortical connectivity, EEG and Gait Analysis in motor complete paraplegic patients post epidural spinal stimulator implantation
abs: Background: Complete spinal cord injury (SCI) has always been a devastating, life-altering event due to the near-permanent loss of essential neurological functions which affect multiple facets of a person’s life. Long-term effects of complete SCI include health complications, reduced quality of life and increased care burden, translating to increased socioeconomic costs. Aims/hypothesis: Our hypothesis in this clinical trial is that electrogoniometers and electroencephalography (EEG) readings correlate well with gait analysis in chronic motor complete SCI patients who have undergone implantation of an epidural spinal cord stimulator (ESS). Coupled with the use of resting state functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (rs-fMRI) and a gait laboratory, we will study the intricate changes in gait patterns and investigate the different aspects of brain-spine neuroplasticity before, during and after ESS implantation. Secondary aims include identifying changes in rs-fMRI, EEG and electrogoniometer patterns that correlate with learned gait analysis, and using these datasets to predict success in locomotion. Methods/Approach: We propose a Human Clinical Trial to study the gait patterns of five (5) patients with chronic motor complete SCI who have undergone ESS implantation. These 5 patients will undergo a specialized pre- and post-operative rehabilitation program at Tan Tock Seng Hospital Centre of Advanced Rehabilitation Therapeutics (CART), whilst EEG and electrogoniometer data will be collected at the Rehabilitation Research Institute of Singapore (RRIS) gait laboratory. 10 data setpoints per patient would be extracted and analysed using a computational software to correlate with actual gait motion and predict gait patterns. Significance Given ESS’ recent international success, understanding the intricacies in gait analysis becomes increasingly relevant. This would help predict success in ambulation and customise the rehabilitation techniques employed in patient-management. This next step, in the paradigm of SCI rehabilitation, is essential to maximise the potential of these individuals with an evidence-based allocation of resources.
kw: Electroencephalogram; Epidural spinal cord stimulation; functional magnetic resonance imaging; electrogoniometer; motor complete spinal cord injury

title: GENEKIDS-PRO: Genomic Enhancement and Patient Engagement in NEphrology through Multidisciplinary KIDney Genetics Clinic Implementation and Integration in Singapore – using PROcess Evaluation Framework.
abs: A multidisciplinary kidney genetics clinic has demonstrated significant clinical utility and cost-effectiveness. However, the degree of clinical utility varies across different healthcare settings, and integrating kidney genomic services globally remains a significant challenge due to the complexity of the process. This study aims to refine and improve a multidisciplinary kidney genetics clinic at a tertiary hospital. We will evaluate the quality of kidney genomic care in terms of effectiveness, timeliness, and patient-centeredness for adult kidney patients and their families with genetic kidney diseases. Additionally, we will use a process evaluation framework to identify key determinants of successful implementation in terms of acceptability, appropriateness, feasibility, and degree of fidelity. We will also study the mechanisms of impact and the context of implementation. This will be achieved using an effectiveness-implementation hybrid type 1 design, quasi-experimental, with mixed quantitative and qualitative approaches. Healthcare providers and researchers acknowledge that the effectiveness of evidence-based interventions often diminishes in real-world settings due to various contextual determinants. Therefore, successful implementation of kidney genomic clinical services is crucial to achieving maximum intervention impact. Poor implementation can lead to less desirable outcomes and negative unintended consequences, known as "Type III" errors, where interventions are deemed ineffective due to improper implementation. The success or failure of these interventions also depends on their impact on three key groups: recipients, deliverers, and decision-makers. Ensuring equitable and ethical impact on all these groups is essential for a successful intervention. This study is critical to ensure maximum impact on both implementation strategies and patient outcomes. The evidence generated can be used to mainstream and incorporate kidney genomic medicine into the Singapore healthcare system, ensuring sustainable and widespread adoption in the future.
kw: Multidisciplinary Kidney Genetics Clinic; Kidney Genomic; Genetic Kidney Disease; Nephrology; Implementation; Process Evaluation

title: Novel Non-Invasive Imaging to quantify blood brain barrier dysfunction in vascular mild cognitive impairment
abs: Dementia is a global health problem with an estimated 55 million patients worldwide with more than half of these patients residing in Asia. Moreover, vascular mild cognitive impairment (VMCI) is highly prevalent in Asia and various pathophysiological processes likely influence its onset and progress. Dysfunction of the blood brain barrier (BBB), the protective gateway to the brain, has been shown to be associated with the onset and progression of VMCI. This represents impairment in the interplay between neuronal activity and blood flow to the brain or neurovascular coupling. BBB dysfunction is also believed to be a crucial process in the acceleration of the amyloid cascade, neuroinflammation and ensuing neurodegeneration. Thus, an in-depth understanding of the role of the BBB in the pathobiology of dementia would allow for development of novel biomarkers and interventions. With recent advances, we are now able to non-invasively measure BBB health using state-of-the-art MRI in humans. These measures show promise in detection of age-related changes in BBB permeability and are emerging as important techniques in clinical research applications. As this is a developing field, the relationship between non-invasive BBB imaging in human subjects and the possible effects on other structural and cerebral perfusion aspects of the brain as well as validation with gold standard BBB imaging need extensive exploration. In this proposal we thus aim to employ novel non-invasive neuroimaging to study neurovascular dysfunction related to BBB impairment in human subjects from an Asian cohort with VMCI. Subjects will undergo BBB Arterial Spin Labelling MRI and cognitive testing along with multimodal brain imaging including structural and perfusion MRI to enable examination of associations between BBB dysfunction, blood flow, brain structure and cognition. A subset of VMCI subjects will also undergo gold standard BBB imaging using dynamic contrast enhanced MRI for validation with non-invasive BBB MRI.
kw: blood brain barrier; vascular mild cognitive impairment; brain imaging; dementia; biomarkers; validation

title: AI-Enhanced Smart Toilet System for Optimal Bowel Preparation in Colonoscopy Patients
abs: Colorectal Cancer (CRC) is a critical global health issue, ranking as the third most common cancer worldwide, with about 1.9 million new cases and 935,000 deaths reported in 2020. In Singapore, CRC accounts for roughly 17% of all cancer diagnoses, highlighting the urgent need for effective prevention and treatment strategies. Colonoscopy is a crucial tool in CRC screening, enabling the removal of premalignant polyps and preventing the progression of cancer. High-quality bowel preparation is essential for the detection and removal of adenomas and polyps. A novel healthcare toilet prototype has been developed, equipped with various health monitoring functions, including urinalysis, uroflowmetry, and defecation monitoring using the Bristol Stool Form Scale (BSFS). This prototype collects stool images for analysis by a machine learning algorithm designed to classify stool images according to the BSFS, ensuring an accurate assessment of bowel preparation readiness. In the first phase of the project, anonymized images of defecated material from 156 subjects undergoing colonoscopy preparation will be collected and annotated. A binary Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) will be trained to classify these images based on the BSFS. The algorithm’s performance will be validated against clinical experts' assessments, with accuracy measured using the Area Under the Curve. In the second phase, the trained model will be deployed in a smart toilet for a randomized, controlled, single-blinded study involving 50 subjects in both control and intervention groups. Subjects in the intervention group will receive an additional purgative if their BSFS score indicates inadequate preparation. Clinical outcomes will be evaluated using BBPS scores, adenoma and polyp detection rates, and patient satisfaction. This system addresses unmet needs in CRC screening. This innovative approach has the potential to revolutionize bowel preparation protocols, reduce healthcare costs from repeat procedures due to inadequate preparation, and ultimately improve early detection and prevention of colorectal cancer.
kw: Smart Toilet System; Colonoscopy; Bowel Preparation; Bristol Stool Form Scale;  Boston Bowel Preparation Scale; Adenoma Detection Rate

title: Developing a Multidisciplinary Intervention Program for prevention of dementia
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Dementia is a common degenerative neurological symptom that affects cognition, behavior, and daily activities. Prevention of dementia has been a top priority in the aging society due to its profound impact on the health care system. Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) is an intermediate state between normal cognition and dementia, which is commonly present in Parkinson Disease (PD) patients even in the early stage. The presence of MCI in PD increases the risk of developing early PD dementia. Previous study demonstrated that modifying multiple risk factors concurrently can reduce the likelihood of participants with dementia. However, there is limited study to show the effectiveness of multidisciplinary approach to prevention of cognitive decline in PD-MCI patients. To address the gap in knowledge, we propose to develop a Multidisciplinary Intervention Program for prevention of cognitive decline in PD-MCI patients. We hypothesize that multidisciplinary intervention will improve neurocognitive performance in PD-MCI patients during the 2-year study period.
kw: Multidisciplinary Intervention Program; Prevention; Cognitive decline

title: Integrating ArtificiaI Intelligence, Phenotypic Analysis, and Genomics to Elucidate the Systemic and Genetic Foundations of Drusen Subtypes in our Population
abs: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is a leading cause of vision loss, characterized by early-stage drusen deposits. This proposal integrates artificial intelligence (AI), phenotypic analysis, and genomics to explore the systemic and genetic origins of drusen subtypes in AMD. Specific Aim 1 focuses on developing and validating a convolutional neural network (CNN) to identify and classify drusen from color fundus photographs and optical coherence tomography (OCT) images. We hypothesize that the CNN can accurately subtype drusen based on multimodal retinal imaging features. Specific Aim 2 aims to validate associations between drusen subtypes and systemic phenotypic measurements like BMI, lipid profiles, and blood pressure. Our hypothesis suggests significant links between drusen presence/subtype and these phenotypes. Specific Aim 3 involves genetic studies to uncover biological pathways linked to confirmed drusen associations. We anticipate that specific genetic variations influence drusen development by impacting crucial molecular processes shared with other systemic diseases. Utilizing the Health for Life in Singapore (HELIOS) dataset, which includes retinal imaging, systemic measures, and genetic data, we will train CNN models and conduct statistical analyses for phenotype associations. Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) will identify genetic variants associated with drusen subtypes. Preliminary results demonstrate high CNN accuracy in drusen classification from color fundus photographs, and manual grading confirms drusen subtype prevalence feasibility in elderly subsets of HELIOS. Our interdisciplinary team of ophthalmologists, AI specialists, geneticists, and epidemiologists ensures comprehensive expertise for this study. This research promises new insights into drusen prevalence, systemic relationships, and genetic foundations, particularly in Asian populations. Findings could inform personalized AMD management, preventive strategies, and novel therapies, potentially alleviating the burden of vision loss.

title: A novel isolation room model based on culture-independent Hi-C metagenomics for tracking antimicrobial resistance transmission between patients and hospital environmental reservoirs
abs: Background: Limiting the global spread of antimicrobial resistance is vital to reducing disease burden, especially in the post-antibiotic era. Hospital surfaces harbor diverse microbial communities that can transfer antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) via mobile genetic elements like plasmids to pathogenic bacteria. There is a significant lack of information on the spatial, temporal, and phylogenetic relationships between different bacterial taxa on hospital surfaces and the patient microbiome. This includes understanding the physical colocalization and horizontal gene transfer between multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria and environmental bacteria, which hinders infection-control efforts even in high-resource settings like Singapore. Traditional shotgun metagenomics cannot link the extrachromosomal mobilome to individual host cells. Methods: A culture-independent, high-throughput chromosome conformation capture (Hi-C) metagenomics approach is proposed. This method, deployed in an isolation ward set-up to exclude external microbiome influences, will track the exchange of carbapenemase-encoding and other ARGs between patients and their immediate hospital environmental reservoirs in situ. Aims: Firstly, we seek to establish a novel contact-precaution isolation room model that enables the directionality of gene transfer to be determined, Secondly, to optimize and validate a Hi-C metagenomics pipeline for patient and hospital environmental samples. Thirdly, to determine microbial diversity and genomic contexts of ARGs in patient and environmental microbiomes. Fourthly, to analyze spatiotemporal transmission dynamics of ARGs between patients and their environment. Lastly, to compare metagenomics with whole genome sequencing of cultured bacterial isolates for detecting resistome transmission between patients and the hospital environment. Significance: Understanding the ecology of antibiotic resistance and the pathways of ARG transmission between patients and environmental reservoirs is crucial for designing effective infection-control strategies. The isolation room model with an integrated Hi-C metagenomics pipeline could be used for clinical testing of decontamination protocols targeting uncovered environmental reservoirs, transforming medical practice and clinical research through effective knowledge translation.
kw: Hi-C metagenomics; shotgun metagenomics; hospital environment; microbiome; antimicrobial resistance; plasmid transmission

title: UNVEIL study – UNcovering therapeutic Vulnerabilities in EGFR and HER2 Exon 20 Insertion mutated Lung cancer
abs: Background: EGFR and HER2 exon 20 insertion mutations, together accounting for up to 10% of all NSCLC patients, are associated with poor response to EGFR and pan-HER TKIs that have activity against ‘classical’ EGFR mutations. There is substantial diversity in exon 20 insertion variants. There remain limited in-depth integrative studies on the clinicopathologic and multi-omic (genomic, transcriptomic and structural protein) characterization of this molecular subset. Hypothesis: We hypothesize that EGFR and HER2 exon 20 insertion mutated NSCLC constitute distinctive subtypes within the spectrum of NSCLC. This has historically posed therapeutic challenges. This complexity necessitates combined analyses integrating comprehensive genomic, transcriptomic, structural protein and clinicopathologic datasets to recapitulate this unique tumor biology and unveil therapeutic vulnerabilities, particularly for individual insertion variants. Specific Aims & Methods: 1. To uncover genomic, transcriptomic pathway and immune therapeutic vulnerabilities, including combination approaches for EGFR and HER2 exon 20 insertion mutated NSCLC – elucidated through deep multi-omic profiling with whole exome and transcriptome sequencing of resected tumors to identify how different insertion variants influence pathway and immune activation 2. To understand how specific insertion mutation variants affect drug binding and therapeutic efficacy – through the application of established machine learning models of in silico drug binding to predict TKI drug binding to the most common insertion variants with validation using patient derived organoids and in vitro drug screens 3. To identify key clinicopathologic features for individual insertion variants determining response and resistance to systemic therapies including EGFR targeted therapies – through the interrogation of an extensive Pan-Asian real-world patient dataset annotated with clinical and treatment outcomes Significance: EGFR and HER2 exon 20 insertion mutated NSCLC remains a molecular subtype of NSCLC with high unmet medical need. Deep multi-omic characterization and integration with clinical datasets is needed to identify novel therapeutic vulnerabilities and improve patient outcomes.
kw: EGFR; HER2; non-small cell lung cancer; exon 20 insertion mutations; therapeutic vulnerabilities

title: Development of preference weights for the 10-item Singapore Caregiver Quality Of Life Scale
abs: Singapore is an aging society with an increasing burden of debilitating illnesses. The demand on family caregivers has grown larger than ever before. Healthcare agencies have emphasized the importance of family caregivers’ quality of life (QoL) and have recommended the use of preference-based instruments to assess family caregivers’ QoL for the computation of utility value. Utility value is an essential component in calculating quality-adjusted life years, an important measure in health economic evaluations. Due to the sociocultural differences between the East and the West, existing caregiver-specific preference-based QoL instruments developed in Western countries are not appropriate for evaluating the utility of caregivers in Singapore. Hence, a caregiver-specific preference-based QoL instrument suitable for local use is required. However, such an instrument is currently not available. This proposal aims to develop preference weights for a locally developed, culturally appropriate, profile-based QoL instrument for family caregivers, namely the 10-item Singapore Caregiver Quality Of Life Scale (SCQOLS-10), so that a SCQOLS utility value can be calculated. We hypothesize that the SCQOLS utility value will show a better discriminative ability than the utility value obtained from a generic preference-based QoL instrument. We will examine other measurement properties such as concurrent validity and test-retest reliability of the SCQOLS utility value. We will conduct a discrete choice experiment incorporated in a cross-sectional online survey. Samples of 1,000 family caregivers of an adult person and 1,000 individuals from the general public will be recruited. Each respondent will self-administer an anonymous questionnaire, including the SCQOLS-10. Conditional logit models and anchoring methods will be performed to develop the preference weights. The availability of preference weights for the SCQOLS-10 will be invaluable for health outcome assessments and health economic evaluations, aiding in decision-making and the design of policies and healthcare innovations relevant to family caregivers.
kw: Caregiver; Quality of life; Utility value; Preference weights; SCQOLS

title: Navigating feeding decisions in dementia: development of a caregiver decision aid
abs: Background: Eating difficulties are nearly universal in advanced dementia. Though tube feeding is discouraged among older adults with advanced dementia, caregivers often find feeding decisions challenging to navigate due to emotional, cultural, and ethical implications. Decision aids have been shown to provide support for caregivers making significant decisions in dementia care, however, none currently exist to support dementia feeding decisions in the Singapore context. Study Aims: 1) To develop a digital decision aid to support feeding decisions for caregivers of community-dwelling older adults with advanced dementia; 2) To test the feasibility, acceptability and usability of the decision aid among dementia caregivers. Methods: We will convene an advisory panel of clinicians, dieticians, speech therapists and caregiver representatives to guide content development for the decision aid using qualitative in-depth, semi-structured interviews to gather the essential information practitioners and caregivers need to make an informed decision about feeding options for older adults. Based on expert interviews, we will develop the decision aid content in accordance with international standards, including using a systematic process, presenting information in a balanced manner, drawing on evidence, including methods for clarifying and expressing values and using plain language. Following development of a prototype decision aid, we will conduct cognitive interviews with members of the advisory panel to elicit feedback to inform revision and refinement of the prototype. Finally, we will recruit a convenience sample of 30 family caregivers to older adults with advanced dementia to review the decision aid and respond to a questionnaire assessing its feasibility, acceptability and usability. Feasibility and Importance: This proposal builds on our team’s extensive prior work and clinical and research expertise. We aim to address a critical gap in existing dementia palliative care research specifically affecting Singaporeans and provide a solution for many caregivers navigating difficult feeding decisions in advanced dementia.
kw: dementia; caregivers; decision aid; feeding difficulties, tube feeding, careful hand feeding

title: An AI weight management program in type 2 diabetes: development, validation and evaluation of the Wabi program
abs: Background: Digital weight loss interventions require human behavioural intervention for successful weight loss, limiting scalability due to cost and manpower constraints. Recent advancements in large language models (LLM) technology offer improved accuracy, multi-step task execution, and dynamic responses. The Wabi program leverages LLM communication capabilities for engagement and empowerment, integrating user clinical data, self-monitoring, geolocation, and national food databases for personalized dietary guidance. Aims: The Wabi research program aims to develop an innovative LLM-supported weight management program that is user-centric, accurate, safe and effective in supporting weight loss and behavior change in overweight/ obese individuals with type 2 diabetes. Methods: The research program comprises 3 phases: (1) user co-development, (2) multi-faceted validation using simulated data and a pilot feasibility study, and (3) efficacy evaluation through a pragmatic RCT conducted in primary care settings. Wabi’s development will include clear program theory, required databases integration and safety measures aligned with MOH guidelines. Conclusions: A multi-disciplinary approach, user co-development, and rigorous validation will ensure Wabi meets user needs, maintains accuracy, and addresses LLM-related safety concerns for clinical implementation. Wabi has potential for population-wide application in addressing overweight/obesity in type 2 diabetes. In addition, this research will provide valuable insights into generative AI use for health behavior change.
kw: Artificial Intelligence; Weight Management; Type 2 diabetes; population health

title:
Does Green Urbanism Work Together with TOD?
A Spatial Analysis of Energy Consumption, Transit Ridership, and Price Appreciation
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: In recent years, Asian cities have progressively adopted “green urbanism” elements (e.g., energy-efficient green building and electric vehicle [EV] sharing service systems) in urban development and management practices for climate change mitigation. On the other hand, contemporary urban spatial planning and environmental design practices have continued to stress the importance of “transit-oriented development (TOD)” principles (e.g., compact, dense, mixed-use, and pedestrian-friendly built environment features around rail transit stations) in changing automobile-dependent lifestyle and travel behavior, reducing vehicle kilometers traveled and greenhouse gas emissions, and creating property price premiums for enhanced accessibility and agglomeration benefits. Conceptually, the combination of green urbanism and TOD, called “Green TOD,” can create synergetic benefits beyond the sum of what green urbanism and TOD generate separately. Nevertheless, there is almost no scientific evidence on the combined effects of green urbanism and TOD features on urban development and management outcomes due largely to the lack of Green TOD project implementations at scale in many Asian cities. This proposed research aims to empirically investigate the possible synergies and/or tradeoffs between green urbanism elements and TOD principles by conducting three sets of spatial data analyses in Singapore as one of the global best TOD city cases. The first set of spatial data analyses will statistically explain differences in energy consumption across buildings with and without green mark certification and EV sharing service systems around rail transit stations and beyond station catchment areas. The second set of spatial data analyses will inspect the influences of green urbanism elements and TOD principles on travel behavior changes by estimating direct ridership models across rail transit stations citywide. The third set of spatial data analyses will extensively measure the combined capitalization effects of Green TOD on commercial and residential property transactions around rail transit stations and beyond station catchment areas by applying both linear and non-linear regression modeling techniques (e.g., machine learning methods). Empirical findings on building energy consumption, rail transit ridership, and property price appreciation are expected to help Asian cities employ innovative green technology solutions, promote clean public transport modes, and leverage land value capture (or land-based finance) techniques and private real estate investments for carbon neutrality in strategic urban development and management locations.
kw: Green Urbanism, Transit Oriented Development, Urban Climate Change Action, Urban Spatial Planning, Environmental Design, and Evidence-based Policy

title: Chemoselective enrichment and mass spectrometry (MS) profiling of the gut microbiota-derived N-acetyl-2-amino carbohydrate metabolites
abs: The gut microbiota produces a trove of small molecules and metabolites that strongly influence the host's health. Notably, the gut microbiota-derived carbohydrate motifs represent an emerging class of signaling molecules in the microbiota-host crosstalk. Changes to the compositions and quantities of these bioactive carbohydrate metabolites may have significant implications on the host's health status. However, due to the structural complexity and poor MS ionization of carbohydrates, the soluble glycan chemotypes are often neglected in the current metabolomic profiling analysis of gut microbiota-derived metabolites. Recognizing the widespread presence of N-acetyl-2-amino saccharide as the reducing unit in diverse gut microbiota-derived glycans, we propose a chemoselective strategy via oxazoline chemistry to irreversibly capture and enrich N-acetyl-2-amino sugars from the complex biological matrix for LC-MS profiling. The chemoselective enrichment and MS profiling of the gut microbiota-derived N-acetyl-2-amino sugar metabolites in bacterial culture and host will not only offer fundamental knowledge of the identities and quantities of these carbohydrate metabolites but may also uncover novel biomarkers for potential diagnosis and treatment of microbiome-associated human diseases.
kw: chemoselective probe; N-acetyl-2-amino sugars; oxazoline chemistry; bio-orthogonal chemistry; gut microbiota-host interaction; mass spectrometric profiling

title: Advancing Nutrient Removal from Wastewater by Innovative Biofilm Reactors with Specialized Microbial Consortia to Realize Low- Energy and Carbon Footprint
abs: Escalating concerns about pollution and water resource scarcity have brought the need for efficient reclamation of water from wastewater into sharp focus. In tropical regions, where high nutrient concentrations and elevated temperatures pose unique challenges to conventional treatment technologies, innovative solutions are imperative. This project will evaluate the feasibility of a ground-breaking biological treatment system with the potential for achieving complete removal of nitrogenous compounds. The system will be developed to operate with minimal net energy consumption, produce negligible sludge, and achieve net-zero greenhouse gas emissions. Our innovative work involves discovering and harnessing novel nitrifying, denitrifying, and anammox bacteria with novel pathways within purpose-built biofilm reactors. Applying bacterial cultivation techniques pioneered by my research group, we will enrich nitrifying, denitrifying and anammox bacteria from diverse ecosystems and explore their metabolic pathways using a multi-omics approach. Insights gained from these cultures will inform the development of adaptable microbial consortia tailored for specific treatment objectives. Performance evaluations will be conducted in bench-scale bioreactors treating synthetic and real wastewater, with a focus on monitoring microbial community dynamics and retaining functional redundancy. Furthermore, a comprehensive assessment of carbon/energy balance and greenhouse gas emissions will be undertaken to gauge the economic and environmental sustainability of the system. This project challenges conventional wastewater treatment paradigms by unravelling complex microbial interactions and biochemical pathways involved in nitrogen transformation; revolutionizes bioreactor design/operation by establishing resilient microbial consortia. Through laboratory-scale experiments, molecular analyses, and computational assessments, the proposed system will be developed and evaluated. Key steps include the enrichment and cultivation of bacteria, establishment of defined microbial consortia, and integration into advanced bioreactors. Computational models will optimize nutrient removal conditions, aiming to reduce energy consumption and greenhouse gas emissions. The project's outcomes hold significant academic and industrial implications, shedding light on microbial interactions, biofilm formation, and nutrient cycling in established microbial communities. These findings will provide valuable insights for next-generation sustainable water reclamation globally.
kw: nutrients removal; sustainable wastewater treatment; low energy; low carbon emission; specialized microbial consortia

title: Open-World 3D Scene Understanding with Neural Fields
abs: There are two main research goals in this grant proposal. First, we will investigate the use of neural fields to circumvent the limitations of the commonly used 3D point clouds for scene representation towards three important 3D scene understanding tasks: 1) 3D object detection; 2) 3D semantic/instance segmentation; 3) 3D Question and Answer (3D-QA). In comparison to 3D point clouds, neural field scene representation has the advantage of continuous representation of the 3D scene and thus alleviating the sparsity and irregularity issues of 3D point clouds without scarifying versatility and conciseness of the scene representation for 3D scene understanding tasks. Second, we will study the use of large foundation models for open-world 3D scene understanding with neural field representation. Existing large foundation models are mostly trained on large amounts of data and thus can be considered to contain vast information including open-world classes that are not seen in the training of the 3D scene understanding task. We will explore the use of two types of foundation models coupled with neural field representation for the open-world 3D scene understanding tasks: 1) Language-vision model when the closed and open-world object class text labels are available; 2) Vision-only model when the object class text labels are not available. To these ends, we will focus on solving the following challenges that are common to all three 3D scene understanding tasks for neural fields open-world learning with large foundation models: 1) 2D-to-3D Modality Gap; 2) Task Transfer Learning; 3) Open-world Generalizability; 4) Modes of Supervision; 5) Feature Representation and Learning.
kw: 3D Scene Understanding; Neural Radiance Fields; Deep Signed Distance Fields; Open-world;

title: Holographic MIMO for 6G Wireless Communications and Beyond
abs: The development of metamaterials/metasurfaces and advanced antenna technologies encourage the emergence of holographic multiple-input and multiple-output (H-MIMO), which shows great potential to support the sixth-generation (6G) and beyond wireless communications in boosting spectral efficiency, improving energy efficiency, and supporting a multitude of rising functionalities and upper layer applications. We expect that H-MIMO systems can achieve 200% higher spectral efficiency compared with the currently deployed Massive-MIMO systems but at lower hardware cost. Moreover, from the energy efficiency perspective, we aim to achieve at least 30% energy consumption reduction at the same spectral efficiency as Massive-MIMO. In this project, we will investigate three critical aspects of H-MIMO in the physical layer. First, we will develop tractable channel model from the fundamentally physics perspective, which captures the inherent electromagnetic (EM) characteristics in wave propagation across the space domain. With these proposed models, we will be able to delve into the performance of H-MIMO systems, such as the channel capacity. Next, we will investigate effective channel estimation approaches in H-MIMO systems to deal with the high complexity induced by densely placed antenna elements. Finally, the beamforming design of H-MIMO is introduced to fully utilize the H-MIMO systems in various scenarios, such as spatial/polarization interference cancellation in multi-user cases, and spectral efficiency maximization. Our research efforts will bring H-MIMO one step closer to reality, as H-MIMO appears to be a transformative technology that is capable of fundamentally changing the way wireless networks are implemented nowadays, this project also has the potential to transform the future landscape of wireless communications.
kw: Holographic MIMO; Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface; Massive MIMO; channel modelling; channel estimation; beamforming design

title: NOVEL ANYON PLATFORMS FROM PARTIALLY FILLED TOPOLOGICAL BANDS
abs: Realizing different types of anyonic quasiparticles in 2D quantum materials is one of the most exciting endeavours in condensed matter physics. Theoretically it pushes the boundary of our understanding about emergent quantum behaviours, sometimes offering tantalizing opportunities to study elusive high-energy elementary particles with low-temperature and even tabletop experiments. Experimentally, observing topological phases hosting such quasiparticles is the strong motivation behind much progress in material synthesis, realization of ultra-low temperature environment and innovative probing methods. From the application point of view, anyonic quasiparticles hold great promises as building blocks for the robust storage and processing of quantum information. This project aims to discover new topological phases, and more realistic ways of stabilizing non-Abelian topological phases hosting exotic quasiparticles, that emerge from strong interaction between multiple species of electrons. More specifically, we will develop a comprehensive set of analytic and numerical tools to systematically identify universal topological features of 2D quantum fluids, and to compute the dynamical and statistical properties of their low energy quasiparticle excitations. Working with our experimental collaborators, the tools we develop will also be applied to design and compute novel tuning knobs in heterostructures and moiré systems, for stabilizing fragile non-Abelian topological phases that so far have proved to be elusive in experiments. For many of the studies for the experimental realization of non-Abelian quantum fluids from single-component electronic systems, the experimental evidence is scarce and controversial. To address such gaps, our approach is to endow electrons in topological bands with internal degrees of freedom (i.e. pseudospins) from spin, valley, layer or other unconventional indices (e.g. Landau level and Chern number indices). Enriching the correlated topological bands with multiple fermion species will allow us to propose diverse experimental platforms, new theoretical tools to tackle the complexity of many-body systems, and advanced numerical recipes to simulate and compute quantitatively the quasiparticle properties for experimental control. The pursuit of this project is also timely given a number of recent theoretical works developed by the PI, and the advent of experimental platforms especially from recent advances in multilayer graphene and TMD moiré materials, where pseudospins from a myriad of physical origins are readily available. Close collaboration with experimentalists and strong numerical capabilities from the PI and the co-PI allow us to address outstanding theoretical and experimental questions with three inter-connected aims: A. proposition and characterization of new topological phases from additional degrees of freedom, and their experimental signatures from local and transport measurements; B. exploiting pseudospins as additio

title: X-ray nanophotonics for next-generation ultrafast coincidence timing resolution in positron emission tomography
abs: Overcoming the 10-picosecond challenge is a holy grail in time-of-flight positron emission tomography (TOF-PET), a medical imaging modality known for its picomolar sensitivity in cancer diagnosis and therapy response monitoring. The accuracy of this measurement is determined by the coincidence timing resolution (CTR), the record value of which is approximately 69 ps. The 10-picosecond challenge is to realize a CTR of less than 10 ps, which would enable millimeter-level precision in imaging and thus safer (lower dose), faster (reconstruction-free) and more accurate medical diagnostics. In the proposed project, we will theoretically explore and experimentally demonstrate unprecedented nanophotonics phenomena in high-light-yield and ultrafast perovskite materials, with the ultimate ambition of overcoming the 10-picosecond challenge. In particular, we will (1) develop proposed ab initio Monte Carlo software XPONENT (X-ray Photonics On the Nanoscale for Emerging NanoTechnologies) that fully captures nanophotonic phenomena, which existing particle–matter interaction solvers do not consider; (2) harness cutting-edge nanophotonic concepts in emerging perovskite scintillator materials to uncover new fundamental mechanisms for achieving still higher light yields and decay rates in these materials; and (3) experimentally demonstrate substantial light yield and decay rate enhancement using nanophotonics in ultrafast (ns and sub-ns) perovskite scintillator materials to realize a sub-10 ps CTR. The feasibility of our proposal is backed by our preliminary studies and proof-of-concept experiments, which include our unprecedented experimental demonstration of the ability of nanophotonics to enhance the light yield and decay rate of ultrafast perovskite scintillators. Our proposed project will be highly multidisciplinary, combining a broad range of expertise in computational X-ray nanophotonics, perovskites and materials science, ultrafast optics, and positron emission tomography. The project will pave the way to next-generation scintillator devices having ultrahigh light yields and ultrafast responses, for applications in TOF-PET and beyond.
kw: X-ray photonics; nanophotonics; scintillators; perovskites; light-matter interactions; ultrafast optics

title: Hybrid Seawater-driven Geothermal Energy Piles for Thermal Storage and Sustainable District Cooling in Southeast Asia
abs: Energy pile technology shows great potential for extracting geothermal energy from the ground to support sustainable space heating and cooling. However, the direct application of energy piles in cooling demand-dominated regions, such as Singapore, can be problematic as the continuous operation of energy piles can inject excessive heat into the ground, thereby leading to thermal imbalances or even system failure. Moreover, cyclic thermal loads can induce additional radial/axial deformation in piles and adversely affect the engineering properties of fine-grained materials at the pile interface. Therefore, how to leverage energy pile technology for sustainable space cooling and flexible thermal storage without compromising the structural integrity of piles is an interesting and challenging topic. This project proposes a seawater-driven energy pile system to prevent thermal imbalances and promote decarbonization in the energy sector. The system can effectively harness both seawater energy and shallow geothermal energy for sustainable space cooling while also providing flexible energy storage in the ground to meet thermal needs across different time scales. The research will develop an integrated thermodynamics model to evaluate the long-term thermal storage and efficiency of the hybrid energy system. Additionally, a multiscale framework will be established to investigate the fundamental thermo-mechanical soil behaviors under cyclic thermal loading, and surrogate models will be developed to predict the thermomechanical pile-soil interaction under complex loading paths. The obtained insights will be leveraged to create a techno-economic and lifecycle assessment model for cost and performance optimization. The outcomes of this project will enhance our fundamental understanding of the complex thermodynamics and thermomechanical interactions of energy piles. This, in turn, will promote the application of energy geostructures in Southeast Asia, contributing to the region’s transition towards carbon neutrality, and benefiting mankind.
kw: Energy geostructure; Machine learning; Sustainable district cooling; Thermo-mechanical interaction; Thermal balance

title: Modelling the evolution of punishment and exploring the challenges to metaethics
abs: The evolutionary of morality raises philosophical questions about its foundations. Some philosophers argue that the evolutionary origins of morality show our moral judgements would be the same even if they were not true – and from this, conclude that our moral judgements are not justified. This is known as an evolutionary debunking argument against our moral judgements. Such arguments exemplify a tension between a view of ourselves as beings with evolved moral instincts, and a view on which we are moral agents responding to objective, morally relevant features of actions and institutions. As an example, consider punishment: it seems reasonable to believe that punishing wrongs is morally justified. But if it turns out that we would have evolved to believe that punishment is morally justified even if it were not, then the justification of these beliefs is undermined. To address these issues, this project brings philosophers together with evolutionary game theorists in an interdisciplinary collaboration. Evolutionary game theory provides us with models of possible paths for the evolution of punishment and morality, which may then inform the philosophical debate about the justification of punishment and morality. We will use evolutionary game theory to explicitly model possible scenarios for the evolution of punishment. We will then use these richer models to assess evolutionary debunking arguments against our moral judgements in general, as well as their application to normative ethical disputes over punishment in particular. By modelling in detail some possible ways punishment may have evolved, including various punishment mechanisms and kin selection effects, we will explore more-detailed and realistic models of the evolution of ethics than hitherto discussed, thus providing new insights into ethics. Q1: From an evolutionary game-theoretic perspective, how could punishment have evolved? We will model punishment mechanisms proposed in both the scientific and philosophical literatures with a focus on plausible evolutionary trajectories. Whereas previous models have tended to assume for simplicity that members of a population interact with each other at random, we will explore relaxing this unrealistic assumption to consider evolutionary models in which interaction is more likely with kin, especially early in evolutionary history (without assuming that this is the only possible path of human evolution). We are particularly interested in understanding the influence of kin selection, including the likely role kin interactions could have played to facilitate the first emergence of punishment in human societies. But we are also interested in modelling how punishment can persist even as social environments shift from interactions with mostly kin to interactions with strangers. title: Advancing Consumer Behavior Research through Generative AI and Large Language Models
abs: Advances in artificial intelligence (AI), such as large language models (LLMs), present opportunities to fundamentally transform scientific research about human behavior. Modern LLMs are increasingly capable of understanding and generating human-like text. Utilizing a network of neurons inspired by the human brain, these advanced models process massive text corpora of natural language to detect patterns within texts, allowing LLMs to predict and generate texts that are contextually relevant and syntactically coherent. The primary objective of this research project is to examine how LLMs can be leveraged to augment scientific study of consumer behavior for causal inference. Consumer behavior plays a critical role shaping the economy, as private consumption constitutes about two-thirds of all economic activities in many countries. An understanding of the drivers of consumer behavior is crucial for businesses and policymakers alike. GPT series and similar LLMs are trained on a vast array of internet text data, which may include product descriptions (e.g., manufacturers’ websites, e-commerce websites, specialized industry reports, patent descriptions) and consumer reviews (e.g., social media, review websites). By training on such diverse sources, modern LLMs should encompass a broad understanding of various aspects of products and consumer perceptions, enabling LLMs to generate informed and relevant responses in these contexts. Specifically, we identify two areas in the research pipeline to focus on in this proposed project. In the first part, we aim to examine the capacities of LLMs in complex and specialized domains. We are interested in the extent to which LLMs acquire specialized knowledge and emulate a human expert’s reasoning ability. We will: 1. Evaluate the extent to which LLMs can develop hypotheses about consumer psychology and behavior. 2. Test the performance of LLMs as a tool for theory development and refinement for consumer psychology and behavior (prior to experimentation). Our hypothesis holds that, when we prompt a LLM to provide a hypothesis about consumer behavior in a specified decision context, the responses it provides reflect the learned distribution of responses from the consumers that are a part of the LLM’s training data. In the second part, we plan to use LLMs to augment current scientific practices in experimental design and analysis. An inherent challenge lies in balancing the complexity and richness of real-world product descriptions with the scientific necessity for precision. To facilitate causal inference, experimental designs need to isolate specific factors for precise measurement while eliminating extraneous variables. However, real-world product descriptions can be elaborate and diverse, and consumers are often presented with many product options. title: Artificial Intelligence + Data Assimilation (AIDA) for weather and climate models
abs: Accurate medium-range (up to 2 weeks ahead) weather forecasts are crucial to avoid extreme-weather induced disasters, or at least to mitigate them. Additionally, time scales ranging from extended range (up to 8 weeks ahead), to yearly and decadal, are crucial to implement effective climate mitigation strategies. The key driver to accurate weather forecasts in the medium range is strictly related to the underlying predictability of the Earth system (including the atmosphere and the ocean, among other physical processes). It has been established that overall atmospheric conditions are predictable for up to two weeks ahead, due to the highly nonlinear and chaotic nature of the Earth system. Yet, weather forecast performance tends to deteriorate rapidly for few days predictions, and they are highly sensitive on the location and initial conditions adopted. Tremendous effort is being made to increase the forecast performance to the theoretical 2-week predictability horizon. Many of these efforts are related to a crucial aspect of any weather forecasting system: data assimilation, or briefly DA. Data assimilation consists of combining different sources of information to have an accurate estimate of a system as it evolves in time. In weather prediction, this usually means combining observations of the Earth system (arising from probes, sensors, satellites, etc.) with the mathematical model used to describe the evolution of the weather, to obtain a reliable initial state of the atmosphere. DA systems are usually believed to be the discriminative factor between more and less accurate weather forecasting systems. This speaks alone on the importance of the DA component on the overall weather forecasting workflow. In addition to this, it has been suggested that DA may provide a pathway for improving physical process models at climate scales, by reducing model error. Indeed, climate predictions (e.g., yearly, decadal) are tied to model errors. Therefore, having an effective DA system has two direct benefits: (i) increases the predictability for medium-range weather forecasts, (ii) reduces the biases and model error in climate projections, thereby improving their accuracy. In this project, we aim to use artificial intelligence (AI) and deep learning in particular, to generate fast surrogate weather models (also referred to as emulators). Emulators are accurate approximations of the weather system that use a reduced number of degrees of freedom than the full high-dimensional model used to simulate the system of interest (in this case the weather system). Indeed, the full high-dimensional model usually contains millions if not billions of degrees of freedom. Using the high-dimensional model for DA has some practical limitations mainly related to the computational costs incurred, that in turns limits its accuracy and deployment.
