title: ​​DiffuseM2 - Prompt-based Extremely Controlled High-quality Generative Music Models ​
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: Music generation models have been around since the 1950s, when Hiller and Isaacson programmed the Illiac Suite string quartet on the Illiac computer. The last few years, tremendous progress has been made when it comes to generative models. The field of music AI is catching up with field such as computer vision and natural language processing. Due to advances in diffusion models, direct audio generation (instead of MIDI) generation is possible since this year. This, combined with the attractiveness of text-prompt AI interfaces has led us to propose this grant on prompt-controlled music generation. We aim to develop the first large-scale dataset with music and text captions, thus facilitating progress for the field of text-to-music models. This will be achieved by leveraging recent advances in the field of music information retrieval as well as by training a music-to-prompt model. Secondly, we aim to build an efficient text-to-music model that is able to: 1) train efficiently, with a lean, effective architecture; 2) generate full-length songs, not just 10s fragments. Finally, we aim to add music-theory text controllability to the generative model, so that the user can `talk’ to the model using domain-knowledge terminology. All of the models and new dataset will be extensively evaluated through both objective metrics as well as expert listening studies. Both the investigators have extensive experience in generative models. The PI has worked on music generation models for over 10 years, and the co-PI is an expert on generative models and NLP. They have worked together on preliminary research to build the Mustango controllable text-to-music system. Mustango is able to generate 10s music fragments and outperform state-of-the-art models like MusicGen by Meta. This project is situated in the digital music industry, which is worth over 26 Billion USD per year, and has the potential to disrupt the industry, much like DALL-E and chatGPT are disrupting computer vision and NLP. The academic impact is significant, as the developed efficient and long-term controllable architectures may be useful for adjoining fields such as computer vision as well as time-series prediction and speech synthesis. In addition, the new dataset will empower other researchers to advance their music research.

title: Deciphering flower morphological divergence mediated by DOSE in orchids
abs: Orchids are members of the family Orchidaceae, one of the largest and most diverse families of angiosperms. They are widespread in most of the habitats with broad economic impact for their ornamental and medicinal values in the world. To cater for their special pollination and adaptive strategies required for different habitats, orchids display several unique reproductive features, among which a highly modified petal, called lip or labellum, is one of the key characteristics that distinguish orchids from other flowering plants. Lips are morphologically distinct from the other perianth organs (sepals and petals) and usually serve as the landing platform for attracting insect pollinators, thus playing an essential role in contributing to the unique flower morphology required for orchid reproduction. However, by now the mechanisms of morphological divergence between lips and sepals/petals remain largely elusive. To elucidate the molecular basis of this morphological divergence in orchids, we have performed RNA-seq and single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) analyses of floral organs in Dendrobium Chao Praya Smile, a tractable orchid system for molecular genetic studies. These analyses have revealed that a Dendrobium orchid SERRATE-like gene (DOSE) is considerably upregulated in lips versus sepals/petals and is mainly expressed in the cell cluster contributing to lip morphogenesis. DOSE encodes a zinc-finger protein containing three intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) homologous to Arabidopsis SERRATE (SE) that affects RNA metabolism involved in multiple developmental processes. Through our preliminary studies, we hypothesize that DOSE could mediate metabolism of specific RNAs in lips that determine lip-specific morphogenesis in orchids. This research proposal aims to investigate the molecular function of DOSE and its regulatory network involved in shaping lip morphology in orchids. These objectives will be achieved through testing our hypothesis using a combined molecular, genetic, genomic, biochemical, and bioimaging approaches as later described in this proposal. Successful completion of this project will provide new sights into the molecular mechanisms of floral morphogenesis and the regulatory roles of RNA metabolism in developmental processes. In addition, new mechanisms and regulators to be revealed in this study will enable the development of novel strategies for classical breeding and targeted genome-editing of desirable floral traits for economically important crops.

title: Understanding Mechanisms of Lipoprotein-Derived Cholesterol Distribution: Implications for Brain Health and Animal Physiology
abs: Proper brain function requires a precise combination of lipids within neuronal plasma membranes (PMs). This is because PM lipids play essential roles in synaptic communication and neuronal survival. One of the major lipids in the PM is cholesterol, which represents half of the total PM lipids and plays vital roles in neuronal development and in regulating neuronal morphology and function in the adult. Additionally, cholesterol serves as a major building block for steroid hormones, contributing to the maintenance of physiological homeostasis. Abnormal distribution of cellular cholesterol has been linked to numerous neurodegenerative disorders, including Alzheimer’s disease (one of the major causes of dementia in aging societies, including Singapore). Despite decades of effort, there is still no effective cure for neurodegenerative disorders. Therefore, understanding the fundamental processes underlying the transport of cellular cholesterol may reveal new therapeutic targets for combatting neurodegeneration. Many cell types, including adult neurons, take up cholesterol from lipoproteins, such as low-density lipoproteins (LDLs). However, exactly how cells transport lipoprotein-derived cholesterol to various cellular membranes remains poorly understood. Our overarching hypothesis is that evolutionarily conserved lipid transfer proteins (LTPs) mediate transport of lipoprotein-derived cholesterol to maintain the distribution of cellular cholesterol. To test this hypothesis, we developed a novel cholesterol biosensor based on the GRAM domain of an evolutionarily conserved GRAMD1 LTP (which we named GRAM-W). Lipoproteins are imported into neurons via dedicated receptors, including the LDL receptors, and trafficked to the lysosome before being delivered to other cellular organelles and membranes, including the PM. Using GRAM-W, we successfully tracked the movement of LDL-derived cholesterol from the lysosome to the PM. We will use GRAM-W, in combination with high resolution microscopy, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome-editing, iPSC-derived neurons, and C. elegans genetics, to dissect the molecular machineries responsible for distributing lipoprotein-derived cholesterol to promote neuronal health and physiological homeostasis. Specifically, we will 1) elucidate the role of LTPs in neuronal cholesterol distribution and test whether neurons carrying mutations linked to Alzheimer’s disease show altered cholesterol distribution, 2) build on our novel GRAM-W-based ultrasensitive cholesterol detection system to perform a genome-wide screen to identify the molecular machineries responsible for the delivery of LDL-derived lysosomal cholesterol to the PM, and 3) elucidate the importance of LTP-mediated cholesterol transport for steroid hormone biogenesis and animal physiology using C. elegans as our model system. title: Trigonelline as a novel NAD+ precursor therapeutic for liver aging and NAFLD
abs: Improvements in healthcare and living standards have increased life expectancy in Singapore, but its rapidly aging population faces a surge in age-related metabolic diseases, notably non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), prevalent at over 35%. Currently, there are no approved therapies for NAFLD, apart from dietary and lifestyle habits recommendations; hence there is a clear and immediate need for novel therapeutic approaches. At the cellular level, NAFLD and liver aging share features of metabolic dysfunction, explaining how aging can be a predisposing factor to develop liver disease. In particular, a critical enzymatic cofactor for the majority of metabolic processes, nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+), decreases in liver and other tissues during aging. Importantly, NAD+ decline also plays a critical role in the development NAFLD, with the liver becoming more prone to accumulate fat and inflammation and therefore steatohepatitis. Based on this, strategies to maintain or increase tissue levels of NAD+ with vitamins like NAD+ precursors have become a promising complementary approach to reduce or prevent liver disease. However, issues with bioavailability, sourcing and rapid metabolic degradation of these compounds have limited their clinical application thus far . I recently discovered that a natural molecule present in plants and the human body, trigonelline, is a novel NAD+ precursor linked to muscle aging and sarcopenia in Singaporean elderlies, and that its supplementation may be beneficial via increasing NAD+ (Membrez et al., 2024, accepted in Nature Metabolism). My findings also show that trigonelline increases NAD+ in liver, making it a putative therapeutic approach, yet no studies on its impact as NAD+ precursor on liver aging and disease exist. The overall goal of this proposal is to characterize and validate the therapeutic potential of the NAD+ precursor trigonelline for NAFLD and declined liver function during aging. The specific aims of this project are: 1) Characterize the impact of trigonelline on human liver cells and in aging in C. elegans 2) Evaluate trigonelline as NAD+ precursor for the prevention and treatment of steatohepatitis In Aim 1 I will uncover the conversion route of trigonelline into NAD+ in vitro in liver hepatocytes, and in vivo during aging in the nematode model C. elegans. Genetic or pharmacological approaches and metabolomics analyses will be implemented to functionally map the conserved mechanisms controlling the effects of trigonelline on the NAD+ and lipid metabolome, mitochondrial function in these models, and in vivo on aging phenotypes. title: Investigating the role of angiopoietin-like 4 protein in neutrophil heterogeneity on wound healing.
abs: Poorly and non-healing wounds are a silent epidemic, affecting a significant portion of the global population, especially those with co-morbid conditions such as diabetes. The biomedical and socioeconomic implications of these wounds are anticipated to escalate, emphasizing the need to understand the biological mechanisms underlying wound complications. Traditionally, neutrophils were viewed as a homogeneous population of terminally differentiated cells. However, recent studies have challenged this perspective, revealing significant heterogeneity within neutrophils. These distinct subpopulations exhibit diverse functions and behaviors, revolutionizing our understanding of neutrophils' roles within immune responses, particularly in wound healing. Guided by two unresolved questions concerning the factors shaping neutrophil heterogeneity and the specific tissue-restorative functions of these subpopulations, our research aims to develop innovative therapies that selectively target pathogenic neutrophil subsets without compromising the body's immune defense. A critical piece of this puzzle is the angiopoietin-like 4 protein (Angptl4). Observations in Angptl4-deficient mice, which exhibit delayed wound healing patterns, mirror those in human diabetic wounds. High-resolution single-cell sequencing analysis has identified six distinct neutrophil subpopulations at wound sites, and Angptl4 deficiency may steer the wound milieu towards a highly proinflammatory phenotype, marked by increased infiltration of the pro-inflammatory G6a neutrophil subpopulation.To address these unresolved questions, we propose two structured aims. The first aim will investigate the influence of Angptl4 on the molecular and functional distinctions of specific neutrophil subpopulations, focusing on the G5a and G6a neutrophil subpopulations. These will be isolated from wound biopsies and casein-induced neutrophilia of both Angptl4+/+ and Angptl4-/- mice. Bulk RNA sequencing, functional assays and dual immunofluorescence staining will be conducted to understand these subpopulations in depth. Functional assays including NETosis, ROS measurement, apoptosis, and chemotaxis assays. In vivo investigation will be conducted by topically adding isolated G5a or G6a neutrophils, altering the G5a-to-G6a ratio, in wounds. The second aim will elucidate the mechanism by which Angptl4 guides the transition of G5a to G6a neutrophil subpopulations. This will involve studying the roles of X-box binding protein 1 (Xbp1) and ISG15 Ubiquitin Like Modifier (Isg15) in G5a-to-G6a transition through transplantation of bone marrow stem cells carrying shRNA of the target gene. Post-recovery, neutrophils will be isolated for in vitro reconstituted wound microenvironment study. The regulation of the Xbp1 and Isg15 genes by Angptl4 will be explored by identifying potential regulatory sites using the ENCODE database. These sites will be experimentally validated with a DNAse I hypersensitive (DHS) assay. Further in

title: Sustainable Cathode Recycling from Spent Lithium-Ion Batteries through Electrolyte and Interfacial Control
abs: Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) technology has come a long way from its inception to widespread deployment in a multitude of applications, ranging from micro electronic devices to grid energy storage or electric vehicles. With decades of research and development, the LIB industry remains bogged down by high cost of raw materials, environmental damage and safety concerns. Recently, the increasing production of spent LIBs has attracted attentions on battery recycling research and industry. Despite all the previous efforts, high energy consumption, low recycling efficiency, complex and non-selectivity process still are the key challenging issues in the LIB recycling industry. To tackle these challenges, we propose a novel and sustainable method for extraction of all valuable metals from the cathode materials of spent LIBs. Solid-state electrolyte materials are used as a lithium-ion selective membrane in this innovative approach. We aim to investigate the synergistic combination of electrolyte control and interfacial design to achieve molecular selectivity for the precious metals in the cathodes of LIBs (i.e., lithium, cobalt, and nickel) during potential-dependent electrodeposition. Initially, our team will develop a sustainable roll-to-roll recovery process capable of selectively recovering lithium from spent batteries containing LFP, LiCoO2 (LCO), and LiNi0.8Co0.1Mn0.1O2 (NCM811) electrodes without compromising their integrity. Following this step, the research focus will be extended into the utilization of concentrated chloride facilitates speciation control by inducing the selective formation of anionic cobalt chloride complexes (CoCl42-), while concurrently preserving nickel in its cationic form ([Ni(H2O)5Cl]+). This step will be critical for the multicomponent metal recovery from commercially sourced NCM electrodes. The electrochemically driven technique developed in this research proposal holds promise for overcoming the limitations associated with current recycling methods and offers a pathway towards a more efficient and environmentally friendly cathode recycling process for LIBs.
kw: Sustainable Battery Recycling; Cathode Precious Metal Extraction; Spent Lithium-Ion Batteries Recycling

title: Evaluating Demand and Feasibility for Mobility-as-a-Service (MaaS) at an Urban Scale
abs: This project develops a framework at the intersection of econometrics, deep learning, and simulation for ex-ante evaluation of the new mobility paradigm, namely the Mobility-as-a-Service (MaaS). MaaS integrates multiple travel modes on a digital platform by allowing travellers to subscribe to mobility bundles, facilitating seamless door-to-door mobility without a private car. For example, a mobility bundle could include unlimited use of shared bikes for a fixed monthly cost, with a threshold on ride-hailing usage. The city-level analysis of MaaS requires answering the questions on mobility bundle preference and consumption: (i) How would a traveller create a mobility bundle based on her current travel pattern? (ii) How will she consume the subscribed mobility bundle in the post-MaaS scenario? (iii) Which travel modes will benefit from MaaS (i.e., what is the effect of MaaS on congestion and emissions at an urban scale)? While the preference for mobility bundles is challenging to model due to too many discrete-continuous choice dimensions (i.e., which travel modes and how much of each mode), post-MaaS bundle consumption is equally challenging due to the temporal correlation in travel mode choices. To handle these challenges, theory-based constraints will be integrated into deep learning-based models to develop a new generation of data-driven interpretable choice models with high predictability. For model training, choice experiments will be conducted in Singapore using an in-house designed interactive platform. Finally, these individual-level models will be fused into the city-level agent-based simulation model to analyze MaaS demand at an urban scale. In summary, the proposal develops an innovative survey platform and a novel deep learning-based behavioural model to elicit complex and high-dimensional mobility behaviour, followed by integrating them into system-level simulation models to evaluate the feasibility of MaaS at an urban scale. The proposed approaches for SP experiment design, data-driven personalized choice models, and system-level impact analysis would be crucial in configuring the pricing of MaaS bundles, nudging travellers to adopt it, and analysing the effect of MaaS on transport emissions, accessibility, and social equity. It is the first formal and generalizable framework for the ex-ante evaluation of the individual-level and system-level demand and feasibility of MaaS at a city level, which is critical before the pilot or city-wide implementation to avoid potential failures.

title: AI-Human Creative Collaborations: Challenges and Opportunities
abs: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into creative tasks has become increasingly popular, with the potential to increase productivity and creativity. However, limited research has been conducted to examine the underlying mechanisms of Human-AI creative collaboration in each stage of creativity, from idea generation to idea selection to idea evaluation. This research proposal aims to investigate the role of Human-AI creative collaboration in the three stages of creativity using Amabile's three componential theory of creativity (Amabile, 1983) which proposes that creativity is a result of a combination of domain-relevant skills, creativity-relevant skills, and task motivation. Subsequently, we will examine whether Human-AI collaboration helps to improve efficiency (shorter time), productivity (more ideas), and variety (more categories) in creative thinking. Additionally, given the challenges that women and individuals from tight cultures face during creative work, we explore the enhancing or limiting effects that gender and cultural tightness can have on Human-AI creative collaboration. Lastly, as AI models tend to be trained on data from a specific culture, we will examine the AI tool’s cultural characteristics and effect of cultural fit between Human innovator’s culture and AI tool’s culture. The specific aims of this research are to: 1. Investigate the role of Human-AI collaboration in the three stages of creativity – idea generation, idea selection, and idea evaluation. 2. Examine the role of domain-relevant skills, creativity-relevant skills, and task motivation underlying Human-AI collaboration in each stage of creativity. 3. Explore the potential for Human-AI collaboration to enhance efficiency, productivity, and idea variety. 4. Uncover the effects of gender and culture in Human-AI collaboration. The key hypotheses include: 1. Collaboration between AI and Human will yield more creative outcomes compared to AI and Human working alone. 2. The enhanced effects of Human-AI collaboration on creative outcomes is partially explained by relevant domain knowledge, creativity relevant skills, or task motivation. 3. Collaboration between AI and Human will take less time, generate more ideas, and produce more varieties of ideas. 4. There is a positive correlation between AI and Human evaluators’ assessments on idea novelty and idea usefulness. title: Quantifying nitrogen deposition flux and its effects on nitrogen cycle in terrestrial ecosystems over Southeast Asia: Isotope perspectives for regional ecosystem management
abs: Since the mid-19th century, human activities, such as industrialization and fertilizer use, have significantly increased anthropogenic reactive nitrogen (N) emissions. The potential implementation of renewable ammonia, known as "green ammonia", to replace fossil fuels for achieving carbon neutrality is expected to further elevate N emissions. This surge in N emissions has led to elevated levels of N deposition in ecosystems, altering their functioning and potentially exacerbating ecosystem-level phosphorus (P) limitation and affecting the soil carbon cycle. These changes can result in terrestrial species losses at local, regional, and global levels. While N deposition is well-documented in developed regions, tropical regions like Southeast (SE) Asia have received relatively less attention, leaving gaps in our understanding of N deposition in this area. In this proposed research, we will address this knowledge gap and understand the N deposition and its effect on ecosystems in SE Asian region, including Singapore. Our research presents a comprehensive investigation into the intricate relationship between anthropogenic nitrogen (N) deposition and terrestrial ecosystems, with two primary interlinked objectives. Objective 1: Investigating Atmospheric N Deposition and Emission Sources in SE Asia The first objective entails a comprehensive exploration of atmospheric N deposition dynamics and identification of its emission sources within SE Asia. This involves monitoring and analyzing nitrogen and oxygen isotopes of nitrate in precipitation samples collected across the region. Bayesian isotope-mixing models will be used to estimate the proportional contributions of different nitrogen emission sources. By characterizing the isotopic ratios of key N species, we aim to pinpoint the sources of anthropogenic N emissions. Furthermore, in combination of mathematical models, machine learning techniques and ecosystem service analysis, we will examine spatial and temporal patterns of N deposition in the region, including Singapore. With this knowledge, we can predict the future trend of N deposition in this region. Objective 2: Understanding the Impact of N Deposition on N Cycle and Transformations in Terrestrial Ecosystems The second objective delves into understanding how atmospheric N deposition influences N cycling and transformations within terrestrial ecosystems. This involves conducting a series of field experiments and analyses to assess changes in N transformation fluxes, nutrient availability, and ecosystem responses to varying levels of N deposition. What sets this research apart is the innovative integration of stable isotope models and computational tools to quantify the fractions of N transformation processes in the soils of terrestrial ecosystems and predict future trends, providing invaluable insights into the mechanisms driving ecological shifts. title: Capitalizing (Possibly biased) Offline Data for Sequential Learning: Theoretical Foundation and Algorithm Design
abs: The proposal primarily concerns online stochastic optimization, where a decision-maker (DM) sequentially chooses actions to take over discrete time steps. The process involves maximizing an unknown reward function under model uncertainty. The model finds applications in various domains, from Operations Research to Machine Learning. Our research seeks to unravel the profound implications of integrating offline data—data collected prior to the online optimization process—into an online stochastic optimization model. Crucially, we delve into scenarios where the probability distribution of the offline data needs not faithfully align with that for online data, introducing a fascinating dimension of complexity to our exploration. We aim to shed light on two primary research questions: (Q-well-specified): In the well-specified setting where offline and online data follow the same probability distribution, we aim to identify the optimal regret bound with respect to the number of time steps and the size of the offline dataset. Our aim is to provide a quantitative understanding with data augmentation, considering both full and partial feedback scenarios. (Q-mis-specified): Our primary focus lies in the more intricate mis-specified scenario, where the offline data distribution can deviate from the online data distribution. Within this context, we confront two pivotal challenges. First, we aim to define novel metrics that can effectively quantify the "distance" between these diverging distributions, where the distance shall depend crucially on the optimization objective. Second, we aim to design a near-optimal online algorithm, under the challenge that the offline data does not need to align with the online data. Our mission is to illuminate the intricate trade-offs that decision-makers face when determining whether and how to leverage offline data, and to unravel how these decisions affect the objective value achieved by the DM. Our research is rooted in the belief that deciphering the intricate relationship between offline and online data holds the key to more effective decision-making strategies. By embarking on this journey, we aim not only to advance theoretical understanding, but also to unfurl practical implications that resonate across industries and applications reliant on online optimization algorithms. The potential dividends from this exploration are manifold, encompassing improved operational efficiency, cost savings, and bolstered decision-making capabilities in the face of relentless uncertainty. We show that the DM requires auxiliary knowledge additional to the offline data, in order to outperform the state-of-the-art online sequential algorithms that learn from scratch. title: Empowering Real-World 3D Scene Understanding: Navigating Noise, Distribution Shifts, and Incremental Learning
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: This research endeavors to advance the field by developing robust, generalizable, and resilient 3D scene understanding models for machine perception systems operating in real-world settings. The objective is to transcend the limitations of controlled environments, addressing challenges of noisy data, shifted testing distributions, and incremental learning. The research is organized into three work packages. In the first package, "learning with noisy labels," we hypothesize that noisy labels can arise from model prediction errors in semi-supervised learning or human annotation errors in fully-supervised learning. To combat this, we focus on robust model design through techniques like adaptive sample selection and reliability-guided consistency regularization. These methods aim to handle noisy pseudo labels and noisy human-annotated labels in semi-supervised 3D instance segmentation and 3D object detection, respectively. In the second package, "out-of-distribution generalization", our hypothesis considers the availability or unavailability of unlabeled testing data with distribution shifts during training, leading to unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) or domain generalization (DG). Our goal is to design models capable of generalizing to distribution-shifted testing environments under either setting in both UDA and DG settings, in the context of 3D object detection and 3D semantic segmentation. Techniques like hierarchical domain alignment and clustering instance mix augmentation will be explored. The third package, "continual learning without forgetting" hypothesizes that incremental learning stages are relatively long and that examples for new classes during incremental learning can be either sufficient or limited, resulting in standard sequential incremental learning or few-shot incremental learning. We aim to develop resilient models for continual learning of new classes without forgetting old ones, utilizing a reinforcement learning-based exemplar selection framework and a unified solution for few-shot incremental 3D object detection. The feasibility of this research is supported by the PI's expertise in 3D scene understanding, the team's prior accomplishments in addressing related challenges, and the methodical approach delineated in the proposed work packages.

title: Challenging a 40-Year-Old Assumption: Can Reduced-Scale Experiments Reproduce the Physics of Flows Across Buildings at Full Scale?
abs: Ironically, despite having the keyword “flows”, the research field of flows across built environments has been ignoring the physics of flows and the fundamentals in fluid mechanics. The main reason for this ignorance is that many researchers in built environments are practitioners who do not have a relevant background and training in fluid mechanics. Consequently, results derived from reduced-scale experiments are directly applied to full-scale applications without considering the consequences of scale mismatch. For example, wind tunnel experiment results from reduced-scale building models (length scale of centimeters) have been directly applied to design full-scale, real buildings (length scale of meters). This mismatch in length scale is circumvented by the Reynolds-number-independence assumption, which states that the mismatch can be disregarded provided that the Reynolds number (Re) exceeds 10^4. Re governs the scale of a flow: reduced-scale experiments of flows across buildings have Re ~10^3 to 10^4, while full-scale flows have Re ~10^6 to 10^7. The Re-independence assumption allows experimental results at Re ~10^4 to be generalized to full-scale applications at Re ~10^6 without any validation. Such a generalization is unacceptable in fluid mechanics but has become the norm in the applications of flows across buildings since the 1980s. Ignoring the scale mismatch can result in serious consequences, ranging from wrong model development to the misconception that observations in wind tunnels will also be observed in full-scale built environments, leading to ineffective building design and urban planning. Our preliminary works show that the flow fields are indeed different at Re beyond 10^4, indirectly invalidating the Re-independence assumption. This proposal aims to conduct a systematic set of controlled experiments to derive direct evidence to challenge and rectify the Re-independence assumption, providing new insight into full-scale urban airflow and establishing a database for benchmarking and model validation with full-scale Re for flows across buildings. This project adopts a novel approach by conducting experiments of flows across buildings in the TCOMS Ocean Basin, Singapore’s largest fluid experimental facility. It attempts the first-ever modeling of flows across street canyons (i.e., spaces between buildings) up to the full-scale Re of 10^6 to challenge the Re-independence assumption. Both 2D and 3D street canyons will be modeled to study the impact of Re on the flow fields. The building models will be fabricated with acrylic sheets. The spacing between the building models will be varied to study the effects of Re on flows across street canyons at a height-to-width aspect ratio between 2 and 5. title: Study of Metamaterials for Microwave Metadevices Using Prior Knowledge-guided Deep Learning-enabled Methods
abs: 1. Academic significance: Recently, the advent of 5G marked a monumental leap forward, introducing unprecedentedly high capacity, ultra-low latency, and massive device connectivity. The progress of wireless communication technologies heavily depends on the development of electromagnetic (EM) hardware devices, such as antennas and frequency selective surfaces (FSSs). In general, the advanced properties of materials and design methods are important drivers for further advancements in EM hardware device designs. Besides natural materials, metamaterials (MTMs) are artificial structures designed to have unique EM properties that are not found in nature. Their properties, such as permittivity, permeability, and refractive index, can be precisely tailored by manipulating their geometric structures. Over the past two decades, MTMs have ignited a revolution in microwave device design, enhancing performance and enabling novel functionalities, further promoting the development of advanced communication systems. 2. Research questions: The current state of MTM designs, based on the transformation or combination of basic geometry patterns, limits the potential for further performance improvements. Increasing the degrees of freedom (DoF) of MTM design is a way to explore new and powerful MTMs, but the elaborate designs also increase the complexity of the design process and the time required for design. Meanwhile, the extensive range of possibilities in generating unit cells of MTM often leads to the creation of excessively large datasets, rendering them both inefficient and ineffective. 3. Methodology: In a bid to push the limits of achievable performance and functionalities with EM devices, the advanced characteristics of MTMs are generated through deep learning (DL) techniques, leveraging datasets with notably increased DoF. However, the augmentation in DoF results in datasets that are expansive yet inefficient and lacking in effectiveness, as previously noted. To address the challenges of inefficiency and ineffective of excessively large datasets with increased DoF, the integration of prior knowledge (PK), including both the principles of EM theorems and the expertise gained from previous experience in metadevice design, is proposed to be incorporated into all key stages of DL-based methods to address these challenges. title: Investigating the spatiotemporal control of the master stomatal gene SPEECHLESS
abs: Background In multicellular organisms, developmental master regulators drive the specification of cell types. Addressing how the precise expression of these master regulators is controlled is therefore fundamental to developmental biology. Due to their accessibility and the robust genetics of the model plant Arabidopsis, my research group employs the development of stomata—essential surface pores of plants—as our system to study cell specification and developmental plasticity. Stomata are derived form a specialized epidermal cell lineage called the stomatal lineage. The lineage begins with a self-renewing stem cell-like stage, and the master regulators SPEECHLESS (SPCH) is required for the initiation and proliferation of the stomatal stem cells. The expression of SPCH is tightly controlled and is restricted only to the early stomatal precursors in the aerial tissues. However, how the spatiotemporal expression of SPCH is regulated and how its tissue specific-expression is maintained remain unexplored. Objective, hypothesis and preliminary studies The main objective of this proposal is to investigate the mechanism underlying the precise regulation of the gene expression pattern of the master stomatal regulator SPEECHLESS (SPCH). Specifically, we will test the roles of the DNA-binding VIVIPAROUS1/ABI3-LIKE (VAL) family of transcriptional repressors in regulating this process. Based on our strong preliminary results, we hypothesize that VALs, in particular VAL1, directly bind to the promoter of SPCH and suppress it, restricting SPCH expression within the defined spatiotemporal domain of the stomatal lineage. Through genetic analyses, we have found that VAL1 plays a role in inhibiting stomatal formation in both seedling leaves and stems. Our confocal analyses indicated that VAL1 is broadly expressed in the epidermis including the stomatal lineage, and by specifically driving VAL1 expression in the stomatal precursors in a val1 mutant, we showed that VAL1 can function within these cells to suppress stomatal formation. Further, through both yeast one-hybrid and in vitro DNA-protein pulldown assay, we found that VALs can bind to the promoter of SPCH through its RY motif. Using a transcriptional fluorescent reporter, we observed a substantial enhancement in activity of the RY motif-mutated SPCH promoter. Interestingly, we also detected the expression of this mutated promoter in the root tip, which is normally absent in the WT promoter. These preliminary results indicate that VALs have critical roles in restricting the expression of SPCH and stomatal development. title: Applications of a new integral representation for quantum information measures
abs: A fundamental question at the core of both classical and quantum information theory and cryptography is how to quantify important notions like uncertainty (or randomness), information, correlation, and entanglement. In information theory the study of such measures has been successfully initiated by Shannon who introduced entropy and related measures for this purpose. Studying mathematical properties of such information measures is of conceptual but also practical interest since they appear prominently in security proofs for cryptographic systems. While the properties of classical information measures are well understood, many questions remain when it comes to their quantum generalisations. Recently we have found a new way of expressing quantum entropy and related information measures in terms of liner combinations of simpler quantities that are well understood. This new perspective allows us to lift many of their properties from the classical to the quantum domain in a more straight-forward manner than previous proofs. This project, building in our previous insights, aims to further develop our understanding of quantum information measures in several directions: a) We believe that our definition, currently only valid for finite-dimensional quantum systems, also naturally extends to more general quantum and even post-quantum general probabilistic theories that currently lack well-defined information measures. We want to study the structure of these theories and answer some open questions with the help of these new measures. b) As an exemplary application, we want to use the new techniques we introduced to derive stronger continuity bounds, i.e., bounds that ensure that entropy does not vary too much when we have uncertainty about the underlying quantum state. The goal is to resolve some prominent conjectures in this area. c) Finally, we want to explore the relationship between hypothesis testing and the new information measures that is suggest by our work and hope that it will lead to a better understand of hypothesis testing beyond finite-dimensional quantum mechanics.
kw: information theory, quantum information, entropy

title: Development of scalable pyrolysis-chemical vapor deposition technology for conversion of contaminated and rejected plastics into carbon nanotubes and hydrogen
abs: A significant fraction of plastic waste has substandard quality for mechanical and chemical recycling even after sorting and cleaning. This project leverages the use of pyrolysis-chemical vapor deposition (CVD) technology for converting these plastic waste streams (specifically, contaminated and rejected plastics) into multi-walled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs) and hydrogen. Pyrolysis-CVD technology have shown its flexibility towards the processing of mixed contaminated plastics in laboratory studies. The technology has the potential to reduce direct carbon emissions from plastic waste treatment by ~70% compared to incineration. MWCNTs from the process can find applications in existing and emerging markets, including polymer compounding, construction, coatings and energy storage. Hydrogen released as a by-product is a strategic energy source for decarbonization and an important input in petrochemical and fertilizer industries. Some challenges, limiting implementation of the technology, will be addressed during the project, increasing the technology readiness level from 4 to 6. This will bring the technology closer to industrial application capable of diverting up to 20,000 tonnes/year of plastics from incineration. The innovation of the project lies in development of an improved catalyst with lower cost and higher efficiency towards the processing of contaminated and rejected plastics, a scaled-up system prototype for plastic waste conversion with increased throughput, the investigation of potential safety risks arising from MWCNT incorporation into products and understanding the overall life cycle assessment of the process. The translation of research outcomes into commercial deployment will be facilitated through an intellectual property (IP) licensing model. The developed IPs will be made available for both non-exclusive and exclusive licensing opportunities, with a specific focus on engaging project industry partners and third-party entities interested in scaling up the technology. This innovative waste management approach anticipates a significant positive impact, contributing to sustainable practices and increasing waste recycling rates in Singapore and beyond.
kw: Carbon nanotubes; chemical vapor deposition; contaminated plastics; hydrogen; pyrolysis; rejected plastics

title: Identifying novel microglia-based targets for neurodegeneration using immuno-competent organoids
abs: Neural organoids, particularly spinal organoids, offer a unique platform for studying neurodevelopmental processes and neurodegenerative disorders like Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS). Spinal organoids, comprising various spinal cord cell types, exhibit self-organization capabilities, making them valuable models for investigating neurodegeneration. However, the absence of immune cells, particularly microglia, limits the study of neuro-immune interactions in ALS. To address this gap, we propose the derivation of "immuno-competent" spinal organoids by co-culturing induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived microglia with spinal organoids. Microglia, the resident immune cells in the spinal cord, are implicated in ALS pathogenesis alongside motor neurons (MNs). Dysfunctions in ALS microglia contribute to MN degeneration, yet the precise mechanisms remain elusive. Immuno-competent spinal organoids provide an opportunity to elucidate dynamic microglia-astrocyte-MN interactions in ALS. Notably, no relevant co-culture model comprising human microglia, MNs, and astrocytes exists. Our approach involves co-culturing ALS microglia with wild-type spinal organoids and vice versa to examine microglial activation and the non-cell autonomous effects of diseased microglia in ALS. The proposal's overarching goal is to understand how ALS microglia contribute to MN degeneration, aiming to halt disease progression by targeting microglial pathways. Four specific aims are proposed: 1. Development and characterization of chimeric immuno-competent spinal organoids using iPSCs with and without the TDP43G298S mutation. 2. Dynamic modeling of ALS phenotypes in immuno-competent organoids. 3. Exploration of pathways underlying microglia-mediated neuroprotection versus toxicity in ALS. 4. Investigation of the therapeutic potential of novel microglia targets through microglia-specific knockouts in TDP43M337V mice. This comprehensive approach promises to advance our understanding of ALS pathology and offers insights into potential therapeutic strategies targeting microglia-mediated mechanisms in ALS.
kw: spinal organoids; microglia; neurodegeneration; ALS

title: Effective emotion recognition from neurophysiological signals
abs: The primary objective of this project is to develop novel learning methodologies for multimodal emotion recognition, to enhance the reliability and robustness of existing emotion understanding systems. This effort involves the initial development of an innovative human emotion elicitation and annotation scheme, as well as the collection of a substantial volume of multimodal emotion data. Within this dataset, inherent annotation ambiguities are effectively mitigated through the application of innovative emotion elicitation and annotation techniques. Building upon these foundations, our goal is to attain accurate emotion perception by automatically capturing crucial cues from diverse modalities through advanced deep multimodal learning paradigms. Subsequently, we intend to derive a dependable multimodal recognition model that can be applied across various emotion-dependent systems. The project differs significantly from most existing multimodal learning studies that focus on emotion perception. We aim to mitigate the emotion annotation ambiguity issues inherent in conventional multimodal datasets and explore new frameworks for learning fine-grained multimodal representations for subtle emotion understanding. This will advance both existing emotion elicitation and annotation paradigms as well as a multimodal learning framework for intrinsic emotion understanding.
kw: Human emotion; Multimodal emotion recognition; Emotion elicitation and annotation; Deep learning; Knowledge distillation; Modality alignment

title: Serverless Programming Model and Cloud Resource Virtualization Co-Design for High Performance and Efficiency
abs: The serverless computing paradigm has taken the cloud by storm: more than 50-70% of companies operating in the cloud deploy their software in serverless platforms [Datadog’23]. In serverless, application developers can focus on writing business logic as a workflow of serverless functions while the cloud providers manage the underlying cloud infrastructure, allocating compute and memory resources to these functions. This labor separation allows to cut time to market for applications and unlock potential cloud-wide optimizations for high performance and energy efficiency. Unfortunately, existing serverless architecture fails to deliver the promise of high performance and efficiency because of the complexity of its deep and distributed stack, majorly inherited from the conventional cloud architecture. We showcase that the conventional serverless architecture inherits microservice-oriented cluster management and heavy-weight virtualization technologies for isolating the untrusted code of applications from each other and the cloud infrastructure. We identify that these limitations are due to the existing serverless systems design relying on container abstraction for application programming and deployment and cloud resource management. This proposal introduces a clean-slate serverless design by separating the system abstractions used for the programming model, load balancing and scaling, and cluster resource allocation. We then describe how this separation of concerns can boost the overall serverless system efficiency by passing the application-level information down to the cluster and virtualization infrastructure, opening opportunities for compile and run-time optimizations. We will devise the proposed system architecture by characterizing workload and system implications and prototyping system solutions in three thrusts. In the first thrust, we will explore the co-design of the serverless programming model and the cluster manager to inform placement and load balancing of the application workflow. In the second thrust, we will study the interactions between the application code and the underlying system to devise a novel approach to fine-grain compute, memory, and IO bandwidth resource virtualization across a cloud datacenter. Finally, in the third thrust, we will investigate the design of a distributed serverless control plane that can coordinate IO bandwidth allocation in conjunction with compute and memory at the cloud scale.
kw: Cloud computing; operating systems; serverless; cluster management; distributed applications

title: Polyandry & parasites: Investigating the role of female remating on population structure, gene expression and microbial transmission in mosquitoes.
abs: Polyandry refers to females mating with multiple males and it is widespread across insects. In disease vectors such as mosquitoes, increased female remating in the wild can influence the effective population size and genomic diversity of populations. Polyandry can also affect the evolution of parasites such as Wolbachia. In Singapore, Wolbachia is used as a reproductive manipulator that induces wild females that mate with artificially infected males to lay infertile eggs. However, females that re-mate with naturally non-infected males, may still be able to ‘rescue’ their fertility and produce viable offspring. This can undermine the long-term efficacy of vector control. In addition, higher polyandry increases the genetic diversity of populations, often improving their survival in the wild. The genetic diversity of mosquito populations can differ across landscapes like Singapore, where urban residential areas (frequent exposure to insecticides) are interspersed among forest fragments (no insecticide). Hence, polyandry across different habitats can influence overall ‘genetic’ movement across the island. Heterogeneous landscapes provide a mix of artificial and natural breeding habitats which can influence how far females must disperse to lay eggs. Finally, females that mate with multiple males may also be exposed to various reproductive parasites which can directly affect the evolution and transmission of microbes within mosquitos. Objectives: We will address the following research questions: (1) Do mosquito vectors such as Aedes aeygpti, Ae. albopictus, and Cx. quinquefasciatus differ in polyandry across Singapore? (2) How does polyandry influence genetic diversity as well as reproductive traits in females and males? (3) What reproductive parasites naturally infect mosquitoes in Singapore and how do they evolve across species? Methods: We take an integrative approach using extensive field surveys, molecular screening, laboratory-based mating experiments as well as Next generation ‘omics techniques to answer these questions. Intellectual merits and broader impacts: This project will be the first to investigate natural polyandry and genomic structure of multiple vector species across urban and forested landscapes. Studying reproductive trait variation in both natural populations and lab strains of mosquito vectors will have important practical repercussions for vector suppression. Specifically, the gene expression studies of male testes and accessory glands will shed light on the potential mechanisms of competitive mating between non-infected and Wolbachia-infected males. Finally, meta-barcoding wild-caught mosquitos will highlight naturally occurring reservoirs of microbial infections, which is relevant for long-term surveillance and parasite transmission among potential emergent vectors.
kw: Reproduction, Mosquitos, Wolbachia, Population genomics, Gene expression

title: Control of dual GGDEF/EAL enzymes, role in biofilm, chronic infection, and host interaction
abs: The c-di-GMP messenger is an ancestral signaling system that regulates bacterial behaviours and is of key importance for driving the switch between motile loner cells and biofilm formers. The correlation between high c-di-GMP concentration and biofilm formation and between low c-di-GMP levels and motility was demonstrated in many bacterial species. Levels of c-di-GMP are modified by the rate of its synthesis and degradation. The molecule is synthesized from two molecules of GTP by DGCs and is degraded into pGpG and/or GMP by PDEs. The catalytic domains of DGCs and PDEs have been characterized. The former carries a GGDEF motif, the latter carries either EAL or HD-GYP motifs.Among the DGCs/PDEs a class of enzymes, called dual enzymes, harbour both GGDEF and EAL domains. The molecular mechanisms associate with the activity of these enzymes remains to be fully elucidated, although in few cases it seems clear that binding of c-di-GMP at the GGDEF site triggers the PDE activity from the EAL site. In this proposal we focus on few dual enzymes (PA0285, RbdA, BifA) on which we collected preliminary data to conduct a structure-function analysis. We hypothesize that some of the GGDEF/EAL dual enzymes have a key role during P. aeruginosa infection, and that control and manipulation of their activity could help resolving chronic infections associated with this organism and provide a therapeutic strategy to destabilize biofilms and improve treatment outcomes. We and our Co-I/collaborators have: 1) shown that in our PAO1 strain, PA0285 is a key PDE involved in early-stage attachment; 2) shown that BifA activity is inhibited by interaction with the HecE protein and activated by the small synthetic molecule Disperazol; and 3) resolved the 3D structure of RbdA which could be used as a model dual GGDEF/EAL. In parallel, we engineered single clean deletion mutants for every of the 41 c-di-GMP-related enzymes (i.e. 17 GGDEF, 5 EAL, 16 GGDEF/EAL and 3 HD-GYP proteins.) and started combining all mutations in one single strain (deleted 20 genes as per today), which we call c-di-GMP zero strain (PAOcdg0).We expect that, upon completion of the project aims, the outcomes will include the characterization of key dual PDE enzymes which we use as archetype targets for identifying modulators that would allow manipulating the c-di-GMP network, preventing biofilm formation or inducing biofilm dispersal. Our ambition is to provide basic knowledge in a comprehensive and unambiguous format for future therapeutic applications. Our proposal is timely, because of the surge in antimicrobial resistance and bacterial biofilm resilience in P. aeruginosa chronic infections.
kw: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, biofilm, chronic bacterial infections, c-di-GMP signaling, drug screening, structure-function

title: An improved lipid nanoparticle technology for folded messenger RNA delivery and gene editing
abs: Current genome editing tools, such as CRISPR-Cas9, have been validated as robust and effective approaches in manipulating multiple diseases. However, drawbacks and potential risks of direct protein or plasmid DNA delivery hindered its wide application. The employment of mRNA and lipid nanoparticle (LNP) technology offers greater flexibility for CRISPR-Cas9 mediated genome editing to systemically deliver mRNA/gRNA to targeted tissues. Current challenges in mRNA therapeutics include: 1) CRSPR-Cas9 tool usually requires multiple fold higher mRNA doses than mRNA vaccines to reach the therapeutic threshold, 2) targeted delivery of mRNA therapeutics to other solid tissues aside from liver. In our preliminary studies, we developed a metal-directed folding RNA technology via rapid self-assembly as a generalizable strategy to deliver RNA of any length or origin. When packing the folded RNA with currently approved lipid nanoparticle components, the uptake of mRNA and protein expression was increased by nearly 10-fold over Moderna LNP formulas in vivo. title: Knowledge-informed privacy-preserving modelling and control of urban transportation systems
abs: The era of big data has brought an enormous potential for improving transportation safety, mobility, and sustainability but has raised severe privacy concerns. This project seeks to advance traffic control by developing theories and tools to address privacy concerns in transportation systems while maximising the benefits of big data. Specifically, we develop privacy-preserving traffic modelling and control strategies from the standpoint of Municipal Authorities (MAs) to facilitate data-sharing with individual Connected Vehicles (CVs) and Mobility Providers (MPs) such as ridesharing companies. We investigate two research questions: (1) how to fuse detector data owned by MA with trajectory data provided by MPs and individual CVs for traffic estimation while mitigating the risks of leaking MPs' sensitive operational parameters (e.g., algorithm specifics) and individual travellers' location privacy, and (2) how should traffic control problems be formulated to embrace privacy-preserving mechanisms to achieve a better trade-off between control performance and privacy. These research questions, although significant for maximising the benefits of big data, are rarely explored in transportation literature. We address the first question by developing privacy-preserving data fusion algorithms for traffic estimation while protecting MPs' sensitive operational parameters (e.g., algorithmic specifics) and travellers' location privacy. We devise three algorithms: (i) a statistical parameter privacy filter-based algorithm to enable MPs to share data without leaking sensitive operational parameters, (ii) a privacy-preserving data aggregation mechanism to aggregate and perturb CV information to key traffic variables while protecting individual travellers' location privacy, and (iii) a data-efficient Bayesian physics-informed vertical federated learning (FL)-based data fusion algorithm that enables the cooperation between MA and MPs without requiring any party to disclose its raw data. We address the second research question by investigating two aggregated formulations for traffic control problems that can better handle the noises brought by privacy-preserving mechanisms: (i) a link-based formulation with model reduction and (ii) a hierarchical formulation, whereby the upper-level leverages Data-enabled Predictive Control to optimise regional control variables, and the lower-level optimises signal timings of individual intersections. We theoretically analyse the trade-off between privacy and control performance. The outcome of this project will shed light on how the synergy between transportation and privacy research can help develop methodologies suitable for addressing privacy concerns in transportation systems, as well as provide insights into the fundamental question of how much and what type of data is necessary for transportation modelling and control.
kw: Traffic Control, Data Privacy, Traffic State Estimation, Big Data, Data Fusion

title: Enhancing Privacy Regulation Compliance among Web Applications
abs: In this project, we propose to build a framework for enhancing the privacy compliance of web applications. This is motivated by the currently increased emphasis on user privacy within the software supply chain where the enforced privacy regulations still suffer from insufficiency rooted in factors such as the lack of privacy expertise among application users and developers, the lack of executable and actionable steps, and the complexity associated software development lifecycle. Considering the heterogeneous nature of goals for analyzing and enhancing the privacy regulation compliance, the framework at the very least consists of three work packages The first work package analyses the privacy policy compliance of the applications, by correlating the consistency between the privacy policies from application vendors and the actual runtime behavior of the applications. The second analyses the compliance of data processing principles, by extracting the specific requirements and checking with the actual runtime behavior. The third work package introduces implements a compliance-oriented development assistance system that investigates the correspondence between application-specific functions and privacy policies to automatically generate compliant privacy policies. The expected outcome from this project should further enhance and advance Singapore’s position in leading and nurturing the privacy-aware and privacy-respecting analysis and detection infrastructure, which aligns the city state’s goal of becoming a smart city.
kw: Privacy compliance, web applications, privacy regulation, privacy policy, data processing principles

title: Visualizing and Debugging Training Dynamics of Deep Learning Models via Time-Travelling Visualization: Perspectives of Foundation, Techniques, and Tool Design
abs: Deep Learning based classifiers (or, deep classifiers) are learnable functions mapping a sample to a predefined class. Typical deep classifiers consist of two components: - Representation Learning: A sample (e.g., an image, a sentence, or a piece of voice) is transformed into a representation vector in a high-dimensional space. The transformation can be implemented as convolutional layers, LSTM layers, or transformers. - Representation Predication: The learned representation is further fed into layers for fitting its label as prediction, which can typically be implemented as fully connected layers. A well-learned deep classifier can learn the classification landscape consisting of (1) representations of the samples well distributed in the space and (2) classification boundaries to well distinguish them. When a deep classifier does not meet the expectation, the model developers need to address questions such as “why the representation and the classification landscape are unexpectedly formed?”. However, debugging and understanding how a neural network model is trained has far larger observability challenge. On one hand, the model training process can update tens of thousands of parameters in a single learning step. Observing how those parameters are updated in detail is prohibitively expensive and exhaustive. On the other hand, the representation and classification boundaries are in the form of numeric vectors and formulas, which is hard to observe and understand. In contrast, the conceptual representation and classification boundaries are in the mind of programmers and data scientists, which is intuitive, but hard to describe and specify. The gap between what the mode developers can observe and what they can expect is largely unaddressed by any tools. Thus, we propose to achieve the following research goals: (1) Training Dynamics Observability: We propose to develop time-travelling visualization foundations to transform the model training process into an animation of visualized canvas, to understand how a prediction is gradually formed. We will develop the mathematical properties to project the high-dimensional representations to a visualized canvas with optimal visualization accuracy. (2) Visualization Technique: We will explore the most reliable record-and-replay solutions to (i) preserve the training process by recording the model, (ii) implement the visualization on each of the recorded model checkpoints, and (iii) provide tool support for practitioners to generate and observe the visualization. (3) Interactive Recommendation: Based on the visualization facilities, we will develop recommendation technique to infer user interested events during the training to explain their observation. We will also propose to develop a recommendation system to guide the users to find the training events of interest. title: Engineering Interfacial Microenvironments via Polymers for Robust CO2-to-Fuels Conversion
abs: Upgrading CO2 into valuable fuels and chemicals through electrocatalysis powered by renewable electricity have been recognized as a promising approach aiding to the sustainability transition. To date, significant successes have been achieved for electrocatalytic CO2 reduction, particularly the materials discovery for selective and active catalyst, and the fundamental understandings on the related surface reactions: e.g., the mechanism of C―C bond formation to afford the desired products. However, the practical implementation of this technology is hindered by its unsatisfactory stability (typically < 100 hour under practical relevant operating conditions). Unlike prior approaches that primarily emphasize catalyst development to attain high selectivity towards desired products, our primary focus of this research is on addressing the stability challenge. In response to this challenge, our project revolves around engineering reaction microenvironments through tailored polymer chemistry. We aim to create a protective matrix at the electrode/electrolyte interface, shielding the catalyst and the reaction layer from various of deactivation/corrosive factors during CO2 conversion. This innovative approach holds the potential to significantly extend the lifespan of the electrocatalytic reactor, rendering them suitable for large-scale industrial applications. We will tackle this research challenge at three different scales: the electrode/electrolyte interface, the cathodic catalyst layer, and the membrane-electrode-assembly (MEA). Our primary focus will be on the development and engineering of the robust electrode/electrolyte interface, where the CO2 reduction reaction occurs. The stability of the catalytic process at the electrode/electrolyte interface is often compromised by factors like electrolyte flooding, high local pH, impurities deposition, catalyst substrates decomposition, etc. At the electrode/electrolyte interface, we aim to employ thin protection layers using polymer materials with specific properties, such as robust chemical/physical stabilities, suitable pore sizes, hydrophobicity, and CO2/H2O uptake capabilities. These polymers will envelop the catalyst, shielding it from the above instability factors while maintaining its desired activity and selectivity. Notably, we have obtained promising preliminary results to demonstrate the feasibility of this approach. Building upon these data, our next step is to establish a comprehensive Multiphysics model to study the interfacial kinetics, selectivity, and mass transportations with the polymer coating. These explorations will ensure the high activity and selectivity of CO2 reduction while employing the polymer coatings for enhanced system stability. Currently, gas diffusion electrodes (GDE) used in CO2 reduction are mostly adapted from fuel cells without significant modifications. title: Novel Carbon-Negative Functional Manufactured Aggregates for Sustainable and Resilient Infrastructure
abs: Concrete contributes significantly to carbon emissions, mainly from the Portland cement consumption during construction and operational carbon from rehabilitation during its service life. Constant efforts have been made to reduce the embodied carbon in concrete through low-carbon cementitious materials. The existing approaches have mainly focused on reducing embodied carbon, with their efficiency plateaued in recent years. The current strategies do not address the carbon already released into the atmosphere. Thus, a holistic approach based on carbon sequestration and utilization is proposed to achieve carbon neutrality in construction. The main objective of this project is the development of carbon-negative functional manufactured aggregates and enhance the carbon sequestration potential and properties of the manufactured aggregates via the scientific understanding of the underlying physicochemical mechanisms and parameters. Manufactured aggregates are artificial filler materials with unique attributes whose properties can be tailored. The factors governing the carbon sequestration potential of manufactured aggregates (i.e., raw materials, carbonation kinetics, and carbonates formed) will be studied using chemical characterization, microstructural characterization, and macro-scale properties. The carbon mineralization techniques – gas-solid using carbonation through gaseous CO2 and solid pellets, gas-liquid by injecting CO2 into Ca/Mg-rich solutions, and liquid-solid using supercritical CO2, will be investigated. The effects of processing parameters - binder type, water-to-binder ratio, and curing regime on the physical, chemical, and mechanical properties of manufactured aggregates will be studied, and the pelletization process will be critically explored. The strategies to impart self-healing functionality and its efficiency will be assessed using the mechanical and transport properties of the manufactured aggregate concrete. The mechanical characterization of manufactured aggregate concrete will be performed under compression and tension. The fracture behavior will be characterized using crack-controlled tests and non-linear fracture mechanics principles. A comprehensive environmental sustainability analysis will be conducted to evaluate the enhancement in environmental sustainability. We have recently developed carbon-negative manufactured aggregates through gas-solid carbonation of brucite [Mg(OH)2]. The manufactured aggregates with a maximum nominal size of 4.75 mm showed an average crushing strength of about 25 MPa after carbonation with a carbon sequestration potential of 29% by weight of aggregates. The conventional concrete with a characteristic strength of 45 MPa, produced with 25% replacement of fine aggregates with manufactured aggregates, showed better compressive strength. title: Data-Driven Prediction and Synthesis of Edged Atomic Catalysts
abs: Catalyst goes to atoms. Transition metal (TM) atoms emerge as a type of unique catalyst system that can dramatically reduce the use of precious metals and improve utilization efficiency of metals. TM atoms anchored on the basal plane of the support (generally graphitic carbon and 2D materials) are the promising candidate to compete or even outperform precious metals (Pt, Pd, Ir, Ru, etc). Traditionally, these atoms bonded to the support with theoretically ideal bond structures. However, metal atoms anchored at the edge sites of 2D supports have been rarely considered, despite that fact that edges have been well known as the active centers for many 2D based materials due to the presence of unsaturated dangling bonds. We hypothesize that, by localizing TM atoms at the edge sites of the supports, we will create a new dimension to manipulate the first-, second- and even higher-shell coordination structures for atomic catalysts, leading to improved intrinsic activities for desired reactions. Because of its unique atomic configuration, there lacks systematic investigations on their structural characteristics and the catalytic trends of edge-anchored single atom catalysts (E-SACs). In this project, we aim to employ a data-driven strategy based on high-throughput calculations combined with machine learning to significantly accelerate the prediction and experimental realization of E-SACs. Specifically, the structural stabilities and intrinsic catalytic activities will be first evaluated for possible E-SACs under the high-throughput computing framework. Subsequently, one or two synthesis methods will be developed for the experimental realization of selected promising catalysts structures. The high-throughput prediction together with experimental feedback will allow us to build a database for training machine learning models, which will not only enable us to elucidate the structure-activity relationship of E-SACs, but also accelerate the discovery and realization of E-SACs. This project will be feasible based on our recent preliminary research in predicting optimal E-SACs on graphene support (out of 26 samples) for their oxygen reactions.
