title: A multilineage dependency mapping of the tumour ecosystem in EGFR-mutated Non-small Cell Lung Cancer
abs: Tumour-associated cell state is not only influenced by its genotype, but also the presence of cell types from multiple lineages (multilineage) within its tumour microenvironment (TME). The lung TME is a complex ecosystem, comprising diverse multilineage components including fibroblast, immune infiltrates, endothelial cells, lung epithelial cells, bronchial secretory cells and alveolar cells, where type 2 alveolar has been associated with tumour initiation of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) - the most prevalent form of lung cancer. Currently, targeted therapy is selected through histology and molecular definition, yet, drug resistance remains a major clinical challenge for advanced NSCLC. Reversal of drug resistance by targeting a single gene or a particular tumour cell population has become challenging, as it neglects the impact of various tumour-associated cell states on adaptive response. Relevant “ecotypes” which integrate various aspects of cell-cell interactions surrounding the lung TME may influence cancer progression and treatment response. These processes are currently not well understood for lung cancer. Using massively parallel techniques for single-cell/nuclei and spatial expression profiling with innovative computational tools, this proposal seeks to map and integrate intercellular (receptor-ligand interactions) and intracellular (downstream effectors) signalling networks unique to each ecotype that relies on either EGFR dependency or other oncogenic pathways. We aim to unravel multilineage components influencing tumour ecotype unique to responses or resistance to TKI. Our preliminary findings from more than 60,000 high quality single-nuclei transcriptomes demonstrate early adaptive tumour-associated cell states following the initiation of TKI treatment. Using these datasets as initial benchmark, we aim to define a framework to identify essential multilineage interactions and signalling components in lung cancer ecotypes and experimentally validate relevant crosstalk that are crucial for progression. The resulting multilineage dependency map here will not only impact on biomarker-driven patient selection, but also identify relevant ligands or receptors for targeted modulation.
kw: EGFR-mutated NSCLC; TKI resistance; Tumor microenvironment; Deep molecular profiling; Single cell sequencing; Lung ecological niche

title: Long‐term outcomes of post-TB lung disease following doxycycline intervention
abs: Pulmonary cavitation, a hallmark of tuberculosis (TB), is the site of high mycobacterial burden leading to disease transmission. The cause of tissue destructive cavitation in TB is due to host inflammatory response, leading to post-TB lung disease. A matrix-degrading phenotype develops in TB disease, where the activity of human proteolytic enzymes, specifically matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) is unopposed by their specific inhibitors (TIMPs), driving tissue destruction and cavitation. In our previous Phase 2 double-blinded randomised-controlled trial using MMP inhibition with doxycycline, we showed that lung cavity resolution improved significantly with doxycycline. Using a preclinical murine TB model, we also showed that doxycycline improves leaky blood vessels in TB granulomas potentially improving TB drug delivery. However whether doxycycline improves long term cardio-respiratory outcome is unknown. We hypothesize that 2 months of doxycycline inhibits tissue destruction in patients with pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB) to improve 2-year long-term cardiorespiratory outcomes. The specific aims are to: 1) determine long-term lung function of FEV1% predicted with and without doxycycline 2) characterize the resolution of pulmonary cavities, reduction in host immunological markers of tissue destruction and quality-of-life post-doxycycline. 3) characterize cardiovascular outcomes. Approach: This project is a longer follow-up to 2 years post-randomisation of a fully-powered Phase 3 double-blinded trial. Lung function tests, non-contrast CT thorax to characterise cavity volume and cardiac echocardiography will be performed. Plasma samples from all PTB patients shall be analysed for MMPs, their functional activity and cardiac markers highly-sensitive Troponin T and N-terminal pro-brain natriuretic peptide. Whole blood RNAseq and a subset of patients’ blood will be analysed by single-cell RNAsequencing. This fully-powered trial will evaluate if doxycycline can improve long-term lung function in post-pulmonary TB patients, determine cardiovascular outcomes and dissect the human immunological response to doxycycline intervention. Positive results will impact clinical practice and international guidelines to improve outcomes.
kw: Tuberculosis, Host-directed therapy, clinical trials, experimental medicine

title: The Impact on Population Health Arising from Alterations of the Gut Microbiome Associated with Bile Acid Homeostasis in the Development of Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC)
abs: Background: At 0.92, hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) has the highest case-fatality rate of any solid tumor. HCC is asymptomatic in its early stage when cure is possible and this significantly delays timely diagnosis. Patients at high risk of HCC (chronic hepatitis B and C) are thus offered 6-monthly screening. However currently 40% of HCC patients are non-B-non-C (NBNC HCC) and this proportion is increasing globally due to the growing prevalence of metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease (MAFLD). A robust means of risk stratifying the large NBNC population for HCC is urgently required to identify high-risk patients for surveillance. Concordant with the report by the Singapore Chinese Health Study, our two discovery cohorts, the NMRC LCG-funded PLANet and the A*STAR IAF-ICP funded ELEGANCE, have identified dysregulated bile acids as significant risk factor for HCC especially in NBNC patients and this is associated with changes in gut microbiome profile. Specific Hypotheses: (1) Cumulative gut microbiome dysbiosis leads to bile acid dysregulation and predisposes to the development of HCC; (2) Circulatory metabolomic biomarkers from the dysregulated bile acid metabolic pathway associated with development of HCC will stratify patient risks of developing HCC; (3) Interventions in dietary intake and lifestyle modification will correct dysbiosis of gut microbes related to bile acid homeostasis. Methodology: We propose to (1) leverage on the bio-samples of the PLANet and ELEGANCE programs to determine the molecular biology of dysregulated bile acids and bile-acid metabolizing microbes in HCC pathogenesis; (2) validate these metabolic signatures against bio-samples from the Singapore Chinese Health Study and SG 100K cohorts and derive machine-learning models for risk stratification; (3) conduct a prospective patient cohort with dietary and lifestyle interventions to correct dysbiosis of gut microbes. Summary: Our integrated, multi-pronged approach will provide a unparalleled opportunity for patient stratification, surveillance and disease prevention in HCC.
kw: Population Health; Gut microbiome; Bile acid homeostasis; Hepatocellular carcinoma

title: Clinical Validation of Gene Expression Predictor for Bevacizumab Treatment Response
abs: Bevacizumab is a monoclonal antibody targeting vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF). It has been used in the treatment of several cancers in the advanced stage, including glioblastoma, ovarian, lung, colorectal cancer and nasopharyngeal cancer (NPC). Unfortunately, despite its wide use and inclusion in clinical practice guidelines for cancer, there is currently no accurate biomarker to predict bevacizumab treatment response. We have develop a gene expression predictor for bevacizumab treatment response. The RRB signature (“Reduced Response to Bevacizumab signature”) was established from a discovery cohort of locally-advanced NPC patients treated with bevacizumab on the NCT01309633 phase 2 clinical trial. In this proposal, we will validate the performance of the RRB signature in two independent prospective clinical trials of NPC patients and extend the utility of the RRB signature to predict bevacizumab response across cancer types. To achieve these objectives. We will use a novel RNA-Seq technique to obtain high quality gene expression profiles from FFPE sections of biopsies patient biopsies, and also interrogate existing gene expression datasets from large clinical trial. Finally, we will also evaluate the performance of combining gene signature scores using a "one test, many decisions" approach for precision medicine.
kw: precision oncology, gene expression, RNA signature

title: Target prioritisation and molecular insights from an iPS cell platform for cardiometabolic disease
abs: Heart failure imposes a heavy burden on society, with high rates of mortality, morbidity, and hospitalization. Despite past advances, there is still a need to target other disease pathways in the heart. To discover novel first-in-class targets, we combine disease pathway analysis with population-scale human genetics approaches by profiling heart failure-relevant phenotypes in patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells. This target discovery and prioritization platform is powered by a large (N~500), genetically diverse iPSC biobank (“iPSC diversity panel”) gathered from local and Southeast Asian collaborators. Through the two complementary approaches of quantitative trait loci analysis of profiled phenotypes from "cell villages" and a suite of genetically encoded molecular sensors engineered into genomic safe harbours, we aim to identify genes underpinning cellular phenotypes of interest and prioritize targets by colocalization with genome-wide association studies and other means. In the future, by integrating function and ‘omics data from iPSC-derived cardiac cell-types with matched clinical and lifestyle data from donors, we hope to develop predictive models for risk and response, incorporating an individual’s genetics, lifestyle, and environmental context, culminating in clinical insights and tools for heart failure management.
kw: cardiometabolic disease, heart failure, iPS cells,

title: Deciphering advanced colorectal cancer using new region-specific stem cell-driven mouse models
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a major burden worldwide and particularly in Singapore, where it is the most common cancer in men and second most common in women. Late diagnosis of the disease and relapse after treatment is the major cause of CRC lethality. Colon compartmentalisation translates into different cancer profiles making colorectal cancer a very heterogenous disease that further confounds efforts to develop broadly effective treatments. Current CRC mouse models lack either colon tissue-specificity, limiting progression towards more advanced disease, or preclude evaluation of resident stem cells as cancer origins. The generation of advanced CRC mouse models that accurately recapitulate disease initiation and subsequent progression towards terminal stages is of crucial importance for deciphering underlying mechanisms of disease and for identifying novel biomarkers and therapeutic targets. We have recently developed new stem cell-specific Cre driver mouse lines that facilitate tumour formation in a region-specific manner when relevant conditional mutations are incorporated. These unique mouse models, together with a suite of CRC organoid models will, for the first time, enable us to accurately model regional CRC using mutational signatures being obtained from human CRC samples isolated from corresponding regions of the colon. These models are expected to be invaluable for deciphering clinically-relevant insights into disease progression, reveal novel biomarkers aiding cancer detection and stratification and novel therapeutic targets. Importantly, these models will also facilitate a rigorous functional evaluation of potential CSC populations, which are considered key drivers of tumour relapse following traditional therapies and therefore represent important therapeutic targets. This multifaceted project is expected to deliver both scientific breakthroughs as well as translational opportunities for driving R&D investments and/or collaborations with local healthcare institutions, academic institutions, and pharmaceutical companies.
kw: Colorectal cancer; metaplasia; stem cells; biomarkers; therapeutic targets; mouse models

title: Interrogating Immunogenicity of Adeno-Associated Viruses (AAVs) and CRISPR-Cas for Safer Therapeutics
abs: CRISPR-Cas gene editing and Adeno-Associated Virus (AAV) gene therapy therapeutics present tremendous opportunities for treating human diseases, but the immune responses towards these foreign entities could render treatments ineffective and unsafe. The objective of this proposed research is to map, engineer, and characterise how CRISPR-Cas and AAV systems interact with host adaptive immunity, so as to develop safer nucleic acid therapeutics. In Specific Aim 1, we will comprehensively map immunogenic determinants of AAV delivery vectors with display and affinity technologies, focusing on B-cell epitopes eliciting the more potent humoral immune response. In Specific Aim 2, we will interrogate how CRISPR-Cas therapeutic modalities engage the human immune system, focusing especially on the T-cell epitopes and T-cell cytotoxicity that impose safety and efficacy concerns. In Specific Aim 3, we will demonstrate that AAV and CRISPR-Cas proteins can be engineered to be less immune-reactive, while enhancing or preserving functional activity, and show that reduction of immunogenicity enables new DNA and RNA -editing therapeutic avenues with CRISPR-Cas cargoes delivered by AAV vectors. Upon completion, this proposed research should provide novel biological insights into immunogenicity and new intellectual property assets in safer nucleic acid therapeutics.
kw: Immunogenicity; CRISPR-Cas; Adeno-associated virus; therapeutics

title: Effect of innate immune reprogramming by primary dengue on host response to secondary dengue
abs: Dengue is a acute viral disease that is caused by infection with the mosquito-borne dengue virus (DENVs). There exists four antigenically and genetically distinct DENVs mean; immunity from infection with one does not prevent infection with the remaining 3 DENVs. Moreover, epidemiological observations show that secondary infection with a DENV that is heterologous to that which caused the first (primary) infection increases the risk of severe dengue. Two different hypotheses – the antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE) and T-cell original antigenic sin (OAS) hypotheses – may explain the increased risk of secondary DENV infection to severe dengue. The mutual exclusivity of these two hypotheses has, however, funnelled dengue pathogenesis studies into testing either of these models, never both even though both hypotheses are plausible. This study is aimed directly at addressing this conundrum. It proposes that both hypothesized processes operate simultaneously through an innate immune system that has been reprogrammed by prior DENV infection. We have found in 3 independent cohorts, that individuals with prior DENV infection show reduced expression of genes enriched in monocytes and dendritic cells, which are targets of secondary DENV infection through their expression of Fc gamma receptors, as well as antiviral response. These findings suggest that lasting changes in baseline gene expression in target cells of secondary DENV infection could alter host response to antibody-enhanced infection as well as antigen presentation for T cell responses. We aim to elucidate the mechanisms regulating DENV-induced trained immunity and determine effects of DENV-induced trained immunity on ADE-mediated DENV infection and T-cell responses. We will use primary cells from volunteers with and without prior DENV infection, following informed consent, for our investigations. The findings of this study would fill an important knowledge gap, pave the way for vaccines to be used safely and provide insights into new host-directed therapeutic targets.
kw: Dengue; innate immune cells; reprogramming

title: The pathobiology of tRNA modifications in cardiac development and diseased cell states
abs: The RNA epitranscriptome is an emerging druggable space, led so far mainly by cancer therapeutics on mRNA methylation and pseudouridination pathways. Current epitranscriptomic studies in cardiac systems are narrowly focused on the same mRNA pathways. However, at least 170 RNA modifications exist and the potential epitranscriptomic repertoire in development and diseased cardiac cell states remains to be fully explored. Among all, tRNAs are highly abundant and most diversely modified. The tRNA epitranscriptome controls codon-selective protein translation for targeted changes driving physiology and disease. Our preliminary results highlight a profound and previously unnoticed tRNA-centric translatomic switch underlying cardiac cell differentiation and maturation. We mapped this modification rewiring in tandem with changes in tRNA-modifying enzyme gene expression. 73% of MS-detected tRNA modifications, including N6-methyladenosine (m6A) and 7-methylguanosine (m7G) were transiently downregulated during the formation of ISL1/NKX2-5+ cardiac progenitors. The expression of novel modifications hydroxywybutosine (oHyW) and 5-(carboxyhydroxymethyl)uridine methyl ester (mchm5U) persists from the progenitor state into 37-day maturation. Using Weighted Gene Correlation Network Analysis (WGCNA), gene modules, METTL1 and METTL3 (writer enzymes for m6A, m7G, and mchm5U) were persistently downregulated. Whereas TYW1, TYW3, TYW5, and TRMT5 (enzymes upstream along the OHyW modification pathway) followed another distinct expression trajectory, tracking with OHyW levels during cardiomyocyte differentiation. Moreover, discernable turnover of tRNA pools and tRNA fragments may contribute another layer of gene expression control. Here, we will generate a comprehensive map of intra-sample multi-omics relevant to tRNA modifications across cardiac cell states and disease models. We will test for codon-biased translation and identify the proteomic networks underpinning physiology. Candidate tRNA pools and epitranscriptomic drivers will be perturbed with inducible CRISPRi, prime-editing/base-editing or modulation of tRNA-modifying enzymes to assess causality. This study will reveal new biochemical pathways in cardiac cell development and disease, potentially leading to novel RNA therapeutic strategies.
kw: cardiomyocyte, heart failure, tRNA, modifications

title: Spexin as a novel metabo-inflammation treatment target for heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
abs: Rationale Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is a leading cause of death and disability in Singapore and worldwide with numbers rising given the aging population and the increasing prevalence of metabolic risk factors such as obesity and diabetes. Treatment options for preventing the onset and progression of HFpEF are limited, and new treatments are needed to improve health outcomes in HFpEF. In this proposal, we investigate Spexin as a novel metabo-inflammation treatment target for preventing HFpEF using human stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes and mice models of HFpEF and will elucidate the mechanisms underlying its protective effects. Specific Aims Aim 1: To evaluate Spx as a novel metabo-inflammation treatment target for improving contractile/relaxation function in HFpEF IPSC-CMs. Hypothesis: Spx levels are reduced in HFpEF IPSC-CMs and Spx treatment will enhance myocardial energetics, reduce inflammation, and improve contractile/relaxation function. Aim 2: To evaluate the effects of augmenting Spx levels on myocardial energetics, inflammation/fibrosis, cardiac diastolic function, and development of HF in HFpEF mice. Hypothesis: Myocardial tissue and circulating Spx levels are reduced in HFpEF mice and augmenting Spx levels by either the exogenous administration of Spx or exercise will enhance myocardial energetics, reduce inflammation/fibrosis, improve diastolic function and prevent HF. Aim 3: To elucidate the mechanisms through which Spx improves myocardial energetics in HFpEF. Hypothesis: Spx treatment enhances myocardial energetics by increasing uptake of glucose, decreasing cardiomyocyte uptake of long chain fatty acids and upregulating key components of the glucose oxidation and fatty acid oxidation pathways in HFpEF IPSC-CMs and HFpEF murine cardiomyocytes. Expected results We hope to demonstrate Spx to be a novel metabo-inflammation treatment target for treating HFpEF, a strategy which has the potential to reduce patient mortality and morbidity (less re-hospitalisation for heart failure and improved quality of life).
kw: Spexin, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, metabolism, inflammation

title: Extent and extending tumor-targeting immune repertoire in locally advanced head and neck cancer
abs: In epithelial malignancies such as head and neck squamous cell cancers(HNSCC), there is a constant conflict between the need to ablate tumor draining lymph nodes(TDLN), which are sites of metastases versus preserving tumor-targeting immune function therein. TDLN are key players in the cancer immunity cycle yet the specificity and extent of tumor-specific activation along well-defined lymphatic chains remains undetermined. Moreover, there is significant interest in the role of tumor-associated tertiary lymphoid structures(TLS) and their role in the cancer immunity cycle. We hypothesize that tumor antigen-based nodal activation diminishes with increasing ‘distance’ of the TDLN from the primary tumor which is also a reflection of temporal exposure, but this could be augmented by cytotoxics or immune checkpoint blockade. Our secondary hypothesis posits that TLS provide an additional source of tumor-targeting T-cells. T,o test these we will profile primary tumors along with tumor-adjacent ‘normal’ TDLN, tumor-involved TDLN and tumor distant ‘normal’ TDLN(designated 1P3L) along a ‘lymphoid axis’ using dissociated single cell analyses to uncover subcluster-based signatures for tumor-targeting T-cells, and spatial transcriptomics to identify specific localization, cellular context and niche/architecture associated with these including both the impact of Type 2 and innate immune responses. T-cells will be expanded from various TDLN stations to functionally test for tumor-targeting and used to refine signatures above. Finally we will test the role of pre-treatment of the primary tumor in extending and expanding the immune repertoire by ex vivo treatment of tumor-lymph node explants and spatial profiling 1P3L nodal sets in tissue from patients pre-treated with chemotherapy and nivolumab(PD1-blockade). These analyses will also include spatial dissection of the TLS to understand the role of T-cells within these in the treatment-naïve and neoadjuvant setting. These data will have major impact on the extent of nodal ablation in curative HNSCC therapy and provides additional endpoints in neo-adjuvant protocols.
kw: immune modulation; checkpoint inhibitor; T lymphocytes; tumor targeting T cells; tumor draining lymph nodes; immune exhaustion

title: An Evaluation of the Mechanisms of Allergy to Galacto-oligosacharide, a Supplemental Prebiotic in Food and Beverage
abs: Background and Aims: Galactooligosaccharides (GOS) are enzymatically produced prebiotics, comprising over 100 different structures. Our previous work described acute allergy and anaphylaxis to GOS, and that the dust mite, Blomia tropicalis, is a putative sensitizer. GOS are unique allergens as they are carbohydrates of low molecular weight. The IgE epitopes for GOS and the mechanism of IgE sensitization to GOS remain unresolved. The aims of this study are: 1) To evaluate the molecular mechanisms behind IgE-mediated GOS allergy by: (a) Identifying the IgE epitope(s) of GOS allergen(s) and the natural glycan in the environment showing cross-reactivity with GOS, (b) Identifying the glycan structure(s) of the putative primary sensitizer, (c) Studying how GOS cross-links IgE on basophils 2) To validate the mechanistic pathways of GOS allergy through in vivo animal studies. Methods: Chemically synthesized GOS structures covering all linear and branching trisaccharide, excluding the trehalose series, will be produced. Basophil activation assay and competitive IgE ELISA assay will evaluate the allergenicity of these structures. Monoclonal antibodies against the most allergenic epitope will be generated to detect cross-reactive epitopes using glycan arrays and Western blotting, and to purify glycoproteins from the putative primary sensitizer. Glycan structures of the glycoproteins will be analyzed by liquid chromatography coupled with Orbitrap mass spectrometry. Time-lap microscopy will be used to study how GOS cross-link IgE. Animal models will be used to study the association of Blomia tropicalis sensitization with the development of GOS allergy in vivo. Benefits and Clinical Significance: This study has the potential to discover novel common carbohydrate determinants (CCD) with allergenic potential. The results obtained will lay the groundwork for development of diagnostic tools for GOS allergy, the screening of potential GOS related allergens in new food products, and designing 'safe' or hypoallergenic GOS prebiotic products as supplements for food and beverages.
kw: Galacto-oligosaccharide, IgE epitopes, glycoallergens

title: Investigating the role of UBOX5 in Primary Angle Closure Glaucoma.
abs: Primary angle closure glaucoma (PACG) is a blinding disease that is initiated by occlusion of the trabecular meshwork angle leading to increased ocular pressure (IOP). The disease is highly prevalent in Asia, and will increase considerably in the future due to aging. To deepen our understanding of PACG, our team sequenced >10,000 subjects and found that predicted loss of function (LoF) variants of UBOX5 were significantly associated (P=1 × 10-10) with a 2.3-fold increase in risk of developing PACG. This is the first time in the world an actual risk gene has been found to be associated with PACG. In this study, we will characterize the phenotype of PACG patients with UBOX5 LoF mutations. Our preliminary experiments demonstrate that UBOX5 modulates cellular responses to ER stress. Using this finding, we developed an assay to functionally evaluate UBOX5 variants and found that the actual risk due to carrying a validated UBOX5 variant was much higher. This discrepancy between actual and predicted function necessitates testing of every discovered UBOX5 variant for validation in order to begin tracking patients who carry LoF variants. We will develop a new high-throughput assay to facilitate this, allowing us to ascertain if UBOX5 LoF variants lead to worse PACG disease. As UBOX5 is expressed prominently in the iris and retina, we will study UBOX5 knockout mice to determine where UBOX5-mediated protection is important. Ocular hypertension will be induced to interrogate for changes in both locations in the eye and to uncover candidate pathways for further analysis. Success in our aims will allow us to discover clinically-actionable UBOX5 variants linked to PACG disease outcomes, and develop a new pre-clinical mouse model for PACG. These will eventually pave the way for effective stratification of PACG patients and the development of new PACG therapies to combat this blinding disease.
kw: Glaucoma, Biochemistry, ER stress, Aging, Unfolded Protein Response (UPR)

title: Large prospective cohort to study adiposopathy, sarcopenia and cardiorenal failure among Asians with type 2 diabetes
inst: Khoo Teck Puat Hospital Pte Ltd
abs: Singapore is facing the “dual tsunamis” of rising metabolic burden & a rapidly ageing population. Hence, we need to concurrently address dia-besity (diabetes & obesity) associated adiposopathy (i.e. sick-fat syndrome), ageing-mediated sarcopenia (accelerated by diabesity) & their resultant cardio-renal dysfunction. Diabesity-associated adiposopathy, has 3 cardinal features: (i) excess adiposity, (ii) unhealthy fat distribution (visceral adiposity & ectopic fat) & (iii) mal-adaptive dysmetabolism. Importantly, Asians carry greater adiposopathy at any given body mass index, compared to Caucasians, which may explain Asians’ vulnerability to obesity related adverse health outcomes. Novel data from our group suggest that both adiposopathy & sarcopenia can drive cardiorenal failure. Importantly, the relationship between diabesity & ageing-related sarcopenia is likely bi-directional & hence, challenging to unravel. Given its rich serial phenotypic data & bio-resource collection, our two decade-long type 2 diabetes (T2D) cohorts (total N~4,000) - SMART2D (Singapore Study of Macro-angiopathy & Micro-vascular Reactivity in Type 2 Diabetes) & DORIS (Diabetic Kidney Disease – Onset & Progression Risk Factors), will meet the challenge, to temporally unravel the complex patho-biology, for causal inference. Therefore, leveraging SMART2D & DORIS cohorts, we aim to study the complex relationship between diabesity-associated adiposopathy, ageing-related sarcopenia & cardiorenal failure, using state-of-the-art, targeted (candidate-biomarker) & untargeted (OMICS) molecular epidemiology approaches. We hypothesize that diabesity-associated adiposopathy & ageing-related sarcopenia (both “exposures”) will predict long-term changes (& provide mechanistic insights) in endothelial function, arterial stiffness (“intermediate phenotypes”) & incident cardiorenal outcomes. Additionally, we also hypothesize that diabesity-associated adiposopathy contributes to ageing-related sarcopenia. We will employ advanced analytics e.g. Mendelian Randomization (MR) (including bi-directional MR), to strengthen causal inference, for the discovery of potential therapeutic targets. Importantly, diabesity-associated adiposopathy & ageing-related sarcopenia are amenable to lifestyle, nutritional & pharmacological interventions. Understanding their mechanistic relationship with cardiorenal function, will reveal treatment-targets to prevent cardiorenal failure.
kw: Type 2 Diabetes; Biomarkers; Adiposopathy; Sarcopenia; Cardiorenal failure; lifestyle

title: Histological Validation and Etiological Markers of Small Fiber Neuropathy
abs: Small fiber neuropathy (SFN) is phenotypically and etiologically heterogeneous, with patients presenting with debilitating neuropathic pain and dysautonomia. Diagnosing SFN is challenging due to a lack of specific biomarkers and constantly evolving diagnostic criteria. The current “gold standard” of diagnosing SFN with skin biopsy and testing for the epidermal nerve fiber density (ENFD) comes with diagnostic and technical limitations. The ultimate challenge lies in finding the underlying causes of SFN and subtyping them according to disease presentation. Although the etiology is oftentimes identifiable, the underlying cause remains elusive in around 50% of the cases, and these are classified as idiopathic SFN (iSFN). Autoimmunity has been postulated to be pathophysiologically important in presumed iSFN. In addition, gastrointestinal side effects are a common presentation of SFN in up to 50% of our cohort, but the mechanism is unknown. The primary objective of this project is to validate a new and improved immunohistochemical technique by indirect immunofluorescence (IF) to diagnose SFN in our local Pathology laboratory, and to confirm the presence of autoantibodies in skin and gut mucosa samples. These specific aims will be addressed: Aim 1: Validation of IF on 50 um and comparison with 10 um cryosections of skin for quantification of epidermal nerve fiber density (ENFD) to diagnose patients with small fiber neuropathy. Aim 2: To determine the possible etiology of SFN by the presence of organ-specific markers (cutaneous and GI mucosal) by IF and digital spatial profiling, and correlating it systematically by immunophenotyping of patients’ peripheral blood mononuclear cells. We hypothesize that epidermal nerve fiber density visualized by indirect immunofluorescence is reduced in SFN patients, and novel autoantibody-antigen complexes secreted by B cells may be present in the skin and gut.
kw: skin biopsy, intraepidermal nerve fiber density, small fiber neuropathy, autoantibodies, functional gastrointestinal disorders

title: Leveraging artificial intelligence and whole genome sequencing to unravel transmission dynamics of carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales in Singapore hospitals (CaPES-AI)
abs: Background: Carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales (CPE) pose a major public health threat due to multidrug resistance. Hospitals struggle with hidden reservoirs and complex transmission within their walls. This research will use artificial intelligence (AI) and whole genome sequencing (WGS) to investigate CPE transmission. Aims: i. Identify Reservoirs: Locate hidden CPE reservoirs and map their distribution and transmission patterns. ii. Build Predictive Model: Integrate clinical, genomic, and environmental data to create a model predicting patient susceptibility. iii. Validate Model: Prospectively assess the model's ability to identify high-risk patients and environments. Hypotheses: i. Persistent environmental reservoirs drive uncontrolled CPE spread. ii. Integrating WGS and AI will improve understanding of transmission, enabling high-risk patient/environment identification. iii. The model can significantly improve infection control practices, reducing CPE transmission. Methods: Through a prospective hospital cohort of CPE-negative patients we will identify CPE acquisitions. We will swab hospital environment extensively to identify CPE contamination. Using WGS linkage data, a WGS network (GWGS) will be created, representing potential transmission pathways. Incorporating the hospital’s spatial distribution and potential CPE transmission routes a Graph Neural Network (GNN)-based model will be developed to approximate the probabilities of nodes (patients/environments) being superspreaders. This model will be trained using labeled subgraphs derived from contact tracing simulations and validated. Predictive analyses will then be conducted to identify high-risk human and environmental factors, which will then be validated in the clinical setting. Significance: This study aims to set new standards for infection control practices by providing easy-to-use tools to identify patients at risk of CPE acquisition, which will enable more effective infection control measures, improving patient outcomes and reducing healthcare costs. The findings will have significant implications for clinical practice, healthcare policy, and the development of diagnostic tools, contributing to the global effort to combat antimicrobial resistance.
kw: Artificial intelligence; carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales; infection prevention and control; transmission dynamics; whole genome sequencing; predictive modeling

title: Lean diabetic heart failure: Validation and Mechanistic Insights of Treatment Targets
abs: Background: The heart failure (HF) burden in Singapore is rapidly growing. One out of five patients in Singapore have a lean-diabetic HF phenotype, which has worse outcomes than other patient subgroups. Previously, we identified that this population has increased inflammation and cardiac metabolism markers, particularly myeloperoxidase (MPO). However, the mechanistic role of MPO in this context remains poorly understood. Aim: This proposal explores the mechanistic role of treatment targets in patients with HF with a lean-diabetic phenotype using human induced pluripotent cells (HiPSC), a mouse model, and a systems biology approach. Methods: We will achieve the overall aim according to three sub-aims. First, we will perform an integrated-systems biology analysis to identify pathophysiological pathways associated with MPO in patients with lean vs obese diabetic HFpEF using >1800 proteins, >400 metabolites, and phenotypic and imaging data. Second, we will measure >400 metabolites in >700 patients and controls for independent validation. We will validate pathophysiological pathways identified in sub-aim 1 in sub-aim 2, identify possible genetic regulators using Mendelian randomization, and evaluate the effect of treatment targets on the heart and cardiac fibrosis using MRI-measured extracellular volume (ECV). Finally, we will use HiPSC-derived cardiomyocytes from patients with lean and obese diabetic HF phenotypes to validate potential pathophysiological targets' mechanisms and an HFpEF mouse model to identify small molecules to attenuate the effects of druggable targets. Significance: By identifying novel pathophysiological mechanisms in lean diabetic patients with HFpEF, this study is an essential next step in identifying druggable treatment targets that can be used in phase-1 human clinical trials to improve the outcomes of a vulnerable population in Singapore.
kw: Heart failure, diabetes

title: Metabolic biomarkers for dietary intake and health outcomes in multi-ethnic Asian populations
abs: Improved understanding of diet-health relationships and establishing effective approaches to dietary change for health promotion, are critical needs that underpin efforts to improve prevention and control of multiple chronic diseases. To date, nutritional research and dietary intervention in Singapore has relied on self-reported questionnaire, an approach confounded by low accuracy, poor reproducibility and recall bias. In our preliminary and preparatory work, we demonstrate 20 metabolite panels that enable objective characterisation of Asian dietary intakes, and these metabolite panels better predict cross-sectional health outcomes than self-report. In this proposal, in specific aim 1 (SA1), we will first carry out dose-response controlled feeding studies to validate our Asian dietary metabolite panels, as more objective and accurate measurement of food intakes. We will prioritise 10 Asian food groups, that are highly relevant to Singapore’s multi-ethnic population and 2 healthy eating indices focused on aMED-centric and aHEI-centric diets, that represent composite measures of favourable dietary intakes. In SA2, we will develop quantitative and reproducible laboratory assays for quantifying concentrations of these Asian dietary metabolites. Finally, in SA3, we will test whether our validated metabolite panels identify dietary intakes and predict incident cardiovascular and metabolic outcomes, amongst 10,000 HELIOS study participants, accounting for genetic background and microbiome diversity. This will include comparison of predictive performance for disease outcomes, between our dietary metabolite panels and conventional self-report. Anticipated outputs of these experiments include: i. Improved understanding of quantitative relationships between dietary intakes and metabolic variation; ii. Development of validated metabolite panels for dietary intakes in Asian populations, and iii. A scalable, validated assay platform for clinically relevant evaluation of dietary intakes. Our research will lead to improved understanding of diet-health relationships, as well as objective tools to enable and enhance the development and implementation of effective dietary interventions for cardiovascular disease, diabetes and other chronic conditions.
kw: Dietary exposure; metabolite biomarkers; controlled feeding study; nutritional epidemiology; cardiovascular disease; diabetes

title: The Role of Peroxisome Proliferator-activated Receptors-α Agonists in Promoting Corneal Nerve Trophic Function and Nerve Regeneration
abs: Corneal neuropathy is a common corneal disease, with an incidence of 27-90% depending on etiology. It may evolve into a devastating condition culminating in visual loss, resulting in a high economic burden. However, the greatest unmet clinical need is there are extremely limited treatments available to enhance corneal nerve health and regeneration. The current management is for symptomatic relief only. My team has published that oral fenofibrate, a peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors-α (PPARα) agonist, stimulated corneal nerve regeneration in diabetes, where PPARα expression is down-regulated in corneas. In this proposal, we aim to further investigate the efficacy and detailed mechanisms of PPARα agonists in various forms of corneal neuropathy where the PPARα pathway is or is not impaired (Aims 1&2). We will also formulate fenofibrate into topical eye drops, as well as nano-based eye drops, and evaluate their therapeutic effects in ameliorating diabetic and non-diabetic corneal neuropathy (Aims 1&3). Our central hypothesis is that topical and oral PPARα agonists promote corneal nerve regeneration through the PPARα pathway and standalone neurotrophic effect. The former stimulates corneal reinnervation in the scenarios where PPARα expression is down-regulated such as diabetes, while the latter exerts beneficial effects in corneal neuropathy where PPARα expression is normal. Nanotechnology can enhance the therapeutic effects. We will attest these hypotheses using different animal models. This study will provide a novel therapeutic agent for corneal neuropathy, addressing unmet clinical needs and delivering more effective medical care. It will also identify the pathogenesis and targeted pathways involved in corneal neuropathy, providing the basis for exploring potential biomarkers or new treatments. Additionally, repurposing existing drugs (i.e. fenofibrate) has been an attractive approach to identify therapeutic agents because of the reduced cost, risk, and timeline. Together with our solid preliminary data, we anticipate high translational value and significant clinical applications of this project.
kw: Corneal Neuropathy; Corneal Nerves; Peroxisome Proliferator-activated Receptors; Corneal Nerve Regeneration; Cornea

title: Novel long noncoding RNA interactions with EZH2 as a new strategy to target drug resistance in multiple myeloma
abs: Multiple myeloma (MM) is an aggressive B-cell malignancy that is currently incurable and displays a poor prognosis despite significant advances in new treatments. Understanding the genetic factors contributing to myeloma progression and therapeutic resistance is critical for improving the clinical outcome of MM. Our recent study revealed a novel NF-ĸB/p52 regulated long noncoding RNA (lncRNA), LINCNARA (NFkB Associated Regulator of Apoptosis), in promoting the oncogenic progression and drug resistance of MM. We further identified EZH2, the enzymatic subunit of Polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2), whose overexpression is associated with chemoresistance in MM, to interact with LINCNARA. We hypothesize that aberrant non-canonical NF-ĸB signalling is a major driver of myeloma associated lncRNAs promoting chemoresistance and disease relapse. We further postulate that EZH2 functions as a critical RNA-binding protein (RBP) for such lncRNAs to mediate their chemoresistance and oncogenic functions. In this study, we propose three specific aims to characterize and target the biological functions of EZH2-LINCNARA in the treatment resistance and disease progression of MM. Aim 1: Elucidate the biological roles of EZH2-LINCNARA complex in the therapeutic resistance of MM. In this aim, we will investigate how LINCNARA regulates the stability and activity of EZH2, including the PRC2 complex, to mediate resistance to standard regimen drugs used in MM therapy. Aim 2: Identify EZH2-LINCNARA regulated targets and pathways driving chemoresistance and establish signatures of prognostic value in relapsed/refractory MM patients. In this aim, we will examine and characterize the EZH2-LINCNARA driven gene signatures and signaling mechanisms that are important in the chemoresistance and prognosis of relapsed/refractory MM patients. Aim 3: Design and validate nucleic acid therapeutics targeting the EZH2-LINCNARA mediated chemoresistance functions of MM. In this aim, we will investigate the potential utility of novel antisense oligos for MM therapy, through disrupting EZH2/PRC2-LINCNARA interactions to abrogate myeloma progression and drug resistance.

title: Constructing the organ-immune interface in a human organoid model of kidney disease
abs: Human pluripotent stem cell (PSC) derived organoids represent an innovative model system to replicate key physiological features of the cognate human organ. In the past decade, human PSC derived organoids, alongside iPSC reprogramming and genome editing, have been widely used to study human organ development and disease pathogenesis. Although human organoids are comprised of the principal cell types of the cognate organ or tissue, generic cell types are severely underrepresented, such as vasculature and macrophages. Although the interface between organ and tissue resident immune cells plays a pivotal role in a wide range of pathophysiological processes, the current organoid models are not feasible for studying how macrophage shapes the local tissue microenvironment and pathophysiology. To address this limitation, we aim to construct the organ-immune interface in kidney organoids, via direct differentiation and multi-cellular self-organization. As a proof-of-concept, we will employ this novel immune-kidney organoid model to investigate the intercellular crosstalk between kidney organ specific cells and macrophages in the context of inherited polycystic kidney disease (PKD). We hypothesize that human PSC derived macrophages and kidney organoids can establish a close-to-native intercellular crosstalk in healthy as well as in diseased kidney contexts. This proposal outlines three specific aims to be pursued over the span of 3 years

title: Single-Cell Multiplex Assessment of Cardiac cell-type specific Cis-Regulatory Elements in Human Myocardial Infarction Heart Failure
abs: Background: Heart failure remains the major cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. With the advent of single-cell technology, cardiac disease-associated cell states were mapped to help us better understand the pathogenesis of heart failure at single-cell resolution. Interestingly, the causal contributions of disease-associated regulatory loci in individual cardiac cell types connected to these diseased gene programs are unique and remain to be comprehensively functionalized and determined. Specific Aims: In this proposal, we seek to map out distal elements regulating diseased gene signatures such as RUNX1 in respective cardiovascular cell types and functionally perturbing these elements using a single-cell CRISPR interference system to assess for reversal in diseased cell states restrained in a cell-type specific manner. For discovery, we aim to compile intra-sample single-cell epigenetic and transcriptomic maps using fresh human myocardial infarcted failing heart explants, and cell-type specific chromatin interaction data. For validation, we aim to prioritize a list of disease-associated elements for the systematic genetic perturbation in respective cardiovascular lineages. Hypothesis: We propose the mapping and multiplexed targeting of cell-type-specific disease-associated enhancers to pathologic cell states to assess for disease reversal signatures. Methodology and Approach: We will be leveraging computational workflows such as the activity-by-contact and E2G framework, as well as cell-type specific chromatin maps to build genome-wide single-cell enhancer-gene maps for human heart failure and co-localize with GWAS variants to identify cell-type specific distal regulatory elements implicated in heart disease. To assess causality, we will engineer an inducible " all-in-one" single-cell CRISPR perturbation system using a non-viral safe-harbour knock-in approach for the systematic genetic perturbation of disease-associated elements, following lineage differentiation into respective ES-derived cardiovascular cell types, to identify causal regulatory regions to disease-associated genes in a cell-type specific manner. This could pave the way for cell-specific enhancer-based targeted therapies for heart failure.
kw: CRISPR;Stem-cells;Heart Failure;Cardiac Epigenetics;Omics

title: Designing LanCL1-Targeting Cyclic Peptides to Potentially Improve Chemotherapy of Hepatocellular Carcinoma
abs: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the primary type of liver cancer, causing a serious health and economic burden globally. As one of the most common cancers in the world, this malignancy is often diagnosed at its advanced stage and is noted for poor prognosis with a 5-year relative survival rate of ~20%. Sorafenib and Lenvatinib, both of which function as multi-kinase inhibitors, have been approved by FDA for the first-line treatment of advanced HCC. Nevertheless, the chemoresistance issue has arisen for both drugs. One common mechanism for anticancer drug resistance is the upregulation of the antioxidant system in tumor cells to alleviate drug-induced oxidative pressure. It was recently discovered that the LanCL1 protein was overexpressed in several types of cancer cells to suppress reactive oxygen species (ROS)-triggered apoptosis. Moreover, LanCL1-targeting antibodies have been found to effectively suppress HCC cell proliferation. Based on the previous reports, we propose that new LanCL1-targeting molecules may be designed to boost intracellular ROS signaling of HCC cells, and that those LanCL1 binders can potentially help HCC chemotherapy by alleviating tumor cell proliferation or chemoresistance. Our proposed research includes the following specific aims, 1) to identify LanCL1-binding cyclic peptides by either structure-guided ligand optimization or various display technologies. 2) to investigate whether the LanCL1-binding cyclic peptides can modulate intracellular ROS signaling of HCC cells. 3) to evaluate the effect of LanCL1 binders on HCC cell proliferation and chemoresistance.
kw: LanCL1, hepatocellular carcinoma, oxidative pressure, drug resistance, cyclic peptides

title: Harnessing LYVE1-expressing macrophages as a novel cellular target to manage endometriosis
abs: Endometriosis is an inflammatory gynaecological disorder characterised by the extrauterine growth of endometrial-like tissues. It is associated with debilitating pelvic pain, infertility, and adverse obstetric outcomes. Asian women are at greater risk of endometriosis, compared with other ethnicities. However, the precise etiology of endometriosis remains unclear. Macrophages, a highly heterogenous and plastic immune cell subset, are thought to be a key contributor to the development of endometriosis. Our team previous discovered that the expression of hyaluronic acid receptor LYVE1 is a hallmark for perivascular tissue resident macrophages. LYVE1+ macrophages maintain tissue homeostasis by preventing fibrosis and suppressing inflammation, while their dysregulations contribute to exacerbated pancreatic cancer and vascular ageing. Our preliminary study performed a single-cell transcriptomic analysis on endometriotic disease lesions (ectopic) and the intrinsic controls, endometrial tissues within the uterus (eutopic) from four patients with severe endometriosis. Such preliminary results provided strong evidence that LYVE1+ macrophages are enriched in the ectopic lesions compared to the eutopic tissues, and LYVE1+ macrophages from ectopic lesions have inflammatory, fibrotic and angiogenic transcriptomic features. Therefore, we hypothesise that dysfunctional LYVE1+ macrophages modulate local inflammatory responses, vasculature and extracellular matrix remodelling thus promoting the tissue growth seen in endometriosis. In this proposal, we aim to 1) deeply characterise LYVE1+ macrophages from both human ectopic endometriotic lesions and eutopic endometrial tissues; 2) determine the localisation of LYVE1+ macrophages in both ectopic and eutopic tissues; 3) predict and validate cellular interactions involving LYVE1+ macrophages in ectopic and eutopic tissues. We will use cutting-edge multi-omics techniques, including high dimensional mass cytometry, spatial transcriptomics, multiplex immunofluorescence imaging, to assess LYVE1+ macrophages from both ectopic and eutopic tissues. Completion of this study may establish LYVE1+ macrophages as a critical factor driving the development of endometriosis and pave ways for future treatments against endometriosis by targeting this immune cell population.
kw: Endometriosis; LYVE1; Macrophage; Multi-omics; Immunology; Gynaecology

title: Nur77 agonism reinvigorates natural killer cells for superior anti-tumor immunity in hepatocellular carcinoma
abs: Background & Objectives Nur77 is a potent transcriptional regulator for both innate and adaptive immunity. A recent study revealed that Nur77 is upregulated in memory-like NK cells upon antigenic stimulation. Nonetheless, the influence of Nur77 on NK cell functionality remains elusive. Present proposal seeks to uncover how Nur77 activation enhances NK cell-mediated immunity and to mechanistically determine how Nur77 confers NK cells the resistance to immune suppression. Methods We proposed to use NCR1(iCre)/NR4A1(fl/fl) transgenic mice for a conditional knockout of Nur77 in NK cells to investigate the role of Nur77 in NK cell-mediated immunity against murine hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) study in vivo. Using human NK cells ex vivo, we will next determine the DNA binding sites of Nur77 via CHIP-sequencing and subsequently perform in vitro validation using immunoassays that confirm the underlying mechanisms for enhanced NK cell activation. Preliminary Findings To highlight the feasibility of the proposal, we performed exploratory experiments to find identify that Nur77 expression is associated with favorable NK cell phenotypes within patient HCC tumors. Using cytosporone B which is a agonistic activator for Nur77, we confirmed that Nur77 activation enhances NK cell activation and anti-tumor immunity both in vitro and in vivo. Preliminary CHIP-sequencing revealed several Nur77-binding targets that supports our hypothesis that Nur77 confers resistance to lipid-mediated immune suppression. Conclusion Taken together, we proposed a study using pre-established models to evaluate the therapeutic potential of Nur77 agonism for its integration to conventional NK cell-dependent immunotherapies particularly in HCC. To the best of our knowledge, our proposed study will be the first to demonstrate how Nur77 renders NK cells better resistance to immune suppression.
kw: Immunotherapy, NK cells, Tumor microenvironment

title: Uncovering the role of complex structural variations in the subtelomere for cardiovascular diseases and cancers.
abs: Genetic variations are known to predispose individuals to a wide range of human diseases. However, the role of complex structural variations (SVs) in disease predisposition remains poorly studied due to the technical challenges associated with analyzing these complex genetic events. Our unpublished work indicates that numerous large ( >100,000 base pairs) and previously unreported complex SVs exist in the subtelomeres of more than half of all chromosomal arms. Given the size of these events and their proximity to telomeres, it is plausible that they might modulate telomere length and predispose individuals to diseases such as cardiovascular diseases and cancers, which are known to be associated with telomere length. Our overarching hypothesis is that complex structural variations in the subtelomere predispose individuals to cardiovascular diseases and cancers by modulating telomere length. To evaluate this hypothesis, we will: (Aim 1) perform a comprehensive analysis of complex SVs in the subtelomere across all chromosomal arms and evaluate their frequency in different ancestral groups; (Aim 2) assess the association of these complex SVs with the risk of cardiovascular diseases and cancers in the SG100K cohort; and (Aim 3) determine if these subtelomeric variations modulate telomere length. The completion of this project could lead to the discovery of previously unrecognized genetic variations that predispose individuals to cardiovascular diseases and cancers.
kw: subtelomere; telomere; complex structural variations; cardiovascular diseases; cancers

title: NIT2 Promotes Liver Metabolic Adaptation to High Fat Diet by Enhancing Mitochondrial Activity to Protect Against Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is a major worldwide health concern that is aggravated by the lack of viable drug treatments. To identify factors that regulate progression to NAFLD, we fed an obesogenic high fat diet (HFD) to non-human primates for more than three years. Multi-omics analysis of the liver of these obese monkeys revealed that Nitrilase Family Member 2 (NIT2), was significantly up-regulated in response to chronic HFD feeding. NIT2 catalyses the conversion of asparagine and glutamine into Krebs cycle intermediates, oxaloacetate and alpha-ketoglutarate respectively. Published reports have shown that glutamine-enriched HFDs suppressed overall fat accumulation compared to standard HFD. Our preliminary data indicate that liver-specific NIT2 over-expression in mice attenuated systemic fat stores even when the mice were fed a normal chow diet. Transcriptomics analysis of NIT2 over-expressing mouse livers showed significantly elevated expression of mitochondrial proteins. Although cytosolic NIT2 cannot directly regulate transcription, metabolites such as alpha-ketoglutarate are known obligate cofactors to histone and DNA methylation enzymes, that can alter gene expression patterns. Based on our preliminary data and prevailing literature, we hypothesize that fat-induced NIT2 expression is an important protective adaptation that suppresses liver lipid accumulation by augmenting mitochondrial activity in response to chronic overnutrition. This work will be foundational for the development of NIT2-specific novel targeted drug treatments against obesity-driven fatty liver diseases. To test our hypothesis we propose the following three specific aims: (1) To investigate the physiological function of NIT2 by liver-specific over-expression or knockdown in mouse models. (2) To investigate the epigenetic mechanisms through which NIT2 promotes mitochondrial protein expression. (3) To explore the mechanism of NIT2 up-regulation by HFD and develop NIT2 targeted therapeutics.

title: Investigating the role of NIK in chronic inflammation.
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Colitis is a chronic inflammatory disorder driven, in part, by NFκB pathway dysregulation. Targeting the canonical NFκB arm with anti-inflammatory drugs (e.g., TNF-antibodies) increases the risk of cardiovascular disease and cancer. I hypothesize that inhibiting the non-canonical NFκB arm, which regulates fewer acute responses, is a potential strategy to manage chronic inflammatory disorders while minimizing side effects. Using genetically engineered in vitro and in vivo model systems, I aim to a) understand the molecular details of the immune microenvironment and signaling pathways regulated by the non-canonical NFκB pathway and b) investigate the therapeutic efficacy by using NFκB-inducing kinase (NIK) inhibitors in chemically induced colitis.

title: Enhancing Metacognition in Adults through a Tech-Augmented Learning Programme
abs: This grant proposal aims at enhancing metacognitive skills in adult learners through an interdisciplinary blend of cognitive neuroscience, educational science, artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML). Aligned with SOL2023 grant priorities, our project underscores the necessity of fostering cognitive abilities and understanding adult brain plasticity in the context of lifelong learning, especially pertinent in rapidly evolving career environments and amidst an aging population. Central to our research is the hypothesis that targeted metacognitive training can significantly improve cognitive abilities, brain functioning and career outcomes in adults. We aim to fill a notable gap in the literature by focusing on adult metacognition within the Asian context, particularly in Singapore. Our objectives include developing a tech-augmented Metacognition Learning Programme to address metacognitive deficits, evaluating its impact on participants’ metacognitive awareness, cognitive abilities and career advancement, using ML to identify profiles of individuals who benefit most from the intervention as well as elucidating the neurobiological underpinnings of metacognitive improvements after the intervention. Our initiative begins with the creation and pilot testing of a Metacognition Learning Programme tailored to adult learners, particularly focusing on those in Singapore's context. This programme will encompass a series of interactive workshops and an AI/ML-augmented mobile app. The workshops, designed by educational experts, will cover various aspects of metacognition, including awareness of cognitive processes, regulation and control mechanisms, and metacognitive experiences. The mobile application, powered by AI, will provide personalized learning experiences, track progress, and offer real-time feedback to users. Following that, we will conduct a randomized controlled trial focusing on 200 participants identified with poor baseline metacognitive abilities. This trial aims to evaluate the efficacy of our Metacognition Learning Programme. Participants will be randomly assigned to either the intervention group, receiving immediate access to the programme, or a waitlist control group, thus allowing for a robust comparison of outcomes. The programme’s impact on metacognitive awareness, cognitive abilities, brain functioning and career outcomes will be thoroughly evaluated. This includes pre- and post-intervention assessments using standardized cognitive tests, metacognitive awareness inventories and neuroimaging data analysis. Advanced neuroimaging techniques, such as MRI and fNIRS, will also be utilized to investigate how metacognition is represented and modulated in the brain. These techniques will enable us to identify specific brain regions and networks activated during metacognitive tasks and track changes due to our intervention. title: Enhancing Learning and Transfer of Digital Literacy in Adult Learners
abs: Self-regulated learning (SRL), comprising the preparation-performance-appraisal cycle, has been found to relate to positive learning outcomes. A more competent self-regulated learner is expected to have a greater ability to assess their learning process accurately and adopt better learning strategies. A major challenge in the transfer of learning is the identification of the similarity between the context where learning takes place and the context where the knowledge will be transferred to. Effective instructional strategies are critical in building connections between these contexts directly or indirectly. Artificial Intelligence (AI)-powered tools have become more accessible to the public, but risks of AI such as hallucination, confabulation or just plain making things up have been identified. AI literacy needs to be cultivated and developed in order to harness the benefits and counter the risks of using the technology. With this contextual backdrop, this research project aims to understand the learning process and learning transfer in adult learners so they can tackle better the challenges in acquiring and applying AI literacy. Three studies are proposed. Study 1 aims to investigate the SRL process and factors influencing knowledge acquisition among adult learners in developing their AI literacy. Sixty participants of different age groups will be recruited. They will undergo a short learning session on developing their AI literacy. They will then be asked to perform AI-related tasks and articulate their thoughts and actions following the Think-Aloud Protocol. The participants will also complete a set of questionnaires to measure trait-level and state-level individual differences in cognitive, metacognitive, and psychosocial variables. We hypothesize that the SRL processes and individual differences will impact knowledge acquisition and transfer of learning differently among the age groups. Study 2 aims to survey the instructional and pedagogical methods used by instructors of AI literacy courses. We plan to interview 30 instructors who teach different levels of AI courses to be interviewed. They will be asked to share on the instructional and pedagogical methods they often use and how these methods are implemented specifically in their courses, the rationale behind their choice, and the challenges that they have encountered with the implementation of those methods. Study 3 aims to investigate the effectiveness of instructional designs in promoting training transfer and to identify the impact of individual differences in trait-level SRL on the effectiveness using experience sampling methodology. We intend to recruit a total of 120 participants from at least 15 AI training courses. The participants will be followed up weekly for 12 weeks. title: Adult Learning for Career Change: Motivating Skills Transfer and Reskilling
inst: IHPC - Institute of High Performance Computing
abs: By 2027, significant number of jobs and skill requirements in Singapore are expected to undergo changes (World Economic Forum, 2023). To adapt, Singaporeans need to learn new skills for career change (i.e., transition into a new occupation). This project aims to foster the cognitive and motivational capabilities of Singaporean adult learners, enabling them to overcome skill adoption challenges related to career change, gain confidence in potential transitions, and actively engage in learning for career change. We will first investigate how domain-specific self-efficacy, specifically career change self-efficacy, predicts learning engagement outcomes pertinent to career change. We will then delve into individuals’ beliefs regarding two dimensions of their skills – existing skills (i.e., awareness of skill transferability) and new skills (i.e., confidence in reskilling). We hypothesise that these beliefs significantly predict the resources individuals possess to surmount the learning challenges inherent in career change, thereby predicting their career change self-efficacy and, ultimately, their levels of engagement in the learning process. Our project seeks to connect the science of learning literature to the socially impactful case of adult learning for career change. Framing this as a self-regulated learning challenge, we focus on the motivational precursors that drive relevant learning behaviours. We also draw on wider behavioural theory to identify likely predictive factors. Using questionnaire-based and behaviourally informed methods, we aim to validate these insights and develop measurement instruments, ultimately providing validated targets for future interventions.
kw: skills transfer; reskilling; belief; self-efficacy; learning; career change

title: Operando Imaging-Guided Catalyst Design toward Oxygen Evolution Reaction
abs: Water splitting using renewable electricity is an indispensable technology in green hydrogen production to realize a sustainable energy landscape, which, however, is impeded by the notorious sluggish kinetics of oxygen evolution reaction (OER) in acidic solutions. Currently, the commercial catalysts for industrial OER are Ir-based catalysts featuring a high cost and scarcity as well as an unsatisfactory activity. To address these issues, Ru-based catalysts have been considered a promising substitute for Ir-based catalysts because the price of Ru is ten times lower while its activity is superior. Nonetheless, Ru-based catalysts still have two major drawbacks: high cost and poor stability. In this project, we propose to overcome the above two challenges by innovating a new class of Ru-based catalysts, i.e., Ni@RuFeCoNiCu, featuring a core-shell structure, a high-entropy alloy (HEA) shell, and tuneable crystal phases. Firstly, the material cost can be remarkably reduced by the core-shell structure and alloying with abundant elements. Secondly, we hypothesized the durability issue can be largely mitigated by the strong atomic interactions of multiple elements and the thermodynamically more stable HEA structure. Thirdly, the activity of Ru-based catalysts can be further boosted by the crystal phase control, alloying effect, and composition manipulation. The synthesis of Ni@RuFeCoNiCu HEA catalysts will rely on a template-directed method while the crystal phase control can be achieved simply by using Ni templates with different phases. To rationalize the structure-property relation for guiding OER catalyst design, we propose to quantitatively map the adsorption pattern of reactive oxygen species and the generation/desorption dynamics of formed oxygen gas nanobubbles on single nanocatalysts through operando imaging techniques. A new spectroscopic technique will be developed to in-situ examine the catalyst durability, which can reach a detection limit of parts per quadrillion. Moreover, we will test the performance of the as-developed catalysts in electrolyzers to evaluate their industrial potentials. In our preliminary results, we successfully synthesized Ni templates with diverse crystal phases and completed the proof-of-concept for the in-situ spectroscopic techniques. The proposed research will not only innovate a new class of cost-effective OER catalysts for advancing green H2 production via water splitting, but also enrich the fundamental knowledge of materials science. The advancement in OER catalysts remarkably contributes to the national targets of net-zero emissions by 2050 and advanced manufacturing.

title: Development of Multiscale Subsurface Imaging Techniques for Geothermal Resource Assessment in Singapore
abs: Singapore's geothermal energy potential has gained significant attention following the discovery of the Sembawang hot spring in 1909 and the observation of above-average underground temperature from recent deep drilling activities. This research project aims to establish an extensive suite of mathematical inversion and imaging techniques capable of accurately interpreting multiple types of geophysical data, shedding light on the seismic and resistivity structures beneath potential geothermal reservoirs. Utilizing advanced inversion theory and high-performance computing (HPC), our approach involves probabilistic joint inversion of multi-type passive seismic data, offering insights into shear wave velocity and seismic anisotropy within the upper 10 km of the Earth's crust. Additionally, an efficient adjoint-state imaging method that incorporates seismic and magnetotelluric (MT) data will be developed to refine geological features in prospective geothermal areas. These techniques enable imaging of the upper crust at various scales, from kilometer-scale geothermal reservoirs to meter-wide fault and fracture zones. The project employs data collected from a nationwide portable nodal seismic array, referred to as SingArray, and 1-2 representative geophysical profiles. The resulting subsurface images will elucidate the geometry, location, and volume of Singapore's geothermal energy sources at depth, guide optimal drilling locations for thermal production, and assess potential microtremor hazards associated with future geothermal exploration. This research project seeks to significantly advance geothermal exploration capabilities in Singapore, laying the groundwork for sustainable and efficient utilization of geothermal energy resources in this country.
kw: Geothermal Energy; Singapore; Inverse Problem; Bayesian Monte Carlo; Adjoint Method

title: A New and Versatile Hardware-Software Interface for Software Security
abs: Classically, processor security features are difficult to redesign, as they are often constraints of legacy software and hardware controls by a handful of popular instruction-set designs (e.g. Intel x86, ARM). Thanks to the recent availability of open-source processor designs, like RISC-V, one can now reimagine the security abstractions offered by general-purpose hardware. We propose to study new hardware-software memory interfaces that caters for stronger security on a RISC-V processor. Our proposal builds on recent advances in secure memory-related ISA abstractions using hardware capabilities. These recent advances offer the conceptual promise of providing a unified ISA interface which addresses multiple security goals that have been traditionally been challenging to get right---secure interposition on all memory accesses, flexible trusted execution environments (TEEs), as well as incremental migration to memory safe code. However, this promise has only been a concept so far, without any concrete demonstrations of hardware implementation of the supporting OS and application stack. In this proposal, we aim to develop concrete techniques to realize the ISA specification and enable how to support existing OSes on such hardware. We also propose to explore novel security defenses and techniques for fine-grained memory safety and coarse-grained data isolation of data in memory. The key challenge lies in redesigning the traditional hardware-software boundary, i.e., rethinking whether hardware or software should perform certain security operations for safety and efficiency. The feasibility of both enabling the new security abstractions in real systems software as well as enabling efficient hardware implementations is our central challenge. If shown to be practical, these works would be the first demonstrations of unified processor interface for securing low-level memory access in a wide range of security contexts. It hopes to offer a viable alternative to the current of deploying piecemeal and varied memory security abstractions across processors and its various generations.
kw: Computer Security; Processor Design; Operating Systems

title: Investigating the function of UFO proteins in cap-snatching viruses
abs: The segmented negative-sense viruses (sNSVs) represent an important group of highly pathogenic human, plant and animal viruses, (e.g. Lassa virus (LASV), Haantan virus (HTNV)). Although these viruses have immense social, economic and health impacts across the world, there are few therapeutic or prophylactic strategies available for many of them. Recently, we discovered a new mechanism by which the sNSVs express novel host-viral chimeric proteins from cryptic open reading frames in their mRNA 5’ untranslated regions (UTRs). These cryptic ORFs, termed Upstream Frankenstein ORFs (UFOs), are expressed as consequences of sNSV cap-snatching activities. The UFO proteins are predicted to be relatively well conserved within viral species. They are also predicted to be recognized by the host adaptive immune system. Taken together, our data imply that (1) The functional proteomes of the sNSVs are much larger than previously thought and (2) Given their high conservation levels and potential immunogenicity, the UFOs could present ideal targets for therapeutic modulation. We have previously established that UFO proteins are expressed and impact viral pathogenicity in Influenza A virus (IAV). However, little is known about the exact functional roles of the IAV UFO proteins in infected cells, and how they affect long term host immune responses to virus. Further functional investigation on host and viral determinants of IAV UFO expression, their biochemistry as well as their impact on the host immune system would not only improve our understanding of IAV biology, but also help uncover novel ways to counter other sNSVs. Hence, the goal of our proposal is to deeply characterize and investigate the physiological functions of the UFO proteins generated by IAV during infection. We will do so by achieving the following aims: 1. Generate molecular tools to study IAV UFOs: In this aim, we will generate and validate recombinant IAV PB1-UFO, PB2-UFO, PA-UFO and HA-UFO UFO-null and relevant control viruses using reverse genetics (Aim 1.1). In addition, we will also generate antibodies that allow us to detect the IAV UFO proteins in their endogenous context (Aim 1.2). These tools will form the basis of our study of UFO proteins during infection in Aims 2 and 3. 2. Investigate molecular functions of IAV UFOs in vitro: In this aim, we will use tools generated in Aim 1 to study the role of UFO proteins in infection. We will investigate the role that cell type and timing post infection affect UFO expression at the transcript and protein levels. We will also investigate protein interactors of UFO proteins (Aim 2.1). Finally, we will investigate the impact of UFO expression loss on viral replication and host responses in vitro (Aim 2.2). Integration of data obtained from these sub-aims will provide us mechanistic insights into the functional role of UFO proteins in infected cells. 3. Investigate role of IAV UFOs on infection in vivo.
