title: Elucidating the Role of P-Cadherin as a Guarantor of Mitotic Fidelity in Epithelial Tissues
abs: Tissue cells proliferate by mitotic cell division. However, while cell division is essential for growth, development, and regeneration, in most adult tissues cell division must be stringently regulated, since unchecked cell division leads to tumorigenesis and is a prime precondition for carcinogenesis. While the core machinery of cell division is conserved through evolution, in different tissue types cell division regulatory networks are fine-tuned by myriad signal transduction pathways to adapt to different biological context. Indeed, in recent years the deviation from the ‘textbook’ model of cell division in different cell types are increasingly appreciated. This is highly relevant to cancer therapeutics since a hallmark of cancer is out-of-control cell division. For inoperable cancer, remaining cancer treatment strategy includes the disruption of various steps in cell division. However, given the highly conserved and central roles of cell division in normal physiological functions, such strategy is notorious for harming healthy cells and giving rise to toxic side effects. A better understanding of mechanisms that drive cell division in each specific biological context is therefore of central importance for improving cancer treatment options. Epithelial tissues are responsible for 80-90% of cancer cases. Thus, in this proposal we focus on mechanisms regulating cell division in the epithelial context. Epithelial tissues are formed and maintained by cell-cell interactions mediated by a large variety of transmembrane receptors, with the cadherin superfamily being of foremost importance in animal development and normal physiology. Conversely, mis-regulation of cadherin is well-known in a broad spectrum of cancer. In epithelia, cell-cell interactions mediated by Epithelial (E)-cadherin is by far the best characterized. However, in many epithelial cell types, Placental (P)-cadherin is also co-expressed with E-cadherin. Intriguingly, while E- and P-cadherin are close homologs that are located directly adjacent to each other on the chromosome and with close similarity in their amino sequences, their functional differences are clearly divergent in both normal and diseased conditions. Case in point, while E-cadherin is widely known as a tumor suppressor, P-cadherin is identified as tumor promoters in a wide variety of prevalent cancers including breast, pancreas, colon, prostate, gastric, and ovarian, where high expression of P-cadherin is strongly associated with poor prognosis. However, despite the prominence of P-cadherin among tumor markers, the molecular mechanism underlying P-cadherin functions and what differentiate P-cadherin from its close homolog E-cadherin remain poorly understood. title: Decoding Organizational Ethical Awareness: Unraveling the Formation and Consequences in the Context of Generative AI
abs: In recent years, the rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has driven significant progress in Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI). By emulating human language capabilities, GAI has unlocked a multitude of applications, ranging from chatbots and virtual assistants to translation services and content-generation tools. Undoubtedly, GAI holds the potential to revolutionize the business world and society in unprecedented ways. However, GAI has evolved into a double-edged sword, giving rise to ethical concerns surrounding transparency, privacy protection, misinformation, bias and fairness, job displacement, and environmental impact. In this project, our objective is to quantify and validate firms' ethical awareness of GAI (FEGAI) and employ econometrics models and quasi-experiments to comprehend its determinants and document consequences. Through these efforts, the project makes a distinctive contribution to the promising trajectory of developing responsible and ethical GAI systems in business, ultimately fostering a sustainable society. The project specifically investigates three key questions: 1. Quantify FEGAI. FEGAI refers to the extent to which firms consider their duties and responsibilities towards stakeholders and shareholders when developing and deploying GAI systems in business. FEGAI encompasses aspects such as the protection of privacy, transparency, bias and fairness, misinformation, job displacement, environmental impact, etc. We aim to quantify the ethical awareness surrounding firms’ usage of GAI from firm-level public disclosures (e.g., SEC filings and earnings conference call) through the application of transformer-based language models such as Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) and Generative Pre-trained Transformer (GPT). 2. The determinants of FEGAI. Our project will further examine the determinants of such ethical awareness using econometric models and possible causal inference methods to understand its formation. Specifically, we first categorize GAI application into three phases: Automate, Informate-up/down, and Transform. Our investigation centers on determining how varying uses of GAI influence FEGAI, underscoring the importance of vigilance and awareness to mitigate potential negative outcomes and promote responsible GAI utilization. Second, we focus on both internal and external contingent factors. Internal contingencies might include ownership structure, corporate governance, top management team (TMT) characteristics, etc. In addition, we also hypothesize that FEGAI is also determined by industrial peer effect as well as macro-level policy uncertainty or environmental uncertainty. 3. title: Mastering Hummingbird Flight: Incorporating AI-based Modeling of Unsteady Aerodynamics and Asymmetric Wing-Tail Morphing for Agile Drone Flight
abs: Sustaining biodiversity is essential for human well-being by securing ecosystem balance. Drones offer the potential to conserve biodiversity through monitoring, mapping, and management, but to do so, will require attributes like discretion, compactness, precise hovering, and in-flight agility. Traditional multi-rotor drones can hover but their lift generation technique (rapid spinning propellers) lacks discretion due to propeller noise, limits compactness, and lacks hover resilience to wind gusts. Fixed-wing drones, however, lack agility and cannot perform fixed-point hovering tasks. Hummingbirds, which are nature’s agile pollinators rely on unsteady aerodynamics generated by flexible wings and asymmetric wing-tail interactions to ensure robust hover and agile maneuvering amid cluttered environments. Leveraging these features can create a promising class of flapping-wing drones that make them suitable for promoting environmental sustainability. However, the complexity of understanding and translating these hummingbird flight mechanisms into a functional prototype is challenged by inherent uncertainties and inaccuracies in dynamics. Consequently, leveraging Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly the implementation of a Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN), is proposed to model these uncertainties and inaccuracies using simulation and flight data. The strength of the PINN approach lies in its ability to incorporate these effects within established dynamic frameworks, mitigating the need for extensive labelled datasets. Furthermore, this approach yields nonlinear models distinct from traditional neural networks or data-driven models, allowing for the representation of unsteady aerodynamics and asymmetrical wing-tail interactions within the hummingbird-inspired dynamic model. By capturing these intricate underlying dynamics, the effects of asymmetric flexible wing-tail morphing on hover resilience and agility will be demonstrated in this proposal by means of a hummingbird-inspired drone prototype.

title: Manipulation of Polar Metamaterials for Efficient Nonlinear Pyroelectricity from Non-Static Waste Heat
abs: The project addresses the critical need for distributed and sustainable energy alternatives by harnessing disordered, distributed, and decentralized waste heat from ambient environments. Utilizing pyroelectric materials for non-static waste heat conversion, driven by sustainable and renewable energy solutions, addresses the underutilization of waste heat from various sources. The research group's pioneering efforts in nanophononics/plasmonic light manipulation and the development of transverse pyroelectrics for nonlinear heat harvesting have positioned pyroelectric heat harvesting technology competitively with organic thermoelectrics and ferro-photovoltaics. Despite advancements, the complexity of spatial-temporal dynamics and mechanisms underlying nonlinear heating in pyroelectrics necessitates further exploration, particularly in manipulating spontaneous dipole moment changes in anisotropic pyroelectrics. The project is structured around several objectives aimed at unraveling the fundamentals of nonlinear pyroelectricity, including i) Investigating asymmetrical thermal and electrical transport behaviors in pyroelectrics under nonlinear heating. ii) Examining spatiotemporal temperature profiles and electric dipole moment changes in pyroelectric metamaterials and composites. iii) Probing operando variations of polarization ripple in pyroelectric metamaterials influenced by active metasurfaces. iv) Assessing the flexibility, scalability, multifunctionality, and techno-economic sustainability of pyroelectric metamaterials. The project aims to achieve exceptional benchmarks, including over 20% relative Carnot efficiency and over 40 mW/m2 electrical output power density in pyroelectric devices, underscoring the innovative potential of this research in energy harvesting. This research is significant for its potential to efficiently convert low-grade environmental waste heat into electricity, contributing to sustainable energy solutions and carbon neutrality. It aims to create new knowledge in utilizing thermal nonlinearity in pyroelectric materials for enhanced energy conversion efficiency and understanding the role of material anisotropy and multiscale thermal manipulation in pyroelectricity. The outcomes are expected to drive future research in sustainable energy recovery and inspire the development of new materials and methods optimized for nonlinear thermal processes. The methodology encompasses the preparation and characterization of pyroelectric metamaterials, hybridization with electronic metasurfaces, and mechanistic and modeling studies. This involves synthesizing pyroelectric metamaterials with optimized compositions, exploring the active tunability of pyroelectricity with electronic metasurfaces, and employing finite element modeling to understand thermal and electrical transport under nonlinear heating. title: Understanding and Projecting Natural Hazards That Endanger Food Production in Southeast Asia
abs: This research aims to enhance food security in Southeast Asia by fostering a comprehensive understanding and providing evidence for decision-making support regarding the impact of climate-driven natural hazards on agricultural productivity. The study begins with the construction of a detailed historical reanalysis dataset, capturing intricate details of major natural hazards such as floods, heatwaves, and wildfires in Southeast Asia. This dataset serves as a foundational resource, providing valuable insights into the historical occurrences and patterns of these hazards in the region. Subsequent efforts focus on employing an intricate machine-learning model, tailored to accurately quantify the impact of various natural hazards on food production. By utilizing historical data and advanced modelling techniques, this facet of the research aims to furnish nuanced insights into the specific risks each hazard poses to different crops and regions. The research further introduces an innovative pseudo-global warming (PGW) modelling framework, anticipating the future manifestation of historical natural hazards under varying climate change scenarios. The subsequent quantification of these hazards' impact on food production, utilizing the established machine-learning model, positions the research as a forward-looking effort with substantial potential for aiding in the development of strategies and policies that enhance climate resilience in Southeast Asia's agriculture. By combining historical analysis, machine learning, and innovative modelling, this research seeks to provide stakeholders with essential knowledge for proactive decision-making amid the challenges posed by natural hazards and climate change.

title: Odorous airborne chemicals in Singapore: Sources and atmospheric processes
abs: Odorous incidents are location specific, challenging to detect and identify their origins and ensuing atmospheric processes. Sufficient understandings of odorous incidents are needed to tackle the issues and enhance the life quality of the public. To address the intermittent and recurrent odorous incidents in Singapore, this study characterizes airborne odorous chemicals regarding their properties, atmospheric chemical reactions, emission sources, and potential health impacts. To deliver the abovementioned objectives, the study approach comprises five major research components, starting with building “Singaporized” database of airborne chemicals associated with the past odorous incidents occurred in Singapore. This will establish a foundational knowledge base to carry out the other four components in parallel. In return, the findings rendered from the other four components are expected to enable the continual update of the Singaporized database. The four concurrent components include (1) developing feasible and effective monitoring of potential odorous incidents, (2) investigating the atmospheric transformation and transport of the emitted odorous compounds through chemical-reaction modelling and simulation of plume dispersion, (3) identifying domestic and cross-border emission sources through an in-house optimized method to apportion emission sources, and (4) assessing potential health risks of exposure to transient airborne odorous chemicals based on questionnaire survey and measurements of cardio-respiratory functions. The new knowledge gleaned from the studies can facilitate the development of mitigation strategies, emergency respondent actions, enhanced air quality surveillance, plans for timely communications with domestic and cross-border stakeholders.

title: Evaluating the Impact of Heat Stress on Outdoor Recreational Activities and Mental Health in Urban Environments
inst: IHPC - Institute of High Performance Computing
abs: The proposed study aims to examine how heat stress impacts recreational activities in Singapore, especially how it affects individuals' decision-making and mental well-being under future climate projection scenarios. Despite the widespread use of air-conditioning in 79% of residential households and most public spaces, outdoor recreational activities remain vital for physical and mental health. Most existing research on heat stress focuses on occupational settings, overlooking its influence on recreational activities. Our study aims to fill this gap through a three–step approach. First, we plan to develop a heat stress model tailored to Singapore’s distinctive hot and humid climate, which will include shading and radiant heat exchange in complex built environment. Second, we will conduct surveys to gauge how heat stress perceptions affect people's activity preferences and mental states. By summarising behavioural patterns of both status quo and potential changes, we aim to synthesise people’s heterogeneous responses to an aggregable level with socio-demographics. This will provide insights into how individuals adapt their behaviour in response to heat stress. Finally, using the heat stress model, we will analyze various future climate projection scenarios, including both the best-case and worst-case situations. Insights from surveys will help in determining preferences and well-being in relation to different recreational facility. The goal is to provide urban planners with insights for early-stage facility planning, enhancing urban liveability and creating resilient spaces that are prepared for climate change. This study not only seeks to bridge a significant research gap, but also to inform practical, future oriented urban planning solutions.

title: Development of high-resolution heat stress maps to assess urban heat island (UHI) effect and public heat risk in Singapore
abs: The continuous increase in surface air temperature has resulted in adverse health risks worldwide, particularly in urban regions. Singapore, with its dense urban development and substantial Urban Heat Island (UHI) effects, is anticipated to face an even bigger challenge on temperature-related risks given the increasing hot days and warm nights under projection. Addressing UHI effect and heat stress on individual heat resilience is crucial to mitigate such climate change challenges. Previous studies assessing UHI intensity relied on stational data records. Due to sparse station-based datasets, spatial uncertainties limited our understanding. Also, various heat vulnerability indices (HVIs) were designed for low-exertion settings and may not accurately assess risks during physical labour, highlighting the need for both kind of HVIs specific to exertional settings in Singapore. To implement effective mitigation policies, developing high-resolution country-level heat stress maps is necessary. The map is essential to consider the impacts of urban morphology, land use, upper-level atmospheric dynamics and population dynamics on UHI effect and individual health risk simultaneously. Leveraging high-resolution climate projection data from NEA, this study aims to characterize historical and future UHI intensity in Singapore, providing novel insights nationwide. Heat stress will be quantitatively analysed by constructing both HVIs considering low-exertion and exertional settings in Singapore. A country-level heat stress map that can provide daily heat distribution and public heat risk with a spatial resolution of 500 m or finer integrating Land-use regression model, machine learning and Doppler LiDAR technology is proposed to mitigate UHI impacts effectively. Ultimately, this research aims to equip the government with a scientific method for timely mitigation strategies, safeguarding public health in a projected hotter world.
kw: UHI effect, heat stress maps

title: The Impact of Climate Change and Heat Events on Health in Singapore
abs: Climate change and global warming adversely impact human health and healthcare systems. Singapore will be vulnerable to future climate warming patterns due to its ageing population and the high burden of non-communicable diseases like diabetes, which compromise thermoregulatory capacity. While Singapore is at the global forefront of research on climate adaptation and preparedness, exemplified by the recent Heat Stress Advisory and V3 climate study, a gap remains in directly linking these climate factors to health outcomes. Baseline data on the current burden of heat-related illnesses (HRIs) is also lacking, without which high quality projections of future HRI burden are difficult to assess. Lack of quality baseline data also complicates analysis of how the population can adapt to future heat trends and the impact of potential intervention strategies. The proposed study seeks to address these knowledge gaps by identifying the baseline HRI burden. The project will align with national health preparedness and resource allocation priorities while further strengthening them with empirical data. A two-year prospective study conducted in the emergency departments of all public hospitals in Singapore will encourage a standardised HRI diagnosis and management workflow to actively identify HRI cases and collect key demographic, situational and clinical outcomes data. A retrospective study based on 10 years of health data compiled in the Ministry of Health OMNIBUS database will compile historical diagnostic records into a bespoke HRI database. The prospective and retrospective HRI case counts will be fed into established forecasting models which will be integrated with V3 climate projection data to estimate future HRI burden in response to future climate trends. Potential intervention scenarios will also be factored into the predictive models to establish the quantitative impact of these interventions.
kw: Climate change, Heat events, health impact

title: Innovation of Recyclable Polyolefin Packaging to Achieve Circularity of Plastic Packaging
inst: ISCE2 - Institute of Sustainability for Chemicals, Energy and Environment
abs: Polyolefin is heavily used in food packaging ascribed to its wide range of physical properties, excellent chemical resistance, high process-ability, good flexibility and heat-sealing property. Its production is energy and resource efficient with low greenhouse gas emission. However, the utilization of mono-polyolefin food packaging is hindered by its poor gas barrier. Therefore, it is always laminated with other materials to produce multi-material plastic packaging to meet up to the requirements of food preservation. However, recycling the laminated multi-material plastic packaging with existing recycling infrastructure is next to impossible. Recently, we have developed a silicate/polymer-based oxygen barrier coating to produce high barrier mono-polyolefin food packaging, even at very low coating weight of 0.3 gsm. In light of this promise, we propose to further develop the silicate/polymer-based barrier technology and produce recyclable polyolefin food packaging to achieve circularity of plastic packaging. The project will be executed along four work packages that will run parallelly. 1) developing washable barrier coating and adhesive which can easily be washed off from polyolefin during recycling; 2) designing and manufacturing recyclable mono-polyethylene food packaging with excellent gas barrier against oxygen and CO2 molecules, even used in high humidity environment; 3) developing recycling technology to produce high quality and food grade recycled polyethylene based on the existing recycling process and infrastructure; 4) designing and manufacturing recyclable mono-polyethylene food packaging from up to 30 wt% recycled polyethylene, including primary packaging and secondary packaging. The developed technologies will be integrated into production through a high-fidelity prototype (TRL 6 or high). The project research aims to provide an innovative and yet practical solution to produce recyclable polyolefin food packaging to replace non-recyclable plastic food packaging which also can be easily recycled.

title: Deep understanding of THGM biology and its Critical role in inflammatory autoimmune diseases
abs: Immune-mediated inflammatory diseases (IMIDs) such as multiple sclerosis (MS) and ulcerative colitis collectively afflict approximately 10% of the population and an increasing prevalence was observed globally. While current treatments are effective in reducing the frequency of relapses, it serves only to alleviate symptoms by targeting immune components playing a role late in the disease, along with poor tolerability and worrying safety profile. Therefore, further understanding the fundamental cause of autoimmunity remains important for development of new and effective therapies. Autoreactive CD4+ T helper (TH) cells are known to play important roles in the pathologies. However, the specific roles and mechanisms by which each TH subset contributes to pathogenesis remained less defined. Inflammatory cytokines such as granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) has long been associated with autoimmunity. Studies substantiated the pathogenic potential of GM-CSF, with knockout (KO) mice and neutralising antibody treatments targeting GM-CSF conferring protective outcomes in animal models of autoimmune diseases such as EAE. However, clinical trials observed that non-specific elimination of GM-CSF increases susceptibility to infections and even exacerbated the severity of some ailments such as Crohn’s disease. Thus, such discrepancies represent a translational gap between bench and clinical settings. Therefore, the identification of the primary cellular source of GM-CSF and determining its pathological influences will reveal potential cellular and molecular candidates that can be explicitly targeted for effective interventions. Recently, a new TH subset which predominantly produce GM-CSF designated THGM has been identified. Accumulating evidences showed that THGM-derived GM-CSF play an important role in the pathogenesis of EAE. In this project, we will elucidate the function of THGM in the pathogenesis of both MS and colitis using T cell-specific GM-CSF KO mice and mouse models of MS and colitis. Findings made will not only elucidate the function of THGM cells in pathogenesis of EAE and colitis, but also deepen our understanding on THGM biology.

title: Energy-Optimized, Situated Instruction Comprehension for Pervasive Assistive Agents
abs: Notable advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities such as natural-language understanding and vision-based perception are driving a generational leap in interactive personal agents, transforming them from pure language-driven interaction (e.g., Apple’s Siri or Amazon’s Alexa) to ones that can reason across a multiplicity of visual, verbal, and gestural stimuli. Furthermore, the substantial penetration of low-cost RGB and light detection and ranging (LIDAR) sensors on pervasive devices has enabled new opportunities to capture and use three-dimensional (3D) real-world spatial information for situated reasoning. However, embedding such situated, multimodal interactive agents on pervasive devices, such as smartglasses and assistive robots, remains a formidable challenge for two reasons that we shall tackle. First, spatial sensors such as LIDAR have considerably high energy overhead to support day-long operation on such battery-operated devices. Second, at present, the Deep Neural Network (DNN)-based AI models underpinning such agent reasoning capabilities are computationally too demanding to be executed on such resource-constrained devices. To overcome the high sensing-energy overheads, we propose to develop two new capabilities that enable continuous, ultralow-power spatial sensing and visual perception. (1) A new decoupled-LIDAR-system concept will be developed where stationary emitters will be deployed in a planned manner within an instrumented indoor space. These emitters will generate light pulses containing spatiotemporal information encoded using visible-light communication (VLC) techniques. Wearable and robotic devices can decipher these received light pulses using a simple spatial array of passive photodiodes to reconstruct information about their dynamically changing 3D environment while achieving a targeted 1000× decrease in power consumption compared with current LIDAR sensors. (2) Emerging event-based (neuromorphic) sensors that provide low-power, fine-grained tracking of scene changes and object dynamics will be judiciously used. By refining AI models to combine such event-based sensor streams with sporadic image data captured using conventional, higher-power RGB image sensors, we believe that such agents will support situated visual perception but with ≥100× reduction in sensing energy. Separately, we propose to develop two innovative dynamic-optimization techniques for reducing the prohibitive computational burden associated with DNN-based multimodal instruction comprehension by such agents. The first technique targets video grounding tasks, which are relevant for situated interactions where users’ instructions or queries involve reasoning over events captured by video sequences rather than single images. title: Understanding the motile to sessile transition in bacterial colonies through mechanics and cell behaviours
abs: Bacterial colonies exhibit intricate collective behaviours for survival. One of such behaviours is the formation of biofilms, which are fortresses built to protect the bacteria from external threats. Along with this process, there is a transition in cell motility: the free-moving planktonic bacteria decrease their moving speed and eventually become immobile. This is reminiscent of a fluid-solid phase transition called jamming transition – once the kinetic energy of a particle is insufficient to overcome the confinement due to its densely packed neighbours, the motion will cease. However, living cells are far more complicated than self-propelled particles. Bacteria sense, communicate, and regulate their behaviours correspondingly. Two fundamentally different mechanisms can cause this motile-sessile transition: the cell pushes hard but cannot overcome the mechanical constraints imposed by its crowded neighbours, or the cell decides to regulate its motility to stop generating propulsion. Our hypothesis is that both mechanics and regulation control this transition, so to fully understand it, the key is to quantify not only cell motility but also cell intention. Our model system is a thin layer of a rod-like bacterium M. xanthus, which can change from a motile, fluidic state into a static, jammed state. The team will use two innovative experimental techniques to characterize cell activity. First, microsphere force microscopy will enable direct quantification of intercellular mechanical stresses. Second, our preliminary results demonstrate that certain fluorescently tagged proteins in the cells indicate both the direction (polarity) and magnitude of their active propulsion. In parallel, we will deploy agent-based numerical simulations mimicking the experimental system. To interpret the results and elucidate the underlying phenomena, we will combine models on active matter and a data-driven approach to map out a state diagram connecting the emergence of large-scale collective behaviours and changes in individual cellular behaviours. This interdisciplinary approach, bridging biology and physics, explores the possibility of advancing the physics of active matter to the physics of living matter, which encapsulates the regulated behaviours of living organisms. Lastly, because biofilms are ubiquitous, a comprehensive understanding of the interplay between mechanical forces and bacterial behaviours can potentially lead to novel strategies aimed at mitigating biofilm-related challenges in healthcare, agriculture, ecology, and industry, and thus benefit Singapore society.

title: An electrochemical cross-coupling approach for carbohydrate synthesis
abs: Carbohydrates are prevalent in naturally occurring and synthetic molecules, and have multiple roles in a wide range of physiological functions. In particular, C-glycosyl compounds have attracted significant interest as robust mimics of the native O-glycosides for potential design of therapeutic agents, or to study important biological processes. However, compared to O-glycosides, methods for the stereoselective assembly of C-glycosyl compounds are less developed. Most synthetic methods take advantage of the direct formation of glycosidic C-C bonds using glycosyl donors via the intermediary of electrophilic/cationic species, anionic species, radical species or organometallic species. Among these strategies, C-glycosylation through glycosyl radicals stands out as an attractive platform, providing access to a range of C-glycosyl products with good control of anomeric selectivity. Despite these advances, critical challenges still remain. Many of these glycosyl radical processes rely on toxic and often air/moisture-sensitive organometallic complexes or reagents, require specialized substrates that take multiple steps to make, and/or utilize excessive amounts of additives or harsh conditions. These problems lead to excessive accumulation of toxic waste that need to be treated. On the other hand, C-glycosylation via glycosyl anions are relatively less explored, and the only reported cases necessitated the use of strong bases for reductive metalation under cryogenic conditions, or expensive rare-earth samarium-based reagents. Organic electrochemistry has emerged as a potentially enabling green technology to produce chemicals with reduced waste under mild conditions. In this proposal, we envision to leverage electrochemistry as a tool to unlock a new mode of reactivity for glycosyl donors to construct C-glycosidic bonds. Through controlled two-electron reductions, our proposed electroreductive strategy potentially generates glycosyl anions in a greener manner under mild conditions without excessive waste formation, which could then be cross-coupled with a vast array of carbon-based electrophiles to form stereochemically pure C-glycosyl compounds. This circumvents the need for toxic metallic and non-metallic catalysts/reagents/additives. Successful implementation will significantly expand the scope of C-glycosyl compounds that can be secured through chemical synthesis, potentially accelerating sugar-based drug discovery programs and glycoscience research to investigate important biological processes, as well as create new opportunities for cosmetic ingredient applications. Preliminary investigations revealed that glycosyl aryl sulfide donors can participate in electrochemical cross-coupling to deliver the desired C-glycosyl product under mild conditions, underscoring the feasibility of our proposal. Studies are ongoing to further optimize these results and evaluate the performance of sulfides derived from other sugars.
kw: electrochemistry; drugs; cosmetics; carbohydrate; glycoside; green chemistry

title: Atomic engineering of zigzag-edged graphene nanoribbons towards next-generation spintronics
abs: Spintronics aims to utilize the spin degree freedom of electrons for new forms of information storage and logic devices.1 Recently, there has been great interest in spin logic devices for high-speed, low-power operation, and spin transistors for reconfigurable logic.2, 3 For this purpose, a major challenge is developing a suitable spin transport channel with long spin lifetime and long-distance spin propagation. It has been predicted that the edge-states of hydrogen-terminated zigzag graphene nanoribbon (ZGNR) exhibit a ferromagnetic (parallel) alignment of spins along either edge of the ribbon while the spins on two opposing edges are antiferromagnetically coupled (Fig. 1a).4 Such spin-ordered electronic states give rise to quantum magnetism, making ZGNR a very promising spin channel material. Technologically, inducing magnetic order, or just magnetic moments is the first step of vital importance for ZGNR to meet the demands of ever-increasing magnetic information storage density by engineering ultimately thin, one-dimensional (1D) magnetic materials. To date, there have been many theoretical studies of magnetic moment modulations in ZGNRs as a result of width-control, heteroatoms doping, twisted bilayer stacking, and the application of electrical field.5, 6 Currently, the bottom-up synthesis approach of graphene nanoribbons with armchair edges is not directly suited for ZGNRs, due to: (i) polymerization of monomers via aryl–aryl coupling takes place along the armchair direction rather than the zigzag direction, (ii) dehydrogenative cyclization of phenyl subgroups is not sufficient to form pure zigzag edges.10 Although tremendous attempts have been made for fabricating ZGNRs with different widths and various edge modifications, only the 6-ZGNR (6 carbon atoms laterally across the ribbon) has been achieved experimentally by far, primarily due to the challenges on the precursor design and synthesis. Moreover, the strong hybridization of the electronic edge states of 6-ZGNR with those of the underlying metal substrate, along with the susceptibility of zigzag edges to undergo passivation through atom-abstraction or radical-recombination reactions, represents a veritable challenge to their exploration in spin-related properties.7 One effective strategy is to introduce a superlattice of isoelectronic substitutional dopant atoms along both edges of 6-ZGNR, which can thermodynamically stabilize and electronically decouple the highly reactive spin-polarized edge states. title: Bridging Chemistry and Biology: synthesis, structure, and properties of Mechanically Interlocked Peptides (MIPs)
abs: Significance to science and medicine The study of Mechanically Interlocked Peptides (MIPs) holds transformative potential for both science and medicine by merging sophisticated chemical design with biological utility. In science, MIPs challenge and expand the frontiers of molecular architecture, enabling the creation of complex, functional structures with applications ranging from nanotechnology to materials science. For medicine, their biocompatibility, stability, and responsive nature present new paradigms for drug delivery systems, therapeutic agents, and diagnostic tools, promising more targeted and efficient treatments. This research not only pushes the envelope of what's achievable in synthetic chemistry and bioengineering but also opens up avenues for peptide therapeutics and advanced healthcare solutions, marking a significant step forward in the quest to solve complex biological and medical challenges. Specific aims The goal of this proposal is to develop innovative chemical synthesis methods tailored for MIP construction, enabling the creation of peptides with precise, stimulus-responsive three-dimensional structures, and to conduct comprehensive study of the physicochemical and pharmaceutical properties of MIPs to elucidate their potential as versatile molecular tools in medicine and beyond. Specifically, the proposal aims at: (1) designing and constructing linear MIPs (peptide rotaxanes); (2) constructing mechanically interlocked cyclic peptides (peptide catenanes); (3) investigating structure and dynamic structural exchange between well-defined co-conformations of MIPs; and (4) investigating pharmaceutical properties of MIPs. Hypotheses Mechanically interlocked molecules (MIMs), developed through chemical synthesis, have paved the way for the creation of artificial molecular machines. Mechanically interlocked peptides (MIPs), developed by the nature, possess remarkable stability and a range of biological functions (e.g., antimicrobial activity, enzyme inhibition, receptor blocking, anticancer properties, and HIV antagonism). Therefore, it's plausible to hypothesize that the chemical methodologies applied to small MIMs could be adapted to construct MIPs. These MIPs are anticipated to mirror the dynamic intercomponent motions observed in their small counterparts, potentially leading to the development of biocompatible molecular machines. Additionally, MIPs synthesized through these synthetic methods are expected to possess enhanced pharmaceutical properties akin to those observed in nature. This research proposal aims to explore the feasibility of using chemical synthesis to create MIPs with dynamic functionalities and improved pharmaceutical traits, paving the way for the design of novel biocompatible molecular machines in chemical research and the development of innovative peptide therapeutics with superior properties in pharmaceutical research. title: Projecting Urban Heatwaves and Building Resilience in Singapore and Southeast Asia
abs: A pivotal challenge confronted by Southeast Asia (SEA) is the intensification of urban heatwaves. During April-May 2023, SEA experienced the unprecedented ‘once-in-200-year’ heatwave, during which many countries set new temperature records of up to 49°C. In comparison to rural and natural land cover, urban areas typically exhibit temperatures 1 to 3°C higher due to the Urban Heat Island (UHI) effect. This effect exacerbates heat stress during heatwaves, resulting in urban temperature increases ranging from 2 to 8°C. In SEA, urban expansion is anticipated to double or even triple by 2050 under fossil-fuelled development pathway. Meanwhile, the severity and frequency of heatwaves is being escalated in the context of global warming. Amidst these dynamics, the intertwining factors of a growing and ageing urban population add a complex layer to the region's risk and resilience landscape. The expanding urban population amplifies the vulnerability to heatwaves. Resilience, on the other hand, is challenged by the simultaneous ageing of the urban population. An ageing demographic potentially strains existing healthcare systems and support structures, making adaptive measures against urban heatwaves more intricate. In this evolving context, comprehensive risk assessment and tailored resilience strategies are imperative to navigate the complex interplay between rapid urbanisation, warming climate, and the associated escalating heatwave threats, as well as a growing and ageing urban population. Our proposal has three overarching goals. Firstly, we will build the physics-based and machine learning-based modelling systems to better understand the characteristics of SEA urban heatwaves. title:
Chronic monitoring neurological disorders in brain organoids based on 
microscale opto-electronic tetherless electrodes (MOTEs)
abs: The proposed technology leverages existing, mature technologies and heterogeneously integrate them to create an autonomous microsystem, which is completely untethered hence is powered and communicate without any wires. Notably, the propose autonomous microsystem vertically integrates III-V optical components (diode or VCSEL) on top of conventional CMOS integrated circuits. The ensuing integration fabrication allows an extreme scaling yet sufficiently complex functionalities to record voltage signals as well as pH. This opens up a unique opportunity to chronically and directly monitor the inner workings of organoids, which has been previously impossible as the conventional means of direct measurement often end up destroying the very physiology it is trying to measure due to either the tethered nature or the unwieldy size. Taking advantage of these merits of proposed autonomous microsystems, we plan to chronically monitor (voltage and pH) intestinal organoids for neurological disorders studies, which has a direct clinical implications for future treatment. A successful demonstrate of such recording will not only advance our understanding of neurological disorders, but it will signal a deluge of autonomous microsystems for biological territories that we have not been able to peek into because of the size constraints.

title: The Impacts of Generative AI on Creativity, Decision-Making Performance, and Agency: Human–AI Collaboration in Problem-Solving and Artefact Design
abs: Generative AI, exemplified by the Generative Pre-trained Transformer (GPT) models, has gained attention for its potential utility in education, such as for offering personalised tutoring, supporting automated grading, and creating content. Nonetheless, there are concerns over its impact on students’ future employment and development of critical 21st-century skills such as creativity, decision-making, and agency (Sundar & Liao, 2023; Zhai, 2022). UNESCO (2023, p. 18) has recently emphasised that “the use of AI technologies in education should enhance human capacities for sustainable development and effective human-machine collaboration in life, learning, and work,” underscoring the importance and urgency of understanding human–AI collaboration and its influence on the development of critical 21st-century skills. Studies have suggested that there are diverse types of human–AI collaboration categorised by varying degrees of contribution from each entity (e.g., high AI contribution and low human contribution, low AI contribution and high human contribution; Liu & Bridgeman, 2023; Ouyang & Jiao, 2021; Sowa et al., 2021). However, this has rarely been empirically validated in education settings. In the proposed project, we will embark on a large-scale empirical study involving 6,000 undergraduates to address these research gaps. Specifically, we will examine the participants’ collaborative patterns with a ChatGPT model during problem-solving and artefact design. We have chosen problem-solving and artefact design tasks because these present major challenges for human–AI collaboration and are common contexts for studying such collaboration (Memmert & Bittner, 2022). The project will further delve into the effects of different collaboration styles on students’ creativity, decision-making, and agency and use structural equation modelling (SEM) to examine how these factors collectively affect individual learning performance while controlling for gender and disciplinary background. We will leverage our 3D Maze platform, which is a web-based tool with an integrated ChatGPT, to gather diverse student data, including 3D Maze logs, design reports, surveys on perceived agency, and indicators of individual learning performance. The 3D Maze platform provides a context for students to apply their computational thinking skills to design and solve mazes, while the integrated ChatGPT enables seamless collaboration with the ChatGPT as students work on the tasks. By clustering students based on their behaviour logs during 3D Maze activities, we aim to identify distinctive human–AI collaboration patterns in problem-solving and artefact design. Meanwhile, the design and problem-solving outputs will be analysed to gauge creativity and decision-making performance. A subsequent comparison of students’ creativity, decision-making, and agency across the distinct collaboration styles will highlight the most effective human–AI collaboration pattern. title: Unravelling the cellular biochemistry of the CO2-fixing pyrenoid from red-lineage phytoplankton
abs: In most marine microalgae, the photosynthetic CO2-fixing enzyme Rubisco is sequestered in the pyrenoid, a subcompartment of the chloroplast. This is essential to allow the organism to elevate the CO2 concentrations around the non-specific carboxylase. Diatom photosynthesis, enabled by its pyrenoid, is thought to account for 20% of global primary productivity. In this project we aim to extend our biochemical appreciation of how the pyrenoid of a marine diatom is structured. We have discovered multiple, as yet undescribed diatom pyrenoid proteins. We will use biochemistry, structural biology and cell biology approaches to understand and recapitulate the protein-protein interactions in the pyrenoid. In parallel we will use Crispr-Cas9 mediated gene editing to generate mutant algal strains, and physiologically characterize their photosynthetic phenotype. The work will contribute to a blue-print of a marine pyrenoid to synthetic biology workers hoping to enhance the photosynthetic efficiency of land plants. It also forms part of the frontier of recent work understanding the principles underlying the subcompartmentalization of cells. In these times when the global carbon cycle has been unbalanced by human interference it can be argued that there is some urgency to carefully characterize and understand the diverse molecular machinery that has evolved on our planet to sequester the greenhouse gas CO2.
kw: Photosynthesis, pyrenoid, Rubisco, carbon dioxide fixation, cellular compartmentalization

title:
Pushing the boundaries of single-molecule interferometric scattering imaging
for precision digital molecular analytics
abs: Conventional bioassays can only report the average behavior of a population of molecules. In such ensemble measurements, valuable subtle information and molecular heterogeneity are lost, resulting in limited detection sensitivity. Recently, digital molecular analytics has emerged to address these issues by constructing individual micro/nano-scale partitions and incorporating signal amplification mechanisms through enzymatic reactions. However, these methods suffer from laborious workflows and their inability to conduct true single-molecule analysis. In this project, we aim to develop a novel digital molecular analytic platform utilizing interferometric scattering microscopy (iSCAT), enabling the detection of biomarkers at low concentrations (even down to the single-molecule level) and the determination of their properties (e.g., molecular weight, hydrodynamic radius, binding affinity with antibodies, and charges) from small-volume biofluids (e.g., a droplet of blood). To achieve this goal, we will introduce new optical system designs (high-speed contrast-tunable off-axis configuration and high-precision confocal configuration), establish innovative detection strategies (characterizing biomolecules on surfaces or tracking their three-dimensional trajectories in motion), and develop advanced signal processing techniques, including solving inverse problems through optimization and machine learning for particle recognition and localization. If successful, our efforts will provide unprecedented opportunities in molecular science and disease diagnosis.
kw: Digital molecular analytics; Interferometric scattering microscopy; Single-molecule imaging

title: Function of ARHGAP12 in the regulation and mechanobiology of epithelial tight junctions
abs: The dynamic regulation of the junctional actin cytoskeleton is critical for epithelial tissue morphogenesis, integrity and plasticity, as well as for the regulation of the paracellular permeability barrier. Tight junctions (TJ) control the paracellular flux of molecules via two distinct and individually controlled pathways: the pore pathway (ion transport) and the leak pathway (macromolecule transport). The pore pathway is regulated by charge and size selective claudin pores, whereas the leak pathway is less selective and is believed to be mediated by transient breaks in the TJ strand barrier. Mechanical forces driven by cortical actin polymerization and actomyosin contractility have been suggested to cause, and indeed subsequently repair, such transient TJ breaches. Since a sustained breakdown of epithelial barriers would have severe physiological consequences, junctional tension needs to be balanced to maintain epithelial integrity whilst permitting macromolecular flux across the TJ barrier. How this balance is achieved is not well understood. Central to the regulation of the actin cytoskeleton are the small Rho-type GTPases (Rho, Rac, and Cdc42), whose activities are regulated by a large number of Guanine Nucleotide Exchange Factors (GEFs) and GTPase Activating Proteins (GAPs). We have recently identified a novel TJ-associated GAP called ARHGAP12, which primarily acts on Rac and Cdc42. Our data show that CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene knockout of ARHGAP12 in MDCK cells delays TJ formation and causes severe defects in epithelial tissue morphogenesis in 3D cultures. Importantly, although ARHGAP12 KO cells form a normal TJ ion barrier in fully polarized 2D monolayers, the paracellular permeability to macromolecules (4KDa dextran) is much reduced. This reduced leak pathway activity is accompanied by an increase in junctional tension, as determined by laser ablation experiments. In other words, TJ in ARHGAP12 KO cells are tighter and under higher tension. This suggests that ARHGAP12 regulates the mechanics of TJ to specifically control the TJ leak pathway. We further find that ARHGAP12 interacts with the actin polymerization factors N-WASP and WAVE2. N-WASP and WAVE2 are Cdc42/Rac effectors that activate the Arp2/3 complex, which induces the formation of branched actin networks at cell-cell junctions and elsewhere in the cell. The interaction is mediated by the tandem WW domain of ARHGAP12 and the N-WASP and WAVE2 proline-rich domains (PRDs), which serve as an important regulatory element in N-WASP and WAVE2 complexes. Intriguingly, the tandem WW domain of ARHGAP12 binds to the N-WASP PRD in a multivalent manner, and this is sufficient to suppress N-WASP-Arp2/3-mediated actin polymerization in vitro. Together our data provide strong evidence that ARHGAP12 links Cdc42/Rac signalling to the control of junctional actin polymerization. Specifically, we hypothesize that ARHGAP12 dampens branched actin polymerization at TJ by inhibiting N-WASP/WAVE2 activatio
kw: Epithelial cells, tight junctions, RhoGTPases, actin cytoskeleton

title: Identification and characterisation of novel nascent chain interacting co-translational factors via crosslinking mass spectrometry
abs: A eukaryotic cell produces approximately 106 proteins per minute. Their accurate synthesis, folding, enzymatic processing, targeting, translocation across membrane compartments, and assembly into protein complexes are critically important for cellular homeostasis. Dysregulated protein biogenesis is linked to many age-related human diseases, including neurodegenerative disorders and cancers. A central strategy cells employ to ensure proper biogenesis of proteins is to initiate the key maturation processes co-translationally: co-translational targeting of translating mRNA to avoid the deleterious effect of releasing the free proteins at inappropriate places; co-translational chaperones engages newly synthesized polypeptides to prevent aggregation and assist folding; co-translational assembly of multi-subunit complexes to avoid non-specific interactions; co-translational quality control pathways prevent the release of toxic aberrant translation products. These co-translational pathways are often implicated in human diseases, but the factors involved are poorly understood, owning to the transient nature of the co-translational interactions and the lack of tools for systematic study. Currently, there is no available method for unbiased discovery of co-translational factors. In this proposal, we combine the use of cell-permeable protein crosslinkers with metabolic labelling of newly synthesized NCs to achieve proteome-wide discovery of NC-interacting co-translational factors. Using this novel Nascent Chain CrossLinking Mass Spectrometry (NC-XL-MS) technique on HEK 293 cells as a proof of concept, our preliminary results identified the majority of known co-translational factors and revealed many potential new co-translational factors in HEK 293 cells. Herein, we aim to functionally characterise novel co-translational factors identified from our NC-XL-MS and study their co-translational interactome in cancer cells. We reason that cancer cells have higher dependency on the co-translational network due to their elevated protein synthesis rate. These results will not only provide mechanistic understanding of the molecular and functional roles of these novel co-translational factors, but also shed new lights into their involvement in disease processes and guide development of potential therapeutic treatments.
kw: Protein biogenesis, co-translational interactions, crosslinking mass spectrometry

title: Distributionally robust submodular optimization: Theory, algorithms and applications
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: Distributionally robust submodular optimization models and solves optimization problems with submodular functions where there is distributional uncertainty. Submodularity is a key property that shows up in applications in machine learning and operations research among others. Our work aims to bring together recent advances in distributionally robust optimization with submodular optimization. Advances in distributionally robust optimization have been primarily along two directions: (a) models that are based on ``data driven’’ approaches by building appropriate balls around the data (empirical distribution) that are assumed to contain the true distribution and (b) models that are based on modelling the ``dependence’’ among the random variables directly but not the full distribution. Most of the models and tractable algorithms here are developed exploiting convexity as a key property with random variables defined over convex sets. Much less is known when the functions are nonconvex and random variables are fundamentally discrete. Suppose we want to compute and optimize worst-case/best-case expected value of submodular functions given only limited information among the dependence of the random discrete uncertainties. Previously introduced notions such as the ``correlation gap’’ provide partial characterizations along this line. To the best of our knowledge not much is known about the behavior of submodular functions with more general notions of dependence information. Developing optimization methods that can characterize the extreme values and plan for it is a natural approach that we hope to pursue in this setting. Furthemore studying sets of distributions where bounds on expected values of submodular functions are providedwill help us to derive tractability results for new ambiguous sets of distributions that have been previously not analyzed in the distributionally robust optimization literature. Submodularity can help go beyond convex functions even for continuous random vectors and possibly develop good approximation algorithms for nonconvex problems even in these settings. Such results will have a direct application on solving optimization problems of influence maximization social networks and pricing and assortment planning in discrete choice models.
kw: submodularity; stochastic optimization; distributionally robust optimization; discrete optimization; machine learning

title: Open-world Segmentation in Space and Time for Long-form Video Understanding
abs: Many video-understanding applications (news search and summarization, smart CCTV cameras, smart glasses, and caring robots for the elderly, etc.) often involve long-form videos of hours or days. Understanding long-form videos is a challenging task that needs to recognize previously unseen objects or events and efficiently process a large number of frames. We propose a video understanding system that addresses these challenges by parsing long videos in a bottom-up manner, which is much more efficient. That is, it will perform (1) Diffusion-based open-world object segmentation in space, (2) Efficient Open-world event segmentation in time, and (3) Long-form video understanding based on spatio-temporal segmentation. For each objective, we will develop the methods based on our preliminary studies, including our previously proposed open-world detection method, generic event boundary detection system, and video-language reasoning models. Such an open-world and efficient video understanding paradigm can be adopted by researchers in various video sub-fields including question-answering, video grounding, etc., opening up a new direction for the whole video understanding community.
kw: Video Understanding. Multimedia. Vision+Language. Video Segmentation. Open-world.

title: Unveiling mechanisms and enhancing pulmonary gene delivery using extracellular vesicles
abs: Pulmonary diseases such as surfactant protein deficiency disorders, cystic fibrosis (CF), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and alpha-1 antitrypsin (AAT) deficiency can lead to lifelong morbidity and mortality. Although the genetic origins of these diseases have been identified, an effective treatment option remains elusive. Gene therapy is a promising strategy that enables the correction of a genetic deficiency by replacing the defective protein with functional copies of it. However, the treatment of genetic lung diseases with gene therapy presents numerous challenges, primarily stemming from the inefficient delivery of therapeutic genes to targeted cells in the lung. An important target for pulmonary-disease gene therapy is the gene encoding cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR). CFTR dysfunction plays a critical role in CF and other common airway diseases such as COPD, non-atopic asthma, and non-CF bronchiectasis. Several gene therapy approaches have been tested to deliver functional copies of the CFTR gene in pulmonary diseases with acquired CFTR dysfunction. However, gene delivery vectors, including virus, liposomes, and synthetic nanoparticles have shown limited efficacy in transducing or transfecting target cell types in the lung. The mucosal barrier in the lungs, along with the cellular defense system, impede the successful transport of therapeutic agents to target cells. Ensuring sustained expression of introduced genes within lung cells presents a challenge due to the dynamic and rapidly dividing nature of respiratory tissues. Additionally, immune responses against foreign genetic materials can lead to insufficient transgene expression. Cellular nucleic acid sensors, like RIG-I and cGAS, can robustly detect exogenous payloads, leading to leading to the inhibition of translation or triggering innate immune responses that ultimately clear cells carrying therapeutic payloads. As a result, the effective dose of DNA vectors is severely restricted, making achieving therapeutic expression with manageable doses a major challenge in gene therapy for genetic lung diseases. Overcoming these challenges demands innovative strategies in gene delivery systems. We have developed a new platform for nucleic acid delivery using extracellular vesicles derived from red blood cells (RBCEVs) and demonstrated that RBCEVs have the potential to deliver different types of nucleic acids to various cell types efficiently without causing any cytotoxicity. Our preliminary data show that RBCEVs can be loaded with DNA or mRNA to efficiently deliver these cargoes to epithelial cells in the lung. Importantly, aerosolized RBCEVs maintain their physical properties and delivery efficiency, enabling direct delivery into mouse lungs using a ventilator. We observed gene expression within the epithelial layer of the lung where many critical cells associated with genetic lung diseases reside. We have also developed a new method for conjugation of

title: Development and Clinical Evaluation of a Bimanual Hybrid Robot Therapist (TheraBot) for Stroke Rehabilitation
abs: Stroke is the leading cause of death for people under the age of 65 and the 5th leading cause of death overall. Every year, 15 million people suffer a stroke, and almost 60% of them will need rehabilitation services. However, there is a global shortage of healthcare workers, making it difficult to provide adequate care to all stroke survivors. In most developed countries, the physiotherapist-to-patient ratio is at 50:1,000,000. The low ratio worldwide signifies a clear need of robotics to provide assistive care to an ageing world population. In Singapore, the number of elderly is expected to triple by 2030, with a decreasing old-age support ratio, This means that the number of stroke cases is also expected to increase. In cases where patients are bedridden for a prolonged period, they may need to undergo long and repetitive therapy sessions. This can be a burden on our therapists, who are already facing manpower constraints. Furthermore, stroke patients require delicate assistance by therapists, and it is difficult to automate these therapy exercises well and safely using traditional manipulators. To address this challenge, we propose the development and clinical evaluation of a bimanual hybrid robot therapist (TheraBot). TheraBot aims to be a safe and effective solution to deliver rehabilitation therapy to stroke survivors in place of conventional physiotherapy sessions, especially when manpower remains a major constraint. It will be equipped with hybrid robotic arms and end-effectors that can emulate human therapists. It will have visuo-tactile intelligence that allows it to "observe" the patient during therapy and provide safe movement assistance, patient motion tracking, exercise performance monitoring, and intent detection. TheraBot could help to give stroke survivors their lives back. It could improve patient outcomes, reduce the workload of therapists, and free up resources for other healthcare needs. We propose a randomized controlled clinical trial to evaluate the clinical and productivity outcome measures of TheraBot. We believe that it has the potential to make a significant impact on the lives of stroke survivors and their families. The specific aims of this project are to: (1) Develop modular hybrid robotic arms with end-effectors that can interact safely with patients' limbs to achieve a range of therapy exercises. (2) Implement visuo-tactile sensing to provide intelligent motion learning, assistance, and assessment for the patient. (3) Evaluate clinical efficacy of TheraBot in a randomized controlled trial involving stroke patients. We plan to conduct this research project and achieve the specific aims across three years through three key phases,: Phase 1: Robot Development with Visuo-tactile Sensing Phase 2: Pilot Testing, System Refinement and early health technology assessment (HTA) Phase 3: Clinical Evaluation Given the track record and experience of our team in soft rehabilitation robotics and associated clinical trials, we ex

title: Structural and Functional Studies of Primed-Adaptation-Complexes (PAC) in Type I CRISPR-Cas3 systems
abs: Type I CRISPR-Cas system employs two distinct pathways for spacer acquisition: naive and primed adaptation1-4. Prior studies have demonstrated that Primed adaptation Complex (PAC) requires the coordinated action of Cas1-Cas2, the CRISPR-associated complex for antiviral defense (Cascade), Cas3, and a historical record of infection by a related pathogen5. This process is markedly more efficient and vital than naive acquisition, facilitating the renewal of the immunity against phages that have evolved escape mutations. Although the genetic prerequisites for primed acquisition have been delineated, the biophysical dynamics among Cascade, Cas3, and Cas1-Cas2 have been less understood. In this proposal, our preliminary findings lead us to assemble and categorize Primed Adaptation Complex 1 (PAC1) containing Cascade-Cas1-Cas2 and Primed Adaptation Complex 2 (PAC2) containing Cas1-Cas2-Cas3 in the type I-E CRISPR-Cas3 system. We have obtained a mediate-resolution structure of the PAC1 complex at 19 Å resolution and a 4.4 Å high-resolution structure of the PAC2 complex. These discoveries support two hypotheses: 1. the binding of Cas1-Cas2 to Cascade to form the PAC1 complex facilitates R-loop formation when guide RNA engages with mutated target DNA. This process triggers the activation of Cas3, initiating the degradation of the target DNA. 2. the formation of the PAC2 complex significantly enhances Cas3’s nuclease activity and simultaneously facilitates the coupling of Cas1-Cas2-driven PAM (Protospacer Adjacent Motif) searching and Cas3-dependent generation of short protospacers. To further our understanding and map out the evolutionary patterns, we have also identified a significant complex PAC3 within the Type I-B system: the ability of Cas3 to form a complex with the Cas4-Cas1-Cas2 complex (PAC3 complex). This finding highlights a conserved feature of PAM recognition in systems containing Cas4, particularly during the Primed Adaptation process. With the support of this proposal's funding, we aim to validate our hypotheses and uncover the intricate processes of Primed Adaptation within Type I-E and Type I-B CRISPR-Cas3 systems, crucial for the acquisition of spacers and the reinforcement of immune responses in CRISPR-Cas systems. Achieve high-resolution structures of the PAC1 complex in both Type I-E and Type I-B systems to uncover the conserved functions and mechanisms of the PAC1 complex. 2. Secure high-resolution structure of the Type I-E PAC2 complex alongside longer protospacer DNA sequences to represent the natural coupling state of Cas1-Cas2-driven PAM (Protospacer Adjacent Motif) searching and the Cas3-mediated generation of short protospacers. 3. title: Understanding cross-talk between envelope assembly pathways in mycobacteria
abs: Mycobacterial species assemble a unique double-membrane cell envelope to protect themselves from external insults and antibiotics. A defining feature of this intricate envelope structure is the mycolyl-arabinogalactan-peptidoglycan (mAGP) complex, where long-chain, branched (C70-C90) mycolic acids (MAs) in the outer membrane (OM) are covalently attached to arabinogalactan (AG) polysaccharides, which are in turn linked to the peptidoglycan cell wall. The mAGP complex is essential for cell viability; therefore MA biosynthesis and transport, as well as AG biosynthesis, are critical, highly conserved pathways in mycobacteria. MAs are biosynthesized as trehalose monomycolates (TMMs) and must be transported to the outer membrane (OM), where they become functionalized into the mAGP complex. While the biosynthetic pathway of MAs/TMMs is well characterized, how these lipids get to the OM remains unknown. Of note, recent studies suggest that TMM transport requires modification in the form of acetylation, a reaction believed to be catalyzed by the putative acyltransferase TmaT. The assembly of AG polymers is also relatively well studied – the key transferases mediating the formation of various glycosidic linkages within the AG polysaccharides have been identified. One such arabinotransferase is the AftD enzyme, which is unique in its ability to interact with the cellular acyl carrier protein, possibly reflecting a general link to lipid metabolism. Despite the importance of the mAGP complex in the mycobacterial cell envelope, nothing is known about how MA biosynthesis/transport may be coordinated with AG biosynthesis to facilitate envelope biogenesis. This proposal outlines experiments to elucidate and characterize the mechanisms for cross-talk between MA transport and AG biosynthesis, specifically examining functional implications of a novel physical interaction between the key enzymes TmaT and AftD in these pathways. We hypothesize that TmaT and AftD require each other for their respective functions, effectively coordinating MA and AG biosynthetic pathways to ensure proper mAGP assembly. In Specific Aim I, we will investigate how TmaT requires AftD for function, both in cells and in vitro. In Specific Aim II, we will investigate whether and how AftD requires TmaT for function, both in cells and in vitro. Finally, in Specific Aim III, we will establish the structural and molecular basis of TmaT-AftD interaction and functional regulation. Collectively, these three aims will deliver new insights into how mycobacterial cells coordinate processes to build its complex cell envelope. Both MA and AG biosynthetic pathways are highly conserved among mycobacterial species and are well-validated drug targets, Given the role of the mycobacterial cell envelope in intrinsic antibiotic resistance and in pathogenesis, this proposal will contribute significantly to the ground work towards the development of novel antibiotics to combat the problem of drug resistance in mycob

title: Controllable metal 4D laser powder-bed fusion printing
abs: In recent years, additive manufacturing, popularly known as 3D printing has transformed traditional manufacturing paradigms, enabling the creation of intricate and complex structures with unparalleled precision. Building upon this foundation, the emerging field of 4D printing introduces the additional dimension of time, allowing materials to adapt and morph over time in response to external stimuli. This research proposal presents a cutting-edge endeavour that pushes the boundaries of additive manufacturing by introducing a new concept of controllable 4D metal printing. The major hypothesis of this research is that the precise control of martensite-to-austenite transformation temperature is key to achieve controllable 4D metal printing. The overarching goal of this proposal is to quantitively control martensite-to-austenite reversible transformation temperatures of nitinol shape memory alloy through 3D printing and structural design. The proposed research will delve into the following three aspects: (1) additive manufacturing processes, (2) Design and algorithm development, and (3) Validation and applications. In the long run, aerospace components, biomedical implants, robotics, and beyond will benefit from structures that autonomously adapt to changing conditions, enhancing performance, safety, and efficiency. Controllable 4D metal L-PBF printing holds the potential to revolutionize industries by ushering in a new era of smart materials and structures that evolve in response to the environment. By addressing technical challenges in 3D printing process, design algorithms, and validation processes, we aim to establish a robust foundation for the development of adaptive metal structures that push the boundaries of engineering innovation. This research proposal thus signifies a pivotal step which is the precise control of phase transformation behavior in the 3D-printed nitinol shape memory alloy microstructure.
kw: 4D printing; NiTi alloy; powder-bed fusion; control; adaptive structure

title: Broad-Range Spectroscopic Investigation of Electronic and Quantum Quasiparticle Dynamics in Unconventional Nickelate Superconductors
abs: The recent emergence of infinite-layer nickelate superconductors has positioned them as an intriguing class of high-temperature superconductors. They offer a rich playground for investigating the interplay between electronic structures, lattice dynamics, and emergent phenomena. Serving as an analogous system that resemble that of unconventional cuprate superconductors, infinite-layer nickelates present an exciting realm for scientific inquiry and technological potential. This proposal delves into the complex relationships between charge, spin, orbital, and lattice degrees of freedom, exploring the speculated mediation of unconventional superconductivity by quantum quasiparticles. This proposed study will integrate a diverse range of spectroscopic techniques over a broad spectral range, including synchrotron-based soft X-ray methods, to comprehensively investigate the quantum quasiparticle dynamics of infinite-layer nickelates. By systematically characterizing structural and electronic properties and assessing the impact of sample preparation and synthesis methodologies, the research seeks to uncover the intricate mechanisms dictating the superconductive features of these materials. The ultimate goal is to provide a detailed understanding of the fundamental electronic properties and their intrinsic connection to the rich array of quasiparticle dynamics in infinite-layer nickelates, thus contributing valuable insights to the field of high-temperature superconductivity.
kw: Unconventional Superconductivity, Quasiparticle Dynamics, Electronic Correlations, Spectroscopic Ellipsometry, Soft X-ray Spectroscopy

title: Towards a Foundation Model for Graph Understanding and Question-Answering
abs: Graphs are a fundamental data type for representing entities and their relationships. Many graphs are also of high commercial importance in industry, including e-commerce graphs, recommendation, fraud detection and finance. Most existing graph machine learning models are only trained on data from a single application at a time, and perform one or a few tasks, limiting their utility and generalization. In this project, we aim to develop a foundation model for graph data, which will generalize across tasks and applications while interacting textually via a conversational interface, using which it can explain its predictions in natural language. In contrast to single-task models, our foundation model will support general graphs from a multiple tasks and applications. Moreover, its conversational interface will make the model naturally explainable and interactive by utilizing textual conversations in natural language. To achieve these goals, a key novelty of our approach is to focus on text as a unifying medium or “bridge” across graphs. Many practically important graphs contain textual information on each node, and can be referred to as textual graphs: e.g., social media, knowledge graphs, etc. Text has relatively consistent meaning across different domains; allowing large language models (LLMs) such as GPT to generalize successfully across a wide range of domains. Hence, using textual graphs as input, we aim to start from a pretrained LLM, and further adapt it into a foundation model which is capable of understanding graphs, allowing for effective generalization across many graph tasks.
kw: Foundation model, graphs, machine learning

title: Robust Nonparametric Methods for High Frequency Data
abs: Asset prices contain a great deal of information about the current status of the economy and economic agents' forward-looking beliefs. The financial markets aggregate the agents' individual knowledge through the enormous number of financial transactions of stocks, bonds, real estates, and currencies. As these transactions occur continuously, the resulting high frequency data allows researchers to gauge the pulse of the global financial market in real time. The development of econometric methods for such data has been an interdisciplinary effort contributed by economists and mathematicians. The PI is a leading scholar on the global stage. The proposed activity advances the PI’s ongoing research agenda in various directions. The new methods will be applied to various high-frequency financial data, including stock prices, interest rates, exchange rates, and futures prices, sampled at the one-minute or higher (up to nanosecond) frequencies. Project 1 is concerned with how to use high-frequency candlestick data to optimally test for price burst. Such test is useful for gauging the impact of news and/or demand shocks on asset prices, including macroeconomic policy announcements, social media news events, and corporate earnings releases. The novelty of the proposal is its use of candlestick data, rather than commonly used returns data. The former contains strictly richer information, and so, allows the researcher to zoom into shorter time windows while maintaining the same level of statistical precision. The proposed approach is also practitioner-friendly as it is closely connected to technical analysis. The theoretical goal is to analyze the optimality of such tests. The method will be applied to study the impact of central bank announcements concerning interest rate decisions and forward guidance, using candlestick data for long-term US Treasury yields and stock market index funds. Project 2 focuses on the uniform inference of the drift coefficient in continuous-time asset price models. The drift coefficient captures the instantaneous expected return of asset prices. Under a standard framework for high-frequency analysis, the drift coefficient is theoretically negligible; however, a recent literature argues that drift can be significant, justified by certain microeconomic reasoning. The available statistical evidence for the latter is flawed due to its reliance on inferential methods that do not adequately control the probability for false discovery. A robust procedure shall be developed by extending the PI’s recent research on approximate finite-sample inference and high-dimensional coupling. The procedure will be applied on a broad set of data to shed new light on this topic. Project 3 extends a recent published paper by the PI in the American Economic Review. The problem is to test whether the spot beta of an asset equals to a target value. The method is particularly relevant for monitoring the tracking performance of “synthetic” assets, such as ex
