title: Corporate Environmental Performance, Human Capital, and Information Management
abs: Over the past decade, there has been a mounting call for enhanced corporate environmental performance from academia and governments. Many governments, including Singapore, have established ambitious environmental objectives; however, translating these goals into tangible outcomes has been a challenge, primarily due to the lack of intrinsic motivation among businesses. In particular, managers have always considered responding to environmental problems as a no-win proposition. Although many firms often recognize the costs of environmental issues for external stakeholders, they may overlook the impact of these issues on internal operations. Our project seeks to investigate whether corporate environmental performance affects issues related to a firm’s human capital, including employee retention, recruitment, and talent quality, which are critical components of firm value. Additionally, it aims to examine the potential negative externalities of corporate environmental incidents on the information environment in labor markets. Our first set of research questions explores whether a firm’s environmental performance affects the likelihood of employees resigning from the firm and of job seekers joining the firm. Moreover, we investigate the underlying mechanisms of this effect by examining whether it varies with personal value and financial risk concerns. Subsequently, our second set of research questions explores whether, in response to employees’ reactions to changes in corporate environmental performance, a firm takes real actions in human capital management or strategically discloses workplace information in the labor market, or both. Regarding real actions, we expect firms to offer greater benefits to retain existing employees to mitigate the costs of employee turnover following environmental incidents. Furthermore, we expect the firm to delay job postings after environmental incidents to mitigate the effects of negative sentiment in the labor market. Finally, we expect the firm to provide greater benefits to attract competent employees after losing high-quality employees due to poor environmental performance. Regarding strategically discloses or information management, if environmental incidents reduce a firm’s bargaining power in the labor market, we expect the firm to strategically offer increased positive workplace information to counteract the potential negative effects of environmental incidents on employee retention and recruitment. Specifically, if the costs of real employee benefits are too high, improvement of environmental performance is too slow, or the job recruiting process cannot be delayed, we expect the firm to be incentivized to engage in information management without sufficient support by underlying performance, termed human-capital information management. Enhanced employment packages and human-capital information management have positives and negatives that become evident through labor flows. Our final set of research questions ex

title: Quantitative electron microscopy of quantum defects
abs: SIGNIFICANCE. Atomic-scale quantum defects largely determine the optical and electronic properties of monolayer semiconductors. The density of point defects in two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors can be well-controlled; vacancies and substitutional dopants are now being engineered to tune the transport properties and single-photon emission, particularly in monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs). These highly-confined, yet tuneable materials are now becoming invaluable for energy and quantum information technologies. However, quantitative, atomic-resolution characterization is required to determine the engineered defects in doped-TMDs, but this remains a great challenge. A few host-dopant combinations can already be measured with the help of aberration-corrected scanning TEM (STEM), and they show a large discrepancy between the measured defect quantification and the nominal (intended) defect density, emphasizing the importance of accurate atomic-resolution quantification. Most of these doped-TMD monolayers do not show much elemental contrast in STEM images, posing a pressing challenge for their characterization and for progressing the rational design of single photon emitters (SPEs) and qubits. It has been found that introducing complex defects to strained single layers of transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) can produce extraordinarily pure single photon emissions, which can be manipulated for future quantum devices. Yet, the types of these complex defects that are important for this behavior remain highly speculative. The novel scientific objective here is to create and investigate these complex defects in two TMDs (MoS2 and WSe2) using a form of high-content electron microscopy known as 4DSTEM. Ultimately, we wish to determine which complex defects create high-purity photoemission and understand the mechanisms for such purity. OPPORTUNITY WITH 4DSTEM. The novel scientific objective here is to create and investigate these complex defects in two doped TMD systems (MoS2 and WSe2) using a form of high-resolution, high-content electron microscopy known as 4DSTEM. Ultimately, we wish to determine which complex defects create high-purity photoemission and understand the mechanisms resulting in such purity. However, 4DSTEM is unwieldy because of technical barriers associated with scalability, complexity, and statistical power. This proposal aims to solve these technical barriers of 4DSTEM by developing a scalable, quantitative, and automated approach to recognizing local motifs, reliably quantifying all quantum defects in 2D materials, automatically separating them by type, and computing their concentration and spatial distribution with a precision of >99%. This work will, therefore, deliver for the first time a rapid, reliable, and quatitative characterization tool for this fast-growing family of engineered 2D semiconductors and quantum emitters. title: Ultrafast laser-induced metastable spin order in low-dimensional quantum magnets
abs: In addition to ground-state phases with least energies, quantum materials frequently host metastable states represented as local minima in the potential energy landscape. These states have distinct properties not found in equilibrium but are rarely populated due to thermodynamic constraints. The search for pathways to access these thermally forbidden electronic orders is a fundamental question in condensed matter physics. Ultrafast laser excitations, thanks to their ability to impulsively drive quantum materials out of equilibrium, have been proven effective in transferring population from ground-state orders to their metastable hidden counterparts. However, experimental demonstration of light-induced metastable magnetism has remained elusive, which is majorly due to challenges associated with the driving and the detection protocols of electron spins encountered by earlier studies. Here in this project, we propose to experimentally realize metastable spin orders in 2D quantum magnets, which involves a laser-mediated transition from the ground-state spin order to another order with a distinct magnetic symmetry. By bringing technical innovations including ultrashort tunable pumping light sources, symmetry-sensitive optical polarimetry probes, and broad-range time-delaying protocols, we will explore unique transition pathways that harness the charge-spin and lattice-spin interactions (WP1 & 2), as exemplified by our unpublished findings in Ca2RuO4 crystals. Further, by leveraging the unique compatibility of 2D magnets with emergent device architectures, we aim at demonstrating the application merit of light-induced metastability by fabricating proof-of-concept opto-spintronic devices (WP3). If successful, the project holds the intellectual merit of expanding the knowledge frontier of out-of-equilibrium quantum matter, a topic of current interest among the condensed matter and the cold atom community. Beyond fundamental science, the demonstration of proof-of-concept devices will showcase, for the first time, the prospect of applying new knowledge on metastability to technologically relevant functionalities. This will potentially deliver next-generation high-speed spintronic and optoelectronic components operating based on fundamentally different physics principles, including those optically controllable components that are way more efficient and versatile than the current technology. title: Constructing precise mechanically interlocked polymers for highly dynamic and functional materials
abs: The proposed research involves constructing precise mechanically interlocked polymers such as polyrotaxanes (PRs) with control over molecular weights, dispersity, microstructure, the density of threaded rings, and ring sequences using a chain-growth ring-opening relay metathesis polymerization. A polyrotaxane is a polymer in which many rings (macrocycles) are threaded onto a polymer chain capped with bulky stoppers at both ends. In recent years, the use of movable crosslinks in PR-based networks has shown promise as an effective alternative for the dissipation of applied mechanical energy, leading to the production of highly stretchable and tough soft materials that have found applications in hydrogels, elastomers, battery binders, and flexible electronics. However, approaches to afford well-defined mechanically interlocked polymeric materials are rare. The proposed new syntheses and designs would significantly advance beyond the work already described in the literature toward the controlled synthesis of PRs. This proposal aims to disclose a general synthetic strategy to afford catenane-based monomers and, subsequently, precise PRs, which may provide a sought-after solution for producing dynamic polymeric materials with many desired functionalities. Key to the success of the proposed work includes a) the development of a general synthetic strategy to afford catenane-based monomers that can undergo controlled polymerization reactions and b) the identification and optimization of effective chain-growth polymerization methods to enable the production of various PRs with a broad scope in term of rings and materials architectures in a well-defined manner. In order to realize these overarching goals, we will pursue the following three specific aims: Aim 1: Designing and synthesizing catenane-based monomers. Aim 2: Developing chain-growth polymerization to afford PRs with control over molecular weights, dispersity, microstructure, the density of threaded rings, and ring sequences. Aim 3: Producing slide-ring polymer networks using PRs or figure-8-shaped crosslinks.

title: Pathways to early literacy in bilinguals' non-dominant language
abs: Overview. For young bilinguals in Singapore, learning two languages simultaneously can present significant challenges, particularly against the backdrop of prevailing language shift diminishing their exposure to Mother Tongue Languages (MTL) in the home environment. The lack of early exposure to MTLs has far-reaching consequences for subsequent language and literacy development. In this project, we endeavor to understand the influence of prior exposure to Chinese oral language and writing system on Chinese word learning among English-Chinese bilinguals in Singapore. In particular, we will investigate the relationship between prior Chinese language exposure and the efficacy of Pinyin, a phonetic system used to aid Chinese character pronunciation. Most research on Pinyin efficacy has focused on populations in which Chinese is the dominant language, leaving a significant research gap in understanding its impact on learners with diverse language profiles. This project tackles this gap and seeks to identify factors that critically contribute to the successful learning of Chinese characters alongside the Pinyin system. To address the challenges faced by young learners with low exposure to Chinese, we further seek to devise evidence-based scaffolding strategies to enhance Chinese word learning among English-Chinese bilingual children of varying language backgrounds and aptitude levels. In short, we embark on this project to investigate the Science of Learning in establishing early literacy in bilinguals’ non-dominant language and more specifically, to identify the pathways through which young bilinguals with ranging exposure to Chinese can attain success in learning the language. Specific Aims and Approach. The first aim of the project is to investigate the relationship between learner’s oral vocabulary level and Pinyin efficacy (Aim 1). Pinyin aids self-directed reading in Chinese by providing a pronunciation guide to otherwise unpronounceable Chinese characters, enabling learners to link a visually unfamiliar word to existing oral vocabulary via its pronunciation. It is thus hypothesized that for learners with low oral language exposure, the efficacy of Pinyin may be limited. In Study 1, children participants will be assessed on their Chinese receptive oral vocabulary and its association to their word learning performance with and without Pinyin will be evaluated. The next aim concerns with the observation that the simultaneous presentation of Pinyin alongside Chinese characters can draw attention away from the characters and impede learning for learners of lower language aptitude, suggesting that the attentional draw posed by Pinyin could be larger for learners who have yet to develop sufficient orthographic expertise in Chinese. The second aim is hence to examine how Chinese orthographic expertise, measured through behavioral and neurophysiological markers, shapes attentional patterns to characters vs. Pinyin and impact Chinese word learning (Aim 2)

title: Integrating adaptive forgetting and remembering in experiential learning
abs: As education progressively moves away from direct instruction towards more reflective, experiential type of learning, it is necessary to examine whether our cognitive strategies align with these new forms of learning. While traditional classrooms put a lot of emphasis on remembering information, in this study we argue that forgetting is, counter-intuitively, of relevance to Experiential Learning (EL) as this type of learning includes a concurrent exposure to irrelevant, unimportant, biased and sometimes inaccurate information alongside the information which should be remembered. Research shows that forgetting is not necessarily a negative aspect of memories and is, in fact, necessary for effective learning. Furthermore, as cognitive capacity is limited, in order to learn optimally, the brain would have to make only relevant memories accessible, while leaving irrelevant information more elusive. Given this characteristic of the human brain, it is important to understand the nature of cognitive processing for knowledge acquisition in the context of experiential learning, by identifying which kind of information should be remembered and forgotten and investigate how learners can remember and forget the information accordingly. In this study, we would leverage on the concept of adaptive memory and hypothesise that integrating adaptive forgetting and remembering contributes to effective knowledge acquisition in the mental health education domain. To test this hypothesis, this study will be guided by the following research questions (RQs): (RQ1) What should be forgotten? (RQ2) Are we able to forget what should be forgotten, (RQ3) Does adaptive forgetting and remembering enhance knowledge acquisition, i.e., forgetting peripheral (e.g., irrelevant, unimportant) information facilitates remembering central (e.g., relevant, important) information? We will answer the research questions through a two-stage design that includes a Delphi study followed by an experiment. In the Delphi study, we will build a corpus of central and peripheral knowledge items by using the Delphi method to elicit experts’ opinions and reach consensus on core knowledge associated with psychosocial interventions. This corpus will then inform the list which will be used in the experiment. In the experiment, we will use the directed forgetting paradigm to test our hypothesis that directed forgetting and remembering enhances the recall of central information. Our participants will be randomly assigned to one of the three groups (i.e., one experimental and two control group). The participants will be asked to study the list we create from the corpus that we build in the Delphi study. The experimental participants will be instructed to selectively forget peripheral items on a list while the control participants will be instructed to either forget central items or remember all items during this study period. Both groups will then be tested after this study period, and we will compare how wel

title: Mechanism-based Design of Programmable Nanoparticle Delivery Vehicles for RNA Therapeutics: Controlling Endosomal Escape
abs: This document proposes a 5-year $23.967M programme to develop innovative nanoparticle delivery systems for ribonucleic acid (RNA) therapeutics. Our goal is to design programmable nanoparticle delivery systems to overcome the endosomal escape (EE) bottleneck and achieve non-liver organ delivery. We shall accomplish this through advancing the fundamental understanding of the dynamics of nanoparticle intracellular trafficking and its correlation to particle formulation. RNA therapeutics are believed to have great potential to treat or prevent multiple human diseases ranging from infectious diseases to cancers to genetic disorders. In addition, RNA therapeutics can be personalised, and act on targets that are otherwise “undruggable” by small-molecule or protein drugs. A primary obstacle to the exploitation of RNA nanomedicine is its delivery. Naked RNAs are negatively charged and are generally too large to enter cells on their own. They are also vulnerable to removal by the immune system and by RNases in tissues. Hence, they require suitable delivery vehicles to reach the cytosol, their target site, for downstream actions. Among various families of delivery vehicles explored, synthetic lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), employed in the recent FDA-approved COVID-19 mRNA-LNP vaccines, are one of the most effective systems. Though synthetic delivery nanoparticles, including LNPs, can enter cells (primarily via endocytosis), they are mostly trapped inside endosomal compartments and remain separated from the target cytosol. Typically, only a small fraction (2-4%) can successfully deliver their cargoes to the cytosol while the remainder is subsequently expelled or degraded. The ionisable lipid used in Moderna’s mRNA COVID-19 vaccine results in an exceptional EE efficiency (~10%). Much higher gene knock-down or protein expression levels (1000x higher) are required to fully realize the potential of RNA nanomedicines for therapeutic and protein-encoding applications. It is generally agreed that EE is a major rate-limiting step for RNA therapeutics. Improvement of RNA delivery efficiency has been hindered by poor understanding of the intracellular trafficking and EE process of nanoparticles and how the nanoparticle composition influences these. This is largely due to the interdisciplinary nature of the EE problem and the technical challenges involved. Cell biologists have found that the intracellular trafficking of native cargoes relies on complex networks of proteins and lipids. However, how these intrinsic regulators are tuneable by synthetic LNPs, and the extent to which the LNPs can influence their pathways and eventual fates, are largely unknown. Further, the relevant sizes and time scales of EE are often beyond the spatiotemporal resolution of conventional optical microscopy. title: Subsea cable sensing for anomaly detection and tide sensing
abs: Distributed acoustic sensing (DAS) has emerged as a transformative technology with significant potential to enhance the sustainability of the built environment and marine environment. By monitoring and analysing backscattered light in optical fibers, DAS can identify and locate disturbances and changes in real-time. Subsea cables, which are the backbone of international data transmission, carry approximately 99% of global communication traffic. They hold great potential for sensing applications, particularly through DAS technology, will offer significant benefits for enhancing the sustainability and resilience of the global infrastructure, as well as improving security, environmental protection, and disaster preparedness. The primary focus of this proposal is to harness DAS technology for two key applications using the dark fiber of the subsea cable within the first repeater. 1. Anomaly Detection and Event Detection of Cable Disturbances: This task aims to assess and develop the capability to detect and localize disturbances along subsea cables in Singapore water. 2. Tide Sensing: This research explores the potential and builds capabilities of novel DAS technology for continuous and distributed tide level monitoring using existing subsea cables.

title: Sustainable Production of Cultivated Meat: Media, Scaffolds and Bioprocess
abs: We aim to advance current state-of-the-art technologies for cultivated meat production process by filling the significant technology gaps. The objectives are structured into four work packages (WPs). Firstly, WP1 aims to develop cost-effective, serum-free media formulations that precisely modulate both growth and differentiation stages to upscale functional biomass for gen 2 product development. A suite of platforms will be leveraged to substitute key components of culture media: A) serum replacement using AI and metabolomics-driven pipelines, B) reducing growth factor dependency via novel small molecule synthesis and phytochemicals, and C) reducing reliance of pharmaceutical grade basal media with plant protein hydrolysate and waste valorization. Next, WP2 will explore plant proteins as new edible biomaterials for scaffolds and microbeads with cost-effective extraction process and functional coatings to enhance cyto-affinities. Subsequently, in WP3, scaffold fabrication technologies such as sugar cube template-leaching methodology and electrohydrodynamic printing will be employed to create sponge-like properties with high porosity and fibrous quality, respectively. Lastly, WP4 aims to integrate these novel outputs and fine-tune them in bioprocesses to validate their compatibility with scaling-up processes, with the objective of demonstrating commercial feasibility up to 10 L bioreactors. Overall, all work packages will comprehensively review their technologies synergistically throughout the entire production process. This feedback and iterative loop within this consortium could serve as the differentiator to develop innovative yet practical industry solutions. Overall, we hypothesize that the objectives proposed by this consortium will present a valuable proposition for industry partners, bringing Singapore significantly closer to achieving its 30 by 30 goals.

title: Development of a vaccine against scale drop disease virus to support barramundi aquaculture in Singapore
abs: The barramundi (Lates calcarifer) farming industry in Singapore faces a critical challenge due to viral infections, notably the emergence of the Scale Drop Disease Virus (SDDV), which leads to significant fish mortality. This proposal aims to further develop an SDDV vaccine for Asian seabass based on the rational discovery of viral proteins that are targeted by protective immune responses. The project is divided into three parts. The first part focuses on developing tools for virology research by establishing a primary barramundi cell line. This cell line serves multiple purposes, enabling virus propagation, the development of an antibody assay, and potentially facilitating the isolation of SDDV or other emerging barramundi-specific pathogens. The second part aims to further identify T cell epitopes in immune target proteins using innovative methods. We will then design vaccine candidates by incorporating both B-cell and T-cell epitopes, with clear GO/NOGO decisions based on data generated in our assays and in vivo experiments. The peptide-based vaccine will be obtained commercially, and the recombinant proteins will be produced in-house. Lastly, challenge trials and pilot implementation of the selected vaccine candidates will be conducted in barramundi to assess their effectiveness and safety. This project will lay the foundation for a platform dedicated to vaccine design and tools for propagating pathogens in the marine environment. This will not only benefit SDDV research but also future studies in aquaculture. The goal is to advance vaccine development with commercial potential, protecting fish from diseases. If successful, this research will significantly impact Asian seabass farming by reducing SDDV impact, enhancing Singapore's food security, and supporting a sustainable future.

title: SALSA: Sustainable Aquafeed for Local Singaporean Aquaculture
inst: SIFBI - Singapore Institute of Food and Biotechnology Innovation
abs: The global demand for aquatic food is set to be primarily fulfilled through aquaculture, but recent years have witnessed notable fluctuations in feed ingredient supply, pricing, and quality. In response, there is a pressing need to identify and thoroughly characterize alternative ingredients. Local food processing generates sidestreams which present opportunities for both protein and carbohydrate-rich alternative ingredients for aquafeed (Table 1), but their incorporation leads to specific challenges. Carbohydrates, especially fibre, are poorly digestible by most farmed fish species which also exhibit minimal nutritional requirements for these components (Table 2). To enhance the circular utilisation of these nutrient-rich sidestreams, the project will focus on developing ingredient pre-treatment technologies using enzymes and microorganisms to improve carbohydrate digestibility and palatability of sidestreams. Identifying optimal processing conditions will involve exploring various feed formulations, extrusion processing parameters, and alternative pelletising methods (such as pellet milling, gelation of wet ingredients, and non-thermal drying) compatible with the pre-treatment technologies, maintaining biological activity, and aimed at cost reduction. The project will investigate the shelf-life, nutritional value and digestibility of the feeds and ingredients in vitro and in vivo. Apparent Digestibility Coefficients (ADC) will also be calculated for selected Singapore-farmed fish species-saline tilapia (Oreochromis mossambicus) and barramundi (Lates calcarifer), chosen for their contrasted protein requirements and abilities in carbohydrate utilisation (Table 2). To provide comprehensive insights into environmental and economic impacts, the project will employ eco-Techno-Economic Analysis (eco-TEA) and Life Cycle Assessment (LCA). The project's final phase will involve comparing the performance of fish, alongside the cost of processing feeds composed of over 70% local by-products, aiming for a target cost of SGD 1.5 kg. The ultimate goal of this project is developing a platform feed technology, capable of bolstering farm productivity, implementing circular valorisation of food processing sidestreams, and advancing food production autonomy

title: Mindful High-Intensity Interval Training Sessions (Mindful-HIITS)
abs: In Singapore, one in three adolescents report experiencing depression, anxiety, and loneliness. Negative affect and mood disorders can seriously reduce individual quality of life, ability to learn, or develop positive relationships. Considering the high prevalence and serious impact of negative affective disorders in Singapore, it is critical to equip local adolescents with knowledge and experience to establish patterns of behaviour that protect their health and promote their capacity for lifelong learning. Exercise and mindfulness training are both valuable interventions that can enhance cognitive function, emotion regulation, and well-being. Their low-cost, modifiable, and scalable nature offer economical practices that can be adopted by schools to enhance student learning. Indeed, teachers in Singapore already try exercise or mindfulness with students in efforts to enhance learning and well-being; however, it is unclear how effectively these practices are implemented and whether there are specific barriers for their success in local schools. Moreover, while there is ample evidence supporting the broad benefits of exercise and mindfulness separately, there is little research examining their combined effects. Combining physical exercise with mindfulness could provide individuals with more holistic skills and benefits for managing their cognitive and affective states, which resonates with recent calls for integrated evidence-based interventions that merge top-down (cognitive) and bottom-up (physiological) approaches to address neurocognitive issues, like negative affective disorders. The proposed project aims to develop and test a novel school-based intervention to improve adolescents’ cognitive and affective functioning through a unique combination of exercise (high-intensity interval training [HIIT]) and mindfulness practice that is tailored for secondary school students over several PE lessons. The proposed programme was designed relative to the local O-level PE syllabus so that the research and intervention may be delivered in a way that can integrate, support, and possibly enhance the goals and purposes of PE in Singapore. The combined mindfulness and HIIT sessions (Mindful-HIITS) will be further developed and tested in collaboration with secondary schools to investigate its impact and optimise its potential for scaling and translation in the local context. Chronic (pre- vs post-) and acute (diurnal) intervention effects on lower secondary school students will be evaluated in a cluster randomised control trial using a science of learning approach, incorporating measures of neurocognitive function (EEG), physiological function and arousal (e.g., HRV), classroom behaviour, and momentary self-report questionnaires to investigate how combining mindfulness and HIIT can improve physical and mental processes that support effective emotion regulation and well-being. title: Neutrophil phenotyping in community acquired pneumonia and its association with disease severity and post-infectious sequelae
abs: Background: Community acquired pneumonia (CAP) is a major cause of sepsis and acute respiratory distress syndrome, with high mortality and morbidity. Neutrophils are integral components of the innate immune system, and are increasingly recognised to influence disease trajectory and outcomes in CAP. Specific aims: (i) To characterise neutrophil phenotypes in patients with CAP across varying disease severities; (ii) To investigate neutrophil phenotypes in different etiologies of CAP i.e. viral, bacterial and viral and bacterial co-infections; (iii) To explore longitudinal changes in neutrophil phenotypes from the acute to convalescence phase. Hypothesis: (i) There will be an increase in immature neutrophils in CAP, which correlates with disease severity. These immature neutrophils will display various dysfunctional phenotypes, with both hyperactivated and immunosuppressive profiles; (ii) Viral, bacterial and viral and bacterial co-infections will display distinct neutrophil phenotype both cross-sectionally and longitudinally; (iii) There will be differences in neutrophil phenotypes in patients with severe CAP compared to non-severe CAP on longitudinal follow up. This will be associated with development of nosocomial infections and late post-infectious sequelae. Methodology: Blood and/or respiratory samples from CAP patients in the acute and convalescence phase will be collected from the Respiratory Infectious Research and Outcome (RESPIRO) study. Neutrophil phenotypes will be characterised by: (i) differences in receptor surface expression using flow cytometry; (ii) measurement of neutrophil granular proteins; (iii) cytokines/chemokines; (iv) neutrophil extracellular trap formation; (v) mass spectrometry-based proteomics; (vi) single-cell transcriptomics; and (vii) functional assays such as chemotaxis and phagocytosis. Dynamic changes in neutrophil phenotypes over time will also be examined to determine association with recovery versus development of nosocomial infections and post-infectious sequalae. Clinical significance: Delineating the contribution of the various neutrophil phenotypes to disease severity across various etiologies of CAP over different time points, will allow rational development of adjunctive therapies to attenuate the dysfunctional responses.
kw: neutrophil, phenotyping, community acquired pneumonia, pneumonia severity, post-infectious sequelae

title: GENEKIDS-PRO: Genomic Enhancement and Patient Engagement in NEphrology through Multidisciplinary KIDney Genetics Clinic Implementation and Integration in Singapore – using PROcess Evaluation Framework.
abs: A multidisciplinary kidney genetics clinic has demonstrated significant clinical utility and cost-effectiveness. However, the degree of clinical utility varies across different healthcare settings, and integrating kidney genomic services globally remains a significant challenge due to the complexity of the process. This study aims to refine and improve a multidisciplinary kidney genetics clinic at a tertiary hospital. We will evaluate the quality of kidney genomic care in terms of effectiveness, timeliness, and patient-centeredness for adult kidney patients and their families with genetic kidney diseases. Additionally, we will use a process evaluation framework to identify key determinants of successful implementation in terms of acceptability, appropriateness, feasibility, and degree of fidelity. We will also study the mechanisms of impact and the context of implementation. This will be achieved using an effectiveness-implementation hybrid type 1 design, quasi-experimental, with mixed quantitative and qualitative approaches. Healthcare providers and researchers acknowledge that the effectiveness of evidence-based interventions often diminishes in real-world settings due to various contextual determinants. Therefore, successful implementation of kidney genomic clinical services is crucial to achieving maximum intervention impact. Poor implementation can lead to less desirable outcomes and negative unintended consequences, known as "Type III" errors, where interventions are deemed ineffective due to improper implementation. The success or failure of these interventions also depends on their impact on three key groups: recipients, deliverers, and decision-makers. Ensuring equitable and ethical impact on all these groups is essential for a successful intervention. This study is critical to ensure maximum impact on both implementation strategies and patient outcomes. The evidence generated can be used to mainstream and incorporate kidney genomic medicine into the Singapore healthcare system, ensuring sustainable and widespread adoption in the future.
kw: Multidisciplinary Kidney Genetics Clinic; Kidney Genomic; Genetic Kidney Disease; Nephrology; Implementation; Process Evaluation

title: Developing and Delivering Topical RNA Therapeutics for Inflammatory Dermatoses: focusing on Atopic Dermatitis
abs: Background: ~30% of the world’s population have skin conditions. Inflammatory diseases constitute most of skin diseases, of which atopic dermatitis (AD) is the most prevalent. RNA therapeutics hold great potential for the advancement of dermatological treatments. We have commercialised a siRNA-dissolvable microneedle patch, and our preliminary studies on our anti-sense oligonucleotides (AONs) have demonstrated positive results. Goal: Aim: To develop and validate topical RNA therapeutics that inhibits the TH2 pathway in inflammatory dermatoses, through cellular, tissue and animal studies. We will focus on AD in this project, with the proposed therapies comprehensively addressing the 3 pathogenetic components in AD – inflammation, itch and skin barrier defect. Specific aims: 1. To design and validate small interference RNA(siRNA) nanoplexes embedded in a dissolvable microneedle patch that reduce IL-4, 13 and 31 as a novel RNA therapeutic for AD. 2. To design, validate and formulate liposome-complexed antisense oligonucleotides (AONs) in a moisturising lotion down-regulating IL-4Ra receptors, IL-13Ra1 receptors and lfTSLP (long form of Thymic Stromal Lymphopoietin) as a novel RNA therapeutic for AD. Hypotheses: 1. The siRNAs nanoplexes embedded in the dissolvable microneedle patch can be delivered transcutaneously to T cells and can effectively silence the translation of IL-4, 13 and 31 to ameliorate TH2 inflammation. 2. The liposome-complexed AONs in a moisturising lotion can cross the defective skin barrier in AD and are able to reduce the production of IL-4Ra, IL-13Ra1 and lfTSLP in resident skin cells to ameliorate TH2 inflammation. Impact: The proposed therapies for AD, a highly-prevalent inflammatory skin disease, can create a significant positive impact for patient care in the clinics and healthcare in the population.

title: Brain-computer interface (BCI)-guided upper limb neurorehabilitation for acute stroke with the recoveriX system
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Background: Brain-computer interface (BCI)-based neurorehabilitation has been demonstrated in previous studies to significantly reduce functional impairment in stroke (both hemorrhagic and ischemic strokes). Stroke causes disruption of the corticospinal tract, and BCI offers a means to electrically bypass nervous system lesions by reading out patients' movement intents from their cortical signals through electroencephalography (EEG) and using processed and decoded signals to re-establish control of their own stroke-paralyzed limb through end effectors like neuromuscular functional electrical stimulations (FES) or exoskeletons. Such a closed-loop control system has been shown to induce significant neuroplastic changes to aid stroke recovery. Existing BCI trials included predominantly patients with chronic stroke in whom functional recovery has plateaued despite conventional physiotherapy, but evidence of its efficacy in acute stroke (defined here as the first 3 months post-stroke), where neuroplasticity is at its highest, is still lacking. Hypotheses: We hypothesize that the early introduction of BCI-based neurorehabilitation within the first 3 months post-stroke will be beneficial in reducing stroke-induced upper limb impairment. Methods: We aim to perform a feasibility study for the use of the recoveriX system, a commercially FDA-approved system that has been validated in stroke and multiple sclerosis rehabilitation, to facilitate functional recovery post-stroke. The recoveriX system comprises an EEG head cap, processing software that automatically calibrates and decodes patients' EEG signals during imagined movement (motor imagery, MI), and a functional electrical stimulator (FES) to trigger muscle contractions on the detection of MI. Patients would undergo BCI-based rehabilitation using the recoveriX system for 15 sessions in total delivered over 3 to 4 weeks (4-5 times/week), supervised by trained occupational therapists, in parallel with standard occupational therapy. Efficacy is measured with functional outcomes such as Fugl-Meyer Assessment score, and BCI performance measured through decoding accuracy. The collected EEG signals will be analyzed.
kw: brain-computer interface; brain-machine interface; neural interface; BCI; recoverix; neurorehabilitation

title: Development and Testing of a Digital Psychological Toolkit to improve Symptom Burden in Dermatology Patients
abs: Skin diseases can significantly impact the quality of life (QoL) and morbidity of individuals, causing physical symptoms such as skin flaking, itch and pain, as well as psychological distress. Inflammatory diseases like eczema and psoriasis are chronic and cyclical and the lack of curative treatments highlights the importance of adaptive coping strategies. Our research reveals that QoL impairment in dermatology patients is greater correlated with psychological constructs such as emotional representation of disease, social comparison and resilience, and less with objective disease measures. Despite this, there are limited strategies and interventions available to target psychological constructs in routine dermatological clinical practice. To address this need, we are currently developing and piloting a multimodal digital psychological tool kit to be self-administered on a mobile app. This intervention adapts evidence based psychological and behavioural techniques for dermatological patients, and targets selected constructs and needs identified from our previous study. In this multicentre double blind randomised controlled trial, we assess the effectiveness and implementability of this intervention in 700 patients with chronic inflammatory skin disease. The primary outcome is the DLQI (a dermatology specific QoL measure), secondary outcomes include generic QoL measures, objective disease severity, measures of psychological constructs such as resilience and anxiety, and disease perception including acceptance and illness coherence. Implementing such an intervention can be a useful adjunct to standard medical therapies. Moreover, it is designed to be scalable at low cost, thereby potentially improving not just patient reported outcomes, but also healthcare efficiency and value.
kw: behavioural health; patient-reported outcomes; implementational science; health economics evaluation; mixed method; psychodermatology

title: Characterization of Vehicular Emissions in Singapore
abs: Traffic emissions are widely recognized as major contributors of air pollutants with adverse impacts on public health and climate change. Singapore, characterized by rapid urbanization, a dense population (7,800 people/km²) and a large vehicle population (~1 million) makes vehicular emissions a major air pollution source (NEA, 2023). Therefore, obtaining a comprehensive understanding of traffic emissions, encompassing both exhaust emissions and non-exhaust emissions, is considered a cornerstone of effective local air quality improvement strategies. Traditionally, traffic emission factors, which estimate emissions per distance travelled or fuel consumed, and related emission inventories have been developed through laboratory-based methods. These methods include engine dynamometer tests and chassis dynamometer tests, both conducted in controlled laboratory settings. The tests are based on standardized driving cycles, such as the New European Driving Cycle (NEDC) or Worldwide harmonized Light-duty vehicles Test Cycles (WLTC), which serve as the foundation for emissions testing. However, such standard cycle testing is often considered unrepresentative of real-world driving conditions for two primary reasons. Firstly, conventional test cycles fail to capture the diversity of real-world driving behaviors and local traffic conditions, leading to inaccurate results (Jing et al., 2022). Hence, creating driving cycles tailored to local conditions is of practical importance. Secondly, research has shown significant disparities between parameters measured during standard cycles and real-world journeys, including differences in acceleration trends and frequent off-cycle events (Hu et al., 2023; Hung et al., 2007). This inability to accurately reflect real-world driving can distort emission estimates, especially in areas where off-cycle driving behavior predominates. Emission factors derived from dynamometer-based procedures and conventional test cycles often significantly differ from those observed in field studies, typically underestimating emissions (Liu et al., 2021; Rahman et al., 2021; Ropkins et al., 2009). Pollutant emissions of road vehicles depend on many parameters including vehicle weight, engine capacity, fuel type, exhaust aftertreatment technology, driving pattern, environmental conditions, road gradient and the level of maintenance of the vehicle (Fontaras et al., 2014). Furthermore, dynamometer studies have revealed that engine loading exerts a significant and often nonlinear impact on emissions (Ropkins et al., 2009). This raises uncertainties about whether emission trends observed in dynamometer test cycles would correspond directly to real-world emissions when applied to specific vehicle fleets, given the diverse range of driving patterns in real-world conditions. While much research has focused on engine exhaust particulate matter (PM) emissions, substantial progress has been made in reducing them through advancements in engine combustion

title: Multifunctional and Adaptive Green-Grey Shorelines (MAGGShore)
abs: The global urbanisation of coastal cities, particularly those in Southeast Asia, is rapidly changing how shorelines evolve in function and morphology. Spatial planning must support local ecological health, socioeconomic objectives as well as provide protection against rising sea levels and more intense storms that put low-elevation and land limited countries at risk. In the challenge that is building multifunctional and adaptive coastal defences, designs must stem from innovative research to identify locally-relevant strategies for improving current and future coastal protection. This requires a multi-pronged approach: 1) We will approach construction and engineering requirements for low-carbon multi-functional coastal protection systems using green and lightweight building materials, hydrodynamic modelling, and testing for structural integrity. 2) Our designs will include factors that influence the settlement, colonisation and succession of marine life on sea defences, employing biofilms for larval colonisation, multi-scale biodiversity-complexity relationships, and experimentally transplanting habitat-forming fauna and flora. 3) Current and future coastal defences must provide ecosystem services, such as recreation and education, to ensure both ecological and societal benefits. Assessing the perception of these coastal ecosystem services through surveys and outreach will allow for two-way facilitation of knowledge. 4) With the foundational knowledge collected throughout these projects, the next generation of adaptable retrofitted biodiversity enhancement units can be designed, 3D printed and assessed for use of new applications and materials. Agent Based Modelling will also identify optimal locations for shoreline enhancement. 5) Ultimately, we will prototype full-scale hybrids coastal defenses. Integrating eco-engineered seawalls and the broader waterfront will be achieved via architectural design and technology solutions to improve implementation and functional characteristics. Guidelines for future architectural design strategies for multi-functional coastal protection systems are the overall aim of this proposal to fulfil the end-goal of how Singapore’s future coastal defences can sustainably harbour higher biodiversity, ecosystem functions and human interactions. Leveraging a decade of urban marine research and world-class architectural and sustainable design technologies, our approach will define the relative trade-offs of alternative design options to support decision making. Our overall is to deliver transformative system-wide recommendations and creating innovative designs for adaptive coastal protection while simultaneously placing Singapore on the forefront of sustainable, functional protection systems for both human and ecological communities in the tropics.

title: Targeting tyrosine hydroxylase against alpha-synuclein relevant neurodegeneration in Parkinson's disease
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common age-dependent neurodegenerative disease with progressive dopamine (DA) neurodegeneration in PD brains. PD results in high rates of disability and the need for care, especially for older people. The α-synuclein (α-syn) is an established PD biomarker and therapeutic target. The α-syn protein is prone to form deleterious protein aggregates and it is the primary structural component of Lewy bodies in PD patient brains, including sporadic and familial forms of PD. In our preliminary study, we have shown that the neurotoxicity of wild type (WT) and mutant α-syn to DA neurons can be endogenous DA dependent and inhibition of Tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) by α-methyl-L-tyrosine (α-MT), a clinical grade competitive and reversible TH inhibitor, can rescue α-syn induced neurodegeneration of DA cells. The α-MT is an orally TH inhibitor, which has been used for multiple human disorders, including hypertension-linked phaeochromocytoma and Dystonia, Dyskinesia and Huntington's disease. The low dose α-MT treatment on human subjects has been shown to be safe with no significant side effects even after prolonged time (3 years) usage. Furthermore, the application of α-MT can protect against LRRK2 mutations and other PD factors induced DA neurodegeneration. In this proposal, we suggest for the first time to test and validate whether early-stage application of TH inhibitor α-MT can protect DA neurons against WT and mutant α-syn induced DA neurodegeneration in our transgenic Drosophila and human midbrain organoid PD models. The successful execution of the current study and achievements from this project will help pave the way for future application of TH inhibition as a new therapeutic strategy against DA neurodegeneration in PD.
kw: tyrosine hydroxylase, dopamine, alpha-synuclein, neurodegeneration, alpha-MT, therapy

title: Softer Meals that Impact the Life of the Elderly (SMILE)
abs: BACKGROUND Age-related changes such as taste alterations, xerostomia, reduced mastication, poor dentition, and swallowing difficulties (dysphagia) have been found to adversely influence the consumption of food. Dysphagia, a geriatric syndrome with a prevalence of 30-40% among elderly aged over 65 years, has been linked with impaired nutritional intake. To maintain oral nutrition and prevent aspiration, textured modified diets (TMDs) are recommended for individuals with dysphagia. However, consistent evidence has shown that TMDs have lower energy and protein content, are sensory unappealing and have altered taste. AIMS AND HYPOTHESIS We aim to 1) evaluate food intake among elderly with chewing and swallowing difficulties on TMDs, 2) use a novel enzymatic method to develop a range of TMD soft meals that are visually appealing, tasty and nutritious, 3) evaluate food intake and acceptability of the textured-modified soft meals. METHODOLOGY We plan to conduct the project in 3 phases. Phase 1 aims to profile the community elderly with chewing and swallowing difficulties to understand food choices and taste preferences. Phase 2 involves the development of TMD soft meals based on results from Phase 1, using an innovative enzymatic modification method. Phase 3 involves the conduct of a food intake study to determine food intake and acceptability of the TMD soft meals developed in Phase 2. FEASIBILITY AND IMPORTANCE TO SCIENCE We are working with St. Luke’s Eldercare (SLEC) in this study as they have a range of elderly whom we can recruit for Phases 1-3. Working alongside various healthcare professionals (dietitian, speech therapist as well as kitchen chefs in SLEC), the multi-disciplinary approach enables the integration of various capabilities to develop TMD soft meals that are well-accepted, visually appealing, nutritious and safe for swallowing. The know-how in the development of TMD soft meals can be rolled out and adopted across different healthcare sectors.
kw: Dysphagia; textured modified diets; elderly; nutritious

title: Potential of Artificial Intelligence to Track and Predict Cognitive Impairment in Stroke Rehabilitation
abs: Cognitive impairment is a common consequence of stroke, significantly impacting survivors' quality of life and functional independence. Current approaches to assessing cognitive function in stroke survivors, such as the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), have limitations, including infrequent assessments, subjectivity, and limited accessibility. This project aims to develop an automated system using natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning techniques to enable early detection and longitudinal monitoring of cognitive impairment in stroke survivors. The proposed system will predict MoCA scores from speech samples, allowing for remote screening and tracking of cognitive function. We hypothesize that subtle changes in language usage, discourse patterns, and conversational behavior can serve as reliable indicators of cognitive impairment. The system will employ state-of-the-art automatic speech recognition models to transcribe speech recordings and extract multimodal features, including acoustic and linguistic characteristics. Advanced machine learning models, such as random forests, support vector machines, and deep neural networks, will be trained on the multimodal feature set to predict MoCA scores and detect impaired cognition based on clinically relevant thresholds. The system's performance will be rigorously evaluated using metrics such as correlation coefficients, ROC curves, and classification accuracy. A pilot study involving 20-30 stroke survivors will be conducted to assess the system's feasibility, usability, and ability to capture relevant features. The study will compare the system's predictions with standard cognitive assessments and establish proof-of-concept. The successful development and validation of this automated cognitive assessment system have the potential to revolutionize the management of cognitive impairment in stroke survivors, enabling early intervention, personalized monitoring, and improved patient outcomes. The system's accessibility and potential for remote assessment will address the limitations of traditional cognitive screening tests, ultimately contributing to the well-being and quality of life of stroke survivors in an aging population.
kw: Cognitive impairment, Stroke rehabilitation, Automated assessment, Natural language processing, Machine learning, Predictive modeling

title: Crosstalk between immune-endothelial cells in the pathogenesis of endometriosis
abs: Endometriosis is a debilitating chronic condition that affects one in ten women during reproductive age. Management of the chronic pain patients experience and its associated subfertility incur significant socio-economic burden in par with other chronic diseases such as diabetes mellitus. Endometriotic lesions represent a complex micro-environment comprising several infiltrating cell types, with immune cells and their associated dysfunction featuring prominently. Treatment options are limited due to the poor understanding of the pathophysiology of the disease. Therefore, it is important to delineate the basic units of this disease in order to introduce improved therapeutic interventions and reduce associated ailments. In our proposed study, we aim to map the immune and non-immune cell types pervading the endometriotic lesions (endometrioma) at the single-cell level and determine the interaction of immune cells with the neighboring endothelium and their implications in disease progression and immune-surveillance.
kw: Immunology; cells; endometriosis; pathogenesis

title: Performing Complex Adaptive Tasks More Eﬃciently with Autonomous Quantum Agents
abs: From vehicles navigating busy streets to trading algorithms seeking sustained profit, the tasks we seek to automate are growing ever-more complex. To achieve satisfactory performance, autonomous agents designated for such tasks must make decisions accounting for information in the distant past -- forcing their complexity to grow in tandem. Indeed, recent AI models reflect this trend, where memory requirements have amplified two hundredfold in two years, leading to immense training costs and unsustainable energy demands. All such autonomous agents, however, store relevant past information in classical bits and make decisions using classical computation. Recent advances in quantum computing open the possibility for quantum-enhanced agents, where past features are stored within qubits in quantum superposition, and future decisions are made by leveraging the unique capabilities of quantum information processing. This project will explore this potential via three central questions: To what extent can quantum agents perform complex adaptive tasks with less energy, memory, and data resources than classically possible? How can we employ current and emerging quantum technologies to design these quantum agents? And how might quantum agents reshape what tasks we consider complex, especially those of significant practical or conceptual importance?' By project conclusion, we will have concrete designs of quantum agents that (a) are deployable within existing quantum technologies, (b) perform complex adaptive tasks of practical or fundamental interest, and (c) demonstrate improved performance in memory, energy, or data-limited regimes. Thus we will uncover entirely new domains in which quantum technologies will leave a permanent mark.
kw: Quantum Computing; Complexity Science; Quantum Information Theory, Quantum Thermodynamics; Quantum Machine Learning

title: Merlin: Development of Robotic Systems for Safe and Efficient Facade Maintenance with Close-Range and 100% Visual Inspection Approaches
abs: Facade maintenance is a crucial task for ensuring the safety and longevity of buildings, but it can be difficult and dangerous to accomplish. In this project, we aim to develop two work packages, namely, a) a fleet of drones enabled with intelligent flight automation software customised for 100% visual inspections, and b) a cable driven robotic system (CDRS) for safe and efficient close-range facade inspections using non-destructive testing techniques. The close-range inspection system consists of a cable driven robot equipped with cameras and non-destructive testing techniques (thermal imaging, infrared imaging, and ultrasound) for façade defect detection. The multi-degrees of freedom manipulator arm system can navigate and inspect the facade of a building at close-range through occluded areas. The CDRS enables capturing high-resolution images and data that will enable the accurate identification and mapping of existing defects. Moreover, 100% visual inspection will be enabled through a fleet of drones equipped with optical and infrared cameras. Flight missions will be defined by an automated path planning software enhanced by ground control capabilities to autonomously operate the fleet and capture imagery data. The collected data will be uploaded to the cloud where 3D reconstruction, defect detection and classification, and masking will be performed using AI-driven technologies, including photogrammetry techniques and convolutional neural networks. The resulting defects will be mapped on the 2D (facades) and 3D environment and presented to the user through an online platform. This project leverages on expertise from industry and academia. Our proposal combines the market experience and field expertise of H3 Dynamics leading facade inspection solutions across Singapore and the region, and the research and development expertise in building custom reconfigurable robotic platforms for maintenance tasks at Singapore University of Technology and Design. The solution developed will adhere to the Standard Guide for Conducting Inspections while improving efficiency, reducing time and cost associated with facade maintenance, and ensures safety of the building, occupants, and operators.

title: Dispersion Analysis and Simulation for Handling of Future Fuels
inst: IHPC - Institute of High Performance Computing
abs: Adopting alternative fuels like ammonia, methanol, and hydrogen to decarbonize energy and transportation sectors is vital in combating climate change. Recent trials in Singapore with methanol bunkering and ammonia combustion on ships highlight the progress. However, safety remains a key concern due to the unique risks associated with these fuels, such as ammonia's toxicity and methanol's flammability. This proposal aims to address these safety challenges in handling those future fuels. As molecules, ammonia and methanol are not new in the industries. From cargo to energy source, complexity and consequences of accidental releases increase. Modelling and simulation need to take into account complex multiphysics such as two-phase release, liquid pool formation and evaporation and plume dispersion driven by wind and current. Importantly for risk assessment and mitigation, it entails answering a number of questions in practical operations such as model accuracy, safety boundaries, effectiveness of mitigation measure, speed of response in emergency as well as design of innovative safety features for newly built vessels running on future fuels. To further enhance model-based risk assessment and mitigation of accidental leakages, the proposed programme delves into three key areas. First, it aims to enhance understanding and quantification of two-phase release from accidental leakages providing more accurate input conditions into all the models for plume dispersion in air and water. This involves considerations such as solubility of two-phase mixture in water, vapour-droplet interaction as well as effects of humidity on vapour dispersion process. Secondly, the programme seeks to improve predictability of coupled models for plume dispersion in air and water taking into account input from atmospheric and ocean environmental condition through monitoring stations or forecasted data. Validating these models with experimental data specific to tropical conditions such as those found in Singapore is crucial in building confidence for the model-based risk assessment approach. Thus, a phase gated experiment campaign will be designed and carried out in this project to provide reliable data for validation of the model while ensuring safety and integrity of assets. Lastly the programme addresses challenge of enhancing speed of the prediction and leakage detection to facilitate the development of effective incident response and preparedness in emergency. This involves development of hybrid physics-based and data-driven surrogate models with high fidelity simulation data through data reduction techniques and advanced regression methods. It is believed that the surrogate modelling approach will greatly improve speed of the prediction while balancing the accuracy when training with physics-based high fidelity data. title: Development of a symbiotic ectomycorrhizal community to enhance growth of Dipterocarpaceae species
abs: The relationship between Dipterocarp trees and ectomycorrhiza (EcM) fungi is poorly defined in Southeast Asia, and understanding this axis can improve the both the conservation of the natural ecosystems in Singapore and urban renewal efforts. Composed of three work packages, this proposal harnesses modern metagenomic and transcriptomic approaches to understand the myriad factors affecting the relationship between Dipterocarps and EcM fungi. The first Work Package will produce a comprehensive dataset of Dipterocarp trees and their associated EcM fungi, microbes, and environmental data. Metagenomics will be used to generate reference sequences of fungi and EcM, and root transcriptomics will be used to identify growth-associated biomarkers. An association study will identify specific growth-associated microorganisms, pathways, and environmental factors. The second Work Package will produce a symbiotic community of EcM fungi and microbes that improve Dipterocarp growth. Based on the results of the association study, in vitro assays will test the effects of healthy/unhealthy soil, single organisms, and prototype communities on Dipterocarp growth, using root transcriptomics to monitor growth-associated biomarkers. Finally, the third Work Package will produce a set of guidelines, policy, and application methods informed by in natura assays, in which the symbiotic community is applied to select Dipterocarp trees in forest and urban areas across Singapore, and growth monitored. Not only is this project feasible given the funds and timeframe, but it will also further Singapore's goal to conserve its natural capital and restore natural traits to urban ecosystems. The resulting symbiotic community can be used by Nparks in conservation and restoration efforts, and there is a commercialisation opportunity if the community also enhances crop growth.

title: RISE-M: Regulation Competencies for At-rISk Adolescents: Social Well-bEing & Neurophysiological Markers
abs: One’s regulation competency play a critical role towards positive self-development, and adaptation with changing contexts and represents a core human construct that is positively correlated with direction, meaningfulness, and satisfaction in life. In the context of a post-pandemic world, regulation competencies are more critical than ever as underlying mechanisms of well-being. Recent evidence has highlighted the interconnectedness of social well-being with broader regulatory competencies. The problem is exacerbated in at-risk populations, where individuals facing adversity, such as those from low socioeconomic backgrounds, or with early-life stress, experience unique regulation challenges that have been found to impact the development of self-regulation skills and contribute to increased risk-taking behaviors, externalizing problems, social stigmatization or isolation. In the context of Singapore's educational landscape, the presence of mental health challenges, in conjunction with the rising lifetime prevalence of mental illness, and the economic burden of stress-related illnesses in Singapore (~$3.1 billion), begets a serious need for research and interventions that can contribute to not only individual well-being, but so too informing therapeutic practices and shaping positive social relationships. In this study, we focus on the relatively understudied dimension of regulation competencies and social well-being which stems from their recognized significance as pivotal aspects influencing the well-being of adolescents, given the critical role that social factors play in shaping the developmental trajectory of adolescents. Specifically, we will enact i) a baseline investigation of the regulation competence profiles of adolescents in Singapore, and ii) implement and examine the feasibility and efficacy of a RISE-M intervention across different profiles to provide valuable information for practices and strategies that are targeted towards regulation competence developments in adolescents. Given the notable gap in research that quantifies and delineates the impact of differential regulation competencies on social well-being outcomes, the study also seeks to investigate and validate hypothesized differential neurophysiological markers of regulation competencies.

title: Tree-Root Anchorage and Non-Destructive Tests for Trees in Constrained Urban Planting Spaces
abs: Trees in the urban environment compete with infrastructure for space. Often trees in the urban environment grow in constrained planting spaces and sometimes infrastructural development may further compromise their root systems. In addition, there is a growing trend for skyrise gardens in residential and commercial buildings. Trees in skyrise gardens can grow on a shallow soil substrate or a container. Hence, trees in the urban environment may have less healthy root development and are at greater risk of tree failures due to windthrow. This problem is exacerbated by the stronger winds and heavier storms expected in light of climate change. Hence, it is necessary to evaluate tree anchorage resistance for better management of the trees in the urban environment. There are more studies on anchorage resistances of trees in the forest and less studies on anchorage resistances of trees in the urban environment. A tree is a complex living thing, and the root architecture varies among species and even trees of the same species. The anchorage resistance of a tree is the sum of many components. Hence, the whole tree structure needs to be first mapped. In this project, the below ground biomass (root system) will be mapped using ground penetration radar and sonic tomography using a deep learning framework to develop a 3D model of the root system. The above ground biomass (trunk and crown) will be mapped using photogrammetry and developed into a 3D model. In situ probing tests will be conducted to determine the strength of the soil around the tree. Non-destructive and destructive load tests will be conducted on the tree. Such tests have not been standardised and there is still some controversy on using non-destructive test to determine the tree anchorage resistance. The tree response will be measured using on tree instruments such as inclinometers, triaxial movement sensors, and strain meters and measuring the load and inclination of the applied load. The data acquisition system which is suitable for the non-destructive and destructive tests will be developed as part of the process. The tree response will be analysed and evaluated against the 3D model of the tree. Numerical modelling will be conducted where the non-destructive and destructive tests will be used to calibrate the numerical model. The validated numerical model will be then used to conduct parametric study to determine the influence of various scenarios such as roots constrained against an underground structure, damaged roots, and roots in a container. The results from the numerical study will be used to formulate guidelines and standards for non-destructive and destructive tests. Such guidelines and standard will be beneficial for the community as it provides all the stakeholders (arborists, building authorities, policy makers, and building and landowners) an urban tree management plan with a scientific basis.

title: Aquatic pathogen challenges: investigating innovative solutions for enhanced disease resilience in barramundi and shrimp: non-lethal heat shock, functional feed, and recombinant peptides
abs: Barramundi (Lates calcarifer) and Pacific white shrimp (Litopenaeus vannamei) are key farmed species experiencing rapid growth in production across Asian waters. However, they face the challenge of numerous pathogens. For instance, Singapore's barramundi farms have identified nine persistent harmful pathogens leading to significant mortalities (Fig. 1). Amid the imperative to reduce antibiotic use in animal production, there is an urgent need for new and effective prophylactic and therapeutic measures to sustain production. In tropical aquaculture hatcheries, non-lethal heat shock (NLHS) is the most common preventive approach, involving short-term water-heating protocols (Fig. 2). However, its mechanisms and efficacy are still poorly understood. In recent years, alternative treatments from Singapore companies, such as immune-enhancing functional feeds (Adisseo) and recombinant peptides (Recombinetics) and, have shown promise, but their mechanisms of action and efficiency require comprehensive analysis. The current project is designed to assess the effectiveness of these treatments in enhancing survival rates (Table 1) against two significant industry-related diseases: Scale Drop Disease Virus (SDDV) for barramundi, and Early Mortality Syndrome (EMS) for Pacific white shrimp. The research will explore the associated immunity mechanisms by assessing the gene expression of heat shock proteins (e.g., Hsp70, Hsp90, Hsc70) and several candidate innate immunity genes (e.g., interleukins, Toll-like receptors, interferon-alpha, antimicrobial proteins) using RNA-sequencing. Blood and haemolymph samples will be analyzed to measure immunity markers during infection. Finally, microbiome diversity will be comprehensively examined through DNA sequencing. These disease challenges will be conducted in BSL2 research facilities for which TLL recently obtained authorization from the NUS IACUC committee, marking a significant milestone as Singapore's first authorized aquaculture disease challenge research. This initiative seeks to improve fish disease management in Singapore's aquaculture industry, offering insights into immunity mechanisms and practical solutions for farmers.

title: Microbes hungry for dessert: discovering gut-brain substrates that mediate craving
abs: How can a healthy adult eat ~1,000,000 calories each year, yet experience little or no change in body weight? Our brains not only see, hear, smell, taste and feel the world around us, but also sense our inner self to regulate our internal states. The workings of our internal senses remains a core mystery of biology. To strategically unravel our internal biology, we wonder: how does our gut, and the bacteria within, communicate with our brain? Our preliminary insights hint that gut microbes mediate food craving, and the emerging literature shows that the gut-brain axis has access to pleasure centres in the brain. Indeed, my pioneering work in this nascent field demonstrated that ingested sugars and fats engage the neural conduit from the intestines to the brain, and they coax the brain to want to consume more (Nature 2020; Nature 2022). However, we lack clarity on how neural circuits for food reward are modulated by the expansive biochemical milieu harboured by the trillions of microbes within the intestinal tract. Here, in another bold leap forward, I propose to investigate how microbiota-associated chemicals engage the gut-brain dialogue to tune our motivation for palatable food. I will leverage my expertise on the gut-brain axis and combine state-of-the-art approaches from neuroscience and microbiome disciplines to uncover and characterise gut microbial elements that modify hedonic feeding circuits (Aim 1) that influence food craving (Aim 2) via gut-brain signalling (Aim 3). Once we understand at a mechanistic level how gut microbes influence food craving, I envisage that we can engineer healthier innate eating habits by designing appropriate prebiotic, probiotic, or post-biotic gut interventions that would dynamically moderate our cravings via our internal gut-brain dialogue. Through use-inspired basic research on gut-brain biology, I also envision that modulating the brain from the gut will become a breakthrough therapeutic method in many areas of biomedicine and human potential, including conditions that range from obesity to mental health.
kw: Neuroscience; Microbiome; Gut-brain axis; Food craving; Microbe-host interaction; Neural circuits & behaviour

title: Vertical van der Waals superlattices. Quantum materials and technologies of tomorrow.
abs: The concept of vertical superlattices was proposed by Leo Esaki in 1970. Originally, they consisted of 2D electron gases (2DEGs) periodically stacked on top of each other and separated by thin dielectric spacers. Such superlattices were proposed as a platform for hunting Bloch oscillations induced by the ballistic motion of electrons through multiple Brillouin zones, which should result in tunable radiation including THz and infrared (IR) wavelengths. Currently, it is a big problem for the semiconductor industry to produce effective radiation sources within this wavelength range (THz gap), while these wavelengths are needed for multiple applications ranging from security and medical diagnostics, finishing with vehicular cruise control and remote sensing of the pollutants in the atmosphere. Unfortunately, there was no unambiguous observation of this beautiful effect in classical superlattices. Despite that, this direction itself was incredibly fruitful in terms of novel phenomena and applications. In particular, vertical superlattices were successfully utilized as a main building block for quantum cascade lasers (QCLs) and IR detectors, and such studies also led to the discovery of the giant magnetoresistance effect, which is utilized for computer memory applications. Unfortunately, there are quite a few fundamental problems with existing vertical superlattices which limit research possibilities and further development of functional devices. Those problems potentially can be solved by using van der Waals (vdW) materials. Over the last two decades, the rapid development of the research dedicated to vdW materials has brought to light several hundreds of 2D materials with very versatile electronic properties. They can be combined by the simple stacking technique and form an atomically smooth interface between each other. Here, I propose to utilize the latest developments in the field of vdW heterostructures to create novel artificial three-dimensional (3D) materials based on vertical vdW superlattices. Such superlattices are promising systems to look for robust Bloch oscillations and for the development of novel efficient THz radiation sources (e.g. QCLs) and detectors. Even more, in contrast with previously studied superlattices, by using atomically thin dielectric spacers or interlayer twist angles it is possible to create vertical superlattices with extremely strong interlayer coupling which will allow the formation of the 3D band structure. Our novel artificial 3D materials are the platform to create 3D flat bands, which will result in novel 3D quantum materials including high-temperature superconductors and topological insulators. So far, all the research dedicated to vdW materials was essentially 2D and the availability of a novel completely unexplored class of 3D systems, which are designed based on our knowledge acquired in 2D - will certainly attract the interest of a broad community of researchers. title: Portable multimodal seepage detection and evaluation system by integrating super wide band electromagnetic wave technology with ultrasound technology

abs: This project aims to develop an accurate and comprehensive evaluation method for detecting water seepage and leakage paths in underground (UG) Infrastructures, so that optimal repair strategies can be targeted to the type of leakage diagnosed. title: Studying virus structures inside infected cells
abs: To date, most structural information on viruses are that from in vitro purified samples. Little is known about the virus infection events inside cells. Recent developments in cryoelectron microscopy (CryoEM) has made the determination of in situ structures possible. In this proposal, we will set up the infrastructure and the know-how to determine virus structures inside cells. We will study influenza (IAV) and dengue (DENV) viruses as they are important human pathogens and they represent two distinct structural classes of viruses. The specific aims are (1) to study the virus infection cycle, and (2) to optimize existing procedures and develop new methods for in situ virus structure determination. For IAV, we will study the virus structures during (A) the entry process - attachment and uncoating, and (B) during virus replication, transcription, packaging and budding. For DENV, we will study the structures of DENV (A) during cell entry – cellular attachment and fusion with the endosomal membrane, (B) the virus assembly and (C) maturation processes. Results generated from these studies could help in the design of therapeutics against these important diseases.
