Using fresh CRC patient samples, patient-derived xenografts (PDXs), and CRC organoids and cell lines, we find that high iron-(Fe3+) levels directly drive CRC pathogenesis by reactivating the dormant hTERT promoter, thereby leading to high activity of the immortality enzyme, telomerase. We identify Pirin (PIR), a cellular iron sensing protein as a key regulator of hTERT reactivation in an iron-(Fe3+) dependent manner. We also identify a small molecule inhibitor, SP2509 that competes with iron-(Fe3+) binding to PIR and hence blocks this pathway specifically in cancer cells with high iron-(Fe3+). Blocking transcription by PIR blocks hTERT reactivation and is a novel way of inhibiting this enzyme for which no enzymatic inhibitors are in the clinic. We aim to 1) delineate how iron-(Fe3+)-PIR levels molecularly drive CRC pathogenesis, by spatially resolving the cell type-specific roles of PIR- iron-(Fe3+) dependent transcription in high and low PIR/iron cancers at single cell resolution, 2) recreate and study the changes seen in aim 1 using genetic and organoid models, and 3) identify small chemical inhibitors of this pathway that may be developed for CRCs and other iron driven cancers (such as hepatocellular cancers; HCC).
kw: Cancer; CRC; Fe3+; Pirin; NF kappa B; tumour microenvironment; Telomerase; hTERT promoter mutations

title: Targeting muscular S6K1 to improve muscle function for healthspan extension.
abs: Maintaining muscle functions is essential for healthy longevity. The mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) is indispensable for muscle growth during development. Yet, hyperactive mTORC1 accelerates muscle aging, whereby inhibited mTORC1 by rapamycin in later life improves muscle health with age. Potentially adverse side effects resulting from “off-target” inhibition have prevented the long-term use of rapamycin as a therapy for aging in humans. Thus, identifying the direct target of mTORC1 inhibition-mediated healthy longevity is highly desired. Our preliminary data in old mice demonstrate that muscle-specific deletion of mTORC1 target ribosomal protein S6 kinase beta-1 (S6K1) preserves motor performance and lean body mass resistant to age-related decline. While alleviated motor functions could result from the improved functions of skeletal muscle, heart, or both, aged S6K1 muscle knockout mice preserved muscular capacity and were significantly protected against cardiac hypertrophy, a similarity to lifelong exercise training. Reminiscent of lifelong exercise training, aged S6K1 muscle knockout mice also improve systemic fatty acid metabolism, reducing age-associated obesity and hepatic steatosis. In addition, muscular S6K1 deletion also attenuates cardiac hypertrophy induced by mTORC1 hyperactivation in adult mice coupled with increased survival, signifying the vital role of mTORC1-S6K1 in pathological cardiac hypertrophy development. This proposal aims to explore the therapeutic potential of intervening in S6K1 signaling to promote muscle health. We hypothesize that diminished muscular S6K1 activities preserve metabolic flexibility and promote the survival of myonuclei, maintaining muscle health similar to long-term endurance exercise training (Aim 1). The outcome of this study can validate mTORC1-S6K1 as a therapeutic target to promote healthy longevity (Aim 2). Our preclinical work raises the exciting potential of targeted therapy to improve muscle health.
kw: sarcopenia; exercise; metabolism; cardiac hypertrophy; aging

title: The role of human CRL4 E3 ubiquitin ligase complex in neural stem cell proliferation and brain development
abs: Neurodevelopmental disorders, encompassing conditions such as microcephaly, affect approximately 5% of the pediatric population in Singapore, contributing significantly to intellectual disability, epilepsy and developmental delays. Our prior research, supported by NMRC, underscored a crucial role of the Cullin 4 (Cul4)-RING E3 ubiquitin ligase complex (CRL4) in Drosophila brain development. Furthermore, loss of dcaf1/mahjong, the substrate receptor of the CRL4 complex, led to a microcephaly-like phenotype in Drosophila. However, the role of human CRL4 during human brain development remains unexplored. This study aims to address this gap by unraveling the novel role and mechanism of human CRL4 E3 ligase complex in brain development, with a specific focus on neural stem cell proliferation. Additionally, we propose to model DCAF1 variant-associated microcephaly in human cerebral organoids. Our central hypothesis is that the human CRL4 complex plays a crucial role in neural stem cell proliferation by negatively regulating the tumor suppressor CDC73. To address this hypothesis, we propose the following specific aims: Specific Aim 1. Investigate the function of human CRL4 in neural stem cell proliferation; Specific Aim 2. Model DCAF1 variant - associated microcephaly in human cerebral organoids; Specific Aim 3. Investigate the role of mammalian Parafibromin/CDC73 in neural stem cell proliferation and its functional link to CRL4. The feasibilities of this study are strongly supported by our preliminary studies. The outcomes of this project are anticipated to provide significant and unprecedented novel insights into the functions of the human CRL4 complex and CDC73 during brain development, shedding light on the mechanisms underlying CRL4-associated neurodevelopmental disorders.
kw: Neurodevelopmental disorders, CRL4, Parafibromin/CDC73, neural stem cell proliferation, autism, microcephaly

title: Normative Whole-Cortex Excitation-Inhibition Activity Ratio Trajectory Over the Human Lifespan and its Disruption in Alzheimer’s Disease
abs: Healthy brain function requires a delicate balance between neural excitation (E) and inhibition (I), known as the E/I activity ratio. The homeostatic set point of E/I ratio changes over the lifespan, with deviation from the normative trajectory contributing to many neuropsychiatric disorders. Studying E/I ratio in-vivo in humans is challenging due to limitations in non-invasive neuroimaging techniques. Previous in-vivo human studies of E/I activity ratio utilized indirect putative markers of E/I ratio limited to small portions of the cortex and focused on neurodevelopment. Therefore, normative cortex-wide E/I activity ratio trajectory across the lifespan remains unknown. Here, we propose to collate 8 overseas and 5 local datasets comprising more than 50,000 participants across the human lifespan. We recently developed an approach to non-invasively estimate a putative marker of whole-cortex E/I activity ratio from resting-state functional MRI using a biophysically plausible large-scale circuit model. In AIM 1, we will use our putative E/I ratio marker to estimate normative cortex-wide E/I ratio trajectory over the lifespan. In AIM 2, we will investigate whether deviation from the normative E/I ratio trajectory relates to cognitive ability among healthy individuals. Finally, in AIM 3, we will investigate the hypothesis that abnormal tau and Aβ levels are associated with higher E/I ratio. Furthermore, we will investigate whether higher E/I ratio increases the risk of progression from mild cognitive impairment to dementia. Overall, our proposal provides new insights into how the E/I ratio (1) evolves over the lifespan, (2) relates to cognitive ability in healthy individuals, and (3) is disrupted in AD dementia. Just as growth charts are widely used in pediatric care, our normative E/I ratio trajectory charts might eventually be used to track healthy neurodevelopment and aging. Insights into E/I disruption in AD dementia might also lead to future therapies to rebalance E/I ratio.
kw: MRI; excitation/inhibition balance; growth chart; aging; neurodevelopment; Alzheimer's Disease

title: Assessing the potential zoonotic risk of Alphacoronavirus HKU2
abs: The devastating COVID-19 pandemic, caused by the Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), showed that human and animal health are inextricably linked. In 2006, an Alphacoronavirus, termed HKU2, was discovered in Chinese Rhinolophus bats, but this virus was not investigated further until a series of fatal swine disease outbreaks occurred in pig farms more than a decade later in Guangdong province, China. The virus causing these outbreaks was named Swine Acute Diarrhea Syndrome CoV (SADS-CoV) and turned out to belong to the HKU2 species, suggesting that it spilled from bats to pigs. Since 2016, this virus is occasionally resurfacing in China, raising the question whether this virus or its bat relatives can infect humans and cause a pandemic. There are currently limited tools to evaluate the risk of potentially zoonotic viruses. In the past few years, human organoids, or ‘mini organs’ have proven exceptionally useful for studying viruses. Since organoids accurately model specific aspects of organs and can be grown from a wide range organs and animal species, including bats and pigs, they may be particularly useful for the risk assessment of potentially zoonotic viruses. Here, we aim to use organoid models to assess the potential zoonotic risk of HKU2 coronaviruses. We hypothesize that specific coronaviruses belonging to the HKU2 species can efficiently replicate in human cells of the respiratory and intestinal tract, and elicit detrimental host responses, thereby posing a pandemic threat. Early identification of high-risk pathogens through both genetic characterization and functional studies is key to pandemic preparedness. Addressing their potential to invade human cells can inform the rapid development of diagnostic tests, treatments, vaccines, and control strategies. Such advances increase local and global preparedness for future coronavirus outbreaks to limit their societal and economic impact.
kw: Coronavirus, Organoids, Zoonosis, HKU2, SADS-CoV, Alphacoronavirus

title: Targeting non-tuberculous mycobacteria lung disease (NTM-LD) using anti-infective conjugated oligoelectrolyte
abs: Chronic lung infections caused by non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM) represent a growing global health concern. Common in vulnerable populations with chronic pulmonary conditions (such as cystic fibrosis, non-CF bronchiectasis, and COPD), NTM lung disease (NTM-LD) severely impacts quality of life with high morbidity and mortality and is challenging to eradicate despite rigorous and prolonged treatment that lasts years. Patients with NTM lung disease have limited treatment options, all of which have low cure rates yet possess significant potential for adverse side effects. Barriers to developing novel treatments for NTM-LD, namely the high level of intrinsic antibiotic resistance of NTM and its ability to evade treatment by forming persisters, biofilms or living intracellular, have stifled innovation. There is therefore a critical unmet need to overcome these barriers and provide patients a superior treatment option. Our long-term aim is to develop the first built-to-purpose inhaled therapy to treat NTM-LD based on our novel antibiotic platform, known as anti-infective conjugated oligoelectrolytes (COEs). A synergistic pair comprising an optimized COE molecule and a first line antibiotic will be formulated for localized lung delivery through inhalation with the objective of providing a paradigm-changing therapy for patients with NTM-LD. Relative to current treatments, this proposed innovative therapy has the potential to improve cure rates, reduce time-to-cure, and reduce adverse effects, thereby vastly improving the quality of life for patients afflicted with NTM-LD. As the most prevalent strain causing NTM-LD in Singapore, M. abscessus (Mab) leads to high morbidity and mortality. Hence, we will focus our study on treating Mab lung disease in this proposal. Our specific objectives in this proposal are to (1) improve our understanding of structural-activity-relationships (SARs) and lead-optimization process through a chemical synthesis campaign and (2) formulate synergistic pair of COE and antibiotic into layer-by-layer liposomal nanoparticles (LbL NPs).
kw: bacterial infection, pharmaceutical small molecules, conjugated oligoelectrolyte, antimicrobial resistance

title: Targeting epithelial WWP2 to ameliorate lung fibrosis
abs: Progressive fibrosing interstitial lung disease (PF-ILD) is a group of incurable diseases characterized by decline in lung function, worsening of symptoms and early mortality. PF-ILDs contribute to 0.26% of all-cause mortality worldwide and despite being a rare disease, the Global Burden of Disease Study reported that, between 1990 and 2013, there was an 86% increase in ILD-related years of life lost. Our group discovered a new role of WWP2, a multifunctional E3 ubiquitin ligase, in fibrotic heart disease (Nature Communications 2019 and 2022). In addition to heart disease, we have detected a strong genetic association of WWP2 with respiratory function in >400,000 subjects, and direct evidence of WWP2 upregulation in epithelial cells of fibrotic lesions in PF-ILD lungs. WWP2 deficiency attenuates lung fibrosis in vivo and WWP2 regulates epithelial-macrophage interaction crucial for fibrotic progression. These findings propose a novel hypothesis for WWP2 as a risk gene for PF-ILD and regulator of epithelial vulnerability in fibrotic lungs. Here, we will combine studies in preclinical lung disease models, single cell genomics and “epithelial secretome” analyses with PF-ILD patient-specific in vitro modelling using human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived lung epithelial cells. We propose three aims: (1) determine whether WWP2 function in epithelium is critical for the development of pulmonary fibrosis; (2) determine how WWP2 regulates the crucial epithelial-macrophage interaction during fibrotic progression; (3) explore the therapeutic potential of inhibiting WWP2 in PF-ILD patient-derived lung epithelial cells. Our approach is innovative as it combines generation of novel conditional WWP2 KO mice and PF-ILD patients-derived epithelial cells to evaluate the antifibrotic potential for targeting WWP2 specifically in epithelium to mitigate lung fibrosis in PF-ILDs. Since we have already started developing a new class of inhibitors of WWP2, the long-term goal of this research is to develop new effective anti-fibrotic treatments for PF-ILDs patients.
kw: Lung fibrosis; Pulmonary Fibrosis-Interstitial Lung Disease; Interstitial Pulmonary Fibrosis

title: Targeting urea cycle-EIF5A hypusination (EIF5AH) pathway to treat nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH)
abs: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is a spectrum of liver diseases that affects more than 30% adults in Singapore and worldwide. Nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) is a severe form of NAFLD characterized by hepatic inflammation and fibrosis that can progress to cirrhosis. NAFLD/NASH also increases the risk for type 2 diabetes (T2DM), cardiovascular disease (CVD), and chronic kidney disease (CKD). Currently, there are no FDA-approved drugs for NASH treatment. Recently, we reported that decreased protein synthesis rate led to dysfunctional mitochondria in NASH. Mechanistically, NASH decreased the post-translational hypusination of the translation factor EIF5A (EIF5AH), an elongation factor that is essential for the synthesis of a subset of mitochondrial proteins. These findings showed for the first time that dysregulated protein synthesis played a pathogenic role in NASH, and identified EIF5AH as a potential druggable target. Our preliminary data also showed that NASH decreased hepatic urea cycle activity, which serves as an endogenous pathway providing substrates that affect EIF5A hypusination. Thus, we hypothesize: The decreased hepatic urea cycle-EIF5AH pathway is an important mechanism accounting for dysregulated protein synthesis and mitochondrial metabolism during NASH that can be modulated to provide therapeutic benefits for NASH. Accordingly, we propose the following three Specific Aims: 1) To determine genome-wide translatome and the role(s) of impaired EIF5AH on hepatic protein synthesis and metabolism during NASH progression; 2) To determine the role of urea cycle on hepatic EIF5AH, protein synthesis, mitochondrial function, and NASH progression; 3) To employ pharmacological approaches targeting the urea cycle-EIF5AH pathway to improve protein synthesis and metabolic function during NASH. Protein synthesis is an essential cellular process but poorly understood in NASH and metabolic disorders. Our study will address this knowledge gap and identify novel pathogenic factors for therapeutic targeting, accelerating the development of new methods or agents for NASH treatment.
kw: NAFLD; protein synthesis; EIF5A hypusination; urea cycle; mitochondrial function; SGLT2 inhibitor

title: Comparative in vitro and in vivo alphaviral-host interplay for novel therapies
abs: Viral infections, as demonstrated by the current pandemic, have a vast impact on human health and society in general. Due to the expanding geographical distribution of competent vectors, arthropod-borne viruses (arboviruses) are imposing a substantial economic and public health burden on a growing number of affected countries and are poised as serious contenders for the next outbreak. Currently, Arboviruses are a global threat with 3.9 billion people living in at-risk regions with subtropical and tropical climates. To date, no licensed vaccine or treatment exists against most of these arboviruses. Recognizing this threat, in March 2022, the World Health Organisation launched the global arbovirus initiative, a collaborative effort focusing on monitoring, preparing for, and reducing the occurrence of arbovirus outbreaks. Amongst arboviruses, Alphaviruses often induce chronic debilitating complications for several years post-acute infection. Interestingly, our preliminary data shows that highly genetically related alphaviruses Chikungunya and O’nyong nyong, which are transmitted by different but sympatric mosquito vector species, trigger different immune response in mammals consistent with a different viral-host interplay strategy for efficient viral replication and immune evasion. This proposal aims to use viral-centric comparative systems virology in vitro and in vivo to understand key host-factors involved in the differential viral-hijacking. Using novel tools as well as high throughput multiOmics, in in vitro and in vivo models, we will investigate previously non-visible by standard approaches, key host factors and assess their importance during infection and immune evasion. The main outcomes expected from this project are novel host-factors for broad spectrum antivirals development, novel immunomodulatory drug targets and novel fundamental concepts that could be applied to next generation of self-amplifying vaccines or novel adjuvant strategies.
kw: arboviruses; alphaviruses ; comparative virology ; host-factors ; immune evasion

title: Investigating the metabolic regulation of immune dysfunction during the progression of NASH to NASH-HCC
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Hepatocellular carcinoma is a major contributor to mortality in non-alcoholic steatohepatitis patients. However, poorly understood mechanisms drive the progression NASH towards HCC, leading to a lack of preventive therapies to block this transition. Moreover, systemic therapies for advanced HCCs, in particular HCCs arising from NASH, remain poor. There is therefore, a need to better understand the factors that determine transition from NASH to NASH-HCC for its prevention and to improve on current therapeutic strategies for NASH-HCC. In this respect, immune dysregulation during the progression to NASH-HCC has emerged as a critical determinant driving the transition. In addition, recent studies have begun to elucidate a unique immunological landscape of NASH-HCCs that belies its increased resistance to immune checkpoint inhibitors. However, how these immune alterations are regulated remains relatively unknown. There is increasing recognition of the role of interstitial metabolite composition in regulating immune cell state and function. Yet little is known about the interstitial metabolic profile of NASH livers and its effects on hepatic immune cells during the progression to NASH-HCC. By utilizing a dietary mouse model that mimics human NASH progression, we seek to study the crosstalk between interstitial metabolites and hepatic immune cells and how they evolve over the transition to HCC emergence. Through interstitial metabolite profiling and single-cell transcriptomic analyses, we aim to comprehensively characterize both the metabolic and immunological landscapes of progressors and non-progressors to NASH-HCC. Using this knowledge, we aim to identify and test new therapeutic candidates for preventing the NASH-to-HCC transition and treating established NASH-HCC tumors. We anticipate that our study will not only offer important, fundamental insight into the progression of this highly prevalent disease, but also provide translational opportunities to help alleviate the significant clinical burden and improve patient well being.
kw: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease; non-alcoholic steatohepatitis; hepatocellular carcinoma; immune microenvironment; bile acid; hyodeoxycholic acid

title: Deciphering the neural circuit mechanisms of compulsive eating
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Compulsive eating disorder (CED) or binge eating disorder (BED) is with noted social and health consequences that typically arises in later adolescent and young adult years. Such excessive craving for food of binge eaters is often triggered by external cues. Compulsive eating has been closely linked to obesity and other psychiatric comorbidities, but the neural mechanisms of this eating disorder are still poorly understood. The medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) has been implicated in CED, and appears to be a convergent node for regulating compulsive behaviors in both food addiction and drug addiction. However how mPFC interacts with hypothalamic orexigenic neural network to regulate CED is unknown. By pairing the activation of specific hypothalamic orexigenic neurons with environmental context, we created neural circuit specific contextual feeding conditioning (CFC) paradigm, which could be used to probe neural mechanisms of maladaptive eating behavior. In contrast to other major orexigenic neurons, activating anterior zona incerta (aZI) GABAergic neurons produces long-lasting, compulsive-like eating behavior that could be triggered by external cues. Using brain-wide neural activity and connectivity mapping, we identified medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) as a potential input region that drives CED. In this proposal, we aim to examine the causal relationship of mPFC-aZI connection in CED and provide mechanistic insights of this devastating eating disorder.
kw: compulsive eating; binge eating; zona incerta; hypothalamus; mPFC; neural circuits

title: Harnessing antioxidants and the redox proteome in adoptive NK cell therapy for superior targeting of solid tumors
abs: The suppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) presents a major challenge to infiltrating immune cells such as Natural Killer (NK) and cytotoxic CD8 T cells and affects the efficacy of adoptive cell therapy. One major stress is the reactive oxygen species (ROS) present in the TME. Previously, we established a role for IL-15 stimulated thioredoxin activity in conferring NK cells resistance to oxidative stress. We found that IL-15 increases the cell surface thiol density of tumor-infiltrating NK cells. However, which critical proteins and how thiol-modification of these targets enhances NK cells resilience in the harsh TME is not entirely clear. We hypothesize that thiol-modification of key effector protein(s) and their effects on associated signaling pathways could increase NK cell efficacy against solid tumors. In this proposal, we seek to further elucidate the causal link between antioxidants and the redox regulation of immune effector molecules in NK cell therapy. The specific aims are: (1) Elucidate the redox targets and signaling in NK cells that can enhance anti-tumor response and (2) Identify conditions that can boost NK cell redox defense, to prime for better performance during adoptive cell therapy. Specifically, we aim to (1) identify thiol-enriched proteins with immune effector functions in NK cells, (2) investigate the effects of oxidation on the catalytic activity of candidate effector signaling molecules and to profile the phospho-proteome of NK cells with high surface thiol density, and (3) conduct drug screening to identify means of enhancing the surface thiol density of NK cells and to examine candidate drug-treated NK cell infiltration in human tumor spheroid models. These objectives when accomplished would allow us to understand how thiol-mediated mechanisms and pathways enable NK cells to overcome the harsh TME and potentially offer means to enhance NK cell therapy against solid tumors.
kw: NK cells, Immunotherapy, antioxidants, proteomics

title: Targeting mitochondrial macrophage iron for a better understanding of fibrosis during chronic kidney disease
abs: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) eventually progresses to end-stage kidney disease that requires dialysis or kidney transplantation. Independently of its etiology, CKD has often a common endpoint characterized by tubulointerstitial fibrosis. Macrophages are master regulators of inflammation and fibrosis in CKD and their polarization is tightly controlled by environmental factors such as tissue iron, which accumulates within the fibrotic tubulointerstitial space during CKD. We previously discovered that systemic iron depletion with a mitochondria-permeable chelator reduces the severity of CKD and affects macrophage immunometabolism in a pre-clinical model of crescentic glomerulonephritis. Here we hypothesize that abnormal iron build-up within inflamed kidneys drives fibrosis through polarized macrophages that accumulate iron within mitochondria. We propose to combine highly reproducible pre-clinical models of CKD in the rat with systems genetics approaches to elucidate the biology of interstitial pro-fibrotic macrophages and their modulation via mitochondrial iron. Specifically, we will target macrophage mitochondrial iron in two pre-clinical models of CKD with the aim of preventing inflammation and fibrosis (Aim 1). We will characterize immune and metabolic profiling of interstitial pro-fibrotic macrophages and their functional modulation via mitochondrial iron (Aim 2). We will establish macrophage-fibroblast crosstalk at a single cell level during renal fibrogenesis, in view of identifying and targeting an anti-fibrotic soluble factor (Aim 3). Mitochondrial targeting of iron has not been applied to macrophages in CKD and we propose to undertake a timely research program that will elucidate the cellular mechanisms of tubulointerstitial fibrosis. The proposed studies will target the macrophage – a cell with proficient metabolic activity, increased sensitivity to iron and common features of polarization across multiple fibrotic tissues. The knowledge gained from the biology of pro-fibrotic macrophages is likely to increase the translational potential of the proposal with possibility to extrapolating the results to multi-organ fibrosis.
kw: chronic kidney disease; fibrosis; macrophages; iron; mitochondria

title: Developing Next-Generation Extracellular Vesicle-Based Therapeutic Cancer Vaccines
abs: Immunotherapies have emerged as a promising cancer treatment strategy. Notably, cancer vaccines involve the administration of tumor antigens and/or adjuvants to train the immune system against tumor cells, have gained significant interest in recent years. However, therapeutic cancer vaccines face challenges, including suboptimal antigen delivery to dendritic cells (DCs), inadequate antigen presentation and DC maturation, and ineffective T-cell activation. To overcome these hurdles, we propose leveraging tumor cell-derived microparticles (TMPs) as a novel vaccine platform. Our preliminary data demonstrate high immunogenicity of TMPs and their capacity to activate the cGAS/STING pathway, thereby enhancing DC maturation and antigen presentation. TMPs also show versatility as carriers for various cargoes. This study aims to evaluate TMP vaccines integrated with STING-amplifying manganese phosphate nanoparticles, IL-15:IL-15Rα mRNA, and PD-L1 siRNA for their anti-tumor efficacy. We hypothesize that TMP-based vaccines, with their intrinsic antigen profiles and innate signals, will achieve effective DC activation and antigen cross-presentation; and engineering TMPs with immunomodulators will further boost T-cell priming and expansion, ultimately leading to robust and durable anti-tumor immune responses. The specific aims are as follows: Aim 1: Screen TMP formulations for optimal extracellular vesicle-based cancer vaccines and investigate the innate immunostimulation. Aim 2: Develop STINGVax, investigate the immunomodulation mechanisms for promoting DC maturation, and evaluate anti-tumor efficacies. Aim 3: Develop T-Fuel-Vax, investigate the immunomodulation mechanisms for boosting T-cell activation, and assess therapeutic outcomes in diverse murine and patient-derived tumor models. The research team comprises investigators with extensive expertise in cell-based drug delivery systems, cancer vaccines, cancer/mice model, cancer biology, and cancer immunotherapy, collaboratively aims to significantly advance our understanding of vaccine design, immunomodulation mechanisms, and the therapeutic potential of TMP-based vaccines. Successful completion of this proposal will pave the way for translating these findings into impactful clinical applications, bringing TMP-based vaccines closer to practical use.
kw: cancer vaccines; drug delivery; extracellular vesicles; cancer immunotherapy; nanovaccines; STING

title: Evaluating a screening instrument for the early identification of autism spectrum disorder among young children in Singapore
abs: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) affects 1 in 100 children and is increasing in prevalence. The disease burden of ASD is high; lifelong impairments in social communication affect daily functioning. Effective treatment is available and when initiated before 3 years of age, leads to improved communication and development. Although symptoms are present in the majority by 18 months, the current age of diagnosis is 36-42 months of age, leading to delayed treatment. Systematic screening can facilitate earlier diagnosis and treatment initiation. The Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers, Revised with Follow-up (M-CHAT-R/F) has been used internationally with good sensitivity for ASD screening in meta-analytic studies. Preliminary data from Singapore suggests acceptable sensitivity and feasibility of use within our healthcare system but its definitive performance in our unique cultural and ethnic context is unknown. We aim to 1. Establish sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value and negative predictive value of the M-CHAT-R/F in ASD screening among healthy children aged 18 and 30 months. 2. Compare diagnostic accuracy across two age-groups 3. Evaluate perceived barriers and facilitators to ASD screening among parents and healthcare professionals. We hypothesise that the M-CHAT-R/F will have >80% sensitivity at both 18 and 30 months and sensitivity will be higher at the older vs younger age. This population-based longitudinal cohort study will recruit children from primary care at age 18 months and follow them until 30 months. The M-CHAT-R/F will be administered at both timepoints, with follow-up diagnostic evaluation performed for all who screen positive and for a subset who screen negative at each timepoint. The diagnostic evaluation will entail a gold standard diagnosis for presence of ASD. An embedded process evaluation will ascertain beliefs and perceived barriers to screening among parents, nurses and physicians. This study will inform critical public health policy for the children of Singapore.
kw: Autism; autism spectrum disorder; screening; M-CHAT-R/F; sensitivity

title: Investigating the Role of Glycerol 3-phosphate Acyltransferase in the Pathogenesis of Parkinson’s Disease
abs: The study seeks to investigate the role and mechanisms of an enzyme glycerol 3-phosphate acyltransferase in the pathogenesis of alpha-synuclein-associated Parkinson's disease, utilizing Parkinson's disease models in both fruit flies and mouse primary neurons. Additionally, it aims to assess the effectiveness of the FSG67, a computer-designed inhibitor specific to glycerol 3-phosphate acyltransferase, in alleviating the disease pathology. The hypothesis posits that elevated lipid synthesis activity, lipid peroxidation, and lipidomic deregulations are associated with alpha-synuclein pathology. These effects could be mitigated by targeting the rate-limiting step in lipid synthesis catalyzed by glycerol 3-phosphate acyltransferase. Suppression of glycerol 3-phosphate acyltransferase could also attenuate the formation of pathogenic alpha-synuclein aggregates. Multiple isoforms of the enzyme localized in either mitochondria or endoplasmic membranes may share a common role in alpha-synuclein pathogenesis. Finally, modulating SREBP transcription factors to suppress fatty acid and lipid synthesis may also reduce alpha-synuclein aggregates or neurotoxicity. To test the hypothesis, we will study the effects of mino on alpha-synuclein-induced dopaminergic neuron degeneration, lipid peroxidation, alpha-synuclein higher-order oligomer formation and neuronal oxidative stress. Additionally, we will assess the effectiveness of modulating alpha-synuclein neurotoxicity via targeting SREBP. The potential of FSG67 to mitigate the pathological features of PD in fruit fly and mouse primary neuron models will be evaluated. We will also compare RNAi against mitochondrial mino with other GPATs present in the endoplasmic reticulum to determine if mino’s effects are a common attribute of glycerol 3-phosphate acyltransferases, irrespective of their subcellular localization. The feasibility of the study is ensured by the applicants and collaborators, who possess the necessary knowledge and experience to execute the research effectively. Furthermore, the research will enhance our understanding of pathogenic mechanisms and contribute to the development of novel therapeutic targets and treatments for Parkinson’s disease, ultimately benefiting public health and well-being.
kw: Parkinson’s disease; neurodegeneration; lipid metabolism; glycerol 3-phosphate acyltransferase;

title: Mechanistic dissection of novel biologics targeting PAI-1 via an integrative proteomic and transcriptomic approach coupled with prospective validation of a rapid ELISA companion biomarker panel to infer successful treatment response in peritoneal metastases
abs: Peritoneal metastases (PM) is a common form of metastasis confined to the abdominal cavity that can arise from any intra-abdominal organ. We have previously demonstrated proof of concept of a phenomenon termed “paracrine addiction” and that direct ligand inhibition of a key paracrine factor, plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1), in ascites provides a potential therapeutic opportunity for PM patients. After establishing paracrine addiction as a key biological hallmark of PM and creation of representative mouse models of PM with incorporation of the microenvironment, we sought to create novel biologics targeting PAI-1 to be administered intraperitoneally to inhibit PAI-1 paracrine oncogenic effects. Biologics targeting PAI-1 were identified and generated from a phage display screen with promising biochemical, in vitro and in vivo effects. We also identified and patented a companion biomarker panel to serve as a Laboratory Developed Test (LDT) to select patients for successful PAI-1 therapy. The first aim of this proposal is to integrate data from a large proteomic screen of ascites (n=175) with transcriptomic changes following treatment with patient ascites and our novel biologics. This will serve to decipher the mechanism underlying the inhibitory effects of our biologics in the presence of the fluid microenvironment (ascites) in PM patients. Aim 2 will prospectively validate a 6-biomarker panel which predicts successful PAI-1 therapy and will support the utility of our panel as a companion biomarker therapeutic predictor, laying the framework for a clinical trial in the next step. Our team is committed to discovering novel therapeutic treatment for patients with PM who would otherwise have limited treatment options. With the support of this grant, we will generate data to support the scientific novelty of our biologics and generate a first of its kind biologics targeting PAI-1 in PM along with a predictive companion biomarker panel.
kw: Peritoneal Metastases; Biologics; Companion Biomarker Panel

title: From Nonalcoholic Steatohepatitis to Hepatocellular Carcinoma: Investigating the Molecular Mechanisms for Biomarker Development and Therapeutic Insights
abs: Despite the high burden of nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH)-related hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) in Southeast Asia, the molecular mechanisms behind the development of NASH-related HCC remain unclear. Existing surveillance modalities, such as ultrasound, are inadequate. More than a third of NASH-related HCC manifests before the onset of cirrhosis, posing a challenge to conventional HCC surveillance practices, which focus on cirrhosis. The central objectives of this proposal are to determine the molecular mechanisms underlying hepatocarcinogenesis in NASH and to develop a liquid biopsy to distinguish NASH-related HCC from NASH. The overarching hypothesis is that chronic cellular injury in NASH may drive progressive reprogramming and dedifferentiation of the microenvironment, facilitating the development of HCC. We propose the following key aims: Aim 1: Generate a single-cell spatial atlas to detect serial changes in the microenvironment as NASH progresses to HCC. The PI has generated preliminary data suggesting that chronic inflammation from NASH drives the activation of microenvironmental reprogramming and dedifferentiation, which facilitates the development of an immune-exhausted, pro-tumorigenic niche. We have recruited participants (n=5 in each category) with histologically-confirmed healthy livers, steatosis, NASH without advanced fibrosis, NASH with advanced fibrosis, NASH-related HCC without cirrhosis, and NASH-related HCC with cirrhosis. snRNA-seq and snATAC-Seq will be conducted and integrated with spatial data. Aim 2: Develop a liquid biopsy for NASH-related HCC. The team has developed a liver-specific, extracellular vesicle-based signature that captures serial microenvironmental changes in NASH and can distinguish between the various stages of NASH. The PI will develop a liquid biopsy to distinguish NASH-related HCC from other stages of NASH, using serum already collected from participants (n=120 histologically-confirmed) across the spectrum from healthy to NASH-related HCC. At the end of this project, we would have identified key molecular mechanisms of progression to HCC in NASH and developed a liquid biopsy signature for early NASH-related HCC.
kw: Hepatocellular carcinoma; nonalcoholic steatohepatitis; HCC; NASH

title: Exploiting Candida cell wall interactions with synthetic membrane-active supramolecules for de novo antifungal therapeutics development
abs: Despite available prevention and treatment measures, fungal pathogens, especially the Candida spp., still infect billions of people worldwide, claiming ~2.5 million lives by invasive fungal infections each year. Several fungal pathogens have evolved strong resistance to all classes of antifungal drugs currently available on the market, whereas most new drugs under development use a similar mechanism of action to the existing ones by targeting a specific protein and hence susceptible to the drug-resistance challenge. It is therefore imperative to develop new antifungal drugs with unprecedented mechanisms of action. Synthetic mimics of antifungal peptides have aroused immense interest recently due to their unique membrane-disrupting capability, broad-spectrum activity, and stability under in vivo conditions. Before reaching the plasma membrane, they must cross the (bio)chemically active exoskeleton fungal cell wall. Whether and how these synthetic antifungals interact with the cell wall is unknown. We hypothesize and have preliminarily demonstrated that, the Candida cell wall can be exploited as a target for a panel of in-house synthesized membrane-active cationic supramolecules to recognize and eradicate the target Candida species. Here we propose to expand the preliminary findings to a systematic investigation on the details of the possible tripartite interaction among the structurally versatile antifungal supramolecules, fungal cell wall, and the plasma membrane, aiming to reveal new insights and design principles for developing safe, potent, and broad-spectrum antifungal drugs with a low probability of resistance development. Once new antifungal designs are successfully synthesized, their antifungal activity, mode of interactions with fungal cell wall and membrane, synergy with existing antifungal drugs, and the clinical therapeutic potential will be characterized in detail using a combination of chemical biology, biochemistry, imaging, and computational tools and mouse infection models. This study will provide valuable guidance to expand our antifungal repertoire and open up new opportunities for effective antifungal therapeutics development.
kw: fungal pathogens; supramolecule; fungal cell wall; antifungal therapeutics; synergistic effect

title: Harnessing Microbial SCFAs to Accelerate Mucosal Healing in Ulcerative Colitis
abs: The microbial dysbiosis and intestinal barrier abnormalities are essential contributors in the development of ulcerative colitis (UC). Intestinal barrier re-establishment and mucosal healing have become a focus in current research of UC. Recent studies have found that macrophages, regulated by microbial signals, play an important role in tissue regeneration and intestinal homeostasis, however the mechanism is not yet clear. Our previous studies have confirmed that microbial dysbiosis with a decrease of short-chain fatty acid (SCFA)-producing bacteria, abnormal clearance of apoptotic cells and obstruction of macrophage polarization are key mechanistic features in the progression of UC. Symbiotic SCFA-producing microbial supplementation could regulate the M2 macrophage polarization and promote intestinal mucosal repair. So, does macrophage mediate the protective effect of symbiotic SCFA-producing microbes on promoting restoration of intestinal barrier in UC? And what is the specific regulatory mechanism behind it? In this project, we try to answer these questions at animal, tissue and molecular level. We will apply a series of organoid culture, adoptive transfer of immune cells, fluorescent cell tracing and genetic manipulation methods to clarify the potential effect of macrophage, regulated by symbiotic SCFA-producing microbes, on the process of intestinal repair, and investigate the mechanism of histone deacetylase (HDAC), the core molecular of epithelial restitution, in the protective effect of SCFA-producing microbes mediated by M2 macrophage, further providing theoretical and experimental support for the clinical management of UC from the perspective of gut homeostasis.
kw: Microbiome, Ulcerative Colitis, Inflammation

title: Histone variant H3.3 as a central driver of metastasis and a therapeutic target for rhabdomyosarcoma
abs: Rhabdomyosarcoma is the commonest soft tissue malignancy among young people. Fusion-positive (alveolar) rhabdomyosarcoma (FP-RMS) is the aggressive highly metastatic form, characterized by a single fusion oncoprotein PAX3-FOXO1 but few pathological mutations. To date this oncoprotein cannot be effectively targeted, so survival outcomes remain poor and reliance on cytotoxics increases the burden of toxic late effects among survivors. Having previously identified the signaling axis involving histone variant H3.3 as a critical regulator of metastasis in FP-RMS, we hypothesize that up- and down-stream members G9a and MCAM can be exploited as potential therapeutic targets and treatment biomarkers. Our specific aims are: (1) To define the molecular basis of H3.3’s role as a central driver of metastasis in FP-RMS. Specifically, by identifying interacting proteins and its mutations of H3.3 that affect how it regulates MCAM and other target genes. (2) To determine preclinical evidence for MCAM as a potential therapeutic target in FP-RMS. Specifically, by assessing the impact of its inhibition in patient-derived models of FP-RMS, studying the signaling pathways through which MCAM functions, and investigating its role as an effector of H3.3. (3) To examine the reasons that lead to upregulated H3.3 expression in FP-RMS, by verifying upstream regulators like G9a that activate its expression, then testing if targeted degradation of upstream regulators impacts H3.3 levels and disease progression in vivo. Elucidating the mechanism by which H3.3 drives metastasis will establish foundational target validation data for the development of new therapies directed against members of the G9a-H3.3-MCAM axis, and evidence for the role of H3.3 target genes as putative risk-stratification and prognostic biomarkers in FP-RMS. This translational project synergizes expertise from KKH, NUS, IMCB, and DUMC and all required platforms, clinical samples and preclinical models to address these key gaps in the understanding of disease biology and preclinical therapeutic development for RMS.
kw: Rhabdomyosarcoma

title: Development of biologics targeting PAI-1 towards regulatory approval aided by patient stratification using a vesicular signature on a novel nanotechnology platform (STAR) in peritoneal metastases (PM)
abs: Peritoneal metastases (PM) represent a prevalent form of tumour cell dissemination originating from any intra-abdominal organ. PM occurs in 10%, 40% and 50% of colorectal cancer, gastric cancer and ovarian cancer patients respectively, resulting in a tremendous healthcare burden. Current clinical therapies do not exploit tumour biology for treatment. On the therapeutics front, using integrative proteomics, transcriptomics and single cell analysis, we previously described a key paracrine factor, plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1) which PM cells are oncogenically addicted to. We termed this phenomenon paracrine addiction. To circumvent the effects of systemic absorption via intraperitoneal therapy, we created high molecular weight biologics (1 human antibody and 2 nanobodies) and demonstrated promising therapeutic potential in biochemical and in vitro functional assays. We also harnessed our unique mouse models of PM to demonstrate proof of concept of successful inhibition in the presence of the fluid microenvironment (ascites) with minimal toxicity. Aim 1 of this proposal will focus on improving the specificity and affinity of our biologics via affinity maturation experiments prior to in vitro and in vivo validation in our PDADX models. This will enhance the biologics’ therapeutic potential and facilitate translation to the clinic. Aim 2 will leverage on a successful collaborative effort to test and validate a revised vesicular signature on intra-abdominal fluid obtained from PM patients to predict successful PAI-1 therapy and patient prognosis. This proposed project builds upon our ongoing collaborative efforts among key members of the Singapore Peritoneal Oncology Study Group, harnessing the advantage of combined expertise of the surgical teams from the 3 largest tertiary hospitals (NCCS/SGH, KKH and NUHS) in Singapore and scientific biomedical engineering teams. If successful, we will generate multiple PAI-1 biologics with high affinity to PAI-1 to facilitate translation to clinical trials with potential for extension to indications in PM and other diseases.
kw: Peritoneal Metastases; Biologics; Nanotechnology platform; Biomarkers

title: Folinic Acid as a Treatment for Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) in Children: A Double-blind Randomised Placebo-controlled Trial with Open Label Extension (FOLIN-A Trial)
abs: Background: Autism affects 1% of children and comprises social interaction impairments, with restricted, repetitive behaviours. The 2010 Singapore MOH Burden of Disease Study found that autism was the leading cause of disease burden in children 0-14 years old. Evidence-based autism interventions mainly comprise behavioural and social communication therapies. There are no specific medical treatments to improve the core symptoms of autism, and this represents a huge unmet need. Ongoing clinical trials worldwide are investigating oxytocin, vasopressin, bumetanide, and stem cells in treating autism. The folate cycle is a common critical factor involved in the glutathione oxidative stress pathway, amino acid/DNA methylation reactions, and neurotransmitter synthesis pathway, which have all been implicated in the pathogenesis of autism. Cerebral folate deficiency also results in autism symptoms. Folinic acid supplementation is superior to folic acid as it can function in defective folate metabolism without resulting in high unmetabolised folic acid levels. High-dose folinic acid is already safely used in paediatric oncology. Aims/Hypothesis: Following a successful pilot study, this proposed trial aims to investigate the efficacy of folinic acid in treating autistic children, demonstrate safety, and investigate related biochemical changes in response to treatment. The primary hypothesis is that oral folinic acid improves autism symptoms in children, compared to placebo. Method: 184 autistic children, aged 3 to 10 years old, will be randomized to either folinic acid or placebo for 12 weeks, followed by an open label extension for another 12 weeks. Pre- and post-treatment measures include validated psychometric measures of autism symptoms, language, behaviour, and adaptive skills; physiological eye-tracking responses to social stimuli; and biological measures of amino acid methylation and glutathione redox status. Significance: If found to be safe and effective, folinic acid, which is a relatively inexpensive existing supplement, could be repurposed to improve autism symptoms for many Singaporean children.
kw: autism spectrum disorder; folinic acid; randomised controlled trial; folate metabolism; oxidative stress;

title: Therapeutic Potential of Thrombospondins in Preventing Heart Failure after Myocardial Infarction
abs: Acute myocardial infarction (MI) is a top cause of morbidity and mortality globally. Advances in treatment have reduced short-term mortality but heart failure (HF) occurring after MI has become a major long-term cause of morbidity and mortality among acute MI survivors. We aim to uncover new therapies to prevent ischemic HF by interrogating thrombospondins-2 and -4, soluble proteins discovered from our previous NMRC-funded large-scale plasma proteomics studies of A. patients with recent MI and 7-year longitudinal follow-up for HF events and B. an in-house porcine model of experimental MI. We hypothesise that soluble circulating proteins such as the thrombospondins can be useful drug targets for the prevention of ischemic HF. Indeed, it was the discovery of B-type natriuretic peptide, a soluble plasma peptide, that led to the development of valsartan-sacubitril with global sales revenue of 2.5B USD in 2020 alone. Our methodology is a ‘bedside-to-bench-to-bedside’ approach that leverages bleeding-edge research capabilities at both heart centres in Singapore. First, we will perform CRISPR-directed activation (dCas9-VPR) and interference (dCas9-KRAB) of thrombospondin-2 and -4 activity to investigate their therapeutic potential in the prevention of HF after MI using in vitro 3D heart tissue engineered from human IPSC-derived cardiomyocytes and extracelullar matrix cells. The top protein candidate will then be targeted using an AAV-9-mediated gene therapy approach followed by efficacy and safety testing with in vivo murine models. Increasingly, pharma is pivoting towards high-value gene (and cell) therapies as these assets are not easily replicated by "me-too' competitors. If successful, the new treatment can benefit the 105 million people around the world who suffer acute MI each year by starting an upstream treatment to prevent the onset of post-MI HF. A new treatment for HF can potentially even help the 64 million people around the world suffering HF from different causes.
kw: Acute myocardial infarction; heart failure; proteomics, drug discovery

title: Roles of transcriptional co-factors in drug resistance in T-acute lymphoblastic leukemia
abs: T-acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (T-ALL) is a common, highly aggressive form of blood cancer. Compared to other cancers, T-ALL is driven by very few genetic mutations. Overexpression of the oncogenic TAL1 accounts for the largest molecular subtype (~30% of cases) of T-ALL. TAL1 is a master TF which drives a shared core regulatory circuit (CRC) with RUNX1, GATA3 and MYB. TAL1 induced CRC sustains upregulation of the target genes which the lymphoblasts become dependent on as a form of ‘transcription addiction’. Since TFs are generally undruggable, inhibition of transcriptional co-factors have been one therapeutic option to target this addiction. But resistance to inhibition of co-factors have also since been described by others. It is still unknown which transcription co-factors are crucial to in the propagation and maintenance of the TAL1 CRC. Whether rewiring of TAL1 CRC is essential for resistance to transcriptional cofactors inhibition has not been investigated as well. Our preliminary data demonstrated that the TAL1 CRC responds differently to inhibition of different co-factors. Surprisingly, inhibition of SMARCA2/A4 or CDK9 increased the TAL1 oncogenic signature, although only very weakly in CDK9 inhibited cells, while inhibition of BRD4 reduced TAL1 signature. Furthermore drug resistant cells were consistently observed upon treatment with the respective co-factor inhibitors at high doses. These results suggest that incomplete inhibition of TAL1 CRC could lead to subsequent drug resistance. We hypothesize that specific transcriptional co-factors are required to drive TAL1 CRC and these co-factors could help in rewiring of the CRC to drive drug resistance. Overall purpose of this project is to identify and understand molecular functions of these specific co-factors in driving TAL1 CRC and to establish therapeutic basis for the targeting of these cofactors in TAL positive T-ALL.
kw: T-ALL, Transcription, Co-Factors, Epigenetics

title: SURE-TREAT: Singapore Undiagnosed Research Endeavour: identification and TREATment of splicing variants in patients with neurodevelopmental disorders
abs: Background: Advances in genomics are not only helping clinicians understand risk factors for adverse health, but also providing opportunities to intervene with programmable precision therapeutics. While this field of Precision Medicine is nascent with many challenges, there has been recent progress specifically for monogenic diseases caused by variants that disrupt splicing and have a moderate to severe effect size on health. However, proving the pathogenicity of splicing variants, especially those classified as variants-of-uncertain-significance, as well as developing therapeutics targeting these variants is laborious and time-consuming. Objective: We hypothesise that ~10% of patients with neurodevelopmental diseases have splicing causative variants, and identifying plus functionalizing them through minigene and knock-in analysis would provide potential therapeutic targets for treatment with modalities such as antisense oligonucleotides. Methods: We aim to bring Precision Diagnostics and Therapeutics closer to the clinic for our patients, through two aims: Aim 1: To establish a robust genetic diagnostics protocol to assess the splicing effects of new variants associated with genetic diseases, by validating the effect on splicing via minigenes and/or CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-ins for variants predicted by in-silico tools, followed by assessing the effects on the encoded mRNA and protein, and finally by a mechanistic characterization of cases where the result deviates from the prediction; Aim 2: To identify and optimize splice-switching antisense oligonucleotides (ssASOs) that correct the splicing defects by one of the variants identified so far in the TCF4 gene in a patient with Pitt Hopkins syndrome. We will identify and functionally validate the ssASOs that efficiently rescue the splicing defect, we will characterize their off-target effects and measure their toxicity in mice. Clinical significance: This study will generate new knowledge on splicing mutations causing disease and their therapeutics and will contribute to building a diagnostics and therapeutics pipeline for a subset of patients who previously had none.
kw: genomics, therapeutics, antisense oligonucleotides, precision therapeutics

title: Characterization of the Retinal Microvascular Endothelial Cell Response to Biomechanical Deformation
abs: Our overall hypothesis is that altering the extracellular mechanical micro-environment, or disrupting the intrinsic structure of retinal ECs will result in impaired barrier function and cell-to-cell communication in retinal microvascular ECs. Results from this study will result in an improved understanding of the pathogenesis underlying complex eye diseases associated with biomechanical deformation of blood vessels, such as myopia and glaucoma. We will test our hypothesis with the following Specific Aims: 1. To evaluate the effects of modulating static and dynamic biomechanical properties of the external micro-environment on human retinal endothelial cells (hrECs), in vitro. a) We hypothesize that hrECs grown on stiffer, larger diameter fibers bio-scaffolds will show disrupted barrier function and impaired extracellular vesicle production; b) We hypothesize that hrECs subjected to cyclical cell stretch or hydrostatic pressure will show disrupted barrier function and impaired extracellular vesicle production. 2. To evaluate the effects of endogenous structural changes that alter human retinal endothelial cells mechanobiology, in vitro. We hypothesize that prime genome editing to introduce myopia and glaucoma disease-causing mutations associated with alterations in hrEC structure will result in disrupted barrier function and impaired extracellular vesicle production. 3. To investigate the effects of biomechanical changes on the retinal endothelial cell transcriptome at the optic nerve head using murine models of glaucoma and myopia, in vivo. We hypothesize that molecular pathways that modulate retinal EC barrier function and neurovascular coupling at the ONH will be altered in association with increasing myopia severity and IOP. Preliminary findings suggest that hrECs grown on thicker diameter bio-scaffold fibers are more permeable and produce fewer extracellular vesicles. We have also demonstrated functional vascular changes at the optic nerve head that closely recapitulate clinical observations in glaucoma and myopia eyes, and viral vector-mediated restoration of endothelial cell function in the eye in animal models.
kw: myopia; glaucoma; optic nerve head; endothelial cells

title: The Protective Role of Maternal Immunization in Early Life
abs: During the early stages of COVID-19, we established methodologies to analyze humoral correlates of protection in the breast milk of nursing mothers. Maternal COVID-19 and influenza vaccinations during breastfeeding enhance specific antibodies in breast milk but only protect infants during the breastfeeding window. These current vaccines are not approved for those under six months of age. Beyond antibodies, breast milk contains immune cells whose dynamics vary throughout lactation, suggesting a potential role in infant immunity. However, these immune cells' intricate mechanisms and contributions to the overall protective effects in vaccinated mothers are largely unexplored. This proposal investigates the potential benefits of booster maternal vaccination (i.e., influenza and COVID-19) while breastfeeding to enhance both the humoral and cellular constituents of breast milk. The goal is to extend protection to the infants post-breastfeeding, contributing to preventive healthcare strategies. This prospective cohort study is led by a doctoral candidate collaborating with local and international experts in immunology, lactation, and pediatrics, including Associate Professor Paul A. Macary and Prof Lee Yung Seng. We aim to create an immune breast milk cell atlas, investigate immune cell transfer to infants, and examine antibody changes and associated immune factors following booster maternal vaccinations. The proposed research involves a comprehensive analysis of immune phenotypes using high-dimensional flow cytometry and single-cell RNA sequencing. The study design integrates clinical and laboratory components, aiming to bridge the gap in understanding dynamic immune responses in breast milk after maternal vaccinations. In conclusion, this prospective cohort study is positioned to provide valuable insights into optimizing maternal vaccination strategies for improved maternal-child health. The comprehensive approach to understanding immune responses in breast milk and their implications for infant protection emphasizes the potential impact of tailored immunization strategies on the health of mother-child dyads.
kw: Breastmilk; antibodies; immune cells; COVID-19; Influenza; immunization

title: Evaluation of sleep quality among nurses
abs: Background: Insufficient sleep and sleep disorders are commonly identified health challenges for nurses who work rotating shifts. Prolonged irregular working hours increases nurses’ vulnerability to the development of sleep disorders. Objective assessment of sleep quality is necessary. This study aims to: (i) examine self-reported sleep parameters (sleep quality and pattern) coupled with actigraph data and sleep hygiene habits of nurses undergoing different shift work duties; (ii) examine association between sleep quality and self-reported symptoms of depression among nurses; and (iii) explore sleep concerns among the nurses. Hypothesis: (i) The sleep parameters and sleep quality will be poorer among nurses who are working rotating and night shifts, with shorter sleep time, increased wake after sleep onset, poorer sleep efficiency and worse sleep hygiene habits. (ii) Nurses with worse sleep parameters will report greater depressive symptoms and more sleep concerns related to shift work. Methodology: This prospective cross-sectional study will recruit 84 full-time registered nurses over one-year via convenience sampling. Socio-demographic and work-related information will be collected. Nurses’ sleep characteristics (sleep time, wake after sleep onset and sleep efficiency) will be evaluated for two weeks using actigraph. Nurses’ sleep parameters, sleep hygiene and depressive symptoms will be measured with validated scales. Nurses will compete a sleep diary for two weeks. Descriptive statistics will be used to describe the sleep parameters, and factors affecting sleep. Sleep variables will be compared among nurses with different shifts, using inferential statistics. Regression techniques will be used to explore associations between studied variables. Qualitative data will be analysed using thematic analysis. Project significance: Findings will support development of interventions targeted to improve sleep hygiene of nurses doing shift work, including adjustment of work policies and improvement of roster planning. This will in turn improve job satisfaction and career longevity of nurses in clinical practice.
kw: Sleep quality; nurses; acute care; shifts

title: Predicting anhedonia using naturalistic and lab-based measures of reward
abs: Growing evidence has suggested that a hallmark symptom of adolescent depression is anhedonia. Anhedonia is predictive of the development and persistence of depression, as well as poorer treatment response and increased suicidal ideation and death by suicide even after controlling for other depression symptoms. Consequently, there is a critical need to identify processes that predict individual differences anhedonia risk and maintenance. Impaired reward-related processes have been theoretically and empirically linked with depression generally and anhedonia specifically, yet extant work is mainly cross-sectional. One specific set of relationships of interest is how anhedonia is associated with impaired anticipation versus attainment/consumption of reward. Although lab-based work suggests reward anticipation seems to be impaired in depression, work in adolescents has highlighted that the types of rewarding examined impact findings. For instance, lab-based work mainly employs monetary or food-based rewards, but alternative reward domains (e.g., social) may be more predictive of anhedonia. An under-examined (yet particularly relevant) reward domain for adolescents is education. Academic achievement, in the form of good markings, can serve as naturalistically rewarding experiences and provide a unique vehicle for studying the reward-related processes hypothesized to relate to anhedonia. We propose to identify which reward-related processes measured in the laboratory and in response to the natural (academic) environment prospectively predict individual differences in anhedonia development and maintenance in adolescents transitioning into adulthood using machine learning prediction algorithms. We hypothesize that impaired anticipation of social rewards (measured in lab) and academic rewards (measured in the natural environment) will emerge as top predictors of the development or persistence of anhedonia and depression. Achieving our aims will not only identify potential targets for experimental manipulation and treatment development but also identify easy-to-measure processes that suggest greater risk for the development of anhedonia and other symptom dimensions of psychopathology, thus meriting additional intervention and support.
kw: Anhedonia; reward; positive valence systems; depression; predictive utility; cognitive

title: Blood flow velocity quantification with Spectrally Extended Line Field (SELF) Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) Angiography for early detection of eye diseases
abs: Diabetic retinopathy (DR), age-related macular degeneration (AMD), glaucoma and pathological myopia are the leading causes of vision impairment and blindness worldwide. Abnormalities in retinal and choroidal circulation are critical in AMD, DR, glaucoma and others, because they originate from pathologic changes in the hemodynamics. While the invention of Optical Coherence Tomography Angiography (OCTA) has enabled visualization of the retinal vasculature, it does not provide information on blood flow velocity. We lack a tool for non-invasive and three-dimensional measurement of absolute blood velocity in the human retina and choroid. The objective of this research is to develop novel OCTA technologies to overcome fundamental gaps and establish a tool for robust measurement of absolute blood flow velocities in the human eye in vivo. In specific aim 1, we will develop Spectrally Extended Line Field OCT (SELF-OCT) technologies that overcome the current limitations in flow dynamic range, sensitivity, and speckle contrast. In specific aim 2, we will develop Multiple Inter-Scan Time (MIST) signal analytics and validate absolute blood flow velocity measurements in whole blood ex vivo and an animal model in vivo. In aim 3, we will validate MIST-OCT device for reliable absolute velocity measurements in normal human subjects in vivo. Our preliminary results in phantom studies and human studies in vivo shows that it is feasible to achieve the objective with the proposed method. A robust tool for quantification of absolute blood flow velocity holds the potential to facilitate early detection of vascular-related diseases and help in monitoring disease progression and evaluating the effectiveness of therapeutic interventions.
kw: Optical Coherence Tomography; blood flow velocity; Diabetic Retinopathy;

title: Multifunctional membrane-coated nanoparticles for enhanced osteoarthritis therapy
abs: Specific Aims: To design and develop multifunctional macrophage membrane-coated nanoparticles and characterize their physicochemical and functional properties, and to determine the therapeutic effects of these multifunctional macrophage membrane-coated nanoparticles in a rat knee osteoarthritis model Hypothesis: Macrophage membrane-coated nanoparticles endowed with reactive oxygen species scavenging ability would be able to alleviate OA inflammation and oxidative stress to promote overall joint homeostasis and repair Methodology & Approach: 1) Synthesis and assembly of multifunctional macrophage membrane-coated nanoparticles - rat macrophages (NR8383) will be treated with IFN-γ/LPS to polarize to M1 macrophages, and IL-4/IL-13 to M2 macrophages 2) Characterization of macrophage membrane-coated nanoparticles - the morphology of the membrane-coated nanoparticles will be observed by NanoSight and/or TEM. 3) In vivo study and dose optimization - to determine the optimal dose of macrophage membrane-coated nanoparticles, in 30 rats (8-week-old male), OA will be induced over 2 weeks by intra-articular monoiodoacetate injection in the right knees, before randomly allocated into 5 groups: 1) vehicle, phosphate-buffered saline (PBS); 2) 10μg; 3) 50μg; 4) 100μg; 5) 200μg membrane-coated nanoparticles. 4) Time-course analysis of joint repair - In 36 rats, OA will be induced by MIA injection in the right knees, before randomly allowed into 2 groups: 1) PBS; and 2) optimal dose from steps 1) and 2). At 1, 4 and 8-weeks post-injection, animals will be euthanised and samples harvested for analyses. Blood serum/plasma and synovial fluid samples will be collected for multiplex cytokine analysis. Knee joint samples will be harvested for histological staining, immunohistochemical staining for cartilage matrix proteins, macrophages, proliferative cells, apoptotic cells, cytokines, and histological scorings will be performed. Importance to science/medicine: If successful, our research will birth a novel disease-modifying immunotherapeutic as an early intervention for osteoarthritis and its associated negative impacts, which is expected to gain significant uptake and see wide applications.
kw: osteoarthritis; inflammation; nanoparticles; macrophage; immunotherapy

title: The Geriatric Oncology Supportive Clinic for older Frail adults (GOS-Frail) study
abs: Background Cancer is more prevalent in older adults, but most cancer treatment trials have mainly involved young and healthy subjects. Among geriatric syndromes, frailty is a significant risk factor for negative outcomes such as treatment delays, discontinuation, and treatment-related side effects, as well as functional decline and poor survival. Research has shown that geriatric assessment with appropriate intervention can improve these outcomes, although the impact may be influenced by the inclusion of patients receiving palliative-intent treatment. Supportive care focuses on symptom assessment and treatment to enhance treatment tolerance and quality of life. To date, there have been no studies examining the combined benefits of geriatric oncology and supportive care clinics. We conducted a pilot study called Geriatric Oncology Supportive Clinic for Elderly (GOSPEL), which demonstrated an improved quality of life for older adults with curable cancer. Based on these results, we developed an enhanced care model. Aim The study GOS-Frail aims to assess the effect of an integrated Geriatric Oncology Supportive Clinic on the quality of life of older adults with cancer receiving curative-intent chemotherapy and/or radiotherapy at 1 month. Methods The GOS-Frail study is a multi-centre, open-label, parallel-arm, randomized controlled trial conducted in the specialist outpatient clinics of two university-affiliated tertiary care hospitals. 154 adults aged 65 and above, diagnosed with solid organ cancer and planned for curative-intent chemotherapy and/or radiotherapy, and with a clinical frailty scale score of 4 and above, will be recruited. Subjects will be randomized to either attend a geriatric oncology supportive clinic or receive frailty education material. Quality of life questionnaires will be administered at baseline, 2 weeks, and 1, 3, 6, and 12 months from treatment initiation. Conclusion The GOS-Frail study investigates on the role of a synergistic geriatric oncology and supportive model of care in improving quality of life in older adults undergoing curative-intent cancer treatment.
kw: Geriatric Oncology; Supportive Care; chemotherapy; radiotherapy; models of care

title: AI-powered radiomics for early treatment response prediction and personalised treatment in nasopharyngeal carcinoma: integrating clinical, imaging and biomarker data
abs: Background Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) presents a therapeutic challenge due to its aggressive nature and variable treatment response. Early and accurate assessment of response following induction chemotherapy is critical for personalized treatment planning, prognostication, and adaptive therapy approaches. However, current methods suffer from subjectivity, limited early insights, and delayed information. Hypothesis: We propose that AI-driven radiomics analysis of on-treatment scans can predict both early therapeutic response and long-term prognosis in high-risk NPC patients. Specific Aims: 1. Develop a machine learning model using on-treatment CT scans to predict early treatment response and long-term prognosis with high accuracy. 2. Identify and validate response and toxicity biomarkers, for personalized treatment and minimization of adverse effects. Methods We will acquire data from 150 high-risk NPC patients undergoing induction chemotherapy. On-treatment CT scans will be analysed to extract radiomics features, and matched multimodal data including liquid biopsies (EBV DNA), clinical data (tumour features and demographics), and other on-treatment markers (serum protein markers) will be collected. Machine learning models will be developed for early response, prognosis, and toxicity prediction, comparing individual factor baseline models to those incorporating multimodal data. Preliminary Results: A pilot study on 85 head and neck squamous cell carcinomas demonstrated the feasibility of our approach, with a radiomics model based on 5 key features outperforming clinical models for early response prediction. Significance: By enabling early and accurate prediction of treatment response and long-term prognosis, our AI-powered radiomics approach has the potential to: • Optimize treatment: Guide personalized treatment decisions by tailoring therapy intensity based on predicted response, potentially improving survival while minimizing unnecessary toxicity. • Improve prognostication: Provide more accurate prognostic information to guide patient counseling and resource allocation. • Advance adaptive therapy: Facilitate real-time treatment adaptation based on early response assessment, improving treatment efficacy and reducing side effects to maximize quality of life.
kw: nasopharyngeal carcinoma; radiomics; AI; machine learning; biomarkers

title: A longitudinal study of the immunological and microbiome dynamics in Mycobacterial abscessus complex pulmonary disease.
abs: Non-tuberculous mycobacteria pulmonary disease (NTM-PD) is becoming increasingly prevalent worldwide, with Mycobacterium abscesses complex (MABC) subspecies being the predominant cause of NTM-PD in Singapore. MABC-PD is a chronic and often relapsing infection associated with significant morbidity. The uncertainties surrounding case management of MABC-pulmonary disease (MABC-PD) exacerbate its burden on public health. In part, a poor understanding of the role that the immune system and microbiome plays in MABC-PD pathophysiology hampers advancement in developing effective treatment strategies. Indeed, trials of immunomodulatory treatments in NTM-PD patients show conflicting outcomes and there are uncertainties regarding antibiotic effectiveness in relation to drug combination choices and treatment
kw: Non-tuberculous mycobacteria, transcriptomics, proteomics, microbiome, host-pathogen interactions, immune

title: The Effect of Combined Transcranial Pulse Current Stimulation (tPCS) and Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation (TENS) on lower limb motor function in Subacute to Chronic stroke patients with hemiplegia: A double-blind, sham-controlled, randomized controlled study.
abs:
Stroke is a leading cause of chronic disabilities worldwide. Over 50% of patients with stroke display residual motor dysfunctions and hemiparesis. Unfortunately, stroke rehabilitation programmes have not solved the issues of motor dysfunctions and hemiparesis, especially in the subacute stage and beyond. Current literature on non-invasive brain stimulation (NIBS) use in post-stroke rehabilitation centred largely on transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), which has not demonstrated significant effectiveness in lower limb rehabilitation. Transcranial pulsed current stimulation (tPCS) is a more novel type of NIBS which has been shown to induce greater corticospinal excitability effects than tDCS that may be relevant for promoting stroke recovery. 

We propose to study the efficacy of combined tPCS with Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation (TENS) in treating ischaemic and haemorrhagic stroke patients of their lower limb and gait dysfunction. In this prospective, double-blinded, sham-controlled, randomized control study, the investigators aim to recruit patients in the subacute to chronic stage of stroke (    > 2 weeks and <    6 months) and randomize them into treatment vs control arm. Treatment with tPCS and TENS consists of daily session of 30 minutes whereas the control arm subjects receive sham stimulation of similar
