title: Acute and post-acute multi-system sequelae following non-SARS-CoV-2 respiratory viral infection: a national population-based cohort study
abs: Aim: To assess the acute burden (0-30 days post-infection) of morbidity and mortality arising from non-SARS-CoV-2 respiratory-viral-infection (RVI) in a national cohort of hospitalized Singaporean adults, as well as post-acute (30-365d) incidence of new-onset multi-systemic sequelae following hospitalization for non-SARS-CoV-2 RVI, contrasted against (a)test-negatives; (b)COVID-19 hospitalizations. These results will be nested into analyses to assess cost-effectiveness of vaccination against non-SARS-CoV-2 RVIs. Hypothesis: We hypothesize that non-SARS-CoV-2 RVIs have comparable burden of acute/post-acute sequelae compared to COVID-19, and that vaccination will be largely cost-effective. Methods: Retrospective population-based cohort study, using three cohorts constructed from national healthcare claims data and hospital-level surveillance data: a cohort hospitalized for non-SARS-CoV-2 RVI (2018-2023); a cohort hospitalized (2018-2023) and tested negative for RVI; and a cohort hospitalized for COVID-19 (2020-2023), identified using the national COVID-19 registry. Information on acute/post-acute clinical outcomes will be obtained from national Mediclaims data. Risks of acute sequelae across non-SARS-CoV-2 RVI, test-negatives and COVID-19 will be contrasted using Cox-regression; risks of post-acute sequelae will be compared using competing risk-regressions. Differences in hazard-ratios for acute/post-acute sequelae in vaccinated vs. unvaccinated subgroups will be nested in analyses to understand net cost-effectiveness of vaccination to prevent specific sequelae. Importance and feasibility: Non-SARS-CoV-2 respiratory viral infections (RVIs) account for significant morbidity/mortality; however, detailed data on the disease burden accruing from acute infection are lacking from tropical settings with year-round RVI circulation. Additionally, while COVID-19 survivors are at-risk for developing chronic post-acute multi-system sequelae (“long COVID”), there is less clarity on risks of post-acute sequelae following non-SARS-CoV-2 RVIs, such as influenza/respiratory-syncytial-virus (RSV). This information is crucial in assessing cost-effectiveness of vaccination against non-SARS-CoV-2 RVIs, in particular RSV, for which vaccines were recently approved in older adults. This work builds on prior research published by the PI on long-term sequelae post-SARS-CoV-2 infection, and as such, is highly feasible.
kw: respiratory viral infection; influenza; RSV; COVID-19; vaccination; cost-effectiveness

title: SingCHILD: Evaluating prenatal exposome for healthy neonatal and infant development
abs: Background: The chemical exposome encompasses lifelong exposure to various xenobiotics, including substances from plant constituents, food additives, drugs, pesticides, cosmetics, and environmental pollutants. A critical window of susceptibility towards the toxic effects of chemical exposomes is during prenatal life. The enzyme set for xenobiotic biotransformation processes, the immune system, and metabolism are more sensitive in early life than in adults. Yet, understanding xenobiotic exposure effects in this vulnerable group in Singapore is limited. Closing this gap is crucial, especially as pregnant women and developing fetuses are highly susceptible to exposome effects. Hypothesis: Maternal exposomes will be transferred to neonates during prenatal development and will induce long-term epigenetic changes with enduring impacts on the child's health. Specific aims: To investigate the transmission of exposomes from mothers to neonates and examine the epigenetic implications of exposomes on neonates’ health. Methods: We will recruit 140 mother-child pairs from KK hospitals. A questionnaire will be employed to collect data on prenatal exposures. Saliva samples will be collected from mothers at 30-40 weeks of gestation and neonates within the first week of birth. Utilizing metabolomic experiments, the chemical exposomes in maternal and neonatal saliva will be screened. DNA methylation patterns of neonatal saliva samples will be analyzed using Reduced Representation Bisulfite Sequencing. Bioinformatic analyses will identify correlations between maternal and neonatal salivary exposomes. Associations between maternal exposomes and neonatal DNA methylation will be explored, integrating exposure data from the questionnaire into the analytical models. Significance: Successful completion of this project will provide Singapore’s first biological imprints of the early life exposome, significantly advancing our comprehension of the prenatal exposome's impact on fetal development and epigenetic programming. Additionally, it emphasises the importance of optimizing maternal and fetal health through prenatal care and lifestyle choices, mitigating the risk of adverse effects in future generations.
kw: exposomes, pregnancy, neonatal, saliva

title: Combinational inhibition of inflammasome and LRRK2:  a new therapeutic strategy for Parkinson’s disease
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Parkinson disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder with the hallmark pathological changes of dopaminergic neuron (DA) death in the substantia nigra. Numerous studies support neuroinflammation involve both CNS and peripheral blood immune cells in PD. Therapeutic effect and specificity of inflammatory pathway inhibitors in PD pathogenesis has yet to be determined. The combination of inhibitors targeting PD risk genes such as LRRK2 and inhibitors targeting inflammasome complex may have a specific protective effect in PD pathogenesis and prevent inflammation induced DA neuron degeneration. We have identified significantly increased levels of NLRP3 in plasma extracellular vesicles in PD patients. We have also established that MLi-2 efficiently inhibit LRRK2 and Rab10 phosphorylation and caspase-1 activation in immune cells in PD patients. Our collaborator’s group has identified and patented a novel ASC inhibitor which specifically targets the inflammasome complex to inhibit the caspase-1 and IL-1b cleavage in immune cells. We will further characterize the LRRK2 downstream targets and inflammasome complex in plasma EVs and in immune cells of PD patients. We will then genotype LRRK2 and establish the relationship between Asian specific LRRK2 risk variants and inflammasome activation in immune cells in PD patients. We will also confirm activation of inflammasome pathway in animal models carrying LRRK2 mutations. In addition, we will use a LRRK2 phosphorylation inhibitor and a novel inflammasome inhibitor in in vitro immune cells and midbrain organoid together with in vivo animal models to test if blocking LRRK2 and inflammasome pathways can synergistically prevent dopaminergic neuron death induced by the inflammation. We expect to find that the combination of the LRRK2 and the inflammasome inhibitors have a synergistic effect in preventing inflammation induced dopaminergic neuron degeneration with less off target effect and thus provide a potential novel therapy to stop or slow down the disease progression in PD.
kw: biomarker, extracellular vesicle, LRRK2 inhibitor, inflammasome inhibitor

title: Investigating human immunosenescence in disease and vaccination
abs: Immunosenescence confers disproportionate adverse effects to older adults with infections. This aging immunity shifts from a predominant T-helper(Th) 1 axis to a pro-inflammatory Th2 response, resulting in poorer vaccination responses and impaired defenses against intracellular pathogens such as tuberculosis(TB) and viruses. Interferon-gamma(IFNγ) is a key cytokine in inducing Th1 responses. My preliminary data on COVID-19 mRNA vaccinees across age groups showed that younger adults exhibited a significant increase in IFNγ-secreting CD4+ T-cells to wild-type and Omicron antigens after 2 doses of vaccination, which strongly positively correlated with SARS-CoV-2 neutralisation. This phenotype was absent in older adults and may explain their poorer vaccination response. Therefore, we hypothesise relative CD4+-driven IFNγ deficiency as a potential mechanism for the immunological shift to type 2 responses in aging. A consolidated study looking across different infections for common underlying immunophenotypes is critical in investigating this hypothesis and target discovery of mechanistic pathways contributing to immunosenescence. Our primary aim is to conduct detailed cellular and molecular analyses of longitudinal immune responses in younger versus older adults, with an emphasis on latent TB infection(LTBI) and COVID-19 hybrid immunity. Leveraging on our immunophenotyping data, our secondary aim is to investigate mechanisms underlying these age-associated deficiencies in immune repertoires to diseases with single-cell RNA sequencing. I will recruit 168 participants, 24 in each group: younger adults(21-40years) and older adults(≥70years) with LTBI on treatment, LTBI older adults not on treatment, age-matched healthy controls; younger and older adults pre-4th dose COVID-19 vaccination. Blood samples will be sent for high-dimensional flow cytometry, cytokine analysis, antigen-specific T-cell stimulation assays, CMV seropositivity and aging biomarkers. By investigating for a common link, our findings will have major implications on managing LTBI and COVID-19 infections, and more broadly, infections in older adults. Immunomodulators can then be explored to augment these age-associated immune deficiencies.
kw: immunosenescence; interferon-gamma; latent TB infection; COVID-19 vaccine; COVID-19 hybrid immunity; single cell RNA sequencing

title: Designing highly splicing varied synthetic RNAs to predict alternative isoform detection confidence via machine learning models
abs: RNA profiling is used in understanding diseases at cellular level, identifying cancer biomarkers, and developing drugs for RNA therapeutics. Although there are methods for transcript expression profiling or differential isoform usage, the high complexity of the transcriptome has hindered their evaluation due to a lack of a proper ground truth set. We aim to design synthetic RNA sequences of high complexity and concentration variability to facilitate the optimization of transcript profiling methods. We hypothesize that a systematic selection of reference gene candidates and proper design of isoforms and sequences can generate a cost-effective synthetic RNA set that remains comparable to the real transcriptome at both complexity and expression variability levels [Aim 1]. The new synthetic RNA sets, generated either by spiking in sample RNAs, or produced on its own to serve as a profound validation dataset, can be used to improve the evaluative power of existing transcriptome profiling methods. [Aim 2] Lastly, we also hypothesize that mixing synthetic RNAs at varying ratios allows us to train a machine learning model in recognizing the features of isoforms and identifying isoforms and alternative isoform events that can’t be accurately estimated with the current technology [Aim 3]. The successful implementation of this proposal would increase confidence in isoform expression estimates, directly improving the ability to identify disease associated isoforms and novel RNA based diagnostic markers, and facilitating experimental design of cancer biomarker discovery at isoform level.
kw: synthetic RNA design; machine learning; reference standards; RNA sequencing; transcriptome analysis; alternative isoform events

title: Splice-switching oligonucleotides as a therapeutic modality for hepatic genetic disease
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: The urea cycle is a metabolic pathway in the liver that converts ammonia into urea for excretion. Loss-of-function genetic mutations in any component of the urea cycle cause urea cycle disorder (UCD), which results in hyperammonemia and progressive encephalopathy, culminating in coma and death. Intronic mutations that modify splicing are abundant and often responsible for such genetic disorders. Splice-switching oligonucleotides (SSOs) are fully chemically-modified single-stranded RNA oligonucleotides that can correct splicing aberrations through steric hindrance of RNA binding proteins. In this study, I seek to prove the feasibility of using SSOs as a therapeutic modality for UCD by developing SSOs targeting OTC c.540+265G >A and SLC25A13 c.615+5G >A, two recurrent splice-altering mutations causing UCD. The sequences of the SSOs will first be rationally designed and tested. Effective sequences will then be chemically optimized for enhanced safety and efficacy by combining ribose modifications known to improve stability and target affinity with a screen for positional variations of inter-nucleotide phosphodiester and phosphorothioate linkages. The best candidates will then be conjugated to hepatocyte-targeting N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc) and validated for in vitro phenotypic rescue using induced hepatocytes differentiated from pluripotent stem cells harbouring the pathogenic variants. Mouse models that are responsive to human-specific SSOs will also be generated, either by humanizing relevant introns of the mouse gene or knock-in of an expression cassette interspersed with introns. The models will then be analyzed for manifestation of the UCD phenotype. GalNAc-conjugated SSOs will be tested in vivo for safety and target engagement using these models. If no notable toxicity is observed, the mice will then be analyzed in-depth for rectification of the UCD phenotype upon administration of the SSOs. If successful, this study will have proven the use of SSOs for hepatic genetic diseases and improved the state of SSO design for future RNA therapeutics development.
kw: Splice-switching oligonucleotides; RNA therapeutics; urea cycle disorder; splicing; inborn errors of metabolism; rare disease

title: Developing novel cell therapeutic strategy using gene-edited neutrophils
abs: The advent of immune-modulating therapies for cancer treatment has provided promising breakthroughs for cancer treatment over the past decades. Nevertheless, the efficacy of these therapies for pancreatic cancer remains low and therefore, further research is needed to improve these outcomes. In various cancer types like pancreatic cancer, tumour-infiltrating neutrophils have been implicated in multiple pro-tumoral functions, suppressing current immunotherapeutic treatments, and promoting tumour growth and metastasis. However, our understanding of the underlying mechanisms behind their 'rogue' behaviour remains significantly understudied. This proposal aims to identify and target the key mechanisms driving pro-tumorigenic functions in neutrophils while exploring the responsible signalling cues. Leveraging single-cell transcriptomics, CRISPR-based genome-editing screens, and in vitro assays, we will unravel the essential pathways and factors regulating pro-tumour neutrophil functions in vivo using a preclinical model of pancreatic cancer. We will also validate these findings with human samples and cancer cell lines to obtain a global understanding of the mechanisms perturbing neutrophil functions in cancer. The outcomes of this study will serve as the foundation for developing new drugs and effective neutrophil-specific therapies, ultimately improving treatment outcomes for pancreatic cancer patients.
kw: Pancreatic Cancer; Immune-therapy; Tumour infiltrating neutrophils; CRISPR

title: IMMUNe-mediated diseases: Epigenetic PRediction, biomarker Identification and Novel Therapeutics (IMMUNEPRINT)
abs: We hypothesize that the 2 prototypical immune-mediated diseases (IMDs), Crohn disease and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) possess both unique as well as shared epigenetic correlates that mediate disease susceptibility and outcome, respectively. Our preliminary data suggest that while most disease susceptibility loci in Crohn disease are common across different ancestries, ancestry-heterogenous loci exist. These ancestry-specific loci have distinct regulatory structures which are likely to impact the transcription of genes at these loci. We will assess whether genomic regions at ancestry-specific risk loci are differentially methylated in East Asian compared to European patients with Crohn disease providing an explanation for the differential strength of genetic association seen in both ancestries for Specific Aim 1. Knowing the underlying basis of this ancestry difference may identify therapeutic targets in East Asian Crohn disease. Currently, prognosis in IMDs is made by clinical scoring systems incorporating evidence largely from clinical data and laboratory parameters. However, these disease-specific prognostic models have been formulated without strong immunological rationale. With regards to outcome, there are important novel findings in our preliminary data that require validation. First, the methylomes of purified immune cell types appear to be stable across disease activity, seasonality and time. Second, IMDs of differing prognosis may share similar early immune epigenotypes in naïve CD4+ T cells. Third, hypomethylation of inhibitory receptor genes in naïve CD4+ T cells has not been reported previously. Fourth, a machine learning-constructed model using CpG sites of naïve CD4+ T cells may accurately predict time to first flare in inflammatory bowel disease. Lastly, the exhaustion-associated DNA methylation signature in naïve CD4+ T cells is also found in healthy controls. Therefore, we will stratify patients with Crohn disease and SLE into good and poor prognostic groups using an epigenetic signature of exhaustion in naïve CD4+ T cells for Specific Aim 2.
kw: Immune system diseases; epigenomics; biomarkers; therapeutics

title: Ghrelin as a gut-brain communication messenger shapes non-homeostatic feeding
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Obesity is an increasing global epidemic and environmental factors have been suggested to play an important role in it. Previous research has suggested that environmental factors, rather than physiological needs, critically regulate food intake in obese subjects. In both rodents and human beings, excessive feeding in satiated states could be driven by external cues through a conditioning procedure by pairing palatable food with such cues. We previously revealed the plastic change of the synaptic connection between ventral subiculum (vSub) and tuberal nucleus somatostatin (TNSST) neurons in conditioned feeding paradigm, but the underlying molecular mechanisms are still unknown. Ghrelin, a gut-secreted hunger hormone, not only promotes feeding but also plays a critical role in synaptic plasticity and learning tasks through activating ghrelin receptors expressed in multiple brain regions including the hippocampus. We also found that contextual feeding conditioning (CFC) leads to increased ghrelin secretion when the animals were exposed to contextual cues, indicating a potential involvement of ghrelin in conditioned feeding. Beyond its role in hunger-driven-food consumption, ghrelin could be a mediator of gut-brain communication in shaping non-homeostatic feeding behavior. We hypothesize that ghrelin signaling promotes CFC through facilitating the plastic change of the input neural circuits onto TNSST neurons. To test our hypothesis, we plan to investigate whether ghrelin signaling plays a critical role in CFC (Specific Aim 1) and investigate whether ghrelin signaling is critical for the functional and anatomical plastic change of the vSub-TN circuit in CFC (Specific Aim 2). The successful completion of the proposed research will provide an important molecular mechanism underlying such maladaptive feeding behavior. Furthermore, elucidating the physiological function of ghrelin will advance our understanding of this important gut hormone and lead to better clinical intervention strategies targeting this extensively studied but still illusive peptide, and thus may improve human health and wellness.
kw: Ghrelin Signaling; Synaptic Plasticity; Gut-brain Communication; Non-homeostatic Feeding.

title: Investigating the role of ectopic EBV infection in Natural Killer cells and its contribution towards Immune dysregulation
abs: Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) infects over 95% of the global population and establishes a persistent, lifelong infection. While usually asymptomatic, EBV infection can lead to severe lymphoproliferative and hyperinflammatory conditions, such as secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (sHLH), hypersensitivity to mosquito bites and chronic active EBV. These diseases often result in extensive tissue damage and life-threatening complications. Other than the overt activation of the immune system, ectopically EBV-infected natural killer (NK) cells (EBV+ NK cells) are also present in such diseases. Consistent with published studies, our preliminary analysis of EBV+ NK cell derived from sHLH patients revealed that they displayed a hyperactivated phenotype. This suggests that EBV+ NK cells may contribute to the immunopathogenesis of hyperinflammatory conditions. Despite the strong association, ectopic EBV infected in NK cells remained an understudied field, possibly due to difficulties in patient sample collection and resistance of primary NK cells to in vitro EBV infection posing a challenge to the study of host-pathogen dynamics. To overcome the challenge, we established a model in which primary NK cells acquire EBV receptor CD21 through trogocytosis on CD21+ target cells. Acquisition of CD21 on NK cells makes them susceptible to EBV infection, allowing us to maintain and monitor EBV-infected NK cells in culture. Our research proposal aims to leverage on this model to systematically uncover the development and trajectory of ectopic EBV infection in primary NK cells and their potential contribution to immune dysregulation in both in vitro and in vivo settings. The anticipated findings could provide novel diagnostic biomarkers and pave the way for new therapeutic strategies to disrupt the formation of these cells, potentially transforming the clinical management of EBV-associated disorders.
kw: Immune dysregulation, EBV, EBV-infected NK cells

title: Longitudinal exploration of Extracardiac Adipose tissue and coronary Plaque (LEAP)
abs: Coronary artery disease (CAD) poses a significant healthcare challenge, underscoring the importance of early diagnosis and continuous monitoring. The dynamic nature of extracardiac adipose tissue (EAT) and plaque morphology make predicting its progression a formidable task. Presently, there's no method to identify individuals at risk of rapid plaque progression. By leveraging insights from our APOLLO program, which included 3 million CT images from 5000 patients, we've developed AI algorithms and patented post-processing technologies (US patents: 10,349,910B2; 10,636,146B2; 10,832,492 B2; 10202303513W; 10202303520R) to assess extracardiac adipose tissue (EAT) and coronary plaque at baseline. The LEAP (Longitudinal exploration of Extracardiac Adipose tissue and coronary Plaque) project extends this work by enrolling a sub-cohort from APOLLO for repeated CT scans to track disease progression. LEAP's specific aims are: 1. Refine and evaluate AI technology's efficacy in characterizing EAT and coronary plaque progression. Participants (n=180) will undergo repeated CT scans, with analysis at baseline and follow-up. 2. Test the system with a sub-cohort of patients across three healthcare clusters and assess user experience. Clinical feedback will inform refinements to the AI solution's performance and usability. 3. Develop a minimal viable product with QMS for commercialization, showcasing core AI capabilities and an intuitive user interface to gather feedback and guide future enhancements. Predicting CAD progression with AI is crucial for timely interventions, optimizing patient care, preventing adverse events, engaging patients, efficient resource allocation, and advancing research. Our AI solution significantly reduces scan-to-report time (by ~90%) and costs (with ~45% savings per diagnosis) while maintaining high accuracy at the point-of-care, leading to improved patient outcomes and more efficient healthcare delivery.
kw: Coronary artery disease, Coronary CT angiography, Coronary plaque, Artificial intelligence

title: A Novel Device to Regulate Drainage of Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF) from External Ventricular Drain
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: External Ventricular Drain (EVD) is one of the most common neurosurgical procedures performed to treat hydrocephalus, a condition characterised by the build-up of excessive cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) in the brain. It is a life-saving treatment. Nearly 25,000 EVD's are being done yearly in the United States, with an estimated market size of 5.3 billion in 2019. The EVD is usually left in the brain to drain CSF for several days. The drainage of CSF is currently regulated by a manometer device that release CSF when the intracranial pressure exceeds a certain threshold (usual range of 5 - 25 cmH20). The manometer device will only work accurately when its zero reference point is positioned at the same horizon as the centre of the head (using the tragus of ear as a landmark). The manometer has to be repositioned each time the head move. Nurses have to perform a check at least once every hour. The device will malfunction when the head position change goes unnoticed. Complication of over or under-drainage can lead to detrimental brain damage. We have designed a novel device that will detect the intracranial pressure and automatically release or hold the CSF based on a pre-set pressure value. It removes the need of frequent manometer adjustments and reduce the risk of over or under drainage of CSF. We have completed the proof-of-concept stage with satisfactory lab results. In the next phase, we will assemble the components in a single unit, and perform tests to ascertain its functionality and durability, to de-risk and make it fit for human trial. The system design and algorithm that controls the valve function will form our intellectual properties. We will then form a start-up to take the device through clinical trials and regulatory approval.
kw: External Ventricular Catheter; EVD; Cerebrospinal fluid; CSF

title: Developing a renal detection system for early and accurate detection of silent kidney injury in obesity using shear wave elastography (ReELASTO study)
abs: Our work has shown that early (hyperfiltrating) kidney disease in metabolic states such as obesity are undetected today because of significant limitations in current laboratory testing using serum creatinine-based estimated glomerular filtration rate. 1 in 10 Singaporeans are obese, and even without other metabolic complications, risk progression to end-stage kidney failure. We aim to perform technological enhancement of existing 2-D shear wave elastography, and build artificial intelligence assisted imaging (ReELASTO) to detect kidney stiffness as a marker for early kidney disease. 2-D shear wave involves the perpendicular propagation of ultrasound shear wave through tissue parenchyma, with stiffer tissues having higher shear stiffness readings. 2-D shear wave elastography is well established in the imaging of chronic liver disease (Fibroscan), but renal elastographic literature is immature, due to challenges highlighted by our early work with the technology: Small studies that lack external validity, and Poor measurement reproducibility due to inability to distinguish different kidney microarchitecture and navigate shear propagation direction. Using prior assembled patient cohorts from a bariatric surgery patient dataset, and a large ongoing community cohort with central obesity and subclinical metabolic disease (Project RESET), we will perform longer term correlates between 2-D shear wave with validated renal surrogate outcomes such as albuminuria, and biomarkers established to assess CKD risk for progression: NGAL and FGF-23. We have developed provisional patent-filed software method wireframes for, and will progressively train and validate a computer algorithm, to develop ReELASTO’s artificial intelligence-assisted kidney architecture scanning. Non-invasive kidney stiffness by ReELASTO represents a paradigm shift in how we perceive kidney care, by uncovering hyperfiltrating early chronic kidney disease otherwise falsely reassured to be normal, and facilitating early treatment with pharmacotherapeutics which ameliorate kidney hyperfiltration. This project moves ReELASTO closer in milestone development to product commercialisation and impacting preventative renal care for the mass population.
kw: Hyperfiltration; chronic kidney disease; shear wave

title: The Pilot Implementation Study of the LILAC model for the Detection and Management of patients with Elevated Lipoprotein(a) levels and at High Risk of Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Events
abs: Background: The LILAC model is a novel method developed for the management of elevated lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] to address barriers involving training of healthcare professionals, and laboratory and logistic challenges. It encompasses education, awareness, implementation, and clinical management which can potentially be seamlessly integrated into clinical practice. An important reason for the persistence of atherosclerotic cardiovascular diseases (ASCVD) as the major cause of death is the under-diagnosis of hyper-Lp(a). Hyper-Lp(a) affects 20% of the general population worldwide with a 50% heritability rate. The causal links between elevated Lp(a) and ASCVD have led to 10 international guidelines recommending the measurement of Lp(a) at least once in all patients at high-risk of ASCVD. Yet, Lp(a) is not routinely measured and managed. From our preliminary study, we found that a major barrier in clinical practice is the lack of easy-to-follow clinical recommendations and hitherto non-existent clinical model-of-care for Lp(a). Aims and methods: Using a stepped-wedge design, we will pilot and investigate the feasibility and effectiveness of the LILAC model in five departments of Changi General Hospital: cardiology, endocrinology, vascular, neurology, and internal medicine. A pre-post survey will be administered to assess the impact of LILAC model rollout on 500 healthcare professionals’ knowledge, confidence, and their practice in detecting and managing hyper-Lp(a) in patients at high-risk for ASCVD. Process related outcomes such as provider adherence will be tracked prospectively to assess the effectiveness of implementation. Cost effectiveness of the implementation proposal will be analysed. Conclusion: The findings from this study will offer insights on the feasibility and effectiveness LILAC model as a model of Lp(a) care nationwide to all hospitals, with implications to primary care, medical education, and cascade testing in the general population. They address an important understudied atherosclerotic risk factor and will be timely with ongoing nation-wide scaling of Healthier-SG initiatives.
kw: lipoprotein(a); dyslipidaemia; atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease; model of care; myocardial infarction

title: The Academic Respiratory Initiative for Pulmonary Health (TARIPH)
abs: Each day, we breath 22,000 times inhaling 11,000 litres of air. In health, we take this for granted, however, respiratory disease represents half of the top six causes of global mortality and, significant knowledge gaps exist in Asia as current literature focuses on non-Asians and few clinical trials include Asian participants. Factors unique to the Asian sub-continent include ethnic and geographic diversity, disease heterogeneity, risk exposures, air quality, diet, and latitudinal effects. These factors result in variable clinical, immunological, and inflammatory disease endophenotypes, aetiologies and therapeutic responses between patients hindering early diagnosis, therapy, patient stratification, and clinical trials. Our Singaporean multi-ethnic, multi-racial population represents an opportunity to address such knowledge gaps in Asian respiratory disease. The Academic Respiratory Initiative for Pulmonary Health (TARIPH) was established with the mission of “bringing research to patients through partnerships” and a vision to “generate (preliminary) data by aligning strategic academic expertise across Singapore to benefit Singaporeans living with lung disease through research”. Since establishment, TARIPH has brought together interdisciplinary teams, generated strong preliminary data, and established significant collaborative networks across the basic-translational-clinical spectrum forming the basis of this program. Through five interlinked themes, we will conduct innovative basic, translational, and clinical respiratory science, incorporating multi-institutional, inter-disciplinary TARIPH partnerships to address Multi-ethnic Endo-Phenotyping of Asthma and COPD (MEPAC) (Theme 1) including the Burden and biology of Post-Intensive Care Syndromes (2B-PICS) (Theme 2). CEllular Models of respiratory disease for Asian Phenotyping (CEMAP) will be developed (Theme 3), while FOrecasting COPD and Asthma attendances using Large-scale time Series for patient and policy support (FOCALS) will be pursued (Theme 4) alongside studies focused on Climate change, Allergy, Pollution, and the Environment (CAPE) (Theme 5). Overall, this program aims to enhance the evidence-base of Asian respiratory disease and position Singapore as a key academic respiratory hub for the Asian-sub-continent.
kw: Respiratory; Critical Care; Asthma; COPD; Allergy; TARIPH

title: Photoelectrocatalytic:mediator strategies towards emissions-free e-refining of chemicals
inst: ISCE2 - Institute of Sustainability for Chemicals, Energy and Environment
abs: Chemical manufacturing is an energy- and CO2-intensive sector. More than 0.4 billion tons of CO2 emissions are attributable to the production of oxygenates via the oxidation of hydrocarbons to supply commodity materials for the plastics and textiles industries. To reduce these emissions, I will build novel photoelectrocatalyst:mediator assemblies for the activation of inert hydrocarbons for selective oxidation under ambient conditions, which can be powered by renewable energy. In WP1, I will develop mediators that can facilitate the indirect exchange of electrons between the electrode and the hydrocarbons. The mediator will be electrochemically activated to a highly oxidative state capable of activating the inert hydrocarbons, that which cannot be easily obtained through the usual thermochemical means. The electrocatalyst:mediator configuration buffers the hydrocarbon from excess positive charges at the electrode, thereby enabling selective oxidation even at high potentials and reaction rates. This contrasts with state-of-art electrochemical oxidation of hydrocarbons such as methane and propylene, which operate at near-thermodynamic potentials and are characterized by low reaction rates. For poorly-reactive hydrocarbons such as methane, ethane and hexane, a large amount of energy input is required to cleave the strong sp3 C-H bonds. This can cause the electrochemical system to uncontrollably favor competing reactions such as electrocatalyst dissolution. Hence in WP2, I will explore the combination of photo-irradiation with my electrocatalyst:mediator strategy to generate highly-oxidizing holes in semiconductor-based electrodes or activate mediator species to much higher oxidation capabilities. This can enable C-H cleavage in hydrocarbons with much reduced electric potentials, thereby avoiding destructive overoxidation of other components of the electrochemical system. At the extended heterogeneous:homogeneous reaction space, chemical reactions consume reactant species, form intermediates and release byproduct species1-3. This causes the reaction environment to differ greatly from the bulk electrolyte. Hence for WP3, in-built probes will be integrated to detect chemical signatures of these species in this extended reaction space. In contrast to conventional operando techniques such as Raman spectroscopy which monitors only the electrode:electrolyte interface, the in-built probes can monitor chemical signatures at different length-scales, which is imperative for understanding these photoelectrocatalyst:mediator systems. The positive outcome of the proposed study will make significant headway in the burgeoning field of powering chemical production with renewable energy. The technologies described can reduce a significant fraction of emissions in Singapore’s large chemicals sector and strengthen Singapore’s position as a sustainability powerhouse both regionally and internationally.
kw: electrocatalyst; photoelectrocatalyst; petrochemicals; fine chemicals; C-H activation

title: Going Skin-Deep: Targeting Stem Cells to Tackle Inflammatory Skin Diseases
abs: Our skin is the largest regenerative organ with the ability to expand more than 8000-fold in a month. Such regenerative capacity is accorded by epidermal stem cells and is central to maintaining a defense barrier against external threats. Yet, epidermal stem cells are rarely the focus of current therapies for restoring skin health. Existing strategies to treat common chronic inflammatory skin diseases, such as atopic dermatitis (AD) and psoriasis, are centred on symptomatic management. They either target the non-permanent skin barrier layers to provide temporary relief, or curb inflammation which in turn increases risk of infection. I hypothesize that we can bias the regenerative capacity of epidermal stem cells towards more favourable outcomes by understanding how they modulate their responses when tissue homeostasis is perturbed. This will allow us to harness the capabilities of long-lived epidermal stem cells to construct a healthy skin barrier as a more definitive disease treatment option. To test, I will dissect clonal response of epidermal stem cells towards barrier dysfunction and inflammation. I will map long-term epigenetic changes in epidermal stem cells post-inflammation. I will also determine how epidermal stem cells modulate immune sensing so as to prevent immune overdrive. Findings will reveal epidermal stem cell clonal behaviours and immune sensing modulators that we can influence to curb disease initiation and progression, as well as epigenetic marks that we can manipulate to prevent disease recurrence. These stem cell-centric findings will constitute a novel therapeutic approach that may also be generalized to other diseases at large.
kw: skin; epidermal stem cells; barrier dysfunction; inflammation; inflammatory skin diseases; disease therapy

title: Ethical Approaches to AI-Visualization in Shakespeare Adaptation
abs: The main goal of this project is to create innovative visual adaptations of Shakespeare plays in animation, supported by AI production methods. Given its recent emergence, the focus on AI is the logical next step building from the PI’s previous 2 successful Tier 2 projects. It continues his impactful collaboration with the Shakespeare Institute in Stratford-upon-Avon. The project will not only use AI to maximize the potential of artistic and technological outcomes but also consider the ethical dimension of its use. We posit that the use of AI as an artistic tool needs to be informed by human-driven aesthetics and ethical standards: By creating corresponding working methods, the investigators propose that the project can achieve both: Innovative artistic outcomes and an ethical framework for AI uses in visual adaptation. This two-pronged approach will result in high artistic and scholarly impact as well as suggestions for future policymaking towards AI-application. The emerging methods and techniques can then be applied to uses in filmic animation, games and immersive media/expanded animation. Preparatory discussions with collaborator Prof. Michael Dobson, Director of the Shakespeare Institute in Stratford-upon-Avon have identified research outcomes and deliverables that would serve as testbeds for the implementation of AI-assisted creative production methods: 1.) To create animation in the style of famous classic Shakespeare illustrators (e.g. Delacroix’s famous Shakespeare illustrations). This will be tested through the creation of a 5-minute animated short film. 2.) Creating new performances of famous classic Shakespeare actors in hyper-realistic or stylized designs of bygone times on the basis of photography and photogrammetry – supported by AI-related production methods. This project will not only add new artistic possibilities to the spectrum of digital Shakespeare studies but also create new knowledge beyond the specifics of the field. This will include avoiding plagiarism and giving artists control over AI-tools.
kw: AI; Shakespeare; adaptation; animation; ethics

title: A review of endometrial pathology in women's health and fertility
abs: Endometrial hyperplasia is the precursor to endometrial cancer. Both endometrial hyperplasia and cancer can affect women’s survival, quality of life and fertility. Advancements in cancer treatment and improved survival in oncology patients have also allowed patients to push for more research in the importance of survivorship and long-term quality of life after cancer treatment. Cancer treatment is also costly to the patient and the health system. In 2019, a quarter of the nation's total drug spending was on cancer drugs. Medical advancements mean that these costs are likely to continue to rise. As such, there is a need to consider primary prevention to limit the progression to disease but appropriately identifying and managing modifiable risk factors. The goal of my research is to control modifiable risk factors in patients at risk of the disease, optimise treatment and outcomes in patients with endometrial cancer, in hope to decrease the incidence and severity (late stage) of endometrial cancer, so as to improve outcomes to survival and quality of life.
kw: endometrial cancer; endometrial hyperplasia; oncofertility; survivorship

title: Investigation of Muscle Histopathology in Post-Stroke Spasticity and the Impact of Hyperselective Neurectomy
abs: Introduction Stroke is a common cause of long-term disability in Singapore. A complication of stroke frequently dealt with in hand surgery is upper limb spasticity, which severely impacts patients’ quality of life and functional independence. Recently, hyperselective neurectomy (HSN) has been proposed as an ideal treatment method to reduce spasticity, but the ideal timing of intervention is largely arbitrary. Histological changes in terms of the connective tissue components also remain relatively unknown. Aims Our primary aim is to examine the histological changes that occur over time within the muscle during the development of spasticity in rats after spinal cord transection and after HSN. The secondary aim is to determine the most ideal timing for intervention with HSN to minimise muscle changes of spasticity in rats. We will further develop this study in future by examining the histological changes of upper limb muscles in post-stroke human subjects, and investigating the histological changes and clinical effectiveness of performing hyperselective neurectomy on post-stroke human subjects. Hypothesis We hypothesise that HSN at an appropriate timing (4-8 weeks after spinal cord transection) will lead to reversal of histological changes of spastic muscles. Methodology Spasticity will be induced in rats via spinal cord transection. Muscle biopsies will be taken at 6 different time points and sent for histological evaluation. The histological changes will guide our hypothesis regarding the ideal timing for HSN. At the respective time periods after spinal cord transection, the rats will undergo HSN and muscle biopsies thereafter. The results of the biopsy post-HSN will be compared to the results in the first part of the study to evaluate the changes over time. These results will help guide future practice in terms of operative management for patients with post-stroke spasticity in future. It will also help us gain a better understanding of contracture formation.
kw: hyperselective neurectomy, spasticity, stroke, muscle histopathology

title: AI-Generated Content: Economic Impacts and Implications for Policy and Regulation
abs: Advancements in generative AI’s capability have led to various leaps and bounds in the related applications. For instance, programmers have developed AI systems using natural language processing methods to write news articles that report sports and stock market news. ChatGPT, OpenAI’s language generator, can generate unending, impressive textual content in response to input parameters provided by humans. Platforms such as Stable Diffusion and Midjourney allow artists to generate photo-realistic images given any text input within seconds. As generative AI technologies move into mass adoption, a detailed understanding of consumer responses and producer strategies toward AI-generated content, the economic impacts from the consumption of media content produced or co-produced by AI, and the implications for content production and regulatory policies is needed. We therefore propose to answer the following research questions for this proposal: a) How and to what extent does AI-generated content have demand effects on economic outcomes of content consumers in relation to fundamental AI-generated content attributes (i.e., AI integration, reliability and creativity), and why do these arise? b) How and to what extent do content producers exhibit strategic AI-generated content production behaviors by generating content to cater to consumer preferences for AI-generated content and its fundamental content attributes? c) What are the managerial and regulatory implications of regulating AI-generated content consumption and/or production? Can we balance the competing interests between innovative AI-generated content business, truthful or accurate content, and intellectual property rights? Our research therefore aims to make the following theoretical and practical contributions, in relation to our proposed three research questions above: a) Our proposed research will be among the pioneers to identify the fundamental key attributes, beyond technical considerations (Brown et al. 2020) or related risk issues (Weidinger et al. 2022), that define the central nature of AI-generated content and for which could have key influences on the perceptions and demand/supply responses toward such AI-generated content. This endeavour will thus have significant scope to contribute new knowledge to the various related streams of work in the information systems, economics and marketing disciplines, for example, on user/firm-generated content (Goh et al. 2013), online labor platforms and markets (Möhlmann et al. 2021), and the economics of artificial intelligence (Cockburn et al. 2018), i.e., where the demand effects of AI-generated content have rarely been examined now. b) Beyond current simple demand outcome comparisons of human-only, AI-only and human-AI co-created work or service outputs (Adam et al. 2022; Reisenbichler et al. 2022), and stated preference studies using lab experiments to evaluate consumer preferences towards AI/algorithmic (versus human) services or products in a
kw: Generative AI, Digital Media Content, Digital Labor Platform, Structural Demand and Supply Model, Econometric and Causal Impact Evaluation

title: Modalities of Religious Populism in Asia: How Secularism Shapes Religion and Politics
abs: Our research aims to answer two theoretically and empirically significant questions that have been largely unaddressed in the existing literature: 1) How do the different forms of secularism in Asian countries condition the interactions of religion and populist politics? 2) How can the experience of Asia contribute to our conceptual understanding of religion’s role in populism not just in Asia but in other parts of the world? Our study’s originality and significance lie in considering secularism as a variable and conceptualising religion as both an ideological and cultural resource. Conceptually, we propose four ideal types of state as a new way to analyse the interaction of religion and populism: non-secular; weakly secular; strongly secular; and atheistic. Our project’s advantage over existing methodologies lies in our utilisation of both quantitative and qualitative research methods to explore the interactions of secularism, religion, and populism in Asia. We will develop an innovative time series, cross-national database on religion, secularism, and populism for all the countries in Asia. For our qualitative study, we will focus on one case study country for each of the four types of states: non-secular Malaysia, weakly secular India, strongly secular Singapore, and atheistic China. In these case studies, us examine the contextual and enabling conditions that either hinder or facilitate the rise of religious populism, which our quantitative data cannot capture.This will provide us with rich data to investigate complex causal mechanisms, historical processes, and deeper meanings and understandings that are highly dependent on the contextual specificities of discrete country cases. Our comparative research in Asia will provide a much-needed correction to the existing religious populism scholarship that is predominantly centred on Christianity and politics of democratic states in Europe and the US. Our empirical and theoretical insights from Asia will contribute to the broader scholarship on secularism, religion and populism.
kw: religion, populism, secularism, Asia, politics

title: Machine Learning Enhanced Multidimensional Indexes for Modern Database Systems
abs: Background Indexes are vital for achieving good performance in database systems, and can speed up the execution time of queries by orders of magnitude. The current database systems still have challenges in supporting querying on big data, or a large number of queries posed to a database (e.g., on a promotion day for e-commerce service provider). The need of querying and managing big data and big queries, together with the success of machine learning techniques in other domains, motivate the database community to explore how machine learning can be used to build learned indexes recently. The idea behind learned indexes is to learn a cumulative distribution function (CDF) that maps a search key to the storage address of a data object. Despite the success of these learned indices in improving the efficiency of processing some types of queries, they still have various limitations. Furthermore, they need to replace both the index structures and query processing algorithms currently used by the database systems, and such a radical departure, together with their limitations, make it challenging for them to be deployed in current database systems. Aims and Novelty Rather than learning a CDF for a data to replace the classic indexing structures as it is done in the learned indexes, in our recent work in SIGMOD’23, we consider a fundamentally different approach, i.e., to use machine learning (ML) techniques to construct a better R-Tree, called RLR-tree, for better query efficiency. We call it ML enhanced indexes. The success of our preliminary work suggests a promising open direction in machine learning enhanced indexing construction. But our preliminary work does not consider instance-optimized indexes, which aims to build optimal indexes for a given query workload. Along this direction, we aim to propose new machine learning techniques to build instance-optimized indexes to enhance the querying performance of existing multidimensional or spatial index techniques. Different from the learned indexes, we aim to develop ML techniques to enhance the classic indexing structures without changing the indexing structures. As a result, the existing query processing algorithms based on the classic index structures are still applicable. This would make it easier for the ML enhanced index to be deployed by current databases, compared with learned indexes. This project aims to make the following key research and technical breakthroughs: (1) We will propose new techniques to build ML empowered instance-optimized multidimensional indexes such that the query performance on big data and difficult queries can be significantly improved. Specifically, we focus on three types of existing multidimensional index techniques, including (a) RLR-tree for the dynamic scenarios, where we build and maintain the R-tree in the manner of one-by-one insertion, (b) a new top-down packing R-tree for the batch loading scenarios, where we build the R-tree in bulk loading when the data is alre

title: Attention-based Generative Model for Antibody Sequence-Structure Co-design
abs: To accelerate the computational process for antibody discovery, we will be investigating the hypothesis that the study of antibody-antigen binding affinity is significant and associated with the design of antibodies. A contrastive self-supervised learning model will be adapted for discovering (monoclonal) antibodies with high-binding affinity and specificity for the target antigen. Thereafter, we will be identifying the corresponding features related to discriminating between affinity-labelled antibodies with high and low binding affinity. Lastly, to achieve antibody diversity and conduct rational design of antibodies, we will be applying a cross-attention network model to study pairing preferences between the antibody variable domain of light chain (VL) and variable domain of heavy chain (VH). Adopting rational instead of de novo antibody design reduces cost and at the same time improves computational efficiency and scalability. Last but not least, we will evaluate the generated or predicted structures with molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and experimentally validate or identify high potential candidates suitable for further clinical applications.
kw: antibody; antigen; affinity; features; self-supervised; cross-attention

title: Phase-Type Sieve: Theory and Applications
abs: Semiparametric statistical models – containing both a low-dimensional parametric component which can be easy to interpret scientifically and an infinite-dimensional nuisance parameter which enables flexibility in the model fitting – are widely used in statistics, biostatistics and econometrics. Given a random sample, we often estimate the parameter through maximizing an empirical criterion over the parameter space. However, the maximization is often computationally infeasible when searching over the infinite-dimensional parameter space for the nuisance parameter and the sieve idea has become popular to circumvent the difficulty. Sieve estimators are defined by maximizing the empirical criterion over a sequence of finite-dimensional spaces whose complexity increases with the sample size and the limit space is dense in the original space. when the nuisance parameter space is the class of Holder continuous functions, Fourier series, splines, wavelets, artificial neural network, and Bernstein polynomials are popular choices for the approximation. In many applications, the nuisance parameter space of direct interest is the class of density functions, which are nonnegative with integral one. It has been well recognized that the above sieve tools do not work well in this scenario, mostly due to the unit integral constraint. To address this critical issue, the overarching goal of this project is to promote phase-type distributions as a method of sieve. Phase-type distributions are defined as the distributions of absorption times of a Markov chain with one absorbing state and all other states transient. They are dense in the space of nonnegative distributions, closed under minimum, maximum, and convolution, and compatible with the accelerated failure time model when handling covariates. These properties render them attractive for sieve density estimation for problems with sophisticated data missing patterns. However, the class of phase-type distributions is over-parameterized and non-identifiable, and the phase-type approximation error rate for a given density as the number of phases increases remains unknown. These handicaps hinder theoretical development of phase types as a sieve method. To fill the above gaps, the main objective of this project is to design a sequence of identifiable phase-type density classes with provable approximation error rate for a given non-negative density, and the design should also consider the balance between the approximation error rate and the statistical error arising from random data. We will apply it to sieve M-estimation and establish general theory on the asymptotic behaviour. With modern empirical process techniques, we will first show that the sequence of the semiparametric sieve estimators, under an appropriate metric and reasonable regularity conditions, is consistent; while the rate of convergence is not root-n but depends on the smoothness of the true density function. title: Automated and Efficient Inference for Bayesian Time Series models
abs: Uncertainty is present in most real-world phenomena. Dynamical systems provide us with a principled modeling framework to quantify and reason about uncertainty. Although probabilistic forecasting of complex systems is paramount to many disciplines, general methods for long-term forecasts with calibrated uncertainty are still an open problem. Applications abound in geophysics, finance, weather forecasting, quantitative biology, and a host of additional domains. In practical settings, collected data may be noisy, indirectly observed, and limited in number or resolution. Quantifying the associated uncertainty is an essential part of the inference process, vital to the efficient use of computational models and efficient decision-making. In this project, we focus on a very flexible class of models for time series data known as state space models (SSM) or hidden Markov models. In this project, our computational approach is based on sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) methods that can provide state-of-the-art approximations. Adopting the SMC framework provides a principled approach that offers many advantages such as the ability to learn parameters sequentially and perform model comparisons. From a computational perspective, SMC methods are well-suited to exploit modern parallel computation tools, such as graphics processing units (GPUs) and parallel computing architectures. In this proposal, we aim to push the limits of controlled-SMC (cSMC) methods, a powerful and flexible class of algorithms recently developed by some

title: Functional MR imaging-based brain decoding using large-scale representation learning and generative models
abs: Exploration of the human brain is of fundamental interest. Our perception of the world is determined not only by the objective properties of stimuli but also by our prior knowledge and experiences, leading to complex brain activities. Deciphering these brain activities and recovering the encoded information is an important goal in cognitive neuroscience. It deepens our understanding of the human visual system and builds a solid foundation for bridging human and computer vision through the Brain-Computer Interface. As the most widely used non-invasive brain imaging technology with a high spatial resolution ( >1 million voxels in the brain), functional MR imaging (fMRI) has been playing a major role in understanding how the brain works at the temporal resolution of less than 1 second. fMRI indirectly measures brain activities, often used to recover visual information. However, it remains challenging to decode high-dimensional information from brain fMRI recordings due to the complex representations of brain signals and the scarcity of data annotations. To address this challenge, emerging deep learning approaches including representation learning and generative models are needed. Representation learning involves training algorithms to extract meaningful features from complex data (e.g., brain fMRI), and represent them in a compact and interpretable form. Generative models, on the other hand, aim to learn the underlying distribution of the data and generate new samples (e.g., visual images) that are similar to the original data. Very recently, by leveraging cutting-edge representation learning and generative models, we developed a deep learning model under biological guidance for vision decoding based on very few paired annotations between fMRI and images (CVPR 2023). For the first time, our model can reconstruct images with not only plausible details but also accurate semantics and features. Our approach substantially outperformed the other state-of-the-art deep learning models in both semantic mapping and generation quality. This is a proof-of-concept study that demonstrates the feasibility of vision decoding from brain fMRI recordings. There are still some gaps to be addressed. First, the image generation quality and consistency of the existing approach need to be improved at the pixel level. Second, the pre-training fMRI data should contain more visual stimuli to enhance the learning of relevant brain features. Third, it is unclear whether we can extend the current framework to decode other modalities such as audio or video (see our preliminary results). Brain recordings such as fMRI signals is a set of time-varying observations across different domains (i.e., visual and auditory). How to model the actual spatiotemporal dependence of these observations across domains for accurate decoding of video/audio input remains to be investigated. title: Directed Self-Assembly of Thermoresponsive Magnetic Nanocrystals
abs: The ability to assemble nanocrystal (NCs) into high-order structures offers the opportunity to explore possibly intriguing collective properties that emerge from the spatial association of individual building blocks for a wide range of applications. A host of strategies have been developed to organize NCs, including self-assembly induced by inter-particle forces and directed self-assembly guided by interfaces, templates, or external fields. Notably, self-assembled NCs could easily disintegrate to generate defects (e.g., nanoscopic or microscopic cracks) owing to the weak van der Waals forces or electrostatic interaction between NCs, thereby greatly affecting their properties when subjected to external stimuli. Thus, to create nanostructures via self-assembly with greater structural complexity, in addition to spherical nanoparticles, geometrically intricate building blocks (e.g., nanorods, tetrahedra, etc.) and stronger external forces are invoked. Moreover, the routes to permanently fixing complex nanostructures need to be developed to impart their post-self-assembly harvesting and incorporation into other processes. However, effective strategies for crafting complex yet stable self-assembled nanostructures are comparatively few and limited in scope. In this context, the objectives of this proposal are to (a) rationally design and assemble a new class of multifunctional (i.e., crosslinkable, stimuli-responsive, and magnetic) nanocrystals (NCs), (b) explore their dimension-dependent magnetic properties (i.e., structure-property relationships), and (c) capitalize on these assembled NCs for tailored 3D-structured soft robotic elements with magneto/light-control of actuation and responsive behavior. Intellectual Merit: The intellectual merit of the proposed research is manifested in (1) judicious tuning of inter-nanocrystal distance to regulate magnetic properties of self-assembled chain-like nanostructures via incorporation of thermoresponsive polymer blocks; (2) systematic investigation into shape-dependent magnetic properties of self-assembled chain-like nanostructures with different magnetic building blocks (i.e., nanoparticles and nanorods); (3) scrutiny of the differences in magnetic properties among randomly dispersed NCs, aligned NC chain aggregates, and arrays of NC chains; and (4) creation of nano-actuators based on the arrays of self-assembled NC chains for dual-responsive, remotely controlled actuating designs such as self-propelling nanorobots and soft robotic arms with fast shape morphing triggered by programmed remote stimuli. If successful, this project will result in an intriguing class of multifunctional NCs of different architectures with tunable thermal, magnetic and photothermal properties as well as outstanding structural integrity (i.e., stability) enabled by crosslinking for use in actuators, separation, purification, and sensors, among other areas. title: Novel Polymeric composite resin for 3D printed multifunctional optical waveguides
abs: Stretchable waveguides with low attenuation losses hold great potential for applications such as optical communication in soft robots, surgical tools, and health monitoring devices. Employing 3D printing for fabricating these waveguides offers the advantage of enhanced design possibilities and integration in functional devices, a feat that is challenging in conventional methods. Although there have been reports of polymer-based stretchable waveguides, they are not compatible with 3D printing. On the flip side, existing 3D printing resins lack the necessary attributes for producing stretchable optical waveguides, notably the combination of high elasticity and low optical signal loss. This project's primary objective is to conceive and produce novel UV (ultraviolet) curable compositions suitable for 3D printing stretchable optical waveguides, particularly geared toward soft robotics applications. The first goal of this project is to design and formulate novel UV-curable polymeric composite resins utilizing fluorinated oligomers and polyurethane elastomers with desired optical properties and elasticity. The second goal of this proposal is to design and 3D print optical waveguides using a multi-material 3D printer for optical communication and sensing applications. Our study will inspire the rational design of functional resins for the 3D printing of optoelectronic devices and open doors to novel applications of optical waveguide-based sensors by utilizing Additive Manufacturing (AM) approaches.

title: From Limited Data to Smart Decisions: Identifying and Controlling Agent Behavior in Games
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: With the increasing integration of systems of interconnected intelligent agents in our lives, policymakers require tools to identify and control their dynamic behavior. Current data-driven approaches use vast data and powerful machine-learning algorithms. However, their applicability is limited in time-critical scenarios where quick estimation and control of system dynamics are required in response to unexpected events. This proposal aims to: Develop a theoretical and algorithmic framework for identifying and controlling the dynamical behavior of a multi-agent system, in real-time and with limited data. To address this challenge we introduce the Side Information Assisted Regression(SIAR) method, designed to identify the dynamics governing agent behavior in games, where game-theoretic principles model agent interactions. To enhance system recovery in the face of limited data, we identify and incorporate within SIAR side-information constraints native to game-theoretic applications, thereby narrowing the space of admissible solutions. Our extensive preliminary studies indicate that SIAR accurately recovers the true dynamics across a spectrum of games, natural dynamics, and robust benchmarks—even when the underlying system is chaotic. Moreover, when integrated with control methods, SIAR enables efficient real-time control of multi-agent systems, highlighting its promise as a key facilitator of real-time decision-making and management in multi-agent environments.
kw: Sum-of-squares optimization; system identification; learning in games; game theory; dynamical systems; replicator dynamics

title: Genomic insights into Sea Turtles: Understanding population dynamics and climate change
abs: The marine ecosystem of Southeast Asia is widely recognized as a biodiversity hotspot due to its unique geographic location at the confluence of the Pacific and Indian Oceans, as well as favorable environmental conditions such as warm and nutrient-rich waters. However, this exceptional marine biodiversity is under threat from climate change, causing habitat loss and alterations. The consequences of climate change include population decline, reduction in genetic diversity, and species extinction, which have cascading effects on ecosystem health. To mitigate the loss of marine biodiversity, it is crucial for scientists to conduct comprehensive studies and fill knowledge gaps, considering the regional scale, to develop effective conservation plans, particularly in understudied regions of Southeast Asia. This research proposal focuses on the critically endangered species of sea turtles in Southeast Asia, which play a unique and critical role in both oceanic and coastal ecosystems. Our objectives are as follows: First, we aim to generate whole-genome population datasets to examine the population structure and enhance the resolution of management units for sea turtles in conservation planning. By utilizing these datasets, we will develop genome-wide nuclear genetic markers that will enable us to accurately trace the nesting site of sea turtle samples. This information can be instrumental in promoting population genetic studies, monitoring, and preventing illegal trade. Second, we will assess the vulnerability of each sea turtle population based on their genetic diversity and degree of inbreeding. This assessment will help to understand nesting behavior and identify target populations for conservation efforts. Third, we will infer the demographic dynamics and natural adaptation of the sea turtle populations and examine the impact of past and future climate changes through an interdisciplinary approach combining population genomics, geography, and ecology. We aim to link their population history and adaptation with sea level rise and global warming. The research team consists of scientists with extensive expertise in population genomics and marine ecology, along with international collaborators actively involved in sea turtle research and conservation in Southeast Asian countries. This highlights the potential influence and benefits this project will bring to the region. The project’s outcomes will provide crucial baseline knowledge and revolutionize the global standard for sea turtle studies and conservation plans. Furthermore, the innovative approach to studying sea turtles’ response to sea level rise and global warming will provide insights into the broader impact of climate change on marine ecosystems and biodiversity. Overall, the project holds significant promise for advancing marine conservation efforts, protecting these iconic marine animals, and maintaining a healthy marine ecosystem of immense value to local communities and future generations i
kw: Climate change, sea turtles, sea level rise, global warming, population genetics, conservation

title: Construct kidney organoids with higher-order tissue architecture for studying congenital kidney diseases
abs: The global incidence of chronic kidney disease (CKD) is increasing with an alarming rate due to the high occurrence of cardiovascular and metabolic diseases. As an invisible killer, CKD is affecting more than 10% of the global population, responsible for approximately 1.2 million deaths worldwide each year (GBD Chronic Kidney Disease Collaboration 2020). Hence, there is a pressing need to gain a better understanding of kidney disease aetiology and to develop new approaches for managing CKD. While model organisms are highly useful in revealing the biological underpinning of human kidney development and disease, they are limited in the degree to which they faithfully recapitulate the specifics of human anatomy and physiology. In the past decade, human pluripotent stem cell (PSC)-derived miniature kidneys, termed kidney organoids, have emerged as an alternative for the conventional animal models. While kidney organoids have demonstrated remarkable capability in revealing human renal pathophysiology, the current array of kidney organoids has its limitations. In particular, the current kidney organoids do not have the cellular repertoire and macro-anatomical structure that are reminiscent of the cognate organ. Different from other organs such as liver and pancreas, the principal functionality of which could be accomplished by few critical cell types, the realization of kidney function is heavily dependent upon the highly specialized three-dimensional organ architecture, as well as the full array of intercellular communications. To address these burgeoning issues of the current generation of kidney organoids, we aim to generate a comprehensive repertoire of cell types via direct differentiation from human PSCs, and construct kidney organoids with higher-order tissue architecture that can be further exploited for modelling Congenital Anomalies of the Kidney and Urinary Tract (CAKUT). To achieve this goal, we will 1) synergize CRISPR Cas9 gene editing tools and direct differentiation of human PSCs to enrich the desired renal cell populations; 2) employ in vitro self-organization and in vivo xenotransplantation to enhance the structural and functional maturation of the higher-order kidney organoids; 3) perform genome-wide pooled CRISPR screening to reveal candidate CAKUT genes in the multicellular kidney organoid system. The successful accomplishment of this project will lead to 1) a novel kidney organoid system that demonstrates higher physiological relevance with human kidney; 2) a deeper understanding of the intercellular crosstalk among different renal cell types in human; 3) revelation of unknown risk genetic factors for congenital kidney diseases.
kw: Kidney organoid, pluripotent stem cell, differentiation, CRISPR, pooled screening, CAKUT

title: Unraveling the transcriptional cascade of the stomatal self-renewing cells
abs: Background: Developmental master regulators are transcription factors critical for cell type specification in multicellular organisms. Addressing how these master regulators modulate transcriptomes and control downstream genes is thus a fundamental pursuit in developmental biology. Due to ease of access and the power of Arabidopsis genetics, my lab utilizes the development of stomata—the essential surface pores of plants—in the model plant as our system to study cell specification and plasticity. Stomatal guard cells are the final differentiated products of a specialized epidermal lineage called the stomatal lineage. The lineage begins with a self-renewing stem cell stage, and the master regulators SPEECHLESS (SPCH) is responsible for the initiation and proliferation of this cell stage. We have previously mapped the genome-wide binding sites of SPCH and identified thousands of gene targets, including other transcriptional regulators. However, the topology of the transcription cascade induced by SPCH and how SPCH utilizes these downstream transcription factor genes for stem cell specification and function remain unexplored. Objective, hypothesis and preliminary studies: The main objective of this proposal is to decipher how the master regulator SPCH employs downstream transcription factors to induce a transcription network for the specification and/or activity of the stomatal stem cells. Specifically, we will investigate the roles of two related zinc finger-homeodomain (ZF-HD) transcription factors, HB21 and HB31, as SPCH-induced targets and for their roles in supporting SPCH function. Based on our strong preliminary results, we hypothesize that SPCH-induced HB21 and HB31 drive a secondary cascade of transcriptomic changes that is necessary for the activity of the stomatal self-renewing precursors. We found that both HB21 and HB31 are direct gene targets of SPCH, and our confocal analyses indicated that they are expressed in the stomatal lineage. To study their function, we generated CRISPR mutants of the two genes and obtained the double hb21 hb31 mutant. Interestingly, the double mutant exhibited a dramatic reduction in stomatal number. In contrast, the ectopic overexpression of HB31 led to an overall increase in cell number. Examination of a translational reporter of SPCH in the double mutant background suggests the suppression of stomatal production occurs at the stomatal stem cell stage. Further, using the genetic materials described, we have profiled the transcriptomes affected by the HBs, and through an inducible system and ChIP-qPCR assays, identified a few high-confidence HB-regulated HB direct target genes. These preliminary results indicate that the HBs have critical role in promoting the activity and function of SPCH and the stomatal precursor cells. These data are also consistent with our hypothesis that the two HBs could act as “middle managers” in propagating a branch of SPCH-induced transcriptome. Specific Aims and Approaches: To e
