title: The novel role of p53 in host defence by regulating iron metabolism in macrophages
abs: The emergence of new infectious diseases and the persistent problems of bacterial infection highlight the urgent need to develop new therapeutic approaches to fight against these pathogens. Recent studies have revealed that the tumor suppressor p53 has non-canonical functions, and its function in the immune system is beginning to attract attention. Although p53 is known to be activated by pathogens such as viruses and bacteria, its role in host defence is not yet fully understood. In this proposal, we will investigate the p53-SLC40A1-iron pathway in the context of host defence. We will focus on the role of p53 in regulating iron levels in macrophages, key players in the immune defence and iron homeostasis. SLC40A1 is the only known iron exporter and regulates iron levels in tissue and blood. We identified SLC40A1/Ferroportin as a novel p53 transcriptional target gene. Our preliminary results show that p53-mediated induction of SLC40A1 reduces intracellular iron levels in macrophages, which enhances their ability to induce the pro-inflammatory cytokine IL-1β and phagocytize pathogens. In contrast, p53 or SLC40A1 knockout macrophages have elevated intracellular iron levels, which impairs IL-1β induction and phagocytosis. Furthermore, the addition of exogenous iron to cells decreases IL-1β expression and phagocytosis, suggesting that iron overload is a major obstacle to the functions of macrophages. Based on these findings, we hypothesize that the p53-SLC40A1 pathway is a novel and previously unidentified mechanism for protecting against pathogens by reducing iron levels. We propose three aims to investigate this pathway: 1. To determine whether the p53-SLC40A1-iron pathway contributes to IL-1β expression and secretion in macrophages in response to pathogen signals. 2. To determine whether the p53-SLC40A1-iron pathway enhances phagocytosis of pathogens by macrophages. 3. To evaluate the role of the p53 and SLC40A1 on IL-1β expression, phagocytosis, and clearance of infection by in vivo mouse models. Our studies will provide new insights into how p53 protects against infection. They may also lead to the development of new therapeutic approaches for infectious diseases, such as the combination of p53 activation and iron chelation. The proposed research is highly innovative and has the potential to make a significant impact on the field of infectious diseases.

title: Multifunctional peptide nanonets as novel antimicrobial agents
abs: In Nature, bacteria-trapping is an immune strategy utilized by various species to defend against the invasion of pathogens. Upon recognition of pathogenic intrusion, specialized tissues in the body release peptides or nucleic acids that self-assemble into networks of interwoven “nanonets” to entangle the microbes, preventing their invasion into host cells. The class of peptides responsible for this action is now widely known as host-defense peptides or more specifically human α-defensin 6 (HD6). HD6 is a 32-residue cysteine-rich peptide that is produced in the small intestines as a precursor peptide stored in granules and released into the lumen. Interestingly, although HD6 exhibits unprecedented self-assembly properties, it completely lacks antimicrobial activity observed for other human α-defensins. The entrapped bacteria are subsequently killed or removed by other components of the immune system, such as recruited neutrophils, or excreted. Moreover, HD6 apparently does not have any selectivity for Gram-negative or Gram-positive bacteria, and no preference for a given bacterial invasion mechanism, qualifying essentially as a “broad spectrum” agent. As Orgel’s second rule states, “Evolution is cleverer than you are”; clearly understanding this ingenious strategy designed by Nature and mimicking it may provide us with a viable, alternative therapeutic strategy to tackle the ever-pressing global health problem of antibiotic resistance. Inspired by nature, our team has focused our research on understanding the chemical and biophysical interplays between peptides and bacterial membrane components and developed a toolbox of modifications in peptide chemistry for potential clinical translation of peptide therapeutics. Our long-term goal is to design and develop stable peptide drugs and biomaterials as next generation antimicrobial therapeutics capable of tackling multidrug resistance. The focus of this grant is to characterize and elucidate the mechanism of action of a newly designed class of nanonet-forming AMPs that are hypothesized to act as multi-functional “trap-and-kill” biomaterials. These peptides, known as BTT peptides, are rationally designed and we have obtained early evidence demonstrating antimicrobial, anti-endotoxin and anti-inflammatory effects of these peptides. Additionally, in Gram-negative bacteria, lipopolysaccharide (LPS) was identified as the prominent amyloid nucleator. This interaction is particularly significant since LPS is responsible for a host of immunostimulatory and toxic septic processes in the body. Our hypothesis is that through the physical capture of Gram-negative bacteria via LPS, synthetic peptide nanonets will catalyze their rapid removal and retard the emergence of antibiotic resistance with participation of host immune systems. The aims of this proposal are to (1) examine LPS specificity and Gram-negative activity spectrum of peptide nanonets, (2) evaluate the impact of bacterial trapping on resistance develop

title: Bilingual Metalinguistic Scaffolding as a Pedagogical and Psychological Support for Early MTL Development
abs: In Singapore, the proficiency and usage of Mother Tongue Languages (MTLs) have been rapidly declining. With this project, we endeavour to support the bilingual and biliteracy development of young language learners by harnessing the potential of cross-language influence. While research has shown that competency in one language can facilitate learning in another similar language, studies exploring such relationships between two dissimilar languages are limited. Thus, among the MTLs used in Singapore, this program focuses on Chinese, which is typologically distant from English, the main language of instruction and also the dominant language for most young learners. Notably, there is also a shortage of empirical research utilizing longitudinal and experimental designs in the current literature. Therefore, the first aim of this project is to investigate the development of cross-language relationships between English and Chinese language sub-skills and reading attainment among early readers in Singapore (Aim 1). Subsequently, we seek to determine if these cross-language relationships can be leveraged and amplified through a novel and highly structured bilingual pedagogical practice – bilingual metalinguistic scaffolding, which explicitly highlights structural commonalities between English and Chinese to facilitate the learning of the less proficient language, namely Chinese (Aim 2). Importantly, we will explore how learners’ language enjoyment and anxiety levels may be moderated by bilingual metalinguistic scaffolding (Aim 3). Additionally, we will also examine how cross-language transfer effects may be affected by individual learners’ differing initial proficiency levels and home language backgrounds (Aim 4). We propose two studies to achieve our research aims. Study 1 (addressing Aim 1) will employ a longitudinal design to uncover the development of cross-language relationships between English and Chinese among young readers. Specifically, we will track the bilingual language development of two cohorts of children: a group of Primary 1 children as they progress to Primary 2, and a group of Primary 2 children as they progress to Primary 3. We anticipate identifying bidirectional cross-language influence between language sub-skills and reading proficiency, both concurrently (i.e., within each time point) and predictively (i.e., across the two time points). Study 2 (addressing Aim 2) will comprise an 8-week language training program in which children will be randomly assigned to receive Chinese morphological skill training, either with bilingual metalinguistic scaffolding (i.e., interleaving of English examples demonstrating similar rules) or without (i.e., Chinese-only instruction). A control group of children will not receive active training beyond standard school lessons. Pre- and post-tests will be administered to measure gains associated with the training. title: Uncovering how dynamics and mechanics regulate sperm-somatic interplay during sperm maturation in male reproductive tract
abs: Male infertility and its effects on reduced birth rates are a growing concern worldwide. In Singapore, infertility affects approximately 15% of couples, with male infertility being responsible for around 50% of cases, as reported by the Singapore General Hospital. Recent years have seen renewed academic interest in male infertility focus on the epididymis, a male reproductive organ known to be responsible for sperm maturation. In the epididymis, sperm produced from the testis transit through the long and convoluted duct to receive luminal proteins secreted from the epithelial cells, and eventually mature, characterized by capacity for fertilization and motility. While genetic studies have contributed to the accumulation of knowledge about crucial genes and molecules required for sperm maturation, little is understood about the dynamics and mechanical aspects of sperm maturation under physiological conditions due to a lack of appropriate methods, hindering a comprehensive understanding of how sperm maturation occurs. In other words, how sperm progressively acquire maturity in mammalian epididymis has remained an open question for almost a century since the proposal of the initial conjecture. Therefore, our goal of this proposal is to directly observe the sperm behavior in the epididymis and uncover the fundamental regulatory mechanism underlying the collective sperm dynamics during sperm maturation. To achieve this objective, we have developed a novel intravital imaging system, which enables us to observe the behavior of individual sperm in the epididymis of live mice. Our unpublished key findings, obtained through this imaging technology, demonstrate that sperm collectives in the epididymis display dynamic flow patterns in response to spontaneous contractions of the epididymal duct. Remarkably, this preliminary discovery challenges a long-standing belief, even described in standard textbooks, stating that the sperm behavior in mammalian epididymis is quiescent. Further detailed imaging analysis and preliminary perturbation experiments have led us to formulate a central hypothesis: collective sperm behavior is regulated by a complex interplay of mechanical and chemical feedback mechanisms between the sperm and the epididymal somatic cells, including epithelial cells and surrounding smooth muscles. Here we propose three specific aims to verify the central hypothesis. Aim 1 is to establish the measurement system and quantitatively characterize the collective dynamics of sperm and epididymal somatic cells in vivo. Aim 2 is to reveal the mechanical origin for generating collective sperm dynamics that underlies sperm maturation, specifically focusing on the generation of luminal sperm dynamics by epididymal cell activities within the murine epididymis. Aim 3 is to elucidate mechano-chemical impacts of sperm dynamics on the epididymal duct contraction in order to uncover how the luminal sperm dynamics affects the activities of the epididymal somatic cel

title: Dissecting the therapeutic mechanisms of milk-derived extracellular vesicles in health and metabolic disorders
abs: Bovine milk, as part of the human diet, contains many extracellular vesicles (mEVs). The biological activities of mEVs have been reported in various physiological or pathological conditions, including our own studies, making it an exciting oral therapeutic candidate. mEVs are natural nanoparticles of a size ranging 40-200nm and contain large amounts of immune-related microRNAs and proteins. Notably, mEVs can survive the harsh environment (low pH, high temperature, potent enzymatic activity) in the gastrointestinal tract and protect microRNAs to reach the intestines. More importantly, as natural and edible nanoparticles, mEVs possess potential to interact with gut bacteria, penetrate the intestinal barrier, and be taken up by epithelial cells and immune cells. Indeed, our recent report shows that oral administration of mEVs could restore disturbed gut microbiota and suppress intestinal inflammation in experimental colitis. In line with this, increasing literatures reports the therapeutic effects of mEVs of various species (human, cow, goat, pig, panda, etc) in colitis and gut related diseases. Apart from the gut per se, there are recently few studies reporting potential impact of orally administered mEVs on remote organs, such as the brain, knee, pancreas and kidney. It has been assumed that mEVs pass through the gut barrier to act on the diseased organ or tissue directly like other topical or intravenous administered EVs. In fact, majority of orally administrated mEVs remain in the GI tract with only neglectable amount reaching the circulation or remote organs, which unlikely explain the observed therapeutic effects. Thus, how mEVs impose therapeutic impact on the remote organs remain largely unknow, leaving a huge gap of knowledge about the underlying mechanism(s). The intestinal barrier acts as a selective filter to prevent the passage of harmful entities while allowing the translocation of essential nutrients. Impairment of intestinal barrier can increase intestinal permeability, i.e. “leaky gut”, resulting in vulnerability to various diseases, including inflammatory bowel disease, hepatitis viral infection, and metabolic disorders. Based on our recent discovery that mEVs modulating the gut-liver axis via acting on the gut barrier, we hypothesize that oral mEVs may function in multiple dimensions: 1) influence locally host intestinal tissue and act on remotely other organs via modulating gut microbiome. In the current proposal, we therefore aim to explore the underlying mechanisms in a spatiotemporal manner in health and disease via multidisciplinary approaches.
kw: milk, extracellular vesicle, intestinal barrier, gut microbiome, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, heart failure

title: Embrittlement-tolerant alloys for safe hydrogen transmission and storage
abs: Clean, cheap, storable hydrogen fuel, produced without emissions and leaving only water when burned, is poised to become a reality for the world. In the introduction to the Singapore’s National Hydrogen Strategy [1], it is highlighted that our hydrogen economy has been limited by two factors: “the expense of manufacturing clean hydrogen and concern around the safety of operation”. New technologies are reducing costs, and it is increasingly feasible that the market will meet the government’s stretch goal of producing clean hydrogen under US$1 per kilogram. However, a remaining critical problem affecting equipment durability is hydrogen embrittlement, a phenomenon that can cause sudden, catastrophic failure of stressed metallic components exposed to hydrogen. This project aims to understand hydrogen embrittlement in steels to enable the design and production of safe, hydrogen-compatible gas infrastructure. I will lead my research group to take a new approach, separately assessing the role of hydrogen in the different phases and microstructural features that are commonly found in typical pipeline and vessel steels, building up a susceptibility map that can be applied in the design of metallic materials. This approach will be enabled by access to new, unique-in-the-world, microscopy-based experimental techniques. We will use a state-of-the-art hydrogen-sensitive cryogenic atom probe microscope to observe the distribution of hydrogen in steel microstructures and to identify the microstructural features that attract hydrogen. We will also use microscale mechanical testing to quantify the susceptibility of specific regions of the steel to hydrogen-induced changes in deformation behaviour. Micromechanical tests will be undertaken at both ambient and low temperatures, to relate to the service temperatures of hydrogen pipelines and storage vessels, respectively. To do this, we will need to develop a new cryogenic mechanical testing rig, which will be done in partnership with my industry partner – Microscopy Solutions. To connect the microscale properties to the real-world failure behaviour of the bulk materials, we will incorporate the results into computational models that predict materials properties, with and without hydrogen. We will validate these models by testing samples at intermediate-size scales and connecting with macroscale embrittlement. This innovative approach will provide fundamental information about the distribution of hydrogen, and its effect on deformation, making an important contribution to knowledge in the field of physical metallurgy, underpinning future studies, and allowing retrospective examination of existing mechanical property data. This work will directly facilitate the development of new alloys with less susceptible, and more beneficial, microstructural features. This will enhance the safety and efficiency of Singapore’s hydrogen industry, addressing the impending high demand for hydrogen transmission and storage.
kw: Hydrogen energy; hydrogen embrittlement; metallurgy

title: Improving Collaborations between Clinicians and AI for Head and Neck Cancer Screening
abs: Summary: This project will explore multimodal representation learning, human-centered uncertainty quantification, and interactive explainable artificial intelligence (AI) techniques to enable effective collaborations between clinicians and artificial intelligence (AI) for head and neck cancer (HNC) screening. Specifically, these techniques will allow clinicians to understand which aspects an AI model performs well, which cases should be prioritized to be reviewed, and strategically review AI analyses to make more informed diagnoses while providing their inputs to AI systems to make it more deployable in clinical practice. The recent advance in AI makes it possible to process large quantities of medical imaging data and replicate clinicians’ decisions with competitive performance. These AI-based systems are increasingly being considered for healthcare services, such as processing endoscopic videos for screening HNC. However, the adoption of AI in clinics has been challenging for several issues. For instance, clinicians cannot determine the strengths of an AI model and whether it is ready to be deployed. Also, most AI models involve complex algorithms that function as “black box” models; therefore, clinicians cannot understand the rationale for a recommended diagnosis, correlate AI outputs with clinical contexts, and decide how much they can rely on AI outputs. Thus, clinicians cannot trust and adopt AI systems. This project aims to develop and validate computational techniques and practices to improve collaborations between clinicians and AI in the context of screening HNC. These computational techniques include multimodal representation learning using paired clinical videos and reports, human-centered uncertainty quantification, and interactive AI explanations. Specifically, we will leverage the multimodal representations of clinical videos and reports to make more human-centered uncertainty quantification and interactive AI explanations. For instance, clinicians can review the visualizations of embedding spaces of samples with distance-based uncertainty quantification scores to understand the capabilities and benefits of an AI model and determine cases where it can be used (deployment support). Using uncertainty scores, this project will identify cases that clinicians should prioritize to review (point-of-care triage). In addition, we will utilize multimodal representations to identify relevant clinical cases and highlight image regions of a clinical context (e.g. symptoms, risk factors) in endoscopy images, which will provide clinicians new insights to improve their diagnosis and identify an AI failure while they can provide their inputs to AI to improve it (decision-support). After implementing our computational techniques, we will conduct user studies in Singapore, the U.S., and Vietnam to examine their effectiveness. title: Polymer Combination for Preventing Adhesion of Atmospheric Particulates
abs: Adhesion of dust on surfaces is ubiquitous and causes major problems to society. Dust adhesion can cause damage to equipment, reduction in efficiency of industrial processes, contamination of products, major health problems, and numerous annoyances in our everyday lives. Dust adhesion can jam rotary parts of machineries, block pipes, reduce efficiency of solar panels, and reduce visibility of common appliances (e.g., computer monitors, phone screens, and windows). Dust particles adhere onto surfaces mainly by attractive electrostatic forces generated by contact electrification. There is currently no effective way of preventing dust adhesion onto surfaces. For example, cleanrooms, washing, and protective covers are far from being satisfactory solutions for the vast range of problems of dust adhesion. Dust adhesion is a major problem all around the world, and certainly also in Singapore. It is fundamentally extremely challenging to fabricate surfaces that prevent dust adhesion because of many factors. First, the fundamental mechanism of contact electrification is very poorly understood. It is currently unknown what are the factors that affect the amount of static charge generated on surfaces (i.e., factors that affect adhesion). Second, microscopic dust particles have large surface-to-volume ratio; hence, they tend to adhere onto surfaces readily by electrostatic forces. Hence, dust always sticks onto surfaces and is a widespread phenomenon found everywhere. Third, the composition of dust and dynamics of dust aggregation are complex. Due to these severe challenges, there is currently no report of a surface that prevents dust adhesion in research. This proposal seeks to create for the first time surfaces that naturally prevent dust adhesion. These surfaces thus do not require any external interventions (e.g., washing) for maintenance. The basis of this proposal is due to a fundamental discovery that we obtained recently (i.e., unpublished preliminary results) in our laboratory. The results are highly reproducible and consistent through many experiments across different times and different types of dust. This previously unreported fundamental mechanism is thus scientifically interesting. In addition to these results, we also have other preliminary results and accumulated experience in our laboratory for reducing the amount of charging by contact electrification. In this proposal, we plan to create and develop this novel material that naturally prevents dust adhesion. We plan to collect dust samples from different areas in Singapore, including the CBD, residential, and industrial areas. We will optimize the performance of the material that prevents dust adhesion. We will integrate multiple fundamental mechanisms learnt from our accumulated experience into the single material to enhance its performance. title: Net-Zero Concrete Design Powered by Machine Learning
abs: Concrete is an indispensable material for modern civilization. The gigantic quantity consumed has led to its heavy carbon footprint and demand for natural resources. Substituting concrete constituents with low-grade/waste materials is a common approach to reduce carbon footprint which, however, is limited only to several well-studied materials. There is an urgent need to develop method to guide the usage of non-conventional under-used in producing more sustainable concrete. In this project, we aim to explore a new concrete mix-design scheme that incorporates a broad type of low-grade/waste materials in Singapore, and extendable to under-used materials in neighboring regions. This scheme allows reliable design and efficient evaluation of the performance and sustainability attributes of mix designs containing one or more circulated materials. The key to achieve this is to evaluate the chemical reaction and the resulting cementing capabilities of an exhaustive set combinations of many waste materials. This is not possible only via laboratory measurements. Here we plan to combine lab experiment, reliable thermodynamic modeling and machine learning (ML) algorithm, which allows an effective evaluation of tens of solid materials and thousands of proportioning among them. Scientifically, the work helps extend the concept of cement chemistry towards much broader types of solid materials. Practically, it provides data-based design scheme to complement the conventional experience-based design of concrete, and allows more under-used materials to be circulated for construction.

title: Materials for Room Temperature Exciton Condensates: From Database to Laboratories
abs: The overarching goal in this proposal is to empower the study and application of quantum phenomena at or close to room temperature, in the form of a Bose-Einstein condensate of excitons. This will be achieved by strategically and systematically identifying, from materials databases, materials that can host exciton condensates at or close to room temperature, realising the exciton condensates in the laboratory, and demonstrating the existence of quantum coherence in the condensate. A Bose-Einstein condensate is a state of matter in which a macroscopic number of particles exist in the same quantum state. Such a state is said to demonstrate coherence; all particles in the state are coordinated in space and time. Bose-Einstein condensation has led to several sensational phenomena, including superfluidity, superconductivity, and coherent matter waves; but, generally at rather low temperatures. Signatures of Bose-Einstein condensates of excitons have recently been observed at ~100 K, orders of magnitude higher than the condensation temperature for atoms. Excitons are bound electron-hole pairs in materials; these exciton condensates can give rise to super-radiant luminescence, super-thermal-conductivity, and counterflow superconductivity. The temperature below which exciton condensates are formed is inversely proportional to the exciton mass and the exciton area. Thus far, the materials for studies on exciton condensates have largely been chosen ad hoc. Based on our preliminary studies and our understanding of the critical temperature, we believe that a systematic materials search will uncover experimentally realisable materials that can host exciton condensates at higher temperatures, even close to room temperature. This is because the exciton mass and area can be further reduced, and the energy scales of the interactions in exciton condensates are much larger than those in other quantum coherent phenomena such as superconductivity. Realising an exciton condensate close to room temperature will enable the study of exotic exciton condensate physics, with the potential for translation into applications. To conduct the proposed materials search, we will employ a multi-scale theoretical approach. First, we will establish an approach to predict the critical temperature for exciton condensation, using first principles many-body calculations that take into account details of the crystal structure and many-body Coulombic interactions, without empirical parameters. We will use existing theoretical models for Bose-Einstein condensation, and compute the required parameters from first principles. We were one of the first groups to predict the critical temperature for exciton condensation using first principles, many-body calculations, in the ideal dilute bosonic gas limit, and we will now also explore the weakly interacting dilute regime and the dense exciton regime. title: Polysulfide anions photocatalysis for green synthesis and functionalization of complex small molecules
abs: Driven by public regulations worldwide, pharmaceutical, agrochemical and fine-chemical manufacturers, which together contribute to nearly 6-7% of the Singapore GDP, are increasingly seeking for greener and more cost-effective processes to manufacture key-products. Photoredox catalysis has emerged as an incredibly versatile tool for the generation of various radical and radical ion species through single-electron-transfer events with high energy electronically excited states of visible-light absorbing redox catalysts under milder reaction conditions, advancing current state-of-the-art chemical synthesis. The PI’s group recently developed a potent photocatalytic system employing readily accessible and inexpensive polysulfide anions, which are actively employed as the charge transfer carriers in the Li-sulfur batteries. In these processes, the photoexcited polysulfide dianions (Sn2–) were found to be capable of inducing the single-electron reduction of aryl (pseudo)halides or aryl ketones having reduction potentials (Ered) as low as –2.5 V vs. saturated calomel electrode (SCE) (ref. J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2021, 143, 481-487; Chem. Catal. 2022, 2, 1128). Moreover, polysulfide anion radicals (Sn•–) erived from single-electron oxidation of Sn2– were found to be capable of inducing hydrogen-atom-transfer (HAT) from relatively electron-rich aliphatic C-H bonds. Based on these preliminary results, our objectives in this research project are to harvest solar (visible light) energy using ubiquitous polysulfide anions as photocatalysts to drive greener synthetic processes, which enable the synthesis of complex molecules of pharmaceutical and agrochemical interests. Furthermore, to translate the newly developed polysulfide anions photocatalysis into sustainable manufacturing processes, we will upgrade selected transformations in kg/day scale through innovative reactor designs. Specifically, we would set the following topics as the major project milestones: (WP-1) Photo-Birch reduction of (hetero)arenes to functionalized aliphatic carbo- and heterocycles (WP-2) Alkene functionalization (WP-3) Reductive desulfonylation of sulfonamides and sulfonimides (WP-4) Late-stage functionalization of biologically active complex molecules (WP-5) Accelerated process design and scaled-up reactor development for manufacturing

title: Magnetic oxide heterostructures for oxygen electrocatalysis
abs: Transition metal oxides (TMOs) have raised as promising catalysts for oxygen electrocatalysis which has been involved in many renewable and eco-friendly energy technologies, such as fuel cells and water electrocatalysis. TMOs in perovskite and spinel structures have been recently developed, in which first-row transition metals, such as Ni, Fe, Mn, and Co, can act as catalytically active centres for catalysing both the oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) and oxygen evolution reaction (OER) in alkaline. To improve the catalytic activity of spinel oxides, researchers have found that controlling the cation type and optimizing cation coordination geometry are beneficial for both OER and ORR. Besides the compositional and structural flexibility, another uniqueness of perovskite and spinel oxides is the spintronic properties of some oxides that originate from the unpaired spins of fist-row transition metal cations. More recently, the dependence of oxygen electrocatalysis on the spin channel in TMOs has been sporadically reported and the theoretical origins of spin-enhanced electrocatalysis are raising interests. This is because the conversion between water and the triplet dioxygen molecule involves the spin-polarized electron transfer in ORR and OER. The pertinence of the spintronic properties of magnetic TMOs to the oxygen electrocatalytic activity has been sporadically observed and the potential of manipulating the spin configuration for achieving better activity remains huge. However, it is difficult to alter the spin configuration in single-phase TMOs, e.g., the most active oxide phase is not magnetic. This leads to the construction of magnetic oxide heterostructures, in which the spin current and crystal distortion at the interface of two different magnetic oxides can create a strong force to realign the spin direction and arrangement of unpaired electrons. This is the main hypothesis of this proposal that magnetic oxide heterostructures can fine-tune the spin configuration of the catalytic active phase for promoting oxygen electrocatalytic activity. To date, this has not been systematically studied and constitutes the basis of this research proposal. This project targets to investigate the spintronic phenomena at the interface of magnetic oxide heterostructures and gain fundamental understandings on how the rearranged spin of unpaired electrons in metal cations affects the intrinsic catalytic activities of perovskites and spinels towards ORR and OER. Various magnetic oxide heterostructures will be prepared to pinpoint the optimal spin arrangement at the interface. Although several spin-dependent activities of OER on TMOs have been reported, this is the first systematic study to explore and uncover the fundamentals of spintronic properties in magnetic oxide heterostructures. title: Test of Quantum Equivalence Principle
abs: The equivalence between inertial and gravitational masses is one of the fundamental pillars of Newtonian and Einsteinian mechanics. It is known as the universality of free fall or weak equivalence principle (WEP). Precise measurements using torsion balances, Lunar ranging or Earth-orbiting objects have ruled out WEP violation up to a 10^(-15) level. Less precise measurements using an atomic interferometer in free fall have also been performed at a 10^(-12) level. In all cases, those WEP tests are classical, as opposed to recently proposed quantum WEP tests. Indeed, a torsion balance or Earth's satellite (natural or not) are classical macroscopic objects. Atoms used in state-of-the-art experiments performed so far are also classical because they are in a well-defined mass (or energy) quantum state. For instance, WEP was generality tested using simultaneously two atoms of different masses, or one atom in incoherent superposition of internal states. We propose here to explore WEP in its quantum version, using an atomic interferometer where atoms are in a coherent superposition of different masses. In this situation, we will consider a test theory based on mass-energy equivalence where the inertial and gravitational masses are expressed by operators instead of scalars. The quantum WEP violation appears if those two mass operators do not commute namely, they do not share the same eigenbasis. The quantum WEP test will be implemented on an atomic accelerometer using ultracold gas of strontium. The atoms will be prepared in a coherent superposition of clock internal states. Here, the mass difference is five orders of magnitude larger than the current state of the art, so the sensitivity to quantum WEP violation. We aim to measure quantum WEP with an ultimate sensitivity three orders of magnitude larger than the current state of the art. A violation of WEP in the quantum regime will be a major milestone toward a more fundamental theory of gravity beyond the geometrical approach used in general relativity. Our proposal will also help to develop quantum sensors, a domain of strategic importance for Singapore.
kw: weak equivalence principle; atomic interferometry; quantum physics; ultracold atoms

title: Polarization singularities in metaphotonics for arbitrarily charged vortices
abs: Optical vortexes, serving as a fundamental concept in optics, extend the scope of the optical orthogonal beam set. It has been employed in optical communication, nanoparticle manipulation, quantum calculation, and other fields1. In particular, optical vortices are one of the most promising solutions for enhancing the capacity of data multiplexing to meet an unprecedented growth in big data and internet traffic information2. Distinguished from amplitude, frequency, time, and polarization, orbital-angular-momentum mode carried by optical vortices is a new freedom in light, potentially addressing the challenges of information transmissions in IoTs and 5G/6G communications. As a result, there has been considerable pursuit within the optics and nanophotonics community to develop vortex generators. Currently, there are three main types of mechanisms for generating vortex beams. The first type involves the use of conventional bulky devices, such as spiral phase plates, spatial light modulators, and q-plates, which utilize dynamic phase to generate vortex beams3. However, these devices suffer from the large volume, which limits the potential for integration into fibre-optical communications and on-chip information processing. The second type utilizes subwavelength metasurfaces, taking advantage of geometry phase, to produce vortex beams4,5. However, this method requires sophisticated design, complex manufacture processes, and high-precise nanoscale-aligning technology for the illuminating light and nanostructures. These requirements could pose challenges and inconvenience in practical applications. The third method involves utilizing bound states in the continuum (BICs) operating in momentum space6. These BICs are supported by uniform periodic structures and do not require a real-space centre. In this method, the generated charge of vortices is limited to even numbers. This restriction arises from the integer-charge nature of the BICs and has detrimental implications for the possible range of vortex charges that can be generated. On the other hand, most investigations have been implemented with dielectric materials, leading to limited fundamental frequency in modulating optical vortices and their functionalities of on-chip devices. Two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides is presently attracting increased attention due to the observation of new physical phenomena, such as extraordinary nonlinearities, arising in systems of reduced dimensionality. The nonlinear optical properties of TMDs can be enhanced by decreasing the number of layers. Therefore, TMDs are a promising material for compact vortex devices with tunable frequencies due to their atom-scale thickness. Here we propose a method to utilize the polarization vortex in the momentum space induced by polarization singularities in photonic crystal slabs to generate vortex beams. title: Multi-Modal Reimaginative 4D Generation Engine
abs: Artificial Intelligence Generated Content (AIGC) has become a powerful tool for creativity and accessibility in various fields, including art, music, design, movies, and entertainment. With the growing popularity of 4D content that integrates 3D elements, realistic lighting, and life-like character movements, a 4D generation engine driven by AI has the potential to revolutionize the creation of immersive experiences. The engine can generate 4D content by using simple text descriptions and images as input, creating 3D objects along with authentic lighting and natural character movements. However, developing such an engine is challenging due to the complexities of 3D/4D data, complicated light transports, physics-aware motion generations, and cross-modality issues. While contemporary AIGC systems have limitations in generating high-quality 3D objects with realistic reflectance and vivid movements, the goal of this project is to research and develop a comprehensive 4D generation engine that can generate general 3D objects, 3D/4D reflectances, and 4D motions based on multi-modal instructions. Specifically, three key contributions are made. First, we aim to study hierarchical diffusion models with sparse voxel-based NeRF to achieve high-quality generation for general 3D objects, which generates high-resolution 3D objects conditioned on multi-modal instructions from the users. Second, to learn illumination-invariant reflectance based on 3D structures, we will design learnable volumetric primitives for modeling 3D/4D reflectance, especially for simulating complex light transport for diverse materials. Third, we target to incorporate physical properties into 4D motion generation using hierarchical learning, which generates physical-plausible motions with environmental interactions by considering the surroundings. Our project designs the first powerful 4D generation engine that takes all three major components together, which benefits the research community by offering new insights for future research. Moreover, our 4D generation engine also benefits industries and the wider public with improved entertainment experiences and cost-effective 3D/4D modeling.
kw: Generative AI; 3D/4D Generation; Multi-Modal Learning; Reflectance Modeling; Motion Generation

title: Comprehensive Privacy Auditing in Machine Learning
abs: Addressing privacy risks in machine learning is of critical importance in the domain of AI. This has been underscored by research studies revealing the privacy weaknesses present in machine learning algorithms, and by legal regulations concerning privacy and AI, which require privacy auditing and measures to reduce privacy risks in AI applications. In this proposal, we aim at designing a comprehensive framework to conduct practical explainable privacy auditing of machine learning algorithms. Privacy auditing in machine learning is a process to quantify how much information a model inadvertently leaks about its training data. Existing techniques are predominantly based on membership inference attacks (MIA). MIA methods, originated by the PI's work, determine if a specific data point was included in a model's training set by merely examining the model's parameters or predictions after the training has been completed. Existing methods are very valuable but limited in their capacity to provide detailed explanations of sources of leakage, precisely quantifying privacy risk across a sequence of inference queries, and performing accurate auditing with limited computation resources. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel direction in redesigning inference algorithms to interpret the effective privacy loss for any data record, given any sequence of queries, and to identify the influential features and data points responsible for privacy vulnerabilities with low computation cost. Furthermore, we extend our analysis to the limitations of existing auditing methods for differential privacy frameworks, as they do not perform a tight analysis in the black-box setting. Here is the list of the specific objectives in this proposal: - To design scalable membership inference attacks with high precision and low computational complexity. - To quantify and interpret the privacy loss for any data record, given any sequence of inference queries. - To identify influential features and data points that contribute to a model's privacy vulnerabilities. - To address the potential shortcomings of existing black-box auditing methods for differential privacy. We plan to design novel likelihood ratio tests for membership inference attacks, by maximally utilizing the contrast between members and non-members of the training set, while using only a minimal number of reference models hence reducing the computational cost. Additionally, we will develop adversarial regularization algorithms to identify the specific data attributes that cause algorithms revealing information about their training data. We plan to release the results as a practical tool, extending the ML Privacy Meter open source tool, thereby making a significant contribution to the fields of privacy and explainable machine learning.
kw: Responsible AI; Privacy; Machine learning; Information leakage; Membership inference attacks; Explainability

title: Online Harms, Perpetration, and its Effects on Adolescents' Well-Being in Singapore: A Longitudinal Panel Study
abs: Adolescents are vulnerable to online risks, such as cyberbullying and technology-facilitated sexual violence (TFSV), which can have severe short-term and long-term psychological consequences. Anxiety, depression, conduct problems, and substance consumption are just some of the numerous long-term consequences that victims – and in some cases, even perpetrators – might experience. The social environment surrounding adolescents is known to be one of the most crucial factors in the origin of cyberbullying and TFSV, and the role played by peers and parents are especially influential. However, limited research has examined the development and evolution of normative beliefs and their influence on cyber aggressive behaviours during adolescence. Interactions mediated by digital technology significantly differ from face-to-face interactions, and features such as potential anonymity, a wider audience, and the absence of physical and temporal boundaries can affect the relationship between normative influences and aggressive behaviour. Despite the critical role of social norms in shaping aggressive behaviours, there is a scarcity of longitudinal evidence that tracks the development and evolution of normative beliefs across adolescence. Furthermore, limited research exists on how changes in perceived norms impact adolescents’ behaviours. Theoretical and empirical evidence is likewise scarce on how peer norms shape adolescents’ technology use and interactions in cyberspace, and how, in turn, these interactions impact their psychosocial outcomes and pillars of support. This is one of the few research projects following a panel to better understand local adolescents’ exposure to online harm and the longitudinal impact of norms. The planned study contributes to the body of research on cyber aggression by clarifying the role of social norms and perceived parental mediation in online settings, and filling the knowledge gap concerning the trajectories of online aggression norms during adolescence. Extending the theory of normative social behaviour, this study will examine the theoretical constructs associated with cyber aggressive behaviours (cyberbullying and TFSV) in a longitudinal perspective. In particular, the researchers will investigate the development and evolution of adolescent social norms and behaviours both on the individual level of a person and between subjects, as well as examine the role of perceived parental mediation in cyber aggressive behaviours, across the critical developmental period of adolescence. The present research has the following aims: 1. To investigate the drivers of the development and evolution of cyber aggressive behaviours (i.e., cyberbullying and TFSV) during adolescence, as well as the changes in peer norms and parental monitoring about these behaviours, using an integrative framework of normative social behaviour. 2. To assess the relationship between exposure to cyberharms on social media and adolescents’ social norm perception

title: Addressing Visual Plagiarism in Art & Design: A Multi-stakeholder Investigation
abs: Project Goals We aim to launch a comprehensive and innovative investigation to increase creative integrity by addressing visual plagiarism in art & design, specifically targeting two key stakeholder groups, i., international art & design faculty and ii. Singapore’s communication design industry. To do this, we will explore current understandings of visual plagiarism issues and identify the assumptions that underlie creative integrity. Additionally, we aim to identify ways that higher education establishments and creative industry leaders can support design faculty and practitioners in addressing visual plagiarism and promoting creative integrity. Finally, we will develop and disseminate tools, resources and recommendations for addressing visual plagiarism in art and design education and practice. Visual plagiarism, defined as “the taking of someone else's artwork or design and claiming it as one's own” (Kennedy, 2021), is a complex issue prevalent across various disciplines. It can have significant legal, reputational, financial, and social consequences. However, there is a scarcity of academic literature that examines the factors contributing to the prevalence of visual plagiarism, particularly from the viewpoint of art and design faculty. The issue is significant in Singapore, with several high-profile cases recently exposed in the media. However, an initial literature review of international scholarly databases could not uncover any research on visual plagiarism in the communication design industry, even from a commercial Intellectual Property (IP) or copyright perspective. Furthermore, the advent of artificial intelligence has created new challenges in the detection and prevention of visual plagiarism. Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) can produce high-quality images that are difficult to differentiate from human-generated works, provoking ethical and legal dilemmas in the scope of A.I.-generated image content. Therefore, the proposed research aims to establish knowledge of the current status quo and propose ways to increase creative integrity by addressing visual plagiarism both in Singapore and on a global scale. Approach Over the course of the last five years, the PI’s research into visual plagiarism has uncovered four unique challenges. i. Knowledge of visual plagiarism amongst faculty is inconsistent and, in some cases, misunderstood. ii, faculty often Assume that students are aware of the issues of visual plagiarism and therefore do not directly teach it in class. iii. No Time is allocated within current curricula to teach on the topic, and iv. A lack of Supporting policy that directly addresses visual plagiarism. These four key inciters, acronymed as KATS, provide a framework that will scaffold local and international participatory-design workshops to co-create solutions with art and design faculty for each of the issues. Each of the KATS issues will directly inform a corresponding hands-on activity in the workshops. Concurrently,
kw: Visual Plagiarism; visual communication; participatory design workshops; semi-structured interviews; Creative industry; Art & Design Faculty

title: Navigating co-parenting, parenting stress and child development in a novel Work From Home (WFH) environment: A mix-methods naturalistic on-field investigation
abs: The recent pandemic has necessitated Work-From-Home (WFH) policies. However, WFH poses unique challenges to the new parent who aims for career progression but at the same time must care for their infant. While past studies have found disproportionate negative effects of WFH on mothers, a key reason may be the lack of paternal support. Today, WFH remains popular. Therefore, it is important to build upon previous literature and disentangle the effects of WFH and the pandemic on family functioning, as well as investigate the impact of active fathering on parent and child outcomes. The present study implements a mixed methods quantitative fieldwork experiment and a qualitative semi-structured interview to uncover the effects of (1) child-rearing on mothers’ WFH performance, (2) co-parenting habits at home and (3) their impact on child development, and (4) coping strategies adopted by new parents and their care needs. A total of 80 family units, consisting of Singaporean biological mother, father, and their child aged between 1 to 3 years, will take part in the study. In the first part, a 3x2 mixed-subjects study design with two factors (cognitive load and active fathering) is implemented. Mothers will undergo the n-back task simulating high, medium, and low cognitive loads during WFH conditions. During this part, fathers will either actively support caregiving, or be a passive observer. Child development in terms of language acquisition will be assessed. Simultaneously, fNIRS neuroimaging will be conducted to understand how the prefrontal cortex is activated during challenging moments of juggling work and caregiving. In the second part, a subset of 20 mother-father dyads will be interviewed on their perspectives towards WFH, work-life balance, and care needs. Findings will inform the impact of WFH on mothers, as well as how parenting duties are shared between spouses. These results can be applied to develop appropriate services to address parents’ care gaps in a changing work landscape.
kw: work-from-home, parenting, co-parenting, parenting stress, neuroscience, child development, work-life balance

title: Dynamic in vivo maps of the postsynaptic network
abs: Our ability to learn and remember information is crucial to the human experience. Learning is important throughout our lives, from childhood development and education to aging. Disruptions in learning and memory can impact people at every stage of life, from young individuals with intellectual disabilities to the elderly experiencing cognitive decline. Memories are thought to be created by changes in communication between neurons. Neurons are connected by synapses, which are protein-rich bridges that allow for the transmission of information between cells. During the learning process,synaptic transmission changes via a process called synaptic plasticity. This process is critical for normal learning; patients with various intellectual disorders often have abnormal synapses, and these conditions are sometimes referred to as "synaptopathies". While our understanding of synaptic function is extensive, we are still not at the level where we can, for example, make synapse-targeted pharmaceuticals. We have a good understanding of neurotransmitter release from the presynapse and the composition of the postsynapse. Indeed, numerous protein-protein interactions, multi-molecular complexes, and other functional connections between postsynaptic components have been identified. However, the overall connectivity of the protein network, which is integral for synaptic function, is incompletely mapped. This proposal aims to answer an important question in synaptic neurobiology: What is the arrangement of proteins in the network that forms the postsynaptic density (PSD)? To do this, we will use a biotinylation identification (BioID) in a novel genetic-proteomic strategy in Drosophila to map the structure of this molecular network. By drafting a map of the PSD network, we can improve our understanding of how synapses function and develop more sophisticated models of synaptic activity that will help lead to new ways of improving cognitive health. Two recent breakthroughs have encouraged us to develop this project: deep-learning algorithms that can model the structure of most proteins and protein-protein complexes, and biotin proximity-labeling studies that can map the relative proximities of thousands of proteins in the cell. We consider that deep learning tools will enable the construction of large-scale molecular models of cellular networks, including the PSD and its surroundings. The use of large-scale proximity labeling in synapses in vivo represents an incredible opportunity to investigate a structure with central importance to neuroscience. Aim 1. We will build on our existing proven methodology for BioID in the Drosophila neuromuscular junction and central brain. Having successfully collected data for the canonical PSD factor Dlg1, we will expand our investigations to new PSD baits. title: Decoding the Mechanisms of Lanthipeptide Modification by LankC: A Trifunctional Class III Enzyme
abs: Lanthipeptides are a class of bioactive peptides produced by gram-positive bacteria that exhibit potent antimicrobial, antitumor, and immunomodulatory properties. Despite their therapeutic potential, the mechanisms underlying the modification of these peptides by class III and class IV trifunctional enzymes remain poorly understood. In this study, we aim to address this gap in knowledge by investigating the mechanisms underlying lanthipeptide modification by class III trifunctional enzymes, using LankC as a model system. Our approach combines bioinformatics, structural biology, and biochemistry techniques to elucidate 1) substrate recognition and catalysis, 2) intermediate transfer, and 3) interaction with downstream membrane transporter for lanthipeptide secretion. Through this research, we hope to gain a comprehensive understanding of the molecular basis of lanthipeptide biosynthesis, which can inform the development of new antimicrobial and immunomodulatory agents. Our combined expertise in enzymology and membrane biology has positioned us perfectly to study the challenging biosynthesis of lanthipeptides. To this end, we have successfully reconstituted all key components from the LanP biosynthesis pathway, including the peptide substrate, the highly dynamic modification enzyme LanKC, and the membrane transporter LanT. Using a combination of molecular biology, biochemical assays, and cryo-EM techniques, we have made significant progress in our research. Our preliminary findings suggest that LankC can utilize both GTP and ATP as substrates, with GTP being preferred. Moreover, substrate peptide binding stimulates GTP hydrolysis activity. We have also determined two cryo-EM structures of LankC, one with bound peptide and one without. These structures reveal a shaft between the kinase and lyase domain that coordinates leader peptide recognition and binding, while the core peptide is positioned in a groove between the lyase and cyclase domains. These results provide a strong basis for understanding the catalytic mechanism and potential substrate channelling among multiple domains of LanKC, which is likely a universally conserved process among all lanthipeptide modification enzymes. This study is a collaborative effort between the PI's lab, which will be conducting the major work on protein biochemistry and structural studies, and Dr. Lok-To Sham's lab at NUS, which has complementary interdisciplinary expertise in microbiology and will be responsible for cell genetic and phenotype studies. By combining our expertise, we aim to bridge a significant knowledge gap in the field of lanthipeptide modification by providing new insights into the mechanisms of substrate recognition, intermediate transfer, and export. This will provide a foundation for developing new antimicrobial and immunomodulatory agents. Ultimately, our work has the potential to contribute to the development of new therapeutics to combat antibiotic-resistant pathogens and other diseases.
kw: Lanthipeptides, Multidrug-resistance, peptide modification, substrate channeling, cryo-EM

title: Spatiotemporal analysis of interactions between cytoskeleton and integrin adhesions
abs: The cytoskeleton is a complex of cellular fibrillar structures and numerous associated proteins that is found in the cytoplasm of all cells. It determines cell shape and is involved in many cellular processes from signalling, exocytosis, endocytosis, intracellular transport, to cell division, polarization and migration, and is an essential determinant of cell plasma membrane organization. Mis-regulation or aberrations in cytoskeletal proteins lead to various pathologies including neurodegenerative disorders, cardiovascular syndromes, cancer, liver cirrhosis, and pulmonary fibrosis. The cortical microtubule stabilization complex (CMSC) is a central component of this system. It captures microtubules at their tips and targets them to long-lived cell-matrix adhesions important for cell migration and matrix remodelling. However, the organization and dynamics of the CMSCs and its microtubule interaction are only poorly understood as until now the simultaneous determination of structure and dynamics was difficult, if not impossible, to achieve. Recently, we developed a new microscopy modality, called SRRF ’n’ TIRF, that allows the simultaneous measurement of both, structure and dynamics with millisecond time and ~100 nm spatial resolution. Here, using and further developing SRRF ’n’ TIRF, we will for the first time investigate the spatiotemporal structure of the CMSC and provide insights into the regulation of the connection of microtubules to the plasma membrane, a process which, when mis-regulated, has serious implications for various pathologies. Insights into these processes, therefore, will provide new points of action for disease intervention.
kw: single molecule fluorescence spectroscopy; super-resolution microscopy; machine learning; cell biology; cytoskeleton; integrin

title: Improving Antimicrobial Stewardship and Infection Control in Primary Care
abs: Background: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a significant global health threat, and primary care plays a crucial role in combating it. We aim to assess antimicrobial utilization patterns, identify effective antimicrobial stewardship strategies, and evaluate the impact of physician-centred feedback on antimicrobial prescribing in primary care settings. Methods: 1. Systematic review: Identify novel and effective strategies for antimicrobial stewardship in primary care. 2. Cluster randomized trial: Evaluate the effectiveness of physician-centred feedback on antimicrobial prescribing patterns in primary care. 3. Cost-effectiveness analysis: Evalute the cost-effectiveness of antimicrobial stewardship programme intervention (physician-centred feedback) Significance: - It will identify effective antimicrobial stewardship strategies for primary care settings. - Physician-centred feedback is a cost-effective strategy to improve antimicrobial appropriateness and reduce unnecessary prescriptions. Feasibility: - The research team has expertise in antimicrobial stewardship, systematic reviews, and cluster randomized trials. - The study's findings will inform policy and practice changes in primary care settings, contributing to efforts to combat AMR. Conclusion: These studies are critical steps toward enhancing antimicrobial stewardship in primary care, ultimately improving patient outcomes and reducing the spread of AMR.
kw: Antimicrobial Stewardship; Primary Care; Family Medicine; Infection Control; Antimicrobial Resistance

title: Effectiveness of a new framework ACP-FG in screening to identify patients with palliative and supportive care needs and in increasing the delivery of Generalist Palliative Care, using a surrogate measurement of incidence of conduct of goals of care discussions.
abs: With a rapidly ageing population in Singapore causing a rise in proportion of patients suffering from life limiting illnesses such as cancer and advanced organ failure leading to increased healthcare burden, development and delivery of a generalist palliative care model to address the increased needs is needed. To overcome barriers such as lack of training, knowledge and confidence in our generalist colleagues to do so, a novel framework ACP-FG was developed for screening to identify patients with palliative and supportive needs. This consists of diagnosis, needs and general based domains including poor prognosis, presence of general markers of health decline, conservative patient's preferences towards their care goals and a poor quality of life. In this pilot study. we hypothesize that this tool will have good sensitivity when compared to a gold standard of screening done by an experienced Palliative Care specialist and that by screening using ACPFG, there will be increased delivery of generalist Palliative care compared to an unscreened cohort. This will be measured in the primary outcome of goals of care discussions. Secondary outcomes include addressing symptom control, increased rates of specialist Palliative Care referrals, and appropriate care coordination. An accompanying education and training framework will drive upskilling of healthcare professionals in delivery of Generalist Palliative Care with more widespread implementation of the tool. Pilot data can lead to larger scale studies in implementation, examining changes in clinician behaviour, confidence and attitudes towards providing basic palliative care as well as organizational practice change. Acceptability, feasibility and sustainability of ACP-FG can be further evaluated in both the hospital and community settings in future.
kw: Palliative Care; Generalist; Prompt; screening

title: An open-label phase II study of EGFR TKI in patients with advanced NSCLC harbouring EGFR mutations categorized according to structural based classification
abs:
Lung cancer is the most prevalent carcinoma globally, ranking highest in terms of cancer deaths. Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) comprises 80-85% of cases, predominantly diagnosed at advanced stages. Patients with advanced NSCLC typically have a median overall survival of 10-12 months. Advances in the molecular characterization of NSCLC, particularly adenocarcinoma, have highlighted EGFR (epidermal growth factor receptor) mutations as significant drivers of tumourigenesis. EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) have shown efficacy against common EGFR mutations (exon 19 deletion and exon 21 L858R). Afatinib, a second-generation TKI, is FDA-approved for these common mutations and for certain uncommon EGFR mutations (S768I, L861Q, and G719X). A structure-based classification has categorised EGFR mutations into four groups, with PACC (P-loop αC-helix compressing) mutations showing particular sensitivity to afatinib.

Hypothesis & Specific Aims
We hypothesize that afatinib is active in patients with advanced NSCLC harbouring EGFR PACC mutations. The study aims to evaluate afatinib’s efficacy in this subgroup, primarily through the objective response rate (ORR), and secondarily through progression-free survival (PFS), overall survival (OS),
