title: Optimizing Preoperative Screening and Intervention Strategies for Glycemic Control in Surgical Patients: A Comprehensive Analysis for Enhanced Population Health
abs: Introduction As Singapore experiences a transformative shift in perioperative care amid escalating diabetes rates, this research addresses a critical aspect—preoperative glycemic control. Emphasizing preventive strategies, this study explores the nuanced role of glycemic control in the preoperative context. It builds on existing literature gaps, focusing on the untapped potential of HbA1c screening and the urgent need for evidence-based guidelines. Study Design and Methodology This research employs a two-phase approach—a prospective observational cohort study and a pragmatic interventional trial. The cohort study involves elective surgical patients, examining the relationship between diabetes status and postoperative clinical, patient-centered, and financial outcomes. The interventional trial assesses intervention feasibility, including surgery postponement for diabetes optimization. The study spans adult patients undergoing elective non-cardiac surgeries at Singapore General Hospital, utilizing statistical analyses to determine optimal HbA1c targets. Aims The primary aim is to ascertain the most effective preoperative HbA1c screening strategy, comparing selective to universal screening. Secondary aims involve exploring intervention feasibility and determining optimal HbA1c targets for effective diabetes optimization. Furthermore, this study aims to assess the potential role of preoperative HbA1c screening and intervention in fostering good long-term diabetes control. Study Significance This research addresses three distinct gaps: the utility of HbA1c as a screening tool and intervention target, its impact on short-term perioperative outcomes, and long-term diabetes control. Recognizing the preoperative care period as a strategic window for public health intervention, the study leverages on the “teachable moment” of a significant health episode such as undergoing surgery, and aligning with Singapore's evolving healthcare landscape. Building on our prior research, the study emphasizes the need for targeted interventions, especially for patients with elevated HbA1c levels. The overarching significance lies in refining preoperative screening strategies, advancing perioperative care knowledge, and translating findings into tangible healthcare improvements.
kw: diabetes; glycated haemoglobin; health economics; non-cardiac surgery; perioperative medicine; population health

title: HArnessing the MicrObiome to improve therapeutic outcomes in caNcer patients receiving immunotherapY (HARMONY)
abs: The gut microbiome has been shown to be a potential predictive biomarker for response to immunotherapy in patients with melanoma, renal cell carcinoma and non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). In melanoma, proof-of-concept studies using faecal microbiota transplantation from immunotherapy responders have shown promise in the manipulation of the microbiome to overcome treatment resistance in immunotherapy non-responders. Most of these data however is generated in the Western world and its applicability to Asian cancer patients and other cancer types such as hepatocellular carcinoma and EGFR mutated NSCLC are unknown. We propose a cohort study in Asian cancer patients to discover the predictive potential of the microbiome signature as a biomarker for immunotherapy-treated patients. We also aim to better understand the host-microbiome interactions and its impact of immunotherapy responses in mice models. We will then use the information generated to design therapeutic interventions involving modulation of the microbiome in an attempt to improve treatment outcome in Asian cancer patients on immunotherapy.
kw: Microbiome, Cancer, Immunotherapy

title: A Comprehensive Assessment of Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] in Cardiovascular Risk Prediction, Management, and Detection – to facilitate the formulation of a model of care for Lp(a).
abs: Elevated plasma Lp(a) [Lp(a)] levels is a clinically important and common autosomal co-dominant inherited hypercholesterolemia disorder. Large observational prospective studies across Western populations have shown that elevated Lp(a) is causal risk factor for ASCVD including premature onset of ischaemic heart disease, calcific aortic vascular disease, ischaemic stroke, and peripheral artery disease and cardiovascular mortality. The clinical importance of Lp(a) as an important cardiovascular risk factor has led to the recent European Atherosclerosis Society’s recommendation (2019) and other guidelines that all adults in the general population should have Lp(a) measured at least once in their lifetime. Yet, there is major paucity of research in Asian populations including Singapore. In this RTF proposal, the applicant aims to perform a comprehensive assessment of Lp(a) as a cardiovascular risk predictor, detection strategies and implementation science. The overall aim is to facilitate the formation of model of care for Lp(a) in Singapore and Southeast Asia in the near future using these evidence-based recommendations that our projects will generate. The applicant hypothesises that measurement of Lp(a) at least once in an all adults preferably in their early adult lifetime improves overall cardiovascular risk stratification and risk mitigation. The methods in the RTF and PhD proposal includes (i) using prospective studies of patients with Lp(a) with ischaemic heart disease, stroke, familial hypercholesterolemia and general population, (ii) generating genetic risk score as surrogate marker of Lp(a) for research and clinical purposes, (iii) investigating cost effectiveness and implementation science of Lp(a). This area of research addressed a great unmet need now because an estimated 20% of the world population have elevated Lp(a), implications on cascade testing, actionable management can mitigate overall risk, and there are effective Lp(a)-lowering agents currently in phase II and III clinical trials.
kw: lipoprotein(a); hypercholesterolemia; cardiovascular risk management;cardiovascular risk prediction; stroke

title: Evaluating the clinical applicability of flow-mediated dilation of the brachial artery as a marker of endothelial function
abs: Background: Cardiovascular disease remains one of the top causes of mortality locally. Flow-mediated dilation (FMD) of the brachial artery, a non-invasive ultrasound-based method of assessing endothelial function, may potentially improve early detection of cardiovascular disease. However, implementation has been limited due to a lack of procedure standardisation. Furthermore, there is a lack of data on FMD in our local population. The goals of this project are to: i) develop a standardised protocol for measuring FMD; ii) generate pilot data on FMD values in our healthy local population and individuals with type 2 diabetes mellitus; iii) assess the impact of novel indices such as physical activity, cardiorespiratory fitness, and sleep quality on FMD; and iv) evaluate the utility of FMD as an integrative marker of endothelial response to a personalised exercise intervention. Methods: This pilot study aims to generate preliminary data on brachial artery FMD. Another group of individuals with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) matched for age and sex will be measured and compared against the healthy individuals. Correlations with physical activity, cardiorespiratory fitness, and sleep indices with FMD will be performed. In addition, a subset of sedentary individuals with T2DM will undergo a 6-month personalised exercise intervention using changes in FMD and endothelial regenerative capacity as outcomes. Clinical significance: FMD is a noninvasive measurement that can potentially be integrated to identify endothelial dysfunction in high-risk individuals early. Demonstrating the feasibility of performing FMD measurements in a standardised and rigorous way will be fundamental to establishing reference intervals for our local population, which further research can build upon to identify thresholds for diagnosing endothelial dysfunction. Furthermore, the exercise intervention seeks to demonstrate the efficacy and clinical utility of FMD as a therapeutic marker for tracking responses to interventions.
kw: Endothelial function, flow-mediated dilation

title: Utilising Electronic Health Records Data to Determine Periodontitis Treatment Trajectories in People Suffering from Severe Periodontitis and Its Association with Systemic Multimorbidity Clustering
abs: Background: Severe periodontitis is an inflammatory disease of the gums and leads to tooth loss. It is the sixth most prevalent major disease globally. Local registry-based research in oral health and its oral-systemic relationships has never been performed. Identifying periodontal treatment response patterns through data-driven approaches are also not well investigated. Aim: To use real-world evidence in the local population suffering from severe periodontitis to investigate the influence of multimorbidity clusters, and its effect on treatment response trajectories. Hypothesis: Oral registry data can identify different response trajectories in periodontitis, and poor responders to therapy are more likely to present with multimorbidity and common risk factors. Methodology: The study will utilise data from the Oral Disease Registry. First, real-world treatment outcomes for adults suffering from severe periodontitis from the registry will be compared against pooled efficacy results obtained from systematically reviewing existing literature. Second, exploratory factor analysis will be used to identify patterns of periodontitis phenotypes, and will be clustered into distinct response trajectories. Third, multimorbidity clusters will be identified in patients with differing treatment responses, using artificial intelligence (network analysis). Fourth, structural equation modelling will used to investigate the influence of cardiometabolic multimorbidity clusters, and common risk factors, on treatment responses. Feasibility: The Oral Disease Registry will be operational in mid-2024. This pipeline will extract data records from National Dental Centre Singapore and will be linked with Singapore Health Services Diabetes Registry. Approximately 1,000 unique patients have shared appointments at the NDCS and at the SGH Diabetes and Metabolism Centre yearly. Importance of the study: Investigating real-world treatment responses through a data-driven approach will quantify the chronic oral disease burden in Singapore. This also allows identification of shared risk pathways and modifiable risk factor targets in the same patient, facilitating multidisciplinary coordination of care for the patient.
kw: big data; real-world data; prognosis; oral health; cluster analysis; multimorbidity

title: Identifying laboratory biomarkers and microbiological correlates that prognosticate and monitor the clinical course of Guillain-Barré Syndrome
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Background Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is an acute postinfectious immune-mediated polyneuropathy displaying a wide spectrum of disease manifestations and severity. Variations in clinical phenotype may be an interplay between host and disease factors, including antecedent infections, though specific mechanisms remain to be elucidated. It is conceivable that this immunologically-mediated insult is associated with blood protein profile aberrations, arising from upregulation of inflammatory mediators (e.g. cytokines, complements) and/or products of neuronal injury (e.g. peripherin, neurofilament light chain). Assaying these released proteins generates proteomic signatures that can be correlated with the patient’s clinical phenotype and antecedent infections. This understanding can potentially facilitate discovery of biomarkers for disease activity and elucidate the biological underpinnings of the disease process. Objectives Primary aim: Identify proteomic signatures associated with severe GBS phenotypes (respiratory failure, protracted disease course). Secondary aims: Examine the relationships of: - proteomic signature kinetics with disease course and treatment response. - antecedent infections with clinical phenotype and proteomic signature. Methodology We maintain a database of prospectively recruited GBS patients and controls, with clinical, laboratory and electrodiagnostic data collected at protocolised intervals. We are concurrently exploring the association of antecedent infections and subsequent GBS phenotype via VirScan. Serum samples will be assayed with the SomaScan platform for high throughput multiplex proteomic analysis. Patients will be stratified by disease severity, and intergroup differences in proteomic signatures will be sought via multivariate statistical modelling. Feasibility Our institution provides the majority of neurological care in Singapore, allowing continued recruitment of most locally-occurring GBS patients to our ongoing database. Our close collaboration with biostatisticians will also be invaluable to this study. Impact Findings from this study will help identify patients at risk of deterioration and track disease progression. It would also clarify the underlying pathogenic processes in GBS and their relationship to antecedent infection, informing future management strategies.
kw: Guillain-Barré syndrome; immune-mediated; post-infectious; proteomics; severity; prognostication

title: Longitudinal analysis of non-motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Parkinson’s disease (PD) is one of the commonest neurodegenerative diseases. With Singapore’s ageing population, the prevalence of PD is expected to increase markedly in the coming years. Non-motor symptoms are a major component of PD and contribute significantly to disease burden. Cross-sectional studies have established that the prevalence of non-motor symptoms in PD is much higher compared to healthy controls, with up to 90% of patients with PD displaying at least 1 non-motor symptom. However, there exist only limited cohorts which follow non-motor symptoms longitudinally using detailed, annually assessed clinical measures. As such, it remains unclear how the pattern and severity of non-motor symptoms change over a longitudinal period. Additionally, there have been conflicting results regarding the association of non-motor symptom severity and the motor progression of PD, with some studies reporting an association and others a lack thereof. Previous attempts to characterise PD subtypes have identified that the severity and clustering of non-motor symptoms may be associated with more rapid motor progression and thus more severe disease. These uncertainties can be explored by analysing results from the Early PD Longitudinal (PALS) Study, which is a deeply-phenotyped cohort of 200 PD patients with PD and 100 healthy controls, currently in the 6th year of follow up. Participants undergo annual assessment of motor and non-motor symptoms including anxiety, depression, apathy, and cognition using specific and established clinical scales. Serum biomarker analysis and neuroimaging is also performed. With the benefit of a long prospective cohort with annual data, the longitudinal progress of motor and non-motor symptoms of PD can be closely monitored. I aim to examine the hypothesis that non-motor symptom severity is associated with motor symptom severity, and to understand which specific non-motor symptoms progress with time, so that they can be identified early and aggressively managed in order to reduce disease morbidity.
kw: Parkinson's disease, non-motor symptoms, disease progression

title: Utility of DNA Methylation Markers in Biliary Brush Cytology and Bile Sample in Malignant Biliary Stricture
abs: Specific Aim To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of specific DNA methylation biomarkers in biliary brush cytology and bile samples in malignant biliary stricture. Hypothesis The addition of DNA methylation on biliary brush and bile samples would improve the diagnostic yield of malignant biliary stricture when compared with standard care of cytology brushings. Methods Study Design: Single center prospective cohort study Inclusion Criteria: 1. Age ≥ 21 years 2. Presence of biliary stricture on radiological imaging requiring biliary brush cytology Exclusion Criteria: 1. Presence of malignancy other than cholangiocarcinoma 2. Pregnancy 3. inability to provide informed consent Eligible subjects with biliary stricture for biliary brushed cytology will be approached and recruited. Procedures will be performed by experienced interventionist. Bile juice will be drawn from bile duct and parallel biliary brushing and/or biopsies will be obtained from all patients. The samples will be sent for routine cytological examination and molecular analysis. The outcomes measures will be diagnostic sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV) and accuracy of methylation markers in the evaluation of biliary stricture. Sample Size The sample size estimate/power calculation for the cohort used within this study will be based on a 60% prevalence of malignancy among bile duct strictures and corresponding 40% sensitivity for detecting malignancy using cytological evaluation of ERCP-obtained specimens. We expect a corresponding 85% sensitivity using the DNA methylation analysis. Therefore, a sample size of at least 34 patients would yield a > 80% power with an alpha of 0.05. Feasibility In SGH, our department received at least 50 new referral of biliary strictures per year and hence the study feasibility is high. Significance of Study 1) reduction in need for repeat procedures 2) avoid delays in diagnosis and assist in formulation of a definitive management plan 3) reduction in unnecessary surgery
kw: cholangiocarcinoma;brush cytology;bile;DNA methylation

title: Screening for undiagnosed glaucoma in the community using deep learning algorithms based on retinal photos
abs: Background: Glaucoma is the leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide, characterized by optic nerve damage and visual field loss. Screening for glaucoma is challenging due to lack of a simple, cost-efficient, standardized process. Artificial intelligence, (AI) especially deep learning (DL) algorithms have the potential to improve and standardize glaucoma detection, however these algorithms have to be tested prospectively in real world settings, before public deployment. Aim: To evaluate the accuracy and cost-effectiveness of a DL algorithm based on colour fundus photographs (CFP) as a clinical decision support tool, for detecting glaucoma, in a real-world community setting. Hypothesis: We hypothesize that the AI-assisted clinical model has better screening performance (i.e., sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value) in detecting glaucoma and is cost-effective in terms of costs per Quality Adjusted Life Years (QALYs) saved relative to the current practice. Methods: A single centre, single-blind, pragmatic randomised control trial (RCT) in 1040 eligible patients with diabetes recruited from the Diabetes & Metabolism Centre’s clinics under the Singapore Integrated Diabetic Retinopathy Program (SiDRP). After CFP are obtained, the study participants will be randomized to either arm: grading by AI-supported method vs current grading by graders at the SiDRP reading center (520 subjects in each of the two arms). The performance of both methods will be compared to the gold standard ground truth for glaucoma diagnosis, performed by the study ophthalmologist. These tests include complete ocular examination including intraocular pressure measurement, visual field analysis, optical coherence tomography and dilated fundus examination. For assessing cost-effectiveness, a cohort-based Markov model nested within a decision tree will be developed to simulate the net lifetime cost and incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs) of the two glaucoma screening strategies. Clinical importance: Integrating AI into community glaucoma screening can overcome resource and capability deficiencies in the community.
kw: glaucoma screening, artificial intelligence, deep learning, randomised control trials, cost-effectiveness

title: Clinical characterisation of physical activity, cardiorespiratory fitness, and/or muscle and bone strength on performance of physical and mental health, and/or prevention and control of medical diseases
abs: Aim: To understand the clinical impact of physical activity, cardiorespiratory fitness level, and muscle and bone strength on the promotion and maintenance of physical and mental health in paediatric populations. By investigating these factors both individually and in combination, the study seeks to provide evidence-based exercise prescriptions tailored to each patient's medical background and health goals, enhancing effectiveness and patient safety. Hypothesis: Physical activity, cardiorespiratory fitness, and muscle and bone strength have distinct and interconnected effects on paediatric health. Combining these factors may lead to synergistic health benefits. By studying both healthy children and those with medical conditions, the research aims to identify personalised exercise interventions for various paediatric populations, address evidence-based recommendations gaps, and promote overall well-being. Methodology: Study will take multi-step approach. Initially, a registry of population normative data will be established to determine paediatric reference values for physical activity, cardiorespiratory fitness, and muscle and bone strength in multi-racial populations. Next, investigate current physical activity habits and their relation to health outcomes in healthy children and those with medical conditions. Various exercise programs will be tested on their health impacts. Lastly, a long-term follow-up will explore the relationship between physical activity habits, cardiorespiratory fitness, and disease prevention. Approach: Holistic approach of analysing the physical and mental health effects of physical activity, cardiorespiratory fitness, and muscle and bone strength individually and collectively, in both healthy children and those with medical conditions. Feasibility: This study is supported by available international and local recommendations for physical activity levels in general pediatric populations. Collaborations with healthcare institutions will facilitate the inclusion of pediatric patients with medical conditions. The multi-step approach allows for comprehensive data collection and analysis, leading to a more nuanced understanding of the relationship between fitness factors and pediatric health outcomes.
kw: paediatric; physical activity; cardiorespiratory fitness; muscle and bone strength; physical health; mental health

title: Doxycycline host-directed therapy to improve neurological recovery and clinical outcomes in central nervous system tuberculosis
abs: Although tuberculosis is now considered a treatable disease, central nervous system tuberculosis (CNS-TB) when managed with the current standard-of-care (SOC), still has mortality rates ranging from 30-50% even in tertiary hospital centers. At present, the SOC for the management of CNS-TB is anti-tuberculous therapy with adjunctive corticosteroids. In CNS-TB, the activity of pathogenic host matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) is unopposed to tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMPs), resulting in a matrix-degrading phenotype which may drive worse outcomes in CNS-TB. In our established CNS-TB murine model, we have demonstrated that adjunctive MMP inhibition using doxycycline, a widely available and cheap drug, in addition to standard TB treatment, compared with standard TB treatment alone, improved murine survival. We previously showed that in humans with pulmonary TB, doxycycline with anti-TB treatment is safe, accelerates the resolution of inflammation, and suppresses systemic and respiratory MMPs. Hence, we are now ideally positioned to determine if adjunctive doxycycline in patients with CNS-TB can improve clinical outcomes. We will perform a Phase 2 double-blind randomized-controlled trial (RCT) of adjunctive doxycycline versus placebo with standard TB treatment and steroids for 8 weeks, with the primary outcome of 8-week mortality or severe neurological deficits. We hypothesize that in patients with CNS-TB, the addition of doxycycline to SOC improves clinical outcomes.
kw: Central Nervous System Tuberculosis; Infectious Diseases; Host-Pathogen Interaction

title: Uncovering Protective Mechanism of BCAA Catabolic Activation in Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction
abs: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is “the single largest unmet need in cardiovascular medicine” based on prevalence, poor outcomes and lack of therapies. Abnormal BCAA catabolism is not only a metabolic biomarker but also a therapeutic target for diabetes and heart failure. Our preliminary studies demonstrated that restoring systemic BCAA catabolic flux can effectively ameliorate cardiac dysfunction associated with improved insulin resistance in HFpEF. This led us to propose our key hypothesis that BCAA catabolic defect is a major metabolic feature and a significant pathogenic mechanism of HFpEF, subsequently restoring BCAA catabolic flux is a promising therapeutic strategy to treat HFpEF. However, we have yet to establish whether the therapeutic benefits of BCAA catabolic activation for HFpEF are mediated by a cardiomyocyte specific cell-autonomous mechanism or via a systemic effect. Adipose tissue is a major contributor to systemic BCAA catabolic activities and adipose BCAA catabolic flux is severely impaired under obese condition. However, the specific contribution of cardiomyocyte- verses adipose tissue-specific BCAA catabolic activity to the manifestation of cardiometabolic defects associated with HFpEF has never been investigated. Therefore, in this proposal, we plan to fill this important gap by accomplishing the three specific aims: 1) To determine the cell-autonomous impact of cardiomyocyte specific BCAA catabolic activation on HFpEF pathogenesis by cardiac specific BCAA catabolic activation in animals. 2) To establish the functional role of adipose BCAA catabolic activity in obesity and cardiac dysfunction during HFpEF development by adipose tissue specific BCAA catabolic activation in vivo. 3) To elucidate the mechanisms of action for the therapeutic effect of BCAA catabolic activation for HFpEF in cardiac and adipose tissues by integrating analysis at metabolomic and transcriptomic levels. Overall, the proposal will uncover the mechanism of BCAA catabolic activation in HFpEF, as well as develop a BCAA targeted therapy for HFpEF.
kw: HFpEF; BCAA;BCAA catabolic flux; metabolic disorder; adipose tissue

title: Deciphering the structural basis of SIRT6-Telomere interplay in Aging and Cancer
abs: Like most eukaryotes, human DNA is organized into chromatin in association with a histone octamer core composed of two copies each of H2A, H2B, H3 and H4. This chromatin condenses in association with various protein factors to form chromosomes. At the end of chromosomes are the telomeres characterized by a unique repetitive sequence TTAGGG in humans and variants with a triplet of guanine in most other species. The telomeres shorten with each round of cell division, acting as a biological clock. Cancer cells through mutation and dysregulation of normal biological processes, achieve immortality by elongating or maintaining telomere length through telomerase or ALT pathways. SIRT6 is a telomere-associated protein that has been shown to increase life span in mice. The SIRT6, through its deacetylase activity, facilitates efficient DNA repair, thereby helping maintain genomic integrity. However, the structural mechanism by which SIRT6 interact with short repeat length and columnar architecture of telomeric chromatin characterized by supergroove and open state remains a mystery. The proposed project aims to decipher the structural mechanism of SIRT6 with telomeric chromatin. A complementary approach aims to establish a cryo-EM platform for small molecule drug interaction with telomeric nucleosomes by exploring the feasibility of a cryo-EM structure of cisplatin bound to telomeric nucleosomes. In tandem, the two objectives aims to establish a platform to study DNA damage response at telomeres and a drug development platform aimed at telomeric chromatin.
kw: Cancer;Ageing; Telomere;Cryo-electron microscopy; Drug-discovery;Nucleosome.

title: Delineating crosstalk between NK receptor and CAR signaling to optimize CAR-NK therapy
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-bearing cellular immunotherapies have revolutionized the landscape of cancer treatment: pioneering CAR-T therapies have shown unprecedented efficacy in hematological cancers, and new trials have begun to demonstrate their potential in solid tumors. Natural killer (NK) cells are potent anti-tumor effectors with immense potential to be harnessed in immune therapies, particularly as, compared to T cells, they have an improved safety profile, and enable allogeneic therapy with industry scalability. While CAR-NK therapy is still at its infancy, its clinical success relies on an understanding of how the synthetic CAR functions in an NK cell. Unlike T cells, which recognize their targets via a single rearranged receptor, NK cells utilize a wide array of germline encoded activating and inhibitory receptors; the balance of signaling between these receptors determines their fate. In CAR-NK cells, while the CAR redirects target specificity, endogenous NK cell receptors on these cells continue to contribute to the balance of signaling. We propose that, by identifying native NK cell signaling pathways in the tumor microenvironment, we can adopt these axes into developing CAR-NK cells that can improve the intra-tumoral functional fitness of CAR-NK. Our specific aims are: 1. Define and phenotypically map functionally active and functionally deficient NK cell subsets in the CRC TME. 2. Determine and synergize the activating signaling axes that enhance CAR-NK effector activity. 3. Determine and overcome inhibitory NK receptor signaling that impedes CAR-NK effector activity. Overall, this proposal will address a fundamental knowledge gap regarding receptor signaling crosstalk in CAR-NK cell biology. These findings can be immediately translated into actionable targets to enhance the anti-tumor efficacy of CAR-NK cells, and develop them into a safe and effective therapy for the benefit of patients.
kw: NK cells; colorectal cancer; CAR-NK; chimeric antigen receptor; transcriptomics

title: Investigating the role of the type 2 diabetes risk-associated ZHX3 gene in disease pathogenesis
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: ZHX3, which encodes for a transcriptional repressor, is associated with fasting blood glucose (FBG) levels and T2D risk but its role in cell types involved in glucose metabolism is not well understood. The first aim of this study is to investigate the role of ZHX3 in human hepatocytes and the second aim is to investigate its role in human pancreatic β cells. So far, we have successfully deleted ZHX3 in the human hepatoma line HepG2 and the human pancreatic β cell line EndoC-βH1. The expression levels of gluconeogenic genes PCK1 and G6PC1 were de-repressed when ZHX3 was deleted in HepG2 cells. To investigate the effects of losing ZHX3 in HepG2 and EndoC-βH1 cells, we propose to perform RNA-Seq analysis to identify the target genes of ZHX3 in these two cell types. To evaluate the phenotype of losing ZHX3 in HepG2 and EndoC-βH1 cells, we plan to perform various functional assays such as the hepatic glucose production assay on ZHX3 KO HepG2 cells and the glucose-stimulation insulin secretion assay on ZHX3 KO EndoC-βH1 cells. Given that it is not clear how ZHX3 functions as a transcriptional repressor, the third aim of this project is to identify its binding partners. Co-immunoprecipitation followed by mass spectrometry analysis of ZHX3 in HepG2 cells identified CEBPB, which is a transcriptional activator of PCK1 and G6PC1, as a binding partner of ZHX3. We propose to evaluate if CEBPB is required for ZHX3 to repress its target genes in HepG2 cells by knocking out ZHX3 in a CEBPB-null background HepG2 line. We also propose to perform molecular dynamics simulation analysis study the molecular interaction between ZHX3 and CEBPB. Elucidating how ZHX3 regulates glucose metabolism may pave way for the discovery of novel therapeutic approaches for T2D and precision medicine for patients having mutations in the ZHX3 gene.
kw: type 2 diabetes; ZHX3; hepatocytes; pancreatic β cells; glucose metabolism

title: Function of lysosomal cysteine transport in human brain development
abs: Lysosomes are metabolic organelles that are responsible for the salvage of nutrients particularly in times of nutritional stress. The lysosomal cysteine transporter MFSD12 imports cysteine into lysosomes and melanosomes, where defects in melanosomal cysteine import leads to reduced pheomelanin synthesis affecting skin pigmentation. Cellular cysteine is required for the synthesis of the most abundant antioxidant glutathione (GSH), which reacts readily with reactive oxygen species (ROS) resulting in its oxidation to GSH disulfide (GSSG) when cells undergo oxidative stress. The ratio of GSH to GSSG needs to be delicately balanced to protect cells from oxidative damage leading to cell death. MFSD12 has ubiquitous expression throughout the body but is enriched in brain. This proposal is built upon clinical observations of our first account of patients with compound heterozygous mutations in MFSD12. These patients present with intellectual disability, epilepsy, ataxia and cerebellar hypoplasia. We demonstrate that mouse model of early postnatal Mfsd12 deficiency (iKO) recapitulate some of the saliant clinical features of these patients such as cerebellar hypoplasia and motor defects. How defective lysosomal cysteine import affects brain growth is not known. The central hypothesis of this proposal is that reduced flux of cysteine into lysosomes depletes cellular glutathione production for redox homeostasis leading to reduction in neuron survival. This hypothesis will be tested by two specific aims: (1) to determine the mechanism by which MFSD12 and lysosomal cysteine regulates cerebellar growth, and (2) to determine the contribution of MFSD12 to redox homeostasis and cell survival. Cell models using mouse embryonic fibroblasts and elicited peritoneal macrophages generated from iKO will be utilized to address aim 2. It is anticipated that the understanding of the physiological role of MFSD12 will provide mechanistic insights on the function of lysosomal cysteine and brain development.
kw: lysosome; brain growth; redox homeostasis; transporter

title: Investigating the early-stage colorectal cancer liver metastasis microenvironment to discover novel molecular and cellular targets and dissect the roles of distinct macrophage populations
abs: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the second-leading cause of cancer death in Singapore, and liver metastasis is a major cause of death in CRC patients. The liver comprises several immune cell types, including liver-resident macrophages known as Kupffer cells. Previous studies that investigated the role of Kupffer cells in CRC liver metastasis do not distinguish Kupffer cells from the large number of monocyte-derived macrophages that infiltrate during disease progression. This is an important distinction as these macrophages of different origins exhibit different functions in various contexts, and the ability to target these distinct macrophage populations separately could lead to novel preventive and therapeutic strategies against CRC liver metastasis. Our preliminary data using an orthotopic immunocompetent CRC liver metastasis mouse model in “monocyte-derived cell” fate-mapping transgenic mice shows that in early-stage CRC liver metastasis, the number of Kupffer cells in the liver microenvironment decreases significantly before the outgrowth of CRC liver metastasis which is accompanied by an influx of monocyte-derived immune cells. We therefore hypothesize that Kupffer cells initially protect against disseminated metastatic CRC cells in the liver. However, as the disease progresses, important cellular crosstalk and ligand-receptor interactions take place that decrease Kupffer cell protection and remodel the liver microenvironment, catalyzing the outgrowth of CRC liver metastasis. We propose to study this by: (1) Using single-cell sequencing and spatial omics-sequencing to discover important ligand-receptor interactions and crucial cellular crosstalk in the early-stage CRC liver metastasis microenvironment; (2) Using transgenic mouse strains to determine the respective roles of Kupffer cells and monocyte-derived immune cells in early-stage CRC liver metastasis; (3) Using transgenic mice, pharmacological approaches, and human tissue samples to validate our findings. This approach has not been used to study early-stage CRC liver metastasis to-date, and will lead to novel preventive and therapeutic strategies for patients against CRC liver metastasis.
kw: Cancer; Metastasis; Colon; Liver; Immunology; Microenvironment

title: Rewiring neutrophil responses in chronic lung disease to improve neonatal outcomes
abs: Globally, complications due to prematurity are the leading cause of death in children under five. Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) is the most common prematurity complication, and is a severe lung disease of preterm infants characterized by improper vascularization and destruction of lung architecture. Despite widespread efforts, BPD incidence is increasing and is the most adverse outcome for preterm infants, with impacts on mortality and morbidity continuing on into adult life. Systemic inflammation precedes symptomatic onset, representing a therapeutic window of opportunity to divert the disease course. However, although inflammation is the common pathway driving pathophysiology in BPD, how the immune system initiates or exacerbates disease remain unknown, representing a significant knowledge gap. Neutrophils are the first immune cells to infiltrate the diseased lung, and is highly associated with worse disease prognosis in BPD. Additionally, pro-angiogenic neutrophils also emerge in BPD lungs, but whether they reflect an unsuccessful repair response, or participate in disordered vascularization is unknown. Lastly, neutrophils play crucial roles in maintaining host defence in the healthy lung, illustrating the complexity of neutrophil populations in health and disease. Thus, understanding neutrophil heterogeneity and how their phenotypes and functions are disrupted in BPD will allow rewiring of aberrant neutrophil responses to avoid disease initiation or progression. Using longitudinal flow cytometric profiling, changes in neutrophil composition and function in the blood and lungs of human patients and a mouse hyperoxia model of BPD will be correlated with levels of soluble inflammatory mediators to find disease drivers of BPD. In parallel, spatial transcriptomic mapping of neutrophils comparing steady state and acute/chronic disease lungs will identify how their homeostatic functions are disrupted in BPD. These approaches address the urgent need to understand the disease mechanisms underlying unresolved inflammation, thus providing new and specific immunomodulatory targets to potentiate effective treatments for BPD.
kw: Human Health and Potential; Preterm birth; Early life immunology;Chronic lung disease

title: Associations of metabolic indicators and circadian behaviour changes with reproductive outcomes in overweight and obese women who are trying to conceive
abs: Although human reproduction is tightly controlled by metabolic and circadian signals, the impact of metabolic and circadian alterations on female fertility in overweight/obese individuals, who are inherently at a higher risk of infertility, remains unknown. Our goal is to identify potentially modifiable metabolic and circadian behaviour factors that contribute to impaired fertility, with the intention of developing interventions to improve reproductive health outcomes for women. This proposal aims to investigate the relationship between changes in metabolic indicators or circadian behaviour and reproductive health outcomes in overweight/obese women who are trying to conceive, while also exploring the underlying biological mechanisms. To achieve this, we plan to recruit 240 preconception women with a body mass index (BMI) of 25-40 kg/m2 from a women's care program at KK Women's and Children's Hospital. By adjusting for confounders, we will evaluate the associations between metabolic indicators and circadian behaviour changes with the clinical pregnancy rate over a one-year period of conception attempts. Secondary outcomes include fecundability (defined as the probability of conception within a menstrual cycle, measured by time-to-pregnancy) and the rate of spontaneous miscarriage before 16 weeks' gestation. We hypothesise that within three months from baseline, reductions in BMI, total body fat, insulin resistance, metabolic syndrome score, or circadian behaviour index score will be associated with a higher pregnancy rate and fecundability, and a lower miscarriage rate. We will use modified Poisson regression models to examine associations with pregnancy and miscarriage rates, and discrete-time proportional hazards modelling to estimate associations with fecundability. We will also explore the relationship between circadian behaviour and clock gene expressions in the blood, hypothesizing that women with healthier circadian behaviour will exhibit higher clock gene expressions. This study is crucial for identifying potential novel modifiable risk factors that can help to improve fertility rate in Singapore.
kw: Preconception; obesity; metabolic health; chrononutrition; circadian behaviour; fertility

title: Development and Pilot Evaluation of a Clinical-Decision Support Tool to Manage Patients with Hypertension in Primary Care based on Self-monitored Blood Pressure
abs: Primary care physicians (PCPs) face challenges in managing patients on home BP (HBP) monitoring; these include time-consuming and cognitively overloading tasks to examine HBP data from different sources (paper and digital) and difficulty interpreting the BP, mainly because of BP variability and insufficient knowledge of managing these patients. Thus, the study aims to develop and pilot test a clinical decision-support (CDS) tool to capture and process HBP records from paper and digital sources and prompt PCPs to make decisions in BP management. The study has two phases: Phase 1 will conduct a scoping review to synthesise evidence on CDS integrating HBP records and develop a CDS prototype on a mobile tablet device. Phase 2 will pilot test the CDS in 2 public primary care clinics in Singapore with 8 PCPs and 100 patients with hypertension in a single-blind cluster randomised controlled study with an embedded qualitative study. Intervention group PCPs and patients will be educated on HBP monitoring, and PCPs trained to use the CDS tool. PCPs will use the CDS tool to manage patients, followed by focus group discussions to gather qualitative data on their experiences. Control group PCPs will provide usual care. All patients will be reviewed over two to three visits by PCPs over six months. title: Elucidating the evolutionary drivers of resistance to kinase inhibitors
abs: Tyrosine kinase inhibitors are now widely used in the treatment of solid tumors.  In non-small cell lung cancer, there at least 9 druggable molecular subtypes (EGFR, ALK, ROS1, BRAF, cMET ex14, KRAS, RET, NTRK, HER2), each with a suite of corresponding targeted therapies, ranging from structural distinct small molecules to bispecific antibodies and antibody drug conjugates.  However, drug resistance often develops through a range of mechanisms including on target pathway dependent mechanisms, acquisition of alternate drivers e.g. cMET amplification or lineage transition states. Emerging data suggests convergent mechanisms of resistance across different molecular subtypes, suggesting a common framework towards resistance of targeted therapies, both in NSCLC, as well as other solid tumors.  While several combination approaches have been examined, current clinical experience suggests only modest response rates and durability of response. title: Heart-Brain Connection for Vascular and Cognitive Health
abs: Background: Undiagnosed cognitive impairment (CI) in patients with heart failure (HF) is approximately 40%. To address this blind spot and improve the prognosis in HF, a mechanistic study in heart-brain connection accounting for CI is important. Hence, we aim to extend and expand our Transition Award (TA) project for this. Specific aims: We aim to examine the associations between the heart and brain vascular pathology for CI in HF. And establish longitudinal patterns of cognitive decline and associated factors, and explore the effect of sodium glucose co-transporter 2 inhibitor (SGLT2i) on cognition. Hypothesis: There are associations between cardiac markers [e.g., ejection fraction (EF), NT-proBNP], brain injuries (e.g., white matter hyperintensities) and CI. Lower EF and higher NT-proBNP are associated with cerebral hypoperfusion and reduced cerebral blood flow. HF patients on SGLT2i may have less cognitive decline due to higher levels of ketones and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF). Methodology: We will recruit 400 HF patients. Of these,160 HF patients (80 with CI and 80 without CI) will undergo intensive investigation procedures. These include neurocognitive assessments, blood tests for cardiac markers, metabolomics, holter monitoring, transcranial doppler (TCD) and brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Neurocognitive assessments will be taken at baseline, year 1 and 2, while other intensive measures will be taken at baseline and year 2. Approach of the research proposal and feasibility of the study: The proposed mechanistic study will add 2 new approaches, i.e., metabolomics and TCD, to provide insight on the heart-brain connection for CI in HF. It is feasible based on the TA study. Clinical Significance: Our proposed research will improve diagnosis and treatment of CI in HF based on the mechanistic insights. This will help to modify cognitive trajectory halting decline in HF population.
kw: Heart Failure; Heart-Brain Connection

title: Web-based advance care planning intervention for patients with kidney failure on dialysis: Pilot testing of ‘My Voice’
abs: Advance care planning (ACP) is integral to delivering quality care for patients with kidney failure. Yet, ACP completion rates among patients with kidney failure in Singapore remain notably low. ‘My Voice’ is an evidence-based interactive web-based ACP intervention tailored for patients with kidney failure on dialysis. The specific aims of this study are to assess the preliminary efficacy of ‘My Voice’ ACP web intervention in improving (a) ACP conversations between patient-physician, (b) ACP conversations between patients-family caregiver; (c) patient’s understanding of their illness; (d) patient’s engagement in the ACP process and (e) patient’s preparedness for future EOL decisions. Our hypothesis is that ‘My Voice’ intervention compared to usual care (control) will improve ACP conversations between patient-physician and patient-caregiver, patient’s illness understanding, their engagement in ACP; and preparedness for end-of-life decisions. We will also assess the feasibility and acceptability of ‘My Voice’. Using mixed-methods, we will conduct a 2-arm non-randomized controlled cluster trial at six National Kidney Foundation (NKF) dialysis centers in which n=50 eligible patients with chronic kidney failure (CKD stage 5) on dialysis will receive ‘My Voice’ (intervention arm, 3 centres, n=25) or current standard of care (control arm, 3 centres; n=25). Caregivers of all patients enrolled will also be recruited (n=50). All participants will attend baseline, 1-month and 6-month follow-up visits for outcomes. Among patients and caregivers in the intervention arm, we will assess the acceptability of ‘My Voice’ quantitatively using the Acceptability of Intervention Measure (AIM), and qualitatively assess acceptability of ‘My Voice’ intervention though in-depth interviews on a sub-sample of patients (n=6) and caregivers (n=8) at 1-month visit, and renal health care providers (n=6) at end of study. The proposed study will help address gaps in ACP implementation in Singapore and offers sustainable ways to integrate ACP in the care pathway of patients with kidney failure on dialysis.
kw: Kidney failure, dialysis, advance care planning, end-of-life, communication

title: Towards validating biomarkers and identifying new drug targets for improving treatment-free remission in chronic myeloid leukaemia
abs: Treatment-free remission (TFR) is the ultimate goal of chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML) management. TFRs define a so-called ‘operational cure’ with improved quality of life, and substantially reduced treatment costs. While 40-60% of CML patients are eligible to attempt a TFR, half will relapse upon stopping therapy. Consequently, only ~20% of patients ever achieve a TFR. Two obstacles prevent improvement of TFR rates: accurate biomarkers to identify patients who will relapse and benefit from additional therapies, and effective relapse-preventing therapies. Underlying these knowledge gaps is a near-complete lack of understanding on the fundamental mechanisms driving relapse. Specifically, while CML leukaemic stem cells (LSC) are almost certainly the source of relapse, no studies have directly examined their molecular biology. Accordingly, we performed single cell RNA-sequencing on diagnostic pre-treatment bone marrow (BM) in a uniform cohort of patients who attempted TKI stop, and were annotated for TFR (Remission) vs relapse (Relapse). Among 31 different BM cell types, Relapse vs Remission LSCs harboured the most differentially expressed genes (DEG), whose signature predicted Relapse LSCs with 95% accuracy. Importantly, these genes were expressed on their progeny, and detectable in diagnostic peripheral blood. Further, we found evidence for increased polycomb repressive complex 1 (PRC1) activity in Relapse vs Remission LSCs, predicting increased sensitivity of Relapse vs Remission LSCs to PRC1 inhibitors. We confirmed that Relapse LSCs are 2-fold more sensitive to PRC1 inhibitors in vitro, which also decreased expression of Relapse DEGs. We hypothesize that PRC1-driven epigenetic programming in CML LSCs drives relapse. Our Specific Aims are to: 1. Develop biomarkers for predicting TFR at initial diagnosis and on treatment; 2. Understand the contribution of epigenetic factors to LSC-driven relapse; and 3. Develop new therapeutic approaches to improve TFR rates. The successful completion of our Aims may change practice and potentially enhance TFR rates in CML.
kw: CML; treatment-free remission; leukaemia stem cell

title: Understanding the long-term auto-immune, cardiovascular, cerebrovascular, neuropsychiatric and thrombotic sequelae of dengue
abs: Long COVID-19 highlighted the wide-ranging manifestations of post-acute chronic sequelae after viral infection. Similar syndromes of post-acute chronic sequelae have been observed after infection by other pathogens, such as dengue. However, the long-term risk, excess burdens and functional impact of post-acute dengue complications remain poorly defined and are limited to small-scale studies. This proposal seeks to leverage on electronic health records data to provide a large-scale, high-resolution and high-dimensional characterisation of post-acute sequelae of dengue in the auto-immune, cardiovascular, cerebrovascular and neuropsychiatric domains. Namely, this proposal has 3 specific aims, using Singapore as the study setting to: (1) leverage on population-level electronic health records (n >5,000,000), national dengue surveillance and dengue test-negative/positive data to assess the long-term auto-immune, cardiovascular and neurological consequences of dengue infection overall across 2015 – 2022. (2) Evidence suggests that there may be differences in severity in the acute phase of dengue infection by serotype. We aim to exploit switches in the predominant serotypes responsible for outbreaks over the past decade in Singapore to examine potential differences in long-term complications following infection of different serotypes. Namely, these would employ cohort construction methods developed the first aim but exclusively to comprise DENV-2/3 predominant phases of transmission, as well as data on serotype individuals (3) We aim to examine whether differences in severity in the acute phase of dengue infection lead to differences in risks and excess burdens of long-term complications. As severity status (ambulatory, admission to hospitalization, ICU) are not part of the dengue notifications and test-positive/negative dengue databases used in Aims 1 and 2, we will construct and analyse two retrospective clinical cohorts comprising attendances and/or admission to Singapore General Hospital and Tan Tock Seng Hospital, 2 of 3 flagship hospitals among the healthcare clusters in Singapore.

title: Colo-SCRIPT: Colorectal cancer subtype-specific research informs phenotypes, diagnostics & treatments
abs: Colo-SCRIPT is our national CRC research program, unifying health clusters, universities, and A*STAR. CRC comprises major molecular subtypes with distinct origins in precursor lesions. We focus on subtype-specific biology across this continuum. We hypothesise that understanding distinct biology of different molecular subtypes of CRC can lead to subtype-specific prevention, diagnosis and treatment. Our research themes focus on interrogating subtype-specific biological and clinical underpinnings in CRC. Theme 1 and 2 investigate intrinsic and environmental factors influencing malignant transformation in epithelial compartment. The tumour microenvironment stromal and immune interactions with malignant cells play an increasing role as tumours progress towards invasive and metastatic lesions, thereby influencing oncogenic phenotypes, clinical behaviour and treatment response. Deploying model systems, Theme 3 and 4 evaluate cell-autonomous and stromal/immune-tumour interactions to exploit therapeutic vulnerabilities. Through the above findings, Theme 5 develops tools for accurate clinical diagnosis and patient stratification. Our program will establish "C-bank" - a curated set of in-house and public resources (data, tissue, and patient-derived models) linked at individual subject level. We upscale existing research studies into national cohorts, SCRIPT1 and SCRIPT2, which are leveraged for our five Themes. SCRIPT1 recruits ~20,000 patients undergoing endoscopy, identifying 600 serrated precursors and 1,400 advanced adenomas, with accompanying epidemiological exposures and samples. SCRIPT2 expands recruitment to a national cohort of 1,000 patients undergoing surgery for primary and/or metastatic disease, from whom blood and tissue samples are allocated to respective Themes for generation of pan-omic molecular profiles and patient-derived subtype-specific organoids and xenografts. Resources from C-bank, SCRIPT1 and SCRIPT2 are shared across the Themes and the Singapore research ecosystem, as well as for industry collaborations. Collectively, these efforts will result in measurable advances in building scientific peaks of excellence, clinical translation and trials, human talent development, infrastructure building, international-standing, academic-industry collaborations and IP generation.

title: Translational Asian Age-related Macular Degeneration Program Phase 2 (TAAP-2)
abs:
The overall aim of TAAP is to address the major unmet clinical needs and scientific gaps in age-related macular degeneration (AMD), which remains the leading cause of blindness in elderly people in Singapore, Asia-Pacific and globally. Since the inception of TAAP in 2018, our team has made signficant progress and highly impactful research findings which have achieved the 5-year goal. 

Our multidisciplinary scientific and clinical team propose this renewal program (TAAP-2) comprising of four concurrent themes 
1)	Theme 1 RE-INVENT EYECARE MODELS aims to pivot eye care from the current hospital-centric model, primarily engaged with advanced disease management, towards a community-oriented framework emphasizing early detection and preventative intervention in high-risk individuals
2)	Theme 2 RESTORE SIGHT aims to develop personalized treatment strategies through studying deep genotype-phenotype correlations and their impact on treatment outcome, with a focus on multi-specific therapies and novel anti-fibrotic therapies.
3)	Theme 3 REVEAL PATHOLOGY will optimize a novel polarization-sensitive OCT to evaluate fibrosis development and its correlation to functional outcomes in a clinical trial in neovascular AMD.
4)	Theme 4 REDEFINE THERAPY will elucidate novel molecular mechanisms and develop new generation multi-specific ocular therapies.

Our TAAP-2 proposal brings forward the most promising research outcomes from TAAP-1 from bench to bedside. Key highlights include clinical trials of first-in-man evaluating novel anti-fibrotic therapy (LRG1), novel imaging device to quantify and predict fibrosis (polarization-sensitive optical coherence tomography (PS-OCT)), in-depth evaluation of non-Mendelian genetics alongside disease sub-phenotyping, and the formulation of novel screening and preventive strategies. title: Singapore lYMPHoma translatiONal studY (SYMPHONY) 2.0
abs: This is a renewal of our NMRC-funded LCG program, which was focused mainly on T- cell lymphomas, an area of critical unmet need globally. Accompanied by a rising incidence in recent decades, global challenges in the field remain. In SYMPHONY 1.0, we have built a rich resource of samples and technical expertise, used these to understand the molecular basis of Asian-centric lymphomas, published cutting-edge papers on globally-relevant challenges in lymphoma, and importantly fostered the development of new lymphoma investigators. SYMPHONY 2.0 builds on this foundation with an ambitious program extending beyond genomics and transcriptomics, into phenotypic analyses with multiomics data integration. Theme 1 will focus on accentuating our world-class lymphoma programs to develop and implement a clinically applicable lymphoma NGS panel for Asian use, with a special emphasis on resolving key diagnostic challenges within the current ICC/WHO lymphoma classification. Theme 2 will leverage on early adoption of spatial techniques to push beyond genomics to identify markers of drug resistance to standard and novel treatments for lymphoma. Theme 3 will address challenges in immune evasion, focusing on the roles of tumour immunogenicity and microenvironment in response and resistance to immunotherapy. Theme 4 will develop novel platforms and assets for therapeutic drug discovery such as EZH2 small molecule degraders and T-MoVac platform for cancer vaccines, and new platforms for identification of cell-surface targets for novel immunotherapy. We aim to foster collaboration in biomarker discovery and address limitations of commercial CAR-T, and improve patient access to locally generated CAR-T through proof-of-concept studies. Theme 5 builds on our collaborative network and advances in data integration/analysis to set up a public resource of a multiomic Asian Lymphoma Atlas, incorporating spatial and other -omic data for lymphomas, for machine learning to overcome limitations in subtyping, dynamically evolving prognostication and disease resistance.

title: Novel imaging biomarkers for myopia
abs: Myopia, a prevalent eye disease that emerges during childhood, is characterized by abnormal eyeball elongation. Uncontrolled progression to high myopia increases the risk of severe complications and irreversible visual impairment later in life. While pharmacological and optical interventions are available to slow down early-stage myopia, there is a lack of reliable biomarkers that guide the timing of treatment. Currently, treatment decisions are based on monitoring the spherical equivalent refractive error (SE) over time. However, the progression of SE is not linear. Therefore, there is a critical need for biomarkers that can accurately predict myopia progression in myopic eyes. To address this need, we have developed two imaging biomarkers utilizing optical coherence tomography (OCT). The first biomarker, triple-input polarization-sensitive OCT (TRIPS-OCT), measures the posterior scleral birefringence. Studies on a guinea pig model of myopia have shown that this biomarker is highly predictive of future SE outcomes. The second biomarker involves a novel technique to estimate the shape of the posterior eye using an ultrafast wide-field OCT prototype. In this grant, we aim to refine these technologies and assess their potential as biomarkers for myopia development in children aged 6-8 years and high myopia development in children aged 12-15. Both studies will adopt a longitudinal approach, tracking the baseline biomarker values and correlating them with changes in SE over two years. By refining these imaging technologies and evaluating their effectiveness as biomarkers, we aim to bridge the current clinical gap in predicting myopia progression. If successful, these biomarkers could significantly impact treatment decision-making, allowing for more precise and timely interventions for children at risk of developing myopia or high myopia. Ultimately, our research aims to improve myopia management and reduce the risk of long-term visual impairment associated with this condition.
kw: Myopia; Optical coherence tomography; Polarisation optics; Risk stratification; Children; Predictive biomarkers

title: Genome-scale CRISPR screening for LDLR-independent pathways regulating LDL uptake
abs: This proposal is inspired by the fact that atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease disease (ASCVD) remains the leading cause of death worldwide, and lipid-lowering therapies that act independently of LDL Receptor (LDLR) are urgently needed. To systematically test the contribution of every gene in the human genome to the LDLR-independent LDL uptake in hepatocytes, we performed unbiased genome-scale CRISPR knockout screen and identified 802 genes whose disruption significantly alters LDL uptake in LDLR-/- hepatocytes. Through functional validation of candidate genes in LDLR-deficient hepatocytes, we have confirmed five causal genes whose knockout led to significantly increased LDL uptake. Moreover, we have successfully demonstrated that FDFT1, DR1, and CHP1 play important roles in regulating plasma cholesterol and TG levels in LDLR-deficient mice. In line with animal study, we found that human individuals with loss-of-function variants of DR1 show a trend of reduced plasma cholesterol levels. In the current proposal, we seek to address three fundamental questions about hepatic LDLR-independent LDL uptake, including: (1) how inhibition of cholesterol synthesis by depletion of FDFT1 promotes LDL uptake in hepatocytes lacking LDLR? (2) what are the major pathways that are involved in regulating LDLR-independent uptake of LDL? (3) whether our integrated discovery pipeline would allow us to discover valuable therapeutic targets for HoFH? Correspondingly, if successful, Aim 1 will yield new molecular insights into the mechanistic link between cholesterol biosynthesis and LDLR-independent LDL uptake; successful validation and elucidation of the mechanism of action of FDFT1, DR1, and CHP1 in Aim 2 will substantially extend our understanding of molecular pathways regulating systemic cholesterol and TG metabolism; importantly, development of GalNAc-conjugated siRNA molecules and their subsequent validation in pre-clinical animal model in Aim 3 will pave the way for the future translation of these targets into novel therapies tackling hyperlipidaemia.

title: Identifying regulatory modules potentiating tumor infiltrating γδ T-cells in colorectal cancer
abs: γδ T-cells are a unique subset of T-cells that have shown promising anti-cancer functions in various settings including colorectal cancer (CRC). We hypothesize that distinct clonotypes of γδ T-cells may exhibit varying degrees of functional reactivity against different molecular subtypes of CRC. To test our hypothesis, we will use both single-cell sequencing approaches in combination with functional assays for validation of in-silico findings. In Aim 1, we will define the clonal repertoire of γδ T-cells in a cohort of 63 CRC patients. We will correlate the clonal repertoire with the transcriptomic landscape of γδ T-cells identified in these patients. Additionally, we will correlate the γδ T-cell clonal repertoire with CRC molecular subtype to identify CRC subtypes that can potentially benefit from γδ T cell based immunotherapy. In Aim 2, we will characterize in vitro expanded γδ T-cells showing reactivity against CRC cells. We will use a well-established cord blood γδ T-cell expansion system to study cell-populations showing CRC reactivity. We will also develop optimized bioinformatics solutions for the analysis of multi-omics data from γδ T-cells. The findings of our study and the resources generated will contribute to the development and adoption of γδ T-cells as promising candidates for adoptive cellular therapy in the management of CRC, potentially improving treatment outcomes and advancing cancer immunotherapy strategies in GI cancers.
kw: Gamma-delta T-cells; Colorectal Cancer; Bioinformatics; Immunology

title: Design of polymer-modified lipid nanoparticle systems for lymph node targeted delivery to enhance cancer immunotherapy
abs: Cancer vaccines have emerged as a promising approach in cancer therapy. However, their effectiveness is hindered by inefficient delivery to dendritic cells (DCs) and inadequate cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL)-mediated cellular immunity. In this research, we aim to address these challenges by developing a lymph node-targeted vaccine with Toll-like receptor agonists (TLRa) to enhance DCs' uptake efficiency and improve CTL-mediated anti-cancer immunity. The lymph node serves as a crucial site for the residence, activation, and proliferation of lymphocytes. Targeting a vaccine to the lymph nodes allows direct delivery to lymphocytes, optimizes interaction with DCs, and enhances antigen-presentation to T cells. Moreover, the activation of Toll-like receptors on immune cells can further enhance cellular immunity to improve cancer treatment. A library of polymer-modified lipid nanoparticles (PLNPs) will be developed to encapsulate cancer antigen-expressing mRNA. A total of 54 lipid-based polymers with various lipid tails, functional headgroups, and polymer chain lengths will be carefully designed and constructed. By modifying lipid nanoparticles with these polymers at different composition ratios, the particle size, surface charge, and compositions of PLNPs could be fine-tuned for optimum delivery efficiency to lymph nodes. The incorporation of suitable TLRa into the developed system will further enhance DCs' maturation and CTL-mediated cellular immunity. To assess efficacy, a comprehensive evaluation will be conducted, including lymph node accumulation, mRNA transfection in DCs, DCs’ maturation, CTL-mediated immune responses, and anti-cancer treatment effect will be conducted. The success of this research holds the potential to significantly improve cancer treatment outcomes. The screening platform utilizing a comprehensive library of lipid-based polymers will help us better understand the fundamental mechanisms of LNPs and their potential for various therapeutic applications. It will advance our understanding of cancer vaccine design and provide valuable insights for the development of improved cancer treatments.
kw: Cancer vaccine, mRNA, lymph node, lipid nanoparticle

title: Elucidating the molecular mechanism of fatty acid uptake in mycobacteria and its role in pathogenesis
abs: Mycobacteria are the cause of severe infections including tuberculosis, leprosy, and non-tuberculous infections. Tuberculosis claims more than 1 million lives out of over 10 million new cases annually. Mycobacterial infections especially those caused by < i >Mycobacterium abscessus< /i >, are difficult to treat, typically requiring a six-month regimen with multiple antibiotics. The rise in resistance to extant drugs further compounded the situation, significantly lowering the treatment success rate and necessitating the use of more toxic drugs. Therefore, new anti-mycobacterial strategies are urgently needed. It is known that during infections, mycobacteria utilize host fatty acids as a major carbon source. However, the molecular mechanism of fatty acid uptake and its role in pathogenesis are poorly understood. We have identified MSMEG_5008/9 in < i >Mycobacterium smegmatis< /i > as a putative ATP-binding cassette transporter important for fatty acid uptake. Herein, we propose the experimental outline to unveil the molecular mechanism of the transporter’s function and to probe how fatty acid uptake impacts mycobacterial virulence. First, we will reconstitute the protein complex into liposomes to test its function in fatty acid flipping within the lipid bilayer. Next, we will use cryo-electron microscopy to obtain high-resolution three-dimensional structures of the complex in different functional states. We will conduct mutagenesis studies based on the structures to reveal the transport mechanism and potential means to inhibit the transporter. Finally, we will test whether homologs of MSMEG_5008/9 in < i >M. abscessus< /i >, a common causative species of non-tuberculous mycobacterial infections, also function in fatty acid uptake. We will use a zebrafish model to probe how the homologs and more generally how fatty acid uptake impacts the pathogenicity of mycobacteria. The proposal will provide key insights into fatty acid uptake in mycobacteria, contributing to development of novel anti-mycobacterial strategies and diagnostic tools.
kw: fatty acid uptake; ATP-binding cassette transporter; cryo-EM; mycobacteria; virulence

title: ADEPT: Atopic DErmatitis research Program for patienTs
abs: Background Atopic Dermatitis (AD) is a disease of high prevalence, with significant economic, social, and personal cost. It is the most common skin disorder in Singapore and despite the high prevalence, there has been a dearth of innovation and treatment options. Aim. The overall objective of this program is to establish Singapore as a global leader in AD through better understanding of the epidemiology and pathogenesis of AD, and to develop cutting-edge tools and therapies to improve health outcomes. Methodology. This program will bring together dermatologists, basic scientists, and biomedical engineers across Singapore in 3 interconnected/complementary themes. Theme 1 will build a longitudinal AD cohort of 500 patients with ages ranging from paediatrics to elderly, with the collection of comprehensive datasets to stratify atopy, allergies and AD. Theme 2 will build upon our work on the 3 main pathogenic mechanisms of barrier, innate inflammation, and epithelial-dermal-immune crosstalk. From Theme 1 cohort, we will study circulating biomarkers and skin surface profiles to characterise the skin barrier and initiating innate immunology of AD. The AD cohort will provide patient demographics as well as the biological samples needed to drive this theme and the mechanistic insights will be derived from in vitro and in vivo models. Theme 3 will focusing on molecular endotyping. Specifically, we will be looking at metabolomics, microbiome as well as immunoprofiling of patients from Theme 1, with an aim to better endotype them into specific subgroups to prognosticate and individualize therapy for patients. This research will significantly contribute to scientific excellence as many areas of our proposed work is novel and pioneering. This programme will improve quality of life of patients through novel therapeutics, as well as prognostication, treatment stratification and monitoring.
