title: Novel Extraordinary Electronic Devices for Super-fast Processing and Extreme Exchange of Data (NEED for SPEED)
abs: The exchange and processing of massive amounts of data has become essential for the future of our society due to the widespread adoption of emerging technologies such as virtual reality (VR) and autonomous vehicles (AVs) , as well as the explosion of social media, mobile devices, and the internet of things (IoT). Shrinking transistors has been the primary way to make electronics faster, however, this approach is reaching its fundamental limits. The proposed research project uses a totally different approach and aims to develop new types of electronic devices that can outperform the speed of currently-existing components, such as transistors and diodes, and integrate them into functional chips for ultrafast communications and computation. The project has two main objectives: ultrafast telecommunications for 6G and beyond and high-speed memory and neuromorphic computation. For ultrafast telecommunications, the project will develop terahertz electronics based on the innovative “meta-transistors” to achieve a complete set of fundamental functionalities, including modulation, demodulation, and amplification, on CMOS and III-V platforms. This is a new concept for electronics, in which a gate terminal controls a sub-wavelength propagative mode between two ports. In addition, the project aims to realize electronics operating at infrared frequencies (IR) ( > 10 THz) by proposing the new concept of meso-scale devices which outperform the speed of traditional compact devices such as transistors and diodes, to achieve unprecedented speeds (terabits per second) for wireless data transfer for beyond 6G telecommunications. Such ultrafast IR electronics can reshape the future of wireless communications. For high-speed memory and computation devices, the project will focus on two main areas. Firstly, the realization of ultra-dense nanosecond memories using a new effect observed in vanadium dioxide. The goal is to overcome the “memory wall”, which is a severe limit in the computation speed of existing processors. Secondly, the project will demonstrate integrated nanoprocessors based on the unique electronic effect observed in vanadium dioxide, which exhibits similarities to the computational processes of the human brain, at much higher speeds. This approach enables extreme miniaturization and powerful computation, which can provide a platform for human-level artificial intelligence.
kw: Electronic devices; terahertz; 6G telecommunications; Infrared electronics; Artificial intelligence; Nanoprocessors

title: Phase-Separating Peptides as a General Platform for Intracellular Delivery of Antibody Therapeutics
abs: Antibody (Ab)-based therapeutics, including Ab mimics such Abs fragments and nanobodies, hold enormous potential to treat a wide range of diseases, from cancer to neuropathologies to infectious diseases, with a market value projected to US$ 300 Billion by 2025. While most Ab therapeutics target extracellular antigens, there is an estimated 6000 potential intracellular targets that are currently considered “undruggable” due to the limitation of Abs to cross the cell membrane. Abs can in principle be designed to target virtually any protein or DNA targets, with high-precision and greatly reduced off-target toxicity compared to small molecule drugs. Thus, a platform technology that would enable intracellular delivery of functional Abs would be a game-changer both from therapeutic treatments and business value perspectives. Our team has recently developed (Sun et al, Nature Chemistry 2022) and filed IP on a new class of phase-separating peptides (PSPs) assembling into coacervate microdroplets (CMs) that can: (i) quickly encapsulate (within seconds) a wide range of large macromolecular therapeutics (including in preliminary experiments Abs); (ii) cross the membrane of a broad range of mammalian cells via non-classical endocytic pathways, which alleviates endosomal degradation of the payload; and (iii) deliver functional payloads once in the cytosol triggered by endogenic glutathione (GSH). Separately, members of our team have developed a ligase-based conjugation method enabling efficient and versatile production of antibody drug conjugates (ADCs) that can be engineered against a wide range of potential targets, including inside the cell. Furthermore, through our industrial collaborator, we have access to proprietary monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) that exhibit very high affinity against intracellular targets. The objectives of this project will be to: (1) combine our unique delivery platform to deliver functional mAbs and ADCs targeting intracellular targets with high specificity and affinity; (2) develop custom Abs and ADCs for intracellular targets; (3) demonstrate bioactivity and functionality of mAbs and ADCs using live cell assays; (4) establish the in vivo potential of the combined platform in animal models. More broadly, the project will lead to an entire new intracellular delivery platform that can not only deliver functional Abs and ADCs, but also other large macromolecular therapeutics (proteins, mRNAs, CRIPSR/Cas9, etc..) that are all met with the common challenge of crossing the cell membrane.
kw: Antibody; intracellulalr delivery; peptides; microdroplets; in vivo testing

title: Intelligent AIRC Robotics System (IARS)
abs: Our proposed design provides a complete solution for auto-detecting a full bin, auto chute door opening and collection of waste at IRC, transportation of collected waste to the bin centre, loading and unloading trash at the bin collection centre. The localized fleet management system is scalable to control multiple robots and be integrated into the Robot Middleware Framework (RMF) with the following features: • Open source: localized fleet management system integrated with Robot Middleware Frame. The software packages integrate individual modules' core algorithms and data structures into a ROS2-based distributed system; • Modular design: The electronics system and the hardware mechanical structure are modular for easy maintenance and troubleshooting; • Built-in refuse bin-compactor on the refuse AMR robot. This will increase the capacity of collected waste by at least 15%. • Innovative wheel-spring mechanism design (Patent file no: S102201709761U) to provide better ground traction for localization and positioning. The AMR base platform drive-wheel system is omnidirectional and equipped with multi-axis actuators. Our research approach is to automate the whole process with a Smart AIRC Robotics System (SARS). The collection time can be scheduled or “on-call” basis. When the bin waste reaches pre-set full level, the sensor in the bin will send an alarm signal to the control centre. Then, the fleet management control system will activate a refuse AMR to perform the collection job.
kw: Autonomous Robot; Outdoor Robot; Robot Navigation; Automatic Lifter; Mecanum Wheel

title: SB: Singapore Biodesign Innovation Fellowship Training Programme
abs: The Singapore Biodesign Innovation Fellowship is an intensive 6 months hands-on multidisciplinary team-based training on the entire biodesign process of health technology innovation, focused on developing new health technologies for unmet clinical needs in Asia. The Fellowship will provide a holistic experience of the health technology innovation journey based on the Biodesign pedagogy founded by the Stanford Byers Centre for Biodesign and adapted by Singapore Biodesign for the local and regional landscape. The Biodesign methodology has a proven track record; more than 53 health technology companies have been founded directly from the Stanford Biodesign programme, with >US$1Bn funding raised and >4Mn patients helped. 19% of the companies have been acquired. The Fellowship will kick off with a pre-fellowship preparation phase where we will spend time to research and understand the Clinical theme of the year, as well as a deep dive on the Biodesign Process. After which, we will focus on applying the Biodesign process and uncovering local and regional healthcare needs towards developing a solution for our top identified need. Fellows will get a unique opportunity to immerse in regional countries i.e China to investigate unmet clinical needs and develop a deeper understanding of the native healthtech ecosystems. In addition, my training will include time spent with Singapore Biodesign’s Silicon Valley partners to further refine and develop implementation plans for our top projects. I plan to leverage on the access to seasoned commercialization domain experts to increase the chances of securing follow-on funding for the Fellowship project.
kw: Medical Innovation; Health Technology; Medical Devices; Digital Health; Artificial Intelligence

title: “Weaving” Hydrophobic Polymers into Hydrophilic Network: Toward Ultra-tough Hydrogels
abs: Polymer gels are polymeric networks swollen by large amount of fluid. Owing to their high water/fluid content and flexibility, polymer gels, such as hydrogels are widely used as functional smart materials and find many important applications in biomedicine, wearable electronics, solid state electrolytes and soft robotics. However, the inherent weakness and fragility of traditional hydrogels seriously hamper their potential applications. According to Lake-Thomas theory, loose hydrogel networks are soft and weak, while dense networks are rigid and fragile. To overcome this stiffness-toughness conflict in hydrogels, many approaches are adopted and they are mainly based on hydrophilic networks with sacrificial bonds. While these approaches could improve the toughness of hydrogel, they also suffer many drawbacks, such as low tensile modules, and fully hydrophilic characteristic. In this research, we propose a novel toughening strategy for hydrogels by introducing a “complimentary” hydrophobic polymer as reinforcement, in which the semi-crystalline hydrophobic polymer chains are thermodynamically “woven” into a hydrophilic network via entropy driven miscibility. Our hypothesis is that: when the interaction between a hydrophilic polymer and a ‘complementary” hydrophobic polymer, either attractive or repulsive, is very small, the entropy dominated Gibbs free energy of mixing. This not only leads to miscible blend of the two polymers, but also promotes the formation of entanglement between the hydrophobic and hydrophilic polymers. In-situ cross-linking hydrophilic polymer components results in formation of a hydrophilic network which is highly entangled with hydrophobic polymer chains . When swelled in water, partial aggregation of hydrophobic polymer leads to in-situ formation of crystallites domains which is tightly entangled with the hydrophilic network. This unique morphology could stiffen the hydrogel network due to the hydrophobic crystalline domains, while the highly entanglements between the hydrophobic polymer and the hydrophilic network enable large deformation of the hydrogel before failure. The resultant hydrogels could be stiff, tough and durable against shear. Moreover, they could also effectively encapsulate both hydrophobic and hydrophilic molecules for applications owing to its amphiphilic characteristic. Our recent investigation on polyethylene oxide (PEO) - polylactic acid (PLA) system support our hypothesis. PEO and PLA are hydrophilic and hydrophobic polymers, respectively. Furthermore, the PEO has weak interaction with PLA and the entropy dominates free energy of mixing. By blending crosslink-able PEO (polyethylene glycol diacrylate, PEGDA) with PLA, the hydrophobic polymer intertwines with the hydrophilic polymer to form a dense chain entanglement due to entropy effect. title: Mechanistic investigations of peptidoglycan fragments (PGNs) uptake and recognition in Candida albicans for novel anti-virulent strategies against fungal infections
abs: Candida albicans is a major fungal pathogen that can cause serious infections in humans. The key virulent characteristic of C. albicans is that, upon sensing external stimuli, it changes from the commensal yeast state to the filamentous hyphal form, where the hyphal form facilitates C. albicans’ invasion across the host mucosal barrier and renders resistance to host immune phagocytosis. Notably, C. albicans mutants lacking the ability to grow hyphae are avirulent, implying that the inhibition of the yeast-hyphae morphological transition in C. albicans is a promising anti-virulent strategy. Among the numerous hyphal-inducing signals, bacterial peptidoglycan fragments represent the most potent hyphal inducers, which are naturally present in the host gut niche and blood circulation (i.e., the physiological relevant reservoirs for C. albicans infections). Peptidoglycan molecules were known to bind to the cytosolic sensor, adenylyl cyclase Cyr1 in C. albicans, which in turn activates the downstream pathways for hyphal growth. Thus, understanding the peptidoglycan uptake and recognition mechanisms in C. albicans is paramount for discovering potential anti-virulent drug targets in C. albicans. Our lab has recently developed novel chemoenzymatic peptidoglycan probes that possess different functionality such as fluorescent, photoaffinity or bio-orthogonal moiety, which are valuable tools for probing fungal biology. We have revealed that peptidoglycan fragments enter C. albicans via receptor-mediated endocytosis and localize into the vacuole compartments, raising important questions regarding the identities of the cell surface receptor(s) and the vacuolar egress mechanisms of peptidoglycan in C. albicans. In this proposal, we will combine chemical biology tools with our expertise in microbiology and biochemistry to address the mechanistic details of the peptidoglycan uptake and recognition mechanisms in C. albicans. The insights from this work will not only answer long-standing questions in fundamental C. albicans biology, but also discover novel cellular targets for thwarting C. albicans’ yeast-hyphae transition for potential anti-virulent therapeutics development.
kw: chemoenzymatic peptidoglycan probes; chemical biology; chemoproteomics target identification; receptor-mediated endocytosis; C. albicans hyphal growth

title: Scalable Estimation of Multivariate Hurdle Model for Network Inference in Single Cell and Multi-Tissue Atlas Studies
abs: Gaussian graphical model (GGM) is an instrumental tool for inferring undirected graphs from multivariate data across many fields in natural and social sciences. However, existing estimation methods and shared memory-based software implementation thereof are no longer scalable for emerging ultrahigh-dimensional data sets, which normally feature more than tens or hundreds of thousands of variables. Past decades of high-performance statistical computing research have now enabled a genuinely scalable regularized pseudolikelihood framework for sparse inverse covariance matrix estimation. This is best exemplified by the parallel proximal gradient optimization algorithm that takes advantage of distributed memory systems and communication-avoiding linear algebra, called HP-CONCORD (High-Performance CONvex CORrelation selection methoD). This innovative method bypasses expensive communications needed for distributed matrix multiplication and reduces the multivariate likelihood problem into a more manageable pseudolikelihood maximization problem, rendering network estimation on high dimensional data sets considerably more feasible, and opens the door to network inference with more complex constraints. While CONCORD is applicable to any continuously scaled multivariate data, emerging large-scale omics data sets generated in contemporary biomedical research present an unforeseen challenge: zero inflation in the observed data. In molecular profiling experiments in isolated single cells or across multiple types of tissues, many variables are unobserved due to the limit of detection issue and this phenomenon is attributable to either the absence of molecules in the samples or the lack of depth in the respective measurement modalities. For such data sets, the current HP-CONCORD framework must specifically address the non-negligibly large proportion of zero data points by changing the objective function (likelihood function). A promising solution can be found in a recently proposed multivariate hurdle model, which incorporates the distribution of zero data point as a point mass and uses neighborhood selection via penalized regression framework for network identification thereafter. However, the method again suffers from the scalability issue in ultrahigh-dimensional data, and we aim to address this problem by adapting the hurdle model into the HP-CONCORD algorithm. In this proposal, we will develop the hurdle model version of HP-CONCORD in collaboration with the original developers, called Hurdle-CONCORD, and validate its performance through rigorous and realistic simulation studies. We will also demonstrate the tool’s utility in two different systems biology applications: (i) single cell omics data analysis and (ii) multi-tissue, multi-omics animal model, both of which are representative cases of zero inflated data. In single cell omics data, we will generate gene-gene and cell-cell networks in fly brains using single cell and single nuclei transcriptomic profili

title: Identifying protective mechanisms of butyrate-producing gut bacteria against atherosclerosis
abs: Gut microbes significantly influence cardiovascular health, impacting atherosclerosis and disease susceptibility. Notably, our preliminary studies found that Roseburia intestinalis, a potent butyrate producer, interacts with dietary fibres, improves gut barrier function and reduces atherosclerosis in gnotobiotic mice. Moreover, we identified that colonization with R. intestinalis increases β-hydroxybutyrate, a ketone body that hinders inflammasome activation, and that administration of β-hydroxybutyrate reduces the development of atherosclerosis. However, the role of β-hydroxybutyrate in the athero-protective action of butyrate-producing bacteria remains poorly understood. Our study aims to unravel the nexus of dietary fibres, butyrate-producing bacteria, and ketogenesis. We will investigate whether dietary fibers and butyrate-producing bacteria impact ketogenesis (Aim 1), probe the role of HMGCS2, the key rate-limiting enzyme of ketogenesis, in atherosclerosis (Aim 2), and elucidate the role of ketogenesis in the athero-protective action of butyrate (Aim 3). These insights into host-microbe interactions could provide a basis for innovative strategies against cardiovascular diseases, leveraging dietary modulations and probiotics administrations.
kw: Gut microbiome; Atherosclerosis; Butyrate; Dietary fibre; Ketone body

title: Advanced Cell Therapy and Research Institute, Singapore (ACTRIS)
inst: Advanced Cell Therapy and Research Institute, Singapore
abs: ACTRIS was established in April 2020 to meet the increasing clinical demand for cellular therapeutics to treat various life-threatening diseases. Its vision is to be the national and regional centre of excellence for facilitating discovery, process development, and manufacturing of cellular-based therapeutics across the broad spectrum of immunotherapy and regenerative medicine, encompassing both investigational and clinical-use products for Singapore. Through its specialised infrastructure and skilled workforce, ACTRIS aims to promote and support the entire value chain of the cell therapy ecosystem by enabling translational research and development, manufacturing, clinical service provision, and commercialisation by serving the healthcare, academic and industrial sectors. In addition, ACTRIS will also provide value-added services such as workforce training, regulatory support, and the standardisation of ancillary materials and product testing pertaining to the delivery of cellular therapy to patients. ACTRIS is a programme of CRIS.

title: TEACHING MACHINES TO SEE OUR 3D WORLD
abs: The first part of my research goal is to reconstruct high quality geometric 3D digital models of humans, animals, objects and the general scenes from perceptual sensory input data such as RGB images, point clouds, RGB-D images, etc; Specifically, I will investigate the following to holistically achieve high fidelity, scalable and efficient 3D reconstructions. 1) Scalability and efficiency to design an efficient neural field model that is capable of large-scale 3D reconstruction. We will tackle this problem using the divide-and-conquer approach, where the large-scale scene is split into multiple parts and multiple neural field models are learned efficiently in parallel to encode each part of the scene. 2) Controllability and editability to investigate neural field models that can edit or control general scenes or objects. We plan to design an auto-decoder to encode the dynamics of the editable parts with latent codes that can then be used to control the shapes. 3) Quality of reconstruction to enable neural field models to achieve better 3D models that can capture complex topology and appearance modeling, where we aim to circumvent the lack of details in the 2D training data by proposing better physics-based models and priors. 4) Robustness and generalizability for generalizable 3D reconstructions on video from a single hand-held camera or sparse multiple views of the scene. The main challenge of doing sparse view 3D digital modeling is to establish feature correspondences across different video or image frames. We plan to leverage the unique mesh vertex indices of SMPL (for human modeling) and semantic labels (for general scenes) obtained from every video frame or the sparse multi-view images to establish feature correspondences. 5) 5D reconstruction that models a dynamic world (4th dimension of time) with semantic meaning (5th dimension of semantics). We will investigate deformable explicit and implicit scene representations such as point clouds, meshes, SDFs, occupancy field for 4D reconstructions. Furthermore, we will study the learning of priors to enforce global consistency in the semantic labels generated from the neural field model. The second part of my research goal is to do (out-of-distribution) OOD learning for 3D scene understanding (semantic). Specifically, I will focus on the following to enhance the ability of 3D machine learning models for long-term operation in the dynamically changing world. 1) Robustness to noisy and outlier training data, and OOD test-time data. We will study the use of geometric consistency, i.e., a sample under different spatial transformation should give the same output, to detect samples with clean labels, in-distribution noisy labels and OOD outlier labels. 2) Data efficiency to enable effective learning without the need for a lot of hard-to-get labeled data. Specifically, we will improve in-distribution object detection/semantic segmentation with in-the-wild unlabeled data while preventing the detrimental

title: AI-Human Collaborative High-Quality 3D Content Generation
abs: The main goal of this project is to develop generative AI algorithms that allow humans and AI to collaboratively create high-quality 3D content. To achieve this goal, we will investigate interactive methods that can automatically generate 3D content based on intuitive user guides. The generation of 3D content is based on state-of-the-art diffusion models that serve as a strong prior to perform multi-view supervision. Based on this pipeline, several open problems towards an interactive 3D generative AI system will be studied including: 1) Shape-guided generation. We will develop a conditional pipeline that supports 3D content generation based on a coarse shape from the user. 2) Interactive shape editing. The AI system will be further extended to support user-friendly interactive shape editing like point-to-point deformation. 3) Text-guided editing. We will investigate flexible editing of 3D objects based on text guidance and evaluate the combination of all the aforementioned methods for AI-human collaborative 3D content generation. Advances in these directions will give rise to new methodologies for AI-generated content (AIGC), providing better ways for AI-human interaction, and could revolutionize the way how 3D content is created.
kw: Generative AI; 3D Content Generation; AI-Human Collaboration; Generative Models

title: Design of synthetic DNA regulatory elements for precision gene therapy
abs: This research aims to develop a suite of new computational and molecular methods to enable the design synthetic DNA regulatory elements for use in nucleic acid therapeutics. These technologies will have important applications in limiting the expression of gene editing components to specific cell states, reducing the potential for off-target mutations in patients undergoing therapeutic gene editing. This research program will involve completion of three aims: 1) I will develop sensitive and low-cost methods for single-cell epigenomics, using a combinatorial indexing approach, and apply these methods to construct a large-scale single-cell epigenomic dataset for the blood; 2) using data generated in aim 1, I will build machine learning methods based on large language models to generate synthetic DNA sequences to drive gene expression in individual cell types; 3) I will experimentally test the cell-type-specific activity of generated sequences in a novel high-throughput assay using a diverse population of human cell types. Together, completion of these aims will build a platform for the rapid development and experimental screening of synthetic regulatory elements with desired properties, with broad applications for human health and basic research.

title: Long-life solid-state batteries by intelligent composites with active interfaces
abs: All-solid-state batteries (ASSBs) that combine energy-dense Lithium anodes with non-flammable, thermally stable solid-state electrolytes (SSE) eliminate the safety hazards of Lithium-ion batteries, reduce the need for heavy enclosure, and their electrochemically stable SSEs enable to exploit the 5-10 times higher specific capacity of Li or alloy anodes. While ceramic SSEs with Li+ conductivities comparable to those of liquid electrolytes are available, serious challenges remain at both the fundamental and the manufacturing technology levels to realize competitive ASSBs. The key bottlenecks are large and quickly rising interfacial resistances that limit energy efficiency, rate capability and capacity retention. To overcome these, we will develop novel ASSBs with these globally unprecedented features: (1) Ultrathin, light-weight SSE ceramic-in-polymer composite membranes enable cells, where 2/3 of the total mass is active cathode, so that energy densities >450 Wh/kg become achievable with highly stable cathode materials. (2) The high conductivity membranes and low resistances at stable interfaces will enable cycling with high current densities of 5 mA/cm2 at overpotentials < 50 mV. (3) An innovative integration of intelligent features empowering active control of the interface evolution lead to cycle life exceeding 10,000 cycles and an average Coulombic efficiency exceeding 99.95%. Our confidence in achieving these globally competitive goals is raised by breakthrough results from our preliminary work, where we demonstrated 10 μm thin ceramic-in-polymer SSEs on the composite cathode and Li anode layers by scalable in situ UV-curing of spin-coated precursors. Our non-flammable SSE feature fast ionic conductivity, wide electrochemical window, and high thermal decomposition temperature. When cycling with high rate over 500h, the overpotential remains stable and no dendrites are observed. Besides licensable composite and interface design, advanced fabrication nanotechnologies, smart materials, component and battery development, the key deliverable will be a working prototype and scalable fabrication method for our novel ASSBs.
kw: Energy Storage

title: Transfection-Free in situ Engineering of Receptors and Protein-Based Signaling Molecules
abs: Proteins and peptides are the basic building and functional blocks of all life. They perceive and process information, then interact with each other to govern the biological activities. Even more so, in multi-cellular eukaryotes, cells work together in a highly coordinated manner, facilitated by intricate protein-protein interactions and signaling networks involving surface receptors and their signaling counterpart. The roles and functionalities of cells are often categorized or labelled according to the presence of their signature surface receptors. Thus, manipulating these protein-based receptors and signaling molecules represents a powerful approach to modulate cellular behaviour and has tremendous potential in both research and therapeutic applications. Indeed, engineered chimeric receptors or modified signaling proteins have demonstrated tremendous therapeutic potential. For example, Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells are a promising form of immunotherapy for cancer treatment, where T cells are engineered to express a chimeric antigen receptor targeting tumor-specific antigens, as well as treating other diseases. However, current CAR T cell production methods involve time-consuming and inefficient gene transfer procedures, which can also pose safety concerns such as potential genotoxicity and off-target effects. Hence, there is an unmet need for developing fast, efficient, and safe methods for in situ engineering of proteins and peptides in their native context. In this proposal, we aim to develop a new class of protein ligases that can perform direct, biorthogonal conjugation of functional cargoes onto target proteins, without requiring transfection or genetic manipulation. We will engineer protein ligases that can recognize specific target proteins and catalyze site-specific covalent modification with high efficiency and selectivity. We will optimize the design and performance of these protein ligases using both rational design and directed evolution approaches and evaluate their utility in a range of biological applications. The overarching aim of this proposal is to garner and advance the necessary tools for such approaches.

title: Soft interconnects in stretchable electronic devices: overcoming the Achilles’ Heel for extensive deployment
abs: Stretchable electronic devices with the resilience against mechanical deformation, could enable various application domains as the next generation of microelectronics, including sense digitization, digital healthcare, and intelligent systems. However, the fragile nature of the soft interconnects within stretchable devices significantly impedes its overall durability and widespread implementation. Therefore, this proposal aims to develop soft interconnects that can reliably assemble multifaceted stretchable electronic systems, to accelerate its extensive deployment. The first aim of the proposal entails the development of soft interconnects between stretchable modules. Supported by preliminary data, strategies including bi-phasic nano-dispersed interface, ionotronic-electronics coupling, and mechanical interlocking are proposed to solve the core challenge of mechanical mismatch. Subsequently, the second aim focuses on establishment of hybrid interconnects between stretchable devices and silicon-based rigid electronics, through technological pathways including conformal adhesive coating, wire bonding, and liquid metal. Based on the previous two aims, the third aim focuses on achieving multi-functional integrated stretchable systems, with technical advancements in inter-layer interconnects, soft encapsulation, and multi-functionality development. Collectively, the proposal endeavors to address the soft interconnect challenge in stretchable electronics, which could significantly enhance its technology readiness level for lab-to-fab transition, therefore promotes the economic growth, technological leadership, and global competitiveness of Singapore in the field of hybrid integrated next generation microelectronics.
kw: Stretchable electronic devices; Soft interconnects; Mechanomaterials science and engineering; Nanofabrication and processing; Multi-functional integrated stretchable systems; Sense digitization

title: Unravelling the Age-old Question on How Neurons Distribute Cholesterol within the Cell
abs: Proper brain function requires robust mechanisms to maintain a precise lipid composition in the neuronal plasma membrane (PM). This is because PM lipids play critical roles in neuronal communication and survival. In particular, cholesterol contributes to almost half of the total lipids in the PM and is essential for normal brain function. Importantly, the dysregulation of cholesterol has been associated with numerous neurodegenerative disorders, including Alzheimer’s disease (AD). However, we know very little about how neurons (or any cell type) maintain appropriate levels of cholesterol in the PM. Thus, understanding the molecular machineries responsible for this process will provide new therapeutic targets for neurodegenerative conditions. Our overarching hypothesis is that neurons use evolutionarily conserved lipid transfer proteins to maintain an appropriate distribution of cellular cholesterol, thereby promoting cell viability and function. Building on our exciting preliminary data, we will: 1) elucidate the molecular machineries that transport cholesterol to the PM, and 2) characterize the distribution of cholesterol in neurons and investigate the impact of disrupting intracellular cholesterol transport machineries on neuronal function. These analyses will significantly impact the fields of cell biology and neurobiology and enhance our understanding of neurodegenerative processes.
kw: Lipid biology / Cholesterol / Phospholipid / Membrane contact sites / Neurological disorders

title: Development of a scalable and versatile platform in enabling the facile production of cultivated fats
abs: Cultivated fat is critical in replicating the texture, sensory attributes, and nutritional profile of traditional animal meat. Currently, either plant-based fats or cultivated fats from animal cells are used as alternatives. As of now, the former could not replicate the organoleptic quality of animal fats while culturing fats from animal cells involves expensive adipogenic cocktail to differentiate stem cells into adipocytes (fats). Such adipogenic cocktail consists of basal media supplemented with fetal bovine serum and other small molecules namely isomethylbutylxanthine (IBMX), insulin, dexamethasone and rosiglitazone which are expensive. Of these, IBMX and rosiglitazone are toxic and non-food compatible. Herein, we propose to use mechanotransduction to differentiate stem cells into fats in a facile manner via usage of 3D scaffolds made of cheap, abundant and edible materials, without requiring the use of adipogenic cocktail. This project employs a mechanotransduction platform that confines encapsulated cells within a 3D environment with the aim to direct cell fate towards adipogenesis. As this strategy does not require specialised differentiation media, it is versatile and cost efficient. In our preliminary work, porcine adipose-derived stem cells were encapsulated in microspheres fabricated via electrospray. The cell-laden microspheres were then cultured without any adipogenic media. The microspheres upregulated lipid production by ~3 fold as compared to cells in 2D culture, and a significant increase in the number of cells stained for lipid marker from 65% to 97% within a week. This highlights the potential of the 3D platform as an enabler to produce cultivated fats without the use of specialized differentiation media.

title: Quantum-Inspired Protocols for Light Engineering of Correlated Materials
abs: The past decade has witnessed a surge of interest to dynamically engineer properties of quantum materials by applying light radiation. This proposal aims at exploring the experimental frontier of light-driven phase transitions in correlated materials – materials with electronic correlations so strong as to host an array of emergent phenomena. Driven by the prospect of exploiting quantum advantages in next-generation electronic technologies, efforts will be made to accomplish two tasks rising to the forefront: (1) pushing the speeds of dynamical phase switchings to their physical limits, and (2) stabilizing novel far-from-equilibrium electronic orders that are inaccessible in equilibrium. To combat laser-induced thermal effects as the most significant challenge, the PI plans to bring approaches inspired by quantum optics, a field traditionally focusing on atomic and molecular systems, to engineer correlated materials. The PI envisages these approaches, dubbed quantum-inspired protocols, holding the key toward strengthening the role of light as a quantum (as opposed to thermal) control knob in a number of settings. Based on an advanced ultrafast tunable-pump multi-messenger-probe system, concrete experimental pathways are designed. Impulsive excitation of the charge, spin, and lattice degrees of freedom will be applied for achieving the fastest phase switchings in situ. Cavity quantum electrodynamics devices, where correlated materials are embedded in photonic cavities, will be leveraged to stabilize unusual electronic phases. Developments along the quest pave the way for future devices, ranging from high-speed quantum transducers to nonvolatile memory units, to operate based on a new set of physical principles that can potentially break bottlenecks in current technology. Upon harnessing the diverse collaboration opportunities with local universities and the vibrant innovation ecosystem in Singapore, the project has the potential to deliver scientific findings that deepen the understanding of nonequilibrium quantum matter, to fabricate novel materials and devices with unprecedented optical controllability, and to implement education and traineeship programs for future research talents.
kw: condensed matter physics; optics; laser spectroscopy

title: Future Ship & Systems Design (FSSD)
abs: This program aims to develop capabilities in these three domain areas: • CA1: Ship and System Design for Sustainability • CA2: Intelligent Ship and Operations • CA3: Charging Infrastructure and Onshore Microgrid CA1: Ship and System Design for Sustainability Today’s ship design practice is dominated by the traditional spiral design approach which often leads to non-optimal sizing decisions due to its sequential and iterative nature over a large parameter space. To overcome this, Project 1-1 proposes a model-based holistic design approach that integrates multi-objective optimization and multi-disciplinary co-simulation in the form of the Ship Simulation and Optimization (SSO) software platform. Additionally, three specific ship design challenges are addressed: namely shipboard electrical power distribution system, hull form and structure. The integration of battery and power converter systems on a full electric ship with the shore charging infrastructure requires proper design, system control and coordination. To ensure power system reliability and stability as well as optimal energy management, Project 1-2 proposes an assurance framework for the power system simulation. The development of validated and qualified power system models is a key enabler for automatic design optimization, performance test verification and risk analysis for full electric ships. Project 1-3 proposes the development of an automated and efficient design optimization procedure for ship hull design by using accurate and validated reduced-order models that were derived from ship physics, simulation, model tests and operational data. This will improve the efficiency and feasibility of high-fidelity CFD simulations for ship hull design optimization. The design of lighter-weight vessels through a combination of optimized structural elements and advanced materials is essential to compensate for the lower energy density of batteries. To optimize the structural design and enable the safe operation of a lighter harbour craft, a structural digital twin model with a sensor-based structural health monitoring program is proposed in Project 1-4. As Lithium-ion batteries become the main power source onboard harbour crafts, a better understanding of fire risks, mitigation and emergency response is needed. P1-5 looks at battery fire dynamics, gas monitoring, fire suppression solutions, explosion hazards and vapour cloud dynamics to improve battery room design, monitoring capability for risk indicators and emergency situation awareness and management planning. For CA1, MPA Guardian and MRV Red Dolphin will be used as research vessels for the validation of models and simulations for a catamaran and monohull respectively. Operational challenges arise from conflicting objectives such as minimization of voyage time, risk and missions. Project 2-1 proposes to enhance ship management capabi

title: Miniaturizing Higher-Dimensional Structured Light for Information Security
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: Information security is crucial for modern society to function, by protecting confidential data from unauthorized access and manipulation. For example, the commercial world relies heavily on conventional encryption algorithms in daily internet transactions. The apparent security in conventional encryption algorithms is based on the computational difficulty in solving certain mathematical problems, such as factorizing the product of two very large prime numbers (Rivest–Shamir–Adleman algorithm) or searching in a very large key space (Advanced Encryption Standard algorithm). However, conventional encryption algorithms are deterministic, vulnerable to hackers, and ultimately breakable with the rise of quantum computers. The fall of conventional encryption algorithms can have devastating consequences such as the loss of revenue, reputation, and trust in established institutions. Furthermore, breaches in information security can compromise Singapore’s total defence against military, civil, economic, social, psychological, and digital threats. We seem to be witnessing an end to the algorithmic approach to information security. Though quantum-resistant encryption algorithms based on more complicated mathematical problems can be implemented, they require greater amounts of computational resources and increase latency in information channels. Hence, an efficient yet unbreakable information security system based on new optics hardware is urgently needed to overcome the weaknesses of conventional encryption algorithms, in preparedness for the “year to quantum”. In this proposal, we aim to achieve compact, efficient, and unbreakable information security based on higher-dimensional structured light. The term “higher-dimensional” refers to a nascent field in optics involving the “entangled states” of the multiple degrees of freedom of light, e.g. amplitude, phase, polarization, spin and orbital angular momentum, frequency, time, space, coherence, and angle. Higher-dimensional structured light promises larger bandwidth for encoding information with unique optical signatures that are currently untapped. As compared to conventional encryption algorithms that are based on electronic computing, our proposed encryption approach is based on state-of-the-art optical methods to compute mathematical operations (e.g. Fourier transforms, nonlinear functions, quantum entanglement) more efficiently. The use of higher-dimensional structured light in encryption offers greater information capacity, noise resilience, and robustness against eavesdropping and copying. This investigation will fuel the development of new platform capabilities and inventions that align with Singapore’s growth areas in advanced manufacturing and information technology. title: Community Ageing in Place Ecosystem (CAPE)
abs: To support a rapidly ageing population with manpower and land constraints, Singapore has adopted the policy of 'ageing in place' to facilitate healthy ageing. This places emphasis on strengthening community-based health services and social assets to enable seniors to age well in their communities before institutionalization becomes the last resort to care. The proposed Community Ageing in Place Ecosystem (CAPE) will be implemented at two of the oldest estates in Singapore, Bedok South and Marine Parade. Interventions to be delivered include (i) integrated health and social care by SingHealth HealthierSG teams and community partners, (ii) assistive technologies by Government Technology Agency, (iii) built environment (BE) modifications such as retrofitted community kitchens and rehabilitation units to expand the functionality of communal spaces, and (iv) remote assistance through the 24-hour CareLine to provide social befriending and help to seniors in the community. These bring essential and innovative health-social care functions closer to the homes of seniors of varying frailty statuses and empower them through enhanced community participation and social support. The primary aim of this study is to assess the effectiveness of CAPE in reducing healthcare utilization (HCU), retarding the progression of frailty and improving the health-related quality of life (HRQoL) among community-dwelling seniors, compared to standard of care, using a quasi-experimental study with 1840 senior participants in 2 intervention and demographically similar control sites at Telok Blangah, Bukit Merah and Chinatown. The secondary aim of this study is to model the contributions of social, BE and behavioural predictors, and functional ability, on HCU, progression of frailty and HRQoL. Wwe will also evaluate the implementation of CAPE using CFIR 2.0 and RE-AIM to produce actionable improvements. Findings from this study will inform the effectiveness, implementation and scale up strategies of this care model to support seniors to age well and reduce institutionalization.
kw: ageing in place; health and social care; technology; built environment; population health; gerontology

title: INdividualized proFiling Of Recurrence risk using Multiomics for EGFR-mutated non-small cell lung cancer (INFORM-EGFR)
abs: Background Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) mutations represent the most common subtype of non-small cell lung carcinoma (NSCLC) in Asia. Three years of osimertinib has improved survival in resected EGFR-mutated NSCLC but has significant toxicities including cost considerations. Importantly, our institutional data demonstrated that 37% of these patients remain disease-free at 5 years without adjuvant osimertinib, underscoring the importance of individualized risk stratification. Genomic and transcriptomic features such as co-mutations and gene signatures can improve prognostication in early-stage lung cancer. Our preliminary data from 86 patients illustrated the ability to integrate molecular and clinicopathological features to improve recurrence risk prediction among EGFR-mutated NSCLC and we aim to expand on these findings through whole exome (WES) and RNA-sequencing of a larger dataset. Hypothesis The addition of genomic and transcriptomic features to routine clinicopathological staging can improve recurrence risk predictions in resected EGFR-mutated NSCLC Specific Aims 1. To perform a comparative molecular landscape analysis of resected stage IA-IIIA EGFR-mutated NSCLC to identify features significantly associated with disease-free survival (DFS) 2. To identify and longitudinally track somatic mutational events in peripheral blood that predict for recurrence and relapse patterns in resected stage IA-IIIA EGFR-mutated NSCLC 3. To build multiomic risk prediction models incorporating clinicopathologic, genomic and transcriptomic data that reliably classify resected stage IA-IIIA EGFR-mutated NSCLC into “low risk” or “high risk” Approach/Methods WES and RNA-sequencing will be performed on 350 stage IA-IIIA EGFR-mutated NSCLC patients. Plasma ctDNA levels will be measured longitudinally and correlated with clinical outcomes. Multiomic risk prediction models incorporating clinicopathologic and molecular features will be build to predict individualised recurrence risk. Significance Given the healthcare burden of adjuvant osimertinib and heterogeneity of patient outcomes, there is an urgent need to risk stratify patients to individualise adjuvant treatment recommendations. This would translate into improved treatment outcomes and significant healthcare savings.
kw: EGFR; NSCLC; recurrence risk

title: Defining innate immune drivers of T cell responses to mRNA vaccination in children
abs: As the innate immune system initiates the adaptive immune response to vaccination, components of innate immune responses to vaccination determine antibody- and T cell-mediated immunity. Systems vaccinology studies have revealed pre- and post-vaccination innate immune drivers of antibody responses, but those for T cell responses remain scarce. T cell-mediated immunity is useful; in fact, in our paediatric cohort study of SARS-CoV-2 mRNA has demonstrated that T cell response is the most important vaccine-induced immunological correlate of protection against symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection. Knowing the innate immune drivers of T cell response can thus guide the development of better vaccines. Moreover, there is a lack of such studies in children and so the drivers of paediatric vaccine responses remain poorly understood. Children are immunologically distinct from adults, yet represent a critical target group for vaccination. Filling this knowledge gap is thus urgently required. The objective of this proposal is to elucidate the molecular determinants of T cell response to mRNA vaccination in children, using existing clinical samples from the same cohort of 110 healthy 5- to 12-year-old children who underwent SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccination. We will apply unbiased RNA sequencing along with antigen-specific T cell cytokine profiling to intricately dissect the innate immune and T cell responses to mRNA vaccination. We will define not only the post-vaccination responses but also examine for pre-vaccination innate immune endotypes that correlate with vaccination outcome. Knowledge on how innate immune endotype could shape development of personalized vaccination, such as those against cancer. title: Identification and management of progressive pulmonary fibrosis
abs: Interstitial lung disease (ILD) is dichotomised to idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF)and non-IPF ILD. Progressive pulmonary fibrosis (PPF) describes the subgroup of non-IPF ILD patients that manifest a progressive-fibrosing phenotype. Anti-fibrotic therapy has been effective in retarding progression among PPF patients, not just IPF patients. Immunosuppressive therapy has also been effective in a subgroup of PPF patients, but evidence remains lacking. In addition, the definition of PPF remains unclear and need further refinement. The research aims (a) To refine and improve the identification of those patients with PPF using novel approaches applied to clinical investigations including pulmonary function and high-resolution CT scans; (b) To better understand the epidemiology of and clinical approach to patients with PPF in the Asia-Pacific region through the evaluation of real-world registry data; (c) To understand the role of immunosuppressive therapies among PPF patients. For aim 1, I will leverage on the Australian ILD registry to (a) study the impact of the new spirometry guidelines in 2022 on spirometry interpretation; (b) determine the threshold of serial change in spirometry indices to determine the progressive-fibrosing phenotype. I will also look at the serial radiological changes and utilise both human scoring and artificial intelligence technology to predict radiological progression. I hypothesize that a relative decline of FVC of > 10% over a time interval of 3-6 months would identify this group. For aim 2, I will be working with other regional ILD registries to determine the prevalence of PPF utilising the refined criteria. In the process, we would also be able to study the behaviour, prognostic factors and define subgroups of progression based on ILD subtypes. For aim 3, I will utilise the Australian ILD registry data to establish prevailing practices of immunosuppressive therapy and anti-fibrotic therapy among those with PPF, and thereafter compare the impact of immunosuppressive therapies.

title: Application of Artificial Intelligence to Improve Patient Care and Resource Allocation in Obstetric Medicine
abs: We have identified key unmet needs in Obstetric medicine amenable to AI and ML deployment. The objective is to develop ML algorithms to predict various unfavorable pregnancy outcomes (Preeclampsia, preterm birth, growth restriction, stillbirth), gestational length of individual pregnancies, as well as labour trajectory and mode of delivery; for the purpose of applying these algorithms as clinical decision support tools throughout each pregnancy journey. There are three stages for this project- (i) retrospective analysis to develop ML models (ii) validation in a prospective cohort (iii) clinical assessment in a controlled trial setting. Several large datasets will be acquired from different populations across the world to develop these ML models. A variety of input variables will be used. The top performing models need to validated prospectively. A local Singaporean cohort study is planned for. Although these models are for predicting different outcomes, each of them can be tested during a single pregnancy journey. The final stage will be the testing of these algorithms in a controlled trial setting to assess their impact on change in clinical practice for high-risk patients. A potential application of such technology is a risk stratification system in real time to assist with subsequent management of pregnancy in terms of personalised care pathways.
kw: Artificial Intelligence; Machine Learning; Obstetrics; Pregnancy; Antenatal Care; Risk prediction

title: Characterization of a novel Cas13-based RNA engineering technology
abs: Recently, CRISPR-Cas13 systems have emerged as a powerful platform for transcriptome engineering. Cas13 nucleases are RNA-guided, RNA-targeting enzymes that can be readily programmed to cleave selected transcripts. In addition, a catalytically inactive Cas13 protein can serve as a scaffold to recruit an effector domain to target RNA molecules to regulate their function or metabolism. Notably, Cas13 can be fused with a deaminase domain from the ADAR family of enzymes for site-directed adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) RNA editing. Since inosines are recognized by cellular machineries as guanosines, A-to-I editing effectively results in a nucleotide change. Programmable RNA editing has attracted considerable attention because it is much safer than DNA base editing and has minimal requirement for a motif at its target site. However, existing site-selective RNA editors are non-ideal as they suffer from a trade-off between on-target activity and specificity. To address this problem, we have invented a novel programmable RNA editing platform, named xPERT, that exhibits both high efficacy and high specificity for its intended target. We rationally modified the Cas13 protein and a deaminase domain from human ADAR2 to achieve both desirable properties. Nevertheless, despite the success, we presently do not understand why our new tool works so well. Hence, in this project, we seek to characterize it in detail. First, we aim to elucidate the three-dimensional structure of xPERT to gain mechanistic insights into how each modification improves the enzyme. Second, we aim to replace the deaminase in xPERT with other effector domains and test the activity of each new fusion construct. This will allow us to broaden the utility of our technology to other aspects of RNA biology. Third, we aim to build a computational model based on machine learning to predict the activity of xPERT guides, which will facilitate the adoption of our technology by other RNA researchers.
kw: CRISPR; Transcriptome engineering; Genomics; RNA editing; Nucleic acid therapeutics; Biotechnology

title: Proteostatic control of muscle rejuvenation with aging
abs: Sarcopenia, defined as a decrease of muscle mass and strength with age, is strongly linked to physical disability, thus shortening human healthspan. The mammalian target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) is an evolutionarily conserved kinase whose activation induces protein synthesis and inhibits protein degradation, thus essential for muscle growth. Although it may initially seem counterintuitive that emergent evidence has revealed that chronic activation of mTORC1 accelerates muscle aging while suppressing it prolongs muscle health with age. mTORC1 inactivation or genetically mutated mTORC1-mediated phosphorylation of Eukaryotic Translation Initiation Factor 4E Binding Protein 1 (4EBP1), actives 4EBP1 and represses cap-dependent translation. While muscle growth is restricted in 4EBP1-activated myofiber, transgenic mice retain their skeletal muscle functions with age. By activating 4EBP1 in myofibers, the number of functional muscle stem cells is increased, and neuromuscular synaptic transmission is enhanced. Yet, how a repressor of cap-dependent translation, 4EBP1, regulates muscle functions and how 4EBP1-activated myofibers enhance the activities of MuSCs and motor neurons in a cell-nonautonomous manner remains unclear. To address the knowledge gap, we will employ 3D muscle-motor neuron-MuSCs co-culture systems to further dissect the action of 4EBP1 in regulating muscle microenvironment. We hypothesize that 4EBP1 activation alters the global translational profile by switching translation from being cap-dependent to being cap-independent, on which genes responsible for muscle health. Here, our specific aims are to (1) determine whether genes involved in protein quality control are regulated by cap-independent translation in a 4EBP1-dependent manner, (2) elucidate how improved protein quality control contributes to muscle rejuvenation, and (3) decipher the signals exchanged between skeletal muscles and motor neurons to augment neuromuscular synaptic transmission. Collectively, the outcomes of this project are expected to establish mTORC1-4EBP1 as a novel therapeutic target in muscle aging and identify the underlying mechanisms integrated through altered mTORC1-4EBP1 signaling for muscle health. Furthermore, the effectual recreation of the myofiber niche in vitro will provide the physiologically relevant platform for future drug screening to combat sarcopenia or various muscle disorders.
kw: sarcopenia; exercise; aging; muscle stem cell; 3D culture

title: COMPACT: Continuous Megacity-Scale Pandemic Prediction and Intervention
abs: The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic caused by SARS-CoV-2 motivates this project. We want to leverage the techniques from data science, deep learning and reinforcement learning to help the government make efficient non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPI) to mitigate the pandemic. This is a multi-disciplinary project, as it will involve computer scientists, medical professionals, and government agencies. There have been various research works about COVID-19 and we only assess the research related to this project. The first line is the epidemic modelling and prediction where there are four subcategories: 1. Compartmental models consider a single population divided according to health statuses and in some cases age structure]; 2. Metapopulation models are based on a network of subpopulations (i.e., cities, regions, countries) connected by mobility; 3. Statistical models capture the evolution of the epidemic inferring key parameters and behaviors from data; 4. Agent-based models capture the spreading patterns at the level of single individuals. The different models can provide the simulation of the pandemic at different levels. However, the first three kinds of models are not data-driven and cannot take the heterogeneous information of the population, e.g., geographical information and interactions among the population, and the fourth kind of models require a large amount of data to estimate the parameters of individuals, which often cannot be obtained, and suffer the scalability issues for the simulation and prediction of the megacity, e.g., Singapore. Therefore, novel techniques are required for accurate predictions of the pandemic.The second line is the optimization of the government intervention policy. There are only a few works, where Miralles-Pechuán et al. applied deep Q learning and genetic algorithms into an SEIR epidemiological model (Susceptible-Exposed-Infected-Recovered), and Colas et al. developed a Python toolbox EpidemiOptim to facilitate the optimization of the interventions based on the SEIR model; on the other hand, Thiagarajan et al. applied machine learning-based methods to both SEIR model and the agent-based model EpdiCast and Kompella et al. applied the soft actor-critic to an agent-based epidemic model Pandemic Simulator. Most of these works focus on specific kinds of interventions and small-scale populations. Therefore, these methods cannot provide a comprehensive solution for the government on a megacity scale. One critical problem which is ignored in previous works is the explainability of the solution. Most of the previous works take advantage of the powerful expressiveness of deep neural networks (DNN) to represent the intervention policies. However, DNN cannot be understood by humans, which brings difficulties to apply the policies to critical domains, especially the intervention of pandemics. Therefore, most of the previous works cannot be deployed into the real world, because the government cannot believe the policy and justi
kw: Pandemic Intervention, Reinforcement Learning, Explainability

title: ACTBIG: On Analysing Career Trajectories using Big Data
abs: 1. Specific Aims. In this proposal on Analysing Career Trajectories using Big Data (ACTBIG), we propose to use a computational social science approach to analyse career trajectories using very large resume datasets. Our first research goal is to adopt a new methodology in which social scientists can integrate statistical and AI methods (i.e., GPT, ChatGPT, knowledge graph-based techniques, and representation learning techniques) in their career trajectory research to derive new findings of social science relevance. Our second research goal is to develop new AI-based analytics methods required for the study of career trajectories, and to conduct the required basic research to enable these methods. 2. Research Questions and Hypotheses. The data-driven career trajectory analysis aims to study how we can combine career trajectory analysis methods of social science researchers with AI methods to generate granular insights and findings which are useful input to government policies and worker’s career planning. The first set of research questions to be investigated are: RQ1.1: How do we characterize the career pathways of different groups of workers such as by age, ethnicity, gender, education, occupation, and industry? How different are the career trajectories from different geographic regions? How different are these pathways which may suggest issues faced by the affected workers? RQ1.2: How do we distinguish high-growth career from low-growth ones from the career trajectories? A worker on a high-growth career experiences rapid job advancement and ample opportunities to learn as well as to practise new skills. How do we measure career growth of a worker based on his/her individual career movements (e.g., promotion, lateral career change, and skill required by different jobs? RQ1.3: What is the impact of the Covid-19 pandemic on career trajectories? Are workers experiencing their career stalled by the pandemic? Are they able to recover the career progress after the peak of pandemic? The proposed project also investigates into second set of research questions on the gaps between what the career trajectory analysis requires and what existing AI methods can offer, and the technical challenges to overcome these gaps. The project therefore includes a set of analytics and basic research tasks to address these technical challenges. The questions are: RQ2.1: How do we infer missing attribute labels and career movement labels for analysing the career trajectories extracted from resume data? How do we leverage the state-of-the-art large language models in these inference tasks? How can knowledge graph be used to improve the prediction accuracy of these tasks? RQ2.2: To perform computations on career trajectories, they are often required to be represented as numerical vectors. The derivation of such vectors is known as representation learning. How do we design new representation learning techniques for career trajectories which is a kind of temporal sequence data

title: Exploiting the anisotropic transport of Layered Sb2Si2Te6 for advanced thermoelectric applications
abs: Thermoelectric (TE) devices, which use Seebeck effects to generate electric directly from heat, offer a promising technology to recycle waste heat from fuel consumption and industrial manufacturing. The efficiency of TE devices depends on the performance of their constituent materials, which can be evaluated by the dimensionless figure of merit, ZT. From the definition of ZT, ZT=S2σT/κ, the thermoelectric performance is governed by both electrical and phonon transport. However, electrical and phonon transport properties are intrinsically interconnected, which makes the improvement of ZT a major challenge. Here, we propose to utilize the anisotropic transport properties of layered compounds to overcome this challenge, developing advanced thermoelectric materials and devices with a novel layered material, Sb2Si2Te6, which was first introduced as a high-performance thermoelectric material by our group. In addition to its high TE performance, this compound is rather stable due to the absence of phase transition. However, its anisotropic transport characteristics and the full thermoelectric performance potential have yet to be demonstrated. Therefore, a systematic study of Sb2Si2Te6 will be performed in the following perspectives: (1) demonstrating the anisotropic transport properties of Sb2Si2Te6 nanosheets using microdevices as measuring platforms, which demands significant efforts and expertise, signifying the high novelty of this proposal, (2) investigating the physical transport characteristics of charge carriers and phonons, (3) modulating carrier and phonon transport through defect-control, and (4) synthesizing single-crystal-like textured polycrystalline pellets and fabricating prototype TE devices. Due to challenges in growing large Sb2Si2Te6 crystals, its anisotropic transport properties are to be measured on Sb2Si2Te6 nanosheet using microdevices. By combining experimental measurement with first-principles density functional theory (DFT) modeling, the underlying mechanisms dominating the anisotropic carrier and phonon transport can be elucidated. With a well-understood anisotropic behavior, the thermoelectric potential of Sb2Si2Te6 can be uncovered by simulating its electrical and thermal properties using physical models. The lattice thermal conductivity can be obtained via the Debye-Callaway model, considering the phonon dispersion and scattering mechanisms. The potentially high carrier mobility can then be interpreted by the phonon-electron coupling. Combining the phonon and carrier transport, the blueprint to obtain high ZT in Sb2Si2Te6 can be decoded. Following the established blueprint, the physical transport properties of Sb2Si2Te6 can be modified accordingly by controlling the defects. The carrier concentration and type can be adjusted by introducing aliovalent dopants such as Sn4+, as well as tuning the concentration of the intrinsic Sb3+ vacancy defects. The effective suppression of thermal conductivity can be realized by introduci

title: All antiferromagnetic Magnetic Tunnel Junction for non-volatile Memory
abs: In post-Moore law period, static power consumption (SPC) which is caused by the leakage current due to small feature size and volatility of the SRAM and DRAM, accounts for more than half of the total power consumption in mainstream CMOS-based chips and is a key issue hindering the performance of current computing architecture. Non-volatile spintronic device is widely considered as the most promising technology to reduce or even eliminate the SPC, e.g. spin orbit torque (SOT) based magnetic random access memory (MRAM) is considered as the most potential candidate to replace the SRAM, where the writing is based on the spin orbit torque (SOT) generated from adjacent spin source layer and reading relies on the resistance change in the magnetic tunnel junction (MTJ) device. To date, the basic structure of MTJ is ferromagnet (FM)/MgO/FM sandwich structure. However, towards a better performance, FM materials have brought several inextricable obstacles: 1) the intrinsic precession frequency of FM materials is limited at the order of GHz, which sets an operation speed ceiling for FM-MTJ; 2) the large net magnetization of FM materials induces a strong stray field, which would affect the nearby device and thus does not favour high density of memory. To solve these issues, antiferromagnetic (AFM) materials have recently been intensively investigated. The intrinsic antiparallelly coupled magnetic sublattices provide AFM materials with zero stray field and ultra-fast magnetic dynamics (frequency at the order of Terahertz), which naturally overcomes the performance bottlenecks that FM-MTJ is facing. Theoretical works have predicted the existence of sizable tunnelling magneto-resistance (TMR) in AFM-MTJ. And in 2023, researchers have experimentally observed TMR in AFM-MTJ, either in Mn3Sn/MgO/Mn3Sn or in Mn3Pt/MgO/Mn3Pt heterostructure. However, due to the vanishing net magnetization and insufficient material investigation, the reported TMR in AFM-MTJ remains limited, i.e., less than 100% at 300K, which is far from the standard circuit design requirement ( > 200%). Moreover, there lacks effective method to write information in AFM-MTJ, which is also an essential issue. Therefore, it is desirable to explore feasible plans to realize reliable reading and writing functions in AFM-MTJ, both at material choice level and physical mechanism level. In this project, we aim at experimentally realizing AFM-MTJ based non-volatile memory. Firstly, we will achieve sizable TMR in AFM-MTJ. We propose non-colinear AFM materials to replace the FM layers in FM-MTJ. By first-principles calculation, we will search the best tunnel barrier material candidate that is suitable for the non-colinear AFM Mn3Sn and Mn3Pt. We will further improve the TMR ratio in AFM-MTJ by investigating the impact of the tunnel barrier crystal orientation (spin filtering effect), the tunnel barrier thickness (resistance area value), etc. Then, we will demonstrate the energy efficient switching of Néel vecto

title: Engineering Superballistic Electron Flow in Graphene
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: Geometric diodes use the shape of their structure and ballistic electron transport to create diode behaviour – an asymmetry in the geometry of the material (on the order of the mean free path of the charge carrier) creates an asymmetry in forward vs. reverse bias current (a.k.a. a diode). This project aims to study and engineer ballistic and superballistic electron flows in a two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG) of a nanopatterned graphene system via geometric control, targeting both nonlinear and rectification effects. The proposed work culminates the experimental and simulation tools that both PIs have developed in the past years, and we are confident to demonstrate the new phenomena. Specifically, we will extend the geometric diode concept to the superballistic regime by adding electron-electron collision effects to our theoretical model. Upon confirmation, our simulations will lead to optimized geometric designs, which will subsequently be fabricated for experimental demonstrations. Specifically: (I) Fabricate geometric diodes from graphene films via nanopatterning. (II) Demonstrate superballistic electron transport in graphene via electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) at ultrahigh spectral and spatial resolutions.
kw: Ballistic; Superballistic; Graphene; Particle-in-cell (PIC); Electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS)

title: Monolithic spintronic devices based on a magnetic topological insulator.
abs: One of the central topics of condensed matter physics is the search and manipulation of novel quantum phases and the further integration of them into novel device architectures, where quantum degrees of freedom could be fully harnessed. Among those, recently emerged magnetic topological insulators (MTI) offer an exciting platform for the manipulation of charge, spin, and band topology. MnBi2Te4 is a van der Waals MTI that has garnered attention due to its high spin density, strong spin-orbit coupling, out-of-plane magnetic anisotropy, and low levels of disorder. These characteristics have facilitated the emergence of Chern insulator and quantum anomalous Hall (QAH) states at elevated temperatures. However, most experimental studies to date have only focused on quantization phenomena using non-magnetic contacts, leaving the unique spin transport degrees of freedom of this emerging quantum material largely unexplored. The intrinsic connection between the magnetic state and band structure of this material opens a new frontier for experimental explorations for new control knobs in tuning spintronics devices. One of the key aspects of MnBi2Te4 is the spin polarization of the band structure imprinted in the surface state and edge state spin polarization. Despite extensive experimental efforts in both nanoscale device communities and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) communities little is known about the relationships between spin and momentum of electrons in surface state and in chiral edge modes and its dependence on doping, electric field, and magnetization in atomically thin devices. Understanding and exploiting surface and edge modes in MnBi2Te4 for spin transport and spin torques would be the central theme of the proposed research and will enable multiple future applications of this material. In this research program, we focus on having two interconnected work-packages (WP) to develop an experimental framework for the novel detection and manipulation of intertwined spin, magnetic, and topological degrees of freedom in MnBi2Te4. They involve several individual tasks and each task alone will provide important scientific milestones in spintronics research. In WP1, we will focus on probing the intrinsic in-plane spin polarization of MnBi2Te4 and realizing novel spin valve devices. In WP2 we will explore spin transfer torque (STT) effects in MnBi2Te4 by using the induced in-plane spin polarization and modulating the signal in our dual-gated devices. Taking advantage of the inherent characteristics of the material will result in the development of monolithic spintronics devices that were previously unattainable. Despite its ambition, the project is highly feasible because it builds upon our prior discoveries and expertise. Our team has achieved important milestones in highly-related areas such as low-dimensional spintronic devices, the properties of atomically thin MnBi2Te4, and spin torque phenomena. title: Thin Film Bulk Acoustic Wave Resonators Based on Atomic Piezoelectric Layers at Millimetric Frequencies
abs: To efficiently control data transmission in high-speed communication, radio frequency (rf) filters constructed with high-frequency and wideband resonators are essential. The rf filters based on thin film bulk acoustic wave resonators (FBARs) are of high operation frequencies, high electromechanical coupling coefficient (kt2), high-quality (Q) factor and compact architectures, dominating the rf filters in the high-speed communication kingdom. To meet the requirement of the operating frequency band for the 5G/6G communications, FBARs need millimetric resonant frequencies (or from a few GHz to several tens of GHz). As the resonant frequency is inversely proportional to the thickness of the piezoelectric film, the core component in an FBAR, the millimetric resonant frequencies could be in principle achieved only with a few hundred nanometer conventional piezoelectric films, like ZnO, AlN, PZT and other piezoelectric ceramics etc. Unfortunately, the piezoelectric properties of such thin conventional piezoelectric films are very poor due to inconsistency of the crystalline orientation, high defect density near the surfaces of the piezoelectric films, leading to large degradation in kt2 value and Q factor of the fabricated FBARs. To conquer this technical challenge, two approaches are adopted recently. The first is to make use of the higher harmonic resonance modes, rather than the fundamental resonance mode, of the resonators without reducing the thickness of the piezoelectric layer involved. Nonetheless, the higher modes have a very poor kt2 value, resulting in a large insertion loss. The second approach entails a thin piezoelectric crystal layer fabricated by ion implantation-exfoliation method or a periodically poled piezoelectric film to achieve resonances at millimetric frequencies. The major problem associated with these techniques lies in the conventional fabrication processes for the thin piezoelectric layers, such as metal organic chemical vapor deposition, sol-gel deposition, RF sputtering, or vapor deposition etc, which could not ensure the necessary crystalline orientation and sub-nanometer flatness for the piezoelectric layers. In this proposal, we propose an unprecedented approach to tackle this challenge by introducing novel two dimensional (2D) piezoelectric crystals, like. 3R MoS2 or 3R-WSe2 atomic layers to FBARs. 3R MoS2 atomic layers are of the excellent piezoelectric, mechanical and thermal properties and atomic level flatness. Our recent experimental observations suggest that 3R-MoS2 atomic layers are of strong piezoelectricity from a single atomic sheet up to a few hundred nanometre thick, regardless of the number of the atomic sheets (H. Hallil et al, Strong Piezoelectricity in 3R‐MoS2 Flakes, Adv Electronic Mat 2022, 2101131). This is obviously a big advantage over conventional piezoelectric materials for FBARs.
