title: Topology-enhanced physical models for biopolymer structure and interaction analysis
abs: Understanding the structure-function relationships of biomolecules is an active area of research due to its fundamental importance in biology, physics, and engineering. Our research will answer fundamental questions such as “what is the shape of a biopolymer?”, “why is a biopolymer shaped the way it is?”, “how is structure related to function?”, and provide new perspectives into the geometry and topology of a biopolymer. We will utilize recently developed mathematical tools from algebraic topology, combinatorial topology, computational topology, and differential geometry to characterize and model the shape of biopolymers such as DNA and RNA, and translate the findings into practical applications such as molecular dynamics simulations. The project has three specific aims: Aim 1: Characterize the shape and topology of biopolymers. Aim 2: Formulate models of biopolymers encoded with molecular and structural information. Aim 3: Develop many-body interactions force-fields amenable for molecular dynamics simulations. Our research will provide new ways to encode and characterize structural motifs of complex biopolymers responsible for folding pathways and biological functions in nature.
kw: Biopolymers; biophysical models; Geometry and Topology; Many-body interactions; Molecular Dynamics simulations; Simplicial Complex

title: Convergent evolution in South East Asian rainforests and its association with soil, identified through population metagenomics analyses
abs: Understanding the ecological drivers behind forest succession is important for conservation, forestry and landscaping purposes. We have previously sequenced 499 flowering plant genomes from Bukit Timah Nature Reserve, representing 76% of the entire plant biodiversity in the forest reserve. Data analysis of the genome sequencing data, combined with spatial analysis of the forest structure identified a surprising biochemical stratification in the primary versus secondary rainforest types. The analysis of biochemical potential of the plant assemblage identified pathways with significantly fewer genes than by chance, suggestive of purifying selection, but also pathways where the enzyme coding space was significantly expanded. This suggests positive selection and diversification of these biosynthetic pathways. Since the traits are shared by an entire forest type, our hypothesis is that the evolution of biochemical diversity results from shared belowground microbiota, and/or allelopathic interactions. This proposal will test this hypothesis by i) carrying out high quality reference genome assemblies of ten highly abundant species from each of the two forest types, ii) identifying tissue types the diversified biosynthesis pathways are active and the compounds produced by the pathways, and iii) carry out root metagenomics analysis of the representative forest tree species, and iv) linking the the root microbiome data with the host biosynthesis pathways using population metagenomics. The aim of the project is to provide concrete hypotheses that can be tested with plants in controlled experiments with subsequent funding. Depending on the identified pathways and secondary metabolites the work may have applications in sustainable farming, food security and medicine, as well as in forest management through identifying conditions that accelerate forest succession.
kw: ecology, genomics, population metagenomics, plant-microbe interaction

title: Quantum Geometric Advantage
abs: Exploiting truly quantum phenomena at device scale promises to unlock a range of quantum functionality with no classical analog. Yet directly harnessing such coherences is challenging: quantum coherences are often delicate and highly susceptible to minute changes in device environment and fabrication process. Over the past decade, a different quantum platform has emerged -- quantum geometric and topological materials. In these, robust quantum phenomena (e.g., anomalous Hall effect without magnetic field, orbital magnetic states without spin, giant valley-selective Hall effect, quantum-geometry-induced circular photogalvanic effect) can persist over long and realistic device length scales. Robustness of these quantum phenomena arises from their dependence on the “winding” of wavefunctions in materials (characterized by quantum geometry and topology) that persist even in the presence of disorder and device imperfections. This dramatically expands the possibility horizon of material response enabling highly unusual and useful properties that include the symmetry-protected helical edge modes, topological non-Hermitan skin effects that provide extreme sensitivity to boundaries, and quantized photocurrents under circularly-polarized pump light in a chiral Weyl semimetal. Our program aims to harness quantum geometry for device “advantage”: namely to create or enhance new functionalities for a new type of quantum materials engineering and technology. Traditional device technology has been largely based on the "classical" particle-like properties of electrons in materials. Recently quantum geometric effects were observed in different classes of materials, from topological insulators, to Weyl/Dirac semimetals, to transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs), and also controlled by periodic driving with light. The above materials have opened up a distinctly different avenue ⎯ unconventional responses that are activated by the intricate pattern and winding of electronic wavefunctions, and hence vastly enriched the phase space for material response. Given this exciting context, a key question is: what "advantage" can devices utilizing quantum geometry provide? Our vision is to clearly enunciate the advantage that exploiting quantum geometry can provide (quantum geometric advantage). In particular, we aim to demonstrate how and where quantum geometry can enhance/enrich material response over conventional devices. Just as entanglement is the key resource for quantum information and computation, we envision that wavefunction-winding-sensitive responses in recently discovered topological materials can form the basis for a new quantum geometric device technology. title: Developing Insect-derived Products for Sustainable Management of Plant Pathogens in Urban Farms
abs: In a rapidly urbanising world, urban farms, especially those in indoor controlled environments, have become crucial for sustainable food production. However, managing plant diseases in these urban environments without overusing harmful synthetic pesticides remains a challenge. Our research proposes innovative solutions by harnessing the untapped potential of natural insect-derived products to protect crops and promote plant growth in urban farms. Studies have indicated that some insect species naturally produce antimicrobial compounds that have significant antibacterial and antifungal properties. While some of these compounds have been identified and synthetically produced, their application in agriculture is currently limited, and the cost of production is high. Our project seeks to address these challenges by developing and optimising two new cost-effective approaches for the production and extraction of such compounds. Firstly, methods for enhancing and extracting antimicrobial compounds from the Blow Fly (BF) and Black Soldier Fly (BSF) secretions and excretions will be developed and optimised. Secondly, a high-throughput transient over-expression method for specific antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) production in plant system (similar to a “biofactory”) will be developed, followed by extraction of the AMPs. These extracted products will be tested against Singapore's local plant pathogens and crops, to develop tailored insect-derived products for plant disease management and growth improvements. By transferring these methods to our collaborators, we aim to significantly contribute to sustainable agriculture, while ensuring plant health and production in urban farms. If successful, the insect-derived products can serve as sustainable, eco-friendly alternatives to synthetic pesticides. Urban farms will be able to reduce their reliance on harmful, synthetic pesticides, while consumers can enjoy fresh, chemical pesticide-free local produce. Ultimately, it is envisioned that the products from this research will transform the local urban farming sector to become more productive, sustainable, and environmentally friendly, while contributing to the Sustainable Development Goal 2 (Zero Hunger), 11 (Sustainable cities and communities), and 12 (Responsible consumption and production) of the United Nations.

title: intelliCARE : Empowering Seniors with AI-Driven Personalised Assistance
abs: IntelliCARE: Empowering Seniors with AI-Driven Personalised Assistance IntelliCARE is a groundbreaking project that aims to revolutionize ageing-in-place for seniors in Singapore through data science, machine learning, and IoT technologies. By addressing falls prevention, medication adherence, cognitive health, and home environmental stressors, IntelliCARE seeks to deliver personalized and proactive care for seniors, enabling independent and safe living. The project involves preliminary studies to identify fall risk factors, evaluate existing interventions, and understand adherence barriers. Leveraging data from wearable devices, electronic health records, and home sensors, IntelliCARE will develop predictive models and algorithms for personalized interventions. The user-friendly application will provide real-time risk alerts, recommendations, and support networks, enhancing seniors' quality of life. Engaging healthcare and community care stakeholders, IntelliCARE fosters collaboration and promotes local SMEs' technological capabilities in the healthcare industry. With significant commercial potential, the project aims to manage and protect intellectual assets effectively. The two-year project plan encompasses research, development, testing, and commercialization, delivering research reports, predictive models, algorithms, UX design guidelines, and comprehensive datasets. The budget includes manpower, equipment, software platforms, and consumables. IntelliCARE's visionary approach empowers seniors with AI-driven personalized assistance, transforming ageing-in-place interventions and elevating the well-being of seniors in Singapore. This initiative opens avenues for healthcare technology advancement and community care improvement.

title: Six-Dimensional Data-Driven In-Vivo Estimation of Joint Kinetics for Gait Analysis
abs: Gait analysis potentially detects muscle weaknesses that are caused by non-gait activities. For instance, individuals who participate in sports or activities that require one muscle group to work more than others may experience muscle imbalances that can affect their gait pattern. By detecting these imbalances, gait analysis can help develop targeted exercise programs to strengthen these muscles and correct any misalignments in the body. Through anatomical joint forces and moments analysis, healthcare professionals can identify abnormal patterns or movements, potentially contributing to the development of injuries and chronic conditions. Joint kinetics analysis of the lower back and lower limb can also determine the efficiency of interventions such as orthotics, physical therapy, or surgery. Additionally, joint forces and moments estimation during gait analysis can assist athletes and active individuals in improving their performance and avoiding injuries by identifying areas of weakness or imbalance. Corrective movements or strengthening exercises can then address these areas. Overall, clinical gait analysis is an essential tool in injury management, rehabilitation, and prevention. It provides valuable insight into joint mechanics and movement patterns, helping healthcare professionals, athletes, and active individuals achieve their optimum health and performance goals. However, systems that enable such analysis, utilizing joint forces and moment measures, are costly and require specialized personnel to operate. They are not portable and their setups require large amount of space. Thus, such useful gate analysis has yet become routine tool in clinics and community. Increasing the accessibility of such systems help provide valuable insights for healthcare professionals in making analysis and design more effective treatment plans. Regular follow up and re-evaluation can be done via accessible quantitative gait analysis will increase relevant individual compliance and effectiveness of such treatment. The objective of this project is to innovate a data-driven gait analysis approach, called “KinemAIticWizard”, for quantifying lower back and limb six-dimensional (6D) joint kinetics using a hardware setup comprising of a single camera connected to a CPU-driven portable device such as a PDA or a laptop. “KinemAIticWizard” will be affordable, ultra-portable and easy to operate without the presence of a specialist, providing healthcare professional easy, frequent access to essential gait assessment tool to improve their analysois and prescription plan. “KinemAIticWizard”, a data-driven approach deployed in a single-camera enabled device, can be used at various points of person’s pain or rehabilitation journey, from assessment, analysis, to treatment and education on posture, body mechanics, ergonomics, and lifestyle modifications to prevent future recurrence of injury or pain. title: Verifying the Verifiers: Trustworthy Proofs for Critical Computer Systems
abs: Formal methods are being applied in numerous safety- and mission-critical application domains, ranging from classical use cases in software and hardware verification, to emerging use cases in AI verification or even computer-aided mathematics. However, scaling formal methods to modern computer systems requires the use of powerful automated reasoning techniques with highly complex tool implementations. Curiously, there are occasionally examples of flawed automated reasoning techniques and implementations, which calls into question the trustworthiness of formal methods, especially when they are used to verify critical computer systems. My research is about systematically scrutinizing the trustworthiness of automated reasoning, by providing rigorous correctness justifications throughout the design, implementation, and application of automated reasoning tools. The aims of this proposal are threefold: 1) to build extensible and light-weight proof certification frameworks as a general-purpose enabling technology for eliminating errors in automated reasoning tools, 2) to develop proof certification techniques with formal guarantees for new, state-of-the-art techniques in automated reasoning, and 3) to apply proof certification, alongside other domain-specific techniques, towards trustworthy hybrid systems verification. The key to achieving these aims will be the use of deductive reasoning verification techniques, which have been shown to be amenable to highly rigorous justification and trustworthy implementation in computational tools. I will apply my prior research work, including in verified proof checking, verified compilation, and deductive verification for continuous and hybrid systems, to answer novel challenges in trustworthy automated reasoning. This research will demonstrate that trustworthiness can be readily built into automated reasoning development from the outset. It will also lead to reusable insights, tools, and techniques for the development of logical systems and trustworthy proof tools throughout various formal methods application domains. This added trustworthiness will bring about greater adoption of formal methods in both academic and industrial applications, bringing truly trustworthy proofs to critical computer systems.
kw: formal methods; trustworthy automated reasoning; proof certification; verified compilation; hybrid systems verification

title: Mechanistic studies and applications of RNA modifications using ‘designer’ RNA
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: RNA modifications play fundamental roles in the structure and function of non-coding and coding RNAs. The field currently relies on genetic knockout or overexpression of modification readers, writers, and erasers to deduce their function. However, this approach suffers from several weaknesses and technical challenges. Rather than using genetic manipulation, I will build synthetic mRNA with precisely defined modifications and determine their activity in biochemical assays. I will first focus on N6-methyladenosine (m6A), which is an abundant mRNA modification that is crucial for human development, and the progression of deadly diseases such as acute myeloid leukaemia. m6A is correlated with increased transcript turnover, yet its mechanism of action remains poorly defined. Leveraging my expertise in protein engineering, I will develop CRISPR-Cas enzymes that precisely install m6A in transcripts of interest. I will then use these modified RNAs to test the hypothesis that the number, density, and positions of m6A modifications in a transcript dictate RNA turnover. Specifically, I will reconstitute key m6A pathways in vitro using site-specifically modified RNA and purified effector proteins. This system will enable me to rigorously determine how specific m6A configurations and reader proteins dictate RNA turnover. Modified mRNAs have also emerged as a promising modality for vaccines, gene therapy and somatic reprogramming. This is attributed to their high stability and translation, and low immunogenicity. What is the code of RNA modifications that maximizes these properties? Current methods uniformly incorporate modified bases through in vitro transcription. This is not ideal as RNA modifications can exert contrasting impacts on stability and translation, depending on their position and sequence context. Here, I will build custom modification patterns that maximize RNA stability and translation, and minimize immunogenicity (Aim 3). This reduces the required dose (and therefore cost and toxicity) of mRNA-based applications. The ability to tailor RNA modification patterns will fuel the global market for mRNA therapeutics, which was valued at >US$30 billion in 2021 and is projected to more than double by 2030. My proposed work is important because it answers two outstanding questions in the RNA modifications field: 1) What is the function of RNA modifications, individually and collectively? 2) How can modification patterns be designed to confer maximal potency of synthetic mRNA in human cells? I will build mRNA with tailored m6A modification patterns to directly determine how m6A impacts RNA turnover. In addition, I will construct optimal patterns of RNA modifications to maximize the potency of mRNA beyond what is currently possible in the field.
kw: RNA modifications, synthetic mRNA, m6A, somatic reprogramming

title: Next-generation atomically-precise quantum emitters
abs: The development of a quantum communications network has evolved into active research. To establish a quantum communications network, a multitude of components that are not yet available must be developed, including quantum memories and switches, as well as coherent wavelength converters that match the 'flying qubits' to the 'stationary qubits' within quantum processing units. The solid-state single-photon quantum emitter (SPQEs), also known as a single-photon emitter (SPE), is widely considered an excellent candidate to serve as the source of flying qubits. The performance of SPQEs is defined by key characteristics, such as photon emission rate, single-photon purity and indistinguishability, and photon lifetime. Practical implementations of SPQEs necessitate highly controllable, scalable, and reproducible fabrication processes, as well as the capability for tunable photon wavelength and room temperature operation. Apart from RT operations, SPE emitted in the telecom regime is preferred for the larger distance quantum communications, due to its lower attenuation loss in fiber transmission as compared to shorter wavelengths. Currently, the most promising functionalities of SPQEs have been achieved with solid-state-based SPEs, including fluorescent defects and quantum dots (QDs). Among these, the nitrogen-vacancy (NV) and silicon-vacancy (SiV) color centers in diamond are the most extensively studied, demonstrating relatively high photon count rates of up to 3x106 s-1, and offering the potential for room temperature single-photon generation5, 7. However, the main drawback of color centers is their susceptibility to local electric fields, lattice strains in the diamond, and proximity to other defects, resulting in broadening of the emission line. The most promising quantum emission characteristics achieved to date have been demonstrated by quantum dot-based SPQE structures, such as InAs/GaSe QDs, which exhibit photon count rate values of 1x107 s-1, superior photon purity, and photon indistinguishability. However, the fabrication of these QD-based SPQEs requires high-quality materials and relies on technologically demanding processes, making it highly challenging to create fully identical SPQE structures with predefined and well-controlled quantum emission characteristics. The range of solid-state emitters expanded significantly in 2015 with the discovery of the cryogenic SPQE properties of QD-like defects present in two-dimensional materials (2D materials), specifically transition-metal dichalcogenides (TMDs). In 2016, I. Aharonovych and colleagues reported the room-temperature SPQE properties of QD-like defects present in hexagonal boron-nitride (hBN). The wide band gap of hBN renders non-radiative recombination of electron-hole pairs negligible, resulting in strong SPE emission at room temperature across a range of energies from near-infrared to ultraviolet wavelengths. Consequently, hBN-based SPQEs show immense promise for applications in quantum

title: Introducing Intelligence into Automated Synthesis of Metal Nanoclusters
abs: The production of functional nanomaterials with customized properties is a challenging task that requires the integration of multiple disciplines and cutting-edge technologies. To address this need, materials scientists seek to develop innovative and intelligent platforms to produce functional nanomaterials. The aim of this project is to create the first-ever smart synthesis platform of customized metal nanoclusters (MNCs, Figure 1 in Detailed Research Proposal) using high-throughput nanocluster synthesis instruments and data-efficient deep learning frameworks. In this project, we will introduce an innovative approach for the rapid production of customizable atomically precise MNCs, which serve as our representative model nanomaterials. These nanoclusters, containing both inorganic and organic components, are synthesized through a state-of-the-art integration of high-throughput nanocluster fabrication instruments and data-efficient deep learning frameworks. The end goal is to unveil the first-of-its-kind Smart Synthesis Platform for Metal Nanoclusters. Imagine this platform as a highly advanced analogue to a 3D printer in the realm of nanomaterials, with the crucial addition of machine learning algorithms for self-optimization. This enables us not only to accelerate the creation of atomically precise structures, but also to improve and innovate the synthesis process iteratively, thus revolutionizing the advanced manufacturing of functional nanomaterials. MNCs have garnered significant interest in both basic and applied research due to their intriguing physical and chemical properties. Gold (Au) and silver (Ag) nanoclusters, for example, have promising applications in fields such as catalysis, sensing, and bio-imaging, despite bulk gold and silver being chemically inert. These atomically precise MNCs exhibit size-dependent physical and chemical properties, making them ideal for a wide range of downstream applications with diverse physicochemical property requirements. However, rapidly developing MNC synthetic protocols customized for user-designated characteristics requires numerous trial-and-error experiments to adjust reaction conditions, such as reagents used and their concentrations, temperature, stirring, and reaction time, to fabricate the desired MNCs. This process becomes even more challenging when the MNC species with the desired characteristics has yet to be discovered and a new protocol is required. To facilitate the rapid and custom production of MNCs, a novel MNC smart design approach is highly desirable. Such an approach would provide suggestions and make optimizations of feasible synthesis recipes to obtain adequate MNCs for a variety of applications. Our project aims to address this need by creating the smart synthesis platform of customized MNCs, leveraging the power of high-throughput synthesis instruments and data-efficient deep learning frameworks. This project focuses on the synthesis of aqueous Au and Ag nanoclusters, which t
kw: Deep Learning, High-throughput Experimentation, Metal Nanoclusters, Metal Nanomaterials, Advanced Manufacturing, Smart Production

title: Steering data-driven algorithms into effective decision-making with granular and sharp statistical evaluation
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: How should we train machine learning (ML) models such that the predictions they yield, beyond just carrying high predictive accuracy, can also be certified as effective and reliable for use in decision-making tasks of the scale required to run business and manufacturing operations? This project aims to develop a statistical framework for answering this question and leverage the insights to design modular learning procedures that are both statistically efficient and computationally flexible for integrating into the data-driven decision making pipeline. Recent years have witnessed much excitement in responding to the above question. In particular, most of this activity has centred on developing new training methods which strive to become aware of the trade-offs captured in optimization models deployed by the firms to run their operations. Just as how important it is to develop new methods, it is equally crucial to have a clear-eyed view of the quality of decisions they lead to and be capable of discerning the differences in their effectiveness. Generalization and regret error bounds, which are typical in the ML literature, have NOT been able to explain something as elementary as, say, for example, why one should favor a sophisticated “optimization-aware” regression procedure over something as simple as the least-squares regression (or) the celebrated lasso estimators which are not optimization-aware. Bridging a gap of this nature requires modeling that goes beyond constructing instant-specific ML and optimization models. To make this leap and constructively contribute to the design of “optimization-aware” algorithms, this project aims to investigate the following two basic research themes for both static and online resource allocation problems affected by uncertainty: 1) (Granular statistical evaluation) How can we embed the integrated learning and optimization problems in an appropriate asymptotic framework capable of delineating the effectiveness of different optimization-aware schemes with granular characterizations of the gaps in their optimality and data requirement? We propose to embed the first-step prediction problem explicitly in a high-dimensional statistical setting that has proven rich enough to bring out the complexities in model selection and yet sufficiently tractable to characterize the selected model. A key innovation here is the shift of focus from predictive accuracy to model selection, as the chosen prediction model has an outsized role on downstream decisions. 2) (Design of algorithms) Most optimization-aware methods presume 100% flexibility in training. This view ignores the repeated task-dependent training costs incurred when a firm has to solve not just one but several optimization problems by building on the predictions. Considering this repeated high training costs, we propose the novel use of debiased predictions as a modular, light-touch approach to be optimization-aware. We will quantify if there is any price paid for t
kw: Operations Research, Decision-making under uncertainty, Applied Probability, Diffusion approximations, Data-driven optimization

title: Emerging Disruptive Trends in Accounting: Implications for Stakeholders, Governance and Regulation
abs: In this project, we investigate how accounting rules and disclosure regulations influence key stakeholders’ response to three emerging disruptive trends in the financial markets: (1) the use of blockchain and digital assets such as cryptocurrency, (2) the use of data analytics, and (3) firms’ climate and sustainability impact. Within each of these three trends, we conduct a series of experiments to (a) identify the impact of the trend on various stakeholders, (b) test the cognitive and affective mechanisms responsible for these responses, and (c) determine how accounting rules/disclosure requirements could impact stakeholders’ response to these disruptive trends. We study the effects of each disruptive trend on relevant stakeholder groups separately, and conduct 6 main studies with 11 experiments in total: blockchain/digital assets (Studies 1a/b and 2a/b: 4 experiments), data analytics (Studies 3a/b/c/d: 4 experiments), and climate/sustainability (Studies 4, 5ab/b, 6a/b: 5 experiments). Studies 1a/b examine the impact of blockchain technology. In Study 1a, we recruit jurors to examine their judgments of auditor liability when an audit failure occurs in a blockchain audit context with a 2 (audit method – real-time audit, periodic audit) by 2 (blockchain type – public blockchain, private blockchain) between-participants experiment. We manipulate the audit method and the blockchain type as part of the audit failure scenario and solicit investors’ judgments of auditor liability. Study 1b will recruit corporate managers to examine their reactions to the same two factors but in an auditor-client negotiation setting where they decide whether to accept audit adjustments made that differ based on these two factors. Study 2a/b examines the impact of digital assets and cryptocurrencies on investors and managers respectively. In Study 2a, we will recruit experienced investors to examine how they respond to a company’s accounting treatment for cryptocurrencies. We will conduct a 3 (cryptocurrencies’ categorization on financial statements – intangible assets, cash equivalents, trading securities) by 2 (industry of the company – traditional industry, digital industry) between-participants experiment. Investors read background information about a company and how the company categorizes cryptocurrencies before providing their investment judgments. In Study 2b, we will recruit corporate managers to examine their chosen accounting treatment for cryptocurrencies. We will conduct a 2 (reversibility of cryptocurrency’s previous impairment – reversible, irreversible) by 2 (cryptocurrencies’ categorization on financial statements – intangible assets, trading securities) between-participants experiment. We manipulate how cryptocurrencies are categorized in the financial statements and provide information on the reversibility of previous impairments. Managers will then provide their decisions on whether to remove the impairment loss of cryptocurrencies when reporting non-

title: Deepen the understanding of nucleic acid-small molecule interaction and search for more selective nucleic acid-targeting small molecules
abs: Cancer and neurodegenerative disorders (NDs) constitute prominent global causes of mortality. Despite its adverse side effects, chemotherapy remains a primary therapeutic modality for cancer management. The effective medications against NDs remain limited. The etiology of both cancer and NDs is rooted in DNA mutations, prompting researchers to explore the potential of targeting mutated DNA sequences using small molecules to develop novel therapeutic interventions. However, comprehending the intricate mechanisms underlying DNA-small molecule interactions remains constrained due to the dearth of methodologies enabling facile and quantitative profiling of nucleic acid-small molecule recognition events with both high resolution and high-throughput capacity. To bridge this knowledge gap, we have conceived a highly sensitive turn-on type fluorescent probe that facilitates expedient reporting of the binding affinity and binding site of nucleic acid-small molecule interactions in a high-throughput format with base resolution. This innovative probe enables us to amass unprecedented datasets pertaining to nucleic acid-small molecule interactions, thereby facilitating the characterization of "druglikeness" attributes applicable to nucleic acids. Leveraging these insights, we aim to identify druglike small-molecule binders targeting DNA repeat expansion and R-loops through high-throughput screening (HTS). The overarching objective of this proposal is to deploy the recently developed fluorescent probe as a means to deepen our comprehension of nucleic acid-small molecule interactions and exploit the acquired knowledge to identify more selective small molecules with potential as efficacious anti-cancer or anti-ND therapeutics.
kw: Nucleic acid-small molecule interaction, druglikeness, DNA repeat expansion, DNA-RNA hybrid, chemotherapy

title: The role of sound in courtship and male-male competition in Bicyclus butterflies
abs: Butterflies have been shown to rely on visual signals in the form of wing patterns and on pheromones to exercise mate choice. The role of sound, however, in butterfly intraspecific communication has never been assessed. Many butterfly species display ritualized rapid wing flickering during courtship to attract mates. These wing flicks can lead to production of sound signals inaudible to human ears but potentially audible to butterflies. In recent years, there is growing evidence of increasing anthropogenic noise affecting invertebrate populations. Given the lack of evidence of acoustic communication in butterflies, they are not considered for this area of study. Many butterfly species are important pollinators and fulfil many ecosystem services, making it imperative to explore their reliance on acoustic cues for reproduction. We aim to fill this gap by exploring acoustic communication in the African satyrine butterfly species Bicyclus anynana. In this research proposal we first demonstrate a possible role of acoustic signals in courtship in Bicyclus anynana, wherein we show that the males may be listening to conspecific male sounds in male-male competition. We then propose a series of experiments to understand acoustic communication in the context of mating in Bicyclus anynana and investigate the molecular correlates of sound perception in the brain. Specifically, we aim to 1) Determine the sounds produced by males during courtship and investigate the role of male courtship sounds in male-male competition and female mate choice; 2) Investigate the role of male-specific silver scales in courtship sound production; 3) Determine the vibrational characteristics of the tympanal membrane (hearing organ) in WS and DS forms; 4) Determine the molecular mechanisms of courtship sound perception and identify the regions in the brain involved in sound processing. Follow up experiments should 1) examine whether anthropogenic sounds might be interfering with butterfly communication and contributing to the worldwide butterfly population decline; 2) use knowledge generated in this proposal to help develop biocontrol methods of interruption of intraspecific communication in pests using acoustics along with trapping and monitoring of pests.
kw: insects, sound, laser vibrometer, courtship behaviour, tympanal membranes, sexual selection

title: Breaking the Box -- On Security of Cryptographic Devices.
abs: a) Significance One of the significant challenges in the modern era of cryptography was the emergence of side-channel attacks. These attacks don’t break the mathematical foundations, which are too strong. Instead, attackers started exploiting vulnerabilities in the implementation or doing things beyond the scope of formal security definitions. Previously, cryptographic devices were thought of as black boxes with a secret key and a strictly defined input/output interface. However, no device is truly a black box, since it consumes electricity, emits electromagnetic radiation, has a heat signature, and a running time, which were not accounted for in the clean black box security model. This gave rise to the first wave of passive attacks, where attackers could exploit side-channel information like the aforementioned factors and use them to break the security of the device. Such side information is often called leakage, and attackers who exploit it are known as passive adversaries. Active attacks, on the other hand, involve the attacker actively interfering with the system. For example, an attacker may maliciously modify some part of a device or flip values on specific gates of a device circuit. These attacks can be particularly devastating for embedded systems, such as smart cards or IoT devices, which have limited resources and are often used in critical applications. Our goal is to provide security against passive adversaries, tampering attacks, and joint leakage and tampering attacks. We propose a three-prong approach to tackle these problems, via study of Leakage, Non-malleability and Randomness. Those angles are fundamentally connected. We aim to make progress in every of the three fields. Finally, we note the new, unique challenges those fields face with the emergence of new technologies like blockchain or artificial intelligence. b) Research Questions First angle is the study of Leakage: In order to provide a formal security analysis in the presence of leakage we first need a precise definition and model of leakage. There is a large body of models that can be partitioned into two groups: efficient and theoretical models. Efficient models reflect very closely the power of leakage (as observed in practical experiments) but lack the mathematical elegance that would allow for easy construction of protocols secure in those models. We have already started a work in unifying those models and showed various reductions between them. Ultimately, we’d like to propose and experimentally test the new leakage models that offer a better balance between efficiency and ease of use. Then we’d like to deepen our understanding of leakage resilience of basic objects like secret sharing etc. Second angle is the study of Non-malleability: Non-malleability is a natural extension of error correction and error detection codes. Non-malleability captures exactly what we require to prevent related key attacks and guarantees that data after tampering is either preserved or
kw: Tamper-resilient cryptography, leakage-resilient cryptography, randomness

title: Towards Harmonious Transitions to Post-Quantum Cryptography: Technical Challenges and Innovative Approaches
abs: Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) refers to conventional cryptosystems that are secure against both quantum and classic attacks, and can interoperate with existing communication protocols and networks. The main aims of this project are to address several prominent technical challenges regarding the ongoing transitions to PQC over communication infrastructure or contemporary devices. There are billions of old and new devices that need to transition to the PQC suite of basic algorithms, leading to a multidecadal transition process that has to account for aspects such as security, algorithm performance, ease of secure implementation, compliance, and more. Furthermore, the transitions to PQC need to be conducted and implemented at the same pace across platforms, systems and applications. However, the current state-of-affairs of the transitions are not satisfactory. On the one hand, there are still unresolved mathematical and cryptographic gaps in understanding and deploying the basic PQC primitives. On the other hand, the existing advanced PQC primitives such as multi-party computation protocols and zero-knowledge protocols – which are essential components for many applications in cloud computing, big data and blockchains – are still underdeveloped, compared to the basic primitives. In other words, the transitions to PQC so far are not harmonious, due to the gaps between existing PQC systems and their classical counterparts as well as the gaps between the basic PQC primitives being standardized and the underdeveloped advanced PQC primitives. The present project precisely aims to fill in these gaps. In the process, these technical challenges will be tackled via novel ideas innovative approaches.
kw: Cryptography; Post-quantum; zero-knowledge proof; secure multiparty computation; Security Analysis; Side channel attacks

title: Long-time Simulation of Open Quantum Systems for Spin Chains and Non-relativistic Particles
abs: Open quantum systems refer to quantum mechanical systems that interact with external quantum systems, which are known as the environment or the bath. In reality, all quantum systems are more or less coupled with the environment, causing an irreversible evolution of the system due to loss of information to the bath (quantum dissipation). Particles in an open quantum system are also less entangled due to the interaction with the bath, which is termed as quantum decoherence. Open quantum systems have wide applications in many fields including quantum computation, chemical physics, quantum optics and quantum sensing. An accurate simulation of system-bath coupling is of high importance in order to obtain an accurate understanding of quantum systems. As Singapore is investing a large amount of fund to support the development of quantum technologies, the study of open quantum systems will also contribute to the theoretical understanding of behavior of quantum systems. Additionally, the numerical methods of open quantum systems have not yet been widely studied in the mathematical community. It is meaningful to discover more mathematical insights in this field, and the results may also shed some light on other areas in computational mathematics. However, the numerical simulation of open quantum system is highly challenging. The path integral method is a classical and very general method for such simulations, but an infinite series of high-dimensional integrals must be evaluated. In this project, we take the following hypotheses which are widely accepted: 1. The bath is modelled by non-interacting harmonic oscillators. 2. Earlier history has weaker effect on the evolution of the system. 3. The system is a spin chain or some non-relativistic particles modelled by the Schrödinger equation. The aim of this project is to develop efficient algorithms for long-time simulations. For spin chains, we target at a chain of at least 20 spins, and for non-relativistic particles, we expect to perform simulations for at least one particle in the three-dimensional space. The simulation should be done on a cluster supporting 1280 processes. The feasibility of the study is mainly based on our extensive preliminary study of open quantum systems. The major difficulties in the simulation of open quantum systems include 1. The path-integral formulation contains high-dimensional integrals. 2. The state space of the system is of high dimensionality. 3. The computational cost for the integrand grows factorially with respect to the number of dimensions. 4. The evolution depends on the entire history. In our preliminary studies, we have developed algorithms to tackle or alleviate all these problems, including: 1. title: Genome mining for peptide natural products and biosynthetic enzymes
abs: Natural products and their derivatives are the source of more than half of the antibiotics that are currently used. Genome-sequenced bacteria and bioinformatic analysis has informed us that the majority of natural products have not been characterized and represent next-generation antimicrobial agents. To gain access to these new and potentially therapeutic small molecules this project will focus on a large and diverse natural product class known as ribosomally synthesized and posttranslationally modified peptides (RiPPs). A significant number of these peptide natural products have been found to contain broad and narrow spectrum antimicrobial activities. Since the majority of RiPP natural products in bacterial genomes have not been characterized and their true number remains enigmatic strategies to uncover their biochemistry, chemical structures and bioactivities are important for drug discovery efforts. We will use innovative and multidisciplinary chemical, biochemical, and biological techniques to dissect two chemically different RiPP biosynthetic pathways encoding new peptide natural products. During this project we will biochemically characterize the key posttranslational modifying enzymes and produce and elucidate the structure of the natural products. These studies will yield new sequence-function space to study a novel class of enzymes and new chemical space for antimicrobial screening. The outcome will provide new classes of peptide natural products which can then be screened in various biological assays. Antimicrobial natural products from this project will serve as important lead compounds and intellectual property for further development.
kw: natural products, peptides, enzymes, biosynthesis, antibiotics

title: Computational light and image sensors enabling ubiquitous and beyond-visible sense of color in standard CMOS systems
abs: Image sensors and their single-pixel form of light detectors are well known to be among the classes of sensors with highest growth (10.3% CAGR from 2020 to 2025 – see Markets&Markets market research report, March 2021), in view of the fast-rising demand for vision and physical context awareness in a wide range of silicon chips. The demand is driven by prominent applications ranging from visual scene monitoring, to machine vision and light spectral quality monitoring (e.g., human health, plant growth tracking), among the many others. More recently, such demand includes multi-spectral sensing beyond visible in near infrared (NIR) and near ultraviolet (NUV) to enrich feature extraction for substantially improved machine vision (e.g., detection of small features/irregularities in NUV, features uncovered from fog in NIR). Standard CMOS image and light sensing are easily embedded in common silicon systems via inexpensive integration with any other sub-system on the same silicon chip (e.g., machine learning for scene analysis, radiofrequency circuits for wireless communications with the cloud), without requiring any large-volume manufacturing process change. However, standard CMOS image sensors are inherently monochromatic and indiscriminately combine light from near ultraviolet (NUV) to near infrared (NIR) range. On the other hand, color discrimination is achieved by adopting special CMOS Image Sensor (CIS) processes with color filters deposited on top of the chip to discard unintended spectral content (e.g., NIR-cut filter to sense the visible range only, color filter array (CFA) to isolate red-green-blue RGB spectral components). Unfortunately, color filters added through CSI processes are 1) inflexible with a rigidly fixed choice of wavelength ranges (e.g., NIR) and/or sub-ranges (e.g., RGB), prohibiting spectral reconfigure-ability based on the sensing task at hand (as required in machine vision) 2) offer limited spectral component availability (e.g., three RGB colors), prohibiting sensing at user-specified wavelengths and any feature extraction quality improvement for machine vision (e.g., extracting features visible in a specific band to overcome limited visibility/lighting conditions) 3) prohibit low-cost standard CMOS manufacturing and single-chip integration with any other silicon sub-system (e.g., post-processing, machine learning, radios), due to the requirement of CIS-specific process such as CFA and wafer stacking to integrate photosensors with other necessary circuitry. In prior art in standard CMOS technology, color filter-less imager sensors were introduced by Caltech/Sigma based on wavelength-dependent absorption, although at a rigidly fixed and limited spectral response (visible, RGB). title: Universality of Kardar-Parisi Zhang physics in quantum platforms: Random Quantum Circuits, Anderson localization and Exciton-Polaritons.
abs: The Kardar-Parisi-Zhang (KPZ) equation was introduced in 1986 to describe the growth of rough surfaces and has since become an exciting area of research due to its striking universality. KPZ physics has been shown to govern very different classical physical phenomena, and recently has been even observed in quantum systems, where it has been shown to correctly describe the growth of correlations. The study of KPZ universality in quantum systems has only just started. It has been found recently in numerical investigation in certain class of quantum circuits, and in Anderson-localized wavefunctions, and both theoretically and experimentally in a many-body state of light akin to a condensate. These systems are very different in nature and yet, the findings and approaches developed in a given platform can be used as a guide to acquire new knowledge in the other platforms. Owing to the notion of universality which is at the heart of the KPZ physics, we expect this cross-fertilization process to be particularly fruitful. The potential results have important implications for a wide range of fields, including condensed matter physics, quantum information science, and quantum optics. This project aims to explore the physics of KPZ universality in three different quantum platforms: quantum circuits, Anderson localization, and exciton-polaritons. Quantum circuits have been utilized to investigate important aspects of quantum information processing, as well as quantum many-body systems, including the growth of entanglement. Anderson localization stands as a crucial condensed matter phenomenon that impedes diffusive transport in the presence of disorder. Exciton-polaritons offer a paradigmatic example of a driven-dissipative quantum fluid, which can exhibit condensation similar to ultra-cold atoms. Despite their inherent differences, these platforms have all recently demonstrated signatures of KPZ physics. This project aims to bring together experts from these platforms in Singapore, fostering collaborative exploration and characterization of the profound analogies between these systems provided by KPZ physics through a cross-fertilization process. Within the Anderson localization platform, which holds the most advanced analogy with KPZ physics and will serve as a guiding principle for progress in the other platforms, this project aims to delve into dynamic glassy properties suggested by the KPZ physics analogy. The project will also explore the interplay between classical KPZ effects and quantum effects induced by factors like magnetic fields or topological properties. In the realm of quantum circuits, our strategy involves initially establishing more deeply the analogy with KPZ physics using Clifford gates, followed by an investigation into the connection with glassy physics as in Anderson localization. Subsequently, we intend to probe how KPZ physics influences the stability of clean circuits against noise. This investigation will encompass both Clifford ci

title: Droplet and spray combustion of liquid ammonia as a fuel
abs: With the aim of achieving carbon-neutral energy solutions, this project investigates the feasibility of employing liquid ammonia as a direct combustion fuel for power. The research objectives include: (a) Design experiments to study the combustion of ammonia droplets and sprays and utilize mathematical modelling and high-fidelity simulations to analyze the intrinsic physical phenomena; (b) Investigate the mechanism of atomization, stable combustion, and pollutant formation of liquid ammonia under typical operating conditions; and (c) Develop a fundamental theory of liquid ammonia evaporation and combustion. The project employs a multidisciplinary approach involving experimental investigation, numerical simulation, and theoretical analysis. Experimental efforts focus on specialized setups for studying single droplet and spray combustion of liquid ammonia, yielding detailed insights into combustion characteristics, flame dynamics, and emissions. Concurrently, high-fidelity numerical simulations are conducted to model the complex inter-process interactions under varying conditions. Additionally, theoretical analysis formulates a dedicated theory for liquid ammonia combustion by integrating experimental data and numerical simulations. Key deliverables of this project include enhanced numerical codes for droplet and spray combustion simulations, detailed experimental datasets and fundamental theories customized to liquid ammonia, as well as the advanced measurement and imaging techniques. The significance of the proposed research lies in its contribution to advancing low-carbon emission technologies through the utilization of liquid ammonia as a direct combustion fuel. The project novelty emerges from its innovative methodology, incorporating modular experimental setups and specialized diagnostic tools, high-fidelity simulations, and formulation of fundamental combustion theories for liquid ammonia.
kw: Ammonia, droplet evaporation, spray combustion, constant-volume chamber, high-fidelity simulation, asymptotic theoretical analysis

title: Design of enzyme-like DNA catalysts for asymmetric catalysis
abs: Catalysis plays an indispensable and multifaceted role in our contemporary society. It underpins a myriad of essential functions ranging from the large-scale production of chemical compounds on megaton scales to the meticulous synthesis of life-saving pharmaceuticals. Furthermore, catalysis serves as the driving force behind a diverse array of foundational research disciplines and their practical applications, including drug discovery and development, the advancement of environmentally sustainable and renewable energy technologies, and more. At the heart of catalytic processes lies the catalyst, which operates as the linchpin within a catalytic cycle. By lowering the activation energy and expediting chemical reactions, the catalyst exerts control over reaction pathways and selectivity. A striking dichotomy emerges when comparing the catalyst design strategies employed by nature and human. Nature employs intricate enzyme architectures, where active sites intricately engage with reactants through a spectrum of interactions—such as electrostatic attraction, hydrogen bonding, hydrophobic interactions, and π-π stacking. This orchestration results in remarkable enhancements in reaction rates, precise selectivity, and heightened substrate specificity. However, this high degree of specificity constrains the scope of reactions and substrates that enzymes can catalyze. Conversely, man-made catalysts exhibit simpler structures, fewer interaction modalities, and diminished specificity. As a consequence, while human-designed catalysts find extensive utility across various reaction types, they generally fall short in achieving the efficiency and selectivity exhibited by enzymes, particularly in specific reactions. To reconcile the superior attributes of enzymes with the versatile nature of small-molecule catalysts, we propose a synergistic approach. This approach involves fusing the programmable, intricate, and chiral attributes of DNA with carefully selected small-molecule catalysts, culminating in the creation of enzyme-mimicking DNA catalysts, with a specific focus on asymmetric catalysis. The distinct molecular recognition capabilities of DNA, facilitated by Watson-Crick base pairings and complementary interactions, permit facile and tailored structural modifications to accommodate diverse substrate geometries within bespoke chiral environments. Pioneering a novel "mutagenesis" methodology, we aim to systematically probe the interplay between DNA sequence and structure, and the resultant outcomes of chemical reactions, encompassing both reactivity and selectivity. This deepened understanding will guide the strategic design of enzyme-like DNA catalysts, poised to address a wide spectrum of asymmetric transformations. The overarching ambition of this proposal is threefold: firstly, to establish a universally accessible enzymatic conjugation technique; secondly, to expand the horizons of DNA-mediated asymmetric catalysis; and finally, to enhance our comprehen

title: Unravelling the Role of Native Probiotics Mixture in Conferring Disease Resistance across Fish Species in Aquaculture
abs: Singapore is taking purposeful steps toward fulfilling her audacious “30-by-30” vision – to increase local food production to 30% by 2030, with fish as one of the key food source. With an increasing demand for food fish, along with a depleting supply of marine-harvested fish, food fish industries are now shifting their focus towards aquaculture production. However, aquaculture fish is constantly exposed to environmental fluctuations and pathogens, making them susceptible to diseases, especially at its early life stages. Pathogenic infections raise fish mortality, affect their growth rates, thus impacting aquaculture productivity. In aquaculture, antibiotics, vaccination and probiotics are three strategies for disease management. However, the use of antibiotics and vaccinating juvenile fishes have their challenges. Probiotics on the other hand is starting to show promise to boost fish immunity when supplemented into feeds. However, most commercial probiotics used in aquaculture are from terrestrial sources, which are expensive and unstable in an aquaculture environment. On the other hand, native probiotics derived from the gut of fish is considered a better alternative because of their ability to adapt and better perform in their native environment. This project therefore seeks to address two key research questions: 1. Will a mixture of anti-pathogenic native probiotics perform better than a single strain?; and 2. Can this native probiotic mixture be used across other fish species against diseases? Addressing these questions will enable the concoction of a native probiotics mixture that can be universally employed across different fish species against emerging infections. In addressing these hypotheses, our aim is first, to investigate the impact of native probiotics isolated from freshwater and marine species and their combination against fish pathogens; and second, to evaluate if an optimal combination can confer maximal disease resistance across other fish species. To achieve these aims, this project will address the following five objectives, in a sequential manner: 1. Identifying and isolating native probiotics from gut microbiome of healthy fish; 2. In vitro evaluation of single and combination native probiotics against three pathogens of V. harveyi, A. hydrophila, and S. iniae; 3. Encapsulation of single strain probiotics and combination probiotics; 4. In vivo challenge test of single and combination probiotics against pathogen; 5. Gut microbiome and immunity assessment of juvenile fish of Asian seabass and Mozambique tilapia after pathogenic challenge.Meeting these objectives will allow us to address to the hypothesis if a combination of native probiotic mixture in fish feeds will enhance disease resistance of aquaculture fish because of suitable native probiotic colonization of their guts. The supplementation of fish feeds with probiotics is an approach that will have greater acceptance and significance as this can be applied to all fishe

title: Cellular and molecular explorations of blood stage dormancy of malaria parasites and its role in drug resistance.
abs: This research proposal will focus on the newly emerging aspect of malaria infection, blood stage dormancy. It has been long speculated that the recrudescence of malaria infection after a seemingly successful course of chemotherapeutic treatment rises from a latent parasite stage that remains in the patient's body as a hidden reservoir. Our preliminary study developed a robust laboratory model for a putative latent dormant stage of the deadliest malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum. Here we will capitalize on this and carry out comprehensive molecular and cellular characterizations of the P. falciparum dormancy to evaluate its significance for key aspects of malaria epidemics including transmission and drug resistance. For that, we will carry out systems-wide (omics) characterizations and genome-wide screens to categorize metabolic and cellular processes driving dormancy and at the same time identify key factors (genes/proteins) that regulate its induction, maturation, maintenance, and re-emergence to proliferation. With this knowledge, we will develop a quantitative assay to estimate the potential for dormancy in distinct P. falciparum strains induced by varying external conditions and stimuli. This assay will be particularly applied to a panel of malaria parasites with various degrees of drug resistance to assess the role of dormancy in drug resistance. Using the Mass Spectroscopy-linked Cellular Thermal Shift Assay (MS-CETSA) we will also evaluate the druggability of the P. falciparum dormant stages. Altogether, the successful completion of this project can bring invaluable insight into a crucial, previously undetermined blood stage dormancy and its role in the overall patterns of malaria infections.

title: Structural and morphological adaptations of influenza A viruses to facilitate high transmissibility
abs: Influenza A viruses (IAVs) cause persistent global threat. We will investigate their structural adaptations underlying transmissibility. Employing a multidisciplinary approach, it delves into IAV pleomorphism, deciphering mechanisms and implications for viral fitness and immune recognition. By using cryo-electron tomography, air-liquid interface culture, and mutagenesis, we will study the ultrastructure of IAVs and determine high-resolution structures of viral proteins in situ, which will allows us to uncover their impacts on viral replication, transmissibility, and assembly. Insights gained in this study will inform strategies to disrupt viral dynamics and mitigate infection, offering a multifaceted understanding of transmissibility and pathogenesis for improved public health outcomes.

title: Pathogenicity islands bypass the SOS response to induce prophage activation.
abs: The Staphylococcus aureus pathogenicity islands (SaPIs) are a family of highly mobile genetic elements that carry genes for superantigens and toxins. They are prototypical members of the phage-inducible chromosomal islands (PICIs) found in gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria, and they are regarded as molecular parasites because they exploit bacteriophages (phages), the viruses of bacteria, for their reproduction and dissemination. Normally, SaPIs reside quiescently in the chromosomes of their S. aureus hosts under the maintenance of their master repressor Stl. Their life cycles are activated by the phages that they parasitize, following the formation of a complex between Stl and “helper” phage-encoded antirepressor proteins that lift Stl repression and initiate the SaPI excision-replication-packaging (ERP) program. To date, numerous helper phage-encoded SaPI antirepressor proteins have been identified. However, there are currently no reports of SaPI-encoded proteins that trigger prophages to initiate the lytic cycle. Herein we report the discovery that SaPIs can induce prophage activation. We discovered that when SaPI1, SaPI2, or SaPIbov1 were introduced into strains that were lysogenic for specific phages (ΦNM1, Φ52A, and Φ85), the prophages became extremely unstable and were rapidly cured from the SaPI-containing cells. Mutants of SaPI1 that lost the ability to induce prophage instability were isolated, and the mutations mapped to SaPI1 open reading frame (ORF) 18. Furthermore, the expression of SaPI1 ORF18 alone in a strain lysogenic for ΦNM1 was sufficient to induce prophage activation, independent of the SOS response that is normally required for prophage induction. Based on these early findings, we hypothesize that the SaPIs encode proteins that bypass the bacterial SOS response and directly induce prophages to enter the lytic cycle. The primary objective of this study is to fully characterize and understand the process underlying SaPI-induced prophage induction. To achieve this objective, a set of carefully designed genetic selections will be employed, along with protein biochemistry, to elucidate how SaPIs relieve the repression of lysogenic prophages at the molecular level. Specifically, we will begin by verifying the SaPI1 ORF18 homologs present in SaPI2 (ORF7) and SaPIbov1 (ORF16) as SaPI phage inducers (spi) genes by mutational analysis. We will also set up a genetic selection to identify mutants in phages ΦNM1, Φ52A, and Φ85 that are no longer inducible by Spi proteins to identify the phage de-repression target (pdt) genes. Second, we will identify non-synonymous point mutations in Spi proteins (Spi*) that are incapable of inducing prophage activation. We will then use these Spi* mutants to screen for Pdt suppressors (PdtSup) that restore protein interactions. Lastly, we will confirm Spi-Pdt and Spi*-PdtSup interactions by bacterial two-hybrid and affinity tag pull-down analyses, followed by determining the protein crystal struc

title: Automated, low-chemical, spent Lithium-ion batteries processing system for sustainable metal and leachate recovery
abs: The global demand for lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) is projected to witness a significant upsurge from 500GWh to over 2000GWh between 2023 and 2030, primarily driven by escalating demand for electric vehicles (EVs). This rapid adoption of EVs will lead to the cumulative generation of 11 million tons of spent LIBs by 2030, which must be handled as electronic waste according to end-of-life Vehicle Management laws. Recycling spent LIBs is therefore critical to sustain resources, economy, and the environment by reducing dependence on fresh mining and minimizing the amount of toxic waste disposal. Currently, less than 5% of spent LIBs are recycled into valuable resources. The low recycling rate is mainly attributed by the challenges associated with existing recycling processes such as high temperature, chemical consumption and generation and discharge of toxic wastes that negatively impact the environment. In addition, conventional recycling methods such as Hydrometallurgy necessitate a series of energy, cost, and labour-intensive chemical and physical treatment processes. Hence, in this project, we will develop a membrane-integrated spent LIB processing system that is modular, automated, and low-chemical. The proposed integrated system will consist of a three-step sequence: pre-treatment, separation, and purification. First, the pre-treatment unit will be based on a sequencing batch reactor (SBR) and an ultrafiltration (UF) process to remove solids and fine particles. This automated pre-treatment unit will simplify the labour-intensive pre-treatment process and will help in enhancing the purity of final products (metal & leachate). Then, the separation unit will comprise of a proprietary positively charged nanofiltration membrane to retain and concentrate the multivalent salts (e.g., nickel) for selective precipitation using less chemicals. This proprietary charged membrane will also promote the selective separation of Lithium from other multivalent ions, enabling high purity Lithium recovery. Finally, the purification unit will be an ion exchange membrane separation process for lithium extraction. The purification unit enables the recovery of lithium as well as the leachate that could be reused back in the pre-treatment step. The proposed integrated system is expected to improve the economics of LIB recycling by reducing the labour reliance, chemical consumption by at least 20% and waste generation by up to 70% compared to the conventional recycling methods. Our approach is sustainable as by-products are upcycled (where possible), thus embracing circular economy.

title: EzHolo: the ultimate solution for glasses-free 3D displays
abs: Virtual Reality (VR) and Augmented Reality (AR) have attracted much attention from academics and industry in recent years. However, for VR/AR applications, the users need to wear head-mounted displays which normally come in bulky size and is difficult for users to carry around. This limits the applications of VR/AR for full-day applications, especially in public spaces. Glasses-free 3D display technologies allow viewers to directly view and perceive 3D image without wearing glasses. However, although glasses-free 3D displays have been developed for years with commercial products available in the market, there are still two remaining key challenges that hinder their wide adoption. First, glasses-free 3D displays normally achieve satisfying 3D viewing experiences for only a few specific fixed viewing regions (sweet spots) due to the static and regular pattern of the optical layer placed on top of the 2D display and it is also a challenge to achieve high-accuracy requirements for the manufacturing process to achieve the sweet spots. Secondly, glasses-free 3D displays require the raw content to be in 3D format in order to synthesize images from different viewing directions. The 3D content can be created in a manual manner or through 3D scanning but both methods lead to high cost. In this project, we aim to develop the ultimate solution for glasses-free 3D displays (named “EzHolo” in short) to address the abovementioned two key challenges. To allow 3D viewing experience for all visible regions, we will develop a deep-learning empowered method for universal and efficient spatial calibration of glasses-free 3D displays. A deep neural network (DNN) will be trained to obtain the mapping relationship between the viewer’s eye position and each display element (e.g., a pixel on an LCD) on a given glasses-free 3D display). With the trained DNN, the positions of the viewer's eyes will be tracked and the image on the glasses-free 3D display will be updated in real time such that the view’s left and right eye will perceive stereoscopic 3D images for 3D experience respectively. To facilitate the content generation for glasses-free 3D displays, we will develop a deep-learning empowered method to automatically convert normal 2D content (e.g., photos or videos taken from a smart phone) into 3D content suitable for the target autostereoscopic 3D display. In this way, the user can simply select 2D content and our method is able to automatically convert it to 3D content and then generate the final high-quality content suitable for the target glasses-free 3D display. Our proposed EzHolo solution represents the ultimate breakthrough solution for glasses-free 3D displays and stands a high chance for huge economic and social impact for applications in a wide spectrum of sectors, such as gaming, entertainment, education, medical visualization, design, etc. It can be deployed to empower the existing glasses-free 3D displays or can be used to develop a new glasses-free 3D dis

title: Soil Conditioning Design for Earth Pressure Balance Machine in Tunnelling
abs: Earth Pressure Balance (EPB) shields are widely employed in tunnelling projects in Singapore, especially in cohesive soils, soft grounds, and mixed-face conditions. The effectiveness of soil conditioning in EPB tunnelling is pivotal for ensuring safety, stability, and efficiency. However, the lack of standardized methods for soil conditioner selection has led to trial-and-error approaches, hindering the reliable and optimized design of conditioning agents. To address this critical knowledge gap and enhance tunnelling operations in Singapore, this research proposes a comprehensive quantitative soil conditioner selection framework based on rigorous laboratory testing and the development of a specialized Screw Conveyor Extraction Test (SCET) equipment. The framework aims to determine the optimal mixes and quantities of commercial soil conditioners suitable for local soils encountered during tunnelling. Extensive laboratory testing will be conducted, including slump tests and foam stability tests with different conditioning sets. By quantifying the plasticity, workability, and stability of conditioned soils, the framework will establish valuable design charts and empirical correlations. Notably, this research will focus on assessing the technical performance of eco-friendly soil conditioners, aiming to promote sustainable tunnelling practices. Given the upcoming Cross Island Line's prevalence in the Old Alluvium (OA) formation, particular attention will be given to soils from this formation to establish quantitative links between different foam types and specific ground conditions. The SCET equipment, a key component of this research, will replicate dynamic tunnelling conditions and facilitate the assessment of conditioned soil extraction. Designed with adjustable inclination angles, the equipment can closely resemble actual tunnelling scenarios, where changes in face pressure directly impact the extraction rate and required foam injection control. This innovative equipment will enable the evaluation of the conditioned soil's ability to control and apply confining pressure within the bulk chamber, providing valuable insights into the torque of the screw conveyor and the conditioned soil's control of pressure inside the screw conveyor. The feasibility of this research is supported by the well-established laboratory testing methods used worldwide to quantify conditioned soil behaviour. Collaborative efforts with Shanghai Tunnel Engineering Co (Singapore) Pte Ltd (STECS) ensure access to sufficient Old Alluvium (OA) soil samples for testing, validating the equipment's performance. Moreover, the SCET equipment will not only enhance research capabilities at the Centre for Infrastructure and Tunnelling Engineering (CITE) at the Singapore Institute of Technology (SIT) but also offer potential commercial testing services to the industry. The significance of this research to the tunnelling industry in Singapore cannot be overstated. The quantitative soil cond
