title: Knowledge graph-based AI closed-loop management system (KG-AICLM) for urban farming to improve crop yield and risk management.
abs: Farming efficiency will be improved if there is a certainty in the seed’s quality and automating the farming management process. Although there are research papers showing that there is a relationship between the seed appearance and their physiological performance, this specialised farming knowledge is usually not used in current farming due its complexity and difficulty in implementing. In using AI, we could collect, train, implement and automate the process seamlessly. We proposed a Knowledge Graph-based Artificial Intelligence Closed-Loop Management System (KG-AICLM). The data is collected using high precision camera with robotics to automate the data collection process. The damaged area on the seed or poor physiology crop will be identified using you only look once (YOLO) object detection. The area of interest will be segmented into different domains (micropyle, seed coating, yellowish spot on the leaf etc.) with segment anything models from META (formerly known as Facebook). These classified domains will be stored in the graph database with AI reasoning assigning the weights to establish the possible relationship and outcome. The main challenge is that, under limited supervision, it is extremely difficult to synthesize photo-realistic and highly diverse images, while acquiring representative characters of the target, which we could resolve during the first few cycles in our investigation. Two modules will be imported to the generator and the discriminator respectively. An attribute adaptor into the generator freezing the parameters from existing academia study, the prior knowledge could be reused to a certain extent, maintaining the synthesis quality and diversity. A well-learned discriminator backbone with an attribute classifier ensures that the generator captures the appropriate characters from the reference and new information from our data. With the limited data in prior works, the method shows that it works well even with large domain gaps, and robustly converges within a few minutes for each experiment.
kw: Artificial intelligence (AI), Agriculture, Robotics, Computer Vision, Knowledge Graph

title: Harnessing mast cells to improve antigen presentation and adaptive immune responses
abs: Antigen-presenting cells (APCs) uptake antigens and present them to T cells, providing contextual cues that drive immune activation and the clearance of harmful substances, such as infections or tumors. This crucial process is primarily carried out by professional APCs, such as dendritic cells (DCs), which transport antigens to draining lymph nodes for presentation. In contrast to DCs, mast cells (MCs) are primarily known as immune sentinels. They are found in peripheral tissues and at the host-environment interface, often undergoing degranulation upon triggering by exogenous antigens. Here we hypothesize that MCs are an unexpected partner in the communication between professional APCs and T cells. Our preliminary data show that MCs not only directly interact with T cells in vivo forming immune synapses with them, but that their granules bind to antigens and facilitate their uptake by DCs. Granules are primarily formed of MC-specific proteases that are known to cleave proteins at unique sites in comparison to the proteases used by DCs, which raises the possibility that proteins could be cleaved into unique antigenic peptides in the presence of MCs. Thus, we will also evaluate the hypothesis that MC-specific proteases generate novel peptide antigens and deliver them to DCs for subsequent antigen presentation to T cells. Additionally, we will employ advanced spatial transcriptomics techniques to identify the communication networks among MCs, DCs, and T cells during the initiation of adaptive immune responses. Finally, this knowledge will be leveraged to evaluate novel MC protease-based immunotherapeutics with potential applications in combating infections and treating cancers.
kw: Mast cell; antigen presentation; protease; antigen

title: Understanding and remodeling microbial communities to prevent the spread of antimicrobial resistant pathogens
abs: The global rise in antimicrobial resistance (AMR) rates for common pathogens (e.g. ESKAPE) is recognized as a pre-eminent threat to healthcare systems. As the range of effective antibiotics shrinks we approach a tipping point where no antibiotic works for a pathogen, putting at risk the lives of millions of vulnerable patients in hospitals worldwide. Our current approaches to tackle AMR are largely reactive, waiting for infections to happen rather than proactively targeting key pathogen reservoirs to prevent infections (e.g. hospital environments or the human gut). We propose an ecological approach to target environmental and human reservoirs of antimicrobial resistance by leveraging microbial competition to suppress pathogens. To do this we plan to synergize advances in metagenomics, single-cell technologies and AI to understand how microbial communities assemble in a Deconstruct-Model-Reconstruct framework. Specifically our objectives are to: (i) Deconstruct complex microbial communities into constituent strains, genomes and functions, (ii) Model ecological rules of community assembly via high-throughput combinatorial culturing, and (iii) Reconstruct stable community configurations in vitro and in vivo that robustly inhibit multiple pathogens. By understanding how microbial communities naturally suppress pathogenic species, we hope to catalyse an alternative strategy for tackling one of the greatest challenges facing humanity in the form of antimicrobial resistant pathogens and their reservoirs. In addition, by designing and utilizing microbial consortia effectively, mixing and matching existing strains as parts in our toolbox, we can effectively leverage the rich microbial diversity present in Singapore that is adapted to our environment and lifestyles for a range of applications including agriculture (biofertilizers), food production (fermentation and food safety), bioremediation, manufacturing of speciality chemicals and biotherapeutics. The foundational technologies developed as part of this proposal will thus serve as resources for the scientific community in Singapore working in these diverse fields. Finally, the technologies developed in this proposal can contribute to understanding how microbes colonize different parts of the body, communicate with host cells, respond to perturbations and influence disease biology, thus having a transformative impact on biomedical research.
kw: Antimicrobial Resistance; Metagenomics; Microbial Ecology; Biotherapeutics

title: Computational Hardness of Lattice Problems and Implications
abs: A lattice L ⊂ Rn is the set of all integer linear combinations of linearly independent basis vectors b1, . . . , bn ∈ Rn. The most important computational problems associated with lattices are the γ-Shortest Vector Problem (γ-SVP), and the γ-Closest Vector Problem (γ- CVP) which are parameterized by an approximation factor γ ≥ 1. Given a basis for a lattice L ⊂ Rn, and a bound d > 0, γ-SVP asks us to approximate the length of the shortest non-zero vector in the lattice by a factor γ. Given a basis for a lattice L ⊂ Rn, a target vector t ∈ Rn, γ-CVP asks us to approximate the distance of the target vector from the lattice by a factor at most γ. Here, we define length and distance in terms of the Euclidean norm (though, in the sequel, we sometimes work with arbitrary norms). Another computational problem that is very closely related to these lattice problems is the integer programming problem. The problem asks to find integers x1, . . . , xn that satisfies a system of m linear inequalities in x1, . . . , xn. Integer programming is one of the most important problems in discrete optimization.

title: Multifunctional Organic Materials with Persistent Luminescence
abs: The generation, stabilization, and transfer of triplet excitons in organic molecular and hybrid systems could create breakthroughs in the development of organic light-emitting diodes, organic semiconductor lasers, and photodynamic therapy, among many others. For most organic luminescent materials, triplet excitons are generally dark states due to the spin-forbidden nature of intersystem crossing (ISC) between singlet and triplet states and non-radiative losses of the excited energy. The proposal aims to establish a new principle in effectively harvesting and utilizing triplet excitons, which will allow us to develop multifunctional organic materials with persistent luminescence. Specifically, we will focus on creating charge-separated states through a machine-learning guided and precisely designed doping process to develop (i) materials with ultralong lifetimes and time-dependent tuneable emissions; (ii) materials with persistent mechanoluminescence; and (iii) afterglow photosensitizers for emerging applications in security marking, anti-counterfeiting, information encryption, and theranostics. This study will also allow us to reveal the impurity conundrum in organic luminescent materials and correct many structural-property mistakes in the literature.

title: High-resolution, Portable, Microwave Holographic Imaging (MHI) system for real-time visualization and analysis of concealed structures & defects in Engineered Facades
abs: By advancing the radar imaging technology and signal processing algorithms, we aim to develop portable and safe NDT equipment that is applicable for real-time scan & data analysis of engineered facades. We aim to achieve this by 1. Our current scanning technology has an operating frequency from 400 MHz to 6 GHz. The accuracy in range and cross-range is close to 1 cm. However, for engineered facades, there is a requirement for finer accuracy to accurately detect the profile of objects/ defects and quantify them. 2. Development and enhancement of signal processing algorithms, including multi-layered focusing algorithms and diffraction tomography techniques, to enable unprecedented image fidelity. 3. Further optimization to package the scanner in a smaller form factor suitable for handheld usage and enabling real-time visualization of results. 4. Development, customization, and enhancement of AI engine to automate the process of object detection and defect detection. 5. Adding more software features to ease the deployment of engineered façade inspection applications.

title: PhENoTyping And Genotyping of yOuNg stroke in Singapore (PENTAGON-SG)
abs: Stroke is a leading cause of death and disability. Ischemic stroke in young adults accounts for 15% of all cases and carries a disproportionately high socioeconomic burden. Many young patients are unable to return to work following a stroke, with a significant proportion developing post-stroke cognitive impairment. Our preliminary study revealed that 20% of young stroke patients in Singapore have intracranial atherosclerotic disease (ICAD). ICAD is a debilitating disease and carries a high recurrent stroke rate of 20% per year even with best medical treatment. Beyond cardiovascular risk factors, recent studies have suggested an underlying genetic basis of ICAD. Several genetic variants identified in small ICAD cohorts have been implicated in angiogenesis, inflammatory, homocysteine and lipid metabolism, and renin-angiotensin aldosterone system pathways. Genes differentially expressed in ICAD are important for understanding these associated pathways. Observing the transcriptomic effects of genetic variation is an additional approach to understand the biological effects resulting from rare genetic variations. We propose the following aims in our study: 1. To characterize the genetic profile of young ischemic stroke patients with ICAD from a Singapore cohort using whole-exome sequencing (WES) to explore causative or susceptibility variants for ICAD. 2. To evaluate distinctive gene expression profiles and signatures of peripheral whole blood in ICAD patients compared to age-matched controls. 3. To perform a GWAS analyses in a large pooled cohort of ICAD patients obtained from collaborators in the International Stroke Genetics Consortium. Whilst the current understanding of ICAD genetics is limited, it is more likely that ICAD is a heterogeneous disease, with a subset of ICAD due to rare variant monogenic causes, and the majority being polygenic in nature. Precise classification of ICAD by genetic signatures will be crucial to tailoring treatment strategies and developing novel drug targets in a disease with no effective therapy.

title: Universal Design Principles for Multivalent-Ion Batteries
inst: IMRE - Institute of Materials Research and Engineering
abs: Li-ion batteries have transformed our everyday lives, powering a multitude of applications ranging from cell phones and laptops to electric vehicles and smart grids. However, the limited energy density of Li-ion batteries, together with the low abundance and high cost of Li, are spurring intensive research on beyond-Li-ion technologies. Multivalent-ion batteries such as Mg-, Zn- and Al-ion batteries are compelling candidates due to their high energy density, high abundance, low cost and improved safety. However, there is a severe lack of suitable anode, electrolyte and cathode materials for multivalent-ion batteries, which arises from a poor understanding of how nanostructures evolve and affect battery function at the electrode-electrolyte interfaces. Therefore, in this project, we propose to uncover universal design principles for multivalent-ion batteries to create a unified framework that can guide their development more generally. The big question we aim to answer is: What makes a favorable solid-electrolyte interface and cathode-electrolyte interface in Mg-, Zn- and Al-S batteries? To do so, we will investigate the composition and structure of key interfaces connecting the Mg, Zn, Al anode; electrolyte; and sulfur cathode in non-aqueous electrolytes. Advanced characterization techniques, such as near-ambient pressure X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy and cryogenic transmission electron microscopy, will be used to study non-aqueous Mg-, Zn- and Al-S batteries for the first time. The overarching aim is to create new fundamental knowledge on electrode-electrolyte interfaces and uncover broader scientific insight for the development of high-performance multivalent-ion batteries with energy density of 750 Wh/kg and cycle life of 1,500 cycles.
kw: Batteries; Energy Storage; Electrochemistry; Materials Chemistry; Interfaces

title: Harnessing distant resident memory T cells to prevent breast cancer metastasis
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Metastasis is a major cause of mortality in breast cancer patients, demanding the development of innovative prevention strategies. We made a surprising discovery that resident memory T cells (TRM) develop in distant tumor-free tissues prior to the onset of metastasis. These TRMs, derived from CXCR6+ effector T cells, provide substantial protection against metastasis. Therefore, we hypothesize that expanding the population of CXCR6+ precursor T cells and promoting their engraftment in distant tissues will enhance immune surveillance and prevent metastasis. This study aims to elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying CXCR6+ TRM formation, develop strategies to enhance their engraftment in distant tissues, and assess their clinical significance in protecting against metastasis. We will utilize single-cell RNA sequencing analysis to map the differentiation pathways of CXCR6+ TRM precursors in both animal models and human triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) samples. Tumor models employing transgenic and immunocompetent mice will be utilized to identify critical transcription factors and signaling pathways that support TRM precursor differentiation and distant engraftment. Immunogenomics analysis will validate the clinical relevance of this unique T cell population in patient cohorts. Our research team possesses extensive expertise in cancer immunology, T cell differentiation, immunogenomics, bioinformatics, and translational medicine. We have already established all necessary animal models, profiling platforms, and computation pipelines. Collaboration with physician scientists will provide clinical samples and disease expertise, while our world-class bioinformatician will support computational needs. This comprehensive study holds great potential for advancing both basic science and medicine. It addresses a critical knowledge gap in tumor immunology by investigating the distinct differentiation pathways of TEFF/EMs within the tumor microenvironment. By focusing on the unique subset of CXCR6+ TRM precursors, this research project has the potential to inform the design of neoadjuvant therapies and cell therapies for breast cancer metastasis prevention. The findings and therapeutic approaches identified may also have broader implications for metastasis prevention in diverse cancer types, contributing to the advancement of precision medicine in cancer treatment.

title: Development of Secured Components & Systems in Emerging Technologies through Hardware & Software Evaluation
abs: In this programme, 4 projects will be led by NTU and their outline is briefly elaborated as follows. Project A builds on our achievements from the CHFA core projects that investigate on techniques and approaches in evaluating the hardware security of advanced devices using failure analysis and side-channel analysis, as well as conducting forensics through these developed techniques. In this new project, the focus will be to (1) identify and study undocumented features in electronic devices such as microcontrollers, and evaluate the potential security risks through non-invasive methods; and (2) study the content extraction of memories with advanced electronics packaging technology, which will include sample imaging, image enhancement, sample preparation, and data extraction techniques. The objective of project B is to design and develop novel and practical defence methodologies and systems for strong protections over DNN accelerators. This builds on the CHFA seed project teams that studied the Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) of microprocessors and DNN hardware. Our key insight is to leverage software-hardware co-design to achieve defence in depth. For each security threat identified in the accelerator’s lifecycle, we will devise advanced algorithms in the software level for effective attack detection and mitigation, and implement lightweight modules in the hardware level to guard the DNN executions reliably. The interactions between software and hardware components can well trade-off the efficiency and reliability. With the vast potential that quantum computers may usher in, it also brings about the looming threat that it presents towards public key cryptography. Notable challenges which require immediate action include designing secure implementations for different platforms, conceptualizing evaluation and certification approaches, and detecting and migrating existing hardware and applications to be quantum resistant. In Project C, we will address these challenges by exploring the side-channel resistance in the implementation of the winners of the post-quantum cryptography (PQC) and also utilizing deep-learning (DL) for side-channel analysis (SCA). Another focus is to investigate the PQC compliance of a given software implementation or protocol, and the migration of the secure hardware and software to a quantum-safe environment. In Project D, we build on our understanding of secured design from CHFA and SOCure projects, and address the security requirements by construction through designing a high-bandwidth encrypted memory. The security requirements by construction cover four levels, (1) data encryption with a high-bandwidth architecture, (2) SCA mitigation with low area and power overheads applied to that high-bandwidth architecture, (3) hardware logic locking to enable authorization control as a preventive measure for security risk mitigations within the Integrated Circuit (IC) supply chain, and (4) camouflage IC to prevent reverse enginee

title: Host-microbial interaction pathways predictive of atopic dermatitis disease severity
abs: Background: Atopic Dermatitis (AD) is the most common skin disorder in Singapore and affects up to 20% of the population. The pathogenesis of AD is modulated through host genetics, immune dysfunction and microbial imbalances. Aims & hypotheses: We hypothesize that microbial factors and immune dysregulation exacerbate AD in a cohort of infection susceptible individuals. Differentially abundant microbial species from baseline and corresponding changes in expression of host factors and virulence genes during infections can then be used to develop point-of-care diagnostic assays for clinically relevant decision making. Aim 1: To construct and evaluate a predictive signature for disease severity and cutaneous infections in AD by associating baseline variability in in vivo host and microbial gene expression with clinical markers. Aim 2: To enable point-of-care diagnostic assays for virulent species/strains and gene products associated with infectious complications in AD by characterizing longitudinal changes in abundance of viable microbes and host/microbial gene expression changes during infectious AD flares. Methodology This is a multi-omic approach integrating clinical phenotyping, skin metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, skin barrier physiology measures and culture-based techniques to characterize skin microbial-barrier-immune dysregulation pathways in a discovery AD cohort of 40 adolescents & 40 adults with prior cutaneous microbial infections, and age-matched AD controls without prior infections, and validate these in a separate cohort of n=80 adolescents and n=80 adults. Expected outcomes are predictive and diagnostic biomarkers for infectious flares, and characterization of mechanisms and strains to develop diagnostic assays for clinical microbial biomarkers. Clinical Significance Rapid diagnostic platforms and point-of-care assays will facilitate subsequent clinical trials investigating efficacy of therapeutic strategies in at-risk patients. It will additionally support decentralised diagnostic testing, reduce turnaround time and burden on clinical laboratories, develop clinically-relevant biomarkers and novel intervention strategies such as biotherapeutic approaches to reduce the burden of microbial infections in at-risk AD patients.

title: Geo-referenced Mapping And Positioning System (GMAPS) for Automatic Generation of As-Built Building Information Model (BIM) of Underground Assets
abs: Today, the alteration works on underground assets require prior scans using Ground Penetrating Radar (GPR) and digging of trial holes. Skipping such preparations can lead to cutting of utilities, causing damages, disruption and sometimes grave danger, in the case of cooking gas. We propose to build a set of Geo-referenced Mapping And Positioning System (GMAPS) prototypes to accurately map the underground assets before they are covered during construction. These scans are then automatically converted to as-built Building Information Model (BIM), referenced to Singapore's standardized geospatial coordinate system (SYV21), so that another set of contractors can accurately relocate the underground assets with less than 100mm of error. The specific aims are to 1) design, calibrate, and measure the accuracy of GMAPS prototypes, using combination of lidar, Global Navigation Satellite Systems Real Time Kinematic (GNSS RTK), RGB+Depth cameras to map underground assets. Four variants of prototypes are handheld, excavator mounted, ground tracked robot mounted and aerial drone mounted. 2) Software is used to generate new or modify existing BIM for as-built documentation, using GMAPS with minimal to no user input. This is to automatically create as-built BIM of the assets with relevant construction information, accurate within 100mm in the SVY21 and Singapore Height Datum for x/y and z coordinates, respectively. 3) Test automation of scanning by mounting onto the excavator and using both ground robot and aerial drone that can self-navigate using existing BIM models of the construction sites. The ground and aerial robots are tested both independently and cooperatively for autonomous navigation using the building BIM as the initial map. 4) Build GMAPS Mixed Reality (MR) tablet prototype to accurately project the underground assets to the ground surface as visual aids for A&A works. 5) Review current site practices, and quantify improvement in productivity. The GMAPS hardware and software are designed to require minimal user effort and inputs to operate robustly. This is expected to reduce the manpower, such as registered surveyors and BIM modelers, and time for both initial scanning and preparations for alteration work. This is to achieve the productivity gains compared to current practices. The approach is to build and test four variants of GMAPS prototypes and use software algorithms and AI image analysis to automate the documentation processes. All prototypes use the Global Navigation Satellite Systems Real Time Kinematic (GNSS RTK) system to obtain the standardized WGS-84 geospatial positions relative to the Earth with 1cm accuracy with clear view of the sky. The reduces the need for registered surveyors and is then automatically converted to the SVY21 coordinate system. title: Achieving Coherence in Opto-Mechatronic Levitation Systems for Precision Quantum Sensing
abs: Levitation is the suspension of an object against the gravitational field without any physical support. While levitation has been demonstrated in a variety of settings, from frog levitation to Maglev trains, most levitations rely on scattering interactions that destroy coherence. In this proposal, we propose three platforms that levitate via coherent scatter-less interactions. Maintaining coherence in levitation has advantages. First, these platforms are ideally closed quantum systems where the total “information content” are self-contained within and decoupled from the environment. Second, the interactions used for levitation are reversible coherent operations that produce no noise. This enables the possibility of mapping quantum information between the two interacting systems.

title: Radiolabeled Albumin-binding Somatostatin Analog 177Lu-DOTA-EB-TATE for Peptide Receptor Radionuclide Therapy of Recurrent or Metastatic Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma
abs: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) is a malignant epithelial tumor originating in the nasopharynx and has a high incidence in Southeast Asia. It is by far the most common type of head and neck cancer in Singapore. Despite the excellent local control with external beam radiation therapy, distant failure remains a key challenge. The outcome of patients with advanced metastatic NPC remains poor. Peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (PRRT) with radiolabeled somatostatin analogues has demonstrated remarkable success in the management of somatostatin receptor (SSTR)-positive neuroendocrine tumors. More recently, SSTR has been confirmed overexpression in NPCs. This project aims to explore a theranostic pair of 68Ga-radiolabeled SSTR agonist Tyr3-octreotate PET/CT, followed by beta-particle emitter 177Lu-labeled novel long-acting albumin binding octreotate peptide derivative 177Lu-DOTA-EB-TATE for PRRT in patients with advanced metastatic NPCs. The EB moiety provides reversible, medium affinity binding of 177Lu-DOTA-EB-TATE to albumin in vivo to prolong its half-life and thus provides an extended therapeutic time window. We hypothesize that 177Lu-DOTA-EB-TATE will achieve remarkable tumor uptake with significant tumor retention, favorable dosimetry profile and will lead to a significant benefit in tumor response for patients with advanced metastatic NPCs. We will evaluate the biodistribution and dosimetry following each cycle of 177Lu-DOTA-EB-TATE and evaluate the safety and therapeutic efficacy in patients with advanced metastatic NPCs. We will also utilize 68Ga labeled SSTR-binding derivative PET/CT imaging to further evaluate the diagnostic value in NPCs and for patient selection for PRRT and monitoring therapeutic effects. This novel theranostic approach will provide a precise and individualized SSTR-targeted radionuclide theranostic system in NPCs. 177Lu-DOTA-EB-TATE for PRRT may open up new applications in NPCs to achieve remarkable tumor uptake and tumor retention, and higher tumor response as compared to other treatment modalities, and more importantly, rendering a significant benefit in survival in patients with advanced metastatic NPCs.

title: National Healthcare Group Investigational Medicine Unit
abs: IMUs provide supporting infrastructure for clinician-investigators, such as a dedicated space and beds for inpatient and outpatient research, computer hardware, and software systems for data management and analysis, as well as manpower infrastructure such as clinical pharmacologists, clinical research coordinators, specialised research nurses/clinical research nurses, and biostatisticians. IMUs focus on early phase trials (Phases 1 and 2), preferably first-in-human studies while also supporting late phase trials, and encourage collaborative efforts across trial units, institutions and clusters in Singapore as well as outside Singapore to develop innovative thought leadership and global competitiveness.

title: Development of a rapid molecular assay for rapid identification of antifungal resistance
abs: Invasive candida infections results in significant mortality and morbidity despite current available antifungal therapy. Treatment may be delayed due to limitations in diagnostic modalities. Antifungal resistance is also increasingly reported, with evidence of in-hospital transmission including in Singapore context. However, there remains a dearth of knowledge with regards to effective infection prevention measure. The primary aim of this study is to develop and validate a molecular test for rapid identification of acquired antifungal resistance in Candida spp. Retrospective isolates will be collected from multiple tertiary hospitals in Singapore, with whole-genome-sequencing performed to identify mechanisms of antifungal resistance in Singapore, and to investigated genetic relatedness and epidemiology of major drug-resistant Candida spp. These will be used to develop and validate a rapid molecular test in Singapore context. A molecular for rapid identification of antifungal resistance will enable earlier diagnosis/confirmation of antifungal resistance and better direct medical care in a clinical context. The test is also required as a step in furthering research in infection control contexts to better understanding nosocomial transmission of drug-resistant Candida spp. such as its risk factors and route(s) of transmission, followed by studies on effective interventions to minimize spread.
kw: Antifungal resistance; Diagnostic testing; Rapid diagnostics; Genomic epidemiology

title: Targeted covalent Inhibitors against key epigenetic proteins
abs: Epigenetics studies heritable phenotype changes in gene expression that do not involve DNA sequence changes. Of various epigenetic factors that control the post-translational modification of histones, acetylation, methylation and phosphorylation are the most prevalent types. These dynamic and reversible processes play an essential role in many physiological processes, and are controlled by epigenetic proteins known as writers, erasers and readers. DNA methyltransferases (DNMTs), histone methyltransferases (including protein lysine methyltransferases or PKMTs, and protein arginine methyltransferases or PRMTs) and histone acetyltransferases (HATs) are writers that add epigenetic marks into DNA and histones. DNA/histone demethylases and histone deacetylases (HDACs) are erasers that remove these marks. Amongst readers that bind to epigenetic marks, bromodomains (BRDs) are the ones that recognize acetylated lysines. Epigenetic dysregulation causes various human diseases, most prominently cancer. Drugs targeting epigenetic regulators for cancer therapy has attracted significant attention. Eight epigenetic drugs are FDA-approved, but all of them target epigenetic erasers, including DNMTs and HDACs, with one exception – tazemetostat, which is a first-of-its-kind PKMT inhibitor for cancer therapy. No FDA-approved drugs against other HMTs, HATs and BRDs are available. We will focus on developing novel targeted covalent inhibitors (TCIs) against HATs, PKMTs, PRMTs and BRDs by targeting conserved/non-conserved ligandable, nucleophilic residues (K/E/D/M/R) present in these proteins. Despite recent advances in the development of small-molecule epigenetic drugs, no covalent drugs are available. The proposed chemistries are unprecedented in epigenetic inhibitors, but our preliminary results have proven their feasibility. Our strategies are universal against virtually all epigenetic targets. The key innovation of this proposal lies in its complementarity to existing cysteine-targeting TCIs, and can be applied to most non-covalent epigenetic inhibitors, either FDA-approved or in clinical trials, thus obtaining leads with improved activities – such a “piggybacking” strategy provides a “shortcut” to develop new epigenetic drugs with minimal resources and faster approval window.

title: Sirtuin 1 as the endogenous inhibitor against NETosis: Translation to a novel anti-NET treatment for accelerating diabetic wound healing
abs: World Health Organization ranks diabetes within the top 10 leading causes of death. Amongst all diabetic complications, non-healing wounds constitute a perpetual clinical issue with unmet solutions. Singapore is one of the countries with the highest prevalence of diabetes-related lower extremity amputation. There is a pressing need in developing efficacious therapeutics for hard-to-heal wounds before the onset of irreparable damages. Neutrophils are found to extrude their cytotoxic chromatin upon activation, forming neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs). NETs are detrimental in diabetic wound healing, and anti-NET treatments have been demonstrated for their therapeutic potential. However, such findings have limited clinical utility thus far due to the lack of effective inhibitors against NET formation (NETosis) and an effective drug delivery system. We recently identified Sirtuin 1 (SIRT1) as an endogenous inhibitor of NETosis and found that SIRT1 becomes dysfunctional in diabetes. SIRT1 reactivation that suppresses aberrant NETosis in diabetes would be instrumental for enhancing wound recovery. The specific aims of this proposal are to (1) dissect how resveratrol reactivates this natural “brake” of NETosis in diabetes, and to (2) develop a drug delivery system that enables high bioavailability of our novel anti-NET combination formulation (resveratrol, DNase, and bactericide) for topical application on wounds. We will test the therapeutic effect of the novel anti-NET treatment in animal models of diabetic wounds and chronic wounds with human relevance. We also aim to (3) define the timeline of NET emergence in the wounds of our local diabetic patients to attest the best window for anti-NET treatment. The current proposal is novel and innovative in terms of scientific concepts, technology advancement and translational approach, and may transform standard of care for diabetic wounds locally and worldwide. The ultimate goal of the project is to enable diabetics to live independently with quality and a retainment of human potential.
kw: Diabetic complications; wound healing; neutrophil extracellular traps; NETosis; drug delivery system; topical treatment

title: Multi-targeted Approach to Advance Clinical Implementation of Nephrogenomic Testing in Singapore
abs: Singapore has a very high burden of chronic kidney disease. Up to 30% of patients with chronic kidney disease has monogenic disease. Genetic diagnostic yield does not differ significantly between pediatric and adult patients. Earlier genetic diagnosis can lead to earlier interventions and improved kidney outcomes. Genetic diagnosis has clinical impact in 73% of patients, including management changes and avoidance of further investigations. Genetics testing is rarely performed locally. Successful nephrogenomics clinical implementation requires a multidisciplinary programmatic approach, backed by translational research. We have setup Renal Alliance for PrecIsion Diagnosis in Singapore (RAPIDS), but current gaps include lack of pipelines for unsolved cases and unclear sequencing strategies. Due to Singapore’s small population and the rare disease prevalence, we will leverage on our existing “Deciphering Diversities: Renal Asian Genetics Network (DRAGoN)” consortium to increase sample size. Our specific aims are to: 1. Provide advanced research platforms to increase genetic diagnostic yield though: a) Establish pipelines for functional studies for variants of unclear significance: minigene splicing/reporter gene assays, collagen IV assays, surface trafficking of genes in polycystic kidney disease, patch clamp studies and ex vivo urine tubuloid cell lines b) Long-read/ whole genome sequencing for unsolved cases 2. Estimate population prevalence of pathogenic variants in key kidney genes using genomic data of 10,000 healthy Singapore individuals Our work can increase diagnostic yield in genetic testing and increase the cost-effectiveness of a nationwide large-scale clinical genomics testing program.
kw: genetics; kidney; glomerular; ciliopathy; cystic; tubulopathy

title: Molecular understanding of ergothioneine cardioprotection
abs: Doxorubicin (DOX) is an anthracycline class of antibiotic that is used in the treatment of cancer, yet its use is limited due to the development of chemotherapy related cardiac dysfunction (CTRCD). Strategies targeting these deregulated pathways have had limited effects or interfere with the anti-cancer effects of the drug. These concerns have limited the use of FDA-approved cardioprotective drug dexrazoxane. In a prospective cohort of breast cancer patients that accounted for echocardiography, we monitored 318 small molecule signatures and 74 functional pathways. Among the top differentiated oxidative stress cardioprotective metabolite, ergothioneine (EGT) was found to be significantly downregulated. Can pharmacological cardioprotection avoid subclinical damage in patients who are undergoing cardiotoxic therapy or with ischemic damage? Therefore, there is a critical need for new strategies to mitigate cardiotoxicity without comprising its therapeutic efficacy. In our pre-clinical mice study, we have discovered a potent cardioprotectant EGT. Converging evidence suggests that treatment with exogenous natural antioxidants can protect heart form cardiotoxicity and acute myocardial infarction (AMI). EGT seem to protect against both these conditions and improves left ventricular ejection fraction decline, upregulates OCTN1 ergothioneine transporter, inhibits ferroptosis and aberrant heart remodeling. Remarkably, in our preliminary study we found that a novel SLC7A11 transporter activity is upregulated and is strongly associated with glutamate and cystine antiporter that is involved in abrogating ferroptosis via SLC7A11-GSH-GPX4 antioxidant pathways. In this proposal, we seek to understand the molecular mechanisms that underpin the protective effects that we have validated in animal studies. To date, studies with CTRCD and AMI have focused on age and genetic factors. Unfortunately, these are non-adaptable factors and are difficult to translate into clinical treatment. Among the modifiable factors, several dietary interventions studies and gut microbiota derived metabolites have been beneficial in preventing the development of cardiometabolic disease and mortality.

title: Strategy for controlling confounding in real-world evidence research on palliative care for patients with advanced cancer
abs: Real-world evidence has an important role in medicine and healthcare. A major challenge in the analysis of real-world data is the control of confounding, especially by unobserved confounders. The prior event rate ratio (PERR) has been proposed to control confounding in real-world evidence research with repeatable event outcomes, such as emergency department visits. It does not mandate the assumption of absence of unobserved confounders and it does not require extensive covariate information. Nonetheless, the current PERR approach is reliant on several important assumptions, such as non-differential mortality/drop-out. Addressing these assumptions could enhance the value of the PERR approach. Randomized controlled trials of palliative care interventions have only indicated small benefits on patient-centred outcomes and inconclusive evidence on acute healthcare utilisation. Previous investigators have hypothesized that this observation of small effect and inconclusive evidence, as opposed to stronger effect and conclusive evidence, is largely due to the differences in how palliative care is delivered in the trial setting versus the real-world setting. Furthermore, high degree of mortality in the palliative care context accentuates the bias generated by differential mortality. Last but not least, outcomes of interest in palliative care extend from repeatable events to quantitative outcomes such as quality of life. We propose to (1) develop and evaluate a new version of PERR based on analysis of multiple events for generation of real-world evidence of treatment impact on event rates, (2) extend the new PERR approach to the analysis of longitudinal quantitative outcomes, and (3) evaluate the impact of hospital-based specialist palliative care for patients with advanced cancer in Singapore on healthcare utilization and patient-centred outcomes. We will develop the analytic methodology, evaluate it by simulation, develop software programs, and apply the new methodology to analyse real-world data from the National Cancer Center Singapore and a cancer cohort study.
kw: Palliative medicine; electronic health records; data analytics; confounding

title: Identification and characterization of novel cellular factors that license the human NLRP1 inflammasome to sense dsRNA
abs: Double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) is a pathogen-derived pattern molecule that is conserved in viruses. The presence of dsRNA in the cytosol of mammalian cells is a harbinger of viral invasion and/or disruption of immune homeostasis. In response, mammalian cells encode a cadre of sensor proteins to detect dsRNA. Genetic or acquired defects of dsRNA-sensing cause immunodeficiency, uncontrolled viral dissemination as well as destructive systemic auto-inflammation (Lee et al. 2022; Zhang et al. 2020). A detailed understanding of the dsRNA-driven innate immune pathways will help elucidate the pathogenesis of viral diseases and develop better anti-infective and anti-inflammatory agents. Human NLRP1 was recently identified as the long sought sensor that triggers pyroptotic cell death and IL-1 driven inflammation in response to dsRNA (Bauernfried et al. 2021). Remarkably, this important immune function is not shared by rodent NLRP1 (Robinson et al. 2020; Jenster et al. 2022; Planès et al. 2021). The mechanism by which human NLRP1 couples dsRNA binding to inflammasome activation still remains unknown. In this proposal, we report unpublished data that identify two novel endogenous proteins that license NLRP1 to sense long dsRNA. We propose to elucidate mechanistically how these two cofactors enable NLRP1 to couple dsRNA sensing to rapid inflammasome activation via ubquitinylation and proteasomal degradation of the NLRP1 auto-inhibitory domain. Furthermore, we aim to ascertain the contribution of the NLRP1 inflammasome in chikungunya (CHIKV) pathogenesis in primary human cells as well as a novel mouse model with a humanized NLRP1 gene. Due to the proven druggability of one of the cofactors, we will further repurpose a clinical-grade molecule to simultaneously inhibit viral replication and dampen dsRNA-triggered inflammation. Taken together, these experiments will lead to a greater understanding of the fundamental biology of host-virus interaction, as well as open new avenues to develop better therapeutics for viral infections.
kw: virus; infection; immunity

title: Development of Bladder Cancer mRNA Vaccine Targeting MAGE family antigens
abs: Bladder cancer (BLCA) is one of the most prevalent urinary system malignancies, with high mortality and recurrence. Cancer immunotherapy, especially cancer vaccine, has emerged as a promising approach to induce antigen-specific antitumor immunity. However, the effectiveness of these vaccines has been hindered by challenges such as the lack of high-quality tumor-specific antigens and inefficient presentation of these tumor antigens by dendritic cells (DCs). Therapeutic mRNA vaccines encoding tumor specific antigens derived from genetic mutations through precise sequence or tumor-associated antigens (TAAs) can induce tumor specific T cell response. Recent research from our team and other groups has revealed that depleting YTHDF1 in DCs can epigenetically downregulate lysosomal cathepsin proteases. This downregulation reduces the degradation of fragmented peptides into free amino acids, thereby enhancing the presentation of MHC-antigen complexes and improving immune responses. Building upon these findings, we hypothesize that by targeting the RNA m6A epigenetic regulation of lysosomal cathepsins, we can enhance the efficacy of mRNA vaccines. This enhancement will involve optimizing the endosome/lysosome pathway for improved MHC-I and MHC-II-based mRNA antigen presentation, ultimately leading to potent anti-bladder cancer immune responses. In this proposal we aim to generate mRNA vaccines against the MAGE family members and test their potential therapeutic effect in bladder cancer murine models. We will use the top candidate, MAGEA10 as an example to illustrate the experimental design. The main objectives of this proposal are as follows: Specific Aim 1: Development of a DC-targeting lipid nanoparticle (LNP) system to effectively co-deliver mRNA encoding antigens and siYTHDF1 to DC cells. Specific Aim 2: Optimization of mRNA sequences encoding the MAGEA 10 antigen to enhance MHC presentation on DC cells. Specific Aim 3: Evaluation of the potential therapeutic effect of the MAGEA 10 antigen-encoded mRNA-siYTHDF1-LNP vaccine for bladder cancer and investigation of the underlying mechanisms.
kw: Bladder Cancer； mRNA vaccine; MAGE familiy antigen; m6A epigenetic regulation; lysosomal cathepsin; DC-targeting effect

title: Determination of mechanisms underlying TDP-43-mediated oligodendrocyte biogenesis and myelination in health and disease
abs: TDP-43 aggregates as the defining pathological hallmark for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) coupled with ALS/FTD-causing mutations in TDP-43 indicate that TDP-43 dysfunctions incur damage to both the motor and cognitive system. Furthermore, TDP-43 pathologies are present in other neurodegenerative diseases and traumatic head injuries. In diseases associated with TDP-43 proteinopathies, TDP-43 aggregates are found in neurons and glia. We and others have showed that TDP-43-mediated damages occur in multiple cell types of the central nervous system (CNS) and act through a cell-autonomous and non-cell-autonomous fashion, including oligodendrocytes. Oligodendrocytes are derived from oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs), which is a renewable progenitor population in the CNS, and make myelin that provides neurons with energy and metabolic support, Myelin changes in respond to neuronal activities and this myelin plasticity is required for learning new motor skills and memory consolidation. Furthermore, the ability to generate new OPCs and myelination and/or modification of existing myelin underlie the myelin plasticity and remyelination. Here, we hypothesize that TDP-43-mediated damages within OPCs may contribute to the impairment of both the motor and cognitive systems. To test this, we will establish the normal physiological functions of TDP-43 in OPCs. Our preliminary data suggests that TDP-43 sustain the expression of a critical transcription factor for oligodendrocyte biogenesis and myelination via a novel splicing mechanism. Furthermore, this TDP-43-dependent splicing alternation is reversed by antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) treatment. In parallel, we will determine how an ALS/FTD-linked TDP-43 mutation may incur damage in OPCs using a transgenic TDP-43 ALS/FTD mouse model. The remarkable adaptability and dynamics of the oligodendrocyte lineage cells may be one of the key determinants in maintaining brain health and adaptability to the ever-changing environments. Elucidating TDP-43-dependent mechanisms underlying oligodendrocyte biogenesis and myelination will provide novel insights into disease mechanisms, therapeutic avenues, and regenerative medicine.
kw: TDP-43, myelination, oligodendrocytes, plasticity, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), frontotemporal dementia (FTD)

title: Dysregulation of circadian rest-activity rhythm in the loss of RNA editing CaV1.3 mice: a novel perspective on estrogen-protection of female mice against obesity
abs: From our recent published work, we demonstrated that loss of Cav1.3 RNA editing enhanced spatial learning and memory in the male Cav1.3ECS mice. As RNA editing is a dynamic process that is not hardwired like in genetic mutation, we expected trade-offs and discovered that the male Cav1.3DECS mice were prone to over-weight tending towards obesity, and showed disturbance in sleep. In contrast, the female Cav1.3ECS mice were protected against obesity and have better metabolic health. Our preliminary data led us to pursue the possible role estrogen may play in this gender difference observed in the Cav1.3ECS mice, given that in rodents and humans, estrogen has been shown to play a pivotal role in the control of body weight. We hypothesize that the circadian regulation of RNA editing in CaV1.3 IQ-domain influences the SCN pace-making activity and loss of CaV1.3 RNA editing leads to male-specific circadian rhythmic disturbance. In this proposal we will be investigating firstly, the role of CaV1.3 IQ-domain RNA editing in pace-making activity in SCN neurons in a gender-specific manner and the potentially protective effects of estrogen in female CaV1.3∆ECS mice. Secondly, we will examine the circadian rhythmic regulation of CaV1.3 RNA editing in SCN and the effects of disrupted Ca2+ homeostasis on Ca2+-dependent signalling pathway and global gene expression for day/night differences, gender differences and across genotypes by using Smart-seq3 single-cell RNA sequencing and proximity labelling. Thirdly, we will evaluate potential interventions with antisense oligonucleotides and CaV1.3 channel blocker for possible therapeutic treatment of rest-activity disturbances. This proposal will provide new insights not only on the role of RNA editing of CaV1.3 channel in regulating SCN pace-making activity but also the link between estrogen and its protective effect against obesity in females by reducing calcium currents flowing through the Cav1.3 channels either directly or indirectly.
kw: Cav1.2 channel, supra-chiasmatic nucleus, RNA editing, circadian rhythm, ADAR2

title: CYP8B1: A novel target for cardiometabolic diseases
abs: Inadequate therapies exist to impact diabetes, evidenced by the current global epidemic. The bile acid (BA) gene CYP8B1 determines the relative amounts of the two primary BAs, cholic acid (CA) and chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA), with reduced CYP8B1 increasing CDCA. We identified that human carriers of heterozygous complete loss of function CYP8B1 mutations show significantly improved insulin sensitivity, likely driven by increased skeletal muscle glucose uptake. The activity of the bile acid associated transcription factor FOXO1 is increased when human skeletal muscle myotubes are exposed to mutation carrier CDCA levels. FOXO1 is the transcription factor for the insulin receptor, and insulin receptor expression is increased in these cells, resulting in increases in the muscle insulin signalling pathway. Administration of CDCA to wild-type mice specifically and solely increased glucose uptake in skeletal muscle. Our findings indicate a novel paradigm shift, where BAs signal directly in the skeletal muscle, through a FOXO1 mediated pathway, to increase whole body insulin sensitization. In addition, our preliminary data find that increased CDCA levels associate with a significant decrease in myocardial infarct, and atherosclerotic lesions are decreased in Cyp8b1-/- mice, suggesting that, in addition to protecting against diabetes, reduced CYP8B1 may also protect against the leading cause of death in diabetics, cardiovascular disease. This present study aims to further identify the mechanisms conferring increased muscle insulin sensitivity and decreased CVD susceptibility in the face of reduced CYP8B1. Successful completion of these aims will more deeply inform on the suitability of CYP8B1 inhibition as a drug target for T2DM and CVD. Most drugs fail to reach the market due to lack of efficacy in humans. Our studies, conducted in humans, suggest a high likelihood of success of CYP8B1 inhibition as a novel therapeutic target for T2D and associated CVD.
kw: bile acids;diabetes;cardiovascular disease;target validation

title: Blood-based combinatorial monitoring of cancer treatment response
abs: Measuring specific drug–target interactions provides a promising opportunity for activity-based evaluation of targeted cancer therapies. Nevertheless, current analytical approaches require invasive tissue biopsies and lack clinical utility. There is thus an intense interest to develop a blood test to characterize drug–target interactions for personalized treatment monitoring. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) have recently emerged as an attractive blood biomarker. They contain drug-bound proteins and present a transformative approach to characterize drug–target interactions, even of solid tumors. Despite such clinical potential, EV detection remains challenging, primarily due to the vesicles’ nanoscale features. We have recently developed a nanotechnology platform to measure drug–target interactions in EVs, directly in patient blood samples. The technology utilizes bio-orthogonal probe amplification on plasmonic resonators to measure drug–target interactions in EVs. The platform is thus well-suited for blood analysis; it enables sensitive measurements in native plasma samples and its results faithfully reflect patient treatment outcomes. Based on these developments, we aim to advance the technology for combinatorial profiling of EV drug dynamics. Using a panel of distinguishing probes, we will test the hypothesis that combinatorial analysis of EV drug changes through multiplexed probes can improve treatment monitoring. This hypothesis stems from our growing understanding of EV composition but has yet to be validated due to a lack of compatible technologies. The goal of this proposal is thus two-fold. First, platform development. Through integrative plasmonic engineering and assay expansion, we will develop a new platform for high-resolution profiling of EV drug changes. Second, clinical validation, we will perform a translational study to profile EVs in lung cancer patients undergoing targeted treatments. We will correlate the blood EV measurements with clinical evaluation of tumor mutation and treatment response. These advances will significantly expand our understanding and clinical applications of EV drug changes for personalized treatment monitoring.
kw: Blood test; combinatorial assay; plasmonic sensor; extracellular vesicle; drug-target interaction; treatment monitoring

title: Unraveling Candida albicans’ mechanisms for balancing growth forms and rate to sustain virulence through metabolic adaptation
abs: Fungal diseases affect over one billion people annually, causing 150 million severe cases and 1.7 million deaths. The World Health Organization recently published the first-ever Fungal Priority Pathogens List, with Candida albicans classified as a Critical Priority pathogen. For decades, C. albicans has been the most prevalent fungal pathogen, causing life-threatening infections in immunocompromised patients with high morbidity and mortality. Critical virulence traits of C. albicans include its transition between yeast and hyphal growth and its metabolic flexibility. Hyphae are invasive, allowing them to penetrate host tissues and evade the immune response. Many hyphae-defective mutants are non-virulent. Therefore, inhibiting hyphal growth has been explored as an antifungal strategy. However, some hyphae-defective mutants remain virulent and, in some cases, are even more virulent than the wild-type strain. We uncovered a gene, CTM1, whose deletion blocks hyphal growth. CTM1 encodes a protein methyltransferase that methylates cytochrome c (Cyc1), specifically at lysine 79. Unmethylated Cyc1 binds to and inhibits the activity of Protein Kinase A (PKA), shutting down the cAMP-PKA pathway, which is responsible for promoting hyphae. Surprisingly, mutants such as ctm1∆/∆ and cyc1K79A, which cannot methylate Cyc1, maintain their virulence by accelerating proliferation through metabolic adaptation in mice. Another hyphae-defective mutant, eed1∆/∆, has been reported to exhibit a similar phenotype. However, the underlying mechanisms that control the switch to a fast-growth mode through metabolic changes are unknown. We hypothesize that the mechanisms that govern the yeast-hyphae decision and metabolism are intricately linked and can be dynamically shifted to enhance C. albicans’ ability to survive in the host, thereby sustaining its virulence. This proposal aims to uncover the molecular mechanisms that coordinate hyphae-promoting signaling pathways and metabolic activities to maximize C. albicans’ capability to survive and proliferate in the host. The findings will unveil new drug targets for developing antifungal therapies.
kw: Fungal disease, pathogenic Candida, antifungal drug resistance, antifungal therapy, bacterial-fungal interaction

title: Circular RNA are an alternative source of immunogenic antigens for developing cancer vaccines.
abs: Neoantigen cancer vaccines have shown promising results in the treatment of cancers with high tumour mutational burden (TMB) such as melanoma but not in solid tumours with low TMB. Moreover, the current neoantigen cancer vaccines are highly personalized and hence cannot be used to vaccinate a wide range of patients. Most of these neoantigens selected for cancer vaccine generation are derived from somatic mutations. But the majority of the cancers that do not respond to existing immunotherapies, such as the checkpoint inhibitors, have low TMB and hence, do not have sufficient number of predicted immunogenic neoantigens from somatic mutations. This greatly limits the ability to develop effective cancer vaccines to treat such tumours. In this proposal, we explore the possibility of identifying immunogenic neoantigens from cancer-specific circular RNAs (circRNAs). CircRNAs represent a diverse class of covalently formed RNA structures formed through back splicing of linear RNA leading to the formation of new exon-exon junctions that could give rise to neoantigens. Many independent studies have also shown that circRNAs displayed tumour-specific expression. Reports have also demonstrated that circRNAs, which bear unique exon-exon junctions due to back splicing, can also be translated through the internal ribosome entry sites (IRES). Translation of the new exon-exon junctions could give rise to neoantigens. A recent report found that circRNAs can be presented as antigens bound to antigen-presenting complexes on the cells. In this proposal, we aim to explore if cancer-specific circRNAs can be an alternative source of neoantigens for cancer vaccine development. To this end, we will identify and validate the immunogenicity of antigens arising from the translation of cancer-specific circRNAs and to explore the potential use of these antigens for the generation of cancer vaccines and T-cell therapies.
kw: Cancer Vacines; Neoantigens

title: Investigating role of potassium channel, KCNJ15, and associated potassium homeostasis during Mycobacterium infection
abs: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) circumvents the immune system by remodelling the host’s protective and and pathological immune responses. We recently conducted a histone acetylome-wide association study (HAWAS) of tuberculosis (TB) to understand the dynamics of host cell chromatin changes during Mtb infection in humans. Analysis of differential chromatin peaks associated genes in monocytes revealed an overall enhancement of voltage-gated potassium channel family members. Most notably, differential acetylation was enriched near the inwardly rectifying potassium channel subfamily J member 15 (KCNJ15) gene locus, which was upregulated upon infection. KCNJ15 gene codes for an understudied Kir4.2 potassium channel. We hypothesize that: 1. Mtb-infection mediated induction of the expression of KCNJ15 gene is dependent on TLR2/TLR4 signaling and related transcription factors, which might affect K+ influx and inhibition of NLRP3 inflammasome activation in monocytes / macrophages. 2. Necrotic mycobacterial granuloma has high extracellular K+ "[K+]e" which result in increased intracellular K+ "[K+]i". Increased [K+]i regulates mitochondrial ROS and AKT-mTOR signaling mediated autophagy thus limiting Mycobacterium growth. We will perform in vitro, and animal experiments (using wildtype and KCNJ15-KO mice-Mtb and zebrafish-M. marinum model) to test these hypothesis. We aim to identify the molecular mechanism(s) governing upregulation of KCNJ15 upon mycobacterial infection and how this mediates myeloid cell anti-microbial and anti-inflammatory properties. Furthermore, we will characterize the effect of K+ on Mtb infection and TB disease, in mice and zebrafish, resulting in generating the preclinical data on dietary potassium mediated reduction in TB pathology, similar to what has been observed in inflammatory bowel disease. Thus a broader translational implication of our findings.
kw: Tuberculosis, potassium, macrophages, autophagy, granuloma

title: Understanding LLPS in hematopoiesis and leukemia: a perspective from FUS and RUNX1
abs: FUS, an RNA binding protein, is involved with multiple key biological functions. FUS is well documented and studied in neurodegenerative diseases; however its role in hematopoiesis and leukemia remains largely unknown. Preliminary studies utilizing Fus conditional knockout mice (Fus cKO) demonstrated that Fus inactivation results in B cell defect and, when stressed, lead to severe defects in both hematopoietic stem and progenitor cell (HSPC) and lymphoid progenitor populations. Furthermore, we also demonstrated that deletion of Fus and Runx1 lead to myeloproliferative disorder (MPD). ChIP-seq analysis showed FUS and RUNX1 co-bind throughout the genome at super-enhancer loci of HSPC and DNA repair genes. Mechanistically, preliminary in vitro experiments suggest controlled liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) as the molecular basis for Fus and Runx1 mediated hematopoietic maintenance, and dysregulation of LLPS lead to leukemogenesis. In this proposed study, biological significance of Fus will be further examined by: i) performing comprehensive stress study using various stress inducing agents, ii) employing sequencing techniques on sorted HSPC and B cells. Significance of Fus will also be examined by comparing the transcriptional changes within the HSPC population sorted from aged Fus cKO, Runx1 conditional knockout mice (Runx1 cKO) and DKO mice. For mechanistic studies on LLPS, we will be employing in vitro and ex vivo techniques, which will be performed using in-house developed tagged WT and LLPS mutant proteins. In this study, we also propose hyperactive LLPS driven by overexpression of FUS and RUNX1 lead to leukemogenesis, and it serves as a novel therapeutic target. To address this, we will be performing efficacy check using selected commercially available LLPS inhibitors against PDX mouse models and AML cell lines. The results of this proposal will help advance our understanding on the previously unappreciated role of FUS in hematopoiesis and establish LLPS as a novel target for leukemia therapy.
kw: RUNX1; FUS/TLS; Hematopoiesis; Leukemia; LLPS; Molecular therapy

title: Unraveling the functions of the TNF⍺-NFkB signaling axis in cell death and immune response of the developing liver
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: The liver plays a crucial role in processing and breaking down both internal and external substances, as well as eliminating unwanted cells like those that are damaged, genetically mutated, or infected by viruses. Inflammatory diseases such as liver injury-derived cirrhosis and hepatitis impair the function of the liver and its regenerative capacity. Upon inflammation, the NFkB transcription factors drive expression genes associated with cytokine response, pro-survival, and cell death. Inflammatory cytokines, such as tumor necrosis factor (TNF)α and interleukin-6 (IL-6) can trigger various cellular responses like proliferation, survival, and death. However, it is not clear how these distinct responses are initiated, regulated, and ceased in a timely manner. Studies on mice lacking components of the NFkB pathway have shown increased hepatocyte apoptosis following TNFα stimulation both during embryonic development and in adulthood. However, this phenotype cannot be fully rescued by the knockout (KO) of the TNF receptor, suggesting a TNF-independent role of NFkB in liver cell death, but the molecular mechanism is poorly understood. In line with the literature, my preliminary results indicated that RelA-/-Tnfr-/- mice survived several days before then died at day 10 due to acute hepatitis and hepatic infiltration of mature neutrophils. Although these mouse models have been studied extensively, this observation was probably missed due to a lack of high-resolution assays like single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-Seq). Since NFκB activity during fetal liver development is crucial for shaping the adult immune system to create a strong barrier against liver injury, I hypothesize that NFκB regulates immune cell homeostasis to protect the TNF-induced cell death. I will utilize KO models of various NFκB and TNF pathway members and perform single-cell analysis to identify the key regulators involved in embryonic development and to investigate the immune-epithelium cell interaction during embryonic development.
kw: embryonic development; TNF; NFkB; liver diseases; immune development

title: Rapid diagnosis of peritoneal dialysis-related peritonitis by point-of-care Vis/NIR optical spectroscopy and machine learning algorithms
inst: Khoo Teck Puat Hospital Pte Ltd
abs: Peritoneal dialysis (PD)-related peritonitis is a major infectious complication in patients receiving PD. Early and accurate diagnosis of PD-related peritonitis is important, as delaying the initiation of appropriate antibiotics increases treatment failure and mortality. Currently, there is a lack of tools for point-of-care and rapid diagnosis and identification of the microorganism. Our collaborator (industry counterpart) has developed a bedside prototype spectroscopy to detect visible light / infrared spectra for body fluid analysis of biomarkers and bacteria in the combination of artificial intelligence algorithms. In this study, based on the detection methodology and machine learning algorithm with further training and modifications by incorporating variables on inflammatory biomarkers and bacteria spectra library, we are going to evaluate the diagnostic ability of the prototype by detection of pathological changes in PD dialysate samples, compared to standard bacteriological diagnosis by conventional culture method. We aim to provide a rapid and low-cost point-of-care diagnosis of PD-related peritonitis by accurately identifying specific microorganisms.
kw: End stage kidney disease; peritoneal dialysis; optical spectroscopy; peritonitis; diagnosis

title: 27-Hydroxycholesterol acts on estrogen receptor α expressed by pro-opiomelanocortin neurons in the arcuate nucleus to modulate energy homeostasis
abs: Obesity is a global epidemic, and obesity-related diseases, such as type 2 diabetes and hypertension, are two of the most prevalent chronic diseases in Singapore. This proposal focuses on 27-Hydroxycholesterol (27HC), the most abundant circulating cholesterol metabolite that has been identified as an endogenous selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) for both estrogen receptor α and β (ERα/β). Importantly, the net flux of 27HC into the brain suggests 27HC acts as a ligand of ERs in the brain. In addition, cumulative evidence demonstrates that estrogenic signalling is essential for modulating both energy intake and energy expenditure. I hypothesize that 27HC regulates energy homeostasis through ERα expressed by pro-opiomelanocortin neurons. To test the hypothesis, I will pursue the following three specific aims: Aim 1: Define the effects of the central administration of 27HC on metabolic outcomes. Aim 2: Determine if active POMC neurons in the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus (POMCARC) via ERα (ERαPOMCARC) is required for the metabolic effects of 27HC. Aim 3. Establishment of the neuronal and molecular mechanisms underlying the action of 27HC/ERα in POMC neurons. As a proof-of-concept application, I will use the Cre-loxP strategy to generate unique mouse models with genes of interest, including ERα (esr1), steroid receptor coactivator 1 (SRC1), and small-conductance Ca2+-activated K+ channel 3 (SK3), manipulated in specific brain regions or populations of neurons at the time of choice. These mouse models are supplemented with chemogenetic, optogenetic, and electrophysical approaches to manipulate or determine the activity of specific neural populations in a real-time manner. I have extensive experience performing all of these key techniques, and I do not anticipate any technical issues. The potential outcomes of my project will provide novel central targets for developing therapeutic strategies or discovering drugs to combat global health issues, such as obesity and diabetes.
kw: Energy homeostasis; 27-Hydroxycholestrol; estrogen receptor alpha; hypothalamus; proopiomelanocortin neuron; feeding behavior.

title: Therapeutic and biomarker discovery for lysosomal acidification dysfunction in Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias
abs: Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias (ADRD) are neurodegenerative diseases without known cures. They are characterized by the presence of hyperphosphorylated tau tangles in affected brain regions. Both cellular and animal models of tau-induced AD and FTD (frontotemporal dementia) have indicated that lysosome impairment and associated autophagy dysfunction contribute to tau accumulation and play a key role in neuronal death. Specifically, it has been reported that lysosomal acidification is impaired in neurons from AD mouse model and several FTD-associated genes are implicated in lysosomal pH elevation. We have also shown that lysosomal acidification is impaired in tauP301S overexpressed SH-SY5Y cells. Lysosomal acidification is central to lysosomal functions, and direct lowering of lysosomal pH to enhance its luminal acidification represents an effective strategy in restoring its functions for clearance of toxic tau aggregates in AD/FTD. However, there is currently no available pharmaceutical agent in the market to induce lysosomal acidification for AD/FTD treatment. In our preliminary studies, we demonstrated that a lysosomal vacuolar (H+)-ATPase (V-ATPase) specific targeting small molecule (C381) is capable of lowering pH in tauP301S overexpressed SH-SY5Y cells and showed that restoration of lysosomal acidification activates autophagy function, reduces tau accumulation and rescues tauP301S-induced cell death. In this proposal, our goal is to investigate the effect of C381 in more physiologically relevant models, including the use of tauP301S primary neurons from mouse and patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells. We will also investigate whether C381 can reverse neurodegeneration and cognitive impairments in a tauP301S mouse model of AD/FTD. Furthermore, we will identify neuron-derived exosome-based biomarkers that correlate with lysosomal acidification dysfunction in the mouse brain with tauopathy. Based on our preclinical data, we will provide an assessment of the potential use of C381 as a pharmaceutical agent in future clinical trials for tauopathy related AD/FTD.
kw: defective lysosomal acidification; autophagy dysfunction; V-ATPase targeting small molecule; tau pathology; neurodegeneration; Alzheimer's and frontotemporal dementia

title: Study longitudinal trajectory of brain structure-function decoupling underlying cognitive development from preschool children to adolescents
abs: Childhood and adolescence are critical periods for cognitive development, influenced by biological changes, genetics, and the environment. The brain is functionally organized into large-scale networks, supported by white matter structural connectivity. Converging evidence suggest that structure-function relationships are organized along a hierarchical gradient spanning unimodal to transmodal cortex, with strong coupling in unimodal sensorimotor cortices and weaker coupling in transmodal association regions. However, the relationship between the structural connectivity and brain functional dynamics supporting cognitive development is not well understood. This study aims to investigate the developmental trajectory of brain structure-function decoupling and its association with cognitive development and genetic risks in typically developing children and adolescents. By analyzing longitudinal data from Singapore cohort (GUSTO) and North American cohorts (NKI-RS and HCP), we will examine the structure-function decoupling using a novel measure - structural-decoupling index (SDI), which measures the smoothness of functional signals on the underlying structural connectome using graph signal processing technique. We hypothesize that the developmental trajectories of SDI will vary across different brain regions (i.e., transmodal versus unimodal), with different rates of change across ages. We also expect that the association between SDI and cognition would be region- and age-dependent. Additionally, we predict that early regional SDI will predict future cognitive performance. Furthermore, we anticipate that developmental changes in SDI would be linked to the maturation of microstructural and morphometric features, including cortical thickness, myelination, and the excitatory-inhibitory ratio. Lastly, we hypothesize that the polygenic risk score for educational attainment and dopamine transporter would moderate the association between the SDI and cognition. Our preliminary study has revealed increased SDI, especially in the executive control network, supports cognitive flexibility improvement in preschool children, providing a strong foundation and motivation for this proposed project. This research will have significant implications for early detection and treatment guidance in neurodevelopmental disorders.
kw: Typical neurodevelopment; magnetic resonance imaging; brain structure-function decoupling; brain-cognition association; polygenic risk score

title: Investigating male factors and their relationships with reproductive health outcomes in Singapore: Towards improved Fathering, Fertility, and Fatherhood
abs: Paternal contributions to fertility and reproductive health outcomes have been understudied, despite promising evidence from animal studies. This proposal aims to investigate the male contribution to pregnancy likelihood and explore the underlying biological mechanisms. Specifically, we aim to (1) identify male factors associated with pregnancy rate; (2) develop a fertility index combining modifiable factors for both males and females to predict pregnancy rate; and (3) explore the relationship of male modifiable factors with semen physical and molecular characteristics. We hypothesize that successful pregnancy depends not only on female factors but also on male factors, with altered sperm epigenetic signatures and seminal fluid oxidative status playing a role in explaining the link between male exposures and fertility. To test the hypotheses, we will conduct a case-control study with 240 fertile couples (men with female partners who are currently pregnant) and 240 infertile couples where the female partner does not have an infertility diagnosis, recruited from KK Women’s and Children’s Hospital. We will use questionnaires to collect data on socio-demographic characteristics, clinical, lifestyle, and environmental factors; analyse metabolic and stress biomarkers from blood samples; and measure semen parameters including sperm motility, density, morphology, volume, DNA fragmentation, DNA methylation, gene expression, and seminal plasma oxidative status. Using the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator method, we will identify predictive male factors while taking account of female factors. A logistic regression model incorporating male and female factors will be built to derive the fertility index, which will be evaluated using cross-validation on subsets of those studied. Additionally, we will perform multivariable linear regression to explore the relationship between male modifiable exposures and semen quality. Findings from this proposed study will pave the way for developing lifestyle-based or medical interventions to enhance male and couple reproductive health, and potentially benefiting future offspring health.
kw: Father; Male fertility; Modifiable factor; Risk score; Reproduction; Semen quality

title: Understanding and triangulating interventions to mitigate healthcare-associated infections and multi-drug resistant organisms burden
abs: Healthcare associated infections not caused by multidrug resistant organisms (HAIs) and hospital-acquired MDRO infection caused by a specific MDRO (HA-MDRO) incur a large excess number of bed days, ICU usage and mortality rate compared to hospitalized individuals who are not. They are complex patients who require extensive treatment and more antibiotics. This proposal seeks to understand the excess burdens incurred by HA/HA-MDROs infected individuals, current approaches to mitigate HA/HA-MDROs and better optimize current approaches to alleviate nosocomial transmission.
