This will be done by: (1) estimating the difference in clinical outcomes between admitted patients who acquired HA/HA-MDROs infection (2) estimating the intervention efficacy of ASP and/or IPC measures individually or as a combinatorial intervention strategy, to reduce HA/HA-MDROs incidence and their effect on antibiotics defined daily dose (3) compute the excess cost-burden per HA/HA-MDROs (4) estimating the cost-effectiveness of ASP/IPC interventions to mitigate HA/HA-MDROs (5) adapting an already developed microsimulation platform, we would triangulate novel screening, isolation and other intervention strategies to better mitigate HA/HA-MDROs, as well as design strategies to alleviate nosocomial transmission for emerging pathogens where no therapeutics are yet available for pandemic preparedness. By employing an interdisciplinary approach comprising clinical epidemiology, statistics and transmission dynamic modelling, we would ascertain whether our proposed strategies can be cost-effective versus alternatives, as well as whether they are reasonable in clinical practice. In collaboration with clinicians, these findings will be directly translated into clinical guidelines and health policy for mitigating HA/HA-MDROs burden.
kw: Healthcare associated infections; multi-drug resistant organisms; interventions; economic evaluation;

title: Technology-enabled anticipatory guidance and peer support in empowering parents to prevent early childhood caries: A randomized controlled trial
abs: Specific aim: To test the effectiveness of technology-enabled anticipatory guidance and peer support in empowering parents to establish proper childcare practices and prevent early childhood caries (ECC). Hypothesis: Technology-enabled anticipatory guidance and peer support is more effective than conventional oral health education in enhancing parental efficacy, establishing proper childcare practices (dietary, feeding and toothbrushing), and preventing ECC. Methods/approach and feasibility: This is a two-arm, parallel group, assessor-blinded, randomised controlled trial. 490 parent-child dyads will be recruited and randomly assigned to receive conventional oral health education (control), and technology-enabled anticipatory guidance and peer support, respectively. Anticipatory guidance and peer support will be delivered through 4 unique online sessions, when child turns 3, 6, 12, and 18 months, to match the developmental milestones and parental needs for childcare support. Outcomes will be assessed through a questionnaire and food diary (at 12, 24 and 36 months of child’s age) and a dental examination for the child (at 24 and 36 months of age). The effectiveness of the intervention will be evaluated using psychological outcomes (parental efficacy), behavioural outcomes (dietary, feeding and oral hygiene practices), clinical outcomes (oral hygiene and ECC), and quality of life outcomes. Process evaluation and cost-effectiveness analysis will be included. This multidisciplinary research involves experts from relevant fields. Access to the target population via collaborating hospital/clinics and social media has been confirmed. Our pilot study supports the feasibility. Significance: ECC is a significant clinical and public health challenge that the world and the Singapore population are facing. Despite 60 years of water fluoridation, health promotion, and access to health care, ECC prevalence is higher in Singapore than in most developed countries. By delivering appropriately timed, immediately actionable and ongoing guidance and support, this parent empowerment program is likely to reverse this trend and set the right trajectory for children’s health.
kw: Early childhood caries; anticipatory guidance; peer support; parent empowerment; randomised controlled trial

title: Impact of caregiving for older adults on employed informal caregivers
abs: Background: As Singapore’s population is ageing, family members often care for older adults who need assistance with daily living. Many of these informal caregivers are also simultaneously employed in paid work. The demands from juggling paid work and informal caregiving adversely impacts both health (e.g. stress, physical health) and work-related outcomes (e.g. work interruptions, reduced performance) of employed caregivers, which reinforce each other and may affect caregivers’ healthcare utilization. However, there is a dearth of literature in Singapore to fully understand the complex pathways and draw causal inferences between caregiving and caregivers’ personal and work-related outcomes. Objectives: We propose a theoretical framework to understand how caregiving characteristics (e.g., caregiving hours, intensity, care recipient’s status) affects the personal (e.g., physical and mental health) as well as work-related outcomes (e.g., job changes, work interruption) and resulting healthcare utilization of the employed caregivers and the extent to which this relationship is moderated by caregiver (e.g., gender, education) and workplace (e.g., flexibility, supervisor support) characteristics. Specifically, we aim to 1) assess the association between caregiving characteristics and the personal and work-related outcomes of employed caregivers 2) Compare the healthcare utilization, personal and work-related outcomes of employed caregivers with employed non-caregivers 3) Understand the mechanisms through which caregiving is associated with personal and work-related outcomes of employed caregivers. Importance: Caregivers by providing unpaid care, provide a significant portion of long-term care, reducing the burden on the healthcare system. Poor physical and mental health of caregivers could lead to discontinued caregiving, higher likelihood of institutionalization and healthcare utilization of the care recipient and the caregivers themselves which threatens the sustainability of the healthcare system. Understanding how caregiving affects the working caregivers’ work-life interface will help in designing workplace interventions which can help to ease caregiver burden which can ensure the sustainability of care for older adults.
kw: employed informal caregivers; older adults; mental health; family-work conflict; workplace characteristics; Singapore

title: Multi-centre prospective validation of machine-learning models that systematically identifies patients with advanced cancer at risk of one-year mortality and facilitates earlier palliative care (PROTECH)
abs:
Background 
Palliative care (PC) is appropriate for any individual living with advanced cancer, but most impactful in their last year of life, as these individuals face over-medicalized care, high needs, and decreasing quality of life. Current delivery of PC is unmethodical, relies on clinical discretion, and occurs too late. We have developed machine-learning models using routine data to identify the “last-year-of-life”. However, more model testing is needed.

Specific Aims and Methods
Specific Aim 1: Improving and validating machine-learning models to achieve robustness for future implementation trial.

Aim 1a: Conducting multi-centre prospective validation of machine-learning models. 
Hypothesis: Model maintains discrimination (AUROC     > 0.80), accuracy (     >75%), and precision-recall (AUPRC     > 0.70) across four sites.

Aim 1b: Ascertain algorithmic fairness by validating model performance within demographic groups: gender, ethnicity, age, and cancer stage.
Hypothesis: True positive rate should be equal across groups.

Aim 1c: Validate model capability in handling actual data volumes by batch processing weekly cohorts over continuous 6-month
kw: Oncology; Palliative care; Machine Learning; Electronic Health Records; Screening

title: Implementation of palliative care screening criteria in cancer, heart failure and chronic kidney disease
abs: Patients with advanced serious illnesses such as cancer, heart failure and chronic kidney disease have high symptom burden, poor quality of life and high acute healthcare utilisation. Palliative care improves outcomes for patients with advanced serious illnesses such as cancer, heart failure, and chronic kidney disease. However, less than half of the patients with terminal illnesses in Singapore receive palliative care. Furthermore, most patients who accessed palliative care did so only in the last weeks of life – too late in their illness journey. In order to identify which patients are likely to benefit from palliative care, several screening approaches have been suggested in recent years. International Delphi studies have been conducted for cancer and heart failure to identify consensus criteria for referral of patients to palliative care. Patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) can also be used to proactively screen for problems that may benefit from additional support. Examples of relevant PROMs are the distress thermometer and problem list (DTPL) and the Integrated Palliative Care Outcome Scale (IPOS). The overall aim of this study is to assess the implementation and gather data on the effectiveness of palliative care screening criteria among patients with cancer, heart failure and chronic kidney disease. Based on literature and consultation with local clinician stakeholders, the study team have formulated a list of possible palliative care screening criteria. To assess implementation, we will use selected implementation outcomes in Proctor’s taxonomy – acceptability, adoption, appropriateness, feasibility, and implementation cost. To assess effectiveness, we will assess if these palliative care criteria are associated with subsequent healthcare utilisation, survival and end-of-life outcomes.
kw: Palliative care; Screening; Neoplasms; Heart failure; Renal insufficiency

title: Preventing Depression: Investigation in Cohorts of its etiology and Trajectory - The PREDICT study
abs: Background: Globally, depression affects approximately 4% of the population annually, translating into about 280 million people with depression. The COVID-19 pandemic has exacerbated mental health conditions worldwide, and significantly added to the prevalence and burden of depression. Major depressive disorder (MDD) is the most prevalent mental health disorder in Singapore, with a lifetime prevalence of 6.3%. Currently, data on the long-term course and outcomes of depression are extremely limited in Singapore and few studies have systematically examined interventions that can potentially prevent depression. Aims: We aim to establish a well-phenotyped cohort to describe the long-term prognosis of depressive disorders i.e., dysthymia and MDD in Singapore. We will also examine biopsychosocial determinants of the long-term course and consequences of depressive disorders. Furthermore, the study will examine the course of sub-syndromal depression in Singapore and will pilot and evaluate interventions that can prevent progression to depression among those with sub-syndromal depression. Methods: We will establish a cohort (n= 3200) of those with depression, subsyndromal depression and those without depression or sub-syndromal depression by leveraging several recruitment strategies. Patients with depression will be recruited from a tertiary hospital (IMH) and a primary care clinic (NHGP). To recruit those with sub-syndromal depression and those without depression, the study will leverage existing cohorts in Singapore, as well as participants from large-scale epidemiological studies conducted by the Institute of Mental Health. Participants will be followed up for a period of up to 5 years. Assessments will include questionnaires to determine psychopathology, psychosocial risk factors and well-being, physical health examinations and biological assays. Clinical Significance This would be the first mental health cohort in Singapore, and by focusing on depression, much-needed local data on both causes and outcomes associated with depression will be made available that can help in both the prevention and management of depression.
kw: Depression; Sub-syndromal depression; Cohort; Biopsychosocial factors; Intervention; Prevention

title: Extended follow-up to examine the impact of a multidomain lifestyle intervention for the prevention of cognitive decline and frailty – SINGER extended follow up
abs: Dementia is a multifaceted and complex neurological disorder. The complex and multifactorial nature of dementia requires a multidomain approach to prevention and treatment strategies in order to comprehensively address the underlying mechanisms involved. The SINgapore GERiatric intervention study to reduce cognitive decline and physical frailty (SINGER) is one such multidomain prevention trial currently underway and expected to complete recruitment of 1200 participants by the end of 2023. SINGER is a 2-year multi-site randomized controlled trial consisting of multidomain interventions: dietary advice, exercise, cognitive training, and vascular risk factors management. The primary outcome of SINGER is global cognition measured by a neuropsychological test battery. Other outcomes include domain-specific cognition and function, neuroimaging changes, incidence and progression of chronic diseases, blood biomarkers, quality of life, mental health and cost-benefit analysis. The overarching objective of this current proposal is to elicit evidence on the long-term benefits of multidomain lifestyle programmes on cognitive and vascular health in an at-risk population by leveraging on the available SINGER cohort, while examining the barriers and facilitators to sustained healthy lifestyle behaviors. We expect to translate the evidence into practice via collaborations with community providers to implement evidence-based community programs. We propose to extend the follow-up period for SINGER participants post the 2-year intervention period, to continue to have outcome assessments at year 3 and year 4. We will examine long term benefits of the multidomain intervention, maintenance of healthy lifestyle behaviour and elicit barriers and facilitators to maintenance of healthy habits. Community stakeholders will also be engaged via focus group discussions to map community resources that may contribute to maintenance of evidence-based lifestyle behaviours for dementia risk reduction. By generating real-world data post-intervention settings, this proposal responds directly to calls to research on eliciting evidence on approaches to reduce risks before the manifestation of disease.
kw: Dementia;Alzheimer’s Disease;mild cognitive impairment;multidomain intervention; extended follow-up

title: Exploring the effects of the imR sElf-management prOgramme for people experiencing MajoR depressive disorders in Singapore: The REcOvERy programme
abs: Background: Over the last decade, more people have been diagnosed with major depressive disorders (MDDs). This has resulted in many years of life with a disability compared to other medical conditions. Although recovery in mental health has always been framed through the biomedical model, the acceptance and insight towards disabilities as part of oneself proposed by person-oriented recovery has started to gain traction. Aim: to examine the effects of an evidence-based self-management program specifically for people experiencing major depressive disorders in the community. Methods: This study consists of three phases; Phase one looks into developing the self-management program based on the Illness Management and Recovery (IMR) program toolkit. Based on the preliminary works by the Principal Investigator, the program will be contextualised for people with MDDs. Mental Health Experts and members from Participant Patient Involvement will be enlisted to ensure relevance and adequacy for the local population. Phase two is a single-centre, unblinded, two-arm parallel-group pilot randomised controlled trial (RCT) where 72 participants will be randomly allocated to the interventional or Treatment as Usual Group to test the effects of the self-management program. The outcome measures will be taken at baseline, the fifth week, and at the end of the intervention. Phase three will be a process evaluation for the program. Outcomes: The outcomes explored in this study include: Illness Self-Management, Depressive Symptoms, Mental health recovery, Perceived Stigma, and Sense of Hope. Data analysis: Quantitative data will be analysed using IBM SPSS 25. Descriptive statistics and either parametric or non-parametric inferential statistics will be used. An intention-to-treat approach will be used to reduce the effects of participant drop-out from this study. Qualitative data obtained in this study will be analysed using the Braun and Clarke six-phase thematic analysis approach.
kw: Mental health; People with major depressive disorders; personal recovery; community reintegration

title: Maximizing the effectiveness of public health messaging to improve adolescent mental health in Singapore
inst: IHDP - Institute for Human Development and Potential
abs: This research project aims to investigate the importance of positive health messaging in promoting youth mental health, with a particular focus on adolescents in Singapore. Adolescence is a critical developmental period when individuals undergo significant transitions, making it a pivotal time to foster mental resilience and emotional flourishing. To achieve this, our multidisciplinary approach draws upon the integration of surveys, experiments, and content analysis of media to comprehensively understand the influence of positive mental health messaging on adolescents' lives. Through surveys and experiments, we aim to gain profound insights into how positive mental health messaging shapes adolescent well-being, attitudes towards seeking help, and their perceptions of mental health. By exploring these dimensions, we can identify the critical factors that impact young individuals' mental health, providing a deeper understanding of the mechanisms through which positive messaging exerts its effects. Moreover, we recognize the significance of media portrayals in shaping social perceptions, hence delving into content analysis of news articles, TikTok videos, and Instagram posts to unveil the dominant framing of mental health in mainstream and social media. This investigation will be instrumental in comprehending the broader societal influences on adolescents' mental well-being. Our research also leverages the powerful tool of network analysis to explore the interconnectedness of different mental health dimensions among adolescents. By mapping the complex web of associations, we seek to unravel the intricate relationships between various aspects of mental health, shedding light on potential pathways to fostering holistic well-being in this vulnerable population. The anticipated findings of this research will hold substantial significance for informing evidence-based interventions. Armed with a deeper understanding of the impact of positive mental health messaging, we can design targeted interventions and public health strategies tailored to Singaporean adolescents' unique needs.
kw: youth mental health; positive mental health messaging; social perceptions; resilience

title: Advancing the understanding of biological mechanisms influencing atopic dermatitis and skin barrier function.
abs: Background: Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a common chronic inflammatory skin condition with complex disease mechanisms. Despite improved understanding in recent years, there remain important knowledge gaps. Aims: To use our existing population based clinical and genomic data, coupled with experimental models, to investigate the mechanisms influencing skin barrier function, itch and atopic dermatitis (AD). Specific Aims: SA1) To identify host genetic factors associated with skin barrier function, modulation of itch and AD using genome wide association. SA2) To correlate polygenic risk scores of skin barrier function, itch and AD with real world clinical data of AD diagnosis, onset, severity and complications through data linkage to national electronic health records (NEHR) via MOH TRUST platform. SA3) To validate the identified potential molecular mechanisms linking candidate genes to skin biology to advance understanding of mechanisms of AD in a skin organoid model. Hypothesis: Mechanisms of AD are complex and may be more than immune dysregulation and a disrupted skin barrier. Our experiments could identify potential mechanisms for development of AD and its symptoms. Methods: I will leverage on an observational epidemiology experiment conducted among participants from a general population cohort (n=~40,000). Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) analysis will be performed based on available genotype information. Various omics data are also available from European and Asian populations to identify plausible candidate genes in SA1. Calculated polygenic risk scores (PRS) will be associated with real world clinical data via linkage with the national electronic medical records (SA2). A pilot basic science experiment using skin organoid models based on specific prioritized genetic and molecular targets identified from SA1 is then designed to address the specific aim SA3. Clinical significance: A better understanding of molecular targets and pathogenesis of AD with further validation in skin keratinocytes model would provide important therapeutic target candidates for future development.
kw: atopic dermatitis; genetics; keratinocytes; barrier function

title: Immunosenescence, Frailty, and their Influence on COVID-19 Immunity in Older Adults
abs: Immunosenescence is a physiological process that influences an individual’s vaccine response as they age. Whilst the underlying processes that driving this phenomenon remain poorly defined, particularly in those who are frail, cellular senescence in immune effectors has been strongly implicated by previous studies in mainly Caucasian patient cohorts. COVID-19 is a good model to conduct a detailed cellular and molecular analysis of aging-influenced immune pathways and how they impact upon vaccine efficacy. We have preliminary data conducted on older adults who have been vaccinated with 2 doses of the BNT1626 vaccine. We showed that younger adults exhibited a significant increase in their interferon(IFN)-γ-secreting CD4+ T-cells to wild-type and Omicron antigens in response to vaccination, which positively correlated with the functionality of SARS-CoV-2 neutralising antibodies. This relationship is markedly absent in older adults, illustrating a relative IFNγ deficiency may explain poorer vaccination responses in older adults. Hence, we aim to investigate the effect of 1) age and 2) physical frailty on repeated COVID-19 mRNA booster doses and hybrid immunity on the adaptive immune response. We will recruit 40 participants, 20 young and 20 older adults. Participants will be recruited prior to taking their 4th dose vaccination and bloods will be taken before vaccination, at 6 months, 1 year and 2 years. These will be processed for SARS-CoV2 neutralization, B and T cell immunophenotyping, and antigen-specific stimulation studies. All participants will undergo annual medical questionnaire, functional and cognitive assessments. Blood biomarkers for biological age and frailty will be measured. Comparative analyses using two-way ANOVA of immune markers over time between young vs older adults will be conducted. To be pandemic ready, we need to have better understanding of the immune response of the older adult to develop novel strategies for immune augmentation.
kw: immunosenescence; frailty; COVID-19 vaccine; COVID-19 hybrid immunity

title: Advancing Clinical Insights from Wearable-Generated Data and Digital Phenotyping in Dermatology
abs:
The advent of value-based healthcare has precipitated a paradigm shift from healthcare quality as delineated by physicians to a patient-defined framework. This evolution is anchored in a patient-centric approach, emphasizing metrics centered on the patient's experience, like quality of life and satisfaction, as pivotal indicators of treatment efficacy.

Progress in wearable technology and digital phenotyping has enabled the extensive collection of Patient Generated Health Data (PGHD), which is multi-faceted and rich, at a heightened frequency. The clinical significance of these data types within dermatology, however, remains to be fully elucidated.
This study aims to fill this knowledge gap by conducting a 8 week-long data collection exercise using wearable technology on 30 dermatology patients. Concurrently, these patients will interact with a mobile application that gathers data on various aspects, such as itch intensity, life quality, mood, and skin condition. The data amassed will encompass physiological parameters like heart rate, body temperature, and electrodermal activity, alongside proxies for wellness such as sleep
kw: digital technology; wearable; patient generated data; patient reported outcomes; quality of life; itch

title: WeeCare – Providing cost-effective home monitoring of urinary flow for men with Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms (LUTS)
abs: The clinical evaluation of patients with LUTS and males with benign prostate enlargement (BPE) involves history taking, clinical examination and investigations including uroflometry (measuring peak urine flow rate), both at the time of initial diagnosis and subsequent follow up visits.LUTS form the bulk of referrals from primary care physicians to tertiary urology centres. These referrals are usually made with reference to patients' subjective complaints of voiding and storage symptoms, without any objective clinical parameters, This is mainly due to the lack of affordable and available equipment (i.e. clinic setting uroflometry machines). We aim to develop a portable device which can empower the primary care physician in the assessment and monitoring of patients with benign prostate enlargement (BPE), a chronic condition prevalent in the ageing population of Singapore. The primary physician can use this device easily to follow up these patients. Using the initial CIDA grant, the team has designed and built from scratch a flow simulator, against which the prototypes were tested for accuracy, reproducibility and consistency. Our device achieved a high specificity (81.5%) and negative predictive value (83%) in the evaluation of a poor urinary flow rate of less than 12.5ml/s (Table 1). Given a low rate of false negatives, WeeCare was shown to be effective as a simple test in the ambulatory setting, with reassurance that a formal urology consult might not be required with a consistent “pass” reading. Furthermore, patient experience surveys performed demonstrated that WeeCare was easy to use, safe and provided reproducible results. We then engaged Racer medical technologies to enable the prototypes to be ready for mass production. The current grant application , if successful, will help fund the mass production of the protoype and bring it for clinical trial at the SGH Urology Centre. We believe primary care physicians and patients will be ready to use the device with confidence after the Urology Centre adoption.
kw: Urinary flow measurement

title: Remote monitoring of swallowing function using a mechanoreceptor sensor system
abs: Oropharyngeal dysphagia is a swallowing disorder affecting safe and efficient transport of food/drink from the mouth to the stomach. Delay in managing oropharyngeal dysphagia may result in choking, aspiration pneumonia and/or malnutrition. Speech therapists conduct bedside feeding assessment, fluoroscopy and/or endoscopy to make diet and fluid recommendations until the next reassessment which may be days to months away. Developing a non-invasive swallowing sensor system can potentially provide objective data on swallowing function during this gap, thus augmenting clinical decision making in short- and long-term management of dysphagia. Our pilot engineering prototype has demonstrated the feasibility of capturing swallowing-related signals using an ultrathin, carbon-coated sensor patch adhered over the neck surface. Next, we aim to improve the composition, design, fabrication, and signal processing algorithm of the sensor system, to determine its clinical usability for monitoring swallowing function remotely in oropharyngeal dysphagia management. We hypothesize that the improved engineering prototype has potential to identify changes in swallowing function over time, and/or differentiate between normal and disordered swallowing function between healthy participants and those with oropharyngeal dysphagia. We will develop the mechanical properties of the sensor system by testing different material compositions, fabrication methods and sensor array designs to maximise signal-to-noise ratio for capturing swallowing movements during eating and drinking. Signal processing methods will also be developed to identify change vs. no change in swallowing function over time in patients and healthy participants. This technology has direct translational applications into clinical practice as we develop it into a remote monitoring tool for home and hospital use in between routine clinical reviews. Through early detection of changes in swallowing function for a variety of oropharyngeal dysphagia etiologies, we can potentially reduce healthcare burden by reducing adverse patient outcomes and saving additional hospitalization costs incurred due to choking, poor oral intake and/or aspiration pneumonia.
kw: dysphagia; telehealth; wearables; remote monitoring; rehabilitation

title: The development of a novel ear surgery toolkit
abs: Eardrum perforations are common, and affect 330 million people worldwide. It causes recurrent ear infections and hearing loss, particularly in developing countries, where it is the leading cause for permanent childhood hearing loss. The definitive treatment is surgical repair of the eardrum (myringoplasty), where a graft is placed as a healing scaffold to induce closure of the perforation. Current myringoplasty techniques suffer from significant limitations. An operating microscope is traditionally used to provide illumination and magnification as the eardrum is a small structure located deep in the ear canal. However, as the ear canal is extremely tortuous, a long incision around the ear is required to accommodate the straight-line passage of light. This is invasive, requires general anaesthesia, and is associated with significant post operative complications. Endoscopic ear surgery has emerged as an alternative, but it forces surgeons to perform one-handed dissection since the other hand is occupied holding the endoscope. This leads to difficulty performing key tasks such as bleeding control and accurate graft placement. There is therefore an unmet need for a surgical platform that enables myringoplasty to be a 1) minimally invasive, 2) two-handed, 3) natural-orifice surgery that can be performed as an in-office procedure under local anaesthesia. We have developed a novel ear surgery toolkit that addresses these needs comprehensively, through the use of three devices – an endoscope holder (EH), a graft delivery device (GDD), and a tympanic membrane suction punch (TMP). In this project, our specific aims are to: 1) To refine the EH and TMP through benchtop iterations, and demonstrate proof-of-concept in a cadaver trial, and 2) to conduct a first-in-man trial of the complete surgical platform, to generate preliminary data for further refinements of all three devices. Through these activities, the PI will be further developed as a Clinician Innovator.
kw: Ear surgery;Surgical innovation;Medical device;Minimally invasive;Surgical platform

title: High Fidelity Personalised Liver Digital Twin for Surgical Planning and Intraoperative Navigation
abs: Introduction: Patient safety during surgery is of paramount importance. Although surgical skills are taught and trained based on a surgeon’s experience and their own technical skills, navigational aids have been shown to increase efficiency, improve safety, and reduce complications in surgeries. Using surgical navigation systems and tools in deformable organs has been extremely challenging. Till date, there is no commercially available system that is clinically validated and certified for soft organ surgical navigation. Aims: The overall aim of this project is to create a customised structural digital twin of a patient’s liver based on the patient’s own liver’s biomechanical data. This digital twin will be an accurate representation of how the patient’s liver will react to external forces, thus providing a real-time image map for the surgeon. This digital twin will be superimposed onto the patient during a surgery to act as an image navigation tool. Impact of Study: The ability to have a structural digital twin of the liver to provide real-time surgical navigation will be invaluable. With a personalised structural digital twin of the liver, a surgeon can have an overlay of the patient’s pre-operative imaging that is extracted from their own CT or MRI scans superimposed onto the patient’s liver during the surgery. With real-time simulation of liver deformability using the biomechanical properties extracted, the liver deformability computational model will allow the surgeon to see a dynamic image that will adjust as the surgery progresses, based on the real-time physical location and cutting of the patient’s liver. The superimposed image will conform to the contour of the liver, with the image structures adjusting based on real-time feedback from the cameras in the operating field. This enables the surgeon to see where critical structures are, and how close the tumours are to the cutting line in real-time.
kw: Artificial Intelligence; Machine Learning; Digital Twin; Surgical Navigation; Medical Technology; Mixed Reality

title: Digital imaging using optical and thermal sensors to scale the general inspection for kaki ailments and promote healthy feet in people with diabetes (DigiKAH Experience)
abs: One in 10 Singapore residents has diabetes; 25% of people with diabetes develop foot ulcers in their lifetime, and severe infections result in 1,500 local leg amputations annually. Screening to detect early diabetic foot disease prevents complications and amputations, but the current process is staffing intensive and burdens patients with more appointments that risk poor compliance. We have developed a compact prototype (DigiKAH) incorporating thermal and optical sensors for digital foot imaging. DigiKAH may detect foot ulcers, deformity, vasculopathy, and neuropathy, by assessing the heat distribution of the foot and capturing skin or contour abnormalities. This solution enables foot screening to be performed rapidly like any clinic parameter with minimal staffing; expansion of screening becomes feasible beyond clinics and more accessible to patients. We aim to perform technological enhancement of DigiKAH and build its imaging AI classification model to detect diabetic foot disease. We will refine DigiKAH with optimised image processing techniques. We propose a dual-site deployment at the hospital and polyclinic to recruit 250 people with diabetes attending foot screening and 50 healthy volunteers for DigiKAH imaging. We will perform stratified sampling to adequately represent the subgroups of foot ulcers, deformity, vasculopathy, neuropathy, and normality. We will adapt the recruitment strategy based on the progressive model training and interim assessment with every 30 patients and obtain the best-achieved mean average precision for disease detection. We can deploy DigiKAH widely in all public and private clinics and community health posts nearer to homes as a convenient mass screening tool for diabetic foot disease. We can retrain our AI classification model with contemporaneous data to improve its disease detection accuracy over time. Our device will reduce the staffing to screen the projected 870,000 residents with diabetes by 2030 and facilitate our upstream efforts in preventing diabetic foot complications in Singapore.
kw: Artificial intelligence; Community health services; Diabetic foot; Digital signal processing; Optical devices; Thermography.

title: Human Joint Motion & Load Sensing Using E-textiles
abs: Soft, wearable electronic textiles (e-textiles) have recently shown promise in healthcare settings. However, little research has been done on how to integrate stretchable circuits. In response, we are working to create stretchy, conductive knits that can be tuned for optimal electrical and mechanical performance. We made highly stretchable piezoresistive strain sensors by changing the yarn combinations and stitch arrangements at the mesoscale. This gave us sensors that could handle more than 120% strain with a sensitive gauge factor of 8.47, lasting over 100,000 cycles. Strategically placed interconnects can withstand strains above 140%, while resistors show resilience to strains exceeding 250%, allowing for a very stretchable sensing circuit. We used a computer-numerically controlled knitting machine, which is inexpensive and scalable, to create the wearable with minimal post-processing. A wireless circuit board developed specifically for this project allows for continuous transmission of data acquired in real-time. This grant will support the study in two phases to continue this product's potential commercialization. Phase 1 focuses on validating the knee brace sensor and establishing a fundamental model, and Phase 2 is dedicated to rigorous sensor validation and reliability research. Our overarching objective is to substantiate the efficacy of the knee brace sensor in diverse human health and wellness applications. The comprehensive dataset gathered from this study will bolster the development of medical products and lay the foundation for future applications in remote rehabilitation for musculoskeletal and mobility-related conditions. Through this meticulously designed project workflow, we aspire to make significant strides in wearable healthcare technology.
kw: E-textiles; telerehabilitation; gait motion; wearable sensor; kinematic;kinetics

title: Project Pensieve II – A Proof-of-Concept Study on an AI Tool to Detect Delirium among Hospitalized Older Patients
abs: Delirium is a condition akin to acute brain impairment, whereby a person displays acute and transient impairment of brain activities in the face of serious medical conditions. Undiagnosed delirium is a significant unmet medical need among hospitalized older patients, affecting an estimated 56,000 older Singaporeans every year. Despite occurring in 30–80% of hospitalized older patients, 70% of delirium cases are undiagnosed because of the (1) subtleness of cognitive disturbances in attention and other cognitive domains, and (2) impracticality of conducting routine cognitive testing in busy ward settings. Consequently, undiagnosed delirium leads to increased mortality, morbidity, cost and suboptimal care. In our previous study (Project Pensieve – Phase 1), we have developed an AI tool that, based on preliminary testing, has good performance in detecting cognitive impairment among older persons. The AI tool takes < 5 minutes to complete; is designed to be administered by lay volunteers; and captures the clinically-relevant cognitive domains. In this Phase 2 of Project Pensieve, we aim to train the AI tool to distinguish delirium from non-delirium among hospitalized older patients, hypothesizing an AUC of ≥80% in the AI tool’s diagnostic performance. We will administer the AI tool to 500 hospitalized older patients with delirium. Data from these 500 recruited participants will be merged with a preexisting dataset of another 500 controls without delirium (from Project Pensieve – Phase 1), and the combined dataset (n=1000) will be used to train deep neural networks to discriminate between delirium and non-delirium. At present, no similar AI solution exists in the market globally. If proven useful, the new AI tool can provide a more scalable and sustainable approach to address undiagnosed delirium and reduce adverse health outcomes.
kw: delirium; artificial intelligence; hospital admission; older persons; health services research; machine learning

title: Innovative m(mobile)Health-based program to facilitate exercise and self-management in knee osteoarthritis: A non-inferiority randomized controlled trial
abs: Background and Aims With an ageing population and rising obesity prevalence, the prevalence of knee osteoarthritis (OA) will increase with time. In Singapore, although outpatient physiotherapy is a key component of conservative OA management, regular outpatient rehabilitation is costly and inconvenient for patients. As a m(mobile)Health-based rehabilitation program potentially provides the best access to affordable OA care, we aim to (i) co-design with stakeholders to create a locally contextualized OA self-management program and (ii) compare the clinical- and cost-effectiveness of this innovative program with that of standard hospital-based rehabilitation among patients with knee OA in a randomized controlled trial (RCT). Hypotheses We hypothesize that a 24-week mHealth-facilitated exercise and self-management program will not be clinically inferior to a 12-week hospital-based rehabilitation program at 6 months post randomization, in terms of improving physical functional outcomes, and that the mHealth-based program will be more cost-effective than the hospital-based rehabilitation program. Methods This will be a single assessor-blinded, parallel design, RCT. Two hundred patients with knee OA will be randomly assigned to either a 12-week hospital-based, physiotherapist-supervised rehabilitation program or a 24-week mHealth-based program. To support personalized exercise progression, the mobile app will interface with a force-platform system that we have developed to provide criterion-based exercise progression recommendations. Outcome measures will be collected at baseline and at 3 and 6 months post randomization. The primary outcome will be physical function. Secondary outcomes include healthcare costs, knee pain intensity, knee impairments, physical activity, and quality of life. Significance This study is the first in Singapore to develop and examine an innovative and affordable solution for delivering guideline-recommended care to a large segment of patients with knee OA. If successful, the mHealth-based program has the potential to reduce or delay the need for an expensive total knee replacement surgery.
kw: digital health; knee osteoarthritis; self-management; physical therapy

title: Using Patient-Reported Outcome Measures to Improve the Use of Elective Orthopaedic Surgeries: Development and Evaluation of a Treatment Decision Support Intervention for Patients with Knee Osteoarthritis
abs: The increasing global utilisation of elective orthopaedic surgery and concerns about suboptimal patient outcomes and satisfaction call for improved decision-making in clinical practice. This project aims to develop and evaluate a novel patient decision support intervention (PDSI) for patients with knee osteoarthritis (OA). This PDSI comprises an application for providing individualised health outcome predictions of total knee replacement (TKR) surgery, a widely used surgical treatment for knee OA, and an implementing plan. We hypothesise that this PDSI can be used in local clinical practice and will improve the treatment decisions, care experiences, and outcomes of knee OA patients. This project will be carried out in two phases, including a development phase (Phase 1) and an evaluation phase (Phase 2). In Phase 1, the core of the application will be developed, including a qualitative study to understand patient and surgeon perspectives on knee OA treatment decisions and prediction models for post-operative patient-reported outcomes (PROs) of TKR surgery. The analysis will be based on data collected from three PRO measures (PROMs) at the National University Hospital Department of Orthopaedic Surgery (NUH-DOS) since 2009. A web-based application and an implementation plan will be collaboratively developed with a multidisciplinary team of patients and clinicians. In Phase 2, we will assess the effectiveness of this PROM-based PDSI using a cluster-randomised crossover trial. In this trial, we will prospectively recruit 210 knee OA patients (intervention group: 105; usual care group: 105) who visit the NUH-DOS for consultation and treatment. We will follow all patients up to 1 year to evaluate their treatment decision processes and outcomes, satisfaction, and post-treatment health outcomes. This project will lay the foundation for a new research programme that has the potential of improving patient experience and outcomes as well as the efficiency and cost-effectiveness of healthcare delivery in Singapore.
kw: Patient decision support intervention; Osteoarthritis; Total knee replacement; Shared decision making; Patient-reported outcomes; Decision quality

title: Phase 1/2 trial integrating allogeneic NK cells in high-risk advanced stage III-IV nasopharyngeal cancer patients
abs: Natural Killer (NK) cells are lymphocytes innately programmed to recognize and eliminate virally infected or mutated cells without the need to engage class I MHC molecule. This property enables them to play a crucial role to eliminate circulating cancer cells, which is essential to prevent carcinogenesis or minimize cancer relapses following definitive cancer treatment. It is therefore unsurprising that both quantities and functions of NK cells are frequently compromised in cancer patients. In locally endemic nasopharyngeal cancer (NPC) that is ubiquitously associated with the Epstein Barr Virus (EBV) infection, the presence of detectable post-treatment circulating EBV-DNA has been well-documented to represent minimal residue disease (MRD), which portends a high risk of relapse following definitive treatment and thus a worse prognosis. We hypothesized that infusing adjuvant functional activated NK cells eradicates post treatment circulating EBV-DNA completely, from currently presenting in 30% of advanced NPC patients to 10%. To this end, our laboratory has developed a robust technique of expanding allogeneic NK cells from peripheral blood mononuclear cells to nearly 350-fold increase over a 21-day expansion protocol. These expanded, enriched NK cells demonstrated in vitro potent cytotoxic ability against NPC cells. Furthermore, they were proven to be highly effective in vivo on suppressing NPC tumors and exerting an additive tumor suppressive effect when combined with cisplatin chemotherapy in NPC rodent model. Building on these preliminary data and our previous success in applying autologous NK cell therapy in NPC patients, we propose a phase 1 leading to phase 2 clinical trial to evaluate the safety and preliminary efficacy of adjuvant, allogeneic NK cell treatment for locally advanced NPC patients. If successful, this pre-emptive strike using “off the shelf” allogeneic NK cells to eliminate MRD among advanced NPC patients will reduce their risk of relapses and invariably improve survivals of these patients.
kw: Off the shelf allogenic NK cells; Locally advanced nasopharyngeal cancer (NPC); chemoradiation; Minimally residual disease (MRD); Phase 1 and 2 clinical trial, plasma EBV-DNA, immunoprevention

title: Pilot study of the Serious Illness Care Program in Singapore
abs: Background: High quality conversations between clinicians and seriously ill patients about their values and goals are associated with improved outcomes but occur infrequently. The Serious Illness Care Program (SICP) is a system-level care delivery model aimed at ensuring every seriously ill patient can have more, better, and earlier conversations with their clinicians. The SICP was developed in the United States and is a multi-component program, comprising education of clinicians in serious illness communication (SIC) skills, use of a serious illness communication guide (SICG), and support for leaders and champions to support change. However, the effectiveness of a program such as SICP depends on the context in which it is delivered. Whilst SIC might be seen as universally important, acceptance of communication around serious illness is likely to differ amongst healthcare settings that are sited in different geo-cultural environments. Aims and Hypothesis: Our overall aim is to pilot the SICP program locally in Singapore to determine suitable program parameters that will facilitate subsequent large-scale implementation of the SICP. Specifically, we will evaluate the comparative feasibility and appropriateness of different SIC triggers and also the acceptability of SIC amongst patients, caregivers and healthcare staff. We hypothesize that the feasibility and appropriateness of specific conversation triggering criteria will differ, though SIC will overall be acceptable. Methods: This will be a non -randomized pilot study that will recruit at least 30 patients, 30 caregivers and 20 clinicians from the National Cancer Centre Singapore and the National Heart Centre Singapore. We will collect quantitative survey data on participant communication experience, time from SIC to death, and perform semi-structured interviews to understand barriers and facilitators to SIC. Study feasibility: The study is feasible as the team already has experience teaching SIC and adapting SICG locally. Significance: A successful SICP will improve patient and caregiver outcomes.
kw: serious illness conversation; heart failure; cancer;

title: National University Health System Investigational Medicine Unit
abs: IMUs provide supporting infrastructure for clinician-investigators, such as a dedicated space and beds for inpatient and outpatient research, computer hardware, and software systems for data management and analysis, as well as manpower infrastructure such as clinical pharmacologists, clinical research coordinators, specialised research nurses/clinical research nurses, and biostatisticians. IMUs focus on early phase trials (Phases 1 and 2), preferably first-in-human studies while also supporting late phase trials, and encourage collaborative efforts across trial units, institutions and clusters in Singapore as well as outside Singapore to develop innovative thought leadership and global competitiveness.
