title: The Singapore Epidemiology of Eye Diseases (SEED) Study 4: Prospective multi-ethnic cohort study of 20-year incidence, progression, and risk factors of major eye diseases in elderly Asians
abs: Asia bears a disproportionate burden of visual impairment (VI), representing 75% of global primary angle-closure glaucoma and high myopia cases. As the region experiences a demographic shift towards an aging population, the prevalence of eye diseases is expected to rise. To address this issue, we propose a 20-year longitudinal study focusing on major eye diseases in Asia, particularly primary angle closure disease (PACD) and myopic macular degeneration (MMD). This research builds on the landmark Singapore Epidemiology of Eye Diseases Study, a multi-ethnic population-based study conducted the baseline visit from 2004 to 2011, which examined 10,033 Malays, Indians, and Chinese Singaporeans aged 40-80 years. We subsequently conducted the 6-year follow-up (SEED-2, 2011-2017) with 6,762 participants and the on-going 12-year follow-up (SEED-3, 2017-2023) with approximately 5,100 participants to date. Now, we propose SEED-4 to re-examine this cohort two decades after the baseline study. Our primary objectives are to determine the 20-year incidence, progression, and risk factors of VI and major eye diseases, particularly PACD and MMD. Additionally, we aim to create a digital virtual cohort to enhance prediction and management of these eye diseases. Using advanced ocular imaging technology and analytic methods, we seek to discover novel imaging biomarkers, understand aging-related retinal changes, and assess the impact of polypharmacy on eye disease. We will also analyse and compare longitudinal data across ethnic and age groups, including the super-aged. With an experienced team of epidemiologists, clinician-scientists, computer scientists, and imaging specialists we have comprehensive access to high-quality, deep-phenotyped ocular and systemic data, ocular imaging, preserved bio-samples, and genomic data. The forthcoming completion of the proposed 20-year follow-up visit promises invaluable insights into the long-term natural progression of major eye diseases in the elderly Asian population. This data will inform public health strategies to mitigate visual impairment not only in Singapore but throughout Asia.
kw: Aging; Age-related eye disease; Epidemiology; Digital Health; Artificial intelligence; Myopia

title: The Pre-clinical therapeutic validation of tyrosine hydroxylase inhibitor in LRRK2 Parkinson's disease models.
abs: In our preliminary study, we have shown that PD-linked LRRK2 mutations deregulate TH-DA (Tyrosine hydroxylase-dopamine) pathway, resulting in up-regulation of DA (Dopamine) early in the disease which subsequently leads to neurodegeneration. We found that LRRK2 mutation deregulate TH-DA pathway in human neurons, transgenic LRRK2 Drosophila, mouse and human middle brain organoid PD models. However, the LRRK2 induced DA toxicity and neurodegeneration can be reversed by low dosage application of a clinical grade drug, α-methyl-L-tyrosine (α-MT), a TH inhibitor, in transgenic drosophila PD models. α-MT is an orally competitive TH inhibitor, which has been used clinically. In this proposal, we suggest to test and validate whether early stage application of TH inhibitor α-MT can protect DA neurons and abrogate PD onset in LRRK2 G2019S TG mouse model and human middle brain organoid model carrying G2019S mutation. The successful execution of the current study and achievements from this project will help pave the way for future application of TH inhibitor as a new therapeutic strategy against LRRK2 mutation induced DA neurodegeneration in PD.
kw: Dopamine, LRRK2, Neurodegeneration, Parkinson's disease, tyrosine Kinase, PINK1

title: A functional genomic study to identify therapeutic targets for abdominal aortic aneurysm
abs: Population-scale genetic analyses have discovered many genomic loci associated with abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA). However, for most of these loci, the biological mechanism linking the genetic variants and the disease remains unknown, hindering therapeutic translation from these important findings. There is emerging evidence indicating that some of the genetic loci promote AAA by primarily acting on vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs), a major cell type of the arterial wall and a key player in AAA development and progression. We hypothesize that: 1) some genetic loci promote AAA through influencing causal gene expression in VSMCs and thereby altering VSMC phenotypes; 2) targeting the causal genes at such loci can modulate VSMC behaviour and inhibit AAA development and progression; and 3) some causal genes at these loci represent potential therapeutic targets for AAA intervention. In a recent study, we performed a systematic, integrative analysis of genetic and transcriptomic data from a large biobank of VSMCs, to interrogate genetic variants at the AAA loci in relation to genetic influence on gene expression in VSMCs. The study identified 55 candidate causal genes at AAA loci that may act through VSMCs. Here we propose a follow-up study with the aims to: 1) ascertain effects of these AAA candidate causal genes on VSMC apoptosis and phenotypic changes; 2) investigate the cognate molecular mechanisms; 3) test effects of selected candidate causal genes on aortic aneurysm development in an animal model; and 4) screen for compounds that can modulate VSMC apoptosis via a selected AAA causal gene. The research team and collaborators collectively have expertise and experience on the methods to be used. The findings from this project will provide a better mechanistic understanding of genetic influence on AAA risk and nominate novel targets for further therapeutic development.
kw: Cardiovascular disease; genetics; vascular smooth muscle cells

title: Mapping and characterising NF2-YAP and motins family mediated cardiomyocyte cell renewal and cardioprotection
abs: Heart failure is incurable because the loss of cardiomyocytes (CMs) is not overcome by any substantial innate reparative capacity for the heart to repair itself. Over the past decade, renowned research groups have reported that CM-specific activation of the Hippo Effector YAP induces pro-proliferative gene programs and cardiac repair. As such, inhibiting negative regulators of YAP, such as SAV1, a component of the canonical hippo-kinase regulatory pathway, improves cardiac function following myocardial infarction. However, the role of NF2/AMOT-mediated non-canonical hippo signalling, upstream and at the adherens junction borders of CM, has not been noticed or characterized in cardiac development and disease. Our preliminary findings establish the importance of the NF2-AMOT scaffold regulation of YAP in early CM differentiation. Specifically, we found that a 7 amino-acid “blue-box” motif in the NF2 FERM domain, and specific post-translational modification of AMOT Serine-175 may serve as targets region for designing novel dominant-negative decoys and CRISPR based approaches to induce YAP activation and CM regeneration. To deepen these initial findings, we will comprehensively map out the interactions and post-translational modification of the players. We will use high-content screening and the FUCCI cell system to test and validate a small series of novel decoy peptides and existing YAP activators, with the aim of uncovering all the necessary and sufficiency factors of this important CM pathway. Leading candidates will be tested on in vivo mouse and human engineered heart tissue models for their translational value on CM regeneration and/or cardioprotection.
kw: cardiomyocyte, heart failure, YAP, motins

title: A Model for Myopic Traction Maculopathy Progression Based on Retinal Biomechanics
abs: High myopia (HM), or extreme nearsightedness, is a leading cause of blindness worldwide when HM progresses to pathologic myopia (PM). PM manifests clinically in two forms — tractional (namely, myopic traction maculopathy: MTM) and degenerative (myopic macular degeneration). The two forms often occur concurrently, and we recently reported tractional PM predisposes an eye to degenerative PM. By 2050, it is predicted that 1 billion people worldwide will have HM, almost a quarter of whom may have MTM. MTM is a spectrum of tractional macular complications ranging from retinoschisis (splitting among the layers of the photoreceptive retina) to macular holes with end-stage foveal retinal detachment and permanent vision loss. At present, there is no preventive treatment for MTM and surgical treatment is reserved for end-stage MTM eyes. MTM has been strongly associated with tractional forces on the retina in both the anterior-posterior and coronal planes. All stages of MTM progression are associated with Müller cell anatomic stretching within the retina layers. However, the biomechanics at the tissue level (retina) and cellular level (Müller cell) have not been fully described in MTM. We will use state-of-the-art engineering tools to measure in vivo biomechanical properties that have previously remained elusive: 1) retinal tissue strain (deformation in response to elevated intraocular pressure) and 2) Müller cell stiffness (or resting tone). More specifically, the proposed studies will examine the hypothesis that retinal tissue strain and Müller cell stiffness are predictive of functional changes (as measured by microperimetry) and MTM progression. These, along with posterior ocular curvature and other myopia-related measurements will be used to train a deep neural network to classify HM, stable MTM or progressive MTM. The culmination of this work will allow us to direct surgical timing and location of mechanical-releasing interventions, and also elucidate potential novel therapeutic targets for MTM.
kw: Myopic Traction Maculopathy; Pathologic Myopia; Muller Cells; High Myopia; Inner Limiting Membrane

title: CRISPR/Cas-powered point-of-care testing for rapid identification of antibiotic resistance in urine bacteria
abs: Urinary tract infection (UTI) is one of the most common bacterial infections especially among women. Antibiotic/antimicrobial resistance (AMR) of bacteria makes UTI harder to treat and increase the risk of disease spread and severe illness. AMR it is a major global health threat and requires urgent measures. Classic methods for AMR analysis are laborious and time-consuming, thus rapid and reliable test methods are needed by clinicians. In this project, we will develop a point-of-care testing (POCT) system for urinary bacteria AMR analysis. The system utilizes CISPR/Cas-based molecular diagnostic assay for multiplex identification of bacteria species and their antibiotic resistant genes. Microfluidic modules are designed for each key steps in the test including DNA extraction, amplification and AMR genes detection. Individual components are integrated to automate the whole process. Total test time is significantly shorter than standard methods and the results will provide information on types of antibiotics the patient may have resistance to. The POCT system provides sample-to-answer AMR analysis solution which can be deployed at frontlines of UTI diagnosis. It will help the clinician to determine personalized and effective antibiotic therapies, meanwhile minimize the unnecessary use of medicine and the spread of resistance microorganisms.
kw: point-of-care, bacteria, urine, antibiotic resistance, antimicrobial resistance, CRISPR

title: Targeting metabolic vulnerabilities in breast cancer brain metastases
abs: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is a heterogeneous disease with a poor prognosis due to the lack of targeted therapies and its propensity for brain metastases (BrM). The blood-brain/tumor barrier (BTB) further limits the efficacy of therapeutic agents. Identification of novel therapeutic targets and the development of molecules capable of crossing the BTB are critical advancements. Recent studies have revealed metabolic vulnerabilities in TNBC, including the upregulation of de novo lipid synthesis pathways to adapt and grow in the lipid-poor brain microenvironment. Notably, upregulation of the transcription factor SREBP1, a master regulator of lipid synthesis, has been implicated in BrM growth and survival in HER2+ and TNBC BrM. MNK inhibitors (MNKi) have demonstrated the ability to modulate lipid metabolism and inhibit SREBP1 function. Thus, we hypothesized that MNK activity contributes to SREBP1-dependent growth in neurotropic TNBC. Our preliminary data show that neurotropic TNBC upregulate MNK and critical lipid biosynthetic genes, including SREBP1 and FASN, compared to their non-neurotropic counterparts. Neurotropic TNBC cells exhibited robust growth in lipid-depleted conditions mimicking the brain microenvironment. Strikingly, a brain-penetrant MNKi, ETC-501, significantly inhibited their growth and induced apoptotic cell death in vitro, and completely prevented the establishment of CNS metastases in vivo. Mechanistically, MNKis impaired the nuclear translocation of SREBP1 and inhibited lipid droplet formation. These results highlight a novel and essential MNK-SREBP1 axis in the establishment and growth of TNBC in the brain microenvironment, and demonstrate that MNKis are highly effective in preventing TNBC BrM. Our specific aims are to: 1. Validate the activity of MNKis in TNBC BrM, 2. Determine the mechanism of action of MNKis in TNBC, and 3. Identify MNKi combinations that prevent and combat therapy resistance. The completion of these Aims will validate the targeting of MNK in TNBC BrM, and provide a thorough understanding of their mechanism of action.
kw: Breast cancer; brain metastases; metabolism

title: Making Further Inroads into High Risk Myeloma
abs: Multiple myeloma is the second most common haematologic malignancies and has a rising incidence in Singapore. Significant advances have been made in the treatment of myeloma over the last decades with an improvement in overall survival from 4 years to more than 10 years now. However, there remain a high-risk group of myeloma patients whose survival is still at about 2-3 years despite this improvement. In recent years, the following high-risk phenotypes have emerged that are still significant unmet medical needs. 1) Patients with double genetic hits including 1q21 amplification and 17p13/p53 loss; 2) Patients who are multi-drug refractory with those who are refractory to lenalidomide and immunotherapy targeting CD38 and BCMA as being particularly associated with poor outcomes; 3) Patients who progress within 18 months of induction therapy, the so-called functional high-risk myeloma patients who does not harbor any of the known high-risk genetic factors. In these patients, the presence of resistant clones manifesting as residual disease may be a clinically relevant source of relapse. In this proposal, we aim to build on the work that we have previously done to tackle these areas of unmet needs. We will target nodes of vulnerabilities that we have previously identified in patients with 1q Amp and 17p13 loss. We will study a novel mechanism of Lenalidomide resistance and develop multi-targeting antibody-based treatment to better eradicate myeloma cells and prevent loss of efficacy due to heterogenous antigen expression of 1 antigenic target. Lastly, we will utilize single cell techniques to understand residual and drug resistant cells as well to understand the microenvironment of functional high-risk patients. I believer but targeting these 3 areas of significant challenge and unmet medical needs in clinic will bring about the next leap in outcome improvement in myeloma.
kw: multiple myeloma, therapeutics, 17p13, ADAR1 over-expression, drug resistance, genomics

title: Elucidating Heart-Brain Interactions of Functional Significance in Older Adults
abs: The critical heart-brain connection is underscored by the intricate relationship between cardiovascular health and cognitive functions. Advanced brain and cardiac MRI techniques have proved pivotal in furthering our understanding of this connection. Our recent research among asymptomatic community-dwelling older adults has revealed significant associations between reduced cerebrovascular and cardiac functions. This sheds light on the alarming prevalence of silent cognitive and cardiac deterioration in our community, and emphasizes the potential of advanced MRI techniques for early intervention. Despite these promising discoveries, there remains a need for rigorous validation through controlled studies. Particularly, exploring the influence of the heart-brain connection on ageing represents a significant gap in current research. To address these challenges, we propose a prospective study, nested within a larger clinical trial, that leverages diet and exercise intervention to investigate the functional implications of heart-brain alterations in older adults with cardiac issues. Our aim is to investigate the heart-brain connection in older adults with cardiac problems, focusing on the impact of a diet and exercise intervention on both cerebrovascular and cardiac functions. Through this, we hope to enhance our understanding of the role this connection plays in ageing and cognitive decline. The proposal will test the following hypotheses: i) Diminished cardiac function is associated with cerebrovascular alterations and cognitive deficits, without specific intervention; ii) a diet and exercise intervention can slow the progression of cerebrovascular and cardiac dysfunction compared to a control group; iii) changes in the brain and heart will occur simultaneously post-intervention. If substantiated, our research could highlight early intervention strategies, delay cognitive and cardiac deterioration, and improve the quality of life and longevity in older populations. The potential of this proposed study to transform clinical practices, emphasizing the heart-brain connection and proactive interventions, holds significant and extensive implications.
kw: Brain Heart Connection; Ageing; Cardiac MRI; Brain MRI; Cognition; Intervention

title: Ultrasonic control of multiplexed gene expression to enhance adoptive T cell therapy
abs: Engineered T cell therapies such as T cell receptor and chimeric antigen receptor T cells have achieved remarkable success in treating blood malignancies, but challenges remain to treat solid tumour due to insufficient T cell activation. Nonetheless, non-specific activation causes on-target, off-tumour adverse effect. Thus, there is a high demand for the development of more precise, non-invasive, and tunable control of cell therapy. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC), a prevalent head-neck malignant tumour in south Asia, still lacks effective treatment, especially for patients with recurrent or metastatic disease. Engineered T cells targeting Epstein Barr virus antigens, often expressed in NPC patients, have shown promising but limited success in recent clinical trials. Strategies to improve the efficacy and safety of EBV-specific T cell therapy are needed. Sonogenetics is an emerging but under-explored field using ultrasound to regulate cellular activity. We propose to develop new approaches to employ ultrasound for multiplexed gene modulation in EBV-specific T cells to improve treatment against NPC by enhancing T cells’ anti-tumour activity in a temporal and spatial specific manner. We hypothesize that we can reply on the thermal effect of focused ultrasound through the CRISPR-Cas system. To achieve this, we plan to conduct experiments in the following three stages: 1) Develop thermosensitive CRISPR-Cas tools in cell lines; 2) Apply these tools in primary human T cells to show multiplexed gene activation; 3) Demonstrate enhanced T cell activity in NPC cell or tumour models. These experiments will build the foundation of using ultrasound as a highly specific and safe method to improve immunotherapy in general. We have shown some preliminary data with a heat/ultrasound-sensitive Cas12a system for transcriptional activation and achieved simultaneous activation of four genes (Aim 1). We have also demonstrated thermosensitive CRISPR-Cas activation for reporter gene activation in primary human T cell and mouse tumour model.
kw: Cell therapy; Sonogenetics; Genome engineering; Nasopharyngeal carcinoma; Immunotherapy

title: Artificial enzyme-regulated probiotics for self-adaptive tumor therapy
abs: Probiotics have shown potential in shifting the tumor environment to inhibit tumor growth, but their therapeutic accuracy and efficacy are limited. To address this, the proposal introduces a redox regulatory strategy using pH-dependent artificial enzymes. These enzymes can generate reactive oxygen species (ROS) specifically within the tumor while remaining safe in normal tissues. Responding to the TME, these artificial enzymes can selectively produce ROS, guiding the metabolism of probiotics and promoting the increased production of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs). These SCFAs plays a dual role in this strategy. On one hand, the SCFAs can regulate the tumor immune microenvironment, promoting an anti-tumorigenic response. On the other hand, as SCFAs accumulate within the TME, they create a more acidic environment, which enhances the catalytic activity of the artificial enzymes and facilitates the generation of higher levels of ROS. The study aims to: 1) Investigate how artificial enzymes regulate probiotic behavior. 2) Explore the tumor-targeting ability and assess the safety of engineered probiotics. 3) Investigate the anti-tumor potential and immunoregulatory mechanisms of engineered probiotics with artificial enzymes in colorectal cancer models. The feasibility of this work is supported by the researcher's expertise in artificial enzymes and successful studies using antioxidant enzymes to protect probiotics in treating colitis. Preliminary data shows that engineered enzymes can modulate probiotic behavior and exhibit anti-cancer effects at the cellular level. However, further evaluation is needed to understand the underlying mechanisms, therapeutic effects, and immunomodulatory mechanisms involved. Nonetheless, the team's experience in probiotic research and tumor immunology supports the feasibility of this work. The importance of this research lies in its potential to develop more effective probiotic-based therapies for controlled cancer treatment, leading to improved therapeutic outcomes and patient well-being.
kw: artificial enzymes, probiotics, cancer, immunotherapy, metabolic regulation

title: EBV-specific immunity across the healthy human lifespan and in nasopharyngeal carcinoma
abs: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) latently infects >90% of adults and is associated with multiple inflammatory and malignant disorders, including nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC), which is endemic to Singapore. Increased EBV DNA titres are associated with poorer NPC outcome, suggesting a role for lapsed control of the virus in the pathogenesis of this disease. Similarly, EBV reactivation is observed in the elderly. It is currently unclear how EBV-specific immunity changes with age, and if reduced immunosurveillance could be associated with subsequent cancer incidence or other pathology. Hypothesis: Dysregulated EBV-specific immunity in ageing and EBV-associated malignancy results in lapsed viral control and disrupted interactions with the systemic immunome Specific Aims: We propose to investigate 1) longitudinal changes of EBV-specific immunity across the healthy human lifespan, 2) differences in EBV-specific immunity in NPC vs. healthy individuals and 3) the mechanistic basis of derangements in EBV-specific immunity in ageing and NPC Approach: We will utilise mass cytometry to compare high-dimensional immunophenotyping of healthy human donor PBMC across the human lifespan, and diseased PBMC from NPC patients. Network analyses will be used to infer interactions between antigen-specific and nonspecific immunity. The mechanistic basis of derangements in EBC-specific immunity in ageing and NPC will be assayed using functional assays, single-cell transcriptomics, and spatial transcriptomics of NPC tumours. Feasibility: Our in-house immunome resource and analysis pipeline will facilitate high-dimensional analyses. Most healthy and NPC PBMC samples have already been collected. We have also determined that EBV-specific T cells are readily detected in the circulation. Importance to Science/Medicine: These studies will establish a reference of healthy EBV-specific responses throughout the human lifespan and identify dysregulated immune components in NPC, thereby facilitating the design of effective, tailored therapies against EBV.
kw: infectious disease; cancer; translational research; immunology; nasopharyngeal cancer; EBV

title: HOPE (Helping to Optimize Potential & Experiences) after Pediatric Critical Illness Cohort Study
abs: In tandem with improvements in supportive care provided in the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU), decreasing mortality from pediatric critical illness comes at the cost of increased morbidity. Poor survivorship after pediatric critical illness is associated with long-term health sequalae, increased medical needs and hospital readmissions. Our current understanding on how to optimize the potential of these survivors is limited by the inability to identify patients who are at the highest risk for physical and cognitive sequalae and identification of modifiable risk factors that are associated with poor outcomes. To address this unmet need, we propose the first long-term longitudinal PICU study across two centres in Singapore that will collect in-depth data with the overall aim of investigating patient demographics and medical interventions that influence physical and cognitive outcomes in a child up to 18 months after PICU admission. This prospective cohort study have the following aims: (1) To characterize the 6 to 18 months physical (e.g., Pediatric Evaluation of Disability Inventory Computer Adaptive Test) and cognitive health outcomes (e.g., National Institute of Health Toolbox Cognition Battery) of PICU survivors; (2) Investigate for subgroups of patients who are at the highest risk of bad physical and cognitive health outcomes; and (3) Elucidate modifiable risk factors within PICU supportive care (e.g., mechanical ventilation, nutrition, sedation and early mobilization) that are associated with poor health outcomes in PICU survivors. Upon completion of this study, we will have a comprehensive dataset that will reveal a detailed trajectory of physical and cognitive outcomes of PICU survivors in Singapore. These data are essential to help us understand how to optimize survivorship of our youngest critically ill patients. Leveraging on the insights provided by this study, future studies can investigate the efficacy of specific interventions that target the highest risk patients for poor outcomes.
kw: Pediatric critical care; pediatrics; survivorship; morbidity; functional outcomes

title: The Novel Role of a Peptide in Promoting Neural Stem Cell Reactivation
abs: The balance between proliferation and quiescence of stem cells is crucial for development and tissue homeostasis. Most neural stem cells (NSCs) in the adult mammalian brain exist in a quiescent state, but can be reactivated upon physiological stimuli. Dysregulation of NSC reactivation is associated with neurodevelopmental disorders. Drosophila larval brain NSCs have emerged as a powerful in vivo model to study quiescence and reactivation. Micropeptides are small polypeptides encoded by short open reading frames (sORF) and are essential regulators of various cellular processes. Dysregulation of the sORFs is linked to human diseases including cancer and neurodegenerative diseases. However, the role of sORFs during NSC reactivation and brain development is poorly understood. This proposal aims to establish a novel function of a peptide named Fp1 (fat body sORF-encoded peptide 1) in quiescent NSC reactivation during brain development. The central hypothesis of this proposal is that peptide Fp1 functions in the fat body to facilitate NSC reactivation via activating the Wingless/Wnt pathway. In specific aim 1, I will determine the role of the sORF Fp1 during NSC reactivation. I will validate the expression and localization pattern of Fp1 and identify the cell type(s) where Fp1 functions in NSC reactivation. I will also test the effects of gain-of-function of Fp1 during NSC reactivation. In specific aim 2, I will identify downstream targets of Fp1 peptide in promoting NSC reactivation by methods such as Mass Spectrometry. The causal relationship between Fp1 and the Wingless/Wnt pathway in NSC reactivation will also be examined by genetic analysis. I propose to establish a novel role of Fp1 and Wingless/Wnt signaling in promoting NSC reactivation. In conclusion, the outcome of this proposal will provide important insights into mechanisms of NSC reactivation and brain development, which may ultimately contribute to our understanding of mechanisms underlying small polypeptide-associated neurodevelopmental disorders.
kw: neural stem cells; reactivation; small polypeptide; Fp1; Drosophila

title: Investigation of the role of BATF in regulating hypoxia-induced T cell exhaustion in solid tumors
abs: Solid tumors are known to have a hypoxic tumor microenvironment (TME) that is immunosuppressive and poses a substantial barrier to the efficacy and persistence of anti-tumor immunotherapy. A wide range of transcription factors, including TOX, NFAT, TCF1, et.al, are extensively documented to regulate T cell differentiation and exhaustion in cancer. However, it is largely unknown how these transcription factors and associated gene expression programming determine the cell fate of tumor-infiltrating T cells (TILs) in the context of tumor hypoxia. My previous work has shown that tumor hypoxia promotes TILs effector dysfunction and terminal exhaustion upon repeated tumor antigen stimulation. In this study, we found that hypoxia-induced factor 1α (HIF1a) is required to inhibit T cell effector activity by suppressing immune effector expressions like IFNγ and TNFα. However, hallmarks associated with hypoxia-induced T cell terminal exhaustion do not seem to be dependent on HIF1a. This observation has prompted us to propose that hypoxia can promote infiltrating T cell exhaustion through a mechanism independent of HIF1α activation. In search of an answer to this question, we utilized a pre-established hypoxia-promoted tumor antigen-specific T cell exhaustion assay to screen for genes whose expression is associated with T cell exhaustion progression but not affected by HIF1α inhibitor treatment. This preliminary study has revealed that BATF, one of the critical transcription factors known to regulate T cell fate, is progressively downregulated during hypoxia-induced T cell terminal exhaustion. Given the known role of BATF in chromatin remodeling and the increasing knowledge that T cell exhaustion is highly associated with epigenetic regulation, we hypothesize that hypoxia-induced suppression of BATF may play an important role in promoting T cell exhaustion. This proposal investigates whether hypoxia-induced BATF downregulation contributes to T cell exhaustion and how it occurs in a HIF1α-independent manner.
kw: Tumor hypoxia; immunotherapy; T cell; BATF; terminal exhaustion

title: Mapping Human-Specific Immune-Microbiome Interactions for Microbiome-Based Therapeutics in Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Utilizing a Dual Humanized Immune and Gut Microbiome Mouse Model
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a chronic immune-mediated condition with increasing global prevalence. Despite advancements in IBD treatment, a therapeutic ceiling exists, with low clinical remission rates and diminishing drug efficacy. This research aims to utilize a humanized immune and gut microbiome (HIM) mouse model to study the interactions between the human gut microbiome and immune system in the context of IBD. The specific aims are as follows: 1. Characterize the immune response to IBD microbiome: The study will examine the transcriptomic and phenotypic changes in immune cells from the intestines and peripheral blood of HIM mice engrafted with IBD or healthy gut microbiome. Flow cytometry and transcriptomic analysis will be performed to identify immune cell alterations. 2. Investigate the association between immune changes and bacterial communities: The research will identify bacterial species overrepresented or underrepresented in HIM mice engrafted with IBD microbiome compared to healthy controls. Shotgun sequencing of fecal samples will be conducted, followed by bioinformatics analysis to determine differential abundance and pathway analyses. 3. Assess the effectiveness of bacterial replacement therapy: The study aims to identify combinations of live bacterial species that can reverse dysbiosis and alleviate IBD pathology in HIM mice. The project builds upon the development of the HIM mouse model, which enables the investigation of human-specific immune-microbiome interactions. Preliminary studies have shown successful engraftment of human fecal matter, stability of human B and T cells, increased secretion of human IgA, and reproduction of colitis symptoms in HIM mice. The research will contribute to the development of microbiome-based therapeutics for IBD and advance the field of microbiome-targeted therapies. Additionally, the HIM mice technology fills a translational gap, providing a valuable tool for studying microbiome-immune system interactions and accelerating the commercialization and adoption of microbiome-based therapeutics.
kw: Microbiome; IBD; Humanized Mouse

title: Using Spike-in RNA probes to train Machine Learning models: an approach to validate and improve RNA detection accuracy in Spatial Transcriptomics assays
abs: Spatial omics technologies, which profile the molecular content of single cells within the context of tissue architecture, hold immense promise for biological discovery and clinical application, especially in the areas of cancer and neurology (2 of the 7 national priorities for HHP research), by enabling a deeper understanding of disease etiology, progression and heterogeneity in treatment responses. Multiplexed fluorescence in-situ hybridization (MERFISH) methods are a major subset of spatial omics technologies, and form the basis for numerous recently released commercial platforms (e.g. 10X Xenium, Nanostring CosMx and Vizgen MERSCOPE). All use oligonucleotide probes to target and image 100s to 10,000s of different RNA species. RNAs are then decoded from stacks of noisy images, requiring stringent filtering that lowers sensitivity. There are currently no methods to directly validate the accuracy of RNA decoding, a critical step preceding all downstream analysis and impacting biological interpretations. We hypothesize that we can design “guide” probes targeting a subset of RNA to serve as a ground-truth controls and use the resulting data to validate the accuracy of existing decoding methods (Aim 1). This additional data will allow us to design machine-learning algorithms to substantially improve RNA detection accuracy and sensitivity (Aim 2). Finally, the accurate identification of cell types and their spatial relationships is critical for understanding tissue function. We hypothesize that we can use the same “guide” probe approach, but with careful selection of cell-type specific genes, to validate cell-types identified in spatial transcriptomic data (Aim 3). The proposed work will greatly enhance the key analysis step in FISH-based spatial transcriptomic assays – RNA decoding, and hence improve overall quality and reliability of such assays. This will potentiate the use of spatial omics in exploratory research on the molecular underpinnings of disease and enable the development of more accurate clinical diagnostics.
kw: Spatial Transcriptomics, Machine Learning, Computer Vision, Single cell omics

title: A multimodal learning framework to stratify cancer patients for immune checkpoint blockade
abs: Immune checkpoint blockade(ICB) is an established class of immunotherapy that induces significant tumor shrinkage and long-term disease control in many cancers. However, ICB can cost over $20,000 per month and most patients do not benefit from expensive ICB treatment. Existing biomarkers of ICB are inadequate for treatment stratification in many cancer types. Here, we hypothesize that a data-driven machine learning approach that integrates multiple data modalities from ICB patients would substantially improve patient stratification for ICB. First, we will develop a noise-robust deep learning (DL) framework that accurately predicts ICB outcome from tumor transcriptome. Then, we will tap into a clinical database of >3,000 local patients who have received ICB, to investigate the clinical-demographic predictors of ICB response in the local context. Finally, we will generate a multimodal patient cohort with complete clinical, transcriptomic and genomic data, to build an integrated learning framework based on all data modalities for improved ICB response prediction accuracy. In summary, we aim to deliver a multimodal learning framework that accurately predicts patient response to ICB based on transcriptomic, clinical and genomic data, and evaluates its utility in clinically relevant patient subgroups. This framework could significantly improve clinical decision-making on ICB treatment, and guide future clinical trials to enhance the efficacy and cost-benefit profiles of ICB agents.
kw: immune checkpoint blockade, immuno-oncology, machine learning

title: A multi-proteomics approach to elucidate mechanisms of drug resistance in the frontline treatment of sarcoma
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Soft tissue sarcoma accounts for more than 20% of paediatric and young adult malignancies. Frontline treatment, chemotherapy with doxorubicin has poor treatment outcomes with less than 20% of patients responding to treatment and an overall median survival of less than 1 year. Despite several large-scale efforts to characterize sarcoma with genomics and transcriptomics and some small studies with single proteomics approaches, the molecular mechanisms underlying doxorubicin resistance in sarcoma remain unknown. To address this knowledge gap, we propose to perform proteomics profiling on patient-derived sarcoma cells and a multi-proteomics approach on sarcoma cell lines. Proteomic profiling can identify protein abundance changes and response to treatment across the proteome. Comparison of the proteome profile of resistant and sensitive sarcoma cells will facilitate identification of biomarkers to predict patient response to doxorubicin treatment. Poorly responding patients can then be treated with alternative therapeutic strategies instead of suffering the side effects of doxorubicin with a small chance of therapeutic efficacy. The multi-proteomic approach will enable deciphering of the molecular mechanisms contributing to resistance, with information about protein abundance, protein abundance changes in response to treatment, protein binders to doxorubicin and identifying protein interaction partners of protein binders. Proteins contributing to doxorubicin resistance can then be validated in knockdown assays of patient-derived sarcoma cells. Identification and validation of proteins as potential therapeutic targets will help the development of treatment strategies for patients who do not respond to doxorubicin treatment. The proposed multi-proteomic approach will further our understanding of the molecular drivers of sarcoma and response to current frontline treatment, improving patient stratification, avoidance of unnecessary toxicity and ultimately better treatment outcomes for patients through discovery of novel targets. Future applications of this multi-proteomic approach can also be applied to other cancers to improve treatment outcomes for cancer patients.
kw: Proteomics; Mass Spectrometry; Sarcoma; Drug resistance; Drug mechanism; Predictive marker

title: In Vivo Spatial Perturb-Seq for the Functional Characterization of Alzheimer’s Risk Genes
abs: Perturb-seq is a scalable genetic screening approach that takes advantage of single-cell transcriptomics to profile CRISPR-edited cells on a massively parallel scale, allowing genetic interrogation in a compact and high throughput manner. However, perturb-seq is usually done cell culture systems. As a first-of-its-kind study, we applied perturb-seq in the adult mouse brain, to functionally evaluate neurodegeneration risk genes in their native environment, across different cell types. Spatial transcriptomics is a rapidly emerging method that has greatly accelerated biological discovery. We hypothesize that by integrating our in vivo perturb-seq CRISPR screen with spatial transcriptomics using our spatial barcode design, and applying it in the adult mouse brain, we will understand how a cell’s genetic perturbations affect its tissue environment, and how a cell’s response to perturbations is affected by its environment. Our goal is to determine genetic factors and pathways that modulate glial function from a neurodegenerative to homeostatic state, thus identifying therapeutic avenues to delay the onset of neurological decline. We propose expanding our capabilities in spatial phenotyping and to be one of the first to spatially characterize the CRISPR-perturbed mouse brain. We aim to study loss-of-function of 18 neurodegeneration risk genes in a biologically relevant, native tissue setting. As such, we have generated an AAV-CRISPR-knockout library and optimized a pipeline to feasibly address the following specific aims: 1. Technology pipeline establishment: Integrate in vivo perturb-seq with spatial transcriptomics 2. Application of spatial perturb-seq in the mouse brain 3. Statistical modelling and analysis of spatial genetic perturbation data
kw: Neuroscience; Spatial Transcriptomics; Perturb-seq; Microglia; Alzheimer's

title: Structural and mechanistic insights into G4 recognition and unwinding by Pif1 helicase
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: G-quadruplexes (G4s) are four-stranded DNA structures that can cause genome instability and cancer. Pif1 is a DNA helicase that can unwind G4s and regulate various cellular processes. However, the molecular mechanism of eukaryotic Pif1-mediated G4 unwinding is still unclear. We hypothesize that Pif1 helicase recognizes and unwinds G4 structures by a unique mechanism that differs from other G4-unwinding helicases. To test this hypothesis, we have two specific aims: 1) To determine the crystal structure of Pif1-G4 complex and identify the key residues involved in the interaction; 2) To elucidate the molecular mechanism of G4 unwinding by Pif1 using in vitro and in vivo assays. We have already solved the preliminary structure of Pif1-G4 complex, which reveals how Pif1 interacts with G4 mainly through the wedge region in domain 1B. We will further refine the structure and test the importance of key residues by mutagenesis and binding assays. We will also determine the kinetics of G4 unwinding by Pif1 and its mutants using in vitro unwinding assays. Moreover, we will examine the function of Pif1 mutants in Okazaki fragment processing and mitochondrial maintenance using yeast models. This research will provide novel insights into the structural and mechanistic basis of Pif1-mediated G4 unwinding, which is essential for maintaining genome stability and preventing cancer. This research will also facilitate the development of new strategies to modulate Pif1 activity and function, which could have potential applications in biotechnology and medicine.
kw: helicase; Pif1; G-quadruplexes; unwinding mechanism

title: Investigating the liver-brain vagal pathway underlying liver fibrosis for therapeutic discoveries
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Liver fibrosis is a crucial pathological precondition for liver cirrhosis, the top 20 causes for years of life lost in Singapore, and its severity is directly associated with the risk of liver cancer. While progress has been made to understand the cause of liver fibrosis, the contribution of the nervous system via hepatic innervation to disease progression remains largely unknown. In this work, we propose to investigate whether liver inflammation in a bile duct ligation (BDL) mouse model leads to activation of liver-innervating vagal neurons and neuronal activation in the synaptically connected brain regions (Aim 1). Additionally, we will determine if liver inflammation drives a counterregulatory pro- or anti-inflammatory gene transcriptional program in vagal neurons using a scRNA-seq approach. Knockdown or overexpression of the identified gene(s) of interest for evaluating the prognosis on BDL mice will be performed subsequently (Aim 2). Lastly, chemogenetic approaches will be utilized to inhibit or activate the liver-specific vagal pathway to evaluate the contribution of vagal nerve manipulation on the process of liver fibrosis (Aim 3). We hypothesize that increased liver inflammation in the BDL model activates liver-innervating vagal neurons as well as neurons in the connected downstream brain regions, liver inflammation activates the vagal neuronal gene transcriptional program towards an anti-inflammatory state to counter-regulate the immune response and stimulation of the vagal neural circuit reduces the inflammatory reaction and retards disease progression. Some preliminary data is provided to support the feasibility of the studies. Overall, this work offers new insights into the neural mechanisms on how the vagal nerves modulate liver inflammation in the BDL mouse model. This knowledge will also shed light on the interventions that can be done to delay the progression the liver fibrosis. Importantly, these findings can provide an opportunity for discovering novel neuro-immune targets for liver fibrosis treatment.
kw: Liver fibrosis; Liver-brain axis; vagus nerve; vagal neural circuit; single cell RNA sequencing

title: Profiling the Extracellular Milieu in Colorectal Cancer Tumors for Targeted Therapies
abs: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a growing health care burden in Singapore, with high incidence rates and low survival rates at later stages of the disease. Despite development of therapies that target specific cells within the tumor microenvironment (ME), there remains limited efficacy. In order to design better interventions, we propose to deeply characterize the tumor ME across a large patient cohort using high resolution spatial proteomics technology, multiplexed ion beam imaging (MIBI-TOF). Efforts to study MEs in CRC have been limited to cell types. However in order for coordinated tumor promotionto occur in the ME, there needs to be intercellular communication between cells. Here, alongside cell type and functional state delineation, we capture the extracellular milieu comprised of functional signaling and structural proteins that influence cancer progression through cell-cell communication and adaptive tissue scaffolds. By investigating the extracellular proteins and cells involved in forming pro-tumorigenic MEs, we aim to identify putative drug targets to modulate cancer progression. Consequently, we will validate anti-tumor effects of inhibiting extracellular protein activity in patient-derived organoids and syngeneic CRC mouse model. Together, this work aims to elucidate drivers of CRC progression within the extracellular milieu and thereby identify novel drug targets for CRC.
kw: Colorectal cancer; Tumor microenvironment; Extracellular proteins; Signaling

title: Investigating the pathogenesis of the Notch2nlc polyG expansion in neurodegenerative diseases
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: NOTCH2NLC (N2C) with GGC repeat expansions have been identified to be a cause of neuronal intranuclear inclusion disease (NIID), a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by ataxia, dementia, parkinsonism, and neuropathy. The pathogenic ( >60GGC) and intermediate (40-60xGGC) have also identified in patients with Parkinson’s disease and essential tremor. The GGC repeat is located within the 5’ UTR region of NOTCH2NLC gene, however, the exact pathogenesis underlying N2C-GGC repeat expansion-linked neurological disorders remains unknown, and the pathophysiologic role of intermediate repeats and AGC interruption have yet to be reported. We have generated several lines of N2C-GGC repeat expansion knockin (KI) mice carrying different GGC repeat sizes and AGC interruption. We highlight for the first time that the intermediate repeat with AGC interruption forms aggregates in mouse cortex and shows motor deficits. Hypothesis: We hypothesize that GGC repeat expansion sizes influence the degree of neurotoxicity in N2C-polyG-associated pathogenesis and AGC interruption can accelerate the pathogenic phenotypes. Objective: To investigate the pathogenicity of GGC expansions in human iPSC-derived neurons and transgenic mouse models, and to identify compounds that can inhibit N2C-polyG protein aggregations. Methodology: We will investigate the function of N2C-polyG in N2C repeat expansion-associated neurotoxicity in patient induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) using cell-based assay. We will elucidate the pathophysiology of the expansions in customized KI mice carrying pathogenic or intermediate repeats. Spatial transcriptomics with bulk-seq and single cell RNA transcriptomic profiling will evaluate cell-cell interaction and identify spatiotemporal gene expression pattern in N2C-polyG KI mouse model. We will also screen and identify inhibitors of N2C-polyG using a biosensor-based high throughput screening system and investigate the rescue effects of the hid-to-lead drugs in KI mouse models. Scientific/Clinical Impact: Our study will provide new pathophysiologic insights and identify novel compounds that can potentially treat N2C-GGC repeat expansion-linked neurological diseases.
kw: Notch2nlc, NIID, GGC repeat expansion, mouse model, patient iPSC

title: Decoding the Enigma of Postnatal Cardiomyocyte Maturation
abs: Cardiac development continues after birth when cardiomyocytes undergo dramatic changes which are collectively described as cardiomyocyte postnatal maturation. These changes are critically important for heart to adapt major changes in cardiovascular system during perinatal transition and postnatal growth. Despite of this obvious significance, little is known about the regulatory scheme responsible for the postnatal reprogramming in the new-born hearts. In the meantime, almost all stem-cell derived cardiomyocytes share the same deficiency in lack of maturity which is a major limiting factor in cell therapy and stem cell-based modeling for human heart diseases. Therefore, fundamental knowledge in postnatal cardiac maturation can have significant implications in better understanding the full continuum of cardiac development as well as addressing a major challenge in the field of stem-cell based therapy, mechanistic studies as well as drug development for human cardiomyopathies. Findings from our lab lead to our current hypothesis that postnatal maturation is contributed by RBFox1 mediated RNA-splicing in cardiomyocytes, and RBFox1 expression promotes specific features of stem-cell derived cardiomyocyte maturation and improves stem-cell based therapy and disease modeling for heart failure. In this proposal, we will rigorously investigate this novel hypothesis by accomplishing the following three specific aims: Aim 1. To uncover the molecular mechanism of RBFox1 mediated cardiomyocyte maturation by identifying responsible downstream targets. Aim 2. To identify upstream maturation specific transcriptional network for RBFox1 induction during perinatal cardiac reprogramming. Aim 3. To demonstrate the translational impact of RBFox1 mediated cardiomyocyte maturation in human stem-cell therapy and cell-based disease modeling.
kw: gene regulation, myocyte maturation, stem cell, cell therapy, heart disease, disease modeling

title: Using spatial transcriptomics of cerebral thrombus to uncover the biological mechanisms that underlie ischaemic stroke
abs: Spatial transcriptomics is a novel approach that precisely identifies the location of mRNA expression within intact biospecimens. Applying spatial transcriptomics to analyse cerebral thrombi may uncover the molecular mechanisms underlying ischaemic stroke and influence treatment decisions for secondary stroke prevention. In our preliminary analysis, we optimised analytical methods for cerebral thrombi and studied spatial transcriptomics in thrombi from two patients undergoing endovascular treatment - one with cardioembolic stroke and the other with intracranial large artery disease. This analysis provided a detailed digital profile of analyte abundance in the thrombi, revealing increased activation of certain pathways which was verified through protein analysis. We hypothesise that spatial transcriptomics analysis of retrieved cerebral thrombi could unveil stroke-specific gene expression profiles, explaining molecular differences between stroke mechanisms and those with post-stroke complications. To achieve this, we propose to: 1. Conduct spatial transcriptomics analysis of cerebral thrombi to create a comprehensive whole transcriptome atlas to describe stroke-specific gene expression profiles within different cellular components of the thrombi, and 2. Identify differentially expressed genes in individual cellular components that distinguish patients based on their stroke mechanism (cardioembolism and large artery disease) and those with post-stroke complications (e.g., symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage and malignant cerebral oedema). Findings from this study could offer essential molecular insights into stroke pathogenesis that may have important clinical and therapeutic applications.
kw: Stroke; spatial transcriptomics; RNA profiles; stroke mechanisms; stroke complications

title: Change in insulin sensitivity, insulin secretion and beta cell function from 24 to 28 weeks antepartum to 6 to 12 weeks and 52 to 56 weeks postpartum in women with gestational diabetes.
abs: Gestational diabetes (GDM), defined as hyperglycaemia during pregnancy, affects one in five pregnant women in Singapore. Maternal hyperglycemia arises due to the decline in insulin sensitivity during pregnancy. Although insulin resistance typically normalizes after pregnancy, a substantial proportion of women progress to dysglycaemia and develop type 2 diabetes (T2DM) within 12 months of delivery. However, the magnitude of change in insulin sensitivity from pregnancy to postpartum has not been clearly defined. Pancreatic β-cell function expands during pregnancy to increase insulin secretion and counteract the decline in insulin sensitivity during pregnancy. This change in β-cell function between pregnancy and the postpartum is also not well-understood. Reproductive hormones such as prolactin and human placental lactogen (hPL) stimulates β-cell proliferation and glucose stimulated insulin secretion whereas progesterone and adiponectin decrease glucose uptake and attenuate insulin signaling predisposing to insulin resistance. Physiological factors which influence the change in β-cell function, insulin sensitivity or insulin secretion are also not clearly evaluated. Furthermore, it has not been established if the β-cell function post-partum is determined by genetic factors that influence β-cell function in non-pregnant adults. Therefore, in this research proposal, we prospectively study the changes in insulin sensitivity/secretion and β-cell function following an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) in women with GDM from 24-28 weeks gestation up to 52-56 weeks postpartum. We study the association of insulin secretion/sensitivity and β-cell function with glucose tolerance status in women with GDM at 6-12 weeks postpartum. More importantly, we evaluate the contributions of hormonal and metabolic hormones to the change in insulin sensitivity/secretion and β-cell function before and after pregnancy and consider how these might differ from women with GDM who are normoglycaemic postpartum. Lastly, we determine the impact of partitioned genetic risk score for T2DM on insulin sensitivity/secretion in women with GDM.
kw: Gestational diabetes, pregnancy, type 2 diabetes, insulin sensitivity, insulin secretion

title: Defining proinflammatory metabolomic biosignature -using multiple sclerosis as a disease model.
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Neuroinflammation is the common thread that underpins all neurological diseases, (example stroke, Parkinson disease, Alzheimer dementia) with prototypical CNS neuroinflammatory disease being Multiple Sclerosis(MS). To date, there is no easily accessible and reliable biofluid marker informing on the extent of neuroinflammation in these diseases. Inflammation/neuroinflammation is a catabolic state, resulting in energy deficiency in chronic inflammation as measured by metabolomics. Further, specific immune cell types undergo metabolic programming during neuroinflammation, example activated microglial preferential use of glycolysis. Using MS as a representative disease, we aim to perform targeted metabolic analysis of energy-related metabolomes (TCA, glycolysis, lipid) and correlating to cytokines during clinical relapse and remission, defining metabolites that inform on neuroinflammation phases. We hypothesis that there are discriminatory energy metabolites during different neuroinflammatory phases determined by clinical parameters, neuroimaging, and cytokine profiling. Primary aim of this study is to identify discriminatory CSF neuroinflammation biosignature by comparing CSF metabolomes to cytokines between MS relapse and non-inflammatory controls. There are previous reports of similar differentiating TCA cycle-related metabolites e.g., isoleucine in CSF and serum which supports the plausibility to correlate CSF and serum metabolomes. Secondary aim(SA)1 is to identify serum neuroinflammation biosignature by comparing CSF neuroinflammation-specific metabolites with corresponding serum metabolites within MS relapse patients. For SA2, we would refine the serum biosignature by using paired sera from individual patients in relapse and remission and perform external validation using MS patient cohorts from United Kingdom and South Korea (SA3). Elucidation of neuroinflammation biosignature will provide direct measurement of neuroinflammatory intensity in MS patients allowing for expedient initiation of immunomodulatory therapies potentially ameliorating neuroinflammation and downstream deleterious effects on neurons. This also set the platform to interrogate other neurological diseases neuroinflammatory state and impact on future research to characterize neuroinflammation in other neurological disorders and identification of a therapeutic window for immunomodulatory therapy.
kw: Neuroinflammation, Biomarkers, Metabolomics, Neurology, Multiple sclerosis

title: Effectiveness of a Self-Administered Digital Psychological Toolkit to reducing Symptom Burden and Morbidity in Dermatology Patients: A Multicentre Randomised Controlled Trial
abs: Skin diseases can significantly impact the quality of life (QoL) and morbidity of individuals, causing physical symptoms such as skin flaking, itch and pain, as well as psychological distress. Inflammatory diseases like eczema and psoriasis are chronic and cyclical and the lack of curative treatments highlights the importance of adaptive coping strategies. Our research reveals that QoL impairment in dermatology patients is greater correlated with psychological constructs such as emotional representation of disease, social comparison and resilience, and less with objective disease measures. Despite this, there are limited strategies and interventions available to target psychological constructs in routine dermatological clinical practice. To address this need, we are currently developing and piloting a multimodal digital psychological tool kit to be self-administered on a mobile app. This intervention adapts evidence based psychological and behavioural techniques for dermatological patients, and targets selected constructs and needs identified from our previous study. In this multicentre double blind randomised controlled trial, we assess the effectiveness and implementability of this intervention in patients with chronic inflammatory skin disease. The primary outcome is the Skindex-16 (a dermatology specific QoL measure), secondary outcomes include generic QoL measures, objective disease severity, measures of psychological constructs such as resilience and anxiety, and disease perception including acceptance and illness coherence. Implementing such an intervention can be a useful adjunct to standard medical therapies. Moreover, it is designed to be scalable at low cost, thereby potentially improving not just patient reported outcomes, but also healthcare efficiency and value.
kw: quality of life; behavioural health; digital health; mental health; dermatology; psychological strategies

title: Investigating the Role of Humoral Innate Immunity in MSC Exosome-Mediated Alleviation of Osteoarthritis: Targeting Complement Activation
abs: Knee osteoarthritis is a diarthrodial wear-and-tear disorder of local cartilage and bone that is a global health burden and a major cause of disability in the elderly. Modern strategies have shifted to seek and provide joint preservation that is minimally invasive, with outcomes comparable to arthroplasty. The lack of adequate clinical outcomes with the currently available intraarticular injections may be because the focus should instead be chondrogenic for longevity, with a multipronged approach of combined extracellular matrices and growth factors to facilitate optimal joint conditions for multifaceted chondrogenesis that is ultimately hyaline. Mesenchymal stem cell (MSC) exosome intraarticular injections may allow superior joint preservation via synergistic chondrogenic extracellular matrix networking and growth factor signalling. There has been limited knowledge regarding complement activity in the pathogenesis of osteoarthritis and even more limited knowledge regarding exosomes/extracellular vesicles in modulating complement activity of this. The literature gap is clear; no studies revealed if MSC exosomes can play a role in complement activity regulation for knee osteoarthritis. The understanding of this can facilitate the involved protein cargo selection in the therapeutic doses to optimise joint homeostasis, notably for prime chondrogenesis. We propose a study protocol that involves MSC exosome injections in the rat knee osteoarthritis model to investigate the MSC exosome mechanism of action in complement activity regulation, including joint homeostasis.
kw: Complement; exosome; extracellular vesicle

title: Elucidating and therapeutically targeting the mechanisms of Interferonopathy against severe influenza and coronavirus infection
abs: Frequent viral mutations often render current influenza and COVID-19 therapeutics ineffective There is no treatment that prevents severe diseases and protracted illnesses such as long-COVID. Interferons (IFNs) are crucial antiviral factors that circumvent dissemination of viruses. Uncontrolled IFN levels are associated with severe influenza and COVID-19, and long-COVID. The underpinning mechanism of this pathogenic IFNs or “interferonopathy” is unknown. Understanding the molecular processes that contribute to severe disease pathogenesis would facilitate the development of effective treatments. Using our highly relevant ex vivo human nasal epithelial cells (pNECs) and CRISPR-Cas9, we show for the first time that host factors DHX40 and DDX52 play a key role in driving elevated IFN expression. We show that DHX40/DDX52 inhibits type I IFN expression potentially by disrupting a key signaling factor MAVS. DHX40/DDX52 levels are markedly reduced in severe influenza and coronavirus infection. Infection in DHX40- or DDX52-deficient pNECs leads to substantially higher IFN production and surprisingly more extensive epithelial damage. Reduced DHX40 / DDX52 expression is likely driven by highly up-regulated expressions of micro-RNA (miR)-302c and miR-181 family. These miRs are predicted to inhibit DHX40 and DDX52 expressions, thus increasing IFN production. We will combine our expertise with spatial transcriptomics/proteomics to 1.) define the mechanisms DHX40 and DDX52 mediated MAVS inactivation and IFN production; 2.) to elucidate the roles of DHX40 and DDX52 and IFN in severe epithelial damage; and 3.) to therapeutically target DHX40 and DDX52 using synthetic miR inhibitors and nanoparticles to treat influenza and coronavirus infection. These ground-breaking studies will provide novel insights into the role and therapeutic targeting of host factors that drive severe diseases by influenza and coronaviruses, including future emerging novel viruses. This is important since there is no effective treatment available that 1.) prevent and/or reduce infection severity, and 2.) are resistant to viral mutations.
kw: Influenza; coronavirus; innate immunity; airway epithelium; interferon

title: Functional and structural analysis of the sub-cellular localization of dengue NS5 protein and its impact on host response and pathogenesis
abs: Most studies on DENV and its non-structural (NS) proteins have been based on DENV serotype 2 (DENV2), despite the fact that the four DENV serotypes have well-characterized differences such as the subcellular localization of their NS5 protein. While the flavivirus NS5 protein plays its primary virus enzymatic role in the cytoplasm of infected cells, we have found that flavivirus NS5 proteins have distinctly different subcellular localizations, although the functional consequences are still not fully elucidated. We hypothesize that the subcellular localization of the flavivirus NS5 plays a crucial role in directing its interactions with the host and in virus-induced pathogenesis. In this proposal, we will utilize molecular, biochemical, and virological approaches to identify the molecular determinants of flavivirus NS5 subcellular localization, with a focus on how nuclear localization signal sequences and post-translational modifications regulate DENV3 and DENV4 NS5 localization respectively. We will then use cell biological and animal models to determine their effect on virus viability, replication and pathogenesis. The outcome of dengue infection is driven by the complex interplay between the host response to virus infection, and the virus’s attempts to counter it. In particular, the DENV serotype 2 NS5 protein antagonizes the host innate immune response, but it is not known whether the other DENV NS5 proteins function similarly and whether DENV2’s nuclear subcellular localization is involved. We will use cell biological approaches to directly test this. In addition, we will use complementary systems approaches to characterize how changes in NS5’s subcellular localization impacts the virus-host protein interactome, and the host response to DENV infection at both the proteome and transcriptome levels. These studies will be followed by cell biological and animal studies to interrogate the importance of these host factors and pathways on virus replication and pathogenesis.
kw: Dengue; non-structural protein 5 (NS5); virus-host interactions

title: Preclinical development of innovative T cell-directed immunotherapy for sustainable immune memory and tumor clearance
abs: Immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) has revolutionalized cancer therapy, yet some patients failed to achieve positive clinical outcomes. Emerging evidence has shown that the failure of ICI is primarily attributed to the high amount of exhausted T cells and the lack of progenitor T cells in the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). Although anti-PD1 could revitalize exhausted T cells, it does not impact the proliferation of progenitor T cells, leading to a deficiency of T cells in TME due to the apoptotic susceptibility of exhausted T cells. We have identified a new regulator of T cell differentiation and exhaustion, namely PHLH. We showed that PHLHhigh/PD1+/TIM3+/CD8+ exhausted T cell subset is highly correlated with ICI resistance in both mouse and human tumors. Interestingly, inhibiting PHLH mitigates T cell exhaustion and simultaneously enhances the self-renewal capacity of progenitor memory phenotypes. Using CAR T cells, we showed that ex vivo treatment of PHLH inhibition greatly enhanced in vitro and in vivo expansion, increased memory and reduced exhausted of T cells, leading to effective tumor clearance in different solid tumor models. Crucially, long-term tumor suppression of tumor recurrence and higher survival rate were observed in a synergic mouse model treatd with PHLH inhibitor that induces sustaining T memory activity. This proposal seeks to identify the molecular mechanism of PHLH in modulating T cell memory phenotypes and its contribution in T cell exhaustion and validate the PHLH-targeting therapeutic utility in inducing durable T memory immunity for long term cancer clearance.
kw: T cell, immunology, targets, immunotherapy

title: Diffuse optical tomography near Infrared Imaging ( (DOT-NIRS)  for acute stroke diagnosis and monitoring with feedback for non-invasive augmentation of ischemic collaterals.
abs: Aims: We use a novel method of Near Infrared Spectroscopy imaging termed Diffuse Optical Tomography (DOT-NIRS) to detect anterior circulation large vessel occlusion (LVO) ischemic stroke. The DOT-NIRS will be used to modulate therapeutic limb compression to improve cerebral perfusion and preserve tissue, therefore extending the time-window for thrombectomy. Hypothesis: DOT-NIRS will be able to detect anterior circulation LVO acute ischemic strokes. In addition, NIRS technology will integrate with automated limb compression systems to improve blood flow to the vulnerable ischemic penumbra. Methodology & Approach: We will conduct a 2-stage study with suspected stroke patients. In the first stage we will use a patented DOT-NIRS headset with high density sensor array with signal processing techniques correlated with the pulse to lower the image noise by orders of magnitude. The primary outcome will be to show diminished brain perfusion and diagnose LVO stroke. Preliminary data using the device from 8 LVO stroke patients had sufficient signal-to-noise resolution and found a large side-to-side difference (29 ± 18 ml/100g/min). For the second stage of the study, we will use a patented machine-to-machine interface to control external limb cuff pumps to reduce the difference in perfusion between the stroke and unaffected cerebral hemispheres. The outcome measure is 10% improvement in the hemisphere-to-hemisphere difference in cerebral blood flow. In preliminary studies on 5 healthy volunteers, the improvement in cerebral flow was 20±11% over baseline. Clinical impact: This portable DOT-NIRS based device will diagnose LVO ischemic stroke in a pre-hospital environment deployable in an ambulance or pre-hospital setting. It reduces healthcare cost significantly by correctly triaging LVO strokes to thrombectomy-capable centres faster, resulting in better functional outcomes and reduced rehabilitation time. The therapeutic compression device will help maintain cerebral perfusion and limit the infarct tissue size, thereby allow for more patients to be eligible for thrombectomy.
kw: Acute stroke, diagnostic, pre-hospital, near-infrared imaging, compression, counterpulsation

title: Evaluation of An Artificial Intelligence Model For The Combined Diagnosis And Treatment Of High-Risk B3 Lesions Detected On Breast Ultrasound
abs: Background. Abnormal lesions detected on breast US are biopsied if there is a suspicion of cancer. Almost 20% return as a high-risk B3 lesion and surgery is often done to exclude malignant upgrade. Minimally invasive vacuum assisted excision (VAE) is increasingly done, but open surgery is still preferred for B3 lesions with atypia. We developed an Artificial Intelligence model (AIUS) that can identify B3 lesions as a distinct category and hypothesize that this helps optimise the use of VAE in B3 lesions. Primary Objectives are to validate AIUS model performance, evaluate VAE in B3 lesions with atypia, and to conduct prospective clinical evaluation of VAE for AIUS predicted high-risk B3 lesions. First, we validate accuracy of AIUS 3-category classification into benign, high-risk B3 and cancer, and specifically examine whether B3 lesions with upgrade are correctly classified as cancers. A combined set of 3000 images will be used; lesion histology to serve as groundtruth. Concurrently, we evaluate VAE in 10 women with B3 lesions with atypia and determine the accuracy of assessment of upgrade and the completeness of lesion removal on VAE. Once the AIUS model performance is satisfactory, we will proceed to recruit 100 women predicted by AIUS to have a high-risk B3 lesion. These women will undergo VAE, instead of a biopsy; this will not be followed by open surgery unless indicated by the surgeon. Accuracy of AIUS classification will be assessed against tissue diagnosis. Frequency of upgrade, completeness of lesion removal on VAE and VAE complications will be evaluated. As a secondary objective, we compare the accuracy of cancer detection on AIUS with the Koios DS. Outcome. The 3-category lesion classification is unique to AIUS and facilitates the evaluation of VAE as a means to combining tissue diagnosis and definitive treatment of B3 lesions into a single encounter.
kw: Artificial Intelligence, Breast Ultrasound, High-Risk B3 lesions, Vacuum assisted excision

title: Tumor micro-environmental evolution and niche conditioning of gastro-intestinal peritoneal metastasis
abs: Background Gastrointestinal cancers, such as gastric/colon cancer, often metastasize to the peritoneum and are resistant to systemic chemo/immunotherapy. The tumor (epi)genome and immune microenvironment have been identified as areas for discovery of novel therapeutic targets. Hypothesis By characterizing the peritoneal metastatic gradient, we hypothesize that the analysis will reveal biological underpinnings of transcoelomic metastases, identify molecular and epigenetic determinants of transcoelomic metatasis and novel therapeutic targets. Specific Aims First, we aim to build the NICHE cohort – a prospective cohort that encapsulates the peritoneal metastatic gradient, characterizing the temporal evolution of niche conditioning in the process of transcoelomic metastasis. Second, we aim to undertake spatially resolved molecular multi-omic profiling of these samples, to identify molecular and epigenetic determinants of transcoelomic metatasis and interrogate the tumor-microenvironment for therapeutic targets. Third, we intend to functionally validate the molecular determinants of GI transcoelomic metastasis through perturbed humanized mouse models and intra-peritoneal protective therapeutics. Methodology 1. Building a prospective cohort that encapsulates the peritoneal metastatic gradient (NICHE cohort). The peritoNeal evolutIonary meCHanisms in transcoElomic metastasis (NICHE) cohort will include peritoneal tissue from patients without cancer, patients with GI cancer without peritoneal metastasis and patients with GI PM in order to fully characterize the changes that occur in the peritoneum. 2. Comprehensive molecular multi-omic profiling. a. Identify molecular and epigenetic determinants of GI transcoelomic metastases. b. Interrogate the TME of peritoneal metastases and the reprogrammed peritoneal niche for therapeutic targets. 3. Functional validation of molecular determinants of transcoelomic metastases. a. Through humanized mouse models with perturbed cell lines or organoids b. Intra-peritoneal therapeutics in humanized mouse models Impact This study will provide significant insights into the molecular mechanisms involved in peritoneal metastases of GiCPM and the effect on tumor immunity, leading to the discovery of novel treatment strategies.
kw: gastric cancer; colon cancer; peritoneal metastases; genomics; precision oncology
