title: Evaluating a novel locoregional immune-modulator in an immune-resistant mouse model of peritoneal metastasis
abs: Peritoneal metastases (PM) from gastrointestinal malignancies are debilitating and frequently resistant to immunotherapy. Recent advances in combinatorial strategies including intraperitoneal (IP) immune modulation may cause tumour microenvironment (TME) alterations and potentially increase susceptibility to the immune system. However, most ongoing studies include accessible tumours e.g. cutaneous or head & neck malignancies but have not studied abdominal cancers. Hence, we aim to evaluate the peritoneal TME in a mouse model of immune resistant PM, with the addition of an intra-peritoneal Toll-like receptor (TLR) agonist and in combination with systemic immunotherapy. This would allow a comparison of the peritoneal immune microenvironment to evaluate if IP immune modulation converts the TME of PM from immune-resistant to immune-susceptible. To achieve this, we propose to utilize MC38 and CT26 colorectal cell-lines that exhibit a mesenchymal-type immune resistant phenotype in an immunocompetent syngeneic mouse model. The TME in controls would be compared against mice treated with intraperitoneal TLR agonists alone and in combination with systemic immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI) using immunohistochemistry, flow cytometry and multiplex assays (LEGENDplexTM Mouse inflammation panel) to evaluate the peritoneal immune and inflammatory milieu. The anti-neoplastic activity of the TLR agonist and/or ICI would be evaluated by bioluminescence imaging, survival data as well as quantifying the degree of PM burden at sacrifice. This proposed study would give novel insights into the peritoneal TME response after immune-modulation and justify the need for peritoneal-directed studies in larger animal models and subsequently first-in-man trials. This study leverages established PM models with a well-characterized immune-resistant phenotype within the Ceelen laboratory which has sufficient resource and expertise to complete the proposed project in the stipulated time-frame
kw: peritoneal carcinomatosis; immunotherapy; immune modulation; locoregional therapy; intra-tumoral immune modulation; peritoneal microenvironment

title: Deciphering the neoantigen landscape and T cell recognition in microsatellite stable colorectal cancer using a novel high throughput TCR: antigen screen.
abs: Immune evasion is a hallmark of cancer. Cancer cells evolved under selective pressure from the host’s immune system during progression, enabling them to evade recognition by the cytotoxic CD8+ T lymphocytes, the main anti-tumour effector immune cells. Neoantigens arising from mutations in cancer cells are critical targets for tumour recognition and eradication by CD8+ T cells. Neoantigen-specific CD8+ T cells, are not subjected to central tolerance and were found to be the most potent T cells in tumour eradication. Notably, the clinical response against immunotherapies, such as checkpoint inhibitors, is also strongly correlated with tumour mutation burden, suggesting that the diversity and frequency of immunogenic neoantigens is a strong predictor of immunotherapy response. Interestingly, microsatellite stable (MSS) colorectal cancer, which accounts for 80-85% of all colorectal cancers – a highly prevalent cancer worldwide – does not respond to checkpoint inhibitors despite having intermediate levels of tumour mutations. Despite the lack of response to checkpoint inhibitors, tumour-infiltrating effector T cells were found to be present within MSS colorectal tumours. However, the function of these intratumoral CD8+ T cells and their ability to recognise tumour neoantigens are not well understood. Notably, in published reports of tumour infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) analysis, intratumoral neoantigen-specific T cells recognition and response were only inferred through T cell receptor (TCR) clonality and gene expression analysis and were not measured experimentally. In this proposal, we seek to understand the neoantigen landscape and recognition of tumour neoantigens by TILs in MSS colorectal cancer. To study the function and neoantigens recognition of Cd8+ T cells in MSS colorectal cancer, we will probe the unbiased recognition of intratumoral TCR repertoires, independent of the dysfunctional state of the T cells, against the entire repertoire of predicted neoantigens from each patient using our established granzyme reporter cells. This will enable us to identify paired tumour TCR: neoantigen in a high throughput manner thus enabling the comprehensive investigation of neoantigens-recognition of TILs. Analysing gene expression of the neoantigen-specific T cells at the single cell level would yield further important immunological insights into the mechanism of T cell dysfunction in the neoantigen-specific T cells. Lastly, we hope to determine the spatial interaction of neoantigen-specific T cells with the tumour microenvironment to identify mechanisms leading to T cell dysfunction. This study will allow us to empirically analyse the recognition of neoantigens by TILs and identify mechanisms leading to their dysfunctional state to facilitate the understanding of how cancers evade recognition by neoantigen-specific CD8+ T cells.
kw: Cancer vaccines, immunotherapy, colorectal cancer

title: Experimental study of the doping evolution of band structures and superconducting observables in the infinite-layer nickelates
abs: Following the discovery of ‘high-temperature’ (high-Tc) superconductivity in layered cuprates four decades ago, intense efforts in searching for ‘cuprate-analogue’ have led to new superconductors such as cobaltates and ruthenates, which share similar planar structure, but none better mimics cuprates’ physics than the newfound infinite-layer nickelates [Nature 572, 624-627 (2019)]. The realization of superconductivity in nickelates through hole doping into the 3d9-x electronic structure closely resembles strongly correlated systems such as cuprates and magic-angle Moiré graphene superconductors. Infinite-layer nickelates, therefore, has reignited excitement in the community to march closer to the secret makeup of high-Tc pairing mechanism – the ‘holy-grail’ of condensed matter physics. In this aspect, we have successfully produced the phase diagram and superconducting dome of (Nd,Sr)NiO2 and (La,Ca)NiO2 as a function of hole doping with Sr2+/Ca2+ [Phys. Rev. Lett. 125, 147003 (2020); Science Adv. 8, eabl9927 (2022)]. Investigation on the electronic band structure and interpretation of the role of each Fermi surface in the emergence of superconductivity, magnetism, charge order, etc. are the first steps in dissecting a new material. However, due to the lack of atomically clean surface for powerful tools such as angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES), the experimental study on the Fermi surfaces of nickelates superconductors are non-existing, despite the large discrepancies between theoretical calculations. Therefore, we propose to develop an in-situ topotactic reduction process to create infinite-layer nickelates which surface is free of contaminants or adsorbates. Understanding the nature of the Cooper pairing, such as the symmetry of the order parameters, is fundamental to the deduction of the unconventional pairing mechanism. We have performed preliminary penetration depth measurements and observed a possibly distinctive pairing between Nd- and La- nickelates, which Nd-nickelates are nodeless and La-nickelates have nodal order parameter [arXiv:2201.10038]. Recently, we also reported the Pauli-limit violation in the La-nickelates, which can be an indication of a rare type of superconductivity: spin-triplet pairing [arXiv:2204.12606]. Such behaviour resembles some similarities to both the cuprates (nodal) and magic-angle twisted trilayer graphene (spin-triplet) [Nature 595, 526–531 (2021)]. Further studies on the pairing symmetry of nickelates are crucial, and we propose using phase-sensitive techniques. The emergence of superconductivity from multiple competing orderings such as magnetism and charge orders is a longstanding puzzle. We propose to study the presence and evolution of these phases as a function of hole doping 3d9-x using spectroscopic and transport characterisations. This will improve the understanding of the mechanism behind the universality of these phenomena across various strongly-correlated superconductors. At the end
kw: Infinite-layer nickelates, high-temperature superconductivity, electronic-structures, angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, topotactic reduction, spin-triplet pairing

title: Enabling ultra-low power software-defined radios for flexible/updatable wireless sensor node communications down to the pJ/bit and uW range
abs: Next-generation connected sensor nodes for the Internet of Things and massively distributed sensing are required to exhibit a small form factor in the scale of millimetres (for unobtrusive deployment), low cost well below the dollar range (for low total cost in many-sensor systems), low power in the uW range (for long battery life, typically solid-state micro-battery), long lifetime in the order of a decade or longer (due to typically difficult physical accessibility and cost in maintenance operations), and functionality adaptation to a wide range of evolving operating conditions and system requirements (to prevent premature obsolescence, which would otherwise translate into higher and dominant maintenance cost due to replacement). Wireless transmissions are well known to largely dominate the above sensor node power budget due to mW-range consumption in conventional radios for relatively short-range communications at common Mbps datarates (e.g., WiFi, BLE, Zigbee), whereas wake-up receivers in the 10 nW range are available (IEEE 802.11ba standard), and silicon demonstrations of all other sub-systems with much lower power have been widely shown in the recent scientific literature and commercial chips. As further challenge, low-cost, mm-scale and long-lasting energy sources for self-powered operation can support only limited peak power in the 1-10 uW range, as set by the high internal resistance of solid-state micro-batteries ( >10 kOhm), and power density of common energy harvesters (uW/mm2 or uW/mm3). This has led to the recent research effort to reduce transmitter power down to the 10-uW (e.g., [W20]) and uW range (e.g., [LAS21]) via backscattered transmitters, based on an inflexible and highly-customized architecture. As further challenge, support for large volume manufacturing and adaptation to changing communication needs across the long lifespan of most connected sensor nodes mandate flexibility in terms of 1) wireless transmission protocol for integration in existing environments (MAC, physical layer), 2) modifications of the protocol across the device lifespan (e.g., BLE coded-phy release in 2020). Currently, very limited protocol flexibility at tens of uWs is offered by best-in-class transmitters (e.g., WiFi+BLE in [K22] at 39-88 uW). For true adaptation to existing and upcoming standards and device lifetime preservation over changing communication requirements, software-defined radios (SDRs) would be required, as their baseband and physical layer can be updated over-the-air. However, the large power (mW and higher) of conventional SDR architectures and their complexity leading to a cost of hundreds of dollars makes them unsuitable for the above applications. As a result, bridging the power gap between flexible SDRs and the best-in-class power of backscattered transmitters requires the introduction of fundamental advances to enable backscattered software-defined radios (here named BSDRs) with energy in the pJ/bit range for uW-power in Mbp

title: Uncertainty Quantification for data-driven modeling of dynamical systems
abs: Uncertainty is present in most real-world phenomena. Dynamical systems provide us with a principled modeling framework to quantify and reason about uncertainty. Although probabilistic forecasting of complex systems is paramount to many disciplines, general methods for long-term forecasts with calibrated uncertainty are still an open problem. Data assimilation from noisy observations, a ubiquitous problem in science and engineering, is concerned with the incorporation of observational data into mathematical models. Applications abound in geophysics, finance, weather forecasting, quantitative biology, and a host of additional domains. In practical settings, collected data may be noisy, indirectly observed, and limited in number or resolution. Quantification of the associated uncertainty is an essential part of the inference process, and vital to the efficient use of computational models and efficient decision-making. When analyzing modern complex systems such as those found in epidemiology, biology, or neuroscience, deriving models from first principles is a formidable task that is often impossible. In these situations, data-driven methods (as opposed to modeling from first principles) are becoming increasingly attractive to practitioners. Thanks to the vast amount of data collected by sensors and measurement tools, models can be directly created to circumvent or complement/enhance first-principle modeling. Although this paradigm-shift is becoming increasingly popular in various disciplines, comparatively little attention has been devoted to the problem of uncertainty quantification associated with these methods. The overarching goal of this research proposal is to extend and build upon these modern data-driven methods in order to produce robust and well calibrated probabilistic predictions. For this purpose, we are planning to leverage recently proposed differentiable formulations of uncertainty quantification pipelines (eg. differentiable particle filtering / ensemble Kalman filtering). When combined with modern extensions of Koopman-based approaches, a methodology that has recently demonstrated its usefulness and versability for the data-driven analysis of complex and high-dimensional stochastic dynamical systems, as well as with recent advances in unsupervised representation learning proposed in the machine-learning and computer-vision literature, our hybrid methodology will allow the assimilation/prediction of complex stochastic systems without relying on first-principle modeling. In contrast to most existing data-driven approaches, uncertainty quantification will be a built-in feature of the method (as opposed to being a secondary concern, or by-product). The project will provide new theoretical and methodological tools to the research community in statistics, machine learning, and data science. These new methodologies will also be helpful to practitioners in several fields of data science. Importantly, in order to ground the project in a rea

title: Learning time-varying networks from limited data, and beyond
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: With the advent of big data analytics, matrix-variate observations (i.e., two-dimensional grids of observations) are becoming prevalent in various domains including spatial-temporal data analysis, financial markets, genomics, imaging processing, psychology and social sciences. Due to the pervasiveness of matrix-variate observations, it is important for us to understand the embedded structure in these observations, wherein the precision matrix is of particular interest as it encodes conditional independence patterns among variables. Structured precision matrices are called for due to the challenges coming from the extremely high dimensionality, the probably small sample size and the vital row and column structural information. A novel and important Kronecker-sum (KS) structure of the precision matrix comes into our attention. Specifically, the precision matrix of the matrix-variate observations is assumed to be in the form of the KS of two precision matrices, which correspond to the row and column independence patterns, respectively. An appealing property of the KS structure is that the KS of two networks represents their Cartesian product, which is arguably the most prominent of graph products and is essential to network estimation in the low sample regime. In order to deal with the big data challenge, we need efficient algorithms for computing the maximum likelihood estimator of the KS-structured precision matrix, especially for large-scale cases. Current state-of-the-art solvers, such as TeraLasso and EiGLasso, are limited to median-scale problems and are generally unable to cope with problems having dimensions beyond one thousand within hours. The challenges mainly come from 1) the extremely high dimensionality; 2) the complicated regularized log-likelihood objective function; 3) the non-identifiability of the diagonal elements of row and column networks. In this project, we are going to take advantage of the novel KS structure to learn time-varying networks from limited matrix-variate data, including building meaningful models, designing efficient algorithms and solving interesting application problems. One essential of our model design is that we consider the maximum likelihood estimator of the precision matrix based on the attractive KS structure, with additional positive definite constraints on two precision matrices associated with the rows and columns of the observations. The imposed KS structure is vitally important for handling limited matrix-variate data and the additional positive definite constraints are going to be posed for two reasons. One is that we can treat our problem of learning a large time-varying network as jointly learning two subnetworks - one for rows and one for columns. The other reason is that it will automatically avoid the non-identifiability challenge of the diagonal elements of row and column networks arising from the nature of KS structure. title: Identifying type-2 diabetes risk genes with single-nucleus RNA-seq in adipose tissues from Asian populations
abs: Type-2 diabetes (T2D) affects nearly 500 million people worldwide. Singapore has the highest incidence of T2D (11.6%) among developed countries and this rate is projected to reach 14.3% by the year 2045. It is widely accepted that individuals of Asian descent develop type-2 diabetes at a lower body mass index (BMI) and at a younger age of onset compared with other ethnic groups. A recent GWAS meta-analysis with more than 400,000 East Asian individuals identified 61 new loci associated with T2D. Functional genomic data for these loci are needed to elucidate their functional mechanisms. Unfortunately, Asian ethnic groups are underrepresented in functional genomic association studies. Large-scale QTL projects, such as GTEx, have generated comprehensive QTL maps in tissues relevant to T2D. Although these projects detected an abundance of QTLs in adipose tissues, they suffered from the following two limitations. First, the remarkable cellular diversity in adipose tissues - including distinct sub-types of adipocytes, rich representation of immune cell types, and pluripotent stem and progenitor cells - has been masked by homogenization for bulk RNA sequencing. Furthermore, Asian individuals are severely underrepresented in these projects. To address these limitations, we propose to conduct cell-type specific QTL mapping using single-nucleus RNA sequencing from adipose tissues in Asian individuals. We hypothesize that a cellularly resolved Asian-specific QTL map will identify T2D risk genes and contribute to the understanding of elevated T2D susceptibility. Specifically, we propose the following three aims: Aim 1: To generate matched expression (bulk & single-nucleus) and genotyping data using adipose biopsies from 500 Asian donors. Aim 2: To map cell-type-specific QTLs and identify T2D risk genes by jointly analyzing QTL and T2D GWAS. Aim 3: To systematically validate high-priority risk genes in human preadipocytes and mature adipocytes using reporter assays and CRISPR/Cas9-based genome editing.

title: Multiple organ transcriptomic analysis of bamboo sharks reveals the mechanism of early adaptive immune response
abs: Apart from bony fishes 450 million years ago, cartilaginous fishes, including bamboo sharks, possess many unique features, like cartilages, early adaptive immune systems, and adaptive and efficient propulsion of sperms. The adaptive immune system of cartilaginous fish comprises IgM, IgW, and heavy-chain immunoglobulin new antigen receptors (IgNAR), which generate high-affinity antigen-specific single-domain antibodies (nanobodies). Due to its advantages in molecular weight, size, stability, and cost compared with double-chain antibodies, IgNAR attracts much interest from the industry and the academy. Bamboo sharks are small cartilaginous fish and are easy to farm. We decoded the whole genome of a white-spotted bamboo shark (chiloscyllium plagiosum) to the chromosome level. Next, we mapped the detailed genome sequence over IgNAR at chromosome 44 by PacBio and next-generation sequencing. Then we demonstrated that bamboo sharks developed robust immune responses after antigen immunization and generated IgNARs with high affinities and specificities. We confirmed that the diversity of IgNAR was mainly from the complementarity-determining region 3 (CDR3), even with the low V(D)J recombination. However, the mechanism of the IgNAR hypermutation remains unclear. Here, we performed the transcriptomic analysis over twenty tissues isolated from three adult and three junior bamboo sharks. And we identified 15227 mRNAs with 44837 isoforms and 2942 long non-coding RNAs (LncRNA) with 3635 isoforms. The conservation analysis revealed that 10% of bamboo shark genes were conserved across bony fishes, humans, and mice. And bamboo sharks shared a higher conservation rate with other sharks suggesting cartilaginous fishes developed a distinct evolution trajectory from bony fishes and mammals. Conservation analysis between bamboo sharks and catsharks, which do not possess humoral immune responses, revealed that bamboo sharks had many unique genes related to immune response. 1) To uncover the essential genes related to antibody hypermutation in sharks, we expect similar essential genes to have similar expression profiles in immune-related tissues, including the spleen, blood, and gills. Thus, we propose to analyze our transcriptomic data by gene expression profiles in different tissues and select vital genes that might be critical in antibody hypermutation for functional studies. 2), Interestingly, the essential gene Activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AICDA) in mammalian antibody hypermutation also appears in sharks but with an extra C-terminal domain. We propose to study the function of this unique shark AICDA. 3) different bamboo sharks might possess different naïve immune repertoires like nurse sharks. Therefore, we propose to generate a mega shark naïve single-domain antibody library for antibody discovery from many bamboo sharks. Without animal immunization, we expect this library to create antigen-specific shark antibodies in 20 days. If successful, our research

title: Integration of Physics and Artificial-Intelligence: Deriving synergies to Capture Aeroelastic Phenomenon
abs: Aeroelasticity (or aero-servo-elasticity) is a phenomenon resulting from the interaction between elastic, inertial and aerodynamic forces, and is ubiquitous where flexibility is involved. This is commonly found in aerospace, biological processes, infrastructure, energy and marine applications, etc. Due to the flexibility of the structures, they can run into risks of excessive loads, uncontrolled vibrations or even catastrophic failures. As such, fast and accurate aeroelastic predictions are needed for loads and stability predictions both offline and online to enhance performance, design and safety. Yet, current approaches to solving aeroelastic problems are still extremely time and resource intensive, and lacks robustness to capture uncertainties in the actual physical systems. Separately, aeroelastic experiments are destructive and very costly. Fortunately. with recent advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) approaches, exciting opportunities arise to fundamentally investigate its adoption and push the boundary for AI to address aero-servo-elastic problems. In this project, we propose the use of data-driven approaches that are guided by physics (governing equations) to obtain reduced order descriptions for efficient time-marching simulations, frequency domain analysis and controls. As (i) data driven model lacks physics resulting in unrealistic results and (ii) governing equations fails to capture uncertainty in physical systems, we seek to integrate them. The outcome is a methodology capable of capturing large operating conditions (generalization), increased accuracy and with reduced requirements of datasets. The project will first involve experiments of aeroelastic phenomenon (e.g. flutter, stability, loads, etc.) where data will be extracted and used for training and validation of the data-driven models. Next, a multitude of network and feature-based approaches include CNN, GNN, PINN, etc. will be explored. Following which, fundamental governing equations for aerodynamics and structures will be used alongside these data-driven approaches for improved generalisation and reduce the burden on having massive datasets needed to cover large operating conditions. Often, limited aeroelastic experimental data is available but a large operating space is required for analysis, safety and to cover the operating envelope. This is where the combination of data and physical governing equations can complement each other in deriving and reinforcing learning to provide accurate machine learning models that remains general (through physics) and yet captures uncertainties (through data) in the physical systems. Furthermore, the resulting more accurate reduced order models can be used for controller synthesis (servo in aero-servo-elasticity) to control the physical system. title: A Flexible Optoacoustic Blood Stethoscope for Non-invasive Multiparametric Cardiovascular Monitoring
abs: Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) are the leading cause of death globally, taking an estimated 17.9 million lives each year. CVDs are a group of disorders of the heart and blood vessels and include coronary heart disease, cerebrovascular disease, rheumatic heart disease and other conditions. More than four out of five CVD deaths are due to heart attacks and strokes, and one third of these deaths occur prematurely in people under 70 years of age. In Singapore, 21 people die from cardiovascular disease (heart diseases and stroke) every day. Cardiovascular disease accounted for 32% of all deaths in 2021. This means that almost 1 out of 3 deaths in Singapore is due to heart diseases or stroke. Regular monitoring multiple physical and chemical blood dynamics properties is critical for preventing the damage of cardiovascular diseases on human. Current blood analysis methods are typically restricted to invasiveness, bulky instruments and complicated clinical procedures. The cost of a single device is around S$300 and the annual cost of testing strips for each patient is around S$800. A non-invasive device that can be used for continuous blood analysis will therefore present as a technological and market feat. A plethora of attempts had been devoted to the development of non-invasive devices using different technologies yet none of those devices lasted the test of the markets due to the limited performance and accuracy. Quantitative and multiparametric blood analysis is of great clinical importance in cardiovascular disease diagnosis. Although there is a plethora of methods to extract blood information, they are typically restricted to invasiveness, non-continuity, bulky instruments, and complicated testing procedures. Flexible sensors can realize on-skin assessment of several vital signals but generally exhibit limited blood analyzing functions. Here, we propose a flexible optoacoustic blood ‘stethoscope’ (OBS) for noninvasive, multiparametric, and continuous cardiovascular monitoring, free of complicated procedures. The OBS features the light delivery elements for blood illumination and the piezoelectric acoustic elements capable of capturing light-induced acoustic waves. OBS can adhere to the skin for continuous and non-invasive in-situ monitoring of multiple cardiovascular biomarkers, including hypoxia, intravascular exogenous agent/drug concentration decay, and hemodynamics, which can be further visualized with the tailored 3D algorithm. Demonstrations on both in-vivo animal trials and human subjects would highlight the OBS's unique potential to provide a new avenue for cardiovascular disease diagnosis and prediction. More specifically, taking advantage of optical spectral specificities and high acoustic resolution, the OBS allows imaging to quantitatively analyze multiple physiological vitals of blood to solve several unmet clinical needs in atherosclerotic cardiovascular diseases, including coronary heart disease, peripheral ischemia, atherosclerosis

title: 3D Geometric Tiling for Modeling and Realization of 3D Tileable Assemblies
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: This research deals with assemblies that can be built from instances of a small set of building blocks (i.e., 3D tiles), called 3D tileable assemblies. The main advantage of these assemblies is that 3D tiles can be reused not only in a single assembly (e.g., replace a lost/broken tile instance) but also across multiple different assemblies (e.g., deconstruct an assembly and reuse tile instances for building another assembly), resulting in a reduction in resource consumption, material waste, and fabrication cost. Modeling 3D tileable assemblies can be viewed as a form of tiling the three-dimensional space, or simply 3D geometric tiling. In computer graphics, 2D geometric tiling has been extensively studied, and used in the contexts of texture synthesis, decorative pattern generation, sampling, and visualization. However, 3D geometric tiling remains a challenging research problem that has not been well studied. Only a few recent research works addressed the problem of 3D geometric tiling of surfaces by computing 3D tiles with primitive shapes like triangles or quads. However, these existing works deal with special cases in 3D geometric tiling, and their modeled 3D tiles have relatively simple shape. In this research, we aim to carry out a comprehensive study on 3D geometric tiling of given shapes for modeling and realization of 3D tileable assemblies. The challenge is two-fold. First, the geometric tiling happens in 3D instead of 2D space; the 3D tiles have more complex geometry and higher degree-of-freedom in terms of placement and the contact among the 3D tile instances are more complicated, thereby incurring much higher complexity for computing the 3D tiles. Second, our goal of realizing the modeled 3D tileable assemblies requires that the generated 3D tiles have to be fabricable and the resulting 3D tileable assembly has to be buildable and structurally stable. This realization-oriented geometric tiling has not been studied in the literature yet are essential for fabricating 3D geometric tiling results and making use of them in real world. The research objectives are thus: 1) to establish computational foundations for 3D geometric tiling of shapes, to generate reusable 3D tiles for modeling 3D tileable assemblies; 2) to advance 3D geometric tiling theory and techniques to fabricable tiling, buildable tiling, and structurally stable tiling; and 3) to develop innovative techniques and practical algorithms for modeling 3D tileable assemblies, and explore their potential applications in engineering, architecture, and recreation. To achieve these objectives, we conduct our research by investigating three major directions outlined below: 1. 3D geometric tiling of a single shape • Computational framework of 3D geometric tiling • Optimizing 3D tileable assembly for realization • Variations of 3D geometric tiling 2. 3D geometric tiling of a family of shapes • Co-decomposition of multiple shapes • Generating 3D tiles from co-decomposed parts • Approximat

title: A Scalable Comprehensive Framework for Formal Verification of Quantum Programs
abs: Quantum computing (the use of quantum mechanics for sophisticated computation tasks) promises an enormous impact on real-world applications, e.g. cryptography, machine learning, system simulation, and computational biology. With the rapid progresses on quantum technology recently, giant tech companies such as Google and IBM have started to build the core hardware architectures for quantum computer. On top of that, a number of programming languages and compilers for quantum computing have been developed, such as QWire, Quipper, Scaffold, Microsoft’s LIQUi$| >, Q#, IBM's OpenQASM, Google’s Cirq, ProjectQ, Chisel-Q, and Q|SI >, etc. As quantum computers are operated in extreme physical conditions and thus the cost per run is significantly high, it is desirable to verify the correctness of a quantum programs before the execution. However, the verification task of quantum programs is challenging due to the following reasons: (1) Quantum programs (even written at high-level languages) are complicated to comprehend as it requires a good understanding of quantum mechanics and the relevant advanced mathematics. (2) The quantum states are exponentially huge in size because the state of a classical bit is either 0 or 1 at any time, while the state of a quantum bit (qubit) can be in the superposition, in which both states 0 and 1 can co-exist simultaneously. This induces the state-space explosion problem for brute-force-like methods. (3) Quantum states are naturally probabilistic thus may yield different results on different runs, which is challenging for the testing and debugging methods. In this project, we aim to build a scalable and comprehensive framework to develop and verify quantum programs. We propose the following goals and aims: 1. [Intermediate Language]. We plan to propose an intermediate language to model quantum programs. The proposed language would be complete to describe all of the desired characteristics of quantum computing while at the same time simple enough to be understood by most programmers. More importantly, other high-level quantum languages can be complied into the proposed language so that their correctness can be proved/verified uniformly using our verification framework, as mentioned in our next goal. 2. [Formal Verification Framework]. We plan to develop a formal verification framework for the correctness of quantum programs written in our intermediate language. To avoid the state-space explosion problem, our verification strategy utilizes a high-level assertion language to construct the correctness proof. Moreover, the assertion language is infused with Separation Logic to support local reasoning and keep the verification task tractable. 3. [Mechanization]. We plan to mechanize our framework formally using state-of-the-art theorem provers such as Coq or Isabelle/HOL. title: Perovskite Solar Concentrators Optimization through Radiative Engineering (SCORE)
abs: Halide Perovskites, the wonder optoelectronic material, has captivated the imagination of scientists, engineers, and the public. With their outstanding photovoltaic performance, perovskite solar cells (PSCs) are now at the cusp of commercialization. Equally impressive are perovskite light-emitting devices (PeLEDs) in a parallel development, whose meteoric rise in performance (from < 1% to >20% emission efficiency within a decade) rivals that of their solar cell counterparts. Rising from the intersections of these two contrasting perovskite fields, perovskite luminescent solar concentrators (LSCs) present fresh opportunities for combating climate change. LSCs are an integral component of building integrated photovoltaics (BIPV) in net-zero energy buildings for sustainable urban power generation. However, LSC has been on the backburner as state-of-the-art incumbent LSC chromophores (e.g., undoped and doped II-VI quantum dots, dyes, conventional PNCs, etc.) face numerous challenges spanning poor ambient stability, low quantum efficiency, reabsorption issues to inefficient solar harvesting. Ultrastable, strongly absorbing yet reabsorption-free, high-efficiency chromophores hold the key to transcend these challenges. Recently, the PI discovered the secret recipes to making undoped ultra-stable aqueous colloidal perovskite nanocrystals PNCs (Patent Pending) with PLQY >80% despite being soaked in water for >12 months. This know-how presents tantalizing opportunities for the incipient perovskite LSC field to tackle the challenges facing incumbent chromophores. Unlike conventional PNCs which suffer from poor ambient stability, our novel core-shell PNCs will provide an extraordinary host system for a deep interdisciplinary dive into the myriad of interrelated challenges present in LSCs chromophores. Using specific doping processes to extend their emission ranges from VIS to IR, our broad approach is compatible with a wide range of solar cells (Si, CIGS solar cells, etc.). Reports on Yb-doped conventional PNCs attaining a luminescent quantum efficiency >190% via quantum-cutting and our preliminary simulations and experiments strongly support the viability of this idea. A theoretical maximum of 17% boost in Si solar cell efficiency is estimated from our preliminary calculations for the Yb system (assuming 100% conversion efficiencies). Nevertheless, there remain significant knowledge gaps over the basic photophysical mechanisms and structure-function relations between the perovskite host, and the guest (e.g., transition metals, rare-earth dopants, etc.) for efficient energy transfer and radiative emission. Herein, we harness our novel aqueous core-shell PNCs (undoped) platform (Patent Pending) as the host system and the exceptional optoelectronic properties of perovskites to engineer ultra-stable reabsorption-free doped PNCs for high-efficiency perovskite LSC applications. title: Predicting the stress resilience mechanisms in the plant kingdom
abs: This abstract describes a proposed study aimed at generating a comprehensive stress gene expression, metabolic and phenotypic atlas for 9 major monocot crops and Brachypodium distachyon, a model crop for grasses. The crops will be exposed to drought, heat, and a combination of the two abiotic stresses. The study aims to elucidate the stress resilience mechanisms in plants, predict which crop varieties are resilient/susceptible, and engineer stress resilience in susceptible crops. The proposed study involves a multipronged approach to analyze the data, including building machine learning models to predict gene expression and metabolite levels in combined stress, predict stress resilience from gene expression and metabolite levels, and predict stress resilience in combined stress. The study also involves genetic engineering of Brachypodium distachyon to validate the role of identified marker genes in heat and drought resilience. Additionally, the study will construct a Plant Stress Database, providing public access to the data and models, thus allowing crop researchers worldwide to study how plants respond to stress in a complex environment. The ability to predict gene expression in combinations of stresses will significantly reduce the time and effort required to identify stress-resilient plants, which otherwise takes extensive time, resources, and effort in the field. Identifying genes essential for stress resilience opens up possibilities for engineering stress resilience. Consequently, the work in this proposal will be highly impactful in academia and industry. The results from this study will serve as a valuable resource for plant breeding and engineering for crops with better performance in the future climate.
kw: crops; stress; abiotic; yield; gene expression; metabolism; machine learning; artificial intelligence

title: Synergizing online and offline social participation to advance health and digital research among older adults
abs: The use of digital communication technologies have proliferated in the last decade, drastically changing how we interact with each other and how we conduct population health research (i.e., through digital trace data, online surveys, and administrative records). Yet two important gaps remain. First, while online technologies can facilitate social participation, we do not fully understand how it interacts in tandem with offline aspects of social life to shape older adult health and well-being. This is crucial in a world where the spread of health information online can influence health behavior (e.g., vaccination), and where offline social support is key to adoption of online health technologies such as telehealth. Second, it remains difficult to accurately assess how older adults are faring at the population level in a timely and cost-effective manner through online methods. The possibility of future pandemics (like the COVID-19 pandemic) may mean that in-person research can be suddenly restricted, limiting our ability to monitor the well-being of the older adult population in a responsive and cost-effective way. Online survey and recruitment methods present a novel way to overcome this, but tends to suffer from selection biases. The broad vision of this project is thus to understand whether and how synergies in older adults’ online and offline social participation can be used to enhance the reliability of online research and to investigate its associations with health and well-being among older adults. The project has two key research questions and four specific objectives: First, how do older adults’ online and offline social participation jointly shape their health outcomes? Specific Objective 1: To explore the various ways in which older adults mix online and offline social participation. This includes the use of social media and video conferencing tools not just to interact with friends and family, but also the ways in which they organize and engage the community (e.g., arts, sports, volunteering, politics). Specific Objective 2: To establish whether and how online and offline social participation work together to affect older adults’ health and well-being (e.g., through factors such as health behaviour, use of telehealth services, chronic disease management). Specific Objective 3: To establish the factors that influence online social participation among older adults (e.g., health difficulties, lack of ability/skill, lack of interest, lack of access). Second, how can information about older adults’ online and offline social participation help to enhance the reliability of online research among older adults? Specific Objective 4: To establish the sources and degree of bias in local online non-probability samples of older adults, and if it can be reasonably corrected for using information about their social participation. title: Design and Additive Manufacturing of Robotic Metamaterials with Embodied Intelligence
abs: The tight coupling of shape transformation, stiffness tuning, self-sensing, and closed-loop feedback that biological organisms exhibit (e.g., octopus’ arms) is an inspiration for next-generation robotic systems. Today, however, robots rely on the assembly of separate actuators, sensors, and computing units connected by wires to achieve functions, resulting in bulk volume and poor manufacturing scalability. Advanced manufacturing of multi-materials with programmed functions in a tightly integrated body without mechanical failures or delamination, which mimic biological organisms, has long remained a challenge. Here, we propose to design and manufacture a new class of robotic metamaterials with hierarchical multi-material architectures which can realize embodied intelligence by achieving shape-morphing, stiffness-variation, self-sensing, and closed-loop feedback. These proposed functions are programmed into the metamaterials’ composition and architecture, while a magnetically assisted drop-on-demand 3D printing technique (MDOD) will be used to manufacture the metamaterial building blocks. We will demonstrate their applications by creating self-sensing deployable structures, adaptive robotic grippers, morphing electrical devices, etc.

title: Development of next-generation organic micro/nanocomposites for ultrafast co-thermoregulation of lithium-ion batteries
abs: The aggressive pursuit of high-energy-density of lithium-ion battery cells in electric vehicle applications has led to serious safety concerns, triggered by excessive internal heat generated during cathodic-anodic-electrolytic exothermic co-reactions. When the accumulated heat within a cell cannot be effectively removed in time, an exponential rise in its internal temperature results in thermal runaway in which the cell enters an uncontrollable self-heating state, leading to catastrophic combustion and explosion. Hampered by their sluggish thermoresponse and poor thermal efficiency, existing thermal management strategies are unable to effectively arrest the rapid spike in cell temperature under extreme conditions, such as overcharging/discharging and internal short circuiting, to prevent thermal runaway. To overcome these challenges, this proposed research aims to (1) couple organic phase change materials (PCM) with micro/nanoengineering strategies to develop new PCM-based micro/nanocomposite materials with ultrafast thermoresponse and (2) establish their implementation framework to provide undisrupted thermoregulation of lithium-ion batteries, without compromising their electrochemical performance. Both interior and exterior thermoregulation strategies shall be developed to co-regulate the cell’s temperature. For exterior thermoregulation, flexible PCM nanocomposite materials that are leakproof, form stable and have high effective thermal conductivity shall be the focus of this proposed project. Different from existing PCM composites works which focus only on thermal conductivity improvement, the new flexibility function of our PCM composites shall enable pressure-induced dynamic close contact melting of high thermal efficiency and response due to the active removal of thick liquid layer between the heat source and PCM. Furthermore, good shape recovery and high capillarity characteristics of this material shall also enable the re-absorption of liquid PCM for continuous thermocycles. For interior thermoregulation, this project shall focus on the development of in-built (1) battery separator consisting of nanofiber encapsulated PCM and (2) micro-spherical hollow shell encapsulated PCM dispersed in battery electrolyte. The direct implementation of these micro/nanoengineered components within battery cells shall eliminate undesirable parasitic thermal resistance, facilitating the ultrafast response of the material to absorb exothermic heat. This project shall involve material development and thermal, mechanical and electrochemical characterization to further tailor micro/nanometric parameters for the performance optimization of individual thermoregulators. A design guideline for the synergistic integration of interior-exterior co-thermoregulation for lithium-ion batteries shall be then developed. If successful, this work will lead to the first undisrupted thermoregulation solution for lithium-ion batteries with ultrafast thermoresponse and prolonged

title: Pushing the Limits of Highly Efficient Single-Actuator-Single-Wing Nature-inspired Aerial Robots
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: The monocopter is a unique single-wing unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) platform that achieves controlled flight by replicating the spinning nature of falling maple seeds. Recent research breakthroughs in SUTD have allowed this nature-inspired flying platform to achieve fully controllable sustained flight with only a single actuator for propulsion, allowing for unrivalled flight efficiency and endurance. The goal of this research is to continue this fundamental push in advancing single-actuator flight through enhancements of key components and functionality of the single-actuator monocopter. Currently, the single-actuator monocopter utilizes a 2D ‘flat’ wing and basic open-loop speed control for the propulsion and employs a basic feedback flight controller using only intrinsic sensors. This research will provide the technical foundation for design, analysis and optimization of next-generation high-performance single-actuator monocopters that will feature 3D airfoil wings with embedded compact extrinsic airspeed and ranging sensors, precision servomotor propulsion and learning-based autopilot flight control.
kw: Robotics, Mechatronics, UAVs, Monocopters, Nature-inspired

title: PREP-NexT: Pathways for REsilient Planning of water-energy-food Nexus Transformation
abs: This project aims to address the grand WEF security challenges in Singapore and SEA to guide the development of robust and climate-resilient adaptation pathways into policy support. These adaptation pathways are composed of a variety of investment and policy instruments, such as cascade reservoir development, renewable energy penetration, and agricultural trade (e.g., for staple foods). To identify the most appropriate combinations, we will leverage recent proliferation of geospatial big data and methodological advances in biophysical models, machine learning, and decision analytics to achieve the following specific goals: (1) Advance and accelerate our scientific understanding of cross-scale linkages between drought/flood risks and WEF security outcomes; (2) Identify robust and adaptive development pathways within the context of plausible future scenarios that minimize WEF trade-offs and conflicts, maximize synergies, and promote resilient and sustainable development; (3) Develop a decision support framework for managing risks and impacts arising from hydrologically related natural hazards, especially considering their scaling effects and the role of interconnected infrastructures. Such a system will contribute to enhanced WEF resilience to hydroclimate shocks over the entire SEA and will further benefit Singapore’s national and economic security beyond its WEF sectors.
kw: Climate change, extreme events, water-food-energy nexus, resilience, sustainability

title: Hardware efficient algorithms for simulating topological phases on near term quantum processors
abs: By harnessing the powers of quantum mechanics (quantum superposition and quantum entanglement), quantum computers are expected to perform tasks that cannot be done in realistically on any classical computer (quantum supremacy). This will have wide ranging applications in every field from cybersecurity to developing smart materials for technological applications. After nearly 40 years of development, quantum computers have finally been realised. Google and IBM have launched their Sycamore and IBM Q machines; many others are expected to follow suit. While the number of working qubits is still modest (~100), it is expected to grow rapidly in the near future. IBM's roadmap envisages the availability of quantum processors with ~100,000 qubits within a few years, making it possible to use them to solve real life problems. This opens up a new avenue to study complex quantum states that are difficult to simulate on classical computers, and there is an urgent need to develop efficient algorithms for this purpose. Motivated by our recent success in developing a quantum algorithm to simulate quantum spin chains, we propose a comprehensive study to (i) develop full-featured, hardware efficient, quantum algorithms to simulate quantum spins with complex interactions, and (ii) use the algorithms developed to study microscopic models of interacting topological phases in quantum spin systems. Properties such fractionalized excitations and robustness against local defects make topological phases interesting for both fundamental and practical reasons. Understanding, and more importantly, controlling the emergence of these complex phases is one of the most active frontiers of contemporary condensed matter research. Topological phases are often realized in frustrated lattices and are characterized by non-local order parameters both of which make it challenging to probe them on classical computers. Significantly, as we discuss later, our proposed quantum algorithms are able to overcome both hurdles, making it possible to study microscopic Hamiltonians of topological phases in a controllable manner in the near future. Our present research is motivated by the prospect of availability of adequate quantum computing resources in the near future as well as the ability to test our algorithms directly on Singapore’s first superconducting qubit-based quantum computer being built by the Co-PI at NTU. Importantly, the current generation of quantum computers are not fault-tolerant; they belong to the class of Noisy Intermediate State Quantum (NISQ) computers and it is necessary to optimize any algorithm to minimize the effects of noisy qubits and logic gates. At every stage of the project, we shall use feedback from the tests of our algorithms on the quantum computer at the Co-PI's lab to optimize the circuits to mitigate the shortcomings of NISQ hardware. title: Nonlinear random matrices and generalization errors of the large multi-layer feed forward networks
abs: The past decade has witnessed the remarkable practical success of deep learning in a variety of tasks like computer vision and natural language processing, yet the mechanisms behind the powerful generalization capabilities of these models remain largely opaque. Recent progress in theoretical understanding of over-parameterized neural networks has revealed the important role of the spectral properties of some specific high-dimensional nonlinear random matrices in the study of generalization performance of neural networks. As a result, a large number of open problems have been raised in both the communities of random matrix theory and machine learning. The main aim of this project is to investigate the spectral properties of some nonlinear random matrices involved in the large multi-layer feedforward networks and study the generalization errors and random weight initialization of the large multi-layer feedforward networks based on these results. Specifically, we plan to investigate bilinear forms of resolvents and linear spectral statistics of nonlinear random matrices including conjugate kernels, neural tangent kernels and the input-output Jacobians, and study benign overfitting of neural network classifiers for nonlinear data. We will also examine the generalization dynamics of neural networks trained by gradient methods, particularly for the gradient steps in the early training stage and their relationship with some kernel matrices determined by training sample and random initialization of weights. Moreover, we will explore the generalization dynamics for a variety of data distributions under different parameterizations and learning rate settings so that we can uncover the mysterious phase transition between different generalization mechanisms. The main approaches we will adopt include the linearization method, central limit theory for martingale difference sequence, comparison between functionals of resolvents based on Lindeberg’s strategy, moment methods based on the cumulant expansion, graph enumeration techniques, and orthogonal polynomial decomposition. The academic significance of this project may be summarized as follows. (i) It will lay down a solid theoretical foundation for understanding the generalization performance of deep learning, (ii) It will reveal the transition mechanism between different generalization behaviors of neural networks and provide reliable theoretical guidance for practitioners in the machine learning community, (iii) It will facilitate new techniques for investigation of complicated random matrix ensembles involving nonlinearity, (iv) It will strengthen the international collaboration with well-renowned figures and promote Singapore's reputation in the field.
kw: Random matrices; extreme eigenvalues; eigenvectors; generalization errors; multi-layer feed forward networks

title: Optimal adaptive finite elements for Bayesian inverse problems and multiscale problems
abs: The project develops optimal numerical methods for Bayesian inverse problems and multiscale problems where the coefficients of the underlying partial differential equations are discontinuous. These problems arise in many critical real world applications such as detecting tumors in medical imaging using the Electrical Impedance Tomography method, and in composite materials. The optimal methods developed so far in the literature do not apply to these classes of problems. Bayesian inverse problems play important roles in many practical and engineering applications, where quantifying uncertainty in the model and in the physical properties of the physical media is necessary. The complexity of sampling the posterior probability measure by the Markov Chain Monte Carlo method is enormous, as a large number of realizations of the forward partial differential equations needs to be solved accurately. To overcome this obstacle, the PI and his collaborators develop the Multilevel Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods to approximate the posterior expectation of quantities of interest, which only require an optimal level of complexity to produce an approximation within a prescribed level of accuracy. The methods are successfully developed for the case of uniform prior where the coefficients are uniformly bounded for all the realizations, and the log-Gaussian prior where the coefficients are not uniformly bounded. The optimal convergence is mathematically rigorously proved (see, e.g., V. H. Hoang, Ch. Schwab and A. M. Stuart, Inverse Problems, Vol. 29, 085010, 2013, and V. H. Hoang, J. H. Quek and Ch. Schwab, Inverse Problems, Vol. 36, 035021, 2020). The methods use finite elements with different levels of resolution to solve the forward partial differential equations. The number of samples in the Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling procedure is chosen judiciously according to the level of resolution. However, these methods are not applicable in the case where the coefficients are discontinuous, for example, in the inverse problems for detecting an inclusion, such as a tumor, in the medium. The project develops the optimal Multilevel Markov Chain Monte Carlo method for this case using an adaptive approach for solving the forward equation. A typical approach for solving the forward equation adaptively is developed by A. Bonito, R. A. Devore, R. H. Nochetto, SIAM Journal of Numerical Analysis, Vol. 51, 3106-3134, 2013. This adaptive approach avoids discretizing the domain beforehand with a mesh that fits the discontinuity of the coefficients, thus simplifying significantly the sampling procedure. We study Bayesian inverse problems for the forward elliptic equation, the Electrical Impedance Tomography problem, and the time dependent parabolic equation. For locally periodic multiscale problems, the PI and his collaborators develop the sparse tensor product finite element method to obtain all the macroscopic and microscopic information of the solution. title: Accessing Uncharted Chemical Space of Chiral Medium-Sized Heterocycles by Metal-Catalyzed de novo Cycloaddition
abs: The chemical and pharmaceutical industry is one of the largest contributors to Singapore’s manufacturing output and therefore a key pillar of Singapore’s economy. Innovation in chemical production process that delivers novel structures and functions with high efficacy will contribute greatly to the local market and promote a future-ready sustainable society. Medium-sized (8 to 12-membered) heterocycles, despite of their great significance in nature, are severely under-represented in commercial synthetic small-molecule drugs. 9 to 11-membered heterocycles, in particular, found zero presence out of the >600 commercial heterocyclic drugs. Such an unusual absence of medium-sized heterocycles is a missed opportunity of their potentials for drug development and functional material science. The major bottleneck is lack of efficient synthesis of such structures to overcome their inherent ring strain and high entropy cost for cyclization. Recognizing this significant gap in synthetic chemistry, we propose to establish de novo synthesis of medium-sized rings by developing catalytic higher-order cycloaddition of simple building blocks known as the dipoles and the dipolarophiles. These transformations represent formidable challenge in synthetic chemistry, achieving which will offer a powerful entry to uncharted chemical space and find broad applications in drug discovery. In order to achieve the overarching goal, we will pursue the following four specific aims: Aim 1: Develop novel dipoles for modular, systematic construction of 8–12 membered heterocycles using palladium- or nickel-catalysis. Aim 2: Introduce new dipolarophiles for building diversely functionalized medium-sized rings. Aim 3: Establish unprecedented divergent synthesis of E- or Z-alkene-containing medium-sized rings and even macrocycles. Aim 4: Incorporate CO2 as feedstock in construction of diverse medium-sized lactones/carbonates. Key to success of the proposed work includes a) the introduction of novel dipoles and dipolarophiles and the incorporation of feedstocks such as 1,3-dienes and CO2 to participate in efficient and stereoselective cycloaddition and b) the identification of effective palladium- or nickel-based catalytic systems to enable such transformations. Very promising results have been obtained for all the three aims in this proposal. Not only have we established the validity of the proposed novel building blocks for the preparation of various sized heterocycles, but we have also made exciting discovery on the divergent control of either E- or Z-alkenes in 11- or 12-membered rings. Incorporation of CO2 to access medium-sized lactones/carbonates has also seen promising hits. Further optimization of the conditions and achieving a general divergent alkene geometry control in various medium-sized ring formation will result in a landmark advance in stereoselective synthesis.
kw: New chemical space; medium-sized heterocycles; de novo cycloaddition; enantioselective catalysis; base metal catalysis; CO2 fixation

title: Solvent-free Mechanosynthesized PerovskIte Light Emitters (SMILE)
abs: The primary objectives of this proposal are to accelerate the incorporation of metal halide double perovskites into affordable indoor optoelectronic devices by combining sustainable, solvent-free mechanosyntheses and fabrication methods with state-of-the-art, in situ functional monitoring, time-resolved and temperature-dependent ultrafast spectroscopy, multimodal microscopy, and electronic structure calculations. Metal halide perovskites have received worldwide attention over the past decade because of their exceptional optoelectronic properties with promising applications such as solar cells, light-emitting diodes, lasers, photodetectors, and X-ray scintillators. However, the best performing perovskites used in the devices contain the highly toxic lead or tin, and are easily damaged by air, moisture, or heat. Meanwhile, majority of the latest research has focused on mitigation strategies by encapsulation and improvements on the device performances, instead of overcoming the fundamental problems. This raises the risk of widespread environmental pollution if they are deployed for outdoor applications (e.g. solar cells) that are exposed to extreme weather conditions. Moreover, most perovskite devices are solution processed now, meaning that the reproducibility and the quality and purity of the perovskite films can be very sensitive to the solvents and conditions used. Since most of the high performance perovskite devices require N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF) as the solvent, but DMF has been included in the European Union’s substance of very high concern list and its use will be restricted in Europe from the end of 2023, the perovskite community faces a severe crisis if it persists in depending solely on solution processing. In this proposal, we intend to surmount all these problems through three sub-projects: (i) We will apply solvent-free mechanosyntheses to prepare less toxic, lead-free double perovskites. Our team has customized the only system in the world that can be used for the in situ observations of the reflectance and photoluminescence during mechanochemical ball milling reactions. Although modern automated mechanosyntheses have been used to prepare perovskites, there have been no examples of functional time-resolved in situ techniques for monitoring them since they are usually conducted in sealed, opaque, steel milling jars. Thus, we will use our unique capability to monitor the solvent-free mechanosyntheses of metal halide double perovskites and focus especially on the candidates that exhibit the widest spectral absorption ranges and the highest photoluminescence quantum yields. (ii) We will perform detailed structure-function photophysical experiments to quantify the photoluminescence quantum yields, and measure the dependence of the optoelectronic properties on temperature, power, time, and structure to understand the origins of the performances and provide insights for further improvements. title: Non-Invasive Online-Self-Correcting Closed-loop Brain Computer Interface for Decoding and Control of Motor Imagery Hand Movement Kinematics
abs: Motor Imagery Brain Computer Interface (MI-BCI) exploits the knowledge of neural correlates of motor activities and provides a novel tool to further explore the neural mechanisms underlying Motor Imagery, i.e., mental rehearsal or imagination of motor activity. Neurofeedback training using MI-BCI promotes neural plasticity through repeated recruitment of motor neurons and helps to improve motor dysfunction. Motor Imagery modulates the brain activity in the motor cortex, which can be decoded from Electroencephalograph (EEG) and translated to control commands to interface with rehabilitation or prosthetic devices. State-of-the-art non-invasive MI-BCIs perform only decoding of discrete movements such as left-hand versus right-hand imagery or MI of the dominant hand in two directions, which offer only a limited number of control commands. Online (real-time) MI-BCI that can provide high-dimensional motor control is essential for the deployment of MI-BCI systems in the real world. In this project, we aim to develop an online EEG-based MI-BCI for decoding imagined hand movement kinematics (directions and speed), which will offer higher degrees of freedom facilitating a more natural control. Further, we will exploit the use of Error-related potential for improving the direction/speed decoding accuracy. Error-related potentials are neurophysiological signals elicited in the brain associated with error processing, in response to an erroneous feedback stimulus presented to the user when the decoded result is different from the imagined direction or speed. The hypothesis is that error processing in the brain evokes distinct EEG activity that can be detected and used to correct and adapt a MI-BCI decoder. To improve the direction and speed decoding accuracy, the respective Motor Imagery decoding module will be integrated with an Error-related potential-based automatic self-correcting module. The specific aims are: 1. Identify the neural mechanisms and EEG signal patterns reflected in sensorimotor rhythms associated with Motor Imagery of center-out hand movement in four orthogonal directions in a vertical plane (left, right, up and down) and two speeds (slow and fast). 2. Adaptively decode imagined hand movement directions and speed. 3. Single-trial detection of Error-related potentials triggered by erroneously classified direction and speed presented in the form of visual feedback, characterization and identification of Error-related potentials corresponding to different directions and speeds, and extraction of the self-correction feature. 4. Integrating all the above, design and implement an online self-correcting MI-BCI that decodes the imagined hand movement directions and speed from EEG and combines it with Error-related potential detection to develop a closed-loop system for controlling the robotic arm movement of the user in the imagined direction and speed. 5. Design an experimental paradigm of the proposed online closed-loop self-correcting BCI system
kw: Brain Computer Interface; Neurofeedback; Motor Imagery; Error-related potential; Single-trial detection; Feature classification

title: Liquid Metals as Carbon Dioxides Hydrogenation Catalysts for High-value Products
abs: This project aims to find innovative carbon dioxide (CO2) hydrogenation catalysts to afford various high-value and easily marketable fuels and chemicals containing two or more carbons (C2+ species), such as dimethyl ether (DME), olefines, and higher alcohols. To activate the extremely inert CO2 and overcome the huge C-C couple barriers and mass transfer, these reactions are generally required high temperature (300 - 700 degree Celsius) and high pressure (0.5 – 10 MPa, or even above 30 MPa). Many competing reactions lead to the formation of C1 products, such as the so-called even dead-end CH4. The state-of-the-art catalysts are usually transitioning metal-based solid matrices and have low selectivity toward the desired product (below 30%). They are easily deactivated by structure deformation or coke deposition under harsh environments and have an extremely short lifetime (< 50 h) during operation. The C2+ production is still in the preliminary stage. In contrast to TM, Liquid metals (LMs) are referred to as metals whose melting point can be achieved by kitchen appliances (< 350 oC), such as K, Na, Hg, Mg, Ga, In, Sn, Pb and Bi. The advantages of LMs in thermal catalysis are obvious, such as no particle sintering, minimizing coke deposition and much cheaper prices than TMs. However, the development of LMs catalysis has been very slow both experimentally and theoretically during the past century, yet no LMs are reported for effective C2+ production to date. We propose to design novel catalysts by taking the advantage of liquid metals (LMs), whose electron/phonon dynamics and unique liquid-solid interface are seldom correlated with catalysis but no doubt an important degree of freedom in thermal catalysts. We aim to answer three questions in the proposal (1) how to efficiently prompt the C2+ selectivity since most LMs are inert in the bulk form and TMs are poisoned by C1 product? (2) how to find long-lived catalysts under harsh conditions (450+ oC and 1+ bar) or facilize productivity under low temperatures (below 100 degrees Celsius) and ambient pressure (0.1 MPa)? (3) Phonon dynamics has been longly ignored in thermal dynamics, how to understand it and decouple it with electronic effect? To this end, we intend to design a series of LM-based nanoparticles (NPs) from monometallic to LM-TM binary and multiple-elemental system and LM NPs/Porous supports the hybrid system, which results in unique liquid-solid interface and electron/phonon dynamics that not existing in the conventional solid catalysts. The nanomaterials will be synthesized using a wet-chemistry method to control their composition with optimized crystal structure, shape, and size at an atomic level. Operando measurements and theoretical calculations will be used to study the electron/phonon structure changes and their impact on catalytic behaviour. title: Deconstructing neural mechanisms of social intelligence
abs: Cooperation and competition are two pillars in the evolution of human societies. Self-interested agents, including humans and other animals, often work together to achieve a shared reward or compete for limited resources. In artificial intelligence, multi-agent deep reinforcement learning (RL) has been extensively studied for its potential to model emergent behaviour that arises from multiple agents co-evolving together. Multi-agent deep reinforcement learning has been successfully applied to complex game domains and biological behaviour simulations involving cooperation and competition. This research direction is important because multi-agent deep reinforcement learning may provide novel solutions to a variety of societal issues. In contrast, studies of multi-agent systems in neuroscience have been mostly limited to innate behaviour, such as mating and fighting, leaving the neural mechanisms of social intelligence in more complex environments largely unknown. In this proposal, we aim to study the neural mechanisms of cooperation and competition in mice using multi-agent deep RL algorithms. These algorithms will provide theoretical predictions for the emergence of neural representations of social values over learning. We will test these hypotheses experimentally by recording neural activity in mice performing the same task as artificial agents, focusing on brain regions important for cognitive functions. Additionally, leveraging the power of mouse genetics, we will study the neural circuits underlying cooperation and competition. Our hypothesis is that social intelligence involves the emergence of social-value-encoding neurons in a neural circuit composed of the medial prefrontal cortex and striatum. The successful completion of this research will provide new insights into the neural mechanisms of social intelligence in mice and potentially offer better algorithms and neural network architectures to improve machine intelligence in multi-agent settings.
kw: Social intelligence; Systems neuroscience; Two-photon calcium imaging; Electrophysiology; Deep reinforcement learning

title: Terahertz-to-Imaging Integrated Circuit for Security and Health Monitoring
abs: In this project, we will aim to enable technologies for fully integrated hardware solutions for security screening, food safety, gas spectroscopy, and contactless health monitoring. The successful completion of the project will facilitate the replacement of existing expensive instruments with at least a thousandfold reduction in cost and size. Industry and consumers will be able to access these functionalities through mobile devices. Such technologies would have significant security, safety, and economic benefits for the world and particularly Singapore. Recent research on terahertz (THz) electronics has demonstrated many exciting applications, including 1) THz imaging for security [1] and food safety [2], 2) rotational gas spectroscopy [3], 3) frequency-modulated continuous-wave radar and positioning for drones [4], and 4) wireless health monitoring [5]. Unfortunately, many of these products are bulky and expensive, and most importantly, cannot be accessed easily or timely by consumers at low or no cost. For example, security screening at airports requires machines that cost millions of dollars. Food safety detection and gas spectroscopy can only be performed with expensive equipment at the relevant agencies. Advanced contactless health assessment is attractive for patients with skin problems, but it typically requires expensive equipment that can only be accessed at medical centres, which can be costly and time consuming. The bulk and cost of existing THz-band (0.1 GHz to 10 THz) electronic instruments are mainly due to their discrete and power-hungry circuits/systems, which may also require complex cooling systems. Despite their exceptional performance at THz frequencies, these circuits/systems rely on advanced and expensive semiconductor technologies (e.g., gallium arsenide or indium phosphide devices). Each device may be from a different company, making their integration difficult. Combining all of these devices, with additional components and complex packaging, requires significant effort. Therefore, there is an urgent need in the consumer market to integrate all of these devices/systems into a single chip that can perform the above functionalities, to significantly reduce the overall cost and power consumption. The integration of these devices could yield the following benefits: 1. Elimination of path loss and crosstalk due to on-board wiring. 2. Great reduction in the cost and complexity of packaging. 3. Reduction of system complexity and power consumption of the whole system (through removing the need to connect each discrete component). 4. Simplification or removal of cooling systems (due to the reduced power consumption). 5. Cost and size reduction as a result of the above benefits. title: Harnessing In-Fiber Extreme Mechanics: Advanced Sensory Fabrics Enabled by Ultra-Long Continuous Semiconductor Fibers
abs: Recent advances in flexible optoelectronics have enabled the realization of a wearable full-body sensing system to monitor various physiological signals and detect chemical compositions of body fluids. Fiber-based platforms have been proposed and demonstrated to provide various functionalities at the fiber length scales. However, previous studies have indicated the challenges of fabricating standalone ultra-long semiconductor fibers. Both cracks and deformation in the semiconductor core due to the stress development and capillary instability in the fabrication process have significantly affected the performance of these functional fibers in various applications. Here, we propose to control the in-fiber extreme mechanics to enable the formation of ultra-long continuous semiconductor fibers by fundamentally addressing two major challenges (cracked core and capillary breakup). First, the realization of standalone ultra-long semiconductor fibers is achieved through a detailed stress analysis and understanding of the capillary instability in the process of thermal drawing, resulting in kilometer-long continuous semiconductor-core fibers with unprecedented control over architectures, compositions, and sizes, while maintaining the flexibility of fibers. Then, a newly developed convergence thermal drawing method will be applied to confine semiconductor cores in a well-defined metal-semiconductor-metal structure and further integrate them into a single flexible fiber to achieve diverse functionalities. The produced fiber-based devices thus have all the necessary functions built into them and do not require any further processing steps and packaging. We plan to demonstrate various applications in healthcare, wearable communication, and assistive technology. The achieved high-performance fiber-based devices exhibit many unique and extraordinary characteristics such as lightweight, ultralong, highly flexible, and mechanically stable. More importantly, the hierarchical nature (fiber - yarn - fabric) of these fibers makes them particularly suitable for the fabrication of wearable functional fabrics. The successful execution of the proposed work will not only yield new fundamental insights in semiconductor material science and extreme mechanics with the geometries and parameters that are not accessible in traditional platforms, but also essentially address the increasing demand for high-performance wearable electronic, photonic, and optoelectronic devices to engage a broad range of applications.
