title: Cellular and molecular mechanisms of necroptosis during extracellular bacterial infection
abs: Innate immune cells such as macrophages express a repertoire of pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) to rapidly detect microbial danger. Ligation of PRRs induces a variety of proinflammatory functions including the production of reactive oxygen species, chemokines/cytokines, phagocytosis, and initiation of lytic cell death pathways. While important for host defence, activation of the innate immune system is increasingly associated with a variety of sterile inflammatory diseases including aging, rheumatoid arthritis, cardiovascular disease and neurodegenerative disorders. Programmed necrosis including pyroptosis and necroptosis are emerging as key drivers for both of these processes, however, the molecular regulation of necrosis, and mechanisms by which necrosis promotes host defence is not completely understood. For example, while programmed necrosis is a simple and straightforward host defence mechanism that destroys the replicative niche of intracellular pathogens, whether and how necrotic cell death promotes host defence against extracellular pathogens is unclear. Here, we provide strong preliminary data that necroptosis is a novel and exciting host defence mechanism against the diarrheagenic extracellular bacterium, Citrobacter rodentium. Mechanistically, we demonstrate that C. rodentium injects a bacterial cysteine protease, EspL, into macrophages to cleave the pro-necrotic kinase, RIPK3 to subvert macrophage necroptosis. In agreement with that, mice infected with espL-deficient bacteria display enhanced phosphorylated MLKL, a hallmark of necroptosis in colonic tissues; Ripk3-deficient mice that are unable to trigger necroptosis display heighten susceptibility to C. rodentium infection compared to wild type controls. However, the molecular mechanisms by which C. rodentium triggers necroptosis, and the cellular mechanisms by which necroptosis drives host defence against extracellular pathogens in vivo remains unclear. Therefore, the aims of this project are: (1) to determine the molecular mechanism by which C. rodentium triggers macrophage necroptosis; (2) to define the biochemical composition and subcellular location of the necrosome following bacterial infection; and (3) define the cellular mechanisms by which necroptosis protect against extracellular bacterial infection. Successful completion of this study will significantly improve our understand of necroptosis during extracellular bacterial infection, which is a fundamental biological questions. Knowledge gained from this study will also be relevant in a broader context, since necroptosis is heavily implicated in other infectious disease (e.g., SARS-CoV-2), inflammatory disorders (e.g., inflammatory bowel syndrome), neurological degeneration (e.g. sporadic amyotrophic lateral sclerosis), and aging (e.g., sterile low-grade inflammation).
kw: Innate immunity, cell death, necroptosis, host-pathogen interactions, bacterial infection

title: Mechanistic Understanding of Signal Peptide Secretion for Quorum Sensing
abs: Quorum sensing (QS) controls group behavior in bacterial pathogens for virulence and the formation of biofilm and sporulation, its interference has become a novel therapy in fighting bacterial infections. The first step of this process in Gram-positive bacteria involves the maturation and secretion of QS signalling peptide, or competence stimulating peptide (CSP), which is in charged by an ABC-type efflux pump with assistance from another associated protein. Owing to the lack of structural and biochemical data, the molecular mechanisms underlying CSP process and secretion in QS are still not clear, limiting drug development targeting this key process. In this proposal, we aim to establish a detailed mechanistic understanding of signal peptide secretion for quorum sensing involved by ComA and ComB, and provide novel targets and mechanisms for drug targeting in combating Gram-positive pathogens. This will be achieved by 1) biochemical reconstitution of Com proteins in vitro for the following functional and structural characterisations, 2) exploring the unknown role of ComB in CSP secretion, 3) in-vitro and in-vivo study of ComA/B for an overall understanding of their functions, and 4) determining a series of structures to uncover the detailed mechanism of ComA/B underneath CSP processing and secretion at a molecular level. A major bottleneck that delayed this study for decades is the three-dimensional (3D) structure determination of a challenging membrane efflux pump ComA. Through a series of preliminary studies, we have reconstituted all key proteins in vitro and resolved the first high-resolution structure of ComA. Multiple in-vitro and in-vivo assays have also been established for functional characterisation. Utilising these methods, we characterised the kinetics of ComA and for the first time, established the essential role of ComB in the secretion of CSP. Three cryo-EM maps of ComA have been determined, from which a novel binding pocket for two CSPs was elucidated; as it is located at the outer leaflet of the membrane with easy access to drugs, this pocket contains a high potential for drug targeting. In addition, the translocation pathway is uncovered with three patches of charged residues identified with a potential role in the binding and translocation of CSP. These results proved the high feasibility of this project and framed a novel site from ComA for drug targeting. In this project, we will further characterize the process of CSP secretion for QS, at both cellular and molecular level, through membrane biology, single-particle cryo-EM methods, combined with in vitro and in vivo functional studies. The major work on protein biochemistry and structural study will be performed in the PI’s lab; cell genetic and phenotype study will be carried out by our collaborator Dr. Lok-To Sham’s lab at NUS, which has complementary interdisciplinary expertise in microbiology. title: Investigating Kindlin-3 as an adaptor protein that modulates interleukin 2 receptor localization and signaling
abs: The expansion of T cells during infection is crucial in adaptive immunity. On the other hand, deregulated proliferation of T cells can lead to leukemia. Homotypic interaction between T cells has been shown to promote T cell expansion by enhancing cytokine interleukin 2 (IL-2)/IL-2 receptor (R) autocrine and paracrine signaling. The mechanism by which the IL-2R accumulates at the T cell-T cell homotypic synapse is unclear. Derived from our preliminary studies, the hypothesis of this proposal is that the focal adhesion protein Kindlin (K3) is an adaptor protein that binds to the ß subunit of IL-2R. K3 stabilizes IL-2Rß and modulates IL-2Rß signaling by recruiting a scaffold protein that assembles downstream signaling components of IL-2Rß. Finally, detailing the mode of interaction between K3 and IL-2Rß allows targeted disruption of their association, which will inhibit T cell proliferation, thus having potential therapeutic value in disease treatment, for instance Adult T cell leukemia. To test this hypothesis, the aims of this proposal are: 1: Investigating the dynamic behaviour and interaction trajectories of K3 and IL-2Rß 2: Investigating the K3-IL-2Rß signaling node: Assembly, scaffolding, and stabilization 3: Characterizing small molecule-mediated disruption of K3 and IL-2Rß interaction

title: The novel role of two micropeptides in the reactivation of quiescent neural stem cells
abs: Micropeptides/peptides are small polypeptides encoded by short open reading frames (sORFs) that are less than 100 codons long. Given their small size, sORFs were initially overlooked by genomic studies, and functional studies on micropeptides are far behind those on larger proteins. Emerging evidence indicates that micropeptides are essential regulators of various cellular processes such as cell growth, metabolism, and development. However, the role of micropeptides in brain development is poorly studied. Drosophila neural stem cells (NSCs) in the brain enter into quiescence at the end of embryogenesis and subsequently become proliferative again (reactivation) in early larval stages. Here, we propose that two previous uncharacterized Drosophila micropeptides Simba1/2 play a novel role in promoting quiescent neural stem cell reactivation (re-entering the cell cycle). Our central hypothesis is that Simba1 and Simba2 promote NSC reactivation by regulating Wingless signaling. We propose to address this hypothesis with the following 3 specific aims: 1. Establish the novel role of Simba 1/2 in NSC reactivation. We have identified Simba1 and Simba2 from a reverse-genetic screen for their novel role in quiescent neural stem cell reactivation. In addition, knocking down of either simba1 or simba2 in glial cells results in defects in NSC reactivation, suggesting that they may function in glial cells to control reactivation. To understand their role in NSC reactivation, we will overexpress or misexpress Simba1/2 in glia and NSCs and examine the effect on the cell cycle re-entry. We will also generate antibodies against Simba1/2 and transgenic flies expressing Simba1/2 tagged with HA and examine the subcellular localization of these micropeptides in the Drosophila brain. In addition, we will perform tissue-specific rescue of the KO phenotypes by expressing Simba1/2 in various brain cell types. 2. Determine the novel role of the Wingless/Wnt signaling pathway in neural stem cell reactivation. Our preliminary data suggest that Wingless (Wg), a well-studied Wg ligand, is required for the reactivation of NSCs. Interestingly, we observed Wg in the blood-brain-barrier (BBB) glia and underlying NSCs in the Drosophila larval brain. We propose that Wg is produced in the BBB glia to activate the Wg pathway in the underlying NSCs prior to their cell cycle re-entry. To test this hypothesis, we will examine the loss-of-function phenotypes in major canonical Wingless/Wnt pathway components during NSC reactivation. We will also perform in vivo RNAi for wg and other canonical Wg/Wnt pathway components in glial cells and NSCs and determine within which cell types Wg signaling is required for NSC reactivation. We will also identify downstream targets of the Wg pathway in NSC reactivation. 3. Investigate the link between Simba1/2 and Wingless/Wnt signaling pathway in neural stem cell reactivation. Our preliminary data suggest that wg mRNA levels were decreased in simba1/2 KOs.
kw: Drosophila, neural stem cells, reactivation, larval brains, micropeptides, Wingless

title: How does earnings management affect employee mental well-being?
abs: Employee mental well-being has become an important global issue in recent years with more and more companies directing attention to understanding how to reduce workplace stress, something that negatively affects employee productivity and increases voluntary turnover. For example, Singapore employees have the highest turnover rate in Asia, with 46% expected to leave their job within a year. Demand for higher pay and a desire for better work-life balance are often the primary motivations employees mention for their voluntary exits. Voluntary employee turnover is costly as firms must incur additional costs to acquire and train new talent for the organization. Similarly, a recent study finds that Singapore spends about S$3.1 billion a year, or 18% of its total annual healthcare costs, on stress-related illnesses. Likewise, mental health problems, such as depression and anxiety disorders, affect more than one in six people across the European Union in any given year. Besides the impact on people’s well-being, the EU spends over 600 billion Euros – or more than 4% of GDP across the 28 EU countries, on mental-related illnesses. In general, data from different countries around the world suggest that work-related stress is a global issue and it is thus not surprising that “Good Health and Well-being” is one of the United Nation’s sustainable development goals. To understand how to improve employee well-being requires an understanding of the cause of their lack of job satisfaction and factors behind their work-related stress. In this proposed international study, we examine whether pressure from senior management to meet short-term earnings benchmarks is associated with employee attitudes towards work and their overall well-being. The need to meet or beat earnings expectations is a deeply entrenched notion in today’s corporate world, and prior studies in accounting and finance have examined extensively the effects of firms’ earnings management behavior on operating performance and capital market consequences. While these studies show that firms enjoy a trading premium, in the short run, for meeting or beating earnings benchmarks, there is also evidence suggesting this myopic behavior is not sustainable in the long run and can lead to negative capital market consequences. More importantly, there is scarce academic evidence on the impact of this myopic behavior on employees, an important stakeholder group of the company. This is alarming because growing evidence suggests more and more employees are unhappy at work. While traditional theories on the organization of the firm suggest that maximizing shareholder value should be a company’s main objective, it has been increasingly argued that companies must also consider the impact of their operations and success on other stakeholders. title: Hidden Treasure Walks – A Virtual Immersive Cultural Experience in Singapore
abs: Hidden Treasure Walks is art-based research that offers an immersive virtual experience from an app and a 360-degree video to guide its users to discover historical and cultural stories at familiar locations along the route of Bus 166 in Singapore. Using the field findings in the natural and cultural communities around the route, the research combines augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR) technology to produce an immersive experience for the local stories to be heard, seen, and sensed. Working with faculty members, students, and collaborators from two previous research projects, the primary investigator produces a virtual, immersive cultural experience in the context of Singapore’s urban space. Hidden Treasure Walks is exceeding the limits of traditional arts and bringing forth awareness of Singapore’s rich cultural heritage. The research project is based on the hypothesis that art and technology can jointly improve social life. Through the narrative of sensory inputs, voiced by different ethnicities, communities, and social groups and equipped with new virtual technologies, the intangible cultural heritage of hidden treasures in Singapore can, therefore, be identified, interpreted, and reintroduced. The project explores the city as a spatial practice, reflecting one’s subjectivity to ecological, urban, social, and cultural surroundings. The immersive experience will take place on a bus and a walking tour of nearby communities and historical sites, exemplifying how art can engage the mind to understand what lurks in everyday life. The research project aims at delivering two results: (1) The Hidden Treasure Walks app is designed as a GPS-triggered audiovisual guide. The soundscape is the main carrier of the narrative experience, punctuated by a site-specific AR experience. (2) A series of 360-degree videos based on the same storytelling. Participants will be able to access cinematic virtual reality episodes without being on the site. The research results are intended to demonstrate how artistic knowledge can contribute to the field of humanities. The outcome can be seen as a prototype for an art project to affirm the cultural branding of Singapore, which can be applied to further use for cultural tourism and community service.
kw: Performative arts; digital cultural heritage; electronic arts & multimedia; Architecture and urban environment; Transportation; Tourism.

title: The Capital Market Consequences of ESG Reporting Divergence
abs: The past decade has witnessed an increasing demand for firms to undertake more environmental, social, and governance (ESG) activities, particularly in the area of sustainability. A growing number of governments, including Singapore, and firms have set sustainability goals and are working towards achieving them. However, such goals are easier set than met because of the high costs involved and the difficulty in holding governments and firms accountable. At the same time, there is also a growing demand for information on firms’ ESG activities. Investors need ESG information for investment screening and asset allocation, and ESG funds need ESG information to make portfolio allocation decisions. Hence, many firms voluntarily disclose ESG information. However, the lack of comparability of ESG information across firms (referred to as ESG reporting divergence) poses a big challenge to the users of ESG information. For example, Mr. Tan Boon Gin, the CEO of SGX RegCo, has emphasized that making ESG information comparable is essential in fighting greenwashing and holding firms accountable for unsustainable practices. In response to the call for comparable ESG reporting, in November 2021, the International Accounting Standards Board announced the formation of the International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB) with the mission of setting sustainability disclosure standards and improving the comparability of ESG reporting. Since its formation, ISSB has issued two proposals on sustainability reporting. The SGX plans to incorporate the forthcoming ISSB standards into its listing rules as mandatory disclosure requirements. Against the backdrop of the increasing demand for the comparability of ESG reporting, it is important to understand the capital market consequences of the current ESG reporting divergence in the absence of mandatory ESG reporting requirements. As such, in our first research question, we will examine the effect of ESG reporting divergence on ESG information users – ESG rating providers, ESG fund managers, and investors. To the extent that less comparable ESG reporting reduces the overall quality of ESG information and ESG rating providers’ reliance on publicly available ESG information, it can increase the disagreement in ESG ratings across different rating providers. Therefore, we predict that ESG reporting divergence is positively correlated with ESG rating disagreement. Furthermore, ESG information, along with ESG ratings, are used by ESG fund managers and investors to make portfolio allocation decisions. The lack of comparability of ESG information and the disagreement in ESG ratings across rating providers are frequently regarded by investors as the biggest impediments to ESG investing. To the extent that ESG reporting divergence reduces the usefulness of ESG information and ESG ratings, we expect it to weaken the positive association between ESG ratings and ESG fund allocation as well as the market reaction to ESG news. title: Building a Deeper Long-Term Climate Understanding of Rainfall Trends in Singapore, West Malaysia, and Northern Sumatra
abs: Water security represents a major future challenge in the face of predicted climate changes, with risks to water supply ranked by the World Economic Forum (2020) as among the most likely threats with the biggest impact globally. Regions such as southeast Asia, where much of the water for agricultural, industrial and human consumption is supplied by rainfall, are particularly vulnerable. Rainfall-related extreme events such as floods and droughts are set to increase in both frequency and severity in southeast Asia as a result of climate change. Flood events are relatively common today, but can have devastating impacts for populations, resulting in power-outages, damage to property and infrastructure and, in extreme cases (e.g., the floods of 1969 and 1978 in Singapore), loss of life. Droughts are also surprisingly frequent. Despite its tropical climate, Singapore is considered to be one of the most water-stressed countries in the world, such that prolonged dry spells can lead to water shortages. Whilst it is possible to use climate models to project the likelihood of rainfall-related extreme events in the future, our understanding is limited by our inability to contextualise the frequency and intensity of floods and droughts historically. Even in Singapore, where meteorological data has been collected since 1815, there are major gaps in coverage (e.g. between the late 1900s and 1920s, where continuous daily rainfall data are only available for two stations). Without spatially- and temporally-extensive datasets – or substitute proxy evidence for the pre-instrumental period – it is difficult to attribute major flood and drought episodes to climate change with any confidence. The overarching goals of this project are to (i) enhance the dataset underpinning regional water security, by reconstructing rainfall variability and the frequency of rainfall-related extreme events in Singapore, West Malaysia, and northern Sumatra between 1815 and 1960, and (ii) explore the socio-economic consequences of extremes to investigate patterns and strategies of risk and resilience. We will achieve these goals by examining a body of untapped historical instrumental and documentary sources of weather and climate information. Collectively, these sources will allow us to address four aims: 1. title: Pulmonary Circular mRNA Nanovaccines
abs: The growing elderly population in Singapore and worldwide highlights the urgent need for effective vaccination strategies to protect against diseases and infections, particularly in light of the increased vulnerability of this demographic due to age-related changes in immune defences. Mucosal vaccines have the potential to generate immune responses at the primary site of pathogen entry, providing protection against infections. However, the development of mucosal vaccines is hindered by the poor uptake of vaccines across the epithelial and mucus lining. Therefore, there is a critical need for vaccines that induce potent and durable immunity while efficiently targeting mucosal sites. To address this challenge, we propose to develop a novel mucosal vaccine technology using lipid nanoparticle (LNP) systems for the pulmonary delivery of small circular mRNA (circRNA). Our preliminary studies have shown that LNP can effectively deliver circRNA to the lungs, resulting in more robust immune responses compared to benchmark mRNA in young and aged mice. Furthermore, pulmonary delivery of small circRNA nanovaccines has demonstrated effective immune protection against influenza. Based on these findings, we hypothesize that pulmonary delivery of circRNA vaccines will generate durable and potent immune responses against dangerous infectious diseases, such as influenza, due to their inherent immunostimulatory properties and prolonged biostability. We will evaluate our hypothesis through the following aims: 1) designing and optimizing an LNP library for the screening of LNP-mediated pulmonary delivery and antigen presentation of circRNA, 2) studying the immunomodulation mechanisms and efficacies of pulmonary circRNA nanovaccines in young adult and immunosenescent aged mice, and 3) developing universal influenza pulmonary circRNA nanovaccines and testing their breadth and effectiveness of influenza prevention in young adult and immunosenescent mice. The successful completion of this study will provide valuable insights into mucosal circular mRNA vaccines and pulmonary drug/nucleic acid delivery. Additionally, the immunomodulation mechanisms uncovered may lead to the rational design of vaccines for various diseases, including infectious diseases and cancer, especially for immunosenescent individuals.

title: Dissecting the Mechanisms Underlying Pediatric Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome
abs: Pediatric Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (PARDS) occurs in approximately 2.2-5.7 cases per 100, 000 person-years and it is associated with an unacceptably high mortality of approximately 24-33%. In Singapore, PARDS has been reported to confer a mortality of 21% and a prolonged burden of mechanical ventilation. Pathologically, it is associated with intense pulmonary inflammation, proteinaceous alveolar exudation and fibrosis which impairs the oxygenation function of the lung. The pathogenesis of ARDS, studied mainly in adults, involves a dysregulated and over exuberant immune response. However, PARDS is distinct from adult ARDS in epidemiology, mechanical properties/ physiology of the lung, ultrastructure and stage of immune maturation. Therefore, PARDS likely has a completely different pathogenic mechanism from adult ARDS. To date, there are no clinical or laboratory predictors which can reliably discriminate whether a child will develop PARDS, or the likelihood of progression in those diagnosed with PARDS. There is a lack of understanding of the immune pathogenesis of PARDS and currently no targeted therapies for PARDS. This proposal addresses the gap in the understanding of the immunopathogenic diversity of Pediatric Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (PARDS) and consequently, the unmet need for a lack of specific diagnosis, patient stratification and targeted treatment. The over-arching hypothesis is that immune dysregulation contributes to persistent pulmonary inflammation with resultant respiratory failure in viral-induced PARDS. Through a greater understanding of the immunopathogenesis, this research will benefit children and families by improving the diagnosis of PARDS and aiding stratification into functional patient groups for targeted therapies.

title: Timely Interventions to Enable and Reach patients with Heart Failure, and their caregivers, with Palliative Care (TIER-HF-PC)
abs: Background Palliative care (PC) improves quality-of-life (QOL) and reduces inappropriate hospitalizations. However, PC is currently delivered “too little, too late” in heart failure (HF). Aims and Hypothesis TIER-HF-PC is a novel, tiered, nurse-led model of PC that aims to improve the timeliness of PC initiation. We will compare the effectiveness of TIER-HF-PC against usual care for improving patient and caregiver outcomes. We will also evaluate implementation outcomes (including acceptability, timeliness, and appropriateness of PC) for further fine-tuning of TIER-HF-PC. Methods: In TIER-HF-PC, patients will be screened regularly for symptoms, concerns, and distress. The PC nurse will direct PC treatments, based upon severity of detected problems. All participants will receive PC education resources. Participants with moderate-severity problems will receive PC nurse coaching. Participants with severe problems will receive a PC physician consultation, on top of PC nurse coaching. Patients in usual care are not screened but can be referred to a PC physician based upon cardiologist discretion. We will recruit 240 patients with HF and up to 240 caregivers, from 2 acute-care hospitals. Participants will be randomized in a 1:1 ratio to TIER-HF-PC or usual care. We will utilize an intention-to-treat approach for data analysis. Our primary outcome is patient QOL on Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire at 24 weeks. Secondary outcomes include patient healthcare utilization, caregiver QOL, and cost-effectiveness of TIER-HF-PC. All participants on the TIER-HF-PC arm will receive a validated service evaluation survey. Additionally, a sample of participants on the TIER-HF-PC arm, and their treating healthcare staff, will be purposively recruited for semi-structured interviews that evaluate their experience in TIER-HF-PC. Interviews will be thematically analyzed. We will evaluate protocol fidelity through audits of case notes and study processes. Significance An effective, satisfactory TIER-HF-PC model allows more timely PC initiation, which will improve QOL and other health outcomes.
kw: heart failure; palliative care ; population health; quality-of-life; implementation science

title: Isolating functional T cells from patients that recognize KRAS mutations and can exert cytotoxicity.
abs: Genetic abnormalities in cancer lead to the production of cancer antigens, which can be presented on human leukocyte antigen (HLA) as immunogenic cancer peptide fragments. These peptide-HLA (pHLA) complexes are detected by the T cell receptors (TCRs) of cytotoxic CD8+ T cells, driving clinically relevant and meaningful anti-cancer responses. Some cancer mutations, like KRAS mutations, are shared across patients and offer opportunities for off-the-shelf TCR-based therapies. The hypothesis is that responses in patients with mutant KRAS lung cancer (mKRAS-LuCa) treated with ICI/ICI-Chemo are driven by KRAS-specific T cell (mKRAS-T cells). Those T cells may serve as a precise biomarker for treatment response and disease progression. This study will focus on cancer patients with HLA types that are high in frequency among local and global populations. Building upon preliminary experiments that have identified novel HLA-C*08:01-mKRAS G12D-T cells and HLA-A*11:01-mKRAS G12C-T cells, the specific aim is to identify and characterize mKRAS-TCRs. The study seeks to establish a library of at least 50 distinct mKRAS-TCR sequences and prioritize lead TCR candidates with potent cytotoxic activity. Firstly, flow cytometric analysis of MHC Tetramer staining intensity will be conducted. Next, cell-based binding assays will be carried out using Jurkat cells transduced with TCR and K562 cells transduced with appropriate HLA. Furthermore, soluble TCR-based binding assays will be utilized to identify the lead TCRs. The establishment of this diverse mKRAS-TCR library holds implications for immunotherapy strategies and biomarker identification, potentially leading to improved treatment responses and patient outcomes. Moreover, exploring mKRAS-TCRs within specific HLA types, including those prevalent in Asian populations, may pave the way for the development of region-specific therapies. This study may contribute to the advance of personalized cancer immunotherapy and enhance our understanding of the immune response to KRAS mutations in lung cancer.
kw: T cells, TCR, Cancer, KRAS

title: Elucidating the neural basis of emotional dysregulation and other factors via a transdiagnostic approach: A longitudinal follow-up of mood disorder patients in the Cohort Health study In Mood and Emotional regulation in Singapore (CHIMES)
abs: Background Mood disorders are the most disease-burdening psychiatric disorders. High symptom heterogeneity among patients suggests dimensionality to mood disorders uncaptured by categorical diagnoses. Local data on factors influencing disease progression, treatment response, and outcomes are scant. Emotional dysregulation is frequently observed and could be a transdiagnostic risk factor. Aims (i) Identify common and unique neural, psychological, sociodemographic, and behavioural factors that differentiate mood disorders and influence disease severity, progression and outcomes. (ii) Examine the association between emotional dysregulation and neural variability in a transdiagnostic mood disorder cohort and ascertain if it can be a biomarker. (iii) Correlate functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) brain patterns with functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) signals and investigate the clinical utility of fNIRS in diagnosing and monitoring mood disorders. Hypotheses (i) Mood disorders have common and unique transdiagnostic factors that differentiate between disorders and are associated with disease severity, course and outcomes. (ii) Emotional dysregulation is a transdiagnostic factor associated with neural variability in the fronto-limbic circuits that can serve as a biomarker. (iii) fNIRS is a viable neuroimaging tool for differentiating and monitoring mood disorders in clinical practice. Methodology This one-year naturalistic observational study will recruit 280 new and existing mood disorder patients with unipolar depression or bipolar disorder (age 21-50) at the National University Hospital or Institute of Mental Health and 70 healthy controls. After baseline questionnaires, fMRI and fNIRS scans, participants will be monitored at 3-month intervals with 6- and 12-month fNIRS and 12-month fMRI scans. Multivariate analysis will identify latent components connecting clinical, cognitive, and personality measures to functional connectivity patterns and investigate neural patterns, disease outcomes, and treatment responses. Significance This study will elucidate the neural basis of emotional dysregulation and influencing factors of disease trajectory and outcomes, thus guiding improved diagnoses and developing targeted interventions for mood disorders.
kw: Mood disorders; Emotional dysregulation; Neuroimaging; Transdiagnostics

title: Exploring the role of the mTORC1-SMAD pathway in ovarian ageing to extend ovarian lifespan and health-span of women
abs: The first organs to undergo ageing in women are the ovaries. Senescence of the ovaries results in infertility and culminates in menopause. This estrogen-deficient state is associated with cardiovascular disease, osteoporosis, neurocognitive decline, sexual problems and immune-senescence. Reproductive ageing in the woman, with its detrimental health effects, leads to reduced health-span (i.e. being in good health) and lifespan. This phenomenon is exemplified by premature ovarian insufficiency, affecting 1% of all women globally, where women experience premature menopause before the age of 40 years accompanied by loss of fertility, increased risks of neurocognitive decline, cardio-metabolic diseases, osteoporosis and frailty leading to premature morbidity and mortality. The functional unit in the ovaries which maintain reproductive lifespan and health-span are the ovarian follicles, comprised of the oocyte and its surrounding somatic cells – granulosa and theca cells. There are intra-ovarian pathways that are vital to maintain ovarian lifespan such as the mTORC1 and AMH-SMAD signalling pathways, collectively, provide the energy, nutrients, and microenvironment for the development and maturation of the oocyte. Age-associated senescence of these somatic cells leads to atresia (degeneration) of the follicles and results in reproductive ageing and the loss of oestrogen vital for reproductive healthspan in women. This proposal aims to discover the positive interactions between the molecular targets in mTORC1 with SMAD pathways, which act via AMH, to halt ovarian ageing. This may offer an ovary- and cell-specific therapy targeted at rejuvenating aged ovaries through enhancing granulosa cell functions to achieve the positive biological effects on reproductive health-span. This will lead to impactful discovery of precise diagnostics to accurately assess the true reproductive lifespan of women to ensure optimal health-span, and novel therapeutics in the prevention of the increased risks of chronic diseases due to menopause and ovarian ageing with the loss of ovarian follicles.
kw: ovarian ageing, mTORC1 signalling, SMAD signalling, women healthspan

title: Elucidating ImmuNe ReprogrammIng in NasopharynGeal CarcinoMA - Resolving an ENIGMA
abs: EBV-associated nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) is Asia-endemic. Treatment resistance in NPC is poorly understood and as paradigms change to incorporate immunotherapy (IO), opportunities arise to interrogate immunobiology and test therapeutics in NPC. We hypothesize that cell-cell interactions, signaling nodes and spatial organization shape tumor immune microenvironment (TIME), setting the stage for development of immunotherapy resistant/sensitive states. We will elucidate cellular, molecular & spatial determinants of response/resistance to immunotherapy and develop biomarkers that can help in therapeutic selection utilizing the methods and approach outlined in the specific aims below: Aim 1: Characterize de novo untreated and on-treatment TIME in nasopharyngeal cancer. Serial pre-/on-treatment samples of tumor from IO-treated clinical cohorts will be immunophenotyped using scRNAseq, spatial profiling and mIHC; paired blood will undergo flow cytometry and cytokine analysis. These will be correlated with biopsy site-specific responses/clinical endpoints, allowing us to dissect and compare differences in spatial organization/signaling nodes across disease stages, and that modulate response to immunotherapy. Aim 2: Characterize resistant TIME in patients who relapse after primary chemoradiation and in treatment refractory disease. Serial tissue and blood samples obtained from relevant clinical cohorts will be immunophenotyped as in Aim 1, and correlated to biopsy site-specific responses/clinical endpoints, allowing us to dissect differences between early and late secondary resistance, understand immune escape across time and different therapeutics, and map the development of resistant TIME in a curated cohort of LA disease who relapse. Aim 3: Establish NPC-PDX mouse models to functionally validate resistance/response mechanisms and test therapeutics. A diverse panel of humanized NPC-PDX mice, will be established from tissue biopsies, immunophenotyped as above, and used as in-vivo models to study immune escape mechanisms and test novel therapeutics. This proposal addresses knowledge gaps in NPC from immune biology to translational science, synergize with ongoing research programs, and keep Singapore competitive in NPC research.
kw: Nasopharyngeal cancer; tumor immune microenvironment; spatial biology; patient-derived xenografts; mouse models

title: Elucidating the drivers of ethnic disparities in breast cancer to improve outcomes
abs: Breast cancer (BC) survival outcomes have improved with earlier detection and better systemic therapies. However, outcomes are worse in Malays compared to Chinese in Singapore, even after adjusting for treatment, tumor and patient characteristics. The drivers of these disparities are currently unclear. Hypothesis: There is a multifactorial basis for the ethnic disparities in BC survival outcomes, including intrinsic differences in host and/or tumor biology. Aim 1: To identify the drivers of inferior survival outcomes in Malay patients, based on cohort of Chinese, Malay and Indian women diagnosed with BC from 2000 to 2017 at our healthcare cluster. We will characterize ethnic differences in BC clinicopathological features, patient characteristics (including socioeconomic status) and treatment compliance (including timeliness), and quantify the extent to which ethnic differences in outcomes are mediated by these factors. Aim 2: To evaluate whether the inferior outcomes in Malay patients have persisted over time. We will characterize ethnic differences in tumor and patient characteristics plus treatment factors according to year of diagnosis, evaluate differences in the time trends of various survival outcomes by ethnicity, and compare against overall trends from the national registry. Aim 3: To elucidate ethnic differences in tumor biology beyond standard pathological variables. Through bulk RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) of invasive BCs, we will identify gene expression signatures and tumor microenvironment differences by ethnicity, and correlate with clinicopathological characteristics and outcomes. Significant findings will be validated with multiplex immunohistochemical profiling. Significance: The new in-depth knowledge generated can help to promote equity in BC outcomes. Several of the potential drivers are modifiable eg better education and health-seeking behaviour, healthier lifestyles with reduction in obesity, greater financial and other support for optimal treatment. Improved understanding of tumor biology may lead to discovery of novel therapeutic targets or strategies in future, and biomarkers for prognostication and selection of therapy.
kw: ethnicity; breast cancer; outcomes; biology

title: Investigating the molecular basis of endosomal membrane dynamics and its impact to neurodegeneration
abs: By 2050, the number of dementia patients in Singapore is expected to reach 187 thousand, which means that one out of thirty Singaporean will suffer from dementia. Therefore, the establishment of its treatment is an urgent issue. The most common cause of dementia is a neurodegenerative disease, including Alzheimer’s disease and Parkinson’s disease. Interestingly, many mutations responsible for these neurological disorders have been identified in endosome-related genes. However, how endosome dysfunction can lead to the progression of these diseases has not been well characterized. Endosomes are specialized compartments for sorting membrane proteins. They utilize distinct molecular machinery, ESCRT and retromer, to determine the fate of membrane proteins, degradation or recycling. However, my recent work revealed the involvement of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) in endosomal sorting and a novel recycling pathway, which indicate endosome membrane dynamics are much more complex than previously thought. As a principal investigator, I will utilize multidisciplinary approaches to define the molecular mechanism of previously unappreciated endosomal membrane dynamics. I will specifically ask how ER contributes to endosomal sorting (Aim 1), how the activity of the endosomal coat complex is spatially and temporally regulated during vesicle formation (Aim 2), and how the endosomal recycling pathway is linked to Alzheimer’s disease (Aim 3). Since these aims focus on specific genes responsible for neurodegeneration, my ultimate goal is the identification of critical molecular mechanisms that can be therapeutically manipulated to treat these diseases.
kw: Neurodegeneration; Alzheimer's disease; Endosome; Membrane remodeling; Yeast

title: iNvestigation of wAve aTtenUation over mangRoves and sEagrass (NATURE)
inst: TCOMS - Technology Centre for Offshore & Marine Singapore
abs: The NATURE proposal aims to deepen our understanding of the potentials of mangroves and seagrass meadows in protecting our coastlines. The main objective is to characterise the functional baselines and the effectiveness of mangroves and seagrass meadows in attenuating wave energy and contributing to sediment accumulation through combinations of prototype-scale physical experiments and numerical simulations. Characterising the effectiveness of these nature-based solutions is an area of active research. Field measurements are conducted to obtain detailed flow characteristics over vegetation, especially in extreme conditions, but these are limited due to the challenges to operate under such scenarios and uncertainties associated with the field environments. Physical experiments are proposed as an alternative. However, most of the studies were conducted at reduced-scale in wave and current flumes. Because wave attenuation and energy dissipation are scale-dependent, there are uncertainties in interpreting the results obtained from reduced-scale experiments and in whether they are truly representative of the field conditions. Prototype-scale experiments in TCOMS Ocean Basin facilities are proposed to bridge the gap and address the uncertainties. The outcomes from physical experiments will be fed into numerical modelling and simulations to assess how we can further enhance the effectiveness using solutions that can be adopted or adapted into contemporary Singapore’s coastal and marine ecosystem, and to formulate engineering design guidelines that can assist industry and government agencies to design technically sound and economically viable nature-based solutions.
kw: wave attenuation; mangroves; seagrass meadows; drag coefficient; sediment accumulation; climate change

title: Solution-based Synthesis and Assembly of Large-Area Complex 2D van Der Waals Heterostructure Composites for Large-Scale and Low-Cost Optoelectronic Devices
abs: Since the advent of graphene, two-dimensional (2D) crystals, ranging from semiconducting to superconducting materials have captured the imagination of many to enable new applications. As the field advances beyond understanding the monolayer physics, increasing interests shift towards heterogeneous combination of these materials in the form of van Der Waals heterostructures (vdWH) to engineer material functionality beyond what can be achieved in bulk crystalline heterostructures. However, current “grow-and-transfer” approaches, with mechanical layer transfer of chemical vapor deposition (CVD) grown 2D sheets are still far from enabling complex heterostructures at large-area scale due to the mechanical fragility of current “pick-and-place” stacking methods. Hence, the exploration of large-area complex vdWH to manipulate electronic and photonic interactions are largely precluded. Solution-synthesized and deposited 2D films, albeit discontinuous, overcome the fundamental issue of large-area assembly on wafers. Such techniques may show great potential to achieve low-cost low-temperature deposition conformal to sub-micron-sized topographical features, allowing for integration ease with advanced semiconductor technologies. Moreover, judicious mixing of the 2D nanosheets by size, type, or order allow for novel vdWH composites not achievable by “grow-and-transfer” methods. However, there are technological gaps that detract the precise control of film morphology; due to the uniformity of synthesized flake dimensions and large-area composite film assembly. There is also poor understanding of the defect, electronic, and optical properties due to the intrinsic discontinuities of the vdWH flake network. Here, we propose the development of a high-yield with enhanced flake uniformity solution synthesis method for large-area deposition. The method enables complex vdWH composites that allow us to investigate electronic and light-matter interactions for novel opto-electronics functionalities. Our approach is organized in 3 work packages as follows: (1) Develop gas-assisted exfoliation combined with a cascaded centrifuge separation method to improve the monodispersity of 2D materials (I.e., MoS2, WSe2, h-BN and graphene) dispersions, increasing the uniformity in shape, size and electronic purity. (2) Improve the film uniformity by developing spatially controlled assembly of vdWH with surface functionalization to enhance large plane-to-plane alignment. (3) Implement physical-charge-based characterization (atomic force microscopy) with detailed modelling of percolation transport and light-matter interaction study with time-resolved photoluminescence (TRPL) and continuum full-band quantum transport models for the vdWH films.
kw: 2D materials, van Der Waals Heterostructure, Optoelectronic Devices, Semiconductors

title: Discovering large and unconventional spin Hall effect materials by high-throughput computations, symmetry analysis, and experiments
abs: Technology will be the key driver of the future world economy. Some major technological challenges can be solved by clever engineering; others cannot because of fundamental limitations. Conventional computers store much of their information using electric charge, but these memories are volatile, and miniaturizing components - to build laptops with high memory capacity - increases their power consumption. Information can be more stably encoded magnetically, using the spin (analogous to charge) of electrons to bypass the fundamental limitations, in a form of electronics known as spintronics. To avoid applying external magnetic fields in devices, modern spintronic technology requires all-electric control of magnetization with low energy consumption. An emerging technology, spin-orbit torque (SOT), enables the field-free manipulation of spintronics devices via the charge-to-spin current conversion. While SOT holds promise for applications in magnetic random-access memory (MRAM), until today, it has been limited to the low efficiency of charge-to-spin conversion, resulting in high power consumption of devices. New technology requires new materials. In trial and effort, several materials and their spin Hall effect (SHE) have been experimentally studied for high conversion efficiency of charge-to-spin current, such as metals, oxides, topological materials, 2D materials. Unfortunately, most of them have low spin Hall angle (θ_SH) as shown in Table I. Note that θ_SH is a figure of merit of charge-to-spin conversion, which is given by the ratio of the spin Hall conductivity to the charge conductivity. Clearly, such a trial-and-error method for finding highly efficient SHE materials is highly impracticable because there are around 0.3 million real crystals that have already been experimentally characterized and stored in Inorganic Crystal Structure Database (ICSD), and around 12,000 new materials are synthesized and added in this database every year. In contrast, previous work on (AI-aided) high-throughput computation suggests that large-scale screening is in principle much more straightforward. It is because simulation with proper models will greatly reduce the experimental effort in trial and error, as well as narrow down the scope for experimental exploration. An additional advantage of high-throughput calculations is that they can provide further insight into the physics of SHE and suggest general guidelines for designing SHE materials and SOT devices. The aim of this project is to find nonmagnetic materials with high spin Hall conductivity ( >1000 ((ℏ)⁄e)(S⁄cm)), large spin Hall angle ( >0.4) and unconventional out-of-plane SHE from ~0.3 million crystals in ICSD. Since all these materials have been synthesized experimentally before, this project/platform is to revisit “old” materials for discovering “new” properties. Thus, the chance to re-synthesize the SHE material candidates is high. In this project, we will fully develop high-throughput algorithms

title: Quantum energetics beyond ideal conditions: role of strong coupling, external noise and finite size baths
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: Recent years have seen significant advances in the modelling and experimental realization of thermodynamic devices for the control and conversion of energy transport. In particular, there have been proposals for diodes of the size of a few atoms with remarkable rectifying properties, and realizations of single atom engines. Various approximations are typically done in the modelling of these systems, and the experimental realizations also are performed in ideal conditions. With this proposal we aim to go beyond these ideal/proof-of-concept scenarios so as to bridge the gap with future realizations in devices. We are going to focus on few atom diodes, transistors and engines and we are going to consider non-ideal scenarios for the system (dephasing noise), for the baths (finite size) and for their coupling (strong coupling).
kw: Quantum thermodynamics, quantum transport, many-body quantum systems, pure state statistical mechanics

title: High-frequency exploration of twist-controlled moiré structures: from interaction effects to quantum geometry
abs: Strongly interacting electronic systems with unusual band topology have recently emerged as a candidate to search for new states of matter as well as the foundation for novel quantum devices. Heterostructures composed of novel low-dimensional materials offer a unique setting in which to experimentally realize and study such systems in a controlled manner. In such materials, all atoms are available for interaction with the adjacent layer, making it possible to fine-tune their electronic properties without changing chemical composition, by stacking different atomically thin crystals, using electrical gates, and changing the relative orientation between their crystallographic axes. The latter has been especially impactful as it led to the discovery of various phenomena governed by an interplay between interactions, quantum geometry, and band topology in twist-controlled moiré structures (TCMS) such as twisted bilayer graphene, superlattices based on rhombohedral graphene, twisted graphene multilayers, and more. While previous experiments have illuminated many features of TCMS, full comprehension of interaction-, quantum geometry- and topology-driven quantum effects in TCMS remains difficult. For example, the problem of the superconducting state genesis, its quantum geometric origin, and the nature of phase transitions in twisted graphene multilayers call for extensive exploration. Not only does the resolution of these problems require the knowledge of the normal state characteristics such as bands dispersion, effective mass, and Fermi velocity that, at low twist angles, is hard to determine using conventional approaches, but it has also proven challenging to access them in standard transport experiments. Also, the existence of sound-like collective modes in electron fluids (e-fluids) hosted by TCMS and their entrainment by the current flow has remained largely unexplored. Moreover, understanding electron-electron and electron-phonon interactions in TCMS has proven challenging. Finally, it has been scarcely realized that TCMS offer new opportunities to develop practical devices. In particular, the response of TCMS to external electromagnetic fields can be engineered on demand through the control over their underlying symmetry and quantum geometry that, in turn, can be exploited for the development of alternative principles of terahertz detectors where conventional devices perform poorly. We propose to address these challenges through a novel multi-messenger approach involving radiation-driven magnetotransport experiments on high-quality TCMS spanning across the sub-THz and THz frequency domains. In our program, we target to explore THz photoresponse of various TCMS to reveal the role of interactions (i) and quantum geometry (ii) in electron transport. We will probe the single-particle effective mass of charge carriers and phase transitions using THz-driven magneto-absorption experiments (iii) and characterize collective modes in e-fluids hosted by TC

abs:

Stochastic computing is one candidate, which can accelerate the solution of various practical problems such as combinatorial optimizations, resource allocation, image processing, and tour planning. title: Toward Ubiquitous 3D Perception and Recognition via Generation and Adaptation of Point Cloud Data
abs: Different approaches have been explored for mitigating the data constraint in 2D deep computer vision research via image synthesis, unsupervised learning, transfer learning, few-shot learning, etc. As a comparison, 3D point cloud is facing much more severe data constraint, but the point cloud data problem is far under-explored. In this project, we will investigate point cloud collection and adaptation problem, one very fundamental challenge in the deep learning and the prevalent point cloud research where the lack of large-scale point-wise annotated point cloud data has hindered related deep learning research and the exploitation of point clouds in various visual perception and recognition tasks. We will address the point cloud data problem via three approaches: 1) point cloud generation that derives large-scale point-wise annotated point clouds via synthesis in virtual scenes and stereo reconstruction from annotated 2D videos; 2) point cloud transfer that adapts synthetic or previously collected point clouds for handling various unannotated new point cloud data; 3) weakly supervised learning that learns strong point cloud models from a tiny amount of annotated new data and a large amount of unannotated new data. Our preliminary studies (published in AAAI 2022 and NeurIPS 2022) has shown that point cloud synthesis and point cloud adaptation have great potential to mitigate the point cloud collection and annotation challenge. The proposed research will leverage our prior studies and open a new door for a long list of point cloud related deep learning research, and it will greatly mitigate the data constraint while exploring deep learning and point clouds in various visual perception and recognition tasks.
kw: Lidar point clouds, point cloud synthesis and generation, photogrammetry, unsupervised domain adaptation, domain generalization, weakly supervised learning

title: Monitoring Indonesian Democracy with High-Frequency Data
abs: Amid both a global democratic recession and heightened regional geopolitical instability, Indonesia will hold its fifth presidential election since the fall of Suharto in 1998. The election will be the single largest same-day voting event in human history. Against this backdrop, we propose to conduct 56 weekly online public opinion surveys—comprising over 80,000 unique interviews—in the buildup and aftermath of the 2024 Indonesian elections to monitor and study the health of its democracy. As both a validation and an experimental exercise, we will supplement these weekly surveys with a monthly longitudinal survey tracking the same 1,500 respondents over an identical time frame. Our proposal constitutes the largest coordinated scholarly effort to capture the evolving attitudes of the Indonesian public. The chief virtue of our approach is its scale: by collecting high-frequency data on synchronized questions over an unusually wide time frame, we will be positioned to conduct fine-grained analyses to understand the drivers of political attitudes in the world’s third most populous democracy. But we are principally motivated by questions of substantive and theoretical interest of social scientists and policymakers alike. Given the scope of our project, we register eight hypotheses across five thematic areas: (1) democratic consolidation, (2) identity politics and polarization, (3) misinformation, (4) external and foreign policy events, (5) civil-military relations. We anticipate three core outputs from this initiative. First, for social scientists broadly, our proposed data collection and analyses will shed light on the real-time causes and consequences to questions of broad interest, including how political polarization, identity politics, and democratic consolidation evolve in response to the dynamic and unexpected events that unfold over the course of a political campaign. Second, for policymakers, we anticipate that the data we collect will reveal important insights into how the public responds to salient foreign and domestic events. Included in our proposal is an initiative to conduct “data learning” days in which we hope to encourage a data-driven perspective on Indonesia’s political discourse by inviting policymakers, journalists, and researchers to learn how to analyze the data we collect. Finally, third, we hope that the ambition of our initiative will draw in interested external collaborators from top institutions around the world to help establish NUS as a global hub for the data-driven study of Asian politics.
kw: Indonesia, Democracy, Data Science, Public Opinion, Identity, Misinformation

title: Developing methods to reduce functional loss in Transplant kidney: using non-invasive Shear Wave Elastography as a predictive tool
abs: Background: Kidney transplant (KTX) interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy (IFTA) is the end-result of many injurious processes afflicting KTX, associated with poor KTX survival. IFTA can only be diagnosed via invasive biopsy and if severe, may not be amenable to intervention. Two-dimensional (2D) ultrasound shear-wave elastography (SWE), a non-invasive diagnostic tool, has been shown to be useful in detecting liver fibrosis, and has the potential revolutionise the diagnosis of KTX fibrosis. Hypothesis: SWE can detect early KTX fibrosis and can be used in the surveillance of KTX along with traditional ultrasound imaging and eGFR biomarker to monitor longitudinal changes in KTX for improving KTX outcome. Aims: This study aims to identify a threshold for diagnosing fibrosis based on SWE measurements. Based on longitudinal temporal SWE changes, transplant patients will be triaged by monitoring SWE as a surrogate for KTX fibrosis, and differential changes of fibrosis to reduce eGFR drop off by 20% in 100 patients. Methodology: This study will include 4 stages: 1) Obtaining the optimal threshold and validating across multicentre (SGH + NUHS) 2) Determining the correlation of quantitative values of SWE with clinical biomarkers and the permutations of kidney transplant pathology biomarkers known as BANFF lesion scores 3) Evaluate the possible factors affecting errors in SWE measurement and variability between the different vendor technology 4) Evaluate the cost-effectiveness in adopting SWE screening on interval US examinations in the care of KTX compared with non-screening KTX Clinical Significance: SWE has the potential to be used as a non-invasive screening and diagnostic tool for the evaluation of kidney allograft dysfunction. SWE diagnostic cut-offs and accuracy for KTX fibrosis will be determined and compared against gold-standard biopsy. This will be invaluable to reduce the rate of invasive biopsy and reduce risk of graft loss.
kw: Ultrasound; Elastography; Transplant; Kidney

title: The role of Setd3 in regulation of B cell activation and differentiation
abs: Previously, we proposed a potential cytosolic function for histone lysine methyltransferase (HKMT) EZH2 in receptor-stimulated polymerization of actin (1). Our recent report further demonstrates that EZH2 regulates adhesion dynamics and migration of leukocytes through direct methylation of the extra-nuclear protein, Talin1 (1,2). EZH2-mediated methylation of Talin1, a key regulatory molecule in cell adhesion, disrupts Talin1 binding to F-actin and thereby promotes adhesion turnover and cell migration (2-4). It is likely that cytosolic methylation plays a more important role than initially expected in cytosolic signaling cascades. With this in mind, we identified Setd3, a HKMT and critical regulator of muscle differentiation, predominately localized to cytoplasmic compartment of various immune cells, including B cells. Our data revealed that Setd3 protein level was upregulated upon BCR stimulation likely due to inhibition of GSK3ꞵ-regulated proteasome-dependent degradation6. However, in vitro activation of B cells via anti-IgM F(ab’)2 antibody stimulation was not affected by Setd3 deficiency. Interestingly, in vivo immune response against sheep red blood cell (SRBC) or NP14-Chicken Gamma Globulin (NP14-CGG), was significantly compromised. To further characterize the function of Setd3 protein in B cell immunity, we propose three complementary Specific Aims, which will make use of biochemical and proteomic approaches, in vitro culture systems and in vivo conditional knockout mouse models. References: (1) Su, I. et al. Polycomb group protein Ezh2 controls actin polymerization and cell signaling. Cell 121, 425-436 (2005). (2) Gunawan, M. et al. The methyltransferase Ezh2 controls cell adhesion and migration through direct methylation of the extranuclear regulatory protein talin. Nature Immunology 16, 505-516 (2015). (3) Loh, J.T. et al. Ezh2 Controls Skin Tolerance through Distinct Mechanisms in Different Subsets of Skin Dendritic Cells. iScience 10, 23-39 (2018). (4) Lim, T.J.F. & Su, I.H. Talin1 Methylation Is Required for Neutrophil Infiltration and Lipopolysaccharide-Induced Lethality. J Immunol 201, 3651-3661 (2018).

title: Personalized and Global Context-aware Sequence Recommendation
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: This project studies the problem of sequence recommendation by considering the perspective of both the individual user as the consumer of the item/service and the POI operator as the producer. Many existing work focuses on either personalised recommendation from the individual user perspective or the overall fair allocation of resources from the entire population perspective. However, there has been a lack of work that examines both personalisation and fairness as a joint problem, which is a complex task due to the two potentially contrasting objectives. In this project, we address this limitation by the following approaches. Firstly, we introduce a novel problem formulation that jointly models both personalised recommendation from the individual perspective and fair allocation from the global perspective, in the context of both item and sequence recommendation. Secondly, we will develop models that consider heterogeneous features, such as spatial-temporal dependencies and user-related information holistically, and use this integrated knowledge to jointly optimise for individual preferences and overall fairness. This involves a non-trivial development of deep learning models that incorporate these different aspects. Thirdly, we will develop a joint model for personalised and fair itinerary recommendations by using a multi-head attention transformer to personalise recommendations to user interest preferences and design an over-demand cut policy and under-demand add policy to ensure fair POI allocations. Lastly, we will collect and curate various datasets of user trajectory patterns in the form of POI visit histories across different locations. These datasets will be useful for general research in item recommendation and sequence recommendation, and both advance and provide a common benchmark for future research in this general area.
kw: Recommendation Systems; Personalisation; Sequence Recommendation; Itinerary Planning

title:
A transcriptional repressor orchestrates secondary cell wall formation and seed
shattering
abs: Fruits are important in human diets, nutrition, and health. Fruit dehiscence (seed shattering) is a natural process that negatively impacts seed harvesting and yield in crops. The global demand for food is escalating quickly. Improving seed or crop yield is vital because simply expanding food crop acreages would significantly increase problems associated with environmental contamination and depletion of natural resources, such as land and water. Hence, to produce more nutritious and resilient crops with improved yield, we need to improve our understanding of the regulatory mechanisms controlling fruit developmental process. However, such exploration is by no means trivial in the absence of a detailed scientific framework regarding the transcriptional regulation of plant fruit development. An attractive approach is by characterizing essential regulators (e.g. transcriptional factors) that modulate fruit and seed development and subsequently use these regulators to improve desired agronomic traits. Here, we propose to determine the function of a newly identified transcriptional factor, ZFP2, involved in mediating fruit development and secondary cell wall (SCW) biosynthesis. Our preliminary studies found that ZFP2 is predominantly expressed in silique valves and plays a role in regulating expression of genes involved in SCW biosynthesis. We found that ZFP2 functions as a transcriptional repressor and its loss-of-function mutants exhibit increased expression of several key genes for fruit SCW biosynthesis in Arabidopsis. In silico analysis indicated that ZFP2 contains multiple intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs). It is known that IDRs and multivalent interactions are important for liquid-liquid phase separation. Protein phase separation is vital for gene regulations and various cellular processes. Protein phase separation has only recently been demonstrated in plant cells, thus becoming an emerging topic in plant science. Our preliminary evidence suggested that ZFP2 can form nuclear puncta (resembling phase separation) in planta. We believe that ZFP2 is a key regulatory hub that responses to upstream signals (e.g., phytohormones) and regulates downstream regulatory or structural genes. We obtained evidence that ZFP2 is induced by the phytohormone auxin and directly activates another transcription factor, NST1 which is known to regulate silique development. However, the detailed regulatory roles of ZFP2 remains inefficiently understood. Even less known is the interacting networks of ZFP2 at the protein or gene levels. Therefore, we propose the following specific aims: 1) Identification of the essential protein motif responsible for ZFP2 repression, 2) Detailed analyses of Arabidopsis silique phenotypes of ZFP2-knockout and inducible overexpression lines, 3) Exploration of ZFP2 phase separation and establishment of ZFP2 interactome, 4) Generation of a gene expression atlas of Arabidopsis silique valves. title: Nonlinear Integrated Optics: Creating, manipulating and harnessing classical and topological modes of light.
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: The fundamental driving force behind Photonics, the study of light stems from its unparalleled speed of three hundred million meters per second. On this basis, enormous amounts of information are constantly transmitted through fiber optic networks, without which the internet would not function as it does today. Light may also influence the properties of the propagation medium, introducing a nonlinear component to its refractive index. First discovered as an absorptive phenomena in 1931, nonlinear optics evolved slowly through the 1900s, making accelerated progress only when the Ruby laser was invented. Thereafter, nonlinear optics underwent significant progress, with studies focusing on bulk crystals such as KTP, BBO and LiNbO3, followed by significant work in optical fiber starting in the 1980s, largely fueled by the discovery that optical fiber modes provide an intensity scaling of the light interacting with the silica material. Thereafter, a whole suite of nonlinear optical phenomena leveraging the augmented nonlinear interactions availed in fibers vs. crystals were demonstrated, including soliton formation, nonlinear wave mixing, Brillouin and Raman scattering, eventually expanding to cover applications in all-optical switches, Raman amplifiers and soliton-based data transmission. A salient development in optics was the ability to easily create on-chip, photonic waveguides, thus heralding the birth of the field of nonlinear integrated optics. Photonic waveguide devices manufacturable using electronics infrastructure receive special attention for their integrability with application specific integrated circuits. We have developed photonic platforms and waveguides which augment the nonlinearity by six orders of magnitude over optical fiber, greatly facilitating the observation and applications of nonlinear optical phenomena, while being compatible with electronics manufacturing. Consequently, our work in nonlinear optics aims to operate in a regime requiring far lower power, availing the observation of nonlinear effects not possible in either bulk crystals or optical fiber. Nonlinear optical device classes encompassing novel on-chip soliton states and their use in slow light, optical buffers and light storage, parametric processes towards but not limited to high gain amplification, ultrafast information processing and light generation using both resonant and non-resonant phenomena. In addition, beyond classical modes of light, our project aims to study nonlinear optical phenomena in the context of topological modes of light, leveraging the rich underlying physics brought photonic analogues of topological insulators, interactions of such systems with nonlinear perturbations and how these may then be harnessed for new classes of photonic switches, modulators, light sources and optical information processors. title: Delineating long-term implications of climate change on endemic and emerging vector-borne disease transmission in Singapore
abs: Many mosquito-borne diseases are increasing in incidence and geographical distribution, reinvading into areas once previously eradicated and emerging in new regions due to climate change. This proposal takes Singapore as the study setting as well as fine-scale climate change projections to: (1) understanding long-term environmental and anthropogenic drivers of major mosquito vectors (2) understanding the implications of climate change on endemic and emerging mosquito-borne disease transmission and (3) understanding the resultant economic impacts of endemic and emerging mosquito-borne diseases conditional on different climate change scenarios. This will be done by building (A) integrated process-based models to project future mosquito abundance (B) spatially-explicit, climate driven vector-borne models (C) economic costing framework which nests estimates from A and B. The successful execution of this proposal will provide the first integrated baseline study on the long-term implications of climate change on the burdens of hyperendemic and emerging mosquito-borne diseases in Singapore.
kw: Mosquito-borne diseases; climate change; long-term burden; high-dimensional modelling; high-resolution spatial modelling

title: Temporal-Spatial Impact Analysis of Climate Changes on Renewable Energy and Load Demands
abs: Climate changes can significantly affect the availability of renewable energy power supply and the temporal-geospatial behaviours of power energy demands. This project aims to develop new temporal-geospatially models and perform advanced analysis for analysing technical, economic, and social impacts of climate changes on renewable energy production and user-specific energy consumption patterns in Singapore context. The temporal-geospatial models will simulate the interaction between climate changes, renewable energy resources, and energy demands, taking into consideration of dynamic aspects of local climates, renewable energy technology advancements, consumer behaviour, and market mechanisms. Specifically, the project will examine the effects of climate change on the availability and stability of renewable energy sources in South East Asia, including the impacts of extreme weather events and changes in wind and solar patterns, as well as load patterns and criticality. Additionally, the project will investigate the influences of climate change on different user energy demand in Singapore, including changes in energy usage patterns and energy efficiency. Furthermore, the project will analyse the risks of extreme scenarios and uncertainties for robust decision-making, which considers potential flooding, hurricanes, drought, different emissions scenarios and global energy policies. This multi-disciplinary research will provide valuable insights into the complex relationships between climate change, renewable energy, and energy demand for supporting energy security and sustainability in the face of a changing climate. The specific research outcomes can be applied by government agencies (such as Energy Market Authority), renewable power plant investors (such as generation companies), and power utilities (such as SP Group) for decision-making support in overseas power import project investment, planning, and power grid expansion, etc.
kw: Climate-resilient Singapore, energy systems, climate changes, temporal-geospatial modeling, uncertainties

title: Estimating future mortality and morbidity from the exacerbation of chronic diseases across different climate change scenarios
abs: Climate change is harming chronic health in all populations via additional heat-related stress. Singapore is expected to face a chronic health crisis that is exacerbated by increasing heatwave incidence where maximum daily temperatures could potentially go up to 40°C by 2045. Multiple studies globally have shown that ongoing and future heatwave events have and will further increase both chronic disease burdens and the number of Emergency Department (ED) visits for acute myocardial infarctions (AMI), chronic kidney diseases (CKD) and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). The degree of impact for Singapore’s population health however remain largely unknown. This study therefore seeks to (1) Project population level AMI, CKD and COPD incidence and prevalence until 2100 via an agent-based model where relative risk of an individual’s trajectory of developing or worsening disease, or the occurrence of acute events, are determined by using applied conditional logistic regressions which ascertain the role of the sociodemographics, comorbidities and environmental geospatial exposures, (2) Estimate the population-at-risk, DALYs, YLLs, of disease complications, as a function of both the number and severity of future extreme heat events projected to occur from SINGV-based V3 climate projection data, and literature estimates and statistical relationships observed in national cohorts of the relative risk of complications occurring during or post extreme heat events, (3) Estimate the excess number of past ED admissions attributed to extreme heat events for a wide set of chronic diseases and conditions with associated societal costs, and carry out projections based on observed trends and expected climatic changes, (4) Assess the savings in DALYs and YLLs of a heat health warning system which advises patients-at-risk of having complications from aforementioned diseases to stay indoors and not be exposed to additional risk of complications from extreme heat events.
