title: Multi-scale impacts of climate change on tropical forest dynamics in Singapore
abs: Anthropogenic climate change will have a profound impact on both the diversity and functioning of tropical forest ecosystems globally. Long-term changes in precipitation and temperature, as well as the frequency of extreme weather events (e.g., strong winds, drought) have already begun to influence tropical forest dynamics. In Amazonian and African tropical forests, changes in the frequency and magnitude of drought have driven increases in tree mortality and diminished their role as carbon sinks. Changes in climate are also projected to lead to substantial losses in climatically suitable habitat for a wide range of species. In Singapore, however, the effects of climate change on forest ecosystems remain poorly understood, due to the prevalent secondary and disturbed nature of much of the vegetation and the relative dearth of plant functional studies locally and regionally. Here, we propose a research program that will evaluate the impact of climate change on Singapore’s tropical forests at a range of ecological scales, by combining insights from i) the experimental and functional characterisation of demographic responses in a wide range of locally occurring tree species, ii) dynamic ecosystem models that can evaluate changes in demographic parameters and disturbance regimes on stand level attributes such as functional composition, biomass and stem density, and iii) species distribution models that can evaluate the long-term extinction risk of species. Our findings will have significant implications for nature-based climate policy, sustainable ecosystem management / restoration and biodiversity protection of tropical forests in the region, at a crucial time when the effects of biodiversity loss and climate change are intensifying.
kw: Forest demography, forest simulation models, tree mortality, plant functional traits, environmental suitability modelling

title: Harnessing Big Data to Plan a Climate-Resilient Food Bowl for Singapore
abs: The proposed research project aims to create a data-driven framework to enhance the resilience of Singapore’s food system against the impacts of climate change and attain its goal of meeting 30% of its nutritional needs through local food production by 2030. This will be achieved by improving the understanding of direct and indirect impacts of climate shocks on the food supply. With a focus on vegetables, palm oil, and fish, the two main objectives of the project are to: (1) determine the physical risks posed by climate shocks to major agriculture and aquaculture regions of import and their direct impact on food security, and (2) understand how climate shocks cause indirect disruptions to the food supply chains through changes in trade and infrastructure dependencies. The proposed approach and methodology for the project are built on publicly available data of climate, food production/yield, trade, and critical infrastructure. The project will not rely on economic modelling assumptions and will instead learn directly using a novel approach that dynamically links climate shocks, crop/fish production, food trade, and infrastructure systems models in a single framework. This approach aims to overcome limitations in current research by considering the dynamic interplay of these factors and accurately representing the network structure and spatial dependencies of infrastructure. The hypothesis of the project is that a data-driven framework incorporating climate, food production/yield, trade, and infrastructure data can provide a comprehensive understanding of the impacts of climate shocks on food system resilience and support decision-making to enhance the resilience of the food supply. The proposed methodology will involve compiling and analyzing granular data to meet the objectives of the project.
kw: food security and resilience, climate shocks, crop production, aquaculture, supply chain, critical infrastructure

title: The Climate Resilience and Threshold of Trees in Singapore
abs: Trees provide critical ecosystem services (e.g., carbon sequestration, urban cooling, biodiversity conservation) to mitigate global climate change. With future increases in the frequency and intensity of climate perturbations (i.e., heat wave, water stress), however, these critical services are increasingly likely to be interrupted. Such interruption is most prominent for tropical trees, including those in Singapore, as tropical trees are reported to already function outside their optimal climate space and are losing climate resilience to perturbations. To guide tree planting and preservation for a climate-resilient Singapore, it is important to understand the climate resilience and threshold of trees nationwide. However, tree-level resilience is largely elusive not only for Singapore but also for other parts of the world, as previous studies often focus on ecosystem-scale resilience and lack examinations of tree-level processes. Here, we propose to use a combination of a novel automatic tree health monitoring system, satellite remote sensing and controlled experiments to quantify the resilience and threshold of trees in Singapore. We aim to identify the main biotic (e.g., species, stand age, height) and climatic factors that determine the spatial-temporal variations in resilience and threshold of multiple tree health indicators (i.e., photosynthesis, transpiration, biomass growth and canopy structure). We plan to use a large amount of tree-level observations (i.e., long-term monitoring of 300 trees during the project) to develop a machine learning model for resilience and threshold predictions. By applying the high-resolution climate outputs from the Third National Climate Change Study (V3) to the machine learning model, we will quantify the climate resilience and threshold of any trees at any time up to 2100 in Singapore. Using resilience loss as an early warning signal, we can identify the hotspots and time range for potential tree mortalities in Singapore under various climate scenarios.

title: Developing a risk assessment and communication platform to translate climate projections to policy
abs: The Third National Climate Change Study (V3) for Singapore projects changes in climate variables under three Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5) and allows for a detailed understanding of the future impacts of climate change. In principle, detailed projections should enable policymakers and other stakeholders to plan for a comprehensive set of scenarios and develop effective mitigation and adaptation strategies. In reality, translating climate projections to policy remains a significant challenge for two main reasons. First, climate change projections are characterised by complex human-ecological interdependencies and a relatively high degree of uncertainty. Second, the psychological distance to climate change makes it difficult to communicate the severity of future climate impacts. We will make two significant contributions to overcome the barriers to effective translation of climate projections to policy. First, we will ascertain the solution space for climate adaptation and mitigation policy and identify potential cases of maladaptation by translating projected downscaled climate impacts in Singapore into a risk assessment framework. We do this by examining climate-driven impacts, identifying and assessing human-ecological compounded and cascading risks, and modelling changing risk profiles from different SSP scenarios. By developing a risk assessment framework, policymakers and other stakeholders will be able to navigate the complexity and uncertainty inherent in climate projections. Second, we will develop a platform that operationalizes and communicates the risk assessment framework through immersive virtual reality narratives. This approach will reduce the psychological distance to climate change and make the future impacts of climate change, along with the solution space, highly salient to policymakers and other stakeholders. We will develop proof-of-concept immersive virtual narratives to demonstrate and evaluate the effectiveness of our risk assessment and communication platform as a tool for translating climate projections to policy.

title: Towards Reliable, Data Efficient, and Privacy-Preserving 3D Human Digitization
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: 3D human digitization, which aims to create the 3D virtual human (e.g., 3D mesh of the body/hand) based on visual data (e.g., RGB images), plays an important role in a wide range of applications, such as mixed reality (MR), virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), and film/game production. More recently, there has been a further surge in interest in 3D human digitization due to the enormous potential displayed by the Metaverse, of which human digitization is a crucial component. However, existing computer vision (CV) techniques face challenges that limit their utility in practical applications. Specifically, there still exist important challenges that need to be addressed: 1) To facilitate more application scenarios (e.g., AR/MR/Metaverse applications), especially the in-the-wild scenarios, instead of using restrictive configurations (e.g., relying on multi-view systems or depth sensors), the paradigm of 3D human digitization from a single RGB image attracted much attention recently, since single RGB images are much easier to be obtained. However, accurately constructing 3D human models from single-view 2D images is highly challenging due to the inherent depth ambiguity and potential occlusion. Moreover, in some scenarios, we need to create 3D human models for multiple people in the same scene. To provide timely response, it is important to develop multi-person digitization models that are able to accurately digitize all people in one shot, instead of separately performing digitization for each person. 2) A lot of annotated data (e.g., images with corresponding 3D meshes) is often required to train 3D human digitization models. However, the cost of collecting such annotated data (image-3D mesh pairs) in the wild can be potentially overwhelming. 3) There exist security (privacy) concerns with current 3D human digitization methods when involved in AR/MR/Metaverse applications, since some applications tackle vision tasks by sending captured human images to servers/cloud for processing, bringing privacy issues. This project aims to handle several crucial challenges to effectively improve vision techniques for monocular 3D human digitization in the wild. We will develop new methods that improve 1) prediction accuracy in terms of both single-person and multi-person digitization, 2) labour efficiency involved in collecting and annotating data, and 3) security of the human digitization model. In this project, we will create novel techniques involving diffusion models, characteristic functions, and meta-learning, introducing new insights and expanding upon the current collective understanding. Moreover, we will investigate domain adaptation, data efficiency, and privacy concerns of human digitization, which are important research problems. By working on these aspects, our project shall make significant contributions to the research field and real-world applications involving AR/VR/MR techniques, Metaverse and human-robot interaction.

title: Neurosymbolic AI for Commonsense-based Question Answering in Multiple Domains
abs: (1) We propose a multi-layer commonsense knowledge base under the hypothesis that commonsense reasoning could depend on a concise core of concepts. To our best knowledge, this is the first work incorporating the idea of conceptual primitives into a general-purpose commonsense knowledge base to provide a generalizable, effective representation of commonsense knowledge for AI tasks. (2) We construct a novel commonsense knowledge base based on conceptual primitives, named ProtoNet. It contains approximately 488K nodes and 1M relations, covering entities in the domains, e.g., manufacturing, medical science, natural science, and social science. Despite being smaller than widely used public knowledge bases designed to convey commonsense knowledge, our ProtoNet advances them in terms of generalizability, semantic similarity and analogy. (3) We develop a QA system to exploit ProtoNet, supporting explainable AI research communities in different domains to leverage commonsense reasoning efficiently and effectively. The QA system allows humans to access the analogical process of ProtoNet, so that the decision-making of machines can be interpreted by humans in natural language.

title: Exploring visual signal representation towards machine uses
abs: In this new AI era, big visual data is from everywhere at anytime. More and more machines are replacing humans and acting as the final users of massive visual data to perform visual analysis and decision-making in more and more scenarios. Therefore there is an urgent call (like the recent Call for Proposal by MPEG Video Coding for Machine (VCM) workgroup, JPEG AI workgroup, etc.) for a new scheme of comprehensive visual signal representation to address the said new requirements, i.e., to cater for the needs of the deep machine vision (DMV), effectively and efficiently, and to end the existing separation of visual intelligence (such as image classification, object detection, instance segmentation, pose estimation, image retrieval, and image captioning; and the list can go on and on) and visual signal representation (including pre-processing, compression, transmission, decompression and post-processing). The team has performed some pioneering work exploring the feasibility of visual signal representation for machine uses; there has not been systematic investigation toward a comprehensive scheme for visual representation toward machine uses yet. To be more specific, aiming at a new scheme of visual signal representation of machine uses based upon a systematic investigation on the emerging requirements in the new AI era, the proposed project is among the first attempts in this area internationally. The represented visual data should be able to facilitate deep-learning-based visual machine intelligence tasks. In this new scheme to be devised, deep visual features are regarded as the new coding base. In particular, we will explore along the following directions: feature-level just-noticeable difference (JND) modelling for machines to facilitate different aspects of the proposed scheme; formulation of the new scheme to enable massive visual signal representation with deep-learnt visual features; exploration of visual feature extraction, selection, pre-processing (filtering), transmission and optimization for the proposed scheme; a novel feature codec for machine uses; possibilities of international standardization of the resultant technology. We expect the proposed scheme to be a catalyst for a wider revolutionary shift to make visual data representation for serving visual intelligence better in terms of edge computing/collaboration, representation accuracy, integration of signal representation and visual intelligence, signal transmission and storage, flexible system configuration, computational load distribution, privacy preservation, system resources, and energy saving, and so on. Due to the fundamental nature of the proposed scheme, the scopes of meaningful application scenarios include but are not limited to connected vehicles, intelligent traffic/security control, smart visual surveillance, health monitoring and care, and many other smart-city building related functionalities. title: MXene-Enabled Jaumann Absorbers
abs: 1. Goal and Specific Aims The overarching project goal is to study the mechanisms of electromagnetic (EM) absorption in MXene, and then develop MXene-based Jaumann absorber for EM absorption in C to Ku band that are crucial for civilian and military applications, and of great interest (for Radar application) to our industrial partner Thales. Our specific aims include (1) MXene-based functional component design and fabrication, (2) resonant EM absorber design, and (3) fabrication of MXene-based resonant EM absorbers. 2. Hypothesis EM absorption of MXene is largely underexploited to date; let alone MXene-base resonant EM absorbers. Superior to graphene, MXene has metal atom terminated surfaces, endowing it rich surface chemistry. Surface functionalization can thus readily change the properties of MXene in a wide range from insulator to metal and from nonmagnetic to magnetic, leading to tunable response to EM waves from completely lossless to highly lossy. Herein, we propose to increase EM absorption of MXene via atomic level functionalization of MXene to leverage both electric and magnetic losses. Both permittivity and permeability will be modified by amending its surface dipoles and intercalating agents. Then, the functional materials will be employed to construct resonant EM absorbers. 3. Academic Significance and Innovation Innovation: Surface atoms of nanomaterials are advantageous for EM wave absorption compared to their bulk counterpart because under-coordinated surface atoms are easy to be engineered with various surface dipoles since they are chemically active. 2D nanomaterials are particularly promising for EM absorption owing to their layered structure to maximize the interaction between surface dipoles and EM wave. Graphene is a great candidate for EM interference shielding owing to its high conductivity; however, its inert carbon surface is difficult to engineer. To this end, graphene-like MXene is more promising due to its reactive surface arising from its metal dangling bonds. We have developed various functionalization processes for MXene to control its surface dipoles systematically in order to vary its conductivity, work function, and magnetic properties. To date, there is no report on thin Jaumann absorber which have high absorption and broad bandwidth using MXene or other nanoparticles. The team’s capacity of controlling MXene properties and rich experience in theoretical design/modelling offer us the opportunity to make printable thin EM absorber with lightweight, efficient, and broadband absorption. EM absorbers with wide frequency bands near the transmit / receive antenna or around sensitive components can absorb undesired surface waves, which is critical for automotive industry. title: Identifying math learning difficulties with video-evoked brain activity
abs: Aims and Objectives The proposed project addresses Challenge Statement 1 of leveraging Science of Learning to ensure that children are well prepared and ready to learn when they are enrolled in school. Here, we aim to combine state-of-the-art neuroimaging – educational video evoked brain activity – and machine learning approaches to identify children who may be at risk of mathematical learning difficulties (MLD) as early as Kindergarten Year 2 (K2) rather than adopting a wait-to-fail approach in the first half of Primary 1, thus justifying the importance of our project as well as the novelty of our proposed techniques. Beyond identifying this group of students, we also aim to level up students who may face difficulties in learning mathematics in Primary 1 and even informally before Primary 1 by focusing on a core skill that has been shown to be predictive of later mathematical success – place-value understanding, even if it is an approximate one (i.e., knowing that 63 is larger than 36 without a full understanding of tens and ones). Aim 1 (what): To compare the concurrent performance of resting-state brain networks (specifically, functional connectivity between regions) and educational video-evoked brain networks in identifying risk of MLD in Primary 1 children. Aim 2 (when): To validate the predictive models developed in Aim 1 with brain scan data from an independent cohort of children acquired before formal schooling. Can the brain scans in K2 can allow us to successfully predict with good sensitivity and specificity whether a child will be identified as having risk of MLD later in Primary 1? Aim 3 (why): To explain why the brain features in Aims 1 and 2 may be predictive of MLD risk with numeracy, literacy and cognitive variables, as well as environmental and demographics variables. Methodology This project proposes complementary cross-sectional and longitudinal designs, each with an independent cohort of children. To address Aim 1, we will recruit Primary 1 children with MLD (N = 50) and without MLD (N = 50) (Cohort 1). We will acquire both resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and video-evoked fMRI to compare their relative efficacies in predicting the concurrent group membership of MLD status. To address Aim 2, we will acquire both resting-state fMRI and video fMRI from Kindergarten 2 children with risk of MLD (N = 50) and without risk of MLD (N = 50), and follow them up to Primary 1 a year later (Cohort 2). To address Aim 3, we will collect from both Cohorts 1 and 2 a comprehensive battery of numeracy (e.g., numeral reading, numerical magnitude comparison, numeral ordering), literacy (e.g., phonological awareness), cognitive (e.g., language skills, executive functions), environmental (e.g., home literacy and home numeracy) and demographic (e.g., ethnicity, socioeconomic status) variables. The co-PI has access to these students based on his existing network and research agreements with these schools. Novelty Our project

title: Health Technology Assessment of Population Oral Health Strategies
abs: Aim: The key aim of the study is to develop, deliver and evaluate the cost-effectiveness of technology-enabled programmes to enable individuals and communities to improve their oral health. Hypotheses: The hypotheses are: (1) Tele-screening for oral diseases using the store-and-forward method is effective and cost-effective in improving population oral health as compared to in-person examinations. (2) Key drivers of the cost-effectiveness of digital oral health strategies include effective design and patient compliance. (3) Digital health solutions are effective in reducing oral disease burdens and the cost of care, and are cost-effective across developed countries. Methodology/ Approach/ Feasibility: The study will develop a protocol for image capture, image transfer, image processing and assessment. Intraoral images will be captured by community partners and caregivers using mobile phone cameras, and transmitted via a store-and-forward method to clinicians based remotely. The effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of tele-screening to detect oral disease in the population using intraoral images, compared to in-person intraoral screening will be evaluated in a sample of 250 children. The study will also assess the cost-effectiveness of digitally-enabled initiatives tracking caries risk assessments and assessments of dietary habits, oral hygiene practices, oral health status, healthcare utilisation patterns, and oral health-related quality of life over time, including through a pilot mHealth intervention. Finally, the cost-effectiveness of digital oral health promotion initiatives will be compared across countries, using data from trials in Singapore and UK. Decision tree and Markov modelling will be carried out to compare the cost-effectiveness of digital oral health initiatives. Significance: Digital oral health interventions have great potential for scalability, and can reduce manpower costs and resources required for in-person screening and examinations. The assessment of factors that influence the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of digital health interventions can enhance the utility of these interventions in improving oral health on a population-wide scale.

title: Investigating Therapeutic Targets in Parkinson's disease
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Background: Parkinson’s disease (PD) is a common neurodegenerative disorder. Leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) mutations cause both autosomal dominant and sporadic PD, with a common recurrent mutation accounting for 30-40% of sporadic PD cases in some races, and Asian specific common coding variants have been found to increase PD risk. Identifying physiological substrates of LRRK2 will provide vital leads in identifying new drug targets. Objectives: We have identified an autophagy regulator as a novel LRRK2 interactor. Leveraging on this discovery, we aim to determine the physiological significance of its interaction with LRRK2, identify the downstream pathways that are involved using transgenic animal and human organoid models that we will develop. We will test a monoclonal antibody targeting the phosphosite of the interactor and drug inhibitors we have identified in the in vivo models. Methods: The effects of the interaction between LRRK2 and the autophagic protein and its effects on downstream biological pathways will be examined using mammalian and human models (mouse and human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs)/organoids). Phenotype (including behaviour and motor functions), biochemical and immunohistochemistry studies will be carried out. We will test the therapeutic efficacy of a customised monoclonal antibody that we have developed, and also specific inhibitors that target the autophagic protein we have identified (from a screen of 12 000 compounds) in the mice and human models. Rescue of neuronal death and improvement of motor and non-motor functions will be demonstrated using different techniques in the various PD models. Conclusion: Our proposed study will unravel novel pathophysiologic clues and can potentially lead to identification of biomarkers and new therapeutic targets that may help better monitor Parkinson’s disease and provide curative treatment.

title:
Granzyme B-Targeting PET as a Predictive Imaging Biomarker of Cancer
Immunotherapy Treatment Response
abs: Cancer immunotherapy (CIT) harnesses the immune system for effective and durable tumour control. However, response rates remain variable and treatment is often associated with significant adverse effects. One major challenge with correct triaging of patients into responders and non-responders is that CIT stimulates immune infiltration of tumours, causing paradoxical apparent disease worsening on conventional imaging which is indifferentiable from true disease progression until further follow-up. Consequently, non-responders suffer unnecessary costs, side effects and delay of more appropriate treatments, while responders prematurely stop effective treatment. Granzyme B (GZB) is a key downstream effector of CIT-mediated cancer kill. By GZB-targeted imaging (GZB-PET), we can perform non-invasive, whole-body, per-lesion quantification of GZB as a direct and specific marker of CIT activity, to accurately predict CIT response. Our prototype probe (GZPGEN1) has been designed to target GZB successfully. We hypothesise that further specific modifications to GZPGEN1 will enhance its in vivo performance, and thereby diagnostic efficacy of CIT response. We aim to design our next-generation advanced probe (GZPGEN2) with improved stability and pharmacokinetics while preserving GZB-specific binding. We will confirm its improved properties in vivo preclinically, and validate its predictive value in patients. Firstly, we will generate candidate peptides using in silico and rational drug design techniques for in vitro testing. Secondly, we will image GZPGEN2 against GZPGEN1 in syngeneic mouse models to compare in vivo stability, pharmacokinetics and targeting; and perform ex vivo biodistribution and tissue immunoprofiling for GZB and immune correlations. Thirdly, we will evaluate the diagnostic efficacy of GZPGEN2-PET in patients on CIT by correlation with disease outcomes. This proposal is supported by GZPGEN1 preclinical pilot data, and a multidisciplinary team with complementary skillsets and resources. If validated, GZB-PET will allow more effective and safer use of CIT, and potentially be applied to other GZB-based therapies against viruses or autoimmune diseases.

title: Enhancing Perioperative Cardiovascular Risk Predictions with Static and Dynamic Physiological Data and Interpretable Deep Learning - A study with smart wearable devices.
abs: Accurate perioperative evaluation is essential to optimize patient outcomes and streamline clinical workflows. However, current clinical decision-making processes rely on manual assessments and static guidelines, leading to inefficiencies and variability in care. To address these limitations, this study aims to develop and evaluate PEACH (PErioperative AI CHatbot), a specialized AI-driven Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS). PEACH integrates large language models (LLMs) with institutional perioperative protocols to generate accurate, evidence-based recommendations tailored to real-world clinical workflows. By leveraging AI-driven natural language processing, PEACH seeks to enhance decision-making, improve documentation efficiency, and ensure guideline adherence. The study will be conducted in two phases. Firstly, PEACH will undergo development and refinement using institutional perioperative guidelines and clinician feedback. Secondly, a randomized, cross-over trial in a perioperative evaluation clinic will assess PEACH’s accuracy, operational efficiency, and user acceptance. Quantitative metrics, including concordance with expert recommendations, documentation time, and hallucination rates, will be evaluated, complemented by qualitative user feedback. This study has the potential to transform perioperative clinical workflows by reducing decision-making time, minimizing errors, and improving standardization of care. The integration of AI-driven CDSS in perioperative settings represents a significant advancement, facilitating scalable AI adoption across healthcare disciplines. By demonstrating PEACH’s effectiveness, this research will provide a blueprint for AI-driven innovations, ultimately enhancing patient care and healthcare resource optimization. Key concepts: - Efficient perioperative decision-making is crucial for optimizing patient outcomes and reducing clinical inefficiencies. - Current manual assessments are time-consuming and prone to variability. - AI-driven clinical decision support systems can enhance perioperative workflows. - Integrating LLMs with institutional protocols ensures accurate and tailored recommendations. - AI-powered solutions like PEACH may improve healthcare scalability and cost-effectiveness.

title: A Greener, Healthier Future for Our Children: Pioneering Sustainable Paediatric Practice Through Implementation Science
abs: Climate change poses a substantial threat to global health, and healthcare itself contributes to a significant portion of carbon emissions. Children, who bear the bulk of disease burden from climate change, are particularly vulnerable. Paediatrics, being a critical area of child health, holds enormous potential for sustainable healthcare solutions. This research proposal aims to address the implementation gap in integrating sustainable, low-carbon practices in paediatric care through rigorous implementation science methodologies. The project seeks to reduce the environmental footprint of paediatric healthcare while optimizing patient outcomes through exploring evidence-based interventions. Specific aims include: (1) Investigating the carbon footprint of pressured metered dose inhalers (pMDIs) in paediatric practice; (2) Developing and identifying low-carbon interventions in paediatric care, particularly asthma and bronchiolitis, to mitigate carbon emissions while improving patient care; (3) Evaluating the feasibility and effectiveness of implementing sustainable inhaler prescribing in paediatric healthcare settings; and (4) Developing evidence-based implementation strategies to facilitate the adoption of sustainable inhaler prescribing in paediatrics. The research will involve a systematic review of relevant literature, qualitative studies through interviews and focus group discussions with key stakeholders and assessing patient outcome and environmental footprint assessments. Intervention development and implementation strategy identification will be tailored to the paediatric setting using implementation science frameworks. A pilot implementation of the intervention will be conducted, and feasibility will be assessed using a quasi-experimental mixed-methods design, with iterative enhancements made before broader implementation. In summary, this novel project aims to foster the integration of environmental sustainability within paediatric practice through rigorous implementation science methodologies. By identifying and developing evidence-based interventions, developing strong context-specific implementation strategies, and holistically evaluating the impact of low-carbon practices, a model for greener and higher-value paediatric healthcare is possible.

title: Navigating Charge Separation at Designer Conjugated Polymer/Perovskite Nanocrystal Interface
abs: In stark contrast to conventional organic ligand-capped counterparts, the ability to create stable metal halide perovskite nanocrystals (PNCs) strongly tethered with conjugated polymers (CPs) represents an important endeavor towards tailoring charge carrier dynamics at their interface that critically underpins applications of this unique class of all semiconducting, organic-inorganic nanomaterials for optoelectronics. This, however, has yet to be largely explored. In this context, the objectives of this proposal are to (a) develop a general and robust platform for crafting an array of uniform PNCs intimately and permanently ligated with CPs of different compositions and molecular weights (i.e., CP-ligated PNCs), (b) scrutinize their optoelectronic properties and stabilities that are dependent upon the structural parameters of CPs and the size of PNCs, and (c) explore their utilities for photo-induced living radical polymerization. A series of polythiophene (PT) derivatives with distinct structural parameters and cesium lead bromide (CsPbBr3) will be selected as model CPs and PNC, respectively, where the structural parameters of CPs (i.e., composition of side chains, MW of PT, grafting density of PT chains on the surface of PNC, and chain conformation) and the diameter of CsPbBr3 NCs will be systematically varied. Intellectual Merit: The intellectual merit of the proposed research is manifested in (i) the ability to craft a host of PT-ligated CsPbBr3 NCs with precisely controlled size of NCs and readily tailorable compositions of side chains, chain length, grafting density, and chain conformation of PTs, (ii) investigation into the dependence of optoelectronic properties (in particular, energy level alignment and charge carrier separation at the PT/CsPbBr3 NC interface) as well as stabilities of PT-ligated CsPbBr3 NCs on the PT structural parameters and the size of CsPbBr3 NCs, and (iii) development of high-performance photocatalysts for p-ATRP enabled by PT-ligated CsPbBr3 NCs of optimized optoelectronic properties and stabilities. The central hypothesis of this research is that the use of amphiphilic star-like block copolymers composed of inner hydrophilic PAA blocks and outer hydrophobic CP blocks as nanoreactors provides a robust platform for creating monodisperse PNCs of varied diameters directly and stably ligated with CPs of readily tunable compositions, MWs and grafting densities, thereby affording unique opportunities to examine the synthesis-structure-property relationship of PT-ligated CsPbBr3 NCs. Such fundamental knowledge derived from the success of the proposed project will in turn render their appealing utilities in photo-induced polymerization via directly exploiting solar energy through a charge/energy transfer process from PT to CsPbBr3 NC for the synthesis of polymers of interest under mild reaction conditions. title: Electrochemical Bicarbonate Conversion to Formate: A Promising Approach towards Capture and Conversion of CO2
abs: Carbon-based fuels and precursors are foundational to the growth of modern society, yet there is a critical lack of industrially scalable approaches to recover and valorise carbon dioxide (CO2) into useful chemical fuels and feedstocks. The development of these industrially scalable approaches is vital because global net negative CO2 emissions are required to limit CO2-driven climate change to less than 1.5°C. Hence, there is tremendous interest in developing new technologies to capture and convert CO2 and its equivalents to valuable chemical fuels and precursors. One such promising technology is electrochemical bicarbonate reduction, which is paired with CO2 capture. For this pairing, CO2 can be captured using wet scrubbing with an alkaline absorbent (such as sodium hydroxide) to form bicarbonate (HCO3-) from CO2. Subsequently, bicarbonate can undergo an electrochemical reduction reaction to value-added products such as formate. This paring is a promising route towards developing scalable technologies for integrated CO2 capture and conversion. This process can be powered by renewable energy sources, operate at ambient temperature, and scale to smaller CO2 emission sources. However, the current record report for bicarbonate reduction Faradaic efficiency is only 64% at 100 mA/cm2 and < 50% for more commercially relevant current densities >150 mA/cm2. Moreover, the record energy efficiency is < 10% at ≥400 mA/cm2 for electricity to formate, and solar to formate efficiency is yet to be reported. Here, further developments and innovation are urgently needed to enable scalability. To address these challenges, this proposal develops new platforms and materials to convert bicarbonate to formate using electrocatalysis and unveils the relevant reaction mechanisms. Overall, in terms of scope and scientific merit, this proposal combines (1) catalyst materials development to improve activity, faradaic efficiency, and energy efficiency, (2) mechanism investigation, and (3) solar-driven platform development to maximize energy efficiency. In terms of broader impacts, this research is crucial to unlocking our global CO2 capture and utilization strategy and is aligned with the objectives of RIE 2025. Thus, this program consists of three innovative and interdisciplinary specific aims that will inform each other: 1. This proposal will develop new state-of-the-art materials for the conversion of bicarbonate to formate with increased activity. This effort will establish new records for faradic efficiency compared to the previous state-of-the-art, metallic bismuth. Our preliminary studies support the feasibility of this aim. 2. This proposal will investigate the mechanism of the electrochemical conversion of bicarbonate to formate via in operando Raman spectroscopy. Currently, the mechanism for the electrochemical conversion of bicarbonate to formate has not been proven. title: Controlling Solid-Electrolyte-Interphase for High-Performance Anode-Free Sodium Batteries
abs: The rapid development of electronic devices and vehicles is essential to Singapore due to the gradual consumption of fossil fuels and the increasing environmental issues. However, the low abundance of lithium (Li) resources in the earth’s crust (0.0017 wt%) makes the state-of-the-art Li batteries increasingly expensive. Compared to Li, sodium (Na) displays similar chemical and physical properties, and most importantly, ~1400 times higher natural abundance of Na resources in the earth (2.3 wt%). Hence, Na batteries have been attracting tremendous attention to supplement Li batteries in the field of massive-scale energy storage. Carbon anode-based Na batteries has been successfully commercialized in 2021, however, the low capacity of carbon anode (~ 300 mAh g-1) limits the energy density below 160 Wh Kg-1, much lower than that of commercial Li counterparts. Comparatively, Na metal anode reveals great advantages over carbon anode due to its high theoretical capacity (1166 mAh g−1) and low redox potential (−2.71 V vs SHE). However, due to the soft and sticky properties of metallic Na, it is very challenging to produce the ultra-thin Na metal anode via mechanical rolling. Sodium metal batteries (SMBs) with thick anodes that contain excess Na can sacrifice energy density. Another issue is the poor air stability of Na metal (even in dry room conditions), which greatly hinder the large-scale manufacture of SMBs. The anode-free sodium batteries can increase the energy density via avoiding fabricating ultra-thin Na metal anode and reducing the usage of excessive Na. In anode-free sodium batteries, the ‘real anode’ is the electrochemically deposited Na on the current collector during the charging process with active Na+ shuttling completely from cathode materials. However, during the charging process, the anode side suffers from an uneven deposition of Na, which can cause serious Na dendrite growth problem and the failure of the anode-free sodium batteries. Besides, the developed porosity and instability of organic solid-electrolyte-interphase (SEI) components can lead to the continuous consumption of active Na, which will accelerate the battery capacity decay. Therefore, it is of great necessity to construct a stable and rigid SEI on the deposited Na metal surface via adjusting electrolyte compositions, which is a fundamental and cost-effective method to alleviate the Na dendrite growth and increase the usage efficiency of active Na. Adding electrolyte additive is effective to fabricate rigid and stable SEI on the deposited Na via modulating the solvation structure of solvated Na+. In this proposal, XPS and cryo-TEM will be adopted to characterize and understand the nucleation sites, lattice ordering, nanostructures of SEI, and interface between SEI and metallic Na, which will be beneficial for the fundamental perception and rational design of efficient SEI. title: Scalable computation and model misspecification in highly structured statistical models
abs: Modern applications of statistics and machine learning involve datasets which are both large and high-dimensional. Latent variable models having observation-specific parameters are commonly used for structured modelling of complex datasets, and this project considers new Bayesian methods for specifying and computing with such models. The contribution of the proposed work is in three aspects; computational methods, modified Bayesian inference methods in the presence of model misspecification, and the modelling of complex dependence in high dimensions. In terms of computation for Bayesian inference, we will consider approximate but scalable variational inference methods which are attractive when conventional exact Monte Carlo methods such as Markov chain Monte Carlo are impractical. An interesting recent innovation in the variational inference literature is the development of variational boosting methods which approximate a Bayesian posterior distribution with a Gaussian mixture, where mixture components are added one at a time to an existing approximation. The modular boosting approach simplifies optimization, and facilitates an attractive computation/accuracy trade-off where the sequential process of adding new components can be terminated once a fixed computational budget has been used up. Two challenges in the application of variational boosting methods are the development of better optimization methods, and the development of boosting steps which exploit conditional independence structure in the model specification. In terms of the optimization, we will consider natural gradient methods for the optimization which reflect the underlying geometry of the space of approximating distributions, and which are not sensitive to the often arbitrary way that the approximating variational family for the posterior distribution is parametrized. We will consider new natural gradient methods for variational boosting with mixtures. Current boosting methods also do not respect conditional independence structure in the true posterior distribution in the approximations, and we will extend current variational boosting approaches by making them more modular in terms of the boosting components being able to improve certain components in a hierarchical decomposition of the true posterior density. We also consider flexible variational approximations in cases where some model components may be misspecified, and where it is desired to limit influence of possibly misspecified model terms on inferences while still propagating uncertainty. One method for dealing with misspecified components in complex structured Bayesian models is called “cutting feedback”, and this approach applies when models are constructed from a collection of interacting modules representing different aspects of the data. title: ProExpan: Proactive Ontology Expansion for Conversational Agents
abs: One major scourge of current conversational agents developed is the huge performance gap between training conversation models using static corpus and serving end users in a dynamic environment. Models trained on fixed training datasets often fail easily in practical application scenarios. Existing methods for the fundamental task of conversation understanding rely heavily on training slot-filling models with a predefined ontology. For example, given an utterance such as “book a table for two persons in Blu Kouzina,” the models classify it into one of the predetermined intents book-table, predict specific values such as “two persons” and “Blu Kouzina” to fill predefined slots number_of_people and restaurant_name, respectively. The agent’s inherent conversation ontology comprises these intents, slots, and corresponding values. When end users say things outside of the predefined ontology, the agent tends to misunderstand the utterance and may cause critical errors. The aim of this project is to investigate how conversational agents can proactively detect new intents, values, and slots, and expand their conversation ontology on the go to handle unseen situations better during deployment. This project has three primary research objectives: (1) detecting new intents or values within existing slot ontologies (e.g., a new check-vaccination-status intent or a new "TAI ER" value for the restaurant_name slot for the same restaurant booking assistant after 2019), (2) automatically discovering new slots to enrich existing ontologies (e.g., vaccination_status and ART_results), and (3) integrating these new discoveries into an interactive expansion process that allows the agent to actively select uncertain cases and leverage a limited amount of human guidance during deployment. To accomplish these aims, our hypothesis is that conversational agents can acquire these abilities through training with deep learning models and algorithms. To test this hypothesis, we propose the following methods. (1) We will develop a deep learning model based on large pretrained language models to detect out-of-vocabulary values and new intents. This model will employ a comprehensive understanding of utterances and incorporate world knowledge to handle inconsistent conversation context across different levels of granularity. (2) We will design an adversarial semantic perturbation mechanism and explore a semi-supervised clustering algorithm to leverage existing ontology by propagating knowledge from known slots to unknown slots. This method aims to capture the inherent variation of slot values and handle unknown numbers of new slots. (3) During deployment, there will be situations where new values or slots appear. title: Machine Learning Force Field–assisted Computational Framework for Molecular Crystals and Van der Walls Heterostructures
abs: Accurate and fast calculation of phonon dispersions is indispensable for understanding the various phenomena in materials science. However, the phonon calculations for molecular crystals and two-dimensional (2D) van der Waals (vdW) heterostructures, where the non-local vdW interaction plays an important role, are very expensive, leaving many properties and various spectrums unexplained. The proposed research aims to develop a machine learning force field (MLFF) assisted computational framework for phonon calculation of molecular crystals and 2D vdW semiconducting heterostructures. There are two methods for phonon calculation: the density functional theory (DFT) and molecular dynamics (MD). DFT is considered an accurate method for phonon calculation, but the O(N4) (N is the number of atoms in the system) scaling, strong functional dependence, and incomplete consideration of various interactions limit its application in complex systems. On the contrary, the MD method can be easily employed for phonon calculations of complex systems, like molecular crystals, vdW heterostructures, or even biological materials. However, the accuracy of MD calculation cannot be guaranteed since the key factor in the MD method, force field (FF) potentials, are generated from intuition or experience. Fortunately, the DFT and MD methods can compensate for each other with the link of the newly developed machine learning (ML) method. The basic idea of the ML method is to extract the key features of the targeted problem by learning from the existing results (supervised) or training new calculations (unsupervised). In particular, the gaussian approximation potential (GAP) based MLFF method targets the generation of FF potentials for molecular dynamics. Our preliminary investigation shows that the MLFF has much better behavior than the general DFT methods. In our phonon calculation framework developed in this proposal, the FF potential can be generated with the ML method by learning from a highly accurate DFT or even many-body calculations with the non-local vdW interaction fully considered, and such force field potential can be employed in the MD calculation for phonon dispersions. The whole procedure will be capsuled into an automatic module based on an atomic simulation environment, with a full test and benchmark for auto-generation of the hyperfine parameters and the cut-off radius for multi-body kernel for molecular crystals and 2D-vdW semiconducting heterostructures. title: Connections between Automata Theory, Computational Complexity and Recursion Theory
abs: The grant aims to investigate various aspects of interplay between automata theory, computational complexity and recursion theory in the following four areas: I. Automatic complexity. This field is motivated from the search for a complexity measure which is on one hand similar to Kolmogorov complexity and on the other hand feasible, that is, based on finite automata. Shallit and Kjos-Hanssen with various coauthors have pioneered this area. Their research has left open several important questions which are to be addressed within the framework of this grant. First, whether the two common versions to define automatic complexity based on nondeterministic finite automata are different. Second, whether there is a linear bound q n + q’ with q < 1 for the automatic complexity using deterministic finite automata of all strings of length n. Third (and this question is more accessible than the others), given a rational q between 0 and ½, what abstract properties does the set of all words x of automatic complexity below q times length(x) have, for example, what is its level in the Chomsky hierarchy and what is the circuit complexity of a circuit computing it (which is well defined for the binary alphabet and needs some tweaking for larger alphabets). Kjos-Hanssen corresponded with the investigators on these questions and is willing to work with them on this research; he has for all questions preliminary published results. Furthermore recent work of the investigators touched the notion of unambiguous automata and their properties discovered in recent research recommends the usage of these as an alternative to an nfa and dfa for defining automatic complexity; the investigators would also like to look into this new direction. II. The investigators have with local coauthors in Singapore studied the impact of the choice of primitive steps in machines on complexity notions. Their recent finding allowed new characterisations of the polynomial hierarchy using alternating computations. The investigators seek to extend these studies and are in particular interested how the notions of primitive steps between Presburger arithmetic and full arithmetic influence the characterisations of complexity classes using the corresponding machines. Furthermore, they seek to refine the notions of alternating computations for being able to characterise complexity classes which are not closed under complement. III. The investigators furthermore seek for special representations of the natural numbers where + is automatic but equality and order might only be semiautomatic; their goal is to take the additive monoid of k-tuples of natural numbers and let each tuple represent the sum of its components. Preliminary unpublished explorations for this project showed that this approach is promising and allows to represent more sets than the usual automatic representations of natural numbers with automatic addition and equality. title: Meta-Learning for Fast-Adaptive Control of Aerial Robotic Systems
abs: Air taxis, cargo delivery aircraft, and other revolutionary new aircraft are emerging to form the future urban air mobility (UAM) system. Autonomous aerial robots such as delivery drones are being gradually integrated into the airspace to increase the connectivity and sustainability of cities. However, the existing aerial robotic systems still fall short of the stringent safety requirements needed for UAM integration. To improve safety and achieve enhanced autonomy, it is imperative to develop more intelligent aerial robots that are robust and fast-adaptive to dynamic and complex environments. Control system theory and techniques have been the powerhouse behind robotic applications to enable key autonomies such as localization and navigation, path planning, trajectory tracking, control, etc. However, conventional control techniques suffer from modeling complexity and conservative controller structures. They are typically tuned to excel at controlling a single task in a relatively isolated environment but lack the advanced autonomy of fast adaptation to dynamic environments. On the other hand, deep neural networks (DNN) based machine learning achieved state-of-the-art artificial intelligence (AI), which has great potential to enhance robot autonomy. This project proposes to combine deep learning and control techniques to develop novel planning and control algorithms that are expected to achieve the best of both worlds. We draw inspiration from meta-learning research to learn high-level DNN policies that orchestrate the low-level optimal control algorithms to perform adaptively and robustly. Overarchingly, our goal is to develop a general meta-learning control framework that seamlessly fuses high-level AI with low-level optimal control to empower more intelligent aerial robots. We pursue four specific aims under the proposed framework, which are focused on the estimation, planning, control, and team cooperation of aerial robots, respectively. These aims represent the cutting-edge challenges in aerial robot research. Our first aim is to develop a fast-adaptive neural moving horizon estimator (NeuroMHE) that estimates various disturbances for robust flight control against challenging adversarial environments and abrupt flight condition changes. We plan to utilize DNN to parameterize the weighting matrices in MHE such that it can estimate the disturbances optimally and achieve robust and accurate trajectory tracking. We plan to train the DNN hyperparameters in a particular way such that rapid online adaptation is promoted. To this end, we plan to develop efficient algorithms to differentiate through NeuroMHE for backpropagation training. This shall seamlessly embed the MHE policy in the DNN for joint training. Our preliminary studies developed a recursive implicit differentiation of MHE, we plan to further develop more efficient gradient descent algorithms. title: Structural and Functional Analysis of a Lysosomal Phospholipid Transporter
abs: The lysosome is central to the degradation of proteins, carbohydrates and lipids and their salvage back to the cytosol for reutilization. The myriad forms of lysosomal storage diseases highlight the crucial role that catabolism and export of lysosomal macromolecules play in cell and organ functions and the importance in elucidating transport pathways for understanding lysosomal storage diseases. Lysosomal transporters for amino acids, sugars and cholesterol have been identified, and the metabolic fates of these molecules in the cytoplasm have been elucidated. Remarkably, it is not known whether lysosomal salvage exists for glycerophospholipids, the major constituents of cellular membranes. In this grant proposal we utilized a transport assay screen against orphan lysosomal transporters to identify the Major Facilitator Superfamily protein Spns1 that is ubiquitously expressed in all tissues, as a proton-dependent lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC) and -ethanolamine (LPE) transporter. LPC and LPE are the lysosomal breakdown products of the most abundant eukaryotic phospholipids, phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylethanolamine, respectively. Spns1 deficiency in cells, zebrafish embryos, and mouse liver resulted in lysosomal accumulation of LPC and LPE species with pathological consequences on lysosomal function. Patients with loss-of-function mutations in SPNS1 present with very similar liver pathologies as seen with mouse Spns1 deficiency. Flux analysis using stable isotope-labeled phospholipid apoE-nanodiscs targeted to lysosomes showed that LPC was transported out of lysosomes in a Spns1-dependent manner and re-esterified back into the cytoplasmic pools of phosphatidylcholine. Our findings identify a phospholipid salvage pathway from lysosomes to the cytosol that is dependent on Spns1 and critical for maintaining normal lysosomal function. However, the mechanistic basis of Spns1 LPC/LPE transport and its physiological function in phospholipid salvage and lysosomal function remain to be determined. Built on strong preliminary data coupled with success in solving the structure and physiological functions of Mfsd2a, a sodium-dependent LPC transporter that we discovered, this proposal will focus on elucidating the structure and physiological function of Spns1 through the following two specific aims: 1) To determine the mechanism of LPC transport by Spns1 and 2) to determine the physiological role of Spns1-mediated lysosomal transport of LPC/LPE. In our opinion, this proposal is innovative because it aims to elucidate the biochemical and structural basis of this newly discovered phospholipid lysosomal salvage pathway utilizing novel biochemical approaches and animal models. The fundamental information generated in this research program is expected to provide mechanistic understanding of how lysolipids are transported across membranes by Spns1 and the roles of the Spns1 pathway in physiology.
kw: lysosome; metabolism; transporters; phospholipid

title: Self-regulatory mechanism of ADAR1 and its implication in cancer immunity
abs: Although there has been a tremendous progress in the field of cancer immunotherapy, most patients still do not respond to immunotherapy or develop resistance. Unfortunately, there are currently no effective options to overcome this acquired therapeutic resistance. Researchers have recently discovered that inhibiting adenosine deaminase acting on RNA 1 (ADAR1) could stimulate production of interferons (IFNs) and other pro-inflammatory cytokines to induce immune responses intrinsically (particularly in immunologically ‘cold’ tumours). More importantly, ADAR1 was characterized as an inhibitory checkpoint and inhibiting its expression overcomes resistance to PD-1 immune checkpoint blockade therapy. ADAR1 is a primary RNA editing enzyme catalysing adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) RNA editing of double-stranded RNA (dsRNA), which marks endogenous RNAs as ‘self’. Loss of ADAR1 triggers excessive RNA sensing and IFN production. Such regulation establishes the role of ADAR1 as an immune protector/repressor to regulate self-tolerance to endogenous RNA ligands. As such, inhibition of ADAR1 (either alone or in combination with immunotherapies that have limited efficacies) becomes an attractive therapeutic approach, though clinical ADAR1 inhibitors have yet to be developed. The race for developing ADAR1 inhibitors is a current ongoing priority. My team has recently uncovered a novel self-regulatory mechanism of ADAR1 by which ADAR1 positively regulates expression of its canonical forms (ADAR1-p110 and p150) by repressing intron 13 (In13) retention, which would otherwise produce two truncated ADAR1 protein variants (herein referred as p90 or p130) that are devoid of a significant portion of the functional catalytic deaminase domain. We hypothesize that two truncated variants, which are repressed by canonical ADAR1 isoforms in multiple cancer types, may function as editing-incapable dominant negative variants that not only trigger immune response intrinsically to overcome ADAR1-mediated immune suppression in tumours, but also sensitize tumour cells to immunotherapies. In this study, we will first delineate the mechanisms of how ADAR1 and other splicing regulatory proteins that participate in regulating intron 13 (In13) removal and then characterize the functional role of truncated variants p90 and p130 in vitro and in vivo. Lastly, we will restore the expression of p90/p130 isoforms in tumours using splice-switching oligonucleotides (SSOs) and observe the immune activation and the inhibition of tumour growth. We hope to develop novel strategies for overcoming patient’s unresponsiveness and resistance to immunotherapies.
kw: ADAR1, cancer immunity, intron retention, splice-switching oligonucleotides

title: Characterization of the molecular and physiological roles of Mfsd7b as a transporter for choline
abs: MFSD7b belongs to the Major Facilitator Superfamily (MFS) of transporters that transport small molecules. Two isoforms of MFSD7b have been identified and they are reported to be heme exporters that play a crucial role in maintaining the cytosolic and mitochondrial heme levels, respectively. Global knockout mice of Mfsd7b is embryonically lethal due to multiple defects such as haemorrhages, edema, and whole body maldevelopment. Conditional knockout of Mfsd7b using Mx1Cre also exhibited anemia due to a block in progenitor cells’ proliferation. Mutations of MFSD7b (also known as FLVCR1) has been reported in patients with symptoms of retinitis pigmentosa (RP), posterior column ataxia with RP (PCARP), and hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy (HSAN). Although Mfsd7b functions have been linked to heme detoxification by exporting excess heme from erythroid cells, it is ubiquitously expressed with a high level in the gastrointestinal tract, lungs, liver, and brain. By analyzing gene expression during erythropoiesis, we found that the expression pattern of Mfsd7b is similar to that of the genes in the lipid biosynthesis pathway. Mfsd7b expression is negatively correlated with the genes in the heme biogenesis pathway. These observations suggest that Mfsd7b plays additional roles beside heme export function. In this proposal, we plan to test whether Mfsd7b also transports choline, an essential molecule, mainly used for phospholipid synthesis. The overarching goals are to understand the mechanisms by which cellular substances are transported by different membrane transporters. The long-term goals are to harness the roles of these membrane transporters for treatment of diseases. The broad objective here, is to reveal the additional molecular and physiological roles of Mfsd7b besides its reported role as a heme transporter. Our central hypothesis is that Mfsd7b transports choline as a ligand independent from heme export function. The rationale for the proposed research is that revealing the main molecular functions of Mfsd7b will inform us basis of the disease mechanisms due to Mfsd7b mutations. Although Mfsd7b is ubiquitously expressed and the missense mutations of Mfsd7b cause several unrelated diseases, we focus to understand its roles in the blood vessels using cell-based and mouse models. The Significance of this study is that we will reveal an uncharacterized function of Mfsd7b and gain insights into this new role and the pathogenesis of the diseases caused by the mutations of the gene that has left uncharacterized. This study may also generate new knowledge about the important roles of Mfsd7b and its ligands for the integrity of the blood vessels.
kw: Mfsd7b, Choline, Phospholipids, MFS Transporters, Retinitis Pigmentosa (RP), Posterior Column Ataxia with Retinitis Pigmentosa (PCARP), and Hereditary Sensory and Autonomic Neuropathy (HSAN)

title: Biogeography, functional ecology, and resilience of photosynthetic microbial communities under extreme environmental stress
abs: Photosynthetic microbial communities are important because they underpin the food webs of many environments. They are increasingly facing multiple and simultaneous environmental challenges (poly-extreme stress) due to anthropogenic forcing, yet surprisingly little is known about how they may respond to increasingly poly-extreme conditions. Hot springs photosynthetic microbial mats offer a highly tractable natural poly-extreme model system with large environmental gradients that enable clear measurement of dose-response relationships. They are well suited to testing hypotheses related to biogeography under poly-extreme stress due to their island-like and readily characterized habitats, and their functional ecology under environmental stress has broad application for informing future response in other terrestrial and marine photosynthetic microbial communities facing increasing environmental stress. Singapore lies at the foot of an extensive geological fault system extending ~3,000km through Southeast Asia that supports geochemically diverse poly-extreme hot spring habitats, and we propose their use as a large-scale natural model in this study. The research will employ a combined multi-omics and ecophysiology approach to interrogate the ecology of hot spring microbial mats along an unprecedented scale of geographic and geochemical variation. The findings will provide novel insight on how microbial communities assemble and function under stress, and their response to disturbance. The aims and outcomes of the study are: 1) Apply metagenomic and genome-resolved phylogeographic analysis and ecological modelling to gain insight on the role of stochastic and deterministic drivers on spatial distribution of photosynthetic microbial mat communities, and pangenome evolution across poly-extreme stress gradients. The findings will be highly relevant to resolving the mechanistic basis of large scale microbial distribution patterns under poly-extreme stress in other ecosystems, and will provide the first major regional atlas of hot spring microbial metagenomic diversity. 2) Develop metatranscriptomic and functional ecophysiological approaches (photosynthetic yield and carbon assimilation) to provide insight on metabolic pathways and productivity under poly-extreme stress, mechanistic insight on the basis for taxa-specific tolerance ranges, and wider application including novel method development and predicting how extreme stress may impact microbial productivity in a changing world. 3) Assess metatranscriptomic and ecophysiological response and recovery from disturbance in order to provide novel insight on resilience of photosynthetic microbial mats under poly-extreme stress. This will have direct relevance to management and conservation strategies for tropical hot springs that are highly valued culturally and commercially. title: Drug occupancy in extracellular vesicles: multiplexed profiling in vesicle subpopulations
abs: Measuring defined interactions between drug compounds and target molecules (drug–target interactions) has broad applications for the monitoring of various cancer treatment effects (e.g., on-target therapeutic effects and off-target side effects). Nevertheless, conventional approaches for measuring drug–target interactions have limited clinical utility. These approaches include thermal shift and chemical proteomics assays. Thermal shift assays measure changes in thermal stability of drug–protein interactions; as such changes are subtle and nonspecific, the approach requires a large sample amount, and can only be applied for high-abundance proteins that display large stability changes. On the other hand, chemical proteomics uses chemically-modified small molecule probes to enrich interacting proteins for mass spectrometry analysis; the approach too requires extensive processing and a large sample amount. As a result, these conventional assays are universally complex, require extensive sample processing on large sample amounts (i.e., repeat invasive tissue biopsies for tumor monitoring), and cannot be readily applied for clinical care. There is thus an intense interest to develop a blood test to characterize drug–target interactions for personalized, high-resolution treatment monitoring. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) have recently emerged as an attractive blood biomarker. EVs are small membrane vesicles released by a variety of mammalian cells. They abound in blood and carry diverse molecular contents of their parent cells. Importantly, recent studies found that they carry drug-bound proteins; capturing this repertoire of blood-borne information could thus present a transformative approach to map drug–target interactions across different parent cell systems and reflect various treatment effects. Nevertheless, EV detection remains a challenging task, primarily due to the vesicles’ nanoscale features. We have recently developed a nanotechnology platform to measure drug–target interactions in EVs, directly in patient blood samples. The technology utilizes bio-orthogonal probe amplification on plasmonic resonators to measure drug–target interactions in EVs. In this approach, EVs bearing different amounts of drug–target interactions are labeled with drug-competitive click probes; this labeling is further amplified and measured through plasmonic resonators to enable quantitative assessment of drug–target interactions in EVs. The technology is well-suited for blood analysis: 1) it measures EV drug changes to faithfully reflect parent cellular drug changes, and 2) it can be performed directly in patient blood samples (5 μl of plasma in 1 h). Based on these developments, we now seek to advance the ExoSCOPE technology to develop an integrated platform for multiplexed profiling of drug dynamics in EV subpopulations derived from different cell origins. title: Transformative nanotechnologies for molecular profiling of extracellular vesicles
abs: The growing emphasis on precision medicine increases the need to measure key molecular markers to enhance patient stratification, guide treatment decision and monitor drug efficacy. Conventional approaches, including tissue biopsy and tumor volumetric imaging, are either too invasive or insensitive to molecular changes. There is thus an intense interest to develop a blood test for accurate disease detection and high-resolution monitoring. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) have recently emerged as an attractive blood biomarker. They are nanoscale membrane vesicles secreted by a variety of cells. A robust biomarker, they abound in blood and carry rich molecular contents from their parent cells (e.g., proteins and drug–target interactions). Capturing this repertoire of blood-borne information could enable reflective mapping of different cellular systems and treatment effects. Nevertheless, EV detection remains challenging, primarily due to a lack of compatible technologies to match to the vesicles’ nanoscale features. To address these challenges, we propose to develop transformative nanotechnologies for robust profiling of circulating EVs and establish reflective blood signatures for personalized disease detection and treatment monitoring. Specifically, we have previously developed the first generation ExoSCOPE technology for real-time monitoring of EV drug effects directly in patient blood samples. While the technology enables proof-of-concept clinical monitoring, as it relies on subtle EV-induced refractive index changes, it generates small nanometer spectral signals and requires sophisticated optical setup for detection. To improve the technology translatability, we propose to develop transformative nanotechnologies to enable robust and expanded EV detection. The goal of the proposal is thus two-fold. First, through integrative assay development and nanosensor engineering, we will develop transformative nanotechnologies for multiparametric EV profiling. The digital nature of these transformative assays – switching on and off dramatic property changes – can be robustly measured by simple miniaturized devices, thereby enhancing the technology’s translation and commercialization. Second, employing the proposed platform, we will perform translational studies to evaluate patient blood samples. We will apply the EV measurements to accurately identify patients and distinguish various treatment effects. The intersection of these developments creates unprecedented opportunities to empower technology translation and innovate clinical applications for precision medicine.
kw: Transformative nanotechnologies; mode-switching optics; extracellular vesicles; multiparametric profiling; blood test; personalized medicine

title: Directed Energy Materials (DEM) for Advanced Manufacturing
abs: The Industry 4.0 revolution is now upon us with future goals of increased production, sustainable methods, and new possibilities of rapid agility/resilience. Demand on the material side has not paced with the new connective and intelligent technologies. Smart materials, which respond to specific external or internal stimuli, have had limited innovations with respect to the 4.0 agility and resilience that is sought. We aim to fill this research and industrial gap with novel platform technology based on Directed Energy Materials (DEM)—an emerging discipline at the interface between physics and materials science. Current plastics are based off legacy formulations—no electronic activation or automation possible. In contrast, directed energy materials allow remote activation, real-time feedback, and external digital manipulation for a new paradigm of design intents. This innovative transformation creates new platforms aimed to remove laborious manufacturing methods. Alignment of Industry 4.0 renaissance is proposed through retooling of static, resin/plastics to dynamic materials that can be activated through the directed energy spectrum. The new modus operandi for Directed Energy Materials (DEM): (1) Magnetic field responsive thermoplastics, where induction-based directed energy allows advanced manufacturing methods of thermoplastic composites, for the first time. (2) Voltage/current electrochemical induction of semiconductive resin/plastics for instantaneous electro-setting composites. (3) Sustainable composite lifecycles that exploits DEM attributes for composites repair, post-consumer recycling and ‘cradle-to-grave’ product lifecycle directives. DEM platforms have the following design intent: (1) impart remote, on-demand functions, (2) integrate with automated assisted manufacturing, (3) provide real-time processing feedback, and (4) address unmet industrial needs of post-consumer sustainability. Mapping the platform structure property relationships of DEM-composites constitutes the translational science and intellectual framework of this CRP proposal.
