title: Comparison of litterfall nutrient cycling between forests and parks in Singapore
abs: Fundamental links between stand biomass, canopy production and litterfall nutrient release rates (mineralization and sequestration) are well understood in the literature, but the effects of plant traits on canopy productivity and invertebrate and microbe communities, and the effects of these invertebrate and microbe communities on mineralization and sequestration rates, are poorly studied. The proposed project aims to: (1) describe patterns of litterfall and detritivorous microbes and invertebrates; (2) develop litterfall nutrient (C, N, P, K) budgets using leaf and wood nutrient traits of dominant plant species; (3) investigate how litter quality and mixing interact with detritivorous invertebrate and microbe communities to drive mineralization (C, N, P, K) and sequestration rates across different vegetation types in Singapore. Litterfall traps will be deployed across different vegetation types in Singapore, in existing vegetation plots wherever possible (such as the Nparks long-term forest ecological monitoring plot network). Soil and litter invertebrates and microbes will also be surveyed at locations where litterfall traps are deployed, and these would be identified through metabarcoding. Major litter-producing species in each vegetation type will be selected for plant trait and nutrient concentration measurements. Traits will also be measured from invertebrate groups found across all vegetation types. Litterfall nutrient (C, N, P, K) budgets for the different vegetation types will then be estimated, and association patterns between litter traits and invertebrate and microbe communities identified. Field mesocosm experiments will also be conducted in major vegetation types in both natural (forests) and managed (park/streetscape) areas. Reciprocal exchanges of litter and microbe and invertebrate communities will be performed between mesocosms found in different vegetation types. Mineralization and sequestration rates will then be determined at the end of the one-year experimental duration. Mesocosm experiments will reveal the interactions between habitat, litter quality and mixing, and invertebrate and microbe communities on mineralization and sequestration rates. The findings from this project would influence standard industry practice in urban park plant selection and litter management protocols, and evaluate the feasibility of soil/litter invertebrate rewilding for the restoration of urban vegetation ecosystem functioning.
kw: leaf litter; nutrient cycling; inverebrates; micrbes; urban parks; tropical forests

title: Assessing the long-term viability of nature-based climate solutions to future sea level rise and marine heatwaves in Singapore
abs: Our research aims to understand how climate-related sea level rise and ocean warming will drive changes in the spatial distribution and habitat functionality of Singapore’s coastal and marine ecosystems. We will provide the first quantification of the survival thresholds and ecological tipping points for mangrove and coral reefs in Singapore to assess the long-term viability of nature-based solutions under different Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP) scenarios (e.g., SSP1-1.9; SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5). Our multi-disciplinary approach combines sedimentary geological archives and field ecological surveying in Singapore with high-resolution climate models. We will: (1) use mangrove cores collected at sites in Singapore to establish the upper tolerance limits of mangroves to sea-level rise on Singapore’s urbanised coastline by measuring past elevation gains and carbon sequestration. title: Integrated framework to characterize local wave climate through non-contact wave monitoring, numerical modelling and vessel tracking
abs: Coastal defence, particularly in light of climate change requires an understanding of the present and the ability to monitor and assess impacts now and in the future. Waves generated by wind and/or moving ship vessels is one of the potential stressors to coastal defences. A long-term, reliable and cost-effective means to monitor and understand the combined impact of such stressors will be useful for planning future coastal protection needs. With this in mind, this project aims to introduce an integrated framework to monitor, model and assess the local wave/wake climate in a cost-effective and sustainable manner in the long-term. The monitoring method is designed to reduce maintenance costs while providing both water level and current measurements. The proposed framework will gather vessel information through the use of Automatic Identification System (AIS) messages as supplementary information to be combined with wave-focused numerical models to simulate and understand the combined effects of wind waves and ship wakes in the local environment. The framework will incorporate Machine Learning (ML) techniques in conjunction with the observations (wave and AIS) and wave-focused models to highlight potential coastal protection areas that may come under stress. To deepen understanding and to future-proof the framework, development of a computational fluid dynamic (CFD) model to study wave-current and coastal processes interaction and assess their near-shore impact on coastal protection will be carried out.
kw: waves, sensors, models, coastal protection

title: Intelligent topological engineering of single-molecule quantum π-magnets
abs: Topological engineering of zigzag-edged molecular graphenoids offers a rich playground in design and fabrication of a new class of single-molecule quantum π-magnets (SMQMs) hosting robustly coherent spin centers and non-trivial π-magnetism with giant exchange coupling. This renders them as appealing candidates for developing emergent quantum information technologies. Realizing this goal is not a simple task as it requires the ability to achieve on-demand fabrication and precise engineering of SMQMs with tunable π-magnetism that lays the cornerstone for their device integration towards on-chip quantum technologies. Unfortunately, conventional fabrication strategies including on-surface synthesis or atomic manipulation with scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) cannot offer such a high-level on-demand engineering and intelligent scalable manufacturing. The current fabrication strategy of SQMQs has relied on the design of elegant organic precursors to undergo surface-catalyzed cyclodehydrogenation on judiciously chosen substrates (4-7). Such a one-pot surface-assisted route with competing reaction pathways often leads to a relatively low yield of target products and lacks the ability for on-demand fabrication and precise engineering of π-magnetism at the single-molecule level. Alternatively, atomic manipulation (8-12) utilizing probe chemistry has the capability to achieve the site-selective fabrication of desired SMQMs. However, this goal has been limited to tackling relatively simple reactions for creating zigzag edges within the existing carbon network (13-15). Extending the π-electron topology along the zigzag orientation via atomic manipulation is crucial to realizing site-specific engineering and manipulation of multiple spin centers in SMQMs. However, this remains an open challenge, as it requires new capabilities to tackle complex single-molecule reactions involving multiple-bond cleavage and seamless bond reformation. In addition, single-molecule reactions promoted by probe chemistry often rely on the knowledge and experience of the operators to improve the success rate, which typically compromises efficiency and scalability, a major hurdle for practical applications. On the other hand, the application of artificial intelligence (AI) in nanotechnology has gained considerable attention as it offers a powerful tool for making predictions, recommendations, and decisions by applying neural network-based machine learning models in the microscopic world (16). Current implementations of AI in this area mainly focus on offline data extraction and analysis, while the real-time operation-level implementation remains in its infancy with few explorations (17-21). Moreover, the ultimate goal of such multidisciplinary implementations is not only limited to performing autonomous operations to increase efficiency by adopting and converting expert knowledge but to unveiling deeper information through data mining that could provide additional and explainable i

title: Morphologically complex particulate photocatalysts for solar-driven H2 production
abs:
Photoelectrochemical water splitting using semiconductor photocatalysts represents a promising solar-to-fuel technology for green H2 production from water, capitalizing on surface activities of photogenerated charge carriers (holes and electrons). The charge carrier behaviors often limit the reaction kinetics on catalyst surfaces, and the overall photon-to-current conversion efficiency and eventual conversion efficiency to fuels. An outstanding challenge is to elucidate charge carrier behaviors of morphologically complex particulate photocatalysts – anisotropically shaped particles with multiple different facets and cocatalyst modifications, which recently emerged as a class of highly promising, economically viable materials for green hydrogen generation, with recently demonstrated water splitting performance with a 100% quantum efficiency.
Here we propose to study morphologically complex particulate photocatalysts by quantitative, operando, multimodal functional imaging to optimize their performance toward solar-driven H2 production. Scientifically, this project will provide fundamental knowledge to rationally engineer the particle morphology and cocatalyst pattern to improve water splitting performance. Technically, it will lead to novel catalyst characterization tools, applicable to other (photo)(electro)catalytic processes such as CO2 reduction and N2 fixation, and a novel single-entity-level analytical framework for studying shaped semiconductor particles and elucidating the exact role of cocatalysts, an area of active debate. This project will contribute to the global effort in using renewal energy to meet larger-scale longer-

title: Bayesian approach to irreversibility
abs: This is a proposal in theoretical physics. Its goal is to develop the conceptual and mathematical potentialities of a new approach to irreversibility, introduced by the PI in the last two years. In stochastic thermodynamics, irreversibility is quantified by entropy production, a statistical comparison between the physical process and its “associated reverse process”. The latter is easily defined as “the movie played backward” only for reversible processes. But the more irreversible a process appears to us, the less straightforward it was to define its reverse – and thus, to study irreversibility in a quantitative way, by means of fluctuation theorems. The disruptive idea has consisted in replacing the reverse process with Bayesian retrodiction. This is the logical inference of the causes (inputs) from observing the effects (outputs). The recipe is unequivocal, recovers past results, and can be applied beyond the physical setting of thermal processes, both in classical and in quantum theory. In this proposal, which spans three years, we have three Aims (each leading to three Milestones, one per year): 1. Quantifying irreversibility for quantum processes with a complex structure. We shall start with the basic open system setting and its "dilations" (closing the system by adding an environment), then we move on to processes consisting of repeated interactions and hidden Markov models. Lastly, we plan to apply our tools to the study of entropy production by a black hole. 2. Unify notions of entropy across unrelated processes. We have preliminary connections of our retrodictive approach with the theory of expected utility in economics, and with the notion of "observational entropy". We conjecture that our definition of entropy is actually fully general, encompassing those obtained form specific processes as special cases. 3. Reassess the role of time reversal in physics, both in mathematical frameworks (theory of "process matrices" without definite causal order) and in philosophical arguments (what is the definition of time reversal, and how it relates to the perception of an "arrow of time"). The budget of the proposal caters for the hiring of two post-doctoral researchers (one with expertise in quantum information theory; the other with a possibly broader background in classical process theory, Bayesian networks, black hole physics, or foundations and philosophy of physics). The EOM is complemented by travel fees, to attend conferences and maintain discussions with experts worldwide; and publication fees.
kw: Irreversibility; entropy; Bayesian logic; retrodiction; quantum information

title: Space-time-engineered topological photonics
abs: Crystals generally refer to structures with periodicity in space. This has inspired Yablonovitch and John in late 1980s to propose the concept of photonic crystals, which are spatially periodic photonic structures exhibiting photonic bands for electromagnetic waves. The recent discovery of band topology in topological quantum matter (e.g., topological insulators) has stimulated the explosion of research into topological photonic structures, especially the photonic topological insulators that have found impactful applications in topological lasers and robust communication chips. So far, the nontrivial photonic band topology has largely been limited to spatial crystallization, with little consideration from time. It is thus worth noting that, recently, time has been proposed as the dimension of crystallization in “photonic time-crystals”, which are photonic structures with periodically varying refractive index in time. Unlike conventional frequency bandgaps, such photonic time-crystals can generate bandgaps in momentum, leading to fundamentally new mechanisms of light-matter interaction. For example, a laser can be designed to extract energy from time modulation rather than from gain media. Hence, it can be envisioned that the time degree of freedom is able to shift the current paradigm of topological photonics from space-engineered to space-time-engineered. In this project, we will systematically investigate time as a fundamental degree of freedom in constructing topological photonic structures in space-time. The specific aims include: (1) Demonstration of a temporal topological insulating phase. We plan to design and realize for the first time a “temporal topological insulator” whose topological edge states are localized in time. The previously unexplored wave amplification mechanism will also be demonstrated. (2) Realization of time-periodic topological states breaking discrete time-translational symmetry in an optical lattice. Unlike quantum “time crystals” that rely on quantum many-body interaction to stabilize their periods longer than the driving period, topological protection can also stabilize the doubled period (as in realized time crystals) and even longer periods (still difficult in time crystals). Most proposals for time-periodic topological states remain on the theoretical level. We will design and demonstrate such time-periodic topological states with doubled and even longer periods for light in an optical lattice. (3) Design and implementation of topological space-time crystals and their boundary states. Space-time modulation will form not only moving boundaries but also space-time symmetries. We will design and demonstrate some topological space-time crystals that cannot be realized with only spatial symmetries. We will also study the topological phases associated with different velocities of boundaries, and demonstrate the topological edge states moving together with the boundary. title: Genetic Dissection of Host Factors Critical for Flavivirus Infection
abs: Mosquito-borne flaviviruses, such as dengue virus (DENV), Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV), West Nile virus (WNV), yellow fever virus (YFV), and Zika virus (ZIKV), infect up to 400 million people worldwide each year, causing significant morbidities and burdens on the global economic, social, and public healthcare systems. Hitherto, approved antiviral therapeutics against flaviviruses remain absent. Extensive efforts have been invested in unlocking the biochemical properties of flaviviruses. Each flaviviral particle is highly organized, ~50 nm in diameter, containing a copy of ~11 kb single-stranded, plus sense RNA genome that encodes for ~10 viral proteins. In contrast, very little is known about host factors essential for the infection and transmission of flaviviruses. As an absolute requirement for existence, flaviviruses must hijack cellular factors to enter host cells, replicate progeny virions, and exit host cells to spread. On the contrary, host cells are well equipped with restriction factors as the utmost front-line defense to counter viral invasion. Hence, a better grasp of flavivirus host factors can illuminate the molecular details of viral infections and diseases, which are crucial for novel antiviral strategies. Genome-wide loss-of-function (LOF) genetic screens, such as Haploid Genetic screens and CRISPR knockout (KO) screens, have been proven as powerful approaches for the discovery of virus host factors. Multiple lists of hits have been reported, albeit only for a few flaviviruses, such as DENV and ZIKV. However, flaviviruses are composed of >50 virus species that are distantly related; DENV and ZIKV may not accurately inform on the host factors required by other flaviviruses. Furthermore, due to finite capacities and resources, a few top hits from each hit list were typically validated and published, and the remainder of unvalidated hits are usually buried in the supplementary information. Minimal efforts were observed to consolidate these datasets to reveal human genes that scored with the most specificity for flaviviruses because no practical tools are currently available. In addition, due to variabilities in the experimental conditions (e.g., cell lines, CRISPR libraries, virus isolates, bioinformatic analyses), some discrepancies among hit lists are often observed, further restricting the utility of these datasets. Hence, despite the accumulation of sizeable genetic screening datasets, the majority of reported hits have yet to be validated. Consequently, the knowledge we can glean from such screens for combating flaviviruses, especially antiviral therapeutic development, has been disproportionately limited relative to the cost of such studies. Our grant is tailored to address this gap in the comprehensive identification of host factors critical for flavivirus infection. title: Cellular metabolism as a developmental regulator of microglial fate and function
abs: Cellular metabolism affects all aspects of cell function and life. Classically, metabolism was thought to respond to the energy needs of a cell following commitment to a specific fate. Challenging this notion, growing evidence suggests that metabolism has an instructive role in determining cell fate through mitochondrial-nuclear crosstalk (1, 2). Here, we ask whether metabolism could provide the key to understanding development and function of microglia, the resident innate immune cells of the brain. This knowledge is urgently needed, as dysfunctional microglia contribute to a wide range of neurodevelopmental, neuropsychiatric and neurodegenerative diseases. Specifically, we will test the hypothesis that metabolic reprogramming drives critical transcriptional and epigenetic changes in microglia, leading to their differentiation and functional specialization in brain development. Our preliminary data show that changes in metabolism, coined ‘metabolic reprogramming’, are observed in developing microglia during embryogenesis. We will focus on two major microglial metabolic programs – aerobic glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS). Firstly, we will determine the spatio-temporal sequence of microglial metabolic, epigenetic, transcriptional and functional changes during embryonic development, as well as the key intrinsic and extrinsic environmental cues that trigger microglial metabolic reprogramming during development. Secondly, we will test whether switching the metabolic program is sufficient to direct microglial differentiation and function. To address this in vivo, we will use genetically encoded, light-controlled metabolic switches that enable non-invasive, precise temporal and spatial control of glycolysis and OXPHOS in living animals. Thirdly, we will define how metabolic reprogramming directs microglial fate, determining if metabolic reprogramming drives epigenetic modification and transcriptional states. This project will advance our fundamental understanding of how microglia attain different fates. The knowledge developed here will be immediately relevant to human disease. Novel molecular pathways controlling microglial fate will provide new avenues to reprogramme dysfunctional microglia in disease, and new targets for in vitro generation of microglia, which is an essential precursor for development of microglia replacement therapies. Our project will also develop novel experimental models enabling precise in vivo control of microglial metabolism, an advance that overcomes technical challenges currently faced in investigating energy metabolism in health and disease. Our application of optogenetic tools to understand microglial development and function represents a world first. These models will open new avenues of research to understand disorders characterized by microglial metabolic dysfunction. abs: Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) has been identified as one of the first signs of more severe neurological disease and is considered a prodromal state to clinical Alzheimer’s disease (AD). The main symptoms of MCI are loss of short-term memory, attentional processing and visual/spatial perception. There is presently no proven pharmacological treatment for MCI. Hence, there is increasing interest in the use of Brain Computer Interface (BCI)-based Neurofeedback Training (NFT) that could potentially regulate brain activity underlying the symptoms of MCI, targeting slowing down the deterioration of cognitive functions. title: Investigating Associations Between Biological Age measured by Blood-Based DNA Methylation, with Cognitive Performance, Neuroimaging Markers and Conversion to Dementia – A Nested Case Control Longitudinal Study
abs: Specific Aims 1) 1a)To study associations between biological age measured by blood-based DNA methylation clocks with cross-sectional cognitive performance, longitudinal conversion to dementia (subtypes), and neuroimaging markers and; 1b)Its comparison with existing biomarkers for dementia 2) To identify methylation signatures of cross-sectional cognitive performance, longitudinal conversion to dementia (subtypes), and neuroimaging markers. Hypotheses 1) 1a)DNA methylation clocks are associated and; 1b)Add incremental predictive value to existing circulating biomarkers for dementia in predicting cross-sectional cognitive performance, longitudinal conversion to dementia(subtypes) and neuroimaging markers 2) Characteristic methylation signatures underpin cognitive performance, longitudinal conversion to dementia(subtypes), and neuroimaging markers. Methodology This proof-of-concept study will leverage upon a subsample of a deeply-phenotyped existing memory clinic cohort, with 5-year longitudinal data collected. 360 patients stratified into 3 groups will be included: 60 dementia converters, 150 cognitively normal controls, 150 with baseline dementia. The primary outcomes are 1)Cross-sectional cognitive performance, 2)Neuroimaging markers, and 3)Longitudinal conversion to dementia with 4)Stratification for dementia causative subtype. For specific aim 1: High-throughput measurement of DNA methylation on a genome wide scale will be performed using the Illumina EPIC BeadChip. Four machine-learning derived blood-DNA methylation aging clocks (Hannum, Horvath, Phenoage, Grimage) will be calculated. The Differences in DNA methylation clocks will be evaluated on cross-sectional and longitudinal analysis of the primary outcomes. The incremental predictive value of DNA methylation clocks will be compared with existing circulating biomarkers for dementia (ie. p-tau, NfL, amyloid-beta). For specific aim 2: Differentially methylation region analysis and gene pathway analysis will be employed to identify significant differences in methylation profile with regards to neurocognitive and neuroimaging outcomes. Feasibility and Importance Taken together, this study will 1)Investigate biomarkers of biological age which may add predictive value to current markers for dementia, 2)Uncover mechanistic insights between the epigenome and dementia pathophysiology; and 3)Identify potential therapeutic targets for dementia.

title: Drug discovery and mechanism investigation in novel 3D systemic in vitro model for Alzheimer’s disease
abs: Human life expectancy has been rising drastically over the past two centuries, healthspan does not increase to the same degree as lifespan due to chronic diseases accompanying aging. For example, Alzheimer’s disease is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the profound loss of cognitive functions and behavioral abilities. The number of affected individuals is growing rapidly due to the aging of human populations, and the severe effects of such diseases on the quality of life have increased the burden on healthcare systems and societal support systems. Currently, there is neither effective treatment nor a clear understanding of the disease’s pathophysiology. It is crucial to build a new model for Alzheimer’s disease that is both human origin and systemically representative. In this proposal, we aim to develop a medium-throughput assay to validate chemicals we previously identified to extend the cellular lifespan in an Alzheimer’s disease model. We also aim to combine previously available iPSC cells, 3D organoids, and fluidic systems to construct an integrated system that provides a highly accurate model for Alzheimer’s disease in vitro. This novel model will be used to analyze the mechanism of action of chemical compounds, providing new insights into the disease's pathophysiology.

title: DNA methylation status in human pancreatic islets as a function of biological metabolic health
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Ageing is a major risk factor for diabetes, with one in three elderly Singaporeans having diabetes. However, the link between ageing and beta cell failure in diabetes remains unclear. Increasingly, there is substantial evidence pointing to epigenetic alterations that are associated with ageing, giving rise to age-related diseases. A small number of studies have started to evaluate the link between DNA methylation in islets and diabetes in ageing. However, the studies suffered from low sample size or lack of tissue-specificity. Here, we hypothesise that as pancreatic islets age, key functional genes are differentially methylated, altering gene expression and metabolic function/health. We aim to 1) determine the DNA methylation status of human pancreatic islets and their correlation with chronological age, and 2) correlate the transcriptome of human pancreatic islets with DNA methylation status and identify key beta cell genes that are dysfunctional with ageing, leading to beta cell functional decline. Using machine learning, we will derive an islet-specific algorithm (epigenetic clock) to predict beta cell biological age and metabolic health of an ageing individual. We will also identify beta cell genes that can potentially be altered to improve beta cell functional decline in ageing. Overall, the improvement of metabolic health of ageing individuals will delay the onset of metabolic disorders such as diabetes.
kw: DNA methylation, human, pancreas, islets, beta cell, metabolic health, ageing

title: Brain structure and function underlying sarcopenia and cognitive decline in ageing – the SG70 study
abs: Sarcopenia and cognitive impairment are two prevalent causes of disability in the aging population of Singapore and worldwide. Sarcopenia is a condition of physical frailty marked by loss of muscle mass, strength, and function. Importantly, sarcopenia is associated with an increased risk of cognitive impairment and often co-occurs with neurologic diseases including cerebrovascular disease and dementia. It has been suggested that convergent age-related changes in brain structure and function may underlie this relationship between physical frailty and cognitive function in older adults. However, such possible overlapping neural mechanisms remain poorly elucidated, especially in Asian populations. Although a number of studies have demonstrated that sarcopenia is associated with brain grey matter and white matter tissue degeneration and cerebrovascular burden (e.g. white matter hyperintensities), few studies investigated brain functional network and microstructure changes and their potential links with domain-specific cognitive function. Therefore, in this study, we aim to examine brain structural and functional underpinnings of sarcopenia and cognition in 250 Singaporean community-dwelling older adults (aged 65 to 79 years) from the SG70 cohort, nested in the prospective Singapore Chinese Health Study cohort. We hypothesize that the objective measures of sarcopenia (handgrip strength, muscle mass, and gait speed) would be related to specific brain microstructure (via diffusion MRI), cerebral blood flow (via perfusion), and functional network measures (via resting state functional MRI), particularly in the sensorimotor and attention networks. We then seek to test whether such physical frailty-related brain integrity measures would relate to domain-specific cognition and midlife lifestyle risk factors. This study is the first step to understand the neural mechanisms underlying the possible bidirectional relationships between physical frailty and cognition. Outcomes of this study could pave the way for future longitudinal characterisation of brain-physical-cognition trajectories and facilitate the development of new interventions to mitigate age-related cognitive and physical decline.
kw: Cognition, brain structure and function, sarcopenia, older adults, aging

title: Spatial Multiome Cartography in Human Thymus to Guide NextGen Cell-based Therapies (SPECTRA)
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: The overarching goal of the proposal is to advance our understanding of the regulatory mechanisms of proliferation, differentiation, and cell fate decisions during T cell maturation. We are endeavoured to determine the phase-specific transcription factors, epigenetic modifications and cell-cell communications governing the process, as a mean to empower the development of NextGen T cell-based therapies. The penetrative understanding illuminated from the thymic spatial multimodal cartography will help revolutionize the development of fully functional and potent T cells from iPSCs, for ‘off the shelf’ cell therapy. The proposal centred on two interconnecting themes. In theme 1, we seek to build a ‘state-of-the-art’ single-cell resolution, spatial multiomic platforms, combining mRNA modifications, protein expression and Transcriptomics, to gain unprecedented comprehension of thymic biology. Integrative analyses will be performed for cell-cell interactions, ligand-receptor interactions, tissue architecture and thymocyte migration We envision a granular understanding of T-cell maturation in thymus, as well as underlying mechanisms of thymic involution during ageing. The penetrative understanding illuminated from Theme 1 will help guide Theme 2, which is the derivation of mature T-cells from iPSCs in culture. We will engineer the step-wise directed differentiation of the cells using the intrinsic central lineage genetic/epigenetic factors, at the same time, providing the extrinsic spatial micro-environment, through the development of stage specific thymus epithelial/T-cell progenitor co-culture system. We anticipate to achieve high differentiation efficiency of bona-fide T-cells and TECs which will be deployed. Overall, we envision to build a spatial multiomic cartography of human thymus across different ages at a single cell resolution and develop innovative cell products for future cell-based therapies.

title: Climate Change Impact on Erosion Failure Risk of Slopes in Singapore
abs: Rainfall-induced erosion failure of the slope is a severe concern in many tropical countries as it can harm public safety and/or infrastructure. The impact could be especially severe in Singapore as our population density is high and our infrastructure development is very dense; hence, some of these slopes are near to the infrastructure development and residential areas. In some instances, while the heavy rainfall may not cause the entire slope to fail completely (i.e. no deep-seated or toe slope failure), but may still soften the surface soils, causing the soil particles detachment due to the impact energy of the raindrop, and followed by sheet erosion of the shallow soil surface. This will generally result in some form of “surface erosion failure” (till a certain shallow depth). Typical examples of this kind of failure were found to have happened on 2nd January 2021, where some shallow surface erosion took place along some section of the slope by the side of TPE and at the hillside of a hotel near Havelock Road The heavy rain on July 15th, 2021, also caused surface soil erosion, and subsequently, a huge amount of water gushed down the slope in Bukit Batok, causing delays in traffic at the downslope location. Soil erosion failure at 5 Jalan Khairudhin, threatened the safety of residents of the adjacent property to this eroded slope. The erosion failure can also lead to high repair costs. Many such similar soil erosion instances have occurred in Singapore. Hence, it is important to identify the slopes prone to this kind of soil erosion failure. The overall goal of the research is to develop a set of criteria to identify slopes with high erosion failure risk in Singapore that could lead to public safety concern and/or property damage, and to study the climate change impact on such slope erosion failure. The specific objectives of the research are categorized into 4 parts: Part 1: Develop Reliable Method to Quantify Erosion Failure Probability in Singapore by establishing the key parameters responsible for slope erosion failure in Singapore (via lab testing and modeling) and developing technical analysis probability based models for “Erosion probability Index”. Part 2: Develop Slope Erosion Risk Assessment Model and Set Criteria to Evaluate Impact of Slope Erosion Failure, and Climate Change Impact Assessment by establishing key factors for impact assessment on public safety and/or damage to building from slope erosion failure. Thus establish the risk factor using various criteria and appropriate weightage for risk ranking based on public safety and/or damage to building caused by slope erosion failure, using fuzzy Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) risk assessment Model. title: Next-generation geminal-atoms catalysis as a disruptive technology for the sustainable fine chemical manufacturing
abs: The chemical manufacturing sector continues to grow and thrive worldwide. Driven by an increasing demand for organic chemicals, the combined global market size of the fine chemicals and pharmaceuticals industries, now exceeds US$2 trillion annually. In Singapore alone, the energy and chemicals sector is the nation’s second largest contributor to manufacturing output, having accounted for over S$60 billion in manufacturing output in 2020. However, a global shortage of energy and resources, and the push for clean manufacturing processes, means that economical and sustainable production methods of fine chemicals are urgently needed. A particular priority is in catalyst development, as this is fundamental to the discovery of more efficient and selective transformations, which can be implemented with lower cost, less energy input and less waste generation. Transition metal-catalyzed cross-coupling reactions are fundamental to organic synthesis, however, they require homogeneous catalysts which are associated with high production costs and are detrimental to the environment due to the need for repeated product separation and purification steps, and catalyst recovery. Metal contamination in products and waste streams must also be addressed [ref]. As an alternative, the heterogeneously-catalyzed processes are highly attractive as they would allow simplified catalyst recovery, circumvent metal contamination, and offer improved adaptability for continuous flow synthesis, especially in large-scale chemical production. However, existing heterogeneous catalysts often feature inherent limitations that include site diversity, poor surface-area-to-volume ratio and a lack of molecular precision, which consequently lowers overall atom utilization, catalytic activity and selectivity. In addition, catalysis is not sustainable due to the requirement of precious metals, and the generation of side-products that require energy to separate. Therefore, there is a compelling need to develop stable solid catalysts that are sustainable, recyclable, and capable of mediating complex coupling reactions with minimal metal leaching. The overarching goal of this CRP programme is to develop a pioneering class of heterogeneous geminal-atom catalysts (GACs) consisting of pairs of adaptive low-valence single-atom metal sites as a disruptive technology for sustainable fine chemical manufacturing, where cost and environmental impact is dramatically reduced.
kw: Geminal atoms catalysis; sustainable manufacturing; fine chemicals; pharmaceuticals; scalable synthesis; flow technologies

title: Harnessing randomness and chaos in complex disordered photonic systems
abs: Driven by emerging applications, a new generation of miniaturized spectrometers and high-performance hyperspectral imaging systems is required, featuring reduced physical dimensions, cost, and power consumption, while maintaining high resolution and reconstruction speed. Disordered photonics is an emerging approach for both spectrometry and imaging, due to the key merits such as high compactness and high spectral resolution can be simultaneously achieved; the spectral resolution can be finely controlled, and robustness to fabrication error or optical misalignment. Advanced spectrometry and snap-shot HSI still face significant limitations, such as limited understanding about the fundamental limits in terms of spectral reconstruction efficiency, resolution, and losses; typical disordered structures scatter light strongly in all directions; their operation wavelength has thus far been limited to the near-infrared and visible regimes, not the “fingerprint” molecular spectra; and HSI requires thicker disorder media to achieve higher spectral resolution, which reduces the memory effect region and limits the field of view for imaging. We will address the above limitations in this program. The aim is to engineer the disorders based on advanced algorithms and non-Hermiticity and develop disorder-based high-performance spectrometer and snap-shot HSI system. In WP1 we aim to surpass the limitations in existing optimisation algorithms for disordered spectrometry and HSI by investigating the use of machine learning; In WP2, we aim to enhance the performance of disorder-based spectrometry by engineering disorders, and to use random metasurface with judiciously designed random phase distribution to enhance the intensity of field at the detector plane, thereby boost the performance of imagining system. In WP3, we aim to realize the mid-infrared/THz disorder-based spectrometer based on ML algorithms developed in WP1. In WP4, we aim to realize an advanced snapshot HSI system with a simple optical configuration but integrated with sophisticatedly engineered disorders and proprietary signal processing algorithm.
kw: Photonics; disordered photonics; randomness; micro-spectrometer; snapshot hyperspectral imaging

title: Optimising Value in Surgical Care: Cost Analysis of the Implementation of Choosing Wisely Campaign to Reduce the Overuse of Preoperative Chest X-Rays
abs: Introduction The overuse of preoperative clinical investigations can result in unnecessary costs and risks to patients. To address this, the Choosing Wisely Preoperative Chest X-ray (CXR) bundle (intervention) was implemented in Singapore General Hospital (SGH) to reduce unnecessary preoperative CXRs. This study aims to evaluate the overall cost-savings, clinical impact, and sustainability of the intervention. Study design and methodology This quasi-experimental study will be conducted over a 12-month period and will involve collecting data on the costs and outcomes of elective surgical patients undergoing pre-anesthetic evaluation at SGH. The data collection period will consist of 3 phases, with the first 6 months serving as the pre-implementation phase, the next 6 months as the implementation phase, and the final 6 months as the post-implementation phase. Data from the pre-implementation phase will be collected retrospectively, while data from the implementation and post-implementation phases will be collected prospectively over a 12-month period. Aims and hypotheses The primary aim is to evaluate the change in total costs by comparing data from the pre-implementation and implementation phase, hypothesizing a reduction in overall cost due to a decrease in unnecessary preoperative CXR testing. The secondary aim is to compare the incidence of postoperative pneumonia between the 2 phases to demonstrate that patient outcomes are not adversely affected by the intervention. Additionally, a process evaluation will be conducted 6 months after implementation to assess the mid-term sustainability of the intervention. Study significance The study findings are expected to provide evidence for potential cost savings of the Choosing Wisely Preoperative CXR bundle without any negative impact on clinical practice. Lessons learned can be applied to other areas of healthcare over-consumption, leading to a more sustainable healthcare system. Overall, this study is significant as it aims to promote value-based healthcare by reducing unnecessary costs and risks to patients.
kw: Health Services Research; Health Economics; Value-Driven Care; Perioperative Medicine

title: Unlocking Motivations, Confidence, and Positive Outcomes for Adult Learners:  Empirical Characterization and Digital Interventions
inst: IHPC - Institute of High Performance Computing
abs: With digitalisation and the rapidly evolving nature of jobs, it is more important than ever to ensure that the working population is motivated to acquire new skills to navigate new and rapidly evolving job roles and work environments. There is also a growing need to build a culture of lifelong learning to improve individual quality of life, socio-economic mobility in Singapore, and the nation’s economic resilience and productivity. Yet, most adults are not actively engaged in learning. According to OECD’s 2021 Skills Outlook report, the main reason preventing adults from participating in learning is a lack of willingness to engage in learning opportunities that are currently available to them. Factors affecting willingness to learn may include one beliefs about the monetary returns of training, attitudes towards learning, psychological traits and mindsets, social environment, or past schooling experiences. The well-established theoretical and empirical research in the learning sciences focuses predominantly on school-based, pre-employment training (PET). These theories and strategies to encourage learning may not map well to adult learners due to stark differences in hurdles, motivations, cognitive processes, and learning styles between young and adult learners. Within the literature on adult learning, there has been recent interest in understanding how intrinsic motivation and dispositional barriers explain differences in willingness to learn. Yet, policies to encourage adult learning that are implemented around the world have largely focused on tackling practical barriers such as shortage of time and financial resources, without addressing the lack of motivation. At the same time, advances in social sciences have offered effective strategies to encourage and enable behavioural and lifestyle changes by individuals. Despite the success in using behavioural approaches to address policy challenges in several domains, such as health promotion, retirement savings, and sustainability, little work has been done to study issues in adult learning from a behavioural change perspective. Through this project, we establish a multi-disciplinary research programme formed by investigators with expertise in psychology, economics, computational sciences and neuroscience, to push the frontiers of knowledge in the Science of Learning (SoL). The objectives are three-fold: (1) Characterize the motivations to engage in adult learning. We seek to empirically identify and analyse the psychological, socio-ecological, and neurobiological factors that contribute to the motivations and impediments in adult learning, and to examine how they vary across groups of individuals in Singapore. (2) Connect with the behaviour change literature. Our empirical characterizations of adult learners’ motivations and hurdles will guide the selection and design of theoretically-sound and evidence-based digital interventions to encourage adult learning. title: NATIONAL CYBERSECURITY R&D LABORATORY PHASE 3
abs: This proposal seeks renewal funding for National Cybersecurity R&D Labs (NCL) and the CSA-National Cybersecurity R&D Lab Scholarship (NCLS): Programme for 3 years. This program is part of the Singapore Cybersecurity R&D Laboratories (SGCL) initiative which also includes our sister lab, iTrust in SUTD. Together, both NCL and iTrust seek to provide high quality physical virtual testbeds made available to local and international cybersecurity communities for the purposes of research, education, and training. The funding will go towards support of NCL, specifically, maintenance and upgrade of Cybersecurity Compute Infrastructure (CCI) and cybersecurity exercises, supporting a group of specialized cybersecurity technology engineers, with a view of NCL’s path towards eventual self-sustainability. The main objective of NCL is to support local and international cybersecurity efforts towards the design and use of safe and secure critical cybersecurity compute infrastructure (CCI), rapid experimentation/investigation relating to Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) and Advanced Persistent Threat (APT). These efforts are made possible by a variety of cybersecurity activities under NCL: (1) R&D; (2) Technology Testing, Deployment and Validation; (3) Cyber Exercises; (4) Education and Training.

title: iTrust Labs Phase 2
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: iTrust testbeds have supported and validated numerous experiments in iTrust-led and -funded National Satellite of Excellence (NSoE) in Design Science and Technology for Secure Critical Infrastructure (DeST-SCI) projects. They provide an accessible, safe and realistic environment for researchers to test their theories and tools to a reasonable level of fidelity and assurance. Indeed, the testbeds have been a key element in helping some of these projects achieve higher technology readiness levels (TRLs), so that the R&D results can be translated into commercially viable products for market adoption. As federated labs with NCL, as was the case in 2022, the provision of a combined IT-OT facility as a service will accentuate and amplify the realism of the platform and users’ experience, as well as increase the use cases for cyber-related activities. The testbeds have been provided as a service to the academia, government agencies, and private companies for a variety of use cases, summarized below: 1) Government: Cybersecurity solution validation, professional training, cyber exercise, R&D 2) Private companies: Cybersecurity solution validation, R&D, cyber exercise 3) Academia: Cybersecurity solution validation, R&D, cyber exercise, education, internships Cyber exercises SWaT, WaDi and EPIC have – at various points in time – been integrated into cyber exercise platforms organised and conducted by iTrust. Since the first cyber exercise in 2015, we have added and integrated more testbeds to create an ever more complex and realistic exercise playground for cyber defenders and attackers alike. The main goals of the cyber exercises are three-fold: to (1) tease out real-world attack vectors and surfaces, (2) improve the robustness of iTrust’s in-house anomaly detectors and (3) provide training to critical infrastructure operators and regulators in understanding CI security and developing action plans to mitigate cyber attacks. A positive trickle-down effect of organising such cyber exercises is that they also support iTrust’s ascendency into a leading centre for research in critical infrastructure security. A case in point would be iTrust’s increased role in the annual Exercise Locked Shields conducted by the NATO Cooperative Cyber Defence Centre of Excellence (CCDCOE), where iTrust has contributed red
