title: Clonal analysis of antigen-specific T and B cells in stomach cancer to guide personalized immunotherapy and vaccine design
abs: Stomach cancer is one of the most common cancers worldwide and despite recent advancements in immunotherapy, overall mortality remains high. Up to 80% of stomach cancers is associated with H. pylori infection, classifying H. pylori as a Group 1 carcinogen. However, how chronic H. pylori infection, which affects over 50% of the global population, influence anti-tumor immunity remains poorly understood. One major challenge has been the lack of a systematic approach to identify and distinguish H. pylori-specific from neoantigen-specific lymphocytes. The overall objective of this proposal is to isolate and characterize the repertoire of antigen-specific T and B cells in three groups of stomach cancer patients: H. pylori-naïve, H. pylori-recovered, and those with active H. pylori infection. This comparative and comprehensive clonal analysis will address the fundamental question of how chronic H. pylori infection impacts the priming, differentiation and functions of the anti-tumor T and B cells. This study will also provide several translational applications that will be explored in this study. First, the identification of neoantigen-specific T and B cell receptors (TCRs and BCRs) will facilitate the conception of bispecific antibody therapeutics, chimeric antigen receptor-T cells (CAR-T) and TCR-engineered T cells for adoptive cellular therapy, which has shown clinical efficacy in solid malignancies. Second, the identification of their corresponding antigens will inform the design of therapeutic, neoantigen-based, personalized stomach cancer vaccines to improve survival outcome. Finally, the isolation of H. pylori-specific T and B cells will enable a better understanding of the immunogenic epitopes that should be considered in vaccine design against H. pylori, which, in contrast to other oncogenic pathogens such as human papillomavirus (HPV) and Hepatitis B, still has no clinically approved vaccines despite its global disease burden.
kw: T cells; B cells; antigen-specificity; stomach cancer; H. pylori

title: Robust Polygenic Risk Score for Metabolic Syndrome of Asian Women
inst: IHDP - Institute for Human Development and Potential
abs: Metabolic syndrome (MetS) is the co-occurrence of central obesity, insulin resistance, hypertension, and dyslipidemia. It increases the risk of developing pathologies like cardiovascular diseases and type 2 diabetes. While MetS is known to be related to both lifestyle and genetic susceptibility, genetic risks are ever-present throughout life. However, genetic studies can be challenging due to the need for extensive clinical measures and genotype data. Women’s MetS is significantly different from men's due to the impact of pregnancy and menopause across the life course. This project aims to investigate the genetic basis of MetS in Asian women, who are at a higher risk of cardio-metabolic diseases compared to women in the West and lack genetic analysis. Our study will develop a MetS polygenic risk score (MetS-PRS) using primary genotype and phenotype data from 1,500 women in two maternal cohorts in Singapore (~30 years old). Our goal is to show that MetS-PRS, formulated with predictive genetic variants, can detect cardio-metabolic diseases up to 20 years before onset. We will test this by predicting metabolic disorders in two independent groups: ~5,000 Asian women age ~53 from the UK Biobank, and ~1,000 Singaporean women aged ~57 with comorbidities of T2D, hypertension, stroke, and heart failure. Successful development of the MetS-PRS could enable risk stratification, early detection, and clinical interventions for women in Singapore and other Asian countries. This approach involves a low-cost genotyping panel that includes only the genes in the MetS-PRS, lifestyle interventions for high-risk individuals, and follow-up to reduce poor health outcomes and hospital admissions. The tool could be provided cost-free to individuals who have undergone genomic testing in SG10K, SG100K, and other screening programs. This study will improve understanding of MetS in Asian women, inform public health policies, and contribute to the field of personalized medicine and public precision health.
kw: polygenic risk score, metabolic syndrome, early detection, CVD, T2D,  Asian women

title: Evaluation of the Acute Myocardial Infarction allied Health-Oriented Patient-centered technology-Enabled (AMI-HOPE) Care Program
abs: Acute myocardial infarction (AMI) affects 11,000 Singaporeans each year with a 5% compound annual growth rate. As the incidence of cardiovascular disease rises across Asia due to rapid ageing, sustainable models of care are needed in place of traditional in-person physician-led care. The Acute Myocardial Infarction - allied Health-Oriented, Patient-centered and digitally-Enabled care (AMI-HOPE) program (AMI-HOPE), an innovative care model supported by the MOH Health Services Development Program, was co-created with the Ministry of Health Health Services Integration Division and will be implemented in a step-wedged trial of 3660 patients with AMI across all 3 healthcare clusters in Singapore. AMI-HOPE has upskilled 36 hospital and polyclinic pharmacists to lead transitional care of complex cardiovascular diseases like AMI, thereby taking over the majority of these roles from cardiologists and family physicians. We have built secure digital health tools, remote vital signs monitoring and telehealth capabilities to support pharmacist decision-making and enable patient self-care within H-cloud, Singapore's enterprise-grade healthcare cloud. The HSDP grant supports pharmacist headcounts and IT subscription costs. The cardiovascular National Clinical Translational program (NCTP) will support AMI-HOPE in integrating national big-data sources within a ‘learning healthcare system’ to inform program evaluation. However, we still need program coordinators for patient enrolment, consent-taking and onboarding of patients to the digital health and remote monitoring tools. The NCTP can support program coordinators at NUHCS, NHCS and TTSH for 3 years. This thematic PHRG grant will provide additional support for program coordinators at CGH, KTPH, NTFGH and SKH. This thematic PHRG grant will also support the ‘end-to-end’ program evaluation of AMI-HOPE including quantitative outcomes, qualitative outcomes, cost-effectiveness and value-based analyses to co-create, with the MOH Health Services Division, a financial sustainability roadmap for program mainstreaming.
kw: Acute myocardial infarction; digital health; allied health; pragmatic randomised trial

title: WORKING TOWARDS NEXT-GENERATION ALLOGENEIC CAR-T THERAPIES FOR RELAPSED/REFRACTORY NEUROBLASTOMA AND OTHER CHILDHOOD CANCERS
abs: Chimeric Receptor Antigen (CAR)-T therapies, T cells genetically modified to kill cancer cells by targeting a tumour-associated antigen, have revolutionised treatment for r/r B-lineage leukaemia/lymphoma, but have not been successfully applied to other devastating r/r childhood solid cancers. High-risk neuroblastoma (NBL) has one of the highest treatment burden and poorest survival. 50% of cases eventually relapse despite anti-GD2 antibody therapy. The overarching aim of the research proposal is to develop a Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR)-directed T-cell therapy for relapsed/refractory solid tumours, using neuroblastoma as a prototypical cancer to start with. We identified 3 gaps to address: poor T cell function, poor persistence in an inhibitory tumor microenvironment, and the lack of a clinically effective target. We lay out two specific aims to work towards a next-generation allogeneic CAR-T with enhanced persistence targeting B7-H3, the IL7Rα-armoured allogeneic anti-B7H3-BBZ-CAR-TEM, in order to address these gaps. In specific aim (SA) 1, I will study the effects of IL7Rα co-expression with CAR on the proliferative ability of allogeneic B2MKO CAR-T effector memory cells (CAR-TEM). We hypothesise that co-expression of a novel IL7Rα enhances proliferative ability of CAR-T cells which may predict persistence in the inhibitory tumour microenvironment. In specific aim 2 (SA2), I will develop a B7-H3-BBZ chimeric antigen receptor and evaluate the in vitro cytotoxicity and persistence of IL7Rα-armoured anti-B7-H3-BBZ allogeneic CAR-T cells against 2D and 3D neuroblastoma cell cultures. We hypothesise that, in vitro, armoured anti-B7H3 CAR-T has potent cytotoxicity against neuroblastoma in conventional 2D cell culture and enhanced persistence to eradicate neuroblastoma in spheroid models. The two independent components with high translation potential in this proposal are: The IL7Rα -armoured allogeneic CAR-T as a universal immune effector cell with enhanced persistence, and the next-generation allogeneic B7-H3-BBZ CAR-T as an Investigational New Drug (IND) for a biomarker driven basket trial.
kw: CAR-T, Relapsed Refractory, Neuroblastoma, Solid Tumours

title: Targeting Novel Macular Pigment Analysis and Therapy to Improve Vision-Related and Patient-Centred Outcomes for Epiretinal Membrane Surgery
abs: Epiretinal membrane (ERM) is a common age-related eye disease that can cause significant visual impairment with adverse impact on quality of life. Surgery remains the mainstay treatment for patients with ERM and vision loss. Although ERM surgery has become the most frequently performed retinal surgery, its visual outcomes can be highly variable. In fact, only about half of the patients could achieve significant gain in vision after surgery. Therefore, improving the visual outcome for ERM surgery is a major unmet medical need. Membrane peeling is the key step in ERM surgery. It involves the use of surgical forceps to physically remove the ERM at the macula. This surgical manoeuvre is the most delicate part of the surgery, with potential to cause retinal damage that may contribute to the variability of visual outcome. Specifically, it may inadvertently remove some or most of the macular pigment along with the ERM during membrane peeling. Macular pigment, consisting of carotenoids lutein and zeaxanthin, has important neuroprotective functions for the macula. Based on analysis of fundus autofluorescence images, macular pigment can now be quantitatively and reliably measured as macular pigment optical density (MPOD). Previous studies suggest that lutein supplement may increase MPOD in healthy eyes and in eyes with age-related macular degeneration (AMD). More importantly, such increase in MPOD has been associated with significant improvement in visual function in patients with AMD. Although the role of macular pigment in ERM is less well understood, there is emerging evidence that changes in the MPOD are correlated with visual outcome after ERM surgery. Herein, we propose to conduct a double-blinded, randomized, placebo-controlled trial to determine whether the loss of macular pigment during ERM surgery could be replaced, with the use of oral lutein supplement, thus restoring the neuroprotective functions and improve visual outcome after ERM surgery.
kw: epiretinal membrane, retina, vitrectomy, vision loss, age-related eye disease

title: Thromboinflammation and Cerebral Dysfunction following Acute Myocardial Infarction (TICAMI) Study
abs: Acute myocardial infarction (AMI) is the leading cause of cardiovascular mortality worldwide. It is increasingly recognised that AMI is also associated with non-cardiovascular complications involving the central nervous system (CNS). While the more common cerebrovascular complications such as thromboembolic stroke are well-understood, the mechanisms underlying associated complications of neurocognitive decline and mood disorders are poorly defined. Having previously demonstrated that AMI is associated with a systemic prothrombotic and proinflammatory state, we hypothesise that this systemic prothrombotic and proinflammatory state may have a deleterious effect on the CNS, leading to various forms of cerebral dysfunction. We therefore aim to prospectively phenotype a unique cohort of patients to investigate longitudinal associations and mechanisms between AMI and cerebral dysfunction over 12 months after an AMI. We aim to first, quantify targeted thrombotic and inflammatory biomarker profiles in a cohort of patients assessed at the time of AMI and at one-month post-AMI, second, characterise the changes in cerebral dysfunction in acute myocardial infarction patients at the time of AMI and at one year after the AMI and third, identify early predictors of cerebral dysfunction at one-year post-AMI. Elucidating neuropathological mechanisms that underlie post-MI cerebral dysfunction will hopefully lead to further work that culminate in new neuroprotective interventions in the post-MI patient. Several anti-thrombotic and anti-inflammatory drugs are already being studied for therapeutic use and can potentially be repurposed to prevent cerebral dysfunction after AMI. We aim to reduce the twin burden of cardiac and neurological disease that will become increasingly prevalent in ageing populations.
kw: thrombosis, inflammation, cognitive impairment, myocardial infarction, mood disorders, imaging

title: Deep learning pipeline for augmented reporting of MRI whole spine
abs: Back pain is a very common complaint and is estimated to affect up to 80% of adults in Singapore with a considerable impact on livelihood. MRI spine is often employed to detect and grade stenosis along the spine, detect spinal cord compression and assess for spinal instability (fractures and spondylolisthesis). MRI spine is a very commonly requested investigation in the management of patients with back pain and constitutes a significant workload in a radiology department. In Singapore, there are an estimated 120000 MRI spines performed per year, and the number of studies is increasing. Reporting MRI spine is time-consuming for the radiologist because stenosis needs to be quantified on axial and sagittal planes at each level along the cervical (7 vertebrae), thoracic (12 vertebrae), and lumbar (5 vertebrae) spine. In addition, the presence of fractures, spinal cord compression, and spondylolisthesis needs to be detailed in the report. This study will develop a deep learning pipeline to automatically triage MRI spine for radiologist review, and provide augmented reporting of the whole spine. This will improve the reporting accuracy and improve radiologist productivity, enabling more timely diagnosis with reduced healthcare costs. Aims: Develop a multitask deep learning (DL) pipeline tool to improve radiologist assessment of whole spine MRI. This will triage spine MRI for urgent reporting and augment reporting. Aim 1: Develop DL models for the detection and grading of stenosis along the cervical and thoracic spine. This will build on our existing DL model for lumbar spinal stenosis. Aim 2: Develop a DL model for the detection and grading of spinal cord compression (whole spine). Aim 3: Develop a DL model for the detection and grading of fractures along the whole spine. Aim 4: Develop a DL model for the detection and grading of spondylolisthesis along the whole spine.
kw: Spine; MRI; Deep learning; Artificial intelligence; Back pain; Radiology

title: Reducing false-positive diagnoses and biopsies from breast screening: a novel noninvasive and clinically integrable ultrasound-guided optoacoustic imaging system
abs: While current breast screening programs reduce the mortality rate from breast cancer by up to 40%, they result in large number of indeterminate lesions stemming from the overlapping structural information between benign and malignant lesions, thus requiring invasive biopsies to confirm the diagnosis. In Singapore, > 75% breast biopsies advised through screening programs are false-positive. These unnecessary biopsies increase the burden on healthcare system, cause distress to patients and discourage women from attending subsequent breast screening. To reduce the false-positive cases, we hypothesize that additional information on biochemical distribution of the intrinsic chromophores (lipid, haemoglobin, collagen, etc.) from optoacoustic (OT) images on top of the clinically familiar ultrasound structural information will aid better risk stratification of the indeterminate lesions by confirming the benignity of the tissue. Our overarching aim is to develop an imaging based objective approach to accurately and noninvasively risk stratify breast lesions that can reduce biopsies resulting from breast screening. The sub-aims are: 1. Develop hybrid ultrasound-OT system and software which provide clinical grade structural image and high-resolution biochemical information of the breast including oxy- and deoxy-haemoglobin, lipid, collagen, melanin and water at a clinically relevant depth. 2. Develop an objective diagnosis method based on the ultrasound overlaid OT images offering distribution patterns of the chromophores in vivo 3. Correlate findings with histopathology analysis of the biopsy lesions Employing the developed diagnostic method, we expect to screen out > 50% of the indeterminate lesions and negate biopsies. Such reduced biopsies, in turn, could save the time and stress of the patients, man-hours of the clinicians and pathologist performing the biopsies and subsequent processing. The pain-free definitive diagnosis experience, in turn, will encourage more women to attend breast screening. Monetarily, it could save 9 million SGD for Singapore and 300 million SGD globally every year.
kw: Ultrasound; Optoacoustic Tomography; Breast

title: Continuous non-invasive haemodynamic monitoring
abs: Estimation of right atrial pressure is a critical step in management of patients in heart failure, have pulmonary hypertension, or other heart problems. The gold standard of measurement is invasive pressure transduction through the venous system into the heart chambers and measuring direct pressure through a fluid-filled channel. This is invasive with a risk of potentially life-threatening complications. Naturally, patient uptake of the above procedure is limited. Non-invasive estimates of right atrial pressure have been limited in accuracy and temporal resolution. Additionally, current methods of continuous arterial blood pressure monitoring are via insertion of invasive lines into peripheral arteries. This is fraught with risk of bleeding and complications. Through funding from NUHS-NHIC JointMedTech 2019 and NMRC-CIDA Nov 2020 grants, we have developed a unique sensor that is able to transduce intravascular pressures continuously and non-invasively. Through application of the above sensor the skin at pre-designated sites, we are able to provide a complete haemodynamic monitoring solution for measurement of cardiac filling pressures and output. This system has gone through several iterations, and in its current form, is based off a piezoelectric sensor mounted in a PDMS patch applied to the surface anatomy of the internal jugular vein and peripheral radial artery. Peripheral arterial transduction has shown excellent correlation with blood pressure measurements in early testing. Phantom models of the internal jugular vein with simulated atrial waveforms has also shown excellent ability to transduce and reproduce the above pressures. This system provides a unique opportunity to improve patient outcomes and reduce complication rate and healthcare costs. The aim of this round of grants is to further strengthen the team of engineers, and subsequently, to embark upon clinical trials for correlation against the gold standard of invasive pressure measurements. The mid term goal is for commercialiasation intent after clinical data is acquired.
kw: Cardiology; Right Atrial Pressure; Pulmonary Hypertension; Heart Failure

title: Nanoparticle mediated complete synthesis of biological therapeutics
abs: Proteins and peptides are the most abundant biomolecules, with wide range of functional and structural roles in a living organism's physiology. They are excellent therapeutic candidates due to their high specificity and potency in binding to their targets. Although site-directed mutagenesis has revolutionized therapeutic research by producing macromolecules with novel functions, these methods are limited in that substitutions can only be made between 20 naturally occurring proteinogenic amino acids. As a result, the expanding therapeutic protein market is drawn to chemical synthesis, which allows for the creation of macromolecules with precisely controlled structures and functions. This is accomplished by combining unnatural amino acids and/or post-translational modifications (PTMs) at specific sites. These modifications provide them stability against degradation, increased affinity for receptors, and non-immunogenicity. Despite being a well-established method, chemical synthesis and ligation of polypeptides has remained a difficult endeavor, particularly for the production and folding of large cysteine-rich proteins. Furthermore, any attempt to fold these molecules can frequently result in a loss of functional activity due to aggregation and misfolding. Using our patented platform technology 'thermostable ExoShell (tES),' we have already addressed challenges in folding large cysteine-rich proteins in vitro. The revolutionary nanoparticle has the unique property of enclosing macromolecules, prevent aggregation, and folding them into functional molecules via electrostatic charge complementation. Simply removing the shell allows for the release of a fully functional biological product. We hypothesize that by combining a comprehensive strategy of synthetic chemistry and tES technology, we can synthesize and fold ‘designer’ therapeutic molecules. We will test the utility of these methods to chemically synthesize proteins such as antibodies and nanobodies, tumor suppressor protein p53, and cystine-knot containing proteins. Finally, we will study the role of non-coding amino acids and PTMs in enhancing the therapeutic efficacy of these molecules.
kw: Nanoparticles; Thermostable Exoshells; Chemical Protein Synthesis; Protein Folding; Antibodies; Therapeutics

title: Genetics of Treatment Resistance in Schizophrenia
abs: Schizophrenia is associated with high levels of social burden as well as immeasurable pain and suffering to afflicted individuals and caregivers. About 30% of these individuals fail to respond to treatment, i.e. ‘treatment-resistant schizophrenia’ (TRS). Although clozapine is the gold standard for treating TRS, globally, its utilisation is low and very often delayed, which leads to poorer clinical outcomes and an increased likelihood of developing clozapine-resistant schizophrenia (CRS). Treatment guidelines beyond CRS are sorely lacking; hence, optimising antipsychotic and prompt clozapine use remains the current pragmatic approach to improve clinical outcomes. At present, it is not possible to reliably predict how individuals will respond to antipsychotic treatment. Recent studies have attempted to apply genetics in TRS prediction. In our preliminary analyses on a small but well-characterised dataset from Singapore, we constructed a genetic risk score for TRS that has shown promise in identifying TRS (OR 3.29). However, our findings highlighted the importance of ancestry in the development of valid genetic risk scores for the target population. Therefore, in the present study, we aim to: (1) expand the current biorepository of individuals with schizophrenia to enable further neurobiological investigations of schizophrenia and its pharmacological subtypes, (2) identify genetic variants for both antipsychotic and clozapine resistance in schizophrenia, and (3) develop and validate a locally derived genetic risk score for TRS. These aims can be achieved by enrolling individuals with schizophrenia-spectrum diagnoses, seeking their consent for bio-specimen collections and linkage to electronic medical records, together with genomic sequencing to identify genetic variants. Taken together, this information will augment clinicians’ antipsychotic treatment selection, which will enable a prompt initiation of clozapine in TRS and lead to improved clinical outcomes. This is an important step towards the development and eventual implementation of precision medicine in psychiatry.
kw: Treatment Resistance; Schizophrenia; Genetics

title: A bioengineered probiotic approach for immunoregulation and restoration of skin barrier function in Atopic Dermatitis
abs: Background: Atopic dermatitis (AD), a chronic inflammatory skin condition which affects 20% of the population, is characterized by skin barrier disruption, Th2 cytokine dysregulation and overgrowth of pathogenic microbes. Probiotics are known for their immunoregulatory properties and safety in humans but wild type probiotics have not been shown to be fully effective as AD therapeutics. Methodology: We hypothesize that an engineered probiotic Lactobacillus will attenuate immune dysregulation, restore skin barrier function, and inhibit the growth of opportunistic pathogenic organisms in AD. The engineered Lactobacillus will produce indole-3-aldehyde at a concentration that will trigger immunoregulatory responses via the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (Ahr) pathway; as well as increase expression of the glycerol dehydratase gene, which is responsible for the production of reuterin, a potent antimicrobial compound that inhibits growth of opportunistic pathogenic organisms on the skin. Biological activity of I3A will be confirmed in cytokine-stimulated immortalized keratinocytes (HaCaT cells) in co-culture assays, transcriptomics analysis, targeted RT-qPCR, and quantitative protein analysis. The engineered probiotic’s antipathogenic activity will be assessed through antimicrobial assays, keratinocyte co-cultures and reconstituted human skin models. Skin barrier restoration will be quantified through measuring skin barrier protein expression using RT-qPCR and quantitative proteomics. Efficacy will be validated in a reconstituted human skin (RHS) models and calcipotriol-induced AD murine model to assess its ability to alleviate AD symptoms, eliminate opportunistic pathogens and restore skin barrier function. Significance: This novel therapeutic approach is a valuable adjunct to conventional AD management, which integrates antibacterial effects against major pathogens associated with AD flares, with immunoregulatory properties for restoration of skin barrier health. Its non-invasiveness aids pathways to clinical translation through potential deployment through a skin cream vehicle, minimizing systemic effects and enhancing end-user acceptance.
kw: atopic dermatitis; bioengineering; probiotic; S. aureus; multi-omics; in-vitro and vivo models

title: Singapore Oral Population Health Initiative (SOPI): hypothesis-driven research to inform policymakers and health professionals and improve the oral health of Singaporeans
abs: The Singapore Oral Population Health Initiative (SOPI) aims to close the gap in epidemiological knowledge of the causal links between oral and general, non-communicable chronic diseases (NCD), the impact of population-based oral health policies, interventions, and the current mode of delivery of dental care on the burden of oral diseases in Singapore. The program's findings will directly impact Singaporeans' health and well-being by providing tangible solutions to address the causes and consequences of oral diseases. The aims of this programme are: Aim 1: To investigate the link between oral and NCDs. Hypothesis: Periodontal disease is a risk factor for increased levels of systemic blood markers of inflammation, subclinical signs of atherosclerosis, and CVD morbidity and mortality. Hypothesis: More than acting as disease modifiers, diabetes and dyslipidemia commonly occur as comorbidities, synergically affecting the destruction of the structures around the teeth. Hypothesis: Individuals with oral frailty have a higher risk of being physically frail. Hypothesis: Tooth loss is causally associated with cognitive impairment and brain damage. Aim 2: To assess the impact and cost-effectiveness of policies to reduce the burden of oral diseases. Hypothesis: Front-of-food labeling is cost-effective to significantly prevent dental caries and tooth loss and less significantly to reduce the burden of inflammatory signs of periodontal diseases. Hypothesis: Tobacco control is cost-effective in significantly preventing periodontal disease, tooth loss, and oral cancer. Hypothesis: HPV vaccination is cost-effective and significantly prevents incident mortality of oropharyngeal cancer and less cost-effective in preventing incidence and mortality of oral cancer. Aim 3: Quantify the cost-effectiveness of dental services in Singapore. Hypothesis: The cost-effectiveness of some of the most common dental procedures is questionable and must be redefined. We will use population-based cohort data, datalinkage, nationwide surveys, and administrative data employing cut-edging epidemiological and statistical approaches never used in Singapore in oral health research.
kw: Oral Health; Epidemiology; Health Policies; Causal inference; Cost-efective analyses; Risk factors

title: tReatment Individualisation By eBy stratificatiON in Locoregionally Advanced Nasopharyngeal carcinoma: A multi-arm platform study (RIBBON-LA-01)
abs: RIBBON-LA-01 is a Phase 2 platform clinical trial designed to evaluate the feasibility of treatment individualisation by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) DNA levels, and the efficacy and safety of maintenance tislelizumab and metronomic capecitabine in patients with "high-risk" locoregionally-advanced nasopharyngeal carcinoma (LA-NPC). The study consists of 2 components: (1) to allocate patients with LA-NPC to 3 treatment arms of different intensities based on their EBV DNA levels pre-treatment and post-induction chemotherapy (IC); and (2) to incorporate an open-label, single-arm, Phase 2 trial within the platform for patients who are deemed to be at high-risk of relapse, defined by a persistently detectable EBV DNA following 3 cycles of IC. For Part 1, patients will be allocated to two arms of standard of care (SOC) treatments based on their pre-treatment EBV DNA levels. Patients with a pre-treatment EBV DNA of < 4,000 copies/mL AND T3N0-1 or T4N0 NPC will be assigned to concurrent chemo-radiotherapy (CCRT) with adjuvant chemotherapy (Arm I), while patients with a pre-treatment EBV DNA of >4,000 copies/mL OR N2-3 or T4N+ NPC will be assigned to upfront IC. For patients assigned to upfront IC, patients with UNDETECTABLE EBV DNA following 3 cycles of IC will receive CCRT with metronomic capecitabine (Arm II). For the third group of patients who have DETECTABLE EBV DNA following 3 cycles of IC, they will receive maintenance tislelizumab and metronomic capecitabine for 12 months following the completion of CCRT (Arm III). We plan to recruit a total of 140 subjects; 16 subjects to Arm I, and 62 subjects each to Arms II and III. Primary endpoint is 2-year disease-free survival (DFS). We will also be evaluating a novel biological objective response rate (bORR) as a secondary endpoint for its surrogacy to DFS. This will expedite go-no go decisions for future investigational regimens in LA-NPC.
kw: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma; Individualised treatment; Precision medicine; Epstein-barr virus (EBV); Liquid biopsy; Immune checkpoint blockade; Immunotherapy; Tislelizumab

title: Singapore-Malaysia Renal Trials in Nephrotic Syndrome (SMaRT-NS): Dupilumab maintenance therapy in steroid idiopathic nephrotic syndrome
abs: Idiopathic nephrotic syndrome (INS) is the most common glomerular disease in childhood and acquired cause of paediatric chronic kidney disease. While most children respond to high-dose steroids, 50% have a frequently relapsing course often persisting into adulthood, leading to irreversible steroid toxicity. Steroid-sparing agents currently in use have limited effectiveness or significant safety concerns with prolonged use. We have demonstrated that (i) T-cell IL-13 production is increased during nephrotic relapse, (ii) IL-13, signaling via the IL-13 receptor on podocytes, results in rearrangement of the podocyte cytoskeleton which normally maintains slit diaphragm integrity, and (iii) overexpression of IL-13 in a rat model recapitulates clinical and molecular features of INS. Dupilumab is a subcutaneously bioavailable monoclonal antibody that antagonizes the IL-13 receptor. It is licensed for use in asthma and eczema, including in children, with an excellent safety profile. We hypothesise that Dupilumab will be an effective steroid-sparing agent in INS. We propose a multi-centre double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial to investigate the efficacy of Dupilumab in maintaining nephrotic remission. Patients between 5-18 years old with frequently relapsing or steroid-dependent INS will be recruited while in remission, and randomized to either receive Dupilumab (per licensed dosing for eczema) or placebo. Existing immunosuppression will be weaned per protocol starting 2-weeks after the first dose. The primary efficacy outcome is time to relapse. Secondary endpoints include average urine protein excretion during the study, reduction in maintenance immunosuppression, and translational endpoints. Based on a relative risk reduction of 0.56 (similar to calcineurin inhibitors), we require a sample size of 66 patients (β=0.2, α=0.05), which is realistic in this multi-centre study. Participating centres have ongoing collaborations as part of the regional nephrotic syndrome study network (DRAGoN). Importance: Dupilumab, if effective, will be the first steroid-sparing agent in INS that is effective and safe for long-term use.
kw: Dupilumab, interleukin-13, nephrotic syndrome

title: A novel individualized connectome-guided approach for precision intermittent theta burst stimulation for depression: a double blind, randomized controlled trial
abs: Intermittent theta burst stimulation (iTBS) is an approved transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) therapy for treatment resistant depression. Standard iTBS utilizes a one-spot-fits-all anatomical approach to determine a prefrontal stimulation location. However, anatomical localization does not account for inter-individual variability in brain connectome. Recent studies suggest that using individualized functional connectome guided stimulation locations can yield significantly improved accelerated iTBS treatment efficacy in Caucasian populations. Given brain differences between races, these approaches must be validated in local populations. Furthermore, we recently developed a machine learning algorithm that yielded more reliable functional network localization than previous approaches, which might further improve target localization. We propose a randomized, double-blind study to compare the treatment outcome of (1) our novel individualized connectome-guided localization and (2) standard anatomically-guided localization for accelerated iTBS among Asian patients with depression. 70 patients will undergo resting-state functional MRI (resting-fMRI) scanning to identify individualized connectome-guided locations. The patients will then be randomized to receive either individualized connectome-guided or anatomically-guided accelerated iTBS with 10 treatment sessions every day for 5 consecutive days. In both groups, iTBS will be applied with a precise robotic neuronavigational system. Patients will also undergo resting-fMRI scanning after treatment to compare iTBS induced connectivity changes between the two groups. Patients and assessors will be blinded to treatment assignment. The primary outcome is the response rate defined by ≥50% decrease of the Montgomery-Asberg Depression Rating (MADRS) Scale. Exploratory outcomes of changes in patients’ quality of life, general functioning and resting-fMRI will also be assessed till three months after treatment. Health economic evaluation will be conducted to assess the impact on health services utilization and associated costs. This study will determine whether individualized connectome-guided accelerated iTBS is superior to anatomically-guided accelerated iTBS for patients with depression. The optimal treatment system for this population can be immediately translated to practice.
kw: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation; precision medicine; Connectomics; depression; treatment response

title: Development and preliminary evaluation of a brief Stepped-care Telehealth Early intervention Protocol for Adolescent (STEP-A) emergency department patients with panic-related anxiety: An early stage multi-site single-arm hybrid effectiveness/implementation trial in Singapore
abs: Background: Approximately 33% of adolescent Emergency Department (ED) patients with noncardiac chest pain meet criteria for panic-related anxiety (i.e., panic attacks or panic disorder), but they are rarely diagnosed or treated in the ED. Missed diagnoses and a lack of early interventions typically result in worsening of panic symptoms, frequent re-admissions, and costly referrals to cardiologists or adolescent medicine providers. Early interventions delivered via videoconference have the potential to reduce costs and unnecessary attendances at the ED while simultaneously improving quality of life and functioning for adolescents with panic-related anxiety. Our team has developed a brief stepped-care protocol consisting of psychoeducation and cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) for adults with panic-related anxiety, but it has not been tested for telehealth delivery in adolescent ED patients. Objectives: The proposed project has the following specific aims: Aim 1) to utilize treatment co-design principles to modify an existing brief stepped-care intervention protocol and improve its appropriateness for telehealth delivery to adolescents with panic-related anxiety; Aim 2) to conduct a multi-site single-arm open trial to evaluate the preliminary clinical effectiveness of the co-designed STEP-A intervention for reducing severity of panic symptoms in a sample of adolescent ED patients; and Aim 3) to explore early stage implementation-related outcomes from multiple stakeholder perspectives. Methods: Participants for Aims 1-3 will be recruited from ED’s located within the SingHealth Regional Health System, the largest public healthcare cluster in Singapore. A multi-method design (quantitative and qualitative) will be used to evaluate the preliminary effectiveness of the STEP-A intervention and to evaluate potential for implementation (i.e., appropriateness, acceptability, feasibility, fidelity, costs) from the perspectives of patients/caregivers and providers. Significance: The results will be used to further improve the STEP-A intervention, develop appropriate implementation strategies, and build the foundation for a nation-wide study to evaluate its effectiveness using a randomized controlled trial design.
kw: panic attack; panic disorder; early intervention; adolescent; emergency department

title: ENABLE-SG (Educate, Nurture, Advise, Before Life Ends for Singapore) as a proactive palliative care model: Evaluation and implementation preparation
abs: The current model of interdisciplinary specialist palliative care focuses on supporting patients with advanced cancer who have complex problems in the last weeks of life. This model has two big problems: First, palliative care is delivered very late in the patient’s disease trajectory. Second, as the initiation of palliative care is triggered by uncontrolled symptoms typically in a time of crisis, patients and families are often in distress and end up being passive recipients of services. Models of palliative care ought to move beyond the current reactionary illness-stress paradigm to a proactive health-wellness approach that is integrated early in the patient’s serious illness trajectory. ENABLE (Educate, Nurture, Advise, Before Life Ends) is a proactive early palliative care model that aims to coach patients and caregivers on how to cope effectively with serious illness via developing self-management skills, including problem-solving, decision-making, advance care planning, symptom management, self-care, communication, and life review. Although ENABLE has demonstrated effectiveness in the U.S., we do not know whether or not ENABLE would be effective when implemented in contexts that have different organisational, social, and cultural norms. The PI and her team have piloted a culturally-tailored ENABLE-SG care model in Singapore and found it to be both acceptable and feasible. This proposal aims to test the effectiveness of the adapted ENABLE-SG model in patients with recently diagnosed advanced cancer and collect data on real-world implementation. To evaluate effectiveness, we will conduct a randomized wait-list controlled trial comparing clinical outcomes at 6 months between those receiving early ENABLE-SG and wait-listed individuals receiving usual care (the wait-list group will begin receiving ENABLE-SG at 6 months post-randomization). To evaluate ways to improve implementation, we will use the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) to underpin this part of the study and systematically identify processes that influence implementation outcomes.
kw: Palliative care; Neoplasms; Quality of life; Self-management; Telemedicine; Caregivers

title: Gastric Bypass via Natural Orifice Trans-luminal Endoscopic Surgical (NOTES) approach: Towards clinical translation
abs: Bariatric gastric bypass surgery has significantly improved metabolic outcome of persons with type II diabetes mellitus (DM) and obesity over the last decades. Despite its effectiveness, only 1% of eligible patients underwent bariatric surgery in North America. The primary reason for this low take-up rate is due to significant mortality (0.5-1%) and morbidity associated with traditional laparoscopic bariatric surgery. Endoscopic bariatric therapies (EBT) are emerging as an effective alternative approach for managing overweight. Unfortunately, most of the current endoscopic procedures only restrict gastric volume without altering the underlying metabolism that is seen in gastric bypass surgical patients. We have developed a novel endoscopic procedure to efficiently replicate the anatomical features and physiological effects of gastric bypass surgery via a flexible endoscopy, termed Natural Orifice Trans-luminal Endoscopic Gastric Bypass surgery (NOTES-GB). We have successfully performed & published the feasibility studies of NOTES-GB in both porcine and cadaveric models. The aim of this project is to validate the durability and efficacy of NOTES-GB up to 7-months post-procedure. Fifteen female miniature pigs will be fed obesogenic diet and then randomised to control, endoscopic sleeve gastroplasy (current best endoscopic therapy) or NOTES-GB. We will compare the metabolic outcomes of plasma glucose, insulin, GLP-1 & liver panels at 0 (prior to surgery), and 1, 3, and 6 months after surgery. We will assess oral Glucose Tolerance Test, insulin resistance & metabolomics at 6-months, and perform histopathological assessment of liver at necropsy. The durability and patency of anastomosis will be evaluated using endoscopy and contrast study at 6-months and necropsy 4 weeks later. NOTES-GB meets the requirements of an ideal bariatric intervention: painless, scar-less, safe, reversible, effective, shorter hospitalization and lower cost. Clinical application of NOTES-GB can potentially extend beyond obesity, including non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, infertility, dyslipidemia, hypertension and cardiovascular complications.
kw: NOTES; gastric bypass; Natural Orifice; Metabolomic; Bariatric; Metabolic Surgery

title: Functional evaluation of Parkinson’s disease-associated SMPD1 variants in substantia nigra cell types
abs: Parkinson’s disease (PD) is a common age-related neurodegenerative disorder with the hallmark of aggregated α-synuclein protein inclusions (Lewy bodies) in the midbrain. We recently uncovered exome-wide significant association of rare pathogenic variants in SMPD1 (sphingomyelin phosphodiesterase 1) with PD. The function of SMPD1 in the midbrain and the potential functional aberration caused by SMDP1 genetic variants require exploration. We hypothesize that PD-associated SMPD1 variants adversely affect activity level of the encoded acid sphingomyelinase protein (ASM) in converting sphingomyelin into ceramide in physiologically relevant cell types, and contribute to increased α-synuclein aggregation. We propose to evaluate the functional effects of PD-associated rare pathogenic SMPD1 variants that result in catalytic deficiency and potential localization deficiency to ascertain their contribution to PD pathogenesis. We will first evaluate which cell types in the substantia nigra express SMPD1 by analysing publicly available single cell transcriptomics datasets. We will then establish canonical SMPD1 and SMPD1 variant-expressing cell models based on available cell lines or primary cells. We will assess the effect of the PD associated SMPD1 variants on ceramide metabolism within the background of substantia nigra cell type(s) and its contribution to PD pathogenesis by assaying SMPD1 variant-encoded ASM activity and its cellular localization, the potential alteration of sphingomyelin and ceramide species and levels, effects on metabolomics profile, and α-synuclein total protein and α-synuclein aggregate levels. These assays will allow inferences to be made between ASM aberrant activity and PD pathology. Our work addresses gaps in the field by focusing on defining SMPD1 function in the context of disease relevant genetic variants and cell types, delves into systemic assessment of alterations in ceramide metabolism due to altered SMPD1 function and the eventual consequence on PD pathology. Our findings will thus be impactful for PD research as well as the general field of neuroscience.
kw: Parkinson's disease; Lysosome

title: Gut microbiota-derived metabolites: the link between gut microbiota and development of gestational diabetes
inst: IHDP - Institute for Human Development and Potential
abs: Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is affecting approximately 16.7% of pregnant women worldwide, which leads to various obstetrical and metabolic complications in both mothers and neonates. Diagnosis and prevention of GDM in early pregnancy or even preconception could reduce its incidence and associated morbidities and enhance human potential. Accumulating evidence implies that gut microbiota plays a pivotal or even a causative role in GDM pathogenesis. Nonetheless, the underlying mechanisms of how gut microbiota involves in the onset of GDM remain obscure. Gut microbiota-derived metabolites have been proven to help enrich the knowledge of microbiota-host interactions in obesity and type 2 diabetes. Several recent studies identified microbial metabolites such as trimethylamine-N-oxide to be associated with GDM during pregnancy. However, previous studies failed to characterize the dynamic remodeling process of the gut microbiome and its metabolites before the onset of GDM due to a scarcity of longitudinal studies following from preconception until late pregnancy. Therefore, the overall objective of the proposal is to define the role of gut microbiota-derived metabolites in the link between gut microbiota and the development of GDM in the local longitudinal preconception cohort S-PRESTO. Hypothesis: We hypothesize that dysbiosis of gut microbiota-derived metabolites due to imbalanced gut microbiota at preconception or early pregnancy leads to insulin resistance and is involved in the development of GDM. Specific objectives: 1. To establish the trajectory of the gut microbiota-derived metabolites from preconception to late trimester and identify the factors affecting microbial metabolites 2. To identify the gut microbiota-derived metabolites associated with insulin resistance and GDM 3. To assess the interplay between key gut microbes, microbial metabolites, and insulin resistance in the development of GDM with an integrative multi-omics approach
kw: Gestational diabetes mellitus; gut microbiota; metabolomics; integrative multi-omics; machine learning; longitudinal cohort

title: Novel Gastrin-releasing peptide receptor (GRPR) and Integrin αVβ3 Dual-targeting Probes for Radiotheranostics of Prostate Cancer
abs: Accurate diagnostic and staging of prostate cancer (PCa) is of utmost significance for effective therapy, which currently largely relies on radiolabeled prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA)-based theranostic pairs. However, pitfalls exist in diagnosing and treating PCa with low to nil PSMA expression. This has triggered the development of other theranostic molecules for PSMA-independent PCa targets. One example is the gastrin-releasing peptide receptor (GRPR)- and integrin αVβ3- dual targeting heterodimer RGD-GRPR agonist (RGD-BBN) designed by our lab. Although it has been translated into its first-in-human application for imaging purposes, the suboptimal metabolic stability, compromised tumor retention and fast clearance prevented effective treatment of PCa. This project aims to develop an RGD-GRPR antagonist by substituting the BBN in the heterodimer with its antagonist counterpart to develop a better GRPR- and integrin αVβ3- dual targeting heterodimer for PCa theranostics, and further modify the structure of RGD-GRPR antagonist through multiple strategies, including cyclization of GRPR antagonist peptides, PEGylation, insertion of cell penetration peptide sequence and selection of the well-suited macrocyclic chelator. In this study, we propose a library of 60 RGD-GRPR antagonist heterodimers to be labeled and tested. 30 compounds with the best docking potentials will be selected for further in vitro cellular binding assay and in vivo screening, giving rise to 2 potent 68Ga-labeled RGD-GRPR antagonists that will provide superior stability and specificity, enhanced tumor uptake and tumor-to-background contrast in PET and SPECT imaging. The 177Lu-labeled RGD-GRPR antagonist heterodimer with the best therapeutic effect will be selected and further evaluated. This new dual-targeting RGD-GRPR antagonist is expected to have remarkable metabolic stability, specificity, and prolonged tumor retention for diagnosing and treating PSMA-negative PCa, and early-stage PCa; due to these predicted advantages and a strong scientific rationale, translational studies are likely to be initiated in the future.

title: Cancer-specific antigen discovery platform using Ribosome profiling
abs: Cancer immunotherapies have become increasingly popular with significant improvements in patient survival and life quality compared to traditional therapies. Immunotherapies like CAR-T cells, mRNA vaccines and monoclonal antibodies all feature an essential commonality: They require identifying tumour-specific peptides, and subsequently epitopes, to target the cancer and trigger a specific cytotoxic response. While these treatments show high-efficacy, non-specific expression of these peptides can lead to a severe toxic response. One major obstacle remains; The accurate identification of peptide inventories in both cancer and healthy cells to determine highly-specific peptides in cancers. Current techniques to identify peptides such as proteomics and RNA-seq come with inherent limitations in being able to determine the complete repository of peptides. Ribosome profiling (Ribo-seq) allows a high-resolution view of RNA translation and thus is a powerful tool to determine protein inventories. I recently developed the largest-to-date atlas for RNA translation in humans using Ribo-seq. Building on this, my central goal is to develop a platform technology for the identification of cancer-specific peptides. To achieve this, I have three aims: 1) to profile RNA translation of clinical cancer samples, 2) To develop computational algorithms to generate peptide inventories using comparative translatomics, and 3) To identify and prioritize single- and pan-cancer specific-antigens. This study will provide insights into tumour-specific antigens that have been previously missed due to lower resolution of peptide identification as well as allow an accurate view on specificity of antigens at an unprecedented level across the healthy and cancer cells. The outcome of this study will be a cancer repository of RNA translation and peptide inventories that are highly-specific to a given cancer or groups of cancer for both personalized and generalized therapies. Thus, taking me a step closer towards my long-term goal of developing powerful immunotherapies with high efficacy and minimum toxicity.
kw: RNA; Translation; Ribo-seq; Tumor-specific antigen; Cancer; Immunotherapy;

title: Expanding the Toolbox for Therapeutic RNA Editing of Inherited Retinal Disease
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Stargardt disease (STGD1) is one of the most common types of rare inherited retinal disease (IRD) that leads to early visual impairment, affecting roughly 1 in 10,000 people globally. However, there are currently no FDA-approved treatments for STGD1. STGD1 arises from a biallelic point mutation in the ABCA4 gene that encodes for a transporter protein found on the membrane of retinal pigment epithelium. Point mutations that result in defective ABCA4 leads to accumulation of toxic N-retinylidene adducts in the lumen. If left untreated, prolonged accumulation of adducts can impair photoreceptor function and lead to irreversible loss of central vision. Given that ~21% of the mutations associated with STGD1 are G-to-A conversions, ADAR-mediated RNA editing could be used for early-stage adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) conversion within the ABCA4 transcript to restore expression of healthy ABCA4 protein. To overcome the challenges of variable editing efficiencies, RNA instability, and off-target activity, this proposal aims to generate stable and programmable guide RNAs for highly efficient A-to-I correction of STGD1-associated mutations. The number of disease targets available for RNA correction is partly limited to the constrained preference of endogenous RNA-acting adenosine deaminases (ADAR). Previously engineered ADAR variants are highly active but prone to off-target activity. To increase RNA targeting specificity, we will apply AI-assisted protein design to engineer ADAR variants that are specific to a single 5’-NA context, in which N=A, U, C or G. RNA editing is currently limited to A-to-I or cytosine-to-uracil conversions. To correct mutations arising from insertions, deletions, and base transversions, protein replacement therapy could be used in place of RNA editing. We plan to develop a new protein-based method to generate long stable mRNAs in vitro for robust translation. These efforts will collectively accelerate the field of therapeutic RNA editing and RNA-based drugs against a variety of ocular and non-ocular genetic disorders.
kw: RNA editing; Stargardt; ADAR; circular RNA; AI protein design; inherited retinal disease

title: AI deep learning approach for predicting cancer immunotherapy response in hepatocellular carcinoma using marker-free H&E images
abs: Our main goal is to develop an effective, clinically feasible, and extensible artificial intelligence (AI) solution for predicting cancer immunotherapy (IO) response, through novel strategies that (1) measures and localizes 30 tissue immune markers in the same tumor microenvironment (TME) using high-plex multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF), (2) accounts for the spatial characteristics of IO-response determinants, and (3) enables hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-based in-silico molecular staining of the 30 tissue markers via deep learning (DL). Using the baseline tissues obtained from 100 IO-treated hepatocellular carcinoma, and the hypotheses that (1) multiple tumor immune factors and their spatial relationship collectively impact tumor response to IO, and (2) the tumor immune factors manifest as differential histomorphological features in H&E images, we propose three specific aims as follows. (Aim 1) Identifying novel spatial biomarkers using 30-plex mIF. (Aim 2) Building DL models for predicting mIF-quantified markers from H&E images. (Aim 3) Building an IO-response prediction model using in-silico spatial biomarkers constructed from DL-predicted tissue markers, via machine learning. The performance of the IO-response prediction model will be compared with existing non-spatial biomarkers including PD1/PD-L1 overexpression. Our proposed study represents an important step to address the bottleneck issue of IO, i.e., the lack of effective biomarkers to avoid unnecessary toxicities and treatment delay for non-responsive treatment. The proposed study offers important clinical significance: (1) the ability to increase the availability of multi-marker data using low-cost and ubiquitous H&E images enabled by DL, ensuring clinical feasibility, (2) enhanced IO-response prediction accuracy through accounting for TME spatial characteristics omitted by existing biomarkers, (3) the ability to map multiple molecular data onto the same H&E image, enabling flexible and extensible usage of the spatial data, and (4) the ability to discover novel IO determinants as potential new therapeutic targets given the de novo nature of the in-silico spatial biomarkers.
kw: Deep learning; spatial biomarker; multiplexed immunoprofiling; cancer immunotherapy; molecular staining; marker-free H&E image

title: Investigating the role of COVID19 vaccine in regulating tumor associated macrophages and related trained immunity for re-invigorating their anti-tumor response
abs: Besides controlling adaptive immunity, vaccines can also regulate the long-term response of innate immune cells (such as monocytes, macrophages) through a phenomenon known as trained immunity. Considering this and the fact that macrophages are key regulators of tumor immunity, we hypothesized that vaccines should regulate the functions of these cells in a cancer setting and thereby influence tumor immunity. This idea is timely and relevant in view of the widespread COVID19 vaccination which also includes cancer patients. We aim to investigate the role of COVID19 vaccine in regulating tumor associated macrophages (TAMs), their associated trained immunity and how this influences cancer progression and treatment. The effect of COVID19 vaccine (Pfizer BNT162b2) on in vitro generated human TAMs (e.g. for pancreatic and lung cancer) will be studies at the transcriptional, epigenetic and functional levels using state-of-the-art technologies (RNA-seq, ATAC-seq, deep immunophenotyping) to ascertain vaccine-induced changes on TAMs and how it’s impact their pro/anti-tumor functions. Second, we will perform mechanistic studies to identify pathways of vaccine-induced alteration (or training) in TAMs. Third, vaccine-induced alterations in TAM signature and key mechanistic findings will be validated in vivo in preclinical tumor models (e.g. pancreatic cancer, lung cancer) and it’s effect on modulating standard-of-care treatment regimens. We believe that the findings from the present proposal will have potential biological/clinical relevance as it should yield i) mechanistic targets for COVID19 vaccine-induced trained immunity that can be used for rationale design of combinatorial treatment to re-invigorate TAMs for enhanced anti-tumor immunity and ii) COVID19 vaccine-induced myeloid signatures for assessing trained immunity in vaccinated cancer patients and hence any need for boosting anti-tumor immunity. Such findings are of direct relevance to Human Health Potential.
kw: Tumor associated macrophages, Trained Immunity, Cancer Immunology

title: Development of temperature-responsive pseudorotaxane carriers for delivery of Camptothecin
abs: The goal of this proposal is to design, develop, and utilize pseudorotaxane (PR) platform to furnish temperature-controlled delivery of anticancer drug – Camptothecin (CPT). We believe the thermal-sensitive PR-based drug carriers will display a unique potential and prospective application in targeted thermo-chemotherapy, which contributes to increasing drug concentration, enhancing drug efficiency, lowering effective dose and alleviating side effects. Our first hypothesis is that the disassembly of a PR-CPT conjugate can be controlled by structural modification and temperature change. This is proposed on the basis of our preliminary work (unpublished work). Secondly, we hypothesize that the bioactivity of CPT can be caged by the mechanically interlocked architecture of PR and then released with the disassembly of the PR-CPT conjugates in vitro and in vivo. Thus, this type of molecular architectures could be developed into a novel controllable Drug Delivery System (DDS). This hypothesis is based on our preliminary data (unpublished work). Specifically, the proposal aims at: (1) designing and constructing temperature responsive PR-CPT conjugates (underexplored); (2) PR-CPT thermal release test and cell viability assay (underexplored); (3) In vivo imaging, biodistribution and thermo-chemotherapy of PR-CPT (underexplored). The successful demonstration of the proposed project would 1) provide a new platform for directed chemotherapy allowing “real time” drug release at the tumor site in vitro and in vivo rather than systemic chemotherapy; 2) provide potential and prospective application of CPT in targeted thermo-chemotherapy, which contributes to increasing drug concentration, enhancing drug efficiency, lowering effective dose and alleviating side effects.
kw: drug delivery system, temperature controlled, pseudorotaxane, Camptothecin, anticancer drug, thermo-chemotherapy

title: Functional identification of small molecule suppressors for deficient AMPK activity with cellular aging
abs: Metabolism is linked with cellular aging. The decline of metabolic functions with aging is associated with several age-related ailments, including cancer, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, neurodegeneration, and sarcopenia. One of the major regulators of metabolism is AMPK (AMP-activated protein kinase) which is highly conserved and integrates with multiple biological processes in the cells. AMPK redirects metabolism towards increased catabolism and decreased anabolism through the phosphorylation of key proteins in multiple pathways, including Target of Rapamycin Complex 1 (TORC1), lipid homeostasis, glycolysis, and mitochondrial homeostasis. Emerging studies indicate that AMPK activity and AMPK responsiveness decrease with age, which may explain the altered metabolic regulation, resulting in unnecessary product accumulation due to reduced autophagic processes, an increase in oxidative stress, and decreased resistance to cellular stress. Such changes eventually increase the vulnerability to age-related pathologies in the older population that affect health for the remaining life. Since AMPK activity declined with age, that affected cellular metabolism and connected several intracellular signaling pathways that require proper functioning of the cells. To keep the cells healthy for proper functioning while aging requires interventions that suppress the deficient activity of AMPK. We have identified >30 small molecules (FDA-approved drugs and natural products) that rescue the accelerated aging of yeast deficient in AMPK activity, a powerful model organism to study cellular aging. The major goal of this research proposal is to characterize and elucidate the mechanism of action of identified suppressors using various functional and integrated analyses. Subsequently, we will evaluate the efficacy of suppressors in normal human dermal fibroblasts (NHDF) and lung fibroblasts (WI-38) that have a finite lifespan. Subsequently, we will evaluate the activity of potential suppressors in the accelerated aging model system Hutchinson–Gilford progeria syndrome (HGPS) cells.
kw: Metabolism, AMPK, Aging, Anti-aging, Small molecule suppressors, Multiomics

title: Deploying omipalisib as an anti-cancer drug in head and neck cancer
abs: This project will collect preclinical data on using omipalisib to reduce tumour burden and metastasis in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC). HNSCC primary tumours can seriously impair speech, swallowing, and breathing. Metastasis is common and a major cause of treatment failure. Dysregulated signalling through the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) is prevalent and activates pro-oncogenic regulatory pathways including phosphoinositide-3-kinase (PI3K)/AKT and extracellular signal-related kinase (ERK). We have also identified a third pathway through which EGF signalling drives metastasis in HNSCC. The Follistatin-like 1 (FSTL1) transcript functions as a molecular switch regulating keratinocyte migration. It encodes two alternative products with opposite functions – pro-migratory FSTL1 protein and anti-migratory microRNA miR-198. In HNSCC, persistent EGF signalling downregulates miR-198 and upregulates FSTL1 encouraging cell invasion. Omipalisib, a potent inhibitor of PI3K/AKT signalling, also blocks ERK signalling. Furthermore, our preliminary data indicate that omipalisib concurrently restores miR-198, downregulates pro-invasive genes, and impedes HNSCC cell invasion. This proposal will fully characterize omipalisib’s effect on survival and proliferation in a panel of ATCC and patient cell lines. Dose-response studies measuring cell viability, cell cycle arrest, and apoptosis will be performed and LC50 values for each cell line established. We will also investigate omipalisib at sub-LC50 concentrations to assess its use as adjuvant anti-metastatic therapy. Functional effects of omipalisib on invasion will be assayed using 2D and 3D migration assays and microfluidic models. In vivo data will be gathered using an orthotopic mouse model. Data collected from this project will secure industrial investment for future drug development including formulation and drug delivery. I also intend to expand this project with future grant applications exploring omipalisib’s use in other squamous cell cancers. This research is in line with the HHP goal of maximising human potential by protecting health amidst population ageing and concomitant increases in cancer incidence.
kw: cancer; metastasis; drug discovery; HNSCC

title: Repurposing belinostat analogues as a novel therapeutic for atopic dermatitis
abs: Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a highly prevalent chronic inflammatory skin condition. A defective skin barrier and exposure to allergens are known to initiate the development of AD. A rational approach to treat AD that focuses on restoring barrier function is therefore needed. We identified a microRNA, miR-335, as a key-driver of keratinocyte differentiation and cornification, a requisite for the establishment of a healthy skin barrier. miR-335 exerts this effect by directly repressing SOX6. Recruiting SMARCA complex components, SOX6 suppresses epidermal differentiation and epigenetically silences the critical genes involved in keratinocyte differentiation. In AD lesional skin, miR-335 expression is aberrantly lost. SOX6 is consequently abnormally expressed throughout the epidermis, where it impairs skin barrier development. miR-335 is epigenetically regulated by histone deacetylases (HDACs), and drug screening has led to the identification of belinostat, a broad spectrum HDAC inhibitor, which can restore epidermal miR-335 expression in pre-clinical human skin models. Our objective is to repurpose belinostat as a therapeutic for AD and develop a topical cream. We hypothesize that analogues of belinostat, which can be easily degraded upon entering the bloodstream, can be used to treat AD with high efficacy and minimal toxicity. We will achieve our objective through the following specific aims. Specific Aim-1: Design and validation of belinostat analogues Specific Aim-2: Identification and validation of belinostat analogues in-vitro, ex-vivo, and in-vivo. Specific Aim-3: Formulation and clinical assessment of the lead analogues. We anticipate this novel therapeutic to effectively rescue the defective barrier in AD, leading to improved patient outcomes.
kw: Atopic dermatitis; belinostat; analogues; miR-335

title: Matrix metalloproteinase inhibition to improve neurological and mortality outcomes in Central Nervous System Tuberculosis
abs: Tuberculosis remains a leading infectious cause of death. Central nervous system tuberculosis (CNS-TB) even with effective anti-TB treatment has mortality rates of up to 50%. In CNS-TB, the activity of pathogenic host matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) is unopposed to tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMPs), resulting in a matrix-degrading phenotype. We previously showed that adjunctive MMP inhibition using doxycycline, a widely available and cheap drug, with standard TB treatment improved murine survival. Now, we will perform a Phase 2 double-blind randomized-controlled trial (RCT) of adjunctive doxycycline versus placebo with standard TB treatment and steroids for 8 weeks. We hypothesize that in patients with CNS-TB, the addition of doxycycline to standard-of-care (SOC) improves clinical outcomes. The specific aims are to determine: 1) Whether the primary outcome of mortality rates or severe neurological deficits in CNS-TB patients in the doxycycline arm improves at 8 weeks. 2) Whether MMPs and inflammatory gene transcriptomics in the doxycycline arm are reduced. 3) Whether concurrent SOC treatment and doxycycline for CNS-TB are safe. This is a multinational study with sites spanning Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia. 190 CNS-TB patients will be randomised to receive either 8 weeks of doxycycline or placebo with concurrent follow-up. Neurological deficits is defined using a modified Rankin scale score of 3 or higher to measure disability or dependence in the daily activities. Plasma and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) MMPs and TIMPs will be measured by luminex bead array technology. The functional activity of CSF MMPs will be assessed using Dye-quenched (DQ) Gelatin degradation. Inflammatory gene transcripts will be measured using whole-blood bulk RNA sequencing and single-cell RNA sequencing. CSF will be profiled using single-cell RNA sequencing. The results will be a platform for a Phase 3 randomised-controlled trial of CNS-TB to positively impact clinical practice and international guidelines.
kw: central nervous system tuberculosis, randomised controlled trial

title: Therapeutic targeting of the pulmonary microbiome in chronic respiratory disease
abs: Our understanding of the pulmonary microbiome has advanced over the past decade. The lungs contain varied and functional microbial communities with roles in maintaining health and promoting disease. This “respiratory ecosystem” represents an unsung source of biological and clinical heterogeneity across patients with acute and chronic lung disease. Unlike other sources of heterogeneity, such as comorbidities and host genetics, the pulmonary microbiome is readily modifiable by clinical interventions such as antibiotics and corticosteroids. Use of a single course of antibiotics has demonstrated acute and persistent effects on the gut microbiome including altered diversity, resistance, and composition, collectively termed “antibiotic scarring”, a phenomenon that remains unexplored in the lung. In work performed by the PI, understanding microbial networks in the lung and across the gut-lung axis, through integration of inter-kingdom microbiomes is critical to understanding microbial interactions (the interactome) which strongly predicts clinical outcomes, exacerbations, and explains antibiotic-related effects, more so than traditional models evaluating only microbial identity and implicating individual microbes rather than microbial interactions to explain clinical phenomena. In this proposal, we extend our studies to determine the effect of commonly prescribed agents in respiratory medicine: antibiotics and corticosteroids, on the pulmonary microbiome. We further assess effects on the pulmonary interactome, antimicrobial resistome and the gut-lung axis using a combination of next generation sequencing, systems biology, state-of-the-art analytical pipelines, clinical trial sampling and humanized gnotobiotic mouse models subjected to “paired” gut-lung microbiota transplantation. To realize the pulmonary microbiome as a potential “treatable trait”, this novel translational study represents a key first step in understanding how standard therapeutic interventions, commonly used in respiratory disease, affect the pulmonary microbiome, with the longer-term ambition to deliver fresh approaches for precision intervention, prescribing and improved clinical trial stratification based on microbial dynamics.
kw: microbiome; COPD; bronchiectasis; gut-lung axis; metagenomics

title: A bioinspired and photoprotective scaffold for retinal stem cell therapy
abs: The incidence of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)-related retinal degeneration diseases including age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is growing with an aging population. There is still a lack of treatment options for end-stage AMD patients. Given that AMD is characterized principally by retinal cell loss, retinal stem cell therapy represents an intuitive therapeutic approach for patients. The survival of transplanted RPE cells is sensitive to the microenvironment, especially the laminated extracellular matrix between RPE and choroid, called Bruch’s membrane (BrM). At the disease state, BrM lacks adhesion due to age-related deposition of anti-adhesive molecules, which results in poor transplanted cell attachment and survival. One unmet clinical need is the absence of suitable biomaterial to support RPE growth as healthy BrM. Here, we hypothesize to use tissue engineering strategy to improve cell survival and function by transplanting polarized RPE monolayer on bioactive scaffolds. Limitations of current RPE scaffolds include (1) Incompatible structural and mechanical properties. (2) Lack of bioactive function. (3) Lack of long-term biocompatible evidence in large animals. To overcome these, we aim to construct a bioinspired scaffold with a photo-protective feature that structurally mimics endogenous BrM to support retinal cell growth, delivery, and long-term survival. Aim 1: Use 3D print + electrospinning to fabricate a bioinspired scaffold with sufficient mechanical strength to support cell growth and delivery. Aim 2: Incorporate photoprotective functions with melanin to reduce light damage to RPE. Aim 3: Validate long-term biocompatibility of RPE with designed scaffolds in large animal models. The current proposal builds on the team’s established track records in RPE scaffold fabrications, retinal stem cell biology, and retinal cell transplants in large animal models. If successful, this proposal represents an unprecedented opportunity to validate a bioinspired and biocompatible RPE scaffold with the ultimate goal of enhancing retinal cell therapy outcomes.
kw: Age-related macular degeneration, Retinal pigment epithelium, 3D print, electrospinning, stem cell therapy, non-human primates

title: Brown Fat as Therapeutic Strategy for Obesity and Associated Metabolic Diseases via Functional Food/Nutraceutical Approach - Molecular Mechanisms of Pentacyclic Triterpenes (BRACE)
abs: Obesity and associated metabolic diseases including type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypertension and cardiovascular diseases have become fast-spreading public health problems worldwide. PPARγ agonists, Thiazolidinediones (TZDs) developed as synthetic insulin-sensitizing drugs have been used for the treatment of type 2 diabetes. However, the use of such drugs has been restricted due to the adverse side effects. Thus, there is an unmet and urgent need to develop a novel class of PPARγ agonists that can retain the beneficial effects while minimize the side effects. Ursolic acid (UA), a natural pentacyclic triterpenic acid present in a variety of traditional medicinal herbs and fruits has a wide spectrum of pharmacological activities including anti-obesity and anti-diabetic effects. UA has been shown to increase energy expenditure and brown fat mass but the underlying mechanism is not known. In this study, we discovered that UA directly binds to PPARγ and acts as a partial agonist to promote its transcriptional activity. We have determined the structure of PPARγ in complex with UA, which shows that UA binds to a pocket distinct from that occupied by TZD. The structure information and subsequent functional assays will not only help us to understand the mechanistic mode of action of UA on PPARγ in brown fat development and function but also will allow us to develop novel UA-based therapeutics with better pharmacological properties than TZDs for managing obesity-mediated metabolic diseases.
kw: Nutraceutical, Functional food, Browning, Pentacyclic triterpenes, Ursolic acid, Maslinic acid

title: Detection and quantification of Na/K redistribution disorder in patients with primary aldosteronism
abs: Background: Hypertension due to autonomous elevation in aldosterone production (primary aldosteronism; PA) is not responsive to usual antihypertensive medications, and is dramatically underdiagnosed in standard clinical routine. Currently, only 0.1% (1,280,000 worldwide and 1,140 Singaporeans) are diagnosed, much lower than the 5-20% (64,000,000-256,000,000 worldwide and 57,000-228,000 Singaporeans) of all patients with arterial hypertension that are estimated to suffer from PA. Approach: An evolving alternative view on the principles of salt and water physiology may help to achieve this goal: in preclinical studies, we have shown that animals with mineralocorticoid receptor (MR) activation lose large amounts of K+ and store large amounts of Na+ in skeletal muscle. This aldosterone-specific Na+ accumulation process is undetectable in blood or urine, and reflects an aggregation of chronically elevated aldosterone level in conjunction with low-K+/high-Na+ intake, which we found to be the predominant dietary pattern in Singaporeans. We have developed a 23Na+ magnetic resonance imaging (23NaMRI) protocol to detect and quantify skeletal muscle Na+ storage non-invasively in humans. In this project, we propose to use 23NaMRI to transfer our preclinical research into the clinical arena. Aims: We will use 23NaMRI to for the first time test the hypotheses that PA increases muscle Na+ by 10-20% (Specific Aim 1), that high K+ intake reduces muscle Na+ in patients with PA (Specific Aim 2), that MR blockade reduces muscle Na+ in patients with PA (Specific Aim 3), and that compared to MR blockade, adenoma surgery more efficiently reduces muscle Na+ in patients with PA (Specific Aim 4). Expected Outcome: Improved diagnostic and clinical management of patients with PA by quantitative data-driven precision medicine. Increased awareness of the adverse effects of the low-K+/high-Na+ pattern in the Singaporean diet. Demonstration of the potential of increasing K+ intake to prevent cardiovascular disease, even independent of blood pressure level.
kw: Primary aldosteronism, Na storage, hypertension, cardiovascular disease, arrhythmia

title: A novel way to manage reperfusion injury in ischemic stroke
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Reperfusion therapy such as the tissue plasminogen activator, tPA, is currently the only potent treatment for acute ischemic stroke.
