However, administration of the drug has a very narrow time window (< 4.5 hrs after stroke onset). After that, risk of reperfusion injury increases dramatically, causing damage to the vasculature. Therefore, only a small portion of stroke patients can benefit from this therapy. Over the past 14 years, we and others have identified that TRPM4 channel plays a critical role during vascular injury in stroke. Hypoxia was found to induce TRPM4 expression and enhance channel conductance, leading to excessive sodium influx and subsequent cell swelling and death. We have developed a polyclonal antibody M4P that could bind to and block rodent TRPM4 from extracellular space. In animal model of stroke, M4P could attenuate reperfusion injury in both early (3 hr) and delayed reperfusion (6 hr), potentially extending the time window to 6 hr. We further generated a mouse monoclonal antibody M4M targeting human TRPM4. M4M could block human TRPM4 in primary cultured human vascular endothelial cells, protecting the cells from hypoxia-induced cell swelling. Based on the sequence of M4M, a series of humanized antibodies were recently produced. In this proposal, we will examine the therapeutic effect of the humanized antibodies in stroke. Transient middle cerebral artery occlusion is created on transgenic rats carrying human TRPM4 sequence. Reperfusion injury will be evaluated following the treatment with the humanized TRPM4 antibodies. Once proved effective, the humanized TRPM4 antibody can be tested in clinical trial to treat stroke patients. The clinical significance of TRPM4 blocking antibody is prominent if the time window is extended. Our patents of TRPM4 antibody for stroke treatment have been granted in US and Europe.
kw: stroke, reperfusion injury, ion channel, antibody

title: Identification and evaluation of novel PI3K-inhibitor based drug combinations using patient-derived organoids from refractory metastatic breast cancers
abs: Breast cancer is the commonest cancer among females globally and one of the commonest causes of cancer mortality. Although many drugs are available to treat breast cancer, drug resistance invariably develops in metastatic cancers underscoring the need to widen the treatment repertoire for these patients. Only two agents targeting the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway have been approved in breast cancer: mTOR inhibitor everolimus and PI3K inhibitor alpelisib, both in combination with endocrine therapy. Recently, we successfully generated patient derived organoids from fresh tumor biopsies from refractory metastatic breast cancer patients with 60% success rate (25 organoids growing from 42 fresh tumor samples). Median time from tumor cell plating to organoids growth was 9 weeks (range 5-14 weeks). Preliminary drug sensitivity testing on primary tumor cells or organoids followed by QPOP analysis for effective drug combinations was carried out in 10 patients. 33 unique combinations were identified, including 10 unique PI3K inhibitor alpelisib-containing combinations. We plan to expand the number of patient-derived avatars to confirm the most frequently occurring effective alpelisib-containing combinations in refractory breast cancers. In-depth molecular and protein profiling of PDOs in relation to sensitivity to these novel combinations will be performed to identify predictive biomarkers for response. We will conduct a pilot therapeutic trial on patients with successful organoids generated and who have a QPOP-guided effective alpelisib-containing combination, treating them with the predicted combination to validate clinical efficacy. This proposal will build a valuable resource of breast cancer PDOs that can contribute to development of novel therapeutics and predictive biomarkers. PDO generation from fresh tumor biopsy followed by QPOP analysis to predict drug combinations has the potential to be developed into a clinical grade test for real-time guidance of personalized therapy. Novel combinations uncovered may be tested in larger clinical trials, potentially adding to future treatment armamentarium in breast cancer.
kw: QPOP; PI3K-inhibitor; Refractory metastatic breast cancer

title: Risk of advanced fibrosis in first-degree relatives of patients with nonalcoholic fatty liver disease-related hepatocellular carcinoma
abs: The systematic screening of family members of patients with nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD)-related hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is not recommended due to limited data. The central objective of this proposal is to fill this gap in knowledge by prospectively determining the prevalence of advanced hepatic fibrosis in the first-degree relatives of probands with NAFLD-related HCC and the factors responsible for this increased risk. We propose two key aims and the following testable hypotheses: Specific aim 1: To test the hypothesis that first-degree relatives of probands with NAFLD-related HCC have a significantly increased risk of advanced fibrosis compared to first-degree relatives of non-NAFLD controls. We propose a 3-year prospective, cross-sectional, single-site clinical study in 25 adult patients who have NAFLD-related HCC and their first-degree relatives, 25 NAFLD patients without advanced fibrosis and their first-degree relatives, and 25 non-NAFLD controls and their first-degree relatives. We will use advanced magnetic resonance imaging modalities to accurately phenotype families with NAFLD-related HCC to assess the risk of advanced fibrosis in first-degree relatives. In a pilot prospective study that recruited five families with NAFLD-related HCC, we demonstrated that 40% of first-degree relatives of patients with NAFLD-related HCC had advanced fibrosis, compared to 0% in first-degree relatives of non-NAFLD controls (p=0.048). Hence, we demonstrate that this project is feasible. Specific aim 2: To investigate major genetic and environmental factors among families of patients with NAFLD-related HCC. We will test whether the difference in the prevalence of advanced fibrosis between first-degree relatives of NAFLD-related HCC patients and first-degree relatives of non-NAFLD controls can be explained by environmental factors and risk variants in PNPLA3, TM6SF2, GCKR, MBOAT7, HSD17B13, MTARC1, and GPAM. Successful completion of this project may lead to a change in clinical practice and support a recommendation for screening of first-degree relatives of patients with NAFLD-related HCC.
kw: Hepatocellular carcinoma; nonalcoholic fatty liver disease; NAFLD; heritability

title: Translating Macrophage Membrane-Coated Nanoparticles into Therapeutics for Sarcopenia
abs: Sarcopenia is a progressive skeletal muscle disorder defined by the accelerated loss of muscle mass and function. It is strongly linked to adverse health outcomes such as falls, frailty, loss of independence, and increased mortality. Current treatment options of nutrition, exercise, and pharmacological interventions have limited clinical effectiveness and hence, highlight an urgent need for more targeted, disease-modifying therapies. Recent advances in nanomedicine have introduced biomimetic strategies with promising therapeutic potential. One such platform, macrophage membrane-coated manganese dioxide nanoparticles (MnO₂@MM), offers a unique combination of immune-mimicking and antioxidant properties. These nanoparticles are capable of scavenging reactive oxygen species (ROS), modulating inflammatory responses, and restoring mitochondrial function, which are key features of sarcopenic muscle degeneration. While MnO₂@MM has shown therapeutic benefits in other inflammatory models such as atherosclerosis and ischemic injury, its potential in age-related muscle loss remains unexplored. In this study, we propose to evaluate the therapeutic efficacy of MnO₂@MM using the TSC1 muscle-specific knockout (TSC1mKO) mouse model, which exhibits progressive muscle degeneration and shares pathological similarities with human sarcopenia. Specifically, our aims are to synthesize MnO₂@MM nanoparticles, evaluate their therapeutic efficacy in alleviating disease severity in the TSC1mKO mouse model of sarcopenia, and elucidate the underlying mechanisms of action, with a focus on inflammation and oxidative stress. This study will provide foundational insights into the potential of MnO₂@MM as a next-generation nanotherapeutic for age-related muscle degeneration.
kw: mesenchymal stromal cell exosomes; sarcopenia; TSC1mKO mouse

title: An open label, single arm study of the efficacy of accelerated intermittent theta burst stimulation in schizophrenia patients with persistent negative symptoms
abs: Schizophrenia patients commonly present with persistent negative symptoms which remain the main reason for dysfunction after recovery from an acute episode of psychotic symptoms. Negative symptoms in schizophrenia exact significant burden with no effective pharmacological treatment options thus far. Neuromodulatory modalities present a novel and alternative treatment approach and recent trials have shown preliminary evidence for the efficacy of intermittent Theta Burst Stimulation (iTBS) to treat negative symptoms in schizophrenia. In this study, we aim to examine the effectiveness and safety of an accelerated iTBS treatment protocol as an augmentation treatment regime for patient in rehabilitation care with persistent negative symptoms. We propose a pragmatic, open label and single arm clinical trial. Forty patients with diagnosis of schizophrenia, who had been stabilized from psychotic symptoms and currently suffering from dominant negative symptoms will be recruited and undergo accelerated iTBS treatment for 5 consecutive sessions each day for 5 working days. Participants will be followed up immediately, 1 month and 3 months after the end of treatment. Clinical assessment includes Scale for the Assessment of Negative Symptoms (SANS), Positive and Negative Symptoms Scale, Calgary Depression Scale for Schizophrenia, the Clinical Global Impressions Scale (severity), Global assessment of functioning, Montreal Cognitive Assessment scale and EQ-5D quality of life assessment. The primary endpoint of the trial is the change of negative symptoms as assessed by SANS scale immediately after the treatment. This study will determine whether accelerated iTBS is effective and safe to be delivered as an augmentation therapy for patients with persistent negative symptoms. The optimal treatment system for this population can be immediately translated to clinical practice and benefit patients in need.
kw: Accelerated Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation; Schizophrenia; Negative Symptoms; Treatment outcome

title: Pharmacogenomics of Immune Related Adverse Events from Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors in Asian Patients – Genomic Sequencing and Replication Study
abs: Specific Aims/Hypotheses In Singapore, an estimated 41 people are diagnosed with cancer every day, claiming the lives of 16 Singaporeans daily. Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have significantly improved clinical outcomes but have also ushered in a unique entity known as immune related adverse events (irAEs), that can be severe, debilitating, and fatal. It is estimated that 15-90% of patients experience one or more irAEs, with up to 42.7% experiencing at least a severe irAE (NCI-CTCAEv5 ≥ Grade 3). Given that human genomic variations underlie both disease susceptibility and drug response, there is reasonable cause to believe that germline genetic alterations are predictive of irAEs. Therefore, the goal is to perform a pioneering pharmacogenomics study to uncover the genomic biomarkers associated with irAEs. Methodology/Approach Immuno-oncology Registry is prospectively recruiting patients from NUH and TTSH. IrAEs clinical characterization/grading will be done using NCI-CTCAEv5. Genotyping will be carried out by targeted and unconstrained genome-wide and sequencing analyses. Statistical analysis strategy has been designed to account for all confounding factors a priori and to select for appropriate genetic association methods. Preliminary Studies/Progress Report Our initial study on 286 Singaporean Chinese patients shows that irAEs are frequent, severe, debilitating, and fatal and show high phenotypic variation that cannot be explained by clinical factors alone. Genome-wide association analysis (GWAS) uncover 2 and 6 genetic variants associated with ICI-induced pulmonary toxicity and ICI-induced hepatoxicity, respectively. Interestingly, some of these variants are, mapped to unique genes (FGF1 and SLC25A47) involved in the pathogenesis of the respective irAEs. Taken together, our initial studies establish our ability to recruit and phenotypically characterize patients and provides strong support for a full pharmacogenomic investigation. Clinical Significance Genomic biomarkers enabling risk assessment and stratification of patients will allow the tailoring of clinical/therapeutic decisions to an individual’s risk-benefit profile.
kw: Pharmacogenomics; Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors; Immune-Related Adverse Events; Genome Sequencing; Genome Wide Association Study; Asian Patients

title: Clinical validation of novel systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) biomarkers for therapeutic and diagnostic development: nucleolar alarmins and their reactive B cells
abs: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) became known as an autoimmune disease 70 years ago. Antinuclear autoantibodies (ANA) were identified as a major pathogenic cause for SLE 50 years ago. However, what causes ANA production remains unclear. Dead cells accumulate in SLE patients. In mice, injection of dead cells induce ANA but what molecules in dead cells cause ANA production and which B cell types they activate to trigger ANA production are unknown; otherwise these molecules and B cell subset provide specific targets for the development of specific therapy for SLE and effective diagnostic/prognostic tools for patient management. Since 2012, Our collaborator Prof. Lu Jinhua’s group progressively investigated the ANA-triggering molecules in dead cells and the B cell subset that respond to these molecules to produce ANA. Through a series of hypotheses and experimental validation, 3 nucleolar alarmins were identified as ANA triggers and a subgroup of nucleolus-reactive B cells as potential ANA producer. The objective of this project is to: 1) identify alarmin-specific B cells, validate their pathogenic roles in SLE patients in relation to disease onset, severity and treatment response, and screen for specific biomarkers on (multicolour flow cytometry) or inside (RNA-seq) these cells for developing antibody- and small molecule-based therapeutic drugs 2) validate changes in 3 novel nucleolar alarmins and their antibodies in SLE patients in relation to disease onset, severity and treatment responses for developing these alarmins into effective SLE diagnosis/prognosis tools. At the conclusion of this project, we hope to identify one or more B cell biomarkers for developing specific and effective drugs for SLE treatments and establish effective alarmin-based diagnosis/prognosis tools for patient management.
kw: systemic lupus erythematosus; biomarkers; nucleolar alarmins; reactive B cells

title: Therapeutic Targeting of the Autotaxin-Lysophosphatidic Acid Axis as an Immunomodulatory Strategy in Ovarian Cancer
abs: Background: Ovarian cancer remains the most lethal form of gynaecological cancer. An urgent unmet need remains for effective and novel therapeutic approaches in ovarian cancer. Targeting the autotaxin (ATX)- lysophosphatidic acid (LPA) axis is an emerging strategy in cancer medicine. Elevated LPA levels and ENPP2 gene expression have been associated with cancer-associated fibrosis, treatment resistance and immune evasion, and is a hallmark of ovarian cancer stem cells and chemotherapy-resistant ovarian cell lines. ATX-LPA targeting may modulate anti-tumour immunity through two mechanisms. Firstly, LPA operates as a negative regulator of intrinsic type I interferon responses in advanced ovarian cancer and its abrogation can restore innate immune signalling via cGAS-STING activation. Secondly, ATX-LPA targeting holds promise as an immune modulatory strategy by extrinsically targeting the fibrotic tumour microenvironment. IOA-289 is a highly potent and selective first-in-class ATX inhibitor for cancer therapy developed by iOnctura (Geneva, Switzerland), with preclinical efficacy in cancer models defined by a fibrotic tumor microenvironment. Hypothesis/Aims: Our central hypothesis is that ATX-LPA targeting is a relevant and novel strategy to modulate and promote anti-tumour immunity to improve ovarian cancer responsiveness to anti-PD(L)1 immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) strategies. The overall aims are to characterize the ATX-LPA axis in the progression of clinically advanced ovarian cancer and establish proof-of-concept for pharmacological ATX inhibition using IOA-289 as an immunomodulatory strategy, in vitro and in vivo. In parallel, we aim to develop clinically-relevant biomarkers and pharmacodynamic markers of ATX inhibition. Approach: In this proposed project, we will combine cell biology, genomic/transcriptomic and bioinformatic approaches to test this hypothesis by using both clinical and laboratory resources, including relevant ovarian cancer models and patient-derived tumour and blood samples. These data will provide robust rationale to fuel one or more future investigator-initiated clinical trials of ATX inhibition in advanced ovarian cancer.
kw: Ovarian Cancer, Drug Development, Novel Targets

title: Deciphering cellular and molecular markers in diabetes polyneuropathy (DPN) and chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (CIDP) through corneal nerve imaging, serum and tear cytokines profiling
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: We propose to perform a cross-sectional observational study to establish corneal dendritic cell density(DCD), serum and tears cytokines as novel predictors differentiating diabetic polyneuropathy(DPN) from chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy(CIDP), the commonest inflammatory neuropathy among patients with diabetes mellitus(DM). DPN and CIDP may co-exist, leading to disability and healthcare burden. However, no diagnostic biomarker is available. The rising DM prevalence, increased risk of CIDP in DM and improved outcomes with immunotherapy in CIDP emphasizes the need to differentiate them. Corneal nerve imaging is shown to quantify denervation and inflammation early and noninvasively in peripheral neuropathy, while cytokines help clarify pathomechanisms. Our primary aim is to test the hypothesis that corneal DCD (quantified using in-vivo confocal microscopy) is elevated in 50 CIDP compared to 50 DPN patients recruited from neurology clinics. Secondary aim(SA) 1 is to analyse molecular differences in specific serum and tear cytokines (using multiplex assays) between the groups, independent of corneal DCD. This is untested and is a novel aim that will deliver supportive evidence towards this clinical conundrum. We hypothesize that specific serum/tears Th1 cytokines are upregulated while specific non-Th1 cytokines are downregulated in CIDP; the inverse pattern expected in DPN, supported by our preliminary data (tear IL-6 raised in DM). SA2 is to clarify confounding by co-existing DM on corneal DCD and serum/tear cytokines in CIDP patients; we hypothesize that corneal DCD is similar in CIDP with (CIDP-DM) and without DM, while an overlap in Th1/non-Th1 cytokines is observed in CIDP-DM. As exploratory aim, we will characterize sensitivity and specificity of a statistical model combining corneal DCD and specific serum/tear cytokines in differentiating CIDP from DPN. We anticipate that a combination of cellular and molecular markers will enhance prediction of CIDP in DM patients, guide appropriate immunotherapy, advance understanding of inflammatory pathomechanisms and identify novel therapeutic targets.
kw: diabetes mellitus; DM; inflammation; corneal dendritic cells; CIDP variants; CIDP

title: Dissecting in vitro the immunological mechanisms driving cutaneous adverse drug reactions
abs: Cutaneous adverse drug reactions (CADR), especially severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SCAR), are rare and life-threatening hypersensitivity reactions that result in prolonged hospitalization and dermatological and ophthalmological sequelae. To prevent the reaction from recurring, it is imperative to know the culprit drugs that resulted in the reaction. However, identification of culprit drugs in CADR is a complex and challenging task. At present, there are no accurate means of identifying culprit drugs in CADR apart from deduction based on clinical history and drug chart in our local setting. We aim to investigate the precise cellular and immunological mechanisms in CADR through secretion patterns of cytokines/chemokines by drug-specific mediator releasing cells via enzyme linked immune-absorbent spot (ELISpot) and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), evaluate intracellular cytokine (T-helper, Th1, Th2, Th17 and cytotoxic CD8 T cells (CTL) staining to detect drug-specific T cell response and cellular activation profile including CD69, HLA-DR and CD45RA/RO for naïve/memory subsets via flow-cytometric methods in various phenotypes of CADR throughout the disease
kw: Severe cutaneous adverse drug reactions; Enzyme linked immune absorbent spot; Allergy

title: Imaging-transcriptomics of essential tremor brain phenotypes (ETIX)
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Essential tremor aetiology is heterogeneous and poorly understood. It is known that most of the risk is genetic, and that two brain-imaging phenotypes are often present: degraded cerebellar microstructure and abnormal functional connectivity of the cerebello-thalamo-cortical circuitry. To better understand essential tremor aetiology, we need to determine how genetic expression regulates the differentiation of associated brain phenotypes. To address the need for improved differential diagnosis and subtyping, we must identify new biomarkers and aetiologically-defined subtypes. In this study we aim to determine whether the two key brain imaging-derived phenotypes for essential tremor are associated with genetic expression, and whether this association differs between inherited or idiopathic essential tremor, and healthy controls. We hypothesise significant correlations of gene expression which will vary across study groups. Secondly, we will apply a novel unsupervised machine learning algorithm to generate new spatial-genetic markers and define new subtypes. We hypothesise that this will be possible through the integration of MRI and transcriptomic data. To accomplish this, we will perform a three-year observational cohort study of Singaporean essential tremor patients and healthy controls. We will gather brain MRI, blood and clinical tremor assessment data in a single session. After RNA-sequencing, we will use a machine learning tool trained on cross-tissue correlations to infer brain genetic expression. Our study team comprises leading experts in their respective fields (movement disorder genetics, neurology, radiology, bioinformatics and image analysis). Logistically, the study is designed to easily fit our existing infrastructure for on-going studies with recruitment, approvals, imaging protocol, data storage and analysis in-place. Understanding how gene expression modulates the differentiation of tremor brain phenotypes would enable more aetiologically-informed diagnosis and subtyping, while aiding to identify new drug repurposing and imaging biomarker candidates.
kw: magnetic resonance imaging; human; brain; neuroimaging; transcriptomics; neurological

title: Gut microbiota communication with bone marrow in cardiometabolic disease
abs: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is a condition characterised by the accumulation of fat in the liver, leading to non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), liver cirrhosis, and eventually hepatocellular carcinoma. However, despite the increasing prevalence and potentially serious clinical consequences of NAFLD and NASH, there are currently no approved treatments for these diseases, and the only management option available is lifestyle modification. There is growing evidence showing that the gut microbiome plays a critical role in human health and disease. Several clinical studies have identified associations between the presence of NAFLD/NASH and gut microbial species. However, the causal role of identified gut microbial taxa in disease development has not been investigated. Using gnotobiotic mouse models, we have previously identified bacterial taxa that influence cardiometabolic phenotypes. For example, we have shown that colonisation of germ-mice with the prominent butyrate producer Roseburia intestinalis improves intestinal barrier function and reduces systemic inflammation and atherosclerosis in a dietary fibre-dependent manner. Moreover, our preliminary data showed that a high-fat (HF) diet increased the number of inflammatory monocytes in the blood and mature monocytes in the bone marrow and that microbiota ablation reversed the HF diet-induced monocytosis and haematopoiesis, suggesting that gut microbiome is a causal factor affecting the HF diet-induced skewing toward myeloid cell production, which may lead to chronic inflammation and the progression of NAFLD. In summary, our preliminary work suggests that modulation of gut microbiota influences cardiometabolic disease and that bone marrow myeloid cells play a key role in connecting the gut microbiome and NAFLD. Here we propose to follow up these exciting observations to gain novel mechanistic insights into how modulation of the gut microbiota by i) antibiotics and ii) butyrate-producing bacteria could be a novel therapeutic target for NAFLD, given their effects on bone marrow myeloid cells and chronic inflammation.
kw: Gut microbiome; NAFLD; Bone marrow immune cells; Haematopoiesis

title: Investigating the genomics of racial/ethnic disparities in toxicities and survival outcomes in Asian children with childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia
abs: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is the most common childhood cancer. Despite good outcomes with contemporary therapy, stark racial and ethnic differences persist in this cancer. Asian children, particularly South Asians, do especially well with contemporary treatment compared to other populations, but the biological basis of these differences are unknown. Additionally, disparities in drug-related toxicities have also been observed across racial and ethnic groups, but these are not well characterized. This is further exacerbated by significant differences in the global burden of ALL, where the highest incidences of ALL lie in South and East Asia, but yet these Asian children represent only a small fraction of existing genomic studies. To address these disparities, we aim to comprehensively characterize the genetic variation underlying ALL toxicities and treatment outcomes in Asian children. Our overarching hypothesis is that differences in somatic and germline genetic variations contribute to these racial and ethnic disparities. We will perform comprehensive germline genomic profiling through whole genome single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) genotyping, and somatic profiling through whole-transcriptome (RNA) sequencing across a large cohort of Asian children (N=500) to identify ancestry-associated genomic variants that are associated with different toxicities across racial and ethnic groups. Additionally, across specific selected subtypes, we will perform deep somatic genomic sequencing (whole genome sequencing and whole exome sequencing) to investigate differences in fusion genes, structural variation, and gene expression profiles across racial and ethnic groups, which may explain differences in treatment outcomes and survival. Identification of these genetic variations associated with drug toxicities, and survival outcomes will not only advance the understanding of etiology and pharmacology of ALL, but importantly also become potential biomarkers and/or reveal biological pathways that can be therapeutically targeted to reduce global racial disparities in ALL in the long term
kw: childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia; race; ancestry; ethnicity; genomics

title: Using a humanized antibody to manage cognitive decline during chronic hypoxia
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: During hypoxia, excessive activation of glutamate receptors such as the N-Methyl-d-aspartate receptor (NMDAR) causes calcium overload, leading to neuronal death. This process is known as excitotoxicity. Direct blocking NMDAR has been extensively investigated for managing brain disorders with hypoxia. However, NMDA antagonists have often been found to yield side effect by inhibiting NMDARs on healthy neurons. Here, we show that blocking TRPM4 channel using an antibody could specifically inhibit calcium influx via glutamate receptors in hypoxic neurons by repolarizing the membrane potential. Healthy neurons are not affected by the antibody as TRPM4 expression and activity are low. Over the past few years, we have generated a series of TRPM4 blocking antibodies ranging from the polyclonal antibody M4P against rodent TRPM4, to the monoclonal antibody M4M against human TRPM4, and more recently, multiple humanized antibodies against human TRPM4. Several patents on TRPM4 antibody have been filed or granted for various diseases. In this proposal, we will investigate the functions of the humanized TRPM4 antibodies on primary cultured transgenic rat neurons expressing human TRPM4 and on human iPSC neurons. Using a transgenic rat line carrying the human TRPM4 sequence, the therapeutic effect of the humanized Abs is examined in an animal model of chronic hypoxia by occluding bilateral common carotid arteries. This translational study could pave the way for a novel therapy to treat brain diseases with chronic hypoxia such as vascular dementia. Once proved effective, the humanized antibody can be tested in future clinical trial.
kw: humanized antibody; dementia; hypoxia; ion channel

title: Splicing Regulation and Cancer-Related Cellular Functions of Antiviral ZAP Isoforms
abs: We aim to study the regulation of the Zinc Finger Antiviral Protein (ZAP) by alternative splicing versus intronic polyadenylation, and characterize its emerging cancer-related functions. As a broad antiviral that restricts retroviruses and SARS-CoV-2, ZAP targets viral RNAs for degradation or translational repression. The ZAP long (ZAPL) isoform is generated by the full-length mRNA while the ZAP short (ZAPS) is a Carboxyl terminus-truncated isoform made by intronic polyadenylation. We previously characterized some cis-acting elements and trans-acting factors regulating the mutually exclusive ZAP splicing vs intronic polyadenylation. Using isoform-specific knockouts (KOs) in HEK293T, we unveiled a role of ZAPL/S in epithelial to mesenchymal transition (EMT). Furthermore, we identified few splice-switching antisense oligonucleotides that alter the ZAPL/S ratio. In Aim 1 we plan to identify all regulators of ZAPL/S via splicing vs intronic polyadenylation, by genetic screens in cells with fluorescent knock-ins for ZAPL and ZAPS. By using a genome-wide short hairpin RNA library, we will isolate genes whose knockdown affects the ZAPL/S ratio as measured by flow cytometry, including RNA Binding Proteins and Interferon Stimulated Genes. In Aim 2, we will generate ZAPL/S KO cells in EMT relevant breast cancer cell lines to identify their regulated endogenous RNAs using RNA sequencing, their bound RNAs by native RNA ImmunoPrecipitation, their interacting proteins by pulldown and mass spectrometry, and their subcellular localization by immunofluorescence. In Aim 3, we will characterize the functions of ZAPL/S in EMT and migration, invasion, tumor formation and metastasis, using cellular assays and mouse xenografts of breast cancer cells. We will integrate Aims 2 and 3 with public data for a model of the ZAP isoforms in cancer. This project should elucidate the new cellular roles of ZAP with relevance to cancer, and perhaps establish certain ZAP isoform(s) or their regulated genes as targets for cancer or other diseases.
kw: Alternative splicing; intronic polyadenylation; antiviral genes; ZAP; epithelial to mesenchymal transition

title: NF1-derived extracellular vesicles as a therapeutic agent for glioma
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most notorious tumor to treat. Mutation or loss of the NF1 tumor suppressor gene is observed in ~23% of GBM and is one of the drivers for GBM mesenchymal transition. We and others have shown a higher percentage of tumor-infiltrating microglia/macrophages (TAMs) in GBM with mutant NF1 compared to those with wildtype NF1, suggesting that downstream signaling associated with dysfunctional NF1 remodels the glioma microenvironment. We previously identified the neurofibromin leucine-rich domain (NF1-LRD) that inhibits GBM invasion and promotes therapeutic sensitivity. Our preliminary results demonstrated that conditioned media or extracellular vesicles (EVs) derived from glioma cells expressing NF1-LRD inhibit TAMs infiltration in vivo and in vitro. Importantly, LRD-EVs repolarized TAMs into the pro-inflammatory phenotype with augmented phagocytic activities, filopodia densities, and pro-inflammatory cytokines expression. Since TAMs constitute ~30-50% of the entire GBM and NF1-LRD reverse therapeutic resistance, we hypothesize that therapeutic strategies combining TAMs targeting and a standard-of-care treatment could improve GBM patient outcomes. Our aims are (1) to characterize the non-cell-autonomous effect of LRD-EVs on microglia/macrophage signaling. We will use RNAseq and integrative bioinformatics to analyze microglia/macrophage signaling alteration when treated with LRD-EVs. (2) To determine the effect of the LRD-EVs-primed microglia/macrophages on the glioma stem cell states. We will elucidate what happens to the GBM when exposed to LRD-EVs-primed microglia/macrophages. (3) To evaluate LRD-EVs in the context of standard-of-care treatment in syngeneic mouse and PDX human glioma models. We will investigate the biodistribution and stability of the EVs in vivo. We will also test the efficacy of combining LRD-EVs and TMZ in an orthotopic syngeneic mouse glioma model. Results obtained will shed light on how LRD-EVs reprogram TAMs and may lead to the discovery of actionable targets and the development of novel treatment regimens in the long term.
kw: NF1, Glioma, extracellular vesicles, microglia, tumor microenvironment

title: Characterization of DNA repair pathways in the regulation of H3K27ac-bound c-MYC, YY1 and CTCF-associated 3D genome organization loops in high-c-MYC myeloid leukemia
abs: Introduction: 3D genome organization between enhancers, super-enhancers (strong enhancers that can strongly drive gene expression) and target genes is important in regulating oncogene expression in cancer cells. In this grant, we wish to ask whether targeting DNA repair pathways will target c-MYC, YY1 and CTCF, leading to general perturbation of cancer-acquired enhancer-promoter chromatin interactions at oncogenes in high-MYC cancer, leading to loss of oncogene expression and cancer-specific cell death. Hypothesis: c-MYC works together with YY1 to increase chromatin interactions and regulate c-MYC-specific cancer pathways at cancer-acquired enhancers and superenhancers in high c-MYC myeloid leukemias. The c-MYC/YY1 and CTCF pathways which regulate H3K27ac-bound chromatin interactions (putative superenhancer and enhancer-promoter loops) are regulated by DNA repair pathways, perturbation of which will lead to losses in MYC-gained 3D genome organization, which leads to specific cancer cell death. Innovation & Novelty: We will develop new methods and potential treatments. Methodology and Approach: Specific Aim 1: Characterize how c-MYC works together with YY1 to increase chromatin interactions and regulate c-MYC-specific cancer pathways in high-c-MYC myeloid leukemia. In this aim, we will investigate how overexpression of c-MYC seen in high c-MYC myeloid leukemias can lead to increased chromatin interactions and increase oncogene expression through c-MYC/YY1 gained chromatin loops. Specific Aim 2: Characterize DNA repair pathways as upstream regulators of c-MYC/YY1 and CTCF chromatin interactions in high-c-MYC myeloid leukemia. In this aim, we will investigate upstream regulators of H3K27ac-associated chromatin loops, which we have found to be mainly c-MYC/YY1 and CTCF-associated. We propose to use a novel barcoded spike-in quantitative HiC approach to analyze small molecule inhibitors of DNA repair pathways and chromatin loops. Significance: We hope to be able to identify small molecule inhibitors that will be of clinical utility in the treatment of high c-MYC Leukemia subtypes.
kw: 3D genome organization; leukemia; c-MYC; cancer

title: In situ Therapeutic Nanovaccine for Personalized Cancer Immunotherapy
abs: Cancer remains a major public health threat in many parts of the world including Singapore. Immunotherapy has shown tremendous potential in cancer therapy in recent years. Despite considerable efforts to develop cancer immunotherapy, it is still a major challenge how to initiate robust anti-tumor immunity in patients already afflicted with cancer, mainly owing to the tumor heterogeneity within and between tumors, and the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. Generally, conventional cancer therapeutic strategies, such as radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and phototherapy, trigger large amounts of cancer cell apoptosis. Unfortunately, these apoptotic cancer cells are silently cleared by tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) through the interaction between the phosphatidylserine (PtdSer) on the apoptotic cancer cells and the phagocytic TAM receptors (Tyro3, Axl and MerTK) on TAMs (“efferocytosis”), which further supports immune tolerance. We hypothesize that if this efferocytosis process could be inhibited, the tumor immunogenicity will be enhanced and the anti-tumor immune responses can be potentiated. To this end, in this proposal, we seek to: 1) Develop a clinically translatable nanoplatform to co-deliver Annexin A5 (for PtdSer blockade) and anti-MerTK antibody (for TAM receptor blockade) for tumor stroma-targeted delivery and tumor microenvironment-specific burst release. 2) Validate the possibility of PtdSer and TAM receptor co-blockade in preventing phagocytic clearance of apoptotic cancer cells induced by radiotherapy by tumor-associated macrophages. 3) Evaluate the therapeutic outcome of the in situ therapeutic cancer vaccine platform in vivo, and investigate the underlying mechanism of initiating anti-tumor innate and adaptive immunity.
kw: Cancer immunotherapy; in situ therapeutic cancer vaccine; tumor associated macrophages; TAM receptor; phosphatidylserine; efferocytosis

title: Investigating the role of BRD4 isoforms in embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma
abs: The goal of this project is to understand the role of BRD4 as an epigenetic vulnerability in embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (ERMS). BRD4, is a bromodomain and extraterminal (BET) protein. It has two main isoforms BRD4S and BRD4L. BRD4 is deregulated in multiple cancers and has surfaced as a promising drug target. However, the function of the two main isoforms (BRD4L and BRD4S) has not been analyzed in most cancers. This complicates determining therapeutic efficacy of pan-BET inhibitors. Using functional and transcriptomic analysis of isoform-specific knockdown cells, we found that BRD4L likely has an oncogenic role and inhibits differentiation. Depletion of BRD4L impairs tumor progression but does not impact metastasis. On the other hand, depletion of Brd4S has no significant impact on tumor growth, but unexpectedly promotes metastasis. Since the two isoforms play distinct roles, it is paramount to elucidate the roles of BRD4L and BRD4S and examine the therapeutic efficacy of pan-BRD4 targeting in ERMS. We propose two Aims: Aim 1: Pre-clinical studies to examine the impact of pan-BRD4 targeting on tumor progression and metastasis. We will examine the therapeutic efficacy of the BETi and a PROTAC in mouse xenograft, tail vein metastasis models and PDX models. This is relevant to unravel any undesired outcome of the drugs. Aim 2: Examine mechanisms underlying distinct functions of BRD4S and BRD4L. Using biochemical and molecular tools we will identify targets that are unique and shared between the isoforms. Direct gene targets of BRD4S and BRD4L will be identified by ChIP-sequencing and the interactomes will be identified by IP/Mass Spec. Molecular targets of each isoform will be validated by loss-of-function studies. This work will unravel BRD4 function in tumour progression and metastasis. The distinct roles of BRD4L and BRD4S have important implications on BRD4 targeting approaches in ERMS.
kw: cancer, epigenetics, metastasis, therapeutics

title: Investigating the relationship between lipid metabolism defects and astrocyte-mediated toxicity in neurodegeneration
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Astrocytes are one of the most abundant cell types in the central nervous system and play important homeostatic roles. In neurodegeneration, astrocyte dysfunctions have been shown to contribute to neuronal dysfunction and death in a process known as astrocyte-mediated toxicity. Using Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS), a progressive disease affecting spinal cord and cortical motor neurons as an example of a neurodegenerative disease affecting the central nervous system, we aim to uncover the molecular mechanisms underlying astrocyte-mediated toxicity. To do so, we differentiated healthy and ALS patient induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) into spinal cord astrocytes, and analyzed their secretome components. Our co-analysis of metabolomics and transcriptomics datasets revealed that several lipid molecules, specifically those in the linoleic acid metabolism pathway, were highly secreted by ALS astrocytes, and potentially contribute to ALS-like defects in motor neurons. The overarching goal of this proposal is to identify novel astrocyte-secreted toxic lipids, and provide mechanistic insights into how these lipids lead to neuronal dysfunction and death. Mapping out the molecular underpinnings of astrocyte-mediated toxicity would allow us to identify new druggable targets to treat neurodegeneration.
kw: Neurodegeneration; Astrocyte-mediated toxicity; Lipid metabolism; Induced pluripotent stem cells

title: Arf senses and prevents dysplastic changes during metaplasia and colonic epithelial regeneration
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Arf is a major tumour suppressor that functions as a potent inducer of p53 stability and activation via inhibition of Mdm2. Arf restrains abnormal cell growth and maintains genomic stability involving p53 dependent or independent pathways. Emerging as a new player, Arf is part of a tumour surveillance mechanism that regulates the inflammatory response and innate immunity. The precise role of Arf and the underlying mechanisms regulating its activity during tumourigenesis and the inflammatory response to tissue injury remain poorly understood. Metaplasia and regeneration are tissue healing processes that frequently occur in multiple tissue locations in response to various stimuli and following tissue injury. These processes create a microenvironment and immune milieu that helps facilitate tissue repair, but which can simultaneously promote cancer initiation when something goes wrong, such as a mutation of the tumour suppressor p53 (occurs in half of all human cancers). Using a mutant mouse model, we have observed the frequent occurrence of mutant p53 highly accumulated (mutp53Hi) lesions with aberrant differentiation and profound immune infiltration that involve tissue regeneration, metaplasia and malignant transformation. In these lesions we have discovered (for the first time) Arf expression in non-dividing cells, providing new insights into its role in response to tissue injury and inflammation. We will investigate the mechanisms regulating the coordinated spatiotemporal induction of Arf expression in aberrantly differentiated epithelium during metaplasia and epithelial regeneration arising from mutp53Hi lesions in our mouse models and humans to develop a histopathological diagnostic tool for identifying early dysplastic changes among benign human diseases using identified Arf, p53 and cancer biomarkers. Our models will provide a tool for identifying precancerous dysplasia from metaplastic and regenerative lesions and monitoring possible early oncogenic changes during clinical usage of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) and their derivatives in regenerative medicine.
kw: p53 tumour suppressor; Arf tumour suppressor; metaplasia; tissue regeneration; colorectal cancer; pre-cancer

title: AI-assisted wearable undergarment stethoscope for early detection of heart failure
abs: Heart failure (HF) is one of the leading causes of death and disability worldwide affecting >64 million patients, causing 9.9 million/year lost due to disability, and imposing a global economic burden of US$346 billion/year. A major contributor to this disability and costs are attributed to rehospitalisation for HF, the risk of which is increased in the first 90 days following hospital discharge of HF and occurs in ≈30% of patients. As such, novel strategies for detecting early signs of HF decompensation before overt symptoms of HF develop in the post-discharge period would allow adjustments to be made to the patient’s HF medication and avoid rehospitalisation for HF. The global remote patient monitoring market was valued at $1.9 billion in 2021, and is projected to reach $8.5 billion by 2031, growing at a CAG+R of 16.3% from 2022 to 2031 [Source: Allied-Market-Research]. In this regard, several remote monitoring approaches have been evaluated to detect early signs of HF decompensation, but these require either the implantation of invasive monitoring devices or the application of wearable multisensory devices – however, these are expensive and have had issues with patient compliance. To address these barriers, we will develop an AI-assisted wearable undergarment ‘fabric stethoscope’ which continuously monitors heart and lung sounds to detect early signs of HF decompensation. This is based on innovative fibre technology seamlessly woven into the garment fabric comprising novel acoustic fibre sensors, digital fibres with integrated computer and AI technology, and a fibre battery as a compliant power source. This acoustic-sensing fibre will take advantage of piezoelectricity, nanotechnology, and diaphragm fibre concept. As such, this AI-assisted wearable technology solution will be inexpensive and user-friendly for the target population of middle to older aged HF patients thereby increasing patient compliance, improving health outcomes, and reducing the risk of rehospitalisation for HF.
kw: heart failure; wearable technology; digital health; hospitalisation; remote monitoring; medical techology

title: Investigating the circuitry underlying prosocial behaviors to gain insights into social disorders.
abs: Normal social behaviors require integration of cognitive processes that include attention, memory, motivation, and reward. Computations underlying these cognitive processes are integrated within specialized ‘hub regions’ of the brain which are positioned to process information coming from different sensory and cognitive streams. Previous work has established roles for two major hubs- 1) Medial amygdala (MeA) for processing information pertaining to social cues such as aggression, allo-grooming and sexual pursuit, and 2) Nucleus accumbens (NAc) for processing information pertaining to reward obtained from various hedonic pursuits including consumption of food, alcohol and drugs of abuse. However, if the ‘social hub’ - MeA has functional projections to the ‘reward hub’ - NAc is not known. If the MeA does send projections to the NAc, then what are the cellular, molecular and synaptic properties of these projections? Do these projections mediate prosocial behaviors, including social reward? These open questions, along with our discovery of novel projections from the MeA to the NAc form the base for this proposal. Thus, we hypothesize that reward associated with social behaviours (social reward) emerges from the circuitry between the medial amygdala and the nucleus accumbens (MeA→NAc). Using a combination of circuit mapping, intersectional genetics, opto/chemo genetics, rodent behaviour, in vitro electrophysiology and functional imaging, we intend to determine the role of MeA-NAc projections in mediating prosocial behaviours and social reward. For this, we will characterize the molecular, synaptic, and cellular properties of cells in this circuit, their role in mediating social behaviours, and examine the dysregulation of this circuit in animal models of disease. Characterizing this circuit will give us a greater comprehension of the circuit-level mechanisms of how social information is processed during social behaviors and social-reward.
kw: social reward, social disorders, schizophrenia, ASD, Nucleus accumbens, medial amygdala, synapse,  chemogenetics

title: Energizing Mitochondria in Heart Failure : Revving Taurine Metabolism with Microprotein CRISTA
abs: Small open reading frame (sORF)-encoded proteins (SEPs) are an emerging class of microproteins with largely explored function and untapped potential. Over the last decade, our lab has developed a suite of bioinformatic and experimental tools to discover and functionalize microproteins from this mini-proteome, with a focus on SEPs required for metabolic processes such as amino acid metabolism. Taurine is a conditionally essential -sulfonic amino acid that is found abundantly in mammalian excitatory tissues such as the heart, muscles and brain. Although Taurine can be synthesized from cysteine derived from 1-carbon pathways, dietary supplementation of Taurine has been shown to augment mitochondrial bioenergetics and protect against degenerative diseases caused by defective mitochondrial function, particularly cardiomyopathy, which is a prominent manifestation of Taurine deficiency. Despite its proven beneficial effects, few studies have attempted to study and target Taurine biosynthesis in cardiac biology. By performing a genome-wide CRISPR screen for SEPs required for survival in the absence of exogenous cysteine or serine – precursors for Taurine synthesis -- we have uncovered a novel microprotein CRiSTA that is required for 1-carbon and Taurine metabolism. CRiSTA knockout animals die in utero, which can be completely rescued by exogenous Taurine administration. Because CRiSTA expression is the highest in the heart, as well as the fact that Taurine is critical to cardiac health, we hypothesize that CRiSTA is essential to prevent cardiomyopathy and can be targeted to improve cardiac mitochondrial health during heart failure. In this proposal, we aim to understand the underlying molecular mechanism of CRiSTA in promoting taurine metabolism. Our long term goal is to promote taurine metabolism through the use of microprotein CRISTA in order to boost mitochondrial health in the context of heart failure.
kw: Cardiomyopathy, Microproteins, Mitochondria, Metabolism, Heart Failure

title: Identify novel antimicrobial targets by high-throughput profiling of genetic interactions in human respiratory pathogens.
abs: With the rapid advancements in sequencing technologies, there is an explosion of genome information in the public database. Yet, even in the simplest of cells like Escherichia coli and Streptococcus pneumoniae, about one-third of the genes remain poorly characterized. As phenotyping knockout mutants are usually time-consuming and labor-intensive, annotations of the genes were mostly done by inference based on sequence similarity. In addition, since many genes are functionally redundant, the single mutants may lack any detectable phenotype. To overcome these issues, we developed two new approaches called dual RB Tn-seq and E-seq. These tools enable us to empirically determine the fitness of millions of double mutants, thereby establishing the genetic relationships of a bacterial genome for elucidating their functional roles. Aim 1 of the project is to profile the genetic interaction landscape of the major human pathogen S. pneumoniae. We will also challenge the double mutant pools under various environmental conditions that mimic the host to uncover factors that are likely required for pathogenesis. In Aim 2, we will extend dual RB Tn-seq and E-seq to clinical isolates of pneumococcus and related Streptococci to study the pangenome. We hypothesize our system approach will uncover many good drug targets by annotating these “proteins-of-unknown-functions”. The genetic interactions identified will be used to design pathway-directed screens outlined in Aim 3. Here, we will search for molecules that specifically kill/spare a selection of mutants to find compounds that target a particular biochemical pathway. This approach will eliminate unwanted Pan-Assay Interference compounds (PAINS) that are commonly found in chemical libraries. Together, the proposed study promises to elucidate the genetic network of an important pathogen and informs efforts for the development of therapeutics against multidrug-resistant pathogens.
kw: Microbiology; Streptococcus pneumoniae; Microbial genetics; Chemical genetics; Transposon sequencing

title: Artificial intelligence (AI)-powered platform for discovery of novel FDA-approved drug combinations against multi-drug resistant Enterobacteriaceae species
abs: The rising bacterial resistance to antibiotics has caused the World Health Organisation to issue the Global Priority List of Antibiotic Resistant Bacteria in 2017, classifying carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales under the critical Priority 1 list of bacterial species in urgent need of new treatments. Antimicrobial drug development is beset with a long runway, high costs and failure rates. We leverage on the Artificial Intelligence platform developed for drug discovery (IDentif.AI) to identify novel combinations of drugs that will be broadly effective against multidrug resistant (MDR) and carbapenem-resistant (CR) Enterobacteriaceae isolated from patients. This strategy involves careful selection of FDA approved drugs with no a priori data on their bactericidal activity nor mechanism. Data of dose-response curves and maximum serum concentrations of the drugs will be experimentally derived and fed into the IDentif.AI platform to sample a possible parameter space of 531,441 combinations from a panel of 12 drugs with three concentrations to generate a list of 155 drug combinations to identify the top-ranked synergistic drug combinations. The orthogonal array composite design wedded to empirical testing workflow significantly shortens the discovery process and circumvents the translational hurdles related to unfavorable drug profiles. Our preliminary study identified two synergistic two-drug combinations that exert rapid and potent bactericidal activity on a several isolates of MDR-CR bacteria within clinically actionable drug concentrations. This effort and success of the AI platform in identifying novel drug combinations for cancer and COVID19 treatment supports the feasibility of our approach which not only surveys active but also inactive drugs that could perform well in combinations despite showing no in vitro antibacterial activity. We hypothesize that this approach would lead to discovery of novel synergistic drug combinations that are effective and safe against a broad spectrum of the most prevalent MDR-CR Enterobacteriaceae species that can be further tested in animal models.
kw: bacteria; Enterobacteriaceae; antibiotic-resistant; synergistic combination; artificial intelligence

title: The network structure of the Fragile-X neuronal granule
abs: Human wellness is closely connected with cognitive function, which depends on learning and memory. Learning is fundamental to the human experience, linked to child development, education, and aging. In autism and mental retardation, normal cognitive function and learning are disrupted. The most frequent monogenic cause of mental retardation is Fragile X syndrome, which also has extensive comorbidity with autism. Recently, it was found that the Fragile X protein (FMR1) is connected to the neuronal RNA granule (NRG), a cluster of RNA-binding proteins that regulate translation of numerous transcripts. This presents an opportunity to analyze the relationship between the Fragile X protein and other NRG components. This is challenging in mammalian cells, due to the extensive redundancy of multiple paralogs of FMR and other NRG factors. Using the Drosophila model system, which has less redundancy, our analysis will comprise three Aims. First, we will conduct proximity mapping of the NRG using the BioID biotinylation method. Second, we will conduct rescue and modifier screens to understand the temporal, anatomical, and protein-network dependencies of FMR1 protein. Findings from these fly screens will be applied in a translational model using patient-derived neurons. Third, we will conduct functional analyses on the behavioral and physiological function under different NRG genetic states. The knowledge acquired by these experiments will be critical to understanding the basic mechanisms of the Fragile X NRG complex; over the long term it will improve our understanding of how learning disorders affect the NRG and may even guide efforts for cognitive therapies and enhancement.
kw: Muscle, synapse, myocyte, postsynaptic, Drosophila, proximity mapping

title: Capturing the role of SATB2 in cortical neuron development and mental health with advanced human in vivo cellular models.
abs: The expansion of the cerebral cortex is thought to underlie the unique cognitive abilities of humans, and defects in the development of cortical neurons and resulting network deficits likely cause many neurodevelopmental disorders associated with mental illnesses such as Down syndrome (DS) and schizophrenia. Using a novel human in vivo graft model of DS (Real et al Science 2018), we recently identified that impaired network activity is associated with a reduction in upper layer cortical neurons, which express the transcription factor and chromatin regulator Special AT-rich sequence-Binding protein 2 (SATB2). In mouse models, SATB2 deficiency impairs the generation of upper layer cortical neurons, while in humans, SATB2 mutations cause the SATB2‐associated syndrome (SAS), characterised by DS-like clinical features such as microcephaly, developmental delays and intellectual disability. This suggests that a reduction in upper layer neurons may be a common pathological feature of DS and SAS, and that SATB2 activation could be used as a novel therapeutic strategy to re-specify lower layer neurons into upper layer neurons and restore the upper neuronal layer in both disorders. However, the functions of SATB2 in human neurodevelopment and the molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying its role in SAS is not well-understood. In this project, we aim to determine the role of SATB2 in the development and function of human cortical neurons in vivo, and how impaired SATB2 function contributes to SAS and DS pathogenesis. By clarifying the physiological role of SATB2 in human neuron development and synaptic and neural network activity, our approach could lead to the design of more effective therapies for other common human mental health diseases, such as epilepsy and schizophrenia where SATB2 is already implicated.
kw: Mental health; SATB2 associated syndrome; Schizophrenia; Synapses; Patient-derived iPSCs; In vivo optical imaging

title: Oncogenic non-V600 BRAF Mutants and Their Precise Targeting for Cancer Therapy
abs: Hyperactive RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK signaling has well-defined role in cancer biology. The Ser/Thr protein kinase, RAF is a core component of this signaling pathway, which includes three isoforms, ARAF, BRAF and CRAF. Among them, BRAF is a dominant target of oncogenic mutation, whose mutations are highly prevalent in some type of cancers such as melanoma, papillary thyroid cancer, histiocytocysis, microsatellite-instable colorectal cancer and hairy cell leukemia. There are over 300 mutations of BRAF have been identified in cancer genomes, which function as oncogenic driver mutations. Although the most frequent BRAF mutation, V600E can be targeted by using the first-generation RAF inhibitors in clinic, there's no medicine/approaches for treating cancers driven by non-V600 BRAF mutations. In this study, we’ll firstly understand how BRAF is regulated under physiological condition by its cycling between inactive monomer and active dimer status, and then how non-V600 mutations alter this regulation and thus trigger the oncogenecity of BRAF. According to the action modes of non-V600 mutations, we’ll classify them into different groups and hence develop precise interventions for targeting different groups of non-V600 BRAF mutations in cancer. This study will not only improve our scientific knowledge about the regulation of RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK signaling, a central pathway for cell biology, but more importantly contribute significantly to the precise therapy of cancers with oncogenic BRAF mutations.
kw: RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK signaling, BRAF, non-V600 mutations, precise therapy, cancer, oncogene

title: Protein-centric prioritising predictors for cancer antigen discovery
abs: The ability to identify good cancer antigens is a key determinant, and pre-requisite, for successful cancer vaccination. Such antigens are short peptides, that are preferably mutated and tumor-specific in sequence, and are sourced from intracellular proteasome degradation, as part of routine protein turnover. To date, vaccine targets are largely predicted based on nucleic acid sequencing data. This leaves many questions unaddressed in the vaccine target shortlisting process; for instance, if the mutant sequence is actually made into a protein, if the mutant protein is sufficiently degraded to provide raw material peptides for antigen presentation, and if mutation-containing peptides exist in quantities that can compete for probabilistic loading on Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA) molecules. Without considering these, the attrition rate remains very high, from nucleic acid level prediction to actual working vaccines that can elicit T-cell responses. To augment this inefficient prediction process, we hypothesize that protein-centric prioritizing predictors can significantly improve the efficiency of cancer antigen discovery. This is based on the fundamental understanding that proteins are further down the antigen processing assembly line, compared to DNA and RNAs, and as such are more accurate predictors of peptide availability for antigen presentation. In this rationale, mutated proteins that prematurely terminate in sequence, potentially misfold, or have reduced stability would be enriched in the cellular ubiquitinated degradome, the obligatory processing center prior to antigen loading. If true, this would imply that the proteome and ubiquitinated proteome could be better prioritising predictors of tumor antigen presentation. If proven, this can significantly alter the neoantigen prediction route to identify a correct payload for cancer vaccine design.
kw: antigen presentation; cancer vaccine; targeted mass spectrometry; ubiquitination; post-translational modifications

title: Accounting for allosteric effects of mutations in diagnostics and personalised treatment within SG10K project
abs: The launch of SG10K project opened a new chapter in Singapore’s efforts in improvement of health care and societal wellness, benefiting from the power of emerging precision medicine in different biomedical applications and clinical setting. This proposal is aimed to contribute an important but not yet fully appreciated aspect of working within the paradigm of personalized medicine – allosteric effects of mutations in expansion of cancer (and other genetic diseases) landscape and their role in diagnostics, in emergence of drug resistance, and, eventually, in developing allosteric drugs and biologics. Two major goals of this proposal are: (i) further general development of the Allostery Platform, which allows to tackle a wide range of diagnostics/prediction and drug design tasks; (ii) using already existing elements of the platform for the analysis of group-specific SNPs in SG10K project, and for the case studies on the role of allostery in specific cancer landscapes and emergence of drug resistance. To achieve these goals, we will build a new network-based sequence-dependent version of structure-based statistical mechanical model of allostery (SBSMMA), which will be coarse grained, providing an opportunity for high-throughput analysis of big sets of proteins. Another modified version of SBSMMA will also be developed in order to gain all-atom resolution using output of molecular dynamics (MD) simulations as an input. The second direction in general development of Allostery Platform will be a machine learning (ML) based framework focusing on DPD - Diagnostics, Prediction, and Design models. Immediate implementations and planned developments of the Platform will be performed concurrently for the analysis of allosteric effects of SNPs in originating genetic pathologies (with case studies of K-Ras oncoprotein and data from the SG10K project) and for exploring mechanisms of the drug resistance and allostery-based therapeutics to alleviate the issue.
kw: Allosteric effects of mutations, diagnostics, SG10K project, K-Ras, allosteric drugs, drug resistance, machine learning (ML)

title:
Digital Information Resilience:
Restoring Trust and Nudging Behaviours in Digitalisation
abs: It is widely accepted that vulnerabilities in the digital information pipeline, especially those that enable MDM to be propagated in news or hamper the dissemination or accessibility of varied and trustable content, must be mitigated or remediated. However, to achieve long term resilience in information digitalisation, it is imperative to understand the antecedents and consequences of vulnerabilities in digital information pipeline. This can only be achieved using the lens of ‘consumer behaviour’, where factors like belief systems or biases influence the motivations and decisions driving digital media consumption. Thus, we have devised a holistic programme on digital information resilience that benefits from sociotechnical perspectives and integrates expertise in behavioural economics, computer science, communications, and law and governance. The programme encourages close collaborations that address common problem statements, and emphasise the sharing of resources. The framework for the programme incorporates three research spheres. At its core is Research Sphere 1 (RS1) on ‘consumer behaviour’. Here, behavioural economics methods, including Bayes’ Theorem and decision-theoretic modelling, will be employed to assess the motivations and decisions that determine what information consumers seek, digest and share. Understanding why vulnerabilities in the digital information pipeline are so readily exploited will guide the research of Research Sphere 2 (RS2), which is divided into three Technology Domains (TD1-3). These represent major stages of the digitalisation pipeline. In TD1 we will examine vulnerabilities in the creation of MDM in text-based and visual media. Here we will focus on vulnerabilities that allow falsity to masquerade as legitimate facts. In TD2 we will focus on vulnerabilities leading to the dissemination of MDM, particularly those that exploit consumer biases and belief systems. Algorithms behind recommender systems or search engines, which function off data derived from consumer’s historical or social media behaviour, will be investigated. We will examine their consequences on opinion and affective polarization at the individual level, and on developing echo chambers at the community level. In TD3 we will focus on vulnerabilities in the consumption of digital information. With online citizens increasingly using social media platforms to receive news and information, we will synthesize and apply information vignettes, through content analytic and experimental methods, to study vulnerabilities in information consumption, and seek mitigation strategies that emphasise consumer reasoning and empowerment. Finally, Research Sphere 3 (RS3), on regulation and sociotechnical policy, integrates with both RS1 and RS2 to study the potential impact of mitigation strategies and interventions on human and community behaviour, and consider the role of regulation or policy in their deployment at a population level. title: Mobile Team-care Deprescribing Application to Improve Health Outcomes and Workflow in Nursing Homes
abs: With a rapidly aging population in Singapore, there is an increasing need to ensure that everyone can age well and be provided with good end-of-life care. With longer life expectancy, more older adults would require nursing home care. Older adults in nursing homes are often frail and taking many medications, but many of which are no longer appropriate. Deprescribing is a clinical process of tackling and reducing these unnecessary inappropriate medications, and previous studies led by our team have found that deprescribing could reduce the pill burden (number of pills that the patient consumed daily), medication cost, fall risks, hospitalizations and death in the few nursing homes. Despite the evidence of these multiple benefits, implementation on a wide scale in Singapore is limited mainly by the lack of trained personnel, cost, as well as high nursing staff turnover in this setting. This is worsened by the COVID-19 pandemic which prevents face-to-face training. To address this issue, our team intends to develop and test a mobile application to support clinical decisions. Doctors, pharmacists, and nurses would be able to launch the team-care deprescribing application from any nursing home and hospice in Singapore. Using the user-centered design framework, this project consists of 3 work packages over 2 years. Work Package 1: A survey with end-users to consolidate and analyse the requirements and user needs of the mobile team-care deprescribing application, and a focus group discussion with key stakeholders. Work Package 2: To design and develop the application using data collected from Work Package 1. Work Package 3: To evaluate and consolidate feedback through test-bedding and a satisfaction survey with end-users. This project will be able to benefit the end-users, doctors (from both public and private sectors), pharmacists (from both public and private sectors) and nurses, by improving their workflow and communication in nursing homes. Four nursing homes that we have approached have already expressed interest in the application. When completed this mobile application could be rolled out at up to 77 nursing homes and more than 16,000 nursing home residents, reducing pill burden, hospitalization, death and medication costs. This project would also help in the digitalization of our healthcare sector, and also promotes sustainable healthcare practices in Singapore, aligning with MOH’s vision of delivering better care at lower cost by reducing manpower time and cost.
kw: Deprescribing; older adults; nursing home; polypharmacy; multidisciplinary; clinical decision support system

title: Smart Climbing Robot for Camera Installation & Maintenance on Lamp-posts
abs: In this research project, there are innovation areas involved, which consist of 1) the robot’s unique climbing technique, 2) the active alignment solution via the computer vision approach to assist the operator in the process of docking and undocking between the camera holder and the top plate fixture post-mounted at the top of the Tapered lamppost, and 3) the Jig & Fixture design of the camera holder with the top plate fixture. The robot’s unique climbing technique By mimicking the climbing strategy of the climbing robot’s arms movement like an umbrella open and close movement on the 10-meter Octagonal Tapered lamppost, the motion of climbing can be controlled to overcome the bending curve at the top of the lamp pole, as well as the changing circumference of the octagonal tapered lamppost. The active alignment solution The operator standing at the ground level may have poor visibility and judgment in controlling the climbing robot to render maintenance services for the CCTV camera on top of the 10-meter tall lamppost. Hence, the active alignment solution is to assist the operator on the ground to dock and undock between the camera holder and the top plate fixture at the top of the lamp pole via the computer vision approach. The tracking camera will start to compare the detected cross symbol image captured on the top plate fixture with its post-calibrated symbol image pre-stored in the robot system as it approaches the top plate for docking or undocking. The operator can control the robot with better accuracy and visibility based on the error between the actual and detector symbols’ images reflected continuously on the guidance monitor on the ground. The real-time images from the wireless monitor on the ground will also assist the operator to make a better judgment in controlling the robot during the docking and undocking process. The active alignment approach provides a well-binding affinity between the camera holder and the top plate fixture position and orientation during the attachment and detachment process. The Jig & Fixture design of the Camera holder The CCTV cameras on the lampposts are not connected to the Wi-Fi network; they are connected to the LAN network. To power up the CCTV surveillance camera through docking, we used a magnetic RJ-45 female connector terminal for our Camera holder and a magnetic RJ-45 male connector terminal located on our post-mounted top plate fixture at the top of the lamppost. The Jig and Fixture housing design of the camera holder can be modified to contain different types of CCTV cameras, should the needs and requirements arise in the future. Our proposed solution can be reused easily with modification to accommodate different tasks including some cutting-edge technology devices on the camera holder housing for some pilot tests and evaluation purposes. title: Burden of COVID 19 infection in CKD patients
abs: The COVID-19 pandemic has led to mortalities and morbidities among those with chronic kidney disease (CKD), part of which were contributed to by acute kidney injury (AKI). However, the long-term effect of COVID-19 infections on CKD and its progression has not been widely studied. This study aims to examine the effect of past COVID-19 infection on CKD progression independent of AKI. We aim to examine the progression of CKD pre and post COVID infection by enrolling adults with CKD undergoing regular follow up under the department of renal medicine in Changi General Hospital who have had prior COVID infection. Retrospective cross-sectional data will be obtained from the electronic medical records for two years prior to COVID infection and prospective data will be obtained two years from the point of COVID infection. We will examine outcomes such as GFR slope, GFR decline, doubling of serum Creatinine and incidence of initiation of renal replacement therapy (RRT) pre and post COVID infection. title: Hateful Content Moderation in Low-Resource NLP
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: LowResHateNLP will be the first comprehensive intelligent system to detect and explain low-resource hate speech in Southeast Asia. This project will advance the state-of-the-art hate speech analysis and detection techniques proposed in NLP, text mining, and computational social science research communities. title: Single Particle Cryo-Electron Microscopy: Reconstruction and Uncertainty Quantification
abs: The three-dimensional (3D) structure of a biological macromolecule (particle) is key to understanding its biological function. At present, the data available are represented as two-dimensional (2D) images. Thus, the reconstruction of a particle's 3D structure from a given set of multiple 2D images is of utmost importance in structural biology. Single particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryoEM) is a modern technique that produces 2D images of biological particles. In cryoEM, the particles are placed in an aqueous solution, and with the aid of cryogens, are rapidly frozen in a thin layer of vitreous ice. Prior to vitrification, these particles are allowed to diffuse and rotate freely in the solution. Different biological particles can exhibit different levels of structural variation, or conformational variability due to different stages of assembly or function. Taking into account the different conformations of the particle provides more insight into its biological function. However, to our knowledge, current reconstruction algorithms only produce a single output (that is, a single reconstruction from many 2D images). What should be done instead, is to capture the different conformations of the particle, together with their relative frequencies. This motivates us to statistically model the three-dimensional structure particles in a dataset with a degree of uncertainty. Overall, we aim to quantify the conformational fluctuations while attempting true reference-free reconstruction. Specifically, we aim to model its conformational variability by placing a probability measure on the particle's 3D structure. To do so, a number of techniques need to be developed. These include (1) probability measures on classical Lie groups, (2) sampling methods in high dimensions, and (3) probability measures on functions with bounded domain (i.e., manifolds [19-22]). We then evaluate and verify our algorithm, by testing it on real large datasets, and analyze it from a theoretical standpoint. With this project, we will provide a method that is free of any ad-hoc steps or user-specified bias. It should allow us to estimate the degree of variability in the dataset and provide 3D reconstructions of possible states, that can be used to uncover the biological and structural details, as well as starting points for further, high resolution studies of each of the state.
kw: Fourier Slice Theorem, Manifold, Projection, Uncertainty Quantification.
