title: Revisiting Memory Defences Through Hardware-Software Co-Designed Approaches
abs: Attacks exploiting memory errors have been known from the 1970s. Despite much research and advances in software and hardware, a memory attack is the main avenue for which serious and exploitable attacks occur. Unfortunately much of the critical software (operating systems, browser, networking, etc.) is continuously attacked and the success can be seen in the security patches which occur like clockwork. There are many tradeoffs in the deployment of defences against memory attacks. Overheads and compatibility are the primary impediments in the complex tradeoff between a security mechanism, to prevent a potentially undesirable memory access versus correctness which is based on how the code is written and works. Generally, software-only defences have too high overheads for usage in production settings. Can hardware acceleration with architecture extensions work well? Existing experience with Intel MPX and ARM PAC suggest that the answer is No. Many hardware proposals also have limitations in that they are incompatible with general programmer assumptions and the needs of complex software such as browsers. In this proposal, we want to investigate both the software-only and hardware assisted defences to understand what are the core operations which are to be in hardware while achieving lower overheads while having high compatibility including working on complex software such as browsers. We want to devise a new framework which can apply to diverse processors such as minor extensions of current processors to more different ones architectures such as the CHERI capability-based architecture. We want to look at a range of defences against memory attacks including spatial memory errors (aka. buffer overflow), temporal memory errors and memory isolation such as Software Fault Isolation (SFI) and Trusted Execution Environments (TEE), e.g. Intel SGX. As we have developed existing state of art software-only defences for certain memory attacks, we intend to build on that experience to understand what is a foundation for hardware-software co-designed defences and the appropriate architecture extensions which can address both the problems of efficiency and compatibility. We highlight that this problem is very challenging since after 40 years, it is nowhere close to being achieved for the kinds of critical software for which modern life and society relies on. As part of this work, we will devise benchmarking to evaluate various software-only and hard-software combinations of defenses against memory attacks. We believe that the reason why attacks are still very successful is because existing work is to wedded to conventional architectures. The CHERI project tries for a significant direction change but there are still many impediments which remain and this project will investigate what kinds of hardware extensions are suitable to remove the impediments to real world deployment and dealing with requirements of complex software.
kw: Security; Memory Attacks; Memory Defences; Control Flow Integrity; Isolation; Hardware-Software Co-Design

title: Interrogating relapse mechanisms in rhabdomyosarcoma
abs: Rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS) is an aggressive pediatric soft tissue sarcoma. The lack of effective targeted therapies poses a major problem, as high doses of combinatorial chemotherapy (Vincristine, Actinomycin-D, Cyclophosphamide (VAC) is associated with significant side effects and long-term co-morbidities in children. While extensive clinical trials have been conducted to optimize dosing based on risk stratification, thirty percent of patients experience recurrence, with a stagnation of five-year survival rates at approximately thirty percent for the past decades. Due to the lack of understanding towards recurrence mechanisms in RMS, relapsed RMS patients are usually treated with salvage chemotherapy, which unsurprisingly shows little efficacy. As cyclophosphamide is the main agent used at significantly higher doses in VAC chemotherapy, a previous clinical trial attempted to lower cyclophosphamide dosing in RMS treatment but was unfortunately met with a double in the number of expected recurrences. The molecular mechanisms underpinning this phenomenon remains unexplored. Delving into recurrence mechanisms in RMS against a backdrop of decreased cyclophosphamide dosing may kill two birds with one stone – it allows for the development of more targeted approaches to reduce recurrence rates, while simultaneously decreasing chemotherapy dosing to reduce cytotoxicity by combinatorial therapy. RMS is characterized by low mutational burden. Prior studies have failed to identify consistent mutations arising from chemotherapy. We postulated that non-genetic changes may be involved in chemoresistance and there may be small cellular subpopulations that evade chemotherapy-induced death by exhibiting cellular plasticity and changing cellular states. To better characterize the single cell landscape of this rare cancer, we first performed single cell RNA-Sequencing (scRNA-Seq) of eleven diagnostic and relapsed RMS Patient-Derived Xenografts (PDXs). This would allow for the discovery of unique transcriptomic states in RMS recurrence samples. Further, to track transcriptomic changes that occur during the dynamic relapse process in RMS, we created a longitudinal RMS chemorelapse mouse model to mimic clinical relapse from lowered cyclophosphamide dosing. We performed single cell RNA-Sequencing at various timepoints of the chemorelapse mouse model to identify cells that could survive treatment to cause recurrence. Our preliminary studies provide compelling evidence that chemotherapy induced epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition in surviving cells. These mesenchymal-like cells are characterized by increased inflammatory response and upregulated JNK MAPK pathway. Chronic inflammation has been shown to play critical roles in pro-tumorigenic roles, from cancer initiation through increasing ROS and mutations, to aiding cancer cell proliferation, survival, and migration. Meanwhile, the JNK MAPK pathway is implicated in various cellular processes and is often hijacked by cancer

title: Cellular mechanisms of a novel risk gene SV2C in Parkinson’s disease pathogenesis
abs: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the most common neurodegenerative movement disorder, characterized by selective loss of dopamine (DA) neurons in the midbrain and dopamine deficiency in the target brain region striatum. Genetic studies have identified more than 20 genes responsible for familial PD and 90 risk loci in sporadic PD. Several of these genes encode proteins that play a role in synaptic vesicle (SV) trafficking, supporting that the impaired synaptic transmission observed in the early stages of PD could be caused by dysfunctions in these genes. Most recently, synaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2C (SV2C) has been identified as a PD risk factor via genome-wide association studies (GWAS). However, the normal function of SV2C in SV trafficking and the mechanisms underlying SV2C dysfunction in PD pathogenesis are largely unknown. In this project, we will address this knowledge gap and test the hypothesis that SV2C dysfunction leads to impaired synaptic transmission in different types of synapses in striatum, resulting in selective neurodegeneration of DA neurons. To accomplish this, we will study the physiological and pathological functions of SV2C in SV trafficking in DA neurons. In addition, we will examine SV2C’s novel functions in striatal cholinergic interneurons (CHINs) and its potential role in regulating the crosstalk between dopaminergic and cholinergic signals in the striatum in both healthy and PD conditions. By lending fresh insights into SV2C’s role in SV trafficking and determining the cellular mechanisms by which SV2C dysfunction leads to PD pathogenesis, this study will help in the identification of potential drug targets in synaptic trafficking pathway for designing therapeutics that could cure PD in its early stages.
kw: Parkinson's disease; SV2C; synaptic vesicle trafficking; dopaminergic; cholinergic

title: Unravelling the role of FtsEX in the regulation of bacterial cell division
abs: Cell division is a fundamental process in bacteria. Understanding the mechanism underneath is a major goal in bacteria biology and has a high impact on human health. A central process in cell division is the hydrolysis of septal peptidoglycan (PG) mediated by amidases, such as AmiB in E. coli. Amidases in cell division are self-muted and regulated activation is needed at the constriction site for daughter cell separation. Toward this, bacteria utilize an essential membrane complex FtsEX as a conserved regulator in amidase activation, either by direct interaction or mediated by a periplasmic factor, such as EnvC. As PG is one of the most successful targets for antibiotics, FtsEX-regulated PG remodeling in cell division has direct implications for discovering novel antibiotics. However, the molecular details of how FtsEX regulates this process are still unclear, largely blocking the development of new therapy targeting this central pathway. In this proposal, our primary goal is to unravel the conserved regulation of PG hydrolysis by FtsEX, and establish a systematic understanding of its mechanisms in cell division. This will be achieved by 1) Unravelling the regulatory role of FtsEX in the activation of PG hydrolysis, by combining protein interaction studies, in-vitro ATP and PG hydrolysis assay, cell growth, and genetic approaches; 2) Elucidating the structural basis of EnvC recruitment, activation of AmiB, and conformational dynamics of FtsEX in the regulation of PG hydrolysis, through determining high-resolution information using nanodisc and cryo-EM methods; screening of small molecule inhibitors targeting the key enzymes in PG hydrolysis will be explored as well. As a major topic in bacteria biology, PG hydrolysis in cell division is no doubt a challenging process to study. Through close collaboration with Dr. Lok-to Sham’s lab at NUS, enormous progress has already been achieved from our preliminary studies, proving the high feasibility of this project. First, utilizing membrane biology and homologous screening, our research group has established the biochemical reconstitution of all key protein complexes for PG hydrolysis activation, including the binary complex of FtsEX, ternary complex of FtsEX/EnvC, and the quaternary complex of FtsEX/EnvC/AmiB, this paved the way for the following structural and functional characterization. By combining protein interaction and in-vitro functional assay, we further refined the current working model in the recruitment of EnvC and AmiB by FtsEX. We have also determined a 3.8 Å cryo-EM structure of FtsEX which showed a noncanonical fold in its periplasmic region, suggesting a novel mechanism in its regulatory role in signal transduction. As the key player in transducing signals across the membrane, this long-sought snapshot represents a milestone in the structural studies for PG hydrolysis research. title: Impacts of light pollution on tropical arthropod diversity and ecology
abs: Urbanisation is among the greatest threats to existing biodiversity. Recent studies reveal a worldwide decline of arthropods, threatening the sustainment of essential ecosystem services such as pollination and food webs. Habitat loss and light pollution through artificial light at night (ALAN) are thought to be the most important consequences of urbanisation that contribute to loss of arthropod biodiversity. This insight derives almost exclusively from research on species from temperate Europe and North America, which show that ALAN can negatively affect traits such as the immune response of field crickets or the life history of nocturnal spiders and other organisms that interact with arthropods, thus influencing the dynamics of interspecific interactions. Other biologically crucial aspects, such as the mechanisms by which ALAN affects arthropod signalling, remain largely unknown. Additionally, the long-term impacts of ALAN on arthropod ecology are poorly understood, with some studies showing negative impacts in the long-term but not necessarily in the short-term, making ALAN potentially an agent of evolutionary change. Since colonialization of Singapore in 1819, more than 95% of the original vegetation cover have been cleared and less than 10% of the remaining forest is primary forest. While Singapore has been listed as the most light-polluted city in the world, our understanding of the effects of ALAN on the diversity and abundance of terrestrial arthropods within an urban context in tropical Southeast Asia is conspicuously lacking. This will be the first integrative, comparative and multidisciplinary study to investigate the effects of ALAN on arthropods and the underlying mechanisms within such an urban environment. Using a combination of techniques such as field surveys, morphological analyses, DNA barcoding and behavioural experiments, our proposed research will advance current understanding of the impacts of ALAN on arthropods, thus opening up new lines of research in several fields – arthropod ecology, behaviour and evolution. Furthermore, this project will provide both postgraduate and undergraduate students with experience in multidisciplinary and cutting-edge research in environmental and life sciences, in support of Singapore’s research and development goals. Intellectual merit: Reveal the impacts of ALAN on arthropod assemblages in a tropical, urban landscape, and its effects on key fitness-related parameters in model arthropod systems. Broader impact: Integrate insights on the impacts of ALAN on arthropod assemblages, which can be used for policy and planning recommendations within a sustainable urban development framework. Singapore will lead as a case study, providing the opportunity for leadership in conservation and practice.
kw: light pollution, artificial light at night, arthropod biodiversity, nocturnal arthropods

title: Unraveling novel non-equilibrium states of matter for electronics and circuits
abs: The harnessing of new states of matter for novel device applications is a major scientific and technological challenge. From graphene to acoustic metamaterials, they have traditionally been associated with topological states, which are paradigmatic exotic states of matter associated with the 2016 Nobel Prize in Physics. However, the idea of topological phases is already over a decade old. Recently, there have been breakthroughs in more novel non-equilibrium phases that thrive beyond the topological paradigm. In this proposal, we aim to discover fundamentally new states in robust non-equilibrium phenomena, and experimentally realize them in electrical circuits, which recently emerged as promising platforms for hosting sophisticated states beyond traditional materials and metamaterials. This project will offer new non-equilibrium physics insights and paradigms for device applications like information processing and sensing. Well-known states like liquid, solid and ferromagnetic phases are equilibrium phases, meaning that they exist in closed systems that do not exchange energy with the environment. However, recently, the physics community have shifted their attention to more exotic non-equilibrium (also called non-Hermitian) states in open systems, as found in lasers, gain/loss media and feedback mechanisms. Unlike ordinary equilibrium phases, they can host exotic behaviour, such as “action- at-a-distance” (non-local) properties, which refers to the fact that the system can be very sensitive to selected disturbances or disorder, even if they are so far away such that they cannot normally have a significant influence. For instance, in conventional materials, removing one atom from the sample cannot possibly change the aggregate properties of the whole sample. But in non- equilibrium media, that one atom or meta-atom may indeed profoundly affect the spectral and response properties of the whole system, in a controlled manner that is still subject to much research under the topical name dubbed the “non-Hermitian skin effect “. Among the frontier topics in non-equilibrium physics, we shall investigate new non-equilibrium states arising from the novel combination of three of the most promising mechanisms: (i) asymmetric gain/loss, (ii) time-dependent (Floquet) driving and (iii) nonlinear feedback. Asymmetric gain/loss refers to energy being pumped anisotropically towards one end of the system, time-dependent driving implies that the system is not static, say by excitation by an external laser, and nonlinear feedback mechanisms lead to new correlated states with no analogies in conventional ionic materials. Separately, each aspect (i-iii) has already inspired intense recent research efforts. However, their simultaneous complex interplay remains poorly understood, given the young field and the lack of established frameworks. title: A Novel Efficient Task and Motion Planning Algorithm Based on Bio-Inspired Action Grammar for Robot Bimanual Manipulation of Daily-living Objects
abs: The world population is ageing; hence, an increasing number of older adults will suffer geriatric syndromes, preventing them from achieving daily living activities. Therefore, the elderly will need caregivers to assist them. However, caregivers experience job burnout since looking after an aged person is physically and emotionally draining. Service robots are a promising solution to assist older persons and reduce the caregivers' workload. These service robots should have bimanual manipulation capabilities as many activities of daily living involve using both hands to manipulate objects. Current service robots exhibit limited bimanual manipulation capabilities because their Task and Motion Planners present these drawbacks: 1) Existing Task Planners spend significant time finding all the actions to accomplish a goal; 2) Most conventional Task Planners require a pre-discretization of the entire robot's operating environment by a human expert using a planning domain language, which reduces the robot’s adaptability; 3) Most Task and Motion Planners provide robots with unimanual manipulation capabilities, but disregard bimanual manipulation. This research proposes a novel learning-based efficient Task and Motion Planning algorithm, using a bio-inspired action grammar, for Service Robots to achieve bimanual manipulation of daily living objects. This work accomplishes three scientific objectives: 1) Collect a dataset of human bimanual manipulation actions by asking subjects to perform daily living activities. A camera records the hands' movements, and an expert annotates the videos following the rules of a bio-inspired grammar; 2) Train an action prediction model (i.e., the Task Planner) using the Long Short-Term Memory algorithm (LSTM). The resulting model infers an optimal action plan to realize a daily living activity. The action prediction model is coupled with a Motion Planner that derives the motor control parameters for each action; 3) Integrate the Task and Motion Planner into a service robot. The research has intellectual merit since it proposes an efficient novel Task and Motion planning algorithm at the intersection between Neuroscience and Robotics to address bimanual manipulation. This research's impact is three-folded: 1) It impacts academic research as it contributes to the nascent fields of Cognitive Robotics and Neuroscience; 2) It is socially significant as it solves a critical limitation that hinders service robots' deployment in society, their lack of bimanual manipulation skills; 3) It can help bimanual robots in industrial environments to planning their actions more efficiently.
kw: Task and motion planning; Service Robotics; Bimanual-Manipulation; Bio-inspired; Machine Learning; Human Skill transfer

title: Interaction-Aware Predictive Decision-Making for Human-Like Autonomous Driving: A Hybrid-Learning-Based Codesign Approach
abs: In the near future, autonomous vehicles are believed to share public roads with human-driven vehicles, which requires autonomous vehicles to be smart and able to act like human drivers, being predictable and interpretable to other road users. However, due to their limited smartness, current autonomous vehicles are still lack of robust situation understanding, interaction prediction and intelligent decision-making abilities when interacting with others, particularly in complex and emergency situations involving humans. This would lead to unnaturalistic decisions and behaviours that may confuse and even endanger human road users, imposing a negative impact on the public acceptance and quick penetration of autonomous vehicles. In order to break through the current limitations and enhance the smartness, safety, as well as user-friendliness of autonomous vehicles, this project will take one step forward to develop advanced human-like autonomous driving with predictive decision-making ability by introducing human intelligence into machine via a novel hybrid-learning-based codesign approach. More specifically, we aim to build up the following two key intelligent human-like capabilities for autonomous vehicles: 1) interaction-aware motion prediction of multi-modal agents using heterogeneous-graph-based deep learning for enhancing the situation awareness; 2) human-like predictive decision-making using novel deep reinforcement learning with online human guidance. The theoretic results generated in this project will expand the current theories and methodologies of intelligent decision making and reinforcement learning. The technical outcomes will contribute to Singapore, strengthening its position as a centre of excellence for the development of artificial intelligence and autonomous vehicles. The technology development trend is likely to include not only the novel autonomous vehicle and artificial intelligence I features, but also the adjacent automation and robotics components and spin out into other related sectors. End-users in Singapore will enjoy a greater level of automated driving technology with more user-friendliness and enhanced safety. From a wider social perspective, these benefits translate into more intelligent transport and traffic efficiency and will help the public uptake of future smart mobilities.
kw: Human-Like Autonomous Driving; Interaction Prediction; Intelligent Decision-Making; Deep Learning

title: Characterization of the role of gut microbiota and immune system in cancer immunity of N-WASP knockout mice
abs: Cancer remains one of the leading causes of morbidity and mortality in many countries, including Singapore, despite concerted efforts to treat cancer. Our immune system has the ability to suppress cancer growth and cancer develops when cancerous cells evade the immune system. Recent advances in cancer immunotherapy using checkpoint inhibitors have proven to be effective in the treatment of some cancers, but they are very expensive. Thus, it is necessary to identify other avenues to activate the immune system to treat cancer and prevent cancer relapse among patients in remission. N-WASP (Neural-Wiskott Aldrich Syndrome Protein) regulates the actin cytoskeleton. We found that N-WASP knockout mice developed an Atopic Dermatitis (AD)-like skin condition with an activated immune system and were resistant to chemically induced skin cancer and suppressed the growth of transplanted skin cancer. We hypothesize that the epidermal barrier defects in N-WASP KO mice caused changes in the gut and skin microbiota, which activate the immune system to induce immunity to skin cancer. Our preliminary results suggest that transplanting the gut microbiota from N-WASP KO mice to wild-type (WT) mice induced a cancer suppressive phenotype in WT mice. Bacterial-induced anti-tumour responses may be a cost-effective alternative strategy in cancer treatment. Hence, further understanding of the relationship between bacteria, immune response and tumours is needed to explore this possibility. Thus, we propose three complementary aims, which will make use of molecular techniques and conditional N-WASP KO and germ-free mice. 1) Characterize the role of microbiota in Cancer immunity of N-WASP KO mice. 2) Identify and validate the immune cells and cytokines responsible for Cancer immunity in N-WASP KO mice. 3) Identify the combination of bacteria which can induce cancer immunity in wild type mice. Data from this proposal will allow us to identify components of the immune system critical for cancer surveillance and identify a combination of bacteria that can be used to suppress cancer growth.
kw: Gut Microbiota, 16s rRNA seq, Cytokine profiling, Immune Profiling, Skin Cancer, Colorectal Cancer

title: Structural basis for the interaction mechanism of receptors and antibodies on O’nyong-nyong virus
abs: Background:- Arboviruses are major disease-causing pathogens such as flaviruses and alphaviruses that are transmitted by mosquitoes. Alphaviruses such as Chikungunya virus (CHIKV), O’nyong-nyong virus (ONNV), Mayaro virus (MAYRV), Ross River virus (RRV), Semliki Forest virus (SFV) and Sindbis virus (SINV) are known to cause fever, rash, joint pain, rheumatic disease, headache and persistent fatigue. These viruses have caused many epidemics globally and continue to be a public health concern. The recent CHIKV epidemic in 2014 and in 2016 infected over 2.4 million people with 1,310 and 440 deaths respectively. Singapore had major outbreaks of CHIKV in 2008, and again in 2013-2014. ONNV is antigenically, genetically and clinically related to CHIKV. ONNV has been responsible for several major epidemic outbreaks of disease in Africa since the early 1980s. Its spread in Europe in 2013 through the travellers returning from Africa highlights the need to consider the potential re-emergence of the virus. Given that Singapore has a tropical climate suitable for mosquito breeding, and as a travel hub, this could potentially lead to outbreaks here if similarly brought over by travellers. Moreover, a single mutation in CHIKV and ONNV envelope proteins could affect their vector specificity and epidemic potential. For example, the year 2005/2006 epidemic in Reunion island that resulted in 266K human cases was associated with a strain of CHIKV with a single mutation in the envelope protein. Presently no antiviral treatment or effective vaccine is available for alphaviruses infections. The most prolific vectors of arthritogenic alphaviruses are Aedes and Anopheles species. These mosquitoes effectively transmit and infect the human. Thus, mosquito-borne diseases remain a constant threat for the world as well as for Singapore. Our long-term objective is to design and develop novel strategies to overcome vector-borne infectious disease by gaining a fundamental understanding of the interactions among the partners of vector-pathogen-host in arboviral transmission and infection by exploring their structure–function relationships and mechanisms of action. The current project focuses on the alphavirus ONNV. Specifically, we will investigate the ONNV-receptor interactions, and explore its interactions with neutralizing mAbs, as it presents unique modes of action, and compare these interactions with other alphaviruses (CHIKV and MAYRV). Objectives:- To date, only two alphavirus receptor proteins have been identified in humans: matrix remodeling-associated protein-8(MXRA8) and human CD147. The mechanism of alphaviruses binding to these receptors is not fully understood. Most of the neutralizing mAbs reported in the literature are human antibodies raised against CHIKV, and a few of them are shown to have cross-reactivity against MAYRV. Notably the antibodies raised against ONNV (preliminary studies of this proposal) show only reactivity and neutralization against ONNV but not

title: Understanding evasion of the innate immune system by malaria parasites
abs: Examining early splenic innate immune responses during Plasmodium parasite infection are the focus of intense studies as it been indicated to be essential in determining host infection outcome. The current information in this area showed that expression profile of different parasitic factors such as variant surface antigens, encoded by large multigene families, can have crucial immune evasion and modulatory interactions against individual innate immune cell subpopulations in vitro. This intricate relationship between the various splenic innate immune cells and the largest variant surface antigens family in Plasmodium however have been greatly understudied due to the challenges involved in obtaining a homogenous parasite population expressing a single member. In this proposal, we will utilize an established technical approach to overcome these challenges to study the biological roles of specifically defined Plasmodium interspersed repeats members across a range of Plasmodium species. We will focus our study on yirs in P. yoelii, the rodent malaria infection model, and kirs in P. knowlesi, the zoonotic parasite causing significant human morbidity in Southeast Asia. Understanding the interplay between the host innate immune responses and the parasitic factors involved will not only deepen our understanding of Plasmodium pathogenesis, but it will also directly contribute to novel intervention strategies and possibly better clinical management against P. vivax, P. knowlsei, and other potential zoonotic infections in humans.

title: Van der Waals structures for ultra-tunable X-ray sources and free-electron quantum optics
abs: X-rays are pervasive in modern society, being used in medical imaging, industrial inspection, security scanning, forensics, and many other applications. The global X-ray imaging market is valued at over $13 billion USD. A major drawback of the conventional X-ray tube (used as the X-ray source in imaging systems) is its lack of tunability: peaks of the emitted X-rays arise when bound electrons move from higher to lower energy levels, and their photon energies are thus fixed for a given anode material. Tunable X-rays, which are crucial in high-contrast imaging and spectroscopy applications, are currently available only at large facilities such as synchrotrons and free-electron lasers. However, such facilities are expensive and bulky, making them impractical for widespread commercial use. The advent of nanophotonics has unlocked new prospects for solving this long-standing problem, by enabling the compactness of conventional X-ray imaging systems to be combined with the versatility of large-scale synchrotron and free-electron laser facilities. Our proposed project will aim to fulfil this objective as follows: 1. In the first phase, we will theoretically study and experimentally demonstrate free-electron-driven van der Waals (vdW) materials as sources of table-top ultra-tunable narrowband X-rays. We will achieve tunability by using free electrons directly as X-ray emitters, instead of relying on the transitions of bound electrons as conventional X-ray tubes do. We will use vdW materials because a wide range of atomic compositions is available when stacking them, which enables the output X-rays to be spatially shaped and tuned as desired by controlling the atomic lattice geometry. Furthermore, the high in-plane thermal conductivity of vdW materials simplifies thermal management. Our proposed X-ray source will feature the tunability of free-electron-based facilities such as synchrotrons, but with a much smaller footprint (in fact, it will be over 1,000 times smaller). In contrast to the conventional X-ray tube, it will be possible to vary the peak photon energy of our proposed source dynamically (i.e., in real time) and continuously, allowing for more discriminating X-ray imaging and selective X-ray photon generation. 2. In the second phase, we will explore an elusive fundamental effect that will manifest in our proposed ultra-tunable X-ray source: quantum shifts in the output photon energy. These shifts arise because the classical assumption – that the free electron remains unperturbed during its interaction with the periodic medium – no longer holds. Although theoretically predicted as early as 1940 by Physics Nobel Laureate Vitaly Ginzburg, these quantum shifts have never been experimentally demonstrated, despite active, ongoing research into free electron–light interactions over the past 80 years. title: Perovskite light-emitting metatransistors
abs: In this project, we will explore a radically new light-emitting device concept, the perovskite light-emitting metatransistor, that enables unprecedented control of electroluminescence parameters at the subwavelength regime (spectrum, polarization, luminosity, wavefront and directionality) and light-matter interaction by embedding monolithic dielectric nanostructures in the active region of the device. Research will develop on the light-emitting transistor (LET) platform, a device that combines the light-emitting properties of LEDs with the switching capabilities of FETs, providing independent control of electron and hole injection and much higher accumulated charge carrier densities. In the past few years, we have demonstrated the first hybrid perovskite LET, optimizing materials morphology and device operation to achieve bright and stable electroluminescence up to room temperature. Concurrently, we have shown that the high refractive index of hybrid perovskites, combined with their excellent luminescence properties, could be used to realize dielectric metamaterial structures that confine light within sub-wavelength volumes, enhance luminescence brightness, and tune color, polarization and spatial emission profile of light emission. All these demonstrations, however, were limited to the optical domain and required external light sources. This proposal outlines the exciting opportunities offered by the “lateral” device architecture of LETs for direct incorporation of functional metamaterial structures in the active region of electrically driven light-emitting transistors. Preliminary results have shown the feasibility of this concept for electroluminescence polarization control without disrupting the device transport characteristics, and even observation of exciton-polariton electroluminescence in the strong coupling regime. In this project, optimization of the light-emitting transistors suitable for metamaterial integration will include incorporation of multidimensional perovskites (2D, mixed-dimensional and quantum dots) and operation under different electrical biasing schemes. As proof-of-principle demonstrations, we will design and develop perovskite dielectric metamaterial structures enabling electromagnetic field confinement at subwavelength scale for Purcell enhancement of luminescence, emission polarization tunability, and wavefront and directionality control. Finally, we will incorporate such metamaterial structures in the active region of the LETs to achieve electrically driven perovskite metatransistors with active functionalities, and optimize their electroluminescence and resonant characteristics towards the realization of current injection and polariton lasers.

title: Circuit Quantum Electrodynamics with Spins: Expanding the Quantum Toolbox
abs: The goal of this project is to develop new theoretical tools and techniques for the study of a hybrid architecture which couples a semiconductor spin quantum bit (qubit) with a superconducting resonator. This is a promising platform for a scalable processor of qubits encoded in the spin states of electrons localized in semiconductor quantum dot and donor systems. In particular, spin qubits have long coherence times in silicon, but their scalability has been limited by nearest neighbour couplings and the high density of wiring and interconnect requirements as qubit count increases. A resonator cavity overcomes this by long-range coupling of spin qubits through photons in the cavity. This allows quantum states of light and matter to be created, a field known as circuit quantum electrodynamics (QED). In addition, qubit measurement, control and entanglement can all be performed with a single resonator, allowing scaling up while minimising additional complexity. This project addresses the major challenge of scalability to both quantum dot and donor­-based semiconductor spin qubits. A proposed long­ term goal of a large­ scale quantum processor is a sparse array of spin qubit modules, interconnected by long­ range superconducting resonators. To achieve this requires a basic understanding of the interplay between spin­photon coupling and charge decoherence, as well as the range of interactions that may be engineered. These are primary aims of the project which, if successful, should result in new knowledge creation that improve the understanding of potential paths to the realization of the long­ term goal. The goals of the project are: Aim 1: We will conduct a systematic exploration across the range of achievable interactions available between the superconducting resonator cavity and spin qubits. We plan to focus on the double quantum dot hybrid qubit and donor­-based flip­-flop qubit, aiming to under­stand how strong spin­-photon coupling may be achieved. Both dc pulse­-gating, and ac driving in both weak and strong regimes will be studied, with the goal of identifying the op­timal working points and scaling behaviour of coupling strength, especially in the presence of realistic decoherence rates for both resonant and dispersive regimes. Aim 2: We will develop platform­-specific schemes for cavity­-based qubit measurement, control and entanglement. This involves the analytical characterisation of the performance of such schemes with realistic experimental parameters and noise models, and the development of protocols for experimental implementation when one and two qubits are coupled to the same cavity. Aim 3: We will study and characterize the generation of photonic states in the cavity, with a focus on how nonclassical states of light can be engineered, e.g. superpositions of coher­ent states (Schrödinger cat states) and superpositions of even/odd photon number states (binomial states). These states are the basic building blocks of the encodings for q

title: The liquid-liquid phase transition (LLPT) of water - influence on mineral solubility
abs: To understand the chemical and physical processes that occur in subduction zones, as well as during diagenesis and metamorphism in sediments and the deeper crust, an understanding of the composition and behaviour the fluids present is essential. These fluids are dominated by water, the properties of which are dependent upon pressure and temperature, amongst many other factors. Recent findings indicate that a liquid-liquid transition, from a low- to a high-density structure, takes place in water. The pressure and temperature dependency of this transition is uncertain, but appears to be relevant to pore fluids in sediments, hydrothermal fluids in the crust, and may also take place at depth within a subduction zone. This prevents simple extrapolation of properties such as solubility (which determines fluid chemistry) from low to high pressure and temperature conditions. Quantitative observations in situ at high pressure and temperatures must be made. Here, such experimental observations are proposed, using diamond anvil cell techniques coupled with Raman and X-ray spectroscopy, in order to determine the influence of the liquid-liquid transition of water on the properties of water in Earth’s interior. As the LLPT of water is likely to occur at high pressure and high temperature, its influence in hydrous systems towards supercritical conditions such as in metamorphic and melting processes in the Earth's crust and mantle may play an important role in volcanic processes, changing the physical characteristics of the subsurface. For instance, the transport of carbon in subduction zones is driven by fluids thought to be H2O-rich relative to other volatiles. These aqueous fluids liberated during metamorphic devolatilization in subducting lithosphere act as agents of transport of solutes into the overlying wedge of Earth's mantle inducing physico-chemical modifications of slab and wedge. As the most abundant volatile and a very effective solvent, water controls the properties of subduction zones fluids. These are the very fluids that result in the destructive volcanism of subduction arcs such as the Indonesian and Philippine islands. The solvent properties of water depend on the density, structural order, hydrogen bond strength and the dissociation character of H2O molecules which, in turn, is strongly related to the pressure and temperature environmental conditions. As a consequence, the modifications of the physico-chemical properties of water under pressure and temperature conditions relevant to the Earth's lower crust and upper mantle should affect the mechanisms of carbon transport in Earths subduction zones. title: Machine Learning Aided Multi-Scale Droplets Evaporation Model for Engineering Applications
abs: Accurate prediction of droplets evaporation is fundamental to many applications and is crucial to health and safety assessments, for instance relating to disease or toxic chemical transmission. Capturing this droplet evaporation rate is also key to the development of important engineering applications and technologies such as combustion processes, inkjet printing, coating technology, medical diagnostics and microelectronics cooling. Following the Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) outbreak, the importance of droplet and aerosol dispersion transmission was emphasized, with increased attention given to the study of droplets dispersion behaviour. However, till today, the ability to accurately predict and quantify the evaporation process of droplets is still lacking. For example, one fundamental research question in COVID-19 disease transmission is the viral-containing droplets’ trajectories. As these droplets shrink (leaving just the virions solid residue in the droplet nuclei, the dominant factor of their dynamical behaviour might well transit from gravity to hydrodynamic drag. More crucially, would the infected droplet, shrinking to its core due to evaporation, remain infectious? Accurately predicting and capturing this droplets evaporation behaviour is fundamental to address this question. Droplets evaporation is a multi-scale phenomenon, with droplets initial size ranging from millimeter to nanometer scale, and transiting through the various scale as the droplets evaporate and interact, finally disappearing at the nano-scale level into water vapor. It is a theoretical gap today that a droplet model that can well predicts the behaviour of micro to nano-scale droplets in reasonable computational time is still lacking. This project aims to address this gap by using a combination of validated transitional computational fluid dynamics (CFD) methods, molecular dynamics (MD) and machine learning (ML) to establish a micro-to-nanoscale droplets model that can predict droplets behaviour in a variety of environment applicable to today’s engineering problems. This includes varying temperature, humidity, droplets composition and cross-wind. It is also a research goal to eventually integrate this micro to nanoscale droplet model with the current macro-scale model to provide a seamless multi-scale description of droplets behaviour. title: The genetic basis for differences in cuticle polarization and regionalization in butterfly wing scales
abs: The scale cells that make up the pixels of colour on the wings of butterflies have the most complex skeletons in the natural world. These skeletons are made of insect cuticle, containing a mixture of the polysaccharide chitin, pigments, and a variety of cuticular proteins. Currently it is unclear how these complex skeletons are built and deposited both inside and outside a live scale cell (Figure 1). In particular, the mechanism of how insects deposit cuticle inside cells is almost completely unknown. It is also unclear what factors control variation in this process across scales with different skeleton morphologies. We propose to approach this almost complete black-box by focusing our attention on the most distinct scale types on the wings of Bicyclus anynana butterflies, silver and brown scales (Figure 1). Silver scales have an upper and lower lamina of equal thickness, whereas brown scales display an open morphology, lacking an upper lamina and having a thicker lower lamina. Silver scales also display more angled pillars in between the two laminae, whereas these pillars are vertical in brown scales. We have identified multiple differentially expressed genes between the two scale types. These include cuticular proteins, transcription factors, sclerotization factors, and genes involved in vesicular trafficking. Our aims are to 1) use either RNAi or CRISPR-Cas9 to down-regulate or disrupt each of these genes, and to observe how this affects scale-specific morphologies, in particular in the scale type where the gene is expressed at higher levels; 2) develop new machine-learning imaging tools for a novel form of electron microscopy that will allow us to precisely characterize variations in cuticle density and morphology across the skeleton of WT and crispant/RNAi scales; and 3) develop a tool to label chitin and smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER) with fluorescent proteins, and also use EM of scales during development, to observe how cuticle is deposited on the inside and exterior of these developing scales over time. This will be the first time that live imaging will be performed on a developing scale cell with a reporter construct. Insights from this work will contribute to a basic understanding of how cells produce intricate photonic structures during development, and the role of multiple classes of genes in the process of creating variation in chitin transport, deposition, and sclerotization at the single-cell level.

title: Are you tired? Wearable digital biomarkers to detect, evaluate, and predict cognitive fatigue for healthcare professionals
abs: Background: As many as 91% of healthcare professionals (HPs) complain of cognitive fatigue (CF). This familiar psychocognitive condition appears when the individual, after sustained mental engagement, suffers from lower attention, concentration, and motivation. Aim: The goal of this project is to understand, evaluate, monitor, and predict CF and recovery from CF (CF&Rc) in HPs. Current status: The negative effects of CF for HPs (errors, poor decisions, low satisfaction) are well-established. Yet, the nature, temporal properties and mechanisms of CF&Rc are less understood. A key reason is that CF&Rc are dynamic, adaptive, partially unconscious, and continuous. However, the metrics used (mostly surveys, observations, or controlled tasks), especially in situ, are non-dynamic, static, subjective, and fragmented. Heart rate variability (HRV) can reliably detect CF&Rc, but is currently assessed using equipment that is inappropriate in real-life settings. Objectives: Research Objective 1 (RO1) capitalizes on recent advances in wearable technology measuring HRV (w-HRV) to (i) unobtrusively, dynamically, and objectively assess CF&Rc 24/7 and (ii) to evaluate whether physiological signals can act as biomarkers of CF&Rc. RO2 expands RO1 in terms of ecological validity, time (over hours and days), and complexity of decisions and environment by assessing CF&Rc of HPs in real-life decisions and work environment. RO2 combines the breadth of traditional methods (questionnaires, interviews) with the depth of wearable technology to holistically understand, assess, and predict CF&Rc for HPs in situ. The objectives are to (i) evaluate and validate the limitations of w-HRV and (ii) test context-specific individualized CF&Rc algorithms and models akin to biomarkers. Methods: RO1: w-HRV indexes will be cross-validated using six methods (standard electrocardiogram, eye-tracking, brain responses, performance, reaction time, subjective assessment) in a controlled lab environment with standard CF&Rc (vs. active and passive control) protocols. RO2: We will record CF&Rc metrics of HPs at KK Hospital for 21 days. Seven (7) metrics will be used, encompassing subjective (self-assessment questionnaires, experiential sampling), objective (performance based on records), and physiological indicators (w-HRV, activity, sleep quality). Significance: The proposed study demonstrates and advances measurement and understanding of CF&Rc in an unobtrusive, continuous, objective, real-time, and computationally tractable manner. There is great potential for personalized intervention (akin to precision medicine) and even integrating with the Internet of Things toward interactive and smart buildings.

title: Future Transportation Network with Autonomous Vehicles and Human-driven Vehicles: Capacity Estimation, Mode/Route Choice Modelling and Lane Planning
abs: Autonomous vehicle (AV) technology should lead to an urban mobility revolution and yield various benefits in societal, environmental, and economic aspects. Incorporating new emerging AVs into an existing urban transport network will result in remarkable impacts on road capacity and the equilibrium behaviours of users in route choices. This is because the inclusions of AVs will give rise to different types of vehicular headway, and consequently cause a high variance of road capacity subject to the AV penetration rates. In addition, there is a compensation on the value of time (VOT) of AV users, as these users are released from human manoeuvrings by enjoying the in-vehicle time for entertainment or productive activities. These new features will definitely reshape the behaviour of users on their mode/route choices. Given the potential of AVs in pushing up road capacity and impacting users’ travel behaviour, it is imperative for us to rigorously analyse road capacity and model users’ mode/route choice for a near foreseeable urban transportation network with both AVs and human-driven vehicles (HVs). Moreover, these analyses will enable us to develop useful models/tools for advanced urban transportation planning and various transportation policy evaluations, including but not limited to, urban mobility system performance assessment and road lane planning. This 3-year project will mainly focus on the following three correlated research topics for a near future urban transport network with both AVs and human-driven vehicles (HVs): random road capacity analysis, travel behaviour modeling, and dedicated AV lane planning and accessibility management. To in-depth understand the implications of introducing heterogeneous AVs into road capacity, the first work package (WP) of this project is to examine the random capacity for both single-lane and multi-lane cases. For the single-lane case with HVs and multi-class AVs, the random capacity will be studied from the three facets: the lower and upper bounds estimation, mean and its relation to AV penetration rate, and probability distribution determination. First, we will analytically derive the lower and upper bounds of lane capacity and propose a novel method to estimate these two bounds. We will further explore to what extent the AV heterogeneity in terms of vehicle-pair headway distributions will affect the mean capacity and examine the possibility/eligibility of using a function of an overall penetration rate of all kinds of AVs to formulate an approximate mean capacity. Thirdly, a simulation approach will be adopted to sample vehicle platoons with mixed AVs and HVs. Using the simulated vehicle platoons, we can identify the appropriate probability distributions for the random lane capacity. For the capacity of a multi-lane road, we will use a microscopic traffic simulation based method that integrates car-following/lane-changing models to estimate the multi-lane road capacity with heterogeneous AVs. title: Mechano-regulation of Ovarian Follicle Development
abs: In early mammalian development, the development of functional eggs in the follicles (folliculogenesis) is arguably one of the most important events since it is essential for successful reproduction and hormonal regulation during early pregnancy. While past histology and molecular genetics studies have identified genes that are critical for folliculogenesis, the underlying mechanisms regulating follicle growth remain enigmatic. Interestingly, new studies revealed that the follicle growth is highly sensitive to its mechanical environment, where extracellular matrix (ECM) stiffness has been shown to influence follicle activation and maturation. These studies demonstrate that mechanical signals could mediate the crosstalk between the oocyte, somatic cells and the stroma across multiple scales. Yet, two knowledge gaps remain: 1) How does mechanics influence follicle morphogenesis and oocyte growth? 2) How are these mechanical forces being generated within the follicles? A major bottleneck in addressing these questions is the multiscale complexities in vivo and the lack of appropriate tools to ‘visualise’ cellular dynamics and mechanical forces in living tissues. To investigate if mechanical forces play a significant role in follicle development, we developed an in vitro bottom-up approach based on isolated follicles and primary cell culture. These tractable models allow us to decouple the many interdependent factors in vivo, so that we could assess the functions of each factor and identify possible feedback mechanisms. Experimentally, they also facilitated quantitative imaging and biomechanical measurement and manipulations. Based on these in vitro assays, counterchecked with immunostaining in vivo, we revealed that the theca cells (TCs), which are the outer cells encapsulating the follicles, are highly contractile and can generate significant compressive stress to control follicle growth and oocyte size. Furthermore, cell stretch and substrate stiffness can trigger changes in TC proliferation rate and YAP signalling, suggesting that the TCs are mechanosensitive and may adapt to the changing tissue geometry and basement membrane properties in vivo. We also found that physical and biochemical manipulations of mechanical stress suppress somatic cell proliferation and oocyte size, which can potentially alter the degree of molecular crowding and affect downstream oocyte functions. Based on these preliminary data, we hypothesize that mechanical stress plays a critical role in instructing robust follicle morphogenesis and oocyte maturation, through multi-tier feedback interactions between TCs, extra-cellular matrix (ECM) and tissue pressure. To test this hypothesis, we propose three approaches. First, we will elucidate the mechanical functions of TCs, by characterising TC compressive stress using in vitro reconstitution and 3D co-culture systems. title: HARNESSING ORGANIZATIONAL CULTURE CAPITAL: MULTIPLE ORGANIZATIONAL CULTURES REPRESENTATIONS AND THE IMPACT ON WORKPLACE BEHAVIORS
abs: Due to changing jobs, holding multiple jobs, or experiencing organizational changes, people are increasingly influenced by multiple organizational cultures (MOC). These organizational cultures can be experienced either sequentially or simultaneously and either within or across organizational boundaries. In this grant, we propose a series of studies to examine what gives rise to various prototypes of MOC representations and how individuals can harness organizational cultural capitals by unpacking the workplace behaviors associated with each MOC prototype. First, we provide a classification to outline different kinds of MOC experiences, using a temporal dimension (sequential or simultaneous) and a spatial dimension (within or across organizational boundaries). Second, we organize the MOC prototypes along two dimensions: perceived cultural difference and relative cultural salience among the organizational cultures. Third, we identify how various MOC representations are associated with the utilization of cultural capital that people have accumulated from their experiences in multiple organizations or through multiple cultures within an organization. We propose and test three sets of hypotheses on how MOC representations affect professionals’ identity management, creativity, and networking behavior. Specifically, we propose that the way individuals make sense of their current professional identity and navigate and form new professional identities is influenced by the multiple organizational cultures they have experienced. And different combinations of prior organizational cultures that people have experienced or are experiencing can give rise to differentiated behaviors (e.g., creativity, networking) at work. We further propose four studies to test these hypotheses in four contexts that give rise to multiple organizational culture experiences, including job hopping (Study 1), multiple jobs hopping (Study 2), organizational sub-culture (Study 3), and organizational cultural change (Study 4). In doing so, we advance the literature on organizational culture by understanding how organizational cultures can have long-lasting impacts on individuals across temporal and spatial boundaries, as well as how multiple organizational cultures jointly influence individuals at the workplace.

title: Engineering of truncated sodium iodide symporter as a novel nuclear imaging reporter protein
abs: Despite the tremendous growth in the development of cell therapies, such as the chimeric antigen receptor expressing T cell (CARTs) therapies, they have limited clinical antitumor activity in treating solid tumours, and significant on target/off cancer toxicity. Nuclear medicine imaging modalities like SPECT and PET can be used to monitor cell therapies in real time using integrated reporter genes (RG) expressing its protein gene product as a proxy for therapeutic gene expression/cell function. One leading example includes the human sodium iodide symporter (hNIS), which can be paired with a variety of readily and easily accessible radioactive hNIS imaging probes. With hNIS RG technology, there is the potential to rapidly and non-invasively monitor cell therapies, and guide their optimisation for maximal tumour homing and penetration, with limited adverse events. However, due to its large 1.9 kb gene size, the genetic integration of hNIS into cell therapies is very inefficient. Using wildtype hNIS (hNISWT) as a template and other related NIS homologues (NISH), we propose to engineer “NanoNIS”, a truncated NIS variant which will be up to 50% reduced in length but displays equal or even superior efficiency in iodide and radiotracer transport compared to hNISWT and related protein homologues. We hypothesise that preserving the key protein features driving sodium/iodide transport will allow for identification of NIS-like proteins with a smaller size and preserved function (NanoNIS), to enhance its universal utility as an imaging RG. We will employ three parallel protein engineering approaches, which, combined with continuous iteration, will provide the team with the most suitable candidates for NanoNIS for subsequent experimental validation: Aim 1. Computational Protein Design (CPD) comprising of rational sequence-based as well as homologous templating design facilitates in situ calculations on structure and function of truncated versions of hNISWT; Aim 2. PCR-driven directed evolution of NanoNIS using hNISWT as a template gives us a library of a potentially infinite number of randomly introduced truncations to be screened and selected for in in vitro functional assays; Aim 3. 3-D-structure based design following the first experimental identification of the 3-D structure of hNISWT using cryogenic electron microscopy (CryoEM). This proposal will be an immense step forward for the field of NIS research in general as well as support our efforts in predicting the protein folding, conformation and function of generated NanoNIS constructs. Resulting NanoNIS candidates will then be functionally analysed and further selected for beneficial characteristics in vitro. The most promising targets will be sequenced and run through a second round of protein design iteration to fully optimise length, structure and ion transport efficiency. title: Decoding the Membrane-Associated Assembly of Viral Replication Complex in Live Cells Using Nanotopography Engineering
abs: Many detrimental RNA viruses, including SARS-COV-1 & -2, Dengue virus, and Zika virus, have been found in generating specialized membrane compartments in host cells to provide a protective microenvironment for viral genome replication. These membrane compartments only require a few non-structural proteins (nsPs) of viruses to form but exist in a variety of shapes with curvatures ranging from tens to hundreds of nanometers. However, the molecular mechanism of how nsPs bind and assemble around the membrane to induce or stabilize such highly curved structures in the host cells is largely unclear. It is mainly due to the technical challenges to manipulate the interaction between nsPs and nanoscale curved membranes in live cells that are too small to resolve by conventional fluorescence microscopy. In this proposal, we propose to introduce nanofabrication-enabled membrane topography engineering in cells to dissect the mechanism of how viral nsPs dynamically assemble on the curved membranes. Specifically, we will utilize the state-of-the-art high-resolution nanofabrication technologies (e.g. electron beam lithography, reactive ion etching, and super-resolution imaging) to engineer the host cell membrane into a variety of shape designs in nanoscale resolution and identify the key regulators for efficient assembly of functional viral RC in live cells. Specifically, we still focus on the following three research aims: 1) Identify viral nsPs and their domains that can sense and modulate their interaction with the curved membrane in cells; 2) Validate the key regulatory factors for curvature sensing and generation by reconstituting the membrane binding of viral nsPs in vitro; 3) Evaluate the impact of membrane topography on the formation and function of viral replication compartments with both nsPs and RNA template. Successful implementation of this project will provide new mechanistic insights on how membrane topography facilitates or interferes with the assembly of nsPs for functional viral replications in host cells. The evaluated nanochip designs will be critical to establishing a new platform for viral replication characterization in cells and in vitro, and the key regulators identified can serve as new targets for anti-viral therapeutics development.

title: POSEIDON: Predicting cOaStal brEakIng waves with advanced Data-driven turbulence mOdelliNg
abs: Combining state-of-the-art in computational fluid dynamics (CFD), experimental methods and machine learning (ML), POSEIDON aims to produce the first engineering turbulence model capable of accurately simulating the entirety of the coastal wave breaking process and the morphological sediment transport processes beneath. In the past decades, despite major advances in computational power, turbulence modelling of the realistic fluid mechanics problems involving turbulence, e.g. coastal breaking waves, has remained relatively stagnant. A recent breakthrough was made by the Applicant/PI (Li et al. 2022, Journal of Fluid Mechanics) using so-called Reynolds stress turbulence model (RSM) which for the first time successfully capture the development of the undertow velocities throughout the entirety of the surf zone of spilling breaking waves using a Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) approach. However, there are still disagreements between the RSM predictions and the experimental measurement for the plunging breaker - which is a more violent breaking type. This may be due to the simplistic formulation of the pressure-strain terms in the model equations, for which more comprehensive closure could potentially make further improvement for the undertow predictions for plunging breakers. Another possible reason could be the large number of (empirical) closure coefficients used in the RSM equations, which were tuned individually based on basic steady flow experiments, thus requiring formal investigations. In tandem to the development in turbulence modelling of breaking waves, the formal use of data-driven machine learning (ML) methods to improve or replace turbulence models have just started to emerge in the past several years. While promising, such ML-enhanced turbulence modelling applications have to date typically been limited to rather canonical flow situations, involving steady flows with smooth wall boundaries. Applications to unsteady flows, let alone multi-phase flows (e.g. air-water as in breaking waves) on rough beds, are lacking. A most recent data-driven study of Eeltink et al. (2022, Nonlinear wave evolution with data-driven breaking, Nature Communications) discussed the recent work of the PI (Li and Fuhrman, 2022, using RSM model to simulate and predict wave breaking from modulation) and marked the turbulence model in Li and Fuhrman (2022) as a promising candidate to tackle the challenge in future work – to capture the most important feature of wave breaking in various scenarios with high-fidelity modelling. Motivated by this, combined with our recent breakthrough in the analysis and coastal applications of RSM, the proposed study will consider novel physical-driven ML applications based on RSMs for simulating breaking waves and related coastal engineering problems. title: Functional Quantum Geometric Opto-electronics
abs: The transduction of light into electrical signals lies at the core of opto-electronics necessary for a range of technologies that include photodetectors, optical modulators, and photovoltaics. In conventional semiconductors, opto-electronics is dominated by the electrodynamics of carriers at p-n junctions. As a result, opto-electronic device action is often directly tied to the quality and structure of the junction and interface. In contrast, in a range of recently discovered quantum materials, a new type of opto-electronics is emerging: quantum geometric opto-electronic responses that are determined by Bloch band quantum geometry and topology (this encodes the complex winding of electronic wavefunctions) that manifest even in the absence of p-n junctions. Given its nascent stage, little is known about how quantum geometric opto-electronics can function beyond the initial pioneering (but relatively rudimentary) demonstrations of quantum geometric photocurrent. Our proposal stems this gap with a view to understand how exploiting the winding of wavefunctions in electronic materials can lead to a “quantum geometric advantage” in opto-electronics devices. We will establish the principles of quantum geometric "metallic" photovoltaics using p-n junctionless metals, new types of electro-optic modulators based on the geometric phases accumulated along the Fermi surface, push the limits of quantum geometric opto-electronics into the non-local light-matter interaction as well as cavity limits, and unveil how and what types of quantum geometric opto-electronics can manifest in correlated matter.

title: Climate-driven changes in the terrestrial carbon sink of tropical Asia
abs: Anthropogenic emissions of heat trapping CO2 are the major reasons for contemporary climate change, which is an existential threat to Singapore. Terrestrial ecosystems – such as forests – have been acting as a carbon sink that offsets about one quarter of human CO2 emissions in the past decades. To preserve and enhance the terrestrial carbon sink is therefore critical to the success of climate mitigation plans, including the realization of carbon neutrality in ~40 years and curbing temperature increase below 1.5-2.0°C. Albeit its importance to the climate agenda, the fate of the terrestrial carbon sink remains uncertain as multiple lines of evidence demonstrate contrasting climate controls over the sink variability. Recent studies have suggested that a major source of uncertainty in the terrestrial carbon sink estimate is tropical Asia, where the ecosystems host some of the densest carbon stocks and the largest land-atmosphere CO2 exchange in the world, and yet are under the most direct influence of climate anomalies driven by El Niño–Southern Oscillation and the most intensive land use change of the 21st century. The terrestrial carbon sink in tropical Asia, however, has been historically understudied. The lack of accurate quantifications of tropical Asia carbon sink size and its responses to climate change hinder our prediction of future ecosystem responses and the implementation of climate mitigation plans (i.e., efficient conservation and reforestation for maximum carbon sequestration). Therefore, the proposed research aims to 1) examine the historical change in tropical Asia terrestrial carbon sink, to 2) assess the climatic sensitivities of the sink and to 3) identify parts of the region that should be prioritized for reforestation and conservation to sink carbon, as the climate continues to change. To do so, we propose to use state-of-the-art Terrestrial Biosphere models (TBMs), in combinations with observational constraints from leaf and soil traits, remote sensing and eddy covariance to establish a credible account of tropical Asia carbon sink in the past 20 years. TBMs are the principal tool to estimate land-atmosphere CO2 exchange by simulating the growth of vegetation using mathematical representations of plant functions, however, those mathematical representations contain a high degree of empiricism and are often generalized from observations at non-tropical sites. To address the lack of observational constraints in tropical Asia, we will take advantage of the recent developments in machine learning to upscale in-situ observations and new remote sensing derivatives to inform regional modelling work. This data-informed TBM will equip us with the capacity to estimate tropical Asia carbon sink with unprecedented accuracy and anywhere over the last 20 years and also in near real-time following data availability. title: Executable AI Semantics for AI Framework Analysis
abs: Neural networks can be regarded as a new programming paradigm, i.e., instead of building ever-more complex programs through (often informal) logical reasoning in the programmers' mind, complex ‘AI’ systems are built by optimizing generic neural network models with big data. In this new paradigm, AI frameworks such as TensorFlow and PyTorch play a role which is as essential as a compiler for traditional programs. It is known that the lack of a proper semantics for programming languages (such as C), i.e., a correctness specification for compilers, has contributed to many problematic program behaviours for decades. While it is in general hard to have a correctness specification for compilers due to the high complexity of languages and the abundance of language features, we have a unique opportunity to do it right this time for neural networks (which have a limited set of functions, and most of them have well-understood semantics). Hence, in this project our goal is to develop a correctness specification of neural network libraries (or frameworks) such as TensorFlow and PyTorch. We plan to specify the semantics of all commonly adopted deep learning layers, as well as other essential AI library components, in order to facilitate a variety of potential applications. To name a few, we will develop and improve different test case generation methods for testing AI libraries. For example, we will build a fuzzing engine, which features a strong oracle and a systematic specification guided way of generating valid deep learning models. Moreover, we aim to develop bug localization and repair approaches, which will allow us to systematically find bugs in AI models and suggest potential fixes. For yet another example, we will establish the correctness of various optimization techniques proposed in frameworks such as the TVM compiler based on preserving the high-level semantics of the neural networks. Finally, our executable specification will enable a range of other potential applications. Regarding related works, existing approaches on testing deep learning frameworks such as TensorFlow and PyTorch often rely on simple patterns for generating neural network models and weak oracles such as simple algebraic properties (such as adding certain kind of layer does not change the prediction) or differential testing (e.g., comparing the output of TensorFlow and PyTorch given the same model and input). We argue that such less-than-ideal approaches are what contributed to the long history of C program vulnerabilities (due to the lack of a semantics for the C language, or equivalently, the specification of the C compiler). This project is particularly relevant now as there are many deep learning frameworks which have been developed and many platforms (such as the TVM compiler) that aim to incorporate sophisticated optimization in compiling deep learning programs. title: Mobile-friendly Data Visualization
abs: Data visualization is ubiquitous for data exploration and analysis. With the explosive popularity of mobile devices, they have become one of the major platforms for people to view, explore and analyze data visualizations of different sources such as online articles and smartphone apps. A recent report by World Advertising Research Center have shown that about 72.6% of Internet users (about 3.7 billion) all over the world will access the web only via their smartphones by 2025. However, existing data visualizations suffer from critical mobile-friendly problems when they are transformed from desktop computers to mobile devices. According to our survey, there are two major mobile-friendly problems that originate from the intrinsic difference between mobile devices and desktop computers in terms of their screen size and interaction inputs. First, most visualizations are mainly designed for a desktop or laptop, and readability problems, such as visual clutters, tiny texts and overflowing content, arise when they are shown on mobile devices (e.g., smartphones) with a relatively-small screen size. To fix such readability issues, visualization developers and practitioners need to manually adjust or redesign the visualizations, which is tedious and time-consuming. Second, mobile devices have no access to mouse-based interactions and suffers from some well-known mobile interaction issues (e.g., the fat finger problem), making it difficult to conduct fine-grained selection and filtering on mobile data visualizations. In this project, we aim to address the three major problems of data visualization on mobile devices. We will develop and implement a series of novel visualization and interaction approaches to achieve mobile-friendly data visualization, which can benefit both visualization designers/practitioner/developer and common users of data visualizations. Specifically, to address the readability problems of mobile data visualizations, we will propose an AI-powered approach to automatically generate desirable mobile data visualizations across different mobile devices for a given visualization. Such an approach will be informed by a systematic investigation on the design considerations and guidelines for responsive mobile data visualizations. We plan to leverage and augment the LayoutGAN approach to model the relationship among different visual elements in a visualization and further generate desirable visualizations across different mobile devices. For the mobile interaction issues, we will develop intuitive and generic multimodal interactions for mobile data visualizations. Specifically, we will propose an expressive natural language (NL) based interaction framework for accurate filtering and selection interactions with static visualizations on mobile devices, and leverage tilting interactions to help users trigger and control animated visualizations on mobile devices. Further, we will investigate how speech, touch, tilting interactions can be combined in
