title: Stochastic gradient descent type of algorithms for sampling and optimization problems in machine learning and their convergence analysis
abs: In this study, we focus on the development of numerical algorithms for the sampling problem and the optimization problem (involving, e.g., neural networks). The two problems are closely related in the sense that investigating the sampling behavior of numerical algorithms contributes to the development of convergence results for the optimization problem. In the first part of the study, we consider the problem of sampling from a high-dimensional target distribution whose potential is non-convex and has a super-linearly growing gradient. These conditions naturally appear for distributions relevant in practice. We plan to develop new sampling algorithms based on the tamed unadjusted Langevin algorithm (TULA) and the higher order Langevin Monte Carlo algorithm (HOLA) by proposing a new class of taming factors. Convergence results of the proposed algorithms in Wasserstein distances will be provided with improved rates of convergence, compared to those in the existing literature. These results are obtained under a convexity at infinity condition of the potential, and under the condition that the gradient of the potential is locally Lipschitz continuous. Numerical experiments will be provided on various distributions including the Gaussian mixture model, the double well potential distribution, and the Ginzburg-Landau model, as well as on Bayesian regression problems, aiming to further support our theoretical findings. In the second part of this study, we focus on non-convex optimization problems where the objective functions have discontinuous stochastic gradients, which naturally appear in practice, e.g., for optimization problems with ReLU neural networks or CVaR minimization in financial risk management. We plan to propose new optimization algorithms which generalize the Tamed Hybrid ε-Order POlygonal Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm (THεO POULA) and the stochastic gradient Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (SGHMC) algorithm. Non-asymptotic error bounds of the newly proposed algorithms will be provided in Wasserstein distances under a local convexity at infinity condition and a continuity on average condition of the stochastic gradient. These results, which describe the sampling behavior of the algorithms, enable us to further derive a non-asymptotic estimate for the expected excess risk associated with the optimization problem. To illustrate the applicability of the main results, we plan to apply the proposed algorithms to optimization problems involving ReLU neural networks and to CVaR minimization in financial risk management using real-world datasets. We expect to observe their superior performance in terms of stability and training accuracy compared to popular optimizers.
kw: Stochastic gradient descent algorithms; machine learning; sampling problem; optimization problem; Bayesian statistics; convergence analysis

title: Computation Guided Materials Discovery of Heavy-Atom-Free Organic Fluorophores with Room Temperature Phosphorescence (RTP)
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: Room-temperature phosphorescence (RTP) in heavy-atom-free organic materials has been attracting significant research interest, for both fundamental photophysics and their promising applications (i.e., electronic displays, security inks, and bioimaging applications). Doping host molecules (majority) with guest emitters (minority) through simple mixing represents one favorable method to generate RTP with an ultralong lifetime (or afterglow). Yet, host-guest RTP materials with distinct emission colors, varied lifetime, and tailed photophysical and biochemical properties remain lacking. Additionally, the detailed RTP working mechanism for host-guest systems is still controversial. Laborious trial-and-error is often unavoidable in developing such organic materials. In the proposed research, we aim to employ quantum chemical calculations and experimental characterizations to (1) establish and refine descriptors that allow efficient screening and effective predictions of organic host-guest RTP materials; (2) conduct large-scale in silico screening of host and guest molecules with enhanced RTP performances, based on commercially available low-cost materials; and (3) investigate the RTP mechanism of host-guest molecule pairs and deploy promising candidates in various applications (i.e., anti-counterfeiting labels). Our recent work and preliminary data have demonstrated the feasibility of computation-guided RTP materials screening, via the discovery of one “universal” host molecule and three new guest emitters.
kw: Room temperature phosphorescence; high-throughput virtual screening; molecular engineering; quantum chemistry calculations; sustainable chemistry;

title: Toward 3D Global Aromaticity Rules
abs: Aromaticity is one of the most important concepts in organic chemistry to understand the electronic properties of cyclic π-conjugated molecules. Over a century, different aromaticity rules (e.g., Hückel, Möbius, and Baird aromaticity) have been developed, which are dependent on the topological structures and spin states. However, these rules are only applicable to two-dimensional (2D) monocyclic pi-conjugated systems. The fundamental rules for three-dimensional (3D) molecules remain poorly understood mainly due to synthetic challenges. In recent years, the PI’s group has systematically investigated the global aromaticity in a series of open-shell macrocyclic polyradicaloids in which multiple frontier π-electrons are intermediately coupled with each other in a cyclic mode. Global aromaticity was generally observed, and it was found that both Hückel’s rule and Baird’s rule were applicable depending on the spin state (see summary in Acc. Chem. Res. 2019, 52, 2309-2321). More importantly, the team recently reported the first 3D global aromaticity in pi-conjugated open-shell molecular cages (Nature Chem. 2020, 12, 242-248; Chem 2021, 7, 3442-3453). They also pointed out a possible noble gas atom-like 2(N+1)2 spherical aromaticity rule. These assumptions, however, need further validation and exploration. Therefore, the major objective of this project is to explore the unknown 3D global aromaticity rules in fully pi-conjugated molecular cages with different topologies, and 3D through-space interacting systems. Two series of 3D molecules were designed to address the issues: (1) polyhedron-like polyradicaloids with different symmetry, and (2) 3D mechanically interlocked catenanes and trefoil knots. Both can answer the fundamental questions on how the -electrons interact with each other either through bond or through space in three dimensions, the basic rules, and the correlation with the electronic properties. The proposed works include challenging synthesis and theoretical analysis. The findings of this project will start a new chapter of the concept of “Aromaticity” in Organic Chemistry. It will also help us to eventually formulate a universal aromaticity rule for any type of conjugated (either pi- or σ-) molecules with any kind of 2D or 3D topology. The materials have promising applications for 3D superconductors and quantum spin liquids.

title: Remote non-covalent interactions enable long-range stereocontrol of catalysis and molecular recognition
abs: Significance to science and medicine As the demographic shifts towards an ageing society, accelerating the discovery and manufacturing of next-generation pharmaceutical drugs is at the centre of chemical and pharmaceutical research. High-throughput screening campaigns of traditional combinatorial libraries for drug discovery are particularly powerful in identifying chemotypes within the existing libraries. However, the explorable chemical spaces using available molecular libraries designed for identification of lead compounds are limited. First, traditional combinatorial libraries employed for drug discovery are dominated by architecturally flat molecules owing to their synthetic feasibility and rapid assembly via metal-mediated cross-coupling reactions. Second, the small dimensions of these molecular structures lacking stereochemical features across large distances have greatly restricted their success in interacting with extended, diffuse binding pockets and areas. Specific aims The proposed research aims to address the first limitation through innovating synthetic methods to access molecular structures where diverse substituents are positioned at distant points along the vertices of chiral scaffolds. The proposal aims to address the second limitation through profiling stereospecific intermolecular recognition patterns of the long-range spatial arrangements of functional groups built on diverse chiral scaffolds. Specifically, the proposed studies include (1) designing and constructing novel ionic ligand–metal catalysts; (2) creating remote core quaternary chirality and axial chirality; (3) expanding the asymmetric induction to mechanically interlocked chirality and inherent chirality; and (4) elucidating long-range interaction patterns for stereospecific intermolecular recognition. Hypotheses Enzymes demonstrate remarkable ability in utilizing noncovalent binding interactions with distant, nonreactive groups of the substrates to accelerate chemical reactions and modulate selectivity. In particular, remote electrostatic interactions play an indispensable role in steering substrates into the enzyme’s active site, and orienting the reactive groups towards the catalytic site (e.g., nonreactive, distal phosphate group of phosphorylated biomolecules is essential for metabolism enzymatic activity). Furthermore, selectivity of many enzymatic transformations is controlled by charge-charge interactions away from the catalytic site (e.g., trypsin selectively cleaves peptide bond at the carboxyl side of lysine and arginine, directed by ion-paring with an aspartate residue in the binding pocket.). Therefore, it is reasonable to hypothesize that ionic interactions between a small-molecule catalysts and substrates can be utilized to achieve long-range stereocontrol of chemical transformations, even though ionic interactions are considered less-directional than widely used covalent and hydrogen bonds in catalysis. title: Organic solvent reverse osmosis membranes for energy-efficient separation of complex hydrocarbon mixtures: towards low-carbon petroleum refining
abs: In this project we propose to develop a new generation of organic solvent reverse osmosis (OSRO) membrane and to use it in a non-thermal reverse osmosis (RO) process, as an alternative to the energy-intensive distillation-based separation process or even hybridization with distillation, for the fractionation of high-value small hydrocarbon molecules from light crude oil. The overall goal of this project is to dramatically reduce energy consumption and greenhouse gas emissions for hydrocarbon processing industry. The specific objectives are to: (1) develop new materials and optimize material synthesis routes for the proposed OSRO membrane; (2) develop new approaches to fabricate a high-performance OSRO membrane using the newly synthesized materials; (3) demonstrate the high separation efficiency and energy saving of the new OSRO membrane for the fractionation of light crude oil mixtures to produce high-value hydrocarbon products; (4) study mass transport mechanisms and optimize performance-limiting factors for OSRO membranes. These objectives can be achieved via the synergistic efforts and multidisciplinary approaches of synthesizing new membrane materials, developing new membrane fabrication approach, investigating fundamental mechanisms of mass transport, and optimizing OSRO membrane performance-limiting factors and OSRO process operation. Specifically, we propose to synthesize polyimide-based polymers of intrinsic microporosity (PIM-PI) integrating spirobifluorene building blocks (i.e., SBF-PIM-PI) as new materials for the proposed OSRO membranes. Electrospraying 3D printing method will be innovatively used to fabricate the OSRO membranes. The new SBF-PIM-PI materials will have high rigidity to resist swelling and plasticization during membrane filtration of complex hydrocarbon mixtures, while the novel 3D printing method can help precisely control the thickness of the membrane active layer. Therefore, the resultant membrane is expected to be able to break the trade-off between permeance and selectivity and will achieve high performance for the fractionation of high-value small hydrocarbon molecules with molecular weights < 200 Da from complex light crude oil mixtures. The success of this project can address an important academic significance on organic solvent membrane development. It will create new materials for organic solvent membranes via new chemical synthesis, advance the membrane fabrication approaches to develop high-performance, cheap and scalable membranes for separating complex hydrocarbon mixtures, and drive a new research direction from developing reverse osmosis membranes for large-scale seawater desalination towards large-scale organic separations (e.g., crude oil) in hydrocarbon processing industry.
kw: Organic solvent reverse osmosis (OSRO); complex hydrocarbon mixtures; energy-efficient separation; thin-film composite membrane; solvent resistant membrane;  organic separations

title: Electrochemical polymerization of carbon dioxide and its reduced intermediates to C6- C20 hydrocarbons
abs: C6-C20 hydrocarbons are ubiquitous used as transportation fuels and chemicals. These molecules are typically produced from the refining or cracking of fossil fuels such as crude oil, or to a smaller extent, from the thermally-driven Fischer-Tropsch (F-T) reaction. Both of these processes are highly polluting and unsustainable. Herein, we propose to develop a process by which carbon dioxide or its reduced intermediates undergo electrochemically-initiated coupling to give C6-C20 linear and branched hydrocarbons, such as hexane, iso-octane, 1-octene, etc. Ambitious but realistic Faradaic efficiencies and current densities of respectively 50% and 50 mA/cm2 for these molecules are targeted as figures-of-merit. Water will be used as the hydrogen source. CO2 (carbon dioxide) + H2O + electrons - > CxHy (x = 6-20) + OH- A distinguishing feature of this proposal is that we shall steer away from the usual copper-based catalysts. Instead, we plan to explore catalysts based on the F-T metals, such as iron, cobalt, ruthenium, or their composites. This approach is taken based on our latest results (Nature Catal. 5, 545. 2022) showing (a) an unprecedented production of C1-C6 hydrocarbons on Ni catalysts, and (b) previous works on all forms of copper catalysts have failed to produce any hydrocarbons larger than C4, which indicates that the potential of copper for CO2 polymerization is nearly exhausted. Apart from optimizing the composition of the catalysts, we shall also investigate the effect of their micro-environment by changing the type of binders, electrolytes, membranes, and configuration of the electrolyzer used, etc. We further aim to elucidate the fundamental relationships between the structure and composition of the catalysts / catalytic environments and their performances. Density functional theory calculations will be performed to complement and explain the results, and to predict what might be an active catalyst. If successful, we shall be the first to electrochemically couple CO2 to give linear and branched C6-C20 hydrocarbons. Another innovation is to detect the reaction intermediates and elucidate the mechanistic pathways. Both are unprecedented in the field of CO2 electro-conversion. Oil cracking / refining and thermally-driven F-T processes are competing technologies. These processes are commercialized by major companies, such as Shell, Sasol and Exxon-Mobil. Thus, if successful, our project has the potential to become a ‘highly-disruptive’ technology. Our work will impact the chemical/energy sector in Singapore.
kw: Electrochemistry ; Catalysis ; Carbon Dioxide ; Multi-Carbon Hydrocarbons

title: Capitals of the Future: Place, Power and Possibility in Southeast Asia
abs: Imaginations of the future play an important role in planning innovation in Asia. Governments and planning agencies are concerned with building the city of the future, while societal and market actors contribute to the imaginations of the future as they seek to influence and take a stake in urban development. These actors often reference other cities as positive and negative examples, aspirational models or warnings of pathways gone wrong. Our research seeks to understand the interaction between imaginations of the future, discourses of urban planning and pathways of urban development in Southeast Asia. How do sites of urban planning reflect and generate imaginations of the future? What roles do references to other cities and sites play in these imaginations of the future? How do inter-referencing discourses influence the development of the city of the future? We examine these questions through a discourse and historical analysis of three case cities in Southeast Asia, focusing on three key dimensions of planning and development. The administrative capital cities of Putrajaya in Malaysia, and Nusantara in Indonesia have been or are being planned from scratch. The third city, Singapore, stands out as a different type of capital of the future, one which we define in a broader sense as an established centre of planning innovation that has been widely referenced as a model for futures elsewhere and seeks today to be an international knowledge hub of urban futures and solutions. The three dimensions of the future comprise (1) the embracing of technological disruptions as opportunities for R&D and industrial reforms in the contemporary digital age, (2) the environmental calibration of the relationship between humans and nature, and (3) imaginations of past civilizational and cultural symbolisms that connote ideas of cosmopolitan social harmony. We have developed an interdisciplinary theoretical framework encompassing the relational geography of place-making imaginations, the sociology of urban power and the history of pathways of city development. Our theoretical framework focuses on the networks of discourses of the future that are located within and extended across the planning of the three cities. Capital cities have long been identified as sites of memory articulating both dominant and alternative narratives, but we theorize the ways in which new capital cities also serve as imaginative sites of possible urban futures and urban solutions for anticipated future problems. State and non-actors engage in debates, discussions and deliberations over the planning and development of capital cities and redevelopment of existing zones within them. Their relations of discursive power—the power to persuade others that the imagined city is a viable and desirable site of the future—drive the development of the capital city. Two factors influence the relations of discursive power. We examine how truth spots referencing other places as negative or positive example

title: Analyses and Projections of Households and Living Arrangements in Six ASEAN Countries (HOUSEHOLD-ASEAN)
abs: Households and living arrangements are changing rapidly around the world, prominently featured by the decline of traditional households of three-generation coresidence, rise of one-person households, and continuously/quickly increasing numbers of households all over the world. Among numerous issues related to household changes, the living arrangement of older adults stands out as a salient topic. This is especially true in Singapore and other countries of Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), in which most older adults rely on family members in later life. While the future changes of household and living arrangement have been extensively studied in certain countries such as the United States and China, little is known about this topic in Singapore and many other ASEAN nations. This project aims to analyze and project the transformation of household and living arrangement in six major ASEAN nations, including Singapore, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, the Philippines, and Vietnam. These six countries combined are home to about 600 million people, approximately 90% of the ASEAN’s total population. This project has a strong theoretical motivation. The transformation of household and living arrangement is now at the core of the demographic transition theories. Specifically, the theory on the second demographic transition (SDT) focuses on household-related dynamics such as the decline of marriage and the rise of alternative living arrangements, and predicts that some new types of households and living arrangements may prevail in our world such as cohabitations, solo-living, childless households, and single-parent households. The empirical evidence of the SDT is still mixed, mostly coming from Europe. Thus, the theoretical goal of this project is to test the SDT theory in Singapore and the broader ASEAN region. Regarding the household and living arrangement, the SDT theory hypothesizes the rise of alternative living arrangements beyond marriage and the increasing prevalence of individualistic families. Accordingly, our baseline hypothesis is that special types of households and living arraignments is and will be prevailing in the ASEAN nations, including but not limited to cohabitations, one-person households, single-parent households, childless households, as well as empty-nested older adult households. The project also has a strong methodological goal, which is to innovatively develop and apply two methods in this project to enhance the testing of the SDT model. We will develop and apply the DemoRates program, which is a R package, capable of estimating the key demographic rates of marriage/union formations and dissolutions, births, migrations, and any other transition rates, classified by demographic characteristics such as age, sex, marital/union statuses, education, rural/urban residence, and race. title: Robust Scenario Reduction, When Duality Fails.
abs: Traditional operations research studies assume that all parameters in an optimization problem, besides the decision variables, are completely known. However, it has been widely documented that such a know-it-all approach often results in poor decisions being made. On the one hand, we may simply not possess enough data to be able to replace adequately all problem parameters by known values. For instance, even if some experts may claim to have predicted the occurrence of the current pandemic, it is unfathomable that anyone would have been capable of predicting the scale and the severity of Covid-19. On the other hand, while the amount of data may be substantial and thus not pose an issue, incorporating it into an optimization problem certainly is. This is because the more data we have, the more complex our operations and the corresponding optimization problems become. Besides, while data could be stored and recalled efficiently using distributed infrastructures, optimization problems still rarely benefit from such technological advances as most optimization algorithms cannot work in parallel. Because we could only use limited information in optimization problems, it is important to safeguard against errors that arise from data inaccuracies, and robust optimization is a branch of mathematics that has been developed for this particular propose. In robust optimization, we are allowed to have some unknowns, which are collectively referred to as uncertainty. Unlike deterministic approaches, which assume that all uncertain parameters take a single value, robust optimization seeks to find a solution that is robustly feasible and that optimizes the worst-case objective function in view of all possible realizations of the uncertainty from the so-called uncertainty set. Decision makers then have the flexibility to adjust the level of protection by varying the size of the uncertainty set according to the confidence they have in their data. The uncertainty set plays a crucial role in determining whether a robust optimization problem is solvable in polynomial time. The usual tractability-ensuring assumption is that the uncertainty set should be a convex and compact set, such as a polytope or an ellipsoid. These choices of the uncertainty set have been boosted by well-known statistical results, such as Central Limit Theorem. Nowadays, we have established results on how to deal with convex uncertainty sets, largely thanks to the convex duality theory. The duality theory ensures that we can eliminate uncertain parameters from a robust optimization problem by adding a modest number of auxiliary decision variables. As a result of such an elimination, we obtain a deterministic optimization problem which is known as a robust counterpart and which can be solved by many off-the-shelf solvers, such as CPLEX and GUROBI. title: Adaptive bus network scheduled by deep reinforcement learning
abs: The optimal scheduling of buses is a complex problem that is NP-hard. If we were to include the real-time dynamical demand of the commuters, the problem of optimal bus scheduling becomes even more complex. Our aim in this proposal is to solve the complex problem of bus scheduling with heterogeneous commuters' demand at the scale of a city by combining the methods of deep reinforcement learning (DRL) and statistical physics (SP). To do so, we will build a general agent-based simulation platform by modelling a transportation system with a weighted complex network. This framework is general, where the adjacency matrix of the underlying graph can be prescribed according to synthetic or real data and even be time-dependent. Such a generic platform that we develop would then allow us to design an intelligent optimisation framework to discover the best routing and scheduling of the bus system based on DRL+SP. DRL had made great progress recently with its demonstration of superhuman ability in mastering the game of Go which is of complexity EXPTIME-complete. DRL then further extended its prowess through multi-agent reinforcement learning algorithms when it reached Grandmaster level against human in the online game of StarCraft II. Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is a nascent field currently under active development. While MARL is plagued by issues of non-unique goals, non-stationarity, and scalability, it has already shown great promises in addressing the bus bunching problem by coordinating the holding actions of the bus agents. In this proposal, we shall design an MARL framework known as the Deep Centralised Multi-Agent Actor Critic (DCMAC) to yield novel optimal bus scheduling strategies. Unlike past MARL work in this area, which focuses on controlling the buses to adopt a staggered configuration, our approach is more general where even a bunched configuration could be selected if it optimises the overall waiting and travelling time of the commuters. The reason being that our technique processes additional information such as the commuters’ arrival time at the bus stop, and the commuters' origin and destination bus stops, as input states to our algorithm. The consequential increased granularity of the data gives the bus agents opportunity to zoom in on the right combination of actions to undertake. Moreover, the concomitant expansion of the state space has motivated the use of deep neural network as function approximator in our actor-critic reinforcement learning algorithm. By using a centralised architecture such that all the bus agents have access to the overall state information, our scheme overcomes the issue of non-stationarity of the MARL framework. However, this expansion of state space negatively affects the computational efficiency of the algorithm especially at the scale of the city level. title: Smart Industrial IoT Kit with Configurable Advanced Battery Temperature Management System (BTMS) for Enhancing Lithium-ion Battery Performance in Subzero Temperature Environment
abs: Despite the widespread usage of Li-ion batteries, there are still major unsolved problems in the aspects of safety, cost, and recycling. Meanwhile, under low-temperature operation conditions, Li-ion batteries have lower charge and discharge capacity, lower rated voltage, shorter cycle life, and if charging is forcibly performed, Li-ions are inclined to deposit on the surface of negative electrodes, causing lithium plating or even the formation of dendrite that may induce internal short and trigger thermal runaway events. These issues can easily occur in winter-driven vehicles, especially in Europe, Canada, northern parts of China, USA, and in certain regions in the southern hemisphere. Although Singapore has a warm climate, Li-ion batteries can still find applications under subzero conditions in cool rooms. Cool rooms are used for storage and distribution of fresh goods, medicine and industrial materials. In many cool rooms, the temperature can be -30 °C or lower. This subzero condition is not ideal for Li-ion batteries. Most of the time, the battery is frozen, resulting in difficulties to start up. When it is running, the battery pack needs to be changed frequently because of poor performance. Even so, the demand for cool rooms is rapidly increasing, with more cool rooms built for storage purposes, especially during COVID-19. The Russian-Ukraine war further aggravates the supply chain disruption, resulting in more food and goods being stored in face of shortages. The discharge capacity of Li-ion batteries at subzero temperatures significantly reduced. At -10 °C, a 2.2 Ah 18650 cylindrical cell could only retain approximately 1.7 Ah discharge capacity at 1C discharge rate, and the discharge capacity is even lower, when using a higher discharge rate (about 0.9 Ah at 4.6C). The decrease in discharge capacity would lead to a reduction of energy provided by the battery. The primary objective of the project is to develop an IIoT kit with configurable advanced BTMS for enhancing performance of Li-ion batteries of commonly used sizes in subzero temperature environments. The aim is to help battery system users alleviate their pain points of startup difficulties and poor performance in the subzero temperature conditions, by maintaining the battery temperature in optimum working range. With attainment of the desired operating temperature range, capacity loss and battery degradation could be prevented, and the life cycle of battery cells could be prolonged. Besides fulfilling the requirements of Li-ion battery pack of different sizes, the configurable advance BTMS could also be applied to other types of batteries in the cold working environments in the future.

title: Evaluating the efficacy of a digital feeding and lifestyle behaviour intervention for infants: a randomized controlled trial.
abs: Aims and Hypotheses: The first 1000 days of a child’s life is a critical period which influences lifelong cardiometabolic health. Early childhood lifestyle, activity, and appetitive behaviours sets this pivotal foundation. Our team has developed and validated a digitalized tool, called Feeding, Lifestyle, Activity Goals (FLAGs) to assess lifestyle and feeding behaviours of young infants, simultaneously providing guidance and tailored advice for parents on ideal practices specific to their children. The study objective is to determine the effects of FLAGs intervention on infant’s lifestyle behaviours, growth, and metabolic health outcomes. The central hypothesis is that infants whose caregivers are exposed to FLAGs intervention will exhibit healthier lifestyle behaviours, leading to optimal physical growth and metabolic health status at 12 months of age, compared to those without FLAGs intervention. Methodology: This is a prospective, two-arm, parallel group, randomized controlled trial in KK Women’s and Children’s Hospital, conducted over 12 months. We will recruit 130 infants, and they will be randomized in 1:1 ratio to i) the control group, receiving standard routine infant care, and ii) intervention group, where they will additionally receive access to the FLAGs assessment tool together with the real-time feedback and advisory provided by the digital application, complete with mobile nudges. We will examine efficacy of the FLAGs intervention through i) measuring indicators of good feeding and lifestyle behaviour at 12 months old using validated questionnaires, and ii) longitudinal growth trajectories and markers of infant metabolic health (anthropometry, body composition, diurnal variation in salivary cortisol). Conclusion: Demonstrating the benefits of using FLAGs will highlight the importance of integrating this digitalized assessment and advisory tool into the screening and evaluation of well children, with the potential to be upscaled and adopted in both tertiary and primary care settings. Its utilization can also be integrated practically into community-based health programmes.
kw: Metabolic health; developmental origins of health and disease; maternal and child health; population health

title: Immunoprofiling and Microbiome Analysis of Gestational Immunity For Transfer cohort Against Common Neonatal Respiratory Pathogens
abs: Background: The level of immune change in response to the health of the lactating mother-child dyad in human milk is complex. The complexity of breast milk composition means that most researchers explore only a few factors and rarely determine the composition in depth. Aims: Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that antiviral and immunomodulatory components of Human Milk Oligosaccharides (HMOs), human milk microbiome, cytokines and immune factors are altered after COVID-19 vaccination. Aim 1: To determine temporal changes in human milk oligosaccharides, microbiome composition, human milk cytokines and immune factors after receiving COVID-19 vaccination. Hypothesis 2: Enrichment of human milk with secretory immunoglobulin A through maternal vaccination could help infants combat targeted pathogens. Aim 2: To study the effect of immunization during pregnancy and lactation on induction of vaccine-specific immunity in human milk after delivery in the presence of maternal Tdap (tetanus, diphtheria, acellular pertussis), influenza and COVID-19 vaccination. Hypothesis 3: There are maternal vaccine specific T cells in human milk which may provide an under-recognized form of passive protection. Aim 3: To investigate if human milk T cells are modulated after maternal vaccination with potential implications for infant passive protection. Methods: Immune profiling and microbiome analysis will be performed on collected human milk samples from our 100-member GIFT-2 (Gestational Immunity For Transfer) cohort of COVID-19 vaccine-naive lactating mothers before and after receiving 2 doses of COVID-19 vaccinations. The applicant will be supervised by an established lab mentor who has methods ensuring feasibility. Impact: The applicant will examine how changes in the human milk immune factors of vaccinated mothers’ have the potential to impact infant health. By doing so, the applicant would be able to further explore the role of human milk and its compositional differences as a therapeutic in modifying respiratory infections, including COVID-19.
kw: COVID-19, neonatology, human milk, respiratory viruses, immunology

title: Towards Precision Medicine in Systemic Sclerosis: Identification of Immune Signatures Associated with Disease Activity and Predictive of Treatment Response in the Systemic Sclerosis Cohort Singapore
abs: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is a multi-systemic connective tissue disease that is characterized by complex interplay between autoimmunity, vasculopathy and fibrosis. It has high morbidity and mortality, particularly among Asians, and ethnicities were shown to play role in clinical manifestations. The classification of SSc subsets have relied mainly on the extent of skin involvement (diffuse vs. limited), and autoantibodies. However, due to the heterogenous pathological processes contributing to heterogeneity of disease, it is challenging to identify the right treatments for the right patients. Incorporation of molecular signatures that reflects pathological processes into clinical stratification is a promising approach to develop a more granular stratification system to personalize therapeutic approaches in SSc. In the proposed study, we aim to identify peripheral blood-derived immune signatures that are associated with disease activity and predictive of treatment responses in the Systemic Sclerosis Cohort Singapore (SCORE). We hypothesize that (1) peripheral immune signatures derived from circulating blood reflect disease activity, and (2) peripheral immune signatures derived from circulating blood predict response to immunosuppressive treatment in SSc. To address these hypotheses, our aims are (1) to identify peripheral immune signatures associated disease activity, and (2) to analyse peripheral immune signature predictive of response to immunosuppressive treatment in SSc. Peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) will be analysed by mass cytometry using a panel of cell surface and intracellular markers known to play pivotal role in SSc pathogenesis. Transcriptome analysis (single cell RNA sequencing) will be performed on differentially represented immune cells identified by mass cytometry, followed by unsupervised clustering analysis and correlation network analysis to reveal segregation/ correlation of immune cell subset, features and functions. The long-term goals are to discover and validate peripheral blood-derived immune signatures for SSc that will enable personalised therapeutic approaches, ultimately leading to improved outcomes of SSc patients.
kw: Systemic sclerosis; patient stratification; precision medicine; disease activity; treatment

title: Detection and optimization of treatment of severe cases of dry eye disease
abs: Dry eye disease (DED) is a common condition which ranges from idiopathic dry eye which reduces quality of life and work productivity, to sight threatening conditions such as DED related to cicatrising conjunctivitis, autoimmune disease like Sjogren’s syndrome, and DED secondary to graft vs host disease. To address this problem we propose a project with two major themes. Firstly, we want to develop a method of screening that can accurately detect more severe DED that requires specialist care. This will increase the accessibility of the current care since the screening and treatment of mild cases are performed in community settings by optometrists. This will also increase efficiency of care, still severe cases can be treated earlier, and avoid unnecessary hospital referrals. Since there is no effective way to screen the severe cases of DED in the community at the moment, we want to use a method based on imaging of the cornea that uses relatively simple and low cost equipment that is already available in primary care. In our preliminary findings with data scientists from ASTAR, we have achieved good results using an artificial intelligence algorithm. Now, we intend to evaluate the screening to non-Asians with eyes that have potentially issues with screening, and to incorporate symptom questions in conjunction with imaging in a two stage process. The second theme of this project deals with improving the treatment of severe DED. Currently, we are using umbilical cord plasma eyedrops produced by the collaborator from Singapore Cord Blood Bank. This is shown to be clinically safe and efficacious in our preliminary results. We intend to pursue further studies to see if incorporating the platelet lysates to the plasma at various concentrations will increase the health of the ocular surface cells. This will help DED patients that are refractory to current approach.
kw: ocular surface inflammation; personalised medicine; immunology; tear lipids; dry eye; community care

title: Adipocyte browning by near infrared or alternating magnetic field exposure on subcutaneously implanted nanomaterials containing chemical agents (ANTENNA)
abs: Specific Aims and Hypotheses: In contrast to well-established brown adipose tissue (BAT) activation and browning of white adipose tissue (WAT) by cold stimulation, the browning of WAT using localized heat is a new pathway discovered recently. We hypothesize that heat generated from interaction between near infrared radiation (NIR) and copper sulfide nanodots (CuS-ND) or from interaction between alternating magnetic field (AMF) and superparamagnetic iron oxide nanoparticles (SPION) can also trigger WAT browning. Methodology and Approach: We will exploit a novel bioengineered browning protocol in mice using subcutaneous injection of CuS-ND hydrogel followed by NIR exposure, as well as subcutaneous injection of SPION hydrogel followed by AMF exposure. This will inform the design and optimization of a pilot WAT browning protocol in humans. We will next recruit obese volunteers scheduled for bariatric surgery (n=20-30) to test the browning efficacy of both methods in humans. The optimized human protocol will subsequently be utilized in two parallel-arm, randomized, placebo-controlled clinical studies of obese subjects treated with CuS-ND/NIR or SPION/AMF respectively to evaluate the efficacy of browning and the magnitude of any favorable metabolic effects. Importance to Science or Medicine: This research will offer insights into a first-in-class once-weekly subcutaneous injection strategy of obesity treatment based on WAT browning. If successful, we may be one step closer to managing obesity, metabolic syndrome and type 2 diabetes using a BAT-based paradigm. Clinical Significance: In our obesogenic environment where energy dense food and physical inactivity are major factors driving the rising scourge of metabolic disorders, it fits our national interest to develop promising, cost-effective, non-pharmacological and safe BAT-activating approaches that tackle obesity and diabetes. Establishing a novel technique of harnessing BAT to increase energy expenditure as a counter against high energy intake can prove clinically feasible and worthwhile exploring as an important public health priority.
kw: Adipocyte browning; Nanomaterials; Near infrared; Alternating magnetic fields; Obesity; Metabolic syndrome

title: Investigate the potential function of telomeric variant sequences in allele-specific telomere protection and cardiovascular aging
abs: The ends of human linear chromosomes are capped by telomeres that consist of long tracts of hexa-nucleotide DNA repeats (5’-TTAGGG-3’)n with short single-stranded G-rich 3’ overhangs. Telomeres are bound by the shelterin complexes that are essential for the protection and stability of the chromosomal ends. Progressive shortening of steady-state telomere length in normal human somatic cells is a well-established biomarker for aging-associated diseases. Recently, we developed a novel workflow to capture full-length telomeres and subject them to single-molecule real-time (SMRT) sequencing. This new method provides the necessary accuracy and throughput to measure absolute telomere length with nucleotide resolution in human culture cell lines as well as clinical patient samples. Our results reveal the presence of telomeric variant sequences (TVSs) that are dispersed throughout the telomeric region, with larger and more abundant TVSs proximal to the subtelomeric region. The exact sequence and distribution of TVSs are unique to every chromosomal end in each individual. Our preliminary data have shown that even TVSs with only one nucleotide deviation from the canonical telomeric repeat dramatically reduced the binding affinity of the shelterin complex. We hypothesize that telomeric variant sequences (TVSs) lead to allele-specific telomere shortening and contribute directly to cardiovascular aging. Accelerated telomere shortening has been linked to premature human aging and aging-related diseases, such as cardiovascular disease. Using an established cohort of older adults (N=1000) who have been extensively evaluated for cardiovascular function, we will phenotype for telomere length and sequence to determine how TVSs influence the progression of cardiovascular aging and diseases.
kw: Telomere, allele-specific telomere length,aging, cardiovascular aging and diseases, biomarker

title: Cardiac Remodeling and Heart Failure Progression in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus and Co-existing Hypertension (REMODEL-2)
abs: The pathophysiology of heart failure depends on the etiology and risk factors. Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and hypertension have direct influence on the myocardium and are prevalent cardiometabolic risk factors of heart failure. With an increased prevalence in cardiometabolic risk factors, the burden of heart failure in Singapore is expected to increase further. Heart failure progression is characterized by cardiac structural and functional adverse remodeling, which progresses from an asymptomatic phase to an advanced stage where clinical symptoms occur. I lead an on-going observational study of Singaporeans with cardiometabolic risk factors who did not have other cardiovascular diseases at baseline (REMODEL; NCT02670031). We reported that hypertensive patients with T2DM had a higher prevalence of impaired left ventricular function and myocardial fibrosis compared to age- and sex-matched hypertensive patients without T2DM. Novel protein markers of increased inflammatory response and immune cell activation were associated with myocardial fibrosis in patients with hypertension and T2DM. One of these markers was growth and differentiation factor 15 (GDF-15), which has been associated with apoptosis, fibrosis, inflammation, adverse cardiac remodeling and a worse prognosis in heart failure. While the mechanisms mediating the adverse impact of T2DM in heart failure are not clear, metabolic changes in the heart may precede the abnormal structural and functional signs of heart failure. In this regard, flux of pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) was reduced in T2DM rats and correlated negatively with diastolic dysfunction, supporting a mechanistic link between metabolic and structural/functional cardiac remodeling in cardiometabolic diseases. Our over-arching hypothesis is adverse cardiac remodeling in patients with cardiometabolic risk factors is complex. Beyond the hemodynamic consequences of elevated blood pressures, we suggest that heart failure progression may be mediated by activation of pathways promoting cardiac fibrosis, inflammation and/or abnormal glucose metabolism in the heart.
kw: cardiac remodelling; myocardial fibrosis; diabetes mellitus; hypertension

title: Investigating effects of Roseburia intestinalis on colorectal carcinogenesis and its dietary modulation for cancer prevention
abs: Recent research has shown that altered gut microbiota is causally linked to the development of colorectal cancer (CRC). While certain microbes have been shown to promote cancer, some microbes can inhibit carcinogenesis. Thus, modulating the gut microbiome by diet or other means has great potential in preventing and treating CRC. Analyzing microbiota composition in multiple cohorts, we identified Roseburia intestinalis, a common gut commensal bacterium, to show consistently decreased abundance in CRC patients. Our preliminary data demonstrated that treatment of R intestinalis was able to produce anti-tumor effects to suppress tumour growth in both in vivo and in vitro studies. Furthermore, a high-fiber diet was also shown to assist R intestinalis growth in the murine intestine. Our findings from patient cohorts, CRC mouse models, and microbiota-associated diet support the hypothesis that a specific diet enriches R intestinalis to suppress colorectal carcinogenesis. We propose three specific aims to test this hypothesis: 1. To determine the anti-tumour effects and mechanisms on CRC development 2. To profile the metabolome from R intestinalis and identify its bioactive metabolites in inhibiting carcinogenesis 3. To determine the efficacy of a specific Roseburia-enriching high-fibre diet in preventing CRC Determining the anti-cancer effects of R intestinalis and testing the dietary modulation in preventing CRC will uncover a new direction to prevent carcinogenesis. Such an evidence-based approach not just demands a mechanistic understanding of the functional microbial species but also leads us toward novel microbiome-based biotherapeutics to prevent CRC. The outcome of this proposed study will provide a specific and effective clinical impact in terms of CRC prevention.
kw: colorectal cancer; microbiome; bacteria; cancer prevention; diet

title: Evaluation of biomarkers of tuberculosis treatment response, disease cure and relapse detection in the TRUNCATE-TB trial
abs: Many new drugs and combination TB treatments await testing in TB clinical trials. Microbiological outcomes measured in phase 2 TB trials are poor predictors of response in phase 3. Phase 3 TB trials require large numbers of participants and long follow-up to detect clinical outcomes and are slow and expensive. Because of these barriers, few trials are conducted and this impedes the development of new TB regimens. We aim to develop biomarkers for monitoring treatment, identifying people who are cured at the end of treatment and identifying early TB relapse in people who have completed treatment. We will use samples stored in the TRUNCATE-TB trial that evaluated a strategy of treating TB for just 8 weeks using novel drug combinations, with close follow-up to identify and retreat (with a full 6-month course) the minority who relapsed. It is the first ever large randomised controlled trial of 8-week treatment for TB and provides a perfect (and unique) opportunity to develop and assess biomarkers for determining success of 8-week treatment regimens. We will do transcriptomics and proteomics assays on blood samples collected and stored at baseline, week 4 and week 8 in 540 trial participants, and at the time of suspected relapse in a further 214 participants. Using advanced bioinformatics and statistical analysis approaches we will identify new biomarker signatures and risk scores that can be used to monitor the response to TB treatment; to differentiate between cure and non-cure during and at the end of treatment; and differentiate between relapse and no relapse in patients after the end of treatment. We will validate these new biomarkers and published biomarkers and provide the definitive global data on the value of biomarkers with 8-week treatment. Such biomarkers could transform the pace of clinical trials and also have clinical management applications.
kw: tuberculosis; clinical trial; biomarker; transcriptomics; metabolomics; proteomics

title: Investigating the function of β-cat-TCF4 responsive transcription (CRT) in promoting an immune tolerant microenvironment in colorectal cancers (CRC)
abs: Background: Recent studies suggest that increased nuclear β-cat-responsive transcription/CRT may inhibit T cell infiltration into Wnt-associated tumors, alluding to its immune-suppressive role. We recently developed GB1874, a specific and selective small molecular inhibitor of β-cat-TCF4 interaction. We demonstrated that GB1874 can block Wnt-dependent tumor-intrinsic properties, such as stemness, and growth/proliferative potential of Wnt-addicted CRC cells both in vitro and in vivo. Motivated by the promising anti-tumor effects the β-cat-TCF4 inhibitor, and given our preliminary but promising data suggesting that GB1874 treatment can reverse the immune exclusion phenotype in syngeneic models in vivo, our research objective is to study how β-cat-TCF4 inhibitors might affect tumor immune microenvironment (TiME) in CRCs. Hypothesis: We hypothesize that small molecule inhibitors of nuclear β-cat-TCF4 interaction will reverse immune tolerance by promoting increased infiltration of effector tumor infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) (such as CD8+ T cells), thereby re-sensitizing immune-cold CRCs to immunotherapy to produce a favorable anti-tumor immune response. Methodology and approach: We will utilize multi-dimensional single cell approaches (including single cell RNA-seq, high-dimensional flow cytometry, CyTOF, spatial transcriptomics and multiplex-immunohistochemistry) to characterise the tumour immune microenvironment, in both syngeneic and humanized mouse xenograft models of patient-derived CRC, upon treatment with either CRT inhibitors as monotherapy or in combination with ICB. Specific Aims: 1) Determine the biological effects of β-cat-TCF4 responsive transcription (CRT) inhibition on tumor immune microenvironment (TiME); 2) Characterize alterations in cellular composition and cell-states (phenotypes) within the tumor microenvironment (TME) upon CRT inhibition at the resolution of single cells; 3) Interrogate the effect of CRT inhibition on response to immune checkpoint blockade in syngeneic and humanized mice models Importance to science and medicine: Successful development of nuclear β-cat-TCF inhibitors have tremendous promise in the generation of novel, nuclear β-cat-targeting drugs that could be combined with current immunotherapy modalities to improve the anti-tumour immune response.
kw: colorectal cancer, Wnt signalling, b-catenin, immunotherapy

title: Targeting Stress Granule-associated RNA Structure and Interaction in Cancers Cells
abs: Stress granule formation is associated with cancers. However, the mechanism by which RNA structures and interactions mediate stress granule formation remains elusive, making it challenging to target therapeutically. We propose to study RNA structure and interaction under stress conditions in cancer cells, thereby providing a foundation of knowledge on developing novel cancer therapeutics to overcome drug resistance.
kw: RNA Structure; RNA Interaction; Stress Granule; Cancer; Drug Resistance

title: Development of biomarker and epigenetic priming strategy to overcome CAR T cell therapy resistance in HER2+ breast tumor
abs: With the success of chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy in hematological cancers, there is increasing interest in applying CAR T cell therapy to treat refractory solid tumors. However, most of these clinical trials in solid tumors, including HER2-targeting CAR T therapy in refractory breast cancer, have been unsuccessful. While most attempts have been made through the amelioration of CAR T cells, the intrinsic resistance mechanism within solid tumors has been overlooked. In our recent study of anti-HER2 resistance and metastasis in breast cancer, we found interferon-gamma receptor 1 (IFNGR1), which mediates the interferon-gamma (IFN) signaling in antitumor immunity, is markedly downregulated in trastuzumab-refractory HER2+ breast tumors. Moreover, our preliminary data have shown that the downregulation of IFNGR1 is associated with reduced HER2-targeting CAR T-killing efficacy of HER2+ breast cancer. Notably, an FDA-approved EZH2 inhibitor, tazemetostat (EPZ-6478; EPZ), can restore IFNGR1 expression in HER2+ breast cancer and increase CAR T efficacy in vitro and in vivo. Interestingly, we find that IFNGR1 is not only downregulated in breast cancer but also in other solid tumors as well. Based on these observations, we hypothesize that the downregulation of IFNGR1 expression in tumors contributes to CAR T cell therapy resistance in solid tumors. This proposal seeks to utilize HER2+ breast cancer as a model to validate this hypothesis and develop a biomarker and therapeutic strategy to overcome CAR T cell therapy resistance in IFNGR1-low tumors.
kw: CAR T cell therapy, HER2+ breast tumor, biomarker, epigenetic

title: Functional Characterisation of Enhancers of ALX1 and Beyond in Human Craniofacial Enhanceropathies
abs: Craniofacial malformations affect a third of all congenital diseases, affecting key sensory organ development, with increased risk of neonatal mortality when essential life activities such as feeding and breathing are compromised. Such craniofacial abnormalities arise due to disrupted gene networks underpinning the development of facial tissues during the first two months of pregnancy from their embryonic precursors – the cranial neural crest. Mutations in the neural crest transcription factor ALX1 are known to cause severe Frontonasal Dysplasia (FND3), a rare disease characterized by severe facial clefting and extreme microphthalmia (small eyes with vision loss) with frequent lethality. We have identified two independent consanguineous families presenting with disease fully phenocopying FND3. However, the ALX1 gene is not mutated in both cases. Instead, we identify large non-coding genomic deletions upstream of ALX1. Based on our preliminary work encompassing reanalysis of published omics datasets and functional modeling of the disease lesion in vivo in zebrafish, we hypothesise that the large non-coding deletions identified in our patients contain putative regulatory enhancers for ALX1, thus representing a novel craniofacial enhanceropathy. In this proposal, we aim to functionally assess the putative craniofacial-specific enhancers of ALX1 and other craniofacial genes in a physiologically relevant human in vitro model, and understand the cause of the genomic lesions. More specifically, we will functionally assay the putative enhancers of ALX1 in wildtype and patient-iPS-derived human Cranial Neural Crest Cells (hCNCCs) via gain- and loss-of function assays. Then we will characterize and generate a hCNCC enhancer-gene connectome of ALX1 and all other craniofacial genes – linking all functional craniofacial enhancers to their target gene promoters. This will yield a powerful diagnostic resource of non-coding candidate loci potentially implicated in craniofacial disease. Finally, we will decipher the mode of deletion underlying the enhanceropathy’s genomic lesions in an in vitro assay amenable to drug inhibition.
kw: enhancers; craniofacial; rare-disease; stem-cells; omics; epigenetics

title: Investigating the unknown molecular players in colitis driven inflammation.
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Chronic inflammation conditions like colitis often have high disease and economic burden with very limited treatment regime. Understanding the major key players regulating this inflamed state could provide better therapeutic candidates. While telomere attrition has been correlated with colitis progression and chronic inflammation, whether telomerase controls the presentation, differentiation, and maturation of any specific immune cell population during colitis is unknown. In this regard, telomerase reverse transcriptase (Tert) has been reported to have significant non-canonical extra-telomeric roles too play in inflammation. In this proposal, we hypothesise that the Tert molecule has additional inflammation-associated regulatory functions that can be telomere-independent, and which may act as new targetable candidates to treat colitis and other inflammatory disorders. We generated a novel catalytically inactive Tert mice that will help to understand telomere independent function of Tert compared to whole body Tert KO mice. The current proposal exploits the most frequently used DSS-induced colitis model to understand the non-conventional partners of Tert and its ability to modulate inflammation in the colon. Specifically, we aim to (i) : identify telomere-dependent and independent inflammatory responses and (ii) deconvolute the mechanisms of telomerase-associated immune regulation and (iii) develop genome-wide screening tools to identify TERT-dependent novel immunotherapies against colitis and beyond. We will be reporting probably the first in vivo evidence for Tert’s non-canonical function using a catalytically null Tert mice. This mice model will be favourable for future studies regarding Tert’s canonical role in disease context. Preliminary results show that Tert KO leads to dampened inflammatory response compared to the WT or catalytically inactive mice. This gives a strong proof that Tert may activate/modulate the immune cell type or the signalling pathway in colitis model. This study makes use of advance technique like sc-RNAseq that will provide new insight on inflammatory regulatory mechanism in colitis progression.
kw: Colitis; Inflammation; Tert; Immune cell; Cytokines; Telomerase

title: Engineering CRISPR-associated transposons for precise RNA-guided DNA integration in gene therapy
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Gene therapy involves the functional replacement of a defective gene copy in host cells. Current methods rely on i) random integration of functional genes into the host genome, which carries the risk of insertional oncogenesis, ii) introduction of functional genes in a non-integrating episome, which is not inserted into the host genome and therefore constitutes a non-permanent rescue of function. Here, we propose a novel approach for gene therapy involving the use of CRISPR-associated transposons (CASTs) for precise, high-efficiency integration of therapeutic genes into human cells. Currently, CASTs are widely used for genome editing in bacteria, but not human cells. We hypothesize that CAST systems have not been successfully applied to human cells due to insufficient basal activity, and the lack of knowledge about accessory proteins necessary for CAST activity. Since CAST elements are native to bacteria, these accessory factors may be specific to the bacterial host and are therefore absent in human cells. To this end, we will: i) perform a mutagenesis screen on CAST proteins to engineer them for improved activity and specificity, ii) identify host factors that augment CAST activity using E. coli gene deletion libraries, iii) apply our optimized CAST system, together with beneficial host factors, for rescue of SMN1 deficiency in human cells.
kw: CRISPR; transposon; gene therapy

title: Develop a Real-world Evidence-based, Flexible Decision-Making Evaluation Framework for Optimizing Precision Medicine in Severe Asthma
abs: Background: The world, including Singapore, is moving towards precision medicine (PM) as an alternative to traditional reactive medicine. However, the question remains how to turn PM from theory into practice. Aims: This study aims to address this issue by using asthma as a case study to build a real-world data (RWD)-based decision-making evaluation framework to estimate the clinical utility and cost-effectiveness of machine learning (ML)-based risk prediction tools in real-world scenarios, and to guide patient-level clinical decisions. Methods: First, we will perform a Bayesian network analysis to estimate the causal interactions of core predictors that lead to severe exacerbation in patients with severe asthma, and incorporate decision and utility nodes and “what-if” scenarios into this prediction process. Second, a decision curve analysis will be applied to assess the clinical net benefits of a robust new risk prediction model in guiding asthma treatment escalation across a range of clinician-preferred risk thresholds and test harms. This analysis informs the desirable prediction accuracy for the model to be clinically useful. Third, a novel, RWD-based, patient-level simulation model with dynamic decision-making will be deployed to estimate the cost-effectiveness of asthma risk prediction model in guiding treatment escalation, considering the heterogeneous decision-making process and downstream patient outcomes in real-world scenarios. Finally, we will implement the asthma risk prediction model into a user-friendly, freely-accessible Web App to inform personalized one-year risk and rate of severe asthma exacerbation, accompanied by a human-machine interface for counterfactual analysis to support clinical decision making. Feasibility: The study team has obtained all the necessary data and has a strong track-record in building risk prediction models and cost-effectiveness analysis, and has done a significant background work on methodology and predictor selection. Importance: This proposed research is a critical step towards adopting digital PM in the context of noncommunicable diseases worldwide.
kw: clinical decision making, clinical utility, cost effectiveness, machine learning, risk prediction, severe asthma

title: Rebuild corticospinal tract by cell transplantation in Ischemic Stroke
abs: Stroke is the second leading cause of death and third leading cause of disability globally. Cerebral ischemia triggers the ischemic cascade and quickly results in irreversible neuronal injury. The current treatment of ischemic stroke is limited to rapid reperfusion by intravenous thrombolysis and endovascular thrombectomy, but this therapeutic strategy is restricted to a narrow time window of up to 6 hours from stroke onset. After that, there are no effective therapeutic options. I propose to develop a cell therapy to replace the lost neural cells and reconnect the neural circuit. The bottleneck of stroke cell therapy is the poor survival of transplanted neural cells due to the hostile environment and the inability of nerve growth from the survived neurons in the disease brain to repair the neural networks. I have developed a chemical cocktail to promote the survival of grafted human neural progenitors by providing physical support to human neural progenitors and by overcoming the harmful inflammatory environment. In the present proposal, I will examine if the grafted human neurons project to the target brain regions and rebuild the neural circuits by circuit mapping and cellular profiling (Aim 1). By using stem cell lines engineered with chemogenetic switches, I will ascertain if the circuit reconnectivity is responsible for the behavioral recovery of the stroke animals (Aim 2). I hope that my proposed study will set up a foundation for developing a new therapeutic option for repairing the irreversibly damaged stroke brain, offering hopes for stroke patients.
kw: Cell transplantaion, neural regeneration, neural progenitor, corticospinal tract, stroke

title: The functional contributions of tissue-specific viral variants in Zika virus disease pathogenesis
abs: Zika virus (ZIKV), which was initially classified as an innocuous member of the flavivirus genus, has re-emerged as a viral disease of international concern due to the correlation of the infection with severe neurological abnormalities in newborn babies. Replication error rate of RNA viruses combined with viral protein/RNA structural plasticity can lead to evolution of virus-induced pathogenicity that is critical to identify and validate. Preliminary studies revealed a tissue-specific expansion of non-consensus ZIKV variants only in the brains of infected mice but not in other tissues such as testis or blood, that appeared to correlate with the lethal neurological phenotype. However such tissue-specific expansion of ZIKV variants is not well-understood. Therefore this proposal aims to use established mouse models supported by insectary and human-brain organoid infections models to test the hypothesis that within-host selection pressure could favour the dominance of specific viral sequence variant(s) in the virus swarm, thereby resulting in the unusual ZIKV-associated tissue pathologies. Specifically this proposal seeks to unravel the molecular mechanism underlying the unique brain-associated variants in ZIKV disease pathogenesis through state-of-the-art proteomics to identify the critical host-factor(s) in mediating the ZIKV-induced tissue pathologies. Collectively this study could provide new insights into the dynamics of virus evolution and disease pathogenesis.
kw: Zika virus; neuropathogenesis; viral variants; animal models; brain organoids; proteomics

title: Real-time Quantitative Evaluation of Cancer Therapy Efficacy by NIR-IIb Luminescence Lifetime Imaging
abs: Traditional methods to evaluate cancer therapeutic efficacy are based on tumor size measurement by CT or MRI, which need weeks or months post-treatment to identify the shrinkage of tumors. Thus, quantitative evaluation of therapeutic efficacy in real-time is in urgent demand to greatly benefit cancer patients, realizing personalized precision treatment at the reduced cost. In this proposal, we aim to build an integrated lanthanide-dye nanoplatform, which can achieve cancer phototherapy and, at the same time, non-invasively and quantitatively evaluate the therapeutic efficacy in real-time in the second near infrared b (NIR-IIb, 1500-1700 nm) window by luminescence lifetime imaging. The main method is to precisely regulate the energy transfer in lanthanide nanoparticles (LnNPs) and select functional molecular E1057 as photothermal agent, as well as energy acceptor, to realize NIR-II (1000-1700 nm) phototherapy and NIR-IIb luminescence lifetime regulation for real-time quantitative evaluation of phototherapy. Specifically, in mouse tumor metastasis lesion, E1057 acts as energy acceptor can regulate NIR-IIb luminescence lifetime of LnNPs beyond 1500 nm, meanwhile, E1057 exhibits photothermal effect, which will be used for NIR-II photothermal therapy (PTT). Then reactive oxygen species (ROS) in tumor cells will significantly increase response to heat stress during PPT treatment, resulting in the destruction of E1057 and cut off the energy transfer from LnNPs to E1057, finally leading to the NIR-IIb luminescence lifetime recovery of LnNPs. The correlation between NIR-II luminescence lifetime and the final therapy efficacy can be built to evaluate and predict the therapeutic efficacy in real-time, which in the future can provide guidance for personalized precision PTT treatment, increase survival rate, save time and medical cost for both patients and government.
kw: Luminescence lifetime imaging; Second near-infrared b; Quantitative in vivo sensing; Cancer therapy; Efficacy evaluation

title: Generating an MS-CETSA footprint to capture the dynamic interactome of autophagy and dissect complex drug-induced cellular responses on a proteome-wide scale
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: It is well accepted that dysregulation of autophagy is linked to human diseases including neurodegenerative diseases, diabetes, or liver diseases. Over the past decade, autophagy has gained increasing interest in the context of cancer development and resistance. Due to the lack of available tools for systematic studies, detailed insight into the molecular mechanism and regulation of autophagy are only fragmented. This restricts the understanding of disease progression or resistant mechanisms and hampers the development of novel compounds. Using Mass Spectrometry coupled CEllular Thermal Shift Assay (MS-CETSA), a high-resolution interaction proteomic methodology, I aim to generate an autophagy footprint to identify unique key players of autophagy and to dissect drug-specific cellular responses. Two different modes of induction and two time points will capture the time-dependent processes involved in autophagy activation and progression. The unique feature of the CETSA heating step captures changes within the cell in situ, and responses in already established autophagy markers will be used as proof of concept. Additionally, the unbiased proteome-wide approach will provide an integrated view of the whole cellular interactome. In subsequent studies the established autophagy footprint can be used to further characterize subtypes of autophagy or to study autophagy-inducing drugs where modes of action are still poorly understood. When applied to clinical samples, the cellular state of tumour cells can be determined, which in turn can guide towards a combination therapy specifically tailored to each patient.
kw: CETSA; mass spectrometry; autophagy

title: Large DNA genome editing by “Prime-exchange” with Enhanced Efficiency and Safety
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Despite herculean efforts have significantly improved CRISPR toolkits, programmable edits of gene-size length are current limited to homology-directed repair (HDR). However, limitations in efficiency, precision, and potential indels seriously jeopardize its clinical application. We propose Prime-Exchange, an innovative technology allowing gene-size genome edits without double-stranded breaks (DSB). In contrast to the Cas9-HDR approach, we prime the genomic locus for HDR by prime editing, creating capturing DNA flaps that facilitate HDR without DSB. Our project will employ bioengineering techniques, next-generation sequencing, classical molecular and biochemistry assays to develop and evaluate Prime-Exchange. This development promises therapeutic genome editing with enhanced safety and efficacy.
kw: Genome editing; CRISPR; large DNA insertion; Prime editors

title: Rational design of broad-spectrum fusion inhibitors
abs: Flavivirus is a family of more than 70 single-stranded RNA viruses vectored principally by arthropods. More than 400 million people are infected by flaviviruses annually, with 20,000 deaths. Flavivirus infection can cause a spectrum of severe illness, including hemorrhagic fever, Guillain-Barre syndrome and encephalitis. Effective vaccines are only available for a few flaviviruses, such as yellow fever virus and tick-born encephalitis virus. Current anti-flavivirus drug discovery largely focuses on nonstructural proteins, to disrupt virus assembly and replication by interfering with their enzymatic functions. Despite decades of intensive efforts, therapeutic candidates targeting these proteins has yet to perform satisfactorily in the clinic. To identify effective broad-spectrum anti-flavivirus drug candidates, I will leverage on an antibody-guided drug screening strategy to search for small molecule inhibitors targeting flavivirus E protein. E protein is the sole antigen on the surface of flavivirus, responsible for viral entry into host cell. It is a major target of immune system, captured by many potent neutralizing antibodies, indicating a critical function. Due to a high conservation in protein sequence and structure, many E protein-targeting antibodies have cross-reactivity across different types of flaviviruses. Here, I hypothesize that the E protein of flaviviruses is a potential druggable target that can be captured by small molecule inhibitors with pan-flavivirus potency. Utilizing broadly neutralizing antibodies, I will carry out high-throughput screening to search for E protein-directed small molecule inhibitors able to block infection by mimicking the antibody, followed with mechanistic study using NMR and cryo-EM approaches. The best hit compound will be validated in vivo using IFN-αβR- mutant mice. Together, this work will produce pan-flavivirus small molecule inhibitors with high translational value. In addition, the antibody-guided drug screening platform will be a robust tool for antiviral drug discovery.

title: Singapore Biodesign Innovation Fellowship Training Programme
abs: The Singapore Biodesign Innovation Fellowship, housed under the Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR), is an intensive 6 month hands-on, multidisciplinary team-based training programme on the entire biodesign process of health technology innovation. The aims are to train the next generation of leaders in health innovation, and to develop new health technologies for unmet clinical needs in Asia. To date, more than 53 health technology companies and US$ 1 billion funds have been founded or raised directly from the programme. The Biodesign pedagogy and methodology are founded by the Stanford Byers Centre for Biodesign, and includes 3 iterative phases, “Identify”, “Invent” and “Implement” applied via a clinical theme (no further details regarding theme are available at this point), which is designed such that it may not reflect the Fellows’ prior clinical expertise or research focus. The assembled team and I will undertake local and regional country immersion to experience various health technology ecosystems. This is followed by a period of product invention, then implementation by formulating a business development and technology commercialisation strategy, in collaboration with domain experts in the Silicon Valley, USA. The critical design thinking and knowledge in scaling innovation, as well as the partnership and networks forged after completion of the Fellowship, will enable me to develop innovation designs and care models, that accelerate achievement of process indicators in chronic kidney and metabolic disease management, and enable more effective health navigation. I forsee a future role as a Clinician Innovator, actively contributing to the local health ecosystem by dual leveraging a Biodesign framework on healthcare coupled with prior proficiencies in informatics, to develop more cost and service quality efficient and effective care in chronic and metabolic diseases to foster a healthier Singapore.

title: The Efficacy and Mechanism of Controlled Microtrauma on Human Hair Regrowth and Regeneration
abs: AIMS In this project, I aim to show that controlled microtrauma is effective in reversing hair follicle miniaturisation in androgenetic alopecia (AGA). I will use single-cell RNA sequencing to identify cellular interactions specific to controlled microtrauma which results in hair regrowth. HYPOTHESIS I hypothesize that microtrauma may stimulate hair regrowth in AGA, and that this mechanism is mediated through distinct interactions with immune cells. METHODOLOGY 75 male AGA patients will undergo a randomized split-scalp double-phase study with controlled microtrauma. Microtrauma will be induced with either monthly fractional CO2 (fCO2) laser, or twice-weekly customized microneedle (MN) patches to half the temporal hairline. Patients will be randomized to receive standard medical therapy (topical minoxidil and oral finasteride) alone, microtrauma alone, or topical minoxidil and split-scalp microtrauma. In Phase 2 (next 6 months), microtrauma treatments will cease. This design will show if controlled microtrauma can stimulate hair regrowth in AGA, with or without current standard treatments, and how long this effect is maintained. In selected patients, 3mm scalp biopsies will be obtained from both temporal hairline and the vertex at baseline and +3m into treatment. Single-cell RNA sequencing and CellChat analysis will be used to infer intercellular communications to identify potential interactions associated with reversal of HF miniaturisation during AGA treatment, particularly between immune and non-immune cell types. These will be validated with spatial imaging and ex vivo organ culture. IMPORTANCE Hair loss is a common and potentially devastating condition. AGA is the most common form of hair loss, and its prevalence will rise with Singapore’s ageing population. Work in this project will uncover the mechanism of hair regrowth in regeneration in our local population, a field which has been underfunded and represents a significant unmet need.
