title: The role of primary angle-closure glaucoma (PACG) susceptibility gene, EPDR1 in clinical PACG severity and intraocular pressure susceptibility
abs: Primary angle closure (PAC) glaucoma (PACG) is the major form of glaucoma and visual loss in Singapore. Current strategies for patient stratification do not identify PAC suspects (PACS) who may progress and develop advanced PACG. This unmet need has led us to identify EPDR1 as a potential biomarker of such high risk PACG patients. Reports have suggested that the EPDR1 (ependymin related 1) gene, a recently identified PACG susceptibility gene, is associated with the PACS phenotype and increased PACG severity. How EPDR1 is associated with PACG severity is unclear. EPDR1 is expressed in the retinal ganglion cells (RGC), the site of glaucoma damage and EPDR1 expression is loss in human lens capsules of PACG patients compared to PACS patients. Epdr1 knock out (KO) mice exhibit PACS features and loss of RGC Epdr1 expression, and are thus ideal for studying the effects of raised intraocular pressure (IOP) and Epdr1 loss. Our hypothesis is that " loss of EPDR1 in lens epithelium, and serum correlates with PACS disease phenotype (Aim 1A). Patients with greater reduction in lens epithelial and serum EPDR1 may have more severe glaucoma damage on visual field (Aim 1B). Epdr1 loss in Epdr1 KO mice increases its susceptibility to raised IOP (Aim 2A). This RGC damage may be mediated through increased endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress secondary to EPDR1 loss (Aim 2B).” Our specific aims are: Aim 1A: To correlate the gene and protein expression of EPDR1 in patients with PAC spectrum. Aim 1B: To compare the visual field changes in age-matched PACG patients with and without reduced EPDR1 expression. Aim 2A: To determine if Epdr1 KO mice have increased glaucoma susceptibility using the magnetic bead induced experimental glaucoma (EG) model. Aim 2B: To determine the molecular signature of EG on RGCs of Epdr1 KO mice.
kw: primary angle closure glaucoma, EPDR1, PACG susceptibility, PACG severity,

title: Evaluating the Role of Tumour-Associated Macrophages in the Response to Anti-CD38 Monoclonal Antibody Therapy in Multiple Myeloma
abs: Background Immune dysregulation is a key mechanism of resistance to anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody (mAb) therapy in multiple myeloma (MM). Tumour-associated macrophages (TAM) have been proposed to promote resistance to immunotherapy but have not been well characterized in MM. MM plasma cells (PC) also evade CD38 mAb induced antibody-dependent cellular phagocytosis by CD47 expression. It remains unknown whether TAMs or PC CD47 expression play a role in the response to CD38 mAb therapy. Specific Hypotheses 1) TAM infiltration, as assessed by full spectrum flow cytometry (SFCM) and 2) PC CD47 expression are associated with an inferior response at 1.5 years following anti-CD38 mAb therapy. We also hypothesise that TAMs in patients with inferior responses have a distinct gene expression profile. Proposed methodology We propose a prospective cohort study of newly diagnosed MM patients planned for treatment with anti-CD38 mAb based regimens. Peripheral blood (PB) and bone marrow (BM) samples will be collected at diagnosis, achievement of complete response, and relapse. Response to treatment will be assessed based on the International Myeloma Working Group uniform response criteria. At the 1.5-year time point, patients who achieve a very good partial response or better will be classified as having a “ good response” while those with a partial response or worse will be deemed to have a “ poor response”. BM and PB samples will be analysed through SFCM, using an antibody panel designed to characterise TAMs. The same technique will be used to identify clonal PCs and quantify their CD47 expression. Correlation analysis will be performed to investigate if PC CD47 expression impacts treatment response and the degree of BM TAM infiltration. Lastly, we will use single-cell RNA sequencing to study the GEP of TAMs in good and poor responders at diagnosis and relapse.
kw: multiple myeloma;tumor associated macrophage; anti CD38 monoclonal antibody; immunotherapy;CD47

title: Modelling the Disease Burden of Cancer in Singapore
abs: Aims: Cancer ranks as a leading cause of death in several countries globally, and may soon be the leading cause of premature death in most countries within the next century. These trends are mirrored locally, where between 2017 to 2021, cancer was the leading cause of death in Singapore, accounting for almost one-third of all mortalities. The primary aim of this project seeks to anticipate the burden of three major preventable cancers, including breast cancer, colorectal cancer, and cervical cancer in the long-term, taking into account changes in demographic and population factors. We also seek to study the impacts of changes to current national screening programmes on the incidence of these cancers, and its effects on the healthcare system and cost. Hypotheses: We hypothesise an initial rise in cancer incidence given the changes in our population structure, particularly with the ageing population in Singapore. This may lead to an increase in both direct and indirect healthcare expenditure. Lastly, an increase in cancer screening uptake will lead to cancer stage migration with a rise in early stage disease, however should eventually plateau and potentially decrease over the medium to long-term as these pre-cancers would have been treated appropriately before progressing to cancer. Methodology: This study will employ a Bayesian evidence synthesis to pool data from various date streams, including the NRDO (1968 to 2022), NCCS, national health surveys, as well as other available data sources. This will then be used to conduct incidence projections forward to 2050 using an individual-level simulation model. We aim to obtain health finance data from various sources such as OMNIBUS to estimate direct costs. We plan to recruit cancer patients of all stages for the three cancer types, to conduct detailed structured interviews and surveys to ascertain the indirect costs that patients potentially incur. Clinical implications: The use of modeling techniques can help forecast future trends in cancer incidence, prevalence, mortality, and survival rates in Singapore. This information will be crucial for stakeholders at all levels, including policymakers, healthcare leaders, physicians, researchers to allocate resources effectively and develop targeted interventions. Importantly, by incorporating dynamic demographic changes into the model, this study can analyze, for instance, the impact of Singapore’s ageing population on the incidence of cancer, which we will project to rise in the future.

title: SB: Singapore Biodesign Innovation Fellowship Training Programme
abs: The Singapore Biodesign Innovation Fellowship is a rigorous training program that provides first-hand experiences in the innovation, design, and development of novel health technologies to address unmet healthcare needs in Asia. At least 53 health technology companies have been founded by the Stanford Biodesign program, raising more than USD 1 billion and benefiting more than 4 million patients. Along with a focused multidisciplinary team (e.g. engineers, health care professionals, corporate professionals), I will be trained using the well-established Stanford Byers Centre for Biodesign pedagogy and closely mentored by experts in Biodesign. The program consists of three main phases - (1) Identify; (2) Invent; and (3) Implement. In the Identify phase, Various cognitive processes such as design thinking will be taught to identify crucial clinical needs. Extensive research will then be performed through various modalities (e.g. clinical immersion, stakeholder interviews, policy review) to understand the problem and identify the pertinent pain points. In the Invent phase, the team will generate novel ideas and apply various strategies to shortlist the most viable solutions, considering implications concerning regulatory and technical feasibility, business model and sustainability, and intellectual property. A prototype will also be generated, tested, and optimised. In the Implement phase, a commercialisation and sustainability plan will be developed and implemented. Throughout the 6 months fellowship, I will also be immersed in the relevant regional (i.e China and Indonesia) Healthtech settings to gain an in-depth understanding of the healthtech ecosystem. I will also be attached to the program partners in Silicon Valley to refine and develop implementation plans for our top projects. This fellowship will provide me with the opportunity to connect and learn from various healthtech domain experts to enhance my ability to develop and implement novel and scalable solutions to improve the healthcare landscape in Singapore and beyond.

title: Muscle Quality Assessment in Sarcopenia: Examining the role of shear wave elastography in sarcopenia assessment and diagnosis
abs: Background Operationalisation of sarcopenia diagnosis in clinical setting has been difficult due to the challenges in establishing consensus criteria for sarcopenia. Emerging literature has demonstrated that decreased muscle mass alone does not consistently predict impaired mobility and poorer physical performance. Evaluation of muscle quality in sarcopenia diagnosis is potentially useful with advantages in utilisation of shear wave elastography (SWE) for muscle quality measurement such as wide availability including at the bedside and relatively low cost. Clinical applicability of SWE is limited at present due to underlying challenges that impact its validity. Aims Our research objective is to determine the potential of SWE as a diagnostic tool for sarcopenia by further investigating its construct validity in terms of concurrent validity with MRI spectroscopy measured muscle quality and blood biomarkers relevant to sarcopenia as well as predictive validity for muscle strength measures, muscle performance measures and clinical measures such as activity level and quality of life. Methods We will conduct a cross-sectional analysis of 100 participants in the Muscle Ultrasonography for Diagnosing Sarcopenia in Community-dwelling Older Adults Study. Correlation between SWE determined muscle quality and MRI spectroscopy measured muscle quality and blood biomarkers will be determined using Pearson’s correlation. Association of SWE determined muscle quality and measures of muscle strength, physical performance, level of activity and quality of life will be determined using linear regression analysis adjusted for age and gender. Contribution to medicine Our purpose is to add to current understanding of the concept of sarcopenia and sarcopenia diagnosis beyond muscle mass to muscle quality. This in turn will provide further evidence for the conceptualization and operationalizability of sarcopenia to allow better implementation of community-based sarcopenia case-finding, diagnosis and management that can be realised in a more upstream manner at an earlier stage where sarcopenia interventions can be implemented more effectively.
kw: Sarcopenia, Shearwave, Elastography, Diagnosis, Validity

title: The adOlescent Acne STudy (TOAST): assessing quality of life and improving management
abs: Acne vulgaris is one of the most common inflammatory dermatoses globally. It typically presents in adolescence, can persist in adulthood, and may have long-lasting adverse implications. There are limitations identified in the current approach to adolescents with acne. The local prevalence is unclear. There is insufficient evidence pertaining to predictive factors for severe acne with scarring, and its psychological effects have been under-estimated. Furthermore, assessment of acne severity is subjective. We aim to determine the prevalence of acne, identify the risk factors for severe disease, delineate its psychosocial impact on our adolescent population, and develop an artificial intelligence (AI) tool to grade acne more objectively. We hypothesise that acne is common and has a significant psychosocial impact on our local adolescents. Our study population will be from the GUSTO (Growing Up in Singapore Towards healthy Outcomes) cohort. There are approximately 600 adolescents of ages between 12 to 13 years old in the cohort, enabling an estimate of the prevalence of acne. A 6-part questionnaire that evaluates the epidemiological characteristics and quality of life will be administered to all participants. The first 4 sections consist of several questions that assess the participant's demographic and socio-economic profile, family history and lifestyle. These components will be taken into account when evaluating for predictors of acne severity. With regards to quality of life, 2 validated questionnaires will be used: Children’s Dermatology Life Quality Index (CDLQI) Questionnaire and The Cardiff Acne Disability Index (CADI) Questionnaire. Acne severity will be assessed clinically and scored using the Global Acne Grading System (GAGS). In addition, standardised clinical photography and subsequent AI will be performed to assess acne severity. Overall, this study will help identify patients who are at increased risk of acne-related complications and consequently facilitate more holistic and tailored treatment strategies for prompt and effective management.

title: ENdocuff and Computer Aided Detection of polyps in colonoscopy (ENCAD)
abs: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a leading cause of cancer-related morbidity and mortality worldwide, with rates of CRC predicted to increase. Currently, colonoscopy is the gold standard of screening for CRC and polyp detection/surveillance and has been shown to decrease the risk of CRC-related mortality. The adenoma detection rate (ADR) is an established quality indicator for colonoscopy, but subjected to missed rates of up to 25%. This has led to the use of colonoscopy-assisted devices such as Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Endocuff aiming at improving the ADR. AI is seen as one of the solutions to bridge this gap in adenoma detection. These AI systems utilise deep neural networks to enable computer-aided detection (CADe). Prospective studies have shown that AI improves colonic polyp detection rate, paving a new strategy in the CRC screening with colonoscopy in the future and also an improvement in cost effectiveness. Another factor accounting for the high missed rate is poor visualisation of lesions blocked by the mucosal folds. Endocuff (Olympus), an endoscopy device that is mounted to the end of the colonoscope, has the ability to manipulate and flatten the colonic folds to enhance the view of the mucosa. By doing so, it has proven to mitigate the issue of missed rates by permitting better visualisation behind the folds and hence, polyp detection. This had led to an improvement in ADR and naturally, a decrease in the risk of interval CRC. While these individual tools have effectively improved the ADR, it remains uncertain whether their combined use during colonic examination could potentially further improve the ADR. We plan to conduct a randomised, prospective clinical trial at our centre to compare the difference in ADR between AI-assisted colonoscopy plus Endocuff and AI-assisted colonoscopy.

abs: Cyber security is one of the most important concerns in the modern digital society. The smart nation initiative launched by Singapore government makes cyber security even more important. title: Interpretable and Automated Cryptanalysis for Tailor-Made Cryptographic Design
abs: With the endless digitalisation of our lives and the growing amount and impact of data breaches around the world, cyber-security has become a necessity for most businesses and a top-priority concern for governments. Cryptography, the science of creating and breaking encryption schemes, is one of the main links of the global security chain. Symmetric-key cryptography primitives (when the same secret key is used between the two communicating parties) are among the most important components in cryptography, backbones of security processes in various industries such as telecommunications, banking, cryptocurrencies, access control, supply chain, military, etc. and used in everyday applications such as PC, phones, smart-cards, the Internet, control systems, cars, satellites, etc. For most use-cases, performance and cost are key aspects of a product and cryptography can have an important impact on this efficiency, whether the efficiency is about throughput, latency, energy/power consumption, memory, code size, hardware area, etc. Better cryptography performances can lead to cost savings, improved user experience, and even create new market opportunities (when security becomes available in situations where performance remained a technological lock). Cryptographic primitives are applied to many different scenarios with various security expectations and performed on different platforms with very diverse efficiency constraints. Yet, despite the variety of needs, most of the symmetric-key cryptography we are using today is composed of a handful of standardised primitives. The standardisation bodies have been promoting these designs via public worldwide competitions that spanned over several years and that required a lot of efforts from the research community. This one-size-fits-all situation is mainly due to the fact that designing and analysing cryptographic schemes is a very difficult, tedious and error-prone task, performed largely by humans. Overall, the confidence in their security gained by the cryptanalysis is a crucial and costly asset. In a nutshell, the objectives of this project are twofold: 1) to create for the first time fully automated and interpretable tools to conduct advanced cryptanalysis 2) to leverage these tools to design cryptographic primitives tailored for the various real-world use-cases, improving performances (speed, area, energy, etc.), and explore in particular a new cryptographic design paradigm (so-called Tweakable Block Ciphers or TBC) that we foresee will greatly outperform existing design trends. Computer programs have long been used to help cryptographers perform their analysis and we have seen an important acceleration in the development of automated tools, mainly based on SAT/SMT, MILP or CP solvers and very recently on new AI tools like deep neural networks, albeit with an interpretability that remains difficult. title: Understanding the metabolic milieu of the tumor microenvironment for niche-based therapy
abs: Dysregulated cellular energetics is a rapidly re-emerging paradigm in cancer. It affords novel insights into the biology of cancer cells and how they use nutrients to fuel biosynthetic growth, regulate epigenetics and maintain homeostasis. Investigations into the metabolic derangement in cancer has primarily focused on the cell-autonomous nutrient requirement of cancer cells, but the influence of the tumor microenvironment metabolic milieu has remained underappreciated. Tumor niche cells are important co-conspirators promoting malignant progression such as therapy resistance and metastasis. The diverse roles of niche compartment in providing contextual signaling molecules, especially cytokines and growth factors to promote tumor growth, resistance and metastasis, are well-established. Cancer cells utilize nutrients in cell-autonomous manner, but more recently, cell-extrinsic factors arising from the tumor microenvironment are observed. The notion that stromal and tumor cells engage in metabolic exchange is very nascent. For instance, lactate produced as a by-product of fibroblasts can be used as an energy source by lung carcinoma cells to fuel their biosynthetic needs, while alanine secreted by fibroblasts is being taken up by pancreatic cancer cells. Understanding the extent and nature of such metabolic exchanges between tumor and microenvironment cells can inform on strategies to target niche-based metabolic vulnerabilities. Conversely, the activity of niche cells is increasingly appreciated to be influenced by metabolic reprogramming. Some cancer or niche cells may express ectopic enzymes into the microenvironment and modulate nutrient levels. Metabolic-based therapies remain powerful therapeutic avenues for altering the behaviors of niche cells to boost the success of therapy response. In-depth understanding is needed, especially for other critically important but underappreciated cell types such as cancer-associated fibroblasts. Learning how these cells may be influenced by the niche metabolic milieu will be equally important for providing another perspective of niche-based therapy, beyond immunotherapy. To provide an in-depth understanding of unique metabolic exchanges between cancer and niche cells, we will generate a rich resource of patient-derived cancer cells along with their stromal compartment. Through the genetic engineering of reporter cell lines and using our curated metabolic drug libraries, cancer-stromal co-culture organoid systems will be adopted to understand how cancer-associated fibroblasts program metabolic addiction in cancer cells. We will focus on pancreatic, liver and lung cancers, which are populated by dense stromal compartments. Spatial transcriptomics and metabolite mass spec imaging will aid in visualizing and validating interactions in tumors of human patients and mouse models of cancers. Aim 1 seeks to discover metabolic exchanges in the tumor microenvironment using functional organoid co-culture perturbations.

title: A Blue Carbon Framework for Singapore’s national climate change policy (BlueCarbonSG)
abs: Blue carbon ecosystems are gaining rapid interest by the public and privates sectors because of their potential to sequester greenhouse gas emissions from the atmosphere and store them in the vegetation and soils at rates that far exceed those of terrestrial ecosystems. The global potential of blue carbon in the fight against climate change is substantial, with our research showing that global conservation and restoration can avoid 304 Tg CO2 emissions per year, while drawing down a further 841 Tg CO2 per year from the atmosphere. Recently, a dozen countries (mostly small island states) incorporated blue carbon targets into their Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) under the Paris Agreement. Singapore currently does not do so, but we expect the conservation and restoration of blue carbon ecosystems to be able to contribute to meeting our climate change mitigation obligations. We have brought together an internationally recognised and multi-disciplinary team that aims to show the potential for blue carbon to contribute to Singapore’s greenhouse gas reporting and climate change targets. We do this by providing the evidence base for blue carbon at the site scale and across Singapore, and we show how this information can be incorporated into Singapore’s current greenhouse gas accounting mechanisms, and what constraints currently exist in doing so. We will achieve this through 3 interlinked and complementary Work Packages. Work Package 1 quantifies blue carbon stocks and fluxes across different sites in Singapore, and tests the influence of various environmental gradients such as geomorphic setting, ecological community, and disturbance history. Such gradients are known to influence blue carbon at global scales, though has not been tested at the scale of Singapore. While Singapore only has 2 recognised blue carbon ecosystems (mangroves and seagrasses), we will also take carbon measurements in mudflats, to show their potential as a blue carbon ecosystem. This will contribute evidence to similar scientific debates occurring internationally. Work Package 2 upscales site measurements of stocks and fluxes to the national level. Firstly, we will create a novel soil carbon predictive model based on relationships between stocks/fluxes and environmental variables. Such modelling has only been conducted on continental to global scales, but is important for us to downscale to Singapore since the soil carbon pool accounts for at least 60% of total blue carbon stocks. Secondly, we will use novel global LiDAR (the NASA GEDI mission) and hyperspectral remote sensing data to create national maps of total blue carbon distribution. Finally, we will calculate habitat loss across Singapore for the last 70 years, and link them to our blue carbon models to estimate historical emissions from coastal development. title: Improving the efficiency of computational algorithms for fitting multilevel models to large data using augmentation techniques
abs: As datasets increase in size and complexity, statistical models with greater flexibility and depth are required to gain useful insights from these data and simultaneously, more efficient algorithms are necessary for fitting these models. This proposal considers the use of augmentation techniques for improving the rate of convergence of iterative algorithms, such as the expectation maximization (EM) algorithm, Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods and variational approximation methods for fitting hierarchical models in the classical statistics or Bayesian framework. Given a statistical model for the observed data, an augmentation scheme introduces unobserved or missing data, which are carefully designed so that ease of computation or faster rates of convergence can be achieved in the algorithms used for fitting the augmented model, while preserving the likelihood of the observed data. In the Bayesian framework, data augmentation is also known as model reparametrization, and two well-known parametrizations are centering and noncentering. The data augmentation scheme or parametrization of the model can have a huge impact on the performance of the algorithm used for model fitting. In extreme cases, the algorithm may not even be able to converge within a reasonable time period due to a poor augmentation scheme. We propose to conduct an in-depth study of augmentation techniques and build upon existing techniques to develop novel algorithms for fitting complex models to large data sets. One focus is on variational approximation methods, which provide an important alternative to computationally intensive MCMC methods for posterior approximation, and can reduce computation by up to several orders of magnitude. Although data augmentation techniques remain largely unexplored for variational methods, they can be used to improve not just the convergence but the posterior approximation accuracy as well. As the convergence rates of the EM, MCMC and variational algorithms are closely connected, we wish to explore how augmentation techniques for improving one class of algorithms can be modified or adapted to work for another. We focus on time series models for financial data and hierarchical spatial models for areal data, where the observations are correlated either across time points or spatial locations. Such models have wide applications, for instance in financial econometrics, epidemiology, ecology and forestry, and the data are often available in large quantities. The development of more efficient algorithms will enable useful insights to be drawn from these data, which can facilitate more informed planning and decisions in related applications.
kw: Data augmentation schemes; Multilevel models; Rate of convergence; Expectation maximization algorithm; Variational approximation; Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm

title: Synthetic lethal targeting of MYC-driven multiple myeloma with nucleoside analog/IMiD-based combinations
abs: Multiple myeloma (MM) is the second most common haematologic malignancy worldwide and remains incurable. Approved treatment for MM is largely driven by proteosome inhibitors (PIs), immunomodulatory drugs (IMiDs) and monoclonal antibodies, given in various combinations. Despite combinatorial therapy with these potent novel agents, relapse is inevitable and patients eventually succumb to their disease. Refractory and relapsed MM (RR MM) results in empiric treatment where combination therapies switch to a new drug class or to a second or third-generation drug of the same class. While several pathogenic genomic alterations in MM are well characterised, the majority of genetic alterations that drive MM are currently not targetable. One such genomic alteration, MYC rearrangements, occur in 20-50% of MM and are associated with adverse outcomes independent of risk status based on IGH translocations. Thus, there is an urgent need for more precise therapeutic options against MYC-driven MM. Pom, a third generation IMiD, is currently used in combination therapies for MM patients who have received at least two prior treatments, including lenalidomide and proteosome inhibitors. None of the current Pom-based combinations are linked to a predictive biomarker, including MYC rearrangement. Nucleotide analogues, including purine analogues, continue to gain interest in haematological malignancies, including MM. Of particular interest is 8-chloroadenosine (8-ClA), which has shown preclinical efficacy in a range of MM studies and is currently being clinically evaluated for chronic lymphocytic leukaemia. While the potential of 8-ClA in MM has been shown, it has not been evaluated clinically in MM due to the lack of a clear and effective 8-ClA-based combination therapy strategy in MM. Utilizing our quadratic phenotypic optimization platform (QPOP), we have recently identified the combination of 8-choloroadenosine (8-ClA) and pomalidomide (Pom) to be synergistic against MM cell lines with increased MYC gene expression. We hypothesize that the combination of 8-ClA/Pom may effectively treat MM patients bearing MYC rearrangements through inhibition of MYC synthetic lethality targets, particularly metabolic synthetic lethality. In this proposal, we aim to validate this combination in patient samples with known MYC translocations as well as elucidate the specific synthetic lethality mechanisms that drive 8-ClA/Pom efficacy. Preliminary studies suggest that 8-ClA/Pom can target MYC-dependent MM through downregulation of multiple MYC synthetic lethality targets. Of note, 8-ClA/POM appears to affect glutamine metabolism, a key survival mechanism in MYC addicted cancers. We will interrogate the scientific rationale of this therapeutic strategy through the following Aims. Specific Aim 1: Analysis of 8-ClA/Pom in MM patient samples with MYC translocation. title: Building a Versatile System Infrastructure for In-Network Computing
abs: We are witnessing a paradigm shift in computing: with the end of Moore's Law and Dennard scaling, the computing industry is searching for alternatives to general purpose processors to further scale computational performance. One attractive research direction is in-network computing, in which selected computation is offloaded to specialized network hardware, such as new generation programmable data plane switches, that offer orders of magnitude higher performance than modern CPUs. Unfortunately, existing system infrastructures for in-network computing are highly restrictive: they only expose a small amount of data plane memory to in-network applications with restrictive memory access requirements; the hardware is only capable of performing limited number of simple arithmetic operations per packet; and in-network computation developed for one hardware model is not portable to a different platform. These limitations forced existing in-network acceleration solutions to make hard trade-offs among performance, consistency, complexity, and generalizability. More importantly, they rule out a large class of applications that could benefit from in-network computing. The goal of this project is to address this gap by developing highly versatile system infrastructures for in-network computing, enabling a wide range of computational tasks to be offloaded to network hardware. We will identify key limitations in existing software and hardware components of programmable data planes, and propose both architectural changes and new system software to address those limitations. The project will also demonstrate the versatility of the proposed infrastructures by building new distributed systems with in-network acceleration that show significant speed-ups and scalability improvement. Specifically, we will pursue three main research directions in this proposal: - We will build a transparent hierarchical memory system for programmable data planes. The system exposes large address spaces to in-network applications, eliminating the memory constraints they are facing in existing systems. We will leverage off-chip accelerators to provide a hierarchy of data plane memory, and design system software to transparently manage memory caching across layers. - We will design a new switch architecture for in-network computing that tightly couples FPGA co-processors with the main switch chip. This new architecture transparently offloads computations that are not supported by the switch chip to the FPGA co-processors, permitting new classes of applications to enjoy in-network acceleration. We will investigate system designs that can efficiently and transparently manage the entire offloading process. - We will co-design new distributed applications with in-network computation that leverage our proposed infrastructures. The first application is a permissioned blockchain system that offloads message authentication and ordering into the network to implement a Trusted Ordered Multicast pri

title: Characterizing the role of the 'ribotoxic stress-inflammasome' (RSR-I) pathway in skin antibacterial immunity
abs: All kingdoms of life rely on ribosomes to translate messenger RNAs (mRNAs) into proteins. Although much is known about the housekeeping function of the ribosome, its roles beyond protein synthesis, especially as active participants in cellular signaling, are still poorly defined. In 2021, my lab identified a novel signaling pathway that triggers inflammasome-driven inflammatory cell death in response to specific types of ribosome perturbations. We termed this pathway ‘ribotoxic-stress-response-induced inflammasome activation’ (RSR-I) and identified its key sensors and effectors using chemical genetics approaches (Robinson et al, Science, 2022). The role of RSR-I in vivo is currently still unclear. In addition, our recent unpublished results demonstrated that certain activities of RSR-I are controlled by unknown cellular factors. In this proposal, we will combine in vitro biochemistry, human organoid culture and murine models to 1) test the hypothesis that RSR-I is required for immune defense against bacterial skin infections in vivo and 2) identify additional RSR-I regulators. These experiments will advance our understanding of the connection between the ribosome and innate immunity, and help develop better approaches to treat bacterial infections and inflammatory disorders. SPECIFIC AIMS To investigate the role of RSR-I in ribotoxin (e.g. Pseudomonas aeruginosa exoA)-induced inflammation in in vitro and ex vivo human skin culture To test the in vivo role of RSR-I using murine models of Pseudomonas aeruginosa skin wound infection To identify additional regulators of Pseudomonas aeruginosa exoA-induced RSR-I in human skin keratinocytes

title: Egocentric Vision-based Activity Analysis in the Wild
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: Egocentric videos, which are videos captured in a first-person perspective with a wearable camera or virtual reality glasses, are highly relevant to a series of applications. An important application is robotics, where robots’ front-facing cameras are used to aid navigation and completion of other tasks (e.g., performing actions of object grasping). In recent years, there has been a further surge in interest in egocentric videos, due to the enormous potential displayed by the metaverse, which is driving the rapid development and adoption of augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR) technologies. These applications are highly reliant on the analysis of egocentric videos, and in many of these applications, a good understanding of activities occurring in the captured egocentric video is crucial, because actions/gestures/poses within the video often first need to be correctly identified, before other downstream system software can perform as intended. However, existing computer vision (CV) techniques, including our previous works involving egocentric videos and activity analysis, face certain challenges that limit their utility in modern egocentric activity-based applications. Specifically, several challenges still need to be addressed: 1) The performance of existing methods are still unsatisfactory in terms of fine-grained discriminative capabilities and computational efficiency. Fine-grained capability is crucial in various applications in our daily lives, such as AR kitchen assistants, where performed actions can be very similar (e.g., turning on vs turning off the stove) with only fine-grained differences. Meanwhile, computational efficiency is also important because many modern applications require a timely response for good user experience. 2) There can be safety and security concerns with current methods when they are used in AR/MR applications. For example, some applications can process vision tasks by sending captured egocentric videos to the cloud, so using them can raise privacy concerns. Furthermore, some safety-critical applications, e.g., medical surgery assistance or factory work, require methods to be robust, to avoid accidents or targeted attacks. 3) A lot of annotated video data is often required for training activity analysis models, and the cost needed for annotation can be potentially overwhelming. In summary, this project aims to tackle several crucial problems to allow improvement of CV techniques for modern applications of egocentric videos. We will develop methods that improve 1) fine-grained discriminative capabilities and computational efficiency, 2) safety and security, and 3) data efficiency of existing methods. Our project shall bring significant impact in academia and also industry. We will design novel techniques involving dynamic architectures, efficiency-accuracy attacks, meta-learning, and diffusion models, introducing new insights and expanding upon the current collective under- standing.
kw: Computer Vision; Action Recognition; Video Analysis

title: Modeling and Design of 3D Freeform Gears for Exact 3D Motion Generation
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: Motion generation is a fundamental task of designing mechanisms, aiming to realize user-prescribed motion usually specified as a set of sequential rigid-body poses. Motion generation mechanisms can perform repetitive motion reliably and precisely driven by a single actuator by embedding motion of the actuated part into the mechanisms geometry, making them widely used in a variety of applications including machines, mechanical automata, and robotics. Existing motion generation mechanisms are mainly based on linkages and can only generate a few prescribed rigid-body poses, due to the finite number of design parameters of linkages. However, the mechanisms that can exactly generate an infinite set of 3D rigid-body poses have been rarely studied, and this problem is known as exact 3D motion generation. In this proposal, we aim to address the exact 3D motion generation problem by proposing and studying a new class of gears called 3D freeform gears. Gears are the first choice for transferring motion in many applications due to their nice features like compact layout, high efficiency, reliability, and ability to transmit high torque. Conventional gears have circular shape and are used for transmitting rotary motion from one shaft to another. Our 3D freeform gears generalize conventional gears with freeform 3D shape and ability to transfer more complex motion (e.g., from 1-DOF rotation to 3-DOF rotation). Thanks to the recent advance in additive manufacturing, these 3D freeform gears can be 3D printed easily and inexpensively, even by non-professionals. In a mathematical sense, a gear pair is a pair of conjugate surfaces. According to the theory of conjugate surfaces, the contact entity between two conjugate surfaces may be a point, or a line segment, or a surface patch. Conventional gears principally rely on line conjugation to transfer 1-DOF rotation to another 1-DOF rotation. In contrast, our 3D freeform gears will make use of multi-point conjugation to transfer 1-DOF rotation to 𝑁-DOF motion, where 1 ≤ 𝑁 ≤ 3. Modeling and designing a pair of conjugate gear surfaces to satisfy the multi-point conjugation requirement is a challenging task. In this project, we will carry out a comprehensive study on 3D freeform gears, guided by the theory of conjugate surfaces, in order to use them to build the next generation of motion generation mechanisms. The research objectives are thus: 1) to establish theoretical and computational foundations of 3D freeform gears, which are necessary to fully understand 3D freeform gears; 2) to investigate modeling of 3D motion generation mechanisms, taking 3D freeform gears as the core building blocks; and 3) to explore innovative techniques and practical algorithms for designing 3D freeform gear-based motion generation mechanisms, and explore their potential applications. To achieve these objectives, we conduct our research by investigating three major directions outlined below: 1. Modeling and analyzing 3D freeform gears • Geom

title: Nontoxic carbene photoinitiators for sustainable biomaterials
abs: Proposed research consists of three research thrusts: RT1- Carbene initiator utility: The structure-property relationships (SPR) will be mapped for carbene precursors initiating a range of common and sustainable resins. For the first time, the fundamental scientific investigation will explore carbene initiation of ring opening polymerization for synthesis of biodegradable polyesters and petrol-free, sustainable resins from renewable sources (e.g. itaconic acid). RT1 Objectives: Create a platform of novel, light activated carbene-initiated resins with known material properties, benchmarked against commercial competitors. RT2- Mechanism of photoinitiation: Carbene precursors with known singlet/triplet carbene ratios will be correlated with respect to the reaction mechanism of monomer degree of conversion and kinetic parameters. Active species, most efficient for polymer synthesis, will be determined as a function of carbene transient, precursor structure, and resin chemistry. RT2 Objectives: Optimize initiator efficiency with respect to carbene precursor design, reaction mechanism, resin monomer, exposure dose (joules), UVA/visible irradiation, and mol %. RT3- Minimizing toxic leachates: For the first time, the carbene photoinitiation intermediate (diazoalkane) will be investigated as a chemical absorbent of unreacted monomers after light activation. The reduction of leachates aims to improve biocompatibility of tissue contacting resins. GLP compliant, OECD biocompatibility tests will serve as an unbiased benchmark. RT3 objectives: (i) Exploit diazoalkane scavenging of unreacted monomers; (ii) Perform quantitative analysis of leachates; (iii) Biocompatibility risk assessment.

title: Optimal Configurations in Finite Geometry
abs: Consider the problem of finding lines through the origin of Euclidean space such that the smallest interior angle is as large as possible. This problem of finding optimal configurations of lines is fundamental in the discipline of geometry. Approximate solutions to this problem appear in nature, e.g., the distribution of pores on a spherical pollen grain. Other fundamental geometrical objects such as the Platonic solids provide particular solutions to this problem. Furthermore, its solutions bring substantial implications to various important areas, including modern communication theory and quantum information theory. Recent developments in the above problem have emerged in the context of frame theory, where one seeks to find a set of unit vectors such that the maximum absolute value of the inner product of any pair of vectors is as small as possible. This maximum absolute value is called the coherence and is lower bounded by the so-called Welch bound. In this context, the optimal configurations correspond to equality in the Welch bound and are known as equiangular tight frames (ETFs). ETFs enjoy applications in many disparate areas of mathematics e.g., waveform design for wireless communication, compressed sensing, quantum information theory, and algebraic coding theory. The study of ETFs dates back to the first half of the 20th century and, while their definition stems from functional analysis, the known families of ETFs are constructed from combinatorial designs. Furthermore, the study of ETFs is a nexus between otherwise apparently disjoint areas of mathematics. This area of study is an emergent, exciting, and rapidly developing field whose community is steadily growing. Indeed, ETFs have been the focus of a large number of conferences and workshops in only the last five years. In many cases these events brought together researchers from various different disciplines for the first time. There are two main aims to this proposal. The first aim is to find new constructions for ETFs and SICs. The second aim is to develop the understanding of when ETFs of a given size can exist in each dimension over a given field. For the first aim: There is a wealth of literature on modifying structures and concepts from algebraic combinatorics in order to construct an ETFs, however, the connections between ETFs and algebraic combinatorics have not yet been fully exploited. Indeed, since most researchers interested in ETFs are engineers and physicists, the techniques from algebraic combinatorics and number theory that have been used so far are relatively elementary compared to today's cutting-edge technology. Our main approach, therefore, is to use current techniques from combinatorial and algebraic design theory to find new constructions of ETFs and new necessary conditions for the existence of ETFs. title: Toughening PHB and PLA via Entropy Driven Miscibility: Toward Sustainable Plastics
abs: This project aims at developing a facile yet scalable approach to drastically reduce the brittleness of typical commercial biodegradable plastics such as polyhydroxybutyrate (PHB) and polylactic acid (PLA), giving them a competitive edge over petroleum-based plastics. Petroleum-based plastics are associated with many environmental problems. In the environment, microplastics may persist for centuries before being fully decomposed, causing profound detrimental consequences for ecosystems, the environment and human health. Although significant progress has been made in plastic recycling, so far only a small percentage of plastics are recycled due to its high demand for socio-economic inputs, and global warming makes incineration of plastics an unfavourable option. Biodegradable plastics from biomass have long been claimed as a promising way to solve the plastic pollution problem, whereas so far only a few percent of annual consumption of plastics are biodegradable plastics. A key challenge faced by us is how to enhance their toughness and elasticity to the extent that could rival that of petroleum-based plastics in an economically viable way. PLA and PHB are the two most promising biodegradable plastics derived from biomass, whearas their widespread applications are hindered by their inherent brittleness. Reported toughening methods for PHB and PLA involved chemical modifications of the resins, tailor-synthesis of compatibilizers, etc., which are tedious and costly. The proposed toughening approach in this project is based on our newly discovered entropy driven miscibility in polymer blends, which utilizes commercial polymers and involves no chemical reaction. In a polymer blend, the free energy of mixing (G) is determined by enthalpy (H) and entropy (S) of mixing, i.e. G = H + TS. The enthalpy component is considered as the most important factor in intermixing while entropy is often ignored since it is relatively small in polymer blend. In contrast to this convention wisdom, our proposed project centers on selecting and/or designing suitable polymer pairs that when blended, |TS| > |H|, i.e. enthalpy H is very small (H ~ 0). Our hypothesis is that under this condition, the good miscibility due to G < 0 leads to small domain size and large interfacial surfaces, while the polymer chains could easily overcome the intermolecular attractive or repulsive forces to adopt a more random and entangled conformation at the interface since S is dominated. The morphology of resulting polymer blends exhibit two unique characteristics: 1) a huge amount of interface due to good miscibility of two polymers, and 2) a highly entangled interphase, both could lead to mass crazing and plastic deformation, hence ultra-ductility. Our preliminary study on PLA-PMMA system support our hypothesis. PLA and PMMA are two very brittle polymers with strain at break < 6%. The PMMA has weak interaction with PLA (H ~ 0) and the entropy dominates G which also lead to a miscible polymer

title: A mirror-image form of peptidyl asparaginyl ligase for D-protein engineering
abs: Peptide asparaginyl ligases (PALs) are plant-derived enzymes that catalyze peptide ligation reactions at an Asn or Asp (Asx) residue. The ligation reaction can occur intramolecularly which leads to peptide cyclization or intermolecularly for joining two peptides together. PALs are very powerful enzymes with a catalytic efficiency that is 4 orders of magnitude higher than sortase A, a previous gold-standard enzyme. Since the discovery of the first PAL in 2014, these enzymes have found numerous applications, including the preparation of macrocyclic peptides or proteins, site-specific protein ligation, and cell-surface protein labelling. In this project, we propose to prepare the mirror-image form of a peptidyl asparaginyl ligase and use it to synthesize proteins and peptides of the unnatural D-configuration for applications in biochemical studies and drug discovery. Many exciting applications of such a D-PAL are possible, such as macrocyclization of D-peptides and the total synthesis of D-proteins. Cyclo-D-peptides have attractive therapeutic potentials. D-proteins are useful in mirror image phage display (MIPD) for the identification of D-ligands in drug discovery. They can also be used for racemic protein crystallography whereby mixtures of L- and D-protein isomers at a 1-to-1 ratio would facilitate the formation of well-diffracting crystals which are achiral, thus avoiding the phase problem in data analysis. Because of their resistance to protease degradation, D-proteins have enhanced stability in vivo and consequently superior pharmacokinetic properties as therapeutics compared to their natural L-protein counterparts. Therefore, the availability of a mirror image PAL enzyme will open many possibilities in basic and translational research. The specific aims of the proposed project are: 1) to synthesize a D-PAL by combined use of solid phase peptide synthesis and chemoselective peptide ligation techniques; 2) to use the chemical prepared D-PAL for the synthesis of D-proteins, including the D-PAL itself, 3) to use the D-PAL for the macrocyclization of enantiomeric natural cyclic antimicrobial peptides and their analogs for structure-activity relationship studies; 4) to conduct racemic crystallography on the synthetic D-PAL and natural L-PAL to solve the structure of the active enzyme.
kw: Enzyme; Peptide asparaginyl ligase; D-Proteins; Protein synthesis; D-Amino acids

title: Novel optogenetic inhibitors of synaptic circuits
abs: Brain functions including locomotion, memory and feeding all rely on the neuronal connections: synapses. Neuroscientists manipulate physiology using optogenetic channelrhodopsins that can alter membrane potential and neuronal excitability. However, channelrhodopsin actuation typically impacts activity across an entire cell or groups of cells. Many neurons have divergent axons that output to different targets in multiple brain regions, so cell-resolved intervention can be impossible to interpret. Synapses represent a critical unit of analysis. What is needed are neurogenetic tools that definitively target the synaptic interfaces between two genetically defined sets of neurons. Current tools cannot be used to genetically target synaptic interfaces. This proposal works to develop and test novel inhibitory tools that can be used to build a new generation of interventional methods oriented towards the synapse. Here, we propose to implement and test a series of neurogenetic tools that build towards genetically encoded inhibitors with synaptic-interface specificity. First, we will use our expertise in developing optogenetic tools for inhibiting neurons to generate and test the latest optogenetic inhibitory molecules. Our preliminary data indicate that potassium-conducting ‘kalium’ channelrhodopsins (KCRs) are effective in vivo inhibitors. Second, we will test two high-conductance opsins, an optoGPCR and a long-acting KCR which would allow reduced illumination and may be suitable for incorporation into luminogenetic designs. Third, in human cells and flies, we will test new luciferases and fusions between luciferase and channelrhodopsins, termed ‘luminopsins’. These experiments will use both known luminopsins and novel inhibitory luminopsins that use the new inhibitory opsins listed above. We will explore the development of bipartite inhibitory luminopsins (BILMOs), whereby luciferase and channelrhodopsin are produced in separate, synaptically connected cells and are brought together via heterodimerization domains across the synaptic cleft. Heterodimerization across the synaptic cleft will allow for the formation of lumino-optogenetic effectors capable of inhibiting specific synaptic interfaces. Statements of (i) intellectual merit and (ii) broader impact: (i) The development of inhibitors targeted to the synaptic interface would be a new concept in neuroscience, opening up novel methods of analyzing neural circuits. (ii) While neuroscience has made excellent progress in building knowledge of synaptic connectomes at the anatomical and ultrastructural levels, bipartite synaptic inhibitors would inform the functional analysis of connectomes, and would represent a critical tool.
kw: Neuroscience, synapse, brain, optogenetics, channelrhodopsin, Drosophila

title: Quantum information processing with confined many-body localized states (c-MBL)
abs: Many-body localized (MBL) states are a new quantum phase of mater in systems with strong disorder and strong correlations. One property of MBL states is the violation of the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis i.e. these quantum states do not mix with each other even at infinite temperature. Following intense theoretical and experimental investigations in the past decade, there is now a general consensus that these states can be realized – at least on experimental timescales [see e.g. (Nandkishore and Huse, 2015; Alet and Laflorencie, 2018; Abanin et al., 2019)]. Given the practically infinite dephasing times, it would seem obvious prima facie that MBL states would be excellent for quantum information storage and processing. However, MBL qubits face several previously unsurmountable challenges including the need for dynamical manipulation of disorder, the inability to encode information in a single quantum state among exponentially many such states, and the ability to spatially move MBL qubits adiabatically. Based on preliminary results, our proposal overcomes each of these challenges. Specifically, we have demonstrated that the eigenstate-to-Hamiltonian construction works for MBL states (Dupont and Laflorencie, 2019; Tang et al., 2022), and in particular addressees only a single quantum state (Tang et al., 2022); and that a confining potential can be used to both reliably turn on and off MBL states (Foo et al., 2022), and that these states are stable to perturbations in both the disorder and confining potential. We propose using our eigenstate-to-Hamiltonian construction on an Ising-Majorana chain that is stabilized by MBL (Laflorencie, Lemarié and Macé, 2022) to demonstrate the encoding of quantum information. The robustness of our confined MBL qubits will be probed experimentally using established technologies with ultracold quantum degenerate gas of fermionic lithium atoms (Dieckmann et al., 2002) in an upcoming setup that should be ready later this year. Armed with the theoretical and experimental characterization of single qubit properties, we will propose both new qubit architectures as well as how to stabilize existing architectures by harnessing the properties of many-body localization.
kw: Many-body localization, quantum information processing, magneto-optical trapping

title: Sand mining in Southeast Asia: Monitoring system, the first budget and sustainable harvesting
abs: Sand mining activities have accelerated in recent years due to rapid urbanization, resulting in sand being stripped away from riverbeds of many rivers globally, particularly in Southeast Asia (SEA). While sand mining has caused riverbank erosion, riverbed scouring, and reduced flood frequencies, studies on sand mining rates remain scarce due to difficulties associated with monitoring, either in-situ or long term. Here, we seek to enable a step-change in our understanding of riverbed sand mining rates and facilitate sustainable sand harvesting across the rivers in SEA. Our proposal has two overarching aims: First, we intend to develop a novel remote sensing-based monitoring system capable of systematically mapping sand mining activities in large rivers. We will use the Mekong River as a “testbed” to implement a field-calibrated Deep Learning model for estimating the sand mining budget of the Mekong River. Our Deep Learning method will subsequently be calibrated with field survey data from ten major rivers across SEA to obtain the first sand mining budget for the entire region. Second, the morphodynamic model (MIKE 21C) will be used to identify sediment sinks and investigate the environmental impacts of different sand mining scenarios in all the rivers of SEA. Multiple Criteria Decision-Making (MCDM) will then be used to identify fluvial reaches in SEA where sustainable sand extraction can be carried out. Our results will provide local governments with the first-ever science-based research to inform regulatory frameworks for sustainable sand mining, as well as provide baseline information for environmental impact assessments. We envision that the novel Deep Learning approach we develop in this project can be adapted to other large rivers across the world, overcoming the methodological challenges associated with monitoring sand mining activities.
kw: Sand mining; Southeast Asia; Remote sensing; Deep Learning; Sustainable development; Environment

title: Identifying BCL-2 inhibitor resistance mechanism in TP53 mutated leukemia
abs: It is now well understood that most tumors exhibit dysfunction in TP53 due to frequent mutations. TP53 mutations are found in 70-80% of Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) patients with complex karyotype and 35% of therapy-related AML patients. Compared to TP53 WT, AML patients with TP53 mutations show resistance towards both conventional chemotherapy (median OS 12.5 months vs 6.7 months) and newly approved venetoclax plus azacytidine combination therapies (median OS 23.4 months vs 5.1 months). While the tumorigenic mechanism of TP53 mutated cancer is studied predominantly, the mechanism by which mutated TP53 exerts therapy resistance remains unknown. This urges for urgent need to understand mechanisms of poor outcomes in TP53-mutated AML and to identify therapeutic strategies that can target this subpopulation. Using patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models of in vivo acquired resistance to venetoclax, we previously reported that venetoclax resistance is invariably accompanied by decreases in mitochondrial apoptotic priming (Bhatt et al 2020, cancer cell). Our preliminary data showed that TP53 mutant and WT AML patients show comparable threshold (mitochondrial priming) to undergo apoptosis at the pretreatment phase, measured via BH3 profiling (unpublished data). Yet using CRISPR-Cas9 edited TP53 mutant isogenic AML cells (MOLM-13), we found that in a long-term clonogenic assay, TP53 mutants outcompete WT cells in venetoclax and azacytidine combination therapy. Mechanistically, we found that long-term venetoclax treatment led to persistent DNA damage in TP53 mutants that showed reduced apoptosis compared to WT. TP53 mutant cells showed increased senescence compared to WT (unpublished data). This suggests that venetoclax-induced senescence may give selective survival advantage to TP53 mutant clones by preventing complete mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization (MOMP). Based on these findings, we hypothesize that defects in mitochondrial signaling pathway in TP53 mutated AML result in poor outcomes to venetoclax-based combination therapy. Our goal is to identify the mechanism of therapeutic resistance in TP53 mutated AML and to overcome the resistance by identifying novel agents. To study this, we propose to utilize a novel paradigm in apoptosis biology to answer critical clinical needs of (a) determining the involvement of mitochondrial sensitivity to apoptosis in driving leukemia resistance in TP53-mutated AML primary tumors and patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models (b) characterizing molecular pathways selectively enriched in TP53 mutated isogenic cell lines (c) identifying targeted therapies based on early death signaling measured using dynamic BH3 profiling assay that can overcome therapy resistance.
kw: TP53 mutations, venetoclax, acute myeloid leukemia, BCL-2 family, apoptosis, CRISPR

title: Compositional representations for multi-task and transfer learning
abs: Cognitive flexibility is one of hallmarks of biological intelligence exhibited by the brain, an evolutionally optimised system capable of acting in multiple environments ("multi-task learning") and transferring prior knowledge to novel situations ("transfer learning"). The biological system is in stark contrast to the artificial system, which suffers from lack of generalisability despite its supra-human performance in single-task domains. Expressing such unique features of the biological intelligence in machines is one of main objectives in research of artificial intelligence (AI). However, although there is rich behavioural evidence for the cognitive flexibility underlying multi-task and transfer learning in the biological system, their neural mechanisms are poorly understood. Deep reinforcement learning (deep RL) is a field of AI, integrating theories of RL with expressive, general-purpose function approximators such as artificial neural networks (ANNs). Deep RL has been successfully applied to a wide range of decision-making and control tasks, such as learning to play video games and robotic control. However, unlike the brain, one ANN typically learns to solve one specific task and serial training of the same neural network in new tasks leads to forgetting of old ones, a phenomenon known as “catastrophic forgetting”. Thus, it is important to design neural network architectures and algorithms that can generalise across multiple tasks without losing pre-learned information. Recent progress in deep RL has demonstrated that compact representations of behaviour policies shared across multiple tasks are important for generalisation. However, whether there exist such shared representations in the brain remains to be uncovered. In this proposal, leveraging on theoretical frameworks established in the field of deep RL, we aim to study neural mechanisms underlying multi-task and transfer learning in the brain. We will address the hypothesis that the brain learns modular, decomposable and compact representations of tasks that can be re-used and combined in a novel way to solve a suite of tasks with minimal additional training. Successful completion of the project will shed a new light on how the brain implements multi-task and transfer learning and may provide novel opportunities to improve machine intelligence via neuroscience-inspired algorithms.
kw: Multi-task learning; Transfer learning; Systems neuroscience; Deep reinforcement learning; Artificial intelligence

title: An Integrated “Imagenomic” Framework for Quantifying Phase Separation-Mediated Chromatin Remodeling and Re-organization in Single Cancer Cells
abs:
The ability to alter genomic architecture, accessibility and expression constitutes a defining hallmark of cancer. Among the cellular processes that modulate the genome, one of the most fundamental yet under-explored is chromatin remodeling, carried out by remodeler proteins that control genomic accessibility at the nucleosome level to provide access to the underlying genome for other chromatin-based processes. Importantly, misregulation of remodeling is implicated in a wide range of human cancers across tumor types. However, beyond biochemical/mutational levels, our understanding of how remodeling is organized and regulated in space and time at ultra-high resolutions inside the cell remains very limited (largely due to technical constraints), nor do we understand how quantitative changes in its organization and dynamics can serve as a diagnostic tool by informing on the physiological/pathological state of the cell in vivo. We hypothesize that biophysical changes in the nanoscale dynamics of chromatin remodeling and re-organization in their in situ genomic contexts, as mediated by phase separation, can provide uniquely valuable insights for cancer diagnosis. Leveraging our extensive expertise in single-molecule/super-resolution microscopy, chromatin biology and imaging/genomic technology development, we will use the SWI/SNF family of chromatin remodelers as model system to accomplish the following specific aims: 

Aim 1: Develop integrated “imagenomic” strategies for probing chromatin remodeling and re-organization with ultra-high spatio-temporal resolutions and sensitivity over extended

title: Activation mechanism of a protein water channel by cardiolipin: implications for the fabrication of block copolymer nanosheets
abs: Optimization of biomimetic membranes that incorporate membrane proteins for their use in desalination, filtration, dialysis or drug discovery applications is still challenging. In these systems, amphiphilic block copolymers (BCPs) are often used instead of lipids, because of BCP’s far higher chemical and mechanical stability. For example, high water flux has been successfully demonstrated in BCP nanosheets incorporating a bacterial porin and other similar architectures (Tu et al. Nature Materials, 2020). Despite this artificial environment, many membrane proteins also require tightly bound native lipids for optimal function. Tetrameric aquaporin Z (AqpZ) from E. coli has been used as a workhorse for water purification/desalination systems for the last 15 years. Binding of the lipid cardiolipin (CDL) to AqpZ more than doubles water permeability and increases stability (Laganowsky et al., Nature, 2014), and we found recently that this activation by CDL binding may be highly cooperative (Tan, C.L.J. and Torres, J., BBA-Mol Cell Biol Lipids 2021). Although in some proteins lipid-binding can allosterically modulate binding affinity of other lipids, our model suggests that in AqpZ, CDL binding induces a concerted conformational change that affects not one, but the four monomers in the AqpZ homo-tetramer. Also, the efficacy and compatibility of these tightly bound lipids (CDL) in BCP environments has not been addressed at the molecular level. Herein we will address these two issues by exploring the conformational changes induced by CDL binding, and its enhancing effect on AqpZ activity and stability, in the presence of both lipid or BCP environments. If CDL activation is cooperative, only two observable types of tetrameric structure will be observed, instead of gradually varying conformations with increasing CDL. We will use single particle cryo-electron microscopy (nanodiscs) and solid-state NMR, to extract this information in both lipidic and BCP environments. The AqpZ activation promoted by CDL will be tested in the context of AqpZ-based BCPs polymersomes (liposome-like particles made of BCPs)and also planar nanosheets, following published protocols. The conclusions of this project will be key to optimize membrane biomimetics when applied to AqpZ and other MPs that also use lipid modulators. (i) intellectual merit. It is known that tightly bound lipids can allosterically modulate the binding affinity for other lipids (e.g., in the E. coli ammonia channel, AmtB), but this allostery was not observed for AqpZ [1]. Lipid-binding events can also modify protein-protein interaction affinity [2], but the conformational change induced by CDL on AqpZ, responsible for its increased activity and stability is not known. Thus our aim is to determine how CDL is able to change protein structure, in native and synthetic lipidic environments, and also in a polymeric context (BCPs) that is relevant for bioengineering applications. title: Towards direct and rapid mapping of RNA modifications with nanopore sequencing
abs: A deep knowledge of how the transcriptome is regulated is key to understanding normal and diseased cells. Specifically, dynamic control and interpretation of chemical marks on RNA molecules serve as a fundamental gene regulatory mechanism in all living organisms. While over 150 RNA modifications have been found to date, the distribution and prevalence of these modifications in most biological systems are still unclear, especially on messenger RNAs and long non-coding RNAs. A major bottleneck is the lack of a general, direct method to map these chemical marks throughout the transcriptome rapidly. Here, we plan to leverage on single-molecule, long-read, native RNA sequencing on nanopores to study RNA modifications. In this technology, a native RNA strand is threaded through a membrane-embedded pore under a voltage bias. Each nucleotide will perturb the electrical current in a unique manner, allowing the sequence of the RNA to be determined by changes in the ionic current. Importantly, a modified nucleotide is believed to alter the current differently from its unmodified counterpart. Hence, by monitoring the current over time, we can in principle deduce the location and identity of any RNA modification using machine learning techniques. We seek to develop new methods to comprehensively study the epitranscriptome with nanopore sequencing. First, we aim to build new software to generate site-level predictions for various chemical marks in the transcriptome. Here, we will aggregate signals across multiple reads to overcome experimental variabilities in nanopore sequencing. Second, we aim to train machine learning models to detect specific modifications on single RNA molecules. Third, we aim to develop a new base-caller that can identify unmodified and modified nucleotides directly from raw current intensities. We envision that the methods developed can be broadly deployed in many areas of biomedical research, thereby strengthening Singapore’s position as a global genomics hub.

title: Active and Passive Monitoring of Realtime Internet and 5G Evolution
abs: The Internet today supports a large variety of applications with often competing requirements. These requirements can range from low latency for gaming and live streaming, to high throughput for large file downloads. Moreover, close to 65% of the Internet’s downstream traffic today is video traffic, which usually tends to optimize for even more complicated network metrics like jitter and variation in bandwidth. Soon, we can expect this diverse set of performance requirements to further evolve with the deployment of high-speed 5G networks and the emergence of virtual reality (VR) and self-driving cars. While the Internet has remained relatively stable since the last major Internet congestion collapse in 1986, the rapid and unmanaged proliferation of new congestion control algorithms in the wild could potentially give rise to the next major Internet congestion collapse. We argue that it is hence imperative for us to understand these changes as they happen. If we can do so, we will be in a position to develop new congestion control algorithms to support the evolution of the Internet and provide safety guarantees in a timely manner. To this end, We propose a new research programme to develop new measurement techniques based on dataplane-programmable switches. We will design and implement both a passive measurement testbed and an active measurement testbed. The passive measurement testbed will continuously collect fine-grained real-world data from the links connecting the NUS School of Computing (SoC) network to the Internet. Since our proposed passive measurement strategy involves live user traffic for thousands of real users, the main concerns include doing it safely (without affecting the live traffic) and in a privacy-preserving manner. To address the issue of safety, we will perform measurements on a copy of the live traffic instead of the actual traffic. We will also be anonymizing the copied traffic by replacing the user IP addresses and port numbers from the packet header and also truncating the packet payload which may contain any other personally-identifiable information to ensure the privacy of the users is respected. The anonymization will however preserve the relationships between the packets belonging to the same flow so as to allow us to perform meaningful measurements. All the traffic tapped from the network would pass through a dedicated anonymizing switch placed under the control of our network operator. The anonymizing switch would also perform packet truncation. We (the researchers) would only have access to the anonymized packet headers for our measurements. Our proposal along with further details on the anonymization setup would be sent for ethics review. Our active measurement testbed will perform active measurements on both wired and our local 5G cellular networks. title: Holistic AI-augmented elderly movement monitoring and alert system
abs: This project aims to develop a holistic assistive solution to augment existing human-centric monitoring approach in ensuring a safe and conducive environment for the elderly at non-institutional care centres. It leverages upon existing CCTV camera surveillance system installed at these centres which it is currently used only for forensic investigations when required. The proposed deep learning AI-based spatial-temporal 3D convolutional neural network (3D-CNN) for video analytics is uniquely designed to detect unattended elderly movement such as walking, sit-stand posture transition and multiple attempts of sit-stand transitions. Respective movements of different joints at human skeleton model are measured and used as features in training the 3D-CNN. A hybrid colour-based image processing and 2D-CNN AI-based classification model is also incorporated to better differentiate the elderly from the centre’s care assistants and the elderly’s domestic helpers stationed at the centre. To overcome the occlusion or obstruction posed by the CCTV camera, a smart pressure sensing mat with wireless connectivity is being proposed for monitoring high-risk elderly sitting on a wheelchair or normal chair. Both AI-based video analytics and pressure sensing mat are integrated seamlessly with synchronized and localised alarm alert for the care assistants to approach the identified elderly promptly.

title: A Holistic Innovative Approach To Boost Local Fish Production
abs: Rapid expansion of aquaculture has led to intensification practices which have led to more frequent disease outbreaks costing up to ~ US$6 billion loss per year. Similarly, local farmers also suffer from emerging and existing disease outbreaks which can wipe out all their fish stocks, thus hampering production capacity. In spite of technological advances in fish health R&D in salmon and trout, R&D in tropical fish disease is in its infancy. This lack of knowledge and working solutions is evident in local fish hatcheries and nurseries and grow out farms whereby thousands of fish still die at the fry to fingerling, and fingerling to market ready size. To protect the fish fry to fingerlings fish stages, we plan to investigate the use of yeast lysate (rich in beta-glucans) and Chlorella vulgaris extract to boost fish immunity. The immuno-stimulants (yeast lysate & Chlorella vulgaris) fed fish will also be examined for trained immunity markers and also to see if the fish can resist certain common pathogens. For fingerlings, our project intends to develop a Quick Response Procedure (QRP) to detect fish pathogens in 3 local fish species, Asian seabass, red snapper and grouper. After identifying the pathogen, effective autogenous vaccine prototype will be developed to protect the fish fingerlings from such diseases. With this holistic approach to tackle fish diseases from fry to fingerling, and fingerling to market size, this will boost local fish production and built seafood resilience and sustainable aquaculture in Singapore.
kw: Immunostimulants, fish diseases, fish pathogens, diagnosis, autogenous vaccines, fish immunity

title: A Paradigm Shift in Kinase Drug Discovery – Development of Lysine-Targeting, Cell-Active Covalent Inhibitors (CIs) with High Potency and Selectivity
abs: Reversible phosphorylation mediated by kinases and phosphatases plays a key role in regulating essential cellular functions. The human kinome is composed of 500+ protein kinases that are divided into several major groups (e.g. tyrosine kinases, or TKs, and others). Since the 1980s, these enzymes have been recognized as potential drug targets against major human diseases, especially cancer. Despite initial skeptics, remarkable progress has been made in the discovery of small-molecule kinase inhibitors (KIs) possessing good potency and specificity. To date,      >70 kinase-targeting drugs are on the market, but most are non-covalent inhibitors and cover <      20% of all targetable kinases. Key challenges remain in kinase drug discovery, especially in light of the rapidly emerging drug resistance. Targeted covalent inhibitors (TCIs) have emerged as validated drugs to overcome acquired resistance in cancer treatment.  Covalent kinase inhibitors (CKIs) are generally considered to be one of the best strategies to solve drug-resistance dilemma in kinase drug discovery. Among them, reversible covalent kinase inhibitors (RCKIs) in which a covalent but reversible inhibitory mechanism was used, have shown even more effective kinase inhibition with minimized toxicities, prolonged
