title: Chinese voluntary associations in transition: China's rise and the remaking of ancestral communities in Southeast Asia
abs: The proposed program of research adopts an interdisciplinary, multi-sited and translocal approach to study the transformations of Chinese Voluntary Associations (CVAs) in Southeast Asia. This project regards CVAs as dynamic ancestral communities that are composed of diversified relations and networks among people having common ancestral ties of the same religion, locality, language, surname, occupation and other affinities. These ancestral ties not only bridge the linkages between China and Southeast Asia but also become the basis of community formation in host societies. In Southeast Asia, CVAs, along with Chinese schools and Chinese media, have been called one of the ‘three pillars’ of Chinese societies that play pivotal roles in developing Chinese diasporic communities. While often lamented as outdated social institutions in decline, CVAs in Southeast Asia are vibrant communities that are currently undergoing complex, multi-dimensional transformations, driven by both internal and external forces. This project interrogates the ways that CVAs reconstruct themselves and forge new processes of community (re)making amidst shifting dynamics in both domestic environments and within changing China-Southeast Asia relations while China rises as global superpower. This program of research will advance knowledge about the contemporary transformations taking place within CVAs as the collective identities of ethnic Chinese communities in Southeast Asia are negotiated through renewed transnational connections with China in the contemporary era. The research will advance knowledge in the study of Chinese social institutions, Chinese diaspora, and Sino-Southeast relationships in the following ways: (a) the project moves beyond the dominant political-economic interpretation of CVAs by exploring the embodied experiences and socio-cultural perspectives of CVA members in order to understand the effects of China’s rise on local communities in Southeast Asia; (b) it goes beyond merely documenting empirical findings and policy implications by developing a theoretical agenda for the study of CVAs from the perspective of “ancestral communities”; (c) it will constitute the first interdisciplinary, multi-sited and longitudinal investigation of CVAs in the Sino-Southeast Asia cultural sphere and bring multidisciplinary researchers into dialogue to expand the research spectrum of the field; (d) it forges local, regional and transregional inter-Asian connections within the framework of Chinese ancestral communities and employs multiple frames of reference in the understanding of Asian subjectivities. The research employs a dual framework of transnationalization and localization to explore the reconfiguration of CVAs in Southeast Asia. These two dimensions are not only analytical divides but are inextricably intertwined processes operating under specific historical circumstances. This dual framework is conceptualised around three interrelated aspects - state, (non) human act

title: Aromatic Hydrocarbon Belts
abs: Aromatic hydrocarbon belt (AHB) as well-defined fragment of carbon nanotube (CNT) can be considered as one of the Holy Grails of Organic Chemistry. The synthesis is extremely challenging mainly due to large strain generated at the final synthetic step. After half a century’s efforts, chemists are now able to synthesize a few such type of molecules and one can foresee a new era of AHB chemistry in the coming years. The PI and co-PI’s groups recently made breakthroughs in this area. Particularly, they developed efficient synthetic methods for the synthesis of highly strained cylindrical [12,0]CNT fragment and figure-eight twisted carbon nanobelts. On the basis of those findings and some of our preliminary results, the major aims of the proposal are: (1) to design and synthesize a series of AHBs with different sizes, shapes, and edge structures; (2) to understand the fundamental structure-electronic property relationships especially in view of the edge structure; (3) to explore their applications for optoelectronic devices, persistent circular polarized luminescence, and supramolecular materials. The proposed systems include: (1) AHBs with elongated sidewall structure; (2) AHBs with all-armchair edge structure (Vögtle belts); (3) Dewar benzene containing AHBs as analogues of all-zigzag cyclacenes; and (4) twisted AHBs with a Möbius-type structure showing persistent chiroptical properties. Different synthetic strategies are proposed on basis of our rich experiences on polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons. At the end of the project, we are confident to put Singapore at the forefront of AHB chemistry.

title: Machine-Learning-Assisted Topological and Geometrical Data Analysis of Extreme Events in Complex Systems
abs: Higher-order information processing by a complex system involve the reorganization of its constituents and their interactions. These changes, frequently in terms of the fusion of distinct clusters, or the fission of a large cluster into multiple smaller clusters, are accompanied by topological and geometrical signatures. To derive deeper mechanistic understanding of information processing pathways at multiple scales, we aim to (WP1) use topological data analysis(TDA), Laplacian eigenmap analysis (LE), and Ricci curvature analysis (RCA) to classify persistent features associated with extreme events; (WP2) with the aid of machine learning, classify causal sequences of topological and geometric changes associated with these extreme events; and (WP3) develop these insights by working with stock markets and scientific citation networks, two contrasting real-world complex systems we have extensive experience working on. Besides checking whether information processing pathways involving fusion-fission-rearrangement are universal across the two complex systems, we also aim to use the understanding derived to re-design rules on the stock market, so that traders can process information without causing bubbles or crashes, thereby making financial markets more robust and resilient. Using similar insights, we aim to create more cross fertilizations between disciplines and

title: Food Recognition: Causality-driven Cross-modal Cross-lingual Domain Adaptation
abs: This project will research on open-set cross-domain adaptation for food recognition. Given a source domain (a cuisine) with parallel training examples, the problem is to transfer the knowledge learnt in the source domain to a target domain (a different cuisine) with limited resources. The parallel data refers to pairs of multi-modal objects that capture the cause-and-effect relation between text-rich document (cooking recipes) and visual examples (dish images). The relation is not narrative but causal. The visual impact changes depending on the series of actions (cooking methods) on different objects (ingredient compositions). The process is textually described in a natural language and the language differs across domains (cuisines). Consequently, these introduce domain gap due to change in data distribution, modality gap due to disparate representation of data from visual and textual aspects, and lingual gap due to use of different languages in detailing cooking process. This project will research on and develop new algorithms to model the complex causality change across the borders of domain, modality and language in the context of food recognition. The main issues to investigate are model robustness and representation learning. Specifically, the project will research the confounding factors that hinder the learning of a generalized model robust to environment change. The problem is complicated with the facts that the data-of-concern are multimodal within a domain and multilingual across the domains. Furthermore, a single image (of cooked dish) alone is inadequate in capturing the evolving cause-and-effect changes during the course of cooking. This project will research cross-modal representation learning that captures time-evolving causal relationship between visual effect and text descriptions of different languages. The project will address the general challenge of domain adaptation in learning invariant representation not only across domains but also across modality and language gaps. The existing works perform adaptation to address the change of data distributions and class labels in a target domain. The solutions cannot be trivially applied to the scenario when a “class label” is described with rich text in a language different from the source domain. Particularly, the text provides descriptions not mainly about visual appearance but the series of actions that could impact the visual effects. Furthermore, the descriptions are written in free style with different languages. Recipe is not a Dirac delta function but a distribution capturing variation in language expression, content composition and processing. To model the complex alignment between visual and text, the project frames the problem of domain adaptation from the angle of learning invariant representations across domain, modality and language. title: Unleashing the Power of Pre-trained Models for VisualQA: A Skill-based Framework
abs: This project aims to develop a new methodological framework to harness the power of large-scale pre-trained vision-language models for visual question answering. Visual question answering (VisualQA), a technology that enables machines to answer questions based on visual data, is the core of human-like interactive intelligent agents and many other applications. With the current trend in artificial intelligence (AI) to directly utilise large-scale pre-trained language models, such as GPT-3, for downstream tasks, there is similarly great potential to use large-scale pre-trained vision-language models trained on millions of image/video-text pairs for VisualQA. However, the community lacks a deep understanding of what capabilities of pre-trained models can be transferred to VisualQA and what capabilities are missing. This severely hinders the design of effective transfer learning solutions to best utilise pre-trained models for VisualQA. We propose to close this research gap using a skill-based framework based on the observation that VisualQA requires different types and levels of perception and reasoning skills. For example, to correctly answer the question “What is the colour of the lamp on the nightstand,” given an image of a room with multiple lamps, a VisualQA model needs to have object recognition skill to locate lamps and nightstand in the room, spatial reasoning skill to identify the lamp on the nightstand, and colour recognition skill to give the final answer. It is unclear whether the current pre-trained models possess all these skills. We first propose to identify the basic skills required by VisualQA and use a “probing approach” to identify the “skillsets” of pre-trained vision-language models (WP1). We will then design novel methods based on adapter modules, which are lightweight additional neural network layers, to augment the pre-trained models with additional skills (WP2). Finally, we will design a new multi-prompt method to decompose a question into sub-questions based on skills and jointly utilise complementary pre-trained models to answer the question (WP3). Intellectual merit: Using large-scale, pre-trained models (also known as foundation models) for transfer learning has emerged as a new paradigm of learning. Many large companies, including Google, Facebook and Microsoft, invest heavily in developing large-scale pre-trained vision-language models. Our project rides on this wave of a paradigm shift in AI but takes an underexplored, skill-based approach to offer both (i) a deep understanding of what pre-trained models can transfer and (ii) new technical solutions to bridge the skill gap between pre-trained models and what is required by VisualQA. Broader impact: VisualQA has practical value in many applications, particularly for multimodal interactive service bots, such as airport/hotel kiosks and shopping assistants. Our developed technologies can greatly reduce the R&D effort to build customised VisualQA models by effectively lev

title: High-Performance Thermoelectric Polymer Blends by Molecular Energy Filtering for Waste Heat Harvesting and Sustainable Development
abs: This project aims at developing high-performance thermoelectric polymer blends via the molecular energy filtering. These thermoelectric polymer blends can be used in thermoelectric generators (TEGs) to harvest waste heat into electricity. Hence, this project will be of great significance for the sustainable development because of the abundant waste heat on earth. Heat has been the primary energy for human society. However, the heat utilization efficiency is only about 30-40%, that is, the majority of the heat is dissipated to environment as waste heat. Plentiful heat is generated in natural process such as geothermal and photothermal processes as well. In addition, fossil fuels are usually burned to generate heat. CO2 is emitted during the combustion of fossil fuels, and CO2 can cause the global warming and disasters like sea level rising. To harvest waste heat can reduce the consumption of fossil fuels and the CO2 emission. Thus, this project can be of great significance for sustainable development. The thermoelectric properties of thermoelectric materials depend on the Seebeck coefficient, electrical conductivity and thermal conductivity. To have a high figure of merit (ZT) value, a material should have a high Seebeeck coefficient, high electrical conductivity while low thermal conductivity. The conventional thermoelectric materials are inorganic semiconductors or semimetals like Bi2Sb3 and its derivatives. But they have problems of scarce/toxic elements, high cost, and poor mechanical flexibility. Recently, thermoelectric polymers emerged as the next-generation thermoelectric materials owing to their advantages of low cost, low thermal conductivity, abundant elements, light weight, high mechanical flexibility and ease to process. Nevertheless, the thermoelectric properties of polymers are saliently inferior to their inorganic counterparts today. In particular, thermoelectric polymers usually exhibit a Seebeck coefficient lower than that of the inorganic counterparts by 1-2 orders in magnitude. We propose to significantly enhance the Seebeck coefficient of thermoelectric polymers via the molecular energy filtering in this project. Although lowering the charge carrier density can increase the Seebeck coefficient, it simultaneously lowers the electrical conductivity. A remedy to improve the thermoelectric properties is the energy filtering that can remarkably increase the Seebeck coefficient while does not lower the electrical conductivity too much. The conventional ways to induce the energy filtering are to blend nanometer electronic materials such as metal nanoparticles, carbon nanotubes or graphene into thermoelectric materials including thermoelectric polymers. However, these nanomaterials may not dispersed well in the thermoelectric matrix, and they have high thermal conductivity and limited contact area to the thermoelectric matrix. title: Quantum single photon emitters in silicon emitting at telecom wavelengths
abs: Single photon emitters (SPEs) that are intrinsically coupled to waveguides remain highly desired in quantum photonic information processing and communication owing to its potential for scalable quantum photonic technologies. At present, defects in solids such as nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers and silicon vacancy (SiV) in diamond are well studied and have proven to be excellent candidates for various quantum optical applications. However, their photoluminescence spectrum remains outside of the telecom range, preventing the implementation to existing optical fiber infrastructure. Very recently, a specific class of carbon-related defects in silicon, also known as G centers, have gathered increasing attention due to its bright photoluminescence in the telecom range (~1270μm, O band), remarkably narrow linewidth emission in the zero-phonon line (ZPL), and high spectral stability over hours. Another possible application for G centers in silicon is quantum memory qubit through the coherent control of the nuclear spins. Coupled with the presently highly mature CMOS-technology process, the research in G centers may potentially lay the foundation for the realization of integrated quantum photonic chip suitable for quantum communication with long quantum memory times. In this proposal, we propose to generate such G centers in deterministic location with addressable knock-in implantation. We will investigate their photonic integration into the optical cavity and waveguides. The proposed research lies at the intersection of topics in quantum optics, nanofabrication, confocal microscopy and material science. The result of this research would facilitate in-suit SPEs gereration and integration techniques not only for technological applications, but also fundamental studies in condensed matter physics. These research efforts would likely lead to new applications in practical quantum communication and room temperature quantum technology.
kw: Quantum emitters, silicon photonics, quantum communications, photonics circuits

title: AntiMicrobial resistance Research & Intervention Alliance Singapore (AMRITAS)
abs: Background Carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative bacteria (CR-GNB) constitute a global public health threat, with a tremendous health impact in Singapore and the region. Advances in the treatment and prevention of such infections will significantly reduce morbidity, mortality and healthcare costs. Aims and Hypotheses 1. Establish a regional clinical trial platform that utilizes a novel adaptive trial design to identify and implement optimal treatments for severe CR-GNB infections. We hypothesize that current clinical trial models for CR-GNB infections pose significant barriers to translation. This can be addressed by innovative trial design which is adapted from the network meta-analysis method. 2. Understand factors impacting transmission in the human gut and develop strategies to prevent infections. We hypothesize that the key genetic elements for antimicrobial resistance (AMR) evolution and transmission in the gut microbiome will be distinct from those in the environment. The healthy human gut microbiota harbours an ecosystem of commensals key to providing colonization resistance and interaction with the host to prevent infections. Approach and Methodology We aim to pilot a novel adaptive clinical trial design based on network meta-analysis that allows continuous evaluation of existing and new antibiotics. This will leverage on the Asian drug-resistant infection network ADVANCE ID to scale up for a large perpetual platform trial for CR-GNB management. Our second theme aims to identify key genetic elements for AMR evaluation and transmission in the gut via metagenomic analysis of clinical samples collected in the abovementioned trial, followed by laboratory testing and infection challenge in mini-bioreactor arrays and gnotobiotic mouse models. Potential Impact/Relevance High-quality evidence for the best treatments for severe CRE infections will transform clinical practice locally and globally. Our research outputs with better understanding of gut transmission and colonization resistance may lead to further clinical trials as well as academic and industry interest and investment.

title: Diabetes StudY in Nephropathy And other Microvascular cOmplications II
abs: DYNAMO was created to address the problem of diabetic nephropathy (DN), the leading cause of end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) in Singapore where the incidence of DN-associated ESKD is among the highest in the world. Despite its prominent global prevalence, the molecular pathogenesis of DN is not clearly defined. The major objective of DYNAMO is to identify the root causes of DN to provide a basis for new approaches to prevention, risk stratification, and treatment. To achieve this objective, we have assembled a team of world-class multi-disciplinary researchers who are focused on unravelling causal mechanisms of DN. The key nucleus of the team is based in Singapore but it comprises collaborating investigators from 6 countries and >20 institutions. A major focus has been deep-phenotyping of carefully curated Singaporean cohorts enriched for diabetic kidney and eye disease. This work has leveraged on “omics” technologies as powerful, scientifically agnostic approaches for solving the complex pathophysiology of diabetic complications. Organizing these cohorts and carrying out thousands of genomic, metabolomic, and proteomic assays were a major accomplishment during the first phase of DYNAMO, generating a large data set that will be an enduring resource for understanding DN in the Singaporean population and beyond. DYNAMO II builds upon the foundation of our previous findings, our outstanding team of basic and clinical researchers, and capitalizes on the large data sets we have generated. It is structured around 5 themes designed to achieve our major objective of translating our discoveries into new approaches for prevention, risk stratification, and treatment of DN. We have also refreshed our Biomedical Cores to support and facilitate the work to be carried out within the highly interactive Themes.
kw: Diabetes; diabetic nephropathy

title: Decoding cortical and spinal signals through ultrafast functional ultrasound neural interface
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Background: Central nervous system (CNS) is unable spontaneously regenerate injured neurons, and once injured, there is currently no way for disconnected regions of the brain to re-establish connections with the rest of the body. Brain-computer interface (BCI) is a technology that uses miniature bioelectronics to capture motor intents from neuronal signals, and uses the decoded signal to guide output systems such as prosthetic limbs, electrically stimulate one's own paralyzed muscles, or even control robotic systems. Currently, most neural interface systems record the weak electrical or electromagnetic signals that neurons generate. This approach faces problems such as noise interference, electrode shift or degradation, or surgical implantation risks. Ultrafast focused ultrasound (FUS) is a new imaging modality which uses ultrasound, mounted from a miniature probe, to distantly image the microvasculature of the cortex. These arterioles regulate cerebral blood flow proportionally to neuronal activities, a well-described phenomenon known as neurovascular coupling. Preclinical studies in non-human primates have demonstrated that such cerebral hemodynamics contain adequate information to allow real-time control of a screen cursor. Aim: We will evaluate FUS in deciphering motor intents from descending corticospinal signals. Hypothesis: Corticospinal signals contain adequate information to infer motor intents and for use as control signals for external effectors Methods: We will intraoperatively record neural signals in patients who are undergoing standard-of-care lumbosacral spine surgery. We will record sensorimotor (e.g. proprioceptive and sensory) signals as well as micturition signals from the spinal cord. Ultrasound is non-invasive and will present minimal additional risks to the patient. We hope that this will inform future translational development of real-time closed-loop neural control systems.

title: Characterizing the immune microenvironment to inform stratified immunotherapeutic approaches in MSS metastatic Colorectal cancer (MSS-mCRC)
abs: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the third most common cancer globally. ~95% of mCRC are microsatellite-stable (MSS), MSS-mCRC is refractory to PD1/PDL1 immune checkpoint inhibition with near 0% objective response rates. Current trials generally evaluate 1 combination across all patients with MSS-mCRC, taking it as a single disease entity. MSS-CRC is a heterogeneous disease. In July 2022, we used single cell & bulk omics to update the classification system of CRC, the IMF classification, comprising MSI-H cancers and 4 distinct subsets of MSS-CRC, defined by 2 malignant epithelial cell states and the extent of fibrosis. The 4 molecular subsets of MSS-CRC are characterised by distinct unique molecular features and different component cell types within their tumor microenvironment (TME). Continuing our team’s work , the overall objective is to inform stratified immunotherapeutic approaches, tailored to different subsets of MSS-mCRC, through spatial biology, humanised mouse models and histopathological stains. We aim to characterise the cellular composition, spatial organisation & tumor-stromal-immune interactions of different subsets of MSS-CRC & at different metastatic sites. We aim to establish humanized mouse models for pre-clinical evaluation of immunotherapy combinations in different subsets of MSS-CRC. We aim to identify antigen targets that can be further developed into clinical assays.

title: Enhancing urban coral reef resilience to climate change across biological scales
abs: Coral reefs are driven by complex processes with various connections and interactions that may convey ecological resilience. While short-term disturbances allow for recovery, this may not always be possible with longer term stressors such as climate change, so resistance against degradation and adaptive capacity are critical. In the urban context of Singapore, a resilient reef ecosystem is one that can respond to environmental shocks, protect its resource provision, and adapt to rapidly changing conditions. Singapore’s marine environment consists of urbanised coastal waters bordering dense human populations alongside high levels of shipping and anthropogenic activities. Therefore, traditional models of ecological resilience as applied to natural ecosystems may not be appropriate as the built environment exerts a strong influence on ecosystem function. The focus of this project is to develop scientific understanding and applications to secure the ecological resilience of coral reefs in the context of a tropical urban port environment. Our project has two core objectives, which will, for the first time for any reef system, integrate community, population, microbial and management approaches based on aquarium and field experimentation to enhance reef resilience against climate change. The first objective is to develop resilient coral holobionts that would better withstand climate change conditions under locally relevant environmental thresholds and global projections. We will first identify and culture naturally thermal resilient corals that will then be inoculated with beneficial microorganisms for corals (BMC) to further enhance corals’ tolerance against more frequent marine heatwaves. Specifically, we will isolate potentially beneficial microbes from naturally occurring coral microbial communities, test the effects of the isolated BMC on corals under stress conditions, and experimentally investigate the mechanism(s) by which the BMC deliver benefit to the coral through a combination of manipulation experiments and genome sequencing of bacterial isolates. The second objective is to design ecological and microbial solutions to enhance reef resilience for deployment on urban coral reefs based on a novel risk management and decision framework. For the resilient coral holobionts to be successfully transplanted and integrated into the natural reef environment, it is crucial to consider site-specific factors such as local environmental conditions, connectivity with other reef sites, and microbial pathogenic risks. A comprehensive framework for selecting and managing reef enhancement sites will therefore benefit reef resource management agencies such as the National Parks Board. This project will integrate community, population, microbial and management approaches based on aquarium and field experimentation to enhance reef resilience against climate change. title: ECO-Cycling: Environmentally-friendly Catalytic Oxidations for Upcycling Waste Polyethylenes into Chemical Commodities
inst: IMRE - Institute of Materials Research and Engineering
abs: Polyethylenes (PEs), the single largest class of plastics disposed worldwide, are non-biodegradable and the vast majority are incinerated after use. With no viable biodegradable alternatives available, societal demand of PEs will continue unabated for the foreseeable future. Instead of disposing them, waste PEs can be given a new ‘lease of life’ by converting them into useful chemical feedstock. However, the chemical inertness of PEs limit the possibilities to only high-temperature pyrolysis that transforms PEs into hydrocarbons for use as fuels, solvents and lubricants. To improve the attractiveness of waste PEs as a resource, this proposal aims to transform them into oxygenated molecules such as organic acids, which are commodity chemicals of massive industrial demand and excellent value-addedness. Holistically sustainable oxidation methods, utilising clean oxidants (oxygen or hydrogen peroxide, which only generates water as a side product), renewable or aqueous solvents, and catalysts synthesised using green chemistry methods, will be employed to turn PEs into oxygenated commodity chemicals with minimal waste and energy input. A range of dicarboxylic acids of different lengths, aromatic acids and small oxygenated molecules will be produced, representing an unprecedented variety of useful chemical commodities from upcycling PEs alone. With ready markets and strong existing demand in vital industries which include chemical, polymers, food and beverage, coatings and pharmaceutics, successful oxidative transformation of PEs into these oxygenated chemicals via sustainable means will truly establish a viable post-use waste plastics economy, whilst simultaneously impacting multiple sectors of society for a more sustainable future.
kw: Green chemistry; waste plastic valorisation; sustainable materials economy; sustainable manufacturing; Organic acids; zero-waste

title:
Spinning Towards a ‘Bright’ Future: 
Energy-Harvesting with Spin-Triplet Excitons in Luminescent Materials
inst: IMRE - Institute of Materials Research and Engineering
abs: As Singapore, and the world, faces an environmental energy crisis, the ecosystem is working towards sustainable, energy-efficient solutions, and locally there are national schemes such as the Singapore Green Plan. In this proposal, our goal is to contribute towards novel approaches in utilising common energy resources efficiently with minimum loss and usefully for targeted applications, by harnessing energy inter-conversion processes in organic luminescent materials. We address several types of energy inter-conversions: between different colours of light, electrochemical energy to light, and between electrical and light energy, targeting use-cases of agritech, flexible electronics, lighting, display and biosensing. Organic semiconductors have the unique presence of (Frenkel) excitons, or Coulombically-bound electron-hole pairs, formed when photons are absorbed or when charges are injected. The excitons are spin-dependent, i.e. there are spin singlet, triplet, or quintet excitons. Central to this proposal are two processes regarding the behaviour of triplet excitons, namely spin-state interconversion (SSI) and triplet-triplet annihilation (TTA), in a range of organic materials. We aim to harness them for energy-efficient and energy-harvesting outcomes with: 1. Inter-converting between colours of light: to achieve photon energy upconversion at low optical powers for practical purposes 2. Harnessing such low-power photon upconversion (from (1)): to enable dual-colour conversion from a single system, which will in turn enable two targeted demonstrations: a. A passive spectral-tailoring dual colour converter for green plants, without external energy input b. A new approach to generate white-light for lighting devices 3. Converting electrical and chemical energy into light: developing brighter, better electrochemiluminescence devices using new materials and designs, for display and sensing applications. We will combine versatile materials processing, device design and engineering, and various photophysical (and electrochemical) characterisation techniques. In sum, this highly inter-disciplinary proposal strives to bring about valuable insights and demonstrations on versatile control and manipulation of excitonic behaviour in organic luminescent materials, for energy-harvesting processes and energy-efficient applications.

title: Fuzz Testing
abs: The project will develop new techniques in testing and analysis, for detecting security vulnerabilities, specifically for concurrent, stateful and reactive software systems. Traditionally these systems have been checked via verification methods which store the state space in some form. Since common usage of the verification methods is in bug finding, we propose to develop smart fuzzing methods to validate stateful systems. Technically this will involve various innovations in (a) identifying state variables in programs (b) inferring stateful behavior and state machines even when state variables may not be accurately identified, (c ) being able to fuzz concurrent systems to capture the space of interleavings and (d) taking advantage of fuzzing distributed data processing systems by opportunistic mutations of data formats. Being able to validate concurrent / distributed / stateful systems, allows us to deeply test the impact of a vendor provided component on (stateful) software. The proposed research is of importance in the context of recent well-known supply chain attacks, such as Solarwinds. Fuzz testing and binary analysis techniques can be employed to prevent such attacks (and others) - to mitigate their impact. The project also looks at sound statistical basis for comparing evaluation of fuzzer tools, so that practitioners can choose fuzzers which are useful for their specific application set-up to find vulnerabilities effectively. This can also impact the way fuzzer evaluations are currently conducted in well-known computational infra-structures including Google’s Fuzzbench. Last but not the least, we will seek to build a fuzzer collaboration platform for combining fuzzers with other validation tools such as model checkers and symbolic execution engines, to make the task of checking stateful software systems more manageable and tractable in the future. This can be investigated concretely potentially under a well-known tool competition such as SV-COMP, to further enhance the impact of the technologies to be developed.

title: From Tough Pollen to Soft Matter
abs: Often regarded as the diamond of the plant kingdom, the pollen – as a class of material – is at once tough and soft. However, our understanding of how this structural adaptation allows pollen to deliver its biological functionality while displaying the stunning longevity, which often extends to geological time scales remains limited. Thus, the overarching intellectual and scientific vision for this proposal is to develop materials science of pollen. Specifically, we aim to systematically map fundamental relations between processes, structures, and properties spanning full range of relevant multiple length scales and produce comprehensive descriptions of the structure-dynamics-function relations characterizing pollen. We will implement a tightly integrated, highly collaborative, and a narrowly focused research strategy by focusing on a small sub-set of natural and engineered pollen and launching a systematic investigation to arrive at a quantitative map consolidating key structure-dynamics-properties-function relations that characterize the pollen as a material. To systematically alter material composition and structure of the pollen, we will engineer a natural variant using environmentally benign chemical methods. We will investigate the stability and environmental adaptability of a selection of natural and engineered pollens. We hypothesize that the pollen morphology must adopt folding pathways that maintain routes of communication and exchange with the environment, while preserving the structural integrity of the pollen grain. We reason that the fundamental understanding of how the material organization enables the pollen to generate negative feedback loops that respond to environmental assaults will not only provide basic understanding of pollen as a dynamic, responsive material but also yield fundamental design principles for the synthesis of novel pollen-mimetic matter. This will eventually lead to pollen-based materials for applications in drug delivery, tissue engineering, 3D printing, biosensing and beyond.

title: A New-Generation Envelope Tracking Modulator for Radio-Frequency Communications Devices (including the Internet-of-Things): Higher Power-Efficiency, Wider Bandwidth and 'Open' Platform
abs: The Problem Wireless radio frequency (RF) communication devices are globally some of the most ubiquitous electronic devices, ranging from feature and smartphones, 2-way radios (walkie-talkies), DECT phones, etc. Their use reaches nearly all of humanity – more than 90% of humanity own a smart/feature phone, virtually all police and civil defence employ 2-way radios, etc. RF communications are enabled by an RF power amplifier to transmit wireless signals. Despite the maturity of RF power amplifiers and their supply modulators, three perennial real technical issues remain unresolved. One, the power-efficiency remains insufficient. Two, for operation with wide-bandwidth/high-speed, the power-efficiency is further compromised. Three, state-of-the-art supply modulators (to provide a means for substantially improved power-efficiency of RF power amplifiers) are ‘closed’ platforms, rendering them inapplicable to general wireless devices. In other words, supply modulators are presently limited only to ‘closed-platform’ 3G, 4G and 5G smartphones, and inapplicable to other RF communications devices. The inapplicability to other RF communications devices renders them power-inefficient because they cannot employ a supply modulator. Collectively, these three unresolved issues are particularly imperative because the RF power amplifier is typically the dominant power dissipation block in wireless RF communication devices, i.e., their battery lifetime remains insufficient. Our Proposal We will investigate to resolve some of the most fundamental issues – the aforesaid three unresolved real issues – pertaining to the design and realization of power supply modulators for RF power amplifiers. Specifically, we propose a novel ‘Open-Platform’ High-Bandwidth High Power-Efficiency Envelop Tracking Modulator (ETM). The innovations/solutions proposed are beyond the state-of-the-art, where the proposed ETM features simultaneously: (i) Unprecedented reduced ETM losses by 50%. This translates to improving the power efficiency of a typical RF power amplifier by a significant 20% – this is equivalent to a 4-year lead in battery technology (batteries improve by 5%/year). This further translates to improved reliability due to the ensuing reduced heat in the RF power amplifier; (ii) Unprecedented bandwidth extension by 2x (200MHz vs 100MHz in the state-of-the-art) without compromising power-efficiency; and (iii) First-ever ‘open’ platform (vis-à-vis the ‘closed’ platform in the state-of-the-art that can hitherto only be applied only to 3G, 4G and 5G smartphones) for universal application. The open platform, for the first-time, allows an ETM to be universal – applicable to virtually all RF power amplifiers that otherwise cannot embody an ETM. Put differently, all RF power amplifiers can hence feature significantly improved power-efficiency by adopting an ETM – not just limited to ‘closed-platform’ ones today. The potential outcomes of the proposal are very impactful – a technologica

title: The feasible aspects of mathematical structures
abs: The abstract notion of a computation is a fundamental concept in modern scientific research. This project aims at applying the theory of computation to gain more insight into various mathematical structures and targets at advancing the frontiers of computational theory. The general model of a computation allows for an algorithm to take finite but otherwise unrestricted time and resources. Applying algorithmic restrictions on mathematical structures and processes result in the study of computable mathematics. The PI and coauthors pioneered a research program in which a feasible model of computation was used. Applying feasible algorithms to mathematical structures and processes result in the study of punctual mathematics. This proposal describes research to advance the understanding of the role of algorithms in two broad areas of mathematics, via both the computable and punctual approach. Algorithms in discrete mathematics - The tools of computable and punctual mathematical theory are used to define how much algorithmic information is present in a discrete structure. We aim to advance this study by studying the degree structure induced by the isomorphism type of a discrete structure. We will also attack fundamental problems in punctual equivalence relations and online graph colouring. Algorithms in continuous mathematics - The tools of computable and punctual mathematics can also be used to calibrate the algorithmic body of countably based topological and metric spaces. This direction is less developed than that for discrete structures and there is much potential for groundbreaking work here. The proposal describes research to set new trends in this area by studying computable and punctual topological categoricity. The PI has extensive experience working in the topics of the proposal and has a proven track record of strong technical ability and abundant success in creating new techniques to solve intricate problems in the subject. The successful completion of this project will advance the understanding of the role algorithms play in mathematics. The project will shed intuition downstream to other areas of mathematics such as descriptive topology, functional analysis, graph colouring problems, infinitary combinatorics and discrete mathematics, to name a few.
kw: Mathematical structures, Feasible computation, Computable mathematics, Topological spaces

title: All-Optical Perovskite Polaritonic Circuits with Robustness
abs: Exciton-polaritons are an exemplary man-made system for fusing together the physics of light and matter. These systems are coherent and display ultrafast (picosecond scale) dynamics, similar to photonic systems, while they also show nonlinear behaviour and a sensitivity to applied fields better known in electronic systems. Their mixed nature makes them ideal candidates for novel optoelectronics. They are well placed to interface with electronics and photonics, while the continuous mixing of photonic and electronic properties, which can be done with controlled fractions, allows an optimization of desired properties. This has led several pioneering research groups in the field to develop a range of different transistor and optical switch prototypes, moving in the direction of realizing polaritonic circuits. There are two key problems that must be addressed though, before completely functioning polaritonic circuits with high stability can be realized. The first key problem is the choice of material system, where most earlier works have focused on using III-V semiconductor technology. They demanded liquid helium cooling to sustain stable polaritons, which is enormously expensive in relative energy terms. It is necessary to move to systems with more stable polaritons, such as perovskites or organics, which have seen rigorous development in NTU in recent years. The second key problem is the stability of the polaritonic circuits, where earlier works of polaritonic circuit elements, such as transistor and optical switch prototypes, are usually sensitive to backscattering and perturbations including defects and disorder. They could easily degrade or even destroy the performance of polaritonic circuit elements. For a polaritonic circuit platform to be stable and practical, it will be crucial to endow it with strong protection, such as giant topological robustness against backscattering and perturbations. Herein, we intend to overcome above challenges and build on our previous studies of polariton nonlinearity, spin phenomena, and topological physics with emerging perovskites. We aim to achieve robust propagating topological polariton states in perovskites with a wide topological gap and bandwidth, thus strong topological protection. Combined with its sizeable nonlinearity, our final goal will be to achieve a prototype of an all-optical polaritonic circuit with strong topological protection for robust logic operations, that can work at room temperature. The outcome of this proposal will produce profound knowledge in nonlinear topological polaritons with perovskites and will lead to practical and unprecedented functionality in ultrafast photonic circuits with low energy consumption.
kw: Exciton polariton; Perovskites; strong light-matter interaction; photonic crystals; nanophotonics; optoelectronics

title: Dynamical characterization of the spin-to-charge conversion mechanisms in 2D heterostructures
abs: Spintronics is an approach to electronics where not only the charge degree of freedom of the electron is used as a way to store and transport information, but the electron’s spin is used as well. The strength of the approach comes from the unlocking of the possibility to use the best of the two degrees of freedom to implement different electronic processing. Such idea however relies on the capacity to transform one type of information into the other. This can be achieved due to the relativistic effect of spin–orbit coupling (SO). In materials, like heavy metals, where SO is strong, a very efficient charge-to-spin conversion, as well as its reciprocal process spin-to-charge conversion (SCC) can be achieved. Due to its pivotal importance to a number of applications, the SCC phenomenon has been intensely studied, yet only close to equilibrium: little is known about the ultrafast out-of-equilibrium analogous. As electronics pushes to break the GHz barrier to achieve faster microprocessor’s clock rates, spintronics is supposed to follow into the THz regime. At these extreme speeds, less time is left to the electronic system to thermalise and out-of-equilibrium states start weighting more on the measured dynamics. Far from being an undesired effect, the role of excited carriers can be of great use to access and utilise beneficial characteristics of bands even away from the Fermi energy, unlocking new potential avenues for optimisation, manipulation, and often new emergent phenomena. One spectacular result of out-of-equilibrium SCC is the development of the popular spintronics THz emitters (of which the PI has been co-developer and theory leader). Yet, it remains unclear how SCC is modified when pushed to extreme frequencies and is triggered away from the Fermi level. Furthermore, while the role of intrinsic (due to band structure) and extrinsic (due to scatterings, usually defects) contributions to SCC is relatively understood close to equilibrium, the same cannot be said when the electronics system is excited. In particular, laser excited electrons undergo several (electron-electron and electron-phonon) scatterings during their thermalisation. It is still unclear if these electron-electron scatterings can give a contribute to the SCC process (contribution which is instead absent close to equilibrium). In this project, we will then address the following questions: • How do out-of-equilibrium electronic distributions triggered by femtosecond lasers affect SCC? • Is it possible to leverage out-of-equilibrium population away from the Fermi level to enhance SCC? • Can the scatterings during thermalization provide an extrinsic-like enhancement to intrinsic SCC? We will investigate both experimentally and theoretically the temporal, spatial (bulk vs surface) and energy features of the THz SCC in 2D materials. title: Mast cell promoted T cell functions during primary and secondary viral infections
abs: Mast cells (MCs), granulated immune cells, are immune sentinels positioned strategically in the skin and mucosal tissues as first responders to pathogen challenge. MCs recognize and respond to many types of pathogens, including viruses. To promote pathogen clearance, MCs coordinate early immune events such as recruitment of cytotoxic cells to the site of infection. MCs also accelerate adaptive immune responses by promoting trafficking of dendritic cells (DCs) to draining lymph nodes (DLNs). Recently, we defined the subsets of T cells that are recruited by MCs in response to dengue virus (DENV) infection and made the surprising observation that MCs appear to interact tightly with T cells in the skin, suggesting immune synapse formation. Furthermore, we showed that activation of certain subsets of T cells, such as gammadeltaT cells, by MCs can promote efficient early clearance of DENV. This raises several questions, including whether the phenotype of the activated T cell is imprinted through the process of MC-interaction. Another intrinsic property of T cells is the ability to adopt a memory phenotype. To date, studies examining MC interactions with T cells have mostly focused on their interactions during the acute phase of a primary immune response to infection or vaccination. In contrast, our knowledge is limited on MC-T cell interactions during memory formation (when activated T cells convert to a memory phenotype) and memory recall, as occurs during a secondary challenge. Our preliminary data support that MCs play a role in this process. Here we aim to define how MC regulation of the skin microenvironment influences early T cell trafficking and activation during viral infection, to subsequently impact immunity. Understanding MC/Tcell/pathogen interplay will increase our basic knowledge and may discover novel targets for early disease intervention. We also question whether human MCs are capable of antigen presentation to T cells, which would have implications for the design and implementation of vaccines against human viral pathogens.
kw: mast cell, T cell, adaptive immunity, immune memory, dengue virus

title: Examining the altered immunological and molecular landscape of the jaw following bisphosphonate treatment to define mechanisms of bone homeostasis
abs: Bisphosphonates (BPs) are central drugs of the orthopaedic clinic, used for treating a variety of diseases of the bone. Through targeting osteoclasts, they have strong anti-resorptive effects, and improve bone density in skeletal diseases including osteogenesis imperfecta and osteoporosis. However, despite well documented reduction in fracture rates in patients, all bisphosphonates suffer from adverse clinical complications and side effects. Commonly, bisphosphonates induce osteonecrosis of the jaw (ONJ), presenting as non-healing exposed bone in maxillofacial areas. ONJ poses significant complications to clinical treatment regimes. Bisphosphonate related ONJ (BRONJ) is not understood mechanistically. Proposed cellular and molecular mechanisms proposed to explain BRONJ are highly discordant and lack consensus. It is unclear what cellular effect bisphosphonates are having at the jaw and why they specifically target this region. We have recently established a robust model of BRONJ using adult zebrafish, which, unlike current animal models, is highly consistent, rapid, and permits easy assaying of the relevant tissues. This offers a completely novel and unique method to interrogate the cellular, genetic, and molecular changes underlying BRONJ. We have established transgenic lines able to label relevant cell types and have already identified a mutant strain which is resistant to BRONJ, giving us direct and testable hypotheses. This proposal has 3 major aims. 1. We will apply microCT and genetic cellular labelling approaches to define the tissue defect and the cells present in the jaw contributing to BRONJ onset and determine their origin. 2. We will use molecular genetic tools and RNA-Seq approaches to identify molecular alterations over the course of disease progression, leading to relevant cell changes. 3. Test the implicated cell and molecular culprits through cell ablation and pharmacological interventions to define pathomechanism in our zebrafish BRONJ model. Our proposal will thus identify how cellular resorptive behaviour in the jaw is constrained under steady-state conditions, furnish new understanding about how this regulation becomes deranged in the BRONJ patient, and offer molecular pathways for future clinical testing, confirmation, and pharmacological targeting. Ultimately this proposal exploits a novel preclinical model for understanding BRONJ pathomechanism.
kw: Bisphosphonate; Osteonecrosis; Jaw; Bone; Zebrafish; Immune

title: High-Resolution Flood Risk and Impact Modeling
abs: Floods are the most frequent natural hazard globally, and flood-induced losses are expected to grow with future climate and land-use changes. In this context, quantitative flood-risk analysis models are critical to understanding, planning for and promoting resilient cities and communities, particularly in the face of climate change and sea-level rise. Such models have been crucial for underpinning flood mitigation planning by water management agencies (e.g. PUB), as well as the catastrophe insurance sector (e.g. flood insurance programs). Yet flooding events continue to regularly overwhelm protective infrastructure and insurance reserves because of gaps and inaccuracies in flood risk analysis models. In particular, while most research and development in flood risk analysis has focused on the flood hazard component of risk analysis, little attention has been placed on the consequences component (exposure and vulnerability) or on the link between the geophysical process of flooding and the statistical models used to represent them in risk analyses. This study aims to address these gaps through three main objectives (1) the development of new techniques for high-resolution flood exposure making use of street-view imagery analysis techniques, (2) the development of building-component-level damage models to capture complexities of flood damage dynamics more accurately than current building-level damage models, and (3) the use of spatial statistics to account for missing drivers of flood damage that are not captured in hydrodynamic process-models of flood hazard. These aims are linked, and collectively will enable the better identification and characterization of assets at risk (aim 1), better modelling of their vulnerability to flooding (aim 2), and with reduced bias through the use of statistical correction (aim 3). The results of this project will contribute to better understanding of floods and better quantifying their impacts on society. This will produce significant benefits to the flood management, planning and insurance industries, and is particularly relevant to Singapore and other cities facing the challenge of increasing flood impacts driven by climate change and sea-level rise.
kw: flood modelling, climate change, probabilistic methods, spatial statistics, reliability analysis

title: Ammonia-fed solid oxide fuel cell as a power source for maritime industries
abs: The International Maritime Organization (IMO) adopted an initial strategy in April 2018 on the reduction of GHG emissions from ships, which sets goals to reduce total annual GHG emissions by at least 50% by 2050 compared to 2008 and eventually fully eliminate harmful emissions from the global maritime industry. Thus, there is an urgent need for the maritime industry to invest in clean fuels and efficient energy conversion technologies. Hydrogen is viewed as the future fuel to decarbonise the maritime sector. However, the mode of delivery and form of storage is still being debated on its safety, technical and economic viability. In Singapore’s context, the country is constrained by limited land and natural resources, thereby leaving the option to import hydrogen gas as the reasonable choice. The hydrogen can be imported in the form of liquid hydrogen, ammonia and alternative hydrogen carriers. In particular, ammonia has attracted great attention as a hydrogen carrier because of its advantages including high energy density (5.2 kWh/kg), high hydrogen content (17.7 wt.%), ease in liquefaction (boiling point –33.4°C at atmospheric pressure), and narrow flammable range (16-25% by volume in air). A recent report by DNV estimated that the demand for ammonia as a bunker fuel could lie between 35.9 to 71.7 million tonnes by 2050. The carrier can be converted into heat and power through combustion engines or fuel cells. Between these two energy converters, fuel cells, in particular the solid oxide fuel cells (SOFCs), have the advantage that the energy conversion is done through electro-chemical path and at relatively lower temperatures (compared with internal combustion engines), where conditions are less favourable to produce NOx that has global warming potential (GWP) 265 to 298 times that of CO2 for a 100-year timescale. Moreover, such ammonia-SOFC system has no moveable parts, hence possible leaking of ammonia during operation is less an issue. With the shipping ports as the potential landing points for imported ammonia, it would make sense to use the ammonia to decarbonise the port’s operations while serving as a holding and distribution point. The notion to start with port applications and land applications is supported by our industrial partners, Jurong Port (JP) and Surbana Jurong (SJ), who are in good positions to see through the developments within Singapore and outside of Singapore, respectively. This project shall explore the use of ammonia with SOFC system in the port to efficiently and effectively generate low-carbon power and heat for port operations. The waste heat from SOFC shall drive the cracking process in the integrated ammonia cracker, serving as a waste heat recovery device (~14.2%). The project shall focus on 1) the development of self-supported non-precious iron-group metal-based catalysts for ammonia cracking, 2) the development of ammonia reactor, and 3) integration of ammonia reactor into SOFC system.
kw: Ammonia Cracking, Solid Oxide Fuel Cell, Catalyst

title: TrustedSEERs: Trusted Intelligent Work Bots for Engineering Better Software Faster
abs: The proposed project – TrustedSEERs (Trusted Software Engineering Expert advisoRs) – will realize trusted and intelligent automation work bots that act as concierges and interactive advisors to software engineers. The bots will help engineers ensure the high quality of software and the sustained and rapid pace at which it should be built and updated. TrustedSEERs will realize such automation by effectively learning from domain-specific, loosely-linked, multi-modal, multi-source and evolving software artefacts (e.g., source code, version history, bug reports, blogs, documentation, Q&A posts, videos, etc.). These artefacts can come from the organization deploying the automation bots, a group of collaborating yet privacy-aware organizations, and from freely available yet possibly licensed (e.g., GPL v2, GPL v3, MIT, etc.) data contributed by many, including untrusted entities, on the internet (e.g., on StackOverflow, GitHub, etc.). TrustedSEERs will bring about the next generation of Software Analytics (SA) – a rapidly growing area in the Software Engineering research field that turns data into automation – by establishing two initiatives: First, Data-Centric SA, through the design and development of methods that systematically engineer data needed to learn more effective SA bots from diverse software artefacts, many of which are domain-specific and unique. Second, Trustworthy SA, through the design and development of mechanisms that engender software engineers' trust in SA bots considering intrinsic factors (explainability) and extrinsic ones (compliance to privacy and copyright laws and robustness to external attacks). TrustedSEERs has three Work Packages (WPs): WP1. Data-Centric Software Analytics This work package will design and develop a human-in-the-loop data-centric software analytics (SA) approach. Specifically, it will realize new methods that can better select, label, synthesize, link, and transform data from diverse software artefacts to learn better SA models and tackle their weaknesses. My prior works have proposed methods that can make sense of software artefacts of diverse modalities to learn SA solutions to automate various software engineering tasks. Although many of my prior works were model-centric, I have recently investigated domain-specific data-centric methods. For example, I have designed methods that: (i) repair programs by selecting high-quality patches that developers made in thousands of repositories on GitHub and learning a suitable AI model from the high-quality data; (ii) systematically help domain-experts label data with higher quality and less quantity to allow for better identification of actionable static analysis warnings through an AI classification model. In WP1, I will generalize these studies to create a framework that can systematically engineer smart-sized data to address SA solutions' weak points for various software engineering tasks. title: Developing a new platform for assessing volcano hazard through analysis of globally acquired monitoring data
abs: In their fight to mitigate the threats of volcanic eruptions, volcanological observatories and research institutions must process and interpret an increasing amount of monitoring data in order to make timely decisions when advising authorities, civil protection agencies and other stakeholders. This project aims at closing the gap between increasing monitoring capacity and lacking interpretation capability by testing existing, and further developing automated computer algorithms to formulat a generalised and standardised model of volcano-seismic unrest. This project will combine many datasets recorded at volcanoes in different geological settings with different types of volcanic activity in a holistic approach, resulting in the first unified model that classifies volcano-seismic events, allowing us to identify common patterns across volcanoes, and linking certain seismic event types to specific volcanic processes. New approaches in data processing will have to be developed to overcome this challenge. This project will achieve impact by developing and disseminating open-source tools, complemented by associated training courses. At the scale of a single observatory, this will ensure automation and consistent interpretation, while at a larger scale, this project will boost our understanding of volcanic processes and our ability to forecasting eruption style and size, and therefore better mitigate their impact. This project is in line with international initiatives underwritten by the IAVCEI Commission for Volcano Seismology and Acoustics and the World Organisation of Volcano Observatories.

title: Interface Engineered Ferroelectric 2D Materials for Artificial Synapses and Neuromorphic Computing
abs: The conventional von Neumann computing architecture has limited computation speed and drastically increased energy consumption because of the physically separated processing and memory units. Inspired by the human brain, neuromorphic computing possesses great advantages of high fault tolerance and ultralow power dissipation for complex learning, recognition, perception, and memory functions, making it a promising alternative to alleviate the existing computing bottleneck. 2D materials, such as 2D transition metal dichalcogenides, have been rapidly established as promising building blocks for the neuromorphic computing devices. The 2D atomic layered structure enables their immunity against the short channel effects, while the mechanical strength and structural flatness allow their integration into flexible and wearable circuits. However, the realization of 2D materials based neuromorphic devices faces many challenges. For example, the existence of large contact resistance at the interface between the 2D semiconductor and any bulk (or 3D) metal makes the power mainly dissipated at the contacts, and this largely impedes the development of the ultralow power neuromorphic computing devices. Unlike the bulk materials, atomic-thin 2D materials are essentially interface-type materials and the performance of their devices are controlled and determined by the interface, such as charge injection/collection at metal/2D interface, charge carrier trapping at the dielectric/2D interface. Moreover, the effective control of these interface properties can also offer the great opportunity to significantly improve the device performances and to realize the devices with novel functionalities. Our aim is to develop interface engineered 2D materials including 2D ferroelectric materials for neuromorphic computing or brain-inspired computing, to address the stringent scaling requirement (energy, size and device complexity) for the traditional von Neumann architecture based CMOS technology. The project has three main objectives: (1) Development of large-scale growth of high-quality 2D materials including 2D ferroelectric materials with controlled interface properties; (2) Development of air-stable Ohmic contact (both holes and electrons) approaches for 2D materials; (3) Fabrication of 2D materials based neuromorphic computing devices with ultralow power consumption. Our group has been focusing on the interface research for over 15 years and pioneered the development of interface engineering for 2D materials-based electronics and optoelectronics. Very recently, our group systematically investigate the interface engineered 2D materials for memory devices and discovered unique multibit optoelectronic memory devices using 2D materials-based heterojunctions, which demonstrates great potential to realize neuromorphic computing and forms the basis of the proposal for this NRF Investigatorship Award.
kw: Interface Engineering, 2D Materials, Neuromorphic Computing, Artificial Synapse, Surface Science, Epitaxy

title: Robust Bayesian inference of characterization and spread of infectious diseases by integrating genomic, serological, and epidemiological information
abs: The broad aim of this research proposal is to integrate genomic, serological and epidemiological information from an infectious disease outbreak into a single Bayesian framework to inform public health strategy. We are experiencing an unprecedented opportunity in pathogen genomics research, where from a few thousand sequences available worldwide for each pathogen, we now have 100 or 1000-fold this number. This huge volume, especially during the COVID-19 pandemic, means that models will be fundamental for interpretation and analysis of these data. This proposal will contribute to this research, and operationalize the tools so that they can be used in real-time to inform public agencies. Very few current frameworks integrate analysis pipelines, and those that do tend to be disjointed. The methods and tools developed in this proposal would be at the forefront of the current ‘state-of-the-art’ and will specifically focus on three scientific aspects: Effectively integrating genomic data into transmission models to improve inference of the virus’ epidemiological dynamics by using methods from information theory and Bayesian evidence synthesis. Applying modern deep generative modelling as the inferential scheme to handle the current surge in volumes of data. Existing methods are entirely unable to perform inference over millions of genomes, let alone also include other epidemiological data jointly. Understand the factors that shape the establishment and subsequent spread of various diseases and its variants. These three themes, taken together, will create a suite of tools that can utilize as many relevant data sources as possible to create a near real-time snapshot of the epidemic with informative summary metrics to facilitate policy decisions. New and emerging infectious disease tools need to balance historical experience with new contemporary science.
kw: Infectious Disease Modelling, Outbreaks, Phylogenetics, Bayesian Inference, Statistical Machine Learning
