title:
Targeting novel genes to overcome drug resistance in EGFR-mutant
Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC)
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Activating mutations in the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) is the commonest oncogenic driver in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) with a preponderance for East Asians and targeting this pathway with EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) represents a major advance in precision therapy. However, despite initial responses, resistance to TKIs typically develops with median progression-free survival of 12-18 months. The emergence of EGFR mutations e.g., T790M or C797S are major mechanisms for TKI resistance and remain a major unmet need. Therefore, there is an unmet need to find strategies to overcome TKI resistance for NSCLC. We and others have found that EGFR mutant receptors are more stable than the wild-type. Our study of screening a set of human G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) has found some novel genes whose knockdown resulted in a decrease of EGFR mutants, which prompted us to formulate a novel hypothesis that the EGFR mutants have acquired intrinsic property to leverage on the cellular pathway to avoid their degradation, resulting in their enhanced stability and accordingly oncogenic signaling. Here, we propose using unbiased high-throughput analyses using genome-wide RNAi screen to identify genes in the cellular pathway exploited by mutant EGFR for their enhanced stability and TKI resistance. Targeting these genes, essential for mutant EGFR stability, may offer novel targets for overcoming drug resistance due to additional EGFR mutation and/or for combination therapy with TKIs. Candidate genes will be validated in NSCLC cell lines and stable cells expressing the mutants, and further validation will be conducted in patient-derived xenograft (PDXs) having mutant EGFR. We will select those genes that are highly expressed in EGFR mutant patients and/or druggable. Their underlying mechanism in maintaining the stability of EGFR will be investigated, aiming to define druggable targets that can be used for further drug screening and development for overcoming TKIs resistance.
kw: Lung cancer; NSCLC; EGFR-mutation; Tyrosine-kinase-inhibitors; Drug resistance

title: THE GENESIS STUDY – discoverinG novEl blood-based biomarkers aNd protEomic SIgnatureS of neurocognition and aging
abs: Specific Aims: 1. To identify novel blood-based biomarkers in predicting neurocognitive decline. 2. Using a proteomics analytic approach, to a) unravel novel protein signatures; and b) to characterize candidate biomarkers which are associated with longitudinal neurocognitive decline. 3. Using a machine-learning augmented approach, to develop a novel multi-domain biomarker index for prediction of neurocognitive outcomes. Hypotheses: 1. Novel non-amyloid and non-tau related proteins related to systemic aging processes (ie. IGFBP-7, GDF-15, MMP-10) can predict neurocognitive outcomes. 2a) Mechanistic protein signatures underlying cognitive impairment identified using proteomic analysis comprise a mix of neurodegenerative, inflammatory, and vascular aging processes. 2b) Using a proteomics analytic approach, candidate biomarkers associated with neurocognitive decline include CXCL-9, MMP 10, IL-6, and the IGFBP superfamily. 3) An exploratory machine-learning augmented multidomain blood-based biomarker index will identify neurocognitive outcome risk strata, and provide incremental predictive value, compared with existing risk factor models. Methodology: This PhD will leverage upon an existing memory clinic cohort, with longitudinal data (neurocognitive assessments, neuroimaging, biological sampling) collected over 5 years (N=700). The primary outcome is the 5-year incidence of neurocognitive decline and conversion to dementia. For specific aim 1: Blood-based biomarkers including GDF-15, MMP-10 and IGFBP-7 will be quantified using dedicated immunoassays. For specific aim 2: The O-link proteomic analytic platform will be used to identify novel candidate proteins and proteomic signatures of neurocognitive decline. Statistical analytic approaches include Logistic regression, canonical correlation analysis and Gaussian graphical models. For specific aim 3: Exploratory analysis using Machine-Learning algorithms will be conducted, cross-validated using a training set (80%) and validation set (20%), to develop a multidomain blood-based biomarker index for dementia. Feasibility and Importance: Taken together, this study will 1) uncover new pathophysiological processes, 2) develop novel biomarker indexes, and 3) shed insight into novel therapeutic targets of neurocognitive decline.
kw: neurocognition, dementia, biomarkers, proteomics

title: Singapore Microsimulation Model to Assess Interventions to Improve Diet
abs: To tackle the sharp rise in the prevalence of chronic diseases and its risk factors, the Singapore government has embarked on a series of initiatives aimed to improve diet quality. Other food policies implemented elsewhere may also be up for consideration here. This study proposes to develop a microsimulation model to quantify the short and long-term costs and benefits of these interventions. The model will be tailored to Singapore’s ethnically diverse population and can evaluate a wide range of diet interventions from multiple stakeholder perspectives. To meet this objective, we conduct four key aims: (1) We will use data from the Multi-Ethnic Cohort (MEC) and existing literature to estimate the short-term effect of excess caloric intake and poor diet quality on key biomedical measures, and the longer-term effect on risk of developing type 2 diabetes, chronic kidney disease, and cardiovascular disease. (2) Linking MEC to MediClaims data, we will estimate the incremental per capita direct healthcare costs and indirect productivity costs associated with these chronic diseases. (3) Using outcomes of earlier aims, we will develop a microsimulation model, which takes as inputs the impact of select food policies on key measures of caloric intake and diet quality, to simulate the health and economic outcomes for a representative population of Singapore residents and for selected population subsets. (4) We will use this model to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of promising food policies identified in partnership with the Health Promotion Board. This effort will contribute to a greater understanding of actionable and cost-effective interventions that promote healthier foods and healthy eating habits among Singaporeans. It also has significant potential to reduce Singapore’s disease burden and extend healthy and functional lifespan of the population by identifying policies most likely to be good value for money.
kw: food policy; cost-effectiveness; microsimulation; diabetes; cardiovascular disease; chronic kidney disease

title: Formal and informal care among persons with cognitive impairment or dementia: projections of utilisation and societal costs over time
abs: Worldwide, it is estimated that 46.8 million people live with dementia and is expected to double every 20 years. In Singapore, about one in ten elderly persons aged 60 and above have dementia, while the proportion of older adults with cognitive impairment is 6.9% for Chinese, 10.6% for Malays, and 12.5% for Indians. Yet, little is known about the distribution of formal and informal care among persons with cognitive impairment or dementia, and if these care models are sustainable in light of our rapidly ageing population. Such questions are of critical relevance to the provision of sustainable integrated long-term care, as they contribute to the identification of policy gaps, the potential for capacity development in the community, and the projection of the future mental health burden attributable to ageing. To answer these questions, we propose to construct a Future Elderly Model (FEM) for cognitive impairment and dementia, a dynamic Markov micro-simulation model that predicts future health status and healthcare costs for the older adults of Singapore up to 2050. Forecasting future cognitive impairment and dementia for older adults in the presence of multiple related co-morbidities is highly challenging. Estimating formal and informal care is even more difficult, as utilisation and cost are a function of many factors including health status, age, gender, diseases, family structure, and insurance coverage. We will estimate cognition, health states, and utilisation using existing population cohorts, prevalence studies and administrative data on medical claims. In the long term, we will also model the impact of various policies or interventions on population mental health. The FEM thus offers the potential to answer pressing questions regarding the long-term impact of mental disorders on health and economic outcomes for Singapore.
kw: Community Mental Health; Cognitive impairment; Dementia; Long-term care; Caregiver; Economics of Ageing

title: GLOBICS - Global Consortium of Oral Health Birth Cohort Studies: from global evidence to local action
abs: This project is a response to the Lancet Series on Oral Health (2019) which has pointed out the need to shift the global oral health agenda. In 2021, the Borrow Foundation supported the establishment of a consortium on oral health-related birth cohort studies (OHRBCS). The National Dental Research Institute Singapore (NDRIS) has established the GLOBICS, a Global Consortium of OHRBCS. Key OHRBCS were identified as the first step toward pooled analysis. The group also identified two research questions for pooled analysis based on previous collaborative work findings and consequent gaps in the literature. This project aims to disseminate findings from this international collaborative research group to leverage existing longitudinal data and generate more impactful health outcomes. The specific aims include (i) consolidating a long-lasting international collaborative research group (GLOBICS) and disseminating the collaboration’s findings through scientific meetings, journal articles, and, more broadly, (ii) establishing a global research agenda for the future of the OHRBCS; (iii) to identify what is the optimal exposure to breastfeeding that protects against Early Childhood Caries and the role of sugar intake in this process by pooling data; (iv) to analyse the impact of the first dental visit during the first year of the child’s life on Early Childhood Caries considering the fluoride exposure by pooling data. We intend to disseminate our findings among clinicians, the local and global community, and policymakers to help make decisions and implement actions based on our findings. The pieces of dissemination will be adequate for each public.
kw: Birth Cohort Studies; Population Oral Health; Life-course Epidemiology; Oral Health Promotion and Prevention; International collaboration; Implementation Science

title: Precision Care Pathway through frailty and cognitive assessment among older adults and development of Care4Senior App, Intensive Aerobic Resistance Training and Brain Health program in the Community
abs: Aging is associated with frailty, cognitive decline and increased prevalence of chronic diseases. The rapidly growing aged population is in dire need of innovative preventive healthcare programmes that cater for such chronic conditions. Hence, there is a pressing need to discover fundamental mechanisms that underlie pathophysiological processes and formulation of translational concepts that can guide ageing research and age care practices. We hypothesise that an Immunological, Skeletomuscular and Neurological (ISN) triangle underlies the ageing process whereas C1q and myokines are the key mediators, and that lifestyle interventions can improve the balance among the three aspects in the ISN triangle in the aging process. This study consists of two phases. Phase 1: a cross-sectional study to investigate biological changes in older adults and evaluate their frailty and cognitive status. A Precision Care Pathway is then developed based on frailty, cognitive assessments and inflammatory biomarkers – such that the older adults at risk of progressing to frailty and cognitive impairment will be identified, and recruited for the targeted intervention in Phase 2. Phase 2 involves a cluster randomised controlled trial of older adults to evaluate the precision and targeted intervention on the Care4Senior Intensive Aerobic Resistance Training and Brain Health (CIRTAB) program. This program focuses on muscle strength training, lifestyle consultation, and brain health education. This app combines the strength of mobile phone application technology, with standard physical and cognitive exercises. In the long term, this new service model has the potential to transform care, contain healthcare cost inflation and increase the efficiency of the lean manpower. It will translate knowledge into practice, and result in impactful outcomes, such as better self-management and healthy longevity. The CIRTAB program will raise the awareness of health behaviour, thus attracting more older adults to engage in preventive health, in a way, better preparedness for healthy ageing.
kw: Frailty; Cognitive Impairment; e-health Intervention; exercise; Cognition, inflammatory biomarkers; older adults.

title: Developing a patient-centric tool for measuring the quality of end-of-life care among Singaporean patients with advanced illnesses
abs: Measurement is key to accountability. To improve the quality of healthcare delivery, health systems should measure and report outcomes that matter most to patients. When it comes to patients with advanced illnesses, such measures that adequately assess the quality of care do not yet exist in Singapore. To fill this gap, our team has recently developed an instrument, termed Quality of Care for Patients with Advanced Illnesses (QCPAI), which comprises all key domains for assessing the quality of end-of-life (EOL) care from the patient’s perspective. The proposed study aims to build on prior QCPAI work by conducting validity and reliability tests among patients with advanced illnesses in Singapore to ensure it can be used in multiple sectors and patient populations. We will also conduct a patient preference study that will define relative weights for each QCPAI domain based on the areas of EOL care that respondents most value. QCPAI will address the unmet need for evidence-based indicators for measuring the quality of EOL care and evaluating the effectiveness of healthcare interventions aiming to improve the EOL experience. QCPAI has the potential to be a part of the minimum dataset for the collection of quality indicators for EOL care provided by institutions across Singapore. By comparing and contrasting EOL care delivery across institutions over time and identifying areas for improvement, this tool will help improve EOL care delivery in Singapore in areas that matter most to patients.
kw: end-of-life care; palliative care; quality of care; instrument validation; patient preference

title: Real World Evidence Evaluation of Singapore’s New Front-of-Pack Beverage Label
abs: Many Singaporeans fail to meet recommendations for a healthy diet, with unhealthy beverage consumption a primary contributor. According to the 2018 National health survey, Singaporean adults consumed an average of 60 g of sugar daily (10 g above the daily recommended intake), more than half of which came from sugar-sweetened beverages. As a result, rates of obesity, diabetes, and other risk factors for chronic diseases are increasing. To address these concerns, the Health Promotion Board (HPB) recently proposed a new front-of-pack label, called Nutri-Grade (NG), grading pre-packaged and freshly-made non-alcoholic beverages based on sugar and saturated fat content. The proposed study aims to use proprietary longitudinal data on household beverage purchases, called Nielsen HomeScan, pre- and post- implementation of the new policy to quantify the net effect of the new labelling policy. We will quantify the effects on consumer purchases, beverage prices, product offerings, and diet quality of beverages purchased in total and separately for lower and higher income households taking both demand and supply effects into account. We hypothesize that consumers shift their demand towards healthier beverages (NG A and B), which leads suppliers to increase (decrease) the prices of the healthier beverages (less healthy beverages) and bring a greater proportion of new NG A and B beverages to market relative to C and D beverages. We expect a positive net effect of NG on improved diet quality, but that this effect is greater for higher income households who are more health-conscious and less price-sensitive than lower income households. Given rising rates of non-communicable diseases (NCDs), this study is both timely and has high potential to have a significant public health impact in Singapore.
kw: Front-of-Pack labels; Sugar-sweetened beverage; War on diabetes; Diet quality; Reformulation

title: Implementation of a Generalist-Specialist Palliative Oncology Care Model amongst Advanced Cancer Surgical Patients: A Pilot Cluster Randomized Control Trial
abs: Palliative considerations are essential in surgical oncology. However, most surgeons lack basic palliative education and training and are heavily reliant on specialist palliative care (SPC) physicians in the management of terminally-ill patients. While our conventional specialist-centric approach is ideal to provide quality palliative care, it is unsustainable in the long-run as growing demands for end-of-life services in our ageing population will outstrip the supply of specialist providers. As such, there is a need to consider an alternative approach to deliver quality palliative care to a wider population. To address this, we propose a novel integrated generalist-specialist palliative surgical oncology (PSO) care delivery model where surgeons trained and educated in primary palliative care (PPC) deliver basic end-of-life services to palliative surgical patients in consultation with a multi-disciplinary palliative team. This is in contrast with current usual care where ‘untrained’ surgeons provide surgical-centric care whilst SPC services are sought at an ad-hoc basis. We aim to conduct a pilot cluster randomized control trial to compare palliative outcomes amongst advanced cancer surgical patients receiving PSO and usual care. We hypothesize the PSO model results in a) improved delivery of palliative care, b) improved health related quality of life (HRQoL), c) reduced SPC resource utilization and d) is acceptable amongst participating surgeons. Care delivery will be measured using four validated palliative surgical quality indicators and patient reported outcomes measured using health-related quality of life (HRQoL) questionnaires. We also compare SPC resource utilization metrics between the two groups. Acceptability of the PSO care model amongst surgeons will be assessed qualitatively through semi-structured interviews. The PSO model, if successfully implemented, has the potential to improve access to palliative care in patients with life-limiting diseases. It is also scalable and may be adapted easily amongst other non-SPC physicians.
kw: Palliative care, palliative surgical care, surgical oncology, end-of-life

title: Elucidating Effectiveness, Perception and Barriers of Primary Eye Care Model in Singapore
abs: In Singapore, the number of attendances at specialist eye care clinics have grown at 8.6% per annum since 2002 but ophthalmologist numbers have not increased proportionately. To ensure long-term sustainability, a shift towards a community-based, allied health-led eye care model, in the form of optometrists-led service delivery, is needed. A well-functioning system of optometrist-delivered community eye care model will detect eye diseases earlier, reduce avoidable disease burden and improve sustainability of the healthcare system. In 2019, Singapore’s three regional healthcare clusters developed a pilot primary eye care(PEC) model which deploys upskilled optometrists to right-site stable and non-complex eye patients in the community. Within the National Healthcare Group, the PEC model currently operates at three sites (Ang Mo Kio specialist center, Geylang polyclinic, Hougang polyclinic). Preliminary data from these sites demonstrated that the PEC model provided quality eye care and reduced unnecessary referrals to tertiary hospitals. However, real-world evaluation on operational viability and stakeholders’ perception of PEC have yet been performed. These evaluations are important as in-depth understanding of stakeholders’ experience and perspectives will be key to ensure long-term sustainability and scalability of this PEC model. In this proposed project, we aim to holistically examine the real-world effectiveness and implementation process of PEC by adopting a mixed-method design. This study will identify current barriers or areas(patient acceptability or provider barriers) that could be improved to increase PEC’s operational efficiency and enhance its service utilisation. Importantly, key lessons and strategies derived from these evaluations will help to facilitate future cluster-wide implementation of PEC. Overall, this project’s focus on preventive eye health is in line with MOH’s long-term focus on preventive care among elderly Singaporeans(beyond healthcare to health). This implementation research project resonates with NMRC’s vision and mission to promote excellence in translational clinical research and enhance health outcomes for our elderly population.
kw: Health Services Research, Primary Eye Care Model, Implementation Science, Sustainable Implementation

title: Development of Humanized mouse peritoneal metastasis model for immunotherapeutic biology and drug discovery
abs: Gastric cancer (GC) is the 5th most frequently diagnosed cancer with significant mortality and morbidity. Peritoneal metastasis (PM) occurs commonly in GC, confers a poor prognosis, and responds poorly to systemic chemotherapy. An improved understanding of the tumour microenvironment (TME) in GCPM will allow better utilization of immunotherapy. This remains challenging as the peritoneal cavity requires surgical access. Humanized mouse models are immunodeficient mice engrafted with functional human immune systems. This provides a novel platform that can closely replicate the interaction between cancer and the human immune system within the peritoneum, providing the opportunity to study the TME of GCPM with greater accuracy. However, the creation of a humanised mouse model is technically demanding. Importantly, such a model to study the TME of GCPM has not been reported in existing literature. Hypothesis and Aims 1. To create viable orthotopic models of GCPM in humanized mouse 2. Downstream analysis of the GCPM and immune microenvironment and comparison with previously described reports of TME response phenotypes in human GCPM Humanized mice are created by introducing human CD34+ embryonic stem cells in immune-deficient mouse pups and confirming the engraftment of human immune system by downstream flow cytometry. Humanized mice will then be injected with NCC59 (MSI-H) and SNU1750 (Diffuse type) GC cell lines in the flank, stomach and peritoneum. We seek to develop a replicable model of GCPM via orthotopic inoculation in humanized mice, which will allow better understanding of the TME and mechanisms driving GCPM. The creation of a replicable orthotopic GCPM humanized mouse model will provide a robust platform for the analysis of the TME changes seen in human GCPM. Furthermore, the model allows for further study to identify potential therapeutic targets and testing of potential therapeutic modalities, including both immunotherapy as well as peritoneal-directed therapies.
kw: Gastric cancer

title: The role of epigenome as biomarkers for hepatitis B versus metabolic associated fatty liver disease (MAFLD) - driven hepatocellular carcinoma
abs: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the third most common cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide. Asia carries the highest burden of liver cancer where the 5-year survival was less than 30%. Several lines of research have demonstrated significant genomic and molecular heterogeneity within HCCs, limiting the development of reliable biomarkers and targeted therapies. Most HCCs develop from chronic liver disease, such as viral hepatitis and increasingly, metabolic (dysfunction)-associated fatty liver disease (MAFLD) which includes alcoholic and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). Epigenetic alterations are emerging as crucial contributing factors to HCC initiation from a background of chronic liver disease at the preneoplastic stage. Patients with hepatitis C infection have genome-wide epigenetic modifications that are associated with HCC development, which persist even after direct-acting antiviral treatment. To date, most epigenetic studies in HCC focused on DNA methylations and little is known about the role of chromatin alterations in HCC carcinogenesis from different aetiologies. Recently, our collaborator discovered significant differences in the transcriptomic and lipidome profiles from hepatitis B versus diabetes mellitus-associated HCCs (manuscript in preparation, study supported by NMRC/CSA-SI/0018/2017/Pierce Chow), without corresponding changes at the genomic level. This has led to our hypothesis that epigenetic dysregulations underpin the distinct HCC phenotypes from different aetiologies. We will examine this hypothesis by exploring the epigenetic landscape of HCC at the promoters and suppressors in hepatitis B and MAFLD-driven HCCs. We will approach this by performing chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing (ChIP-seq) of modified histone marks (H3K4me3 and H3K27me3) from primary HCC tumour samples and matched non-tumoural liver parenchyma. By integrating our results with the existing transcriptomic and metabolic findings from the same tumour samples, we can identify epigenetic signatures that mark the HCC development and prognosis in viral versus non-viral aetiologies.
kw: HCC epigenetic, MAFLD-HCC, HBV-HCC, ChIP-seq, Histone modifications

title: Towards Precision Medicine in Systemic Sclerosis: Identification of Immune Signatures in Early Disease and Progressive Interstitial Lung Disease in the Systemic Sclerosis Cohort Singapore
abs: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is a multi-systemic connective tissue disease that is characterized by complex interplay between autoimmunity, vasculopathy and fibrosis with high morbidity and mortality. One of the leading causes of death in SSc is interstitial lung disease (ILD), which affects up to 80% of patients with SSc and has varied clinical course between individuals. There remains an unmet need to identify the subset of SSc patients at early disease stage (prior to organ damage) and those with progressive phenotypes (for earlier therapeutic interventions). Incorporation of molecular signatures that reflects pathological processes into clinical stratification is a promising approach to develop a more granular stratification system to guide therapeutic approaches in SSc. The proposed study aim to identify peripheral blood-derived immune signatures reflective of early disease stage and associated with progressive SSc-ILD in the Systemic Sclerosis Cohort Singapore (SCORE). We hypothesize that (1) peripheral immune signatures derived from circulating blood reflect disease stage (early vs. late SSc), and (2) peripheral immune signatures derived from circulating blood reflect disease trajectory in ILD (progressive vs. stable phenotypes). To address these hypotheses, our aims are (1) to characterize peripheral immune signatures in early SSc (vs. late SSc), and (2) to characterize peripheral immune signature in progressive SSc-ILD (vs. stable SSc-ILD). Peripheral blood mononuclear cells will be analyzed by mass cytometry using a panel of cell surface and intracellular markers known to play pivotal role in SSc pathogenesis. Single cell RNA sequencing will be performed on differentially represented immune cells identified by mass cytometry, followed by unsupervised clustering analysis and correlation network analysis to reveal segregation/ correlation of immune cell subset, features and functions. The long-term goals are to discover and validate peripheral immune signatures that will enable personalized therapeutic approaches, ultimately leading to improved outcomes of SSc patients.
kw: Systemic sclerosis, patient stratification, precision medicine, disease stage, interstitial lung disease

title: Project RESET: Redirecting immune, lipid and metabolic drivers of early cardiovascular disease
abs: In Singapore and globally, cardiovascular disease (CVD) morbidity and mortality remain relentless. Despite medicines for hypertension and hyperlipidemia, we still face an urgently unresolved need to tackle early detection and prevention, ideally dealing with modern disease drivers, and using modern approaches. Our team have thus far characterised the unique Asian heart disease phenotype, commonly lean and yet centrally obese, ~10yrs younger than patients in the west, and with left ventricular decompensation driven dominantly by metabolic dysfunction, often independently of ischemic heart disease or myocardial infarction. Here, responding to the research objective to go upstream, we propose to characterise subclinical CVD, critically triangulating cardiac, vascular, and fatty liver phenotypes, together with metabolic flexibility, and refreshing new dimensions of molecular and digital, physiological and psychological lifestyle biomarkers. We hypothesise that lipid, metabolic and immune factors drive pathology in the myocardium independently of their well-known roles in the vessel wall, and that CVD trajectories can be tracked longitudinally by the cost-effective selection of CV-metabolic-digital biomarkers. In a nested randomised controlled trial, we will test if lifestyle intervention and AI-symbiotic health coaching regresses/halts myocardial fibrosis. Finally, studies of economic feasiblity, behavioural science and implementation will serve to assess scalability and applicability of CVD prevention.
kw: Cardiovascular disease, digital medicine, cardiometabolic disease

title: Understanding and Engineering Immunity to Combat Plant Infection: Molecular Condensation at the Interface of Plant-Microbe Communication
abs: One of the global challenges of sustainability is the increase in plant resilience in the context of biotic and abiotic stresses. Understanding plant signaling pathways and synthetic engineering of plant signaling circuits are at the heart of current and future sustainable agriculture research. Fundamentally, precise plant signaling on demand requires the phase separation of biomolecules, in space and time, into multivalent biomolecular condensates (BCs). BCs serve as incubators for biochemical reactions, thereby confining and controlling signaling transduction for development or defense. The physicochemical properties of BCs determine the inter- and intramolecular interactions and, thereby, the activation of plant signaling. Over the past decades, biomedical research has progressed rapidly by improving the identification of human immune signaling molecules (1950s - 1980s), to the reconstitution of the signaling circuits (2000s), until the era of engineering immune cells to combat disease (2010s - now). Although there is a global need to transform agricultural protection research into innovative agri-technologies toward greater sustainability and food security, our ability to control and rewire plant signaling pathways remains primitive, particularly for defense against pathogens. Plant immune signaling is sophisticated and comprises pathogen-associated molecular pattern (PAMP)-triggered immunity (PTI) via plasma membrane (PM)- bound pattern recognition receptors (PRRs), bacterial type-III effector (T3E)-triggered immunity (ETI) via ETI receptors, and PTI-ETI crosstalk, as recently proposed by four Nature papers (Fig. 1A). The activation of individual immune signal transduction in plants requires the formation of BCs at the nanometer scale, which are derived from a diverse array of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) at the cell– cell interface (Fig. 1A). Our understanding of how these plant signaling hubs are formed during infection on the host PM for immune activation is still in its infancy. To fill the knowledge gaps in plant immunity and enable synthetic engineering of plant immune signaling, a few plant immunity labs, including the Miao laboratory, have recently contributed significantly by identifying the essential components that drive the macromolecular assembly of BCs and the underlying biophysical cues in controlling BC-mediated signal transduction. The interdisciplinary research of the Miao laboratory has recently discovered a series of novel plant-microbe communication mechanisms by which BC formation upon microbial attack activates plant immune responses and BCs mediate filamentous growth of pathogenic fungi. It is important to point out that a holistic biochemical and biophysical view of biomolecular condensates for plant immune signaling at the host-pathogen interface is the key and major challenge to understanding plant immunity for future agriculture and sustainability. The Miao laboratory is uniquely positioned to tackle t
kw: phase separation; plant immunity; signal transduction; synthetic engineering; sustainable agriculture

title: Towards Building Autonomous Genomics: AI-Driven Omics to Drug Discovery
abs: Conventional drug discovery and development relies on targeting only the protein-coding genes. However, these druggable genes make up less than 3% of the human genome. My interest is in seeding the development of a completely new class of therapeutics that target noncoding RNAs and noncoding gene regulatory elements, which together make up ~80% of the genome (the ENCODE project). The major challenge is that these noncoding elements are poorly characterized. In most cases one does not know which gene is regulated by nearby enhancers in a 3-dimensional space. Understanding how enhancers contribute to specific gene regulation has become an active area in cancer, drug resistance, and immune checkpoint deregulation. Through my deep experiences leading the FANTOM and the Human Cell Atlas international consortiums, I can bring new capabilities to build single-cell genomic technologies in understanding noncoding regulatory elements in disease and create untapped opportunities in Singapore to target regulatory noncoding RNAs using nucleic acids. Here I propose a unique strategy to discover and target cancer-associated noncoding RNAs involved in chromatin interactions and build a robust and structured genomic database necessary for developing AI-driven omics for drug discovery.
kw: Single Cell Omics; Drug Discovery and Development; Automation; Regulatory Enhancer RNAs; Artificial Intelligence

title: Creating SERS Chemical Space to Identify Unknown Chemical/Disease X
abs: Rapid and accurate identification of unknown species such as diseases/chemical X is the crux of most research problems and is relevant to various fields including biomedical, chemical synthesis and defence. While current chromatographic and spectrometry are powerful for laboratory-based research, their lack of portability and bulky instrumentation limits their use for on-the-spot detections. Surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS) emerges as a powerful nanomaterials-based sensing platform technology that provides highly sensitive molecular detection qualitatively and quantitatively at trace ppm to ppb levels. It is also a portable and non-invasive technique. However, the translation of SERS from laboratory research to real-life applications is hampered by three main challenges. Firstly, SERS lacks a universal spectral database that correlates the molecular structure and function with its key vibrational region (structure-to-function property). Secondly, current SERS platforms typically suffer from poor batch-to-batch reproducibility due to its manual fabrication process. Finally, traditional approach to manually analyze SERS spectra visually is inept and cannot elucidate spectra-to-function information promptly and accurately, especially in complex sample matrix. This proposal aims to build the world’s first SERS-based chemical database as an academic resource, and to use this database to accurately and rapidly identify unknown chemicals/disease “X” in the case of emergency. We will: 1) create a comprehensive dataset of molecular SERS fingerprint by integrating an automated fabrication of various SERS platforms and high-throughput SERS profiling of diverse chemical species 2) use artificial intelligence (AI) to drive the correlation of SERS spectra with the corresponding chemical functions, and construct of predictive chemical signature-to-structure models. 3) accelerate the translation of SERS research for targeted biomedical applications, e.g. chronic respiratory disease screening. From the academic perspectives, our program will curate the world’s first SERS-based chemical signature database. By integrating high-throughput automated experimentation with AI-driven data analysis and predictive model building, we will be able to use SERS to deconstruct chemical molecules into a multidimensional chemical space akin to the mapping of the human genome, which is previously unattainable. The proposed SERS resource can overhaul current challenges in molecular identification to better position us to be the first mover into new, disruptive technologies to efficiently tackle problems in multiple fields from biomedicine to environment and catalysis.
kw: Surface-enhanced Raman scattering; Machine Learning; Automation; Disease detection

title: Developing high throughput technologies to study RNA structure and function
abs: RNA structures are key to the ability of RNA viruses to replicate, translate and package. While individual elements have been shown to be important, it is unclear how the rest of the genome is structured and dynamic during different stages of the virus lifecycle. In this proposal, we aim to develop and utilize new high throughput technologies to study the structural determinants of RNA viruses and their host transcriptomes to identify functional viral structures so that we can target them. Specifically, in the next five years, we aim to: 1) study RNA structure dynamics and their functions during different stages of the virus lifecycle to identify candidates for drug targeting, 2) study RNA structural determinants in single host cells that impact virus growth, and 3) study RNA structural heterogeneity in viruses at single-molecule level to identify functional structural populations and their functions. Collectively, we aim to deepen our understanding of the molecular and structural basis of RNA virus infection.
kw: RNA, structure, genomics, infectious diseases, drug targeting

title: Topological Quantum Photonics
abs: Over the past decade, topological photonics has flourished as a research topic, growing into one of the major sub-fields in photonics. Its essential insight is to apply concepts from the theory of topological insulators to photonics, using light waves in place of the electron wavefunction. The resulting photonic devices have unprecedented properties, such as disorder-free light transport. Compared to the condensed matter systems in which topological states were first discovered, photonic structures have the advantage of room temperature operation and ease of fabrication, making topological photonics a rich and accessible playground for exploring the physics of band topology. At the same time, the unique features of photonic topological states has enabled promising applications that are now coming to fruition, such as robust waveguides for use in lasers, quantum optics chips, and WiFi chips. Thus far, most efforts in topological photonics research have focused on the manipulation of classical electromagnetic waves, which is the regime of interest for most current-day technological applications of photonics, such as telecommunications. Quantum effects (i.e., the fact that the electromagnetic field is quantized) are ignored. We aim to develop quantum topological photonics as a new research direction at the intersection of topological photonics and quantum optics. This involves developing topological photonics solutions for controlling quantum effects such as photon blockade, quantum amplification, and photon condensation. We will focus on photonic systems that are nonlinear and/or non-Hermitian, as these are the ones in which quantum effects most readily manifest. If successful, this research will extend the reach of topological photonics into quantum optics and photonics, with potential benefits for a range of emerging quantum technologies including quantum communications, quantum sensing, and quantum computing. We will create new concepts such as topologically enhanced single-photon sources and quantum amplifiers. We will also establish quantum topological photonics as a leading platform for accessing fundamental phenomena that are difficult to achieve even in classical photonic metamaterials, such as tunable imaginary vector potentials.
kw: photonics; topological photonics; quantum technology

title: Non-equilibrium Many-Body Physics and Quantum Information Science in the age of Programmable Quantum Systems
abs: There is an intense, ongoing effort to realise new technologies arising in the form of programmable quantum systems -- systems whose constituents we can individually control at the quantum level. Examples include cold atoms in optical lattices, trapped Rydberg atoms and ions, and arrays of superconducting qubits. These systems usher in a host of possibilities, like the ability to realize novel physical phenomena in new dynamical regimes, to simulate complex many-body problems, and to implement improved, quantum-enhanced algorithms for information processing. At the same time, these systems are still not perfect: they often operate with noise and a restricted range of controls, and the central challenge is to understand how to extract the maximal wealth of physical information from such nascent technologies. This proposal aims to develop ways to fully capitalise on these new technologies. It will involve developing new theoretical frameworks, rooted in quantum information theory, that allows discoveries of fundamental phenomena in unexplored physical regimes like far-from-equilibrium dynamics, which go beyond existing theories. It will also involve designing robust control methods to steer dynamics to realize desired, target Hamiltonians for simulations, utilizing drive controls or geometrical rearrangements of individual constituents. To aid in such studies, novel algorithms to prepare quantum states efficiently and to learn the system's physical properties will be developed, leveraging programmable quantum systems' unique capabilities like measurements at the single-site resolution. The successful completion of the project will lead to a deeper understanding of quantum matter far-from-equilibrium, which has implications in condensed matter, quantum statistical mechanics, quantum chaos and quantum thermalization. Quantum simulation and advanced data acquisition techniques will give fresh insights to outstanding problems like the origin of superconductivity. Lastly, the development of robust control methods will feed into the development of better-controlled, future generation quantum technologies, important in our ultimate quest for a universally controllable quantum computer.
kw: Quantum technologies; Nonequilibrium quantum many-body dynamics; Quantum information science; Quantum simulation; Quantum algorithms

title: Cardiopathy MRI and PET: A novel protocol to investigate embolic stroke of undetermined source (ESUS) patients
abs: Background: Embolic stroke of unknown source (ESUS) is a common and frustrating entity. It is reported to account for 17% of all ischemic strokes, and has an annual recurrence rate of close to 5%. Although up to 30% of patients with ESUS are eventually found to have atrial fibrillation, other potential sources of embolism include atrial cardiopathy, inflammation and ascending aortic plaque. Therapeutic trials in this cohort have all been negative. Hypothesis: we hypothesised that the use of a novel hybrid cardiac and aortic arch PET-MRI is feasible to evaluate key potential sources of ESUS in the same setting: namely left atrial cardiopathy (as measured by left atrial fibrosis), left ventricular disease and Aortic arch disease. We estimate that up to 63% of ESUS stroke aetiology can be diagnosed with this protocol. With adequate phenotyping, a targeted trial of therapy such as anticoagulation for suspected atrial cardiopathy, or SGLT2-I to reduce atrial fibrosis, may be tried, whereas for aortic plaque inflammation aggressive statin and anti-inflammatory medication may be efficacious. methods and approach: We aim to perform a pilot project to prospectively recruit 11 patients with ESUS who have underwent our hospital protocol for stroke work-up and have a implantable loop recorder inserted. These patients will undergo a cardiac MRI-PET with a Philips 3-Tesla system and 18fluoro-2-deoxy-d-glucose (18FDG) positron emission tomography magnetic resonance imaging (PET MRI) at NUS CIRC within 4-weeks of acute stroke, to accurately detect high-risk carotid plaques with active inflammation. We would also include aortic arch sequences to assess aortic atherosclerosis and inflammation. These scans will be reported by a CMR/PET trained radiologist or cardiologist. Finally, the patients will also have Nt-proBNP tested at recruitment and at the 1-year mark. We will follow the up to 1-year for recurrent ischemic stroke, TIA, myocardial infarction and death

title: Process Development Methodology for the Spray Drying of Future Food Powder
abs: In the near future, food options will expand beyond what we are currently familiar with, where ‘fancy’ food such as alternative protein, functionalised food, and personalised nutrition will become more widespread. These future foods frequently require the use of food powders as ingredients. The production of food powder, however, is non-trivial. The powder must achieve certain requirements depending on its application – solubility in oil/water, flowability during processing, particle size, and compatibility with other food components, among many others. Such food powder properties can be tailored to individual applications through formulation and particle engineering using the spray drying technique. However, the usual spray drying process development is empirical and thus experimentally driven. These methods are usually time-intensive, require large quantities of materials, and the resultant process is commonly not well-understood or lack robustness. Considering the new food materials that will be converted into powder for the first time, the large amounts of materials required for experimentation and the limited understanding of the process are not acceptable. The goal of this project is to rapidly meet companies’ requirements for spray drying formulation and process development expertise with high precision. Specifically, we aim to define a user-friendly spray drying formulation and process development methodology that will quickly lead to an efficient initial process definition, with a focus on future food materials. Using a hybrid empirical-theoretical methodology, formulation and process definition will be resource efficient (in terms of time and materials required), streamlined, and robust. Fundamental engineering models and various process characterization tools will be used to develop the methodology, resulting in a methodology superior to the traditional experiments-based spray drying process development methods. The outcome of this project is a spray drying formulation and process development methodology that has been validated on different future foods, and can be applied on other future foods from the food industry. The methodology will be of particular interest to local small and medium enterprise (SME) food manufacturers looking to transform their food materials into powder with the required characteristics for onward processing. Such local food manufacturers (and even start-ups) will benefit from the rapid formulation and process development afforded by our methodology as time and materials are frequently the bottlenecks in their expansion and development plans.
kw: Process development; spray drying; future food; particle engineering; powder

title: Structure-Function Understanding of Activation and Inactivation of a Bitter Taste Receptor
abs: Bitter taste receptors, well known for alerting us to bitter compounds, are also actually crucial for other physiological functions like immunity and hormone secretion. Hence their dysregulation results in diseases such as cardiovascular diseases, airway infections, neurological diseases, cancer and diabetes. No high-resolution structure is currently available for this class of receptors, and thus there is limited mechanistic understanding of how various ligands transduce different signals. Building on my expertise on membrane protein biochemistry, mammalian protein production, high-resolution single-particle cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structure determination, and cryo-EM method development, I propose to study the structure and function of TAS2R38, a representative member of the bitter taste receptor family. Structural biology through cryo-EM will provide fundamental insights into their mechanism of action and enable development of chemical probes and therapeutics against these targets.
kw: Membrane protein; structural biology; bitter taste receptor; innate immunity; cryo-EM; functional assay

title: Towards AIoT – Building Intelligence into Sensing, Networking, and Data Analytics of IoT
abs: Recent technology advances in Internet-of-Things (IoT) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) provide unique opportunities for deep and broad instrumentation of the physical world so the merge of real world and cyber space can best benefit people’s smarter life. A promising solution sits in the intersection of AI + IoT a.k.a. AIoT, where the massive instrumentation of people and their things translates to knowledge through advanced machine intelligence and may guide the engineering of the physical world. AIoT may transcend technologies in both AI and IoT. On one hand the unprecedented data scale and prevalence from IoT magnifies the power of AI; on the other hand the machine intelligence from AI helps excel every aspect of sensing, computing, and communication in nowadays IoT. Devising viable AIoT, however, is technologically demanding to the state-of-the-art of today’s AI and IoT, and faces the following fundamental challenges: (i) Massiveness of devices – building scalable AIoT foresees the deployment of hundreds of billions of networked sensors in the physical world, which may exhaust computing and communication resources in terms of energy consumption, wireless spectrum, network bandwidth, etc; (ii) Intrusion to people and their things – improper design of the IoT instrumentation may lead to disruptive sensing, and as a result the technology intrusion impairs the harmonious co-existence of people and the machine intelligence; and (iii) Data Plethora – unprecedented scale and prevalence of the IoT data not only contributes to training powerful AI but also sets obstacles for distilling, verifying, adapting, and transferring the machine learning processes across people and different cyber or physically engineered systems. The objective of the proposed study will focus on addressing the above challenges and achieve scientific and technological breakthrough in devising viable AIoT – (i) We will study how AI can be applied to optimize the allocation and shared usage of the throttled resources for scalable AIoT. In particular we will study the co-existence of massive IoT wireless technologies that share radio spectrum. We will also explore network federation of regional low power wide area networks and more efficiently utilize the sensing, computation, and energy resources. (ii) We will continue our pioneering study of novel sensing interfaces with wireless radio frequency (RF) signal which is essentially non-intrusive. We will explore the adoption of AI to significantly complement conventional signal processing techniques, which may lead to technology leapfrogging into super-resolution and support new applications in human health monitoring. (iii) We will carry on knowledge and experience gained from our existing data analytical research and tackle challenges due to data plethora. We will particularly look into how massive heterogeneous data from IoT scenarios can be best leveraged to strengthen AI. Domain adaptation and self-supervised learning techniqu
kw: AIoT, Internet of Things, Sensing, Data analytics

title:
What AI cannot do but humans can: 
Closing gaps in visual search efficiency between AIs and humans with neuroscience-inspired approaches
abs: Visual search is a common daily visual activity that we engage in, exemplified by looking for a friend in a crowd. During the search, we examine the entire scene efficiently with a sequence of eye movements. Visual search has two characteristics. First, it is invariant, where the target object may vary with numerous transformations, such as rotation, scale, and occlusion. Second, it carries both a spatial (searching for keys most likely to be on the table rather than on the ceiling), and a temporal context (episodic memory of boiling water with kettle an hour ago modulates our search for kettle at the current time). These spatiotemporal contextual cues allow us to narrow down feasible search areas and reduce ambiguity in object recognition, and hence, improve our search efficiency and robustness. While visual search seems effortless to humans, a lack of prior contextual knowledge and memory guidance makes AI inferior to humans in visual search. Despite recent successes with attention-based transformers, these AI models fail to retain memory over lifetime. In reinforcement and continual learning, external episodic memory for replays has been widely adopted to facilitate learning or prevent catastrophic forgetting during training. However, these memories are often excluded during the inference process. The question of how memory is organized and guides visual search is largely under-explored. Thus, there is an urge to turn to neuroscience to seek for answers. In neuroscience, most studies primarily focus on fixation patterns when participants search for perfect matches of a target in simplified artificial stimuli. However, we have little knowledge of the interaction between memory and eye movements in complex real-world scenes. The aim of this proposal is to answer the following question: what are the memory computations in the human brain that modulate eye movements to ensure a time-efficient and transformation-invariant visual search in complex real-world scenes? The methodological approaches in this proposal are primarily multidisciplinary, at the intersection of neuroscience and AI. I will first design and conduct human behavioral experiments that help us benchmark human and AI performance in visual search tasks, identify research gaps, and hence bootstrap modern AI for visual search. I will then use AI models to further our understanding of brain computations during visual searches and in turn, translate these insights into AI. I break down the visual search problem into three sub-problems with corresponding aims. Aim 1 is to study the memory efficiency and organization of humans and AI models when they are asked to search for multiple objects. These memories are used for storing unique features distinguishing targets among themselves and distractors. In Aim 2, I will study how humans and AI learn spatial contextual cues incrementally over time and incorporate them in visual search tasks. In Aim 3, I will examine episodic and procedural memory

title: Mitigation Technology And Environmental Impact From Ammonia Bunkering Release
abs: a. Description and Methodology The project is a knowledge creation process based heavily on the modelling, simulation and professional inputs from partners of high industrial relevance. Each work package will be executed with a specific method. i. Mitigation technology. The work will start with evaluating and improving conventional measures, such as water curtains and other physical means. The diffusivity of ammonia vapour in presence of an absorption media or a physical obstruction will be the primary focus of the study, followed by an in-depth understanding of the reactions between ammonia pool, ammonia vapour, moisture and surface water. The overall development can be translational; however, innovative elements and new concept will be added. Similar to the tools used for modelling and simulation, CFD, PHAST and CHEMMAP software will be used as validation tools to demonstrate the effectiveness. We expect to run a physical experiment to achieve more reliable verification. ii. Modelling and simulation. For near-field simulation, computational fluid dynamics (CFD) is the primary tool. And for far-field simulation and large-scale dispersion of ammonia in sea water, PHAST and CHEMMAP software will be chosen. In the near-field simulations using CFD method, the key focus will be on development and integration of a phase change model for ammonia into the Navier-Stokes flow solver to take into account the effects of ammonia changing from liquid during storage into gas upon releasing into the environment. Another challenge in modelling of ammonia releases relates to the capability of accurately handling mixing of ammonia with water either from direct release on water surface or its interaction with a water curtain. As gaseous ammonia is highly soluble in water, accurate prediction of mixing and dispersion of ammonia in water has direct impact on risk assessment as well as understanding the effectiveness of the mitigation measure on limiting the ammonia vapour cloud from dispersing into the environment. It has been shown that mixing and dispersion of ammonia in water is highly sensitive to turbulent models commonly used in CFD tools; therefore, evaluation of different turbulent models and improvement of their performance for ammonia mixing will be carried out in this work. Coupling the near-field simulations using CFD method with far-field models is another important focus of this proposal. Information from CFD prediction will be fed as input conditions to the far-fields model for more accurate representation of actual scenario; thus improving the predictability of far-field dispersion models. iii. Environmental impact. The environmental impact in case of accidental spill will be assessed beyond the typical simulation that includes only physical mixing and air-sea partitioning; but also include the key biogeochemical transformations (e.g. nitrification and annamox). title: Precision oncology approaches for hepatocellular carcinoma
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: HCC is a deadly malignancy with 60% of cases found in Asia. 5-year-survival for patients with advanced disease is a dismal 3%, largely due to therapy resistance. There is a dire need for new therapeutic approaches. Complex tumor heterogeneity is a hallmark of HCC, due to multiple etiological factors. I hypothesize that there is significant inter-tumor heterogeneity among HCC therapy-resistant tumor cells. Establishing a precision oncology pipeline identifying and targeting these subpopulations will improve overall survival in HCC. Currently, a lack of well-validated biomarkers for patient assignment, insufficient molecular understanding of therapy resistance mechanisms, and an unfulfilled need for in vivo models that allow rapid preclinical validation of predicted therapy has significantly deterred the development of a precision oncology pipeline. In recent years, the zebrafish has emerged as a powerful tool for xenotransplantation preclinical studies. My postdoctoral work has created the first adult immunocompromised zebrafish xenograft models capable of engrafting human cancer cells. These mutant animals are especially suitable for large-scale preclinical drug discovery studies and single-cell resolution imaging of therapy responses. However, current iterations of immunocompromised zebrafish cannot engraft primary human cancer cells or peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs). Aim 1. Humanized immunocompromised zebrafish xenograft model as patient-derived avatars Aim 1 will develop a new humanized immunocompromised zebrafish that expresses a set of human cytokines, facilitating engraft of human primary HCC patient cancer cells and whole blood PBMCs. These animals will be used as patient avatars for large-scale preclinical modelling of HCC combination therapies. Aim 2. Dissecting HCC first-line therapy resistance using single cell sequencing and patient avatars Aim 2 uses single-cell sequencing approaches and preclinical zebrafish and mice xenograft modelling to 1) identify first-line therapy resistant HCC subpopulations; 2) understand HCC resistance mechanisms; and 3) perform preclinical modelling of combination therapies targeting identified resistant HCC tumor subpopulations. Aim 3. Establishing precision oncology pipeline for HCC patients. Aim 3 leverages on identified biomarkers, combination therapies and zebrafish patient avatars to establish a robust HCC precision oncology pipeline. I will create a multi-biomarker array to identify therapy resistant tumor cell in HCC patients. Preclinical early-endpoint assays leveraging on zebrafish avatar engrafted with the patient’s own tumor will be used to validate efficacy of predicted combination therapy. The net result will establish a clinically relevant precision oncology pipeline for HCC patients, potentially transforming how precision medicine is performed.
kw: Precision oncology; hepatocellular carcinoma; patient avatar; therapy resistance; preclinical modelling; combination therapy

title: Solidified Natural Gas (SNG) Storage Technology
abs: In Singapore, natural gas (NG) currently contributes to about 95% of the electricity generation, making it a critical resource in maintaining Singapore’s competitiveness. Moreover, NG is expected to drive key petrochemical and industrial processes as we move into a global natural gas-based economy from oil. It is noted that, Singapore, deprived of its own NG reserves depends heavily on international imports to cover and sustain these steep needs. The major sources of NG imports into Singapore are Piped Natural Gas (PNG), Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) that is imported and re-gasified at the SLNG terminal. However, with the growing population and predicted irregularities associated with PNG and LNG imports into Singapore, there is a need to develop cost effective technological solutions that can provide an integrated national energy security system against unforeseen incidents to keep the lights on for both community and industry needs. In such an integrated system, one needs to look at a portfolio of NG storage (storage in molecular form) along with the portfolio for energy storage of electrons (batteries, grids etc.). In this project, we propose to develop one such novel and cost-effective technology – storage of NG as solidified natural gas (SNG) via clathrate hydrates. SNG can be formed in large quantities at moderate temperature and pressure conditions making it a promising candidate for cost effective stationary energy storage application. The overall objective of this project is to develop SNG technology by demonstrating technical and economic feasibility and long-term stability in the context of Singapore’s projected energy landscape to enable energy security and resilience. We thus seek to establish further breakthroughs for the technology by adopting a radical and methodical approach to address the problem at hand, and implementing the same through focussed, contemporary lab-scale experimentation. In addition, we propose to successfully design-build-validate and demonstrate lab-scale integrated process for the SNG technology. More specifically, the three specific research objectives are: fundamental breakthroughs (identification and evaluation of dual-action promoters); to develop lab-scale fully automated and integrated SNG process prototype; to develop process simulation models for techno-economic analysis and technology deployment. This research project will build on our momentum on both fundamental and translational aspects of SNG storage technology and will make significant contributions to UN Sustainable Development Goals of 7 and 13.

title: National Satellite of Excellence in Design Science and Technology for Secure Critical Infrastructure [Satellite DeST-SCI]: Phase II
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: Physical Critical Infrastructure includes water treatment and distribution plants, electric power rgid, oil and natural gas systems, and maritime systems. Over the past decade these systems have been under cyber attack. Some of these attacks has caused significant damage to the targeted plant while other have had an instantaneous impact on the country's economy. The NSoE Phase II proposal is focused on the creation of technologies to ensure that attacks launched on such systems are detected rapidly and the plant is protected against damage. Significant foundational research has been done in Phase I of NSoE. Phase II will focus primarily on the creation of tools at TRL 5 and above based on technologies developed in Phase I. Maritime is a new sector that has been added as a critical infrastructure domain. Research in this domain will focus on methods and tools for protecting ships from cyber attacks.

title: Development of Individualized Cancer Vaccines
abs: Cancer vaccine is a validated and critically important approach in cancer immunotherapy. Our program is focused on continuous innovation in platform technologies in the field of cancer vaccinology. Our team nucleate thought leaders in medicine, gene engineering, chemistry and immunology from NUS, NUH, Duke-NUS, and A*Star and have gained international competitiveness in cancer vaccine innovation. With a strong base at NUS and partner institutions, we will utilize the extensive experience in vaccine development, computational modeling, chemical synthesis, nanomedicine and cellular therapeutics of our researchers, clinical partners, and state-of-the-art research facilities to establish the program of excellence in cancer vaccinology. We aim to develop a pipeline of neoantigen-based vaccine technologies for the treatment of cancer. We will build a high-throughput methodological model to identify alternative neoantigen candidates for the treatment of nasopharyngeal cancer. We will develop a robust lipid nanoparticle (LNP) library to enhance delivery of mRNA neoantigens. We will also reprogram dendritic cell nanovesicle (DCNV) vaccines via biomimetic nanotechnology to optimize efficacy, minimize toxicity, and broaden the application of immunotherapies based on DCs.

title: Agriculture Specialised Facilities Hosted at NUS
abs: Fruited crops form a major part (30%) of the expanded food mix for the revised 3030 goal, but there is a lack of indoor agri-tech R&D facilities with specialised growing systems to support R&D in seed genetics and breeding of fruited crops. Existing R&D facilities are tailored to leafy vegetable R&D and are not easily converted to fruited crop systems. For example, fruited crops require larger inter-tier spacing and deeper troughs than leafy vegetables in a multi-tier growing rack, making existing racks tailored for growing leafy vegetables not suitable. A facility with specialised growing systems for fruited crops R&D would build new capabilities to help push productivity of fruited crops from annual production of 30 tonnes (in 2020) to target of 25,000 tonnes (by 2030). As such, SFA proposes to partner with NUS to establish a specialised facility to support fruited vegetable research.

title: Integrating Wideband Tuneable Acoustic Filters on Silicon for High-speed Wireless Communication
inst: IMRE - Institute of Materials Research and Engineering
abs: With the deployment of the fifth generation (5G) mobile network worldwide, high-speed wireless networks are being increasingly recognized as a key foundation for the future highly connected society. However, the current speed of wireless communication is still not sufficiently high to enable disruptive shifts in applications such as autonomous vehicles, telemedicine and smart factories. The crucial factor that limits the speed is the bandwidth of radio frequency acoustic filters, which are essential to select the desired frequency bands and filter out unwanted bands. The aluminium nitride (AlN) film-based acoustic filters that currently dominate the market cannot meet the bandwidth required in future high-speed 5G and beyond wireless networks, due to the fundamental limits of the material properties. Moreover, these commercial acoustic filters are not tuneable, thus cannot be reconfigured to the multiband and multi-standard operations that are increasingly desired in 5G and future sixth generation (6G) wireless networks. In this proposal, we will develop the next generation acoustic filters with wide bandwidth and tunability based on high performance NaNbO3 thin films we recently invented and integrate them on silicon wafers towards large scale manufacturing.
kw: Radio Frequency Filters, Wireless Communications, 5G, Thin Film, Electronic Devices

title: Characterization of Tropical Urban Air Quality
abs: To continually improve air quality in Singapore and achieve relevant national targets, this project aims to identify major emission sources and build more knowledge of existing, emerging and persistent airborne pollutants. To further control PM2.5 and O3 in the tropical urban environment, this proposal characterizes plastic-originated components, nanosized particles, and secondary aerosols (SAs) in PM2.5, volatile organic compounds (VOCs), and persistent airborne per- and poly-fluoroalkyl substance species (PFASs) for their increasing concentrations in the environment and health impacts. To refine source apportionment of PM2.5, particularly among stationary combustion, traffic and commercial cooking exhausts, this project will explore more indicators and molecular tracers (e.g., dimethyl phthalate emitting from plastics). Nanosized particulates, accounting for >70% of the number concentrations of PM2.5 in Singapore, will be characterized to understand their sources and formation processes. SAs, one of the most abundant fractions in PM2.5, will be investigated through a suite of advanced instrumentations (including aerosol mass spectrometers) and newly developed methods. To identify the associated emissions sources of O3 and SAs, a near-explicit chemical reaction box model will be optimized to identify the potential reaction pathways and precursors, including those originating from volatile chemical products (VCPs) due to massive production and daily use. The parameterized chemical reaction model will also serve to optimize implicit chemical reactions to be coupled with a transport model to differentiate locally formed O3 and secondary organic aerosols (SOAs) from transported influences. Land-use regression models will be developed to generate high spatial resolution maps of PM2.5 and O3 concentrations in Singapore. Available analytical methods of molecular speciation will be streamlined to quantify gaseous and particulate PFASs for regulation assessment. Results will provide references and scientific knowledge for assessing the effectiveness of control measures and devising short- and long-term mitigation plans to continually enhance the tropical urban air quality.
