title: Point-of-care Nocturia Evaluation - Improving the diagnosis and treatment of nocturia
abs: Aim: We aim to further establish on a previously provisionally patented device to determine urine osmolality through a portable electrical impedance device (SG provisional patent 10202006783R). The main aim of this project is to miniaturize the urine osmolality device, so that it can be used as form of POC test by both patients and physicians to determine and characterize the aetiology of patients who have nocturia.. Hypothesis: Nocturia is a common urinary complaint and is defined by the International Continence Society as the interruption of sleep one or more times to void. Various urological and non-urological conditions can cause nocturia; one cause in particular where the correct diagnosis is crucial for effective therapy is nocturnal polyuria. In a prior study performed by Goessaert, participants with nocturnal polyuria had a significant decrease in night-time urine osmolality as compared to daytime. Hence, our hypothesis is that a POC urine osmolality device could help diagnose a patient with nocturnal polyuria and avail correct treatment. Methodology & Approach: We have previously performed a proof-of-concept study demonstrating the use of an impendence model to determine urine osmolality (NTUitive gap fund NGF-2020-08-003). This was performed through a an impedance model with 96.1 ± 1.8 % accuracy as compared to the results obtained from a standard biochemistry laboratory with a freezing-point osmometer. This technology will be further calibrated and improved, and most importantly miniaturised so that it can fulfil the aims of a palm-sized POC device that is cheap and cost effective. Feasibility: With the POC urine osmometer, we would be able to diagnose nocturnal polyuria in an objective fashion, without depending solely on bladder diaries. This would allow urologists to treat more patients with desmopressin (the primary treatment of nocturnal polyuria) and monitor their side effects, hence improving their quality of life.
kw: Nocturia, Point-of-care device

title: Singapore Primary Angle Closure Evaluation and Diagnostics (SPACED) study
abs: Primary angle closure glaucoma (PACG) is a major form of glaucoma and cause of irreversible blindness in Singapore and Asia. It is a disease spectrum with starts with primary angle closure suspect (PACS), the earliest disease stage, which then progresses to primary angle closure (PAC) characterized by elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) and culminates with PACG. PACG is potentially preventable by prophylactic intervention such as laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI) if performed in the early disease stage (PACS). Although most PACS eyes are at a low risk of converting to PAC/PACG, however, some PACS eyes continue to progress despite a patent iridotomy. Current strategies for patient risk assessment are inadequate to identify those PACS eyes who are likely to develop elevated IOP/PACG, and are mainly based on structural features. In this proposal, we hypothesize that impairment of the aqueous outflow facility, which is the main mechanism for development of elevated IOP in open angle glaucoma, also occurs in angle closure; where PACS eyes with impaired outflow facility are at a higher risk of developing elevated IOP/PACG. To address our hypothesis, we will characterize the outflow facility in angle closure, and evaluate responses to provocative tests and prophylactic interventions (Aim 1). Next, we aim to build a multimodal patient-stratification model using machine-learning approaches to identify earlier those individuals at risk of developing PAC/PACG (Aim 2). Finally, we will build a well-characterised longitudinal cohort of angle closure patients (currently lacking for angle closure) who are treatment naïve patients at enrolment. This cohort will facilitate future development of ‘precision-medicine’ strategies to tailor management strategies that is unique to an individual’s characteristics. It is hoped that this project will lead to improvements in risk stratification of angle closure, and facilitate early administration of prophylactic treatments to those at the greatest risk of developing PACG.
kw: Primary angle closure glaucoma; aqueous outflow facility, water drinking test, patient stratification; anterior segment imaging; artificial intelligence

title: EXPLAINABLE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE FOR GLAUCOMA DETECTION
abs: Glaucoma is the leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide. Early detection of glaucoma remains challenging. By the time the current method of visual field testing detects glaucoma, at least 25% of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) are lost. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) imaging is commonly used to aid glaucoma diagnosis, but its ability for early detection remains inadequate. Artificial intelligence (AI) has the potential to provide earlier detection of glaucoma through the discovery of new disease-related patterns. Although AI models in glaucoma have demonstrated performance nearing human levels of accuracy, there is hesitance in adoption as AI models are difficult to interpret and have limited generalizability. We have pilot data showing that the use of anatomy-based compensation reduced the aspect of ocular peculiarities from OCT data and significantly improved the performance of AI models for glaucoma detection in an independent external dataset of different ethnicity. We propose to use explainable AI methods and anatomically corrected OCT data in AI models to improve their interpretability and generalizability, respectively. The main objective of this proposal is to develop explainable AI methods to improve glaucoma detection and improve the robustness of AI algorithms across ethnicities, which will also provide an additional level of insight into an AI model's decisions. We hypothesize that our novel approach will significantly improve diagnostic performance in the early detection of glaucoma and optimize the role that OCT imaging plays in glaucoma management. Early glaucoma diagnosis is essential to improving patient outcomes, as earlier treatment can prevent or slow the disease progression and thus preserve patients' visual function. Given that glaucomatous damage irreversibly leads to blindness at late stages, the outcome of this study, a novel method to advance glaucoma diagnosis, will greatly impact the prevention of blindness in Singapore and worldwide.
kw: artificial intelligence; explainable AI; glaucoma; detection; progression

title: Programme for Ocular Inflammation & Infection Translational Research (PROTON)
abs: Intraocular inflammatory diseases account for a significant proportion of visual impairment, decrease in quality of life of patients and substantial economic cost for countries worldwide. Yet, much remains unknown about this heterogeneous disease. Often times, different conditions present with overlapping clinical signs, posing diagnostic challenges. Furthermore, the treatment for IOID, such as corticosteroids, immunosuppressive agents, or biologics, have therapeutic responses and side effect profiles that vary greatly from patient to patient, making it difficult for ophthalmologists to weigh the risks and benefits for individual patients. In recent years, a new area of interest known as biomarkers has come into the spotlight. Biomarkers such as proteomes, cytokines and inflammasomes have been increasingly observed to be secreted or activated in specific patterns in different conditions, acting as condition-specific signatures. For example, in the work done so far from the CSAINV grant on ocular tuberculosis, we have observed differential cytokine and proteomic profile in patients with tubercular uveitis. The Programme for Ocular Inflammation & Infection Translational Research (PROTON) aims to build up on the CSAINV grant awarded in 2020 and expand the use of uveitis registry to determine the specific clinical phenotypes based on imaging patterns and biomarkers profile from ocular fluid and peripheral immune cells associated with individual uveitic conditions. By identifying these, we can better predict the likelihood of a specific diagnosis and the probability of treatment response. Current proposal is continuation of the prospective multicentre cross-sectional study (CSAINV grant) and will additionally evaluate inflammasome and specific pathogens through VirScan testing besides clinical-image data collection, cytokine analysis, proteomics study and peripheral blood leukocyte immunophenotyping, These parameters will then be compared between subjects of varying diagnoses and treatment responses. In the future, biomarkers may allow for precision medicine and tailored treatments for individual patients with uveitis, leading to improved patient outcomes.
kw: Uveitis; Ocular inflammation; Artificial intelligence; precision medicine; infectious uveitis; biomarkers

title: Paracrine factors and their inhibitors: A novel therapeutic strategy for peritoneal carcinomatosis
abs: Peritoneal carcinomatosis (PC) is a form of localised metastasis arising from any intra-abdominal organ, affecting up to 70% of colorectal cancers and 40% of gastric and ovarian cancers. There is a paucity of efficacious therapeutics and current therapy does not harness tumour biology. This proposal builds upon key findings from my Transition Award project (NMRC/TA/0061/2017) that led to a novel and recently published clinically actionable phenomenon “paracrine addiction”, i.e. cancer cells depend on key paracrine factors within the fluid microenvironment for formation of PC. We identified plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1) as a key paracrine factor in PC, irrespective of histology, and demonstrated that PAI-1 ligand inhibition lowers tumour burden using unique models of patient-derived ascites-dependent xenografts (PDADXs), which incorporates the PC paracrine microenvironment. Here, we seek to utilise both targeted and unbiased approaches to develop novel PC therapeutics, decipher mechanism underlying successful PAI-1 inhibition in PC via a CRISPR screen and identify additional druggable paracrine factors shortlisted via our CAPTIVATE platform. We hypothesize that paracrine factors drive PC progression and confer metastatic potential within the peritoneal cavity, and thus inhibition of key paracrine factors via intraperitoneal instillation of therapeutic agents is a novel and efficacious therapy for PC. This proposal is built upon well-established collaborations and is supported by consortia that the PI has embedded himself within to combat PC. This proposal will generate robust scientific data that would form the foundation and rationale for our translational therapeutics program targeting PAI-1, which will be the critical starting point for the inception of a first-in-human clinical trial to improve survival outcomes of PC patients via PAI-1 ligand inhibition. Further, we will uncover other paracrine factors amenable to paracrine inhibition in PC, paving the way for future research in the development of PC therapeutic strategies and potentially other cancers and disease indications.
kw: Peritoneal carcinomatosis; paracrine factors; therapeutics; precision medicine

title: High-Dimensional Approach to Understanding Immune Dysregulation in Lupus Towards Novel Therapy
abs: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) is a polygenic, systemic autoimmune disease with immune dysfunction driven dually by a lowered activation threshold for immune effector cells and an impaired immunoregulatory axis. Modulated by myriad mechanisms and interactions among varied immune cells, SLE’s immunopathogenic complexity results in the marked heterogeneity of lupus clinical manifestations and responses to therapy. The childhood-onset disease is often more severe than the adult-onset disease. Current treatments aim mainly to dampen the effector immune responses in which incomplete remission and flares after drug tapering are common. There is therefore a critical unmet need to interrogate this disease spectrum, systematically and holistically, to identify the mechanism of tolerance loss in SLE such that strategies for the dual targeting of the effector and regulatory immune axes to restore immune homeostasis and achieve sustained remission can be developed. We aim to identify, in childhood and adult-onset SLE, the intracellular signalling milieus that reduce the activation threshold of effector immune cells and mechanisms that drive the defective compensatory immunoregulatory responses by regulatory B (Breg) and T (Treg) cells. These pathognomonic immune signatures will be validated in a humanised lupus mouse model for follow-on preclinical development with intervention studies. As proof of concept, we have previously observed a reduction of cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated protein 4 (CTLA4) expression in the effector CD4+ T cells and an abnormal expansion of Treg-like T cells without the Treg phenotype marker, CD25, in our discovery adult lupus cohort. With a theragnostic approach, this proposal addresses a translational framework for childhood and adult-onset SLE where we seek to identify immune signatures and therapeutic targets for preclinical development by studying primary patient samples and validated animal (humanised mouse) models.
kw: Paediatric; Adult; Systemic Lupus Erythematosus; Immunome

title: Evidence-based lifestyle interventions for the delay of cognitive decline among older Singaporeans: cohort study and randomized controlled trial
abs: We propose a study that combines observational and interventional study designs to investigate the relationship between lifestyle factors and cognitive decline among older Singaporeans and assess the feasibility and efficacy of lifestyle interventions in delaying cognitive decline. The cohort component will leverage on an existing cohort, the Diet and Healthy Ageing (DaHA) cohort which have recruited over 1,000 participants with comprehensive lifestyle and cognitive data collected. The intervention component will focus on the promotion of a brain-healthy lifestyle, with special attention paying to common problems among local older adults. The interventions include the promotion of physical, social, and cognitive activities, the control of cigarette smoking and alcohol intake, dietary modification based on local guidelines, increase in consumption of tea, mushrooms and vegetables, better management of hypertension, diabetes, metabolic syndrome and overweight through lifestyle changes, and early detection and management of depression and stress. Interventions will be delivered in two forms, with or without individualization. 120 older adults age 60-75 years, who are at risk of dementia will be randomly allocated to one of the two intervention arms and control arm. Primary outcome is change in processing speed. Secondary outcomes include epigenetic age, systemic chronic inflammation and other health-related measures. We hypothesize that lifestyle factors are associated with cognitive decline, epigenetic age and systematic chronic inflammation and lifestyle interventions focusing on common problems among local population can delay cognitive decline, slow epigenetic ageing and produce favorable changes on inflammation markers. The study will provide evidence on the role of lifestyles in ageing and the biological changes after lifestyle interventions. The translation of our work into clinical practice could lead to heathier ageing population and reduced incidence of cognitive decline and subsequently result in sizable savings on the direct and indirect cost of dementia care in Singapore.
kw: Ageing, cognitive decline, lifestyle intervention, DNA methylation, systemic chronic inflammation, cohort study, randomized controlled trial, Asians

title: Different strokes for different folks - Leveraging on community social networks for public health education on antibiotic use and antimicrobial resistance
abs: Antibiotics are the cornerstone of modern medicine. However, the inappropriate use of antibiotics has driven the emergence and increase in antimicrobial resistance (AMR). AMR occurs when the bacteria no longer respond to antibiotics. Infections with antibiotic-resistant bacteria result in excess healthcare costs, morbidity, and mortality. Poor knowledge of antibiotic use and AMR are respectively associated with the inappropriate use of antibiotics. “One-size-fits-all” campaigns have little impact on increasing public awareness on AMR and antibiotic use. Whilst healthcare providers are the public’s trusted sources of health information, only half of the population have a healthcare encounter annually. To increase accessibility to information on antibiotic use and AMR, community-based non-healthcare influencers should be mobilized. The proposed research will be conducted over two phases in a neighborhood comprising 20,000 residents. The Exploratory Phase will involve social network analysis using qualitative and quantitative methods that include in-depth interviews and a questionnaire survey to comprehensively map out the key social networks in the community and identify healthcare and non-healthcare establishments with high degrees of centrality who can be harnessed as health advocates. Based on findings from the Exploratory Phase, a cohort study will be conducted in the Intervention Phase to evaluate the comparative effectiveness of health education via multimedia online and offline platforms facilitated by non-healthcare establishments and healthcare establishments in increasing Singaporean’s knowledge on antibiotic use and AMR, and improving behaviors on antibiotic use. Harnessing sociometric social network analysis to design and implement antibiotic use and AMR educational interventions is a novel approach yet to be explored internationally. Furthermore, the engagement of highly-accessible non-healthcare advocates in the community for health communication on antibiotic use and AMR has not been trialed. In the long-term, the identified influential non-healthcare advocates can be harnessed for other health communication and promotion efforts to augment Singapore’s Healthier SG strategy
kw: Community social network analysis; Antimicrobial resistance; Antibiotic use; Health communication; Non-healthcare advocates; Comparative effectiveness research

title: Eradicating minimal residual disease using "off the shelf" Natural Killer (NK) cells for advanced nasopharyngeal cancer
abs: Natural Killer (NK) cells are lymphocytes innately programmed to recognize and eliminate virally infected or mutated cells without the need to engage class I MHC molecule. This property enables them to play a crucial role to eliminate circulating cancer cells, which is essential to prevent carcinogenesis or minimize cancer relapses following definitive cancer treatment. It is therefore unsurprising that both quantities and functions of NK cells are frequently compromised in cancer patients. In locally endemic nasopharyngeal cancer (NPC) that is ubiquitously associated with the Epstein Barr Virus (EBV) infection, the presence of detectable post-treatment circulating EBV-DNA has been well-documented to represent minimal residue disease (MRD), which portends a high risk of relapse following definitive treatment and thus a worse prognosis. We hypothesized that infusing adjuvant functional activated NK cells eradicates post treatment circulating EBV-DNA completely, from currently presenting in 30% of advanced NPC patients to 0%. To this end, our laboratory has developed a robust technique of expanding allogeneic NK cells from peripheral blood mononuclear cells to nearly 350-fold increase over a 21-day expansion protocol. These expanded, enriched NK cells demonstrated in vitro potent cytotoxic ability against NPC cells. Furthermore, they were proven to be highly effective in vivo on suppressing NPC tumors and exerting an additive tumor suppressive effect when combined with cisplatin chemotherapy in NPC rodent model. Building on these preliminary data and our previous success in applying autologous NK cell therapy in NPC patients, we propose a phase 1 leading to phase 2 clinical trial to evaluate the safety and preliminary efficacy of adjuvant, allogeneic NK cell treatment for locally advanced NPC patients. If successful, this pre-emptive strike using “off the shelf” allogeneic NK cells to eliminate MRD among advanced NPC patients will reduce their risk of relapses and invariably improve survivals of these patients.
kw: Adjuvant allogenic NK cells; Locally advanced nasopharyngeal cancer (NPC); Concurrent chemoradiation; Minimally residual disease (MRD); Phase 1 and 2 clinical trials, plasma EBV-DNA

title: Developing Individualised Bacteriophage-Antibiotic Combinations for Difficult-to-treat Bacterial Infections
abs: Carbapenem-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa (CRPA), a highly-virulent pathogen, have resulted in debilitating infections despite long term antibiotics combination therapy and repeat surgeries. Phage therapy in combination with antibiotics have demonstrated success clinically for drug-resistant bacteria infections. Upon phage exposure, phage-resistant and antibiotic-susceptible bacterial variants became dominant and replaced the entire bacterial population. These bacterial variants have acquired mutation adaptation to evade phage infection (phage-resistant), resulting in restoration of antibiotic sensitivities, as illustrated in one drug-resistant PA. It is unknown if other outbreak CRPA strains behave similarly under phage pressure. In current phage-antibiotic combination treatment, while the choice of phage is customised according to its effectiveness against the resistant bacteria, the choice of antibiotic remains empirical. Also, phage-antibiotics interactions have not been systematically evaluated. The lack of a scientific rationale in the choices of antibiotics to complement the customised phage therapy, and limited understanding of phage-antibiotics interactions, greatly restrict the utility of phage-antibiotic combined therapy to treat drug-resistant bacterial infections. I propose to establish a systematic and individualised approach to recommend appropriate phage-antibiotics combination therapies to achieve the best clinical outcomes through the following study aims: 1) To evaluate whether the hypervirulent outbreak strains of CRPA (phage-sensitive) become phage-resistant and antibiotic-susceptible subpopulation dominant after being exposed to phage, and if so, evaluate the genetic/ transcriptomic changes associated with CRPA dominant population changes; 2) To explore bacteriophages and antibiotics interactions in terms of therapeutic effects on different hypervirulent CRPA strains. We hypothesise that: 1) After phage exposure, the CRPA population is dominated by phage-resistant subpopulation that are sensitive to antibiotics, confirmed by its genetic/ transcriptomic trade-off changes; 2) Phage-antibiotics interactions as to treatment efficacy are bacterial strain-specific. Individualised, appropriate phage-antibiotic combination is an ideal therapy approach for patients with persistent, drug-resistant bacterial infections, given the escalating crisis of antimicrobial resistance.
kw: bacteriophage; antimicrobial resistance; antibiotics; combinations; individualised therapy

title: Using sensors to detect mild cognitive impairment, early dementia and frailty among older adults living in the community: A proactive approach for healthy ageing
abs: Mild cognitive impairment (MCI), a pre-dementia stage, is a window for treatment to delay dementia onset. Multi-domain interventions can effectively delay further cognitive decline. Frailty is another potentially reversible geriatric syndrome that is often comorbid with cognitive decline. Affected individuals frequently present late in the course of their disease and thus miss the ideal time for intervention. More proactive detection is needed. To detect MCI and pre-frailty cases early, we propose deploying sensors in homes of 200 elderly (aged 65+ years) with no frailty and no dementia, to monitor their behaviour change patterns over 3 years. We hypothesize that specific behaviour change patterns in performing daily activities signal MCI/ early dementia, or pre-frailty/ frailty, which distinctly differ from age-related behaviour change patterns. Activities (e.g., medication intake, forgetting personal items, step count, % active and sedentary time, gait speed, room transitions, outings and sleep quality) will be tracked using sensors installed in senior’s homes. Cognitive, psychometric and physical function assessments will be performed annually using consensus diagnoses for cognitive status and the established criteria for diagnosing frailty status. Group-based trajectory modelling will be used to classify distinct behaviour change patterns in performing each individual task over time. Deep recurrent neural networks (an artificial intelligence approach) will be used to differentiate age-related behavior changes from MCI or pre-frailty-related behaviour changes, and to build prediction models. We have established the feasibility and acceptability of sensors in homes of 49 community dwelling elderly persons who were living alone, with over 80% of participants giving positive feedback. As a smart nation, sensors are already used in seniors’ homes to detect for falls or death. With this proposed study we evaluate if the technology can yield more meaningful information that can translate directly to early detection of MCI/ dementia or frailty, to enable timely patient care.
kw: Digital Health; Artificial Intelligence; Dementia; Frailty; Healthy Ageing

title: Transforming Population Eye Health Research (Transformer) Program: From Data and Algorithms to Precision Health
abs: Visual impairment is a major global public health problem, further exacerbated with rapid aging worldwide. Asia, home to 60% of the world population is particularly affected. More effective ways and strategies for detection and management of diseases are needed. This warrants for more ‘precise’ identification of risk factors and biomarkers of eye diseases to optimize screening and risk-stratification models in Asian population. In this regard, epidemiological studies provide valuable insights. However, decade-long epidemiological eye cohorts are lacking worldwide. Furthermore, ‘traditional statistical modelling’ may no longer suffice in unlocking the full potential of population data, and novel approaches are needed. Hence, to transform the population eye health landscape, our program aims to advance precise population eye health through enriching population data and leveraging on advanced digital innovations and analytics. In Specific Aim 1, we will build on the foundation of the Singapore Epidemiology of Eye Diseases (SEED) study (a multi-ethnic Asian cohort with Malays, Indians, Chinese), and complete its 12-year follow up. In Specific Aim 2, through hybrid federated learning approaches, we will establish an integrative data-sharing platform for seamless data analysis across centers, forging wider interdisciplinary collaborations within and beyond Singapore. In Specific Aim 3, by leveraging on advanced analytics and big data, we will develop deep learning algorithms to predict major blinding eye diseases, and refine our current models for detecting disease-related visual impairment and visually significant cataract. In Specific Aim 4, to translate our algorithms into deployment for screening, we will evaluate the performance of our AI model for detecting visual impairment as a clinical decision support tool via a pragmatic randomised controlled trial. Overall, our program is uniquely positioned to formulate precision health initiatives through granular population data and world-class digital innovations. Collectively, these multipronged action plans will culminate in healthy longevity for our aging society.
kw: Population health, Epidemiology, Data Science, Digital Health, Artificial Intelligence, Age-related eye disease

title: The Singapore Platform for Controlled Human Infections with SARS-CoV-2 ('Sing-CoV')
abs: The primary aim of this pilot controlled human infection study (‘Sing-CoV’) is to confirm the safety and infectivity of the nasal inoculation of an infectious dose of a SARS-CoV-2 Delta variant in twenty seropositive healthy volunteers with a history of having received mRNA vaccination and Omicron variant infection. Specifically, this study aims to: 1. Establish a SARS-CoV-2 controlled human infection (CHI) model in previously vaccinated and infected seropositive volunteers in Singapore with an infection rate of 50-70%. 2. Characterise the clinical, virological and immunological responses following controlled inoculation of Delta variant SARS-CoV-2 in Singaporean volunteers. 3. Identify determinants of breakthrough infection and correlates of protection in individuals with pre-existing immunity. 4. Explore antigenic imprinting and the effects of pre-existing immunity on response to infection with an immune escape variant. 5. Examine time-course of the generation of respiratory aerosols containing infectious virus from inoculation onwards. We hypothesise that the infective SARS-CoV-2 dose determined in an ongoing study in seropositive individuals in the UK (Development of a SARS-CoV-2 Delta variant human infection challenge model (COVHIC002)) will have an acceptable safety profile as measured by the occurrence of adverse events (AEs) and serious adverse events (SAEs) from the viral challenge (Day 0) up to Day 28 follow up; and that it induces laboratory confirmed infection in a comparable proportion of participants in a Singapore setting. The key secondary aim of this pilot study is to establish the framework for the safe conduct of CHI studies in Singapore and to build a multi-disciplinary consortium committed to pursuing CHI studies in COVID-19 and other infectious diseases for the development of novel vaccines and treatments in collaboration with local and international academic and industry partners.
kw: COVID-19; SARS-CoV-2; Controlled Human Infection; Immunology; Virology; Transmission

title: Giving the right treatment for the right patient. To define frailty in elderly cancer patients and to understand their preferences for care
abs: In a population with increasing elderly patients, we are seeing a corresponding increase in cancer incidence. The current definitions for frailty are not accurate especially for those who are in the intermediate or prefrail group. This can lead to over- or under-treatment of patients. This study aims to define frailty in elderly patients more accurate by incorporating biomarkers into the clinical assessment. We also aim to assess the quality of life of patients post treatment as the hypothesis that if elderly cancer patients are correctly stratified as fit, prefrail or frail, the patients would be able to tolerate the treatment offered (curative or palliative or supportive) and their quality of life would be maintained or even improve post treatment, with the understanding that QoL generally deteriorates as patient progresses along cancer treatment. We would further want to explore elderly cancer patient preferences to aid physicians in offering treatment. Shared decision-making has been shown to improve patient satisfaction, treatment adherence, self-rated health, confidence in the decision, patient trust in physicians and healthcare costs. We aim to recruit 250 newly diagnosed or relapsed acute myeloid leukemia, non Hodgkin lymphoma, multiple myeloma, non small cell lung cancer, and colorectal cancer patients who are planned to undergo chemotherapy. NCIS sees 3000 cancer patients yearly and with a study period of 2 years (including 1 year follow up), it is feasible to recruit the patients required. We aim to increase the quality of the treatment patients received by identifying what local cancer patients value and any discrepancies between preferred and perceived control over decisions. Insights gained from this study will be used to promote shared decision-making, value-centric care and better patient-physician-caregiver communication. Stratifying patients accurately will enable physicians to offer personalized treatment to ensure that patients maintain a good quality of life post treatment.
kw: Patient preferences; geriatric haematology; geriatric oncology; Frailty; Chemotherapy toxicity; Quality of life

title: Urban care farming on living well and productive engagement of older adults
abs: In Singapore, one in five elderly persons aged 75 and above have shown signs of depression, and the proportion who committed suicide rose from 23% in 2000 to 30% in 2014. This may be contributed by older adults who suffer greater physical and mental deterioration due to low self-esteem, loss of independence, financial limitation, and a lack of social network. These numbers are set to increase in the wake of COVID-19 and its social distancing measures. In line with national efforts, productive ageing in recent years has called upon the need for both efficacious and cost-effective upstream interventions. This study plans to utilise an urban care farming programme as a viable, productive activity to improve health outcomes and impart practical horticulture skills and knowledge. We will be assessing the cost-effectiveness of this programme using a dynamic Markov micro-simulation from a societal and healthcare provider perspective. In addition, a person-level cost-effectiveness analysis will be carried out to compare outcomes and costs incurred. This study will provide insights into the short-term relationship between urban care farming on mental health, physical health, and healthcare utilisation and cost. In addition to establishing the potential sustainability, our study is expected to impact policy and act as a modelling tool to assess the cost-effectiveness of public health interventions. In the short term, the programme provides older adults with a better nutritional diet and an opportunity to learn new skills while forming social connections to improve their physical and mental well-being. In the long term, the programme hopes to reduce the disease burden among older adults and slow down the rate of hospitalisation and nursing home institutionalisation.
kw: Community gardening; Health promotion; Productive ageing; Productive engagement; Older adults; Health outcomes

title: Oral Nutritional Supplementation with HMB enhance muscle quality in sarcopenic surgical patients (HEROS) – a pilot interventional cohort study
abs: Specific Aims & Importance: Clinical frailty severely impacts the physical, functional and physiological reserves necessary for the recovery after surgery. Sarcopenia, a multifactorial, multi-organ process which leads to loss of muscle mass over time, eventually resulting in clinical frailty. These 2 entities result in an increased morbidity and mortality from surgery. They also lead to a slower recovery from surgery with some patients never reaching baseline function after their surgery. It is, therefore, important to optimize patients with sarcopenia prior to surgery to reduce the incidence of morbidity and mortality. Nutrition and resistance training have been shown to be able to curb the effects of sarcopenia. However, the type and regime of nutrition is still unknown. Hypotheses: The study team hypothesize that Ensure Plus Advance + HMB (beta-hydoxy-beta-methylbutyrate) would reduce the amount of IMAT (inter and intramuscular adipose tissue) in sarocpaenic patients after 2-4 weeks of prehabilitation. This effect would be sustained even after surgery and would continue to improve up to 3-months post-surgery whilst participating in rehabilitation. Taking Ensure Plus Advance + HMB would also improve functional parameters after prehabilitation, ensure a similar QoL 1-month post-surgery even if biochemical parameters may not show a significant improvement. Methodology & Feasibility: We would be conducting a pilot interventional cohort with an institution with an established prehabilitation programme (SKH) to evaluate the effect of the use a high protein, high calorie oral nutritional supplement (ONS) with HMB on muscle quality, using a device with Automated Intelligence (AI), in sarcopenic patients undergoing gastrointestinal surgery. Primary outcomes will be changes in Intermuscular Adipose Tissue (IMAT) while secondary outcomes include changes in functional parameters, quality-of-life (QoL), surgical outcomes and biochemical results.
kw: sarcopenia; prehabilitation; rehabilitation; surgery; leucine; muscle health

title: Impact of Machine Learning-based Clinician Decision Support Algorithms in Perioperative Care  - A Randomized Control Trial (IMAGINATIVE Trial)
abs: About 17% of patients develop at least one major complication after surgery. Predicting at-risk patients facilitates specific risk/benefit analysis, targeted preoperative optimization to risks, perioperative management planning, and accurate informed consent. Usage of machine learning (ML) techniques for creating such models are increasing worldwide. However, despite the importance of real-world clinical validation studies for ML algorithms, knowledge of its effectiveness in improving outcomes is lacking. Our team has developed ML models to predict the risk of postoperative mortality and Intensive Care Unit (ICU) admission, called CARES. We aim to investigate the models’ effectiveness for reducing 1-year postoperative mortality and optimizing ICU bed utilization as our Specific Aims (SA) 1 and 2, respectively. Our SA 3 is to assess adoption, acceptability, user experience, and concerns regarding ML-based prediction models in clinical use. We will also explore the models’ impact on important health service outcomes such as length of hospital stay, operating theater utilization rates and etc. The hybrid type 1 effectiveness-implementation Randomized Controlled Trial study design will be used, where patients undergoing surgery are allocated in a 1:1 ratio to CARES-guided (unblinded to risk level) or unguided (blinded to risk level) groups. Patients undergoing elective and emergency surgeries in SGH will be eligible for enrollment. We will recruit 4548 participants in each group to detect a reduction in 1-year mortality from 3.5% to 2.5%, with 80% power and a 2-sided 5% alpha. The success of SA 1 & 2 will provide the case for adopting CARES in other institutions in Singapore and beyond. Most importantly, SA 3 will inform the best path for deployment and uptake of the other ML models. These would include cost-effectiveness, practical barriers to implementation, and strategies to improve the buy-in from clinicians.
kw: surgery; machine learning; perioperative

title: Supporting at-risk Mothers across perinatal period: A Randomized controlled Trial (SMART)
abs: Aims: The proposed study aims to develop and evaluate the effectiveness of a Supporting At-risk Mothers across the perinatal period: A Randomized Controlled Trial (SMART), a mobile-health application (M-Health App) based intervention on maternal depression at 6 months postpartum. It is also aimed that SMART will influence vulnerable mothers’ emotional well-being, self-efficacy, help-seeking behavior (social support), attachment, and interactions with their infants. Lastly, we aim that emotionally well mothers will ultimately influence their newborn’s physical, social and emotional development. Hypotheses: When compared with those in the control group receiving standard care: 1. mothers receiving SMART intervention will have better - emotional well-being (Reduced depression and anxiety); - parenting self-efficacy; - social support; - attachment and interaction with the newborns. 2. new-borns of mothers receiving SMART will have better; - physical development; - social development; and - emotional development. 3. It will be more cost-effective to provide SMART than the standard care Methodology: A randomized controlled two-group pretest and repeated posttest experimental design will be used. Mothers (n = 200) recruited from a tertiary hospital and polyclinics will be randomly assigned into the two groups. Data will be collected by questionnaire surveys using locally validated and reliable instruments, semi-structured face-to-face interviews, blood samples, videos and telephone interviews. Data will be analyzed using SPSS27.0 and thematic analysis. Significance of the study: This study will identify a clinically useful and potentially effective and cost-effective SMART intervention to improve maternal and newborn outcomes. The widely accessed M-Health App will be used to enhance mother-infant attachment and prevent postpartum depression, one of the debilitating conditions that influence new mothers, their children, and the overall family dynamics. Receiving evidence-based timely support may eventually lead to more positive parenting experiences which may then influence the psycho-social well-being of both mothers and their newborns.
kw: mental Health; perinatal period;postpartum depression; psychosocial risks; social support; mother-infant attachment

title: Defining how dengue virus "makes haste slowly" to enable a rational approach for engineering new live attenuated vaccine candidates
abs: Dengue is a mosquito-borne acute viral disease that debilitates an estimated 100 million people each year. It is caused by any one of four dengue viruses (DENV1-4), all of which are expanding their geographic footprint from the tropics to the subtropics. Patchy knowledge of the molecular determinants of clinical and epidemiological fitness of DENV has complicated dengue vaccine development. Studies have shown that clinically fit DENV avoids prematurely activating the innate immune response that limits intrahost infection dissemination. Studies from the applicant’s laboratory have found that wild-type DENVs evade immune activation, in part, through slowing its replication rate and “make haste slowly”. However, how DENV infection is regulated, especially through virus-host interactions instead of mutations in the viral polymerase, is not understood. The goal of this proposal is to define the DENV-host interactions that regulate virus replication rate. This study will build on our recent findings of two DENV mutants that serve as exquisite tools to interrogate how DENV replication is regulated through virus-host interactions. The first is an attenuating mutation in the prM gene found in DENV2 PDK53 - a phase III clinical trial tested vaccine candidate - that has impaired interaction with human high mobility group box 1 (HMGB1) protein that plays critical roles in regulating gene expression. The second is a novel mutation in a conserved region of the DENV NS2B gene. Both mutants show accelerated replication and attenuated infection dissemination compared to their wild-type parents. The specific aims of this study will use these mutants to delve into the mechanisms that operate to regulate DENV replication and hence attenuation. It will also aim to discover new mutations that accelerate DENV replication and use these as well as others to engineer new strains with suitably attenuated phenotype for further development as dengue vaccines.
kw: Dengue virus; replication rate; innate immune activation; interferon; attenuation; vaccine.

title: Nanoparticle-assisted antisense oligonucleotide targeting Parkin as potential therapeutics for Parkinson’s disease
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Parkinson’s disease (PD) is a common neurodegenerative disorder. parkin gene is frequently mutated in autosomal recessive PD. Of note, elevated Parkin have been found to be neuroprotective by rescuing defective mitochondrial dysfunctions, alleviating motor defects in experimental models. Through binding to RNA by Watson-Crick base pairing, antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) may affect RNAs in various ways, regulating protein functions. Antisense drugs hold potential for the treatment of neurodegenerative diseases, with antisense drug, nusinersen, having been approved for the treatment of spinal muscular atrophy. However, delivery of ASOs to the targeted cells remains a challenge. Spherical nucleic acids (SNA) represent a nanoparticle-based delivery strategy, in which the hydrophilic oligonucleotides are attached to the hydrophobic core nanoparticle to achieve efficient transmembrane intracellular delivery. We have designed and validated ASOs which may significantly upregulate Parkin level in culture cells. To translate the discovery to a potential therapeutic option for local PD patients, it warrants further study of the ASOs in the neurons derived from induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) of PD patients with Asian-related gene mutations. Our hypothesis is that ASOs packed onto nanoparticles may be delivered into human neurons and upregulate endogenous Parkin protein level, having potential for PD therapeutics. To test our hypothesis, we will synthesize and validate ASOs which are conjugated to the surface of the nanoparticles via thiol linkages. Next, we will examine nanoparticle-assisted ASO delivery to neurons and midbrain organoids derived from iPSCs of local PD patients. Eventually, effects of enhanced Parkin on neuronal health of PD patients will be evaluated. The proposed work will bring in nanotechnology to assist the delivery of ASOs into iPSCs-derived neurons and organoids. Enhanced endogenous Parkin through nanoparticle-conjugated ASOs may rescue PD pathogenesis in local patient iPSC-derived neuronal models, thereby representing a promising therapeutic option for PD.

title: Precision BRAin COnnectivity Profiling of Learning Difficulties (BRACO-LD)
abs: Background: Learning difficulties (LDs) are associated with problems of health, productivity and well-being throughout life. However, our limited understanding of the neural mechanisms that underlie LDs constraints our ability to develop a more sophisticated diagnosis necessary for personalized treatments and innovation in therapeutics. Objective: Our primary aim is to characterize the neurocircuitry basis of the core domains of learning (executive function/emotional regulation, language, literacy and numeracy) using MRI-based brain connectivity profiling. We have two specific aims; (1) To identify “brain connectivity signatures'' associated with the core domains of learning and (2) To identify potential “patterns'' that will allow stratification of children with LDs into connectivity-based subtypes. Methods: We will analyze brain connectivity profiles and measures of learning skills from 1680 young children (age 4-7 years); 280 with LDs and 1400 typically developing children from pre-existing cohort studies (GUSTO, S-PRESTO). To identify “brain connectivity signatures” associated with the core domains of learning, we will employ both conventional statistical methods (Spearman’s rank correlation coefficients followed by canonical correlation analysis) and deep learning methods (‘meta-matching’). We will then perform exploratory analysis to identify potential “patterns'' that will allow stratification of children with LDs into connectivity-based subtypes using hierarchical clustering technique. Significance: Our proposed study will be the largest cohort of young children with comprehensive brain connectivity profiling and deep phenotyping of learning skills. Our results will significantly improve our understanding of the neural mechanisms which underlie different domains of learning skills. This will form the basis of precision brain connectivity profiling that could complement existing clinical assessments and refine the clinical care of children with LDs. Our project is considered relatively upstream at the proposed stage. However, its successful establishment would form the critical scaffold for future translational research.
kw: brain connectivity; learning difficulties; magnetic resonance imaging

title: The Role of Novel Auto-Antibodies in Idiopathic Small Fiber Neuropathy
abs: Specific Aims & Hypothesis Small fiber neuropathy (SFN) is phenotypically and etiologically heterogeneous, with patients presenting with debilitating neuropathic pain and dysautonomia. Diagnosing SFN itself is a challenge due to a lack of diagnostic tools and effective diagnostic criteria, but the real challenge occurs in finding the cause of SFN.which remains elusive in around 50% of the cases and are classified as idiopathic SFN (iSFN). Autoimmunity has been postulated to be pathophysiologically important in presumed iSFN, but few associated autoantibodies have been described. We recently published preliminary proteomics results showing 3 autoantibodies, namely anti-MX1, anti-DBNL and anti-KRT8, with significant differences in protein fold changes for iSFN. Overall findings suggest the involvement of an immunological mechanism in the pathogenesis of SFN. The primary objective of this project is to determine the role of anti-MX1 antibody and other proteins in iSFN, that may actually be autoimmune, and to further validate the findings in biopsy-confirmed "Definite SFN". In this dual-center study, we will address the following specific aims: Aim 1. To identify autoantibodies against MX1 in patients’ sera by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and/or indirect immunofluorescence. We hypothesize that anti-MX1 antibody is at higher titers in iSFN patients, compared to sSFN. Aim 2. To use a multi-pronged approach to decipher other immunological targets that may be involved in iSFN. These include immunophenotyping of iSFN patients’ peripheral blood mononuclear cells, multiplex analysis to test for cytokines and complement, mass spectrometry to validate initial findings, and further validation of other putative autoantibodies in their original conformation with a custom proteomics array. We hypothesize that other putative autoantibodies and immunological pathways may be involved in iSFN.

title: SCARCE Phase 2 (RT 2):Recycling of Laminated Solar Panels
abs: As the photovoltaic industry continues to grow, it is essential to develop efficient waste management for the projected end-of-life (EoL) solar panels. The effort to design proper waste management for these solar wastes are still at an early stage. Most of the established processes today revolve around the removal of the aluminium frames and tempered glass – typically by thermal or mechanical treatment. In terms of sustainability, the noxious gas emission generated from thermal treatment and, the negligence on recovery and repurposing of the high-purity silicon substrates makes these recycling processes less attractive. In SCARCE Phase 1, we have devised solvent delamination as a replacement of thermal treatment to separate the glass from solar waste. Alternative crush-and-sieve operation demonstrated segregation of valuable metals from polymeric components via particle size differences. This allows focused hydrometallurgical effort for recovery of valuable metals and avoid the need for thermal treatment to remove the polymers. Sequential selective leaching and single-reagent approaches have been designed and tested as parts of hydrometallurgy developments. The team has also explored and validated potential upcycling applications with the recovered materials from solar wastes, namely metal-organic frameworks (MOF) and lithium-ion batteries. This has resulted in 4 technology disclosures (including 1 in preparation), published articles and an industrial research collaborative agreement. Moving forward, SCARCE Phase 2 will build on this success and continue developing sustainable technologies. The key focus will be to build on the collected data and further scale up each individual technology to pilot scale. Low-temperature delamination operation and greener hydrometallurgy strategies will be employed to minimize carbon emission and mitigate hazardous operation. Mechano-chemical principles will be incorporated into the process to exploit the benefits of enhanced performance and improved efficiencies. Overall, SCARCE strives to work towards the sustainable future by developing green strategies for solar waste recycling that can be easily scalable, deployable and adaptable as a standalone operation or complementary to existing plants.
kw: Green Methodology; Recycling; Solar Panels; Laminated E-wastes

title: SCARCE Phase 2 (RT 3): Recycling and Recovery of strategic metals and rare earth from PCBs and beyond
abs: Since August 2018, the joint CEA/NTU SCARCE laboratory demonstrated, in Phase 1, with 1-10 kg/h prototypes, a recycling strategy of wasted PCB based on (i) first their disassembly/dismantling, followed by the world first elemental sorting of individual wasted electronic components (ECs), (ii) enabling simplified recovery sub-processes targeting precious, and/or critical metals. The latter use greener hydrometallurgy approaches that are more easily to deploy. In Phase 2, we will further develop these technologies to increase their TRL and achieve their translation to industries. We will therefore seek industrial partners to jointly: (i) to work on larger prototypes for dismantling system/process as well as for the elemental sorting of electronic components for specific element segregation beneficiation; (ii) to demonstrate economical viability at much larger scale for our proposed hydrometallurgy processing that enable closing the loop thanks to the recovery of precious and/or critical metals from waste PCBs. Overall, these processes will be greener with output in forms of marketable elemental metals, metal oxides, or metallic ion complexes. Such process development will be accelerated thanks to our world first liquid-liquid separation microfluidic platform integrated with on-line X-ray Fluorescence spectrometer, which allows quicker determination of process parameters windows. Furthermore, we will develop further and scale up: (i) metal ions separation membranes using MOF or 2D materials; (ii) liquid-liquid separation using supercritical fluid toward a zero-waste goal. The goal, time line and deliverables are listed in each work packages within 5 years.
kw: Dismantling, sorting, beneficiation, green solvent, waste reduction

title: SCARCE Phase 2 (RT1) - Recycling of Batteries including Lithium ion
abs: Lithium-ion batteries (LIB) have experienced an exponential demand owing to the rapid growth of its energy storage applications in consumer electronics, electric vehicles and wing/solar energy storage. The global lithium battery market demand is expected to reach ~ $690 billion in 2025. Such huge demand and consumption of LIB would lead to generation of mountains of spent LIB waste which if left in the landfill will cause irreversible pollution and damage to environment and human health. Spent LIB also contains large amounts of valuable and strategic metals such as Li, Co, Mn, Ni, Cu, Al, Fe in higher concentration than in the respective ores. Hence, recycling of spent LIB is of importance for both critical metal supply and environmental protection. State of art LIB recycling using pyrometallurgical process and conventional hydrometallurgical processes employ higher temperatures (1000degC) and/or strong corrosive acids that lead to secondary pollution, lower recycling efficiency, higher cost and energy/water intensive processes. In this project, we focus on alternative green technologies to recycle spent lithium-ion batteries. We will focus on employing weak solvents and waste from other streams such as plastics, food waste and bio-organisms to extract valuable metals from spent LIB. In addition, closed loop and open loop process of repurposing and reusing elements extracted from spent LIB to create economic value will be explored.
kw: E-waste, Recycling, Hydrometallurgy, Circular economy

title: Fungal sensitization as a potential contributing factor to Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) deterioration
abs: COPD is a common respiratory condition resulting in significant morbidity, mortality and socioeconomic burden. COPD is the the 3rd leading cause of death worldwide and is the 10th leading cause of death in Singapore. COPD is a heterogeneous disease with a significant inter-individual variation in disease progression and treatment responses. The precise mechanisms leading to COPD susceptibility and subsequent progression remain to be fully understood. Despite treatment, COPD progresses with no reliable cure. One potential mechanism relevant to the role of fungi remains understudied. Emerging evidence supports the important role of infection (bacteria and viruses) in the pathogenesis of COPD. However, the significance of detecting fungi in the airway of COPD patients remains poorly understood, despite the high abundance of fungal spores in the outdoor air. Limited studies, however, do suggest some important associations with disease severity and clinical outcomes which is further attested by my preliminary work with high fungal sensitization in South-East Asian COPD. We hypothesize that fungal sensitization is clinically relevant in COPD with association to persistent colonization and disease progression. This has potential implications for clinical management. Our objective is to interrogate fungal sensitization and colonization and the involvement of autosensitization in COPD and the impact on disease progression. This is important as it has the potential to uncover avenues amenable to precision medicine approaches specific to COPD patients. A prospective study of 166 patients with COPD and 50 healthy controls will be undertaken. We will assess the sensitization profile, cytokine and sputum for mycobiome and fungal polymerase chain reaction. This work will significantly enhance our understanding of the role of fungi in COPD and potential novel diagnostic and/or therapeutic approaches specific to our population. This will permit more targeted precision medicine approaches to COPD management in the Asia-pacific region.

title: Evaluating the REal-World PAtient-ReporteD and Economic Impact of Combined PHACO-MIGS Surgery (REWARD)
abs: For patients with mild-moderate primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) and concomitant cataracts, many clinicians now combine phacoemulsification (PHACO) and a new procedure called minimally invasive glaucoma (MIGS) surgery (PHACO-MIGS). Aside from a slightly greater and longer-lasting intraocular pressure reduction however, the lack of a clear clinical benefit offered by this combined procedure over PHACO alone means that it is still unclear when PHACO-MIGS should be performed over the latter; or if the patient should instead continue to be treated non-surgically with medication. With the increasing focus on value-based care, assessing the patient-reported and cost-effectiveness of this combined procedure using real-world patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) can be utilized to inform clinical guidelines and healthcare policy decisions. To date, however, there are very few studies evaluating these outcomes in patients undergoing PHACO-MIGS. To address these knowledge gaps, my main objective in this HCSA-INV submission is to determine the patient-reported and economic outcomes associated with PHACO-MIGS in comparison with (a) continued topical medication use only; or (b) PHACO alone, in a real-world cohort of patients with mild-moderate POAG and cataracts using sensitive and validated glaucoma-specific PROMs (GlauCATTM and Glau-U) that have been developed by our research group. GlauCATTM is a novel and comprehensive glaucoma-specific scale encompassing multiple patient-identified QoL domains that presents targeted questions to respondents using a type of secure cloud-based artificial intelligence. Glau-U is a preference-based utility measure that has been found to be more sensitive than the widely used EuroQoL 5-Dimension scale in quantifying utility values across the glaucoma severity spectrum. Data from this submission will thus provide a clearer understanding of the patient-reported and economic benefits of PHACO-MIGS over the two traditionally utilized treatment modalities for mild-moderate POAG and concomitant cataracts in a representative clinical population, and aid in informing clinical recommendations for the use of this combined procedure.
kw: Glaucoma Management; Quality of life; Phacoemulsification; Minimally invasive glaucoma surgery; Cost effectiveness;Real-world study

abs: STCC was established in 2020 as a nationally coordinated consortium to synergise cancer research capabilities in Singapore. title: Preclinical Intrauterine Nanoparticle-based Gene Editing for Genetic Diseases
abs: Inherited monogenic diseases pose a significant clinical, socio-economic burden, many of which cause irreversible damage in-utero, is an urgent unmet clinical need. Intrauterine gene therapy (IUGT) has shown tremendous promise in providing a cure, but prone to problems with viral toxicity and integration, and use of a non-physiological promoter. A potential solution would be to perform intrauterine gene editing through nanoparticle (NP) based delivery. In this proposal which builds on our internationally-recognised success in IUGT and immune ontogeny, we will deliver intrauterine gene editing using advanced NPs. Our long-term objective is to develop the scientific, technical, and safety foundations for the clinical translation of intrauterine gene editing technologies for inherited monogenic diseases using a clinically and ontologically-relevant non-human-primate (NHP) model. Our hypothesis is that a NP-based gene editing platform is safe and effective to treat monogenic diseases. Specifically, we will (A) develop and identify the most efficient NP system for mRNA-based gene-editing tools, (B) demonstrate the efficiency and safety of NP-based intrauterine gene editing targeting PCSK9 and HPD, and (C) map the immune ontogeny and perturbations with NP-based gene editing through high-resolution assays. The goal of this programme is to develop an optimised NP-based intrauterine gene-editing platform of relevance for the treatment of monogenic diseases of significant socio-economic burden. The data derived here, especially from the translationally relevant NHP studies, will inform on the development of a clinical protocol, which may be applicable to almost half of human pathogenic genetic variants, which are caused by point mutations. Concurrent studies of human immune ontogeny funded through NMRC/CIRG/1484/2018 will further identify the ideal time for intervention in tandem with efforts to do the same in the NHP. This proposal brings together a team of internationally-competitive Clinician- Scientists, Scientists, and Maternal-Fetal Medicine Specialists to build on the clinical translation of intrauterine gene-editing.

title: Developing an improved nanopore-based RNA structure probing method to study the structure and function of dengue viruses
abs: The dengue virus is an RNA virus from the family Flaviviridae and infects more than 390 million people around the world each year1. As of June 3rd 2022, more than 12000 cases of Dengue has been reported in Singapore this year and result in relatively mild dengue fever to potentially fatal dengue hemorrhagic fever. The dengue virus consists of ~11kb RNA genome that can fold into complex structures for viral replication, translation, and packaging2,3. In addition to the full-length genome, the virus also produces a short ~450 base subgenomic RNA at the end of the genome, which is important for its infection4,5. Studying the structure and function of subgenomic RNA and the full-length genome is key to understanding dengue infectivity. Unfortunately, current short-read high throughput structure probing cannot distinguish structures that are unique to subgenomic and full-length dengue genomes. By using direct RNA sequencing, we had previously developed a method to couple structure-probing with the long-read nature of nanopore sequencing to determine RNA structures in highly similar sequences6. However, the lack of training data limits the accuracy and sensitivity of our method. In this proposal, we aim to develop a more accurate and sensitive version of our high throughput RNA structure probing method using nanopores to study the structural heterogeneity and function of dengue genomes. Specifically, we aim to 1) chemically synthesize modified nucleotides to generate training datasets for structure probing using nanopore sequencing; 2) study the RNA structures of dengue full-length and subgenomic RNAs, and 3) identify alternative secondary structures along the dengue genome using single-molecule RNA structure clustering. Collectively, this proposal identifies functionally important regions along the dengue virus to enable downstream drug targeting.
kw: RNA structure, nanopore sequencing, dengue virus

title: Host, environmental, and mycobacterial determinants of Mycobacterium abscessus infection
abs: Non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM) such as Mycobacterium abscessus are genetic cousins of Mycobacterium tuberculosis but have distinct mechanisms of pathogenesis and host interaction. Knowledge of how M. abscessus constructs granulomas has previously been restricted because of a lack of an appropriate model of chronic infection. We have developed a novel model of chronic M. abscessus infection using adult zebrafish that outperforms existing mouse models by replicating high bacterial burden during chronic infection and uniquely facilitates the study of M. abscessus-mediated granuloma formation in an intact animal host. We will use a candidate gene approach in the adult zebrafish-M. abscessus infection model to dissect the roles of host immunopathology and M. abscessus ESX secretion systems in granulomatous infection. We will take advantage of the experimental tractability of our model to investigate three important known susceptibility factors to M. abscessus infection: prior tuberculosis infection, inhaled corticosteroid usage, and cigarette smoking. We will determine if these factors increase susceptibility and then pull apart the molecular mechanisms responsible for increased infection susceptibility. To discover new host susceptibility and bacterial virulence factors we will perform dual host-pathogen transcriptomics to perform the first census of host-M. abscessus gene expression during granuloma formation. This transcriptomic analysis will provide a unique dataset of granuloma-associated gene expression signatures for future mechanistic investigation. In a unique approach, we will use adult zebrafish as avatars of human infection with a pool of M. abscessus clinical isolates. This screening approach will identify isolates with extreme phenotypes for genome sequencing and facilitate the identification of novel virulence genotypes for mechanistic investigation.
kw: Mycobacterium abscessus; immunopathogenesis; environmental susceptibility; bacterial virulence factors

title: Simultaneous inhibition of mutant KRAS and activation of RIG-I pathway for the treatment of pancreatic cancer
abs: Pancreatic cancer is one of the most lethal cancers. KRAS G12D and G12V are major mutations in pancreatic cancer. Therefore, there is an urgent need to develop a novel therapeutic approach targeting mutated KRAS for improving the clinical outcome of pancreatic cancer patients. A new approach is to employ antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) that target KRAS G12D/V specifically. Recently, our research group has developed a new platform for nucleic acid drug delivery by employing red blood cell-derived extracellular vesicles (RBCEVs). We demonstrated that RBCEVs are safe and efficient carriers for the delivery of ASOs. We also delivered an immunomodulatory RNA (immRNA) to activate Retinoic acid-inducible gene-I (RIG-I) and trigger anti-cancer immune responses in primary tumors and metastases. Here, we aim to simultaneously target KRAS mutants and activate the RIG-I pathway in pancreatic cancer using nucleic acid therapeutics delivered by RBCEVs. We observed that a combination of KRAS-G12D ASO and immRNA, synergistically triggered interferon release and suppressed pancreatic cancer cell survival. Hence, we sought to further validate the efficacy of this combination in co-culture of pancreatic cancer cell lines and patient-derived organoids with immune cells. We will subsequently validate the combination in xenografted mouse models of subcutaneous pancreatic cancer and experimental lung metastasis. Secondly, we will develop systemic treatments of pancreatic cancer with RBCEVs containing KRAS ASO and immRNA in orthotopic cancer models, including immunocompetent Kras-LSL-G12D mice. To increase the circulation half-life of RBCEVs, we will develop a method for EV hitchhiking onto blood cells. The biodistribution and efficacy of the new formulated EVs will be validated in orthotopic models of pancreatic cancer. Thirdly, we will examine the biodistribution and safety of RBCEVs with nucleic acid payloads in macaques as a non-human primate model.
kw: cancer, pancreatic, KRAS, immunotherapy, drug delivery, extracellular vesicles

title: The SenseHealth Research Programme: Untangling the complex relationship between the severity/laterality of age-related sensory decline, and frailty in elderly Singaporeans through  novel risk factors, non-invasive biomarkers, patient-centred impact, and potential intervention targets to improve frailty outcomes.
abs: Age-related vison and hearing impairments (VI and HI) alone, notwithstanding combined (dual sensory impairment [DSI]), are potential risk factors of physical frailty in older adults. However, the contribution of the severity and laterality of VI, HI or DSI in the development and progression of frailty remain unclear in elderly individuals at a population-based level. Similarly, prospective data on the factors underpinning the VI/HI/DSI-frailty relationships, and the patient-reported impact and economic burden of concomitant frailty and sensory impairments remain scarce, while the effectiveness of sensory treatments to prevent frailty are non-existent. Addressing these knowledge gaps is the focus of this submission, through four inter-related objectives. First, we will recall participants of the PopulatION HEalth and Age-Related SEnsory Decline PRofilE (PIONEER) study, comprising multi-ethnic Singapore residents aged ≥60 years, and evaluate the temporal relationship of the severity and laterality of baseline VI, HI and DSI with frailty at their 4-year follow-up visit to determine their potential as risk factors and susceptibility and prognostic biomarkers. Second, the factors mediating the association between VI/HI/DSI and the incidence/progression of frailty will be investigated in the same population. Third, we will explore the longitudinal impact of concomitant frailty and sensory impairment on several important patient-related outcomes, including falls, loneliness, functioning, quality of life, personal and economic hardships, thereby providing novel in-depth insights into the consequences of combined frailty-sensory losses from the patient’s perspective. Finally, we will determine the real world effectiveness of commonly available sensory treatments for correctable sensory losses in reducing frailty incidence and progression in individuals following sensory treatment gains; and using a mixed-method research design, we aim to identify the barriers and facilitators to the uptake, and short- and long-term adherence of these treatments and formulate evidence-based recommendations to improve the uptake, and adherence of real world sensory treatments.
