title: Lung-Gut-Liver Axis in the pathogenesis of Klebsiella pneumonia infection
abs: Klebsiella pneumonia (KP) is a major pathogen causing antimicrobial resistance (AMR) infection in the community and hospital both globally and in Singapore. KP could be broadly divided into classical KP and hypervirulent (Hv) KP based on clinical phenotype. Classical KP is the most predominant carbapenem-resistance hospital acquired infection. Conversely, HvKP primarily cause community acquired infection associated with severe pyrogenic liver abscess (PLA). Epidemiological evidence in Asia suggests an increasing trend of AMR acquisition in HvKP. Together, there is a need develop new non-antibiotic-based treatment. However, progress has been slow as KP pathogenesis remains poorly understood. In this project, we aim to decipher the lung-gut-liver axis in the pathogenesis of KP infection. Using relevant clinical KP isolates we have developed mouse models for both classical (ST258) and HvKP (ST23) that mimics clinical infection in terms of route of infection, lung pathology and KP gut colonization in the absence of antibiotic pre-treatment to establish infection. Preliminary data from these models suggest that KP adaptation in the lung is required for downstream gut colonization and dissemination into the liver to induce PLA. Using these models, 3 specific aims will be studied: (i) To define the virulent genes of KP that are activated in the lungs that support gut colonization through transposon mutant library approach; (ii) To understand the host cellular interaction partners with KP in the gut that leads to leaky gut and liver dissemination by performing the kinetics of histopathology assessment, immunohistochemistry (KP and epithelia) and immune phenotyping of the intestinal tissue; (iii) To determine the role of KP–hepatocytes–immune cells interactions in the liver by performing infection in humanized-hepatocyte, humanize immune system and dual humanized mice. This study could reveal new targets on the bacterial or the host for development of new antibacterial therapeutics and host-targeted adjunct therapy respectively.
kw: Bacteriology; Pathogenesis; Klebsiella; Anti-microbial resistance; host-bacterial interaction

title: Dissecting the contribution of oncometabolism during tumour-initiation and metastasis-initiation.
abs: Metabolic alteration is a cancer hallmark that provides for crucial functional adaptations along the course of disease progression. Cancer cells can rewire their metabolism to gain competitive advantage over their non-neoplastic counterparts to adapt to tumour microenvironment. At distinct stages of cancer progression, cancer cells may have different metabolic adaptations due to metabolic plasticity and reprogramming. Tumour-initiating cells (TICs) help spawn the early phases of tumour and metastasis-initiating cells (MICs) seed metastatic colonies in secondary organs and function as TICs in microenvironments distinctly different from the primary tumour. There is therefore a clinical need to target TICs and MICs specifically to reduce occurrence of relapse and metastatic spread of the disease. We hypothesize that specific metabolic programs confer tumour-initiating and metastasis-initiating abilities and interfering with these metabolic adaptations might be useful for sensitizing them to chemotherapy, reduce relapse and metastasis. As proof of concept, we employed a novel whole-metabolome in-vivo inducible CRISPR-Cas9 screen with site-directed genome integration to uncover metabolic vulnerabilities in TICs. This system is advantageous for reducing off-target effects and complicated analysis due to copy number variation of guide RNAs. Validation of hits revealed that TICs are dependent on two key enzymes involved in fatty acid metabolism and glutathione biosynthetic pathway which could be targeted to eliminate TICs. We propose to elucidate and target the most effective effector of the tumour-initiation phenotype. Triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) is one of the most devastating cancer subtypes, often prone to metastasis and chemotherapeutic resistance. This is largely attributed to the presence of TICs and MICs. We propose to uncover metabolic vulnerabilities of MICs in TNBC using our whole-metabolome CRISPR-Cas9 screen during metastasis-initiation. Finally, we will also elucidate the mechanisms of action for metabolic enzymes important for metastasis-initiation, to drive MIC-directed pharmaceuticals for improving clinical outcomes of TNBC patients.
kw: Cancer; Metabolism; CRISPR; Tumour-initiating; Metastasis

title: Spinal Cord Bioelectronic Bypass: Towards Restoring Volitional Motor Function after Acute Spinal Cord Injury
abs: Spinal cord injury (SCI) can lead to severe paralysis but current treatment is supportive without effective motor restoration. Advances in epidural electronic stimulation (EES) have enabled patients with SCI to walk. However, this stimulation requires external input that does not represent the patient’s volitional motor intention. To achieve a closed-loop electronic bypass of SCI to restore volitional motor activity, recording volitional motor signals proximal to the SCI site is essential. We have developed flexible electrode arrays that can record motor evoked potential (MEP) signals following electrical stimulation of the motor cortex and decode the signals as triggers for EES to bypass a site of SCI, enabling hindlimb motor activity in paralyzed rats. In this preclinical in vivo study, we aim to establish the safety of spinal cord electrode array implantation and the ability to record motor signals around the spinal cord in awake, behaving pigs. We will first validate the ability of the array to record MEP signals around the thoracic spinal cord of pigs (n=3) and the ability of the decoded MEP signals to trigger EES to enable hindlimb movement in pigs with SCI (n=3) under terminal anaesthesia. Subsequently, the array will be implanted around the thoracic spinal cord of pigs (n=3, no SCI). The hindlimb kinematics of the implanted pigs walking on a treadmill will then be correlated with neural signals recorded from the spinal cord. We hypothesize that electrode arrays implanted around the spinal cord can record motor signals in pigs that correlate with hindlimb kinematics, demonstrating that: 1) implantation of electrode arrays does not result in SCI, and 2) motor volition can be decoded from the spinal cord using the electrode arrays. The establishment of the feasibility of spinal cord electrode array implantation in pigs will pave the way for clinical translation in patients with paralysis.
kw: Spinal cord injury; Spinal cord recording; Neural interfaces; Epidural spinal stimulation; Implantable Neuroprosthetics

title: Functional roles of plasma micronutrients in overweight and obese women receiving nutrition intervention during preconception and early pregnancy
abs: Micronutrient deficiencies can result in reproductive failure. Given that overweight and obese women are particularly vulnerable to micronutrient deficiency and at-risk of impaired reproductive health, an intervention consisting of healthy eating and supplementation to optimize micronutrient reserves among these women, commencing in the preconception and continued throughout pregnancy, may contribute to a successful and healthy pregnancy. Herein, we propose a single-arm trial, which will be embedded within a newly established model of care program called Healthy Early Life Moments in Singapore (HELMS), to evaluate the impact of this nutrition intervention from preconception and early pregnancy, in improving the micronutrient status, and thus resulting in positive reproductive outcomes among overweight and obese women. Specifically, we will examine levels of one-carbon metabolites (e.g. folate, B6, B12, methionine, choline, homocysteine), vitamins D and E at baseline, post-intervention during preconception. These micronutrients are commonly reported to be involved in reproductive functions. We will recruit 300 women with body mass index 25-40 kg/m2, aged 18-45 years, who are trying to conceive. Trial visits will be conducted in KK Women’s and Children’s Hospital. Nutrition education, healthy eating guidance and multi-micronutrient supplementation will be provided throughout preconception and early pregnancy phases. Our outcomes are to measure changes in micronutrient concentrations and how it affects clinical pregnancy rates. An observational preconception cohort (S-PRESTO) will be the control arm for this study, given its similar study schedules, studied micronutrients and outcome variables. Our proposed trial will provide greater insight on the prevalence of micronutrient deficiencies among overweight and obese women, and more importantly, the impact of intervention on fertility which will support routine supplementation for these at-risk women.
kw: micronutrients, overweight, obese, nutrition, preconception, pregnancy

title: Mechanism of empagliflozin to improve myocardial relaxation in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction through inhibiting sodium-proton exchanger 1
abs: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is poised to be the predominant cause of HF in the near future. However, therapeutic approaches to improve clinical outcomes in patients with HFpEF have been limited due to its complex pathophysiology and diverse phenotypes. The sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor, empagliflozin, is the first therapeutic agent demonstrated to improve clinical outcomes in patients with HFpEF, but the exact mechanisms underlying the salutatory effects of empagliflozin on cardiac function remain unclear. Lack of proper in vitro and in vivo models of HFpEF have severely hampered the study of HFpEF. In this research proposal, we will use a novel human iPSC-derived cardiomyocyte model generated from patients with HFpEF and a recently described two-hit mouse HFpEF model to investigate the mechanisms through which empagliflozin mediates its beneficial effects in HFpEF. Considering that NHE-1 inhibition has been proposed to mediate the cardiomyocyte-specific effects of empagliflozin, we will investigate whether empagliflozin can (1) improve myocardial energetics and (2) decrease myofibril stiffness through NHE-1 inhibition in human and mouse HFpEF cardiomyocytes, as both mechanisms could potentially improve myocardial relaxation. Results from our study may provide insights into the mechanisms through which SGLT2i reduces the risk of hospitalization for HF in patients with HFpEF.
kw: heart failure; diastolic dysfunction; iPSCs; relaxation; myocardial energetics; myofibrils

title: Targeting glutamatergic and GABAergic signaling pathways as novel immuno-modulatory therapies against arboviral diseases
abs: Neurotransmitters have been shown to modulate host immunity, as part of the neuroimmune circuitry In this proposal, I hypothesize that glutamate affects immune cell functions and I want to understand how glutamate modulates crosstalk between the immune cells in arboviral infections. Glutamate is the most abundant neurotransmitter in the body and is capable of acting on T cells and macrophages. Using a well-defined murine model of the arbovirus chikungunya virus (CHIKV), I have shown that virus infection induced high levels of blood glutamate levels. I have also recently demonstrated the importance of crosstalk between CD4+ T cells and CD64+MHCII+ macrophages in driving CHIKV pathogenesis. Interestingly, glutamate is also a precursor of -aminobutyric acid (GABA), a pre-dominant inhibitory neurotransmitter, and can be converted to GABA, through the actions of glutamate decarboxylase. GABAergic signaling affects multiple immune functions and was reported to reduce IL-6 and IL-12 production in macrophages. IL-6 and IL-12 are key cytokines associated with CHIKV disease severity. GABA can also downplays the antigen presentation capacity of peripheral macrophages. Given that glutamate is also a precursor of GABA, I hypothesize that initiating GABAergic signallings in CD64+MHCII+ macrophages will be crucial given that they present CHIKV antigens and prime CD4+ T cells during CHIKV. Using both in vitro infection systems and in vivo murine models of CHIKV, I will aim to first identify the cellular targets affected by glutamatergic and GABAergic agents. Secondly, I will study the immunomodulatory effects of the glutamatergic and GABAergic compounds on CHIKV-specific CD4+ T cells and macrophages. Lastly, drugs that specifically target these pathways will also be assessed as possible novel therapeutics against arboviral infections. The success of this project will open new transdisciplinary research paradigms involving neuroimmunology and infectious diseases in combating arboviral diseases.
kw: neurotransmitters; glutamate; gaba; Chikungunya; immunopathogenesis; immunomodulation

title: Investigating how metabolic-epigenetic interconnection regulates inflammasome activation
abs: A common strategy used by pathogens to evade immune response and induce pathology is by manipulating host’s metabolic and epigenetic reprogramming. Lactylation, a novel histone modification elicited by hypoxia and bacterial challenges, regulates the expression of homoeostatic genes that assist in repairing. However, the relationship between lactylation and inflammation remains elusive. This proposal will investigate how lactylation and interconnected acetylation modulates inflammasome activation. Our hypothesis is that 1) lactate-mediated lactylation inhibits inflammasome activation by posttranslational modification; 2) lactylation and acetylation play distinct roles in regulating inflammasome activation; 3)SIRT1, a NAD+-dependent deacetylase, could perform immunomodulation by coordinating lactylation and acetylation. We will perform biochemical, proteomic and transcriptomic studies to decipher the underlying molecular mechanism and explore the potential of lactate and lactylation in designing host-directed therapies for diseases caused by dysregulated inflammasome activation.
kw: Lactylation, Acetylation, SIRT1, Inflammasome

title: Function and Basis of Disease in Lysosomal Amino Acid Transporters
abs: The lysosomal protein Mfsd12 was recently identified as a transporter of the amino acid cysteine. Our overseas clinical collaborators recently identified two patients from two separate pedigrees carrying compound heterozygous mutations in the MFSD12 gene. The clinical presentation of the MFSD12 patients were reminiscent of the Batten diseases neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis 3 and 7 (CLN3, CLN7), resulting from mutations in the CLN3 and MFSD8 genes respectively which also encode lysosomal transporters. While animal models of CLN3 and CLN7 disease are well characterized, which ligands they transport remain unknown. This is contrary to Mfsd12, for which the ligand is known but the disease has yet been studied in animal or cell models. Based on the similar disease presentation, structure, and lysosomal localization of these proteins, my central hypothesis is that they are lysosomal amino acid transporters and that their genetic diseases result from defective amino acid transport out of lysosomes. We will use patient-derived lymphoblast cultures and knockout mice to determine the physiological function and basis for genetic disease in Mfsd12. In parallel, we will identify the ligands of Mfsd8 and CLN3 by testing uptake of radiolabeled amino acids in HeLa cells overexpressing the transporter. Understanding how amino acids are transported out of lysosomes is important not only to accelerate development of therapeutic interventions for lysosomal storage diseases, but because this transport pathway can be a major susceptibility target in cancers reliant on lysosomal protein salvage.
kw: protein; biochemistry; transporter; lysosome; amino acids

title: Investigating the role of SATB2 in serrated colorectal cancer.
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Over 15% of sporadic colorectal cancers (CRC) develop via the serrated pathway. Histologically, early serrated lesions present with disordered crypt architecture and proliferation, but without dysplasia. Detection and removal of these serrated lesions during colonoscopy is challenging due to their inconspicuous appearance within the proximal colon. However, progression to invasive CRC is rapid and unpredictable. Thus, understanding the genetic events that drive the progression of precursor serrated adenoma or polyps into frank serrated CRC is essential to determine CRC risk and identify potential therapeutic targets. In this proposal, I hypothesise that decreased expression of the Special AT-rich binding protein 2 (SATB2) - which functions as a nuclear matrix protein to regulate gene expression – is an essential cooperating event for serrated CRC progression. My preliminary data demonstrates that SATB2 expression is significantly lower in BRAF mutant, mismatch repair deficient, microsatellite instable and CpG island methylator phenotype CRC, which are features strongly correlated with serrated CRC. Indeed, analysis of gene expression data that profiled both conventional and serrated CRC revealed a trend for lower SATB2 expression in serrated tumours. Knockdown and overexpression experiments suggest that SATB2 functions as a tumour suppressor gene in advanced CRC cell systems. Interestingly, SATB2 overexpression in the HT29 cell line - which harbours the BRAFV600E mutation - showed marked reduction in the expression of ANXA10 - an established marker of serrated CRC. Furthermore, exploratory analyses revealed that SATB2 expression is inversely correlated with CD8+ T cell migration and CD274 expression, that may have potential implications for response to immune checkpoint blockade agents. Taken together, these findings provide a strong rational to gain a detailed understanding as to how SATB2 functions in serrated CRC, with the goal of translating this knowledge into improved diagnosis and treatment of this CRC subtype.
kw: serrated colorectal cancer; tumour immunology; mouse models; PD-L1; single cell analysis

title: Investigation of a Cortical-Hypothalamic Circuitry that drives Continuous Feeding
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: The aetiology of obesity is highly variable in the human population, characterized by a wide array of maladapted feeding behaviour. There is a cognitive element in the control of appetite that can influence the susceptibility to over-feeding. Neuroimaging studies have shown a correlation between a decrease in cortical functionality and obesity. The central cognitive pathways have also been postulated to override homeostatic feeding regulation from the hypothalamus, although the mechanisms and neural correlates are not well elucidated. From a previous work, we generated an obese model by deleting synaptic active zone proteins, ELKS 1 and ELKS2, from the hypothalamus using an Nkx2.1-Cre mouse line; and termed the knockouts NkxEKK. Along with synaptic perturbations, they displayed a persistent and continuous feeding drive that lasts throughout the day. This feeding behavior has distinctions from other murine models of obesity like the diet-induced obese mice and the Lepob/ob mice model. When resting state fMRI scanning was conducted on the NkxEKK mice, along with preliminary brain activity quantifications, we saw a reduction in the volume and activation at the prefrontal cortex (PFC) of the NkxEKK mice. This model allows us to investigate the role of the cortical and hypothalamic circuitriesin voracious appetite and the dysregulation during obesity. After confirming the reduction in activity of the PFC through whole-brain light-sheet fos activity measurements, we will further characterize the cellular subtypes and endogenous role of these PFC neurons in appetite. We will also trace the connections to or from the hypothalamus using tracing tools and MRI-DTI, to understand the functional importance of these circuitries in proper feeding. The findings from this study will offer new mechanistic insight into the role of higher cognitive areas and their interaction with sub-cortical hypothalamic homeostatic regulation in the maintenance of energy homeostasis.
kw: Obesity; Neural; Prefrontal Cortex; Hypothalamus; Appetite

title: Design of nucleic acid immune agonist delivery platform technology to elicit potent and safe anti-tumor immunity
abs: Specific aims This project aims to develop a nucleic acid nanoplatform for TLR9 agonist targeted delivery and evaluate the safety, efficacy and mechanism of synergy between TLR9 agonist and radiation therapy. Hypotheses The nucleic acid platform will enable potent and safe anti-tumor immunity of TLR9 agonist and synergistically sensitize cancer radiation therapy. Methodology & approach We will establish a pooled single strand DNA (ssDNA) library for TLR9 agonist optimization. A novel DNA nanoplatform using screed TLR9 agonists will be constructed via DNA self-assemble technology. Dendritic cell (DC) targeting molecules will be screened from exponential enrichment (SELEX) platform and chemically modified to DNA nanoplatform for precise DC delivery. The safety, efficacy and mechanism of synergy between TLR9 agonist and radiation therapy will then be determined in mouse tumor models. A multiphasic treatment will be carried out, wherein the first phase involves tumor debulking with radiotherapy, while the second phase involves TLR9 agonist which is expected to reactive the suppressive TME to eradicate residual cancer cells. TME immune phenotypes will be analyzed by multiplex flowcytometry and immunohistochemistry. Feasibility Nucleic acids represent a major class of immune agonists in pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) mediated cancer immunotherapy. In this proposal, a novel nucleic acid delivery platform will be developed to improve TLR9 agonist cancer immunotherapy, spanning TLR9 agonist screening, self-assembly DNA nanotechnology for DC targeted delivery and combining TLR9 agonist with radiation therapy for synergistic cancer therapy. With a powerful base at NUS and strong expertise of the research team, we will utilize the extensive experiences in cancer immunotherapy, nucleic acids nanomedicine, and state-of-the-art research facilities to establish a powerful new strategy for immune agonists screening and delivery. The combination with radiation therapy will be studied which further enhances the clinical and translational relevance of the proposed studies.
kw: Nucleic acids nanotechnology; TLR9 agonist; radiation therapy

title: Understanding broad coronavirus neutralisation with high resolution structural definition of conformation-dependent B cell epitopes
abs: The spike (S) protein of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) is the major target for neutralising antibodies and also most currently available vaccines. While the majority of neutralising antibodies in COVID-19 patients were found to block receptor-binding of S1 subunit, antibodies binding to the well-conserved S2 subunit, which mediates the fusion between viral and host membranes, were found to be produced from memory B cells. These antibodies have cross-neutralisation activity against multiple coronaviruses including the seasonal human coronavirus (HCoV) OC43. However, the mechanism of cross-neutralisation is elusive due to the intrinsic flexibility of S2. In this project, we aim to develop new methods to determine the in-situ structures of S proteins directly on the viral membrane with cross-reactivity antibodies targeting the S2 subunit. We attempt to identify conformation-dependent and highly conserved epitopes bound by broadly cross-reacting antibodies in SARS-CoV-2 convalescent patients. By performing site-directed mutagenesis on spike protein and antibody depletion experiments, we would determine if each of the above novel epitopes are bound to neutralising antibodies in COVID-19 patient plasma. This project will establish a high-resolution structural approach to study cross-neutralising antibodies that are rapidly recalled in COVID-19 patients and define conformation-dependent and highly conserved epitopes in the S2 subunit of betacoronavirus. This will provide insights into the roles of new functional motifs in mediating viral entry and has important implications for the development of pan-coronavirus vaccines.
kw: human coronavirus, antibody, cross neutralisation, SARS-CoV-2, cryo-electron tomography, subtomogram averaging

title: Developing a chemically locked neural interface for longitudinal single-unit electrophysiology
abs: In vivo electrophysiological recording suffers from a short stable window of a few days due to micromotion at the neuron-microelectrode interface. Developmental and longitudinal electrophysiology studies are limited by the recording instability and therefore unable to chronically interrogate neural circuits at the single neuron precision. Extending the same-unit electrophysiological recording from days to a month, and even years has paramount importance for both neuroscience studies and clinical applications. Our overarching goal is to develop a neural interface that continuously and stably interrogates single neurons without signal drifting and enable knowledge generation in fundamental neuroscience and understanding of neurological disease mechanism, particularly in developing neural circuits. We hypothesize that in situ covalently bonding microelectrodes to neurons and adjacent extracellular matrix can address the challenge above. Specifically, we will chemically lock the microelectrode to specific neurons post-implantation, allowing the microelectrode to physically adapt to micromotion, and therefore eliminating the source of neural recording instability. The longitudinal neural recording technique proposed here is expected to be applied in the neuroscience community, for the study of single-cell electrophysiology longitudinally over months to years. It is particularly useful for study of developmental electrophysiology at single-cell precision. The proposed research also offers a necessary tool for studying of neurological and psychiatric diseases. We envision the longitudinally stable brain-machine interface (BCI) can be applied for treating patients with stroke or amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and pave the way for pediatric BCI.
kw: Brain-computer interface; electrophysiology; neurological diseases

title: The role and therapeutic application of ergothioneine in age-related macular degeneration and other eye disorders.
abs: The present proposal aims to shed light on the role of ergothioneine (ET) in the healthy eye and potential therapeutic efficacy against age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and other eye diseases by investigating: • The levels of ET in human (commercial cadaver eye) and animal eyes • Correlation of peripheral ET levels with eye levels in humans (plasma and aqueous humor) and rodent models • Investigating levels of ET in the eye of AMD patients versus normal controls (aqueous humor) • Investigating the mechanisms of protection by ET using cultured retinal epithelial cells exposed to relevant forms of stress • Using an animal model of blue light-induced retinal injury to establish whether oral supplementation or topical application may slow or prevent the progression of retinal injury We hypothesize that lower levels of ET in the eye predispose individuals to high risk of AMD and other ocular diseases and thereby supplementation of ET may prevent, slow, or mitigate the progression of degenerative eye diseases by protecting the eye from oxidative damage and inflammation, especially in the retinal pigment epithelium.
kw: Ergothioneine, macular degeneration, antioxidant, oxidative stress

title: Targeting WRN helicase as a synthetic lethal target in ARID1A deficient cancers
abs: Faithful duplication of the genome depends on accurate DNA replication. As several endogenous and exogenous insults cause genotoxic replication fork stalling, cells have a plethora of proteins to stabilize, repair, and restart stalled forks. Dysfunction of this process causes replication stress, which is a common feature in cancer and an emerging target for novel targeted therapies. This work aims to investigate the nature of stalled replication forks in ARID1A deficient cancer cells, and the role of the Werner (WRN) helicase in stabilizing/restarting stalled forks in the absence of ARID1A. ARID1A is a subunit of the chromatin remodelling BAF complex and is a frequently mutated gene in variety of cancers (~10% of all cancers). Mutations in ARID1A typically result in loss of function making it a difficult target. Understanding compensatory mechanisms in ARID1A-deficient cancer cells are vital to uncover synthetic lethal strategies for therapy. ARID1A deficiency has been shown to be associated with replication stress and loss of mis-match repair (MMR) pathways. However, it is not known if there are specific regions in the genome that show patterns of replication stress, nor is it known how stalled forks are restarted in ARID1A deficient cells. Based on preliminary in-silico data showing dependency of ARID1A deficient cells on the Werner (WRN) helicase, we hypothesize that, like cells with microsatellite instability (MSI), ARID1A deficiency causes excessive stalling of replication forks in a site-specific manner with dependence on WRN helicase for their stabilization, protection and restart. We propose to study this phenomenon in ARID1A wild-type and deficient isogenic cell lines, with inducible knockdown of WRN. This work is expected to identify a synthetic lethal therapeutic vulnerability in cells lacking ARID1A and clarify the nature of replication defects in cancers with loss of this frequently mutated tumor suppressor.
kw: gastric cancer; replication stress; genome instability; ARID1A; WRN helicase; synthetic lethality

title: Placental tryptophan metabolism: the link between maternal mood and offspring neurodevelopment
inst: IHDP - Institute for Human Development and Potential
abs: Intrauterine signals of maternal stress received by the fetus via the placenta are thought to program the fetal brain during pregnancy and influence subsequent neurodevelopment. Nonetheless, the exact mechanisms by which the effects of antenatal maternal stress are transmitted to the fetal brain to alter developmental trajectories remain unclear. Tryptophan is an essential amino acid that is vital for healthy growth and development. In the placenta, tryptophan is catabolised via the serotonin or kynurenine pathways that can generate metabolites with neuroactive functions among many others. Various rodent models of maternal antenatal stress (eg. sleep deprivation and physical restraint) further implicate placental inflammation with altered placental or fetal brain tryptophan processing, which could program anxiety-like behaviour and social behavioural deficits in offspring. However, whether this is also the case in humans is unclear. We hypothesise that high maternal mental stress leads to inflammation-induced dysregulation of the tryptophan pathway in the placenta, which has detrimental consequences for offspring neurodevelopment. We aim to associate altered placental expression of tryptophan metabolic pathway genes and tryptophan metabolites with the inflammatory cytokine profile of high maternal antenatal mental stress and available offspring neurodevelopmental outcomes in the GUSTO cohort by using a wide range of experimental techniques including qPCRs, protein assays, high-performance liquid chromatography and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, and statistical analysis. Furthermore, to understand tryptophan processing between the mother, placenta and child, we will also examine the relationship between the placental tryptophan metabolites with the tryptophan metabolites previously measured in the maternal circulation and cord blood. Possible mediating factors such as sleep will be explored as well. The proposed study will be the first to define the relationship between maternal stress, placental tryptophan metabolism and offspring neurodevelopmental outcomes in humans.
kw: placenta; tryptophan; kynurenine; pregnancy; neurodevelopment; mental health

title: Deciphering the biological functions of mRNA pyrimidine-rich tract and its putative binders in regulating insulin-controlled translation
abs: The adipose tissue serves as an endocrine organ and the major site for regulating energy expenditure and storage, and when dysregulated leads to metabolic disorders. Our understanding of adipocyte biology is primarily derived from the studies of its transcriptional cascades, however, the translational control of gene expression in adipocyte has barely been explored. Translation has emerged as a crucial phase for cells to modulate gene expression during stress response. We have developed a platform integrating polysome profiling, spike-in and RNA-seq to study nutrient-controlled translation in adipocytes. We have depicted the insulin-stimulated translatome in adipocytes, revealing a discordance between the mRNA abundance and the translational efficiency of a subset of genes. In this proposed study, we aim to decipher the biological functions of the interaction between the pyrimidine-rich tracts on the mRNA and its RNA binding proteins. Our preliminary data shows that insulin-control of translation drives energy metabolism in mouse adipocytes. Insulin also increases the translation of several adipokines, suggesting that these adipokines are regulated at post-transcriptional level. Taken together, we hypothesize that insulin selectively enhances the translation of AdipoQ (adipokine) and Pgk1 (glycolysis) through modulating the interaction between pyrimidine-rich tract at the 5’UTR and RNA binding proteins. To test the hypothesis, we will perform reporter assay to characterize the regulatory elements on the UTRs in adipocytes. Thereafter, we will perform functional studies on the RNA binding proteins in adipocytes. Finally, we will test our hypothetical model in human primary adipocytes. The successful completion of this proposal will enhance our understanding of how the untranslated regions on the mRNA controls protein synthesis implicated in adipokine production, carbohydrate metabolism and energy homeostasis. The study will also lead to the discovery of RNA binding proteins and RNA motifs, thus contributing to the search of translation-controlling therapy for metabolic disorders associated with insulin resistance.
kw: mRNA translation; Adipokines; Polysome profiling; Insulin; Glycolysis; Oxidative phosphorylation

title: 4D neural organoid model to study the response of glial cells towards dynamic biophysical changes and aging
abs: The insufficient understanding of the tissue microenvironment changes due to aging or degeneration reduces the effectiveness of potential therapeutic approaches. In particular, tissue biophysical changes are found to be correlated with aging and diseased nerve tissues but there is a lack of a good model to understand the mechanisms better. More specifically, how dynamic changes in the extracellular matrix affect the functions of human oligodendrocytes remains unknown. Here, we propose an approach of using a combination of dynamic hydrogel and organoid to model after the dynamic micro-environmental changes to the human nerve tissues. The overall objective of this project is to establish a 4-Dimensional organoid platform to study the effect of dynamic microenvironment changes on glial functions, with a focus on myelination. We will develop a new organoid platform based on a 3D dynamic hydrogel whose properties change over time as the fourth dimension, to simulate the dynamic changes in vivo. We hypothesize that the biophysical changes in a human neural organoid model are similar to aging where the matrix stiffness decrease gradually over time. We will also manipulate the hydrogel stiffness adjacent to the organoid to simulate local degeneration or tissue damage through stiffening or softening the hydrogels. Through this platform, we will investigate the effect of dynamic stiffness changes on oligodendrocyte differentiation and myelination in an organoid and thus identify how matrix stiffness changes contribute to the age-related impairment in myelination. This work will provide a unique approach to model microenvironmental changes after the nerve tissues are damaged due to aging, diseases, or injuries. The results will help understand the glial cells' role under these changes. Subsequently, potential novel therapeutic targets may be identified to slow down the disease progression and aging process in the brain and spinal cord.
kw: organoid; hydrogel; dynamic; stiffness; aging; neurodegeneration																						organoid; hydrogel; dynamic; stiffness; aging; neurodegeneration

title: Genomic study on the structural conformations and epigenetic landscapes of Epstein-Barr virus associated malignancies.
abs: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) has been implicated with multiple malignancies such as Burkitt lymphoma (BL), Natural-killer/T-cell lymphomas (NKTCL), gastric adenocarcinoma (GA), peripheral T-cell lymphoma-not otherwise specified (PTCL-NOS), diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL), aggressive NK-cell leukemia (ANKL) and nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC). Since these malignancies are virus-associated, the malignant cells must have developed adaptive immunity against the innate immune of the host, and this has refocused much research on how immune evasion was achieved and could be targeted. It was also reported that PD-L1/PD-L2 genetic aberrations was observed in high frequencies within NKTCL (23%), ANKL (57%), EBV+ DLBCL (19%) and PTCL-NOS (15%). Within the same study, not-always EBV-associated malignancies were found to harbor significantly (P=0.0001) more PD-L1/PD-L2 genetic aberrations within the EBV+ (33/148) than EBV- (12/236) samples. This suggests that EBV could reshape the structural landscapes and regulatory marks of cancer genomes and allow the preferential occurrence of structural rearrangements at the PD-L1/PD-L2 loci. Thus, Aim 1 tries to understand if there is any interplay between EBV positivity and topological-associated domains that could explain the higher occurrences of PD-L1/PD-L2 genomic rearrangements in EBV+ malignancies that might be relevant for immune checkpoint therapy. In addition, Aim 2 aims to explore the consequential effect of a structurally altered genome for any dysregulated pathway and regulatory marks that could be relevant for tumorigenesis and drug targetability. Consequently, we also examine extrachromosomal DNA, a subclass of structural rearrangements, that drives tumor evolution and genetic heterogeneity in these human cancers and never in normal cells. Lastly, Aim 3 investigates if any of the human/EBV’s oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes are involved in the formation of ecDNA that could associate with the prognosis of patients and potentially be exploited as a biomarker of clinical response to current treatments.
kw: genomics; Epstein-Barr; epigenomics; chromatin conformation, ecDNA

title: LIquid Biopsy EaRly to expedite Targeted therapY (LIBERTY) in newly diagnosed advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC)
abs: Background: The discovery of therapeutically targetable oncogenic driver alterations has led to marked improvements in NSCLC outcomes. Targeted agents have been approved for an expanding list of biomarkers, including BRAF, EGFR, HER2 and KRAS mutations, MET alterations and ALK, NTRK, RET and ROS1 fusions. Consequently, the accurate and timely identification of targetable alterations with diagnostic molecular profiling is crucial. Previously, we demonstrated the utility, feasibility and cost-effectiveness of upfront tissue next-generation sequencing (NGS), and approximately 75% of advanced NSCLC patients in Singapore harboured a targetable alteration. However, significant limitations with tissue NGS remain such as insufficient tissue, scheduling limitations, need for repeat biopsies and long turnaround times. This leads to delays in commencing appropriate first-line therapy, including in patients without a targetable alteration. Liquid biopsies, using plasma circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA), has the potential to overcome these issues. Hypothesis: Early plasma genotyping will significantly shorten the time to initiation of first-line therapy in advanced NSCLC. Specific Aims: (1) To demonstrate the clinical utility of liquid biopsy in newly diagnosed advanced NSCLC; and (2) to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of incorporating liquid biopsy in the diagnostic testing paradigm. Methods: Prospective single-arm clinical study of LIquid Biopsy EaRly to expedite Targeted therapY (LIBERTY) in newly diagnosed advanced NSCLC. Patients with suspected advanced lung cancer, at the time of or prior to diagnostic tissue biopsy, will have plasma NGS testing. NGS results will be returned to treating clinicians using a rapid assay (turnaround time < 1 week). Primary endpoint is time from diagnosis to targeted therapy initiation compared with historical control. Significance: This study may improve clinical outcomes through earlier initiation of first-line therapy in metastatic NSCLC. In addition, there may be significant reductions in healthcare costs by identifying the most cost-effective interventions in the diagnostic testing paradigm of NSCLC.
kw: Circulating tumour DNA; Diagnostic Testing; Liquid biopsy; Lung cancer; Non-small cell lung cancer

title: Role of mesenchymal stromal cell exosomes in meniscal repair
abs: The failure rates of meniscal tear suture repairs remain high despite continued advancement in surgical techniques. This is primarily due to limitations imposed by the inherent poor blood supply in the meniscus which results in compromised healing. With poor healing and loss of meniscus function, existing symptoms from the meniscus tear are likely to persist, and subsequent secondary osteoarthritis is predisposed to occur with the increased tibiofemoral pressures. Mesenchymal stromal/stem cells (MSCs) possess immunomodulatory and regenerative properties and have demonstrated efficacy as a cell-based strategy for repair of meniscal tears. Increasingly, the therapeutic efficacy of MSCs is attributed to its paracrine secretion, particularly exosomes, which serve as intercellular communication vehicles with the ability to interact with multiple cell types and to elicit diverse cellular responses. Our preliminary findings have observed that MSC exosomes dose-dependently enhance cell migration, proliferation, and tube formation of endothelial cells, which are cellular processes relevant to angiogenesis during meniscal repair. Additionally, we have demonstrated that MSC exosomes promote cell migration, proliferation, and matrix synthesis of meniscal chondrocytes. With poor vascularity limiting the healing potential of the meniscus, we expect that future repair techniques will need to address the need for vascularization to enable mobilization and proliferation of host cells for optimal tissue repair. We therefore hypothesize that MSC exosomes could interact with resident cell types such as endothelial cells and meniscal chondrocytes at the lesion site to promote well-orchestrated processes of angiogenesis, migration, proliferation, and matrix synthesis to bring about repair and regeneration of meniscal tears. In this proposed study, we aim 1) to investigate the effects of human MSC exosomes for meniscal repair in a rat meniscus defect model, and 2) to investigate the cellular processes modulated by MSC exosomes and the associated mechanisms underlying exosome-mediated meniscal regeneration.
kw: Mesenchymal stromal cells; Stem cell; Exosomes; Meniscal injury; Meniscal repair

title: Developing bioengineered microbe to secrete GLP-1, PYY, Oxyntomodulin and butyrate to reduce appetite for treatment and prevention of obesity and diabetes.
abs: Obesity poses a huge global public health problem. Growing evidence suggests that the gut-brain axis regulates appetite via gut peptides like glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), peptide YY (PYY) and oxyntomodulin (OXM). In addition, it has been proposed that microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids such as butyrate play a part in preventing and treating obesity by promoting fatty acid oxidation, inhibiting fat accumulation and stimulating gut peptides secretion. Hence, increasing GLP-1, PYY, OXM and butyrate production are promising therapeutic strategies against obesity and obesity-associated comorbidities, such as diabetes mellitus. Human and mice studies using parenteral administration of these gut peptides in combination have shown that delivering a combination of these gut peptides at lower doses (than if used singly) to target multiple hormonal pathways had a greater impact on body weight and appetite, with lesser side effects. However, these therapies are mainly parenteral and invasive. A few published works have demonstrated that microbes can be engineered to secrete GLP-1 or OXM, or increase butyrate production, and these had been administered in mice. These studies showed better glucose and lipid profile of treated mice. However, none had studied the effect of secreting multiple gut peptides in bioengineered microbes. In this study, I hypothesise that administration of bioengineered microbes secreting GLP-1, OXM, PYY and butyrate can render a synergistic effect to reduce food intake and body weight. I aim to evaluate the effect of bioengineered microbe secreting GLP-1, PYY, OXM and butyrate on food intake, body weight and glucose homeostasis in mice models, both as prophylaxis and treatment. The outcome of this research will serve an important foundation of using bioengineered microbe to modulate hormonal and butyrate level to mitigate obesity and treat diabetes, which are fast becoming huge global health crisis.

The two most common cognitive syndromes in PD, PD dementia (PDD) and PD mild CI (PD-MCI), were operationally defined in diagnostic and assessment guidelines by the International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society (MDS).
