title: 68Ga-FAPI-46 PET/CT of Peritoneal Metastases in Patients with Gastric Cancer
abs: Peritoneal metastasis is one of the most common and life-threatening metastases in gastric cancer (GC) patients. However, despite the significant advancement of technology, the diagnosis of peritoneal metastases remains challenging. Exploring new imaging modalities for early detection and accurate assessment of peritoneal metastases are crucially needed in the clinical management of patients with GCs. Fibroblast activation protein (FAP), a type II transmembrane cell surface serine proteinase belonging to the dipeptidyl peptidase family, is highly expressed on cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) of over 90% of epithelial cancers and is rarely expressed in normal tissues. Thus, targeting FAP is a promising approach for tumour imaging in various types of cancer. This project aims to explore a precise FAP-targeted molecular imaging in patients with peritoneal metastases of GC. We hypothesize that 68Ga-FAPI-46 PET/CT will outperform other existing imaging methodologies in the detection of primary tumors and peritoneal metastases, and make an important impact on clinical practice in patients with advanced GC. We will define the biodistribution of 68Ga-FAPI-46 in normal and cancer tissues including primary and metastatic lesions in patients with GC, determine the sensitivity, specificity and positive predictive value of 68Ga-FAPI-46 PET/CT for the detection of primary tumors and peritoneal metastases confirmed by histopathology of biopsy, as compared to the high resolution CT, determine the correlate between SUV from 68Ga-FAPI-46 PET/CT and expression level of FAP from IHC, and determine To determine the proportion of patients in which the addition of 68Ga-FAPI-46 PET/CT to the current management algorithm leads to a change in treatment strategy. The proposed project will promote excellence in translational and clinical research on FAP-targeted molecular imaging, and benefit patients in more accurate staging and to improve treatment decision making, with the goal of improving clinical outcomes for GC patients.
kw: gastric cancer; peritoneal metastases; fibroblast activation protein (FAP); tumor microenvironment (TME); 68Ga-FAPI-46; PET/MR

title: Deciphering the role of MACIR/C5orf30 in diffuse large B cell lymphoma
abs: Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma (DLBCL) is the most common haematological cancer worldwide and in Singapore. ~40% of cases relapse despite initial responses to standard first-line chemoimmunotherapy, highlighting the need for strategies to identify and treat “high-risk” DLBCL. Using an in-silico screen to analyse protein-coding transcripts across 8 independent patient cohorts for consistent survival prediction, we identified a novel and unobvious prognostic indicator, MACIR/C5orf30. The association of MACIR/C5orf30 overexpression with poor survival was consistent across 3931 DLBCL patients from 13 cohorts, and stronger than DLBCL biomarkers in clinical use. Little is known about MACIR/C5orf30, except that it regulates macrophage function in rheumatoid arthritis. Our preliminary data suggests that MACIR/C5orf30 is expressed within DLBCL cells but appears to primarily mediate cell-extrinsic phenomena after chemotherapy (interaction with the microenvironment). In this proposal, we intend to characterize MACIR/C5orf30 in DLBCL, specifically interrogating its role in tumorigenesis and modulation of the lymphoma microenvironment. We propose to create MACIR/C5orf30-modulated transgenic mouse models to determine its effect on lymphomagenesis and chemoresistance in vivo. Simultaneously, we propose to characterise a MACIR/C5orf30-scultped microenvironment using samples from clinically annotated DLBCL cohorts and state-of-the-art high-dimensional microscopy with spatial analytics. This will elucidate the nature of the immune infiltrate and its interaction with lymphoma cells in MACIR/C5orf30 high and low cases. Finally, we will delve into the molecular role of MACIR/C5orf30 in modulating the microenvironment of DLBCL by studying the effects of MACIR/C5orf30 knockdown and overexpression on a) the membrane and secreted protein compartment of lymphoma/ normal B-cells and b) phenotypes in tumour-immune cell co-culture systems, in the setting of chemotherapy. We expect this project to: outline the mechanistic basis for MACIR/C5orf30 as a clinically applicable biomarker in DLBCL; identify avenues for therapeutic intervention for MACIR/C5orf30-high DLBCL; and expand our general understanding of cell-intrinsic features in cancer that influence the tumour microenvironment.
kw: MACIR; DLBCL; immune microenvironment; spatial; high-dimensional microscopy

title: Pathogen/Pathway to Vaccine Development to Enhance Singapore’s Pandemic Resilience (PrepVax) Stage 1 Funding
abs: PrepVax aims to enhance Singapore's pandemic resilience by leveraging existing capabilities and build up local capabilities to progress pandemic vaccine asset(s) from antigen design to early phase clinical trials.
kw: Pathogen/Pathway to Vaccine Development to Enhance Singapore’s Pandemic Resilience, PrepVax

title: An elucidation in KRAS-driven lung cancer patients of circulating T cells that are KRAS specific.
abs: Somatic mutations in cancer presented by major histocompatibility (MHC), neoantigens, are targets for cancer vaccine-based therapy. Antigen-specific cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTL) from peripheral blood or tumor tissue of cancer patients have demonstrated CD8 T cell-mediated anti-tumor immunity in many successful clinical trials. Identification of immunogenic neoantigens and their cognate T cells represent the most crucial and rate-limiting steps in the development of personalized cancer immunotherapies. The overall aim of this study is to identify circulating T cells in patients with KRAS-mutated lung cancer that are immune-reactive against patient-specific KRAS mutations. The identification of such cells has several potential downstream applications such as the development of a peptide to TCR sequence pipeline, as well as serial monitoring of the immune reactivity of patients to their cancer antigen. Specifically, in patients with KRAS mutant lung cancer, the aims of this study are: 1. To identify the immune reactivity of circulating CD8 T cells from a fresh blood draw to patient-specific 8, 9, 10, 11, and 12-mer KRAS mutant peptides on T cell interferon-gamma elispots and flow cytometry 2. To perform expansion with KRAS mutant peptides of T cells (ex vivo peptide vaccination) to further establish patient immune reactivity to patient-specific KRAS mutation 3. To perform HLA typing, evaluation of peptide MHC (pMHC) complex stability to identify pMHC multimers that can then be used for identification of KRAS-specific T cells through alpha beta T cell receptor sequencing 10 patients will be recruited and their PBMC will be isolated then tested for immune-reactivity towards KRAS mutant peptides using elispots, flow cytometry and peptide MHC binding assays. Additionally, patients found to have immune reactive cells will have cell sorted selection of antigen specific T cells for TCR sequencing.
kw: Neoantigen, KRAS, TCR, T Cells

title: Developing a tunable matrix to investigate mechanosensing functions of Yap in gastric cancer
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Gastric cancer is one of the most prevalent and deadliest cancers worldwide, necessitating the development of new treatment methods tackling its progression. Current research is centred around the biochemical pathways governing disease progression, but much less is known about the contribution of mechanical properties exerted by the tumour microenvironment and how cancer cells respond to these mechanical features. Yap is a transcriptional regulator overexpressed in gastric tumours that is sensitive to mechanical changes, making it a potential mediator of tumour-environment interactions. To investigate the role of Yap as a mechanosensor in gastric cancer, we propose to develop a 3D gastric cancer organoid system capable of recapitulating key biological features of human gastric cancer that is amenable to controlled modulation of matrix stiffness across a physiological range measured in human gastric tumours. This system would support the direct evaluation of changes in matrix stiffness on organoid morphology, tumourigenic behaviour and bulk gene expression profiles. We will concurrently generate Yap knockout organoids to assess if loss of Yap can block the changes in organoid tumourigenicity in response to matrix stiffness, which would support the role of Yap as a mechanosensor in this system. Finally, we will validate the transcriptomic profiles generated through this study using primary mouse and human gastric tumours to determine the clinical translatability of our identified targets. Together, this project should yield a physiologically relevant 3D tunable organoid system combining both biological and mechanical features of gastric cancer capable of disease modelling and therapeutic efforts, and support the development of novel drug targets downstream of Yap activity that can be exploited for the treatment of gastric cancer.
kw: Gastric cancer; organoids; synthetic matrix; mechanobiology

title: Exploiting the Clec9A targeting vaccine platform to develop a safe and effective dengue vaccine
abs: Despite decades of research, dengue continues to represent a significant public health threat in Singapore and the Asia-Pacific region, with climate change contributing to its expansion beyond the tropical and subtropical belts. With no effective treatment against dengue, vaccination represents the most economically viable approach. Two tetravalent live attenuated virus vaccine formulations have reached the market and late clinical development stage respectively, but these vaccine candidates have met with shortcomings including complicated manufacturing processes, safety concerns and/or imbalanced protection against the four dengue virus (DENV) serotypes. Our limited understanding of the immune correlates of protection has hampered our ability to undertake a rational approach to design live virus-based dengue vaccines. The development of subunit dengue vaccines overcomes those limitations. However, candidate vaccine molecules are generally poorly immunogenic, and delivery systems and adjuvants are needed for an effective vaccination strategy. In this project, we will exploit a powerful vaccine delivery platform that targets vaccine antigen candidates to surface molecule Clec9A expressed by a dendritic cell subset that is common to mice and humans. The Clec9A targeting strategy consists of fusing the antigen vaccine candidate to the heavy chains of a proprietary anti-Clec9A monoclonal antibody (mAb). Our previous work has shown that this platform is particularly effective at delivering weak immunogens and inducing exceptionally sustained immune responses in both murine and non-human primate animal models. Here, Clec9A Ab constructs harbouring domain III of the Envelope protein (EDIII) of DENV will be engineered, using serotype-specific or consensus EDIII sequences. We will characterize in mice the immune responses and protective efficacy upon prime-boost immunization. The effect of dengue pre-existing immunity on vaccination efficacy will also be evaluated. Lastly, we will explore the immunogenicity of a bivalent Clec9A mAb construct that harbours both EDIII and a conserved CD8 T cell protective epitope.
kw: Clec9A vaccine targeting; dengue virus; envelope domain III; consensus EDIII

title: Targeting RNA methylation for sarcopenia
abs: Skeletal muscle is the largest organ in the human body that is critical for mechanical activity. The progressive loss of muscle mass and strength associated with biological aging, known as sarcopenia, leads to decreased lifespan and quality of life. Although several aging-related biological changes have been linked to sarcopenia, little is known about its genetics and molecular basis. Our preliminary results suggest that m6A RNA methylation is regulated by FOXO, a key regulator of longevity, and acts as a driving force for the aging-induced muscle wasting. Increased m6A activities lead to proteotoxicity in aging muscles while inhibition of m6A pathway alleviates the aging-induced muscle defects. Consistent with animal results, we also observed high levels of m6A and aggregated proteins in the muscles of sarcopenic patients. To further elucidate the regulation of RNA methylation in aging muscles, we will: 1) Characterize the FOXOs-m6A signaling in aging muscles; 2) Identify the m6A methylated RNAs that trigger sarcopenia; and 3) Validate the roles of m6A methylation in sarcopenic patients. Together, our study will uncover an unexplored mechanism of how RNA methylation triggers sarcopenia and propose a potential strategy to improve therapeutic efficacy by suppressing m6A activities.
kw: Sarcopenia, m6A RNA methylation, FOXO

title: Aetiology of Idiopathic Scoliosis and mechanism of spinal cord regeneration
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: The spine consists of the vertebral column encasing the spinal cord. Idiopathic scoliosis (IS) represents a common debilitating spine disorder. Abnormal spine curvatures in IS result in defective posture and gait, chronic back pain and breathing difficulties, severely limiting the quality of life. Current treatment options are limited to physiotherapy, bracing and invasive surgical interventions. Consequently, research into IS is warranted to uncover the pathobiological mechanisms for better therapeutic strategies. Another common affliction of the spine is spinal cord injury. The mammalian spinal cord has limited regeneration capacity, and patients often suffer from varying degrees of paralysis. We and others have established that the zebrafish is a very good in vivo model for investigating the biological basis of scoliosis as well as spinal cord regeneration. In particular, our pioneering work established ciliary motility-driven transport of catecholamines in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and assembly of a glycoprotein fiber called Reissner fiber (RF). RF binds catecholamines and presents to CSF-contacting neurons (CSF-cNs) for induction of Urotensin peptides which signal via their receptor on trunk skeletal muscles to bring about spine straightening. Here, we have proposed to investigate 3 important aspects that will further inform us how the cilia-CSF-RF-Urotensin axis acts and uncover novel mechanisms driving spinal cord regeneration. First, we will investigate how precisely Urotensin signaling causes proper spine morphogenesis using zebrafish carrying mutations and transgenes for the Urotensin pathway. Secondly, using mice unable to make RF or mutants for cilia motility, we aim to examine whether the zebrafish pathway is conserved in mammals. Finally, we will exploit the regenerative potential of the zebrafish spinal cord to examine CSF flow, RF and ciliary transcription factors for spinal cord regeneration. Our findings will provide the much-needed insights into mechanisms causing IS and provide new directions that could be exploited for efficient spine cord regeneration.
kw: Idiopathic scoliosis; cilia; Reissner fiber; Urotensin; spinal cord; regeneration

title: Influence of metabolic disease on mast cell physiology and antiviral function during dengue
abs: Dengue virus induces a wide spectrum of disease from mild and self-resolving febrile illness to severe disease characterized by vascular leakage and organ/tissue damage. Although the mechanisms that lead to severe dengue are not fully understood, several risk factors have been identified that make a patient more likely to experience complications, including metabolic diseases such as diabetes and obesity. Severe dengue has also been linked to activation of a specialized type of immune cell, the mast cell (MC), which are granulated cells found lining blood vessels and at the host-environment interface. Intriguingly, MCs have been independently implicated in metabolic disease and they increase in density during metabolic disorders. Our previous studies also identified that metabolic pathways are significantly perturbed in vivo in mice during therapeutic targeting of dengue disease with MC-stabilizing drugs. These observations raise questions of whether metabolic perturbations in MCs could exacerbate dengue disease severity. We hypothesize that diet-induced changes in the density/distribution of MCs in vivo and metabolic reprogramming that results from metabolic disorders could influence downstream proinflammatory mediator release by MCs. We propose here to address these questions first by combining mouse models of metabolic dysregulation, mast cell sufficiency/deficiency, and dengue infection. Furthermore, we will corroborate these findings in human samples from donors with metabolic disease and from a clinical trial testing MC-stabilizing drugs in humans with dengue. The resulting information will allow us to understand how metabolic diseases influence MC antiviral responses and the functional role of MCs in dengue disease severity during metabolic disease. Our results will also provide insights into metabolic pathways that could be targeted to reduce the risk of developing severe dengue and may lead to improved therapeutics for those at highest risk of developing severe disease.
kw: Dengue virus; metabolic disease; mast cell

title: Engineered Tumor Slice Cultures for Personalized Drug Testing
abs: Patient tumor-derived tissue slices represent a highly attractive ex vivo model for personalized drug testing as the model preserves, at least transiently, the original tissue architecture as well as cancer and stromal composition in the native extracellular matrix of the patient’s tumor. However, these models are currently limited by reduced viability of the tumor slices after few days in culture. We hypothesize that viability of patient-derived tumor slices can be prolonged using engineered hydrogels to provide optimized mechanical and biochemical support. To date, this has not been investigated. Our data (patent filed) reveals that hydrogels with tunable properties not only support tumor slice cultures generated from head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) patient tumors, modular investigation into material parameters also indicates that certain material properties can further enhance the viability of these tissue slices in culture. We further posit that these engineered tumor slice cultures also preserve the composition of patient tumors for the derivation of accurate response to immune checkpoint inhibition (ICI) reflective of that in vivo and in patients, as well as generate novel readouts that may be predictive of ICI response. As these organotypic models represent the closest representation possible to patient tumors, these models would be highly valuable for rapid and accurate assessment of the likelihood of a patient responding to drugs, especially ICI therapies. The proposed Aims are: Aim 1. To successfully establish ex vivo HNSCC humanized PDX tumor slice models using hydrogels for at least 1 week in culture Aim 2. To establish ex vivo HNSCC tumor slice models direct from patient tumor tissue using hydrogels and deeply characterize the composition and molecular profile of engineered tumor slice cultures over time Aim 3. To conduct drug testing on engineered tumor slice cultures and correlate responses to humanized PDX models and HNSCC patients
kw: tumor slice, personalized drug testing, cancer, immune checkpoint inhibitors, biomaterials

title: Role and therapeutic potential of LRG1 in rheumatoid arthritis
abs: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a systemic chronic autoimmune disease characterized by destructive polyarthritis and extra-articular manifestations. Over 50% of RA patients are forced to stop working within 6 years of being diagnosed, which not only affects the sufferers’ quality of life but also imposes a substantial economic burden on their family, healthcare systems, and society. Current guidelines and outcome measures for RA focus on RA as a single disease, whereas comorbidities are often underdiagnosed and undertreated. Unfortunately, around 74% of patients do not respond well to the standard of care. Furthermore, a variety of side effects have been reported for existing antirheumatic drugs. Leucine-rich α2 glycoprotein 1 (LRG1) is a multifunctional protein. We and others have demonstrated LRG1’s roles in endothelial cell activation, extracellular matrix (ECM) homeostasis, immune cell function, and cell senescence, all of which contribute to the development and progression of RA. Indeed, LRG1 polymorphism has been reported in patients with RA, and LRG1 is significantly induced in the serum and synovial tissue of RA patients. Importantly, Lrg1-/- mice are resistant to collagen-induced arthritis in vivo. We, therefore, hypothesize that LRG1 drives RA progression by modulating broad spectrum pathological processes. To test this hypothesis, we aim to 1) establish the association of serum LRG1 levels with the development and progression of RA and RA-associated cardiovascular complications; 2) investigate the role of LRG1 in RA pathophysiology; 3) evaluate the treatment efficacy of novel LRG1 blocking antibody using a wide range of histopathological, molecular, and biochemical techniques as well as various preclinical experimental models. We anticipate that the outcome of this study will lead to the identification of reliable serum biomarkers for RA progression and the development of cardiovascular comorbidities, provide novel insights into the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying RA and assist the development of more effective therapeutics for RA.
kw: Rheumatoid arthritis, synovial fibroblasts, Lrg1, senescence, therapeutics, biomarkers

title: Preclinical evaluation of candidate PKD drugs in kidney organoid xenograft model and genetic animal model.
abs: Polycystic kidney disease (PKD) represents one of the most common genetic kidney diseases, which still has no cure. Autosomal dominant (ADPKD) and autosomal recessive (ARPKD) polycystic kidney diseases represent the most prevalent forms of PKD. ADPKD, typically manifests in adulthood, has an occurrence of 1:1000. While PKD1 accounts for approximately 80% of ADPKD cases, PKD2 is responsible for around 15% of ADPKD cases. ARPKD, mainly caused by mutations in PKHD1, has an estimated incidence of 1:20,000, commonly manifests in utero or during neonatal stage. Although ADPKD and ARPKD are caused by different types of genetic lesions, both diseases share a myriad of disease phenotypes, as well as many common mechanistic underpinnings. Revelation of disease pathways that are commonly shared by ADPKD and ARPKD will help identify targetable pathways for developing novel drugs. In our previous OFIRG project (NMRC/OFIRG/0076/2018), we have developed a patient induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived kidney organoid model that can recapitulate principal disease phenotypes of both ARPKD and ADPKD in a dish. This PKD kidney organoid model revealed regulatory pathways that can be commonly harnessed for managing cyst severity. Employing ARPKD patient iPSC-derived kidney organoids and gene-edited human embryonic stem cell (ESC)-derived ADPKD kidney organoids, we have tested the effects of 22 compounds on cyst formation. We have identified two candidate drugs that showed remarkable effects in cyst inhibition in both ARPKD and ADPKD kidney organoids. In this project, we will employ both in vitro and in vivo models to perform preclinical evaluation of these two candidate drugs. The success of this project will deepen our understanding of the pathogenetic mechanisms of human PKD, as well as develop prospective treatment options for PKD patients.
kw: Kidney organoid; polycystic kidney disease; drug validation; preclinical animal model; organoid xenograft

title: Wide-field multicolor fluorescence dynamic imaging for real-time delineation of tumor resection margins in the head and neck
abs: Complete surgical resection of the tumor for Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) remains challenging, given the devastating side effects of aggressive surgery and the anatomic proximity to vital structures. To address the clinical challenges here, we propose a wide-field, label-free imaging tool that can assist surgeons delineate tumor margins real-time. We assume that autofluorescence lifetime is a natural indicator of the health level of tissues and ratio-metric measurement of the emission-decay state to the emission-peak state of excited fluorophores will enable fast, wide-field fluorescence lifetime mapping of tissues. We assume autofluorescence lifetime mapping will minimize influence of inhomogeneous illumination, tissue scattering, and other factors confounder the accuracy of fluorescence intensity imaging. We also hypothesis that the rapid macroscope imaging will better adapt to irregular surfaces of tissues at a reasonable distance and fits best in a clinical scenario. Specifically, we will first develop the imaging system, Widefield Multicolor Fluorescence Dynamic Imaging (WMFDI), with our novel relative fluorescence lifetime algorithm, using a rigid endoscope to enable easy access to all regions of the oral cavity, a dual wavelength excitation and a multichannel optics module to enable fast acquisition of hyperspectral information to allow for deep-learning evaluation. We will then pursue a pilot trial where WMFDI imagery will be acquired of surgical bed both prior to and following surgery in patients undergoing head and neck surgeries. Statistical image analysis will be performed to identify image features and generate classifiers for sensitive and specific cancerous, pre-cancerous, and normal tissue detection. Once good agreement is achieved between histological analysis of biopsies and the image classifiers, we will perform a preliminary clinical trial, enabled by online, real time processing of imaging results that evaluates the utility of WMFDI in guiding additional (as needed) sections that are missed by standard visual assessment and palpation.
kw: wide-field fluorescence dynamic imaging; tumor decarcation; precision surgery and therapy

title: Determining the molecular basis of Noddosome activation in human
abs: Noddosome complexes, composed of innate immune receptors, NOD1 or NOD2, and its downstream adaptor protein, RIP2 (also known as RIPK2, RICK, etc), are well known for their roles in various pathological conditions. High resolution atomic structures of the NOD1/2-RIP2 complex would help elucidate Noddosome’s signaling and regulatory mechanism. Based on a few Noddosome related complex structures we recently resolved, we identified a surprisingly non-canonical architecture of the Noddosome complexes, a stark contrast to all the previous predictions. Thus, we propose to further investigate these Noddosome complexes, gathering more biochemical and cellular support of our findings. A detailed and validated molecular model of Noddosome complex would provide the critical functional insights about these signaling complexes, paving ways to new methods to manage autoimmune diseases that are related to NOD1/NOD2 receptors. Aim1: To obtain the atomic resolution structures of the NOD1-RIP2 and NOD2-RIP2 activation complexes. We will use biochemical and structural approaches (in vitro reconstitution of the signaling complex and visualization using cryo-EM) to obtain electron densities to build models of these active Noddosome signaling complexes. Aim2: To expand the structural analysis to full length NOD1/2 complexes. Despite educated guesses of their structures based on the closely related innate immune receptor NLR family CARD domain-containing protein 4 (NLRC4) and NLRP3, the actual functional conformations of NOD1 and NOD2 remain unknown. Aim3: Direct identification/visualization of the bound substrates of NOD1/2, and validate these key complex composition using biological approaches. This would serve as an ideal platform for screening of chemical and biological regulators/inhibitors of Noddosome, providing critical structural feedback for development of therapeutics.
kw: NOD2; RIP2; NOD1; CARD domain; cryo-EM; innate immune receptor

title: Exploring hydrogel encapsulation of polyamines to treat chronic wounds
abs: Older adults are disproportionately affected by chronic wounds which impose substantial morbidity and mortality. Wound healing slows with age, but these changes are poorly understood. Thus, few effective therapies are available to treat patients. Wound healing is tightly regulated and must be turned off following wound closure. Molecular switches coordinate multiple pathways to work in concert during wound healing. A defective/dysregulated switch can lead to a failure-to-heal, scarring or cancer. Exploring the mechanisms underlying these control switches could lead to the development of novel therapeutics and diagnostics. We identified polyamines, as critical regulators of wound healing. Intracellular polyamine levels are tightly regulated by biosynthesis and catabolism. Their levels are reduced by 50% in aged skin but the significance of this on wound healing remains elusive. We found that polyamine metabolism is transiently upregulated during wound healing. Inhibition of polyamine catabolism impaired the epithelial to mesenchymal transition that was essential for re-epithelialization and also showed negative feedback on biosynthesis. Furthermore, we found a novel polyamine metabolism-based pathway that functions as a molecular switch to coordinate the healing processes. Polyamine metabolite acrolein transiently inhibits caspase-3, which cleaves RNA-binding protein HuR to regulate the mRNA stability of key factors in wound healing. We hypothesize that, the polyamine-acrolein-caspase-3-HuR pathway functions as a master regulator which is turned on early to initiate healing and switched off once healing is complete. This pathway is prone to be defective in aging due to the reduced polyamine levels. To test our hypothesis, we aim to characterize the role of polyamine catabolism and investigate the mechanisms underlying the polyamine-acrolein-caspase-3-HuR pathway during wound healing using a combination of in-vivo, in-vitro and ex-vivo models. We aim to explore hydrogel encapsulation of polyamines and metabolism modulators as therapeutics in treating chronic wounds
kw: wounds, polyamines, acrolein, treatment

title: DUSP16 in tumor resistance to chemotherapy and in anti-tumor immunity
abs: Cancer is a main public health problem globally and a main hurdle for human life expectancy. Chemotherapy remains the back bone of cancer treatment. In addition, increasing knowledge in molecular and caner biology and anti-tumor immunology has led to the development of molecular targeted therapy and immunotherapy which have shifted the paradigm in cancer treatment. However, many challenges including lacking of biomarkers to identify suitable patients, acquired resistance to therapies of cancer and severe side effects of the treatment need to be met in order to improve treatment outcomes. Continuous elucidation of druggable genomic alterations in cancer and immune regulatory mechanisms will help to overcome the limitation of these therapies and to develop novel strategies for cancer treatment. In our study on a molecule known as DUSP16, we found that it targets on ERK, the effect molecule of the RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK pathway. This pathway is a major downstream signalling of EGFR and its members including RAS and RAF are frequently mutated in various caner to promote cancer development and mediate response to therapies. We showed that DUSP16 mediates cancer resistance to chemotherapy through JNK/p38-Bax axis and could be a biomarker for cancer sensitivity to chemodrugs. In addition, we also found that DUSP16 plays an important role in T cell activation and function. We hypothesize that DUSP16 negatively regulate anti-tumor T cell response and is an important molecule mediating chemoresistance in tumor cells, therefore could be targeted to improve both anti-tumor immunity and cancer chemosensitivity. This project aims to elucidate the function of DUSP16 in anti-tumor T cell immunity, its function in CAR-T signaling and develop therapeutic strategies to improve both CAR-T efficacy and cancer chemosensitivity. We expect that the outcome of this project will contribute to our endeavour to overcome cancer.
kw: DUSP; cancer; chemotherapy; cancer immunity; CAR-T; signaling.

title: MILK (Macrophages In LacK-tation): Decoding mammary macrophage heterogeneity to optimise treatment of breastfeeding disorders
abs: Mammary tissue is an important exocrine gland in female mammals that provides critical nutrients and passive immunity in the form of breastmilk to their offspring after delivery. Women who develop gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) during their pregnancies experience breastfeeding challenges associated with lactation insufficiency and are thus more likely to cease breastfeeding early. Nevertheless, the mechanisms that lead to lactation insufficiency are poorly defined and as a result, there are currently no clinically proven treatments till date to resolve these challenges in postpartum mothers, let alone women who have GDM. Immune cells such as tissue-resident macrophages (TRMs) are located in the mammary tissue and have been recently described to partake in morphogenesis, alveologenesis and involution. Furthermore, lactation involves significant remodeling of the mammary tissue that is associated with high susceptibility to an inflammatory condition called mastitis that further impedes lactogenesis. However, how specific TRM subsets function in these processes and the effect GDM has on their downstream mechanisms in the mammary tissue remains unresolved. Our proposal aims to address these gaps of knowledge by utilizing state-of-the art experimental techniques and analytical tools such as spatial transcriptomics, metabolomics, in silico modeling and in vivo preclinical mouse models to unravel heterogeneity and the specific cellular interactions between mammary TRMs and their tissue niche. We will also investigate the response of mammary TRM subsets towards inflammation and metabolic perturbations and identify dysregulated pathways that results in lactation insufficiency. Since breastfeeding confers critical benefits not only to the mother but also to the infant, understanding these mechanisms that lead to lactation insufficiency will provide a framework to discover alternative intervention candidates from the immune front, which will serve as a paramount step towards tackling the low exclusive breastfeeding rate in the Singapore population.
kw: Macrophages, Mammary Tissue, Lactation, Gestational Diabetes Mellitus

title: A bispecific antibody agonist of the IL-12 heterodimeric receptor for cancer therapy
abs: Cytokine-based immunotherapy is a promising field in cancer treatment. Preclinical studies in mice revealed that interleukin-12 (IL-12) had a dramatic effect on shrinking syngeneic tumors. However, systemic delivery of IL-12 in cancer patients resulted in severe toxicity, which narrows the therapeutic window and limits the potential response rates. This proposal aims to create first of its kind bispecific antibody IL-12 receptor (IL-12R) agonist with tailor-made immune modulating functions for cancer therapy. The bispecific antibody will ligate the two subunits of IL-12 receptor, IL-12Rβ1 and IL-12Rβ2, and mimics native IL-12p35/p40 activity yet with reduced toxicity through skewed immune subsets activation. The engineered bispecific antibody IL-12R agonist can be used in monotherapy against tumors or in combination with existing cancer immunotherapies to improve the efficacy and response rates. The proposed deliverables will be the discovery and development of a bispecific nanobody (BsNb) IL-12R agonist derived from llama immunization and antibody engineering techniques. Various in vitro assays and in vivo mouse studies will be carried out to identify and assess the potential leads that have desired tolerability and efficacy. The mechanism underlying toxicity reduction, such as the correlation between agonist affinity and the immune responses/cell populations it induces, will be studied for further engineering and lead optimization. Furthermore, non-human primate study will be conducted to evaluate the safety profile and therapeutic window of the top lead. The approach combines the favorable drug-like properties of antibodies with cytokine’s functional behavior against tumor. If successful, the program will place Singapore at the front runner position of the field and the economic impact is enormous.
kw: IL-12; bispecific nanobody; IL-12 receptor agonist; Immune modulation; T cell; Cancer

title: Dissecting the role of Asparagine synthetase (Asns) in the cardiomyocyte cell state
abs: Heart failure remains a top cause of mortality and morbidity worldwide. It is a worsening healthcare burden, especially with increasing ageing populations in Singapore and elsewhere today. The lack of any reparative mechanism in the heart lies at the root of the problem. Cardiac damage is not reversed by current therapy, and lost cardiomyocytes (CMs), even through ageing, are not replaced due to their limited proliferative capacity. Cardiac regenerative approaches are therefore urgently sought, promising to reverse the course of disease, rather than only slow down disease progression. Exciting and high-profile discoveries in recent years have revealed defined molecular means that enhance endogenous CM proliferation. Careful molecular characterisation confirm that CMs are induced first to undergo dedifferentiation, follows by proliferation, showing features including upregulated cell cycle genes, sarcomeric and cytoskeleton reorganization, re-expression of embryonic cardiac genes, loss of CM-CM junction and a metabolic switch from fatty acid to carbohydrate oxidation. Our lab has been studying CM cell states for several years, and now discovered a candidate gene marker (ASNS) which we show through preliminary data to track closely with CM dedifferentiation. Here, we propose through a novel genetic mouse model and human Engineered Heart Tissue studies, to establish the molecular mechanisms by which ASNS functions in CM cell state changes. We will uncover if ASNS (and/or asparagine) related CM dedifferentiation is necessary for proliferation, whether ASNS itself induces cell state changes, and whether this observation is translatable to human, and hold clinical implications. If successful, a bona fide marker for CM dedifferentiation will add significantly to the growing body of literature accumulating around cardiac regenerative research. Our aim is to contribute towards paving the ambitious route to deliver regenerative therapy for patients with heart disease.
kw: cardiomyocyte, heart failure, regeneration, dedifferentiation

title: Role of KIF1A in Neurodevelopmental Disorders: Modelling Microcephaly for Therapeutic Target Discovery
abs: Background: Neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) are socially debilitating disorders affecting ~5% of the paediatric population in Singapore. NDDs also affect the adult population, due to considerable overlap with adult neurological disorders. However, currently, there is little or no treatment available for NDDs. A common cause of NDDs is KIF1A-Associated Neurological Disorder (KAND), first reported in 2011. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying KAND, such as microcephaly, are not established. Objective: This proposal aims to establish the causal link between the KIF1A variant and microcephaly (aim 1), and evaluate a potential treatment for KAND by activating Wnt signaling (aim 2). Methods: Through our Undiagnosed Disease Programme, we have identified a heterozygous variant in KIF1A (p.Glu253Lys) in a patient with developmental delay and microcephaly. Our preliminary data suggest that neural stem cell proliferation is decreased and neural rosettes are smaller in patient-derived cerebral organoids. In aim 1, we plan to investigate the novel role of KIF1A in brain development in human cerebral organoids and the mouse developing brain to establish the causal link between the KIF1A variant and microcephaly. Our preliminary data suggest that beta-catenin, a core component of Wnt signaling, is downregulated in KIF1A patient-derived human cerebral organoids. In aim 2, we will use scRNA-seq as well as modalities to modulate Wnt signaling (either pharmacological or overexpression of wild-type or stabilized beta-catenin) in human cerebral organoids and mouse developing brain to establish the novel link between KIF1A and Wnt signaling, to identify potential novel therapeutic targets. Clinical Significance: Given the significant clinical and economic burden of NDDs, establishing the causal link between KIF1A and microcephaly through the Wnt signaling may identify potential therapeutic targets, which may be applicable not only to KAND, but also to other neurodevelopmental disorders like autism spectrum disorder as well as adult neurological disorders.
kw: Neurodevelopmental disorders; Microcephaly; KIF1A; Pathophysiology; Therapeutic Target discovery

title: Investigating the role of bile acids in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease and insulin resistance
abs: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is the leading cause of liver-related morbidity and mortality in developed countries. The hepatic insult in NAFLD is potentiated by insulin resistance (IR). A key signalling molecule involved in both IR and NAFLD are bile acids (BAs). Gut modified BA’s (GM-BA’s) have been shown to play a key role in the severity of NASH. BAs are also intrinsically linked to the development of insulin resistance. However, existing studies are correlative and not causal, making it difficult to develop new, effective therapies especially combinatorial approaches which might be more effective in treating these comorbidities. We hypothesize that 1) specific bacterial produced secondary BAs, when in excess, exacerbate NAFLD and drives IR and 2) restoring their balance can regress NAFLD and IR progression. We aim to characterize unique bacterial produced secondary BAs (GM-BAs) in NAFLD using ex vivo gut microbiota model and apply them to a hepatic in vitro model and skeletal muscle model to investigate the direct effects of GM-BAs on progression of NAFLD and IR respectively. We will then apply liver processed GM-BAs to the skeletal muscle model to study their effects under NAFLD conditions in IR pathogenesis. Skeletal muscle cells and hepatic model will be treated with BA modulators to assess if they can alleviate GM-BAs induced NAFLD and IR pathogenesis progression. New scientific information derived could drive novel treatment strategies modulating gut microbiome with food-based strategies and targeted nutrition for metabolic diseases. It would also open avenues for individualized therapies for metabolic diseases.
kw: NASH, insulin resistance, bile acids, microbiome

title: A functional study of candidate coronary-heart-disease causal genes to identify novel therapeutic targets
abs: Population-scale genetic studies have discovered many genomic loci associated with coronary heart disease (CHD) susceptibility. However, for most of these loci, the biological mechanism linking the genetic variants and the disease remains unknown, hindering therapeutic translation from these important findings. There is emerging evidence indicating that some of the genetic loci promote CHD by primarily acting on vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs), a major cell type of the arterial wall and a key player in the development of atherosclerosis, the pathological condition underlying most CHD cases. We hypothesize that: 1) some genetic loci promote CHD by primarily modulating the expression of causal genes at these loci in VSMCs and influencing VSMC behaviour; 2) altering the levels of these causal genes can modulate VSMC behaviour and impact on the development of atherosclerosis; and 3) the causal genes at these loci represent potential therapeutic targets for CHD intervention. In a large-scale integrative analysis of genomic, transcriptomic, and cellular phenotypic data from VSMCs, we recently identified 84 candidate causal genes at CHD susceptibility loci. Here we propose a translational research project to: 1) test if altering the level of any of these 84 candidate causal genes can change VSMC behaviour, by performing a pooled CRISPR screening assay followed by validation experiments; 2) investigate the molecular mechanisms that regulate the expression of the candidate causal genes, through interrogating Hi-C sequencing data; 3) ascertain the effects of selected candidate causal genes on the development of atherosclerosis in an animal model; and 4) screen for compounds that may modulate VSMC behaviour via a selected causal gene. The research team and collaborators collectively have expertise and experience on the methods to be used. The findings from this project will provide a better mechanistic understanding of genetic influence on CHD and nominate novel targets for further therapeutic development.
kw: Coronary heart disease; atherosclerosis; genetics; vascular smooth muscle cells

title: Quantifying the risk of gut microbiome disruption and disease due to antibiotic therapy by leveraging on the Singapore-led multicentre INVEST trial
abs: Antibiotic consumption is a key driver of gut microbiota disruption, which may lead to detrimental consequences such as antibiotic-associated diarrhoea (AAD) and Clostridoides difficile colitis. Antibiotic consumption also selects for multidrug-resistant organisms (MDRO), which create a reservoir for transmission of antibiotic resistance genes such as ESBL, AmpC and carbapenemases. It is therefore crucial to examine the degree of gut microbiota perturbation associated with different antibiotics, the speed and extent to which the microbiota recover post antibiotic treatment, as well as their associations with risk of developing AAD or colonization/infection with C. difficile and MDRO. Additionally, it is important to identify microbial species that aid in gut microbiota recovery to facilitate the development of a live biotherapeutic product (LBP). The LBP may be helpful particularly for patients undergoing prolonged periods of antibiotic therapy and/or broad-spectrum antibiotic treatment, which is likely to cause severe gut microbiota perturbation that may take a long time to recover. This prospective observational study will leverage on the INVEST trial to gain insights to the aforementioned objectives. INVEST is an international multicentre trial led by the Singapore Infectious Disease Clinical Research Network. INVEST aims to compare the clinical efficacy and economic impact of early stepdown to oral fluoroquinolones such as ciprofloxacin versus continuing/prolonged intravenous standard of care therapy for uncomplicated Gram-negative bacteraemia. The hypothesis of this study is: (1) early switch to a narrow spectrum antibiotic such as ciprofloxacin may result in less dysbiotic gut microbiota and greater speed and completeness of microbiota recovery, and (2) less dysbiotic microbiota associated with a narrow spectrum antibiotic may result in a lower risk of colonization/infection with MDRO and C. difficile. The knowledge gained can help optimise antibiotic prescribing practices in healthcare institutions to improve patient and economic outcomes as well as aid in the development of a LBP.
kw: Gut microbiota; metagenomics; antibiotics; antimicrobial resistance; bacteraemia; Gram-negative bacteria

title: DISCerning biomarkers and nOVel therapeutic strategies in hEpatocellulaR carcinoma (DISCOVER)
abs: Recent success in immunotherapy has revolutionized the treatment landscape for advanced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) patients. However, modest response rate of around 20% and common incidence of immune-related adverse events (AEs) from monotherapy anti-PD-1 immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) limit optimal patient outcome. Combination atezolizumab and bevacizumab while increasing response rate (30%), is associated with higher rates of treatment related adverse events. This highlights the urgent need to understand and improve on various immunotherapy strategies. Research efforts in understanding the mechanisms of action of immunotherapy in HCC, an asian centric disease remain sparse. Here, we aim to perform multi-dimensional immune-profiling of the peripheral blood from HCC patients collected before and at various time points after ICB treatment (both monotherapy and combination therapy) in order to identify circulating biomarkers predictive of clinical response and immune-related AEs. We will study the mechanistic link between immune response and clinical outcome. The tools employed in this study include mass cytometry by Time-of-Flight (CyTOF), single-cell transcriptomic sequencing as well as intensive in-vitro and in-vivo mechanistic studies. These advanced technologies followed by in-depth mechanistic studies are crucial in biomarker identification and better understanding of both local and systemic immune response after immunotherapy. They would aid us in identifying key pathways or molecules which could be modified with novel therapeutic interventions in order to achieve optimal clinical response with minimal AEs. Finally, we will develop and use an innovative in-vitro 3D microfluidic co-culture device (patient tumours on the chip with immune microenvironment) as well as in-vivo immunocompetent murine models to perform preclinical testing of these novel immunotherapeutic strategies. With this project, we aim to provide predictive biomarkers of response and AEs from ICB and devise innovative immunotherapeutic strategies to improve patient outcome by enhancing the clinical response and reducing the incidence of AEs.
kw: Immunotherapy, biomarkers, response, adverse events, combination immunotherapy.

title: Simple Non-cultured Endothelial Cell (SNEC) Replacement Therapy for the Treatment of Corneal Endothelial Dysfunction
abs: The main objective of this proposal aims to create a conducive environment for the translational development of a “Simple Non-cultured Endothelial Cells (SNEC)” harvesting technique for corneal endothelial cell injection (CECI) therapy. With regulatory acceptance in mind, the development of SNEC-based CECI as a minimally-manipulated Class 1 Cell, Tissue or Gene Therapy Product (CTGTP) will be refined towards establishment of a therapeutic work-flow towards regulatory approval as a clinical service. We hypothesize that primary corneal endothelial cells (CEnCs) isolated using the SNEC-harvesting technique do not undergo any cellular expansion. To show that these cells had been minimally manipulated, the transcriptomic profile and cell-cycle status of the donor-matched samples between the SNEC-harvested CEnCs and their cellularly expanded counterparts will be analysed and compared across the various donor-matched samples. Here, expansion of CEnCs will be carried out using a dual media culture approach. Transcriptomic profiling will be perform using single-cell smart sequencing followed by bioinformatics analysis and validation using quantitative polymerase chain reaction of genes of interests; whereas cell-cycle status will be assessed using a Nucleocounter and flow cytometry. We also hypothesize that a GMP-compliant workflow can be developed for the SNEC-harvested CEnCs, and can be clinically adapted. For process refinement of SNEC-harvesting technique, the use of non-compliant components will be refined, with additional focus on the substitution of the rho-associated protein kinase inhibitor Y-27632. Specific work-flow to be established include the accurate determination of isolated cell numbers, as well as the handling of the harvested CEnCs prior to CECI. Finally the functionality of the GMP-compliant SNEC-harvest CEnCs will be assessed within a rabbit and a non-human primate model of bullous keratopathy.

title: Biofabrication of freestanding blood vessel surrogate as a platform to study vascular disease
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: We propose to fabricate freestanding, cell-laden vasculature models with complex architecture using 3D-printed porous molds that enable spatiotemporally controlled crosslinking of hydrogels. Blood vessels are one of the key components of the circulatory system responsible for transporting nutrients and oxygen throughout the human and animal body. Physiological blood vessels consist of endothelial cells, vascular smooth muscle cells, and fibroblasts, which collectively plays an important role in maintaining vascular functions in health and disease. For example, vascular dysfunction causes common underlying phenomenon for cardiovascular diseases such as diabetes or hypertension, where the ability to facilitate vasodilation is impaired. To this end, vascular models that offer controlled dimensions, three-dimensional (3D) cellular arrangement, and biomimetic motions will be critical in advancing the understanding of vascular biology. To address this problem, multiple engineering approaches have been developed to create vascular analogs in vitro. Microfluidics and sacrificial 3D printing allow creating perfusable channels in hydrogels. However, the attainable vascular channels are typically embedded in bulk hydrogels, and freestanding vascular models cannot be realized in these methods. Alternatively, co-axial bioprinting enabled fabricating multilayer arrangement of cell-laden hydrogels as a continuous tubular construct. However, because the method relies on continuous materials extrusion, branching (or more complex) vascular architecture cannot be achieved. Overall, despite recent advances in biofabrication, recapitulating complex architectures of cell-laden vascular analogs remains challenging. Specifically, biofabricated vascular models have not yet achieved four fundamental attributes of native vasculatures simultaneously: (1) freestanding, (2) branching, (3) multilayered cellular alignment, and (4) physiologically relevant functions such as myogenic properties and vascular reactivity. To bridge the gap, this proposal aims to develop a unique engineering approach that enable fabricating complex structures of freestanding and cell-laden vascular analogs. Our proposed approach involves the use of 3D-printed porous microchannels that facilitate the crosslinking of enclosed materials (e.g., alginate hydrogels) from outside to inside unidirectionally. Controlled quenching of crosslinking will enable fabricating unique hollow structures inside the mold that serve as complex vascular models. The use of biocompatible hydrogels (e.g., collagens, gelatin methacrylate) along with alginate enables cell encapsulations in multilayer structures. The release of the fabricated vasculature from the mold gives freestanding vascular models that can be mechanically manipulated in radial and axial directions. title: Statistical Theory and Methods for Data-Driven Multi-Period Inventory Problems
abs: Periodic review stochastic inventory control is a fundamental problem in operations management (OM). In this problem, the decision maker (DM) must review the inventory levels and then make ordering decisions. A good ordering policy can significantly reduce operating costs and can also improve overall business performance. Because of the randomness in the customer demand and the multi-period nature of the inventory problem, dynamic programming (DP) is the main tool to determine the optimal ordering policy. Traditional inventory models typically assumed that the DM knows the exact distributions of the random demands. Under such an assumption, the DP problem is well studied and the base-stock policy and the (s, S)-policy are well-known solutions. In almost all real applications, however, the demand distributions are unknown and the DM has to infer them from either survey, expert knowledge, or historical demand data. As such, much attention has been paid to take into account the uncertainties in the demand distributions over the last decade. When historical data are available, a natural data-driven approach to a general T-period inventory problem is to minimize the empirical cost-to-go functions backward in time, leading to an empirical DP (EDP) solution for the inventory control. Such EDP solutions for the policy and for the optimal expected cost are call M-estimators in statistics. However, weak convergence of the EDP estimators, which are useful in interval estimation and hypothesis testing of vital parameters in the inventory system, are surprisingly hard to establish. To explain, weak convergence of an M-estimator is usually established via the advanced theory of empirical process that deals with weak convergence of i.i.d. sum n^{-1/2} \sum_{i=1}^n h(X_i) uniformly over h in a functional class H. In the multi-period inventory problem, when we minimize the empirical cost-to-go function at a certain period, the estimation errors of the EDP estimators in later periods will propagate to this period, due to the backward nature of DP. Because of the error propagation, the empirical cost-to-go function is no longer an i.i.d. sum, but rather a multi-sample U-statistic. As a result, weak convergence of the EDP estimators must established via multi-sample U-processes rather than empirical processes. However, the general theory of multi-sample U-processes is highly complicated and underdeveloped. The objective of the proposal is fourfold. First, we will establish the general theory of multi-sample U-processes and apply it to general multi-period inventory problems, including capacitated inventory with a constraint on the ordering quantity. Next, we will derive the semiparametric efficiency bound for the policy and compare the bound with the asymptotic variance of the EDP estimators. The comparison would tell us how much the EDP estimators can be improved in terms of efficiency. Third, we will consider the more realistic scenario where the demands in differ

title: Formation of Black Holes in Gravitational Collapse
abs: My research in mathematical general relativity is motivated by a long-standing and central question: the dynamical formation of black holes and singularities. The objects of study are 4-dimensional Lorentzian manifolds (M, g) called spacetimes. The evolution of spacetimes is governed by the famous Einstein field equations. One of the most fascinating features of Einstein field equations is that it admits solutions containing black hole regions. Black holes are spacetime domains, where even light cannot escape. And they are invisible to far-away observers. Famous explicit static or stationary solutions to Einstein vacuum equations containing black hole regions include the Schwarzschild and Kerr families. At present, however, understanding the dynamical formation of black holes and singularities remains one of the most important unfinished tasks in the theory of relativity. The question Can ``black holes'' form dynamically in vacuum? was totally open for more than forty years, until a recent 589-page breakthrough result of Christodoulou in 2008: with a novel short-pulse method he proved without any symmetry assumption, a black hole region (trapped surfaces) can form dynamically in the Cauchy development of vacuum initial data. In my previous work joint with Luk, we extended Christodoulou's result to the scale-critical regime. Recently, in 2019 I gave a simplified proof of Christodoulou's breakthrough result with 55 pages. Based on my previous works, I aim to explore further along this direction. Two remaining open questions are the dynamical formation of black holes and the formation of central singularities. I am developing mathematical tools and proofs. In this proposal, I aim to give some answers to these questions. In particular, I plan to address the following open questions in the field: 1. To prove the dynamical black-hole formation for Einstein vacuum equations via using short-pulse method and the stability of Kerr black holes, and to solve the complete apparent horizon; 2. To prove Ashtekar's conjecture on black hole thermodynamics for the general case and to establish global dynamics of apparent horizon; 3. To prove the weak cosmic censorship conjecture for the Einstein-Maxwell-charged scalar field system under spherical symmetry; 4. To prove the naked singularity censoring under anisotropic perturbation. The proofs and answers to these questions will be important to both mathematics and physics communities.
kw: hyperbolic partial differential equations, Einstein’s field equations, black holes, formation of trapped surfaces, weak and strong cosmic censorships

title: XMM: Towards Explainable Multimodal Deep Learning
abs: Multimodal learning has been playing crucial roles in various artificial intelligence applications and delivering gratifying results. Despite the encouraging advances of multimodal learning, most approaches have been treating multi-input neural networks as black boxes; very few endeavours attempt to investigate the interpretability of multimodal learning. The goal of this project is to develop plug-and-play tools to understand the underlying mechanism of multimodal learning, and to devise explainable deep neural networks to strengthen our understanding, confidence, and task performance to surpass the state of the art. Specifically, we aim to accomplish three objectives: 1) Establishing a principled framework to interpret the complementary roles of the multimodal input in making the final decision of a designated task; 2) Developing a generic solution to disentangling intra- and inter-modality representations and operations to transparentize multimodal neural networks; 3) Devising lightweight interpretable models deployable on edge devises, via conducting knowledge transfer from pre-trained based models with arbitrary and opaque architectures. The three objectives cover three different angles of multimodal interpretability and complement one another while remaining intrinsically coherent: our fundings in Objective 1) can be readily adopted in Objective 2), and together, they can be utilized in Objective 3). The proposed XMM is expected to advance the frontiers of deep learning research, to enrich the fundamental knowledge on multimodal learning, and to bring a significant impact on explainable AI. Unlike any prior work, the proposed XMM project will deliver the first general-purpose platform for both interpreting pre-trained multimodal models and enhancing the explainability of a base model. The tools to be developed in this project will not be limited to specific tasks but readily applicable to various network architectures and domains, such as autonomous driving, Internet of Things (IoT), and edge computing.
kw: Machine Learning, Artificial Intelligence, Computer Vision

title: Process Intensification of Nanofiltration by Functional Porous Membranes
abs: The biomedical and chemical industries contributed more than 28% of Singapore’s total manufacturing output in 2019. Catalyst recovery is a highly valuable operation in these industries, whereby most of the catalysts (such as enzymes and homogeneous catalysts) used are expensive, rare, and strictly regulated. Membrane-based nanofiltration presents a high value-added approach for catalyst recovery due to its low energy demand and minimized damage to heat-sensitive molecules. However, conventional dense polymeric membranes demonstrate limited flux, selectivity, and chemical stability. In this project, we aim to achieve process intensification of high value-added nanofiltration for catalyst recovery by developing advanced functional porous membranes, thus furthering sustainability efforts in the biomedical and chemical establishments within, and perhaps, beyond Singapore. This project consists of three main stages. The first stage involves the de novo design of application-oriented functional covalent organic frameworks (COFs) by employing appropriate reticular chemistry. After developing COF skeletons with robust linkages, we will tune the pore sizes, topologies, and functionalities of the resulting COFs to meet the requirements of a range of practical separation processes. In this regard, we propose some novel strategies, such as exploring multivariate-component COF synthesis and triggering interlayer shifting to manipulate the pore sizes of the COFs. Exploring novel topologies and interpenetration numbers in COFs is also on the agenda to develop these application-oriented COFs. In the second stage, we will develop advanced functional COF membranes for catalyst recovery via nanofiltration. For one, we aspire to enhance the chemical stability of commercially-available polymeric substrates by carbonization. Moreover, as opposed to conventional solvothermal syntheses, we will be preparing functional COF membranes by milder approaches such as interfacial polymerization. Through interfacial polymerization, we seek to optimize the key properties of the COF membranes, inclusive of their porosities, homogeneity, thickness, and crystal orientation. Furthermore, to address the trade-off between reaction time and the crystallinity of the COF membranes, we will also explore novel strategies such as the addition of active protons, photon-assisted condensation, and secondary error correction. The last stage of the project involves integrating these membranes into industrial vessels for catalytic reactions. We will scale up these COF membranes, design the plate-and-frame and hollow fiber membrane modules, and test their catalyst recovery performance under industrially relevant conditions. The modification-evaluation feedback loops will be implemented until membrane performance has been optimized for the applications of interest. title: Mechanisms of Hebp1-associated neurotoxicity in Alzheimer’s Disease
abs: An estimated 20 to 45 million people presently suffer from Alzheimer’s Disease (AD), the most prevalent form of dementia in the elderly. With cases expected to triple by 2050 and no effective treatment or cure in sight, AD constitutes one of the biggest socioeconomic challenges of the 21st century, exerting tremendous strain on healthcare, economy and society. While there is consensus on the critical need to identify and treat AD patients at the earliest opportunity (preferably asymptomatic), this is confounded by a comparative lack of knowledge and understanding of early AD pathophysiological mechanisms that are of diagnostic value and amendable to therapeutic intervention. A significantly better understanding the sequence of early events in AD pathogenesis and the accompanying molecular mechanisms driving its progression is desperately needed for the development of more effective approaches for therapeutics and early diagnosis. a) Background, hypothesis and research Questions to be Address We observed early elevation of Hebp1 in the brain of asymptomatic AD transgenic mouse model and in post-mortem brains of AD patients. Hebp1, a mitochondria-associated protein, plays a critical role in sensitizing neurons to apoptosis over the course of AD progression. Deleting Hebp1 expression in neurons protects them from heme- and amyloid beta 42 (Aβ42)-induced apoptosis, both of which are mechanisms driving AD1. Moreover, our preliminary data uncovered links between Hebp-mediated mitochondrial dysfunction, increased oxidative stress and destabilisation of the mitochondrial respiratory chain complexes upon exposure to heme. Taken together with our earlier report, these findings further strengthen our central hypothesis that Hebp1 plays integral roles in heme- and Aβ-associated mitochondrial toxicity leading to neuronal cell death starting from early stages of AD. As such, elucidating how Hebp1 is involved in the signalling mechanisms affected not only contributes to our understanding of early AD processes, it also allows for the design of therapeutic strategies to circumvent AD progression. Furthermore, given that Hebp1 up-regulation is detectable at the asymptomatic stage at least in AD transgenic mice, the protein is a potentially useful biomarker for early diagnosis of AD. Specific aims to be addressed in the proposal include: 1. Elucidation of mechanisms and signalling pathways used by Hebp1 to trigger neuronal apoptosis. 2. Elucidation of Hebp1’s role in neuronal survival and function in Hebp1-knockout (KO) mice. 3. Use of Hebp1 as a potential biomarker for early AD diagnosis in patients. b) Methodology, Approach and Feasibility of study For Aim 1, we will first interrogate Hebp1’s role as a potential mediator of oxidative stress. title: Endocytic trafficking: common and divergent mechanisms in neurodegeneration
abs: Although neurodegenerative diseases exhibit divergent pathological features and clinical symptoms, synaptic endocytic dysfunction has been recognized as an early event that is shared by several of these neurodegenerative conditions, including Alzheimer’s disease (AD), Down syndrome (DS) and Parkinson’s disease (PD). In this study, we will focus on synaptojanin 1 (SJ1), one of the endocytic proteins that is commonly linked to these conditions. SJ1 is a phosphoinositide PI(4,5)P2 phosphatase enriched at synapses and plays a critical role in clathrin-mediated endocytosis at nerve terminals. Loss-of-function (LOF) mutations of SJ1 have been identified in PD, while gain-of-function (GOF) of SJ1 linked to AD/DS. However, how an imbalanced SJ1 homeostasis leads to different pathologies in PD and AD/DS through a common endocytic pathway is largely unknown. We hypothesize that dysregulation of SJ1 affects endocytic trafficking of specific cargos in a neuron-specific manner, leading to selective degeneration in PD or AD/DS. We will test our hypothesis through biochemical, cell biological, and functional analyses that will examine the endocytic trafficking of potential cargos in SJ1 mutant mouse models as well as human neurons derived from patient iPSCs and/or genetically engineered stem cells carrying SJ1 LOF/GOF mutations. In particular, we will examine if 1) SJ1 LOF inhibits dopamine transporter (DAT) endocytosis and vesicular monoamine transporter 2 (vMAT2) recycling, resulting in impaired dopamine sequestration and the accumulation of oxidized dopamine in the cytosol of dopamine neurons, and 2) SJ1 GOF promotes the endocytic trafficking of two AD hallmark proteins in cortical neurons: amyloid precursor protein (APP) endocytosis and A production/deposition or extracellular tau uptake/pathology spreading. Our proposed project, will validate endocytic dysfunction as a common mechanism across neurodegenerative diseases. It will also reveal the specific targets of SJ1, and how they functionally interact, in different neuronal types. The findings will fill a major knowledge gap on how different neurodegenerative conditions are caused by the selective degeneration of neuron subtypes, opening up avenues for the development of novel therapeutic interventions.
kw: Parkinson's disease; Alzheimer's disease; Down Syndrome; endocytic trafficking; synaptojanin 1

title: Multifunctional Modular Self-assembled Nanocarrier (MMSN) Systems for Protein Delivery
abs: Anticoagulant therapy is widely used to prevent and treat arterial and venous thrombosis in patients with cardiovascular disease, cerebrovascular disease, and cancer. Venous thromboembolism is the third most common cause of cardiovascular death, following acute coronary artery disease and stroke. This project aims to address the major need for efficacious anticoagulant therapy that incurs the lowest possible bleeding risk. The team of our co-PIs has developed and patented a new type of high affinity antithrombin peptide, variegin and its variants. We have obtained extensive and promising preclinical efficacy and safety data, showing variegin and its most outstanding variant ultravariegin (UV) can inhibit thrombin much more potently than unfractionated heparin and bivalirudin and have superior selectivity for thrombin. More importantly, we have demonstrated that UV achieved greater antithrombotic efficacy with far less bleeding. The extremely high potency and specificity, and low bleeding rate of UV warrant our proposed development of a new therapeutic strategy for achieving much improved efficacy and higher safety for the patients in various fields. However, the short half-life remains the main limitation for its clinical translation, which must be urgently improved for reduced injection frequency and increased patient’s compliance and comfort level. Herein, we propose to design the innovative multifunctional modular self-assembled nanocarrier (MMSN) systems where a few rationally designed polymeric building blocks are integrated and self-assembled into a single nanostructure carrying the UV peptide for its sustained delivery with a prolonged half-life. Firstly, the size of MMSN is between 10 – 100 nm, which is within the ideal range for long circulation in blood. Secondly, unlike traditional PEGylation using large PEG for shielding, the shielding blocks of MMSN are based on our previous studies on the superior shielding effect of comb-shaped short PEG or zwitterionic phosphorylcholine-based polymer poly(2-methacryloyloxyethyl phosphorylcholine) (PMPC), providing safe and excellent efficiency to reduce nonspecific interaction with blood components and avoid fast recognition by the immune system. Thirdly, the large variety of adjustable parameters of the shielding blocks, such as molecular weight, molecular architecture and shielding density, guarantee the highly tuneable property of our proposed MMSN to meet our goals to deliver UV. Further, the core of MMSN is composed of biodegradable polyesters, which can degrade to release and re-activate UV for maximizing its antithrombotic efficacy. title: Validating and Improving Satellite-based Forest Carbon Estimation in Southeast Asia
abs: Conservation and restoration of carbon-rich Southeast Asian forests are of tremendous ecological and economical importance to ASEAN countries to combat climate change. Yet exact spatial distribution, health status and carbon stock of these forests remain poorly known. While a great many conventional satellite data sets have been used to estimate forest carbon stocks, most are not accurate enough to ensure the credibility and integrity of the marketplace for nature-based climate solutions. Here we propose to improve current aboveground biomass estimation capabilities by using a set of new instruments on the International Space Station (ISS), including lidar and hyperspectral sensors. A multi-dimensional data framework will be developed to achieve this goal by linking these ISS observations to ground measurements of representative forests in Southeast Asia. This new development will reduce uncertainties in carbon trading activities and provide technical support for Singapore’s ambition to be a carbon services hub, while reaching its climate and sustainable development goals.

title: Data-Driven Distributed Algorithms
abs: A critical challenge in system design is balancing the trade-off between common-case performance and worst-case performance. A design that focuses too heavily on the common case may be prone to catastrophic failures; while a system that focuses only on worst-case performance may perform poorly most of the time. The goal of this proposal is to develop new algorithms and new technique for managing this trade-off in distributed systems. Over the last several years, there has been significant progress in using machine learning models to optimize traditional algorithms. These models are often quite good at optimizing for common case performance; when trained on real-world data, they yield high performance data structures. At the same time, these machine learning models often fail catastrophically when they are exposed to situations for which they were not trained. Performance often suffers when the training data does not match reality. Thus the challenge in using machine learning model is achieving strong common case performance when the model is good, and guaranteeing adequate worst-case performance when the model is bad. This observation has led to the development of “Learned Data Structures” and “Learning Augmented Algorithms”; it has led to new “data-driven algorithms” and ‘algorithms with advice.” (The topic is sufficiently new that terminology remains malleable.) The key idea is to combine a traditional algorithm with a “model” that provides “advice” or “predictions.” When the advice/predictions are good, then the algorithm should perform well; as the advice/predictions degrade, the performance will degrade; when the advice/predictions are bad, the algorithm should perform no worse than a classical algorithm with no advice at all! This approach has proven quite successful in the context of sequential algorithms, and in particular, for online algorithms. The goal if this project is to develop this approach for distributed algorithms, i.e., for algorithms designed to run on large-scale networks of devices that communicate over a network. In this context, it seems clear that additional advice/predictions should enable better performance. For example, the machine learning model might provide advice (based on historical data) as to the topology or size of the network, the frequency or types of requests that will be sent over the network, the future load on the network, etc. All of this information would help to achieve better typical performance than an algorithm strictly focused on worst-case performance. First, we will explore distributed resource allocation problems (such as contention resolution or load balancing) where devices have to cooperate to use or share a resource; here, typical advice must consist of information on the network itself, or information on the workload to be shared.
