title: Elucidating the Contribution of Respiratory Supercomplexes to Immunity and Inflammation
abs: Electron Transport Chain (ETC) complexes are a series of 5 enzymes in the mitochondrial inner membrane that facilitate chemiosmotic production of ATP via oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS). Traditionally thought to be free-standing entities, ETC complexes are now known to form higher order supramolecular structures called supercomplexes or respirasomes. Respirasomes are thought to enhance bioenergetic efficiency and ATP production, and reduce harmful reactive oxygen species (ROS) associated with oxidative metabolism. Promoting respirasome formation is therefore an attractive way to bolster OXPHOS. Intact OXPHOS is crucial for mounting productive and protective immune responses against pathogens. Promoting respirasome formation is therefore an attractive albeit unexplored way to enhance host immunity. However, the role of respirasomes in immunity is unknown. We will do this by leveraging a unique animal model that has enhanced respirasome formation – the “RespirasomePLUS” mouse. BRAWNIN (BR) is a 71 a.a. nuclear-encoded mitochondrial localized small endogenous peptide (Mito-SEP) discovered recently by our lab. Loss of Brawnin (Br) in mice stimulates the formation of an extra-large and energetically efficient supercomplex called the SC-XL, making the Br KO mouse the first gain-of-respirasome-function model to our knowledge. Our preliminary results demonstrate that Br KO mice have enhanced resistance against viral infection. Using this mouse model, we will determine if respirasome formation potentiates host innate immunity and disease tolerance during influenza infection. We will further elucidate the underlying mechanisms of respirasome in enhancing innate immunity and develop therapeutic strategies to recapitulate the beneficial effects of respirasomes during infection. Our study will generate new knowledge on the physiological roles of respirasomes in vivo and pave the way for "metabolo-therapeutics" to ameliorate infectious and non-infectious inflammatory disorders.
kw: mitochondria, influenza, infection, immuno-metabolism, metabolomics, bioenergetics

title:
Anticipating Robots. 
Improving Human-Robot Communication Using an Artistic Approach.
abs: Due to the expanding use of non-humanoid robots in a close vicinity with humans, functional human-robot communication and cooperation becomes increasingly important, especially in countries with a high robot-to-employee ratio such as Singapore. In 1981 the Disney animators Olli Johnston and Frank Thomas published the book ‘The Illusion of Life’. In it they formulated the ’Twelve Principles of Animation’ which since then have become the standard for applied artistic animation. Animators using the Twelve Principles in their animation do not aim to imitate realistic movement and physics - they create an artistic, abstracted impression of movement and by doing so create a body-language for their animated characters that is expressive, intuitively readable and – if intended by the animator – confidence building. In contrast, robotic movement typically is neither expressive, intuitively readable nor confidence building. In fact, it is quite the opposite. Humans interact and communicate in different modalities: Verbally, (e.g., through speech), and nonverbally, (e.g., through gestures and poses) with the nonverbal part crucial in the areas of emotion, intuition, and trust. However, the nonverbal communication between humans and robots remains neglected, especially for non-anthropomorphic robots, which make up for the majority of robots employed in areas such as healthcare, elderly care or manufacturing. We propose a research project that investigates the potential of applying principles of animation into robot movement paths, thereby achieving an improvement of human-machine interaction. Our previous research (conducted by animating a robot-arm model), which fathomed the potential of different principles of animation on non-anthropomorphic, articulated robots, showed that the principle ‘Anticipation’ has the biggest statistical effect on human perception. The proposed project would be the next step: Applying ‘Anticipation’ on a real robot, measuring the human perception quantitively and qualitatively and developing basic algorithms, to be in cooperated to robot’s movement paths. Our research would bring together the arts, communication studies, robotics, and mathematics in four consecutive stages: - Designing movement patterns suitable for robots from an animator’s perspective in a virtual environment. - Applying these movements on a real robot while measuring the effect on and response of humans. - Quantifying and interpreting the collected data of the response group. - Using the collected quantitative data for machine learning implementations to improve human-robot communication in autonomous systems.
kw: Robots; Animation; Communication; Human-Robot-Interaction; Machine-Learning; Automation

title: Enabling μW-Scale, On-Chip Acceleration with Compute-In-Logic for Deep Neural Networks
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: Nowadays, how to design scalable, compute efficient Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) accelerators free from noise and non-idealist is still an open question. In this project, we are proposing innovative digital accelerator circuitry that is tailored for ultra-low power, energy-efficient DNNs workloads with enhanced scalability compared to state-of-the-art. To be concrete, the core of the proposed project is to design non-von-Neumann, ultra-low power circuits that co-locate data storage and Multiple-Accumulate (MAC) operations for in-situ computing. In this manner, computations are executed at the location where data resides that the energy spent to fetch data from memory could be tremendously decreased, eventually improving energy efficiency. We target to achieve DNN acceleration with W-scale power dissipation, up to 6 improvement in energy efficiency. To obtain that goal, we propose a novel technology, namely Compute-In-Logic (CIL) to resolve von-Neumann bottleneck and overcome some of the most crucial limitations our counterpart, Compute-In-Memory (CIM) circuits possess. We choose Binary Neural Networks (BNNs) as the backbone of our computation, design a Latch-XNOR cell to fulfill CIL in BNNs, extend it to multi-bit DNNs and further improve the energy efficiency by holistic design optimization. Specifically, we aim to (i) design non-von-Neumann, CIL circuitry with novel standard cell structure that fuses data storage and XNOR function together for in-site computing; (ii) deploy the CIL paradigm in BNNs and extend it to multi-bit DNNs with bit-serial technique; (iii) formulate parallel, input-reusable, weight-stationary dataflow for on-chip acceleration to suppress data movement and enjoy energy saving; and (iv) fabricate the accelerator chips after holistic optimization and demonstrate their efficacy via real-world applications. The project features three individual yet tightly coupled phases. We will start by applying CIL paradigm to BNNs (i.e., single-precision DNNs) via dedicated Latch-XNOR cell and facilitate efficient bit-count operation with Look-up Table. Subsequently, we extend the precision from single-bit to multi-bit by leveraging bit-serial approach on top of CIL paradigm with well-defined dataflow and Processing Element (PE) cluster partition. Lastly, we further enhance the energy efficiency of the accelerators from micro-architecture and circuit perspectives to foster energy efficient memory access and reliable ultra-low voltage operations. We see the efficacy and feasibility of the proposed methodology through successful BNN model training, standard cell circuit verification, layout design and BNN chip synthesis.
kw: Compute-In-Logic, DNN accelerator, ultra-low power, energy efficiency

title: Single-Pixel Photon-Counting TR Raman Spectroscopy for Field Deployable Sensors
abs: When photons interact with molecules, scattering of several forms occur. The highest proportion are elastically scattered photons (Rayleigh scattering), which has the same wavelength as the incident photons. The remaining proportion are inelastically scattered photons, also known as Raman scattering. Raman scattering consists of both Stokes and anti-Stokes shift, with the former resulting in an increase in wavelength and the latter resulting in a symmetrical decrease in wavelength about the Rayleigh wavelength. Compared to Anti-Stokes, Stokes Raman scattering has a stronger scattering peak and is therefore the scattering commonly collected for analysis in Raman spectroscopy. The Raman shift can be calculated from the change in wavelength of the scattered photons, thus producing a broadband Raman shift spectrum, which is very valuable as it reveals vibrational modes of molecules and provides characteristic peaks of the tested sample that allows the tester to identify its constituent components. Raman spectroscopy has a number of outstanding advantages compared with infrared (IR) spectroscopy. These mainly include the use of widely-available and more efficient visible (or near IR) lasers and detectors, no or minimum sample preparation, superior for biological and liquid samples owing to the fact that water is a weak Raman scatterer, and its non-destructive nature of testing. Raman spectroscopy is hence considered promising for a wide range of applications in homeland defense, environmental monitoring, pharmaceutical testing, healthcare, biological science, and many others. However, Raman spectroscopy has two major technical challenges, namely, weak Raman scattering signal and strong fluorescence emission background noise. This project hence aims to address these challenges and provide a solution to enhance the Raman spectroscopic sensing capability through a series of technological developments. These include: (1) Development of a new type of optical spectrometers that has an extremely-high optical throughput for gathering weak Raman signal using a large encoded entrance aperture instead of a narrow slit in traditional optical spectrometers. (2) Use of time-gate (TG) and/or time-resolved (TR) Raman signal to suppress the background fluorescence noise. This time domain method uses pulsed laser excitation and is based on the fact that Raman scattering is ultrafast (almost instantaneous) while fluorescence emission is relatively slow and has a time delay of typically a few nanoseconds. Our innovation here is to use single-pixel imaging technology to replace expensive intensified CCDs or streak cameras commonly used in TG/TR Raman systems. title: DEFORMABLE SOFT ELECTROMECHANICAL DIELECTRIC ACTUATORS
abs: The proposal aims to to realize soft electromechanical dielectric actuators with high performance using ionic materials. Ionic based conductors are intrinsically highly deformable, high stretchability and high optical transparency. The conductivity is sufficiently high in providing conduction to the low current, electric field-driven electro-actuator devices. The mechanical deformability and compliances of the ionic conductors are highly desirable for soft electroactuators. The smooth surfaces of the ionic conductors are critical in preventing the electrical breakdown of the underlying dielectric elastomer layer, which is often related to the conductive pathway induced by the roughness or protrusions of the conventional electrical conductive pastes in soft actuators. The outcome of the proposed work is to create a new class of soft and deformable electromechanical actuators utilize the ionic-elastomer interface with electrical double layer which couples the voltage effectively into the dielectric elastomer layer. Simultaneously, the compliant ionic layer will maximize deformability and free-up the constraints imposed by a rigid electrode, thereby enhancing a higher output performance in actuation. Finally, dual-functionality of integrated electroadhesion surfaces with deformable actuating device will be demonstrated for wearable and interactive human-machine interfaces for virtual reality applications.
kw: electromechanical actuators, deformable electronics

title: Multi-stated organic photocatalysts for sustainable molecular transformations
abs: Current mainstream approaches for the chemical production of the active ingredients in the pharmaceutical and agrochemical industries utilize thermal energy to drive conventional ionic two-electron transfer events. Employment of other forms of energy can allow for development of new synthetic processes, thus resulting in a vast expansion of the chemical spaces. Our primary objectives in this research project are to use ubiquitous energy of visible light to create highly efficient catalytic processes driven by single-electron transfer (SET) and/or energy transfer (ET). Visible-light photocatalysis has advanced the state-of-the-art chemical synthesis via harnessing of mild energy visible light to productively drive various types of useful molecular transformations. Homogeneous photocatalysts such as ruthenium (Ru)/iridium (Ir)-based polypyridyl complexes or complex organic dyes can be excited under irradiation with visible light that will induce SET to/from organic substrates or ET via triplet-sensitization to provide reactive open-shell radical intermediates. However, there are several points that should be addressed to enable translation of these photocatalytic methods into more practical and sustainable chemical processes. First, rare transition metal-based photocatalysts such as Ru- and Ir-based ones are not suitable for sustainable chemical processes due to their cost and toxicity. Second, the irradiation of transition metal-based photocatalysts produces longer-lived triplet excited states that can induce outer-sphere SET or ET events with the substrates. However, the electronic excitation process is typically based on a metal-to-ligand charge-transfer (MLCT) band (commonly observed at 450-500 nm) so that only triplet excited states of lower energy (ET = nearly 45 kcal/mol = 2 eV) will be involved in the SET or ET events. The long-lived excited states are indispensable for intermolecular substrate activation processes via SET or ET, because the diffusion rate constant of molecules in solution are about 10*9-10 /s. Their redox windows, however, inevitably restrict their engagement in the redox processes of the readily available substrates having highly negative reduction potentials [such as organic halides and carbonyl compounds, E(red) = –2 V or less vs saturated calomel electrode (SCE)] as well as those with highly positive oxidation potentials (such as non-activated arenes and alkenes, E(ox) = 2 V or more vs SCE). On the other hand, to avoid the rarity and toxicity of transition metal-based photocatalysts, organic photosensitizers such as eosin Y, rhodamine 6G, acridinium salts and 10-phenyl-phenothiazine which have electron-donating and/or -withdrawing groups in pi-conjugated systems have been employed as photocatalysts. title: Molecular basis of protein quality control by membrane protease FtsH complex
abs: Membrane proteins not only are major components of cell membrane, but also carry out essential and diverse functions. Notably membrane proteins account for almost one third of the total proteins in cell. In contrast to this significantly importance, our understanding of membrane protein for the structure, function, and biogenesis lags far behind compared with that of non-membrane protein due to its handing difficulty in experiment. Ribosome and translocon take a major role in membrane protein biogenesis through a process called co-translational translocation. Compared with cytosolic protein biosynthesis, membrane protein biogenesis is much more complicated, cells have evolved delicate systems to control the quality of these proteins. Of these systems, the membrane AAA protease FtsH paly an indispensable role in protein quality control in bacteria, by degrading misfolded, misassembled, aggregated, and dysfunctional proteins. FtsH is capable of degrading both membrane and cytosolic proteins. Recently, more and more substrates of FtsH have been identified. In addition, another protein complex HflKC, is composed of two membrane subunits HflK and HflC, interacts with FtsH to finely modulate its proteolytic activity. In contrast to the large number of protein substrates and the essential function for FtsH, limited information is available regarding molecular mechanisms and structural details of i) how these three players are organized to be an entire complex that subsequently become active in an ATP-dependent manner; ii) how FtsH specifically recognizes and degrades its protein substrate; iii) how HflKC regulates the enzymatic activity. To address these issues, here we put forward to a research propose that aims to elucidate the molecular basis of protein quality control by membrane protease complex FtsH-HflKC. Firstly, we will try to determine the structure of an entire FtsH holoenzyme at atomic resolution by Cryo-EM approach, which enables us to understand how these three membrane subunits are assembled as well as to uncover structural basis of enzymatic activity regulation by HflKC. Next, we will determine structures of the complex FtsH-HflKC trapped in different functional states by employing a combinative strategy (mutating catalytic residue mutation E252Q and adding non-hydrolyzable ATP analogue). Structural comparison of the FtsH holoenzyme in ATP-free and ATP-bound states would elucidate how ATP hydrolysis to trigger conformational change which is required for proteolytic activity. Furthermore, we will target the Cryo-EM structure of nucleotide bound FtsH-HflKC with its substrate, like cytosolic protein LpxC and membrane protein YccA, to elucidate molecular basis for substrate binding and recognition mechanism. title: Tightening Bounds for Submodular Optimization: Algorithms and Analyses
abs: Submodular optimization is an important building block for developing algorithms in many areas such as data mining and machine learning. Submodular optimization problems are normally NP-hard. Various heuristic algorithms have been devised to address these optimization problems. Some algorithms provide theoretical approximation guarantees on the worst-case ratio between the solution produced and the optimal solution over all instances of the problem. But these constant factors usually leave a significant gap between the solution obtained and the optimal solution of a particular problem instance because they consider the worst-case scenarios only. For other heuristic algorithms without strong worst-case guarantees, it remains unknown how close these algorithms perform to the optimum which is hard to estimate due to the NP-hardness of the problem. If we are able to find a close upper (resp. lower) bound on the optimal solution of a particular maximization (resp. minimization) problem instance, we can then derive a good approximation guarantee for any solution obtained. Motivated by this target, the main goal of this project is to conduct a comprehensive study on (i) developing effective and efficient algorithms to tighten the upper/lower bounds for various submodular optimization problems, and (ii) applying these bounds to several applications, such as finding the exact optimal solutions using the branch-and-bound approach and constructing approximate solutions for large-scale problems. The research outcomes of this project will include new fundamental techniques for establishing bounds, constructing solutions and deriving solution quality for submodular optimization. The significance of this project lies not only in its high scientific values but also in its great potential of applications in many domains. The bounds developed in this project can be used to benchmark and better characterize the actual performance of any algorithm for any problem instance. In addition to providing tighter approximation guarantees, these bounds are also useful for branch and bound procedures to find the exact optimal solutions for combinatorial optimization problems. Moreover, to scale to humongous data, advanced techniques such as sampling, streaming and sketching have been proposed for various real-world applications. Our bounds can be used to speed up these techniques for achieving a predefined approximation guarantee on the solution quality. Furthermore, the approximation guarantees certified by these bounds are useful for developing interactive processing algorithms whereby the user can check the approximation guarantee of the solution produced at any time and decide when to stop the algorithm with a solution of satisfactory quality.
kw: Submodular optimization; algorithms; approximation guarantee

title: Ultrafast Coherent Spectroscopy and Control of Nano-plasmonically coupled Complex Molecular Energy Landscape and Transfer Dynamics
abs: We aim to characterize and control the energy landscape and the energy transfer network of complex molecular systems that are coupled to tailored nanoplasmonic structures. The complex systems that we mean here are systems having multiple energy levels that are coupled to each other, giving rise to a complex energy/population transfer network at the femtosecond to picosecond timescale. To control, we mean to be able to shift the energy levels as well as strengthen/weaken the couplings between these states, thereby changing the excitation energy transfer (EET) pathways and network of the complex systems. One important example of such complex systems is the plant light harvesting complex II (LHCII), the main pigment-protein complex in higher plants responsible for harvesting photons from sunlight and channelling of excitation energy to the photochemical reaction centre. We intend to use this system as our main test subject system and simpler molecular systems, such as chlorophylls for our initial studies. We will manipulate the complex molecular energy landscape and transfer dynamics by selectively coupling the LHCII’s excitonic levels to tailored plasmonic modes (PM) arising from metal nanostructures, via strong light-matter coupling. Eventually, to achieve higher spectral specificity and optimized EET, we will aim to couple the excitonic states to plasmonic modes arising from lattices of noble metal nanoparticles, known as surface lattice resonances (SLR) To characterize these complex systems coupled to the nanostructure plasmonic modes, we will use ultrafast coherent multidimensional optical spectroscopy. This is the most powerful tool available to characterize complex system energy flow and coupling at the ultrafast timescale. We will study and understand the ultrafast energy transfer network in the strongly coupled systems to guide the designs of the nanoparticle lattice arrays to manipulate selected excitation energy transfer channels in the LHCII. These will then be applied to achieve the following scientific application aims: 1) To further clarify the natural EET network in LHCII, important in understanding these biologically important systems 2) to induce long range and fast energy transfer between different excitons which are originally uncoupled via strong coupling to PMs. These can then be a platform to explore the possibility of using the LHCII-nanoplasmonic hybrid device as a model system to design other related molecular photonic structures for optimized transport of excitons.
kw: Two-dimensional Electronic Spectroscopy; Plasmonics; Ultrafast Spectroscopy; Strong Light-Matter Coupling; Excitation Energy Transfer; Light Harvesting Complex; Plasmonic Modes

title: LLPS of the Effector-Guardee Complex Generates Signaling Hubs of Plant Immunity
abs: Plants activate sophisticated immune responses during bacterial pathogen infection. In general, two steps of the plant immune system, pathogen-associated molecular pattern (PAMP)-triggered immunity (PTI) and bacterial type-III effector (T3E)-triggered immunity (ETI), are activated at different stages of bacterial infection. The activation of both immune pathways depends largely on the macromolecular assembly of the respective plant surface-associated receptors. However, the underlying inter- and intramolecular interactions to form signaling complexes of PTI and ETI receptors are largely unclear. In addition, mutual potentiation of PTI and ETI was recently found to be critical mechanisms that fully activate plant defense, indicating physical interactions between PTI and ETI complex on the plasma membrane, which is, however, remain unknown. Although >30% of bacterial T3Es, which interact with ETI receptors, target the host PM during host invasion, we have limited knowledge of the molecular mechanisms by which T3Es might orchestrate biomolecular interactions between PTI and ETI complexes and leverage their communication at the cell surface. Recently, we identified novel molecular mechanisms underlying plant-pathogen interactions, by which the liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) of Xanthomonas T3Es condenses multiple host immune regulators and hijacks host immunity. Our efforts also revealed that the Arabidopsis guardee protein RIN4 participates in the LLPS of Xanthomonas XopR and regulates T3E- and RIN4-regulated ETI responses through complex coacervation between XopR and RIN4. The guardee is the plant immune regulator that inhibits T3E-triggered ETI by binding with both NLRs and T3Es1,2. Here, we hypothesize that both intrinsically disordered proteins, Arabidopsis RIN4 and bacterial XopR, form macromolecular complexes via LLPS that serve as signaling hubs, regulating the various plant immune responses underlying PTI, ETI, and their crosstalk by tuning the physical-chemical properties of the phase-separated protein complex on the plant cell surface. We envision studying the new mechanisms underlying plant-bacteria interactions, and next, a holistic understanding of the complex mechanisms underlying T3E guardee-mediated host immune signaling would guide the rational design of strategies in enhancing plant resilience against bacterial infection. By the end of the project, our research will illuminate the fundamental mechanisms of plant pathology and biotechnology development in sustainable agriculture.
kw: Host-microbe interaction; Liquid-liquid phase septation; Plant innate immunity; Effector-triggered immunity; Type III effector, Guardee

title: Towards A Better Understanding of Beating Cilia and Flagella in Complex Environments
abs: Oscillating cilia, or interchangeably flagella, function in various biological processes, ranging from locomotion of microorganisms, feeding of marine invertebrates, airway defense against viruses to the mobility of ova and sperms in mammalian reproduction. A proper understanding of ciliary beating would benefit various activities, e.g., exploiting algae for efficient CO2 capture, developing novel therapies of ciliary dysfunction-induced human diseases, and informing novel utilization of synthetic cilia. Due to its importance, tremendous work has been conducted to understand the mechanisms of ciliary beating. Early theory and simulations commonly considered ciliary beating as a purely mechanical process, regarding the cilium as a filament executing a prescribed waveform or being actuated by an imposed periodic forcing at its basal end (like whipping a rope). However, this modelling strategy of prescribing ciliary kinetics/kinematics is inconsistent with the biological observation that they are not fixed but vary significantly according to the changing environment. In this project, we will study oscillating cilia/flagella by incorporating a multi-disciplinary mechanobiological model, aiming to better understand their behaviours in complex biological environments. Unlike most studies imposing a ciliary beating/forcing pattern a prior, we allow the cilia to oscillate spontaneously from a coupling between their biochemical activity, structural deformation and fluid flow. This allows us to consider the biological spontaneity as a crucial element to depict the ciliary response to the changing environments. We will characterize ciliary/flagellar beating in three typical scenarios featuring 1) rheology of bodily mucus as complex fluids, 2) structural coupling between flagella, and 3) metachronal waves generated by collectively beating cilia, which cannot be reasonably probed without mimicking the biological spontaneity. While it remains challenging to experimentally decouple these biochemical and physical mechanisms, modelling and simulations that can conveniently switch them on/off will not only improve our biophysical understanding but also inform future experimentation.
kw: Mechanobiology; oscillating cilia and flagella; low-Reynolds-number flow; hydrodynamic interaction; numerical simulation; non-Newtonian flow

title:
Shape Memory-Based Smart Adhesive Systems 
through Harnessing Fracture Regimes
abs: Smart adhesive systems – those that provide on-demand strong attachment to irregularly shaped objects and on-demand detachment with ease – present a challenge that has attracted attention of researchers. Recent theoretical studies show that the adhesive strength of fibril structures is governed by two fracture regimes --- an interfacial strength-limited regime with uniform detachment leading to strong adhesion, and a crack propagation-controlled regime giving rise to weak adhesion. This research project aims to develop robust, one-level fibrillar smart adhesive systems with both strong adhesion and on-demand detachment by harnessing the two fracture regimes. Switching of adhesive fibrils between the two regimes can be modulated by their geometrical, elastic, viscoelastic and adhesive parameters. We propose to use shape memory polymers (SMPs) as the adhesive fibril material, whose elastic modulus and adhesive properties can be changed dramatically by external stimuli such as heat, light or electric field. Utilizing the drastic differences in SMP’s elastic moduli in the glassy and rubbery states as well as its shape memory features, we will develop robust methods to form conformal contact between the adhesive and adherend for strong, theoretical interfacial strength-limited adhesion, and to recover non-conformable contact for weak, crack propagation-dominant detachment, on-demand. The project involves identifying and characterizing the right SMPs for smart adhesives, exploring various external stimuli to trigger the transition between glassy and rubbery states, designing the fibrils and the devices, fabricating the adhesive systems with embedded stimulation functions, and optimizing the design for best attachment-detachment performances. We will employ an integrated approach involving experimentation, modelling and simulations, and design optimization. We will also use a few application examples to demonstrate the performance of the smart adhesive systems. The proposed research represents a paradigm shift in making switchable smart adhesives. The success of the project has the potential to significantly impact on many applications including, but not limited to, releasable structural connectors, reusable superglues, soft grippers for heavy objects, perching components for large Unmanned Aerial Vehicles, and smart adhesive skins in biomedical applications.
kw: Smart adhesives; fracture regime switching; shape memory polymers; fibrillar structures;

title: CONCH: Ceramic resilience OptimizatioN with Complex Hierarchical structure
abs: This research project aims at extending the crack path in bio-inspired, hierarchical ceramics using a microstructural design inspired by the conch seashell. Significance of the research: Although crack engineering and toughening of ceramics with oriented particulates is not new, bio-inspired approach with grain orientation, multilayers, and controlling the atomic diffusion during the sintering open up new opportunities. The key aspect of the research project is its multidisciplinarity from chemical surface modification and dispersion of ceramic powders, colloidal control of the orientation of those powders via magnetic fields, ceramic densification, mechanical testing, and the underlying theory and mechanisms to explain the experimental observations using computational methods. Although the proposed project aims at addressing fundamental research questions, the scientific method, tools and results are anticipated to contribute to field of near net shape processing of structural ceramics and additive manufacturing in general. The results and methodologies developed during the research could be applied to other ceramic and ceramic composite chemistries. Hypotheses and research questions: The central hypothesis of the proposed research is that appropriate composition and microstructure can limit the diffusion of atoms during pressure-less sintering, leading to weak interfaces where cracks can propagate in specific directions, as observed in natural materials like the conch seashell. Achieving tortuous cracking with high strength grain boundaries will increase the work of fracture of the ceramics, leading to its tolerance to flaws and reliability. Using anisotropic powders as the initial raw material, this general hypothesis will be narrowed down to several research questions. First, what are the crystallinity, composition and mechanical properties of the grain boundaries in the ceramics and how additives can influence these properties by tuning the diffusion of atoms? Secondly, is there an optimum interface length and roughness to obtain grain pull-out instead of grain fracture during a crack event and how is this length varying with the properties at the boundary? Thirdly, what is the relationship between interface properties and angle of deflection of a crack in ceramics with aligned microstructures (hierarchical design)? And finally, using the answers to these questions: how should the microstructure of the ceramic be designed to channel the propagating crack into specific directions? Approach: To tackle the research problem, the proposed project will use Al2O3 as a ceramic model and the conch seashell as the natural inspiration. title: Analysing Present and Future Compound Hydroclimate Extremes in Southeast Asia
abs: Compound hydroclimate extremes are (a) co-occurrence of two or more extreme events, (b) combinations of extreme events with underlying conditions that amplify the total impact, or (c) combinations of events that are not themselves extremes but when combined lead to an extreme event. Recent studies have shown that the risk due to compound extremes is much higher than the risks from component extremes occurring in isolation. However, research on compound hydroclimatic events occurring at urban scales, their predictability and future behaviour is still in nascent stages. Under this project, we plan to firstly analyse the physical processes driving these compound extremes and their potential changes under climate change. We will focus on three specific compound events, (i) concurrent rainfall and wind extremes, (ii) concurrent rainfall, flood, and storm surge events, and (iii) concurrent dry spell and temperature extremes, as particularly relevant natural hazards for the recently urbanized coastal cities of South East Asia. Multivariate frequency analysis for delineating effect of dependency amongst compound event drivers on their joint occurrence probabilities will be undertaken. Secondly the direct and cascading economic impact of these extremes on identified vulnerable urban areas of South East Asia will be studied. This will be via Input-output models that enables assessment of how a disruption in one sector propagates into the rest of the economy. Besides adding significantly to our scientific understanding of such events, the results are also expected to inform on city planning and public preparedness.
kw: Compound Extremes; Hydroclimate; Urban Risk; Climate Change; Machine Learning

title: Cardiovascular Disease National Collaborative Enterprise (CADENCE)
abs: Established in February 2023, CADENCE is a national clinical translational programme aimed at synergising cardiovascular research and technology capabilities across Singapore. Its goal is to integrate existing research capabilities by bringing together the strongest basic, clinical, and translational talent and expertise across Singapore and its institutions. This aims to establish a focused and impactful national cardiovascular disease research and translational programme with world-class peaks of excellence. To achieve this, CADENCE has established four national joint platforms focused on data science, clinical trials, and artificial intelligence or digital health, together with a business intelligence and development unit to attract industry collaborations and external investments. CADENCE is a programme of Consortium for Clinical Research and Innovation, Singapore.

title: Advancing population viability analysis for an increasingly variable world
abs: Background: Natural ecosystems across the planet are increasingly threatened by human-driven environmental change, including deforestation and climate change. Substantial numbers of species are at risk of extinction. Population viability analysis (PVA) is the use of ecological modelling to project species’ population dynamics into the future in order to inform sustainable management and conservation. Applications of PVA typically aim to identify the optimal strategy for minimising the extinction risk of native species. Intellectual merit: A current limitation of PVA is its overly simplistic treatment of the effects of a temporally variable environment on population dynamics. The primary aim of the proposed work is to address this knowledge gap by building on recent advances in mathematical ecology and integrating them into PVA. Improving PVA in this way is a global imperative, given the increasingly variable environments to which species’ populations are subject due to human-driven environmental change. We hypothesise that adequately accounting for temporal environmental variance (TEV) in PVAs will yield more-accurate extinction risk estimates, which in many cases would be higher than previous estimates and thereby imply the need for more-vigorous conservation efforts. Broader impact: Our new techniques will be broadly applicable to species of conservation concern across the planet. To demonstrate their use, we will carry out case studies for key species of conservation concern in Singapore, which will inform management strategies aimed at minimising extinction. This ties in with Singapore’s focus on becoming a “City in Nature” as part of the Singapore Green Plan 2030. The results of our case studies can point to management strategies likely to be of broad efficacy in the coming decades, as habitat destruction and climate change subject more species’ populations around the world to increasingly variable environmental conditions.

title: Investigating the role of SMCHD1 in forming an epigenetic memory
abs: Epigenetic memory is the ability of cells to retain and transmit gene expression information from one cell division to the next. Stable epigenetic memories are used in processes such as X inactivation, and in the establishment of barriers that prevent de-differentiation. Epigenetic memory can occur by many mechanisms including DNA methylation, histone modifications or the use of histone variants. However to date, only a handful of proteins have been shown to be able to set up and maintain epigenetic memory. This project aims to understand how an epigenetic memory is set up. Understanding this can also help in the development of a genetic tool for long-term epigenetic repression. We focus on the epigenetic repressor SMCHD1 as a model. Initially discovered as an important protein for X-inactivation, SMCHD1 also regulates select autosomal genes. Interestingly, our preliminary data in zebrafish shows that SMCHD1 is required for epigenetic repression of developmentally important hox genes in early embryogenesis, after which it is dispensable for sustained repression. Similar effects were observed in cultured human fibroblasts where germline knockout of SMCHD1 causes HOX misexpression but somatic knockout does not. Together this points to an ability of SMCHD1 to set up an epigenetic memory on HOX genes early in development. In this project we aim to study the nature of this epigenetic memory and to understand the role of SMCHD1 in this process. We further aim to develop SMCHD1 as a tool for programmable long-term epigenetic repression. We leverage on our expertise of SMCHD1 genetics, a zebrafish and cell culture model that we have generated to address the following aims. Aim 1. Identify the epigenetic marks laid down by SMCHD1 in early embryos Approach: hox genes are marked by DNA methylation in oocyte, histone variant H2AZ before zygotic genome activation (ZGA) and bivalent chromatin marks H3K4me3/ H3K27me3 post-ZGA. Genome-wide bisulphite sequencing and chromatin immunoprecipitation against the histone variants and modifications above will be performed in wildtype and smchd1-/- zebrafish embryos at the respective stages to determine whether these marks are misplaced in the absence of Smchd1. The marks will be examined at a later stage when hox genes transcriptionally active to determine which are involved in the epigenetic memory. Feasibility: We have strong phenotypic and expression data of hox de-repression when smchd1 is lost in oocytes. We have also performed targeted bisulphite sequencing on one hox gene and showed that it is hypomethylated in smchd1 null oocytes. This shows that it is feasible to isolate good quality nuclei and DNA in early embryos for mechanistic experiments. Aim 2. Characterize the sequence of events upon SMCHD1-mediated gene repression Approach: A fusion protein dCas9-SMCHD1 and the appropriate guide RNAs (gRNAs) will be used to bring SMCHD1 to the beta-globin locus in K562 cells, where it does not usually bind. title: Development of a single-shot universal flu vaccine
abs: Influenza, commonly referred to as “flu”, is a top global public health concern worldwide. Current influenza vaccines are based on the very immunogenic but highly variable hemagglutinin (HA) and need to be updated annually to match the circulating strains. Increasing effort and interest have thus been devoted to developing broadly protective “universal” flu vaccines, based on highly conserved antigens across all influenza strains. Accordingly, these vaccines are expected to provide basal pan-flu protection that boosts the effectiveness of seasonal, strain-specific flu vaccines. They are also expected to confer some protection against outbreaks/pandemics caused by newly emerging flu viruses. The highly conserved ectodomain of influenza A M2 protein (M2e) is a leading universal flu antigen vaccine candidate. However, the clinical development of M2e-based vaccines has faced roadblocks due to M2e poor immunogenicity, despite strong adjuvant and multiple dose regimen. Thus, clearly, novel vaccine approaches are needed to improve the protective potential of M2e. We have been developing a powerful vaccine targeting approach that effectively enhances the immunogenicity of weakly immunogenic vaccine candidates. The strategy consists of shuttling these antigens to the Clec9A+ dendritic cell population by the means of a Clec9A-specific monoclonal antibody (mAb). We have applied this technology to M2e and engineered a recombinant anti-Clec9A mAb fused with M2e. We have shown that the single administration in mice of a small amount of the Clec9A-M2e construct triggered an exceptionally long-lasting anti-M2e antibody response that was accompanied with the generation of long-lived plasma cells, and resulted in up to 80% protection upon lethal influenza challenge. Thus, these findings supported that the Clec9A-targeting strategy allows antigen and dose sparing, and addresses the shortcomings of current M2e vaccine candidates. Building on these exciting results, we propose here to develop the second generation Clec9A-M2e vaccine candidate that will be able to induce simultaneously a humoral and cellular protective immune response. We will also optimize the vaccination regimen to stimulate effectively older immune systems, and we will investigate the nasal route of vaccination. Beyond influenza, the Clec9A-targeting strategy represents a “plug-and-go” vaccine platform that can be rapidly deployed and applied to any infectious and non-infectious diseases, the latter includes cancer. Thus, pre-clinical optimization of the Clec9A-targeting vaccine platform is an important endeavor that paves the way for the clinical development of this novel and promising vaccine approach.

title: Rationally designed immunotherapeutics for joint disorders
abs: Osteoarthritis (OA) is the leading cause of chronic progressive joint pain and damage amongst the world population. There is currently no effective treatment for OA, thus consequently, the need for new disease-modifying therapies is urgent. It is well-established that inflammation is the major driver of OA disease pathology and progression. However, recent therapies targeting IL1β and TNFα to decrease inflammation have not been successful. As OA pathological inflammation is driven by a plethora of inflammatory mediators, inhibition of one or a few inflammatory mediators may not be sufficient to halt or reverse the disease progression. Given that these inflammatory mediators are mostly produced by the innate immune cells at the early stage of disease, and in general interact via receptor-ligand binding, the immune cells must have the known and unknown cognate receptors on their membranes to bind to these inflammatory mediators. In our preliminary studies, we generated nanoparticles coated with membranes derived from different macrophage subsets, namely naïve (M0), pro-inflammatory (M1) and anti-inflammatory (M2) macrophages. Amongst all, M2 macrophage membrane-coated nanoparticles had the highest potency in binding inflammatory cytokines, IL1β and TNFα, and alleviating IL1β-induced nitric oxide production and matrix degradation in chondrocytes and cartilage explants. As OA inflammation is preceded by activation of innate immune cells, deciphering the profile of innate immune cells and their activities during OA would allow us to rationally design immune cell membrane-coated nanoparticles for effective OA treatment. We hypothesize by deciphering the cell membrane profile of innate immune cells activated during OA, immune cell membrane-coated nanoparticles can be rationally designed and manipulated for broad spectral capture of inflammatory mediators to reduce OA inflammation and promote joint repair. In this proposed study, we aim to 1) first profile the innate immune cells, their activation and cytokine production, as well as the complement activities during OA development and progression at both local joint and systemic levels; 2) design immune cell membrane-coated nanoparticles and hybrids based on the profile of innate immune cells activated during OA and characterize their physicochemical and functional properties; and 3) determine the therapeutic effects, biodistribution and fate of immune cell membrane-coated nanoparticles in a mouse OA model.

title: Statistical Reinforcement Learning for Mobile Health Interventions
abs: Mobile health (mHealth) interventions, broadly defined as health and behavioural interventions delivered via mobile and/or wearable devices, offer a powerful vehicle to improve health outcomes in today’s technology-enabled world. In recent years, healthcare providers and governments are excited about the opportunities mHealth offers in terms of improving efficiency and reducing cost of healthcare systems. Stakeholders in Singapore are no exception. In the era of “big data”, with the increasing volume, quality and accessibility of mHealth data, statistics/data science has a key role to play in the development of data-driven, personalized, adaptive, just-in-time mHealth interventions, and thereby in advancing this modern field. Hence methodological research on mHealth intervention studies is a very timely enterprise. mHealth interventions often consist of sequences of text-messages or other prompts that often aim to adapt to an individual’s time-varying context (e.g., location, weather, past behaviour, past treatments, evolving health status, etc.), and thus optimizing them is a multi-stage decision problem. Contextual multi-armed bandit (MAB) type reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms from the field of artificial intelligence have been employed in such decision problems, wherein a system must repeatedly choose among a set of actions (interventions), in an effort to maximize a reward (outcome). In the current proposal, we will focus on a popular MAB algorithm called Thompson Sampling (TS) – deeply grounded in Bayesian statistics, particularly useful in case of small amounts of data, and often operationalized via a regression model for the reward. The goal of employing such algorithms is to develop the so-called optimal just-in-time adaptive interventions (JITAIs), the optimally contextualized intervention decision rules that deliver the right type/amount of intervention at the right time. The current gold-standard data source for constructing JITAIs is a novel sequentially randomized experimental design called micro-randomized trial (MRT). JITAIs are often learned by longitudinal data analysis after the MRTs are completed. While this is a sound randomization-based developmental approach, trial participants do not get the benefit of receiving the optimized JITAIs. Thus, an even more attractive approach is to conduct adaptive MRTs wherein JITAIs are learned online via TS algorithm. The PI is currently involved as a collaborator in three MRTs in the United States, where some version of TS algorithm has been employed; these collaborations have helped the PI develop the current methodological research proposal. Despite their growing popularity, a number of open questions about optimal JITAI development via TS algorithm remain, demanding urgent attention. A key problem in mHealth is that only a small percentage of users use behaviour change apps over a long period of time. title: On the origin of droughts in Mainland Southeast Asia—implications for water and energy security
abs: In Mainland Southeast Asia, socio-economic progresses related to electricity production, crop cultivation, and power grid decarbonization are chiefly controlled by the availability of water resources. The strong seasonality of rainfall influenced by the Asian monsoon and the recent changes in local water availability demand for a better understanding and attribution of the origins of past hydrological droughts, as well as detailed projections of the impacts of future ones. This aim, combined with the analysis of drought consequences on electricity production and vegetation functioning, frames the scope of the project. Specifically, we plan to address the following questions: How did the water fluxes in the hydrosphere and biosphere change in response to changes in land use and hydro-climatological conditions in Mainland Southeast Asia? Have water management interventions altered the spatial distribution of water availability? How will drought characteristics evolve in response to future changes in climatological conditions and anthropogenic interventions? Currently, there is limited knowledge of how water management and vegetation response affect the spatial distribution of water availability across Mainland Southeast Asia. In this regard, the proposed project will create a knowledge basis to describe in detail Mainland Southeast Asia from an ecohydrological and water resources management perspective. In particular, we will use state-of-the-art process-based models (run at high spatio-temporal resolutions) to (1) simulate water fluxes in the hydrosphere (blue water) and biosphere (green water), and (2) explain and how these fluxes have changed in response to alterations of land uses, construction of hydraulic infrastructure, and natural climatological shifts. After having characterized past patterns, we will study how future climatic, land use, and management pathways are likely to modify the occurrence and intensity of droughts. The project will provide new knowledge about hydrological and carbon cycles in tropical and subtropical Mainland Southeast Asia, which have been understudied so far. We therefore expect it to generate new findings in tropical ecohydrology and water resources management. Beyond their scientific relevance, the problems addressed here have also paramount practical implications for the management of natural resources (crops, energy, and water) on which Southeast Asian countries, including Singapore, depend. A case in point is international power trading—a solution adopted by countries like Singapore to decarbonize their power grids—which is largely affected by droughts. Disentangling the origin of droughts in Southeast Asia is thus a first, necessary, step towards informing the management of interconnected resources. Another practical example are regional climate policies, which should ideally be informed by a deep understanding of the hydrological and carbon cycles of the different countries. title: A Catalyst-Controlled Blueprint for Enantioselective Alkene Functionalization
abs: Enantioenriched organic entities containing tri- and tetrasubstituted stereocenters are crucial for natural product synthesis and drug discovery programs. The spatial arrangement of atoms around stereocenters often dictates the overall shape of a molecule and influences its biological activity or toxicity. As such, the ability to exert exquisite control over the absolute stereochemistry is of utmost importance in pharmaceutical and agrochemical research. An attractive approach to assemble enantioenriched compounds in modern organic synthesis involves the regio- and enantioselective carbofunctionalization of readily available alkenes. Despite the advances reported thus far, major challenges remain unresolved. Catalysts containing precious noble metals continue to be regularly employed in synthetic processes, which inadvertently raises the cost of chemical production. Also, unnecessary chemical bond transformations are sometimes required, which contributes to excessive waste generation. In addition, the direct incorporation of two different carbogenic groups across alkenes, especially unactivated alkenes, suffer from poor regioselectivity due to weak electronic/steric bias and usually require pre-installation and removal of specialized directing auxiliaries. Furthermore, most dicarbofunctionalization reactions generate racemic molecules due to the lack of suitable chiral catalysts. For the analogous hydrocarbofunctionalization processes (addition of a hydrogen and a carbogenic unit), only trisubstituted stereocenters could be generated with limited scope. Therefore, we propose to develop a general nonprecious nickel catalyst-controlled blueprint (without activating/directing groups in the substrate) for enantioselective alkene carbofunctionalization transformations, in order to provide a more direct approach to access enantioenriched target compounds. This approach is expected to be more practical and sustainable to address critical synthetic challenges in enantioselective synthesis across academia and industry.

title: Tracking sea surface temperature change in the tropical Indian Ocean over the past five centuries
abs: Over the past two decades, sea surface temperature (SST) has increased significantly faster in the tropical Indian Ocean than the tropical Pacific and Atlantic oceans. The anomalous warming can intensify climate-related impacts, including rising sea levels, more frequent mass coral bleaching events and cyclone strengthening, and hence, has created serious concerns on marine biodiversity and human populations living around the Indian Ocean. The newly released Sixth Assessment Report by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR6) has concluded that the observed rapid ocean warming is driven by anthropogenic climate change, yet such human-caused climate change can be amplified or muted by natural internal variability in the climate system. title: A kingdom-wide study of genes, pathways, metabolites, and organs of plants
abs: The water-to-land transition of plants (plant terrestrialization) occurred ~500 million years ago, and the initially morphologically primitive land plants had to evolve complex organs, lifestyles, and specialized metabolites to adapt to an array of new challenges such as drought and desiccation. Understanding these molecular adaptations would be of tremendous interest, as we would better grasp how plant organs evolved and adapted to the different environments, allowing us to better tailor plant crops to our needs. However, the majority of current studies show two significant limitations. Firstly, they focus on studying genomes, which often cannot reveal when and where the different genes are active and which genes work together. Secondly, compared to flowering plants, the non-flowering plants are largely understudied and pose a significant knowledge gap. This proposal aims to address this gap and reveal which genes, biological pathways and metabolites are found in the plant kingdom, and study how these traits evolve. Our main hypothesis is that genes work together in pathways, which can be discovered with gene expression data. Thus, by comparing gene expression data of different species, we can gain an understanding of how pathways are born, multiply, or are lost. To address these gaps and take advantage of Singapore's tremendous biodiversity, we will generate 150 gene expression atlases for non-flowering plants and use this data to identify genes and gene expression patterns, which will form a basis for kingdom-wide comparative studies. By including the publicly available gene expression data of >200 plant species, we will compare the organ transcriptomes, biological pathways, and specialized metabolism biosynthetic pathways of ~400 plant species. This analysis will tell us which genes are essential for the function of plant organs, gene function, and which pathways appeared or were lost as plants became more complex. Furthermore, due to their importance in ecology and medicine, we will focus our analysis on the discovery of biosynthetic pathways producing specialized metabolites, which will be achieved by combining gene expression and metabolomic analyses.

title: Elucidating the Molecular Interactions of Engineered Protein Nanoparticles in Imaging Atherosclerotic Plaques
abs: Conventional atherosclerotic plaques diagnosis using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) modality is challenged due to the requirements for an ultra-sensitive contrast agent that allows early detection for improved prognosis. The FDA approved MRI contrast agent, superparamagnetic iron oxide nanoparticle (SPION), requires a long time (i.e., 2 days) to concentrate at the plaque site with limited and untargeted accumulation. The consequence is extended waiting time for patients and possibly administrative burden on the healthcare system. Furthermore, these contrast agents are typically monofunctional and do not allow for longitudinal tracking of the plaque’s progression. In previous work, we have shown that protein nanoparticles (PNPs) based on archaeal ferritin, a thermostable natural iron storage protein, can serve as a dual functional platform for both contrast agent in magnetic resonance (MR) imaging and molecular carrier [1, 2]. PNPs with magnetic iron nanocores of ~8 nm show high contrast enhancement in MR imaging [3], while loading of cyclodextrin shows reduction of lipid content in foam cells [4]. The reduction is comparable to standard statin treatment. These in vitro studies demonstrate the potential of the PNPs both as diagnostic agent and carriers for therapeutic molecules. We have also demonstrated cellular targeting via conjugation with reporter moieties, such as antibody, antibody fragments, and peptides, on the surface of the PNPs [5, 6]. Recently, we have started exploring PNPs for atherosclerotic plaque imaging. In a preliminary study, we confirm that fluorescently-labeled PNPs accumulate at the plaque sites using the ApoE-/- mouse model and they enhance the contrast in MR imaging. PNPs do not elicit acute immunological response as determined by immunodiffusion method and preliminary in vivo studies. Despite these promising material properties, the potential of PNPs with iron nanocore as a multi-functional carrier for staging of atherosclerotic plaque is relatively unexplored. No studies have been reported on their pharmacokinetics, improved accumulation at plaque sites, and molecular/cellular understanding on the fate of the PNPs in the plaque and their interactions with the resident macrophages. Understanding these interactions are important for future designs of better MR imaging contrast agents and improved diagnosis on atherosclerotic progression. In this proposal, our goal is to elucidate PNP molecular interactions with atherosclerotic plaque to better inform the design and engineering of the PNPs for faster targeted accumulation and better MR imaging contrast enhancement at the plaque sites. Hence, paving ways for the design and developments of future contrast agents. Particularly, in identifying vulnerable atherosclerotic plaques for the prevention of myocardial infarction or stroke. title: Understand and Predict: Marine Concrete Degradation under Climate Change
abs: Coastal reinforced concrete structures often suffer from accelerated corrosion. The degradation rate-controlling micro-processes, such as reactive transport of chemicals, corrosion product formation and mechanical disintegration are largely influenced by environmental conditions such as temperature, rainfall frequency, abundance of moisture and chloride. In the era of a more volatile climate, there is an urgent need to predict the environmental change and its influence to rebar corrosion. This is key to an enhanced structural resilience and a better maintenance planning that balances cost and safety. In this project we aim to investigate the degradation of reinforced concrete exposed to a variety of plausible climate change scenarios. This goal will be achieved by the synergized work from three investigators. Dr. He (Co-PI) will carry out high-fidelity regional climate modelling, the key outcome of which will be a set of projected climatic variables in the coming decades that are known to largely affect the corrosion degradation. Using Dr. He’s output, Dr. Geng (PI) will investigate the degradation mechanism of reinforced concrete exposed to both the current and future projected climate conditions. Using cutting-edge synchrotron-radiation probes coupled with laboratory-based methods, knowledge of phase-assemblage and microstructural evolution during corrosion will be provided to understand the ingress of chemicals, the formation of corrosion products and the accompanied mechanical damage. Dr. Poh’s (Co-PI) expertise in micro-mechanical modelling will be used to establish a coupled hydro-electro-chemo-mechanical model, with physics-informed parameters extracted from the experimental data of Dr. Geng, to set up a predictive virtual platform for the determination of damage and remaining service life of the degraded concrete. Supported by NUS College of Design and Engineering, and the Department of Civil and Environment Engineering, the PIs have necessary experimental facilities and the intelligence accumulations to conduct the project. The three PIs have solid experience and preliminary work to justify that they are capable of conducting the planned research. The novelty and impact of this project are three-fold. 1) It adds fundamental knowledge to marine concrete degradation throughout all stages of corrosion at unprecedented spatial-phase resolutions. 2) Predicted climate conditions, particularly extreme events are used as input for accelerated test, which may inspire future design of infrastructural durability. 3) A multiscale mechanical modelling calibrated & validated by experimental data will be established for serviceability prediction, in contrast to conventional modelling based on stationary material properties. title: Deterministic and scalable quantum systems in hybrid condensed-soft matter
abs: We are fast approaching the limits of the silicon technology, when it becomes increasing harder to reduce the size of transistors and optoelectronic structures. Quantum technology is an enticing candidate to enrich and vastly improve our capabilities in the domains of computation, telecommunication, information storage, optoelectronics and many others. The fundamental requirement for meaningful quantum technologies is the ability to control the state of individual particles, such as electrons, holes, excitons or photons. This can be done in a variety of structures and materials systems in a laboratory setting in extreme physical conditions utilizing complex characterization techniques. This project will enable step-by-step development of optical quantum chips that are technological in nature. Our structures will be fabricated via scalable and affordable printing process, polymer deposition and wet chemistry. The optical chips will operate at ambient conditions and will allow for selective optical and electrical excitation of individual quantum emitters, coupling of distant quantum emitters through polymer waveguide interconnects and will exhibit adaptive, quasi-intelligent response of the environmental variations. The ability to take advantage of quantum properties of matter to enrich modern technology is limited by the lack of appropriate material systems. For example, nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond is a flagship condensed matter system for realization of a qubit and single photon emitters. The diamonds are however very expensive and difficult to process due to their hardness and 3D crystal structure. In this project we will use the properties of hexagonal boron nitride (e.g., stable single photon emission at a limit of a monolayer thickness in ambient conditions) in combination with cheap and scalable growth techniques to create hybrid condensed-soft matter quantum systems/chips. The demonstration of electrically, optically, chemically and mechanically controllable quantum systems will bridge the gap between fundamental research and technology. Through our heterostructure and device architecture we will also demonstrate novel phenomena such as electrical excitation of defect centres in hBN, waveguide integration leading to microscale interdefect coupling. We envisage that the outcomes of this project will encourage scientific community to incorporate quantum technologies into novel domains of material research and enable development of quantum technologies. title: Changing Redox Center from Metal to Oxygen in Ni-based Catalysts under Light
abs: Achieving a comprehensive understanding in the electron transfer process during oxygen evolution reaction (OER) is crucial in the development of efficient and durable OER catalyst. Adsorbate evolution mechanism via metal redox center (AEM) and lattice oxygen mechanism via oxygen redox center (LOM) have been used to describe the electron transfer process in most of the OER catalysts. In particular, LOM-based catalysts have attracted significant research interest due to their superiority in terms of OER activity, when compared to AEM-based catalyst. With the escalating attention focusing on the development of LOM-based catalysts, researchers have been attempting to unearth the origin of lattice oxygen in LOM-based catalyst. Even though the presence and the quantity of accessible non-bonding oxygen (ONB) in the materials can be used to explain the adaption of numerous materials towards LOM route, it remains inconclusive for some LOM-based catalysts with low amount of accessible ONB. Thus, it is with upmost importance to provide a more comprehensive study on the triggering factor towards LOM, which is clearly lacking at the current stage. In our preliminary studies, it was found that LOM could be triggered and unusual OER performance with an extremely low overpotential of 133 mV at 10 mA cm-2, which is the best reported OER performance to the date, was achieved in strain-stablized NiOOH nanoribbons (NR-NiOOH) under simulated solar light. Although there have been quite a number of research works reporting the LOM phenomenon in various materials recently, the photon-triggered LOM has never been reported. It has been well agreed that the rich density of the accessible non-bonding oxygen (ONB) is the key factor towards LOM, but it is well known that Ni(OH)2 based materials lacks accessible ONB. Based on our previous study, the NiO6 unit cell in NR-NiOOH has a certain degree of distortion. Our hypothesis is that the distorted NiO6 unit cell in NR-NiOOH can be changed from the conventional octahedron to the square planar configuration under light irradiation. As a result of the formation of square planar, two accessible ONB states are generated, and hence the LOM mechanism is triggered. If this hypothesis can be verified, we are able to provide a new insight towards LOM in those materials with low quantity of accessible ONB, which will definitely contribute to the full understanding of LOM and add a new layer of designing mechanism for more efficient LOM-based OER catalysts. title: Chromium-Catalyzed Selective Hydrofunctionalization of Unsaturated Hydrocarbons
abs: The drive for replacing precious metals with abundant, cheap, and low-toxic first-row transition metals in catalysis has great promise for sustainable chemistry and has been practised by academic and industrial groups worldwide. Chromium is an early first-row group 6 metal and it ranks among the most abundant elements in the Earth’s crust. In contrast to the common view of chromium as a highly toxic metal, biological evaluation of toxicity for widely used metal salts in catalysis has confirmed the low toxicity of chromium(II) salts. Accordingly, there is a recent growing interest in developing chromium-catalyzed organic reactions. However, chromium compounds have never been employed to catalyze hydrofunctionalization reactions of unsaturated hydrocarbons previously. Unsaturated hydrocarbons are ideal starting materials to build complex molecules because they can be readily accessible or commercially available from major chemical suppliers. The development of hydrofunctionalization reactions of unsaturated hydrocarbons, such as alkenes and alkynes, has been considered to be a very promising push towards “greener” chemical synthesis as these transformations are completely atom-economical and produce minimum waste. For example, hydrosilylation and hydroboration of unsaturated hydrocarbons provide effective approaches to prepare versatile organosilicon and organoboron compounds, which can serve as important building blocks to construct medicines or pharmaceutical candidates. Our group’s recent work has disclosed the first example of chromium-catalyzed hydroboration of allenes and has demonstrated that chromium compounds have unique catalytic activity and selectivity for hydrofunctionalization of unsaturated hydrocarbons compared with the corresponding reactions catalyzed by other first-row transition metal catalysts. With chromium catalysts, unprecedented chemo-, regio- and stereoselectivity for hydrofunctionalization of unsaturated hydrocarbons can be achieved. The current research proposal focuses on developing highly effective and selective chromium-catalyzed hydroboration and hydrosilylation reactions of various types of unsaturated hydrocarbons, including but not limited to alkenes, alkynes, enynes, diynes, and 1,3-dienes. In addition, we will also study the asymmetric hydroboration and hydrosilylation of enynes to prepare chiral densely functionalized silicon- or boron-containing compounds. Furthermore, we will conduct mechanistic studies to identify catalytically active chromium intermediates and understand the achieved selectivity by studying the selectivity/ligand-structure relationships. The specific objectives of the proposed research are listed below. For each objective, we have gained solid preliminary results that strongly support the feasibility of the proposed research. title: Deciphering the roles of NuSAP in governing centrosome biogenesis
abs: During cell division, several proteins tightly control the dynamics of microtubules to ensure the precise alignment of chromosomes at the centre of the cell. Our group made seminal contributions to the characterisation of a group of microtubule-associated proteins (MAPs) that include HURP (Hepatoma up-regulated protein), HMMR (Hyaluronan-mediated motility receptor), and NuSAP (Nucleolar Spindle-Associated Protein) on their roles in chromosome oscillation, segregation, and cell division. In particular, NuSAP plays a vital role in mitosis as a microtubule stabiliser. In addition, NuSAP is a regulator of the chromokinesin, Kid. Depletion of NuSAP significantly suppresses the amplitude and velocity of chromosome oscillation. Moreover, NuSAP regulates the dynamics and depolymerisation activity of MCAK (mitotic centromere-associated kinesin) in an Aurora B kinase-dependent manner. Hence, our previous studies have provided new insights into the position of NuSAP in chromosome segregation during mitosis and cell division. Although previous studies have shown that NuSAP plays a role in the spindle assembly during mitosis, given its centrosome localisation, the function of NuSAP on centriole/centrosome biogenesis has not yet been studied. To explore the function of NuSAP in the regulation of centrosome biogenesis, in our preliminary results, we first established NuSAP-KO in HeLa cells by CRISPR/Cas9 system. Interestingly, we observed that depletion of NuSAP could induce centriole aberrations, including multi-centrosome with pericentriolar material (PCM) disorganisation, elongated centriole, and precocious disengagement. Remarkedly, several centriole/centrosome aberrations observed in the NuSAP-KO cells are similar to those in CEP57 (Centrosomal protein 57 kDa)-depleted cells. We went on to demonstrated that NuSAP could interact with CEP57. Depletion of NuSAP significantly delayed the recruitment of CEP57 onto daughter centriole during S/G2 phase, suggesting that NuSAP is likely to be critical in regulating centriole/centrosome biogenesis. Given that CEP57 plays a crucial role in recruiting CEP63-CEP152 to form a complex interface between centriole core and PCM, it is logical to question how NuSAP might regulate CEP57 and its complex in maintaining centriole biogenesis. To recapitulate the cellular functions of NuSAP in vivo, we aim to take advantage of the Mink (NuSAP homolog) mutant in Drosophila and investigate its centriolar/centrosomal phenotypes. Interestingly, we observed significantly longer basal bodies in Minkf02851 flies than of the control flies in our preliminary studies. Collectively, these preliminary results lead us to hypothesise that NuSAP may play a critical function in governing centriole/centrosome biogenesis.
