title: Cerebellin 2 and 4 signaling at synapses underlying memory-guided behaviors
abs: Synapses are fundamental to complex cognitive processes including the formation of memory, and the ability to use past experiences to make informed decisions, which lead to desirable outcomes. The prefrontal cortex particularly is intimately involved in the formation, modulation and retrieval of memories. Within the circuits centred around the prefrontal cortex, synapses between different neurons exhibit diversity in synaptic properties, including presynaptic release and postsynaptic receptor composition. This diversity enables circuits to perform precise computations in a reliable and fool-proof manner, resulting in normal behavioural output (Hestrin et al., 1990; Reyes et al., 1998). Abnormal synaptic function caused by mutations in synaptic proteins results in abnormal behavioural outcomes that are associated with a multitude of neuropsychiatric disorders including intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorders and schizophrenia(De et al., 2014). What gives rise to this diversity in the form and function of synapses? One class of molecules - synaptic cell adhesion molecules (SCAMs), which organise ‘adhesion’ of the pre- and the postsynaptic compartments are known to play a role in the generation of this complexity, owing to the diversity of their interactions in the synaptic cleft. Some of these proteins are implicated in neuronal synapse formation, synapse maintenance and activity-dependent strengthening of synapses(Sudhof, 2017a; Sudhof, 2018; Sudhof, 2021). Cerebellins (Cbln) are one family of recently discovered SCAMs. Mutations and variations in Cbln isoforms are penetrant in a wide variety of brain disorders including Tourette’s syndrome and schizophrenia(De et al., 2014) The impetus for this proposal is that mutations in Cbln genes, and in the complexes they form are found in patients with a variety of neurological disorders including schizophrenia and Tourette’s syndrome. Mouse models carrying constitutive brain-wide deletions of Cbln isoforms show severe cognitive and memory deficits. However, the precise mechanisms these molecules are recruited to are yet vastly unknown(Otsuka et al., 2016). Our preliminary data, generated using cutting-edge tools in molecular neuroscience, electrophysiology, mouse genetics and rodent behaviour suggests that Cerebellin isoforms, Cbln2 and Cbln4 play critical roles in both glutamatergic and GABAergic synapse formation/maintenance in the PFC circuits, and in turn, these molecules enable selective aspects of learning and memory This project will use a number of innovative tools that we have developed including the use of genetically engineered conditional knockout mouse lines carrying conditional deletions for multiple alleles, combined with circuit manipulations, in vivo and in vitro electrophysiology and mouse behaviour. This project will also employ the use of optogenetic technology to investigate synaptic function, including synaptic plasticity. Only a handful of labs carry out complete investig
kw: Cerebellin, neurexin, synapses, prefrontal cortex, excitatory synapses, inhibitory synapses, optogenetics

title: Perovskite-Based Heterostructures with Tunable Novel Optoelectronic Properties and Applications
abs: Two-dimensional (2D) hybrid organic-inorganic perovskites have been extensively studied in the last decade due to the naturally formed quantum-well structure and tunability. The other 2D materials including transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) have attracted a lot of attention since graphene was discovered. Combining two and more 2D materials in heterostructures brings up new physics: atomically thin p–n junction, non-linearity, many-body phenomenon, interlayer valley exictions, etc. As a result, it broads the applications in photodetection, light emission, electro-optic modulation, polariton devices. However, works on perovskite-based heterostructures have started to be published very recently are still rare. Combining perovskites with the other 2D semiconductors will help to address the current problems of the perovskite applications. First of all, it will allow investigating the interlayer charge and energy transfer. A better understanding of the mechanisms will allow molecular engineering of the perovskite materials with desirable properties for solar energy harvesting, light emission, and detection applications. Additionally, it will bring about new physics of the interfaces as has been achieved in TMDs heterostructures. In this proposal, we aim to combine the various hybrid halide perovskites layers and 2D materials in heterostructures in order to extend the already fascinating properties of the components. This novel approach has been first applied recently and has already demonstrated its potential. In this project, three types of heterostructures will be considered: two different perovskites, perovskite-TMD, and 2D perovskite superlattices. We plan to investigate excitions, phonons, energy and charge-transfer mechanisms, and other phenomena, evolving Raman and optical spectroscopies in a wide temperature range and under high pressure along with theoretical simulations. We will demonstrate the improved properties of such materials through prototype devices. This proposal builds on our considerable core expertise in the study of both hybrid perovskites and 2D materials, especially of light emission properties, electronic and atomic structures, simulation and device study, as well as high pressure and variable temperature.
kw: Hybrid Perovskites; low-dimensional materials; light emission; heterostructures; high pressure; simulation

title: Understanding and Closing Gender Gaps in Workplace Outcomes
abs: Achieving gender parity in workplace outcomes, whether leadership attainment or fair pay, is one of the pre-eminent challenges of our time. Although organizations in some developed countries have made progress in implementing more gender-balanced hiring practices (e.g., Schaerer et al., 2021; Williams & Ceci, 2015), large gender gaps persist in the promotion and compensation of female relative to male employees (Auspurg, Hinz, & Sauer, 2017; Bar-Haim, Chauvel, Gornick, & Hartung, 2018; Goldin, Kerr, Olivetti, & Barth, 2017; McKinsey & Company, 2021), both internationally and in Singapore as well (Straits Times, 2020; Channel News Asia, 2021). Past research on understanding why gender discrimination in workplace settings occurs has been extremely valuable, but holds some limitations. Although it can effectively estimate overall gender disparities in outcomes (e.g., gaps in leadership attainment), observational and archival research is unable to draw causal inferences and therefore provides limited insight into the underlying psychological processes behind gender discrimination. On the other hand, the current conclusions by past experimental research on gender discrimination are undermined by two challenges. First, growing evidence indicates that a disturbingly high proportion (up to 60%) of laboratory experimental investigations fail to replicate when the same methodology is repeated using new participants (Open Science Collaboration, 2015). Second, foundational gender bias effects may not emerge again if the cultural population in question has undergone shifts in the relevant beliefs, norms, and social roles (Eagly et al., 2020; Schaerer et al., 2021). Thus, carrying out contemporary replications and theoretical extensions of key findings in the gender discrimination literatures is critical, as is sampling as wide a variety of cultures as possible. This is exactly what we intend to achieve via the present initiative. Our proposed project will use state-of-the-art crowdsourced (Uhlmann et al., 2019) and open science methodologies (e.g., Nelson, Simmons, & Simonsohn, 2018) to systematically capture the factors that predictably trigger and deactivate discrimination against women and men in professional settings. We seek to understand the causal underpinnings of discrimination and inequality in order to identify theoretically and empirically informed interventions that can be used to combat them. The project will examine gender discrimination in three important work contexts: hiring/promotion decisions (Part 1), performance evaluations (Part 2), and salary negotiations (Part 3). In Part 1 of the proposed project will identify the most robust and generalizable contemporary contributors to gender discrimination in selection and promotion decisions. We will carry out both direct replications (same method, new samples of participants) and conceptual replications (new method, new samples) of foundational experiments on gender bias, collecting data across

title: Scaling up Graph Neural Networks – Theory and Algorithms
abs: Graphs are ubiquitous in modeling entities and their relationships. In recent years, graph-based applications have become increasingly popular in many disciplines, ranging from social networks, medical health, financial banking to road networks, and biology. Graph neural networks (GNNs) are known to be the most effective method to learn knowledge from data. However, training GNNs is resource-demanding, hindering its applications to industrial-level graphs. This project aims to address this issue by improving the GNN training and inference time costs, as well as storage overhead. We will employ multiple technical approaches such as advanced graph data management techniques and new parallel-processing frameworks. We will explore four specific directions. First, we will study how to design novel graph data management techniques in improving GNNs. Second, on top of the algorithmic improvements, we plan to explore the trade-off between efficiency and accuracy in both theoretical and algorithm aspects, to scale up GNNs at a proper expense of the accuracy. Third, we plan to design new techniques for parallel and distributed computation in the training of GNNs to improve scalability. Fourth, we plan to design online GNN algorithms to continuously handle the graph updates while maximizing the accuracy of GNNs spanning a long period of time.
kw: Graphs; Graph Neural Networks; Data Management

title: Numerical Methods and Analysis for the Dirac/Nonlinear Dirac Equations
abs: This project is devoted to design and analyse the most efficient and accurate numerical methods for the Dirac/nonlinear Dirac equations arising in the relativistic quantum mechanics for the mathematical description of complex physical systems with relativistic and quantum effects. In fact, the Dirac equation is a relativistic wave equation derived by British physicist Paul Dirac in 1928 in order to integrate special relativity with quantum mechanics for the mathematical description of the motion of relativistic spin-1/2 massive particles, such as electrons and quarks. It is consistent with both the principles of quantum mechanics and the theory of special relativity, and was the first theory to account fully for special relativity in the context of quantum mechanics. It was validated by accounting for the fine details of the hydrogen spectrum in a completely rigorous way. The equation also implied the existence of a new form of matter, antimatter, previously unsuspected and unobserved and which was experimentally confirmed several years later. Needless to say, the Dirac equation is the fundamental theory and the most important equation in atomic, molecule and optic (AMO) physics and particle physics. Recently, the Dirac/nonlinear Dirac equations have been extensively adapted to investigate theoretically the structures and/or dynamical properties of graphene and graphite as well as other two-dimensional (2D) materials, to study the relativistic effects in molecules in attosecond lasers, to simulate the neutron interaction in nuclear physics, and to model Bose-Einstein condensation with chiral confinement, etc. Due to the dispersive nature and highly oscillatory of the solutions in space and time as well as singular potential and nonlinearity, the Dirac/nonlinear equations at different parameter regimes become mathematically challenge and numerically complicated as well as scientifically important. The highly oscillatory nature in the solutions provides severe numerical burdens, making the efficient and accurate numerical computation for the Dirac/nonlinear Dirac equations extremely challenging. Thus it is very important to design and analyse efficient and accurate multiscale methods for the Dirac/nonlinear Dirac equations, which are uniformly accurate at different parameter regimes. The main aim of this project is to propose and implement the most efficient and accurate multiscale numerical methods and establish their uniform error bounds for solving the Dirac/nonlinear Dirac equations and the Maxwell-Dirac system in different parameter regimes. The questions to be addressed are: (a) to design and analyze multiscale methods for the Dirac/nonlinear Dirac equations in the semiclassical regime; (b) to establish uniform error bounds of time-splitting spectral methods for the long-time dynamics of the Dirac equation with small electromagnetic potentials; (c) to establish improved uniform error bounds of time-splitting spectral methods for the long-time

title: Seeing Is No Longer Believing: Examining Deepfake Identification, Impact and Instruction
abs: Deepfakes are synthetically generated media that pose as actual video recordings. A quintessential example is the face of a person in a video being replaced by someone else who is originally not in it. While deepfakes can be used positively, the majority are ill-intentioned for the purposes of pornography and misinformation dissemination. Consequently, deepfake identification is now an emerging area of research where most work is on the use of machine learning techniques that identify audio-visual imperfections. While such research is useful, a critical gap is that the human perspective of deepfake identification is missing. This is because despite advances in research, identification algorithms are currently not performing at a level where human judgement is unneeded. Further, deepfakes are relatively new to many people who may then fall prey to such misinformation, unaware that videos could be so well doctored. Set in this context, the proposed research is underpinned by three I's, namely identification, impact and instruction, and its specific objectives are to: (1) establish baseline deepfake identification strategies undertaken by people; (2) ascertain factors that impact the effectiveness of these baseline strategies; (3) examine the impact of deepfakes on people; and (4) create an instructional program to teach people about deepfakes. These objectives are accomplished through three streams of work. Each stream will be buttressed by theoretical frameworks drawn from fields such as information science, psychology, game design, and instructional design. Stream 1 addresses the first objective and encompasses two studies, one that requires participants to identify real and deepfake videos in a naturalistic setting and elucidate their strategies in an interview, and another that compares their performance against existing deepfake identification algorithms. The work will employ Hilligoss and Rieh's (2008) framework for information credibility assessment (FICA). It presents a unified conceptualization of three levels of credibility judgments, but whose potential has not been harnessed in the deepfake context. Complementing this framework is the Elaboration Likelihood Model (ELM), which will be used to understand how people process videos in their attempt to identify their authenticity. Stream 2 addresses the second and third objectives. One study employs a large-scale experiment to determine influential factors on deepfake identification strategies, and people's resulting perceptions of trust in online media and self-efficacy. It will be underpinned by both the FICA and ELM, as in Stream 1. Recognizing that the impact on deepfake victims have not been systematically investigated, the other study employs a survey and interview to understand the potential harms faced by deepfake victims. It will employ Carlson and Dalenberg's (2000) framework for the impact of traumatic experiences, which comprehensively characterizes the responses of people experi
kw: Deepfake identification; Impact and perceptions; Deepfake education; User-centered design; Information behavior

title: Building a fluxomic toolkit for strain improvement, with application to scCO2-tolerant Bacillus SR7 as a novel platform organism for bioproduction
abs: The goal of this project is to advance the development of non-model environmental microorganisms into platforms for production of biofuels and value-added bioproducts. The project will be centered on work with Bacillus megaterium strain SR7 (Bm_SR7), isolated from formation fluids of the McElmo Dome (Colorado) CO2 field that grows under supercritical (sc) CO2. However, the approaches developed will be applicable to development of additional strains with “extremophilic” properties, such as are currently being discovered in PI Thompson’s team at the Sembawang Hot Spring, Singapore (a separate ongoing project). The unusual physiology of Bm_SR7 enables its use as a biocatalyst in scCO2-based process environments that are inhospitable to most organisms but are beneficial for fuel and chemical production. In this work, we propose to use metabolic modelling to improve isobutanol and isopentanol production in a genetically engineered strain of Bm_SR7 that we have previously shown can produce biofuel with in situ product recovery with scCO2. We will characterize strain metabolism through genome scale metabolic modelling (GSMM) and metabolic flux analysis (MFA), to identify factors limiting growth and biofuel product titres under ambient and high CO2 partial pressures. Our specific aims are as follow: 1) Curate and test a metabolic model for strain Bm_SR7 using flux-balance analysis (FBA); 2) Probe 13C labelled metabolic fluxes to validate the model, and finally 3) Develop and test a roadmap for improved growth and production of isopentanol and isobutanol. This work will move us closer to sustainable fuel production from protein-rich waste streams accessible to Bm_SR7, advancing technology for a circular economy. However, beyond improvement of isobutanol and isopentanol bioproduction in Bm-SR7 the fluxomics toolkit developed in this project will represent a significant advance of the technical capacity in the two project PI’s laboratories and development of this know-how at NTU. Thus, a broader impact of this project will be the training of 2 PhD students and 2 Research Fellows in fluxomics methods and establishment of this method as part of the tool-box to study cell metabolism and enhance bioproduction of non-model organisms through analysis of metabolic fluxes at the Singapore Phenome Centre (SPC).
kw: Metabolic flux analysis; stable isotope; metabolomics; Bacillus; biofuel; isopentanol

title: Algorithms for High-dimensional Data Streams: Theory and Applications
abs: Data streams are models for data that are too large to be stored completely and can be updated arbitrarily. The rise of machine learning and data mining has resulted in an explosion of large-scale numerical linear algebraic problems. A core algorithmic technique is dimensionality reduction, which compresses a linear algebraic problem to a smaller version of itself, making the slow classical algorithms affordable. The techniques from traditional data stream algorithms have surprisingly led to several time-efficient dimensionality reduction constructions, applicable to a wide range of numerical linear algebra and optimization problems such as regression, low-rank approximation, tensor decomposition, etc. The proposed project pursues further study of dimensionality reduction techniques from both theoretical and applied perspectives, including pushing the limits in general guarantees and creating bespoke designs for concrete applications. Specifically, the proposed project considers the following two major directions. (1) Non-oblivious subspace embeddings. A foundational technique in dimensionality reduction is subspace embedding. Given an n-by-d matrix A (n > > d), a subspace embedding for A is a random m-by-n matrix S (m < < n) such that with a large probability, S preserves up to a (1+/-eps)-factor the ell_2 norms of all vectors in the column space of A simultaneously. There has been a good understanding of a few different oblivious constructions of S. However, in most numerical experiments, the target dimension m can be chosen to be much smaller than the theoretically guaranteed bound, and little research has been done to explain the phenomenon. A major thrust of the proposed project is to provide at least a partial answer to this question. A preliminary result of the PI and his collaborators show that if the matrix A only has a few rows of a large leverage score, it is possible to achieve a Count-Sketch-type embedding (column sparsity s = 1) with m = O~((d + log(1/delta))/eps^2), improving on m = O(d^2/(eps^2*delta)) for Count-Sketch, where delta is the failure probability. This can be regarded as a first step towards designing better non-oblivious subspace embeddings, and the PI intends to understand the trade-offs between the target dimension m and the leverage scores or other quantities of the data matrix A, similarly to how the Johnson-Lindenstrauss Transform, which can be viewed as subspace embedding for d = 1, is now well understood for feature vectors. The question above is about a specific matrix. In real-world problems, the data tend to follow certain patterns. This motivates the problem called distributional subspace embedding. Here it is assumed that A is sampled from some distribution D and the task is to design a subspace embedding matrix S that works for A with probability at least 0.9. title: Efficient modelling, inversion and imaging methods for site selection and reliable monitoring of CO2 sequestration
abs: To achieve the goal of net-zero emissions by 2050 to limit the global temperature rise to 1.5 degree Celsius, the massive amounts of carbon dioxide (CO2) produced by the combustion of fossil fuels and natural gases have to be largely and permanently stored in deep underground. To find a suitable place to store CO2, a high-resolution image of the detailed subsurface structure is highly demanded to provide guiding information. We propose to develop a novel joint inversion scheme using multiple types of seismic data and apply it to produce high-resolution 3-D subsurface images. Firstly, we will build a high-quality seismic dataset including body-wave traveltimes, receiver functions, P-wave polarization, Rayleigh-wave phase velocity, and Rayleigh-wave ellipticity. Then we will develop a joint inversion scheme that can make full use of the information embedded in seismic data. Finally, we will conduct a joint inversion of those seismic data to generate a seismic reference model of the upper crust (from the surface to about 10 km depth) beneath each test site or possible CO2 storage site. The seismic reference model will provide valuable insights into the hydrological, thermal, compositional, and other geodynamic processes of the near-surface underground, and therefore supply the necessary information to decision makers to select a suitable place for CO2 storage. We also propose to develop a reliable monitoring tool to detect underground microseismicity possibly related to CO2 injection, migration and leakage. In detail, advanced earthquake location method and adjoint-state traveltime tomography method will be developed to solve the coupled hypocenter-velocity problem. Starting from the seismic reference model mentioned above and iteratively improving model accuracy, particularly of the local complex media surrounding the CO2 reservoir, we can precisely locate microseismicity. We aim to reliably monitor microseismicity induced by the migration of CO2 in the subsurface and the temporal change of subsurface properties due to the interactions of CO2 with rocks and water. Reliable microseismic monitoring of the 3-D subsurface structures is very much needed to avert dangers to humans, animals, plants and prevent water aquifers from contamination. The success of this project will make direct and significant contributions to the development of carbon capture, utilization and storage (CCUS) technologies, which can remove CO2 from the atmosphere and have significant value in the road toward a net-zero future.
kw: Net zero by 2050; CO2 Sequestration; Site Selection; Monitoring; Joint Inversion; Adjoint-state traveltime tomography

title: Molecular underpinning of endothelial-immune crosstalk in the progression of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease
abs: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is the most common liver disease in developed countries, affecting up to a third of western populations, and up to 40% in South East Asia. The mechanisms underlying disease progression in some NAFLD patients remain unclear but likely involves a complex interplay between metabolic abnormalities with a vascular etiology. Concordantly, cardiovascular complications, but not liver-related disease, represent the main cause of death in NAFLD patients. Harnessing the replicative potential of blood outgrowth endothelial cells, we developed NAFLD patient personalized endothelial cell model to facilitate transcriptomic analysis and functional studies. Our preliminary data support that NAFLD implicates endothelial dysfunction through immune effector cell cytotoxicity-induced injury. To reduce the burden of NAFLD and associated vascular complications, we aim to elucidate molecular basis of endothelial dysfunctions and its contribution to disease progression. For this, two areas will be explored. Aim 1: To intervene chemokine-receptor interactions between endothelial cells and immune effector cells in order to restore vascular health: We propose to evaluate the therapeutic potential of inhibitors of chemokine and/ or chemokine receptors in in vitro human endothelial-immune coculture assays, as well as in vivo mouse model of diet-induced NAFLD. Aim 2: To elucidate the contribution of liver sinusoidal endothelial cells to NAFLD progression: Circulating endothelial cells (CECs) dislodged into bloodstream following vascular injuries can be used to establish correlates of vascular burden. We will employ single-cell RNA sequencing to derive molecular insights of liver-originated CECs from patients, and corroborate the findings with spatial transcriptomic analysis of mouse NAFLD livers. The identification of various transcriptomic states associated with cell types found in the liver, along with their spatial information, will provide a blueprint for deconstructing dynamic alteration of cellular interactions and pathologies during NAFLD progression.
kw: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease; endothelial dysfunction; chemokines; endothelial-immune crosstalk; single-cell analysis

title: Human-Interpretable Math Word Problem Solving with Reasoning-based Structured Prediction
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: Enabling machines to automatically solve maths problems written in natural language text is one of the most fundamental tasks in the field of natural language processing (NLP) and artificial intelligence (AI). Solving such math word problems requires deductive reasoning over the quantities in the text. Existing research efforts mostly relied on sequence-to-sequence or sequence-to-tree approaches to generate math expressions without explicitly performing relational reasoning among quantities in the given context. While empirically effective, such approaches typically do not provide explanations for the generated expressions. We aim to propose a novel approach that presents explainable deductive reasoning steps to iteratively construct target expressions. Each step in the reasoning process involves parsing text into a mathematical equation that captures the complex relations amongst quantities and entities. The algorithms are designed based on a novel deductive reasoning graph built based on an extended version of the structured prediction framework that we proposed. In this project, we aim to make the following major contributions: ● We build some new foundational understandings on top of transition-based structured prediction. ● We propose a novel, extensible model that is able to extract complex structured information from the text, which would be useful for math word problem solving. ● We propose a novel algorithmic approach to produce human-interpretable explanations to the deductive reasoning process, which can serve as a useful guide to human math learners. ● We deliver high-quality research papers and release useful software packages to the community. We believe the success of this research would lead to a new way of conducting research in the domain of math word problem solving – to the best of our knowledge, ours is the first effort that learns an explainable deductive reasoning process for such a task. We hope that our research could not only lead to significant scientific outputs but also be used to develop real applications useful for helping student learners (in Singapore and beyond) to fulfill their practical needs in learning mathematics.
kw: Natural Language Processing, Machine Learning

title: The River of Cooperation and Competition - The Effects of Upstream Dams on Downstream Countries in the Mekong River Basin
abs: Water has become an increasingly important and contestable natural resource, with conflicts often occurring over major rivers that flow through several countries. Worldwide, there are 263 such rivers that cross national borders, and some have been at the heart of disputes between neighbouring countries. In order to gain control of water resources, dams have been a widely used instrument through which countries upstream can either provide a source of hydropower or supply water. Recently, considerable attention has been paid to China’s construction of eleven dams along the stretch of the Mekong River within its borders, which has drawn massive concern over their potentially devastating impact on downstream countries. The environmental costs associated with dam construction, such as the disruption of the river cycle and the impact on the local ecology, have attracted some academic attention. However, we still know very little about the economic consequences of dams, and the limited research has mostly focused on the consequences of dams built over domestic rivers where coordination is possible (Duflo and Pande 2007; Strobl and Strobl 2011; Chen et al. 2021). Different from the existing studies, this project is the first to examine the economic and ecological impact of dam construction on international rivers where upstream and downstream coordination between countries is limited. To investigate this research question, we focus on Chinese dams built along the Mekong River that provide an ideal setting for several reasons. First, the two Chinese dams we examine in this project are among the largest dams in the world, and therefore the consequence of their operations, arranging from water flow patterns to economic impact on millions of people’s livelihoods, could be substantial. Second, the lack of coordination between the upstream and downstream over international rivers is particularly true in this setting, because the Chinese dams are built right next to the Chinese border with Laos, leaving China with little incentive to internalize the cost imposed on the downstream. That is probably why China has no role in the Mekong River Commission, an inter-governmental organization that works directly with governments in the downstream countries to jointly manage the shared water resources of the Mekong River. Last but not least, the segment of the Mekong River that lies just outside the Chinese border provides a quasi-experimental setup where a major tributary of the Mekong River, Nam Ou River, flows parallel with Mekong mainstream but was not affected by the two Chinese dams during the study period. To casually identify the economic impact of Chinese dams on the downstream countries, we compare croplands close to the Mekong River to those nearby Nam Ou River before and after the dams were built (a difference-in-differences estimation strategy).
