title: A Phase I/IIa Study of Dual Anti-CD22/CD19 Chimeric Antigen Receptor-directed T cells for Relapsed/Refractory B-Lineage Acute Lymphoblastic Leukaemia
abs: Anti-CD19 chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy is a promising curative treatment for relapsed/refractory B-ALL (r/r B-ALL) which may obviate the toxicities of radiation and allogeneic stem cell transplant used in standard salvage. Antigen-escape relapse is a major limitation of anti-CD19 CAR-T therapy, accounting for up to 50% of late relapses. Our clinical goal is to provide a cure for r/r B-ALL with less acute and long-term toxicities through our investigator-initiated treatment protocol which uses a pipeline anti-CD22-CD19 CAR-T therapy (named CART2219.1) in an upfront setting to replace chemotherapy intensification, transplant and irradiation. We propose that simultaneously targeting CD22 and CD19 will reduce antigen escape and improve leukaemia-free survival. Towards this goal, we will specifically evaluate the safety and efficacy of CART2219.1 in adult and paediatric cohorts with unmet needs ie. patients with persistent measurable residual disease (MRD) after front-line chemotherapy (Specific Aim 1) in place of transplant; and patients with relapsed/refractory extramedullary B-ALL in place of irradiation and transplant (Specific Aim 2). Our translational goal is to generate correlative data that predict dual CAR-T failures. The clinical significance of this research is the potential to achieve better leukaemia-free survival with less chronic health issues, improved quality adjusted life years, and significantly less health care expenditure. Our programmatic goal is to build a sustainable academic CAR-T programme in Singapore addressing the needs of relapsed/refractory leukaemias. In delivering our proposed therapy, we were the first group to have driven CliniMACS Prodigy® technology transfer, talent development and collaborative networks across our national GMP manufacturing teams, adult and paediatric clinical teams and scientific teams. We anticipate that such academic CAR-T therapies will improve patient access to cost-effective cell therapies manufactured in close proximity to the patient (point-of-care manufacturing).The multi-site clinical trial will also establish critical national collaborations and networks for academic cell therapies.
kw: CAR-T, Relapsed Refractory, Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, CART2219

title: Oncogenic roles of SWI/SNF complex in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia
abs: T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) is a hematological malignancy arising from immature thymocytes. Dysregulated expression and activation of oncogenic transcription factors, such as TAL1, NOTCH1 and MYC, is frequently observed in this disease, which initiates and maintains the cellular program of T-ALL (“transcription addiction”). However, it is still unknown how these transcription factors co-operate with chromatin remodellers to regulate different steps of transcriptional processes. Our preliminary study demonstrated that SMARCA4, one of critical subunits of the SWI/SNF chromatin remodelling complex, is aberrantly upregulated in T-ALL cells. Depletion of SMARCA4 by genetic knockout or by the treatment with ACBI-1, a PROTAC drug that specifically degrades SMARCA2/A4 protein, results in apoptosis induction in multiple T-ALL cells. Notably, depletion of SMARCA4 reduces the open chromatin regions (OCRs), majority of which are enriched for the DNA binding motifs of regulatory partners of TAL1 and NOTCH1. In particular, NOTCH1 and its target genes, such as MYC, are primarily affected by ACBI-1 treatment. These results indicate that SWI/SNF subunits potentially serve as an oncogenic factor in T-ALL, which is a marked contrast to its potential role as a tumor suppressor implicated in other cancers, suggesting the context-specific roles of SWI/SNF complex. Specifically, we hypothesize that, in the context of T-ALL where the cells are addicted to oncogenic transcription factors, SMARCA4-dominant SWI/SNF complex coordinates with these factors to remodel the chromatin and thereby efficiently provide OCRs at critical gene loci, by which leukemic cells are able to sustain malignant gene expression program. Overall purpose of this project is to understand the molecular functions of the SWI/SNF complex in co-operation with oncogenic transcription factors and their roles in cellular maintenance and transformation processes of T-ALL. We also aim to establish molecular basis for the application of SWI/SNF inhibitors for clinical trials.
kw: Cancer, transcription factor, chromatin remodelling, T-ALL, SWI/SNF

title: Precision Medicine PDOX (Patient-derived orthotopic xenograft) Modelling of Brain Tumor Microenvironment in Craniospinal-Metastasizing Brain Germinoma Phenotypes for Preclinical Testing (PreCIsionMOdELS 1.0)
abs: PROJECT BACKGROUND: Pediatric brain cancer is the leading cause of death in childhood cancer. Intracranial germ cell tumor is an Asian-centric disease, and majority (50-70%) are germinomas. No effective molecular inhibitors have been used in this disease - a lack of tumor models impeded preclinical drug development. SPECIFIC AIMS: The goal of this proposal is to develop Precision PDOX (patient-derived orthotopic xenograft) Mouse Models of metastasizing brain germinoma, capable of re-creating patient’s sequence of metastases in the craniospinal axis in-vivo, to provide biological tumor material from both primary (within brain) and metastatic sites during real-time in-vivo evaluation of drug efficacy. Specifically, we will evaluate differences in the drug response of 2 clinical stage molecular inhibitors, between primary site versus metastatic sites within a single mouse system, and elucidate distinct mechanisms in each site. HYPOTHESES: Based on our preliminary data, our working hypothesis is that there exist new secondary targets in tumor microenvironment promoting metastases, which can be exploited for treatment strategies. METHODOLOGY/APPROACH: We have successfully repositioned our PDOX Models from static (non-metastasizing) to dynamic (metastasizing) tumor models in-vivo, by changing the macrophage microenvironment. These Models efficiently replicates the metastasizing process of tumor cells in patients. Our panel of Precision Models provides an In-Vivo Toolbox encompassing a spectrum of 4 new in-vivo parameters representing a continuum of patient-relevant clinical features for preclinical testing. This will be an invaluable asset to the neurooncology community and pharmaceutical industry. IMPORTANCE: FDA-review of new anti-cancer drugs now includes assessment for substantial relevance to pediatric cancers. Our preclinical data will be crucial for driving FDA-approval for molecular inhibitors for germinoma and metastases – which currently there are none. Metastases cause 90% of cancer deaths worldwide. Drugs with tumor killing capabilities may not have an equal ability to control metastatic spread - a major determinant of survival outcome.
kw: Metastasizing Disease; Germinoma; Patient-Derived Orthotopic Mouse Models; Re-Purposing; Tumor Microenvironment Modelling; Dual Compartment Preclinical Testing

title: Determining the Hepatic Function of Lysolipid Transport by the Liver
abs: Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD) refers to a spectrum of worsening disorders progressing from mild steatosis (NAFL), to Non-Alcoholic Steatohepatitis (NASH), to cirrhosis, and might progress to hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). The development of NAFLD is driven by excessive uptake of dietary fat that contributed to lipotoxic lipids accumulation in the liver. The response of the liver to dietary fatty acids is to store them as triglycerides in cytosolic lipid droplets (LDs), export them as Very Low-Density Lipoprotein (VLDL), or oxidize them in mitochondria. Notably, both LD formation and VLDL secretion require a source of phospholipids. Intriguingly, lysolipids, namely lysophosphatidylcholines (LPCs) have been shown to augment VLDL secretion and LD formation in cells. However, the mechanism by which the liver acquires LPCs that could mediate these effects remains enigmatic. Here, we discovered a pathway that relies on exogenous uptake of phospholipid through the sodium-dependent LPC transporter Mfsd2a. The circadian expression of Mfsd2a is regulated by glucocorticoid receptor (GR) action at the onset of mealtime. Remarkably, mice with Mfsd2a liver deficiency (L2aKO) exhibited a robust NASH-like phenotype within just two weeks of high fat feeding (NASH diet). Lipidomic analysis of the L2aKO mice fed with NASH or choline deficient NASH diet showed significant reduction in phosphatidylcholine and phosphoethanolamine containing polyunsaturated fatty acids, and many species of LPCs. Intriguingly, treatment of LPC-18:1 and LPC-18:2, in Mfsd2a expressing human hepatoma cells, promote LDs formation. Taken together, we hypothesize that GR regulated Mfsd2a expression transports LPC to promote LD biogenesis and VLDL secretion in the liver in response to dietary induced stresses, thereby limiting the development of NAFLD.
kw: lysophosphatidylcholine; Mfsd2a; phospholipids; NAFLD; NASH

title: Probing Cellular Senescence in an Undiagnosed Disease with IVNS1ABP Mutation
abs: Ageing is a biological process characterized by cellular senescence and degenerated tissue function. It is often accompanied by debilitating disorders like Alzheimer’s disease. We have encountered an undiagnosed family whose teenagers display progeria (premature ageing) and severe neurological symptoms, including dyschromatosis, gray hairs, progressive motor deficits, and intellectual developmental delay. Whole genome sequencing revealed a homozygous mutation in the IVNS1ABP gene. As an influenza virus nonstructural binding protein, as well as an E3 ligase adaptor protein, the association between IVNS1ABP and ageing or neurological deficits has never been reported. By generating human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) from the skin cells of the family members and correcting the mutations via CRISPR/Cas9, I examined the cellular behaviors of the iPSCs and their differentiated progenies. I found that the mutant (MT) IVNS1ABP iPSCs and their differentiated neural progenitor cells (NPCs) display a greatly reduced growth rate. Their cell cycle time is extended and, in particular, the cytokinesis is disrupted, leading to mislocalized centrosomes and dysregulated spindle orientation and consequently mitotic failure. Furthermore, proteomics analysis with IVNS1ABP immunoprecipitated cell lysate revealed actin and actin-binding proteins as IVNS1ABP’s potential binding partners. Actin as a major player to set the fundamental cytoskeletal structures and cell framework is crucial for cell division. I, therefore, hypothesize that mutant IVNS1ABP dysregulates actin filaments and cytokinesis, leading to DNA damage and subsequent cellular senescence. I will first identify cellular and molecular changes underlying dysregulated cytokinesis in MT IVNS1ABP NPCs (Aim 1) and further define the molecular mechanism of how IVNS1ABP mutation dysregulates actin during mitosis (Aim 2). The information gained from this study will not only explain how IVNS1ABP mutation results in premature ageing, thus aiding the diagnosis and potentially development of therapeutics for the disease but more importantly reveal fundamental mechanisms for the normal ageing process.
kw: IVN1ABP; ageing; senescence; actin; cytokinesis

title: The Role of G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) Signaling in Quiescent Neural Stem Cell Reactivation
abs: The decision on the switch between quiescence and proliferation of stem cells is fundamental for tissue development and homeostasis. Most neural stem cells (NSCs) in the adult mammalian brain exist in a quiescent state but can undergo reactivation (exit from quiescence) upon physiological stimuli. The failure of NSC reactivation is associated with neurodevelopmental disorders. Recently, Drosophila neural stem cells have emerged as an ideal in vivo model for studying quiescence and reactivation. G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) and heterotrimeric G proteins transduce signaling cascades for various neural functions, and variants of GPCRs are associated with neurological disorders. However, the function of GPCR signaling in the quiescent NSCs is not established. This proposal aims to fill in this gap of knowledge by unveiling the novel role of GPCR signaling in quiescent NSC reactivation during brain development. The central hypothesis of this proposal is that the GPCR signaling promotes NSC reactivation via a small GTPase Rho1-mediated actin dynamics. In specific aim 1, I will determine the role of the GPCR-Gaq signaling during NSC reactivation. I will validate the role of GPCR Smog and G protein Gaq in NSC reactivation during larval brain development. The causal relationship between Smog and Gaq in NSC reactivation will also be examined by genetic analysis. In specific aim 2, I will investigate the role of Rho1 in Gaq-mediated NSC reactivation. I propose to establish the novel role of GPCR-Rho1-Formin (Dia) axis in promoting NSC reactivation via regulating actin remodeling. In conclusion, this proposal will discover the novel role of the GPCR-Rho1-Formin signaling in NSC reactivation during brain development, which may ultimately contribute to our understanding of the mechanisms underlying GPCR signaling-associated neurodevelopmental disorders.
kw: Neural stem cell, GPCR, Gaq, RhoA, Actin

title: Investigation of the circuit and molecular mechanisms underlying Synaptojanin 1 (SYNJ1) related epilepsy
abs: A homozygous missense mutation (R258Q) in SYNJ1, which encodes for Synaptojanin 1, results in early-onset atypical parkinsonism and severe treatment-resistant epileptic encephalopathy. Using SYNJ1 R258Q knock-in (KI) mice, a previous study established a mechanistic link with Parkinson-related phenotype, but it is unknown how the defective Synaptojanin 1, a presynaptic phosphatase involves in synaptic vesicle endocytosis and recycling, results in epileptic encephalopathy, which is evident in these KI mice. Using SYNJ1 Ki mice, I observed specific activation of neuronal population in the subtantia nigra pars reticulata (SNPR), which contains mostly GABAergic projection neurons and has been implicated in epileptogenesis previously. More importantly, my cell-attached recording of these neurons showed elevated spontaneous action potential firings. Based on these data, I hypothesize that increased SNPR neuronal activities result in epileptic encephalopathy in SYNJ1 KI mice with circuit-specific mechanisms and want to identify underlying circuit mechanisms of how SNPR neuronal hyperactivity drives epileptic encephalopathy in SYNJ1 KI mice by employing multidisciplinary approaches such as chemogenetic and optogenetic neuronal activity modulation as well as electrophysiology. Outcomes from this proposal will broaden our understanding of how dysregulation of SYNJ1 results in epileptic encephalopathy via a specific circuit mechanism and eventually provide a novel therapeutic opportunity for treating epileptic encephalopathy.
kw: Neuroscience; Synapse; Circuit; Epilepsy;Electrophysiology

title: The role of human fetal antigen presenting cells in tolerance and immunity
abs: There is still much unknown about how the immune system develops in early life. Defining the key moments when functional immune units develop during gestation and how it interacts with its environment has important clinical implications for a range of conditions. Our Long-Term goals are to pursue our work in the fetal immune ontogeny and to understand the general mechanisms of fetal immunosuppression, and the influence of the maternal-fetal interface in health and disease. We have previously made important discoveries of the fetal antigen presenting cell network that promotes T-regulatory cell development published in Nature (2017) and provided evidence of the phenomenon of fetal immune priming by live-bacteria found in the early fetal gut published in Cell (2021). In this renewal, we shift our focus towards the fetal gut, and will (I) continue to build a fetal immune atlas through state-of-the-art technologies in single cell sequencing and spatial transcriptomics, (II) generate a single cell spatial atlas of the fetal gut through integrating datasets from us and others, and (III) interrogate the preterm immune perturbations in necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC). Mapping the human immune system at the single cell level with crucial spatial information will enable us to develop a detailed understanding of the ontogeny of immune cells and their functional status during development that impacts on long term heath and disease in postnatal life. In turn, this may (i) enable more effective strategies for intrauterine molecular therapy to be developed, (ii) shed further light on fetal susceptibility to severe complications from intrauterine infections, (iii) develop new knowledge on the possible role that fetal immune play in the induction of fetal-maternal tolerance, and (iv) improve our understanding on how immune dysregulation early in life can lead/contribute to NEC, a devastating condition with high mortality and morbidity.
kw: Immune ontogeny, dendritic cells, T cells, necrotizing enterocolitis, single cell

title: Modelling and Evaluation of Retinal Stem Cell Transplants in an In-vivo Humanised Immune System
abs: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and Inherited retinal dystrophies (IRDs), are the main causes of currently untreatable blindness worldwide. In advanced AMD and IRDs, irreversible loss of central vision occurs due to death of retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) and photoreceptor cells. Given that AMD and IRDs are characterized principally by retinal cell loss, cell-based therapies represent an intuitive restorative approach. However, several key challenges remain before retinal cell therapy can be adopted as standard-of-care in clinical practice. This includes (i) Poor survival post-transplantation due to immune response in diseased host retinal micro-environment, and (ii) Limited integration for functional synaptic connection with host retinal tissue. This proposal aims to model and evaluate retinal stem cell transplant in an in-vivo humanized mice immune system. More specifically, we seek to understand host-immune response, cell fate maturation and functional integration of iPSC derived RPE and photoreceptor precursor cells, using a novel combinatory single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomic approach. If successful, this proposal represents an unprecedented opportunity to develop a somatically pristine, hypo-immunogenic cord-lining derived iPSC cell resource, and to improve our knowledge of retinal graft-host immune response – with the ultimate goal of enhancing retinal cell therapy outcomes. Findings from this study will help advance the field of regenerative cell therapy and develop novel therapies for otherwise incurable and blinding retinal degenerative disease.
kw: Retinal Degenerative Disease , Retinal Stem Cell Therapy , Humanised Mouse Models, Single Cell RNA Sequencing and Spatial Transcriptomics

title: The roles of non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH)-induced hyperhomocysteinemia (HHcy) on insulin resistance, visceral adiposity, and atherosclerosis
abs: Visceral adiposity, insulin resistance (IR), and cardiovascular disease (CVD) are risk factors that are highly associated with non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), a major complication in patients with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) which affects 30% of adult Singaporeans. We recently found that hyperhomocysteinemia (HHcy) increases in parallel with NASH severity, and that Hcy itself induces NASH. Elevated intrahepatic Hcy concentration led to Hcy-lation and down-regulation of key proteins, including Stx17, a SNARE protein involved in autophagy. Remarkably, vitamin B12 and folate (Vits) therapy decreased Stx17 Hcyl-ation, restored autophagy, and reversed the inflammation and fibrosis in NASH by promoting Hcy conversion to Met in the liver. Surprisingly, we also found that HHcy changed the visceral adipose tissue (VAT) distribution, homocysteinylation (Hcy-lation) of adipocyte proteins, and browning gene expression in in vivo and cell culture models of HHcy and NASH. Remarkably, Vits supplementation reversed these changes. Since HHcy and NASH both are associated with cardiovascular disease (CVD), it is possible that Hcy also promotes atherosclerosis by inducing protein Hcy-lation in vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs). Thus, we hypothesize: 1) HHcy has direct effects on VAT and vascular smooth muscle cells to increase IR and atherosclerosis, respectively; and 2)Vits supplementation reverses IR and atherosclerosis due to NAFLD. We will study the effects of NASH and Hcy on IR, protein Hcy-lation, cell signaling, and metabolism in VAT using genetic, dietary, and cell culture models of HHcy and NASH and the ability of Vits to reverse these changes. Similar studies will be performed in a mouse model of restenosis after wire injury and cell culture systems to determine whether HHcy causes cell proliferation and protein Hcy-lation in VSMCs. Vits supplementation to reduce IR and atherosclerosis associated with NASH could lead to major reductions in the health and economic burdens in Singapore.
kw: NAFLD, NASH, insulin resistance, obesity, visceral fat, muscle

title: Elucidating the mechanism by which Tjp1/ZO-1 deletion suppresses liver cholestasis and a possible involvement in biliary atresia
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Liver-specific inactivation of Tjp1/ZO-1 shows no overt phenotype but suppresses liver injury in several mouse cholestasis models via unknown mechanism(s). This protection can be recapitulated using AAV8 Tjp1 shRNA-mediated silencing, potentially opening a novel therapeutic approach for cholestatic liver diseases. We aim to elucidate the mechanisms by which Tjp1 deletion is protective using bile duct ligation (BDL) and Yap cKO mouse models. We will explore if Tjp1 expression correlates with biliary atresia severity or therapeutic outcome, and if gene expression changes in disease tissue are common with genes regulated by Tjp1 deletion in the mouse models. Since Tjp1 deletion leads to increased Cyp2b6/CYP2B10 expression, we hypothesize that protection may be due to enhanced bile detoxification. Cyp2b6/CYP2B10 expression is mediated by the transcription factor Sp1, and Tjp1 may bind and inhibit Sp1. Since bile ducts, absent in Yap cKO mice, are restored by Tjp1 inactivation, improved bile flow may contribute to protection. We postulate that Wwtr1/Taz, upregulated in Yap cKO liver, compensates for Yap to restore bile ducts, but only if Tjp1 is inactivated. Tjp1 binds Taz to restrict it to the cytoplasm. Taz can drive hepatocyte to cholangiocyte transdifferentiation and may thus also mediate bile duct regeneration in the adult, Tjp1-deficient, liver. Biliary atresia is a progressive pediatric cholestatic disease that requires surgery, often associated with modest success. We will determine of Tjp1 expression levels in biliary atresia liver correlate with disease severity or therapeutic outcome. Expression profiling will determine if genes affected in biliary atresia are common with those regulated in response to Tjp1 inactivation in the mouse models. The team has the expertise to successfully tackle the project. Required methods and mouse lines are available in the PI’s laboratory. The collaborators have banked biopsies from patients with biliary atresia (and other pediatric cholestatic conditions).
kw: cholestasis; biliary atresia; liver cancer; tight junction protein 1; signalling; regeneration

title: 23hr laparoscopic colectomy: From dream to reality? A step wise approach.
abs: Specific aims and hypotheses Aims: 1. To examine key stakeholders’ perceptions, receptibility, barriers and facilitators towards novel models of next day discharge post-colectomy in selected patients 2. To evaluate clinical-, patient reported-, safety and feasibility outcomes comparing the novel models of next day discharge with current post-laparoscopic colectomy inpatient care. 3. To estimate the potential cost-savings between the novel models of next day discharge with standard care Hypotheses: 1. Concerns and barriers exist amongst key stakeholders towards next day discharge following laparoscopic colectomy, which can be addressed prospectively 2. Next day discharge after laparoscopic colectomy is safe and achieves comparable clinical and patient reported outcomes as standard care 3. 23-hour colectomy can lead to considerable healthcare cost-savings compared to standard care Methods and approach This is a collaborative effort across three public hospitals (NUH, NTFGH, SKH) and the Schools of Medicine and Public Health, NUS. Study 1 will examine attitudes, perceived barriers, and facilitators surrounding 23-hour colectomy from the perspectives of eligible patients, caregivers of eligible patients, and healthcare providers. Study 2 will retrospectively examine pre-, intra- and post-operative outcomes in a defined cohort of laparoscopic colectomy patients aged 65 and below in the last 5 years. Study 3 will pilot a proof-of-concept establishing feasibility, safety, and uptake of this 23-hour colectomy model firstly with patients in NUH, and then subsequently with NTFGH and SKH. Lastly, Study 4 will economically evaluate the pilot 23-hour colectomy programme compared to the corresponding cohort of eligible patients who opted instead for standard care. Importance to science and medicine This study epitomizes NMRC’s vision for more self-ownership of health. Through the use of more tailored or targeted health services pathways, in this case for the lowest risk post-operative patients, we seek to free up precious tertiary healthcare resources to cater to more complex cases.
kw: health services research; healthcare manpower sustainability; implementation science; laparoscopic colectomy; early discharge; new models of care

title: Dopamine treatment of Myopia (DTOM): Assessing the efficacy of levodopa eye drops in the control of childhood myopia.
abs: This study will assess the safety and efficacy of a novel pharmaceutical treatment for controlling myopia progression in childhood. Myopia is a chronic progressive condition arising from excessive elongation of the eye during development. It is the leading cause of visual impairment and low vision world-wide. Although the visual blur can be easily corrected, this does not address the sight-threatening pathological changes associated with excessive eye growth. There are a range of interventions (atropine eyedrops, glasses and contact lenses) available to control myopia, but each has its limitations. Importantly, treatment efficacy can be variable, especially in younger children with a strong family history of myopia. Therefore, significant efforts and being undertaken to develop novel treatments to combat the onset and progression of myopia. One of the most consistent molecular changes implicated in myopia development is a reduction in the levels of dopamine, a major retinal neuromodulator. This prompted our team to reformulate the drug levodopa into an ophthalmic solution for topical application to the eye as a treatment for myopia. Levodopa is the naturally occurring precursor molecule to dopamine and has been used clinically for over five decades as the primary treatment for neurological disorders involving depleted dopamine levels. Our preclinical findings show that an ophthalmic levodopa solution can prevent the onset and progression of experimental myopia in a dose-dependent manner, providing greater efficacy than atropine, the primary pharmacological treatment for human myopia. Consistent with pre-clinical animal testing, a Phase 1 tolerability and safety trial observed no adverse effects of levodopa on ocular surface tolerability, visual function, ocular health, cycloplegic refraction and ocular biometry. This randomized, placebo controlled, double masked 12-month Phase II clinical trial will determine the safety and efficacy of daily levodopa eyedrops in controlling myopia progression in 90 6–12-year-old children over 1 year.
kw: dopamine myopia intervention

title: Function of the omega-3 fatty acid lysolipid transporter Mfsd2a in epidermal homeostasis
abs: The skin functions as a protective barrier against microbial, chemical and mechanical insults from the external environment and is essential in preventing the loss of water and electrolytes, contributing to thermoregulation. Disruption of the epidermal skin barrier is a common clinical feature for prevalent diseases such as atopic dermatitis and psoriasis. The epidermis is completely reliant on exogenous delivery and uptake of the essential fatty linoleate for the synthesis of acylceramides, critical for barrier formation. The pathway for acylceramide biosynthesis and barrier formation has been largely elucidated. Epidermal barrier formation demands a high amount of phospholipid, yet very little is known regarding the function of epidermal phospholipids and the pathways by which the epidermis obtains phospholipids. In this proposal, we leverage our knowledge of the biology of Mfsd2a, a sodium-dependent lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC) transporter, and demonstrate that Mfsd2a is expressed in epidermal keratinocytes where it mediates LPC uptake. We show that epidermal-specific deficiency of Mfsd2a leads to reduced epidermal phospholipids associated with hyperkeratosis and defective desquamation. The central hypothesis is that uptake of plasma-derived LPCs via Mfsd2a is quantitatively important for maintaining normal phosphatidylcholine pools that is important for keratinocyte differentiation. Guided by strong preliminary data that supports feasibility of this project, the goal of this application will be achieved by three specific aims: (1) To determine the role of Mfsd2a-mediated LPC transport on epidermal lipid homeostasis. (2) To determine the relative contribution of the Mfsd2a pathway and the Kennedy Pathway on epidermal lipid homeostasis and differentiation. (3) To determine the importance of Mfsd2a and LPCs in reepithelization and wound healing. The proposed research is designed to fill major gaps in fundamental knowledge on the role of phospholipids in epidermal homeostasis and differentiation and provide key proof-of-principal experiments in mice for the development of LPC-based agents for wound healing.
kw: transporters; lipids; omega-3 fatty acid; phospholipids; epidermis

title: A combined museomic and ‘Earth history-guided’ field approach to discover the world’s last undetected centers of species endemism
abs: Current rates of species extinction are ~1000 times the likely background rate, and the conservation of biodiversity has been recognized as "a common concern of humankind" by all 196 signatory nations of the Convention on Biological Diversity. Most species are range-restricted endemics that are more likely to be threatened than wide- ranging species. Conservationists can target a disproportionate share of biodiversity by focusing on centers of endemism, especially of birds, as good taxonomic data on most other organisms are lacking. But recent avian discoveries have shifted the main arena of undescribed diversity away from South America and into the Asia-Pacific region, suggesting many centres of endemism have not yet been detected. Vertebrate species discovery in the 21st century is challenging and requires a confluence of capabilities involving field experience, taxonomic expertise and genomic know-how combined with requisite funding, and my lab group is uniquely positioned for this challenge. I propose a massive integrative effort, involving museomics and the implementation of an ‘Earth history-guided’ discovery approach as first championed in my Science paper (14) that would enable a single lab group to produce a breakthrough in the discovery of the planet’s last unknown centres of avian endemism. The described program has the realistic potential to increase the count of centers of endemism in the Asia-Pacific region by 10- 20%, which is a quantum leap in our knowledge on endemism in the 21st century, and shift global conservation focus on areas in Southeast Asia that have remained neglected for centuries.
kw: biodiversity discovery; centres of endemism; museomics; NGS; earth-history

title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) Based Vessel Risk Profile Estimation and Classification
abs: With the rapid development of shipping industry in recent decades, the number of vessel traffic accidents has also been increasing, resulting in environment pollution, economic loss, and human fatality. To support a smart and advanced decision making of various stakeholders in the shipping industry, such as ship owners, charterers and insurers, it is imperative to develop cutting-edge methodologies and efficient tools to assess vessel risk profiles and make vessel risk classification from the perspective of vessels as well as vessel traffic conditions. This project aims to investigate vessel risk profile estimation and classification using Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based approaches. The first research focus is to establish a multi-source vessel risk data mall. The multi-source data fusion approach will be conducted to establish a comprehensive vessel risk data mall. The unstructured text data will be mined with Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques. To reduce the dimensionality and remove redundant information on the vessel risk profile, feature selection methods will also be utilised. The second research focus is to develop an AI-based vessel risk level assessment engine. An AI-based vessel risk assessment model will be developed, and the most significant contributing factors to vessel risk level will be identified. We will also augment the vessel risk profile and risk assessment model with the historical voyage information of vessels, subject to historical AIS data availability. The research methodologies proposed by this project include multi-source data fusion, text mining, feature selection, and AI-based classification algorithms. With these methodologies, this project will estimate the vessel risk profile and develop viable models for vessel risk assessment. In addition to the academic merits, the deliverables of this research project are with practical significance, which could help policy makers design related countermeasures on vessel risk mitigation, aid on the commercial decisions of shipping industry stakeholders, and reduce vessel incidents’ severity/frequency.
kw: Vessel risk profile; vessel risk classification; multi-source vessel risk data; AIS data; data fusion; Artificial Intelligence based approaches

title: Coupled Engine-Vessel Physics with Data Driven AI Models for Carbon Emissions Estimation
abs: This Proposal relates to the Maritime R&D Grant Call on Maritime Artificial Intelligence, on the Topic of Decarbonisation and the AI Challenge To estimate and calculate CO2 emissions of a vessel based on available datasets by Wärtsilä. Scientific Abstract This project couples comprehensive principle- and physics-based engine and vessel models with Artificial Intelligence to structure, dynamically adapt and evolve the models through data assimilation and machine learning techniques. A mapping function that predicts the various types of data will be first developed for CO2 emission estimation. Knowledge distillation or pruning techniques will be used to reduce the model size of a pre-trained model to arrive at an updated model with few parameters and a faster inference speed. Concurrently, a physics-based model for quantitatively simulating carbon emissions under various operational conditions is developed. The total power consumption and engine load are calculated using the vessel's hydrodynamic model, the carbon emissions based on the engine model and total emissions based on the voyage or voyage segment. The prediction model will be further refined for better accuracy using methods such as Adaptive Artificial Neural Network (ANN) through the coupling of the principle and physics-based model. The ship engine and vessel data will be assimilated into the physics-based model and coupled with the AI estimation models with an adaptive neural learning engine.
kw: Decarbonization; Artificial Intelligence; Machine Learning; Adaptive Neural Network

title: Smart ship fuel consumption and emission estimation: AI-based approaches and assessment of energy-saving devices and technologies
abs: The international maritime organization (IMO) and many governments have recently adopted several restrictions and control policies on ship emissions. Thus, ship operators and owners need to deploy energy-saving technologies and devices for reducing ship emissions and fulfilling emission control requirements. To facilitate the investment and management of energy-saving devices, it is of crucial importance to accurately estimate fuel consumption/emission before and after installing energy-saving devices. This 2-year project aims to develop AI-based approaches for estimating ship fuel consumption and emission and propose evaluation methodologies for ship energy- saving devices and technologies. Based on the multi-source sensor data of ships, the first work package (WP) of this project is to develop a methodological framework of data fusion and pre-processing procedures to build a holistic ship- related data mall. We will conduct relevance analysis and principal component analysis (PCA) to identify the key data items and refine them as standardized and normalized datasets. The second WP of this project is to develop machine learning (ML) based models for fuel consumption and emission estimation respectively using the processed datasets in WP1. We will consider and test different types of ML models and ensemble different model results for better estimation performance. Special consideration will be paid to the impact of ship types and energy-saving devices. The third WP focuses on the cost-effectiveness evaluation of energy-saving technologies and devices. We will assess the efficiency of multiple energy-saving devices in terms of fuel consumption/emission based on the ML estimation results and put forward various cost-effectiveness measurements to rank energy-saving devices in terms of economic and environmental benefits. Overall, the project will provide valuable managerial insights on ship energy- saving devices for decision-makers. The developed models and algorithms can form a cutting-edge decision tool for the investment and application of energy-saving technologies and devices.
kw: ship fuel consumption and emission estimation;  multi-source sensor data of ships;  data fusion;  energy-saving technologies and devices;  machine learning based modes;  cost-effectiveness evaluation

title: Baseline data collection and projections of the impacts of Climate Change on Singapore’s offshore water resources
abs: Singapore is a highly water-stressed nation which has turned to technology to optimize all available water sources. Desalination is the key method for the future, which together with NEWater, is projected to meet 85% of Singapore’s water demands by 1961. However, desalination is energy intensive (3.5 kWh/m3), with high operating costs due to membrane scaling/fouling. Additionally, brine discharge may pose considerable threat to marine faunal and floral communities. Future climate change and sea-level rise will inherently affect the water quality, sedimentation flux and geochemistry of the intake water source – the Singapore Strait. Beyond hydrological modelling, we currently know little of the water quality, sedimentation flux, geochemistry and ecological health within the Singapore Strait. This comprehensive study aims to ground truth modelled outputs by collecting baseline water parameters (i.e., salinity, turbidity, temperature, current), bathymetry, subsurface geology and sedimentological data (i.e., grain size, organic content, geochemistry) critical for projecting the effect of climate change on Singapore’s offshore water resources. Through a systems-thinking approach, we will produce key deliverables aimed to optimize the desalination process, quantify and reduce ecological damage and identify potentially identify alternative offshore water sources. Deliverable one is the temporal and spatial identification of offshore sites with low salinity, sedimentation and organic loads with reduced (sub)surface heavy mineral/geochemical concentrations to not only reduce desalination costs but provide empirical data which help to predict impacts on the Singapore Strait through future climate change. Deliverable two will deliver quantitative baseline data on the sea floor faunal assemblage of key sites where water may be either extracted or discharged from the desalination process. These deliverables are achieved systematically through four sub-projects, comprising (1) desktop study/synthesis, (2) seafloor and subsurface mapping, (3) coring and sedimentological analysis (4) micropaleontological analysis. This project will significantly benefit any agency (e.g., MPA) with operations/infrastructure in the Singapore Strait.
kw: Marine geology; benthic survey; seafloor morphology; sedimentology; micropalaeontology; climate change

title: Conjugated Oligoelectrolytes: A New Molecular Platform for RNA Encapsulation and Delivery
abs: Cationic conjugated oligoelectrolytes (COEs) interact with RNA to form well-defined spherical nanocomplexes. Preliminary work has demonstrated that in the case of small interfering RNA (siRNA), these COE nanocomplexes protect against RNase degradation, achieve RNA transfection efficiencies comparable to those of commercially available lipid reagents, enable efficient silencing of relevant genes in pancreatic cancer, and inhibit tumour growth. These opportunities led us to propose this study program, which seeks to understand the full potential of COEs as RNA transfection agents, with a special emphasis on mRNA. A key enabler of the effort is the diversity of COE molecular structures afforded by the modular and versatile nature of their synthesis. The collective effort will provide guidelines on how to design the chemical structures of the COEs (Project 1), the best formulation conditions for controlling nanoplex self-assembly with messenger RNA (mRNA) (Project 2), and an evaluation of COE nanoplexes as mRNA transfection agents through a set of in vitro studies (Project 3). These Projects are individually summarized below. Completion of the overall program will provide the first systematic study of COEs as a platform for the design of mRNA transfection carriers. Project 1: We will take advantage of the modular chemical structure of COEs and their established synthetic methodologies to identify molecular features that improve overall COE-mRNA nanoplex properties. These features include length of the conjugated framework, total number of charges per molecule, and introduction of pH-sensitive end groups. Cytotoxicity and haemolytic activities of all new COEs will be measured to determine safety profiles for comparison with commercial counterparts. Project 2: COE-mRNA nanocomplexes will be prepared by microfluidic techniques using the outputs from Project 1. The objective is to determine the most reliable formulation for consistently achieving spherical nanoplexes with diameters in the 50-150 nm range, positively charged surfaces, and low polydispersities. We will also examine the function of COEs as optical dopants in conventional mRNA-lipid nanoparticles with the intent of using the emissive properties of COEs to untangle mechanistic questions. Microfluidic approaches are particularly appealing to prepare nanoplexes and LNPs in view of scalability and reproducibility, and preliminary studies show that this is the case for COEs. For all nanoplexes, we will determine size distributions and surface charge by using a Zetasizer instrument, morphological features by cryo-TEM. Knowing these structural features as a function of COE structure will reveal the logis of COE-mRNA assembly. Project 3: The cellular entry and desired function of COE-mRNA nanoplexes from Project 2 will be determined by using custom-made mRNA sequences that contain a tracking dye (to determine its location) and produce eGFP (to determine intracellular transfer expression efficiency).
kw: Conjugated Oligoelectrolyte, Self-Assembly, mRNA delivery, Supramolecular Organization, Transfection Reagents

title: IntelliStream: Towards Highly-Optimized, Ultra-Scalable, and Self-Adaptive Data Stream Analytics in the Heterogeneous IoT Environment
abs: The arising heterogeneous IoT system, which contains hundreds of loosely coupled heterogeneous IoT devices (e.g., powerful sensors/mobiles, gateways, and edge computing infrastructures), and millions of ad-hoc and continuous running data-intensive analytic applications will require significant changes to the current design and implementation of big data processing paradigms. Traditional batch processing mechanisms are often not suitable, while state-of-the-art stream processing mechanisms are commonly designed for cloud-centre architecture with tightly coupled commodity servers. As a result, high-performance stream processing in the heterogeneous IoT system remains a still open and challenging research problem. Despite the development of next-generation networking and computing infrastructure is currently in progress, little attention has been paid to revising the design and implementation of stream operations and the next-generation data stream processing systems (DSPSs) to take advantage of the emerging heterogeneous IoT system. To respond to this situation, we propose the first systematic approach in designing and optimizing stream operations and DSPSs from the bottom-up. In particular, we have the following inter-related goals: 1) develop a highly-optimized stream processing engine for representative stream operations on modern hardware architectures with a software-hardware co-design paradigm; 2) develop an ultra-scalable workload scheduler leveraging novel mathematical modelling and AI techniques; 3) propose self-adaptive mechanisms to handle fluctuating IoT environment. This proposal is timely, and we address the fundamental research issues in designing efficient stream operation algorithms and scalable DSPSs for the emerging heterogeneous IoT system with a prototype implementation and empirical evaluation. The outcome of this research is also timely with the popularity of real-time artificial intelligence (AI) applications, where stream processing (e.g., filtering, summarization, transformation, cleaning, continuous learning and inferring) for large scale online machine learning and stream data mining, especially in the large scale heterogeneous IoT system, is becoming crucial and will soon become a mandatory task for AI experts. The proposed research will yield novel methodologies to facilitate a fundamental understanding of the challenging problem of designing highly-optimized, ultra-scalable and self-adaptive DSPS for the emerging massive scale IoT applications. The results of this research proposal can be translated directly into working prototype that will benefit the data analytic industry. Moreover, the theories and methodologies developed by this research will be integrated into teaching materials, tutorials, and textbooks, benefitting a cadre of students and engineers.
kw: Stream Processing; Heterogeneous Architectures; IoT Systems; Query Optimization, Edge Computing; Modular Design

title: Tackling Disruptions to Frailty Interventions: Developing Personalized Interventions Targeted for Older Persons with Cardiac Frailty
abs: Background: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is a formidable disruptor of frailty interventions related to exercise or dietary modification. Patients and physicians face uncertainty about dispensing exercise programs to frail patients with CVD. This hesitancy is found across acute to step-down care to community settings. We found that skeletal muscle sarcopenia, deteriorations in handgrip strength are closely linked to deterioration in cardiovascular structure resulting in overall functional cardiac frailty. Exercise interventions effected changes in mitochondrial pathways, muscle energetics and cardiovascular function. This 5-year proposal seeks to develop interventions in exercise and diet that are targeted for older adults with cardiac frailty. To achieve greater impact in primary and secondary prevention, this proposal seeks to test interventions in exercise and diet targeted towards cardiac frailty, across healthcare settings (acute care, community hospitals, primary/outpatient clinics). Methods: Using a multi-centre clinical trial study design (first 2.5 years), cardiac frail participants from each healthcare setting will be randomized to receive Intervention Sets or usual care. At pre-defined time points, participants will undergo assessments for frailty, cardiovascular function, nutrition, quality of life and behaviour. We will determine if the Intervention Sets can reverse or retard cardiac frailty, compared to usual care. In next 2.5 years, we will implement cardiac frailty screening and assessment at these healthcare settings. Artificial intelligence will be used to screen large volumes of patients going through these facilities. The special diet will be incorporated as part of diet order system in hospitals. The exercise program will be incorporated into hospital or community hospitals and linked to community partners. Our proprietary cardiac health mobile application will serve to allow self-evaluation of physical activity on cardiac health. Significance: Randomized investigations are urgently needed to reverse or delay frailty. This proposal will provide definitive evidence and executable care plans to incorporate frailty interventions in CVD prevention.
kw: prevention; aging; cardiovascular; sarcopenia; biomarkers; metabolic

title: Optimising INtrinsic Capacity for Functional INdependence and to Impede FrailTY in Older Adults: Adaptation of the WHO-ICOPE for Healthy Ageing in Singapore (INFINITY-ICOPE)
abs: This study (Optimising INtrinsic Capacity for Functional INdependence and to Impede FrailTY in Older Adults: Adaptation of the WHO-ICOPE for Healthy Ageing in Singapore) integrates concepts of intrinsic capacity (IC, composite of physical and mental capacities) and frailty in a systematic screening approach linking with targeted referral pathways to support healthy ageing in community-dwelling older adults, leveraging technology for automated measures of frailty characteristics and self-management of IC. The primary objectives are (i) to maintain functional independence in older adults, measured using life-space mobility, and (ii) implement INFINITY-ICOPE with high fidelity, penetration and sustainability. Our secondary objectives are to (iii) promote adherence to regular screening for frailty and IC decline, (iv) prevent frailty progression or onset, (v) improve health-related quality of life for seniors, (vi) deliver a cost-effective model for healthy ageing with reduced healthcare utilization. The study will progress in 4 phases, with a hybrid type 2 implementation-effectiveness study design. In proof-of-concept, we will validate our working prototype for automated frailty measures (SCREENii), adapt an existing mHealth platform (EMPOWER) to accommodate self-monitoring of IC with IC-domain specific and lifestyle interventions, and assess feasibility of integrated frailty and IC screening by trained community providers. The proof-of-value phase will pilot INFINITY-ICOPE in 60 older adults, validate automated algorithmic frailty measures and self-monitoring of IC, and survey stakeholders to understand participant and provider experience. The implementation phase will involve a cluster randomized control trial of 540 older adults across 8 eldercare/ active ageing centres, with 6-monthly follow-up over 1 year for functional performance, frailty (Fried), IC and health-related outcomes. Implementation outcomes will be evaluated using Proctor’s conceptual framework in a mixed method approach. The deployment phase will scale INFINITY-ICOPE across SingHealth, and amalgamate the self-monitoring app with SingHealth’s patient-fronting app to support integrated information and care.
kw: Frailty; Intrinsic capacity; Functional ability; Healthy ageing

title: Integrative Threat Modeling, Risk Assessment, and Security Control Management for Government Settings
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: In today’s web application landscape, many applications leverage big data and advanced AI technologies to deal with critical information and business processes. At the same time, their design (e.g., the use of microservices and zero-trust architecture) and deployment options (e.g., cloud, on premise, hybrid) are fast evolving. Building security assurance into those applications early on in and throughout the DevOps lifecycle and ensuring that those applications comply with organization policies is a key challenge faced by developers. To address the limitations of existing threat modeling tools, we propose an integrative threat modeling, risk assessment, and security control management tool that is customized to the government setting and can support a holistic and streamlined process for achieving high security assurance and compliance. Our project objective is to support project managers and risk consultants to perform threat modeling and risk assessment with automation while navigating the evolving threat landscape and compliance policies. To achieve our objective, we intend to deliver a system with the following capabilities: (1) a smart system able to ingest data from project managers and other tools (e.g., cloud architecture scanner) to build a comprehensive model of the target application's data and ecosystem, (2) a unified framework that correlates various widely-accepted threat knowledge bases and agency-specific threat knowledge bases, (3) a scalable threat assessment engine able to leverage the generic risk scenarios in a knowledge base to generate an application-specific risk profile of the target application, and (4) an intelligent security checker that produces actionable recommendations to remediate identified threats on the target application. This project comes with a unique set of research challenges: (1) the disparate structure, syntax, and scope of various risk knowledge bases (i.e., risk registers, ATT&CK framework) and project application documentation that needs to be integrated into a cohesive framework for performing risk assessment, (2) the fast-changing facets of cyber risk assessment including the threat landscape, regulatory compliance, and security trends, and (3) the huge variations of risk profiles and required mitigation controls due to the diversity of project applications across the private sector and government agencies that differ in terms of features, deployment strategies, and target consumers. We address those challenges by performing semantic analysis and data fusion on the diverse information sources to build expressive and scalable models that are adaptable to the evolving security trends, threat landscape, and compliance policies. Then, we transform and compose those models in a systematic manner to build up a tailored risk profile of the target application. Finally, we design behavior contracts that can be used to automatically develop application-specific security tests which ensures the security and c
kw: Threat Modeling; Risk Assessment; Security Control Management; IM8 compliance

title: Quantitative NIR-IIb Lifetime Imaging of Glutathione in Metastatic Melanoma
abs: The overarching goal of this proposal is to build a fluorescence lifetime nanosensor in the second near-infrared b (NIR-IIb) window that can image and quantify glutathione level with high reliability, sensitivity and high resolution. The main method is to precisely regulate the energy transfer pathway in erbium (Er3+) doped rare-earth nanoparticles (ErNPs) and select novel energy acceptor manganese oxide (MnOx) to realize NIR-IIb lifetime regulation beyond 1500 nm for glutathione (GSH) quantification. Then the lymphatic GSH level and the degree of tumor metastasis will be correlated in a melanoma model. To this end, in this proposal, our specific aims are: Specific Aim 1: To develop NIR-IIb fluorescence lifetime sensor based on ErNPs and MnOx. Specific Aim 2: To validate the NIR-IIb fluorescence lifetime imaging with quantitative GSH response of the lifetime sensor ErNP@MnOx in vitro and at cellular level. Specific Aim 3: To quantitatively measure lymphatic GSH level and correlate with the degree of melanoma metastasis in mice. If successful, the novel NIR-IIb lifetime nanosensor will achieve non-invasive and quantitative in vivo GSH sensing, and correlate lymphatic GSH level with the degree of melanoma metastasis in mice. This NIR-IIb lifetime-based strategy for GSH measurement shows great potential for in vivo quantitative sensing, and the same principle can be extended to quantify other disease associated biomarkers.

title: Unravelling the Hydraulic Regulation of Plant Stem Cells.
abs: Water is a limiting resource for all life forms, and it creates considerable fluid flux and physical pressure in animals and plants, that must be sustained by tissue-generated forces to ensure tissue integrity. Such forces, generated by cell contraction and tissue tension, can relay biomechanical signals, which are then sensed and transduced in the cells to drive growth and programmed cell fates. Biological forces are relevant in many physiological and pathological processes, including embryogenesis, organogenesis, and tumorigenesis. Animal and plant tissues obey the same physical principles, but animal tissues are very soft and more delicate, whereas plants generate much higher biological forces thanks to their rigid cell walls, thus are easier to measure and manipulate for biomechanical studies. At tissue level, plant cells experience two major biomechanical forces, an internal water pressure called “turgor pressure” and the subsequent mechanical stress accumulated in the cell walls. We and others have shown that the long-term plant stem cells within the plant shoot apical meristem (SAM) tissue have stiffer cell walls, meanwhile cell wall softening is both sufficient and necessary to induce organ formation in the SAM. These demonstrate the developmental functions of cell wall mechanics. Turgor pressure is the “driving force” of cell wall stress, however the decisive roles of turgor pressure in plant development are often overlooked, largely due to technical limitations and oversimplified assumptions. Indeed, since most plant cells are interconnected, it was widely assumed that cellular pressure is equal. Recently, we broke this misconception and demonstrated for the first time that plant cells in the SAM of Arabidopsis thaliana have very different turgor pressure between neighboring cells. Such turgor pattern is also involved in growth control and tissue homeostasis. This implies that turgor pressure is not an inert property, but may carry cell-specific biomechanical information to trigger biological responses. Given the context of plant stem cells, turgor pressure may link the mechanical and biological regulations of plant development. The objective of this project is to investigate the developmental function of turgor pressure in plant stem cell, with the following specific aims: Aim 1. Characterize tissue hydraulic dynamics by 4D (3D + time) correlative mechanical-optical microscopy in two stem cell populations of Arabidopsis thaliana. Aim 2. Perturb tissue hydraulic patterns by synthetic approaches by bioengineering inducible, tissue-specific hydraulic manipulations in and around stem cells. Aim 3. Investigate the hydraulic – cell type feedback by interrogating their up/downstream relations. We have generated preliminary data experimentally and theoretically. Our new 3D physical model reveals that turgor pressure and cell size are controlled by cell wall mechanics and water fluxes into and between plant cells. This water flux, or “tissue hy

title: Understanding the structural basis of dengue NS1 in causing vascular leakage
abs: Dengue virus (DENV), which contains four serotypes (DENV1-DENV4), could cause diseases ranging from the mild dengue fever to the severe dengue hemorrhagic fever/dengue shock syndrome (DHF/DSS). Dengue Non-structural protein 1 (NS1) is a multi-functional protein and it exists as dimers intracellularly (hereafter referred to as iNS1) and when secreted outside the cell (hereafter referred to as sNS1) exists in multimeric forms. iNS1 participates in replication of the viral genome while sNS1 plays an important role in causing endothelial disruption leading to vascular leakage, one of the major symptom in DHF/DSS. Structure of iNS1 is available, but not sNS1. Thus it is important to understand the structural basis of how sNS1 causes endothelial cell hyperpermeability. We will aim to understand (1) the oligomerization states and the structures of the sNS1 from different DENV serotypes, (2) how sNS1 interacts with endothelial cell surface e.g. with attachment factor (heparan sulphate) and lipid membrane, (3) how it affects the endothelial cell structure integrity, and (4) identify the epitopes on sNS1 bound by the different human monoclonal antibodies that could block endothelial cell hyperpermeability. Results from this proposal will provide fundamental understanding on the structures of sNS1, how it binds and affect the endothelial cells and identify epitopes on sNS1 that contribute to their pathogenic functions. We will also identify possible therapeutic antibodies that will prevent development of DHF/DSS. The knowledge gain from this proposal will contribute towards treatment of DHF/DSS to reduce mortality rate caused by DENV infection.

title: Exploring New Unconventional Dopant-Free Ferromagnetic Mott-Insulator in s-Band
abs: Our research programme is driven by our recent discovery on a novel low-dimensional gold, namely highly oriented single crystalline gold quantum dots (HOSG-QDs). Interestingly, unlike gold in all existing forms such as bulk, film and nanoparticles, the novel HOSG-QDs show potentially unusual ferromagnetic Mott-insulator, which are among our main hypothesis-to-be-proven in this research program. Importantly, this discovery opens a new path to address an outstanding, important “53-year question” in condensed matter physics: (1) Could one generate Mott-insulator in s band? (2) If so, could one generate ferromagnetic insulator in Mott-Insulator s band? In this research program, we aim: (1) to fabricate novel low-dimensional gold heterostructures with high-symmetry-structure, (2) to generate the first Mott-insulator based on s band of the novel low-dimensional gold heterostructures, (3) to explore and establish the fundamental physics of new unconventional dopant-free ferromagnetic Mott-insulator in s band of novel low-dimensional gold heterostructure, (4) to study and manipulate its spin (magnetic), charge (electronic), and optical properties, and (5) to explore its potency for highly efficiency spin-to-charge conversion. To show the feasibility of our research programme, in this proposal, we show our recent discovery and preliminary results on the new unconventional dopant-free ferromagnetic Mott-insulator based on low-dimensional gold. Ferromagnetic insulator has recently attracted a lot of interests because of its rich fundamental physics and applications such as highly efficiency spin-to-charge conversion. Of particular interest is a dopant-free ferromagnetic insulator. Unlike ferromagnetic metals that exhibit high damping due to spin scattering processes from conduction electrons, dopant-free ferromagnetic insulator materials carry information through spin waves and prevent charge displacement, inelastic scattering centers and Eddy current losses, which cause power loss and determine the spin-wave damping, necessity for spin-to-charge conversion. Indeed, for applications and integrations into devices, a dopant-free ferromagnetic insulator material with high-symmetry structure and high Curie temperature is critical. However, our understanding on the ferromagnetic insulator is still lacking and dopant-free ferromagnetic insulator materials are still very limited. All existing dopant-free ferromagnetic insulator were based on complex d- or f-system, have extremely low Curie temperature and low-symmetry structure, and therefore grew only on limited substrates but not directly compatible with industrial relevance. Clearly, it is important for both fundamental science and applications to search for a new dopant-free ferromagnetic insulator material, which has higher Currie temperature and high-symmetry structure, and is able to grow on substrates directly compatible with industrial relevance such as MgO, and it would then allow us to understand compet

title: Mechanism Design for Weakly Structured Environments
abs: The mechanism design literature hinges upon several assumptions, including (1) strategic sophistication - the ability of the individuals to think in complex ways, and (2) detailed knowledge of the environment. While these assumptions are standard in mechanism design, they are nevertheless very strong. ``Real-life'' economic agents are not as rational as typically modeled. When agents have limited strategic sophistication, economists lose confidence in the performance of mechanisms that force participants to engage in complicated mental tasks. Furthermore, in realistic settings, the designer typically does not have detailed knowledge of the environment. Thus, a mechanism that performs well under strong assumptions of the environment might perform poorly when these assumptions turn out not to be true. The projects we propose here aim to further the understanding of mechanism design when the above-mentioned assumptions are relaxed. Our aim for Project 1 is to propose a systematic framework for thinking about the issues of strategic simplicity and complexity in settings with agents that are strategically unsophisticated. We relax the assumption about the designer’s knowledge of the strategic reasoning process of the agents and only make a minimal rationality assumption about what the agents can do. These assumptions are minimal, as we only assume that the agent avoids K-dominated actions, where K corresponds to the solution concept that we are working with. In other words, we do not assume any strategic reasoning process of the agent to reach an optimal decision; we only assume that the agent is able to rule out some K-dominated actions. Within the framework outlined in the previous paragraph, theoretically, we aim to (1) study environments in which there is a foundation for the use of simple mechanisms, (2) identify structured environments in which complex mechanisms are superior, (3) solve for the optimal complex mechanism. We then build on the theoretical analysis and complement it from an experimental perspective. Through lab experiments, we seek to understand the behavior of real-life economic agents in a variety of settings. We plan to run the experiments in two prominent economic environments: (1) the single-unit auction environment, and (2) the bilateral trade with ex-ante unidentified traders environment. The data has the potential of either supporting the theoretical results or highlighting additional perspectives that are missing from our theory model. We believe the theoretical analysis and the experimental analysis would complement each other and provide a fuller understanding of mechanisms design with unsophisticated agents. Projects 2 and 3 study the design of mechanisms when the designer does not have detailed information about the environment. Traditional models in mechanism design assume that the designer has detailed statistical information about the environment, such as the distribution of the agents' private information or the ag

title: Power Efficient Spin-Devices via Orbital Current driven Electronics (Orbitronics)
abs: Spin-based devices, which function based on maneuvering spins in a ferromagnet, hold promising potential in the future. These spin-based devices have been useful in memory and neuromorphic-computing applications because of their eminent properties like non-volatility, high storage-density, and high switching speed, combined with the practicality of implementation in mass-production. These devices, being non-volatile, do not require standby power. However, for writing information, much power is consumed. Writing of information, which is carried out by manipulation of magnetization in such devices is currently achieved by the application of current-induced spin-transfer torque. Spin Hall torque, another type of spin torque, which provides the most efficient conversion of current to spin torque is also under investigation. For commercial applications, higher efficiency of charge current to spin torque will be required for fabricating power efficient spin-devices. Therefore, a lot of work has been carried out to improve the efficiency of spin torque. In this sense, our project uses “Orbital Torque” as the novel “scientific approach” to overcome writing power consumption. Recently, a few theoretical studies have been published that claim the generation of an orbital torque from Nonmagnetic/Ferromagnetic bilayer. The orbital torque is produced due to a phenomenon called Orbital Hall Effect (OHE). Unlike the spin Hall effect (SHE), where an electric current through the nonmagnetic heavy-metal layer generates a spin current, the orbital Hall effect can be generated in a light metal (low atomic mass) nonmagnetic layer. When a current is applied in a nonmagnetic layer, a transverse orbital current is generated due to OHE. The generated orbital current enters from nonmagnetic layer to the ferromagnetic layer, where an orbital torque is transferred to the magnetic moment of a ferromagnet. Impressively, the orbital Hall angle (ratio of input charge current to produced orbital current) for some materials (V, Mn, Cr) has been calculated to be exceeding their spin Hall angle (ratio of input charge current to produced spin current) by 60 to 70 times. At the time of submitting the first version of this proposal a year ago, there were not enough experimental work carried out specifically on orbital torque. We aimed to a pioneer in this field by quickly getting into this field and producing experimental evidence. Within the past one year, there have been some experimental evidence of Orbital torque. However, this area is still in its primitive stages and lots of experimental understanding has to be made. Besides academic interest, our results will be also useful from a commercial perspective. Therefore, in this proposal, we aim to study experimental generation of pure orbital torque in a light-metal nonmagnetic/ferromagnetic layer system. title: Universal Pre-training of Graph Neural Networks
abs: The proposed project studies the pre-training of graph neural networks (GNN). Graph-structured data are prevalent in real-world scenarios, including financial networks (e.g., fund transfers between entities), e-commerce graphs (e.g., users clicking or buying products), supply chains and job-skill networks. A plethora of graph analytics tasks exist, such as fraud detection and anti-money laundering on financial networks, product recommendation and user segmentation on e-commerce graphs, container demand and shipping prediction on supply chain networks, and talent match on job-skill networks. While GNNs have been extensively studied for their superior ability to learn graph representations that empower a wide range of downstream tasks, they are limited by a critical issue: the need of large-scale task-specific labelled data, which are often unavailable or expensive to obtain. That also means a separate GNN must be trained for each task and graph to attain optimal performance. GNN pre-training aims to address this critical issue of GNNs, by leveraging more readily available label-free graphs (i.e., graphs without task-specific labels) in a domain. In particular, GNN pre-training learns intrinsic graph properties that intend to be general across tasks and graphs in a domain. Intrinsic graph properties include node connectivity, neighbourhood context and attribute patterns, which do not rely on any task-specific label. That is, the pre-trained GNN model constitutes a form of prior in a domain, which can be used as model initializations to bootstrap a new task or graph in that domain through a quick fine-tuning step on a small amount of task-specific labels. This is analogous to how human beings learn—even toddlers can quickly recognize a new mammal species they have never seen before (i.e., a new task), after showing them just a few pictures (i.e., task-specific labels), owning to their prior knowledge that mammals generally consist of a head, a torso and four legs (i.e., the pre-trained model). In other words, they can efficiently bootstrap from the general knowledge and focus on the finer differences between different mammal species, such as the stripes of a zebra or long neck of a giraffe. Thus, GNN pre-training would not only improve task accuracy given limited task-specific labels, but also avoid training from scratch for every new graph and task. To date, GNN pre-training is still a nascent research direction and a few pioneering studies show promising results. However, existing works often make over-simplified assumptions on the graphs and tasks. Specifically, we identified three major gaps in state-of-the-art GNN pre-training approaches: 1) The semantic gap from the heterogeneity of real-world graphs; 2) the temporal gap from the evolving dynamics of real-world graphs; 3) the task gap from the different families of downstream tasks. Bridging the three gaps is crucial to enabling the full potential and applicability of GNN pre-training. Our pro
