title: Developing tailored solutions based on multi-trophic interactions for pest management in urban farmed crops
abs: Current chemical control measures for pest management, including application of chemical insecticides, have limitations and may not be relevant and effective in long-term for the urban farms in Singapore due to high-density living. Resistance to insecticides have already been reported for several pest species in Southeast Asia. Parasitoid wasps have been intentionally released to control certain pest population with varied success in Southeast Asia. To develop tailored solutions for pest management, it is imperative to evaluate the local biogeographical distribution of pest population/species, their characteristics and disease potential in order to build efficient, resilient crop protection strategies that build on ecological principles and learn from systems-level approaches. We propose here, such strategies that rely on discovery of multi-trophic interactions between the pest species with plant hosts, microbial communities and surrounding environment. Information on selected contrasting associations can then be used to rapidly develop ecology-inspired solutions for integrated pest management. Through this project, we aim to (i) discover diversity within local pest communities; (ii) evaluate multi-trophic interactions (between plants-microbes-pests) for selected variants; (iii) utilize this knowledge to develop tailored chemical and biological pest management solutions. For the purpose of this project, we will focus on lepidopteran and hemipteran insects, such as diamondback moth larvae and aphids, which are the most widespread group associated with crop damage, especially in leafy greens. This proposal builds on our recent findings of multi-trophic microbial interactions with plant hosts and their hemipteran pests, which leads to biorepulsion of hemipteran insects from plants. We will deliver a robust platform that identifies pest and microbial communities associated with vulnerable crops that can be applied to other crops. This platform is based on our current capabilities in utilizing multi-trophic interactions, from where novel microbial and chemical solutions will be readily developed.
kw: Pests, microbiomes, environment, nature-based solutions

title: Improving the shelf-life and nutritional quality of kai lan and lettuce using 405 nm LED illumination and moistureresponsive antimicrobial packaging
abs: Locally grown leafy greens such as Brassica oleracea var. alboglabra (kai lan) and Lactuca sativa (lettuce) have short shelf-lives due to their high moisture content and nutritional profile, which leads to the growth of bacteria such as Pseudomonas spp. and molds such as Botrytis cinerea. Currently, their distribution chain, which consists of transport, retail, warehousing and domestic storage, relies exclusively on refrigeration to preserve their quality. However, refrigeration does not kill microorganisms. Hence, we propose the use of two methods to complement refrigeration at different distribution stages to kill microorganisms and protect the leafy greens from spoilage. During on-farm storage, transport, retail and warehousing, we propose using moistureresponsive antimicrobial packaging (MRAP), which our team has demonstrated previously to extend the shelf-life of strawberries. For enhancing quality during retail, in addition to MRAP, the application of 405 nm light-emitting diodes (LEDs) will also be developed, as it has been previously shown by our team to extend the life of strawberries, tomatoes and bananas. The project will be executed along four work packages that will run parallelly – 1. Testing the efficacy of selected antimicrobial volatile organic compounds (Am-VOCs) against the major spoilage bacteria and molds in leafy greens, 2. Delivering these Am-VOCs into the headspace of kai lan and lettuce in a moisture-triggered manner by synthesizing a packaging composite based on inclusion complexing with - cyclodextrin and mesoporous silica particles, 3. Studying the effect of 405 nm LEDs on the microbial and physicochemical quality of kai lan and lettuce, 4. Delivering the 405 nm LED illumination through a high-fidelity prototype (TRL 6) of a retail refrigerator that integrates these LEDs. With the two aforementioned hurdles, the project aims to extend the shelf-life or reduce the wastage of these vegetables in the distribution chain by at least 50%.
kw: photodynamic effect; volatile organic compounds; active packaging; vegetable spoilage; food preservation; antimicrobial

title: Delivery of nature-identical antifungal crop protectants for indoor urban farming in Singapore
inst: ISCE2 - Institute of Sustainability for Chemicals, Energy and Environment
abs: Improved crop protection strategies in urban agriculture settings are needed to minimise crop loss, while avoiding the use of harmful pesticides. In Singapore these mainly comprise Asian leafy greens (Brassica sp.), which are often susceptible to fungal infections. We have the technological capabilities to employ nature-identical glucosinolate (GSL) crop protectants for use in urban farms. GSLs are plant secondary metabolites with natural crop protection properties, activated upon predation by insects to undergo enzymatic hydrolysis to release bioactive isothiocyanates. They are present throughout the family Brassicaceae (brassica greens, mustards, and root vegetables). Activation of the GSL defence by the myrosinase enzyme only occurs upon plant tissue damage (i.e. predation) as both components are present internally. External application of GSLs, coupled with myrosinases known to exist in both the phyllosphere and rhizosphere will provide crop protection without damage to the plant. Using our sustainable gram-scale synthesis of GSLs, coupled with our existing portfolio of delivery technologies will provide GSL formulations ca. 100-10,000x less costly than natural GSL extracts. GSLs and their hydrolysis products have shown strong antifungal activities, which we will confirm for our prepared GSLs in the presence of pathogenic fungi such as Fusarium sp. and Verticillium sp. fungi. Based on principles of crop rotation and biofumigation, GSL activation will occur upon interaction with the plant and soil microbiomes, known to contain myrosinase. We will study the ecological relationship between the GSLs and the plants. We expect this method to reduce crop losses within urban agriculture applications. Finally, we will compile existing toxicological safety data for GSLs and conduct preliminary tests for food safety evaluation and regulatory approval to explore commercialization of these natural food-borne chemicals.
kw: crop protection; antifungals; urban farms; glucosinolates

title: Harnessing hybrid vigour and genome guided breeding for improved vegetable production in Singapore
abs: A long-standing solution to crop loss is to develop crop varieties harbouring stress resilience and robust growth. To provide crop protection technologies for indoor farming, this proposal aims to utilize hybrid vigour to generate elite varieties of Brassica vegetable crops with enhanced yield and resilience suited for indoor/urban farming. We propose to employ advanced genomics, hybrid seed technology and metabolomics tools to improve currently available germplasms. Our competitive advantage lies in the utilization of genome-guided next-generation selective breeding strategies to diversify currently available germplasm and to develop new elite varieties of Choy Sum. We propose to employ successive rounds of hybridization to generate lines with mosaic sectors of four-parental origins, which have great potential to combine beneficial traits in multilayers. Genome sciences will then help fast-forward the vegetable breeding practices as follows. First, by using the proposed hybrid panel, hybrid vigour with stress resilience and growth will be associated with genome and metabolome data. Second, genetic interactions contributing to hybrid vigour will be identified to the level of single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) markers. In particular, we will develop high-quality green leafy vegetable varieties/tester lines with enhanced biomass yield and nutrient content. Identified tipping points for balancing growth and defence metabolism will help fine-tune the overall yield aligned with robust nutrient content. Full utilization of available genetic resources with novel mosaicism will provide a focal point to increase food independency in an urban city setting. As plant disease outbreaks are on the rise, our versatile elite lines will provide solutions to increase food security in urban farms. Upon the completion of this project, we will obtain genomic and metabolic signatures of improved hybrid performances, and superior vegetable tester lines (with at least 15-20% improvement in overall yield) which will serve as readily deployable suitable germplasms for advanced indoor cultivation.
kw: hybrid vigor, genomics, metabolomics, RADseq, breeding

title: Pre-harvest treatments for shelf-life extension and nutrient preservation of fresh produce
abs: Harvested produce undergoes constant physiological changes and gradually loses its freshness and nutritive quality during post-harvest processing. A recent study indicates that Singapore’s one-fifth of the locally produced and imported food is lost during production and post-harvest handling. Minimising food loss is important to Singapore as it aims for 30 by 30. Despite advancements in postharvest technology, losses are high owing to inappropriate postharvest management and unfavourable climatic storage conditions. While various post-harvest approaches such as maintaining low storage temperature, or exogenous application of chemicals like hypochlorite, oxalic acid, benzyl aminopurine, gibberellic acid etc, have shown to extend the shelf life of leafy vegetables, but they require additional resources. Studies suggest, changes to growth conditions, such as temperature, relative humidity, light, etc., has direct impact on quality of the produce. Plants with higher quality can withstand unfavourable conditions better by triggering internal biochemical pathways to delay the tissue degradation. Thus, managing preharvest factors would be the ideal solution to minimize post-harvest quality loss. The proposed project aims to: 1) optimize the light recipes by combining the light intensity, spectral quality and photoperiod in the cultivation of Asian greens such as bak choy, nai bai, Choy sum etc to increase the growth and nutritional quality, 2) apply a biostimulant such as Ascophyllum extract to maximize the growth in order to impart tolerance to adverse condition, 3) evaluate the effect of light and biostimulant on postharvest qualities by analyzing the morphometric, physiochemical and organoleptic traits and 4) gain knowledge on the changes in cellular pathway of chlorophyll degradation and membrane solubilization through proteomic and metabolomic approach. The project builds on our ability to precisely control growth environment of plants and use of LED as preharvest treatments. Findings of the study will benefit local growers and retailers as the proposed strategy can be applied during the production and end-of production cycle reducing need for extra post-harvest treatments of leafy greens.
kw: Preharvest, shelf-life, LED, light-recipe, ascophyllum

title: Engineering Plasmons in Atomically-Thin Metals
abs: A new class of materials is emerging: metallic monolayers. The optical properties of these materials are predicted to be drastically different from those of any other material: theoretical simulations indicate that they have the potential to very efficiently absorb light, slow it down to a fraction of its original speed, and by doing so, focus the light energy to unprecedented levels. Due to the novelty of these materials, experimental investigations are only just starting. At the same time, initial experiments are hampered by the oxidation-sensitivity of the first generation of these metallic monolayers. This project first aims to control the growth of these materials, to form high-quality monolayer films, and to develop a platform for oxygen-free handling and transfer of these materials, starting in the growth chamber, all the way to optical spectroscopy and aberration-corrected, atomic-resolution electron microscopy. Subsequently, these materials will be patterned, followed by spectroscopical investigation and atomic resolution imaging, to demonstrate that the unique optical properties can be controlled: we will demonstrate control over the light frequency and the local light concentration. The unique properties of these materials arise due to the extremely low-damped surface plasmons that are created when they are illuminated by light. We will control these surface plasmons down to sub-10 nm to demonstrate the giant optical field enhancements in these materials. The ability to controllably engineer light in monolayer films, slowing it down, and designing sites with extreme light energy concentration has broad applicability, from photovoltaics to sensing and electrochromic devices. This project aims to place Singapore at the forefront of this emerging discipline.
kw: Conductive monolayers, Nanoplasmonics, Electron spectroscopy, 2D materials

title: Giant Magnetostriction in Bulk and Nanocomposite Oxides
abs: Magnetostriction (MST) refers to the physical deformation of a material when it is magnetized. The deformation can be isotropic (volume change) or anisotropic (length change) or shear. Magnetostrictive materials can convert magnetic energy into mechanical energy in a time-varying magnetic field[1,2] and hence they have potential applications as transducers, actuators, linear motors, to create mechanical force or sense stress/torque/and magnetic field via the inverse phenomenon known as the Villari effect[3-8]. MST arises from the coupling of the electrons’ s spin to orbitals via spin-orbit coupling (SOC) and orbitals to the lattice via the crystalline electric field[1,3]. When the spin of an electron rotates towards the field direction, the orbital associated with the electron’s spin also reorients if the SOC is strong, causing the lattice to deform. Thus, SOC is the atomic origin of the MST and it also is the mechanism for the magnetocrystalline anisotropy in a solid. The SOC is large in heavy rare-earth ions such as Tb, Dy, and Ho due to the aspherical shape of the 4f- orbital which also have non-zero total spin. The rare earth alloy called “Terfenol-D” (Tb0.7Dy0.3Fe2) shows the highest MST (λ = 2000 x10-6 or 2000 parts per million (ppm) at room temperature) among all magnetic alloys. However, this alloy is expensive due to the cost of heavy rare earth metals (Tb, Dy). They are brittle which limits the temperature range of their applications. Since they are metallic, eddy current limits their applications to frequencies below 1 kHz. Less expensive, easy to manufacture, mechanically robust over a wide temperature range, and electrically insulating or semiconducting materials are desired for many applications. Transition metal oxides that are mechanically stable over a wide temperature range could fill up this gap. However, SOC is usually weak for transition metal ions (B = Fe, Co, Ni, Cu etc.) in perovskite oxides (ABO3 type oxides where A can be a divalent alkaline earth cation or trivalent rare earth ion) because the orbital angular moment of B cations is usually quenched by the crystalline electric field arising from surrounding oxygen ions. Because of the perceived notion that the SOC is weak in transition metal ions, magnetostriction in ABO3 type perovskites and its derivative A2B’B’’O6 double perovskites has been largely overlooked until recently. Although the PI reported giant magnetostriction in a metallic cobalt perovskite (Sr-doped LaCoO3) in 1998 [9], not much progress has been made to explore MST in other oxides[10,11]. MST is also expected to play a major role in the magnetic-field induced ferroelectricity in some oxides [12], however, studies of MST in multiferroics are very few so far. It is worth mentioning a recent result: a giant MST (λ= 1000 ppm) is found in CaBaCo4O7 that exhibits the highest magnetically tunable (but not switchable) electrical polarization of all oxides[13]. title: The Impacts of On-demand Platforms under Individual Choice Endogeneity
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: The rise of sharing-economy is largely supported by the emergence of various on-demand platforms which connect owners of idle resource (in terms of durable goods and/or service) with others who need these idle resource. The most popular sharing economy appears in door-to-door transportation services in terms of ride hailing/sharing platforms such as Grab, Uber, and Didi. These platforms have been developing in an irresistible trend as they have brought considerable benefits to stakeholders, such as enabling car owners/renters to monetize their idle car resource and time and providing travelers with efficient and affordable car travelling service. However, the emerging business has also brought in new social, economic and regulatory challenges. One of the controversies is related to the platforms' impacts on car demand. While the platforms argued that their sharing business could help reduce the total car demand, researchers have different findings. Theoretic research has indicated that the hailing/sharing platforms bring in two competing effects on car ownership: while they would reduce individuals' incentive to own a car through providing more convenient car-traveling service, they might also boost car demand by providing extra income for car-owners serving the platforms. Similarly, a study on new vehicle registrations in China suggested that Uber entry is significantly associated with 8% increase in car ownership (Gong et al. (2017)). To further understand how car demand are affected by these platforms, it is essential to understand how the presence of hailing/sharing platforms affects each individual's decision making on buying a personal car or not. Through studying individuals' car purchasing behavior, we could further capture the role of each factor in affecting the aggregate car demand, as well as the total need for car-parking spaces, total traffic on the road and carbon emission to the environment. Individuals' car purchasing decisions have been excessively complicated by the existence of ride-sharing/hailing platforms due to the following reasons. First, an individual's decisions on car purchasing is often coupled with one's choice on transportation modes, which has become more diverse due to the new option of hailing service provided by the platforms. Second, the car purchasing decision might also be affected by the car owners' opportunities to earn extra income from serving the platforms, thus the decision is also coupled with one's decision to be a platform driver or not (i.e., employment choice). Last but not least, the two decisions regarding to using or providing platform service are interacted in the sense that the incentive to use the platform hailing service depends on the number of platform drivers available, and the return from being a platform driver depends on the amount of demand for the platform service. title: Characterising the role of the sea-surface microlayer in regulating microbial dispersal, human exposure, and pollutant transformation
abs: The sea-surface microlayer (SML) is the topmost 10mm of a marine body of water. It mediates all the gaseous, particulate and chemical exchanges between the seawater and the atmosphere. As a transitional ecosystem, it is uniquely characterised by the accumulation of hydrophobic chemicals, oil slicks and extreme physical parameters (e.g. high UV irradiation, large temperature fluctuations) and has been shown to support unique assemblages of microbes that can be either beneficial or harmful for humans, plants and animals. Understanding the SML is therefore essential for identifying and quantifying ecosystem threats in any coastal marine community. This proposal aims to fill a critical knowledge gap and employ a multidisciplinary approach, ranging from molecular taxonomy to ecological modelling, to understand, for the first time, the fundamental role of the SML in the tropics. The project will leverage the complementary expertise of the two PI’s in the ecology of the atmosphere and the hydrosphere and will employ the latest advancements in sampling methodology and genomic sequencing. Using a recently developed method for single cell viral characterisation we aim to enumerate the virally infected cells in the SML and will use laboratory microcosms for manipulative experiments of air-sea exchanges under future climate scenarios. All the results will be mapped back to specific anthropogenic impacts and integrated into ecological models that will help quantifying the risk that the SML might have on the health of humans, plants and animals on the Singapore coastline. In doing so, this research will not only answer fundamental questions in microbial physiology, adaptation to extreme environments and evolution, but also the way for effective global strategy of a sustained, multidisciplinary and integrated observation of the SML in tropical waters.
kw: Atmospheric microbiology; Marine microbiology; Microbial ecology; Planetary health; Pollutant transformation

title: Spin Hall Effects in Topological Two-dimensional Semimetals
abs: The spin Hall effect is an all-electrical mechanism to achieve charge-spin interconversions. It has significant relevance to both fundamental understandings of spin physics and technical applications in memory and computing devices. This proposal aims to develop new spin Hall sources with exotic mechanisms to overcome current limitations in terms of the efficiency and manipulation of spin Hall effect. Within this context, three specific objectives are formulated as 1) topological engineering for record-highly efficient and electrical tunable spin generation / detection; 2) symmetry engineering to achieve a novel spin Hall effect that is highly desired for high-density memory technology; 3) non-volatile low-energy (attojoule) and ultra-fast (picosecond) switching of the spin Hall effect. The hypothesis to address these problems is that novel spin-orbit physics and effects may be engineered by modifying trivial spin-orbit coupling with additional ordered states. To test this hypothesis, our approach is to explore the spin Hall effect in topological 2D semimetals, where strong spin-orbit coupling coexists with three ordered states (topology, symmetry, and ferroelectric order) in a very rare way. Our previous studies of Weyl semimetals, including high-quality growth, spin transport and spin Berry curvature calculations and ferroelectric switch, strongly support the feasibility of this proposal. Achieving these objectives extends current understandings of spin-orbit physics and establishes new knowledge of correlation between spin-orbit effects and various ordered states. In a broader sense, it also opens new frontiers in engineering spin-orbit coupling related effects and lays a promising route towards high-performance spintronic devices and an insightful approach to understand various spin physics.
kw: Spintronics; Spin Hall effect; Topological semimetal; 2D materials; Spin manipulation

title: Social Interactions and the Cross-Section of Expected Stock Returns
abs: After decades of research, it has become clear that stocks frequently become overpriced and subsequently earn unusually low returns (Barberis and Thaler, 2005; Barberis, 2018). "Bubbles" in the stock market can lead to economic distortions. Bubbles can also lead to poor long-run investment performances, particularly among ordinary citizens. Explaining what forces cause mispricing in the stock market represents one of the biggest questions in financial economics. This research aims to study a possible new and important source of mispricing. Prior literature documents that when individuals purchase a particular stock, the likelihood that their close neighbours and coworkers buy the same stock increases significantly (Kaustia and Knüpfer, 2012; Hvide and Östberg, 2015; Pool, Stoffman, and Yonker, 2015; Huang, Hwang, and Lou, 2021). The literature views this pattern as evidence that investors share investment ideas with one another and that investor conversations trigger stock market investments. In addition to providing supplementary evidence that (a) investors obtain investment ideas through social interactions, this research extends the literature by examining (b) what information investors share with each other, (c) what the consequences of investors' social interactions are on the quality of their investment decisions, and (d) what the effects of their social interactions are on the stability of financial markets. This research has a conceptual and an empirical component. In the conceptual component, this research draws from extensive work in neuroscience and social psychology and spells out why investors discuss investment ideas with one another. More importantly, this research notes that investor conversations only impact market prices and, by extension, investor performances and financial market stability *if* investor conversations are systematically biased towards certain types of stocks. If there is no such bias, "investor chatter" largely washes out and does not materially affect market prices. Again drawing from extensive neuroscience and social psychology work, this research offers strong reasons to believe that there are such systematic biases in investor conversations. Among others, this research predicts that investors prefer conversing about stocks that have recently risen in value, experienced high sales growth and are accompanied by high return volatility. As investors synchronously discuss and purchase stocks with these characteristics, these stocks become overpriced. These stocks subsequently earn unusually low returns in the long run as overpricing becomes corrected, and investors who purchased these stocks based on conversations end up suffering from poor long-run investment performances. The empirical component of this research evaluates these possibilities. (1) The PI obtained proprietary server-log data from one of the largest investment-related websites in the world. title: Enhancing light-matter interactions in all-hollow fiber-optic cavity
abs: The Project aims to develop all-hollow fiber-optic cavity as a versatile device for staging light-matter interactions. The cavity is created by inscribing a pair of hollow core fiber Bragg gratings separated by a cavity length directly in the path of a single-piece hollow core fiber, while keeping its two ends open for easy filling of matter. It promotes photons of a specific wavelength to circulate multiple roundtrips between the gratings, presenting an additional means to control their interactions with matter. The all-hollow-core-fiberized cavity retains benefits of hollow guidance, such as ability to handle high optical power and fiber-optic guidance in non-conventional spectral regions, e.g., in deep-ultraviolet and mid-infrared. Coupled with the fiber geometry, which tightly confines both light beam and matter in the core over an extended and mechanically bendable length, the cavity will be one-of-a-kind matter cell, offering outstanding performance and seamless integration into hollow core optical fiber network. Its simplicity, flexibility, and small footprint are well-aligned with current research trend of streamlining and miniaturizing existing systems. The all-hollow fiber-optic cavity is expected to create unique opportunities in various areas in science and engineering, including spectroscopy, metrology, nonlinear science, as well as laser and quantum technologies. The main highlight of the Project is the fabrication of hollow core fiber Bragg grating. A fiber Bragg grating has a periodically modulated optical mode index along the length of the fiber. In conventional optical fiber, this is obtained by illuminating the core in an ultraviolet interference fringe to produce a permanent alternating pattern of high and low material indices. This method cannot be used in hollow core fiber as its core is empty. Our solution is to induce regular modulations in the effective index by periodically deforming the microstructured cladding surrounding the core. We will explore femtosecond laser- and focused ion beam-enabled silica micromachining techniques to meet the high level of precision required. The first ever realizations of (i) hollow core fiber Bragg grating, (ii) all-hollow fiber-optic cavity, and (iii) cavity-based mid-infrared lasing in a single-strand hollow core fiber platform will be presented in the Project.
kw: Hollow core optical fiber; Optical cavity; Fiber Bragg grating; Light-matter interaction

title: Using Deep Learning to Overcome the Complex Acoustic–Physical Limitations and Computational Requirements of the Anti-Noise Window.
abs: Finding a sustainable and practical solution for controlling the propagation of noise into naturally ventilated buildings is challenging, especially in densely populated, high-rise tropical cities. Owing to the impracticality of erecting noise barriers for high-rise buildings, façade elements play an especially critical role in urban noise mitigation. Paradoxically, the demand for naturally ventilated buildings is exacerbating the noise problem by providing more points of entry. Only the plenum window strategy has shown promise for noise control in dense high-rise cities, but its deteriorative effect on natural ventilation is yet to be overcome. Thus far, the proposed noise mitigation solutions for fully opened apertures have been largely based on active control techniques. In the latest revision of the World Health Organization’s Environment Noise Guidelines for the European Region, there is strong evidence linking noise exposure to increased risks of cardiovascular diseases and metabolic illnesses [1]. Although the guidelines were intended for the European region, they are based on data collected from across the globe, including Asia. Excessive noise exposure has also been likened to “secondhand smoke” [2]. We propose an anti-noise window (ANW) in which a window frame equipped with compact active noise control (ANC) units generates anti-noise waves to cancel noise from the city without compromising ventilation. Compared with the traditional single-channel ANC technique, such as that used in active noise-controlling headphones, the ANW belongs to a complex class of multiple-in and multiple-out (MIMO) systems characterized by numerous practical challenges. To overcome the computational complexity and performance limitations of the MIMO system based on conventional linear signal processing techniques, a deep learning approach (i.e., convolutional neural network) will be applied to improve the noise reduction performance of the ANW, perform real-time inference on the noise types, and select the best set of noise control filters. Moreover, the artificial intelligence (AI)-based ANW can intelligently select the noise to be removed while allowing critical sounds, such as alarms or natural sounds to pass through without attenuation. Furthermore, for a multichannel ANC system, the placements of microphones and loudspeakers considerably influence the noise reduction performance. A modified reinforcement learning method will be adopted to seek the optimal positions of speakers and microphones in the ANW in different window settings and environments. To enhance the ANW performance in canceling high-frequency or dynamic noises, which are difficult to attenuate using conventional ANC, a new AI technique known as the conditional generative adversarial network method will be developed to generate masker sounds according to different environmental factors. These masker sounds can mask or reduce the perception of these noises. [1] World Health Organization Regio

title: History & Sustainability of Animal-Based Drugs in Asian Traditional Medicines
abs: Our project aims to answer the following question: How has the expansion in the use and trade of animal-based Traditional Medicine (TM) products in East and Southeast Asia been shaped from the 1950s until today, and how has this impacted the sustainability of the resource on which it depends? The question is important because the expanded use of animal parts and tissue for medicinal purposes over the last seventy years has contributed to the threatened extinction of many species, and indirectly to zoonotic disease (by contributing to the trade in wildlife). While the wildlife trade is coming under increasing scrutiny across many academic domains (conservation biology, ecology, criminology, public health, public policy etc.), we know comparatively little about the cultural, social, economic, and historical processes that have shaped one if its main drivers, faunal medicalization. Our project will greatly advance knowledge of how animal-based medicinal use has developed across East and Southeast Asia, and provide information which can help in crafting policy to check its more dangerous trends. Our initial focus or baseline will be animals linked to the largest of the Asian traditional medicines (TM), namely Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), but will involve cross-referencing the use of faunal drugs in other regional TMs (Japanese Kampo, Tibetan Sowa Rigpa, Vietnamese Thuốc Nam, and Laotian and Cambodian medicines) to provide a unique and holistic picture of faunal medicinal use across all these domains, a project not previously accomplished within the social science of TM. The key product of our research will be a publicly accessible, open-access, digital scholarship product: the TM Faunal Resource Database. This will document 1) which animal parts and tissues have been designated as medicinal, when, for what purpose, and according to which authorities; and 2) the types and quantities of medicinal animal parts and tissues gathered, traded, and used within and between East and Southeast Asia countries spanning a 70-year period (1950s-2020s). This will be the first-ever regional database of the types of animal-based medicinals identified in written source-material as traditional and traded across borders, with the aim of revealing patterns of change in both processes (naming and trading), as well as their linkages. It will draw upon a wide variety of published and unpublished references, some still in archives. Our baseline will be published and unpublished TM pharmacopeia of the 1950s/60s and extending forward as close as possible to the present day. It will initially cover faunal resources in (and trading between) China, Hong Kong, Taiwan, Singapore, Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam, and Japan, but will be designed for expandability to other countries in the region, and further back in time. title: Atomistic Understanding and Controlling the Phase Segregation of Wide-bandgap Perovskites: towards the Next-generation Triple-junction Tandem Solar Cells
abs: The current mainstream solar technology, silicon, is reaching its practical and economic photovoltaic efficiency limit of 27%. We need a quantum leap forward. Combining silicon with a wide-bandgap perovskite in a triple-junction tandem device offers a promising pathway to overcome the performance limitations of conventional silicon and reach a higher power conversion efficiency (PCE) potential of 50%. Double-junction perovskite/Si tandems have shown rapid PCE progress since 2015, and many research groups, including ours, have already reported PCEs of >26%, with a current record value of 29.8%. Notably, this current record efficiency already surpasses the best market-dominant silicon solar cell. It is very likely that triple-junction perovskite/perovskite/Si tandems will follow a similar efficiency improvement trend but could obtain even greater efficiency if supported by research and development. However, matching the current of perovskite middle cells (1.5 eV) and Si bottom cells (1.1 eV) is challenging, as the ideal top perovskite cell requires a much wider bandgap between 1.9 eV to 2.0 eV. The most relevant ultra-wide-bandgap perovskites rely on Cs- and Br-rich composition to enlarge the bandgap, but this usually leads to inhomogeneity (chemical and physical) and thermodynamic phase instability. Moreover, these wide-bandgap perovskites suffer from low phase transition/segregation activation energy. The microscopic understanding of the impact of phase energetics on wide-bandgap perovskites and the regulation of local chemical and physical inhomogeneity remains limited, and efficient perovskite-based triple-junction tandems have not been achieved. To overcome these above challenges, this project will address three main, interconnected themes: 1) gaining microscopic insights into phase segregation in mixed halide perovskites and correlating the intrinsic properties of perovskite to local inhomogeneity. 2) Regulating phase segregation in mixed halide perovskites. 3) Building next-generation triple-junction tandems with high efficiency and longevity. The scientific aims are to correlate the intrinsic properties of perovskite to local inhomogeneity (e.g., bulk and surface defects, strain, compositions), which can be readily probed using state-of-the-art non-invasive scanning probe microscopy; decipher the possible origins of phase segregation at dark and light conditions; transfer microscopic knowledge and atomic insights obtained to device fabrication for a high-level control of the processing of wide-bandgap perovskites; and finally deliver a perovskite-based triple-junction tandem with high efficiency on industrial textured Si wafers. The success of this project may pave a way towards a more powerful, reliable, and broadly accessible green energy harvesting technology with major impacts on atomistic understanding of perovskites and supporting the future sustainable energy infrastructure.
kw: STM/AFM, Perovskite, Phase segregation, Optoelectronics, Tandem solar cell

title: Subversion of non-canonical inflammasome activation by Gram-negative bacteria
abs: The non-canonical inflammasome is activated upon detection of cytosolic lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and is an important innate immune defence pathway against bacterial infection. However, the mechanisms by which pathogenic bacteria subvert cytosolic LPS sensing is unclear. Pathogenic Yersinia are a group of Gram-negative bacterial pathogens that cause disease ranging from gastroenteritis to plague and were traditionally believed to replicate extracellularly. Surprisingly, we found evidence of vacuolar and cytosolic Yersinia in macrophages. However, cytosolic Yersinia did not trigger non-canonical inflammasome activation, suggesting the presence of an uncharacterised bacterial subversion mechanism. Indeed, we found that deletion of the bacterial acetyltransferase, YopJ, triggered robust non-canonical inflammasome activation in macrophages. Therefore, the aim of this proposal is to: (1) characterise host and microbial factors that enable cytosolic Yersinia replication; (2) dissect the molecular mechanisms by which YopJ inhibit non-canonical inflammasome activation in vitro and in vivo; and (3) determine whether subversion of non-canonical inflammasome activation by bacterial acetyltransferase is a conserved mechanism used by other Gram-negative bacteria such as Salmonella. Successful completion of this study will improve our basic understanding of non-canonical inflammasome signalling as well as the corresponding host subversion mechanism by pathogenic Yersinia and Salmonella.
kw: innate immunity; inflammasome; cell death; host-pathogen interaction; Yersinia

title: Atomic scale understanding of heterojunctions between ferromagnetic and semiconducting 2D transition metal dichalcogenides
abs: Selected two-dimensional ferromagnetic transition metal dichalcogenide (TMDC) materials have attracted much attention due to their intrinsic ferromagnetism with high Currie temperature, excellent environmental stability and potential application in spintronic devices. In particular, the recently discovered stable phases of ferromagnetic TMDCs such as CrSe2, CrTe2 and VSe2 are mostly metallic, which hinders the manipulation of both electron charge and spin by an external electric field. Fabricating the heterojunctions between ferromagnetic and semiconducting TMDCs with atomically sharp interfaces is a feasible strategy to combine the complementary functions of ferromagnetic and semiconductor materials. Atomic structures and electronic properties such as interface states and band alignments at the interface will be investigated by scanning tunnelling microscopy/spectroscopy. The heterojunctions with highly compatible work functions and well-matched lattices will decrease the contact resistance and facilitate carrier injection at the interface, thereby improving the electrical transport properties. Realization of the manipulation of electronic spin by an external electric field could give rise to the possibility of reading and writing non-volatile magnetism information. In this project, we propose to perform in-situ growth and atomic characterization of the heterojunctions between ferromagnetic and semiconducting TMDCs with atomically sharp interfaces, using the ultrahigh vacuum facilities at the Surface Science Laboratory (SSL). The molecular beam epitaxy technique enables reliable and atomic control over scalability, crystallinity and thickness of the heterojunctions. We will grow lateral and vertical heterojunctions by the sequential epitaxial growth of MoSe2 and CrSe2 or MoTe2 and CrTe2 on different substrates. In-situ atomic characterization will be performed scanning tunnelling microscopy/spectroscopy (STM/STS) to reveal the interface structures and electronic properties at the interfaces of lateral and vertical heterojunctions. The ferromagnetic properties and magnetic proximity effect will be explored by the element-specific technique of X-ray magnetic circular dichroism (XMCD) at the Singapore Synchrotron Light Source (SSLS) in NUS. An important issue is the measurement of transport properties and manipulation of electronic spin in the low-dimensional devices based on the MBE-grown heterojunctions. For the device fabrication and measurements of transport properties, the lateral and vertical heterojunctions will be directly grown on insulating sapphire or mica. A movable metal shadow mask will be specially designed to grow large-scale lateral heterojunctions in order to facilitate the device fabrication. We will use an existing Physical Property Measurement System (PPMS) in an NUS collaborator’s lab to explore whether or not the heterojunctions can improve the electrical transport properties and realize possible spin injection from a ferroma

title: Innovating multi-bioinspired composites via novel centrifugal freeze casting
abs: Modern product designs for high-end applications rely on developing advanced strong and lightweight structural composites. Various routes in material designs have been explored; amongst all, the most promising with demonstrated successes is multi-hierarchical bioinspiration. The biostructures of living organisms, such as the shell of marine species, bones, etc., have ingeniously evolved to consist of functional gradients (local optimisation) and heterogeneities (structural toughening). These allow biostructures to be strong yet tough, to withstand the harsh environment in nature. The translation of these concepts into man-made materials undoubtedly provides feasible pathways for the design of advanced materials with potentially unprecedented properties and functionalities. Nevertheless, it is challenging to transcribe the concept of gradient heterogeneity into synthetic materials, primarily due to the lack of a facile and effective manufacturing process. To overcome such challenges, herein, we propose to develop a novel technology – centrifugal freeze casting (cFC)– followed by secondary-phase infiltration for the fabrication of multi-bioinspired composites with simultaneously gradient and heterogeneous characteristics. This technique can provide multiple degrees of design freedoms – ranging from (i) heterogeneous design with the use of feedstock materials, (ii) an additional degree via the introduction of functional gradients, to (iii) an overall microstructural control through varying process parameters. Furthermore, it is versatile given that composites of any combinations of feedstock materials and structures are possible. With a thorough understanding of the underlying forming mechanisms, we can leverage these as a design guideline for composites – to design composites on-demand through selecting initial process parameters. Three specific aims associated with our proposed work include: (i) development and setup of the cFC process for composites with multiple bioinspired structures, (ii) detailed process mechanisms study to understand how to control the structure via process parameters, and (iii) experimental and simulation studies of the materials composition-microstructure-properties relationships. Nonetheless, being an entirely new concept, much of the scientific issues, notably those associated with centrifugation, are currently unknown. As such, this imposes many scientific questions for us to address. Advances in materials science from understanding multi-bioinspired hierarchical structures and centrifugal freeze casting process are assured. Materials fabricated from the cFC are also expected to find use in various applications, from biomedical to structural materials in tooling, aerospace, automobile, etc. Apart from these, the possibilities brought about by cFC also open a new door for product designs, in particular novel material concepts previously unachievable from being hindered by the lack of advanced manufacturing routes. title:
Humid Air-Stable SoLid Electrolytes For Roll-to-roll solid-statE battEries 
(HASSLE-FREE)
abs: Over the past three decades Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) revolutionized the space of mobile device applications and started to transform urban transport because they are lightweight and have relatively high energy density. However, today’s LIBs use graphite anodes and flammable liquid Li+ electrolytes, which represent significant safety hazards. All-solid-state batteries (ASSB) combine non-flammable fast-ion conducting solid electrolytes with energy-dense Li or Na metal anodes, which represents a promising path to address the safety concerns associated with LIBs, while simultaneously offering up to 70% higher energy density. The key bottlenecks for a wider market penetration are rate capability for fast charging which for ASSBs translates into the requirement for ultrafast ionic conductivity and to retain the high performance over a long cycle life, which requires deeper understanding and tighter control over the chemical and physical processes at the electrode-electrolyte interfaces that otherwise cause premature performance degradation. Among the ASSB systems intensely explored to address this urgent demand, those employing fast sodium ion-conducting sulfides show particularly great promise to yield safe, low‐cost energy storage systems for large‐scale applications. An ideal solid electrolyte must not only have high ionic conductivity, it should also have good stability against environmental influences during processing (such as humidity or air) and high kinetic electrochemical stability. Among the candidate compounds, materials availability and low‐cost synthetic as well as processing methods will finally decide on a commercial adoption. Achieving a high score in all of these criteria is a major challenge for the synthesis of sulfide‐based solid electrolytes. Among the candidate systems here we focus on Na3SbS4 (NAS) as it is particularly promising in terms of high ionic conductivity and compatibility with humid air. In this project we aim to introduce a new low-cost aqueous solution halide doping procedure and rational interfacial engineering. Thereby we will strongly increase the conductivity of the solid electrolyte as well as the cycling stability of the interfaces with sodium metal or sodium alloy anodes. Based on a deepened understanding of processes at the electrode:electrolyte interfaces over cycle life, we aim to rationally design ASSBs with enhanced rate performance and capacity retention employing our solid electrolytes. For the cost-effective integration of such solid electrolytes into safe high performance all solid-state batteries, we will elaborate an organic-inorganic composite membrane suitable for roll-to-roll fabrication processes and thus ideal for industrial uptake.
kw: Solid State Batteries; High safety energy storage; Computational Materials Design; Advanced Manufacturing Engineering

title: Teacher-Child Neural Scaffolding for Executive Function & School Readiness
abs: The transition into primary school marks a major change in a child’s life. With this transition comes increased demands on cognitive control and executive function (EF) (priority area: cognitive abilities and functions). School readiness is an important predictor for later academic success and EF skills underpin school readiness, yet children’s EF skills at school-entry vary widely. The neural circuits that support EF undergo considerable maturation during early childhood. During this time, preschool education, in particular teacher-child social interactions are an important social driver of EF development, providing “neural scaffolding” that can positively shape children’s emerging EF skills. Here, we leverage neuroscience-based theories of social learning to address how teachers can scaffold children’s EF development during the preschool and primary years. Further, we will study social scaffolding mechanisms in children who are typically-developing or have neurodevelopmental disorders (ASD or ADHD), providing insights into how developmentally-disadvantaged children can be supported for school readiness. Specifically, we address the following research questions: Q1: How do teacher-child social interactions scaffold children’s emerging EF and support consequent school readiness? Q2: Do the same or different neural mechanisms apply for typically developing (TD) children and children with (or at risk for) ASD or ADHD? The proposed project will be an accelerated longitudinal study tracking EF development and school readiness in TD children and in children with (or at risk for) ASD or ADHD between 2-8 years of age. Each child will be followed for 2 years and assessed 3 times at 1-year intervals. Five groups of TD children will be measured cross-sectionally at starting ages of 2:0 – 2:11, 3:0 – 3:11, 4:0 – 4:11, 5:0 – 5:11 and 6:0 – 6:11 years respectively. Each age group will consist of N = 40 children (total N = 200) and their teachers (N =50). A further sample of N = 100 children with or at risk for ASD or ADHD (N = 50 each) in the same age range will be tested. Children will be assessed three times each at one-year intervals to measure teacher-child interaction and the classroom environment using behavioral observations. We will further measure the teacher’s and child’s physical proximity and child’s linguistic input using wearables. We will also employ a state-of-the-art social brain imaging technology, dyadic-EEG, to measure teacher-child neural scaffolding, and collect EEG and cardiac data during standardized tasks to measure the child’s executive functions and school readiness. To examine how teacher-child social interactions scaffold children’s emerging EF and support consequent school readiness (Q1), we will test the unique and joint contributions of different neurophysiological and behavioral interaction-based measures in predicting a child’s later EF and school readiness outcomes. title: Understanding Brain Networks of Reading and Math to Inform Diagnostics and Interventions (Brain-NORM)
abs: Significance: Our research programme takes on the grand challenge to prepare our children well in learning to read and reason mathematically in their early school years by leveraging on the Science of Learning through the use of neuroimaging methods together with cognitive measures to inform practice. Uncovering the underpinnings of brain networks related to literacy and numeracy to allow earlier identification of difficulties in learning with existing screeners, will help differentiate whether these learning difficulties stem from weaknesses in reading, mathematical or other cognitive abilities, such as working memory. The long-term goal of this research is to value-add and enhance the existing learning support programmes with precise measures to monitor development of literacy and numeracy from the start of primary school. This enables earlier characterization of difficulties in learning, provide targeted remediation, level-up disadvantaged students and bring their learning trajectory closer to that of their peers. Aims and Objectives: Although there is growing evidence showing that learning difficulties in literacy and numeracy may stem from common factors, current diagnostic approaches and interventions treat learning difficulties in these two domains independently. This research will join recent global efforts in developing transdiagnostic approaches to understand developmental learning disabilities not only by providing novel evidence to validate different subtypes of learning difficulties in literacy and numeracy, but also by conceptualizing an exemplary model of how such evidence can be translated into educational practice to augment current approaches in diagnostics, monitoring and interventions. The goals of the research programme are: 1. To identify the core deficits and behavioural indicators for learning disabilities (LD) in the areas of reading (RD), math (MD) and their co-morbidity (RMD) development within a local bilingual sample of Singaporean children. 2. To provide precise whole-brain mapping using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the functional and structural networks supporting reading, math and working memory (where working memory is hypothesized to be the underlying domain affected in RMD) from preschool to lower primary children, as well as to elucidate how these networks are compromised by the respective difficulties. 3. To uncover the differences in functional networks of reading, math and working memory (visuospatial and verbal) between RD, MD and RMD, and provide neural evidence from ecologically valid tasks to validate the neurocognitive tests that are sensitive in distinguishing RMD from RD and MD. 4. To examine purported subgroups of RD and MD and RMD enrolled in learning support programmes using identified sensitive neurocognitive measures to (a) check the sensitivity and specificity of the school screeners based on the assignment of students to the LD groups (RD, MD, RMD) according to the neurocognitive measure

title: Early Support for Foundational Skills of  Preschool Children at Socio-economic Risk in Singapore
abs: Significance: Children from disadvantaged homes in Singapore enter kindergarten with poorer skills (pre-academic and cognitive), and they maintain poorer learning rates over the kindergarten years (Ng et al., 2014; Ng et al., 2021). The impact of socio-economic risk is heightened in the preschool years (e.g., Mollborn, Lawrence, James-Hawkins, & Fomby, 2014), indicating that this is a key sensitive period for intervening with additional supports in order to prepare children prior to kindergarten entry. This proposal takes a SoL approach to prepare young disadvantaged children by developing and evaluating early interventions aimed at four core skills necessary for later success in school: literacy, numeracy, social-emotional learning, and self-regulation. Objectives and Specific Aims. This programmatic proposal aims to develop and trial the efficacy of targeted interventions for preschool children at Nursery 2 in Singapore to build their foundational skills – both academic and non-academic. Early childhood is a critical period, which contributes significantly to longer range outcomes in student achievement and career attainment; therefore, many nations are investing in early childhood care and education (ECE). While high quality ECE reaps positive effects, family factors (such as socio-economic status - SES) also weigh heavily on child outcomes. The effects are wide-ranging, from academic (reading and math) to executive functioning to socio-emotional development, and studies within Singapore reflect these findings that SES impacts academic skills at entry into kindergarten even after controlling for IQ and age (Ng et al., 2014). The Singapore Kindergarten Impact Project (SKIP) further showed that kindergarten entry level skills explained children’s rate of learning throughout kindergarten and into primary school. Building on the previous findings from SKIP and the GUSTO study, the overarching aim of the current project is to improve children’s essential skills before they enter kindergarten, with a focus on literacy, numeracy, socio-emotional, and self-regulation skills for children at socio-economic risk . Approach: A three-phase programme of research includes an intervention-development process informed by collaborative input from preschool practitioners, followed by a randomized controlled study implementing the interventions with a preschool sample, and finally a production phase of teaching packages for future effectiveness studies in preschool classrooms. Feasibility: The set of projects draws on the deep expertise within the Centre for Research on Child Development (CRCD) for early childhood development specifically for each of the four core skill areas.The PIs have extensive experience successfully conducting early education research in Singapore. Combining the set of projects into one programmatic research proposal yields cost savings within a manageable five-year project.
kw: preschool intervention ses risk

title: SLIONS: an AI-enabled Platform to Promote Personalized Chinese language Learning for Adult Language Learners
abs: Bilingualism is a cornerstone of Singapore’s education system (MOE, 2010), with most students taking classes in English and a second language. 90% of 15 to 24 year-olds in Singapore report literacy in two or more languages (Singapore 2020 Census). However, proficiency in second languages can differ greatly: young adults who receive more/earlier Chinese exposure in their early years report higher Chinese proficiency relative to their peers (Wu et al., 2020), and early language exposure also results in changes to the auditory system that modulates later language learning (Pan, Ke & Styles, 2021). This leads to a two-fold challenge: How to best support basic perceptual skills for robust language learning in Singaporean children with limited exposure to mother tongue in their early years (Priority area 3.2.4)? And how to promote neuroplasticity in adult learners who did not develop early acoustic representations for the sounds of their second language (Priority area 3.2.5)? The project team believes the solution to both challenges lies in the application of technology-enhanced learning (Priority area 3.2.6) that promotes neuroplastic change through real-time feedback on how a learner’s spoken language aligns with perceptual targets of the language they are learning. Over the past 3 years, the PI’s team have developed and tested an AI-powered system called Singing and Listening to Improve Our Natural Speaking (SLIONS) (Murad, et. al., 2018), a multimedia processing system that uses a microphone to track a learner’s voice as they sing or speak, providing real-time feedback on their pronunciation accuracy. In this proposal, the project team aims to develop SLIONS-Plus, an enhanced app designed for adult learners, with built-in fun activities to enhance engagement, and micro-dosed learning strategies for integration into adult learners’ schedules. This proposal describes how the powerful AI-driven multimedia processing engine SLIONS will be developed and tested in a real-world learning environment. The proposal also includes (1) neuroimaging studies needed to assess how well the app leverages neuroplasticity to enhance learning outcomes (Challenge 4) and (2) behavioural tests to show how the app achieves transfer of learning to new contexts, such as healthcare students and professionals at NUS Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine (NUS Medicine) and the National University Health System (NUHS) who need to communicate with Chinese-speaking patients. In the first two years of the project, the Technology team led by PI Ye Wang (Computing, NUS) and Co-PI Shengdong Zhao (Computing, NUS) will lead the technology development phase of the project in consultation with collaborators Tang Ching Lau (Medicine, NUS), and Rebecca Starr (English Language and Literature, NUS). This phase will culminate with evaluation of the app’s impacts on learner outcomes, engagement and motivation, by the Behavioral team, led by Co-PI Suzy Styles (Psychology, NTU). title: Inflammation, metabolism and body composition as physiological markers of homeostatic capacity in a ‘vitality index’ of ageing: a study of the vitality domain of intrinsic capacity and its impact on frailty, activity levels and life-space mobility
abs: The World Health Organisation proposed reframing the concept of healthy ageing to emphasise intrinsic capacity (IC), a key determinant of an individual’s functional abilities. However, amongst the five domains comprising IC (cognitive, sensory, locomotor, psychological and vitality), there are critical gaps in our current understanding of the definition and measurement of vitality. Currently, vitality is conceptualised as the capacity to maintain homeostasis in the face of stressors. To operationalise vitality, nutritional status is often used as a surrogate, but nutrition alone does not holistically capture the vitality construct. In this proposal, our central hypothesis is that vitality is represented by core physiological systems required to maintain an individual’s homeostasis. Age-related dysregulation in these physiological systems leads to decreased IC, culminating in frailty and functional decline. The central hypothesis will be tested via three specific aims: (Aim 1) To investigate inflammation, metabolism and body composition as core physiological markers comprising the vitality domain; (Aim 2) To compare vitality versus nutrition in the causal pathway leading to the one-year outcome of frailty; and (Aim 3) To examine the predictive ability of IC for one-year outcomes of activity limitation and reduced life-space mobility, comparing between vitality versus nutrition for the vitality domain. We will conduct a prospective cohort study in healthy community-dwelling older adults. Biomarkers of inflammation, metabolism and body composition will be measured at baseline to determine the components comprising the vitality construct. Construct validity will be investigated by factor analysis and longitudinal outcomes analysed using structural equation modelling. The proposed research will illuminate concepts that define vitality, determine measurable attributes of vitality and characterise the role of vitality and IC in early risk stratification for frailty and functional decline. The long-term goal is to develop new preventative strategies targeting vitality and IC to prevent frailty and achieve healthy longevity.
kw: vitality; intrinsic capacity; frailty; ageing; healthy ageing; healthy longevity

title: Duke-NUS Medical School Master of International Translational Medicine Degree
abs: My personal research focus will be on atopic dermatitis, genetic skin conditions, vascular anomalies, immune-dermatological conditions, cutaneous lymphomas, skin cancer syndromes and the histiocytosis. The “Master in International Translational Medicine” (MITM) course will further enhance our research expertise by helping our understanding and capability to progress our laboratory or clinical research towards patient-based solutions. It will helps us to understand key events and requirements necessary to progress research beyond our own expertise, as well as to develop our ability to interact with key stakeholders to further develop our solutions. Upon completion of the MITM course, we hope to further develop our research capabilities by developing and collaborating with more research, clinical and industry partners, to bring more of our laboratory, clinical and innovation research to patient-based solutions in the real world. Apart from elucidating deeper understanding of the pathogenesis of various dermatological disease, we hope to develop more strategies to treat and manage these conditions through drug discovery and the use of more digital innovations, such as artificial intelligence and deep learning platforms to better care for our paediatric and women’s dermatology patients. Beyond this, we hope to work with industry partners to commercialize our discoveries.

title: Developing betA-lactam pharmacodynamic taRgets in Gram-nEgative bacTeraemia using Physiologically based pharmacokinetic modelling (TARGET)
abs: Background The syndromic diagnosis of infection, lack of pathogen data and tissue levels at the infection source could had led to variations in beta-lactam plasma pharmacodynamic (PD) targets of clinical significance. Classical pharmacokinetic modelling has been used commonly and there is potential for applicability of physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) which are able to mechanistically predict tissue levels, physiological conditions, and populations which there were initially untested in. Piperacillin-tazobactam is a common antibiotic used. Specific aims We aim to compare the plasma piperacillin-tazobactam pharmacodynamic targets that is associated with clinical response and mortality in gram negative bacteraemia patients and develop dosing regimens needed to achieve these targets using PBPK and classical pharmacokinetic modelling. Depending on the distribution of the source of gram-negative bacteraemia, plasma targets for different sources (e.g. Lungs, liver) of bacteraemia will be estimated. Once these targets are established, source specific empiric dosing regimens for piperacillin-tazobactam will be developed using the selected PK modelling program Hypothesis The hypothesis is that PBPK models can be used to construct pharmacokinetics models for beta-lactam antibiotic and following that plasma pharmacodynamic targets accounting for site of bacteremia associated with clinical response and mortality can be developed. Methodology Patients with gram negative bacteraemia and receiving empiric piperacillin-tazobactam therapy will be prospectively enrolled in an observational study. PBPK and classical PK models will be used to together with CART analysis to develop source specific pharmacodynamic targets. Empiric piperacillin-tazobactam regimen that achieve the optimal targets will then be developed to suite the variety of clinical scenarios and patient populations. Clinical significance This evaluation of PBPK and classical PK models which considers plasma and tissue levels as well as a variety of clinical scenarios and patient populations can provide a more specific target that can be used to improve treatment outcomes of gram-negative bacteraemia.
kw: beta-lactams; gram-negative bacteremia; therapeutic drug monitoring; pharmacodynamics

title: Understanding the trans-kingdom metagenomic interactions of the human microbiome on obesity and metabolic syndrome
abs: The twin epidemics of obesity and diabetes mellitus are an emerging global health issue. Though bariatric surgery has had reasonable success, there is an unmet need to better personalise anti-obesity treatment. The human metagenome play an important role in obesity. The gut bacteriome, and more recently the virome is shown to be significantly correlated with the obese phenotype. In other chronic inflammatory diseases, there is emerging evidence that trans-kingdom interactions, rather than the effect of a single entity, may be responsible for the alteration of the host phenotype. The study aims to: 1. Characterise the metagenomic signatures unique in obesity and metabolic syndrome. 2. Identify changes in the human metagenome following weight loss treatment. 3. Identify the microbial metabolites responsible for influencing obesity. 4. Characterise trans-kingdom interactions involved in influencing obesity. Hypotheses: 1. The human metagenome differs in composition between individuals with obesity in contrast to non-obese controls. 2. The metagenome of an individual with obesity, will undergo alterations following weight loss treatment. 3. Microbial metabolites play a role in influencing the obese phenotype of the host. 4. Trans-kingdom metagenomic interactions influence the obese phenotype of the host Methods: A cohort study utilising shotgun metagenomic sequencing of human salivary, gastrointestinal, fecal, urine and serum samples will be performed from obese individuals and controls. Bioinformatics analyses will then be performed. Proof-of-concept studies via metagenomic pattern analysis utilising murine models. Metabolomic analysis will also be performed to identify fecal metabolites of microbial origin that influences the obese phenotype. Feasibility: The study team has various expertise in clinical, phenomics, metabolic disease and microbiome research. The findings will shed light on the impact of the metagenome and their cross-kingdom interactions on the obese phenotype, which is a rising public health issue globally. Study will be in the new Centre for Microbiome Medicine, NTU.
kw: Obesity; Metagenome; Microbiota; Metabolic Syndrome; Virome

title: Nano-enabled Adsorptive Membrane Scaffolds as Harvesting Devices for Precious Lithium Metal Recovery
abs: Lithium (Li) is a high-value resource that sees >1000-fold higher amount in seawater than on land. In Singapore, we produce a massive amount of seawater reverse osmosis (SWRO) brine, which puts us in a good position to recovery this resource. However, the challenge is that the Li concentration remains low despite SWRO brine being a concentrated by-product. Herein, we propose a nano-enabled nanofibrous membrane scaffold as an adsorptive harvesting device to address this pervasive problem. Adsorption is to date the most promising technology for low concentration Li recovery and nanofibrous scaffold can help mitigate the low efficiency due to granulated compaction in a fixed-bed packed column. The amalgamation of both adsorption and nanofibrous membrane technology will be supported by tailored design and synthesis of a new class of porous covalent- and metal-organic frameworks as high-performance chemically-stable nanoadsorbents with unique pore functionalization for high Li selectivity. Nanofibrous membrane scaffolds will be supported by the electrospinning technique to optimize fiber diameter, porosity and surface area for maximizing loading and mechanical strength. In total, we propose four work packages (WPs) with WP1 and 2 focusing on nanoadsorbents design and synthesis, WP3 on nanofibrous scaffold fabrication, nanoadsorbent integration and assembly into harvesting devices and WP4 on performance evaluation, process design and techno-economic analysis. Unlike other studies, this proposal sees through the entire course of Li recovery from capture right to the conversion to battery-grade lithium carbonate. Our techno-economic analysis will cover every single aspect to give PUB a holistic cost-benefit insight into our technology. Beyond SWRO brine, we will also demonstrate the potential of our harvesting device for synthetic Salt Lake brine mining. For this reason, our proposal has garnered tremendous support from corporate heavyweights including Li mining and chemical industries as well as an NRF-backed early-stage technology investment company for potential future commercialization.
kw: Lithium recovery; Adsorption, SWRO brine; Covalent organic framework; Metal-organic framework; Electrospinning

title: Traversing Geodesics in Discovery-Development Space - from Novel Electrophotocatalysis to Sustainable and Scalable Manufacturing Processes
abs: Current mainstream approaches for the chemical production of active ingredients in the pharmaceutical and agrochemical industries utilize thermal energy to drive conventional ionic processes (transfer of two electrons). Employment of other forms of energy can lead to the development of new synthetic and production processes, thus resulting in a vast expansion of the chemical spaces. Our primary objectives in this research project are to combine solar energy and electricity to create innovative process technologies driven by single electron transfer (SET) events. We will design and develop novel electrophotocatalysis capable of precise control of electrons and ions to enable the desired syntheses of various active pharmaceutical and agrochemical ingredients. Furthermore, to translate the newly developed electrophotocatalysis efficiently into sustainable manufacturing, we plan to concurrently develop new workflows, including high-throughput screening, and groundbreaking reactor designs by combining chemistry, engineering, multi-scale modelling, and data science. The proposed work will be enabled by the synergy of the multidisciplinary expertise in the project team, spanning synthetic chemistry, catalysis, electrochemistry, photochemistry, materials chemistry, computational modelling, and chemical engineering, supported by strong collaborations with our industry partners in Syngenta, a world-leading agrochemical company.
kw: Electrophotocatalysis; Organic free radicals; High-throughput screening; Scalable Reactors; Active pharmaceutical and agrochemical ingredients

title: Abiotic-Biotic Composites for Bioelectrosynthesis
abs: Nature has evolved a highly successful biochemical process to capture and utilize CO2, in the conversion of solar energy into chemical energy. Through a set of transformations characterized by high selectivity but low efficiency, photosynthesis has ultimately sustained plant life for millions of years. In contrast, although operationally simpler, chemical, and electrochemical reduction of CO2 often yields a variety of multicarbon products with low selectivity. We propose here an innovative solution to tackle the low efficiency in bioelectrochemical systems by designing biocomposites that enable 3D electron transport, and injection of electrons into large populations of electroactive microbes, genetically engineered to undertake the chemical synthesis of multi-carbon products, with high specificity. The proposed research will allow us to understand electron transfer across biotic and abiotic interfaces and provide fundamental insight on how living or artificial materials can be designed to facilitate this process. Genetically engineered microbes offer unique advantages over wild stains, such as significantly accelerated electron transfer, improved CO2 transport and fixation, and the presence of specific synthetic pathways with high selectivity and yield. This novel genetic engineering approach to CO2 conversion will provide solutions that mitigate anthropogenic carbon emissions and establish a basis for integrating the selectivity and milder reaction conditions characteristic of biochemical cycles into chemical manufacturing platforms.
kw: CO2 to fuel, synthetic biology, bioelectrosynthesis, biotic-abiotic interface

title: Identifying functional RNA tertiary structures in dengue virus
abs: Dengue is an important human pathogen with high social and economic burden. While decades of work have focused on studying how dengue proteins work to result in pathogenicity, the virus genome is also known to fold to orchestrate various virus functions such as replication, translation and packaging. However, our lack of understanding of dengue genome structures and how they function in different stages of the virus life-cycle prevent us to be able to effectively target this virus. Here, we develop and use a combination of experimental and computational methods to determine dengue virus tertiary structures and their functions during the virus life cycle. These studies provide first insights into the nature of higher order dengue structures to enable them to be targeted by small molecules in the future. In addition, the methods developed in this proposal can be widely applied to other biological and disease systems to interrogate the structure function relationships of RNA.

title: Development of Three Key Sub-Systems for Automated Quay Crane
abs: Automated quay crane operation can be more intelligent given the advancement of robotics technologies. In this proposal, sophisticated robotics technologies are deployed to the automated quay crane system. There are two major open problems, 1) the key challenge is to detect and track any workers in the designated area in all-weather conditions. Current video analytics is able to detect and track workers but the results could be unstable when the lighting and weather conditions are not ideal. 2) This challenge is to integrate multiple technologies, including real-time precise 3D mapping of the environment, real-time path generation and robust control algorithm, etc. These challenges can be addressed using robotics technologies on perception, target detection and tracking, as well as point-cloud based 3D modelling of operation environment. Advance control algorithms and path planning algorithms will be developed to ensure smooth running of the crane operation.
