title: Climate and Land-Use changes: Effects on nutrient inputs to Singaporean reservoirs (CLUE)
abs: The projected increases in temperature and atmospheric CO2 concentration, and changes in rainfall intensity and frequency are expected to modify how nutrients are cycled in the soil, transported through runoff over pervious and impervious surfaces, and finally enter water bodies including water reservoirs. The quantification of how climate affects the nutrient cycles and modify loads of nitrogen and phosphorus to the Singaporean reservoirs is essential to understand future risks of eutrophication of water bodies as well as to delineate mitigation strategies or to re-think reservoir operations in case of increased risk. As nutrient flushing is a process that occurs at relatively short temporal scales, methodologies for downscaling precipitation at high-temporal resolutions (hourly scale) are needed and will be implemented in the project. Local-scale effects of climate and land use changes will be analyzed by means of a mechanistic terrestrial biosphere model that will provide quantification of soil biogeochemical cycles and time series of nutrient leaching and nutrient concentration in runoff as a function of land-cover, soil texture, and meteorological forcing. The parameterization of the terrestrial biosphere model will be refined through targeted measurements of soil biogeochemical processes collected in the project. Climate and land-use scenarios of nutrient inputs to all major reservoirs of Singapore will be generated by means of numerical simulations to evaluate the total impact of future changes on nutrient loads in the reservoirs. Subsequently, the effect of modified nutrient inputs on lake eutrophication and reservoir water quality will be analyzed using existing water quality models that will be revised to allow simulating long-term scenarios. Finally, an assessment of alternative reservoir management strategies will be studied to mitigate some of adverse water quality impacts that are expected to occur in the future.
kw: Water Quality; Nutrient loads; Eutrophication; Reservoirs; Climate Change; Soil biogeochemistry

title: Multimodal imaging of brain reorganisation as a function of recovery of movement quality after stroke: A longitudinal fMRI and kinematic study
abs: The high morbidity associated with stroke places a huge burden on individuals, families and societies worldwide. Rehabilitation approaches targeting restitution have the potential to optimise stroke recovery. This is because such approaches focus on neural repair to regain normal motor control (i.e. true recovery) rather than simply compensate with the intact limbs. Understanding how the brain recovers through restitution after stroke offers the first step towards developing efficacious and cost-effective rehabilitation approaches. To accomplish this goal, this project proposes to use multimodal imaging (i.e. task-based fMRI, resting-state fMRI and diffusion tensor imaging) and 3D motion kinematics to study recovery of upper limb (UL) movement quality after stroke. In this project, longitudinal changes in imaging biomarkers and extent of recovery of movement quality will be tracked in 20 stroke participants from acute to chronic phases of stroke (i.e. ≤2 weeks, 3 and 6 months after stroke onset). 10 healthy controls will be similarly assessed to enable comparative reference. The specific aims are to 1) identify imaging biomarkers for predicting recovery of UL movement quality after stroke, as well as 2) investigate if longitudinal changes in patterns of brain activation associate with recovery of UL movement quality from acute to chronic stroke. We hypothesise that 1) gains in UL movement quality after stroke associate with i) changes in blood oxygenation level--dependent (BOLD) activity in motor areas of both hemispheres as well as ii) greater functional connectivity between ipsilesional M1 and contralesional M1. We further hypothesise that 2) longitudinal changes in i) blood oxygenation level--dependent (BOLD) activity in motor areas of both hemispheres as well as ii) functional connectivity between ipsilesional M1 and contralesional M1 differ between stroke participants presenting initially with better UL movement quality and stroke participants with poorer UL movement quality.
kw: kinematic; motor control; functional MRI; neuronal plasticity; connectivity; stroke recovery

title: A Multi-Centre Randomized Clinical Trial of Exercise to Retard Cardiovascular Ageing
abs: Background: In ageing, deleterious alterations in cardiovascular (CV) structure and function increase risks of ageing-related cardiovascular disease (CVD). We found that these CV alterations were associated with circulating serum metabolites linked to tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle activity and beta oxidation of fatty acids, suggesting a metabolic basis to CV ageing. Additionally, these CV alterations correlated with exercise levels and changes in metabolite profiles. We hypothesize that modification of these metabolites by intervention, such as exercise, may retard CV alterations and reduce CVD in ageing. Methods: Using a multi-centre clinical trial study design, participants with CV alterations (total N=450) will be stratified based on their serum levels of metabolites (high versus low serum levels of TCA cycle and fatty acid metabolites). Participants from each stratum will be randomized to receive either a 3-month exercise program intervention (2 times per week 60 minutes each session) or no exercise. At the start and end of study, participants will undergo cardiovascular imaging and metabolic profiling. We will determine if exercise can reverse high-risk metabolic profiles and improve cardiovascular structure and function. Secondary outcomes include physical skeletal muscle function and frailty scores. Associated factors such as dietary, comorbidities, quality of life and related habits will be tracked simultaneously by questionnaire and proprietary cardiac health mobile application. An explainable artificial intelligence-based cardiac network tool that incorporates medical imaging data, biological/blood measurements and clinical information will be used for data analysis. Significance: Without clear mechanisms to explain cardiovascular ageing nor interventions known to retard cardiovascular ageing, our approach will provide much needed translational evidence to incorporate targeted interventions aimed at reducing cardiovascular disease risk in older populations. This trial would provide more definitive evidence for abnormal metabolism as a driver of cardiovascular ageing and offer a blueprint for measures to prevent and treat ageing-related cardiovascular disease (CVD.
kw: cardiovascular ageing; metabolomics; exercise; clinical trial

title: Role of blood-based inflammatory markers in predicting cognitive function among community-dwelling older persons: a proof-of-concept study
abs: Dementia incurs a huge socio-economic burden to ageing populations. However, to date, there has not been an established disease-modifying drugs for dementia due to limited understanding of the disease processes. Recent evidence highlighted the central role of chronic, systemic inflammation on age-related diseases such as dementia. Yet, it is still unclear how peripheral immune system can affect diseases of the central nervous system such as dementia, given prevailing understanding that the central nervous system is largely an immune-privileged organ. This proof-of-concept study will examine whether a panel of 15 inflammatory markers related to ageing may potentially be useful in predicting cognitive function (measured using a battery of neuropsychological tests) among older individuals. This study will collect blood specimens from up to 1000 community-dwelling older individuals, and is an add-on component to an ongoing research project that captures detailed neuropsychological tests in the same individuals. The 15 inflammatory markers will be presented to machine-learning models to predict cognitive function (i.e. global Z-score of the neuropsychological tests). The sample will be split into Training:Validation:Test dataset (60:20:20); and predictive performance of various machine-learning models will be compared using R-squared. All-in-all, this proof-of-concept study is part of a larger effort to examine the relationship between systemic inflammation and age-related diseases. If the findings show promise, our next course of action will be to apply for a national grant, where we intend to utilize a recently available, high-throughput technology to measure up to 1000 blood-based inflammatory markers to enrich our understanding on systemic inflammation and cognitive function. If our hypothesis is proven true, inflammatory markers may potentially be used in future (along with other established biomarkers) to provide a simpler and cost-effective approach in tracking cognitive function among older individuals; as well as provide mechanistic information to aid the development of disease-modifying drugs for dementia.
kw: dementia; inflammation; ageing; biomarker

title: An evaluation of the validity, reliability and acceptability of a virtual reality system in assessing cognitive function using mixed methods.
abs: Introduction: Dementia is increasingly prevalent in aging populations. Early identification of cognitive impairment is important, so that interventions can be initiated to retard the decline of cognitive function. However, current paper-and-pencil-based cognitive screening tests like the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) have limitations. Virtual reality (VR) is a potential alternative, but existing VR systems are limited in evaluating all cognitive domains. We developed a novel fully-immersive VR system (CAVIRE) to assess all six cognitive domains: perceptual-motor function, executive function, complex attention, social cognition, learning and memory, and language. CAVIRE will be available in three languages: English, Mandarin and Malay. Aims: This study aims to evaluate the validity, reliability and acceptability of CAVIRE among older individuals. We hypothesise that CAVIRE is a valid and reliable screening tool for cognitive impairment, and the participants are acceptable towards its use in primary care. We also hypothesise that the three language versions of CAVIRE are comparable in performance. Methods: The study will be conducted at two polyclinics in Singapore. Participants aged 55-84 years will be recruited. In Visit 1, an assessor will conduct the CAVIRE assessment for the participants. Subsequently, a second assessor, blinded to the participants’ CAVIRE score, will conduct the MoCA. Participants will return for Visit 2 to repeat the CAVIRE assessment, followed by an interview and questionnaire to capture their feedback. To encourage return of participants, more reimbursement will be given at Visit 2. Validity will be evaluated via factor analysis of the CAVIRE segments, Receiver Operating Characteristic analysis of the CAVIRE scores, and Pearson correlation of the CAVIRE and MoCA scores. Reliability will be assessed via Cronbach alpha and Intraclass Correlation Coefficients. Acceptability will be evaluated using mixed methods via interviews and feedback questionnaires. Performance of the three language versions of CAVIRE will be compared via Analysis of Variance.
kw: Dementia; Virtual reality; Assessment; Cognitive Domains; Validity; Reliability

title: Artificial Intelligence modelling approach to Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment for Haematology-Oncology patients
abs: With an increased life expectancy and a low birth rate, our ageing population will be the key demographic change that will impact our country for the next 50 years. There will be a concurrent increase in the number of older adults being diagnosed with cancer. We already have in place a geriatric oncology service with provision of care for older cancer patients helmed by physicians with expertise in both oncological and geriatric issues. These patients will undergo comprehensive geriatric assessment (CGA) which can identify impairments and gaps that may contribute to vulnerability and adverse outcomes. The ability to identify patients that are fit, pre-frail or frail is of paramount importance as we do not want to short-change our older cancer patients. Fit older cancer patients that receive similar chemo-therapeutics as younger patients have an increased life expectancy and enjoy similar benefits to their younger counterparts. However, pre-frail or frail patients treated with intensive treatment do suffer from higher rates of toxicity and hospitalizations. The correct identification of this group of vulnerable patients will enable the oncologist to use a non-intensive regiment and avoid excessive toxicity whilst the patient can still enjoy a stable quality of life (QoL). Little has been explored on using AI models to assess the medical fitness of cancer patients which helps the primary oncologist to determine the treatment intent, regimen selection and intensity of the cancer directed treatment for their patients. This proposal aims to develop an artificial intelligence (AI) model based on machine learning (ML) algorithms to assess the medical fitness of geriatric oncology patients as a replacement to the traditional CGA. We aspire for the AI model to perform at least, as well as current CGA tool but utilising significantly less resources in terms of manpower and time.
kw: Artificial intelligence; CGA; Oncology-Haematology; Geriatrics; Fitness; Classification

title: Development of a personalized medicine strategy for age-related macular degeneration (AMD) therapeutic
abs: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is the leading cause of irreversible blindness in the elderly, yet treatments are lacking due to an incomplete understanding of the pathogenesis. Because lipid metabolism is involved in the AMD pathophysiology, statin has been thought to be of possible interest for AMD therapeutic. However, studies have shown discrepant results, some reporting decreased, other increased risks of AMD associated with statin treatment. Therefore, this question does not have yet a clear answer despite the important clinical implications. Recent studies suggest that the two main pathways of the diseases, lipid and complement system (CS) metabolisms, might be inter-connected. We hypothesized that the effect of statin on the risk of AMD depends on the complement system (CS) genotype profile. Preliminary analyses conducted in the Singapore Epidemiology of Eye Diseases (SEED) cohort indicated that the effect of statin could vary according to one genetic variant located in the C3 gene. In this grant, we first propose to replicate these analyses in two external cohorts (Australia and Ireland). Secondly, we will measure the level of 26 CS proteins in a subset of SEED cohort using mass spectrometry proteomics technique. We further hypothesize that the variation of effect of statin on AMD could be associated with different patterns of correlations between lipids and CS proteins. Some correlations might be associated with a decrease level of inflammation and therefore a decrease risk of AMD. Machine learning algorithms will be used to identify these patterns between lipids and CS proteins. If successful, this will open up the avenue for a possible personalized AMD treatment based on genotype profile.
kw: Age-related macular degeneration, statin, lipid metabolism, complement system, personalized medicine, machine learning

title: Lenvatinib and Pembrolizumab in Endocrine Resistant Breast Cancer with Letrozole in the Advanced setting - a Phase II Study
abs:
Treatment resistance is a major problem for advanced hormone receptor-positive (HR+) HER2-negative breast cancer (BC). Although HR+ BC may be less immunogenic than certain cancers, the role of immune checkpoint inhibitors needs to be explored by combining with other agents. We propose a phase 2 trial using pembrolizumab (PD-1 antibody) and lenvatinib, a multi-kinase inhibitor that has activity against vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) receptors 1-3, fibroblast growth factor receptors 1-4 (FGFR1-4) and ret protooncogene (RET), in HR+HER2- advanced BC with letrozole, an aromatase inhibitor, to suppress the HR pathway concurrently. We hypothesise that lenvatinib will enhance the immunogenicity through normalisation of the tumor vasculature, suppression of myeloid-derived suppressor cells and regulatory T cells, increased T-cell infiltration of the tumor and apoptosis.

Up to 40 patients with advanced HR+HER2- BC that has progressed on standard endocrine therapy will be recruited. Lenvatinib (14mg) and letrozole (2.5mg) will be given orally daily from Day -14, while pembrolizumab (400mg) will be administered intravenously during week 1 of each 6-weekly cycle from Cycle 1 Day 1 (C1D1). The study treatment will be continued until disease progression, intolerable toxicities, patient’s withdrawal request, or up to a maximum of 18 6-weekly cycles (approximately 2 years) per patient. 

The primary objective is to determine the efficacy of pembrolizumab, lenvatinib and letrozole in terms of the objective response rate (ORR). A Simon’s 2-stage design will be used to allow early stopping if there is no strong evidence suggesting that the treatment regimen is active. After enrolment, patients will be reviewed at regular intervals with safety blood and urine tests, with efficacy assessments by CT scans.  Secondary objectives include progression-free survival,

title: Variable Stiffness Wrist Brace for Parkinson’s Tremor Suppression
abs: In Singapore, three out of every 1000 individuals aged 50 and above have Parkinson’s disease (PD). This number is expected to go up with the rapidly ageing population. Statistically, about 80% of PD patients suffer from tremor, which is manifested by unconscious shaking of the hands or arms at rest and is aggravated during emotional stress. In this proposal, we present a novel wrist brace to suppress hand tremors for PD. The brace is composed of a 3D printed fabric with variable stiffness which can be controlled by pneumatic pressure. In the soft state, the brace offers very little resistance to the daily movements of their wrist. When the embedded sensors detect shaking movements, the brace rapidly stiffens and provides additional damping to the wrist, thus suppressing the tremor. Then, the patient’s normal activity can be performed.
kw: Assistive Device; Parkinson's Disease; Soft Robotics; Adaptive Fabrics; 3D Printing

title: Screening for therapeutic targets of NOTCH2NLC gene non-coding CGG repeat expansions associated dopamine neurodegeneration
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Recently, pathogenic non-coding CGG repeat expansions in the neuroblastoma breakpoint family member 19/ notch 2 N-terminal like C (NOTCH2NLC) gene are found to the cause of Neuronal Intranuclear Inclusion Disease (NIID). Furthermore the non-coding CGG repeat expansions in the NOTCH2NLC gene can be the pathogenic factor of comprehensive neurodegenerative conditions, including dementia and Parkinsonism. However, the pathophysiological mechanism of non-coding CGG repeat expansion diseases remains to be elucidated. No therapeutic targets have been identified and no therapies have been developed. In our current study. we will perform high throughput single cell sequencing (SCS) of neurons from transgenic (Tg) NOTCH2NLC gene CGG expansion mice to search for therapeutic targets of non-coding CGG expansion associated neurodegeneration. SCS analysis of transcriptome (mRNA sequencing, scRNA-seq), translatome (ribosome profiling sequencing, scRibo-seq) and methylome (epigenetic sequencing, scMT-seq) will be performed. Potential therapeutic target identified from SCS study will be further validated in our NOTCH2NLC gene CGG expansion patient cells derived human neuron models. Our study aims to enhance clinical diagnosis, treatment and prognosis assessment of CGG expansion neurodegeneration and finally improve our life quality.
kw: Single cell sequencing, therapeutic targets, CGG repeat expansions, NOTCH2NLC, neurodegeneration

title: Can Gait Parameters Obtained Through 3D-printed Smart Insole/Footwear Predict Mild Cognitive Impairment?
abs: Dementia is one of the greatest health challenge of the modern world, and there is no cure. By 2050, it is estimated that 135 million will be suffering from the disease. Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) is a transitional phase of cognitive decline between normal aging and dementia, and a known precursor of dementia. MCI is prevalent in 20-30% of adults where more than 60% of the individuals will progress to dementia in their lifetimes. While dementia may be irreversible, progression of MCI to dementia can be delayed or prevented through lifestyle modification such as diet, exercise, lifelong learning, hearing and vision restoration and stringent chronic disease management. Gait and cognition share a common neural pathway, and any neurodegenerative processes will affect both simultaneously. Gait and balance disorders have been observed in persons with MCI but data to date is scanty. In addition, there is no gold standard diagnostic test for MCI. The crux of our idea is to collect baseline gait data for healthy and those with MCI through smart 3D-printed insole with an embedded pressure sensor layer to address gait and balance variability within their own footwear. Early identification of these signature hallmarks may enable early identification of those at risk, and with appropriate preventive efforts, possibility of preventing or delaying the onset of dementia. While it is known that gait speed decline can precede dementia by 10 years, progression of gait pattern and balance changes in older adults with MCI has been under investigated. The personalised 3D-printed smart insole has the potential to be used at population level for early identification of MCI, and other related conditions such as frailty and sarcopenia where all are precursors for dementia and disability. Our hypothesis being MCI and healthy controls can be differentiated through gait pattern variability and postural control.
kw: mild cognitive impairment, 3D-printed smart Insole, gait

title: Peptide-based eye drop as non-invasive treatment of age-related macular degeneration (AMD)
abs: This project develops the first topical non-invasive formulation (in the form of eye drop) to treat age-related macular degeneration (AMD), which is one of the major causes of avoidable blindness for people aged 50 and above, affecting 1.8 million people per year globally. New therapeutics are needed urgently to address the challenges faced by the current anti-VEGF therapy, namely low patient compliance to the monthly intravitreal injection for a prolonged period, and limited efficacy (i.e. 30-50% of patients do not respond or have poor response, while ~51% of patients still have active disease after 2 years). Our eye drop is based on the therapeutic peptide developed by the co-investigator, A/P Rajamani Lakshminarayanan that has shown effective inhibition on multiple aspects of VEGF- and basic fibroblasts growth factor (bFGF) – induced angiogenesis in mice as well as non-human primate models (preliminary data showed that the peptide reduced the mean area of leakage in Kimba mice (n=3 eyes) significantly more effectively than the state-of-the-art anti-VEGF compound, Eyelea (i.e. from 38872±8086 to 5316±1963 vs from 42698 ± 8794 to 13899 ± 8750). This therapeutic peptide is modified in the current project to be multi-targeting (i.e. VEGF and bFGF), long-acting, cell penetrating (through the tagging with peptide fragments such as polyarginine) and highly bioavailable (through substitution with D-amino acids) to achieve better sequela. The composition of the eye drop is optimised to prolong the storage stability at temperatures that can be conveniently achieved in normal households (i.e. 4 - 25 °C). Our project has two hypotheses based on peptide science literature: 1) peptides are more cost-effective than proteins and 2) modification of the parent peptide through tagging with cell penetrating peptide fragment and D-amino acid substitution does not create adverse side effects and does not reduce the efficacy of parent peptide.

title: Cross-species drug screening for sarcopenia
abs: Sarcopenia, as characterized by the progressive decline in muscle mass, function and quality, commonly occurs with aging and is associated with increased risks of falls, morbidity, and mortality. Increased aging populations, coupled with the adverse effects of sarcopenia, further underscores the importance of identifying therapeutics to prevent muscle weakness. Age-related loss of skeletal muscle mass and strength is associated with the progressive accumulation of protein aggregates, and alleviation of protein aggregates has been shown to improve lifespan. To identify potential inhibitors against sarcopenia in vivo, we will 1.) screen compounds with therapeutic potential in sarcopenia by using the Drosophila as an in vivo drug screening tool, followed by verifications in mice; and 2.) functionally characterize the effect of candidate drugs in mice. Our results will establish a new drug screening platform for sarcopenia combining two model systems, Drosophila and mice. Drosophila is an efficient and effective animal model for large-scale drug screens. Subsequent verification and characterization in mice and mouse myocytes can further confirm that the candidate drugs apply to mammals. Together, our cross-species drug screening approach will provide a genetic and mechanistic basis for sarcopenia and contribute to an effective treatment for sarcopenia patients.
kw: Sarcopenia, drug screening, cross-species

title: Developing modelling infrastructure to establish the population at risk of frailty and the effectiveness of nationwide interventions until 2050
abs: The aim of this study is to create an individual based model designed to test the efficacy of interventions which reduce frailty among older individuals, including resistance-based exercise, nutrition supplementation and hormone supplementation, which can allow for small scale studies to be tested at a national scale to ascertain health burden savings. The model utilises censuses and clinical cohort data to establish risk factors and scale up estimations for the whole population. At the base, we already have a model framework called DEMOS, which operates as a synthetic yet realistic representation of Singapore's population in terms of its sociodemographics, epidemiology, behaviour and environmental heterogeneities. We will build on this to incorporate frailty with a greater focus on the wellbeing of the older population where different suites of interventions will be applied. Similar efforts have been conducted for other public health problems spanning both the infectious and chronic disease domains, exploring the effects of interventions at a national scale. title: Ageing in Solitude: Perception and Health among Older Adults
abs: Being alone can be a negative or positive experience. While health risks associated with loneliness have been widely reported, less is known about the health benefits associated with solitary experiences which may involve positive emotions, spiritual or mental renewal. The current research aims to delineate solitary and loneliness experiences among older adults in the context of eating, working, physical and recreational activity participation, and examine the health correlates between perceived solitude and loneliness. Effectiveness of health messaging relating to solitary and social activities will also be investigated. Approximately three hundred older Singaporeans will be recruited for a survey eliciting the amount of time they spent alone and with family and friends for activities including eating, working, and physical and recreational activities. In addition, the participants will report whether they have any medical conditions and mental disorders, their satisfaction with life and quality of life. Following which, the participants will be randomised into one of four experimental conditions to determine which method of health messaging aimed to promote solitary and social activities is most effective based on the Self-Determination Theory. Each health promotional advertisement is rated for its affective quality, meaningfulness, and persuasiveness. Multiple linear regression analyses will be conducted to examine the correlations between perceived solitude and loneliness, and the health correlates and the effectiveness of health messaging across the experimental conditions will be examined. The present findings provide insights on the qualitative differences between solitude and loneliness experience among older adults and their health outcomes. In addition, the effectiveness of health messaging through visual advertisement will be assessed. The research findings can inform policymakers, and healthcare and social care professionals in terms of the activities (e.g., physical and recreational activities) that could support and promote positive solitude experiences and potentially better health among older adults.
kw: Solitude; loneliness; health; quality of life; positive psychology

title: Nanoscale Nuclear Patterning to Detect Nuclear Envelope Remodeling During Skin Cell Aging
abs: A significant hallmark of aging is the deterioration of the nucleus in cells, where aged and senescent cells are commonly observed to have nuclei with abnormal morphology and architecture, such as enlarged size, wrinkled and invaginated nuclear membrane, loose heterochromatin, etc. A better understanding of how aging-related genetic and epigenetic altercations is triggered by or leads to the physically mis-organized nuclear morphology is important for the discovery and evaluation of anti-aging therapeutics. However, a reliable and quantitative detection of the abnormal nuclear morphology is technically challenging. This is due to the fact that most of the abnormal features are randomly distributed across the entire nuclear space and appear in tens to hundreds of nanometers in dimension, beyond the detection limit of conventional microscopic imaging. To overcome these difficulties, we propose to introduce nanofabrication-enabled nuclear patterning to deliver quantifiable readouts of the abnormal nucleus in aged and senescent cells. Nanopillar-enabled nuclear patterning has been recently developed by the Zhao lab of the team to differentiate cancer cells with high and low malignancy. Here in this proposal, we aim to study whether or how the nuclear deformation patterns on nanopillar arrays can differentiate young and aged nucleus. Uniquely, we will focus on the aging of human fibroblasts and keratinocytes as the skin is an accessible, well-characterized and optimal model system to translate potential in vitro findings towards clinical application. Using the inducible premature aging and senescence cell models developed by the Dreesen lab of the team, we will compare different nanostructure designs and nuclear morphology markers to build assays affording quantification of nuclear alterations in aging.The success of this proposal will establish nanostructure-based nuclear patterning as a new strategy to detect cellular aging and open a new angle to develop anti-aging therapeutics.
kw: nuclear deterioration; nanopillar; premature aging; cell senescence; skin aging; anti-aging therapeutics

title: Maritime AI Program
inst: IHPC - Institute of High Performance Computing
abs: Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools have enhanced the speed, precision and effectiveness of human efforts. Developing such AI tools is a necessity in the maritime sector, considering its importance for the industry and global trade. Efforts to develop such tools in the local maritime ecosystem have been sporadic and unfocused, highlighting the need for an optimised and collective development programme. The proposed Maritime AI Programme would be a hub for AI R&D that outlines potential opportunities and develops key capabilities to advance maritime AI research in Singapore, with the use of domain knowledge and scientific data to support maritime development into the next generation locally and beyond. In the programme, 4 key research pillars are proposed to govern research development: (1) maritime data excellence; (2) AI modelling excellence; (3) computing excellence, and (4) applied AI excellence. To fully establish these 4 pillars, two research phases are planned. In phase 1, we focus on data excellence and AI modelling excellence research. This phase will develop enabling technologies for maritime big data handling capability and platform-type AI technologies for automating and streamlining maritime AI development that are also compliant to specifications and standards for the maritime industry. After building a solid foundation for maritime AI development in Phase 1, the focus in Phase 2 will be on intensifying research and application development with industry partners towards AI computing and applied maritime AI excellence development. Research in Phase 2 of the programme is to scale up maritime AI capability building and adoption and develop Maritime AI Test Centre. In Phase 1, multiple use cases will be carefully selected and studied based on the inputs from industry and agency partners. These will be used for verifying the developed technologies and establishing research and practical values of the programme. In parallel, landscaping investigation to provide inputs for the maritime AI roadmap and long-term planning development will also be conducted in Phase 1. More use cases will be included for the scaling-up development in Phase 2. The proposed programme will be a central node to drive a coordinated approach for maritime AI R&D projects. This will minimise unnecessary duplicated efforts, develop the maritime AI ecosystem and promote maritime AI cooperation among research performers and industry partners. The program lead will steer local and international collaboration of core AI initiatives and collectively deliver AI algorithms and tools for their adoption by the industry. The programme will play a core role in AI research to support the development of next-generation maritime technology, support establishing an international Maritime AI Test Centre and strengthen the leading position of Singapore as a key global maritime logistics hub, by promoting maritime AI capabilities and innovative AI models with interoperability and translat

title: Impact of climate change on water quality and pipeline failure in water distribution network
abs: The impact of climate change on water security and quality is projected to be more severe in the coming few decades due to change in intensity and magnitude of precipitation, soil water content, atmospheric water vapor and temperatures. Water distribution network plays a vital role in transporting clean and safe water to the consumers. Climate change can impact the quantity and quality of total residual chlorine, organics, microbial activity (formation of biofilm) and disinfection-by products. The combined effects may cause pipeline failure in water distribution system. However, prior studies only incorporated limited effects of climate change on the distribution network. This study investigates the potential changes of water quality occurring within water distribution network with the exploration of various chemical and biological aspects under various climate change situations. Hence, this proposal systematically provides a better understanding on the impact of climate change and the inter-relationship between climatic change and water quality in distribution network. This proposed study focuses on both lab- and pilot-scale studies to investigate the effect of climate change. Modeling works will also be carried out to forecast the impact of climate change on water quality and pipeline failures. The artificial neural network (ANN) and techno-economic analysis (TEA) will be designed and developed in this study. This study will help understand how water distribution network will change under climate change situation with reliable simulation and modeling projections. Adaption strategies will also be recommended based on the results from this study to mitigate the impact of increasing climate change on water quality and potential pipeline failure risk.
kw: Climate change, total chlorine decay, natural organic matter, biofilm, water distribution system

title: Developing RNA vaccines for dengue virus
abs: Dengue viruses (DENV) are important human pathogens with significant social and economic burden worldwide. Globally, DENV infects ~400 million people each year, leading to ~25,000 deaths1. In Singapore, we recorded 35,315 cases in 2020, a steep jump from 15,998 in 2019, highlighting their sustained importance in our society. As the current vaccines in development have limitations and there are no treatment options available, advances in new dengue vaccines are crucial to protect our society. DENV consists of 4 serotypes, DENV1-4, that are clinically relevant1. A major challenge in developing dengue vaccines is to generate cross-protection against all four serotypes. This is because antibodies towards one serotype do not cross-protect against a second serotype and can result in more severe disease, a phenomenon known as antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE) of infection2–4. As such, dengue vaccines are designed against all four DENV serotypes and need to control dosing for equal protection against each virus. The traditional vaccine strategy of passaging in non-human host cells attenuates the virus but has potential safety issues. The exact genetic composition and properties of such attenuated viruses can vary, resulting in the potential of unexpected vaccine properties in humans. Studies also showed that both B and T cell responses are important in mounting immunity towards DENV, and vaccines that only activate B cells showed poor efficacy5. Here, we aim to leverage on the recent success of mRNA vaccines to develop effective dengue vaccines. We will 1) develop strategies to activate both B and T cells; 2) optimize RNA designs for structural and non-structural proteins of all four serotypes; 3) develop cost effective strategies to encapsulate and deliver mRNAs; and 4) optimize the vaccine formulation to balance protective responses against all serotypes, allowing us to assess vaccine immunogenicity, efficacy, and safety in animal models.
kw: Dengue; serotypes; RNA vaccine; vaccines

title: Targeting energy of life for the development of drug combination to eradicate antibiotic-tolerant Mycobacterium abscessus, a clinical nightmare
abs: The incidence and prevalence of non-tuberculous mycobacterial (NTM) infections have been increasing worldwide. Among rapidly growing NTM, Mycobacterium abscessus (Mab) is the most common pathogenic one in Singapore and the most drug resistant opportunistic one. Mab can cause pulmonary diseases, cutaneous- and catheter-related infections. The process of oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) is the major process for the pathogen to synthesis the currency of life, ATP, making the pathogen vulnerable to potential drugs targeting this pathway. The enzyme complexes cyt-bc1-aa3 oxidase and F1FO-ATP synthase of Mab’s OXPHOS pathway are essential for growth. Our team has deciphered that a) Mab’s F-ATP synthase prevents ATP-waste by latency of ATP hydrolysis, and identified the regulative and Mab specific elements, providing novel compound targets. b) Described the essential role of the mycobacterial subunit δ in ATP synthesis, leading to the inhibitor DeMF1. c) Designed the anti-Mab compounds GaMF1 and (±)-C-118-F1. d) Determined the atomic solution structure of Mab F-ATP synthase subunit ε and the cryo-EM structure of the mycobacterial F1-ATPase, shining light on mechanistic features and Mab specific epitopes for novel compounds to bind. e) Deciphered critical amino acids of Mab’s cyt-bc1-aa3 oxidase for enzyme inhibition. The proposal describes a research program that will combine understanding and translation of OXPHOS operation of the pathogen Mab by forming a network of experts, whose overall goals are: a) To archive structural, enzymatic and mechanistic insights of the Mab’s cyt-bc1-aa3 and F-ATP synthase for novel target and hit identification. b) To design hit molecules of our unravelled DeMF1, GaMF1 and (±)-C-118-F1 F-ATP synthase inhibitors for the development of advanced lead molecules. c) To archive synergistic efficacy of multi-drug combination for drug resistant Mab, including the novel developed Mab F-ATP synthase and/or cyt-bc1-aa3 leads. d) To develop a preclinical development candidate. e) To establish an international clinical Mab network.
kw: non-tuberculous mycobacteria; Mycobacterium abscessus; anti-mycobacterial drug discovery; Bioenergetics; cytochrome oxidase; F-ATP synthase

title: Investigation of drug induced toxic optic neuropathy using human stem cell derived retinal ganglion cells
abs: Drug induced toxic neuropathy is a widespread clinical issue faced by neurologists and ophthalmologist alike. Multiple antibiotics and chemotherapeutic agents are the commonest culprits and cause significant morbidity including pain, paraesthesias; and with the optic nerve - blindness. Retinal ganglion cells (RGC) are highly specialized neurons, similar to central and peripheral neurons, that traverse the optic nerve. They transmit visual signals from the eye to the brain and any dysfunction of these cells results in partial or total blindness. Backed by our clinical neuro ophthalmology experience in drug induced optic neuropathy and the fact that we have successfully established a stem cell derived human retinal ganglion cell model (schRGC) to study optic nerve/ retinal ganglion cell disease; in this proposal we intend to address the problem of drug induced neurotoxicity using this schRGC model. Together with evidence from previous work in animal models and our own results in schRGC, we now have evidence for the first time that when exposed to toxic drugs like ethambutol one of the earliest effects of the drug exposure in schRGC is mitochondrial dysfunction. We hypothesize that mitochondrial dysfunction is a key mechanism causing drug induced toxicity in retinal ganglion cells; and interrupting the pathways that result in drug induced mitochondrial dysfunction will prevent neuronal toxicity. To investigate this hypothesis and identify key features that diagnose and could prevent/treat drug induced toxic neuropathy, we intend to use a comprehensive functional, proteomics and genomics approach to develop an in vitro diagnostic assay for drug induced toxic optic neuropathy, identify key metabolic pathways that can be modified to reduce or prevent drug induced toxicity in patients where drug cessation is not possible and identify genes that prevent/ promote toxicity when modified, with potential for development of future therapeutics for drug induced toxic neuropathy.
kw: drug induced toxic neuropathy; retinal ganglion cells; mitochondrial dysfunction

title: Using immunological methods and modelling to evaluate infection risk in children against SARS-CoV-2 variants (IMC study)
abs:
There is an urgent need to address knowledge gaps in understanding the protection conferred by current vaccination strategies, past-infections, combination of both vaccination and infection, and future multivalent COVID-19 vaccines especially in children. There is ongoing emergence of SARS-CoV-2 variants with mutations which can escape the protection conferred by vaccination and/or past infections. 

The study aims:
1.	to monitor natural infection and SARS-CoV-2 variants specific seroprevalence in the paediatric population
2.	to investigate immunological and population risk factors of symptomatic infection in children
3.	to develop mathematical modelling of infection risk in the paediatric population against current and future SARS-CoV-2 variants

The primary hypothesis states that seroprevalence of hybrid immunity (natural infection and vaccine induced) in the paediatric population is 70%.

Cohort 1 will be composed of n=400 anonymized residual blood samples every 6 months from the two public paediatric hospitals in Singapore. 
Cohort 2 will be a prospective cohort of n=400 children who will be followed up for symptomatic COVID-19 over 2 years with 6 monthly blood sampling.
Data from both cohorts will be used to provide 6 monthly variant specific immunity profiles of children in Singapore. It will also be used to develop an extended susceptibility- infected – recovered- vaccinated (SIRV) differential equation model with multiple immune classes through which people transition. This model will project the magnitude of future waves of COVID infection given current population immunity to the variants circulating at that time.

title: Data and Theory Driven Artificial Intelligence to Boost the Science of Learning
abs: Traditional research on teaching and learning often starts with hypotheses generated from empirical observations (observation-driven) or by analyzing gaps in learning theories (theory-driven). This approach is often limited by sensory systems and cognitive abilities of humans. Artificial intelligence has emerged as a powerful tool for improving education in recent years. Education platforms can now take over some teaching tasks from teachers and interact with students to help them learn contents. These education platforms have produced huge amount of data for assessing and understanding teaching and learning in online environments. This proposal adopts the Conjecture Mapping Framework of design-based research as the overarching methodology to iteratively and discursively integrate the data- and theory-driven approaches. The proposed work leverages on recent advancements of AI technologies and big data generated from online education platforms to generate insightful design conjectures (i.e., how designed elements such as tools, materials, activity structures, and discursive practices generate mediating processes in learning) and theoretical conjectures (i.e., how mediating processes produce desired learning outcomes), and test whether the expected mediating processes and learning outcome do emerge and whether the desired learning outcomes can be traced back to designed elements. The goal is to develop, test and refine AI-enabled interventions/recommendations (which embody actionable knowledge in optimizing teaching and learning) and to boost the Science of Learning. The pursue of both AI-enabled actionable knowledge and its theoretical underpinning contributes to Science of Learning and explainable AI in education.

title: CSA-National Cybersecurity R&D Lab Scholarship (NCLS) Programme
abs: This proposal outlines a plan to provide scholarships to approximately 40 to 50 Masters students in NUS, pursing degrees and careers related to cyber security, during the 2022-2025 period. The objective of this scholarship is to drive and support the development of professionals in Singapore’s cybersecurity sector and support the National Cybersecurity R&D Lab (NCL) initiative. This scholarship is open to students who: (1) are Singaporeans or Singapore Permanent Residents; (2) are admitted into NUS Masters programme with emphasis on cybersecurity (full-time or part-time). It provides (1) Tuition fees; (2) Monthly stipend of $2,000 (full-time students only); and (3) A project grant of $5,000 to the academic supervisors. Students who are awarded the scholarship must: (1) Maintain their Cumulative Average Point (CAP) at average 4.0 and have good academic standing; (2) Post-graduation, be employed at NCL for a period of at least 1 year, or embark on their PhD studies in a Singapore University, or be employed in Singapore’s cybersecurity industry for at least 1 year

title: Advanced Membrane-based Lithium Mining from Seawater
abs: This project aims to develop an on-site prototype for ion-selective membrane extraction process for lithium mining from the brines of seawater reverse osmosis (SWRO) to produce pure lithium salts (such as lithium carbonate and lithium phosphate) at PUB seawater desalination plants. We will design a high-flow-through electrochemical prototype integrating with lithiophilic ceramic membranes to allow selective lithium extraction among other competing ions. This also combines with state-of-the-art membrane processes such as high-pressure reverse osmosis (HPRO) and disk tubular reverse osmosis (DTRO) which can produce a highly concentrated lithium mother liquid with a Li+ concentration of 12,000 ppm. Special objectives include the development of cutting-edge lithiophilic ceramic membranes, advanced high-flow-through electrolyser, as well as the process know-hows on the production of purified battery-grade lithium salts (purity of 99.5%) from concentrated lithium mother liquids (i.e., crystallization), which can be integrated into the state-of-the-art seawater desalination process in PUB’s desalination plants.
kw: Resource Recovery, Brine Mining, Li-La-TiO3 Composite Ceramic Membrane, Li Battery

title: Carbon-Negative Minerals Recovery from Waste Streams for Concrete Applications
inst: ISCE2 - Institute of Sustainability for Chemicals, Energy and Environment
abs: Combined with carbon abatement, a novel electro-assisted method is proposed to produce mineral precipitates from waste streams such as seawater reverse osmosis brine, NEWater Brine, wastewater from industry, and even pristine seawater. An electron-assisted flow system containing cathode chamber and anode chamber will be specially designed to facilitate the process. Cathode chamber and anode chamber are physically connected but electrically insulated. The waste streams will firstly pass-through anode side then through cathode side. Valuable chlorine gas will be produced from the anode side of the flow reactor system, which can be used for water disinfection. Meanwhile, on the cathode side of the specially designed flow reactor system, electrochemical derived catalytic reduction of oxygen directly from the air was used to generate hydroxide ions (OH-). Hydroxide ions react with carbon dioxide from any source (such as biogas, natural gas power plant, or captured CO2) and mineral ions (such as Ca2+, Mg2+, and Al3+) in the waste streams and produce valuable minerals precipitates (such as CaCO3, MgCO3, and Al(OH)3). The precipitates will be separated from the treated waste streams by sedimentation separation method. A multi-talented team in ICES, A*STAR and Pan-United Pte Ltd (LLE) including experienced experts in flow reactor system design, CO2 mineralization, electrocatalysis, and process modelling will work together to implement this research plan. Taking 120,000 m3/ day seawater RO brine as an example, 43,285 tonnes/year CO2 can be captured and mineralized. 98,442 tonnes/year CaCO3 can be produced. Carbon footprint is negative even though we count the CO2 generation from the electricity for the process. This novel technology combines the minerals recovery, carbon abatement, and wastewater streams treatment together, giving strong impacts not only from economic competitiveness, but also from decarbonization and global environmental benefits.

title: Perovskite Multi-Quantum Well Metastructures for Optoelectronics
abs: Metal halide perovskites (MHPs) have established themselves as exceptional semiconductor materials with solar cell (SC) power conversion efficiencies (PCE> 25%) rivaling those of silicon solar cells and light emission external quantum efficiencies (EQE>20%) approaching those of organic light-emitting diodes. As witnessed in III-V semiconductors, Multi Quantum Wells (MQW) exploit the principles of quantum confinement to deliver breakthrough performance. MQW are multi-layered thin structures that enable quantum confinement and profoundly affect the density of states for the confined charge. MQWs are an indispensable optoelectronics component, deployed in commercial light-emitting diode (LED), laser diodes, SC, and other optoelectronic devices. The gold standard in semiconductor, III-V group materials (GaAs, InGaN, AlGaAs) have employed MQW in their devices achieving a 53% enhancement in light output power in LEDs and the record PCE of 28.3% for SC. Quantum confinement has been investigated in MHPs nanostructures (quantum dots/nanowires) and in layered MHPs; however pure MHPs MQW metastructures have not been sufficiently explored yet. MQWs in MHP can leverage the intrinsic compositional and structural versatility of the perovskite materials to exploit unexplored capabilities. We hypothesize that the energy transfer process in MHP MQW’s would be significantly more efficient, resulting in carrier localization, reduction in trap-induced non-radiative recombination, leading to unprecedented gains in photoluminescence quantum yields (PLQY) and stability. The vision of the proposed research is to design MQW meta-structures based on MHP delivering optoelectronic properties beyond the intrinsic limit of these exceptional semiconductors. Our strategy is a combined theoretical and experimental approach toward the design of materials, structure, and fabrication procedures. Only vacuum processes guarantee precise control of the growth process of MHP layers and the possibility to grow interlayers additively. We will create MQWs completely by thermal evaporation to finely control layers’ thickness and reach excellent growth reproducibility. This will mimic epitaxial growth in MPH. We will investigate fully perovskite-based MQWs with barriers and wells with variable dimensionalities and compositions to create homojunction (THRUST 1) MQWs. Differently, heterojunction MQW’s will alternate MHP and organic small molecules or inorganic semiconductors (THRUST 2). The impact of frontier phenomena (as hot carrier cooling) in MHP MQW’s will be identified to be exploited in SCs and LED (THRUST 3). This project will leverage on MQWs induced phenomena to explore uncharted areas of fundamental optoelectronics and utilize them to maximize optoelectronic performance.
kw: Quantum well, Hetero-structures, Metal halide perovskites, Molecular doping, Defect passivation

title: Integrating Volcano and Earthquake Science and Technology (InVEST) in Southeast Asia
abs: The “Integrating Volcano and Earthquake Science and Technology (InVEST) in Southeast Asia” project will take a multi-faceted, interdisciplinary approach to examining the science and societal impacts of volcanoes and tectonics -- and their related hazards -- around the Southeast Asian Ring of Fire. The project will combine modelling and state-of-the-art observation techniques to reveal how earthquakes interact with volcanoes, how together these events can trigger landslides and tsunami, how the hazards that arise from these linked systems have impacted regional societies, and how we can best foster regional resilience and sustainable development. InVEST is based around three primary research questions: (1) How do physical processes link together to drive geohazards?; (2) How do we innovate technology to monitor and understand geohazards?; and (3) How do geohazards affect societies in Southeast Asia? These questions are addressed by eight interrelated components, that range from a focus on obtaining better understanding of the underlying physical processes (e.g., building a new, kinematically consistent tectonic framework for Southeast Asia, and investigating more about how we can identify a potential caldera eruption), through innovation of observation and modelling techniques (e.g., investigating the use of quantum technology for volcano monitoring), to developing new ways to map the impacts of disasters, estimate risks to society, and catalogue past impacts of earthquakes and volcanic eruptions (e.g., remote-sensing based imaging of earthquake building damage). The project is unique in its plans for deep collaboration and synergy between
