title: AI-Assisted Visual Impairment Screening Model: Community-based Implementation and Evaluation of Performance, Feasibility and Costs.
abs: Visual impairment (VI) is a major public health problem, associated with reduced quality of life. Globally, 600 million people suffer from VI. In Singapore, one-fifth of elderly aged ≥60 years (~180,000) suffer from VI. Among them, half were due to uncorrected refractive error (i.e. can be corrected with spectacles), and the other half were attributed to various eye diseases. With timely detection and intervention, vision can be improved or halted from worsening. Hence, screening for VI is crucial for healthy ageing and productive longevity. Currently, as part of the Ministry of Health (MOH)-operated Project Silver Screen (PSS), community vision screenings are conducted for elderly nationwide. However, there remains gaps in the current PSS model as it requires 2 visits, multiple eye tests, substantial manpower and resources. These factors limit the program’s screening capacity, efficiency, and long term sustainability to meet the demand of annual screening for Singapore’s elderly. A more efficient screening model is needed. Artificial intelligence (AI) technology offers unique opportunities to revolutionize healthcare. We have developed a novel retinal photograph-based AI which can detect disease-related VI. When coupled with a simple vision test, these two tests alone, can detect both refractive error- (e.g. myopia) and disease-related VI (e.g. cataract), forming a new AI-assisted screening model. This game-changing, one-stop solution offers the potential to substantially reduce time, resources and cost. In this proposed project, using a randomized controlled trial design, we aim to prospectively perform a hybrid effectiveness-implementation study to evaluate and compare the performance, acceptability, operational efficiency and cost differences between the proposed AI-assisted screening model and the current PSS model in a community screening setting. In line with MOH’s long-term focus, this innovation will contribute towards high-value health service delivery (beyond quality to value) and promote better preventive care among Singapore’s elderly (beyond healthcare to health).
kw: Vision; Screening; Artificial Intelligence; Preventive health; Implementation

title: Developing a Core Real WOrld Dataset for Economic Evaluations of Oncology Therapies (RODEO)
abs: The treatment landscape in oncology is a rapidly evolving one, with an increase of over 60% in new drug developments in the past decade. Health technology assessment (HTA) is increasingly being used to inform resource allocation. HTA has traditionally used efficacy data from randomized clinical trial, a study design that minimizes bias. However, real-world data (RWD) are increasingly being incorporated in HTA due to a need to increase the representativeness of the data beyond the trial population. There is growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) in healthcare but the untapped potential is huge. Electronic medical records (EMR) is an important source of RWD but has been underutilized because of a lack of trained analysts and concerns over data privacy and security. In this proposal, we aim to curate an accurate and valid oncology real-world dataset to facilitate HTA and other health decision making by (1) cleaning, processing and characterizing EMR data and (2) developing use cases to demonstrate the value of this curated oncology real-world dataset. Specifically, we will 1. Assess data quality by characterizing completeness and nature of missing data from real-world sources 2. Process unstructured data using machine learning (ML) algorithms to facilitate data analyses and achieve standardization 3. Demonstrate the use of the core real-world dataset through the following studies: a. Comparative effectiveness of selected novel therapies b. Electronic phenotyping of responders to treatments
kw: real-world data; oncology; electronic phenotyping; machine learning

title: Protecting feet at risk in people with diabetes (PREFERD)
abs: Singapore has a high incidence of diabetes related lower extremity complications (DRLEC: foot ulcer, infection or gangrene), which contributes to the high rate of amputations. Despite efforts for early identification and improved management of active foot problems, cost of care remains high, as does the consequent disability and mortality burden. Primary prevention is likely to be cost-saving; however, little is known about the risk and protective factors involved in the development of a first ulcer in people with diabetes, and consequently on effective interventions for primary prevention. This is an critical and unmet healthcare need. Hence, this proposal aims to 1. Identify patient- and foot-related risk and protective factors for the development of a first ulcer in people with diabetes 2. Improve prediction of those at higher risk by combining clinical, patient, foot and footwear data using an AI-based deep learning algorithm 3. Pilot interventions for protecting feet at risk to evaluate their feasibility and acceptability We will recruit 1000 participants with diabetes at risk of first DRLEC with follow up for three years. All participants will undergo detailed assessments at baseline and annually on patient factors (including social support, self-efficacy, self-care, psychological wellbeing, barriers for preventive footcare utilization), foot status (including thermometry, thermography, plantar pressures, muscle strength and range of motion), and footwear. The new knowledge generated will be combined with available EMR data to build an AI-based prediction algorithm to improve the identification of those at higher risk. Findings will also be used to design and test new interventions for primary prevention. By focusing on primary prevention and interventions in primary care, our proposed work will substantially augment Singapore’s capacity to reduce the health and economic burden of DRLECs. The insights on the pathways to first ulcer and the factors involved will also have substantial international relevance.
kw: Diabetes Mellitus; amputations; diabetic foot ulcers; risk factors; prediction algorithms; preventive interventions; lower extremity complications

title: SMARTRx (Safe Medication management platform augmented by ARTificial intelligence for Prescribers[Rx]) - A focus on Diabetic Patients
abs: Medication errors can result in prolonged hospitalization, elevated risk for morbidity and mortality and significant healthcare spending, with an estimated cost of up to USD$40 billion in the United States. Locally, Ministry of Health reported medication error as the 5th most common error type between 2002 - 2010 and 2nd top Serious Reported Events in 2013. Diabetes mellitus is a chronic disease fast increasing in global prevalence and is associated with significant morbidity. Oral hypoglycemic agents (OHGAs) and insulins are prescribed in up to 85% of adult diabetic patients, but carry a high risk for causing patient injury when used in error. Current strategies adopted by healthcare institutions eg. rules-based prescriber order entry (CPOE) and manual pharmacist review of medications were not successful in fully eliminating errors. As COVID-19 accelerated maturation of digital innovations including artificial intelligence (AI), we postulate that AI systems can accurately and consistently detect medication errors. The overall objective of this proposal is to develop, validate and test a multi-modal machine learning AI system to detect diabetes medication error. Our specific aims include: 1. To develop and validate a novel AI model to detect errors in insulin and OHGA prescriptions in a tertiary hospital setting using a 3-year historical training dataset (2018 - 2021) 2. To prospectively test the performance of the AI model in detecting prescribing errors using an independent 1-year dataset (2022-2023) 3. To simulate reduction in pharmacist intervention workload and direct healthcare cost savings over 1 year by preventing adverse events that could arise from these prescribing errors. Historical data of DM patients, together with domain knowledge of endocrinologist and pharmacists, will be utilized for building the AI model. Different classification algorithms will be assessed; we will also utilize deep learning, a novel AI technique, to improve model performance.
kw: Diabetes; Medication Safety; Artificial Intelligence; Errors

title: Bringing iGauze, a prototype AI-vision based medical device from bench to bedside, in order to prevent Gossipyboma, reduce potential morbidity and mortality and improve patient safety
abs: Background of the need Retained surgical gauzes result in patient harm and mandate surgical re-exploration for removal of said gauzes. The consequences are potential patient anxiety, morbidity and mortality and can culminate in costly lawsuits with damage to hospital reputations. Such occurrences are inevitable even despite the substantial effort invested in preventing such occurrences, and near-misses from count-discrepancies can occur in up to 12.8% of cases, although most are caught leading to the published rate of occurrences of only 0.3 to 1.0 per 1000 cases. Current technologies fail to address the problem well and adoption is poor. Our team comprising a surgical device innovator, clinicians and engineers has designed and trained a prototype system that utilizes ML and AI visualization to recognize surgical gauzes and keep a real-time running tally which is constantly displayed back to the surgical team. Aim and methodology To reiterate the current prototype into a state ready for field trials and pilot test it in a "live" operating theater performing complex, prolonged surgery (e.g. oncologic resection), then reiterate it based on stakeholder evaluation and feedback to address specific concerns and constraints while further improving the accuracy of the system, then re-evaluate it in the same setting to ensure all requirements are met. The downstream impacts are prevention of patient harm from Gossipybomas and surgical reopenings, and reduction in requirements for onerous and time consuming counts and recounts upon gauze count discrepancies occurring, and further adjuncts e.g. on-table X ray, all of which occur while the patient kept under GA, or else at the worst case scenario may result in reintubation and re-induction for surgical reopening. Reduction in such overhead for staff will also allow the to divert more attention to other issues pertaining to the operation or logistics surrounding it.
kw: gossipyboma; serious reportable events; device innovation

title: Antimicrobial resistance in severe healthcare-associated infections - proposal for a patient registry
abs: Antimicrobial resistance is a universally recognised public health crisis. Highly-resistant bacterial infections increase morbidity and mortality given limited treatment options. Current understanding of multidrug-resistant infection epidemiology is largely based on ad-hoc observational studies and microbiology data with no linkage to clinical outcome. As such, it is not known which organisms/resistance contribute to clinically relevant infections in Singapore, and how much are the excess mortality/morbidity and healtheconomic costs. Obtaining this data through a systematically designed database with longitudinal follow up will be a vital first step towards interventional strategies. During my PhD at Oxford, I led a multinational randomised trial which optimised treatment for ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP), the commonest healthcare-associated infection (HAI) in intensive care units. To build on this, this proposal will also be on HAIs, specifically bloodstream infections (HA-BSI) and VAP. The hypotheses are i)there is high prevalence of multidrug-resistant HA-BSI and VAP in Singapore, ii)carbapenem-resistant HA-BSI and VAP are associated with more excess mortality and healtheconomic costs compared with other drug-resistant and drug-susceptible infections, and iii)specific antibiotics are associated with improved outcome depending on resistance phenotype and genotypes. The corresponding objectives are to i)evaluate disease burden in terms of patient outcomes, ii)understand treatment practices to guide clinical decisions, and iii)inform interventions such as antibiotic stewardship policies and motivate clinical trials. Study participants will be enrolled based on clinical suspicion of HA-BSI or VAP and positive microbiology culture. Bacterial isolates will be collected for whole genome sequencing. Importantly, a novel registry system will integrate patient-level clinical (infection syndrome, mortality and functional outcome), microbiology, bacterial genomic and healtheconomic cost data. I plan to implement the registry in three major local hospitals. The direct benefits of the registry are generating clinically-relevant data that can guide treatment to optimise patient outcomes, and lay the foundation for subsequent nested randomised trials.
kw: Antimicrobial resistance; treatment; disease burden

title:
Nanoradiosensitizers Target Cellular Energy Metabolism to Reverse 
Tumor Radioresistance and Immunosuppression
abs: Cancer is the number one cause of death in Singapore, accounting for around 29 % of all deaths every year. Radiation therapy is used in the treatment of approximately 50% of all malignancies and shows synergistic effects with immunotherapy. However, treatment resistance to radiation therapy and immunotherapy, intrinsic or acquired, is still prevalent, which is largely attributed to the aberrant cancer energy metabolism. Cancer cells predominantly metabolize glucose for ATP generation and biomass synthesis. The glucose can be metabolized through glycolysis with generation of lactate in the cytoplasm, or through the initial steps of glycolysis followed by further metabolism of pyruvate via the tricarboxylic acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) in mitochondria. Both pathways reduce extracellular pH, which orchestrates systemic and local immunosuppression. Meanwhile, ATP production may promote the synthesis of DNA repair enzymes poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP), which adversely affects radio-enhancement from heavy metal nanoparticle-based radiosensitizers. Herein, we propose to employ heavy metal Hf-based metal organic frameworks (Hf-MOFs) to co-deliver glycolysis-inhibiting Au nanoparticles and OXPHOS-interfering nitric oxide (NO) prodrugs. We hypothesize that by leveraging nanotechnology to dual-target glycolysis and OXPHOS, cancer metabolism would be reprogrammed to reduce PARP generation and tumor acidification, thus preventing DNA repair and eliciting immunosupportive TME and finally overcoming the resistance to radiation therapy and immunotherapy. Our Specific Aims are: 1) To design and synthesize a Warburg effect and mitochondrial OXPHOS dual-targeting nanoradiosensitizer Hf-MOFAu/NO. 2) To investigate the in vitro Hf-MOFAu/NO-mediated cellular energy metabolism inhibition and synergistic radiosensitization. 3) To explore the in vivo Hf-MOFAu/NO-mediated reprogramming of cell metabolism and immune TME and evaluate the efficacy of the radio-metabolic cancer immunotherapy. We expect this proposed research will greatly add to our understanding of cancer metabolism modulation in the reversal of resistance to cancer therapies, with the goal of translating our findings into clinical practice.
kw: Nanomedicine; Nanoradiosensitizer; Radioresistance; Immunosuppression; Drug Delivery; Tumor Microenvironment Modulation

title: Clinical relevancy of non-criterion A traumatic events to mental health and clinical utility of transdiagnostic affective factors in identifying subgroups of trauma-exposed patients with severe mental illness
abs: Specific aims: The present study aims (1) to compare the impact of exposure to DSM-5 non-criterion A traumatic events on mental health in relation to DSM-5 criterion A traumatic events; and (2) to determine the clinical utility of combining transdiagnostic affective factors (i.e., global emotion dysregulation, rumination, worry, and expressive suppression) and mapping them onto trauma exposure and co-occurring symptoms of PTSD, depression, and psychosis in order to identify subgroups of trauma-exposed patients with severe mental illness. Hypothesis: We hypothesize that (1) between three groups of patients with severe mental illness (i.e., no trauma; exposed to criterion A trauma; exposed to non-criterion A trauma), both groups of trauma-exposed patients will have similar effect sizes and severities of PTSD, depressive, and psychotic symptoms; (2) latent profile analysis of transdiagnostic affective risk factors will identify a latent high-risk group (i.e., elevated levels of emotion dysregulation) and a latent low-risk group (i.e., low levels of emotion dysregulation); and (3) the latent high-risk group will be associated with more trauma and more severe PTSD, depressive, and psychotic symptoms than the latent low-risk group. Methodology and approach: This cross-sectional study aims to recruit 500 outpatients with severe mental illness from the Institute of Mental Health (IMH). We will employ both structured clinical interviews and self-report measures. Latent profile analysis will be conducted to determine subgroups of trauma-exposed patients. Feasibility: The study team has clinical research experience and access to a large pool of patients with severe mental illness at IMH. It is expected that this study will be completed within three years. Importance to science or medicine: This study aims to develop a novel trauma assessment tool for trauma-exposed patients with severe mental illness. A reliable, valid, and transdiagnostic assessment tool is needed to address symptom complexity and guide trauma-focused interventions in this vulnerable group.
kw: transdiagnostic; trauma; PTSD; severe mental illness; mood disorders; schizophrenia spectrum disorders

title: Unveiling the molecular mechanisms of coding variants associated with type 2 diabetes for precision medicine
abs: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) is a leading cause of death worldwide. Patients are usually treated initially with a combination of lifestyle changes and oral medication, and eventually exogenous insulin, which is associated with poor patient compliance and carries a high risk of hypoglycaemia. There is a pressing need to develop alternative and orthogonal therapeutic options to complement these existing approaches. Large-scale genetics studies have identified a large number of gene variants that are associated with T2D. This offers the promise of targeted therapies that are tailored to the individual's genetic background for enhanced effectiveness of treatment. However, it is often not clear how this information can be translated into actionable clinical decisions. This may be facilitated by studying the effect of the risk allele on the structure of the encoded protein at the atomic level, which will then inform the development of targeted medicine to mitigate its deleterious effects. This study aims to reveal the molecular mechanisms of coding variants that are associated with T2D through computational structural biology and bioinformatics methods, which will then help guide the development of a structure-based predictive model for as-yet-unknown T2D-associated mutations and the design of novel anti-diabetic drugs for targeted therapy. Functional studies will subsequently be carried out to verify the molecular mechanism of selected T2D-associated coding variants and validate predicted mutations. This study is expected to advance precision medicine in T2D by providing insight into its molecular pathogenesis and improve the prevention and treatment of T2D by the development of personalised therapeutic strategies that target specific coding variants.
kw: diabetes; precision medicine; molecular dynamics; biomolecular modelling; computational structural biology

title: Handheld magnetic imaging for monitoring of suture integrity in deep surgical wounds
inst: IBB - Institute of Bioengineering and Bioimaging
abs: Deep surgical wound monitoring is a compelling clinical need as estimates on postoperative wound dehiscence in the USA are 0.5–3.4% of abdominopelvic surgeries and carries a mortality of up to 40%. Anastomosis, which is the surgical connection between two biological structures, accounts for most of the deep surgical suturing performed. However, anastomotic leaks or dehiscence are usually detected late-stage when life-threatening complications occur in patient presentation. Currently, ultrasound cannot image the sutures directly, and implanted bioelectronic sensors are not biodegradable. We propose to use a portable magnetic imaging device (same size as ultrasound) for direct visualization of sutures in deep surgical sites post-operation using a new method called Magnetic Particle Imaging. The biodegradable sutures typically used for internal procedures such as anastomosis will be minimally functionalized with iron oxide nanoparticles that are also biodegradable and FDA-approved as imaging agent, with essentially no change to the clinical workflow and expected biodegradation of the suture. This simple modification allows direct positive-contrast visualization of the sutures deep inside the body by a portable handheld magnetic imaging device to assess for suture integrity and predict wound dehiscence. Imaging is anticipated to be robust since the imaging agent is bound to the suture and not diluted into the blood volume. The same locally-concentrated magnetic nanoparticles can be heated by external alternating magnetic fields to suppress nearby infection or any leftover cancer cells. Specifically, our aims are to: (1) investigate early-detection of suture failure using handheld magnetic imaging and (2) investigate the localized cancer-suppressive properties of magnetically-heated sutures in the context of anastomosis after surgical resection of cancerous tissue.
kw: Magnetic Particle Imaging, Sutures, Deep surgical sites, Wound dehiscence

title: Evaluation of the Efficacy and Safety of Antibiotic Therapeutic Drug Monitoring (TDM) in Patients with Difficult-to-Treat Gram-Negative Bacterial (DT-GNB) Infections
abs: Sepsis remains a major cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide in the face of antimicrobial resistance especially in patients with Gram-negative bacteria (GNB) infections. Limited new antibiotics for GNB infections pose a severe threat to clinical management of these patients and thus call for old antibiotics to be repurposed. Dosing regimens of old antibiotics often fail to achieve therapeutic drug concentrations in some septic patients. Septic patients commonly have significant hemodynamic changes and/or undergo extracorporeal interventions that may increase patients’ susceptibility to treatment failure and increase the chance of more resistant bacteria emergence, or toxicity from the antibiotic. Hence, the “one size fits all” dosing principle for antimicrobial treatments of suspect sepsis due to infection by antibiotic-resistant- or less susceptible-GNB [collectively known as “difficult-to-treat” (DT)-GNB infections] is no longer viable. This will require therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) to inform if the dosing is adequate to treat such infections. To this end, we have developed a novel TDM that covers eleven antibiotics for DT-GNB infections with a turnaround time of less than 8 hours. A prospective, open-label, randomized controlled trial will be conducted to evaluate a novel TDM-guided therapy in management of DT-GNB infections. We hypothesize that TDM-guided antibiotic therapy will reduce 14-day all-cause mortality by 6% (absolute risk reduction) in septic and acutely-ill patients with DT-GNB infections, when compared to standard therapy. TDM for 11 antibiotics will be performed for all trial patients although test information will be withheld for the standard therapy arm. The primary aim is to compare the 14-day all-cause mortality rates of novel TDM-guided antibiotic dosing versus standard therapy. This proposal seeks to provide evidence supporting the application of TDM-guided antibiotic therapy on reducing mortality and morbidity among septic and acutely-ill patients with DT-GNB infections and significant hemodynamic changes, which can potentially shift current practice paradigms.
kw: Therapeutic drug monitoring, Randomized controlled trial, Antibiotic, Beta-lactam, Fluoroquinolones, Fosfomycin

title: Immunological approaches to Chronic Hepatitis B Functional Cure
abs: Globally, 296million have Chronic Hepatitis B(CHB) leading to increased deaths and cancer mortality. These can be reduced by 70% if patients achieve HBsAg loss or functional cure(FC). This rarely occurs with current antiviral therapies hence new therapies are needed. These either target the virus or boost immunity to clear the virus. However the immune mechanisms by which FC occurs is not well understood. High levels of virus may exhaust immune cells but if virus levels decrease (esp HBsAg levels) recovery of immune exhaustion may occur. This is supported by the high rates of FC in CHB on antiviral therapy who stop treatment. Consequently methods and strategies of how low HBsAg levels can lead to immune recovery and FC are crucial. Preliminary data from our liver biopsy study suggests that HBV specific CD4 cytotoxic T-cells were increased in patients with FC. In Theme 1 of our proposal we will use stored samples from our study of stopping antivirals in CHB patients with low qHBsAg< 100IU/ml, where 9/57(16%) patients achieved FC to comprehensively (cytokine-chemokine analysis, immune cell phenotyping, HBV specific T cells using pooled peptides, single cell transcriptomics) characterize immunological changes longitudinally. In our previous grant we discovered a potent anti-HBV monoclonal antibody (mAb006-11, Singapore patent application:10202107784Y). In theme 2 we aim to improve its antiviral efficacy by antibody engineering to enhance its half-life and antiviral efficacy to assess its potential. In theme 3 CHB patients with low qHBsAg(< 100IU/ml) will be treated with a highly immunogenic HBV-CPG vaccine approved as a prophylactic vaccine(Heplisav-B), in a randomised control trial (2:1 randomisation, n=74, 80% power for 30% difference) in treated/untreated CHB patients to evaluate FC, and assess the immune mechanism of FC. This proposal will lead to novel findings that advance the understanding and strategy to achieve FC.
kw: Hepatitis B

title: Tackling Fibrosis in Glaucoma Surgery (FiGS)
abs: Disordered scarring is at the root of many diseases and conditions, and its pathogenesis remains one of the biggest challenges in modern medicine. Previous approaches based on studies involving fibroblasts as effector cells of scarring in glaucoma surgery, have failed to deliver improvements to inhibit scarring despite the generation of much promising data. A new approach to reducing pathological scar formation as the underlying cause of surgical failure is much needed. An emerging concept is that scarring occurs when immune cells stimulate fibroblasts to produce excessive collagen during the repair process. In addition, chronic eyedrops also lead to a profibrotic state of the conjunctiva. This link between immune cells and differential scarring phenotypes in filtration surgery has been alluded to in the past but never fully examined to date. In this proposal, the scarring phenotype in glaucoma subjects will be investigated. Whole genome exome sequencing of patients undergoing surgery aim to look for major genes and mechanisms underlying the scarring process. A better understanding of the relationship between genetic predisposition and environmental influences on the conjunctival tissues at the surgical site, will be explored. This translational research programme will integrate scientific investigations (genomics, bioinformatics, molecular biology and experimental surgical models) with clinical research to establish a framework for a personalized approach to the identification and management of high risk to scar glaucoma patients. We propose to start with a DNA-based approach to stratify patients with the highest risk of scarring. The data generated constitute a resource that will empower the development of a personalized medicine approach to surgical management for the first time.
kw: glaucoma; surgery; fibrosis; Asian

title: The Effect of Mesenchymal Stem Cell (MSC) Exosomes on Enhancing Meniscus Repair: A Translational Study towards Clinical Application
abs: Meniscus injuries (meniscus tears) are common among physically active persons and those in occupations requiring high physical demand. If untreated, the affected persons will have worsening knee pain, restricted motion and secondary osteoarthritis (OA). Mesenchymal stem/stromal cell (MSC) therapies have demonstrated beneficial effects on meniscal healing in pre-clinical studies. There has been a paradigm shift in understanding the action mechanism of MSCs in tissue repair: from cell differentiation shifting to paracrine secretion. Among the wide myriad of trophic factors, extracellular vesicles (EVs), particularly exosomes, have been increasingly shown to replicate the wide-ranging therapeutic efficacies of MSCs. In this proposal, we aim to establish the pre-clinical, proof-of-concept for MSC exosomes as a novel cell-free therapeutic for meniscus injuries. We hypothesize that MSC exosomes enhance the cellular migration, proliferation and matrix synthesis of rabbit meniscal chondrocytes in a dose-dependent manner, and augment meniscus repair via increasing angiogenesis of the perimeniscus capillary network, increasing meniscus cellular proliferation and increasing ECM compositions and immunomodulation of the cytokine expressions in a dose dependent manner; and that MSC exosomes mediate phosphorylation of AKT and ERK signalling pathways in rabbit meniscus chondrocytes via CD73/ecto-5’-nucleotidase activity. Finally, using a rabbit meniscus repair model, we hypothesize that compared to a conventional suturing technique with fibrin glue only, the addition of MSC exosomes in treating meniscus tears leads to improved anatomic healing in terms of continuity of microstructure, maintenance of biomechanical function and less damage on adjacent cartilage. If successful, this study will break the clinical dogma that healing of meniscus injuries within the avascular zone is impossible. MSC exosomes as an off-the-shelf, cell-free therapeutic for meniscal repair will overcome the current limitations associated with cell-based therapies and be potentially a practice-changing procedure, adopted easily with improved clinical outcomes and reduced incidence of secondary OA as well as healthcare costs.
kw: meniscus; exosomes; mesenchymal stem cells; repair; regeneration

title: A novel approach to identify Serious Bacterial Infections (SBIs) among febrile young infants: the Serious bacterial Infections in Febrile infants Toolkit (SIFT)
abs: Early identification of serious bacterial infections (SBIs) among febrile young infants (less than 3 months old) remains a diagnostic dilemma. Due to the fear of missed SBIs and a lack of accurate diagnostic tools, clinicians subject many febrile young infants to unnecessary hospitalisations, painful invasive tests and intravenous antibiotics. There is an unmet need for an effective risk stratification tool. I previously demonstrated that addition of heart rate variability (HRV) parameters to traditional triage tools improved the prediction performance for SBIs in a pilot population. We aim to incorporate HRV and other biomarkers into a novel diagnostic tool in the emergency department (ED), termed Serious bacterial Infections in Febrile infants Toolkit (SIFT). First, SIFT-1 aims to stratify febrile young infants into low risk versus non-low risk of SBIs, thereby identifying infants who will benefit from hospitalisation and further investigations, as compared to those who deserve a less aggressive approach. Next, SIFT-2 stratifies those at non-low risk of SBIs into infants with or without high-risk of developing adverse outcomes, thereby identifying infants who will benefit from urgent empirical antibiotics. We intend to derive and prospectively validate SIFT in two separate cohorts of 500 infants each. Based on the simulated application of SIFT in the validation cohort, we will compare the proportions of infants being hospitalised and receiving broad-spectrum antibiotics between SIFT and standard-of-care. We anticipate that (1) SIFT-1 will improve early discrimination between infants who will benefit from hospital stay and extensive laboratory tests, compared to those who will not; (2) SIFT-2 will prioritise resources to infants with likely SBIs at high risk of developing adverse outcomes so as to reduce delays in time-to-antibiotics; (3) SIFT-1 and SIFT-2 will have the potential to reduce unnecessary hospitalisations, invasive investigations and empirical antibiotics in this febrile infant population.
kw: Infant sepsis; clinical decision rule; heart rate variability; serious bacterial infection

title: NEUROprotection via optimizINg cerebral blood flow afTer cArdiaC arresT (NEURO-INTACT) study
abs: Background Global outcomes of patients resuscitated following out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) are dismal with brain injury accounting for most of the mortality and morbidity. Optimizing cerebral blood flow through an adequate systemic blood pressure early after return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) is key to neuroprotection. Current practice of a ‘one-size fits all’ approach to systemic blood pressure management does not account for varying impairment of cerebral autoregulation and phasic variations in cerebral blood flow after ROSC. Aims and Hypothesis We aim to compare with standard-of-care, the effect of an individualized blood pressure strategy which targets person- and time-specific cerebral blood flow on brain injury (primary), cardiac and renal injury (secondary) as well as physician- and patient-reported outcomes (secondary). We hypothesize that this strategy, compared with standard-of-care, will reduce brain injury (using neuron-specific enolase as a surrogate marker), and cardiac and renal injury (circulating blood and urine biomarkers) at 72 hours. We also hypothesize this strategy will improve neurological function at hospital discharge, and function, cognition and quality of life at 6 months. Methods We will conduct a proof-of-concept randomized study in 90 resuscitated OHCA patients with blood and urine collection at stipulated timepoints. In the intervention arm, hemodynamic optimization is performed to a target arterial pressure corresponding to optimal cerebral blood flow, serially assessed using non-invasive transcranial Doppler ultrasound and near-infrared spectroscopy in the first 72 hours after ROSC. Those allocated to standard-of-care will have a target arterial pressure of 65mmHg throughout. Survivors to hospital discharge will be followed up to 6 months to assess their physical function, cognition and quality of life. Clinical Significance If successfully validated in a definitive study, this precision medicine approach could be incorporated into a protocol-driven, bundle of post-OHCA care and extended to other critical conditions, revolutionizing hemodynamic management in the critically ill.
kw: out-of-hospital cardiac arrest; individualized blood pressure strategy; cerebral blood flow; neuron-specific enolase; near-infrared spectroscopy; transcranial Doppler ultrasound

title: Proteomic profiling of exosome molecular signatures in alpha-synuclein induced Parkinson’s disease
abs: Parkinson’s disease (PD) is the second most common progressive neurodegenerative disorder that affects 6.1 million individuals over the world and more than 8000 people in Singapore. PD is characterized by the loss of dopaminergic neurons and the presence of alpha-synuclein (α-Syn) aggregates in Lewy bodies in the brain. There are many species of α-Syn aggregates, including dimers, trimers, or higher-order aggregates which are considered pathological species in PD. However, the question of how α-Syn confer different pathogenicity to PD patients remains unknown. Hence, characterizing their impacts on PD progression is critical for developing rational and urgently needed treatment targets. Recently, studies have shown that oligomeric and fibrillar aggregated species of α-Syn spread from cell to cell, mediated by exosomes. Autophagic pathway dysfunction, especially lysosomal dysfunction, has been shown to contribute to exosome mediated α-Syn propagation and spreading. However, the precise mechanism of α-Syn exocytosis via exosomes, the nature of released α-Syn in terms of aggregation, and how different species of α-Syn mediate toxicity or spreading pathogenicity via exosomes in recipient cells remain outstanding questions. Mass spectrometry (MS) based proteomic methods are increasingly being used for the analysis of exosomes, and have revealed that exosomes each contain specific sets of proteins specific for the biological source and experimental condition, which can provide crucial information regarding the molecular mechanisms related to disease pathogenesis. Currently, there are no approved diagnostic biomarkers for PD. Previous analysis of disease-related constituents of exosomes isolated from the blood of PD patients suggests that exosomes can be efficient biomarkers of PD, and can correlate with disease progression. This research proposal sought to use comparative knowledge of exosome proteomes from various diseased and clinical conditions to decipher different α-Syn species induced pathogenic mechanisms in PD, as well as develop potential biomarkers for early PD diagnostics and disease progression.
kw: Alpha synuclein; exosome; Parkinson's disease; autophagy; pathogenic mechanisms; spreading

title: Dual burden of early-life metabolic risk and suboptimal neurodevelopment: multi-omic etiologic discovery and clinical prediction modelling
inst: IHDP - Institute for Human Development and Potential
abs: Adolescents with type 2 diabetes (T2D) showed lower cognitive scores; however, the relative roles of genomic versus modifiable factors are unknown. Moreover, evidence is critically lacking among Asian populations who are at increased metabolic susceptibility than European populations. This project will be based on the deeply phenotyped birth cohort, Growing Up in Singapore Towards healthy Outcomes (GUSTO) study. We aim to investigate the relationship between genetic risk of T2D and executive function, a higher-order cognitive skill critical for health and human capital, and with a primary focus on the development of spatial working memory (SWM). We hypothesize that a higher genetic risk of T2D is inversely associated with SWM development, and the effect may be mediated by early-life epigenome and proteome. Specifically, we will construct conventional polygenic risk score (PRS) and brain-specific expression-based PRS (ePRS) using a large-scale genome-wide association study (GWAS) of T2D in East Asian. We will conduct epigenome-wide association study (EWAS) and proteomic analysis for T2D PRS/ePRS to identify relevant molecular biomarkers. Mediation analysis considering candidate epigenetic and proteomic markers simultaneously will be performed to elucidate the mediating role of molecular mechanisms. We will also develop a risk prediction model to help identify individuals at higher risk of poor metabolic and suboptimal neurodevelopment. Better understanding of intervenable mechanisms and the prospect of early risk prediction can provide tools to alleviate the dual burden of early life T2D risk and suboptimal neurodevelopment in Singapore and other Asian populations. In the longer run, promoting neurodevelopment in early childhood is not only relevant to educational outcomes but also has far-reaching impacts on improving lifelong learning capacity, reducing the risk of cognitive decline, and promoting healthy longevity.
kw: metabolic risk; neurodevelopment; multi-omics; etiology; polygenic risk score

title: Developing a biologically-informed measure of brain health during neurodevelopment
inst: IHDP - Institute for Human Development and Potential
abs: Mental health disorders have neurodevelopmental origins, underscoring the importance of early intervention during childhood as a window of opportunity to improve future outcomes. However, there is currently no objective measure that predicts the risk of poor mental health outcomes at the level of the individual child. Recent research has focused on brain age as a biomarker of brain health that reflects brain developmental trajectories. Existing brain age models are trained to predict chronological age from neuroimaging data. However, few studies leverage data from more than one imaging modality to derive brain age. Moreover, chronological age does not reflect environmental exposures or genetic background. There is also a paucity of data on brain developmental trajectories from early to late childhood. This study aims to derive and validate an objective measure of brain health predictive to the individual during the crucial neurodevelopmental period by addressing the aforementioned limitations. MRI scans and buccal swabs were collected over childhood (ages 4.5 to 10) in a population-based cohort to obtain neuroimaging data and DNA, respectively. We will first model MRI-based brain age utilizing multi-modal neuroimaging data (900 scans), and predict brain age in a test dataset (400 scans). DNA-derived biological age reflects environmental exposure, and is commonly estimated by telomere length and DNA methylation. Next, we aim to evaluate which measure best represents brain age – DNA methylation, telomere length, or chronological age. Finally, we will validate the utility of our MRI-based brain age and biological age measures by comparing between case cohorts (learning difficulties, high depression scores), and typically-developing individuals. A biologically-informed metric for brain health could help in the early identification of children at risk for poor mental health outcomes, with the opportunity for timely intervention. Long term impact includes the integration of neuroimaging into clinical practice by providing an automatable and interpretable output.
kw: Mental Health; Neuroimaging; Epigenetics; MRI; Statistical modelling; Brain age

title: Elucidating Dok3-calprotectin axis in neutrophils to identify potential therapeutic targets for management of severe COVID-19
abs: COVID-19 is an on-going pandemic caused by SARS-CoV-2, with a significant mortality rate of approximately 2%. While mass COVID-19 vaccination program is currently underway worldwide, a significant proportion of the population remains unvaccinated, and there exists a risk of emerging variants of concern with immune evasion potential surfacing in the future. Hence, urgent efforts are warranted to rapidly expand our therapeutic toolbox against SARS-CoV-2 infection. Severe illness can arise in minority of the patients due to dysregulation of their innate immune system, and they frequently exhibit signatures of neutrophil activation and dramatically increased calprotectin levels in their blood as compared to patients with mild disease. However, the precise mechanism underlying calprotectin production upon SARS-CoV-2 infection remains elusive. Our preliminary data suggests that Dok3, an adaptor protein which functions downstream of immune receptors, mediates the suppression of calprotectin production by neutrophils in response to the trimeric spike protein of SARS-CoV-2. Hence, we aim to decipher the role of Dok3 and its associated signal transduction pathway regulating calprotectin production during SARS-CoV-2 infection, thereby uncovering potential strategies and candidates for therapeutic intervention in severe COVID-19 patients.
kw: neutrophils, immune signaling, COVID-19, calprotectin, Dok3

title: PDIA6-deficiency induced ER-stress: A novel driver of hepatocellular carcinoma
abs: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the 5th most common cancer in Southeast Asia and is responsible for ~11% of cancer related deaths. In our team's efforts to unravel the genetic determinants of liver disease, we have identified PDIA6, encoding a protein disulfide isomerase of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), as an essential gene that maintains liver homeostasis. Germline PDIA6 loss-of-function mutations give rise to constitutive ER-stress and heritable liver fibrosis. In parallel, we have also found recurring somatic PDIA6 mutations in HCC and thus hypothesize that these variants, and by extension ER-stress, may drive the emergence of HCC. This is supported by our zebrafish model of HCC in which pdia6 mutations increase the incidence of severe liver carcinoma. Markers for ER-stress and small molecule chemical chaperones to alleviate ER-stress exist, suggesting that tools to detect and blunt an oncogenic stress are available or can be developed in the future. Therefore, we have devised a comprehensive study to determine the contribution of PDIA6 loss and ER-stress to the formation of HCC. We propose to characterize the effect of liver-cancer associated PDIA6 mutations, to quantify increased cancer predisposition and to describe the modes of cancerogenesis with respect to the cancer genome and the microenvironment. We believe that this effort will form the foundation for novel diagnostic and prophylactic approaches for this widespread and deadly form of liver cancer.
kw: Hepatocellular Carcinoma, Liver Cancer, Hepatology, ER-Stress, Protein Folding Stress, PDIA6

title: Characterization of metabolic vulnerabilities in aggressive fumarate hydratase (FH)-deficient renal cell carcinoma (RCC) for therapeutic opportunities
abs: Loss of function germline mutations in fumarate hydratase (FH), the enzyme that converts fumarate to malate in the TCA cycle (tricarboxylic acid cycle), can lead to a variety of syndromes, one of which is hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer (HLRCC)-associated renal cell carcinoma (RCC), a lethal subtype of RCC with young age of onset but no effective targeted therapies. Such unmet clinical needs require further research on its molecular mechanisms. Kidney is a metabolically very active organ, and RCC has been recognized as a metabolic disease. Although all classified as type 2 papillary RCC histologically, HLRCC- associated RCCs are heterogeneous, where FH has different types of mutations, including frameshift deletions (FH_fs_del, complete protein loss) and missense mutations (FH_missense, altered protein). Thus, we hypothesize that targeting metabolic shifts caused by FH loss can be effective for treatment; and different FH mutations can lead to varied drug responses. We performed high-throughput in vitro metabolism compound library screening and identified BAY-876, a GLUT1 (Glucose Transporter Type 1) inhibitor, showing 99% growth suppression in RCC cell lines with FH frameshift deletion but much reduced efficacy (46%) in those with FH missense mutation. Such differences in drug response may be due to the underlying dependency on alternate metabolic pathways for survival. Therefore, we propose to elucidate how different types of FH mutations affect downstream pathways and drug responses using metabolomic profiling, protein structure modelling and virtual screening. The proposed study in the long term can be readily applied to other less common cancers, e.g., other kidney cancers with mutated TCA cycle enzymes, many of which still lacks treatment, representing high socioeconomic burden.
kw: Renal cell carcinoma; fumarate hydratase; metabolism; drug library screening; protein structure modelling

title: Epstein Barr Virus in ENKTL: Molecular Pathogenesis and Therapeutic Opportunity
abs: Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma (ENKTL) is an EBV-associated, aggressive lymphoma prevalent in Asia and shows dismal treatment outcomes. EBV infection is thought to play a crucial role in the pathogenesis of ENKTL, but the precise mechanistic roles of the EBV latent genes and miRNAs in instigating aberrant NK-cell proliferation remain unclear. Defects in DNA damage response (DDR) and replication stress (RS) are established cancer hallmarks and our preliminary data has revealed enrichment of DDR signalling in ENKTL. EBV has been implicated in DDR in solid cancers but it remains unknown how different EBV latent genes/miRNAs may modulate DDR signalling and lead to lymphomagenesis in ENKTL. Meanwhile, accumulating evidence suggests that derailment in global DNA methylation may play a critical role in ENKTL pathogenesis. EBV infection is known to induce genome-wide gene methylation in cancer but it is currently unknown how EBV may modulate DNA methylation in ENKTL, and whether insight into EBV’s effect on DNA methylome landscape may be of clinical importance. For the current study, we aim to (i) unravel the mechanistic link between EBV and fundamental hallmarks of lymphomagenesis that may inform therapeutic directions for ENKTL by perturbing the expressions of specific EBV latent genes and miRNAs in in-vitro ENKTL models; (ii) elucidate the mechanistic association between EBV and DDR by studying DDR gene and protein expression and mutation in ENKTL patient samples, as well as investigate the effects of perturbing EBV latent genes/miRNAs on DDR signalling and DNA replication dynamics in vitro; (iii) investigate the differentially methylated regions of prognostic and therapeutic significance and examine the effect of EBV latent genes/miRNAs on the global methylation pattern of ENKTL. We foresee that an in-depth understanding of EBV’s potentially diverse effects in driving lymphomagenesis may lead to more effective treatment options and diagnostic/prognostic modalities for ENKTL.
kw: EBV; extranodal NK/T cell lymphoma, DNA damage response; miRNA, methylation

title: Diabetes mellitus and dysregulated angiogenesis in pulmonary tuberculosis
abs: Diabetes mellitus (DM) worsens tuberculosis (TB), one of the leading causes of death from an infectious disease. Uncontrolled DM-TB patients are more likely to die and remain infectious longer despite effective treatment. The reasons underlying the worse DM-TB phenotype is unknown. Angiogenic factors (AF) are upregulated in TB patients without DM. The effect of clinically-approved angiogenic inhibitors on survival, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) burden in DM-TB has not been determined. We hypothesise that targeting dysregulated angiogenesis from uncontrolled DM reduces immunopathology in pulmonary TB. Our specific aims are to determine: 1: whether the expression of AF is increased in DM-TB patients compared to TB patients without DM. 2: the regulation of AF in the DM-pulmonary TB murine model. 3: the effects of clinically-approved anti-AF drugs on immunopathology in the DM-pulmonary TB model Methodology: First, AF will be phenotyped in an existing cohort of 60 DM-TB and TB patients recruited in Singapore. AF proteins and gene expression will be analysed using Luminex bead array and single-cell RNA sequencing. Lung granulomas from ten DM-TB and TB patients will be examined for AF expression and 3-dimensional granuloma vasculature. Expression of AF on immune cells will be analysed by flow cytometry in a DM-TB murine model. 3-dimensional granuloma vasculature and intracellular signaling pathways regulating angiogenesis will be examined using chemical inhibitors. Finally, the effects of angiogenesis inhibition on improvement of TB immunopathology will be examined. Mtb-infected DM mice will be administered two candidate angiogenic inhibitors with standard TB drugs. The effects of TB drug penetration into the murine lung, morphology of granuloma vasculature and hypoxia markers will be assessed. This project determines if angiogenesis inhibition will improve TB-DM immunopathology. The results will positively impact the launch of a Phase 2 clinical trial to improve the treatment outcomes of DM-TB patients.
kw: Tuberculosis, diabetes mellitus, matrix metalloproteinasa

title: Macrophage mediated role of Yap/Taz in pulmonary fibrosis
abs: Pulmonary fibrosis (PF) is an incurable interstitial lung disease with increasing mortality, characterized by the chronic inflammation, progressive scarring of lung due to excessive accumulation of extracellular matrix between the alveoli’s or air sacs, and destruction of lung parenchyma. This results a decline in oxygen exchange function of lung, breathlessness and that eventually leads to organ failure. Number of factors are known to trigger PF including ageing, genetic disorders, autoimmune diseases, radiation, environmental factors and most recently the SARS-CoV-2 infection. When the underlying cause of PF is unknown it termed as idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF). Infiltration of inflammatory cells such as neutrophils, dendritic cells, leukocytes and macrophages into the injured site after organ injury including IPF are common. Whether inflammation contributes to IPF remains under debate, since anti-inflammatory agents are ineffective to improve clinical outcomes. For example, nonselective depletion of both tissue-resident and monocyte-derived macrophages might worsen the fibrosis through further recruitment of monocytes that affect tissue homeostasis. Therefore, understanding the contribution of specific cell populations and their interactions in the fibrotic niches are essential to prevent the pathogenesis of PF/IPF. Growing evidence indicates macrophages are crucial regulator of PF and ontologically distinct populations of macrophages differentially contribute to PF; however, the regulatory mechanisms and pro-inflammatory/reparative behaviour of distinct subpopulations underlying disease pathology remain poorly understood. To understand the macrophage biology in IPF, we propose following aims: Specific Aim 1: To investigate the role of Yap/Taz in the distribution and phenotypic plasticity of alveolar and interstitial macrophages in the lung of multiple phases of bleomycin-induced PF mouse model. Specific Aim 2: To explore the macrophage-specific implications of Yap/Taz in the development of bleomycin-induced inflammation and PF. Specific Aim 3: To examine the regenerative potential of alveolar epithelial cells due to inactivation of Yap/Taz in macrophages of mouse lung exhibiting PF.
kw: pulmonary fibrosis, alveolar macrophage, interstitial macrophage, Yap and Taz

title: Application of chemical kinetics to unravel the molecular mechanism of bispecific antibody aggregation in biotherapeutic processes
abs: Antibodies have become one of the most important classes of biomacromolecules that have achieved significant therapeutic success in many human diseases. However, their optimisation process as suitable clinical candidates remains challenging due to the need for extensive favourable biophysical properties apart from affinity and functionality. One such important parameter is the antibody’s propensity to aggregate, where monomers self-associate to form unwanted multimers. Upon therapeutic administration, antibody aggregation has been known to greatly reduce efficacy and trigger immunogenicity, causing serious safety issues for patients. As such, there is substantial interest in understanding the fundamental mechanism of aggregation in antibodies, in order to develop strategies to control it and ensure therapeutic safety for patients. Recent advances in chemical kinetics that combine experimental kinetic bulk measurements with theoretical global fitting of rate equations have allowed us to elucidate the molecular mechanism of pathological protein aggregation in human diseases. By extending such approaches to the study of antibody aggregation, we aim to introduce novel approaches within the biopharmaceutical pipeline to prevent the antibody aggregation process, in order to extend their shelf-life and ensure the safety of their therapeutic administration. More generally, the chemical kinetics approach can also be further extended and applied to other fields associated with protein aggregation, such as the development of other biologics, as well as other proteins pathologically involved in human diseases. This provides us with a new general avenue to combat protein aggregation in order to preserve human health.
kw: Protein aggregation, Antibody developability, Bispecific antibodies

title: Rechargeable Light Delivery Device for Wireless Optogenetics Interrogation in Ageing Brain
abs: A challenge for conventional optogenetics is that most of opsins are responsive to UV or visible light only, which is unable to penetrate deeply into tissues. Tethered, invasive and chronic implantation of bulky optical fiber set up is usually required for light delivery to neuron cells, restricting the movement of the animal and reducing its practical applicability. Furthermore, maintenance of a port in the scalp and cranium through which an optical fibre is inserted exposes the risks of infection. Although optogenetics offer optical mode of neural circuitry, delivering light wirelessly and enabling animal unrestricted roaming has yet to be achieved. Use of small-size LEDs for photodynamic therapy and optogenetics has recently been demonstrated, however, implantation of LEDs requires surgery. Furthermore, LEDs are rigid, not degradable and cause pain, bleeding and infection when being inserted. Near-infrared (NIR)-excited optogenetics have been explored by our group and other groups using deep tissue penetrating NIR light for excitation and upconversion nanoparticles (UCNP) as a light nanotransducer to convert NIR light to visible light for activation of opsins. However, the penetration of NIR light is still limited (< 1cm) and the retrieval of the UCNP in suspension form is almost impossible which may cause toxicity. Here, we propose to develop an injectable hydrogel fiber implant encapsulating persistent luminescence nanoparticles (PLNP) at the tip of the fiber as a rechargeable light delivery device or power bank for optogenetics. The hydrogel fiber is formed in-situ by injection using a biopsy needle. The hydrogel material is FDA-approved and biodegradable. This technology overcomes long-standing light penetration limitations of optogenetics and its advantages are multifold: wireless, rechargeable, maintenance-free, and biodegradable. We will use this new technology for first demonstration of wireless excitation-inhibition of neurocircuitry and optogenetic neuromodulation on orexin neurons in aged mice with unrestricted movement.
kw: Rechargeable; Light Delivery; Hydrogel; Wireless; Optogenetics

title: Agrin-driven microenvironment offers an attractive therapeutic strategy in hepatocellular carcinoma
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: It is increasingly recognized that corrupted Extracellular Matrix (ECM) is intimately involved in the establishment and maintenance of the tumor microenvironment. The tumor microenvironment is one of the hallmarks of cancer that is not only important for cancer pathophysiology but also a limiting factor for effective cancer therapy. Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the predominant form of liver cancer with high mortality rates in Singapore. Regretfully, therapeutic interventions targeting the HCC are limited partly due to its tumor microenvironment, for which we have limited knowledge of ECM proteins regulating its tumor microenvironment. We demonstrated that proteoglycan Agrin is overexpressed in HCC cells, integrates outside-in signaling to promote cell proliferation and migration. It also stimulates tumor angiogenesis as well as acts as an ECM sensor and mechanotransduction signal to orchestrate the interplay of cancer cells with the tumor microenvironment. In view of the dual roles of Agrin in cancer cell proliferation and orchestrating the interplay of the tumor microenvironment and cancer cells, we here propose to study the molecular mechanism and therapeutic opportunity of Agrin in HCC through the following specific aims. 1) Determining the molecular pathways underlying Agrin overexpression in cancer cells and tumor microenvironment. 2) Defining Agrin’s role in mediating a ‘dynamic mechano-reciprocity’ between cancer cells and tumor microenvironment that impacts immune surveillance and tumorigenesis. 3) Developing novel therapeutic candidates to inhibit Agrin via antibody and antisense oligonucleotide (AON) therapeutic approaches. Significance: i) understanding the role of Agrin in the corruption of the HCC microenvironment by the ECM sensing, tissue stiffening will offer insight into the resistance mechanisms of HCC to targeted therapies and mechanisms of immune cell regulation within the tumor tissues; ii) Agrin antibody/AON-mediated therapy will offer new monotherapy and combinatorial treatment strategies for HCC treatment as it targets both cancer cells and tumor microenvironment.
kw: Agrin; HCC; Tumor microenvironment; Mechanotransduction; Therapeutics; Hippo pathway

title: Development of Armoured Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR)-Tγδ cells for Effective Cancer Targeting
abs: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cells represents an exciting new paradigm in cellular immunotherapy. Nevertheless, there remains challenges pertaining to its clinical application, including cost-effective production of efficacious CAR-T cells at clinical scale, persistence of the treatment response as well as management of CAR-T cell induced adverse events. While significant effort has been dedicated to improving the core design of CAR, it is now apparent that properties of specific T cell subsets used for CAR-T cell generation also dictate the fitness and potency of the resultant CAR-T cell. Given the growing body of literatures documenting the promise of γδ T cells in targeting cancer, our team had previously characterised and explored the potential of human cord blood derived γδ T cells (CB-GDT) in targeting acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Based on our proprietary in vitro expansion protocol, we had achieved clinically relevant expansion and activation of γδ T cells. A significant proportion of these cells display central memory T cell (Tcm) and effector memory (Tem) phenotype, exhibiting both in vitro and in vivo cytotoxicity against a range of human AML cells. In contrast, they showed minimal cytotoxicity against normal hematopoietic cells. Despite of these findings, we found that the in vitro expanded γδ T cells require a high effector to target cell (E:T) ratio in order to produce clinical efficacy. In the current study, we hypothesize that developing armoured CAR-Tγδ cells shall offer a safe, effective and sustained cancer targeting. To identify gene candidates for CB-GDT engineering, we shall perform high dimensional sequencing analysis coupled with advanced functional validation systems to dissect the molecular programs governing the functional states of CB-GDT. Leveraging on our well-established CB-GDT expansion protocol, we aim to develop an optimised platform to produce potent armoured CAR-Tγδ cells for rapid translation.
kw: Immunotherapy, gamma-delta T cells, chimeric antigen receptor T cells,  cord blood, genetic engineering

title: Targeting RNA exonuclease XRN1 to potentiate immune checkpoint blockade therapy
abs: The remarkable achievement of immune checkpoint blockade antibodies has altered the therapeutic landscape of many types of cancer. However, the response rate is relatively low (20-30% in melanoma and even lower in other types of cancer) and only a fraction of patients can benefit from the treatment. Therefore, comprehensively understanding the genes and molecular mechanism controlling the efficiency of immunotherapy is an urgent need. We recently identified several key genes (LNK, SETDB1 and XRN1 etc.) regulating the response of immune therapy using murine melanoma models. In this study, we will focus on the most likely druggable target we identified, RNA exonuclease XRN1. Specific Aims & Hypothesis: XRN1 regulates aberrant-RNA mediated interferon (IFN) signaling and innate immune response; therefore, inhibiting XRN1 can potentially enhance the response of immunotherapy. Aim 1 To examine whether our finding of role of XRN1 in potentiating immunotherapy in melanoma models can be extend to other major cancers which are currently been treated with anti-PD1 antibody. Aim 2 To identify the target RNAs which are degraded by XRN1; and to elucidate mechanism of how downstream sensors recognize accumulated aberrant-RNA and activate anti-viral IFN signaling. Activated downstream RNA sensors will be systematically identified using a small customized CRISPR library. Rescue experiments will be conducted in XRN1 silenced cells to examine whether knockdown of the identified sensors can abolish the aberrant RNA induced IFN signaling. We will also examine whether XRN1 silencing enhances the antigens/neoantigens presentation and T cell response. Aim 3 Potential XRN1 inhibitors will by identified by using small molecule library screening, and their potential therapeutic effect will be evaluated.
kw: cancer immunotherapy, PD1 resistance

title: Mathematical modelling and health economic analysis of dengue vaccination strategies in Singapore
abs: Dengue transmission is increasing in Singapore, with more deaths from dengue last year than from COVID-19. There a number of vaccines on the horizon for dengue and the rational use of these vaccines could be a useful part of future dengue control. Phase 3 trials will not be happening in Singapore and therefore it is important to determine how to interpret the current results and what they mean for use in Singapore. The approach in this grant is the use of mathematical models, combined with empirical data such as clinical, epidemiological, cost, and programmatic data to provide evidence to support decisions about the future use of dengue vaccination in Singapore. The process will start with characterizing the epidemiological patterns of dengue in Singapore that are relevant to vaccination. With state-of-the-art statistical model-fitting techniques this data will be used to parameterize a mathematical model of dengue transmission and all possible vaccination strategies. The results of this modelling analysis will then be coupled with a health economic analysis using the most up-to-date health economic analysis techniques including information on the health system and disease control. All the work will be underpinned by continual stakeholder engagement to incorporate the relevant parameters of vaccine uptake and the realities of a future dengue vaccine program in Singapore.
kw: dengue, vaccination, cost-effectiveness

title: Local and global immunomodulation by conventional type 1 dendritic cells in myocardial infarction
abs: Chemokine-chemokine receptor networks coordinate immune cell trafficking from hematopoietic organs to sites of tissue injury, yet, how those immune cells communicate with each other and therefore orchestrating local immune response to cardiac injury and systemic immune response beyond the injured heart remain largely unknown. Dendritic cells (DCs) are unique antigen-presenting cells being part of the innate immune system. Their roles in MI has been controversial largely due to their high heterogeneity and complexity. We now find that conditional depletion of a specific a subset of DCs, cDC1s, limits post-MI cardiac immune response and preserves cardiac function. Surprisingly, cDC1s also modulate MI-induced immune activation in remote organs including the lung and liver. These unexpected findings lay the foundation of this grant proposal. Our central hypothesis is that cDC1s regulate both local inflammation within the injured heart and systemic inflammation in remote organs. In addition, cDC1s may affect the susceptibility of remote organs to subsequent infection or injury. To test our hypotheses, we will employ various cutting edge approaches including high-dimensional flow cytometry analysis and single cell sequencing to elucidate the mechanisms by which cDC1s regulate inflammatory responses in the infarcted heart and in the remote organs (lung and liver), and evaluate the impact of cDC1s on post-MI cardiac remodeling as well as its impact on susceptibility to pneumonia and drug-induced liver injury. Clinically relevant mouse model, porcine model, and human samples from MI patients will be used for this study. The uncovered mechanisms by which cDC1s control local inflammatory response within the infarcted heart (local) and systemic inflammatory response in remote organs (global) will lay a foundation for developing new therapeutic approaches for MI. The knowledge obtained on pneumonia and drug-induced liver injury will address the clinical problem of increased multi-organ vulnerability in the post-MI setting.
kw: Myocardial infarction, dendritic cells, inflammation, lung infection, drug-induced liver injury

title: Deciphering the role of metabolic reprogramming during nutrient stress in lung cancer
abs: Metabolic alteration is a hallmark of malignancy recognized almost a century ago, and now represents is a re-emerging paradigm. However, the gaps in knowledge remain significant. Recent landmark studies have revealed that carcinoma cells possess metabolic plasticity to increase nutrient influx for growth, rewire metabolic pathways or reshape the tumor microenvironment. Tumors are inherently heterogeneous; the metabolic differences between different cellular fractions remain underappreciated. Tumor-initiating cells (TICs) represent a subpopulation responsible for tumor-initiation and driving resistance. They tend to reside in tumor regions that are poorly vascularized or help spawn the early phase of tumor- or metastasis-initiation events; they are thereby expose to considerable nutrient stress. The manner by which they tolerate nutrient-poor environments through reprogramming their cellular metabolism is not well-understood. We reason that TICs possess unique metabolic adaptations and a degree of metabolic plasticity compared to bulk or differentiated/non-tumor-initiating cells. By subjecting TICs to specific nutrient-depleting conditions, key features of their metabolic adaptations can be uncovered. In ultra-low glucose environments that mimics the cancer stem cell niche, we hypothesize that TICs may undergo metabolic reprograming to utilize other nutrients. Our preliminary data suggest that TICs appear able to utilize ketone bodies under glucose-limiting conditions for maintaining stemness, survival and tumor growth. Since the monocarboxylate transporter 1 (MCT1) and its ancillary protein cluster of differentiation 147 (CD147) are key regulators of ketone transport between the tumor and its microenvironment, they may be useful biomarkers and therapeutic targets for cancer intervention. Interfering with their ability to activate metabolic reprogramming or restricting their access to specific metabolites may provide a therapeutic avenue for improving anti-cancer responses, and providing new metabolic targets for drug development. Since diet is associated with cancer, we hypothesize that ketogenic diet might play a role in shaping the behavior of tumor cells or their response to therapy.
