title: Machine-learning based detection of cancer and drug resistance from non-invasive liquid biopsies
abs: Early detection of cancer or treatment relapse from cell-free DNA (cfDNA) has implications for both early and late-stage cancer patients, and could generate considerable cost savings in the health care system. Furthermore, the ability to quantify and continuously track tumor growth dynamics from levels of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) in blood, provides a promising non-invasive approach to track disease progression during therapy and clinical trials, offering a real-time tool to adjust therapy. However, current solutions for quantification of ctDNA levels in the blood are expensive, tailored for individual patients or cancer types, or cannot easily be combined with standard clinical-grade gene panel sequencing. Here, we hypothesise that epigenetic footprints at specific nucleosome depleted regions (NDRs) can be used to quantify ctDNA levels across distinct cancer types (Aim 1). We propose to develop a machine learning model that jointly models cfDNA patterns at these NDRs, in combination with cfDNA fragment properties, to estimate the ctDNA burden in a blood sample (Aim 2). The model will be trained and validated using >1000 cfDNA samples from patients with distinct cancer types. As a proof-of-concept study, the model will be applied to profile ctDNA dynamics and stratify treatment responses in lung cancer patients receiving EGFR TKI treatment (Aim 3). Overall, our proposal aims to both study fundamental properties of cfDNA in cancer patients and use these insights to develop a new low-cost, general-purpose, and non-invasive method for tracking of disease progression in cancer patients.
kw: Cancer; Bioinformatics; Genomics

title: Predictive Identification of Cancer Biomarkers and Drivers via the Delineation of Novel Topological Domains involving SETDB1 and Cohesin (DiSCs)
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Cancer remains one of the most pervasive afflictions to plague humankind consistently across the global spectrum. Despite the delineation of a wide plethora of biomarkers, genetic markers and drug therapies against cancer, its detection, early diagnosis and subsequent treatment still remains a major roadblock. Along these lines, our group discovered a novel cluster of topological sites in the mouse stem cell genome that are co-occupied by the histone methyltransferase SETDB1 and the topological regulator Cohesin complex. These sites were characterised to be unique since they were involved in topological and transcriptional regulation of the genome. In the mouse stem cell system, these sites were involved in maintenance of the stem cell fate and homeostasis and were also engaged in regulating differentiation programs encoded into the stem cell genome. Further studies on these sites which we named DiSCs (Domains involving SETDB1 and Cohesin) allowed us to infer that the key topological regulator at the DiSCs was SETDB1 – which directly influenced the Cohesin enrichment at these sites. Moreover, we have also detected DiSCs in the chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) derived K562 line. SETDB1 has often been talked of as a target in multiple cancer models, but the exact nature of its contribution to the etiology and development of cancer still remains to be divulged. The genes regulated by SETDB1 via the DiSCs in K562 seem to be critical contributors to CML and AML (TAF1, MLL1 etc.) thus unearthing the potential of DiSCs in this cancer type and others to be used as a robust tool for profiling and identifying new markers/targets. Additional exploration and characterisation of these DiSCs in cancer can therefore be used as a discovery-based approach for mapping key contributors to the cancer and subsequently will be used for the development of molecular drugs for attenuating cancers.
kw: Cancer; Genome topology; Histone modifications; Molecular therapy

title: Overcome RAFi resistance in targeted cancer therapy by developing advance allosteric inhibitors
abs: Hyperactive RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK signaling is a well-defined cancer signaling pathway and exists in over 80% cancer cancer cases. Although targeting this pathway has achieved a promising outcome in cancer therapy, significant challenges remain unresolved. RAF inhibitor resistance is a major problem that impairs the efficacy of clinical cancer treatment. Clinical RAF inhibitors belong to Type I or I1/2 kinase inhibitors and have been developed to target BRAF(V600E) mutation that is highly prevalent in some cancers such as melanoma and hairy cell leukemia. These inhibitors have very high efficacy in initial treatment phase, but which is broken by quick-rising resistance. Moreover, Ras-mutated cancers exhibit intrinsic resistance to RAF inhibitors. Recent studies have revealed that RAFi resistance primarily arises from enhance RAF dimerization, which can be induced upon RAFi loading in cancers with active RAS or by alternative splicing of N-terminus of BRAF(V600E) as well as other alterations. However, why enhance RAF dimerization or other alterations results in RAFi resistance is unclear. In this study, we’ll figure molecular mechanism that underlies enhanced dimerization as well as other alterations-driven RAFi resistance and hence develop novel advance allosteric inhibitors that target sites other than ATP-binding pocket for treating RAFi-resistant cancers with RAS or RAF mutations.
kw: RAF inhibitor, RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK signaling, RAS, RAF, drug resistance, Cancer

title: Exploiting the metabolic vulnerability of cancers to mitochondrial uncoupling
abs: We recently discovered that mitochondrial uncouplers induce metabolic catastrophe and enhance apoptosis in p53-defective cancers, elucidating a first-in-class mechanism exploiting mitochondrial uncoupling (MU) against p53 deficiency. Sensitivity to mitochondrial uncoupling is linked to alterations in calcium signalling, defects in arachidonic acid (AA) catabolism, and consequently a lethal accumulation of lipid metabolites in the arachidonate pathway. The objective of the project is to discover molecular signatures predicting the MU-sensitive cellular state. In the first part of the project, we will use a focused cohort of cell lines carrying p53 mutations to identify specific molecular targets in the mitochondrial calcium signalling pathway that mimic mitochondrial uncoupling. The second part of the project uses machine learning to discover predictive molecular signatures of the MU-sensitive cellular state, by combining response to mitochondrial uncouplers and molecular targets identified herein. This will expand the use of MU-related therapeutics to a broader cancer cohort, in addition to those bearing p53 mutations. Finally, we will apply and further validate the signatures of MU-sensitivity using a vast range of public molecular data on tumours in order to identify clinical opportunities for MU-based therapeutics, both alone and in combination with existing therapy. This proposed project presents a unique opportunity to exploit our recent discovery of a novel cancer vulnerability by using a combination of experimental tools and artificial intelligence to rapidly identify opportunities for first-in-class novel anti-cancer therapeutics. By combining experimental tools and artificial intelligence, The outcomes of this study will both have a direct impact on the identification of new therapeutic targets and empower the development of a valuable pipeline and workflow for exploring AI technology in drug response prediction.
kw: Mitochondrial uncoupling; Therapeutics; Machine learning; Cancer; Precision medicine

title: Molecular Characterisation and Biomarkers in Detection of Patients with Increased Risk of Oesophageal Cancer
abs: Approximately 1% to 3% of gastric cancer arises in the setting of hereditary diffuse gastric cancer (HDGC) which is an autosomal dominant condition mainly attributed to germline mutations within CDH1. CDH1 is a tumour suppressor gene and encodes for the transmembrane glycoprotein E-cadherin essential for cell-cell adhesion. Notably, the loss of E-cadherin increases the risk of proliferation and metastasis. This syndrome is dominated by highly penetrant diffuse-type gastric cancer and an elevated risk of lobular breast cancer. Given the high cumulative gastric cancer risk in HDGC at 70% and 56% for men and women respectively by 80 years old, patients are counselled to undergo risk-reducing gastrectomy (RRG). However, this procedure is associated with significant side effects which have an adverse impact on the quality of life of patients. As such, endoscopic surveillance can be offered as an alternative to surgery. Cambridge is a pioneer in the surveillance of HDGC and has developed “Cambridge Protocol” adopted by centres worldwide where pale areasharbouring signet ring cell (SRC) foci are identified endoscopically for biopsy and followed systematically over time. The natural history of these early lesions is not entirely understood and it has been proposed they may remain indolent with a latency period of many years. A key challenge is to distinguish between indolent lesions and those at high risk for cancer progression. Hence, there is an urgent clinical need to better understand the pathogenesis of SRC into DGC amongst HDGC patients which will facilitate risk stratification and uncover novel therapeutic targets. As loss-of-function mutations are challenging to target therapeutically, the synthetic lethal approach could be adopted in CDH1-deficient cells where simultaneous loss of both genes induces cell death. The potential of this therapeutic approach using CRISPR-Cas9 based gene editing has demonstrated promising results on druggable vulnerabilities in CDH1-mutant cancers and profound anti-tumour effects of ROS1 inhibitors in E-cadherin defective cancer cell lines.
kw: oesophageal cancer, Barrett's oesophagus, risk stratification, biomarkers

title: Refinement of a Whole Child Panel to assess school readiness risks
abs: School readiness risks not addressed during early childhood beget critical downstream problems with human capital and health of society. Our main aim is to develop a unified approach in Singapore towards reliable early childhood screening in children ages 3 to 6. This project capitalises on a comprehensive screening tool, also referred to as the Whole Child Panel, developed locally with data from the Growing Up in Singapore Towards Healthy Outcomes (GUSTO) cohort. This Whole Child Panel captures the multi-dimensional aspects of school readiness beyond traditional pre-academic skills. We will evaluate this existing tool with three proposed refinements in early childhood settings, specifically in preschools. A major refinement is the digitalization of this tool with machine learning capabilities, which will be key to launching this screening strategy at scale. We hypothesize that this mode of administration will be superior to pencil-and-paper methods in terms of metrics accuracy, cognitive accessibility to this generation of young children, and reduction in manpower. We will collect data from children through our partnership with researchers and psychologists overseeing the Development Support and Learning Support (DS-LS) Programme. In this new population of preschool children, we will refine the screening tool further into a tiered approach (i.e., more in-depth profiling only for children with a positive first screen), which allows for time efficiency, yet improved psychometric properties and more clarify on risk stratification. This approach is not for diagnostic purposes. Rather, whole child profiles are apt in ascertaining risks with accuracy, and thus allowing effective interventions to start and preventing more severe sequelae in the future.

title: MariOT: A Maritime Testbed of Shipboard OT Systems for Cybersecurity Research, Training, Exercise and Education
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: Maritime industry is one of the key engines of Singapore’s economy. It has showed an increasing trend of adoption of more ICT technologies in maritime industry. On the other hand, similar to other critical infrastructures, maritime infrastructure faces an evolving array of cyber threats, which may come from insiders, criminals, terrorists, or other hostile sources. In this project, we aim to create a maritime testbed of shipboard OT systems (MariOT) and the ship-shore interfaces for cybersecurity research, training, exercise and education. It will be a hybrid platform that includes the essential components of shipboard OT and ship-shore interface systems. Considering the rapid development of new technologies, the platform will also have interface with digital twins. It will adopt common industry communication protocols and have an open and realistic framework that provides the interfaces for launching various cyber attacks as in a real system and is also able to deploy and demonstrate detection and defence mechanisms to validate their effectiveness against those attacks. This testbed will complement and work together with the software-based bridge simulator hosted by CEMS at the Singapore Polytechnic (SP). To ensure there is no duplication of efforts or overlapping scope, SUTD’s will focus on maritime cybersecurity while SP’s will be on maritime safety. A remote connection of SUTD’s testbed and CEMS’s simulator will be established to enhance the human factor relevant R&D, training and exercise with respect to cyber attacks, creating synergy and complimenting each other’s platforms. MariOT will be the first of kind to be created in Asia on cybersecurity research for the maritime industry. It allows cybersecurity researchers to design and validate new cybersecurity technologies that can be deployed in shipboard OT systems. This will further cement iTrust’s international standing as a world-leading research centre in cyber-physical system security and a national satellite of excellence on secure critical infrastructure. MariOT will be used as a platform for research, including design and validation of new (and existing) cybersecurity technologies that can be deployed in shipboard OT systems. It will also be used for training of maritime cybersecurity professionals such as through cyber ranging exercises, conduct of readiness exercise, etc. for Singapore maritime stakeholders, such as MPA, port and port facilities, cybersecurity solution providers/vendors, ship owners and classification societies to install and validate cybersecurity technologies in a safe, controlled and realistic environment as well. Maritime researchers and educators would be also keenly interested to use the testbed for experiments and development of manpower capability in maritime cybersecurity, respectively.

title: Unconventional Spin Transport in Layered Quantum Materials for Low-power Electronics
abs: For the development of spin-based electronics, it is essential to find new materials with long spin relaxation lengths. There have been many advances in the field of metal and semiconductor spintronics with traditional materials (e.g. Cu, Al and Si, GaSe) such as evidence of spin injection and transport in the non-local geometry by utilizing electron or hole as a carrier. It has even been shown in Cu-based non-local devices that such pure spin current can reverse the magnetization direction of a tiny detector magnet by a process called the non-local spin-transfer torque (STT). This advancement is the building blocks of non-volatile, low power all-spin logic (ASL) devices with built-in memory as this permits the output state to be controlled with current rather than external fields. Regardless of these initial successes, the progress for the development of proposed such ASL circuits has been very slow as this STT effect could be only observed at low temperatures (10K) using high d.c. currents of ~ 5 mA. These major problems can be overcome by creating new-generation room-temperature spin valves that have improved interfaces by combining atomically thin magnets with highly efficient spin transport materials (Objective I & II) or by using alternative unconventional approaches to carry spin information more effectively (Objective III & IV). In this research programme, I will devise spintronic devices with atomically sharp interfaces by combining our synthesized magnetic material with highly promising spin-conducting channel materials. In these devices, I will control the magnetic states by STT effect at room temperature. Here, I will demonstrate a complete set of Boolean logic operations that will have key advantages of non-volatility and low-switching energies. To further reduce the input power in these devices, I will realize spin transport and STT phenomenon by using quasiparticles found in superconductors and magnetic insulators instead of electrons. Realization of such nonvolatile, green electronic devices is mandatory for the continuation of the further growth of computation efficiency.
kw: Spintronics; Quantum materials; Magnetism; Magnons; Novel devices; Heterostructures

title: Early Cancer Intervention Initiative (Eψ)
abs: Premalignant cells bearing cancer-promoting genetic or epigenetic alterations accumulate and persist in apparently normal tissues, and can be triggered by further changes to initiate tumours. Similarly, dormant cancer cells persist after therapy; reactivation may cause relapse and drug resistance. Being able to identify, suppress or eliminate such cells would, in turn, permit early intervention to detect, delay or prevent cancer. But how premalignant (or dormant) cancer cells arise, persist or progress in different tissues is enigmatic. We conceptualize from mounting evidence that premalignant (or dormant) cancer cells are in a ‘poised’ state distinct from normal cells, wherein their cancer- promoting alterations evoke many cell-intrinsic or -extrinsic, tumour suppressive, biological responses. Recent scientific and technological advances embodied in our research team provide a timely opportunity to multi-dimensionally characterize the features that define the ‘poised’ state in different tissues, promising transformative insight into the mechanisms of early cancer evolution. Using this information, the functional dissection of the ‘poised’ state by an approach we term ‘epistatic targeting’, using new experimental models and patient-derived systems available to our research team, creates an exceptional opportunity to discover the fundamental mechanisms for persistence and progression in these settings. A spectrum of gene-environment interactions drives cancer progression. Our model systems – BRCA2-mutant breast cancer, APC/Wnt-mutant colorectal cancer, and non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH)-driven liver cancer –refl ect key principles in this spectrum, are founded on well-established expertise, experimental & clinical platforms in our research team, and represent health priorities in Singapore and globally. We will MEASURE, MAP, and MANIPULATE premalignant cells in these carefully chosen models, and in adjunct studies, extend our efforts to post-therapy dormancy in the same tissues. We will: (1) computationally integrate multi-dimensional profiles at bulk and single-cell resolution to extract ‘hallmark’ phenotypic features and correlated molecular alterations that define premalignant (or dormant) cells (MEASURE); (2) use molecular imaging to chart the in situ topography of premalignant & interacting cells during cancer evolution (MAP); and (3) target hallmark phenotypes arising from epistatic interactions (‘epistatic targeting’) to discover & interfere with the mechanisms underlying persistence and progression (MANIPULATE). We will validate key findings in a range of clinical samples accessible to our research team. The feasibility of the proposal is evidenced by the leading scientific expertise & resources available to the team, our integration into programmes focused on common scientific objectives, and preliminary work that has already established the key model systems and methodology required for this initiative. title: Overcoming drug resistance in Chronic Myeloid Leukaemia by computationally predicting cellular responses to perturbations from single-cell data
abs: Single-cell transcriptomics (scRNA-seq) has impacted clinical practice largely through its ability to accurately dissect different populations of cells isolated from patients. However, current analysis does not exploit the increase in single-cell data to deploy complex machine learning models. This proposal aims to develop a machine learning framework, named Drugnamics, to build an in silico model of the patients’ cells from scRNA-seq. This tool will be able to accurately predict how cells respond to drug perturbations transcriptionally even if they have not been experimentally performed. Similar to how animal models are used to mimic the various aspects of a disease, Drugnamics will provide an alternative, cost-effective in silico approach to disease modelling to aid in time-efficient testing of hypotheses. Furthermore, Drugnamics can be extended to transfer the single-cell data of new patients into Drugnamics to predict how these new patients will respond to any given drug treatment at a molecular level. To demonstrate this framework, I will apply it to identify drug(s) to target quiescent cancer stem cells in chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML). Quiescence in leukaemic stem cells (LSCs) leads to increased drug resistance and these cells often escape treatment and reestablish the disease after therapy. These drug-resistant quiescent LSCs represent a rare cell population that needs to be targeted to cure CML. Targeting this root cause of CML will overcome drug resistance and remove the need for life-long therapy, which is required by most CML patients. The Drugnamics framework will be applied to a CML scRNA-seq data generated by my clinical collaborator to predict how different LSC populations, especially quiescent LSCs, respond to drug treatment. Also, the framework will be extended to incorporate single-cell data from other leukaemia to construct a pan-leukaemia in silico model of LSCs, allowing us to compare the treatment response of drugs across different leukaemia.
kw: Drug perturbations; Combination drug therapy; Single-cell RNA-seq; Gene regulation; Leukaemia

title: Targeting innate immune response in blast crisis, CML
abs: CML is a hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) malignancy caused by the oncogenic BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase. Over the last decade, treatment of CML patients with the tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI), imatinib has significantly increased survival and resulted in long-term disease control. However, ~10% of CML chronic phase patients are unresponsive to TKI treatment and instead transform into a fatal condition called as blast crisis. As epigenetic modifiers have been shown to be critical for BC transformation, we profiled the epigenome of BC samples by carrying out BMI1 and H3K27Ac ChIP-seq. Analysis revealed a gain in super enhancer status for genes bound by BMI1 and controlled by NFkB - Master regulator of Inflammation. Interestingly, scRNA-seq of BC samples also revealed convergence of the samples at IRF3 driven STING pathway of inflammation. Hence in this proposal we wish to decipher the epigenetic and transcriptomic regulation of inflammation in blast crisis transformation. We wish to identify additional regulators of inflammation that are critical for BC transformation and TKI resistance. We will target these nodal points using a CRISPR screen against the identified master regulators of inflammation and pharmacological inhibition, using H151, STING inhibitor . We believe the proposed work can open various new lines of investigation, both along basic research and clinical perspectives with potential impact on patient outcome and improved clinical understanding.
kw: CML, Blast Crisis, Epignetics, Innate Immunity, Inflammation, Enhancers

title: Designing Type I Photosensitizers for Photo-immunotherapy against Tumors
abs: Photodynamic therapy (PDT) holds great promise for cancer treatment due to the lack of initiating resistance, low systemic toxicity, and minimal invasiveness. However, reliance on O2, insufficient tissue penetration depth and photobleaching of photosensitizers (PSs) limit the widespread clinical use of PDT. Therefore, alternative approaches to solve the problems by designing unique functional platforms that can minimize O2 consumption, enhance penetration depth while maintaining negligible side-effects to the normal tissues are urgently needed. Furthermore, despite the advances in the treatment of cancers based on PDT, the antitumour efficacy by PDT is unsustainable. It is now well known that monotherapies of PDT and killing cancer cells simply by inducing apoptosis is not, by itself, particularly effective for treating cancer to avoid metastasis and relapse. PDT can cause tumour cell death in an immunogenic way. Immunogenic cell death (ICD), which is characterized by release of tumour-associated antigens (TAAs), danger associated molecular patterns (DAMPs), elicits an antigen-specific immune response against a broad spectrum of solid tumours. In this proposal, we will design BODIPY-based photosensitizers for type I photodynamic therapy that do not require oxygen to produce cytotoxic free radicals for cancer treatment. More specifically, we will: 1) Design highly efficient type I photosensitizers for PDT to reduce O2 dependence, which will also be able to work under hypoxia condition; 2) Design photosensitizers for PDT with high ability to elicit immunogenic cell death to prevent metastasis and relapse; 3) Combine type I PDT and IDO inhibition to further enhance ICD and cancer photoimmunotherapy.
kw: Cancer, type I photodynamic therapy, immunotherapy, NIR-II imaging

title: Oncogenic roles of CIITA in mature T-cell neoplasms
abs: Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATL) is a mature T-cell neoplasm with poor prognosis. The tumorigenesis involves HTLV-1 infection and subsequent accumulation of complex genetic abnormalities. My preliminary study with enhancer and gene expression profiling identified that CIITA, which plays a central role in antigen presentation to T-cell receptor (TCR) by inducing MHC class II expression, is aberrantly expressed in malignant T-cells but not in normal T-cells. My data indicated that a loss of CIITA downregulates MHC class II genes and also inhibits the survival of ATL cells. Therefore, I hypothesize that CIITA plays a non-immunological and oncogenic role by activating driver pathways, which are mediated via the cell-to-cell interaction between MHC and TCR expressed on ATL cells as well as via intrinsic mechanisms in an MHC-independent manner. ATL cells may utilize machineries that are normally required for immune response for their malignant transformation and maintenance. The overall purpose of this project is to identify molecular mechanisms and roles of CIITA as well as clinical significances underlying aberrant expression of CIITA in ATL and other T-cell malignancies. Specific aims include: 1) elucidate the roles of CIITA in molecular pathogenesis of ATL, 2) analyze molecular mechanisms by which CIITA and its downstream targets contribute to ATL pathogenesis, and 3) analyze the clinical significance of aberrant expression of CIITA in ATL and other T-cell malignancies. For Aim 1, I will establish CIITA knockdown or overexpression to assess how it affects cellular phenotype and tumor formation in MHC class II-dependent or -independent manners. For Aim 2, I will comprehensively identify CIITA target genes and interconnecting pathways. I will also focus on CD74, a direct target of CIITA, and identify its interacting proteins. For Aim 3, I will reveal the association between CIITA expression and clinical characteristics in ATL and other T-cell lymphomas.
kw: CIITA, transcription factor, mature T-cell neoplasms, adult T-cell leukemia

title: Identifying the coordinative role of the SNpr in the motor and sleep symptoms in Parkinson’s Disease
abs: Parkinson’s Disease (PD), a movement disorder caused by degeneration of dopamine (DA) neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNpc), is often accompanied by sleep disorders. How DA neuron degeneration results in both motor and sleep symptoms remains a mystery. A recent optogenetic study shows that the substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNpr), commonly regarded as a movement related region, is involved in sleep regulation. In the preliminary data, I discovered our 6-OHDA induced PD mouse model developed both motor and sleep abnormalities and presented hyperactivity in the SNpr neurons. Inactivation of the SNpr neurons by chemogenetic means normalized the motor and sleep symptoms. Thus, I hypothesize that degeneration of DA neurons in the SNpc causes dysregulation of neuronal activity in the SNpr, leading to motor and sleep deficits in PD. I will first dissect the SNpr neuronal networks that are altered in the PD mouse model by using immunobiology, in vivo calcium imaging, electrophysiology, chemogenetics, and behavioral test (Aim 1), and then correct both the motor and sleep dysfunctions by transplanting human GABA neuron to restore the SNpr activity (Aim 2). Accomplishment of the proposed studies will likely not only solve the mystery of PD pathogenesis for combined motor and sleep deficits but also open a novel avenue for PD therapy.
kw: Parkinson's Disease, SNpr, Cell Therapy, Sleep Disorders

title: Understanding the function and phenotypes of tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes in the tumour microenvironment of liver metastases in microsatellite stable (MSS) colorectal cancers
abs: Colorectal cancer with liver metastases (CRLM) is a type of cancer that is potentially curable with resection, but with high relapse rates. Tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) in colorectal cancer (CRC) and liver metastases have both been shown to prognosticate for recurrence and survival. Neoantigen-specific TILs are identified in CRC but display the exhausted phenotype for microsatellite stable (MSS) CRCs. We hypothesise that neoantigen-specific T cells are present, potentially functional (but immunosuppressed or evaded) and have biological relevance in the liver metastases and colorectal primary tumours. We aim to investigate the presence, specificity and function of these neoantigen-specific TILs using a transgenic HLA-matched granzyme reporter cell line and artificial antigen presenting cell (aAPC) platforms. Ten patients with resectable CRLM will be recruited before surgery for tissue and blood collections and followed up for two years. The paired liver and CRC tumours will undergo whole exome and RNA sequencing, followed by bioinformatic neoantigen predictions. The TILs isolated from the paired tumours, and PBMCs, will undergo FACS analysis for phenotyping. We will then create neoantigen variant library and transfect the reporter cells with these variants. We will screen for neoantigen-specific TILs and expand these TILs using the neoantigen-expressed aAPC system. These T cells will undergo TCR sequencing, phenotyping as well as functional co-culture with patient-derived organoids to confirm if they can perform cytotoxic killing. We will then perform co-culture experiments with the presence of other tumour-derived immune cell. We will perform multiplex immunohistochemistry on the formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissues to confirm TIL density and the presence of these neoantigen-specific T cells in these tumours. We will correlate these translational results with patients’ clinical outcomes. We hope that this strategy can help improve our neoantigen screening and validation of CRLM and also help identify key TCRs that may help develop future therapeutics in CRLM and beyond.
kw: Colorectal cancer; liver metastases; tumour infiltrating lymphocytes; T cells; tumour microenvironment

title: Targeting miRNA-138 in recurrent Glioblastoma (MIRaGe)
abs: Glioblastoma (GBM) continues to be a lethal and ravaging disease, and uniformly recurs despite surgery, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy. The median survival in patients with recurrent GBM is 6 months, with no effective salvage therapy. It has been shown that the oncogenic microRNA (miR-138) is plays a key role in treatment-resistance. Therefore, our hypothesis is that miR-138 is a marker of poor prognosis in recurrent GBM. Secondly, we hypothesize that suppressing miR-138, through a targeted approach, will improve survival. We will test our hypothesis in the following manner – we will obtain resection samples from patients with recurrent GBM to quantify the expression of miR-138 using qRT-PCR and correlate the miR-138 levels with clinical outcomes. Where available, we will obtain paired samples (primary vs recurrent samples, from the same patient) to demonstrate that miR-138 is over-expressed in the recurrent setting. Secondly, we aim to evaluate the therapeutic potential of targeting miR-138, using anti-sense oligonucleotide (antagomir-138 oligonucleotide AMOs-138), testing its efficacy (via systemic administration) on PDX glioma models. We acknowledge the challenges posed by the blood-brain barrier (BBB), in effective delivery of the payload. Therefore, we will first design a novel AMOs-138 packaged into albumin nanoparticles, modified with Apolipoprotein E, to leverage on receptor-mediated transport systems. We will test AMOs-138-nanoparticle in-vitro, and subsequently in-vivo using intra-cranial PDX mouse models. This will include bio-luminescence imaging and bio-distribution studies to characterise the intra-cranial activity of the novel compound. We feel this is imminently feasible through our neuro-oncology tumour group infrastructure and collaborators. The thrust of this proposal is to improve the clinical outcomes of patients with GBM, which remains unmet, by developing novel targeted agents which can cross the BBB.
kw: glioma; miRNA; antisense oligonucleotide

title: Heart-Brain Changes in Acute Myocardial Infarction: Investigating the Association between Acute Cardiac Injury and Cognitive Decline
abs: We aim to characterize the impact of background risk and acute cardiac injury on the prevalence of cognitive impairment early after acute myocardial infarction (AMI), the incidence of cognitive decline after AMI at 12 months and investigate potential risk factors and biomarkers via concurrent quantitative heart-brain imaging. We hypothesize that poorer risk factor control, larger AMIs and worse baseline cardiac and brain structure and function are associated with worse cognitive impairment after acute AMI and cognitive deterioration over 12 months. This is a prospective cohort study of 150 AMI patients. At recruitment (Visit 1), patients will have systematic data collection, evaluation of haematological parameters, electrocardiographic and advanced echocardiographic analysis. Cerebral haemodynamics will be assessed via cervical duplex ultrasound (CDU) and transcranial Doppler ultrasound (TCD). At 30±7 days (Visit 2), MRI brain will help evaluate global and regional brain volume, cerebral blood flow, white matter microstructure and whole brain functional connectivity analyses. Cognitive testing will be done using the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) and a comprehensive neuropsychological test battery. At 12±2 months (Visit 3), repeat CDU, TCD and cognitive testing will be performed. Descriptive and correlative analysis of baseline and longitudinal parameters (advanced echocardiographic analysis, MRI imaging, blood biomarkers, questionnaire scores, CDU/TCD parameters) with cognitive scores will be performed. The team has experience in performing MRIs in AMI patient cohorts safely. We can perform advanced echocardiographic analysis, cognitive testing, and do quantitative analysis of MRI brain scans. We target recruiting 150 out of approximately 1200 AMI admissions annually. Dementia and AMI both pose huge medical, economic, and societal burdens. Understanding the prevalence of cognitive impairment and factors leading to cognitive dysfunction after AMI will lay the foundation for future studies that aim to manage and mitigate cognitive deterioration, improve quality of life, and reduce mortality.
kw: acute myocardial infarction, cognitive impairment, magnetic resonance imaging of the brain, echocardiography, cognitive testing, risk factors

title: Therapeutic efficacy of mesenchymal stromal cell exosomes for intervertebral disc regeneration
abs: The study aims to 1) investigate if human mesenchymal stem cell (MSC) exosomes can repair the intervertebral disc (IVD) in a rat IVD puncture model, and to 2) identify the cellular processes modulated by MSC exosomes in IVD repair and regeneration. Given that inflammation is a major player mediating the progression of IVD pain and degenerative changes, we hypothesise that MSC exosomes could exert an immune-based mechanism to suppress pain and inflammation, reduce tissue degeneration, and facilitate overall IVD regeneration. In the first study aim, 36 rats will be used. In 30 rats, IVD puncture will be performed to induce IVD degeneration before allocated into 5 groups: untreated; vehicle, phosphate-buffered saline (PBS); 10µg; 50µg; and 100µg exosomes. Six rats serve as sham controls. Analyses include weekly pain behaviour, live MRI of disc height and hydration at 0, 3 and 6 weeks post-treatment, and post-euthanasia histological scoring to assess the severity of IVD degeneration at 6 weeks post-treatment. Here, we will have determined the optimal dose of MSC exosomes for IVD regeneration. In the second study aim, a time-course analysis will be performed. A total of 54 rats will be used, with needle puncture performed in 36 rats before allocated into 2 groups: PBS; and optimal dose of MSC exosomes (from Aim 1). Eighteen rats serve as sham controls. Analyses in addition to the above, will include immunohistochemical staining for pro- and anti- inflammatory cytokines, neuropeptides, and macrophages (CD68, CD86, CD206). Given our previous works on rat spinal fusion models, and MSC exosomes in rat models of osteochondral defect and osteoarthritis, we have the expertise required. If successful in proving its efficacy, our continued work may result in a “first-in-class” exosome-based therapeutic to alleviate IVD degeneration in early treatment of LBP. Patients could potentially avoid surgical procedures and their complications.
kw: MSC exosomes; intervertebral disc; regeneration; therapeutic efficacy

title: DREAMS-OT Trial: Delirium Reduction through Early Activation in Motivating and Sleep Promoting Routines: A randomized controlled trial of Occupational Therapy for ICU patients after Coronary Artery Bypass Graft (CABG) surgery
abs:
Delirium following cardiac surgery is associated with cognitive decline, longer hospital stays, loss of functional independence and most importantly, death. In fact, delirium predicts increased mortality up to 10 years after cardiac surgery. It is characterized by acute, fluctuating levels of altered consciousness and it is a common problem. Some studies have found that more than 50% of patients undergoing coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery experience delirium. Modifiable delirium risk factors include immobility, sleep deprivation, and emotional distress. Current evidence supports the use of early mobilization protocols following cardiac surgery, but very few studies address sleep deprivation and emotional distress. 

Occupational therapy (OT) interventions promote sleep and reduce emotional distress and have been shown to significantly reduce delirium in ICU patients not receiving mechanical ventilation. However, ICU patients following CABG always receive mechanical ventilation, therefore the impact of OT interventions to reduce delirium in CABG patients is unknown. We hypothesize that early and intensive OT will significantly reduce delirium compared to usual care for patients undergoing CABG surgery. 

We propose testing this hypothesis in a randomized controlled trial. Three hundred adult patients receiving elective CABG surgery will be recruited and randomized to receive occupational therapy three times per day or usual care in the ICU. The primary outcome will be the incidence of delirium, and secondary outcomes will include

title: RESTORES trial: RESToration Of Rehabilitative function with Epidural spinal Stimulation
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Background/ hypothesis Spinal cord injury (SCI) leads to significant and often catastrophic permanent dysfunction and disability to the individuals’ physical and mental health, with limited neuro-restorative interventions. The downstream secondary health conditions translates to reduced quality of life, caregiver burden and high socioeconomic costs. Recent research with spinal cord stimulation (SCS) in patients with SCI suggests potential malleability of the neuronal networks for neurological recovery. Our team from NNI Neurosurgery, TTSH Neurorehabilitation and A*STAR propose a Phase I SCS Implantation trial to be conducted at the National Neuroscience Institute (NNI). The hypothesis of this pilot trial is that SCS in conjunction with neuro-rehabilitation can improve neurological function in patients with SCI. Aims/Methods The primary aim is to assess the synergistic potential of SCS with advanced robotic neuro-rehabilitation in restoring volitional motor activity in three patients with chronic motor complete SCI. Secondary aims are assessing the safety of off-label SCS usage, achieving further clinical improvements in autonomic functions and independent locomotion, as well as using artificial intelligence to understand and modulate neuronal recovery. Multi-site nationwide recruitment will be performed. Three selected patients will undergo surgical implantation of SCS electrodes into the epidural space and a customized perioperative rehabilitation program utilizing robotic technology. Neurophysiological assessments using non-invasive surface electromyography (sEMG) will aid in optimization of stimulation parameters. Computational techniques will be applied to sEMG signals to chart neuronal recovery and develop further algorithms for improved SCS efficacy. Neurological, autonomic, cognitive, and quality of life assessments will be performed at pre-determined intervals. Significance SCS provides very exciting promise in a field currently devoid of disease-modifying therapies. Success of this pilot trial will provide clinical evidence that the human spinal networks can be transformed post chronic injury with a multifaceted approach of targeted neurotechnology using SCS, advanced personalized neuro-rehabilitation and customized engineered computational algorithms.
kw: Spinal cord injury; Neuromodulation; epidural stimulation; Neurorehabilitation; Robotic technology; Artificial Intelligence

title: PINNACLE : Precision ImmuNotherapy for Nash And Conquering Liver CancEr
abs: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) typically develops on a background of chronic inflammation, with risk factors including HBV/HCV and increasingly non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH). Indeed, different HCC aetiologies may influence the tumour microenvironment (TME) with implications for immunotherapy response, such as immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy. Emerging evidence suggests a poorer immunotherapy response for NASH-HCC versus viral HCC, yet no therapies exist for NASH and associated liver fibrosis. We have pioneered research into the transcription factor GATA4, the loss of which occurs in ~50% of HCC cases. Our data has highlighted the importance of GATA4 loss in fatty liver and HCC development, suggesting that targeting pathways downstream of GATA4 loss may expand our treatment options and offer early therapeutic intervention. We hypothesise that HCC of different aetiologies or GATA4 status requires differentiated treatments. Therefore, we aim to study GATA4-deficient and NASH-related HCC to characterise the tumour and TME comprehensively, identify pathways and biomarkers of response/resistance, discover and validate therapeutic targets, and assess novel immunotherapy combinations. With our expertise in organoid and mouse models, we will conduct mechanistic and therapeutic studies with preclinical models that accurately recapitulate the biology of GATA4-deficient and NASH-related HCC. In parallel, we also leverage our expertise in performing deep profiling of HCC patient samples to identify clinically relevant targets and biomarkers. Furthermore, we are developing next generation cell therapies with neoantigen-specific dendritic cell vaccine (in phase 2 trial) and engineered γδ-T cells, based on findings elucidated from preclinical and clinical studies. Our strategy is to position cellular immunotherapies earlier in the adjuvant setting and pre-cancerous NASH/liver fibrosis. With over two decades of experience in translational immuno-oncology and a broad network of academic, clinical and industry collaborations, we are poised to address the unmet need for precision immunotherapies for HCC and NASH to benefit patients locally and beyond.
kw: hepatocellular carcinoma; precision immunotherapy; cell therapy; tumour microenvironment; NASH; GATA4

title: Identifying novel miRNA therapeutic targets in Parkinson's disease
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Parkinson’s disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disease, characterized by alpha-synuclein deposition in Lewy bodies, and dopaminergic neuronal loss in the substantia nigra (SN), leading to movement disorders including speech and body language. The prevalence of PD is about 0.3% for the population aged 50 and above, which accounts for 6,000 – 8,000 patients in Singapore. Currently, there is no reliable diagnostic biomarker and no cure for PD, which calls for greater awareness and intervention fighting against PD. Here we found that miR-103a-3p is downregulated in PD plasma and brain tissue and is associated with ER-stress-related responses. Arf-GAP with FG repeats protein 1 (AGFG1) was identified as a downstream target of miR-103a-3p. AGFG1 is upregulated in PD post-mortem SN and can rescue miR-103a-3p-inhibition-induced ER-stress signaling. Hypothesis: The miR-103a-3p-AGFG1 regulatory axis is associated with ER stress-induced neurodegeneration and modulators of miR-103-3p and AGFG1 could be novel therapeutic drugs for PD. Objective: To identify and validate modulators of the miR-103a-3p-AGFG1 regulatory axis as therapeutic drugs for PD. Methodology: we will first use a novel high throughput fluorescence-based biosensor system to screen for small molecule modulators of miR-103a-3p and AGFG1 from the FDA-approved drug library and the Chip-GIS high throughput platform. Next, we will study the effect of the hit-to-lead compounds on the modulation of dysregulated miR-103a-3p-AGFG1 regulatory axis in PD patient iPSC-derived neuronal cells. Further, we will explore the hit-to-lead compounds on the modulation of dysregulated miR-103a-AGFG1 regulatory axis in an ER-stress, 6-OHDA-induced, and the A53T αSyn PD mouse models. Scientific/Clinical Impact: The elucidation of the novel miR-103a-3p-AGFG1 regulatory axis in ER stress-associated PD will help to understand PD pathogenesis. The modulators of the miR-103a-3p-AGFG1 regulator axis will shed lights on the novel treatment of PD, which will help to relieve the physiologic and economic burden of PD patients.
kw: Parkinson’s disease,  miRNA, therapeutic targets, mouse model, pathogenesis, therapy

title: Understanding the role of nucleic acid induced immunity in liver diseases
abs: The liver immune system demonstrates high tolerance to harmless self and non-self (foreign) moieties to maintain homeostasis in the healthy liver. Loss of tolerance to self-nucleic acids can result in an increased risk of chronic liver inflammation, tissue damage/repair, fibrosis/cirrhosis, and even hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). ADAR1-mediated adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) RNA editing establishes self-tolerance to endogenous duplex RNA through marking them as ‘self’, which may otherwise trigger duplex RNA accumulation, excessive RNA sensing (primarily through MDA5/MAVS pathway) and interferon (IFN) responses. It is known that Adar1-knockout (KO) mice are embryonic lethal with liver disintegration and upregulated IFN signalling, indicating an indispensable role of ADAR1 in liver development. Our team recently established a liver specific Adar1/Ifih1 (encoding MDA5) double KO murine model and found concurrent depletion of Ifih1 in Adar1-KO mice was unable to rescue inflammatory response and hepatic damage, indicating the involvement of hitherto undiscovered immunoregulatory signaling pathways/mechanisms in such pathological conditions. Moreover, as ADAR1 is often upregulated in cirrhotic livers and HCC tumors, it is very likely that these identified nucleic acid-associated immunoregulatory pathways may be suppressed during the progression from cirrhosis to HCC, contributing to immunologically “cold” HCC. In this research, we aim to understand hitherto undiscovered nucleic acid-associated immunoregulatory pathways/mechanisms and decipher how they drive disease progression from chronic inflammation, hepatic damage, fibrosis/cirrhosis, to even HCC. We hypothesize that following ADAR1 depletion, there are non-MDA5-involved immunoregulatory mechanisms recognizing unedited self-duplex RNAs and inducing IFN response (hepatocyte-intrinsic changes); cell extrinsic mechanisms may also be involved in the inflamed hepatic milieu; hence a complex interplay between intrinsic and extrinsic pathways contribute to nucleic acid-induced liver pathogenesis. Results from this study can improve our understanding of mechanisms underpinning nucleic acid-induced inflammatory responses which eventually lead to liver diseases. We hope our findings can be translated for prevention and treatment of these diseases.
kw: liver disease, nucleic acid immunity, ADAR1

title: In-depth mechanistic study of cognitive dysfunction in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus using multi-modal neuroimaging
abs: Cognitive dysfunction (CD) is prevalent in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) – a multi-systemic autoimmune condition that chiefly affects young women and carries excessive mortality and morbidity. While around 80% of SLE patients with clinically-overt neuropsychiatric events such as stroke and seizures have CD, up to 54% of SLE patients without a history of major neuropsychiatric events experience a varying degree of CD across different domains, including impairment of attention, working memory and executive function. CD negatively impacts vocational capability, household income and health-related quality of life of SLE patients. Indisputably, thorough understanding of the pathogenic mechanisms of CD is indispensable to accurate diagnosis and development of effective therapies targeting CD in SLE patients. Believed to be complex and multifactorial processes that involve enhanced access of neurotoxic mediators to the brain via blood-brain barrier (BBB) leakage and/or microglial-induced cerebral inflammation, the pathogenic mechanisms leading to CD in SLE patients remains elusive. The current standard cognitive function assessment in SLE patients that is not pathophysiologically based further contributes to the stagnant trajectory of knowledge gain regarding the mechanisms of SLE-related CD. In this proposal, multi-modal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) techniques will examine how the structures (grey and white matters), microstructural integrity (white matter microstructure, functional connectivity and structural-functional coupling) and neuronal function differ cross-sectionally and change longitudinally, and how these changes relate to CD in SLE patients. The proposal allows examination of how BBB integrity measured by dynamic contrast enhanced-MRI and extracellular white-matter free water influence the structural and functional MRI signals, and their relationships with SLE-related CD cross-sectionally and longitudinally. Furthermore, the relationships between glucocorticoid dose, neurotoxic biomarkers, structural, functional and BBB integrity of the brain and CD will be studied, aiming to further unravel the pathophysiological processes of SLE-related CD, and ultimately improve the life of our SLE patients.
kw: cognition; neuroimaging; autoimmunity; systemic lupus erythematosus; magnetic resonance imaging; blood-brain barrier

title: Novel dual targeting CAR T approaches against AML
abs: Acute Myeloid Leukaemia (AML) is a highly heterogenous hematologic cancer with complex molecular landscape. The difficulties in achieving long term remission have been attributed to the presence of the leukemic stem cells (LSCs), which are insensitive to the chemotherapy and thought to be the origin of relapse. Chimeric Antigen Receptor T cells (CAR T cells) has emerged as the next generation cancer therapy in the recent years. To cure the AML patients, CAR-T therapies will have to target the highly heterogenous and genetically variable leukemic cells and be able to eradicate the LSC population without causing significant off-tumour toxicity. In this study, we will evaluate the anti-leukaemia potency and efficacy of two strategically designed CAR-T formats: A tandem CAR design where recognition of either antigen can fully activate the T-cell for killing, or a split CAR design where the T cells can only be fully activated when they simultaneously engage the two antigens. For the tandem design, CLL-1 and TIM-3 were chosen as targets, as they have been found on ~80% of the AML blasts and ~78% of LSCs express TIM-3 in the patients, whereas their expression in the normal tissues are nearly negligible. This will broaden the cancer cell coverage such that tumour antigen escape can be avoided or reduced. In split CAR approach, we choose to target CD33 and TIM-3. CD33 is highly expressed on >99% of the AML blasts in almost all patients but also expressed in hepatic Kupffer cells with risk of significant hepatotoxicty. To increase tumor specificity, TIM-3 is chosen as the 2nd target because it is selectively expressed on LSCs but not normal haematopoietic stem cells (HSCs). In addition, targeting TIM-3 will greatly improve the remission rate via eradication of the chemo-resistant LSCs.
kw: Leukemia, CAR-T, therapy, immunotherapy

title: Mechanisms of SALL4 Dysregulation in Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC)
abs: The transcription factor and oncofetal protein SALL4 plays an essential role in maintaining the pluripotency of embryonic stem cells and in fetal limb development. It is silenced in adult tissues, but aberrantly re-activated in a significant subset of almost every human cancer, including hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Those cancers which reactivate SALL4 are dependent on it for self-renewal, and knocking down SALL4 results in rapid apoptosis. Therefore, understanding the mechanisms of how SALL4 is aberrantly expressed in cancer is a critical question. Surprisingly, however, almost nothing is known about SALL4 gene regulation in normal or cancer cells. In this proposal, we will study SALL4 dysregulation in HCC. These findings will support a potential therapeutic approach in SALL4+ cancers. One mechanism of augmented expression of oncogenes is activation of new enhancers in tumors, especially larger groups of enhancer elements known as super-enhancers. Our preliminary data has identified a presumptive SALL4 super-enhancer located upstream of the SALL4 coding region present in SALL4+ HCC cells but not in SALL4+ embryonic cells. Treatment of SALL4+ (but not SALL4 ) HCC cells with inhibitors of super-enhancers led to loss of loss of SALL4 expression and selective killing of SALL4+ relative to SALL4 HCC cells. Therefore, we hypothesize that an alternative enhancer is responsible for SALL4 expression in normal versus cancer cells, leading to a potential novel therapeutic approach in HCC. In this proposal, we will further investigate mechanisms of SALL4 re-expression in cancer, focusing on the novel super-enhancer in HCC and drugs that target it.
