title: Dynamical and Mechanical properties of epithelial cell tissues: from the bottom up
abs: Epithelial tissues are a critical component of living animals that protect, shape and deform organs and glands and whose malfunctioning leads to pathological conditions. This proposal uncovers the physical and biological processes that regulate tissues transition from a flowing to a solid-like state, e.g., enabling wound healing and tissue spreading, and how tissue deform and fracture in response to applied forces. We integrate experiments, theoretical models and computational investigations to describe tissue behaviour as emerging from those of a collection of living cells and their interactions, following a bottom-up approach whose viability is suggested by recent experimental breakthroughs. These experimental advancements indicate that the emergentist approach demands a description of subcellular and intracellular processes more detailed than that provided by current models, e.g. Vertex and Voronoi, and their recent generalizations. Henceforth, we introduce a conceptually new computational model with an unprecedented subcellular resolution to first realistically link subcellular features and macroscopic tissue properties. Using this model, we investigate how contact inhibition of locomotion, microscopic features of the lamellipodium induced pulling motility and cell deformability allow tissues to flow and solidify while retaining confluency, exploring an analogy between tissues’ solid/liquid transition and the liquid/attractive-glass transition of sticky colloidal particles. Integrating numerical simulations and novel experimental setups, we investigate how subcellular and intracellular processes endow tissues with spectacular mechanical properties, e.g., stretched tissues may double their length before fracturing. The proposal leverage PI, co-PI and collaborator expertise in the numerical, theoretical and experimental study of epithelial cell tissues. Preliminary investigations demonstrate the viability of the proposed high-resolution computational approach and of the novel experimental setups to probe tissue mechanical response. Our research questions are of biological and medical relevance, as the disruption of normal tissue mechanical response leads to diseases. Furthermore, the proposal focuses on the emergent behaviour of a many-particle system out of thermal equilibrium, pushing the boundary of knowledge of physics and complexity science.
kw: epithelial tissues; jamming; glass transition; mechanical response;

title: Self-Assembly and Transient Laser Heating Experiments of Ordered Mesoporous High-Entropy Metals (STEM2) as Efficient Stable Electrocatalysts
abs: The broad objective of the proposal is to develop an integrated approach combining wet-chemistry self-assembly with transient laser heating to generate highly ordered mesoporous architectures of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) consisting of 5 and more nonprecious elements with well-defined 3D connectivity and novel property profiles for the first time. This will be achieved through three scientifically interesting work packages (WPs) focusing on nonprecious metals of Cu, Ni, Co, Mo, Fe, Al, Ti. Such metallic combinations are highly desirable for various catalytic environmental and sustainable energy-related applications such as water splitting. In WP1, we will first investigate HEA structure formation via the well-established polyol route with transient laser heating. We will expand the approach in WP2 to write well-defined block copolymer-directed mesoporous 3D carbon nanostructures as hard templates to cast HEA nanostructures deterministically. We will employ lateral gradient laser annealing to enable simultaneous generation of various 3D HEA nanostructures in a single laser scan. The materials structures and functional properties of HEA structures will be studied via high-throughput characterization techniques such as spatially resolved X-ray diffraction and scanning droplet cell electrochemical measurements. This will enable the correlations of various design parameters such as active metal composition, nanostructure architecture, surface area and pore accessibility for optimum electrical and catalytic properties, to establish the composition–structure–process–property relationships at both atomic and mesoscale scales. In WP3, we will use the materials characterization and property libraries for machine learning analysis, generating generate smart data as feedback to design and discover new HEA catalysts. We will further perform advanced materials characterization for the most promising ordered mesoporous HEA materials and verify their performance in electrochemical hydrogen/oxygen evolution reactions. Our preliminary results of laser-induced FeNiCuAuPd HEA nanoparticles and mesoporous hexagonal cylinders demonstrate the novelty and feasibility of the proposed approach. The integration of self-assembly with laser heating represents a paradigm shift in metal processing as a new programmable synthetic platform for the creation of advanced 3D hierarchical multifunctional metallic materials suitable for fundamental studies and broad technological applications such as water splitting for clean energy generation.
kw: High entropy alloys; 3D ordered nanostructures; transient laser heating; multicomponent metals; self-assembly; catalysis

title: Resistive Memory Endurance Enhancement Utilizing Smart Mitigation and Recovery Techniques
abs: Flash memory technologies have been the primary non-volatile memory solutions over the last few decades, opening up the development of electronic systems requiring high memory density and non-volatile characteristics. However, flash memory shows limitations in read/write speed, power consumption, and endurance, which prevents them from being adopted as computing random-access memory (RAM). Besides the advent of internet-of-things (IoT) connecting numerous computing devices and sensors requires low-power non-volatile memory solutions. Since the IoT devices employ batteries and energy harvesting devices as the main power supply, their power/energy efficiency is one of the topmost requirements. Various non-volatile memory devices, including magnetic RAM (MRAM), phase-change RAM (PCRAM), ferroelectric RAM (FRAM), and resistive RAM (RRAM) have been investigated to tackle the limitations of the flash memory and meet the high power/energy efficiency of IoT devices. Among the aforementioned non-volatile memory devices, RRAM has been considered as the most promising non-volatile memory for IoT devices because of its excellent scalability, compact device structure, and CMOS compatibility. However, RRAM suffers from various reliability issues such as endurance degradation, limited data retention, etc. These technical obstacles prevent RRAM from being deployed to many IoT devices. In this project, we will develop various integrated circuit techniques for mitigating RRAM endurance degradation over time and revitalizing the RRAM to extend its lifetime. To achieve this goal, we will first study the endurance characteristics of RRAM and design endurance sensing circuits. Each key RRAM endurance parameter, such as resistance values and programming bias conditions, will be investigated by a dedicated sensing circuit to isolate the impact of other endurance parameters. This will allow us to understand the endurance degradation characteristics. We will then develop RRAM endurance monitoring circuits to track the parametric degradations in actual RRAM operating conditions. The monitoring circuits will provide the degree of the reliability degradation that needs to be mitigated or compensated so that the RRAM can still work reliably after degradation. Finally, self-reconfigurable techniques will be developed to optimize the RRAM operating conditions for endurance enhancement or endurance recovery. This task will utilize the data generated by the RRAM endurance degradation monitors and control voltage levels, signal polarities, and pulse widths automatically through the developed control strategy.
kw: Resistive memory; Endurance; Resistance degradation; Smart circuits; Reconfiguration

title: Ultrasonic Imprinting of Plasmonic Nanostructures for Surface-Enhanced Raman Spectroscopy
abs: 1. Goal and Specific Aims The overarching project goal is to investigate and develop a cost-effective and unconventional ultrasonic nanoimprinting technique for making ultrasensitive biosensing platforms. We propose to study the detailed mechanisms of our newly patented ultrasonic nanoimprinting technique (namely nanojackhammer), and then to develop our patented ultrasonic nanoimprinting technique (namely nanojackhammer) for fabrication of complex plasmonic nanostructures for quorum sensing (QS) using surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS). To achieve this goal, we propose the following specific aims: (1) Identification of the detailed working mechanism of nanojackhammer. Under ultrasonic frequency impact, the nanojackhammers deform the substrate step-by-step swiftly, and controllably deliver the stress to the focused area. Under the extremely high vibrational local stress, the substrate would experience repeated severe plastic deformation that enables metal flow into the mold. A clearer physical picture will be obtained with complementary atomic scale microscopy imaging and theoretical modeling. Moreover, the impact of ultrasonic frequency and local heating on the fabricated structure will be investigated. (2) Fabrication of plasmonic nanostructure of multi-segment nanorods with embedded nanogaps. Taking QS as an example, we aim to fabricate a wafer-scale array of nanorods with built-in nanogaps, which will be carefully designed to maximize the plasmonic effect for specific sensing targets. (3) Monitoring of QS in biofilms using the fabricated plasmonic structure and screening of QS inhibitors. We aim to design a SERS platform for detection of QS-regulated molecules in biofilms with multiple nanogaps embedded in multi-segment nanorods. Quantitative QS sensing will be pursuit. 2. Hypothesis Plasmonic nanostructures that control molecule-light interaction via confined electric field arising from excited localized surface plasmon resonance have led to the development of advanced biosensing platforms. This forms the fundamental basis of surface-enhanced optical methods, e.g., SERS, which is capable of producing enormous signal amplification at single-particle level. QS is crucial to biofilm formation and physiological regulation, and was previously analyzed in situ by using SERS on complex plasmonic nanostructures in a non-invasive and label-free manner. However, the precise and reproducible fabrication of the complex plasmonic nanostructure is very challenging. Conventional fabrication method suffers from long processing time, low-yield, and high cost. In contrast, our fabrication method leverages the unique features of ultrasonic energy flow and precise physical vapor deposition to fabricate multi-segment nanorod arrays with embedded nanogaps for highly-sensitive SERS detection and imaging. title: Holistic Allocation of Edge and Wireless Resources for Time-Sensitive IoT Applications
abs: Resource provisioning and scheduling for edge and cloud architectures have gained a lot of attention in the recent past both in academia and industry. This interest is primarily driven by the enormous success of two technologies in the field of computing: 1) Artificial Intelligence (AI), and 2) Internet of Things (IoT). Cloud architectures play a central enabling role for AI due to the significant demand that this technology imposes on computational resources. Orthogonally, IoT has enabled an unprecedented decentralization and deployment of applications across domains, including several in which AI (at the edge) is gaining prominence. As a result, the edge and cloud hardware architecture is poised to dominate the field of computing across application domains in the future. The general objective of this project is to minimize the power consumption of end devices by offloading their computation intensive workload on edge and cloud servers. Formulated as such, this problem has already received a lot of attention in the literature on mobile and edge computing. However, the originality of our work lies in the consideration of timing constraints associated with the workload: in building cooling systems for example, some of the software services such as real-time control are indeed time-sensitive which means they must be performed within predefined deadlines. This aspect has also been studied in a few research works, but most of them consider simplistic hypothesis when it comes to modelling timing interference among workload. The problem we propose to address is thus a resource allocation problem with the following objectives: (i) To minimize power consumption of end devices; (ii) To minimize the average response times of non time-sensitive workload; and (iii) To enforce end-to-end deadlines of time-sensitive workload with guarantees. As opposed to existing works, which study a subset of the infrastructure, we aim at a holistic approach considering (i) the wireless communication resources, (ii) the computation resources of edge and cloud servers and end devices, as well as (iii) the communication resources of the backhaul network. This problem is ambitious and will require finding a trade-off between optimality and reactivity: on the one hand, resource allocation problems are usually difficult to solve optimally because of their combinatorial complexity. On the other hand, service workload characteristics vary over time (notably because of mobility of devices), which means the resource allocation framework must run online together with the system in order to adapt resource allocations to these variations. In this project, we aim to address this complex resource allocation problem using a decentralized divide-to-conquer strategy. The infrastructure will be divided into segments depending on the architecture of the backhaul network, with each segment comprising a set of potentially different resources. title: Machine Learning Driven Query Optimizers for Big Database Systems
abs: Background: Query optimizers are vital for achieving good performance in database systems, and can speed up the execution time of queries by orders of magnitude. However, building a good query optimizer today takes huge amounts of efforts. Moreover, query optimizers need to be tediously maintained, especially as the system’s execution and storage engines evolve. As a matter of fact, the current database systems still have huge challenges in supporting querying on big data (e.g., telecom data), or a large number of queries posed to a database concurrently (e.g., on a promotion day for e-commerce service provider), despite the huge success of database systems on the market. The need of querying and managing big data and big queries, together with the success of machine learning techniques in other domains, motivate the database community to explore how machine learning can be used to improve query optimizers very recently. Most of the recent work typically focuses on optimizing one component of a query optimizer using machine learning techniques, such as join ordering, and shows that machine learning models can usually help to improve the performance of a specific component of the query optimizer. However, it is not clear whether the learned module can achieve a consistent or significant improvement on actual query performance. Aims: In this project, we aim to tackle the problem of bridging the area of deep learning with the area of querying big data. We aim at utilizing and developing deep learning models for query optimizers with the following specific aims: 1. Develop a benchmark to evaluate the effect of machine learning based selectivity estimation techniques on the end to end query processing time under representative query optimizers. 2. Develop new machine learning based selectivity estimation techniques for a wide type of SQL queries, such as queries involving continuous attributes. 3. Develop a new machine learning based algorithms for cost estimation of queries under an index configuration. 4. Develop new machine learning based algorithms for query optimizers, which return better query plans, based on the techniques developed in Objectives 2 and 3. 5. Build a system component on top of PostgreSQL with the learned query optimizer. Significance: The relational query optimization problem has been around for more than forty years and is one of the most studied problems in database management systems. Yet, query optimization is still an unsolved problem. This success of this project will bring the two areas (querying big data, and deep learning) together. This will not only result in new techniques to build big data management systems, but also open new research directions. The success of this project will advance these areas significantly. The outcome from this proposed research is highly relevant to industries, as it will improve the performance of tens of thousands of applications that use databases. title: Ricci curvature based deep learning model for polymer informatics
abs: Polymers, which have extraordinary diversity in their structural, physical, and chemical properties, are arguably the most important materials in modern times. The plastic industry, whose major task is to manufacture polymer materials, has a size of around 549.5 billion in 2020 globally. The ubiquity of polymers in our everyday life and technology is due to the reason that polymers are not only highly stable and non-toxic, but also easy and cheap to process and manufacture. However, the traditional Edisonian approach of trial-and-error for polymer discovery is not only expensive and time-consuming, but also extremely inefficient. The ever-increasing demand for new polymers to solve various challenges from climate change to future energy calls for innovative ways of polymer design and discovery. With the development of artificial intelligence (AI) techniques, advancement of computational power, and accumulation of polymer information, data-driven polymer informatics has enormous potential to fundamentally change the way of polymer discovery and design. Currently, one of the central challenges for AI-based polymer informatics is efficient polymer representations and descriptors. In this project, we propose, for the first time, persistent Ricci curvature (PRC) based molecular representations and their combination with machine learning models for polymer informatics. Discrete Ricci curvatures, including Olliver Ricci curvature and Forman Ricci curvature, are used for quantitative polymer structure characterization. Filtration-based multiscale topological representations, in particular, simplicial complexes, will be developed for polymer structures and interactions. PRC-based persistent attributes will be systematically calculated and further used as molecular descriptors. Further, we propose to systematically collect, consolidate, and pre-process polymer structural and experimental datasets. The accumulation of high-quality polymer data is essential to all learning models. Currently, various polymer databases are established, including PolyInfo, Polymer properties Database, Khazana, CAMPUS, etc. The polymer information will be gathered from these databases and further pre-processed together with private in-house datasets, and ab-initio calculations to establish a large databank for the training of our learning models. Moreover, PRC-based machine learning models and end-to-end deep learning models are proposed. PRC-based persistent attributes can be discretized and concatenated into a long vector, i.e., molecular fingerprint. The polymer fingerprint will be combined with machine learning models, in particular, random forest and gradient boosting tree, for polymer property prediction. We will also develop end-to-end deep learning models with PRC-based polymer 1D sequence and 2D image representations. title: Learning Latent Structure of High-Dimensional Data with Adversarial Training
abs: A key task of modern data scientists is to discover complex dependencies among variables present in large datasets. For example, one might ask how factors, such as genetic conditions, interact to cause childhood asthma? Graphical models use graphs to capture such dependencies probabilistically. Nodes index random variables, while edges represent statistical relationships. Such models have been studied extensively in applications including computer vision and gene regulatory networks. If the model is sparse, it provides a succinct visualization of the underlying dependencies. Another useful formalism to encode high-dimensional data is matrix factorization. Indeed, it has been well-recognized that large matrix-valued datasets can be well-approximated by low-rank ones because there is typically only a small number of latent or hidden phenomena governing the data. For example, there is usually a small set of topics present in a bag of documents. Another aspect of contemporary machine learning pertains to the fact that even the most sophisticated and well-trained models may be susceptible to and be fooled by well-crafted (but small) adversarial perturbations to the observations. This has become hazardous in high-stakes applications such as medical diagnoses and autonomous vehicles. However, it has also been well-recognized that if the learner is cognizant of the presence of adversarial corruptions and takes this into account in the learning process, the learned models will be more robust and can generalize better on test samples, improving the overall performance. This proposal lies at the intersection of statistical inference and adversarial training. These concepts have been studied in isolation in most works. We believe that studying them in unison has the potential to revolutionize the way we think about learning models with latent variables whilst being aware of adversarial actions. Preliminary numerical studies have shown promise and the project aims to advance the algorithms we have proposed from the theoretical perspective. Our specific aims are as follows. 1) Learning Latent Graphical Models with Adversarially Corrupted Observations In graphical model selection, we use a set of vector-valued samples to learn the structure of the graph that encodes the dependencies of a set variables. While this is a classical problem that has been extensively studied, the problem in which latent (hidden or confounding) variables exist in the model is significantly more challenging. Here, the underlying graph may be simple—for example, a tree—however, we may only have access to observations that are sampled from a subset of the variables and these observed variables in general admit a complicated graphical structure. Such models with latent models are extremely rich; in contrast models without latent variables have limited modelling power. title: Deep Generative Modeling of 3D Data
abs: Objects and scenes are essentially 3D data with delicate and hierarchical internal structures and parts. In this proposal we aim at answering the question: can we directly model the manifold of objects and scenes in the 3D space by designing novel generative models? To this end, we will devise different models for rigid 3D objects, non-rigid 3D objects and scenes, according to the characteristics of different objects. Specifically, we will investigate new models for generative modeling of rigid 3D objects such as tools and furniture. While their structures cannot deform in general, based on the developed models novel learning methods will be investigated to study the connections between object structures and object functionalities. We will design new models for generative modeling of non-rigid 3D objects such as human bodies and garments, where the models are capable of learning object deformations at different granularities. We will formulate new models for generative models of 3D scenes, that employ the compositionality of scenes to efficiently handle the variations of scene layouts as well as the variations of objects in the scenes. Unlike existing works that model objects and scenes in the 2D image domain, the proposed projects understand them directly in the 3D space, where structures and properties of objects and scenes are fully preserved, and undesired noises brought by the 3D-to-2D projections are avoided intrinsically. Through a series of new generative models that respectively focus on a specific category of 3D data, the proposed projects will significantly broaden the applicability of generative models. Issues encountered along our investigation may also challenge existing solutions from brand new angles and lead to breakthroughs in related fields like adversarial learning and probabilistic learning. In terms of 3Ddata processing, by modeling 3D data in a generative way, we move beyond analyzing the characteristics of different instances in isolation. In contrast, we are forced to treat a group of instances from an overall perspective, which may encourage important common patterns to emerge from instance-level variances. This will provide new tools and sparkles to advance the frontier of 3D data processing.

title: 3D Geometry and Semantic Modeling for Human-Scene Interaction
abs: Modeling 3D human-scene interaction has been a crucial technology in many digital media applications such as augmented/virtual reality, gaming, and computer animation. It requires computers to 1) accurately reconstruct the environment in 3D when only partial point clouds are given, 2) understand the semantics of each part in the complex 3D scene, and 3) generate meaningful, realistic interactions in the form of 3D humans. However, existing methods are often vulnerable to data variations, hence being unscalable in practice when deployed in different environments; lack informative supervision for learning semantic representations; and do not take into account the relation between people and scenes, which often leads to unrealistic generations that violate physical laws, such as a mesh interpenetration. In this work, we for the first time study 3D geometry and semantics jointly, aiming to solve the problem of 3D human-scene interaction. Specifically, three major contributions are made. 1) First, to address 3D partial point clouds registration for accurate reconstruction, we propose to learn transformation-invariant features from partial point clouds via hierarchical point graphs. 2) Second, to improve semantic inference to allow computers to make sense of the 3D world, we will leverage external knowledge graphs that encode rich information about the composition of objects and scenes to supervise the model learning. 3) Finally, 3D human generation will be achieved by a novel spatial-temporal reconstruction approach based on dynamic knowledge graphs to simultaneously reconstruct fine-grained garments and human bodies. Altogether, these three approaches lead to a comprehensive 3D human-scene interaction framework. Our work will not only advance 3D modeling and generation and bring new insights to the research community, but also benefit the wider public with improved experiences in human-computer interaction.

title: Technocratic Regionalism in Southeast Asia: The Translational Politics of Smart City Knowledge Transfer
abs: Specific aims This project seeks to understand the translational politics of smart city knowledge transfer, and how these politics implicate urban environments throughout Southeast Asia. We will explore the emergence of “technocratic regionalism” as a strategy through which power and inequality is (re)produced at both the macro (or regional and national) and micro (or local) scales. Technocratic regionalism refers to the technology-driven forms of regional integration and consolidation that are being implemented throughout the member states of ASEAN (the Association of Southeast Asian Nations). The ASEAN Smart Cities Network (ASCN) is the political framework through which technocratic regionalism is implemented. It is being used to spur urban development through the rollout of smart city plans, policies, and projects throughout Southeast Asian cities. Specific aims are to consider how smart city initiatives can lead to: 1. Vertical and horizontal (non-)integration 2. Divergent infrastructural developments 3. The emergence of (in)formal spaces of the smart city By addressing these aims, this project will be multi-scalar, and will interrogate the effects of knowledge transfer at the regional, national, and local levels. In addition, it will explore the processes of negotiation that exist at every point at which the “smart” or the “new” intersects with the “material” or the “old”, and will therefore seek to illustrate the translational politics of smart city knowledge transfer. Research questions The following research questions fall within each specific aim: 1. Vertical and horizontal (non-)integration • At the regional level, how are smart city policies formed, transferred and applied between members of the ASCN? • At the national level, how do national, regional (i.e. sub-national) and local governments reinforce and challenge each other vertically (i.e. up and down different scales of power and implementation) and horizontally (i.e. across different departments, ministries, stakeholders) when implementing smart city projects? • At both the regional and national levels, how does the private sector (or the government-linked, or quasi-private sector) help to shape, influence, or otherwise enable smart city knowledge transfer? 2. Divergent infrastructural developments • At the national and local levels, how are smart city policies prioritised within the urban “policy mix”? • At the local level, how are smart city projects designed to integrate (or not) with pre-existing urban infrastructures? 3. The emergence of (in)formal spaces of the smart city • At the local level, how can smart city projects be seen to “formalise” the city, and how can formalisation paradoxically lead to the emergence of new spaces and economies of informality? • At the local level, how do different social groups benefit (or not) from smart city projects, and may these effects lead to new forms of social stratification and organisation? title: Noble Metal-Based Oxygen Electrocatalysts For Sustainable Energy Conversion
abs: Oxygen (O2) electrochemistry is a description of the electrocatalytic reduction and evolution of molecular oxygen, which has been intensively studied because of its fundamental complexity and importance in many practical technologies and industrial processes. However, due to the sluggish reaction kinetics and poor durability under harsh operating environments, it is highly imperative to develop highly active and stable oxygen electrocatalysts with new structures and compositions to enhance the energy conversion efficiency in practical technologies, such as water splitting, metal-air batteries, fuel cells, and other industrial applications. Currently, the state-of-the-art noble metal platinum (Pt) and iridium/ruthenium oxides (IrO2/RuO2) are widely recognized as the benchmark electrocatalysts for the ORR and OER, respectively, but their scarcity and high cost have impeded their large-scale commercial applications. Although extensive efforts have been devoted to developing alternative noble-metal-free ORR/OER electrocatalysts, their synthetic methods are complex and time-consuming, and the obtained activity and durability are still insufficient to meet the standards for practical applications. Besides, due to the thermodynamic instability of transition metals in acidic media, noble metal compounds have been primarily utilized as electrocatalysts in water splitting and reversible fuel cells. Therefore, reducing the noble metal usage while maintaining or even improving the catalytic performance is an important cost reduction and utilization enhancement lever. Potential approaches to improving the oxygen electrocatalytic performance of noble metal-based electrocatalysts include: 1) developing external field-assisted rapid synthetic strategies for noble metal oxides, alloys, and their composites with low loading but high utilization efficiency; 2) designing and synthesizing metal-organic framework (MOF)-derived functional supports with high surface area and abundant anchor sites for a better loading/dispersion/stabilization of noble metal-based nanocrystals; 3) optimizing and developing high-efficiency loading methods of noble metal-based nanomaterials for easy manipulation of catalyst-support interactions, achieving the high catalytic activity and durability of composite oxygen electrocatalysts; 4) engineering surface and interface of noble metal-based electrocatalysts towards highly efficient oxygen electrocatalysis in practical energy conversion technologies; 5) clarifying the cooperative catalytic mechanism and the long-term stable operation mechanism of the catalytic sites under working conditions based on the advanced in-situ techniques along with theoretical calculations, and deepen the understanding of the limit dosage of noble metal, and screen novel noble metal-based oxygen electrocatalysts. title: Examining the impact of communication media on the outcome of negotiation
abs: Since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, online video-conferencing – notably the Zoom platform – has assumed unprecedented significance, prompting great interest in the impact of videoconferencing and other communication media on the negotiation outcome. Earlier studies examining this issue have largely focused on comparing face-to-face communication with text messages, e-mail and phone calls. Comparatively less attention has been paid to video and audio, despite their increasing relevance in negotiation. There has also been limited exploration of the boundary conditions that moderate the impact of communication media on negotiation outcomes, such as the individual’s conflict management style and personality type. This study seeks to address these gaps through examining the impact of four communication modes – Zoom videoconferencing, Zoom audio call, WhatsApp text messaging, and face-to-face interaction – on the negotiation outcome. The experiment involves 200 dyads randomly allocated to one of 4 communication modes and required to negotiate according to the instructions of a negotiation simulation. Negotiation outcomes will be measured holistically in terms of value creation in the economic outcome, process outcomes such as trust, rapport and accurate understanding of the other party, and procedural justice. In addition, the study explores the potential moderating effects of five negotiator traits – conflict resolution style, communication style, familiarity with the relevant media, self-interest orientation and personality type – on the media effects on negotiation. The study’s findings will cast light on the impact that different media have on diverse aspects of negotiation. In addition, this will be the first such research project conducted within Singapore, which serves as a microcosm of other multi-ethic societies in Asia. This research is also timely as general preferences towards communication media could have evolved considerably in the wake of the unprecedented reliance on video-conferencing and development of new technology and media. This study is meant to be stage one of a three-part research endeavour that explores multiple facets of the interaction effects between communication modes and negotiation outcomes. While this preliminary research focuses on the moderating impact of negotiator traits, research in stage 2 will investigate other moderating variables that are common to commercial and legal negotiations, including time limitation in negotiation, the use of multiple negotiation sessions, and the nature of the prior relationship between negotiators. Stage 3 will explore the impact of using a combination or sequence of communication modes, such as using text messaging followed by video-conferencing.

title: Understanding China's Agricultural Modernization and Rural Development
abs: Origin: When we began researching agriculture change in China in 2007, we noticed a revolution quietly unfolding: agribusinesses were entering the countryside and beginning to organize agricultural production in a variety of novel ways, while the smallholding family farmers were interacting with agro-capital in different ways and transforming themselves into new social actors from doing so. In our pioneering study, we conceptualized this change as the “rise of agrarian capitalism,” and contemplated whether this marked the “beginning of the end” of the Chinese peasantry. Since then, this revolution has greatly accelerated. In the past decade, in particular, national statistics and academic research have been reporting new trends that appear to represent a radical departure from our earlier findings. For example, in 2009, 64.6 million rural families operated small pig farms, and another 49 million raised broiler or layer chickens. By 2017, the size of these two populations has declined by 45% and 40%, respectively: only 35.7 million small pig farmers and 29.5 million small chicken farmers are left, a total decrease of 48.4 million households. Not coincidentally, agribusinesses of the most massive scale (producing more than 50,000 heads of pigs annually) quadrupled in number over a similar period. Aims and questions: If what puzzles researchers in other developing countries in Asia is the continued persistence of smallholders, in China now, what researchers must answer are questions about the rapid disappearance of smallholders: Who replaced them, and how did they acquire the capital and scale up their operations? What happened to the displaced smallholders? How are the remaining smallholders dealing with increasing competition from large producers and interacting with the latter? This project has two main research aims. First, we intend to discover the newest trends in China’s agricultural change, analyzing their dynamics and effect. Second, and more importantly, we aim to investigate a range of theoretical questions made salient by developments in the past decade and that have emerged in recent scholarly debates. For this, we will focus on the three classes of actors at the center of this massive transformation—the expanding agrarian capitalist class, the laboring classes now relying on wage jobs, and the class of smallholding family farmers—and organize the inquiry around four thematic issues that are significant to social science theories: accumulation and dispossession, class relations, the role of the state, and institutional change. With this framework, we derive nine clusters of research questions to guide our investigation. Gaps: Four different academic camps have emerged in the study of China’s agricultural change, each adopting incompatible positions regarding the fate of smallholders, as well as differing assessments of the nature of that change: agricultural modernization, trapped transition, neo-populism, and agrarian capitalism. title: Automated Program Repair
abs: Software systems are amenable to change, and the process of software construction is error-prone. As a result, debugging and fixing of errors in any complex software project takes up significant time, manpower and investment. Today, a common way to produce correct software for critical software systems is via formal methods, where the intended behavior of the software is explicitly captured as a formal specification and the correctness is accomplished via a formal proof. This requires a workflow completely outside the normal software construction workflow used in the industry, requires the writing of formal specifications, is often not scalable to very large software projects, and is typically not sustainable due to the formal proof being invalidated by future changes in the software. The vision of our research program is to retain the workflows of software construction as they exist today in the form of Continuous Integration (CI) systems, and yet support correct software evolution. In today's Continuous Integration systems used in companies, a developer will make changes to a code base and will seek to deposit them in the form of code-base commits. Even though the developer typically conducts unit testing prior to submitting the commits, the commits may fail system level tests when submitted. The developer is then tasked with manually fixing the errors so that at least all given tests pass, by informally following a "chain" of reasoning starting from an observable test failure. Our goal in the proposed research program is to retain this software development workflow and yet alleviate the developer burden by automating trustworthy program repairs. The main research challenge is to make sure that the repair constructed automatically can be trustworthy, and works for usage scenarios outside of those foreseen by the supplied tests. We note that trust in automated program repair involves various issues including whether the patch is overfitting, the origin or provenance of the patches, absence of new errors, and so on. We plan to investigate these issues in our research program. Since, in general, we do not want to demand formal specifications from the programmer, we will strive to infer adequate specifications to drive the program repair process towards correctness, and integrate such specifications into repair technologies embedded inside Continuous Integration systems. Specifications may be inferred from program artifacts such as static analysis summaries, failed proofs and automatically generated (not manually-provided) tests via a systematic test generation method. Repairs thus generated come with partial or full evidence of their correctness. We will explore forward-looking applications of program repair such as enhancing trust in automatically generated code, automated transplantation of patches from one program version to another, as well as intelligent tutoring for teaching of programming at NUS.

title:
Channel Coding and Signal Processing for Emerging Non-Volatile Memory
for Future Data Storage and Computing
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: In recent years, the solid-state non-volatile memory (NVM) technologies have been developed rapidly which offer lower power consumption, faster read access time, and better mechanical reliability than the hard disk drives, and non-volatile data retention over the volatile memories such as the dynamic random access memory (DRAM) and static random access memory (SRAM). Among the various emerging NVM technology candidates, the resistive random access memory (ReRAM) has significant advantages such as simple structure, nanosecond speed, excellent scalability, long data retention, and compatibility with the current CMOS technology. It is widely believed to be able to provide a competitive solution across all the layers along the memory hierarchy- used as on-chip caches; serving as memory replacement for big data analytics and in-memory databases; adopted in massive storage devices, and so on. Furthermore, it also demonstrates great potential for neuromorphic computing. Despite its great potential for both future data storage and computing, currently, the reliability of ReRAM is severely affected by several critical factors. These factors mainly include the random variations of the switching voltages and cell resistances, the sneak path interference (SPI) occurred in the ReRAM crossbar array, and the channel offset caused by the read disturb and change of operating temperature. The above issues will affect not only the reliability of data storage, but also the accuracy of neuromorphic computing. In particular, the sneak path problem is a major problem for all the resistive crossbar arrays which serve as a key design of the next-generation memory architecture. The detection and correction of errors occurred in neuromorphic computing lead to a completely new problem in the history of error correction coding. Channel coding and signal processing have played a critical role for mitigating different types of noise and interference and ensure fast and reliable data recovery for various data storage systems. However, up till now, the research on channel coding and signal processing for ReRAM is very limited and insufficient, and it remains a very challenging problem for the research community worldwide. Therefore, the objective of the proposed research is to design and analyze novel and efficient channel coding and signal processing algorithms and techniques to effectively improve the reliability of ReRAM and support its applications for future data storage and computing. title: Elucidating the Molecular Function of GPR146 in Regulating Nonalcoholic Steatohepatitis
abs: Nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) is a more serious form of nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) that is under global prevalence, and it is one of the most important causes of liver disease worldwide. NASH is a chronic inflammatory liver disease caused by excessive accumulation of fat in hepatocytes. It can slowly progress to hepatic fibrosis, cirrhosis and even hepatocellular carcinoma, which causes large burden to public healthcare. Therapeutic development in NASH has been demonstrated as a difficult task. Numerous therapeutic strategies targeting different pathological processes of NASH, such as fat accumulation, inflammation and fibrosis, are currently in clinical testing, yet there are no approved therapies. This highlights the urgent need to gain deeper understanding of pathogenesis of NASH for the future development of new therapies. Many lines of evidence collected from my previously published work, ranging from human genetic analysis to experimental models, have unequivocally established an important role of orphan G protein-coupled receptor 146 (GPR146) in regulation of hypercholesterolemia and atherosclerosis. In addition to its function in regulating cardiovascular traits, our preliminary studies in the current proposal showed that GPR146-deficient mice were resistant to high-fat diet induced obesity and fat accumulation in the liver. Moreover, the level of circulating liver enzyme alanine aminotransferase (ALT) was significantly reduced in the mice lacking GPR146 compared to control littermates. Consistent with mouse phenotypes, our human genetic analysis in UK Biobank( 300,000 individuals) showed that lower expression of GPR146 is associated with decreased levels of circulating liver enzymes (alanine aminotransferase, alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyltransferase), and verse versa. These data together suggest that GPR146 might regulate NASH in both human and mouse. Deorphanization of GPR146 through identifying its endogenous ligands is one of the most important missions in GPR146 study as it will uncover novel biology regulating systemic lipid metabolism as well as providing the natural agonists for future screening of antagonists inhibiting GPR146 activity. The approach that uses GPR146 as bait to identify its ligands requires the establishment of two technologies: (1) monitoring GPR146 activity through a cell-based high throughput assay and (2) preparing tissue extracts with active endogenous ligands. title: Generation of Heterogeneous Tumor-Associated Macrophages Using Engineered Tumor Niches
abs: Tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) are a major constituent of solid tumors and contribute to tumor progression and drug resistance. The functional significance of TAMs in the tumor microenvironment (TME) makes them highly attractive targets for cancer therapy. However, broadly targeting TAMs through reprograming or elimination is now challenging as recent single-cell analyses of various cancers have unveiled the presence of a spectrum of different TAM subpopulations with unique transcriptomic profiles, spatial distribution and possibly diverse functions in the TME. Accordingly, there is a need to greatly increase our limited understanding of TAM phenotypes to more precisely target TAM subpopulations with pro-tumoral functions while maintaining those with anti-tumoral roles in the TME. However, present studies still rely on in vitro protocols that leverage cytokine cocktails or 2D cancer cell-conditioned media to differentiate monocytes and generate TAMs, highlighting that the simplified binary M1/M2 macrophage polarization paradigm arises from how little we understand of polarization cues in the TME and how grossly we are underestimating the inherent heterogeneity of TAMs in patient tumors. This underscores the need for improved approaches to generate TAM subpopulations found in vivo to increase the specificity of TAM-targeting strategies for both drug development and personalized drug testing. Paralleling recent studies, our own preliminary single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq) data of head and neck squamous cell carcinomas (HNSCC) have also revealed several TAM subpopulations with distinct transcriptomic profiles. Additionally, several murine studies have now confirmed the ability of different tumor niches to differentially regulate the phenotype of TAMs. By leveraging engineered hydrogels to recapitulate HNSCC tumor niches in vitro and using patient-derived HNSCC organoids, matched cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), and endothelial cells, we propose to investigate the following hypotheses: 1. Distinct TAM subpopulations exist in HNSCC tumors with unique gene signatures, spatial distribution and functions in the TME. 2. TAM subpopulations can be recapitulated in vitro by using engineered niches of the TME (representing the tumor nest, tumor stroma, perivascular niche and areas of cancer cell invasion) to EDUCATE co-cultured peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC)-derived monocytes; these niche-educated TAM subpopulations would better recapitulate the molecular profile of TAM subsets in patient tumors compared to conventional methods used to obtain TAMs in vitro, and exhibit different functions. 3. Different TAM subpopulations would respond differently to TAM-targeting drugs and targeting specific TAM subpopulations in combination with immune checkpoint inhibitors would result in enhanced cancer cell kill. title: Identifying novel targets and designing new anti-TB agents through understanding the Mycobacterial stringent response to stress
abs: The stringent response in Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) is mediated by the so-called Rel protein (MtRel), an GTP pyrophosphokinase which works as a bifunctional (p)ppGpp synthetase/hydrolase. During amino acid starvation MtRel senses a drop in amino acid concentration and synthesizes the messengers pppGpp and ppGpp, collectively referred to as (p)ppGpp. Synthesis of (p)ppGpp changes bacterial physiology, including down-regulation of rRNA synthesis, affecting poly-phosphate metabolism, gene regulation, purine metabolism, up-regulation of protein degradation and amino acid biosynthesis, as well as shifting the bacteria to a non-replicating state. Deficiency of MtRel blocks the pathogen from entering into quiescence, affects persistence of infection and reduces antibiotic tolerance. The multi-domain MtRel (738 residues) harbors the catalytic domains with opposing activities for the hydrolysis and synthesis of (p)ppGpp in its N-terminal domain (NTD; residues 1-394). While the NTD contains the catalytic domains, the C-terminal domain (CTD) represents the regulatory elements, including the TGS-, AH-, RIS- and ACT domain. The TGS domain is proposed to be crucial for (p)ppGpp’s synthesis regulation and it has been predicted that activation of the synthetase domain occurs via an TGS-deacylated tRNA bound form. In contrast, the ACT is predicted to regulate the hydrolysis-ON state in conjunction with specific valine-binding. In solution, MtRel is discussed to be in a steady-state of monomer- and dimer formation, which may alter in the presence of nucleotides, uncharged tRNA and branched amino acids (BCAAs). Besides the oligomer equilibrium the enzyme forms a ribosome-tRNA-Rel complex during amino acid starvation leading to (p)ppGpp synthesis and increased amino acid biosynthesis. We resolved the first atomic structures of the MtRel NTD, -TGS- and ACT domains. Most recently, we unravelled the specific binding of valine to the ACT domain and revealed that uncharged tRNA binds to the TGS domain even in the absence of the translation machinery, and identified the tRNA binding-epitope in the MtRel TGS. Production and purification of an MtRel NTD construct and the entire MtRel formed the platform for successful crystallization of both proteins. In addition, a protocol to isolate a mycobacterial ribosome complex and to generate an active ribosome-tRNA-MtRel ensemble provided first electron micrographs. title: Interplay of RNA editing and oxygen-sensing mechanism on Filamin A function
abs: In Singapore ischemic heart diseases and hypertensive diseases are two of the top three prevalent cardiovascular diseases that account for 23.4% of total deaths in 2020. In addition to surgical intervention, there remains no available pharmacological treatment option, especially for myocardial infarction. The CaV1.2 calcium channel, a major pathway for Ca2+ influx in both smooth and cardiac muscles, has been considered an important therapeutic target since the 1980s for common hypertension. However, calcium channel blockers have not been successfully used to treat pulmonary hypertension and ischemic heart diseases due to the incomplete understanding of the roles of CaV1.2 in heart failure. Recently, we identified Filamin A, a dimeric actin crosslinking protein, as a novel CaV1.2-binding protein partner. We showed that Filamin A interacted with the I-II loop of CaV1.2 channel and increased the current density of CaV1.2 channel through an unknown mechanism. We have additional data to show that Filamin A is significantly up-regulated in left ventricles of pig and non-human primate models of cardiac diseases. These results suggest that Filamin A may contribute to the pathogenesis of cardiovascular diseases via modulating CaV1.2 channel function. Intriguingly, Filamin A is sensitive to ADAR2-catalyzed RNA editing and the oxygen sensor PHD2-mediated proteasomal degradation. Our preliminary data showed that, compared to wild-type Filamin A, edited Filamin A (Filamin A-Q2341R) had lower binding affinity to CaV1.2 channels, and was degraded more by PHD2 in transfected HEK 293FT cells. These results indicate that Q2341R substitution may inhibit the binding of Filamin A to CaV1.2 or PHD2, and interfering with the editing level of Filamin A may provide a promising therapeutic approach for cardiovascular diseases via regulating CaV1.2 channels. In addition, Filamin A binds to dopamine D2 receptor (D2R) and increases the trafficking of D2R to cell surface, thus, we predict that Filamin A scaffolds D2R to be adjacent to CaV1.2 channels to up-regulate CaV1.2 channel function, as dopamine has been shown to increase action potential duration in pig cardiomyocytes. The Filamin A-D2R axis may be a novel molecular mechanism underlying Filamin A-mediated CaV1.2 up-regulation. title: Platform Technology for Bacterial Surface Modification and Rapid Detection of Antimicrobial-Resistant Bacteria
abs: We propose to develop metabolic labeling-mediated controlled radical polymerization on living bacteria as a platform technology to realize 1) ultrasensitive detection of multidrug-resistant bacteria within 4 h and 2) flexible modulation of surface properties of living bacteria and hence associated biological activities. With the rapid emergence of antimicrobial-resistant (AMR) bacteria, the slow turnaround of cultivation-based antimicrobial susceptibility testing has become a major barrier in managing bacterial infection and effectively containing the spread of resistance. Early detection of resistant bacteria and rapid identification of effective antibiotics hold the key to improve patient care and reduce the overall healthcare cost. On the other hand, it is essential to tailor the surface properties of engineered bacteria that have found widespread uses in emerging applications such as human microbiome engineering and microbial production of bioactive nature products and biologics. Our proposed strategy is fundamentally based on two key technologies that we have developed recently: antimicrobial susceptibility-dependent metabolic labeling of bacteria and surface-initiated photoinduced electron transfer-reversible addition-fragmentation chain-transfer (PET-RAFT) polymerization on living bacteria. We will take advantage of metabolic labeling to selectively install click chemistry handles into peptidoglycan and lipopolysaccharides of Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, respectively. PET-RAFT allows for rapid, controlled polymerization of monomers of diverse chemical characteristics under light-regulated biocompatible conditions. Therefore, subsequent introduction of chain transfer agents on bacterial surfaces via click reactions provides the opportunities to graft polymers of tailored functionalities and chain architectures on metabolically labeled bacteria, offering the possibility of tailoring their surface physiochemical properties and tolerance of external stress. Based on the systematic evaluation of polymerization kinetics and the contributing factors for controlled synthesis of functional polymers of different chain architectures on living bacteria, we will investigate the impact of polymer modification on surface properties, viability, growth characteristics, metabolic status, and genetic responses of different bacteria of interest, and explore the use of polymer modification to improve the bacterial tolerance of external stress, such as low pH. Of particular interest for the rapid detection of AMR-bacteria, we have found that metabolic labeling in presence of bactericidal concentrations of antibiotics for susceptible strains results in favorable labeling of AMR-bacteria that are metabolically active and undergo continuous growth, in contrast to drug-susceptible strains that are inhibited or killed by the antibiotics. title: Unraveling the impacts of environmental change and restoration initiatives on biodiversity and species interactions in Southeast Asian ecosystems
abs: Human-modified habitats, from secondary forests and oil palm plantations to cities, are now dominating tropical landscapes, causing changes to biodiversity, and impacting ecosystem services. Restoration initiatives, such as tree planting and green corridors, are a key component in helping to reverse biodiversity declines and maintain functioning ecosystems. The impacts of environmental change on invertebrates in tropical systems is still relatively unknown, despite their huge importance for ecosystem functioning and provision of key ecosystem services, such as pollination and nutrient recycling. This is particularly true in Southeast Asia where there is a huge data gap in our knowledge of the taxonomy, natural history, distributions, and traits of many important invertebrate groups. This project will address how environmental change and restoration initiatives impact invertebrate biodiversity and interactions, providing a solid scientific evidence-base on which to inform future conservation planning. Through combining field surveys and experiments with cutting-edge population genomic approaches, predictive modelling, and conservation prioritization techniques, we will examine the drivers and impacts of environmental change and restoration initiatives for invertebrates in the region. We first aim to address the data gap on invertebrates by building distribution, DNA barcode, and trait databases alongside identification guides, and checklists for two key invertebrate groups: dung beetles and soil arthropods. Alongside this we will investigate the interactions between invertebrates and mammals, plants, fungi, and microbes, and how changes in species composition can cascade through ecosystems of linked species, ultimately affecting ecosystem functioning. Finally, through using state-of-the-art population genomics we will instigate the importance of landscape connectivity and green corridors for insect movement, gene flow, species divergence, and population structure across fragmented landscapes. This project will underpin our future capacity to monitor several key invertebrate groups and help to inform effective habitat management and restoration in Southeast Asia, while providing a fundamental understanding of the processes and mechanisms underlying species responses to environmental change.

title:
REBOT
Rethinking underwater robot manipulation
abs: Despite the helpfulness of underwater robotics in many different industrial and scientific fields, underwater robot manipulation is still a minor sector in this field. The typical approach used for underwater manipulation is based on the installation of a robot arm on an underwater vehicle, treated in a similar way as it is done outside of water. However, movement efficiency in water is profoundly different, for the effect of water drag, reduced gravity, perturbations, high pressure, and many more environmental factors. In this project, we aim at proposing more efficient and effective movement strategies for underwater robot manipulation. We propose a bioinspired approach where we can learn unusual movement strategies from marine species. We focus on Octopus vulgaris, a mollusc with remarkable manipulation abilities. This animal uses its soft body and the water action on it to obtain effective and energetically efficient movements. Its typical reaching movement consists of a bending wave that propagates from the base to the tip of the arm. The bending is pronounced and the arm is sort of folded in two parallel segments. The propagation of the bending point unfolds the arm till its final position. This is the most efficient extension movement in water, as it minimizes water resistance. What we consider most important in the bioinspired approach is the transformation of observed principles into mathematical models. For this reason, this project is focused on obtaining a full mathematical insight of the octopus arm reaching movement, especially focused on the fluid dynamics involved. We will develop a model of the octopus arm and couple it with the fluid dynamic one. We can then demonstrate the efficiency of the octopus arm movements, qualitatively and quantitatively. Based on this model, and capitalizing on the PI’s experience in soft robotics technologies and the expertise in materials in the team, we will build a robot arm that can implement a reaching movement similar to the octopus one, i.e. based on a bending wave. In this way, we can ultimately demonstrate experimentally, with the models and with the robot, in simulation and in water, that and to what extent the octopus strategies are more efficient in water. The results we aim at can bring a revolutionary impact on underwater robotics. Efficient and effective grasping movements can increase significantly the current limited use of underwater robots in manipulation tasks. Efficient movements reduce energy requirements also contributing to a wider underwater robot adoption. Possible applications span from off-shore industry to biology and oceanography. title: Towards an intelligent, data-driven strategy for hydrodynamic manipulation of particles in microfluidics
abs: Microfluidics is a technique initially developed to control a low volume of fluid constrained in a small-scale (typically sub-millimeter) chamber. Its capacity for precisely manipulating fluids makes it an increasingly prevalent facilitator for applications in different fields ranging from engineering, physics, chemistry, biology, to nanotechnology. This expansion into various domains has imparted the multi-physical merit to microfluidics: encompassing the physics of soft matter (e.g., droplets, biological cells) in complex fluids (e.g., polymeric fluids with nonlinear rheology) and the use of diverse external fields (e.g., electrical, magnetic, optical or acoustic) for flow and particle control. Nevertheless, the sheer amount of knowledge required in different physics branches renders a systematic design approach intractable, aggravated by the growing complexity of microfluidic applications. To rise to the challenge, this proposal conceives a novel approach to design a data-driven, intelligent, automated microfluidic chip that learns complex physics from the data—historical operations and the resulting fluid motion, and then evolves optimal strategies informed by the assimilated physical rules. Hydrodynamic manipulation of particles is a non-perturbative method that steers the particle in microfluidics by hydrodynamic forces alone. It possesses several advantages over other perturbative methods. Prior hydrodynamic manipulations have been limited to idealised setups owing to their critical reliance on a physical model that predicts the particle motion, which is however unavailable in generic setups. We will remove this limitation by substituting an artificial neural network (ANN) as a data-driven approximate model for the hard-to-attain physical counterpart based on the historical microfluidic operations and the associated particle motions. This data-driven approximation combined with advanced controllers will enable automated particle manipulations in a general microfluidic setting. Our preliminary results using this approach have indeed achieved effective control of three particles' trajectories without any prior knowledge of hydrodynamics. By interfacing the ANN-integrated controller with microfluidic experiments, we will tackle several tasks of automated particle manipulation traditionally unattainable for the inability to capture the physical ingredients. The proposed AI-powered control strategy has never been adopted in prior microfluidic research to the best of our knowledge. By opening transformative avenues of automated microfluidic operations, our research outcome will facilitate the development of intelligent microfluidic devices for manipulating various particulate samples such as cells, droplets/bubbles, and vesicles. Versatile manipulations of these samples will largely improve the performance of diagnostics, biological and chemical analysis extensively demanded in biomedical, pharmaceutical, and food sciences. title: Understanding the Transmission Risks of SARS-CoV-2 and the Fundamental Rethinking of HVAC System Design in the Post-Pandemic World
abs: COVID-19 is a newly emerged viral respiratory disease first reported in Wuhan, China, in December 2019. It is caused by the severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), which belongs to the same family as SARS-CoV and MERS-CoV that are responsible for the SARS and MERS outbreaks in the last two decades. While the fatality rate of SARS-CoV-2 is significantly lower, it is highly contagious and still spreading relatively uncontrolled in some countries. One key reason is the occurrence of asymptomatic cases, who show indistinguishable viral load compared to those who are symptomatic. The rapid rise of the Delta variant (B16172) is another major concern that shows 100- to 1000-fold higher viral load than the original version of the virus, and it has now become the dominant strain globally. In essence, the current engineering control measures that are used to mitigate the transmission risks, such as face-covering, social distancing, and increased air ventilation rate still appear to be an ongoing experiment without compelling scientific evidence. The research questions that we propose to address in the state-of-knowledge of SARS-CoV-2 transmission routes and their relative contributions to the infection risks in both hospital and non-hospital environments, and to propose and evaluate the effectiveness of different air-conditioning and mechanical ventilation (ACMV) design strategies that can be potentially incorporated in the post-pandemic building designs to mitigate any future airborne viral outbreaks. Some fundamental questions that we aim to examine include: (1) How do the various expiratory processes and viral load of an infected person influence the virion concentration and transmission, and subsequently the infection risks?; (2) How do we fundamentally obtain and quantify the impacts of air ventilation strategies, room layouts, ambient environment, face-covering, and the passive engineering control measures on the droplets’ dispersion and deposition patterns, and their effectiveness in interdicting the transmission pathways?; and (3) How can we safely and effectively deploy UVGI technology for airborne viral disinfection in air-conditioning and mechanical ventilated spaces? To answer these questions, in Work Package 1, CFD simulations will be carried out using ANSYS Fluent software to accurately predict the virus-laden respiratory droplets’ emission by an infected individual via breathing, talking, singing, coughing, or sneezing, with consideration to the flow dynamics of the respiratory processes and viral load. The contrasting effects of natural or forced ventilation, ambient air temperature and humidity, room layouts, face covering, and engineering control measures such as physical barriers, partitions, and redesign of furniture layout on the droplets’ evaporation, dispersion, and deposition processes will be investigated. title: Integrated Control Algorithm for Autonomous Spacecraft Formation Flying
abs: Spacecraft formations, flying in tight configurations have the capability of enabling a wide range of new applications. Nevertheless, controlling the movement of spacecraft in formation poses difficulties, such as in-orbit high-computing demand and collision avoidance capabilities. These challenges escalate as the number of units in the formation is increased, complicated nonlinear effects are imposed to the dynamics, and uncertainty which may arise from the lack of knowledge of system parameters are considered. The objective of this project is, therefore, to develop new control methods to allow spacecraft in formation, with circular/elliptical reference orbits, to efficiently execute safe autonomous manoeuvres, and embed them into the control and propulsion systems of the satellites. The controllers that will be investigated will merge guidance laws and collision avoidance capacities into a single control strategy: linear optimal regulation, linear optimal estimation, and adaptive nonlinear control. In general terms, the proposed control approaches command the dynamical performance of one or several followers with respect to a leader to asymptotically track a time-varying nominal trajectory, while the threat of collision between the followers is removed by repelling accelerations obtained from the collision avoidance scheme during the periods of closest proximity. To evaluate the design of the controllers, test cases based on the physical and orbital features of existing cubesatellite missions will be implemented, extending the number of elements in the formation into scenarios with reconfigurations and on-orbit position switching in elliptical low-Earth reference orbits. The controllers will then be integrated into the attitude, orbit and propulsion system to allow for autonomous on-board operations.

title: Visualizing and interrogating secretory transport within the Golgi
abs: The Golgi complex plays a central role in eukaryotic protein glycosylation and intracellular protein trafficking. The structure of the mammalian Golgi is complex; it contains multiple stacks of flattened membrane sacs called cisternae. Each stack can be further divided into four regions, the cis-, medial- and trans-Golgi regions and the trans-Golgi network. Newly synthesized proteins enter the Golgi stack at its cis-region, transit the medial region, and exit at the trans side of the Golgi stack. It is not fully understood how proteins are transported through the multiple Golgi cisternae and how the intra-Golgi transport works; indeed proposed mechanisms remain highly controversial and under heated debate. Imaging intra-Golgi transport using light microscopy is extremely challenging and a tool that enables such imaging is highly sought-after. In this proposal, we will first develop such an imaging method and subsequently apply it to investigate trafficking within the Golgi stack. The proposal has two aims. The first aim is to develop an imaging tool that uses light microscopy to visualize intra-Golgi secretory trafficking (Aim 1). The tool will semi-automatically align, resize, and average multiple super-resolution images of the Golgi ministack that are taken from the side-view. Averaging is introduced to effectively suppress the noise in the image caused by random morphological features. Our tool is expected to not only produce images with a sub-Golgi cisternal resolution but also generate numerical localization data with an accuracy comparable to that of immuno-electron microscopy. With the aid of this new tool and our previously developed imaging tools, our second aim is to understand the dynamics of secretory trafficking within the Golgi (Aim2). We have confidence that the following three challenging questions regarding secretory intra-Golgi transport can be addressed. 1) How are protein and lipid cargos transported within the Golgi (Sub-aim 2.1)? 2) How are cargos sorted within the Golgi (Sub-aim 2.2)? 3) How are membrane carriers assembled at the trans-Golgi to deliver cargos to the plasma membrane (Sub-aim 2.3)? The proposed research is backed by sufficient preliminary data and will be carried out by a team of researchers who are very experienced in Golgi research. Therefore, the risk of the proposal is low. The successful completion of our proposal will make light microscopy the instrument of choice for imaging the Golgi and open new research avenues for Golgi research. We will gain further molecular and cellular insights into intra-Golgi secretory transport (Sub-aim 2.1), sorting (Sub-aim 2.2) and the biogenesis of exocytic carriers (Sub-aim 2.3) within the Golgi. Most importantly, our study will provide experimental evidence that is crucial for evaluating and assessing the three proposed models of Golgi transport — cisternal maturation, stable compartment, and rapid partitioning models — which are currently hotly debated in the Golgi fi

title: The mechanism of a small GTPase Rab2B in Trypanosoma brucei cellular differentiation
abs: Cellular differentiation involves activation/inactivation of various signaling pathways and remodeling of transcriptional, translational and metabolic activities, and is important for the life cycle and development of all living organisms. While cellular differentiation is mostly studied and best understood in multi-cellular models during development, single-cellular eukaryotic organisms also undergo cellular differentiation, and exhibit significant differences to higher eukaryotes in the signaling pathways and regulatory network involved. A deeper understanding of the differentiation pathways in single-cellular organisms, particularly those responsible for important human and animal diseases, can also provide insight to the pathogenesis, the transmission and eventually the control of these pathogens. Trypanosoma brucei subspecies are the causative agents for African Sleeping Sickness in humans and nagana in cattle. Its life cycle alternates between mammalian hosts and tsetse fly vectors, with the parasites taking on different forms in adaptation to different environmental niches (Fig.1). Within this complex life cycle, the slender-to-stumpy differentiation step that occurs in mammal blood is of particular interest, and has been researched extensively as a main point of therapeutic intervention to control these deadly parasites [1]. At least three pathways have been found to induce slender-to-stumpy differentiation (Fig.1). The best characterized is the stumpy inducing factor (SIF)-induced stumpy formation through a quorum sensing mechanism [2]. Activation of T. brucei adenosine monophosphate kinase (TbAMPK) via AMP analogs or oxidative stress also induce stumpy formation, possibly via concomitant inhibition of an unconventional Target of Rapamycin homolog, TbTOR4 [3, 4]. Recent studies on the expression of variant surface glycoproteins (VSGs) that are crucial for parasite immune evasion also found a link between VSG expression suppression and stumpy formation [5, 6]. While each of these pathways could function during parasite differentiation in vivo and together ensure stumpy formation and parasite transmission, it is not clear if there is crosstalk among these pathways, and how these different pathways all converge to the same cell fate determinants leading to stumpy formation. In a recent RNAi screen for Rab small GTPases functions in T. brucei autophagy, we identified TbRab2B as a regulator of autophagosome degradation (Figs. 2 and 3), likely via a specific function on the lysosomes (Figs. 4 and 5). Most surprisingly, depletion of TbRab2B in slender form cells led to efficient transition to functional stumpy forms (Figs. 6 and 7). Based on these results, we hypothesize that TbRab2B acts as a negative regulator of slender-to-stumpy differentiation, possibly via its function on the lysosomes.
