title: Tandem activatable molecular reporters for real-time longitudinal optical imaging of cancer immunotherapy
abs: In Singapore, cancer accounts for 28.4% of all deaths. Cancer Immunotherapy has revolutionized oncology and provided a promising treatment option particularly for patients with resistance to chemotherapy. However, the response rate to immunotherapy is low and different patients often respond differently to a same immunotherapy. To understand this issue for improved cancer immunotherapeutic outcome, development of analytic methods to evaluate and monitor dynamic tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) is essential. Current approaches to assess TIME include flow cytometry, histological staining, and mass cytometry of biopsy tumor tissues. However, single-site biopsy is invasive, static, risky to cause metastasis and only able to reveal regional information on TIME, while peripheral bloods inevitably contain biomarkers released from organs other than tumor. In contrast, molecular imaging offers a real-time and non-invasive way for longitudinal monitoring of overall TIME. However, limitation of “always-on” signaling feature for most contrast agents prevents precise signal correlation with the status of TIME. This project aims to develop a library of tandem activatable molecular reporters (TAMRs) for real-time optical imaging and semi-quantitative analysis of TIME with the purpose to guide cancer immunotherapy. The unique dual-lock activation design ensures that TAMRs only switch on their optical signals in the presence of both tumor and leukocyte biomarkers but remain inactive in normal or even inflammatory tissues. Thus, the signals of TAMRs are highly specific to tumor-infiltrating leukocytes (TILs), permitting accurate signal correlation with the status of dynamic TIME. TAMRs will be applied to establish the functional relationship between signals and therapeutic outcomes and screen for new combinational immunotherapeutic treatment in murine tumor models. The high renal clearance of TAMRs enables facile multiplex urinalysis, holding translation potential for high-throughput optical analysis of TIME. Successful implementation of this project can fundamentally help us understand the relation of immune contexture with immunotherapeutic outcome, preclinically provide a noninvasive and sensitive high throughput method for optimizing combinational cancer interventions, and clinically serve as a potential way for clinicians to stratify patients towards personalized cancer immunotherapy.

title: The Role of Pro-viral Host Factors in Alphavirus RNA Gymnastics.
abs: Alphaviruses are a genus of positive-sense viruses that contain many medically important pathogens transmitted by arthropods. Old World alphaviruses like chikungunya virus (CHIKV) and Sindbis virus, cause febrile inflammatory diseases characterised by a rash, polyarthritis and myalgia. The New World alphaviruses like Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus, cause potentially fatal encephalitis and other neurological manifestations like convulsions in humans. Often considered the most medically important alphavirus, CHIKV outbreaks have been continuously reported across different continents since 2004, infecting millions. Despite the global medical threat they pose, there are no vaccines or antivirals against alphaviruses available for humans. Antiviral compounds targeting viral factors often show a decrease in efficacy over time due to drug resistance, which emerges due to rapidly evolving viral genomes. Instead of targeting viral proteins, one strategy to decrease the chances of resistance is to target host factors essential to viral replication. An in-depth understanding of virus-host interactions is therefore necessary in order to identify potential targets for antiviral development. Our preliminary studies have identified SFPQ (splicing factor, proline- and glutamine- rich) as a novel host factor involved in the replication of CHIKV and other alphaviruses. SFPQ is a highly conserved RNA-binding nuclear protein that is involved in numerous cellular processes. SFPQ was identified as an interacting partner of the CHIKV capsid protein in an immunoprecipitation (IP)-based screen on CHIKV-infected cells using anti-CHIKV capsid antibodies. Immunofluorescence and western blot assays showed that SFPQ egresses out of the nucleus upon CHIKV infection. IP performed using CHIKV-infected cells that were fractionated into nuclear and cytoplasmic fractions showed that the interaction between SFPQ and the CHIKV capsid occurs in both compartments. SFPQ knockdown reduced virus titres, indicating that SFPQ is a pro-viral factor. CHIKV capsid proteins overexpressed in uninfected cells were unable to pull down SFPQ, suggesting that the viral RNA mediates the interaction between capsid and SFPQ. When biotinylated CHIKV RNA fragments were used to pull down SFPQ, the 3’UTR was identified as an SFPQ-binding site. Bioinformatic analyses identified three potential SFPQ binding regions within the 3’UTR and mutagenic studies showed that all three regions are important to SFPQ binding. To determine the role of SFPQ in CHIKV replication, we used a temperature-sensitive luciferase reporter construct of CHIKV which does not undergo genome replication at 37⁰C, but is translated by the host translational machinery to produce proteins. The decrease in luciferase signal upon SFPQ knockdown suggested that SFPQ is involved in CHIKV protein translation. title: Mechanistic transports of sphingolipids in the lysosomes by Spns1
abs: The brain is enriched with different types of lipids. These lipids are essential components of membrane structures and functions in neuronal cells. Cholesterol and polar lipids including phospholipids and sphingolipids constitute the majority of lipids in the brain with little neutral lipids such as triglycerides. Of particular interest is sphingolipids, which are key components of myelin sheaths in the white matters. These sphingolipids such as gangliosides can be de novo synthesized from simple precursors in the brain. Importantly, it has been well documented that a defect in the remodelling of sphingolipids often leads to the ectopic accumulation of sphingolipids in the lysosomes in sphingolipid lysosomal storage diseases (SLSD). These diseases including Gaucher, Sandhoff, Fabry, Tay-Sachs, and Niemann-Pick type C are inherited metabolic diseases characterized by the accumulation of toxic materials in the cells. The brain is the most severely affected organ in the SLDS patients. There is no effective treatment available, leaving an unmet needs for healthcare. It is unclear as to why sphingolipids are specifically recycled in the lysosomes and why a defect in any enzymes in this pathway often results in SLSD, leaving a huge gap of knowledge in understanding the roles of sphingolipid remodelling in the brain. We identified Spns1 as a potential gene candidate that we hypothesized is involved in the recycling of sphingolipids in the cells. Spns1 shares 54% identities with Spns2, which is a sphingosine-1-phosphate transporter. Our preliminary data show that Spns1 is a lysosomal protein. Lack of this protein results in severely delayed development in mice. Sphingolipids are accumulated in the brain tissue of Spns1 knockout mice and Spns1 deficient cells. Guided by these strong preliminary data, we hypothesize that Spns1 plays a key role as a gateway for sphingolipid transport from the lysosomes. The overarching goals are to understand the mechanisms by which cellular substances are recycled in the lysosomes and how these molecules are released to regulate cellular functions. To test our hypothesis, we will pursue these specific aims: 1) Determination of physiological roles of Spns1. 2) Identification of the ligands for Spns1. 3) Determination of stage-specific functions of Spns1 in adult mice. 4) Determination of molecular roles of Spns1 in cell models. The long-term goals are to harness lysosomal transport pathways to mitigate lysosomal storage diseases. The broad objective here, which is the next step to achieve these goals, is to unravel the mechanisms by which Spns1 functions in the lysosomes.
kw: Sphingolipids, lysosomal storage diseases, transporters

title: Understanding Chikungunya virus cell entry pathway
abs: Some important human pathogens such as the flaviviruses (e.g., dengue, zika, yellow fever viruses) and alphaviruses (e.g., chikungunya virus), utilized the class II fusion protein to gain entry into cells. Entry of the class II fusion viruses into the cell begins with the virus particles engaging their respective cell receptor(s). After the receptor:virus complex are being endocytosed, the low pH environment of the endosome will induce the viral surface proteins to undergo dramatic rearrange to facilitate fusion between the virus and the endosomal membranes. It is important to study the virus fusion process, as they are important for cell entry and thus are targets for neutralizing antibodies and drug design. In this proposal, we used Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) as a model to understand the fusion process used by the class II fusion virus. We will first understand how CHIKV interacts with its cell receptor and attachment factors by determining their complex structures using cryo-electron microscopy. We will then investigate whether binding to the receptor and attachment factors will help enhance fusion of virus to endosomal membrane. Finally, we will determine the fusion transitional structures of CHIKV by using a combination of cryo-tomography and subtomogram averaging. Results from this study can help us understand the important structural elements allowing alphavirus, in particular, CHIKV to gain entry into cells. These structures can be used for drug design or selection of antibodies for inhibiting virus infection.
kw: Chikungunya, class II fusion, virus fusion, cryoEM

title: Novel Antimalarial Cyclic Peptides and Enzymes from an Unusual Biosynthetic Pathway
abs: Naturally occurring peptides constitute a niche of clinically important drugs for treating both infectious and chronic diseases. The discovery and development of cyclic peptide natural products as therapeutic drugs remain a fertile research field today with two to three new peptide drugs entering the market annually. As the genome sequencing of microbes and plants continues to disclose an astoundingly large number of peptide biosynthetic pathways, the pace of discovering therapeutically valuable peptides is expected to accelerate in the next decade. Within this context, our lab recently discovered tasikamides, a family of structurally distinctive cyclic peptides produced by a microbe isolated from a quarry lake on the island of Palau Ubin, Singapore. Remarkably, tasikamides feature a heavily modified cyclic pentapeptide scaffold connected to a lipophilic moiety through a highly unusual hydrazone (NH-N=C) functionality. Naturally occurring hydrazone functionality is very rare despite many synthetic hydrazone compounds are considered commercially valuable synthetic precursors and ingredients today. The enzymes responsible for the biosynthesis of hydrazones remain unknown as of now. The discovery of tasikamides from the genetically tractable microbe offers an outstanding opportunity for us to disclose the mysterious hydrazone-synthesizing enzymes. In addition, three of the tasikamides exhibited promising antimalarial activity (Half maximal effective concentration EC50 = 1.1 ~ 2.5 µM) by inhibiting the development of the parasitic Plasmodium falciparum in blood cells, raising the prospect of developing tasikamides as novel antimalarial agents. Motivated by the potential of discovering novel biosynthetic enzymes and antimalaria drug leads, we propose a research project with the aims of (1) elucidating tasikamide biosynthetic mechanism and identifying the novel hydrazone-synthesizing enzymes and (2) generating tasikamide derivatives with enhanced antimalarial activity by pathway engineering and chemical modification. The outcome of the research work will not only shed light on the biosynthetic mechanism of a family of structurally unique hydrazone-containing cyclic peptides, but potentially yield novel antimalarial drug leads and enzyme biocatalysts that can be exploited for the production of commercially valuable hydrazone-containing chemicals.
kw: Natural product, antimalarial compound, enzyme, cyclic peptide, biosynthesis

title: Synthesis of Novel and Complex Molecules through Selective Coupling
abs: The project has three distinct but related Aims: 1. To achieve a mechanistic understanding of the selective coupling of the two isomeric 1,2- dichloroethylenes and of trichloroethylene by computational means. The results will inform the choice of catalysts for experimental studies and will be implemented for the other two Aims. Disagreements in the literature about the regioselectivity of the coupling of trichloroethylene will be resolved by experimental studies in conjunction with theoretical work. 2. We will use sequential and selective Suzuki coupling of both cis-1,2-dichloroethylene and of trichloroethylene to synthesise, first, cis-stilbenes and triarylethylenes with a diverse range of substitution patterns. Then these will undergo oxidative cyclisation to phenanthrenes. This methodology will be extended to the synthesis of picenes by employing an extended coupling startegy followed by tandem cyclisation. In all cases, we will include a diverse set of substitution patterns on the molecules. We will include synthesis of the scarcely known aza-picenes and othert heteropicenes. In parallel, we will develop a novel route to picenes using the Bergman cyclisation and a route to corranulene using the hexadehydro-Diels-Alder reaction. Both of these routes rely on the selective coupling of chloroethylenes. The library of molecules thus produced will be submitted for preliminary testing of materials properties. 3. Using the same selective coupling methodology, we will synthesise two families of natural products: phenanthroizidines and onydecalins. For the phenathroizidines, we will draw upon the understanding of triarylethylene and phenanthrene synthesis of Aim 2, as well as developing methods for cyclisation, asymmetric hydrogenation and asymmetric hydroamination. For the synthesis of the onydecalins, after the selective coupling chemistry, we will employ an intramolecular Diels-Alder reaction, building upon our earlier synthesis of allahabadolactone. The library of molecules thus produced will be submitted for preliminary testing of biomedical properties.
kw: Coupling; catalysis; materials; polycyclic; alkaloid; decalin

title: Exploring Chiral Induced Spin Polarization With Chiral Nanostructures For Enantio-recognition and Asymmetric Synthesis
abs: Recent studies on the chiral induced spin selectivity (CISS) effect have uncovered a new pathway for the discrimination of enantiomers based on electronic, rather than spatial, effects. Yet, many open questions remain as to how this effect may be manipulated or amplified for the purposes of asymmetric organic synthesis. This project therefore seeks to employ state-of-the-art 3D printing technology for the nanoscale engineering of chiral materials, in order to probe the mechanisms behind this effect, as well as to shed light on the nature of chirality in various forms – namely, structural and molecular chirality. Secondly, we endeavour to design and fabricate a highly sensitive enantiomeric excess (ee) detector, that operates based on this new enantio-sensing principle. In addition to providing considerable advantages over existing techniques for measuring ee, this proof-of-concept device would be the first of its kind and would open the door to further progress in chiral separation technology. Finally, we will investigate how chiral materials may be engineered and optimized for asymmetric catalysis, with the goal of demonstrating that enantioselective hydrogenation of a-keto esters can be achieved using electron spin and/or structural chirality for chiral induction.

title: Post-Pandemic Growth and Career Adaptability for School-to-Work Transition
abs: The effects of the COVID-19 have been found to be especially tumultuous for young adults navigating through the developmental stage of emerging adulthood. Using a prospective longitudinal cohort research design for surveying a sample of about 2,000 university students, this proposed project has three main aims. First, specific COVID-19 stressors will be identified and tested in the short-term and long-term for the predictive validity on mental health outcomes. As the link between identifiable stressors and stress response is an important basis for the category of Trauma and Stressor-Related Disorder in the DSM-5 nosological system of mental disorders, the research findings will provide important evaluative evidence for the conceptualization of the adverse psychological impact of COVID-19 within this framework. Second, longitudinal monitoring of university students will allow us to investigate the psychological recovery process following the acute phases of the pandemic. The construct of Post-Pandemic Growth will be explored for its theoretical parallels to posttraumatic growth which is defined as positive transformational personal changes that may result from the experience of severe stress and adversity. Third, career adaptability in university students will be investigated for its role in promoting employment self-efficacy and successful employment outcomes when students transition from school to work during this period of economic uncertainty. This investigation will test the applicability of the Career Construction model of Adaptation during the pandemic and identify any moderating effects of COVID-19 stressors. Overall, findings from this proposed project will help us test and extend psychological theories related to stress and coping in the context of COVID-19. Our understanding about the psychological impact of a pandemic will help us develop evidence-informed prevention and intervention programmes for young adults to help them recovery from the adverse impact of COVID-19 and attain the milestones of their developmental stage, including transitioning from school to work. Thus far, we have demonstrated the feasibility of this project by successfully recruiting about 2,300 university students for our cross-sectional study. We have also submitted a manuscript for publication and we continue to analyze the data as part of student projects and collaboration with overseas collaborators. The successful application for this grant will help us extend our work to a longitudinal study.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Augmenting Medical Information Dimensionality: The Future of Work in the Medical Profession
abs: The impact of machine learning and AI in knowledge work is inevitable. We observe an increasing use of AI in clinical areas for prevention, screening, diagnosis, and treatment, particularly in healthcare. Specifically, in Singapore, the use of AI in these areas is typically ad-hoc, opportunistic, and largely driven by the availability of digitized clinical data from healthcare providers. This proposal presents a framework to classify the four major types of clinical work (preventing, screening, diagnostic, and treatment) that can benefit from AI use and propose ways to solve these clinical problems along the lines of effort and expertise augmentation. We argue that clinical tasks can be divided broadly into tasks that require extensive information foraging and tasks that are equivocal. Both forms of tasks benefit differently from AI and data analytics. Specifically, information foraging tasks require high data variety with increased processing breath, while equivocal tasks require greater data velocity processing depth. Finally, we examine how AI augmentation of healthcare work impacts the underlying work processes, the decision-making process of healthcare workers, and the team dynamics among physicians. We situate the application of this AI Augmentation framework in the real-life clinical environment and propose two studies to illustrate the benefit of AI augmentation. First, we examine the cancer screening processes in National University Hospital and argue that AI use results in effort augmentation. Second, we propose an AI-based new way of managing of ICU patients on mechanical ventilation in Ng Teng Fong General Hospital and argue that AI use results in expertise augmentation.

title: Mitotherapy for Retinal Pigment Epithelium (RPE) regeneration in Age-Related Macular Degeneration (AMD)
abs: Specific Aims 1)To investigate and develop in-vitro models to recapitulate mitochondrial dysfunction in AMD 2)To investigate efficacy of mitotherapy in an in-vitro and an animal model of AMD Hypothesis: Strong experimental evidence suggests that RPE mitochondrial defects drive AMD pathology. As AMD is primarily caused by RPE dysfunction, rescuing the degenerating RPE cells offers promising treatment. Therapeutic potential of transplantation of isolated, metabolically active mitochondria has been demonstrated in several in vitro and in vivo experimental models of cardiac, hepatic, and central nervous system diseases. We hypothesize that mitotherapy has the potential to rescue damaged mitochondria in the degenerated RPE in AMD. Methods: We aim to study mitochondrial uptake by RPE and functional improvement in the in-vitro model of AMD. To study its effectiveness in-vivo, we will administer mitochondria intravitreally in mouse model of AMD. Approach: We aim to develop novel therapeutics for AMD, whereby the underlying pathology of RPE dysfunction is addressed, thus arresting the disease progression early. This approach can potentially reverse the disease phenotype, prevent RPE atrophy and progressive vision loss which ensues despite anti-VEGF therapy. Clinical Significance: Currently, the sole therapy for neovascular AMD only aims to regress the CNV but fails to address the underlying pathology which is mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE cells. Mitotherapy addresses the root of the problem and has the potential to revive the degenerating RPE from intrinsic mitochondrial damage that continues to occur despite regular anti-VEGF therapy. Mitotherapy could also be a putative treatment for ‘dry’ AMD, which lacks any treatment currently. Thus, mitotherapy has several advantages compared to current treatment modalities – it can be used to treat RPE dysfunction early in disease before significant damage occurs, can prevent disease progression which is not achieved with anti-VEGF therapy and be used as a therapeutic agent for both early and late AMD.
kw: mitotherapy, retinal pigment epithelium, age-related macular degeneration

title: Discovery and validation of transcriptional changes in Soft Tissue Sarcoma responsible for therapeutic effect of Doxorubicin
abs: Soft tissue sarcoma (STS) is a malignancy that disproportionately afflicts young people, thus posing a high risk of mortality and morbidity especially in the young. Half of patients with localized disease develop metastases. Cytotoxic chemotherapy with Doxorubicin remains the mainstay for most STS, but prognosis is abysmal with a median overall survival (OS) of one year. As STS are a heterogeneous group of tumors originating from mesenchymal precursors, the overall response rate of unselected STS patients to Doxorubicin is only 20% in clinical trials, leaving 80% of patients merely experiencing toxicity without therapeutic efficacy. We have generated patient-derived STS cells (PDSC) from tumours which capture the characteristics and behavior of the original tumour. Importantly, responses to Doxorubicin in these cells mirror the clinicoradiological responses to Doxorubicin in the patient. Here, we propose to use a functional approach in PDSC to understand why some patients respond to Doxorubicin while others do not. We hypothesize that: (i) Doxorubicin treatment in STS results in transcriptional changes; (ii) by understanding the transcriptional changes in PDSC following treatment with Doxorubicin, we can identify biomarkers that predict whether individual STS patients will respond to Doxorubicin treatment. We aim to validate the findings in vitro and ex vivo, as well as correlate these findings with clinicoradiological responses of STS patients. These biomarkers may be used to accurately match appropriate patients to Doxorubicin, the standard of care in advanced STS, while sparing those who would not respond. Our work would additionally serve as a proof-of-concept in using PDSC as a screening platform to discover other drugs that could be more effective than Doxorubicin, as well as to identify their associated predictive biomarkers for response. This could finally allow accurate matching of more STS patients to effective treatment, improving survival in this devastating disease.

title: Cardiovascular Manifestations and Prognostic Outcomes of Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (Master of Clinical Investigation)
abs: Aims: The current knowledge of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD)-related prognoses is reliant on population-based studies that are limited by the absence of histologic information, or by small sample sizes. This study will be the first longitudinal cohort study to generate comprehensive assessments of cardiovascular outcomes in a large population of NAFLD patients. Hypotheses: 1. NAFLD patients will likely have higher all-cause, liver-related and/or cardiovascular-related mortality compared to the expected background age-related rates, even after adjusting for metabolic confounders. 2. The severity of cardiovascular diseases (CVD) will increase with increasing fibrosis stages and NASH disease activity. Methodology and Approach: This will be a retrospective observational cohort that includes consecutive adult patients diagnosed with NAFLD at NUH between 1st January 2011 and 1st November 2021. NAFLD will be diagnosed clinically by imaging or liver biopsy, with the absence of alcohol consumption. Patients who had liver disease other than NAFLD, had received a liver transplant or had hepatocellular cancer before enrolment will be excluded. Noninvasive grading of NAFLD will be evaluated by ultrasound hepatobiliary system, vibration-controlled transient elastography, magnetic resonant imaging. Invasive histological grading of steatosis and fibrosis via liver biopsy will be retrieved. The principal outcome is cardiac-related mortality. Secondary outcomes include all-cause mortality, liver-related mortality, and major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events (MACCE). Cardiovascular events will include coronary heart disease, arrhythmia, cardiomyopathy, valvular heart disease and stroke. Associations between the severities of NAFLD and CVD will be examined. Independent predictors of MACCE will be identified through Cox regression. Feasibility: The study is feasible as it an observational study of NAFLD patients, and it does not involve additional investigations or interventions. Elucidating the incidence of CVD in NAFLD patients is crucial to highlight the large burden of morbidity and mortality in the local population and its public health implications.
kw: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease; cardiovascular diseases; incidence; prognostic outcomes

title: Development of a multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging radiomic signature-based pre-operative scoring system for predicting risk of post-operative cerebellar mutism syndrome in paediatric medulloblastomas.
abs: Study importance/feasibility: Post-operative cerebellar mutism syndrome (pCMS) affects about half of children undergoing surgery for posterior fossa tumours, particularly medulloblastomas. Although several pre-operative clinico-radiological predictors of post-operative pCMS have been identified, accurate risk prediction of pCMS remains challenging. The latest pre-operative risk scoring model proposed by Bae et al. (2020) utilises standard structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data, but with limited accuracy and lack of prospective large cohort validation. Medulloblastoma molecular subgroups are recently reported to be strong predictors of pCMS, independent of tumour volume and midline location, highlighting the need for subgroup-specific analysis. Currently, a robust risk prediction model integrating subgroup information with structural imaging data is lacking for clinical use and early identification of high risk patients. Aims: To validate the Bae et al. pre-operative risk prediction model for pCMS on our local medulloblastoma dataset and to develop an easy to use, reliable, and sensitive preoperative risk prediction model for pCMS incorporating MRI radiogenomic pre-operative prediction of medulloblastoma subgroups. Hypotheses: Incorporating molecular subgroups into risk modelling improves the accuracy of predicting pCMS occurrence. Machine learning algorithms demonstrate high predictive potential of medulloblastoma subgroups non-invasively. Applying this into a pCMS risk stratification model is useful for patient counselling and aiding in clinical management decisions. Methodology: Clinical and imaging data from paediatric medulloblastoma cases treated at our local tertiary children’s hospital from 1999-2021 will be retrospectively reviewed. The study cohort will be characterized by descriptive statistics. Imaging features are measured and scored according to the Bae et al methods. Morphologic features and quantitative grey-level radiomics features extracted from manually segmented tumour regions of interest will be selected. A machine learning predictive model will then be developed and evaluated. Finally, a new pCMS risk prediction model will be developed by assimilating selected radiomics features and applied to our study cohort.
kw: radiogenomics; magnetic resonance imaging; medulloblastoma; posterior fossa tumours; cerebellar mutism syndrome; paediatrics

title: Robotic Mastectomy - A Pilot Study Assessing Surgical Outcomes, Health-Related Quality of Life and Patient Satisfactions
abs: Conventional nipple and/or skin-sparing mastectomy (NSM/SSM) is one of the standard surgical treatments for breast cancer or as a risk reducing option in high-risk ladies. While this technique provides satisfactory outcomes, its disadvantages include skin flap and/or nipple-areolar complex (NAC) necrosis as well as visible scar(s) on the breast. In terms of technical aspects, NSM/SSM has its inherent challenges in view of limited incisions and thereby difficulties in dissection. Since 2015, a number of institutions worldwide had adopted a new technique of NSM/SSM using robotic surgical system. Institutional experiences worldwide demonstrated feasibility and safety of this technique coupled with improved patients’ satisfactions. There are a few aspects in the conduct of nipple sparing mastectomy and breast reconstruction which can be improved with the robotic approach. For example, better visualization and thereby preservation of blood supply to the nipple areolar complex using robotic surgical system would lead to lower incidence of nipple areolar complex necrosis. In addition, robotic approach allows for smaller/fewer incisions and the demand for smaller/hidden incisions is higher in Asian ladies. To date, there is no center in Singapore offering robotic mastectomy. The investigators believe that robotic mastectomy is a feasible and safe technique that can be utilized in our patient population and it provides superior aesthetic outcomes with less morbidity and higher patient satisfaction. The aim of this study is to conduct a single-arm pilot study to investigate surgical, aesthetic and health related quality of life outcomes as well as satisfaction in patients undergoing robotic mastectomy. Further prospective multi-arm trials comparing conventional and robotic mastectomy will be conducted after the initial pilot study. This will enable the long-term outcomes of both techniques to be compared in a head-to-head comparison thus paving the way for a potential paradigm shift in the surgical management of breast cancer.
kw: breast cancer; breast surgery; robotic mastectomy; breast reconstruction; minimally invasive breast surgery; patient satisfaction

title: Validation of a Hospital Frailty Risk Score and Association with Clinical Outcomes in Older Adults in Singapore
abs: Background: The Hospital Frailty Risk Score (HFRS) is a validated geriatric comorbidity measure derived from routinely collected administrative data. The HFRS is increasingly being validated and deployed across various settings, although there is scant work done in Asian settings. Hypothesis: The HFRS can be used to predict clinical outcomes such as length of stay, mortality, readmission and institutionalisation and can guide clinical service programmes to target high risk individuals and improve these outcomes. Methodology: The HRFS will be derived from hospital data using International Classification of Diseases (ICD-10) codes. We may try to validate a subset of the data against frailty scoring systems if available for some groups of patients. There is also potential to explore subsets of patients such as specific chronic comorbidities. This information could be used to identify those that might benefit from holistic assessment, aid prognostication, commissioning and service planning. Feasibility: The study is feasible in that it relies on electronic hospital records. We will need to work with the medical informatics department to obtain such data. The main concerns would be the reliability and accuracy of the ICD-10 coding data and also further work such as frailty where risk scoring systems may not be widely used. Importance to science: The HFRS is a novel risk stratification and frailty assessment tool that has only been recently developed internationally. It uses electronic hospital records unlike many other frailty scoring tools which are manually done. The potential for its clinical applications as well as characterisation in Asian populations leave much room to be studied.
kw: frailty; clinical outcomes; risk score

title: Using health technology assessment to assess direct and indirect impacts of life-course vaccination and increase adult vaccination compliance in Singapore
abs: Carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales (CPE) represent a critical threat to healthcare systems globally. Infections caused by CPE are associated with substantial mortality and economic impacts due to costly treatments, with costs surpassing SGD $24 million annually in Singapore alone. The incidence of CPE in Singapore has been rising since 2011 and urgently demands effective infection control strategies to mitigate transmission and consequently reduce adverse outcomes. However, current standardised international guidelines for CPE transmission control are not sufficiently evidence-based, often resulting in limited efficacy. Asymptomatic carriers, environmental reservoirs, and resource-intensive measures pose additional complications. The inherent genetic diversity of CPE and especially the unique phenomenon of plasmid-mediated gene transfer has also conferred significant challenges to early and accurate outbreak detection and control. Traditional methods of microbiological culture-based testing often exacerbate delayed detection of linked clusters or misidentification of unrelated cases as outbreaks. A national surveillance study in Singapore has correspondingly highlighted that traditional epidemiological methods fail to detect a significant portion of CPE transmissions. Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) has emerged as a pivotal tool in outbreak detection, providing high-resolution granular genetic data that outperforms conventional testing methods. WGS enables the accurate identification of transmission networks and distinguishes between true outbreaks and sporadic cases, optimising downstream infection control efforts. The implementation of WGS in routine surveillance has been demonstrated to improve infection control programmes internationally. However, there are still technical and cost barriers to its widespread adoption in Singapore. This study aims to assess the effectiveness of WGS in detecting and managing CPE outbreaks specifically in the Singapore context, additionally addressing the nuances of local infection control practices and offering valuable insights for policymakers. A life-course vaccination approach, which includes completing recommended adult vaccinations, has increasingly been recognised as a crucial discipline in public health policy. In line with Singapore’s healthcare landscape shifting towards emphasis on healthy ageing and population health maintenance, the role of robust adult vaccination programs becomes more essential than ever. Life-course vaccination offers not only improves individual health by preventing morbidity and mortality from preventable infectious disease, but significant public and population health benefits. Apart from health benefits, an equally important domain is the societal and economic value gained through healthcare and social care savings resulting from reduced incidence of disease. title: Deciphering the molecular basis of LINE-1 repression by RUNX1 towards novel anti-aging and leukemia treatments
abs: A retrotransposon, long interspersed nuclear elements (LINE-1 or L1), is the most dangerous endogenous source of DNA damage, as nearly a million of LINE-1 copies occupy ~17% of the human genome and ~100 copies of them are movable, thereby causing DNA damages and human diseases including common maladies such as premature aging and cancer. Therefore, the repression of LINE-1 is critical in maintaining our genome integrity; however, its molecular basis remain elusive. We recently found that a stem cell factor RUNX1 plays a central role in transcriptional suppression of LINE-1 by forming a previously unknown repressive complex, named transcriptional repressive complex for LINE-1 (TRCL), with STAT5, PU.1 and CTCF. In this proposal, we will further investigate the molecular mechanism of LINE-1 repression by RUNX1 through TRCL formation by employing two novel experimental systems: i) mouse models in which LINE-1 reactivation can be readily reproduced and captured, and ii) long-read third generation sequencing and downstream bioinformatics workflow to efficiently detect LINE-1 elements amongst a huge number of repetitive sequences in human genome. Furthermore, pharmacological inhibition against awaken LINE-1 will also be tested as novel therapeutic methods for premature aging and tumorigenesis. The molecular basis for LINE-1 repression by TRCL complex including RUNX1 would deepen our understanding of widespread tumorigenesis and premature aging, and the best performing LINE-1 inhibitor(s) selected in this study would lead to a novel clinically-applicable drug.
kw: LINE-1, Runx, aging, leukemia, DNA repair, animal model

title: Understanding and targeting the IL11/LKB1/AMPK/mTOR axis to extend healthspan
abs: We recently discovered that interleukin 11 (IL11) is upregulated in ageing organs, to control key ageing signalling pathways and to underlie cardiometabolic dysfunction in old age. Our preliminary data in old mice shows IL11-stimulated ERK activity to inhibit LKB1/AMPK resulting in mTORC1 activation and cell senescence, causing disease. Up till now LKB1 was thought to be constitutively active and it has no known role in ageing. Here, in four Aims, we will explore IL11 as an ageing gene and therapeutic target for multi-morbidity and dissect disease mechanisms and cell-type specific effects: Aim 1. To perform cardiometabolic phenotyping in mice with germline deletion of IL11. We hypothesise that germline deletion of IL11 in the mouse inhibits critical ageing pathways across tissues and that this preserves organ function and metabolic health in old mice. Aim 2. To therapeutically target IL11 in mice to prevent and reverse diseases of ageing. We hypothesise that IL11 is an accessible drug target in ageing mouse tissues and that a neutralising IL11 antibody can prevent ageing diseases in old mice, reverse disease in very old mice and extend lifespan. Aim 3. To identify the cells expressing IL11 in aged kidneys and aorta. We hypothesise that IL11 is upregulated in specific cell types in the kidney and aorta and that autocrine IL11 activity in these cells contributes to age-dependent loss of renal and aortic function. Aim 4. To establish STK11/LKB1 as a signalling nexus for ageing diseases. We hypothesise that a primary signalling pathway underlying diseases of ageing is mediated via an axis of IL11-regulated ERK/LKB1/AMPK/mTORC1 activity across tissues. This project explores large new biology with a strong translational focus. If our hypotheses are proven and anti-IL11 therapy translates, the health and economic benefits could be large.
kw: ageing, health, old age, metabolism, inflammation

title:
Elucidating the role of inflammasome as pathogenic factors, biomarkers and
therapeutic targets for Alzheimer's disease and vascular cognitive
impairment
abs: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and vascular dementia (VaD) are the two most common forms of dementia. Given that there is often comorbidity of AD and VaD among the elderly, “vascular cognitive impairment” (VCI) is termed to cover a wider spectrum of cognitive impairment involving cerebrovascular disease, including mixed dementia which expresses both the AD and vascular pathologies. It is evident that AD and VCI share common risk factors and underlying mechanisms, including neuroinflammation. Inflammasomes are intracellular multi-protein complexes expressed abundantly in the brain and immune cells, playing important roles in detecting cellular damage and mediating inflammatory responses during disease pathogenesis. Our preliminary findings demonstrated that several upstream activators and downstream effectors of inflammasomes were deregulated in the human brains of AD, supporting the involvement of inflammasomes in disease pathophysiology. Although numerous pre-clinical studies had showed the relationships between inflammasomes and disease pathology of AD and VaD, their potentials as clinical biomarker and therapeutic target are unclear. Thus, we aim to adopt an inter-disciplinary approach to elucidate the roles of inflammasomes as (i) pathogenic factors using a postmortem neurochemistry study, (ii) clinical biomarkers using a longitudinal study cohort, and (iii) therapeutic targets using animal models of AD, VaD and mixed dementia. We hypothesise that activated inflammasomes are correlated with the neuropathological features of AD and VCI, making them potential clinical biomarkers and therapeutic targets for the diseases. The hypothesis will be examined in three separate yet highly complementary studies, leveraging on the existing human cohorts as well as animal models of AD and VCI established at the Memory Ageing & Memory Centre (MACC). It is expected that these studies will provide further insights into the pathogenic role of inflammasomes in cognitive impairment and dementia, and discover novel and clinically useful biomarkers for disease mechanisms, prognosis and treatment.
kw: Alzheimer’s disease; Vascular cognitive impairment; inflammasome; neuroinflammation; biomarker; therapeutics

title: Increasing uptake of cascade testing in families with familial cancer syndromes: A randomized controlled trial of a registry-aided outreach model.
abs: Approximately 10% of cancer patients possess germline pathogenic/ likely pathogenic variants in cancer predisposition genes. Family members harbouring these pathogenic/ likely pathogenic variants are at elevated risk for cancer compared to the general population. Cascade testing for at-risk family members will broaden the current focus of cancer care from a purely reactive service model to encompass a pro-active surveillance and preventive model. Currently, reliance on probands to inform his/her family members to undergo genetic testing results in a 15% uptake rate in Singapore, compared to 30% in Western countries. There are significant barriers that could hinder a proband in Singapore from disseminating this critical information to his/her family. To improve the uptake rate of cascade genetic testing in families at high risk of cancers, we propose a registry-aided outreach model to contact at-risk family members, avoiding the barriers inherent with the proband-dependent approach. We plan to conduct a cluster randomised controlled trial to compare cascade testing uptake rates between the current proband-dependent versus our proposed, registry-aided outreach approach. We hypothesise that cascade testing uptake of at-risk family members would increase from 15% to 30% with the implementation of a registry-aided outreach approach, compared to the current proband-dependent approach. We also aim to conduct in-depth interviews to identify barriers to cascade testing among at-risk family members who decline cascade testing despite the outreach approach, using thematic analysis to determine dominant themes. If successful, this novel registry-aided outreach model will facilitate the expansion of current cancer care to incorporate proactive surveillance and preventive measures, and thus reduce cancer care burden, healthcare demand and costs in the long run.

title: Singapore Biodesign Innovation Fellowship Training Programme
abs: The Biodesign innovation fellowship training over 6 months is segmented into 3 main phases: Identify, Invent, and Implement with a further deep dive into each sub-segments. In the Identify phase, the Biodesign innovation process begins with the team identifying a series of unmet needs, preferably through on-the-ground observations in the healthcare setting that can be further validated through interviews with the right stakeholders including patients, payor and provider. The Biodesign methodology addresses the importance of choosing a ‘good’ need with appropriate needs characterization from a multi-disciplinary perspective. With this in mind, we are trained to develop our needs-driven mantra as follows: 1. A well-characterized need is the DNA of a great invention 2. A “good” need looks for insights beyond the immediate technical problem In the Invent phase, the process will require the team to brainstorm and generate possible concepts without bias. They will follow up with multiple layers of screening to narrow down to the top concept, considering the various parallel strategies concerning intellectual property, regulatory, technical feasibility/product development, business model/reimbursement. In the Implement phase, once the final concept and prototype are created, the team will look into formulating a development strategy and plan to move towards technology commercialization.

title: Study of secondary squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck after definitive radiotherapy+/-chemotherapy for nasopharyngeal carcinoma
abs: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is a prevalent disease in Southeast Asia. Unfortunately, as NPC is characterised by a relatively younger peak incidence between 30-50, survivors of NPC post radiation are susceptible to development of secondary cancers of the radiated fields years after ending treatment. Second primary tumours generally reported to be more advanced and lethal and reirradiation is not an effective regime and there is no standard treatment. The emergence of cancer immunotherapy with potential for durable responses and extended survival is an attractive strategy to explore for this group of patients. We aim to describe the demographics, clinical characteristics, and outcomes of patients with RISCCO and analyse the pathological, immunological and genomic characteristics of tumours at baseline and after treatment with immunotherapy. We hypothesize that the tumour microenvironment is primed for immune activation. These may include conventional biomarkers for immune response like high expression of programmed death ligand-1 (PD-L1), high tumour mutational burden (TMB); and expression of wide repertoire of tumour neoantigens and immune suppressive cell states. This study is both retrospective and prospective. We will retrospectively collect clinical and demographic data for patients who are deceased or lost to follow up. Leftover tissues for patients consented into N-CABS Registry will be used (Protocol number 2018/01048). For patients still coming for clinic visits, we will consent them for medical data collection and leftover tissue. Where feasible, biopsies will be taken of recurrent tumour (1 FFPE and 1 frozen) at baseline and after 1 treatment of immunotherapy to analyse immune modulatory effects and cell states in the tumour microenvironment. This study provides an opportunity to pioneer future studies in this area. We will be able to understand the sensitivity of these secondary cancers to immunotherapy and uncover the mechanisms underpinning immune escape to shed light on future directions of research.

title: Development of prognostication models for outcomes following resection of hepatocellular carcinoma using multi-modal healthcare data.
abs: Introduction Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a leading cause of cancer deaths worldwide, with liver resection as the mainstay of curative treatment in the majority of cases. In spite of technical advances in liver surgery and improved perioperative management, long-term disease recurrence remains a significant problem. The ability to prognosticate the likelihood of disease recurrence would help inform initial treatment decisions (whether to transplant or resect upfront when both are potential options, and if for resection, whether to proceed with aggressive anatomical resection or parenchyma-sparing resections) as well as follow-up adjuvant treatment decisions (which is currently still not well-established for the treatment of resected HCC). Machine learning has been increasingly used in building prognostication models in healthcare, and has shown to offer significant advantages over conventional methods especially when combined with data science and image analytics. While there are a handful of existing studies which have applied machine learning in the prognostication of outcomes following resection of hepatocellular carcinoma, they are each primarily focused on limited data types per study, with a paucity of studies which have applied it on multi-modal healthcare data. Aims To develop prognostication models for outcomes following resection of hepatocellular carcinoma using multi-modal healthcare data. Hypotheses An integrated model based on multi-modal healthcare data developed using machine learning algorithms will offer superior prognostication for outcomes following resection of hepatocellular carcinoma as compared to conventional statistical methodologies. Methodology Multi-modal healthcare data of patients who underwent resection of hepatocellular carcinoma ranging from clinical patient data from a prospectively maintained clinical database to radiographic and histopathological images will be analysed to build prognostication models for long-term outcomes. Prognostication models using conventional statistical methods will be compared with various machine learning algorithms to determine relative prognostic accuracy. Outcomes of interest which will be examined include overall survival and disease-free survival.
kw: Hepatocellular carcinoma; machine learning; prognostication; artificial intelligence

title: Single centre prospective evaluation of Gallium-68 FAPI-46 PET/MRI in Hepatocellular Carcinoma compared to standard of care evaluation
abs: Introduction: Fibroblast activation protein (FAP), a transmembrane serine protease, is overexpressed on cancer associated fibroblasts, a key cell in the tumour stroma which have diverse functions including tumour growth, angiogenesis and metastasis. FAP expression is seen in the majority of epithelial neoplasms and promotes tumour invasion in vitro while levels correlate with poor prognosis some studied malignancies. In light of FAPs rare expression in healthy tissue it is potentially an attractive imaging and therapeutic target with the synthesis and testing of various radiolabelled FAP inhibitors (FAPI) reported. Emerging studies show the potential of FAPI-PET tracers in tumour imaging, with reported advantages over the most commonly utilised PET-tracer 18F-FDG. Here, we aim to assess the PET tracer Gallium(Ga) 68-FAPI-46 in a hybrid PET/MRI scan, in the context of the diagnostic pathway in patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Methods: We will conduct single arm study assessing the utility of whole body 68Ga-FAPI-46 PET/MRI in comparison to standard of care imaging (contrasted multiphasic MRI liver, CT thorax) in 100 patients with a diagnosis of HCC and no prior cancer directed treatment. Consented patients will undergo study imaging on a hybrid PET/MRI scanner which includes a contrasted (primovist) multiphasic MRI liver and whole-body hybrid PET/MRI with, Ga-68 FAPI-46. Following imaging patients will undergo standard of care treatment for HCC per their treating physician. Images will be reviewed by two independent experienced radiologists. The study’s primary endpoint will be estimating the sensitivity for intrahepatic HCC lesion detection of FAPI-PET-MRI versus multiphasic MRI. Secondary endpoints will assess specificity of Ga-68-FAPI PET/MRI versus multiphasic MRI and rate of staging difference (using TNM and BCLC criteria) between FAPI PET/MRI and standard of care imaging. Translational studies will use spatial transcriptomics to assess mRNA expression in regions of interest in patients with histological specimens available.

title: Multiomic analysis, Immune Profiling and T-cell Immunity in Persistent Human Papillomavirus (HPV) Skin Infection and Cutaneous Squamous Cell Carcinoma (cSCC) among Immunocompetent Hosts and Organ Transplant Recipients (OTRs)
abs: Organ transplant recipients (OTRs) receive life-long immunosuppressive medications to ensure the survival of the newly grafted organ. Such treatment leads to dampened T cell immune response which can result in failure to control viral infections. One such complication is persistent cutaneous human papillomavirus (HPV) infections. Importantly, the mortality rate in OTRs with cSCCs is twice that in the general population. I propose to study the role of T cell immunity in the pathogenesis of cutaneous HPV infection and subsequent cSCC development in OTRs. The primary goals of this study are to investigate the effects of long-term immunosuppression on the quality and quantity of T cells in OTRs and how these changes differ among OTRs with cSCC as compared to immunocompetent hosts with cSCC. I will also further define the differences in HPV-specific T cells targeting the HPV epitopes in OTRs with disseminated HPV and cSCCs and compare these with the HPV-specific T-cell response of their immunocompetent household members who carry similar HPV subtypes, but who can eradicate the HPV infection. In addition, I will perform the characterization of immunosuppression in the tumor microenvironment (TME), both in immunocompetent and immunosuppressed hosts. The key areas of interest include analyzing the tumor mutation burden (TMB) as well as the dominant Ultraviolet (UV) damage mutational signatures. Through integrating next-generation multiomic sequencing, NanoString gene expression platforms for immuno-oncology profiling, and multiplex IHC, I aim to investigate cSCC in detail by simultaneous examination of their genomic, transcriptomic, and immune landscape. Findings from this study may also potentially pave the way forward for the development of personalized medicine, where HLA-matched, HPV-specific T cell replacement therapies can be used to prevent and/or treat HPV-associated SCC in OTRs.
