With this in mind, we are trained to develop our needs-driven mantra as follows: 1. The foundation of innovation is shaped by starting with a “good” clinical need 2. A well-characterized need is the DNA of a great invention 3. A “good” need looks for insights beyond the immediate technical problem In Phase 2 – Invent phase, the process will require the team to brainstorm and generate possible concepts without bias. They will follow up with multiple layers of screening to narrow down to the top concept, taking into account the various parallel strategies concerning intellectual property, regulatory, technical feasibility/product development, business model/reimbursement. In Phase 3 – Implement phase, once the final concept and prototype are created, the team will look into formulating a development strategy and plan to move towards technology commercialization.
kw: Singapore Biodesign

title: Perioperative Preservation of Renal Function in the Non-Cardiac Surgical Population
abs: Perioperative acute kidney injury (AKI) occurs in 18% to 47% of surgical patients and is associated with morbidities and mortality. The development or progression of chronic conditions after an episode of AKI increases socioeconomic costs and majorly impacts public health. Also, with an ageing population and an increase in the number of patients with underlying chronic kidney disease presenting for non-cardiac surgery in Singapore, the incidence of perioperative AKI is likely to increase with time. There is, however, a paucity of studies of AKI, its risk factors, trajectory of recovery vs non-recovery, and evaluation of prevention and treatment modalities on our local non-cardiac surgical patients. Considering that at least 800 000 surgical procedures done annually in Singapore, the potential public health impact is likely to be phenomenal with the perioperative preservation of renal function of our non-cardiac surgical patients. Given that AKI treatment options are controversial and limited, early identification of the at-risk non-cardiac surgical patient is key so that early management strategies can be employed. Therefore, we aim to develop a robust predictive perioperative AKI risk score for our non-cardiac surgical Asian patients. Perioperative data of non-cardiac surgical patients, aged 21 years old and above, will be extracted for retrospective analysis to identify the at-risk AKI patient. A multi-variable predictive perioperative AKI risk score will then be developed from the derivation cohort with the best-performed machine-learning regression model, and further tested on the validation cohort. SHAP values obtained will also allow us to determine the important AKI risk factors so that clinical resources can be concentrated to these areas. The development of the predictive perioperative AKI risk score will lay the foundation for future works in this arena, with the final aim of perioperative preservation of renal function for our non-cardiac surgical Asian patients.
kw: Perioperative, Acute Kidney Injury, Surgery

title: The role of immune modulation in spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
abs: Background Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) can occur in patients with decompensated liver cirrhosis, with local data showing high 30-day and 90-day mortality rates of 30.8% and 51.3% respectively. In patients with cirrhosis, the integrity of the gut mucosal barrier is impaired as a result of systemic cytokine release and portal hypertension, providing an avenue for bacterial translocation into the ascitic fluid. Translocation is also promoted by immune abnormalities such as deficiency in bactericidal and opsonic function and defective monocyte activity. Concurrently, bacteria and bacterial products are associated with marked immune response, shown by elevated levels of proinflammatory cytokines. The high inflammatory response further induces derangement of both mucosal integrity and the intestinal immune system. Aim We aim to better understand the role of immune modulation within the ascitic fluid microenvironment in bacterial translocation and development of SBP. Knowledge gained from this study will potentially allow better identification of patients at risk for SBP, prognostic indications for treatment response and identification of novel molecular targets for therapy or prevention of SBP. Methods In clinical practice, patients with decompensated cirrhosis and refractory ascites undergo regular paracentesis. The ascitic fluid drained is routinely discarded. We plan to obtain the ascitic fluid and perform analysis (e.g. immunophenotyping, molecular analysis). Hypothesis We expect that there will be both up and down-regulation of various molecular pathways during the process of bacterial translocation from the gut into the ascitic fluid. Analysis of ascitic fluid will allow identification of these pathways and improve management of patients at risk for SBP. Feasibility Patients with decompensated cirrhosis (of any etiology) and refractory ascites undergo regular large volume paracentesis (frequently more than 5L during each session). The ascitic fluid is routinely discarded. On average, -5 patients undergo paracentesis weekly. Obtaining ascitic fluid for analysis is deemed to be feasible.
kw: Immune modulation, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, decompensated liver cirrhosis

title: The role of the faecal microbiome in immune modulation in an Asian Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) population.
abs: Background Inflammatory bowel disease(IBD) is a chronic systemic inflammatory disorder that primarily targets the gastrointestinal tract. It encompasses two primary disease phenotypes, ulcerative colitis(UC) and Crohn’s Disease(CD). The pathogenesis results from a complex interplay between genetic, environmental, intestinal barrier and immune response factors. Hypothesis The role of the gut microbiome is being studied in its contribution towards chronic inflammation. Diet, antibiotics, age, environmental and nutritional factors can alter the gut microbiome. IBD patients have an underlying gut microbiome dysbiosis. Studies show differences in concentration biologically active metabolites and gut microbiome profiles between patients afflicted with IBD and healthy subjects. Some differences in IBD patients’ microbiota profile features increased abundance of Pasturellaceae, Fusobacteriaceae sp, and a converse decrease in abundance of Bacteroides, Faecalibacterium sp. With current knowledge, it is not possible to establish a direct cause and effect link between dysbiosis of the microbiome and disease activity. There are limited studies evaluating the gut microbiota profile in Asian IBD patients. The different environmental and nutritional factors in Asia suggest that data from Western studies may not be applicable. There may be differing microbiome patterns within our Asian population. Aims This study is a population based observational study of IBD patients in Singapore. Primary objective of this study is to evaluate the gut microbiome profile of IBD patients in Singapore for patterns which may differ from existing literature. Secondary aim is to establish a causative link between disease activity and the gut microbiome. Feasibility The study involves collection of stool from patients within the SGH IBD Clinic. Patients will submit stool at various timepoints during their clinical course, such as during a flare or during remission. IBD patients have stool calprotectin measured during their clinical course and will be compliant to collection. Sequencing and analysis of stool will be performed by collaborators.
kw: Inflammatory Bowel Disease, Faecal Microbiome

title: Developing molecular biomarkers for dementia staging in a Singapore cohort of geriatric patients
abs: Dementia is a syndrome which results from a variety of diseases and/or injuries that primarily (e.g. neurodegeneration) or secondarily (e.g. stroke) affect the brain. It is now increasingly recognised that mixed, or a multifactorial cause of, dementia is common worldwide. While we can stage dementia confidently using well-validated clinical scales, such as the Global Deterioration Scale, there are currently few clinically established molecular biomarkers. Molecular biomarkers are complementary to clinical scales under certain circumstances, and have advantages, for example, when testing interventions targeting specific disease processes. Indeed, most studies using such molecular markers have been hypothesis-driven and are typically focused on specific mechanistic aspects of dementia. The recent rapid development of machine learning and data-science tools suggests a new way to identify general molecular markers in a hypothesis-free, data-driven fashion. These techniques are based on an initial comprehensive set of biomarkers and are aimed at reducing the resulting large feature space into a smaller subset of biomarkers that maximises information content relevant to dementia stage while reducing cost and complexity. Chronic inflammation has not only been recognised as a central mechanism in Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and stroke, but also contributes significantly to cognitive decline, immune dysfunction, and systemic ageing itself. We therefore plan to develop such a data-driven marker starting from a comprehensive set of candidate biomarkers related to inflammation, including routine clinical biochemistry, lipidomics (focusing on inflammatory mediators), and proteomics (to measure cytokines and chemokines). Using a data-driven approach based on classical dimensionality reduction, machine learning and modelling tools, we will then identify correlated sets of features (biomarkers) to clinical dementia stage. The goal is to develop an optimised, reduced “essential” panel that can provide actionable information and directly correlated to the stage of dementia, including that of AD and vascular-related pathology, in a Singapore cohort of geriatric patients.
kw: biomarkers; dementia; staging

title: Prefrontal cortical activity, impulsivity, and executive function in bipolar disorder: a functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fnirs) study
abs: The aim of the study is to examine neural activity measured by functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), impulsivity, executive function (inhibitory control, and working memory) in bipolar disorder. It is hypothesized that there will be significant differences between bipolar disorder and healthy control groups, and significant associations between impulsivity ratings, prefrontal cortical activity, and scores on tasks of executive function. This study employs a 2 (bipolar disorder, matched controls) by 2 (positive, neutral mood induction) between-subjects matched case-control experimental design. A pilot study of 10 individuals will be conducted first to ascertain the feasibility of the experimental design, followed by the actual study which will involve another 70 individuals. Inhibitory control and working memory are operationalized using an fNIRS-adapted Stroop colour-word task and an n-back task respectively; impulsivity is determined by individuals' report. Participants will be randomized into two conditions (positive and neutral) of a mood induction paradigm. Those randomized in the positive condition will be tasked to complete a modified Go-task for the purpose of inducing positive mood as a distractor for the cognitive tasks. Results will address prominent gaps in research pertaining to individual differences in impulsivity, executive function, and prefrontal cortical activity, in bipolar disorder. More importantly, results will bring added knowledge to address the long-term goal of determining reliable neurocognitive markers for cognitive screening and/or for intervention targets in psychopathology.
kw: fnirs; prefrontal cortex; bipolar disorder; working memory; executive function; inhibitory control; impulsivity

title: Sequencing for pathogens in patients with suspected central nervous system infections
abs: Meningoencephalitis, often infectious in origin, is a neurological condition associated with significant morbidity and mortality. However, the etiology of 42% of meningoencephalitis cases in Singapore remains inconclusive despite testing. Current methods of pathogen identification comprise culture-based methods and polymerase-chain reaction (PCR) screens. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) involves the use of sequencing technology for the unbiased metagenomic identification of pathogens. Unlike conventional testing methods, it does not rely on a priori selection of targeted pathogens. Therefore, diagnoses not considered in conventional testing can be made, which is especially helpful in the diagnosis of infections caused by novel, rare or unexpected organisms not included in the current limited panel of infective PCR screens and cultures. Recent studies show an increasing role of mNGS in diagnosing meningoencephalitis caused by unusual organisms missed by routine diagnostic algorithms. Identifying the aetiology helps direct targeted treatments, supports clinical decisions to stop unnecessary empirical treatments and aids in ending the diagnostic odyssey that meningoencephalitis patients undergo. However, the epidemiology and treatment of meningoencephalitis is highly variable across geographical locations and the utility of metagenomic sequencing in a Southeast Asian population is currently unclear. We hypothesize that unbiased mNGS technology will identify a pathogenic infective aetiology in a subgroup of patients with meningoencephalitis of previously unknown aetiology. Our objective is to compare the clinical utility of mNGS against current standard of care diagnostic methods. This prospective study aims to recruit inpatient adult neurological patients with suspected meningoencephalitis in whom cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) testing is routinely performed. CSF obtained will undergo mNGS for the detection of pathogens. The results from this will be compared against routine tests performed for the patient. Findings from this study will be important to evaluate the utility of a novel diagnostic technology to improve the diagnostic algorithm of patients with this severe disease.
kw: central nervous system; meningitis; encephalitis; metagenomic sequencing

title: Decoding ischemic stroke mechanisms through a detailed analysis of the microstructure and composition of retrieved blood clots
abs: Stroke continues to be a leading cause of disability and mortality worldwide. Improving our understanding on why strokes occur could lead to better preventive treatment to reduce the burden of stroke in the community. Present methods to assign stroke mechanisms are based on collection of investigational results days and weeks after strokes occur which are retrospectively pieced together to classify patients according to their likely stroke mechanism. Despite the rigor of investigations (e.g., prolonged cardiac rhythm monitoring, echocardiogram and angiographic studies), the search for stroke mechanisms often returns negative in up to 30% of patients (undetermined or cryptogenic stroke mechanism). Blood clots retrieved from stroke patients during endovascular treatment could serve as an important resource of stroke biomarkers and mechanisms. We hypothesize that ex vivo examination of retrieved blood clots using microCT and 7-tesla MRI methods would allow better characterization of the microstructure and composition of blood clots with respect to stroke etiology. By leveraging on an existing repository of blood clots and materials, we propose to employ advanced imaging methods incorporating microCT and 7T MRI to characterize the microstructure and composition of blood clots retrieved from patients with acute ischemic strokes. We aim to measure the various volumetric properties of these clots ex vivo, and correlate with histological, clinical and radiological aspects of ischemic stroke, with the eventual goal to utilize these volumetric parameters to determine the underlying stroke mechanisms. Findings of this study would allow clinicians make more informed choice and personalize the selection of antithrombotic agent for stroke prevention.
kw: Ischaemic stroke; mechanical thrombectomy; clot; volumetric assessment; microCT; high resolution MRI

title: A study of epidemiological trends, transcriptomic and immunological profiles of early-onset colorectal cancer in Singapore
abs: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the third most commonly diagnosed malignancy and one of the leading causes of cancer mortality worldwide. 80% of CRC is sporadic and occurs in individuals above 60 years of age. In sporadic CRC, environmental factors such as diet and carcinogenic exposure play a greater impact on tumorigenesis as compared to genes. However, genetic variants that influence response to environmental insults in an individual may result in small but cumulative effects which result in CRC tumorigenesis. Globally, the incidence of CRC has a slight decreasing trend, however, there is worldwide observed increase in early onset CRC (EOCRC) especially among Western countries. In Singapore, CRC incidence is rising across the entire population though age specific patterns are not yet described in detail. Sporadic EOCRC is defined as CRC diagnosed before 50 years of age with the absence of familial syndromes such as familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) or Lynch syndromes. By 2030, it is estimated that 1 in 8 CRCs will be sporadic CRCs diagnosed amongst patients less than 50 years of age. When compared to patients with CRC diagnosed above 50 years (LOCRC), EOCRC is associated with less favourable histopathological characteristics and of poorer prognosis as reflected in inferior cancer-specific survival. As the underlying factors that contribute to the rise of EOCRC are not well established, therefore it is essential to evaluate the trends and epidemiology of EOCRC in Singapore as well as to investigate the biological differences between EOCRC and older patients which may lead to an understanding of the biology of EOCRC and informed development of prevention strategies, diagnostics and treatments for EOCRC.
kw: early-onset colorectal cancer, epidemiology, transcriptomics, immunology

title: Engineered extracellular vesicles for enhanced bone regeneration
abs: Background: Critical size bone defects remain a major clinical challenge, requiring the use of bone grafts to achieve defect healing. Existing bone grafts are unable to fulfil the increasing clinical demand due to their inherent drawbacks. Mesenchymal stem/stromal cells (MSCs) and their secreted extracellular vesicles (EVs) have been explored as adjuvants in combination with bone grafts to improve bone healing and integration. N-Acetyl Cysteine (NAC) is a small molecule that enhances the capacities of osteoblasts and MSCs towards bone formation. However, the effects of NAC-preconditioning of MSCs on the secretion of MSC-EVs and their therapeutic properties remain to be elucidated. Hypothesis & Specific Aims/Outcomes: Our goal is to generate engineered EVs through N-Acetyl Cysteine (NAC) preconditioning of MSCs for enhanced bone repair and regeneration. We hypothesize that optimized NAC preconditioning of MSCs will generate high yield of engineered EVs endowed with potent properties in promoting angiogenesis and osteogenesis, as well as enhancing M2 over M1 macrophage polarization to promote overall bone regeneration. Methods & Approach: We will optimize NAC-preconditioning of MSCs and characterize the yield, presence of exosome-associated markers, and size distribution of the engineered MSC-EVs. We will culture human bone marrow MSC lines in growth medium supplemented with varying concentrations of NAC and characterize the effects of NAC on osteogenic differentiation. The conditioned medium will be collected and NAC in the EV preparations will be determined, together with particle size and concentration. We will evaluate the capacity of engineered MSC-EVs to modulate the cellular functions of principal cells involved in bone repair. Cell proliferation, migration, osteogenic differentiation assays of human bone marrow MSCs and osteoblasts will be performed. Using the THP-1 human monocytic cell line, we will differentiate these cells to macrophages and determine the immunomodulatory effects of engineered MSC-EVs on M0, M1 and M2 polarized macrophages.
kw: Bone regeneration, Exosomes, Extracellular vesicles, Mesenchymal stem cells

title: A pilot study on feasibility and efficacy of modified Crohn’s disease exclusion diet in Asian adults with Crohn’s disease
abs: The mainstay of treatment in adults with Crohn’s disease (CD) is immunosuppressant, which are associated with significant side effects and cost. Diet is implicated in the pathogenesis of CD which leads to intestinal dysbiosis and gut inflammation. Diet therapy is an attractive alternative to treat CD due to its safety profile. Exclusive enteral nutrition in adults were poorly tolerated due to poor palatability. The CD exclusion diet (CDED) is a novel whole-food diet designed to reduce exposure to dietary components which drives intestinal inflammation. CDED has been shown to be well tolerated and effective in mild-to-moderate CD, mostly in the West and paediatric population, with paucity of data in Asia. As CDED is designed based on Mediterranean diet, it is unclear if there is similar findings in the Asian CD patients. This is a single centre pilot study to explore the tolerance and efficacy of CDED, a novel dietary intervention in adults with CD. Our hypothesis is CDED is well tolerated and effective at induction of remission in CD. Adults with CD on optimal and stable dose of immunomodulators and/or biologics who has persistently active disease will be who opted for nutritional intervention over escalation of therapy will be recruited. Eligible participants will be placed on 12 weeks of CDED. To improve the tolerance of CDED, we will modify the diet to suit Asian population. Primary outcome will be tolerability of CDED at 6 weeks. Secondary outcomes include disease remission at week 6 and 12; effect of CDED on gut microbiome. If dietary intervention is proven to be effective, this will provide a safer treatment option for CD and contribute to reduced healthcare cost.
kw: Crohn's disease, Crohn's disease exclusion diet

title: Evaluating the Role of Tumor-Associated Macrophages in the Response to Anti-CD38 Monoclonal Antibody Therapy in Multiple Myeloma
abs: Background Immune dysregulation is a key mechanism of resistance to anti CD38 monoclonal antibody (mAb) therapy in multiple myeloma (MM). Tumour associated macrophages (TAM) have been proposed to promote resistance to immunotherapy but have not been well characterized in MM. MM plasma cells (PC) also evade CD38 mAb induced antibody dependent cellular phagocytosis by CD47 expression. It remains unknown whether TAMs or PC CD47 expression play a role in the response to CD38 mAb therapy. Specific Hypotheses 1) TAM infiltration, as assessed by high-dimensional profiling and 2) PC CD47 expression are associated with inferior response at 1.5 years following anti-CD38 mAb therapy. We also hypothesise that TAMs in patients with inferior response have a distinct gene expression profile. Proposed methodology We propose a prospective cohort study of newly diagnosed MM patients planned for treatment with anti-CD38 mAb regimens. Peripheral blood (PB) and bone marrow (BM) samples will be collected at diagnosis, achievement of complete response (CR), and relapse. Response to treatment will be assessed based on the International Myeloma Working Group uniform response criteria. At the 1.5-year time point, patients who achieve a very good partial response or better will be classified as having a “ good response” while those with a partial response or worse will be deemed to have a “ poor response”. BM and PB samples will be analysed using high dimensional flow cytometry and cytometry by time of flight, using an antibody panel designed to characterise TAMs. The same techniques will be used to identify clonal PCs and quantify their CD47 expression. Correlation analysis will be performed to investigate if PC CD47 expression impacts treatment response and the degree of BM TAM infiltration. Lastly, we will use single-cell RNA sequencing to study the GEP of TAMs in good and poor responders at diagnosis and relapse.
kw: multiple myeloma;tumor associated macrophage; anti CD38 monoclonal antibodies;cytometry by time of flight; flow cytometry

title: Trustworthy AI Centre NTU (TAICeN)
abs: The importance of cybersecurity is on the rise. Fundamentally, our society is more dependent on technology than ever. Data leaks that could lead to identity theft has now been posted publicly on social media accounts. Sensitive information like social security numbers, credit card information and bank account details are now stored in cloud storage services like Google Drive. Whether you are an individual, a small business or a large multinational corporation, you almost rely on computer systems every day. Pair this with the rise of cloud services, poor cloud service security, smartphones and the Internet of Things (IoT), we have a lot of potential security vulnerabilities. Governments around the world are bringing more attention to cybercrimes. For example, GDPR is a great example that is a regulation in EU law on data protection and privacy in the European Union and the European Economic Area. how to detect the cyber threats, cyber criminals and defend the cyber attacks is very important and urgent. With the rapid development of AI, it has been employed as a solution for many different cybersecurity tasks. This proposal mainly firstly focuses on developing AI-based solutions for cybersecurity. This project will develop the advanced techniques, including supervised/unsupervised learning, data augmentation, domain adaptation, on malware detection, anomaly detection, crypto attribution and insider threat detection. On the other hand, to ensure the cybersecurity, the AI-based solutions should be secure, robust and explainable. Machine learning is the field of study in which computers are given the ability to progressively improve performance on a specific task, without being explicitly programmed. In particular, deep learning is an artificial intelligence function that imitates the workings of the human brain in processing data and creating patterns for use in decisions. To continue and even further accelerate Singapore’s rise in AI adoption, related applications call for trustworthiness to have lasting positive and human-centric effect on the public and industry. The efforts in growing trustworthiness of AI systems, enable a strong support for cyber security applications which are one of the main safety-critical applications of this proposal. This project will develop the techniques to enhance the trustworthiness of the AI-solutions in the cybersecurity tasks. Specifically, we will propose techniques for the security, robustness and explanation from the perspective of the ML lifecycle.
kw: Artificial Intelligence, Trustworthy AI, Cyber Security, Malware, Anomaly Detection

title: Less is More: Addressing Mobile Application Security and Privacy through Debloating
abs: # Specific Aims and Hypotheses More-and-more apps are installed in mobile devices (many of which are pre-installed and cannot be uninstalled), but only a few of them are being used frequently. Moreover, mobile applications (apps) are getting larger in size, with many features that are often unused (e.g., Grab app offers not only ride-hailing service but also many other services, such as insurance, etc.). These unused features *increase the attack surface without creating benefits* to end users. Unused code can be exploited by attackers through, for example, code reuse attacks such as Return Oriented Programming (ROP). To help protect end users against privacy and security risks in a mobile operating system (OS), this project will develop a new approach named MINIMA; MINIMA is designed to *debloat mobile apps so that only code units required by an end user are loaded to the memory; other code units are frozen, locked, so they do not pose possible harm to the end user*. Our approach relies on the following observation: The less code is loaded to memory, the less is the attack surface. With MINIMA, only required parts of Android apps will be loaded to memory following the motto: “Just what you need, and nothing you don't”. This two-year project focuses on debloating apps that run on the Android OS -- the most popular mobile OS with more than 70% market share -- but the technologies to be realized can potentially be adapted to other mobile OSes (HarmonyOS, iOS, etc.). # Methodology and Approach The overall process in which we envision MINIMA to be used is as follows: The process starts with an end user who wants to reduce the attack surface of a target app (at version n). MINIMA first elicits (or recommends) features of the app that are (potentially) desired by the end user to produce a feature specification (Step 1). This feature specification is then inputted to the next step (Step 2) that maps the desired features to required code units in the target app. The set of required code units and another set of code units “to lock” form a debloating schema. This schema is then used by our customized Android OS to create a blocking sandbox to selectively load only required code units specified in the schema (Step 3). To deal with changes in the behaviours of the app user and the app itself (e.g., version n+1 of the app is released), we have an incremental update step that can produce a revised blocking sandbox (Step 4). The 4 steps of MINIMA will be realized through 4 Work Packages (WPs): (WP1) Elicitation and Recommendation of Desired Features; (WP2) Mapping of Desired Features to Debloating Schema; (WP3) Selective DEX Code Loading and Dynamic Instrumentation of Native Libraries; and (WP4) Incremental Updates to Address Changes. MINIMA will satisfy the following requirements: it will (i) consider unique features of Android (e.g., permission); (ii) able to work on low resource environment and incur low overhead; (iii) able to work without breaking common

title: Fine-Grained Cryptography
abs: A major concern in cryptography is the lack of diversity in the computationally hard problems that are used to construct advanced primitives like public-key encrpytion. Most of the assumptions that we have fall into two closely connected families, one of which is easily solved by quantum computers, rendering systems based on them insecure once such computers are developed. The objective of this program is to broaden and diversify the foundations of cryptography by identifying new plausible computational hardness assumptions that can be used to construct cryptosystems. We plan to do this by studying and constructing fine-grained cryptographic primitives based on the conjectured hardness of various well-studied algorithmic problems. In fine-grained cryptography, security is required only against adversaries that are moderately more powerful than the honest parties. This is in contrast to standard cryptography, where security is required even against adversaries that are exponentially more powerful than honest parties. This relaxation of the modelling of the adversary allows for the construction of meaningful cryptosystems based on computational problems that are not exponentially hard, but are still moderately hard. This allows us to draw on a whole new set of hard problems, and even to bypass several impossibility results in standard cryptography. The moderately hard problems we intend to use are well-studied algorithmic problems from the area of fine-grained complexity theory, such as k-SAT, the Orthogonal Vectors problem, k-SUM, etc.. Based on established hardness conjectures about these problems, we hope to construct average-case hard problems, one-way functions, and public-key encryption.
kw: cryptography, fine-grained cryptography, one-way functions, public-key encryption

title: Activatable Metabolic Glycoengineering in Cancer Cells for Bioorthogonal Targeted Cancer Therapy
abs: Malignant tumors are highly heterogenous and prone to monoclonal evolution, both of which would compromise the efficacy of conventional targeted therapies. Current targeted cancer therapeutics could only be applied to a small proportion of the total patient population. Consequently, new tumor targeting strategies are urgently needed, which should be able to differentiate tumor cells and healthy cells in a generally applicable and efficient manner. The aim of this program is to develop a generic and universal approach for the targeted delivery of antineoplastic agents to tumor site using a sialic acid-based carrier system. Based on glycoengineering technology and bioorthogonal chemistry, the proposed therapeutic system could artificially label tumor cells with azido or cyclopropene groups to enable the subsequent click reaction with the alkynyl- or tetrazine-modified macromolecular carrier. This strategy would open up new avenues for the treatment of a variety of tumors that were previously considered non-targetable or non-druggable. This program will cover the following main tasks: 1. Construct azido- or cyclopropene-bearing glycoengineered biological agents using the sialic acid-based carrier system. The metabolism of the sialic acid system in tumor cells enables the expression of azido group on the plasma membrane, therefore achieving the artificial labeling of the tumor cells. 2. Investigate the bioorthogonal copper-free click reaction with alkynyl- or tetrazine-modified prodrug formulation. The specificity, delivery efficiency and therapeutic efficacy of the formulated therapeutics will be evaluated across multiple tumor cell lines. 3. Establish animal models of tumor indications to investigate the labeling efficiency and monitor the treatment response of metabolically reprogrammed tumor cells by bioorthogonal drug delivery. The discoveries in this program could drastically enhance both the efficacy and safety of antitumor drugs, and facilitate the future clinical translation of novel treatment modalities.
kw: bioorthogonal chemistry, glycoengineering technology, sialic acid system, targeted cancer therapy, tumor treatment

title: Investigating the Psychology of Consumer–AI Interaction for the Design and Development of AI-based Products and Services
abs: I. Background and Academic Significance Artificial intelligence (AI)—the science of designing and building intelligent systems that can think, learn, and perform actions in response to what they sense and their objectives—is revolutionizing the modern marketplace and may represent the largest economic opportunity in our lifetime (PwC 2017). Although the business deployment of AI is still in a relatively early stage globally, more businesses are experimenting with AI technology with plans to include it in their operations going forward (Thomas 2020). Much of the global economic opportunity from AI depends on consumers, with 45% (over US$7 trillion) of the total economic gains estimated to come from AI-based products and services (henceforth, “AI systems”; PwC 2017). In marketing applications, AI systems interact directly with consumers on a wide range of tasks including recommending products, offering customer support, and placing orders. For example, Netflix uses recommendations AI to suggest movies based on consumer viewing and the time, location, and device used; Amazon’s personal assistant, Alexa, uses conversational AI to simplify purchase. We focus on these two classes of AI in marketing—recommendations AI (AI-based product recommendations and content curators) and conversational AI (voice assistants and service chatbots)—as they are increasingly prevalent in the marketplace. How do consumers perceive and interact with these AI systems? Anecdotal and emerging evidence suggests that the psychology of consumer–AI interactions—how consumers perceive, feel, and respond toward AI—is complex. The extant academic literature provides limited guidance into consumers’ receptivity toward recommendations AI and conversational AI, for two reasons. First, consumer–AI interactions is a recent phenomenon. It is unclear as to what extent prior insights can be extended to consumer–AI interactions, as AI systems differ vastly from earlier technologies in scale, performance, and dynamics. Second, the nascent literature has focused on people’s lay beliefs of automation (Granulo et al. 2019) and algorithms (Castelo et al. 2019), with the studies conducted in the US and the Netherlands. Not only do consumers experience more richness and dynamics in interacting with AI systems in the real-life marketplace, but it is unclear the extent to which prior findings apply to Singapore, as the socio-cultural context is different. Therefore, this research addresses this important gap in examining the psychology of consumer–AI interaction to inform the design of AI-based products and services in Singapore. II. Aims and the Main Questions to be Addressed We aim to answer the following research questions (RQs): RQ1. What is the psychological effect of AI-based product recommendations on consumer decision-making? title: Handling Massive Data under the Edit Metric: Clustering, Finding Median and Computational Hardness
abs: Handling massive data set over high-dimensional metric spaces is one of the fundamental challenges in theoretical and applied big data analysis. One such important metric is the edit metric which plays a central role in several domains, including computational biology, speech recognition, text processing, classification, and information retrieval. The edit distance between two strings is the minimum number of elementary edit operations required to transform one string into another. Elementary edit operations vary with the applications. The most standard one considers character insertion, character deletion, and character substitution as elementary operations. Despite being a central string similarity measure, not much work has been done from the theoretical big data perspective. Clustering with the edit distance is highly significant in real life, mostly due to applications in DNA, RNA, and protein sequencing, document classification, DNA storage system, ranking web pages returned by search engines, and many more. In most of these applications, researchers currently use heuristics to solve these problems, mainly because only a little is known from the theory side. Due to such a wide-ranging application, the problems related to the clustering of strings under the edit metric demand a comprehensive and systematic theoretical study. This project will study various big data problems with edit distance as the underlying space, mainly from a theoretical viewpoint. This project will also invest a significant amount of effort to turn those theoretical results into practice. To achieve these goals, we will pursue the research in three broad directions, mostly in parallel. 1. The first question is to partition (into many clusters) a given data set containing a massive number of strings according to their edit similarity. We will study this problem by allowing various measures of accuracy depending on applications. The main target is to design as efficient a procedure as possible with the accuracy as high as possible. We want to establish a clear trade-off between accuracy and efficiency. We will not just look into the arbitrary input for this task but go beyond the worst-case by considering certain restrictions on the input data. More specifically, we will consider the inputs arising in a particular application of DNA storage system. We hope the restricted input will help us design faster solutions that could also be implemented and used in real life. 2. Another indispensable problem is to find a representative of a data set. title:
M2CardAGE
MOLECULAR AND MECHANOBIOLOGY UNDERPINNING CARDIAC AGEING
abs: The overarching goal of this proposal is to gain a mechanistic understanding into how molecular and mechanical functions of heart cells and tissue change during ageing. Knowledge gained aims to springboard innovative diagnostic methods and treatments for age-related cardiovascular disease (CVD) of direct applicability to the Singaporean population. Singapore is among top nations with rapidly ageing populations. CVD is a significant barrier to healthy ageing, accounting for ~30% of chronic conditions in the old, and contributing substantially to the healthcare burden of chronic diseases in Singaporean elderly. The heart is therefore a key focus if Singapore is to achieve healthy longevity. Here, we propose to tackle an overarching hallmark of ageing hearts: cardiac stiffness. As the heart ages, it undergoes (a) intracellular changes, including deterioration of force-producing/bearing structures, protein aggregation and mitochondrial dysfunction, (b) biophysical, compositional and structural changes of the extracellular matrix (ECM), and (c) altered cell-cell and cell-ECM interactions involving the different cardiac cell types, especially cardiomyocytes. We hypothesize that chronic mechanical and metabolic stressors lead to significant molecular and mechanobiological changes, which in turn result in cardiac stiffness, contributing to accelerated pathologies of cardiomyopathy and heart failure. Our proposal is built on 3 converging and interactive PROJECTS, based on increasing scales, from molecules to cells and tissue, culminating in an integrated framework explaining age-associated cardiac stiffness: (1) Molecular characterization of cardiac ageing, (2) Intracellular mechanics in cardiomyocyte ageing, and (3) Extracellular interactions and architecture in ageing hearts. This ambitious and highly interdisciplinary research brings together basic biomedical and clinical research units at NUS Faculty of Science, Faculty of Engineering, and YLL School of Medicine, and the CVMD programme at Duke-NUS. Collectively, our fully integrated effort will lead to a new paradigm of cardiac ageing research in Singapore, with a unique conceptual framework for age-associated cardiac diseases.

title: Developing the world’s first biological camera that captures and stores images in DNA
abs: DNA data storage is an emerging field that is poised to revolutionize the data storage space, due to its high density, biological relevance and longevity. However, the current paradigm of storing data into DNA is limited by the amount of sequence-specific DNA that can be effectively synthesized, which is untenable with existing synthesis methods. The throughput of the process is also long and slow due to the bottlenecks in DNA synthesis and sequencing. There is thus significant space to explore and develop new biological techniques/approaches which can lead to a new paradigm shift in DNA data storage and lead to its increasing viability in the future. We propose that to obviate the need to synthesize DNA de novo for each time new data is stored, we can encode data into DNA using alterations in existing genetic material, such as that in living bacteria cells. This can be done using various enzymatic tools such as recombinases and CRISPR to directly edit or cause a change in DNA at specific locations and this can be programmed beforehand. This encoding technique can be controlled using various methods such as light and electricity, opening the door for direct-to-DNA data storage at a rate that cannot be matched by existing DNA synthesis methods. By combining light-responsive gene-editing systems with appropriate barcoding techniques, we will develop the first-ever biological camera that is able to capture images into DNA, which can then be decoded in a computer to retrieve said images. To do so, we intend to develop a set of novel light-responsive DNA editing systems, along with barcoding techniques that can barcode individual cellular populations, which can allow us to separate them during the decoding steps. Importantly, this would enable us to spatially encode and decode an image. These two advances will then be combined together to allow for recording of light stimuli into DNA, which is then barcoded for separation and deconvolution, akin to pixelization of an image in a computer. The set of systems to be developed include a base editing CRISPR system with different guide RNAs that are produced upon exposure to different wavelengths of light to edit at predetermined differing locations of the ‘recording’ DNA, which can be deconvoluted accordingly, resulting in the storage of colored images. We have conducted preliminary studies which show the feasibility of the proposed workflow and methods. Firstly, we have shown an initial proof of concept in 96 well plates containing bacteria with blue light-sensitive DNA-editing recombinases, whereby multiple patterns were tested and reconstructed in silico, obtaining an accuracy of ~92% across multiple images. This shows that it is feasible to encode image data via gene editing and through direct shining of light. title: ISM1 in airway homeostasis, inflammation, and allergic asthma
abs: The airway mounts robust immune responses to combat airborne pathogens while also remains tolerant to common allergens and innocuous environmental microbes. Abnormal airway sensitivity to external stimuli underscores the development of chronic inflammatory diseases such as asthma. Airway epithelial dysfunction is a critical etiological factor driving airway inflammation in asthma. We identified ISM1 to be highly expressed in mouse airway epithelium. Ism1-/- mice present airway epithelium remodeling and inflammation under ambient environment. ISM1 is consistently downregulated in both human asthmatic airways and house dust mite (HDM)-induced mouse asthma, with Ism1 deficiency exacerbates HDM-induced asthmatic pathogenesis. These preliminary data led us to hypothesize that ISM1 is an inflammation/immune modulator important for airway epithelium homeostasis and impacts asthma pathogenesis. In this proposal, we aim to answer the following two questions: (1) Is ISM1 important for airway epithelium homeostasis and integrity? If yes, how? Using both loss-of-function and gain-of-function approaches, we will study ISM1’s role in epithelial integrity and signaling transduction. Recombinant ISM1 will be supplemented to Ism1-/- airway epithelial cells in culture and Ism1-/- mice to monitor if airway epithelial abnormalities can be restored. We will further determine how ISM1 impacts cytokine/chemokine secretion and identify the cell surface receptor(s) that mediate ISM1’s function in airways. (2) How ISM1 deficiency exacerbates asthma pathogenesis and what is the underlying mechanism? Using HDM-induced mouse allergic asthma model, we will study how ISM1 deficiency exacerbates inflammation by analyzing gene expression alterations through RNA-seq and proteomics of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid. We will further investigate if and how ISM1 impacts regulatory T cells, cytokines/chemokines and whether ISM1 can function as a therapeutics to suppress airway inflammation. This proposal is novel and highly important for human health. Identification of new inflammation/immune modulator for airway homeostasis and allergic asthma pathogenesis will generate new knowledge and facilitate therapeutics development for asthma.

title: Characterizing myofibroblast regulation by WWP2 as target for kidney fibrosis
abs: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a growing health problem, affecting about 10 percent of the world’s population. Renal fibrosis is a final, common pathway and hallmark in CKD, characterized by the formation of internal scar tissue, and can cause devastating effects and ultimately lead to end-stage kidney failure. However, there are relatively few therapies in development for the treatment of CKD. The development of new and effective antibiotic drugs will require more sophisticated scientific understanding of fundamental molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying kidney fibrosis. Myofibroblasts represent the main source of ECM during kidney fibrosis, but the cellular heterogeneity of myofibroblasts in kidney is complex and remains controversial; in particular, the specific regulation of different renal myofibroblast subpopulations in fibrogenesis is still debated. Our preliminary studies provide new insights into the regulation of the myofibroblast populations during renal fibrosis. Using human CKD data and pre-clinical kidney disease mouse models, we identified the E3 ubiquitin ligase WWP2 as a regulator of pathological fibrosis in the kidney. We show that WWP2 is upregulated in association with renal fibrosis in injured kidneys from patients with different CKDs, including IgA nephropathy, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS), and membranous nephropathy, suggesting a role for WWP2 in human kidney disease. Furthermore, using two murine renal fibrosis models, unilateral ureteral obstruction (UUO) and folic acid (FA) induced fibrotic models, we demonstrated for the first time that inhibition of WWP2 function protects from kidney fibrosis in vivo. At the cellular level, scRNA-seq analyses in UUO-induced fibrotic kidney discovered two ACTA2+ myofibroblast populations: an ACTA2+Col1a1+ cell cluster (termed as collagen producing, enriched in ECM genes), and an ACTA2+ Col1a1-NG2+ cell cluster (termed as non-collagen producing, enriched in repair processes genes). WWP2 deficiency (WWP2-/-) suppressed the collagen-producing myofibroblasts, but retained non-collagen producing myofibroblasts in vivo, which we confirmed in vitro using cultured myofibroblasts. Mechanistically, the Twist 1 and Hes1 transcription factors (TFs) function as key molecular drivers of the transcriptional programs regulated by WWP2 in ACTA2+Col1a1+ and ACTA2+Col1a1-NG2+ myofibroblasts, respectively. However, the specific regulation of these functionally distinct myofibroblast populations and downstream TF signaling by WWP2 in the development of kidney fibrosis remains to be elucidated. In this proposal, we aim to carry out systemic investigations of how WWP2 regulates these myofibroblast functions during the development of renal fibrosis. title: Sonic crystals with built-in meta-structures
abs: Sonic crystals or periodic structures have been reported for applications as noise barriers for noise mitigation, or for shock and vibration mitigation. Various features in particular Helmholtz’s resonators have been incorporated into the design for enhancing the performance. More recently, an acoustic metamaterial capsule consisting of c-shape sonic crystal columns was reported to reduce the noise emission of several stage machinery drive trains while still allowing the ventilation required for cooling. The idea of coiling up space was originally conceived to obtain high refractive indices in different directions and to obtain band folding at low frequencies at which both the effective density and bulk modulus can be well defined. This approach does not require the use of features with local resonances to achieve double negativity, density near zero, and very positive refractive indices. Similar idea has been incorporated into meta-surface for perfect sound absorbers for tuneable bandwidth. The coiled up space could also be replaced by an array of Helmholtz’s resonators of various shapes and sizes to expand the bandwidth. In the proposed research, the team would attempt to incorporate more complex meta-structures within the sonic crystal structures for enhancing the performance of noise mitigation of sonic crystal structures in the form of noise barriers or sonic cage. The main focus will be on the low to medium frequency range from 100 Hz to 2500 Hz in which human sensitivity to noise is high. The design will go beyond the simple C shape cylindrical shell as reported by others and will incorporate features such as labyrinth structures and multiple compartmental structures which enhance the noise mitigation at specific frequency range as well as to broaden the bandwidth for the intended noise mitigation, in particular for lower frequency noise mitigation which is usually more difficult to be achieved by typical noise barrier or noise absorption materials. The main objective is to investigate the incorporation of meta-structures in the form of labyrinth, multiple partitions, or coiled-up space within each element or column of a sonic crystal structure for noise mitigation. The sonic crystal structures can be in the form of noise barrier or cage for the mitigation of environmental noise by creating a quiet zone within the structure, or for the insulation and reduction of noise emitted by noise sources in the form of machines or processes. The approach for the proposed research will be in a closed-loop process involving design, numerical modelling and simulation, prototyping, experimental studies, review and optimization till a good design with superior performance could be obtained. The team would attempt to construct a demonstrator showcasing the interesting acoustic performance of the final design as a grand finale for the project. title: Algorithmic Solutions for Fair Resource Allocation
abs: My goal in the proposed research is to develop algorithms and procedures for practical resource allocation problems in order to achieve socially fair outcomes. These problems are ubiquitous in our everyday lives and range from dividing housing space among the population to selecting candidates for university admissions. Several existing fair division protocols rely on the assumption that any allocation of the resources to the agents can be chosen. However, in real-world applications there are often restrictions on the allocations that we desire. How can we make the collective allocation decisions in a fair and efficient manner, taking into account these restrictions as well as the possibly conflicting preferences of the parties involved? I aim to address this question in three pervasive application domains: 1. Group resource allocation. The resource allocation literature almost always assumes that each interested party consists of a single agent. In many practical situations, however, the resources are allocated to groups of agents---the agents in each group receive the same set of items but may have differing valuations on the items. This is the case, for example, when a city council divides the available resources among various districts, or a university allocates its supplies to different departments. My objective is to design algorithms that compute outcomes with provable guarantees in these settings, and investigate the compatibility of fairness with other benchmarks such as social welfare or strategyproofness. 2. Fair division with constraints. Several resource allocation problems that arise in practice involve constraints on the set of feasible allocations. For instance, when one assigns conference center time slots to conference organizers, each organizer typically wants a contiguous block of time slots for their conference. Similarly, when dividing objects among art museums, it is preferable for each museum to receive objects of different types so that it can offer a variety of exhibitions. Most existing protocols do not take such factors into account and may therefore assign disconnected time slots or unbalanced collections, leading to suboptimal outcomes. My aim is to devise procedures that can be tailored to accommodate various real-world constraints. 3. Housing assignment. The problem of allocating housing space differs from the traditional fair division setting in a number of ways. Not only do we typically want to match each agent or family to exactly one house, but sometimes there are also diversity considerations such as the ethnic quotas in the integration policy of the Housing and Development Board (HDB) in Singapore. Each agent submits a preference over the houses, and the goal is to find a fair assignment, for example one in which as few agents as possible envy another agent for their house. I seek to understand the interplay between fairness, diversity, and economic efficiency in this setting based on both theoretical insight

title: Photocatalytic conversion of renewable feedstock into amino acids with bio-/chemo-induced chirality
abs: The primary objective of the project is to establish new manufacturing protocols for value-added chiral amino acids from inedible lignocellulosic biomass feedstocks via photocatalysis. We intend to explore, optimize and understand catalytic systems that effectively transform a series of organic acids derived from cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin into chiral amino acids. Two specific aims are: 1) photocatalytic production of a series of chiral amino acids from biomass-derived organic acids employing chiral-imprinted photocatalysts; and 2) synthesis of chiral amino acids from biomass-derived organic acids via photocatalytic amination combined with enzymatic catalysts. Formation of L-alanine from lactic acid will be used as a model reaction to understand the interplays among various structural parameters of the catalytic system, reaction parameters and activity. We have already obtained achiral amino acids from biomass-derived organic acids via photocatalysis amination reaction with ammonia under ultraviolet visible (UV-Vis) light irradiation. In this current proposal, we plan to carry out in-depth, systematic study on developing effective methods for chiral amino acids production via photocatalysis by introducing chiral functionality. Towards the end of the project, we intend to develop new protocols for the synthesis of at least 6 natural chiral amino acids with high optical yield (> 80% ee, L configuration) from woody biomass derived organic acids.

title: Learn to Augment and Represent Spatial Urban Data
abs: Urban computing, which corresponds to a process of sensing and analyzing urban data for solving urban city problems such as traffic congestion and air pollution, is becoming a common practice nowadays. Among different types of urban data that fuel the urban computing applications, road networks, addresses/point-of-interests (POIs), and regions are the most commonly used ones. Road networks are the critical infrastructure supporting the mobility activities within a city, POIs and regions represent places and areas where people live, work, consume and live, respectively. These urban data types all involve some spatial information and thus they are called spatial urban data. There are two issues that need to be solved first before the power of spatial urban data can be fully unleashed for urban computing applications. The first one is the data completeness issue, i.e., spatial urban data is sometimes not complete and/or lack of some useful information. For example, the road networks data from OpenStreetMap (OSM), which is mainly contributed by volunteers, is far from being complete. Another example is that the delivery location information of an address, i.e., the location at which a parcel is delivered by a courier to the address, is usually inferred via a Geocoding procedure and not always accurate. The second one is the data representation issue, i.e., spatial urban data needs to be first embedded before it can be fed to machine learning models in urban computing applications yet there is no standard practice for embedding spatial urban data. Motivated by this, this project aims to develop new data-driven techniques for augmenting and representing/embedding spatial urban data. Specifically, this project will develop techniques for augmenting road networks and addresses and for representing road networks, POIs and regions. Compared with existing solutions, some techniques to be developed will be the first of their kind (e.g., those for road networks augmentation) and some others will be more advanced (e.g., they consider more views of the data and/or adopt newer network architectures/learning frameworks). These techniques will be immediately applicable to various urban computing applications that involve spatial urban data, including arrival time estimation, road traffic inference, route planning, customer availability prediction, region function analysis, and the region popularity prediction.
kw: Urban computing; spatial urban data; augmentation; representation learning

title: AI-driven Low Latency Volumetric Media Delivery with 5G Networks
abs: The last 18 months have seen a significant transformation of many activities as people reinvent their way of life given constraints such as social distancing and remote work. Volumetric media is one emerging media format that provides a highly immersive and interactive user experience for many applications. Different from traditional 2D and 360-degree videos, a volumetric video consists of a three dimensional (3D) representation of objects, enabling users to watch a scene from various directions, i.e., with six-degrees-of-freedom (6DoF). While volumetric media has great potential for new applications (e.g., remote medicine, real estate, tourism, historical spaces preservation, entertainment (e.g., sports)), it introduces tremendous new challenges at all stages of media production, distribution and consumption. In the proposed project we aim to address all stages of the distribution of volumetric, immersive media. While volumetric media provides a user unheard-of fidelity to explore a scene freely from various directions, such media also require vast amounts of bandwidth for their network distribution. We plan to address these issues in the context of new, high-speed mobile networks such as 5G. While novel networks can provide high throughput, this is achieved by utilizing very high radio frequencies (e.g., mmWave at 28 GHz in Singapore). Unfortunately such radio waves have low range and poor propagation qualities, i.e., they are easily blocked by walls, buildings, and even the human body. This means that 5G cells need to be densified and a mobile user will constantly switch between cells, and even worse, sometimes alternate between 4G (or 5G/6GHz) and 5G/28GHz. Often when a user enters a building her mobile device will need to urgently switch to WiFi (high speed WiFi 6), or 5G microcells/femtocells need to be deployed close by or indoors. So while we can expect some very high peak bandwidth there will also be significant volatility and a large difference between the minimum and maximum bandwidth that a user may experience. We will focus on four key challenges in the distribution of volumetric media, given the new network realities. Therefore, the goals of this project are to address four main interrelated task areas (T1-T4) holistically together: how to (T1) optimally package 6DoF media to allow (T2) flexible and robust quality adaptations under extremely (T3) varying bandwidth conditions (5G, 4G, WiFi 6) and with (T4) very low latency. The research will be built upon a foundation of novel packaging standards such as the Common Media Application Format (CMAF), HTTP adaptive streaming (HAS), and AI-driven adaptation algorithms. The PI and his team have previously built adaptive bitrate algorithms based on self-organizing maps (SOM), game theory and reinforcement learning. title: An integrated genomic, epidemiological and intervention program for NPC early diagnosis, stratified therapeutics and prevention
abs: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) is a head and neck malignancy around the surface and line of the nasopharynx. NPC has remarkable geographic distribution, with high prevalence in Southern China and Southeast Asia. Patients diagnosed with early-stage NPC have excellent long-term prognosis with a ten year survival rate above 90%, whereas patients with advanced disease harbor a higher risk of metastatic relapses (~20-30%). Unfortunately, due to the lack of specific clinical presentations, most patients are diagnosed with late-stage disease and suffer from poor survival. Multiple factors including genetic susceptibility, EBV infection and environmental carcinogens have been implicated in NPC tumor formation and progression. Our group and some others have discovered 7 human susceptibility genes (explaining ~10% of overall risk) and two high-risk EBV variants (contributing 80% of overall risk) for NPC in Southern China. These discoveries have prompted us to investigate whether: 1) NPC development is also driven by specific EBV strains in Singapore and Southeast Asia 2) EBV risk variants/strains can be used as biomarkers to empower family/population screening and early diagnosis of NPC 3) EBV variants/strains can be used as biomarkers for personalized treatment and response monitoring 4) BALF2 can be used as a target to design RNA molecules such as vaccine candidates against EBV risk strains for NPC therapeutics and prevention. We propose an integrated program that will combine basic research on EBV and NPC genomics with translation research on family and population screening for early diagnosis, biomarker discovery for treatment monitoring, and NPC prevention through RNA vaccination against EBV risk strains. We believe that these efforts will not only improve patient stratification for recurrence risk and personalized treatment for better survival but also further transform NPC into a disease of an early-stage diagnosis type with an excellent cure rate through population screening and early diagnosis.

title: TAckling & Reducing Glaucoma Blindness with Emerging Technologies (TARGET)
abs: Glaucoma, the leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide, is primarily a disease of the elderly afflicting >110 million people worldwide. Population-based studies have found that glaucoma is a major cause of visual impairment and blindness in Singapore. The healthcare burden for managing glaucoma in Singapore is several billions of dollars annually; this will rise further due to aging and increased life expectancy. Despite the significant research progress made over the past decades, there remains outstanding clinical and research gaps that result in at least 20% of patients with glaucoma still going blind from the disease. This proposal will address the 5 key challenges that we believe will make a significant contribution to reducing avoidable glaucoma blindness in Singapore and worldwide: (1) the pathobiology of glaucoma remains poorly understood; (2) there are high rates of undetected glaucoma (in Singapore, 70% are currently undiagnosed); (3) We are unable to accurately identify which patients are at greatest risk of progression to blindness; (4) Adherence to glaucoma eyedrop medications is poor; (5) Existing intraocular pressure lowering treatments fail to halt disease progression adequately in many patients. The main objective of this TARGET proposal is to address these unmet clinical needs through a broad-based, inter-linked multi-disciplinary “bench to bedside” approach. We propose to develop innovative methods and technologies to identify and more effectively treat individuals who are most at risk of vision loss from glaucoma. Our program will investigate genetic and molecular mechanisms underlying glaucoma, establish better ways for community screening, develop improved methods to identify rapid progressors who are at highest risk of blindness, and advance novel medical, laser and surgical treatments for glaucoma. Our overriding long-term goal is to make a significant impact toward reducing avoidable vision loss from glaucoma globally; and specifically, to reduce glaucoma blindness in Singapore by 30% in 10-years.

title: Investigating neuronal mechanisms of obesity and its treatment by bariatric surgery for future therapeutic strategy
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Survival pressure leads to a co-evolution between the human brain and the digestive tract, yet this elegant co-evolutionary outcome is now challenged by our over-engineered modern society, which leads to increasing worldwide prevalence of obesity and metabolic disorders that represent a major social economic challenge. How to harness the gut-brain communication to regulate metabolic health is an important yet poorly understood field. Bariatric surgery represents the most effective treatment for obesity and diabetes, but the mechanism is still unclear, and the complicated surgery makes this option not easily accessible to general population. Initially thought to be due to restricted food intake, more studies revealed profound changes in nutrient sensing, gut hormonal secretion and sensing by the central nervous system and also perception of palatable food, all of which indicate a dramatic change in the gut-brain axis in sensing and perceiving nutrients. However, it’s still poorly understood how and what neural circuits are changed so that multiple aspects of food perception and consumption behaviors are altered in obesity and rescued by bariatric surgery. Through a combination of cutting-edge multimodal imaging tools and genetic sequencing in mouse models, we hope to provide a neuronal perspective of both the detrimental impact of obesity and the beneficial effect of bariatric surgery. We will utilize our custom-built whole-brain imaging and analysis system to examine the input-output change of major hypothalamic feeding regulation neurons (specific aim 1), and examine how the brain-wide neuronal response to palatable food is changed in obesity and after bariatric surgery (specific aim 2); we will also investigate the change of genomic profiles of major ganglia neurons (specific aim 3) for bridging the knowledge gap in gut-brain axis and better designing future therapeutic interventions. The proposed study will fully utilize our world-leading research systems in studying neural regulation of metabolism and will lead to future collaboration possibilities for local neurometabolic community (i.e. new mouse lines, collaboration on neuro-immune or neuro-microbiota crosstalk). Successful completion of this proposal will strengthen Singapore’s position in metabolic research, which aligns well with the national interest of metabolic diseases in RIE2025. Through this proposal, some younger generation scientists will also be nurtured for Singapore’s future research.

title: Deciphering the mechanism(s) underlying adipose tissue remodelling in secondary lymphedema
abs: Secondary lymphedema is a chronic and debilitating clinical condition caused by impaired lymphatic transport leading to the accumulation of lymph in the subcutaneous tissue. The major cause of secondary lymphedema is cancer surgery and radiotherapy. It is becoming more common owing to increasing cancer rates and is estimated to occur in 24-49% of cancer patients after receiving cancer treatment. Progression of lymphedema involves the extensive swelling of the regional tissues and the self-perpetuating cycle of adipose tissue expansion, inflammation and fibrosis. To date, there is no cure or disease-modifying therapies for this chronic and progressive condition causing discomfort, impaired mobility and ultimately a poor quality of life in lymphedema patients. Therefore, there is a need to better understand the mechanisms underlying the tissue transformations of lymphedema to identify potential new therapeutic targets. Based on our previous work revealing the critical role of lymphatic drainage in preventing cholesterol interstitial accumulation and our preliminary data contained herein on human pathophysiology of lymphedema, we hypothesize that as a consequence of impaired lymphatic drainage, the undrained cholesterol from the affected tissue results in adipose cholesterol overload which leads to unhealthy adipose tissue expansion and subsequently adipose dysfunction, inflammation and fibrosis. Specifically, we propose to characterize the phenotypical and functional changes of adipose tissue in lymphedema by interrogating the morphology and the function of adipose tissue in tissue biopsies from healthy and lymphedema subjects presenting in early and chronic stages of the disease (Aim .1). Since we have preliminary evidence that lymphatic insufficiency in lymphedema patients is associated with cholesterol accumulation in the affected tissue, we will assess whether cholesterol accumulation mediates unhealthy expansion of adipose tissue in lymphedema (Aim. 2). As a first approach, we will test whether lipid-rich lymph from lymphedema patients can alter healthy adipocyte in vitro. In a second approach, we will investigate whether removing cholesterol from tissue can reverse adipose tissue expansion and the other pathological changes such as swelling, inflammation and fibrosis in lymphedema. In a proof-of-concept study, we will assess the application of cyclodextrin, a nontoxic drug in humans that has been shown to solubilize cholesterol and improve reverse cholesterol transport in experimental atherosclerosis. We have preliminary evidence that cyclodextrin can restore lymphatic drainage in mouse. The effect of cyclodextrin on lymphedema will be investigated in preclinical mouse models simulating the pathophysiology of human secondary lymphedema, and ex vivo in human lymphedema tissue explants. title: Scalable Production of Energy Efficient Flexible Aerogels and Aerogel Composites for Thermal Insulations
abs: Aerogels are a class of advanced ultralight nanomaterials with a high degree of porosity, high specific surface area, lower density, and unparalleled thermal insulation performance. With lower thermal conductivity than any known solid materials on the planet. Aerogel materials can deliver thermal insulation performance several times better than any conventional material (lower the thermal conductivity, better the thermal insulation performance). Besides thermal insulation, aerogel's impressive properties can also serve numerous other markets in energy storage, drug delivery, filtration, separation, and wound care and fire protection. Aerogels can be produced in various forms such as blankets, boards, film, and particles. Aerogels can be divided into three categories based on their composition - (i) inorganic aerogels: made from silica, metal oxides; (ii) organic aerogels: made from polymer and carbon; (iii) aerogel composites: made from a combination of both inorganic and organic precursors. Owing to their outstanding insulating properties, silica aerogels are the most common and widely studied aerogels. Currently, silica aerogels are produced in the form of non-flexible forms such as monoliths, blankets, nanoparticles, and boards. This resulted in poor mechanical properties, high production costs, excessive usage of hazardous solvents, and dust formation during commercial usage. The flexible aerogel mats available commercially and researched have high thermal conductivities limiting their applications as high-temperature insulation material. To overcome these issues, this project will focus on the following specific aims to fabricate the flexible aerogel and aerogel composites with high mechanical and low thermal conductivity: 1. To develop a novel and scalable process to fabricate flexible aerogel and aerogel composites. 2. To impart structural integrity, flexibility, and mechanical strength to silica aerogels through novel formulation and fabrication techniques. 3. To apply advanced material chemistry to formulate completely eco-friendly non-toxic dustless aerogel products 4. To fabricate a flexible aerogel mat prototype of 50 cm * 30 cm with a thickness range from 2 mm to 30 mm for commercial usage with high mechanical tensile strength >1 MPa and thermal insulation properties of thermal conductivity (Tc) < 0.023 W/m. K. The electrospun nanofibers exhibited high mechanical strength but their application in silica aerogel was not explored much. The project team had expertise in electrospinning and produced different polymeric, metal-oxide, and composite nanofibers. In addition, EWTCOI developed a commercial continuous electrospinning machine and patented (Patent no.: WO2015034431A1) for the production of various polymeric nanofibers. title: Topological Polymers
abs: This project aims at developing “Topological Polymers”. Conventional polymers such as plastics, fibres and rubbers are electrical insulators. This limitation was broken by developing π building units to prepare a new type of polymers, i.e. semiconducting polymers in 1970s. The resulting polymers are π-conjugated, possess linear chains with extended π overlap along the backbone and reduce the band gap to become semiconductors. This discovery breaks through the paradigm of traditional polymers (Alan J. Heeger, Alan G. MacDiarmid and Hideki Shirakawa were awarded with Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2000 “for the discovery and development of conductive polymers”). Despite the progress in polymer chemistry during the past one century, none of polymers has been discovered to show topological properties and functions. Topology is a branch of mathematics to study properties of objects that are invariant under smooth deformations. Materials which are invariant in properties under topological transformations are called topological materials. These materials are quantum materials with the existence of Majorana, Weyl and Dirac fermions and are identified as topological insulators, Weyl or Dirac semimetals and topological superconductors. Since their unique electronic states are applicable to various game-changing technologies including the fault-tolerant quantum computation, searching for topological materials is one of the central challenges in chemistry, physics and materials science. Topological materials are characterized by an electronic band structure that exhibits a special band topology to possess topologically protected surface states. The quantum states and electronic properties of the topologically protected surface states provide a rich playground to reveal fundamental interactions of correlated electrons under topological protection and are attractive for future electronic applications. For example, the linear dispersion between momentum and energy is promising for high-speed electronics, the locking of spin and momentum for spintronics and the helical nature of the electrons for low-dissipation electronics (in which helical means that the direction of motion of the electrons depends on their spin direction). For device applications, thin-film topological materials are attractive as artificial, design-specific heterostructures that interface topological materials with other functional materials, such as superconductors or ferromagnetic insulators, can be fabricated with atomic precision. Device applications that are being explored include topological field-effect transistors based on the quantum spin Hall state, which can be rapidly switched off and may be useful for low-power quantum electronics, low-power topological magnetic memory devices that exploit the spin-polarized topological surface current and perhaps most excitingly robust quantum bits (qubits) that do not suffer from decoherence.
