title: Versatile Edge-based Facility Management through AI driven Dynamic 5G Network Slicing
abs: Industrial enterprises that adopt IoT and 5G technology can reduce their costs by a third, among other competitive advantages. However, a key factor preventing the adoption of these technologies is a lack of clarity on how to proceed with implementation. We propose the development of an Industry Demonstration Platform (IDP) that demonstrates a realistic large scale industrial scenario of IoT use for facilities management, comprising and an implementation software for organisations to use as an envisioning tool. The capability of 5G technology will be enhanced by the introduction of dynamic slicing, based on artificial intelligence (AI) technology. AI will also be used to intelligently adapt the network slicing parameters and action trigger points in the edge systems, training the various parts of the IDP to respond to situations that may arise in facilities at an industrial site. Preliminary work and existing infrastructure support our capability to develop the proposed system. The significant technical development of this project between the background IP and possible translation outputs is TRL 3 to TRL 6.

title: Smart Cooling Surface Solution
abs: The Singapore Green Plan 2030 was announced as a national sustainability movement to tackle climate change and strengthen Singapore’s commitment to the United Nation’s 2030 Sustainable Development Agenda and the Paris Agreement. A key pillar of the Green Plan is “Energy Reset” which targets large-scale improvement in energy efficiency of buildings and mass market adoption of electric vehicles. One of the strategies to achieve increased energy efficiency in buildings is through the use of passive cooling technologies, thereby reducing air conditioning requirements. Solar reflective coating is an important passive cooling technology but factors such as aging, weathering, dirt accumulation and microbial and algae growth are known to reduce the effectiveness of solar reflective coatings by as much as 60% with time. Reliance on solar reflective mechanisms may also give rise to unwanted glare from reflected solar radiation and limits the colour choices of available solar reflective coatings to largely white or silver. According to the United States Department of Energy, running a vehicle’s air conditioner can increase fuel consumption by anywhere between 5% and 25%. The effect of using air conditioner is even more pronounced in electric vehicles, which can decrease driving range by as much as 40%, which is one of the major factors limiting the adoption of electric vehicles in the market. The key objective of this project is to develop an anti-infrared (IR) coating that incorporates the use of alternate IR removal mechanisms such as up-conversion and emittance enhancement in addition to the conventional IR reflecting mechanism to minimise IR transmittance. As of now, there are currently no coating products in the market that utilises the IR up-conversion process as a mode of minimising heat absorption. The performance durability of the resulting functional anti-IR coating will also be enhanced by incorporating the use of photocatalysis and anti-microbial functionalities. A cocktail of hybrid nanofillers, comprising nanoparticles of lanthanide phosphate, silicon dioxide and silver, together with metal oxide-based photocatalysts, will be dispersed in novel formulated binder systems such as silicones and polyurethanes to form the coating. The synergistic action of the different nanofillers will enable sustained high performance and tunability of properties for the functional coating to passively cool electric vehicles, automotive vehicles, commercial buildings, data centres, solar panels and greenhouses. The performance of the proposed anti-IR coating, that goes beyond using existing solar reflective mechanisms, will be benchmarked against commercially available solar reflective coatings. The proposed project will build upon three background intellectual properties (IPs) developed by this research team from Republic Polytechnic (RP), which has already been licensed out to local SMEs. title: Modelling for Prediction of Antioxidant Efficacy - Applications in edible oils
abs: Natural antioxidants are viable alternative to synthetic antioxidants in terms of oxidation-delaying effects in processed food. To meet the increasing market demand for green label as “all natural ingredients”, natural antioxidants as food preservatives have gained more popularity, but there are still many hurdles that limit their wide use. One of the greatest challenges is the great variation of natural sources, resulting in uncertain efficacy when used as food preservatives. Chemical composition is the ultimate deciding factor for the observed activity, but how to well correlate the chemical identity, consisting of hundreds of compounds in a single natural extract, with the desired activity, remains an issue needing addressed. Machine learning is able to learn different complex patterns to come up with models that predict new events with high accuracy. It has already been extensively used in drug discovery for the prediction of biological activity of single pure chemical entity, however its application in unknown chemical mixture is rather limited. Only in petroleum industry, computer-aided analysis has been used on mixture, to guide the formulation of petroleum in order to achieve ideal flash point, melting point or net heat of combustion. Machine-learning adopted in antioxidant extracts is rather scarce. A variety of natural extracts, such as green tea, rosemary, oregano and grape seeds, have already been applied to edible oil or other processed food as preservative. Our previous study has demonstrated that rosemary extract was as effective as BHT (butylated hydroxytoluene) in protecting fish oil from oxidation. To further our effort in bringing more natural antioxidants as preservative to food products, we turn to machine learning algorithms that are able to predict the peroxide value, a diagnostic parameter of oil oxidation, by importing the relevant chemical information of natural extracts. The proposal aims to deliver machine learning algorithms that accurately predict the antioxidant efficacy of natural antioxidants in edible oil, and also one or more formulations that could best protect oil from oxidation at the lowest cost. Specifically, 8 common natural extracts are to be permuted to generate 255 formulations, singly or in combination, which would be added to rice bran oil. The bench mark for oxidation protection would be the combined use of tocopherol and BHT. These 255 formulations will be evaluated for their chemical properties that are most relevant to the antioxidant efficacy in oil, i.e. total phenolic content, total carotene content, total antioxidant capacity and lipid solubility. The oil’s oxidation stability would be assessed using peroxide value after an accelerated experiment. These data are imported to Python with the scikit-learn package. title: Thermal Insulative Building Envelope with Silica Aerogel Additives
abs: With its tropical equatorial climate, Singapore faces the challenge of adequate building cooling, as air-conditioning forms a significant part of building electricity consumption. It is estimated that up to 80% of a building’s energy consumption can be saved, through the use of high-performance insulation and energy-efficient systems. Building envelope design is a specialised area of architectural and engineering practice. A building envelope is the separation between the interior and the exterior environments of a building, and serves to protect the indoor environment and facilitate its climate control. To improve energy efficiency, insulation materials are applied as coatings to the building envelope to reduce thermal transfer. An ideal coating solution would have a low k-value (low thermal conductivity), high thermal emissivity (rapid cooling of heat built-up on external surfaces), is colour-insensitive (no performance variation between light or dark coloured paints) and exhibits high mechanical strength, while still being thin and low-cost enough for economic feasibility. The various existing solutions do not fulfil all the above requirements. We propose to develop a heat insulative building envelope for sustainable buildings, in which a super insulation additive, silica aerogel (SA) powder, has been incorporated into thermal insulative paint and cementitious plaster. Aerogel is the world’s lightest solid material and it exhibits the lowest thermal conductivity, resulting in previously unattainable insulating performance, among other useful properties. However, as an insulation additive incorporated into paint and plaster, its fragile structure results in reduced compressive strength. Its hydrophobic but oleophiliac nature results in weak bonding to paint and plaster. In addition, it is a high cost material that is currently unfeasible for industry adoption. We intend to adapt SA for use in energy efficient building envelope products. Our SA will be fabricated with waste material to reduce costs by up to 50~60%. It will be treated with fluorinated silanes to obtain omniphobic silica aerogel (OSA) with super hydrophobic and oleophobic properties. It will be reinforced with glass fibre for improved compressive strength. The technical feasibility of this approach has been demonstrated by preliminary data. The proposed developed OSA-incorporated water-based paint, and glass fibre-reinforced SA aggregate cementitious plaster will be applied to the building envelope on real sites. Pending successful materials characterisation and optimisation, we will scale up a manufacturing trial run, and test-bed to validate the technology for energy efficient building insulation. By reducing building energy consumption, our project will have a positive impact on the building and construction industry, as well as being aligned with Singapore’s roadmap for securing our energy future and addressing climate change challenges. title: EXPLORING SLEEP AS A THERAPEUTIC TARGET FOR IMPROVING OUTCOMES AFTER ACQUIRED BRAIN INJURY
abs: Trauma and stroke are the 2 commonest causes of acquired brain injuries (ABI), together contributing 25% of the total disability-adjusted life years (DALYs). Advances in acute treatment modalities have significantly improved survival and reduced mortality rates, leading to a growing community of survivors living with permanent physical cognitive and neurobehavioral impairments. Hence, there is a critical need to improve neuropsychiatric outcomes after ABI and reduce overall disability in these patients. Sleep is a fundamental neurobiological behaviour that is vital for normal functioning of the central nervous system and is postulated to have a restorative function that is important for optimal cognitive functioning. Sleep disturbances are highly prevalent after ABI, but the prevalence and nature of abnormal sleep following ABI and the associations with clinical outcomes remain inadequately characterized. Our study aims to explore the possibility of abnormal sleep as a therapeutic target to improve outcomes after ABI by recruiting a sample of ABI subjects and age and gender-matched healthy controls, and following them up prospectively for 12 months post-injury with both subjective and objective sleep measurements. We will first measure the prevalence of the different types of sleep disturbances as measured by the different modalities, then examine the strength of the association between abnormal sleep and neuropsychiatric outcomes such as mood, anxiety, cognitive function and quality of life. We will then explore the neuroimaging characteristics associated with abnormal sleep to identify possible neuroanatomical substrates that will generate hypotheses for future research. Results from our study will potentially change clinical practice by providing a basis for the evaluation and treatment of sleep disturbances in the early stages of ABI, and will also provide crucial preliminary data for future interventional trials.

title: Noise-immune Wireless Biosensors based on Nonlinear Parity-Time Symmetry
abs: Wireless biosensors provide the opportunity to detect medical conditions wherever and whenever they occur. The use of such sensors to monitor physiological signals on and within the body, however, is often limited by our ability to wirelessly extract data from the sensors. In particular, many biosensors currently in clinical use – including smart contact lenses and implantable pressure sensors – are based on a wireless and battery-free architecture in which the sensor is remotely interrogated at radio-frequencies using an external device. This process introduces fundamental constraints on the size, range, and sensitivity of the sensor in order to detect the signal over noise. This proposal aims to overcome these constraints using concepts in nonlinear parity-time symmetry. Recent breakthroughs have shown that linear parity-time symmetry can greatly enhance the sensitivity of certain wireless sensors, although the utility of such concepts have been limited by the amplification of noise. We aim to study the interaction of noise with nonlinear PT-symmetry and create new biosensor architectures that exploit these effects to robustly detect physiological parameters in the presence of noise. These architectures will used to realize new sensor designs, including a wearable noise-robust physiological sensor and a wireless and battery-free wound sensor. If successful, this research will address long-standing challenges in wireless sensing in noisy biological environments, and open new opportunities to harness the miniaturization of electronics to address challenges in healthcare.
kw: Sensors, nonlinear systems, parity-time symmetry, wireless technology

title: Two-dimensional Organic Dirac Quantum Materials
abs: The discovery of graphene triggered an immense research effort in the field of two-dimensional (2D) crystals. Graphene consisting of a single layer of carbon atoms arranged in the honeycomb lattice has led to Dirac Cone band crossings and the emergence of a new paradigm of quantum relativistic phenomena and novel device characteristics.1 However, the absence of an energy gap in graphene has motivated the researchers to search other 2D Dirac-like quantum materials beyond graphene that offer a greater degree of tunability and a non-zero bandgap while retaining high carrier mobility, or 2D flatlands with non-trivial quantum states and quantum effects, which would open new frontiers for both fundamental research and quantum technological development. Graphene also can be considered as one prototype 2D polymer (or 2D covalent organic frameworks-2D COFs). 2D polymers are a rather new family of synthetic 2D crystals where molecular units are stitched together with strong bonds. Among them, 2D organic frameworks with particular topologies (such as honeycomb, Kagome, Kagome-honeycomb lattice) have drawn increasing attention as they often possess intriguing electronic structures and exotic quantum states/phenomena arising from topology-controlled Dirac Cones or flat bands, which constitute a new class of 2D organic Dirac quantum materials (2D-ODQMs). Therefore, 2D-ODQMs with regular crystal lattices can be constructed to comprise all collective phenomena that are known from solid-state physics, however, with a much richer diversity due to the essentially infinite number of molecules that can be considered.5 Despite rapid progress, there are several challenges to be addressed: (i) 2D-ODQMs including honeycomb and Kagome lattices have been reported but, in most cases, experimentally demonstration of their intriguing electronic properties and exotic quantum states/effects have not yet been achieved; (ii) One of the grand challenges that remain to be solved is to develop a new on-surface synthetic route that allows for the coupling of the rationally designed molecular building blocks into highly crystalline 2D-ODQMs in a relatively large domain. The ability to form large domains with high crystallinity serves as the precondition for the investigation of the intriguing quantum properties of 2D-QDQMs; (iii) The intermediate organic radicals are typically chemically reactive, thus prevent the large-size domain growth. It therefore remains a significant challenge to design and synthesize stable organic radical building blocks for the construction of stable 2D covalent organic radical frameworks with different quantum states/phases via engineering the desired topologies. title: Mechanochemical Synthesis of High Electron Affinity Curved Nanographenes
abs: The goal of this proposed research is to reduce the use of environmentally unfriendly, hazardous, and costly organic solvents in the manufacturing of nanographenes (well-defined cutouts of graphene with nano-scale dimensions). We will apply eco-friendly and solvent-free mechanochemical synthesis methods to achieve this goal. In targeting nanographenes, we will focus on the curved structures with potential to be used as electron acceptors in organic electronic devices. This will allow us to have novelty on two different levels: application of mechanochemical synthesis to electron deficient nanographenes. These novelties will be crucial in protecting the intellectual properties generated through this project. Finally, our goal is to transfer the knowledge to the energy sector of Singapore to realize the full-scale potential of the developed processes and the utility of the final materials. The specific aims of this project, therefore, are as follows: I) Development of general mechanochemical methods for the synthesis of nanographenes with a molecular curvature. II) Studying the properties and applications of the curved nanographenes. III) Protecting the intellectual properties and developing collaborations with the sustainable energy sector of Singapore to transfer the generated knowledge and realize the real-life applications.

title: Friction and Order: Great Powers and Globalizing China 1854-1949
abs: The most pressing geopolitical issue of our time is clear: how can China fit into a global ‘rules-based order’? This question is not new. What is new is that this time China will play the decisive role in answering it, from a position of strength. But how it does so will be heavily influenced by the baggage of history it set on its shoulders – because the last time the question arose, China found itself in a position of weakness. For more than a century, from 1839 to 1949, China was the object of efforts by foreign Great Powers to answer that question. They tried to do this by fitting China into a new, truly global order of geopolitics, on their terms. The Communist Party of China now describes this experience in a state narrative that lies at the very centre of its claim to legitimacy. This was ‘the century of humiliation,’ defined by the imposition on China of the ‘unequal treaties’ and all that flowed from them. The narrative runs in four parts. First, a declining Qing China was exploited by rapacious foreign powers that sought crass commercial advantage from Chinese weakness. Second, Chinese efforts to push back produced only the age of ‘high imperialism’: a systematic international effort to dismantle the very long-standing regional Sinic Order and pull China into a new global order – organized around Western principles and built by Western imperialism and power. Third, this led to China being carved up in territorial, political and economic terms, exploited while being globalized. Fourth, from 1911 China gradually overcame this coercion, navigated through its own internal turmoil, expelled foreign influence, and restored its sovereign integrity and agency. By establishing the Peoples Republic, China finally ‘stood up.’ This narrative is subjected to relentless complicating and questioning by scholars, at least outside China. But the vast scope of the question has created a problem. Studies of modern international relations, imperialism, globalization and geopolitics are daunting worlds of their own, with layers of themes and connections. Trying to combine the study of China’s history with such studies of global ordering has produced a serious imbalance. For too long, too many have approached this problem by trying to apply specific expertise on a regional question to draw wider conclusions about a global question. These vast questions have often been engaged within silos of research. Specialists in Chinese history discuss Western imperial behaviour in China, and regarding China, without often knowing very much about the Western entities they discuss. Where, for example, did the Opium War fit into global British policy in the 1840s? Looking at that problem only from vantage points located in East Asia will not answer that question, because global British policy was made in London by people looking at problems ranging far beyond China. title: A rapid, non-destructive and on-site method for the determination of nitrite, nitrate and heavy metals content in edible bird’s nest (EBN) using near Infrared Spectroscopy (NIRS).
abs: Edible bird’s nest (EBN) is widely consumed as functional food which is believed to have many medicinal properties and nutritional values. However, in recent years many alarming food safety issues associated with EBN e.g. presence of high nitrate and nitrite contents and contamination of heavy metals were highlighted. Current conventional methods for investigating nitrate, nitrite and heavy metals content in EBN are based on wet chemical analysis which are relatively expensive and time-consuming. The aim of this project is to study the use of NIRS for the detection of nitrate, nitrite and heavy metals concentration and further identification of the spectral basis of the calibration. In this work, the prediction models were developed by chemometric analysis of the NIR spectra using Partial Least Square regression algorithms. Once calibrated, the platform was used to predict samples acquired in the market and validation was performed by comparing results with those obtained from the chemical analysis. The NIRS technique will provide a rapid and non-destructive method with reliable results in the determination of nitrite, nitrate and heavy metals content in EBN.

title: Multi-purpose Hybrid Aerial-Terrestrial Autonomous Robots
abs: In this project, we aim to develop a multi-purpose hybrid aerial-terrestrial autonomous robot system that is configurable for different industry needs. This system consists of a pair of tethered autonomous aerial and ground robots, an intelligent tether winding control system and integrated power management system. The physical tether link between aerial robot and ground robot serves three purposes, 1) the aerial robot draws power from the ground robot via the tether link, 2) information can be exchanged between aerial and ground robots securely via a dedicated communication link, 3) constraining an uncontrollable aerial robot in case of system or motor failure. The aerial robot will be stored internally within the ground robot and integrated power management system is put in place to guarantee uninterrupted power supply to both robots. The aerial robot is also equipped with modular payloads such as inspection camera or scanning LIDARs for different functions. The tethered aerial and ground robots collaboratively perform mapping and localization by fusion of aerial and ground sensory data, including 2D LIDAR scan, 3D pointcloud, wheel and visual odometry, using a multirobot, multimodal SLAM (Simultaneous Localization And Mapping) algorithm. Consensus algorithm will also be developed to coordinate the control action of the aerial and ground robots for joint navigation and trajectory planning. Besides performing the typical tasks on ground, the tethering concept enables the ground robot to reach to a higher altitude to perform tasks such as stock counting, high ceiling inspection using the tethered aerial robot.

title: Automated Multimodal Pain Detection for Paediatric Patients Using AI
abs: Specific Aims: This research aims to design and develop an automatic multimodal AI system to detect pain level of a paediatric patient based on facial expression, body activities, and physiological measures. Hypotheses: Pain management is a fundamental aspect of clinical care. However, pain assessment for paediatric patients is very challenging, as they are unable to communicate their pain level effectively. Currently, observer-based pain assessment is being used in hospitals for paediatric patients pain assessment. however, observer-based approach is very labor-intensive and inaccurate. Inspired by the the successful application of AI in facial expression and posture detection, and the success of physiological measure in pain assessment, a fully automatic multimodal AI pain detection system is proposed with data fusion of facial expression, body activities, and physiological measures. Methodology: The proposed system consist of the following major modules: facial expression detection, body activity detection, and integration of physiological measures. 1. Facial expression detection: Firstly, facial landmarks are extracted from a sequence of frames. After that, perspective transform is applied to the images so that they are aligned properly. And then, a spatial-temporal convolutional neural network is used to extract the facial express of the patient. 2. Body activity detection: To overcome the challenges of having limited facial datasets, we propose to increase the dimension of our solutions, by including body activity and physiological measures into the hybrid model approach, to improve the performance of the deep learning model. A real-time pose estimation system was adopted for pose detection. The posture information will feed into our hybrid model to improve pain estimation performance. 3. Fusion of physiological measures: Recent research works have shown that physiological measures may also play an important role in determine the pain level of a paediatric patient, for instance: blood volume pulse (BVP), electrocardiogram (ECG), and skin conductance level (SCL). The above-mentioned physiological measures can be obtained using medical grade wearables. Feasibility Study Done: 1. A proof-of-concept pilot study was conducted in KKH on 26 patients presenting for major gynaecological surgery. The pain intensity estimation mobile application demonstrated 20% improvement in performance when compared to alternate approaches (Area Under the Curve (AUC) = 0.83 for estimating high versus low pain) . 2. title: Intelligent and Sustainable Container-Based Aquaponics System
abs: Food security is a major concern worldwide. Singapore imports over 90% of its food. To ensure a resilient food supply, Singapore Food Agency identified three local food productions (i.e., eggs, fish, and leafy vegetables); Singapore Parliament announced to raise the food self-production level from the current 10% to 30% of total food needs by 2030. Most local commercial farms produce either fish or vegetables and are in permanent agricultural sites. Hence, they are inflexible and unportable. Shipping container farming is increasingly popular; however, majority grows only vegetables. Two containerised aquaponics farms exist, but their container designs are tailored for overseas climate and their farm operations remain laborious, time-intensive, and costly due to limited adoption of digital technologies. To fill these gaps and, with the motivation of accelerating local food production, while maximising the scarce resources of land, water, and labour, we propose to design and develop an innovative intelligent and sustainable Container-based Aquaponics System (CAS) for healthy and liveable Singapore. Singapore Institute of Technology (SIT), Temasek Polytechnic (TP), and Metro Farm Pte Ltd will jointly accomplish three specific aims. (1) We will design and construct a two-storey container-based multi-loop aquaponics system appropriate for Singapore’s tropical climate. The multi-loop aquaponics allows flexibility to separate or join aquaculture and hydroponics, strengthening economic feasibility. Passive design strategies towards high-performance CAS will be incorporated. Semi-transparent building-integrated photovoltaics panels for solar energy production will be installed over crops. (2) We will monitor, control, and automate aquaponics operations using reliable green Internet of Things (IoT). A cyber-physical system with sleep scheduling mechanism and selective sensing will be implemented. A IoT dashboard with widgets regulating water quality and microclimate data will be created. (3) We will optimise fish and vegetable yields through precision water and nutrient management with Artificial Intelligence (AI). Multi-parameter aquaponics data will be analysed using descriptive and inferential statistics and machine learning algorithms. AI-driven optimisation models for fish and vegetable yields, and predictive and prescriptive models of CAS behaviour will be derived. Notifications and early warnings, with failure prevention recommendations, will be established. Laboratory testing and analysis will be conducted to ensure high quality and safe yields of fish and vegetables. Our high-yield and high-tech CAS can produce fresh fish (600 kg/year) and organic vegetables (4666 kg/year) simultaneously. With agrivoltaics, green IoT, and AI, the CAS can help increase productivity and efficiency, and reduce labour, operating, and environmental costs. title: Data-driven multi-scale modelling of thermal stress in additively manufactured parts
abs: Thermal stress and distortion is one of the bottleneck problems in additive manufacturing. It is critical to accurately and rapidly predict thermal stress and distortion of the additively manufactured parts, but the existing models are rather inaccurate and low-efficiency. To address these, we propose an integrated data-driven multiscale modelling approach. To ensure accuracy, we will develop physics-based multi-scale models: 1) a meso-scale thermal-stress model by implementing the accurate temperature profile and geometry of melt tracks from the meso-scale thermal-fluid flow model; 2) a macro-scale thermal-stress model for complex-shaped parts, by sequentially activating the representative elements of melt tracks with thermal strains from the meso-scale model. To improve the computation efficiency, we will utilize regression and machine learning methods to develop: 3) a data-driven surrogate model of the meso-scale temperature field to rapidly predict and transfer accurate thermal data into the meso-scale thermal-stress model;4) a data-driven surrogate model of the meso-scale thermal strain, to be implemented into the macro-scale thermal stress model. All the models will be validated by a series of experiments. In our previous works, the meso-scale thermal-fluid flow model has been proven to be accurate against the in-situ X-ray imaging observation, which forms a strong foundation for this proposal. (i) intellectual merit: To the best of our knowledge, this will be the first comprehensive multi-scale modelling of thermal stress in metal additive manufacturing with high efficiency ensured by integrating with data-driven surrogate modeling. We will achieve accurate and rapid prediction of thermal stress in additively manufactured parts, which is currently absent. (ii) broader impact: the accurate and rapid prediction of thermal stress in additively manufactured parts, is an urgent need and will greatly facilitate the wide applications of additive manufacturing in various industries, e.g., aerospace and marine sectors. A bunch of software companies will be very keen to commercialize this intellectual property.

title: Nanofluidic transport in sub-nanometer channels
abs: Nanofluidics – the study of transport of water and ions at the scales of few nanometers – has spurred a revolution in the last few years due to availability of new materials and experimental techniques. When confinements reach scales of several nanometers (or less the nanometer) the continuum hydrodynamics and electrodynamics breaks down and molecular and interfacial details become important. Reduced dimensions lead to new phenomena, such as strong water flow enhancement, increased charge selectivity, edge current enhancements, dehydration effects, low-dielectric water phase, etc. Many biological processes depend on transport of ions and water in extreme confinement, smaller than hydration shell of ions, where only few layers of water molecules could fit in. Related biological structures – such as aquaporin water channels and piezo mechanosensitive sensors – have impressive properties unmatched by artificial counterparts. In this project we will investigate nanofludics transport at the extreme, sub-nanometer confinement scales that has been inaccessible until recently, employing unique physical model system – ultra-clean, atomically smooth graphene nanochannels with height as low as 0.7 nm. In our laboratory, we have developed a method for fabricating such nanochannels with height ranging from 0.7 nm to 30 nm. Using this unique nanofluidic system, we have recently observed a curious phenomenon – as the channels become narrower, instead of dropping, mobility of different ionic species progressively increases, reaching value that is many times higher than in the bulk. We showed that this phenomenon of mobility engineering could be used to develop new type of ion exchange devices for osmotic energy harvesting. Within this project, we will investigate ionic transport in sub-nanochannels – exploring different structures, and physical and chemical environment – to understand the curious phenomena with far-reaching implications. Additionally, we will test two hypotheses: (a) ionic transport is affected by water ordering in extreme confinement; and (b) ions in nanochannels is affected by structures and electronic properties of particular 2D materials. To address this challenge, we will rely on our state-of-art nanochannel fabrication expertise, and our unique, custom-built instrumental setups: nanofludic cell with voltage and pressure driven transport, micro-pervaporation chamber, variable-temperature nanofluidic setup, multi-electrode nanofluidics system for investigating gated devices. Based on our insight is ultra-confined nanochannels, we will develop new types of active nanofluidic devices – nano-harvester for powering nanoscale devices, and ionic diode and nanofluidic switches, and demonstrate their integration in integrated in complex neuromorphic circuitry. title: Islet macrophages control inflammation and β-cell dysfunction during diabetes.
abs: We recently showed that pancreatic islet resident macrophages represent their own niche, replicating during the early phase of diabetes to support insulin secretion. These macrophages are present from the embryonic stage and are distinct from monocytes (bone-marrow derived circulatory pre-macrophages). We showed that their presence within this specific microenvironment (i.e. pancreatic islets comprising of hormonal cells, blood vessels and neurons) conferred an advantage by promoting islet remodelling and thus islet compensation in response to insulin resistance. We were the first to show that islet resident macrophages supported islet compensation during pre-diabetes. While the homeostatic role of islet macrophages in pre-diabetes is clear, the same cannot be said about late-stage diabetes. With continued peripheral insulin resistance, the systemic milieu in both humans and rodents becomes progressively pro-inflammatory leading to life-threatening complications. In such a milieu, we hypothesize that islet resident macrophages continue in its fight to mitigate stress and help islet cells cope in such a hostile environment. Eventually islets decompensate and this further exacerbates diabetes. The transition from compensating to decompensating islets needs further scrutiny for its mechanisms hold promise for novel therapeutics. Armed with new molecular tools, we are now ready to elucidate macrophage dynamics within the decompensating islet of type-2 diabetes (T2D). Our hypothesis is based on preliminary studies that show the importance of islet macrophages in keeping pro-inflammatory immune cells out of the islet and at bay. Based on our preliminary studies also propose to probe underlying mechanisms of islet macrophage and β-cells crosstalk with the pursuit of TLR4 and TGFβ-related signalling pathways in decompensating islets of T2D. We will address our hypothesis by leveraging on three current research capabilities. First, we have a mouse model that recapitulates human T2D pathogenesis closely and this includes islet decompensation with β-cell dysfunction and β-cell death. Second, we have the ability to specifically remove only islet macrophages at any timepoint during T2D pathogenesis and we can compare these islets with those having intact macrophages. Third, we can monitor immune cell movement in vivo, both into and around pancreatic islets longitudinally and non-invasively. We will briefly outline how all these three strengths feed into our experiments aimed at addressing our hypothesis. We intend to pursue three specific aims over four years. First, we aim to extend our islet macrophage phenotype analysis to include Lyve1, MHCII, CD11c, CD64, SiglecF and MertK in Db/Db -BKS.Cg-Dock7m +/+ Leprdb/J (Db BKS) mice as they deteriorate from pre-diabetes to overt diabetes. title: Chemokine control of osteoclast recruitment – new insights into bone remodelling
abs: Bone is a highly dynamic tissue that undergoes constant remodelling to maintain its structural integrity. To achieve homeostasis, extensive communication is needed between bone-forming osteoblasts and bone-resorbing osteoclasts to balance degradation of old bone matrix and formation of new bone. Deficiencies in this balance lead to bone disorders, such as osteoporosis, which is characterized by excessive osteoclast formation. Several pathways that control differentiation of macrophages into osteoclasts have been targeted for osteoporosis therapy. Importantly, however, mediators that control the recruitment of osteoclast progenitors to sites of bone remodelling are largely unknown. Chemokines have been shown to be highly expressed in osteoporotic bone but their roles in recruitment of bone progenitor cells remain unclear. A better understanding of proteins that control progenitor recruitment to bone matrix will therefore help to design novel therapeutic avenues that target recruitment rather than the activity of osteoclasts. Recently, we identified a druggable chemokine pathway with essential functions in osteoclast recruitment (Phan et al., 2020). Using a medaka fish osteoporosis model, we showed that osteoblast progenitors up-regulate expression of the chemokine ligand Cxcl9l under osteoporotic conditions while the chemokine receptor Cxcr3.2 is expressed in a distinct subset of macrophages. Live bioimaging revealed that upon Cxcl9l up-regulation, Cxcr3.2 positive macrophages get activated, migrate to bone matrix and differentiate into osteoclasts. Importantly, mutations in Cxcl9l and Cxcr3.2 impaired this macrophage recruitment and prevented osteoclast differentiation. Furthermore, Cxcr3.2 inhibition by the clinically tested chemical antagonists AMG487 and NBI-74330 also efficiently reduced osteoclast recruitment in a dose-dependent manner and protected bone integrity from osteoporotic insult (our patent No. PCT/SG2021/050147; filed 16 April 2021, see attached file). Our in vivo data therefore identified Cxcl9l and Cxcr3.2 as novel druggable regulators of bone homeostasis and osteoporosis. Importantly, our preliminary data furthermore showed that the corresponding chemokine ortholog is significantly elevated in human serum samples obtained from patients prone to develop hip fractures (see preliminary findings outlined below). In the present proposal, we therefore aim to better understand the mechanisms that lead to chemokine-induced macrophage activation. Based on our preliminary findings, we hypothesize that chemokines play essential roles in controlling bone remodelling and homeostasis. We propose the presence of distinct subsets of macrophages that besides their roles as osteoclast progenitors also serve to create a permissive environment for subsequent bone formation and repair of osteoporotic lesions. title: Immune receptor activation by a self-compartmentalized protease complex in plants
abs: Understanding how host cells detect invasive events from pathogens and trigger immune responses is a central theme in immunity research. The plant innate immune system relies on various types of immune receptors that take part in recognizing pathogenic molecules both at cell surface and within the cell. Like in animals, nucleotide-binding domain leucine-rich repeat (NLR) proteins serve as prominent intracellular immune receptors in plants in recognizing various cellular events caused by invasive pathogenic molecules, so called effectors. Despite recent progress in our understanding on NLR receptor activation by oligomerization upon effector perception, we still lack a comprehensive understanding on the kinds of host cellular processes that lead to NLR receptor activation. This knowledge is critical as most NLRs are believed to be activated upon perceiving a disturbance of cellular homeostasis by pathogenic invasion rather than directly associating with effectors. Investigation of a host factor, so called guardee, that are being monitored by a guarding NLR receptor and cellular events that the host factor governs in the cell can advance our understanding on NLR-mediated immune activation. In this proposal, we will implement an overarching research program to investigate an autoimmunity-triggering pair of plant protease and matching NLR receptor. Our preliminary data include a high-resolution cryo-EM structure of DM3 protease, showing that DM3 forms a self-compartmentalized hexameric complex. Further biochemical characterization of DM3 revealed that the complex stability affects DM2h NLR-mediated immunity and the catalytic activity of DM3 is associated with immune activation. Based on these results, we hypothesize that DM3 functions as a self-compartmentalized immune protease in the plant cell and its complex stability that affects the accessibility to catalytic site is a critical checkpoint for DM2h NLR activation. We aim to test these hypotheses by 1) defining protease function of the self-compartmentalized DM3 complex; 2) investigating the mechanism by which DM3-mediated proteolysis regulates NLR immune receptor activation; 3) characterizing DM3 immune function by identifying matching effectors. Complimentary approaches covering cell biology, proteomics, biochemistry, structural biology and genetics will likely elucidate a comprehensive mechanistic action of the DM3 complex in the plant immune system. Together, these efforts will uncover mechanisms by which proteolytic activities are regulated during pathogen invasion in the plant cell and uncover molecular basis on how these activities lead to plant immune receptor activation. Given that proteolysis plays critical roles in the innate immune systems, defining regulatory modes of a self-compartmentalized immune protease complex within the cell will ultimately generate a tool to engineer immune responses. Future application of this knowledge is expected to improve disease resistance traits in plan

title: Quantum Modelling of Carrier Tunnelling Injection in 2D Semiconductor Device Contact Heterostructures
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: The performance of 2D semiconductor devices is sensitively influenced by the quality of their electrical contacts – a key component omnipresent in modern electronics and optoelectronics devices. Despite tremendous research efforts devoted to study the carrier injection phenomena in 2D material contact heterostructures, the physics of interfacial carrier injection in the quantum tunnelling regime remains largely incomplete thus far. This problem is further complicated by the presence of multiple fundamentally distinctive contact configurations and the highly nontrivial quantum interactions between contacting materials. In this Project, we aim to address these academic challenges by performing a combined theoretical, first-principle modellings and experimental investigations on the physics of quantum mechanical carrier tunnelling injection in 2D contact heterostructures. The charge injection models developed in this Project will be employed to improve the contact resistance modelling of 2D semiconductor nanodevices. The specific aims of this Project are: (i) To uncover the atomistic interfacial properties, such as structural, electronic and transport properties, of various 2D/2D and 2D/3D contact interfaces; (ii) To develop quantum theory of carrier tunnelling injection and contact resistance model for various 2D/2D and 2D/3D contacts, such as metal/semiconductor (MS), metal/semiconductor/metal (MSM), metal/insulator/metal (MIM), and other technologically important contact heterostructures; and (iii) To construct theoretical ‘toolboxes’ and contacts resistance ‘libraries’ that can be readily accessed by the research communities for device design, analysis, and experimental investigations. The developed charge tunnelling injection and contact resistance models will be further refined and verified in proof-of-concept experimental studies, so to concretely establish the technical soundness of this Project. The outcomes of this Project shall provide an important step forward in the fundamental understanding of 2D materials interface physics and shall offer new insights on the design of 2D semiconductor devices.

title: Towards Better Sybil Defenses in High-Throughput Distributed Systems
abs: -- Sybil attacks -- Many large-scale distributed systems today are permissionless — namely, they do not have a central authority that regulates admissions into the system. Prominent recent examples include various permissionless blockchains, as well as blockchain-based cryptocurrency systems such as Bitcoin. To join a permissionless system, any user can simply create a free identity (or id), and then run the prescribed software using that identity. We call such an instance of the software (using the given identity) as a node. A node is honest if it runs the prescribed algorithm. A node may be controlled by an adversary, in which case the node may run arbitrary malicious code and is malicious. Permissionless systems are vulnerable to sybil attacks, where the adversary creates many fake identities, all of which join the system, resulting in a large number of malicious nodes. Researchers have long recognized the importance of defending against such sybil attacks. Fundamentally, addressing sybil attacks is crucial because proper sybil defense is a prerequisite for many other security mechanisms to work. -- Resource-challenge -- An important class of sybil defense mechanisms are based on the idea of resource-challenge. These mechanisms exploit the fact that the adversary has limited resource, despite that it can create unlimited number of malicious nodes. Among this class, Proof-of-Work challenges nodes' computational resource, by asking nodes to do non-trivial computational tasks (e.g., mining in Bitcoin). Conceptually, a node's influence over the system is proportional to the number of such tasks it completes. If the adversary (i.e., all its malicious nodes) has less computational power than the aggregate computational power of the honest nodes, then the adversary will not be able to gain a majority influence. Proof-of-Space-Time and related designs challenge nodes' storage space, by requiring each node to store a non-trivial amount of data. Similarly, there have been a few initial high-level thoughts on Proof-of-Bandwidth, which challenge nodes' communication resource. (But these all lack concrete designs, let alone formal security guarantees.) -- Wasted resources -- Resource-challenge-based sybil defense designs, by definition, force all nodes (especially, including all the honest nodes/users) to consume resources. In some of the above sybil defense designs, the resource consumed is simply wasted. For example, other than serving as sybil defense, the outputs of Bitcoin mining have no meaning/value. Globally, Bitcoin mining is estimated to consume almost the same energy as the whole country of Ireland. Naturally, there have been broad concerns about such huge amount of wasted resources. Some other resource-challenge-based sybil defense designs do aim to avoid such resource waste. For example, Proof-of-Useful-Work requires nodes to search for certain prime numbers. Using the resources for such external purpose (e.g., finding prime numbers) is clearl

title: From iteration on multiple collections in synchrony to fast general interval joins.
abs: Background Comprehension syntax is widely adopted in modern programming languages, as an easy-to-use means for manipulating "bulk" data types such as lists, tables, and vectors. Comprehension syntax provides an iteration construct that is simple enough for programming with bulk data types that data objects of a relational database management system (RDMBS) have been mapped to and is explicit enough to admit a direct translation to the query language of the RDBMS, thereby permitting queries to the RDBMS to be embedded simply and naturally into a programming language. However, when queries written in comprehension syntax for manipulating these objects are not translated to the query language of an underlying RDBMS for execution, but are executed directly in the programming language, they typically correspond to nested loops. This gives rise to a disparity. Many queries when translated to their database equivalent can be executed by the underlying database system very efficiently. Yet when they are executed directly as comprehension syntax, they are not efficient. Consider this query, { (𝑥.dept, 𝑥.stf) | 𝑥 ∈ DeptStaff , 𝑦 ∈ Staff , 𝑥.stf = 𝑦.stf , 𝑦.age > 65 }, which retrieves departments and their staff who are above 65 years old. Suppose a staff belongs to only one department. This query would be a low-selectivity equijoin. It would be executed by an RDBMS via merge-join, with time complexity Θ(𝑛 +𝑚) assuming DeptStaff and Staff have size 𝑛 and 𝑚 and are both sorted by their stf field. In contrast, the same query would typically have time complexity Θ(𝑛 ∗ 𝑚) in the programming language. This linear-vs-quadratic time complexity difference of low-selectivity joins can be called an intensional expressiveness gap between comprehension syntax and an RDBMS, i.e., a gap between the algorithms expressible using comprehension syntax and an RDBMS. As far as the RDBMS is concerned, the relational join and the relational intersection and relational difference constitute the intensional expressiveness gap as all other relational query operators, in the absence of indices on the input relations, have similar time complexity whether executed in the RDBMS or in the programming language as queries in comprehension syntax. Objectives It is open whether this intensional expressiveness gap is a real gap. Our first objective is theoretical, and comprises two main subgoals. The first subgoal is to prove the intensional expressiveness gap, by showing that all subquadratic algorithms expressible in a first-order setting using pure comprehension syntax cannot compute low-selectivity joins. A follow-up question is then what exactly is missing from comprehension syntax that prevents efficient algorithms for low-selectivity joins, relational intersection, and relational difference to be expressed. title: Deep Ear for Hearables (DEHE): Applying Deep Learning Techniques for Hearing Devices
abs: Deep learning has been widely applied and tested in a range of visual, image, and speech applications, and has reached a level of accuracy and maturity suitable for real-life deployment. However, deep learning methods for extracting key information from indoor and outdoor environmental sounds remains in its infancy despite steady progress in the detection, extraction, classification, and localization of acoustic scenes and events. Sound signals carry a large amount of information regarding the everyday environment and physical events. To complement the development of hearables (i.e., assisted listening devices), it is therefore vital to also craft signal processing and deep learning methods that can automatically detect the occurrence of sound events or sound sources, extract their information (e.g., source, direction), and classify or recognize activities in the environment. With the advent of low-cost, low-power embedded processors, the information obtained from deep learning models can be integrated into hearables to transform these devices into powerful and wearable acoustic sound engines that can be used to monitor the environment and provide timely decisions for users to have greater adjustment control. However, a significant amount of research is still required to improve the reliability and robustness and reduce the power consumption and latency of smart sound sensing in realistic indoor and outdoor environments [1], where multiple sound sources are simultaneously presented and often modified. This project aims to (i) formulate a research and development (R&D) framework for devising smart sound sensing that can be implemented in real time for hearables (or headphones), and (ii) establish intelligent control and rendering features for these hearables. Some of these intelligent control and rendering features include the ability to: • selectively enhance desired sound sources (e.g., a person’s voice at a party) • attenuate noise for focused activities (e.g., for a businessman working on an airplane) • augment the acoustic environment with virtual sound objects (e.g., make a noisy environment appear more pleasant) • teleport users to another aural environment (e.g., as part of a virtual reality game) To achieve the goal of deploying lightweight deep learning models in hearables in real time while achieving their desired aural performance, we must investigate the following key research questions. • How can full deep learning models be pruned or trimmed to fit within the relatively low processing and low energy budget of hearables? • What are the most suitable deep learning models for end-to-end processing on intelligent hearables? • Can deep learning models augment conventional digital signal processing (DSP)-based methods to establish a lightweight and energy-efficient deep learning model that can be implemented into a real-time embedded solution? • Can an end-to-end integrated deep learning model be developed for all functionalities (e.g., l

title: Colour centre engineering in wide band-gap semiconductor membranes using ion implantation
abs: Colour centres are optically active defects, impurities or clusters in crystals that absorb and emit light. Colour centres are usually introduced into the crystal lattice during growth and as a result are randomly distributed. One of the only ways of creating colour centres in a controlled manner is through ion implantation. Energetic ions can be used to generate vacancies, interstitials or to dope a crystal with impurity atoms. The energy of the ion beam determines the depth at which the material modification occurs. The ability to focus and scan the ion beam enables one to directly pattern a material thus spatially controlling the distribution of colour centres. At the Centre for Ion Beam Applications (CIBA), a world leading spatial resolution of 20 nm has been achieved for mega-electron volt (MeV) ions. Wide band gap semiconductors such as diamond and boron nitride (BN) have previously been identified as suitable host crystals for colour centres. Diamond has more than 500 documented colour centres and more are still being discovered. Of these colour centres, only a few have been identified as being suitable for quantum applications. In diamond, the nitrogen vacancy centre (NV) is the most promising due to its photostability and the ability to operate at room temperature. In our own studies, we have been able to demonstrate the ability to create NV centres in bulk diamond using MeV protons. Our recent unpublished work on ion beam irradiation of BN has shown that both single photon emission and optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) can occur at room temperature. This proposal will endeavour to develop a platform technology for engineering colour centres in a spatially controlled manner using MeV ion beams in diamond and BN. Fundamental questions regarding the generation yield will be answered using a unique experimental geometry. By using thin diamond membranes or BN 2D materials, the ion beam will traverse the material and be detected behind the sample using a particle detector. This method will enable us to count every ion that has impinged on the sample thus allowing for quantification of the efficiency with which the defects are created. This cannot be achieved in bulk materials. Once the ion implantation method and diamond membrane fabrication has been optimized, two application areas will be explored. The first involves the use of ODMR for magnetic sensing and the second will focus on the electrical excitation of single photons from diamond and BN colour centres. Some prototype devices will be developed and characterized.
kw: Ion implantation, colour centres, quantum sensing, diamond, boron nitride

title: Precision reflectance sensing in noisy environments via quantum illumination
abs:
The precision measurement of a target sample's reflectance has diverse applications, including imaging, microscopy and photodetector calibration. A key technique of doing this is via illumination: we probe the target sample with coherent light and monitor the proportion that it reflects. However, many situations dictate that the energy of our probes be constrained (e.g. delicate biological samples, convert imaging), which constrains the ultimate precision (measured by mean-squared error) of our measurement. To what extent can the use of non-classical light, such as those featuring entanglement, enable enhanced precision? 

We will explore this potential by assembling teams led by Assoc.Prof Mile Gu, an established expert in quantum illumination and Assoc. Prof Gao Weibo, an experimental leader in photonic technologies. Together with a team consisting of two research fellows and one PhD student with a mix of theoretical and experimental expertise,  we will rigorously explore the role of non-classical light in precision sensing of reflectance using a combination of theory and experiment. Our objectives are to:

1. Determine the ultimate performance advantage of non-classical light in sensing reflectance to higher precisions.
2. Design protocols that can exhibit that quantum advantage and verify this advantage conclusively by experiment using present-day photonic technology.

We will organize a project into three phases of 12 months
