title: Wireless Power Transfer: The Next Generation
abs: Wireless charging technologies have reached commercialization stage since 2010 when the Wireless Power Consortium (WPC) launched the world's first wireless charging standard Qi, which has incorporated a group of inventions of the Lead PI. The first generation of Qi focused on compatibility among manufacturers of transmitter and receiver circuits in order to attract support from industry to use the same standard. The transmitter circuits and receiver circuits could be designed and made by different manufacturers without considering optimal charging performance. After 10 years of implementation, the Lead PI proposes to re-examine the current status of wireless charging technologies and shift the existing paradigm from "compatibility" to "optimal performance" in terms of energy efficiency and charging time. The Lead PI proposes that the change to the new paradigm can be achieved by shifting most of the control functions to the primary (transmitter) side so that the designs of the wireless charging pads should be responsible for optimal charging performance. This approach is feasible with the recent advancements of primary-side control method and fast method in determining the mutual coupling coefficients between the transmitter and receiver coils (also pioneered by the Lead PI). This project will explore the combined use of these ideas to develop a new set of design protocols so that the transmitter circuits and receiver circuits can always achieve both "compatibility" and "optimal performance", even if they are made by different manufacturers. The proposed technologies have the potentials of improving existing Qi and SAE standards, and could become key technologies for wireless charging standards of the next generation.
kw: Wireless power transfer, wireless charging, electronics

title: All-fibre approach for multi-photon imaging ultrafast laser development
abs: This project aims to provide a scalable technical path to attain µJ-level <100 femtosecond (fs) pulses from in-house thulium (Tm) fibre innovation for multi-photon deep-tissue imaging applications. A multi-photon imaging technique requires a fs high-pulse-energy excitation source to facilitate the three-photon absorption. Hence, a high-energy ultrafast laser at a 1.7 µm region is in high demand as an enabling light source for deepest tissue imaging in dermatology, brain study, and drug delivery monitoring, just to name a few. However, energy scaling of ultrafast fibre laser in an anomalous region is fundamentally limited by the area theorem that sets a maximum allowed energy, such as ~ 1 nJ in a 100 fs pulse in a telecom fibre. A state-of-the-art laser system utilises a rod-type large mode area (LMA) photonic crystal fibre to delay the limit, but its low conversion efficiency (<10%) saddles the system with a heavy pump source from a complex pulsed laser system. Consequently, this approach is not practical for wide adoption of the multi-photon imaging in healthcare. We will develop a normal dispersion Tm-fibre that is free from the pulse energy limit, and cultivate a molecular-level local environment for Tm ions to obtain highest optical gain in the desired multi-photon imaging wavelength. Laser dynamics in the specialty Tm-fibres will be studied in the most promising laser architectures including parabolic amplification and Mamyshev cavity under the goal of offering an affordable ultrafast laser in healthcare and biomedical study. Hence, the successful outcome will be represented as an ultracompact ultrafast fibre laser that is fully compatible to an optical microscope. The project outcomes will push local capabilities of photonics front that is in perfect accordance with Singapore’s key technology domains of precision engineering and biomedical manufacturing sectors.
kw: ultrafast fibre laser, specialty fibre, nonlinear imaging process, multi-photon imaging

title: Manufacturing PET radiopharmaceuticals using selective C-F activation
abs: Fast generation of 18F labelled aliphatic polyfluorocarbon positions is extremely challenging, but vital for synthesis of 18F PET radiotracers. As such, the wider use of many fluorocarbons in radiotracer applications is limited. Particularly the use of CF3 groups, which are commonly utilised in many synthetic biomolecules. Recently, we discovered a way to selectively activate a single fluorine atom in aliphatic polyfluorocarbons and subsequently replace it with a variety of nucleophiles, a long standing challenge in fluorine chemistry. We have since demonstrated that we can reform the polyfluorocarbon starting material by using fluoride as the nucleophile. This proposal hopes to build upon this initial proof-of-concept (which we have a patent application for) by exploring the possibilities this method offers in generating 18F PET reagents in high yield. Some of the advantages of this technique over existing technologies include the ability to substitute fluoride positions in fluorocarbon products (as opposed to introducing fluorine synthetically) and to use off-the-shelf compounds (e.g. existing drugs which contain fluorine), the introduction of 18F is done at a very late stage (normally the final step) so the radioyield of the short half-life isotopologue is maximised, the C-F activated compounds are bench stable and can be used when desired, this technique works for many different aliphatic fluorides, not only trifluoromethyl groups, and using chiral Lewis bases/acids we may be able to generate enantiomeric 18F PET reagents, which would allow a new field of research to develop. We will be developing the chemistry component of this project and working in collaboration with Dr Edward Robins and Professor Xiaoyuan Chen (NUS – Clinical Imaging Research Centre) to ascertain the radioyields of our isotopologues and study radiotracers in vivo.
kw: PET radiotracer; C-F activation; trifluoromethyl; difluoromethyl; 18F labelling

title: Revealing Nanoscale Photocatalytic Heterogeneity on 2D and its Composite Materials using Super-Resolution Microscopy
abs: Functional 2D materials have attracted extensive research attention due to the unique properties, which have been widely applied for efficient photocatalytic energy conversion and environmental purification. However, a direct visualization of the generation, diffusion and distribution of photoactive species on 2D and its composite materials at nanoscale level have been scarcely reported. In this proposal, we intend to apply super-resolution microscopy technique to investigate the photocatalytic heterogeneity on these materials. With the assistance of fluorescent probes, the distribution of the photogenerated electrons and holes on different structures of photocatalysts (e.g., interfaces, defects, edges, basal planes and wrinkles) can be identified. This would provide a deep insight into the understanding of locations of reactive sites and catalytic heterogeneity on the 2D materials. Combined with the bulk measurement, this research will construct a bridge between the catalyst structure and the photocatalytic activities. It would benefit the morphology design, defect control, surface and interface engineering of the photocatalysts, intended for a variety of photocatalytic applications.
kw: Catalysis; Spectroscopy; Renewable Energy; Sustainability and the Environment; Materials Chemistry; Multidisciplinary

title: Fabrication of large size composite structure dysprosium-doped yttria laser ceramics and high-power mid-infrared ceramic laser development
abs: Due to multi-phonon decay, mid-infrared laser oscillation critically relies on the gain material properties. Only materials with low phonon energy could be used. As low phonon energy materials normally also have low mechanical strength and low thermal conductivity, it is very difficult to obtain high-power mid-infrared laser oscillations. Although it is known that yttria has low phonon energy of ~591cm-1 and very large thermal conductivity, which is attractive for high power 3µm mid-infrared laser operation, yttria also has very high melting temperature of >2400C, which leads to the growth of yttria single crystals very challenge. Recently, we have developed a technology for fabricating high quality transparent yttria ceramics. With the technology high efficiency yttria-based laser ceramics operating at the 1 and 2µm wavelength regimes were successfully developed. In the project we will extend the technology to further fabricate yttria-based ceramics for 3µm wavelength lasers. Specifically, large size end-caped dysprosium ions (Dy3+)-doped yttria lase ceramics will be produced and the first high power Dy3+-doped 3µm ceramic lasers will be demonstrated.
kw: Transparent Ceramics; Mid-infrared lasers; Laser Ceramics; high power ceramic lasers; Composite structure laser ceramics

title: Room-temperature quantum emitters from hexagonal boron nitride
abs: Room-temperature, ultrabright single-photon emitters (SPEs) from hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) create a major paradigm shift towards applications in quantum communication and information technologies. However, microscopic origin of SPEs from hBN and large-scale fabrication of high-quality SPEs from hBN is challenging. This project aims to first decipher the atomic structures of different types of SPEs from hBN and then establish new protocols for precise atomic engineering of SPEs with controlled structure and density. Finally, we will also develop new wafer-scale growth technology and integration of SPEs from hBN with micro-cavities for improved brightness and purity, suitable for future on-chip quantum technologies.
kw: Electronic, Optical and Magnetic Materials,  Atomic and Molecular Physics, and Optics, Condensed Matter Physics, Materials Chemistry; Surfaces and Interfaces

title: Development of more robust and recyclable thermoset polymer
abs: We plan to design recyclable thermoset polymeric materials by incorporating intrinsically recyclable moieties such as -O Trimethylsilyl (-OTMS) or -O β-Methoxyethoxymethyl ether (-OMEM) protected cleavable groups that are able to undergo electronic cascade to release monomers via self-immolative release mechanisms upon activation. The monomer-releasing reaction will be done in ionic liquid, a useful green alternative to toxic organic solvents. We aim to synthesize a novel curing agent, that will lead to more robust thermoset polymer networks, by adopting the allenamide linker technology already developed in by our group, that can replace maleimide groups. Preliminary results show that allenamide can overcome the drawbacks of bismaleimide resins, such as the retro-Michael reaction or depressed glass transition temperature arising from the rotational flexibility of the thiol-maleimide adduct.
kw: Recyclable Thermoset;Circular Economy;Prodrug Mechanism

title: Phase-Change Optical Nanoantenna Enhanced Single Photon Emitters with Tunability and Chirality
inst: IMRE - Institute of Materials Research and Engineering
abs: Quantum photonics is a crucial enabler for quantum technology sector, which has a potential market of ~S$430 billion. Single photon emitters (SPEs) are indispensable in quantum photonics, akin to electrons in electronics. However, an ideal SPE with high efficiency, ultra-miniaturized footprint, transform-limited linewidth, chirality control and tunable emission still remains unrealized. Here, we will develop a SPE as integrated with phase-change optical nanoantenna with bound-states-in-the-continuum resonance, which enables a Purcell-factor enhanced, chirality controlled as well as wavelength tunable photon emission. This proposed project could potentially be used for a wide range of quantum and flat optics research activities in Singapore.
kw: Atomic and Molecular Physics, and Optics; Flat Optics; Nano Photonics; Nanofabrication; Quantum Photonics

title: Development of Sustainable Main-Group Element Catalysts for Industrial Processes
abs: Catalysis is a key technology in industry and increases the output of chemical synthesis without spending unreasonable huge amount of energy necessary in the production of new materials. In the chemistry of catalysis, a catalytic center necessitates to possess a vacant and donor coordinate site with small energy difference, which enable it to transform substrate into product through oxidative addition-insertion-reductive-elimination processes. In the periodic table, precious transition metals, namely rhodium, palladium and platinum beautifully fulfil this requirement and hence they are major industrial catalysts nowadays. However, there are drawbacks. These metals are expensive and low-abundant, leading to supply disruption. They are toxic, which cause problems when they are used to synthesize pharmaceuticals. When sustainable manufacturing is a long-term industrial goal in Singapore, fundamental research on finding an alternative to precious metal catalysts is indispensable. In this project, we develop sustainable main-group element catalysts as an alternative to precious metal catalysts. It is because main-group elements, namely boron, silicon and phosphorus are cheap, high natural abundant, balanced globally available, and low toxic. To unlock catalytic capability of main-group elements, low-oxidation state derivatives will be constructed, where they have a lone pair of electrons and a vacant orbital with small energy difference. This electronic structure is similar to that of precious metals and hence sustainable main-group elements can perform transition-metal-like reactivity in catalysis. Their performance on catalytic transformations will be compared with existing industrial catalysts. The experimental results in term of reaction condition, yield, product selectivity and TON will provide solid evidences to Singapore industry that sustainable low-oxidation state main-group element catalysts are a promising alternative, which will ease the current problems in removing toxic precious metal in production, as well as the threatening from supply disruption of “strategic’’ precious metal catalysts. Hence, high monetary saving is expected to be achieved.
kw: main-group elements; low oxidation state; transition metal-like reactivity; sustainable catalysis; industrial processes; organometallic chemistry

title: Untethered Jammable Robotic Structures Driven by Electrochemical Pneumatic Batteries
abs: The proposed research aims to create untethered, silent, safe, lightweight and energy efficient soft robotic structures enabled by jamming transition and driven by electrochemical pneumatic batteries. We will design and manufacture robotic structures with controllable stiffness and programmable actuation, powered by onboard pneumatic batteries. The proposed device can be used for joint assistance, rehabilitation, exoskeleton, and body protection applications. In particular, the device will help to address the physical needs of the aging population and patients.
kw: Jamming enabled soft robots, pneumatic battery, untethered actuation, biomedical manufacturing

title: Silicon photonic dispersion management systems for error-free transceiver (data center) communication.
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: Globally, transceiver companies serving the intra-data centre (Up to 2km), inter-data centere (10km – 80km+) and core/metro (40km – 80km+) markets need to continuously scale their bandwidths to match the burgeoning developmental pace in cloud computing services, e-commerce, supercomputing and future 5G networks. Multi-source agreements (MSAs) amongst companies allow alignment of technological strategies and architectures. MSAs including the PSM4, 100G Serial Lambda MSA/Ethernet Alliance, OpenEye, IEEE 802.3bs, IEEE P802.3cm and IEEE P802.3cn standards, are opting for Pulse Amplitude Modulation (PAM) to scale to higher data rates. The decision to adopt PAM by these companies arises from the 2x, 3x, 4x (PAM4, 6, 8 respectively) higher data rates compared to non-return-to-zero (NRZ) while maintaining direct detect schemes, significantly reducing cost, power and latency. Both NRZ and PAM data suffer for dispersion limitations, with increasing severity for higher level PAM. Without proper consideration or management for dispersion in the system, transmitted data suffers from a dispersion penalty due to the closure of the NRZ or PAM eye and increased bit error rates. Left unmitigated, the dispersion penalty causes inter-symbol interference leading to high bit error rates at the receiver and data loss. Silicon photonics dispersion management systems are a highly promising pathway towards solving dispersion impairments, allowing data transmission over longer reaches, and increases in the transmission rates for intra-data centre, inter-data centre and core/metro high speed data movement hardware. As testament to the criticality of dispersion management, the PI has previously received funding from Inphi Corporation for the development of dispersion management devices designed and tailored for use in their transceivers. This proposal aims to provide robust technological solutions to dispersion impairments, using silicon photonics-based dispersion management systems which the PI has thus far been able to demonstrate integrated systems with promising performance and record high dispersion - loss metrics.
kw: Electrical and Electronic Engineering (2208), Atomic and Molecular Physics, and Optics (3107), Silicon Photonics, Chromatic Dispersion Compensation Systems, Data Center Interconnects, High-Speed Data Movement

title: Additive manufacturing of advanced microtissue-encapsulating devices for cellular therapy
abs: Cellular therapy offers a promising avenue as a clinical cure for the treatment of protein-deficiency diseases such as insulin-dependent diabetes. Encapsulating insulin-secreting cells in a semi-permeable hydrogel protects these cells against the immune attack of a transplant recipient without the use of immunosuppressants while allowing cellular metabolic exchange. However, the cellular graft often suffers from poor survival due to the low oxygen availability at the transplant site, resulting in limited therapeutic outcome. Using a manual lithography-based fabrication process, we have previously designed a proprietary micropatterned device that improved oxygen exchange and hence increased survival of encapsulated insulin-secreting cells to potentially enhance their performance in diabetes therapy. This proposal aims to establish a 3D-printing procedure for semi-automated and scalable fabrication of cell-encapsulating devices with similar design. The proposed computer-aided transfer process for 3D-printing would help automate the process for device fabrication, reduce manual steps to minimize associated errors or inconsistencies. To this end, we propose the following specific aims: AIM 1: To 3D-print and characterize a device encapsulating toroid insulin-secreting microtissues in vitro AIM 2: To evaluate the in vivo efficacy of 3D-printed device encapsulating therapeutic microtissues in diabetic mice AIM 3: To evaluate the feasibility of fabricating devices with scalable size for encapsulation of a clinically relevant cell source
kw: Multidisciplinary; Biomedical Engineering; Endocrinology, Diabetes and Metabolism; Biomaterials

title: Developing community-friendly diagnostics for glaucoma monitoring
abs: Glaucoma is one of the most common causes of irreversible blindness in the world and is expected to affect more than 100 million people worldwide by 2040. The global ophthalmic diagnostic market was valued at USD2.6 billion in 2017 and is expected to reach USD3.9 billion by 2025. As a chronic disease, glaucoma requires long term follow-up investigations that are critical in detecting deterioration in order to provide timely intervention to prevent blindness. The challenge is keeping up the supply of investigations with the demand from an ageing population in which the glaucoma disease burden is expected to increase by close to 50% in the next 20 years. During the COVID pandemic, this supply-demand mismatch is further exacerbated. There is a pressing need to develop a solution to improve efficiency and de-centralize point-of-care for glaucoma investigations. Current gold standard ophthalmic investigations limits accessibility due to poor sustainability and scalability – they are bulky, expensive, require high level of expertise to operate and there is poor integration of results for telemedicine. We have developed a suite of glaucoma diagnostic devices which aim to overcome the shortcomings of the corresponding gold standards, to enable community-based follow-up of stable glaucoma patients. Our preliminary studies have shown that each individual device correlates well with their corresponding gold standard. The current study will seek to validate the diagnostic performance of the new devices in routine monitoring of stable glaucoma and the acceptance of these devices by patients. Firstly, we will determine the diagnostic performance of a suite of novel devices including measuring visual acuity, tonometry and automated perimetry to detect glaucoma progression in 72 glaucoma patients from the National University Hospital over 1 year. Secondly, we will compare the adoptability of the new diagnostic devices and their corresponding gold standards by glaucoma patients using administered questionnaires.
kw: medical technology; artificial intelligence; digital health; data science and data analytics

title: Precision Therapy for Gastric and Hepatocellular Cancer
abs: Gastric and hepatocellular cancers represent the 5th and 6th most prevalent and the 4th and 3rd most lethal cancers respectively worldwide. Both cancers have the poorest the 5-year survival among the most common cancers endemic to Singapore, contributing to a high healthcare burden. The value of precision medicine cannot be over-emphasized, as there is a price to pay when the wrong drug is selected, both by the patient as well as the society at large. Moreover, administration of futile treatment stretches the already limited healthcare resources. The research program focuses on i) precision drug selection, ii) precision drug delivery, and iii) precision drug dosing. In Aim 1, we will conduct prospective studies to assess the value of realtime phenotypic drug screen using patient-derived organoids to predict treatment response. We will incorporate our novel autologous immune cell/cancer organoid co-culture system to screen the response to immune checkpoint inhibitor. Finally, we will evaluate a 5-azacytidine based therapy uncovered by AI-assisted cancer organoid-based drug screen in ‘predicted’ responders. In aim 2, we will conduct 2 studies using a minimally-invasive drug delivery system that can deliver drugs into the peritoneal cavity as aerosolized droplets, giving better local tissue penetration and minimizing systemic exposure and treatment toxicity. These study will evaluate the efficacy of PIPAC oxaliplatin and IV nivolumab; and to test electrostatic application of PIPAC with paclitaxel in patients with peritoneal metastases. Finally, in aim 3, we will evaluate the use of AI-base dose decision support tool to personalise drug dosing, with the goal to reduce treatment cost and toxicity.
kw: Gastric cancer, hepatocellular cancer, personalised therapy, peritoneal metastasis, artificial intelligence, interventional pharmacoeconomics

title:
Integrated Psychological Program for Management of Postnatal Depression and Persistent Postpartum Pain after Childbirth 
CODEPAD − II (Collaborative Outcomes of DEpression and Pain Associated with Delivery− II)
abs: The childbirth process is associated with the risk of developing postnatal depression (PND) and persistent postpartum pain (PPP), which could contribute to maternal morbidity. There is a lack of routine structured and effective programs in current practice to monitor and effectively manage PND and PPP. Our pilot study found specific pain and psychological vulnerability factors associated with increased risk of PND after childbirth. We propose an integrated psychological program (IPP) consisting of mindfulness mobile application, music listening, digital health video counselling and mobile electronic survey to effectively prevent, detect, monitor, and treat PND and PPP. The primary aim is to determine whether the use of the IPP will result in lower incidence of PND after childbirth. We will also determine whether the use of the IPP will result in lower postnatal Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) scores in a subgroup of laboring women (with outcomes of vaginal or emergency Cesarean delivery) that may have increased risk factors for PND. The interplay of psychological and pain factors during the use of the IPP will also be determined using patient centric outcomes (mother-child bonding, breastfeeding self-efficacy, quality of life). We will recruit 1480 women undergoing childbirth at KK Hospital in this randomized controlled trial. This proposal has the potential to recommend guidelines in community care and to incorporate digital health in management of PND and PPP. The IPP will also provide patient-centered care tailored to the individual’s needs and will have an immediate potential to improve transition of hospital to community care in postnatal women health.

title: Moving Towards Personalized Medicine in Managing Diabetic Patients with Chronic Limb Threatening Ischemia (CLTI) in Singapore: Subtypes, Trajectories and Diagnostic Tools (VALOUR)
abs: Hypothesis: Diabetic patients with chronic limb threatening ischaemia (DM-CLTI) and predominantly diabetic microvascular disease (DM-MVD) have poorer post-revascularization prognosis, compared to those with predominantly large artery stenosis or blockage. Revealing perfusion to the microvasculature of the foot is a vital step to optimize management outcomes for DM-CLTI patients. Overall Vision: Understand CLTI subtypes (with and without MVD) and validating clinical tools to diagnose foot perfusion deficiency will enable implementation of treatment guidelines for personalized medicine and cost-effective management of DM-CLTI patients with different CLTI subtypes. Aims: To identify clinical characteristics of DM-CLTI patients associated with good vs poor prognosis 12 months after revascularization surgery, and evaluate the potential of indocyanine green (ICG) angiography (imaging marker indicative of foot blood perfusion post-revascularization) in differentiating DM-CLTI subtypes (MVD present or not) and post-revascularization trajectories. Methods: We review 400 DM-CLTI patients records, all had endovascular revascularization for limb salvage in SGH and identify patients’ clinical features (including MVD in other organs) associated with good (successful wound healing) vs poor (limb loss/mortality) prognosis 12 months post-revascularization. Based on these data, we construct and validate a prognostic prediction model for DM-CLTI patients undergoing revascularization. We shall perform ICG angiography on prospectively recruited 100 DM-CLTI patients pre- and post-revascularization surgery, and correlate patients’ clinical profiles with ICG imaging data to determine microvascular perfusion thresholds for the presence of MVD and predicting successful wound healing. Complemented with ICG imaging data, we shall construct an improved prognostic prediction model and prospectively validate it in another cohort of 100 DM-CLTI patients undergoing revascularization. Significance: Facing ever increasing healthcare costs, a personalized approach in managing DM-CLTI patients is required urgently. Recognising and correctly diagnosing subtypes of DM-CLTI with different underlying DM complications, and establishing a validated prognostic prediction tool is essential to guide clinicians and patients in their treatment decision-making.
kw: Chronic Limb Threatening Ischemia, Peripheral Artery Disease, Microvascular Disease

title: Prognostic significance of novel multimodal imaging for diabetic retinopathy: Can we improve diabetic retinopathy staging?
abs: Diabetic retinopathy(DR), is one of the leading causes of blindness worldwide. Current DR classification is based on the Early Treatment of Diabetic Retinopathy Study (ETDRS) severity scale which evaluates the risk of progression to proliferative DR (PDR) from color fundus photography(CFP). In the recommended paradigm of care, patients are managed based on DR severity. Those with referable diabetic retinopathy are referred to specialist clinics, where they are monitored for the development of vision threatening retinopathy (VTDR), which includes PDR and diabetic macular edema(DME), that requires active treatment (e.g., laser, anti-VEGF therapy) to prevent vision loss. However, fewer than 10% of referred diabetics require immediate intervention resulting in a high burden of care, and the current DR classification does not predict the risk of endpoints like DME which has emerged as the main cause of visual impairment. Novel imaging modalities can improve our assessment of DR. Optical coherence tomography angiography(OCTA) allows non-invasive imaging of the retinal vasculature delineating true capillary non perfusion and retinal ischemia. Ultrawide field(UWF) imaging captures changes in the peripheral retina not seen on CFP. Imaging features identified on these modalities have are associated with incidence and progression of DR and DME. Despite the success of these current classification systems, there is a pressing need to improve current staging and classification of DR in order to better stratify the risk of VTDR, to enable early identification and treatment, and facilitate cost effective management of DR. In this proposal, we aim to conduct a long-term prospective study to evaluate the prognostic significant of multimodal imaging biomarkers for diabetic retinopathy progression and develop a novel DR staging algorithm based on these biomarkers to improve the staging for DR. We hypothesize that the multimodal DR staging can better predict the risk of development of VTDR compared with ETDRS classification.

title: The role of G6PC2 in glucose homeostasis and diabetes in East Asians
abs: Variants at the G6PC2 locus are reproducibly associated with fasting glucose (FG). G6PC2 is specifically expressed in the pancreatic islets and hydrolyses glucose-6-phosphate (G6P) to glucose and inorganic phosphate. However, G6pc2 knock out on insulin secretion in mice lowers fasting glucose and increases insulin secretion at moderate levels of glucose, whereas the glucose lowering alleles at the G6PC2 locus are associated with lower insulin levels during an oral glucose tolerance test. It has been hypothesised that, in humans, these variants alter the pulsatility of insulin secretion which can improve insulin action and lower glucose despite lower insulin levels. However, this hypothesis has not been tested. To better understand the role of G6PC2 in humans, we will determine the impact of a variant, rs2232326 (p.S324P) at the G6PC2 locus, on the pulsatility of insulin secretion an GSIS in humans. This variant is strongly associated with FG, has been demonstrated to result in low protein expression of G6PC2 in vitro, and has a minor allele frequency (MAF) ten times higher in Asians (MAF=4.6%) than in Europeans (MAF=0.17%). We will carry out a recruit by genotype study to examine insulin pulsatility and GSIS using a graded glucose infusion in 48 individuals, half of which will carry the S324P allele. In parallel, we will evaluate the effect of G6PC2 haploinsufficiency, knock out and the S324P variant in human derived beta-cell models on GSIS and evaluate the mechanisms for any effects. We will further evaluate the hypothesis that the S324P variant, or G6PC2 deficiency could increase endoplasmic reticulum stress which in turn could impair beta-cell function. Finally, we will evaluate the interaction between the S324P variant and glucose lowering drugs that also act on GSIS (GLP-1 agonists) or act on the same pathway as G6PC2 (glucokinase activators) both in vitro and in vivo (human studies).

title: Transforming Clinical Care of Patients with Chronic Disease through Precision Medicine, Person-Centred Care and Complex Interventions
abs: NUH is an academic hospital that exists within a network that is formed by the NUHS. Research within the NUH has traditionally brought together our clinicians and clinician scientists with investigators at the NUS (particularly the basic science departments at the Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine) and the Saw Swee Hock School of Public Health. This has enabled our clinicians to participate in a broad range of research ranging from discovery science to drug development, epidemiology, and human genetics. In 2020, the newly appointed chief executive of the NUHS initiated "CARE PLAN," which defines the roles that each institution plays within the NUHS in providing services required to support the health of our population. Within CARE PLAN, the NUH focuses on acute and tertiary care, while the NUHS focuses on population health. Thus, the research activities that were previously supported by the NUHS CG in RIE 2020, which pertain primarily to basic research for complex diseases, have transitioned to an NUH application for CG in RIE 2025. For this reason, although the institution hosting the CG has changed, we have prepared this application as a renewal of the previous CG. We will also shift our focus from basic science to health outcomes, while specifically addressing challenges related to patients seeking acute and tertiary care. We feel that this plays an important role in improving health outcomes while keeping per-capita cost manageable. This shift in research focus aligns with the 1st Human Health and Potential (HHP) strategic goal under RIE 2025 ( Transform health system to deliver better health and healthcare outcomes ). Although patients seeking acute and tertiary care comprise a relatively small proportion of Singapore population, these patients consume an outsized proportion of healthcare resources and funding, incurring an enormous per-capita cost.

title: SingaPore NEuroscience Clinical Translational Research ProgrAmme - SPECTRA
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: The National Neuroscience Institute (NNI) was established in 1999 and remains to date as the sole national specialist centre for the management of patients with diseases of the nervous system. NNI provides neurological services to more than 80% of patients in the public health sector. NNI also co-ordinates and provides clinical neuroscience training and conducts basic/translational and clinical neuroscience research. NNI has more than 400+ staff, with about 300+ in clinical care and academia and 100 full time research staff. NNI's mission and corporate goals rest firmly on our tripod of strengths in clinical services, education and research. Research at NNI focuses mainly on discovering new ways to treat specific neurological disorders that are relevant to our population, like age-related neurodegenerative diseases and stroke, which is in alignment with Singapore s goal of developing translational medicine to benefit patient s care. These disorders are also the top causes of disability that exact a huge toll on healthcare and socio-economic burdens. As our country population rapidly ages, neurological and related mental diseases will account for ~50% of the overall disability among all diseases in the nation, which highlights the urgency to discover new treatment modalities to effectively mitigate their associated burdens.

title: DEVELOPMENT OF NOVEL THERAPEUTICS AND PREDICTIVE BIOMARKERS IN GYNAECOLOGICAL CANCERS
abs: Background: Gynaecological cancers having been rising in incidence amongst Singaporean women. Endometrial, ovarian and cervical cancers now represent the 3rd, 5th and 10th most common cancers amongst women in Singapore respectively. Most of these cancers are treatable at diagnosis with a potential for cure, but the majority of cases presenting at advanced stage will relapse and subsequently develop treatment refractory disease. Hence, there is an urgent need to develop more effective therapeutic options for primary and recurrent gynaecological cancers. Hypothesis: Evaluating the clinical efficacy of novel therapeutic approaches in gynaecological tumours, combined with molecular profiling platforms for therapeutic stratification and in-depth analysis of the tumour microenvironment to identify novel predictive biomarkers, has the potential to result in greater therapeutic gain. Aims: We aim to studying novel therapeutic strategies in gynaecological cancers through clinical trials, establish a clinical platform to perform comprehensive molecular profiling of gynaecological cancers to identify actionable molecular aberrations to match patients to relevant biomarker driven clinical trials; and develop a spatial immune-profiling platform to identify a) pharmacodynamic changes in the tumour microenvironment and b) predictive biomarkers for immunotherapeutic strategies in gynaecological cancers. Methods: We will set up a gynaecological cancer precision oncology programme involving several early phase trials of novel therapeutic strategies for patients with recurrent gynaecological cancers, in conjunction with a comprehensive genomic and transcriptomic profiling platform for therapeutic stratification, and develop a tumour microenviroment profiling platform using Imaging mass cytometry technology and the GeoMX spatial RNA profiling platform to identify novel predictive biomarkers and new therapeutic targets.

title: Multi-PRonged Approach to Improving and Maximizing HEalthspan: PRIME
abs: Sengkang General Hospital (SKH) is the newest regional hospital with its official opening in the North-East of Singapore on 23rd March 2019. The younger demographics of this region (82% aged 40 to 64 compared with 72% nationally) provides an optimal window of opportunity for preventative health interventions. Adopting a life-course approach to health, SKH has established a track record of working closely with the community to target key stages of the life-course. Our Millennial Kids Programme aims to create healthy communities by targeting primary school children and their families to inculcate healthy lifestyles through education. On the other end of the spectrum, we have been working actively with our community partners to promote active ageing through frailty screening, education and intervention for community-dwelling older adults, through various individual grants - Individual Physical Proficiency Test for Seniors (IPPT-S), Promoting Health Longevity through Mitigation and Prevention of Frailty in Community-dwelling Elderly (Pro-LIFE) and Ageing Successfully in Place- Independent Rewarding Lives (ASPIRE). Amongst those requiring acute hospital care, the Programme for Enhanced Elderly Recovery@Sengkang (PEERS) provides pre-habilitation for older adults undergoing elective surgery, and ensures care continuity post-hospitalization, with ongoing efforts to evaluate programme efficacy. Thus, despite being a new establishment, SKH s vision of Healthy Living. Fulfilling Life. is already well aligned with RIE2025 focus areas for Human Health and Potential Population health & preventive health, Good healthcare outcomes at sustainable costs and Productive Longevity. These existing studies have enabled us to build up well-characterized cohorts for tracking health trajectories longitudinally and across different care settings, while offering a platform for piloting and test-bedding of interventions targeting improved health-related outcomes. SKH is part of the SingHealth-Duke NUS Academic Medical Centre (AMC) and SingHealth Regional Health System (RHS). We have a strong commitment to advancing clinical service and care, alongside basic/translational and clinical research in collaboration with our partners.

title: Building the ARCHIVE - Alexandra Research Centre for Healthcare In a Virtual Environment
abs: The National University Health System (NUHS) took over Alexandra Hospital (AH) in 2018 with the aim to reimagine healthcare for the future through new, innovative care models. The integrated care model at AH aims to reduce care fragmentation, especially for those with multiple comorbidities, whilst improving manpower and financial sustainability. This model is known as One patient (focus on patient-centred care), One bed (care without disruptive transfer across settings), One care team (holistic multidisciplinary approach), One principal doctor (care consolidation across specialties), One with the community (seamless integration with the community and the home), and Healthcare redesign (zero-based approach to rethinking healthcare) or OOOOOH!. As the designated hospital for care model sandboxes in NUHS, AH s experiments provide valuable lessons for the design of future healthcare institutions in Singapore, including the future new Alexandra Campus (first phase due for completion in 2028) and National University Hospital Campus (first phase due for completion in the 2030s). To ensure that the solutions are future-ready, many of these experiments incorporate digital technology. The current research team is too small to match the hospital s ambitions for a programmatic push towards vCare over the next several years and the opportunities this offers for high impact publications. We propose the formation of a new Alexandra Research Centre for Healthcare In a Virtual Environment (ARCHIVE) which will house a larger team with twofold aims: 1) internationally competitive in the research arena, and 2) build a repository of research data that will be used both for academia and future interventions in vCare. The overarching purpose of the ARCHIVE is to create the data-, analytical-, and hypothesis-testing infrastructure to support the design of innovative experiments in hospital-supported community-focused patient-centred vCare models. The ARCHIVE is designed to significantly increase the capacity and capability of this emerging research group with resources that could not be made available by the hospital due financial priorities for clinical service. Project level grant funded research is, by definition, resource constrained, short-lived, and outcome focused. Without an organising centre, the impact of specific projects is limited. Yet, even with limited resources, the RIE team has been able to make progress on at least five important projects related to the virtualisation of healthcare at AH.

title: Comparing the efficacy of dual Autologous Protein Solution (APS) and Hyaluronic Acid (HA) therapy with APS-alone therapy in the treatment of knee osteoarthritis: a randomized controlled trial
abs: Knee osteoarthritis is the most prevalent degenerative joint disease associated with chronic pain and stiffness. It is associated with significant disability and economic burden. This is likely to increase due to an aging population and increasing incidence of obesity. Although the gold standard treatment for knee osteoarthritis is total knee arthroplasty, this is for end stage osteoarthritis and not all patients are suitable for this due to their younger age or existing comorbidities. Thus, there needs to be more non-invasive options for patients with mild-moderate osteoarthritis. Currently, intra-articular hyaluronic acid (HA) injections are recommended in international guidelines as a moderate term solution for osteoarthritis, with effects lasting up to 6 months. Autologous protein solution (APS) injections are an emerging novel therapy that potentially provides a longer-term solution, with small trials reporting pain relief up to 3 years following a single injection. APS and HA have been studied individually and their benefits in improving pain and function outcomes in knee OA is well documented. However, there is a lack of knowledge whether combination therapy has an additive effect in terms of improving longevity of therapeutic benefit, or whether there will be no difference or even a dilutional effect. We aim to illustrate the effect of APS and HA dual therapy versus APS-alone therapy through this study. If shown to have additive effect, combination injection therapy could be potentially used to slow the progression of cartilage destruction in knee OA, provide longer term pain relief and delay or prevent need for total knee arthroplasty.

title: Transforming Oral Health in Singapore – A National Research Programme
abs: National Dental Centre Singapore (NDCS) is the largest referral centre for specialist oral healthcare in Singapore. Its research mission is to conduct high impact clinical and translational research to transform care and improve clinical outcomes. It assumes the responsibility of setting the nation s standard of care for oral diseases by being at the forefront of research and advanced medical technology, practising evidence-based dentistry and organizing nationwide oral health education and preventive programmes. NDCS is part of the SingHealth healthcare cluster. SingHealth partners with Duke-NUS for Academic Medicine with the mission to improve patients lives through excellent clinical care, teaching and research. The partnership combines the collective clinical strengths of SingHealth and Duke-NUS research and medical education capabilities. Since the formation of this partnership, 15 cluster-wide Academic Clinical Programmes (ACPs), each based on a clinical discipline, have been established to catalyse multi-institutional synergy. The Oral Health ACP was formed in 2014, with NDCS as its host institution. Under the ACP framework, NDCS and its satellite and partner clinics (located in Singapore General Hospital, Changi General Hospital, Sengkang General Hospital, KK Women and Children s Hospital and SingHealth polyclinics) collaborate in research, education and clinical innovation. All ACPs have access to shared research support services and core platforms. The SingHealth Duke-NUS Joint Research Masterplan, updated every 4 years, provides a common framework for research work plans in all SingHealth institutions, Duke-NUS Medical School and ACPs. The 3rd Joint Research Masterplan (2021-2025) is aligned with the national RIE2025 Human Health and Potential domain and the Ministry of Health Healthcare Research Strategy 2020, i.e. to collaborate with internal and external stakeholders to generate world-class research leading to health and economic outcomes for the country, and ultimately benefits for patients. To achieve this, it is essential to build up and sustain research talents as well as have enablers and processes in place to support the work.

title: Advancing Dermatological Healthcare through Research, Innovation and Enterprise
abs: As the national tertiary academic centre for dermatological diseases in Singapore, it has been NSC s mission to engage in high-quality, clinically-relevant research to advance dermatological knowledge and practice. The goals are to build NSC as an established and self-sufficient research centre and to distinguish NSC as a reputable, leading opinion leader for skin diseases in the international arena. This has been reflected by Singapore being selected to host the World Congress of Dermatology in 2023, the largest dermatology congress in the world, outbidding cities including Sydney, Beijing and Dubai. Centre Grant 2013 provided the start-up funding for numerous of our research programs. In particular, the skin imaging program has resulted in many new collaborations, scientific publications, research grants and provisional patents which has helped propelled Singapore to being one of the leading countries outside Europe in the field of skin imaging. RIE2020 Centre Grant has been used to develop the core facilities and manpower for the conduct of research, to build up disease cohorts and tissue and cellular biobanks to enable longitudinal research, and to initiate projects such that preliminary results can be used to acquire extra-mural project grants. For RIE2025, we will be building on our current CG s research foci of Atopic Dermatitis (AD, or eczema) and Skin Imaging, and in addition, develop further themes in which we have built capabilities over the years. These are to facilitate our goals to meet future challenges in healthcare, through (i) improvement of healthcare outcomes, (ii) preventive healthcare, and (iii) cost-effective and sustainable implementation.

title: Developing a Population-based, Unified, Learning System for Enhanced and Sustainable Health – the PULSES II Centre Grant
abs: The national population health strategy of the Ministry of Health (MOH), Singapore, co-developed with the wider healthcare family, entails a whole-of-society approach to address the wider determinants of health. Aligning with this strategy, the vision of the SingHealth Regional Health System (RHS) recognises that the Singaporean population can be empowered to keep well, get well and live well in their communities and homes. Under its human health and potential domain, the emphasis of the Research, Innovation and Enterprise (RIE) 2025 is to make Singapore a leading hub in transforming and protecting health, advancing human potential and creating economic value through research and application. Aligning with the MOH population health strategy, the RIE2025 mandate and the SingHealth RHS ethos, our vision for a Learning, Integrated Regional Health System (LIRHS) encompasses research that i) aims to improve population health as measured by the Quadruple Aim; ii) is driven by a cyclical process of evidence generation, innovation, rigorous evaluation and care improvement; iii) adopts a holistic approach encompassing health, social, economic and environmental factors; and iv) has significant potential to generate economic value.

title: Programme for Research in Epidemic Preparedness And Response (PREPARE) - Stage 2
abs: PREPARE is a national research programme set up by Ministry of Health to support and strengthen Singapore s key essential pandemic research capabilities. It focuses on enhancing translational platforms and expertise to develop tools, methods and products that can be tapped on to detect, respond to, and contain future infectious disease threats. Infectious disease outbreaks are a continuous threat to Singapore. As an international travel hub with a high population density, Singapore is particularly vulnerable to imported and local transmission of novel infectious diseases and the re-emergence of established ones. Developing cutting-edge research capabilities to prepare for and respond well to future epidemics is thus a crucial national priority. PREPARE seeks to enhance research capabilities for early detection and sense-making to prepare Singapore against future infectious disease threats; develop and strengthen key enablers in data infrastructure, analytics, and behavioural science research to respond to public health crises; strengthen research capabilities to enhance our national resilience in diagnostics, therapeutics, and vaccines; and develop a strong infectious diseases research collaboration network across countries in our region to respond to epidemics and facilitate multi-centre clinical trials. PREPARE is a national programme under the Communicable Diseases Agency.

title: Understanding human dopamine neuron degeneration in Parkinson’s using brain organoids
abs: A major challenge in developing an effective PD therapeutic is the lack of a human-based physiological model recapitulating cardinal pathological changes in PD neuronal circuit. We have previously developed a 3D human midbrain-like organoid (MLO) model that gives rise to functionally mature DAN. However, two missing parts remain to be addressed: 1) astrocytes, an important cell-type in brain and in PD pathogenesis, are rarely present in MLOs; 2) this model lacks striatum and cortex, key components of the PD circuit. This proposal will address the two aforementioned major issues, to develop a more physiological human neural model to deconstruct PD pathogenesis. Firstly, I will utilize the astrocyte-friendly media formulation I have recently developed (patent pending) to generate organoids containing astrocytes; this improved model system will better enable me to investigate pathophysiological neural function [Aim 1]. I will also recapitulate the PD circuit by fusing organoids of different brain regions, focusing on studying DAN axons making self-organized contact with physiological postsynaptic striatal partner, along with the DAN–MSN synapse, in a midbrain–striatal organoid fusion model [Aim 2], and on studying cortico-MSN synapse and MSN activity in a pioneering, world-first tripartite cortical/ striatal/ midbrain organoid fusion model [Aim 3]. This highly novel, physiologically integrated yet modular human-based PD model will allow me to dissect the cellular and molecular sequences of DAN degeneration and examine the resultant changes in the rest of the PD circuit, as well as in conjunction with other brain cell-types. To demonstrate the validity and utility of the proposed model, I will study the effects of both well-established (GBA) and novel PD genes (CHCHD2), and also utilize PD-associated neurotoxins to recapitulate DAN degeneration. In addition to constituting a new paradigm for modeling circuit deficits in neurological and other diseases, these proposed tools will also open up new avenues for therapeutics development, and along with iPSC technology, can also be adapted for use in personalized medicine.

title: Back to the future: Integrating multiscale coral reef functions in Southeast Asia
abs: The aim of my research programme is to address the urgent need for systematic evaluations of Southeast Asian (SEA) coral reefs and provide real-world guidelines for coral conservation that safeguard coastal communities. Coral reefs support critical habitat for fisheries and are a physical barrier to wave energy, protecting shorelines and infrastructure during storm events. Human activities have radically altered living coral populations and their environments from those that originally formed reefs. The absence of scientific data in the SEA region makes it challenging to predict how stressed reef systems will continue to grow and respond to climate change. I will collect new multiscale ecological and geological datasets to understand how recent coral reef deterioration has affected coastal resilience across the region. Holocene reef core records will be compiled to quantify pre-human reef conditions using coral subfossil material retained inside cores. Present-day reef calcification and vertical growth potential will be assessed using observations of living coral communities. A predictive model of future reef morphology and ecosystem change will then be developed utilizing integrated field data. An understanding of natural reef functions will allow for the optimization of hard engineering structures to provide both commercial purposes and ecological benefits. Specifically, I aim to quantify eco-geological functions of coral reefs across three key time-scales (past, present, future) with the following objectives: i. Reconstruct past reef growth histories and paleo-coral communities from Holocene reef cores to understand regional coral reef degradation ii. Calculate carbonate budgets of living coral ecosystems to evaluate present-day eco-geological reef functions iii. Integrate multiscale field datasets to construct models of future reef growth and ecosystem change under climate change iv. Optimize artificial structures using insights from natural reef systems to enhance functions within degraded coastal areas My sophisticated approach will have significant scientific and societal impact because SEA has the greatest reliance on coral reefs for food security, income and coastal protection. The multi-disciplinary research that I propose includes biologists, geoscientists, engineers, and policy researchers to target the full complexity of issues SEA countries are facing in the Anthropocene. Collectively, we will contribute a better understanding of how coral reef health affects coastal resilience. High impact research outputs will highlight the benefits of nature-based solutions for mitigating climate change impacts and protecting coastal communities.
kw: coral reefs, environmental change, geomorphology, Southeast Asia, carbonate budgets, coastal resilience

title: All-optical electrophysiology: function-associated cellular deformations as intrinsic biomarkers for all-optical functional imaging at the cellular scale
abs: The goal of the proposed research is to develop a new technology for all-optical cellular-scale functional imaging that is applicable in humans. Leveraging the exquisite precision of optical interference, our technology relies on detecting two types of function-associated cellular deformations: the cellular electromotility that induces a fast nanometer-scale cellular deformation accompanying the action potential, and the osmotic swelling that deforms the photoreceptor outer segments by hundreds of nanometers. In terms of cellular electromotility, we will characterize and model the spatiotemporal dynamics of neuronal deformations during the action potential using optical diffraction tomography (ODT) and interferometric scattering (iSCAT) microscope. We will then demonstrate interferometric imaging of individual neuronal action potentials in primary neuron cultures and ex-vivo retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) by signal enhancement through scattering nanoparticles. Moreover, we will implement an all-optical non-fluorescent neural interface based on nanoparticles that allows simultaneous near-infrared readout and photothermal input. For in-vivo functional retinal imaging, we will build a high-speed line-scan optical coherence tomography (OCT) that records individual photoreceptors’ dynamics in the retina. Using rodent animal models, we will investigate the underlying mechanism and explore how different steps of the phototransduction cascade contribute to the photoreceptor deformation. We will also demonstrate quantitative imaging of scotopic sensitivity while examining the link between our imaging results and different types of retinal degenerative diseases. If successful, our observations will provide key insights into the fundamental biophysical mechanisms of both types of function-associated cellular deformations. From the engineering perspective, we will demonstrate optical imaging of nanometer-scale movements within a few milliseconds in vitro, ex vivo, and in vivo. More importantly, our technology will provide an entirely new and transformative approach for the study, diagnosis, and treatment-monitoring of retinal diseases that often lead to severe blindness.
kw: functional imaging; action potential; electromotility; optoretinogram; interferometric imaging; optical coherence tomography

title: Learning why do we do what we do through abductive and deductive understanding of human actions using Neurosymbolic AI.
inst: IHPC - Institute of High Performance Computing
abs: Recognising “what we do” or “what we will do” has been well investigated under action recognition and anticipation literature in the Computer Vision (CV) and Machine Learning (ML) research communities. However, computational learning of “why do we do what we do” is not well investigated. The objective of this project is to develop Artificial Intelligent (AI) models to process videos and learn “why do humans do what they do?” by reducing the gap between neural and symbolic representation through novel neurosymbolic AI. These neurosymbolic AI models can see what we do and then reason about our behaviour to interpret, justify, explain and understand our actions. To develop models that can learn “why do humans do what they do?”, we break down the challenging problem into eight sub-problems which are also the specific aims; 1. situation understanding, 2. learning association between situations and actions, 3. abductive action recognition, 4. learning action preconditions, 5. learning action effects, 6. latent goal inference, 7. action motive recognition and 8. personalised behaviour learning. We develop CV and ML models to solve these high-level reasoning problems using both neural and symbolic representations. How to develop models that can effectively communicate between neural and symbolic representations remains a challenging AI problem, arguably the most challenging one. We develop new algorithms to bridge the gap between neural and symbolic representations which is an important scientific contribution of this project. Specifically, we extend deep learning to perform logical inference and develop new similarity measures, loss functions, divergences over logic programs, symbolic representations so that we can train neurosymbolic programs to reason about human behaviour. We develop deep learning models to generate symbolic representations of functions, novel differentiable logic, differentiable grammar, and differentiable graphs to solve those eight sub-problems using neurosymbolic AI models. AI and robotics fields have made significant progress in the last decade. Somewhat surprisingly, general purpose robotics have made less progress compared to application specific robotics. There are several robotics applications that effectively use AI for solving specific problems such as automated assembly. However, it would be difficult to have some dedicated AI-based robots to solve each and every daily task in our households and we need AI powered general purpose assistive robotics in the future. These general purpose assistive robotics should be able to answer the question "why do we do what we do?". It should be able to understand our needs, routines and expectations. We restrict our scope to daily household human activities. Moreover, computational understanding of “why do we do what we do” would help us to develop specific robotics in the areas of assistive robotics, AI for monitoring, smart homes and shops. title: A green, high-throughput and universal solution for spent lithium-ion battery materials recycling
abs: Herein based on the “redox-targeting concept” that the team has advanced in the field more recently, we propose to develop an innovative high-throughput electrolytic flow system to continuously break down the spent battery materials into valuable chemicals at ambient conditions without secondary pollutions. Such a system operates upon a complementary reductive leaching in conjunction with oxidative leaching of LiFePO4 (LFP) and is applicable to the commercially more dominant while compositionally more complex materials LiCoO2 and NMC. Our preliminary study on LFP has laid solid ground to the success of the proposed approach towards a close-loop, green and low-cost recycling technology universally applicable to all mainstream spent LIB materials. By virtue of the innovative process, the recycling efficiency of LFP could reach up to 99.8% at ambient conditions and high purity LiOH (99.9%) is obtained from the spent LFP material without additional chemicals consumption and waste generation. Following this strategy, this program aims to generalise the approach applicable to all LIB materials (i.e. LiCoO2, NMC, etc.), and to develop an integrated solution for continuous processing of spent battery materials for industry use in large scale.
kw: materials recycling, spent Li-ion batteries, redox electrochemistry, pollution free

title: Perovskite Quantum Emitters (PQE)
abs: Photonic quantum systems are prominent candidates for quantum information processing and provide great versatility to encode quantum information. Deterministic generation of single- and multi-photon states holds the key to large-scale applications including quantum key distribution (QKD), quantum computing and metrology. Despite immense progress, facile, solid-state scalable single photon sources (SPS) and detectors remain elusive. Halide perovskites are exceptional optoelectronic materials for solar cells and LEDs. Recent evidence of novel single photon, many-body cooperative effects in perovskite nanomaterials at both room-and low-temperature reveal colour-tunable system with large oscillator strengths and unity photoluminescence (PL) quantum yield, ripe for integration with emerging quantum technologies. The goal of this programme is to develop a new family of luminescent, high fidelity & stable perovskite quantum emitters (PQEs) for optical quantum technologies through rational materials design, backed by strong fundamental science, proof-of-concept testing & prototyping. The project will target applications of scalable SPS for ground-based and satellite-to-ground quantum communications, solid-state superradiant laser, and quantum-enhanced gyroscope. Our team comprises leading experts in perovskite and quantum technologies. Preliminary findings confirm exceptional single photon purity, absence of inhomogeneous emission broadening, broad wavelength tunablity, superradiant behaviour, and facile cavity integration. These findings underscore the suitability of this research hypothesis that perovskites can overcome a key bottleneck in optical quantum technology; viz. scalable, high purity and brightness solid-state quantum light sources. This project will demonstrate the use of PQEs as a source for compact cavity-enhanced radiation resistant SPS in quantum communications, superradiant lasing and quantum sensing.
kw: Halide Perovskites; Single Photons; High Fidelity; Indistinguishability; Quantum Communications; Quantum Metrology and Sensing

title: Robotic and Intelligent Systems for Securing/Un-securing of Containers in Vessels
abs: With the constant increase of intercontinental commerce and worldwide shipping, sea travel is only going to continue growing both in terms of importance and of gross product transported each year. One of the main bottlenecks is the on-vessel operations for securing and un-securing containers. In this proposed work, we will develop several methods to automate and revolutionize the sea shipping process, by proposing innovative mechanical and robotic solutions to the securement and un-securement of containers on container ships, with a focus on the mega-vessels of the future. Our first effort (thrust 1) will focus on the thorough study of the current operations and existing solutions, pain points, and will also aim at proposing mathematical and physical models of container lashing and locking. Thrust 2 will investigate the automation of existing container securement/un-securement operations, with a focus on decreasing the manpower need and physical aspect of the work, while maintaining or even improving the resulting safety and robustness of the final cargo securement. These methods will mainly focus on the lashing operations, and will involve the use of autonomous or semi-autonomous robotic solutions as well as intelligent systems. In parallel to this, Thrust 3 will develop novel methods to approach the securement/un-securement of containers, by drawing from the team’s expertise in mechanical design, engineering, and advanced robotics. In particular, we seek to remove the need for lashing bars and their manual installation/removal by replacing those with 1) an actuated system which can automatically raise from the ship’s deck and secure multiple stacks (to each other and to the deck), and 2) a novel manner of both reinforcing the integrity of a stack and securing this stack to the vessel by “wrapping” it around its main dimensions with a flexible, yet robust material, using autonomous robots. Moreover, we will also work on developing a smart corner-casting lock to replace the conventional twist locks in order to improve the efficency of coning/deconing process. Through thrusts 2 and 3, our goal will be to thoroughly formulate, investigate, and prototype our different novel ideas, to assess their efficiency and inter-operability with existing vessels and port capabilities in Singapore and around the world. Finally, the fourth thrust of the proposed work will be the commercialization of our final developed solution(s) with PSA and our commercial partners.
kw: robotics; intelligent robotic manipulation; human-robot collaborative systems with optimized autonomy; machine intelligence; integrated perception, planning and control; intelligent inspection

title: Supercharging barramundi production through advanced selective breeding for improved disease resistance, growth and fillet traits
abs: Genomic selection is the “gold standard” in livestock, crop and aquaculture breeding programs. The breeding approach, which is based on genome-wide markers (SNP) trained to predict the genomic breeding value (gEBV) of an individual, increases selection accuracies and is particularly powerful when multi-trait selection for hard to measure traits is desired. The basic principle for implementation of genomic selection involves large-scale genome-wide genotyping and phenotyping of individuals in a training population, and then development of a statistical model accounting for SNP marker effects in determination of a particular phenotype. Once models are established, the gEBV of a selection candidate can be determined with high accuracy through genetic testing without directly phenotyping the individual. Barramundi, or Asian seabass, Lates calcarifer, is an important Singaporean aquaculture species that will benefit from implementation of an advanced genomic-informed breeding program simultaneously targeting improved resistance to scale drop disease (SDD - the major disease of farmed barramundi causing 40-75% mortality losses in Singapore), growth and carcass traits. No breeding programs for barramundi currently target improvements in SDD resistance and fillet traits (yield/colour) as important traits in their breeding objective. This project will develop the genomic and phenotypic data to implement on-farm, and in a commercial setting, a genomic selection program targeting simultaneous improvements in SDD resistance, growth, and flesh traits (fillet yield, flesh colour). It will achieve this objective through a) developing a 70K Axiom SNP array to genotype breeding candidates and progeny; b) conducting industrial-scale phenotyping for traits of commercial importance, along with SDD disease-challenges (including using AI and machine learning to rapidly phenotype fish), and 3) linking genomic information with phenotypic data to produce genomic prediction models. Outcomes from the project will be barramundi that have average SDD survival of 60%, grow 15% faster, and have increased fillet yields and white flesh colouration.
kw: barramundi, genomic selection, selective breeding, disease tolerance

title: Thermogels for Therapeutic Applications (THETA)
inst: IMRE - Institute of Materials Research and Engineering
abs: Charged amphiphilic polymers which are capable of forming thermogels constitute a class of almost completely-overlooked and under-developed biomaterials. There is a need to develop motifs that allow for functionalisation and structural diversification without compromising on their desirable thermogelling behaviour. Whilst a number of zwitterionic thermogelling polymers have been reported, they have thus far remained as academic curiosities with little demonstration of practical biological applications. Their structures are mainly limited to non-biodegradable polymers, or end-capping of polymeric precursors with the zwitterionic motifs which result in low charge densities on the polymers. Furthermore, to the best of our knowledge, no polyanionic thermogels are known, which is a significant deficiency for delivery of biologics considering that many therapeutic agents, such as antibodies,16 are cationic at physiological pH. To address this glaring deficiency, this proposal will feature the design, synthesis and biological studies of novel multiblock copolymers bearing either cationic or anionic groups (Figure 2), randomly incorporated into the polymer backbone. These innovative polyelectrolyte thermogelling polymers will contain cationic functionalities such as quarternary amines and guanidiniums, or anionic groups including carboxylates and phosphates derived from common biocompatible commercially-available precursors. In addition to the charged groups, each polymer will comprise of hydrophilic domains that confers water solubility, hydrophobic domains that bring about self-assembly and thermogelling behaviour, as well as biodegradable linkages that allow natural breakdown and clearance of the polymers from the body after in-vivo applications. These thermogelling polyelectrolytes will combine the inherent advantages of thermogels (temperature-responsive injectability, biocompatibility, ease of synthesis) with the unique bioactivities of polyelectrolytes, opening up a vast new biomedical application space beyond those traditionally achievable using either class of biomaterial individually. The highly biocompatible polymers comprising of FDA-approved precursors such as poly(ethylene glycol), poly(propylene glycol), as well as poly(ethyleneimine) and L-tartrate to confer cationic and anionic functionalities on the polymers respectively, make it safe for medical applications down the line. The material should be safe for biomedical applications: gelation is driven solely by non-covalent interactions between the polymers’ hydrophobic domains in water, with no potentially-hazardous chemical crosslinkers necessary to form the gels. Furthermore, the straightforward and low cost polymer synthesis, comprising of simply joining various commonly available polymer precursors together makes these strategies attractive and ensures that production costs can be kept affordable even during scale-up GMP contract manufacturing.
