title: Green amines for a sustainable future
abs: At present, the prevailing industrial processes to manufacture amines start from non-renewable fossil resources. They also suffer from other limitations such as production of large amounts of chemical waste, need for harsh reaction conditions and highly toxic or hazardous intermediates, and relatively low product yield. Along with the ardent desire to transform the chemical industry into a more sustainable manner with low carbon footprint, it is of high interest to explore alternative routes to make amines efficiently from renewable sources, such as using biomass-derived chemicals as carbon feedstock, as well as green NH3, organic nitrogen fixed in biomass (such as chitin) and ultimately N2 as nitrogen feedstock. In this project, we intend to establish three new pathways from these unconventional feedstocks to access a range of amine products, with three work packages conducted in parallel. In the first work package, new amination chemistry will be developed to convert bio-based alcohols into amines via the development of novel single-atom catalysts and high entropy alloy catalysts. In the second work package, novel conversion routes for a range of amine products from chitin derived platform compounds via tailor-designed catalytic systems will be established, while in the last one, N2 as nitrogen source to make amines from alcohols and hydrogen under the concept of dynamic catalysis will be explored. Using bio-based feedstock, these synthetic routes not only mitigate the carbon footprint, but may also lead to a “short-cut” to complex products by taking advantages of the inherent functionalities in the starting material. Along this journey, new catalysts and new catalytic systems to activate inert chemical bonds will be established to contribute to sustainable chemistry and engineering at large.
kw: Green Chemistry; Amines; Renewable Chemicals; Catalyst design; Nitrogen activation

title: Pilot Tests for using a New Foundation System for Tuas Container Port
abs: New container terminals have being constructed on reclaimed land at Tuas. The foundations used for container yards in the past consist of steel reinforced concrete (RC) piles connected to pile caps. However, this type of foundations is very difficult and costly to be demolished. As such it will incur a huge amount of cost for future port redevelopment. This is what the Pasir Panjang Port will be facing. Furthermore, the use of RC piles through a thick layer of sandfill and well improved ground is also an expensive option. To overcome the above limitations, a new design and construction method for foundations of container yards has been established through an existing SMI project. This new design method adopts a load transfer platform approach through the use of rigid inclusion columns & T-Beams to improve the bearing capacity of soil and control the post-construction deformation. The rigid inclusion columns are made of plain concrete and can be demolished easily in the future. Furthermore, the new method is also more cost-effective and faster to install with a potential saving of 19% in construction cost and 50% in construction time for the foundations. The new construction method consumes less energy (up to 30%) and thus is greener. The new foundation type can also be used for other types of infrastructural development and thus benefits the whole construction industries. However, as the proposed new foundation type has not been used for container ports before in the world, we propose to carry out a pilot test at the Tuas Port container yard to evaluate the performance of the new foundation type, verify or optimise the design parameters and establish the construction method. A small-scale, but full-size foundation will be constructed using this new method and its performance will be evaluated through load tests by simulating the different types of container loads. Finite element analyses will also be carried out to predict and compare with the monitoring data from the pilot tests. Based on the pilot test and numerical analysis, design guidelines will be established for the construction of container yard foundations using this new method. This small pilot test will provide the necessary assurance for the proposed method to be used for the next phases of construction for the container yards at Tuas to reduce the construction cost and more importantly avoid difficulties for future demolition.
kw: pilot test; container port; new foundation; rigid inclusion

title: Decentralized and Accelerated Vehicle Fleet Management System Prototype
inst: IHPC - Institute of High Performance Computing
abs: In the present state, PSA has a centralized fleet control system that can manage the fleet of AGVs in terms of routing, holding buffer management, deadlock detection/prevention/resolution, space granting to prevent collision and trajectory planning. However, due to the system being centralized, it is not adaptable to the scale-up of fleet with more AGVs. The responsiveness will be degraded by the scale-up of fleet due to increasingly intensive computational load incurred on central servers, and consequently, the total number of AGVs that can be controlled will be limited. To solve this issue, the objective of this proposal is to build a decentralized fleet management system prototype such that it is able to adapt to the scale-up of fleet by enabling each AGV to autonomously negotiates via gossiping, routes, prevents deadlock/collision and synchronizes map updates. In addition, the system needs to interface with PSA’s Terminal Operating System (TOS) and Navigation System (NS) to demonstrate that they can collaborate systematically in a simulation environment. This decentralized system prototype will be deployed to servers in lab or in cloud such that AGVs can be realized by their digital twins in servers and communicate with one another via network. This project is an important manifestation of applying advanced computing techniques, such as decentralized computing and acceleration of computing, to solving complex real-world problems, in this case the fleet management. The methodology involves the survey of relevant gossiping network and consensus algorithms, datastore, and consensus-based AGV control logics. The approach includes investigating state-of-the-art consensus algorithms (such as Hashgraph, Raft and Paxos) and selecting one of them, implementing AGV agents on servers, exploring potential acceleration solutions (such as multi-core CPUs, GPUs), and simulating the fleet management.
kw: Decentralized system; AGV fleet management; Consensus algorithm

title: New treatments and strategies to prevent heart failure in diabetes
abs: Rationale The prevalence of diabetes is on the rise in Singapore and currently affects 10% of the general population. Patients with diabetes are at increased risk of developing heart failure (HF) and have worse outcomes once HF is established. Studies in Asian populations with HF have identified a lean diabetic phenotype common in Southeast Asia which presents at a younger age and has worse clinical outcomes but the reasons for this are unclear. The leading causes of HF in diabetic patients are acute myocardial infarction and diabetic cardiomyopathy. The overall aim of this research proposal is to understand the pathophysiology and risk factors underlying the development of HF in the Asian lean diabetes phenotype. We hypothesise that understanding the mechanisms underlying the development of HF in lean diabetic patients will identify novel targets and new treatments for preventing the onset and progression of HF. Specific Aims Aim 1: To discover new treatment targets for protecting the lean and obese diabetic heart from AMI and diabetic cardiomyopathy using diabetic mice and human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) models. Aim 2: To investigate whether targeting the mitochondrial fusion protein, Mfn2, can prevent cardiac dysfunction in lean and obese diabetic mice and human iPSC models Aim A3: To discover new metabolic treatment targets in lean and obese diabetic AMI patients and diabetic cardiomyopathy using cardiac magnetic resonance imaging and spectroscopy and metabolomics. Aim A4: To generate a patient risk score that predicts the risk of HF in lean and obese diabetic AMI and diabetic cardiomyopathy patients to guide patient management and improve health outcomes. Expected results We expect to discover novel treatment targets and new treatments for preventing the onset and progression of HF in obese and lean patients with diabetes which have the potential to improve health outcomes.
kw: Diabetes; Heart Failure; Induced pluripotent stem cells; Metabolism; Mitochondria

title: Risk Stratification of Neuropathic Ocular Surface Dysfunction Using Neural Imaging Metrics, Molecular Biomarkers, and Artificial Intelligence
abs: Neuropathic ocular surface dysfunction (OSD) is the leading cause of corneal morbidity. The current unmet need and challenge is the early diagnosis and risk stratification of these patients, as patients with early-stage disease are frequently asymptomatic, and current clinical assessments are insensitive to monitor the disease progression precisely. This leads to delayed diagnosis and under-diagnosis, and results in a high economic burden. In the proposal, our central hypothesis is that specific imaging-based features of corneal nerves, together with specific ocular surface molecular profiles in the neuroinflammatory pathway, are associated with patients’ clinical severity of neuropathic OSD. We firstly aim to identify the corneal neural imaging and ocular surface molecular biomarkers that are associated with clinical phenotypes of neuropathic OSD (Aims 1&2). A total of 515 patients with neuropathic OSD due to either refractive surgery or diabetic mellitus will be recruited. Detailed ocular surface clinical assessment, in-vivo confocal microscopy imaging on corneal nerves, and multi-omic analysis of tear samples, will be performed over an 18-months follow-up period. By incorporating the multimodal longitudinal data, including the clinical characteristics, corneal nerve imaging features and ocular surface multi-omic profiles, we will build a risk stratification algorithm using machine learning techniques (Aim 3). The development of a risk stratification system will allow clinicians to identify those subclinical cases who are at risk of development of OSD, and those cases at risk of progression to moderate and severe OSD. Stratified and strategic management can be delivered, enhancing evidence-based clinical practice and precision medicine. The study will also provide a novel integrated approach to better understand the pathogenesis of neuropathic OSD. Furthermore, the proteomic and metabolomic markers identified may open new avenues for novel treatment and diagnostic kits for neuropathic OSD.
kw: Corneal neuropathy; Risk stratification; Artificial Intelligence; Corneal imaging

title: Using Flow Cytometry to guide a multi-antigen targeting of Relapsed Refractory Diffuse Large B cell Lymphoma with a combination of CD-19. CD-22 and Antibody-Coupled T-cell Receptor (ACTR) CAR-T cell therapy
abs:
Background: Patients with multiply relapsed or refractory Diffuse Large B cell Lymphoma (RR DLBCL) have a poor prognosis. CD19 chimeric antigen receptor T cell therapy has provided a promising alternative for treatment but antigen-escape relapse has emerged as a major challenge for long-term disease control after CD19-directed therapies
Hypothesis:  The use of flow cytometry to select the target antigens for effector T-cell therapy, in r/r DLBCL, will improve the overall response. 
Methodology: We propose phase II study with the primary objective to determine the overall response rates (ORR) of flow cytometry based effector T cell targeting of  CD19/ CD22/ CD20/CD38 in patients with high risk Relapsed Refractory DLBCL. Flow cytometry from tumor biopsies at the time of relapse will be used to guide selection of a panel of antigen targets, aiming for a total target expression of > 99%. title: A Phase 1 first in class trial of GE-CAR-BiTE cells in patients with glypican 3 (GPC3) expressing refractory tumours
abs: Glypican 3 is a highly tumour specific antigen expressed on the cell membrane of many cancers but not in adult normal tissue. In particular, hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), lung, breast, gastric and ovarian cancers express GPC3, affecting more than 2.7 million new cancer cases globally. There is much interest in targeting GPC3 for cancer treatment using monoclonal antibodies or antibody drug conjugates, vaccine technologies and chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR T) cells. Apart from analysis of tumour sections for GPC3 expression, soluble GPC3 can be detected in the plasma of patients, potentially serving as a selection biomarker. Though CAR T cells have made an astounding impact in B cell malignancies through CD19 targeting, they have yet to show breakthrough in solid cancers. Reasons for these include toxicity from off-target antigen engagement, deficient cell trafficking into tumours and poor survival in the hostile tumour microenvironment resulting in limited immune activation. To address these issues, we have developed GE-CAR-BiTE, a GPC3-targeted Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR) T cell that secretes EpCAM, an epithelial cell adhesion molecule expressed in almost all epithelial cancers. Upon target engagement, CAR Ts will destroy cancer cells, express EpCAM Bispecific T cell engagers, which will bring surrounding T cells to bind to carcinoma cells, further amplifying cancer cell eradication. Off-target engagement leading to toxicity is reduced by 1. Tumour-directed T cell expansion, 2. Tumour restricted BiTE secretion. This gives a measure of safety to these therapeutic CAR T cells. Our preclinical work has demonstrated the superior efficacy of this CAR T to eradicate HCC cells compared to GPC3 targeting CAR T cells alone, as antigen escape is reduced. In this proposal, we are developing a first in human clinical trial of this novel GE-CAR-BiTE in patients with refractory cancers to establish its clinical safety, tolerability and preliminary activity.
kw: CAR T cells; hepatocellular carcinoma; glypican 3; EpCAM; phase 1 trial

title: Future-Ready Interventions for Survival after Cardiac Arrest (FRISCA)
abs: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) occurs when there is sudden cardiovascular collapse. While Singapore has made significant advances in improving outcomes for OHCA, there is considerably more to be done: 1) We need a comprehensive long-term registry and quality of survival data; 2) Community Response needs to be enhanced with improved bystander CPR quality; 3) Ambulance/System Response can be optimised further 4) We need to increase capacity/capability of health systems to deliver quality OHCA care regionally/globally. The overall objective of this STaR application is to increase the number of cardiac arrest survivors with good neurological function by 20% by implementing a bundle of interventions over 5 years. We will further develop and expand our internationally established clinical/implementation science research program in OHCA by 1A: Building a Registry of OHCA Long-term Survivorship and Quality of Life (QoL), 1B: Optimising OHCA Triage and Transport using Artificial Intelligence (AI) Decision Support for Early Risk Stratification, 1C: Modelling the impact of Optimizing Transport Policies to Specialized Cardiac Arrest Centres (CACs) using a decision science model, 2: Developing and Implementing Future Ready Smart Community interventions to improve the quality of Cardio-Pulmonary Resuscitation (CPR), 3A: Conducting a Cluster Randomized Controlled Trial (cRCT) on Pre-hospital Targeted Temperature Management using a Novel Cooling Vest, 3B: Conduct a Prospective Cluster Randomized Controlled Trial on Head-Up CPR, 3C: Implementing Transport Policies for Cardiac Arrest Centers (CACs) in a real-world implementation trial and 4: Developing an Assessment tool for Developing Pre-Hospital Emergency Care systems in collaboration with the Global Resuscitation Alliance (GRA). This program targets a priority disease in Asia and is aligned with the population health, Health Services Research, and AI focus areas in Singapore. Evidence from our program in Singapore will impact OHCA management not only in Singapore but also in the whole of Asia and globally through the GRA.
kw: out-of-hospital cardiac arrest; prehospital emergency care; data science and data analytics; population health and implementation science; emergency medical services

title: T-cell Immunity in Persistent Human Papillomavirus (HPV) Skin Infection and Cutaneous Squamous Cell Carcinoma (cSCC) among Organ Transplant Recipients (OTRs)
abs: Organ transplant recipients (OTRs) receive life-long immunosuppressive medications to ensure the survival of the newly grafted organ. Such treatment leads to dampened T cell immune response which can result in failure to control viral infections. One such complication is persistent cutaneous human papillomavirus (HPV) infections. HPV DNA has been detected in up to 90% of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma cases in OTRs, suggesting HPV may play a significant role in the pathogenesis of cSCC in OTRs. Importantly, the mortality rate in OTRs with cSCCs is twice that in the general population. I propose to study the role of T cell immunity in the pathogenesis of cutaneous HPV infection and subsequent cSCC development in OTRs. The primary goals of this study are to investigate the effects of long term immunosuppression on the quality and quantity of T cells in OTRs and how these changes differ among OTRs with cSCC as compared to immunocompetent hosts with cSCC. I will also further define the differences in HPV specific T cells targeting the HPV epitopes in OTRs with disseminated HPV and cSCCs and compare these with the HPV specific T cell response of their immunocompetent household members who carry similar HPV subtypes, but who can eradicate the HPV infection. This proposed multi-center study builds upon an existing prospective study, where blood sera will be systematically collected from patients diagnosed with cSCC in OTRs and non-OTRs. The findings from this study will clarify the immunomodulatory roles of HPV infections in cSCC carcinogenesis in OTRs. Findings from this study may also potentially pave the way forward for the development of personalized medicine, where HLA-matched, HPV-specific T cell replacement therapies can be used to prevent and/or treat HPV-associated SCC in OTRs.
kw: human papillomavirus; squamous cell carcinoma; T-cell immunity; organ transplant; precision medicine, skin cancer

title:
Using 11C-Metomidate PET-CT in Primary Aldosteronism
To Identify Curable Hypertension due to an Aldosterone-producing Adenoma
abs: Hypertension afflicts 1 in 4 Singaporeans, of which 10-20% have the treatable condition of Primary Aldosteronism (PA). PA can be either bilateral (treated with lifelong medications), or unilateral (curable with laparoscopic surgery). However, identifying unilateral PA requires an invasive test, adrenal vein sampling (AVS), which often yields inconclusive results. Hence, many patients remain undiagnosed, leading to uncontrolled hypertension and preventable heart attacks and strokes. In our prior NMRC New Investigator Grant, we piloted the first-in-Asia 11C-Metomidate PET-CT scan to identify patients with unilateral surgically-curable PA. PET-CT is non-invasive, non-operator-dependent and scalable. We are the first to demonstrate that PET-CT detects more patients than AVS. We will validate our findings in this larger-scale clinical study, where we aim to: 1. Demonstrate that 11C-metomidate PET-CT is more accurate than AVS in identifying unilateral PA as established by cure of disease post-surgery (primary aim) 2. Correlate 11C-metomidate PET-CT uptake with immunohistochemical staining for aldosterone synthase (CYP11B2) of adrenal tissue Our multi-centre collaboration will recruit 100 patients with PA in total (40 supported with this grant) who are keen for surgery. All patients will undergo subtype testing with both PET-CT and AVS. All results will be reviewed at a multi-disciplinary meeting to determine clinical diagnosis (unilateral or bilateral PA). Management (surgery or medications) will be decided by the clinician and patient. All patients will be assessed for cure post-surgery at six-months. Adrenal tissue from all patients who underwent surgery will be assessed using immunohistochemistry to identify the underlying histopathology. 11C-metomidate PET-CT can change the way PA is managed worldwide. It is imperative for Singapore to leverage on our pilot study success and demonstrate that functional imaging with PET-CT can replace invasive venous sampling. This will identify more patients with curable hypertension, and establish Singapore as a world-leading centre in hypertension.
kw: Hypertension; Functional Imaging; Surgery; Adrenal Endocrinology; Resistant Hypertension; Diagnostic testing

title: Widefield and Multi-modal Corneal Imaging to Investigate Corneal Endothelial Cell Loss following Descemet Membrane Endothelial Keratoplasty (DMEK)
abs: Corneal transplantation is the most common solid-organ transplant performed worldwide. Descemet membrane endothelial keratoplasty (DMEK) selectively replaces diseased corneal endothelial cells (CECs), producing better visual outcomes and substantially lower graft rejection compared to traditional corneal transplants. Despite a successful DMEK, transplanted CECs continue to degrade, leading to graft failure in up to 20-30% of the patients in 5 years. The exact mechanisms of CEC loss post-DMEK, observed in 99% of eyes at various degrees of loss with no obvious signs of graft rejection, remain unknown. Currently, CEC loss after DMEK is monitored via imaging a small (<1%) central area of the endothelium. We aim to use widefield endothelial imaging to examine peripheral CEC morphological changes associated with central CEC loss post-DMEK, and hypothesize that early-damaged CECs may occur in the peripheral areas before central regions of the cornea. We will also use a deep-learning (DL) method to derive CEC imaging parameters, and then use machine-learning to evaluate multi-modal cornea imaging parameters for their association with central CEC loss post-DMEK. We hypothesize that CEC and imaging parameters may predict which eyes will suffer excessive CEC loss post-DMEK. We plan to conduct a prospective clinical study of patients undergoing DMEK at the Singapore National Eye Center with 2-year follow-up. We will perform (1) serial widefield endothelial imaging to document peripheral morphological changes antecedent to central CEC loss, and (2) study multi-modal corneal imaging parameters for their associations with high CEC loss 2-years post-DMEK. In a future study, we will validate a DL-derived algorithm to predict CEC loss and endothelial failure post-DMEK. Findings from our study may help developing management protocols tailored to individual patients based on imaging biomarkers to prevent CEC loss, and ultimately, prolong DMEK graft survival - a key solution to an increasing global cornea donor supply-demand mismatch.
kw: Cornea transplantation; cornea endothelial cells; Descemet membrane endothelial keratoplasty; Cellular senescence; Aqueous humour

title: Development of Algorithm-driven 3D-Printed Personalised Biocompatible Eye Masks for Infraorbital Edema Treatment in Healthy and Aged Volunteers
abs: Hypothesis: Algorithm-driven 3D printed personalized biocompatible masks are effective in reducing infraorbital eyebags edema and improving infraorbital appearance in different patient groups who follow a standardized treatment protocol: 1) Healthy volunteers below age 50 2) Aged Healthy volunteers more than age 50. Aims: 1) To validate the effectiveness and proof of concept of 3D-printed compression masks in infraorbital edema treatment 2) To obtain a baseline cohort analysis of volunteers’ eyebags and periorbital facial aesthetics through 3D scanning and baseline relevant medical history; so as to drive the mask AI (Artificial Intelligence) algorithm optimization. Methodology: At least 25 volunteers aged below 50 and 25 volunteers aged above 50 ,without comorbidities, will be recruited. They will first undergo a comprehensive 3D facial scanning via the validated mobile app to establish the baseline. Subsequently, a 3D mask will be printed for them. This will be worn daily at night and tracked for compliance. Daily pictures and facial volume scanning will be done up to a treatment protocol period of 1 month to assess efficacy. Feasibility: The trial is safe as there is no invasive intervention. There is a preliminary prototype that has shown clinical efficacy in reducing periorbital edema in a few test subjects. The trial will be multi-centre to facilitate patient recruitment.
kw: 3D Printing; Infraorbital edema; Medical Device; Compresssion Mask

title: Development and evaluation of ACP-HEART: A randomized controlled trial
abs: Advance care planning is a widely discussed intervention to improve quality of end of life care. However, our previous work found that the existing model of ACP is labour-intense, conducted as a one-time rather than a continuous process and does not facilitate end-of-life care consistent with patient preferences. To address these gaps, we aim to develop and evaluate a novel web-based dynamic ACP intervention (ACP-HEART) among patients with advanced heart failure and a prognosis of less than a year. ACP-HEART will educate patients about their illness and treatment options. It will include a structured approach for patients to think about end-of-life care choices, coach them to communicate preferences with their surrogates and incorporate systems to encourage routine review of preferences. We will evaluate the intervention through a 2-arm randomized controlled trial with 192 eligible patients. Patients in the intervention arm (n=96) will receive the ACP-HEART intervention at least every 3 months for a period of 1 year. They will have their ACP document recorded and updated in the National Electronic Health Records by a trained ACP facilitator. Patients in the control arm (n=96) will receive usual care. We will compare patients’ end-of-life care preferences, ACP documentation, decisional conflict, psychological distress, health care costs and receipt of end-of-life care consistent with preferences, between intervention and control arms. We will also assess the reach, fidelity and patient satisfaction with the intervention. If found to be effective, ACP-HEART will be the first web-based ACP intervention to systematically implement a dynamic model of web-based ACP among patients with heart failure.
kw: heart failure; end-of-life care; advance care planning; decision aid

title: EMPOWERing Patients with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) in Primary Care through App-based Motivational Interviewing PLUS Artificial Intelligence powered Diabetes Management (EMPOWER-PLUS) – A Pragmatic Randomised Controlled Trial
abs: There is an urgent need for better control and prevention of complications in T2DM. Behavioural change is critical, and while literature suggests that motivational interviewing (MI) may be effective in improving glycemic control, none has explored app-based MI designed specifically for T2DM. The overall objective of this project is to determine the effectiveness of primary care model combining app-based MI and AI-powered personalised nudges delivered through a mobile application (app) for diabetes management (EMPOWER-PLUS). Our specific aims are (1) Co-design and develop a mobile app-based MI module on our existing EMPOWER app; (2) Evaluate the clinical and cost-effectiveness of MI and nudges through EMPOWER-PLUS to deliver diabetes management through a randomised controlled trial (RCT); (3) Evaluate the implementation of the app-based MI. We will achieve this goal by firstly co-designing a mobile app-based MI module with T2DM patients and healthcare practitioners. After rapid prototyping of the app-based MI, we will conduct a 3-arm RCT with primary outcome measure being the difference in HbA1c level at week 36 between the intervention and control arms. Secondary outcome measures include cost-effectiveness, quality of life, medication adherence, diet, and physical activity. Eligible poorly controlled T2DM patients with T2DM in polyclinics will be randomized to intervention arm who will receive EMPOWER-PLUS and smartwatch wearable on top of their usual clinical care. The first control group will have access to nudges delivered through app and smartwatch wearable in addition to usual clinical care but will not receive MI. The second control group will receive usual care (no access to MI, nudges and smartwatch wearable). This study is important to improve T2DM outcomes and reduce healthcare utilization by providing scientifically evaluated and transformative primary care model. Leveraging on digital technology and artificial intelligence to drive personalised care, behavioural change and empowerment has huge potential for scale up.
kw: Empowerment; Elements of Motivational Interviewing; Personalized diabetes management; Artificial Intelligence; Automated counselling interactions; Models of care

title: Refinement and Prospective Validation of a Deep Learning Algorithm for Detecting Chronic Kidney Disease Using Retinal Images (RetiKid)
abs: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a major public health problem associated with significant morbidity, and mortality. Screening for CKD is challenging in community and primary care settings, even in high-income countries because of the need to obtain serum levels of creatinine, or testing urine for protein. The retina being accessible to non-invasive imaging and retinal changes have been shown to provide information on systemic vascular and metabolic diseases, we developed and validated an artificial intelligence deep learning algorithm (RetiKid) to detect CKD (corresponding to stage 3-5) from retinal images to complement existing CKD screening strategies. The algorithm showed good performance with area under the curve of 0.91 in internal validation and 0.73 and 0.84 in external tests sets. This proof-of-concept study showed the feasibility of using retinal photography as an adjunctive and/or opportunistic screening tool for CKD in community populations. Building upon this study, in this current proposal, we aim to 1) refine and externally validate RetiKid across several populations using retrospective data as well as in a prospectively recruited community cohort; 2) to evaluate the incremental cost-savings of extending the annual serum creatinine screening to biannual and triennial for diabetic patients identified as low-risk by RetiKid and 3) develop a new “early” CKD DLA for screening early CKD (stage 1 and 2) using retinal images from local and validate it in external cohorts. The RetiKid if found to be robust and effective, we envision deploying RetiKid as a triage tool, i.e., those who tested positive by RetiKid go for blood test to confirm CKD status by serum creatinine and those who tested negative will leave the pathway with recommendation for annual screening. This will avoid invasive phlebotomy and shorten the turn-around time considerably besides reducing the demand on human resources involved in CKD screening.
kw: Chronic kidney disease; retinal image; deep learning; validation; community; high risk;

title: Investigating the kinetics, pathogenesis and host responses of SARS COV-2 Omicron variant in in vitro and in vivo infection models
abs: The emergence of SARS-CoV-2 since late 2019 resulted in the COVID-19 pandemic and is still constantly causing major outbreaks around the world due to the rapidly evolving variants from the virus. Most recently, the emergence of the Omicron variant of concern (VOC), with major changes in the spike protein RBD, show signs of reduced vaccine efficacy, possibility of reinfection, and altered infection biology that once again threaten to escalate into a major outbreak similar to when Delta VOC first emerges. Therefore, it is important to quickly re-establish the infection biology of the Omicron VOC to remain ahead in the devising of management strategies and treatment to this new variant, for minimizing the damage it can cause. This can be achieved via the specific aims of: 1) Investigating infectious viral shedding via virus isolation and culture from patient samples in correlation to virus load via qRT-PCR, with animal model infection to study early pathology and cytokines. The completion of the specific aim will allow us to further our understanding on the SARS-CoV-2 Omicron variant and assess the impact that it brings to the pandemic.
kw: SARS-CoV-2, Infection models, Omicron, Host responses, Pathogenesis

title: SUREFIND-NDD: Singapore Undiagnosed Disease Research Endeavour For Identification of Novel genetic Discoveries in NeuroDevelopmental Disorders
abs: Background: Neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) are a socially debilitating disorder affecting ~5% of the paediatric population in Singapore, and have considerable overlap with adult neurological disorders. Although there is a strong genetic component to NDD, due to extreme genetic heterogeneity, a cause cannot be identified in the majority of individuals by traditional methods of genetic testing. Recently, the advent of complementary genetic tools such as whole-genome sequencing (WGS), transcriptome sequencing, and long-read genomic sequencing have emerged to allow one to comprehensively study genetic variants efficiently and cost-effectively in complex genetic disorders including NDD. Objective: The over-arching goal of this research is to use multi-omics analysis to improve our understanding of NDD and use this knowledge to gain insights to identify potential biomarkers and therapeutic targets. Methods: Over the past 7 years, the applicant and team have recruited over 100 families referred to our Genetics clinic across SingHealth, including KK Women’s and Children’s Hospital and National Neuroscience Institute, and National University Hospital for evaluation for NDD, the majority of whom remain undiagnosed despite whole-exome sequencing. This CSA proposal will help the applicant continue to have protected time and fund infrastructure to continue this program for recruitment, phenotyping, and analysis of patients with undiagnosed diseases. We will apply WGS, blood transcriptome sequencing and long-read sequencing to define high-risk genes within our local population. Bioinformatic algorithms and in-house analytical pipelines will be utilised to identify the causal genes and drive novel gene discoveries. Clinical Significance: The use of these complementary technologies will allow us to identify the underlying aetiology for NDDs. Elucidating the genetic causes will allow us to understand molecular pathways and provide insights into potential biomarkers and therapeutic targets. Given the overlap with adult neurological disorders, understanding from these rare disorders can be applied to the commoner adult disorders.
kw: Neurodevelopmental disorders, genomic sequencing, long read sequencing, undiagnosed diseases

title: Prognostic significance of RNA signatures to predict major complications following acute reperfusion treatment for ischemic stroke
abs: Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage (SICH) and malignant cerebral oedema (MCO) are two dreaded complications of reperfusion treatment in patients with acute ischemic stroke. Using existing resources of the NUHS Stroke Tissue Repository, we sequenced small and long non-coding RNAs using a RNA sequencing (RNA-Seq) method in whole blood samples of 20 ischemic stroke patients (mean age, 69 years; 50% men) who underwent reperfusion treatment at the National University Hospital, Singapore. These RNAs were subsequently analysed for the development of events (a composite of SICH and MCO). We identified unique RNA expressions that were differentially expressed between these groups. We hypothesise that brain-specific RNAs are released into the circulation following cerebral ischemia and detection of these RNAs could signal an increased likelihood of major bleeding and swelling complications following acute stroke therapies. We further hypothesise that the ability to identify these RNAs will allow neurologists and Emergency Room physicians to expeditiously classify patients according to their risk of complications. The overarching objective is to investigate RNA signatures to predict major complications in ischemic stroke patients following reperfusion treatment. Specifically, we aim to: 1. Derive an RNA signature of adverse treatment outcomes 2. Develop a customised technological platform to profile the derived RNA signature 3. Independently validate the performance of the derived panel of RNA signatures to predict adverse events between the customised platform and PCR-based methods This study will deliver: 1. A validated panel of adverse candidate RNAs associated with major complications. 2. A customised technological platform to profile these candidate RNAs. This study builds on compelling preliminary data, creates new knowledge on stroke mechanisms and leverages on multidisciplinary expertise to address an important clinical question.
kw: ischaemic stroke, reperfusion treatment, complications, RNA, device

title: Non-adherence to cancer treatments and the survival gains observed in pivotal phase 3 trials and expected in routine practice
abs: Obtaining an appropriate estimate of a treatment effect of interest (estimand) from a clinical trial to inform research, clinical, and/or policy decisions can sometimes be surprisingly challenging. For example, how should the true efficacy of a treatment be estimated: (1) from a trial in which some participants did not adhere to the randomly assigned treatment (or switched to another treatment); (2) from a trial that was halted early based on an interim analysis; or, (3) if the treatment of interest was permitted to be used concurrently with randomized treatment with the decision left to the preference of the responsible clinical investigator? In each case, a simple comparison between two groups will yield a biased estimate of the treatment effect of interest. This PhD project investigates approaches for addressing such questions using casual inference and other methods. Existing trial datasets will be used to conduct the research. Once disseminated, the findings of the work undertaken will help ensure that high-quality clinical trial data are appropriately used to obtain valid estimates to address important questions.
kw: Clinical trials; Oncology; Epidemiology; Population Health

title: Genotype Guided Antiplatelet Therapy In Ischemic Stroke
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Aims: To determine the feasibility and clinical impact of genetic testing guided antiplatelet therapy in ischemic stroke patients on the prevention of major adverse cardiovascular or cerebrovascular events (MACCE). Hypothesis: We hypothesize that genotype guided therapy would result in a reduction of 10 events /100 person-years in the prevention of a composite MACCE outcomes over 12 months compared to standard medical treatment. Study design: Prospective randomized open blinded end point study Methods: Clopidogrel naïve ischemic stroke or TIA patients aged 21 and above will be randomized to genetic testing guided antiplatelet therapy or standard medical therapy within 1 week of their index stroke. Patients allocated to testing group will have blood drawn for diagnosis of CYP2C19 LOF mutations. Patients who test positive for an LOF mutation will be offered alternative antiplatelet therapy in the form of aspirin (for those who need monotherapy) or ticagrelor (for those with monotherapy that are unable to take aspirin) or aspirin plus ticagrelor (for those who need dual antiplatelet therapy). Patients who test negative for LOF mutation will continue on clopidogrel. Platelet reactivity index (PRI) will be measured at baseline, at steady state, and also at follow up. Primary outcome: The primary clinical outcome is the composite MACCE over 12 months from recruitment following the index stroke. Secondary outcomes: Secondary outcomes include clinically significant bleeding as per GUSTO criteria (Global Use of Strategies to Open Occluded Arteries)6 of severe/life threatening bleeding event, ischemic events (ischemic stroke or TIA, myocardial ischemic events, or death from vascular causes), and PRI.
kw: Stroke; Precision Medicine; Antiplatelet; Genetics

title: Characterizing Pathogen Associated Molecular Patterns (PAMPs) propogating Non-Alcoholic Steatohepatitis (NASH)
abs: Non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) is an unmet medical need with no available non-invasive biomarkers and limited therapeutic options. We recently found that our local NASH patients have distinct luminal microbial dysbiosis (imbalance of beneficial and harmful bacterial species) and corresponding gut barrier dysfunction. Our murine models further suggest a causal relation between microbial dysbiosis and NASH, whereby animals fed antibiotics were found to have attenuated NASH, and transplant of microbial NASH patients’ microbiota into these mice re-induces NASH. Other groups have also demonstrated that, in NASH, there is increased intestinal permeability induced by gut dysbiosis with subsequent translocation of bacterial products, primarily endotoxins, derived predominantly from Gram-negative bacteria, inducing low-grade systemic inflammation. However, we also found a gross enrichment of Gram-positive bacteria in patients with NASH, and therefore we hypothesize that other pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs), such as bacterial peptidoglycans (PGN), which are present at a significantly higher amount quantity in Gram-positive bacteria, also play a key role in propagating NASH. Previously, due to a lack of appropriate detection methods, the diversity and spectrum of the endogenous PAMPs in the host’s gut and systemic circulation are poorly characterised. Our proposal thereby, seeks to first profile the microbiome and PAMPs in 20 NASH patients, compared to 20 patients with fatty liver without NASH and 20 healthy controls, using in-house state-of-the-art high resolution mass spectrometry. Putative PAMPs contributing to NASH would be further verified in silico through paired metagenomics of the patients’ stool and fecal samples, as well as validated in vitro through deep metabolomic characterisation of the isolated bacterial isolates from NASH patients. Next we aim to validate the causal role of these putative PAMPs on NASH propagation in-vivo, through introducing these putative PAMPs and their contributing microbes into pre-existing gut-decontaminated NAFLD murine models we have previously developed.
kw: Microbiome; NASH

title: Identification of pathophysiological processes in lean-diabetic patients with heart failure
abs: Background. Heart failure (HF) is a global public health problem, affecting one in five men and women in their lifetime, and the prevalence is increasing in Singapore. Unfortunately, half of the patients with HF die within five years of diagnosis. Asian patients with HF have a unique ‘lean diabetic’ phenotype, which is poorly understood. Aims. This proposal uses an integrated systems biology approach to identify treatment targets and mechanistic pathways in Asian patients with HF and a lean diabetic phenotype. We propose a novel ‘bedside to bench approach’: We will (1) characterize lean-diabetic patients with HF, (2) elucidate treatment targets in lean diabetic patients with HF and (3) study treatment targets and mechanisms in a cellular model. Methods. First, we will characterize patients with heart failure and a lean diabetic phenotype and compare these patients to controls without HF in a large, richly phenotyped case-control study. Second, we will use systems biology techniques to identify pathways and treatment targets related to disease based on phenotypic (clinical characteristics and imaging data), proteomic and genetic data in patients with HF. Lastly, we propose to validate possible pathways and treatment targets using human induced pluripotent stem cells derived cardiomyocytes. Significance. Results of this proposal will provide much-needed insights into the pathophysiology of HF, specifically in Asian patients. Identified treatment targets have the potential to impact treatment and long-term outcomes of patients with HF.
kw: Cardiovascular disease, heart failure

title: Optimizing Tendon Healing with Functionalized Sutures and Modified Fibrin Gels
abs: Tendon and ligament injuries make up over 50% of all musculoskeletal injuries. Healthcare cost incurred from tendon injuries has been estimated to be valued at 30 billion US dollars per year in the USA and over 115 billion euros per year in Europe. Surgical repairs are considered for patients who have complete ruptures of the rotator cuff tendon. These tears can be repaired primarily by end-to-end suturing or be augmented with the biceps tendon or commercially available grafts. Of the tendon ruptures that are amenable to surgical repair, complete repairs have been reported to fail over 50% of the time. In addition, re-tear rates of commercially available graft-augmented repairs have been reported to be as high as 90%. In view of these limitations in clinical management, research in this field is targeted at a combination of factors that influence tendon healing and regeneration. Two major limitations impede advancement of surgical strategies in tendon reconstruction. Firstly, the use of non-absorbable sutures are areas of high stress with a higher re-tear rate and can compromise vascular supply to the tendon tissue that is already known to be relatively avascular. Secondly, most nonabsorbable sutures have low bioactivity. Mesenchymal stem cells (MSC) exosomes have arisen as a potential cell-free nanoparticle therapeutic strategy with potent immunomodulatory and regenerative properties. However, the therapeutic efficacy of MSC exosomes for tendon repair, and the associated cellular processes and mechanisms remain to be clarified. This proposed study, we aim to develop an MSC exosome-loaded scaffold for localized release of exosomes at the tendon defect site, and to demonstrate its therapeutic efficacy for tendon regeneration, through in vitro cellular assays utilizing tendon cells and macrophages, as well as in vivo rat tendon defect model.
kw: Suture; Fibrin gel; Functionalisation; Tendon;

title: Unravelling the cell lineage origins of EGFR mutated non-small cell lung cancer
abs: Our understanding of the underlying biology of NSCLC has transformed with the identification of molecular subtypes of disease. These are defined by mutated or translocated oncogenic drivers and are therapeutically tractable with highly effective targeted inhibitors. EGFR activating mutations are the most prominent example, prevalent in over half of all lung adenocarcinoma patients in Asian populations. Despite this, emerging evidence indicates even within EGFR mutated NSCLC, there exists significant heterogeneity with further molecular subtypes that may influence clinical and treatment outcomes. Recently, through a comprehensive description of the EGFR TKI resistance landscape, we identified deeper genomic and transcriptomic traits that may characterize these further molecular subtypes. Notably, validated TCGA transcriptomic subtypes were intimately correlated with treatment resistance and underpinned by histologic and cell lineage plasticity. In addition, the cell of origin and genetic driver lesions are increasingly suspected to play a critical role in shaping the phenotypes of lung tumors. Consequently, we hypothesize that in EGFR mutated NSCLC, malignant transformation, oncogenic dependency, phenotypic plasticity and response to therapy, may all be influenced by cell of origin and epigenetic drivers of pulmonary epithelial differentiation. We propose a study to elucidate cell lineage with deep multi-omic profiling of normal lung tissue and paired pre- and post-treatment EGFR mutated lung tumors to provide an integrative understanding of the tumor evolutionary history. This will incorporate deep sequencing technologies, including genomics with whole exome sequencing (WES) and transcriptomics with RNA sequencing (RNA-seq). Integrative clustering will reveal the degree of lineage plasticity and provide a deep understanding of tumor biology to ultimately identify therapeutic vulnerabilities.
kw: Cell lineage; EGFR mutation; lung cancer; novel biomarkers; tumour biology

title: History and syntax of the languages of Borneo
abs: The primary goals of this project are to: (a) document and understand the diversity of the syntax of languages of Borneo, through original fieldwork on these languages, (b) conduct detailed syntactic analysis on specific languages, contributing to the development of the “functional bundling” theory of syntactic variation, and (c) develop models of historical grammatical change in Borneo over the past several thousand years, including the emergence of Malayic language group’s distinctive syntactic features which began roughly two thousand years ago. The project will contribute not only to the primary documentation of these critically understudied languages, but will also contribute to central topics in linguistic theory, including the theory of Austronesian “voice systems,” the nature of syntactic variation, and possible directions and motivations for historical grammatical change. There are two primary motivations that necessitate this study of the languages of Borneo. (i) The Austronesian language family is one of the largest of the world. The western Austronesian languages are conventionally divided into two grammatical types: the Philippine/Formosan-type languages of Taiwan, the Philippines, and northern Borneo (Malaysia), and Malay/Indonesian-type languages located in the remainder of Malaysia and western Indonesia. The diversity and history of the languages of Borneo suggest that their detailed study holds the key to understanding the synchronic and diachronic relationships between these two major classes of Austronesian languages, since Borneo is the only area in the western Austronesian-speaking area where both types of languages are found in abundance. (ii) Linguistic and anthropological evidence suggest that Borneo is the ancestral homeland of the Malay people and the origin of the Malayic language group, who then spread to the Malay peninsula and the Nusantara archipelago, including Singapore, and Borneo is still home to the greatest diversity of Malayic languages. Our planned contributions include work into the historical development of the Malayic language group, including through comparison of the grammars of Malayic languages of Borneo with the grammar of the contemporary Singapore Malay language. We propose to bring together a world-class team of emerging experts on the languages of Borneo, linguistic theory, and language change under “one roof.” Taking advantage of the great young talent that currently exists on the study of Borneo, we propose to hire Postdoctoral/Research Fellows, for which have compiled a preliminary list of exceptional candidates who have first-hand experience with the documentation and analysis of diverse languages of Borneo. These PDF/RF candidates all have direct contacts with different language communities in Borneo through prior linguistic fieldwork, and necessary Malay and Indonesian language backgrounds, which ensure the successful execution of the project’s primary data collection goals. title: From Digital Numismatics to a New History of Ancient Empires
abs: In the era of data-driven humanities, digital numismatics has the potential to transform historical research, by contributing an invaluable source of evidence. Technological advances in the last few decades have provided an unprecedented opportunity to understand and explore humanities in the 21st century through the digitization of the world’s knowledge, tradition, heritage, cultural expressions and artefacts. As such, the discipline of humanities is undergoing a revolution in its methods of enquiry. Tedious and often practically infeasible groundwork underpinning core humanistic research endeavours, such as analysing text corpora or clustering archaeological artefacts, can now be accomplished in a relatively short time using modern data-science techniques coupled with high computing power. As such, digital humanities, with its origins in the 1950s, is still an emergent field: new techniques, resources, challenges and advancements come from the interface between humanistic disciplines, mathematics, statistics and computer science. The process of digitization has produced an incredible amount of data (Big Data revolution) leading to a point where manual analyses are impractical. This is due not only to the huge amounts of data available, but also to their heterogeneity and complexity, which require tailored analysis tools. For instance, in numismatics the interest in sophisticated statistical methods has been fuelled by the increasing availability of digital archives of coin images. Singapore’s cultural and educational institutions are experiencing remarkable success in several ambitious digital initiatives, as highlighted in a recent media commentary (www.channelnewsasia.com/news/commentary/essential-workers-services-singapore-artists-arts-humanities-12851622). These initiatives involve a large spectrum of humanities, from its traditional disciplines (e.g., languages, literature, philosophy, geography, history, art history) to anthropology, heritage studies, museum studies, performing and visual arts. The Singapore-based research community is increasingly engaging in Digital Humanities as demonstrated by Digital Humanities Singapore (https://digitalhumanities.sg/) which promotes the integration of qualitative and quantitative approaches. Other examples include the 2018 creation of the NTU Institute of Science and Technology for Humanity, or the wealth of research and teaching topics at the intersection of computing and humanities supported by NUS (https://libportal.nus.edu.sg/frontend/web/resources/library-initiatives/digitalhumanities). This proposal perfectly places itself in this new research landscape, by enhancing the potential of digital numismatics as a history research tool. Coins offer a crucial source for the political and economic history of ancient states, particularly when other evidence is limited. Millions of ancient coins have been excavated and significantly outnumber other groups of remains such as ceramics and inscriptions. Th

title: Plastic Waste and Women’s Household Practices in Asia and Australia
abs: This proposed research aims to document how women, in different roles as homemakers, career professionals and workers, migrant domestic workers and environmental activists, are shaping the management of household plastic waste in the Asia Pacific. This provides the empirical context to examine the implications of household gendered labour in the consumption and disposal of plastic waste from social, historical and digital perspectives. This is a timely project as it captures a significant moment in which many nation-states are implementing various measures to reduce domestic plastic waste after China’s ban on foreign plastic waste import in 2018. It also documents local practices at the point of origin within the transnational chain of plastic waste, giving attention to household dynamics which are responsible for the generation of a large share of plastic waste. Given that women take primary responsibilities for the care of the household in Asia and beyond, this project fosters an in-depth understanding of the role of gender, intersecting with class, occupation and nationality, in shaping household plastic waste management. Efforts to manage plastic waste have been instituted at a variety of scales including interventions by governments, industry producers and individual consumers. In recent times, proponents in the global and local environmental movement have increasingly hailed the household as the locus of change. State policies have aimed to shift people’s behaviours at the household level, by introducing, for instance, a ban on single-use plastic bags in supermarkets or introducing stricter sorting rules for household waste. Online activism which encourages green consumption and zero-waste has also identified the household as an important target. Yet, while research on plastic waste has expanded in recent decades, a disproportionate share of the scholarship attends to the consequences of plastic waste on environmental and human health; much less is known about the social and historical factors shaping household practices of waste management. Training the analytical spotlight on the household as a critical part of environmental discourse also foregrounds the importance of attending to gender roles and relations within and beyond the household. This is an under-researched area in studies on plastic waste. While there are a few reports by international development organisations that have pointed out that women in developing countries are more likely than men to be subjected to adverse effects of plastic waste originating from developed counties (Lynn, Rech, and Samwel-Mantingh 2017), there has been little attention on how gender shapes consumption and disposal of plastic waste at households in developed countries in the Asia-Pacific region. This proposed research hence fills a gap in the scholarship by investigating gender and household plastic waste in three Asia-Pacific developed countries: Singapore, Japan and Australia. The three countries

title: Chinese Popular Cultures in Post-War Singapore and Malaya (1945-1965)
abs: This research project will explore the cultural and social forces, networks and institutional factors that shaped the everyday life of ethnic Chinese in Singapore and Malaya in the two decades following World War II by exploring a neglected topic: Chinese popular cultures. Thus far, studies of Chinese-language cultures in Singapore and Malaya have focused mostly on literary or intellectual culture—the culture of the elite. Our project aims to document and analyse manifold aspects of Sinophone popular cultures: storytelling, street opera, pop music, folk artists, performance troupes, pulp fiction, entertainment magazines, mosquito papers and tabloids. In short, this project is an attempt at doing cultural history from below. In order to accomplish our goals, we are undertaking the creation of the first-ever online database for primary sources pertaining to Chinese popular cultures in Singapore and Malaya, ranging from printed materials and ephemera to photographs and film clips, audiorecordings and oral histories. Our documentation of the cultural products consumed by the Chinese general public during the post-war period will spur new inquiries as well as re-evaluations of post-war and post-colonial cultural histories in this region. A key strategy in our endeavour is partnering with local collectors. We aim not only to preserve the local Sinophone cultural heritage, but also to learn about the community values represented by that heritage from the perspective of non-academic specialists, and to re-frame those values for a wider audience, including the global academic community. Our project falls under the heading of Sinophone Studies, but this discipline has thus far concentrated on the study of products of elite culture. By reconsidering the many diverse popular cultural experiences on the ground—especially the Chinese dialect cultures in their transcultural and transmedial contexts—our project aims at a reconceptualization of the Sinophone, leading to the creation and promotion of new knowledge in studies of post-war Singapore and Malaya. Overall, this project aims to uncover local and folk epistemologies of Sinophone Southeast Asian cultures. By surveying a wider socioeconomic dimension of the everyday lives of Singapore-Malaysian Chinese, and investigating the extent to which the quotidian is shaped by both colonial forces and intra-Chinese agency, we hope to yield a more nuanced understanding of cultural structuration at work, that is, a different account of forces which are not congruent with the hierarchies that current Sinophone literary debates seek to challenge. Also, conceptualized in this fashion, the project contributes to the interdisciplinary evolution of Sinophone Studies (“Sinophone Studies” 2019), which has embarked on conversations beyond literary studies, cinema studies and queer studies (Chiang 2013, 2019) to seek broader alliances in history, anthropology, musicology, linguistics, art history, dance studies, etc., while reta

title: CONCERTED DANCE OF PROTEIN AND DNA; CHOREOGRAPHY IN CROWDED AND CONGESTED CONDITIONS
abs: Protein transport on DNA and target search are fundamental aspects in DNA metabolism (replication, repair, gene expression regulation, etc.). Accordingly, it has been widely investigated with a range of experimental methodologies and theoretical approaches. In particular, fluorescence microscopy has allowed to track a myriad of proteins moving on DNA. Target search is facilitated by a combination of one-dimensional sliding along DNA and three-dimensional hopping and jumping between different binding sites. An almost ignored, yet important aspect of the dance of protein with DNA is the role of DNA motion and, in particular, how this is related to confinement and crowding as being critical aspects of the native, congested state. The aim of this proposal is to fill this lacuna by systematic investigation of the mobility of a series of proteins with different binding modes, using DNA substrates with specific target sequences and confined to nanofluidic channels in the presence of crowding agents and/or ligands. A key feature of our experimental approach is the measurement of DNA internal motion through analysis of fluorescence correlation and fluorescence imaging and tracking of the protein moving on DNA in the same experimental condition. This previously proven methodology will give unprecedented information about the dynamic coupling of protein mobility and DNA motion. The results will be interpreted with diffusion models including the effects of intermittent binding, 1D sliding along DNA, and 3D diffusion through the interior of the DNA coil. We surmise that the foreseen results on the dynamic coupling of DNA motion, protein mobility, and in conditions bearing resemblance to the native state, will have important implications for the understanding of the machinery of life.

title: Ocean Mining: A Fluidic Electrochemical Route for Lithium Extraction from Seawater
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: The overall goal of this proposal is to design and develop a novel, low-energy lithium extraction technology capable of recovering Li resources directly from seawater. Lithium ion batteries (LIBs) technology has come a long way from its inception to widespread deployment in a multitude of applications, ranging from micro electronic devices to large scale deployment, such as grid energy storage and electric vehicles. Despite decades of research and development, the production of LIBs remains bogged down by high costs and limited resources of lithium (Li) metals. In recent years, the growth of electronics and electric vehicle markets have spurred a concomitant increase in demand for LIBs and could hasten the extinction of lithium resources1. As such, there is an urgent need to diversify lithium production. One promising option is to extract lithium from seawater. However, mining lithium from ocean is an arduous task and so far, only adsorption and electrochemical strategies have been investigated. Adsorption methods are relatively simple to implement but are grossly limited by low adsorption rates and dissolution of adsorbents. On the other hand, the electrochemical method is effective but only works well for lithium enriched brine solutions. Lithium concentration in seawater is extremely low at only 0.17 ppm and is accompanied by a variety of other ions including sodium (11000,000 ppm), calcium (420,000 ppm), magnesium (1300,000 ppm) and potassium (400 ppm). Thus, the separation of Li from seawater is not met by existing methods and this calls for a new cost-effective and highly selective method to be developed. In order to extract lithium efficiently from seawater, we propose a novel and effective fluidic electrochemical extraction (FEE) device. This FEE system comprises of an oxygen evolution cathode, a MnO2 working electrode and an oxygen reduction anode. During operation, a voltage will be applied across the electrodes to insert Li+ into MnO2 and release it as LiOH. We have identified 3 key objectives for our project. The first objective is to design and synthesize redox-active nanomaterials (i.e. MnO2, FePO4, TiO2) to realise maximum Li extraction capacity while maintaining stable cycling performances; the second is to design a Li extraction electrode with high selectivity; the third is to design an optimized FEE system which can be operated to extract Li, K and U with high efficiency. This FEE system is highly tunable, modular and simple to scale up. At present, ion-mining from seawater is a concept far from real-world applications and our FEE system provides an excellent opportunity to narrow that gap. Ultimately, we aim to develop this technique to become a premier ocean mining technology. Not only will this project nurture a generation of specialists with skillsets incorporating ocean mining ideas, it also has the potential to establish Singapore as a pioneering ocean technology hub and improve the economic prosperity of the nation.
kw: Ocean Mining, Fluidic Electrochemical Device, Lithium Extraction

title: Critical role of Neuropilin 1 in left ventricular non-compaction (LVNC)
abs: Many forms of congenital cardiac defects result from abnormal cardiac trabeculation and compaction. For example, left ventricular noncompaction (LVNC) is a cardiomyopathy caused by impaired myocardial compaction. LVNC is the third most common cardiomyopathy after dilated cardiomyopathy and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. LVNC is characterized by excessive trabeculation and impaired myocardial compaction during fetal development. It usually affects both ventricles but is more prominent on the left in humans. Patients with LVNC are at higher risk of developing systolic and diastolic dysfunction leading to heart failure, arrhythmias, and sudden cardiac death. Multiple genetic mutations have been identified in LVNC patients, but the molecular mechanism underlying LVNC remains elusive. In this study, our preliminary results demonstrate that cardiac-specific deletion of Neuropilin1 (Nrp1) leads to ventricular hypertrabeculation and non-compaction. We will test our hypothesis that Nrp1-PDGFRb signaling is essential for myocardial compaction. Our data support the hypothesis that LVNC is a distinct genetic cardiomyopathy with a developmental basis. It establishes the causal relationship between Nrp1 loss of function and LVNC in mice and provides insight into the mechanism underlying the disease. Our study suggests that Nrp1 might be considered as a candidate gene when screening LVNC patients for gene mutation.

title: To motivate human-in-the-loop learning of complex traffic networks
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: Today Singapore has one of the highest road densities (4.8 km of road per square km) and traffic flow (281 vehicles per km) in the world, and it is difficult to enlarge the roadway capacity due to constraints in space and budget. The resultant congestion threatens future economic growth and lowers each road user’s qualify of life. This is the same story in many other urban areas. Taking Los Angeles, which has a similar area and population to Singapore, as an example, each mobile user there spent an average of over 100 hours in traffic jams during peak congestion hours in 2018, costing the city billions of direct and indirect costs (including air pollution, wasted time and fuel, and business operating costs from commercial vehicles idling in traffic). On the other hand, it is found in recent studies like Braess paradox that there is still a good amount of road capacity left even during rush hour, though many users tend to choose similar routes (e.g., the shortest paths) to jam themselves or are unaware of dynamic traffic information. It is crucial to make best use of the limited road network and reduce the social travel cost for all citizens, and how to dynamically learn time-varying traffic information and adaptively route mobile users is a key question. We propose to employ the power of the crowd in information learning to negate their induced congestion effect. Thanks to recent developments in ICT technologies and mobile social networks, now it is possible to create such traffic crowd-learning systems as a public good. Millions of mobile sensors installed on individual vehicles and smartphones are powerful and affordable, enabling full network coverage for real-time traffic monitoring. Further, many mobile users are intensively interconnected, and they sense and share location-based information with each other when travelling on different routes and visit different areas. The information collected is aggregated over all users’ trips and make publicly available as public good. The availability of this public good has the potential of dramatically improving network efficiency, but only if it is used intelligently given users’ selfishness in sensing and routing. This project proposes new mechanism designs for motivating human-in-the-loop learning (HILL) of live traffic information, by aggregating all users’ trip observations and developing an intelligent trip advisory that benefit all. Our HILL platform will apply multi-agent reinforcement learning to data from all those users that have used these paths in the past and recommend paths to new travellers, by creating nudge incentives to gather new data to optimize the exploration-exploitation learning cycle. This is very different from the current practices in industry. Google Maps and Waze are the major mobile social networks that help users collect and share real-time in-vehicle sensor data about the driving conditions they experience on the travelled paths. title: The Interface of Geography, Demography, Human Mobility and Genetics on Dengue Transmissions within South-East Asia
abs: An estimated 390 million dengue infections occur annually, creating considerable health and economic burdens. Dengue is widespread across Southeast Asia (SEA) and is classified as super-endemic due to all four serotypes being in active circulation. Widespread ongoing urbanization and greater host movement rates via both domestic and international travel have increased transmission, particularly across highly major global and regional aviation hubs such as Singapore and Bangkok which may play a key role in increasing dengue transmissions across borders. Heightened local connectivity also drastically eases access between provinces within SEA countries, which likely heightens dengue transmission. Favourable climate and increasing human mobility have led to well suited conditions for dengue transmission in SEA. Lastly, rapid demographic changes through increased life expectancy in SEA may lead to long-term implications on the economic burden of dengue. Vector control has consistently been the primary control method against the two dengue-transmitting mosquito vectors, Aedes aegypti and Ae. albopictus. The low seropositivity rates in Singapore1, and the elevated risk of severe infections among seronegatives more generally, make the implementation of prophylaxis measures such as vaccination with Dengvaxia (CYD-TDV) and potentially other vaccines under development challenging. Instead, techniques such as releasing Wolbachia-infected mosquitoes, and reducing mosquito-breeding sites are employed. Although significant, the limited resource availability in SEA makes an inquiry into vector control effectiveness to be imperative. Such analysis should also account for breeding and infection dynamics of mosquitoes and cases in populations with shifting demography and mobility, but this has not been evaluated. Little is known about the interface of demography and human mobility on dengue transmissions and its associated burden within Singapore and more broadly, SEA. In this proposal, we will characterize (i) the relationship between dengue serotype composition, (ii) cross border dengue transmissions, (iii) flight patterns on the incidence of dengue transmissions across space and time, and (iv) estimate the cost effectiveness of various vector control methods while considering local connectivity, climate and breeding dynamics. We will build a geospatial model of background herd immunity levels using seroprevalence data and an existing individual-based model of Singapore. We will then develop a statistical model using incomplete dengue serotype samples and complete case notifications to predict the serotype composition of nearby and recently infected individuals. The fully inferred composition will first be used to infer the factors affecting the genetic variability of Dengue and the probability of being in an epidemic given past dengue cases. We hypothesise that there is a substantial variation across space and time between dengue serotypes clustered across demog

title: Privacy-Preserving Human-Interpretable Explainable AI
abs: Increasing regulatory requirements for artificial intelligence (AI) in many domains of decision making mandates their responsible use, particularly in decision justification and data privacy. For example, a bank loan model should both obfuscate an applicant’s personally identifiable information (PII) for privacy protection, and provide decision explanations since the outcome directly impacts the applicant’s livelihood. Indeed, many AI applications can benefit from the simultaneous provision of privacy and explainability; however, satisfying both leads to conflicting tradeoffs, where providing explanations harms privacy and preserving privacy distorts explanations. Despite the importance of model explainability and data privacy for responsible AI deployment, current research focuses on Explainable AI and Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning as separate domains. Specifically, current methods for privacy protection focus on maintaining model performance while preserving sensitive information (e.g., obfuscated data), and current techniques for model explanations assume models that are well-trained on clean data. The integrated and synergistic deployment of privacy and explainability thus entails a delicate balance to ease the tension, but it remains a topic under-explored. In particular, there is a critical lack of understanding of the privacy-explainability trade-offs and a paucity of AI explanations that are both privacy-preserving and human-interpretable. This proposal aims to simultaneously satisfy both requirements by examining the privacy-explainability conflicts, developing and evaluating privacy-preserving and faithful explainable AI. In contrast with research in AI focusing on proposing single explanation techniques to improve faithfulness, or research in HCI on validating the human understanding of existing explanation techniques, we have been developing and evaluating explanations that are balanced and optimized with other factors. Specifically, we have conducted a series of work to address the trade-offs between faithfulness and simplicity, explanation under uncertainty, and monotonicity perception in multi-attribute sorting. In this proposal, we will draw on our established approach to study the dual-requirement of explainability and privacy in AI to evaluate issues arising due to providing explanations and preserving privacy, and propose solutions that balance and optimize for these requirements. We will further evaluate outcomes through data-driven simulation studies and scenario-driven user studies. Our specific aims are: Aim 1: Evaluate privacy risk due to model explanations. We will determine various approaches to exploit explanations from target models to train inversion attack models to reconstruct sensitive information. We will train attack models using multi-modal, multi-task architectures with attention transfer. This will shed light on the privacy risks of various nascent explanation techniques. title: Symbolic Reasoning Based Resilience of Critical Infrastructure
abs: Critical infrastructures are among a nation’s most valuable assets whose disruption usually results in large-scale economic losses and inconvenience to its citizens. Thus, the protection and resilience of critical infrastructure are a matter of national priority and necessitate the development of tools and techniques to evaluate and enhance their robustness against natural and man-made (both accidental and adversarial) factors. Increasingly, such models also have to consider risks from cyber-attacks along with reliability given the increased use of information and communication technologies in critical infrastructure, thereby raising the complexity. Traditional approaches to evaluating the reliability are limited by their computation complexity, scalability issues, and their inability to accommodate the temporal correlations in the system dynamics. This project proposes a new approach to solving this problem building on advancements in symbolic reasoning over the past two decades. The objective of this project is to develop more effective, accurate and efficient methodologies for reliability and cyber-security risk assessment of critical infrastructure. The expected outcomes of the project include novel techniques to evaluate the reliability and security of critical infrastructure as well as strategies to enhance their robustness. As a starting point, our approach is based on reducing the resilience and risk evaluating problems to discrete integration problems. We will then explore the use of universal hashing and symbolic techniques to tackle the computational intractability. The paradigm of automated program synthesis that use our symbolic techniques to compute resilience will then be used to develop strategies for enhancing the resilience of critical infrastructure.
kw: Symbolic reasoning; critical infrastructure
