title: Project MixREADY: A unifying framework for Mixed-initiative, REsponsible, DynAmic Decision making under uncertainty
abs: We aim to develop a set of new AI agents toward meeting the following long-term research objectives: 1) Support mixed-initiative decision making and reinforcement learning, where human and AI can separately or collaboratively decide on subsequent actions or policies; 2) Incorporate ethical and governance considerations and to anticipate potential regulatory compliance requirements; 3) Enable multiple modes of reasoning, learning, planning, and decision making capabilities, including causal reasoning, context-depending learning, hierarchical planning, and real-time decision making; and 4) Accommodate changing objectives and functions of the targeted tasks and varying structures and resources of the operating environments. We propose a new approach to mixed-initiative reinforcement learning (MIRL) (pronounced as “mirror”), that combines ethical values and adaptive capabilities, and make decisions based on prior knowledge, tactical reactions, and/or online observations. The search space can be reduced by incorporating control structure or domain knowledge, by applying heuristics based on past experiences to guide learning under uncertainty, or by operating at an abstract level and only instantiating the relevant part of the solution space when needed. We can selectively and sequentially focus on the problem in a relevant context, or transform the problem space to formulate a new model. This project comprises three major parts: 1) Design a general Dynamic Decision Language (DyDeL) that represents the relevant decision elements for responsible human-AI collaboration and define the language properties. DyDeL is knowledge representation system that support intelligent, cognitive level operations in knowledge-based reinforcement learning – reasoning, learning, planning and decision making in real-world situations, with unexpected disruptions and changing conditions. The main objective is to design an adaptive, epistemic 2) Develop a basic architecture of a Mixed-initiative, RAsponsible, dynAmic Decision making under uncertaintY framework (MixREADY) that supports human-AI collaboration. MixREADY includes the basic components of a decision-theoretic, human-AI collaborative framework for guiding and supporting decision process with socio-technical mechanisms that reflect important aspects of responsible AI behavior –fairness and bias, security and privacy, trust and accountability, responsibility, and transparency (ART). The main objective is to incorporate ethical values and definitions as part of the decision making objectives and attributes. 3) Examine the effectiveness and efficiency of the DyDeL and MixREADY for mixed-initiative, collaborative human-AI reinforcement learning in the domains of assistive agents for personalized guidance, and strategic games for resource management, by simulation. The main objective is to assess the major considerations of applying the proposed technologies in changing, uncertain, and open environments and tasks.

title: Memory Efficient Graph Accelerators on HLS-based FPGAs
abs: As graphs are de facto data structures to represent different relationship of entities in many emerging big data applications, graph processing systems have become a hot research topic in both academia and industry. Despite many previous studies having developed software solutions in many-core architectures such as CPUs and GPUs [1-6], the potentials on performance and energy efficiency of graph processing are still bounded to the mismatch of graph processing and current hardware architectures. The irregularity in graph processing inherently falls short in exploiting memory- and instruction-level parallelism on current many-core processors. Though GPUs have demonstrated compelling performance on graph processing, they still suffer from key issues in terms of control and memory divergence, load imbalance and superfluous memory accesses. Another increasingly important issue in data centers is that CPUs and GPUs are known for their relatively high energy consumption. Using pure software solutions on CPUs/GPUs is often extremely difficult to fill the significant gap in the graph-specific computation for energy efficiency. Data centers use an estimated 200 terawatt hours (TWh) each year, and attributes to 1% of the global electricity usage [7]. Even worse, the data center industry has been rapidly growing. Therefore, there is an urgent need to improve the performance and energy efﬁciency of graph analytics. Encouraged by the recent successes of domain-specific architectures (DSA) in deep learning and other applications [8-12], this proposal focuses on research of DSAs for graph processing – graph accelerators. The topic of graph accelerators is still in an emerging status for the research community. There have been two main campuses of developing such accelerators: on ASIC [13-18] or on FPGAs [19-28]. In this proposal, we focus on FPGAs, which offer reconfigurability and can be more suitable for various graph systems and system deployment scenarios (such as in IoT and in the cloud). HLS (High Level Synthesis) offers high programmability and usability for large-scale systems, which we believe that it is more promising for large-scale system development in comparison with low-level HDL (Hardware Description Languages). Thus, we focus on HLS-based FPGAs as our research platform. Despite that there have been some previous studies on FPGA-based graph processing [14, 19-27, 29], we witness the following emerging trends of graph processing that little existing work has addressed. First, most existing studies are based on HDL, which hardly offer user-friendly programming interfaces. Second, in addition to some popular graph processing operations like BFS (Breadth First Search) and shortest paths, graph tasks are becoming more diversified and complex in many graph applications of different domains such as finance and social network. Considering the increasing volume and wide adoptions of graph processing, we need a scalable, low-latency and programmable graph

title: inPMdb: An in-Persistent-Memory Database System
abs: In the last decade, growing demand for fast, power efficient and cost effective memory solutions have prompted major players like Micron, Intel, Samsung to invest heavily in their R&D for advanced memory technologies. In particular, there has been much anticipation for a next generation of non-volatile memory (NVM) that are byte addressable, persistent, high storage capacity and has near-DRAM read/write latency. This has also prompted forward-looking (software) researchers to develop novel programming models, memory architectures, data structures, query processing algorithms, recovery techniques, file systems and databases that exploit these features and characteristics to optimize the performance of such NVM technologies. However, as NVM hardware was not available prior to April 2019, the design decisions made in most of these works were largely based on certain anticipated behaviors of NVMs and evaluated on emulators/simulators. In April 2019, non-volatile memory DIMMs are finally commercially available with the release of the Intel® Optane™ DC Persistent Memory Module (we shall use “Optane” for short). Since then, there has been a proliferation of research studies that evaluate this technology as well as re-evaluate prior art on the real Optane. The results of these studies showed that some of the earlier assumptions on NVM are not applicable to Optane, and existing emulators fail to capture the details of Optane’s behavior (in fact, they deviate drastically from real Optane). For example, in Optane, data are accessed in blocks of 256 bytes. This is in contrast to the DRAM where the cacheline access granularity is 64 bytes. This translates to a higher read latency for Optane than DRAM. As another example, the bandwidth of Optane for both read and write is limited which leads to poorer scalability than expected. In addition, studies have even shown that techniques that perform well under various emulators can become inferior to their counterparts on Optane. In this project, we seek to develop a novel system, called inPMdb, a single-level persistent memory-based database system. We will focus particularly on the App Direct Mode of the Optane which supports in-memory persistence. While today’s software operates under the assumption that data can only be persistent if it is written to slow storage (SSDs, HDDs, the cloud, etc.) this mode allows the processors to directly persist data at memory speeds on the persistence memory. To develop inPMdb, there are several intellectual research challenges to be overcome. Some of these include: a) Unlike traditional persistent storage (e.g., SSD, hard disk) that is block-based, persistent memory is byte addressable. How can we manage the non-volatile memory and its allocation to meet the needs of a DBMS? How can we mitigate the risk of memory wear-out? b) Besides the asymmetric read/write performance of persistent memory, there is a need to deal with wearing out of the memory cells. title: Tunable and Topological Thermal Metamaterials
abs: The project aims at establishing the comprehensive perspective of dynamic thermal systems with the additional freedoms induced by thermal convections, to realize the flexibly tunable conductibility and investigate the unexpected topology in heat transfer. The above two aspects are interesting open questions in heat transfer. Among the state-of-art researches of thermal manipulations, most investigations are implemented with rigid and static components, leading to limited degrees of freedom in modulating the thermal conductivity and their functionalities consequently. Here, we will employ the dynamic system to expand the “tunability territory” of thermal manipulations. The convective effects induced by component motions are to be considered to access these unexplored territories. We propose three basic paradigms in the presence of thermal convection, including the single-spinning system, double-spinning system, and multiple-spinning system to carry out this pilot study on tunable and topological thermal metamaterials The pioneering wave-dynamic works exhibiting mode-switching features through rotating structures, including the whispering-gallery microcavities in photonics (Nat. Phys. 10, 394-398 (2014), Nat. Phys. 16, 334-340 (2020)), would provide inspirations for our diffusive counterpart. However, the governing physics mechanisms significantly differ. Moreover, the rotation has not been applied to heat transfer biasing, and the related theoretical analysis and experiments are absent. We will build fundamental theoretical models and fabricate prototypes for the heat transfer in the forms of the single-spinning and double-spinning systems to study the tunable conduction. The single-spinning system is to be executed by rotating a fluid layer. Considering the difference in fluid deflection and thermal coupling strength at various velocities, the tunability of effective conductivity is expected to be achieved and evaluated with the modulating conductive velocities. Additional degrees of freedom would be obtained in the double-spinning system with one more convective component. In addition to the tunable conductivity effectively, the double-spinning system is also expected to simultaneously reshape the exterior temperature fields and switch the internal temperature distributions. Such accurately quantifiable and easily tunable thermal conductivities could greatly enhance the capability of thermal metamaterials. The multiple-spinning system is to be used to investigate the unexplored heat transfer topology. Such a system naturally satisfies the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian with multiple imposed convections (oscillations) and inherent conductions (dissipations). In principle, nontrivial transitions possessing a quantized integer invariant would be observed when the pair of exceptional points (EPs) is encircled in a complex plane of the parameter space. We propose to open up a new research direction on heat transfer topology, and perform theoretical, numer

title: All electric switching of perpendicular magnetization by a new spin torque
abs: Among non-volatile memory technologies, Spin-Transfer-Torque (STT) MRAM is considered as a credible candidate to replace SRAM in low level caches due to its scalability and low power, as well as compatibility with scaled CMOS processes and voltages. However, STT-MRAM cannot reliably operate at sub-ns scales due to large incubation delays. It suffers from reliability issues due to the shared read/write terminal and large write voltage stress, making it an unsuitable for tackling SRAM cache replacement and non-volatile logic. Spin-orbit torque (SOT) is seen as a promising solution due to its faster writing and separated read/write terminals. SOT induces switching of the free layer by injecting an in-plane current in an adjacent SOT layer, typically with the assistance of a static in-plane magnetic field to ensure deterministic magnetization switching. However, practical product requires all electric switching, namely, “field-free switching”, of the perpendicular magnetization. Several solutions, e.g. shape asymmetry, unidirectional coupling with anti-ferromagnets, interface induced perpendicular spin polarization by extra magnetic layer, stray field from extra magnetic hard mask have been proposed to circumvent it. All these solutions suffer either scalability and/or CMOS process incompatibility and/or reliability. In addition, the magnetic recording layer used in both STT and SOT MRAM is CoFeB thin layer with 0.9-1.2 nm. The interfacial perpendicular anisotropy between CoFeB and MgO is used to maintain the thermal stability of the recording layer. It is well believed that the CoFeB thin layer with interfacial perpendicular anisotropy cannot support the memory size smaller than 20 nm. In this project, we propose a new spin torque can be induced by an interfacial point symmetry of a heavy metal and ferromagnetic layer with R3 ̅m symmetry. Our preliminary results with L11 CoPt/L11 CuPt bilayer demonstrated that the new spin torque can enable a free field switching of perpendicular magnetization. L11 CoPt has a large magnetocrystalline anisotropy of 107 erg/cm2 which can support memory size scaling down to below 5 nm. However, symmetry analysis only reveals what torque is allowed, but does not provide any quantitative information. What physical parameters quantitatively control this new torque is still unknown. The first objective of the current project is to further verify the validity of the mechanism of the generation of the new spin torque we currently proposed. This will include modify the interfacial symmetry by inserting intermediate layers such as Pt or Cu (3-fold symmetry), Ru (6-fold symmetry) and changing the magnetic layer such as CoFeB (amorphous). The second objective is to evaluate what physical parameters controls the new torque and to engineer those parameters to improve the efficiency for further reducing the switching current. title: Topolectrical circuits: Fundamentals and applications
abs: In 2018, it was shown that conventional RLC circuits can harbour topological modes. This proposal builds on this surprising discovery in topolectrical (TE) circuits to bridge the seemingly different disciplines of electrical circuits and topological condensed matter. We will investigate the direct correspondence between the current transport in the TE circuits with quantum transport behaviour. This equivalence would allow more efficient computation of the quantum transport properties of topological materials, and a bottom-up approach of engineering materials with desired topological properties, based on the parameters of the corresponding TE circuit networks. Significance: Topological condensed matter is a vast expanding field, covering well-known materials like graphene and newly discovered ones like Weyl semimetals. These materials exhibit stable properties, e.g., high conductance with no backscattering and robustness to perturbations, and are thus useful for future applications. The pursuit of topological phases has expanded beyond material systems to platforms such as atomic gases. In comparison to material and other platforms, TE circuits offer flexibility and accessibility in terms of realization. Conversely, having designed TE circuits with desired topological properties, we can analyze the circuit properties to design materials with similar properties. Besides serving as models, TE circuits constitute a breakthrough in circuit design on their own right. Their outputs are quantized, highly-directional and robust, and are suited for applications. TE circuit representations of higher-order topological insulators and non-reciprocal systems also have novel features such as corner modes hitherto unknown in electrical circuits. This opens the way for applications such as waveguiding, sensors and multi-level logic. Finally, TE circuits serve as testing grounds for synthetic Hamiltonians, i.e., non-linear, non-Hermitian or hyper-dimensional, Hamiltonians. Non-linear TE circuits can incorporate loss-gain mechanisms, leading to self-sustained and self-organized topological modes. There is fundamental interest in investigating novel forms of topological protection, invariants, and concepts are likely to emerge from the interplay of dissipation and periodic driving, with robust properties to be harnessed. The TE circuits allow us to access richer set of topological behaviour afforded by synthetic Hamiltonians, and unconstrained by material limitations. Objectives: 1) Develop the transport models of TE circuits. Presently, there is little work to analyze the transport behaviour of TE circuits. We aim to establish the correspondence between currents and fluxes in TE circuits with quantum transport in real matter. This will enable us to use TE circuits to model topological transport such as Fermi arcs, tunneling across interfaces and chiral currents. We will also study transport between topological phases across interfaces, highly localized transport alo

title: Blood plasma viscoelasticity and its impact on microhemodynamics
abs: Blood plasma has always been regarded as a purely Newtonian fluid, and any shear thinning behaviour of whole blood is ascribed to the shear-dependent dynamics of the suspended red blood cells (RBCs). However, over the last decade, a handful of studies have utilized high sensitivity rheometers to reveal the slight elastic characteristics of plasma. While the origin of this elasticity has yet to be established, it is speculated that the constituent proteins directly contribute to this rheological property. Like dilute solutions of long and branched polymers, proteins stretch and uncoil in shear flows, from which shear gradient-dependent elastic forces arise. This elastic force will have bearing on RBC dynamics in the microvasculature, where local cell concentrations are reduced, and large shear gradients exist across the vessel. In this mechanistic study, we will investigate the source of plasma elasticity, and the implications of plasma elasticity on hemodynamics and perfusion in microcirculation. In the first part of this study, we will investigate the relative contributions of the most abundant plasma constituent proteins (albumin, fibrinogen and globulin) to the bulk elastic properties of the solution. Engineered solutions containing physiological concentrations of the abovementioned proteins will be characterized by highly sensitive extensional rheometry, from which we will establish the range of fluid relaxation times across pathophysiological protein concentrations. Our findings will be validated by measuring the viscoelasticity of donor plasma samples and correlating the rheological measurements to the measured serum protein concentrations. An artificial intelligence technique (principal component analysis) will be applied to identify confounding factors that may modulate plasma viscoelasticity. In the second part of the study, in vitro microfluidic experiments will be performed to examine the effect of plasma viscoelasticity on hemodynamics in typical microvascular geometries. We will test our hypothesis that elevated plasma viscoelasticity increases the thickness of the cell-free layer at the vessel walls through augmented inward lateral migration of RBCs. Factors such as cell size, deformability, shape and concentration will be evaluated parametrically. We will further investigate how plasma viscoelasticity contributes to the observed displacement of RBCs after arteriolar bifurcations. In the final part of the study, we will expand our findings from part 2 to better understand the cumulative effects of elevated plasma elasticity on microcirculatory perfusion. In order to exclude the effects of physiological variability (such as in the vessel density and tortuosity), an in vitro study will first be conducted in a biomimetic replica of the microcirculation. title: Superconductivity in infinite layer nickelates
abs: The enthusiasm for high-temperature superconductivity soared last year with the discovery of superconductivity in doped infinite-layer nickelate Nd0.8Sr0.2NiO2 thin films [D. Li et al., Nature 572, 624 (2019)]. In contrast to the antiferromagnetic (AF) order in the cuprates, the parent compound NdNiO2 shows no sign of magnetic order down to a temperature of 1.7 K, despite its similarities in the crystalline and electronic structures to the high-Tc cuprates. This severely challenges the scenario of AF spin fluctuation as the superconducting pairing mechanism, which is prevalent in the cuprates [P. W. Anderson, Science 235 (1987)]. The nickelate may represent a new type of superconductivity, and its similarities and differences to the cuprates have motivated intensive effort in reproducing this new superconducting compound and understanding its properties. However, this has been found to be very challenging, and to our knowledge, there have been only three research groups thus far in the world that have been able to reproduce superconductivity in this new compound family, including our group at the National University of Singapore [Zeng et. al., Physical Review Letters, 125, 147003 (2020)]. Our preliminary results suggest that the main challenge lies in the precise tuning of the compound stoichiometry and infinite layer phase as well as the choice of dopants to ascertain the degree of orbital hybridization among the ions. The oxygen reduction step after the growth also risks incorporating hydrogen that can act as a dopant. With their over two-decades experience in thin film growth and synthesis of complex oxide compounds, the PI and his team have nevertheless successfully realized and synthesized the superconducting Nd1-xSrxNiO2 thin film with different doping levels and constructed a phase diagram and demonstrated its superconducting dome as reported in [Zeng et. al., Physical Review Letters, 125, 147003 (2020)]. This achievement has been highlighted in Nature Physics, 16, 1090 (2020). Here, we propose to develop a robust process and to design and synthesize new infinite-layer nickelates RNiO2 (R = rare earth element) to search for new nickel-based superconducting compounds and understand their physical properties through a variety of experimental methods. The design of the superconducting nickelates can mimic that of the cuprates. The key point for superconductivity is to achieve the infinite-layer structure. First, we will develop a robust process to fabricate the high-quality infinite-layer Nd1-xSrxNiO2 films. This process includes the synthesis of pure perovskite Nd1-xSrxNiO3 thin films by pulsed laser deposition technique and then transforming to infinite-layer films through a chemical reduction process using the calcium hydride (CaH2) as the reagent. title: Topological Silicon Photonics
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: Cornerstones of efficient high speed data transmission are the minimization of loss in line with small link budgets, faster device speeds and better robustness. To keep pace with projected bandwidth requirements to match the sophistication of cloud services, approaches to overcome intrinsic limitations in photonic manufacturing yield, loss limits and more augmented functions are required. Growing interest in the field of topological photonics is driven by the potential and desire to provide powerful and commercially relevant solutions, and could perhaps provide an answer to applications which currently exist in other domains. Essentially analogues of topological insulators where high conductivity exists only at the edges, topological photonics exhibit similar behavior where light propagates around edges and not within. In 2016, seminal work on topological phase transitions and the discovery of topological phases of matter from D. Thouless, M. Haldane and J. M Kosterlitz was cemented by their receipt of the Nobel prize in Physics. The field of topological insulators had also progressed with a number of important discoveries: In 2005, Kane and Mele postulated that the topological edge states are defined by the topological invariants of a system. In 2008, a report from Haldane and Raghu predicted unidirectional light propagation in a photonic crystal, a “photonic manifestation” of the quantum-Hall-effect, thus bringing the concept of topological insulators firmly to the photonics domain. This system however required the use of magneto-optic materials and a magnetic field in order to break time-reversal symmetry, and was essential to the topological photonic behavior studied in the paper. Fortunately, a number of systems have emerged since then that greatly simplify the requirements. One special subset involves purely dielectric systems, which offer only an effective breaking of time-reversal symmetry. In turns out that this is sufficient to observe many features of topological photonics, including photonic routing, unidirectional light propagation and importantly, immunity to certain types of disorder/randomness. It is worthwhile to note that all-dielectric systems are sought after, for they allow effective topological insulating behavior to emerge without the requirement of magneto-optic materials or the application of magnetic fields. On the other hand, silicon photonics is a field which has spawned a multitude of critically important applications. These include optical transceivers, on-chip diagnostics, future exascale supercomputers, LiDAR and quantum information processing. Manufacturing of the photonic chips rely on CMOS technologies, and continuous advancements in speeds and functional sophistication need to take place. title: The role of mammalian ARL2 in neural stem cell proliferation and brain development
abs: Neural stem cells (NSCs) play a central role in the development of the mammalian brain. Defects in NSC proliferation cause neurodevelopmental disorders. Arl2 is an evolutionarily conserved small GTPase that interacts with tubulin-specific chaperone proteins to regulate microtubule assembly. Previously, we were the first to demonstrate a pivotal role of Drosophila Arl2 in brain development and neural stem cell proliferation by regulating microtubule growth. Currently, the function of ARL2 in the developing mammalian brain is not established. Our central hypothesis is that mammalian ARL2 governs NPC proliferation by regulating the centrosome assembly and microtubule growth. We propose to address this hypothesis with the following three specific aims: 1. To determine the role of mouse ARL2 in NPC proliferation and asymmetric division during neurogenesis. We will generate dominant-negative and dominant-active forms of mouse ARL2, overexpress these constructs in the developing mouse brain, and investigate the consequence of NSC proliferation, differentiation, and asymmetric division. 2. To investigate the role of mouse ARL2 in regulating centrosome assembly and microtubule growth in NPCs. We will analyze whether overexpression of ARL2T30N and ARL2Q71L have any impact on centrosome assembly and microtubule growth in mouse NSCs in vitro and in vivo. We will examine whether mouse ARL2 regulates centrosomal proteins in NSCs. 3. To investigate the role of human ARL2 in regulating the proliferation of NSCs using human cerebral organoid models. We will knockout ARL2 in human ES cells by CRISPR/Cas9- mediated gene editing and investigate whether human ARL2 regulates the proliferation, asymmetric division, and microtubule growth of NSCs in the organoid models. Variants in Arl2 and tubulin specific chaperones have been reported in multiple neurological disorders and retinal diseases. Results from this project have broad implications for developing potential therapeutic strategies for the treatment of neurodevelopmental disorders and/or retinal disease.

title: How to build a functional cilium? – selective transport of ciliary components into the cilia.
abs: Flagella and cilia are cellular extensions widely present in eukaryotes, essential for sensory and motility functions. Ciliary defects have been found associated with a group of human genetic diseases including Bardet-Biedl syndrome (BBS), polycystic kidney diseases, retinal degeneration etc., collectively known as ciliopathies. Biogenesis and maintenance of functional cilia requires selective transport of ciliary proteins that are synthesized in the cytoplasm. The best studied transport mechanisms are the intraflagellar transport (IFT) and the lipidated protein intraflagellar targeting (LIFT) pathways, both of which are highly conserved among ciliated organisms with rare exceptions. IFT involves movement of multimeric protein complexes forming the IFT trains that carry both structural and signalling proteins in and out of the ciliary compartment. In the LIFT pathway, cargo carriers (PDE6d and UNC119b) bind and solubilize myristoylated and farnesylated cargoes in the cytosol and transport them into the cilia. Cilia-localized Arl13b acts as a guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) on Arl3, activating Arl3 to GTP state inside of the cilia. Arl3-GTP allosterically binds to cargo carriers, resulting in cargo release. With the exceptions of tubulins and a few lipidated, signalling molecules, how IFT and LIFT work together in selective transport of ciliary components is still poorly understood. The unicellular parasite Trypanosoma brucei is responsible for human sleeping sickness. A long, stable flagellum is present in each parasite cell and is essential for parasite survival and pathogenesis in the hosts. The IFT pathway has been extensively studied in T. brucei, but the presence of a conserved LIFT pathway was only recently recognized. Our previous studies identified TbArl13, a single Arl13b ortholog in T. brucei that is essential for flagellum biogenesis and cell viability. Notably, TbArl13 binds to two distinct TbArl3 homologs, TbArl3A and TbArl3C, and catalyzes guanine nucleotide exchange on both Arl3 proteins. Further functional studies showed that TbArl3A, but not TbArl3C, binds to the lipidated protein carrier TbUnc119, which is essential for the flagellar targeting of a myristoylated arginine kinase TbAK3. Together these studies demonstrate the presence of a conserved and functional LIFT pathway in T. brucei, which involves TbArl13, TbArl3A and TbUnc119. Interestingly, neither TbUnc119 nor TbArl3A is essential for parasite survival, suggesting that TbArl13 has other essential functions, likely mediated by TbArl3C and its effectors. Arl13b is a highly conserved small GTPase that could be traced to the last eukaryotic common ancestor (LECA). It is one of >30 proteins implicated in human Joubert Syndrome, and it has been found required for a myriad of important ciliary and cellular functions including regulation of ciliary signalling pathways, ciliogenesis, IFT stabilization and endocytic trafficking. title: Spectral-domain stimulated Raman scattering tomography for stain-free demarcation of brain tumor margins in video rate
abs: 3D accurate demarcation of brain tumor margins for complete tumor removal is critical to improving prognosis of brain tumor patients in neuro-surgery. The available biomedical imaging techniques (e.g., preoperative MRI and fluorescence microscopy) fail to pinpoint the precise location of brain tumor margins during surgical operation. The current gold-standard for identification of brain tumor margins is based on haematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained cryosections of tissue samples for histopathology, which is unsuited for real-time applications due to its labor-intensive and time-consuming nature. There is a clinically unmet need for developing advanced optical imaging techniques to facilitate real-time, in vivo detection and demarcation of brain tumor margins for precise brain tumor surgery. Stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) microscopy is an emerging molecular vibrational imaging technique that is capable of generating stain-free molecular images identical to the H&E images by imaging the biochemicals distribution in tissue and cells. In comparison with H&E counterparts, SRS microscopy has additional advantages: (i) sample preparations are not required to drastically shorten the imaging time due to its label-free nature. (ii) offering rich biochemical information to diagnose brain tumor with high accuracy. However, several technical challenges in the current state-of-the-art of SRS microscopy remain unsolved for brain tissue 3D imaging, e.g., 3D imaging speed of SRS microscopy is too slow (~a few minutes) due to the use of stepper motor for z-scanning mechanically; (ii) penetration depth into tissue is only up to tens of micron without an aid of external contrast agents, limiting its depth of view for deeper brain tumor imaging. To tackle the challenges, the main objective of this project is to develop a novel spectral-domain stimulated Raman scattering tomography (SD-SRST) imaging technique enabled by double-rainbow (DR) spectral focusing and optical beating technique (OBT) associated with non-diffracting Bessel beams to significantly improve both the 3D imaging speed and light penetration depth for determining brain tumor margins at the subcellular level without labelling for precision neuro-surgery. The specific aims of this project are: (1) To develop a novel epi-detected DR-OBT-based SD-SRST imaging technique that retrieves the depth information instantly in super-broad spatial frequency domain for high-speed (>20 fps), label-free 3D volumetric SRS imaging of brain tissue; (2) To characterize the optical performance of SD-SRST imaging on brain tissues with Bessel excitation beams in terms of image acquisition rates, spatial resolution (lateral and axial resolutions), field of view, depth of field, penetration depth and probing volume of SRS signals of brain tissue; (3) To investigate SRS 3D spectroscopic properties and SRS volumetric images of brain tissues for better understanding of the variations in morphology and biochemical distributions

title: Developing monoclonal antibody and nanobody to conserved epitopes in spike and nucleocapsid of newly emerged coronaviruses and bat-borne coronaviruses and exploiting them to deal with future spillover events
abs: Significance of the research Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome coronavirus (SARS-CoV) is the etiological agent for the SARS outbreak in 2003. Subsequently, the first human infection of Middle East respiratory syndrome CoV (MERS-CoV) was identified in 2012. These viruses have reservoirs in wild bats and were transmitted via intermediate animal hosts to humans. In March 2020, COVID-19, which is caused by another newly emerged virus named as SARS-CoV-2, was declared as a pandemic; today, it continues to cause major health problems and socioeconomic disruption worldwide. Given that 3 different bat-borne coronaviruses (BtCoVs) have crossed the species barrier to infect human in the past 19 years, there is an urgent need to develop strategies to defend against potential future outbreaks that may be caused by spillover of another BtCoV. One strategy is to identify well-conserved viral epitopes in a diverse panel of BtCoVs so that we can exploit this knowledge to design new assays for detecting future spillover events as well as develop pancoronavirus therapies. Research questions to be addressed and approach We hypothesize that the two largest structural proteins of coronavirus (CoV), namely spike (S) and nucleocapsid (N), contain B cell epitopes/antigenic sites that are well-conserved between newly emerged CoVs and BtCoVs. In order to identify highly conserved epitopes, we will use multiple methods to generate monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) and nanobodies (Nbs) with broad cross-reactivity. Then, we will perform detailed epitope mapping and structural analysis to determine the breadth of the cross-reactivity of each mAb/Nb and understand the correlation with the genetic diversity of BtCoVs. Finally, we will develop sandwich ELISA to allow sensitive detection of N or S in SARS-CoV-2 and evaluate if our newly developed S-binding mAbs and Nbs have neutralizing activity against SARS-CoV-2 in vitro and in vivo. Thus, we will use innovative approaches to achieve the respective aims: Aim 1: Express full-length, subunits and peptides of SARS-CoV-2 N and use them to generate mAbs and Nbs that can bind to multiple strains of BtCoVs. High throughput screening will be performed to identify mAbs that can bind to multiple strains of BtCoVs. The N proteins of endemic human CoVs will be used for counter-screening to ensure specificity. In parallel, we will generate Nbs by using a novel screening method patented by NUS. title: Investigating the uptake and intracellular trafficking mechanisms of red blood cell derived extracellular vesicles
abs: Recent discoveries in cell biology have highlighted the important role of extracellular vesicles (EVs) in intercellular communication and their applications in gene therapies: EVs facilitate the cellular uptake of encapsulated RNAs while protecting the cargos from degradation and undesirable immune responses. However, EV-based therapeutics are still limited by the small scale of EV production and the risk of horizontal gene transfer from parental to recipient cells. To address these issues, we have developed a new method for RNA drug delivery using EVs from red blood cells (RBCs). Primary enucleated RBCs are readily available, thereby allowing scalable production of RBC-derived EVs (RBCEVs) that are suitable for drug delivery without any risk of horizontal gene transfer. Our study demonstrates that RBCEVs deliver therapeutic RNAs to cancer cells more efficiently than commercial transfection reagents while not causing any cytotoxicity. Delivery of antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) that target oncogenic miR-125b using RBCEVs significantly reduces miR-125b expression and cell proliferation. Our in vivo experiments demonstrate robust delivery of miR-125b ASOs to breast cancer and leukemia cells via local or systemic injections, leading to suppression of tumor growth. Together, these data suggest that RBCEVs can serve as a novel and efficient RNA drug delivery vector for effective cancer therapy. More recently, we have also developed a simple and robust method for conjugation of EVs with peptides and nanobodies using protein ligases, facilitating targeted delivery of therapeutic molecules to target cells, resulting in increased drug efficacy. Our preliminary data reveal that endogenous RNAs in RBCEVs have limited endosomal escape capacity, but exogenous RNAs are able to partially escape endosomal compartments and exert their functions in cells. Antibody-conjugated RBCEVs can mediate specific delivery and functional release of therapeutic RNAs both in vitro and in vivo. However, it is still unclear how the dynamic of RBCEV uptake and RNA release varies in different cell types and how the functional release of RNA payloads can be improved. Thus, we propose to investigate the uptake and intracellular trafficking mechanisms of RBCEVs in different types of cells. We aim to 1) identify the routes of RBCEVs uptake in different cell types; 2) determine the mechanism by which RNA cargoes travel from RBCEVs into the cytosol of recipient cells; and 3) modify the surface of RBCEVs to enhance the endosomal escape of RNAs from RBCEVs. This line of research will reveal new information on the mechanism of RBCEV trafficking and functional cargo release. Such insights will facilitate the rational design of EVs’ surface to improve the efficacy of the RBCEV-based drug delivery platform.

title: Unravelling how the nervous system interacts with the skin microbiota to make a superorganism
abs: The lives of multicellular organisms are closely intertwined with bacteria, fungi, viruses and archaea, collectively known as the microbiota. These microbes can be found in abundance on surfaces, such as mucosal epithelia, where they form a complex community that generates unique metabolites. When the composition of these communities is disrupted, multiple aspects of life, from neural development to metabolism, behaviour, immunity and reproduction, are impacted. Host organisms have therefore evolved a number of mechanisms to regulate their microbiota and utilize its metabolites. Although the immune system mediates the response to microbial infection, loss of key components of adaptive or innate immunity does not fully disrupt microbiota composition. Thus, other systems must be involved. Here, we will investigate the hypothesis that sensory neuroendocrine cells both regulate the microbiota and mediate their effects on the host; we postulate that this depends on their ability to (i) detect microbial ligands, (ii) secrete anti-microbial molecules and (iii) signal to the central nervous system. To test this hypothesis, a novel experimental system will be used: the sensory neuroendocrine cells in the skin of the zebrafish. The skin is an exposed organ and thus sensitive to environmental perturbation. From an experimental perspective, these cells have the advantage of being easily accessible to manipulation and observation within the context of an intact animal, due to their superficial location. This proposal has two major aims. First, to establish the role of skin neuroendocrine cells in regulating the composition of the microbiota and second, to determine if skin neuroendocrine cells enable the microbiota to influence the central nervous system (CNS). To address the first aim, GAL4 and Cre-based transgenics will be used to manipulate these cells selectively. The effect on microbiota composition will be determined by in-depth metagenomic sequencing, ensuring documentation of bacteria, archaea, fungi and viruses. To define specific molecular pathways that modulate the microbiome, neuroendocrine cells will be characterized using data from transcriptomics and proteomics. Candidate pathways will be manipulated genetically and pharmacologically. Resulting effects on the microbiota composition and on pathogen resistance will be determined, to assess function. To address the second aim, functional connectivity of skin neuroendocrine cells will first be established by optogenetic stimulation of these cells and two-photon calcium imaging of the CNS. The effects of mucus and specific microbial ligands on neuroendocrine cell signalling will then be tested. To assess the effects on larval behaviour, such as response to stress and hunting ability, we will determine whether loss of these cells, as compared to gut neuroendocrine cells, mimics the effect of development in germ-free conditions, or prevents rescue by specific bacteria. title: Near-Atomic Resolution Structures of Reconstituted Heterochromatin Fibres
abs: The eukaryotic genome is packaged into chromatin by an approximately equal mass of histone proteins, which provide a foundation for modulating gene expression, maintaining genomic stability and regulating DNA transactions in general. Histone octamers composed of H2A, H2B, H3 and H4 core histones assemble variable expanses of roughly 160 to 240 DNA base pairs (bp) into nucleosomes, the repeating units of chromatin. This nucleosome fibre, which can consist of more than one million nucleosomes in tandem for a given chromosome, can in turn be further compacted into higher order structures through the action of a variety of chromatin architectural factors. These include linker histones, cohesins, condensins, HP1 (Heterochromatin Protein 1) and CTCF, amongst other factors, which appear to act at different levels of structural hierarchy in condensing the nucleosome fibre. In this manner, modulatable structural and chemical features of chromatin— epigenetic factors— collectively dictate cellular differentiation state and activity. And yet our comprehension of how architectural factors operate to maintain the organizational integrity of chromatin lags significantly behind that of the role of other epigenetic regulatory factors in this regard. Moreover, chromatin higher order structure at the level of the organization of interacting/proximal nucleosomes has remained unclear because of conformational and compositional heterogeneity in the cell and dynamic properties that also limit achievable resolution in vitro. Recent advances in imaging and analytical techniques have permitted more detailed insight into chromatin in situ as well as that isolated from natural sources or reconstituted in vitro. This has resulted in an understanding that compact chromatin structure generally consists of irregular interdigitated nucleosome fibres with zigzag features, thereby challenging the long-standing view that higher order structure pertains to folded, helical conformations, referred to as ‘30 nm fibre’. Nonetheless, 30 nm fibre structures may occur in specialized genomic contexts. An improved comprehension of the structural characteristics of nucleosome fibres and the factors that influence local architecture would help clarify the conformational and dynamic behaviour of chromatin in the cell. Recent advances in single particle analysis by cryo-electron microscopy have made it possible to obtain structures for different nucleosome-chromatin factor assemblies. However, the inherent conformational freedom of these systems tends to significantly limit the resolution that can be achieved. Moreover, the structural heterogeneity of poly-nucleosome systems, such as arrays, imposes further limitations, especially when the interest is in condensed or aggregated states of chromatin under salt conditions similar to in vivo. title: INVESTIGATING THE ROLE OF cAMP SIGNALLING CONSERVATION DURING MALARIA PARASITE INVASION
abs: The essential nature of host cell signalling during Plasmodium merozoite invasion makes it an attractive target for novel intervention methods for the disease. At this stage, the exact mechanism of this signalling process has not been elucidated but preliminary studies have indicated that calcium signalling is a critical and conserved part of this signalling cascade across the different Plasmodium species during their invasion into human erythrocytes. In P. falciparum, the responsible ligand-receptor pair triggering calcium influx has been identified as PfRh5 and Basigin respectively, but this information is lacking in other species. The absence of a PfRH5 orthologue in other Plasmodium species and the lack of dependence of Basigin as an erythrocyte receptor indicates that these parasites have evolved other ligand-receptor interactions that mediate this signal. In eukaryotic cells, the induction of calcium signalling is tightly regulated and involves extracellular stimulus, cell surface molecular interaction and signal transduction for the activation of calcium channels on the cell surface. Thus, this mechanism may involve the GPCRs, G-proteins, adenylyl cyclases, intracellular kinases like PKA and PKC. How the malaria parasite manipulates these host cell pathways during invasion is not known. We have established in our preliminary studies that PfRH5 binding to Basigin induces a transient host cell cAMP flux that is critical for the subsequent calcium influx. This suggests the involvement of GPCR signalling pathway that leads to the activation of adenylyl cyclase and the observed cAMP spike. Here we propose to compare and contrast the activation of cAMP in a parasite (P. falciparum) that uses PfRH5-Basigin and one (P. knowlesi) that uses a different but so far unknown mechanism to trigger this signal. Therefore, the focus of this proposal is to understand the specific host signalling mechanism across these two Plasmodium species by firstly identifying the parasite ligands and receptors interactions that leads to the activation of GPCRs and G-protein signalling pathways. As G-protein activation leads to the activation of cAMP, this proposal would like to understand the specific role of different molecular players required for this induction. As at this stage the parasite ligand -erythrocyte receptor combination that is responsible for triggering the equivalent signalling cascade in P. knowlesi is not known, the second aim focuses on the identification of these critical ligand receptor interactions. With this information, we then will aim to identify the molecular players that trigger the cAMP and subsequent calcium signalling in P. knowlesi. Successful completion of these aims will provide new fundamental insights on how parasites manipulate the host cell signalling processes and provide new information for the future development of novel therapeutic intervention approaches. title: Decomposition and environmental impacts of terrestrial organic carbon in the Sunda Shelf Sea, Southeast Asia
abs: The flux of dissolved organic carbon (DOC) from soils on land through rivers to the ocean remains a poorly understood aspect of the global carbon cycle. This flux is quantitatively significant and has increased in many parts of the world as a result of human activities, including the conversion of natural ecosystems to other land uses. However, it is still unclear how much of this terrestrial DOC decomposes to carbon dioxide in the ocean, how rapid this decomposition is, and how it is controlled in different parts of the world. Global carbon cycle models do not represent this flux at all. Consequently, we have a poor understanding of how changes in land–ocean DOC fluxes impact the global carbon cycle and marine ecosystems. The proposed project will track the fate of DOC from Southeast Asian peatlands, which contribute around 10% of the global land–ocean DOC flux, across the Sunda Shelf Sea. We will test the hypothesis that most of this DOC decomposes to carbon dioxide (CO2) within the shelf sea. We will additionally test the hypotheses that (1) undecomposed DOC absorbs environmentally significant quantities of sunlight underwater, and (2) that the decomposition of this DOC causes environmentally significant levels of ocean acidification. We will measure dissolved organic and inorganic carbon at the three locations where peatland DOC can be transported off the Sunda Shelf into the Indian Ocean, and in the Singapore Strait, which is close to major peatland DOC sources. We will use optical spectroscopy and stable carbon and hydrogen isotopes to quantify terrestrial DOC and its decomposition to CO2. We will measure the seawater carbonate system to quantify ocean acidification, and measure underwater light attenuation and inherent optical properties to quantify the absorption of sunlight by terrestrial DOC. We will measure the decomposition rates of terrestrial DOC by both photo-oxidation and microbial decomposition in laboratory experiments. We will then use a numerical ocean model to simulate the input and decomposition of terrestrial DOC across the Sunda Shelf. The model will predict in detail how much terrestrial DOC is decomposed within the Sunda Shelf, and which areas are impacted to what extent by sunlight absorption and by ocean acidification. The study is feasible, because many of the techniques are individually well established, the PI and collaborators have substantial experience of conducting the necessary field work, and a suitable model has already been applied to other aspects of the carbon biogeochemistry of this region. The novelty lies in combining several established and novel field and laboratory techniques with biogeochemical modelling to resolve the fate and environmental impacts of terrestrial DOC in an important, but little-studied region of the world. This study will significantly advance our understanding of terrestrial DOC in the ocean, as well as our ability to measure it and model its biogeochemistry.

title: Investigating triple oxygen isotopes in precipitation over Southeast Asia
abs: The on-going temperature rise is projected to alter the distribution of global freshwater (e.g., rainfall, runoff, and groundwater), with some regions anticipating seasonal flooding while others severe droughts. Such changes to the hydrological systems have significant ramifications for sustainability and socio-economic stability, particularly in densely populated regions like Southeast (SE) Asia. Forecasting the impact of climate change on freshwater is of great importance to this region, as it will allow local governments to prepare appropriate mitigation and adaptation policies, which is also one of the major themes of Singapore’s Research Innovation and Enterprise 2025 plan (RIE2025). However, such projection requires a better understanding of the factors that control regional precipitation. The global hydrological cycle, as well as the past and present climate change, has long been studied using water stable isotopes (i.e., d18O and d2H). As natural tracers of hydrological processes, water isotopes record climate parameters, such as temperature, evaporation/condensation processes, precipitation history, and atmospheric processes. To further our knowledge of regional to global hydrological processes and climate, a Global Network of Isotopes in Precipitation (GNIP) has been built by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) in cooperation with the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) since the 1950s. Recently, isotope-enabled atmospheric general circulation models (GCMs) have provided reasonably accurate simulations on the global distribution of the mean annual isotope ratios of precipitation. However, model simulations are inconsistent with observations in the tropics, where the GCMs predict a clear negative relationship between stable isotope ratios and rainfall, the amount effect. In contrast, this effect is not observed in recent studies of daily precipitation, which suggests the existence of other factors such as moisture source, transport patterns and regional organized convection. This inconsistency shows our limited understanding of the spatial and temporal variations in stable isotopes of present-day precipitation and the complexities of atmospheric and climate processes in the tropics. Recently, with advancement in analytical techniques and instruments, 17O-excess (17O-excess = ln(d17O+1) - 0.528×ln(d18O+1)) has been used as a new tracer in hydrological studies. However, observations show that controls of 17O-excess are much more complicated than experiments and theory suggested. Further observation and modelling are needed to understand what controls the variability of 17O-excess, particularly in the tropics, where studies of 17O-excess are sparse. Isotopic data from the GNIP suffer from insufficient spatial-temporal resolution in the tropics because its stations, largely located in the mid-latitude in the Northern Hemisphere, mostly collect monthly precipitation. title: The role of Ezh2-regulated thymic dendritic cells in thymic involution
abs: Dysregulation of Ezh2, one of the key epigenetic regulators, is known to affect gene expression patterns via H3K27 methylation and associate with several human diseases. However, our recent reports identified a non-canonical role for Ezh2 in regulating integrin-dependent migration through talin1-methylation in dendritic cells (DCs), the professional antigen presenting cells. Our preliminary data further suggest that Ezh2 expression in thymic DCs regulates T cell development by preventing premature thymic involution. To determine the role of Ezh2-regulated thymic DCs in thymic involution, we propose four complementary specific aims, which will make use of cell-biological, biochemical, proteomic and single cell transcriptomic approaches, in vitro culture systems and in vivo mouse models. Mechanistic insights identified in this study may help to slowdown or reverse the progress of thymic involution, to reduce age-related disease incidences such as autoimmunity, infectious diseases and cancers. Specific Aim 1: To identify DC subsets regulating thymocyte differentiation and thymic involution. As three DC subsets are present in the thymus, conditional cell ablation strategy will be utilized to identify the Ezh2-deficient thymic DC subset(s) that is (are) responsible for accelerated thymic involution. The identified DC subset and its interaction with developing T cells will be further characterized functionally as well as biochemically. Specific Aim 2: To characterize alterations in developing T cells imposed by Ezh2-dificient DCs. Our results suggested that Ezh2 expression in DCs influences thymopoiesis at two distinct developmental stages. T cell intrinsic and extrinsic changes in the presence of Ezh2-deficient DCs will be further investigated. Specific Aim 3: To determine how Ezh2-regulated DC functions affect crosstalk between various cell types in the thymus. Our preliminary data revealed that the premature thymic involution in mice with Ezh2-deficient DCs was accompanied by disrupted thymic architecture. To determine the molecular signature contributing to the altered thymic structure and T cell development, we will perform single cell RNA-sequencing experiments to determine molecular changes and crosstalk between various cell types in the thymus. Metabolic properties of Ezh2-deficient DCs and their influences on different cell types in the thymic microenvironment will be further investigated. Specific Aim 4: To determine age-related factors influencing Ezh2-dependent DC functions in regulating thymopoiesis. Our data revealed that Ezh2-deficient DCs are able to support normal T cell development during the first 8 weeks after birth. The thymopoiesis only deteriorated between 8 and 10 weeks. It is feasible that specific age-related thymic environmental factors induce abnormal functions of Ezh2-deficient DCs in promoting declined thymopoiesis. title: Quantum Neuromorphic Computing
abs: The rapid rise of machine learning is providing a growing number of research fields with powerful tools for the recognition of patterns in data and the ability to make predictions based on those patterns. Often machine learning techniques are built on neural network platforms, where power is derived from representing data and making operations in high dimensional effective or feature spaces. This concept sounds very familiar to the motivation behind quantum computers, which derive power from operating in a high dimensional Hilbert space. It is perhaps then no surprise that the field of quantum machine learning has recently emerged. Within the field of quantum machine learning, one can already distinguish three different paths of research. A first path aims to use well-known classical neural networks to help model quantum physics problems, where neural networks indeed offer a useful compact approximation of a state in a large Hilbert space. A second path aims at replacing the elements of neural networks with quantum entities, which, through allowing quantum correlations in the large dimensional Hilbert space, may speed up the solution of classical problems. A third path aims at showing how neural network architectures can enhance future quantum computers or quantum annealers, to form quantum neural networks capable of addressing non-classical tasks. In a recent work, we have introduced the concept of quantum reservoir processing, which allows quantum neural networks without the initial need for quantum computers or quantum annealers. We do this by merging the concepts of reservoir computing with quantum physics. Classical reservoir computers are recurrent neural networks based on randomly connected elements or network nodes. They are particularly good architectures for implementing with hardware as, unlike other neural networks, one requires very little control of the strengths or weights of connections between network nodes. One can operate with completely random weights and network structure, and the network functionality is fully determined by training a single set of weights in a single output layer. In analogy, a quantum reservoir processor would be constructed from a network of randomly connected quantum modes (e.g., quantum dots or nonlinear photonic modes), which avoids the challenges of careful site positioning (typically a problem with quantum dots) and tolerates a wide range of disorder. Remarkably, we have found theoretically that this system can perform quantum tasks such as the classification of quantum states as entangled or separable (a fundamental task in quantum information processing), even without needing to perform any correlation measurements. It can also handle states of different dimensionality, making it a relevant tool in quantum information. However, we believe this is just the first example of what quantum reservoir processors can achieve. The aim of this project is to develop the concept of quantum reservoir processors

title: Halogen Bonding-Based Free Radical Solid Phase Polymerization as Novel Polymer Engineering Technique to Create Advanced Polymer Materials
abs: This project aims to explore halogen-bonding (XB)-based free radical solid phase polymerization (SPP) as a platform technique for designing polymer materials. XB-based radical SPP is an original technique recently developed by PI. The novelty of this technique is the use of XB, which is an unprecedented development in the field of radical SPP and can open up new materials. The specific aims of this project are (1) the expansion of the monomer scope of this technique for a range of applications and also the use of this technique to create new useful materials, i.e., (2) novel stimulus-responsive polymer actuators, (3) dual polymer sensors of gases and liquids, and (4) flexible electron conducting polymer materials. These materials are uniquely accessible by this technique. These materials take advantage of scientifically novel polymer structures derived by XB, i.e., double porous structures, novel polymer covalent organic framework (COF) structures, and first conjugated polyacetylene networks. This project will give significant scientific impacts. XB-based radical SPP is our new chemistry and its scientific originality is primarily high. Because of the wide monomer scope and accessibility to a range of polymer structures, this technique can be an enabling platform technology for designing polymer materials. XB also provides novel polymer structures (double porous, COF, and conjugated network structures), opening up previously inaccessible actuators, sensors, and electron conducting materials. This project also provides practical impacts. This technique uses inexpensive vinyl monomers commonly used in industry and can be a low-cost manufacturing process for high-value polymer products. This project may lead to a range of industrial use and provide value in Singapore. Overall, this project drives new scientific and technological development and will significantly contribute to polymer chemistry and material sciences in academia and industry.
kw: Polymer; Halogen Bonding; Solid Phase Polymerization; Actuators; Sensors; Electron Conducting material

title: Design and development of conformal all-solid-state Na-ion batteries
abs: Aim of the proposed research is to develop a conformal all-solid-state Na-ion battery technology for EV applications with (i) improved energy density, (ii) non-flammable, (iii) flexible for integration into the structure of EVs thus utilizing available footprint of the structure, and (iv) appreciable mechanical strength to achieve impact resistance. Such a technology will guarantee safety and increased drive range of EVs (40-50kWh) almost 1.5-2 times as compared to the Na-ion battery technology using liquid electrolytes. Major challenge is to develop all components of the cells such as solid electrolyte, positive/negative electrodes and current collector to be stretchable with robust interfaces between different layers to tolerate mechanical abuse without delamination during harsh driving condition of EVs. We propose to integrate flexible components to fabricate conformal all-solid-state Na-ion cells. Each flexible components including composite ceramic/polymer electrolyte, positive electrode, negative electrode and current collector will be newly developed in this project addressing charge and mass transport at various interfaces. Several characterization techniques (Operando X-ray diffraction, XPS, XANES and HRTEM) will be used to investigate structural changes as well as interface properties of the composite electrodes such as cathode or anode materials homogenously mixed with solid electrolytes as well as conductive carbon forming positive electrode or negative electrode respectively on flexible current collectors. The physical, chemical, structural and interfacial properties during cycling in half-cell (against Na metal) and full cells will be closely investigated. Besides electrochemical storage performances, we will examine and report heat generation at different working conditions and the associated internal resistance of the proposed all-solid-state Na-ion full cells. The impedance data collected on such full cells at selected SOCs will be analyzed using Distribution of Relaxation Times (DRT) method for deconvolution of various contributions to the total internal resistance of the full cells. Such a deconvolution using Fourier transform analysis by DRT method will provide a guideline for the analysis of complicated impedance data collected on the all-solid-state batteries since the proposed conformal battery contains many components. Additionally, we will investigate in-plane mechanical deformation and tensile stress-strain behaviours of various elements of the conformal all-solid-state Na-ion batteries at various SOC conditions to ensure non-deformation in the event of inevitable crash or impact for vehicles during traffic accidents. Suitable tensile and compression test specimens will be examined and these mechanical properties will be used as inputs for the computational modelling and simulations. title: Uncertainty quantification and multi-objective optimization of additive manufacturing
abs: Additive manufacturing shows promising potentials in various industrial sectors. To facilitate its wide applications, we plan to tackle two bottle-neck problems: 1) quality inconsistency and 2) low-efficiency quality optimization limited by trial-and-error experiments. Thus, this proposal is focused on uncertainty quantification (mainly with material and machine) and multi-objective optimization under uncertainties, where the multi-physics simulations and experiments are to generate data points and provide validation. While the input parameters (e.g., laser power) in real experiments are unavoidably subject to uncertainties, our multi-physics simulations have the freedom to precisely change and set most of the parameters and thus are ideal for quantifying the impact of input uncertainties on output uncertainties (i.e., error propagation) by varying the input parameters within the ranges that are anticipated in real experiments. In experiments, at least two laser powder bed fusion machines will be used to investigate the uncertainties due to machines, and a series of high-strength low-alloy steels with minor differences in the compositions will be used to investigate the uncertainties due to material parameters. Supersaturated Design of Experiments will be adopted to design an affordable and efficient data set to be generated via multi-physics simulations and experiments. Based on the simulation and experimental data, uncertainties will be quantified considering both the input uncertainties and experimental errors, and particularly the interactions of input uncertainties in the error propagation will be studied. Finally, we will develop a multi-objective optimization algorithm incorporating uncertainties, with multiple quality criteria being included, e.g., porosity, surface roughness, and energy and time consumptions.
kw: additive manufacturing; uncertainty quantification; multi-objective optimization; Multi-physics modelling; Experiment; Design of experiments

title: Unleashing Terahertz Photon Pairs from Ultrastrongly Coupled Light-Matter Hybrids in Superconducting Metamaterial Cavities
abs: Recent progress in studying the interaction of quantized light with quantum matter systems has led to the emergence of a variety of physical phenomena under the realm of cavity-quantum electrodynamics (c-QED). In particular, the solid-state systems involving the cooperative enhancement of light-matter coupling and large dipole moments at terahertz (THz) frequencies have provided new opportunities for entering the uncharted regimes of light-matter interactions, termed as ultrastrong and deep-strong coupling regimes. In the ultrastrong coupling regime, the coupling strength of the light-matter interaction becomes comparable to the bare transition frequency in the system, where the antiresonant terms become more significant, leading to many intriguing quantum properties of the ground state polaritons. Due to the presence of antiresonant terms in the Hamiltonian, the higher-order perturbative effects hybridize the states with the different number of excitations and hence the ground state is predicted to be a two-photon squeezed vacuum state consisting of a finite photonic population of virtual photons. These photons stay virtual because the ground state being the lower energy state, it cannot radiate. However, their presence can be revealed by converting them to real photons when the system parameters are nonadiabatically modulated in time. This approach is analogous to the Moore-Fulling-Davies effect, according to which rapid modulations of boundary conditions of a quantum field can induce vacuum amplification effects, leading to the creating of real particles out of vacuum fluctuations. Currently, these phenomena are being theoretically investigated and various experimental approaches for emission and detection of vacuum photons are being sought. In this proposal, it is our goal to uncover, examine and understand the nonclassical behavior of ground state polaritons in the ultrastrong coupled light-matter system and to unleash the terahertz photons from the two-photon squeezed vacuum of the ground state in the ultrastrong coupling regime at terahertz (THz) frequencies. Our approach to generating these THz photon pairs would involve rapid and nonadiabatic modulation of the ultrastrongly coupled light-matter system in a superconducting metamaterial cavity. We propose to use the high electron density and mobility quantum well structures integrated with superconducting metamaterials to reach the regime of ultrastrong coupling at THz frequencies. Superconducting metamaterial cavities possessing ultrafast modulation dynamics together with low photon decoherence rates and low-mode volumes provide favorable conditions for unleashing the virtual photons through rapid modulation of cavity parameters in the ultrastrong coupling regime. These photons are emitted as bunched and correlated photon-pairs showing strong correlations in momentum, frequency, and time. title: PERFLEXO: a PERsonalized, FLExible, and controlled Output-size framework for multi-objective preference queries in large databases
abs: With the advent of e-commerce, users are presented with numerous alternatives to satisfy their everyday needs. Choosing from the available options generally entails the consideration of multiple, often conflicting aspects, the tradeoff among which is assessed differently by different users. At the same time, due to the number of available options, generally it is impractical for a user to examine them all. For example, local review portal HungryGoWhere lists over 25,000 restaurants, rated on four aspects: food, value, service, and ambience. To assist in decisions of a multi-objective nature from a large number of alternatives, database research has considered ways to shortlist the most promising options for the user. Specifically, two alternative paradigms have emerged. In the first paradigm, an option is considered superior to another if all its attributes are more preferable. For instance, in the context of HungryGoWhere, a restaurant is said to dominate another if it is rated higher on all four aspects. The set of non-dominated restaurants is called the skyline, and serves as a general purpose shortlist to interested diners. The dominance-based paradigm is intuitive, however, it suffers from two palpable flaws. First, the skyline is the same for all users, i.e., the shortlist is not personalized. Second, the output size (i.e., the length of the shortlist) is uncontrollable, and often overwhelming. In the second paradigm, each available option is associated with a utility score. The utility function is user-dependent and, most commonly, defined as a weighted sum of the option’s attributes. The weights in the scoring formula represent the relative significance of each aspect to the user. In our restaurant example, there would be four weights (one per rated aspect). These weights together form a weight vector w, which encapsulates the user’s preference profile. Ranking options by score according to such a (linear) utility function has been shown by user studies to resemble closely the way humans make multi-objective decisions. Moreover, in the form of a top-k query, it enables control over the output size too. Its weakness, on the other hand, lies in specifying the “correct” weights, since a miniscule change in w may produce a totally different top-k result. We propose PERFLEXO, a new methodology for multi-objective querying that aims to bring the best of both worlds. Specifically, motivated by the drawbacks of the two traditional paradigms, we center our proposal around three hard requirements, i.e., personalization, flexibility in the preference input, and output-size control. We substantiate the need for these properties and explain that, although the bridging of the dominance and the ranking by utility paradigms has been attempted in past studies, there is still a lack for a methodology that satisfies all three hard requirements.
