title: Fairness and Efficiency for Distributed Job Execution
abs: In big data analytics, jobs typically consist of many computation tasks that process different data partitions and can run in parallel. With the growing geo-distributed deployments of datacenters and edge clusters by major service providers like Amazon, Google and Microsoft, it has become routine for massive amounts of data to be generated and stored at many geo-distributed sites around the globe. To collectively analyze such geo-distributed data, it is increasingly common for jobs to be executed in a distributed fashion across multiple compute clusters or datacenters to take advantage of data locality and avoid enormous bandwidth costs. Given the limited amount of resources available at each cluster or datacenter, the jobs inherently compete for resources with each other. Therefore, it is essential to design fair and efficient algorithms for sharing resources among concurrently running distributed jobs. This project addresses fundamental resource allocation problems for distributed job execution. Distributed jobs with data-parallel tasks have salient characteristics such as they do not need to acquire resources from various sites simultaneously in any fixed proportions and a job is completed only when all of its tasks are finished. These characteristics introduce new research challenges to resource allocation. We focus on the fairness and efficiency aspects of resource allocation in distributed job execution. For fairness, we plan to define new fairness policies on the aggregate resources acquired by each job from all the sites and develop efficient resource allocation mechanisms that possess widely accepted fairness properties including Pareto efficiency, envy-freeness, strategy-proofness and sharing incentive. For efficiency, we plan to develop algorithms for determining the processing site of each task based on data availability and scheduling the task execution at each site with the objective of optimizing the completion time performance of the jobs. Our solutions will address the inter-dependency of task placement and scheduling for distributed data-parallel jobs. In addition, we shall also study balancing the tradeoff between fairness and efficiency for distributed job execution. The success of this project will advance the state-of-the-art of resource allocation in distributed systems and benefit the practice of big data applications.
kw: distributed systems; fairness; resource allocation; scheduling

title: A Framework for Intellectual Property Protection of Deep Learning Applications
abs: Deep learning models and applications become important Intellectual Property (IP) for Artificial Intelligence (AI) companies due to the valuable designs and huge cost of training such production-level models. It is of paramount importance for these companies to protect the IP of their models and prevent copyright. Different techniques have been designed for end users to verify the model ownership even with only black-box accesses. However, it is unknown whether existing watermarking schemes are secure and robust. In this proposal, we will conduct an in-depth and systematic study towards the vulnerabilities as well as opportunities of watermarking DL models. (1) We will design a novel attack, which can invalidate all existing watermarking approaches and steal the model stealthily. In addition, we will introduce three new methods for digital watermarking of DL applications with higher effectiveness and efficiency. Specifically, (2) we will design a novel scheme based on the data augmentation technique to enhance the robustness and generalization of DNN watermarks; (3) we will design a novel scheme to generate temporal watermarks rather than spatial watermarks adopted in prior works; (4) we will design a novel scheme to embed watermarks into the model architecture rather than model parameters adopted in prior works. Our attack design can help researchers better understand the mechanisms and limitations of current solutions for DL ownership verification. Our new solutions can also be readily used by AI companies and practitioners to protect the IP of their applications. With the trend of DL commercialization, we expect this study can contribute to building a more trustworthy eco-system for the smart nation.
kw: Deep Learning; Deep Neural Network; Watermarking; Intellectual Property; Ownership Verification

title: Codebooks for Data Reconstruction with Biological Applications
abs: In today’s Information Age, we are witnessing an unprecedented explosion of data in all sectors of society. For example, in the healthcare sector, genetic data of hospital patients are routinely being collected due to the rapid development of high throughput sequencing technologies and this information together with other health records are now being stored electronically in numerous countries. As the amount of available data grows, the problem of managing the information becomes challenging. To address the problem, various research groups are developing new media to store these huge datasets. An example that have gained widespread attention is the DNA-based data storage. Interestingly, DNA-based storage media rely on technologies that provide users with multiple reads that are cheap but may also contain errors. So, we ask: are we able to accurately reconstruct data from these noisy reads? More importantly, can we take advantage of the multiple reads to increase the information capacity in this new storage media. More generally, can the techniques developed here be used to enhance other biological applications? In this proposal, we explore a myriad of coding strategies for these storage scenarios and provide a comprehensive investigation via both theoretical and experimental approaches. Our specific aims are as follows. (A) In our first aim, we plan to study the fundamental limits of these storage systems. Specifically, given some reliability guarantee and coding scheme, we study two important performance metrics. The first metric is codebook size which measures the number of information bits stored, while the second metric is read coverage is correlated to the number of (possibly) noisy reads provided by the storage system. Ideally, we want to store many messages while using little reads to reconstruct the data. However, this is often not possible and we want to examine the trade-off between these two metrics and study the combinatorial limits of these coding schemes. We remark that our problem of interest may be viewed as a variant of the sequence reconstruction problem defined by Levenshtein (2001). In the latter definition, we fix a codebook and ask how many noisy reads are required to uniquely determine the data. However, in most storage scenarios, the number of noisy reads is a fixed system parameter. Hence, in such cases, we should then reduce the size of the codebook so that unique reconstruction is possible. Therefore, we rephrase the problem as such: given a fixed number of reads, what is the size of a largest codebook that allows unique reconstruction? (B) In our second aim, we analyse algorithms associated with the implementations of such codebooks. In determining fundamental limits in Aim (A), one usually turn to random coding arguments that do not give the explicit codewords. title: Protecting Critical AI Assets for Edge Intelligence
abs: This research focuses on protecting the confidentiality of AI models (algorithms) when they are deployed on the edge (e.g., mobile devices, IoT, embedded systems, etc). The protection of critical AI assets from model extraction attacks will soon become a major security concern with recent transition trends from cloud-based AI services to edge-based AI computing (edge intelligence). This will make AI model theft easy exploits due to the pervasiveness, ease of accessibility, and the low security offerings of the edge devices. Successful attacks will allow adversaries to: (a) gain business advantage over the original model owner, and/or (b) find transferable adversarial examples that will maliciously cause the original AI model to produce devastating outcomes. Our main research question is: How to implement complex AI models securely on low-cost edge devices to prevent AI model theft, while ensuring the Quality of Service (QoS) of the AI applications is not compromised? These edge devices include modern heterogeneous systems such as FPGA based SoCs, which is cost-effective and enables real-time edge intelligence through hardware acceleration. In addition to security challenges faced by traditional microcontroller based embedded systems, modern heterogeneous systems expose larger attack surfaces due to the myriad of interconnecting computing and storage resources. Our target platform in this research will be an FPGA based SoC, which not only subsumes other non-FPGA based heterogeneous systems (e.g., multicore) but also typical microcontroller based IoT systems. The research will be carried out in three stages: 1) Creating a new knowledge base of attacks: We will investigate new model extraction attacks that exploit various side-channel leakages e.g., timing/power traces, memory access patterns, hardware performance counters (HPC), etc., when AI algorithms run on the edge device. We will also explore combined attacks involving cache attacks, hardware Trojans, power, and timing analysis, etc. which targets the heterogeneous processing and storage elements of the edge device, as well as their communication channels. 2) Model-specific DNN obfuscation and mapping: Protecting against AI model theft is challenging as the presence of attacks is not observable from the intermediate or final system outputs. We hypothesize that the proposed countermeasures must be tailored to the specific AI model since different model structures exhibit unique properties that can be exploited in the attacks. We will propose an automated model centric Deep Neural Network (DNN) obfuscation framework that would transform the original DNN into a new functionally equivalent structure that is resilient to reverse engineering and piracy attacks. In addition, the proposed framework will map the DNN structure onto the edge device to take full advantage of the available security and hardware acceleration resources. title: How do depressed and anxious maternal moods shape infant affective cognition?
abs: Depression and anxiety collectively affect ~20% of mothers in the postnatal period. Parental mood disorders severely impact affective qualities of parent-child interaction and confer increased risk of mental illness in later life. Although several social and neurocognitive mechanisms contribute toward intergenerational risk transmission (e.g. stress), one important pathway is still poorly understood: developmental “mistuning” of affective cognition (the emotion-cognition interface). Maladaptive biases in affective cognition that are acquired during infancy may play a fundamental and sustained role in the aetiology of later mental illness. Yet little is known about how maternal moods “tune” the emotion-cognition interface during early sensitive periods of life. This project will systematically examine how maternal depression and anxiety influence infants’ attention allocation, learning and decision-making in emotional contexts, and the inter/intra-personal neurobiological mechanisms that mediate parental influences. 150 infants with typical, clinically-depressed or anxious mothers (N=50 per group) will be assessed twice on tests of affective cognition over the first year. Dyadic-electroencephalography (EEG) will be used to capture bi-directional mother-infant neural influences during these tasks. Understanding how maternal mood influences infant affective cognition could, in future, lead to dyadic (parent-child) interventions that improve mental wellbeing in both parent and child by modifying their emotional biases.

title: Archiving the Underclasses: Knowledge, Law, and Everyday Agency in Modern Southeast Asia
abs: [This is the complete and original project abstract.] Once thought to be passive repositories of objective knowledge, archives are now understood to be the subjective products of a range of institutional actors. As a result, historians, anthropologists, and other researchers increasingly subject the archives of major institutions (like state bureaucracies, court systems, and universities) to critical analysis. We now recognize that archivists, bureaucrats, and academics shape archival knowledge by selecting, organizing, and interpreting documents (Trouillot 1995, Cohn 1996, Stoler 2009). Some theorists even caution that archives may used as instruments of governmental control through their role in crafting what we, as a society, think we know about our neighbors and the world (Foucault 1970, Derrida 1996). So, most scholars no longer accept archival texts as inherently objective sources, and they do not hesitate to question assumptions about the authority of archival evidence (Guha 1983, Dirks 2001). With so much attention on institutions and their functionaries, however, the everyday players in the construction of archival knowledge are too often neglected. The proposed research project, "Archiving the Underclasses," focuses on everyday Southeast Asians, past and present. By searching the archival record to recover the lives of the region’s marginal peoples, we unearth evidence of their varied roles in the provision and collection of information, the constitution of archival records, and—indirectly—the production of knowledge itself (Rafael 1999, Schaffer et al 2009, Saha 2013, Reynolds 2019). We also highlight the agency of underclass communities in the construction of archival information. Marginal peoples can produce data for the state, for example, and they can appropriate government data to file claims for state recognition and services (Bandyopadhyay 2010). Unlike most conventional studies of knowledge production, we focus on the marginal figures who have provided and collected the information that fills the archives. They are a motley cast of characters: suspects, witnesses, smugglers, swindlers, captives, criminals, rebels, migrants, interpreters, guides, and gang members. Through critical examinations of their testimonies and other evidence preserved in the archives, we address questions that still puzzle scholars and policy-makers today: • How is information—evidence, intelligence, stories, data—collected on the ground? • When do everyday peoples engage with efforts to collect information? When do they resist? • How is information transformed even before it reaches the archives or another repository? • How reliable is the information that reaches the archives? Or the desks of state officials? • How can we recover marginal voices from official reports, court records, and other materials? title: Beyond-lead lamellar perovskite-based nano-scintillators
abs: Radiography, i.e. imaging using X-rays, relying on scintillators, is an essential technology in today's world with many vital applications. Low cost, low exposure dose and portable imaging equipment are always desirable. Lead-based perovskite materials are emerging as a low-cost alternative due to their solution processability, but their performance is still a fraction of conventional crystals. By replacing lead with some heavy cations in this project, we expect to maintain the excellent stopping power for ionization radiation and enhance the conversion efficiency from high energy radiation to visible luminescence. We will focus on beyond-lead lamellar perovskite scintillators from material modelling to experimental synthesis and characterization. The choice of 2D perovskite structures with strong confinement in 1 dimension allows high quantum yield luminescence compared to bulk (3D) structures and excellent stability compared to nanocrystal (0D) structures. After understanding these materials' scintillation mechanisms and light emission under X- and gamma-ray excitation, we will utilize nanophotonic strategies to enhance the extraction efficiency of the scintillating photons to gain the highest light yield. Besides the fundamental research outcomes on material development and understanding the underlying physics of the scintillation process, we also aim to demonstrate a large (≥ 6x6 cm2) scintillating panel for X-ray imaging from lamellar perovskite materials with some key specifications (light yield ≥ 66,000 photons/MeV, similar to commercial scintillators; lifetime ≤10 ns, two orders faster than the commercial scintillators of the same light yield; and no afterglow). The extremely fast response makes it an excellent candidate for high-frequency applications (e.g. X-ray computer tomography or fast X-ray imaging with spectral functionality). Such technology demonstrator will have tremendous potentials to revolutionize scintillators and X-ray imaging technology. The strong expert background of the research

title: Advancing van der Waals Heterostructures for High Frequency Tunnel Devices
abs: To answer the demand for increasing services, today information and data communication society requires ever higher data rate transmission networks and processing. This in turn appeals for high frequency (HF) of gigahertz or even terahertz operation for which tunnel devices potentially offer superior performances than thermionic-based ones. Indeed, band-to-band carrier tunnel is mostly determined by the band alignment and intrinsic semiconductor properties of the material heterostructure and does not suffer from limitations due to thermal activation. Moreover, it can lead to negative differential resistance (NDR), which is a unique and key feature for the development of HF sources and detectors.1 However, tunnel diodes suffer from issues when fabricated using traditional Si, Ge or III-V semiconductors, due to the inevitable covalent bonding at the interface. Indeed, 2D van der Waals heterostructures offer some unique properties and have shown potential application in tunnel diodes. However, in previous reports, the devices are mainly fabricated on exfoliated 2D flakes with severe issues regarding: i) the tunnel interface integrity, which is of paramount importance for tunnel diodes; ii) the precise rotational alignment between successive layers; iii) the process scalability and reliability when working on flakes. This project aims at assessing the capabilities of TMDs for tunnel devices. To this end, two kinds of tunnel devices will be fabricated at wafer scale using scalable growth techniques as well as device processing and fully characterized at low and high frequency. The objectives of this project are: i) the preparation of van der Waals heterostructures using chemical vapor deposition (CVD) and development of the preparation method for scalable growth of wafer scale samples; ii) the comprehensive characterization of the heterostructures, including interface properties and band alignment; iii) the design of tunnel diodes based on DFT calculations of material properties and transport in devices; iv) the fabrication of TMD-based tunnel diodes; v) the benchmarking of the resulting TMD-based diodes versus conventional 3D semiconductor-based ones.

title: Fostering Change in Our Foodways: The Perception and Acceptance of Alternative Proteins Among Consumers in Singapore
abs: This study aims to improve understanding of Singapore consumers’ perception of alternative protein and subsequently, foster their acceptance of this novel food technology. The term “alternative proteins” refers to animal-free protein alternatives that can be organised into three distinct categories: “plant-based proteins, edible insects, and a group referred to as ‘cellular agriculture’. This latter group encompasses products commonly referred to as ‘cultured’ or ‘clean’ meat, milk and other animal products, created either through culturing stem cells outside (in vitro) animal bodies, or through the genetic modification and fermentation of yeast cells” (Sexton et al., 2019, p. 48). More specifically, this study aims to answer the following research questions: 1. What are Singapore consumers’ perception of alternative proteins? 2. What message frames are most effective in fostering consumers’ acceptance of alternative proteins? 3. Which type/s of social media influencers (SMI) are most effective in influencing consumer acceptance of alternative proteins? 4. What are the effects of the message frames on Singapore consumers’ attitudes and behavioural intentions (or behavior) in relation to alternative proteins? The study will answer these research questions through an analysis of three datasets: RQ1 will be answered using six focus group discussions comprising participants from each of the following consumer categories: “(1) hedonically motivated meat eaters uninterested in meat substitutes; (2) health-oriented meat eaters open to some meat substitutes; and (3) ethically conscious meat avoiders positively oriented to most meat alternatives” (Bryant et al., 2019). Our approach to RQ1 will be guided by theories on risk and benefit perceptions (e.g. Slovic, 2000; Frewer & Van Trip, 2007;). RQs 2 and 3 will be answered using results from experimental studies comprising 1,000 participants. The study will utilize the controlled experimental design by randomly assigning participants to read one of the 21 message frames (7 message frames x 3 types of social media influencers). Our approach to RQs 2 and 3 will guided by theories on heuristics, message framing, and social influence (please refer to attached research proposal for details). RQ4 will be answered using data from a Wave 2 survey to be conducted six months after the Wave 1 experimental study. As per the survey used in Wave 1, Wave 2 will capture participants’ attitude and behaviourial intentions (or behaviour) with regard to alternative proteins. Together, this study will be able to provide important insights on both the immediate and sustained effects of message framing on people’s receptivity to alternative proteins.
kw: Alternative protein; novel food technologies; message framing; social influence; social media influencers.

title: Uncovering the Mechanical Coupling of Nanoparticle and Extracellular Matrix Elasticities for Enhanced Tumor Targeting
abs: The limited success in the clinical translation of nanoparticle-based drug delivery systems in the past couple of decades motivates improved fundamental understanding on the interaction between nanoparticle and biological systems. Among all the barriers that nanoparticles encounter en route to target a tumor cell, the mechanical resistance by the three-dimensional (3D) extracellular matrix in tumor interstitial space and the plasma membrane of the tumor cell remains the least understood. In this proposal, we hypothesize that there exists an intimate mechanical coupling among the extracellular matrix elasticity, mechanics of tumor cells and nanoparticle elasticity during both the transport and cellular uptake of nanoparticles, which should be taken into consideration when identifying the optimal nanoparticle design to target tumor. To test our hypothesis, we propose to first determine the coupled effects of nanoparticle and extracellular matrix elasticities on the transport and the cellular uptake of nanoparticles (Aims 1 & 2) and then to identify the optimal design of deformable nanoparticles by integrating the coupled effects together into a two-step optimization problem (Aim 3). We will synthesize hydrogel-based nanoparticles of various elasticity, and their capability of penetrating through the 3D extracellular matrix of various elasticity to reach tumor cells and their capability of entering tumor cells through endocytosis will be systematically evaluated and rationalized. The optimal NP elasticity will be predicted by considering the sequential order from tumor penetration to endocytosis as a two-step optimization problem and will be validated using a 3D cell culture system. Successful completion of the proposed work will lead to a potential guideline for precisely tailoring the design of deformable nanoparticles to achieve enhanced drug delivery to tumors at various stages. We expect that our improved understanding of the mechanics at the nano-bio interface would largely benefit the nanomedicine community.

title: CMOS-Compatible Resonant-Cavity-Enhanced GeSn Single-Photon Avalanche Photodiode – Material, Design and Device
abs: The end goal of this proposal is to develop a manufacturable, high sensitivity and high operation temperature germanium-tin (GeSn) single-photon avalanche photodiode (SPAD), which is able of detecting single-photon in the short-wave infrared (SWIR is defined as 1,100~2,500 nm) region for a plethora of quantum photonic and sensing applications. While silicon (Si) SPAD has demonstrated high performance in the spectral range below 1,000 nm, however, there are strong demands to extend the detection capability of Si SPAD detectors into the above SWIR range, which remains a challenge. The proposed SPAD is based on GeSn absorption layer and Si multiplication layer coupled with a vertical optical cavity. Thanks to the group-IV GeSn alloys, the photon absorption wavelength can be extended to the SWIR range and the absorption coefficient is increased significantly compared to Ge. Furthermore, in contrast to conventional photodiodes, by coupling the GeSn SPAD with an optical cavity, SPAD with even a thin absorption layer is able to demonstrate respectable quantum efficiency, resulting in a high-sensitivity and low-noise SPAD. Based on our preliminary modeling and characterizations, we estimate that the GeSn SPAD would have high detection efficiency and its noise can be reduced significantly by novel substrate engineering method. Low-noise SPAD allows operation at higher temperature, which is important for transferring the device from labs to practical applications. In addition, since the fabrication of the proposed SPAD is compatible with mainstream silicon CMOS technology, the cost of the device is expected to be lower than the currently used III-V material SPAD. High-performance SPAD devices in the SWIR regime are key enablers for a myriad of emerging applications include communication, quantum computing, LIDAR, fluorescence medical imaging, and others. The success of this proposal would greatly impact social-economy, healthcare, communication, autonomous system, and the related industries. The educational plan includes development and training of graduate students and researchers in the semiconductor optoelectronic device modeling and fabrication technologies. The expected impacts are relevant to Singapore and beyond.

title: Sustainable Chemical Transformations using Iron Catalysis
abs: Iron is environmentally benign and the most abundant transition metal in the earth's crust. Naturally, the use of iron-based complexes as catalysts to facilitate chemical synthesis is highly desirable. Despite the associated benefits, developments in organoiron chemistry are less advanced compared to other transition metals, partly owing to the difficulty of controlling the multiple oxidation and spin states accessible to iron. This inadvertently leads to over-reliance on other more expensive metal-catalyzed reactions which have various limitations in scope, consequently leading to overpopulation of certain molecular structures. To address these challenges, we believe that the unique electronic properties of iron can be exploited to develop new iron-based catalysts with tunable reactivity and selectivity profiles that are not accessible by other metal catalysis. This will enable us to discover new molecules and chemical space to meet the rising demands of the chemical industry. An important application in chemical synthesis is the sustainable conversion of readily available and abundant chemical feedstock such as alkenes to high-value products such as organoboron and organosilicon compounds which have wide utility in various industries. Although catalytic protocols that install boryl and silyl groups within alkenes have been described, few have shown that simple raw materials can be utilized as substrates, and integration of these methodologies into industrial applications/processes such as drug synthesis remains poor. Regio- and stereoselective convergent and divergent reactions as well as multicomponent processes that give rise to synthetically useful functionalized B- and Si-containing products are scarce. Our proposal aims to devise scalable Fe-catalyzed strategies that are reliable, broadly applicable and conveniently convert readily available feedstock chemicals (e.g. alkenes, alcohols, carbonyl compounds) to the desired chiral organoboranes and organosilanes with exceptional efficiency and selectivity. To achieve our objective, we propose the development of three programs: (i) regio- and enantioselective synthesis of boron- and silicon-containing products by site-specific proto-functionaliztion of alkenes; (ii) regiodivergent and enantioselective synthesis of organoboronates and other products by remote proto-functionaliztion of alkenes; (iii) multicomponent assembly of organoboronates from alkenes and organohalides. We will adopt a three-pronged approach that combines experiments, spectroscopic studies and theoretical computations to develop the proposed programs. These transformations are expected to enhance the way with which many chemicals of interest (e.g. fine chemicals and specialty chemicals) are currently prepared. The question remains whether suitable Fe-based catalysts with appropriate ligands can be identified to promote these transformations. title: Reveal Catalytic Fundamentals of Single Gold Cluster at Single-Molecule Level
abs: In this project, we propose to combine atomically precise gold nanoclusters (Au NCs) and single-molecule fluorescence microscopy (SMFM) to reveal the fundamentals of nano-gold catalysts at the atomic, single-molecule and single-particle level (or traceable NC catalysts). Since Haruta et al. discovered the catalytic activity of nano-gold in the 1980s, the catalysis based on Au nanoparticles has attracted tremendous interest. Although design of catalysts has achieved great success in the past few decades, there is still a lack of atomic- and molecular-level understanding of nano-gold catalysts (e.g., adsorption/desorption/activation/deactivation behaviour, the origin of the active sites, the precise correlation between the size/composition/structure of nano-gold catalysts and their catalytic performance, and the catalytic reaction kinetics/dynamics). Given that nanoscience is entering the era of atomic precision, insufficient atomic-level understanding has increasingly hindered the development of nano-gold catalysts. The establishment of atomic-level catalytic principles requires not only atomically precise Au nanoparticles, but also the ability to monitor the catalytic events (e.g., adsorption, conversion, and desorption) of a single substrate molecule on the surface of single Au nanoparticle. However, traditional Au nanoparticles (> 3 nm) are extremely difficult (if not impossible) to be synthesized and characterized with atomic precision, and conventional optical and magnetic spectroscopy methods can only measure their ensemble behaviour in catalytic reactions. Therefore, there is an urgent need to develop novel model catalysts (stable, with a definite number of metal atoms and protecting ligands, and a well-defined atomic packing structure) and catalytic reaction tracking technology (at the single-molecule and single-particle level) to shed fundamental lights on nano-gold catalysts at the atomic level. In this project, we propose to address this technical challenge by developing a core-in-cage model catalyst (see Figure 1 in the detailed proposal), in which a single Au NC (with atomic precision and adjustable gold atom number) is encapsulated in hollow microporous silica nanoparticles (m-SiO2). This core-in-cage model catalyst (fluorescent Au NC catalyst) will be used in conjunction with single-molecule fluorescence microscopy (SMFM), which can monitor fluorescent species at the single-molecule level, to clarify the basic principles of nano-gold catalysis. Au NCs are a family of ultra-small particles with a metal core of ~1 nm. They can be produced with molecular purity (with a definite number of Au atoms and well-defined cluster structure at Å resolution). Due to their protein-like hierarchical structure and strong quantum confinement effect, Au NCs exhibit interesting molecular-like properties, including discrete electronic energy levels, strong fluorescence, and customizable catalytic activity and selectivity. title: Green and economical chemical production by new stereoselective redox-neutral catalysis
abs: Innovation in chemical production aiming towards higher efficacy and less waste generation has great potential of reforming pharmaceutical manufacturing and benefiting our society in Singapore and worldwide. One particularly effective strategy in catalytic method development is cascade catalysis, which combines multiple steps into one operation to achieve high step-economy with minimized solvent use and workup/purification operations. The concept of redox-economy is also of great significance, which entails less use of redundant oxidation and reduction steps to focus on complexity-generation for chemical production. In addition, the use of early-abundant base metals (instead of precious metals) as catalysts to promote chemical reactions has also been recognized as part of the key solutions for sustainable chemical synthesis. Combining the advantage of all the above mentioned (cascade catalysis with redox economy promoted by abundant base metals), redox-neutral cascade catalysis has demonstrated great potential in promoting green and economical chemical production. In the past few years, my group has pioneered the development of catalytic enantioselective redox-neutral processes in achieving a few highly efficient, catalytic “substitution” of alcohols using amines and enolates. These processes use feedstock racemic alcohols, and deliver valuable chiral amines and alcohols in excellent yield and enantioselectivity. In this proposal, we plan to take our chemistry to a whole new level: instead of substituting the alcohols to access another mono-functional products, we have designed a range of new redox-neutral catalytic processes that will couple alcohols and a few classical building blocks to access complex structures bearing multiple functionalities. Many of these structures are proven, privileged building blocks for accessing valuable bioactive entities. In particular, our approaches include: a) We plan to develop new catalytic borrowing hydrogen processes to incorporate aldol addition, Baylis-Hillman reaction, etc. The products of these transformations are highly valuable acyclic building blocks in the preparation of polyketide family of natural products and pharmaceuticals. Our methods can provide significant advantages in comparison to classical approaches in terms of step-, atom- and redox-economy. b) We also plan to incorporate a dearomatization step into our borrowing hydrogen catalytic cascade to prepare valuable enantioenriched saturated heterocycles from readily available arene precursors. The efficiency and economy of these synthesis compare favourably with previous synthesis of these valuable compounds. c) The success of the above-mentioned processes relies on the development of effective and selective catalysts, especially sustainable, base-metal-derived catalysts. title: Extremely high-density grain boundary of wafer-size atom-thin materials for hydrogen production
abs: Low-cost catalytic materials are very desirable to practical energy applications. As promising materials, atom-thin transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) have emerged as fascinating materials and key structures for electrocatalysis. So far, their edges, dopant heteroatoms and defects have been intensively explored as active sites for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) to split water. However, grain boundaries (GBs), a key type of defects in TMDs, have been overlooked due to their low density and large structural variations. To date, many methods employed to synthesize atomically-thin polycrystalline TMDs include chemical vapor deposition (CVD), physical vapor deposition (PVD), and metal-organic chemical vapor deposition (MOCVD). However, it is found that these methods deliver poor control over the density and structure of GBs, which stems from the fast gaseous-kinetic processes. Therefore, how to control the growth process and limit grain size at an ultra-small region (2D limit i.e.10 nm) will be challenging for applying GB in hydrogen production. On the other hand, current-reported TMD catalysts are nano-size structures like nanoparticles or nanosheets and lack a scale fabrication method, resulting in that their corresponding hydrogen production is limited in a lab. With a view of practical application, the large-scale fabrication of TMD materials (e.g., wafer-size) and the concept of large-scale hydrogen production in TMD catalysts will be desirable to demonstrate the enormous potentials in electrocatalysis. In this proposal, we aim to develop a universal and scalable method to produce wafer-size (up to 2 inches), atom-thin (down to 1 nm) and sub-10 nm grain TMD films. Such film will consist a world-record ultra-high grain and GB density up to 1012/cm2 and will realize the high-performance hydrogen production on a wafer-size (2 inch) TMD film, demonstrating the potential of large-scale hydrogen production in practice and in a lower cost compared to Pt. Moreover, single-GB’s HER activity will be examined in micro-cell as well as single-molecule fluorescence microscopy for the first time. It will serve as a highly efficient catalyst site, with performance comparable or even better than other active sites.
kw: high-density grain boundary, micro-electrochemical cell, wafer-size atom-thin materials, hydrogen production.

title: Sensing gravitational force with light storage in hollow-core fibres
abs: This proposal aims to investigate and develop a high spatial resolution gravitational force sensor based on light storage in an ensemble of cold-atoms optically trapped in a hollow-core optical fibre for applications of studying fundamental physics and mobile inertial sensors. Current state-of-the-art quantum inertial sensors utilise atomic interferometers in free space. Their sensitivity heavily relies on preparing a narrow velocity width (typically one-tenth of the sub-recoil velocity) of the atomic ensemble, which requires a sophisticated cooling sequence. Besides, the atomic cloud's size, typically a few millimetres, limits the spatial resolution of the sensors and is the main systematic effect of the force gradient measurements. Here, we propose to use light storage in optically trapped atoms in an optical fibre as a gravitational force sensor. Our proposed method does not require a sub-recoil temperature of atoms. The signal is detected by measuring the retrieved light pulse's phase shift instead of the atoms' population. This provides a versatile route for processing the signal with direct noise rejection. Moreover, the small core size (~100 μm) of the fibre permits high spatial resolution and can bring the test masses close to the atoms to boost the signal as the gravitational force scales with 1/r^2, where r is the distance between the source masses and the test masses. At the end of the funding period, the expected result is a compact gravitational force sensor in a hollow-core optical fibre with a sensitivity of 10^(-7) m/s^2. The proposed method combines quantum communication and quantum sensing to impact both precision measurements of fundamental physics and mobile quantum sensors. In precision measurement, the fibre gravitational force sensor we develop in the proposal can be used to measure Newton's gravitational constant G and test the gravitational Aharonov Bohm effect, which could lead to studying the deviation of Newton' inverse square law. On the mobile quantum sensors side, our scheme's compactness could provide a high spatial resolution of the gravity gradient mapping for field survey and resources exploration.

title: From 3D to 2D All-Organic Perovskites
abs: Perovskites materials have so far amaze researchers with their superlative performance in applications ranging from solar cells, OLED to ferroelectrics. Most reported perovskites are either purely inorganic or consist of mixed organic and inorganic components. Perovskites made entirely of organic components are uncommon, and among these, the ferroelectric sub-class is even rarer. Ferroelectric materials, which have spontaneous electric polarization that can be switched with an external electric field, are central to electronic and memory devices owing to their applications as capacitors, sensors, and data-storage devices. Conventional ferroelectrics are dominated by inorganic perovskite oxides such as BaTiO3 and LiNbO3, however, these ceramics are brittle and expensive to produce as high-quality thin films, and they often contain heavy metals such as Pb2+, which raises health and environmental concerns. Replacing heavy metals with organic components in the perovskite lattice is appealing because the organic version can be flexible, fracture-resistant, environmentally friendly, and potentially easier to synthesize than the inorganic (eg. Pb based) counterparts. The subject of ferroelectric and/or dielectric organic material has received long standing interests from the community because of their importance in semiconductor passivation and dielectrics to minimize RC delay. Ferroelectric PVDF polymer has relatively low spontaneous polarization values and high coercive voltages compared to inorganic perovskites, yet molecular ferroelectrics can have high polarization values and low coercive voltage due to ease of displacing hydrogen bonded-polar centres. Thus, it is interesting to explore the fundamental structural chemistry of ferroelectricity in all-organic perovskites, with a view of achieving polarization values comparable with inorganic perovskites. The objective of this proposal is to design and synthesize a new family of all-organic perovskite materials, and to understand the structural and compositional changes needed to obtain high relative permittivity values or ferroelectricity in these materials. The successful synthesis of all all-organic perovskites not only enriches the diverse family of perovskite materials, but also opens up possibilities for flexible electronics and organic-based memory devices. The challenge in synthesizing all-organic 3D perovskites stem from the need to comply with Goldsmith’s rule, which dictates that only a certain ratio of cation size to anion size can fit into the cubic or tetragonal lattice; the difficulty is exacerbated in the case of organic perovskites because most molecular ions are too large. In addition, global charge neutrality has to be maintained; these limiting conditions restrict the range of cations and anions that can be used in organic perovskites, making them difficult to synthesize. title: Resolving Star Formation in the Early Universe
abs: In order to understand the populations of galaxies that exist today, astronomers use computational simulations that rely on empirically observed correlations to approximate physics occurring on scales too small to resolve. One of the most important pieces of sub-grid physics is the star formation law (known as the Schmidt-Kennicutt relation) that ties galaxies’ star formation rate to the density of molecular gas in the interstellar medium. The Schmidt-Kennicutt relation has been well constrained in the local Universe, but has only been measured in a handful of galaxies ~10 billion years ago—the epoch when the cosmic star formation rate was at its highest and galaxies built up the majority of their stellar mass. Measuring how the star formation law varies across cosmic time is critical to models of galaxy evolution and therefore fundamental to understanding the origin of galaxy populations that exist today. As one of the few to have successfully measured the Schmidt-Kennicutt relation in the early Universe, we are proposing to (1) better calibrate the gas mass and star formation rate tracers used to measure the Schmidt-Kennicutt relation in the early Universe, and (2) nearly double the number of high-redshift disk galaxies on the Schmidt-Kennicutt relation in order to build a statistical sample of the most abundant galaxy population. These goals fill important gaps in both methodological practices and in our understanding of star formation across cosmic time. Not only will this work be critical for establishing best-practices in future observational studies, but it will also produce a novel tool for translating multi-wavelength galaxy images into maps of their physical properties (such as star formation rate, dust mass, etc.). Our previous work has proven the feasibility of studying the star formation law in the early Universe for individual systems, and we are now poised to take advantage of new cutting-edge facilities to create the first statistically valid Schmidt-Kennicutt sample in the peak epoch of galaxy assembly. The proposed research is the essential first step towards creating a gold-standard measurement of the spatially resolved Schmidt-Kennicutt relation in the early Universe, ensuring its relevance to the field by enabling the efficient development of even larger samples and samples of rare/peculiar galaxy populations. To accomplish these two goals, we will leverage the significant amount of data in-hand for a prototypical star-forming galaxy in the early Universe (SDSS J0901+1814; J0901 hereafter) and conduct new observations for a sample of strongly lensed galaxies analogous to J0901. title: The role of lipid-accumulating macrophages in aging and disease
abs: Recent reports have identified lipid-accumulating macrophages (LAMs) in several tissues, including white adipose tissue (WAT) and the brain, but their exact roles are still elusive. Here we aim to understand whether these LAMs support or restrain the progression of diseases characterized by abnormal lipid metabolism, including obesity and Alzheimer’s disease. We hypothesize that LAMs could have a crucial role in both disorders. To prove our hypothesis, we will generate transgenic mouse models in which tissue-resident macrophages are unable to effectively accumulate lipids. To do so, we will adopt the mouse Cre/lox recombinase system to disrupt Fit2 gene expression specifically in macrophages and will generate two novel transgenic mouse lines (CX3CR1CreERT2Fit2fl/fl and CD11cFit2fl/fl mouse lines). We will then expose these mice to a high-fat diet to promote obesity. From here, we will analyse how reduced lipid accumulation in macrophages affects WAT remodelling during aging and obesity progression. In parallel, we will develop a preclinical mouse model of Alzheimer’s disease in our transgenic mice. We will achieve this by crossing a APPKI Alzheimer’s mouse strain with our CX3CR1CreERT2Fit2fl/fl and CD11cFit2fl/fl mouse lines. Then, we will evaluate the contribution of lipid-accumulating microglia in aging and age-related neurodegeneration. Our analyses will be founded on state-of-the-art techniques, including RNA sequencing of Fit2-/- and Fit2+/+ LAMs as well as single cell RNA sequencing, multi-dimensional flow cytometry, and lipidomics/metabolomics of WAT in presence and absence of Fit2-/- and Fit2+/+ LAMs. Given our extensive experience in harnessing these techniques, and expert knowledge on macrophage biology we are confident that we will clarify the relevance of LAMs in obesity and neurodegenerative disorders.

title: Suppression of Heart Failure through Regulation of DNA Repair
abs: Mammalian cardiomyocytes (CM), exiting their cell cycle shortly after birth, are difficult to be reactivated upon cardiac injury, thus limiting heart repair through cardiac regeneration. We and others demonstrated that enhancing CM proliferation is beneficial for heart recovery from heart failure (HF) models caused by myocardial infarction (MI), pressure overload (PO) and angiotensin II infusion (Ang II), the most common HF models. Interestingly, perturbing the Hippo signalling pathway, which normally prevents adult CM proliferation and regeneration, reversed MI HF model. Moreover, activation of YAP1, the terminal downstream effector of the Hippo signalling pathway, improved cardiac function and survival in the mouse MI model. The proliferation markers for the different stages of cell cycle were enhanced by YAP1 activation. However, the quantification of cardiomyocyte renewal after heart damage is still challenging due to infiltration of inflammatory cells, proliferation of non-cardiomyocytes (non-CM), and cardiac fibrosis. Therefore, it remains elusive whether CM undergo complete cell division cycles to generate new cells in damaged heart. Furthermore, it is also unknown whether there is a regeneration independent role of YAP1 in suppressing HF. DNA damage response (DDR) is an important mediator of postnatal cell cycle arrest in CMs. Additionally, DDR also play a significant role in the pathophysiological of heart failure. Accumulation of DNA damage including single-strand breaks (SSB) or double-strand breaks (DSB) in CM was observed in pressure overload (PO), MI or Ang II HF models as well as patients with HF. Importantly, HF was modulated by genetically targeting the related DNA repair genes responsive to SSB or DBS, suggesting a causative role of DNA damage in the pathogenesis of HF. Apart from regeneration, cell cycle is tightly interconnected with DNA repair, especially DNA DSB repair. It is unknown whether activation of CM proliferation suppresses HF through promoting DNA repair. Here, we propose to address these gaps using our recently developed new HF model caused by Lmna insufficiency in CM (Lmna HF) Pathogenic variations in A-type lamin gene (LMNA) leads to familial Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM), one of the most common causes of HF defined by the presence of left ventricular (LV) enlargement and contractile dysfunction leading to reduced cardiac contraction. Our Lmna HF model demonstrated impaired cardiac contraction, enlarged heart chamber of left ventricle (LV) and reduced LV wall thickness coupled with massive interstitial fibrosis. Studies using laminopathies mouse models as well as muscle biopsies from patients with LMNA-related muscular dystrophy showed that Lmna mutations reduced nuclear stability, leading to DNA damage and DDR activation. title: Mechanisms of progesterone antagonism of estrogen action on the endometrium
abs: Progesterone is a master regulator of endometrial function through coordinated synergistic and antagonistic interplays with estrogen. Timely antagonism of estrogen action by progesterone is critical not only for optimal endometrial receptivity for embryo implantation, but also for the prevention of endometriosis and endometrial cancer. However, the mechanism of the antagonism is poorly understood; the gene and tissue selectivity of the antagonism is not known; the endometrial pathobiology associated with impaired progesterone signalling is not well-defined. Importantly, there is a lack of a suitable in vivo model for the study of impaired progesterone receptor (PR) signalling. PR knockout mice are infertile due to ovulation failure and hence offer no utility in the mechanistic study in the endometrium. We have established the first PR mutant mouse model with mutations at three critical residues of the activation function 1 (AF1) domain. AF1 is in the intrinsically disordered N terminal domain of PR and is believed to mediate the gene- and tissue-specific function of PR. Preliminary studies indicate that progesterone is unable to antagonize estrogen action on the uterus of AF1 mutant mice. The overall hypothesis of the proposal is that AF1 mediates progesterone antagonism of estrogen action in the endometrium. The hypothesis will be tested with the following specific aims: 1) to delineate gene- and tissue-specific roles of AF1 in the antagonism of estrogen on the uterus and to identify novel AF1-regulated molecular networks critical for embryo implantation; 2) to identify endometrial and plasma biomarkers predictive of endometrial receptivity in patients with recurrent implantation failure; 3) to elucidate novel mechanisms of AF1-mediated antagonism by determining whether activated PR/AF1 disrupts ESR1-directed chromatin interactions and by clarifying how AF1 is involved in Pg regulation of target genes in endometrial stromal cells. Completion of the study will achieve a major advancement in the understanding of Pg antagonism of Es action in endometrium. The study will reveal biomarkers for predicting endometrial receptivity. The knowledge will inspire further studies to improve clinical management of endometrial diseases.

title: Molecular mechanisms and spatio-temporal control of epithelial lumen formation
abs: Many major organs are composed of tubes of polarized epithelial cells enclosing a central gas- or liquid-filled lumen. The formation of epithelial lumens plays a fundamental role during embryogenesis and is critical for organ development and function. Defects in lumen formation are also responsible for a variety of human diseases, including microvilli inclusion disease, renal tubular acidosis, and polycystic kidney disease (PKD). Kidney diseases, in particular, affect millions of people worldwide and thus represent a major health care burden. Understanding the molecular and cellular mechanisms that control the morphogenesis and integrity of tubular organs is key for the development of strategies to combat disease. This proposal aims to produce novel molecular and temporal insight into how renal epithelial cells form an apical luminal surface de novo. De novo lumen formation is a highly dynamic process that relies on the precise coordination of cell polarity development and apical membrane assembly. Central to de novo lumenogenesis is the formation of an apical membrane initiation site (AMIS) via membrane trafficking and its subsequent maturation into a luminal precursor, the pre-apical patch (PAP). The AMIS-PAP transition is driven by the spatial segregation of AMIS components, leading to the formation of a free apical luminal surface, the assembly of cell-cell junctions, and apico-basal polarity development. How this remarkable remodeling of the epithelial cell cortex is coordinated and regulated in time and space is unclear, in particular in vivo. In this proposal we will address this question by focusing on one of the major regulators of epithelial tissue morphogenesis - the Crumbs polarity complex. The Crumbs complex is conserved from flies to humans and plays a fundamental role in epithelial polarity development and apical membrane assembly. Loss of the Crumbs complex causes severe defects in lumen formation in 3D epithelial cultures and in vivo, which in mice and zebrafish culminates in various developmental defects including cystic kidney phenotypes that resemble the pathophysiology of PKD. Although this clearly indicates a fundamental role for the Crumbs comples in kidney development, we know very little about how the complex functions on the molecular level, and how its activity is regulated during lumen formation. The aim of this proposal is to study the spatio-temporal regulation and function of the Crumbs complex during renal lumen formation in an established and genetically tractable 3D cell culture model and in the zebrafish pronephric kidney. This project is timely because we have recently discovered that the Crumbs complex defines a hitherto unidentified and distinct membrane domain at the epithelial apical-lateral border. title: Regulation of TSPAN8 cell surface expression and its role in tumor microenvironment and metastasis
abs: Tetraspanins constitute a superfamily of evolutionarily conserved proteins with four transmembrane domains. Tetraspanin-enriched microdomain (TEM), often formed by multiple different tetraspanin members, along with other proteins in the plasma membrane, has been proposed to play critical roles in diverse physiological and pathological functions. Tetraspanin-8 (TSPAN8) was originally discovered as a tumour-associated membrane antigen. It has recently been found to be overexpressed in a wide variety of epithelial cancers. However, the molecular regulation and pathophysiological function of TSPAN8 remain largely unclear in cancer. We hypothesize that cell surface TSPAN8 plays an indispensable role in cancer development and progression. Like all other tetraspanins, TSPAN8 protein lacks a signal peptide sequence and the mechanism for its trafficking to the cell surface has not been well studied. We have recently conducted an unbiased genome-wide loss-of-function CRISPR/Cas9 screen based on cell surface expression levels of TSPAN8. Candidate genes identified from the screen not only reveal that N-glycosylation modification is important for cell surface trafficking of TSPAN8, but also provided us with a powerful platform to elucidate the molecular details in the regulation of ER targeting of tetraspanin and perhaps other membrane proteins, their modifications at the Golgi and subsequent trafficking to the plasma membrane. Preliminary results from in vitro functional studies, based on antibody blocking and knockout approaches, clearly indicate that TSPAN8 plays a non-redundant role in the migration and invasion of multiple cancer cell lines. To gain mechanistic insights, a novel protocol has been successfully developed for profiling and comparing the transcriptome of isogenic cancer cells with and without TSPAN8 expression when they are undergoing acute invasion. Unexpectedly, we found that TSPAN8 appears to act as a master coordinator for multiple signaling pathways during cell invasion. In this project, we will further address how TSPAN8 orchestrates these pathways by validating and characterizing the candidate genes identified in the RNA-seq analyses. We will also use other open strategies, including BioID and Split-Ubiquitin Yeast Two-Hybrid, to identify interacting partners and mediators of TSPAN8 function during cell invasion. Integration of the comprehensive data obtained from multiple approaches used to address TSPAN8-mediated cell invasion would potentially provide new insights into the molecular regulation of cancer cell invasion and metastasis. To address the in vivo role of TSPAN8 in cancer development and progression, we have established a mouse HCC model. Remarkably, preliminary data suggest that knockout of TSPAN8 inhibits tumour burden in this mouse HCC model. title: Cross-species dissection of underlying molecular mechanisms in synucleinopathies
abs: There are no available treatments that prevent or slow down the course of Parkinson's disease (PD) and dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB). These common and devastating "synucleinopathies" are characterized by neurodegeneration associated with abnormal inclusions in nerve cells named Lewy bodies. How Lewy bodies (LBs) form and what roles they play in selectively killing dopamine-producing nerve cells in the midbrain thus causing PD remains a mystery. We hypothesize that genetic perturbations and specialized cellular physiology contribute to dysregulated processing of alpha-synuclein protein, the main constituent of LBs, resulting in the formation of LBs and ultimately neuronal demise, which is revealed by our multimodal strategy that integrates the high throughput, genetic and cellular screening of yeast with human midbrain-like organoids (hMLOs) that enable continuous observation of steps involved in LB formation and related molecular processes. We will first dissect out the fine structure and molecular makeup of LBs in our hMLOs. By introducing mis-processed alpha-synuclein in yeast, we will then screen out genes that are involved in the formation of LBs and toxicity and validate identified genes and genetic mechanisms back to hMLOs to finally tease out how the molecular changes during the formation of Lewy bodies impair and ultimately kill the nerve cell. Successful completion of our proposed research will help us understand the processes leading to the formation of LBs and ultimately the demise of dopamine-secreting nerve cells, which would enable us to develop strategies to halt or slow down the progress of PD and related synucleinopathies.
kw: alpha-synuclein; proteinopathy; lewy-body; brain organoids; electrophysiology

title: Macromolecular assembly of the polarisome complex modulates actin cable polymerization for the establishment of cell polarity
abs: Spatially and temporally restricted actin polymerization is the basis for cell polarization required in multiple processes across all life forms. The dynamic assembly of a large macromolecular protein complex called the polarisome is critical for subcellularly localized actin polymerization in budding yeast and filamentous fungi. The polarisome complex forms via multivalent interactions between several actin-binding proteins (ABPs) at the bud-tip during vegetative cell growth in budding yeast. These inter- and intramolecular interactions are spatiotemporally regulated to ensure production of polarized actin cables at the bud tip when needed during the cell cycle. The polarisome complex is composed of five central members: Spa2, Bni1, Bud6, Aip5, and Pea2, all of which contain long intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) in addition to structured (folded) domains. Past research, including work from my laboratory, has addressed the functional characterization of individual polarisome members with a particular focus on the molecular structure of their folded domains. However, we have had little insight into how the large IDRs of each polarisome member function to regulate polarisome assembly and activity, due in large part to the technical challenges involved in studying unstructured protein domains (knowledge gap). Our past Tier 2 project focused on IDR-mediated contributions to polarisome function and their phosphoregulation by the cell cycle regulator cyclin-dependent kinase 1 (Cdk1). Our more recent research has extended this work in two ways. 1) We have shown that the folded domains of Bud6 and Aip5 interact simultaneously with the Bni1 C-terminal IDR to form an actin nucleation complex core that promotes Bni1-mediated actin nucleation. These findings establish the foundation for the current proposal to study the entire polarisome complex quantitatively, both in vivo and in vitro. 2) We have shown that the IDRs of polarisome members facilitate multivalent interactions that regulate polarisome assembly and function via protein phase separation. On the basis of these findings, we propose a first hypothesis, namely that polarisome assembly and function are tuned by regulating the interaction of multiple IDR-containing proteins required to recruit and pack five core polarisome components (Spa2, Bni1, Bud6, Aip5, and Pea2) at the bud tip. Our results further suggest an exciting mechanism by which the assembly and function of the polarisome is finetuned to both promote actin polymerization and be responsive to the state of actin polymerization in a feedback manner sensitive to cell signaling and the state of the cell cycle. Thus, our second hypothesis is that the mechanical or pulling force generated by actin treadmilling would regulate the motility and equilibrium of proteins in and out of the polarisome in a feedback manner. title: Decoding the connectome by deep encoding on graphs
abs: The aim of this project is to develop technologies for encoding and decoding the human brain network or the connectome in order to investigate cognitive functions and brain diseases. The connectome is detected as the structural connectome (SC) and the functional connectome (FC) from diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) brain scans, respectively. The SC captures the strengths of white-matter fibres connecting brain regions while the FC captures the strengths of functional interactions as temporal correlations of activations of brain regions. The connectome (i.e., the SC and FC) is mathematically represented as a graph where nodes are represented by brain regions and the interactions between brain regions by weighted edges. Brain regions of interests (ROI) are defined by parcellation of the cortex into functionally and structurally relevant regions. When a subject performs a sensory or behavioral task, the brain attains a cognitive state specific to that task whereas the connectome of a patient suffering from a brain disease possesses a disease state as opposed to the healthy state. Cognitive states emerge from neuronal activations and interactions leading to alterations in the FC whereas disease states are manifestations of implications of both the SC and FC. We hypothesis that encoding and decoding the connectome with Graph Neural Networks (GNN) that explicitly operate on graph-structured data and learn deep representations lead to accurate detection of cognitive and disease states and discovery associated biomarkers. We propose to develop Techniques and Tools that facilitate effective encoding and decoding of the connectome with GNN. By encoding, we mean learning compact representations of the connectome, leading to classification of brain scans (i.e., classification of subjects into groups). We aim to develop novel techniques based on recently introduced GNN models such as Graph Convolutional Networks (GCN), GraphSAGE, and Graph Attention Networks (GAT) to encode the connectome. GNN models are specifically designed to learn hierarchical representations of graph-structured data. Though Deep Neural Networks (DNN) models have been widely used for investigation of the connectome, such models are unable to capture the graphical nature of the connectome as they operate on a linearized vector equivalent of the connectome. We hypothesize that a more accurate analysis of the connectome is achieved when its graph structure is explicitly taken into consideration by GNN that are specifically designed to operate on graph-structured data. In particular, we will investigate three most promising GNN models: GCN, GraphSAGE, and GAT. GCN are based on spectral graph theory and the most popular one. GraphSAGE extends applications to inductive learning while GAT is designed to operate on arbitrary structured graphs. title: Neural Basis of General Intelligence in Biological and Artificial Neural Networks
abs: General intelligence (GI) is a term used to describe a specific set of abilities possessed by a physical system, which includes the ability to reason, use strategies to solve tasks, represent commonsense knowledge, plan actions, learn efficiently, and integrate all these skills towards achieving goals. There are a number of cognitive building blocks that are essential to GI, including the capacities to maintain thoughts “in-mind” and manipulate these thoughts flexibly (working memory), to ignore task-irrelevant distracting information (selective attention), to evaluate the subjective reward or punishment associated with stimuli and actions (reward processing), and to prepare and execute actions (motor control), among others. However, to date, we lack an understanding of how these different cognitive operations are implemented in the brain. This is reflected in our inability to replicate GI in man-made systems, including state-of-the-art artificial intelligence systems. Thus, the goal of this proposal is to provide a mechanism that explains how different cognitive operations are implemented in the brain. In particular, we propose to test the hypothesis that brain regions leverage the high dimensionality of their activity to selectively convey information to downstream regions. More specifically, we will test whether a population of primate lateral prefrontal neurons conveys selective information to visual and motor downstream regions using subspaces of activity. To test this hypothesis we will analyze the activity of multiple neurons collected simultaneously from prefrontal, visual, and motor brain regions of macaque monkeys performing a complex behavioral task. Existing analytical methods are limited, which is why we will also be developing novel analytical tools with the help of artificial neural networks, and leveraging inference methods employed in other fields of engineering to develop these tools. Overall, the aims outlined in this proposal will advance our understanding of GI and reveal novel computational mechanisms of its implementation through interactions between neuroscience and artificial intelligence research. These results will be of relevance to our understanding of normal brain function, brain dysfunction, and artificial intelligence.
kw: Cognitive flexibility; artificial intelligence; working memory; intelligence; prefrontal cortex; monkey

title: Epigenetic mechanism that controls the activation of neural stem cells
abs: The broad objective of the proposed research is to study the epigenetic mechanism that promotes brain stem cell proliferation, with a focus on the lysine demethylase, Phf2 (Plant homeodomain finger protein 2). Neural stem cells (NSCs), capable of self-renewal and multi-lineage differentiation, are responsible for the cellular complexity and proper development of the mammalian central nervous system. An emerging view is that the NSCs represent a heterogeneous population that comprises cells with varying depths of cellular quiescence. In particular, we have very little knowledge of the newly identified shallow quiescent (or primed activated) NSC subpopulation. While numerous RNA-Seq studies have revealed that the switch from quiescent to activated NSCs involves the coordinated upregulation of cell cycle, ribosome biosynthesis and RNA synthesis pathways with the accompanied downregulation of extrinsic signaling pathways and differential transcription factor expression, the molecular explanation to this phenomenon remains poorly understood. To investigate the role of Phf2 in brain homeostasis and development by regulating NSC proliferation, I propose to (i) examine NSC subpopulations in postnatal mice and embryos from a Nes-Cre;Phf2(f/f) mouse model by using single cell transcriptomic and histological analyses; and (ii) conduct epigenomic analysis of Phf2 and its interactor, Ddx21 (a RNA helicase), using mouse NSC cultures. Given that impaired NSC proliferation (due to a block in the exit of NSC from quiescence) has been linked to the aged brain, this proposal will expand our knowledge of the mechanisms that regulate NSC proliferation and guide the development of mechanism-driven therapeutic intervention that may reverse/retard brain aging in human.
kw: Neural stem cell activation, epigenetics, PHF2, neurogenesis

title: Probability models to infer cell type contribution and site of origin for total molecular changes in omics data
abs: Single cell omics technologies have become a new cornerstone of contemporary molecular cell biology research, providing unbiased mapping of constituent cell populations and their underlying molecular profiles in complex tissues. In addition, omics-scale molecular atlas for multiple types of tissues have become available and these data resources opens the possibility to infer the origins of circulating proteins and small molecules in blood and urine. These advances undoubtedly call for development of novel data analytic strategies. While bioinformatics approaches in the current literature are mainly focused on the data processing, identification of constituent cell populations, and cell lineage inference, methods for deconvoluting the changes observed in the bulk samples based on single cell and tissue specific experiments are scarce. In the first part of the proposal, we aim to develop a statistical approach for incorporating single-cell RNA-sequencing data into the differential gene expression analysis of bulk tissue data. We will develop a novel statistical method to calculate the gene-specific confidence score of each cell population contributing to the total expression change observed in the bulk analysis, accounting for the overall shift in cell population composition in different samples. We will implement modelling approaches to fully characterize the posterior distribution of cell-type specific latent states of differential expression via parametric and non-parametric Bayes. The models will be calibrated and validated by an existing transcriptomics data set for a mouse model, where genetic disruption of a functional domain of a key cell cycle gene in liver results in a hypertrophic phenotype and both isolated pure hepatocytes and whole liver were analyzed separately. The approach will also be evaluated in other data sets in the analysis of heart, lung, and liver tissues as well as peripheral mononuclear cells in blood. In the second part of the proposal, we will develop a latent variable model for circulating marker data and organ-specific gene expression data. The “site-of-origin” latent variables for organ systems / tissues will be inferred from the circulating marker data, with priors and hyperpriors for latent variables reflecting the organ-specific expression data in an intrinsic manner. For markers significantly associated with disease phenotypes, we will compute the posterior probability that each endocrine organ system is responsible for the altered marker levels in circulation. title: Autonomous Urban Driving using Road Context, Driver Intent and Driving Styles
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: Autonomous urban driving among human-driven cars requires a holistic understanding of road rules, short-term driver intents and long-term driving styles. This is a challenging task given the stochastic intents and driving styles of the on-road users. In addition, dynamically changing environments such as road intersections and traffic signals further increase the complexity with the pedestrian traffic. In this proposal we aim to develop an interactive behaviour planning and control algorithm for a range of scenarios varying from normal to adversarial situations for autonomous urban driving application. Specifically, we propose a road context, driver intent, and driving style aware planner which infers beliefs over the latent states of surrounding exo-vehicles and uses a specialized Partially Observable Markov Decision Process to provide risk-averse decisions and smooth control commands for a self-driving car. We aim to validate our proposed interactive behaviour planner and controller in simulation as well as on full-size autonomous vehicles. Our preliminary experimental results show that our algorithm can enable safe and time-efficient autonomous driving capabilities even in adversarial scenarios.
kw: Autonomous Urban Driving; Driver Intent and Behaviour Inference; Planning under Uncertainty; Risk-Averse Decision Making; Interactive Behaviour Planning

title: Complex structures in Statistical Physics and the Math of Data
abs:
The classical theory of large scale random systems, particularly in application domains, generally embodies a very simple interaction structure between its constituents. While this makes the models analytically tractable, it also limits their efficacy to capture significant real-world phenomena. With recent advances in the empirical sciences and the development of new analytical machinery, stochastic models with structural constraints have emerged as objects of fundamental scientific importance, spanning a wide array of domains from statistical physics to the mathematics of data. Such structural constraints can be of diverse origin, ranging from statistical, algebraic, combinatorial or physical considerations. These are often latent in character, with a natural ques- tion being inferential problems based on observed data or measurable macroscopic parameters.

title: Data Driven Dynamical System (D3S): Model Uncertainty, Learning and Decentralized Optimization
abs: This proposal on stochastic dynamical system studies two core challenges in this field: “Model Uncertainty and Learning” and “Decentralized Optimization”. We first address the topic on data-driven optimization. Data driven optimization is concerned with developing methods for effective decision making with optimization models that use data. The use of data to calibrate models and a concern about out-of-sample performance raises several issues: (i) the in-sample model is generally misspecified because of simplifications in the model-building process and erroneous assumptions about the statistical properties of the data that is used to calibrate the model, and (ii) there is parameter uncertainty because models are calibrated with limited data. These are important concerns because decisions obtained by optimizing a data-driven model that ignores model error can perform poorly out-of-sample. The broad objective of this research is to understand how model uncertainty, parameter estimation, and learning can be accounted for and integrated in a data driven model to improve out-of-sample performance. We are interested in data driven problems involving one-shot decisions as well as multi-period problems where data is collected and decisions are made sequentially over time. We propose to explore aspects of the following three issues both theoretically as well as in applications: (i) the notion of “worst-case sensitivity”, its connection with “worst-case optimization”, and showing how it can be used to select both the family and size of uncertainty sets in “worst-case optimization” so that the resulting decisions are less sensitive to model error yet perform well in terms of expected reward when applied out-of-sample; (ii) developing models for new product forecasting that accounts for cannibalization effects in settings where there is no historical data about the new product, and (iii) approximate methods for Bayesian dynamic portfolio choice with learning and applications to long-term investment with demand predictability models. Applications in retail and insurance, where the lack of data and concerns about model accuracy are central, will be considered. The second topic is Decentralized Optimization in Stochastic Dynamic Systems, where the focus is on optimizing systems that are controlled by multiple decentralized agents. Such a situation arises in many organizations, as well as in engineering and economic systems, where different parts of the system are controlled by “domain experts”, each optimizing his/her own “local” operations, while the performance of the system as a whole depends on the collection of all these local decisions. It is well known, however, that the performance of the aggregate system may be inefficient relative to that of a single centralized decision maker if local agents are not coordinated.
