title: Ultrafast Coherent Comb Lasers Based on Integration of III-V Compound Semiconductor Quantum Dots and Si Photonics
abs: Coherent ultrafast comb lasers as light sources have many applications including: coherent light detection and ranging (LIDAR), compact optical atomic clocks, transceivers in data centres, optical coherence tomography, microwave photonics, and spectroscopy for gas sensing. The above-mentioned various applications have placed a demanding requirement of the optical frequency comb lasers’ performance, including low phase noise (i.e., low timing jitter), high repetition rate, high output power, wide wavelength coverage, narrow optical linewidth and most importantly, compactness, robustness, as well as low cost. Furthermore, the high-capacity optical transmission systems in data centres (like, Google, Amazon, Facebook, etc) are creating an increasing demand for low cost, low power consumption, high speed, highly reliable coherent optical lasers at original (O) bands between 1260 and 1360 nm. One of the further developments to effectively address above requirement is the use of semiconductor quantum dot (QD) material and its integration with Si photonics circuits. The integration of semiconductor QD lasers with Si-photonics has the following benefits, to name a few, and can offer a perfect solution for the increasing demand for data transmission with both high speed and high capacity: - Leveraging on the advantages of both QD lasers and Si technologies to realize the best comb lasers with (1) low threshold current, (2) narrow optical linewidth and RF linewidth, (3) temperature insensitivity (i.e., potential cooler free), (4) wide gain spectrum, (5) feedback insensitivity (i.e., isolator free), etc; - Taking advantage of Si infrastructure and process which offers low fabrication cost, high yield and compactness; - Providing the opportunity to converge communication and computing on one platform. Motivated by above scenarios, the proposal will combine the best of the two worlds, i.e., Si photonics and QD lasers to realize new III-V/Si integratable comb lasers as the low cost, compact, and high performance light sources for communication and sensing applications. This proposal involves intensive Simulation, Design, Fabrication and Characterization of III-V semiconductor QD lasers, Si photonic devices as well as III-V/Si integration. These are built on the group’s recent work on Si-photonics platform which has been used for demonstration of state-of-the-art III-V/Si tunable lasers, narrow linewidth quantum well (QW) lasers, narrow RF linewidth mode-locked QW lasers, etc. In addition, the group is well equipped with full process and test facilities for the fabrication and characterization of QD comb lasers.

title: Promoting anti-catalysis effect to stabilize interface in aqueous batteries
abs: Aqueous batteries are highly promising for both static energy storage and consumables because of their advantages of low-cost, high safety, and ease of recycling compared to the current lithium-ion batteries. However, the development of aqueous batteries has been largely restricted by the limited output voltage (and thus inadequate energy density) due to the risk of water decomposition reactions (i.e., water splitting). Under high voltages, water molecules will split to hydrogen and oxygen on the anode and cathode side of the battery, respectively. This will cause degradation of electrode materials and battery failure. Therefore, in order to effectively increase the voltage window of the aqueous battery, it is important to suppress the water splitting reactions by improving the potential barriers. And this is exactly opposite to what people are doing in water-splitting hydrogen generation technology, where researchers are trying to designing efficient catalysts to lower the overpotentials. The PI has rich experience in both electrocatalysis water splitting and aqueous batteries. In this proposed project, the team will tackle the problem from the fundamental side and intend to systematically investigate the anti-catalysis effect in aqueous Zn batteries with the aim of improving the voltage window up to 3.0 V or more. This will be achieved by tailoring the electronic structures of the electrode/electrolyte interface to increase the overpotentials for water splitting reactions. By theoretical modelling and experimental rational synthesis and surface atomic engineering, we aim to achieve the optimized electrode materials that can achieve an effective battery-catalysis harmony - suppressed water splitting reactions at high-voltage window on both electrodes. The success of this new project will not only provide deep understanding of the interface physiochemistry and push the competitiveness of the high-promise aqueous Zn-ion batteries, but also provide a generic solution to enhance the energy density performance of other aqueous batteries as well as aqueous supercapacitors. The scope of this project contains three major parts: (i) Theoretical screening to identify feasible approaches to promote anti-catalysis effect in well-established oxide electrode materials, which include anion/cation vacancies, atomic surface reconstruction, energy barriers by surface redox couples, degree of crystallinity. Different from traditional electrocatalyst materials for water splitting, in this project we will lower the catalytic effect for water splitting by increasing the overpotentials during the battery operation. (ii) Synthesis of the optimized materials and systematic electrochemical characterization. title: vdW technology for atomic-scale investigation of 2D magnets and devices
abs: The recent discovery of intrinsic magnetism in two-dimensional (2D) materials combined with van der Waals (vdW) technology offers vast opportunities for creating atomically-thin magnetic materials with unique spin textures for next-generation spintronic devices such as voltage switching, spin filtering and spin transistors. Among all the 2D magnetic materials discovered, the family of chromium trihalides, CrX3 (X = Cl, Br, or I), has garnered growing attention. Of particular interest is the layer-dependent magnetic ground state in atomically-thin CrI3. For example, monolayer CrI3 shows the ferromagnetism perpendicular to the 2D plane, while its bilayer exhibits interlayer antiferromagnetism. These magnetic materials are considered as key components for future quantum devices because they host numerous intriguing physical phenomena including giant tunnelling magnetoresistance in spin-filter magnetic tunnel junctions, the electrical control of 2D magnetism, and giant nonreciprocal optical second-harmonic generation. Despite rapid progress, many fundamental and technological issues remain unsolved. Further progress in this field hinges on atomic-scale understanding of structural, electronic and magnetic properties of 2D magnets, and gaining the ability to control magnetism at the nanoscale. Although local electronic properties and magnetism can be probed ideally by scanning tunneling microscopy/spectroscopy (STM/STS), a direct implication of this technique to investigate 2D magnetic insulators remains elusive due to the lack of a complete conducting path for electrical current and their extreme air sensitivity. Recently, engineering van der Waals heterostructures (vdWHs) promoted itself as a versatile tool to modify and study the electronic and magnetic structures of various 2D materials: insulators, semiconductors, metals, superconductors, ferromagnets. Here, we propose to apply vdW technology to the STM to study magnetic insulating materials and gaining the ability to control magnetic ordering at the nanoscale for future spintronics application. This proposal aims to achieve the following objectives. • We aim to develop a general strategy for the atomic-scale investigation of a family of 2D magnetic insulators using vdW technology combined with STM/STS. By exploiting graphene transparency to tunnelling electrons (supported by preliminary results), we aim to obtain atomic-scale characterization of the structural, electronic and magnetic properties of 2D magnet and their vdWHs based devices. The application of vdW technology to the STM will dramatically expand the capabilities of the latter, allowing it to study magnetic insulating materials and uncovering crucial issues such as stacking order and interlayer magnetic coupling in a device-oriented vdWHs. • We will develop new capability to control the correlation gap and interlayer magnetic coupling in magnetic vdWHs via a combination of in situ STM and gate-tunable devices. title: Understanding Therapeutic Resistance in Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors Beyond Genomics
abs: Background. Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors (GISTs) are a group of mesenchymal tumors defined by gain-of-function mutations in KIT (80%) or PDGFRA (10%). In advanced cases, most patients benefit from the tyrosine kinase inhibitor Imatinib, though acquired resistance associated with the development of secondary mutations usually occurs after 18 to 24 months. Despite the simple molecular landscape of GISTs, heterogeneity in clinical outcomes have been observed, including small but distinct groups of long term survivors on Imatinib therapy as well as exceptional responders to subsequent therapies despite acquired Imatinib-resistance. Hypothesis and specific aims. We hypothesize that apart from tumor genetic factors, distinct differences are present in the epigenetic landscape, tumor microenvironment and/or host immune responses in GISTs. These features may affect treatment response and development of acquired resistance, and impact on survival outcome. Therefore we aim to (1) define the epigenetic and immune landscape of GISTs in relation to treatment response and survival outcome, and (2) investigate circulating molecular profiles and host immune response of GISTs. Methodology and approach. This proposal involves a multi-omic sequencing approach in tissue and blood analytes. Somatic mutations in tissue and circulating tumor DNA will be identified using a custom Anchored Multiplex PCR-based targeted sequencing platform. The DNA methylome and promoter landscape will be profiled using cfMeDIP-seq and nano-ChIP-seq, respectively. Host immune responses will be profiled using RNA-sequencing, including single cell and spatial transcriptomic technologies. Information from Aims 1 and 2 will be integrated to identify tumor-relevant biomarkers for both tissue and liquid biopsy-based approaches to predict treatment and survival outcomes. Clinical and scientific significance. The integrative analysis across multi-omic platforms is anticipated to derive novel insights into GIST biology and therapy. This study will facilitate the discovery of novel biomarkers to aid longitudinal surveillance of GIST patients, while refining current methods on prognostication and treatment guidance.
kw: rare cancers; sarcoma; precision oncology

title: Elucidating the mechanisms by which TNF and RIPK1 promote GSDMD activation and inflammatory disease
abs: Receptor-interacting protein kinase 1 (RIPK1)-dependent cell death promotes host defence but is also emerging as an important driver for a myriad of tumour necrosis factor (TNF)-driven diseases. TNF signalling under conditions of transforming growth factor-β-activated kinase 1 (TAK1) inhibition, including microbial infection, aging, metabolic disorders, or pharmacological treatment triggers the formation of a death-inducing complex that requires RIPK1 kinase activity and the protease caspase-8. We recently demonstrated that RIPK1/caspase-8 cleaves the pore-forming protein, gasdermin D (GSDMD), to drive a lytic form of cell death known as pyroptosis to defend against bacterial infection. Since TNF and RIPK1 are implicated in a variety of human immunopathologies, we examined whether this novel pathway contributes to TNF-driven diseases and observed that Gsdmd-deficient animals are remarkably resistant to TNF challenge. While further characterising the cellular regulation of GSDMD cleavage, we made the surprising observation that loss of RIPK1 kinase activity has no impact on GSDMD cleavage, but totally abrogated pyroptosis, indicating that RIPK1 kinase activity sensitises cells to GSDMD-dependent cellular rupture. In this proposal, we will characterise and dissect the mechanisms by which RIPK1 kinase sensitise macrophages to pyroptosis, and the involvement of this novel pathway in driving TNF-mediated disease, such the metabolic disorder, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). The specific aims of this proposal are : (1) To establish the mechanisms by which VPS4A cleavage promotes pyroptosis and NAFLD; and (2) to identify novel RIPK1 substrates that sensitise macrophages to pyroptosis.
kw: inflammation, TNF, RIPK1, pyroptosis

title: Epigenetic targeting of EZH2-regulated IFN-STING signalling to overcome anti-HER2 resistance
abs: Human epidermal growth factor receptor (HER2)-positive breast cancer is an aggressive breast cancer subtype overexpressing HER2, comprising 15- 20% of all breast cancers. Anti-HER2 therapies plus chemotherapy-based neoadjuvant treatment (NAT) have significantly increased the pathological complete response rate (pCR) in HER2+ breast cancer. However, there is still considerable proportions of patients (up to 50%) who have residual disease after NAT, which is associated with subsequent disease recurrence and death. HER2-targeting antibodies not only antagonize the oncogenic HER2 signaling but also elicits antitumor immunity. Our preliminary work has found that histone methyl transferase EZH2-mediated epigenetics plays a role in modulating the interferon related immune response to anti-HER2 therapy through directly repressing the activity of IFI16-dependent STING pathway. Based on this finding, we have developed a robust epigenetic approach showing EZH2 inhibition, when further combined with HDAC inhibition, can give rise to a maximal IFN response and sensitizes anti-HER2 response. We thus hypothesize that an EZH2-based targeting strategy may provide a useful approach to increase anti-HER2 response and that the expression of IFI16-STING signaling can serve as biomarkers to predict and guide the treatment. To facilitate the translation of the pre-clinical findings, we seek to investigate the role of IFI16-dependent STING pathway in anti-HER2 therapy. We also seek to conduct clinical validation to evaluate the impact of our proposed epigenetic treatment in anti-HER2 therapy refractory patients.
kw: breast cancer, anti-HER2 therapy, epigenetic, interferon gene response, biomarkers, therapeutics

title: Investigating the role of isoprenylcysteine carboxylmethyltransferase (ICMT) in breast cancer metastasis mediated by TGFβ signaling
abs: Many advanced cancers, particularly those of breast origin, favour bone as the site for distal metastasis. Bone is often the first site of dissemination and disease relapse that results in significant morbidity and mortality. The specificity of this tissue tropism relies on cytokine modulation of tumour microenvironment (TME) - the result of complicated interactions between cancer cells and various stromal cells. TGFβ signalling has a major role in the cytokine modulation of cancer progression, including bone metastasis. The activation of canonical TGFβ signalling, through R-SMAD and SMAD4, regulates the transcription of many genes essential for cancer metastasis. Isoprenylcysteine carboxylmethyltransferase (ICMT) is an enzyme in the post-translational prenylation pathway whose substrates include multiple oncogenes. From our recent preliminary studies, we found that inhibiting ICMT reduced breast cancer cell colonization and invasive proliferation in the bone, and further metastasis to the lung. We also discovered that this role of ICMT is mediated through canonical TGFβ signalling in modulating the cytokine milieu. Based on the preliminary studies, this project will investigate: (1) the mechanism of ICMT regulation of TGFβ-SMAD activation; (2) the target genes and major events downstream of TGFβ-SMAD canonical signalling accountable for the regulation of breast cancer bone metastasis; (3) microenvironment changes in bone, both the cell and cytokine profiles, when ICMT is inhibited; and (4) the identity of the ICMT substrate(s) that mediate the regulation of TGFβ-SMAD signalling axis. Successful completion of these studies will significantly contribute to our understanding of ICMT regulation of TGFβ and its downstream signalling, and provide support for targeting ICMT in the treatment of metastatic solid tumours, particularly those with the propensity for bone metastasis.
kw: Bone metastasis; TGFβ signalling, Interleukin-11; Breast cancer; Isoprenylcysteine Carboxylmethyltransferase (ICMT); RAB4A

title: Personalized RNA-based Cancer Vaccine for AML Immunotherapy
abs: Cancer immunotherapy has become an exciting and promising field in the battle against cancer. However, there are still many limitations in the current strategies including the lack of cancer-specific targets in the Chimeric Antigen Receptor T (CART) cell therapy and the absence of immune infiltrates in some patients undergoing immune checkpoint antibody therapy. Cancer vaccine has gained attraction in recent years. Many algorithms have been developed to predict personalized neoantigens which have been proven to be therapeutically effective in cancer vaccines. We hypothesize that personalized RNA-based cancer vaccine, coupled with immune-checkpoint inhibitors delivered in the form of RNA, can be an effective treatment option for Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) patients. We will combine the approaches of computing algorithm prediction, T cell activation screening, linker sequence and adaptor protein design, murine leukemia model, and proof-of-concept validation with patient PBMCs in four specific aims. The results generated in this proposal will provide supporting evidence for patient-based study in the future and eventually pave the way in providing effective immunotherapy to cancer patients. The proposed study will solve two major challenges in developing cancer vaccines: inaccuracy in predicting tumor antigens and immune suppression by the tumor microenvironment. Our novel algorithm pipeline will increase prediction accuracy and include neoantigens from somatic mutations, iPAS, and retained introns. Using RNA-platform to combine immune epitopes and scFvs of the checkpoint blockade antibodies, we can overcome immune suppression to enhance the therapeutic efficacy of the vaccine. We select AML as a model disease for this vaccine development. However, the same strategy can be extended to other cancer types. The successful development of this novel cancer vaccine will benefit cancer patients by providing immunotherapy that can induce tumor-specific immune responses and result in improved clinical outcomes.
kw: immunotherapy; AML; RNA; vaccine

title: Understanding White Adipose Tissue (WAT) formation as a therapeutic target for obesity
abs: Obesity is associated with increased type 2 diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, hypertension, cancer, and cardiovascular disease along with increased susceptibility to and poor outcomes from infectious diseases, including COVID-19. Obesity is caused by excess White Adipose Tissue (WAT) with the accumulation of fat in internal organs, such as the liver, vessels, and muscle tissue. Expansion of WAT, or adipogenesis, involves increasing the size of existing adipocytes (hypertrophy) and adipocyte numbers (hyperplasia), with the precursor cells differentiating into mature adipocytes. Regulating these adipogenic processes represent critical therapeutic targets to controlling obesity. While many signalling pathways, regulating key transcription factors that determine WAT formation/loss have been identified, the influence of the cytoskeleton, nucleoskeleton, and extracellular matrix in regulating WAT formation is understudied. Understanding this nexus of control for WAT formation is vital because obesity is associated with alterations in the ECM and those changes correlate tightly with disease. Therefore, studying the role that the ECM-cyto-nucleoskeleton plays in adipogenesis provides a potential new set of therapeutic targets . This proposal will characterize an entirely novel pathway centred on how the nucleo-cytoskeleton regulates adipogenesis. Using a mouse model that we derived, that reproduces many of the aspects of FPLD2 (caused by mutations in LMNA), we have identified the gene Arhgap12 as a necessary regulator of adipogenesis. We aim to characterize and elucidate the molecular mechanisms by which Arhgap12 misregulation contributes to WAT loss and to identify the signaling pathways that Arhgap12 acts upon in adipogenic progression
kw: Obesity, lipodystrophy, adipogenesis

title: Generating decellularized pancreas scaffolds to support the culture and function of human pancreatic β cells
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Diabetes is a disease that affected approximately 463 million people worldwide in 2019, and is expected to affect 700 million people by 2045, according to the International Diabetes Federation. The most common types of diabetes are Type 1 (10%) and Type 2 (90%) diabetes (IDF). While most cases of Type 2 diabetes can be managed by lifestyle and diet modifications, to date, the only durable therapy to achieve stable euglycemia in Type I diabetes patients and severe cases of Type II diabetes is islet or pancreas transplantation. However, this is limited by donor shortages. As such, alternative strategies have to be developed to overcome this shortage of donor pancreases. The use of decellularized pancreata in combination with stem cells is a promising solution to this problem. During decellularization, cellular components are removed from the organ of interest while leaving the structure and ECM of the organ intact. The decellularized organ can then be recellularized with relevant cell types. Our hypothesis is that culturing human pancreatic β cells on these scaffolds or differentiating hiPSCs to β cells on these scaffolds may yield increased numbers of functional beta cells in vitro, compared to current β cell differentiation protocols, as decellularized organs retain native ECM components that are required for proper β cell differentiation and function. The aims of this study are to (1) determine the optimal protocol for decellularization of mouse pancreata, (2) to demonstrate that decellularized mouse pancreas scaffolds can support and maintain β-cell function, (3) to differentiate human iPSCs to β-cells on these scaffolds and to measure their functionality compared to iPSC-derived β-like cells generated in suspension culture. This study has clinical significance as it has the potential to develop more efficient β cell differentiation protocols, which may translate to more effective cell-based therapies for diabetes treatment.
kw: decellularization, pancreas scaffold, beta cells

title: DISSECTING AML WITH NOVEL SINGLE-CELL MUTATION ANALYSIS AND INTEGRATIVE MULTI-OMICS TECHNOLOGY
abs: An urgent challenge in current medical oncology is patient resistance to targeted drug treatment. The root cause of this is that many tumours have highly heterogenous genetic and cellular makeup. However, the lack of coverage of mutation sites is a limitation of current single-cell technologies, such as droplet and nanowell-based technologies, as they are biased to 3’ or 5’ ends of RNA transcripts. Tellingly, direct clinical impact of current single-cell genomic and transcriptomic analyses has thus far been limited in their translational applicability, due to the lack of ability to acquire robust, targeted genotype information at the single-cell and clonal level. In this study, we will be devising a new technology that can provide genotype information, including somatic mutations, indels and chromosomal translocations, at the single-cell level in a manner. The technology will be able to be integrated in a complementary multi-omics manner, thus enabling the multimodal detection of genotype, transcriptome abundance and surface protein markers for tens of thousands of single-cells simultaneously. We plan to apply this technique to the genetically complex AML disease model. Through identification of single cell genotype, such as SNV, indels and fusion gene, we aim to apply our technique to 1) identify rare subclonal changes in AML patients at diagnosis, treatment and relapse, 2) characterise profiles of leukemic stem cells for possible targeting therapeutics, 3) study use of our method for a sensitive minimal residual disease assay and 4) study the effects of malignant cells on the tumour micro environment for signs of T-cell exhaustion. We anticipate this technology will be of value to clinicians and researchers studying cancers that present with complex tumour heterogeneity.
kw: Multi-omics, Single-Cell, Heterogeneity, Leukemia, Genotype

title: Deciphering the metabolic roles and neoplastic potential of p53 in the liver
abs: Development of Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC), the most common type of liver cancer, is a complex process that often involves progression from chronic liver diseases. The p53 gene is one of the most frequently mutated genes in HCC. Apart from its canonical functions, emerging evidence suggests that p53 is also an important regulator of different metabolic pathways in a highly cell-type-dependant context. Nevertheless, its roles in key metabolic processes like glucose metabolism in the liver is still debatable, largely due to a lack of meticulous in vivo models. The current models involved p53 deletion in the whole liver, which failed to address the key question of contributions of p53 in distinct lobular zones of the liver, given that metabolic processes are stringently orchestrated in a highly zone-specific manner in the liver. My preliminary data showed that p53 deletion in pericentral Lgr5+ hepatocytes, in combination of chronic liver injury, led to liver tumour formation. These findings provide the first evidence that targeted deletion of p53 in a defined subset of hepatocytes in mice facilitate HCC development. I hypothesize that p53 deletion in hepatocytes within specific zones of the liver lobule have distinct impacts on the metabolic functions of the liver, and thus play an important role in dictating the outcomes of HCC development. I will test my hypothesis by using multiple novel mouse models generated in our laboratory that allow simultaneous induction of p53 deletion and cell-fate tracing in 3 different zones in the liver lobule. This project aims to address the molecular changes resulting from p53 deletion in different metabolic zones in the liver, which may lead to different outcomes in HCC development. The outcomes will refine current knowledge on the role of p53 in pathophysiological processes resulting in HCC, and aid in delivering precision medicine to patients with liver diseases.
kw: liver, p53, metabolic roles

title: Same but different: ELABELA and APELIN activate APLNR with divergent biological outcomes
abs: Understanding how blood vessels form and how this process can be modulated is crucial in advancing therapeutic success for common diseases involving pathologic neo-angiogenesis such as cancer and age-related macular degeneration. Although anti-VEGF therapy has been very effective to date, existing anti-angiogenic drugs do not work for a large proportion of patients, indicating the need for alternative targets. APELIN and its receptor APLNR have received widespread attention in the last 20 years following its discovery due to its potent role in promoting angiogenesis. But to date, the APELIN-APLNR axis has not been successfully targeted clinically. In 2013, we discovered another ligand for APLNR, called ELABELA (ELA). These two agonists of APLNR have overlapping yet non-redundant roles which are to date still very poorly understood, preventing the effective translation of either ligand-receptor axis into clinical use. The prevailing notion is that ELA and APELIN constitute a spatiotemporal double ligand system to control APLNR signalling with similar outcomes. However, we found that ELA and APELIN differ in their biological effects, beyond a simple difference in spatiotemporal expression. Using mouse retinal angiogenesis as a model, where both ligands and APLNR are concurrently expressed, we found that APELIN is required for establishing the primary vascular plexus, whereas ELA is required for establishing a stable vessel network. APLNR also has ligand-independent stretch-dependent function, and in the retina, we observed that APLNR is required initially for angiogenesis but subsequently switches to enforce endothelial quiescence. These intricacies surrounding the ELA-APELIN-APLNR axis must be resolved in order to effectively exploit the Apelinergic system as a therapeutic target. Here, we aim to 1) decipher the molecular basis of the differences elicited by ELA and APELIN through APLNR; 2) understand how APLNR enforces endothelial quiescence and 3) whether ELA-APELIN-APLNR can be effectively targeted to improve ocular neoangiogenic disorders.
kw: Apelinergic system; Elabela; Apelin; Angiogenesis; Vascular development

title: Rewiring core regulatory networks in acute myeloid leukemia to rescue normal hematopoiesis
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) is a hematopoietic malignancy characterized by the failure in terminal myeloid differentiation, therefore the accumulation of abnormal myeloid progenitor cells. This process is heterogeneous by the virtue of a high variety of alterations in transcription factors regulatory networks. Efforts have been taken in the development of therapies targeting the elimination of abnormal cells or overcoming of differentiation barriers, whereas these therapies are limited to a minority of AMLs due to the lack of understanding of the heterogeneity in the AML hematopoiesis. Here, we propose an integrative analysis utilizing multiple single-cell techniques to determine the contribution of different regulators in establishing the AML transcriptional networks. Three specific aims are as follows. AIM 1. Reconstruction of TF Regulome in the Expansion and Differentiation of Normal and AML Hematopoietic Stem Cells (HSCs) AIM 2. Delineation of the role of key AML regulators attributing to the HSCs expansion, preleukemic HSCs (pHSCs) characteristics and AML Development AIM 3. Elucidation of the RNA epigenomic landscape of TF downstream networks Single-cell RNA sequencing provides unbiased transcriptome and RNA epigenetic profiles of individual cells that could infer cellular heterogeneity and developmental trajectories. Thus, we have considered an integrative approach incorporating transcriptomics, lineage tracing, clonal dynamics, and RNA epigenetics in a single-cell resolution, enabling an improved comprehension in the comparative study of hematopoiesis in the normal and AML condition. This would be able to provide a comprehensive resource on the transcriptional networks in the early hematopoiesis regulating the HSC expansion and AML development, highlighting the new directions to future therapeutic approaches. Also, instead of only focusing on an immediate alleviation of AML through overcoming the differentiation, our approaches would allow sustainability in therapies, conceptually the selective support of the normal HSCs expansion in AML, and to bring economic advantages in the long run.
kw: Acute myeloid leukemia; Epigenetics; Cell fate control; Transcription factor; Single-cell RNA sequencing; m6A RNA modification

title: Assessing the impact of adiposity, low muscle mass and metabolic health on bone health in reproductive age Chinese women
inst: IHDP - Institute for Human Development and Potential
abs: The recent recognition that the risk of fracture is increased in individuals with obesity and type 2 diabetes challenges the traditional view of positive association between obesity and bone mineral density (BMD). Compared to men, women have lower BMD and higher rate of fractures. Current research in bone health focuses on bone loss later in life and the focus on bone health in younger age is almost neglected. The main aim of the proposal is to gain knowledge about the complex relationship between fat mass, lean mass and metabolic health in relation to bone health in women of reproductive age. It will also further assess the possible link with intestinal health by studying its association with gut microbiota. A total of 210 Chinese women, 25 to 40 years old will be recruited. Chinese ethnicity has the highest incidence of osteoporotic fractures and a higher proportion of low lean mass compared to Malay and Indian women. Women will undergo dual energy x-ray absorptiometry scans of femoral neck, lumbar spine and whole body to measure BMD and body composition. Questionnaires on lifestyle will be administered and biosamples (stool) will be collected for analysis of the microbiome composition. The study will test the relationship between adiposity, lean mass, metabolic profiles and BMD simultaneously taking into account modifiable risk factors and the role of gut microbiota. This area of research on bone health in younger women is highly relevant in Singapore as it is one of the countries with increasing incidence of type 2 diabetes and osteoporotic fractures. Better understanding the factors contributing the bone health in younger women will enable to identify women with higher risk of osteoporosis and design intervention studies earlier in the life course. This research will serve as the first step towards translational research in bone health.
kw: Adiposity; Muscle mass; Bone health; Metabolic profile; Reproductive age women

title: DEFINING BIOFILM MECHANISMS OF INNATE IMMUNITY MODULATION IN INFECTIVE ENDOCARDITIS
abs: Infective endocarditis (IE) is a life-threatening biofilm infection of the heart valves. Bacteria form vegetations on the valve leaflets, a mass of bacterial biofilm, fibrin, platelets, and inflammatory cells. Despite bacteria enclosure in this seemingly antimicrobial environment, the immune system cannot clear the infection. Our preliminary in vivo data show that E. faecalis, one of the most common causative agents, forms well-established biofilms, which are often devoid of neutrophil infiltration. Our central hypothesis is that biofilm modulates the key innate immune responses of neutrophil phagocytosis and NETosis. We aim to (i) define the role of complement opsonization, phagocytosis, and NETosis in IE and identify the trigger that shifts the neutrophil response towards NETosis, and (ii) identify bacterial factors that modulate innate immunity and give rise to biofilm heterogeneity in IE. To that end, we will employ a rat model of IE and a 3D cell culture model that mimics the vegetation microenvironment to delineate the interplay between the key innate immune responses of opsonization, phagocytosis, and NETosis, and understand how the neutrophil response in IE is regulated. We will also apply spatially resolved transcriptomics on vegetations by combining laser-assisted capture microdissection and RNAseq to identify bacterial factors involved in immune evasion and modulation. We have already established the in vivo model, workflows for flow cytometry, tissue immunofluorescence, western blot, as well as a workflow for RNAseq analysis. Relevant ethics approvals are already in place. We anticipate that this study will provide insight into the fundamental mechanisms of the largely overlooked IE pathogenesis and identify potential therapeutic targets in bacteria and the host.
kw: infective endocarditis; biofilm; infection; cardiovascular; innate immunity

title: Functional transcriptomics of viral protein-host RNA interactions
abs: The COVID-19 pandemic was caused by a positive sense RNA virus SARS-CoV-2. Recently, we discovered ~5,000 host RNAs interacting with SARS-CoV-2 proteins, representing an underexplored dimension of viral-host interaction. Some of these interactions enhanced the translation of pro-viral genes, which are then identified as potential druggable targets. Virus infection induces alternative splicing to promote viral replication. However, little is known about the underlying mechanism. While single-cell RNA-seq analyses of airway epithelial cells are informative of infection dynamics, our knowledge of host translatomics across different cell types or at the single-cell level is limited. I hypothesize that changes in host translation and splicing are directly caused by viral protein–host RNA interactions in a cell type dependent manner. In Aim 1, I will investigate virus-induced changes in host translation at single-cell resolution in human lung organoids. A ribosomal protein-RNA base editor technology will be used to identify actively translating transcripts in SARS-CoV-2 infected cells. RNA base editors will also be fused to viral proteins of other RNA viruses to rapidly profile viral protein–host RNA interactions to derive broad viral-host interaction principles. In Aim 2, I will investigate splicing perturbation caused by direct interaction of viral proteins with host RNAs. I will also develop a single-molecule RNA-editor based sequencing approach to determine the relationship between alternative splicing and RNA-protein interaction. Despite global drug repurposing efforts, effective antiviral drugs to treat COVID-19 remain elusive. In Aim 3, I will develop minimally invasive and highly versatile RNA therapeutics such as antisense oligonucleotides to disrupt viral protein-host RNA interactions. Further, I aim to generate RNA aptamers that target viral proteins using an automated SELEX platform. This proposal aims to shed light on the functional implications of viral protein–host RNA interactions, and generate new modalities of antiviral therapeutics to help safeguard against future pandemics.
kw: Viral host interactions; SARS-CoV-2; COVID-19; Single-cell transcriptomics

title: Developing a robust cardiometabolic wearable device for continuous non-invasive Blood Pressure and Blood Glucose monitoring: Beyond single time-point measurements to time-in-range
abs: The goal is to develop a robust cardiometabolic monitoring Artificial Intelligence(AI) system for continuous and non-occluding Blood Pressure(BP) prediction and Blood Glucose Level(BGL) estimation, using Photoplethysmogram(PPG) signals in ambulatory individuals via a wristwatch wearable device. Photoplethysmogram is obtained using a light source and a detector, to identify blood volume changes in the microvascular bed of tissue, the same concept used by the pulse oximeter. The PPG signal reflects the blood movement in the blood vessel through a wave-like diagram, for which features can be extracted to predict blood pressure and blood glucose levels. Hypothesis Continuous bio-signal monitoring is as valid as current standards for BP monitoring and Continuous Glucose Monitors. Specific Aims 1. Deploy our novel 2PPG sensor wearable to obtain robust high-fidelity motion-resistant continuous multi-channel PPG signals from ambulatory individuals, even during activity and exercise. 2. Validate the 2PPG derived BP measurements in a pivotal pilot study involving ambulatory individuals in compliance with clinical grade standards (in accordance with US Association for the Advancement of Medical Instrumentation (AAMI), the British Hypertension Society, the European Society of Hypertension (ESH) Working Group on BP Monitoring, and the International Organization for Standardization (ISO). 3. Correlate the PPG signals with continuous BGL measurements with our Convoluted Neural Network (CNN) AI development, and enable PPG-based BGL readouts. Methods: Patients will be consented for the following activities, while wearing our device 1. Blood pressure readings at rest for 3 minutes, with sphygmomanometer readings every minute 2. Treadmill exercise test with automated occlusive BP readings every 2 minutes 3. 24 hour ambulatory blood pressure readings 4. Continuous blood glucose monitor for 14 days Clinical Importance The concept of time-in-range is gaining popularity for management of chronic conditions, such as diabetes. This wearable has potential to assess this concept in the management of hypertension and facilitate delivery of telemedicine.
kw: Wearable device; Time-in-Range; Plethysmography; Continuous monitoring; Hypertension; Diabetes Mellitus

title: Discovering novel molecular targets for immunotherapy of hepatocellular carcinoma using functional in vivo CRISPR screening in tumour-specific CD8 T cells
abs: The overall aim of this project is to discover and characterise novel inhibitory molecules in T cells with anti-tumour activity against hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) for evaluation as potential targets for immunotherapy. Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the most common form of liver cancer, accounting for more than 800,000 deaths per year worldwide. In Singapore, HCC is the fourth most common cancer in men with an age-standardised incidence rate of 17.7 per 100,000 males. Cancer immunotherapy with immune checkpoint blockade therapies (ICBs) using monoclonal antibodies to block the inhibition of anti-tumour T cells has shown clinical success as treatments for many solid tumours. While ICBs have recently achieved major clinical breakthroughs in treating advanced HCC (aHCC), about two-thirds of aHCC patients still do not respond to any combination of ICBs or ICBs + targeted molecular therapies. Furthermore, the molecular pathways targeted by approved drugs for aHCC are largely limited to the PD-1, CTLA-4, and VEGFA signalling pathways, highlighting a pressing need for novel target discovery to drive the development of new therapeutics and synergistic combinations for aHCC to treat non-responding patients. We hypothesise that anti-tumour T cell responses in HCC are impaired by additional molecular pathways and factors beyond the PD-1 and CTLA-4 inhibitory pathways (targeted by ICBs) and beyond VEGF-driven pathways (targeted by molecular therapies). We therefore propose to discover potential targets for immunotherapy and characterise their mechanisms of action through the following specific aims: (Aim 1) Identify candidate inhibitory molecules on HCC tumour-specific T cells via high-throughput focused CRISPR screening in a purpose-built mouse model of HCC. (Aim 2) Validate selected candidates in vivo under conditions where disrupting PD-1 signalling alone is insufficient to treat HCC tumours in our mouse model. (Aim 3) Characterise the cellular and molecular effects of validated hits in vivo using genetic and pharmacological approaches.
kw: Hepatocellular carcinoma; T cells; Immunotherapy; CRISPR screening; Target discovery

title: The function and mechanism of non-coding RNAs in the aging of adipose tissue
abs: The advance in biomedicine technology has significantly extended the human lifespan, but the escalating growth of the aged population is posing a serious challenge to our modern societies. A major driving cause for the aging-related metabolic decline is the aging-related adipose tissue dysfunction, so investigating the mechanism underlying adipose aging is needed for our full understanding of aging. Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) are emerging as novel regulators in a variety of adipocyte biology. However, the role of lncRNAs in adipose tissue aging remains unknown. To address this knowledge gap, we conducted comprehensive RNA sequencing analyses in adipose tissues across the mouse lifespan. We identified an aging-regulated lncRNA (AR-lncRNAs), lncPrdm16os, which is enriched in brown/beige fat and downregulated during aging. We have generated a mutant animal model to abolish the transcription of lncPrdm16os and found that the mutant mice have manifested several aging hallmarks even at their young age. In contrast, transgenic overexpression of lncPRDM16os in adipose tissue ameliorates the aging-associated metabolic decline. Based on our preliminary observations, we hypothesize that lncPrdm16os is a critical regulator during adipose tissue aging. We propose to comprehensively characterize the influence of lncPrdm16os deficiency and overexpression on adipose tissue and on systemic aging health using our mouse models (Aim 1) and dissect the underlying molecular mechanism employed by lncPrdm16os using RNA molecular approaches (Aim 2). The success of our proposed project will advance our knowledge about the mechanism underlying aging and pave a new path to the ultimate development of RNA-based therapies for aging and its related metabolic diseases.
kw: adipocyte; obesity; adipose; non-coding RNA; aging; RNA

title: Investigating the Role of Polarisome Complex in Filamentous Growth of Pathogenic Fungi
abs: The macromolecular assembly of a protein complex called the polarisome, locating at the hyphal tip, is essential for polarized actin polymerization to support the hyphal growth of filamentous fungi. The polarisome complex comprises five central members: Spa2, Bni1, Bud6, and Aip5, all of which contain long intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) and structured (folded) domains that directly nucleation actin polymerization. Our recent works have addressed the functional characterization of individual polarisome members in budding yeast and pathogenic Candida albicans, with a particular focus on the molecular structure of their folded domains1-6. The scaffolder Spa2 recruits Bud6 and Aip5 that interact simultaneously with Bni1 to form an actin nucleation complex core that promotes Bni1-mediated actin nucleation. These findings establish the foundation for the current proposal to study the polarisome complex of different pathogenic fungi and clinical isolates. Polarisome complex proteins are only conserved in the fungi kingdom without human homologs, making them excellent targets for potential therapeutical treatment (Clinical Significance). The recent outbreak of filamentous fungal infection during COVID-19 pandemics raised vital needs for effective antifungal solutions and knowledge of invasive fungal behaviors. However, how polarisome members regulate protein complex assembly and function in different pathogenic filamentous fungi remains elusive (Knowledge Gap). On the basis of our recent findings, we propose a first hypothesis, namely that polarisome assembly (Spa2, Bni1, Bud6, and Aip5) at the hyphae tip and regulate filamentous growth of different invasive fungi through polymerizing actin cytoskeleton. Our second hypothesis is that the inhibition of C-terminal folded domains of Spa2 and Aip5 of invasive filamentous fungi, which regulate polarisome complex formation and activities, will block actin polymerization and thereby hyphal production for invasion. We aim to integrate interdisciplinary works to study the mechanisms of most life-threatening fungi’s polarisome and identify effective strategies to inhibit pathogenic hyphae growth.
kw: Filamentous fungi; hyphal growth; actin polymerization; polarisome complex; macromolecular assembly; intrinsically disordered region

title: Exercise-induced Stress Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance for Evaluation of Chest Pain (EXCEL)
abs: Aims: CMR has evolved as a highly accurate and cost-effective non-invasive diagnostic and prognostic test to guide coronary revascularization in stable CAD patients. We are the first research group that developed the in-scanner ExCMR protocol and showed that multiparametric “4-in-1” approach (viability, perfusion defects, regional wall motion abnormalities and exercise capacity) was accurate in diagnosing significant CAD, compared with gold-standard invasive FFR (EMPIRE Trial). We hypothesise that: 1. The multiparametric ExCMR prediction model can accurately diagnose CAD. We will validate this approach in a validation cohort of suspected CAD (EMPIRE-2). 2. The combined assessment of both global and regional ExCMR measures can differentiate between coronary microvascular disease (CMD) and obstructive CAD. We explore the role of ExCMR in CMD. 3. Exercise triggers an interplay between metabolic demand, neurohormonal changes, coronary haemodynamics and vasodilator response that can unveil subclinical functional changes. We examine how ExCMR can monitor changes in asymptomatic cardiometabolic disease patients before progression to heart failure or microvascular angina. Methods: Aim 1 is an extension of EMPIRE trial (NMRC OF-YIRG funded). CAD prediction model will be derived from 120 patients in Derivation cohort and tested in another 120 patients in Validation cohort. In aim 2, we explore if the combined assessment of ExCMR global measures (fibrosis, quantitative perfusion, exercise responses) and regional abnormalities can differentiate patients with CMD from obstructive CAD in a subgroup EMPIRE-2 cohort. 30 patients will be recruited into each group: 1. obstructive CAD (FFR-positive), 2. CMD (IMR-positive) and 3. controls (FFR-normal, IMR-normal). In aim 3, we will study the interrelationship between fibrosis, exercise capacity, inflammatory and fibrosis markers in 130 asymptomatic patients with cardiometabolic disease recruited to biobank registry (REMODEL cohort). Expected result: To demonstrate the role of ExCMR as a powerful non-invasive tool for risk stratification of patients with chest pain.
kw: exercise stress, non-invasive imaging, chest pain, coronary artery disease, microvascular disease

title: Systematic isolation of bacteriophages from the gut microbiome: revealing and mining the global phageome.
abs: Here we propose a collaboration between NUS, MIT and Singapore-MIT Alliance for Research and Technology (SMART) to mine human fecal matter samples and isolate phages targeting selected gut bacterial species. In three aims, we propose to develop a high-throughput method to isolate phages targeting selected anaerobic (aim 1) and anaerobic (aim 2) bacterial species, and to deploy that technology on the Global Microbiome Conservancy biobank (aim 3) to reveal the global phageome. This proposal builds on our combined expertise in gut microbiome and phage biology, and leverages the tools we developed for bacteria/phage isolation, characterization and screening. Eric Alm’s group at MIT is an establish leader in the field of gut microbiome biology and is the co-founder of the Global Microbiome Conservancy, a non-profit organization that has collected over 4,000 bacterial strains from individuals living in under-represented populations. Benoit Malleret’s group in SIgN has collected stool samples from over fifty healthy individuals in Singapore and has developed phage analytical tools in collaboration with Wilfried Moreira. Wilfried Moreira has developed a phage screening and engineering platform that banked over 300 phages with antibacterial activity against over 10 pathogens including multi-drug resistant bacteria from the WHO priority list of critically important pathogens. This collaborative project will support the development of the next generation of phage-based products ranging from microbiome-tailoring tools to antibacterial therapeutic targeting antibiotic-resistant bacteria.
kw: Gut Microbiome; Bacteriophages; Repository

title: Evaluating the GAR/RGG alarmin motif in autoimmunity and cancer vaccine development
abs: Autoimmunity is the mistargeting of the immune system to self-antigens. Tumor cells evade such immune attacks to develop cancers. Autoimmunity could be retargeted to tumor cells as effective cancer immunotherapy. Prostate acid phosphatase (PAP) is an autoantigen which was translated into the first FDA-approved therapeutic prostate vaccine. In systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) patients, the nucleus and especially the nucleolus is targeted by autoantibodies. In mice, syngeneic necrotic cells induced antinuclear autoantibodies suggesting that the nucleus contains endogenous adjuvants for its autoimmunogenicity. We indeed discovered that a major nucleolar autoantigen, nucleolin (NCL), is also a strong adjuvant molecule. The adjuvant activity was mapped to a poorly antigenic GAR/RGG motif which activates TLR2/TLR4. In this project, we will examine whether injection of NCL into mice is sufficient to induce autoantibodies and accelerates SLE disease (Aim 1). A synthetic 36-AA GAR/RGG peptide (NCL-P2) replicates the NCL adjuvant activity. Unexpectedly, this peptide also possessed cell-penetrating peptide (CPP) activity. Both activities were improved in a NCL-P2 mutant P2M6, which can carry cargo protein into dendritic cells (DC) and activates DC maturation. This led to our fusing P2M6 to real and surrogate cancer antigens to determine whether P2M6 makes them potent vaccines (Aim 2 and 3).
kw: Nucleolin, GAR/RGG motif, autoimmunity, cell-penetrating peptide, adjuvant, cancer vaccine

title: Elucidation of the mechanism of action of the global stress regulator, DINOR, in the super fungus Candida auris
abs: The global emergence of multidrug-resistant fungal pathogens poses severe public health threats. Candida auris is an emergent fungal pathogen, which has been reported in over 40 countries across six continents since its first isolation in 2009. This pathogen is inherently resistant to the azole class of antifungal agents and can deftly evolve resistance to other drugs as well. Clinical isolates resistant to all three classes of antifungals approved for treating invasive fungal diseases have emerged, causing infections with high mortality. C. auris can also withstand hostile environmental conditions such as high temperature, high osmotic pressure, and disinfectants, rendering it a hardy bug to eradicate in hospitals and healthcare facilities and causing person-to-person transmission. However, as a new pathogen, little is known about how C. auris governs drug resistance and stress response. We recently discovered a long noncoding RNA (lncRNA) in C. auris, named DINOR, whose inactivation causes DNA damage and increased susceptibility to antifungals, reactive oxygen species (ROS), macrophages, and membrane stress, and reduced virulence, suggesting that DINOR is a global stress regulator that orchestrates cellular response to diverse stresses. Consistently, DINOR is upregulated upon exposure to the above stresses. DINOR genetically interacts with TOR signaling, an evolutionarily conserved pathway governing stress response in eukaryotes. Currently, how DINOR exerts its function and interacts with other signaling pathways remains unclear. Here, we propose to (1) identify DINOR’s direct interacting partners and investigate their biological significance; (2) identify the transcription factors that control DINOR expression in response to various stresses; (3) elucidate how DINOR communicates with other signaling pathways during the stress response; and (4) evaluate the impact of disrupting DINOR-controlled processes on C. auris virulence. This study will elucidate new drug resistance and stress response mechanisms in fungal pathogens and open up opportunities to identify specific targets for developing effective therapeutics.
kw: Fungal pathogens; multi-drug resistance; stress response; antifungal drug targets; management of fungal infections

title: Supercharging Mitochondria : Promoting Respirasome Formation with Small Peptides
abs: The Electron Transport Chain (ETC) is a series of 4 enzymatic complexes I-IV in the inner mitochondrial membrane that generates cellular energy. ETC complexes can associate to form higher-order supramolecular structures called respirasomes, which enhance bioenergetic efficiency and protect cells against oxidative damange. Common degenerative conditions such as cardiovascular, metabolic and neurodegenerative diseases are frequently accompanied by mitochondrial dysfunction and reduced respirasome formation. Promoting respirasome formation is therefore an attractive albeit unexplored way to boost mitochondrial health. However, our understanding of how respirasomes form and work is still rudimentary, due to the lack of tools to study and manipulate them in vivo. This project aims to overcome this impasse by discovering and characterizing new proteins that promote respirasome assembly. Previous efforts have relied on the serendipitous discovery of 2-3 supercomplex assembly factors discovered over a decade that remain poorly understood. Here, we propose a systematic plan integrating bioinformatics, proteomics and genome-wide Crispr screening to find and characterize hitherto unknown respirasome regulators. We will search specifically for these regulators amongst a mini-proteome consisting of peptides encoded by small open reading frames (sORF-coded peptides or SEPs), which we have previously demonstrated to be a repository of ETC regulators. We will first develop and implement a “sORFome-wide” crispr screen to find mito-SEPs that are respirasome regulators (mito-R-SEPs). Hits arising from this screen will then be subjected to functionalization and therapeutic investigation. We present, as proof-of-concept, 3 validated examples of mito-R-SEPs from our preliminary candidate approach-based screen. We will decipher the molecular mechanism and physiological significance of these mito-R-SEPs, and target them in mouse models of cardiovascular disease to improve disease outcomes. If successful, our work will provide major advances in the field of metabolism, and we will be first in the world to promote respirasomes using small peptides to boost mitochondrial function.
kw: Cardiovascular; Mitochondria; Metabolic; Aging; Electron Transport Chain; Micropeptides

title: Understanding telomere-induced chromothripsis by locus-specific proximity labeling quantitative mass spectrometry analysis
abs: Telomeres are nucleoprotein structures at the end of linear chromosomes. Telomeres solve two fundamental challenges of linear genomes: (1) They serve as a cushion to prevent loss of genetic information due to incomplete replication of linear DNA and (2) they prevent chromosome ends from being recognized by the DNA repair machinery. Both aspects are of fundamental importance to carcinogenesis and progression of tumor growth. The incomplete replication of DNA ultimately leads to cellular senescence when one or a few telomeres reach a critically short length. Each cancer cell would ultimately share this fate. However, they rely on two mechanisms to defy telomere shortening: 85% of all tumors reactivate the expression of telomerase, while the other 15 % use a recombination-based mechanism, termed Alternative Lengthening of Telomeres (ALT). In addition, the ‘end protection problem’ essentially leads to telomere-telomere fusions if telomeres are not efficiently hidden from the DNA repair machinery. While usually the shelterin complex mediates telomeric protection, the result of telomeric deprotection is chromosomal fusions and subsequently breakage-fusion-bridge cycles that drive telomere-induced genome instability. More recently, it has been demonstrated that the resolution of such dicentric chromosomes can lead to chromothripsis, a mutational phenomenon leading to thousands of clustered chromosomal rearrangements. Indeed, signatures of chromothripsis can be found in about half of all cancers frequently involving telomeres, suggesting telomere-driven genomic instability as a recurrent feature of carcinogenesis. We recently described novel telomere-binding proteins and discovered that the overexpression of one such factor can lead to persistent chromatin bridges reminiscent of events leading to chromothripsis upon expression of a dominant-negative version of the shelterin member TRF2. Here, we aim to characterize these fusions by dCas9-based locus-specific proximity ligation. Our research will provide mechanistic insights into telomere-driven genomic instability with important implications for human health and disease.
kw: Telomeres, Cancer, Chromothripsis, quantitative mass spectrometry, proximity labeling

title: Spatial memory in the primate hippocampus
abs: The hippocampal formation has been shown to be critical for long-term episodic and spatial memory in humans, and pathologies of the hippocampus are immensely costly to well-being and public health. Current treatments have been limited due to a poor understanding of the functional circuitry. A promising treatment, inspired by findings in rodents, is the use of neuroprostheses that grossly modulate field potentials in the region, but the results have been inconsistent. Additionally, data is accumulating that the primate and rodent hippocampus differ in cellular and network properties. Place, head direction, and border cells that represent occupied location, heading, and environmental boundaries, respectively, in rodents, have not been replicated in recordings in humans, with place cells found in smaller percentages, and neither head direction nor border cells have been observed. Conversely, the human hippocampus appears to contain cells sensitive to the location of gaze. Theta-frequency (5 to 10 Hz) oscillations in the local field potential, a constant feature of movement in rodents, also appear to be much more transient. Some of these differences may be due to the human recordings being performed on bed-bound epilepsy patients using virtual reality, with restricted vestibular and proprioceptive information. They may also be because visual acuity and the tendency to explore the environment visually is greater in humans. For these reasons, the non-human primate offers an ideal platform, as they, like humans, rely heavily on vision to explore and remember the environment. In this proposal, we aim to compare neural activity from the NHP hippocampal formation as the animals navigate both virtual and real-world environments, while concurrently monitoring eye movements to understand the use of vision. These insights will allow us to formulate better hypotheses for validation in human experiments, and help to improve the effectiveness of neuroprostheses in the short and long term.

title: Rational Design and Effectiveness of Cell-selective Antimicrobial Peptides (ROADMAP) for Fungal Keratitis
abs: The widespread evolution of antimicrobial resistance exhausts all available therapeutic options. A recent review in the prestigious Lancet Infection Diseases (2020;20:e216-e230) attested the need for focused peptide-based drug design and development strategies in combating the antimicrobial resistance. Fungal keratitis is a severe infection in which the pathogenic fungi invades corneal surface and then progress to ulceration and opacification of the cornea. The increased expression of matrix metallo proteases in response to hyphal invasion result in substantial degradation of the extracellular matrix as well. The available antifungal regimes fail in significant number of patients, leading to one and sometimes repeated corneal transplants. Furthermore, effective management of fungal keratitis is hampered by the limited number of antifungals available, their narrow spectrum of activity, poor tissue penetration, toxic side effects, fungistatic (rather than fungicidal) nature and increased emergence of drug resistance. The central goals of this proposal are to address the antifungal void through the development of proteolytic-resistant branched peptides. We hypothesize that assembling multiple copies of short e-lysine residues on branched lysine scaffolds would further enhance the stability of peptides hence their bioavailability in ocular tissues. The overall objectives of this proposal are to design short antimicrobial peptides, based on the structure of ePL and investigate their antimicrobial activity, mechanism of action and preclinical evaluation of their safety and efficacy in established animal models in two specific aims. Aim I will investigate in vitro and in vivo safety and effectiveness of the designed peptides while Aim II probes the mechanism of action. The combined use of ocular bioimaging, high resolution proteomics tools and clinical assessment by experienced
