title: Spatial Multi-Omics and Functional Characterisation of Fibroblast Interactions in the Colorectal Cancer Tumour Microenvironment
abs: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the most common cancer in Singapore, and the third most common cancer in the world. CRC can be classified into 4 major transcriptomic subtypes. Of these, the fibroblast-rich CMS4 sub-type is associated with the highest risk of metastases and mortality. Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are a heterogeneous population of cells within the tumour microenvironment (TME) that have been hypothesized to interact with both tumour and other stromal cells to modulate tumour growth and metastases. They are also emerging targets for anti-cancer therapies. Previous work has identified 2 major cell-states of CAFs within the TME via single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq). However, how CAFs interact with other cells to modulate cancer has not yet been fully characterised as scRNA-seq does not collect spatial information regarding the physical localization of CAFs within the TME. State-of-the-art spatial multi-omics technologies such as multiplexed ion beam imaging by time of flight (MIBI-TOF), the 10X Genomics Visium Spatial Gene Expression technology, and multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridisation (MERFISH) enable the study of cell-type localization and cell-cell interactions via spatially-resolved measurements of genes or proteins. Hence, to fully characterise CAF interactions in the TME, we propose to perform each of these spatial multi-omics technologies to survey the spatial distribution of CAFs and to study the association of their localization properties with molecular and clinical phenotypes. Then, by integrating our spatially-resolved maps of the CRC TME with existing scRNA-seq, we propose to recover signaling interactions previously identified in literature, as well as infer novel signaling interactions. Finally, we propose to functionally validate these interactions through in vitro experiments. We expect that comprehensive spatial characterization of the CRC TME will enable discovery of targetable interactions between CAFs and CRC cells, and hence lay the foundation for a new class of fibroblast-directed anti-cancer therapies.
kw: colorectal cancer; cancer associated fibroblasts; spatial omics; MIBI; Visium; MERFISH

title: Type 2 diabetes-associated HNF4A and HNF1A gene variants contribute to diabetes progression by affecting pancreatic beta cell development and function
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Diabetes is a major health problem affecting millions of adults, costing billions of healthcare expenditure, and the ultimate root problem for diabetes lies in the poor health of insulin-secreting pancreatic beta cells. Thus far, while genetics is known to contribute extensively to the development of type 2 diabetes (T2D), the implications of many diabetes gene variants associated with pancreatic beta cell biology remain unclear. Here, we focus on two genes, HNF4A and HNF1A, known to give rise to monogenic diabetes characterized by defective insulin secretion function, and that T2D-associated coding gene variants are reproducibly found on these two genes. Gene targets of HNF4A and HNF1A in pancreatic beta cells, and how these coding variants affect insulin secretion remain unclear. We aim to perform ChIP-Seq analyses to identify HNF4A and HNF1A gene targets, and evaluate how T2D variants in HNF4A and HNF1A affect these beta cell genes that contribute to insulin secretion function. These newly-identified HNF4A and HNF1A target genes will also be genetically perturbed to ascertain their contribution to pancreatic beta cell development or function. Overall, the identification of these new targets and pathways will lead to actionable therapeutic outcomes to improve pancreatic beta cell health in T2D. This is highly important given that pancreatic beta cell dysfunction is a key feature of T2D in Asians, especially in Singaporeans.
kw: diabetes; HNF4A; HNF1A; gene variants; pancreas; beta cell

title: Investigating the roles of p52:ETS1, a new member of NFκB family of transcription factors
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Dysregulated NFκB signaling is a hallmark of many types of human ailments including cancers. Despite its apparent promise, targeting NFκB pathway in the clinic has been unsuccessful till now. Five DNA binding subunits of the NFκB family, homo and hetero dimerize amongst themselves to activate a number of physiologically relevant genes. However, whether these NFκB subunits can functionally interact with transcription factors from other families, especially in some contexts such as cancers is not fully understood. Furthermore, apart from their roles in certain well studied cell types, if and how NFκB dimers drive cellular composition in normal tissues and tumor niches is also not well understood as yet. We have recently identified that NFκB p52 subunit, independent of its interactions with other NFκB members, complexes with ETS1, a subunit of the ETS family of transcription factors. The p52:ETS1 complex was found to activate a mutant TERT (telomerase reverse transcriptase) promoter, in cancers. Since mutant TERT promoters do not drive TERT in normal physiology and TERT reactivation by these promoter mutations is seen in only 20% of cancers, this project aims to mechanistically delineate the physiological roles of p52:ETS1, in B cell development and malignancies. The reason we choose the B cell compartment to begin to analyze this novel transcription factor is because p52 and ETS1 null mice, both have been documented to have defects in B cell development. These studies, which if funded could be the first to spatially map the transcriptional profiles of cells that define the splenic architecture, will also be the first to delineate the role of any NFκB or ETS1 signaling member at single cell resolution. Studying the mechanisms and consequences of potential new interactions of NFκB subunits will allow us to develop the next generation drugs for targeted therapies in immune disorders and cancers.
kw: NFkB; ETS1; cancer; signaling; p52; B cells

title: Functional Epigenomic Interrogation of Altered Chromatin States in Gastrointestinal Cancer
abs: Epigenetic alterations are fundamental hallmarks of cancer genomes, profoundly influencing foundational features of tumors including aberrant proliferation, chromosomal instability, and metastasis. Clinically, cancer epigenetic changes are also associated with patient prognosis, treatment response, and drug resistance. Previous work has revealed that epigenetic alterations in cis-acting regulatory elements (CREs; eg enhancers and promoters) comprise an essential biolayer linking hardwired genomic alterations to cancer gene expression and signature phenotypes of malignancy. Our own work on CRE cartographies in gastric cancer (GC), a leading cause of global cancer mortality, has led to multiple senior/co-senior publications in Cell, Nature Genetics, Cancer Cell and Cancer Discovery. Here, we propose to deploy an integrated suite of novel technologies to identify functionally impactful CREs driving molecular and clinical features of GC, and to interrogate how these driver GC-associated CREs are regulated along with their downstream transcriptional programs. We seek to a) identify CREs and CRE target genes functionally required for GC malignant phenotypes using CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) in bulk populations and at the single-cell level (CROPqtl); b) identify CRE-associated trans-binding complexes regulating expression of GC driver genes via CRISPR-based mass-spectrometry (CRISPR-MS), and c) use icSHAPE to generate genome-wide RNA structure atlases of GC (an area where knowledge is almost entirely absent) and to link variations in RNA structure to cancer phenotypes and driver molecular alterations. The proposed work, which builds upon an already successful preexisting translational GC research infrastructure (Singapore Gastric Cancer Consortium) will yield basic insights into the spectrum of epigenomic configurations, transcriptional states, and genetic variants contributing to GC development, particularly in non-protein coding genomic regions which occupy 99% of the human genome. Our results will have translational impact by revealing biomarkers linked to GC initiation and progression, and highlight new therapeutic approaches for GC via targeting tissue-specific CREs necessary for maintaining GC cell survival.
kw: Gastric Cancer, Genomic Alterations, Regulatory Elements

title: Doxycycline host-directed therapy to improve lung function and decrease tissue destruction in pulmonary tuberculosis: Investigating patient outcomes and biological responses (Doxy-TB)
abs: Tuberculosis (TB) is a global pandemic that despite successful treatment and bacterial eradication can cause chronic ill health, also known as pulmonary impairment after tuberculosis (PIAT). We have recently performed a Phase II double-blind randomised-controlled clinical trial funded by the NMRC showing adjunctive doxycycline therapy is safe, accelerates resolution of inflammation, suppresses tissue damaging enzyme activity and decreases pulmonary cavity volume after this intervention. Here, we will perform a fully-powered Phase III trial of 8 weeks of adjunctive doxycycline alongside standard TB treatment. We hypothesise that doxycycline inhibits tissue destruction in patients with pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB). The specific aims are to determine: 1) Improvement in lung function as measured by FEV1% predicted in PTB patients with doxycycline versus those without. 2) Resolution of pulmonary cavities, reduction in host immunological markers of tissue destruction and sputum culture conversion with doxycycline. 3) The safety profile of doxycycline with concurrent standard anti-tuberculous treatment. In this Phase 3 double-blind randomised-controlled trial, doxycycline or placebo shall be given to 75 PTB patients in each arm for two months with a further follow-up of four months. Study sites are in Singapore and Sabah in Malaysia. Lung function tests and non-contrast CT thorax will be performed. Induced sputum and plasma samples from all PTB patients shall be analysed for MMPs, TIMPs and monitored for sputum mycobacteria culture conversion. Whole blood RNAseq will be analysed while a subset of patients’ blood will be analysed using single-cell RNAsequencing. Accomplishing these specific aims will determine if doxycycline will decrease PIAT by improving lung function, reducing pulmonary cavities and accelerating sputum culture conversion. The results will positively impact clinical practice and international guidelines including the World Health Organisation that we collaborate with, for the treatment of pulmonary TB.
kw: Tuberculosis, Matrix Metalloproteinases, Tissue destruction

title: Exosomal biomarker predictor of post-surgical peritoneal recurrence to infer treatment strategies
abs: This proposal builds upon the ongoing collaboration within the Singapore Peritoneal Oncology Study (SPOS) Group and the Peritoneal Division of the Singapore Gastric Cancer Consortium. Based on the hypothesis that biomarkers within the intra-abdominal microenvironment after primary surgery can predict PC and local recurrence with therapeutic implications, we aim to improve and validate a nanotechnology platform (TPEX) that can determine the specific levels of exosomes within clinical biofluids to predict PC/local recurrence after primary surgery. The first objective of our proposal is to test and validate a revised TPEX exosomal signature on intra-abdominal fluids obtained after primary surgery to predict PC and local recurrence. This would be achieved via three steps. We will first confirm and extend the differential abundance of exosomal biomarkers in intra-abdominal fluid between patients undergoing surgical resection (extensive tissue trauma) and patients undergoing diagnostic laparoscopy (minor trauma) during primary surgery. Next, we will optimize the selected biomarkers to allow multi-parametric profiling prior to inclusion on our nanotechnology platform on an existing predictive biomarker panel. Lastly, we will apply and validate the revised panel of exosomal biomarkers on our TPEX platform to predict PC/ local recurrence in patients with advanced ovarian and high-risk colorectal cancers undergoing primary surgery. The second objective is to identify and validate potential novel therapeutic options for patients at high-risk of developing local recurrence/ PC via performing a drug screen of FDA-approved drugs and validate our results in in vivo therapeutic experiments. At the conclusion of this study, we will have a nanotechnology platform that can predict patients at high-risk of developing PC and local recurrence, and also has the potential to be applied across multiple fields of biology. Our findings could also provide insight into the biological rationale for therapeutic strategies.
kw: Exosomes; biomarkers; peritoneal carcinomatosis

title: Drugging the undruggable- targeting wild type EGFR with exosomal therapeutics
abs: Despite its potential, targeting epidermal growth factor receptors (EGFR) never achieved significant impact on the majority of cancers driven by this pathway, limiting their use to a subset of lung cancer with specific activating EGFR-mutations. Squamous-cell cancers (SCCs) represent one of the commonest lethal malignancy worldwide with an incidence of over a million cases. Majority of these are addicted to EGFR-signalling but with limited response to EGFR tyrosine-kinase inhibitors (TKIs). In exceptional responders, we r demonstrated that genetic alterations in a lncRNA led to changes in EGFR-splicing resulting in sensitization to TKI therapy. Our current data indicates that a specific splice variants, isoform D lacks in the intra-cellular domain and is secreted in exosomes/extracellular vesicles. Importantly, transfer of these exosomes, is able to promote TKI-sensitivity in a dose-dependent manner in tumor-cells that are intrinsically resistant. Manipulating this single EGFR-variant shows that it is necessary and sufficient to promote this phenotype. In this grant, we aim to expand this discovery across a range of pre-clinical tumor models (in vitro and in vivo) to test the efficacy of exosomal-isoform D as a co-drug for TKI-therapy. These experiments are also aimed at uncovering cellular mechanisms for sensitization through its effect on cellular trafficking of EGFR, and identification of biomarkers predicting responders to this strategy. Finally, as an alternative to delivering loaded exosomes, we intend to exploit the current explosion of mRNA-therapeutics by re-introducing isoform D in vivo as an mRNA. This could obviate the need for exogenous sources of exosomes, and instead promote autochthonous expression, packaging and secretion of exosomal-isoD, which can then sensitize tumor cells to EGFR-blockade. Through these strategies, our eventual objective is to develop a co-drug that will enable cancers that are ‘EGFR-dependent’ to become ‘EGFR-TKI targetable’, fulfilling the true potential of drugging EGFR in an unmet clinical scenario.
kw: EGFR isoform; Extracellular vesicles; RNA therapeutics; Tyrosine kinase inhibitors; cellular trafficking; squamous cell cancer

title: Development of Novel Therapeutics and Biomarker-Directed Strategies in Refractory Solid Tumors and Haematological Malignancies
abs: NCIS is a medium-sized academic cancer centre in Singapore with a relatively short history, being designated one of two national cancer centres only in year 2008. Despite this, NCIS has steadily built a reputation as a centre that not only delivers quality clinical care, but also excels in academic translational medicine to advance patient care. Although smaller-sized than its counterpart National Cancer Centre Singapore, NCIS distinguishes itself as the only tertiary cancer centre in Singapore providing comprehensive cancer care to all specialties under one roof, boasting a full-fledged Haematology Division that provides tertiary care for haematological malignancies that has a stem cell transplantation program that is first in Asia to receive internationally-recognized accreditation by the Foundation of the Accreditation of Cellular Therapy (FACT), a Paediatrics Oncology unit that is a regional referral centre, as well as an internationally well-networked Gynae-Oncology unit. The main strengths of NCIS include long-standing collaborative ties with bench and translational scientists, a cohesive group of motivated clinician-investigators, a clinical trial unit with strong reputation among industry and academic partners, and one of the best phase I cancer therapeutic trial units in Asia. Being affiliated to the university, NCIS has multiple productive collaborations with academic partners within and outside the NUHS family, including the Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, the Cancer Science Institute, Singapore (CSI), NUS Biomedical Engineering, Duke-NUS, A*STAR institutes including Genome Institute of Singapore, and Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology, just to name a few. NCIS has also over the years fostered and maintained multiple regional and international academic networks for clinical trials and cancer research.

title: The application of carbon capture technology for the reduction of GHG emission from ships
abs: Shipping plays an important role to the global economy, transporting more than 80% of total trade volume. However, ships also generate emissions containing pollutants including carbon dioxide (CO2), as a result of burning fuel as the source of the power for propulsion. International Maritime Organization (IMO) aims to halve GHG emissions by 2050 based on 2008’s level of GHG emissions (or to reduce carbon intensity of the fleet by at least 70%). Carbon capture, utilisation and storage (CCUS) has been identified as one of potential abatement technology to facilitate industrial sector to reduce GHG emissions to the environment. However, there are still many questions needed to be answered as well as technical challenges for the exploitation of the CCUS for shipping industry. The proposed project consists of three phases. In Phase 1, the study of CCUS exploitation for maritime application will be conducted using a holistic approach with simulation and modelling (i.e. Aspen HYSYS, SimaPro, ocean carbonate system computation and techno-economic analysis). The evaluation includes the entire chains, ranging from fuel used, components of exhaust gas generated, post-combustion carbon capture (with treatment of exhaust gas to remove other pollutants, if needed), storage of CO2 onboard (or dispose into the sea, if possible) and logistic for CO2 transport to final handling (utilisation or permanent storage underground or in the ocean). The evaluation will be conducted with consideration of shipboard data, various fuels (and price fluctuations), market-based measures (such as bunker levy) and CCUS technologies. Ultimately, the study aims to clarify questionable issues, especially on sustainability of CCUS for maritime industry with the identification of viable pathways. In comparison with pre-combustion and oxy-fuel capture technologies, post-combustion capture has potential for shipboard application due to its applicability to the existing engine technology (i.e. without modification (or replacement) of combustion chambers) and its technology readiness level. Although post-combustion technology using amine-based solvent (particularly Monoethanolamine (MEA) has been used with power plants worldwide, there are still huge challenges when applied onboard ships . With limited resources onboard ships, the major challenges include (but not limited to) space requirement, power requirement and cost involved. It should be noted that there is no existing benchmark for maritime CCS (only available for land-based application). As a result of Phase I, the benchmark for onboard CCS will be contextualised with the setting of performance parameters and targets (desirable but realistic) for onboard CCS technology. These will be used as a basis for the development of onboard CCS technology in Phase 2. In order to overcome existing challenges, there is a need to explore (or to develop) material(s) for CO2 capture as well as the regeneration method to be suitable for onboard CO2

title: Building quantum networks of superconducting circuits mediated by telecom photons
abs: Building large-scale networks of quantum processors connected via optical links is a crucial step towards harnessing the full potential of quantum technologies. Such networks offer the possibility to realise scalable and delegated quantum computing, device independent quantum key distribution, and quantum-enhanced sensing. While prototypical superconducting quantum processors have achieved rapid progress in recent years, linking them in a quantum network remains an unsolved challenge that we aim to tackle through this proposal. This task is the main missing part to enable practical quantum networks. The main remaining difficulty resides in creating high-quality entanglement between local processors, here operating at microwave frequency, and optical photons, ideally in the telecom C-band, for which communication infrastructures and commercial technologies already exist. Among the myriad of proposed techniques aimed at performing this entanglement, ensembles of rare-earth ions in solid-state have emerged as one of the most promising candidates. My unique background, which combines a strong track-record in superconducting circuits and an in-depth knowledge of atomic physics and quantum control, equipped me with the expertise to develop an innovative protocol to entangle superconducting qubits with telecom photons through large ensemble of rare-earth defects. We make use of our recent finding that such ensembles can overcome their disorder and synchronise to emit photons collectively at both microwave and telecom frequencies. My proposal leverages the existing strengths and infrastructure of Singapore's quantum community. In particular, the ability to fabricate superconducting circuits, integrated photonics, and rare-earth doped substrates are well established both through Singapore's highly mature micro-fabrication facilities as well as with the quantum foundry project, started under the Quantum Engineering Programme (QEP) in 2019. Furthermore, this proposed research is a coherent addition to the pursuits of local scientists, whose expertise in key building blocks of this scheme will significantly accelerate its implementation. Finally, this proposal also addresses a few objectives of the ambitious QEP 2.0 initiative, which aims at developing Singapore's capabilities in delegated quantum information processing and more generally in designing the future quantum internet. This project, together with my expertise within the local quantum ecosystem, provides a promising opportunity to place Singapore at the forefront of research and development of practical quantum networks. The technologies developed here can rapidly benefit related fields such as on-chip quantum enhanced sensing. As this proposal taps into technologies that are rarely used together in a same project, it offers a unique avenue to develop a quantum-ready talent pool with a diverse and valuable skill set. title: Evaluating Health-Related Quality of Life Instruments in Children and Adolescents with Heart Diseases for Health Economic Evaluation in Singapore
abs: Congenital heart disease (CHD) is one of the top five leading causes of disease burden among children in Singapore, with a long-term impact on health-related quality of life (HRQoL). Measuring HRQoL accurately is important to understand the impact of the disease, its treatment, or related side-effects on a patient’s health. Generic preference-based HRQoL instruments measuring health status will be needed for health economic evaluations to make reasoned reimbursement decisions across therapeutic areas on new but more expensive treatments. On the other hand, cardiac-specific HRQoL instruments are desirable to assess the unique challenges of heart diseases. Most of such instruments are developed for the Western populations. So far there are no HRQoL instruments assessed for its measurement properties in Singaporean pediatric patients with CHD. Because of cultural and other differences between countries, locally validated instruments using scientifically sound methodology will be needed. We aim to evaluate the measurement properties of two most promising preference-based pediatric HRQoL instruments (EQ-5D Youth version and Child Health Utility 9D) and one of the commonly used cardiac-specific pediatric HRQoL instruments (PedsQL Cardiac Module) in pediatric patients (age 8-18 years) with CHD in Singapore. Following the cultural adaptation and pilot testing of all the instruments in 10-15 patients, the study will recruit another 160 patients for psychometric validation from pediatric cardiology outpatient clinics of two major public hospitals in Singapore. The patients will self-administer the instruments at baseline, 2 weeks (for assessing test-rest reliability) and 6 months (for assessing responsiveness). Measurement properties (discriminative ability, test-retest reliability, convergent validity, ease of use, and responsiveness) will be evaluated and compared among the instruments. The findings of our study will identify the most appropriate HRQoL instruments for clinical research and reimbursement policy decision-making in Singapore.

title: A Longitudinal Assessment of Children’s Advertising Guidelines on Child Food Consumption and Preferences in Singapore
abs: This research is a longitudinal extension based on previously completed projects, which longitudinally assessed the impact of Singapore’s food communication regulations on children’s food consumption. This study will extend the scientific assessments on multiple fronts with particular emphasis on the impact of the policy measures introduced in 2020 to reduce sugar intake from pre-packaged sugar-sweetened beverages (SSBs). This research aims to assess the effects of the existing and recently introduced policies on Singapore population’s food consumption behavior, as well as on the food advertising landscape on new media platforms. We plan to utilise multiple (four) research methods to provide a holistic framework and assessment. Firstly, nationwide surveys will be conducted with school children to assess their attitudes, intentions, consumption, and other behavioral measures towards different types of food and SSBs. Secondly, a family study consisting of surveys of parents and children, as well as food inventory of home pantries, will be conducted to understand the effects of the recent regulations on the food preferences, perceptions, and consumption patterns of a typical Singaporean family unit. Thirdly, in-depth family interviews will be conducted to understand how family dynamics can shape nutritional knowledge, perceptions, and food consumption behaviors. Together with the family study, the family interviews will help triangulate results and provide qualitative insights. Lastly, data mining of food advertisements on social media platforms will be performed to study the content and types of advertising tactics Singaporeans are exposed to. Data collected in this project will be compared against previous data that has been collected over the past 6 years, bringing the dataset period to almost a decade. Overall, this multi-faceted, multi-sample assessment of the population’s food and SSB consumption can equip policy makers with greater insights that can help shape and initiate more effective policies in nudging the population towards healthier living.
kw: Health; Communication; Advertising; Children; Nutrition; Family

title: Beyond Association, Seeking the Causal Relationship of Oral Frailty and Frailty Among Elderly Singaporeans- A Population-based Study
abs: “Oral frailty” is defined as a decline in oral function, which manifests as difficulties in chewing, swallowing and speaking. It is determined by six domains: (i) number of natural teeth, (ii) chewing ability, (iii) articulatory oral motor skills, (iv) tongue pressure, (v) subjective difficulty in eating tough foods, and (vi) subjective difficulty in swallowing. Tanaka et al. 2018 found that oral frailty was associated with physical frailty and mortality in community-dwelling elderly. Early identification of oral frailty could play a vital role in the prevention of frailty among the elderly. The cross-sectional analyses of this cohort study aims to 1. Ascertain the prevalence of oral frailty in Singapore, 2. Determine if there is a causal association of oral frailty on physical frailty using a novel analytic approach with marginal structural models, after taking potential confounders into account, and 3. Assess for agreement between the clinical presentation and oral frailty score. THE SIGNS (Transitions in Health, Employment, Social engagement and Inter-Generational transfers in Singapore) study is a longitudinal national study of community-dwelling older Singaporeans. We will be riding on its next wave commencing in June 2021. A sample size of 3,000 (out of a finite target population of 4,549) will be sufficient to study the prevalence of oral frailty in Singapore and will achieve a 95% confidence level with a precision of 2%. The prevalence of oral frailty is assumed to be 16% (Tanaka et al. 2018). Oral frailty will be determined using a modified oral frailty scale. Physical frailty will be assessed using the Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS). The oral assessment would include the number of teeth, periodontal and caries status, and articulatory oral motor skills. Data will be analyzed by using counterfactual causal inference approaches allowing the estimation of the impact of oral frailty on physical frailty.
kw: Oral frailty; Frailty; Oral function; Elderly; Oral health

title: Geometry, probability, and deep learning
abs: The overarching goal of this proposal is to use geometric and probabilistic methods for analyzing and improving the effectiveness of deep learning; to use deep learning methods for improving algorithms in probability and geometry; and to advance the mathematical theory which constitutes the foundation of these methods. These results can be subsumed under the title geometric data science. They will be instrumental for the targeted applications in mathematical finance and biomedical shape analysis, as well as for a wide range of further applications where stochastic modeling, data analysis, and deep learning are successfully applied. Geometry and probability are ideally suited for investigating the abstract issues involved in complex learning tasks: high-dimensionality, nonlinearity, and randomness. My combined expertise in geometry and probability, traditionally disparate disciplines, will be essential for the success of the project. I have a strong record of publications in these areas, with a focus on data analysis and modeling in nonlinear and/or infinite-dimensional spaces. Singapore, like no other place, provides a research environment where expertise in the diverse areas of this proposal is condensed in a single city. The targeted results will widen the applicability and improve the understanding of stochastic modeling, data analysis, and deep learning. Advances in this direction have high leverage thanks to the ubiquitous real-world applications of these methods. The novelty of this proposal consists in the combined geometric and probabilistic approach, which is able to describe nonlinear and random effects in high dimensions. The results will drive scientific and technological innovations in artificial intelligence, finance, and the life sciences—areas of strategic importance to Singapore.
kw: geometry, probability, deep learning, mathematical finance, shape analysis

title:
Predicting Survival in End Stage Organ Disease: 
Developing and Validating Prognostic Models
abs: Patients living with end stage organ disease suffer unmet needs from physical suffering, psychosocial and emotional burdens of living with chronic illness and spiritual distress which would benefit from palliative interventions. A reason for the differential access to palliative care in end stage organ disease is the difficulty in prognostication. In non-cancer patients, the pattern of decline is characterized by “entry-re-entry” death trajectories where patients suffer acute exacerbations, hospitalizations, and stabilization in the midst of steady decline. In the midst of such clinical uncertainty, particularly in the context of current available technology and treatment, it makes referral to palliative care all the more challenging compared with cancer. Simple, accessible and well validated prognostic models are urgently needed to objectively identify patients and their caregivers who would benefit from an interdisciplinary collaboration with palliative care. At present, non-cancer prognostic models that attempt to estimate survival of ≤ 6 months have poor discrimination, reflecting the unpredictable nature of non- malignant disease. The primary aim of this study is to identify predictive variables in end stage renal, cardiac and pulmonary disease which would indicate survival of less than 1 year. The secondary aim is to develop prognostic models incorporating both generic and organ specific variables which would be validated for predictive accuracy in end stage renal, cardiac and pulmonary disease. Greater refinement in prognostication for non-cancer would raise awareness for patients who would benefit from an interdisciplinary collaboration with palliative care. It allows clinicians to plan and deliver care which aligns realistic medical goals and resources with patient’s hopes and wishes. End of life discussions have always been difficult, but a better understanding of a patient’s prognosis helps ease the uncertainty of these discussions, enabling the setting of achievable goals in a timely manner.
kw: End Stage Organ Disease; Prognostication

title: Advancing Preventive Health Research in Primary Care
abs: SingHealth Polyclinics (SHP) comprise a cluster of 8 polyclinics located in the eastern region of Singapore. The institution is the key primary healthcare provider in the SingHealth Regional Health System (RHS) and an accredited Family Medicine training center. The polyclinics manage 2.2 million patient attendances and 4.6 million services were rendered in 2020 across all ages. An estimated 60% of patients in Singapore with chronic non-communicable diseases (NCDs) such as hypertension, dyslipidemia and type-2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) are managed in the polyclinics due to the comprehensive continuous care provided by the trained primary care (PCPs) and family physicians (FPs). Aside from NCDs, the polyclinics are sentinel centers to identify emerging strains of influenza viruses in the community. Aside from being the first line of contact with most people with health concerns, the polyclinics also manage outpatients convalescing from infectious diseases, backed by in-house vaccination, laboratory and other support services. SHP is the lead in the SingHealth-Duke NUS Family Medicine Academic Clinical Program (FM ACP) and has strong research collaborations with Family Physicians and Specialists in SingHealth institutions such as Singapore National Eye Centre (SNEC), Singapore Eye Research Institute (SERI), National Heart Centre Singapore (NHCS), National Cancer Center Singapore(NCCS), KK Women s and Children s Hospital (KKH), Singapore General Hospital (SGH), Changi General Hospital (CGH), Sengkang General Hospital (SKH), institutions in other RHS such as National Centre for Infectious Diseases (NCID), National Healthcare Group Polyclinics (NHGP) and National University Polyclinics (NUP). SHP is also a pioneer member of the Asia Pacific Academic Primary Care Research Group (AAPCG) and collaborates with NUS Yong loo Lin School of Medicine, NTU Lee Kong Chian School of SHP, University of Malaya, University Putra Malaysia, University of Melbourne (Australia), University of Hong Kong, Chinese University of Hong Kong and Fudan University (PR China). SHP also works closely with industrial research partners, who contribute their expertise in the fields of mobile health, telehealth, smart sensors, gamification, artificial intelligence, augmented and virtual reality (VR) technologies. title: The SALIENCE Programme: A Singapore ALliance towards an Integrated rEsearch platform for NeuroCognitive DisEases
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: The SALIENCE programme will see five major clinical-research centres coming together for the first time to further research into Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI). The five centres which include neurology, geriatrics and psychiatry represent centres that manage more than 80% of MCI patients in Singapore. National Neuroscience Institute (NNI) is the national centre that provides neuroscience related care to 70% of Singapore. NNI has a database of 5000 individuals with neurocognitive disorders. Over the last 5 years, 30-40% of patients attending the NNI memory clinics have MCI. NNI has expertise in cognitive and behavioral evaluation platforms, neuroimaging for cognitive disorders, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) evaluations for amyloid-tau, blood-based biomarkers, genotyping as well as clinical trials for cognitive disorders. NNI has dedicated cognitive laboratories, 3-Tesla MRI machines, image post-processing expertise, research laboratories that process and analyze CSF and blood, -80C freezers as well as a dedicated clinical trial research unit. The dementia and cognitive neuroscience programme has six cognitive neurologists, a team of neuropsychologists, advanced specialist nurses trained in dementia, post-doctoral fellows in neuroimaging, biomarkers as well as a large team of clinical research coordinators. The cognitive neuroscience programme has attracted grant funding from national agencies, foundations as well as international organizations such as the Alzheimer s Association International to validate novel cognitive evaluation tools and research into cerebrovascular contribution to cognitive disorders. Khoo Teck Puat Hospital (KTPH) Geriatric Service is one of the largest geriatric centres in Singapore and has distinguished itself in both clinical & community care and research. Their niche lies in the clinical assessment of MCI, dementia as well as frailty. The memory clinic has seen a progressive increase in patients with MCI and physical frailty in the past decade. Patients visiting the clinics will go through an extensive range of neurocognitive assessment, neuroimaging, psychosocial, lifestyle and behaviour, medical, biological, physiological, diet and nutrition, physical and, health status variables. The team has expertise in biomarkers especially blood-based biomarker and genotyping, as well as digital biomarkers of physical and cognitive decline obtained through wearable and ambient sensors in smart home environments. Additionally, the team is also well versed in providing physical, cognitive and psychosocial interventions which are the key multicomponent intervention in cognitive frailty prevention as well as management. In collaboration with the Geriatric Education and Research Institute, the team has secured the NIC grant to successfully implement a community based multi-component intervention of subjects at risk of cognitive impairment. title: Epigenetic drivers of TKI resistance and disease progression in EGFR mutated NSCLC
abs: Despite development of several generations of EGFR TKI, drug resistance inevitably develops. While on target EGFR resistance mutations, off target bypass oncogenic drivers and histologic transformation have been described, the mechanism of resistance for a fair proportion of tumors - in particular T790M negative tumors - remain unaccounted for, at least genomically. Recently, we presented one of the largest unbiased integrative analysis of EGFR TKI resistant tumors, highlighting how lineage transitions and a stem-like state underlies T790M negative resistance. Further, in an independent cohort of resected EGFR mutated NSCLC, we found a subset (approx 10%) harboring co-alterations in chromatin modifying genes. Finally in a genome wide CRISPR screen in four independent EGFR mutant TKI resistant cell lines, SIRT1, an NAD-dependent deacetylase (class III HDAC) emerged as a convergent mechanism of resistance. Our preclinical and clinical observations underscore the need to look beyond somatic genetic alterations, to identify chromatin regulatory mechanisms and potential therapeutic targets to circumvent or overcome resistance.
kw: Epigenetic drivers; EGFR mutated; NSCLC; TKI resistance

title: Neoantigen screening and validation using engineered artificial reporter cell and artificial antigen presenting cell (aAPC) platform in patients receiving adjuvant dendritic cell vaccine and anti-PD1 therapy (nivolumab) post resection of colorectal cancer with liver-limited metastases (CRLM) and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC)
abs: My PhD project focuses on translational research that is part of an ongoing industry-sponsored phase 2 trial for which I am also a co-investigator. My aim is to learn more about translational science as I transition into the role of a clinician scientist, which dovetails with my clinical subspecialty in gastrointestinal cancers. I will be conducting research experiments under the supervision of Dr Gloryn Chia from National University of Singapore, who is an NRF fellow with funding for the set-up of these research. We hypothesise that there is pre-existing neoantigen-specific anti-cancer immunity in patients with resected colorectal cancer with liver-lmited metastases (CRLM) and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and this may be augmented through neoantigen-loaded Dendritic Cell (DC) vaccine and anti-PD1 therapy. We aim to perform neoantigen screening and validation using transgenic HLA-restricted granzyme reporting cells and artificial antigen presenting cells (aAPC). 293T cell lines will be transduced with lentivirus carrying specific HLA haplotypes while other HLAs are deleted through CRISPR technique, with an IFP-signal releasing granzyme reporter system to confirm T cell recognition of immunogenic neoantigens. Post DC vaccination, antitumour immunity and neoantigen immunogenicity can also be interrogated with a transgenic HLA-restricted K562 aAPC platform. Engineered aAPCs are co-cultured with neoantigens and patient-derived peripheral CD8 T cells. If neoantigen-specific T cells are encountered, T cell activation will occur and outcomes measured with eLISpot assays. Functional killing assays may then be carried out through co-culture of autologous neoantigen-specific T cells with tumour cell lines or organoids. Overall, this platform may be developed for high throughput neoantigen screening and validation. It also allow us to validate the outcome of the neoantigen DC vaccine and may eventually lead to the identification of neoantigen-specific T cell populations for future therapeutic purposes.

title: Advancing RNA-based Therapeutics for Inherited Retinal Dystrophies
abs: Inherited retinal dystrophies (IRDs) encompass a genetically heterogeneous group of diseases characterised by dysfunction or degeneration of photoreceptors. More than 300 genes have been implicated in IRDs with approximately 1 in 1380 individuals affected worldwide. Due to a paucity of effective treatments, IRDs remain a major cause of irreversible vision loss. Gene therapy using adeno-associated viral (AAV) vectors is being investigated for a few recessively-inherited IRDs. However, several of the most frequently mutated IRD genes have a coding sequence that exceeds the AAV cargo capacity, limiting application of this strategy. RNA-based therapeutics which alter gene expression at the transcript level are an alternative approach. Antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) are a type of RNA-based therapy which have entered phase I/II clinical trials for three different IRDs. In our pilot study, we have identified a patient with an ABCA4 mutation that can be addressed with ASOs. We hypothesize that a sub-population of our IRD patients carry pathogenic mutations that are amenable to modulation with ASO therapy. This longitudinal study will capture informative biomarkers and the disease trajectory for a spectrum of IRDs in a multi-ethnic Asian cohort. Disease-causing variants will be identified using whole exome sequencing, then computational and statistical models will be applied to simulate the properties of the transcribed RNA molecule. ASOs will be rationally designed to target the specific genetic variant and tested using retinal organoid models derived from the patient’s induced pluripotent stem cells. The ASO efficacy and efficiency will be assessed by in vitro reversal of disease pathophysiological hallmarks. The small number of patients affected by each IRD present a major hurdle for drug development. However, even for IRDs patients who harbour extremely rare disease-causing genetic variants, ASOs can potentially be custom-designed to halt or even reverse the retinal degenerative process and vision loss.

title: Malnutrition and Frailty: Integrated Community-based and Clinic-supported Screening and Lifestyle Interventions
abs: One third of older Singaporeans are at moderate to high risk of malnutrition and one half of older Singaporeans are either pre-frail (45%) or frail (4.5%).The major cause of frailty is malnutrition: 66% of frail individuals and 40% of pre-frail individuals are at risk or malnourished. Nearly all (91%) of malnourished older people are frail (27%) or pre-frail (64%). We will develop and evaluate simple, effective and generically appropriate algorithms and protocols to screen and assess, prevent and treat malnutrition and frailty for use in an integrated care model in both community and clinic settings. 1.Community-based screening and interventions based in senior activity centers (SAC) performed by non-healthcare professionals trained to use simple ‘pen-and paper’ tools will identify low-moderate nutrition risk and pre-frail older persons for nutritional and physical exercise lifestyle interventions. Community-based lifestyle interventions will employ NCSS-inspired Our Kitchen Programme (OKP) and KTPH Share-a-Pot Programme communality approach for dietitian-guided shared food resourcing, preparation and meal participation to empower and enable frail older persons to improve the quality and quantity of protein and calorie and micronutrient intake, in conjunction with physical exercise intervention using key elements of high velocity resistance training (power training) and dual tasking. 2.Clinic-based program. High risk (malnourished) and frail individuals identified from SAC screening above will be referred to a designated geriatric outpatient service unit in one community hospital providing clinic-based programs for stepped-up clinical assessment, intensive nutritional and physical therapy, and management of multi-morbidity and polypharmacy. A 3-month randomized controlled trial will determine whether the community-based and clinic-supported integrated multi-sector service model to screen and treat malnutrition and frailty will improve nutritional status, physical and functional status, quality of life, and reduce falls risk, hospitalization and need for long-term care.
kw: Frailty; Malnutrition; Elderly; Lifestyle intervention; Integrated care and service

title: Protein supplementation in critically ill children: A pilot randomized controlled trial
abs: Protein malnutrition is prevalent among critically ill children and associated with poor clinical outcomes. Current guidelines for provision of protein in daily management of critically ill children in pediatric intensive care units (PICUs) are based on limited and not high-quality evidence. The current protein supplementation approach, “one-size-fits-all” nutrition prescription, may not be appropriate for every critically ill child. Given the heterogeneity of the patients admitted to the PICU, a targeted approach based on individuals’ needs represents a potential advancement in PICU care. Our central hypothesis is that protein supplementation in PICU care leads to improved clinical outcomes in subgroups of patients only. We propose a dual-centre pilot randomized controlled trial in Singapore with two major aims: (1) To obtain key information for planning and conducting a large-scale multicentre study in Asia; and (2) to evaluate the benefit of protein supplementation to critically ill children with body mass index (BMI) z-scores on PICU ≤ -2. The main clinical outcome of interest is total number of days of hospital stay (from PICU admission to hospital discharge). Two protein supplementation regimes (≥ 1.5g/kg/day vs. standard care) will be randomly allocated to PICU patients with body mass index (BMI) z-scores ≤ -2. We will determine the effect of protein supplementation on total length of hospital stay and other clinical outcomes, and assess the impact of protein supplementation on acquired functional impairment of PICU survivors 6 months after hospital discharge. In addition, we will explore whether muscle ultrasound is a biomarker for protein balance in pediatric critical illness. Upon completion of this study, we will have strong preliminary data to plan, refine our study approach, and execute a future large multi-centre study across Asia. title: Modeling the immune suppressive solid tumor microenvironment for immunotherapy optimization
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Immunotherapy aims to redirect the patient’s immune system to fight against a specific pathology and holds great promise as a novel cancer treatment.While the investment in research and pharma is at an all-time high in the immunotherapy and cell therapy sector, these new strategies are more likely to fail in a solid tumor context during clinical trials. The critical role of the tumor microenvironment (TME) in adoptive cell-mediated cancer immunotherapy is now recognized in the research and clinical community. However, our understanding of the relationship between the TME components and the immune system is limited.3D microfluidic multicellular assays with real-time imaging and precise control over spatiotemporal parameters are poised to help elucidate the roles played by each cell type involved in this complex domain. Therefore, we propose a multidisciplinary strategy to model solid human liver cancer microenvironment in vitro. The final goal is to reach the clinical trial stage with a higher percentage of successful treatment to reduce the cost of research and drug development process. In particular, we’ll focus on the investigation of engineered tumor-specific T cell combined with immune checkpoint inhibitors in a TME microfluidic model which has a remarkable feature of monitoring cell-cell interactions and dynamics. The model could represent an efficient preclinical tool to be potentially used during clinical trials to match the optimal drug and technique to individual cancer patients. Indeed, proposed here is a novel approach by using primary human tumors to investigate patient-specific responses and use the assay as a preclinical tool. Since there are currently no validated methodologies to study immunotherapy response in patient-derived cancer specimens, this proposal has the potential to provide a state-of-the-art technology with wide ranging implications and have the potential to be clinically and economically impactful.

title: Novel palliative care model for advanced cancer patients: A randomized controlled trial study
abs: Cancer is the leading cause of death in Singapore, accounting for 30% of deaths in 2017. Advanced cancer patients have poor quality of life and high utilisation of acute healthcare services. When provided alongside standard oncology care, early access to palliative care improves quality of life of patients with advanced cancers and their caregivers, as well as reduces acute healthcare utilisation and costs by these patients. Yet, in Singapore and elsewhere around the world, palliative care is delivered to a minority of advanced cancer patients shortly before death, with a median time from first consult to death of only 30 days. We propose to conduct a randomized controlled trial of the ‘Supportive and Palliative care Review Kit in Locations Everywhere’ (SPARKLE) intervention, an outpatient-based model of early palliative care. The SPARKLE intervention comprises regular symptom monitoring using questionnaires, early identification and prompt treatment of problems identified. Proactive screening for problems facilitates earlier palliative care interventions for advanced cancer patients, whenever needs arise. The SPARKLE intervention extends palliative care to a larger number of advanced cancer patients and delivers palliative care before terminal phase of life, whenever patients have physical, psychological or social needs. We hypothesize that the SPARKLE care model results in a) improved quality of life of both advanced cancer patients and their caregivers, and b) reduced acute healthcare utilization and costs by these patients.
kw: Cancer; Palliative; Quality of Life; Patient Reported Outcome Measures

title: The Skin Microbiome in Early Childhood Atopic Dermatitis
abs: Background: Atopic dermatitis (AD) is an chronic, incurable skin disease afflicting 20% of children in Singapore and is associated with allergic rhinitis, asthma and food allergy. Studies suggest that prophylactic administration of emollients from birth in infants with a family history of atopy might prevent AD development in a small proportion. It is, however, not known if there are predictive non-invasive skin biomarkers of AD present in early life which could more precisely identify infants at risk of AD and the atopic march, for whom preventive interventions might be specifically tailored towards. Aims: Primary Aim 1) To identify unique characteristics of the newborn’s skin microbiome at 7 days of life which predict development of AD and its severity, allergen sensitization and allergic rhinitis by 18 months in comparison to healthy controls. Secondary Aims 1) To elucidate the relationship between the newborn’s skin microbiomes in relation to the mode of delivery and to correlate this with the development of AD by 18 months of age. 2) To define the maturation patterns of the healthy infant skin microbiome with age by tracking the skin microbiome signatures of healthy infants longitudinally from birth to 18 months of age. Methods: Clinical data collection, skin tape stripping, AD examination and skin prick tests will be performed for mother-offspring dyads in the ongoing Singapore PREconception STudy of maternal and child Outcomes (S-PRESTO) cohort at multiple time-points from birth to 18 months. Whole metagenome sequencing and bioinformatics analysis will be carried out for skin microbiome analysis. Clinical significance Identification of predictive skin biomarkers in the pre-disease phase will identify at-risk infants who would benefit from implementation of early interventions, such as prophylactic emollients from birth in high-risk infants or modification of the skin microbiome for the primary or secondary prevention of atopic dermatitis and its associated co-morbidities.
kw: atopic dermatitis; skin microbiome; allergy; childhood; developmental origins

title: Development and Validation of a Myopia-Specific Item Bank Administered using Computerized Adaptive Testing: The MyoCAT Study
abs: Myopia imposes a massive public health burden, with almost 85% of young adults having this disease. People with myopia not only suffer from impaired vision, but also experience side-effects from corrective therapies and are at increased risk of developing sight-threatening complications such as pathologic myopia (PM). Therefore, understanding the impact of un- or under-corrected myopia, PM and the effectiveness of myopia corrective therapies from the patient’s perspective is becoming increasingly important, with many governing authorities mandating the use patient-reported outcomes data to guide and improve clinical management, support medical decision-making, and inform policy decisions in healthcare measures and resource allocation. While several questionnaires exist to measure myopia-related quality of life (QoL), there are serious psychometric short-comings with these instruments with issues related to conceptualization, generalizability, validity and responsiveness. Moreover, current myopia-specific questionnaires are paper-pencil based, and are therefore static, inflexible and burdensome to administer and answer. Evidently, a culturally valid instrument that allows a rapid, accurate and comprehensive assessment of the impact of myopia and its associated complications and corrective therapies from the patient’s perspective in Asia is urgently required. Fortunately, these problems can be overcome by using item banking (IB) and computerized adaptive testing (CAT). An IB is a large pool of questions calibrated for difficulty based on participant response and the use of modern psychometric techniques. IBs are operationalized by CAT, which is ‘smart’ technology that adapts the items asked based on participants’ responses to previous items, enabling a precise and reliable assessment while minimizing measurement error and reducing test length. The main objective of this project is to develop, validate and evaluate the clinical applicability of a novel IB and CAT system for myopia (MyoCAT) that is able to comprehensively assess the QoL impact of un/under-correction, PM and the different corrective therapies, in a multi-ethnic Singaporean population.
kw: Patient reported outcome measure; Digital Health; Myopia; Population Health and Implmentation Science

title: Real-time modelling of rare cancers and therapeutic screening using ex vivo models
abs: Rare cancers collectively represent a major healthcare problem worldwide, and remains a neglected group of diseases with poorly defined therapeutic strategies and dismal outcomes. From our recent studies on angiosarcoma, an Asian-centric rare cancer, we identified 3 subtypes defined by distinct mutational signatures and gene expression profiles, as well as unique immune signatures. In addition, further work on other rare cancer subtypes have led to discovery of novel molecular pathobiological mechanisms and identification of new therapeutic biomarkers. Based on these results, we hypothesize that comprehensive molecular profiling of rare cancers enables discovery of actionable targets with potential pathobiological or clinical relevance, including novel oncological drivers and therapeutic biomarkers. In addition, our preliminary results suggest the feasibility of creating study models for rare cancers, such as patient-derived xenografts and cell-lines, which provide a valuable resource for discovering novel pathobiology and clinical applications. In this proposal, we aim to 1) delineate the clinically-actionable target landscape of rare cancers via comprehensive molecular profiling and 2) create ex vivo rare cancer models in real-time. This will involve whole genomic and transcriptomic sequencing of rare cancers, and curation of therapeutic targets through in silico bioinformatic analyses. Modelling of rare cancers will be performed using patient-derived xenografts and cell-lines created in real-time for opportunistic pathobiological inquiry and biomarker discovery. Through this study, the results will support the future set-up of a Rare Cancer Clinic emphasizing a precision oncology strategy for all rare cancers in order to guide personalised therapy and facilitate clinical trial matching.
kw: rare cancers, sarcoma, precision oncology

title: Guided transposition bisulfite sequencing as a novel approach to efficiently assess DNA methylation states in heterogeneous cell population
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: The dysregulation of the epigenome is implicated in a myriad of disorders. DNA methylation (5mC) is the best studied epigenetic mechanism to date and has been found play major roles in transcriptional regulation, particularly in the silencing of repetitive elements, X-chromosome inactivation and genome imprinting during organismal development. Aberrant 5mC profiles has been described many forms of cancers and more recently in neurological disorders. Therefore, there is a great interest on the potential use of DNA methylation states as diagnostic biomarkers to discriminate between diseases states and gain insights into the underlying disease biology. For such studies, single cell based bisulfite sequencing (SCBS) is required because 5mC differences at potential biomarkers are concealed by bulk signals in conventional sequencing approaches. However, present SCBS are suboptimal and costly, prompting a need to develop new methodology. Herein, this proposal describes a droplet-based single cell bisulfite sequencing termed guided transposition bisulfite sequencing (GTBS). In GTBS, 5mC immunoprecipitation is immediately coupled to a Tn5 mediated transposition which simultaneously fragment genomic DNA and inserts sequencing adapter in a single droplet reaction. This method enriches for CG sites which reduces the required sequencing depth and thus cost savings, and libraries are immediately amplified with a set of universal primers which can reduce and prevent PCR amplification biases. I anticipate that GTBS may potentially overcome limitations of current SCBS, and can be applied to assess 5mC states in a wide variety of heterogeneous samples
kw: Epigenetics, Single Cell, NGS

title: Strategic Multi-Theme AppRoach to Translational Medicine III (SMART III)
abs: Established in 1821, Singapore General Hospital (SGH) is the oldest and largest acute tertiary hospital in Singapore. Comprising 40 clinical specialties and 18 identified areas of clinical excellence (working in synergy with six SGH research themes), it not only serves the entire nation but is also a key regional and international referral centre. SGH is a member of Singapore Health Services (SingHealth), which is Singapore s largest healthcare cluster. Leveraging SingHealth s network of healthcare institutions, the SGH campus provides close proximity and access to national specialty centres, community hospitals and polyclinics. SGH manages tertiary and inpatient care for all the national specialty centres in the Outram campus (except National Heart Centre Singapore), facilitating multi-disciplinary, inter-professional and seamless continuum of patient care ranging from emergency, acute, chronic, disease-based, surgical, rehabilitative and palliative to community care. Annually, this campus alone provides care for over one million patients. In its earlier years, SGH was focused on providing excellent medical care. In recent decades, to meet the challenges of the ageing population and growing healthcare demands in Singapore, there was a need for SGH to transform itself to incorporate excellent medical education and clinical translational research to enhance care delivery for better patients health. Around the same period, the Singapore government also invested in biomedical sciences as the fourth pillar of Singapore s economy to develop Singapore into a world-leading nexus for biomedical sciences. To this end, SGH and SingHealth formed a strategic partnership with Duke-NUS to establish the SingHealth Duke-NUS Academic Medical Centre (AMC) in 2005. The AMC s vision is defining tomorrow s medicine , with the mission care to heal, educate to empower and innovate to advance . With this vision and mission, SGH has transformed itself into one of the largest teaching and clinical training hospitals in Singapore, training the nation s pipeline of medical undergraduates, postgraduate specialists and surgeons, nurses and allied health professionals. Additionally, this academic medicine transformation is achieving significant results in research, with a growing pool of clinician scientists and researchers, an increasing amount of grant and industry funding, and an increasing number of facility cores and research programmes (Sections 2.1c and d). Notably, in Newsweek s ranking for the best hospital globally, SGH was ranked among the top eight for three consecutive years (i.e. 2019-2021) and is the only hospital in Asia ranked among the top 10. SGH also produced research outcomes comparable to these top 10 hospitals. SGH s RIE2015 and RIE2020 Centre Grants (CGs) have been instrumental in enabling SGH to achieve this exceptional international standing, and the RIE2025 CG is critical to sustain and grow SGH s research in a competitive and rapidly evolving enviro

title: THE ROLE OF IL11 IN ALVEOLAR EPITHELIAL CELL DYSFUNCTION: IMPLICATIONS FOR LUNG REGENERATION IN SEVERE RESPIRATORY DISEASES
abs: Severe respiratory infections and fibrotic lung diseases including Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF) are associated with defects in epithelial repair and irreversible loss of Alveolar Epithelial Cells (AEC) which ultimately leads to the decline in lung function. Thus, it is important to understand the disease mechanisms leading to defective epithelial repair to enhance lung recovery and prevent and/or reverse respiratory diseases. In the lung, Interleukin 11 (IL11) is highly upregulated in fibroblasts from patients with IPF and its expression correlates with disease severity. IL11 is also upregulated in the damaged lung epithelium of patients with IPF, asthma and in response to viral infections including COVID-19. The effects of IL11 on the injured distal lung epithelium are unclear but thought maladaptive and anti-regenerative. Our proposed experimental plan will address the overarching hypothesis that IL11 causes AEC dysfunction and triggers maladaptive repair through several mechanisms involving epithelial-mesenchymal transition, cellular senescence and disrupted epithelial-stromal homeostasis, which prevents lung regeneration. Our first aim focuses on defining the expression of IL11 expressing cells in lung diseases using an in vivo tracing approach with newly developed IL11-EGFP reporter mice. We will perform RNA-sequencing based transcriptomic analysis of sorted EGFP expressing cells to identify mediators of IL11 function during lung disease. Additional mechanisms by which IL11 induces AEC dysfunction will be defined using in vitro cultures of human alveolar type II (AT2) epithelial cells. Lastly, we will leverage AT2-specific IL11 inhibition using new genetic mouse models to study the impact of IL11 loss-of-function on AEC repair and lung regeneration in models of experimental lung injury. This proposal has important translational implications in defining critical factors that regulate AEC homeostasis, as well as for the development of novel therapeutic strategies to promote effective lung repair for patients with lung disease.
kw: Lung, Fibrosis, Inflammation, Regeneration, Interleukin-11

title: Determining the Function of Live-Attenuated Vaccine Induced Pro-Inflammatory Responses in Eliciting Vaccine-Associated Adverse Events and Immunogenicity.
abs: Vaccination to prevent infectious diseases has been hailed as the greatest public health achievement in the 20th century. Increasingly, vaccines are being used to prevent chronic infections and cancers. Moreover, World Health Organisation (WHO) has advocated for vaccines to be used as countermeasures to prevent antimicrobial resistance. Despite these successes, however, there is growing public concern on vaccine safety. Although no causal link has been established between vaccination and conditions such as autism, segments of the public have reduced vaccine uptake, resulting in re-emergence of what were once well-controlled infections, such as measles and mumps. Such mistrust in vaccines stems, at least in part, from the lack of detailed understanding of the molecular basis of vaccine safety. Such understanding is needed for an evidence-based approach to public education. It would also form the molecular basis for the development of vaccines with fewer adverse events. We propose that such understanding is now possible due to recent findings from our group. We have shown that the molecular correlates of vaccine-induced immunity are distinctly separated from the correlates of adverse events (AEs) by the time in which the innate immune and pro-inflammatory responses are induced. Herein, we propose a study that demonstrates the functional relationship between an early innate immune and pro-inflammatory response with AEs. We will use an experimental medicine approach with detailed molecular investigations to demonstrate the functional specificity of our molecular correlates of AEs. We will test the hypothesis that inhibition of the molecular correlates of AEs, which are expressed in the first 24 hours post-vaccination, will reduce the rate of vaccine-associated AEs by 50%. We will also show that AE suppression will not impact the molecular determinants of robust vaccine-induced immunity. If successful, this study will fill a major gap in knowledge on the determinants of vaccine safety.
kw: Vaccine; Live attenuated; NSAIDs; Randomised; Single-blinded

title: A study to identify markers of early retinal cell fate commitment in pluripotent stem cells in vitro
abs: Clinical trials in patients with age related macular degeneration (AMD) have now shown that stem cell based retinal cell replacement therapy can successfully restore visual function. However, production of clinical grade retinal cells from pleuripotent stem cells (PSC) is a complex, time consuming and formidably expensive process. As a result retinal stem cell therapy remains inaccessible to most patients. To produce retinal cells, mixed PSC are subjected to retinal differentiation conditions until retinal cells are formed. This is followed by an extensive purification process to remove non-retinal cell impurities which escalates the time and cost of cell production. This purification process could be eliminated from the cell production protocol if committed retinal progenitors were selectively isolated from mixed PSC before differentiation, It has not been possible to use this approach thus far due to lack of selective surface markers of early retinal progenitors. Using an in vitro model of retinal development and single cell RNA sequencing analysis, we have now identified a list of cell surface targets that are differentially expressed in early committed retinal progenitors. Through this work, we propose to validate these cell surface targets as early committed retinal progenitor markers, by evaluating their ability to yield pure retinal cells in vitro if used for selective cell isolation from mixed PSCs. We have also identified novel transcription factors differentially expressed in early retinal progenitors, and part of this proposal will aim to understand the significance of these genes in early retinal cell fate commitment. Not only will this work enhance our understanding of retinal development; successfully validated cell surface markers of early retinal progenitors will pave the way for automation and up-scaling of retinal cell production, bringing down costs and making retinal stem cell therapy accessible to the growing cohort of patients who need it.
kw: retinal cell fate committment; pleuripotent stem cells

title: Defining the Immune Landscape in the Pathogenesis of Endometriosis through single cell analyses
abs: Endometriosis affects 6-10% of women during their reproductive age, resulting in significant morbidity and economic burden on the patient. Current modalities for both diagnosis and treatment is sub-optimal resulting in unsatisfactory management options for pain, infertility and adverse obstetrical outcomes. Part of this reason is due to the lack of understanding of the patho-aetiology and pathogenetic mechanisms in this disease, for which the immune system plays an important role. Current studies on immune cell types in endometriosis have been conflicting likely due to differing methods of sample preparation, immune cell isolation and characterisation, and lack of strict clinical phenotyping. Another limitation in the data generated to-date is the use of low-resolution flow cytometric and genomic methods, which has an inherent inability to deeply phenotype immune cells. Thus there remains a wide gap of knowledge of the immune landscape in endometriosis. Our hypothesis is that the immune dysfunction interacts to promote lesion establishment and progression. We propose to map out the immune cell types infiltrating the endometriotic lesions, and determine the significance of their interactions with immune as well as other cell types by state-of-the-art Flow cytometry, CyTOF, CITE-seq, scRNAseq techniques. Specifically, we will: (1) Map the global cellular landscape of endometriotic (both immune and non-immune) lesions using high resolution multi-parametric single-cell techniques like flow cytometry, CyTOF, scRNA-seq and CITE-seq. (2) Elucidate the dynamic cross-talks between diverse macrophage populations and the adjacent endothelial cells which are essential for the integrity and function of the endometrium. (3) Validate the crosstalk between immune-endothelial cells and identify their implications on the ‘immuno-surveillance’ and disease progression in severe endometriosis. The successful elucidation of distinct immune aberrations in endometriosis may allow us to classify different subtypes of endometriosis, identify early biomarkers and therapeutic targets for disease interventions.
kw: Endometriosis; Immune cells; Macrophages; Estrogen

title: Roles of the novel stem cell factor IQGAP3 in cancer
abs: Cancer is a major cause of mortality in Singapore. There is a pressing need to study the fundamental mechanisms underlying cancer initiation and maintenance to improve detection and treatment. Tumors are likely to originate from dysregulation of stem cells or acquisition of stem potential by differentiated cells. Identifying the cell-of-origin is problematic because of the broad specificity of various known stem cell markers, multiple stem cell reservoirs and cellular acquisition of plasticity. Our recent discovery that IQGAP3 is specifically expressed in proliferating stem cells provides us with a highly specific molecular tool to study the cancer initiation and proliferation in multiple tissues. Using mouse models, we found that targeted expression of oncogenic Kras expression in IQGAP3+ stem cells resulted in rapid formation of precancerous lesions. Moreover, IQGAP3 is induced following tissue damage and associated with acquisition of stem and proliferative potential in terminally differentiated cells. Tumors are described as wounds that do not heal. Our work indicated that IQGAP3 is the common denominator in stem cell proliferation, wound healing and cancer initiation. We will use IQGAP3 to identify tumor-initiating cells and characterize downstream targets in cancer. Because of the strong detection of IQGAP3 in multiple cancer types, we will extend our findings on IQGAP3 to proliferating cancer cells in the colon and breast. Importantly, we found that IQGAP3 is required for maintenance of stem cell potential and that its ablation led to cell differentiation. We will evaluate the effectiveness of inhibiting IQGAP3 in cancer therapy using patient-derived organoids, particularly in the inhibition of proliferation and induction of terminal differentiation. Our work will contribute to early detection and guide treatment of multiple cancer types.
kw: Proliferating stem cells; IQGAP3; wound repair; chronic tissue damage; dedifferentiation; cancer initiation and proliferation

title: 3D Printed Scaffold Device for Ridge Preservation after Tooth Extraction - A Randomised Controlled Clinical Trial
abs: Following tooth extraction, the socket heals naturally with bone in 1 to 2 months. This healing process occurs with substantial reduction of the original height and width of the alveolar ridge. In a significantly resorbed ridge, bone augmentation procedures are necessary before dental implant placement. Autogenous bone is the gold standard for this purpose but the harvesting procedure results in additional morbidities and expenses. Ridge preservation techniques have been introduced, using xenografts, allografts or synthetic materials to fill the tooth socket immediately after extraction. While the current materials used have improved ridge dimensions to various extents, their osteoconductivity is suboptimal and unpredictable. They do not reduce vertical resorption of the bony walls and often interfered with the normal healing process. Polycaprolactone-tricalcium phosphate (PCL-TCP) is a bioactive, bioresorbable composite polymer that is non-toxic and tissue compatible. This study aims to test the use of a novel 3D printed PCL-TCP device for ridge preservation, levaraging on its 3D shape that fits snugly in the tooth socket, high porosity and bioactivity to promote osteogenesis and reduce resorption. The hypothesis is that the insertion of a PCL-TCP scaffold in extraction sockets allows normal bone healing and better maintenance of ridge dimensions after 6 months compared to extraction sockets without a space filler. This will be a prospective, randomised controlled clinical trial in patients who require single tooth extraction and replacement with a dental implant. The study will compare the ridge dimensions and the quality and quantity of bone formed in tooth sockets, using histology and microcomputed tomography, in both groups after 6 months. The PCL-TCP scaffold to be used in this study will be fabricated by a local company, Osteopore International Pte Ltd. The market potential for this device is tremendous due to a growing demand for tooth replacement from an ageing population worldwide.
kw: 3D printing, bioresorbable, scaffold, polycaprolactone-tricalcium phosphate, ridge preservation, bone bioengineering

title: Targeting Brain Tumors: Improving Lives through Precision Medicine
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Patients with grade IV glioblastoma (GBM) often show a median survival period of fifteen months despite advanced surgical intervention with chemotherapy and radiation treatment. Among the reasons for this highly infiltrative and recurrent disease lies in the molecular heterogeneity of tumors. The Cancer Genome Atlas effort recently showed that histologically identical GBM tumors can be molecularly subtyped, with each class corresponding to unique genomic aberrations and clinical outcome. While computational efforts reveal regulatory pathways of GBM, functional validation and the ability to stratify patient cohorts most likely to receive treatment benefit is lacking. We hypothesize that patient stratification methodologies will lead to improved clinical outcome. This forms the basis of precision medicine, where the NNI Brain Tumor Resource plays a key role. Our national resource contains patient-derived glioma cells, with the ability to create orthotopic xenograft mouse tumors that recapitulate the patient’s original tumor morphology, transcriptomic and karyotypic hallmarks.
