We will utilize a 3-theme approach of: (i) Testing stratification methods to identify key mechanisms corresponding to tumor cell invasiveness and proneural-mesenchymal transition, frequently observed in recurrent tumors, (ii) Establishing molecular profiling information of recurrent GBMs, which will create a “molecular reference baseline” crucial to guide treatment decisions, and (iii) Developing novel imaging probes and predictive biomarker profiles capable of distinguishing patient molecular subtypes. Complementing these imaging capabilities, we will develop real-time guided surgical technologies where maximal tumor resection will be explored through a combination of Raman spectroscopy and intraoperative magnetic resonance imaging, a capability established in very few clinical centers internationally. Collectively, our program will develop capabilities to identify patient cohorts most likely to receive treatment benefit from targeted therapy. This will in turn spare nonresponders of chemotherapeutic side effects and financial cost. Our program seeks to improve clinical outcome through the application of precision medicine approaches.
kw: Glioblastoma; Precision medicine; Patient stratification; Guided surgery; Molecular imaging; Predictive biomarkers

title: Singapore Gastric Cancer Consortium – Bringing Discoveries to Patients
abs: Gastric cancer (GC) is the 5th leading cause of cancer mortality globally. While GC age-adjusted incidence is declining, the absolute number of GC cases is expected to increase due to overall population growth and aging. Importantly, GC is prevalent in Asian countries and in Singapore, GCs represent the 4th/5th highest causes of cancer death in males/females respectively. The Singapore Gastric Cancer Consortium (SGCC) is an integrative multidisciplinary national research program, which over the past decade has established Singapore as a global leader in GC research and treatment, establishing unique population cohorts, novel GC molecular classifications, insights into GC carcinogenesis, and innovative investigator-initiated clinical trials. In this renewal, we seek to take these discoveries back to patients, through five investigational themes in precision prevention, precision therapy and data-driven target identification. First, as early diagnosis is a major factor to improving GC outcomes, we have developed and will be validating novel methods for early detection and risk stratification in high-risk patients, with implications for population screening. Second, for advanced GC patients, we will combine information from molecular biomarkers, organoid platforms, and artificial intelligence to guide the rational and data-driven selection of optimal combination therapies and dosing. Third, we will deeply study the clinical challenge of GC peritoneal carcinomatosis, representing the deadliest and most treatment-refractory presentation of this malignancy. Fourth, using lineage-tracing technologies, we will probe potential GC cells-of-origin (“cancer stem cells”) to identify new therapeutic targets. Fifth, as intra-tumour heterogeneity (ITH) is a major barrier to successful GC treatment, we will apply single-cell technologies to comprehensively demarcate ITH evolution through distinct stages of gastric carcinogenesis and across different intra-tumour cell types. Findings from these themes will apply directly to GC patients, maintain Singapore’s leadership role in the GC field, form a rich training ground for new researchers/clinician scientists, and opportunities for industry partnerships.
kw: Gastric cancer

title: TAAP: Translational Asian Age-related Macular Degeneration Program
abs: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is a major cause of blindness with significant socioeconomic and healthcare burden in rapidly aging populations in Singapore and Asia. An AMD subtype, polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy (PCV), makes up 50% of AMD in Asians, but current treatment options for PCV remains limited. We propose a broad-based multi-disciplinary Translational clinical research program in Asian AMD and Polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy (TAAP), integrating a team of retinal specialists, clinician-scientists, and basic scientists from across major research institutes in Singapore and globally. This “bench-to-bedside-to-population” has 5-linter-linked Themes that address key research questions and is aligned with clinical needs and strong industry interest: Theme 1 (Population Health) will characterize disease burden and identify risk factors of AMD/PCV in Asians to plan future public health policies and preventative interventions. Theme 2 (Pathophysiology) will examine novel pathophysiological mechanisms, metabolic and immune dysfunction and epigenetic changes in AMD with in-vitro and in-vivo experiments. Theme 3 (Novel Imaging Biomarkers) will exploit a multitude of novel imaging technology in collaboration with industry partners to develop and validate imaging biomarkers to guide personalized treatment. Theme 4 (Therapy) will test and develop new therapeutic strategies for PCV through multi-centre clinical trials in Asia. Theme 5 (Quality Of Life) will determine the impact of AMD/PCV through studies in psychometric, behavioural, neuroscience and health economics and investigate the efficacy of a practical problem-solving therapy model on improving patient outcomes. TAAP will build on significant prior work (>10,000 population controls, >800 clinical AMD/PCV cases with biological samples and genetic data), an extensive international collaborative network with SERI and strong industry support. The broad-based research proposed has high potential for commercialization and significant clinical and population outcomes that will lead to blindness reduction from AMD by 20% within 10 years. TAAP is fully aligned to MOH’s priorities in “aging” and “precision medicine”.
kw: Age-related Macular Degeneration; Imaging Biomarker; Population Health; Pathophysiology; Therapy; Quality of Life

title: Singapore PARKinson’s disease Translational Clinical Programme (SPARK, Phase II)
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Background: Parkinson’s disease (PD) with a prevalence of 3:1000 (>50 years) in Singapore will significantly increase as 20% of our population will be > 65 years old by 2030. Objectives: We will develop an integrated clinical, biochemical, and genetic profile identified in several clinical longitudinal cohorts of patients that we have initiated in Phase I so as to develop a model to better manage, prevent development and reduce PD progression. 2. We aim to create cutting edge human brain models, validate new drug targets that we have identified, and unravel key disease mechanisms so as to develop individualized drug and cellular replacement therapies. Methodology Epidemiology/Health Services: To develop an integrated clinical, biochemical, and genetic models to better manage, prevent development and reduce PD progression and identify factors that influence disease progression and drive healthcare costs, so as to improve quality of life in PD. Pathophysiology: To further elucidate the molecular pathways underlying common gene related PD, so as to investigate potential therapeutic interventions through the selection of viable targets using non-human primate and small animal models. Brain Organoids: To develop the next generation human brain organoid model system for innovative and translational research to facilitate screening and validating therapeutic molecules identified in other themes. Regenerative Medicine: To identify and investigate intrinsic and extrinsic factors which would affect the therapeutic efficacy of cell transplant in PD using both non human primate and small animal models. Novel Therapeutics: To conduct a placebo controlled clinical trial in PD involving a propriety compound, to validate the positive autoantibodies identified in PD patients and to conduct experimental therapeutics based on new drug targets. Conclusions: The novelty, international competitiveness and industrial commitment in this Phase II proposal build on our scientific discoveries and achievements in Phase I.
kw: Parkinson’s disease; Clinical studies; Genetics; Animal models; Therapeutics

title: Advancing precision medicine for cardiovascular disease and diabetes in Asian populations
abs: Identification of the mechanisms underlying the increased risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) and diabetes in Asian populations, and developing affordable, effective and scalable strategies for risk stratification and prevention of these major diseases, are urgent national and global public health priorities. To address these challenges, we first create a longitudinal population study of >100,000 Singaporeans (“SG100K”) comprising comprehensive phenotypic characterisation, high quality biological samples, and linkage to national electronic health records. In partnership with the National Precision Medicine programme, we will exploit SG100K to determine the behavioural (including nutrition and physical activity), environmental, genetic and other molecular factors that underpin CVD and diabetes in the multi-ethnic Asian population of Singapore. We will use the knowledge generated to develop and validate algorithms for accurate identification of Asian men and women at risk of CVD and diabetes, taking polygenic information into account. We will strengthen tools for communication of cardiovascular and metabolic risk, taking into account non-genetic and genetic information, and develop personalised approaches to behaviour change for health promotion, that are tailored to social, cultural and environmental context, and delivered by scalable digital platforms. We will evaluate the impact of our risk stratification, communication and behavioural support platforms on engagement with health promotion, and quantify efficacy and cost-effectiveness for prevention of CVD and T2D in community and primary care settings. We will thus advance population and precision health for CVD and diabetes, the leading causes of death and disability in Singapore. In addition, we will deliver SG100K as a unique platform for state-of-the-art epidemiological, translational and precision medicine research, in the genetically distinct and culturally diverse Asian populations of Singapore, which will impact management of a wide range of chronic disease, at national, regional and international scale.
kw: precision; medicine; longitudinal; population; personalized; healthcare

title: The Singapore lYMPHoma translatiONal studY (SYMPHONY)
abs: The proposed programme is a renewal of our NMRC funded TCR program on peripheral T-cell (PTCL) and NK/T cell lymphoma (NKTL), which is more common in Asia. To date, therapeutic interventions are of limited efficacy and there remains a pressing need to improve diagnosis, therapy and patient selection. The current TCR has elucidated part of the underlying complexity of this disease. Identification of mutations in JAK/STAT pathway, epigenetic regulators and structural variations in the PD-L1 gene resulting in immune evasion, amongst others, pave the way towards a biology-driven strategy. Theme 1 aim to (i) target driver oncogenic pathways and genetic mutations previously elucidated using novel JAK inhibitors, PI3K inhibitors, EZH2 inhibitors and histone modifying targeted drugs and (ii) identify rational combinations to overcome resistance. Theme 2 and 3 will focus on novel immunotherapeutic approaches based on novel antibody therapies and immune checkpoint (ICP) inhibitors, respectively. Theme 2 will (i) develop strategies to enhance antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity and complement-dependent cytotoxicity of Daratumumab (anti-CD 38) and (ii) develop novel, next generation hetero-tetrameric IgG bi-specific antibody (BsAb) constructs with broad applications. Theme 3 builds on our findings that suggest ICP inhibition to be a major turning point in NKTL treatment. We will decipher the mechanisms of response and resistance, investigate novel combinatorial regimens and develop next generation biomarkers for patient selection for immunotherapy. Theme 4 will develop more efficient and cost effective diagnostic platforms as well as improve patient prognostication and selection through artificial intelligence, integrative machine learning and algorithm research. Through these 4 intercalated themes, we aim to translate and build on the progress we have made in addressing unmet clinical needs of T cell lymphoma. The expertise and infrastructure we have built will allow us to investigate key strategic areas in B cell lymphoma research where we may be internationally competitive.
kw: Non hodgkin lymphoma;immune checkpoint blockade; drug development; biomarker discovery; artificial intelligence;translational

title: Light-Activatable Theranostic Nanoparticles to Improve the Delivery and Cardioprotective Efficacy of Cytoprotective Peptides in Acute Myocardial Infarction.
abs: Recently clinical studies have failed to demonstrate beneficial effects with different cardioprotective agents in patients with acute myocardial infarction (AMI). This outcome may have, in part, been due to reduced bioavailability and failure to deliver the agent to ischaemic cardiomyocytes within the first few minutes of reperfusion. The goal of this proposal is to develop a theranostic nanosystem that is able to provide fast and on-demand timed delivery of a cardioprotective agent for reducing infarct size together with simultaneous imaging of the ischaemic myocardium. We will load the nanosystem with a novel multi-target cytoprotective peptide, ND-13 (a mimic of the mitochondrial protein, DJ-1), which has been shown to reduce myocardial infarct (MI) size in an ex vivo AMI Langendorff model, but was compromised in an in vivo AMI rodent model due to low systemic bioavailability. Hypothesis: Novel PEGylated multi-functional nanoparticles, which are near-infrared (NIR) light-activatable, and which contain cardiac-homing peptide, will improve the delivery of ND-13 peptide to the ischaemic myocardium, and increase the efficacy of ND-13 in reducing infarct size, when compared to ND-13 alone or conventional nanoparticles. Aims of the proposal: By exploring a theranostic strategy with targeting nanosystems in a AMI murine model, we aim: (1) To achieve a “Burst” drug release upon NIR irradiation localised to the ischaemic area-at-risk; (2) To facilitate AMI imaging and monitor the delivery by targeting the heart ; (3) To achieve superior pharmacological efficacy in reducing MI size via timed/targeted delivering ND-13 into cardiomyocytes. The overarching goal of this project is to develop novel smart nanoparticles for improved drug delivery to reduce MI size, prevent heart failure and improve clinical outcomes in patients with AMI.
kw: Theranostic Nanoparticles, Targeting, Smart Drug Delivery, Peptide, CT, Acute Myocardium Infarction

title: Uncovering the role of nuclear import protein KPNA1 in inflammasome regulation and disease
abs: The inflammasome is an essential arm of the innate immune system in host defence against pathogens. It is a multi-protein complex that induces inflammatory cell death in response to specific pathogenic molecular patterns and physiological stresses. As potent as its activity in pathogen clearance, its dysfunction causes auto-inflammatory diseases and cancers. In our search for novel inflammasome regulators to develop new therapeutic approaches, we identified the nuclear import protein, KPNA1. I found that KPNA1 binds to the inflammasome sensor NLRP1 and mediates inflammasome-induced cell death. I further demonstrated that the expression of a de novo KPNA1 mutant variant alone is sufficient to aberrantly trigger inflammasome activity and account for the pathology of a patient with a skin tumour condition called multiple keratoacanthoma centrifugum marginatum (KCM). Based on these findings, and the established role of KPNA1 in shuttling proteins into the nucleus, I hypothesize that changes in the localization and protein interactions of KPNA1 alter its regulation of inflammasome activity. To test this, I will delineate the inflammasome regulatory mechanism of KPNA1 in healthy, inflammatory and diseased states by 1) mapping the changes in nuclear/cytoplasmic localization of KPNA1 and in turn NLRP1; 2) elucidating the domains of KPNA1 that are critical to its inflammasome regulatory function; and 3) identifying changes in binding partners and cargo proteins of KPNA1. These findings will uncover not only the molecular underpinnings of KPNA1’s role in inflammasome regulation, but also new avenues for the treatment of inflammasome-associated disorders and cancers.
kw: Inflammasome; NLRP1; nuclear import; KPNA1; inflammation; cancer

title: Alpha-synuclein Gene Promoter (Rep1) Polymorphism and Cognitive Decline in Parkinson’s Disease
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by cytoplasmic alpha-synuclein aggregates in the substantia nigra. The alpha-synuclein gene (SNCA) is implicated in familial PD; while polymorphism of the SNCA promoter region (Rep1) i.e. variation in Rep1 allele length, is associated with increased PD risk in multiple studies. The frequencies of Rep1 genotypes in our PD population are ~30% for the shortest allele (allele 0), and ~40% and ~30% for the longer alleles (alleles 1 and 2 respectively). Increased risk of PD may occur via variation in transcriptional regulation of SNCA expression, with longer Rep1 allele lengths displaying increased SNCA expression in both mouse and human brain tissue. Furthermore, clinical studies have shown that longer Rep1 allele carriers show greater motor decline and neuropsychiatric complications compared to shorter allele carriers. However, the association of Rep1 with cognition remains unknown. To address this gap, our primary aim is to investigate the association of Rep1 allele-lengths with cognitive decline in mild- to moderate-stage PD (Hoehn & Yahr score ≤3). We hypothesize that longer Rep1 allele carriers (alleles 1, 2) will show greater decline in cognition based on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) test over 2 years, compared to shorter Rep1 allele carriers. A secondary aim is to determine if peripheral SNCA expression levels at baseline are associated with cognitive decline in longer Rep1 allele carriers. An exploratory aim is to study longitudinal changes in brain structure (grey matter volumes, cortical thickness, and white matter microstructure) and functional connectivity in longer vs shorter allele carriers. We hypothesize that longer allele carriers will show greater decrease in these measures over a 2-year period compared to shorter allele carriers. These will add evidence to the link between Rep1 polymorphism and cognitive dysfunction in PD, identifying Rep1 as a novel therapeutic target for neurodegeneration in PD.
kw: SNCA Rep 1, Parkinson's disease, genetics, biomarkers, cognition

title: Heart-Brain Connection: Cognitive Impairment in Patients with Heart Failure
abs: Vascular cognitive impairment (VCI) is increasingly recognized in patients with heart failure (HF). Data from our preliminary studies indicate a high burden of VCI among HF patients and that existing cognitive tests can be simplified to expeditiously screen patients for VCI. We hypothesize that VCI is prevalent among HF patients and is correlated with cerebral vascular pathology. The primary objective of this study is to determine the burden of VCI among HF patients and to evaluate a novel method of screening VCI in this high-risk population. The secondary objective of the study is to examine the value and feasibility of an intervention that centers on lifestyle changes and cognitive training for HF patients with mild cognitive impairment (MCI). We propose a two-stage study to achieve these objectives: • In stage one, we propose a cross-sectional study involving 300 HF patients who will be screened for VCI using a standardized brief cognitive test and a detailed formal neuropsychological assessment. One hundred patients who consent to an MRI brain will be followed up for a year to assess for the development of cognitive impairment. Additional vascular investigations will be performed to assess for the risk of cardiac arrhythmia and structural cardiac diseases. • In stage two, we propose a randomized control trial design to examine the feasibility of a multi-domain intervention trial in a smaller cohort of 60 MCI patients who will be randomized to receive intervention and control (no intervention) in a 1:1 ratio. Cost-benefit analyses of cognitive screening and intervention in HF patients will be performed. Outcome of this study will provide important insights on the actual burden of VCI among HF patients and risk factors that contribute towards its development. The feasibility of a multi-domain interventional trial incorporating cognitive training will be addressed in this study.
kw: heart failure, cognitive impairment

title: Community-based Screening for Pathological Visual Impairment among Elderly Residents using Artificial-Intelligence Integrated Retinal Imaging
abs: Visual impairment (VI) is a major public health problem, associated with reduced quality of life, and increased frailty risk. Globally, 400 million suffer from VI. Among them, pathological VI (poor vision due to eye diseases not refractive error) accounts for 60%. In Singapore, 12% of individuals aged ≥60 (~90,000) suffer from pathological VI. This number will increase as Singapore population ages. Most causes of pathological VI such as cataract, diabetic retinopathy, when detected early, can be treated and halted from worsening to severe visual/functional loss. Hence, screening for pathological VI is crucial for healthy ageing and productive longevity. Currently, as part of the MOH-initiated functional screening program, community vision screenings are conducted among elderly Singaporeans. The screening model includes 2-tier screening procedures conducted at different days and sites, involves multiple tests and requires skilled manpower, substantial time, to identify pathological VI cases. These factors limit the capacity and coverage of current model. Thus, it is challenging for the current model to operate sustainably to meet the demand of nation-wide annual vision screening for elderly, in the long run. Hence, a simpler, more efficient modality for screening pathological VI is critically needed in Singapore. Artificial intelligence (AI) technology offers unique opportunities to revolutionize current screening model. We propose a novel vision screening modality integrating retinal photography and AI-based algorithm to detect pathological VI. In this proposed project, we will refine, validate this newly developed modality, and pilot its implementation and performance in a ‘real-world’ community outreach screening setting for elderly Singaporeans. This model provides a ‘one-stop shop’ screening using only one objective test, and is time-, labor-efficient and cost-saving. Importantly, this is in line with MOH’s long-term focus of preventive care among Singapore’s elderly (beyond healthcare to health), while adopting a streamlined and sustainable model (beyond quality to value).
kw: Community screening; Visual Impairment; Retinal Imaging; Artificial Intelligence

title: Mapping Cellular and Molecular Pathology in Autism Spectrum Disorders using Human Brain Organoids and Spatial Transcriptomics
abs: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is the top disease burden among children in Singapore and across developed world. Patients struggle with social communication, display repetitive behaviors and have restricted interests. These behavioral hallmarks manifest early in childhood but persist for life, costing society >USD260 billion per year. To date, no drugs target the above core symptoms- existing drugs only alleviate co-morbidities like seizures and hyperactivity, while behavioral interventions provide limited relief. A major roadblock has been a poor understanding of pathology at a cellular and tissue level. Our objective is to define neuropathological substrates in autistic brains and surrogate models, with a long-term goal of developing molecular therapeutics that target core symptoms of ASD. We hypothesize that specific changes in organization, morphology and interactions of particular cell types underlie ASD. Since these cellular features are three-dimensional, we will model ASD in human brain organoids and analyze these features within their tissue architecture. We will first verify patient-derived organoid models against bulk transcriptomes and gross anatomy of postmortem ASD brains (Aim 1). Next, we will identify cell types with altered gene expression in ASD organoid models using single-cell RNAseq (Aim 2). Then, we will determine abnormal arrangement and morphology of cell types in ASD organoids using protein markers and a novel, high-throughput RNA-imaging technology called Multiplexed, Error-robust Fluorescence In Situ Hybridization (MERFISH) (Aim 3). I have tested eight brain organoid protocols and identified the optimal method for reproducible generation of brain organoids. Since application of MERFISH to brain organoids is novel, I optimized sample preparation and performed single-molecule FISH as a proxy for MERFISH, with success. The cellular cartography of autistic brains and ‘mini-brains’ will unveil ASD pathology and identify potential drug targets that can be directly tested on our organoid platform.
kw: Autism; Pathology; Organoids; Human Brain; Transcriptomics

title: Meningeal macrophage and its role in meningeal lymphatics development
abs: Neurodegenerative diseases such as dementia has affected at least 50 million people worldwide and the number is expected to rise. One of the common types of dementia is Alzheimer's disease (AD), which is characterised by early and marked cognitive impairment. One of the hallmarks of AD is the deposition of amyloid plaques in the brain. Recently, meningeal lymphatics were rediscovered and were shown to be involved in the initiation and progression of AD. However, the mechanistic control of tissue-resident macrophages in the regulation and development of meningeal lymphatics vasculature, and how dysfunctional lymphatic vasculature affects neurodegenerative diseases remains unclear. In this proposal, we intend to comprehend the role of meningeal macrophages in the regulation and development of meningeal lymphatic vessels, and also investigate how dysfunctional lymphatic vasculature can affect brain development, and development of neurodegenerative diseases. We hypothesise the meningeal macrophages maintain and regulate the integrity of meningeal lymphatics. Hence, dysfunctional meningeal lymphatics will exacerbate neurodegenerative diseases. To address these questions, we will utilise a variety of techniques such as flow cytometry, microscopy, transcriptomics, as well as the use of conditional genetic mouse models to comprehend the functional role of meningeal macrophages in lymphangiogenesis in the meninges. We believe that this integrated approach will unravel the physiological role of meningeal macrophages in the meninges, thereby enabling us to better comprehend how meningeal immunity can affect brain physiology and its dysregualation. This will also allow us to identify novel mechanistic pathways that can serve as potential therapeutics for neurodegenerative diseases.
kw: neurodegenerative diseases; meninges; macrophages; lymphatics; infection

title: The role of LINC complex-mediated nuclear migration in striated muscle development and laminopathies
abs: The proposal will investigate 2 aspects of LINC complex-mediated nuclear migration in striated muscle relevant to muscular dystrophy and dilated cardiomyopathy. First, we will use live fluorescence microscopy of mNeonGreen-labeled nuclei in differentiating C2C12 myotubes to study nuclear centration, the first stage of muscle fiber formation, where the nuclei of myoblasts fusing with myotubes migrate to the centre of the myotube. To facilitate determination of nuclear centration speed, we are developing computational image analysis tools. We will determine the role of the LINC complex, specifically the KASH domain proteins Nesprin-1 and Nesprin-2, and their potential or known microtubule-associated interactors, dynein, Pericentrin and Akap450, in the speed of nuclear centration. We will use siRNA depletion, chemical inhibition, or dominant negative disruption of these proteins to assess their role in nuclear centration. We will validate potential physical interactions between the Nesprins and the microtubule-associated proteins by co-immunoprecpitation. Second, we will use myotubes as an in vitro model to investigate the role of Sun1 mutations in ameliorating physiological defects associated with lamin A/C (Lmna) mutations in mice. Recent evidence suggests that Sun1-containing LINC complexes preferentially interact with microtubule cytoskeleton proteins to drive nuclear damage in Lmna mutant myotubes, leading to pathology. We propose to dissect the role of Sun1 in this system by Sun1 complementation experiments using constructs with mutations affecting Sun1 tertiary structure and domain swaps with the paralogous Sun2. We will test, via Sun1-dependent recruitment of Pericentrin to the nuclear envelope of myotubes, whether these mutations interfere with Sun1 LINC interactions with microtubule cytoskeleton proteins. We will then test how these mutations influence nuclear damage in Lmna mutant myotubes using established indicators of nuclear rupture (cGAS accumulation) and DNA damage (gH2AX). These studies will enable us to understand both fundamental mechanisms of muscular dystrophy and related cardiomyopathy caused by Lmna mutations.
kw: muscle development; LINC complex; nuclear migration; laminopathies

title: Diet and lifestyle intervention strategies to treat β-cell dysfunction and insulin resistance in Asian Indians
inst: IHDP - Institute for Human Development and Potential
abs: Compared to other races, Indians have a greater risk of developing type 2 diabetes (T2D), increased insulin resistance(IR) and more rapid decline in β-cell function, highlighting the urgency and importance of early intervention strategies for improving insulin sensitivity and preserving/improving β-cell function to prevent T2D and mitigate against the increased vascular disease risk. Preliminary findings show a reduction in glycemic load selectively depletes visceral and ectopic lipid and improves insulin sensitivity and β-cell function in non-diabetic adults. The proposed research will investigate if the phenotypic features increasing T2D risk in individuals of Indian ancestry (IR and impaired β-cell function) can be favorably modified by a low glycemic (LG) intervention, and if the increased IR is attributable to genetic factors regulating adipocyte differentiation and function. These research objectives will be achieved through a 24-week RCT comparing isocaloric LG versus control diets in Indians with prediabetes. Compared to individuals in the control group, those on the LG diet are expected to have greater ectopic (pancreas, liver, visceral and intramyocellular) fat depletion assessed with MRI/MRS, and improvements in first phase insulin secretion and insulin sensitivity assessed with the C-peptide model and oral minimal model, respectively during an OGTT. Reductions in hepatic and pancreatic lipids will be associated with improvements in first-phase β-cell response. Individuals with a greater number of risk alleles from a 53-SNP IR genetic score will have lower insulin sensitivity and leg fat, supporting the notion that impaired adipocyte differentiation leading to limited peripheral adipose expansion capacity is an important etiological factor underpinning IR cardiometabolic disease in Indians. The results will broaden the evidence base for effective prevention strategies in this high risk population by investigating the effect of the proposed diet intervention on underlying physiological and molecular mechanisms implicated in the pathophysiology of T2D in Indians.
kw: Diet, β-cell function, insulin resistance, Asian Indians

title: A novel way of neuroprotection for extracranial carotid stenosis.
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Extracranial carotid stenosis (ECS) is a narrowing of the lumen of the carotid artery. Severe stenosis increases the risk of stroke and chronic hypoperfusion may lead to cognitive impairment. Besides surgical intervention, there is a lack of neuroprotective treatment for ECS. In this study, we propose a novel way of neuroprotection in managing ECS by targeting an ion channel TRPM4. TRPM4 is a monovalent cation channel and our preliminary study has shown that TRPM4 was upregulated in neurons under chronic hypoxia. Importantly, blocking TRPM4 could ameliorate glutamate induced calcium influx in hypoxic neurons and improved learning and memory in ECS animal models and human tissues. Therefore, we propose that TRPM4 can be a novel target for neuroprotection in ECS, and blocking TRPM4 may provide a novel approach in managing ECS. In this proposal, we will examine the expression of TRPM4 under chronic hypoxia conditions using in vitro cultured neurons and in vivo ECS animal model. The functions of TRPM4 are examined by electrophysiological studies and calcium imaging method. We also seek to understand the potential mechanism of blocking TRPM4 by studying the functional interaction between TRPM4 channel and NMDA receptors. Importantly, a patented antibody M4P which has been developed in our lab will be examined in this study to evaluate its therapeutic potential. By completing this study, we hope to identify the therapeutic potential of blocking TRPM4, and provide a novel way of managing cognitive impairment in ECS.
kw: cerebral hypoxia, neuroprotection

title: Novel Intrinsic mechanisms promoting neural stem cell reactivation
abs: Neural stem cells have the potential to regenerate and repair brain damage. However, in the mammalian adult brain, the majority of neural stem cells (NSCs) are in a mitotically inactive, quiescent state with little regenerative ability. Interestingly, in response to extrinsic stimuli, these quiescent NSCs can exit from quiescence and resume proliferation (reactivation) to generate new neurons. However, failure in NSC reactivation may result in the neurodevelopmental disorders. The quiescence state of NSCs is also associated with aging brain. Despite these abundant evidence, how NSCs switch between quiescence and proliferation remains poorly understood. Our work supported by NMRC (July 2015-Jan 2019) showed that the spindle matrix complex, as a key nuclear factor, intrinsically promotes NSC reactivation. Here, we have identified Cullin 4 (Cul4)-RING ubiquitin ligase complex (CRL4) as a new intrinsic factor promoting reactivation of Drosophila NSCs. In addition, mutations in Cul4B, which encodes a subunit of CRL4 E3 ligase, are reported to cause neurodevelopmental disorders including mental retardation syndrome and malformations of cortical development. Given that the Hippo pathway maintains the quiescence (or inhibits the proliferation) of NSCs in both Drosophila and mammalian brains, we hypothesize that CRL4 promotes ubiquitination of Warts, a key Hippo pathway component, to stimulate NSC reactivation. We will investigate the role of both Drosophila and mammalian CRL4 complex in NSCs proliferation/reactivation (Aim 1). We will directly test our hypothesis that CRL4 complex promotes the ubiquitination of Warts, a key component of the Hippo pathway (Aim 2). We will establish the link between CRL4 and Wts biochemically and genetically in Drosophila models. Given the association of human Cullin 4B mutations with neurodevelopmental disorders, the outcomes from this application will provide important novel insight into intrinsic mechanisms that promote NSC proliferation and will ultimately contribute to our understanding on brain development, associated neurological disorders and aging.
kw: Drosophila; neural stem cells; quiescence; proliferation; reactivation; neuroblasts

title: Linking APP and LRRK2 to Pinpoint the Cause of Dopaminergic Neurodegeneration in Parkinson’s disease
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disease in Singapore. Leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) mutations are the most common genetic cause of PD. The G2019S mutation has been shown to elevate LRRK2 kinase activity andinduce dopaminergic neuron loss. Although the role of LRRK2 in PD has been intensively researched, only a handful of LRRK2 substrates have been elucidated that have illuminated the disease pathways involved. Here, we have identified the Alzheimer’s disease (AD)-related Amyloid Precursor Protein (APP) as a novel target of LRRK2. We found that LRRK2 interacts with and phosphorylates APP at threonine-668 (T668). This in turn stimulates the production of the APP intracellular domain (AICD). Hypothesis: APP is a potential downstream target of LRRK2-mediated neurodegeneration in PD, and that targeting APP pathway may provide a novel therapeutic strategy for PD. Objectives: We seek to elucidate the role of LRRK2-mediated APP phosphorylation in association with LRRK2-related PD, and evaluate if the inhibition of APP phosphorylation and processing can rescue LRRK2 G2019S-induced neurotoxicity. Methodology: Engaging LRRK2 G2019S’siPSCs-derived human dopaminergic neurons,post-mortem tissue, mouse dopaminergic neurons, and mice, we aim to 1) elucidate the mechanism on how APP phosphorylation at T668 contributes to LRRK2-mediated neurotoxicity in PD, 2) evaluate if inhibition of APP processing rescues LRRK2 G2019S-mediated loss-of dopaminergic neurons. Using CRISPR/Cas9 system, we will create constitutivelyphosphorylated form of APP T668E and phospho-mutant T668A mice to explore physiological contribution of APP phosphorylation at T668 in LRRK2-mediated neurotoxicity in PD. Scientific/Clinical Impact: We identify APP as a novel substrate of LRRK2 and highlights LRRK2-mediated neuronal loss in PD. It links LRRK2 and APP, and providesa crucial understanding on the pathways connecting the two most common neurodegenerative diseases. The identification of APP as target holds promises to provide a new therapeutic approach for LRRK2-related PD patients.
kw: APP; Neurotoxicity; Phosphorylation; LRRK2; Parkinson's disease; Amyloid Precursor Protein Intracellular Domain (AICD)

title: Rational Therapeutic combinations for Wnt driven Cancers
abs: Pathologic activation of Wnt signaling is found in cancers, fibrosis and other diseases; hence there is considerable interest in blocking Wnt signaling to achieve therapeutic benefit. There are 19 Wnts that couple to different receptors, to activate multiple downstream pathways. At Duke-NUS we have pursued a novel strategy to block all (canonical and noncanonical) Wnt dependent pathways concomitantly by preventing the secretion of all Wnts. In collaboration with Experimental Therapeutics Centre, A*Star we have developed novel, highly potent small molecules that inhibit porcupine, a key enzyme required for secretion of all 19 Wnts. One of these small molecules, ETC-159 has shown remarkable efficacy in pre-clinical models with genetically defined lesions. ETC-159 is Singapore’s first anti-cancer drug to advance to Phase I Clinical Trial. To expand the utility of ETC-159 and other Wnt pathway inhibitors, I propose to pursue the following three Aims: 1) I propose to identify pathways that cooperate with Wnt signaling to drive tumor growth and hence develop rational therapeutic combinations for Wnt pathway inhibitors. 2) While the β-catenin pathway is well studied, understanding of the “non-canonical” Wnts, their specific signaling pathways remains elusive. Exploiting the pan-Wnt activity of ETC-159, I will elucidate β-catenin independent transcriptional networks. This will identify novel markers and provide novel targets for tumors and other diseases with activated noncanonical Wnt signaling. 3) Activation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway is implicated as a key mechanism of resistance in platinum resistant cancers. Given the key role of Wnt signaling in maintenance of stem cells, I will test if inhibition of Wnt signaling can reverse resistance to platinum based therapies. Successful completion of these studies will advance our basic understanding of how Wnt signaling drives cancers, and benefit Singapore’s drug development efforts by expanding the therapeutic applications of ETC-159 and identifying novel targets for future drug development.
kw: Wnt signaling; cancer; Wnt inhibitors; combination therapies

title: Targeting NF1-associated glioma invasion and therapeutic resistance for improved clinical outcome
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Glioblastoma multiforme is incurable with an average survival of less than 1.5 years. Underlying such dismal prognosis is the heterogeneity of the glioma cells, which heightens radio-chemoresistance and promotes tumor infiltration that underpin disease recurrence commonly observed in GBM patients. Our results implicate the loss of the tumor suppressor gene, neurofibromin (NF1), in the transition of proneural GBM to an aggressive mesenchymal state with enhanced invasion and treatment resistance. Since NF1 inactivating mutations or loss of expression is found in 23% of GBM, targeting NF1-loss associated signaling is relevant to glioma therapy. Accordingly, we hypothesize that loss of NF1 promotes mesenchymal transition of gliomas, which results in tumor recurrence and radiochemo-resistance. Our data indicate the leucine rich domain (LRD) functions to suppress motility and invasion in glioma. Thus, our first aim is to investigate whether NF1-loss or mutation confers therapeutic resistance in mesenchymal GBM. We will characterize the somatic mutations identified in GBM patients found in the LRD region and will assess whether they play a role in mesenchymal transition. As a separate, but complementary aim, we will test whether other domains of NF1 mediate mesenchymal regression to a less invasive proneural state to serve as surrogate therapeutic targets. We will investigate whether LRD or other domains of NF1 regulate NF1-loss associated downstream molecules that mediate GPM invasion. We found that loss of NF1 upregulates expression of angiogenic and cell motility related genes, angiopoietin-like (ANGPTL)-4 and ephrinB2 (EFNB2). Accordingly, our third aim is to elucidate how activation of ANGPTL4 and EFNB2 mediate glioma invasion and self-renewal. Results obtained from this proposal will allow us to establish crucial downstream pathways that are required for NF1-loss mediated mesenchymal transition of human GBM that in turn will facilitate the development of novel treatment strategies to target these specific effector for glioma therapy.
kw: glioma; glioblastoma multiforme; neuro-oncology; neurofibromin (NF1); therapeutic resistance

title: Mechanisms of sphingosine-1-phosphate signaling in vascular health and disease
abs: Sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) is a signaling lipid that is essential for blood vessel development and functions. S1P exerts its roles by being a potent ligand for 5 different S1P receptors. Much effort has been made to understand the receptor-mediated signaling mechanisms and S1P synthesis. One major gap of knowledge is how S1P is released for its extracellular signaling. S1P is synthesized from sphingosine by phosphorylation by two sphingosine kinases (SphK1/2). It must be exported out of cells for signaling roles. Blood cells and endothelial cells and are proposed as the main sources for plasma S1P. Nevertheless, the transporters responsible for S1P release were not identified until recently. Spinster homolog protein 2 (Spns2) was cloned by two laboratories as the endothelial S1P exporter which contributes ~25% plasma S1P. My laboratory has recently identified Mfsd2b as the S1P exporter in blood cells and showed that red blood cells (RBC) and platelets contribute ~50% plasma S1P via Mfsd2b (Vu et al., Nature 2017). It is unclear how plasma S1P contributed by blood and endothelial cells for maintenance of blood vessel functions. Here, we plan to determine the mechanisms for S1P release and the molecular roles of plasma S1P for vascular functions. Aim 1: determination of mechanisms for plasma S1P production during development and in postnatal life. Aim 2: determination of mechanisms for physiological roles of plasma S1P in vasculature in normal and pathological conditions. Our central hypothesis is that plasma S1P is a critical factor to regulate blood vessel functions and disruption of its release process will affect vascular functions. The rationale for the proposed research is that the fundamental knowledge obtained will establish the foundation for development of S1P-based therapeutics for treatment of vascular diseases.
kw: lipid signaling, vascular biology, blood vessels, sphingolipids

title: Role of Semaphorin3e-Plexind1 signaling in left ventricular noncompaction (LVNC)
abs: Left ventricular noncompaction (LVNC) is one of the most common forms of genetic cardiomyopathy characterized by excessive trabeculation and impaired myocardial compaction during fetal development. In patients with primary cardiomyopathy of all types, LVNC is the third most common cardiomyopathy after dilated and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. LVNC has been associated with various forms of congenital and adult heart diseases and contributes to cardiac dysfunction. The LVNC phenotype may occur in isolation (22.6%) or associated with other cardiomyopathies such as dilated (58.7%) or hypertrophic (11%) cardiomyopathy. Patients with LVNC are at higher risk of developing systolic and diastolic dysfunction leading to heart failure, arrhythmias, and sudden cardiac death. While key regulators for cardiac chamber development are well studied, the role of Semaphorin-Plexin signaling in this process remains poorly understood. In this study, we propose to use Plxnd1 knockout, endothelium-specific Plxnd1 knockout, transgenic mice overexpressing Plxnd1 in endothelium and Sema3e knockout mice to determine the role of the Sema3e-Plxnd1 signaling pathway in ventricular trabeculation and compaction. Preliminary results demonstrate that genetic deletion of Plexind1 (Plxnd1), a class 3 semaphorin receptor in endothelial cells, leads to severe cardiac chamber defects, as characterized by excessive trabeculation and non-compaction similar to LVNC patients. To further establish the role of Semaphorin-Plexin signaling in ventricular noncompaction, we are doing gain-of-function experiment by generating transgenic mice overexpressing Plxnd1 in endothelial cells. Furthermore, for the first time, we demonstrate that Semaphorin 3e (Sema3e), one of Plxnd1’s ligands is expressed in the developing heart and may be required for myocardial compaction. Collectively, our results demonstrate that the Sema3e-Plxnd1 pathway is essential for myocardial trabeculation and compaction.
kw: LVNC, Semaphorin; Sema3e; Plxnd1; Myocardial trabeculation; Myocardial non-compaction

title: Investigation of the role of polyamines as critical regulators of wound healing
abs: Singapore has a rapidly aging population and the second highest incidence of diabetes globally. Wound healing is compromised with age and diabetic foot ulcers are a significant healthcare problem in diabetic patients. Current treatments to increase the rate of healing in these patients are limited. Understanding the process of wound healing is essential to enable insights into clinically slow-to-heal or non-healing wounds, and to enable the development of therapeutics that will promote healing. We have recently discovered that a group of metabolites called polyamines are critical regulators of wound healing and propose that mis-regulation of polyamines at the wound edge results in a failure or delay in healing which can lead to a chronic non-healing wound. Understanding the cause of and consequence of the changes in polyamine ratios in wound edge cells is essential for their utilization as a therapeutic. This proposal aims to identify the mechanisms by which the polyamines drive wound closure. Polyamines exist largely bound to RNA within the cell so we will determine the molecular targets using genome wide technologies including RNA structural probing, transcriptional and translation profiling. These polyamine targets will then be characterized for their role in cell migration and wound healing. The final aim focuses on determining if the polyamine shift we have shown to be essential for wounding is mis-regulated in chronic wounds. We propose to use a combination of diabetic rat models, human ex vivo wounds and human chronic wound samples to determine if mis-regulation of polyamines is seen in non-healing wounds and if modulation of these levels can promote wound closure. This grant brings together a unique combination of expertise to enable us to examine wound healing in the context of polyamine regulation and RNA biology. This team is ideally positioned to successfully address the unique and challenging questions posed.
kw: Diabetes, Chronic wounds, Polyamines, RNA structure, Gene regulation, Therapeutic targets

title: Modulation of p53 splicing as an approach to improve cancer therapy
abs: Chemo- and radio-therapies are the mainstay of current cancer treatment. Yet, significant side-effects and toxicities are associated with them. Enhancing their therapeutic efficacy will benefit patients tremendously and improve their quality of life. p53 is one of the most-important tumor-suppressers that is activated by, and is required for, the effects of these therapies. Hence, 50% of all patients whose cancers have p53 mutations generally do not respond well to these treatments. Nonetheless, p53 can be activated in the other half of patients with cancers without p53 mutations, to enhance the therapeutic response. In this context, we have recently uncovered that expression of p47, an amino-terminal-truncated isoform of p53, can sensitize cancer cells to cell death in response to cancer drug treatment, due to p47’s ability to selectively transactivate the expression of some apoptotic target genes. p47 is naturally expressed from an alternate p53 mRNA transcript that retains the intron 2 of p53, which represents about 5-10% of all p53 transcripts. Thus, our hypothesis is that inducible retention of p53 intron 2 would lead to enhanced p47 expression in tumor cells and can be a strategy to improve the therapeutic index of standard cancer therapies, especially in cancers with an unmutated p53. Our preliminary results demonstrate an interplay of splicing factors that regulate p53 intron 2 retention. Moreover, based on an initial bio-modelling screen, we have identified several anti-sense oligonucleotides (AONs) that are capable of inducing p53 intron 2 retention. Hence, this proposal aims to perform a comprehensive analysis to characterize the mechanistic basis of p53 intron 2 retention, and to understand its relevance in vivo. Finally, our aim is to exploit the initial findings to evaluate the therapeutic effects of AONs in promoting p53 intron 2 retention, especially in response to therapeutic treatment and tumor growth in vivo.
kw: cancer, intron, p53, splicing, targeting

title: Regulation of monocyte / macrophages metabolism and anti-TB responses by histone deacetylase SIRT1
abs: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the causative agent of tuberculosis (TB), persist within infected cells by hijacking several immune We recently demonstrated that active TB patients have reduced sirtuin 1 (SIRT1) mechanisms. expression and activating SIRT1 by resveratrol induces autophagy and inhibits Mtb growth in mice TB model. SIRT1 is a histone deacetylase and is involved in a range of cellular metabolic and epigenetic processes. Our study indicates the potential of developing SIRT1 activators as an effective and clinically relevant host-directed therapies (HDTs) for TB. We hypothesize that – (i) Mtb mediated reduction in SIRT1 expression result’s in the induction of aerobic glycolysis and perturbation of macrophage metabolism, and (ii) that activating SIRT1 will result in metabolic and epigenetic reprograming, thus negatively regulating TB pathogenesis by suppressing Mtb-induced aerobic glycolysis via targeting mTOR-HIF1a signaling. This will lead to SIRT1-mediated (i) increased innate anti-microbicidal pathways such as autophagy, (ii) dampening of TB pathology, and (iii) increased host-fitness (i.e ability to restrict the growth of bacteria) against pathogen. In this project, we will take parallel and complementary approaches to elucidate the mechanism behind SIRT1-mediated modulation of macrophage metabolism / aerobic glycolysis during Mtb infection. We will perform epigenetic (histone acetylation), transcriptomic and metabolic studies in Mtb-infected human monocytes/macrophages to test whether SIRT1 activation rewires mTOR-HIF1a pathway. Outcome will be validated in mice with targeted disruption of key elements in the proposed pathway. We also hypothesize that the reduced SIRT1 expression seen in TB patients could be linked with SIRT1 gene polymorphisms. Therefore, to understand the role of host genotype on SIRT1-mediated protection against TB we will investigate SIRT1 SNPs (Single Nucleotide polymorphisms) in a Chinese TB cohort. These integrative approaches will help us to identify precise mode of action contributing to SIRT1-mediated enhancement of immunity against Mtb-infection.
kw: Tuberculosis, metabolism, epigenetic, host-directed therapy, sirtuin

title: Non-invasive photoacoustic mesoscopy imaging of clinical skin inflammatory disorders coupled with AI-assisted scoring to evaluate disease prognosis and associated metabolic co-morbidities
abs: Chronic inflammatory skin diseases affect more than 25% of our population and there is strong evidence linking them to metabolic syndrome; putting patients with such dermatoses at risk of cardiovascular events. While metabolic diseases have objective measures to reflect disease severity, chronic inflammatory skin disorders lack such scoring measures and is scored based on clinical questionnaires and are subjected to intra- and inter-observer variations. Non-invasive imaging techniques for assessing the skin vascular structures could potentially serve as objective indicators for these diseases to characterize its severity and understand how inflammation plays a role systemic metabolic co-morbidities. For the first time, we aim to employ photoacoustic (PA) technique- Raster scanning-Optoacoustic Mesoscopy (RSOM) as surrogate clinical measures to objectively characterize the severity of atopic dermatitis and psoriasis. We also aim to automate the classification of disease severity through machine learning and explore vascular features of systemic complications in these inflammatory disorders. Next, we will develop a multiple wavelength-RSOM (Multispectral Optoacoustic Mesoscopy-MSOM) technique to evaluate the saturated oxygen changes in the remodelled vascular networks of the inflammatory skin. To assess and classify these changes and to predict related metabolic co-morbidities, we will be working on the following sub-aims:- 1. Develop customized PAI system, Raster Scanning-Optoacoustic Mesoscopy (RSOM) with optimized transducer frequency for imaging chronic ISD. 2. Develop quantitative new specific RSOM imaging metrics for chronic ISD’s severity and correlate it with the standard clinical scores. 3. Develop Multispectral Optoacoustic Mesoscopy (MSOM) system to evaluate microvascular saturated oxygenation parameters. 4. Develop an artificial-intelligence (AI) approach for accurate and objective classification of ISD from pattern-recognition of MSOM images by using initial RSOM images as training sets. 5. Correlating skin microvasculature and saturation oxygen pattern changes with associated diabetes mellitus using AI to extract disease-specific visual features, which may be used for a downstream classification.
kw: Photoacoustic imaging; Inflammatory Skin Disorders; Metabolic Co-morbidities; Artificial Intelligence; Machine Learning

title: DUSP4 regulates STING-mediated type I interferon production in infection and cancer
abs: Microbial DNA or DNA derived from cancer cells in the cytosol induces potent innate immune responses by inducing the expression of type I interferons (IFNs) and the transcription of type I IFNs is regarded as the dominant response upon the detection of cytosolic DNA. Activation of STING leads to phosphorylation of IRF3 by TBK1 for the production of type I IFNs. Therefore, the STING-TBK1-IRF3 signaling is central for the induction of type I IFNs in response to cytosolic DNA of pathogen- and self-origin. Elucidating the mechanisms that govern the activation and inactivation of this pathway is essential for understanding host-virus interaction, the initiation of anti-tumor innate and adaptive immunity and for targeting this pathway to develop strategies to treat human diseases including viral infection, cancer, as well as autoimmune diseases that are caused by aberrant type I IFN response. However, how this pathway is negatively regulated is unclear. Our preliminary study on a molecule known as DUSP4 demonstrates that this molecule may negatively regulates STING-mediate type I IFN response by inhibiting the activation of both TBK1-IRF3 and ERK. We hypothesize that DUSP4 inhibits STING-mediated signaling including TBK1-IRF3 and ERK to suppress the expression of type I IFNs in response to cytosolic DNA derived from microbial pathogens or cancer cells, thereby playing important roles in anti-microbial and anti-tumor immune responses. In this project, we will address the regulatory roles of DUSP4 in microbial infection and in antitumor immune response. Knowledge gained from this study will shed new light on physiological function of DUSP4 in immune response to viral infection and in cancer immunology, which will help for the development of DUSP4-targeted novel therapeutic methods for treatment of human disease such as cancer.
kw: DUSP; STING; type I interferon; ERK; DNA virus; cancer

title: Using Novel imaging biomarkers to predict Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor inhibitor retreatment load for neovascular Age related Macular Degeneration
abs: Current treatment for neovascular age related macular degeneration (nAMD) requires frequent injections of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) inhibitors. Retreatment strategies are dependent on disease activity assessed at every visit which is defined as a combination of clinical signs and fluid detected in the different compartments of the retina by optical coherence tomography (OCT). This strategy results in large variability of retreatment (4-12 injections per year) and it is currently unknown as to which patients may have higher or lower retreatment requirements. This study aims to use disease features on OCT in the early treatment phase (baseline to month 3) to predict which patient may require low or high retreatment. A “severity score” will be derived by the associations of OCT features detected at baseline and changes of these features at month 3 (assessed by trained graders and with a novel machine-learning (ML) algorithm) with patients with optimal outcomes that have either required high retreatment (≥6 treatments/year) or low retreatment (<6 treatments/year) over 12 and 36 months. This will be a retrospective analysis using data from a comprehensive AMD registry. (2)This score will be validated using a prospective cohort study with patients divided into high/low retreatment groups based on the severity score and treated with standard of care. Primary outcome will be to compare number of injections required over 1 year between groups. Early stratification of patients can help identify those that may require closer monitoring and may have potentially the most benefit from switch in drug. A comprehensive dataset from the validation study can be used to further inform retreatment interval at each visit allowing for even more individualized treatment. Overall these results may change current clinical practice by providing more precision in retreatment decision individualizing management for each patient from visit to visit.
kw: Imaging Biomarkers; AMD; Anti VEGF

title: A Multi-Site Randomized Controlled Trial of a Stepped-Care Intervention for Emergency Department Patients with Panic Attacks and Panic Disorder
abs: Panic disorder is a chronic and disabling psychiatric disorder that is characterized by recurrent panic attacks. Results from our previous studies indicate that up to 50% of Accident and Emergency (A&E) patients with chest pain meet the criteria for panic-related anxiety, but fewer than 1% are currently diagnosed or treated in the local A&E. A stepped-care model, which focuses on providing evidence-based interventions in a resource-efficient manner, is the state-of-the art for treating panic patients in medical settings such as primary care. Stepped-care has not been previously implemented in the A&E setting. This randomized controlled trial (RCT) aims to evaluate the clinical, patient-centered, and economic effectiveness of a stepped-care intervention for patients with panic-related anxiety presenting to the A&E in Singapore’s largest public hospital. The three-year study will follow a two-stage parallel group RCT design with two arms: 1) an enhanced care pathway consisting of a stepped-care intervention for panic attacks and panic disorder; and 2) a control arm consisting of screening for panic attacks and panic disorder in the A&E and discharge. We will randomize 212 patients recruited from the Singapore General Hospital A&E. Screening will be done at the first stage, followed by baseline assessments and blocked randomization in a 1:1 ratio for patients with a confirmed diagnosis of panic attack or panic disorder at the second stage. Masked follow-up assessments will be conducted at 1, 3, 6, and 12 months. Clinical outcomes will be panic symptom severity and rates of panic disorder. Patient-centered outcomes will be health-related quality of life, daily functioning, psychiatric comorbidity, and health services utilization. Economic effectiveness outcomes will be the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of the stepped-care intervention relative to screening alone. The study results will be used to recommend the most cost-effective and clinically meaningful strategy for treating panic patients in the A&E.
kw: panic attacks, panic disorder, stepped-care, cost-effectiveness

title: Pre-empting renal injury ensuing drugs by elucidating microRNA and proteomics of renal tubular dysfunction at its earliest (PRE-EMPTII study)
abs: Drug-induced acute kidney injury (AKI) develops in 13% of patients on nephrotoxic therapy and predisposes to chronic kidney disease. AKI is diagnosed by serial increase in serum creatinine, itself a late biomarker of renal dysfunction. Our preliminary studies demonstrate that urinary KIM1, clusterin, ß2-microglobulin, MCP1, and more recently, select urinary microRNAs, are elevated in days prior to AKI onset in patients versus non-AKI controls, while receiving aminoglycosides or vancomycin. We want to further advance our research by refining the biomarker panel that intercepts drug-induced renal tubular dysfunction at its earliest, well before AKI is evident. First, we will perform exosome analysis of above identified protein biomarkers, to determine if the distinction in levels between cases and controls could be exemplified at >3 days prior to drug-induced AKI, using our biobank urine samples. Next, the selected microRNAs we discovered will be correlated to inducible injury microRNAs in vitro to examine for reproducibility, using a microfluidic human renal proximal tubule cell-model with nephrotoxic insult from antimicrobials, calcineurin-inhibitors, and anti-cancer drugs. The area under receiver operating characteristic curve of these more selective protein and microRNA biomarkers or their combination for AKI prediction at its earliest, will be determined in our current 130 patient-cohort, to derive few better performing biomarkers. Concurrently, we will recruit 150 patients over 1.5 years, prescribed with similar drugs; We will collect urine samples at intervals guided by known AKI trajectory from commencement of respective drugs. Their samples will be batch-analyzed, and the refined biomarker panel for AKI prediction will be validated. The refined biomarker panel would be implemented for real-time analysis to allow fluidity of detecting patients at highest risk of AKI during nephrotoxic therapy. It will be examined in a clinical trial to triage patients for pre-emptive drug cessation or dose reduction to effectively prevent drug-induced AKI.
kw: Drug induced acute kidney injury; urinary biomarkers; exosome proteomics; microfluidic model; microRNA; nephrotoxicity;

title: Preventing limb losses in Singapore through health literacy and healthcare improvements
abs: Diabetic foot ulcers (DFU) are the leading cause of amputations and mortality among patients with diabetes. Worryingly, Singaporean statistics indicate a faster rate of ulcer deterioration and higher rates of amputations compared to most other countries. The current applied care model in Singapore is acute-centric and does not sufficiently consider strategies for prevention and self-care. The aim is to support more efficient prevention and management of DFUs and thereby reduce the number of DFUs and its progression to limb loss. The hypothesis is that this can be achieved through: 1) Evidence-based prevention; 2) Better care co-ordination; 3) Improved understanding about the gaps in the provision and deviations from care guidelines; and 4) Enhanced self-care of people with DFUs or at risk of developing a DFU through an app-based educational program targeting patients, informal caregivers and foreign domestic workers The work by the national Diabetes Prevention and Care Taskforce to fight diabetes will be complemented by focusing on the prevention and management of DFUs. Current everyday care related to DFUs will be investigated to outline treatment pathways and identify possible gaps in the provision of care. Additionally, patients, informal caregivers and foreign domestic workers will be surveyed on their knowledge on preventing and caring for DFU and current care provision and monitoring. An app will be developed and evaluated supporting evidence-based practice through eLearning for the prevention and caring of DFUs directed towards patients, informal caregivers and foreign domestic workers. Health economic modelling will demonstrate potential gains through better healthcare coordination, evidence based prevention and more advanced self-care. Taken together, the proposed research activities will help to maximize the potential of available resources for preventing and caring of DFUs in Singapore, enable earlier identification of patients prone to develop microvascular complications, decrease the number of complications, and demonstrate savings in costs and improvements in quality-of-life.
kw: Disease Management; Self-care; Diabetic foot; Health literacy; Guideline adherence; eLearning

title: Identifying new cell surface receptor(s) for the WNT enhancer R-SPONDINS ligands
abs: The canonical WNT signaling pathway plays crucial roles during embryonic development and cancer. The R-spondin family of secreted ligands (RSPO1-RSPO4) act as WNT enhancers by preventing WNT receptor degradation mediated by the RNF43/ZNRF3 E3 Ubiquitin ligases. Up until now, the R-spondins were believed to exclusively act via their obligate LGR4/5/6 cognate receptors, which together would interact with the RNF43/ZNRF3 ligases to prevent them from ubiquitinating WNT receptors for degradation. However, we recently discovered that the LGR4/5/6 receptors are surprisingly dispensable for RSPO2 and RSPO3 functions during vascular, limb and lung development, suggesting that R-spondins can signal through hitherto unknown receptor(s). In this proposal, we aim to (1) identify these unknown R-spondin receptor(s) using two distinct approaches that will make use of LGR4/5/6 triple-knockout and RNF43/ZNRF3 double-knockout mouse cell lines, and (2) characterize them in vivo, through loss- and gain-of-function studies. Firstly, we will perform a CRISPR-Cas9 screen using the SUPERTOPFLASH luciferase system as a direct readout for WNT signaling, and look for genetic mutations that impact the ability of exogenous RSPO2/RSPO3 to potentiate WNT signaling. In parallel, we will use the Proximity Labeling with Ascorbate Peroxidase (APEX) technique to label and identity the R-spondin receptors. RSPO2/3-APEX fusion proteins will be incubated on LGR4/5/6 triple-knockout and RNF43/ZNRF3 double-knockout mouse cell lines, allowing the identification and quantification of interactions between these ligands and their receptors at the cell surface. These two independent and complementary approaches are expected to lead to the discovery of new R-spondin receptor(s), which in turn will shed fundamental insights on WNT signaling by deciphering R-spondins functions and modes of action. This research will have immediate translational implications in cell biology, development and oncology, and carries the patent potential for identifying new targets for innovative therapies against WNT-associated diseases and cancers such as, but not limited to, colorectal cancer.
kw: R-spondins; LGR; WNT signaling; Development; Cancer

title: A mechanistic study of epigenetic regulation by PBRM1 towards targeted therapy in clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC)
abs: An in-depth knowledge of the epigenetic mechanisms that drive cancer initiation, development and progression can enhance our understanding of tumorigenesis and provide opportunities for better diagnosis and novel therapy. We previously found that polybromo-1 (PBRM1), an accessory subunit of the SWItch/Sucrose-Non-Fermentable (SWI/SNF) nucleosome remodeling complex, is the second most commonly mutated gene in clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC, 40%) (Varela, Nature). Additionally, we demonstrated that the loss of PBRM1 is indispensable for ccRCC initiation in genetic mouse models (Nargund, Cell Reports). Despite its importance, the epigenetic function of PBRM1 remains largely obscure, due to the lack of genome-wide PBRM1- binding profiles and detailed profiling of chromatin changes upon PBRM1 loss. Here, we seek to elucidate how PBRM1 regulates the chromatin with the hypothesis that tumorigenic genes are liberated epigenetically upon PBRM1 inactivation (Aim 1). Consequently, we like to understand how the downstream targets of PBRM1 affect ccRCC development and initiation (Aim 2). Finally, with the deciphered mechanisms we may be able to pinpoint new druggable targets that are synthetically lethal with the loss of PBRM1 (Aim 3). Mechanistic understanding of driver mutations can identify vulnerabilities specific to cancer. CcRCC has two main drivers – VHL and PBRM1. Recent study by our team has showed that the first driver event, VHL loss, epigenetically triggers master regulators of ccRCC through enhancer activation and paved the technical groundwork for this study (Yao, Cancer Discovery). Characterizing the second driver PBRM1 will complete a major milestone in understanding epigenetic malfunction of ccRCC. Our study is also applicable to other cancer types, as the loss of PBRM1 is also one of the top drivers for them. Importantly, we hope that findings from our study can lead to targeted and effective treatment for patients harboring these driver mutations, and translate into better patient survival and life quality.
kw: ccRCC, epigenomics, PBRM1, drugs

title: Investigating the role of the primary angle closure glaucoma (PACG) susceptibility gene, PLEKHA7 in PLEKHA7-/- mutant rats
abs: Glaucoma is characterized by retinal ganglion cell and optic nerve axonal loss resulting in glaucomatous optic neuropathy. Primary angle closure glaucoma (PACG), a major form of glaucoma and visual loss in Singapore and Asia, is defined by the presence of iris-angle contact. Iris-angle contact can cause aqueous outflow obstruction and intraocular pressure (IOP) elevation progressing to PACG. The molecular effects underlying this progression is unknown and represents the current gap in knowledge. PLEKHA7, a recently identified PACG-susceptibility gene, encodes a pleckstrin homology domain containing GTPase-activating protein that is functionally related to cellular adhesion and extracellular matrix (ECM) remodelling. In normal eyes, PLEKHA7 expression is present in PACG-related structures: iris, non-pigmented ciliary epithelium (NPCE), trabecular meshwork (TM), and choroid. In tissues (iris and lens capsule) obtained from PACG eyes, a significant downregulation of PLEKHA7 mRNA expression is present when compared to controls, suggesting that reduced levels of PLEKHA7 may contribute to PACG pathophysiology. Furthermore, we found that in vitro silencing of PLEKHA7 expression led to decreased cellular adhesion in NPCE cells and reduced contractility of TM cells. In our colony of homozygous (Plekha7-/-), heterozygous (Plekha7-/+) and wild type (WT) rats which have ablated and normal expression of Plekha7 respectively, young Plekha7-/- rats compared to WT littermates have a phenotype related to PACG risk—shallower anterior chambers, narrower angles and elevated IOP. Based on these findings, we aim to use Plekha7 mutant rats as an in vivo system to study the ocular effects of PLEKHA7 downregulation. We will study the Plekha7 ocular phenotype, particularly, degree of iris-angle contact with age and provocation (Aims 1 & 2); as well as altered cellular adhesion and ECM remodelling pathways (Aim 3) in PACG tissues specifically related to choroidal thickness and loss of barrier integrity in order to determine the role of PLEKHA7 in PACG.
kw: PLEKHA7; PACG; Cellular adhesion; Extracellular matrix

title: Early Detection and Novel Treatment Through Epigenomic Studies in Endemic Asian Cancers
abs: It is well-known that Asian-prevalent cancers are often associated with a pathogen or carcinogen. For example, hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is associated with Hepatitis B and C viruses, gastric cancer Helicobacter pylori, and nasopharyngeal cancer Epstein-Barr virus. Increasingly, more and more studies are pointing towards epigenomic changes that are associated with chronic carcinogenic exposures – these causative changes may be manipulated not only for diagnostic detection but also for therapeutic intervention using emerging epigenetic drugs. For scientific studies, we propose to study the underlying epigenomic changes related to chronic exposure to their respective carcinogen – liver fluke (Opisthorchis viveriini) for biliary tract cancer (cholangiocarcinoma) and aristolochic acid for hepatobiliary cancer. More specifically we will profile and study DNA and histone modifications as well as RNA-seq (expression) in these cancers and carcinogen exposure in model systems, on both the bulk and single cell level. For translation studies in biomarker development, we will focus on DNA hydroxy-methylation and methylation, non-coding RNA (e.g. miRNA, lncRNA) all of which can be further validated in a very large number of liquid samples like plasma and urine. These biomarkers will have potential for both early detection screening and disease monitoring. For translation studies into novel drug development, we will particularly pay attention to epigenetic targets and epigenetic drugs. These findings, coupled with further molecular, biochemical, proteomic, in vitro and in vivo studies will hopefully shed light on how chronic exposures of these agents contribute to epigenomic changes and subsequently tumorigenesis. Our studies will also allow us to explore the accumulative strength of combining epigenetic drugs and other forms of treatment modalities. Through these studies, we will take our research to a greater height, from making new breakthroughs to translating research findings to clinical applications, and preventing or reducing the cancer risks in different populations.
kw: Cancer; Carcinogen; Epigenomic; Tumorigenesis; Biomarkers; Therapy

title: Identifying distinct immune cell subpopulations in colorectal cancer using single cell transcriptomics and evaluating their spatio-biological interactions in fixed issues
abs: The tumor micro-environment comprises diverse cell populations, ecologically interacting and influencing overall tumor architecture, oncologic phenotypes and clinical behavior. Immune-tumor cell interactions (e.g. PD-1/PDL1 axis) are now viable targets in oncology with unprecedented regulatory approvals of immune checkpoint inhibitors in multiple cancer-types. However, in colorectal cancer (CRC), a globally prevalent cancer, results of clinical trials of drugs targeting PD1/PDL1 & CTLA4/B7 interactions have been disappointing. There is an unmet need to unravel the mediators of the immune millieu in colorectal cancer. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) can identify and characterize distinct immune cell subsets and the transcriptional signatures of these immune cells make it possible to dissect the contribution of different cell types/states within the tumor micro-environment. Recently, we performed a proof-of-concept study with early-generation single-cell transcriptomic technologies(Li, Nat Genet '17) analyzing ~500 cells from 11 patients Building upon this work, we have entered into an academic-industry collaboration to generate single-cell transcriptomes from over 6,000 cells per patient from 50 CRC patients. Using data generated from this dataset, we seek to describe the diversity of immune cell subpopulations in colorectal cancer and their clinicopathologic and molecular correlates (Aim 1). We will FACS-sort major immune cell lineages and generate scRNASeq to describe major immune cell type subclusters and examine distinct gene expression profiles of these immune cell clusters. Next, we will validate these distinct cell states with mass cytometry and then describe the spatial context and interactions of immune cell subpopulations in fixed colorectal cancer tumor tissue (Aim 2) using archival FFPE tissue microarrays from both the 50 patients and a retrospective cohort of 158 genomic-ally annotated CRC patients. Together, we seek to understand the cellular heterogeneity composing the tumor microenvironment which is key to improving existing treatments, discovery of predictive biomarkers, and development of novel therapeutic strategies in colorectal cancer.
kw: single cell RNA sequencing, colorectal cancer

title: Precision oncology approach to identification and expansion of tumor-targeting cytotoxic T-lymphocytes in head and neck squamous cell cancer
abs: Given the limited efficacy of targeted therapy, there is tremendous interest in the role of immunotherapy in treating patients with head and neck squamous-cell carcinoma(HNSCC). Despite the presence of tumor-infiltrating T-cells(TILs), most tumors evade the immune system, suggesting these are dysfunctional. Drugs inhibiting immune-checkpoint receptors(ICB) are intended to reverse this, but are effective in less than 20% of patients.
