Conventional therapy further depletes effective cytotoxic T-cell(CTL) populations, which is evident in trials where neo-adjuvant ICB therapy appears to be more effective than the adjuvant setting. Undoubtedly, there is a need to reconfigure treatment strategies such that ICBs are instituted when effective CTL-populations are more prevalent. Therefore, we hypothesize that untreated tumors contain the most effective source of CTLs capable of targeting more heterogenous populations of cancer cells. We will utilize a number of unbiased and marker-based strategies to identify tumor-targeting T-cells in untreated primary/metastatic lymph-nodes, and matched tumor recurrences using single-cell analysis and high-dimensional flow cytometry. Functional efficacy of specific subpopulations will be tested by expanding these in TIL-cultures, and tested in cytotoxicity assays against matched, patient-derived tumor culture. Markers for tumor-targeting CTLs will also be validated in independent cohorts of treatment-naïve and ICB-treated tumors. Our secondary hypothesis posits that exhaustion status vary between(requiring individualization), and within patients(primary versus metastatic versus recurrent tumors), hence require different strategies to re-invigorate CTL-based cytotoxicity. To address this, we will compare drivers of exhaustion across tumors to identify differences amenable to specific ICB-therapy. Alternatively, we will set up medium-throughput screens to identify drugs that enhance CTL-based killing of matched tumor-cells, to uncover actionable differences between T-cell reactivation in these states. The eventual aim is to identify the best source and CTL sub-population with the ability to maximize tumor kill, either through immunomodulation with drugs, or to effect cellular therapy with expanded, bio-banked CTL populations.
kw: Immuno-oncology; CTL; cytotoxicity assay; Immunotherapy; CD8; T-cell receptor

title: Clinical evaluation of a novel 20-gene signature as a biomarker and metabolic target in breast cancer stem cells
abs: There is much work on developing strategies to target breast cancer stem cells (CSCs), which exhibit intrinsic resistance to conventional treatments. We have recently identified a novel gene signature comprising of 20 genes related to oxidative phosphorylation from functional CSC assays using patient-derived tumourspheres. We hypothesise that this signature is a more sensitive CSC marker than existing ones and may predict tumour sensitivity to oxidative phosphorylation inhibitors such as metformin. We also found metformin to be effective in chemo-resistant cells. Primary objectives are to evaluate this 20-gene signature as an indicator of CSC subpopulation size and to determine the effect of metformin on CSCs. Secondary objective is to establish patient-derived xenografts for future characterisation. The 20-gene signature will be evaluated in non-diabetic women prior to and after completing neoadjuvant chemotherapy in combination with metformin, and will be correlated with known CSC markers using NanoString technology, and with proliferative and apoptotic markers using immunohistochemistry. The association with pathological response will also be examined. Analyses will be stratified according to tumour subtype, to account for variations in chemotherapy regimen. A similar evaluation will be carried out in diabetic women undergoing neoadjuvant chemotherapy, stratified according to whether they receive metformin for diabetic treatment or otherwise. The correlation with CSCs will be further validated in 2 cohorts known for CSC enrichment: pre- and post-chemotherapy pairs and primary and matched recurrent tumour pairs. To validate the association with prognosis, recurrent tumours from the cohort will be compared with matched controls consisting of tumours from women who did not relapse; controls will be matched in terms of disease stage, tumour subtype, histological classification, treatments received. Findings will provide insight into the potential of the 20-gene signature as a CSC marker and as a therapeutic target.
kw: breast cancer stem cells; oxidate phosphorylation

title: Brown fat activation and browning Efficiency Augmented by Chronic COld and Nutraceuticals for Brown adipose tissue-mediated Effect Against Metabolic Syndrome (BEACON BEAMS Study)
abs: Specific Aims and Hypotheses: Having proven that brown adipose tissue (BAT) in adults can be acutely activated by cold and capsinoids, we will now investigate the effectiveness of chronic cold exposure and BAT-activating nutraceuticals in raising energy expenditure, fat oxidation, white adipose tissue (WAT) browning into beige fat to induce weight loss and improve metabolic syndrome regardless of initial BAT status. Methodology and Approach: We will recruit subjects with metabolic syndrome (n=80) and randomize them into 3 parallel intervention arms (n=20 each: daily cold exposure with cooling vest over 1 h, daily intake of BAT-activating nutraceuticals, or a combination of cold exposure and BAT-activating nutraceuticals) together with a control arm. We will employ BAT and WAT assessment protocols including infrared thermography (IRT), fat fraction MRI, 18F-FDG-PET and whole body calorimetry (WBC). The WAT browning mix of functional food spices consisting of capsinoids and curcumin will serve as a ‘food-based’ method to induce thermogenesis through BAT. Subjects will be evaluated at baseline and re-evaluated at 12 weeks, following which all interventions will be discontinued and the subjects re-evaluated at 24 weeks to determine any reversal of browning, BAT, WAT, fat oxidation, metabolic rate and selected biomarkers. Importance to Science or Medicine: This research will reveal the nature of BAT and WAT plasticity under chronic cold and nutraceuticals. It will address establish the safety and efficacy of BAT-activating methods on accentuating metabolic rate and fat oxidation to counter obesity and diabetes independent of food intake and physical activity. Clinical Significance: In our obesogenic environment where energy dense food and physical inactivity are major factors driving the rising scourge of metabolic disorders, it fits our national interest to develop promising non-pharmacological, safe and natural BAT-activating approaches that tackle obesity and diabetes feasibly adopted by the general population.
kw: Brown adipose tissue; White adipose tissue; Browning; Metabolic rate; Imaging; Whole body calorimetry

title: Effects of Dapagliflozin and Metformin on Vascular Function in Newly-Diagnosed Treatment-Naïve Type 2 Diabetes – A Randomized Controlled Trial (DMVascular Study)
abs: The DMVascular study aims to address the impact of early medical therapeutics on vascular function. This stems from the provocative central hypothesis that reduction in cardiovascular risk with glucose-lowering therapies is a result of their beneficial effects on endothelial function, and absolute effect on the vascular risk profile, and is beyond glycaemic control. Recently sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) have been shown to lower cardiovascular risk and mortality within months of initiating treatment, suggestive of early haemodynamic or vascular function enhancements. The primary objective is to determine which vascular processes are specifically enhanced with Dapagliflozin (an SGLT2i) in comparison with Metformin and if its effect is the same in combination treatment in a randomized controlled study involving treatment-naive individuals. Our specific aims are to evaluate the effects of the intervention on: (Aim 1): microvascular and macrovascular function comprehensively inclusive of vascular haemodynamics at retinal and peripheral capillaries, radial artery, brachial artery, carotid artery and aortic artery; inflammation and oxidative stress in order to elucidate the specific pathway which is affected by SGLT2i; (Aim 2): the haemodynamics (involving blood pressure regulation) by studying the sodium equipoise, intrarenal renin-angiotensin and systemic sympathetic and parasympathetic systems; (Aim 3): leukocyte-endothelial interactions using bio-mimetic blood vessel-on-chip in-vitro models. Our proposed study is significant as this study has the potential to reveal SGLT2i and metformin specific vascular processes which can be exploited to uncover novel targets or to personalise/stratify patients who will benefit most from these medications. This approach is innovative as we propose to study all the interrelated vascular and haemodynamic pathways comprehensively using novel methods to evaluate the microvascular and macrovascular functions to gain mechanistic insight into the positive effects of early therapeutics in newly diagnosed T2DM individuals.
kw: Diabetes; Vascular function; SGLT2 inhibitors

title: Patient, Physician, and Organizational Factors Influencing Decision-Making for Antibiotic Use, and N-of-1 Trials of Interventions to Improve the Decision-Making
abs: Upper respiratory tract infection (URTI) is a commonly-cited reason for antibiotic use, although antibiotics are not clinically indicated for the majority. Antibiotic misuse drives antimicrobial resistance. Antibiotic prescribing for URTIs at emergency departments (EDs) is complex and influenced by many patient-, physician-, and organizational-level factors. The proposed research will be conducted over 2 phases in 4 adult EDs that provide Singapore-wide coverage. Phase 1 will involve mixed methods studies on physicians and patients that include questionnaire surveys and in-depth interviews to better understand the multi-level psychosocial, cultural, and systemic determinants of antibiotic prescribing. Based on findings from Phase 1, a multicenter stepped-wedge cluster randomized trial will be conducted in Phase 2 to evaluate the effectiveness of tailored interventions targeting at: 1) patient- (patient education via tailored information leaflets that address local knowledge gaps and misconceptions), 2) physician- (senior physician education through active outreach efforts), and 3) organizational- (clinical decision support tool via mobile or desktop app, based on local epidemiology) levels, in reducing unnecessary antibiotic use. The N-of-1 trials study design will be used to gain a deeper understanding of prescribing practices at the individual physician level in response to the interventions. Unlike conventional methods that evaluate intervention effectiveness for an average physician practicing in an adult ED, the N-of-1 trials will enable the assessment of the interventions that work for individual physicians and allow the design of personalized interventions. With Singapore’s rapidly ageing population, who are more prone to infections and exposure to antibiotics, tailored-interventions after elucidation of root causes for unnecessary antibiotic use that target patient-, physician-, and organizational-level factors in EDs, are necessary to curb the rising tide of antimicrobial resistance amidst the background of a dwindling antibiotic pipeline. This research study will contribute to the limited international understanding of the determinants for antibiotic prescribing in EDs.
kw: Antimicrobial stewardship; Antimicrobial resistance; Antibiotic prescribing; Antibiotic use; Upper respiratory tract infection; Emergency department

title: Innovative Telemonitored Home-Based Program for Post Total Knee Replacement Rehabilitation: A Noninferiority Randomized Controlled Trial
abs: Background and Aims With an ageing population and an increasing prevalence of obesity and knee osteoarthritis, the number of total knee replacement (TKR) surgery will increase with time. In Singapore, although hospital-based outpatient rehabilitation is standard-of-care for patients post TKR, outpatient rehabilitation is costly and inconvenient for patients and their caregivers. A monitored home-based exercise program provides the best access to care and is an alternative for patients who do not require intensive "hands-on" rehabilitation. We have developed a tele-monitored home-based rehabilitation program and aim to compare the clinical- and cost-effectiveness of this innovative program with that of standard hospital-based rehabilitation among post-TKR patients in a randomized controlled trial (RCT). Hypotheses We hypothesize that an 8-week home-based exercise program, combined with tele-monitoring, will not be clinically inferior to an 8-week hospital-based rehabilitation program at 6 months post TKR, in terms of improving physical functional outcomes, and that the home-based program will be more cost-effective than the hospital-based rehabilitation program. Methods This will be a single assessor-blinded, parallel design, RCT. One hundred thirty patients with TKR will be randomly assigned to either an 8-week hospital-based, physiotherapist-supervised rehabilitation program or an 8-week tele-monitored home-based program. To monitor patients’ functional recovery, the home-based program will use rehabilitation tools and monitoring devices that have been validated for use by patients after TKR. Outcome measures will be collected preoperatively and at 1, 3, and 6 months post TKR. The primary outcome will be physical function. Secondary outcomes include healthcare costs, knee pain intensity, knee impairments, and quality of life. Significance This study is the first in Singapore to examine an innovative and affordable solution for delivering post-TKR rehabilitation services. If successful, the home-based program has the potential to serve as a model for managing knee osteoarthritis and other costly, chronic musculoskeletal conditions to which exercise therapy is beneficial.
kw: Total Knee Replacement; Rehabilitation, Cost-effectiveness, Technology

title: Modulating Endoplasmic Reticulum Stress as a prophylactic approach against symptomatic viral infection.
abs: Zoonotic pathogens continue to emerge to threaten human health at an even quicker pace since the turn of this century but vaccines and drugs development lag behind these outbreaks. Therefore it is imperative that we advance our understanding of the molecular basis of host-viral interaction that define clinical outcome to gain insights into how such epidemics can be effectively managed. Using the live-attenuated yellow fever 17D vaccine to induce a mild acute viral illness, we have now shown in two separate studies that baseline adaptive endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress and compensatory reduced tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle activity increased susceptibility to symptomatic infection: Infection in such individuals triggered maladaptive ER stress response with production of reactive oxygen species (ROS). ROS in turn triggered downstream innate immune and pro-inflammatory responses that correlated with symptomatic infection. Metformin, a widely used anti-diabetic drug has recently been shown to act on multiple pathways in the cell, in addition to its anti-glycemia function. One of its functions is ER stress modulation. Our preliminary data also showed that metformin reduced the expression of key intermediates in the ER-stress induced apoptotic pathway, suggesting its potential to reduce maladaptive ER stress and subsequent cell death. The goal of this proposal is thus to show proof-of-concept that modulating ER stress alone with metformin, can reduce the rate of symptomatic viral infection. We will employ a placebo-controlled experimental medicine approach to test the utility and efficacy of metformin as a ER stress modulator to reduce the likelihood of symptomatic YF17D infection, complemented with comprehensive omics-level analyses to define how metformin modulates the host response to YF17D infection and thus alter symptomatic outcome. If successful, this study would clarify a poorly understood but clinically important aspect of host-viral interaction and show a therapeutic pathway to minimize the impact of emerging viral epidemics.
kw: Metformin; endoplasmic reticulum stress; YF17D infection; symptomatic; metabolic; immunometabolism

title: Clinical and Translational Research in Movement Disorders
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Essential Tremor (ET) and Parkinson’s disease (PD) are two of the most common movement disorders and have underlying genetic etiologies. Identification of disease pathogenic variants, followed by studies of these variants in in vivo and in vitro models will shed light on the key molecular mechanisms/pathways and help identify new therapeutic targets. We aim to establish a resource containing prospective clinical and genetic data for different subsets of ET patients from our Asian population. Samples will include those from familial ET, sporadic ET, coexistent ET and PD (those who presented initially as ET but later developed PD), healthy controls and disease controls (enhanced physiological tremor). We will generate induced pleuripotent stem cell (IPSC) derived neurons (Purkinje cells, GABA neurons, serotonergic neurons and dopaminergic neurons) from these subjects, and also transgenic Drosophila models expressing novel and known ET gene mutations (such as FUS and TENM4 etc) and using these iPSC and isogenic lines and transgenic Drosophila models, to conduct RNA-seq and ribosomal profiling to identify potential therapeutic targets. In addition, we will develop cerebellum and midbrain organoids from different subsets of ET patients to uncover any potential deficits in Purkinje neurons and their neural networks, and to investigate any potential degeneration in the midbrain. Separately, we aim to conduct a prospective clinical study to evaluate motor and non motor clinical progression in PD patients who are carriers of the LRRK2 protective variants, compared to LRRK2 risk variants and those carrying both the risk and the protective variants and to conduct RNA-seq of newly synthesized mRNA from dopaminergic neurons in the different groups of transgenic Drosophila expressing these variants and validate the top genes/targets that have been identified using cell based assays, post-mortem specimens from human LRRK2 carriers, human IPSC-derived neurons, transgenic LRRK2 mice and Drosophila.
kw: Parkinson’s disease; Movement Disorders; essential tremor; clinical; treatment

title: Targeting orphan GPR146 to treat hypercholesterolemia and atherosclerosis
abs: Increased circulating LDL-C and TG levels are major causal risk factors for atherosclerotic cardiovascular diseases (ASCVD). Many lines of evidence collected from our previous work, including human genetic association analysis and studies in animal models, have unequivocally established an important role of orphan G protein-coupled receptor 146 (GPR146) in regulating hypercholesterolemia and atherosclerosis. To address the unmet medical needs of lacking potent lipid-lowering oral medication for the treatment of homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (HoFH), in the current proposal, we seek to achieve a critical therapy developmental milestone for GPR146 from three domains, including lipid-lowering mechanism, human genetic association, and tool compounds, all of which will reinforce our studies of GPR146 to a novel oral lipid-lowering medication eventually. Therefore, we propose to focus on three fundamental questions, including: (1) How GPR146 regulates circulating ANGPTL3 levels and whether depletion of them has synergistic effects on lowering plasma lipids? (2) Whether GPR146 plays causal roles in regulating plasma LDL-C/TG levels in human and what is the dominant downstream signaling pathway of GPR146 linked to lipid traits in human (canonical cAMP production or beta-arrestin recruitment)? (3) How to translate GPR146 biology into a new lipid-lowering therapy? Correspondingly, we propose to: (Aim 1) elucidate the molecular mechanism by which GPR146 regulates circulating ANGPTL3 levels, as well as the physiological function of GPR146-ANGPTL3 axis in regulating circulating LDL-C and TG levels; (Aim 2) characterize GPR146 coding variants identified in UK Biobank 200k exomes in a systematic manner; (Aim 3) screen agonists and inverse agonists targeting GPR146. If successful, this study will allow us to achieve a critical milestone for translating GPR146 biology into a new lipid-lowering oral medication, thus addressing the unmet medical need for the treatment of HoFH.
kw: familial hypercholesterolemia; atherosclerosis; genome-wide association study, G protein-coupled receptor

title: Investigation of prefrontal neural circuits that modulates prepulse inhibition, a major endophenotype of schizophrenia.
abs: Prepulse inhibition (PPI) is a phenomenon in which a weak stimulus can suppress the startle response to a subsequent strong startle stimulus. PPI is one of the operational measures of sensorimotor gating, which refers to the process by which the neural system gates extraneous external and internal stimuli to prevent information overload. Although clinical studies in humans have shown that PPI is deficient in Schizophrenia and other neuropsychological disorders, the underlying cellular, molecular, and circuit mechanism underlying PPI mediation and modulation are still elusive. Using our cutting-edge experimental setup that enables simultaneous in situ monitoring of acoustic startle reflex (ASR) and PPI in head-fixed, awake-behaving animals and in vivo Ca2+ imaging using a two-photon microscope, we observed that Ca2+ transients, which correlate with neuronal activities, from the overall neuronal population within the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), are decreased when both prepulse and startle stimuli (PPI) are presented, indicating that the local inhibition within the ACC microcircuit may suppress the startle reflex. And this local inhibition mechanism may underlie the PPI modulation within the ACC. Among multiple types of inhibitory interneurons (INs), we focus on parvalbumin (PV)-positive INs because their dysfunction has been widely implicated in Schizophrenia and our preliminary finding strongly support the modulatory role of PV INs in PPI modulation within the ACC. In this proposal, we hypothesize that PV interneurons in the ACC modulate sensorimotor gating during PPI upon ASR. Outcomes from our proposal will provide a detailed network-level understanding of the neurophysiological alterations that may contribute to Schizophrenia and related psychiatric disorders.
kw: Prefrontal cortex; pre-pulse inhibition; in vivo imaging; schizophrenia; systems neuroscience

title: SINGAPORE ANGLE CLOSURE GLAUCOMA PROGRAM: FROM GENETICS TO PRECISION MEDICINE AND THERAPY
abs: Glaucoma is the leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide, with primary angle closure glaucoma (PACG) a major form of glaucoma in Singapore and Asia. For the past decade, my research program has made substantial contributions to the understanding of the epidemiology, risk factors, genetics, imaging features, clinical phenotype and management of PACG. However, we have almost no data to inform clinical practice about which individuals are at greatest risk for developing advanced PACG and blindness. While we have made advances via genome wide association studies and have identified common genetic variants that increase risk for PACG, there is a need to identify and evaluate more genetic factors for PACG via whole exome sequencing in order to uncover new genetic risk factors, pathways/mechanisms and thus potentially new treatments to prevent blindness. We hope to integrate novel genetic and ocular biomarkers of PACG using a multimodal artificial intelligence approach in order to identify individuals with highest risk of advanced visual loss so as to develop and enhance personalized management strategies for PACG. We will then validate this new algorithm for the prediction of advanced PACG using prospectively ascertained clinic-based cohorts. Finally, with the identification of new genes with deleterious rare variants conferring large effect sizes from whole exome sequencing, we need to understand better the biological impact and physiological relevance of new gene(s) and their role in the PACG disease process. Such genetic findings have the potential to illuminate therapeutic targets. This program will capitalize on the multi-disciplinary team of clinician-scientists and researchers with unique access to clinical data and DNA that we have collected over a decade from on-going studies in Singapore. Furthermore, we have a network of international collaborators with access to global PACG data, and have demonstrated our ability to lead and utilize these datasets for important findings.
kw: Primary angle closure glaucoma; exome sequencing; Ophthalmic genetics; imaging, gene function, risk prediction

title: Precision Medicine in Systemic Sclerosis Gastrointestinal Disease: Evaluating Imaging and Stool Biomarkers for Differentiating Disease Stages and Treatment Responses
abs: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) has one of the highest mortalities among autoimmune diseases (66% 10-year survival), with SSc-associated gastrointestinal disease (SSc-GI) the second highest cause. Intestinal failure leading to malabsorption necessitates costly long-term parenteral nutrition. Although one of the earliest manifestations of disease, SSc-GI is often diagnosed late after fibrosis has occurred. Unmet needs in SSc-GI management are non-invasive biomarkers for (i) early diagnosis (ii) differentiation of SSc-GI stages and (iii) treatment response. We hypothesize that SSc-GI fibrosis is preceded by an early inflammatory stage that represents a window of opportunity for immunosuppressive treatment. Aim 1: Determine if imaging biomarkers differentiate patients with early SSc from those with late SSc. Stool markers will be used as secondary biomarkers supporting inflammation. Aim 2: Evaluate imaging biomarker change over a 6- and 12-month treatment period with mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) in patients with early SSc. Stool markers will be used as secondary biomarkers supporting inflammation. Exploratory aim: To map imaging and stool biomarkers over one year in untreated patients with early SSc Methods: We will use combined 18F-Fluorodeoxyglucose-positron emission tomography and magnetic resonance imaging T1-MOLLI mapping as a novel tool to distinguish inflammation from fibrosis as the predominant pathological process in the bowel wall. Stool biomarkers indicative of an inflammatory state, will be derived using metagenomic analysis of the microbiota, metabolomics and faecal-calprotectin. In a cross-sectional study (Aim 1), we will compare biomarkers between patients with early [pre-scleroderma stage of “Very early diagnosis of SSc” or ≤3 years onset; (n=40)] and late SSc (>5 years onset; n=20). In symptomatic early SSc patients (n=25), we will determine change in biomarkers after 6 and 12 months of MMF (Aim 2). Significance: Non-invasive biomarkers that enable stratification of SSc-GI disease stages and treatment response will greatly advance the field in SSc by enhancing evaluation of SSc-GI.
kw: systemic sclerosis, imaging, microbiota, biomarkers, gastrointestinal

title: Studies on low-cost and novel therapies for NASH
abs: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is the leading cause of liver disease worldwide and occurs in approximately 40% of the adult population in Singapore. NAFLD frequently accompanies obesity and diabetes, and represents a disease spectrum that includes hepatosteatosis, steatohepatitis (NASH) and cirrhosis. While hepatosteatosis is thought to be relatively benign, NASH requires intervention in order to prevent its progression to cirrhosis. Currently, there is no available pharmacologic therapy to treat this condition. Since my last CSA application 5 years ago, we have identified three very promising and low-cost potential treatments for NASH: 1) Thyroid hormone (TH) stimulates hepatic autophagy,b-oxidation of fatty acids, and mitochondrial turnover. Additionally, the intrahepatic concentration of T3, the active form of TH, was decreased in a rodent model of NASH. Our studies in diabetic patients with NAFLD, showed that levothyroxine can decrease hepatosteatosis. 2) Short chain fatty acids (SCFAs) produced by gut microbiota can stimulate hepatic autophagy and oxidative phosphorylation, suggesting that they may be able to reduce hepatosteatosis and improve NASH. 3) Vitamin B12/folate decreased serum homocysteine levels and hepatic inflammation and fibrosis. We also observed hyperhomocysteinemia and hepatic protein homocysteinylation in a mouse model NASH. Accordingly, we hypothesize that TH, SCFAs, and vitamin B12/folate can prevent and/or treat NASH. If so, what are the underlying molecular, cell signaling, and metabolic mechanisms for their beneficial effects? We will employ a dietary rodent model of NASH progression that we developed as well as a primate model of obesity for these studies. Since NASH also involves macrophage and hepatic stellate cell activation to cause inflammation and fibrosis, we also will study the effects of these compounds in these cells during NASH. We anticipate our studies will generate important new insights into the pathogenesis and treatment of NASH, and provide the foundation for future clinical studies.
kw: β-oxidation, NAFLD, Obesity, Short chain fatty acid, Homocysteine, Autophagy

title: Diabetes mellitus and the dysregulation of host proteases in Tuberculosis
abs: The incidence rate for tuberculosis (TB) is rising in Singapore, exacerbated by the increasing prevalence of diabetes mellitus (DM).  DM worsens TB, with patients having a higher mycobacterial burden, more pulmonary cavities, and requiring longer treatment
