title: Optimising Surgical Management and Patient-related Outcomes of Epiretinal Membrane: Predictive Analytics and Randomised Trial
abs: Epiretinal membrane (ERM) is a common age-related eye disease that can cause significant visual impairment with adverse impact on quality of life. Clinical management of ERM is currently hampered by two major challenges. First, it is difficult for clinicians to predict prognostic outcomes for ERM patients being managed conservatively or considered for surgical intervention. A major unmet medical need is therefore to develop a new method to improve prognostic assessment for patients with ERM. Second, surgeons are often faced with a dilemma when they manage patients with concomitant ERM and cataract, because it is unclear which surgical approach is the most appropriate for these patients. Combined cataract and ERM surgery is a popular choice, but this approach may result in unnecessary surgery being performed for ERM that may not contribute significantly to visual impairment. Emerging evidence suggests that cataract surgery alone, which is a cheaper and potentially safer option with faster visual rehabilitation, may achieve similar visual outcome as compared to combined surgical approach for many of these patients. Thus, another major unmet medical need is quality evidence to determine the best surgical approach for patients with concomitant ERM and cataract. In this project, we will conduct a large, multi-ethnic, prospective clinical cohort study of 1,000 patients with ERM. Based on comprehensive clinical and multimodal retinal imaging data, we will develop, with the use of predictive analytics and machine-learning, an algorithm that provides accurate risk prediction for clinically meaningful prognostic outcomes. In addition, we will conduct a pilot randomized controlled trial to evaluate a new surgical approach that may achieve similar visual outcome while reducing the number of unnecessary ERM surgery for patients with concomitant ERM and cataract. Taken together, we anticipate our study to generate impactful data that will greatly optimise the surgical management and patient-related outcomes of ERM.
kw: retinal disease; epiretinal membrane; visual impairment; macular pucker; predictive model; vitrectomy surgery

title: Targeted Cell-Based Therapeutic Program for Corneal Blindness
abs: Visual loss is a global burden. Corneal diseases are the leading cause of vision loss. Whilst the only treatment option is the replacement of damaged corneas through transplantation using cadaveric donor corneas, the global shortage of donor tissue and its sustainability amidst a growing aging population is of utmost concern. Our aim is to develop innovative strategies to treat corneal stromal opacities and corneal endothelial dysfunction. This program will establish targeted cell-based therapy to restore corneal tissue functions and corneal clarity, ultimately aimed at vision recovery. Success of this program will be a paradigm shift to the conventional corneal transplantation. There are two broad themes. (1)Regenerative therapeutic program for corneal stromal opacities using cultivated corneal stromal keratocytes (first successfully cultivated by PI’s team), umbilical cord lining mesenchymal stem cells (UCL-MSC) generated in compliance to good manufacturing practice by an industrial collaborator and MSC exosomes on animal models of corneal stromal haze/opacities. (2)Corneal endothelial cell (CEC) therapy for corneal endothelial dysfunction using cells on bioactive hydrogel as a scaffold carrier for tissue-engineered endothelial keratoplasty, cells cultivated with FDA-approved Rho-kinase inhibitor, Rhopressa, to improve cell quality and regenerated CEC from putative endothelial progenitors identified in transition zone of posterior limbus, for treating bullous keratopathy in a rabbit model, respectively. Experimental outcomes will be instrumental to translate into novel therapeutic approach for corneal diseases and we expect the deliverables to broadly impact on the global shortage of donor tissue in Singapore and worldwide. Our long-term goal is to develop Translational Regenerative Medicine to treat corneal blindness, which can attract multi-disciplinary, entrepreneurial, bio-manufacturing and academic platforms for the benefit of disease treatment and management.
kw: Blindness ; corneal opacities ;  corneal endothelial dysfunction;  cell therapy;  regeneration

title: Studies in chronic myeloid leukaemia
abs: CML is caused by the fusion gene, BCR-ABL1, which transforms normal haematopoietic stem cells into their leukaemic counterparts. While inhibitors of the ABL1 tyrosine kinase (TKI) have turned CML into a chronic condition, several important clinical issues remain. These include the inability of TKIs to eradicate leukaemia stem/progenitor cells (SPC) and cure chronic phase (CP) patients, accurately identify CP patients at risk of transforming into a terminal blast crisis (BC) stage, and the lack of effective BC therapy. To understand the mechanisms mediating SPC TKI resistance, and identify risk factors for BC transformation, we undertook a comprehensive evaluation of the CP to BC progression genome, epigenome, and transcriptome. In CP we identified an RNA binding protein, SRSF1, to mediate cytokine-dependent TKI resistance. We also observed a CML-specific DNA methylation signature, which when analyzed together with transcriptional events, identified a set of methylation-silenced genes predicting aggressive behaviour in CP. In BC, PRC pathway and RUNX mutations occurred in a mutually exclusive manner in 70% of BC genomes, suggesting that either class of mutation is sufficient for BC transformation. Additionally, EZH2, a component of PRC2, marked genes in CP for hypermethylation in BC, while DNA methylation cooperated with activation of the PRC1 complex to silence BC tumour suppressor genes. Together, our studies suggest a model in which a limited set of genetic mutations induce BC transformation through reprogramming of the CP epigenome. Our Specific Aims are: 1. To determine the role of SRSF1 in CP CML, 2. To evaluate epigenetic reprogramming of CP SPCs and identify therapeutic targets, and 3. To determine if recurrent BC mutations contribute to BC transformation. The completion of our Aims has the potential to uncover mechanisms of SPC persistence, identify biomarkers to predict BC transformation, and provide insights into new therapies for both stages of CML.
kw: Chronic myeloid leukaemia, blast crisis, biomarker, iPSC, epigenome

title: Validating biomarkers of myocardial fibrosis and investigating therapies to regress fibrosis (TARGET-FIBROSIS)
abs: Heart failure is a global pandemic. Despite recent treatment advances, the burden of heart failure remains a leading cause of death worldwide. Myocardial fibrosis is a common pathologic manifestation in heart failure, regardless of etiology. Despite its potential clinical value, there are currently no specific treatment approaches targeted at regression myocardial fibrosis. This clinical gap reflects a lack of well-validated biomarkers of myocardial fibrosis to monitor disease progression, risk stratify and assess treatment response in heart failure. Our previous research had identified novel biomarkers (clinical, imaging and circulating) of myocardial fibrosis in aortic stenosis and hypertensive heart disease, both are common causes of heart failure in the adult population. The Clinician Scientist Award proposal extends our previous research and aims to systematically address these critical knowledge gaps. Accordingly, we will determine the association between biomarkers and progression of myocardial fibrosis in a pre-heart failure cardiac condition. In hypertensive cardiac disease, we hypothesize that biomarkers of fibrosis at baseline can predict progression of fibrosis at 3 years (Aim 1). In addition, we will establish and clinically validate a panel of biomarkers (clinical, biochemical and routine clinical investigations) of myocardial fibrosis diagnosed on cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) in patients with heart failure. We hypothesize an integrated panel of clinical markers that diagnoses focal fibrosis also predicts all-cause mortality in heart failure, regardless of underlying etiology (Aim 2). The anti-fibrotic potential of a novel treatment agent (valsartan/sacubitril) will be evaluated in a pilot Phase II randomized controlled trial using CMR to assess treatment response. We hypothesize valsartan/sacubitril is associated with greater regression in myocardial fibrosis volume compared to valsartan after 12 months of treatment in hypertensive patients with left ventricular hypertrophy (Aim 3). Results from these studies will support the role of personalized risk profiling and preventive treatment strategies to improve patient outcomes and reduce the burden of heart failure.
kw: Myocardial fibrosis, left ventricular hypertrophy, cardiovascular magnetic resonance imaging

title: Mapping the trajectory and prognosis of patients with mild-moderate traumatic brain injury – The NEurodegeneration & Understanding of Risk Overlay in Neuroimaging Study (NEURON) 2
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI) will soon be a leading cause of global death and disability; the greatest rise is in the elderly. TBI consequences may be devastating, including physical, cognitive and psycho-behaviours. TBI is now known as a major risk factor for lifelong neurological disorders, including Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s diseases, and other dementias. Although some patients successfully recover and some adapt despite deficits, others continuously decline. Currently, it is not possible to differentiate cohorts as they progress towards either good or poor prognoses. We are unable to characterize the spectrum of processes favouring decline, termed “Chronic Brain Injury” (CBI). Longitudinal data on CBI are severely lacking worldwide. My previous work in normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH), supported by an NMRC TA award, provides proof-of-concept that different cohorts of disease exist with differing degrees of responsiveness to treatments. NPH is one end-point of TBI. Thus, I hypothesize that post-TBI, different cohorts exist, with differing degrees of adaptation to injury. It is possible to find markers and milestones to differentiate such cohorts, and thus manage them appropriately and individually. Modelling such trajectories requires knowledge of the spectrum of reversible to irreversible brain injury. There are no comprehensive data in this regard. To address such gaps, we propose NEURON 2, the first study to confirm CBI, and discover post-TBI markers correlated with good vs. poor prognoses. We aim to explore whether it is possible, prior to any clinical manifestations, to distinguish patients within 3 years of mild-moderate TBI, who will recover from those who will deteriorate from CBI. We shall examine whether advanced brain tissue imaging signatures reflect structural adaptation to injury vs. decline, particularly in those with higher risk of CBI. An experienced team spanning expertise in NPH, TBI and neurodegenerative diseases, and established exemplar datasets, make us well-positioned to deliver NEURON 2.
kw: Traumatic Brain Injury; Chronic Brain Injury; Magnetic Resonance Imaging; Diffusion Tensor Imaging; Biomarkers

title: Scleral Biomechanical Properties in Pathologic Myopia and Myopic Glaucoma
abs: High myopia (HM), or extreme near-sightedness, is a leading cause of blindness worldwide and affects 1 in 12 Singaporeans. By 2050, it is estimated that a billion people will have HM. HM is due to progressive and extreme eye elongation with subsequent eye wall (sclera) thinning, which may allow for focal, ectatic outpouchings called staphyloma. Staphyloma development often occurs immediately before or together with myopic macular degeneration (MMD) and the irreversible vision loss of “pathologic” myopia (PM). The main threats to vision in HM patients are the development of MMD, staphyloma and/or myopic glaucoma. Glaucoma is the most common cause of blindness worldwide, affecting greater than 79.6 million people by 2020, with half being of East Asian origin. Glaucoma is an optic neuropathy with unknown pathogenesis that is related to intraocular pressure, and therefore scleral biomechanical properties. A link between myopia and glaucoma has long been reported. Although scleral changes are believed to underlie both glaucomatous changes and staphyloma development, there are no biomechanical tests available to detect early changes in myopic scleral stiffness and/or reveal whether HM-related biomechanical changes may lead to myopic glaucoma. A fundamental understanding of the biomechanical alterations in scleral tissue may provide a link between pathological pathways in glaucoma and myopia and allow for future therapeutic approaches. We now have imaging technology to assess the eye wall in vivo, providing unprecedented insight into scleral biomechanical properties and allowing us to map regional stiffness. As such, we propose to conduct cross-sectional studies on 200 existing low myopia, HM and PM patients. Scleral biomechanical properties will be compared across cohorts, which allow us to identify and localize scleral regions susceptible to myopia-related remodeling and determine if localized biomechanical weakness in HM is associated with localized functional changes, as well as identify scleral biomechanical changes in myopic glaucoma.
kw: biomarker; myopia; progression; pathologic; staphyloma; sclera

title: Re-invigorating cytolytic tissue resident memory T cells (cTRM T cells) for treating recurrent/relapsed nasopharyngeal cancer
abs: Epstein Barr Virus (EBV) driven nasopharyngeal cancer (NPC) is highly endemic in Southern China, Southeast Asia and Singapore. Up to 80 new cases per 100,000 persons are reported annually in these regions. Despite a relatively good clinical outcome (five-year overall survival of 75-80%), a significant number (~20%) of NPC develops loco-regional failure or distant relapse following definitive treatment. Therefore, newer and more effective treatment options are needed to manage NPCs with recurrences/relapses. Our preliminary study showed that when tumour infiltrating lymphocytic (TIL) T cells were primed with a pool of EBV peptides, they increased tumour specificity and incrementally killed EBV-positive NPC cells by nearly three-fold. We have further identified a specific clone of cytolytic CD8+CD69+CD103+ T cells, termed cytolytic tissue resident memory T cells (cTRM T cells), in approximately 50-60% of our expanded TIL T cell populations. Based on these findings, we hypothesize that our expanded EBV primed cTRM T cells are novel, cellular therapy candidates that can be used either alone or in combination with other immunotherapies, such PD1 monoclonal antibody, to increase treatment efficacy in recurrent/relapsed NPC cases.
kw: T cell therapy; nasopharyngeal cancer; cell therapy

title: Targeting transcription factor pathways in liver cancer
abs: My long-term goal is to translate our knowledge on cancer and transcription factors into clinical applications and therapies. Our overall hypothesis is that it will take a combination of targeted therapies, including those aimed at transcription factors, in order to effectively treat cancer. For this STaR application, I propose to focus on two transcription factors, the oncofetal protein SALL4, and the tumor suppressor CEBPA, for selectively targeted therapies in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), a disease of importance in Singapore with dismal prognosis and no effective drug therapies. SALL4 is not expressed in most normal adult tissues and expressed in approximately 30% of cancers, including HCC. Specifically, I propose the following aims: (1) In order to develop small molecules targeting SALL4 in liver cancer, we will optimize and further develop SALL4 inhibitor compound leads using structure based drug discovery, develop SALL4 degraders, and define the mechanism(s) of the inhibitor and degraders in SALL4-mediated HCC. (2) We will also develop novel RNA based therapies targeting the transcriptional network of SALL4 and CEBPA in HCC, by investigating the mechanism of CEBPA short activating RNA (saRNA) therapeutics in HCC, defining the therapeutic effects of SALL4 siRNA in HCC and compare with small molecule inhibitors and degraders, and defining the therapeutic effects of combination therapy of CEBPA activating RNA and SALL4 siRNA (sasi) as well as CRISPR-based novel RNA therapeutics in HCC. This proposal will involve interactions with basic scientists, clinicians at the National University Hospital, and well as industry partners, and if successful will lead to novel therapeutics targeting pathways not engaged by other therapeutic approaches.
kw: cancer, tumor suppressor, gene regulation, oncofetal protein, liver, HCC

title: Tracking circulating tumour cells and microRNAs in high-risk breast cancer
abs: i. Project Background There is an unmet need to identify patients with breast cancer (BC) who remain at high risk of relapse after standard neoadjuvant or adjuvant therapies, as additional systemic therapies are necessary to maximize their long-term survival. On the other hand, patients who are already cured from standard therapies do not require these additional systemic therapies, since these therapies may provide marginal or no additional benefit to these patients. ii. Hypothesis/Aim Overall Hypotheses: Dynamic changes occurring in CTCs and circulating miRNA reflect the disease burden of BCs Aims To develop assays to monitor the disease burden and predict the risk of relapse among patients with high-risk non-metastatic BCs treated with neoadjuvant (preoperative) chemotherapy before definitive surgery. iii. Methods This study will track the CTCs with single cell gene expression analysis, miRNAs and other circulating markers in high-risk BC patients requiring neoadjuvant chemotherapy before surgery, or adjuvant cases undergoing upfront surgery. At least 60 such patients will be recruited over at least 24 months at National Cancer Centre Singapore (NCCS), Singapore General Hospital (SGH) and Kandang Kerbau Women’s and Children’s Hospital (KKWCH). Blood may be taken at up to 5 or more timepoints. iv. Clinical Significance It will be critical to develop more accurate prognostic biomarkers to ascertain which subgroups of patients need additional systemic therapies, as only a proportion of non-metastatic breast cancers relapse, so that the right treatment can be given to the right patients.
kw: breast cancer

title: Improved Detection of Glaucomatous Structural Damage using Wide-Field Optical Coherence Tomography
abs: Glaucoma is the leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide. Diagnosis of early glaucoma remains challenging. By the time the current method of visual field testing detects glaucoma, at least 25% of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) are lost. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) imaging is commonly used to aid glaucoma diagnosis in clinics but its diagnostic ability for detecting early glaucoma remains inadequate due to the considerable overlap of retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) thickness measurements between normal and glaucoma eyes. Some of this overlap is partly due to the variations in ocular anatomical parameters such as optic disc size, and shape, and the anatomy of the retinal vascular tree, which are important sources of measurement error. We propose a method to mitigate the influence of anatomical ocular parameters on OCT-derived measurements. We have already shown that this anatomy-based compensation method narrowed the variability in RNFL measurements in healthy subjects and reclassified half of the eyes in the 1% high-risk category (with very thin RNFL) to the normal category. The main objective of this proposal is to compare wide-field optical coherence tomography (WF-OCT) combined with compensation for anatomical parameters (termed as WF-OCT plus) and standard OCT in terms of detecting early glaucomatous structural damage and progression in a clinical setting. We hypothesize that WF-OCT plus will significantly improve diagnostic performance in the early detection of glaucomatous damages and optimize the role that OCT imaging plays in glaucoma management. Early glaucoma diagnosis is essential to improving patient outcomes, as earlier treatment can prevent or slow the disease progression, and thus preserve patients’ visual function. Given that glaucomatous damage irreversibly leads to blindness at late stages, the outcome of this study, a novel method to advance glaucoma diagnosis, will confer a great impact on the prevention of blindness, not only in Singapore but worldwide.
kw: Glaucoma; Wide-Field Optical Coherence Tomography

title: Novel genetic and non-genetic risk factors for endothelial dysfunction and diabetic micro-angiopathies – meeting future challenges
inst: Khoo Teck Puat Hospital Pte Ltd
abs: Background Supported by previous NMRC grants, the in-depth phenotyping and serial follow-up of 2,100 multi-ethnic individuals with type 2 diabetes (T2DM) from 2011-2017 have made major contributions to diabetes research (https://www.ktph.com.sg/cru/section_page/494). The cohort also provided rich data and bio-repository to support the operations of national diabetes research consortium. Contemporary epidemiology has informed future unmet needs: (1) increase in longevity related disability e.g. cognitive dysfunction; (2) Amputation due to diabetic foot syndrome (DFS) remains unabated. In this region, our cohort is the only one focusing on these issues. Nonetheless, important gaps in phenotyping remain in our cohort. Thus, we aim to systematically recall all participants from the study-base over ~3 years for re-assessment (including blood and urine collection). Hypothesis Traditional and novel risk factors (RFs) (including genetics), collected at baseline and reassessed serially (to derive their variability), will predict long-term changes in vascular (endothelial) function and incident diabetic complications (including cognitive dysfunction). Methods We will include exposures critical to chronic metabolic disorders: (1) dietary assessment (using the newly-developed web-based platform evolved from the GUSTO cohort, suitable for non-pregnant adults) and (2) physical activities (by tri-axial accelerometer). We will focus on important but under addressed outcomes such as cognitive dysfunction (assessment as employed by the SLAS cohort), and diabetic foot syndrome (DFS) which are in-part attributable to vascular (endothelial) dysfunction. Therefore, our enhanced plan will investigate the long-term relationship between (i) traditional (e.g. hyperglycemia) & novel RFs (e.g. haptoglobinuria) and their variability over time, (ii) endothelial function, (iii) intermediate phenotype (e.g. arterial stiffness) and (iv) extended spectrum of final phenotype i.e. cognitive function, DFS, nephropathy and retinopathy. Significance Collaborating with other major local cohorts (GUSTO & SLAS), we will meet the needs of providing high-quality culturally sensitive local exposures (e.g. nutrition) and outcomes data and biorepository dedicated to T2DM.
kw: Type 2 diabetes; Microvascular complications; Endothelial function; Biomarkers; Cognitive function; Lifestyle

title: Pre-clinical development of brain-penetrant MNK inhibitors for glioblastoma therapy
abs: Adult glioblastoma (GBM) is the deadliest form of brain cancer with fewer than 5% of patients surviving five years, and most succumbing to therapy-resistant disease. To overcome multiple resistance mechanisms, several groups advocate targeting the process of aberrant mRNA translation in GBM, since altered translation represents a final common pathway mediating glioma stem cell (GSC) persistence and therapy resistance. In particular, inhibition of the MAPK-interacting kinase-eFI4E (MNK-eIF4E) axis abrogates translation of resistance-conferring mRNAs in GBM. However, to date, brain-penetrant MNK inhibitors (MNKi) have not been described, an indispensable requirement for effective anti-GBM drugs. Accordingly, we have developed a potent and specific brain-penetrant MNKi, ETC-501, that overcomes temozolomide (TMZ) resistance in a panel of MNK-expressing GSCs. Given that approximately 50% of patients have TMZ-resistant disease, MNKis may have utility in a significant proportion of GBM patients. Our preliminary data indicate that MNKis act via three inter-related mechanisms: (i) augmenting the ability of TMZ to induce DNA double-strand breaks; (ii) synergistically enhancing the senescence-inducing activity of TMZ, while simultaneously inhibiting the pro-tumourigenic ‘senescence associated secretory phenotype’ produced by DNA damaging agents (DDA); and (iii) inhibiting the expression of established GSC drivers, e.g. TGM2. Based on these findings, we hypothesise that MNK-eIF4E-dependent mRNAs contribute to GBM persistence and drug resistance. Our Specific Aims are: 1. To establish efficacy of MNKi and DDA combinations in GBM, 2. To determine the mechanism of action of MNKis in GBM, and 3. To establish efficacy of novel MNKi combinations in GBM. In completing these Aims, we will increase our mechanistic understanding of MNKi activity in GBM, discover novel MNKi combinations effective against GSCs, and identify functional biomarkers for testing in clinical trials. Our work will support and guide the design of MNKi clinical trials, and satisfy a major unmet need in the management of patients with GBM.
kw: Glioblastoma, MAPK-interacting kinase (MNK) inhibitors, drug resistance, pre-clinical drug development.

title: Bayesian Machine Learning Approach to Identify Markers of Progression in Primary Angle Closure Glaucoma
abs: Glaucoma is the leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide, with primary angle-closure glaucoma (PACG) a major form of glaucoma in Singapore and Asia. While we have made considerable advances in understanding the epidemiology, risk factors including genetic susceptibility, and clinical phenotypes of PACG, one of the greatest challenge and unmet clinical need is in identifying which individuals are at the highest risk of progression and development of advanced disease/blindness. The current strategies for patient risk assessment in PACG are inadequate and non-specific. There is lack of long-term clinical data and knowledge of specific determinants for PACG progression. We recently identified some clinical markers for rapid progression; however, the major limitations of our study was that clinical parameters were evaluated in only those subjects who showed progression and not for all who were assessed. Additionally, the possible contributions of PACG-related imaging parameters and genetic markers were not investigated. It is thus not known if there are specific genetic variants and clinical features that predisposes to disease progression and development of advanced PACG/blindness. In this proposal, we hypothesize that disease progression in PACG varies greatly among individuals; and biometric, imaging, and genetic factors contribute to an individuals’ variations. By combining clinical and genetic markers in a Bayesian machine-learning platform, we will develop a clinical tool that will predict the probability/rate of disease progression. To address our hypothesis, we will collect comprehensive clinical and imaging data of patients in whom genome-wide association (GWAS) genetics data is already available; and develop a risk prediction algorithm (Aim 1). Next, we aim to validate the risk algorithm in a separate PACG cohort (Aim 2). It is hoped that this project will give rise to resources that will lead towards precision medicine approaches, which will allow clinicians to stratify patients for more effective customized treatments and management.
kw: Primary angle closure glaucoma; risk prediction; anterior segment optical coherence tomography;  Ophthalmic genetics; imaging; Bayesian machine-learning

title: Role of ARNi in Ventricular Remodeling in Hypertensive LVH (REVERSE-LVH)
abs: In Singapore, one in every two adults in their 60s has hypertension and consequently at risk of hypertensive heart disease, a leading cause of heart failure and cardiovascular death. Currently, management of hypertension relies primarily on achieving peripheral blood pressure targets. However, optimal blood pressure targets are controversial. Given the inherent limitations of peripheral blood pressure measurement and management, a more reliable marker is needed not only for drug development, but also to monitor progression and drug response in individuals with hypertensive heart disease. Consequent to the increased afterload from hypertension, left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) occurs as an adaptive response to maintain wall stress and cardiac output. Ultimately, this initially compensatory response fosters evolution to heart failure as a result of myocyte death and myocardial fibrosis. REMODEL is an ongoing observational study that aims to establish the determinants of cardiac fibrosis in hypertension. All participants recruited have no prior history of heart failure, myocardial infarction or other cardiovascular target organ events. The registry contains the highest quality baseline data including 24-hour continuous ambulatory blood pressure monitoring, comprehensive cardiac and aortic phenotyping with cardiovascular magnetic resonance imaging and tonometry and a biobank of frozen serum and DNA samples. The current proposal, REVERSE-LVH (RolE of ARNI in VEntricular Remodeling in HypertenSivE LVH), is an extension of REMODEL that aims to assess, for the first time, the potential of a anti-hypertensive and anti-heart failure agent (valsartan/sacubitril combination) with anti-fibrotic properties in hypertensive LVH using state-of-the-art cardiac imaging by cardiac magnetic resonance imaging. A total of 200 patients with hypertension and LVH will be randomized to valsartan/sacubitril combination or to valsartan alone. The primary endpoint is regression of myocardial fibrosis volume after 1 year of treatment. REVERSE-LVH will advance knowledge regarding the pathophysiology of myocardial response to hypertension and test a treatment strategy of targeting the myocardium rather than blood pressure.
kw: Myocardial fibrosis, left ventricular hypertrophy, cardiovascular magnetic resonance imaging

title: Extending Health Span through Diabetes Health Literacy and Competency Assessment (HeaLiX health bot)
abs: Life-long patient education and empowerment are key strategies for the successful management of diabetes, recommended by evidence-based clinical guidelines. Currently, diabetes education is provided 1-on-1 or in small groups which are resource intensive and costly. Scheduled education sessions while valued, lack immediacy, timeliness, and flexibility of access. In Singapore, 36% of diabetes patients claim they did not receive diabetes education; and its effectiveness remains questionable. Local studies reported similar rates of general diabetes literacy between people with and without diabetes, raising concerns about patient competency in managing diabetes. Notably, 42% of patients with diabetes had knowledge that did not translate into self-care practices. A better way to provide effective diabetes education is needed. In light of financial and health workforce constraints, two strategies fit Singapore. First, given 100% smartphone ownership and mobile broadband subscription penetration, patient-facing technology such chat bots can be blended with usual care to augment our health workforce and to engage patients. Chat bots are currently used in healthcare for appointment-booking and information provision; and over 70% of consumers are willing to use it for learning about their health condition e.g. diabetes. Second, there are 246,800 domestic carers in Singapore — a significant resource. We hypothesize that carers of seniors with diabetes could be upskilled with diabetes health literacy and competencies via a health bot, to provide better care in line with Singapore’s Home and Community Care Masterplan. We will design, develop and implement a health bot to deliver state-of-the-art diabetes education to carers/patients to improve diabetes health literacy and competency by 80%, and to effect desired behaviour change for 80% of patients, resulting in better health outcomes. As a health intervention for carers/seniors with diabetes the health bot is scalable and low-cost. The future of healthcare is blended care — patients, healthcare professionals, and digital health, working together.
kw: Diabetes; Health literacy; Patient education; Competency; Behaviour change; Health bot

title: EMPOWERing patients with chronic disease using profiling and targeted feedbacks delivered through wearable device (EMPOWER)
abs: Chronic diseases are the leading cause of deaths in Singapore. The rising prevalence in chronic diseases with age and Singapore’s rapidly aging population calls for new models of care to effectively prevent the onset and delay the progression of these diseases. Advancement in medical technology has offered new innovations that aid healthcare systems in coping with the rapid rising in healthcare needs. These include mobile applications, wearable technologies and machine learning-derived personalized behavorial interventions. Our overall goal is to improve health outcomes in chronic disease patients through delivering targeted nudges via mobile application and wearables to sustain behavioral change. Our objective is to design, develop and evaluate an adaptive interventional platform that is capable of delivering personalized behavioral nudges to promote and sustain healthy behavioral changes in senior patients with 3H (diabetes (hyperglycemia), hypertension and hyperlipidemia). Our aim is to assess the clinical effectiveness of real-time personalized educational and behavioral interventions delivered through wearable (FitBit) and an in-integrative mobile application in improving patient activation scores measured using the patient activation measure (PAM). Secondary outcome measures include cost-effectiveness, quality of life, medication adherence, healthcare cost, utilization and lab results. Together with the experts from the SingHealth Regional Health System and National University of Singapore, we will conduct a randomized controlled trial of 1,250 eligible 3H patients. This proposal aims to achieve sustainable and cost-effective behavioral change in 3H patients through patient-empowerment and targeted chronic disease care.
kw: Behavioural nudges; elderly; population health; machine learning; behavioural sciences

title: Diseases as perturbations of the human Immunome: A high dimensionality approach to Translational Medicine in silica
abs: The project proposal entitled “Studying the tolerance-inflammation balance of the human immune rheostat using a deep immunophenotyping approach” aims to address unmet translational clinical needs for comprehensive analyses of clinically well characterised, focussed disease datasets that can be compared against that of robust, age-matched healthy state samples. The study also aims to establish human disease datasets that are hallmarks of opposing ends of pathological immune perturbation represented by autoimmunity on one end and patho-tolerance on the other. We propose to use representative sample sets from various rheumatological diseases to study autoimmunity and to contrast, samples from cancer samples of viral and non-viral etiology to study a state of path-tolerance. The premise being, given sufficient sample sizes and keeping constant several comparator parameters like the baseline healthy cohorts to test against, CyTOF panels that span broad immune cell categories and harmonised experimental protocol, functional and molecular mechanisms that are correct hallmarks of autoimmunity and patho-tolerance as immune perturbances of human disease can be better understood.
kw: Immunomics; Disease datasets; Standardised clinical samples

title: Elucidating the immunobiology of nasopharyngeal carcinoma
abs: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) is endemic in Southern China/South-east Asia. Few disease models exist for NPC and existing cell lines are unreliable. Treatment of NPC with PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors show limited tumor response despite high levels of PD-L1 expression, suggesting checkpoint blockade is not the only driver for immune dysregulation. We propose to investigate the immunobiology of NPC using clinical biopsies (tumor/blood) and humanized mouse patient-derived xenograft models in the following manner: Specific Aim 1: To elucidate the pathobiology of NPC and drug response through extended analysis of paired NPC samples. Integrated molecular analyses of biopsy samples from patients will be done to extensively curate datasets of tumor and blood. These samples are paired and within the context of NPC clinical trials or from patients undergoing standard of care therapy. Clinical data and treatment outcomes for correlative analyses are collected. Specific Aim 2: To establish and expand patient-derived xenografts (PDX) to elucidate the immunobiology of NPC. Fresh tumor biopsies are implanted in NOD SCID mice. Established PDX are compared with primary tumor biopsies for fidelity and EBV status, and expanded in mice with humanized immune background. Successful humanized PDX are studied to understand immune dysregulation using flow cytometry of tumor immune infiltrate, tumor/immune cell checkpoint gene expression, tumor and circulating cytokine levels. Specific Aim 3: To understand the mechanistic basis for response/resistance to immunotherapy/novel therapeutics using the above models. Drug treatment of the NPC humanized PDX will be done. Immunomodulation in the tumor and in mouse circulation are studied using flow cytometry and circulating and intratumoral cytokines. Untreated/treated PDX are interrogated with multicolor immunohistochemistry to investigate changes in tumor microenvironment. Mouse PDX data will be correlated with paired human clinical data where available. This project will establish an inestimable resource of NPC data and human PDX for scientific use and drug testing.
kw: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma; immunotherapy; integrated molecular profiling; mouse models; patient-derived xenografts

title: Tumor-microenvironment interaction and its impact on drug response in advanced pancreatic adenocarcinoma (PDAC)
abs: The underutilization of pre-clinical models incorporating tumor-stroma interactions may explain the lack of clinical translation. Construct of a clinically relevant pre-clinical model may bridge this disconnect. The mechanism of resistance to MEK inhibitors in KRAS mutant (MT) pancreatic adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is mediated via JAK1/2-STAT pathway in preclinical studies. Combined MEK and JAK inhibition demonstrated significant in vivo anti-tumor activity. Both MEK and JAK inhibition is expected to modulate tumor microenvironment. We hypothesize that combination trametinib (MEK inhibitor) and ruxolitinib (JAK inhibitor) is safe and demonstrates preliminary activity in a proportion of patients with KRAS MT PDAC. We aim to determine feasibility of this combination by determining its maximum tolerated dose (MTD)/recommended phase II dose (RP2D), safety, tolerability and preliminary activity in a phase I study in patients with advanced KRAS MT PDAC. Pharmacokinetics would be evaluated. Modulation of gene expression and predictive biomarkers relevant to the MAPK and JAK/STAT pathway would be perused from pre-treatment and ontreatment tumor biopsies. We hypothesize that generation of patient-derived tumor cell models from pancreatic tumor biopsy with distinct tumor and stroma compartment is feasible and represents a more clinically relevant approach. We aim to evaluate feasibility of generating patient-derived tumor cells and organoids (epithelial and stellate cell co-culture) from tumor biopsy. The genetic characterization and anti-tumor activity of this treatment in coculture organoids would be compared with trial subjects in parallel. We aim to study interaction between pancreatic epithelial and stellate cells created and explore other therapeutic vulnerabilities which would inform construct and patient selection of subsequent trials. The ability to generate patient-derived pancreatic tumor and associated stromal cells through tumor biopsies is novel and paradigm shifting providing expedient personalized ex vivo therapeutic screening.
kw: RAS mutant, Tumor micro-environment, pancreatic adenocarcinoma, organoid model

title: Unraveling the evolutionary origin of low vaccine efficacy in the H3N2 influenza virus
abs: Influenza H3N2 virus is the predominant form of seasonal influenza virus. It infects 5-15% of the total population and leads to an estimated half a million deaths annually. Vaccination against influenza viruses is the primary strategy for prevention and control of influenza outbreaks. Despite many years of efforts, there has been an alarming decrease in the efficacy of the H3N2 vaccine in recent years. Both antigenic drift and passage adaptation (substitutions accumulated during vaccine production in embryonated eggs) can result in mismatches between the vaccine and circulating strains, leading to low vaccine efficacy. In our two earlier studies, we observed a strong negative correlation between egg passage adaptation and vaccine efficacy. Accordingly, we plan to employ approaches from evolutionary genetics and computational biologic to achieve the following goals: 1) Characterize the temporal dynamics of passage adaptation across the years and pinpoint major codon positions responsible for low vaccine efficacy, 2)Experimentally validate adaptive alleles through viral culturing and functional studies, 3) Study passage adaptation in other genes and explore the evolutionary link to vaccine efficacy, 4) Develop a computational package guiding vaccine production and link it to the public server (FluSurver) for real-time surveillance, and 5) Construct a computational package for analyzing adaptive evolution over large phylogenies.
kw: H3N2 influenza virus, Vaccine efficacy, Passage adaptation, Mutational mapping

title: Small Molecule Fluorescent Probe Development for Human Liver Stem Cells with High Differentiation Capability into Hepatocyte Lineage
abs: The chronic liver disease involves loss of functional hepatocytes and irreversible scarring of the liver, leading to end-stage liver disease. Although liver transplantation is the curative treatment, the amount of donor organ is limited and alternative strategies, therefore, are needed. A number of studies have shown that human hepatic stem cells are capable of propagating in vitro, can be differentiated into hepatocyte-like cells. Hence, the transplantation of patient-derived hepatic stem cells (PdHSCs) or PdHSC-derived hepatocytes has been offered as an ideal therapeutic option for the treatment of liver disease. However, isolated HSCs seem to come in two flavors. One is more hepatocyte lineage committed, whereas the other is more prone to go in the direction of cholangiocytes. So far the “flavor” can only be determined by costly and time-consuming works. In the current absence of a specific marker for HSCs, especially “flavor” specific a fast translation is limited. Thus, the specific identification and isolation of HSCs from patient tissue would contribute significantly to the effective clinical application of PdHSCs. Development of bio-imaging probes using synthetic small molecules has been explored for a biologically safe and highly sophisticated way to visualize the specific type of cells. Diversity-Oriented Fluorescence Library Approach (DOFLA), which includes a high throughput screening (HTS) step of the synthetic fluorescent compound libraries, have demonstrated various cell type-selective probes through unbiased phenotypic screenings. While DOFLA would be a promising approach for the HSC probe development, unbiased screening requires a reliably established cell model for the HTS step. Fortunately, we have established a PdHSC platform by various patients. Our goal is to identify specific probes for human HSCs using the DOFLA and PdHSCs platform. This study would provide an enormous advance in the field and for the application of HSCs in regenerative medicine for the treatment of chronic liver disease.
kw: Metabolic liver disease; Cell therapy; Liver stem cells; Fluorescent probe; High-throughput screening

title: Alternative 3'UTRs of key cancer genes: Novel regulators and therapeutic targets?
abs: Messenger RNAs (mRNAs) comprise protein-coding regions flanked by untranslated regions (UTRs) that regulate their localization, stability and translation efficiency. Intriguingly, most mammalian genes generate mRNA isoforms with different UTRs. In cancer, 3’UTR shortening can abolish microRNA binding and perturb oncogene expression. In contrast, only a few 3’UTR splicing events have been characterized as the vast majority of splicing research has focused on changes in protein-coding potential. Furthermore, little is known about how different aspects of 3’UTR processing collectively shape the cancer transcriptome and drive carcinogenesis. We hypothesize that alternative 3’UTR processing plays a key role in tumorigenesis, and will focus on liver and colon cancer, where there are still unmet clinical needs in terms of relapsed disease. We will map the global landscape of 3’UTRs in cancers, investigate how alternative 3’UTRs regulate key cancer genes and examine their impact on hallmarks of cancer. Additionally, we will examine the mechanisms underlying 3’UTR heterogeneity and develop a web-based resource for the visualization of these data. Our work will address the following knowledge gaps: (1) No transcriptome-wide analysis of 3’UTR splicing has been performed in cancer to date; (2) Mapping of multiple 3’UTR processing events on a specific transcript cannot be achieved using short-read RNA sequencing data; (3) The few long-read/single cell datasets currently available are insufficient to annotate transcripts of low/moderate abundance or expressed specifically in certain cells. We have assembled a team of world-leading scientists with complementary expertise, established many of the required assays and platforms, and identified promising candidates from our preliminary analysis. This work will deepen our understanding of how 3’UTR processing drives carcinogenesis. Finally, 3’UTR variants and processing factors that are specifically dysregulated in cancer may represent promising new biomarkers for patient stratification, prediction of treatment response, and/or lead to the development of novel targeted therapies.
kw: Non-coding RNA; RNA processing; RNA structure; RNA therapeutics; cancer

title: The Novel Role of the SUMO Pathway in Promoting Neural Stem Cell Reactivation and Brain Development
abs: The delicate balance between neural stem cell (NSC) quiescence and activation is important for adult neurogenesis. Failure of NSC reactivation is associated with neurodevelopmental disorders. Recently, Drosophila NSCs have emerged as a powerful in vivo model for the study of NSC reactivation. Small ubiquitin-related modifier (SUMO) is a posttranslational modification that enables rapid and reversible changes in protein function. Dysregulation of the SUMO pathway is associated with multiple neurodegenerative diseases. However, the role of the SUMO pathway during NSC reactivation and brain development is not established. This proposal will fill in the gap of knowledge by establishing the novel function of the SUMO pathway during Drosophila NSC reactivation and brain development. Our central hypothesis is that the SUMO pathway promotes NSC reactivation via downregulating the hippo pathway. Our preliminary studies showed that SUMO/Smt3 is both necessary and sufficient to promote NSC reactivation. We will further investigate the role of the SUMO pathway during Drosophila NSC reactivation (aim 1). We will test the potential role of various components of the SUMO pathway including the E1 activating enzyme Aos1, E2 conjugating enzyme Ubc9/Lwr in NSC reactivation by gain- and loss-of-function analyses. We will also identify SUMO E3 ligases that are involved in NSC reactivation. We will investigate the role of the SUMO pathway in downregulating the Hippo pathway in NSCs (aim 2). We will determine whether Warts can be SUMOylated and subsequently degraded when Smt3 or Ubc9 is overexpressed. Additional genetic experiments will be performed to approve the novel link between the SUMO pathway and the hippo pathway during NSC reactivation. Our research will provide novel intrinsic mechanisms of NSC reactivation and brain development by establishing the novel role of the SUMO pathway, and will ultimately contribute to the understanding and promising treatment of the SUMOylation-related neurological diseases.
kw: neural stem cell (NSC); reactivation; quiescence; brain development; SUMO pathway; Hippo pathway

title: Immune and dietary control of hypervirulent and multidrug-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae in the gut to prevent disease and transmission
abs: Bacterial multi-drug resistance (MDR) and carbapenem-resistance (CR) is a global health threat. Carbapenems are the last line of effective antibiotics against many bacteria, including Klebsiella pneumoniae. Alarmingly, the convergence of hypervirulent and CR K. pneumoniae has resulted in the creation of “superbugs” that can cause disease in healthy individuals. As hypervirulent strains are prevalent in Asia such as China and Singapore, this problem is of critical relevance. Against the backdrop of COVID19 and future pandemics, controlling these infections is paramount as patients with weakened immune systems rely on prolonged hospital care under the constant threat of hospital acquired infections, especially if patients are already colonized with MDR/CR bacteria. Antimicrobial drug development is beset with a long runway, high costs and failure rates. We hypothesize that understanding the immune and metabolic environment caused by the colonization of MDR/CR and hypervirulent bacteria will enable us to decolonize these bacteria from the intestines. Our goals are to develop a diet and immune modulator regimen to strengthen gut barrier integrity to prevent colonized K. pneumoniae from intestinal translocation to other organs, and to decolonize K. pneumoniae from the gut. Our aims are to firstly examine the immune, microbiome and metabolic landscape in murine models colonized with hypervirulent-CR K. pneumoniae to identify key immune and metabolite modulators and changes in pre-disease and disease states. Secondly, we determine the influence of diet and short chain fatty acids or other metabolites and immune factors (identified in aim 1) in colonization, disease progression and amelioration. Finally, we screen for factors with ability to impede bacterial adhesion and enhance bacterial clearance using a primary human colonic organoid system. Our approach provides a highly feasible path for clinical translation that bypasses bacterial evolution of drug resistance and focuses on diet manipulation and supplementation instead of clinical drug development.
kw: Decolonization; Klebsiella pneumoniae; multi-drug resistance; diet supplementation; metabolite; immune

title: Screening of SARS-CoV-2 Covalent Entry Inhibitors using Photonic Nanowell Plate with Single Virus Resolution
abs: Developing efficient and safe treatment for virus-infected patients is critical for preventing virus spreading and avoiding patient casualties during a pandemic like COVID-19. Unfortunately, it is challenging to perform drug screening for developing timely treatments, due to fast mutation and heterogeneity of RNA viruses. Thereby, current antiviral treatment development is inefficient in isolating virus strain and controlling the micro-environment of infection, lagging behind the risks of emerging new virus mutants. To combat against virus pandemic, a new generation high-throughput platform is highly demanded for selecting inhibitors against SARS-CoV-2 mutants and controlling massive virus population of SARS-CoV-2. This proposal aims to design, fabricate and demonstrate a working prototype of an integrated nanophotonic platform for high-throughput antiviral drug screening at single virus level, by synthesizing chemically modified oligonucleotide libraries and selecting covalent entry inhibitors for SARS-CoV-2 mutants in a massive virus population. For the first time, we propose a photonic nanowell array for real-time single-virus manipulation and host-cell infection, enabling antiviral drug screening in an automated, enclosed microenvironment. We also propose high-throughput selection of covalent entry inhibitors for SARS-CoV-2 using chemically modified oligonucleotide libraries. The program consists of two tasks: Task 1 focuses on the design and fabrication of photonic nanowell array, and its integration with a real-time monitoring and sorting system for antiviral drug screening at single virus resolution; Task 2 aims to establish a high-throughput technique using the photonic nanowell array for the selection of covalent inhibitors based on chemically modified oligonucleotide libraries. By investing in this application-driven research, the integrated nanophotonic platform aims to revolutionize antiviral treatment development. After program, the team will demonstrate working prototype of the integrated photonic nanowell plate platform for antiviral drug screening, and selecting an oligonucleotide library of SARS-CoV-2 entry inhibitors.
kw: SARS; COVID; Photonic Nanowell

title: Smart portable infrared spectrometer for rapid pathogen detection of infectious diseases
abs: In this project, we propose to develop tunable quantum cascade laser spectroscopy technology to record and diagnose the mid-infrared absorption of COVID virus’s biomarkers. The proposed technology has the advantages of small footprint, fast, easy-to-use, accurate, and applicable for other diseases inspection simultaneously as a universal tool. Specific Aim 1: Developing compact spectrometer for fast and accurate detection of viruse pathogens. The pathogens’ fingerprint can be protein, nucleic acid, lipids, etc., which all have broadband and distinct absorption feature in electromagnetic (EM) spectrum. However, it is difficult to identify them in several discrete wavenumber with influence of complex background. Developing electrically pumped semiconductor-based broadband tunable mid-infrared (mid-IR) laser, i.e. quantum cascade laser (QCL), can help to differentiate these mid-IR fingerprints for molecule recognition with a spectral resolution of <0.1cm-1. Specific Aim 2: Verifying the sensitivity and specificity of the detection method using clinical samples. Surface enhanced infrared absorption interaction chip enables high sensitivity detection for pathogen with or without mutations. The ability on the detection of variety of virus mutations is becoming utmost critical for diagnosis, epidemiological record tracing and prevention. Developing a sample loading chip with surface enhancement capability is important to improve the LOD to pico-gram/mL level, whilst considering the device manufacturability at a reasonable cost. Specific Aim 3: Establishing pathogen database for respiratory infectious diseases. Nonlinear deep learning algorithms enables rapid spectra analysis, and cloud-based database for virus monitoring. Linear models such as PCR, PLSR, etc. are usually used for spectra analysis, neglecting the high dimensionality of spectral data. Taking the advantages of AI, we then propose to build up deep learning algorithm based on non-linear function, with a rapid training speed while maintaining high accuracy in terms of >90% sensitivity and >95% specificity. Ultimately, a pathogen database is generated for better diagnosis of respiratory infectious diseases.
kw: Portable; infrared spectrometer; rapid pathogen detection; infectious diseases;

title: Fighting future zoonotic outbreaks by learning lessons from the source of viruses: Antiviral drug discovery based on bat genomics
abs: Bats are natural reservoirs of numerous emerging and re-emerging viruses, such as coronaviruses, henipaviruses, and filoviruses. These pathogenic viruses pose severe threats to global public health, as exemplified by the unceasing COVID-19 pandemic. Unlike humans, bats are generally asymptomatic during viral infections. Unfortunately, bat-borne viruses can often cause severe diseases in humans. A better understanding of bat-virus interactions can shed light on the intrinsic resistant strategies that bats adapted to tolerate virus infections. To expand the repertoire of bat research, we have initiated a collaboration to systematically develop powerful functional genomic platforms (RNAi and CRISPR) to dissect bat host factors critical for viral infections. Our joint efforts have led to the discovery of a collection of novel bat genes that significantly impacted highly pathogenic RNA viruses such as influenza A virus and SARS-CoV-2. Particularly MTHFD1 stood out as one of the promising druggable host factors. MTHFD1 is a unique trifunctional host enzyme known to regulate 1-carbon metabolism, a crucial pathway to support the synthesis of methionine, thymidylate, and purine in cells. We uncovered that MTHFD1 is an essential host factor required for a broad spectrum of RNA viruses to infect bat cells and human cells. Bat cells seem to express significantly lower levels of MTHFD1 mRNA in comparison to human cells. Interestingly, inhibition of MTHFD1 enzymatic functions using carolacton can inhibit virus infections. We propose to investigate the expression and druggability of MTHFD1 in vivo. Furthermore, we will extend our study to validate and characterize additional hits that may serve as targets for developing host-directed therapeutics. Our proposal is a blueprint for uncovering bat factors and the underlying mechanisms that enable bats to co-exist in harmony with viruses. We hope to translate these findings into new antivirals to combat emerging infectious diseases and future outbreaks.
kw: pandemic preparedness; MTHFD1; zoonosis; bat; SARS-CoV-2; functional genomics

title: On-Demand Synthesis of Pharmaceuticals in an End-to-End Fully Automated Fashion and Its Application to Accelerate Drug Discovery Process
abs: Since 2014, the total pharmaceutical revenues worldwide have exceeded US$1 trillion, and the pharmaceutical market continues to flourish due to rising demand for medication as a consequence of increasing global population, increased healthcare needs, and ageing. Organic synthesis represents the most time-consuming aspect of medicinal chemistry so improvements to accelerate and reduce the cost of drug discovery process are of primary importance. Traditional organic synthesis is labour-intensive and generates substantial waste due to repetitive reaction manipulation and downstream purification. The transition from cumbersome manual synthesis to the automated assembly of pharmaceutical molecules has allowed improvements in efficiency, scalability, safety, and reproducibility, and is therefore of widespread academic, industrial, and societal interest. However, other than the well-defined automated synthesis methods for peptides, DNA, oligonucleotides, and oligosaccharides, in which the molecules are composed of repeating functional units, the synthesis of small-molecule-based active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) remains predominantly a manual process due to their structural diversity. Compared to conventional stirred reactor vessels, continuous-flow reactors have several significant processing advantages, which include improved mass/heat transfer, better reproducibility, enhanced safety, reduced equipment footprint, and facile scalability, perfectly matching the future demands for sustainable drug manufacturing in Singapore. Multistep continuous-flow synthesis enable the telescoping of several synthetic steps into a single and uninterrupted process, avoiding purification and isolation of intermediates. However, fully continuous-flow synthesis rarely exceed two steps before offline purification due to issues originating from solvent/reagent incompatibility, the accumulation of side-products, pressure build-up, mismatched time scales, and increased risks of clogging. The overarching goal of this proposed CRP program is to develop a versatile strategy for automated end-to-end synthesis of pharmaceuticals and analogs by leveraging recent advances in flow synthesis and solid-phase synthesis (SPS) to dramatically reduce the cost and time for lead optimization, with the joint force of chemistry, engineering, and biology. The SPS-flow technology enables the simplest and most compact systems for automated multistep synthesis of APIs. We aim to conduct proof-of-concept study of kilogram scale automated production of selected drug molecules, as the developed CRF will enable pharmaceutical production in response to sudden changes in demand or need, and expand the accessibility of medicine in second or third-world countries. Moreover, the generated CRFs can be directly adopted or slightly modified for the automated synthesis of drug derivatives, enabling both late-stage and early-stage diversification. title: Memristive Halide Perovskites for Next Generation Embedded Neuromorphic Computing
abs: Information processing from sensors rely on an approach where signal transduction is separated from centralised computation and decision-making. Such an approach results in power consumption, bandwidth, latency, wiring and chip complexity problems for big sensory systems (eg, smart cities) as well as in sensorized systems that require closed loop feedback for instantaneous decision making (eg. robotics, artificial prosthetics). Biological systems are more efficient- the sensory neurons in the human retina not only sense light stimuli but also conducts first-stage image processing prior to more complex signal processing in the brain. We aim to develop off-chip neuromorphic edge computing platforms (cognitive surfaces) that incorporate both local signal processing and memory capabilities at the sensing elements, emulating and exceeding the peripheral nervous system. The cognitive surfaces would comprise neuromorphic (brain-like) devices that function like elements of the nervous system- (viz. nociceptors or pain receptors for signal processing, synapses for learning and neurons for signal integration). Such cognitive surfaces can (i) process, learn and adapt, allowing for local decision making and fault tolerance; (ii) refine sensor data to alleviate communication bottlenecks. Our results show that halide perovskites with strong ionic and electronic effects can enable memristors with energy-efficient analog switching. These materials offer large degrees of compositional, functional and fabrication freedom, enabling large area memristive neural elements. We will investigate mechanisms and characterise new halide materials and interfacial layers that can enable fine conductivity modulations in memristors (work-package 1). We will accelerate the discovery of such neuromorphic devices through automated data-science driven laboratory workflows - allowing us to navigate perovskites’ large compositional space (work-package 2). We will implement artificial nociceptors, synapses and spiking neurons to realize neural networks that perform optical and pressure sensory signal-preprocessing (work-package 3). These CMOS integrated hardware demonstrators find applications in large area non-invasive monitoring of the elderly and responsive whole- body robotic surfaces.

title: Utilization of freshwater sludge and carbide sludge to produce expansive agent for civil engineering applications
abs: There is ~15,500 tonnes of freshwater sludge produced from waterworks in Singapore per year, which is currently filter pressed to sludge cake and dumped in Semakau landfill, hindering the country’s ambition of “Towards Zero Landfill”. The main concerns for utilization of freshwater sludge include high contents of water, organic matters, microorganisms, aluminium, and sulfate. The other problem related to this project is the disposal of carbide sludge, a by-product generated during acetylene gas production. According to the specific chemical properties of freshwater sludge (aluminum sulfate) and carbide sludge (calcium oxide), this project proposes to utilize them to produce the expansive agent, a high value-added product for various civil engineering applications. In this project, the freshwater sludge and carbide sludge with a proper ratio will be calcined at a proper temperature to produce a mixture of calcium aluminate, gypsum, and quicklime, which can react with water to form ettringite, i.e. the main reaction of most commercial expansive agents. The application of the research results can (1) eliminate the landfilling of freshwater sludge to save the precious volume of Singapore’s only live landfill, (2) eliminate the need of treating carbide sludge, and (3) convert freshwater sludge and carbide sludge to a high value-added product, creating new business and job opportunities.

title: Development and Applications of Next-generation Transcriptome Imaging Technology
abs: Despite rapid advancements in sequencing technologies, we still lack high resolution gene expression data across complex patterned tissues. Spatial information currently obtained via microscopy is limited by the number of fluorophores. Transcriptome imaging technology, such as multiplexed fluorescent in situ hybridisation, fills this critical gap, enables high-throughput data driven image analysis, and promises to transform disease diagnostics. This proposal strives to develop the next-generation multiplexed fluorescent in situ hybridisation technology that is more robust, rapid, and scalable through advanced nucleic acid engineering, hydrogel chemistry, and adaptive optics, and as a proof of concept, demonstrate in toto spatial transcriptomics of model systems for developmental biology, such as zebrafish embryos, human brain organoids, and butterfly wings and brains. The overall goal is to construct the world’s first high resolution and lineage resolved gene expression atlas of a complete organ or organoid. Realization of the proposed program will directly address several fundamental questions in development, such as how tissues are formed through a complex interplay between genes, which control cellular identities, and cellular division mechanisms that drive organ shape and cell movements. Beyond basic science, advancements in the technology will also accelerate its deployment to key translational areas with great relevance to public health, such as pathology and pathogen detection. Finally, as the global spatial-omics market is growing rapidly, resulting intellectual properties from this work could generate significant economic value.

title: REDUCING DIABETIC MACROVASCULAR COMPLICATIONS DUE TO PERIPHERAL ARTERIAL DISEASE - REDUCE-PAD
abs: Background Peripheral arterial disease (PAD) affects >200 million people worldwide and is associated with significant mortality, morbidity, and healthcare costs, especially in diabetic (DM) patients. The REDUCE PAD program will test two novel therapies (antibody to Interleukin-11 [anti-IL-11Ab] and antibody to Lectin-like oxidized low-density lipoprotein receptor-1 [anti-LOX-1Ab]), and develop innovative antibody-delivery systems, to prevent post-angioplasty restenosis, reduce atheroma inflammation/progression, and improve microvascular perfusion, in DM PAD patients. Specific Aims 1 1.1. Use single-nucleus RNA-Seq and mass spectrometry imaging of vascular and atheroma tissue from diabetic and non-diabetic mice and pig PAD models and diabetic and non-diabetic PAD patients to: (a) determine which cell types and regions express IL-11, LOX-1, and their downstream targets; (b) evaluate the effects of diabetes on the expression of IL-11, LOX-1, and their downstream targets; and (c) evaluate the mechanisms underlying anti-IL-11Ab and anti-LOX-1Ab therapy. 1.2. Investigate whether anti-IL-11Ab and anti-LOX-1Ab therapy can prevent femoral artery intima hyperplasia and atheroma inflammation/progression in diabetic and non-diabetic mice PAD models, and elucidate the underlying mechanisms. 1.3. Develop novel diabetic and non-diabetic human ‘arterial wall' and 'stenosis' on-a-chip models to investigate the mechanisms underlying the atheroprotective effects of anti-IL-11Ab and anti-LOX-1Ab therapy. Specific Aims 2 2.1. Develop a novel anti-IL-11Ab nanolipogel formulation for sustained release of anti-IL-11Ab, and investigate whether injecting it into the adventitia can prevent tunica intima hyperplasia in a diabetic and non-diabetic pig model of femoral artery endothelial injury. 2.2. Develop a novel anti-IL-11Ab Sound-Sensitive Multicavity Microparticle formulation, and use an intravascular lithotripsy catheter to deliver anti-IL-11Ab into the vascular wall to prevent tunica intima hyperplasia in a pig model of femoral artery endothelial injury. Specific Aims 3 3.1. Evaluate whether anti-LOX-1Ab therapy can improve lower limb microvascular perfusion (assessed by MRI), and attenuate atheroma inflammation (assessed by 18F-FDG-PET) in DM PAD patients. 3.2. Discover novel plasma biomarkers that reflect PAD disease severity and response to anti-LOX-1Ab therapy in DM PAD patients. Expected outcomes We expect to develop two new antibody-based treatments for preventing PAD complications and improving clinical outcomes in diabetic patients with PAD.

title: Non-Thermal Transformation of Soft Clay into Lightweight Aggregates by Geopolymerization Technology
abs: This project will investigate the treatment and transformation of soft clay for the production of lightweight aggregate (LWA) to be used in non-structural concrete, using our patented ZA-TECHTM reagent and proprietary geopolymerization technology, namely Solidification-Immobilization-Lithification (SIL) process. Multiple streams of industrial by-products such as coal fly ash (CFA) will be used as additives for the production of the LWA due to their synergistic properties. The soft clay and other waste materials will be pretreated, then mixed with ZA-TECHTM reagent using a special mixer. The mixture is then formed into required shape and size, followed by a curing step. The SIL process is able to immobilize the heavy metals present in soft clay and other wastes, solidify and lithify the clay through geopolymerization reaction, transforming it into safe and quality LWA products. The LWA can be used to fabricate concrete pavers, concrete blocks and partitions, etc. The LWAs will be tested in a field trial for their engineering performance including Atterberg limits, particle size distribution, direct shear strength, crushing strength, bulk density, thermal conductivity, unconfined compressive strength, water absorption, microstructure, porosity, permeability, California Bearing Ratio (CBR), etc. In addition, the leaching of pollutants e.g. heavy metals of the LWA will be tested according to local and/or international standards and the environmental impact will be assessed. The technology is robust, scalable, and with high potential for commercialization. In the end, the economic feasibility of commercial production and utilization of the LWA products will be evaluated.

title: Study into the role of Cerebrovascular Disease and Amyloid Pathology on Progression of Cognitive Impairment among Patients with Young Onset Mild Cognitive Impairment (SYNC-Longitudinal)
abs: While cerebral fibrillary beta- amyloid is the pathological hallmark of Alzheimer ’s disease (AD), there is evidence that small vessel cerebrovascular disease (svCVD) co-exists and accelerates the amyloid cascade. Existing studies evaluating the interaction between beta-amyloid and svCVD have been limited to older cohorts with multiple cerebral pathologies, thus not allowing for analyses of the specific contribution of svCVD to beta-amylid pathology. Studies focused on a younger cohort will allow for elucidation of the specific pathophysiological contributions of svCD to cerebral beta-amyloid and AD. Published data from our group has demonstrated that 30-40% of Southeast Asian patients with AD to have a severe burden of svCVD. Thus unravelling the contribution of svCVD to beta-amyloid pathology is of high clinical importance to the Southeast Asian population. In this proposal we will evaluate the interaction between beta-amyloid and svCVD in 250 young subjects (<65 years) with amnestic mild cognitive impairment (a-MCI). This will be a follow-up study to our cross-sectional Singapore Young Onset Dementia Study (SYNC). We will evaluate the interaction between svCVD and beta-amyloid pathology on specific cognitive measures (global cognition, episodic memory, executive function), incident svCVD lesions and integrity of specific functional networks (executive control network, default mode network). As hypertension is a leading mechanism for svCVD, we will carry-out proof of mechanism trial to study the risk-benefit of intensive blood pressure control (<120/80mm Hg) on reducing cognitive decline and reducing svCVD lesions among a-MCI subjects having both svCVD and beta-amyloid pathology. This study will provide novel data on the magnitude of contribution of svCVD to accumulation of beta-amyloid, cognitive decline and functional network integrity. The data would be used to plan randomized clinical trials targeting svCVD for the prevention of AD dementia and to develop novel commercializable softwares to quantify svCVD and to track cognitive performance.

title: The role of human fetal antigen presenting cells in tolerance and immunity
abs: Intra-uterine stem cell therapies are potentially curative treatments for inherited genetic disorders such as haemoglobinopathies, but currently limited by immune-rejection . A key challenge is to determine a window of opportunity that will allow graft tolerance, which is linked intimately with the developing immune system and its functional competence. Antigen presenting cells (APCs) such as dendritic cells and macrophages are critical regulators of immune system, responsible for both self-tolerance directing immune responses. Recently, we defined the temporal and spatial development of APCs during early fetal development and started to address their role in regulating tolerance and immunity. We have now shown that fetal APCs exert a critical role in mediating immunological tolerance and inhibiting T-cell activation through a unique metabolic pathway involving arginine availability. Our aim is to extend our characterization of the fetal immune system and precisely map the development of all immune cells. We will focus on fetal tissue-resident T cells to establish their unique functional properties. Extending our finding on fetal DC immunosuppressive state mediated by Arginase-2, we will investigate how metabolic pathways modulate immune cell differentiation and functions. Firstly, we will first generate a fetal immune atlas through the integration of index sorting single-cell RNAseq and CyTOF analyses, and obtaining combined gene and protein expression analyses to identify novel markers, cytokine and growth factor requirements that will predict their functional specialisations. Secondly, we will characterize fetal immune metabolism through mass-spectrometry, and study how it modulates fetal immunity through in vitro studies to determine activatory/suppressive effects and precursor potential. Detailed understanding of the establishment of the fetal immune system and how fetal APCs exert tolerogenic and immunogenic effects will allow us to develop better strategies for prenatal transplantation, reveal the mechanisms underlying fetal susceptibility to infections and feto-maternal tolerance, and form the basic foundation for future APCs-based immunotherapies.
