title: Wnt pathway in synovial sarcoma: Implications for therapy
abs: Sarcomas are difficult to treat due to a lack of efficacy in conventional chemotherapy drugs. Drugs that target specific tumorigenic pathways offer the potential of having less patient morbidity and more therapeutic efficacy. Our preliminary work has demonstrated synovial sarcoma(SS) may be dependent on the Wnt signaling pathway for survival and growth. In other sarcomas, the Wnt pathway may have an inhibitory effect on angiogenesis. My mentor’s lab has developed an upstream Wnt Inhibitor (ETC159) that is currently in clinical trials. Understanding the role of the Wnt pathway in in these sarcomas will allow us to bring this new drug to clinical use in more cancers. Hypothesis and Aims Our hypothesis is that SS is driven by an upstream Wnt pathway mutation and can be inhibited by an upstream Wnt inhibitor (ETC159). ETC159 inhibits SS by direct inhibition of tumour cell viability as well as disrupting the tumour’s angiogenic potential. We aim to: 1. investigate how SSX-SS18 upregulates the Wnt pathway in SS 2. demonstrate the efficacy of ETC 159 in the treatment of synovial sarcoma 3. investigate the effects of Wnt modulation on angiogenesis in sarcomas Methodology Co- immunoprecipitation of SSX-SS18 will identify the key Wnt proteins, which bind to SSX-SS18. Over expression/ knock down of these proteins will allow us investigate the Wnt signaling pathway in SS. Treatment of synovial sarcoma murine xenografts with ETC159 will allow us to investigate the effects of Wnt modulation on the tumor phenotype as well as transcriptional changes. We will also investigate the effects of ETC 159 on angiogenesis by immunohistochemistry analysis of the treated tumor specimens, as well as chicken chorioallantoic membrane angiogenic model. Clinical Significance Understanding the role of the Wnt signaling pathway in driving sarcomas will allow us to develop a new, locally developed treatment modality for these cancers.
kw: Synovial sarcoma, Wnt pathway, therapy

title: Interrogation of Childhood Onset Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Immunome for the Elucidation of Disease Mechanisms
abs: The pathogenesis of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) involves multiple derangements that perturb the fine balance between immunity and regulation. Traditional investigational approaches focusing on the pathogenic or protective role of individual cell type or molecule independently are inadequate for the study of a complex, multifactorial disease like SLE. The lack of a holistic understanding of the lupus immunome is a critical unmet need. Simultaneously, there are other important knowledge gaps pertaining to the role of B regulatory cells in SLE where there is a lack of specific cell surface and transcriptional factor markers akin to the forkhead box protein P3 (Foxp3) found in T regulatory cells. The over-arching hypothesis is that abnormalities in multiple components of the immune system contribute to lupus pathogenesis. Specifically, we hypothesise that the immune regulatory component is dysfunctional (both quantitatively and qualitatively) during lupus flare. To address such unmet needs, we aim to use a high dimensional approach using mass cytometry to unravel the contribution of the regulatory and inflammatory immunome to lupus pathogenesis simultaneously. This will be achieved with the characterisation of 37 immune markers at the single cell level using mass cytometry, followed by an unbiased and unsupervised analysis with a machine learning custom software based on dimensional reductions followed by automated cells classification and clustering. Subsequently, hierarchical prioritisation of the cell populations based on its strength of association with disease activity for downstream mechanistic characterisation with fluorescence based flow cytometry sorting of the target cells of interest for full transcriptome analysis and in-vitro functional study will be done.This approach has the immediate dual translational potential of identifying immune cell subsets relevant for clinical prognostication and the elucidation of disease mechanisms which will subsequently provide important information for the development of a multi-pronged immunotherapeutic strategy against SLE.

title: A Randomised Controlled Trial Evaluating a Novel Individualised Treatment Strategy for Carbapenem-Resistant Gram-Negative Bacteria Infections
abs: Carbapenem (a potent last-line high therapeutic index antibiotic)-resistant gram-negative bacilli (CRGNB) is resistant to all beta-lactam antibiotics, and likely extensively/pan-drug resistant. Against a background of dwindling antibiotic pipeline effective against these infections, using antibiotic combinations is one of the few viable options left to clinicians. However, evidence for the use of antibiotics is controversial because the mortality reduction associated with antibiotic combination therapy was not consistently observed in all studies. One main reason for this could be the strain-specific effectiveness of different antibiotic combinations. This also underscores the limitation of on-going randomised clinical trials in Europe and the USA, comparing one fixed antibiotic monotherapy against one fixed antibiotic combination. An investigator-initiated, prospective, open-label, randomised controlled clinical trial will be conducted to evaluate a new treatment strategy for CRGNB infections. Termed “guided antibiotic combination therapy”, the study arm will receive the most effective (synergistic and bactericidal) antibiotics combination derived from in vitro antibiotic combination testing (iACT). The comparator arm will receive standard therapy of either antibiotic monotherapy or unguided combination therapy, depending on treating physicians' clinical judgment. The primary hypothesis is that when compared to standard treatment, guided combination of antibiotics following iACT reduces 30-day mortality by 10% in patients with CRGNB infections. The mechanisms of resistance in CRGNB, and patients’ adverse drug reactions will be described. iACT will be performed for all trial patients although test information will be withheld for comparator arm. Instead, results from the iACT will be used to explore the 30-day all-cause mortality rates between patients whose treatments are matched with the iACT result, versus those whose treatments are not matched, within the standard therapy arm. We hypothesis that the mortality rate is 10% lowered in the standard therapy arm among patients whose therapies matched with the iACT results than those whose therapies did not match.

title: Long-term clinical outcomes, cost-of-care, clinical characteristics, re-admission rates, outpatient care and mortality in patients with coronary artery disease, congestive heart failure or atrial fibrillation in Singapore ("SingCLOUD" for Singapore Cardiac Longitudinal OUtcomes Database Study)
abs: SingCLOUD was formed in 2013 for large-scale cardiac analyses of clinical and administrative data across all public health institutions (PHIs). It examines cost-of-care, clinical outcomes, and measures of quality-of-care to help shape national policy making for patients with either proven or suspected coronary artery disease (CAD), congestive heart failure (CHF), and/or atrial fibrillation (AF). It uses the Business Research and Analytics Insights Network (BRAIN) platform - a federated data grid conceptualized by MOH and IMDA, which extracts, harmonizes, and integrates data across all PHIs. SingCLOUD uses BRAIN to federate data from six independent databases covering thirteen subject areas and a total of 7,057 data fields. In April 2015, data extraction for the SingCLOUD Pilot study was completed, and initial analysis completed in November 2017. This examined outcomes from index patients admitted to two hospitals, with outcomes tracked across the whole country, from 2007 to 2014. The next phase of the project is to extend the entire program for index patients across all hospitals and admissions beyond 2014 to 2016 and to include patients with AF, in addition to the current CAD and CHF cohorts. The aims of this proposal are to (1) establish one-year clinical outcomes, cost-of-care, and quality-of-care in patients with CAD, CHF, or AF, admitted to all public hospitals; and (2) study the association between adherence to guideline-recommended therapy and outcomes (including cost-of-care). To do so, this proposal will support the current IT infrastructure for SingCLOUD and extend the current analytics capability of SingCLOUD to SingCLOUD 2.0.

title: Molecular dissection and therapeutic targeting of cardiac fibrosis
abs: Fibrosis is an essential physiological process that is a central to wound healing. However, excessive fibrosis causes disease and is recognized as the final common pathway of cardiac damage. We recently undertook a large genomic discovery program in cardiac fibrosis using RNAsequencing of primary human atrial fibroblasts stimulated with transforming growth factor beta (TGFB) and observed that TGFB most strongly upregulates interleukin 11 (IL11, >10-fold). The true physiological function of IL11 is unknown and we tested the hypothesis that IL11 may act as an autocrine factor in fibroblasts. We found that IL11 is a very potent pro-fibrotic factor and that the action of TGFB, and other pro-fibrotic factors, depends on IL11 activity. This finding is very exciting as it not only reveals new biology but identifies a secreted cytokine, the preferred target for antibody-based therapeutics, as a critical determinant of fibroblast activation. In this study we will leverage our newly created biological reagents that include tissue-specific loss and gain-of-function mice that will be applied to study the effects of IL11 in fibroblasts in vivo by crossing to a Col1a2-CreER line. We will examine the molecular mechanisms underlying cis- and trans IL11 signaling in fibroblasts and dissect the relative contributions of the JAK/STAT and MAPK signaling pathways. We will test the hypothesis that inhibiting IL11 signaling with either anti-IL11 or anti-IL11RA antibodies that we have generated can prevent, arrest or reverse cardiac fibrosis. In molecular imaging and biomarker studies we will examine IL11 detection methodologies as a means of revealing active fibrosis in rodents and humans. These studies will open a new avenue of research in fibrosis, define new biology and explore the possibility of blocking IL11 signaling, directed by biomarker stratification, as a therapeutic approach for inhibiting maladaptive fibrosis, which is an area of unmet clinical need.

title: Precision Medicine in Liver Cancer across an Asia-Pacific Network
abs: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the 6th most common cancer in the world but the 2nd most important cause of cancer death. Because of its highly heterogeneous nature, the current approach to identifying druggable targets have not delivered efficacious therapies in HCC and is a main reason for the high case fatality. Even when surgical resection is potentially curative in early disease, tumor recurrence remains high and long term survival poor because of the absence of useful adjuvant therapy. To address these unmet needs, we bring together internationally recognized scientists from genomics and immunology and established clinician investigators in a synergistic team. This TCR capitalizes on recent collaborative advances made by the PIs in the consortium. We have shown through multi-region sampling of freshly resected HCC and phylogenetic analysis, that significant intra-tumoral heterogeneity exists and have identified the specific positions of known clonal drivers. Simultaneously we have analyzed the immune landscape of the tumor microenvironment with deep immune-phenotyping and found unique inter-patient immune landscapes predictive of clinical trajectory. In this TCR, Phase I is a prospective study that samples resected HCC from multi-ethnic sites within the established Asia-Pacific Hepatocellular Carcinoma (AHCC) Trials Group, which has enrolled approximately 1000 patients through 6 multi-center trials in 35 centers in the region. Clinical trajectories are tracked and genomic and immunological studies are repeated when tumors recur, to confirm clonally dominant driver mutations and immunological processes that are targetable. In Phase II these patients with recurrent tumors are enrolled in a proof-of-principle clinical trial using therapeutics selected or developed on the basis of discoveries in this study. Concurrently, representative pre-clinical models will be developed from the tissues sampled. We aim to combine these approaches to overcome the challenges posed by genomic heterogeneity and to guide the development of therapeutics and precision medicine in HCC.

title: The VICTORY (Virus-Induced Cancer: Translational Oncology Research & immunology) Consortium
abs: The Virus-Induced Cancers: Translational Oncology Research and immunologY consortium (VICTORY) is a national translational team of leading key opinion leaders combining synergistic expertise to optimise immunotherapeutic strategy against virally-driven cancers (VDCs). This will be accomplished by examining host and viral interactions in the tumour microenvironment – specifically how VDCs induce immunosuppression, target discovery and validation, and experimental therapeutics. Major VDCs will be examined, Epstein-Barr virus-driven cancers such as nasopharyngeal cancer (NPC), Human papilloma virus-driven oropharyngeal and cervical cancers, and Hepatitis B-driven hepatocellular carcinoma. The VICTORY team has a proven track record: • 30 joint publications • 9 joint grant applications • 34 clinical trials • 400 recruited patients Virus-induced cancers in Asia account for over 60% of global VDCs, and still expected to increase. The VICTORY consortium harnesses unique, competitive capabilities and resources across academic institutions with industry to establish: 1) The world’s largest collection of functionally, clinically annotated VDC biospecimens. The VDC Biobank forms a centrepiece for the consortium for systematic comprehensive analytics, 2) Deep immunophenotyping and broad omics capability to complete comprehensive characterisation of VDC immune microenvironment including molecular, functional and mechanistic assessment of VDC immune suppression, 3) novel humanised mouse models of VDCs able to host both human solid cancers and a recapitulated human immune system, and shown to harbour oncogenic virus infection, 4) Strong interdisciplinary team of world class clinician-scientists, immunologists, virologists, molecular biologists and metabolism experts, and 5) Robust collaborations with pharmaceutical and biotech companies locally and internationally and with the non-profit Parker Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy. The enhanced understanding of VDCs and underlying immune/metabolic drivers of disease that will result from the VICTORY consortium forms the basis of novel, next generation immunotherapies and discovery of biomarkers informing therapy. The VICTORY consortium creates an unprecedented, coordinated, leading global centre of VDC excellence embracing the biomedical, academic healthcare, and industry sectors.

title: Next-Generation Clinical Trials and Integrative Research for Fighting Lung Cancer
abs: Lung cancer is the most lethal disease in Singapore, but unlike in the West, lung cancer in Asia is far more likely to be driven by mutation of EGFR (epidermal growth factor receptor) and to occur in patients who have never smoked. Many patients respond initially to kinase inhibitor drugs, only to relapse with drug-resistant disease. Our 5-theme proposal harnesses genomics and informatics to predict and direct appropriate interventions, to reduce lung cancer mortality in Singapore. Theme 1 centres around 4 investigator-initiated trials (IIT), 23 pharma-sponsored trials, and observation of non-trial patients, to generate a unique and comprehensive body of clinical data and serial biospecimens for the remaining themes. We have procured substantial industry support for our IITs, including a novel adaptive clinical trial (BESPOKE) which uses genomic profiling to adjust treatments and track response dynamically. Theme 2 clarifies the risks and benefits of immuno-oncology in EGFR-mutant(EGFRm) and EGFR-wildtype(EGFRwt) non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) by interrogating serial biospecimens (blood and tumor) from patients treated with PD-1-related combinations (nivolumab with ipilimumab or metronomic vinorelbine), looking to identify determinants or biomarkers for patient response and toxicity outcomes. Theme 3 provides data processing and analytics for patient-derived data, and performs virtual dissection of tumor heterogeneity to identify molecular changes associated with response and resistance. Statistical methods will identify biomarkers and a clinical decision-support system will cater to the adaptive clinical trial. Theme 4 employs NSCLC-derived model systems for seeking novel therapeutic targets based on stemness and cancer metabolism; for pursuing long-term drug development efforts; and for assessing how combination treatments affect the evolution of drug-resistance. Theme 5 addresses present-day needs in the broader population by testing the feasibility, cost-effectiveness, and psychological burdens of screening people who have never smoked, and by studying environmental exposures in our population.

title: Harnessing LOXL1 as a therapeutic candidate for exfoliation syndrome and exfoliation glaucoma
abs: Exfoliation syndrome (XFS) is a disorder of aging that affects the extracellular matrix (ECM). In the eye, XFS results in obstruction of the trabecular outflow, causing raised intraocular pressure, glaucoma, and subsequent blindness. Although XFS is a major cause of blindness worldwide, it is notable that the prevalence of XFS is low in Chinese people. Genetic studies have shown that common LOXL1 gene variants are strongly associated with XFS. However, the mechanism by which common LOXL1 variants convey differential risk of XFS is unknown. Recently, we sequenced LOXL1 in 5,566 XFS cases and 6,279 controls from nine non-Chinese populations, identifying 63 naturally occurring rare amino acid substitutions. These LOXL1 variants were significantly enriched in normal controls compared to XFS cases, amongst all populations, suggesting a strong protective effect against XFS (Aung T et al., Nature Genetics 2017). We now propose to perform deep sequencing of the LOXL1 locus in Chinese XFS patients and compare them to Chinese controls to define the genetic architecture which could be responsible for the higher degree of protection in the Chinese. We next aim to perform comprehensive functional characterization of all naturally occurring rare genetic variants across the LOXL1 locus. This will first be done by assessing the impact of LOXL1 genetic variants on LOXL1 enzymatic action using a LOXL1 oxidase assay and how it affects downstream ECM components such as elastin, fibrillin, and collagen. We will follow this up with further assessing the manner in which these LOXL1 protective genetic variants affect physiological cell-cell adhesion in human eye tissue cell lines as a direct consequence of altered ECM metabolism. Our proposal will help elucidate the mechanisms by which LOXL1 are involved in XFS biology with the long term aim of designing therapy to halt the disease process and prevent blindness.
kw: LOXL1 genetic; Exfoliation Syndrome; Glaucoma; Biochemistry

title: TCF20 rs932376 genotype-directed dosing of tamoxifen in Asian estrogen-receptor positive breast cancer patients
abs: Tamoxifen is a selective estrogen receptor modulator effective against estrogen-receptor positive breast cancer. Tamoxifen’s therapeutic activity is mainly due to its principal active metabolite endoxifen, which is formed from tamoxifen mostly (>90%) via CYP2D6 mediated metabolism. It is thus hypothesized that low resultant serum endoxifen levels are a harbinger of increased cancer recurrence and poor outcome. Should this be true, it suggests that a critical endoxifen concentration for oncologists to aim for could exist. As preliminary data, we conducted the first genome-wide association study on steady-state endoxifen levels in 154 Singaporean Chinese breast cancer patients, with replication analysis in 290 Germans and 70 Lebanese breast cancer patients. Strong evidence of association was observed between a TCF20 genetic marker and serum endoxifen levels (effect size = -11.15 mmol per-copy of the minor allele; P = 1.19 x 10-40) with no evidence of heterogeneity across collections. Analysis compensating for the canonical CYP2D6 metabolizer genotypes still showed TCF20 to be strongly genome-wide significant over and above CYP2D6, retaining consistent evidence of association across the patient collections. Carriers and individuals homozygous for the minor allele of TCF20 showed poorer clinical outcome (N = 2091 women with 257 events) compared to wild-type individuals (Hazard ratio per-allele = 1.24; P = 0.015; I2 index for heterogeneity=0%). These low-pass GWAS findings herald the presence of genetic variants of higher penetrance and stronger effect with regards to control of endoxifen pharmacokinetics as well as clinical outcome of breast cancer patients following treatment with tamoxifen. The objective of this proposal is to now build on the Singaporean GWAS finding and conduct a prospective TCF20 genotype-based dosing of tamoxifen in Singaporean hormone receptor positive breast cancer patients.
kw: Tamoxifen; Genotype-directed dosing; TCF20 rs932376; CYP2D6; ER-positive breast cancer

title: Unravelling pathway addiction to the long non-coding RNA EGFR-AS1: a basket trial strategy
abs: Squamous-cell cancers (SCCs) represent one of the commonest lethal malignancy worldwide, arising from a range of sites. Despite evidence demonstrating that majority are addicted to Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR)-signaling, targeting with monoclonal antibodies or tyrosine-kinase inhibitors (TKIs) has been met with limited success. We recently published our findings showing that TKI-sensitivity is modulated by the expression of a long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) situated in the antisense strand of EGFR (EGFR-AS1). Mutations in EGFR-AS1 (A/A genotype) and changing lncRNA expression affected TKI-response in patient-derived models and a small patient cohort. Importantly, modest knockdown showed profound effects on TKI sensitivity. Based on our mechanistic insights, we hypothesize that patient-response to EGFR inhibitors is contingent on establishing a comprehensive suite of inter-related biomarkers. To address this, we aim to conduct a proof-of-concept “basket” trial of EGFR-TKI for EGFR-driven solid tumours harbouring the A/A genotype, profiling the entire pathway. Given that these responses can be attenuated due to disruption at each level, analysis of pre-treatment tumour biopsies will provide further insights to the determinants of drug sensitivity. Therefore, our second aim is to identify and validate mechanisms of primary/secondary resistance to EGFR-TKI. This will be done by unbiased profiling of pre- and post-treatment biopsies in trial patients, and understanding these mechanisms in pre-clinical models. Our secondary hypothesis relates to tumors which demonstrate addiction to EGFR-AS1, where effective knock-down of the lncRNA augments therapeutic vulnerability to EGFR-TKIs. The third aim is to target EGFR-AS1 in this cohort, for optimal knock-down in vitro and in vitro. This would be based on medium-throughput in vitro RNA-interference screens along the EGFR-AS1 molecule, in patient-derived lines, with in vivo validation in patient-derived xenografts. Through this grant, we intend to extend this strategy, which started as a clinical observation, into a bona fide therapeutic strategy with widespread clinical ramifications.
kw: LncRNA, Basket trial, Tyrosine kinase inhibitors, Synonymous mutation, TKI resistance, Epigenetics

title: The Singapore Epidemiology of Eye Diseases (SEED) Study 3 – Prospective multi-ethnic cohort study of 12-year incidence, risk factors, and impact of major age-related eye diseases
abs: There is a disproportionate burden of age-related eye diseases in Asians. Specifically, Asia accounts for 30% of diabetic retinopathy (DR) and 60% of glaucoma cases worldwide. There are ethnic variations in the prevalence of major eye diseases in both Singapore and Asia. These observations highlight the need for in-depth evaluation on the long-term incidence and progression of age-related eye diseases in Asians. However, long-term cohort data are still extremely limited in Asia. In 2004-11, we completed the baseline Singapore Epidemiology of Eye Diseases Study (SEED-1), a population-based multi-ethnic study on 10,033 participants (75.5% response rate) of Malays, Indians and Chinese. Subsequently, in 2011-17 we successfully completed the 6-year follow-up examination (SEED-2) in 6,762 baseline participants (78.7% response rate). Data collected from SEED have been used widely by national and international agencies and in clinical guidelines. SEED-3 will re-examine this multi-ethnic cohort 12 years after the baseline examination. We will 1) determine the 12-year incidence and progression of visual impairment (VI) and major eye diseases; 2) employ state-of-art ocular imaging technology; 3) link VI with cardiovascular outcomes via nationwide electronic medical record database; 4) discover new metabolite biomarkers; and 5) evaluate the health impact of major blinding eye diseases in Singaporean adults. The major strengths of SEED-3 include a well-established and characterized cohort at baseline and 6-year visit, an experienced international team of clinician-scientists and epidemiologists, and the highest-quality baseline ocular/systemic data, including high-resolution images of retina and optic nerve, stored serum/blood/urine, and existing genome-wide genotype data. The ultimate completion of 12-year follow-up visits in SEED-3 will provide unprecedentedly comprehensive information on the development of major eye diseases in Asians, covering the 3 major ethnicities in the region. These data will be critical for the planning of public health strategies to reduce visual loss not only in Singapore but across Asia.
kw: population-based study; incidence; progression; glaucoma; age-related macular degeneration

title: A pilot study of intermittent accelerated burst transcranial magnetic stimulation (aTBS) to treat depression: a randomized, single-blind, delayed-start trial
abs: Accelerating the administration of rTMS (aTMS) by delivering multiple sessions of rTMS over a shorter period of time can increase patient acceptability. Various studies of aTMS have been safely conducted with anywhere from 2 to 10 sessions of rTMS a day for a total of 9 – 20 sessions of TMS over 2 to 9 days, showing that aTMS was safe and efficacious, with no significant side effects and a high level of patient acceptability and significant improvements in subjects’ depression. However, there is no data on whether subjects who do not response to aTMS will benefit from more of the same TMS or from changing the mode of rTMS. Our own observations and some preliminary evidence suggest that there may be a delayed response to TMS in some patients. The same outcome may be achieved by giving a shorter period of stimulation (eg 1 weeks), waiting 2-4 weeks, then assessing response and the need for further TMS treatment. Further, giving more than 1 treatment per day has been shown to be effective and may lead to more efficient treatment. This pilot study will contribute to existing knowledge by being possibly the first group in South East Asia to investigate the immediate and delayed efficacy of aTMS in an Asian population and whether continuing or changing the type of rTMS is more efficacious in subjects who do not respond to initial aTMS.
kw: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation; depression; treatment modality; delayed start; response rate; accelerated

title: A Randomized Trial to Slow the Progression of Diabetes (The TRIPOD Study)
abs: A primary focus of the ‘Diabetes’ theme is to identify new models to arrest the rate of deterioration and reduce acute episodes for those with diabetes, and to do so in a cost-effective manner while incorporating elements of secondary and tertiary care aligned with primary prevention efforts. This proposal is highly responsive to those objectives. We will conduct a three arm randomized controlled trial to test whether a low cost mobile diabetes management package (DMP), with or without an incentive program (M-POWER rewards), can improve blood sugar levels at 12 months as measured by HbA1c levels (primary) among those with type 2 diabetes. We hypothesize that DMP will improve HbA1c relative to control but that the greatest improvements will occur for those exposed to both interventions (DMP+M-POWER). Similar hypotheses will be tested for secondary outcomes, including HbA1c at 6 months, proportion of participants initiating insulin, weight, blood pressure, and self-reported weight monitoring, physical activity, blood glucose monitoring, medication adherence and quality of life measures. All outcomes will be tested at baseline, 6, and 12 months. We will also quantify the incremental cost effectiveness of DMP and DMP+M-POWER and the net cost implications of both from a third party payer’s perspective. We hypothesize that DMP will be cost effective compared to control but that despite its higher cost, the incremental cost effectiveness and net costs will be lowest for DMP + M-POWER due to the reduction in medical expenditures that comes through improved blood sugar control. Given the rising health and cost implications of diabetes in Singapore, this application is timely and offers an innovative and scalable model to address Singapore’s diabetes epidemic.
kw: Type 2 diabetes mellitus; Diabetes self-management; Mobile apps and devices; Financial incentives

title: Optimising the assessment of quality of life in glaucoma using item bank and computer adaptive testing systems
abs: Glaucoma is a common and potentially blinding eye condition, disproportionately affecting Asians. Patients with glaucoma have increased risk of falls, and reduced visual functioning, mobility and independence and emotional well-being. Understanding the impact of health conditions and the effectiveness of treatment therapies from the patient’s perspective is becoming increasingly important, and patient reported outcomes data is becoming essential to guide clinical care, support patient-provider decision-making, and for practice improvement, performance evaluation of organizations, and as a metric for value-based payments. While several questionnaires exist to measure glaucoma related quality of life (QoL), modern psychometric methods have revealed serious psychometric short-comings with these instruments. Moreover, current questionnaires in ophthalmology are paper-pencil based, meaning they are static, inflexible, burdensome to administer and answer. Fortunately, item banking and computer adaptive testing (CAT) provide a solution to these problems. An item bank is a large pool of questions calibrated on the same linear scale using item response theory. Item banks are operationalized by CAT, which is ‘smart’ technology that adapts the items asked based on participants’ responses to previous items. CAT minimizes measurement error and reduces test length without loss of precision and reliability. Evidently, a comprehensive, culturally valid and precise instrument is urgently required to assess the impact of glaucoma and efficacy of related treatments from the patient’s perspective in Asia. Fortunately, pioneering work in this area has commenced. PI Fenwick has created 300 glaucoma-specific items housed within 12 QoL domains, globally referred to as GLIBQoLS (GLaucoma Item Banks for Quality of Life in Singapore). The validity, efficiency and clinical applicability of GLIBQoLS are nowr eady to be assessed, resulting in a valuable, highly sought after instrument for use by ophthalmologists, researchers, healthcare organizations and policy planners. Therefore, the objective of this proposal is to psychometrically and clinically validate GLIBQoLS in Singaporean patients with glaucoma.
kw: Glaucoma; quality of life; patient-report outcome measures; item bank; computer adaptive testing; outcomes research; evaluating treatment therapies

title: Panel study Investigating Status of Cognitively impaired Elderly in Singapore (PISCES)
abs: Dementia is a growing epidemic affecting 10% of elderly in Singapore. Caring for patients dying with severe dementia (PDSD) during end of life (EOL) is a medical and economic challenge for the health system and primary informal caregivers. However, to date there is a lack of systematic information regarding EOL care received by community dwelling PDSD, their EOL direct and indirect costs and caregiver burden. This lack of data impedes development and evaluation of interventions to support PDSD and their caregivers. We aim to address this information gap by conducting a first-of-its-kind prospective cohort study of primary informal caregivers of PDSD in collaboration with leading public hospitals and home care foundations caring for PDSD in Singapore. We will assess the EOL care received by community dwelling PDSD and their caregivers, EOL medical and social care costs of severe dementia and caregiver burden; and will develop a risk score to predict 6-month mortality for PDSD. We will survey primary informal caregivers every 4 months for 2 years, or until patient death and then 6 weeks and 6 months thereafter. Presence of severe dementia will be established using the Quick Dementia Rating System. At study completion we will extract and match patient medical and billing data with study survey data for comprehensive assessment of care costs. The study will provide data for improved early decision making by caregivers and physicians regarding EOL care. It will also provide a better understanding of EOL care for PDSD and their caregivers that will lead to cross-sector collaborations to improve delivery of palliative care to PDSD. In the long term this study will improve clinical and public health policy and has the potential to be the foundation for future initiatives for dementia care and improved social and medical infrastructure planning.
kw: dementia; ageing; palliative care; end of life care; cohort; caregiver burden

title: An Intensive, Practical, and Personalized Care Planning to Improve Glycemic Control, Clinical, Ocular, And Patient Centred Outcomes in Poorly Controlled Patients with Diabetic Retinopathy
abs: The prevalence of diabetes in Singapore is increasingly rising as are associated microvascular complications mostly due to poor diabetes management, suggesting that alternative and personalized interventions are urgently needed. Using a multi-site, longitudinal, and single blind RCT, the current proposal aims to evaluate the clinical, ocular, patient-centred and economic effectiveness of a novel, intensive, practical and personalized care planning intervention (DRIPCP) in patients with diabetic retinopathy (DR) and poorly controlled diabetes attending three tertiary hospitals in Singapore. DRIPCP is a patient-centric care model, designed to engage, support and empower individuals with long-term chronic conditions to achieve improved health outcomes. A key component of DRIPCP involves a continuous and active conversation between personalized care-trained doctors and nurse educators with the aim of reaching a mutual understanding on an individualized treatment regimen. The intervention includes 3-way consultations; home visits or phone/Skype calls by trained nurse educators; personalized eye care consultations based on patientsÆ own retinal images; behavior change support strategies; and refresher sessions. Participants will be randomly allocated to receive usual care + DRIPCP or usual care alone. Assessments will take place at baseline, 6, 12, 24, and 36 monthsÆ post intervention. We hypothesize that compared to usual care, those randomized to DRIPCP will have significantly greater improvements in cardio metabolic risk factors including glycated hemoglobin (primary outcome); and due to the sustained improvements in these risk factors, there will be a significantly lower proportion of DR progression and sight-threatening DR incidence at 36 months; with a corresponding decrease in incidence and progression of distance visual impairment in the DRIPCP group. Our personalized approach has wider applications. It can easily be adapted to other diabetes-related complications, such as kidney disease or for use with other systemic health conditions where disease progression can be tracked and behavioral factors can determine progression.
kw: Integrated care; personalized eye care; diabetes management; clinical outcomes; patient-centered; diabetic retinopathy

title: Understanding the Psychosocial, Cultural, and Systemic Determinants of Antibiotic Use and Utilizing a Multilevel Approach to Address Inappropriate Antibiotic Use
abs: The rapid emergence and unimpeded increase in antimicrobial resistance has raised serious concerns about the threat of a postantibiotic era. One major contributing factor is inappropriate antibiotic use. The decision to use antibiotics is complex, involving not only a physician’s propensity to prescribe antibiotics but also the interplay of psychosocial, cultural, and systemic factors among the patient, caregiver, clinical care team, and physician. Antimicrobial resistance, which increases with age, can result in a decreased quality of life, higher morbidity and mortality risks, and increased healthcare expenditure. It is preventable through a successful antimicrobial stewardship program. Most studies on antibiotic use and antimicrobial stewardship have been conducted in developed Western countries, where healthcare provision is a patient-centered model. A relationship-centered model could be the framework for optimal care and antibiotic prescribing in Singapore. However, to date, there is no study evaluating antimicrobial stewardship comprehensively at multiple levels throughout the continuum of care. Through a series of mixed-methods studies involving sequential qualitative and quantitative phases carried out in the community, public and private primary care clinics, and the three largest hospitals in Singapore, the research proposal aims to explore the views and opinions of diverse stakeholders (general public, patients, caregivers, healthcare providers) to gain insights into the multi-dimensional determinants of antibiotic use and prescribing practices. The understanding will guide an evidence-based multi-level intervention that will align the goals of all stakeholders towards a synchronized national antimicrobial stewardship program to reduce inappropriate antibiotic use, prevent antimicrobial resistance, and decrease healthcare costs in Singapore. With a rapidly ageing population, who are more prone to infections and inappropriate exposure to antibiotics due to atypical symptomatic presentations, such an approach is necessary to curb the rising tide of antimicrobial resistance and prevent antibiotic-resistant infections amidst the background of a dwindling antibiotic pipeline and limited healthcare resources.
kw: Antimicrobial stewardship; Antimicrobial resistance; Antibiotic use; Antibiotic prescription; Psychosocial determinants; Singapore

title: Lipid Mediators of Brain Growth and Function
abs: The insulating myelin sheath surrounding axons is vital for optimal computational function of the brain. Demyelination is a hallmark of multiple sclerosis, brain injury, and normal aging. One of the barriers to developing treatments for demyelinating diseases is a limited understanding of the intrinsic factors that regulate oligodendrocyte differentiation and myelination, representing a major unmet medical need. Here we leverage our clinical data, mouse and cell models, and biochemical studies that deficiency of Mfsd2a, an omega-3 fatty acid lysolipid (LPC) transporter, in mice and humans resulted in microcephaly and severe hypomyelination. Remarkably, Mfsd2a is expressed in oligodendrocyte precursors (OPC) and specific deficiency of Mfsd2a in this precursor pool resulted in hypomyelination, indicating that LPC transport by OPC might regulate their proliferation and/or differentiation. Our long-term goal is the development of LPC-based therapeutics for brain health. The objective here, which builds upon our expertise of the Mfsd2a/LPC pathway, is to determine the mechanism by which LPCs regulate myelination. The central hypothesis is that LPC transport into OPCs via Mfsd2a is essential for OPC proliferation and differentiation. The rationale for our proposed studies is that determination of a mechanism of action for LPCs in myelination and demonstration of efficacy in enhancing myelination would catalyse clinical development of LPC-based nutritionals for aging and demyelinating disorders. Guided by strong preliminary data, the goal of this application will be achieved by two specific aims: (1) To determine the biochemical mechanism by which LPC transport via Mfsd2a functions to regulate myelination; (2) To determine if dietary LPC treatment can enhance myelination. The approach is innovative because it is designed to determine a biochemical function of LPCs in myelination. The proposed research is significant because it will provide key experimental information for the clinical development of LPC-based agents to enhance myelination in aging and demyelinating diseases.
kw: transporters; lipids; blood-brain barrier; phospholipids

title: Target RAF Complex for Cancer Therapy
abs: Hyperactive Ras/RAF/MEK/ERK signaling has well-defined role in cancer development, which exists in over 85% cancers and plays a functional role in disease progression. Genetic studies have revealed that the aberrant activation of this signaling pathway mainly arises from the alterations of RAF, Ras, and Ras upstream regulators. In contrast to other components of this pathway, RAF and MEK have been thought as ideal targets for developing anti-cancer drugs, and indeed two RAF inhibitors (Vemurafenib and Dabrafenib) and one MEK inhibitor (Trametinib) have been generated and applied to clinic cancer treatment. However, these drugs have on efficacy to cancers with active Ras and only a short-term efficacy to BRAF(V600E)-mutated cancers. Mechanistic studies have shown that in cancers with active Ras, RAF, MEK and other molecules form a super complex that leads to the inhibitor resistance. The goal of this study is to understand how the RAF complex is assembled and thereby develop approaches to disrupt this complex for achieving better therapeutic efficacy. To reach this goal, we will employ advanced molecular biology, biochemistry, cancer biology and pharmacology methods to explore the compositions of RAF complex and its dynamic characteristics under variable pathological conditions and to construct effective approaches to block the hyperactive Ras/RAF/MEK/ERK singling by disrupting the RAF complex for cancer treatment. We believe the execution of this study will provide us more effective approaches/drugs for the treatment of cancers driven by hyperactive Ras/RAF/MEK/ERK singling, especially Ras-mutated cancers and drug-resistant BRAF(V600E) cancers.
kw: Oncogenic Protein Kinases, Cancer, Cellular Signalling, Ras/RAF/MEK/ERK signaliing, Protein kinase inhibitors, and drug resistance.

title: Structural mechanisms of retinoic acid receptor alpha mutations in breast fibroepithelial tumors and drug discovery
abs: Fibroepithelial tumor of the breast is a group of lesions consisting of the benign fibroadenoma, which is highly common in young women, and the relatively rare but potentially aggressive phyllodes tumors. We have recently demarcated the genetic landscapes of breast fibroepithelial tumors, (Lim et al., Nature Genet., 2014; Tan et al., Nature Genet., 2015), with the discovery of MED12 and RARA mutations as the two most common somatic genetic alterations in all classes of these tumors. RARA encodes for RAR-alpha member of the nuclear hormone receptors, which are well-known to be successful drug targets. While previously known RARA mutations found in acute promyelocytic leukemia are translocations resulting in the fusion with other genes such as PML, this has been the first report of tumor-associated frequent point mutations in RARA. Our in vitro assays revealed a set of functionally distinct properties displayed by mutant RAR-alpha compared to the wild type, which include marked enhanced interactions with transcriptional corepressors. Preliminary analyses based on the published crystal structure of wild type RAR-alpha showed that the majority of the mutations occur at residues that are not directly in contact with ligand or corepressor, suggesting that the mutations may have induced novel structural changes to elicit the altered functions. We have also established isogenic cell lines from patient samples and showed that RAR-alpha agonists inhibit the viability of cells expressing wild-type but not mutant RAR-alpha justifying the specific targeting of latter cells. These lines of evidence supports that mutant RAR-alpha differ structurally from the wild-type protein and require mutant specific agonists to promote their transcriptional activity and growth inhibitory effects. We therefore propose to 1) determine the crystal structures of mutant RAR-alpha to elucidate their structural mechanisms and 2) implement computational and biochemical screening to discover potential mutant-specific ligands to be further developed as therapeutics.
kw: Breast fibroadenoma, Breast phyllodes tumors, Retinoic acid receptor mutations, Crystallography, Structural studies, Novel mechanisms

title: Exploring the Therapeutic Potential of Narciclasine in Treating Metabolic Disorders
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Many countries, including Singapore, are facing a surge of metabolic disorders due to sedentary lifestyle and high-calorie food consumption. As such, there is an urgent need for effective therapeutic approaches for the treatment of these diseases. Recently, we discovered a novel pharmacological strategy in which a natural compound, narciclasine, ameliorates diet-induced obesity (DIO) in mice by promoting energy expenditure. Moreover, narciclasine promotes fat clearance from peripheral metabolic tissues, improves blood metabolic parameters in DIO mice and protects these mice from reduced voluntary physical activity. Further investigation suggested that narciclasine achieves these beneficial effects by promoting a shift from glycolytic to oxidative muscle fibers thereby enhancing mitochondrial respiration and fatty acid oxidation (FAO) in the skeletal muscle. Mechanistically, narciclasine stimulates FAO likely through activating the AMPK signaling pathway. Finally, the beneficial effects of narciclasine treatment in fat clearance and AMPK activation were faithfully reproduced in vitro in cultured murine and human primary myotubes, suggesting its potential use in treating human metabolic diseases. We hypothesize that narciclasine can be developed into efficient therapeutics in treating various metabolic disorders associated with obesity. Moreover, we have synthesized 90 narciclasine analogues and identified one analogue (Ncls-A22) that out-performs ncls in promoting mitochondrial respiration, oxidative metabolism gene expression and AMPK activation. Ncls-A22 also demonstrated stronger anti-obesity activity than ncls. In this study, we propose to fully characterize the beneficial metabolic effects of narciclasine (Aim 1) and decipher the molecular mechanism underlying narciclasine function (Aim 2). We will also explore the therapeutic potential of narciclasine and Ncls-A22 in treating metabolic disorders (Aim 3). Given narciclasine’s distinct chemical structure as compared with other existing metabolic drugs, accomplishing the above proposed studies may lead to the development of a novel class of metabolic drugs for the prevention and treatment of obesity, diabetes, and other metabolic disorders.
kw: Narciclasine, Obesity, diabetes, energy expenditure, fatty acid oxidation, AMPK signaling pathway

title: Structural and functional studies of GABPA/GABPB in complex with mutant TERT promoter DNA and druggable p52/ETS1 and ETS1/DNA complexes
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Levels of catalytic subunit of telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT) are limiting in reconstituting telomerase activity in normal somatic cells. However, cells from 95% of human cancers transcriptionally reactivate TERT and this is necessary for cancer progression. How the WT TERT promoter is shut off in normal cell and how it is reactivated are the most fundamental questions in cancer biology. Highly Recurrent -146C>T and -124C>T TERT promoter mutations have been shown to drive upregulation of TERT in multiple cancers. Since both these hotspot mutations create a binding motif for E-twenty-six (ETS) transcription factors, ETS1/2 and GABPA have been shown to be involved in reactivation of these two mutant TERT promotors. ETS1/2 synergize with non-canonical NF-κB signalling through interaction with p52 to activate -146C>T TERT promoter while GABPA forms a heterotetramer with GABPB to drive the reactivation of both -146C>T and -124C>T mutations. However, the underlying mechanism of this process remains unclear. Built upon the successful structure determination of p52/ETS1 in compex with the -146C>T TERT DNA, we aim to solve the crystal structure of GABPA/GABPB in complex with the mutant TERT promoter DNA for elucidating the mechanism governing the activation of -146C>T and -124C>T mutant TERT promoters. The structures and subsequent functional assays will reveal whether p52/ETS1 and GABPA/GABPB share a unifying mechanism for the activation of -146C>T and -124C>T mutants. Since reactivation of -146C>T and -124C>T mutant TERT promoters only occurs in cancer cells rather than in normal and stem cells, We are interested in identifying small molecular compounds that specifically block TERT synthesis through inhibiting the reactivation of these two TERT mutations. As aberrant proto-oncoprotein ETS1 overexpression have been implicated in various tumours. We are also interested in identifying a small molecule that can disrupt ETS1/DNA interaction. Such a compound may act as a broad spectrum anticancer agent.
kw: TERT reactivation;p52/EST1 interaction;TERT mutation;GABPA/GABPB;ETS1/DNA interaction

title: Rtl1, a neofunctionalized retrotransposon, a novel factor regulating myogenesis
abs: The muscular dystrophies (MD) are a heterogeneous group of genetic diseases characterized by progressive weakness and degeneration of the skeletal musculature, and in some, heart function is also affected. Extensive muscle wasting is also a frequent consequence of other more common diseases such as cancer and diabetes. We identified the paternally expressed retrotransposon-like 1 (Rtl1) gene as being essential for efficient muscle regeneration and is expressed in murine models of muscular dystrophy, including Duchenne’s (DMD) and Emery-Dreifuss (AD-EDMD). In patient biopsies with AD-EDMD, RTL1 regulation is disrupted. We have derived a mouse line carrying a conditional allele of Rtl1 for in vivo studies. These mice will be crossed with inducible Cre lines to either delete or overexpress RTL1 tissue specifically and determine the loss/gain of function of RTL1 on muscle growth and regeneration. The biochemical processes of RTL1 are unknown except that RTL1 overexpression causes muscle hypertrophy in sheep and mice. We will characterize RTL1s’ function concerning myogenesis during the complex process of muscle regeneration. This will be performed in muscle killed by cardiotoxin injection and congenital muscle diseases, DMD and AD-EDMD. We use murine and human muscle cell lines to determine RTL1’s biochemical functions, define RTL1’s subcellular localization, and identify RTL1’s protein interaction partners. Preliminary evidence localized RTL1 to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). RTL1 expression is induced in primary myoblast cultures by treating cells with a proteosome inhibitor, indicating that RTL1 may be involved in the ER stress/Unfolded Protein Response Pathways and autophagy. We have generated antibodies to human RTL1 to validate RTL1 expression in human myogenesis and in muscle from patients with congenital human muscle disease. These antibodies will be used in determining the molecular function(s) of RTL1 and potentially for diagnostic purposes. Understanding RTL1’s role may provide novel approaches to ameliorating muscle atrophy and other myopathic diseases.
kw: Muscle growth; regeneration; muscular dystrophy; RTL1; ER Stress;

title: In vivo 2C-BioID, a new platform technology for interactome analysis
abs: The human genome comprises about 20,000 genes. However, the protein repertoire encoded by these may run to more than a million. Proteins rarely function in isolation since their activities are invariably tightly regulated. It follows, therefore, that how proteins interact with each other in response to both internal and external cues affects every aspect of normal cell physiology and behavior. Because of this, defining protein interactomes has now become an important adjunct of genomics and transcriptomics. Furthermore, it has become clear that the mapping of protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks in a variety of human diseases, from schizophrenia to muscular dystrophy has the potential to identify novel therapeutic targets. While advances in mass spectrometry have revolutionized protein identification, experimental methods to map PPIs, even in cultured cells, are quite limited. Defining PPIs within tissues in vivo containing multiple cell types is even more challenging. We have recently developed an advanced two-component proximity labelling method, 2C-BioID, that can be used to identify PPIs in an unbiased manner. The method takes advantage of a promiscuous biotin-protein ligase (BioID2) that is delivered to a protein of interest by rapamycin-dependent heterodimerization of FKBP and FRB protein domains. While we have validated this method in cell culture systems, there is every reason to believe that it can be adapted to work in vivo. Moreover, since expression of the FKBP-BioID2 component can be rendered inducible in a tissue-specific manner, this raises the prospect of performing tissue-specific interactome analyses. The goal of this proposal is to develop in vivo 2C-BioID as a platform technology. We will validate and refine our protocols on an analysis of a multifunctional nuclear pore complex protein, Nup133, defects in which are associated with Galloway-Mowat syndrome, a rare disease affecting primarily the central nervous system and kidneys.
kw: proteomics; interactome; BioID; Nuclear pore complex;

title: Preventing cardiovascular disease by uncoupling nuclear-cytoskeletal interactions
abs: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) accounted for 30.7% of deaths in Singapore in 2017. Although age is a major contributory factor to CVD, there is increasing evidence that the onset of CVD occurs earlier and in a more severe form in Singapore. To address these issues, we study the premature ageing disease Hutchinson-Gilford Progeria (HGPS) as a reproducible model of CVD. HGPS is caused by the mutant LaminA protein -Progerin, and children with HGPS die in their mid-teens from CVD. We will 1) produce microfluidic 3-D organ-on-a-chip reconstructions of human vasculature using HGPS (and isogenic controls) iPS stem cell-derived vascular smooth muscle and endothelial cells assembled into a vascular system. This will function to model human atherosclerosis and CVD in vitro. 2) We identified two proteins of relevance to CVD, SUN1 and CISD2. SUN1’s expression is increased by Progerin, whereas CISD2 preferentially binds to Progerin, as mice deficient in CISD2 develop diabetes and age prematurely. 3) We will determine whether disrupting CISD2 leads to vascular degeneration, as we hypothesize that Progerin sequesters CISD2 from the ER, so it can no longer regulate ER-mitochondrial Ca2+homeostasis. As a potential therapeutic, we will increase CSID2 levels to determine if this ameliorates atherosclerosis in our microfluidic model. A second therapeutic avenue is that functional disruption of SUN1 prevents lamin induced cardiomyopathy and significantly extends the longevity of HGPS mice. We will determine if disrupting SUN1 in the vasculature prevents CVD. This will be performed in our mouse model of HGPS and our microfluidic system. 4) We will determine if pre-laminA accumulation, which may cause age-related vascular degeneration, like Progerin, is both a biomarker and contributory factor to vascular ageing. Overall, our goal is to identify pathways that both suppress HGPS and be effective in treating CVD on the broader population.
kw: Cardiovascular disease; progeria; ageing; laming; vasculature; CISD2; Sun1

title: Targeting a novel Ca2+‐PP2A‐RIPK1‐dependent cell death pathway in cancer metabolism
abs: Unlike normal cells, many cancer cells generate energy by glycolysis even in the presence of oxygen, termed aerobic glycolysis or Warburg effect. To compensate for inefficient ATP production by glycolysis, cancer cells increase glucose uptake. Thus, cancer cells are more dependent on glucose and glycolysis than normal cells for survival. Therapeutics to selectively target cancer cells by inhibiting glycolysis have been pursued, but the response is mild and varied. We investigated the effect of glucose deprivation on different cancer cell lines, and identified a previously unappreciated cell death pathway. After glucose removal, intracellular levels of glucose become critically low in these glucose-dependent cancer cells, and were associated with an influx of calcium, activation of CAMK1 and the demethylase PPME1, demethylation and inactivation of the phosphatase PP2Ac, and phosphorylation and activation of RIPK1. Unexpectedly, PP2Ac demethylation and cell death are rescued with a glucose analog that inhibits glycolysis. These findings reveal a novel requirement for glucose independent of glycolysis. We hypothesize that glucose acts as a signaling molecule to suppress activation of a novel cell death pathway. In Aim 1 we will elucidate the molecular mechanisms of the cell death pathway through biochemistry and molecular biology. We further hypothesize that this pathway can be targeted by unique combination therapies to selectively eliminate cancer cells, which we will investigate in Aim 2 by molecular biology, cell culture and mouse xenograft cancer models. Successful completion of this proposal will reveal how glucose withdrawal induces calcium influx, CAMK1-mediated PPME1 activation, PPME1-mediated PP2Ac demethylation, PP2Acmediated activation of RIPK1, and cell death. We will also develop strategies to specifically kill cancer cells by combination therapies which block glucose transport and elevate cytosolic calcium levels. The repurposing of FDA approved drugs in unique combinations could translate quickly to the clinic and represent an original therapy from Singapore.
kw: cancer metabolsim; glucose; PP2A; RIPK1; cell death; cancer

title: Mechanisms of enhancer alterations in etiologically-distinct CCAs and their clinical implications
abs: Cholangiocarcinoma (CCA) is a dismal, heterogeneous malignancy with a need for new therapeutic strategies. Enhancers are distal regulatory regions implicated in tumorigenesis, and their studies have generated novel therapeutic targets in various cancers. Our recent study uncovered two CCA subtypes associated with different etiologies and mutations in epigenetic modifiers (liver-fluke-infected CCAs, versus BAP1-mutant fluke-negative CCAs), and subsequent analysis suggested divergent enhancer alterations as well. Since inflammatory signaling leads to enhancer alterations, and biliary tract inflammation is a risk factor for CCA (particularly for liver-fluke-infected cases), inflammatory response may therefore play a role in CCA enhancer dysregulation. The histone deubiquitinase BAP1 has been shown to regulate enhancer activity, thus BAP1 loss may also play a role in enhancer dysregulation. We therefore hypothesize that divergent enhancer dysregulation in fluke-positive and BAP1-mutant fluke-negative CCAs drive distinct oncogenic regulatory circuits and transcriptional programs. Inflammatory response (predominantly in fluke-positive CCA) and BAP1 mutations (predominantly in fluke-negative CCA) play mechanistic roles in enhancer dysregulation, and may underlie divergence in enhancer landscapes. To investigate this hypothesis, we will profile and compare the enhancer landscapes, regulatory circuits, and transcriptional programs, in these CCA subtypes (Aim 1). We will investigate the effect of inflammatory signaling on enhancer dysregulation, and the development of enhancer dysregulation during chronic inflammation (Aim 2). We will investigate the effect of BAP1 loss on enhancer dysregulation, and discover drugs synthetically-lethal with BAP1 mutations (Aim 3). This study will elucidate mechanisms of enhancer alterations in etiologically-distinct CCAs, and allow the identification of regulators of tumor-promoting enhancers as potential therapeutic targets tailored to specific CCA subtypes.
kw: Cholangiocarcinoma; Enhancer; BAP1

title: Physiological Role of Dok3 in Candidiasis
abs: Invasive fungal infection is a serious health threat with high morbidity and mortality, and Candida species are the most prevalent causative agents of such infection. However, current antifungal drugs only demonstrate partial success in improving prognosis. Together with the rapid emergence of drug resistance among Candida species, there is a pressing need to develop novel antifungal therapies to improve clinical outcomes. Understanding the mechanistic interaction between host immune system and fungal pathogens holds the key for uncovering novel immune-based treatments to combat candidaemia. Our preliminary study suggests that Dok3, an adaptor protein involved in immune receptor signaling, acts as a negative regulator of antifungal immunity in neutrophils. As such, we aim to elucidate the underlying mechanisms of Dok3 in antifungal immune response by determining their role in the regulation of neutrophilic antifungal effector functions, which include phagocytosis, secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines, production of reactive oxygen species, release of neutrophil extracellular traps, and the formation of neutrophil granules. In addition, the signaling pathway of Dok3 during antifungal immune response will be examined through microarray, mass spectrometry and biochemical approaches. By dissecting the mechanistic role of Dok3 in antifungal immunity, we will be able to propose the potential utility of Dok3 inhibitors as novel therapies and prophylaxis for invasive candidiasis. Such immune-based approach could act as an adjunctive therapy to current antifungal drugs for further improvement of outcomes in fungal-infected patients. As such, our proposed research will not only extend our understanding about the mechanisms regulating host antifungal immune response, but may also have translationally relevant implications for the development of novel antifungal drugs and infection control.
kw: Infectious diseases, immunology

title: Unravelling the functional dynamics of monocytes at the maternal-fetal interface of the placenta and its consequences during gestational diabetes
abs: Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM) is defined as a state of glucose intolerance with onset during pregnancy that predisposes towards adverse perinatal outcomes. Recent evidence have documented the placenta, which supports the growth and development of the fetus, to be structurally and functionally altered during GDM. However mechanisms that exacerbate these alterations remain unclear. It is increasingly recognized that diabetes is not a sole metabolic and endocrine disorder, and that a dysregulation in the function of immune cells such as monocytes, which are important for the maintenance of tissue homeostasis and vascular integrity, play a pivotal role in the exacerbation of the disease. Nevertheless, their cellular behavior and homeostatic role in the placental circulation remains unclear. In this proposal, we intend to comprehend the functional dynamics of monocytes in the maternal-fetal interface of the placenta and their role in GDM. We hypothesize that maternal monocytes drive vascular and structural abnormalities in the placenta that result in undesired fetal outcomes during GDM. Furthermore, we propose that the placental environment during GDM functionally programs monocytes to alter their trafficking patterns that exacerbates disease progression. To address these questions, we intend to utilize a combination of transcriptomics, intravital imaging, multicolour flow cytometry, functional assays and genetic modified mice models that target specific subsets of monocytes to comprehend their functional role in the placenta during healthy versus GDM-complicated pregnancies. By providing a strong expertise in immunology and state-of-the-art experimental technologies into the largely unexplored field of pregnancy and GDM, we believe that this integrated approach will unravel novel mechanistic pathways that will pave the way towards potential identification of monocyte associated biomarkers and a better comprehension of the dysregulations that occur during pregnancy and GDM.
kw: Monocytes; Macrophages; Placenta; Trafficking; Gestational Diabetes

title: Validation of molecular targets for novel treatment directions in allergic rhinitis
abs: This gene expression study of allergic rhinitis in whole blood included 112 AR cases and 113 controls in Singapore with a replication population of 78 AR cases and 125 controls from Sweden. This is the largest gene expression study for AR till date and also to our knowledge the only study with an independent replication population of this sample size. A recent study has identified that non-modifiable factors such as early allergic sensitisation predict AR in first 2 decades, while early life environment or lifestyle were not identified as primary targets. Since I have identified gene expression association with statistical significance and independent replication, I am now pursuing robust validation in a clinical population of AR patients and controls. I identified 11 genes strongly associated to AR in two independent cohorts. Additionally, these genes have a strong eosinophil signature and thereby provide promising targets which could be further evaluated for treatment of AR. Recent evidence has shown therapeutic potential for drugs targeting eosinophils for the treating asthma. In this context, I aim to perform clinical validation and in vitro characterisation of these targets. Validation of these targets in a clinical population with whole blood and nasal gene expression information will allow to evaluate the relevance of these gene expression candidates for AR. Besides identifying novel targets, our molecular approach has thus also the potential to shed more light on the origin and pathogenesis of AR which could serve provide possible clues for prevention in the future.
kw: allergy, rhinitis, childhood, biomarkers, gene expression, eosinophils

title: Understanding the genetic basis of variability associated with CYP3A4/5 enzymatic activity: A pilot study
abs: Over 60% of current prescription drugs are metabolized by the CYP3A4/5 subfamily of enzymes whereby observed interindividual variability in drug effects may be as high as 4- to 13-fold. The high degree of genetic variation at the CYP3A4/5 locus is mainly responsible for the observed interindividual variability. The probe drug, midazolam, has often been employed to determine CYP3A4/5 enzymatic activity. However, the practical use of the midazolam probe test is deterred by the need for repeated blood withdrawals, inconsistency of sampling time points that correlate with CYP3A4/5 activity and lack in reproducibility in ethnically diverse populations. Although several genetic variants in the CYP3A locus have been purported to predict CYP3A4/5 activity, they remain impractical in the Asian context due to clear differences in CYP3A4/5 variant penetrance amongst different ethnicities. This study proposes the use of an unbiased, comprehensive and global approach such as genome-wide association study (GWAS) to uncover germline marker(s) that may be predictive of CYP3A4/5 enzymatic activity. Blood samples will be taken at 1h and 3.5h from a pilot cohort of healthy volunteers (N=150) receiving a single low dose of midazolam. A GWAS analysis will be performed and correlated with midazolam concentrations taken at these time points. Midazolam concentrations determined at these time points were previously shown to significantly correlate with midazolam clearance in the local population. The functional impact of the genomic positive hits on CYP3A4/5 expression will be further assessed using human liver and intestinal tissues. The robustness of these novel marker(s) will also be validated in a pilot cohort of Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML) patients (N=100) who had previously taken imatinib, a putative CYP3A4/5 drug substrate. Ultimately, this study may provide a deeper insight into the genetic factors involved in mediating CYP3A4/5 activity and thereby improve our ability to better predict drug response.
kw: Midazolam; CYP3A4/5; GWAS

title: Exploring the dynamic processes of psychological resilience and physical     function recovery of elderly hip fracture patients in Singapore
abs: This proposal aims to investigate recovery trajectories of physical function after a hip fracture among the elderly in Singapore and to explore the factors associated with different recovery trajectories, guided by a conceptual model of functional loss and recovery developed by the Duke-NUS Medical School using the system dynamics methodology. The specific aims are to: Aim 1: Assess the relationship between psychological resilience and physical function recovery following a hip fracture. Aim 2: Determine the relationship between psychological resilience and trajectory of recovery following a hip fracture. Aim 3: Test empirically key feedback relationships among physical function, frequency of stressors, expectation of recovery and uptake of rehabilitation services hypothesised in our conceptual model on the dynamics of functional loss and recovery. Hypothesis: Resilient patients are more likely to recover physical function following a hip fracture, and the trajectory of resilient patients is significantly different from their non-resilient counterparts. It is also hypothesised that medically versus surgically treated patients have different outcomes. Methodology: A longitudinal survey of surgically and medically treated hip fracture patients will be conducted over a year to assess hip fracture outcome. A simulation model will also be developed with hip fracture stakeholders to delineate the processes and mechanisms that support or hinder recovery. Importance: As Singapore’s population continues to age, a larger number of older adults are at increased risk of hip fracture due to osteoporosis and falls, which can result in reduced mobility and disabilities. Thus it is of import to understand the determinants of recovery from hip fracture and similar stressors over the life course to develop interventions that promote a resilient pattern of recovery. Given its substantial burden, hip fractures can potentially serve as a model to explore the factors associated with different recovery trajectories from major health stressors among the elderly in Singapore.
kw: Resilience, Recovery, Hip Fracture, Longitudinal Survey, Systems Modelling

title: Role of G9a in embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma
abs: Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (ERMS) is the most prevalent subtype of soft tissue sarcoma in children. While significant advances have been made in understanding underlying molecular and genetic alterations, metastatic disease remains a clinical challenge as drugs that target differentiation and self-renewal of tumors cells have not been identified. Our preliminary data provide strong evidence that the chromatin modifier G9a plays a central role in controlling growth and differentiation in ERMS through regulation of Wnt signaling. Interestingly, ERMS is characterized by down regulation of Wnt signaling that is required for myogenic differentiation and to suppress growth and self-renewal of tumor cells. We therefore hypothesize that overexpression of G9a in ERMS inhibits Wnt signaling resulting in the inability of tumor cells to undergo myogenic differentiation. In this proposal, we will examine the mechanisms by which G9a impacts proliferation, differentiation and self-renewal of tumor cells in vitro and in vivo. The molecular mechanisms by which it regulates Wnt signaling will be examined. Comprehensive analysis of human cancers has revealed pervasive de-regulation of epigenetic writers, readers and erasers. Our studies demonstrating overexpression of G9a in ERMS and its impact on the Wnt- catenin axis provide compelling rationale to target G9a as a therapeutic approach for this deadly cancer. Development of such targeted therapies in combination with conventional therapy could reduce adverse side effects in young survivors and lead to a decline in long-term morbidity.
kw: Cancer, epigenetics, rhabdomyosarcoma, histone methyltransferase, Wnt

title: PRL-3 Basic and Translational Researches
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: In 1998, we identified PRL-3 intracellular protein phosphatase. In 2001, Professor Vogelstein’s team from Johns Hopkins first found that PRL-3 was upregulated in colorectal cancer metastasis. In 2003, we further demonstrated that PRL-3 promotes cancer metastasis. Since then, we and others have been working on the role and mechanism of PRL-3 in various cancers as well as developing potential therapeutics, leading to the development of a vibrant PRL-3 research community. Intracellular PRL-3 oncoprotein normally will be targeted with small chemical drugs that are derived from culture dishes (In vitro), where the conditions are oversimplified from tumor microenvironments (in vivo). Since 2008, we proposed a new concept of using antibodies to target PRL-1 and PRL-3 intracellular oncoproteins in multiple animal models: tail vein, xenograft tumor, spontaneous tumor models, orthotopic ‘seed & soil’ tumor models, such animal models are more clinical relevant and have therapeutic impacts for future clinical trials to demonstrate that antibodies can be used to target intracellular oncoproteins as unconventional immunotherapies that offer enormous opportunities for novel cancer treatments. In this proposal, our objectives are to further study in this forefront area by focusing on 3 specific aims: 1. To understand the role of PRL-3-induced polyploid giant cancer cells (PGCCs) in cancer metastasis and tumor relapse. This novel property of PRL-3 has not been investigated and its underlying mechanism and role in cancer are yet to be established; 2. To target PRL-3 positive tumors and weed out PRL-3 positive “stem cell”-like PGCC with PRL3-zumab as a novel targeted cancer immunotherapy and as a prevention for cancer relapse. 3. To elucidate the mechanism of action (MOA) of how tumors are under inflammation, tissue necrosis/lysis, leaking intracellular PRL-3 antigen into the tumor microenvironment. PRL3-zumab and ‘externalized PRL-3’ antigens result in recruitment of immune effectors and/or classical ADCC- and/or ADCP-mediated tumor clearance.
kw: PRL-3; Clinical useful animal models; new cancer therapies

title: Study Early Asymptomatic Molecular Pathology Of Neurodegeneration In Dementia: Proteomic Identification Of Priority Drug Targets
abs: There are 47.5 million people worldwide affected by dementia, and the social and economic costs of this disorder surpassed those attributed to cancer and heart disease. Despite World Health Organization declarations that dementia now represents a public health priority, disease pathogenesis remains poorly understood and there are still no effective treatments for this disorder. Accordingly, the number of dementia patients is projected to triple by 2050, and there is an urgent need to identify key mechanisms of dementia pathogenesis for subsequent therapeutic targeting. Human dementia is regarded as a ‘proteinopathy’ in which changes in brain protein structure and function promote neurodegeneration. Our laboratory is therefore focused on uncovering the complex molecular pathology of this disorder using proteomics; an unbiased, discovery-driven approach that can identify pathological changes in protein structure and function in human cells and tissues. Over the past 10 years, we have focused on proteomic studies of hypoxic-ischemic brain injury, degenerative protein modifications (DPMs) and aggregation. We discovered for the first time a ‘vicious cycle’ of brain tissue damage induced by hypoxic-ischemic brain injury that critically dysregulated key enzymes mediating protein degradation and repair in the affected tissues, leading to accumulation of DPMs damaged proteins and subsequent protein misfolding and aggregation, resulting in neurodegeneration and dementia. We now propose to conduct a longitudinal proteomic study of dementia pathogenesis in an animal model of inducible vascular dementia. We will monitor dementia progression from the asymptomatic stages to the advanced stages, assess whether active lifestyle and mental activity can modify disease course, and validate potential drug targets by analyzing post-mortem brain tissues from dementia patients and age-matched controls. Taken together, these approaches will generate vital new data on the molecular pathology of early, asymptomatic dementia, and will critically support drug discovery efforts aiming to tackle this major public health problem.
kw: Proteomics; post translational modifications; degenerative protein modifications; dementia; amyloidosis; hypoxic-ischemic injury

title: Single-cell histone modification analysis to study epigenetic heterogeneity and plasticity as a mechanism of tumor chemoresistance
abs: Understanding the underlying epigenetic mechanisms that drive drug resistance is crucial to identifying ways of circumventing resistance in cancer patients. Current bulk epigenetic assays, however, cannot dissect the intratumor heterogeneity and diversity of epigenetic response that lead to acquisition of drug resistance. We propose the novel Single Cell CUT&RUN (sc-CUT&RUN) method, which allows sensitive profiling of histone modifications in single cells, as a tool to investigate the selection and adaptation processes that lead to fixation of drug resistant epigenetic states in heterogeneous tumors.In Aim 1, we will establish sc-CUT&RUN for sensitive histone modification profiling in single cells. sc-CUT&RUN introduces in situ antibody-targeted endonuclease cleavage to solve the key bottleneck of inefficient immunoprecipitation and library preparation steps in chromatin immunoprecipitation.
