title: Guided Symbolic Execution
abs: Symbolic execution (SE) has emerged as an important method to reason about programs, in both verification and testing. By reasoning about inputs as symbolic entities, its fundamental advantage over traditional black-box testing, which uses concrete inputs, is simply that it has better coverage of program paths. In particular, dynamic symbolic execution (DSE), where the execution space is explored path-by-path, has been shown effective in systems such as DART [11], CUTE [18] and KLEE [4]. A key advantage of DSE is that by examining a single path, the analysis can be both precise, and efficient. Yet another advantage is the ability to realize a search strategy in the path exploration, such as in a random, depth-first or breadth-first manner, etc. The key disadvantage of DSE is that the current technology for DSE is unguided giving rise to the path explosion problem: The number of program paths is exponential in the program size in general, and available implementations of DSE do not employ a general technique to prune away some paths. A related area to DSE with interpolation is that of Bounded Model Checking applied to transition systems which model symbolic execution of an underlying program (BMC-SE). BMC-SE differs from DSE in that it is Static Symbolic Execution (SSE), where the main idea is to compile the whole program’s representation into a (single, large) logic formula, and then subjecting the formula to an SMT solver for satisfiability checking. SSE has one key advantage: it can exploit an underlying SMT solver [9], which in turn can exploit its underlying SAT technology and the unsatisfiability core (unsat-core) reduction. As a result, BMC-SE can perform guided symbolic execution. Now the static nature of this method has some disadvantages; for example, it does not have the precision of path-by-path consideration, it does not lead itself to concretization, and also, each loop needs to be bounded upfront. Evidence in testing competitions [3] shows that DSE tools are leading and BMC tools are not very competitive. In this proposal, we propose Guided Dynamic Symbolic Execution to address the key weaknesses of both unguided DSE and static BMC. In the past, we invented the idea of guided DSE in Abstraction Learning [12], also known as lazy annotations [16, 17], which enabled significant optimization of DSE via the use of interpolation. This allows, for the first time, a systematic way to prune the search space of DSE. The core feature is the subsumption of paths whose traversals are deemed to no longer be necessary due to similarity with already-traversed paths. This abstraction is in principle non-lossy in the sense that if a bug is to be found by traversing the subsumed path, the bug should have been found in one of the already-traversed paths. TRACER [13] was the first system to demonstrate guided DSE by implementing Abstraction Learning. However, TRACER only worked on academic examples. e.g. [6, 7, 14]. title: New Directions in Constrained Sparse Learning Problems: Theory and Applications
abs: In the past two decades, big data analysis has played an important role in many real-life problems, leading to the digital transformation of nations. The applications of big data analysis can be found in a wide range of problems such as pattern recognition, bioinformatics, financial engineering, signal processing, marketing research, etc. Big data, characterized by high dimensionality and/or large sample size, promise new opportunities and economic value to modern society but at the same time, bring statistical and computational challenges to data scientists. An effective statistical procedure should address the tradeoff between statistical accuracy and computational efficiency. This project advances the existing theories in high-dimensional data analysis. The underlying themes of this project are high-dimensionality and the constraints that are present in complex scientific data analysis problems. The constraints, presented in the mathematical optimization of the statistical learning problems, usually appear in two ways: 1) part of the problem formulation, such as budget constraint in portfolio selection or website advertising; 2) a derivative of the problem reformulation, such as reformulation of norm objective or support vector machines using slack variables. Very few of the existing high-dimensional data analysis tools can incorporate with the constraints because the unconstrained high-dimensional data analysis has been non-trivial. A prevailing approach is to first obtain an unconstrained solution to the relaxed high-dimensional problem and then take an additional step to amend the solution to make it satisfying the constraints. It is clear that the amended solution is suboptimal to the original constrained problem. Thus, the high-dimensional data analysis with constraints is not thoroughly studied yet and the implication of the constraints in big data analysis is even unexplored. This project aims to fill these research gaps and provide new directions in studying constrained sparse learning problems. In the literature on high-dimensional data analysis, there are two types of formulations: Lasso-type and Dantzig-type estimators. Dantzig selector is a popular statistical estimation tool alternative to Lasso and performs well especially for the ultra-high-dimensional setting. The latest progress with constrained sparse learning is limited to the constrained Lasso for regression problems. This project will explore the theory, algorithms, and applications of the constrained Dantzig-type estimator (CDE). As with the rise of the Dantzig selector, the proposed framework takes into account the statistical and computational tradeoff. It is noteworthy that the Dantzig-type estimators can get rid of the computational issues of Lasso-type estimators while remain a decent and even superior statistical accuracy. title: The Political Participation of Firms in Southeast Asia
abs: Under an ambitious regional integration plan, the AEC is drawing tighter together, lowering trade and investment barriers. This creates new opportunities for firms, while disrupting many previously profitable businesses. Many firms previously affected primarily by domestic politics must respond strategically to a rapidly changing international political environment as well. The growth and stability of national economies, the future of regional economic integration, and the distribution of wealth within and between countries in the region all depend on how firms respond to these novel political conditions. Yet the political actions, investment strategies, and internal functioning of firms are difficult to study. A lack of sufficiently detailed firm-level data has left researchers unable to test key theoretical propositions and resolve urgent questions with implications for both government policy and firm strategies. The core task of this project is to conduct a large-scale multi-country firm survey that will be deployed in Singapore, Indonesia, Vietnam, Cambodia, Laos, the Philippines, and South Korea. In each of seven countries, we will conduct both an online survey reaching thousands of firms and a more detailed, labor-intensive, face-to-face survey of firm managers that focuses on granular, difficult-to-observe information about firm strategy and decision-making. The project covers three major substantive areas: i) the political goals and strategies of domestic and multinational firms; ii) the effects of global production networks on international trade agreements; and iii) the role of social ties in shaping firm capabilities, preferences, and strategies, including their strategies for seeking political influence.

title: Transition Metal-free Cross-Coupling Reactions Catalyzed by Aluminyl Anions
abs: The aim of this research program is to develop an efficient catalytic system for versatile cross-coupling reactions promoted by anionic aluminum species [Al]–M+. Transition metal-mediated cross-coupling reactions are powerful tools for the construction of carob-carbon bonds, and indeed various pharmaceutical and agrochemical compounds are currently manufactured by employing the cross-coupling methods. While a variety of metal complexes that enable cross-coupling reactions have been reported thus far, the cost of transition metal complexes consisted of metal and specific ligands is essentially high, and many metals are often toxic. Therefore, the development of catalysts constructed by earth-abundant cheap elements, instead of expensive transition metals, is highly desirable from both economical and environmental points of view. In this project, we develop a transition metal-free methodology for cross-coupling reactions. By incorporating aluminum into the cyclic (alkyl)(amino) framework, various anionic aluminum species [Al]–M+ can be readily synthesized. The dicoordinate aluminum center of [Al]–M+ possesses both a lone pair of electrons and an unoccupied p-orbital, being isoelectronic with carbenes. The anionic nature of the aluminum center exhibits strong nucleophilicity and it undergoes the substitution reaction with haloarenes Ar-X to afford the corresponding derivative [Al]-Ar. Subsequent nucleophilic attack by organometals R’-M to the neutral and tricoordinate aluminum center of [Al]-Ar yields an ionic tetracoordinate aluminum species [[Al]-Ar(R’)]–M+, from which reductive elimination of the Ar and R’ fragments may give rise to the coupling product Ar-R’, concomitant with the reproduction of [Al]–M+. The elementary step should be applicable to the one-pot reaction and even a catalytic process. Because aluminum is abundant, cheap and not toxic compared with transition metals, the proposed systems for the cross-coupling reactions may be carried out under the economical conditions compared with extant conventional methods. Moreover, the coupling product can be utilized various synthetic building blocks for organic synthesis, drug, pharmaceutical and agrochemical compounds, which will provide a practical opportunity to use our system in industrial processes.
kw: Aluminyl anion, cross-coupling, transition metal-free, main group catalysis

title: Understanding Structure-Function Relationship in Nanocatalysts
abs: Manufacturing, transportation, and chemical industries have been continually transformed by basic and applied research on catalysis. The importance of catalytic research (physical and life sciences) is recognized by 15 Nobel prizes comprising 19% of all Nobel laureates. Today, catalysts are reducing the world's carbon footprint while producing 35% of the global GDP as high energy fuels, chemicals, and foods. The development of efficient, stable, and durable catalysts requires mechanistic understanding at an atomic level of the dynamics at an active site and the reaction pathways. During catalysis, the catalytic surface dynamically restructures at the nanoscale to adopt a geometric and compositional structure set by the reactive gas or liquid environments. Conventional approaches to study catalysts rely either on indirect dynamic spectroscopic methods, which lack the resolution needed to identify structural changes on the surface of nanoscale catalysts, or post-reaction TEM analysis of the reaction products, which lack temporal resolution and fail to capture the details of structural changes during the reaction. Therefore, new approaches that have both the spatial and temporal resolution to directly determine the nanoscale structural change leading to the catalytically active states that exist only during the reactions are needed. In this project, using in situ gas-phase TEM imaging platform developed here in Singapore, we will explore the dynamics of nanoscale catalysts in operando. By simultaneously imaging the nanoscale structural changes and measuring the reaction products, we will identify structural transformations that take place during the catalysis (CO-conversion model reaction) and identify the structures responsible for the activity of nanocatalysts. These fundamental insights into structure–activity relation will pave the way for a rational-design-based approach for the development of future catalysts.
kw: in situ TEM, nanoparticles, catalysis

title: Determine the roles of cholesterol metabolism in TDP-43 proteinopathies-related neurodegenerative diseases
abs: Cholesterol dyshomeostasis is implicated in aging and neurodegenerative diseases. Because of the blood-brain barrier (BBB), the regulation of cholesterol metabolism operates autonomously within the central nervous system (CNS). Although neurons have basal capacity of making cholesterol, the bulk of cholesterol within CNS are produced by astrocytes and oligodendrocytes. For example, neurons uptake cholesterol from the glia to promote synaptogenesis, whereas oligodendrocytes use de novo cholesterol synthesis and the uptake from astrocytes for myelination. TDP-43 is the defining pathological hallmark protein found in neurons and glia of the majority of ALS (amyotrophic lateral sclerosis) and ~45% of FTD (frontotemporal dementia) patients. Furthermore, disease-causing mutations in TDP-43 have been identified for ALS and FTD, highlighting the pivotal role of TDP-43 in the pathogenesis of ALS-FTD spectrum disease. Intriguingly, the hallmark of TDP-43 histopathology comprises of cytoplasmic TDP-43 inclusions that are accompanied by a clearance of nuclear TDP-43 and/or intranuclear TDP-43 inclusions in both neurons and glia. This suggests that the disease mechanism could be at least partially driven by the loss of normal nuclear TDP-43 functions in neurons and/or glia, and glial dysfunctions may contribute to onset and progression of ALS-FTD. Curiously, the functions of TDP-43 in glia, e.g., astrocytes and oligodndeorcytes, and whether loss of TDP-43 in different glia contribute to ALS and FTD pathogenesis remains largely unknown. We have previously shown that TDP-43 is cell-autonomously required for survival and myelination in mature oligodendrocytes. However, the exact mechanisms for the observed demyelination phenotypes remain to be addressed. Using unbiased transcriptomic analysis, we have identified that TDP-43 regulates SREBF2 (sterol regulatory element-binding factor 2)-mediated cholesterol metabolism, which is essential for myelination in oligodendrocytes. Importantly, disruption of cholesterol metabolisms is observed in the oligodendrocytes and motor neurons harboring TDP-43 pathology from FTD and ALS patients. Collectively, our data suggest that (1) loss-of-TDP-43 function approach is able to identify potential targets caused by TDP-43 pathology, and (2) deficit of cholesterol metabolisms in motor neurons may contribute to ALS and FTD pathogenesis. Thus, we hypothesize that TDP-43 is required to maintain SREBF2-dependent cholesterol homeostasis in oligodendrocytes, and that dysregulated cholesterol metabolism may be implicated in TDP-43 proteinopathies-related diseases. To address this hypothesis, we will first determine the molecular mechanisms by which TDP-43 regulates SREBF2-mediated cholesterol metabolisms in oligodendrocytes. This will be followed by assessing the myelination status by the restoration of cholesterol level in primary oligodendrocytes and oligodendroglial TDP-43 deleted mice. title: From protein droplets to oil droplets: understanding the role of WRINKLED1 phase separation in the biosynthesis of vegetable oils
abs: Vegetable oils are an important and versatile resource for human diets, renewable biomaterials, and biofuels. Vegetable oils supply around 25% of dietary calories of the developed countries. Oil crops, such as oil palm, are also of great importance for the economy of Singapore and other Southeast Asian countries. Due to a growing population and expanding industrial applications, the global demand for vegetable oils is escalating quickly, with a market of over 180 million tons in 2016 and an estimated 260 million tons by 2024. Simply further expanding oil-crop acreages would considerably increase environmental stress due to competition with other food crops, environmental contamination, and depletion of natural resources, such as land and water. A more effective and practical way to resolve this challenge is through enhancing oil yield. However, this is not a feasible strategy in the absence of a detailed scientific framework regarding the transcriptional control of plant fatty acid biosynthesis. A proven strategy to boost metabolic outcomes is the manipulation of the transcription factors (regulatory proteins involved in gene transcription) that control metabolic pathway gene expression. Transcriptional regulators often function in concert with other regulatory factors in a combinatorial manner to drive gene expression. Control of gene expression needs the transcriptional machinery to be efficiently assembled. Alteration of transcription factors can lead to remarkable phenotypic alterations, based on evidence from plant domestication and successful synthetic biological engineering using transcription factors. However, the molecular mechanism how transcription factors control plant oil biosynthesis is insufficiently understood, especially in terms of the influence of protein structure-function relationship on regulatory activity. Protein liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) to form membraneless compartments is important for cellular processes and gene regulations. The ability to assemble specific proteins and other macromolecules in a defined volume or concentrated phase can modulate activity and stability of the complexes, which contributes to signal transduction and gene regulation. Multivalent interactions and intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) are thought to be important for LLPS. LLPS of transcription factors and coactivators recruits the transcriptional machinery into nuclear condensates, subsequently enabling transcriptional control. Protein LLPS is an emerging topic in plant biology. Like what has been observed in mammalian cells, membraneless nuclear bodies (nuclear speckles) are found in plants. Currently, there is little direct evidence linking protein phase separation and IDR with transcriptional regulation in plant cells. In this proposal, we focus on the transcription factor WRINKLED1 (WRI1), a key regulator governing plant fatty acid biosynthesis. We have shown that WRI1 contains multiple IDRs and functional domains that are t

title: Build CSI based wireless sensing platforms with commodity WiFi
abs: The radio frequency (RF) signal, after emitted from the transmitter, travels in the air and interacts with intermediate objects/obstacles in the environment before it reaches the receiver. Such interactions (reflection, diffraction, scattering, etc.) lead to attenuation of signal amplitudes and rotation of signal phases, which conveys essential information about the environment and, if measured, can be used to construct key knowledge such as the location or motion of the objects/obstacles in the environment. While existing studies in radar, UWB, time reversal systems, etc. depend on the use of specialized hardware and compute-intensive software solutions (e.g., ultra-high bandwidth radio frontend, software defined radios, special purpose RF signal processors, etc.), recent research suggests promising future of Wi-Fi-based wireless sensing ascribed to the freely accessible channel state information (CSI) measured from commodity Wi-Fi devices, like Intel 5300 NIC or Qualcomm Atheros Wi-Fi NICs. There have been studies that leverage such CSI to locate and track moving objects, detect human activities, and provide human computer interactions. Contrary to its capability in wireless communication, which is advanced and rather mature, the sensing capability of commodity Wi-Fi is fundamentally limited in its signal resolution due to the limited spectrum usage as well as the hardware constraints and imperfection caused by low-cost device manufacturing. In the proposed study, we target at extending the commodity Wi-Fi system in hardware and software, so the RF sensing resolution can be significantly improved. The proposed approach will explore the frequency diversity – with a spectrum splicing method for higher effective RF sensing bandwidth, space diversity – with an antenna stitching method for building a large virtual phased antenna array, and dimension diversity – with a joint signal estimation method for improving path resolvability. The targeted methods and techniques are general hardware or software extensions to existing Wi-Fi architectures, so they can be integrated with commodity Wi-Fi in a plug-and-play mode without any hardware modifications. #Intellectual merit. The proposed study will address the problem of insufficient signal resolution of Wi-Fi-based sensing platforms, which has been deemed as the fundamental bottleneck of Wi-Fi-based remote sensing. We will develop a novel CSI splicing and antenna stitching techniques to allow richer CSI at commodity Wi-Fi devices, providing significantly improved resolution in time of flight (ToF) and angle of arrival (AoA) estimation. On top of that, we will propose a multidimensional joint signal estimation approach to deal with ambiguity encountered in some feature dimensions of the signal, thus improving accuracy in multipath separation. #Broader impact. The success of the research will clear the way for the non-intrusive pervasive remote sensing, since the proposed solutions are general hardware or s
kw: WiFi, wireless sensing, channel state information (CSI), antenna arrays

title: Learning Deep Networks on 3D and 4D Point Clouds for Holistic 3D Scene Understanding
abs: With the advances of 3D sensor technologies, 3D scanners such as LiDAR and RGB-D cameras become very affordable and they have been widely used in many applications such as robotics, autonomous driving and augmented reality. Generally, 3D scanners directly produce point clouds as output. A point cloud is a set of points (3D coordinate values) in the 3D space. Point cloud data are usually multimodal data. Each point is usually associated with other modalities or features, including RGB colour values, sensor intensities, and even 3D point flows in some scenarios. 4D point cloud data is the temporal sequence of 3D point clouds captured by moving 3D sensors, which is also referred to as 3D point cloud videos. How to effectively perform recognition tasks like object detection, semantic segmentation on point clouds, and learning from multimodalities reminds very challenging problems. It is well known that deep learning methods have achieved tremendous success in various recognition tasks on images. However, it is still unclear how to design effective deep learning methods for point cloud data. An image is organized in a regular 2D grid, and thanks to this regular structure, conventional 2D convolution can be efficiently and effectively applied with the support from modern hardware. In contrast, point clouds have some key differences from image data. A point cloud has a sparse structure, and the points are not located in a regular grid. The density of points varies a lot across different regions. Some regions may have many points which are clustered together, while in some other regions there are much fewer points which are sparsely distributed. Conventional 2D convolution cannot be directly applied on point clouds. Various methods have proposed to handle such data including 2D projection, 3D grid projection, 3D convolution, pointwise multilayer perceptron, graph convolution, and point convolution. However, these existing methods are still far from satisfaction and they cannot perform well in many real-world applications such as autonomous driving which requires accurate recognition in complex scenarios. This project aims to develop accurate and efficient recognition methods for point cloud data. Specifically, we will develop novel deep learning methods for semantic segmentation, weakly supervised learning and point flow estimation on multimodal 3D and 4D point cloud data. Our project will bring significant impacts on academics and industrials. 3D deep learning is a recently emerged topic, and most problems remain unsolved. Our project aims to bridge this gap and make significant contributions to this research field. The developed methods will reveal important insights on accurate 3D deep learning and push the performance boundary for 3D point cloud understanding. 3D scene understanding techniques have extensive real-world AI applications, including robotics, autonomous driving, augmented reality, etc, and these applications will be greatly and directly
kw: deep learning, scene understanding, segmentation, point clouds, 3D data

title: Two-sample MR methods accounting for sample overlap in the presence of LD and correlated horizontal pleiotropy
abs: Epidemiological studies have established associations between many exposures and complex diseases. However, unmeasured confounding factors, measurement error, and reverse causation may undermine the robustness of inferred causality. As a large number of genome-wide association studies (GWASs) summary statistics are available, two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) using genetic variants as instrumental variables (IV) present a number of advantages over observational studies, e.g. effective control of environmental confounders, overcoming possible issues of reverse causation and low measurement error in modern genotyping technology. With the availability of large-scale meta-analysis results from completed GWASs, multiple two-sample MR methods that leverage GWAS summary statistics have been developed. However, there are several important issues. Firstly, most existing methods assume that summary statistics for the exposure and outcome are generated from two independent samples. As summary statistics for many traits/diseases are results from meta-analysis, there exist sample overlaps to varying degrees. Secondly, most of them assume that IVs are not in linkage disequilibrium (LD). Methods without considering LD may lose statistical power substantially. Thirdly, all these methods accounting for horizontal pleiotropy assume that the direct effects on the outcome are independent of the effects on the exposure. In practice, this assumption is easily violated due to the complicated networks and pathways shared by the exposure and outcome. Statistical methods failing to consider overlapping samples with LD and correlated horizontal pleiotropy lead to biased estimates and inflated false-positive causal relationships. This proposal seeks to fill the aforementioned gaps by developing statistical rigorous methods that efficiently leverage GWAS summary statistics from overlapping samples accounting for correlated horizontal pleiotropy in the presence of LD. Compared to the existing methods, our proposed methods will utilize a full list of weak genetic variants in overlapped samples as IVs as well as properly account for correlated horizontal pleiotropy among SNPs. To demonstrate the effectiveness of modeling SNPs in LD, in our pilot study, we developed a two-sample MR to use SNPs in LD and further consider independent horizontal pleiotropy (MR-Bayes). A parallel Gibbs sampling algorithm is proposed to ensure computational scalability in large-scale GWAS data. Then we applied MR-Bayes to a validation study with coronary artery disease (CAD) as both the exposure and the outcome, to show the efficiency of the methods. In addition, we applied MR-Bayes to several exposure-outcome pairs, e.g. HDL-CAD, LDL-CAD. Based on the results from pilot studies, MR-Bayes can effectively control type-I error for both weak and strong LD, where other methods fail to control type-I error for strong LD. title: Securing Face Recognition: An Imaging Polarimetry Approach to Face Anti-spoofing
abs: New innovations in almost all areas of human endeavors have heightened human-computer interaction. The most prominent change in these developments is the identity problem that both convolutes and promotes access to private information. With obvious ergonomic benefits, convenience, scalability and reliability, biometric-based identities stand out as an attractive alternative over passwords for access control. Among the most deployed, popular and mature modalities, face images or videos are most easily acquired and reproduced without the target identity’s consent, which results in a plethora of identity theft by face spoofing. Face spoofing is directly performed at the sensor level outside the digital limits of the system. This means that digital protection mechanisms, which are effective against indirect attacks by cyber-criminal hackers or insiders, cannot be used against face spoofing. Without liveness detection, state-of-the-art face recognition systems are vulnerable to different types of face spoofing attacks as they maximize the discrimination between identities instead of detecting the vitality and acquisition origin of a presented face. This research aims to provide a new and coherent face anti-spoofing solution that will satisfy all of the following demanding requirements: (i) it is non-invasive and non-intrusive, and requires no contact with the user; (ii) it is user friendly and requires no involuntary response to the system; (iii) the user can interact spontaneously with the sensor and computer in real time with the detection result generated in a significantly shorter time than the adversaries can synthesize the response to evade liveness detection; (iv) it supplements existing face recognition algorithms to detect fake faces in static and dynamic 2D and 3D spoofing without increasing the false rejection rate of genuine faces; (v) the sensor is cost efficient in mass manufacturing to keep its cost affordable for market adoption. These stringent requirements rule out all known integration of hardware and software-based approaches that rely on emerging technology based sensors, behavioral challenge-response or even multi-modal biometric authentication for liveness detection. Our approach is anchored in polarimetry. There is solid scientific evidence on the distinctive changes in polarization states of light reflected from the surfaces of live tissue compared to other artefacts. Unfortunately, these distinguishable features are invisible to human eyes and undetectable by the CMOS image sensors used pervasively in face recognition systems. To make a CMOS image sensor polarization-sensitive, this project will explore the appropriate formation of a nanometer-scale metal grating based micro-polarizer array on top of the photosensitive pixel array. title: A sustainable and economical binder for construction of low permeable and high durable seepage cut-off wall in marine environment: preparing for sea-level rise in Singapore
abs: Sea-level rise has become a global issue. Singapore is a low-lying island state and is particularly vulnerable to sea-level rise. Among various engineering solutions to protect coastal areas against sea-level rise, the construction of seawalls or dikes, is the most practical and reliable one. Since many coastal areas in Singapore are reclaimed land with sand as the fill material, the sea water can easily flow through the sand layer below seawalls or dikes. Hence, a seepage cut-off wall with a low permeability has to be constructed in the sand layer, for which a cementitious binder has to be mixed with the sand to reduce its permeability. Currently, the Portland cement (PC) is the most commonly used soil mixing binder for the installation of seepage cut-off wall. However, there are several concerns using PC as the binder for seepage cut-off wall in marine environment. First, the production of PC induces remarkable environmental impacts; the production of 1 tonne of PC consumes around 5,000 MJ of energy and 1.5 tonnes of non-renewable resources, and induces around 1 tonne of CO2 emissions. Second, the addition of PC has a negative effect on the workability of fresh stabilized soil. Third, PC is not very effective in reducing the permeability of hardened stabilized soil. Last, but not the least, the PC-stabilized soil is not durable in marine environment, e.g. Na2SO4 in the sea water reacts with PC hydration products and produces ettringite, which is an expansion process and will deteriorates the stabilized soil. Hence, this project proposes a sustainable and economical binder, reactive magnesia (MgO)-activated ground granulated blastfurnace slag (GGBS), for construction of low permeable and high durable seepage cut-off wall in marine environment. GGBS is a by-product during steel making and is commercially available in Singapore, with a price lower than that of PC. The production of GGBS induces significantly lower environmental effects than those of PC, including less energy consumption (around 1300 MJ/t) and less CO2 emissions (around 0.07 t/t), as wells as zero consumption of non-renewable resources. In Singapore, the MgO can be produced from waste brine in desalination plants, turning the harmful waste to a valuable resource. The PI’s previous studies indicate that MgO-GGBS can achieve a much lower permeability for stabilized soil than PC. Additionally, the MgO-GGBS-stabilized soil is nearly inert to Na2SO4 attack, indicating high durability in marine environment. Since there is no existing study on the use of MgO-GGBS for construction of seepage cut-off wall in marine environment, this project will conduct a systematical study on it for preparation of sea-level rise in Singapore. For this application, there are three critical properties of the MgO-GGBS-stabilized soil, including workability, permeability, and durability, which are dominated by three types of chemical-physical process corresponding to different timelines in the service life of

title: Understanding cascading earthquake ruptures on orthogonal faults
abs: Three earthquake cascades in the last decade have highlighted the importance of stress triggering in regions away from plate boundary faults; furthermore, these cascades each occurred on unusual orthogonal fault geometries. We hypothesize that in regions like this, two mechanisms may allow cascading earthquake failure. First, the overall crustal stresses may be higher, putting smaller faults and fractures closer to failure. Second, faults may be misoriented to the overall stress field, and therefore slip in each event may cause a local rotation of the stress field rather than relieving significant stress on the system; this could push nearby faults at different orientations to fail. These mechanisms could act separately or together, and lead to cascading earthquakes due to the dynamic and static stress changes caused by each progressive event. If either or both of these mechanisms is active and can explain such events, this would have implications for how scientists can better communicate earthquake hazard in the period following an earthquake. We propose to study these topics through theoretical and numerical models informed by observational data, with a focus on the 2019 Cotabato earthquake cascade in the southern Philippines, by using the geodynamic setting and the earthquake patterns to constrain the regional stress state. Specifically, we will develop a regional tectonic understanding informed by geological observations (Component 1), and will build a geodynamic model based on the tectonic setting to evaluate the stress state in the southern Philippines and how it has allowed the formation of orthogonal faults (Component 2). We will then use seismic and geodetic observations from the earthquakes to develop 3D models of the faults that slipped and their slip patterns (Component 3). We will calculate the stress transfer following each earthquake and evaluate under what stressing and strength conditions that stress transfer is able to initiate the next observed event (Component 4). We hypothesize that regions away from large, well established faults may be more vulnerable to sequences of similar-sized earthquakes due to a higher level of baseline differential stress and/or misorientation of fault segments to the overall stress field. Our work will explore both regional stress states and fault properties, and may generate useful and societally relevant information about earthquake triggering in the wide regions away from plate boundary faults, including Singapore, by evaluating whether these regions are particularly vulnerable to earthquake cascades (Component 5).
kw: Earthquake; hazard; aftershock; tectonics; fault; geodynamics

title: Integrated Power Management System for the Next-Generation Internet-of-Things
abs: The Problem The number of units and market-size of the Internet-of-Things (IoTs) are gargantuan – 50B units and US$200B, respectively, today – and its precipitate growth is expected to remain unabated. The applications of the Next-Generation IoTs (NG-IoTs) are expected to be increasingly diverse where some of their most imperative attributes include smaller form-factor (size), lower cost, and lower power-dissipation/higher power-efficiency, simultaneously – beyond what is possible or available today. We propose to investigate and resolve some of the fundamental issues for the design and realization of integrated power management systems for NG-IoTs, embodying the following three physically-separate parts: microbattery, DC-DC converter, and passives. Specifically, instead of the said three physically-separate parts in the power-management of present-day IoTs, we propose that the power-management system for NG-IoTs to be either fully monolithically-integrated or integrated as a system-in-package without external passives, i.e., one physical part. Put simply, our overall intentions are to research and investigate, design and realize the power management systems for NG-IoTs that simultaneously feature unprecedented smallest form-factor, lowest cost, and highest power-efficiency attributes – beyond the state-of-the-art. Specifically, we aim to achieve: (a) 2x smaller form-factor – this is important as this expands the application space of IoTs. (b) 3x lower cost – cost is often the main consideration for commercialization. (c) ≥10% higher power-efficiency over the state-of-the-art for the same components – high power-efficiency is imperative for extended battery-life. The collective figure-of-merit (form-factor x cost x power-efficiency) is an unprecedented 6.6x improvement over the state-of-the-art. The outcomes of this proposal are potentially highly impactful – key technological enablers for NG-IoTs. The scope of IoTs in this proposal is ultra-low power NG-IoTs with an integrated-microbattery. The battery is the ‘Thompson battery’ (by our collaborator, Professor Thompson (MIT)) – the only low-temperature processed battery to-date. This, for the time-time ever, allows the opportunity for integrating the microbattery, DC-DC converter and its associated passive elements into an Integrated Power Management System for NG-IoTs – a single-monolithic device or system-in-package without any external passive elements. Fundamental Research #1 From an engineering-science basis, we will analytically investigate and derive analytical models of the power losses of active and passive elements in DC-DC converters integrated in a system-in-package without external passives and of their fully monolithically-integrated counterparts. For a system-in-package solution without external passive elements where we employ the moderate quality-factor (Q) bonding wire and/or packaging lead as the inductor, we will model the inductor AC and DC power losses. title: Magnetic Effects on the Machinability of Difficult-to-cut Materials
abs: Ultraprecision machining technology has significantly matured over the years to produce microstructures and freeform surfaces with an excellent surface finish. Nanometric surface roughness is highly sought after on brittle materials and metallic alloys, which can be produced using single-point diamond cutting tools with an extremely sharp cutting edge. However, the technology is still limited to a certain extent when machining certain types of materials such as brittle ceramics, extremely hard metals with low thermal conductivity, and ferrous metals. Conventionally, the problems presented by each material type can be mitigated through the optimisation of machining conditions, but there has also been the introduction of technological advancements to improve the machinability and productivity of these materials. Among the advancing technologies to augment the ultraprecision machining process, the magnetic field-assisted technique has recently emerged to be a promising method for machining difficult-to-cut materials such as titanium alloys. The explained mechanism for the improvements in machinability under a magnetic field was attributed to the eddy current generation and the consequential Lorentz forces that dampen cutting tool vibrations. Although such an explanation as claimed by other researchers appears sceptical in machining, the concept and its application have already been established in many other rotary mechanical systems. In physics, the application of a magnetic field in the dynamic machining process introduces multiple effects that have never been considered in the previous studies of magnetic field-assisted ultraprecision machining. The physics of the magnetic field and its influence on plastic deformation have been widely studied but were generally only under quasi-static conditions with most loading components directed in one dimension. These phenomena include magnetoplasticity, magnetostriction, enhanced surface oxidation, etc. To date, no research work has contributed to the integration of such effects in magnetic field-assisted ultraprecision machining processes, which would enrich the field of knowledge and enhance the manufacturing technology for processing generally the difficult-to-machine materials. Moreover, research on magnetic field-assisted machining has only been experimented on with descriptions of the phenomenological effects without a thorough theoretical understanding of the magnetic effect in microcutting. This proposal aims to establish the occurrence of the various magnetic effects in the ultraprecision machining process and to develop a quantitative model to elucidate the influence of the magnetic effects according to the machining conditions and magnetic field configurations. A direct investigation on difficult-to-machine materials is deemed unwise given the novelty of this study. Thus, microcutting experiments will first be performed using a precision machining centre on common metals such as copper and alumin

title: Non-volatile Memtransistor Technologies for Edge Devices in the Internet of Smart Things
abs: Multi-terminal non-volatile mem-transistor devices have been recently demonstrated and offer a promising solution to the design issues in resistive RAM (RRAM) technology. Mem-transistors have separate terminals for programming and sensing and can be engineered with improved device-to-device and cycle-to-cycle variations and leakage behavior. Hence, it is a promising alternative to RRAM technology for implementing data storage and machine learning accelerators for future generations of smart edge devices. In this proposed research, we will use a materials-to-system architecture approach to address the scientific challenges in non-volatile 2D materials-based mem-transistor technology for implementing data storage and hardware accelerators that are suitable for future smart edge devices in the Internet of Smart Things. We argue that because mem-transistor technology is in its nascent stages, a vertical approach is needed to provide accurate feedforward and feedback across the layers of design abstraction, which will lead to innovative design solutions that extract the maximum benefits of mem-transistor technology. Our initial characterization of individual mem-transistors demonstrates that 2D materials-based mem-transistors have much better and controllable device variation characteristics for data storage and hardware accelerator applications than their two-terminal RRAM counterparts. This proposed research consists of activities that investigate the relationships between material choice, device structure, modeling and fabrication, and circuit and system architecture design and behavior to develop holistic and innovative solutions to tackle the issues of device leakage and variations. The aim of the proposed research activities is to achieve an experimentally validated materials-to-systems co-design framework and fabrication process for synthesizing highly optimized 2D non-volatile multi-terminal mem-transistor devices that are suitable for implementing for data storage and hardware accelerators in edge devices. The successful completion of our proposed research objectives will have the broader impact of advancing mem-transistor device technology through an improved scientific understanding of the relationships between design issues across the layers of design abstraction and chart a promising pathway towards future generation Internet of Smart Things.
kw: Non-volatile memtransistor, non-volatile memory, edge-AI, Internet of Smart Things, 2D semiconductors

title: The Physics Behind Naturally Evolved Force-Transmission Biomolecular Linkages
abs: The project aims to decipher the physical principles behind the mechanical properties of naturally evolved tension-bearing protein-protein interfaces and protein domains, and use the knowledge learnt from them to guide the design of novel functional materials of unique mechanical properties and potential biomedical applications. The studies will be directed by testing the following main hypotheses: 1) The conserved characteristic structures and topologies of the tension-bearing protein-protein interfaces and protein domains impart them with characteristic mechanical properties and responses. 2) The tension level in a force-transmission supramolecular linkage is “buffered” by tension-dependent conformational and structural changes of protein domains in the linkage. 3) Different tension-transmission supramolecular linkages that contain distinct structural-topological types of domains may maintain tensions at different levels. 4) The physical principles behind the mechanical properties of naturally evolved tension-bearing protein-protein interfaces and protein domains can be used for rational, bottom-up design of novel functional materials of unique mechanical properties. We propose to investigate the hypotheses by classifying typical tension-bearing protein-protein interfaces and protein domains found in cells into groups based on their structural and topological features. Using the magnetic-tweezer based single-molecule mechanical manipulation approach, their mechanical properties will be investigated at a single-molecule level to find out the relation between the mechanical properties and the shared structural-topological features. Steered molecular dynamics simulations will be conducted to obtain insights into the force-dependent conformational changes and to reveal the transition pathways with the atomic level of details. Based on the high-resolution single-molecule experimental data and the insights from the steered molecular dynamics simulations, physical models will be built to understand the physics behind the force responses of the protein-protein interfaces and domains, and their correlation with characteristic structural and topological features. With the above knowledge, Kinetic simulations will be performed to understand the dynamic mechanical properties of force-transmission supramolecular linkages under different mechanical perturbations. Guided by the understanding of the physical and engineering principles learnt from the studies, we plan to design hydrogels with self-healing, tunable extensibility, and mechanical properties.
kw: Protein domain; Protein-protein interface; Single-molecule manipulation; Force transmission; hydrogel

title: Understanding effects of remyelination on functional recovery after CNS injury
abs: Significance: A key characteristic of the recovery process after injuries in the central nervous system (CNS) is a lack of remyelination. A critical question that remains unexplored is how enhancing remyelination affects the recovery of function. Unfortunately, we have not been able to understand this process due to the lack of effective platforms. Here, in the context of spinal cord injury (SCI), we use biomedical engineering methods to enhance CNS remyelination and examine the effects of enhanced remyelination on function recovery after injury. The unique enhanced understanding on myelination that is gained from this study will support the development of future remyelination strategies and nerve injury treatments. Background: Remyelination of the CNS after traumatic nerve injuries is often limited and this chronic progressive demyelination is believed to be a cause of function deficits. Furthermore, although oligodendrocytes (OL) differentiate from oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs) to myelinate neurons during development, evidence suggests that after contusion spinal cord injury, neurons become remyelinated (despite low efficiency) by OPC-derived cells that express markers of Schwann cells from the peripheral nervous system. These findings suggest that while promoting neuronal regeneration after nerve injuries is important, remyelination of these neurons is essential for proper functionality. Unfortunately, there is a lack of effective platforms to enhance remyelination in the CNS and there is also a lack of thorough understanding of how remyelination occurs and affects recovery of function after CNS injuries. Hypothesis: Here, we hypothesize that remyelination of the injured nerve is critical for the regeneration and recovery of function of CNS tissue, and promoting OPC differentiation and myelination by using microRNAs and fiber scaffolds may enhance the recovery of function. Approach: Using SCI as a proof-of-concept, we will use biomedical engineering methods to establish a novel bio-mimetic scaffold to deliver microRNAs (miR-219 and miR-338, i.e. miR-219/miR-338) non-virally to enhance repair and remyelination after injury. We will evaluate the cellular and molecular changes after injury and treatment by single cell RNA-sequencing and Fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS); analyse the structure and stability of the regenerated myelin; and examine the effects of enhanced myelination on recovery of function. Coupled with genetic fate tracing, we will also evaluate if the enhanced myelination is created from OPCs or existing OL in the CNS or Schwann cells in the peripheral nervous system. We will pursue the following specific aims: Aim1: To define the source of remyelinating cells induced by miR-219/miR-338 fiber scaffolds after SCI. title: Genomic approaches to detect somatic mosaicism in Parkinson’s disease brains
abs: Parkinson’s disease (PD) is one of the most common age-related neurodegenerative diseases and is one of the fastest growing in prevalence. Despite years of intensive research, there is still no cure. Recent evidence suggests that somatic mutations, present only in specific tissues and in a fraction of cells, may play a role in neurodegenerative diseases like PD. We hypothesize that these tissue-specific somatic changes may occur later in life and disrupt crucial pathways in cellular and tissue function, and some of these may never be seen in the germline as a result of negative selection in early embryonic development. These may also contribute to individual variation in the age of onset or progression of PD. We propose to use the latest genomic tools combined with next generation sequencing technologies to detect these somatic changes at high sensitivity in post-mortem diseased brain tissue obtained from the Parkinson’s UK brain bank. This study will be carried out in three stages. In the first stage, we will perform high coverage whole exome sequencing of post-mortem substantia nigra tissue from 500 PD patients and 500 age-matched normal controls to identify germline and somatic mutations that are PD-associated using appropriate statistical tests (Aim 1). Next, we will experimentally validate these somatic variants by targeted single cell sequencing and digital droplet PCR to confirm and assess their prevalence and distribution across three brain regions (Aim 2). Finally, we will do clinical and functional investigation of the most significant variants identified in Aims 1 and 2 by correlating with clinical and neuropathological data and functional investigation in a dopaminergic cell and midbrain organoid model (Aim 3). Through these approaches, we aim to identify functionally validated genes affected by somatic variants in PD brains.
kw: Parkinson’s disease; Neurodegenerative diseases; Single cell sequencing; Aging-related diseases; Genetics and genomics; Somatic mosaicism

title: Predisposing lineage specification via precise emulation of 3D embryonic epiblast
abs: Singapore has one of the world’s fastest ageing population, and some of the highest incidences of cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and end stage renal disease. To better accommodate an ageing population, there is an urgent need to develop the next-generation biomedical therapeutic approaches to manage age-associated organ deterioration and/or failure. Recent advances in stem cell biology has revolutionized the way we study and understand human embryogenesis. It is now highly feasible to differentiate human pluripotent stem cells (PSCs) into three-dimensional (3D) miniature organs (organoids) that recapitulates various structural and functional aspects of their in vivo cognates. Despite these major scientific advancements over the last decade, it remains challenging to efficiently and precisely steer human PSCs towards the desired lineages/organoids. Thus, it is of utmost importance to establish approaches that can accurately parallel in vitro human PSC culture with their counterpart in vivo, the embryonic epiblast, in terms of both molecular features and 3D morphogenetic characteristics. We hypothesize that suboptimal differentiation potential of in vitro human PSCs can be efficiently boosted and predisposed towards the desired lineages and organoids via accurately emulating key molecular and structural features of embryonic epiblast. The research strategies of combining a set of stat-of-the-art in vitro stem cell techniques and in vivo analyses in conjunction with systems biology approach represents a unique effort in addressing questions on human development and organoid biology. More specifically, we will use the latest stem cell techniques to conduct in vitro human PSCs differentiation. 3D culture methodology will be employed to generate organoids and early embryonic structures. We will use biochemistry, molecular and cell biology, microscopic imaging, and systems biology approaches to fully characterize the phenotypes of epiblast-like human PSCs that are predisposed towards specific lineages in vitro. We aim to generate a versatile human PSC culture platform that can emulate a spectrum of spatiotemporally dynamic pluripotent states in vitro, thus predisposing human PSCs towards the desired germ layer and lineage. Our laboratory is highly experienced in handling human PSCs, including both ESCs and iPSCs, as well as direct differentiation. Our lab has already established a highly efficient protocol to differentiate human PSCs into vascularized 3D kidney organoids, laying the technical foundation for this proposed project. The participating research teams have diversified expertise, such as stem cell related techniques, metabolomics, transcriptomic and genomics, sufficing the multidisciplinary nature of the proposed research. The realization of this project will fundamentally improve our understanding of the molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying early human embryogenesis and germ layer specification. title: Study of New Unconventional Spin Plasmons in Model Perovskite Cobaltites
abs: Research questions to be addressed. -------------------------------------------------- This research proposal is motivated by our discovery on new unconventional plasmons, namely charge correlated-plasmons, in a correlated electron system of Niobates [Nature Communications 8, 15271 (2017)]. Such a discovery sparks new research directions and interests for both, fundamental physics and new potency applications such as plasmonics photocatalyst [Nature Communications 8, 15070 (2017)], which is also discovered by us. The charge correlated-plasmons occur due to an interplay between short- and long-range interactions, which lead to unusual characteristics in complex dielectric function and loss function (see full proposal). Importantly, this observation of charge correlated-plasmons opens new paths to address an outstanding, important “84-year-old-question”: Do strongly-correlated electron systems contain unconventional spin correlated-plasmons? In this proposal, our main aims are the following. Firstly, we will develop new experimental methodologies and techniques to measure spin correlated-plasmons in strongly-correlated electron systems. Till now there is no reliable technique to directly measure spin correlated-plasmons. Secondly, using our new experimental methodologies and techniques, we aim to address the outstanding, important “84-year question” and to unravel for the first time spin correlated-plasmons in a model strongly-correlated electron system. The success of it will lead to new physics and open new paths for novel technologies, such as, to combine spintronic and plasmonic. We present our preliminary result to show the feasibility of our research program. Academic Significance. ------------------------------- A basic concept of spin correlated-plasmon, a collective mode of spin-density in strongly-correlated electron systems, has been proposed by Sir Mott in 1936. The spin correlated-plasmon is important for both new fundamental physics and opens entirely novel future applications. For instance, it is expected to bridge between the spintronics and plasmonics by strongly confining the photon energy in the sub-wavelength scale within single magnetic-domain to enable further miniaturizing the devices that can be achieved by the recent progress in spintronics and plasmonics. Consequently, the spin-photon interaction in such small-scales is more energy-efficient than the electron-photon interaction. The spin-plasmonics, thus, is believed to take an important role in shaping the future of the fast low-energy high-density data-transfer. However, spin correlated-plasmon is very rarely study and therefore far from understood. Most studies so far are charge-plasmons in metals. Classical models describe the charge plasmons as the collective charge-density mode due to long-range Coulomb effects. Of today, the charge-plasmons have shown a wide range of applications. title: Automating the detection of frailty using Artificial Intelligence(AutoFRAIL): A retrospective observational study of elderly patients admitted to Hospitals in West Singapore
abs: Background: Ageing is sometimes experienced as increased co-morbidity, functional impairment, poor resilience and vulnerability to stressors, with resultant reduced lifespan and health-span. This condition is often referred to as ‘frailty’. There is growing consensus that the consequences of frailty are preventable, or at the very least potentially delayed. Problem Reliable, robust, timely and wide-spread population measurement of frailty remains challenging. The majority of frailty scores are unsuitable for the clinical setting, require manual and resource-intensive assessment processes, are subject to operator error and have not demonstrated benefit in improving patient care. Aim In order to improve care for this vulnerable group, this study aims to automate the widespread identification of clinically relevant frail older patients in Singapore using Artificial Intelligence methods on existing ubiquitous electronic medical records and administrative data. Methods A retrospective secondary analysis of Emergency Department and medical admission records of all patients =>65 years admitted to National University Hospital between 2015-2017. We utilize Natural Language Processing to retrieve information from unstructured data, and other machine learning methodologies from structured data, within the clinically meaningful framework of Frailty Syndromes. We will test this model on patients admitted to Alexandra Hospital between 2018-2019. Outcomes We validate and compare the model against an established frailty score, namely Frailty Index and comprehensive geriatric assessment. We test the predictive validity of this methodology for inpatient mortality, non-elective hospital readmission, long length of hospital stay and future frailty events. Significance This study forms a proof-of-concept for a methodology to automate the identification of frailty in a timely and clinically relevant manner. Understanding a patient’s specific frailty archetype will highlight specific evidence-based personalized interventions compared to standardized frailty scores. If successful, it could form the basis of a reproducible and robust population measure of frailty, providing for intelligent resource planning, and clinical decision making.
kw: Frailty, Ageing, large data, artificial intelligence, machine learning

title: Identifying molecular correlates of radioresistance during chemoradiotherapy for locally advanced non-small cell lung cancer
abs: Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related deaths in Singapore. Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) makes up the majority of lung cancers and a third of patients present in the locally advanced (LA) stage. LA-NSCLC is an intrinsically heterogeneous disease, with distinct molecular and phenotypic sub-types. Radiotherapy (RT) is the core local treatment modality and treatment intensification with concurrent chemotherapy and consolidation immune checkpoint blockade is standard of care. However, nearly half of all patients relapse within the first year, and a significant proportion of these are local in-RT field failures. Existing literature suggests that these local failures (LF) are mainly driven by mechanisms of radioresistance. This highlights the need for early predictive biomarkers, which recognize intrinsic differences in tumour biology and sensitivity to radiotherapy and immunotherapy, to improve patient prognostication and treatment stratification. In this study, we aim to address the problem of radioresistance by first examining baseline treatment naïve biopsy samples through integrative whole exome and RNA sequencing methods. We hypothesise that we will identify genomic and transcriptomic profiles which correlate with radioresistance and LF at 1-year. Next, tumour informed circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) assays can allow accurate detection and quantification of ctDNA and the use of these personalized assays have demonstrated prognostic value in various tumour types. To this end, we have performed a pilot study which demonstrated the feasibility of deploying these ctDNA assays in LA-NSCLC and also their potential as quantitative biomarkers of chemoradiotherapy (CRT) response. In this study, we will leverage longitudinal blood samples to analyse ctDNA levels before, during and following CRT. At the same time, we will determine if the genomic signatures of radioresistance can be detected non-invasively in ctDNA. Through these integrated approaches, this study will provide sound foundational datasets to plan subsequent studies aimed at validating these biomarkers.
kw: Biomarkers; radiotherapy; radioresistance; locally advanced non-small cell lung cancer

title: A Proof-of-Concept Phase 1 Study of RNA Oligonucleotide, MTL-CEBPA In Combination With Atezolizumab and Bevacizumab in Patients with Hepatocellular Carcinoma
abs: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a highly vascularized and immunogenic tumor. Atezolizumab (anti–PDL1) and bevacizumab (anti-VEGF) was recently approved for untreated, advanced HCC as the combination showed improved survival over sorafenib. Anti-VEGF may enhance anti–PD1/-PD-L1 efficacy by reversing VEGF-mediated immunosuppression and promoting T-cell infiltration in tumors. Anti-VEGF also inhibits myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) and MDSCs are associated with poor response to therapy. This is a potential mechanism of resistance and there is lack of therapies which target MDSCs. C/EBP-a is a master regulator involved in cell lineage determination, cell growth and proliferation, and tissue differentiation. In adult liver, C/EBP-a functions in terminally differentiated hepatocytes, while rapidly proliferating HCC cells express only a fraction of C/EBP-a. In MDSCs from tumor-bearing mice, C/EBP-a is down-regulated and upregulation of C/EBP-a in HCC rodent models inhibits tumor growth. MTL-CEBPA is a first-in-class small activating RNA (saRNA) oligonucleotide drug which upregulates C/EBP-a. Upregulating C/EBP-a not only benefits liver function, but inhibits cell proliferation and modulates TME through MDSCs by enhancing anti-angiogenesis, reducing immune suppression and inhibiting tumor growth. We hypothesize that upregulation of C/EBP-a using MTL-CEBPA will “prime” HCCs to VEGF and PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors thus improving response. The research aims are: (1) Conduct a proof-of-concept phase 1a/b clinical trial to determine the safety and tolerability of MTL-CEBPA with atezolizumab and bevacizumab in advanced HCC patients; (2) Determine response from treatment; and (3) Determine pharmacokinetics (PK) and pharmacodynamics (PD) of the treatment combination. A standard 3+3 model commonly used in Phase I oncology studies will be used. Positive results will endorse the proof-of-concept that targeting MDSCs to complement anti-VEGF therapy and checkpoint blockade is synergistic. This will be practice changing for treatment of HCC (a common cancer in Singapore due to the prevalence of Hepatitis B) and potentially applicable to other tumor types.
kw: Hepatocellular carcinoma; checkpoint inhibitor; angiogenesis; MDSC; anti-VEGF; saRNA

title: Establishing a sustainable geriatric-haematology oncology service in a tertiary cancer centre- moving towards CGA-driven home-based interventions, improving quality of life for elderly patients with cancer.
abs: This proposal aims to study an alternate means of medical care for frail elderly cancer patients, to reduce the impact of treatment toxicity due to their multiple comorbidities and frailty, but yet improve their quality of life (QoL). In the short term, the utility of introducing comprehensive geriatrics assessment (CGA) driven home-based interventions will be studied, to provide an alternative treatment option for frail elderly cancer patients. This includes evaluating the utility of the relevant CGA tools, and developing a user-friendly mobile health application to guide the patient/caregiver in administering home-based interventions such as exercise regime via videos, interactive games for cognitive activities, etc. If successful, this will improve patients’ QoL, reduce length of inpatient stay, and hospitalization rates. In the longer-term, this will guide the development of a sustainable, time and cost-efficient multi-disciplinary geriatric haematology-oncology service. This study will adopt a prospective randomized controlled single centre approach, conducted over 2 years, targeted to recruit 250 patients over 65 years old with newly diagnosed haematology malignancy. Patients will be randomized into either the control or intervention arm, using permuted block randomization. Patients in the control arm will undergo the existing standard clinical protocols, while patients in the treatment arm who are identified to have areas of concerns will receive home-based interventions. A post EORTC QLQ questionnaire will be administered for both groups at the end of 3 and 6 months. The number of hospitalizations, length of each hospitalization visit, and compliance of treatment data will be collected. The CGA domain scores and EORTC QLQ questionnaire mean score are compared between both arms by involving the linear mixed effect model. For additional data such as hospitalization rate and its

title: Structural variation and inhibition of key coronaviral ion channels
abs: Coronaviruses (CoV) are vertebrate pathogens that cause human respiratory diseases. Like many other viruses, CoV encode ion channels that are known as viroporins. Several of these viroporins are virulence factors. For example, the envelope protein forms ion channels found in all CoV, including the novel coronavirus (SARS-CoV-2), causative agent of atypical pneumonia disease COVID-19. The channel formed by the envelope protein in SARS and another viroporin, 3a, found in SARS-like viruses have been found to use their channel activity to activate inflammasomes and contribute to pathogenesis. Despite their potential as drug targets, there is so far no effective inhibitor for their channel activity. The paucity of high-resolution structural data, or in some cases complete absence of experimentally confirmed structural models, hampers the progress in the therapeutic development targeting coronavirus encoded viroporins. Rational drug discovery relies on high resolution structures which are not available for envelope proteins. One reason for this is that these channels are dynamic, which makes structural determination difficult for X-ray diffraction or NMR, whereas most of them are too small for electron microscopy. A recent model for SARS-2 3a protein has been obtained by electron microscopy, but this technique is not ideal to screen low to medium affinity drugs. These problems can be overcome with solid-state NMR, but at present a high-resolution structure of CoV envelope protein channels in a membrane environment or even in detergent is not available. Recent progress in solid-state NMR enables structure determination of viroporins in planar bilayers where lipid composition might be adjusted to the corresponding lipid composition of various cellular compartments. Thus, solid-state NMR is our method of choice to achieve structural characterization of viroporins. Thus in this proposal, we aim at resolving the main impediment for the structural charcterization of CoV viroporins by discovering sequence variants that have the necessary stability and rigidity to be suitable for solid-state NMR studies. The availability of these structures will enable the screening of drug libraries, and binding of compounds may further stabilise these structures. We will do that by exploring the conformational space of CoV viroporins, both computationally and experimentally. This will allow us to (1) identify functionally and structurally important amino acid sequence motifs an (2) select and optimize amino acid sequences that will form thermostable channels amenable to structural analysis by both solution and solid-state NMR. The development of these strategies can be applicable to the whole spectrum of CoV viroporins and viroporins in general, making possible to develop antivirals in present and future pandemics. title: Gram+ bacteria derived nanovesicles as new vaccine and antibiotic resistance
abs: The envelope of Gram-positive bacteria is composed of a single membrane below a thick layer of peptidoglycan called the cell wall that is often decorated by capsular polysaccharides. Gram-positive vesicles have only recently been visualized and studied. EVs secreted from Gram-positive bacteria are derived from the plasma membrane and the mechanism initiating this so-called “blebbing” remains unknown. Gram-positive EVs are similar to eukaryotic exosomes and are therefore termed bacterial exosomes in this proposal (BEVs). BEVs have been reported to be produced by a number of pathogenic Gram-positive bacteria for which new vaccines are urgently needed, including group A streptococci (GAS) Staphylococcus aureus (SA) (Lee, E.Y. et al. 2009) and Streptococcus pneumoniae (Pn) (Olaya-Abril, A. et al. 2014). One advantage of using exosomes of Gram-positive origin is the lack of endotoxin, in contrast to OMVs from Gram-negative bacteria where a main constituent is lipopolysaccharide (LPS) with its toxic lipidA moiety embedded in the outer membrane. Nonetheless, similar to their eukaryotic counterparts, BEVs are difficult to isolate and characterize, rendering their study and therapeutic use challenging, especially for future clinical trials. To achieve production of BEVs in large scale needed for vaccine production, we propose to produce them directly from bacteria by a physical process to obtain bacterial extracellular vesicles mimetics (BEVMs). We initially developed this approach for exosomes from eukaryotic cells (Goh et al., 2017) by generating exosomes mimetic called Cell Derived Nanovesicles (CDNs). Using this unique method to produce extracellular vesicles, we demonstrated the capacity to preserve the key proteins responsible for the function and characteristics of exosomes. Similar to CDNs, a quantitative increase of up to few hundred times is expected in the production of BEVs from the same initial number of bacteria. This method will also allow to mix bacteria of different capsular serotypes (ca. 100 different pneumococcal capsular types have been identified so far with different virulence properties). Hence, unlike conventional methods, the inclusion of a large spectra of BEVs that can protect against all pneumococci circulating in the population –and causing disease– will be possible. Towards simplification and standardisation of the methods, a novel microfluidic system is being designed. The new microfluidic setup has two main advantages: 1) it will have a much higher throughput within a shorter processing time, and 2) it will better preserve the integrity of the EVs due to the shorter processing time (few minutes or less comparing to many hours in ultracentrifugation). With this system, we anticipate to be able to purify and prepare samples in reproducible conditions for pre-clinical testing and eventual clinical studies. This microfluidic system will also be tested to isolate vesicles based on their contents (such as proteins, immunogens, e
