title: Dissecting the Chikungunya Virus RNA Replication Process in vitro and in Live Cells
abs: Many positive-sense RNA viruses, such as Dengue, Zika, and the pandemic SARS-CoV-2 viruses, are serious human pathogens to cause severe infectious diseases, of which effective antivirals remain not readily available. Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) causes fever and viral polyarthritis symptoms, which could become a chronic disease. The virus is rapidly spread across the globe by the same mosquito vectors also for Dengue and Zika viruses, causing increasing public health concerns. As an essential step in the viral infection cycle, the viral genome replication process can be targeted to develop specific therapeutics. Indeed, many inhibitors targeting viral proteases and RNA polymerases can effectively stop or slow down the virus replication, thus serve as antiviral drugs to treat HIV and HCV. Success in antiviral development relies on a deep understanding of the virus and how it replicates in the host. The goal of the project is to determine the structure of the CHIKV RNA replication complex and fully understand its molecular function. To achieve this goal, we propose four aims: Aim 1 is to determine the crystal structure of nsP4 RNA polymerase and dissect the structural and functional dynamics of the full-length nsP4; Aim 2 is to determine the structure of nsP1 and characterize the viral 5’ RNA capping machinery; Aim 3 is to probe the 3D membrane association of nsP1 by mimicking the membrane spherule structures via engineered nanoscale biological membrane topography on glass chips; Aim 4 is to determine the overall architecture of the viral RNA replication complex in vitro and in live cells, using complementary cryo-electron microscopy and focused ion beam and scanning electron microscopy (FIB-SEM) methods. Our recent work on the characterization of CHIKV non-structural proteins (nsPs) has built a strong foundation for this project. We have established a library of expression constructs of viral non-structural proteins and RNAs. We reported the first biochemical and enzymatical characterization of the CHIKV nsP4 RNA polymerase. We have also determined the CHIKV nsP2 helicase-RNA complex structure. We recently defined the functional communication between the helicase and protease domains of the full-length nsP2 (Law et al., under review). Here we combine multiple approaches to tackle a big biology problem – structural and functional analysis of membrane-macromolecular complexes which are critical to understand the virus-host interaction. The success of this project will generate long-awaited structural and functional knowledge of the viral replicase complex and how they work together to form the RNA replication nanomachine. The findings from this study represent a major step forward structure-based antiviral development against CHIKV and related viruses.
kw: Chikungunya Virus; Pathogen-Host Interaction; Membrane Nanofabrication; Antiviral Drug Discovery; Structural Biology

title: Developing Bio-inspired Coacervate Adhesives for Flexible Epidermal Electronics
abs: Epidermal wearable devices represent a portable, non-intrusive, and low-cost method for providing reliable and continuous personalized health monitoring. The adhesion between the skin surface and a device is critical for obtaining accurate health information through the skin surface. However, it is still a great challenge for the epidermal electronic devices to achieve conformal attachment to the rough, soft, and textured surface of the skin, especially in hot and humid environments (such as in Singapore) or during exercise as sweat can cause the failure of many synthetic adhesives. Inspired by the marine mussels, we propose to develop redox curable, micro-structured peptidyl coacervate adhesives that can achieve strong and durable skin adhesion in the presence of moisture and sweat. This proposal also aims to solve a critical problem in mussel-inspired adhesives, the oxidation of Dopa in neutral to alkaline pH, by protecting shielding Dopa from oxidation in a peptidyl coacervate environment. The important hypotheses of this proposal are (1) the oxidation of Dopa can be effectively prevented in the mussel-inspired coacervates. (2) the coacervate platform will allow us to tailor the chemistry and redox of the Dopa containing peptidyl coacervate adhesives to tune the adhesion and solidification of the coacervate adhesives, resulting in fine control over the mechanical properties of the adhesives; and (3) the redox curable coacervate adhesives can be utilized to make micro-structured adhesives for on-skin electronic devices. To test the hypothesis, we will use surface force measurements to study the important molecular interactions that govern the formation and properties of the Dopa-containing peptide coacervates. We will also use electrochemistry methods to carefully investigate the redox of the Dopa in the coacervate. Micro-pillar structured adhesives with strong and tunable skin adhesion for epidermal sweat sensors will be fabricated using a micro-templating technique. The adhesion performance of the micro-structured coacervate adhesives on human skin will be carefully characterized and optimized in wet and sweaty conditions by adjusting the properties of the coacervate adhesives and the geometry of the microstructures. Developing such moisture-resistant adhesives is not only critical to skin electronic devices but also important to various healthcare applications, such as surgical glues, medical implants, biosensors, and skin treatments.
kw: Wet adhesives; bio-inspired; peptides; coacervate; micro-structures; epidermal sensors;

title: Transport mechanism of the essential omega-3 fatty acid transporter Mfsd2a
abs: Major Facilitator Superfamily Domain containing 2a (Mfsd2a) mediates the sodium-dependent transport of lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC) across cellular membranes, particularly the endothelium of the blood-brain barrier and eye-blood barriers. Mfsd2a exhibits specificity for transport of LPCs that contain mono- and polyunsaturated fatty acid moieties and constitutes the primary mechanism by which the brain and eye acquires the essential omega-3 fatty acid docosahexaenoic acid (DHA). Mouse Mfsd2a KO models have severe brain DHA deficiency and generalized microcephaly with reduced neuron dendrites, indicating that LPCs are building blocks for membrane biogenesis during brain development. Importantly, patients with homozygous or compound heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in Mfsd2a present with severe microcephaly and developmental and intellectual delay--a disease now categorized as Microcephaly 15, primary, autosomal recessive. Together, these findings indicate that LPC transport via Mfsd2a at the blood-brain barrier is essential for human brain development. Like all other MFS proteins, Mfsd2a contains 12 transmembrane domains. Biochemical and structural studies of bacterial and mammalian MFS proteins that transport water soluble compounds, such as monosaccharides, has supported a rocker-switch alternating access transport mechanism. Because LPCs are polar lipids, our central hypothesis is that Mfsd2a transports LPCs across membranes by flipping the LPC between membrane leaflets, acting as a LPC “flippase”. Currently, there are no known atomic resolution structures of Mfsd2a and a limited understanding of its molecular transport mechanism. This lack of biochemical and structural information precludes the use of structure-based design for the development of small molecule therapeutics that exploit Mfsd2a transport for the delivery of drugs across the blood-brain barrier via Mfsd2a, a major challenge in pharmaceutical development for treating neurological diseases. The central hypothesis of this proposal will be tested by pursuing the following two specific aims: 1) Structure-based determination of the LPC transport path by Mfsd2a and 2) to determine a biochemical mechanism for LPC transport. In this proposal we present several major findings that provide strong proof of feasibility that includes the first atomic structure of Mfsd2a bound to LPC in an inward-open conformation that captures substrate exit from the transporter and novel biochemical assays for quantifying kinetic parameters of LPC transport and activity using purified Mfsd2a in detergent and in proteoliposomes. In our opinion, this proposal is innovative because it utilizes novel biochemical and chemical biology approaches to determine a molecular mechanism of LPC transport. The information generated in this research program is expected to be utilized for structure guided LPC-prodrug design for the delivery of therapeutic compounds across the BBB.
kw: transporters; lipids; blood-brain barrier; phospholipids

title: Tunable Optical Properties of Twisted 3D Materials
abs: Summary and specific aims: Control of the materials properties has been the driving force of modern technologies. Materials that interact strongly with light – i.e. they are either strong light emitters or light absorbers – are particularly relevant for applications such as solar cells, photodetectors, lasers or light emitting diodes (LEDs). So far, optical properties of materials have been modulated by their composition, structure, and sometimes size. In this project, we aim to demonstrate a paradigm-shifting approach to tune optical properties of technologically-relevant materials by changing the twist angle between stacked films. The final goal is to demonstrate that some of the recently discovered quantum phenomena in layered 2-dimensional (2D) materials can be observed, and ultimately explored, in 3-dimensional (3D), bulk-like materials that are technologically mature and can be processed using existing industry-scale technologies. Critical to the success of this program will be an effective combination of experimental and theory work. The unique expertise of PI Gradecak-Garaj and her team in nanoscale synthesis, electron microscopy and in-situ nano-optical spectroscopy will be key to fabricate high-quality twisted heterostructures and achieve a structure-optical correlation of their properties. The experimental work will be complemented by theoretical insights by co-PI Adam’s team in understanding the nature of electronic interactions across twisted interfaces. The specific aims of this program are as follows: Aim 1: To experimentally demonstrate twist-related optical tunability in bulk homojunctions across a range of van der Waals (vdW) materials with the emission ranging from UV, across visible to IR spectral region. This would enable us, for example, to increase light intensity output in spectral regions that are difficult to achieve using conventional methods. Aim 2: To explore novel twist-related phenomena in twisted anisotropic materials and heterojunctions. This approach would enable us to modulate both wavelength and intensity of the light output in a discrete fashion as a function of the twist angle for digitized (quantized) optoelectronic response. Aim 3: To demonstrate proof-of concept optoelectronic devices with the optical response controlled by the twist angle between two bulk 3D materials. This part of the program will serve as a step toward practical implementation of new physical phenomena toward novel semiconductor device concepts. Intellectual Merit: We will study, control, and employ twist-related interface phenomena in bulk-like materials for applications in optoelectronics. Namely, the goal is to achieve wavelength tunability and light intensity enhancement via twist-induced carrier confinement at the interfaces. By combining experiment and theory, our project will be based on fundamental understanding of the mechanisms that govern behaviour of twisted interfaces with the aim of demonstrating practical devices. title: Novel III-V-VI Antimonide Bismide Materials for Ubiquitous Long Wavelength Infrared Photodetectors
abs: Long-wavelength infrared (LWIR) photodetectors operating in the 8–14 μm range have recently gained considerable interest due to development in three key sectors: (a) the Internet of Things (IoT), (b) Big Data, and (c) Artificial Intelligence. These crucial technologies are lauded to be the vital driving force behind the next industrial revolution (Industry 4.0). One of the critical prerequisites to this revolution is the large-scale deployment of sensors to provide critical data gathering for monitoring and automation purposes. Furthermore, photodetectors are used as fundamental components of infrared radiation (IR) imaging cameras typically used in night vision goggles or thermal-sensitive cameras. Infrared radiation photodetectors based on III-V materials can be tuned to be sensitive to different wavelength ranges up to the middle wavelength IR (MWIR) region, making them very versatile in their applications. The ability to detect various infrared windows is considered to have tremendous potential in applications such as pollution, process, environmental control, home-based health monitoring and healthcare, wearable electronics, counter-terrorism surveillance, and sensors to enhance the safety of computer-assisted/self-driving vehicles. These new applications may require a massive increase of IR sensor demand and deployment on an unprecedented scale akin to the exponential deployment of LED lighting and wireless communication products that occurred within the last decade. Currently, there is no ideal detector for LWIR sensing. The silicon-based bolometers, while inexpensive, are plagued with low detectivity and low sensitivity. The mercury cadmium telluride (MCT) technology has raised concerns about the toxicity and environmental impact of the mercury; thus making it inappropriate for mass consumer market deployment. The ratification of the Minamata Convention on Mercury by the European Union in 2017 prohibited the usage of MCT technology for consumer applications and permitted only limited usage for military and space applications. Therefore, MCT technology cannot be deployed in sensors intended for mass consumer markets such as wearables or sensors for smart homes and in the automotive industry. The III-V compound semiconductor products are not affected by these new restrictions. The current drawback of the III-V compound semiconductor technology lies at the bandgap of III-V photodetectors, which is limited to the InSb bandgap energy (0.17 eV at room temperature). This bandgap restricts the detectable wavelength of the III-V photodetector to the MWIR range at 7 μm . The 7 μm cut-off is impractical due to the water molecule absorption gap between MWIR (3 – 5 μm) and LWIR (8 – 14 μm) windows around the 5 – 7 μm wavelength range. In this project, the use of novel III-V-Bi for band-to-band long wavelength IR photodetection towards 8 μm and beyond is proposed. title: Artificial Intelligence Circuits of Hybrid Integrated Photonics System (AI CHIPS)
abs: In recent years, the advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) combining with the Internet of Things (IoT) technology, denoted as AIoT technology, has enabled new applications towards smart sensor networks for smart cities, smart homes, and intelligent industries. Through machine learning, sensor data are processed by data centers with huge computation power, i.e. cloud computing, to provide essential information. The surge in sensor amount in the AIoT era will pose a great challenge to the computation power offered by cloud computing. In fact, each sensor node equipped with an AI processor can help process the data on-chip individually so that only the final decisions are sent to the cloud without the need of further analysis. Such a scheme is called edge computing. While complicated AI processors such as graphic processing units are used in cloud computing, compact low power AI processors are demanded for edge computing because tasks implemented by individual sensor nodes in the edge computing scheme are simpler. Over the past few years, photonic neural networks (NN) have been reported as a complementary platform to the current electronic transistor-based NNs due to its advantages in low power consumption, ultra-high data rate (>100GHz) and immunity to electromagnetic interference (EMI). Nonetheless, the development of photonic NN is still relatively primitive and its potential has not been fully exploited. Firstly, up to now, most research groups have investigated photonic NNs that are based on Mach-Zehnder Interferometer (MZI) structures. The overall footprint of MZI-based NNs is huge. Consequently, the scalability of NNs remains an issue and the current best photonic NN only relies on a 4x4 matrix as its hidden layer. Secondly, while NN with hierarchy can effectively enhance the system efficiency in machine learning, the hierarchy structure has not been realized in photonic NN hardware. Thirdly, the current material platform based primarily on silicon (Si) also has its drawbacks. The power consumption of Si photonic NN is nontrivial due to the thermo-optic effect and the free-carrier dispersion effect based weighting mechanism. Meanwhile, the Si photonic NNs experience high thermal instability so that the NN characteristics will be completely changed as long as there is a thermal perturbation. Fourthly, practical demonstrations of photonic NNs are limited image and voice recognition. Applications involving human actions, which is a crucial aspect in the AIoT era, have not been investigated. In view of the current research and technology status with a focus on the specified limitations, we propose an integrated system featuring a 5x5 micro ring resonator (MRR) based photonic NN (Task A) on a hybrid Si/AlN platform (Task C), together with NEMS photonic switches (Task B) for task breakdown architectures to simplify the photonic NN structure. title: SU(3) non-Abelian physics in ultracold gas
abs: Our proposal aims to generate artificial SU(3) non-Abelian gauge fields acting on an ultracold gas of strontium atoms. Our experimental scheme is a straightforward generalization of the tripod laser scheme already implemented in our lab to study SU(2) systems. Specifically, we will implement controlled geometric unitary transformations acting in the qutrit (three interconnected quantum states) space and characterize their main properties in view of possible applications to quantum devices. Our objectives can be summarized as follows. We will first explore the fundamental properties of the SU(3) symmetry. In particular, we will perform a new type of Aharonov-Bohm experiment in the qutrit space, i.e. involving solely the internal degrees of freedom of the ultracold atoms. We will realize geometric unitary transformations and show the effect of artificially breaking and restoring time-reversal symmetry. For space-periodic systems, it is known that time-reversal symmetry breaking can induce non-trivial topological signatures such as a SU(3) magnetic monopole or nonzero Chern numbers. We will search how these topological effects manifest themselves in bulk systems like ours. Finally, we will explore the dynamics of an atomic qutrit wave-packet subjected to the gauge field structure like a SU(3) spin-orbit coupling, where the Larmor frequency of the spin precession is proportional to the atomic momentum. Here, we expect a more complex pseudo-spin dynamics than for SU(2), bearing similarities with neutrino oscillations.
kw: Laser cooling, quantum physics, geometric transformation, topology, quantum simulation, atomic physics,

title: Moiré engineering of correlated quantum states at oxide/2D-material interfaces
abs: The emerging twistronics is a study of novel electronic properties of artificial materials with a controllable twist in orientation between successive layers. In electronics and optics, the materials utilized to study the twistronics are typically two-dimensional (2D) layered materials, including graphene and transition-metal dichalcogenides. Recently, a number of the artificial materials, also called moiré superlattices, were developed and exhibited unexpected correlated quantum functionalities. Unfortunately, these novel correlation functionalities weakly exist at only extremely low temperature, precluding the moiré superlattices from the practical application at room temperature and exhibiting a variety of the most appealing correlated properties, such as charge/orbit ordering, multiferroics and coexistence of ferromagnetism and superconductivity. We propose that the marriage of correlated functionalities in oxides and the emerging moiré engineering may introduce the unseen correlated functionalities. This is because strongly-correlated electronic materials, in particular oxides, host rich correlated electronic properties and peculiar breaking of symmetries, such as ferroelectricity in strained SrTiO3 arising from the breaking of inversing symmetry and ferromagnetic insulation in LaMnO3 arising from the breaking of the time-reversal symmetry. The feasibility of the hypothesis is experimentally supported by our preliminary results and recent discoveries of oxide-based moiré superlattices, such as MoO3/MoO3 and La1-XSrXMnO3/LaAlO3 moiré superlattices. In this project, we aim to (i) develop a protocol for fabricating a new type of moiré superlattices at the interface of correlated oxides and 2D layered materials, and (ii) explore and manipulate its twist-angle-dependent correlated quatnum behaviours. The success of the proposal is ensured by the preliminary results, complementary team organization, existing experimental and theoretical supports, and an excellent existing scientific environment. This project would bring Singapore to the forefront of condensed matter physics and contribute to Singapore’s future industry of electronics. Scientifically, by demonstrating the moiré superlattice at the oxide-2D interface for the first time, the moiré engineering is generalized to a broader range of material, empowering the existing moiré superlattices with richer correlated electronic phases. Technologically, the development of oxide-based twistronics could potentially promote future electronics in Singapore based on the new types of materials and device structures, including quantum computing devices, microwave/THz devices, and ultralow energy spintronics.

title: Empowering Asymmetric Synthesis of Nitrogen-containing Molecules by Using Azoalkenes as 1,3-Dipoles
abs: This proposal describes a projected investigation concerning the development of azoalkenes as novel carbon-carbon-nitrogen (CCN) 1,3-dipoles, and their applications in asymmetric catalysis for the synthesis of chiral nitrogen-containing cyclic molecules. The intellectual merits of the project lie in: 1) developing new chemistry that is based on unprecedented utilization of azoalkenes as CCN 1,3-dipoles; 2) evolving novel synthetic approaches to access nitrogen-containing cyclic structures which are potentially of biological significance. The broad impacts of the proposed work include: 1) the new modes of activations introduced by azoalkenes may inspire and enable future development of many unknown chemical processes that are based on azoalkenes and the beyond; 2) the catalytic methodologies described in this proposal will allow for effective creation of a wide range of privileged nitrogen-containing molecular architectures, which are potentially significant in medicinal chemistry and biological sciences. Azoalkenes, also known as 1,2-diaza-1,3-dienes, have proven to be versatile synthetic building blocks in organic chemistry. Up to date, their utilizations are limited to serving as acceptors in 1,4-conjugate additions or azo-dienes in [4 + 2] cycloaddition reactions. In this proposal, we intend to explore unprecedented engagement of azoalkenes as novel CCN 1,3-dipoles, as opposed to their common utilization as 4-atom synthons documented in the literature, for effective catalytic asymmetric synthesis of biologically important nitrogen-containing molecules. Remarkably, the reaction modes of azoalkenes described in this proposal are unknown, and we anticipate our studies will enrich the chemistry of azoalkenes and allow for the efficient synthesis of biologically important nitrogen-containing molecules in a conceptually novel manner, thus offering ample new opportunities in organic synthesis. The objective of this research project is to evolve azoalkenes as novel and powerful CCN 1,3-dipoles for effective asymmetric synthesis of useful nitrogen-containing molecules and new molecular architectures. Towards this end, we will develop a range of catalytic asymmetric methodologies, and apply them to the enantioselective synthesis of different classes of nitrogen-containing molecules. The approaches to be taken in this project include the following: • Enantioselective synthesis of pyrroles or 2,3-dihydropyrroles via catalytic asymmetric [3 + 2] cycloaddition reactions of azoalkenes with electron-rich alkenes or enols; • Enantioselective synthesis of multi-nitrogen-containing six-membered ring systems via catalytic asymmetric [3 + 3] cycloaddition reactions of azoalkenes with dipolar partners; • Catalytic asymmetric dearomative [3 + 2]/[3 + 4] cycloaddition reactions of azoalkenes with naphthols/indoles; • Design of intramolecular dearomatization processes to access complex molecular architectures; • Exploring organo/metal cooperative catalysis of azolkene

title: Enzymes that catalyze a new type of peptide macrocyclization
abs: Cyclic peptides are an important chemotype in drug discovery. Prominent uses for cyclic peptides in clinical applications include immunosuppressants, antibiotics, antifungals, antivirals, and anticancer agents. Peptide therapeutics exist in a unique niche in chemical space at the interface of small molecules and larger biologics. Advantageous features include higher affinity binding to biological targets through protein-protein interactions and less toxicity to healthy cells. However, one limiting factor in the development of peptide drugs in their susceptibility to degradative proteases in biological systems. One strategy for stabilizing peptides is the incorporation of a ring or macrocycle by chemical synthesis or by enzymatic catalysis. Methods that create novel cyclic peptide scaffolds in a predictable and robust manner are highly desirable in drug discovery platforms. These technologies can be the basis of drugs with new modes of action or new chemical entities. The translational value in such technologies can be seen in companies such as Peptidream (net worth $17 billion) which is based off technologies to make constrained peptide therapeutics. Our lab has discovered a novel family of bacterial-derived 3-residue cyclophane forming enzymes (3-CyFEs) that create unique peptide macrocycles which stabilize peptides to digestive enzymes. 3-CyFEs catalyze the formation of unprecedented strained cyclophane macrocycles and have the potential to generate natural and engineered peptide libraries. This project is original and innovative because the carbon-carbon bond formed by 3-CyFEs results in macrocycles that have no precedent by synthetic methods or by enzyme catalysis. Our proposal is to broaden our knowledge of 3-CyFEs by the following two aims. The goal of Aim 1 is to develop an atomic level model of three-residue cyclophane formation which will be carried out in three independent parts. 1) Complete the structural assignment for cyclophanes for each of the subclasses of 3-CyFEs. By defining the structure of enzyme products, we will have an overview of the reactions catalyzed across the 3-CyFE family and will guide biochemical studies. 2) Carry out the biochemical characterization of 3-CyFEs and confirm that they act as canonical rSAM proteins. In order to elucidate the individual steps of the catalysis the enzymes will be purified, reconstituted, and characterized in their active form. 3) To carry out crystallization studies on enzymes. Structural information for these enzymes is essential to understanding interactions in the catalytic active site. Our hypothesis is that 3-CyFEs share similar biophysical properties and structure to previously charcterized rSAM enzymes. Collectively, these experiments will provide a detailed overview of the reaction catalyzed by 3-CyFEs at the atomic level which will be necessary to exploit these enzymes for the production of a broad range of cyclic peptides. title: Interface Controlled 2D Materials for Artificial Synaptic Devices
abs: Neuromorphic computing, aiming at effectively emulating the functionality of human brain via the integration of electronic components, has attracted intensive research interest, in order to address the stringent scaling requirement for the traditional von Neumann architecture based complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) technology, i.e., scaling requirement on the energy consumption, device size and device structure complexity. The brain functions in a massively parallel processing mode realized by a compactly interconnected neural network, which contributes to its superior computational and energy efficiency, particularly in dealing with unstructured information. In the biological nervous system, synapses act as processing units for the signal transmission among neurons. In the intelligent artificial neural network, electronic elements are utilized as key building blocks for synapses to emulate the function and efficiency of the brain. A significant amount of research has been conducted to facilitate the development of hardware-based neuromorphic computing. Despite tremendous progress being achieved, the performance of artificial synapse systems is still far from satisfactory when compared with their biological counterparts, particularly on the compromise between the low energy consumption and high operation speed. Two-dimensional (2D) materials, such as 2D transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), have been rapidly established as promising building blocks for the next-generation nanoelectronic devices, showing great potential to extend the scaling limits in silicon-based MOSFETs. The 2D atomic layered structure enables their immunity against the short channel effects, while the mechanical strength and structural flatness allow their integration into flexible and wearable circuits. Very recently, 2D materials have aroused remarkable interest in artificial synapses due to their excellent scalability and desirable electronic transport properties under low-voltage operation. However, it is still a big challenge to realize synaptic device with ultralow energy consumption. The aim of this proposal is to develop artificial synaptic devices based on interface controlled 2D materials for neuromorphic computing. We will focus on the development of optically and electrically stimulated artificial synaptic devices based on the interface controlled 2D materials through the engineering of the mid-gap defect states in dielectric layers (such as the 2D hexagonal boron nitride, h-BN) and the optically tunable interfacial states in the heterostructures of 2D TMDs on complex transition metal oxide films. We also aim to reveal the interfacial and defects state structures at the atomic scale and their roles in synaptic device performance by in-situ x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy and ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS/UPS) and low-temperature scanning tunnelling microscopy (LT-STM) techniques. title: Hodge Laplacian based deep learning models for drug design
abs: Artificial intelligence (AI) based drug design has great potential to significantly change the landscape of pharmaceutical industries. In fact, traditional drug design approaches are laborious, time-consuming, and highly inefficient. Currently, only 10%-14% of drug candidates, which manage to enter clinical trials, can reach the market as medicines. It takes more than 10 years and costs about $2.6 billion to develop a new market-approval prescription medicine. AI techniques have been gradually applied to the whole drug design process, from target discovery, lead discovery, lead optimization, preclinical development, to the three phases of clinical trials. Researchers and biopharmaceutical companies are leading the revolution of AI in drug design. For instance, Pfizer is using IBM Watson to aid immuno-oncology drug discovery. Obama's Cancer Moonshot initiative uses AI for personalization of treatment and early diagnosis. With the ever-increasing accumulation of chemical and biomolecular data, data-driven AI models will usher in an era of faster, cheaper and more-efficient drug design and drug discovery. However, unlike image, text, video, and audio data, molecular data from chemistry and biology, have complicated three-dimensional structures, as well as physical and chemical properties. Efficient molecular descriptors or fingerprints are key to the success of machine learning models in drug design. Traditional molecular/chemical descriptors come from structural measurements and physical measurements. In general, these descriptors tend to focus on specific properties, thus not be able to capture the intrinsic general information. Further, feature vectors made from a simple combination of geometric and physical properties can have dramatically different values under different units, and tend to hinder the performance of learning models even with the normalization techniques. Recently, a series of advanced mathematical models from algebraic topology, combinatorial topology, and different geometry, have been proposed for biomolecular representations. Among these models is topological data analysis (TDA). Using topological invariants as molecular descriptors, TDA-based AI models can reveal the intrinsic global properties of biomolecules, and have found great success in various aspects of drug design. In this project, we propose, for the first time, Hodge Laplacian (HL) based deep learning models for drug design. Hodge theory, which is widely regarded as one of the most important mathematical theories, provides a bridge between differential geometry, algebraic topology, and functional analysis. Spectral graph, spectral simplicial complex, and spectral hypergraph, can be generated from the discretization of HL operator on graph, simplicial complex and hypergraph, respectively. title: Investigate the innate and adaptive immune response against capsular polysaccharides in Streptococcus pneumoniae
abs: Resolving the structure-function relationship of carbohydrates is a fundamental goal in molecular biology, yet this question remains unsolved even in the simplest of cells. In Streptococcus pneumoniae, the cell is encased in a polysaccharide capsule, which is crucial for its survival inside the host. The capsule shields the underlying antigens and interfaces directly with the respiratory tract epithelia as well as immune cells. To counteract the protective effect of the capsule, the host produces opsonizing antibodies via the adaptive immune system. This forms the scientific basis of our vaccine strategy against the pneumococcus. Despite years of study, the glycan motifs that contribute to the immunogenicity of the capsule remain surprisingly ill-defined. This project will build on the state-of-the-art tools that we recently developed to investigate the innate and adaptive immune response when the host cells encounter bacteria expressing different capsule polysaccharides. We will leverage the wealth of structural and genetic information available on the S. pneumoniae capsule pathway to identify polysaccharide regions that are immunogenic. Our first two aims are focused on elucidating the innate response of human airway epithelial cells on isogenic strains of S. pneumoniae displaying various capsular polysaccharides. We will exploit a long-term biofilm model that we have established to measure the reaction of the epithelia when colonized by these capsule-switch mutants and study the effect of environmental factors like viral infections. Experiments in aim 3 will test the hypothesis that the polysaccharide structures affect their antigenicity. Here, we will rank the humoral response of various capsular polysaccharides in mice and identify the potential glycoepitopes responsible. Besides solving important scientific questions, S. pneumoniae is a medically important pathogen in its own right. Our results should significantly impact and inform efforts to generate therapies and vaccines against S. pneumoniae and related pathogens.

title: A novel role for EZH2 in the regulation of polymerase pause release
abs: ACADEMIC SIGNIFICANCE Proper control of transcriptional programs is of fundamental importance for the establishment of cellular identity during differentiation and development, as well as the maintenance thereof in mature tissues. Failures in transcriptional regulation lead to developmental defects and can give rise to cancer initiating cells. Transcription is largely regulated at the level of chromatin, where – together with transcription factors – different protein complexes act as initiators, enhancers or repressors. Among those complexes, the polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2) plays a crucial role in the silencing of genes by depositing histone H3 lysine 27 tri-methylation (H3K27me3) marks at target sites, leading to the generation of inaccessible heterochromatin and gene repression. The enzymatically active subunit of the complex is the methyltransferase EZH2, which is frequently deregulated or mutated in cancers. Chemical inhibitors targeting EZH2 are currently in clinical use and are thought to exert their anti-proliferative effects through their ability to reactivate tumour suppressors. Interestingly, a growing number of recent publications have suggested that EZH2 can also moonlight as transcriptional co-activator, outside the PRC2 complex, and that targeting this “non-canonical” function is key to target certain cancer types which have been otherwise resistant to EZH2 enzymatic inhibitors. HYPOTHESIS/RESEARCH QUESTION While the mechanistic basis for EZH2’s role within the PRC2 complex (canonical function) is relatively well understood, the exact mode of action in its non-canonical role is less clear and we still lack a solid understanding of how EZH2 exerts its role as transcriptional activator. Here, we want to suggest a novel model of how EZH2 can act as a repressor and activator concomitantly. Our central hypothesis is: recruitment of the EZH2-containing polycomb complex (PRC2) to target genes leads to (1) gene repression through H3K27me3 (canonical function), (2) but at the same time it helps to maintain a certain level of expression by facilitating the release of paused polymerase into productive elongation (non-canonical function). This mechanism is crucial for the regulation of bivalent genes, where it helps to avoid the complete transcriptional shutdown, thus keeping them “poised” for activation. We will generate those datasets from wild-type cells as well as upon perturbation of factors of interest for this project (including, but not limited to inhibition and knock-down of EZH2, knock down of other polycomb proteins, inhibition and knock-down of polymerase-pause related factors). The methods of choice will be next-generation sequencing based techniques such as RNA-seq and GRO-seq (“global run-on sequencing”). title: Phosphatases in T cell regulation during autoimmunity and anti-cancer responses
abs: Tyrosine phosphatases play critical roles in regulation of immunity, but the molecular mechanisms are poorly understood. Shp1 and Shp2 tyrosine phosphatases are highly expressed in T cells, but their molecular functions have not yet been fully elucidated. We have recently developed a conditional knockout mouse model with T cell lineage-specific deletion of Shp1 and Shp2, or the individual phosphatases. We discovered that the double phosphatase deficiency resulted in an increase in CD4+CD25+ regulatory T cells (Tregs) and the recently described CD8+CD44hiLy49+ Tregs, suggesting redundant roles of Shp1 and Shp2 in Treg development. We aim to determine the molecular roles of Shp1 and Shp2 phosphatases in development and function of Tregs. We will elucidate the molecular basis of Shp1 and Shp2-dependent control of Treg development. We will determine if the increase in CD4+ Tregs is due to enhanced IL2 and/or TCR signal during thymic development, or enhanced TGFβ signal in mature T cells. As almost nothing is known about CD8+ Treg development, we will identify CD8+ Treg precursors using bone marrow cultures, adoptive transfers and single cell RNAseq analysis, testing if Shp1 and Shp2 modulate CD8+ Tregs by augmenting IL15 signals. We will determine if Shp1 and Shp2 phosphatases control CD4+ Treg and CD8+ Treg suppressive functions in autoimmunity and cancer, using mouse models of multiple sclerosis and melanoma, respectively. We will elucidate the molecular basis of Shp1 and Shp2-dependent control of CD4+ and CD8+ Treg suppression, focusing on T cell receptor and cytokine signals, as well as signals from the inhibitory receptors PD1 and Ly49 in Tregs. We will also use pharmacological inhibition of Shp1 and Shp2 phosphatase activity to validate findings from the mouse systems in human T cells, and to test the translational potential of modulating Shp1 and Shp2 phosphatase activity to control human T cell suppression.

title: Investigating Mechanical Impact of Apoptosis in Compensatory Proliferation
abs: The number of cells in tissues is tightly controlled by cell division and cell death, and misregulation of cell numbers could lead to pathological conditions such as cancer. Programmed cell death, or apoptosis, is a mechanism by which unnecessary, aged, or damaged cells are eliminated. To maintain homeostasis of cell numbers in a tissue, an apoptotic event stimulates the proliferation of neighboring cells. This mechanism is called compensatory proliferation, which was originally observed more than 40 years ago (Haynie and Bryant, 1977). Importantly, during compensatory proliferation it is sufficient for a limited number of the neighboring cells to divide to replace the number of cells lost, meaning that not all the neighboring cells need to divide. However, the origin of this spatially non-homogeneous nature of compensatory growth, in other words why only a small number of cells around an apoptotic cell undergo cell division remains a major open question. Based on our previous studies describing how the apoptotic cell is mechanically expelled from epithelial tissue (Kocgozlu et al., 2016; Saw et al., 2017; Teng et al., 2017; Thomas et al., 2020; Toyama et al., 2008) and our preliminary results, we hypothesize that the spatial inhomogeneity in mechanotransduction in the neighboring tissue, which arises from the non-uniform pattern of mechanical force propagation, accounts for the inhomogeneity of compensatory proliferation. This is complementary to the current biochemical understanding of compensatory proliferation. We will adopt an interdisciplinary approach that incorporates imaging, quantitative analysis, gene manipulation (including CRISPR/CAS9 and optogenetics), biophysical tools (laser surgery, traction force microscopy), bioengineering tools (microcontact printing), and pharmaceutical approaches. All standard techniques and protocols are all well-established or are available in the lab and host institution. All key reagents have been identified and are available without delay. Based on the preliminary results, we are confident that the proposed project will be achieved in due course. We plan to address the long-standing question of why only a small number of cells around an apoptotic cell undergo cell division, which remains unanswered for more than 40 years. We foresee that our proposed approach to developing a simple and robust platform to study the mechanical impact of apoptosis in the neighboring tissue will provide additional insights into basic cellular functions of how tissue maintains its homeostasis. Moreover, because such apoptosis-induced proliferation has been found in a wide range of cancers, including breast cancer, melanoma, and glioma cells (Donato et al., 2014; Kurtova et al., 2015; Mao et al., 2013), uncovering the mechanism of apoptosis-induced compensatory cell division from a new mechanical perspective could be critically important for understanding why some cancer therapies work or why they fail.

title: Deciphering the roles of MOAP-1 in cellular senescence and ageing-associated disorders in liver
abs: The continued and steady rise of the ageing population worldwide will post major challenges to societies for managing the socioeconomic impacts caused by the dramatic increase in ageing-related disease burdens. While exercise and diet are thought to have beneficial effects on preventing certain age-associated disorders, they are insufficient in addressing the problem as ageing is the most significant risk factor for driving the development of chronic diseases in human population. Ageing is mediated, in part, by accelerating accumulation and/or decelerating removal of damaged cells and intracellular components resulting from oxidative stress and oncogenic events triggered by carcinogens or mutations. Cellular senescence, a hallmark of ageing, is an irreversible form of cell cycle arrest that is acquired when cells fail to recover from damages. During senescence, nuclear envelope loses its integrity, resulting in the release of chromatin fragments into the cytoplasm, known as the cytoplasmic chromatin fragments (CCFs). The major impact of CCFs is to trigger inflammatory response. While short-term inflammation can facilitate removal of senescent cells by the immunosurveillance system and initiate tissue regeneration, chronic inflammation is associated with tissue degeneration and cancer development. Understanding how distinct cell types and organs respond to cellular damage may yield novel insights on devising potential therapeutic solutions to mitigate the functional decline associated with the ageing process. While some compounds such as rapamycin and senolytics have shown promising results in slowing down ageing-associated declines in pre-clinical models, in-depth understanding of the ageing process at the molecular, cellular and organ levels is required to permit development of targeted approaches in addressing ageing-associated diseases in specific organs such as liver. MOAP-1 (Modulator-of-apoptosis-1) was originally cloned as a Bax-binding protein enriched in the outer mitochondrial membrane to facilitate Bax-mediated apoptosis signalling. MOAP-1 deficient mice are resistant to Fas-induced liver injury and lethality. Recently, we uncovered additional functions of MOAP-1 in regulating oxidative stress response and autophagy signalling. MOAP-1 suppresses the p62-Nrf2 pro-tumorigenic signalling through binding to the oligomerization domain of p62 to disrupt its protein aggregation function (Tan et. al, manuscript under revision in EMBO Reports). title: Understanding mycolic acid homeostasis in mycobacteria
abs: Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the causative agent of tuberculosis (TB), possesses a complex double-membrane cell envelope structure that renders the bacterium resistant to most classes of antibiotics. In particular, the mycobacterial outer membrane (OM) serves as an effective permeability barrier that prevents toxic molecules from entering the cell. Few drugs can penetrate the mycobacterial OM, and the emergence of resistance to existing antibiotics calls for an urgent need to develop new strategies to combat mycobacterial infections. The OM is essential for cell viability; compromising the structure and assembly of these lipids into the OM kills the bacterium. The OM comprises largely long chain (C60-C90) branched fatty acids, termed mycolic acids (MAs), that pack together tightly to form a membrane bilayer with low fluidity and permeability. MAs are biosynthesized as trehalose monomycolates (TMMs) in the inner membrane (IM) and must be transported across the IM, the aqueous periplasm and to the OM, where they become functionalized onto the bacterial cell wall. The biosynthetic pathway of mycolic acids is well characterized, but how the process may be regulated to achieve control over MA levels and composition is not yet understood. Because the mycolic acid biosynthetic pathway is highly conserved among mycobacteria species and is a well-validated drug target, understanding the mechanisms of MA synthesis, transport, and homeostasis has direct application in the search for novel antibiotic targets and expanding the activity of existing antibiotics against M. tuberculosis and other pathogenic mycobacteria. This proposal outlines experiments to elucidate and characterize the mechanisms for regulation of MA levels and composition in mycobacteria. In Specific Aim I, we will focus on understanding trehalose-dependent regulation of MA biosynthesis and levels, specifically defining and characterizing trehalose-interacting partners within the type II fatty acid synthase (FAS-II) cycle. In Specific Aim II, we will systematically perturb the FAS-II system to investigate the basis of changes in MA composition under various conditions. In Specific Aim III, we will characterize the putative Mce1 transporter to provide a starting point towards understanding how MA recycling and transport contributes to MA homeostasis. Collectively, these three aims will deliver new insights into how mycobacterial cells ensure production of optimal levels and composition of MAs to be assembled into the OM. Given the role of MAs in intrinsic mycobacterial antibiotic resistance and in pathogenesis, this proposal will contribute significantly to the ground work towards the development of novel antibiotics to combat the problem of drug resistance in mycobacterial infections.
kw: Lipid biosynthesis; Lipid transport; trehalose-dependent regulation; FAS; Pks13; anti-microbial resistance

title: Neurobiology of nicotinic acetylcholine receptor subunit chrna3 in addiction and anxiety
abs: The societal impact of addiction is well known. In spite of a long history of research over half a century, addiction to nicotine and alcohol is a growing problem. An advancement is the recognition that a large genetic component underlies the propensity to become addicted, and to overcome withdrawal. A second advancement is the understanding that malfunction in ancient vertebrate neural circuits, such as the habenula-interpeduncular nucleus, normally recruited in risk assessment, is also involved in addictions, anxiety disorders, and depression in humans. However, our knowledge of the genetics and the neurobiology needed to design better interventional strategies is incomplete. The strongest, most consistent evidence to date is an association between polymorphisms in the Chrna5-Chrna3-Chrnb4 gene cluster and addiction in humans. Among these, the role of Chrna3 gene, coding for the α3 subunit of nicotinic acetylcholine receptor, is least well understood due to the lack of suitable animal models. Our study addresses this gap in our knowledge. We build on two recent advancements in my lab – 1) generation of mutant Chnra3 lines, and 2) development of assays to study addictive behaviours in the zebrafish. Using these, our goal is to understand the behavioural, neurophyioslogical, and molecular consequences of Chrna3 dysfunction. We will use in-house developed behavioural assays to study preference for nicotine and alcohol, sleep and arousal, anxiety-like behaviors, and appetite. We will examine neural activity at the level of the whole brain using phosphorylated ERK. At a circuit level, we will perform functional calcium imaging, transcriptomic studies, neuroanatomical analysis, and optogenetic manipulation of the habenula-interpeduncular nucleus. By performing studies at these multiple levels, we expect to obtain a comprehensive understanding of Chrna3’s role in drug dependence, gain an insight into the neurogenetics of addiction in general, and its role in producing symptoms associated with other neuropsychiatric disorders.

title: Learning in MEG/EEG imaging-- from localization to behaviour prediction
abs: Exploration of the human brain is of fundamental interest. How the brain functions is still not well understood; in particular, how the physical functioning of the brain as an organ gives rise to human behaviour remains a complete mystery. As the world’s two non-invasive imaging technology, MEG/EEG have been playing a major role in understanding how the brain possibly works, with the former providing the temporary resolution at 1 millisecond. The traditional problem in MEG/EEG is the so-called source localization problem (namely the inverse problem), which is ill-posed. Behaviour prediction using brain signals is still an open question, where the core is to find a mapping from the MEG/EEG signals to both inter-individual differences and intra-individual temporal fluctuations in behaviour. There have been some major challenges for the analysis of MEG/EEG data arising from the technological limitations. On one hand, it has witnessed that the same behaviour can yield different shapes of MEG/EEG brain signals across individuals, resulting in large intra-class variation when analysing brain-behaviour associations. Such large intra-class variation may worsen the performance of simple and shallow models. On the other hand, the structure of the signal is very complex. Frist, MEG/EEG signal is a set of time-varying observations and the actual dependence of these observations on time is unclear. Existing methods usually describe the temporal structure by certain simple and subjective assumptions. One may assume that the relationship between two successive frames/time points are linearly dependent. However, this simple assumption may not fulfil the temporal structure properly. Second, in fact, the spatial variation of the sensors over time could also lead to the spatial structure variation of the observed signals, which are usually ignored. Third, manual filters may not accurately capture the discriminative features of the signals. In this project, we propose to overcome these limitations by quantifying the intrinsic dimensionality of the brain signals. The big picture is that we propose a paradigm of human behaviour prediction based on the source localization results of the MEG/EEG data, which represent time-varying brain neuronal network fluctuations. The healthy human brain consists of large-scale, distributed, function-critical neural networks. The brain network dynamics change with age and have the potential to predict trial-by-trial task performance and infer individual differences in behaviour. However, such knowledge is still lacking, especially given the difficulty in source estimation. We aim to employ the novel source localization method to reveal how time-varying brain network changes relate to cognitive task performance and vary with age. This project will leverage on the existing MEG/EEG data collected from adolescents, young and older adults. title: Graph Signal Processing for High Dimensional Structures and Spaces
abs: Graph signal processing (GSP) has become an important tool in many applications such as image processing, networking inference and analysis of social network data. In these applications, the data can be represented as a vector in which the relationship between different components of the vector is captured by a graph. Each vertex in the graph corresponds to a signal value that is a complex number or a discrete time series of complex numbers. However, one can assign mathematical objects with richer structures to each vertex of a graph. An example of such a mathematical object comes from a Hilbert space. In this proposal, we develop a mathematical framework to generalize GSP to a much bigger class of vertex signals and practical algorithms for analyzing graph-structured sensor data. Our research objectives are the following: 1. Theoretical development of a generalized GSP framework where the signal associated with each graph vertex is a stochastic process. We aim to develop a rigorous mathematical theory of statistical signal processing taking into account the underlying graph structure relating the signals. 2. Theoretical development of a GSP framework for high dimensional graph structures, including simplicial complexes. In traditional GSP, a graph is simply a one-dimensional simplicial complex. Our goal is to investigate and develop an operator theory for signal processing on high dimensional structures. 3. Application of generalized GSP frameworks and techniques to develop signal recovery methods for sensors in a network with self-reset analog-to-digital converters (ADCs) that produce folded signal samples. The Shannon rate is the minimum sampling rate that guarantees perfect recovery of a bandlimited signal from its sampled signal. To handle the problem of signal clipping that occurs during sampling of high dynamic range signals, self-reset ADCs sample modulo-operated signal values, which are called folded samples. Recovery of the original signals from folded samples has attracted a lot of interest as it allows sensors to have unlimited dynamic range. Current methods however require sampling above the Shannon rate, which makes applying such schemes directly to a large-scale sensor network undesirable. The problem of recovering a graph signal from folded samples across a network is an open problem. In our proposed approach, a spatio-temporal sampling scheme across both the graph and time domain needs to be developed. Our objective is to leverage on the graph (and the underlying signal correlations) to achieve a sampling rate close to Shannon's rate for the whole graph. We aim to design methods based on the graph analytics developed in the previous two objectives to provide fundamental insights into the optimal achievable sampling rates and recovery fidelity. We also develop algorithms to approach these limits. Given the wide applicability of GSP and the use of graph-structured data in different applications, the GSP frameworks developed can lea

title: Automated Synthesis of High-Fidelity Images for Deep Network Training
abs: In this project, we will investigate two image synthesis approaches for synthesizing high-fidelity and annotated images that can be directly applied to train accurate and robust DNN models effectively: 1. Composition-based Image Synthesis: It aims to embed foreground objects into background images for composing annotated new images for DNN training, e.g. embedding cars/pedestrian into street-view images. The foreground objects can have different formats such as editable texts, color images like car pictures, or 3D graphic models. In this project, we will study three problems for high-fidelity image composition: 1) where to embed objects within background images, 2) how to embed objects with realistic geometry in poses, alignment, etc., and 3) how to embed objects with realistic appearance in color, brightness, etc. As the composition is aware of what and where objects are embedded in the background images, this approach generates self-annotated images that can train image classification or object detection models directly. 2. Adaptation-based Image Synthesis: It aims to adapt images from a source domain to a target domain so that the adapted images have target-domain features/attributes and can be more useful for training DNN models for target-domain images. Most existing works focus on adapting image appearance such as colors and styles only. In this project, we will tackle two new adaptation challenges: 1) realistic adaptation of global image geometry, e.g. the pose of face images in face or facial expression generation, 2) realistic adaptation of local image geometry, e.g. local facial expression changes around mouth/eye region in face or facial expression generation. The high-fidelity adaptation of global and local image geometry opens a new horizon for adaptation-based synthesis with numerous applications in various computer vision tasks. Specifically, we will investigate four research challenges for automated synthesis of high-fidelity images: 1. Semantics-Coherent Synthesis: Similar to the human vision system, a well-trained DNN model relies heavily on local and global contexts to classify images or detect objects in images. We conjecture that semantic coherence, the semantic compatibility of objects with their surrounding contexts (e.g. cars should appear on the road instead of trees or sky), is critical to the usefulness of the synthesized images while applying them to train DNN models. It addresses the challenge of where to embed foreground objects in background images in composition-based image synthesis. 2. Object Shadow Generation: Object shadow is an inherent component in natural images. It is critical to the realism and usefulness of synthesized images in DNN training as it forms certain contexts and visual representation of objects. It addresses the appearance fidelity in composition-based synthesis while embedding foreground objects into background images. 3. title: Virulent animals or unsafe meat: The qualification of food safety in live animal 'wet markets' and supermarkets in China
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: The spillover of the Covid-19 coronavirus from animals to humans took place, according to initial reports, in a marketplace in China where fresh food and live animals were sold. Such so-called “wet” markets have long been considered a source of zoonotic disease risks because they enable close contact between humans and animals, and in China there have been widespread calls for their closure and replacement with supermarkets. Yet despite these health risks, many Chinese consumers continue to puchase food at wet markets, including live fish and animals, because these markets are seen as providing healthier, fresher, and safer food. Rather than dismissing consumer perceptions of food safety as misinformed, this study aims to empirically understand how vendors and consumers evaluate food safety and quality. The research asks: how do food evaluations differ when applied to live animals versus slaughtered meats? To do so, the study will conduct a comparison of the “qualification devices” used by both vendors and consumers to evaluate the quality and safety of animal-origin food in “wet” markets and supermarkets. Qualification devices, a concept developed in science and technology studies (STS), are the equipment used to identify, differentiate and evaluate the qualities of a food product, ranging from lab tests to consumer ‘taste’ tests. Crucially, live animal wet markets not only pose completely distinct risks from slaughtered meats (based in interspecies contact, not food ingestion), but also make available different devices for consumers to qualify food safety and quality (for instance, the brightness of a chicken’s eyes as an index of vitality). Therefore, drawing on methods of multispecies ethnography, the proposed study will document how differences in the organization of human-animal relations—whether consumers engage with live or slaughtered animals—alter how food safety is qualified. By recognizing that food is a commodity that may also be a living being, or a “lively commodity,” the proposed study moves interdisciplnary food studies beyond human-centered models of consumption and situates the qualificaiton of food within the political ecology of interspecies communications.
kw: Zoonotic disease, food safety, social trust, science and technology studies (STS), cultural anthropology, Covid-19

title: New machine learning methods with applications in forecasting economic and financial variables
abs: Since the development of economy-wide modeling in the 1950s econometric methods have been successfully used to uncover relationships between response variables and potential explanatory driver variables in many fields of study as well as economics and finance. Such relationships can be specified in parametric form where there is dependence on a set of unknown parameters or in a more general nonparametric form with unknown functions. When a true data generating mechanism (which is more formally known as data generating process or DGP in the literature) exists and is correctly specified in empirical work, the methods of econometric estimation and inference are typically justified by large sample asymptotic properties, including consistency and limit distributional behavior. Consistency is the asymptotic property in which parameter or function estimates approach their respective true values as the sample size of data tends to infinity, thereby yielding the true DGP. Inference is facilitated by using the large sample limit distribution of a suitable test statistic. Reliable forecasting based on observational evidence is useful in individual and firm decision-making, as well as govenmental planning, regulation, and many other activities that rely on future economic projections. Econometric methods have a long history in forecasting macroeconomic and financial variables. Elliott and Timmermann (2016) provide a comprehensive overview of econometric forecasting methods and Xie et al. (2020) review recently developed techniques. When structural instabilities and nonstationarities are in presence in data, a common approach in the econometrics literature is to combine forecasts from different econometric models. This technique is known as forecast combinations. In economics, structural instabilities and nonstationarities are widely expected as the economic environment changes constantly. For example, at the aggregate level, there are business cycles and policy shocks. At the individual level, there are health shocks and employment shocks. When the DGP is expected to be complex, and when the available pool of relevant explanatory covariates is of high dimension, econometric methods face many challenges. DGP complexities typically arise because of the large number of factors and decision-makers that underlie economic and financial data. While big data brings many advantages, users typically do not know in advance whether or not all the available information is useful and which explanatory covariates should be used. This makes it difficult to find the true DGP. Moreover, big data makes the DGP more complicated as there are more relationships to worry about in the big data environment than in the small data environment. Not surprisingly it has been found that traditional econometric methods can be outperformed by automated machine learning (ML) methods in big data environments. title: Understanding Bilingual Dyslexia: Identifying Subtypes for Targeted Remediation
abs: Background & Significance. Reading is the foundation of learning, as it allows access to a wealth of knowledge. Unfortunately, reading is an especially challenging task for children with dyslexia, one of the most common forms of learning difficulty. In Singapore, it is estimated that about 4% to 10% of the population struggle with dyslexia. The consequences of dyslexia are wide-ranging, affecting one’s reading attainment, academic success, and socioemotional wellbeing. Beyond consequences for the dyslexic individual, dyslexia also incurs substantial costs to society. It is imperative to strive for early detection and targeted remediation. Objectives A key challenge to dyslexia management is that dyslexia is a multifaceted disorder that manifests itself differently across individuals and across languages. Our proposed project aims to address specific challenges that bilingual readers in a multilingual society typically face but neglected by the literature, namely, a lack of understanding of bilingual dyslexia, a lack of bilingual-specific norms to allow for accurate and early detection and a lack of targeted intervention programme that is grounded with the latest knowledge in cognitive science. Through a series of studies, we will achieve the following specific aims: Aim 1: To develop a comprehensive language and cognitive assessment tool for young readers in Singapore and establish the bilingual-specific norms; Aim 2: To identify the core deficits of bilingual dyslexia and explore it sub-classifications; and Aim 3: To formulate learning strategies for the different subtypes of dyslexia Approach The research objectives outlined above will be achieved through three studies. In Study 1, we will first conduct a large-scale study to establish norms in cognitive and language development among typically developing young English-Chinese bilinguals. Subsequently, in Study 2, we will administer the same battery of tests to English-Chinese bilinguals who are suffering from reading difficulties. Comparing their performance against the norms established in Study 1 will allow us to identify core processing deficits of each dyslexic reader. We will then conduct cluster analysis to identify subtypes of bilingual dyslexia. In Study 3, the final stage of the project, we will formulate learning support strategies that cater to the cognitive profiles of the subtypes identified via a smaller-scale proof-of-concept experiment. Impact Findings from the proposed research will have significant scientific, pedagogical, and clinical impact. We will provide valuable insights into dyslexia manifestation in bilinguals, which is currently poorly understood around the world, and further our understanding on the nature of dyslexic deficits in general. Our findings can also be used to inform dyslexia detection and intervention practices in Singapore and beyond.

title: Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) and Student Mobilities in China-Southeast Asia
abs: This proposed research aims to document the ways China is shaping tertiary education spaces and new circuits of mobility among youths in Southeast Asia (SEA). We examine the implications of the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) on student mobilities and academic linkages that are shaping young people’s aspirational pathways in moving across places and in expanding the knowledge spaces of the region. This is a timely project as it captures a significant moment in which global and regional education-migration processes are being visibly altered through China’s strategies to take the lead in economic globalisation and to compete for a central place in the world via the BRI. The BRI has also led to an important rise in a Chinese-led regionalisation of Asian tertiary education that seeks to strengthen the positioning of key national universities in East and SEA as well as to invigorate tertiary vocational education and training in the region. Given that BRI linkages are built in hopes of a longer future of co-prosperity based on the assumption of stable ties, this project raises the question of the degree of resilience of education and academic linkages in the face of unexpected turmoil created by larger events, such as health epidemics (e.g. COVID-19) and international relations (e.g. China-US trade war). Young people are often hailed as future drivers of the BRI with a critical role in advancing China’s aspirations in global development and cooperation. Their mobilities in and through BRI-linked projects are also an important feature of the initiative’s emphasis on connectivity and people-to-people bonds. With education and training becoming a recent and critical part of this trans-continental capacity building project, it is ever more important to consider how young people are involved in BRI-linked mobilities (in terms of educational and training opportunities, career prospects and future mobilities), and how such mobilities, in turn, inform their understandings of the region, the world, and their participation in BRI developments. Yet, the rapid growth of scholarship on the BRI continues to pay an overwhelming attention to physical infrastructural development, while little is known about the human mobilities that accompany – as well as youth perspectives towards – BRI’s globe-spanning ambitions. This proposed research fills this gap in the scholarship by investigating education as a site in and through which young people’s mobilities are being reconfigured and articulated vis-à-vis the BRI. The research employs a cross-disciplinary conceptual and methodological approach to study two education tracks in regional student mobility flows: (a) vocational training student mobilities; and (b) elite university student mobilities, that are also augmented by academic linkages between China and SEA. title: Provenance-Based Graph Analytics and Transfer Learning for Intrusion Detection
abs: This project will revolve around the research and development of cutting-edge computational methods and analytic techniques to intrusion detection in cyber security. Traditional methods typically work on system logs which are flat data (system calls, audit logs, etc.) of individual observations, and the detection approaches tend to use basic statistical techniques to identify the inter-relationships between system objects. However, for more sophisticated attacks, such as Advanced Persistent Threats, the threat actors infiltrate a system by incrementally infecting a number of system components which then interact and coordinate in a more stealthy and complex manner. In order to detect the potential existence of such threats, it is useful to explore a new approach to intrusion detection that is capable of analysing data with a richer representation to perform attribution and adapt to unseen attacks. In this project, we will base our exposition on provenance graphs. In contrast to flat data, provenance graphs are structured and linked data that capture the interactions and causal relationships between system-level entities, activities, and users. They model the information flow in the system and thus serve as a perfect data source for intrusion detection. While provenance-graph-based intrusion detection have been proposed recently and demonstrated to outperform traditional system-call-based approaches, the research on this topic is still in its infant stage. Existing methods are primitive, utilizing only a small set of graph properties, and none of them tap on the node/edge attributes in provenance graphs, which carry humongous amount of information about the intrusion activities. This research is the first attempt to explore the full use of attributed provenance graphs systematically and extensively to model root-cause analysis of system activities. We will research and develop (1) graph analytics methods to automatically discover attributed signature patterns of intrusions from historical provenance graphs, and (2) transfer learning techniques for adapting the signatures to unseen attacks. The proposed research will constitute a timely and novel contribution to the field. It aims to significantly advance the best practice currently exercised in the research and industrial applications of intrusion detection. Specifically, the objectives are to produce new intrusion detection methods with higher accuracy and lower false alarm rates, which allows easy root-cause analysis and can swiftly adapt to unseen scenarios as well. Our research will strive to fully utilize the valuable source of attributed provenance graphs to boost the detection performance. The proposed research also aims to fill in the gap when enfacing a completely new attack by adapting and reusing the knowledge of intrusion from the past analysis to its best potential. title: Improving Fairness and Accessibility of Crowd Work
abs: In this Human-Computer Interaction research, we will design a novel system that addresses the low wage of online crowd work. The work is critical for online gig-work to be viable source of income. The past research found that online crowd workers typically earn only US$2.0 an hour on a platform like Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT). This is unfortunate given its potential to offer new work opportunities for people who are forced to stay at home. For example, people with disabilities who find the office environment inaccessible and those who are temporarily unemployed and stay at home could generate meaningful income if crowd work is more lucrative. One of the factors that lowers the wages of crowd work is the presence of workers who submit low-quality work (also known as spammers). The requesters who post work on a crowdsourcing platform lower reward to workers because the output of work may be suboptimal if the workers that they recruit end up the spammers. The reward to worker is also reduced by requesters due to the cost incurred by additional quality control (e.g., hiring multiple workers to perform a same task). The system we build uses machine learning and information visualization to implement mechanisms to encourage workers to submit high-quality work and requesters to compensate workers fairly. The crux for implementing the system that embodies such mechanisms is development of (i) two system components, Requester Tool and Task Templates, and (ii) predictive models that use Bayesian machine learning. The predictive models learn worker profiles (e.g., their abilities to perform crowdsourcing tasks) and task profiles (e.g., task difficulty). We develop Requester Tool, a web-based user interface that allows crowdsourcing requesters to create variety of types of crowdsourcing tasks from templates (Task Templates). Similar to the existing tools like Qualtrics that enable people to create survey tasks, Requester Tool and Task Templates will allow requesters to easily create image segmentation tasks, language translation tasks, video scene description tasks and more, to be published on Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT). A Bayesian method will allow us to combine the prior knowledge about type of a task template used to create the task, as well as worker profiles and task characteristics to estimate expected quality of work and task completion time. The key scientific challenge in this Human-Computer Interaction research lies in the design and evaluation of our system that embodies the mechanisms to nudge workers and requesters to behave in a way that they benefit each other. We use the quality of work and task completion time estimated by the predictive models to design user interfaces that nudge workers to submit high-quality work. We will generate messages and visualizations for workers how likely their work gets accepted or rejected before they submit their work.
