title: IMPACTS OF ENVIRONMENTAL PRESSURES ON LIVELIHOOD TRANSFORMATIONS IN THE MEKONG DELTA
abs: This proposed project seeks to develop a novel conceptual framework, the Socio-ecological Livelihood Pathway Framework (SLPF), which is built upon “Ecosystem Services” (ES) and the “Sustainable Livelihood Framework” (SLF) (DFID, 2000; MA, 2005). The main aim of this framework is to quantitatively evaluate the impacts of environmental pressures on the livelihoods of farmers who are facing the perennial threats of climate change, as well as repercussions from recent surges in human activities. Geographically, the proposed project focuses on the Vietnam Mekong Delta (VMD), the third largest delta in the world and also one of Southeast Asia’s most important food baskets. The project has two objectives (i) to investigate how environmental pressures have triggered VMD’s farmers’ livelihood transformation, and (ii) to find out the sustainable pathways for the livelihood transformations of these farmers. To realize these objectives, the project team adopts methods from multiple disciplines: (i) geospatial analytical methods (GIS and Remote sensing) will be used to measure the biophysical impacts of different environmental pressures across the VMD landscape, (ii) a tri-step social survey campaign (expert in-depth interviews, focus group discussions, and questionnaire-based survey) is planned to investigate the social aspects of the farmers’ livelihoods and explore the livelihood transformation triggers. In addition to directly benefiting the community and local governments of the VMD, the proposed outcomes have two significant intellectual merits: (i) a data portal (hosted by NIE) is targeted to present the key research findings to the international research community and researchers in Singapore, and (ii) the publication of the SLPF manual - one of the main project outputs - in which key methodological implications in adapting the framework for similar studies will be included alongside case studies. As a broader impact, the creation of SLPF contributes to the knowledgebase of both ES and SLF. Specifically, through SLPF, the quantification of ES now contributes to new, yet solid decision making related to sustainable livelihoods. At the same time, SLF can be supported with quantitative measurements in addition to the conventional qualitative approaches. The project has direct relevance to Singapore for the city-state is Vietnam’s largest investor in the ASEAN region, and third largest worldwide. Also, rice imports from VMD take up approximately 28% of the Singapore rice market, and thus any potential disruptions in rice production could have implications for Singapore’s food security. Finally, as NIE will be the host institute for the project, the knowledge crafted from the proposed research will become more impactful as it will be rigorously integrated into teaching materials for NIE’s student teachers who ultimately will educate primary and secondary students in Singapore.
kw: Environmental pressure; Livelihood transform; Ecosystem services; Mekong Delta; SLPF; Sustainability

title: Algorithmic Advances For Program Fuzzing
abs: Software bugs, including exploitable security vulnerabilities, are being discovered at a faster rate in this decade compared to the last one. Part of this recent phenomenon is attributed to improvements to bug-finding tools. In fact, the area of program fuzzing has had a disproportionate influence on large-scale discovery of program bugs in the last five years. Program fuzzing is a collection of techniques which search for test inputs randomly, possibly guided by light-weight observations of the software executions resulting from running test inputs. Despite its evident success over classical deterministic techniques, however, fuzzing is still largely an empirical art. It is riddled with heuristics and intuitive strategies to search an intractably large input space. Researchers and practitioners are often surprised by how well a new strategy works well in real-world programs. It is therefore natural to ask: Which theoretical foundations can predict / explain the performance of program fuzzing and can they be utilized to design better program analysis techniques? We propose to initiate a systematic study of program fuzzing from an algorithmic viewpoint. Specifically, we propose to show direct connections between fuzzing and randomized algorithms, placing fuzzing on formal foundations. In particular, we explain how problems in fuzzing are specialized instances of randomized constraint satisfiability, invariant learning, conditional independence testing, and constrained sampling---each of which have rich theoretical background. Our proposal is to devise new fuzzing algorithms by drawing new insights from theory. These algorithms could be strictly better than state-of-the-art techniques, both for fuzzing and deterministic methods (e.g. symbolic execution). We hope this will generate faster and more scalable program fuzzers both for undirected program testing as well as for directed fuzzing towards specific parts of the program or analysis objectives. We expect these advances to have a direct practical impact. Fuzzing algorithms designed this way can have predictable performance on real-world software and open up analysis of challenging new domains. Our approach would also be helpful in designing “fair” benchmarks which are not susceptible to over-fitting due to experimental bias, and enable comparing generalization of different fuzzing strategies on unseen examples. We can systematically contrast and attribute credit for empirical successes to specific algorithmic choices and devise new optimizations. Our investigation may also advance the general study of randomized algorithms by proposing new models which are observed in the context of fuzzing.
kw: Randomized Algorithms; Security Vulnerabilities; Scalable Program Analysis

title: Vision-based 3D Hand Pose Estimation in the Wild
abs: We consider the problem of vision-based 3D hand pose estimation, which is at the core of many human-computer interactions and augmented/virtual reality applications. Hand pose estimation has been studied for over two decades in computer vision but remains one of the most challenging tasks. This project seeks to advance 3D hand pose estimation ``in the wild'', i.e. from camera footage of the human hand taken in-situ as it performs every-day tasks and interacts with objects. We aim to develop a method for synthesizing realistic hand sequences by imitating real human hand-object manipulations. We also propose explicitly modelling hand-object interactions to capture the relationship between hand articulation and object properties and intended human actions. Such a model is far richer than standard pose priors and or kinematic constraints in current systems and offers a chance to reason about the hand in cluttered scenes and under heavy occlusions. Project outcomes will give insights into synthesizing data for learning, domain adaptation problems, reinforcement learning, and combining generative and discriminative approaches. It will also enable many practical applications such as virtual and augmented reality applications, including those in human-robot interaction, teleoperation, and programming by demonstration.
kw: Hand pose estimation, hand-object interactions, model-based tracking, generative modelling, transfer learning, deep learning

title: Novel Semiconductors Based on Two-Dimensional sp2 Carbon Materials
abs: This project aims to develop “novel semiconductors based on 2D sp2 carbon materials”. Owing to low dielectric constant, semiconductors based on organic compounds and polymers must possess π backbones, which must assemble in a π face-on-π face stacking way to form long-range column stacks as pathways for electron and hole to transport. Traditionally, organic compounds and polymers are difficult to form long-range face-on-face π stacks. For example, traditional self-assembly and solution-based processing methods cannot ensure that each π unit stacks in a face-on-face manner. Moreover, the molecular packing in the resulting material is hardly predictable. Even in single crystals, π units tend to form herringbone-like alignment other than the ideal face-on-face π structure. Despite great progress in chemistry and materials science over the past decades, semiconducting materials that can predesign long-range face-on-face stackings remain a substantial challenge. Targeting on this extremely difficult issue, this project will develop a novel class of semiconductors based on 2D sp2 carbon materials. The reason for developing 2D sp2 carbon materials as novel semiconductors is that they constitute predesignable long-range and face-on-face π stacking structures. One distinct feature is that the 2D carbon materials can be tailor-made by designing building units. 2D sp2 carbon materials are distinct from traditional semiconductors in many aspects. (1) From structural predesignability point of view, 2D sp2 carbon materials are fully predesignable by using the geometry of building units. This is in a sharp contrast to traditional semiconductors in which the assembled structures cannot be predesigned. 2D sp2 carbon materials offer an approach to tailor-made semiconductors. (2) From structural ordering point of view, 2D sp2 carbon materials provide long-range order structure in which each unit can form face-on-face stacking across the material. This feature is inaccessible with traditional semiconductors. (3) From synthetic and manufacturing points of view, 2D sp2 carbon materials are synthesised via one-pot polymerisation without the need of any post synthesis process. In contrast, traditional semiconductors require complicated post synthesis process and thus are more energy demanding. (4) From structural dimensionality point of view, 2D sp2 carbon materials consist of 2D extended sheets and layer frameworks; both of them are ordered and well-defined. This is sharp contrast to traditional organic compound and polymers which are limited to small π domains or only 1D chains. (5) From the viewpoint of interplay, 2D sp2 carbon materials trigger interplays with photons, excitons, holes, electrons and spins both over 2D sheets and layer frameworks, which are inaccessible with traditional semiconductors (6) The difference of interplays enables the 2D sp2 carbon materials to develop unique properties, functions and applications which are inaccessible with traditional se

title: Quantifying Ion Desolvation & Structure Evolution in Carbon Micropores
abs: Ion behaviours in microporous structures are of fundamental importance for supercapacitor. Great research effort has been put to characterize ion migration and distribution in carbon micropore, leading to fruitful progress such as quantification of the uneven ion distribution under nanoconfinement and ion-exchange based diffusion mechanisms. However, little characterization attempt about ions structure information in micropores has been reported due to the limited capability of current characterization techniques. Ion structure information such as quantification of ion desolvation and desolvated geometry is missing. Furthermore, an open question exists that if ions could form ordered structures inside micropores. Lacking ion structure information hinders further exploration in microporous carbon supercapacitor. Thus, new characterizations and simulations are required to address these challenges. X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) is an excellent technique in characterizing structure information of solvated ions, such as ligand species and solvation geometry. It employs Synchrotron X-ray to excite core electron of an atom and measures the X-ray absorption coefficient that can be converted to electron configuration and coordination geometry. For most metallic elements, due to their appropriate excitation energy of core electrons, their XAS signals are easy to obtain with good quality, making them good candidatures for XAS characterization. However, XAS has rarely been applied to microporous supercapacitor to study ion behaviours in micropores, since most of the ions in conventional electrolytes are formed by light elements, such as carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen, and have complex chemical environments. The low electron excitation energy of these element requires ultrahigh vacuum XAS testing environment that is unfriendly to liquid electrolyte, while the complex chemical environments lead to little solvation information from XAS signals since the close coordination is occupied by unchanged covalent bond. Nevertheless, it is possible to capture the desolvation and ion structure evolution in microporous carbon supercapacitor when the ions have good XAS capability. As a result, in this proposal, we propose to investigate structure evolution of transitional metal ion electrolytes in microporous carbon supercapacitor. Both aqueous and organic electrolytes with various transition metal ions in supercapacitors will be characterized by XAS during charging and discharging processes to study their structure evolution. ionic mixture electrolytes and solvent mixture electrolytes will also be investigated, as well as ion structure evolution dependency on temperature and pore size. Our preliminary results of aqueous electrolytes have demonstrated partial desolvation of Mn2+ from octahedral structure to tetrahedral structure as well as the formation of Ni(OH)2-like Ni2+ cluster inside microporous carbon. title: REDOXIVE: Water activated adhesives and antiviral coatings
abs: Discovery of a water-activated, covalent crosslinking reaction heralds a new platform for non-toxic adhesives. The self-curing, redox-based adhesive (Redoxive) addresses the three biggest technological limitations of all bioadhesives; 1) surface-activated crosslinking that transitions from liquid glue into a biorubber, 2) tunable adhesive platform that spans anti-viral coatings to non-toxic tissue bonding, and 3) incorporates scalable production with sufficient shelf life for wide spread industrial application MRT1- Crosslinking Structure Activity Relationships will synthesize CateGlu into liquid formulations that transition into a biorubber upon contact with water (self-curing) or voltage initiation (electrocuring). Recent discoveries in redox paired acceptor/donor groups have yielded a water-free, semi-stable adhesive that begins to bond surfaces in the presence of water/oxygen or with an applied voltage. To optimize reaction kinetics and shelf stability, MRT1 seeks to develop 1) a library of redox adhesives through a click chemistry approach of catechol precursors grafted onto branched polymers, 2) Exploit donor/acceptor redox pairing to achieve rapid bonding upon contact with hydrated surfaces. 3) Optimize redox pairing to achieve liquid to solid gelation time in 5 min or less. Hypothesis: Liquid dendrimers with Schiff base/catechol redox pairs act as electron acceptor/donors that rapidly react upon water into quinone crosslinking functional groups. The redox pair is selected such that curing begins by contact with proton donors (present in water) or induced through an electrochemical voltage gradient. MRT2- Polymer Structure/Biocompatability Structure Activity Relationships will screen polymer backbones and nucleophilic surface groups towards creation of an adhesive platform with broad flexible and tunable material properties. Selection of polymer backbones will focus on yielding water-free, liquid formulations that span the scope of antiviral polyethyleneimine (PEI) coatings to bioresorbable polyesters. Nucleophilic polymer surface groups will be assessed for reaction rates with electrophilic quinones—the reactive crosslinker investigated in MRT1. Hypothesis: Liquid adhesive formulations synthesized with molecular mass dendrimers of 500 – 2,000 Da will crosslink into biorubbers after event initiation. Inherent dendrimer chemical profile combined with on-demand adhesion is exploited for unmet industrial and biomedical needs, such as cationic PEI for antiviral surfaces and Boltorn polyesters for degradable bioadhesives. MRT3- Utility and Risk Structure Activity Relationships will assess the mutagenicity, skin irritation, and viral surface toxicity for future applications in bioadhesives and stick-all antiviral coatings. Congracted GLP laboratories will analyze leachates and surface coatings to prepare a risk portfolio compared against known mutagens and skin sensitizers. title: The novel immunological role of p53 in tumor suppression by inducing immune checkpoint protein ICOSLG
abs: Immune cells continuously circulate throughout the body to detect foreign objects, including transformed cells. The immune system, therefore, works to suppress tumors. Immunotherapy enhancing this immune system has become an emerging strategy for the treatment of cancer. However, immunotherapy is currently useful for treating only a few types of cancers, and the success rate is not very high even in these types of cancer. This is largely due to our limited understanding of the communications between cancer cells and immune cells. Furthermore, a critical barrier exists in translating our knowledge of the immune system using mouse models to successful cancer therapies because there are many differences in the immune system between humans and mice. We recently found that ICOSLG (Inducible T Cell Costimulator Ligand), one of B7 family members, is induced by p53 in human cells but not in mouse cells. ICOSLG expresses at the cellular surface of various types of cells, including antigen-presenting cells, B cells, and non-hematopoietic cells such as tumor cells, and works as a costimulatory molecule to activate T cells. p53 is an important tumor suppressor that is mutated in about half of all cancers. p53 works as a transcription factor to induce cell cycle arrest, senescence, or apoptosis. Besides these canonical functions of p53, the critical role of non-canonical functions of p53 in tumor suppression has been recently appreciated. However, the immunological function of p53 remains understudied. We hypothesize that p53 induces ICOSLG in human cancer cells, B cells, or other immune cells, leading to enhanced activation of T cells that promote immune surveillance of tumors. To test this hypothesis, we will first examine if ICOSLG is a direct transcriptional target gene of p53 in Aim 1. In Aim 2, we will next determine whether the activation of the p53-ICOSLG pathway enhances the ability of tumor-specific T cells to recognize and lyse tumor cells by using 3D in vitro systems. In Aim 3, we will examine whether p53 activating drugs under clinical investigations together with or without clinical immune checkpoint inhibitors, such as PD-1 and PD-L1 inhibitors, can enhance the ability of T cells to kill cancer cells in vitro and in vivo. In Aim 4, we will examine whether the p53-ICOSLG pathway can boost the immune system against cancers in a humanized mouse model. The knowledge obtained from this proposed study will reveal novel future therapeutic strategies to strengthen the p53-ICOSLG signaling pathway to kill cancer cells, potentially leading to the increased success rates of immunotherapy for broader types of cancer patients.
kw: p53; tumor suppression, cancer; ICOSLG; immune checkpoint proteins; T cell

title: A 4D Variational Framework for Constructing 3D Self-Supporting Surfaces
abs: Self-supporting structures are one of the most ancient and elegant techniques in building construction. They can be found in many architectural heritages, due to the efficient use of material and advantageous structural properties. Self-supporting surfaces satisfy the 3D equilibrium equation, which has three balance constraints but there are only two degrees of freedom available on the surface. As an over-constrained problem, constructing SSS is technically challenging. The existing techniques for designing 3D self-supporting surfaces are largely based on thrust network analysis (TNA), which simplifies the 3D equilibrium problem via two types of approximation. First, it discretizes the continuous stress field through uniaxial singular stresses and assumes that the mesh edges carry stresses and the mesh vertices exert vertical loads. By converting the continuous surface into a thrust network, TNA transfers the over-constrained problem to a well-defined linear system. Second, it adopts a 3D-to-2D projection to factor the 3D problem into a 2D horizontal equilibrium and a 1D vertical equilibrium, which are solved separately. TNA is elegant, computationally efficient, and perfect for analyzing beam structures. However, when applying to continuous surfaces, TNA only computes an approximate solution to the equilibrium equation. Furthermore, since TNA forms the equations on the projected vertices, the input surface must be a height function, and it cannot handle the case where the projected boundaries are intersecting or self-intersecting. In this proposal, we present a completely new computational framework to overcome the above-mentioned limitations in the existing methods. We are inspired by two observations in everyday life: an upside down catenary curve (1-manifold embedded in R^2) is self-supporting and catenoid, the rotational sweeping surface of a catenary curve, is a minimal surface (2-manifold embedded in R^3). We discover the relation between 3D self-supporting surfaces (2-manifold embedded in R^3) and 4D minimal hypersurfaces of revolution (3-manifold embedded in R^4). We prove that the hypergeneratrix of a 4D minimal hypersurface of revolution is a 3D self-supporting surface, implying that constructing a 3D self-supporting surface is equivalent to a 4D volume minimization problem. We also show that the energy functional of 3D self-supporting surfaces is the gravitational potential energy, which in turn can be converted into a surface reconstruction problem with mean curvature constraint. Using our theoretical findings, we can easily verify that two historical structures, namely trulli in Italy and Anji Bridge in China, satisfy the equilibrium conditions, hence are self-supporting. Armed with our theoretical findings, we will pursue the following research directions: (1) Developing a variational method for constructing 3D self-supporting surfaces. title: Pre-Processing and Querying Big Trajectory Data with Reinforcement Learning
abs: Trajectory data, which captures the traces of moving objects, is ubiquitous. It has been used in various applications such as traffic analysis, location-based services, sports analysis, etc. Trajectory data has a sequential nature, i.e., each trajectory corresponds to a sequence of time-stamped positions (called points). Many problems of pre-processing and querying trajectory data involve some sequential decision-making process (e.g., trajectory simplification is essentially a process of sequentially scanning the points of a trajectory and deciding whether to drop each point being scanned). Existing algorithms for these problems include dynamic programming based (for exact solutions) or sequential scanning based (for approximate solutions). Nevertheless, the former is usually computationally expensive, and the latter may not always return high quality solutions due to its heuristic nature. Nowadays, reinforcement learning (RL) is becoming a popular tool for solving problems of sequential decision making such as those in control, gaming, and combinatorial optimization. Therefore, an immediate question is: Can RL be leveraged for pre-processing and querying trajectory data, and if so, to which extent and how? To tackle this question, this project aims to develop methods based on RL for various problems of pre-processing and querying trajectory data, including trajectory simplification, trajectory imputation, and sub-trajectory join. To the best of the PI’s knowledge, these methods will be the first attempt of leveraging RL for pre-processing and querying trajectory data. This project will then compare the RL based methods with existing non-learning based algorithms both theoretically and empirically and answer the aforementioned question comprehensively. With the success of this project, it will contribute significant new knowledge including a suite of RL-based algorithms for the problems of pre-processing and querying trajectory data. These methods will be immediately applicable to many real-life applications such as location-based services (e.g., taxi services), logistics (e.g., parcel delivery), infectious disease diffusion (e.g., suspected crowds identification for COVID-19), etc., hence impacting both industry and society significantly.
kw: Trajectory data; reinforcement learning; simplification; imputation; sub-trajectory querying

title: Interplay between Machine Learning and Precision Optical Measurement
abs: A smart nation requires smart manufacturing technology, while smart manufacturing technology relies on smart precision measurement. Fringe-based optical measurement (FOM) is an outstanding technique known for its full-field, non-contact and precise measurement of shape and deformation, and is our research focus. Fringe patterns are mainly formed by optical interference of two coherent beams, one reflected from the specimen being measured, and the other as a reference. These patterns can be understood as a two-dimensional tiny structured ruler net cast onto a specimen. By analysing the fringe patterns, efficient and precise measurement down to a few nanometres can be achieved. This technique is used in the current wafer testing for making IC chips used in every single smart phone in the world, and also needed towards Industry 4.0. With the manufactured pieces becoming smaller and more complicated, the appealing and widely accepted FOM techniques have to be evolved into smarter ones to satisfy today’s demanding environment. In the meantime, it is difficult to ignore that machine learning techniques, especially the deep neural networks (DNN), which have penetrated into various research and engineering areas with an amazing speed, and achieved surprising success. It seems natural to expect that DNN will impact FOM to drastically expand the measurement capability, just as DNN collaborates and succeeds in other areas. This is indeed one of the expected outcomes of this proposal: DNN-enhanced Smarter FOM techniques. However, it is worth noting that, FOM is uniquely distinguished from other areas – while others may be represented as a black box, FOM is hoped to be a transparent box as we need to clearly understand the accuracy and precision of our measurement without any ambiguities. Such a unique characteristic leads to the unique researcher question: how does DNN react to FOM? Finding the answers will deepen our understanding on both DNN and FOM with scientific significance, and help us to advance FOM techniques with practical importance. Based on the above motivation, the following research topics are to be explored, which are classified into three groups according to the anticipated interplay between DNN and FOM. More detailed descriptions, proposed solutions and preliminary results are given in the detailed research proposal. DNN may not help FOM • On measurement principle: the basic technique for fringe analysis is using phase-shifting to extract a phase field which can then be mapped to the measured physical quantity. Although comparisons have been carried out for different phase-shifting algorithms, there is a lack of a thorough evaluation regarding different error sources, leading to the lack of a simple guideline for algorithm selection. There is an urgent demand to clarify and unify algorithms to boost the measurement performance. title: Neurophysiological study of the neural circuits underlying working memory ageing
abs: Working memory (WM) allows us to memorize necessary information for a short time, even in the absence of sensory input, and constitutes the fundamental basis of our cognitive ability. However, our WM ability gradually deteriorates with advancing age, which is the earliest and most common symptom of cognitive ageing. Considerable evidence suggests that the anterior part of the frontal lobe of the brain, the prefrontal cortex (PFC), is a critical hub region that regulates WM maintenance. Neuroimaging and electrophysiological studies show that the PFC displays sustained activity that selectively encodes information maintained in WM and that the PFC interacts with regions widely distributed throughout the entire brain. In the aged brain, reduced synaptic connections and functional connectivity are often diminished in several brain regions, which is hypothesized to underlie age-associated declines in WM. However, it remains poorly understood how the PFC communicates with and controls the relevant brain regions via its projection pathways and how ageing affects the neurophysiological mechanisms involved in PFC-associated pathways. This proposal will employ a mouse model to investigate structural and functional abnormalities in brain-wide circuits that underlie WM decline in ageing and will provide an interventional solution to rescue WM ability. In Aim 1, I will perform a systematic search for the neural circuits that are relevant to WM and determine how their structures deteriorate in the aged brain. Taking advantage of a photoconvertible molecule, I will mark functionally-specified PFC neurons related to WM. Tracing the downstream regions where these neurons send their axon projections, brain-wide WM circuits will be visualized comprehensively. Comparison across different age groups will localize age-associated deterioration of circuit structure. In Aim 2, I will characterize the functional aspects of the identified WM circuits that deteriorate in ageing. Pathway-specific optogenetic inhibition will test the necessity of each neural pathway. Electrophysiological recording of neuronal activity in the PFC and each downstream region will assess how ageing compromises the inter-area neural oscillations that are a landmark of functional interactions. Further, electrical stimulation will be delivered to artificially entrain these oscillations and to determine whether such interventions can rescue WM decline in ageing. The results of this project will advance our understanding of the circuit mechanisms underlying age-associated WM decline and will offer a potential means of restoring WM in older adults.
kw: Frequency-dependent current stimulation; Neural oscillation; Cognitive ageing; Projection pathway; Prefrontal cortex; Working memory

title: Molecular Optical Imaging and Early Diagnosis of Acute Kidney Injury
abs: Acute kidney injury (AKI) with high morbidity and mortality is associated with many other diseases including cancer, diabetes and infectious diseases. Unfortunately, Singapore ranks 4th in the world for incidence of kidney failure with an AKI mortality up to 40%. As ~40% of the AKI patients develop into severe conditions that require life-time dialysis, AKI places an increasing economic burden to Singapore healthcare system. However, it is worldwide poorly diagnosed in hospitals. Early detection of AKI enables timely renoprotective intervention to prevent AKI from progression into severe complications including chronic kidney disease, kidney replacement and death, which also facilitate kidney recovery. However, clinical imaging methods can only image anatomical/physiological changes in kidneys and often fail to sense the early-stage change in molecular level is caused by the onset of AKI. Moreover, clinical diagnostic methods are unable to detect AKI early due to their reliance on insensitive biomarkers of late-stage renal dysfunction. This proposal aims to develop a library of highly renal-clearable molecular sensors, termed as molecular renal probes (MRPs), for real-time longitudinal imaging and multiplex optical urinalysis of AKI. MRPs are designed to exclusively undergo renal clearance, specifically turn on their optical signals towards the potential AKI biomarkers of interest, and noninvasively report AKI. Such a sensing strategy enables MRPs to detect the subtle molecular changes in kidneys at the incipient stage of AKI, which can precede its clinical manifestation: decreased glomerular filtration. With their simple optical detection modality, MRPs can be quickly translated as multiplex optical urinalysis assays to accurately and informatively detect AKI earlier than other methods currently used in clinics. Such molecular probes will be the first kind of imaging agents that permits real-time in vivo detection and screening of AKI biomarkers, providing a dynamic and intact way to precisely evaluate the onset and progression of key pathological events in the course of AKI. Successful development of MRPs will help us better understand the etiology of AKI, identify the most reliable AKI biomarkers, and eventually lead to affordable and high-throughput in vitro diagnostic assays for both in-hospital and at-home monitoring of kidney function.
kw: molecular imaging; optical probes; sensors; acute kidney injury

title: Improving work productivity for patients with rheumatic diseases: An inception cohort study
abs: Rheumatic diseases (RDs) affect approximately one third of the population in Singapore and worldwide. RDs affect individuals in their economically productive working years, resulting in work productivity loss, and account for the most years lived with disability (YLDs) in Singapore. RDs, after cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) and cancers, are the third largest contributor to total disease burden in Singapore. This highlights the importance of the following unmet needs: 1) the impact of RDs on work productivity loss has not been well characterized in Singapore and other Southeast Asian countries; 2) variations in study design, methodology, population studied, disease presentation and contextual factors across published studies mean that findings from existing studies cannot be readily applied to Singapore and other Southeast Asian countries. Our long-term goal is to reduce work productivity loss, societal costs and improve health outcomes of RDs. To this end, we aim to 1) compare work productivity loss, 2) identify modifiable risk factors for work productivity loss, and 3) estimate societal costs among individuals with various RDs and those with no RDs during the first year after diagnosis. We plan to achieve these aims by expanding a recently established inception cohort. This is in line with the RIE 2025 goals of productive longevity and good healthcare outcomes at sustainable costs. Findings from this study will 1) provide fundamental information about the impact of the largest contributor to YLDs in Singapore, namely RDs; 2) identify modifiable risk factors for work productivity loss; and 3) provide a basis for future studies to a) develop interventions to prevent or mitigate work productivity loss, which could help individuals with RDs continue working and/or return to work, thus reducing societal costs; b) evaluate cost effectiveness of such interventions; and c) provide insights into optimization of healthcare resource allocation among individuals with chronic diseases.
kw: rheumatic disease, work productivity, burden of disease, years lived with disability, disability-adjusted life years

title: Evaluation of a Hospital-at-Home Care Model: Deployment of Clinical Manpower to Deliver Acute Hospital-Level Care to the Home
abs: Hospital-at-home programmes provide home-based care to selected acutely ill patients in their own home. They are well-developed internationally as a sustainable way to substitute inpatient care safely and effectively. Shown to improve manpower efficiency, this may be a possible solution to anticipated clinical manpower shortages. The present study seeks to evaluate a recently initiated hospital-at-home programme in NUHS. The aim of the study is to investigate the cost, clinical effectiveness, patient experience and acceptability of deploying hospital manpower to deliver acute hospital-level care to the patient’s home. We hypothesise that hospitalisation at home may reduce the cost of care with comparable clinical outcomes (readmissions, mortality and hospital-acquired complications) and positive patient and staff experiences. The study will first include a quasi-experimental study with a prospective control cohort in order to compare the cost and clinical outcomes of delivering care in the patient’s home compared to traditional inpatient care. We will recruit 147 patients from National University Hospital at Alexandra hospital that are enrolled into the hospital-at-home programme and 147 similar patients who would otherwise be eligible for the programme but are cared for in hospital instead, with a follow up of 30-days post discharge. The primary outcome is mean cost per day of hospitalisation. Second, we will adopt a qualitative approach consisting of interviews and ethnographic studies to understand the experiences of patients, caregivers and staff involved in the programme. Third, we will survey patients who qualified for the programme but opted for inpatient care instead to understand barriers to scaling. Finally, mathematical models will be applied to these results to plan how such a programme can be scaled and impact of a large scale service on our health system. The findings of this study will influence the development and scaling of hospital-at-home programmes nationally.
kw: hospital-at-home; manpower models; manpower sustainability; economic evaluation

title: Evaluating Dynamic Myocardial Blood Flow Quantitation As a Cost Effective Care Model for Diabetic Patients with Coronary Artery Disease: A Randomized Controlled Trial
abs: Background: Diabetes mellitus poses unique problems to detection and management of coronary atherosclerosis. Among the diabetics, certain spectrums of coronary atherosclerosis may be missed on conventional myocardial perfusion imaging, such as early coronary microvascular dysfunction. On the other spectrum, advanced coronary atherosclerosis may result in balanced ischemia, recording falsely negative results on conventional myocardial perfusion imaging. These uncertainties either lead to more downstream testing or under-detection resulting in higher risks of adverse outcomes. Compared to conventional myocardial perfusion imaging (MPI), dynamic myocardial blood flow (MBF) quantitation is a new validated technique that provides additional quantitation across the entire spectrum of coronary atherosclerosis. Hypothesis: We hypothesize that dynamic myocardial blood flow quantitation would be a cost and clinically effective method for management of diabetic patients with coronary artery disease. Methodology and Approach: This will be a prospective randomized clinical trial comprising of n=300 diabetic patients, randomized to either dynamic MBF (n=150) or conventional MPI (n=150) strategy. Healthcare resources utilization of each patient will be tracked for one year because within one year, healthcare testing may be attributable to the index clinical indication for MPI. Patients will be followed up for 12 months for short term outcomes and 36 months for long term outcomes. Short term outcomes: The primary end-point is diagnostic failure, defined as unnecessary coronary angiography (absence of ≥50% stenosis in ≥1 coronary arteries) or any additional coronary testing (example, computed tomography of coronary arteries) within 90 days of the test. Long term outcomes: Major adverse cardiovascular events to be measured include cardiac mortality, acute myocardial infarction, unstable angina, any revascularization, up till 36 months. Health service outcomes achieved by this proposal: Implementing dynamic MBF into our existing clinical service will result in cost savings and clinical effectiveness among diabetics across the coronary artery disease spectrum.
kw: diabetes; cardiovascular disease; clinical services; health outcomes

title: Population’s Preferences for Colorectal Cancer Screening Tests in Singapore
abs: Colorectal cancer screening has been shown to be cost-effective in many countries. In Singapore, a previous study has shown the high level of awareness of colorectal cancer and the benefits of colorectal cancer screening among the local population; however, the screening rate remains suboptimal. This proposed study seeks to understand the barriers preventing the local population from taking colorectal cancer screening by studying the population’s preferences for colorectal screening tests. Each test will be characterized by a bundle of attributes such as preparation procedure required, process invasiveness, preparation time, amount of pain, and accuracy. Each attribute has several levels. The study consists of two stages. In stage 1, qualitative interviews will be conducted to understand the tests’ attributes that people consider as important and the levels that are relevant. Then, we will seek opinions from doctors, nurses, and experts in the gastroenterology department from hospitals. The tests’ attributes and the levels will be refined to guarantee that these are relevant in the clinical settings. In stage 2, the selected tests’ attributes and levels will be used to construct a Discrete Choice Experiment questionnaire and rolled out. Participants’ socioeconomic status and risk factors for developing colorectal cancer will also be collected. Participants’ preferences for the tests’ attributes will be estimated. Subgroup analysis will be conducted to understand the heterogeneous preferences. Given a hypothetical world with certain tests being available, the probabilities of people choosing each test can be derived, which can be used to approximate the population’s screening rate. Different interventions can also be incorporated to examine the policies’ impacts on the population’s screening rate. Optimal policies can be derived for different objectives.
kw: Colorectal cancer; screening uptake; population's preference; discrete choice experiment

title: Managing Cavities in Children and Institutionalized Elderly: Cost-effectiveness and Acceptance of Silver Diamine Fluoride Treatment.
abs: Background: Almost 50% of Singaporean children suffer from cavities, with close to 90% of the cavities remaining untreated. Singaporean elderly also has significant disease, with those living in care-facilities averaging 4 affected root surfaces each. Despite available subsidized/free treatment, utilization remains low in these populations. A possible barrier is the need for caregivers to take time off work or use specialized transportation to bring them to the dentist. Silver diamine fluoride (SDF) is an alternative to traditional restorations, showing 65% effectiveness when treating existing cavities and increasing to 90% for root cavities. It can be provided in community settings such as in childcare and care-facilities without specialized dental equipment. However, there are few studies on SDF cost-effectiveness and the differences in healthcare systems necessitate an evaluation in the local context. Furthermore, previous studies did not account for the acceptability of SDF treatment, which leaves a black discolouration, potentially limiting adoption. Aims: This study will examine the 1) cost-effectiveness of SDF in children and institutionalized elderly and 2) examine the acceptance of SDF treatment among institutionalized elderly. Methods: For aim 1), existing literature on SDF effectiveness, caries prevalence and local clinical data on treatment patterns will be elicited via retrospective chart reviews (2019-2020) of the 2 national oral health centers. The data will be used to construct cost-effectiveness models. Three treatment strategies will be modelled: community-based SDF, community-based conventional fluoride, and traditional restorative treatment. A decision tree model for children (<6 years) and a Markov cohort model for institutionalized elderly (≥65 years) will be used. A cost-effectiveness acceptability curve will be plotted to present the value of the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio across different willingness-to-pay thresholds. For aim 2), an educational video followed by a survey on SDF will be used to examine the acceptance of SDF treatment in 376 geriatric patients.
kw: Dental Care for Aged; Dental care for Children; Costs and Cost Analysis; Preventive Dentistry; Fluorides, Topical

title: Preventing Diabetes via Volunteers Engaging Residents using Technology (P-Divert) : A sequential mixed-method study
abs: This project aims to understand the intention to prevent diabetes among Singaporeans with prediabetes and to develop and examine the effectiveness of a volunteer-led, community-based diabetes prevention program, named Preventing Diabetes via Volunteers Engaging Residents using Technology (P-Divert), in exploring intention to prevent diabetes, diabetes prevention knowledge, health locus of control, self-efficacy, health-lifestyle behaviors, and health-related outcomes, i.e. fasting plasma glucose (FPG), oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT), HbA1c, blood pressure, waist circumference, body mass index (BMI) among Singaporeans with prediabetes. A sequential mixed-method approach, comprising of phase one exploratory descriptive qualitative study to explore the intention to prevent diabetes and phase two on a quasi-experimental two-arm study with process evaluation, is proposed. The P-Divert program offers an intensive diabetes prevention training for selected volunteer trainers in communities, on the basis of findings in phase one, structured with an intensive intervention phase and a maintenance intervention phase. The 12-week intensive intervention phase includes promoting autonomous motivation, updating knowledge (healthy eating, physical exercise and adherence skills), developing behavior change, and ways to deliver the intervention to participants through weekly remote coaching and virtual volunteer-led group-based sessions. The 12-week maintenance intervention phase involves the use of an AI-engineered Chabot to maintain a frequent contact with participants. The community volunteers will be trained to follow up with participants regularly to assist them with problem-solving regarding adherence. This could empower Singaporeans with more diabetes prevention knowledge and improve health literacy through volunteer support and self-care education in a more convenient way, as well as reduce health complications, health service utilization and economic burden in the future. If this P-Divert program is proven to be effective, it can provide evidence for healthcare professionals and the government to consider this program as an alternative health care delivery option in Singapore to complement existing Singapore diabetes prevention services.
kw: Diabetes Prevention; Volunteer-led; Community-based; mHealth; Artificial Intelligence; lifestyle behavior

title: Understanding the longitudinal psycho-social impact of colorectal cancer on young patients and their spouses
abs: Specific Aims & Hypotheses Aims 1. To examine the psycho-socio-economic impact of CRC in young-onset patients and their spouses over their treatment course, using a longitudinal mixed-methods design. Hypotheses 1. Young-onset patients’ quality-of-life (QOL) across the treatment course vary significantly between clinical characteristic groups, and will be moderated or mediated by mental health impact, spousal coping style, and sociodemographic characteristics. 2. The aspects of psycho-social impact faced by spouses are likely different than that faced by the patients Methods & Approach This study is a collaboration across all the 3 healthcare clusters in Singapore. The longitudinal mixed-methods study design will recruit 138 young-onset CRC patient-spouse pairs from the various outpatient colorectal clinics. Patient-spouse pairs will be recruited at point of diagnosis and will be followed up for 12 months over 7 timepoints of administration of the quantitative study measures from pre-operative to 12 months post-diagnosis. Additionally, patients will be interviewed at 2 timepoints. Qualitative data will be analysed using a hybrid inductive-deductive approach. Longitudinal data analysis methods will be used to examine patient and spousal anxiety, depression, dyadic coping, and other aspects of QOL. Associations within and between dyads can be analysed with structural equation modelling. Feasibility of the Study There may be a low rate of recruitment due to the lower proportion of young-onset CRC patients (10 – 15% of the national CRC cohort). Recruitment will be performed in each study site to increase the chances of successfully consenting an eligible patient-spouse pair. Importance to Science or Medicine Our study will examine if the psycho-socio-economic impact faced by young CRC patients and their spouses are considerable and worse amongst spouses than patients. Through identification of the time points where the impact is most significant, we would be able to determine where tailored measures such as psychological support would be beneficial.
kw: colorectal cancer; psychosocial impact; financial toxicity; spousal influence; longitudinal; mixed methods

title: Understanding the knowledge, perceptions, barriers and time-cost of patients towards teleconsultation in primary and tertiary healthcare setting in Singapore
abs: Aims 1. To determine knowledge, barriers and perceptions towards telemedicine amongst patients with chronic medical conditions in primary healthcare setting and low risk colorectal cancer (CRC) patients in the tertiary setting. 2. To map out the aforementioned patients’ journeys in primary and tertiary healthcare between those who adopted teleconsultation versus those who opted for face-to-face consultation using the Time Driven Activity Based Costing (TDABC) methodology. Hypotheses 1. Patients in the primary and tertiary care setting experience similar barriers towards adoption of telemedicine. 2. Patients’ acceptability of telemedicine alternatives in primary and tertiary outpatient care is significantly associated with sociodemographic characteristics (e.g. age, education, socioeconomic status, employment). 3. Telemedicine is feasible even in complex tertiary conditions such as CRC management. 4. Telemedicine is associated with considerable time and cost savings with no detrimental impact on clinical outcomes. Methods & Approach The study will be conducted across tertiary and primary healthcare institutions in NUHS, including NUH, NTFGH, NCIS, Pioneer and Queenstown polyclinics. Mixed methods interviews will be conducted with newly diagnosed chronic patients in the primary care setting and low risk CRC patients on surveillance to validate our technology acceptance questionnaire and fulfil Aim 1 (Sub-studies 1a and 2a). TDABC methodology will be used to chart the telemedicine versus standard face-to-face treatment pathways for newly diagnosed chronic patients in the primary care setting and low risk CRC patients on surveillance, fulfilling Aim 2 (Sub-studies 1b and 2b). Quality of life data for patients in both groups will be collected in order to facilitate cost-effectiveness analyses. Importance to Science or Medicine By identifying key processes through TDABC and identification of facilitators, barriers and cost-effectiveness of adopting telemedicine, this could become a standard of care and significantly reduce overall healthcare cost not just for the patient but for the nation as well.
kw: health services research; primary care; colorectal cancer surveillance; telemedicine; time-driven activity-based costing; cost-effectiveness

title: Development and evaluation of Home-based Care Competency Scale among Singapore nurses: A two-phase study
abs: Background: The Ministry of Health Singapore has implemented several new community care infrastructures to meet the healthcare needs of aging Singaporean. The demands on home-based care are becoming more complex that require an increased range and level of professional nursing competence. A gap seems to exist between the competence expected of home-based nurses and the workforce employed to provide the care. To better understand the educational needs of home-based nurses, there is a need to develop a scale to measure and evaluate their perceived level of competence. Aim: To develop and determine the psychometric properties of a competency-based scale, and to evaluate nurses’ perceived level of competence in home-based care. Method: A two-phase study will be conducted. Phase 1 will involve the development and psychometric analysis of the scale through identification of items from Community Nursing Competency Framework, literature review and an exploratory study, experts’ review using Delphi’s method, and validity and reliability testing. Phase 2 will involve a cross-sectional survey to examine 400 registered nurses’ perceived level of competence in home-based care using the newly developed scale. Implication: The newly developed and validated scale that measures nurses’ home-based care competency can be used to identify nurses’ educational needs for home-based care and inform future development and evaluation of training programmes. Additionally, the scale can be used to evaluate future home-based care related innovation or workforce planning. Feasibility: A multifaceted recruitment approach will be employed to maximise recruitment. The study collaborators in this study will disseminate recruitment materials and facilitate the recruitment process of nurses in the healthcare institutions. While the investigators will disseminate the recruitment information through the department alumni list and online platforms.
kw: Home-based care; Nursing competence; Scale development; Education needs

title: Studying neurorecovery of retinal ganglion cells in ageing after glaucomatous injury
abs: Glaucoma, the leading cause for irreversible blindness worldwide, is characterized by progressive loss of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) leading to optic nerve damage. Next to advancing age, the major risk factor for glaucoma is elevated intraocular pressure (IOP). Lowering IOP is the only proven therapeutic means for preventing vision loss in glaucoma. Unfortunately, sufficient IOP lowering is not always possible and some patients continue to lose vision despite good IOP lowering. Additional therapeutic options providing direct protection to RGCs are thus needed to prevent vision loss from glaucoma. Challenging the dogma that RGCs inevitably die following IOP injury, we published experimental evidence that RGCs enter a non-functional state after IOP injury but retain the ability to recover. The capacity for neurorecovery is tightly linked to ageing, with young animals showing rapid and full recovery whereas older animals recover more slowly and incompletely. We further published evidence that the age effect can be reversed by exercise through BDNF-dependent pathways. The exact mechanisms by which BDNF signaling improves neurorecovery are not known. BDNF is a key modulator of autophagy, a process that recycles damaged organelles in response to injury. The PI recently published evidence that RGC vulnerability to direct axonal damage is substantially increased in aged autophagy-deficient mice. We therefore hypothesize that defective autophagy in older animals delays neurorecovery, and exercise reverses this and promotes neurorecovery to similar levels observed in young animals. This proposal will assess the effect of age and IOP injury on autophagy and then determine whether exercise restores autophagy to promote neurorecovery in older animals. We will additionally conduct a proteomic analysis to identify cellular pathways impacted by exercise. These data will uncover key molecular pathways promoting neurorecovery with the long-term aim of developing new therapeutic targets for protecting RGCs in glaucoma to reduce visual loss and blindness.
kw: Glaucoma; Neurorecovery; Autophagy; Neuroprotection; Aging

title: A Randomised Clinical Trial in the use of Physiological Intra-Cytoplasmic Spermatozoa injection (PICSI) in couples with a previous poor fertilisation cycle in in-vitro fertilisation.
abs: Intra-cytoplasmic Spermatozoa Injection (ICSI) was introduced as an add-on to in-vitro fertilisation (IVF) for couples with male infertility issue. Physiological Intra-cytoplasmic Spermatozoa Injection (PICSI) is a technique used to select sperm to be used in ICSI, which has been reported to result in a better clinical pregnancy rate (CPR) than ICSI in few clinical studies. However, the findings are not consistent and in particular, it is unknown if the efficacy of PICSI versus ICSI can be different in couples with a history of poor fertilisation. This has led to challenges in clinical decision-making and practice for in-service application of ICSI and PICSI. Based on our preliminary data showing higher CPR (65% vs 37%, p<0.001) and lower miscarriage rates (12.8% vs 33.1%, p<0.0001) in couples who underwent PICSI after the first cycle of ICSI, we propose a parallel, single-blind, two-arm randomised controlled trial (RCT) in the KK Women’s and Children’s Hospital IVF (KKIVF) Centre, comparing outcomes between PICSI and ICSI among couples with history of poor fertilisation, defined as less than 50% fertilisation in the first cycle with ICSI. Eligible couples will be randomised to undergo either PICSI or ICSI in a 1:1 treatment ratio. Other standard assisted reproductive treatments are similar between the two groups. Primary outcomes are CPR and miscarriage rates. The secondary outcomes are fertilisation, ongoing pregnancy and live birth rates. To demonstrate a difference of 19% CPR and a difference of 46% miscarriage rates between PICSI and ICSI, at 80% statistical power and 5% α, we need to include 234 couples (117 in each group). We hypothesise that PICSI will improve CPR and reduce miscarriage rates as compared with ICSI, in couples with a history of poor fertilisation.
kw: PICSI, fertilisation, IVF

title: Deep learning pathway for the management of spine metastases
abs: Spinal metastases are common and seen in up to 40% of cancer patients. Up to 20% of these patients develop complications including spinal instability and cord compression which can cause permanent neurological dysfunction if treatment is delayed. Decision-making in spinal metastasis management is challenging and often requires several imaging modalities (MRI and CT) followed by referral to multiple specialists with delays in treatment. Complicated spinal metastases may require surgical decompression, stabilisation, or stereotactic radiosurgery whereas uncomplicated disease can be managed with analgesia and systemic therapy alone. Herein for the first time, we intend to develop a novel deep learning pipeline for automated assessment of spinal metastases and complications on CT and MRI. This will aid earlier diagnosis of cord compression or instability requiring surgery, reduce unnecessary imaging, and identify suitable candidates for stereotactic radiosurgery. The deep learning pipeline will also incorporate clinical data including patient demographics, cancer-related information, comorbidities, local control, and survival to optimize treatment recommendations. To achieve this, we will work on the following aims: Aim 1. To train a deep learning model, using MRI (gold standard), for the detection of spinal metastases and associated complications including metastatic spinal cord compression and spinal instability. Aim 2. Develop a deep learning model for the earlier detection of spine metastases and complications on CT using transfer learning from the MRI deep learning model. Currently, the majority of patients with spinal metastases on CT undergo MRI. A deep learning model on CT in combination with clinical data could prevent unnecessary MRI studies, which will free up capacity for other clinical demands and reduce health care costs. Aim 3. Integrate the deep learning models to form a pipeline encompassing MRI, CT, and clinical data (e.g. age, tumour type) to recommend which patients will benefit from more aggressive treatment (surgery or stereotactic radiosurgery).
kw: Spine metastases; MRI; CT; Deep learning; Spine surgery; Stereotactic radiosurgery

title: Impact of Cancer on Labour Market Outcomes and Workplace Productivity of Survivors and their Informal Caregivers
abs: Cancer imposes a substantial economic burden on society in the form of healthcare spending and productivity losses from morbidity and premature deaths. The share of burden attributable to morbidity can be significant when costs of informal caregiving is considered. Furthermore, this share is expected to grow as survival improves but survivors continue to incur indirect costs. Hence, it is increasingly important to understand cancer’s impact on labour market outcomes of both patients and caregivers when considering how best to design policies to minimize the economic disruption resulting from a cancer diagnosis. This study aims to conduct a cross-sectional survey to compare the labour market outcomes and workplace productivity of cancer survivors and their primary caregivers against similar non-cancer individuals. More specifically we will test the hypotheses that cancer survivors and their caregivers have poorer labour market outcomes (e.g. employment, earnings, workplace productivity, fewer promotions, less job mobility) than those who have no history of cancer and are not caregivers. Furthermore, we will test whether these negative effects are greater for patients who are older, female, less educated, first diagnosed at a later stage, or received more intensive cancer treatment. Our findings will contribute towards informing policies and interventions that help patients and caregivers return to work when ready.
kw: Cancer; Survivor; Breast; Colorectal; Caregiver; Employment

title: Effects of bariatric weight loss on biological aging by DNA methylation and shear wave elastographic evidence of kidney injury in obesity (ELASTO study)
abs: Bariatric surgery represents a unique human model of accelerated metabolic optimization. Preclinical models demonstrated improvements in inflammatory and fibrotic correlates of kidney injury after weight loss, although mechanisms with humans are poorly elucidated without serial invasive kidney biopsies. We detected substantive improvements in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) in obese patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), following bariatric surgery (published work). While this suggests attenuated kidney injury with reduced adiposity, creatinine-based eGFR is confounded by lean muscle loss. Our research in shear wave elastography bridges these gaps by non-invasively quantifying kidney parenchymal stiffness objectively and non-invasively. Additionally, DNA methylation may provide insights on the epigenetic alterations triggered by dysfunctional adiposity and CKD, and serve as a correlate for biological aging in this population. We will test the hypothesis that reversing metabolic syndrome with bariatric surgery is accompanied by attenuated kidney parenchymal stiffness, reduced systemic inflammation and improved biological ageing. We will recruit 50 CKD patients with obesity to undergo bariatric surgery and routine biobanking. Shear wave elastography and body composition analysis by bioimpedance will be performed at baseline and 12 months. Serial sampling of inflammatory proteins secreted by senescent cells in adipose tissues; IL-1β, IL-8, TNF-α, leptin, adiponectin, and salivary DNA methylation will be examined concurrently. Severity in baseline kidney parenchymal stiffness will be correlated with corresponding biomarker changes at baseline, and in their respective changes 1 year post-bariatric surgery. Current guidelines do not recognise CKD as an indication for bariatric surgery. This study clarifies mechanistic associations between excess adiposity, inflammation, biological age and CKD, and advocates for intensive weight loss to be adopted as a means of attenuating CKD progression. Our proposed investigations translate to more effective patient selection and risk stratification in metabolic disease beyond eGFR and albuminuria, cardiovascular benefit and promote healthy longevity in the process.
kw: Obesity; elastography; biological ageing; kidney disease

title: Pharmacogenomics of Bleomycin-induced Lung Injury in South East Asian Hodgkin Lymphoma Patients
abs: Background/Rationale Hodgkin lymphoma (HL) accounts for 15% of all cancer diagnosis in young adults. The standard of care chemotherapy for newly diagnosed classical HL in most countries is ABVD (Adriamycin, Bleomycin, Vinblastine, Dacarbazine), which has resulted in overall cure rates of 70-90%. However, a major complication is Bleomycin induced pulmonary toxicity (BIPT) /Lung Injury which occurs in 0.4-28% and is fatal in 4-5% of treated patients. Currently, there are no effective treatments for BIPT, therefore predicting and preventing BIPT is imperative to improving treatment outcomes, quality of life and the overall survival of patients. Also, understanding the pathophysiology of BIPT could lead to the development of novel and effective treatment strategies. Key Aims/Objectives The current project will perform the first pharmacogenomics studies of BIPT in South-East Asian patients, to uncover biomarkers for the prediction, prevention and treatment of BIPT and for personalizing bleomycin treatments. Research Design and Methods We have recruited 133 bleomycin HL treated patients from NCIS. In our pilot studies on 71 patients, we independently replicated the association of HFE rs1799945 (H63D) via a candidate gene study and uncovered 4 novel loci in a preliminary GWAS investigation. Collectively, these preliminary data establish our ability to recruit and phenotypically characterize patients exposed to Bleomycin-based Chemotherapy and points to a strong genetic predisposition to BIPT. Therefore, the current proposal will expand the recruitment to 300 bleomycin HL treated patients to allow a detailed pharmacogenomics assessment to uncover the full spectrum of the genetic susceptibility to pulmonary complications from Bleomycin-based cancer treatments. Clinical Significance There is a need for pre-emptive pharmacogenomics screening for precision medicine. There are currently no validated clinical-grade pharmacogenomics screening tests for pulmonary complications of Bleomycin-based cancer treatments. Genomic biomarker enabling risk assessment and stratification of patients will allow tailoring of therapeutic decisions to an individual’s risk profile.
kw: Hodgkin Lymphoma; Pharmacogenomics; Bleomycin; South East Asian Patients; Pulmonary Toxicity/Lung Injury; Genomic Biomarker

title: Prospective multi-centre collaborative study of the phenotypic and mutational spectrum of ABCA4 retinopathy in the Asian Population
abs: Specific Aims To study the clinical and genetic profile of ABCA4 retinopathy (aka Stargardt disease), in the East (Korea and Japan) and South East (Singapore and Thailand) Asian populations. (1) Identification of disease-causing variants in a multi-centre cohort of target N=200 suspected ABCA4 retinopathy cases using targeted sequencing of both exonic and intronic sequences of the ABCA4 gene using next generation sequencing (NGS) technology. (2) Clinical follow-up and characterisation of patients with ABCA4 mutations to establish phenotype-genotype correlations. Hypothesis Both the phenotypic and mutational spectrum of the ABCA4 gene in Asians are distinct from those of the Caucasian population due to ethnic heterogeneity and possible founder effects. Methodology & approach Targeted sequencing of the ABCA4 gene of 200 probands from Singapore, Japan, Korea and Thailand with suspected ABCA4 retinopathy will be performed to identify disease-causing variants and determine allele frequency. Genotype data will be correlated with detailed phenotyping using multimodal retinal imaging and functional testing in accordance with international standards. Blood samples of individuals with confirmed ABCA4 variants will be used to derive induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSC) for generation of disease models and RNA therapeutic studies. Feasibility Recruitment from multiple specialist sites with inherited retinal disease (IRD) expertise will facilitate recruitment within a restricted timeframe. Important to science or medicine Identification of Asian-specific disease-causing ABCA4 variants with detailed phenotype correlation will provide the basis for translational research in precision medicine including RNA therapeutics and gene-therapy, as well as identification of the appropriate stage of the disease for therapeutic intervention that will alter the course of this blinding disorder.
kw: ABCA4; Stargardt disease; macular dystrophy; cone-rod dystrophy; inherited retinal diseases

title: Modulatory effects of mesenchymal stem cells-derived extracellular vesicles on conjunctival innate immune responses to viral infections
abs: Ocular surface diseases (OSDs) are a group of disorders that can cause significant morbidity. Severe OSDs can result in chronic debilitating pain; bilateral blindness from complications of chronic inflammation can occur in up to 20% of patients. As OSDs affect individuals of all ages, ranging from young children and adults to the older population, they can result in significant socio-economic burden. Currently, the mainstay of treatment for OSDs are empirical, non-specific immunosuppressive medications. These treatments often produce unsatisfactory outcomes and are associated with significant adverse effects. Hence, there is an urgent need for more effective alternative therapies for OSDs to improve patient outcomes and reduce the socio-economic burden of these disorders. Dysregulated chronic inflammation at the ocular surface is central to the pathophysiology of OSDs morbidity. In order to develop targeted, more efficacious therapies, it is crucial to have a better understanding of the molecular pathways involved in inflammatory processes causing OSDs In this translational study, we hypothesise that mesenchymal stem cells derived-extracellular vesicles (MSC-EVs) can modulate innate immunological responses to alleviate the severity of viral-infected conjunctiva. Using a human adenovirus model and advanced technologies (e.g. digital spatial profiling and RNA-sequencing), we aim to improve our understanding of the molecular pathways involved in ocular innate immune responses by characterizing the immune response of the conjunctiva to adenovirus invasion. We will also evaluate the immunomodulatory effects of MSC-EVs on the innate immune responses of the conjunctiva in a non-human primate model of adenoviral infection. Knowledge gained from this study about ocular surface innate immune responses to viral insults and the modulatory effect of MSC-EVs would be invaluable to paving the way to develop alternative, more effective treatment options for ocular surface inflammation. The immunomodulatory effects of MSC-EVs, if proven, can have wider applications to other ocular surface and systemic inflammatory conditions.
kw: Exosomes; extracellular vesicles; mesenchymal stem cells; virus; ocular surface; immunology

title: Time-in-Range (TIR), a novel continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) based measure, to improve risk stratification of microvascular complications in type 2 diabetes
abs:
Background: Type 2 diabetes is an alarming public health problem in Singapore, affecting 1 in 9 adults, with the prevalence expected to rise to 1 million by 2050. Despite the availability of many novel drugs for T2D in the last decade, complication rates remain high with a third having microvascular complications. HbA1c alone does not fully explain the glycaemia mediated risk of diabetes complications. Continuous glucose monitoring data reveals that people with similar HbA1c have heterogenous glucose profiles, as measured by the percentage of time spent in the recommended glucose range of 3.9-10 mmol/L; the Time-in-Range. Preliminary data suggest that TIR is related to diabetes microvascular complications. 
Hypothesis: Time-in-Range is associated with the risk of microvascular complications independent of HbA1c.
Aims: 	To characterise Time-in-Range of people with type 2 diabetes using continuous glucose monitoring by studying the association of Time-in-Range to diabetes microvascular complications
Methods: A cross-sectional observational study in 300 adult type 2 diabetes subjects. Data on demographics, anthropometry, diabetes complications, type of diabetes therapy, and HbA1c will be collected.  Novel and sensitive methods like optical coherence tomography and corneal confocal microscopy will be employed to assess for diabetes retinopathy and neuropathy, respectively. Time-in-Range will be measured using a blinded 14-day continuous glucose monitoring. 
Statistics: Logistic regression model with Time-in-Range as independent factor for the dependent outcome microvascular complication, adjusted for HbA1c, diabetes
kw: type 2 diabetes, microvascular complications, continuous glucose monitoring, time in range

title: A Novel Drug Delivery Platform for the Treatment of Ureteric Diseases
abs: Urothelial carcinomas are lethal with a 5-year survival rate under 10% in advanced cases. In the upper urinary tract, it causes significant morbidity including bleeding, obstructive uropathy and even kidney failure. Current endourological treatment options are imperfect with high recurrence rates. Adjuvant local delivery of chemotherapeutics can reduce recurrences. However the constant urine flow, the peristalsis and a highly impermeable lining pose unique challenges to effective drug delivery in the ureter. Consequently, there is an urgent unmet need to optimise drug delivery in the ureter to improve treatment outcomes. Ureteric strictures are prevalent in Urology. Success rates post endoscopic management are dismal. Balloon dilatation and endoureterotomy for ureteric strictures are only successful in half of cases. Many patients go on to have more invasive open reconstructive surgeries with attendant morbidities and increased healthcare costs. We aim to study the pharmacokinetics, safety and toxicity of delivering Paclitaxel, which has both anti-cancer and anti-fibrosis properties, using a hydrogel-coated ureteric stent in a porcine model. We hypothesize that Paclitaxel concentrations at the target ureteric tissues can be safely optimised with an expandable drug-loaded stent coating that allows apposition with the ureteric wall to improve drug delivery. A single high dose concentration of Paclitaxel will be loaded unto 6 identical stents and deployed in the left ureter of 6 pigs with the contralateral (right) ureter as a control. These 6 pigs will be used to study the drug release characteristics at Day1, Day3 and Day8. At each timepoint, bilateral ureters will be harvested and assayed for Paclitaxel using liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry. Safety and toxicity parameters include serum creatinine changes, presence of hydronephrosis and histological inflammation and fibrosis. We hope this novel drug delivery platform can improve treatment outcomes, reduce recurrence rates and help reduce morbidity and healthcare costs for patients with ureteric diseases.
kw: urothelial carcinoma; ureter; stent; drug elution; ureteric stricture

title: Pilot Wait-list Randomized Controlled Trial of the ENABLE (Educate, Nurture, Advise, Before Life Ends) intervention for heart failure (HF) patients and their caregivers in Singapore (ENABLE-HF-SG)
abs:
Background
ENABLE (Educate, Nurture, Advise Before Life Ends) is a novel, nurse-led, structured, palliative care coaching program that was developed in the United States. ENABLE improves the quality of life (QOL) of patients (and their caregivers) facing serious illnesses. It is unclear if ENABLE will be efficacious in Singapore, due to differing sociocultural attitudes and expectations regarding healthcare treatments, decision making and care planning. 

Aims
We will pilot a culturally adapted 6 month ENABLE program, using a wait-list randomized controlled trial; to assess the feasibility of trial procedures in the local heart failure (HF) population and the acceptability and preliminary efficacy of the ENABLE program.  

Methods
We will recruit HF patients (and caregivers) from the inpatient and outpatient setting and randomize 30 HF patient - caregiver dyads to each arm. Participants in the intervention arm will start on ENABLE after randomization whilst participants on the wait-list will start after 6 months. Outcome measures will be self-reported. 

Feasibility will be assessed by evaluating the percentage of eligible participant dyads who are recruited and the percentage of recruited participant dyads who participate through the
