title: Integrating community LITE program into a school-clinic-community partnership as a family-based intervention to combat childhood obesity
abs: Background Childhood obesity is on the rise in Singapore with the majority continues into adulthood with serious long-term psychosocial and health complications. Currently available physical activity and dietary education sessions targeting overweight children are ineffective and stigmatising. Family-based multicomponent interventions that incorporate diet, physical activity and behaviour change in a structured programme is a critical missing link. Our pilot study on family-based intervention in the tertiary setting demonstrated feasibility and short-term effectiveness. Here, we propose to integrate our family-based intervention into a school, clinic and community partnership to achieve a sustainable outcome. Due to COVID-19 with safe management measures, we proposed online community Lifestyle Intervention for Everyone (LITE) program which is a structured, group family-based multicomponent lifestyle intervention for overweight children delivered on online videoconferencing platform. We hypothesize that our community Lifestyle InTervention for Everyone (LITE) program will be able to reduce the prevalence of overweight children in Singapore and improve cardiometabolic risk factors and health behaviour Primary aim is to determine whether the community LITE program will lead to 6 month clinically meaningful reduction in Body Mass Index (BMI) z-score of ≥ 0.15 as compared with usual care among overweight primary school-going children (6-10 years old). Secondary aims are to assess whether community LITE program will lead to reduction of cardiometabolic risk factors and improvement in health behaviours. Approach A randomized trial is planned to randomise 100 children into community LITE program and usual care with 1:1 allocation. Recruitment will be through school-based screening. Community LITE program consist of 30 sessions of interventional activities on dietary, physical activities and behavioural changes. The children will be followed up for 6 months for BMI z-score, waist-height ratio, blood pressure, fruits and vegetables intake and activity level outcomes. Significance The community LITE program is a novel way to deliver effective, accessible and scalable treatment for childhood obesity.
kw: Childhood obesity ; family-based interventions; community

title: Oral health, oral microbiome and salivary immunome in gestational diabetes mellitus
abs: Background: There is an increased prevalence of Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) in Singapore. Women with GDM have an increased risk for obstetric and foetal complications. Genetic and environmental factors are known to influence the pathogenesis of GDM, and recently, epigenetic mechanisms have also been implicated. Relatively less is known about the potential role of DNA changes in GDM pathogenesis per se or its utility as a biomarker in diagnosis, risk prediction, and prognosis in the mother. Employing non-invasive diagnostic methodologies using saliva is an urgent endeavour among clinicians and scientists to identify markers, especially in the vulnerable pregnant population. Therefore, we aim to conduct a prospective study to obtain conclusive evidence on the role of salivary markers in the development of GDM using high throughput ‘omics’ technologies. Methods: Pregnant women at 12-14 weeks gestation will be recruited in the study and will be followed up at 24-28 weeks of gestation. OGTT outcome will be used to stratify the groups into subgroups of GDM-positive and GDM-negative patients. The association between the development of GDM in the second trimester and the presence of salivary genomic changes in the first trimester will be evaluated using genomic sequencing. Saliva samples will be subjected to proteomic or metabolomic analysis. Significance: Saliva can be collected non-invasively and painlessly. If we can identify markers in saliva that can predict risk for GDM, it can open the doors to intervention studies to prevent GDM and adverse birth outcomes. Patients can be informed of their risk of developing GDM and can be advised lifestyle modification well advanced in time. This study has the potential to support the development of effective preventive health initiatives and pave the way for future point-of-care diagnostics for pregnant women across Singapore.
kw: gestational diabetes mellitus; pregnancy; microbiome; proteomics; periodontitis

title: Science Health, and Policy Relevant Ethics, Singapore (SHAPES) Programme
abs: CBmE at the Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, National University of Singapore (NUS) is committed to strengthening national capacity and cultivating an ethically responsible scientific community under its Science, Health and Policy-relevant Ethics in Singapore (SHAPES) s initiatives. It drives interdisciplinary research that addresses urgent challenges in public health, health systems, and the governance of emerging biomedical technologies particularly within the Singaporean and broader Asian contexts. CBmE actively collaborates with academic partners across and beyond NUS, as well as key stakeholders in healthcare, biomedical science, and policy, positioning itself as a catalyst for responsible innovation and ethical leadership. CBmE endeavours to keep the research community informed through evidence-based ethical research that upholds professional and responsible standards, reinforcing Singapore s position at the forefront of global biomedical research. The Centre contributes to shaping ethical norms and policy frameworks. Its research outputs are designed to be both relevant and accessible, supporting informed decision-making across the healthcare ecosystem and promoting ethical integrity in clinical and translational research. To further cultivate national expertise, CBmE collaborates with the Bioethics Advisory Committee Bioethics Advisory Committee Secretariat and leading clinician researchers including NMRC grant-holders to convene working groups that produce and disseminate position papers on key developments in translational science and medicine. These papers engage the scientific community in consensus-building and debate, reinforcing CBmE s role as a thought leader in biomedical ethics research and policy.
kw: bioethics

title: Translating Cancer Science into Precision Care – Precise Patient, Location, Biology, Drugs and Dose
abs: National Cancer Centre of Singapore (NCCS) is about to embark on its second and very exciting phase of journey by moving to its new home: a 28-storey brand-new building that will house the $100 million proton beam therapy, Advanced Cell Therapy and Research Institute (ACTRIS) and many other cutting-edge clinical and research facilities. Since its establishment in 1999 with a vision to become a global leading cancer center, NCCS has grown significantly in size and stature with notable clinical and scientific impacts. Today, it boasts over a 1200 staff supporting 5 Clinical Departments: Medical Oncology, Radiation Oncology, Surgical Oncology, Palliative Medicine, and Oncologic Imaging; 3 Research Divisions: Cellular & Molecular Research (CMR), Medical Sciences (DMS), and Clinical Trials & Epidemiological Sciences (CTE); Allied Health Teams: Onco-pharmacy, Stoma and Speech Therapy, Psychosocial Oncology and Nurse Clinicians; Department of Cancer Informatics. To date, we are treating approximately 65% of all cancer patients in the public sector of Singapore with a total of 150,000 outpatient attendances and 7,400 new patients (2020), and is the key regional referral center for patients from South East Asia, and as far as Middle East. Our reputation as a truly global leading cancer center was built and cemented by the combination of world-class clinical care, robust leading-edge research (basic, translational and clinical) and continuing high-quality cancer education. Staffed by 273 members, the NCCS Research enterprise has been organized into 3 divisions, supported by a central Research Admin & Ops department. Its main thrust of research is focused on tackling Asian cancers. By consolidating and strengthening our research efforts to create a seamless, highly collaborative environment, we hope to foster stronger collaboration between groups within NCCS, as well as that with other institutions nationwide such as Duke-NUS, Singapore General Hospital (SGH), National University Cancer Institute (NCIS), Cancer Science Institute (CSI), Genome Institute of Singapore (GIS), Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology (IMCB), and Nanyang Technological University (NTU). Our over-arching aim and emphasis for RIE2025 is to translate our research efforts into precision care (including identifying precise patients, precise cancer location, precise biology, precise drugs and precise doses). Noteworthy, 3 key new developments will profoundly impact NCCS and its research activities: 1) NCCS will soon have a new home (scheduled in 2022) that will provide current NCCS 2.5 times expansion in research space (Annex C); 2) NCCS is championing new therapeutic developments and implementation in the region such as proton beam therapy, immune and cell therapies which are fast gaining importance and acceptance in the cancer field; and 3) NCCS is playing a crucial role of a larger cancer ecosystem by being a major partner of the newly formed Singapore Translational Cancer Consortium

title: PROgram for Transforming & Evaluating outcomes in CardiomeTabolic disease (PROTECT)
abs: Established in 1998, the National Heart Centre, Singapore (NHCS) is the largest national and regional referral centre for cardiovascular diseases (CVD) in Singapore. It provides comprehensive cardiac care ranging from preventive, diagnostic, therapeutic to rehabilitative services, and houses the nation s only Heart and Lung Transplant Programme. Each year, the NHCS handles over 120,000 outpatient consultations, 9,000 interventional/surgical procedures and 10,000 inpatients, and its clinical outcomes are equivalent to international benchmarks. The NHCS is dedicated to providing optimal care through our three core pillars Patient Care, Education and Training, and Research. NHCS continues to pioneer the rapid adoption of leading edge cardiac innovations in Singapore, ranging from Left Ventricular Assist Devices, Percutaneous aortic valve replacement and Mitral & Tricuspid Valve Repair, and Stereotaxis for AF ablation. In 2018, NHCS and Sengkang General Hospital (SKH) collaborated to set up NHCS Cardiology @ SKH, providing cardiac services and expertise at its outpatient clinic and wards for north-east residents. NHCS is committed to developing its research capabilities and has made excellent progress in several key areas of translational and clinical research (TCR), including heart genetics, cardiovascular (CV) imaging, acute myocardial infarction (AMI), heart failure (HF) and data sciences. The National Heart Research Institute (NHRIS) was established in 2013 with the aim to nurture a vibrant translational research environment of basic scientists and clinicians to transform cardiovascular outcomes through patient-centred research. It occupies over 4,000m2 of the NHCS building, and was officially opened by the President in 2014. Over the span of 8 years, NHRIS has successfully restructured research infrastructure to create a seamless "all-the-way" research pipeline that spans across basic science discovery to clinical implementation, creating a translational science environment, typical for an Academic Medicine Research Institute. NHRIS has also established strong collaborations with both local and overseas Universities/hospitals and industry partners. NHCS has leveraged on the RIE2015 and RIE2020 CGs to develop NHRIS into an internationally competitive research Institute as evidenced by increasing numbers of clinician scientists, high impact publications, large quantum grants, patents and licences. NHRIS has fulfilled it aims set out in the short and long-term plans in promoting excellence in TCR, and enabling translation of research into health outcomes. During the RIE2015 CG, we had successfully developed 9 facility cores to support 7 research themes. Subsequently, we refined our program to 5 facility cores and 6 themes in the RIE2020 CG as the centre matured. title: A head-to-head comparison of a novel silicon microsieve device against a cell surface marker-based platform for the isolation of portal vein circulating tumor cells in pancreatic cancer
abs: Circulating tumor cells (CTCs) aid prognostication of cancer by predicting the presence of microscopic metastases. This is important in pancreatic cancer, which is associated with a poor prognosis even in resectable disease, due to microscopic metastases that are not detectable on pre-operative cross-sectional imaging. In pancreatic cancer, blood is sampled from the portal circulation so as to overcome the “hepatic sieve” effect, where pancreatic cancer CTCs are filtered out in the capillary beds of the liver before entering the peripheral circulation. Minimally invasive blood sampling from the portal vein can be done via endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) guidance, allowing CTC analyses to be done pre-operatively. CTCs have traditionally been isolated in various cancers using a cell surface marker-based platform (CellSearch™). This involves the use of antibodies to identify, isolate and quantify CTCs based on presence of specific epithelial cell markers. However, CTCs are now known to undergo epithelial-mesenchymal transformation. The current epithelial cell surface marker-based method of CTC isolation is limited by its inability to detect mesenchymal-type CTCs, potentially underestimating the CTC count, affecting the quantification and subsequent CTC molecular analyses. The use of a novel silicon microsieve device will overcome these limitations. It will simplify the isolation of CTCs by its characteristic size, enable both epithelial and mesenchymal CTCs to be isolated, and also results in greater cell viability, aiding in subsequent cell culture and organoid growth. We will compare a novel silicon microsieve size-based cell filtration device against the cell surface marker label-based CellSearch™ platform for the identification of pancreatic cancer CTCs in portal venous blood obtained via an Endoscopic Ultrasound (EUS)-guided puncture. We will compare the yield of epithelial-type CTCs isolated using both methods. We will investigate whether the isolation of mesenchymal-type CTCs via a sized-based cell filtration device leads to a significant increase in total CTC yield.
kw: Pancreatic cancer; Circulating tumor cells; Endoscopic Ultrasound; Portal vein blood sampling; Fine needle aspiration; Microsieve

title: A Biomarker Enrichment Phase II trial of 177Lu-DOTATATE in Metastatic Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma
abs: Distant metastatic recurrence predominates in nasopharyngeal carcinoma patients who recur following definitive treatment. In this unfavourable subgroup of patients, conventional chemotherapy with gemcitabine and cisplatin represents the standard of care for first-line therapy, but response to this doublet chemotherapy is often short-lived. This highlights the crucial need for novel agents targeting aberrant pathways that drive tumour progression. We have shown that somatostatin receptor 2 (SSTR2) is upregulated in a subset of metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma. We propose a single-arm, prospective phase II clinical trial to investigate the 6 month progression free survival rate with 177Lu-DOTATATE, which is a targeted radionuclide that binds to SSTR2, in metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma patients who have progressed following first-line chemotherapy. Secondary outcomes include overall survival, time to progression and objective response rate. Exploratory aims would be to characterize the changes in tumour immune and inflammatory gene expression signatures and changes in tumour and peripheral blood immune cell composition in response to 177Lu-DOTATATE therapy. We will also correlate blood-based biomarkers (EBV Titres and immune cell composition), transcriptomic, immunomics and dosimetry data with response.

title: Cell Therapy of Cancer
abs: Immunotherapy is gaining increasing prominence in oncology. The overall hypothesis underlying our research is that precisely directed immune cell therapy can yield better outcomes than standard treatment in patients with cancer, and with less toxicity. Research under two previously granted STaR awards resulted in first-in-human clinical trials, publications, awards, patents, and the founding of 3 biotechnology companies. It has also allowed training numerous students and research fellows, and inspired considerable philanthropic support. This application builds on recent ideas backed by extensive preliminary data. It relies on a laboratory with a solid track record in translational research, and a dedicated cell therapy facility managed by a team with proven expertise in the preparation of clinical-grade cell products. Specific Aim 1 is to evaluate a novel chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy for T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia and lymphoblastic lymphoma, aggressive diseases for which effective immunotherapy is lacking. The studies stem from our patented technology, and are supported by very encouraging early clinical results. Specific Aim 2 is to develop a novel cell therapy for acute myeloid leukemia (AML). A major obstacle to CAR-T cell therapy of AML is immunophenotypic heterogeneity of leukemic cells. An existing array of CARs made in our laboratory against CD123, CD70 and CD7, will be complemented by new CARs using an extensive database of AML surface marker profiles, including leukemia stem cells (Aim 2a). The activity of these new CAR-T cells will be studied alone and in combination with natural killer (NK) cells expressing an NKG2D chimeric receptor and membrane-bound interleukin-15 (Aim 2b). These studies will lead to a clinical trial of CAR-T and NK cells in patients with relapse or refractory AML. The research proposed should generate new treatment options for patients with T-cell and myeloid malignancies and, if successful, will revolutionize their clinical management.

title: Indoor air microbiomes as a gateway to exposome-guided precision medicine for respiratory disease
abs: In today’s world, breathing alone: 22,000 times a day inhaling 11,000 litres of polluted air is the health equivalent to that of a heavy smoker. Poor air quality remains a key risk factor for ill health in South Asia reducing life expectancy and contributing to disability. By limiting lung capacity and provoking cardiorespiratory and metabolic disease, ambient (outdoor) and household (indoor) air pollution contribute. Indoor air quality influences chronic respiratory disease and despite this, we know little about microbes inhabiting the urban ecosystem of air. While significant work has focused on outdoor air, limited reports of indoor air exist, and no study has attempted exposome-guided precision-medicine by assessing indoor air microbiomes. This proposal addresses this knowledge gap using novel, prospective and integrative approaches, employing an experienced interdisciplinary team and multi-centre patient recruitment. While human microbiomes are recognised in health and disease, limited knowledge exists on air microbiome composition, a planetary ecosystem with which our lungs interact with every breath. Our central hypothesis is that air microbiomes, within patients’ homes, influence respiratory status and present a novel unexplored target for intervention. If proven, the concept of ‘treating the environment rather than patient’ to alter disease represents a global paradigm shift of significant impact. Manipulating ‘home-exposomes’ is a fresh approach to improve airway health. Through metagenomics, bioinformatics and based on strong preliminary findings, we build on published works that Singaporeans exhibit distinct airway microbiomes reflective of our tropical and urbanised environmental exposures. We will expound home-host-environment interactions by determining indoor air (home), airway (host) and device (environment) microbiome composition explicating interactions (Aim 1) and, develop a novel bioinformatics analytical pipeline to integrate clinical and environmental data for precision medicine (Aim 2). Targeting exposome-associated microbes employs an innovative approach revolutionising the implementation of ‘microbiomics’ into clinical practice.
kw: Respiratory Disease; Microbiome; Environment; Exposome; Metagenomics; Precision Medicine

title: Studying the Heterogeneity of Gestational Diabetes Mellitus: Cardio-Metabolic Alteration and Treatment Response in a Multi-Ethnic Population in Singapore (GDM-CARE)
abs: The transient hyperglycemia firstly identified during pregnancy is also known as gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), and it increases risks of adverse pregnancy and neonatal outcomes like pre-eclampsia and macrosomia. With the phenomenal spread of overweight and obesity and genetic susceptibility, GDM is more prevalent in Asian pregnant women (i.e. 2- to 3-fold greater) compared with European pregnant women, especially ranging from 15% to 30% in Chinese and Indian descendants. Emerging evidence shows that a potential variation in insulin sensitivity, fat deposition and β-cell activity might underlie across heterogeneous GDM phenotypes, which lead to different pregnancy outcomes and maternal diabetic progression. However, current clinical treatment and follow-up strategy against GDM is applying “one-for-all” solution regardless the variation in GDM pathophysiology. Hence, efficiency and efficacy of the current clinical approach during pregnancy and after delivery is poor. In this CSAINV proposal, our objective is to define GDM heterogeneity in terms of cardio-metabolic profiling in vivo and treatment response during pregnancy, by using a set of unique and novel technologies (i.e. continuous glucose profiling and untargeted metabolites profiling). We hypothesize that understanding GDM phenotypes clinically and molecularly will help in tailoring effective treatment strategies to individuals, and even in predicting and preventing postnatal abnormal glucose metabolism. In this proposed 3-year pregnancy cohort, we will conduct a longitudinal study among 800 overweight (23-24.9 kg/m2) or obese (≥25 kg/m2) singleton pregnant women no later than 12 weeks of gestation—without a history of diabetes and composed of Chinese, Malay and Indian ethnicities—in a Singaporean tertiary hospital (National University Hospital, NUH). All of them will be screened for GDM at 24-28 weeks of gestation and followed through until delivery. Our primary outcome is GDM phenotype-specific continuous glycemic profiling and cardio-metabolic biomarkers alteration; and our secondary outcome is GDM phenotype-specific treatment response.
kw: gestational diabetes mellitus; heterogeneity; phenotypes; continuous glucose monitoring; multi-ethnicity; pathogenesis

title: Pathogenesis and novel preventive treatment of pathological cutaneous scarring: role of SPARC and TH2 immunological milieu and treatment with siRNA-embedded dissolving microneedles
abs: Pathological scars, namely keloids and hypertrophic scars, are highly-prevalent conditions arising from excessive deposition of irregular collagen matrix from the highly-proliferative fibroblasts during wound healing. Keloids are disfiguring, itchy, painful and may restrict mobility. At present, existing treatment options are poor and there is no preventive therapy. Keloid pathogenesis is highly complex, with localized chronic inflammation and accumulation of extracellular matrix components, especially collagen, extending beyond the original wound site. In fibrotic tissues, secreted protein acidic and rich in cysteine (SPARC) is significantly overexpressed and is crucial for incorporating soluble collagen into collagen fibrils. The Th2 immune response (IL-4, IL-5, IL-13) during wound healing also causes fibroblasts to differentiate into apoptosis-resistant myofibroblasts, resulting in persistent SPARC and collagen overexpression. We propose here a three-pronged approach to enhance the understanding of keloid pathogenesis and to deliver a novel preventive treatment for pathological cutaneous scarring. This is through (i) elucidating the roles of SPARC and immunological milieu in keloidal scar specimens and studying the therapeutic effects of dissolving microneedles-delivered small interfering RNA (siRNA) in (ii) rabbits and (iii) humans on scarring. To understand the keloid immune microenvironment, we propose to use Visium 10x spatial transcriptomics (ST) as an unbiased screening tool, followed by immunohistochemistry for the Th2 immune response and to validate any leads identified from ST. We will then use three-dimensional (3D) volumetric imaging to understand 3D keloid architecture, particularly the spatial interaction of SPARC protein with collagen and fibroblasts. Next, a preclinical trial to test dissolvable microneedle patches containing siSPARC only, and siRNAs targeting SPARC and IL-4Ra will be tested in a rabbit ear hypertrophic scar model. The aim is to test the efficacy of a multi-target approach to prevent scarring. Lastly, a clinical trial will be conducted with microneedles containing siSPARC, with an identified tangible pathway towards product commercialisation.

title: Personalized rheumatoid arthritis therapeutic strategies incorporating dynamic observation of joint changes using ultrasound and thermal imaging modalities
abs: Background: Despite therapeutic advances in Rheumatoid arthritis (RA), there remains unmet clinical needs for improved disease control within the “window of opportunity” and better selection of Disease-Modifying Anti-Rheumatic Drugs (DMARDs) earlier using a personalized medicine approach. Current clinical practice follows a standard approach, whereby first-line treatment (e.g. methotrexate) is typically given for up to 6 months prior to second-line, more costly, biological DMARDs. Given the response rate to methotrexate is 40-60%, many patients receive suboptimal treatment from the outset and miss the “window of opportunity” with resultant poorer outcomes. Aim(s): To utilize dynamic joint changes detected on ultrasound and thermal imaging to differentiate RA patients’ responses to first-line treatment after the initial one- or three-month treatment period. If true, patients who may benefit from an earlier step-up to second-line therapy can do so without the need to wait up to 6 months as in current practice. Methodology: A clinic-based cohort of 214 RA patients commencing first-line therapy will be recruited and followed up for 6 months. Clinical, ultrasound and thermal imaging joint assessments will be performed at baseline, 1-month, 3-month and 6-month time-points. The therapeutic outcomes and whether or not scaling-up therapeutic decision at 6 months will be used as the “gold standard” to assess the prognostic performance of dynamic changes of imaging after the initial one- or three-month of first-line treatment (e.g. methotrexate). A prediction model will be built to help select patients who may benefit from an earlier step-up to second-line therapy (e.g. biological DMARDs). Significance: If successful, this potentially paradigm changing novel management approach will help address unmet clinical needs by improving RA disease control within the “window of opportunity” and allowing better selection of DMARDs earlier through a personalized medicine approach. It is a part of a Comprehensive Bio-Imaging Program to improve RA/inflammatory arthritis patient care.
kw: Rheumatoid arhritis, Musculoskeletal, Imaging, Personalized medicine

title: Prospective study of biomarkers for diabetic kidney disease (DKD) progression in younger-onset type 2 diabetes – from biology-informed targeted proteomics to trans-omics.
inst: Khoo Teck Puat Hospital Pte Ltd
abs: Background Younger-onset type 2 diabetes (YT2D, onset-age≤40) is increasingly prevalent due to childhood and adolescent obesity. We recently reported that YT2D is associated with rapid DKD progression. However, the reason for such aggressive disease-trajectory is unclear. Data from our group and others have suggested the importance of systemic inflammation, vaso-active factors and renal-tubular injury. However, these factors (likely pertinent for YT2D), have not been specifically studied in this high-risk population. Hypothesis We hypothesize that proteomics targeting the above patho-biology can predict renal-progression among YT2D. Aims We will (i) perform targeted plasma and urine candidate-panel proteomics at baseline and investigate their association with DKD progression prospectively over ~3 year-period among YT2D (with replication); (ii) evaluate potential casual-inference using trans-omic (genomics and proteomics) analysis i.e. Mendelian Randomization (MR). Methods From our prospective diabetic cohorts (DN, SMART2D, DORIS, MODY and YOLO combined N~8,000), we have identified 990 YT2D, defined as individuals with non-type 1 diabetes, onset ≤40 year old. Hypothesis-driven: we will specifically evaluate the following biomarkers for DKD progression (i) systemic-inflammation: TNF receptors 1 and 2 (sTNFR1 and sTNRF2), haptoglobin; (ii) vaso-active factors: pigment epithelium-derived factor (PEDF) and Leucine-rich alpha-2-glycoprotein-1 (LRG1); (iii) Renal-tubular injury: kidney injury molecule-1 (KIM-1) and neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin (NGAL). Discovery and validation: For discovery, five selected OLINK multiplex panels with relevant candidate-peptides will be performed in 400 (200-pairs) DKD progressor and non-progressor, defined according to KDIGO’s (Kidney Disease–Improve Global Outcome) criteria. Novel signals will be validated in the remaining ~300 samples. Together with already-available GWAS data, trans-omics analysis using MR causal-inference will be performed. Scientific and clinical significance. Our data will improve the risk-stratification of DKD, gain insights into its patho-biology and may inform therapeutic targets for YT2D.
kw: Younger-onset type 2 diabetes; diabetic kidney disease (DKD); DKD progression; Proteomics; transomics

title: Mechanisms and therapeutic relevance of the interaction between genotoxic chemotherapy and complement regulators in lymphoma
abs: Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma (DLBCL) is the most common haematological cancer worldwide and in Singapore. Despite good overall responses to the standard first-line regimen of R-CHOP (Chemotherapy and an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody Rituximab), upto 40% of cases will relapse. The majority of these will succumb to the disease despite transient disease reduction with subsequent Rituximab-chemotherapy; highlighting the need for strategies to improve chemotherapy combinations in relapsed DLBCL. Modulating immune clearance of cancer cells after chemotherapy represents a promising approach, as the immune contexture of DLBCL is a critical determinant of relapse-free survival after R-CHOP. We recently discovered that chemotherapy upregulates membrane complement regulatory proteins (mCRPs); which are cell-surface proteins that control the innate immune complement system. We hypothesize that, through modulation of mCRPs, chemotherapy-induced DNA damage in cancer modifies complement-dependent effects on the immune system- both lytic (innate) and non-lytic (innate/adaptive). In this proposal, using DLBCL as our model, we intend to identify mechanisms by which DNA damage leads to the upregulation of complement regulators, and its downstream effects in cancer. We will use clinical-grade inhibitors and CRISPR-based genetic screens to decipher signalling pathways involved in chemotherapy-induced mCRP upregulation. We have optimized an in-vitro assay of Rituximab complement dependent cytotoxicity (CDC) as a functional readout for these experiments. We plan to assess the consequence of chemotherapy-induced mCRP upregulation on complement-related phenotypes/ immune infiltration using in-vitro co-culture assays and dual-humanized mice with a functional human complement system. Finally we will study the relationship between mCRPs and the immune microenvironment of DLBCL clinical samples using single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq) and quantitative multiplexed imaging. Chemotherapy induced changes in mCRPs are hitherto unknown. We expect this project to yield valuable new information on its mechanism and immunomodulatory effect, with the potential for translation to novel therapeutic strategies for relapsed DLBCL.
kw: lymphoma;complement cascade;chemotherapy;immune;mCRP;DNA damage

title: Germline and Somatic Mutational Correlates of Tumour Aggression and Radioresistance in Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma
abs: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) is a unique Asian-specific head and neck cancer affecting ~200 males in Singapore annually. Survival rates of this cancer have improved in the past decade, driven by advances in precise radiotherapy delivery. In locoregionally-advanced patients, treatment intensification with chemotherapy is recommended. Circulating EBV DNA (as a liquid biopsy) has proven utility in NPC for staging and on-treatment monitoring. However, cfEBV DNA remains a quantitative biomarker and yields limited insights on molecular processes underpinning tumour aggression and radio-/chemo-resistance. To fill this gap, we have performed germline and somatic mutational profiling of ~900 NPC patients. We discovered a germline variant (rs1131636-T) localised at the RPA1 gene that predicted for inferior survival following radiotherapy. We elucidated that rs1131636-T conferred a radioresistant phenotype through loss of transcriptional downregulation of RPA1 by altering the binding of miR-1253 to the 3’-UTR gene-region. These observations corresponded to overexpression of RPA1 in post-radiotherapy recurrences compared to paired pre-radiotherapy tumours. Building on these findings, we now propose to investigate for other germline and somatic correlates of tumour aggression in NPC. First (Aim 1), we will expand on our prior discovery and investigate for additional germline and somatic variants that are associated with clinical outcomes. Next (Aim 2), we will explore our paired genome-transcriptome dataset to characterise the regulatory network of RPA1 and other significant genes (from Aim 1), so as to identify aberrant pathways linked to NPC radioresistance. Finally (Aim 3), we will functionally validate these findings using our in-house-derived radioresistant NPC models (RR-C666-1, RR-HK-1). Additionally, we will utilise high-throughput drug screens to derive efficacious drug/drug combinations against radioresistant NPC. This proposal is poised to enable the discovery of a broad panel of biomarkers to identify NPC patients with radioresistant disease, who may be amendable to novel drug-radiotherapy combinations, which will be conceptualised based our findings.
kw: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma; Radiotherapy; Radioresistance; Genomics; Gene expression networks

title: Gut microbiome-derived metabolites linking the gut microbiome to systemic inflammation and neuroinflammation in Asian Multiple Sclerosis and Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorder
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Background Multiple sclerosis (MS) and Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorder (NMOSD) are the prototypical immune-mediated neuroinflammatory diseases. Environmental factors play significant roles in disease causation. Recent evidence suggests that a principal environmental factor is the gut microbiome and its derived metabolites, some of which have been shown experimentally to modulate host physiology, including systemic inflammation and neuroinflammation. Specific aims We aim to investigate: (1) the gut microbiome and its associated metabolome in MS and NMOSD patients as compared to healthy controls (HCs); (2) the relationship of gut microbiome-derived metabolome to systemic and neuroinflammation in MS and NMOSD patients; and (3) the longitudinal changes in the gut microbiome, gut microbiome-derived metabolome and cytokine/chemokine profile during clinical relapses and in remission within the same MS and NMOSD patients. Methods Sixty MS, 40 NMOSD patients and 40 HCs will be recruited. Baseline demographic and clinico-MRI data, and stool and serum samples will be collected. During longitudinal follow-up of patients, clinico-MRI data, stool and serum samples during relapses and in remission will be obtained. The gut microbiome will be profiled using whole genome metagenomics, while the gut microbiome-derived metabolome will be measured using nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy and mass spectrometry. Systemic inflammation will be profiled via measuring serum cytokines/chemokines concentrations, and neuroinflammation will be determined using clinico-MRI confirmed neuroinflammatory events. Multivariate analyses will be employed to identify discriminatory microbes and metabolites, with functional analysis to confirm their biological associations. Correlation between metabolites and indices of systemic inflammation will be assessed, and regression analyses will be used to determine the relationship of inflammation-relevant metabolites to clinico-MRI confirmed neuroinflammatory events. Significance Findings from this project will identify potential metabolite biomarkers for monitoring MS and NMOSD disease activity, and inference into the perturbed metabolic pathways can lead to targeted metabolic engineering as therapeutics to reduce systemic and neuroinflammation.
kw: gut microbiome; metabolomics; neuroinflammation; multiple sclerosis, neuromyelitis optica; cytokines

title: Characterizing early brain changes in midlife – a missing link to cognitive impairment in old age?
abs: Aims and hypothesis: Dementia is the most common age-related disease with a severe impact on elderly, caregivers, and healthcare system. The current lack of effective interventions in ameliorating cognitive decline calls for research into its causes and mechanisms so that novel therapeutic targets can be identified and new therapies developed for effective treatment of this devastating disease before the development of clinical symptoms and signs. Limited data suggests that subclinical brain changes are among the most impactful predictors of cognitive decline as people age. The identification of early subclinical biomarkers for vascular and neurodegenerative changes in middle-age is of interest as brain dysfunction is present many years before overt-symptoms of dementia. Currently, there is no data from Asia including Singapore. Our overall aim is to understand the determinants and aetiology of brain changes in a subclinical phase of cognitive impairment including data on lifestyle factors, brain imaging and blood biomarkers in a middle-aged multi-ethnic population in Singapore. We hypothesize that multi-modal factors measured in midlife can predict future cognitive decline in community-dwelling adults. Methods: This proposal is nested in an ongoing multi-ethnic cohort (ages:45-65 years) in Singapore. 600 participants with an equal distribution of Chinese, Malay and Indian ethnicities will undergo a comprehensive examination consisting of physical, clinical, lifestyle behaviour and neuropsychological assessments at baseline and after 2 years. Of these, MRI and blood assessment will be offered to 200 persons at baseline. Significance: This prospective population-based study provides an ideal platform to study the impact of lifestyle behaviours, MRI and blood biomarkers on cognitive functioning. This research will identify new opportunities to improve public health policies, resulting in better interventions and management of cognitive decline at an early stage. This will also form the basis for future CSA application that will involve larger sample and integrate genetics and metabolomics.
kw: midlife; cognitive impairment; dementia; lifestyle; blood biomarkers; MRI

title: Focal Cryotherapy for Prostate Cancer: Does the Radiological-Molecular Landscape predict Oncological outcomes?
abs: Prostate cancer is the 3rd most incident cancer among Singaporean men. Standard radical treatments such as prostatectomy or radiation are associated with significant impairment to urinary and sexual function. However, not all men require such aggressive treatment – evidence shows that most prostate cancers are low-grade and indolent, and treatment only needs to be reserved for those with intermediate- or high-grade (significant) cancer. Focal Therapy (FT) is a novel concept where targeted ablation is performed to destroy only the area of significant cancer (index lesion) within the prostate, thus reducing collateral damage and morbidity. Our NMRC CS-IRG-NIG-sponsored phase II trial of Focal Cryotherapy (n=30) shows that quality of life is well-maintained after FT. Here we extensively imaged and biopsied the prostate (>30 cores) before FT and 1-year after FT. Our pilot data shows that the recurrence rate of significant cancer after treatment is as high as 33%. Some of these recurrent cancers represent a progression in the index lesion that was targeted for ablation (infield) while others have arisen in areas where imaging and biopsy showed no, or low-grade cancer initially (outfield). We aim to better define these subpopulations where infield or outfield recurrence has occurred and define their transcriptomic and multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging (mpMRI) profiles compared to those patients that have not recurred. We will extract and sequence ribonucleic acid (RNA) from the biopsy samples and export voxel-level mpMRI information obtained before FT of the index lesion and areas of normal tissue or low-grade cancer. Using a known transcriptomic profile for cancer progression risk into low/ medium/ high, we estimate that we will require 60 patients in order to meet our primary endpoint (30 will be obtained from the earlier trial cohort). The findings of this study will help us better select patients for FT of prostate cancer.
kw: Prostate Cancer; Focal Therapy; Radiological-Molecular Signature

title: Interrogating the proteogenomic landscape of pancreatic cancer for therapeutic biomarker discovery
abs: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is an aggressive cancer with a dismal prognosis. In the majority of cases, patients present with metastatic disease, thereby excluding them from potentially curative surgical resection. In addition, the selection of existing chemotherapeutic regimens is based on patient performance status rather than biomarkers. Carbohydrate antigen 19-9 (CA19-9) is the only approved biomarker for diagnosis and therapeutic monitoring but its usefulness is limited by low sensitivity and specificity. In order to identify more robust biomarkers for clinical translation, the characterisation of PDAC at both the genomic and proteomic level is of paramount importance. To overcome the low tumor cellularity in PDAC samples that has hampered -omics analyses, we propose to utilise patient-derived tumor organoids (PDOs) for proteogenomic characterization of PDAC. We will then integrate bioinformatics analysis of publicly available genomic datasets with data from molecular profiling of our PDOs for PDAC subtype classification. In a parallel study, these PDOs will be used for phenotypic screen of current therapies for precision treatment. Quantitative proteomics will be performed to characterise the proteomes of individual lines of PDOs. By classifying PDOs based on their drug sensitivity profiles and comparing their proteogenomic profiles, we hope to identify candidate biomarkers to inform treatment selection. In addition, the high-dimensional proteomic dataset generated will be used to support cross-comparison with transcriptomic-based classification to discern both complementary and unique PDAC subtypes. Information from the current study can also be expanded for future diagnostic and prognostic biomarker identification. Our study will provide key insights into the complex biology of cancer development in PDAC and has the potential to improve outcomes for patients with this devastating disease.
kw: Pancreatic cancer; Precision medicine; Proteomics; Biomarker discovery

title: The Immune Microenvironment in Soft Tissue Sarcomas and Therapeutic Implications for Immunotherapy
abs: Soft Tissue Sarcomas (STS) are a heterogeneous group of tumors with an abysmal prognosis. Median survival is only one year with metastatic disease. Chemotherapy is the mainstay of treatment in STS despite dismal overall response rates (ORR) of 15%. Immune checkpoint inhibition has shown promise in other cancers, but in STS, ORR is only 5% overall. The design of immunotherapy trials has been ineffective, since little is known about the immune microenvironment in STS. Elevated blood neutrophil/lymphocyte ratio (NLR) is strikingly associated with decreased survival in STS. In other solid tumours, immunosuppressive tumour-infiltrating neutrophils contribute to poor immunotherapy response. However in STS, the presence of immunosuppressive neutrophils in the sarcoma tumour itself has not been investigated. We hypothesize that: (1) an immuno-evasive/suppressive immune environment contributed by neutrophils hampers response of STS to immunotherapies, and is altered by chemotherapies; (2) a common signature spanning STS subtypes defines tumours that respond to immunotherapy, the type of immunotherapy that is effective, and whether immunotherapy should be given in combination with chemotherapy. We have one of the largest collections of STS samples worldwide (from which we have identified neutrophils in some) matched to treatment and outcomes. Building on our findings and unique resources, we will use a combination of spatial and high-throughput multiparameter approaches to fully characterize the immune environment in STS, across all clinical settings (pre-chemotherapy, post-chemotherapy, progression) and subtypes. Neutrophils and other immune cells will be identified; their maturation stage and function analysed in matched samples. Immune and transcriptomic signatures will be correlated to patient outcomes and exposure to chemotherapy to determine how the immune microenvironment changes with treatment. Altogether, our findings will allow optimal biology-informed integration of immunotherapies into current treatment, including modification of timing, sequencing and combination of chemotherapies with immunotherapies, for better efficacy in STS.
kw: sarcoma; immune microenvironment; immunotherapy; neutrophils; biomarkers; chemotherapy

title: Immunobiology of advanced prostate cancer
abs: Prostate cancer is one of the most prevalent Uro-Oncological diseases across the Globe. It is the third most common malignancies and ranks the top cancer that showed the highest annual increase in incidence in local men between 1968 and 2017. Standard of care treatment for metastaticprostatecancerusingADThasbeenthecornerstonemodalityforover30years.Clinicaloutcomeofmetastaticprostatecancerhas continued to improve owing to the significant results from several landmark clinical trials looking at additional treatment to ADT. These secondary agents are primarily chemotherapy or androgen receptor antagonists, which carry significant adverse effects on their own rights. Furthermore, most of these patients will ultimately continue to progress and develop debilitating castrate-resistant disease despite the institution of advance treatment. Metastatic prostate cancer remains a health problem in Singapore as our population continues to age. On the other hand, there are also a number relatively young Singaporean men diagnosed with de novometastatic prostate cancer. Prostate cancer screening programme does not exist as no real cancer marker/diagnostic tools are currently available. Here, we are hoping to acquire new insights into the immunobiology of metastatic prostate cancer, which has not been fully elucidated. title: IMMUNO-ONCOLOGY PATHWAYS IN NASOPHARYNGEAL CARCINOMA FOR TARGETED TREATMENT
abs: Nasopharyngeal cancer (NPC) is the third most common cancer among middle-aged males in Singapore. Unfortunately, 35% of patients experience loco-regional recurrence or distant failure. Early clinical trials evaluating anti-PD-1 therapies have demonstrated a response rate of 20.5%, reflecting an urgent need to identify biomarkers to guide patient selection. Using Smart-3SEQ, we will perform micro-dissected gene expression profiling of tumors from patients enrolled in two independent anti-PD-1 clinical trials to identify gene expression signatures associated with treatment response in NPC. Although MHC Class I (MHC-I) molecules are required for antigen presentation to T cells, tumors with intact MHC-I were instead found to have a poorer response rate to nivolumab in the NCI-9742 Phase 2 trial. Our preliminary data suggest that ERAP2, an aminopeptidase that is involved in peptide trimming for presentation on MHC-I, is upregulated in non-responders. By generating a NPC cell line model that expresses only a single HLA allele, we will test the hypothesis that over-activity of ERAP2 results in altered antigen processing and reduced cytotoxicity by T cells and/or NK cells in co-culture. We will evaluate the role of a small-molecule ERAP2 inhibitor in restoring cytotoxicity by effector cells. This grant proposal aims to explain the heterogeneity in response rates to anti-PD-1 therapy and provide a scientific foundation for additional targeted therapies to improve treatment response.

title: Digital Intelligence Research based on Big Data for Improving Efficient Navigation of Vessels to Singapore Port Waters
inst: IHPC - Institute of High Performance Computing
abs: For improving navigation safety and operation efficiency at a port and reducing extra wait time of vessels, deriving operation insights extended beyond a port is critical. Undoubtedly, coordinative and interactive optimization driven by big data intelligence among ports, shipping lines and other maritime stakeholders will lead the next wave of transformation for operation efficiency and safety enhancement in maritime sector. This project aims to develop digital intelligence solutions, leveraging on maritime big data, for coordinative optimization between port and shipping lines, which will help strengthen shipping lines’ operation efficiency and port connectivity with the maritime world and inter-linkages (“Singapore R&D Roadmap 2030: Maritime Transformation” n.d.). For that, AI-based ETA prediction, port berth operation situation awareness and multi-scale optimization techniques will be developed based on historical Singapore port operation data to provide intelligence for the coordinative optimization considering both dynamics in vessel navigation and port operation and future autonomous shipping system’s interaction with ports. The models developed will be evaluated together with port and vessels to provide inputs to OneHandShake portal from PSA Marine (and shipping line (NYK) operation system, i.e. LiVE and Guardian(SCS)), if needed), and enhance its output for future port and vessel navigation safety, efficiency and reliability.

title: Development and Deployment of Advance Shore Power Charger, Vessel Energy Management System and Cyber-Physical Operating System with Sizing Tools
abs: Singapore is a global hub port which is at the crossroad of important and critical tradelines for Asia and the rest of the world. Its port is one of the busiest and most connected to the world, with links to more that 600 ports across 120 countries worldwide. Annually, more than 130,000 ships call at Singapore. All ships and vessels including passenger craft, tugs and cargo vessels docked at Singapore’s yards and ports require power to maintain their lights, heating, cooling, and other essential vessel functions. Typically, this power is provided by running the vessel’s diesel-fuelled auxiliary engines but such engines produce harmful gaseous emissions (CO2, NOX, SO2, others) that pollutes the air. Rapid migration to ports and yard electrification provide avenue to reduce harmful gaseous emissions and ensure achievement of Singapore’s goal for Emission Intensity (EI) reduction by 36% from the 2005 levels. Work Package 1: Shore Power Vessel Charging System Shore power, also known as cold-ironing or alternative marine power, is the process of providing electrical power from the shore to a ship while it’s docked, thereby allowing a ships’ auxiliary engines to be turned off and the burning of diesel fuel to cease. Therefore, shore power is an effective way of reducing air emissions and improving local air quality. Additionally, by providing ship operators with an alternative to running diesel auxiliary engines while docked, shore power technology also reduces ship owners’ fuel costs which increases the competitiveness of Singapore’s busy yards. Work Package 2: Marinized Energy Management System (MEMS) Electric harbour crafts may consume high energy with high operation cost and low reliability for operations in Singapore and thus it is essential to develop an energy management system for optimal and safe operations of the vessel. Our proposed work package would focus on development of Marinized Energy Management Systems (EMS) of electric harbour craft which would provide operational advisory and trip plans as guidelines to operators based on energy usage and environmental conditions. The proposed EMS system would enable informed decision making to both crew and onshore teams and potentially assists vessel operators in the reduction of energy usage and operating costs. Signals from different parts of Harbourcraft such as motors with propellers and signals from different sensors such as GP, IMU and the signal from BMS etc will be collected on-board on a single processor known as an EMS. The proposed EMS system would be able to monitor energy usage of the vessel, assess the ocean sea state and forecast the operating conditions using advanced data analytics techniques, based on which the EMS software would be able to provide an operational advisory of the vessel to the operators. This feature will help operators to plan the number of trips that can be operated per day using the vessel. The proposed EMS system would also provide vessel efficiency and healt

title: Monitoring of tunnel liner performance during construction and operation in local ground conditions
abs: Monitoring of tunnel lining performance is one of the important aspects in tunnel design and construction. This is particularly the case when new types of tunnel liners or new construction methods are adopted. With further development in underground transportation network, larger diameter tunnels are to be constructed. Steel fibre reinforced concrete liners are replacing traditional reinforced concrete liners due to their advantages of reducing construction time and labour costs, increasing the impact strength of the segments, enhancing the durability properties and reducing crack openings. Steel fibre reinforced concrete liners with large diameters will be increasingly used for MRT tunnelling and other underground infrastructure constructions in Singapore. However, there is still a lack of understanding of the performance of steel fibre reinforced concrete liners and design experience with large diameter tunnels. The objective of this study is to carry out a field investigation to monitor the performance of steel fibre reinforced concrete liners during the complete life cycle of a tunnel, from liners casting to installation as well as during operation using embedded fibre optic sensors. Through this research study, we will be able to understand much better the performance of tunnel liners, obtain valuable liners-ground interaction data to verify the design assumptions as well as calibrate numerical methods adopted for the design, and assess any risks associated with the installation of tunnel liners in local ground conditions.
kw: Tunnel liners, fibre optic sensors, steel fibre reinforced concrete, structural health monitoring

title: Next-generation human organoids: Characterization, isolation and combinatorial re-assembly of niche components
abs: This research programme aims to define the optimal conditions for the generation of human organoids that faithfully recapitulate the structural complexity and functional repertoire of their cognate organs. It will address the limitations of current organoids by “deconstructing” developing and regenerating organs in vivo and “reconstructing” them in vitro. The key components of the niche microenvironments that govern the development, maintenance, regeneration and repair of organs in human, mouse and zebrafish will be defined. Single cell RNA sequencing will identify distinct cell types and their roles will be inferred by analysis of their spatial distribution and transcriptional profiles. The lipid and metabolic profiles of the organs as well as their extra cellular matrix (ECM) components and biomechanical properties will be determined. Parallel analyses will identify those niche components missing from the current generation of organoids. The function of niche-specific cells will be explored using targeted in vivo cell ablation techniques in mouse and zebrafish. Critical niche-cell types will be introduced into current human organoids with the aim of enhancing their fidelity and complexity. A novel high throughput combinatorial screening platform will be used to identify optimal combinations of cell types, ECM components, soluble factors and biomechanical parameters for the production of next-generation organoids. The realisation of this programme will enhance the utility of organoids in studies of human development and disease, in personalized medicine, drug discovery and toxicology, and ultimately will pave the way for the in vitro generation of organs for therapeutic use.

title: Determining the impact of SARS-CoV-2 variants and vaccination on close-contact attack rates and acquisition risk factors
abs: Aim: The aims of this study is to determine (i) the impact of SARS-CoV-2 variants and vaccination on close-contact attack rates (household and non-household); (ii) the serologic profile of close-contacts; and (iii) behavioral risk factors associated with SARS-CoV-2 variant acquisition. This leverages on Singapore’s intensive contact tracing and quarantine approach combined with routine entry and exit PCRs. Methodology: The study population will be household and non-household close contacts of cases identified by Ministry of Health from 1st July 2021 to 31st June 2022. Among the household close contacts, secondary transmitted cases (incident cases) will be identified, being defined as those who have a negative entry swab (as well as a negative serology test result, if it was performed) at the start of their Quarantine Order (QO), followed by either a positive exit swab/serology test result at the end of their QO, or a positive “symptomatic swab” if they had developed symptoms during their QO period and were referred for testing. Attack rates of household and non-household close contacts will be determined. Serology testing will be performed at the end of the QO (3 to 8 weeks after completion of quarantine) for household contacts who do not have prior serology test results, to determine prevalence of missed diagnosis. A questionnaire will be administered to all consenting individuals to determine transmission risk factors. Analysis endpoints and clinical significance: The primary analysis endpoints of this study is to determine: (i) the impact of new variants on infectivity (measured by secondary attack rates in close-contact setting); (ii) the impact of vaccination in reducing attack rates among new variants; (iii) whether variants and vaccination have an impact on missed diagnosis using PCR (measured using serologic assays at end of QO); and (iv) the impact of variants and vaccination on acquisition risk factors for SARS-CoV-2.

title: Pathophysiologic Mechanism for MYOcarditis in COVID19 VAccinations (MYOVAx study)
abs: The coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) is an ongoing pandemic which has infected more than 160 million people and caused 3.4 million deaths worldwide till May 2021. With the recent rollout of COVID-19 vaccines globally and in Singapore, reports of rare but serious cardiovascular-related side effects started to appear1-4.  In Singapore acute myocarditis is of particular concern with at least 12 cases reported by the Health Services Authority (HSA)9. The US FDA and EU authorities have confirmed there to be an association between the mRNA vaccines and myocarditis6, 7, 10. The mechanisms through which myocarditis occurs are unknown. Moreover, there is presently no accurate means of predicting susceptibility to SARS-CoV2 vaccine-related cardiovascular toxicity nor predicting recovery. Our study aims to understand the pathophysiology of myocarditis associated with COVID-19 vaccines. In addition to the above, our study hopes to expand in scope to look at myocarditis occurring within 3 months of COVID-19 infection (COVID-related myocarditis). title: UV-C solution for air disinfection in confined spaces
inst: SIMTech - Singapore Institute of Manufacturing Technology
abs: Several SARS-CoV-2 variants have been identified around the world in the COVID-19 patients [1]. Beta and delta variants of the coronavirus are believed to be highly transmissible through both direct contact and airborne routes. The aerosol particles could potentially accelerate the airborne transmission rate in closed rooms. Employing an effective UV-C solution can potentially mitigate airborne transmission. Previously our UV-C device can achieve 99.9% surface disinfection of pathogens in <2sec for E.coli and SARS-CoV-2. This project aims to design, optimize and validate prototype UV-C LED devices to reduce aerosol transmission in various high footfall premises such as passenger lifts, meeting rooms and air ducts of buildings. Modelling and simulation will be used to accelerate design optimization for maximum disinfection and shorten the design cycle, by reducing time for prototype fabrication and testing time and effort. Majority of the existing technologies and products are not evaluated with airborne aerosol droplets but only by surface disinfection. Such claims can be misleading and compromise the safety of the uses. So to build up capabilities in airborne disinfection testing for bacteria/virus, we aim to design and develop a benchtop test setup for establish airborne efficacy relationship (S. pneumonia, MS2 bacteriophage, human corona virus and SARS-CoV-2) with UV dose and dwell time. Finally we would develop a UV-C prototype that can achieve 99.9% disinfection and deployable at confined spaces and air duct with a novel design of UV-C LED engine with enhanced thermal management and maximized LED intensity by using heat pipes as LED carriers. In-field pilot trials for evaluating disinfection rate of the UV-C prototype at confined spaces (e.g. Elevators/MRT) and HVAC air ducts.

title: “Breaking the ground” in Semakau Landfill: technological solutions for site investigation and material reuse
abs: Semakau Landfill (SL) calls for practical solutions to extend its lifetime beyond 2035. Landfill mining combined with material reuse from the waste has been shown as a viable solution to urban landfills, but has never been applied to a landfill containing mixed waste material (MM) consisting of incineration bottom ash, incineration fly ash, and other non-incinerable waste. A series of innovative technological solutions for site investigation (SI) and material reuse aiming at “breaking the ground” in SL are proposed. Our project will be articulated around three key objectives: 1) SI and 3D spatiotemporal modelling of MM; 2) laboratory trial tests on MM processing and material reuse; and 3) decision support tool (DST) for sustainable SL management. In Obj. 1, conventional geotechnical SI techniques with geophysical and geoenvironmental techniques will be combined to provide wider coverage and detailed insights into the MM properties in situ. Subsequently, a series of laboratory characterization and aging tests will be carried out to supplement the 3D MM distribution and evolution model that will inform Obj. 2 and 3. In Obj. 2, a trial treatment train will be designed and tested for the retrieved MM. The processing units will be designed as modules allowing different configurations and sequences. The units will be co-designed between NTU and local industry partners, including Remex, NSC, and JFE. The target reuse applications are road construction, caisson infill, and landfill reclamation. In Obj. 3, a DST will be developed. We aim to deliver: 1) a suite of geotechnical-geophysical-geoenvironmental (SI) techniques and SI datasets of SL; 2) lab characterization and a 3D distribution and evolution model of the MM in SL; 3) treatability assessment of excavated MM and testbed design for treatment train; 4) reusability assessment of excavated and treated MM targeting caisson infill, road construction, and land reclamation; and 5) Optimal decisions for sustainable management of SL based on different decision-making criteria.

title: Development of pan-sarbecovirus vaccine candidates to combat COVID-19 and future coronavirus pandemics
abs: In less than two decades, we have experienced three major human infectious disease pandemics caused by coronaviruses (CoVs), SARS, MERS and COVID-19. All of them caused devastating economic and human loses globally. For COVID-19, the unprecedented speed of developing vaccine and therapeutic monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) led to powerful intervention. However, the recent emergence of SARS-CoV-2 variants has raised real concern that the current vaccines may not be sufficient. We hypothesize that novel approaches to broad spectrum vaccine can greatly enhance our ability to combat not only the current SARS-CoV-2 virus including known and future variants but also pre-emergent CoVs which share the common receptor, the human angiotensin converting enzyme 2 (ACE2). These CoVs are grouped in the subgenus Sarbecovirus (sarbeCoV) and in this proposed project, we aim to develop pan-sarbeCoV vaccines. By examining broad-spectrum neutralizing antibodies (NAbs) using a novel multiplex surrogate virus neutralization (sVNT) platform, we discovered very high level of pan-sarbeCoV NAbs in SARS survivors immunized with the Pfizer mRNA vaccine. This represented the first-in-human demonstration of the feasibility to produce pan-sarbeCoV vaccine. In this project, we will extend our findings to devise a novel cross-immunization strategy which will use the current SARS-CoV-2 vaccines, regardless of the types (it can be mRNA, subunit, vectored or inactivated whole virus), for priming followed by a boosting with a novel “consensus” vaccine covering spike sequences from all known SARS-CoV-1 related CoVs. There will be significant clinical impact from this project not only for the current pandemic, but equally importantly for the prevention and mitigation of future CoV pandemics.

title: The Singapore lYMPHoma translatiONal studY (SYMPHONY)
abs: The proposed programme is a renewal of our NMRC-funded TCR program on peripheral T-cell (PTCL) and NK/T cell lymphomas (NKTL), which are more common in Asia. To date, therapeutic interventions are of limited efficacy and there remains a pressing need to improve diagnosis, therapy and patient selection. The current TCR has elucidated part of the underlying complexity of this disease. Identification of mutations in JAK/STAT pathway, epigenetic regulators and structural variations in the PD-L1 gene resulting in immune evasion, amongst others, pave the way towards a biology-driven strategy. Theme 1 builds on our findings that suggest immune checkpoint inhibition to be a major turning point in NKTL treatment and aims to identify next-generation biomarkers of response and resistance. In addition, strategies to enhance antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity and complement-dependent cytotoxicity of anti-CD38-directed therapy with Daratumumab will be explored. Theme 2 aims to develop novel, next generation hetero-tetrameric IgG bi-specific antibody (BsAb) constructs with broad applications for lymphoma therapy. In Theme 3, we aim to (i) target previously elucidated genetic mutations and the relevant driver oncogenic pathways using novel JAK-STAT inhibitors, PI3K inhibitors, EZH2 inhibitors and HDAC inhibitors and (ii) identify rational combinations to overcome resistance. Theme 4 will develop more effective and cost-efficient diagnostic platforms and optimize drug therapies through computational genomics and integrative machine learning algorithm research. Through these 4 intercalated themes, we aim to translate and build on the progress we have made in addressing unmet clinical needs of T-cell lymphoma. The expertise and infrastructure we have built will allow us to investigate key strategic areas in B-cell lymphoma research where we may be internationally competitive.
