title: MicroRNA-Mediated Neurodegeneration in Parkinson’s Disease
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Parkinson’s disease (PD) is the most common motor disorder and the second most prevalent neurodegenerative disease in the aging population. Owing to many gaps in knowledge about this disease, current treatment methods only provide symptomatic relief and not neuroprotection. Previously, our lab has shown that there is an upregulation of miR-9 and miR-219 in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) in the mouse model of PD (1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine (MPTP)-treated mice. This trend is also similarly observed in the post-mortem SNc of PD patients. We have also demonstrated neurotoxic effect of miRNA-9 dysregulation in dopaminergic neurons using both in vitro and in vivo animal models and identified its target protein V. In this study, we will 1) screen and compare plasma levels of miRNAs and their target proteins between PD patients and health controls in 3 PD case control cohorts; 2) monitor and correlate changes in plasma levels of miRNAs and their target proteins with motor and non-motor symptom progression in PD patients; 3) investigate the toxic effect of miRNA9, miRNA219 and other candidate miRNAs dysregulation on dopaminergic neurons in drosophila; and 4) investigate the functions and mechanisms of miRNA9, miRNA219 and other candidate miRNAs in in vitro PD models and screen their potential proteins. Utilizing 3 case control cohorts, we aim to document that specific miRNAs (such as miRNA9) are dysregulated in PD patients compared to healthy controls. Abnormal expression of miRNA9 and other candidate miRNAs can lead to DA neuron death potentially through interaction with their target proteins. MiRNAs and their target proteins can be used as biomarkers for PD diagnosis and prognosis. They may also serve as therapeutic targets in PD treatment.
kw: microRNA, biomarker, Parkinson's disease

title: Design and testing of a novel respiratory dialysis system to reduce lung injury during mechanical ventilation, a safety and physiology study in a large animal model of hypercapnia
abs: Each year, 20 million patients require mechanical ventilation. Although lifesaving, mechanical ventilation causes lung injury that may develop into acute respiratory distress syndrome. Low-tidal volume ventilation reduces lung injury but leads to harmful carbon dioxide (CO2) accumulation. Extracorporeal CO2 removal (ECCO2R) removes excess CO2, facilitating low-tidal volume ventilation. ECCO2R also helps some patients avoid mechanical ventilation, thus eliminating opportunities for ventilator complications to develop. But ECCO2R is complex, expensive, and unavailable in most hospitals. We are developing an approach of removing CO2 in the form of bicarbonate using dialysis, because dialysis equipment, in contrast to ECCO2R, is readily available in most hospitals. In previous work funded by an NMRC Transitional Award, we demonstrated that removal of bicarbonate using dialysis lowers plasma CO2, but our prototype exposed recipients to excessive dialysis doses. In work funded by an NMRC Clinician Innovator Award, we collaborated with NUS Chemists to design a novel buffering molecule that cannot cross dialysis membranes. This allows us to construct dialysates containing almost no bicarbonate while retaining a physiological pH. The overall goal of the current study is to test the hypothesis that CO2 removal with our new dialysate is safe and efficient, and show we can minimize electrolyte losses by designing personalizing dialysis fluids. We will test this by completing two specific aims. In Aim #1, we plan to show that dialysates containing our new buffering molecule can be used with conventional dialysis equipment to safely remove clinically meaningful amounts of CO2 in a large animal model. In Aim #2, we will measure CO2 kinetics and electrolyte changes during bicarbonate dialysis, and use these data to develop a method for creating personalized dialysis fluids that minimize electrolyte losses. Successful completion of our proposed work will demonstrate our system is efficient and safe enough for translation into first-in-man studies.
kw: ECCO2R, Respiratory Failure, ARDS, Intensive Care

title: A Smart Digital Workflow Towards High Precision and Throughput Production for Removable Partial Dentures
abs: Tooth loss, also termed edentulism, is a major dental problem worldwide, particularly among the senior population. A recent study in Singapore found that 69% of adults aged over 65 are wearing dentures. The high prevalence of tooth loss has resulted in high demands of prosthetic replacements, posing challenges to the public dental care system in Singapore. Removable partial dentures (RPDs) are the most commonly used device to replace missing teeth and restore oral functions. However, the current analogue method to fabricate RPD is a time consuming, complex, error-prone, and expensive process. Due to the inherent inaccuracies in the technique, the fit of the framework and denture base is often undesirable to meet patients’ requirements. We have developed a dedicated “SMART RPD” software to process patient-specific digital intra-oral scan and generate automatically RPD framework designs. These designs can be simply edited and 3D printed through a sintered laser melting technique. We hypothesize that this “Smart workflow” is a more precise and efficient process in fabricating RPDs. This proposal seeks to validate this novel workflow through a randomized clinical trial via comparing the RPDs fabricated through the “Smart workflow” against that through the conventional analogue and partial digital workflows. We will evaluate the metal framework and the final RPDs for 1) adaptation of RPD framework; 2) fit of the RPD denture base and patient satisfaction; 3) cost-minimization of RPD fabrication process. The long-term goal of this study is to reduce treatment cost and time, enhance the quality of RPD fabrication and ultimately improve oral function and overall quality of life of patients.
kw: removable partial dentures; digital workflow; artificial intelligence; software integration

title: Strategies for Kidney Outcomes Prevention and Evaluation - The SKOPE Study
abs: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is an enormous global public health problem affecting thousands of Singaporeans. CKD is associated with dialysis-requiring end-stage kidney disease (ESKD), cardiovascular disease (CVD) and death. Building on the success of our NMRC-funded Singhypertension Trial, we propose a pragmatic, randomized controlled trial of a multicomponent intervention “Strategies for Kidney Outcomes Prevention and Evaluation -SKOPE” versus “usual care” over 3 years among 894 adults (447 per arm) with CKD (estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) <60 ml/min/1.73m2) visiting the polyclinics in Singapore. SKOPE components include: 1) nurses trained as health coaches for CKD specific lifestyle counselling using in-person and remote meetings; 2) training physicians in standardized management of CKD; 3) subsidy on SGLT2 inhibitors; and 4) case review meetings. The specific aims are to: Specific Aim 1: determine whether SKOPE integrated into the primary care system will be more effective than usual care on the primary outcome of preserving kidney function (eGFR slope), and the secondary outcomes of lowering cardiovascular risk, and improving health-related quality of life in patients with CKD. Specific Aim 2: perform a mediation analysis and estimate the extent to which changes in lifestyle, clinical risk factors, and pharmacologic therapy mediate the benefit of SKOPE versus usual care on preserving kidney function. Specific Aim 3: determine the incremental cost-effectiveness of SKOPE compared with usual care on quality-adjusted life-years gained from the health system perspective. We will also perform a budget impact analysis. Specific Aim 4a: assess the facilitators and barriers to and the acceptability of SKOPE from the key stakeholders’ perspectives. Specific Aim 4b: explore the impact of a potential or existing pandemic (example COVID-19) on CKD care delivery. If successful, scaling-up SKOPE in primary care clinics would prevent death and disability related to ESKD and CVD and reduce patients’ sufferings in Singapore and globally.
kw: Chronic Kidney Disease; End-stage Kidney Disease; Cardiovascular Disease; Health Services Research; Primary Care; Cost Effectiveness

title: Uncovering the role of the gut-brain axis in fat preference
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Although humans have an innate preference for fat, which is a macronutrient, this preference can also be maladaptive: over-eating of high-fat food is linked to diabetes, obesity, heart disease, and a plethora of other health problems. The basic mechanism of fat preference must be determined in order for us to manage our unhealthy desire for high-fat food. My preliminary results have revealed an important hint towards answering this question. I found that ingestion of fat robustly activates specific neural substrates of the gut-vagal-brain axis. Here, I test the hypothesis that this novel gut-brain circuit mediates fat preference. Aim 1: I propose to resolve real-time activity of those brainstem neurons by calcium imaging, while the mouse is ingesting fat, or when fat is directly infused into the gastrointestinal tract, bypassing oral consumption. We need to understand the temporal dynamics of those neurons in order for us to find out when does so-called fat perception begin in the brainstem during a meal, and how durable or long-lasting this sensory percept is in the brainstem. Aim 2: In order devise methods to moderate our preference for fat via the gut-brain axis, we first need to understand the role of the gut-brain neurons linking fat sensory input to preference behavioural output. Thus, I will silence the activity of the gut-brain axis neurons, and determine the impairments in fat preference behaviour. Aim 3: For fat chemical stimuli to be transduced into neural signals in the gut, there must be specific receptors. While fat stimuli are infused into the gut, I will add candidate receptor antagonists while assaying for loss of brainstem neural signals. Conversely, infusion of agonists/ activators of those receptors should reliably induce gut-brain neural activity just as fat would. This will be proof of principle that specific chemicals can modulate the gut-brain circuit.
kw: Neurobiology; Molecular Biology; Behaviour; Gut-Brain Axis; Food Preference

title: Role of resident arterial LYVE-1 expressing macrophages in preventing atherogenic vascular remodeling and (underlying) mechanisms
abs: Despite advances in primary and secondary prevention management, cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) was the top leading cause of all death in Singapore last year and contributes to one-third of deaths worldwide. Atherosclerosis is a lipid-driven inflammatory condition characterized by plaque build-up in large and medium sized arteries. Depending on the affected artery can lead life-threatening CVD complications including coronary heart disease, ischemic stroke and peripheral artery diseases. Among immune cells, macrophages emerged as the key cells that drive atherosclerosis progression and regression. Since the discovery of resident arterial macrophages, their involvement during atherosclerosis remains unknown, mainly due to their heterogeneity in origin, phenotype and function. We have recently identified a population of resident arterial macrophages expressing lymphatic vessel endothelial hyaluronan receptor-1 (LYVE-1) that maintain arterial integrity and health. In atherosclerotic preclinical models and human, loss of LYVE-1+ macrophages correlated with disease severity and specific depletion of LYVE-1+ macrophages augments atherosclerosis. According to these preliminary data, we hypothesis that resident arterial LYVE-1+ macrophages prevent atherosclerotic vascular remodelling and the phenotypic/functional transitions of LYVE-1+ macrophages during atherosclerosis progression and regression is investigated in this research proposal using lineage tracing models and single-cell transcriptomic technologies. Endothelin 1 (ET-1) is a potent vasoconstrictor and promotes atherogenesis. Recent studies have demonstrated a novel role of macrophage endothelial receptor type B (ETB) for the clearance of ET-1 via endocytosis in preclinical hypertensive models however, the macrophage population mediating this beneficial effect remains unknown. Our preliminary findings from transcriptomic studies and protein analysis revealed gene enrichment in endocytosis pathways and ETB expression by arterial LYVE-1+ macrophages compared to other macrophage subsets in healthy and atherosclerotic arteries. Here, we will investigate whether LYVE-1+ macrophages ameliorate atherosclerosis via mediating ET-1 clearance. Taken together, the results achieved from this proposal could provide discoveries for new biomarkers or therapies for CVDs.
kw: Cardiovascular diseases; atherosclerosis; macrophage; lymphatic vessel endothelial hyaluronan receptor (LYVE-1); endothelin-1; endothelial receptor type B.

title: Investigating the role of m6A RNA methylation in long term memory and neurodegeneration
abs: A better understanding of biological mechanisms that underlie cognition and neuropathology is of paramount importance to our society. The molecular mechanisms that mediate memory are insufficiently understood and major neurological disorders remain incurable. Along with studies in the literature, our preliminary research indicates that neuronal ribonucleoprotein particles (RNP) facilitate memory. However, in the presence of pathologic stress, disordered RNPs nucleate into misfolded protein seeds that ultimately induce neurodegeneration. The formation of RNP granules is facilitated by the presence of m6A-modified mRNA and the main m6A reader protein YTHDF was demonstrated to stabilize RNP granule assembly. We have recently used Drosophila to show that YTHDF1 function is required for memory. How m6A signalling and YTHDF modulate memory and how RNP granules are mechanistically involved remains to be investigated. We hypothesize that m6A methylation and YTHDF1 play a key role in neuronal RNP function and that local mRNA translation at RNP granules is required for long-term memory. We speculate that under pathologic stress conditions, intrinsically disordered RNP proteins form aggregation clusters that ultimately induce neurodegeneration, potentially by blocking cellular transport. To address these hypotheses we propose to carry out detailed investigations into RNP granule composition and correlate our molecular findings with learning and memory phenotypes. To this end we will employ proteomic BioID labeling approaches in cell culture and aversive odor learning paradigms in Drosophila. Specifically, we aim to investigate 1) whether the RNP network is required for long-term memory; 2) what role does m6A methylation play in physiological RNP function and; 3) what mechanisms drive RNP-induced pathology. Providing answers to these questions will conceptually advance the field of learning and memory and lead to novel strategies for therapeutic interventions against major neurodegenerative disorders and intellectual disability.
kw: Neuroscience; Memory; RNA; BioID; Neurodegeneration

title: Radiation-induced PD-L1 response in cancer – molecular investigations into the roles of KEAP1 and ferroptosis
abs: Inhibition of the tumor immune checkpoint PD-L1 can induce durable responses even in patients with advanced disease, but only benefits a minority of treated patients. Radiation synergizes with PD-L1 blockade in cancer, potentially through the induction of PD-L1 upregulation. However, while this synergy has been validated in several preclinical and clinical studies, its molecular mechanisms has not been clearly elucidated. The increasingly complex cellular role of PD-L1 has also not been fully investigated. To address this scientific question, we performed an unbiased CRISPR screen to identify genes that regulate radiation-specific PD-L1 upregulation. KEAP1, a commonly mutated gene in cancer, and its related cell death pathway ferroptosis, were found to regulate PD-L1 after tumor irradiation. Silencing KEAP1 or inhibition of ferroptosis both upregulate PD-L1 after irradiation of treated urothelial tumor cells, and can potentially be targeted to synergize with radiation and PD-L1 blockade in these tumors. In our first aim, we propose molecular profiling to determine the mechanism of how KEAP1 and ferroptosis regulates radiation-induced PD-L1 expression. Intriguingly, KEAP1 silencing and ferroptosis inhibition led to an increase in DNA damage in treated cancer cells. We thus hypothesized that the upregulation of PD-L1 after KEAP1 silencing might be related to a newly uncovered role of PD-L1 in DNA repair. For our second specific aim, we will investigate the role of PD-L1 in KEAP1 inhibition/ferroptosis inhibition-induced DNA damage. Since KEAP1 and ferroptosis regulate cellular ROS levels, serum or urine-based ferroptosis or ROS biomarkers might also predict patient response to radiation and PD-L1 blockade. Therefore, in our third aim, we propose metabolic profiling of patient blood and urine using a targeted panel of ferroptosis and ROS-linked metabolites to identify biomarkers of response to radiation and PD-L1 inhibition. We will also correlate this to patient tumor PD-L1 expression levels wherever possible.
kw: Radiation, PD-L1, KEAP1, Ferroptosis

title: Neural mechanisms of genetic risk for essential tremor: a multi-cohort, multi-modal, imaging-genetics study
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: The aetiology of essential tremor is unknown. This results in difficulties in diagnosis (including a need for more quantitative, informed subtyping), a lack of “root-cause” treatments and large economic costs. While essential tremor-related genetic loci have been identified, and specific brain abnormalities in an oscillating “tremor network” are known to exist, these do not individually explain clinical status. Instead, it is believed that essential tremor is caused by complex interactions among many genetic, epigenetic and environmental factors. Across imaging studies of essential tremor, there is a lack of power, replicability and use of up-to-date technology. Therefore, we aim to elucidate the neural mechanisms of genetic risk for essential tremor in a robust study design using advanced MRI techniques. To do this, we will recruit people with essential tremor and matched healthy controls from our existing clinical database. Participants will undergo MRI, genotyping and tremor assessment. Using diffusion and functional MRI, we will measure microstructure and connectivity of the tremor network using a novel machine learning “tremor network fingerprint” approach. We will then test whether this can (a) differentiate idiopathic from inherited essential tremor and (b) mediate the relationship between genetic variability and diagnostic status. We will then test whether our findings are replicable in a second large group available from the UK Biobank. This work will identify new aetiologic models and therapeutic targets. This will enable more quantitative, principled diagnosis, subtyping and treatment decisions using new evidence-based guidelines. The effects of this would be lower economic burden, more efficient healthcare and increased quality of life for those with essential tremor. This will be the world’s first imaging-genetics study in essential tremor and the largest such cohort with MRI data. This work will support future integrative multi-omic studies in essential tremor to elucidate its aetiology.

title: Comparison of Focal Inner and Outer Retina Structure and Function to Accurately Diagnose Glaucoma in High Myopia Eyes
abs: High myopia (HM) and glaucoma are leading causes of sight loss worldwide. Present methods for diagnosing glaucoma cannot accurately detect whether structural or functional losses of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs), the predominant cell-type involved in glaucoma, in HM eyes are due to glaucoma or HM alone. HM is associated with generalized retinal thinning involving both inner and outer layers, while glaucoma affects mainly inner retinal i.e. RGC layers. Current diagnostic tests for glaucoma do not differentiate between inner and outer retinal damage. Therefore, I aim to establish normative benchmarks for localized structural measures of both inner and outer retinal thickness and capillary density in HM eyes. I will also investigate the association of glaucoma with localized inner retinal thickness or superficial capillary density, among HM eyes with corresponding visual field defects, after normalizing against outer retinal thickness and deep capillary density in a case-control study sample. I hypothesize that HM eyes with glaucoma will show significant localized thinning in the inner retinal layer and superficial capillary network, after normalizing against outer retina measurements. A prospective case-control study will be performed, where the inclusion criteria are based on retrospective clinical data. Subjects with HM will be classified as 'normal without visual field defects, 'control with non-progressing visual field defects' or 'glaucoma with progressing visual field defects' and undergo automated perimetry (HVF), optical coherence tomography (OCT) and OCT angiography (OCTA). Normative inner/outer retina layer thickness ratios and superficial/deep capillary density ratios will be generated from the 'normal' group, to determine if there is significant deviation of localized inner retinal measurements in the ‘control and ‘glaucoma’ groups after normalizing against outer retinal measurements. The association between glaucoma and localized thinning of the inner retinal layer or capillary density will be examined using mixed effects regression models. Preliminary data suggests this approach is feasible.
kw: myopia; glaucoma; precision medicine

title: Nano-scale structures for versatile transfection of diverse patient-derived immune cells
abs: Significance of research: Cancer is a deadly disease that is estimated to affect one in every five people in Singapore according to the National Cancer Centre. Chimeric Antigen Receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy is a promising treatment for cancer but gold-standard transfection tools using viruses and bulk electroporation to generate CAR-T cells provide low efficiency while compromising cell viability. There is an unmet clinical and commercial need to develop DNA delivery techniques that are efficient and minimally perturbative. Hypotheses: Magnetic nano-scale technology named magnetic nano-electro-injection (MagNEI) can be used for non-viral delivery of DNA to generate CAR-immune cells for cancer immunotherapy with high efficiency and minimal biological perturbations. Research aims: MagNEI platform leverages on nano-structure-localised electroporation and magnetic forces to deliver and transport DNA into the nuclei of immune cells for long-term, stable gene expressions. The first aim of this project is to optimise the MagNEI technology to deliver clinically relevant DNA cargo encoding for CAR proteins such as CD19 to generate CAR-T cells for clinical use. Despite the promise of other immune cell types like natural killer and dendritic cells for cancer immunotherapy, there is no good method to deliver DNA to genetically engineer these cells. The second aim of this project is to optimise MagNEI as a versatile DNA transfection tool for diverse immune cells. Methodology and approach: The physical, electrical, and magnetic parameters of MagNEI to deliver DNA will first be optimised with immune cells from healthy controls, followed by immune cells from cancer patients. The impact of MagNEI DNA delivery on critical biological attributes including proliferation, cancer-killing efficacy, migration, cytokine production and gene expressions will be assessed. The project is expected to generate academic and clinical impact on CAR-immune cell engineering and attract commercial interests to support Singapore’s ambition to become a leader in cell therapy.
kw: Nano-structures; immuno-engineering; chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy; cancer

title: Investigating the functional role of aging-regulated lncRNAs in adipocyte metabolism during aging
abs: Aging is an inevitable physiological process that increases the vulnerability for prevalent diseases such as COVID-19 and cardiovascular diseases. During aging, adipose tissue undergoes significant changes in cellular population, insulin sensitivity, regenerative capacity, etc. leading to the functional decline of adipose organs. Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) are emerging as key regulators in various biological processes including aging, while the function and mechanism of lncRNAs remain largely unknown during aging, especially in adipocyte metabolism. In our preliminary study, we identified thousands of aging-regulated lncRNAs (AR-lncRNAs) in 11 tissues across the mouse life span. Interestingly, most of them are found in white adipose tissues. About two hundred AR-lncRNAs are commonly regulated in both epididymal white adipose tissue and inguinal white adipose tissue. Knocking down one of them, lnc-AdipoAR1 in primary adipocyte culture reveals an essential role of this lncRNA in adipogenesis. We hypothesize that lnc-AdipoAR1 functions as a novel regulator of the aging process by modulating adipogenesis in adipocytes. We aim to determine the function of lnc-AdipoAR1 in adipocyte metabolism in vitro and in vivo during aging (Aim 1) and the molecular mechanism used by lnc-AdipoAR1 to regulate adipogenesis (Aim 2). Moreover, we will also test the function of other novel AR-lncRNA candidates in adipocyte metabolism during aging using in vitro and in vivo models (Aim3). This proposed study will shed light on the function and mechanism of the AR-lncRNAs such as lnc-AdipoAR1 in regulating adipocyte differentiation and metabolism during aging, which will broaden our knowledge about aging and facilitate the development of RNA-based therapeutics for aging and aging-associated diseases.
kw: Aging, long non-coding RNA, adipocyte metabolism, adipose tissue

title: Near-Infrared Flexible Upconversion Implantable for Personalized Remote Phototherapeutics in Cancer
abs: Photodynamic therapy (PDT) comprises a light delivery technology segment and a photosensitizer drug segment to photosensitizes tumour specifically. These two components are highly inter-dependent on one another for effective PDT therapeutic efficacy and range. PDT confers several advantageous to complete standard surgical, chemo and radio-therapies, such as localized treatment which minimizes systemic side effects, ease-of repetitive use and the ability to stimulate the immune system to clear apoptotic tumour cells. One limitation faced by current clinical PDT in the light technology segment, is the low depth penetration efficacy of visible light. By combining multi-disciplinary upconversion nano-science to solve the problem in clinical PDT, we have developed a disruptive near-infrared (NIR) responsive luminescence implantable that is flexible and moldable to fit different anatomical needs as NIR has greater tissue depth penetration as compared to visible light. Clinical PDT is applicable to be used during post-debulking of tumour to target residual cancer cells, as such would require different designs of the implant to fit the cavity. Owing to the flexible and moldable nature of our implant, we are proposing to design personalized implants for each individual cancer case. The feature of such flexible NIR-responsive luminescent implant is a first of its kind, developed by us. This will create a disruptive technology in clinical PDT, where currently interstitial needle is being used to target deep tissue tumour. We have therefore created a new segment of flexible and battery free, light delivery implantable made from hydrogel and silicone that can be applied chronically under the skin to target recurrent tissue with comfort wireless PDT.
kw: Glioblastoma; Breast Cancer; Photodynamic Therapy; Upconversion; Nanotechnology; Near-infrared

title: Genetics and Cell-of-origin Influence Genomic Instability in Cancer
abs: Genomic instability (GI), or the propensity to accumulate mutations within DNA, is a hallmark of cancer. Copy number alterations (CNAs) are a common manifestation of GI. Changes in copy number (CN) can arise due to multiple factors such as diminished capacity to repair DNA double strand breaks or improper chromosome segregation during mitosis. However, the degree and source of CN-based GI can vary widely by malignancy, and our knowledge of the factors contributing to this diversity is limited. We hypothesize that CN-based GI patterns — as measured by genome-wide scores and signatures — are influenced by both cell-of-origin (Specific AIm 1) and germline genetics (Specific Aim 2). To test this hypothesis, we will first generate somatic CN profiles and germline genotypes from a large collection of patients (n = 17,514) representing dozens cancer types (n = 17,514). Bespoke CN signatures will be generated from these patients using non-negative matrix factorization. Numerous GI scores and CN signature activities (scores/signatures) will be estimated for each sample using our SegsToSigs software. These scores/signatures will be compared to one another, across cancer types, and associated with driver gene mutations. We will also evaluate their ability to prognosticate clinical outcomes. In previous work, we were able to associate genetic background with mutation signature activity in breast cancer. Here, using common polymorphisms from SNP arrays and rare, deleterious coding variants from exome sequencing, we will associate inherited variation with scores/signatures to generate pan-cancer quantitative trait loci for GI (giQTLs). Any candidate genes tagged by giQTLs — particularly those harboring rare, deleterious variants — will be validated in vitro with isogenic cell lines. Overall, these efforts will help delineate the underlying biology of CN-based GI while simultaneously providing opportunities to discover clinically-relevant biomarkers.
kw: Cancer, Genetics, Genome Instability

title: Targeting α-synuclein aggregation as a therapeutic strategy for Parkinson’s disease
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Parkinson’s disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative diseases with no existing medication to stop or slow down its progression. Lewy bodies (LBs), primarily composed of fibrillar α-synuclein (α-syn), constitute one of the most prominent pathological features of PD. In our preliminary work, we have established an in vitro α-syn aggregation cell model in which ubiquitin, LAMP1 and phosphorylated α-syn were enriched in α-syn aggregates, faithfully recapitulating the biochemical features of LBs. Utilizing this cell model, we have conducted targeted siRNA screening and identified a few gene hits that may affect the α-syn aggregation. The candidates include three known PD-related genes, EIF4G1, ATP13A2 and PLA2G6, further supporting the relevance of the cell model with PD. Based on our preliminary data, we hypothesize that the newly identified gene hits from the cell-based siRNA screening will modulate neuronal LB-like inclusions, having the potential to represent therapeutic targets for PD. Also, identification of underlying mechanisms by which these genes regulate α-syn aggregation may provide important clues towards PD pathogenesis. In the proposed study, we aim to investigate the genetic hits that regulate α-syn aggregation in human embryonic stem cell (ESC)-derived dopaminergic (DA) neurons. In addition, the effects of α-syn aggregation on the health of DA neurons and the mechanism of a-syn aggregation regulation by the identified target genes will be elucidated in this study. Upon completion of the proposed study, we expect to identify potential actionable drug targets which may reverse or halt PD pathogenesis through regulation of α-syn aggregation in DA neurons. Our ultimate goal is to develop therapeutics for PD, based on the targets identified in this study. Together, our study would clarify the role of α-syn aggregation and its regulation in the pathogenesis of PD and yield potential therapeutic targets to battle against PD.
kw: α-synuclein; aggregation; Parkinson’s disease; Lewy bodies; human dopaminergic neuron

title: “Stop Going Nuts”: Intervention strategies to IgE-mediated mast cell activation from in-depth computational structural modelling and cross-linking Mass Spectrometry
abs: Among food allergies, peanut allergy has become now the top trigger of anaphylaxis in children in Singapore. Type-I peanut allergy is IgE-mediated via interactions of allergen-activated IgE (an antibody) and its receptor FcεRIα on mast cell surface. Interfering with such IgE interactions may intervene the severe allergic responses. This work aims to study these IgE-mediated interaction mechanisms at the atomic level, combining computational structural modelling and experimental cross-linking Mass Spectrometry (XL-MS) for validation. We will use quantitative XL-MS that is not hampered by the size and flexibility on the whole allergen-IgE-FcεRIα system to address our research aims. Through full atomistic models of these movements, we can assess how they explain the measured binding affinities of these components, and thus to guide therapeutic interventions against peanut allergy.
kw: food allergy; peanut allergy; allergen-IgE-receptor complex; structural modeling; cross-linking mass spec

title: Novel Genetic and Neural Correlates of Social Influence of Feeding Behaviour
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Social facilitation of eating is a well-documented phenomenon in psychology. However, the genetic underpinnings of this behaviour are largely unknown, and neuronal mediators even less investigated. Our preliminary data show that, like humans, Drosophila melanogaster males and females fed in groups spent much longer feeding than singly fed animals, and females also consumed higher total volumes of food. This results suggests that manipulating group sizes alters feeding behaviours in laboratory settings in a low-cost genetic model animal and presents an opportunity to study the genetic basis of social facilitation of eating. Drosophila melanogaster in a high-throughput feeding assay, I propose to find genetic and neuronal factors which signal social inputs and influence feeding behaviour in a group setting using a combination of modern neuroscience and genomic methods. Single-cell RNAseq will be utilised to compare the whole transcriptome of singleton feeders and group feeders to isolate candidate genes likely to pay a role in differential feeding behaviour depending on group sizes. Candidate genes are then further studied in loss-of-function and gain-of-function experiments alongside neural circuit tracing techniques for their necessity and sufficiency in regulating social inputs influencing feeding behaviours.
kw: feeding behaviour, social behaviour, transcriptome

title: Human-Centric Lighting Automated Control System for Light Optimization (HALO) at a Singapore Community Hospital
abs: Background Disruption of the sleep-wake cycle is a known hospital stressor. Besides biological complications, disturbed sleep plays a contributory causal factor in the occurrence of many mental health disorders. These effects extend well beyond the hospitalization period. Various interventions have been explored. Environmental factors have consistently shown correlations with sleep quality. In fact, inappropriate lighting has been identified as the sole parameter contributing to poor sleep quality in hospitalized general ward patients upon initial admission. Human-Centric Lighting (HCL) involves not just the elimination of inappropriate lighting to improve sleep quality, but also the duplication and adaptation of natural sunlight to improve sleep quality. However, the circadian rhythm is affected by cumulative light exposure including light sources beyond the HCL intervention. This is of utmost clinical significance for patients who are not in intensive or critical care, and hence not easily confined within the area of the HCL intervention. Furthermore, current HCL interventions do not involve all clinically relevant lighting variables. What is needed is a control system that regulates the network of closed feedback loops for clinically-relevant lighting variables. Overall Aim The overall aim of this study is to achieve Proof-of-Concept (POC) for a prototype Human-Centric Lighting Automated Control System for Light Optimization (HALO) at a Singapore Community Hospital (CH). This will be achieved through a scoping and design exercise, high-level algorithm development, virtual simulation and scenario testing. Specific Objectives O1 Achieve Technology Readiness Level (TRL) 2 by - Scoping and design exercise to gather clinical requirements for HALO - Taking measurements at a typical CH ward O2 Achieve TRL 3 and POC by - Establishing key performance parameters for HALO - Developing high-level algorithm for HALO - Developing virtual simulation for HALO - Validating predictions of the above key performance parameters through scenario testing
kw: Human-Centric Lighting; sleep deprivation; falls

title: Rapid immune-profiling assay for real-time stratification of acute infections and sepsis
abs: Acute infections can incite a dysregulated host response and cause organ dysfunction, leading to a syndrome called sepsis. At the centre of this response is the immune system mediated primarily by white blood cells. Paradoxically, the immune system itself may act as a double-edged sword and induce collateral damage to the host through its over-exuberant activity. The diagnosis of sepsis is often not straightforward clinically due to a myriad of non-specific symptoms and signs patients may present with. Current biomarkers have low diagnostic performance or are laggard, and thus unable to reflect the actual immune activity in the patient. Delay in diagnosis and implementing evidence-based management may precipitate catastrophic outcomes. When activated in conditions such as acute infections, white blood cells undergo changes to their count, size, distribution and deformability. We have developed a prototype using deterministic lateral displacement microfluidic technology to directly interrogate these innate biophysical properties. Measurements can be done rapidly at point-of-care in real-time, label-free using very small volumes of unprocessed direct whole blood sample to derive bespoke immune response signatures. We aim to further develop and optimize the portable integrated automated electronic system, and simultaneously validate the diagnostic performance of immune response signatures on a cohort of patients with different severity of acute infections and sepsis. Our preliminary data support the hypothesis that we can stratify the immune status of patients with acute infections and sepsis in real-time through rapid immune-profiling assay based on white blood cells biophysical properties. This adjunct to clinical assessment could allow better triage and appropriate level of care to be rendered quickly to patients via more precise and individualized immune profiling to guide management. The ability to perform repeated sampling at low cost could enable monitoring of patients’ response to therapy in inpatients and outpatients, in both urban and rural settings.
kw: Infections; sepsis; inflammation; microfluidics; immune profiling

title: Predicting Future Hospital Bed States Using Length of Stay Predictor Based on Admission Text
abs: Modern hospitals have to address evolving needs in bed capacity generated by seasonal variations in the demand for healthcare. This creates surges in bed capacity that are often unpredictable resulting in crowding or long wait times in the emergency department or cancellations of surgeries. Current approaches to address this issue is based on a set of rules that determine the appropriate allocation of beds that often necessitates a tradeoff between emergency vs elective bed admissions. However, these rules only account for present bed states and not projected bed states, which in turn, are affected by a multitude of biopsychosocial factors. Hypothesis: The hypothesis is that a text based, length of stay predictor (LOS) predictor would be able to accurately abstract attributes that predict length of stay, in an explainable manner, so as to enable right siting of care and to implement pre-emptive interventions. Methodology: Primary aim: To train new medical word embeddings using Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT), on a large local medical text dataset. This pre-trained corpus is then used to train the ‘Augurium’ NLP tool to predict LOS using population level inpatient and emergency department datasets. Supplementary aim: To test the ability of this trained model NLP to detect variation in LOS that might indicate the onset of new complications or unexpected prolonged stays in the hospital. This is achieved using a steady state model with continuous incremental learning (IL). Feasibility of study: Given the team’s experience in running large scale neural networks workflows on GPUs, it is hoped that the tests would yield a highly tuneable and explainable LOS model. In addition, the pre-trained medical word embeddings may be used to for other prediction tasks, such as predicting complications, using the same training datasets.
kw: Length of stay predictor; natural language programming; complications predictor; bed optimisation; incremental learning; right siting of care

title: Non-invasive right atrial pressure measurement
abs: Estimation of right atrial pressure is a critical step in management of patients in heart failure, have pulmonary hypertension, or other right sided heart problems. The gold standard of measurement is by invasive introduction of a pressure transducer through the venous system into the heart chambers and measuring direct pressure through a fluid filled channel. This is invasive with a small risk of potentially life-threatening complications. Naturally, patient uptake of the above procedure is also limited. Non-invasive estimates of right atrial pressure have been limited in accuracy and temporal resolution. Our aim is to develop a non-invasive method of estimation of right atrial pressure with high temporal resolution to save patient costs, reduce morbidity, and improve follow up and titration of therapy. When a patient is placed in a supine position, the internal jugular vein is at the same level as the right atrium and direct transduction will allow measurement of right atrial pressures. We have developed a unique sensor consisting of a piezoelectric pressure sensor embedded in a PDMS patch to be applied at the landmarked area of the right internal jugular vein. Early demonstra-tions have shown excellent correlation against non-invasive blood pressure measurements when transduced against the radial artery. In further testing with an internal jugular vein phantom with simu-lated patient waveforms, the sensor has also shown good results and correlation. Software processing will account for movement and competing carotid artifacts. Our intent is to correlate our sensor’s results with the gold standard of invasive right atrial pressure measurement, and as such, provide a cheaper and safer way of providing prognostically significant investigations for better patient outcomes. Eventual direction is industrial collaboration or start-up and push to market with subsequent grants or capital investment.
kw: Cardiology; Right Atrial Pressure; Pulmonary Hypertension; Heart Failure

title: Exosome-infused Device for Enhanced Spinal Fusion
abs: Over 600 million people in the world suffer from lower back pain, causing a significant healthcare burden that is increasing with an aging global population. Most people require surgical spinal fusion with the use of bone grafts to achieve segmental stability and pain relief. However, these bone grafting procedures suffer significant drawbacks such as donor site morbidity, limited healing potential and considerable failure fates. To overcome these limitations, adjuvant therapies using mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) have been supplemented to bone grafts to improve bone healing in spinal fusion. Although the use of MSCs was originally predicated on their differentiation potential, the therapeutic efficacy of MSCs has been increasingly attributed to its paracrine secretion, particularly exosomes. Unlike living cells, exosomes are small, non-living and could be mass-produced from a standardized cell source. These attributes reduce the overall cost through simplified and less costly manufacturing, storage, transport and administration. This proposal seeks to establish the requisite pre-clinical proof-of-concept for clinical testing of MSC exosomes as the next-generation “cell-free” therapeutic for supplementation to bone grafts in spinal fusion. Our preliminary findings have shown that MSC exosomes can be loaded in collagen sponge and that a single implantation of exosome-loaded collagen sponge was able to promote bone regeneration in a rat calvarial defect model. Here, we propose the development of a novel, shelf-stable exosome-loaded collagen sponge for use in spinal fusion. We hypothesize that an exosome-loaded collagen sponge would be effective in sustaining a high local concentration of exosomes required for well-coordinated mobilisation of multiple cell types and cellular responses critical for robust bone formation in spinal fusion. Accordingly, we will optimise the exosome loading, dosing, administration, and investigate the mechanisms of action in our cell culture studies and rat model, before progressing to the pig posterolateral spinal fusion model relevant for clinical translation.
kw: Exosome; Spinal Fusion; Bone Graft

title: Assessing Structural Interactions of Anti Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA) Antibodies with Epitopes on HLAntigens in Transplantation (ASIA_HLA_T)
abs: While kidney transplantation (KTX) is the best treatment for end stage kidney failure, interaction of the transplant patient’s immune system against mismatched donor Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA), results in immune responses that lead to acute and/or chronic transplant rejection and transplant failure. Immunosuppression can abrogate T-cell-mediated transplant rejection but is less effective in preventing B-cell initiated, Donor Specific Anti-HLA Antibody (DSA)-mediated rejection (ABMR) which occurs in 40% of KTX over time. Current assays utilizing single antigen beads (SAB) for Anti-HLAAb detection are unable to discriminate detrimental DSA and have a poor predictive value for ABMR. Our group has previously demonstrated correlations between the structural relationship of a monoclonal Anti-HLAAb (MAb; HLA A*11:01), derived from a non-immune library, to its binding site on A11 with in vitro functional assays of cytotoxicity and affinity of the antibody to its HLA. We hypothesize that structural characteristics of Anti-HLAAb, the relationship between epitopic determinants on HLA with the corresponding complementary determinants on Anti-HLAAb (paratope), and their correlations with functional studies of cytotoxicity and affinity, will lead to identification of characteristics of detrimental, clinically relevant antibodies. MAb generated from isolated memory B cells of sensitized transplant patients (immune library) and from a pre-existing non-immune phage-antibody library will be studied. MAb will be characterized for HLA specificity and reactivity (with SAB on a validated Luminex® platform), functionality (Cytotoxicity, Antibody Dependent Cellular Cytotoxicity), affinity to target HLA (with Quartz crystal microbalance technology) and their structural relationship by X-Ray Crystallography. This proposal will evaluate these structural-functional relationships for Anti-HLAAb to specific Class I and II HLA, especially those derived from KTX whose immune response is anticipated to manifest a deleterious Anti-HLAAb repertoire. This proposal is expected to lead to a more precise and systematic approach to defining sensitization in organ transplantation and offer approaches for mitigating graft injury.
kw: Kidney transplant; Antibody Mediated Rejection; Donor Specific Antibodies; Histocompatibility; Eplets; Immunogenicity

title: Role of Type 2 Innate Lymphoid Cells in childhood idiopathic nephrotic syndrome
abs: Background/Aims: Childhood idiopathic nephrotic syndrome (iNS) is associated with significant morbidity, particularly due to steroid-dependent or steroid-resistant (SD/SR) disease. Existing data implicate a direct effect of Th2 cytokines on podocytes in disease pathogenesis. Recent evidence in asthma suggests that Type 2 Innate Lymphoid Cells (ILC2s) are a relatively steroid-resistant source of Th2 cytokines. We hypothesise that (i) ILC2s contribute to the pathological production of Th2 cytokines in iNS relapse and (ii) SD/SR disease is mediated by ILC2 steroid-resistance. We aim to (a) compare ILC2 number and Th2 cytokine production in relapse compared to remission and healthy controls, both in blood and kidney tissue, (b) quantify ILC2 Dexamethasone-sensitivity in vitro and correlate this with clinical SD/SR, and (c) recapitulate iNS through adoptive cell transfer of patient-specific ILC2s into an immunocompromised mouse model. Methodology: 24 active patients will be recruited and blood sampled in relapse and 1 month after entering remission; their renal biopsy tissue will also be retrieved. ILC2s (CD45+Lin-CD127+CRTH2+) and Th2 cytokine (IL-4, IL-13) production, will be studied in peripheral blood following 48h culture with IL-33±Dexamethasone using multi-parameter flow cytometry, or in renal biopsy tissue using Multiplex Immunohistochemistry (Vectra®). For adoptive cell transfer, NSGTM rats will be injected with 2.5x104 ILC2s from patients in relapse, and followed one-month for the development of proteinuria. Feasibility: Preliminary experiments demonstrate that blood ILC2s are higher in iNS patients in relapse compared to healthy controls (12±1.88% vs 4.10±1.94%, p=0.03). High-dose Dexamethasone treatment reduces blood ILC2s in iNS patients in relapse (p=0.07), but not in patients in remission or in healthy controls. Importance: This study will enable us to use ILC2s as a biomarker of immunological remission in individual patients, and thus titrate immunosuppression to prevent relapses or prolonged over-immunosuppression. Implicating ILC2s may also allow the rational development of a new generation of iNS therapeutics.
kw: innate lymphoid cells; idiopathic nephrotic syndrome; cytokines

title: Cost-Effective Removal and Recovery of Heavy Metals from Non-Incinerable Wastes for Recycling and Reuse with Near-Zero Waste Discharge
abs: In this proposal, we aim to develop a closed waste loop for recovery of heavy metals from toxic industrial non-incinerable waste (NIW) and sewage sludge incinerated ash (SSIA) that will produce near-zero waste discharge. The novelty of this proposal includes: 1) invention of the closed-loop zero-waste heavy metal removal process from toxic industrial sludge, 2) synthesis, characterization and use of novel stationary materials for heavy metals enrichment, 3) development of sequential precipitating reagents to remove and recover heavy metals one-by-one so that the single compound of the heavy metal precipitate can be used as industrial materials, and 4) novel electrochemical process for reuse of heavy metals from NIW and SSIA. This proposal will produce cleaned solid sludge/ash for agriculture, horticulture, and construction use. The process for cost-effective removal and recovery of heavy metals from non-incinerable wastes for recycling and reuse with near-zero waste discharge will have significant environmental benefits including low energy consumption, no carbon dioxide emission, no toxic gases produced, no solid waste generated, and no wastewater discharged. The proposed method serves to remove and recover heavy metals from solid wastes for recycling and reuse and to achieve a significant reduction of amounts of NIW and SSIA. Furthermore, some reovered heavy metal compounds will also be further processed for industrial use. From the cost-benefit analysis for a typical plant, the benefits would be ten times higher than the cost. To ensure successful commercialization of the technologies developed, we have established collaborations with industrial collaborators in the relevant industrial sector. Our key collaborators will provide real samples for evaluation, set up arrangements for pilot tests, and conduct beta-testing of the products developed. They will also be potential customers of the process and products developed in this project. Compared with commercial processes, the method developed in our proposal has competitive advantages in the unique capability to remove of all types of heavy metals by using a combination of chelators and stationary materials to enrich them onto solids, the cost-effective solution to employ acid regeneration to release free metal ions for subsequent sequential precipitation, and the additional benefits of producing individual heavy metals compounds for industrial uses.

title: An Integrated Geophysical and Geotechnical Method for Sinkhole Detection During Bored Tunnelling
abs: This project aims to develop an integrated detection method to monitor the occurrence and propagation of sinkholes above and in front of Tunnel Boring Machine (TBM). This method overcomes the shortages of the current geophysical methods, such as seismic reflection and ground penetrating radar, in terms of detection depth and image resolution. The integrated method includes global detection, coarse detection, fine detection and special detection, depending on the needs in different geological environments and for various tunnelling situations. Global detection will use Singapore 3D geological model with the latest site investigation data to assess the regions of poor geological conditions. A fast and continuous seismic scattering monitoring approach will be conducted as coarse detection to diagnose geological anomalies above and in front of TBM. For fine detection, a well-proven and accurate detection system will be used to visualize the sizes and locations of these anomalies. Special detection is designed to identify potential risks using either a Cone Probing Tool for restricted surface areas or using the detection system inside TBM for the areas beneath building basements. The method provides robust solutions to evaluate excessive over-excavation, to determine mixed-face or cavity conditions within a depth of 20-40 m, and to interpret soil profile variations below existing buildings.

title: A lncRNA candidate in cardiac differentiation and disease pathophysiology
abs: Heart failure (HF) 5-year survival is only ~50%. This is worse than even for some cancers. Contemporary success from molecular-targeted cancer therapy however, is proof of concept that careful molecular characterisation of the failing heart may yet yield game-changing novel therapies for HF. Despite the SERCA2a gene therapy trial that failed at Phase IIb, more advanced molecular candidates such as histone modifiers and microRNAs are now in the pipeline. RNA therapeutics has especially attracted recent attention since FDA-approval for RNAi treatment against amyloidosis, and very soon hyperlipidemia. Moreover, as central gene regulatory factors, long noncoding RNA (lncRNA) may target higher-order gene programmes. From single cell transcriptomes of maturing human embryonic stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes, we have identified and validated the indispensable role of a lncRNA we named VENTHEART in cardiomyocyte specification. VHRT is conserved only in primates, and has muscle-restricted expression. Even in the heart, it is only expressed in cardiomyocytes, not in non-myocytes (fibroblasts, smooth muscle cells, endothelial cells). Having proven its crucial role in late cardiomyocyte development, we have concurrently discovered that the VHRT locus is a significant GWAS and eQTL hit for HF. Integrated genomic analysis suggests that reduced VHRT expression is associated with increased risk for HF. We therefore propose (a) to deepen molecular mechanistic characterisation of VHRT, including resolve conflicting evidence for whether VHRT encodes a putative peptide, (b) dissect out the gene regulatory programme of VHRT and determine upstream regulators, and (c) elucidate the therapeutic value of VHRT using engineered heart tissue constructed with hES-CM. The latter is important because of concordant evidence that VHRT is downregulated in dilated human hearts, and the VHRT knockdown gene profile is largely converse to that of HF. Uncovering the VHRT molecular pathway may therefore open avenues for new co-linear therapeutic options around the VHRT pathway.

title: Precision Medicine on Head CT to Identify Neurodegeneration through Deep Learning-Based Segmentation Empowered with Brain MR Morphometry (PRECISE)
abs: Background Neurodegenerative disorders such as dementia, parkinsonian gait disorders and fall-related traumatic brain injury are a growing public health concern with the aging population. Radiological assessment of neurodegeneration on screening head CT, heavily utilized for older adult fall-related traumatic head injuries, is subjective and expertise-dependent. Automated quantitative brain volumetry aids detection of neurodegeneration and increasingly available on brain MRI, but non-existent on CT. However, MRI is expensive and not widely available. Recent deep learning (DL) approaches showed state-of-the-art performance in complex medical image segmentation tasks, and good results in automating segmentation on head CT. Specific Aims Using a U-Net convolutional network model and paired CT–MRI big data, we will develop an automated segmentation model on head CT, build normative quantitative brain volumes for local target population, and demonstrate the radiological utility of these measures in radiological head CT reporting. Hypotheses We hypothesize that DL will automate CT brain segmentation with robust and accurate results, allow the repository of normative quantitative atlas-based volume outputs to be used as reference normative standards, and facilitate radiological detection of neurodegeneration. Methodology & Approach Paired head CT - high resolution multi-contrast brain MRI scans from 750 subjects aged 55-85 years (550 healthy and 200 patients clinically diagnosed with Alzheimer’s dementia or atypical Parkinsonism) will be acquired. Quantitative brain segmented volume outputs from the DL model will be validated against the MR volumetric gold standards. Value-add from the quantitative indices derived from automated segmentation on head CT will be assessed. Clinical Significance Harnessing novel AI technologies and good quality paired CT-MRI big data to automate accurate segmentation tools on head CT holds promise to provide objective biomarkers to empower precision medicine on head CT as the cheaper and more prevalent clinical neuroimaging alternative with wider scoping and cost-saving impacts on healthcare of our greying nation.
kw: CT; brain; segmentation; volume; MRI; deep learning; image synthesis; neurodegeneration; Alzheimer's dementia; Parkinson's disease

title: Non-invasive Prenatal Diagnosis (NIPD) of genetic disorders using massive parallel sequencing on circulating fetal nucleated red blood cells (FNRBCs) isolated from maternal blood.
abs: There are approximately 7,000 known genetic diseases with >250 new conditions described in medical literature every year. With a worldwide prevalence of ~1%, most genetic diseases are debilitating or even life-threatening. Age-related de novo mutations, especially de novo single nucleotide variants occur more commonly in paternal compared to maternal germ cells and are associated with increased risk of intellectual disability in the offspring. Definitive prenatal diagnoses rely on invasive procedures, which carry a 0.3-2% risk of miscarriage, and which remain the most reliable method of prenatal diagnosis of chromosomal aberrations as well as copy number variants. Current first-tier diagnostics have their limitations. Although well established, G-band analysis cannot detect cryptic translocations <3-5Mb. Chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) has replaced it as the first-tier clinical diagnostic test. However, CMA is limited by the inability to identify balanced rearrangements and is blind to copy-neutral events. We have known for decades that within the pregnant mother’s circulation lies information regarding the wellbeing of her fetus. Whole nucleated fetal cells can be harvested from the maternal circulation noninvasively. However, due to its rarity, fetal cells have to undergo genomic amplification for downstream analysis. Preimplantation genetic testing has shown the possibility of expanding the genome of single/few cells and detecting chromosomal aberrations using next-generation sequencing. We hypothesize that we can determine and detect a range of clinically-relevant genetic disorders during pregnancy by interrogating the genome of fetal cells obtained non-invasively. We envision this technology will enhance current prenatal diagnosis strategies. This opens new avenues/opportunities for individualized therapeutic interventions for condition­specific management that can lead to improved outcomes and quality of life such as genetic counseling/support, future family planning, cascade testing, justifying social and educational services, and connecting to condition­specific support groups. The ultimate goal is to provide autonomy and reproductive choice options to couples worldwide.
kw: Prenatal diagnosis; fetal cell; non-invasive; low-pass whole genome sequencing; de novo mutations; preimplantation genetic diagnosis

title: Defining mInimal residual diSease through major pathologiC response and biOmarker discovery in early stage EGFR-mutated non-small-cell lung cancer treated with neoadjuVant osimErtinib with/without chemotheRapy (DISCOVER)
abs: Background Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) mutations represent the most common subtype of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) in Asia. Patients with early-stage EGFR-mutated NSCLC remain at significant risk of recurrence after curative surgery and adjuvant chemotherapy. Three years of adjuvant osimertinib has been shown to improve disease-free survival (DFS) but long-term outcomes and cost-effectiveness remain undefined. Our institutional real-world data demonstrated that 37% of patients remain disease-free at 5 years without adjuvant osimertinib, underscoring the need to improve risk stratification. Aims DECODE aims to identify tissue-based molecular features that correlate with DFS in resected early-stage EGFR-mutated NSCLC and build recurrence risk prediction models incorporating molecular and clinicopathological data. Hypotheses are molecular features such as co-mutations, copy number alterations and RNA transcriptional changes are predictive of DFS outcomes, and integration of these molecular features with routine clinicopathological data such as stage and lymphovascular invasion can improve individualised recurrence risk predictions. Methodology Patients with stage IA-IIIA EGFR-mutated NSCLC with minimum 3 years follow up post-curative surgery will undergo whole exome sequencing and RNA-sequencing. Main outcome of interest would be 3-year DFS. Molecular features associated with DFS will be identified using Cox regression analysis. These findings will be integrated with clinicopathological data to select features that correlate with DFS on multivariate regression analysis. Risk prediction models will then be developed, for which both internal and external validation will be performed. Approach/Clinical Significance DECODE aims to address the unmet need of improving risk stratification among early-stage EGFR-mutated NSCLC patients to individualise adjuvant therapy recommendations and improve long-term outcomes. Given rising healthcare costs and accelerated regulatory approvals of novel adjuvant therapies based on DFS benefit, insights gleaned from DECODE could promote cost-effectiveness by identifying patients who are cured with surgery alone and distinguish them from those who need further adjuvant treatment such as osimertinib.
kw: EGFR; NSCLC, neoadjuvant

title: PRIME-IOL: intraocular PRessure- and fundus IMage-Exporting IntraOcular Lens for passive continuous monitoring of age-related eye conditions after cataract surgery
abs: Aims Age-related eye conditions such as age-related macular degeneration, diabetic retinopathy and glaucoma are the top causes of irreversible blindness, and they require frequent examinations for both screening and monitoring purposes. Cataract surgery is the commonest intraocular surgery and a permanent intraocular lens (IOL) is typically implanted. This presents an opportunity for miniaturised biosensors to be incorporated into the IOL in the same setting, though none has successfully implemented intraocular monitoring using the IOL. Our project aims to functionalise the IOL to enable continuous monitoring of intraocular pressure (IOP) and on-demand retinal imaging, and transmit this information wirelessly to an external device for remote monitoring of age-related eye conditions. Hypotheses We hypothesise that the IOL is a suitable platform for continuous IOP monitoring by a pressure-sensor on the haptic of the IOL, and we could attach a camera sensor on the IOL to perform retinal imaging, followed by wireless information transmission to an external device. Approach Our approach is to study the feasibility of incorporating miniaturised wireless sensors onto the current IOL design and transmit this information wirelessly to an external device, without compromising the existing optical properties and stability of the IOL. Methodology Our study will be performed in two phases - firstly, the development of IOL prototypes through precise engineering, followed by proof-of-concept in large animal models. By improvising on existing IOL designs, we will integrate an IOP sensor based on microfluidics-sensing technology into the haptic of the IOL to perform continuous passive IOP monitoring, anchor a small imaging sensor on the peripheral IOL optic, and evaluate wireless transmission of data collected onto an external device. We will test the safety, stability and functionality of this modified IOL prototype in large animal models for a period of up to three months post-surgically.
kw: cataract surgery; intraocular lens; biosensor; glaucoma; macular degeneration; diabetic retinopathy

title: Defining a minimum threshold of T-cell immunity for protection against viral infection: An experimental medicine approach
abs: The adaptive immune response to viral infection and vaccination comprises both an antibody-driven humoral immune response, as well as a cellular immune response driven primarily by T cells (T cell immunity). Although, T cell immunity is increasingly recognized to be as important as humoral immunity, it is seldom examined as a correlate of protection for vaccine development. This neglect of T cell immunity has resulted in many vaccine candidates that initially appear promising in pre-clinical or early phase testing based on their ability to elicit robust antibody responses, but fail to protect against infection when they reach late phase, large clinical trials. In order to select effective vaccines, it is thus crucial to define a protective “threshold” of T cell immunity. The overarching goal of my study is to document the role T cells play in protection against viral infection and define a quantitative threshold of T cells needed to protect against subsequent re-infection. I will conduct an experimental study in healthy adult volunteers, leveraging on the immunogenic properties of the licensed yellow fever (YF17D) and chimeric Japanese encephalitis-YF17D (JE-YF17D) vaccines. I will first compare the magnitude of the T cell responses elicited by the YF17D and JE-YF17D vaccines. I will then show that the level of viremia induced by these live-attenuated vaccines correlates with the magnitude of the resultant T cell responses. Finally, I will determine the threshold of virus-specific T cell immunity needed to protect against subsequent challenge infection with YF17D or JE-YF17D. The knowledge gleaned from this study would be would be instrumental when selecting promising vaccine candidates for further clinical development.
kw: T-cells; cellular immunity; flavivirus; vaccine;viral infection

title: Characterizing therapeutically resistant malignant paediatric brainstem gliomas
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Paediatric brainstem gliomas represent a therapeutically challenging group of tumours. In this group, up to 80% are diffuse midline gliomas (DMG) which are highly malignant with extremely poor prognosis. Radiotherapy is the current mainstay of treatment; however, disease recurrence and dissemination are inevitable. In recent years, advances in genomic technologies combinatorically with modern neurosurgical adjuncts have provided valuable insights into the molecular biology of DMGs. Nonetheless, effective treatments remain elusive at this stage. Studies in adult gliomas have highlighted the presence of a therapeutically resistant subpopulation of cells in the tumour that have been postulated to be responsible for the high rate of tumour recurrence and subsequent progression. Extrapolating this concept into DMG, we hypothesize that firstly, a similar subpopulation exists after radiation treatment in affected patients. Next, these surviving cells cause aggressive tumour recurrence and disease dissemination. Characterization of this subpopulation in DMG has never been previously reported. This study aims to characterise this therapeutically resistant subpopulation using patient-derived brainstem DMG cell lines via in vitro and in vivo approaches. Treatment-naïve cells will be treated with radiation with an intention to investigate the surviving population. In-depth molecular and functional studies will be performed on these cells to assess their tumorigenic properties. Overall, results from the project’s endeavours have translational potential for affected children and better disease understanding.
kw: paediatric malignant brainstem gliomas; cytokines

title: Dissection of the genetic determinants of virus attenuation of a clinically-tested live dengue vaccine strain
abs: A tetravalent dengue vaccine development has been challenging due to insufficient knowledge on DENV pathogenesis. Understanding the genetic and molecular basis of attenuation will allow us to develop a targeted mutagenesis approach to derive all 4 attenuated DENVs that is sufficiently safe but immunogenic. We have been studying the molecular properties of a live attenuated DENV2 strain, PDK53, which was derived through 53 serial passages of wild-type 16681 strain, in primary dog kidney cells. PDK53 has successfully completed a phase-3 clinical trial and cannot be transmitted by Aedes aegypti, which is an important safety feature, given that uncontrolled transmission of PDK53 risks acquisition of mutations that revert PDK53 to a wild-type phenotype. PDK53 offers a tractable system to understand the genetic determinants of viral attenuation and this study will focus on defining such genetic determinants in vivo in Aedes aegypti. Using site-directed mutagenesis, we show that only a glycine-to-aspartate substitution on position 53 in the non-structural protein 1 (NS1) attenuated 16681 infection, albeit not to the same extent as PDK53 in mosquitoes. Moreover, reversing this amino acid residue to its wild-type sequence on a PDK53 backbone did not result in full reversion to a wild-type phenotype. Collectively, these findings suggest that the other mutations in PDK53 could be interacting epistatically to contribute to the fully attenuated phenotype of PDK53. Here, we will use the tools our laboratory has established to construct viral mutants to define the combination of mutations that adds to the NS1 G53D substitution to fully attenuate PDK53 in Aedes aegypti, and how they act to attenuate DENV. We envisage that by the end of this study, a more complete overview of the genetic and mechanistic basis of virus attenuation can provide us a foundation to engineer attenuated DENVs to serve as candidates for 2nd-3rd generation dengue vaccines.
kw: Dengue virus; Live-attenuated vaccines; Aedes aegypti; PDK53; Epistasis

title: Understanding a single mutation in DENV NS2B that results in STING-dependent downstream effects that are both anti- and pro-viral
abs: Dengue virus (DENV) is an Aedes mosquito-transmitted virus that is prevalent throughout the tropical world. DENV exists as four antigenically distinct serotypes (DENV1-4) with no licensed antiviral drug to treat dengue and case management relies entirely on supportive care. Thus, any dengue vaccine, which remains an urgent public health need, must effectively protect against disease by all four DENV serotypes. Recent findings from our lab have shown that viral genetic changes in the epidemic strains of DENVs are more successful in evading or suppressing type-I interferon (IFN) responses. Correspondingly, we also found that a live attenuated DENV2 vaccine candidate (PDK53) is unable to evade IFN response, thus preventing the spread and transmission of the virus. This impaired ability to evade host antiviral response has, however, to be balanced by replicative fitness as antigen expression has to be at levels sufficient to induce immunogenicity. Understanding mutations that elicits both increased IFN response while being replicative-fit would enable a mechanistic approach to develop next generation dengue vaccine. Using a IFN-screening method that was developed in the lab, we identified a single DENV NS2B (I114T) mutation that generated a DENV strain that is able to replicate to sufficient levels to induce immune response while being sensitive to IFN, thus preventing dissemination of virus to neighbouring cells. Preliminary data suggests that NS2B I114T acts via stimulator of IFN gene (STING), stimulated through the inability of this mutant to contain DNA damage to host cells thus activating the DNA-sensing cGAS/STING pathway leading to type-I IFN induction. Furthermore, our data suggests that STING has both a known antiviral as well as a hitherto unknown pro-viral function. The combined pro- and anti-viral roles of STING could elicit the desired replicative fitness but retarded innate immune evasion phenotypes.
kw: Dengue; STING; NS2B; DNA damage; ER stress; autophagy

title: Regulating inflammation outcome through modulating mitochondrial metabolism
abs: Inflammation is an essential process to eliminate pathogens but must be rapidly resolved to prevent excessive activation of the immune system. Uncontrolled immune response will lead to hypercytokinemia, resulting in death. Chronic low levels of inflammation will lead to fibrosis and cancer. It is therefore beneficial to reduce inflammation when the body is incapable of resolving it itself. We identified an anti-inflammatory mitochondrial peptide that is expressed only during inflammation. As it incorporates into the complex IV of the electron transport chain, we named it MOCCI, short for Modulator Of Cytochrome C oxidase during Inflammation. Expression of MOCCI in cells leads to reduction in interferon response during viral challenge. We therefore hypothesise that MOCCI works through the election transport chain to modulate inflammation by altering mitochondrial metabolism. We predict that MOCCI-knockout mice will exhibit stronger immune response against viral infection. Using the funding, we will seek to answer the following: 1. Whether MOCCI is required for the resolution of interferon response during acute inflammation using knockout mouse models 2. The mechanism by which MOCCI modulate interferon response during viral infection, using a variety of biochemical methods 3. Whether MOCCI-overexpression by AAV delivery can prevent a cytokine storm during lethal viral infection The upregulation of a respiratory chain subunit during inflammation suggests that the electron transport chain plays a role in regulating the process. We propose that the electron transport chain could potentially be manipulated for immunodulation.
kw: Inflammation; mitochondrial metabolism; infectious disease; viral infection

title: Elucidating the impact of chromatin structure dysregulation in hepatocellular carcinoma development
abs: Although chromosomal structure and nuclear organization is essential to maintain normal cell functions, the consequence of its disorder in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) formation is unclear. In this proposal, we delete zinc finger protein 143 (Znf143), a key regulator of CTCF-bound chromatin interactions, in the liver using the Alb Cre/Znf143f/f mouse model and investigate the impact of chromosomal architecture dysregulation in HCC development. Our preliminary data suggest that ZNF143 maintains normal liver function and prevents HCC formation. Moreover, we found that, through mediating DNA binding affinity of CTCF, ZNF143 regulate expression of genes such as Cebpa through maintenance of chromatin interactions. We will perform systematic analyses to investigate the outcome of global dysregulation of chromatin structures in HCC formation after loss of Znf143. Through comprehensive analyses of expression profile, histone modification, binding of transcription factor, and dynamics of genome topology, we will be able to provide valid information on pervasive architectural changes and their functional significance on gene transcription regulation. Such regulatory mechanism study will provide novel strategies for early detection and therapeutic invention for HCC.
kw: hepatocellular carcinoma; chromatin structure; gene regulation

title: Role of ADAR1 in regulating inflammation and HCC pathogenesis via NF-kB driven lncRNAs
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Chronic inflammation in liver plays major role in the development of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). During the onset of HCC, cells activate immune signaling molecules including proteins and long non-coding RNAs (lncRNA). ADAR1 and p65 proteins are among those and show increased expression in HCC. Since ADAR1 acts on RNA for A-I editing and p65 is a transcription factor, their contribution in the functionality and expression of immune regulatory lncRNA is huge. However, their role in relevance to HCC has not been studied so far. In this proposal, we sought to identify lncRNA regulated by ADAR1 and p65 proteins. We observed increased expression of cytokines in cells lacking ADAR1 and consequently decreased cell proliferation. At the same time, phosphorylated p65, a transcriptional activator for cytokines, is down regulated in cells lacking ADAR1. These intriguing observations led us to hypothesis that ADAR1 exerts negative regulation on cytokines expression through controlling specific lncRNAs which are in turn regulated by p65.
