In the absence of ADAR1, these p65 regulated lncRNA are unedited/misfolded and elicit cytokines expression. In our preliminary data, we identified one such lncRNA called LINC01096. LINC01096 expression is controlled by p65 and its expression is highly upregulated in tumor tissues of HCC compared to adjacent normal tissues. Together our proposal indicates a novel and significant study to address the pathogenesis of HCC and its possible therapeutic targeting using lncRNA.
kw: RNA Editing: NFkB: Liver cancer; lncRNA; Immune signal

title: Investigating the role of lipid peroxidation as an instigator of genomic instability in the progression of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease to hepatocellular carcinoma.
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: The incidence of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) associated with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) progression is on the rise, posing a significant global health and economic burden in the near future. However, curative therapies to either stem the progression of NAFLD or treat HCC, especially in its final stages, remain lacking. This global problem raises an urgent need to develop preventative therapies that block the progression of NAFLD to HCC. However, the molecular mechanisms underpinning the transition from NAFLD to HCC are not well understood. In particular, the source(s) of genomic instability in NAFLD-associated HCC remains unknown. Genomic instability is an enabling hallmark of cancer, driving the acquisition of cancer-causing mutations that initiate carcinogenesis. We, therefore, reason that by identifying the direct causes of somatic mutations in the genomes of HCCs arising from NAFLD, we may design more efficacious therapeutic strategies that prevent the transition of NAFLD to HCC. Lipid peroxidation, a feature of NAFLD to HCC pathogenesis, is a prime candidate for causing DNA damage and mutagenesis in this setting due to the production of numerous reactive molecules capable of adducting and damaging DNA. This, however, has not been formally proven. By exploiting the power of whole genome sequencing and mutational signature analysis, we aim to investigate the role of lipid peroxidation is an instigator of genomic instability in HCCs arising from NAFLD to provide a strong basis for therapeutic measures in the future. Key aims: 1. Elucidate the mutational signature profile of lipid peroxidation using in vitro cellular models. 2. Characterize the mutational landscape of HCCs arising specifically from NAFLD using in vivo mouse models and evaluate the contribution of lipid peroxidation-induced mutagenesis.
kw: lipid peroxidation; hepatocellular carcinoma; non-alcoholic fatty liver disease; genome stability;oxidative stress

title: Accelerating mammalian cell line development for biomedical applications by data-driven systematic identification of “ideal” transgene integration sites
abs: In therapeutic and biomanufacturing applications, transgenes are inserted into mammalian cells for synthesizing the desired protein in vitro. The conventional “random integration” approaches are often subject to undesired effects in host cells, and thus resulting in an unreliable and unpredictable expression of the biotherapeutic. In order to mitigate such uncertainties, 100s of mammalian cell clones are established and then the best performing one is picked through an extensive screening process. This approach is thus uneconomical, as it follows a very laborious and expensive protocol. The advent of targeted genome integration techniques has now enabled the rapid generation of consistent and reproducible clones where the transgene is inserted into the predetermined genomic hotspot, such that it can be expressed in a predictable manner. However, despite the availability of precise gene editing tools, favorable genomic hotspots are still identified using an empirical high throughput screening. In view of these limitations, we hypothesize that it is fundamental to investigate the global transcriptomic, epigenomic and genomic landscapes of mammalian cells using the abundantly available omics data for the rational prioritization of favorable integration sites. Herein, we propose a rational and targeted mammalian cell line development platform based on the knowledge-based approach and demonstrate its applicability in CHO cells. In this approach, we first assess the entire CHO genome and identify the ideal hotspots that intrinsically have a very high transcriptional output and favorable epigenetics. Subsequently, we insert the transgene precisely onto this hotspot using targeted gene editing techniques, and thus establishing best performing cell lines within days as opposed to weeks in the tag-and-exchange screening approaches. Overall, the proposed platform technology will rationalize and speed-up the cell line development campaigns and can be readily applied to any mammalian cell.
kw: biomanufacturing, targeted integration, systems biology, cell line development, genomic hotspot

title: Sebaceous gland biology: Wnt signaling as a therapeutic opportunity
abs: This proposal addresses the most common disease worldwide, acne vulgaris (acne). Acne is characterized by the development of comedones (blackheads and whiteheads) that can turn into inflammatory lesions such as pustules. While the majority of patients have mild disease that resolves spontaneously, up to 20% (in Singapore) develop moderate to severe acne. Due to its visibility, the disease is associated with a significant psychosocial burden and can have life-altering consequences, negatively impacting employability and interpersonal relationships. Others and we have previously proposed that acne formation is fuelled by an excessive proliferation of sebaceous gland progenitor cells. Our recent discoveries indicate that this process is likely to be controlled by stroma- produced Wnt ligands (Wnts). We propose that modulation of acne-promoting Wnts would ameliorate sebaceous progenitor hyperplasia eliminating acne at the initiation stage. This study will use transgenic animal models to label and profile telocytes, novel subtype of stromal cells that are found to reside in skin at the close proximity of sebaceous glands. Telocytes are known to support stem cells by producing Wnts and other differentiation factors in intestine as well as other tissues. We will investigate which of these Wnts and their regulators are relevant in activating sebaceous progenitors and then develop effective targeting methods to ameliorate this activation. We strongly believe that Wnt pathway inhibitors will provide a novel way to treat acne vulgaris effectively.
kw: skin; wnt signalling; sebaceous gland; acne

title: Deciphering the sequence-function interface of the dengue virus non-structural (NS1) protein in pathogenesis
abs: Dengue virus (DENV) infects an estimated 400 million people annually. This Aedes mosquito-borne virus causes acute dengue that, in some cases, evolves into life-threatening severe dengue. The absence of an anti-dengue drugs or sustainable and effective preventative measures demands a deeper mechanistic understanding of dengue pathogenesis to guide therapeutic and vaccine development. The recent discovery of DENV’s non-structural 1 (NS1) protein as a vascular permeability toxin has thus raised much excitement in the field as it suggests a potential antiviral and vaccine target. However, this laboratory-based finding conflicts with clinical observations – NS1 antigenemia is higher and lasts longer in patients with primary compared to secondary infection even though secondary dengue is associated with higher risk of severe disease. We postulate that sequence-dependent and lipid membrane-induced quaternary conformation of NS1 modulates its pathogenic potential and hence bridge the laboratory-based and clinically-observed findings. We have recently found that even minor sequence differences on the NS1 protein effect major differences in its functions. These sequence differences affect both the lipid core composition of hexameric secreted NS1 (sNS1) and also its interaction with ER-resident host proteins. As NS1 is ER-anchored and thus functions on lipid membranes, then any alteration to the lipid composition of cellular membranes could also impact the function of both sNS1 and its role in viral RNA replication and virion packaging. We will examine the impact of different lipid composition of sNS1 on disease pathology using an in vitro vascular leakage assay and correlate this to sNS1 structure and function. Established mosquito infection assays will be used to examine the role of sNS1 lipid core in dengue transmission and disease progression. If successful, this study will reveal the NS1 sequence-function and NS1-lipid membrane interfaces that underpin dengue pathogenesis.
kw: Dengue NS1 protein; NS1-associated lipid; NS1-mediated pathogenesis; NS1 structure and function; NS1-host protein interactions

title: A unique role for ABCB1/MDR1 in tumor suppression and its application to overcome drug resistance in cancer
abs: Resistance to chemotherapy is the main reason for tumor recurrence and cancer patient death. Tumors acquire elevated expression of the transporter ABCB1 after chemotherapy, and ABCB1-mediated drug efflux partly underlies drug resistance. Despite the development of many synthetic ABCB1 inhibitors, none has been demonstrated to be useful in clinical trials due to severe toxicity. Therefore, there is an urgent need to develop additional ABCB1 inhibitors. We discovered that, unlike humans, bats express high levels of ABCB1 ubiquitously in their tissues. We found that high ABCB1 expression protects bat cells from DNA damages caused by genotoxic chemicals and identified tryptophan, whose catabolites are known to promote tumor progression, as a novel ABCB1 substrate. Our preliminary results from computational modeling and in vitro assay showed that tryptophan is a promising lead compound for developing ABCB1 inhibitors. We hypothesized that high ABCB1 activity in bat cells reflects efflux of genotoxic compounds and undesired endogenous substances such as tryptophan, leading to tumor suppression. Developing ABCB1 inhibitors based on tryptophan, a natural compound, is a novel promising strategy to target drug-resistant cancers. In Aim 1, we will use computational approaches for the rational design of ABCB1 inhibitors using tryptophan as a lead molecule and test their ability to inhibit ABCB1 and restore chemosensitivity in drug-resistant cancers. In Aim 2, we will use in vitro cell culture and mouse models that express ABCB1 ubiquitously to test whether high and ubiquitous expression of ABCB1 could be a tumor-suppressive mechanism. Our studies will not only fill the gap in knowledge about the extremely low incidence of cancer in bats but also could be harnessed to develop new cancer therapies for human patients. Our strategy for developing novel ABCB1 inhibitors could represent original cancer therapies emerging from Singapore.
kw: ABCB1;  cancer;  inhibitor; drug resistant; bat; tumor suppression;

title: Combined proton beam therapy and proton beam triggered photodynamic therapy for cancer treatment
abs: Proton beam therapy (PBT) has several advantages over photon therapy for cancer treatment, for example, high penetration depth in tissues, most of the beam energy delivered to tumour at a specified depth with reduced photodamage to surrounding healthy tissues. However, PBT has dosimetric limitation, range uncertainties and its relative biological effect on different tumour and normal tissue types is not well understood. Photodynamic therapy (PDT) is an alternative cancer therapeutic option that involves the administration of light-sensitive photosensitizer drugs. As the drug preferentially accumulates in the tumour through the enhanced permeability and retention effect (EPR) owing to its leaky vasculature, light shone at it activates the drug to release reactive oxygen species, thus leading to tumour eradication. PDT at present relies on the use of low tissue penetrating visible light for activating the photosensitizer drug, which limits its application to surface and endoscopically accessible tumours. Here, we propose a combined PBT and proton excited PDT for treatment of large, deep-seated solid tumours. We aim to develop novel proton-beam excitable nanomaterials with fluorescence emissions for delivery of photosensitizer drugs and activation of the drugs under proton-beam irradiation. We hypothesize that, under proton-beam excitation, proton-beam with appropriate initial kinetic energy can deposit a high amount of radiant energy at tumour site for PBT of large, deep-seated solid tumours. Furthermore, fluorescence emissions generated by proton responsive nanomaterials in solid tumour can activate photosensitizers, allowing PDT to be done in parallel due to higher tissue penetration depth of proton-beam, as an adjuvant treatment option to PBT. This will enable PDT to be used for treating large, deep-seated solid tumours for the first time as opposed to just surface and endoscopically accessible tumour masses, and improve the overall therapeutic efficiency due to the synergistic effect of PBT and PDT.
kw: nanoparticle; proton; photodynamic; therapy; tumor

title: Restoring functional connectivity and memory in hippocampal neural networks impacted by juvenile stress through metaplasticity and epigenetic modifications
abs: Stress during childhood renders potent risk factors for learning and memory deficits resulting in altered cognitive bias and decision making later in adulthood. Since memories are constructs of biochemical and synaptic plasticity changes occurring over time post the learning process, we would like to investigate how the interference of stress during juvenility, even long after the elimination of actual stressors, has a lasting bearing in the adulthood, proffered by an inhibitory metaplastic state upon regulation of synaptic transmission, patterns of gene expression, structural modifications and hence, behavior. Using a combined electrophysiological, behavioral and functional connectivity mapping approach we will target epigenetic marker G9a/GLP complex, ascribed to transcriptional silencing of chromatin, for restoring the long-term plasticity, functional connectivity and long-term memory in animal models of juvenile stress.
kw: Juvenile  Stress, Long Term Potentiation, Memory, Synaptic Tagging, Social memory

title: Tracking and defining the mechanism of plasmid-mediated carbapenem-resistance transmission in Singapore
abs: The rising incidence of infection with carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae (CRE) is a serious global health threat. CRE infections are associated with healthcare settings and poor outcomes. Carbapenems are the last class of safe and effective antibiotics for treating multidrug-resistant (MDR) Gram-negative bacterial infections, the effectiveness of which has been greatly undermined by CRE. Carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae is the most clinically significant member of CRE. The rate of incident CRE clinical cultures among government hospitals in Singapore increased from 2011 to 2013 and plateaued after 2013. We recently discovered 18 isolates of carbapenem-resistant, hypervirulent K. pneumoniae (CR-hvKp) isolates from 7 patients across 6 public hospitals in Singapore. In all these isolates, a blaKPC-2 carrying plasmid (pKPC2) has moved into hypervirulent K. pneumoniae isolates as independent events. Furthermore, our preliminary data indicate that the prevalence of pKPC2 in CRE is rising. As plasmids are the main vector for antibiotic resistance transmission, we hypothesize that pKPC2 has undergone selection for carriage and transmission in K. pneumoniae and does not incur a long-term fitness cost to the host strains. Furthermore, the pKPC2 plasmid favors co-transfer of other hitchhiking multi-drug resistance plasmids. Thus, our second hypothesis is that pKPC2 could drive the transmission of other MDR plasmids. Our goal is to understand the molecular basis for the success of pKPC2 in Enterobacteriaceae species and how this influences the spread of AMR in Singapore. For this, we have developed an effective platform and strategy using a hypervirulent and antibiotic-sensitive K. pneumoniae strain to examine plasmid adaption, evolution, carriage and fitness. This allows the “recreation” of molecular events and factors favoring carriage and persistence of dominant plasmids. Through genetic manipulation, we identify bacterial and environmental factors that govern the transmission in vitro and in mice. We believe this understanding is critical in controlling further spread of these plasmids.
kw: bacteria; antibiotic resistance; carbapenem-resistance; Klebsiella pneumoniae; plasmid; Enterobacteriaceae

title: Targeted delivery of RNA therapeutics for personalized non-small cell lung cancer treatment using extracellular vesicles
abs: Natural extracellular vesicles (EVs) are ideal delivery vehicles for gene therapies. EVs facilitate the cellular uptake of RNAs while protecting the cargos from degradation and undesirable immune responses. However, such therapies are still limited by the small scale of EV production. Our group has developed a new method for RNA drug delivery using EVs from red blood cells (RBCs). Large quantities of RBCEVs can be obtained from a single unit of blood, bypassing the need for in vitro expansion of any cell sources. We illustrated unique properties of RBCEVs that make them an ideal delivery vehicle, including low toxicity, no risk of DNA transfer, simple composition, and robust uptake by many cell types, thus providing efficient delivery for therapeutic RNAs including small RNAs and mRNAs. To develop this platform further, we propose several approaches to make the therapies more specific, firstly by conjugating RBCEVs with peptides and antibodies for targeted delivery and secondly by using gene-specific RNA therapies to target disease-associated genes precisely. As a proof of concept on the clinical application of the platform, we will develop personalized therapy for non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). We will generate RBCEVs coated with peptides or nanobodies targeting surface markers of NSCLC. These peptides and nanobodies will guide specific uptake of RBCEVs by NSCLC and reduce non-specific uptake by normal cells. Secondly, we will develop mutant-specific siRNAs for knockdown of driver oncogenes. We will also add to the siRNAs a 5’ triphosphate modification that activates anticancer immune responses. Thirdly, we will test RBCEV-based therapies in NSCLC patient-derived xenografts (PDXs) in a personalized fashion by customizing RBCEVs with peptides/nanobodies and siRNAs targeting specific markers and mutations in each PDX. The proposed study will advance the specificity and versatility of the RBCEV platform for first-in-class anti-cancer RNA therapeutics.
kw: lung cancer; therapy; delivery; personalized;RNA

title: Versatile and scalable single-cell preimplantation genetic testing for chromosomal aneuploidy and segmental imbalances with/without concurrent Mendelian mutation detection using third-generation single-molecule sequencing
abs: Background: Preimplantation genetic testing for aneuploidy (PGT-A) is proposed to improve pregnancy rate in couples undergoing in vitro fertilisation (IVF). Currently in Singapore, the PGT-A platform used is expensive and inflexible in scaling. PGT-A can also potentially improve the success rate for IVF couples going through preimplantation genetic testing for monogenic disorders (PGT-M) as well, but current procedures are incompatible for testing of both PGT-A and PGT-M on the same embryo biopsy sample. Aims: To develop and validate an inexpensive and scalable third generation sequencing technology platform for PGT of monogenic disorders, segmental imbalances and/or chromosomal aneuploidy. Hypothesis: The Oxford Nanopore Technologies sequencing platform can be used for preimplantation genetic testing of embryonic tissue to identify single gene mutations and/or chromosomal abnormalities. Nanopore-based PGT will lead to lowered test costs and faster turnaround times than other current PGT procedures. Materials and Methods: Single cells from different karyotype-known euploid and aneuploid cell lines will be employed for assay optimization and validation. Also, leftover amplification products of embryo biopsy samples from participants of an ongoing preimplantation genetic screening (PGS) study will be retested, and results compared against previously determined karyotypes for concordance. For combined PGT-A and PGT-M, compatible WGA kits identified will be incorporated into library preparation workflows for Nanopore sequencing. PGT-A and PGT-M analysis will be separated bioinformatically. Finally, workflow will be validated using a. Technical and biological replicates of different cell lines with known aneuploidy or monogenic disorders, then b. Comparison of results from the workflow developed against current PGT-A and PGT-M workflows for concordance analysis.
kw: preimplantation genetic testing; aneuploidy; Mendelian disorders; third-generation sequencing; single-cell; single-molecule sequencing

title: Hypoxia-driven transcriptomic and epitranscriptomic regulation during Enterococcal colonization and infection
abs: Enterococci are members of the healthy human microbiota and are frequent opportunistic pathogens. Most enterococcal infections are biofilm-associated, rendering the bacteria more tolerant to antimicrobials and immune clearance. Despite their prevalence, little is known about how Enterococcus faecalis persists in the host to cause biofilm-associated infections. The normal niche for E. faecalis in healthy individuals is the hypoxic lower intestinal tract, E. faecalis can cause persistent infections within hypoxic environments, and biofilms comprise oxygen gradients with an often hypoxic core. We propose that E. faecalis is exquisitely adapted to thrive in these hypoxic environments, which contributes to its persistence as an opportunistic pathogen. The specific goal of this study is to define for the first time the transcriptomic and epitranscriptomic landscape of E. faecalis in response to host niche- and biofilm-relevant hypoxic states, and determine how this impacts colonization and infection. We hypothesize that E. faecalis responds to changes in oxygen availability that give rise to persistent biofilm-, colonization-, and infection-associated phenotypes in part by translation-based regulation of gene expression. This hypothesis is supported by abundant preliminary data demonstrating that E. faecalis possesses the molecular and genetic components of the translational regulatory mechanism and undergoes tRNA modification changes upon exposure to antibiotics and oxidative stress. We will test this hypothesis and achieve the goals of this proposal through the following specific aims: 1) Characterize transcriptional and translational regulation of gene expression during E. faecalis hypoxic growth in vitro, 2) Functionally characterize predicted RNA-modifying enzymes and two-component systems (TCS) involved in adaptation to hypoxia, and 3) Test hypoxia-associated TCS and tRNA modification mutants in animal models of E. faecalis colonization and infection. We expect these studies will identify novel druggable molecules or pathways required for infection, paving the way for future anti-biofilm and anti-infection therapies for these increasingly common, antibiotic-resistant infections.
kw: Bacterial infection; gut colonization; biofilms; hypoxia; regulation

title: Targeting HIF1α-dependent epigenetic remodeling in immune cells to overcome immune checkpoint inhibitor resistance in triple-negative breast cancer
abs: Although immune checkpoint blockade (ICB)-based immunotherapy such as anti-PD1/PD-L1 has been recently approved for advanced triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), only a small proportion of TNBC respond well to the ICB. Molecular mechanisms underlying immune escape and resistance to immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) in TNBC is poorly understood. Our preliminary study identifies the role of hypoxia immune cell inactivation and resistance to ICB treatment. We found that induction of hypoxia-inducible factor Ia (HIF1α) results in chromatin modifications, including PRC2 and HDAC1-dependent H3K27me3 and H3K27acetylation, leading to transcriptional repression of immune effectors including IFNα, TNFα, and Granzyme B in NK and T cells. Hypoxia-induced immune cell inactivation leads to attenuated TNBC killing and resistance to anti-PD1 treatment. Therapeutic targeting HIF1a and associated epigenetic changes in NK and T cells restores the immune activity of NK and T cells and sensitizes ICB in vitro and in syngeneic mouse models. This proposal seeks to identify the molecular mechanism by which HIF1a induces epigenetic repression of immune effectors and validate the HIF1a targeting strategy in humanized models. This proposal aims to identify hypoxia-induced mechanisms underlying immune evasion in TNBC and develop a new therapeutic approach to enhancing ICB therapy in refractory TNBC.
kw: hypoxia, tumor immune microenvironment, breast cancer, immune checkpoint inhibitor, epigenetics, T cells,

title: Revisiting the structure/function relationship in glaucoma for improved patient care
abs: Glaucoma is a leading cause of irreversible blindness, characterized by a progressive loss of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) and their axons and associated loss of visual field (VF). Lowering intraocular pressure (IOP) is an effective treatment for the disease, but early detection of glaucoma and detection of progression is a major clinical challenge. The diagnosis and follow-up of the disease includes functional testing using automated perimetry and structural imaging using optical coherence tomography (OCT). Relating structural to functional damage in glaucoma is referred to as the structure/function relationship. This may help to integrate information from both structural and functional tests into progression analysis. Current models do, however, only provide relatively weak corrections between structure and function, because of inter-individual variability, measurements errors, dynamic measurement ranges of the techniques and challenges in defining abnormality. Here we propose to improve our understanding of the structure/function relationship in glaucoma with a number of novel approaches: 1. Use of widefield OCTs that cover areas of 12x12 mm or 15x9 mm and therefore contain information from both the macular and the optic nerve head area; 2. Correction of anatomical confounders such as retinal angioarchitecture, fovea-disc angle and optic disc size; 3. Inclusion of vascular density information from OCT angiography (OCTA) measurements; 4. Development of machine learning and deep learning models for advanced structure/function relationship. Our central hypothesis is that the structure/function relationship can be improved using this framework and that this will result in improved prediction of future glaucoma progression in individual patients. This is done in an effort to integrate both structural and functional test results into diagnosis and follow up glaucoma for improved clinical care. A combined OCT/VF outcome may also be considered as an outcome measure for neuroprotection clinical trials.
kw: Glaucoma; automated perimetry; optical coherence tomography; optical coherence tomography angiography; structure/function relationship; artificial intelligence

title: Direct RNA-Sequencing as a scalable method towards quantitative epitranscriptomic markers in cancer
abs: One of the hallmarks of cancer is a change in the transcriptome. Recent advances in transcriptomics research have demonstrated that not only the overall abundance matters, but also that modifications of RNAs can impact the progression and severity of human cancers. However, while abundance of RNAs can be profiled in large scale by standard RNA-Sequencing, current methods to map the epitranscriptome are still suffering from major limitations that prevent their large scale application in a clinical context. In preliminary studies, we demonstrated the ability to computationally identify modified transcripts at a single base resolution from third generation direct RNA-Sequencing data using the Oxford Nanopore platform. Based on these findings, we propose to develop a direct-RNA sequencing based computational method to detect and quantify differential m6A modifications (Aim 1), employ direct-RNA sequencing to map novel cancer-specific modifications beyond m6A (Aim 2), and apply this technology to identify candidate RNA modifications that can act as patient stratification biomarkers for precision oncology (Aim 3). Successful development of a computational method for detection of RNA modifications from direct RNA-Seq data will enable the large-scale profiling of the transcriptome and epitranscriptome in clinical samples using a single, standardised experiment. Combined with the successful identification of new RNA modification-based biomarkers, this has the potential to transform the role of RNA profiling in cancer, opening many new possibilities for quantitative RNA biology in personalized medicine.
kw: computational method, transcriptomics, genomics, RNA modifications, cancer genomics, Nanopore Sequencing, direct RNA sequencing

title: Rapid diagnostic of infectious diseases based on nanopore sequencing and AI methods
abs: We aim to develop new methods for rapid and accurate detection of pathogenic agents based on whole-genome nanopore sequencing. Utilising nanopore sequencing technology advantages such as long read length, lower cost, increasing accuracy, and adaptive sequencing function, we will develop fast diagnostic methods inspired by song recognition software. Contrary to existing sequencing-based methods that use specific short substrings to identify present microbes, we hypothesise that using only reads that are longer than tens of thousands of nucleotides will enable detection on species and even strain levels. To increase the chances of success, we will implement two strategies. One strategy will use raw sequencing signals. Using deep learning methods, we aim to create the best representation of the raw signal, quantise it, and create a dictionary of signal fingerprints that will enable fast detection. Another strategy will transform basecalled nucleotides sequences into distributions of all short substrings of length k (k-mers) and build deep learning models to learn distinct k-mer patterns and identify organisms using a minimal number of reads. To reduce information redundancy in related species and strains, genome sequences for both approaches will be organised in pangenome graphs, and common subsequences will be excluded from the search. Finally, we will conduct multiple experiments to determine the minimal abundance and accuracy of microbial detection in a sample. We deem that developed methods will enable timely and correct diagnosis, resulting in significantly reduced morbidity and mortality, especially in immunocompromised cancer patients, and lead to decreased usage of unnecessary antimicrobial therapy. We deem that developed methods will enable timely and correct diagnosis which might result in significantly reduced morbidity and mortality, especially in immunocompromised cancer patients, and lead to decreased usage of unnecessary antimicrobial therapy.
kw: diagnosis, nanopore sequencing, pathogenic agents, infections

title: Fine-tuning of Cav1.2 channel function by galectin-1 and galectin-3 and its implications in heart disease
abs: Heart failure (HF) is characterized by a defect in contractile and electrical functions, and patients suffer not only from reduced blood circulation but approximately 50% of patients are predisposed to life-threatening ventricular arrhythmia. Excitation-contraction coupling is dysregulated at multiple levels in HF, thus modulating the function of the various channels and transporters, such as L-type Cav1.2 calcium channel, represents a way to restore cardiac muscle contractile function. We have recently identified Galectin-1 and Galectin-3 as a negative or positive modulator of Cav1.2 channels, respectively. However, it remains unknown whether and how this antagonistic regulation of Cav1.2 function by Galectin-1 and Galectin-3 plays a decisive role in HF progression. Our preliminary data showed that in transverse aortic constriction (TAC) induced HF, Lgals1–/– mice displayed significantly reduced ejection fraction, hypertrophied cardiomyocytes, prolonged APD80, suggesting Galectin-1 deficiency may aggravate cardiac dysfunction by up-regulating Cav1.2 activity. In addition, Galectin-3 was identified to strongly bind to the II-III loop that in turn can act as a Galectin-3 decoy and in contrast up-regulated channel function, indicating that Cav1.2-Galectin-3 interaction may contribute to HF progression. Here, we employ 2 mouse models of HF to mimic HF with reduced or preserved ejection fraction (HFrEF/HFpEF), and we have generated cardiac-specific conditional knock-out of Galectin-1 or Galectin-3 to further investigate the roles of cardiac Galectin-1/3 in HF, and will generate Cav1.2DE457&459AA knock-in mice to study the effect of lack of Cav1.2-Galectin-1 interaction on cardiac function. Moreover, we will test specific TAT peptides that directly disrupt Cav1.2-Galectin-1 (Tat-e9c-Cy5) or Cav1.2-Galectin-3 (Tat-II-III loop-Cy5) interactions in human iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes and HF animal models. For translational research, we will employ AAV2/9-mediated cardiac specific delivery of Lgals1 gene and Lgals3 siRNA to overexpress Lgals1 and knockdown Lgals3 respectively in HF animal models, and test the possibility of using circulating Galectin-1/3 as HF biomarkers.
kw: Cav1.2 channel, galectins, heart failure, mouse models, electrophysiology

title: Creating a clinically-relevant skin substitute and source to treat cutaneous wound defects: Use of skin-specific culture platform for growth of umbilical cord lining epithelial cells (CLECs)
abs: Resurfacing critically-large cutaneous wounds due to severe burns, diabetes or genetic mutations, remains a huge clinical challenge despite current capability of ex vivo expansion of autologous human skin keratinocyte (hKC) sheets on mouse fibroblasts from a small skin biopsy to treat these conditions. Today’s skin culture technique is still fraught with limitations for clinical use due to 1) the use of animal cells (xenograft); and 2) unsuitable/unavailable skin donor site (due to infection or mutation) for any meaningful biopsy harvesting and cell culture. We recently described a breakthrough in vitro method using laminin-based chemically defined and fully human platform to expand hKCs without significant loss of regenerative cells [Nat Commun-2018 & Nat Protoc-2020]. It was also demonstrated that autologous oral mucosal epithelial cultures can be used clinically to reconstruct totally depleted corneas (N Engl J Med-2004). Here, we propose a similar approach to develop a skin-specific platform based on biologically-relevant laminins for robust expansion of immunoprivileged human umbilical cord lining epithelial cells (hCLECs) to treat severe cutaneous wounds. Using CLECs is cost-effective due to abundance of cords as “medical waste” and large quantity of cells (six billion) can be derived from a single cord before expansion. Furthermore, this new technique does not incur invasive harvesting or ethical consideration. The CLEC-based skin substitute, cultured in a new clinically-relevant and fully human system will be characterized and compared against KCs cultured in conventional systems. Both systems will be subjected to in vitro comparison followed by in vivo evaluation on animal wound models. An allogeneic line of hCLECs will be co-established and manufactured as a pharmaceutical-grade product once this new skin substitute pre-clinical performance is shown to be efficacious. This will be done in collaboration with industry first to target first-in-man treatment of deep dermal burns and in the nearer future, diabetic wounds.
kw: Cellular therapy; wound healing; burns; diabetic wounds; umbilical cord lining epithelial cells; skin keratinocytes

title: Characterization of a Novel Neutrophil-Mediated Antimicrobial Pathway Involving Gasdermin E.
abs: Neutrophils are short-lived antimicrobial phagocytes that are recruited in large numbers during infection. Exposure to proinflammatory cytokines, growth factors and bacterial ligands at the site of infection rapidly extends neutrophil lifespan to enable the clearance of pathogens via classical antimicrobial programmes (e.g. phagocytosis, degranulation, oxidative stress). Our recent work has identified a novel neutrophil-associated host defence pathway, that involves gasdermin E (GSDME), a pore-forming protein that promotes cell death. Mechanistically, our preliminary findings indicate that GSDME-dependent neutrophil lysis promotes secretion of the proinflammatory cytokine, interleukin (IL)-1b to enable host resistance against infection. In this proposal, we will characterise and dissect the mechanisms by which GSDME-dependent neutrophil lysis drives antimicrobial defence at the molecular, cellular and organism levels. Specifically, we will establish: (1) the molecular mechanisms by which microbial infection triggers GSDME-dependent neutrophil IL-1b production; and (2) the cellular mechanisms by which GSDME-dependent IL-1b promotes host defence in vivo.
kw: innate immunity; cell death; neutrophil; bacterial infection; inflammasomes

title: Mechanisms organizing tumour invasion in heterotypic spheroid-monolayer co-cultures.
abs: Tumour growth is often positively associated with increased invasiveness, but it remains unclear whether cell division is a mere bystander or a driver of invasion. Previously, 3D computational modelling of human tumour evolution predicts that co-occurrence of cell division and migration/invasion at the periphery of tumour is the key to reproduce the size, morphology, growth rate, drug resistance and genetic composition of patient tumours analysed. Thus, targeting the mechanisms linking cell division to invasion is an attractive therapeutic avenue. However, the crosstalk between cancer cell division and invasion remains unclear. Moreover, the consequence of this crosstalk on their heterotypic neighbours is unknown. Thus, we propose to address two questions. First, how do inhibiting interphase and cell-division dependent mechanisms reduce collective tumour cell invasion into adjacent tissues? Second, how does inhibition of the mechanochemical GEF-H1 pathway reduce cancer invasion? Answering both questions would address our hypothesis that activation of the RhoA activator GEF-H1, mechanochemical pathway during the mitosis-to-interphase transition induces invasion of cancer spheroid into neighbouring non-cancerous tissues. This will be the first-ever study to combine Förster-resonance-emission-transfer biosensor, light-sheet microscopy, multiphoton laser ablation, super-resolution structured illumination, and micropatterning to investigate cancer spheroid invasion into normal tissues. We are using the zebrafish model and 3D culture systems to mimic breast cancer extravasation and ovarian cancer metastatic colonization. The two 3D culture systems permit complex manipulations and high-resolution imaging. Our improved 3D culture systems would help gain clearer pre-clinical insights when used for testing of future cancer treatments. The biochemical and physical factors that we have identified in our project are potential diagnostic markers and new drug targets for the treatment of cancer. Our preliminary data and track-record of publications in cell adhesion, cytoskeleton signalling, quantitative analysis with a variety of photonic methods including laser ablation ensure the feasibility of our proposal.
kw: spheroid; cancer; invasion; cell-division; heterotypic 3D cell culture

title: Understanding Tumour Predisposition in Asia (UToPIA) Study: From Patient-Centred Research to the Clinic.
abs: Background: Cancer is a major focus of the precision medicine initiative. While the clinical validity, utility and actionability of testing at-risk individuals for high penetrance tumour predisposition genes (TPGs) is clear, 40% of individuals who undergo clinical testing today are found to have a genetic variant of unknown significance (VUS). Our proposal seeks to address and understand VUS in TPGs identified in Singaporeans through (1) selecting individuals with VUS for functional evaluation and following up carriers with TPG VUS longitudinally to correlate with clinical outcomes. Methods: Mutations in DNA repair pathway genes are responsible for the majority of tumour susceptibility we see in the clinic and are important targets for precision medicine. We will prioritise VUS in the DNA damage and repair Fanconi Anemia (FA) pathway, specifically germline FANCI variants for functional analysis using patient-derived lymphoblastoid cell lines. In parallel, we will also evaluate selected patients with digenic/ oligogenic germline variants in the FA pathway to better understand gene-gene interactions clinically. We will prospectively follow-up patients with a TPG VUS for evidence of overt clinical tumour development. Feasibility: All patient material needed for this study is available. The study team has demonstrated the needed clinical, technical and scientific expertise for the proposed experiments with support from senior members of the study team. Clinical Significance: Our team has shown that successful classification of a VUS not only directly allows affected patients to receive prompt care; but also aids variant classification efforts globally. Data from this study will further inform on the optimal management of individuals with VUS in TPGs and will be used to guide future health policy decision-making.
kw: Precision Medicine; Cancer; Hereditary; Cancer Genomics

title: Personalizing Diabetic Retinopathy Screening Intervals via Risk Stratification using an Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Multi-modal Machine Learning Approach
abs: Nearly 100,000 patients with diabetes are screened annually through the Singapore national diabetic retinopathy (DR) screening program, the Singapore Integrated DR Program (SiDRP). With rising diabetes prevalence and the aging population, the SiDRP is consistently challenged by the increasing DR screening workload. DR screening workload can be reduced with two strategies: 1) automated grading and 2) reduction in screening frequency for persons at low-risk of DR. For strategy 1), we have already developed, and will implement, an artificial intelligence (AI) based, automated DR screening tool. For strategy 2), we will develop a multi-modal DR predictive algorithm, DR-PREDICT, to identify persons with low-risk of DR incidence/progression within 3 years in this proposal (Aim 1). SiDRP retrospective dataset (2010-2019) consisted of patients’ demographic, systemic risk factors and retinal imaging will be the development dataset, split into 80% training and 20% validation. We will use a combination of statistical, machine learning and deep learning techniques. Next, we plan to evaluate the diagnostic performance of DR-PREDICT and workload reduction using SiDRP dataset (2020-2023) for hypothetical modelling, where screening intervals increase from yearly to 2 yearly for persons with mild NPDR and predicted having low risk of DR progression, or 3 yearly for those with no DR and predicted having low risk of DR development (Aim 2). We will also evaluate the generalizability of DR-PREDICT to external datasets of international studies (Aim 3). The diagnostic performance (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, sensitivity, specificity with 95% confidence intervals) of DR-PREDICT will be evaluated against true incidence/ progression. Should DR-PREDICT proven to predict with sufficient precision, DR screening can be personalized based on individuals’ DR risks, accompanied with robust monitoring screening attendance, to sustain local and international DR screening programs for ever increasing DR screening demand.
kw: Diabetic Retinopathy; Digital Health; Artificial Intelligence (AI); Data Science and Data Analytics; Precision Medicine; Population Health and Implementation Science

title:
Novel Precision Technologies to correct β-Thalassaemia Major: 
In vivo Adeno-Associated Viral vector (AAV)-mediated Base-Editing of the commonest Asian IVS1-5 (G>C) mutation in Haemopoetic Stem Cells (HSC), utilising engineered AAV, personalised Humanised Mouse Models and in vitro HSC engineering to address Critical Translational Questions
abs: Major β-thalassaemia impacts significantly on medico-economic resources particularly in populations with high carrier prevalence. This global disease causes 3-4% of early-childhood deaths annually, with severe chronic morbidity arising from progressive disease and inadequate treatment. Gold-standard haemopoetic stem-cell transplantation (HSC-T) is not available to all patients. There is still no universal, affordable and curative treatment for those without a matched HSC donor. Current ex-vivo gene therapy trials are extremely costly and risk myeloablation complications. We investigate in-vivo AAV-mediated base-editing to correct the commonest single nucleotide variant causing transfusion-dependent thalassaemia (TDT) in a proof-of-concept study utilizing personalised humanized mice produced with patient-derived HSC, testing the hypothesis that optimised AAV-mediated delivery of base-editing tools can efficiently correct the IVS1-5(G>C) mutation, the most prevalent in Asian populations. The long-term aim is to enhance cost-effective precision therapy for major β-thalassaemia and make it available to all patients. Our short-term aims are to produce an efficient base-editing strategy for in-vivo correction of IVS1-5(G>C) in engineered human HSC, optimise AAV-transduction of HSC in-vivo using a humanised mouse model, and assess safety and efficacy of in-vivo AAV-mediated base-edited gene correction in the humanized mouse. We will assess transduction efficacy of several AAV vectors including engineered AAV in vitro, select the most effect AAV for further experiments, acquire TDT patient-derived HSC directly or by fibroblast reprogramming, optimise base editing strategies in-vitro, deliver base editing tools in-vivo using a dual AAV strategy to assess long-term safety and efficacy. This research is highly feasible with the team’s collective expertise in gene modification therapies, preclinical models, HSC expansion and engineering, HSC-T in paediatric TDT and perinatal therapy. This novel and innovative study can expedite clinical trials and provide an urgently-needed treatment potentially more accessible and cost-effective than current standards, poised to make substantial global impact.
kw: Engineered AAV; in vivo base-editing; beta thalassaemia major; personalised humanized mouse model; postnatal gene modification therapy

title: Study of epigenetic regulators of the tumor immune microenvironment of gastric cancer peritoneal metastases
abs: Background Gastric cancer often metastasizes to the peritoneum and are resistant to systemic chemo/immunotherapy. The tumor epigenome and immune microenvironment have been identified as promising areas for discovery of novel therapeutic targets. Hypothesis Profiling of epigenetic regulators of the tumor immune microenvironment of gastric cancer peritoneal metastases(GCPM) may reveal therapeutic targets Specific Aims 1) Characterization of the genetic and epigenetic features of GCPM 2) Study the spatial interaction between GCPM and the tumor immune microenvironment, identifying potential therapeutic targets 3) Generate proof-of-principle in vivo data using humanized mouse model of one therapeutic target identified from characterization studies Methodology Our institution has multiple peritoneal-directed therapeutic clinicals trials ongoing. These trials allow access to peritoneal metastases for tissue collection and interrogation. Aim 1): Perform molecular landscaping of peritoneal metastases Samples accessed from peritoneal-directed clinical trials will be processed for DNA and RNA extraction. Integrative analysis of genomic sequencing will be performed, including epigenetic profiling using a novel bioinformatic algorithm. Aim 2): Assessment of tumor microenvironment using multiplex IHC and digital spatial transcriptomics Multiplex fluorescent immunohistochemistry(fIHC) and digital spatial profiling using the NanoString GeoMx platform will be performed for accurate identification and quantitation of distinct immune cell types within the tumor microenvironment Aim 3): Therapeutic translation using humanized mouse model Peritoneal metastatic tissue biopsies will be used to generate immortalized cell-lines. Tumors will be xenografted on humanized mice, generated by engrafting immunodeficient mice with human umbilical cord-blood cells. Using data generated from the landscaping study, a single drug target will be selected and treatment effect on tumor immune microenvironment will be studied in this animal model. Impact This study will provide significant insights into the epigenetic mechanisms involved in peritoneal metastases of gastric cancer and the effect on tumor immunity, potentially leading to the discovery of novel treatment strategies.
kw: Gastric cancer; peritoneal metastases; epigenetics; tumor microenvironment; immunotherapy; precision oncology

title: Advancing therapeutics against squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck and endemic nasopharyngeal carcinoma
abs: Squamous cell carcinoma (SCCHN) and undifferentiated nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) are the most common head and neck cancers in Singapore and carry a significant burden of morbidity and mortality. This proposal brings together a group of highly qualified investigators with critically relevant expertise to collaborate on advancing therapeutics. The group has already established productive collaborations that laying the foundations for this grant and consist of senior as well as junior PIs that ensure diversity of experience and innovation. In SCCHN we will validate 2 projects: 1. We showed that a polymorphism in C-MET gene occurs commonly in East and South Asians and through mutation at the Sema binding domain of MET causes conformational change and increased affinity for HER2 leading to strong oncogenic signalling. METN375S promotes aggressiveness in SCCHN and results in shorter relapse free survival, and we will conduct a clinical trial to study HER2 inhibitors in METN375S positive SCCHN. 2. We showed that the S4 strand of p53 is commonly mutated, and through structural simulations we predict oncogenic gain of function with potential for therapeutic intervention. Through computational modelling of the mutants we will evaluate the hypothesis that binding of chemical groups can reverse their oncogenic phenotype. In NPC we will comprehensively map the tumour microenvironment of treatment-resistant NPC at the single cell resolution and the 3-D chromatin organisation to understand epigenomic regulation. Through this, we would design therapeutic interventions that can be assessed in clinical trials. The proposal will also advance our current efforts in vaccines against NPC through 2 delivery technologies: an efficient CD137L-DC already evaluated in a clinical trial, and a more tractable red blood cell derived exosomes. We will evaluate expressed viral antigens and tumour neoepitopes identified through our transcriptomic profiling of NPCs, prioritising them using an ex vivo high throughput immunogenicity reporter system.
kw: Head and neck cancer, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, therapeutics, cancer

title: Validating Existing and Emerging Multi-modal Biomarkers of Vascular Cognitive Impairment
abs: The focus of this study is on vascular cognitive impairment (VCI) which recognizes that the mechanisms involved in VCI are complex and heterogenous : not only large or small cerebral vessel disease resulting in overt strokes or covert lesions such as microinfarcts, microhemorrhages, and white matter injury, but also neurodegeneration and Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) pathology. Project 1 : Neurobehavioral & structural MRI markers for Cognitive Impairment & Dementia - The specific aims are continuation in the Harmonisation cohort, to examine the potential diagnostic and prognostic value of neurobehavioral and structural MRI markers for cognitive impairment and dementia as well as underlying pathophysiological mechanisms, and building existing as well as new international collaborations. To study, in a cohort of 700 subjects with up to 5 years longitudinal follow up, the independent and joint associations of structural & functional MRI, retinal imaging, blood and neurobehavioural markers with risk of cognitive decline, dementia & vascular events. Project 2 : Multimodal MRI-based network breakdown and progression prediction in Cognitive Impairment and Dementia - To examine longitudinal brain network breakdown and microstructural changes using multimodal MR imaging and evaluate their interactions with AD & cerebrovascular pathology and contribution to cognitive and behavioral decline in patients with no, mild cognitive impairment and dementia. Project 3 : Retinal markers for Cognitive Impairment and Dementia - to determine the relationship of these novel retinal imaging measures over time to progression and development of VCI and other imaging markers of dementia, with a goal to determine the potential diagnostic and prognostic value of retinal imaging. Project 4 : Blood markers for Cognitive Impairment and Dementia - The specific aims are to develop novel blood-based biomarkers of oxidative stress, vascular disease and neurodegeneration, and to examine their potential diagnostic and prognostic value for cognitive impairment and dementia.
kw: Aging;Artificial Intelligence;vascular dementia;biomarkers;Alzheimer’s Disease

title: Evaluating and Decreasing the Socio-Economical Burden of Wound Care in Singapore through Health Systems Innovations and Health Literacy
abs: Background: Wounds present a substantial economic burden to healthcare systems globally with significant reductions in quality of life for those affected. In Singapore, such economic burden data and health economics analysis for wound care is limited. Aim: This project aims to firstly assess the health-related quality of life, healthcare costs and economic burden of patients suffering from wounds in Singapore; secondly, to evaluate the cost-effectiveness and cost-utility of healthcare innovations in improving health-related quality of life, healthcare costs and economic burden of patients suffering from wounds in Singapore; and thirdly, to improve clinical outcomes and decrease disease burden through improved patient and carer health literacy via patient-empowered care. Hypothesis: Similar to Western data, there is a significant clinical and economic burden of wounds to the Singapore healthcare system. By understanding the clinical and economic burden, we can develop and evaluate the cost-effectiveness and cost-utility of healthcare innovations in improving health-related quality of life, healthcare costs and economic burden of patients suffering from wounds in Singapore. This may be achieved through improved patient and carer health literacy via patient-empowered care via an Artificial-Intelligence powered wound imaging ecosystem Methodology: Wounds will be categorized into neuro-ischaemic, venous, pressure-related and surgical wounds. Institutional and national data from primary to tertiary centres on patient characteristics, wound characteristics, healthcare resource utilisation and healthcare costs involved will be analysed. Through health system innovations for each wound type, we will build a predictive model to evaluate the cost-effectiveness and cost-utility of healthcare innovations in wound management using Bayesian network and Markov modelling. Data generated will help guide healthcare resource allocation, healthcare delivery improvement and address current patient and carer needs and education with digital tools and resources, to improve patient and carer health literacy. Patient-centric care-empowerment will be delivered via an Artificial-Intelligence powered wound imaging ecosystem.
kw: wound care; health economics; health systems innovation; artificial intelligence; health literacy

title: Characterisation of Stool Microbiome in advanced HCC patients receiving Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors
abs: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the third most common cause of cancer-related mortality, with most patients diagnosed with advanced disease. Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have been added to the armamentarium of treatment options for patients with advanced hepatocellular carcinoma (aHCC) but response rates remain low with monotherapy anti-PD-(L)1 use. Combination therapies increase response rates modestly but at risk of increased toxicities and costs. Common biomarkers used in other solid tumour types have less utility in aHCC patients in triaging responders from non-responders. We hypothesise that the stool microbiome could be an important biomarker in this cohort of patients, given promising early data in other solid tumour types, and the fact that aHCC patients often have underlying cirrhosis and dysbiosis and as the liver receives a significant blood supply from the portal circulation. We aim to conduct a pilot study in aHCC patients planned for ICI therapy initiation. Longitudinal serial stool collection will be performed in conjunction with data collection on treatment response, toxicities, medication usage, and dietary food frequencies. Stool samples will undergo nucleic acid extraction for shotgun metagenomic sequencing. We aim to assess the feasibility of the collection protocol, as well as obtain preliminary data on microbiome characterisation in this group of patients, in order to plan a larger cohort study and subsequent interventional studies.
kw: cancer; immunotherapy; microbiome; biomarker

title: Pilot study of a “Fast Acting Fentanyl Sublingual Tablet (Abstral) for the Prophylactic Treatment of Episodic Activity Induced Dyspnea in Asian Cancer Patients”
abs: Introduction Episodic activity-induced dyspnea is common in cancer patients and reduces quality of life, however, there are no effective treatments for this symptom. Fast-acting submucosal Fentanyl preparations are an attractive option due to their pharmacological properties. Abstral (given sublingually) is the only available submucosal Fentanyl available locally but it has not been evaluated for dyspnea treatment. Aims/ hypothesis The overall aim is to evaluate the use of Abstral for prophylactic treatment (to reduce dyspnea intensity) of a single episode of activity-induced dyspnea in advanced cancer patients with at least moderate intensity activity-induced dyspnea. The primary aim would be to determine whether a single dose of Abstral (dosed proportionally) is effective for the prophylactic treatment of one episode of activity-induced dyspnea that is induced by a 2-minute walk test. We hypothesize that an Abstral dose (dosed proportionally based on the total opioid daily dose) would be able to reduce the severity of activity-induced dyspnea by at least 1 point on a Modified Borg Scale for Dyspnea (mBorg). Our secondary aims would be to evaluate the tolerability, acceptability of Abstral and the impact of Abstral on walk distance. We will explore the impact of CYP3A4/3A5 pharmacogenetics on the pharmacokinetics (PK) and pharmacodynamics (PD) of Abstral and treatment response. Methods and approach We will recruit 45 participants and evaluate the change in mBorg score after the 2-minute walk test post as compared to pre-Abstral. We will also collect patient views on Abstral acceptability, adverse effects, and 2-minute walk distance pre and post Abstral. Blood will be taken for genotyping and PK/PD studies. Significance This study would give preliminary evidence if Abstral is effective and tolerable for prophylactic treatment of activity-induced dyspnea in advanced cancer patients and allow the investigation of the influence of CYP3A4/3A5 pharmacogenomics on opioid dosing in dyspneic Asian cancer patients.
kw: cancer, dyspnea, fast-acting-sublingual- Fentanyl

title: Neurobiology of Obesity: The role of the prefrontal cortex in mediating childhood obesity risk through changes in executive function and alterations in eating behaviours
abs: The role of the prefrontal cortex (PFC) is to regulate human behaviour through executive functioning and cognitive control. Changes in executive functioning has been described in children and adolescents with obesity. Recently, a bidirectional relationship has been demonstrated between executive function and obesity. PFC changes may be a risk factor that precedes obesity, rather than occur as a consequence of obesity. Aim: To evaluate the role of the PFC in mediating the neurobiology of obesity through changes in executive function and eating behaviours. Hypotheses: 1. Changes in the structure of the PFC precedes development of increased adiposity in children at risk of obesity 2. The PFC mediates increased adiposity in at risk children through changes in executive function, which leads to alterations in eating behaviours, favouring behaviours that promote increased energy intake Methodology: Population: GUSTO birth cohort children who had undergone MRI brain at 0, 4.5 and 6 years. We would study the relationship between: - PFC volume and thickness - Adiposity- BMI, skinfold thickness, quantitative magnetic resonance - Eating behaviour scores - Executive function scores Multiple responses statistical approach to - Compare differences between the various components of the PFC thickness/ volume, executive function and eating behaviours in children at increased risk of obesity vs. those at baseline risk - Evaluate the association between executive function leads to alterations in eating behaviours (e.g. behaviours that promote increased energy intake such as fast eating speed, eating in the absence of hunger or increased portion size and favouring avid appetite traits) Significance: Understanding the neurobiology or scientific basis of food-seeking behaviours, impulse eating and appetite control in those at risk of obesity would be crucial in guiding the prevention and management of childhood obesity with a focus on behavioural modifications targeting impulse control and eating habits.
kw: childhood obesity, prefrontal cortex, eating behaviour, executive function

title: Validation of Donor-derived Cell-free DNA in the Detection of Kidney Allograft Rejection in a Singapore Cohort of Asian Kidney Transplant Recipients Late Post-Transplantation
abs: Antibody-mediated rejection (ABMR) remains a leading cause of late allograft failure in kidney transplantation (KTx). As donor-specific antibodies (DSAs) are implicated in ABMR pathogenesis, their detection has become the cornerstone of immune monitoring post-transplant. However, due to complexity of DSA-Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA) interactions, DSAs have a poor specificity, necessitating invasive allograft biopsies to diagnose ABMR. In the absence of protocol biopsies, for-cause biopsies, triggered by increases in serum creatinine and proteinuria, results in late diagnosis of ABMR. Non-invasive markers to better identify those at risk for ABMR are an unmet need in KTx. In addition, biopsies are expensive and invasive, limiting their repeatability. They are also associated with risks of an invasive test as well as the need for hospital admission, observation and associated costs and morbidity. Plasma donor-derived cell-free DNA (dd-cfDNA, AlloSeq®, CareDx, Brisbane, CA) has been suggested as a novel, non-invasive diagnostic biomarker for graft injury, especially from ABMR. As most previous studies have been performed among KTx at less than 3.25 years post-transplant, it is unclear if dd-cfDNA is a useful biomarker to distinguish ABMR from other causes, when superimposed on non-immune-mediated chronic inflammation and fibrosis. Dd-cfDNA only requires a blood sample. If found to be a good discriminator, it would be especially useful in patients late post-transplantation who may have a higher risk of complications from a biopsy such as those on anticoagulation. Non-invasive biomarkers with better specificity for ABMR are an unmet need in KTx. As dd-cfDNA is novel in Asian KTx, our study may allow extrapolation of international standards of pre-defined cut-off for dd-cfDNA fraction to our cohort with a high prevalence of HLA disparity. Dd-cfDNA has great potential to become standard of care in the future, and we can be the leading center to discover related knowledge for the region.
kw: Kidney Transplantation; Rejection; Donor-derived Cell-free DNA

title: Real-World Validation of an Artificial Intelligence Characterization Support (CADx) System for Prediction of Polyp Histology in Colonoscopy: A Prospective Study
abs: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a leading cause of cancer-related morbidity and mortality worldwide, with rates of CRC predicted to increase. Colonoscopy is currently the gold standard of screening for CRC. The adenoma detection rate (ADR) is an established quality indicator for colonoscopy. A 1% increase in ADR estimated to be associated with a 3% decreased risk of interval CRC. As not all colorectal polyps pose the same risk of CRC, a "diagnose and leave" or "resect and discard" strategy has been postulated to save healthcare costs while not compromising patient safety. Moreover, the size, morphology and predicted histology of a polyp helps the endoscopist determine if a polyp is safe to resect endoscopically and if resectable, the exact modality or technique to use to ensure that complete resection is achieved. However, these ultimately depend on an accurate optical diagnosis of the predicted polyp histology at the time of colonoscopy. Previous studies have shown wide inter-observer variability in accuracy of this optical prediction despite the use of image-enhanced endoscopy (IEE). The sensitivity and specificity also fluctuate between institutions regardless of the modality IEE used for optical prediction. Computer-aided diagnosis (CADx), which utilises deep neural networks, has emerged as a new tool to increase accuracy of polyp histology, but has not been validated in real-word use. We hypothesize that the CADx support tool will increase the accuracy of predicted histology of colorectal polyps in real-time colonoscopy. The aim of this study is to conduct a prospective, multi-centre clinical trial to validate the accuracy of CADx support for prediction of polyp histology in real-time colonoscopy when comapred against polyp histology as the gold standard.
kw: Colonoscopy; colorectal cancer; screening; polyps; optical diagnosis

title: Discordant symptom burden and severity grading in dermatology, a mixed-methods sequential exploratory study
abs: Patients often present with symptoms that are disproportionate to the observed disease state and grade the severity of the disease differently from healthcare providers (HPs). This discordant symptom burden and severity grading (DSG) may result in poorer quality of life, patient dissatisfaction, and increased healthcare utilisation. Due to the lack of an existing guiding framework or theory, we employed the sequential exploratory mixed method approach, beginning with a qualitative study to develop a theory explaining DSG. In the second stage of this mixed method study, we employ quantitative data collection methods to: 1. Quantify the prevalence of DSG in dermatology outpatients 2. Ascertain the strengths and relationships between the factors (independent variables) and DSG (dependent variable) 3. Quantify the impact of DSG on healthcare utilization, quality of life and patient-physician satisfaction 4. Assess and improve ability of physicians to recognize and address DSG Themes identified during the earlier qualitative study will be converted to measurable constructs and measured through questionnaires administered to patients and physicians. Patient-physician pairs will be prospectively recruited from the National Skin Centre and National University Hospital dermatology divisions. Administrative data will be collected to assess healthcare utilisation. Statistical analysis will be performed through a combination of factor analysis, path analysis and structural equation modeling. After discussion with the NUS biostatistics unit, a sample size of 600 patient-HP pairs is targeted (10 observations per parameter and maximum achievable in the accrual period). The current project is important for validating the theory by providing concrete evidence to support the reproducibility and generalizability of the framework. It is also a necessary step toward deriving a valid and reliable instrument to assess DSG that will allow the accurate quantification in subsequent quality improvement and interventional studies.
kw: discordant severity grading; patient outcome measures; perceived severity; patient satisfaction; physician burnout; objective grading

title: Homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) in platinum sensitive triple negative breast cancer (TNBC)
abs: Background: Metastatic triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) is associated with a poor prognosis representing a disease of unmet clinical need. Standard therapeutic options are limited to chemotherapy and PARP inhibitors in 10-15% of TNBC associated with germline BRCA mutations. Recently, inhibition of the PD-1/PD-L1 axis has shown modest efficacy in a subset of PD-L1 expressing TNBC. A major challenge in translating developing targeted therapies or immunotherapy has been the lack of appropriate biomarkers for patient selection and therapeutic targeting. Method: DORA is a multi-center phase II study of Durvalumab and Olaparib in platinum tReated Advanced TNBC. Patients are randomised to receiving either olaparib or olaparib in combination with durvalumab as maintenance therapy following disease response to platinum chemotherapy. The primary endpoint is progression free survival (PFS) with response rates, overall survival, and toxicity as key secondary endpoints. Tumor samples systematically acquired during the conduct of the study will be subjected to multi-platform analysis for: 1) homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) 2) genetic mutational analysis 3) transcriptomic profiling using RNA sequencing. Hypothesis: Compared to unselected breast cancers, TNBC that are platinum sensitive are more likely to be HRD. Patients with HRD tumors are more likely to benefit from PARP inhibitors. The combination of PARP inhibitor with immunotherapy can overcome resistance to DNA damaging agents such as platinum chemotherapy and/or PARP inhibitor. Specific Aims: 1) To compare the PFS of patients with TNBC that are HRD with tumors that are homologous recombination proficient as determined by HRDetect. 2) To determine the mutations in components of homologous recombination pathway through next generation sequencing assays in an enriched population of platinum responsive TNBC. 3) To examine the differences in TNBC molecular subtypes as determined by RNA-sequencing in TNBC that are HRD with tumors that are homologous recombination proficient.
kw: homologous recombination deficiency; triple negative breast cancer; biomarker; parp inhibitor

title: COVID-19 Vaccine Response Across the Ages
abs: The COVID-19 pandemic has a disproportionate impact on older adults. Immunosenescence contributes to worse outcomes in older adults as not only are they more vulnerable to acquiring the infection, they are also prone to developing more severe infections and downstream complications. Even with vaccinations, older adults are still disadvantaged, with suboptimal responses to the vaccination compared to their younger counterparts. Hence, we seek to characterize the differential immune response to the COVID-19 vaccination between younger and older adult. We also aim to explore potential mechanisms for these differences. This study will be a proof-of-concept study. 20 subjects will be recruited, 10 young (21-40 years) and 10 older (71-90 years) adults in equal sex ratio. All subjects will be using the Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine according to the national COVID-19 vaccination schedule. We will examine their pre-vaccination baseline markers and trend them repeatedly over two years. Blood samples will be processed for binding and neutralizing antibodies and T cell responses. We will simultaneously measure gene and protein expression profiles as well as the expression patterns of B cell receptor and T cell receptor sequences. Markers of biological aging will be analysed and correlated to their immunological response. Stool samples will be processed for full shotgun sequencing metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, metabolomics and culturomics. Functional and cognitive testing will be done at baseline and then annually. Comparative analysis will be done to determine differential immunity response to the vaccine across age groups. By dissecting the immunological responses between the young and old, there is potential for targeted therapies to improve vaccine responses in the elderly.
kw: immunosenescence; COVID-19 vaccine; older adults; biological age; microbiota; frailty

title: Identifying exosome biomarkers of response in Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR) mutated lung cancer
abs: Background Tyrosine-kinase inhibitors (TKIs) are the standard first line treatment for Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-mutant lung cancers, but these tumours eventually develop resistance. Previous work suggests that increased reliance on oxidative-phosphorylation is central to this acquisition of resistance, and that intracellular communication through exosomes is part of this process. These exosomes can be readily isolated from body fluids like plasma, and are amenable to sequential sampling over the course of a patient’s disease. Prior research in EGFR-mutant lung cancer cell lines has identified potential candidate exosome biomarkers of TKI resistance, which have yet to be confirmed on plasma exosome testing. Aims and objectives In this study, we aim to isolate and analyse exosomes derived from sequential plasma samples of patients with EGFR mutated lung cancer treated with TKIs, in order to identify potential exosome biomarkers of upregulated oxidative phosphorylation that predict resistance to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors. Methodology, approach and feasibility We currently have sequential plasma samples taken from 50 patients undergoing TKI treatment for EGFR-mutant lung cancer. We will isolate the exosomes through ultracentrifugation, and perform proteomic analysis followed by bioinformatics analysis to identify exosome biomarkers that predict for TKI resistance. This will be done at Professor Goh Boon Cher’s lab at the Cancer Science Institute, which has the technology and expertise to perform these methods. If candidate biomarkers are found, there is potential for a prospective validation cohort amongst lung cancer patients. Importance to Science and Medicine Resistance to targeted therapy is a significant problem in cancer treatment. By identifying exosome biomarkers of resistance to EGFR TKIs, plasma testing could then be used as an accessible, non-invasive method of prognostication and tracking disease response in our lung cancer patients. This research would also allow us to better understand and mitigate the pathways involved in EGFR TKI resistance.
kw: Exosome; Lung Cancer; Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor, Oxidative Phosphorylation

title: Evaluating the Host Microbiome and Cytokine Dysregulation as Predictive factors for Response to Anti CD38 monoclonal antibody-based therapy in Multiple Myeloma
abs: Background Multiple myeloma ( MM) is an incurable blood cancer affecting 100 patients per year in Singapore. While immune dysregulation is key to the pathogenesis and progression of MM, the role of the immune system in response to therapy remains poorly understood. We are currently studying the immune microenvironment of MM patients treated with anti CD38 monoclonal antibodies ( MAB) using the ESCAPE single cell RNA sequencing platform. We hypothesize that the host gut microbiome as well as the cytokine milieu play a role in the response to these agents. Aims Aim 1: Gut microbiome analysis of newly diagnosed MM patients treated with anti CD38 MAB based regimens. Aim 2: Cytokine profiling of newly diagnosed MM patients treated with anti CD38 MAB based regimens. Hypotheses 1. The host gut microbiome at diagnosis affects response to CD38 MAB based therapy. 2. The host gut microbiome at diagnosis affects the cytokine and immune cell profile. 3. Treatment with CD38 MAB based therapy alters the gut microbiome which in turn modulates the cytokine and immune cell profile. 4. The microbiome and cytokine/immune cell profile post treatment correlates with treatment outcomes and toxicities. Methodology We aim to collect blood and bone marrow samples at diagnosis, achievement of complete remission and relapse in 20 newly diagnosed MM patients treated with anti CD38 MAB. These patients will be participants on clinical trials using anti CD38 MAB based combinations. We will perform cytokine profiling at the time points above. Stool samples will be collected at diagnosis, twice a week during the first month, followed by weekly for a month, then monthly for one year. Results of cytokine profiling and microbiome analysis will be correlated with clinical outcomes as well as the immune cell profile generated by the ESCAPE analysis.
kw: multiple myeloma; microbiome;immune dysregulation;cytokine;monoclonal antibody;CD38

title: Assessment of Urban Ecosystem Services in Residential Neighbourhoods in Singapore
abs: The provision of urban ecosystem services (UES) from natural capital in cities is increasingly recognized as an important area that can contribute to enhancing the liveability, sustainability and resilience of cities to external disturbances. Yet, there is a limited amount of scientific studies on provision of UES at the neighbourhood scale, which we argue is important as neighbourhoods affect the well-being of large population of urban dwellers. This project addresses the assessment of UES in neighbourhood landscapes in high-density residential towns in Singapore. This research is a continuation of the research project “Biophilic Town: A Framework for Landscapes to Enhance the Environment of High-Density Towns” funded by the NRF Land and Liveability National Innovation Challenge Grant. It was a multi-agency project led by the PI, with the Housing and Development Board (HDB) as the key collaborator and involving the National Parks Board and Urban Redevelopment Authority. The project was successfully completed in May 2018 and led to the development of a comprehensive set of framework, principles, design strategies and guidelines for designing neighbourhood landscapes to optimize urban ecosystem service (UES) provision . The guidelines proposed five main categories of urban ecosystem services that are relevant at the scale of residential neighbourhood, along with 120 strategies and 28 key performance indicators for the design of neighbourhood landscapes.
