With the adoption and operationalization of the guidelines by HDB since 2018, and the increasing application of the guidelines, there is a recognized need to monitor the extent to which urban ecosystem services are provided in these developments. The overall aim of this project is to develop monitoring protocols for a set of key performance indicators (KPIs) for ecosystem services that are accurate, scalable, and cost-effective, so that they can upscaled to other existing and future areas, in and outside HDB estates, and potentially within and outside Singapore to other cities. This project is thus highly application focused and development driven. The project is organized into 4 stages: review and develop methods to assess UES; apply and validate methods; develop a composite index based on UES identified; and assess performance of design strategies.
kw: urban ecosystem services; assessment; thermal comfort; soil and water quality; noise assessment; recreational service; visual relief

title: Conversion of Spent FCC Catalyst into Value-added Precipitated Silica
inst: ISCE2 - Institute of Sustainability for Chemicals, Energy and Environment
abs: Our process uses acid to leach metals from a silicate material, and then converts the silica-rich residue into high purity precipitated silica using CO2 and calcium oxides/hydroxides. If applied to spent FCC catalysts, then there is an additional opportunity to treat the leachate to recover valuable components such as rare-earth metals. By-products include calcium carbonate (used for land reclamation) and brine, which means that there are practically no residual materials that are to be disposed at the landfill. Our process has been demonstrated to work at the lab scale. We intend to adapt and tailor it to work for spent FCC catalyst wastes, and then scale it up and demonstrate it on a kg-scale prototype to present convincing evidence of its feasibility.
kw: Spent FCC catalysts; precipitated silica; CO2

title: Developing hyperspectral OCT as a clinical test to detect neural dysfunction in degenerative diseases of the optic nerve and retina
abs: The retina and optic nerve are the only parts of the central nervous system that can be easily visualized non-invasively. A limitation with conventional optical imaging technology is that substantial degree of neuronal loss in the retinal and optic nerve structure and function has to occur before the disease is detected. This is true for glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy, as well as ocular changes associated with brain diseases such as Alzheimer’s disease and Parkinson’s disease. Hence, there is a need for novel investigational techniques that can better inform us on the state of neural health status. This will then allow for timely diagnosis of eye diseases and exploit the eye as a “window” to identifying sick and dying nerve cells in the brain. In the present grant, we propose to set up a novel hyperspectral optical coherence tomography (OCT) technique to fill this gap. We have obtained preliminary data using hyperspectral fundus imaging, demonstrating that such characteristic disease signatures can be obtained in principle. However, in contrast to fundus imaging, our approach provides depth resolution thereby increasing sensitivity and specificity. We first plan to set up a custom-built hyperspectral OCT system. Using hyperspectral analysis of the OCT system, we propose to identify characteristic signatures in animal models of the disease. Based on the experience with the initial laboratory-based set-up, we plan to further develop a second hyperspectral OCT prototype that will also be used for the clinical proof-of-concept studies. The final aim of this grant is to establish hyperspectral OCT, as a specific and sensitive biomarker for the early detection of inner retinal changes associated with retinal ganglion cell dysfunction. This may have important implications for early diagnosis and follow-up of neurodegenerative disease, and the technique may also provide a novel surrogate outcome for neuroprotection studies.
kw: Eye; Optical Coherence Tomography; Degenerative Diseases; Neural Dysfunction

title: Non-traditional computing enabled through the Ising model
abs: Many challenging computational tasks are ill-suited for conventional computing architectures such as the von Neumann architecture present on every desktop computer. This is especially true for tasks related to artificial neural networks, where the massive parallelism requirement is incompatible with a traditional central processing unit (CPU). Traditional computing using the high-speed CPU requires precise computation on top of substantial power level demands for overcoming the noise floor to prevent algorithm failure. Machine-learning and neural network emulation tasks, on the other hand, tolerate much higher levels of noise and the importance of every-bit-must-be-calculated-correctly paradigm is diminished. Such computation paradigm relief presents reduction of power requirements for certain computational tasks and consequently enables a much denser level of integration and higher speed. Recently, there has been considerable amount of research efforts devoted to finding such computation models. One such model that has recently garnered significant attention is the Ising model. More specifically, the Ising model presents unique methodology for the mapping of important problems in areas such as finance, drug development, natural language processing, and video/image processing. In this proposal, we turn our attention to deep scientific challenges associated with Ising machines and their implementation. For example, optimization programs related to protein folding, which is an important process for the discovery of new drugs, are executed slowly with traditional hardware implementations. In general, machine learning algorithms executed through neural networks built on software emulated systems suffer from complex abstraction layers compared to application specific (ASIC) hardware implementations. Hypothetically, a well-designed physical realization of an Ising machine would immediately gain performance advantage over the conventional digital system architecture. In particular, we propose a device-level research towards a truly scalable chip-based Ising computer which would pave the way for commercial viability. We also propose research of mapping important computational problems in diverse subject areas using the Ising model. As explained in the subsequent section, experimental Ising implementations carried out elsewhere in the world have typically been constructed by applied physics groups making use of limited or off-the-shelf parts. Such Ising implementations do not ordinarily use transistors or traditional logic gates or circuitry, but rather use a physical system to realize arbitrary coupling topologies between large state networks that must interact with one another in particular ways not possible in traditional digital networks. Examples of such physical systems include photonic networks where states are encoded into the phase co-propagating optical modes, magnetic tunnel junction networks where states are encoded into the spins of arrayed a

title: Enhancement of Regenerative Stem Cell Therapy with Extracellular Matrix Proteins and Novel Small Molecules
abs: Regenerative medicine (RM) is a branch of translational research that develops methods for repair or replacement of damaged cells and tissues. This proposal aims to establish cellular therapy (CT)-based RM to treat blood cancers, ischemic cardiomyopathy and macular degeneration. Our work represents pioneering use of proprietary cell type specific laminins (critical component of extra-cellular matrix proteins which can direct cell type and differentiation) and novel azole-based small molecules (which can enhance cell viability and proliferation) to maintain pluripotent stem cells and differentiate them into CT products (CTPs) for transplantation and subsequent regeneration of the targeted tissues: bone marrow, cardiac muscles and retina. We aim to establish new concepts on using fully human, chemically defined, biologically relevant cell culture matrices in combination with use of small molecules for culturing clinically important cell types for regenerative medicine by (i) optimizing the effects of laminins and small azole-based molecules in generating hematopoietic stem & progenitor cells, cardiovascular progenitors (CVP), and retinal photoreceptors (PRPs) derived CTPs; (ii) performing safety and efficacy studies of these CTPs in appropriate animal models; and (iii) dissecting the pathway of action for the discovery of novel translational technologies and cellular mechanisms. This project brings together established intellectual properties from participating institutes and is likely to generate further novel, patentable innovations that will aid in creating CTPs to advance Singapore’s healthcare capabilities for an aging population. The program team comprises established clinicians, laboratory and clinical scientists along with key industry partnerships. If successful, this work will establish Singapore as a world leader in regenerative medicine in the area of ischemic cardiomyopathy, age-related macular degeneration, and blood cancers.
kw: Hematopoietic Stem and Progenitor Cells; Cardiovascular Progenitors; Retinal Photoreceptors; Laminins; Small Molecules; Cellular Therapy; Regenerative Medicine

title: Discovering new target space for the development of drugs against malaria parasites.
abs: Infectious diseases are a continuous threat for Singapore and the region. While Singapore is considered malaria-free there are regular cases of imported cases seen in Singapore hospitals. The appearance of multidrug resistant malaria poses a threat to Singapore as well, as it increases the likelihood of treatment failure and at the same time increases the risk of spread within the country. The threat that multidrug resistant malaria poses for the world is even greater and it is not unlikely that it would lead to a doubling of malaria deaths each year. This risk has now been further increased due to the significant disruption of health care provisions as a result of the COVID pandemic. The complex and unique biology of the malaria parasite offers new druggable targets that have so far not been explored at the same time our understanding of targets and mode of action of many antimalarials remains limited. We have recently adapted Cellular Thermal Shift Assay (CETSA) to directly identify the intracellular targets of a number of established antimalarial drugs. At the same time we have identified a range of highly promising new chemical scaffolds with strong activity against malaria parasites. The combination of new compounds with attractive therapeutic properties along with the CETSA and other -omic approaches as well as strong medicinal chemistry support provides us with a novel and powerful strategy to survey the potential target space for new antimalarial compounds. The primary aim of this proposal is therefore to leverage on these already developed capacities to rapidly supply the antimalarial development pipeline with unique and clinically-suitable chemical scaffolds which exert their activity on novel cellular pathways to combat drug-resistant parasites in the field. Importantly, the know-how and expertise developed here in would put Singapore into a unique position to become an important player in the development of new anti-infective’s.
kw: Novel targets, Drug development, Plasmodium, CETSA

title: Understanding the low-frequency variability of coastal sea level in Southeast Asia using a regional ocean model and observations
abs: Regional sea level variability is influenced by large-scale climate phenomena across seasonal, inter-annual, decadal and multidecadal timescales. In this proposal, the term ‘low-frequency’ is broadly defined as the seasonal to multi decadal timescale. The superimposition of low-frequency sea level variability on long-term trends may lead to a temporal decrease or increase in regional sea level trend. Hence, along with long-term sea level trends, it is essential to have a realistic estimation of low-frequency sea level variability in both past and future projections. This is crucial for the implementation of better and efficient adaptation policies. The proposed project has two major objectives. Firstly, the project aims at a comprehensive study of the low-frequency sea level variability and underlying physical/dynamical processes, with a particular emphasis on the Southeast Asian region. The study will be performed using a high-resolution regional ocean circulation model (NEMO) simulations supported by tide-gauge and satellite sea level observations. Model hindcast simulations (1958-2020) and sensitivity experiments will be conducted to understand the mechanism/oceanic processes responsible for the coastal sea level variability. Secondly, the study will investigate possible changes to the low-frequency regional coastal sea level variability in Southeast Asia, and underlying physical processes in a warming climate. Dynamical downscaling of atmospheric and oceanic variables from Climate Model Intercomparison Project 6 (CMIP6) coupled model simulations for the historic period (1950-2014), and for selected projection scenarios, will be carried-out.

title: Monitoring and forecasting of land-height change, coastline retreat and coastal flooding around Southeast Asia using geodesy and remote sensing
abs: Alarming numbers of people live in areas of SE Asia that will be inundated by rising seas in the coming decades. Forecasting the exact areas that are likely to be inundated, however, remains challenging, requiring accurate information on how the sea surface will rise, how land heights are changing, and a Digital Terrain Model (DTM) that accurately maps the ground level (not the tops of trees and buildings, as is the case for the commonly used SRTM Digital Elevation Model (DEM)). Here, we propose to apply a state-of-the-art, multi-satellite-sensor approach to filling gaps in knowledge and reducing the inaccuracies for these three necessary datasets. Various recent studies have attempted to correct the SRTM data to true ground level (by correcting for buildings and trees) in order to forecast coastal inundation from sea-level rise (e.g., Kulp and Strauss, 2019). These did not explicitly consider, however, that the SRTM data were acquired in 2000: Over the two decades since, natural and human-driven coastal subsidence in many areas of SE Asia have resulted in considerably lower land levels than captured in the SRTM data. Estimates of future inundation have also ignored the fact that the land levels will continue to sink, taking into account only climate-related sea-surface rise. We will estimate revised forecasts of coastal inundation for all major coastal cities in the region using a combination of (1) time series of land-height change from InSAR and GNSS, (2) a cutting-edge ground-level DTM that incorporates new LiDAR satellite missions, and (3) revised projections of sea-surface change from complementary efforts. We will additionally innovate and test new algorithms to map actual coastal inundation and flooding as it unfolds. These mapping algorithms will be based on SAR, optical remote sensing, and LiDAR, and will be designed such that they can be automated for ongoing monitoring.

title: NOVEL FRAMEWORK FOR PROBABILISTIC SEA-LEVEL PROJECTIONS FOR SINGAPORE AND SURROUNDING REGIONS
abs: Future sea-level rise will generate hazards for coastal populations, economies, and infrastructure of Singapore. Our objective is to develop a novel framework to integrate the probabilistic sea-level projections and their uncertainties for Singapore and surrounding regions by 2100 under different emission scenarios. We will achieve this with a combination of three approaches: (1) Refining the climate models used in our analysis by targeting those which accurately represent regionally important processes including thermal expansion, ocean dynamics, glacier melt, ice sheet contributions, and land water storage; (2) With a focus on regional ocean circulation and its impact on sea level we will validate not only climate models, but also a higher resolution model that resolves more of the relevant regional ocean dynamics; and (3) We will synthesise sea-level rise in a statistical framework (using copulas) that describes probabilistic sea-level projections for the region. The use of copulas is novel in sea-level research. This statistical tool is particularly relevant here because, unlike previously applied methods, it considers the uncertainty and correlations between the component changes of sea level which results in a better description of the combined processes, particularly at the high tail end or extreme sea levels. High-end upper-tail projections are the greatest risk, produce the largest damages, and highest prospective costs in planning adaptation. In addition, we will strengthen our estimates of the confidence interval of the uncertainties by employing graphical copulas to model the statistical effects of downscaling and the collective correlated influences of the spatially dependent components. Our resulting statistical framework couples the uncertainty of sea-level components at different spatial scales, while enabling the evaluation of systemic uncertainties which serve to inform the potential occurrence of regime shifts towards the climatic extreme. It can also handle updated information from CMIP6 simulations at the same time.

title: Retinal microvascular changes in pre-diabetes: Predicting the progression to diabetes and evaluating the response to exercise. The Pre-DICTED EYE study
abs: There are approximately 500,000 pre-diabetics in Singapore, and an estimated 35% of which will progress to diabetes over the next 8 years. It is well established that retinopathy can be observed in persons without diabetes, and these retinal vascular changes can predict incident impaired fasting glucose and diabetes. The Pre-DICTED programme, is a multi-year community-based lifestyle intervention programme plus stepwise addition of metformin to reduce the conversion from pre-diabetes to diabetes. In the current proposal, we aim to apply traditional and novel retinal imaging techniques to assess this cohort of persons with pre-diabetes to achieve the following specific aims: 1. To evaluate the baseline retinal microvascular parameters of persons with pre-diabetes and determine if these biomarkers can predict the progression from prediabetes to diabetes. 2. To develop a multimodal risk classification algorithm based on retinal microvascular changes and traditional risk factors and evaluate if this can improve the risk stratification of patient with prediabetes into those with low and hish risk of progression to diabetes. 3. To evaluate the retinal microvascular changes in response to a systematic programme of interventions using multimodal imaging comparing the intensive treatment and standard of care arm; and assess if these changes are a biomarker for the progression to diabetes that can determine which subjects would respond best to specific interventions. This proposal aims to develop a model to stratify the risk of progression to diabetes among the 500,000 prediabetics and allow targeted intervention to prevent the onset of diabetes and the costly debilitating complications associated with this disease. Therefore this project will address major themes of this research grant call namely the late identification of diabetes and the prevention of the rapid deterioration of diabetes in our population as well as enabling targeted intervention to optimize to use of our limited healthcare resources.
kw: diabetes; pre-diabetes; retinal vasculature; retina imaging

title: Improvement of screening and identifying vulnerable and frail patients in a tertiary cancer centre. Optimising care and improving quality of life through early detection.
abs: With the anticipated increase in the number of older cancer patients in Singapore, a geriatric-oncology service would be timely to address the challenges of treating cancer in the older patients. Distinguishing frail from fit patients is important to ensure optimal treatment and to curtail toxicity. However, the vulnerable patients are a unique group where early intervention may improve their functioning and enable them to receive more intensive chemotherapy. In our preliminary study, elderly cancer patients underwent a comprehensive geriatric assessment (CGA) followed by interventions. The patients’ EORTC-QLQC30 scores were assessed pre- and 3 months post CGA and interventions. Based on the preliminary results for 10 patients who have completed pre and post intervention questionnaires, there was a trend towards improvement in some of the domains of EORTC-QLQC30 scores such as physical functioning, cognitive functioning, social functioning, fatigue and insomnia. To account for the cancer treatment contributing to the improved scores, we further subdivided the 10 patients into 2 groups: those who received the recommended intervention and those who did not. The functional improvement seen persisted suggesting that the CGA was robust at identifying vulnerable patients. This proposal aims to improve the quality of life in elderly cancer patients by evaluating the impact of a baseline CGA and the effect of interventions. We believe that identification of fit, vulnerable or frail patients enable oncologists to optimize cancer care for patients by effective chemotherapy delivery with less toxicity. Our secondary aim is to identify a quick screening test for use in the clinic as we understand the barriers in implementing a full CGA on all elderly patients due to time and personnel constraints. Our long term goal would be to establish a dedicated multidisciplinary geriatric oncology service to cater to the growing needs of elderly cancer patients in Singapore. (298 words)

title: A Novel RNA based approach to Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD) Hepatocellular Carcinoma Oncogenesis
abs: With the obesity epidemic in Asia, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) now afflicts 40% of Singaporeans. The annual incidence of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) in NAFLD cirrhosis is 13%. NAFLD HCC is rapidly rising and is poised to overtake viral hepatitis as the commonest cause for liver cancer. NAFLD HCC is usually detected late and has a worse prognosis compared to viral HCC. Better strategies are urgently required to detect and treat this devastating disease at an earlier stage. While the genomic landscape of HCC has been extensively evaluated, how RNA bridges the gap between individuals at risk and the development of HCC is unclear. RNA biology is one of the most rapidly expanding areas in modern biology, and systematic profiling of the transcriptome in early HCC has not been performed. Specifically, exosomes have been found to be a key mediator of cell-cell interaction in the HCC microenvironment and are essential to hepatocarcinogenesis. Our work has shown that microRNA(miRNA) are dysregulated in NAFLD HCC, and that RNA delivered within exosomes can modulate HCC tumour biology by mesenchymal to epithelial transition. We will evaluate the serum exosomal miRNA in a unique familial cohort of NASH cirrhosis patients in University of California San Diego (UCSD) from 90 individuals with early NAFLD HCC. This will be compared against 90 NAFLD cirrhosis individuals as control. The differentially expressed miRNA will be identified and the top eight miRNAs will be selected by pathway analysis. We will evaluate the mechanism behind these identified exosomal miRNA in tumorigenesis by over-expressing and silencing the miRNA in our in-vivo cirrhotic model. Learning an RNA based approach to NAFLD HCC at UCSD, the leading centre for translational NAFLD research, will help us identify novel biomarkers, evaluate the pathophysiology of hepatocarcinogenesis and identify potential targets for RNA therapeutics in our Singaporean cohort.
kw: Hepatocellular carcinoma; liver cancer; hepatocarcinogenesis; RNA biology

title: Single Cell RNA Sequencing and Protein Expression Analysis of Tumor and Immune Cells of Multiple Myeloma Patients with Early Death and Long Survival
abs: Background: Multiple Myeloma (MM) is the second most common haematological malignancy in the world, characterized by diverse genomic landscape with clonal heterogeneity and complex interaction between malignant plasma cells and the immune microenvironment. Treatment advancement has improved MM survival remarkably over the past decade. However, despite being managed similarly, there are still patients who had early death. Single-cell multi-omics technology is a breakthrough in medicine which have revolutionized the way we study cancer, allowing high-resolution insights into disease biology. Hypothesis: The differences in MM disease outcomes are determined by the balance between aggressiveness and survival advantage of the malignant clones and the immune control exerted by the immune microenvironment. Specific aims: (i) To compare the tumor cell characteristics of MM patients with early death and long survival (ii) To compare the immune microenvironment of MM patients with early death and long survival (iii) To compare the effect of treatment on changes to tumor clones and immune environment using serial samples of MM patients with early death and long survival. Methodology: Single-cell multi-omics study evaluating both the transcriptomic profile and protein expression of the same single cell will be performed using droplet-based 10X Genomics 5’ version 2 platform with DNA-barcoded antibodies. Sequencing will be performed with Novaseq paired-end sequencing platform at 2x150 bases to obtain 50% sequencing saturation. Computational analysis will be done using the R Seurat package version 4.0. Validation studies will be performed based on key markers identified in the analysis. Approach: A total of 300,000 tumor and immune cells from 30 bone marrow samples of MM patients with early death and long survival will be evaluated, including some serial samples of the same patients at presentation, post-treatment, and at relapse.
kw: myeloma; multiple myeloma; single-cell; multi-omics; RNA-seq; protein

title: Deciphering the metabolic and molecular underpinnings of Zika virus pathogenesis
abs: Zika virus (ZIKV), like dengue virus and yellow fever virus (YFV), belong to the Flaviviridae family. Transmitted primarily by Aedes mosquitoes, ZIKV was found to be an important cause of congenital disease and childhood developmental delays. However, the viral and host determinants that provoke disease pathogenesis remains unclear. Recently, we demonstrated clinically that metabolic perturbations underpin susceptibility to symptomatic YFV infection. Our clinical findings hint at the possibility that perturbations in metabolic pathways may also influence ZIKV infection outcome. Indeed, consistent with this notion, we have now preliminary data to support that ZIKV dramatically alters host metabolism, especially glucose and mitochondrial metabolism, resulting in augmented neurovirulence in vivo. Moreover, we found that ZIKV inhibits hexokinase activity, which is involved in the first committed step of glucose metabolism. Bypassing hexokinase inhibition by either pyruvate or glutamine supplementation restored mitochondrial metabolism that was associated with reduced proinflammatory responses. We have also identified how ZIKV manipulates cellular metabolism, where a ZIKV mutant with a phenylalanine-to-leucine amino acid substitution in the Membrane protein, profoundly decelerated both glycolysis and mitochondrial respiration. Therefore, our overarching hypothesis is that the ZIKV Membrane protein is involved in the control of host cell glucose and mitochondrial metabolism, which in turn, is responsible for neurovirulence in vivo. We will combine molecular virology with detailed investigations to pinpoint how glucose and mitochondrial metabolism are perturbed during ZIKV infection. Specifically, we aim to examine how ZIKV Membrane protein represses hexokinase activity and its consequent impact on mitochondria homeostasis. Additionally, we will investigate how repressed hexokinase activity imposed by ZIKV affect metabolic consumption of alternative nutrient sources that may augment viral replication and pathogenesis. We envisage that the identification of specific virus-host interactions critical for perturbing metabolism would guide the development of therapies to reduce the global burden of Zika.
kw: Zika virus; viral host response; viral-host interactions; metabolism

title: Identify the molecular and circuit maladaptation of tuberal somatostatin neurons in obesity
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Overconsumption of palatable food, the leading cause of obesity, involves the intersection of environmental, physiological and genetic factors. Palatable food is rewarding for animals through dopaminergic signaling, and maladaptation of dopaminergic systems has been suggested in contributing to the development of obesity. Because of the rewarding and reinforcing effect of food, Pavlov used food as a cue in classical associative conditioning experiments. Later experiments further showed that associative cues including tone and contextual information paired with palatable food could augment feeding in satiated animals. Indeed, environmental factors has been postulated to play an important role in over-eating and weight gain in human beings. Despite revealing multiple neuronal populations in feeding regulation, it still remains unknown how these neuronal circuits are influenced by obesity. Our previous work showed that somatostatin neurons in mouse tuberal nucleus (TNSST neurons) are a new orexigenic neuronal population. We found that TNSST neurons are the major hypothalamic neuronal population that is more activated after consuming palatable food, and likely receive direct input from midbrain dopaminergic neurons. Moreover, we revealed that TNSST neurons are critical for contextual feeding conditioning, and the ventral subiculum (vSub) is the potential pathway that sends environmental information to TNSST neurons. Such vSub to TNSST show plastic change in conditioned feeding paradigm. Overactivation of TNSST neurons lead to obesity, and contributes to the obesity phenotype found in a mouse Huntington’s disease model. These findings suggest that TNSST neuronal circuit is plastic to consuming palatable food and is likely strongly influenced by chronic high fat diet consumption. Maladaptive TNSST circuit might play a key role in developing obesity. The proposed research intends to examine the change in molecular profile and neural circuit of TNSST neurons, and the results from the proposed research will bring new insights in understanding food overconsumption and obesity.
kw: obesity, tuberal nucleus, somatostatin neurons, feeding regulation

title: Functional investigations of human microbiome secretory enzymes in common dermatological diseases
abs: Skin diseases account for some of the most prevalent human diseases worldwide, with Singapore experiencing one of the highest non-fatal skin disease burden per capita. Disruption of the epithelial barrier is associated with dysbiosis of the resident microbial population, as evident from the dramatic change in microbial composition in many skin conditions. We hypothesize that crucial interactions between the host and the microbes that reside in human are mediated by secretory enzymes produced by these micro-organisms. In this study, we propose to focus on physiologically relevant microbial enzymes of functional importance(proteases, lipases, phospholipases and sphingomyelinases) by first developing metagenomic tools to measure the expression of the microbial enzymes at the transcript level obtained directly from human skin surface. With these targeted sequencing and quantitative PCR-based tools, we aim to first obtain the baseline expression of these functionally relevant microbial enzymes in a healthy cohort using non-invasive sampling methods. To assess whether these microbial enzymes are differentially expressed during epithelial barrier breach, we propose to first perform a cross-sectional study on atopic dermatitis, psoriasis and seborrheic dermatitis. To determine the correlation of disease progression and resolution to the transcription profile of the microbial enzymes, we will focus on atopic dermatitis for our longitudinal study. We will further define the possible functions of these microbial enzymes in influencing skin structure and immunity using 3D skin models and in vivo mouse model. From these studies, we aim to identify a panel of microbial secretory enzymes that can serve as biomarkers of skin health and predictors of disease progression and clinical outcome. Taken together, defining the in situ expression and skin-relevant functions of these key mediators of host-microbial interactions will facilitate design of relevant interventions for alleviation of dermatological diseases.
kw: Microbiome; enzyme discovery; disease biomarker; metagenomics; dermatology

title: Intraoperative detection and demarcation of oral cancer resection margins using hybrid fiberoptic Raman spectroscopy and optical coherence tomography associated with deep-learning
abs: Difficulty in visual identification of premalignant and malignant oral lesions coupled with inadequate cancer margins assessment using conventional white-light imaging is the major cause for the poor prognosis and high recurrence of oral cancer, resulting in disproportionately high mortality rates and poor treatment outcomes. To address clinical challenges, this project aims to develop a novel hybrid fiberoptic Raman spectroscopy(RS) and optical coherence tomography(OCT) technique for improving early detection and diagnosis of oral cancer, as well as intraoperative determination of cancer resection margins for precision surgery. Our hypotheses are that RS is able to characterize biochemical changes associated with oral neoplastic transformation; 2D/3D OCT imaging is sensitive to detect the changes of tissue scattering/vascular properties in oral cancer at microns scales, and hence the hybrid RS-OCT technique containing both tissue biochemical/morphological information will significantly enhance early detection and diagnosis of oral cancer in-vivo for effective surgical procedure. Specifically, we will develop a novel handheld RS-OCT probe with collinear fiberoptic design for both OCT sampling and RS collection that offers compelling advantages for co-localized tissue RS/OCT measurements. RS will remove operators’ subjectivity by enabling in vivo molecular characterization of suspicious lesions, thereby much reducing the sampling errors of tissue biopsies with targeted biopsies. The fast OCT 2D/3D imaging to direct the Raman measurements will further remove operators’ subjectivity on visual recognition of suspicious lesions for tumor margins determination. We will further integrate RS-OCT technique with deep-learning that enables tissue biochemical and scattering/vascularity properties to be extracted and analyzed in real-time during clinical examination. The hybrid RS-OCT technology has potential to become a clinically powerful diagnostic tool for objective,real-time in-vivo detection and diagnosis of oral cancer/precancer as well as for intraoperative determination of tumor margins in surgical operation, which would facilitate oral precancer and cancer detection and effective management to improve patients' outcome.
kw: fiberoptic Raman spectroscopy and optical coherence tomography, oral tumor margin demarcation, in vivo cancer diagnosis

title: Defining the role of zonal hepatocytes in liver homeostasis, regeneration and tumourigenesis
abs: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the second leading cause of cancer mortality worldwide. Currently, there are only limited therapeutic options. New strategies that stem from innovative research on the pathogenesis of this disease at the molecular and cellular levels need to be developed to improve its diagnosis and treatment. HCC mainly originates from the transformation of normal hepatocytes through a series of genetic alterations. However, the role of distinct zonal hepatocyte subsets in cancer initiation in the context of different oncogenic insults is poorly understood. We hypothesize that the target zonal hepatocyte population at the initiation of HCC is a key determinant of cancer phenotypes and plays an important role in HCC malignancy and heterogeneity. Mouse model studies have tremendously improved our understanding of HCC pathogenesis and represent a source of great potential for developing mechanism-based therapies for HCC. In this study, we develop multiple mouse models to systematically trace the fate and function of discrete zonal hepatocyte subsets in liver maintenance and regeneration. These mouse models will be further utilized to selectively deplete distinct hepatocyte populations to examine the dynamics and the relationships between different zonal hepatocyte subsets during liver regeneration. Lastly, to determine the cellular origin of tumours and the correlations in molecular signatures between a normal hepatocyte subset and the tumours arising from it, the zonal hepatocytes-specific mouse strains will be subjected to different oncogenic insults, including (1) overexpression of oncogenes (c-myc, Neu/Her2 and β-catenin), and (2) NASH-driven HCC mouse models. A better understanding of the role of zonal hepatocytes in liver homeostasis and regeneration, and identification of the critical target cell populations and molecular mechanisms for HCC development from this study will potentially lead to novel strategies for early detection, more effective treatment and development of preventative therapies for individuals at high risk of developing HCC.
kw: mouse cancer models; cancer genetics; lineage tracing; cells of origin in cancer; tissue repair and regeneration; tumourigenesis

title: Targeting the dysregulated miR-198 rheostat in chronic diabetic foot ulcers
abs: Non-healing diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs) are one of the most devastating complications of diabetes. DFUs, which commonly occur in approximately 25% of diabetic patients, are the biggest reason for non-traumatic lower limb amputations. Singapore has an exceptionally high rate of amputations due to non-healing DFUs. This globally escalating medical issue lacks approved pharmacologic options. Strategies such as exogenously applying growth factors have almost universally failed in the clinic; this is partly attributed to dysregulation of cellular signal transduction and associated microRNA networks in the local DFU microenvironment. We identified a defective molecular switch in chronic DFUs, which is a consequence of dysregulated TGF-b signalling. The defective switch facilitates sustained expression of miR-198, a microRNA which inhibits keratinocyte migration, wound re-epithelialization and wound healing. Concurrently, expression of pro-migratory factors including FSTL1 and targets of miR-198 are abolished. We hypothesize that, modulation of the defective switch and abrogation of miR-198 expression locally in DFUs, can lead to effective keratinocyte migration, wound re-epithelialization and accelerate wound healing. Addressing our hypothesis, our first objective is to target miR-198 in the wound microenvironment of chronic DFUs using chemically modified antagomiRs. Simultaneously we will design a microRNA-based biosensor system to identify small molecule modulators of the dysregulated pathway by high-throughput screen. Finally following validation of hit-to-lead compounds we will proceed with the preclinical evaluation of combinatorial therapies using 3-dimensional organotypic and ex-vivo organ culture models. All validations will be performed using patient-derived primary cells or skin samples derived from lower limb scheduled for amputation. We will assess the efficacy of the drug on samples from clinically relevant group of diabetic individuals, positioning this proposal for design of new therapeutics. Our objective is to develop a novel therapeutic strategy to accelerate healing of DFUs, thereby mitigating complications associated with chronic open wounds and prevent amputations.
kw: Diabetic foot ulcers;  microRNA; non-healing wounds; amputations; complications of diabetes; chronic wounds

title: Characterization of metabolic pathways and phenotypes in Multiple Myeloma to identify nutrient vulnerabilities as therapeutic opportunities
abs: Multiple myeloma (MM) is a B-cell malignancy that remains incurable despite the recent advances in approved novel drug treatments like proteasome inhibitors. Recurrent chromosomal translocations are central to the pathogenesis of MM, accounting for ~50% of total MM cases. In particular, t(14;16) and t(4;14) translocations represent high-risk groups and very poor prognosis. These translocations displayed an overexpression of the oncogenic transcription factor, c-MAF. It is well-known that metabolic shifts in cancer cells have important consequences and therapeutic opportunities. The field of cancer metabolism in MM is underexplored, and whether primary translocations define certain metabolic features remain undetermined. Our preliminary studies revealed a novel role of c-MAF in the regulation of metabolic genes and metabolite readouts. To comprehensively characterize the metabolic alterations driven by c-MAF, we will perform mass spectrometry-based metabolomics on our stable c-MAF-overexpressing isogenic cells to concurrently measure 116 metabolites, and differential metabolites can be further enriched into metabolic pathways. Given the role of c-MAF as a transcription factor, we will perform RNA sequencing coupled with ChIP-sequencing to analyze the transcriptome for metabolic genes directly regulated by c-MAF promoter binding activity that could be responsible for the phenotype. The altered pathways will lead to the identification of metabolic dependencies and vulnerabilities that could be validated in vitro and translated to pharmacological applications in patients with c-MAF overexpression. Our proposed work helps to further research by establishing a metabolomic framework that can be easily extended to characterize the metabolic profiles of other genetically high-risk MM subgroups. In addition, our proposal has important long-term clinical implications where metabolite concentrations in the blood plasma or serum can potentially act as biomarkers to define high-risk MM.
kw: Metabolomics; Multiple Myeloma; c-MAF; metabolic genes; synthetic lethality; nutrient vulnerabilities

title: Regulation of Circadian Rhythms
abs: Our circadian rhythms are controlled by an internal body clock that regulates internal physiology to optimize life in a world with daily light-dark cycles. This body clock system influences virtually all daily processes. Circadian disruptions due to shift work, inadequate sleep, social jet lag and international travel are an increasingly common feature of Singaporean and international culture. Circadian stresses put us at increased risk for diseases including diabetes, obesity, cancer and mood disorders. A deeper understanding of the mechanisms of circadian clock can provide significant insights into these pathological conditions. Circadian rhythms are controlled by phosphorylation/degradation cycles and so are amenable to therapeutic interventions. We have made substantial progress over the prior grant period in understanding how phosphorylation cycles control the clock, leading to new questions and new opportunities. We described a Casein Kinase 1:PER2 phosphoswitch that controls clock speed by controlling the stability of PER2 and recently validated this by generating a mouse with a mutant PER2 degron. Our finding that CK1δ/ε itself is the elusive priming kinase, and that the phosphoswitch can be controlled by splice variants of CK1δ raises important new questions. Key insights were most recently provided by our collaborative work solving the crystal structure of CK1 with the tau mutation, which identified previously unrecognized CK1 activation loop dynamics regulated by two key anion binding sites. These new findings lead us to a more refined model of the clock control that explains how phosphorylation of CK1 and specific domains of PERs interact to regulate our rhythms. In this proposal we will explore the model that diverse external stimuli converge on the CK1 activation switch via specific druggable pathways to control phosphorylation site choice and hence circadian clock speed. These studies will provide mechanistic insights into the core clock and provide new therapeutic opportunities.
kw: circadian rhythms; kinase; phosphorylation; protein degradation; clock

title: Elucidating the effect of obesity on flaviviral infection and host response to infection.
abs: Dengue is a mosquito-transmitted acute viral disease that afflicts ~100 million people throughout the tropical and parts of the subtropical world. The prevalence of obesity in these places is also increasing. This convergence of dengue and obesity presents fresh public health challenges – obese dengue patients are 2-4 times more likely than non-obese dengue patients to develop severe dengue. This trend not only suggests that current case management may be suboptimal for obese dengue patients, it also indicates that obesity may compound dengue pathogenesis in ways that have not been defined. We have recently discovered that adaptive endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress and reduced tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle activity underpin increased risk of symptomatic outcome in subjects inoculated with a licensed live attenuated yellow fever viral vaccine (YF17D). As YF17D is genetically related to dengue virus (DENV), our finding shed new insights into the molecular pathogenesis of symptomatic flaviviral infection. We now have new preliminary data suggesting that both ER stress and metabolism are also altered in subjects with moderate-to-high body mass index (BMI). Moreover, such elevated BMI subjects also showed higher baseline (pre-infection) level of innate immune activation, which may all contribute to an increased rate of symptomatic YF17D infection with increasing BMI. We thus propose to use YF17D to show that obesity is a susceptibility factor for symptomatic infection and uncover how obesity modifies the host response to flaviviral infection and thus increase the likelihood of acute illness. We will adopt the experimental medicine approach that is coupled with detailed omics-level laboratory investigations, to elucidate the underpinning biology. By unravelling how obesity alters the host response to YF17D infection, we aim to provide a foundational knowledge on how this convergence of dengue and obesity can be effectively addressed to minimize this emerging global health burden.
kw: Flavivirus; dengue; yellow fever; host response, adaptive immune response; innate immune response.

title: Understanding and exploiting natural killer cell activity in chronic myeloid leukaemia
abs: Chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML) is a myeloproliferative stem cell disorder characterized by the oncogenic fusion kinase BCR-ABL1. While treatment of CML patients with tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) against BCR-ABL1 has improved survival, ~90% of patients fail to achieve a treatment free response (TFR) and will require life-long TKI therapy. The inability to cure CML is due to persistent and quiescent stem and progenitor cells (SPC) that may be beyond the reach of current BCR-ABL1-targeting strategies. Accordingly, there is a major need to identify functional biomarkers that predict CML disease outcome at diagnosis, and develop BCR-ABL1-independent approaches to eradicate disease-perpetuating, quiescent SPCs. We used mass cytometry and scRNA-sequencing to interrogate the bone marrow of chronic phase (CP) CML patients at diagnosis. Our preliminary studies reveal striking quantitative and qualitative differences in natural killer (NK) cells between CML patients in three prognostic groups. Quantitatively, NK cells were increased three-fold in patients with optimal TKI responses (Grp A) compared to patients who were destined for blast crisis transformation (Grp C). Qualitatively, in patients with TKI-resistance (Grp B), NK cells were in a resting and terminally-differentiated state, while in Grp C, NK cells had upregulated a major NK inhibitory receptor, NKG2A. Because NK cells have potent anti-leukaemia activity, we hypothesize that NK-CML cell interactions determine TKI responses in CML, and can be therapeutically exploited in a patient-specific manner. Our Specific Aims are: 1. To characterize NK cell differences in Grps A-C; 2. To characterize CML SPC differences in Grps A-C; 3. To functionally analyse NK cells from Grps A-C; and 4. To enhance NK cell-mediated CML SPC killing. The completion of our Aims will determine if NK cells can serve as biomarkers for treatment outcomes at the time of diagnosis, and if these differences may be therapeutically leveraged to enhance TFR rates in CML.
kw: CML; NK cell; leukaemia stem cell

title: Development of Next-generation Transcriptome Imaging Technology for Molecular Mapping of the Tumor Immune Milieu
abs: Progress in cancer immunotherapy has been both exciting and frustrating. While several immunotherapy approaches exhibited stunning and durable clinical benefits for some cancer types, many cancers are not receptive to immuno-oncology treatment. Even for the amenable cancers, not all patients responded to the treatments. Mechanistic understanding of the tumor-immune crosstalk is paramount for the next immunotherapy breakthrough, but its progress is hindered by the lack of precision technology for decomposing cellular responses at the molecular and spatial level. Spatial transcriptomics is an emerging technology that is capable of generating high-resolution cellular maps of multiplexed molecular information of intact tissue samples. We recently advanced our transcriptome imaging technology by enhancing specificity and simplifying the workflow with split-FISH. We want to further develop split-FISH to scale up the number of assayed genes ~10 fold to 3,000 genes (Aim 1). Then, we want to validate our spatial analysis framework by profiling infiltrating and host immune cells in a murine model (Aim 2). Finally, we will use the established framework to profile the spatio-immune zonation patterns and anticancer immune dynamics of human tumor samples, with the goal of correlating them to patient survival and response rate, thereby providing mechanistic models of the observed anti-tumoral phenotypes (Aim 3). This study could reveal previously unknown molecular targets or pathways for designing novel immunotherapy strategy. The technology established through this project could also serve as a platform for the development of new diagnostic tests.
kw: Tumor heterogeneity; Spatial transcriptomics; Gene expression analysis; Fluorescence microscopy; Single cell analysis; Cancer immunotherapy

title: Discovering and Characterizing novel RSPONDIN receptors for WNT Signaling Potentiation
abs: The canonical WNT signaling pathway plays crucial roles during embryonic development and cancer. The R-SPONDINS (RSPO1-4) are a family of four evolutionary conserved secreted ligands. They function as key WNT enhancers by preventing the degradation of WNT receptor complexes triggered by two E3 ubiquitin ligases RNF43 and ZNRF3. Until very recently, RSPOs were believed to execute this role by engaging their obligate cognate receptors LGR4, LGR5 and LGR6. However, we have now genetically and biochemically demonstrated that the LGR4/5/6 receptors are dispensable for RSPO2/3 functions during organogenesis. This unexpected finding has prompted us and others to hypothesize the existence of yet unidentified RSPO2/3 cell surface receptors during embryonic development and oncogenesis. In this proposal, we ambition to identify and characterize these alternative RSPO cell surface receptors. To this end, we will implement three distinct methods. First, we will perform a CRISPR/cas9 screen for genes mediating WNT enhancement by RSPO2/3 in triple Lgr4/5/6-KO cells, using the TOP-GFP system as a readout for WNT signaling. Second, we will use the Proximity Labeling with Ascorbate Peroxidase (APEX) technique to pull-down specific RSPO2/3 cell surface interacting proteins for mass-spectrometry-based identification. Third, we will attempt to identify candidate alternate receptors for RSPO2 using Mendelian genetics by performing whole genome sequencing of unsolved cases presenting with severe limb truncations or duplications. Tentative alternate receptors obtained from any of these three methods will then be subjected to a series of in vitro and in vivo validation tests using cell culture and Xenopus models. This ambitious undertaking is expected to lead to the discovery of new R-spondin receptor(s) and shed new and important insights into WNT signaling. This research will have fundamental implications in cell biology, development and tumorigenesis, and carries the potential for identifying novel targets against WNT-associated diseases.

title: COINing a new mode of collagen regulation
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: The extracellular matrix (ECM) is a key structural and regulatory part of solid tissues. Regulation of ECM is thus essential for human physiology. When ECM production is deregulated, fibrosis ensues and results in the thickening, scarring and loss of function of tissues, with potentially life-threatening consequences. Common fibrotic diseases include cardiac fibrosis, diabetic nephropathy, idiopathic pulmonary disease and liver cirrhosis. Therapeutic options to counter or slow fibrosis progression are limited. Collagen type I is the most abundant and common element of the ECM. Excessive deposition of type I collagen is thus a hallmark of fibrotic diseases. The signaling mechanisms preventing collagen I over-production in fibroblasts are poorly understood. We designed a highly sensitive reporter for negative regulators of collagen expression in human fibroblasts and performed a genome-wide RNAi screen, identifying over a hundred novel regulators. One of them, C2orf69, is a previously uncharacterised protein of 43 kDa, with a secretion signal and no known homology. Depletion of C2orf69, nicknamed COIN (Collagen Inhibitor) markedly promotes collagen synthesis in otherwise quiescent fibroblasts. Recombinant COIN added to cell medium inhibits Collagen I in fibrosis patient-derived fibroblasts. In the extracellular medium, COIN tightly binds to ECM fibers. Based on structure predictions, COIN appears to be a single domain globular protein with distant homology with bacterial esterase enzymes. Here, we propose to characterise COIN’s mode of action and regulation. To better understand its role in vivo, we will probe COIN’s expression patterns and effects of its genetic depletion in zebrafishes and mice. Finally, we will evaluate whether a recombinant and modified form of COIN could be used therapeutically using a bleomycin-induced lung fibrosis mouse model. In sum, we seek to understand better this fascinating uncharacterised human protein and explore whether it could be used to address the major medical problem that is fibrosis.

title: DEVELOPMENT OF NOVEL THERAPEUTICS AND PREDICTIVE BIOMARKERS IN BREAST CANCER
abs: Devising better treatments represents one important broad strategy to reduce breast cancer morbidity and mortality. This breast cancer therapeutics and predictive biomarkers program is centred around therapeutic clinical trials and complemented by systematic collection of biosamples including tissue and blood to study drug pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics, drug resistance mechanisms, and development of predictive biomarkers. There are 3 specific aims. Aim #1 is focused on studying novel therapeutic strategies in breast cancer through clinical trials. Several novel therapeutic trials are planned, some of which represent bench-to-bedside translation of preclinical work done locally, including a trial of lenvatinib + letrozole based on preclinical work at the PI’s lab in Cancer Science Institute, Singapore; a first-in-man autologous antibody coupled T-cell receptor (ACTR)-T cell trial combined with trastuzumab in HER2+ metastatic breast cancer based on work with Dario Campana at the National University Singapore; using an epigenetic drug, tazemetostat, to induce tumor immune gene signature and restore sensitivity to trastuzumab in HER2+ breast cancers based on work with Yu Qiang from Genome Institute of Singapore; and combining a novel immune-oncology drug, ADG106, an agonistic monoclonal antibody against CD137, with chemotherapy in HER2 negative breast cancer, in collaboration with Adagene, USA. Serial tumor biopsies and plasma samples will be collected longitudinally from trial subjects to study biological effects of drugs and for discovery predictive biomarker work. Aim #2 will develop a platform for ex vivo drug sensitivity testing to select rational combinations using patient-derived organoids from breast cancers, aiming for short turnaround time of 4-6 weeks for real-time guidance of treatment in the clinic. Aim #3 will explore the use of exosomes as a blood-based biomarker to prognosticate and track treatment progress in advanced breast cancer, starting first with hormone receptor positive/HER2 negative disease, then moving on to HER2+ disease if resources and budget permit.

title: Reliable measurement of muscle mass, by a D3-creatine dilution assay, to predict risk for osteoporosis and other major health outcomes as Singaporean women age.
abs: From 50 years of age, postmenopausal women are at an increased risk of developing sarcopenia and osteoporosis as a result of deterioration of musculoskeletal health. Both disorders increase the risk of falls and fractures. Fat mass and bone mineral density (BMD) can be measured accurately using two specific energies in dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DXA) scanning. However, reliable measurement of muscle mass remains elusive, due principally to DXA-determined muscle mass as non-bone, non-fat mass which includes intra-abdominal organs which have the same attenuation signals as muscles. This obviously introduces a measurement error in estimation of muscle mass. A novel method to measure muscle mass using the stable isotope deuterated-creatine (D3-creatine) has recently been developed. Muscle mass measurement with this method was recently shown to have strong and consistent associations with physical performance and increased risk of adverse outcomes such as injurious falls and mobility problems in older men. No data is currently available for women. We hypothesize that differences in muscle mass – when measured accurately - can predict trajectories of declines in bone, cardiometabolic, mental and genital urinary health in ageing women. Accurate measurement of muscle mass, without use of DXA, would allow us to dissect the relative effects of fat versus muscle on risk of osteoporosis. The differential effects on women of muscle versus fat mass and with respect to the condition known as sarcopenic obesity are unresolved. To understand the effect of muscle mass on women’s health, we propose to define thresholds for sarcopenia using muscle mass measured by D3-creatine, that predict increased risk for the following critical and debilitating health conditions: osteoporosis, insulin resistance, diabetes, hypertension, depression, anxiety and urinary incontinence. Achieving our aims will bring novel technology to Singapore in the form of a novel, cost-effective and accurate method to measure muscle mass in mid-life women.

title: Poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors modulate immune responses independent of BRCAness in ovarian cancer therapy
abs: Background: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) targeting the PD-1/PD-L1 axis have shown disappointingly low response rates in immunogenically “cold” ovarian cancer (OC). Another class of anti-cancer therapy, Poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors (PARPis) are known to be effective in selected OC which harbour BRCA1/2 mutations or homologous recombination deficiency (“BRCAness”), based on the concept of synthetic lethality. Systematic examination of the change of transcriptomic landscape induced by PARPis led to the discovery that PARPi treatment induces IFN-mediated immune responses in both BRCA1/2-wildtype and -mutant cancer cells. In the presence of PARPi treatment, PARP1 binds to Interferon Regulatory factor 1 (IRF1), a master transcriptional regulator of both innate and adaptive immune responses. PARPi was able to enhance therapeutic efficacy of ICIs independent of BRCAness. We hypothesise that PARPis can trigger anti-tumour immunity through transcriptomic reprogramming, thereby enhancing efficacy of ICIs in OC. Aims: To define the role of PARPis as modulators of anti-tumour immunity, with the goal of turning immunogenically “cold” tumours “hot”, thus effecting a paradigm shift in the clinical application of PARPis and ICIs in OC treatment. Methods: We will employ in vitro, in vivo models and patient specimens obtained from clinical trials to achieve this aim systematically in three parts. Firstly by proving that PARPis trigger IFN-responses via regulating transcriptional activity of IRF-1 independent of BRCAness; Secondly by optimising PARPi-ICI treatment regimens in terms of PARPi choice, dose and sequencing; Thirdly, to identify how PARPi-ICI combinations alter the tumour immune microenvironment, and to look for biomarkers of treatment response/resistance. Rationale: The aim of this fellowship is to acquire skills in translational science of drug combinations used for immune modulation and predictive biomarker development. This will be a firm foundational basis to develop meaningful future clinical trials, and to establish a strong relationship between our institutions for further collaboration.

title:
Endomembrane System Architecture, Dynamics, and Functions in 
Aging Cells and Tissues
abs: Aging, characterised by a progressive loss of structural and functional integrity of tissues and organs, is the greatest risk factor for most adulthood non-infectious diseases in humans .The science of aging is an emerging focus for biomedical research due to the opportunities for novel and ground-breaking discoveries that could potentially lead to new therapies for diseases that are exerting increasing socio-economic burdens globally. For example, age-related macular degeneration (AMD), a human disease that will be directly investigated by our proposed research, is currently one of the leading causes of visual disabilities, affecting ~190,000 (3 in 100) Singaporeans (~170 million people world-wide), yielding an economic burden of >365 million SGD by year 2030. Cellular aging lies at the heart of organismal aging and underpins the functional deterioration of aged tissues and organs. However, what aging means at the molecular and cellular levels remains one of murkiest areas of science. A fundamental property of the eukaryotic cell is the compartmentalisation of the cytosol through elaborate lipid-based endomembrane systems—including the nuclear membrane and membrane-bound organelles such as the Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER), mitochondria, and lysosomes. Such compartmentalisation enables biomolecular reactions to occur in well-defined and separated nanoscale environments with high efficiency and specificity, while providing a hydrophobic environment important for diverse metabolic processes and signal transduction. The centrality of the endomembrane systems in cellular functions critically implicated in the aging process points to an important yet under-explored opportunity for aging research. Given that the endomembrane systems are active biomaterials, a fundamental question is how their biophysical properties change with age. Biophysical changes in the viscosity of the cytoplasm and nucleoplasm, or the fluidity and permeability of the endomembranes, will profoundly influence the transport and diffusion of biomacromolecules. This will in turn directly impact diverse cellular biochemistry such as signal transduction, gene regulation, metabolism, and proteostasis. Since active materials in highly reactive environments can suffer continuous damage, we hypothesise that their replenishment and repair likely lie at the heart of an “anti-aging effort” of the cell; however, certain critical cellular components may not be fully replaceable or repairable, thus leading to a gradual fitness loss for long-lived terminally differentiated cells such as the retinal pigmented epithelial (RPE) cells, a key target of AMD. As such, quantitative descriptions of the dynamic changes in endomembrane properties during aging, and how RPE cells adapt to these changes, will provide important paradigms from which to understand aging and aging-related diseases. title: Human parainfluenza virus: Developing a toolkit to prevent and treat a neglected respiratory viral infection
abs: Acute respiratory tract infection is a major cause of death in children under 5 years of age, accounting for almost 20% of childhood deaths globally each year. In Singapore, there are about 900,000 visits annually to public clinics and hospital emergency departments for acute respiratory infection, with 3,500 cases requiring hospital admission. In comparison, there were 3,300 cases of dengue fever detected in Singapore during 2017. The main causes of acute respiratory tract infection are influenza virus, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and human parainfluenza virus (HPIV)3. By 4 years of age, over 80% of children have been infected with HPIV, and in the United States the virus is responsible for approximately 10% of child hospital admissions. Despite this, there is little fundamental scientific research conducted on HPIVs; the majority of published research consists of epidemiological studies and clinical case descriptions. Furthermore, unlike influenza virus and RSV, no specific vaccine or antiviral treatment is available. Historically, research on HPIV has focused on genomics, epidemiology, and clinical features, although limited characterization of human viruses is published. Most experimental studies relied on the use of Sendai virus, a related mouse parainfluenza virus, that may not reflect the biology of HPIV. Some attempts have been described to investigate vaccine candidates and to characterize the inflammatory response, however, there is lack of research on the immune response and potential for therapeutic development. We are uniquely situated in the field of HPIV research due to a previously-funded project on the global transmission of HPIV, which allowed us to collect virus specimens from diverse geographic locations. Here, we will utilise this virus collection and established experimental systems to characterize host responses after infection to generate methods of treating the disease and new drugs that can be used to target the virus itself. The successful completion of the project would provide a wealth of basic science knowledge on HPIV and strengthen the position of Singapore as a centre for development of therapeutics and vaccines for this important but neglected respiratory virus.

title: The Science of Certified AI Systems
abs: This proposal is based on the view that AI (particularly that based on neural networks) is a new programming paradigm with great promises and challenges, and the challenges faced by AI techniques and systems are not fundamentally different from those that have haunted traditional software systems for decades. In the last decade or so, it has been shown that neural networks could be automatically trained using large datasets to automatically solve problems from a variety of domains (e.g. image recognition and language translation) with impressive accuracy or efficiency. As a result, neural network based AI systems (hereafter AI systems) have been rapidly adopted in an ever-expanding list of domains, including many safety-critical systems (such as self-driving cars). It seems that much arguably neural networks may be regarded as a universal program which could be tuned automatically (through training with abundant data) to satisfy specific domain-specific requirements. Neural networks are far from perfect or safe. Recently, neural networks have been shown to suffer from a variety of problems with security or societal consequences, e.g. adversarial sampling attacks, data poisoning attacks and discrimination. For instance, a neural network well-trained to recognize stop-signs mistakes a slightly tampered stop-sign as a speed limit sign, which clearly causes safety concerns. Furthermore, it has been shown that neural networks may have backdoors, privacy issues or make discriminatory decisions. It is thus clear that quality control, in addition to those standard methods adopted in the machine learning community (e.g. n-fold validation), must be put in place for neural networks which are adopted for safety-critical systems (e.g. self-driving systems) or systems that have societal impacts (e.g. personal credit rating). These problems are however not surprising to someone who regard neural networks (i.e. the model as well as the training data) as a special class of programs. For instance, adversarial sampling attacks simply show that neural networks may have bugs, just like traditional programs (hereafter programs); and backdoors in neural networks are just like backdoors in programs. The good news is that we have decades of experience dealing with these programming problems. First, we have developed a science for analyzing programs based on logics (e.g. Hoare logic, temporal logic, program semantic models and program refinement), which provides the foundation for developing rigorous program analysis techniques and tools. Secondly, we have developed a variety of program analysis tools which have been proven effective in practice, including testing/fuzzing engines, model checkers, and theorem provers. Thirdly, there are efforts like the common criteria [6], an international standard (ISO/IEC 15408), that provides guidelines on how to apply different program analysis techniques to achieve different levels of certification. It is the research arm of Singapore National Eye Centre, and affiliated to the National University of Singapore (NUS) and the Duke-NUS Medical School. SERI has close partnerships with A*STAR Research Institutes, Nanyang Technological University and other biomedical institutions and eye centers in Singapore and throughout the world. title: In-memory Computing based on Multi-terminal Memtransistors for Cognitive Internet-of-Things (C-IoT)
abs: Today, modern computers are designed based on von Neumann architecture which physically separates the storage and computation. Consequently, the operational efficiency is greatly limited by the bandwidth or “memory wall” and a significant amount of energy is wasted in moving data between the memory subsystem and data processors. Clearly, next-generation Cognitive Internet of Things (C-IoT) devices, which hold potential to revolutionise healthcare, urban mobility, and advanced manufacturing, will require a radically different design approach that pushes the envelope for energy efficiency and low power consumption. Artificial intelligence (AI) devices that can achieve human-like performance on cognitive tasks promise to enable C-IoT. Significant research efforts along this direction have yielded a variety of innovations in device technologies, circuit designs and hardware architecture [1-8], but with no universal solution in sight. It is recognized, however, that the origin of the energy-efficiency of these AI devices rests largely on in-memory computing (IMC), which moves data processing circuitry much closer to memory or allows computations to be performed in situ on data stored in the memory [9-11]. Recently, multi-terminal memtransistor (a hybrid integration of memristor and selector transistor into a single device structure) technology based on two-dimensional materials (2DMs) has emerged as a promising solution for enabling energy efficient IMC [12-13]. These 2DMs-based technologies are widely considered to have the potential for enabling highly dense, low operational voltage, and near-zero leakage in performing biological functions such as Hebbian learning, and thereby promise to revolutionize the computing capabilities of current electronic systems. However, several scientific and technological challenges are hindering the pursuit of IMC devices based on 2DMs memtransistors. First, the microstructure uniformity and defect configuration during the growth and transfer of 2DMs must be addressed; Second, the inter-device variability and inhomogeneity across a memtransistor array must be achieved; Third, a new circuit architecture to achieve IMC based on memrtansistors must be designed; And finally, the integration of the non-volatile memory with back-end-of-line (BEOL) CMOS must be developed. In this proposed research, by addressing these challenges, we aim to develop a new device and circuit architecture based on the multi-terminal 2DMs memtransistor to realize efficient IMC for C-IoT applications. By leveraging on 2DMs memtransistor, which is capable of achieving ultra-low operational voltage and avoiding circuit overhead suffered by conventional one-transistor-one-RRAM (1T-1R) design, we will strive to improve the energy efficiency by at least 10-fold. title: A total building performance approach to real-time occupant centric sensing and control for mixed mode ventilation in the tropics
abs: Natural ventilation provides an opportunity to significantly improve the energy and indoor environmental quality of a building. However, the hot and humid climate of Singapore results in little to no natural ventilation potential. Notably, previous attempts in Singapore were also unsuccessful due to concerns with thermal comfort, noise, and air quality. Recent studies in Singapore also suggests that air movement significantly affects thermal sensation and acceptability for tropically acclimatized occupants. Specifically, occupants found high cooling set-point (27°C – 28°C) acceptable when supplemented by elevated air movement. We hypothesize that smart building controls combined with real-time environmental sensing, real-time occupant feedback, and a motorised acoustic ventilation window could be a potential solution for effective mixed mode ventilation in the tropics. The aim is to push occupant sensation and acceptability to the limit while optimising building controls with state-of-the-art algorithms to meet this limit while minimising energy consumption. To achieve effective mixed-mode ventilation, we proposed an integrated approach comprising of the following technologies: - A hybrid air-conditioning system and mechanical ventilation (ACMV) comprising of operable windows, ceiling fans, and dedicated outdoor air system. - A staggered air inlet and outlet double-wall structure with sound absorbers. - A network of IoT sensors combined with a platform for interaction with the occupants through wearable devices to collect real-time environmental measurements as well as thermal and aural comfort feedback. - A hybrid (physics-based and data-driven) control framework optimised for total building performance using real-time data and occupant sensation/preference for modelling and analytics. - Simulation to generalise our findings and identify essential points to note when designing for mixed-mode ventilation. This study will be conducted through a test-bed (phase 1) and a live demonstration (phase 2). The test-bed is an office space located on the third floor of SDE4, the new net zero energy building located at NUS. The space is selected as the test-bed because of the detailed level of metering, the installed air-conditioning and mechanical ventilation (ACMV) system, and the Internet of Things (IoT) infrastructure that is currently being set up. The availability of this infrastructure enhances the feasibility of the proposed research. The novelty of this research lies in the integration between different building related domains and a practical implementation of the proposed control framework. This study would be the first to examine, develop, and implement a control framework that optimises a hybrid system (operable window, ceiling fan, ACMV operation) for total building performance (specifically indoor air quality, thermal comfort, and noise levels) and energy consumption. title: Assessing Cities: A SCoRE (Societal Comprehensive Reflective Estimate) Methodology
abs: The proposed project, therefore, aims to develop and validate a multi-perspective framework and system that would enable the collection and aggregation of select information on various indicators covering distinct aspects of the life of the common Singaporean to derive a composite index indicative of the Singapore Pulse and present visualizations of changes to the index on a real-time basis. More importantly, the system will be gathering and presenting data for different districts in Singapore, rather than at the national level. The more granular level of data will ensure that city planners understand the pulse unique to different regions of Singapore. We present a comprehensive framework covering the economic, societal, environmental, health, and attitudinal dimensions of life, reflected in different districts in Singapore. The types of information gathered are of different temporal basis, thus representing the velocity of changes in the pulse of each region. The information would range from static data such as geospatial information including maps to semi-dynamic data such as economic growth and health-care quality indicators which may be subjected to change although at a slower rate, as well as highly dynamic data such a people movement and behaviors including driving, parking, shopping and eating out, participation in community center events, park use to name a few. Finally, the data is captured at high granularity - at the district level, with the ability to be aggregated at different levels of analysis up to the national level.
