title: Combinatorial Stochastic Analysis for the Connectivity of Random Graphs - Applications to Vehicular and Wireless Networks
abs: This project is devoted to new mathematical results for the connectivity of random geometric graphs based on point processes, with applications to the description and management of both wireless interference and traffic flow in vehicular and communication networks. Our approach draws on the links between stochastic geometry, the theory of point processes, and the statistical physics of complex engineering systems. We plan to build on recent developments in combinatorial methods for the computation of moments of stochastic integrals driven by point processes in order to solve new problems in the connectivity of random geometric graphs, such as estimating graph connectivity via the probability of a k-hop path between given nodes. More involved connectivity problems, such as the existence of edges between node clusters, and subgraph counting, will be considered as well. We will also consider the existence and multiplicity of shortest k-hop paths in linear networks, in connection with the concept of betweenness centrality in spatial networks. Communication networks will be a major field of application for our results, via the estimation of the meta probability distribution of the signal to interference ratio (SIR), which gives the spatial distribution of the probability of successful reception. Our combinatorial framework also applies to general point process settings for the random location of vertices, which should also allow us to consider repulsive to attractive interaction between nodes, based on determinantal point processes. We also plan to extend our approach beyond the classical Rayleigh fading, to various connectivity models such as the unit disk model or the log-normal connection model. Still in a communication network setting, we intend to apply our results to the multihop connectivity of Vehicular Ad Hoc Networks (VANETs), which are spontaneously constructed wireless networks of vehicles which self-arrange communication amongst themselves. In this setting, our goal will be to optimize the locations of the nodes in order to maximize the connection probability of the user. Another topic of interest is the application of our results to heterogeneous d-dimensional spatial networks, by providing information on the hidden spatial embedding of subgraphs using probabilistic arguments.
kw: Stochastic geometry; connectivity; random geometric graphs; random-connection model; k-hop count; wireless networks; point processes; moments identities

title: The role of ABCB1/MDR1 and tryptophan metabolism in the aging of hematopoietic stem cells
abs: Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) predominantly reside in the bone marrow, where their self-renewal and differentiation remain under precise and controlled regulation. However, aging triggers an imbalance in HSC homeostasis, which drives a higher risk of malignant transformation and age-related disease. Our current understanding of the mechanisms underlying HSC aging is limited since the responsible genes remain unidentified. We recently found that ABCB1/MDR1 transporter, an ATP-dependent drug efflux pump, is a key upregulated gene in HSCs during aging. Functional insight into the consequences of increased ABCB1 expression in HSCs during aging remains unknown. By studying the long-lived mammal bat, we revealed that tryptophan is an endogenous substrate of ABCB1. Reducing the availability of tryptophan or its metabolite, kynurenine, in cells prolongs the lifespan in multiple invertebrate and vertebrate animal models. Thus, we hypothesize that increasing ABCB1 expression in aging HSCs extrudes several adverse metabolites, including tryptophan, as a self-protective mechanism against aging-related stresses. To test this hypothesis, in Aim 1, we will determine the protective role of ABCB1 in HSCs during aging using knockout mice and cells of Abcb1a/b and human HSCs with knockdown of ABCB1. In Aim 2, we will study the contributions of tryptophan and its metabolites to HSC aging. Our pioneering proposal will elucidate the protective role of ABCB1 in maintaining healthy HSCs and reveal the impact of tryptophan metabolism on HSC aging. Understanding the mechanisms underlying both the maintenance and the aging process of HSCs will provide a novel tool to prevent the functional decline of HSCs during aging. The knowledge from this proposal will inform future therapeutic strategies to treat leukemia, other cancers, and blood disorders and improve the quality of life for elderly people.
kw: ABCB1, MDR1, hematopoietic stem cells, HSC, aging, tryptophan

title: Microplastic-associated persistent organic pollutants: fate & ecological impacts
abs: Microplastics have been estimated to account for up to 80% of marine litter and may persist in the environment for hundreds to thousands of years. It seems inevitable, therefore, that the level of microplastics pollution will continue to increase as time goes on. Although studies have demonstrated the potential for different persistent organic pollutants (POPs) to sorb from oceanic and estuarine waters to plastic waste, the environmental implications of this phenomenon remain poorly described. Concerns have been raised about the effects of interactions between waterborne microplastics and persistent organic pollutants (POPs) on the global distribution (including Southeast Asia) of emerging and legacy pollutants. Waterborne microplastics also represent a viable matrix for bacterial attachment and can harbor microbial communities that are notably distinct from the surrounding environment. These microbial communities may contribute to the fate of microplastic-associated POPs. Thus in this proposed project we will investigate the role of biological transformation in the dispersal and degradation of POPs associated with microplastics and evaluate the environmental risks of this pollution. To achieve this goal, we will first investigate the incidence and nature of representative POPs (i.e. brominated bisphenol-A compounds (BBPAs), polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), and polybrominated diphenyl ethers (PBDEs), etc.) associated with suspended and beached microplastics in marine, estuarine and terrestrial environments in Singapore. As one measure of ecological impact, we will determine the effects of these compounds on the structure of the microbial communities present on microplastics by comparative analyses of contaminated and uncontaminated samples. Since partial degradation of halogenated organic pollutants can result in formation of different, sometimes more toxic, compounds with different physical and chemical properties, we will also identify functional microbial populations on microplastics that are capable of dehalogenating BBPAs, PCBs, and PBDEs, etc. Ultimately, we will use the data collected to develop a risk profile that describes the potential environmental impacts of POPs associated with microplastics.
kw: Microplastics, persistent organic pollutants, biofilms, biotransformation, migration

title: Exploring Paradoxical Parrondo Effect in Computer Networks
abs: This is the first time that the Parrondo effect is being investigated on computer networks. The throughput and latency bottleneck in accessing system resources is near-ubiquitous in modern computer systems. Similarly, communication overhead in modern SoCs and computing clusters are major fundamental limiting factors in their performances. Addressing these problems enables very significant performance improvements to general computer systems without incurring hardware cost and is a viable way of sustaining performance growth in computing technologies amidst the present slow-down in the development of new semiconductor nodes. Network simulation model based closely on real-world systems has been carried out. The preliminary results are very promising and indicate that the project is in the right direction and deserves to be pursued. There is a potential of two patents to be filed if the proposal proceeds as planned. The patents can lead to licensing or spin-off as many IT companies will be interested in the technological advancement. Our work is also likely to attract industry partner like Microsoft, Google and Intel. Our project focuses on two primary areas of application: switching access-allocation algorithms in the interface layer between processing units (CPUs/GPGPUs) and shared resources such as disks, random-access memory (RAM), and communication buses; and switching communication protocols between components on SoC (system-on-chip) hardware, and between processors on high-throughput computing clusters. In both of these scenarios, the hypothetical maximal computing performance is limited by key bottlenecks. In the former, accessing shared system resources incurs latency, and data transmission rates are limited by bus throughput, therefore resulting in the accumulation of waiting queues as the processor requests accesses; typical allocation schemes are either first in first out (FIFO), or employ fair sharing schemes—but these are optimal only in the local sense, in that the computational load incurred upon resource release and the subsequent impact on resource requests are seldom considered. In the latter, interconnects between processors or computing nodes are by far the most significant limiting factor in performance, typically forcing software architectures to be specifically optimized to reduce communication loads, with typical protocols unable to respond effectively to real-time loads and service demands. The limitation remains that these factors are difficult to predict or otherwise adapt to, and robust deterministic measures are therefore largely infeasible; it is, however, precisely in such scenarios that stochastic switching strategies may yield the best results, as indicated by the success of Parrondo-like behaviours in analogous deadlocks studied in eco-evolutionary systems. title: Towards Next-generation Video Intelligence: Training Machines to Understand Actions and Complex Events
abs: Aims. We aim to develop the next-generation video intelligence system that can: (1) predict future and infer intention of atomic actions, (2) learn knowledge of high-level complex events, and (3) rapidly understand actions and events. Hypothesis & Approach. To accomplish these aims, we hypothesize that we can train machines powered by deep learning models and algorithms to acquire these abilities. To validate this hypothesis, we propose the following approaches. (1) For aim 1, we will create a deep learning model that learns to predict future 3D shapes of actors. Based on this, we will design a novel framework for analyzing the results of an action which corresponds to its intent. (2) For aim 2, understanding how to complete an event is reflected as human knowledge. We propose to establish a multimodal video event graph representation and design algorithms to discover common graph patterns that reflect knowledge. (3) For aim 3, to efficiently process massive video data and deploy our model on computationally-restricted devices, we will design efficient framework that can operate in the compressed domain and design learning algorithms that can search for lightweight model architecture. We have developed the first deep learning framework called Segment-CNN for detecting action segments and its improved versions which won first prize in the International Challenge on Activity Recognition 2017 and Best Student Paper Nomination in IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition 2017. title: Design of intelligent reflecting surface for reconfigurable wireless propagation
abs: This project aims to investigate a fundamentally new approach to achieve competitively high-performance and low-cost millimetre wave (mmWave) wireless communications, termed intelligent reflecting surface (IRS), by smartly reconfiguring the wireless propagation environment with the use of massive low-cost, passive and reflective elements. Different elements of an IRS can independently reflect the incident electromagnetic wave or signal by controlling its phase, thereby collaboratively achieve a fine-grained three-dimensional (3D) passive beamforming for signal enhancement or interference suppression. In this project, a joint investigation of antenna design, signal processing and communication/information theory will be carried out to address the various new technical challenges that arise from the design, implementation, performance analysis and optimization aspects for realizing new and efficient IRS-aided mmWave wireless communication systems. This project is particularly significant as it will lead to a fundamental paradigm shift of wireless communication from today’s “active component solely” network to a new hybrid “active and passive” network in the future. Theoretically, it aims to address the important open question of whether a new wireless network architecture with optimally mixed active transmitting and passive reflecting elements would achieve the optimal energy and spectrum efficiencies, which will make a deep and long-lasting impact to the future wireless system design and implementation. On the other hand, the proposed research also has a high industry value as it aims to solve the most critical coverage issue in mmWave communications, especially for indoor users, thus paving the way for its successful commercialization in the near future. The proposed IRS is of very low cost and power consumption (battery-powered), and easy to be installed and integrated into existing cellular or WiFi networks without the need of any hardware/standardization change. As such, it is a practically appealing solution and has a high potential to be implemented in future wireless systems.

title: Understanding cell fate transition during stomatal development
abs: Understanding cell fate transition during stomatal development Background: The differentiation of stem cell is when a stem cell gives rise to a more specialized cell, leading to a loss in self-renewing potential. Stem cell differentiation thus is a key process that impacts cell type production and general development. My lab employs the development of stomata—essential surface pores for plants—as our model system to study how cell lineage progresses and how cell type production is influenced by intrinsic and external signals. The stomatal guard cells are the final differentiated products of a specialized epidermal lineage called the stomatal lineage. The lineage begins with a self-renewing stem cell stage and transits through an intermediate differentiated stage (i.e. the guard mother cell, or GMC, stage) before its division to form a pair of guard cells. Master transcription factors, including SPEECHLESS (SPCH) and MUTE, are critical in driving each of these processes: SPCH controls the initiation and proliferation of the stomatal stem cells, and MUTE drives their differentiation into GMC. However, it is not known how the fate transition from stomatal precursors to GMCs, i.e. the exit of the stomatal stem cell stage, is controlled. In addition, a recent study reported the existence of a gradient of auxin, a critical plant hormone that can act as a morphogen, along the stomatal lineage, where auxin level is highest in the stem cell stage and decreases as the lineage progresses. These results suggest the potential involvement of auxin gradient and signaling in the control of stomatal lineage progression. Objective, hypothesis and preliminary studies: The main objective of this proposal is to decipher how stomatal stem cells know when to exit its self-renewing stage and differentiate. Specifically, we will investigate the roles of two related AUXIN RESPONSE FACTORs, ARF6 and 8, which are transcription factors mediating auxin signalling, in modulating MUTE and stomatal fate transition. Based on our strong preliminary results, we hypothesize that auxin-activated ARF6 and ARF8 directly bind and suppress MUTE in inhibiting premature differentiation of stomatal stem cells. We found that both ARF6 and 8 are transcriptional targets of SPCH, and our confocal analyses indicated that they are expressed in the stomatal lineage. Interestingly, mutations in arf6 and 8 result in an increase in GMC cells in young seedlings, suggesting defects in the fate transition to and/or maintenance of the GMC stage. Further, bioinformatic analyses identified a DNA binding motif of ARFs in the promoter of MUTE. Through EMSA and DNA pulldown assays, we demonstrated that ARF6 can directly bind to the motif-containing promoter fragment of MUTE and that the association is dependent on the motif. title: Integrating functional and molecular profiling in single cells for personalized immunotherapy
abs: Adoptive Cell Therapy has demonstrated remarkable efficacy in treating patients with various cancers, offering lasting remission in many cases. However, there is large variations in patient responses and side effects, which arise from patient specific heterogeneity of T-cells and the concomitant differences in cell manufacturing outcomes. Understanding the molecular gene regulation that correlates to specific immune cell effector function is important to establish effective cell manufacturing process as well as ensure cell therapy product potency and safety. Single cell RNA-sequencing is a powerful tool to decipher the molecular cell types in heterogeneous populations, yet molecular classification of single cells is of limited value until a clear relationship to functional cellular properties is demonstrated. To bridge this gap, we propose to create a comprehensive platform for high-throughput integrated transcriptome and functional measurement of single cells. In Aim 1: Develop a novel platform for highly multiplexed secretome and proteogenomic profiling of immune cells, we will develop the Pheno-seq strategy that allows transformation of each cell into its own reaction vessel for secretome assay. This “Lab-on-a-cell” concept is realized by grafting antibodies on cell surface to facilitate capture and detection of cytokines and other secreted factors. By utilizing DNA-barcoded detection antibodies, the secretome can be simultaneously profiled with surface phenotype and transcriptome of each cell through next generation sequencing. In Aim 2: Develop single cell analysis method for assaying cytotoxic effector function of individual immune cells, we will develop microfluidic platforms to sort cells capable of cytolysis for downstream molecular analysis. We will also develop capability to tag individual cells that involved in cell killing with DNA-barcodes, for integration of cytotoxicity measurement into Single Cell Pheno-seq. In Aim 3: Application of Single Cell Pheno-seq for personalizing immunotherapy, we will apply Pheno-seq for in depth functional and molecular characterization of Hepatitis B redirected TCR-T cells for treatment of Hepatocarcinoma patients. Our assay will unravel the gene regulation that is necessary for rapid effector functions of mRNA-electroporated TCR-T cells, and molecular circuitry that promotes expansion and persistence of lentiviral-tranduced TCR-T cells, for rapid cancer cell killing and tumor surveillance. Using Pheno-seq, we will also establish a universal screening platform to select the most optimal TCR tailored for individual patient tumor. Our preliminary results have shown that the proposal is feasible. Integration of multidimensional data that address the “What” and “How” of a cell will be the final frontier in understanding gene regulation, form and function. Our vision for a unified platform for single cell sequencing and functional analysis will fuel many new discoveries at the domain interfaces.

abs: MOE encouraged the PI to submit a proposal for a renewal of his current Tier 2 project “From Print to Digital: Re-Defining Narrativity for Interactive Digital Media”, ending January 2, 2020. title: An Execution Trace Alignment Based Approach to Locating Regression Bug with Explanation
abs: Regression faults, faults which make working code stop functioning, are often introduced when developers make changes to the software. Many regression fault localization techniques have been proposed. However, issues like inaccuracy and lack of explanation are still obstacles for their practical application. Inaccuracy wastes the efforts of software programmers during locating the fault, while lack of explanation makes programmers lose confidence in the results of the tool. In this work, we aim to develop a trace-based approach to identifying not only where the root cause of a regression bug lies, but also how the defect is propagated to its manifestation as the explanation. In our approach, we keep the trace of original correct version as reference and infer the faulty steps on the trace of regression version so that we can build a causality graph of how the defect is propagated. To this end, we need to overcome two technical challenges. First, we should align two traces derived from two versions of programs to know how each step on the program execution trace on original correct version corresponds to one on current regression version. Second, we need to construct causality graph (i.e., explanation) by inventing a technique called alignment slicing and mending to isolate the failure-inducing changes and explain the failure. We will develop a software tool which takes as input a program with its original correct version and current regression version, and generate as output (1) the root cause of the regression fault and (2) a causality graph explaining how the root cause propagates the defects to the observable fault. The tool will present an interactive user interface for the programmers to explore, understand, and confirm our reported results.

title: Understanding the Role of Transglycosylase in Bacterial Cell Wall Synthesis
abs: Significance: Bacterial infection has been a major cause of death in human civilization until the discovery of antibiotic in the last century. Nevertheless, the continuing mutations of bacteria accumulated over decades to give rise to antimicrobial resistant strains, which are far more complicated and lethal in turn, and no antibiotics with new killing mechanism or a broad spectrum have been reported for the past decades. Transglycosylases (TGase), responsible for knitting strands of bacterial cell wall, present an opportunity to address this concern as a conserved and ubiquitous target for treatment. Albeit the bright prospect, the investigations associated with the enzymes have been constantly overshadowed by the limited availability of enzyme substrate, when the reported lengthy synthetic route easily amassed to enormous cost. Our recent advances in methodology development allowed us to gain access to substrates of varying sizes in an efficient and practical manner. Hence, we will, for the first time in the world, capitalize on the privileged compounds to explore the role of TGases in bacterial biosynthesis of cell wall. The mechanistic details would pave the way for development and complementation of new antibacterial agents belonging the family of TGase inhibitors. Research questions to be addressed: In line with our long-term efforts on carbohydrate synthesis and biological studies, in this proposal we will prepare PG precursors with varying molecular structures for in-depth investigation of bacterial transglycosylase mechanisms. With the diverse PG precursors, we will study their structural-activity relationships with bacterial TGases and thus gaining insights into how we can enhance or weaken the binding affinity. With the aid of computer modeling, we will be able to identify optimal structures of TGases’ substrate or inhibitor. This would allow us to investigate the mechanistic details of PG biosynthesis with great promise. Moreover, the inhibitory profiles will pave the way for translational researchers to develop new antibiotics targeting TGases, which is present in most bacterial species and has yet to see any resistance evolved in bacteria. Approach: Based on our expertise in glycoconjugate construction, structural biology and computational simulation, we plan to tackle the task by taking the following approaches: a) We propose to synthesize a library of peptidoglycan oligomers (PGOs) with varied sugar chain length and peptide compositions. b) We propose to investigate the detailed molecular mechanism of diverse PGOs as substrate of TGases – Binding mode, kinetics and thermodynamics through combinative approaches, including structural, biophysical and biochemical methods. c) We propose to rationalize the results in Aim 2 and establish the catalytic model of TGase in combination with computational modelling approach. d) We propose to develop new generation antibiotics by designing PGOs as TGase inhibitors. title: Neutrophil Digital Twin (NeuDT): A multi-parametric biophysical cell model to predict cardiovascular risk in Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
abs: BACKGROUND: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is a growing healthcare burden worldwide. The major causes of mortality and morbidity in T2DM are the micro- and macrovascular complications including cardiovascular diseases (CVD). Neutrophils are the most abundant leukocyte subtype in our blood, and have been widely implicated in T2DM and CVD. However, clinical assessment using parameters of circulating neutrophil for CVD risk remains inadequate. There is an unmet need to identify novel neutrophil-based biomarkers for CVD. ACADEMIC SIGNIFICANCE: The proposed study first focuses on developing a novel label-free impedance-deformability microfluidic cytometer for neutrophil testing. Single cell biophysical properties such as cell deformability and impedance are commonly linked to cell biology and pathology, but it is technically challenging to quantify both intrinsic parameters simultaneously due to different sensing modalities (optical vs. electrical). Hence, a multi-parametric biophysical cell model which can potentially achieve unprecedented prognostics capabilities remains unexplored. This issue is further aggravated in neutrophil studies due to laborious cell isolation and preparation methods which can activate neutrophils, if not done properly. Herein, we will develop a novel optics-free electrical-based microfluidic cytometer for high throughput and label-free biophysical (size, impedance and deformability) phenotyping of single neutrophils from whole blood directly. This platform technology will be optimized for human and mouse neutrophil studies, and can be readily translated to other diseases and cell types with poorly-defined surface markers (e.g. cancer stem cells). Secondly, we will apply industry 4.0 concept of digital twin, aiming to monitor and predict neutrophil health in T2DM. The proposed Neutrophil Digital Twin (NeuDT) is an electrical-based representation of neutrophil native and functional state, and will be characterised in patients with T2DM, as well as in mouse models of T2DM and atherosclerosis, the main pathological process of CVD. Research findings from our study will elucidate new insights on the pathological role of neutrophils and NETosis (a key neutrophil function) in T2DM and atherosclerosis to identify novel neutrophil biomarkers related to early stage CVD development. HYPOTHESES: We hypothesize that neutrophil size, deformability and cell impedance are associated with neutrophil activation and dysfunction in T2DM and atherosclerosis. Multi-parametric and dynamic biophysical characterization of neutrophils (~10-15 neutrophil parameters) will enhance prognostics capabilities of CVD risk in T2DM. title: Cultural tightness in Asian firms and its impact on creativity and innovation.
abs: Creativity is the generation of novel and useful ideas whereas innovation is the effective implementation of these creative ideas. Recent research has linked cultural tightness – the extent to which a society or group is characterized by rules and norms and individuals are sanctioned for deviating from them – to creativity and innovation. Scholars have thus far studied how cultural tightness at national and regional levels might affect creativity and innovation (Chua et al, 2015; Chua et al 2019; Harrington & Gelfand 2014). Despite growing investigation of how cultural tightness affects creativity and innovation, our understanding of how cultural tightness operates at the organizational level remains limited as little systematic research has been conducted. How organizational level cultural tightness interacts with national level cultural tightness is also unclear. In this research project, we aim to take the construct of cultural tightness to the organizational level to examine how the tightness of an organization’s culture might influence its creativity and innovative capabilities. This inquiry is important because national and regional culture is typically not within the control of an individual or a small group of people, regardless of how motivated they are. It is extremely unlikely for an organization or a CEO to change the culture of a country or a province/state. Yet, CEO’s and senior executives have the power to directly influence and shape the culture of their organizations. By understanding the effect of cultural tightness at the organizational level, we can help organizations better harness the creativity and innovation benefits of their organizational culture. Specifically, knowledge gained from our research can help companies develop the appropriate set of rules, policies, and norms to maximize creativity and innovation. We focus our investigation in the Asian context because despite economic growth in Asia, this region still lags the West in terms of innovation. Research has suggested that this might be because Asian cultures tend to be relatively tight compared to western cultures (Chua & Zremski, 2016). Thus, we aim to shed light now how cultural tightness might differ across Asian companies and how it interacts with national culture to influence creativity and innovation. We propose that organizations differ in their level of cultural tightness even if they are embedded within the same country (Hypothesis H1). Differences in cultural tightness among organizations can arise from a myriad of factors ranging from management philosophy and leadership style to the type of industry that the firm is in. To examine the impact of organizational cultural tightness, we differentiate between creativity and innovation. title: Biophysical fingerprinting of single cells with AI-empowered microfluidics
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: Overall objective The overall objective of this proposal is to develop and validate artificial intelligence (AI)-empowered microfluidics for analysing and identifying a large number of individual cells without labelling. We will develop a new generation microfluidics-based flow cytometry, termed biophysical cytometry, to measure and characterize multiple types of biophysical properties of individual cells in a single microfluidic interrogation. These cellular biophysical properties will be fed into artificial neural network (ANN) algorithms for machine learning to discover unique biophysical fingerprints for specific cell subtypes, termed biophysical fingerprinting. Discovered biophysical fingerprints will be used to discriminate different cell subtypes in naturally heterogeneous biological samples without labelling. Current challenge Flow cytometry is the current standard for large scale single cell analysis based on the recognition of molecular phenotypic biomarkers (e.g. protein antigens on the cell surface) labelled by fluorescent tags. The use of these antibody-based labels not only involves labour-intensive sample preparation, but also have possibility to damage or even kill cells, which precludes further analysis that requires these analysed cells to be viable. In particular, there are a lack of specific surface molecular biomarkers to effectively discriminate subtypes of a number of important cell types, including human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes (hiPSC-CMs). The solution for the lack of specific molecular biomarkers is to embrace cellular phenotypic biomarkers for single cell analysis. As an example, patch-clamping is the only effective approach to discriminate cardiomyocyte (CM) subtypes based on their distinct difference in action potential measured at the single-cell level. There are two major challenges of cellular phenotyping for single cell analysis: 1) Throughput of cellular phenotyping (i.e. the number of cells measured within an acceptable time duration) by existing technologies is extremely low (e.g. patch-clamping can process up to tens of cells at most). 2) Although microfluidics holds great potentials to solve the throughput issue, the current microfluidic strategy is however to focus on one single type of cellular phenotypes. A wide range of existing studies have shown that microfluidic label-free cell analysis based on one single type of cellular phenotypes is still lack of sufficient specificity to make it practically less useful in analysing real complex biological samples. Research questions and hypotheses This proposal will address the inherent challenges of specificity and throughput for label-free single-cell level analysis based on cellular phenotypic biomarkers (also called biophysical properties/biomarkers). title: Enabling Synaptic Logic Transistors by Gate-Dielectric Defect Characterization
abs: Artificial intelligence (AI) is globally recognized as the way towards better quality of life and greater efficiency and security of businesses. The ultimate aim of AI is to develop intelligent systems capable of taking over complex data analytical tasks from humans. A major component of such systems is the artificial neural network (ANN), which comprises a complicated network of micro-computational circuits or nodes, much like the way neurons in the brain are interconnected by biological synapses. Information processing occurs in a massively parallel way, with each node performing a small calculation and passing the data simultaneously onto subsequent nodes. Frequent and closely-timed communications between nodes strengthen interconnections and create preferential signal transmission paths that leads to a fast convergence to the result. However, due to the lack of a suitable hardware platform, ANNs are implemented as software algorithms on von-Neumann machines which, ironically execute instructions and store data in a sequential manner. To-date, this incompatibility has largely been mitigated by performance gain achieved via Moore's law scaling and system-level workarounds (e.g. multi-core processor). Moving forward, such an approach is deemed unsustainable with Moore's law scaling hitting a physical limit, and with growing ANN complexity needed for handling unstructured big data. The development of hardware-based ANNs has been hindered by the lack of a suitable artificial synaptic device (ASD) for emulating the biological synapse, which controls memory formation and learning in the brain by continuously regulating the strength of neuron connection. Recent effort on ASD research is centered on the memristor, which comprises a thin dielectric sandwiched between two electrodes. Non-volatile modulation of the dielectric conductance could in principle be realized by electrically inducing changes in the material stoichiometry via the displacement of constituent ions. Although synaptic-like behaviors in the conductance change have been demonstrated, several difficult issues remain, two of which, namely scalability and variability, are particularly critical. Among the numerous memristor variants, only a few could show the analog-like conductance modulation needed for ASD application and most tend to exhibit large and abrupt conductance change when the dimension is scaled down. Another critical problem is the significant performance variation observed even in a single memristor, which greatly diminishes the prospect of achieving reliable performance in a large-scale ANN, such as one aimed at emulating the human cerebral cortex, having ~10,000 trillion synapses. title: Direct observation of a toroidal transition in atoms
abs: This project aims to observe and characterize a toroidal transition in atomic spectrum. Nowadays, it is usually admitted that light-matter interaction is well-captured using electric and magnetic multipolar expansion. This assumption is exact in the electrostatics and magnetostatics limits where any charge and current distributions can be expanded into electric and magnetic multipole components. The situation is more complex in electrodynamics where a full description shall include toroidal moments, which are independent of the electric and magnetic multipole expansion. Toroidal dipole emission corresponds to a vortex ring of light similar to what it could be found in fluid mechanic when a burst flow of gas or liquid is going across a circular aperture. Thanks to the advance in nanotechnologies and nanophotonics, structure with resonant toroidal moments have been generated in the radio frequency and optical domain. However, in contrast to their fluid mechanic counterpart, which are stable propagating forms, the electromagnetic structure, generated by a toroidal source, will keep its toroidal form only in the nearfield. In the farfield, the radiation pattern is same than the one generated by an electric dipole moment, however phase shifted by pi. As an important consequence, the coherent superposition of a toroidal dipole moment and an electric dipole moment could lead to a complete suppression of the emission in farfield. The group of C. Wieman has revealed this configuration, called an anapole moment, in the cesium nuclear moment. In atomic physics, the general belief is that only electric and magnetic multipole expansion are relevant. Indeed, in a given multiplicity (fixed total electronic spin), all known transitions are allowed for at least one electric or magnetic multipole components. As a result, toroidal moments have been disregarded, because they are weak and cannot generally be isolated from their electric or magnetic moment counterpart. However, in large static magnetic field environment, when the electronic spin is decoupled to the nuclear spin (Paschen-Back regime), the direct observation of toroidal moment is more favorable. Here, the atomic spectra degeneracy is removed and some transitions, which used to be electric dipole allowed at low magnetic field, turn out to be electric forbidden at all orders but toroidal allowed. Since the expected coupling amplitude of the toroidal transition is weak – ~10-5 weaker than an electric dipole transition- a dedicated phase sensitive fluorescence detection scheme will be developed. title: Relative sea-level changes along the Northern Sea Route: from patterns and rates to drivers and mechanisms
abs: The rapidly changing climate, rising temperatures and declining Arctic sea ice have the potential to open up the Northern Sea Route (NSR). Sailing routes between Europe and East Asian ports such as Singapore through the Arctic Ocean along the NSR are about 6000 nautical miles shorter (43% shorter) than the routes around the Cape of Good Hope and are about 2700 nautical miles shorter (25% shorter) than the Europe to East Asia routes via Suez Canal. To design appropriate and operate coastal infrastructure and minimize potential risk information on future relative sea-level (RSL) and bathymetry changes in the Arctic are required. RSL projection relies on an accurate understanding of the mechanisms driving its complex spatio-temporal evolution, which must be founded on an understanding of their history. Future RSL changes along the NSR in the Eurasian Arctic are controlled by the increase in ocean mass and volume and vertical land motion from glacial-isostatic adjustment (GIA). GIA is the response of the solid Earth and gravity field to ice mass redistribution during a glacial cycle. Models of the GIA process link the cryosphere, hydrosphere and geosphere. However, the robustness of GIA models relies on the accuracy of their input parameters: ice-sheet histories and mantle rheological properties. Geological RSL data provide critical constraints on these input parameters. There is an urgent need for high-quality geological RSL data from the Russian Arctic because global GIA models such as ICE-6G_C (VM5a) and ICE-7G_NA (VM7) have not been tuned to post Last Glacial Maximum (LGM) datasets (26,000 years ago to present) from this region. Furthermore, the thickness and extent of the Eurasian ice complex, which has a first-order control on patterns of uplift vs. subsidence in this region is poorly understood. Therefore, the ability of the current generation of GIA models to fit geological RSL data – and thus predict future RSL and bathymetric changes for the NSR – remains untested. In this project, we will update and expand observations of RSL change along the NSR to achieve the following research objectives:  Determining the rates, mechanisms and geographic variability of RSL along the NSR from instrumental and proxy data;  Refine input parameters of GIA models to develop a comprehensive model for regional vertical land motion for NSR from GIA that can be incorporated into sea-level projections;  To produce projections of RSL and bathymetry change in the 21st century along the NSR. The proposal has three approaches. First, we will expand our post-LGM RSL database of the Russian Arctic using published data from Svalbard and Scandinavia, and unprocessed and new field data from Severnaya Zemlya and the Kara Sea. We will follow standardized international geological protocols to produce Eurasian Arctic RSL database with a full consideration of altitude and chronological uncertainties. title: Theory guided Accelerated Discovery of printable P-type transparent conductors
abs: Smart electronic devices relies on smart screen technology which is enabled by the discovery of n-type transparent conductors. Despite the wide usage of n-type transparent conductors such as Indium Tin Oxide, p-type transparent conductors is not commercially available because their transparency and conductivity values do not meet the requirements of the industry. The absence of good p-type transparent conductors currently limits the development of smart transparent devices which requires selective contacts for efficient opposite charge extractions. These devices ranges from semi transparent solar cells, electrochromic glass windows, light emitting diodes and sensors. The primary factor for poor p-type performance is due to the high effective mass and thus poor hole mobility in many metal oxides commonly investigated for this purpose. The top of the valence band for most oxides consists of tightly bound oxygen 2p orbitals in a non-bonding state. These orbitals overlap poorly making it difficult to form a hole conduction path and consequently lower hole mobility. Chemical modulation of valence band is usually done by hybridization of O-2p orbitals with d or s orbitals of the metal cations. Despite numerous efforts, this method does not appear to be effective in improving the hole mobility at the desired transparency level. In this proposal, we propose a new approach to solve this issue. We hypothesize that the chemical modulation of the VB can be achieved by substituting Oxygen with other anions such as Nitrogen or Sulfur to form Oxynitride or Oxysulfides. We hypothesize that these oxyanion chemistries may tune the valence band curvature and level to a perfect compromise of low hole effective mass and high bandgap for high transparency.As the chemical landscape of oxynitrides and oxysulfides is vast and mostly unexplored, we use an innovative integrated combination of high-throughput computational screening and high-throughput experimental synthesis and optical and electronic characterizations. Both high-throughput computation and experiments will be done in parallel and in series with input given to each other to further fine-tune the selection process. The high-throughput computational approach will focus on stability, hole effective mass, band gap, dopability and band alignment. title: Disorder-induced colossal magnetoresistance and pseudomagnetic quantum Hall effect in terraced two-dimensional materials
abs: The main objective of this proposal is to realize room-temperature colossal magnetoresistance (MR) and to explore the possibility of pseudo-magnetic quantum Hall effect in graphene by disorder engineering. Disorder-induced linear MR effect is quadratic at low perpendicular magnetic fields and linear at high fields, which gained the attention about 20 years ago for understanding the linear MR in silver chalcogenides. This effect is technologically appealing, in particular in the advent of two-dimensional (2d) materials like graphene since 2004, because this 2d system offers potential applications in magnetic sensors with nanoscale resolution. However, to realize 2d-material-based magnetic sensors utilizing this effect is challenging due to the limited understanding of and the lack of technology for controlling the spatial distribution of the disorder in the material. This has resulted in a limited value of MR, in particular in a single-layer regime of graphene, usually ranging between 60-775% at 9 T and 300 K. In 2009, A. K. Geim theoretically proposed that a non-uniform triangular strain aligned along three main crystallographic orientations can induce pseudo-magnetic fields in disordered graphene. This is because the non-uniform strain can affect the two sub-lattices of bipartite graphene differently, shifting the Dirac cones in opposite directions. This pseudo-magnetic field behaves like a real applied magnetic field and can induce pseudo-Landau levels in graphene without applying external magnetic field, and consequently, lead to a zero-field analog of the quantum Hall effect (QHE). However, even though pseudo-magnetic fields have been identified in a variety of disordered systems, such as graphene bubbles, nanopillars, and heterostructures, a clear signature of pseudomagnetic QHE is still missing. Instigated by our preliminary study, this project is about studying and tuning the magneto-effects in a 2d single layer material by artificially creating disorder in the material by means of laminating the layer on an atomically controlled terraced substrate such as SrTiO3 (STO). After the lamination of the graphene on the terraced STO, the van der Waals interaction between the graphene layer and the substrate is expected to be enhanced due to the elastic deformation of graphene, inducing strain both in the terraces and steps. Here we propose to realize and investigate such terraced graphene and focus our study around two main aspects: 1) Realization of room temperature colossal MR effect and understanding the underlying physics of this disorder-induced MR effect, and 2) Realization of strain-induced pseudo-magnetic fields and investigating the potential of pseudomagnetic quantum Hall effect. title: A Multicenter, Adaptive, Randomized Blinded Controlled Trial of the Safety and Efficacy of Investigational Therapeutics for the Treatment of COVID-19 in Hospitalized Adults
abs: COVID-19 is a respiratory disease caused by a novel coronavirus (SARS-CoV-2) and causes substantial morbidity and mortality. There is currently no vaccine to prevent infection with SARS-CoV-2 or therapeutic agent to treat COVID-19. Remdesivir (GS-5734) is a broad-spectrum nucleotide prodrug that inhibits RNA-dependent RNA polymerase activity among a diverse group of RNA viruses including filoviruses, paramyxoviruses and pathogenic coronaviruses. Nonclinical in vitro and in vivo data suggests that Remdesivir might be useful for the treatment of COVID-19 for which no medical countermeasures are currently approved and support testing the efficacy of Remdesivir treatment among hospitalized adults with COVID-19. This study is an adaptive, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial to evaluate the safety and efficacy of novel therapeutic agents in hospitalized 394 adult patients diagnosed with COVID-19. The study is a multicenter trial that will be conducted in up to 50 sites globally. All subjects will undergo a series of efficacy, safety, and laboratory assessments. Blood samples and oropharyngeal (OP) swabs will be obtained on Day 1; 3, 5, 8, 11; and Day 15 and 29. The proposed primary outcome, a 7-point ordinal scale at Day 15, will be defined based on blinded review of data from the first 100 subjects. This study utilizes an adaptive design that maximizes our efficiency in identifying a safe and efficacious therapeutic agent for COVID-19 during the current outbreak. As the a multicenter, multinational randomized controlled study, we will be able to acquire rigorous data about the safety and efficacy of investigational therapeutic agents for COVID-19 that will lead to generalizable evidence. Last, collecting clinical and virologic data using a standardized timeline and collection instruments should provide valuable information about the clinical course of and morbidities associated with severe COVID-19 in a diverse group of hospitalized adult patients.

title: Programme for Research in Epidemic Preparedness And Response (PREPARE)- Stage 1
abs: PREPARE is a national research programme set up by Ministry of Health to support and strengthen Singapore s key essential pandemic research capabilities. It focuses on enhancing translational platforms and expertise to develop tools, methods and products that can be tapped on to detect, respond to, and contain future infectious disease threats. Infectious disease outbreaks are a continuous threat to Singapore. As an international travel hub with a high population density, Singapore is particularly vulnerable to imported and local transmission of novel infectious diseases and the re-emergence of established ones. Developing cutting-edge research capabilities to prepare for and respond well to future epidemics is thus a crucial national priority. PREPARE seeks to enhance research capabilities for early detection and sense-making to prepare Singapore against future infectious disease threats; develop and strengthen key enablers in data infrastructure, analytics, and behavioural science research to respond to public health crises; strengthen research capabilities to enhance our national resilience in diagnostics, therapeutics, and vaccines; and develop a strong infectious diseases research collaboration network across countries in our region to respond to epidemics and facilitate multi-centre clinical trials. PREPARE is a national programme under the Communicable Diseases Agency.

title: Active Topological Photonics towards Robust Lasers and Efficient Sensors
abs: Conventional active photonic devices are designed from manipulating a few degrees of freedom such as frequency, polarization and phase, being susceptible to perturbations occurring in active photonic devices. Topology is a newly discovered degree of freedom, whose use in condensed matter physics has led to the discoveries of topological matter that host robust quantum states, as recognized by the 2016 Nobel prize in Physics. This proposed research programme aims to systematically exploit topology to design improved on-chip active photonic devices over almost the entire electromagnetic spectrum: terahertz (THz), mid-infrared (mid-IR), visible, and ultraviolet (UV). We will investigate active photonic devices that can be classified into three types of designs: time-reversal (T) symmetry breaking photonic crystal structures, T-preserving photonic crystal structures, and non-Hermitian (gain/loss) structures hosting exceptional points. Based on these designs, we will implement devices operating in different regions of the electromagnetic spectrum. The deliverables of this programme will include lasers with unprecedented levels of robustness, and detectors with unprecedented sensitivity. We have done a preliminary experimental study implementing a topological laser at THz frequencies, which proves the feasibility of advancing active topological photonics from concepts to devices. The technology developed by this programme can be incorporated into next-generation photonics products, such as lidar for autonomous navigation and chemical sensors for food processing, which are highly relevant for Singapore’s advanced manufacturing ecosystem.

title: Disruptive Fabrication Processes for Scalable Interconnects
abs: The microelectronics industry is challenged by the demand for smaller, faster, cheaper, and more energy-efficient components. In a typical computer chip, nanoscale wires interconnect billions of transistors and their power sources. As the density and complexity of the transistors on a chip increases, the number and size of the interconnects should scale accordingly. However, reducing the interconnect size is no longer a viable option for the industry for three reasons: 1) Performance of interconnect metals, such as Cu or Co, degrade severely at <10 nm scale. 2) The fabrication cost of smaller and denser interconnects is becoming prohibitively expensive. 3) Most importantly, with every new device generation, we lack the know-how to fabricate smaller interconnects. Thus, to go beyond the practical scaling limits of the conventional approaches, fabrication methods for interconnect architectures from new high-performance metals have to be invented. Unfortunately, as of today, we do not have a good understanding of the underlying nanoscale mechanisms needed to rationally design these fabrication techniques for many promising metals and architectures. In this proposal, we aim to use the disruptive in situ dynamic electron microscopy approach developed by our team to devise and innovate the fabrication processes needed to controllably sculpt high-performance metals into advanced interconnect architectures. Our team has the twin advantage of being pioneers in developing such imaging capabilities, and we are the only one in the world to have mass fabricated industry-relevant 3D nanostructures compatible with these imaging techniques. By imaging the intermediate stages of growth, annealing, adhesion, and etching of these nanoscale metals, we will establish necessary conditions for interconnect fabrication. In-situ real-time imaging, diffraction, and chemical mapping of annealing, wet, and dry etching processes will accelerate the discovery of surface, gas, and solution chemistry that will drive new nanofabrication processes. Together with our industry partners, we will translate knowledge gained here into industrially relevant fabrication processes for the next generations of microelectronics components.
kw: nanofabrication; semiconductor; electron microscopy

title: Real-time crop health monitoring and nutrient analysis system for waste reduction and productivity improvement in hydroponic cultivation
abs: Indoor farming is an alternative to traditional agriculture methods, offering high productivity in a small foot print. This is a promising technology for sustainable food production in developing countries where there is a scarcity of agriculture land. Hydroponics is the most commonly used technique in indoor farming, which incorporates many advanced technologies to optimize productivity. However there are still areas that need improvements and better technologies. The automation of crop health monitoring and nutrient supply is the most important among them. Though there are previous reports on imaging techniques for detecting various symptoms such as plant stress detection, disease detection, chlorophyll monitoring etc., a complete monitoring system that can achieve all these tasks is lacking. For nutrient analysis, electro conductivity and pH meters are used currently to get a feedback loop. However, these techniques can only give an indication of the change in the complex nutrient mixture and are unable to determine the exact nutrient type or deficiency level. The objective of this proposal is to develop a complete quantitative monitoring system for monitoring crop health and nutrient levels. Such a system will help in automating the mitigation tasks which will result in better productivity, reduced wastage and reduction of man work hours. A comprehensive monitoring system consisting hyperspectral imaging (HSI) and laser induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS) is proposed for this purpose. Two HSI modalities, one for leaf health monitoring and one for root health monitoring will be used to create a complete crop health monitoring system. For the nutrient analysis, a real-time monitoring system based on LIBS will be developed. LIBS can provide accurate, in situ quantitative chemical composition analysis utilizing atomic emission spectroscopy. The comprehensive crop health and nutrient supply monitoring prototype developed will be deployed in commercial indoor farming sites for testing and data collection.
kw: Crop health monitoring, nutrient analysis, hyperspectral imaging,laser induced breakdown spectroscopy

title: Genetic Improvement of Indoor Farming Crops
abs: Agricultural production in controlled urban environments offers a reliable alternative to food and nutrition supply for densely populated cities, such as Singapore, and contributes to addressing the impending food insecurity caused by rapid urbanization across the world. Although hardware technologies and solutions have been intensively explored in recent years, innovation of the most essential element in sustainable urban farming systems, the crop itself, has been largely neglected. Nowadays, indoor agriculture mainly relies on legacy crop varieties selected or bred for field conditions, under which breeding for phenotypic stability and the resulting consistent production are the top priorities in a changing environment. Thus, most of the crop varieties currently produced in indoor farms are not the ideal cultivars suited for controlled environments, under which breeding priorities focus on a different set of plant traits, including growth rate, crop yield, nutrient level, low light tolerance and compact plant architecture. This proposal aims to explore advanced breeding strategies, including genomic selection and precise genome engineering using CRISPR-Cas9, to create novel leafy vegetable varieties with desired traits tailored for indoor farming environments so as to maximize the productivity and quality of urban agriculture. The platform technologies developed in this proposal will be integrated with other speed-breeding solutions, such as optimal lighting and temperature, to accelerate breeding of new crop varieties suited for indoor farming conditions. This proposal will focus on two types of popular or high-value crops, including choy sum and kale, for which our preliminary studies have laid a solid foundation, including establishment of various effective experimental platforms. Overall, this highly feasible proposal will not only create improved crop varieties with desired agronomic traits that have immediate commercial values for indoor farming, but also develop research capabilities for breeding of other novel crops for sustainable development of globally competitive indoor farming industry in Singapore.
kw: crop breeding; leafy vegetables; fruits; genome editing; genomic selection; indoor farming

title: Improving yield, cultivating efficiency and nutrient quality of hydroponically-grown crops with rapid testing of growth conditions and gene expression analysis
abs: This proposal aims to translate our knowledge of plant physiology and bioinformatics to achieve (i) increased yield, (ii) increased nutritional values (vitamins, antioxidants), (iii) improved crop protection against diseases and (iv) decreased waste of nutrients and environmental pollution generated by indoor hydroponics systems. In collaboration with ComCrop (growing lettuce and cai xin) and Artisan Green (growing spinach, Spinacia oleracea), we will use computational biology for an in-depth analysis of gene expression in the three plants after exposure to approximately 100 growth conditions. We will then rapidly test and identify the temperature, light quality/intensity and micronutrient compositions that influence the yield of hydroponically-grown plants. Furthermore, we will analyse which genes and pathways are expressed in the different conditions with RNA-sequencing and bioinformatics. This will reveal the activity of metabolic pathways, thus allowing to rapidly infer levels of vitamins and beneficial metabolites, such as antioxidants, in the different growth conditions. The collected data from RNA sequencing will be integrated to generate a reference database used to create an analytical pipeline, DIPPY (Digital Plant Physician). This pipeline will make it possible for the grower to fine-tune conditions for optimal growth in the future, simply upon quick sampling and analysis of a given plant tissue at a given state. For many plants that are of interest to Singapore, particularly local crops, current protocols for hydroponic and indoor systems are not optimized for productive and resource-efficient growth. Consequently, using hydroponics can give low yield and/or decreased nutritional values. The DIPPY gene expression database will benefit urban food production technologies, such as hydroponic indoor systems, as it will enable diagnosing plant health and identifying conditions that boost the yield and nutrient levels of crops. We will initially focus on two indoor-grown crops, but the pipeline can be easily expanded to other plants.
kw: hydroponics; indoor; vitamins; nutrients; gene expression; bioinformatics

title: Combinatorial Supplementation of Fish Feeds through Encapsulation for Enhanced Growth Rates in Aquaculture
abs: Only 10% of the food consumed by Singapore is produced locally. With limited resources and land space, there is increasing impetus for our local farms to innovate with the goal of elevating our self-sufficiency in food fish. This proposal aims to improve productivity of our aquaculture industry by increasing the growth rate and survivability of farmed fish. Earlier studies report that probiotics alone, added into fish feeds, can improve growth rates and survivability. Here, we aim to enhance growth rates and immunity, specifically of fingerlings, through a combinatorial supplementation of fish feeds with encapsulated probiotics and an immunomodulatory nutraceutical (i.e. curcumin), by shortening the period required for stocking of grow-out ponds with healthier fingerlings. We further hypothesize that these desirable traits will be extended through the grow-out phase because of effective probiotic colonization of the gut, during the early fingerling phase. To improve survivability and bioavailability of the probiotic and the nutraceutical, microencapsulation technologies will be employed to achieve targeted delivery in the gut, thereby maximising their efficacy. The Asian seabass is chosen in this study, given its good market acceptance and high economic value in many countries. In this project, a sequential screening and selection of probiotics against the chosen pathogen (i.e. Streptococcus iniae) would be followed by testing of the combinatorial effects of these supplements through in vitro studies. A functional feed supplemented with encapsulated probiotics and curcumin would then be used in a control-environment study to test the growth rate, feed conversion ratio and survivability in the absence and presence of the pathogen. Subsequently, the gut microbiome of the fingerlings would be assessed to verify gut colonization of the probiotic and follow up field studies in the grow-out phase, conducted by our industrial partner – Opal Resources, would be carried out to confirm our hypothesis.
kw: encapsulation, supplements, nutrition, probiotics, functional fish feeds, growth rates, aquaculture, probiotics

title: Oral and Immersion Vaccines against Viruses in Asian Seabass
abs: Viral diseases often cause significant economic losses in aquaculture. Nervous necrosis virus (NNV) is one of the major fish pathogens, while scale drop disease virus (SDDV) has recently emerged in Southeast Asia. To manage the diseases, the best strategy is to vaccinate fish in order to prevent infection. Unfortunately, no vaccines against NNV or SDDV are available for Asian seabass, which is commonly farmed in Singapore. In this project, our objective is to obtain oral and immersion vaccines based on virus-like particles (VLPs). The challenges associated with oral vaccine development include preventing antigens from denaturation in the harsh stomach environment, and enhancing antigen immunogenicity in the gastrointestinal tract. We hypothesise that denaturation can be prevented by encapsulating recombinant antigens inside edible bacterial cells. Meanwhile, mucosal immunogenicity can be enhanced by conjugating the antigens with a strong mucosal adjuvant. We will engineer lactococcus as a system to produce and encapsulate the antigens – NNV and SDDV capsid proteins fused with an adjuvant. The engineered lactococcus cells will be cultured and then incorporated into fish feed as oral vaccines. The challenge for developing immersion vaccine is to increase antigen immunogenicity in gill and skin mucosa. We hypothesise that this immunogenicity can be enhanced by cell-penetrating peptides. Therefore, we will fuse NNV capsid protein with cell-penetrating peptides. The fused proteins will be produced recombinantly, purified and assembled to form VLPs as an immersion vaccine. The efficacies of the oral and immersion vaccines against NNV in larval and juvenile Asian seabass will be evaluated by virus challenge. The immunogenicity and protective immunity of the oral vaccine against SDDV will be assessed in juvenile seabass. The use of our vaccine strategies could bring about long-term economic and societal benefits for Singapore and the region by increasing the sustainability and growth of fish farming industries.
kw: Oral vaccine, Immersion vaccine, Subunit vaccine, Nervous necrosis virus, Scale drop disease virus

title: Achieving a sustainable aquaculture environment by specialized microbes
abs: Aquaculture is a critical component of human nutrition and food security, and facilities that produce a greater volume of fish per unit of land or water area are required to meet current and future demands. Increased production intensity in aquaculture systems can decrease the quality of the culture water, necessitating increased cycling of new water into the system and a corresponding increase in the environmental impact of aquaculture activities. The high levels of nitrate and phosphate characteristic of aquaculture discharge are an important cause of eutrophication and have been known to lead to the collapse of entire affected ecosystems. Recirculation of culture water reduces the potential impact of aquaculture but requires energy-intensive wastewater treatment technologies. The nitrifying reactors that are currently industry standard in aquaculture require supplementation with exogenous carbon sources and oxygenation to sustain growth of aerobic nitrifying bacteria, increasing the cost and environmental footprint of facilities. Furthermore, these reactors remove only ammonia and nitrite, generating nitrate – all of which are toxic to fish. Over time, nitrate builds up in the culture water and must be diluted or purged. In this project, we will investigate an innovative technology that applies a microbial community comprising unique denitrifying phosphate accumulating organisms and anammox bacteria that can sustain high levels of nutrients removal in aquaculture wastewaters. To achieve efficient nutrients removal under the low carbon conditions (e.g., fish farms), we will incorporate nitrogen and phosphate removing bacteria previously obtained in our lab into microcosms exposed to aquaculture discharge to optimize the activity of functional denitrifying-phosphate accumulating and anammox bacterial populations. We will apply these functional populations to a de-nutrient bioreactor – a mobile modular reactor that incorporates the anammox reaction and can achieve high levels of nitrogen and phosphorus removal without aeration or carbon supplementation.
kw: sustainable aquaculture, eutrophication, anammox bacteria, ecology, modular bioreactor

title: Energy Reducing Technology for SWRO Desalination Systems -Closed Circuit Reverse Osmosis Technology
inst: Rohm and Haas Electronic Materials Singapore Pte. Ltd
abs: Conventional membrane-based desalination systems have not evolved much since their introduction in the 1960s. Operational efficiency of RO systems is restricted in these steady-state designs that require strict hydraulic conditions. We propose evaluation and optimization of Closed Circuit Reverse Osmosis (CCRO) technology for the high pressure 1st pass SWRO system in desalination plants. In addition, this same unit would be capable of treating reservoir water at recovery rates of 90-95% recovery at the touch of a button. CCRO technology is a patented technology from Desalitech, which is now a part of Dupont. The CCRO process has been proven successful in groundwater, surface water and municipal and industrial waste water applications for its operational efficiency and flexibility. The technology has not been evaluated for large scale SWRO systems in terms of optimizing for the lowest energy consumption in seawater desalination. CCRO utilizes commercially available RO elements that are designed for traditional RO processes. Simulations show that the CCRO process can reduce energy consumption by 5-18% [1] over a steady-state RO process using an energy recovery device and identical RO elements. In this proposal, we will be evaluating and optimizing the CCRO technology for SWRO to minimize energy consumption while demonstrating the flexibility to adapt to other brackish water sources. Results generated with commercial elements could be used to guide development of new RO elements specifically optimized for adapting to these changes.
kw: CCRO, RO system, IoT, automation, Energy saving

title: Urban-metabolic Farming-module (UmFm): a novel farming module towards eco-resilient megacity farmscape in 2030
abs: The project proposal seeks to attain 30 by 30 target by improving yield via filtered natural lighting via novel coated film with supplementary pulse-width modulated artificial lighting (during sunset) to optimize the morphogenetic stimulus and photo-morphogenetic response of Asian greens grown in urban farmscape. To enhance the utilization of space, an eco-resilient plug and growth Urban-metabolic Farming-module (UmFm) will be built for growth with minimal utilization of energy resources. The nutrients will be fed by irrigation to substrate based growth of crops. Data analytic/ artificial Intelligence competencies will be built into IoT system for evaluation on effectiveness of crop protection technologies and pest management system with tracking of post harvesting cycle to ensure of crops freshness. To address the land constraint, the team will simulate (the air flow dynamics), design and built a vertical modular farming unit with “chimney top ventilation fan” and double skin enclosure suit for operation by commercial farmer in residential areas. This also provides re-skillling and job opportunities for home-makers and retirees at close proximity to their home, fulfilling both food and economic security This allows Singaporean to stay vibrant and promote heathy ageing. The local precinct sales, consumption will cut down on the need for storage and transportation, bringing down costs and making it economically viable. The project will be divided into three work packages (WP-1) Architectural Design and fabrication of UmFm unit for optimal performance of the urban farming module (WP-2) Growth of Asian Greens appropriate to Singapore context with light conversion film and nutrients incorporation (WP-3) An integrated closed loop approach with irrigation and waste recovery system to support a sustainable, scalable, commercially operated farming system. Last but not least, the modular UmFm unit must be aesthetically assimilated into our residential areas to realize the vision of megacity farmscape.
