title: Open & Generic Wireless Structural Health Monitoring System
abs: Reinforced concrete building structures are widely used nowadays. During their service life, these lifeline structures are subjected to material aging, environmental erosion, operational load effect, long-term fatigue, and natural disasters which will inevitably result in damage accumulation and resistance reduction. Nowadays, Structural Health Monitoring (SHM) is characterized by anomaly detection within structures, and therefore owners can make use of these results to provide optimum maintenance and retrofitting. Therefore, the SHM system can be adopted to ensure structural safety and durability by allowing real time evaluation, feedback and timely maintenance/repair. An integrated real-time SHM system which can automatically interrogating the fiber optics sensors, wirelessly transmit, analyse and visualise the building SHM information has been developed and is being trialled at two selected HDB blocks. The developed universal interrogator is able to interrogate various fiber optics sensors installed in HDB blocks, rather than using different proprietary readers. However, it is required to be powered by mains for long term real-time applications, which in turn restrains for large scale deployment. This proposal will address above limitation, enhance the analytic functionalities and validate the predictive diagnosis with finite element modelling. There are five work packages: 1. Versatile Fiber Bragg Grating (FBG) sensors for building structural health monitoring for different parameters such as strain, temperature and vibration, etc.; 2. Low cost battery powered interrogator which can interrogate various FBG sensors: wireless FBG sensor; 3. Real-time data analytic and anomaly detection; 4. Performance and risk analysis and alarming: model updates Finite Element Analysis (FEA) with real-time data analytic results to validate diagnosis and prediction algorithm; 5. System integration and evaluation. At the end, an Open & Generic, Cost-effective Wireless Remote Monitoring System for Structural Health of Building Elements will be prototyped, and hopefully to be tested in the existing two selected HDB blocks, or a new HDB blocks under construction, to provide decision support. The developed wireless FBG sensors, removing the hurdle for its widely adoption and deployment, has huge potential market in structural health monitoring, healthcare and manufacturing industry. Although there are technical challenges and certain risks in development of a real wireless optical interrogator (power consumption to be more than 10 times lower as compared to the state of the art) for fiber optics sensors, we think it is achievable through win-win collaboration and partnership.
kw: Fiber optics sensors (FOS), Structural health monitoring (SHM), Finite Element Analysis (FEA), Data Analytic, Interrogator, Anomaly detection

title: Development of encapsulated starch (ES) products targeted at diabetics
abs: This study focuses on the development of food ingredients that have properties to reduce digestible starch release during human digestion. Asian diets contain highly-processed dense carbohydrates and other refined carbohydrates. These processed refined carbohydrates in starch-based foods are easily digestible, causing spikes in blood glucose levels. This project aims to develop active functional food ingredients that can delay the rate of starch digestion into simple sugars and therefore effectively lower the glycaemic index (GI) of regular starch-based foods. Controlled glucose release is critical for maintaining low blood glucose, which is critical for morbidity and mortality in diabetic patients. We will develop encapsulated starch (ES) formulations by incorporation of hydrocolloids that form gel networks with mono/divalent ions, in which the gel network formed encapsulates starch granules. The resultant ES will be characterised in regards of their physicochemical properties such as textural, rheological and sensorial characteristics, as well as their capacity to lower starch digestion in vitro and in vivo. In preliminary works, the novel ES that we have developed was able to reduce the rate of wheat noodle digestion by 25 - 36%; a more sustained glucose release profile was attained under simulated digestion conditions assessed at various hydrocolloid concentrations. For this grant, we will examine the mechanism of action with regard to microstructural arrangements as results of entrapment of the starch in the gel network system. In collaboration with industry partners, we will explore the ES application to different food products such as noodles, crackers and buns, whilst striving to maintain original textural and organoleptic attributes via physical and sensorial evaluations. This study offers potential opportunities for food manufacturers to expand their existing product lines as well as to optimise dietetic models of diabetic and health management.
kw: Diabetic, functional ingredients, low glycaemic, hydrocolloids, starch

title: Prime-boost vaccine strategy for increased immunogenicity and cross-variant protection (PRIBIVAC)
abs: The ongoing pandemic of a new human coronavirus, SARS-CoV-2 is responsible for a global crisis with a major death toll world-wide. Vaccines with strong efficacy have been developed in record time. The front runners, mRNA vaccines developed by BionTech/Pfizer and Moderna, have shown efficacy over >95%. Other more traditional vaccine formulations, such inactivated viruses developed by Sinovac or nanoparticle formulation based on the S-protein adjuvanted with Matrix M developed by Novavax have demonstrated a lower and variable range of efficacy (between 50 to 90%) depending on the geographical testing sites under various viral strain prevalence. An S-a S-protein-expressing adenovirus formulation has been developed by AstraZeneca and was shown to have an efficacy of 20 to 70%. The lowest efficacy recorded in South Africa was related to the emergence of a new variant, less susceptible to the immune response induced by the vaccine. Singapore has acquired the vaccines mentioned above and may have access though the COVAX program to AstraZeneca vaccine. Vaccination has started for frontline health care workers with the Pfizer/Biontech formulations since the end of December 2020. The final goal is to cover 75% of the population with formulations able to protect against all viral variants. There are limited data so far which indicated that the vaccines mentioned above will be able to do so. Here, we propose to assess a prime-boost strategy by combining different COVID-19 vaccine formulations in Singapore. This will help us to define which combinations provide better immunogenicity against different variants of concern and induce a more durable response. Experiments will be first performed in mice. The best immunogenic combinations will be next further tested in humans. For human experiments, we plan to enroll 50 individuals per vaccine prime-boost combinations (with a maximum of 4 best combinations tested). Mice and humans will be followed at different time post-immunization for up to 12 months. Different immune parameters will be assessed to define immunogenicity.
kw: COVID-19, Vaccine, mRNA, Immunity, Prime boost

title: Integrated Environmental Modeller (IEM) Phase 2
inst: IHPC - Institute of High Performance Computing
abs: This proposal seeks to enhance IEM simulation capabilities by adding myriad environmental and physical models. It involves five Work Packages 1) Multi-physics Urban Climate modelling with advanced urban greenery modelling for Radiative Sheltering, Tree Aerodynamics and Evapotranspiration Process, Wind-Driven Rain with Lagrangian and Eulerian approaches, coupling with Climate model, Utility Tools with local zone overset mesh development and Ventilation Based Design Optimization, 2) Military aircraft noise prediction models based on the Noise-Power-Distance (NPD) curves in which the noise emissions is a function of distance and corrected net thrust, 3) Building Energy Modelling with microclimate effects by adopting open source building energy model such as EnergyPlus to be coupled with microclimate parameters and urban geometry in order to estimate the cooling load demand, 4) Sensor Deployment and Data Acquisition on two HDB estates for model validation work, 5) System Integration and Software Development to include a user-friendly interface which automates most of the tedious steps required to setup the running of the simulations.With the above enhancement of IEM simulation capabilities, we can aim to aid better planning of comfortable living environment with higher resource efficiency.
kw: Multi-physics environmental modeling;Urban greenery modeling;Aircraft noise;Building energy modelling;Wind Driven Rain;System integration

title: A Customizable Oral Device for Faster and Accurate Detection of Bruxism
abs: Bruxism is the involuntary teeth excessive movement, which gradually developing many painful symptoms. Currently, the bruxism diagnosis is mainly based on patients’ complaints, dentists’ visual examination and practical experiences, which is inaccurate, subjective and slow. Measuring teeth occlusal forces during bruxism events, which happen mostly in sleeping time, can greatly provide a core evidence for accurate bruxism diagnosis. However, there is no such a suitable tool available on the market. To solve this problem, we propose a new smart oral device, which integrates a new flexible sensing technologies and dental molding. The device is customizable for real-time recordings of teeth moving forces, highly sensitive with good wear-ability. It is designed for home-based use, the obtained data will be processed intelligently and shared with related physicians for a faster and more accurate bruxism diagnosis, based upon the objective information reflecting teeth activities in real bruxism events, and finally result in a faster and better therapy. The device will benefit bruxism patients that shares about 20-30% of entire population. The flexible sensor technologies derived from this project can be utilized for broad potential applications in other aspects, such as artificial skins, diabetes monitoring, and food safety, etc.
kw: oral device, customizable, bruxism, excessive teeth force, biting force, occlusal force

title: IMC Compartmentalization and its role in maturation and transmission of P. falciparum gametocytes
abs: Malaria is one of the most infectious diseases in the world with P.falciparum malaria responsible for the majority of cases. The recent efforts directed towards its eradication have highlighted the need to target the gametocyte stages of these parasites. The intraerythrocytic development of the gametocyte stage parasites involves sequential morphological changes. These occur in niches such as the bone marrow of the host where the gametocyte remain isolated from the host immune effectors. The morphological changes associated with alterations in the shape and deformability of the gametocyte cells enable effective mechanical sequestration during maturation, leading to the release of the mature late stages parasites into circulation. The Inner membrane complex (IMC), a series of flattened vesicles underlying the parasite plasma membrane and mediating interactions with numerous cytoskeletal structures is differentially associated through these developmental stages. The IMC protein components, their interactions and the specialized functions are largely unknown. This study would 1) reveal the molecular components essential for IMC formation and its various functional roles during the development of P.falciparum gametocytes. 2) The interactions mediated by newly identified protein complexes of the IMC with the parasite cytoskeleton and membranes would be elucidated. 3) The phospho-signalling mechanisms at the IMC and its potential inhibitors would be identified. 4) The biophysical properties contributing to transmission would be evaluated upon disrupting the development of the gametocyte IMC. Firstly, to establish a comprehensive list of essential IMC components, co-immunoprecipitation, conditional gene knockdowns and localization based screens would be performed on transgenic parasites. Further, specialised post-translational modifications specific mass-spectrometry, fluorescence imaging techniques and differential cytoskeleton extractions would help map the essential protein interactions and signalling events at the IMC. Biophysical assays such as micropipette aspiration to measure the stage specific deformability, as well as the capillary flow characteristics would be investigated to measure the contribution of the identified essential interactions towards the physiological behaviours such as sequestration and margination capabilities. This proposal would therefore dissect the essential protein interactions and signalling mechanisms at the gametocyte IMC which confer the stage specific morphology and biophysical parameters mediating the sequestration at the bone marrow of immature gametocytes, the eventual release into the circulation, and the characteristic behaviour in the capillary blood flow leading to successful transmission of malaria. Prioritizing essential targets addresses a critical need to identify gametocyte stage molecular targets and suitable drug inhibitors as only 14% of all identified anti-Plasmodium drugs have gametocytocidal activi

title:
Characterizing the Genome and Epigenome of Congenital Heart Disease and Functional Validation for Disease-related Variants
[PROfiling the Genome and Epigenome of coNgenital heart disease studY (PROGENY)]
abs: A large proportion of congenital heart disease (CHD) is thought to have a significant genetic contribution, and at this time a genetic cause can be identified in approximately 35% of patients.We hypothesise that the epigenetic landscape in CHD will reveal new mechanistic insight into the pathophysiology of CHD, and lead to fresh, personalised therapeutic approaches. The specific aims include: 1) To establish genome-wide maps of enhancers (H3K27-acetylation ChIP-seq), chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), and myocardial transcriptomes for CHD, compared to control “healthy” hearts. These are anticipated to implicate epigenetic (H3K27ac) and transcriptomic mechanisms of disease in CHD. 2) To (a) analyse for chromatin quantitative trait loci (chQTL) from aim 1, (b) establish a genome-wide Enhancer–Promoter Interaction Map (using HiChIP and Hi-C) for paediatric hearts, and (c) integrate chQTL variants and assign their role to the regulation of corresponding gene expression. These are anticipated to prioritise and implicate possible causal genetic variants for CHD in the non-coding genome. 3) To verify the functionality of CHD Enhancers and validate chQTL variants in their role with regulating target gene expression in disease progression.
kw: Congenital heart disease; genetics; epigenetics; chromatin remodelling

title: Developmental Programming of Chronic Kidney Disease- Role of Renal Inflammation
abs: Background: Newborns of low birth weight (LBW), i.e. <2.5kg, have increased risk of chronic kidney disease (CKD) and renal failure in later life. We have recruited a cohort of ex-LBW young adults, and demonstrated that they have incipient nephropathy evidenced by lower eGFR and increased daytime systolic blood pressure load. Hypothesis/specific aims: Ex-LBW individuals are born with reduced nephron mass, and compensate by hyperfiltrating at the level of each glomerulus. We hypothesise that chronic glomerular hyperfiltration results in sustained tissue injury that leads to immune cell infiltration and inflammation. This renal inflammation creates a pro-fibrogenic milieu resulting in fibrosis. To test this hypothesis, we will (i) Isolate urine immune cells and characterise their degree of activation (ii) Characterise the renal cytokine environment, particularly pro- and anti-fibrotic factors, and (iii) Determine early microstructural changes in the kidney. Methodology/Approach: We have recruited 58 young adults (Age: 19.8±1.4 years), comprising 42 ex-LBW individuals (22 premature) and 16 age-matched normal birth weight controls (none premature). Urine immune cells will be isolated and sorted by FACS. RNA will be extracted and subjected to qRT-PCR for subset-specific activation markers and cytokine expression. Urinary levels of relevant cytokines will be determined via ELISA. Diffusion-weighted MRI will be used to quantify the true diffusion constant of renal tissue, which reflects tissue microstructure. Feasibility: Our preliminary data have shown that the subset composition of urine immune cells, as well as urinary cytokine profile, appear to differ between ex-LBW participants and controls. We also have been able to apply diffusion-weighted MRI to derive true diffusion constants in controls. Importance: This study will enable us to risk stratify ex-LBW young adults for follow-up and primary prevention, and provide a rational basis for developing pharmacological agents to prevent or slow progression to CKD, thus reducing the health and economic burden of CKD.
kw: Chronic kidney disease; Developmental Programming; Hyperfiltration; Inflammation; Urine immune cells; diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging

title: Biomarkers of Homologous Recombination Deficiency to Predict Outcomes in Patients with Triple Negative Breast Cancer Treated with Olaparib or Olaparib – Immunotherapy Combination
abs: Background: Triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) has a poor prognosis and no effective targeted therapy representing a disease of unmet clinical need. Standard therapeutic options are limited to chemotherapy alone. Recently, inhibition of the PD-1/PD-L1 axis has shown modest improvement in progression free survival in a subset of TNBC who express PD-L1 on immune cells. A major challenge in translating developing targeted therapy or immunotherapy for use in the clinical setting has been the lack of appropriate biomarkers for patient selection and therapeutic targeting. Method: This proposal will utilize primary and metastatic tumor samples of TNBC to examine potential predictive biomarkers for benefit from PARP inhibitors and/or immune checkpoint inhibition. We aim to interrogate tumor samples systematically and sequentially acquired during the conduct of the phase II multicenter study of olaparib or olaparib in combination with durvalumab. Tumor samples will be subjected to multi-platform analysis for the following: 1) homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) 2) genetic mutational analysis using whole exome sequencing 3) transcriptomic profiling using RNA sequencing. Hypothesis: Compared to unselected breast cancers, TNBC that are platinum sensitive are more likely to be HRD. Patients whose tumors have HRD are more likely to benefit from PARP inhibitors as monotherapy or in combination with immunotherapy.
kw: Triple negative breast cancer; homologous recombination deficiency; whole genome sequencing, RNA sequencing

title: Automated Osteoporotic Score Prediction using Artificial Intelligence
abs: Specific Aims: This research aims to develop an automated AI system to predict osteoporotic score by assessing a plain radiograph of a patient’s femur together with other patient information e.g. patient’s age, gender, etc. Hypotheses: Cortical Thickness Index (CTI) has been proven to have significant correlation with BMD values, which is the golden standard of osteoporotic score, by several studies. CTI has a distinct advantage over traditional BMD measurements as it only requires a quick, readily available inexpensive plain radiograph. Thus our hypotheses is to predict osteoporotic score using CTI and other patient information. Approach: The proposed AI system will first be trained using labelled femur X-ray images through transferred learning, the trained AI system will be able to detect and locate femurs, then subsequently image processing techniques will be used to measure CTI, and the CTI and other patient information will be used to predict osteoporotic score. Feasibility study: A preliminary study has been conducted using 100 retrospective patients data. The preliminary results showed that our proposed approach is able to predict osteoporosis score with reasonable accuracy. Importance: The proposed automated osteoporotic score prediction system using AI can be used as a surrogate measure to the traditional BMD measurements in the assessment of osteoporosis. It is more accessible and less expensive over the traditional method, as it is based on a plain X-ray scan only, which is routinely ordered. The advantages of accessibility and speed of results of the proposed system will help physicians not only in the local context but also globally to screen for and guide management of osteoporosis. The proposed system will also benefit osteoporosis patients through early detection and intervention and prevent osteoporosis fractures which may lead to death.
kw: Osteoporosis, BMD (Bone mineral density), DXA (dual energy X-ray absorptiometry), X-ray, Artificial intelligence, Deep learning, Mask R-CNN

title: The value of blockchain applications – Evidence from asset-backed securities
abs: The last decade has witnessed a great excitement about the blockchain technology and its applications, as exemplified by the popularity of Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies. Due to the benefits of using blockchain – the accuracy and reliability of data maintained on blockchain, many corporations and governments are exploring the applications of blockchain. Given the cost of implementing blockchain technology, it is critical to empirically document the economic value of blockchain applications. However, to our knowledge, there is no academic publication that provides rigorous empirical analysis of the economic value of blockchain applications in a commercial environment. In this research proposal, we exploit the asset-backed securities (ABS) issuance setting in China – where some ABS are issued using the blockchain technology and others are not – to provide empirical evidence on the value of blockchain applications. (ABS are bond securities with interest and principal payments backed by the cash flows from the underlying assets.) Specifically, we investigate whether ABS issued through the blockchain technology are valued differently by the market than those that are not. We will compare the yield of the ABS (the interest rate) and its issuance cost. If blockchain has positive economic benefits – reducing the information asymmetry about the quality of the assets underlying ABS, then it should result in a lower yield and issuance cost, because information asymmetry is the most important factor for both. Being the first study of the value of blockchain applications in the financial markets, whatever the findings turn out to be, the results of this project will be important to the organizations and governments that are interested in the economic impacts of blockchain. The results will also be important to the market participants involved in issuing and buying ABS because issuing ABS with lower yield and lower issuance cost is beneficial to all market participants. Blockchain is a cryptographically secure ledger. It maintains a reliable, sharable and time-stamped record of transactions and ownership. Companies and governments have explored to use this technology in many areas, such as the property registration and record keeping. One particularly important application is security offering, registration, and settlement. However, due to the limited applications in this area, it is unclear whether the blockchain technology can improve the issuance and record-keeping of securities. Given that many governments and stock exchanges are researching the use of blockchain technology in this area, it is important to investigate the value of blockchain. In this research proposal, we aim to provide evidence on the value of blockchain applications by investigating whether ABS issued using the blockchain technology have lower yield and lower issuance cost than other ABS. title: Creation and Analysis of a Digital Asset with the Gibson-Hill Photographic Collection
abs: ABSTRACT Creation and Analysis of a Digital Asset with the Gibson-Hill Photographic Collection The Gibson-Hill archive constitutes a significant cultural heritage asset that holds key data for multiple disciplines including environmental and urban history, zoology, architecture, art, and photography. This research project centers around the photography of the Gibson-Hill archive, which neatly embeds itself in the liminal period of Singapore’s history of the late 1940s to early 1960s. Gibson-Hill’s photographs document a time when rising nationalism in a late to post-colonial society would reveal the tipping point of the start of a new political era and nation-building in both Malaysia and Singapore, seen through the eyes of an expatriate – in effect, a kind of colonial gaze. The research team of this project intends to launch a full-scale and innovative investigation of the Gibson-Hill archive by approaching it from three research perspectives: • A theoretical perspective, which aims at investigating the various lines of inquiry present in the collection, their significance, innovation and impact for the relevant fields of inquiry. This multi-layered project explores how digitalization and new technological uses of photography can enrich our knowledge and rebuild our memories of the period, and reconnect Singapore’s colonial past with the present; • A creative perspective, which aims to provide a new way of approaching the collection and its content, in other words, by revisiting the collection through innovative means such as re-photography, which allows not only to highlight the changes a place, an environment or a scenery has faced over time but also to make them contemporaneous (i.e., a scenery of the past could be a scenery of the present, limiting the effects of time) and create new works of art that stand on their own even if they were created with the support of the collection; and • An experiential perspective, which aims to find innovative ways to display works of art or historical artefacts in a sufficiently attractive way to interest and educate the general public. The team aims to investigate an experience-based curation by employing augmented reality, virtual reality, and also a re-photography mobile app, to highlight the relevance and significance of historical photography in the digital age. To achieve these aims, the team will review, digitize, restore, re-organize, and categorize the archive to create a digital asset so as to facilitate the access to and study of the Gibson-Hill archive for scholars, researchers, institutions and the general public. The research team is collaborative effort of experts from academic institutions including Liverpool University in UK, USC-Shanghai Jiao Tong University in China, and Ehwa Women’s University in Korea, and curators from the National Museum of Singapore and the National Gallery Singapore.
kw: Singapore Social History; Photo Archive; Environmental Humanity; Biodiversity; Digital Content Heritage

title: Smart molecular computers for rapid and visual detection of infections
abs: Detection of pathogen nucleic acids has broad applications in infection diagnostics and management. As an alternative to conventional pathogen culture, which entails long processing time (i.e., several days) and species-specific protocols, nucleic acid technologies have been increasingly adopted in clinical laboratories to provide unprecedented molecular information about infections. Current detection of pathogen nucleic acids, however, is almost exclusively performed in large, centralized clinical laboratories. This limited reach arises from the high complexity and cost associated with conventional technologies. Commercial assays leverage primarily on polymerase chain reaction (PCR) to amplify and detect specific targets. Such systems not only necessitate bulky and specialized equipment, for PCR thermal cycling and fluorescence measurements, but also require trained personnel to operate. Advanced isothermal amplification assays have been developed to relieve the instrument needs for temperature cycling; nevertheless, these assays have their own limitations. For example, loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) has stringent sequence requirements, cannot be easily generalized, and is prone to false-positives (e.g., from primer-dimer formation). As evident in the ongoing outbreak of COVID-19, for prompt detection and efficient management, assay platforms that can bring nucleic acid testing to the patient level (e.g., community clinics and doctor’s offices) are urgently needed to improve disease surveillance, patient stratification and health outcomes. To address these challenges, we have developed a molecular nanotechnology to enable visual and modular detection of diverse pathogen nucleic acids. Instead of relying on traditional target nucleic acid amplification, as in the above-mentioned approaches, the technology exponentially enhances visual signal from direct and independent target hybridization. Termed enzyme-assisted nanocomplexes for visual identification of nucleic acids (enVision), the technology consists of two types of independent enzyme-DNA nanostructures – an easily adjustable recognition element and a sensitive universal signaling element – to decouple target recognition and visual signal enhancement. The built-in enzymatic cascades produce a rapid color readout for the naked eye; the assay is thus fast (as little as 30 minutes), sensitive (<10 amol), and readily quantified with smartphones. The enVision advantages are multifold for rapid clinical applications. First, sensing mechanism. The technology activates immediately upon target hybridization to transduce exponential visual signal enhancement. title: Dynamical Systems, Foliation Theory and Applications
abs: The theory of complex dynamics in dimension 1 was founded 100 years ago by Fatou-Julia and is nowadays a quite developed theory. Several Variable Dynamics emerged in the 90s and is currently a very active research domain. The introduction of Pluripotential Theory in the field was a fundamental breakthrough. Progress in Pluripotential Theory allows us to solve problems from Complex Dynamics but also leads to applications in other domains such as the dynamics of groups, foliations by Riemann surfaces, Nevanlinna theory and homogeneous dynamics. It can also be applied to some areas of Mathematical Physics, such as Random Matrices and Resonances of Schrödinger operators, and it can even serve as a tool to tackle some questions from Algebraic and Differential Geometry. The PI and his collaborators have made significant contributions to the subject and master the necessary techniques to work on these directions. More details are given in Part B below. • Pluripotential Theory. This branch of Complex Analysis was founded in the 50s by Lelong-Oka and is now a powerful technique in many domains. A main object of study are positive currents. Several fundamental questions remain open for higher co-dimension and for non-closed currents. The PI and Sibony have established basic steps for a calculus with the above classes of currents. We will continue to ¬ determine the largest domain where both our theories of super-potentials and densities apply; ¬ study the bi-degree (1,1) case using the theory of densities and revisit known applications. ¬ study non-closed currents, e.g. harmonic currents, central objects in foliation theory. • Holomorphic dynamics in higher dimensions. The PI and collaborators have contributed to the construction and the study of main dynamical objects associated with a complex dynamical system. Challenging problems remain open. We aim to ¬ develop new techniques in order to prove equidistribution of periodic cycles in the quite general setting of holomorphic maps on compact Kähler manifolds in any dimension. ¬ apply our techniques to study the systems perturbed by a small potential. ¬ introduce a new approach to study bifurcation problems. • Foliations by Riemann surfaces. The recent use of positive currents allows one to obtain several surprising results for foliations in dimension 2 with generic singularities. We aim to ¬ study the Lyapunov exponent of a foliation on a compact Kähler surface. ¬ study other singularities and foliations associated with representations of open surface groups. ¬ study the case where the phase space is of dimension larger than 2. • Nevanlinna Theory. This theory has deep connections with Algebraic Geometry and Number Theory. We will apply techniques developed in Complex Dynamics to Nevanlinna Theory and ¬ re-write basic results of the theory using positive currents; ¬ study some of its applications such as Cartan Theory and Kobayashi’s conjectures; ¬ apply Nevanlinna Theory to the setting of foliations by Ri

title: 2D/3D Fully Conjugated Macrocycles and Molecular Cages with Global Aromaticity
abs: The sp2-carbon based nano-structures as 0D fullerene, 1D carbon nanotube, and 2D graphene have shown revolutionary influence in chemistry and materials science. Development of a new type of fully conjugated, all-benzenoid topological structures such as 2D macrocycles and 3D molecular cages would not only help us to deeper understand the fundamental concept of “aromaticity” in different dimensions, but also afford new materials for organic electronics, spintronics, and supramolecular chemistry. However, synthesis of this type of molecules is extremely challenging and so far, there is very limited success. The PI’s research group recently demonstrated that such kind of fully conjugated macrocycles could be easily attained in a simple synthetic protocol involving dynamic Friedel-Crafts alkylation reaction (Angew. Cheme. Int. Ed. 2019, 58, 11742). The obtained macrocycle exhibited annulene-like global antiaromaticity, while two-electron and four-electron oxidation of the macrocycle led to a switch between aromaticity and antiaromaticity. Based on this promising result, herein we propose to synthesize a series of 2D and 3D fully conjugated aza-bridged all-benzenoid macrocycles and molecular cages by using this dynamic covalent chemistry, which are supposed to show global (anti)aromaticity at different redox states. The proposed research includes: (1) synthesis of various complex topological structures such as 2D (nearly) planar macrocycles with different sizes, macrocycle-in-macrocycles (MIM), interlocked figure-of-eight macrocycles and catenanes, 3D conjugated molecular cages, and imine-containing super polycyclic hydrocarbons; (2) investigation of their global (anti)aromaticity at different redox states by both experiments and theoretical calculations; (3) studies of their optical, electronic, and magnetic properties; and (4) exploring their applications in charge transfer complexes, supramolecular recognition, organic ferroelectricity, and organic electronic/spintronic devices. All these designed molecules are long sought-after targets in physical organic chemistry and they will provide important platforms to test some important concepts such as 3D aromaticity. The focus of this proposal will be on synthesis and fundamental physical properties.
kw: physical organic chemistry, aromaticity, macrocycle, molecular cage, dynamic covalent chemistry, organic electronics

title: Single-Crystal Semiconductor Fibers for Wearable Optoelectronics
abs: The demonstration of flexible functional fibers will enable the realization of wearable full-body sensing system to monitor various physiological signals and to measure the chemical compositions of body fluids. This requires the integration of functional materials such as semiconductors, conductors and insulators into a single fiber with complex architectures and diverse functionalities. However, the common use of thermally stable amorphous semiconductors in such fibers generally results in a high density of electronic defects, which subsequently leads to the poor electrical properties of the fabricated fiber-based devices. Moreover, all the previously demonstrated approaches have been restricted to fabricate a single device or a very low density of devices over extended fiber length due to their intrinsic process complexities. The goal of this proposed project is to use laser-induced directional crystallization to enable the precise control on both the crystal structures and the device density of in-fiber semiconductor devices. Specifically, we plan to achieve meter-long single-crystal semiconductor-core fibers with the unprecedented control over architecture, composition, size, and functionality, while maintaining the flexibility of fibers. Our approach is to feed the thermally drawn functional fiber with a semiconductor core through a CO2 laser beam at a precisely controlled feed-in velocity. Thanks to the small heating area under the laser beam, a direct and selective heating will enable the directional crystallization on the semiconductor core. This is a new playing field for the crystal-structure transition and fluid dynamics, with the geometries and parameters that are not accessible in traditional platforms. Studying the fluid dynamics of the thermal drawing of functional fibers and achieving the crystallization of semiconductor cores will yield new fundamental insight to essentially address the following challenges: (1) control and maintain the single-crystal nature of the in-fiber semiconductor wires with the sizes down to tens of nanometers over the entire meter-long fiber, (2) realize process compatibility of thermal drawing crystalline semiconductors and metals confined by the cladding with a wide range of processing temperatures from 300 oC to 2000 oC, (3) maintain a stable processing temperature gradient to compensate the thermal energy loss due to the scattering from different interfaces inside fiber, and (4) achieve the direct contact between semiconductors and metals without the inter-domain diffusion or mixing in liquid phase, while maintaining the single-crystal nature of the semiconductor cores. Ultimately, we will demonstrate a single fiber with the integration of single-crystal semiconducting material and metal electrodes in a precisely defined metal-semiconductor-metal structure, forming in-fiber optoelectronic devices with fast response times, high device densities, large optical bandwidths, and high photon collection eff

title: Chiral Covalent Organic Frameworks for Chiral Recognition and Asymmetric Catalysis
abs: Covalent organic frameworks (COFs), formed by connecting multidentate organic building blocks through covalent bonds, provide a versatile material platform for the exploration of new structures and functions. Owing to their covalent linkages between light elements (H, B, C, N and O), COFs possess lots of unique properties such as rigid structures (two dimensional or three dimensional), low density, high thermal stability and permanent porosity with large specific surface areas, which make them naturally useful in gas storage. The incorporation of suitable functional groups in the building blocks of COFs would open up a new avenue as advanced materials for applications in chiral molecule recognition, separation, and asymmetric catalysis. To meet simultaneously the requirements of crystallinity and functionality, the construction of functional COFs for chiral molecule recognition, separation, and asymmetric catalysis is highly challenging. To address the above issue, the main objective of the proposal is to design and prepare chiral COFs with tunability in composition, structure and chiral function by direct synthetic strategy for chiral recognition and heterogeneous catalysis. The project will focus on the following general tasks: (1) Elaboration of new synthetic approaches for the controlled preparation of proposed chiral COFs. (2) Detailed structural characterizations of obtained chiral COFs by means of relevant experimental and theoretical methods. (3) Performance determination of these chiral COFs for chiral recognition and asymmetric catalysis. The project involves the use of special techniques and analytical facilities: (1) basic characterizations by means of FTIR analysis, SEM/TEM morphology characterization, thermal stability determination with TGA, and HRMS/NMR analysis for compound purity characterization; (2) structure determination using single crystal X-ray crystallography, and powder X-ray diffraction; (3) theoretical studies focused on understanding the structure nature and the host-guest interactions within porous networks; (4) determination of sorption properties for storage and/or separation of small chiral molecules; (5) detailed evaluation on the performance of asymmetric catalysis. Having these experimental and computational studies, we undertake truly interdisciplinary research aiming at correlating structural and physicochemical properties of the synthesized chiral COFs with their unique applications. As a result of the project, we will obtain new types of covalent porous materials capable of efficient chiral separation and asymmetric catalysis. We plan to investigate the proposed systems systematically, starting from the development of new synthetic procedures to the fabrication of novel covalent porous materials for targeted applications. title: Riverine Sediment Load Responses to Climate Change in High Mountain Asia
abs: High Mountain Asia (HMA), the so-called “Asian Water Tower” or “Third Pole”, is the planet’s largest reservoir of ice-snow after the Arctic and Antarctic and the headwaters of over ten large Asian rivers. These headwater rivers are the sources of water, sediment, nutrients, and organic carbon for downstream systems, and hence support and influence approximately 2 billion people living in the downstream river basins. Since the 1950s, air temperature in HMA has warmed 1.9 ℃ at a rate of 0.32 ℃ per decade, doubling the global average (0.16 ℃ per decade) and already exceeding the 1.5 ℃ target of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC). Due to the dramatic climate warming, glacier-snow-permafrost in HMA have been melting at an alarming rate (e.g. there is a doubling of ice loss rate during 2000-2016 compared to 1975-2000). Such fast melting of glacier-snow-permafrost can drastically increase riverine water and sediment load in a medium-term (e.g. till 2050s) before glacial melting reaching a tipping point. The potentially increased sediment load (associated with nutrients, contaminants, and organic carbon) can severely disturb the biogeochemical cycles, aquatic ecosystems, landscapes, and hundreds of constructed reservoirs in the basins of these major rivers. Despite its importance and intense scientific interest, however, less is known about the sediment dynamics in HMA’s headwater rivers due to the difficulty of sediment load modelling. This proposed research aims to address a fundamental research gap in understanding of how climate change affects the sediment load in the headwater rivers of HMA through altering the processes of glacier-snow-permafrost melting and vegetation change. Built upon our ongoing MOE Tier 1 project (2018-2020; “Sediment and carbon fluxes from glacial melting and permafrost thawing: a case study in the upper Yellow River”), this proposed project will select 20 headwater rivers (hydrological stations) in HMA covered by the three types of climate zones (Indian monsoon, East-Asia monsoon, and Westerly (wind)) to study the effect of climate change on sediment load in the cold environments. We will collect the runoff and sediment load data over the past decades from the existing gauging stations across the entire HMA’s headwaters, supplemented by in-situ sediment measurements in the gauging stations that lack sediment monitoring and a detailed case study investigating sediment sources and delivery across a typical river basin covered by glaciers and permafrost. Special attention will be paid to runoff and sediment load modelling in the cold environments with glacier-snow-permafrost. The relative impacts of temperature, precipitation, glaciers, and snow on sediment load will be examined by ‘multiple double-mass-curves’ and cryosphere-hydrological models. title: Optical resonators for high performance laser stabilization and optical atomic clocks
abs: We propose to design, build, and implement two high performance optical resonators to be used to stabilize clock lasers in our current lutetium clock program. Over the past five years we have developed an optical clock system based on singly ionized lutetium. We have demonstrated the superior properties of this atom for optical clock applications and the viability of going beyond the single ion paradigm of all current ion-based clock systems. These two features should enable us to establish lutetium as a globally competitive frequency standard and push the boundaries of atomic clock performance. Currently, our clock performance is limited by the stability of the commercial optical resonator used to stabilize the clock lasers at short timescales. We are now seeking to develop in-house capability for the design and construction of such resonators to extend the performance beyond that possible with our commercial system. Currently there are only a few groups in the world that have established resonators which outperform the best commercially available systems. Such resonators are made from either crystalline silicon or ultra-low expansion glass and both have demonstrated stability that outperforms the best available microwave resonators. Consequently, such resonators can be anticipated to become a core component in future time-keeping industries. Additionally, with optical atomic clocks exceeding the performance of the current Caesium standard, it is anticipated that optical frequency standards will ultimately provide a redefinition of the SI second and this could happen within the next decade. Thus, it is a timely opportunity to establish a world-leading optical clock program with in-house expertise the relevant technologies. Development of the cavities will utilize mechanical simulations of cavity geometries for determining sensitivities of a particular design against low frequency vibrations. A number of reports are available in the literature that illustrate the general considerations, and work has already started to put in place the necessary computational tools. Substrate and mirror fabrication will be provided commercially, and final construction will be done in house. Cavity testing can be done in comparison with our current commercial system and by direct comparison with the atom. We expect to be able to improve the laser system by at least an order of magnitude, which would provide a clock system with sufficient stability to demonstrate clock performance comparable to or exceeding that of the world’s leading clock systems.
kw: Atomic Clocks; Timing Technology

title: Combinatorial DNA-PAINT for the Multiplexed Analysis of Cell Receptor Interactions
abs: Interactions between cell surface receptors and their ligands play an important role in mediating cell signalling pathways, and alterations in their activities have been implicated in numerous diseases. Conventional techniques for probing such interaction activities involve the combinatorial analysis of several receptor targets which generate a huge database of mostly irrelevant images requiring extensive signal deconvolution based on spatial co-localization. Furthermore, the readout signal is based on fluorescence which is limited by the number of spectrally distinct fluorophores with different colours (typically 4 – 5). To tackle the shortcomings of existing analytical methods, we propose to develop a DNA circuit toolbox based on the concept of split proximity circuit (SPC) which acts as a molecular “AND” logic gate to barcode only interaction events, thereby filtering away irrelevant recognition events, e.g. inactivated receptors in their monomeric state. Next, we will encode the DNA barcode as a set of three hairpins, each coding for a different colour channel. This serves as an in-built proof-read function to reduce false positive results which can only be generated when three hairpins tagged with different fluorophores simultaneously bind non-specifically with one another. We then use an optical method known as points accumulation for imaging nanoscale topography (PAINT) to decipher the DNA barcodes simultaneously with nanometer length resolution as “blinking” signals, which reflect the inherent hybridization kinetics of the DNA barcodes with different permutations of probe length and number of repeat units.
kw: DNA circuit, receptor interactions, bioimaging, multiplex detection

title: Complex quantum systems with neural networks: relaxation and quantum computing
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: Many aspects of our everyday life relies on artificial intelligence and thus on neural networks, this due to both theoretical advancements in deep neural networks, and hardware advances in graphical processing units. This has caught the attention of quantum physicists who recently started to use neural networks as a variational ansatz for many-body quantum systems. This novel approach is now known as neural network quantums states (NNQS). As of now, we know that NNQS can represent states which cannot be handled efficiently by other methods, as for example matrix product states. There has also been a large number of applications of NNQS to groundstates. However, few studies have tackled the dynamics of many-body quantum systems, despite many-body quantum systems and their dynamics are key for future quantum technologies, e.g. quantum computers. It is fair to state that the line of research of using neural networks to represent complex quantum systems, and study their dynamics, is still at its infancy. We have not yet fully profited of the experience built by the computer science community, nor of the progress in hardware used for machine learning (GPUs), and it is not clear which is the type of many-body quantum system for which neural networks can be effective. For this reasons, in this proposal we aim to explore the effectiveness of using NNQS to study the dynamics of many-body quantums systems, focusing on scenarios which cannot be addresssed by current methods, e.g. systems with long-range interactions or in dimensions larger than one. We will implement different types of neural networks, e.g. convolutional neural networks, on GPUs and we will study the simulability of different dynamics of many-body quantum systems. This will allow us to learn which scenarios can be best represented by NNQS and by which particular type of neural networks. It is in fact very clear that no classical algorithm can be used to simulate generic many-body quantum systems, however we trust that there are interesting and important scenarios in which NNQS can outperform current methods and thus give us 1) a much clearer insight into the dynamics of many-body quantum systems and 2) possibly open the way to simulate and validate complex quantum devices. To tackle these problems, we have put together a team of physicists and computer scientists with experience at working together and experts in quantum dynamics, many-body quantum systems, quantum computing and classical machine learning.
kw: neural network quantum states; many-body quantum physics; relaxation and thermalization; open quantum systems; quantum computing; matrix product states

title: The Science of High INtensitY (SHINY) Perovskite Emitters
abs: The meteoric rise of perovskite light-emitting devices (PeLEDs) from less than 1% to around 20% efficiency within 5 years is unprecedented and it sparked a worldwide PeLED frenzy. However, beneath the glitter lies the stark reality that their device lifetimes remain abysmal and are still plagued by pertinent issues ranging from halide migration, unstable colour purity, and inefficient blue emission - any of which could derail PeLeDs commercial aspirations. The PeLED field is now at a critical juncture, urgently needing fresh perspectives and approaches to tackle the myriad of multi-disciplinary challenges. Layered multi-quantum well (MQW) perovskites (e.g., Ruddlesden-Popper perovskites (RPP)) are emerging players in the perovskite field with outstanding optoelectronic properties whilst possessing excellent moisture and material stabilities. RPP perovskites are the best bet to address these interrelated challenges. However, significant knowledge gaps over their basic photophysics and structure-function relations between the interacting organic and inorganic subsystems have so far resulted in a trial and error and a piecemeal approach. Without imperative design rules as a compass to guide the development, progress will be painstaking and arduous. In this project, we conceive a creative organic Lego approach to engineer stable, highly luminescent RPPs. RPP, with a general formula (A prime)mA n-1BnX3n+1 (n = 1, 2, 3, 4, ...), comprises of n layers of [BX6]4- octahedral sheets (or layered inorganic base framework) sandwiched by the large organic spacer cation (LC) A prime; while A is a monovalent organic cation, B is a divalent metal cation and X is a halide anion. The LCs are held together by weak van der Waals forces between the repeating n layers. The fine and rational tuning of LCs (from a large library) has a profound impact on both the chemical and photophysical properties of RPPs. Herein, we seek to elucidate the structure-function relations between the large cation (LC) organic spacer building blocks and the layered inorganic octahedral base framework in a bid to simultaneously establish both a wet chemistry MQW perovskite cookbook and a photophysics structure-function playbook to address these interrelated challenges. Our interdisciplinary approach involves revealing photophysical studies, backed by comprehensive first-principles calculations to screen these relations, which correlates with thorough materials and device studies in iterative feedback. title: Longitudinal Immune-Phenotyping of Surgically Resected Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC) following Neoadjuvant and Adjuvant Treatment with Checkpoint Inhibitors
abs: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the sixth most common cancer and the second-most common cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide. Tumour recurrences are common after surgical resection but the mechanisms driving them are not fully elucidated, with risk factors including viral load, vascular invasion, poor differentiation and others. Currently there is no standard of care for HCC neoadjuvant or adjuvant therapy, as no treatment has proven beneficial in randomized studies after potentially curative treatment. The prevention of recurrence via neoadjuvant or adjuvant treatments is thus an important unmet medical need in patients with HCC. Previous studies in other cancer types suggest that effective immunomodulation using checkpoint inhibitors such as pembrolizumab in neoadjuvant-adjuvant setting can re-activating the immune response in HCC, providing immense therapeutic benefit and reduce tumour recurrence rates in patients with HCC. We aim to identify an effective neoadjuvant-adjuvant therapy that will reduce post-resection recurrence by evaluating the efficacy of pembrolizumab as neoadjuvant-adjuvant therapy on recurrence rates of HCC patients at 2-years post-hepatic resection. This study will provide early signs of efficacy of neoadjuvant/adjuvant therapy with pembrolizumab in HCC patients, provide data about changes in HCC immune microenvironment and improve understanding of changes in HBV antigen-specific T cell response following anti-PD1 therapy through crucial tracking of the immune profiles and phenotypes of HBV-specific T cells.

title: A Phase 2a, Randomized, Double-blind, Placebo-controlled Trial to Evaluate the Antiviral Activity, Safety and Tolerability, and Pharmacokinetics of Janssen Dengue Drug in Adults With Confirmed Dengue Fever
abs: Dengue is caused by any of the four (DENV) serotypes which belong to the genus Flavivirus in the family of the Flaviviridae.  Global Public Health R&D group of Johnson & Johnson is developing a dengue antiviral compound, Janssen dengue drug, which aims to treat and/or prevent dengue.  This compound will be tested in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicenter, Phase 2a interventional study in adult participants in Singapore. The study will recruit 150 participants, with the primary objective of investigating the antiviral activity, safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics of study drug, compared to placebo, and evaluate the improvement in clinical signs and symptoms with the administration of study drug.  The primary hypothesis is that study drug is superior to placebo with respect to reduction in viral load in participants with a primary DENV infection, as measured by area under the log10-transformed DENV RNA viral load curve from baseline on Day 1 until Day 5.  As an oral therapeutic agent, it is expected that study drug could be readily used to treat confirmed dengue infection at the outpatient setting or within the hospital in the acute febrile phase of infection. title: PACE: Next-Generation IoT Edge Computing through Efficient Software Programmable Accelerators
abs: Singapore’s Smart Nation initiative is transforming every sphere of our lives from healthcare, transport, homeland security to industrial automation. The primary driver behind this transformation is the Internet of Things (IoT), billions of physical objects connected to the network. IoT system architectures are moving towards edge computing where computational intelligence is added directly to the edge devices at or near the sensors collecting the data instead of the remote cloud for time-sensitivity, security, privacy, and connectivity reasons. At present, the potential of edge computing is severely restricted by the limited compute capability of the power, area constrained edge devices. The overarching vision of the PACE research programme is to unleash the next-generation IoT applications through 50x improvement in edge computing efficiency, i.e., performance per unit power. This is achieved by architecting innovative computing systems that represent a fundamental paradigm shift from the existing inherently sequential von Neumann model of computing to the inherently parallel dataflow model. At the heart of the programme is the design of a reusable, versatile, ultra-low power, software programmable computing chip, inspired by the dataflow model that offers the high efficiency of fixed-function hardware while allowing full configurability through software. The hardware is deliberately kept simple to achieve ultra-low power operations, while the innovative software orchestrates the hardware computation. This software-defined flexibility enables the chip to morph itself on demand to support diverse computations across applications and will open up a gamut of new opportunities that are currently unimaginable. We further improve the energy-efficiency of our system via domain-specific application-level optimizations and low-power circuits optimizations. As a concrete demonstration, we will showcase tiny wearable edge devices powered by PACE accelerator to replace backpack-scale edge analytics solutions currently carried by Singapore law-enforcement authorities for safety, security, and rescue operations.
kw: IoT; Edge Computing; Low Power; Reconfigurable Computing; Accelerator

title: Integrating magnetic resonance spectroscopy imaging modalities with metabolic drug therapy for cancer precision medicine
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Cancer is a leading cause of death worldwide, including Singapore. While significant headways have been made in the development and deployment of therapeutics for some cancers, long-term disease-free responses for most cancers are rare. Current drug development efforts mostly focus on targeted therapy (e.g. kinases and receptors) or immunotherapy. However, most targeted therapies result in bypass mechanisms leading to cancer resistance and relapse, and evidence for acquired resistance to immune checkpoint inhibitors is emerging. Thus, there is significant room to consider other features of cancer that may be druggable and result in longer-term response. Several of the most effective drugs that have been in use for many decades target cancer cell metabolism. In fact, the first chemotherapeutic agent is an anti-metabolite (anti-folate), which is still used as the standard-of-care more than five decades since its discovery. However, research efforts on metabolic therapy have long been complicated by the significant overlap in bioenergetic pathways between cancer and normal proliferative cells, and by the considerable heterogeneity in solid tumors. Our proposal harnesses two innovative technologies – a metabolic gene discovery platform (termed DMITRI, for Deployment of Metabolic Target Discovery), and in vivo metabolic flux measurements using magnetic resonance spectroscopy of hyperpolarized 13C compounds (HP-13C-MRS) – to advance the use of metabolic therapy while minimizing unintended impact on normal tissues. Focusing on liver and lung cancers, we aim to: (1) Implement DMITRI for discovering and validating tractable metabolic targets in tumors and identifying druggable metabolic crosstalk between tumor cells and their niche; (2) Develop first-in-class metabolic probes for HP-13C-MRS to assess metabolic fluxes in tumor and stromal cells; and (3) Build an integrative platform combining metabolic target validation with in vivo metabolic flux measurement and imaging using HP-13C-MRS/MRSI to provide a direct non-invasive approach that predicts and monitors target engagement and clinical responses.
kw: hyperpolarized 13C magnetic resonance spectroscopy; Precision cancer therapy; metabolic cancer therapy; drug resistance; metabolic flux imaging

title: Multipronged approach toward vaccine development against Scale Drop Disease Virus (SDDV) in Asian Seabass
abs: Asian sea bass, Lates calcarifer, is an economically important aquaculture species, with its production increasing within the South East Asian region. However, viral diseases are causing significant production and financial losses to Asian seabass farmers. Recently, an emergent pathogen, Scale Drop Disease virus (SDDV) has been reported to attribute to 50% of the fishes’ mortality in fish farms. As with many pathogens, there is an impending need for the development of a vaccine to protect the fishes against SDDV infection. In this project, we propose to develop a SDDV vaccine formulation based on the identification of immunogenic regions in the viral protein to effectively induce a protective anti-viral immune response. Since little is known about the biology and host immunity against SDDV, the scope of the project will include development of tools to study the virus e.g. development of a cell line for in vitro virus propagation, preparation of viral stocks for challenge experiments and development of assays to functionally assess the immune response after immunisation with various vaccine delivery platforms. This new knowledge will help not only in the development of a vaccine against SDDV but also aid in establishing a framework for vaccine development against new emerging viruses.

title: Development of innovative strategies for disease management in aquaculture to increase production and ensure food safety
inst: IBB - Institute of Bioengineering and Bioimaging
abs: With the intensification of global aquaculture practices to meet the increasing demand of fish protein, diseases are of a major concern in the aquaculture farms. Presently, synthetic chemicals and antibiotics are used for disease management in both land-based and off-shore farms. Moreover, the treatment part is cumbersome and stressful with current approaches. Nonetheless, antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is becoming a major threat facing the aquaculture industry with increasing and inappropriate use of antibiotics, and causing environment instability. In this proposed project, we aim to address these issues with three main strategies. (1) Eco-/bio-degradable antimicrobial polymers that do not develop resistance in bacteria, and can degrade into benign compounds under selected ecological conditions or enzymatically in fish. Thus, the polymers would neither cause harm to the environment nor remain in fish when consumed, mitigating resistance development in human. (2) Broad-spectrum antiviral macromolecules that prevent and treat fish virus infection without inducing resistance development. (3) Antimicrobial and antiviral inorganic composite materials that can be coated onto silica or ceramic particles. These particles would be used to remove microbes and viruses from water in closed-land farms. All antimicrobial and antiviral materials will be synthesized by using methodologies that we have developed. We will focus on optimization of compositions and functionalities for modulating degradation rate, and increasing antimicrobial/antiviral potency and selectivity. The screening and evaluation of these materials will involve in vitro antimicrobial and antiviral activity studies followed by in vivo evaluation of selective promising macromolecules for oral feeding regime to achieve the desirable protective efficacy. Upon successful demonstration of antimicrobial and antiviral properties against targeted pathogens, the products would be scaled up for future farm trials.
kw: Aquaculture; Antimicrobial resistance; Antimicrobial polymers; Antiviral polymers; Inorganic composite materials; Megalocytivirus

title:
Development and optimisation of a robust, integrated, and cost-effective electrochemical
platform for seawater desalination pre-treatment
abs: Pre-treatment processes for seawater desalination are critical for the removal of membrane fouling precursors as well as sustainable operation of the subsequent reverse osmosis (RO) process. Current process performance and economics are heavily dependent on influent seawater quality, with excessive coagulant and chemical dosages required for intake with high foulant contents. Electrocoagulation (EC) is proposed as a robust and cost-effective alternative to chemical coagulation (CC) and dissolved air flotation (DAF), leveraging its advantages of concurrent hydrogen bubble generation. EC has been reported to achieve more than 90% removal of foulants of concern, with the potential for lower volume of waste sludge production. Previous studies have indicated EC can be readily integrated into existing hybrid pre-treatment trains. Preliminary desktop estimations indicate 60% in OPEX savings compared to conventional CC-DAF pretreatment. This joint proposal submitted by NUS and Hydroleap aims to develop a robust, integrated and cost-effective pre-treatment platform, elevating the Technology Readiness Level (TRL) from 3 to 7 for seawater desalination pretreatment based on EC. In Phase 1, lab-scale studies will be used to deliver optimised foulant removal in EC from actual seawater, optimised current efficiency for coagulant generation, evaluation of EC synergy with ultrafiltration (UF) and evaluation of concurrent hardness and boron removal to meet the SWRO feed requirements. Preliminary assessment of the integrated EC-UF treatment performance and cost will be conducted based on the lab-scale studies. In Phase 2, a responsive controlled lab-scale EC-UF system with online intake and treated quality monitoring will be developed and optimised for foulant removal. The optimised lab-scale EC-UF system will be verified at pilot-scale testing. Pilot-scale deliverables include validation of the design scalability and process control, demonstration of long-term integrated process economy and robustness with UF, and detailed cost and energy comparison of EC-UF treatment with the existing pre-treatment process. This proposal will bring together academic, technical and commercial expertise from NUS and Hydroleap. Applied fundamental and process knowledge on this collaboration will catalyse the development, optimisation and operation of EC technology for seawater pre-treatment, enhancing confidence for large-scale deployment and commercialisation achieving the goals of this CRP.
kw: Pre-treatment, Electrocoagulation, Optimisation, Automated integrated EC-UF system, Pilot-scale, Techno-economic Analysis.

title: Rational Design of Catalysts Enhanced by Nanoscale Metal-Oxide Interactions
abs: The chemical industry heavily relies on catalysis to increase the energy efficiency of chemical processes, steer them towards more valuable products and/or decrease their environmental impact. Catalysis is also essential in emerging synthetic fuel and biofuel technologies aiming to lower CO2 emissions and to hinder global climate change. However, the current rate of catalyst discovery through tedious laboratory screening of hundreds of materials is insufficient to limit global warming to 2° C. Although the development of new catalysts can be dramatically accelerated using density functional (DFT) simulations in the “rational catalyst design” paradigm, the latter imposes constraints on maximum activity of the obtained catalyst. The proposed research will circumvent the constraints in the computational catalyst design by enhancing the activity of nanostructured catalysts via tailored metal-oxide interactions. Such interactions are known experimentally to be extremely important for the activity of many heterogeneous catalysts that are composed of transition metal nanoparticles on oxide supports or oxide films on metal supports. Removing constraints in the rational catalyst design via metal-oxide interactions will allow us to engineer new catalysts for the most challenging reactions with a transformative effect on the chemical industry and the world. In the developed work packages, we are going to focus on the design of new catalysts for selective methane conversion to methanol or methyl halogenates, which will enable utilization of methane as an abundant feedstock in chemical industry. We will also design new catalysts for thermal or electrochemical N2 reduction to ammonia, which is required in enormous quantities for the production of fertilizers and global food security. The unique expertise of the applicant, the developed research program together with extensive experimental communities working on catalysis and nanotechnology at NUS, NTU, and A*STAR ICES will put Singapore in the leading position in the development of advanced nanostructured catalysts. Computational catalysis is currently strongly underrepresented in Singaporean Universities, despite being able to increase the efficiency of experimental studies dramatically. Moreover, the goals of the proposed research are in line with Singapore’s effort to develop more sustainable chemical technologies. The applicant contributes to this effort by collaborating with multiple experimental groups within Green Energy Flagship program at the National University of Singapore.
kw: DFT, heterogeneous catalysis, nanostructure, metal-oxide interface, methanol, ammonia

title: Membrane development with enhanced boron removal efficiency in pre-treatment, desalination and post-treatment during brackish water desalination
abs: The purpose of this research is to develop materials and membrane technologies for enhanced boron removal during desalination process. Boron is toxic if its amount exceeds the lethal dose. The acceptable boron level set by WHO is 2.4 mg/L for drinking water. In the semiconductor industry, boron is a p-type impurity which will invert the n-type silicon and cause an adverse effect on the concentration of carriers. Ultrapure water with boron concentration less than 0.05 µg/L has been required for the semiconductor industry in certain countries. Boron removal is challenging because of its small size and fast diffusion rate. Boron in the form of boric acid (B(OH)3 or H3BO3), cannot be easily removed by conventional treatments. Membrane technology is one of potential solutions; however, its removal efficiency still remains a challenge. At neutral pH, boric acid tends to form hydrogen bonds with membranes. Thus, commercial brackish water reverse osmosis (BWRO) membranes are ineffective to remove neutral boron with rejection ratios less than 65%, while seawater reverse osmosis (SWRO) can achieve a better rejection rate of 90%. Some RO processes are modified by multi-step approaches at evaluated pH or with the aid of boron selective resins. Therefore, advances in adsorbent and membrane technologies for boron removal are essential to provide clean water for the public and semiconductor industry. Two approaches are proposed in this proposal to remove boron: (1) develop novel polymers and ultra-filtration (UF) or nano-filtration (NF) hollow fibers for RO pre-treatment and post-treatment with a boron sorption capacity comparable to and greater than that of commercially available resins (i.e., 1-2 mmol/g); (2) design novel RO membranes with dual separation functions for seawater desalination and boron removal to lower the overall energy consumption.
