title: Confinement Mechanobiology: A New Paradigm for Spatiotemporally Controlling Stem Cell Differentiation
abs: Stem cells move through physically confining microenvironments during development, regeneration and repair; thus, confinement is a valuable tool to understand and control the mechanisms involved in differentiation. Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) originate in distinct niches and are capable of directed migration towards sites of inflammation and regeneration. Due to their ability to differentiate towards multiple tissue lineages as a function of the mechanical properties of their surroundings, a number of tissue engineering strategies have focused on providing defined physical microenvironment cues to better understand and control stem cell behavior. Intravital microscopy has revealed that cells migrating in living organisms modulate their migration strategy in order to navigate tight spaces in the ECM. Microchannel-based confinement tools have been used to elucidate the processes underlying immune cell infiltration, cancer invasion, and morphogenesis. While in vivo microscopy has identified long, fluid-filled tracks in the interstitium of several tissues, little is known about which cells migrate through these tight spaces, how they navigate through them, and how this confinement influences their behavior. Furthermore, although fluorescent labeling studies have proven that stem cells are capable of long migratory journeys through multiple tissue layers, the impact of confinement during stem cell migration and subsequent differentiation has not been examined. Currently, a major barrier to controlling stem cell differentiation in vitro is the lack of well-defined microfluidic tools capable of mimicking the mechanical confinements in vivo, in part due to a lack of characterization of these environments in healthy and diseased tissue. To address this barrier, we will design novel, biomimetic microchannel confinement systems informed by measurements of the interstitial spaces in native tissue samples. We will then implement these systems to control the mechanical microenvironment of MSCs and thereby elicit mechanosensitive differentiation. The feasibility of our proposed confinement-based differentiation system is supported by our preliminary data showing, for the first time, that stem cell differentiation towards a specific lineage is enhanced in cells that have migrated through confining microchannels. Our approach has the potential to change the paradigm of stem cell differentiation in vitro and open up new translational approaches for differentiated cell purification and tissue assembly. Based on my experience in both mechanosensitive stem cell differentiation and confined cell migration, as well as the demonstrated field-specific expertise at the Mechanobiology Institute at the National University of Singapore, I believe that we are uniquely suited to accomplish these goals.
kw: stem cells; differentiation; mechanobiology; biomaterials; microfluidics; confinement

title: Defining a bidirectional liver-brain axis in metabolic regulation.
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Maintaining energy homeostasis requires accurate sensing of incoming nutritional substrates and internal metabolic demands, coupled with mechanisms to direct and utilize available resources. As a gateway between the gastrointestinal tract and the body, and also as a metabolizer and store of fuels such as glycogen and lipids, the mammalian liver is uniquely positioned to act as both metabolic sensor and effector. Yet, the liver does not act in isolation and its functions are tightly regulated by the brain through innervation by both branches of the autonomic nervous system. Indeed, hepatic branch vagotomy, which severs nerve communication with the brain, can lead to metabolic dysfunction and physiological changes like reduced food intake and impaired liver regeneration. The bidirectional connection between the central nervous system and hepatic neurocircuitry remains largely undefined, and presents a novel avenue for discovery of targets to manage diseases like obesity and diabetes. This proposal aims to define neural pathways underlying metabolic regulation between the liver and the brain at the molecular, anatomical and functional level. The integrity and alterations of these circuits in mouse models of diet-induced obesity and metabolic syndrome will also be explored. This study will further our understanding of brain communication with peripheral organs and lead to novel strategies for managing metabolic diseases.
kw: Neuroscience; metabolic regulation; hepatic neurobiology

title: Controlling Electrocatalytic Carbon Dioxide Reduction: Towards Sustainable Fuels and Chemicals Production
abs: Electrocatalytic carbon dioxide reduction (ECO2R) has been well recognized as a promising technology for achieving negative carbon emissions. Extensive research efforts have been spent on studying the surface chemistry of ECO2R, predominantly on investigating the intrinsic properties of the electrocatalyst. However, the micro-environments round the catalysts often steer the overall catalytic performance of ECO2R, and fundamental understandings of the interactions between micro-environments and electrocatalysts are still underdeveloped. Here, we propose novel approaches to bridge the intrinsic properties of electrocatalysts to reaction micro-environments (e.g., boundary conditions, pH, electric field, cation, ionomer & membrane, temperature), and further maximize the efficiencies for ECO2R. We will tackle this research challenge at three different scales: interface (molecular) scale, diffusion(micrometer) scale and device scale. At the interface scale, the goal is to establish fundamental understandings of the reaction pathways, kinetics and key intermediates of ECO2R, and to understand how they interact with different reaction micro-environments. At the diffusion scale, sophisticate multi-scale modelling will be built up by introducing electrocatalysts with templated morphology and electrochemical cells with controllable boundary conditions. The goal is to understand how the mass transportation and boundary conditions affect the ECO2R. Finally, at the device scale, a two-step cascade strategy will be used to maximize the CO2 conversion into fuels and chemicals (e.g. ethylene and ethanol). A dynamic feedback loop among materials discovery, kinetic & mechanistic studies, and device design & optimization will be strategically implemented to the whole research, with a focus on understanding the relations between the catalytic performance and the reaction micro-environment in a scale-up configuration. Ambitious and achievable milestones have been set to ensure the success of this research project (see details in the attached proposal). Overall, the proposed research can establish effective design principles for both catalyst and reactor-system for ECO2R. Moreover, the new understandings and insights can be well extended to other electrocatalytic applications, e.g. water splitting to produce hydrogen, oxygen reduction in fuel cell and nitrogen reduction to produce ammonia.
kw: Carbon dioxide reduction, Renewable energy, Electrocatalysis, Fuels and Chemicals, Energy Storage

title: Constructing Event-level Narrative Intelligence from the Ground Up
abs: I propose to develop Artificial Intelligence techniques that achieve narrative intelligence by gradually layering up semantic understanding of simple concepts. Specifically, I will investigate the understanding of a key component of narratives, events and their relations, by jointly utilizing visual and textual media. Previous work aimed that focused on a single modality often faces ambiguity that cannot be resolved from a single modality. For instance, from the sentence “I am looking at a girl with a telescope”, it is impossible to determine who possesses the telescope. Such ambiguity can be resolved from joint modeling of both visual and textual information. In this work, event understanding will be achieved by discovering concepts from representations learned, including story character tracking and reidentification, unsupervised textual semantic role labeling, unsupervised visual action recognition, and visual-textual alignment. Although these tasks have been extensively studied in isolation, little work has explored their connections. By demonstrating that complex semantic concepts can be constructed from simple building blocks, the proposed work has the potential to impact how the scientific community think about and approach general-purpose Artificial Intelligence.
kw: artificial intelligence, machine learning, narrative intelligence

title: Theoretical and Numerical Study of Topological Materials for Applications in Next-Generation Quantum Technologies
abs: The broad objective of the proposed research is to theoretically and numerically study new topological phases and search for related quantum materials for applications in next-generation quantum technologies. Topological phases have opened a new era in condensed matter physics and materials science. These quantum materials are exotic from the perspective of both fundamental physics and practical applications. From the point of view of fundamental interest, topological quantum phases can realize fundamental particles as quasiparticles, such as Dirac, Weyl, and Majorana fermions. On the applied side, the topological insulators with back-scattering-forbidden spin-polarized surface states can be used as high-performance spintronics at low cost. Topological superconductors hosting Majorana fermions are a promising approach towards quantum computation. Despite the tremendous progress, known topological quantum materials have been mainly limited to weakly-interacting single crystals. Moreover, proposed applications usually require extremely low temperatures. This proposal aims to make topological materials applicable to room-temperature next-generation quantum technologies by predictive band theory and realistic simulations of topological quantum materials. The topological band theory combined with predictive numerical calculations is a powerful tool in the field of quantum matter. I propose to theoretically and numerically study new topological phases and related material candidates in low-dimensional materials, superconductors, magnets, and other correlated systems. The objective of the proposed research is to search for new topological phases in real materials and study their striking field (electric, magnetic, and optical) responses to pave the way for further applications. A comprehensive topological quantum materials database of electronic structures and related magnetic and optical responses will be built during this process. This materials database will also be helpful for both theorists and experimentalists in physics, materials science, and engineering.

title:
Thermoelectric Materials by Design: 
Understanding and Extrapolating from Non-Equilibrium Charge and Heat Transport
abs: With climate change and temperatures rising across the globe, there is a pressing need for renewable sources of energy. Photovoltaics and wind energy are options for energy harvesting, while batteries can provide energy storage. However, there are still large industrial processes that operate at high temperatures such as metal, glass, cement and ceramic manufacturing industries and boiler feedwater plants. While heat exchangers and large-scale thermodynamic cycles work well for temperatures larger than 200 deg C, there are no viable solutions for low grade waste heat (T<200 deg C). On the other hand, with 60% of the world’s population living in the tropical belts and only 7% of the population having access to air-conditioning in countries like India, Brazil and Nigeria, the demand for cooling is going to rise up exponentially. The need of the hour is for innovation in technology that can convert heat to power and vice versa. Thermoelectrics are solid state devices, with non-moving parts that can do exactly this, however they suffer from low efficiencies. In order to make thermoelectric technology feasible an efficiency of >10% for waste heat recovery and refrigeration coefficient-of-performance >2 needs to become possible. This a materials challenge, since the efficiency is directly proportional to the figure of merit ZT. To achieve such high efficiencies, the ZT has to approach 2 at T< 200 deg C. Apart from its technological relevance, thermoelectric materials are scientifically extremely interesting and stubbornly difficult to discover. This is because the ZT is defined by a complex interplay of charges and lattice vibrations (phonons). Designing thermoelectric materials requires the ability to manipulate quasiparticles outside of thermodynamic equilibrium when driven by an external temperature field. Much progress has been made in the last few decades by designing material parameters such as bandstructure, phonon engineering and hierarchical nanostructuring to allow charges to move but impede heat: ZT of materials at T>600K has reached values as high as 2.8. In this proposal, I intend to realize similar improvement at lower temperatures, arising from the manipulation of energy-dependent inequilibrium charge and phonon scattering times and inorganic crystal design by building ternary and quaternary alkali- and transition metal-based chalco/halogens with large atomic mismatch, therefore enhancing the powerfactor and reducing the lattice thermal conductivity. The field has thus far focused on “experimentally accessible” parameters and high-T ZT optimization, instead of the parameters that will get us to ZT ≥ 2 at T < 500K. A general framework that addresses quasiparticle scattering times in low bandgap semiconductors will be developed in this proposal. title: You Are What You Eat: Gene-Diet Interactions Regulating Appetite and Food Choice
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Obesity, eating- and metabolic disorders are rising worldwide problems with serious socioeconomic consequences, and stem from complex interactions between our genetic makeup, microbiome, and dietary intake. A fundamental understanding of how each of these factors influences our food choices and consumption, as well as other aspects of behaviour, will be necessary to develop effective interventions and therapeutics for these diseases. The zebrafish is a translational model which shares conserved physiology with mammals and is amenable to high-throughput experimental discovery. I previously used this model to identify new circuit principles for appetite and behavioural control. More recently, I have found that both the palatability and macronutrient content of food can significantly modulate food intake, food choice, and other behaviours in zebrafish, in similar ways as reported in humans. Here, I will continue to leverage the zebrafish system to develop a comprehensive and generalisable gut-brain circuit model of how genetic and dietary factors interact to influence food consumption and feeding decisions, which will inform the treatment of obesity, eating- and metabolic disorders. I will achieve this goal through the following aims: Aim 1: Behavioural and pharmacological interrogation of dietary phenotypes Using high-throughput dietary and pharmacological manipulation of behaviour, including novel machine learning-driven methods, we will systematically dissect the influence of sensory and macronutrient properties of food on zebrafish feeding behaviour and decisions, and further identify molecular mechanisms and therapeutics that can modulate these effects, including gut microbes and metabolites. Collaborators will include Katheline Hua (aquaculture nutrition), Cheng Li & Hwee Kuan Lee (machine learning and data analysis), and Suresh Jesuthasan (zebrafish behavioural neuroscience). Aim 2: Multi-modal mapping of neural circuits underlying dietary phenotypes Using brain (and gut)-wide optical imaging, single-cell transcriptomic and circuit manipulation techniques, we will dissect the neural circuits underlying identified dietary phenotypes. The end product will be a comprehensive molecular-circuit model for appetite control that links sensory and dietary inputs to gut-brain and behavioural state changes. Collaborators will include Suresh Jesuthasan (zebrafish behavioural neuroscience) and Shyam Prabakhar (single-cell transcriptomics). title: Conversations for life: Laying the groundwork for more effective communication in palliative care
abs: Despite the rapidly ageing population and the increasing number of people suffering from terminal illnesses, there is a lack of good quality communication on the topic of death and palliative care options in Singapore. This contributes to the uncertainty of patients and caregivers in the end-of-life process, intensifying negative emotions and paralyzing the decision-making process. Additionally, with the shortage of palliative care specialists in Singapore, equipping other healthcare professionals with skills in palliative care communication has become even more urgent. This research, therefore, aims to conduct an empirically driven assessment of the information environment caregivers in Singapore are exposed to; as well as address the informational and communication barriers that inhibit stakeholders in their decision-making processes for end-of-life care. We plan to pursue a thorough examination of available online resources for end-of-life care. Following which, two large-scale surveys will be administered to understand the information needs, challenges, and gaps among caregivers and healthcare professionals. Based on the insights gained from these two studies, a preliminary set of recommendations and communication guidelines will be developed for health organizations and caregivers/patients. These guidelines will then be comprehensively reviewed and improved through focus group discussions with healthcare professionals and caregivers. Communication is central to the interface between palliative care professionals, caregivers, and patients. By laying this foundation of understanding of the intricacies of religion, race, culture, and other personal beliefs in the journey of end-of-life care, we hope to facilitate the efficacious development of more relevant, concrete training programs; and provide information on palliative communication for healthcare professionals to cultivate a more compassionate and sensitive image of end-of-life care in Singapore. Essentially, our research findings will culminate in a tool for guiding families facing end-of-life decisions through important considerations that will bring less uncertainty and greater peace of mind.
kw: Palliative care; healthcare professionals; caregivers; information; communication guidelines

title: The Role of Caveolin-1 in Inner Retina Neurovascular Coupling in Experimental  Glaucoma
abs: Glaucoma is a leading cause of blindness worldwide. Problems with the blood supply to retinal ganglion cells (RGCs), which are the predominant cell type affected by glaucoma, may predispose to glaucoma. Genome-wide association studies have identified mutations in the Caveolin-1 (Cav-1) gene as an important risk factor for glaucoma. Cav-1 protein, the gene product from the Cav-1 gene, is abundantly expressed in the retina where many neuronal and vascular cells reside, although the role of caveolin-1 in mediating neuronal and vascular interactions in the eye is presently unclear. Specific Aims: 1. To evaluate how the inner retinal neurovascular response in Cav-1 -/- and -/+ mice differs from wild type (WT). 2. To determine if Cav-1 -/- and -/+ mice suffer greater RGC damage from experimental glaucoma, in comparison with WT. 3. To evaluate if intraocular application of caveolin-1 scaffolding domain peptide Cavtratin restores the inner retinal neurovascular response and alleviates RGC damage arising from experimental glaucoma. Hypotheses: Deletion of the Cav-1 gene results in a decreased inner retinal neurovascular response and greater RGC susceptibility to experimental glaucoma. Methodology: Eyes of WT C57/Bl6 and Cav-1 knockout (-/- and +/-) mice will be subjected to light flicker stimulus. Changes in blood vessel diameter and glial calcium signalling will be assessed in vivo, before and after experimentally inducing glaucoma. Markers of RGC injury such as optical coherence tomography and immunohistochemistry will be used to determine the extent of damage from experimental glaucoma, comparing WT and cav-1 knockout mice. Cav-1 scaffolding domain peptide cavtratin will be applied intraocularly, to determine if this alleviates neurovascular dysfunction and protects RGCs following experimental glaucoma. Importance: Developing treatments that are able to restore or alleviate dysfunctional interactions between neurons, glia and blood vessels would augment the current range of available drugs, and potentially preserve vision for more patients

title: Determining the differences in hepatic insulin resistance in Indian and Chinese men
abs: Insulin resistance (IR) describes the impaired action of insulin in maintaining blood glucose and correlates closely with the severity of obesity. Obesity is commonly measured as the body mass index (BMI). Indians have greater IR compared to Chinese individuals with similar BMI. This difference also appears to be more pronounced in the non-obese BMI. However, percentage body fat may be underestimated in Indian individuals with the same non-obese BMI as other ethnicities. In addition to the ethnic differences in body composition, the severity of IR may also be different at peripheral and hepatic tissues. Previously, we found that when both BMI and percentage body fat were matched, non-obese Indian and Chinese men had similar peripheral insulin sensitivity with a standard insulin infusion that completely suppressed hepatic glucose production. Blood insulin concentrations were higher in subjects of Indian ethnicity suggesting that insulin clearance is impaired in Indian individuals. The question of whether there is a difference in hepatic IR is still not known. Assessing hepatic IR requires measurement of endogenous hepatic glucose production during a clamp study with low-dose insulin infusion. We hypothesize that the rate of hepatic glucose production is higher in Indians than in Chinese and that insulin clearance is lower in Indians than in Chinese. We aim to do this by performing a 2-stepped hyperinsulinaemic-euglycaemic clamp with the use of an IV somatostatin pancreatic clamp and the use of glucose tracer isotopes. If we can determine whether IR in Asian Indians is affected at the peripheral or hepatic tissues, we can better understand why certain ethnicities are more predisposed to developing metabolic disorders and we can develop diabetes prevention and treatment strategies that are directed towards the specific metabolic defect(s).
kw: Diabetes mellitus; insulin resistance; hepatic glucose production; insulin clearance

title: War on Diabetes: a policy narrative. The case of Singapore.
abs: In April 2016, the Singapore Ministry of Health (MOH) declared War on Diabetes to rally a whole-of-nation effort to reduce the burden of diabetes in the population and to keep Singaporeans healthy as they age (MOH, 2017a). This declaration of War on Diabetes in Singapore is positioned as a whole-of-nation, whole-of-society effort (MOH, 2017b), and it constitutes a form of policy narrative. Policy narrative views “the policy world through a social construction lens, embracing the notion that policy problems and the whole policy process strongly depend on the meanings attached to them by the actors involved” (Jones and Radaelli, 2015, p. 341). While the efforts and a slew of approaches have been implemented in tandem to tackle the issue of diabetes, it remains unclear how the notion of War on Diabetes, as a policy narrative, has been positioned to bring about changes in its population, and what the challenges associated in the public policy process are. This study seeks to explore the extent to which the ‘War on Diabetes’ can be explained by ideas of narrative policy framework, and it aims to draw implications from its analyses through a qualitative approach. The study design consists of interviews with relevant policy actors and the general public to explore the roles and influences of policy narratives in the War on Diabetes policy process.
kw: diabetes; policy narrative; policy research; health and social care; health policy

title: Mind Matters: A Study of Mental Health Literacy 2020
abs: The current study aims to conduct a national survey to assess the recognition of the condition (diagnoses) and beliefs of the causes, treatment, and outcomes for alcohol abuse, dementia, gambling disorder, depression with and without suicidal ideation, obsessive-compulsive disorder and schizophrenia in Singapore. This cross-sectional study of Singapore Citizens and Permanent Residents aged 18-65 will use a vignette- based approach to determine the level of mental health literacy modeled on the Depression Literacy Questionnaire. The disorders included were chosen after careful deliberation and discussions with various healthcare professionals and policymakers, and guided by the findings of the Singapore Mental Health Study and the Well-being of the Singapore Elderly study. In brief, they were selected on the basis of their prevalence, associated treatment gap, early age of onset, and the loss of quality of life associated with them. While the prevalence of schizophrenia is low in Singapore, it is a particularly devastating and costly disorder causing severe impairment in those affected and affecting society at large. The vignettes will be followed by a series of questions that will establish the level of mental health literacy of the populace. This study will generate actionable knowledge that will: a. Identify and help prioritize mental illnesses to be targeted for mental health promotion. b. Identify the gaps in mental health literacy including deficits in specific areas such as lack of recognition of the signs and symptoms of these disorders and their outcomes, and lack of awareness or misconceptions of the available sources of professional help in the community. c. Track the changes in the level of mental health literacy and stigma over the last 5 years thus providing a measure of the effectiveness of the community mental health programmes and anti-stigma campaigns that have been launched in the interim period between these two studies.

title: Revolutionising the Assessment of Quality of Life in Diabetes Using Item Banking and Computerised Adaptive Testing Systems
abs: Diabetes mellitus (DM) is a global burden with a worldwide prevalence of 8.8%, mostly comprising of Type 2 DM (T2DM), with Singapore having the second highest prevalence of DM (~13%) among developed nations. People with T2DM have an increased risk of developing disabling and life-threatening vascular complications. Understanding the impact of T2DM, its associated complications and the effectiveness of treatment therapies from the patient’s perspective is becoming increasingly important, with many governing authorities mandating the use patient-reported outcomes data to guide and improve clinical management, support medical decision-making, and inform policy decisions in healthcare measures and resource allocation. While several questionnaires exist to measure diabetes-related quality of life (QoL), there are serious psychometric shortcomings with these instruments with issues related to conceptualization, generalizability, validity and responsiveness. Moreover, current DM-specific questionnaires are paper-pencil, and are therefore static, inflexible and burdensome to administer and answer. Fortunately, these problems can be overcome by using item banking (IB) and computer adaptive testing (CAT). An IB is a large pool of questions calibrated for difficulty on the same linear scale based on participant responses and the use of modern psychometric techniques. IBs are operationalized by CAT, which is ‘smart’ technology that adapts the items asked based on participants’ responses to previous items, enabling a precise and reliable assessment while minimizing measurement error and reducing test length. Evidently, a concise, culturally valid and precise instrument that allows a rapid, accurate and comprehensive electronic assessment of the impact of T2DM and its associated complications from the patient’s perspective in Asia is urgently required. The main objective of this project is to develop, validate and implement a novel IB and CAT system for T2DM (DiabCAT) which is able to assess the comprehensive impact of the disease on all relevant QoL domains in Singaporean Chinese, Malays, and Indians.
kw: Diabetes; quality of life; computerized adaptive testing; item banking; patient-reported outcome measures

title: A Dynamical Systems Approach to Deep Learning and its Applications in Science
abs: Despite its empirical success, there lacks a concrete theoretical framework for deep learning. A major roadblock in the development of a mathematical theory of deep learning is the lack of tools to understand how depth, or repeated compositions of layers, affects its effectiveness. This ultimately hinders its expansion to tackle scientific problems where theoretical transparency is essential. This project aims to resolve this issue using a continuum approach, where discrete compositional structures are idealized as continuous time dynamical systems. This allows us to bring in a myriad of tools from continuum analysis, including differential equations, calculus of variations and approximation theory, to solve the pertinent problems faced in deep learning today. I will investigate two complementary theoretical directions, building a theory of deep learning through dynamical systems theory, and a theory of learning dynamical systems from data. Building on the interplay of dynamics and learning, my practical aim is to derive principled deep learning methods for scientific applications, where data naturally come in the form of a dynamical process. This will fundamentally advance our understanding of deep learning and furthermore, expand its influence outside of traditional application domains such as image analysis, natural language processing and game playing.
kw: deep learning; dynamical systems; differential equations; optimal control; materials science; rare events

title: Singapore COVID-19 Vaccine Immune Response and Protection Study (SCOPE)
abs: The SARS-CoV-2 pandemic has caused a global health and economic crisis with an escalating death toll since it started in December 2019. Control strategies have focused so far on preventing/limiting human to human’s interactions and transmission.  However, these approaches are not economically and socially sustainable and the best hope for a return to normalcy is the deployment of effective vaccines. The front runners are two mRNA vaccines developed by BionTech/Pfizer and Moderna that have shown protective efficacy of >95%. Singapore has acquired these two vaccines among others and has started vaccinating frontline healthcare health workers with the Pfizer/Biontech formulation. title: A Network Ecological Approach for COVID-19 Surveillance and Infection Control among Migrant Workers in Singapore
abs: The migrant worker population in Singapore has been disproportionally infected with COVID-19. Majority of migrant workers live in close proximity in dormitories with fellow migrant workers who may work for different employers at different or multiple worksites. However, current research to understand COVID-19 transmissions tended to examine living locations in isolation without adequate attention to the entire ecosystem. We propose to adopt a network ecological approach to study the factors that amplify the spread of COVID-19 among migrant workers. This strategy anchors on two core ideas. First, living locations are inextricably linked to other dormitories, employers, worksites, migrant workers, and the larger community in a complex ecology. A network ecological approach will facilitate a nuanced understanding of risks, channels of transmissions, and how these risks can be mitigated. Second, an approach that amalgamate ideas from different disciplines is critical to represent this complex phenomenon. In other words, an epistemologically and ontologically fluent approach that leverages on the affordances of different concepts, methods, and types of data will allow a multi-model representation and interpretation of COVID-19 outbreak. Different configurations of data provide answers to different research questions. By combining different concepts and modes of analysis, nuanced inferences can be made regarding the dynamics of pathogens, how they spread, what ecological factors matter, and when they matter. We posit the following: • The employer-employee diversity mix and the more central a living location or worksite is, the more likely it would be seeded before CB. • The seeding and extent of subsequent spread at a living location is associated with the size of dormitory, type of dormitory, and centrality of the location in the network. During the CB, we expect the effects of centrality and diversity to be diminished, while we expect other factors (e.g., ensuite/communal, layout examined in RQ2) to play greater roles in the subsequent spread to influence the severity of outbreaks. • We expect to find strains that are more similar to each other to be clustered closer to each other in a network as compared to strains that are more dissimilar.
kw: Network analysis, Ecological diversity, Phylogenetic analysis, Epidemiology, COVID-19, Migrant workers

title: Vaccine communication and messaging:  Addressing COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy and promoting population acceptance
abs: Vaccine hesitancy is a global issue that can affect the spread of diseases. Given the importance of attaining a high rate of COVID-19 vaccination among the population and the release of the COVID-19 vaccine, there is an urgent need for evidence-based strategies for the management of vaccine communication to ensure that health messaging can educate and engage the public to understand the (low) risks and benefits of vaccination. This not only requires strategic communication of health messaging but also the containment of negative (mis)information surrounding the COVID-19 vaccines. This proposal aims to assess attitudes, risk perceptions, and responses to the COVID-19 vaccine and the programmatic rollout in Singapore using four complimentary approaches: 1) Social media surveillance to track online COVID-19 vaccine communication; 2) National surveys with a focus on vulnerable populations to investigate attitudes towards the vaccine; 3) Assessment of healthcare workers to enhance vaccine uptake among patients and investigate confidence in recommending the vaccine; and 4) Human message response experiments to understand messaging and misinformation effects on COVID-19 vaccine uptake. Our findings would provide robust insights to inform both the initial as well as follow-on public messaging strategies, with the aims of increasing the population’s vaccine acceptance and adoption rates throughout various stages of the vaccination programme.
kw: COVID-19 Vaccination, Health Communication, Vaccine Hesitancy

title: Van der Waals High-k Gate Stack in 2D-FET for Energy-Efficient Computing
abs: The continued geometrical and functional scaling of CMOS is driving information processing technology into a broadening spectrum of new applications in big data and IoT. Traditionally, many of these applications are enabled by performance gains and/or increased circuit complexity achieved by classical and equivalent transistor scaling [1]. However, as silicon CMOS is approaching its fundamental physical limit, the exploration of alternative materials and process integration to continue the performance enhancement trend is becoming increasingly non-trivial. This is driving the semiconductor industry in search for new breakthroughs in materials, devices and process technology to enable scaling beyond Moore’s law. Two-dimensional materials (2DM) such as transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) could potentially offer a new pathway owing to their superior material and electrical properties, such as high intrinsic mobility, geometrical scalability, and better electrostatics control over traditional silicon MOSFET technology [2-4]. However, the development of high performance 2D field-effect transistors (2D-FET) is restricted by the challenges in achieving deeply scaled equivalent oxide thickness (EOT < 1 nm) due to the difficulty to grow ultra-thin high-k gate dielectric directly on 2DM channel by atomic layer deposition (ALD). This is primarily attributed to the inert and dangling bond free surfaces of the 2D materials, which impedes the formation of chemical bonds. Although several approaches have been proposed to address this issue, none of them has succeeded in achieving sub-5 nm gate stack integration to date. This proposed research seeks to overcome the challenges by developing an alternative van der Waals (vdW) integration of high-k gate stack to achieve an atomically sharp semiconductor/dielectric interface, leading to carrier transport and drive current performance enhancement in 2D-FET. The vdW integration concept, which relies on pre-fabricating gate stack on an arbitrary substrate and subsequently assembling it on 2D material via polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS)-stamp transfer process, would allow the formation of defect- and pinning-free interface due to the elimination of one-to-one chemical bonds. First, leveraging on the vdW interactions, various high-k dielectrics such as ZrO2 and ferroelectric HfZrOx that have higher dielectric constant even at ultra-scaled thickness (i.e. sub-5 nm) will be screened, which otherwise not achievable using direct deposition technique on 2D material channel. Metal-oxide-semiconductor capacitors (MOSCAPs) will be fabricated on TMDs, including selenide-based (e.g. HfSe2, ZrSe2) 2D semiconductors with high carrier mobility. To date, the experimental demonstration of selenide-based devices is still in the nascent stage, although it was predicted to have superior carrier transport properties than sulfide-based materials [5]. title: Continuous Downstream Purification Platform for High-Value Biopharmaceuticals
abs: Biopharmaceuticals (defined as pharmaceuticals derived from biological sources like microorganisms or animal cells) have revolutionized the treatment of many serious, chronic illnesses, including rheumatoid arthritis, certain cancers and diabetes. Because of the superior specificity and efficacy relative to traditional small-molecule drugs, biopharmaceuticals unsurprisingly account for more than 70% of the revenue generated by the top ten pharmaceuticals. The top-selling is Humira, which is an anti-inflammatory monoclonal antibody that treats arthritis. The growth of the biopharmaceutical market has been explosive in the past three decades, with worldwide sales of monoclonal antibodies alone, which are the dominant class within the biopharmaceutical market, estimated at US$125 billion in 2020. The surging demand for biopharmaceuticals has motivated immense interest in the possibility of employing a wholly continuous processing platform, which is the mainstay for the chemical industries, as opposed to the current practice of batch processing that is less efficient. Specifically, while the upstream bioreactor in the form of perfusion cell culture is well-established, continuous downstream purification processes are uncommon. Continuous downstream purification can not only exploit the economic benefits of cost reduction by 55%, but also the attendant improvement in product quality, as summarized by the Collaborator in two recent perspectives. The current dominant purification method is chromatography, which suffers from low throughput, high cost, and lower product quality. To circumvent these issues, membrane-based filtration is one of the most promising alternative methods. Recent research, including preliminary data by both the PI and Collaborator, has advanced membrane characteristics and process conditions to improve biopharmaceutical purification, but a gap in the knowledge base persists with regards to membrane fouling, which is the progressive accumulation of deposits either within or on the membrane pores that decreases the filtration flux. Compared to batch processing, membrane fouling will be particularly exacerbated by the longer run-times required of continuous processing. Accordingly, a comprehensive understanding of membrane fouling by biopharmaceuticals, coupled with means for mitigation, motivates the proposed research. In membrane-based filtration, membrane fouling is inevitable, which leads to a decrease in efficiency and increase in energy costs to sustain productivity. The understanding of the fouling phenomenon involves addressing the fundamental question of how the foulants interact with the membrane surface and pores. Unsurprisingly, since water treatment largely relies on membrane-filtration, the knowledge base of the mechanisms underlying fouling by various foulants common in water sources (e.g., ions, macromolecules, particulates) is quite comprehensive. title: The chromosomal landscape of genome fusion across replicate natural hybrid zones
abs: The slow and gradual processes of natural and sexual selection are understood to be the primary mechanism leading to biological innovation. However, the recent advent of NGS technology has resulted in a growing realization that some of the most important trait innovations are not necessarily home-grown within a species, but often enter the species’ gene pool abruptly through hybridization and genetic introgression, with prominent examples from many model and non-model organisms, even including humans. Despite these new insights into the importance of hybridization in reshuffling traits and creating novel characters, our knowledge about the process of genome fusion during and after a hybridization event remains in its infancy. The most pressing issue that remains unresolved is whether genome fusion is stochastic or deterministic. Using a whole-genomic approach targeting population samples from across a panel of eight vertebrate model groups in a unique archipelagic setting, we set out to test the following questions: - Is genome fusion in the wake of hybridization a random process in which a hybrid population’s genomic contributions from species A and B cannot be foreseen? - Or does genome fusion follow a trajectory that repeats itself in a predictable manner across replicate hybrid zones? - Is it the same genomic regions that would repeatedly be derived from one parental species versus the other? This project will push the boundaries of current basic knowledge in evolutionary biology by leveraging a rare natural laboratory, the complex Indonesian Archipelago, uniquely allowing us the investigation of multiple replicate hybrid zones involving the same species pairs to test our hypotheses in a natural setting for the first time. We expect that our research will have broad implications for evolutionary biology, adding to the current shift in dogma that points to an underappreciated importance of admixture and introgression in biological trait innovation by extending our horizon of the internal mechanisms of this process.
kw: hybridization; genetic introgression; comparative genomics; genetic admixture; mechanisms of organismic diversification

title: Comprehensive intra-operative assessment of tissue pathology in vivo and ex vivo with high-speed endoscopic microscopy and machine learning
abs: Cancer diagnosis and treatment often require tissue biopsies and resections, which are sent for preparation and microscopic assessment (known as ‘histopathology’), a process that takes days. For organs requiring complex access such as endoscopy, difficulties in tissue sampling are compounded. In vivo optical techniques may be used for imaging regions of interest before excision, and fluorescence microscopy may enable rapid imaging of excised tissue. Real-time visualization that approaches the diagnostic quality and surpasses the speed and coverage of resection histopathology may expedite disease detection and treatment. This proposal aims to develop a comprehensive technology platform for intra-operative optical imaging of tissue before and after excision, alongside powerful machine learning (ML) techniques for enhancing imaging resolution and contrast. Two complementary optical modalities will be leveraged – optical coherence tomography (OCT) for deep imaging of structure and vasculature, and fluorescence microscopy for imaging with nuclear specificity. Recent advances in compact optical scanners, integrated into catheters and tethered capsules, have enabled 2-dimensional scanning for microscopic imaging in vivo. In Aim 1, we will extend the optical resolving power of in vivo OCT devices into the cellular microscopy regime over large fields of view, enabling new pre-clinical studies of tumorigenesis and microvascularization, while yielding insights for clinical early detection. In Aim 2, we will develop fluorescence microscopy and histological techniques for imaging of excised tissue, including staining protocols, compact optical platforms, and computational methods using ML for enhancing resolution of rapid large field imaging. Fluorescence enables meaningful colorization of images to approximate hematoxylin & eosin (H&E) staining, simulating the appearance of histopathology for real-time assessment by pathologists. In Aim 3, we will pursue fluorescence imaging in vivo, by enhancing the nuclear specificity of non-toxic stains with ML, and conceiving an optical fibre-based endoscopic system capable of dual-modality OCT and fluorescence imaging, the ideal in vivo microscopy platform. If successful, this work will pave the way towards a new intra-operative diagnostic pathway, from comprehensive, deep and specific imaging in vivo, to rapid microscopy of excised tissue approaching the appearance of histopathology. This new paradigm of real-time cancer assessment will expedite clinical decisions in the operating room, and bring the practice of pathology closer to patients, potentially achieving more effective screening and cures.
kw: biomedical optics, translational research, applied machine learning

title: Investigation of lower energy consumption for seawater pre-treatment using flat-sheet ceramic membrane with the impact of algae bloom
abs: Ceramic membrane operation for seawater pre-treatment shall be sustainable under negligible impact from algae. Coagulation and direct filtration by ceramic membrane is feasible after the coagulant reduces the fouling potential due to algae and EOM. Therefore, relative operating pressure and energy consumption could be lower than that of polymeric membrane. In the previous study, air scouring was only required during backwash mode and minimally used for ceramic membrane operation and thus overall energy consumption of ceramic membrane system for seawater pre-treatment was relatively low. Net flux as high as 249 LMH was achieved by coagulation and direct filtration in previous study. Due to low operating pressure, ceramic membrane system can also be operated by gravity filtration (without filtration pump). If algae bloom is higher than critical concentration for ceramic membrane operation, enhanced coagulation shall be considered first to reduce the algae and EOM concentration. Coagulation is known to be the most common process in water treatment and plays important role in removing natural organic matter (NOM) and EOM. When algae bloom at high concentration cannot be suppressed by enhanced coagulation, usage of DAF system will be required to reduce the impact of algae bloom on ceramic membrane operation. Impact of algae bloom without using DAF system on operation of ceramic membrane system shall be investigated for better understanding on future design for pre-treatment of seawater desalination system. Suitable cleaning regime and operating condition shall be established. Focus of algae and EOM removal by DAF or different type/dosage of coagulant shall also be investigated initially at lab-scale study. Preliminary study of ceramic membrane performance shall be investigated at lab-scale too. Pilot-scale study at different phases shall be conducted to validate the optimum operating conditions and key findings from the lab-scale study. Newly developed ceramic membrane with improved packing density and surface characteristics will be used in this research study. Evaluation of energy consumption for possible operating conditions will be conducted finally.
kw: Algae bloom, ceramic membrane, direct filtration, energy consumption, seawater pre-treatment

When algae bloom at high concentration cannot be suppressed by enhanced coagulation, usage of DAF system will be required to reduce the impact of algae bloom on ceramic membrane operation. Impact of algae bloom without using DAF system on operation of ceramic membrane system shall be investigated for better understanding on future design for pre-treatment of seawater desalination system. Suitable cleaning regime and operating condition shall be established. Focus of algae and EOM removal by DAF or different type/dosage of coagulant shall also be investigated initially at lab-scale study. Preliminary study of ceramic membrane performance shall be investigated at lab-scale too. Pilot-scale study at different phases shall be conducted to validate the optimum operating conditions and key findings from the lab-scale study. Newly developed ceramic membrane with improved packing density and surface characteristics will be used in this research study. Evaluation of energy consumption for possible operating conditions will be conducted finally.
kw: Algae bloom, ceramic membrane, direct filtration, energy consumption, seawater pre-treatment

title: Integrated Smart Predictive Remote Sensing Technology for Ground Settlement Monitoring
abs: Traditional manual survey on settlement points is labour intensive, time consuming and does not fulfill LTA’s deployment needs during urgent situations e.g. when a potential sinkhole formation is suspected during tunnelling operations. In addition, readings and accuracy of manual surveys are also frequently affected by construction activities which obstructs or disturb settlement markers. Also, manual survey produces only point measurements and is unable to depict a spatial deformation profile of the ground to identify the root of several ground settlement zones. Furthermore, manual survey results are not easily integrated into predictive / analytical IoT technology to enhance productivity and efficiency. Following the proof-of-concept research project titled “Monitoring of Ground Settlement with Remote Sensing”, under the LTA Innovation Fund RE2016-046, it is essential that the processes and analysis be developed into a seamless integrated smart system for settlement monitoring. Apart from simple measurement, this novel system seeks to forecast the final settlement of the ground even before it happens. Such predictive means adopt fundamental engineering principles coupled with IoT platform to capitalise on synergy of resources for intuitive analytics, so as to match or exceed accuracy of time consuming and laborious traditional manual surveying and become the method of choice for settlement monitoring in the near future. In this implementation phase, further field validation trials at selected Cross Island Line (CRL) project sites will be carried out, and a user friendly process developed to measure and report settlement monitoring results. Results would be compared against traditional ground settlement monitoring to ascertain its reliability and efficiency needed to fulfill LTA’s deployment during urgent situations, for example, when a potential sinkhole formation is suspected during tunnelling operations.
kw: Remote sensing, predictive algorithm, IoT, Photogrammetry, LiDAR

title: Climate Crisis and Cultural Loss
abs: This project examines how climate crisis and cultural loss interconnect. It will deploy a research team with transdisciplinary methods to build on emerging environmental jurisprudence in the Pacific region and produce narrative visualisations demonstrating the links between cultural loss and climate change. By combining scholarly knowledge with cultural and artistic practices, the project will develop an innovative framework for addressing the impact of accelerated climate change. Using tools from visual studies and forensic architecture, from ethnography and law, to make scientific evidence on climate change socially robust and impactful, it will also create a relay between local perspectives and knowledge generated in different academic fields. The core objective is the co-production of knowledge that can lead to a changed understanding of environmental justice, which, in turn, will suggest changes in existing legal and policy frameworks. The project hypothesises that a fundamental connection between people and their environments has been lost in contemporary urban contexts, resulting in feelings of indifference towards the climate crisis or unexplained feelings of climate anxiety. Data visualisation and audiovisual presentations of ecological and cultural loss will be instrumental to transform ecological grief and loss into catalysts for climate action. Such narrative visualisations make visible the necessity to re-establish a direct relation between human societies and the environment, especially in the rapidly-changing urban fabric of a metropolis like Singapore. Without such combined knowledge, and dialogue between those at the frontiers of the climate crisis and those in protected urban environments, there is the risk that the gravity and urgency of climate change and cultural loss will not be fully comprehended.
kw: climate crisis; cultural loss; climate action; environmental justice; customary law; data visualisation

title: Big Data and Thick Narratives for Social Science: Study of Political Trust
abs: Qualitative methods in social science research have the power to produce a far more accurate and nuanced picture of public opinion, but are under-used for cost and time reasons. The present project aims to demonstrate that – with the aid of new techniques in computational linguistics and advances in computer processing power – qualitative surveys can be carried out just as quickly and economically as quantitative surveys, and at a greatly reduced cost. This is of particular benefit when analysing subjects that are difficult or impossible to measure using multiple choice approaches, such as identity, trust, democracy, polarization and perception of risk, among others. To show how this can be done, we will produce a detailed breakdown of a concept that is a key factor in political decision-making, but which has proved impossible to accurately interpret and instrumentalise using conventional methods: trust. Using algorithms developed within NUS, we will use open-ended survey data (“thick narratives”) to break the idea of trust down into the various heuristics used by citizens to award or withdraw it (skin-in-the-game, results, qualifications etc.), as defined via linguistic concept maps. These maps can then be used to identify correlations between particular heuristics and political outcomes using historical linguistic corpora, as well as to track current developments using social media. Thus we demonstrate that not only can such concept maps be created as a fast and economical alternative to Likert scores or rankings, they can then be used to track the concept under investigation using social media, thus avoiding the need for costly and time-consuming repeat surveys.
kw: trust;voting behaviour;public opinion;politics

title: Quantitative Design Rules for Developing PET-Based Fluorescent Labels and AIEgens
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: Academic Significance and Hypotheses of the Research: Photoinduced electron transfer (PET) is a fundamental fluorescence quenching mechanism, and has been frequently utilized for developing fluorescence probes. Several theoretical models have been created to aid the rational development of PET-based fluorophores. Nevertheless, these models are either too complicated for practical usage, or are not fully consistent with experimental observations. These limitations lead to slow progress and high cost in searching for novel PET-based fluorescent contrast agents with tailored selectivity and sensitivity, and pose significant constraints on the evolution of advanced bioimaging and medical diagnostic techniques. In this proposed project, we aim to establish one simple theoretical method for predicting the substantial occurrence of photoinduced electron transfer (PET) in organic fluorophores, by a synergetic use of quantum chemical calculations and experimental validations. With the assistance of this prediction method, we aim to design and synthesize PET-based fluorescent labels and AIEgens. We will also explore their bioimaging and biosensing applications. Intellectual Merit: Our work will provide a deep understanding of the structure-property relationship of PET-based fluorophores and renew the current perspective of the PET mechanism. Our work will also offer an effective prediction method for designing PET-based functional fluorophores, and thus accelerate the development of PET probes. Broader Impact: Our research contributes to the transformation of dye chemistry from trial-and-error to molecular engineering. The effective creation of high-performance PET-based fluorophores will expedite the development of biotechnologies, from fundamental research to clinical diagnostics, and facilitate many other applications, such as photocatalysis, photosynthesis, and solar cells. Approaches and Feasibility: (1) We will perform “data mining” in chemical databases and search patterns between molecular structures and quantum yields of PET-based fluorophores and their derivatives. (2) Subsequently, we will rationalize these patterns using both quantum chemical calculations and experimental verifications on representative compounds, thereby generating molecular design rules. (3) Finally, these rational molecular design rules enable us to develop novel fluorescent dyes and sensors with enhanced performance based on the PET mechanism. Specifically, we will develop functionalized wash-free fluorescent labels and AIEgens for bioimaging applications in this project. The effectiveness of this research method has been validated in several of our recent publications: • Discovering twisted intramolecular charge shuttle (TICS), a fluorescence quenching mechanism, using both computational chemistry and experimental validations, and designing a TICS-based glutathione probe (Angew. title: Smart Safe and Robust Motion Control for Multi-Robot Systems
abs: Autonomous mobile robots, such as unmanned aerial vehicles and unmanned ground vehicles, play a key role in industry 4.0. With multiple robots in a system, a multi-robot system, on one hand, can help do labor-consuming tasks, such as completing assemble parts and transportation, cleaning houses, and mowing lawns, in automated manufacturing systems, intelligent warehouses, intelligent transportation systems, household service and so on; on the other hand, can also help do dangerous tasks or tasks that people cannot complete currently, such as search and rescue, humanitarian demining, medical examination and surgical navigation, and underwater exploration. To complete the assigned tasks, each robot should be equipped with an efficient and effective motion controller to avoid any unsafe and insecure situations, e.g., collisions and attacks. Many approaches have been proposed to generate collision-free paths/trajectories for robots. However, due to the dynamic and complex environment, current methods always suffer from high computation load for online planning, leading to low motion efficiency and limiting their wide application in our life. Moreover, current methods usually assume that robots are not at the risk of attacks, and the environment does not exist any adversary. Actually, due to the broad attack surface of robots and environment openness, attacks to robots are common in practice. Hence, this project focuses on smart safe and robust motion control for multi-robot systems against robotic attacks. The targets are threefold: (1) safe motion for each robot is generated efficiently and distributedly in realtime with the aid of machine learning; (2) a compromised robot can continue its motion such that it can move to the desired position as long as its motion functionality can still work correctly; (3) a benign robot can continue its correct motion without the detrimental effects (e.g., collisions and faked communication information) of adversarial robots. First, combined with machine learning technologies and model-based methods, a distributed and efficient planning policy is developed, which can guarantee not only safety preserving but also online computation efficiency. At any time, machine learning models generate high-quality initial motion for each robot so to accelerate the solving procedure of model-based methods (e.g., optimization problems). Second, a robust control policy is developed to guarantee robot motion in case of attacks. If the sensors of a robot are compromised, our proposed algorithms will guarantee the motion of the robot with the cooperation of its neighbors. In case that the control system of a robot is compromised, and the robot becomes an adversary, our proposed algorithms allow benign robots to detect the adversarial one and guarantee their safe motion. Because of smart safe and robust control, a robot can always arrive at the desired position effectively and efficiently in case of attacks. Our objective is to develop

title: Massive, Ultra-Reliable, and Low-Latency Wireless Communications
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: Internet-of-Things (IoT) will connect billions of devices of our everyday life. This will open up new ways to monitor, assist, secure, control with applications ranging from machine-type communications to mission-critical communications in the smart heath care, smart homes, smart factory, autonomous driving, immersive entertainment, and smart city. In fact, massive IoT could change the way we see Internet as a human-to-human interface towards a more general machine-to-machine platform. This interaction includes not just sensing but also simultaneous actuation of numerous connected devices, especially for services with stringent requirements on latency, reliability and availability, e.g. tactile internet. Such tactile services will require ultra-reliable low-latency communications (URLLC) with the reaction time of an object/device be around 1ms since tactile sense is more sensitive to delay compared with auditory and visual senses. In 4G systems, the transmission time interval is 1ms, and the packet loss probability of each link is around 10-3. As such, it cannot satisfy the quality-of-service (QoS) requirements of URLLC. Even though in 5G systems, there are some significant efforts to narrow this gap through the transmit-time interval reduction, processing time reduction, enhanced scheduling schemes, and grant-free access. Nevertheless, the simultaneous provision of low-latency and ultra-reliability with high spectral efficiency and massive connections, which is still very challenging. For instance, to avoid serious traffic accident in a densely populated city like Singapore, huge number autonomous vehicles need to exchange visual and sensing information with extremely low packet loss probability at low-latency at the same time in a single location. In smart factories, massive number of sensors and controllers need to exchange heterogeneous data among each other reliably to make sure there is no accident in an assembly line. Once an emergency event occurs, the controllers need to react to it within a short time. In this proposal, we will develop a framework for guaranteeing both low-latency and ultra-reliability requirements of URLLC in the presence of massive IoT applications. The delay components include transmission delay, queueing delay, access delay, computing delay, backhaul delay, and propagation delay. The overall packet loss come from delay violation due to network congestion, outage of wireless link, and decoding error with short block length channel codes. Therefore, it is important to develop a framework to fundamentally understand low-latency and ultra-reliability design in URLLC as well as establishing different system design trade-offs that can be applied to future mission critical applications. title: Influence of mast cells on antibody quality during dengue virus infection
abs: Mast cells (MCs) are multifunctional immune cells present at the host-environment interface. They modulate immune responses through an array of mediators, surface molecules, and co-stimulatory molecules. MCs are known to influence adaptive immune responses and promote high titer antibody production, but whether they contribute to improving the quality and strength of binding of antibodies is unclear. Affinity maturation is the key process through which antibodies develop increasing affinity for the antigen/pathogen over the course of an immune response and it is critical for generating highly neutralizing antibodies that are capable of clearing infection. Here, we propose that mast cells (MCs) contribute to affinity maturation of antibodies by promoting germinal center (GC) formation during an infection. To test this hypothesis, we will investigate quality of antibodies produced in MC-sufficient and deficient mouse models during infection and determine whether MCs control antibody efficacy through promoting the germinal center response. We will undertake these studies using dengue virus (DENV) as our experimental infection due to its clinical relevance and the unique relationship that antibody quality has on determining outcomes in the context of clinical DENV. During a secondary DENV infection, weakly neutralizing antibodies are associated with an increased risk of immune pathology; thus this model also provides us the opportunity to investigate how MC-driven improvement of the antibody responses can influence functional outcomes of infection, which will be tested in a mouse model of lethal DENV infection. This proposal to investigate the molecular mechanism behind high affinity antibody production during DENV infection and the role of MCs in the process of affinity maturation will generate new scientific knowledge that will be relevant to the goal of improving vaccine efficacies against DENV and other significant viral pathogens.
kw: Mast cell, dengue virus, antibody, antibody-dependent enhancement of infection (ADE)

title: Protein drug target identifications in human malaria parasites
abs: Essentially all antimalarial chemotherapy used currently or in the past was developed by cellular phenotypic screenings and thus is agnostic to the molecular factors of the drug action. Hence, close to nothing is known about the direct protein targets of essentially all antimalarials. This lack of knowledge complicates management of the currently available antimalarial therapy but most importantly impedes any progress in the new drug discovery that is crucially needed for the future of malaria control programs around the world. Here we will employ the newly developed method of Cellular Thermal Shift Assay (CETSA) to identify a set of proteins that have the highest potential to be targeted by chemical agents for new antimalarial drug discovery. Banking on the high information content of the CETSA based assay, we will first explore the basal profile of protein-protein integrations important for growth and development of three species of human malaria parasites, Plasmodium falciparum, P. knowlesi and P. cynomolgi during the blood stage development. Using this as a reference, we will apply CETSA to identify direct protein targets to all clinical antimalarial drugs, hypothesizing their high importance as factors of modes of action of proven chemotherapeutic agents. Next we will identify targets of a set of experimental drug candidates that are publically available as a pert of global effort of malaria elimination. To maximize the information content, the experimental drugs will be selected based on their mode of action diversity that we will analyse using a newly developed high throughput transactional profiling. Biochemical cellar-based studies will be conducted to substantiate the potential of identified proteins as drug targets. Successful completing of these studies will reveal the druggable proteome of the malaria parasites; a well-defined set of protein factors that have the highest potential to serve as antimalarial drug targets for future exploitations

title: Evaluating DP103-PI3K-AKT Axis in Gastric Cancer: Implications for predictive biomarker and targeted therapeutics
abs: Gastric cancer is the second leading cause of cancer mortality and the fourth most common malignancy worldwide. With male preponderance globally, it’s the fifth most common cancer among males in Singapore. Current treatment modalities for GC include endoscopic mucosal resection, gastrectomy along with chemotherapy and radiotherapy to improve the overall survival of GC patients. Despite the advancements in treatment strategies, major limitations towards gastric cancer treatment largely include, lack of prognostic and predictive markers, toxicity at high doses, eventually declining the overall survival rates of gastric cancer patients. The PI3K pathway is mutated and aberrantly activated in gastric cancer and many other cancers and plays a central role in tumor cell proliferation and survival, making it a rational therapeutic target. Until recently, however, results from clinical trials with PI3KCA inhibitors in solid tumors have been largely disappointing. Some of the factors that have limited the success of these agents includes lack of biomarker predictive of clinical response, suboptimal patient selection in trials, and drug-related toxicities. With this in mind and having recently identified a new prognostic and predictive marker in breast cancer (DP103, a DEAD-box RNA helicase), we first show DP103 protein levels are indeed upregulated in gastric cancer and other solid cancers where a relatively high proportion of patients are known to harbor gain of function PI3KCA mutations. Our clinical data showed a positive correlation between expression of DP103 and the PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway associated gene, namely PIK3CA (encodes for p110). To sum up, our preliminary data, we show DP103 physically interacts with PI3KCA to bring about constitutive activation of the PI3K/Akt activity and possibly recruits the PI3K complex to the membrane in gastric cancer. We would further show evidence for possible clinical application from our data showing reduced expression of DP103 decreases PI3K activity and from this study with a better clinical response to PI3K/mTOR inhibitor, NVP-BEZ235. Henceforth, in this study we propose (1) To confirm correlation between DP103 protein expression and PI3K/Akt pathway associated genes in patients’ tissue specimens. (2) Assess the effects of DP103 depletion and overexpression on PI3K/Akt pathway mediated downstream functions in gastric cancer and other cancers (3) Elucidate the molecular mechanism(s) by which DP103 regulates PI3K/Akt pathway in gastric cancer and other cancers (4) To evaluate the role of DP103 in Epstein Barr Virus (EBV)-positive gastric cancer subtype and (5) Demonstrate the role of DP103 in regulating the PI3K/Akt pathway in vivo. In this study, we also propose to examine if DP103-p110 axis regulating PI3K activity is unique to gastric cancer or occurs in other cancers such as breast, ovarian, colorectal and prostate cancers where it is known to have higher percent of patients with gain of function PI3K acti

title: Molecular functions and requisite roles of aldehyde dehydrogenase in T-ALL
abs: Aldehyde dehydrogenases (ALDHs) have been implicated as a stem cell marker both in normal and malignant cells. High level of ALDH activity is observed in hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs). Elevated ALDH activity is also associated with the stemness capability as well as the drug resistance in various cancers. As a notable example, ALDH1A2, one of ALDH family genes, is ectopically expressed in over 50% of T-cell lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL), a hematological malignancy derived from thymic immature T-cells. However, its importance in the T-ALL pathogenesis has not been elucidated yet. In our preliminary study, we demonstrated that the oncogenic transcription factor TAL1 aberrantly induces a specific isoform of ALDH1A2 in T-ALL cells, while normal T-cells do not express this gene. We found that ALDH1A2 has a protective effect from the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS). Additionally, unbiased gene expression and metabolome profiling demonstrated that ALDH1A2 promotes glycolysis and mitochondria respiration, thereby supporting energy production. Thus, high level of ALDH1A2 expression supports the maintenance of T-ALL cells. Importantly, other driver oncogenic pathways including AKT and MYC, which can promote cell proliferation and metabolic processes, are more frequently activated together with ALDH1A2 expression in TAL1-positive T-ALL cases than in TAL1-negative T-ALL cases, suggesting potential collaborative roles. Although activation of these pathways confers a strong growth advantage to leukemia cells, such hyperproliferative and hypermetabolic states often cause intracellular stresses such as ROS, which is toxic to the cells. Hence, we hypothesize that an overexpression of ALDH1A2 may be advantageous for T-ALL cells by promoting metabolic process and also by protecting the cells from stress-induced ROS. This mechanism may serve as a requisite to maintain the hyperproliferative state of T-ALL cells (onco-requisite). We further hypothesize that ALDH1A2 contributes to the stemness capability of leukemia initiating cells. The overall objective of this project is to elucidate molecular mechanisms and requisite roles of ALDH1A2 in the pathogenesis of T-ALL. This proposal is based on the expertise of two

title: Amorphous vs. Crystalline Electrocatalysts for Oxygen Evolution Reaction
abs: Electrocatalysis is a type of catalysis that accelerates the electrochemical reaction occurring on an electrode surface. It plays a critical role in clean and sustainable energy technologies such as fuel cells and electrolyzers. The intrinsic structure of the electrocatalyst determines its performance, i.e. activity, selectivity and stability. Typically, the electrocatalyst is a solid material, which can be arranged in two general ways: a crystalline structure with regular repeating three-dimensional units or an amorphous structure without particular order. Many previous reports have shown that an electrocatalyst with amorphous structure exhibits higher performance than the crystalline counterpart in a reaction, however, opposite results are also observed in another different electrochemical reaction. The origin of this performance gap is still not clear. Moreover, some researchers argue that the bulk phase of the amorphous catalysts can also participate in the reaction together with the catalyst surface while only surface can activate the reaction for crystalline catalysts. However, no direct evidence is shown. In addition, recent studies have shown the original surface structure can change during reaction process. Here come the questions need to be answered in this proposal, (a) What is the origin of the performance gap between amorphous and crystalline electrocatalysts? (b) Why different or even converse results are observed in different electrochemical reactions? (c) Does the bulk phase of the amorphous electrocatalysts participate in the catalytic reaction process? (d) Will the structure of the amorphous catalysts change during reaction process and is the change recoverable after reaction? (e) How to monitor the structure evolution of electrocatalysts during reaction process? To answer these questions, in this proposal, amorphous and crystalline electrocatalysts with same constituents but different arrangement manners will be designed and synthesized. The catalytic performance for oxygen evolution reaction towards electrolyzers will be tested in detail and the structure of the catalysts will be studied firstly by conventional characterization methods. More importantly, the structure evolution or change of the amorphous and crystalline catalysts during reaction process will be comprehensively characterized by various chemical and physical methods such as the pair distribution function (PDF) analysis, isotope labelling experiments, and differential electrochemical mass spectrometry (DEMS) together with a series of in-situ characterizations (IR, Raman, XAS, XPS, and etc.). Density functional theory calculation will be conducted to compare the structure aspect such as model matching degree and performance aspect like catalytic activity trend. It is anticipated that through this project, the above questions can be clarified, and more importantly, the structure evolution process of the electrocatalysts during reaction can be captured in detail.
