title: Understand and mitigate hot cracking in metal additive manufacturing
abs: Some promising superalloys are prone to hot cracking and thus challenging to be additively manufactured. Thus, this project is aimed at elucidating the initiation and early propagation stage of hot cracks at the grain scale in these superalloys fabricated via additive manufacturing. Multi-scale modelling and detailed experimentation will be leveraged to understand and then mitigate hot cracking. The multi-scale modelling will be reproducing the hot cracking incorporating: 1) grain and dendrite growth, 2) local composition variation as well as the resultant low-melting constituents and shrinkage pores, and 3) thermal stress. To validate the simulation and confirm the conclusions, a few experiments will be conducted on an open-architecture selective laser melting system with fully customized parameters. Post-process micro-structural characterizations and residual stress measurement will be performed using cutting-edge techniques, e.g., atom probe tomography analysis of local chemical compositions near the cracks and neutron diffraction measurement of localized residual stress. More excitingly, the collaborator will apply the ultrahigh-speed X-ray imaging at Argonne National Lab to in-situ monitoring of the micro-structure evolution and hot cracking, which looks feasible based on the preliminary study. To explore possible mitigation methods, the multi-scale simulation can not only replace most of the experiments narrowing down the scope, but also attempt some mitigation methods that exceed the current capability of the additive manufacturing machines. (i) intellectual merit: To the best of our knowledge, this will be the first systematic study of hot cracking in metal additive manufacturing using novel multi-scale modelling and cutting-edge experimental techniques. We will achieve comprehensive understanding of hot cracking in metal additive manufacturing, which is currently absent. (ii) broader impact: the thorough understanding and efficient mitigation methods of hot cracking achieved in the proposed work, will greatly facilitate the wide applications of additive manufacturing in producing high-value components of superalloys in aerospace and marine industries.

title: Exploring Spectroscopy of Quantum Degenerate One-Dimensional Electrons and Their Device Applications
abs: 1. Academic significance Materials with the direct realization of 1-Dimensional (1D) electron systems are promising for both fundamental studies, e.g. many body physics, and advanced electronic applications. They behave very differently from those in other dimensions, such as 2D and 3D, which can lead to novel electronic and photonic devices with unprecedented performance in terms of operation speed, compact size and new functionality. In spite of the large number of electrical, optical, and magnetic studies of materials with 1D electron systems in the last decades, most of the predicted exquisite properties of interacting 1D electrons have yet to be observed in these materials due to the lack of single crystal 1D systems and the corresponding probing tools, and some of the reported empirical results remain highly controversial. The main objective of the proposed research is to understand the fundamental properties of quantum degenerate (EF >> kBT) one-dimensional (1-D) electrons in various fabricated single-crystal low-dimensional materials (e.g., carbon nanotubes, InAs nanoribbons, and carbon nanoribbons) using our own developed fabrication method and our own advanced mid-infrared and Terahertz ultrafast spectroscopy tools, and explore their device applications. Excitons in 1D semiconducting systems are expected to act significantly differently from those in other dimensions. In particular, (1) the exciton binding energy becomes infinite in an ideal 1-D electron-hole system. (2) the Sommerfeld factor, the ratio of the exciton continuum to the free electron-hole pair above the band edge, has been predicted to be less than 1 in 1-D systems. (3) unlike ‘conventional’ 1-D metals, the created excitons in semiconductors with metallic behaviour should show unique dephasing and energy relaxation dynamics, the correct understanding of which should provide significant new insight into many-body dynamics on femtosecond time scales. Furthermore, (4) interacting and degenerate 1-D electrons are expected to form an exotic electronic state of matter, the Tomonaga-Luttinger Liquid (TLL). Theoretically, the TLL is one of the most well-characterized many-body electronic states in which electron correlations play a major role. Studying dynamic properties of a TLL would therefore not only be of great interest in their own right, but also provide a paradigm setting to gain insights into the nature of interacting many-electron systems. All these features are highly interesting from both fundamental science and practical application point of view, however, they have not been explored effectively mainly because many of these features in previous studies were obscured due to the many different chiralities present in the low-dimensional material systems. title: Sustainable Cutting of Aerospace Alloys with Mechanochemical Effect
abs: The manufacturing sector is moving towards the implementation of Industry 4.0 and sustainable production systems of the future. One of the key objectives is to eliminate the harmful environmental impact of the manufacturing processes. Currently, governments across the world regulate the use of metalworking fluids (MWF) in machining. The metalworking fluids contribute to over 15-20% of the production cost including disposal of the hazardous chemicals. The conventional MWFs are designed to reduce friction and promote heat dissipation. Significant efforts have been focused on developing environmentally friendly MWF and reducing its usage through improving the performance of MWFs by technology innovation such as minimum quantity lubrication (MQL), nanoparticle enhanced MWFs, etc. However, these new technologies can only partially address the problem; for instance, MQL is based on the atomised MWF droplets supplied by a spray nozzle, which gives rise to a serious health hazard to the operators and fire hazard at the shop floor. In the state-of-the-art machining technologies, the functions of MWF are focused on lubrication at the tool-chip interface and/or cooling of the machining zone; however, the factor of work material property has long been overlooked. Ductile materials, such as copper, low carbon steels, and aerospace-grade aluminium alloys, exhibit excessive plastic deformation during machining leading to excessive heat generation, poor surface finish, and increased power consumption. To date, little attention has been paid to the main source of heat generation due to the work done by plastic deformation in machining processes. In this proposal, an innovative solution will be developed to reduce heat generation in machining by reducing plastic deformation during chip formation. This is accomplished with a surface-active medium to induce a mechanochemical surface effect on the workpiece, which temporarily modifies the surface material properties. The project will encompass the theoretical understanding of the phenomenon with multiscale modelling that is supported with experimental validation, and provide a modern solution of applying the technology in a manufacturing process. Ductile metals (i.e. Cu, Al, Fe) will be studied. Molecular dynamics simulation will first be performed to understand the interaction between surface-active media and the base material at atomistic levels, which includes the change in interatomic energy, lattice spacing, and dislocation dynamics. The modified material properties will be translated to the crystal plasticity finite element method simulations, which is capable of describing experimental findings at its actual length-scale. Micro-tensile/compression experiments along with microcutting tests will be performed to validate the numerical findings on the various metals. title: Resonant Tunneling through 2D and Quasi-2D Interface: Physics and Multi-functional Quantum Tunneling Technology
abs: In recent years, there have been relentless research efforts for developing high performance quantum devices for practical applications such as terahertz (THz) source/detection and multi-valued logic circuits. Resonant tunneling is a quantum process in which electrons or holes tunnel through spatially separated resonant states, formed inside a tunneling layer sandwiched by two barrier layers, at certain energy levels. Electrons or holes with the resonant energy can pass the barriers without being reflected. Among various quantum devices, the quantum devices based on the resonant tunneling have attracted tremendous attention as the best candidate for THz applications including ultra-high speed wireless communications, imaging, and spectroscopy due to its inherently fast carrier transport. However, despite advances in the epitaxial growth of semiconductor layers, it is still difficult to obtain spectrally narrow negative differential resistance (NDR) at room temperature because of carrier scattering originated from interfacial imperfections. Therefore, the realization of semiconductor heterostructures with nearly flawless interfaces has become an essential research topic. Most of the semiconductor quantum well (QW) heterostructures have been realized on lattice-matched substrates by epitaxial growth using metal organic chemical vapor deposition and molecular beam epitaxy. However, interfacial imperfections are not avoidable even by optimizing the growth conditions. It also hinders various combination of semiconductor materials due to stringent requirements such as matches on lattice and thermal expansion of grown layers. This limitation only allows a few material combinations such as GaAs/AlAs, GaN/AlGaN, and SiGe/Si, which result in shallow barrier heights. In addition, incompatibility of mainstream resonant tunneling devices to complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) technology is another major challenge which significantly limits its versatile circuit applications. In this proposal, we aim to address the above-mentioned challenges by developing a completely new hybrid QW heterostructure with pristine interfaces based on unprecedented combination of 2-dimensional (2D) and quasi-2D semiconductors. QWs consist of ultrathin semiconductor layers (i.e., semiconductor wells) sandwiched by barrier layers from which we can observe special properties due to the quantum confinement of charge carriers. These layers, in which both electrons and holes are confined, are typically very thin (10 nm or less) and of high quality to confine excitons (electrons and holes), as well as to avoid unwanted recombination sites. We will develop high quality hybrid QW heterostructures consisting of ultrathin hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) and Si nanomembranes (Si NMs) for quantum barrier and well layers, respectively. title: Visible-Light-Promoted Functional Molecule Synthesis Using Silanes and Silanols
abs: Organosilicon compounds are substances that contain at least one organic group directly bonded to silicon via a silicon-carbon bond. They are an extraordinarily important class of compounds that have found applications throughout all aspects of synthetic molecular, macromolecular, inorganic, coordination, physical chemistry and material science. Organosilicon reagents possess many attractive properties, such as moisture- and air-stable, low toxicity, and are readily available compared with other organometallic reagents, serving as a unique and powerful toolbox for organic synthesis. Silicon polymers range from highly crystalline to amorphous materials, which are normally very soluble in organic solvents, serving as an important class of polymers for material science. Silicon tethers have long provided leverage in organic synthesis as easily installable and removable auxiliaries for a variety of processes. However, omnipresence of organosilanes in synthetic chemistry hides the fact that, except for certain substitution patterns at the silicon atom, their preparation is often far from trivial. The syntheses of organosilicon compounds often involved stoichiometric reactions between prefunctionalized organometallic species and silicon electrophiles, use of expensive and toxic noble metal catalysts, or excess radical initiators. The overarching goal of this proposed research is to develop a general efficient catalytic strategies based on eosin Y photocatalysis for the generation of a valuable organosilane toolbox for organic synthesis and silicon polymer synthesis, enabling compounds otherwise difficult-to-access with existing pathways. Our proposed research highlights nine out of the twelve well-known principles of Green Chemistry. The developed synthetic methods will then be applied to continuous-flow synthesis for the large-scale production of valuable compounds to reach kg/day production. Both the versatility and greenness of the proposed research enable the potential to change the paradigm of the manufacturing of functional silicon compounds. In addition, we propose to achieve a versatile site-selective C-H activation strategy using silanols and silyl alcohols as removable/modifiable auxiliaries via [1,n] intramolecular hydrogen atom transfer (HAT). Site-selective functionalization of ubiquitous C-H bonds is considered the Holy Grail of organic synthesis. In this context, alkoxy radicals derived from alcohols have shown great potential for C-H activation via intramolecular [1,5] HAT or intermolecular HAT. We envision that oxygen radicals derived from silanols and silyl alcohols should possess similar behavior to alkoxy radicals in HAT chemistry. Utilizing silanols and silyl alcohols as removable and modifiable auxiliaries, we plan to realize a versatile site-selective CH activation through modifying the length of the silyl tether. title: Ni-based superconductor - a new family of high-Tc superconductor
abs: Title: Ni-based superconductor – a new family of high-Tc superconductor High-temperature superconductivity (high-Tc), which is a zero-resistance quantum state at a relatively high temperature, is one the most appealing quantum functionalities in material and has potentials in many important applications, such as quantum computation, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and power transportation. However, high-Tc superconductivity is also one of the most mysterious and unknown properties in condensed matter physics. Listed as two of the 125 most important scientific questions announced by the Science magazine in 2005, the questions of “What is the pairing mechanism behind high-temperature superconductivity?” and “Is there a unified theory explaining all correlated electron systems?” remain unsolved till today. The answering of the two important questions is very challenging, because the high-Tc superconductivity is limited to only two families of materials, namely Cu- and Fe-based superconductors. Unfortunately, the Fe-based superconductors, which typically has a toxic As element, are dramatically different from the Cu-based superconductor in terms of stoichiometry, element and structure. In August 2019, Li et al. observed the superconductivity in Nd0.8Sr0.2NiO2 around 9-15 K. Instantly, the new member of the superconductor family, Ni-based superconductor, shocked the condensed matter physics community, because the superconductivity was observed in a material with non-cuprate composition but isostructural to cuprate for the first time over 30 years, and provides a rare insight into the high-Tc superconductivity. We hypothesize that a deeper insight and a road map of high Tc may be achieved by completing the following four initial tasks, namely (i) a higher and more stable Tc by optimizing the fabrication of the Ni-based superconductor, (ii) creation of the first electron-doped Ni-based superconductor, (iii) distinguishing the interplay of electron-hole asymmetry and magnetism, and (iv) the first phase diagram of the Ni-based superconductor. In this project, we aim to contribute to the emerging and urgent topic of Ni-based superconductor from three aspects, namely fabrication, phase diagram and electron/spin modulation, with a purpose of understanding the phenomena and mechanism of the high-Tc superconductivity There are three specific aims in the proposal, and they are: (i) to optimize the growth process to achieve a higher transition temperature of Ni-based superconductor, (ii) to search the unseen electron-doped Ni-based superconductor and identify the phase diagram of the Ni-based superconductivity, and (iii) to investigate the electron-hole asymmetry with magnetic Ni element in the Ni-based superconductivity via ionic liquid gating method. title: Inverse design of radiation-tough high entropy alloys
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: The objective of this proposal is to radically accelerate the development of high entropy alloys, and in particular, identify radiation-tough high entropy alloys for future nuclear fusion reactors. Currently there is no obvious material that can withstand the 14 MeV neutrons, the high gamma ray fluxes, and the 10,000,000 Kelvin plasma that exist in nuclear fusion reactors. It is critical that we discover a material such that nuclear fusion power plants can be developed in time to save our environment from the imminent disastrous consequences of global warming. Recently high entropy alloys composed of W, Ti, Cr, Ta and V have emerged as candidates to contain nuclear fusion plasmas. However, the optimal W-Ti-Cr-Ta-V composition is unknown. A key problem is the enormous composition space for quinary alloys. This deems serial experimentation and density functional theory computation-based search methods orders of magnitude too slow. Therefore, we must completely rethink how to design and optimise alloys in high-dimensional design spaces. The central hypothesis of this proposal is that tough alloys, such as those in the W-Ti-Cr-Ta-V quinary system, can be developed 10,000× faster by combining thin-film combinatorial materials synthesis with high-speed optical techniques to measure the alloy’s elasticity and thermal diffusivity. With the huge amount of data to be revealed by these ultra-rapid techniques, we will not only discover new materials, but also theories, design principles, and property-structure-composition correlations that are related to the complex potential energy landscape of high entropy alloys1. This new academic knowledge will enable new models for the design of new classes of radiation-tough materials for nuclear fusion reactors. We will use co-sputtering to deliberately deposit films with large composition gradients. This means that the composition of a single film will continuously change across the substrate, thus films with different compositions will be grown in parallel at once, rather than sequentially. We will then use transient grating spectroscopy to map the elastic tensor and thermal diffusivity of each material with its composition. The proposed transient grating spectrometer design can measure these properties in seconds with sub-millimetre spatial resolution. We estimate that 10,000 new alloys can be deposited, and then mapped to their thermal diffusivity and elastic tensor within 5 hours. These techniques will be used as a primary screen for promising nuclear fusion plasma containment materials. Materials that pass the primary screen will be exposed to high energy ions to simulate the conditions inside a nuclear fusion reactor. The composition spread samples will be sent to the project collaborator in the Nuclear Science & Engineering department at MIT. title: Mechanism and compartmentalization of CbbQO-type Rubisco activases
abs: Almost all biological carbon dioxide fixation is catalyzed by the enzyme ribulose 1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase (Rubisco). Current problematic increases in atmospheric CO2 concentrations make fundamental research into CO2 assimilation mechanisms a sustainability objective of high priority. In spite of its dominance, Rubisco is a slow catalyst that suffers from a wasteful side reaction with oxygen gas. It also tends to become inhibited by its substrate. Relieving this inhibition requires molecular chaperones known as Rubisco activases (Rca). In recent years we have found that at least three very different Rubisco activase systems have evolved across the tree of life. In plants and red algae, two separate classes of Rca present as hexameric discs that directly remodel the inhibited Rubisco complexes to release the inhibitor. In 2015 we reported the discovery of the third class of Rca, CbbQO, in chemoautotrophic bacteria. This Rca consists of a hexameric cup-shaped particle (CbbQ), and it absolutely requires an adaptor protein CbbO to activate Rubisco. CbbQO Rca-encoding genes are often found associated with gene clusters that encode a bacterial microcompartment, the carboxysome. This Rubisco containing bacterial organelle is surrounded by a protein shell, and enables the manifestation of a powerful carbon dioxide concentrating mechanism. The function of CbbQO in the context of the carboxysome is important for Synthetic Biology projects that want to introduce microbial carbon dioxide concentrating systems into crop plants.In the first objective of this project we will continue our successful structural and biochemical characterization of the CbbQO Rca system in order to develop an ever more accurate mechanistic framework. We will utilize a feedback loop of protein engineering, detailed biochemical assays and cryo-electron microscopy towards delineating the interactions and events that lead to inhibitor release from blocked Rubisco active sites. We will work towards achieving high quality structural models of both the CbbQO complexes in isolation, and when bound to inhibited Rubisco. The most critical target concerns the largely flexible CbbO adaptor protein. Because we are already in a position to achieve high quality maps of the CbbQ hexamer, we aim to alter the conformation of its subunits by binding different nucleotide analogues. Resulting structural snapshots will provide information regarding the force transmission between CbbQ and CbbO. It will also hint at the mechanism by which CbbQ senses the presence of inhibited Rubisco. Critical interactions between Rubisco and CbbQO are transient, and parts of CbbO are flexible. To overcome these difficulties protein engineering approaches will focus on obtaining covalently linked components of the system, utilizing both engineered disulphide bridges and protein fusions. title: Characterization of the roles of the H3K27me3-rich genomic regions as silencers of gene expression in Myeloid Leukemias
abs: Gene transcription is controlled largely by transcription factors that bind to enhancers and promoters to regulate genes. Enhancers distal to genes can loop to gene promoters (“3-dimensional chromatin interactions”). Chromatin interactions tend to be intrachromosomal, and typically have distances less than 1 Mb, and are associated with genome organizing proteins such as CTCF, YY1 and cohesin. Enhancers have been identified in the genome through epigenetic marks such as H3K27ac and H3K4me1. Recently, a new type of genomic element was identified, called “superenhancers”. These are clusters of enhancers, and can strongly activate target genes, can be acquired by cancer cells, and have been identified to be associated with oncogene activation in cancer. Research from my lab has found that superenhancers are highly associated with chromatin interactions. In unpublished work by the lab, we have identified H3K27me3-rich regions (“MRRs”) using a bioinformatics method similar to the identification of superenhancers – MRRs are very long regions of H3K27me3 with very high overall signal strength of H3K27me3. These MRRs show many chromatin interactions (DNA-DNA loops) to gene promoters. In functional testing by CRISPR excising components of MRRs and checking to see the gene expression levels of interacting gene promoters, we have found upregulation of some of these genes, suggesting that MRRs can be involved in silencing. Here we wish to characterize H3K27me3-rich genomic regions as a novel class of genomic elements, and understand their functional significance in cellular regulation. Our overall hypothesis is that H3K27me3-rich regions are distinct genomic elements that are gained in myeloid leukemias and help to maintain the cancer state through control of gene silencing. Here in this grant, our first aim is to understand which H3K27me3-rich regions are gained and lost in myeloid leukemias, their interplay with chromatin loops, and how they respond to EZH2 inhibition. We will characterize how MRRs and MRR-associated chromatin interactions are altered in response to EZH2 depletion. EZH2 is a catalytic subunit of the polycomb repressor 2 complex that deposits H3K27me3 in the genome, and is targeted by several inhibitors some of which are in clinical trials for the treatment of blood cancers. We will characterize how EZH2 depletion leads to altered MRRs, superenhancers, altered chromatin interactions, and altered transcriptional consequences. Our second aim is to characterize the functional roles and mechanisms of functioning of components of H3K27me3-rich regions at target genes in myeloid leukemia (examples of target genes include FGF18 and IGF2, which are two target genes selected from preliminary studies). We will explore whether the constituents of an MRR can work together in a synergistic manner to silence genes. title: Multi-functional and low-cost ophthalmic optical coherence tomography
abs: Throughout the world, eye diseases are a major healthcare burden. In Singapore, tremendous resources and efforts have been invested in the development of diagnostic tools and therapeutic approaches for eye diseases. However, Singapore currently lacks the ability to manufacture optical coherence tomography (OCT) devices, which are essential non-invasive tools for routine ophthalmology research. Thus, we are wholly reliant on external manufacturers for our clinical and research needs, which is far less efficient and cost-effective than having our own research and development hardware capabilities. In addition, there is a need for new-generation OCT with advanced functional imaging modalities, such as polarization-sensitive imaging and speckle-free imaging, as these will enhance our understanding of ophthalmic disease mechanisms, and enable improved evaluation of therapeutic strategies and diagnostic efficacy. It is also desirable that such high-performance devices can be realized via simplified and cost-efficient development. Consequently, our primary objective is to develop a novel, low-cost, multifunctional OCT system that is capable of polarization-sensitive local birefringence and speckle-free imaging. This main objective will be achieved through the following specific aims. Aim 1: Develop a single-detector polarization-sensitive OCT (PS-OCT) which enables local birefringence imaging using the mirror state constraint. We will use the mirror state constraint, a patent pending technology developed by our group, to construct the first ever single-detector PS-OCT that is capable of measuring local birefringence. The existing solutions to the local birefringence measurement require two orthogonal polarization detectors and rather complicated system constructions. Saving one detector and simplification of the system will greatly reduce the bill of materials (BOM) and the manufacturing costs. In addition, we will employ a novel 1-micrometer centre-wavelength low-cost light source, a high-efficiency low-cost spectrometer, and spectrally encoded extended source (SEES) spectral-domain OCT (SD-OCT) technology to enhance the system sensitivity and the penetration depth. All of these devices/technologies were solely developed or co-developed by the PI group. Aim 2: Integrate an ultrafast speckle-modulation unit to PS-OCT developed in Aim 1 to realize video rate speckle-free imaging. Speckles are the primary noise source in OCT images which is a standing fundamental problem that limits the diagnostic accuracy. The proposed method will eliminate the speed issue of the current speckle modulating technique by improving speckle modulation speed by ~4 order of magnitude. Our method will enable reliable video-rate speckle-free imaging for the first time to the best of our knowledge. title: Developing a protease-substrate tracking tool for determining altered protease landscape in cancer
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Proteolytic processing is an irreversible post-translational modification that generates cleaved proteins with altered biological functions. With the neo-proteins regulating a wide array of physiological processes, proteases have begun to be recognized as key signaling modulators distinct from their traditional view of protein degrading enzymes. Despite their deregulations being associated with several pathologies, exploitation of protease-based therapeutics has so far been limited compared to the widely popular kinase-based therapies, especially in cancer. Decoding altered protease activities and their physiological substrates has remained a major challenge in protease research, and this has precluded our understanding of complex protease-substrate networks in many diseases, limiting their broader clinical utility. To this end, we propose to build a strategic pipeline to extract proteolytic information and track protease substrates from complex biological systems by leveraging on massive peptide quantitation data obtained from mass spectrometry experiments. The proposed protease-substrate tracking tool deconvolutes differences in peptide distribution and quantification patterns to track proteolytic events and potential substrates that can ultimately be used to determine altered protease landscape in any biological context. The developed substrate tracking tool will be used to mine proteolytic patterns within breast cancer, a highly heterogeneous disease with aggressive subtypes, to uncover subtype-specific intricacies that can potentially be explored for novel protease-based therapies. In all, the proposed protease-substrate tracking platform offers new perspectives on protease-substrate machinery and holds great promise for exploring protease activity towards next-generation diagnostics and precision therapeutics in cancer and other diseases.
kw: Protease, proteomics, mass spectrometry, substrates, proteolytic processing, cancer

title: Microfluidic Droplet-Based High-Throughput Functional Screening of Single B Cells for Monoclonal Antibody Discovery
abs: Monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) are rapidly emerging biopharmaceutical candidates for therapeutics. However, discovery of new efficacious mAbs is hampered by the inability of current assays and technologies to directly screen mAbs for their functions at high-throughput. This proposal addresses this gap by developing a microfluidic droplet-based high-throughput assay for antibody function (neutralization). As a proof-of-principle, we are developing this system to identify potent anti-chikungunya antibodies. Briefly, single B cells are co-encapsulated with fluorescent CHIKV and susceptible cells in 200pl droplets – antibody clones that neutralize CHIKV will prevent CHIKV multiplication, and show low droplet fluorescence relative to non-functional antibody clones, and can thus be sorted out. Specific Aim 1: Complete development of a high-throughput microfluidic assay for anti-chikungunya neutralizing activity of single B cells. The specificity, sensitivity, and throughput of the assay will be optimized using positive controls comprising transfected mAb-secreting cells, with a fluorescent reporter to monitor antibody secretion quantities in the droplet. Separately, the activation of primary murine B cells will be optimized to achieve sufficient antibody secretion per cell to reach assayable concentrations in droplet, while maintaining B cell diversity. Specific Aim 2: Identify mAbs with neutralization function against chikungunya virus (CHIKV) by utilizing the microfluidic neutralization assay, and determine their potency, epitope specificities, and protective efficacy. The microfluidic neutralization assay will be applied to identify anti-CHIKV mAbs from a pool of immune B cells CHIKV-infected mice. The utility of the assay will be evaluated by determining whether the identified anti-CHIKV mAbs recapitulate the diversity and epitope specificities of published mAbs, as well as determining their potency and protective efficacy in a mouse model. Impact: Successful development will demonstrate a proof-of-concept for a platform that can be utilized for rapid discovery of highly functional mAbs to other targets for applications including infectious disease, cancer immunotherapy, and modulation of autoimmunity.
kw: Monoclonal antibodies; microfluidics; droplet; vaccines; chikungunya virus

title: Evolution of human cells following essential gene inactivation
abs: Cancer is the primary cause of death in Singapore. The leading cause of targeted cancer therapy failure is the emergence of drug resistance. One mechanism of resistance involves compensatory mutations that bypass the cell’s dependency on the targeted essential component. It is advantageous to predict these mechanisms before they occur in patients; however, this remains difficult, especially when the drug treatments are not available for testing in research settings. Because genetic deletion mimics pharmacological inactivation of the corresponding proteins, I hypothesize that cells with genetic perturbations to essential cellular components can rewire cellular pathways to resume growth and this can be predictive of resistance mechanisms to drugs targeting the same cellular function. A promising target to test this concept is the essential Nuclear Pore Complex component, NUP58, because 1) nuclear transport has been demonstrated in yeast to be a physiologically plastic pathway, and 2) nuclear transport is a therapeutic target of both drugs in clinical trials and drugs under development lacking resistance mechanism predictions. In order to address this, the gene NUP58 was disrupted in two cancer cell lines and these were screened to identify rare clones able to survive the deleterious perturbation. To determine compensatory adjustments that facilitate improvement of disrupted nuclear transport in these NUP58 knockout cells, exome sequencing, transcriptomics and proteomics have been conducted and these datasets will now be analyzed using new proteogenomics approaches. Preliminary analysis point toward one possible compensatory mechanism involving karyopherin overexpression. I now propose to test, in vitro, if overexpression of karyopherins is a) sufficient, b) required for survival in a NUP58 knockout background, or c) sufficient to confer resistance to nuclear traffic inhibitors. These studies will reveal the flexibility of cellular networks when cells are faced with life-threatening perturbations and will better inform pathways available to cells to resist targeted therapeutics.
kw: nuclear pore complex; targeted cancer therapy; essential gene; drug resistance; adaptation

title: Targeting a novel mutant TP53-BCAR1 complex to inhibit cancer metastasis
abs: Cancer deaths occur predominantly through metastasis when cancer spreads to secondary sites. However, our lack of knowledge in the molecular mechanisms of metastasis limits developing innovative therapeutic strategies and druggable targets. Tumor suppressor TP53 is mutated in 50% of all human cancers. These mutations frequently occur in highly invasive tumors, suggesting that the mutant TP53 protein possess metastatic properties. Compelling evidence from in vivo and in vitro studies revealed that mutant TP53 lost tumor-suppressive functions while acquiring oncogenic or gain-of-function properties. Mutant TP53 may drive tumor invasion and metastasis by interacting with other proteins, however, underlying mechanisms are still unclear. Our preliminary data uncovered a previously unreported nuclear interaction between a mutant form of TP53 (TP53R273H), commonly found in human cancers, and Breast Cancer Anti-estrogen Resistance 1 (BCAR1). We demonstrated that BCAR1 translocates into the nucleus in a SRC family kinases (SFKs)-dependent manner. We found that inhibiting SFKs disrupted both the TP53R273H-BCAR1 complex formation and cancer cell invasion. When we deleted a domain within TP53R273H that binds to BCAR1, we also inhibited cancer cell invasion. These findings suggest that TP53R273H-BCAR1 complexes in the nucleus may possess transcriptional functions to induce genes associated with cancer metastasis. Therefore, we hypothesize that disrupting the TP53R273H-BCAR1 interacting complex can suppress tumor metastasis in vivo. In this current proposal, we aim to test our hypothesis by exploiting a novel combination therapeutic inhibition that targets mutant TP53 expressing tumors in vivo. We will also elucidate the mechanism underlying TP53R273H-BCAR1 complex-mediated tumor invasion, by identifying its target genes and the DNA binding proteins that can recruit this complex to the promoter of target genes. The completion of this study will lead to a patentable combination drug therapy that targets cancer metastasis in patients harboring mutant TP53-expressing tumors.
kw: Mutant TP53; BCAR1; combination inhibition; metastasis

title: Regulation of the tricarboxylic acid cycle by one-carbon metabolism in Epstein-Barr virus-driven transformation
abs: I hypothesize that oncogenic mitochondrial one-carbon metabolism enhances flux through the tricarboxylic acid cycle (TCA) by promoting TCA enzyme expression at the protein level and exploiting the reverse nicotinamide nucleotide transhydrogenase (NNT) reaction to regenerate NADP+. Specific Aims: The proposed research aims to (1) determine if MTHFD2 activity influences TCA cycle flux, (2) to elucidate the mechanism by which MTHFD2 regulates protein expression of key TCA enzymes, namely mitochondrial NADP+-dependent isocitrate dehydrogenase 2 (IDH2) and 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase (OGDH), and (3) investigate the necessity of NNT for NADP+ regeneration. To address these questions, I will employ chemical-genetic approaches to perturb one-carbon metabolism in cell lines derived from B cell malignancies as well as primary B cell cancer biopsies; CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing will be performed to validate the roles of MTHFD2 and NNT in co-regulating TCA flux, and metabolomic analyses will be conducted to study in fine resolution carbon and hydrogen fluxes through the one-carbon and TCA metabolic pathways. The proposed research will enable us to identify new targets that might exhibit synthetic lethality with mitochondrial FOCM inhibitors e.g. enzymes of the TCA cycle and glutaminolysis, DNA checkpoint inhibitors. Because these pathways are fuelled by sugars and amino acids, the knowledge gleaned from these studies may also inform the way we design dietary regimens to slow down tumour progression e.g. serine/glycine restriction together with redox modulators such as metformin. Ultimately, these findings will allow us to develop better drugs and interventions that improve quality of life and increase life years of patients living with cancer.
kw: One-carbon metabolism, Epstein-Barr virus, B cell malignancies, tricarboxylic acid cycle, redox biology

title: The regulation and function of BAXβ, a potent inducer of apoptosis, in cancer.
abs: Evasion of apoptosis is a hallmark of cancer. BAX, a key pro-apoptotic effector among the BCL-2 family of proteins, defines the gateway to apoptosis. Endogenous BAX proteins encoded by two different splicing isoforms of the BAX gene, BAXα and BAXβ, have been demonstrated in human cells. Interestingly, the pro-apoptotic function of these two isoforms is regulated by distinct mechanisms. Baxα exists in latent form and undergoes conformational changes during activation. In contrast, native Baxβ is constitutively active. However, its expression level and hence pro-apoptotic function, is tightly regulated by ubiquitin-mediated degradation. Nonetheless, the molecular regulators of BAXβ function and degradation, and its role in cancer is yet unknown. Our recent analysis of an RNA-seq database reveals that ~45% of a panel of 935 human cancer cell lines preferentially express BAXβ over BAXα. Given that BAXβ is a potent inducer of apoptosis, this suggests that the dysregulation of BAXβ plays an important role in cancer neogenesis. Based on these findings, my central hypothesis is that key regulator(s) of BAXβ is/are dysregulated in many cancers. The overall objective is to determine how BAXβ-mediated apoptosis is circumvented in cancer cells and to identify the regulators of BAXβ protein degradation. I will utilize advanced genome-wide screening technologies, transcriptome analyses, knock-out and overexpression studies to accomplish the overall objective. The rationale is that once the key regulators of BAXβ have been identified, novel strategies to treat cancer by modulating BAXβ pro-apoptotic function will be possible. I plan to test my central hypothesis by pursuing the following three specific aims: Aim 1: Elucidating the role of cytoplasmic RNA exosome complex in regulating BAXβ protein stability and apoptosis. Aim 2: Identification of E3 ubiquitin ligase(s) of BAXβ protein. Aim 3: Addressing the unique molecular determinants of BAXα and BAXβ-mediated apoptosis.
kw: Cell Death; Cancer; Apoptosis

title: Optimal treatment target identification from longitudinal electronic medical records
abs: Aims Electronic medical records contain vast amounts of clinical information, but much of this information remains unused, partly due to the lack of suitable methodology. An area with such a lack is the derivation of optimal target ranges for longitudinal treatments or biomarkers. This project aims to develop statistical methodology tailored to longitudinal treatments and biomarkers that can derive clinical targets in a data-driven manner. Application of the methodology to medical records from Singapore and elsewhere will provide clinical targets that are better informed by the data and therefore can improve patient care. Approach To capture the dependence between longitudinal data and clinical outcomes, we propose a joint model that allows for accurate quantification of data evidence, which is feasible due to recent advances in statistical methodology. We will use Bayesian nonparametric statistics to flexibly capture the heterogeneity in the patient population, allowing for personalized medicine with treatment recommendations specific to patient subgroups. Bayesian decision theory and optimal design will yield data-driven treatment and biomarker target ranges while taking into account what targets are clinically feasible and relevant. Importance The proposal will yield improved clinical targets derived from large amounts of available, but underused, data. For instance, we will derive a more data-driven oxygenation target in the ICU that has a higher potential to lower ICU mortality than existing analyses. The new methodology will also be applied to elucidate other areas of patient care where there is the most need for a better clinical understanding. Lastly, the proposed methodology will be easily applied by other researchers through its distribution via standard statistical software, and its impact will grow with the increasing use of electronic medical records.
kw: Bayesian decision theory; Bayesian optimal design; Electronic medical records; Longitudinal biomarkers; Patient care improvement; Real world evidence

title: Elucidating molecular mechanisms of cellular viral-hijacking to validate known and novel therapy targets
abs: Arboviral diseases are a major public health concern, with an estimated 3 billion people living in vector-infested areas. Evolutionary pressures have shaped virus interaction with a core of essential host factors sufficiently conserved across mammalian and invertebrate hosts to allow efficient viral replication and immune evasion. We previously identified VCP as a highly conserved protein essential for alphavirus replication. We aim to understand the role of VCP interaction with Viperin, an antiviral protein active against Chikungunya virus, and the links with VCP methylation. Indeed, inhibition of VCP methylation is antiviral, and others showed that it had no effect on the normal development and survival of mice, suggesting it as a viable option for antiviral development. In vivo infection of knock-out mice will validate this possibility, while in vitro assays will elucidate the exact mechanism during virus replication. Cell-free based assays of VCP methylation using recombinant proteins will be used to assess the feasibility and scalability of inhibitory compound screening. Chikungunya and closely related alphavirus, O’nyong-nyong, induce a different adaptive immune response in animal models, likely due to hijacking of immune cells. Limitations in the understanding of these interactions reside in technical limitations with omics approaches requiring quasi-total infection to discriminate false-negative and false-positive from background noise. This proposal will use a novel virus-encoded selectable marker to purify infected cells and allow high-quality omics to be performed. Trial experiment on HEK293T cells identified 183 proteins differentially regulated by the two viruses, including the essential Chikungunya host-factor FHL1. Identified host-factor candidates will be evaluated for their role on viral replication and viral immune-cell hijacking. In addition, chimeric viruses will allow identification of the viral proteins involved. This proposal will yield essential knowledge for the development of antiviral targeting essential host factors, a promising avenue of research with lower probability of escape mutants.
kw: Virus ; host-factors ; viral hijacking ; antiviral ; Omics

title: Mammalian embryonic pluripotency: Characterization of a candidate gene linked to monozygotic twinning.
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: With a worldwide incidence of 1 every 330 live births, identical, or monozygotic (MZ), twinning is more common than any other genetic disease. Not contributing to the diversity of the gene pool and evolutionary not favourable, MZ twinning carries severe pregnancy-related risks for the mother and developing children. While no genetic or environmental factors have been associated with MZ twinning, several reports have documented cases of familial MZ twinning. In a Jordanian kindred with a unique form of autosomal dominant inherited monochorionic MZ twinning, we have identified a small secreted peptide hormone, termed ELABELA (ELA), as a prime candidate gene facilitating MZ twinning. Here, we aim to link ELA gain of function to epiblast expansion in the murine blastocyst as a prerequisite for monochorionic MZ twinning. Ela is transcribed in the inner cell mass (ICM) and particularly the epiblast in mouse embryos; and can be detected with our custom antibodies. Preliminary results suggest that treating early mouse embryos with ELA peptide or Ela mRNA leads to an increase of cells in the Sox2+ epiblast. We hypothesize that a high ratio of epiblast-primed cells in the embryo predisposes for splitting of the ICM in the mammalian preimplantation blastocyst, leading to the most common form of monochorionic MZ twinning. Our line of research will lead to a better understanding of the governance of embryonic pluripotency and have major implications for assisted reproductive technologies that have seen a sharp rise of MZ twinning.
kw: monozygotic twinning; embryonic development; systems biology

title: Machine learning to estimate effects of in vitro fertilization and other assisted reproductive technologies on early adolescent cardiometabolic health
inst: IHDP - Institute for Human Development and Potential
abs: Background: The use of assisted reproductive technologies (ART) such as in vitro fertilization (IVF) are increasing in Singapore and globally. There is conflicting evidence for long term effects on obesity, blood pressure, and diabetes. Mechanisms are unknown and may lead to a mixture of favorable and unfavorable traits in adolescence. Hypothesis and significance: We hypothesize that fetal genomic imprinting and placental effects can be detected in alterations of DNA methylation of respective tissues. Analyses of tissue-specific differences may disentangle mediating mechanisms for ART versus underlying parental infertility which may improve clinical decision making. Machine learning can increase analytic efficiency and reduce bias: critical for clinical datasets. Methodology: Study will be conducted in a nationally-representative, prospective mother-child cohort followed over 11 years. 83 ART-conceived children will be compared to 93 spontaneously-conceived children from subfertile couples. Outcomes include height; weight; body fat percentage; blood pressure; endothelial parameters; glucose, insulin, and lipid concentrations. Existing fetal cord tissue, cord blood, and maternal blood DNA methylation profiles will be leveraged and banked placental tissue will be assayed. Specific Aims: (1) Quantify longitudinal associations between ART parameters (e.g. intracytoplasmic sperm injection) and offspring growth and cardiometabolic function. (2) Investigate the mediating roles of fetal- (cord / chorion) and maternal- (blood / decidua) derived tissue DNA methylation to distinguish ART from infertility effects. (3) Derive a prediction model for adolescent growth and cardiometabolic risk incorporating methylation biomarkers. Feasibility: In preliminary analyses, we have found IVF to result in smaller size, lower blood pressure, and more favourable metabolic profile at 6 years (e.g. lower trigylcerides and fasting insulin, and higher HDL). NECAB3 methylation may mediate blood pressure and fresh embryo transfers may account for some of the effects on stature. Importantly, these discoveries were enabled by our machine learning approach which is both less biased and more precise.
kw: IVF; ICSI; blood pressure; diabetes; epigenetics; machine learning

title: Clone Wars: Investigating clonal interactions and their functional contribution to gastric tumorigenesis and development
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Gastric cancer (GC) is associated with high morbidity and mortality in Singapore. It is often diagnosed late and treatment options are limited. Early detection can significantly improve patient outcomes. However, the molecular mechanisms involved in gastric tumorigenesis and the interplay between somatic mutation burdens, clonal competition and expansion, immunity and phenotypic transformation are largely unclear. This is due to the inherent challenges of studying the early stages of tumorigenesis in situ and tracking changes over time. We hypothesize that tumorigenesis is a product of competitive and/or synergistic interactions between different mutant cell/clonal populations. Hence, while a cell can acquire key oncogenic mutations that alter signaling pathways and physiology, its transformation and establishment of clonal dominance are dependent on dynamic interactions with other mutant cells. We propose to employ patient-derived three dimensional (3D) gastric organoids (GO) in co-culture with autologous immune cells in a novel approach to model early events associated with tumor initiation. We will derive GOs from non-cancer patients and introduce key oncogenic mutations common to GC via genome editing. We will then pit different combinations of mutant cell populations against each other in order to 1)map how competitive or synergistic interactions between these cells promote transformation; 2)elucidate common fitness factors that winning clonal populations possess and how these can be harnessed for translation. We will employ high-throughput, high-resolution imaging techniques to track these spatiotemporal interactions in real-time. We will sequence the exome and methylation profiles of winning populations and validate select targets. To this end, we have already generated GOs with immune co-culture and developed CRISPR-mediated barcodes for tracking of clonal populations. Our study will 1)advance our fundamental understanding of tumorigenesis from the standpoint of clonal competition; 2)uncover potential biomarkers for risk stratification based on clonal cell proportions and expression of fitness targets identified in this study.
kw: Gastric Tumorigenesis; Clonal Competition; 3D Organoids; Immune Microenvironment; Genetic Barcodes; (Epi)genome Profiling

title: Investigating the Role of Top-Down Cortical Control in Feeding Behavior and Energy Homeostasis
abs: Obesity is a health epidemic affecting many developed countries. In Singapore, there has been an increase in overweight and obesity rates in children and young adults. This trend can be attributed to the shift towards a sedentary lifestyle of our population, and exacerbated by an increased availability of calorie-dense palatable foods. Obesity causes a myriad of complications such as diabetes, stroke and cardiovascular diseases, therefore highlighting a need to understand neurobiological processes that regulate food consumption. Previous studies have shown that hypothalamic nuclei regulate food intake for survival, and reward pathways play a role in hedonic food intake (eating for pleasure). However, little is known about the role of higher-order brain regions in regulating feeding behavior. Here, we propose to examine the prefrontal cortex, a region mediating cognition and decision-making, and its role in regulating feeding behavior. Our preliminary data shows that a cortical to hypothalamus pathway regulates high fat food intake. When this pathway is attenuated, mice show increased food intake and weight gain. We hypothesize that the prefrontal cortex regulates feeding behavior by projections to the lateral hypothalamic area via a novel neural pathway and dysregulation of this circuit results in weight perturbation, thus elucidating this circuit will reveal potential therapeutic targets in the treatment of obesity. We aim to characterize the cellular identities of brain regions involved using immunohistochemistry assays and electrophysiology properties, followed by molecular circuit-tracing strategies to identify the connections between the cells. Next, we will establish the behavioral effect of attenuating synaptic transmission by examining metabolic characteristics of the mouse model, and manipulating this feeding pathway using a chemogenetic approach. This study will provide important insights into the role of the prefrontal cortex in feeding regulation and the understanding of neurological causes of eating disorders, thus offering better strategies to treat obesity.
kw: Neural Circuits; Obesity; Metabolism

title: Testing a bio-behavioural toolbox designed to promote self-regulatory eating behaviours in childhood
inst: IHDP - Institute for Human Development and Potential
abs: Children who exhibit eating behaviours that suggest a weaker sensitivity to internal hunger and fullness cues are at greater risk of energy overconsumption and unhealthy levels of adiposity. While all children need to learn to correctly identify different appetite sensations and how to respond to them, the bottom-up salience of internal appetite signals may vary across children depending on their interoceptive skills – the ability to ‘sense’ the physiological state of their bodies that can be captured though heart-rate tracking. The objective of the proposed research is to test an ‘Appetite Toolbox’ designed to improve children’s sensitivity to internal appetite cues using the principles of appetite awareness, directed attention and interoception, and apply it within a clinical setting. The toolbox will incorporate a series of stories and practical activities to help children and caregivers practice attending to body signals, and build awareness of and attention to different appetite sensations. Children (6-11 years old; n = 80) who are above the 85 percentile for their sex and age specific BMI will be recruited with their caregivers through the National University Hospital’s Paediatric Weight Management Clinic. We will assess whether the use of the toolbox (relative to control activities) improves short-term self-regulation of energy intake over a two-week intervention period, and whether this is moderated by individual differences in interoceptive abilities at baseline. We will also characterize the feasibility of the toolbox being incorporated into typical meal times at home and within the family, both during the intervention period and after 1 month follow-up. The results will provide new insights into the underlying factors driving differences in children’s eating self-regulation and their malleability during childhood, and the toolbox will have direct application to current weight management practices and inform recommendations for caregivers and children to cultivate their own eating self-regulation skills.
kw: Obesity; Eating Behaviours; Self-regulation; Attention; Toolbox

title: Neural circuitry underlying compulsive-eating behavior
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Eating is orchestrated by complex motivated behaviors including seeking and consumption of food in response to caloric deficiency. The desire to eat is heavily regulated in the brain under normal conditions, disturbances in this behavior can result in pathological eating behaviors such as compulsive eating. Compulsive eating is prevailing in individual suffering from binge eating disorder, bulimia nervosa and obesity. It is unknown how compulsive eating is elicited but the highly obesogenic environments are implicated. Neuroimaging studies revealed maladaptation of decision making and control centers in the brain in individuals suffering from eating disorders. Prefrontal cortex (PFC) is critical in decision making, control and sensing environmental cues. Earlier studies indicated overactive PFC in compulsive behaviors. In addition, a GABAergic subpopulation in zona incerta (ZI-GABA) has been recently reported to be eliciting binge-eating and repetitive behavior in mice. Therefore, we propose here a novel circuitry from PFC to ZI-GABA that mediates compulsive eating behavior. The hypothesis is also based on our preliminary data showing that recurrent activation of ZI-GABA in an environmental context can generate a context-dependent eating in sated mice. Moreover, our data show that the extinction did not diminish the eating response, instead resulted in habitual eating. Further, the tracing experiments revealed dense connection between PFC and ZI-GABA. Thus, in this proposal we will develop a robust chemogenetics based mouse model to test whether synaptic transmission between PFC to ZI-GABA neurons contributes to compulsive eating behavior. Most importantly, we will test whether blocking this transmission have therapeutic potential for food addiction. Collectively, this proposal will provide the neural substrates underlying compulsive eating which can be targeted for development of better therapeutics against eating disorders.
kw: Neural circuitry, Compulsive eating, behavior, addiction

title: Illuminating neuromodulatory role of primary cilia cAMP signaling in central satiety control
abs: To achieve homeostatic balance in energy intake and expenditure, the typical feeding behavioral pattern of an animal consists of a steady state of satiety intercepted by controlled bouts of hunger. The identification of principal neural circuits encoding hunger and satiety have generated much interest to understand how these neural components orchestrate the temporal pattern of feeding. Notably, loss of satiety regulation results in augmented motivation to eat, which underlies hyperphagia and diet-induced obesity. Recent research suggests appetite-regulating neuropeptides induce long-term modulation in synaptic plasticity that may underlie hunger and satiety behavioral states. G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs) for these appetite-regulating neuromodulators are surprisingly enriched in primary cilia of neurons, yet the function of these organelles within neural circuits have not been unraveled. In humans, genetic mutations compromising primary cilia integrity result in ciliopathy disorders commonly encompassing hyperphagia and obesity. Thus, primary cilia may function as specialized GPCR signaling organelles in neural circuits controlling energy homeostasis, specifically in limiting appetite. Cyclic AMP (cAMP) is likely exploited as second messenger, since most GPCRs identified in primary cilia to-date regulate cAMP synthesis. It is tempting to hypothesize that cyclic AMP signaling within primary cilia may function as a rheostat of neuronal activity in appetite-regulating neural circuits to modulate satiety control. By strategically developing tools and techniques to visualize and manipulate molecular activities in primary cilia, we will investigate ciliary cAMP signaling in an established core satiety center within the brain, namely the paraventricular hypothalamus (PVH). We aim to determine the overall role of primary cilia in PVH control of feeding behavior and illuminate the role of PVH ciliary cAMP signals during different phases of feeding. Elucidation of these relationships will reveal insight into molecular control of neural circuits controlling appetite and facilitate novel strategies in treating neurological and central-regulated metabolic disorders.
kw: feeding regulation,

title: Host cytokine modulation in the amelioration of HFMD neurological complications
abs: EV-A71 is an important causative agent of Hand, Foot and Mouth Disease (HFMD) affecting mostly infants and young children. A substantial proportion of infected patients experience serious neurological complications. Worryingly, the underlying mechanisms remain ambiguous with no effective prophylactic and treatment measures available. Using a novel neuron infection model, we uncovered G-CSF as a neuroprotective cytokine against EV-A71 neuropathogenesis, supporting our hypothesis that aversion of neurological complications is possible via host cytokine modulation to limit EV-A71 replication in the CNS. Here, we will elucidate the protective mechanisms of G-CSF and its use as a treatment strategy to circumscribe severe CNS symptoms. Specific aims are: Aim 1: Examining cooperative effects of EV-A71 non-structural proteins in host cytokine evasion Preliminary findings using neurons singly expressing EV-A71 3D or 2C suggest that both proteins participate in converging pathways targeting JAK2 degradation to subvert G-CSF-mediated responses. To elucidate this, luciferase EV-A71 replicons containing wildtype or mutant viral proteins will be expressed in neurons and their effects on JAK2 and viral replication evaluated. We will evaluate if G-CSF acts by targeting this interaction. Disruption of the 3D-2C pathway is expected to negatively affect viral replication. Aim 2: Evaluation of G-CSF treatment in EV-A71 mouse models The neuroprotective effect of G-CSF in our in vitro model will be evaluated in EV-A71 mouse challenge models. Viremia and neuropathology in G-CSF treated and untreated infected mice will be examined using immunohistochemistry and viral load titering in various organs, including the CNS. Treatment with antiviral cytokines is expected to significantly improve viral clearance. Aim 3: Elucidating cytokine profiles elicited in clinically-defined severe HFMD patients. We will measure and compare cytokine profiles in cerebrospinal fluids of HFMD cases with neurological presentation against our in vitro studies. Corroboration will strongly support G-CSF’s use as a therapeutic in severe HFMD cases.
kw: EV-A71, Hand Foot Mouth Disease, Neurovirulence

title: Functional dissection of SV2C as a novel Parkinson’s disease associated gene
abs: Parkinson’s disease (PD) is one of the most common age-related neurodegenerative diseases worldwide and one of the key research focus areas identified by the National Neuroscience and Sense Disorders Taskforce. In the first large-scale multicenter genome-wide association study of PD to be undertaken in East Asians, we identified a common genetic variant at SV2C associated with increased risk of PD, with consistent effect sizes across Chinese, South Koreans, Japanese and European populations. This genetic variant tags a common nonsynonymous change p.Asp543Asn (allele frequency ~10% in East Asians) within SV2C that occurs within an extracellular/luminal domain and may affect N-linked glycosylation of this domain via the creation of a new glycosylation site (Asn543-X-Thr545). SV2C is the only gene within the associated haplotype, hence we hypothesize that this variant p.Asp543Asn and other rare genetic variants within SV2C have a direct influence on PD risk in humans. SV2C is a brain-expressed gene involved in synaptic vesicle formation and dopamine release and has been shown to interact with α-synuclein. It was also present in intra-and extra-cellular inclusion bodies in PD postmortem brains but not other neurodegenerative diseases. We now propose to identify all common and rare variants within the SV2C locus and to profile all loss of function coding mutations by deep resequencing of over 7,000 PD cases and 7,000 controls from the Asian PD Genetics Consortium. Separately, we will establish a human pluripotent stem cell-derived dopaminergic neuron model to characterize the role of SV2C and its genetic variants in presynaptic vesicle formation and function, especially in the release of dopamine. Given that compounds have already been designed to specifically target SV2C, this work will be an important step towards evaluating the feasibility of developing SV2C as a drug target for the modulation of dopamine release, and for the prevention or treatment of PD.
kw: Parkinson's disease; genetics; stem cells; sequencing; dopaminergic neurons; neurodegeneration

title: Defining the role of NF1 in brain tumor microenvironment
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: NF1 tumor suppressor gene inhibits glioblastoma (GBM) invasion. Previously, we showed that the loss of NF1 promoted transition of proneural glioma to an aggressive mesenchymal subtype with augmented invasion and microglia/macrophage infiltration. Also, exosomes derived from the NF1 leucine-rich domain (LRD) suppresses glioma invasion and impede microglia/macrophage infiltration. Patients with GBM have an average survival of fewer than 1.5 years. Since NF1 is one of the highly mutated genes and a driver of mesenchymal transition in GBM, our findings suggest that targeting NF1 loss may be relevant therapy for a significant number of patients with an aggressive brain tumor. Accordingly, we hypothesize that NF1 modulates the tumor microenvironment by the secretion of exosomes. Aim 1 investigates the key pathways involved in microglia infiltration in GBM. We will use LRD truncation mutants to assess which regions within LRD are crucial for modulating microglia function. We will also investigate the activation state of infiltrative microglia cells exposed to LRD to elucidate key pathways involved in microglia recruitment. Aim 2 will study how the contents of exosomes reflect changes in proneural-mesenchymal transition for potential pharmacological intervention. Our initial miRNA profiling suggests the involvement of families of miRNAs in cell invasion and immune modulation. We will expand our repertoire of miRNAs to include those isolated from the exosomes from six patient-derived gliomas. These miRNAs will be profiled and validated using gain and loss-of-function assay. Aim 3 test the in vivo significance of the miRNAs to reverse microglia/macrophage infiltration in an orthotopic patient-derived glioma xenograft model as a therapeutic strategy. Results obtained from this proposal will allow us to establish crucial downstream pathways that are involved in regulating the immune microenvironment of NF1-loss-associated mesenchymal glioma, which will aid in the development of strategies that repress the recruitment of microglia/macrophage as a therapeutic approach.
kw: Glioma, NF1, tumor microenvironment, microglia, invasion

title: ASC as a new target for fighting inflammatory diseases
abs: Inflammasomes are multi-protein complexes that trigger the inflammatory responses upon recognition of pathogens or ‘sterile’ danger signals. Excessive inflammasome activity has been causally linked to the pathogenesis of a great number of inflammatory diseases. These findings have recently triggered increasing interests to develop pharmacological inhibitors targeting the inflammasomes. However, the few approved therapies targeting downstream cytokines are ineffective with notable disadvantages and there are currently no approved inhibitors targeting the upstream molecules, which are considered more attractive drug targets. Bats, as the only flying mammals, have unique biological features, including very long lifespan and asymptomatically hosting many viruses that are highly lethal in humans. These observations led to our investigation into the altered inflammation control in bats, especially the inflammasomes. Our recent study revealed a potent negative regulator of the inflammasomes in bats, called ASC2. Bat ASC2 is highly expressed at both mRNA and protein levels and highly potent in inhibiting the human/mouse inflammasome in vitro and in vivo. In contrast, human ASC2 is poorly expressed/functional and mouse does not have the ASC2 gene. Importantly, bat ASC2 targets the adaptor ASC, the first convergence of the inflammasome pathways, and there are no existing inhibitors targeting ASC thus far. Our main objective of this project is to develop new inflammasome inhibitors derived from or related to ASC2 and methods of use in the application of treating inflammasome-driven diseases. Our long-term goal is to apply these inventions to improve clinical outcomes in human inflammatory diseases. We hypothesize that the study of bat ASC2 can guide the development of new protein-based therapies and small-molecular inhibitors. It is highly significant to develop novel therapies targeting ASC for multiple inflammasome pathways with potential application in various human diseases including but not limited to autoinflammatory disorders, infectious diseases, metabolic and neurodegenerative diseases.
kw: Inflammasome inhibitor, inflammatory diseases, aging, protein-based therapies, small molecular inhibitors

title: Mapping the signaling pathways coupling mitochondrial functions with the invasive hyphal growth in the fungal pathogen Candida albicans
abs: Candida albicans is the leading cause of bloodstream fungal infections in humans, causing nearly half-million deaths annually. The global emergence of multi-drug resistant strains exacerbates the problem, posing a severe public health threat. A principal virulence trait of C. albicans is its ability to transform from a harmless, commensal yeast to invasive hyphal growth. As mutants defective in hyphal growth become avirulent, both academia and industry have, in recent years, invested significant resources in finding inhibitors that can block hyphal development as an antifungal strategy. Identifying good drug targets depends on a deep understanding of the molecular mechanisms that make the yeast-hypha decision. In recent years, a significant body of evidence indicates that the organelle mitochondrion plays a critical role in linking the cellular metabolic state and the hyphal growth of C. albicans. An emerging concept is that the mitochondrion acts as a metabolic checkpoint for the yeast-hypha decision. However, the components and organization of the checkpoint and how it controls hyphal growth remain unknown. We recently discovered that the trimethylation of cytochrome C, a component of the mitochondrial respiratory chain and famously known as a trigger of apoptosis, is essential for hyphal growth. We hypothesize that Cyc1 could be a central component of the metabolic checkpoint that determines hyphal growth in response to the cellular metabolic state, using Cyc1 trimethylation as a molecular switch. In this study, we will elucidate how Cyc1 methylation regulates the hyphal growth of C. albicans in response to environmental cues and the metabolic state of the cell and investigate its role in pathogenicity and virulence using mouse models of infection. The new knowledge can be expected to reveal drug targets and provide valuable information for designing future strategies for effective treatment of invasive fungal infections.
kw: Fungal infection, Candida albicans, mitochondrion, hyphal growth, metabolic checkpoint

title: Identifying circuit & molecular pathways that underlie tremor using models of Spinocerebellar ataxia 3
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: How does our nervous system coordinate smooth movements, and what mechanisms underlie the disruption of these processes during aging and disease? In humans, neurological disorders like Spinocerebellar ataxias can lead to characteristic movement dysfunctions, such as abnormal gait and/or tremors. Tremors are linked to the underlying disease etiology, and can be debilitating for patients. Despite its prevalence, very little is understood regarding the mechanisms that cause tremor. Detailed molecular and physiological characterization of associated neuronal circuits, and experiments to link gene function to neuronal activity and specific behavioural outputs, can help us to understand fundamental principles of smooth motor control, as well as develop approaches for rational treatments. However, to carry out a comprehensive analysis of the circuitry and brain-body interactions that underlie tremor is currently too challenging to do in models with large and complex nervous systems. The fruit fly (Drosophila) and mouse systems are excellent models for human neurodegenerative diseases. We propose to use fly and mouse SCA3 models in a complementary manner to investigate the circuit and molecular pathways that underlie tremor. Our data show that, like in humans, Drosophila models of Spinocerebellar ataxia 3 (SCA3) exhibit distinct and reproducible gait and tremor signatures, and are hence a good model in which to investigate the neurogenetic mechanisms of SCA3-induced tremor (Wu et. al., PLOS Biology 20191). We hypothesise that aberrations in neuronal circuits and/or cellular-molecular mechanisms cause these distinct movement defects. Hence, we aim to uncover the neuronal populations whose loss of normal function can cause SCA3-induced tremor (Aim 1 – Partially completed), characterise the changes in neuronal activities that lead to SCA3-induced tremor (Aim 2), and identify molecular and cellular pathways that underlie SCA3-induced tremor in the fly and mouse SCA3 models (Aim 3).
kw: Neurodegeneration, Movement disorders, Tremor, SCA3, Spinocerebellar ataxia

title: Direct and multiplexed analysis of circulating RNAs
abs: Detection of circulating RNAs has broad applications in blood-based disease diagnostics and prognostics. Despite such clinical potential, the large diversity of circulating RNAs pose significant analytical challenges. Current RNA analysis requires extensive sample processing and bulky instrumentation; detection of short RNAs (e.g., miRNA) is particularly arduous and necessitates dedicated assay design to modify, amplify and analyze these short targets. We have recently developed a molecular technology to enable direct and visual detection of diverse nucleic acids. The technology utilizes enzyme-DNA nanocomplexes, which function as independent recognition and signaling elements, to form a molecular switch. The switch activates via direct target hybridization and generates exponential visual signal for the naked eye. The platform is thus well-suited for RNA detection: (1) the assay requires minimal sample preparation (no need for DNA conversion), fast (<30 minutes), sensitive (<10 amol), and can be readily quantified with smartphones; (2) its modularity facilitates programmable assay design and multiplexed integration. We aim to address the RNA analytical challenges by enabling direct and multiplexed detection. Using lung cancer as a model system, we will test the hypothesis that multiplexed analysis of different circulating RNAs can improve diagnostic performance. This hypothesis stems from multiparametric analysis of circulating RNA subtypes, but has yet to be validated, due to a lack of compatible technologies. The goal of this proposal is thus two-fold. First, platform development. Through molecular engineering, we will develop and integrate molecular nanocomplexes to detect various circulating RNAs, of different lengths and sequence contents. Second, clinical validation, we will perform a translational study to profile circulating RNAs in patient blood samples and correlate the measurements to clinical diagnoses. These advances will significantly expand our understanding and clinical applications of diverse circulating RNAs for blood-based diagnostics.
kw: Direct detection, multiplexer, circulating RNA, miRNA, visual sensor, molecular nanotechnology

title: FluCluster-AI - Innovations in virus transmission cluster analysis
abs: We propose an alternative approach that is a paradigm shift from the old way of tackling influenza globally going away from chasing the predicted next dominant global vaccine strain (often being 1-2 years too late or regionally inaccurate) to bringing the problem down to more readily traceable higher resolution local transmission chains and shorter timeframes. To achieve this, our aim is to stratify influenza surveillance sequences into closely-connected transmission clusters via genetic distance and analyze clusters for enrichment of epidemiological and geo-temporal data with deliverable of an interactive webtool for near-real-time surveillance/analysis also by non-computer-experts. We hypothesize that this supports local cluster identification and could identify patterns and intervenable routes of transmission. The specific aims are: 1) Identify transmission clusters via genetic distance of influenza viruses from ongoing surveillance efforts in Singapore 2) Enrichment analysis of local epidemiological and geo-temporal data for each cluster including transmission pattern recognition with AI 3) Alert system for rare but relevant mutation phenotypes in clusters with FluSurver 4) An automated pipeline for an interactive webtool for near-real-time surveillance/analysis Our aims provide both easily achievable immediate outcomes from removing manual analysis steps for public health officers to automatically flagging transmission clusters for further investigation and mitigation but also an ambitious moonshot to unveil new angles to tackle transmission in a city-scale context using modern AI methods.
kw: Infectious Diseases; Surveillance; Virus; Influenza; Transmission

title: Targeting Host-Pathogen Synergy in Wound Infection
abs: Wound infections affect between 7% and 15% of hospitalized patients globally.
