Multiple bacterial species, including Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Enterococcus faecalis are frequently isolated from wounds associated with diabetic foot ulcers, burns, and surgical sites. Polymicrobial wound infections are composed of bacterial biofilms that are more tolerant to antibiotic treatment, compared monomicrobial or non-biofilm infections, leading to more frequent treatment failure. Recent evidence from us and others shows that the mammalian unfolded protein response (UPR) promotes the development of bacterial skin and soft tissue infection (SSTI) and impairs wound healing. Therefore, we hypothesize that UPR activation serves as a synergistic node to promote wound infection. Using a combination of multidisciplinary approaches, we will dissect the mechanisms by which the UPR contributes to polymicrobial wound infections by (1) establishing the role of the UPR in wound healing, (2) determining the contribution of the UPR to bacterial infection and growth in vitro, and (3) interrogating and therapeutically targeting the UPR during polymicrobial infection in vivo. Therapeutic targets for infections and the UPR which currently have none, may have long-term health benefits for Singapore.
kw: wound healing; surgical site infections; polymicrobial infection; unfolded protein response; endoplasmic reticulum stress; biofilm

title: Contribution of arterial resident macrophage in abdominal aortic aneurysm development
abs: Cardiovascular disease remains the leading cause of death and disability worldwide including Singapore where it is the leading cause of disease adjusted life years lost and accounts for 30% of all deaths. Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is a focal dilatation of the aorta associated with high morbidity and mortality in the event of aortic rupture. Current treatment for AAA is based on surgical intervention which is associated with a high risk of early or late morbidity and mortality highlighting the need for additional therapeutic strategies. Because infiltration of macrophages has been involved in AAA development and its complications, therapeutic strategies targeting these macrophages are actively being investigated. In contrast, the contribution of aortic resident macrophages in AAA remains unknown. Recently, we identified a population of aortic-resident macrophages that express hyaluronan receptor LYVE-1 and protect aorta from stiffness and excessive accumulation of collagen. Moreover, we showed that experimental and human AAA is associated with a decrease in LYVE-1+ macrophages but an increase in infiltrating LYVE-1- macrophages. Therefore, we hypothesize that aortic resident LYVE-1+ macrophages and infiltrating LYVE-1- macrophages have distinct roles in aneurysm development and progression (Aim.1), with LYVE-1+ macrophages, having an involvement in matrix remodeling (Aim.2). To address this hypothesis, we will employ mouse models lacking specifically LYVE-1+ macrophages and apply an integrated approach of multiple imaging modalities, biochemical and functional analyses. Furthermore, we will investigate whether shifting the balance to LYVE-1+ macrophages or promoting their activity may represent a promising therapeutic option to prevent aneurysm expansion and rupture (Aim.3). By building on prevailing research strengths, unique technology locally developed and clinical competencies in cardiovascular diseases, this project is uniquely suited to make significant scientific and preclinical contributions by accelerating our knowledge on resident arterial macrophage functions and their contribution to the pathophysiology of aneurysm.
kw: aortic aneurysm, macrophage, extracellular matrix remodeling

title: PIM1 Integrates PPARγ Signaling with Epigenomic Reprogramming to Promote Brown Fat Development and Function
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Obesity and its associated metabolic diseases increasingly are responsible for significant economic and social burdens in many countries. Therefore, efficacious obesity therapies are needed to combat this epidemic. Brown adipocytes are capable of burning fat through the process of thermogenesis to prevent and treat obesity in humans. During the process of fat development, PPARγ is considered the master regulator playing a central role in controlling a large number of downstream adipogenic genes. In addition, epigenomic reprogramming is fundamentally involved in regulating brown fat specific gene expression. But whether PPARγ signaling cross-talks to epigenomic reprogramming has been unclear and how this might happen remains elusive. Recently we identified PIM1, a constitutively active serine/threonine kinase, as a novel brown fat activating factor. Moreover, we found PIM1 physically interacts with PPARγ and promotes PPARγ phosphorylation. Given that PIM1 phosphorylates histone H3 at Serine10 which further triggers other site of histone acetylation and promotes gene activity, we hypothesize that PIM1 acts as a key integrator connecting PPARγ signaling with epigenomic reprogramming to control brown fat development and function. We also propose a working model by which PPARγ interacts with and recruits PIM1 to brown fat specific genes, in turn PIM1 phosphorylates PPARγ to enhance its transcriptional activity and promotes epigenomic reprogramming at brown fat genes through phosphorylating histone H3S10. In this study, we will characterize the function of PIM1 in regulating epigenomic reprogramming and PPARγ signaling during brown adipogenesis, and further define the role of PIM1 in promoting the thermogenic program and metabolic homeostasis. In vitro mechanism studies and in vivo functional studies will be carried out to attain our research goals. Accomplishing the above proposed studies will unveil a novel mechanism integrating two prominent signaling pathways in adipogenesis, provide us with novel drug targets and open new avenues for anti-obesity therapy.
kw: Metabolism, thermogenesis, brown fat, obesity, epigenetics

title: Identifying Novel Epigenetic Alterations in Asian Patients with Breast Cancer for Improved Risk Prediction and Molecular Classification
abs: Breast cancer is the most common cancer among women globally and in Singapore. Women with a strong family history of breast and/or ovarian cancer or with early-onset breast cancer are referred for genetic testing of BRCA1, BRCA2 and other predisposition genes. However, a large proportion of these individuals are mutation-negative, suggesting that additional genetic or epigenetic aberrations associated with breast cancer predisposition remain to be discovered. DNA methylation is an epigenetic mark that is heritable. A recent study on 25 Australian multiple-case breast cancer families has identified 24 heritable DNA methylation marks. Furthermore, a preliminary study by our group using epigenome-wide DNA methylation analysis has identified statistically significant differences in methylation levels between BRCA-negative breast cancer cases and matched controls. Based on these findings, we hypothesize that germline epigenetic alterations such as DNA methylation could play an important role in familial and sporadic breast cancer, and may be useful for breast cancer risk prediction and molecular classification. To test these hypotheses, we will utilise epigenome-wide DNA methylation analysis to perform two case-control studies. Firstly, for BRCA-negative breast cancer and secondly, for sporadic breast cancer, each with independent replication cohorts, and with the objectives of (1) identifying novel germline epigenetic aberrations associated with breast cancer susceptibility which could potentially be used for risk prediction, and (2) identifying epi-signatures for molecular classification. In addition, we will investigate if heritable methylation sites previously identified in another study are associated with breast cancer risk in our Asian population. To our knowledge, there are as yet no in-depth studies investigating germline epigenome-wide DNA methylation for breast cancer in Asian patients and the identification of novel epigenetic aberrations in breast cancer could lead to innovative strategies for risk prediction, disease screening, prevention and therapy.
kw: breast cancer susceptibility, hereditary, sporadic, epigenome-wide association study, molecular classification

title: Molecular profiling using CRISPR-Cas9 to reveal the unique metastatic features in human hepatocellular carcinoma.
abs: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is one of the leading cause of cancer-related deaths in Singapore and worldwide. Although surgery and local therapies are available to manage intrahepatic tumors, there is no therapeutic strategies to specifically address HCC with extrahepatic metastases. In consequence, the prognosis of HCC patients with extrahepatic metastases is dismal. Distant metastasis is a complex interplay between tumor cells and the tumor microenvironments and lung is the most common single site of extrahepatic metastasis for HCC. We have developed an orthotropic HCC mouse model of lung metastasis to mimics human disease progression and to provide a system for the functional identification of genes to unravel the complex interactions involved in the metastatic cascade in the physiological state. In this proposal, we aim to decipher the complex HCC metastasis regulatory network(s) through genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 knockout screens with this mouse model to identify and characterize the metastasis-related genes (Aims 1 and 2). We also propose to study the “main” stages involved in HCC metastasis by establishing the transcriptomic landscapes of primary HCC, circulating HCC tumor cells (CTCs) and lung metastases of HCC patients using single cell RNA-sequencing. These studies will provide the molecular basis to delineate the major stages of HCC metastasis and to validate the observations made in the functional identification of metastasis-relevant genes in Aims 1 and 2. Additionally, the tumour microenvironment is formed through interactions between variable cellular components and communications with tumour cells. Immuno-phenotyping of the tumor immune cell filtrates in the primary tumor and lung metastases will therefore be performed to address the intratumoral cellular heterogeneity between the primary and metastatic tumor microenvironments (Aim 3). Collectively, the outcomes of this project will provide valuable insights into the complex interplays between HCC tumor cells and the respectively microenvironment niches that facilitate extrahepatic metastasis in HCC.
kw: Extrahepatic metastases, Hepatocellular carcinoma, CRISPR

title: The role of cytoskeletal microtubule remodeling as a tractable therapeutic target in cancer metastasis
abs: The leading cause of cancer-related mortality for certain major cancers is metastasis. Particularly in breast cancers, metastasis of tumor cells from the primary site to vital distant organs is often fatal. The activation of the epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) program is a major contributor towards the invasion-metastasis cascade. Extracellular and intracellular signaling networks are well-established, often as master regulators, to elicit the phenotype shift in cell state, and cell morphology. While one often assumes that the dramatic change in cell morphology is product of the EMT program that endows the cancer cells with metastatic properties, the precise manner by which cell shape is regulated is often underappreciated and under-investigated. Of the cytoskeletal features (including actin and intermediate filaments), the regulation of microtubule dynamics and rearrangement, comprised on the polymerization and depolymerization of tubulin subunits, appears to be crucial in facilitating the EMT process. Thus, pharmacology inhibition of microtubule organization may be useful in blocking metastasis. We hypothesize that the identification of small molecules that blocks EMT may be therapeutically useful for inhibiting metastasis. Based on our preliminary data, we hypothesize that the regulation of cytoskeletal rearrangement, particularly microtubule depolymerization, is a key step in control EMT. More specifically, we reasoned that Tau protein and the tubulin deacetylase (HDAC6) are major molecular regulators of microtubule stability, and thereby important molecular targets for metastasis. Finally, because of the availability of Tau-binding PET imaging probes (presently used for imaging certain neurodegenerative diseases), we hypothesize that one may repurpose these clinical reagents for tracking metastasis in vivo in animal models. If successful, Tau-binding PET tracers may find potentially utilizing for detecting and tracking metastases in cancer patients.
kw: epithelial-mesenchymal transition; breast cancer; EMT

title: ATORG-003: A single-arm, open-label, phase 2 study of dacomitinib with or without dose titration for the first-line treatment of locally advanced or metastatic non-small cell lung cancer in subjects with an epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) activation mutation.
abs: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is the leading causes of cancer death in Singapore. Our understanding of NSCLC has transformed with the discovery of therapeutically targetable oncogenic drivers, most notably epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) activating mutations, present in 50-60% of lung cancer patients in Singapore. Dacomitinib is a second-generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) which has demonstrated improved progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) compared to gefitinib, a first-generation EGFR TKI. Dacomitinib however, was associated with increased toxicity and higher rates of dose reductions and discontinuation due to adverse events. This trial of dacomitinib aims to demonstrate increased tolerability and safety with a planned dose titration according to toxicity after one cycle of therapy, while maintaining treatment efficacy. This will be a multi-national, multi-centre, single-arm, open-label, phase 2 clinical study of the efficacy and safety of first-line treatment with dacomitinib, with or without dose titration, in patients with newly diagnosed or recurrent EGFR mutant NSCLC. &amp;amp;#13;&amp;amp;#10;This trial will also include significant translational research components, to elucidate the mechanism of acquired resistance and discover novel molecular markers for disease progression. This will be performed in blood and tissue samples using panel-based assays. Furthermore, available tissue at baseline and at the time of resistance will be interrogated with whole exome and transcriptome sequencing, to provide additional in-depth data for discovery of novel biomarkers. It is proposed that this rich dataset of genomic and clinical trial data will be housed on an integrated precision medicine informatics platform. Customizable solutions that can provide a platform for data storage, management and analysis across the basic science, drug development and clinical pipeline are crucial. Ultimately, this may extend to other areas of precision medicine, which will have vast benefits for the healthcare system in Singapore.
kw: Dacomitinib; non-small cell lung cancer; EGFR mutation

title: Targeting the epigenetic circuits in MLL1-rearranged leukemia for telomerase inhibition
abs: Telomere elongation by telomerase is essential for the continual proliferation of >85-90% of human cancers, and make it an attractive target for cancer therapy. However, the potential toxicity resulted from the inhibition of telomerase in normal stem/progenitor cells represents a major challenge for clinical applications. Therefore, current efforts focus on identifying cancer-specific mechanisms for telomerase activation, which may provide opportunities to develop targeted therapies with minimal toxicity to normal tissues. Acute leukemia with MLL1 translocations account for 10% all leukemia and represent mostly incurable diseases. Whole genome sequencing has identified few secondary mutations in MLL1-rearranged leukemia, thereby raising questions on how hTERT is activated in these genetically and phenotypically heterogeneous cancer cells. Our preliminary data indicated that MLL1 oncofusion proteins drive the aberrant epigenetic changes at the newly identified hTERT upstream enhancer to activate its expression. By targeting these cancer-specific alterations in the epigenetic circuits using small molecules, we can inhibit hTERT activation specifically in MLL1-rearranged leukemic cells for cancer therapy.
kw: acute leukemia; telomerase inhibition; epigenetic; transcription; MLL1; cancer therapy

title: Biologics development for immunomodulatory therapy in multiple myeloma
abs: The goal of this project is to develop a set of new biological proteins (‘biologics’) that will be tested for use first as a diagnosis tool and secondly as a prototype for enhancing natural killer (NK) cell-based immunotherapy against multiple myeloma. Multiple myeloma is a form of hematological malignancy that primarily affects the elderly, therefore myeloma is an increasingly important type of cancer in Singapore as well as worldwide in aging societies. Survival of patients has improved to an average of 7-8 years with introduction of a new category of immunomodulatory drugs (Imids) which are assumed to operate through enhancement of the functions of immune cells such as NK cells. These treatments are costly (over $500,000 per patient) and importantly, less than half of myeloma patients benefit from treatment by these drugs. The reason for this is yet unclear, however there is an urgent clinical need to develop methodology to identify the patients who are expected to respond well to Imids, and to develop the means to rescue the patients in which the Imids are expected to be ineffective. This project will develop new engineered proteins to antagonize the immune suppression on NK cells mediated by HLA class I isoforms. This is important in treatment as Imids are assumed to act through NK cells. A first function is their use as probes to detect HLA class I isoforms to enable triage of myeloma patients into responders and non-responder groups. The second use of these proteins is to antagonize HLA class I-mediated NK inhibition by blockade of the HLA-specific receptor-ligand interactions. Aim 1 will develop three biologics, and Aim 2 is a pilot study on clinical samples to investigate the efficacy of these proteins in antagonizing inhibitory receptor signaling in NK cells.
kw: Multiple myeloma; Immunotherapy; Biologics; HLA; NK cell

title: Understanding the pathogenesis of a foodborne strain of Group B Streptococcus unique to Singapore and Southeast Asia
abs: In 2015, Singapore suffered the largest reported outbreak of Group B Streptococcus (GBS) infections. This was caused by a type of GBS termed ST283 (sequence type 283). The outbreak established for the first time that GBS can be foodborne, via consumption of raw freshwater fish. Subsequent studies have shown that ST283 has been causing disease in both humans and fish throughout Southeast Asia since before 2000. ST283 is therefore a locally discovered new disease mechanism caused by a regionally prevalent variant of GBS. As a new disease caused by a new GBS strain, many questions remain. In other work, the regional public health burden and the risk to the aquaculture industry and food safety networks is being examined in collaboration with the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations. An epidemiological approach to re-examine whether other GBS strains can be foodborne is also being conducted. This study will complement these other studies by examining the molecular and genetic mechanisms for how ST283 causes foodborne disease. We have recently developed genetic tools and a proof-of-concept mouse infection model that can now be used to dissect what key differences in ST283 GBS enable foodborne infection. We will do this using modern genetic and genomic techniques on ST283 GBS, tested in the mouse infection model. Understanding how ST283 causes foodborne disease will provide insight into the evolution of this new disease mechanism in GBS; this has importance for understanding whether other GBS or other bacteria may also evolve to become foodborne. Understanding ST283 disease will also enable more specific testing for ST283 in humans as well as in food and farmed fish; this could directly help infected patients but may also provide tools to prevent infections and keep food safe, in addition to facilitating economic benefits from continued (safe) aquaculture development.
kw: Foodborne, Group B Streptococcus, bacterial genetics, animal infection model, Food safety, aquaculture

title: The role of the maternal and infant microbiome/metabolome unit on the development of atopic dermatitis in early life – an integrated multi-omics approach
abs: Background: Atopic Dermatitis (AD) is the commonest chronic childhood skin disorder. We previously demonstrated an impaired developmental trajectory of the infant gut microbiome/metabolome in children with early onset allergen sensitized atopic dermatitis (AD). As an extension of our findings, we hypothesize that the maternal microbiome/metabolome over pregnancy shapes the immunity of the foetus and influence the establishment and developmental trajectory of the infant microbiome/metabolome. The microbiome programming of the immune system, therefore, commences in the prenatal period and extends as a continuum through to the postnatal period into infancy, where postnatal influences would also come into play. In this study, we aim to identify putative gut microbiome and metabolome signatures of prenatal mothers and their infants and define the risk phenotypes (microbiome/metabolome) that predispose to AD. Methods: We will leverage the ongoing S-PRESTO pre-conception cohort to conduct a case-control study to investigate the role of the maternal and infant microbiome/metabolome unit on the development of AD. Serial prenatal maternal stools and infant stools will be analyzed using metagenomics/metatranscriptomics and targeted metabolomics using LC/MS/MS. Maternal serum and cord blood will be profiled using targeted metabolomics. Cytokine profiling will be carried out on the cord blood. An integrative ‘omics’ data analysis will be carried out using multivariate analysis and correlation. The longitudinal data will also be correlated with dietary patterns of mother/infants. Feasibility/Benefits: This study combines the clinical uniqueness of the preconception cohort with extensive multi-omics profiling of biological samples. Its importance lies on providing the insights into the underlying mechanisms between host-microbiome/metabolome during the critical phase of immune development, and relate this to the development of AD. These results would guide the design of cost effective early life intervention studies to reduce the risk of AD and its related allergic disorders.
kw: atopic dermatitis, microbiome, metabolome, maternal, infant

title: Cytokine-induced rat model of minimal change nephrotic syndrome: mechanism of interleukin-27-induced podocyte injury
abs: Our preliminary work on the molecular signature of monocytes from paired patient samples demonstrated IL-27 gene upregulation in unstimulated monocytes in MCNS relapse compared to remission. This was further corroborated by significantly higher plasma IL-27 levels in MCNS relapse. Human and experimental animal studies have shown that podocyte-secreted Angptl4 may play a role in the genesis of proteinuria in nephrotic syndrome. Signaling of IL-27 involves activation of STAT3 and MAPK, with subsequent upregulation of Angptl4 and c-maf-APK respectively. Our preliminary studies have shown that IL-27 was able to cause phosphorylation of STAT3 in human podocytes. Other studies have demonstrated upregulation of c-Maf in T-cells in MCNS relapse, and MAPK-AP1 pathway was shown to be involved in podocyte proliferation. Hence, we hypothesized that IL-27 may play a role in the pathogenesis of MCNS via STAT3-Angptl4 or MAPK-AP1 pathways, resulting in podocyte injury and proteinuria. This study aims to delineate the role of IL-27 in MCNS by creating an IL-27 overexpression rat model of the disease and investigating the biochemical and histological changes, biomarkers of podocyte injury, as well as the downstream pathway of podocyte-specific STAT3-Angplt4 or MAPK-AP1 activation. The direct effect of IL-27 on podocytes will also be validated through in-vitro human podocyte cultures via examination of markers critical for podocyte structure, migration assays and albumin permeability assay in HEK cells. In-vivo and in-vitro reversal of IL-27-induced podocyte injury will be performed through introduction of STAT3 or MAPK inhibitors. Delineating the mechanism underpinning this difficult disease will facilitate the design of more targeted therapy, avoiding adverse effects of current immunosuppressive therapy.
kw: Interleukin-27, Primary nephrotic syndrome, STAT3-Angptl4, MAPK-AP1, podocyte injury

title: In vivo studies of development of ALT tumors and their response to novel ALT-targeted therapies
abs: Ability to elongate telomeres and to bypass replicative senescence is one prominent feature of cancer cells. While most cancer cells achieve telomere elongation through re-expression of telomerase, about 15% of tumors (with high prevalence in sarcomas and gliomas) rely on ALT (Alternative Lengthening of Telomeres). Previous studies have described specific characteristics of ALT cells and proposed involvement of DNA repair pathways in this mechanism, including homologous recombination and break-induced telomere synthesis. However, to date, there is no therapy specific to patients with ALT cancers. Furthermore, in vitro studies have shed light on targetable proteins in ALT cells, but in vivo validation is still missing. Here, by performing genome-wide CRISPR screening and proteome profiling in a model of ALT osteosarcoma xenografts, we assess the genes involved in development of ALT tumors and in the tumor response to novel ALT-targeted therapies that we recently identified. Through this large-scale screening approach, we aim to define vulnerabilities and dependencies for ALT cells in vivo and propose drug combinations tailored for cancers relying on ALT.
kw: Cancer; Telomere; ALT; in vivo; CRISPR-Cas9 screen

title: Novel enterovirus A71 host dependency factors as broad-spectrum host-directed antiviral therapy targets
abs: Non-polio enteroviruses (NPEV) include many disease-causing pathogens, such as coxsackieviruses, echoviruses, enteroviruses and rhinoviruses. NPEV can cause significant health burden in children aged below five. Infections by these viruses generally cause mild gastro-intestinal disease, but can result in severe illness and even death as they possess neuro-invasive capacity. Enterovirus A71 (EV-A71) is a non-polio enterovirus with significant public health threat responsible for millions of EV-A71-related cases and thousands of deaths annually, yet no therapeutic is currently available. In this grant proposal, we aim to identify EV-A71 host-dependency factors as target of host-directed therapeutics. Our genome-wide loss-of-function screen identified glycosaminoglycans (GAG) biosynthesis genes, SLC35B2 and B3GAT3 as EV-A71 host-dependency factors. SLC35B2 transports substrates for GAG sulfation from the cytosol into the Golgi lumen, while B3GAT3 is involved in protein-GAG linker formation. Our preliminary data demonstrated that cells deficient in SLC35B2 and B3GAT3 impacts GAG expression and were resistant to EV-A71 infection. For further development of both molecules as potential drug targets, information on cell-type specificity and the mechanism underlying sulfated GAG mediating EV-A71 infection are required. In this grant proposal, we further explore the role of sulfated GAG in various cell types to EV-A71 infection. The involvement of sulfated GAGs in various steps of EV-A71 replication cycle will be investigated. We also aim, through screening of bioactive compound libraries, to identify (i) polysulfonate compounds as virus-directed therapy; and (ii) sulfation inhibitors as host-directed antiviral therapy. Host-directed therapy possess an advantage in overcoming antimicrobial resistance and have broad-spectrum activity. Our data also showed that sulfated GAG-deficient cells significantly abolished infection by various other highly pathogenic viruses, including pseudotyped Zaire ebolavirus and Nipah virus, highlighting the potency of sulfated GAG as broad-spectrum therapeutic target.
kw: Enterovirus A71, host-directed therapy, Genome-wide CRISPR knockout library screening

title: On-chip Terahertz Topological Photonics for 6G Communication (TERACOMM)
abs: The wireless mode of communication has transformed society and made the world a smaller place by leveraging the potential and power of real-time data. The rollout of 5G communication has made active manifestation for enhanced broadband mobile communications, the Internet of Things (IoT) and virtual reality. However, emerging new services, such as holographic communications, cloud computing, improved healthcare, and artificially intelligent devices, demands a technology to support high data throughput further requires a vision beyond 5G to 6G communication network. In this regard, terahertz frequency region is envisioned for the realization of 6G wireless communication since they offer huge bandwidth necessary for terabits per second (Tbps) link with negligible latency. In order to bring terahertz wireless link into reality, a compact, low-loss and miniaturized platform is required to manipulate and control the terahertz waves. In this project, we will develop terahertz integrated circuits based on Photonic topological insulator (PTI) for rerouting and advance manipulation of terahertz waves which is essential for terahertz wireless communication supporting real-time data rate up to 200 Gbps. The topological protection of terahertz wave in PTI ensures negligible bending loss, zero back-reflection, and low scattering. Miniaturized terahertz devices demand generation and detection of carrier wave; therefore, the planar configuration of the PTI chip will ease the integration of resonant tunneling diodes (RTDs) as THz source/detector. Moreover, to achieve high-speed data rate, on-chip complex modulation schemes will be implemented through active material and RTDs. To unlock the full potential for point-to-point medium-range wireless communications, we will develop directional terahertz antennas to exhibit high gain and wide bandwidth (to support large channel capacity). Hence, PTI based integrated terahertz systems will emerge as new architectures that are multifunctional and reconfigurable and will aid in developing terahertz wireless communication.
kw: Terahertz communication; Topological photonics; On-chip; Bending loss; Bandwidth; Modulation

title: Advanced geological mapping using machine learning technique
abs: Efficient land utilisation is crucial to make a huge metropolitan like Singapore to a compact, effective, and liveable city. Over the past decades, major transportation systems (e.g., MRT) and many service utilities have been already placed underground in Singapore. One of the biggest uncertainties in underground construction works is unforeseen ground conditions and stratigraphial alteration. For example, although the geology of Singapore consists of four main classes of geological units namely the Bukit Timah Granite, the Jurong Formation, Quaternary deposits of Old Alluvium and the most recent Kallang Formation deposit (Sharma et al. 1999), the local stratigraphy within each unit can be very variable. Under such difficult conditions, a comprehensive site investigation is strongly required to map out soil/rock layers and detect non-uniformities in the ground. Traditional site investigation has been conducted by directly drilling boreholes. However, being solely reliant on conventional boreholes drilling (mostly vertical although inclined drilling is also adopted these days) can be inadequate for comprehensive soil profiling. This is because centre-to-centre spacing between boreholes is often dictated by the requirements of the Eurocode 7 or the Client’s specifications and soil profiling only consists of linear interpolation during the desk study. Such simplistic assumptions, though convenient, may lead to surprises during actual construction and result in high costs and time overruns. In this study, we propose to improve predictions of these unforeseen underground variations by using advanced big data analytics and/or machine learning. With the recent advances in artificial intelligence research and computer science, machine learning has developed into a very promising and sophisticated approach to data analysis. In the Singapore context, since every borehole information is submitted to the relevant authorities for approval, the Government possesses an extensive soil database that can be tapped on for ‘learning’. In essence, by using a data-driven approach, we propose that it might be possible to identify strong patterns and relevant correlations contained in existing site investigation data and hence make reliable predictions about the soil stratification at any location in Singapore. This project aims to achieve the following: 1) The development of a machine learning algorithm that is able to identify correlations in the borehole data and make reasonable predictions about the soil stratification – number of layers, soil types and thickness of layers - at ‘unknown’ locations in Singapore. The model inputs are likely to be in the form of borehole location (northing, easting), reduced levels of the soil layers and carefully selected soil features extracted from borehole data (with input from our geological experts). title: Intelligent Lifting Frame for PPVC and Precast Construction
abs: Cranes are typically under-actuated systems where the number of actuators is less than the degrees of freedom, and this makes them difficult to control. The control objective for cranes systems eliminate the payload sway angles, so that the payload can reach the planned destination in a minimum time with less sway. Open loop control schemes are easy to implement as they do not require additional sensors to be installed to measure the sway angle. However, it is not able to deal with external disturbances (e.g. wind disturbance) and changing system dynamics (e.g. different cable length). The approach proposed herein is an intelligent lifting frame that will deploy a closed-loop control scheme for controlling the hoisting operations of precast components, including large PPVC modules on site. The lifting frame features a moving mass and auto-levelling mechanism that combines to provide anti-sway and lateral adjustments and alignment. The research is divided into five tracks: 1) Anti-Sway control & lateral alignment for tower crane hoisting operations; 2) Gyro Stabilization and Yaw Control; 3) Auto-levelling of precast modules; 4) Remote Controller integration with Camera for Bird’s Eye View for close view and control for fine lateral adjustments and alignment; and 5) Alignment of the horizontal 1m datum line with digital sensing devices.

title: Prevention of and Biomarkers for Vascular Cognitive Impairment
abs: Dementia is a major public health challenge globally. Although Alzheimer disease (AD) may be the most common form of dementia, it is likely that vascular cognitive impairment (VCI) play an equally significant role in Singapore because of the high prevalence of cerebrovascular disease (CeVD). There is growing consensus that small vessel CeVD leads to disruption of neuronal conduction and connectivity likely represents the major substrate of cognitive decline, even in the absence of AD, resulting in VCI. Recent advances in positron emission tomography (PET) to image the two pathological hallmarks of AD, i.e. β-amyloid peptide (Aβ) and microtubule associated tau protein in neurofibrillary tangles, as well as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) for CeVD have made premortem diagnosis increasingly possible and provides unprecedented opportunities to gain insights into the pathophysiology of VCI. Blood biomarkers for AD pathology and CeVD have also rapidly developed. This proposal highly focused on VCI, involving multiple institutions and led by well-established and productive PIs, seeks to 1) undertake a multiple lifestyle interventional study to retard VCI-associated disease progression (Theme 1) 2) assess longitudinal changes in brain structure, function (via MRI), and pathology (PET), retinal integrity, as well as novel blood markers in individuals with VCI with and without AD using state-of-the-art imaging techniques and establish their prognostic values (Theme 2) 3) conduct translational studies in mice using the bilateral carotid artery stenosis (BCAS), an accepted model of VCI, to determine the interplay with AD pathophysiology, signaling pathways that contribute to cerebral vascular function, and to correlate changes seen in brains and blood biomarker studies in mice to those detected in the other two themes (Theme 3) 4) link the above research studies (Theme 1 and 2) with health services research (HSR) on healthcare costs associated with VCI to facilitate clinical and policy decision making (Theme 4).
kw: Aging;vascular dementia;biomarkers;Alzheimer’s disease;cerebrovascular disease

title: Implementing precision medicine in clinical practice: The approach for glioblastoma, a neurological disease with unique spatiotemporal complexity
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: In neurological disorders, inter-patient variability to treatment response is a common problem. Several efforts showed that brain tumor molecular heterogeneity dictates prognostic outcome; furthermore, several molecular indicators outperform morphological features used in current diagnoses. There is thus a need to incorporate molecular features to better inform treatment decision. We previously established a STAT3-driven composite signature that stratifies survival and identifies responders to STAT3 inhibition therapy. STAT3 represents the key molecular switch that must be activated prior to tumors assuming an aggressive and recurrent state (proneural-mesenchymal transition, PMT). We demonstrated STAT3-specific subtype switching in recurrent tumors, highlighting the need to serially monitor disease progression to accurately assign appropriate therapy. Our proposal aims to: (1) Serially monitor STAT3 composite signature in blood and cerebrospinal fluid collected from postoperative patients, (2) Define epigenetic enhancer elements unique to H3K27ac in matched, spatially distinct core and peripheral tumors, (3) Develop a nanosensor to measure exosome-secreted RNA, and (4) Implement the N-of-1 clinical trial. To achieve Aims 1 and 2, we will acquire ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data, and identify hallmarks unique to STAT3-specific subtype switching. Our industry partner, BenevolentAI, will evaluate these molecular targets for druggability. In Aim 3, we will provide proof-of-concept that our nanosensor robustly detects the STAT3 profile in recurrent patient fluid biopsies. This will be corroborated by Aim 1 effort. In Aim 4, the clinical trial will involve as a first stage, a proof-of-concept, open-label, pilot study of JAK/STAT3 inhibitor in adult subjects with recurrent malignant glioma using our defined STAT3 gene signature to stratify and identify responders. The following stage will then progress to a multicenter phase II clinical trial at both upfront and recurrent settings. We seek to establish a novel treatment paradigm that focuses on serial monitoring of PMT progression in recurrent patients with targeted therapy in potential responders.
kw: neurological disorder; glioblastoma; STAT3; precision medicine

title: Genetic variants of neurocognitive diseases in Singapore: From discovery to clinical applications
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Alzheimer disease (AD) and vascular dementia (VaD) are two more prevalent subtypes of dementia in Singapore and globally. Although several genetic risk variants have been identified in dementia, only a fraction of the heritability of AD and VaD have been recognised, especially amongst Asians. The advent of high-throughput genotyping arrays has revolutionized the search for candidate genetic targets which could provide novel insights into the neurobiology of AD and VaD. We hypothesize that Asians harbor unique genetic risk variants of AD and VaD that not commonly encountered among Caucasians, and that a detailed interrogation of these variants will facilitate translational and personalisation of recent advances in AD and VaD neurobiology in Singapore. Using existing repository samples, we aim to examine the prevalence of known genetic variants and identify novel variants that predispose individuals to increased risk of developing AD and VaD in Singapore. We will further prospectively validate the identified genetic variants in an independent clinical cohort where diagnoses of AD and VaD are supported by validated amyloid-tau and cerebrovascular biomarkers. Functional annotation, pathway analyses and molecular functional analyses will then be performed on the identified novel genetic variants to evaluate their specific roles in the disease pathophysiology. Elucidating genetic risk variants of AD and VaD is a key step to unravel molecular insights to their pathogenesis in our population. Beyond facilitating diagnosis and subtyping patients into different risk categories of progression, information gathered through this study could substantiate the need for personalised therapeutics and enrolment of patients harbouring high risk signatures into clinical trials.
kw: genomics; genome-wide association studies; functional analysis; neurocognitive disorders; Alzheimer’s disease; Vascular Dementia

title: Spinal Cord-Computer Interfaces (SCCI): Restoring Volitional Motor Activity in a Murine Spinal Cord Injury Model
abs: Spinal cord injury (SCI) is a profoundly disabling disease, preferentially affecting young patients at the peak of their productivity with a poor prognosis for functional motor recovery. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that 250,000 to 500,000 people suffer a SCI every year of which half become tetraplegic with little or no movement below the level of the neck. Besides the profound physical and emotional loss, the financial cost to the society is substantial, reported to be up to US$5 million per patient in the United States. There is currently no effective treatment resulting in functional motor recovery to date. Neuroengineering is an emerging discipline that uses electrical interfaces that can both record signals from the nervous system and stimulate specified regions of the neural system. These neural interfaces are a promising strategy in the restoration of motor function to SCI patients and the University of Cambridge has developed a novel, flexible multi-electrode array (MEA) that is designed to record electrical activity generated in various areas of the spinal cord as well as stimulate the spinal cord to produce evoked motor activity. I aim to implant this MEA in the spinal cord of a murine model to firstly correlate signals recorded from the MEA with volitional hindlimb motor activity. Subsequently, I will simultaneously create a SCI in the animals and implant the MEA distal to the level to spinal cord injury to evoke targeted motor activity. I hypothesize that via the recording of spinal cord signals above a level of SCI and transmitting signals distal to evoke motor activity, this system can restore volitional motor function in a murine SCI model. This strategy will allow a “spinal cord injury bypass” transmission route, potentially restoring functional motor activity in SCI.
kw: Spinal cord injury; Neuroengineering; Bioelectronics; Neuroprosthetics; Brain-machine interface

title: Metabolic Health in Asian Women and their Children
abs: Asia and Singapore are facing an epidemic of type 2 diabetes T2). The high incidence (20-25%) of gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) in Singapore is exacerbated by large differences observed by ethnicity. GDM, a frequent precursor of T2D, carries a high lifetime risk of T2D of up to 70%, with perpetuating consequences into the subsequent generations. There are significant economic, social and human costs to this epidemic. This is a collaborative research proposal by all 3 main healthcare clusters of Singapore together with A*STAR to improve the metabolic health of Asian women and their children. The proposal integrates basic, clinical and translational science to understand the heterogeneity GDM and T2D, and to test new interventions and models of care. It is highly problematic to extrapolate from extensive findings in Caucasians to Asians; in fact, both gender- and ethnic-specific aspects require consideration. We build off our previous research with developmental lifecourse cohorts (GUSTO and S-PRESTO) and studies of ethnic differences in adult male metabolism to explore the pathophysiology and prevention of metabolic dysfunction in Asian women. We will explore differences between Chinese, Indian and Malay women, seek potential biomarkers of GDM and/or conversion to T2D, and evaluate the significance of GDM heterogeneity. Findings will suggest opportunities for population stratification to more effectively identify and target subgroups with interventions designed to reduce the risk of developing GDM or converting from GDM to T2D. We will conduct targeted interventions, leveraging on innovative health devices in particular continuous glucose profiling wearables, healthcare practice advancements, behavioural and lifestyle changes. We will conduct predictive and prescriptive analyses of our GDM population to enhance care and build effective and value-for-money models of care to prevent the development of both GDM and T2D and further apply systems modelling to assess population health, cost outcomes and trans-generational impact.
kw: Diabetes; Gestational diabetes; Prevention; Metabolism; Transgenerational

title: Integrated Innovations in Infectious Diseases (I3D)
abs: Emerging Infectious diseases (EIDs) are major threats to Singapore due to our position as a major global trade and travel hub. EID outbreaks have devastating consequences as seen with the SARS outbreak which claimed 33 lives and caused a 5%reduction of Singapore’s GDP (S$7.8 billion) The outbreak response to such outbreaks, consisting primarily of costly decades old public health interventions. There is currently no licensed therapeutic for any emerging infectious diseases. With lessons learned from SARS and the tremendous advances developed locally, Singapore is now scientifically prepared to make a major contribution in the global response to the next infectious disease threat. Our Large Collaborative Grant (LCG) proposal –_Integrated Innovations in Infectious Diseases (I3D) – is an innovative approach to translate therapeutics that modify disease outcome for unknown and novel pathogens. We will do this through five inter-connected themes that target both pathogens and the host response that drive pathogenic mechanisms. We have focused on respiratory pathogens (Theme 1) since they have been the most devastating in the recent years (e.g. SARS, MERS or influenza); Theme 2 uses novel approaches to pathogen discovery while theme 3 features an adaptive clinical trial design to test repurposed therapeutic agents. We will also develop platforms that rapidly characterize host response, especially those that drive inflammation (Theme 4). Novel immunotherapeutic agents can then be quickly mobilized in the emergency public health response to unexpected epidemics or pandemics (Theme 5). This strategy can also be applied in “peacetime” for the more than 50% of severe pneumonia that are currently undiagnosed. If successful, I3D will provide a framework that accelerates and enables fresh therapeutic strategies that will propel Singapore to a global leadership position in the efforts to break the chains of transmission to reduce the socio-economic impact of these emerging infectious threats worldwide.
kw: Novel therapeutics; Rapid therapeutic antibody translation; Pre-clinical studies; Characterization of emerging pathogens; Host-pathogen interactions; Adaptive clinical trial

title: Digital technology solutions to improve the vision-specific quality of life
abs: Aim: To assess the level of digital readiness and the effectiveness of digital technology solutions (STAAR-Q) on vision-specific quality of life (VS-QOL) and social engagement in visually impaired (VI) older patients. Hypotheses/Background: A robust assessment tool (STAAR-Q) can assess the digital readiness and the impact of various digital technologies on the VS-QOL and social engagement. The VI older population compared to a healthy older population, is likely to have lower levels of digital readiness and hence have more barriers to use digital technology. Customized accessibility feature training can improve the digital readiness of the VI older population and help increase usability of digital technology solutions likely to improve visual functioning, VS-QOL and social engagement. Methodology: We plan to develop, validate and implement an assessment tool (STAAR-Q), which will consist of an electronic questionnaire and pre-specified digital tasks to assess various aspects of digital readiness. Through the implementation of the STAAR-Q in a prospective case control study, digital readiness will be compared between the normal sighted and visually impaired older individuals. The STAAR-Q will also assess the efficacy of various methods of accessibility training for mobile SMART devices, software applications and other assistive technology devices and will evaluate the impact of digital readiness on using digital technology solutions to improve visual function, VS-QOL and promote social engagement. The results of this study can help with planning effective future accessibility feature training programs, provide an objective, standardized manner to assess the impact of digital technology solutions and provide ideas for future development of new devices.
kw: Quality of Life; Digital Readiness

title: 3 Tier Biomarker Discovery Platform for Ageing Frailty
abs: Two principal factors predominantly determine the onset of age-related frailty and morbidity, mitochondrial and muscular function. Muscle is our largest tissue mass and greatest single source of mitochondria. Stimulating muscle energy production, as during exercise, improves overall health and promotes longevity. The homeostatic role of muscle over systemic metabolism and health extends from its evolutionarily-designed capacity to synthesize and release a collection of trophic and metabolic factors, known as myokines, into the systemic circulation. Accordingly, mitochondrial activation induces myokine function. We have developed a non-invasive and efficient method to activate muscle mitochondrial respiration that is capable of promoting in vitro and in vivo myogenesis as well as improve mitochondrial function, downstream survival adaptations and secretome activation with as little as 10 minutes of treatment applied once or weekly, respectively. Our intervention consists of a very low energy magnetic signature that acts on the quantum biological level to stimulate mitochondrial energy metabolism. Our magnetic fields are non-disruptive, being only ~15-times greater than the Earth&amp;amp;amp;amp;rsquo;s standing field. Indeed, we have shown that normal development depends upon environmental magnetism, as shielding cells from all ambient magnetic fields arrests their growth and differentiation. Magnetism is thus an authentic developmental force of underexploited clinical potential. We have demonstrated our magnetic intervention to produce: 1) mitochondriogenesis (Sirt1, PGC-1&amp;amp;amp;amp;#61537;, Nrf2 transcriptional upregulation); 2) mitochondrial survival adaptations (telomere lengthening and reduced apoptosis); 3) improved metabolism (increased mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation, adipose browning, microbiome shifts towards metabolic enhancement, reduced serum ceramide levels, reduced serum insulin and inflammatory markers levels); 4) improved muscle functioning in animals (increased physical performance and reduced fatigue); and 5) enhanced myokine release. In essence, our magnetic fields emulate the mitochondrial effects of exercise, yet without the damaging mechanical stress associated with exercise, having profound clinical implications for the elderly frail.
kw: Electromagnetism; Biomarker Discovery

title: Towards Personalization: Identifying Life-History Patterns of Loneliness as the Basis for Effective Early Interventions
abs: Loneliness is a public epidemic, particularly among older adults (aged 60 years and older). Our proposal is to identify different types of loneliness as a basis for effective interventions. Previous research has shown that loneliness increases the probability of death over and above physical illness and disability. In recent work, our team has shown that being lonely reduces life expectancy by 4 years in the older Singapore population. At present, 53% of older Singaporeans (aged 60+) report being sometimes or mostly lonely using the UCLA 3-item loneliness scale, particularly those living with children only. By alleviating loneliness we can improve healthy longevity. We hypothesise that in order to develop successful interventions for loneliness we must first understand clusters of lonely individuals with particular characteristics. We use a mixed-method design to identify patterns of loneliness and qualitative narratives using a life course approach. We challenge the traditional assumption that older persons living with children in Asian countries are well taken care of and have a higher quality of life compared to older adults in other types of living arrangements. I. We will conduct cluster analyses for the subgroup sometimes/mostly lonely, by gender, ethnicity, education, income, housing type, marital status, personal mastery, social network size, and quality of social network. II. Conduct semi-structured interviews asking participants to define what loneliness means to them using a life-history calendar method. III. Photovoice methods include using images to capture what triggers loneliness in individuals everyday situations Findings from the study will inform the conceptualization of a complex phenomenon: loneliness into key typologies of experience. Next steps are to: (i) cluster older persons at risk of loneliness, (ii) design and develop programmes and intervention with stakeholders and community partners and (iii) match at-risk persons to these programmes and community intervention.
kw: social isolation; loneliness; typology of loneliness; preventive intervention

title: Studying epigenetic ageing and telomere length as possible biological predictors for healthy ageing - the Singapore Chinese Health Study.
abs: We recently showed that telomere length is associated with age, chronic diseases and various mortalities and have highlighted on important ethnic specific genetic loci that control telomere attrition in the Singapore Chinese population. How much telomere length correlates with other ageing biomarkers and whether these interact to affect predictions of future health outcomes is unknown in the Chinese population. We hypothesize that ageing molecular biomarkers are not completely independent but may interactively coalesce to affect ageing outcomes. In this initial proof-of-concept study, we aim at studying two well-characterized ageing molecular biomarkers, telomere length and epigenetic ageing, to determine their associations and correlations with each other (Aim 1) and evaluate if jointly modelling these two biomarkers could improve associations and predictions of prospective health outcomes in the Singapore Chinese population (Aim 2). The Singapore Chinese Health Study (SCHS) has recently characterised the prospective collection as healthy ageing (N=2,834, 20.02% of the sample collection, mean age = 73) defined as the absence of specific chronic diseases, no impairment of cognitive function, no limitations in instrumental activities of daily living, good mental health and overall self-perceived health, good physical functioning and no function-limiting pain after a median 20-year follow-up. For this initial proof-of-concept study we would leverage on the SCHS data to select 100 cases and 100 controls based on pre-defined healthy ageing status and determine epigenetic ageing at baseline (mean age = 53). Readily available telomere length information at baseline from the same study samples will enable understandings on correlation and association patterns of these ageing molecular markers and allow for an initial evaluation on the joint utility of these molecular markers, determined during midlife, to predict prospective healthy ageing status in the Chinese population.
kw: Ageing; epigenetics; telomere length; risk prediction

title: Enhanced Single Cell Transcriptomics for New Biomarkers and Targets in Cardiovascular Ageing
abs: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the primary cause of morbidity and mortality globally. Related annual US healthcare expenditure exceeds $200bn, of which heart disease alone costs $100bn, surpassing all other diagnoses. Age is a fundamental predictor of CVD risk, and as populations age, associated social and economic burden is projected to become increasingly severe. Survivors of acute myocardial infarction (MI) may develop progressive deterioration of cardiac function and heart failure (HF), prognosis for which remains worse than most cancers. New platforms for biomarker and drug discovery are urgently needed. We propose to leverage an advanced sequencing protocol, developed in our lab, to identify novel age-associated and disease-relevant cardiac cell types, states, interactions, biomarkers and drug targets. This will begin with a comparison of MI disease response in young and aged mice, at single cell resolution, with key findings later validated in banked human patient tissue samples. Our protocol is optimised for unbiased, high quality capture and sequencing of dissociated, whole, live cardiac cells, and offers significantly higher sequencing detail than commercial platforms, including a five-fold increase in gene detection. Sequencing of over 2000 cells from young mouse hearts has already demonstrated powerful utility. This innovative approach can thus lead to transformative breakthroughs in understanding, monitoring, management and treatment of age-related CVD. Furthermore, we envisage future applications in a multitude of complex heterogeneous disease settings (vascular, cancer, neurological), unlocking advances in health and longevity research across disciplines.
kw: Single cell transcriptomics, cardiovascular ageing

title: Ergothioneine, the lesser known longevity nutrient?
abs: The naturally occurring thione, ergothioneine, accumulates in the human body at high concentrations primarily from diet. Studies suggest this compound may play an important physiological role, however this has yet to be fully elucidated. We have recently observed that blood levels of ergothioneine significantly decline with age and onset of certain neurodegenerative disorders. We propose that the decline in blood ergothioneine levels may be a factor predisposing elderly to age-related conditions, and as such supplementing this compound may prevent or delay the onset of those conditions and prolong healthy longevity. This proposal will uncover the associations between ergothioneine levels, the onset of age-related disorders, and biomarkers of oxidative damage and inflammation in elderly subjects and help establish a baseline for healthy levels of ergothioneine in the blood. Furthermore, the study aims to investigate the possible mechanisms of protection by ergothioneine using a range of cell and animal models. This proposal lays the foundations for future clinical studies into prophylactic and therapeutic supplementation of ergothioneine for a range of age-related chronic disorders.
kw: ergothioneine, antioxidant, nutrient,

title: Small RNAs: Big Answers to Healthy Longevity?
abs: Humans have long been searching for the path to longevity. Among the latest but less known possibilities being proposed is PIWI-interacting RNAs (piRNAs). These small non-coding RNAs could prevent DNA damage and genomic instability, ones of the key hallmarks of aging and significant players in various age-related diseases. The main function of piRNAs is transposon silencing. A piRNA guides a PIWI protein to its DNA target, including a transposon, resulting in transcriptional repression through epigenetic modifications or by inducing post-transcriptional mRNA degradation. Active transposons, known to increase with age, can lead to aberrant gene expression and cause damage to genomic integrity. Meanwhile, several mRNAs associated with age have been identified. We hypothesize that piRNAs could contribute to healthy aging, possibly by suppressing transposons or other aging-related mRNAs. Although some piRNAs associated with heart failure, cancer or Alzheimer’s disease have been identified, no study to date has reported piRNAs associated with aging. In this proposed study, we will take the first step to identify aging-associated piRNAs using the relatively inexpensive approach. Firstly, genome-wide piRNA expression will be profiled in young (n=6) and old (n=6) mice to identify piRNAs differentially expressed with age. Next, the significant piRNAs that are also expressed in human (using online piRNA database “piRBASE” as a reference) will be shortlisted. Among these, the most differentially expressed piRNA will be overexpressed in human cells, of which genome-wide mRNA expression will be profiled to identify mRNAs potentially targeted by the piRNA. Finally, the pathway analysis will be performed on the list of mRNAs differentially expressed with the overexpressing piRNA. This study will shed light on the potential mechanisms through which piRNAs may regulate aging. The findings will enable researchers to utilize more targeted approaches to confirm the aging-related functions of piRNAs in humans in the future.
kw: small non-coding RNA; PIWI-interacting RNA; transposon; aging; lifespan

title: Deciphering aging-dependent human neuronal activity changes, tissue microenvironment and gene expression patterns
abs: The aging-related decline in brain function is attributed to changes in gene expression patterns, molecular, cellular and synaptic function of the various types of cells - encompassing changes in biophysical properties of neurons and neuronal communication through synapses. This proposal aims to address the question of how changes in neuronal activity, gene expression patterns and cellular function in the human brain correlate with mental aging, and how these changes are exaggerated in pathological conditions. The idea central to this proposal is that examining and correlating changes in the structural, functional and genetic profiles of the human brain will enable us to identify human brain-specific molecular markers of mental aging. This identification (of molecular markers of aging) will advance drug discovery targeted towards delaying and slowing the mental aging process. To achieve the objectives of this proposal, we will perform experiments on fresh cortical tissue extracted from neurosurgery patients of different age groups, at the National University Hospital- Singapore during routine surgical procedures. We will employ a combination of tools in single-cell RNA sequencing, in-vitro electrophysiology, and neurochemistry. This combination of approaches is being employed for the first time to study human mental aging.

title: p75 neurotrophin receptors in forebrain medial septum mediate the enhanced experimental chronic pain in aged rodent?
abs: This proposal tests the hypothesis that the p75 neurotrophin receptors (NTR) in the forebrain medial septum (MS) is a basis of increased chronic pain in aged rodent. Chronic pain affects about 20% of the world population and is debilitating, especially in aged. Indeed, chronic pain is co-morbid with depression, anxiety and cognitive decline and thus affects the lifestyle of patients. Aged rodents, as with humans show enhanced pain on injury in comparison to young. Preliminary experiments from the laboratory suggests that blocking the function of p75 NTR in MS reverses experimental pain due to neuropathy in young rat. However, the role of septal p75 NTR in mediation and enhancement of chronic pain in aged remains unclear. Interestingly, the expression of p75 NTR increases in brain of the aged. Using rodent models, behaviour and cell biology techniques, the proposal will examine (a) the changes in expression of p75 NTR, specifically in MS with age, and (b) the effect of functional antagonism of septal p75 NTR on chronic experimental pain. The function of p75 NTR will be antagonized either with knockdown of the receptor or by microinjection of drugs that antagonize the function of the NTR by binding to it. A demonstration that antagonism of septal p75 NTR effectively blocks pain in aged will be very novel and will be a precursor to a wider investigation into the role of the septal receptor as a common target mediating changes in emotion-motivation in aged of which enhanced chronic pain is one manifestation.
kw: neuropathic pain; expression of p75; peripheral hypersensitivity; intraseptal microinjection; antagonism of p75; knockdown of p75

title: Detecting Parkinson’s disease-associated metabolites with colorimetric sensor array and machine learning
abs: Parkinson’s disease (PD) is a common aging-related debilitating neurological disorder. No drug can reverse disease progression and clinical diagnosis can be challenging during early stages of the disease. There is an acute need for affordable, objective, biomarker-based methods both for diagnosis of patients and for accurate identification of subjects for new drug trials. We propose the use of colorimetric sensor array and machine learning algorithms to discern changes in urine metabolites as a PD diagnostic. Similar arrays have been designed to mimic sophisticated olfactory sensory systems of animals for discerning complex chemical mixtures. We have validated our array on hepatitis B and various cancers, and the current proposal to test it on PD is novel. Our array consists of 70 hydrogel spots; each spot contains a unique combination of derivatized acrylamides and acrylates that undergo distinct color reactions with urine metabolites. The resulting color pattern of the 70 spots is an emergent property of the urine metabolites, which in turn reflects health status. The color pattern of each array is analyzed by machine learning algorithms for diagnosis. In this pilot project, we will test the array with normal urine and urine spiked with 50 PD-enriched metabolites chosen from literature. Normal and simulated PD urine will be profiled and classified using a pre-trained machine algorithm. The performance will be evaluated in terms of sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV. Limit of detection of each metabolite will be assessed. In addition, we have identified colorimetric reactions designed to detect specific metabolites known to be enriched in PD urine and will incorporate these reactions into the array to improve performance. Success of this pilot will lead to a clinical trial for PD diagnostic. We envision that our technology will be generalizable to many aging-related conditions and will enable personalized preventive approaches for healthy longevity.
kw: Parkinson's disease; metabolites; colorimetric sensor array; machine learning; diagnostic

title: Examining evidence for transmissible Alzheimer's Disease (AD)
abs: Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) is known to develop among many individuals in an age dependent manner. A few genetic variants in enzymes or proteins associated with production of amyloid beta (Aβ) peptide from Aβ protein have been identified as potential candidates associated with AD. However, for most part, it is unclear if some individuals are more susceptible than others. In the last 5 years, 2 studies have been published that suggest the possibility for Aβ plaque formation to be associated with seeding of contaminated Aβ plaques to healthy people. This is surprising and it is still debated if AD can be transmitted, just like a prion disease to provide nucleation sites that facilitates further misfolding and aggregation of Aβ peptides and tau proteins in the brain. Only a couple of studies have shown some evidence. Here we take the step to test if transmission can occur via ingestion of Aβ aggregates. We plan to test this transmissibility hypothesis by feeding genetically engineered laboratory model nematode that express the human Aβ aggregates to another laboratory model, the zebrafish. We will then examine the brains by histopathological techniques and the behavior of the fish to evaluate if Aβ associated toxicity and neurodegeneration is detectable due to transmission in a prion-like manner. We also plan to observe inter-generational transmission, if any, and the effectiveness of drug-combinations in attenuating any effects found.
kw: Alzheime's Disease, Amyloid beta, Prion, neurodegeneration, healthy aging

title: Characterizing the role of microglia-mediated cognitive function in aging brain
abs: With a rapidly aging population, an increase in frequency of individuals with cognitive dysfunction and progressive deterioration of memory, represent an enormous socio-economic burden. Recent studies show that microglia, the resident immune cell of the brain, express memory molecules which are involved in synaptic plasticity in the healthy brain. During aging, microglia become dystrophic and may show a reduction in their ability to maintain synaptic functions, thereby resulting in cognitive decline. Given the plasticity of microglial cells in the CNS, we hypothesize that microglia, which have been shown to be involved in learning and memory, can be targeted to complement and enhance neuronal functions by providing memory molecules in the aging brain. To address this hypothesis, we will employ a combination of cutting-edge techniques for morphological (in vivo imaging using 2 photon microscopy and histology), molecular, epigenetic and functional (electrophysiology) analyses to investigate 2 overarching objectives. Firstly, we will characterize microglia in healthy aging brain using single cell RNA sequencing, histone profiling, and morphological analysis using multiphoton microscopy techniques to understand the molecular and epigenetic profile of dystrophic microglia. Further, we aim to develop in vitro models of aging microglia to perform functional analysis of the dystrophy associated genes. Secondly, we propose to explore how dystrophic microglia influence cognitive functions using electrophysiology studies in the aging rat brain, and to evaluate if these cognitive functions can be improved by administration of epidrugs such as HDAC inhibitors. A key outcome of this proposal is a comprehensive understanding of dystrophic microglia in the aging brain which will form the basis for microglia-centric therapies (epidrugs) to improve microglial functions and subsequently delay cognitive decline in the aging brain
kw: aging; microglia; cognition; epigenetics; synaptic plasticity

title: Organismal aging and oxidants beyond macromolecules damage
abs: One prediction of the free radical theory of aging is that oxidative stress shortens organisms’ lifespan because of the damaging effect of oxidants on macromolecules, thereby resulting in loss of tissue/organ functionality as seen in age-related diseases. Based on this prediction, observational studies and small interventional studies accumulated to justify large-scale double-blind interventional trials of antioxidants for many age-related diseases. Unfortunately, by early 2000, sufficient clinical evidence had accumulated to indicate little to no significant health benefits of supplementation with antioxidants. Notably, age-related decline in health and organ functions is also linked to the accumulation of IL-6 secreting senescent cells. While, most interventions using anti-oxidant to benefit human health appear to target oxidants that are implicated in macromolecule oxidation, primarily hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), our recent in vitro work provides evidence for a distinctly different redox milieu involved in the phenotype of senescent cells. We have identified a superoxide/nitric oxide (O2-/NO)-driven redox state which has an effect different from H2O2 on the secretion of the senescence-associated interleukin, IL-6. While inhibiting O2-/NO signaling mitigated IL-6 secretion, scavenging H2O2 increased it. Based on these data, we hypothesize that two distinctly different redox states are at play as the stimulus for human aging. Hence, we propose that for an anti-oxidant approach to have significant benefits on human life-span the antioxidants and/or redox modulators used should mitigate not only the damage to macromolecules but also the accumulation of senescent cells with an age-associated phenotype. As such, this project intends to generate data to get a deeper understanding of the newly discovered redox state in age-related cellular senescence. Moreover, going forward, these results will enable us to establish a cell-based model system that could be used to screen novel redox modulators, able to mitigate both macromolecules oxidation and the accumulation of age-associated senescent cells
kw: oxidants, senescence, antioxidant, redox modulators

title: Uncovering rejuvenation factors in muscle stem cells for the reversal of age-related sarcopenia
abs: Sarcopenia is defined as the progressive loss of muscle mass with age. One major pathophysiology of sarcopenia is the inherent loss of regenerative capacity of skeletal muscle progenitors (SMPs) which is essential for muscle fiber repair and homeostasis. However, less is known on the regulation of the regenerative capacity of aged SMPs. We hypothesized that by identifying longevity factors and subsequently using it to immortalize aged SMPs, we can restore the regenerative capacity of aged SMPs. We aim to identify targets for rejuvenation of sarcopenic skeletal muscle. In order to achieve this, we intend to first replicate our successes with immortalization in aged and sarcopenic muscle. Following isolation, a number of validation studies will be performed to confirm that these isolated cells are indeed SMPs. After validation, sarcopenic and control healthy SMPs will be subjected to transduction of unique cocktail of transgenes using our previously published methods. A successful transgenic combination is one that rejuvenates aged SMPs and maintains the ability to differentiate into myotubes. Once achieved, the rejuvenated aged SMPs and primary sarcopenic aged myoblasts and myotubes will be subjected to RNA-sequencing and metabolomics in order to identify the underlying mechanisms that drive rejuvenation. Upon identification of the pathways involved, we will perform a targeted screen from small molecules that can modulate these pathways. From these investigations, we hope to derive a working model as well as viable targets for the rejuvenation of sarcopenic myoblasts.
kw: Muscle; sarcopenia

title: Metabolic Health in Asian Women and their Children
abs: Asia and Singapore are facing an epidemic of type 2 diabetes T2). The high incidence (20-25%) of gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) in Singapore is exacerbated by large differences observed by ethnicity. GDM, a frequent precursor of T2D, carries a high lifetime risk of T2D of up to 70%, with perpetuating consequences into the subsequent generations. There are significant economic, social and human costs to this epidemic. This is a collaborative research proposal by all 3 main healthcare clusters of Singapore together with A*STAR to improve the metabolic health of Asian women and their children. The proposal integrates basic, clinical and translational science to understand the heterogeneity GDM and T2D, and to test new interventions and models of care. It is highly problematic to extrapolate from extensive findings in Caucasians to Asians; in fact, both gender- and ethnic-specific aspects require consideration. We build off our previous research with developmental lifecourse cohorts (GUSTO and S-PRESTO) and studies of ethnic differences in adult male metabolism to explore the pathophysiology and prevention of metabolic dysfunction in Asian women. We will explore differences between Chinese, Indian and Malay women, seek potential biomarkers of GDM and/or conversion to T2D, and evaluate the significance of GDM heterogeneity. Findings will suggest opportunities for population stratification to more effectively identify and target subgroups with interventions designed to reduce the risk of developing GDM or converting from GDM to T2D. We will conduct targeted interventions, leveraging on innovative health devices in particular continuous glucose profiling wearables, healthcare practice advancements, behavioural and lifestyle changes. We will conduct predictive and prescriptive analyses of our GDM population to enhance care and build effective and value-for-money models of care to prevent the development of both GDM and T2D and further apply systems modelling to assess population health, cost outcomes and trans-generational impact.
kw: not applicable
