title: Production of MgO cement from waste reject brine obtained from desalination plants
abs: The extraction of MgO cement from seawater or brine involves two main steps: (i) the precipitation of brucite (Mg(OH)2) and (ii) calcination of brucite to obtain MgO. Seawater contains an average Mg2+ concentration of ∼1.29−1.35 g/L, which is even higher for reject brine, thereby presenting a vast source for magnesium. Increasing the residence time and the temperature used during this calcination process can reduce the MgO surface area, increase the crystallite size, and reduce the reactivity as a result of sintering. This enables a range of MgO products to be produced, depending on the degree of reactivity required. With the goal of optimising this production process, this study will build on the feasibility of producing reactive MgO from reject brine collected from a local desalination plant in Singapore, via the addition of base materials such as NaOH and NH4OH. Previous studies revealed that the addition of NH4OH into reject brine resulted in MgO with a higher specific surface area and reactivity than the use of NaOH. The final product with the highest reactivity and specific surface area (~79 m2/g) was obtained from the calcination of Mg(OH)2 at 500 oC for 2 hours. This research has currently identified potential routes that lead to the production of high reactivity MgO, which can be used in various applications including the semiconductor and pharmaceutical industries, in addition to the construction sector. The next stage would involve the optimisation of this process, followed by a scaled-up trial of the optimised production procedure.
kw: sustainable cement, reject brine, waste material, cement production

title: Highly efficient boron removal process under ambient conditions using nitrogen-doped graphene  nanocomposites
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: For water-scare countries, desalination is a seemingly obvious choice to increase water supplies since the Earth is approximately 71 % covered by water. SWRO is inefficient in removing boron species in seawater to levels as recommended by WHO hence dedicated post-treatment processes are needed. Boron can be removed via addition of chemical additives to encourage precipitation or through adsorption with IEX resins, however these methods are not cost-effective and usually require further remediation to ensure that the needs of product water quality are met. Another issue with most methods is the need to elevate pH to >9 such that chemical equilibrium is shifted to favour borate ions. Borate ions are charged and larger than boric acid which makes them easier to remove. Our proposed solution involves the use of nitrogen-doped graphene oxide (NGO) to achieve high selectivity towards boron species in water. Nitrogen doped sites are able to alter local pH levels such that the formation of borate ions is promoted whereas hydroxyl functional groups serve as anchoring points for chemisorption to occur. In our experiments, we synthesized NGO nanocomposites as three dimensional (3D) matrices with inherent macropores for efficient ion transport. Thus, an absorption column can function at a lower pressure. We have identified 3 key areas of research: (1) optimization of NGO nanocomposites for maximum boron removal, (2) design of a boron rejection column to be integrated with conventional SWRO plant system and (3) optimization of column operation capacity with lower production/regeneration cost. The proposed solution is easy to implement with cost-effective materials yet boasts a highly efficient boron rejection rate. At present, there are no other solutions in the world which come close to our level of efficiency. The success of this project will further cement Singapore as a pioneering waterhub.
kw: boron removal, water treatment, three-dimensional nitrogen-doped graphene oxide and modified carbon network, adsorbent, chemical bonding.

title: DRIVING MECHANISMS OF PAST AND PRESENT SEA-LEVEL CHANGE TO QUANTIFY PROJECTION UNCERTAINTIES
abs: The limited instrumental and paleo sea-level reconstructions in Singapore and South East Asia hinder the interpretation of sea-level change on global, regional and local scales and limit the possibilities to tune and refine models that predict future changes and their spatial variability. We will develop new records of relative sea-level (RSL) change from mangrove environments and coral microatolls to extend the instrumental records from satellite altimetry and tide gauges. The new regional RSL dataset spanning the last ~2000 years (Common Era) will capture multiple phases of climate and sea-level behaviour for model calibration, provide a pre-anthropogenic baseline for assessing recent trends, and characterize natural variability. To estimate global sea level and the spatio-temporal field of Singapore and South East Asia, the new RSL datasets will be combined with satellite altimetry and tide-gauge measurements in an empirical Bayesian statistical framework. The data and models will be used to test the following research questions: (1) Did sea level in Singapore and South East Asia vary as a consequence of the Medieval Climate Anomaly and the Little Ice Age? (2) Is the rate of sea-level rise since ~1850 CE greater than any other centennial trend during the last 2000 years? (3) Can spatial variability of past and present day sea level be attributed to ocean dynamics and/or vertical land motion? Understanding past and present sea-level changes and their driving mechanisms will provide the foundation for accurately projecting future sea levels for Singapore and South East Asia.
kw: Sea level, paleo, instrumental records, ocean dynamics, vertical land motions, uncertainties.

title: Assessing Extreme Sea Level Exposure for Singapore and the central Sunda Shelf Region
abs: In Singapore and throughout the central Sunda Shelf region, coastal flooding associated with periods of extreme sea level (ESLs) can come from temporary storm-induced sea level highs called storm surges, as well as tsunamis generated by earthquakes, landslides or meteorological events (meteotsunamis). In contemporary Singapore, ESLs cause infrequent nuisance flooding to property and ecosystem disruption. We will examine when, where and how such coastal flooding is likely to change with melting of polar ice sheets (e.g. Greenland and Antarctica) and associated sea level rise. Our assessment of current and future storm and tsunami hazard will help coastal planners and decision makers develop mitigation and adaptation measures for ESLs in Singapore, and throughout the region. We will use numerical models for storm surges and tsunamis within a Bayesian framework to investigate extreme scenarios with a range of return intervals. We will first consider both hazards under present climate and sea level before conduct a stepwise analysis considering potential sea-level rises of up to 2.5m, also factoring in potential climatic increases in storm intensity. We will identify areas where wave setup or currents are an important hazard, and areas of geographical complexity where the broad continental shelf and narrow straits provide amplification or protection. The team will examine the currents generated during storm surge events and potential tsunamis, with a particular focus on major port facilities. We will constrain the non-linear interactions of sea level rise with changing bathymetry and topography in the region and quantify the resulting effects, highlighting areas where changes are found to be large, and examine key sites where inundation events or dangerous currents may be strongly enhanced by rising sea level compared to present conditions. Finally, we will investigate the potential for an integrated ESL warning system for Singapore using floating GNSS buoys and existing GNSS facilities. Collectively our outputs will provide core information for effective coastal development in Singapore and through the region.
kw: Extreme sea level; cyclones; storm surges; tsunamis; sea level rise

title: Bacterial metabolic adaptation during host colonisation and persistence
abs: The rapid emergence of multi-drug resistant pathogens such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis is a serious concern worldwide that urgently calls for the development of new therapeutics. To combat the spread of resistance to the antibiotics currently available, there is a growing interest to explore alternate essential cellular processes in bacteria, including central metabolic and bioenergetics pathways, as target space for the development of next-generation antibiotics. The overall objective of the project is to develop strategies to combat infections caused by bacteria; specifically through the exploitation of their metabolic and bioenergetics pathways that are essential during infection and persistence to design novel therapeutics. We will use a multipronged approach to develop novel strategies to eradicate antibiotic-tolerant hypoxic M. tuberculosis, a concept that promises shorter treatment time for tuberculosis. Furthermore, we will study strategies developed by Staphylococcus aureus and other gram-positive bacteria to scavenge host-derived vitamins, which could uncover their vulnerabilities and identify potential druggable targets. Since metabolic adaptation during host-bacteria interaction must also be important for the establishment and maintenance of the natural microbiota, a related objective is to decipher some basic metabolic principles driving the composition and function of the commensal gut microbiome.
kw: tuberculosis, host-pathogen interaction, bioenergetics, MRSA, microbiota, vitamin metabolism, antimicrobial resistance

title: Microbial transformation of plastics in SE Asian seas: A hazard and a solution
abs: As SE Asian nations are among the top ten global emitters of plastic marine debris, the seas of the region are exceptionally vulnerable to plastic pollution, which is long lasting and deleterious to key marine ecosystems that provision the huge coastal populations of the region. Estimates of the half-life of plastics in tropical seas rely on poorly constrained assumptions and the process of plastic breakdown is only partially understood. The role of biofilm in the process has received limited attention, though we predict that as plastic particle size decreases, microorganism–mediated effects become increasingly important, leading to further plastic breakdown, plus impacts on organisms, and ecosystems. We will investigate the role of biofilm in enhancing animal exposure to microplastics and will use sentinel species to monitor input of microplastic to vulnerable mangrove and reef ecosystems. Singapore-based studies on biofilms on plastic sheeting in industrial processes have inspired ourplanned studies of plastic substrates exposed in seawater in the lab and at sites across the region. We will generate metagenomes from biofilms on experimental substrates, from enrichment cultures and from environmental in order to identify potential plastic-degrading enzymes. We predict that anoxic mangrove soils will be a site of plastic sequestration, but also of microbial cutinases and suberinases – enzymes that in some cases have plastic degradation capability. Promising enzyme sequences will be evaluated through our established pipeline of enzyme discovery, characterisation, engineering and then deployment. Together with other measures, this bioprocessing will form part of a toolbox of mitigation, reduction and removal methods to be developed during this project by the research teams interfacing with stakeholders in workshop, dissemination and consultation activities. Stakeholders engaged with the proposed project include a UN agency, national and local government agencies and environmental NGOs. This teamwork, plus our analysis of governance structures, will ensure that outputs from this project, integrated with those from the other SEAP projects, are taken up at all levels in governance of the seas of the region.
kw: biofilm, plastic debris, plastisphere, depolymerization, plastic pollution

title: Wnt signaling in fracture healing and bone regeneration
abs: Abstract: Wnt signaling 21,2 has an important role in a wide range of developmental and homeostatic processes. Wnts have been implicated in limb development; as well as physiological fracture healing and angiogenesis. Haematopoietic cells within the bone marrow microenvironment is a rich source of Wnts 3. Despite this, the role of haematopoietic Wnts is relatively unknown. The aims of this study are (i) to explore the role of haematopoietic Wnts in fracture healing and angiogenesis in the mouse models that we established, and (ii) to exploit our recent findings that Wnts can synergise to produce effects distinct from single/canonical Wnt ligand activity. Through a genome-wide siRNA screen and biochemical interrogations of Wnt signaling pathways active in haematopoietic cells, mediators/inhibitors of Wnt-dependent tissue repair can be identified and therapeutically modulated through the development of neutralizing antibodies or peptides. This study will allow us to develop various biological modalities for the treatment of fractures which have aberrant healing (non-union or delayed union) 4, especially those which are de-vascularized.
kw: Wnt, bone regeneration, fracture healing

title: Molecular control of totipotency and cell fate plasticity
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Totipotent cells have the greatest potential and plasticity, representing the pinnacle of embryonic stem cell fate potential in mammals. Therefore understanding the molecular foundations of totipotency has strong implications in regenerative medicine and disease. We previously identified a maternal factor, NELFA (Negative elongation factor member A), as the earliest driver of the totipotent-like state in mouse embryonic stem cells (ESCs), and showed for the first time that metabolic manipulation can promote the pluripotent-to-totipotent transition (Hu et al., Nature Cell Biology; accepted). NELFA is best known in the context of a larger complex, NELF (Negative elongation factor complex), implicated in transcriptional pausing. Unexpectedly, we uncovered a moonlighting function of NELFA and showed that it can act independently of the NELF complex to promote totipotent gene expression. Building on these discoveries, we propose a series of follow-up studies to elucidate the molecular underpinnings of NELFA-mediated epigenetic reprogramming towards totipotency. First, through identification and functional assessment of NELFA-interacting partners, we hope to derive deeper mechanistic insights into how NELFA reactivates the totipotency gene regulatory network in ESCs. Second, we plan to conduct a comprehensive metabolic assessment of totipotent-like cells to decipher how modulating ESC metabolic activity can actuate enhanced functional potency. Third, beyond understanding the molecular nature of totipotency, we aim to translate our findings to improve cellular reprogramming strategies. Oocytes are the most powerful reprogramming vehicle in nature, outperforming induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) reprogramming procedures. We hypothesize that maternal NELFA (or its interacting partners) may exert a pioneering-like function to accelerate cellular reprogramming. In summary, our study expands the utility of ESCs and opens up new avenues for translational research in regenerative medicine.
kw: developmental biology; transcription; stem cells; germ cells; totipotency; reprogramming

title: A patented antibody for traumatic brain injury
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Cerebral edema and intracranial hypertension can cause severe secondary injuries following traumatic brain injury (TBI). After TBI, derangements in the blood-brain barrier (BBB) are causally relevant for disease progression by precipitating edema formation and intracranial hypertension. Therefore, protecting BBB integrity will ultimately improve the outcome of TBI. Recently, the non-selective cation channel TRPM4 has been found upregulated in central nervous system injuries such as stroke. Our preliminary study has shown that the expression of TRPM4 is also increased in TBI. TRPM4 upregulation and activation result in an over influx of Na+, causing oncotic cell death, and subsequent BBB disruption and cerebral edema. Our lab has developed a TRPM4 blocking antibody M4P which could ameliorate hypoxia induced cell swelling. A patent on this antibody was recently granted by the US patent office. In this proposal, we will extend the use of this antibody to the treatment of TBI in rodents. Pathological changes following TBI such as cerebral vascular injury, blood-brain barrier leakage, and brain edema will be examined. Functional studies will be performed to evaluate the effectiveness of M4P in TBI. M4P was raised against rat TRPM4 channel. However, there exists a difference in the amino acid sequence between rat and human TRPM4. Recently, we generated a monoclonal antibody version of M4P targeting human TRPM4 channel. In this proposal, we will characterize this monoclonal antibody and examine the potential use of this antibody for managing TBI. Current TRPM4 blockers generate a variety of problems, ranging from lack of specificity to side effects or even toxic effect. Thus, our TRPM4 specific antibody provides a powerful tool not only for studying TRPM4 channel, but also for elucidating the pathophysiology of TRPM4 in TBI. Importantly, TRPM4 blocking antibody can be a novel therapy in managing brain injury following TBI.
kw: Head injury

title: Modulation of chimeric antigen receptor T cell (CAR-T) signalling to enhance anti-cancer T cell function
abs: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell technology has shown great potential to combat cancer. However, several bottlenecks, e.g. cytokine release syndrome (CRS), efficacy in solid tumours, tumour escape etc., have hindered its further development. Fine-tuning CAR signaling may hold the promise to overcome these challenges. Yet, the mechanism of CAR signal transduction is poorly understood. Thus, there has been relatively little attempt to enhance CAR-T functions and innovate CAR-T technology by modulation of CAR signaling. We have found that signaling by CD28-CAR-T but not CD137-CAR-T is LCK-independent. In the case of CD28-CAR-T, signaling relies on another SRC family kinase – FYN – and the traditionally crucial kinase LCK is dispensable. The study proposes to further understand the mechanism and significance of LCK-independent CAR signal initiation in CAR-T technology. Primary human T cells and T cell lines are used to characterize CAR-T cell signalling in the absence of LCK. The findings are important steps towards unveiling the mechanism of CAR signal transduction and to understand how co-stimulatory domains can interplay with downstream signaling. LCK-deficient CAR-T cells can be engineered by knocking out LCK in primary T cells. These LCK-deficient CAR-T cells showed more specific recognition and had a more persistent phenotype than normal CAR-T. The proposed study hypothesizes that LCK-deficient CAR-T cells will have a better performance in vivo and less severe CRS. The in vivo evaluation will be performed with clinical samples both in a xenograft mouse model and an immunocompetent mouse model, where the impact of LCK-deficient CAR-T on tumor immunity will be investigated. In addition, the study will explore the generation of novel CAR-T technologies based on LCK-independent signaling, allogeneic CAR-T and AND-gate CAR-T. The exploration will demonstrate the potential to innovate CAR-T technologies via signaling modulation.
kw: chimeric antigen receptor T cell (CAR-T); signal transduction; LCK independent signaling; allogeneic CAR-T; AND-gate CAR-T; next generation of CAR-T

title: Investigate the viral/host determinant(s) for the vertical transmission of flaviviruses using mouse models
abs: Viral infections during pregnancy have been associated with adverse outcomes and birth defects in the children. Viruses rarely cross the placental barrier, but particular viruses such as Zika virus (ZIKV) are known to infect the fetus, resulting in severe birth defects such as microcephaly or even fetal death. Unfortunately, there is limited therapeutic or preventative tools to protect maternal-fetal transmission of viruses. We recently established a mouse model of ZIKV infection that allows vertical transmission of virus in 40-60% of fetuses when the mothers acquire ZIKV infection in pregnancy. Our preliminary data shows that antiviral treatment completely prevents fetal infection with more than 5-fold reduction in placental viral load, suggesting that suppression of virus infection in placenta can reduce the risk of the vertical virus transmission. Interestingly, however, when focusing on individual placenta of untreated control mice, the placental viral load does not always correlate with the opportunity of for fetal infection, suggesting that the viral burden in placenta is not the only determinant that leads maternal-fetal ZIKV transmission. In addition, we found that dengue virus (DENV) infection in pregnancy also allows fetal infection despite of 2-log lower placental viral load compared with ZIKV infection. We hypothesize that there exists a crucial factor(s) that triggers vertical transmission of virus through placental barrier besides the viral burden in placenta. The ultimate goal of this proposal is to discover the key factor(s) that is responsible for vertical transmission of virus, and discover the therapeutic or preventative tools. We will pursue the following specific aims: (1) Discover the factors that permit virus transmission through the placental barrier, (2) Investigate the mechanism that triggers fetal loss induced by serological status, (3) Develop the therapeutics to prevent maternal-fetal transmission of ZIKV.
kw: Zika virus; dengue virus; mouse model; vertical transmission; placenta; antiviral therapy

title: ASCL1 as an oncogenic master transcription factor and therapeutic target in neuroblastoma
abs: Neuroblastoma is an embryonal tumor of the peripheral sympathetic nervous system. The outcome for the patients with high-risk neuroblastoma still remains very poor, emphasizing the need for more effective treatments. Recently, accumulating studies indicated that a relatively small number of transcription factors cooperate to dominate regulation of gene expression program of a given cell identity (termed “master transcription factors”). They typically form an auto-regulatory loop [also called “core regulatory circuit (CRC)”]. In our recent study, we identified ASCL1 as a CRC member in neuroblastoma, which is directly activated by two major neuroblastoma oncogenes, LMO1 and MYCN. Importantly, depletion of ASCL1 induced the differentiation of neuroblastoma cells. These findings led to our hypothesis: ASCL1 may serve as a master transcription factor in neuroblastoma and be responsible for the maintenance of malignant state and differentiation arrest. Notably, high level of ASCL1 expression was associated with inferior survival of neuroblastoma patients. Hence, we further hypothesize that inhibition of ASCL1 is an ideal therapeutic strategy by inducing differentiation of malignant cells in high-risk neuroblastoma. The overall purpose of this project is to elucidate the molecular functions and oncogenic roles of ASCL1 in the pathogenesis of neuroblastoma and to prepare a scientific basis for future therapeutic option. In Aim 1, we will identify the binding partners of ASCL1 and its downstream pathways as well as its involvement in chromatin organization. In Aim 2, we will establish zebrafish transgenic model, in which ASCL1 is overexpressed in adrenergic neuronal progenitor cells, and analyze its tumorigenic ability by itself and in combination with MYCN. We will also analyze the activity of ASCL1 enhancer during normal neuronal development. In Aim 3, we will optimize a therapeutic condition by which inhibition of ASCL1 in combination with retinoic acid treatment induces differentiation of neuroblastoma cells in vitro and in vivo.
kw: Neuroblastoma; LMO1; MYCN; ASCL1; differentiation; therapy

title: Study designs and analytic methods for improving the evaluation of vaccines and other preventive measures against infectious diseases by using within-unit comparison
abs: Standard clinical trial and observational study designs and analytic methods for the evaluation of vaccines and other preventive measures are powerful in estimating their overall effect during a study period. However, they are limited in ability to reveal the time course of the intervention effects or to differentiate different aspects of intervention effects, including the direct effect (among recipients of the intervention) versus indirect effect (among all persons) and the primary effect (via immunogenicity) versus secondary effect (via modifying a person’s disease event history and level of naturally acquired immunity). When the outcome events are localized in space or time or when there is high level of heterogeneity between persons, the evaluation of the above matters is particularly difficult. We propose a series of study designs and data analysis methods that capitalize on within-unit comparisons and on richly parameterized time course functions to address the aforementioned issues. We will evaluate the proposed methods analytically and by simulation guided by realistic infectious disease scenarios. We will use data from a surveillance system of pneumococcal conjugate vaccines and a stepped wedge trial of seasonal malaria chemoprevention to illustrate the methods. The development of the methods and evidence on their superiority over standard methods will facilitate infectious disease research and public health policy in Singapore and elsewhere.
kw: Clinical trials; Infectious disease epidemiology; Prevention; Statistical methods; Vaccine

title: Defining the super-enhancer landscapes in multiple myeloma and its clinical implication
abs: Multiple myeloma (MM) is an incurable plasma cell malignancy, which is clinically and genetically heterogeneous. Recently, super-enhancers (SEs), referring to a large cluster of enhancers in close genomic proximity, have been identified. Compared to typical enhancer, SEs have aberrant high levels of transcription factor and coactivator binding. SEs are central to drive the expression of cell-fate defining genes and emerging as epigenetic driver of oncogenic program in cancer. Whole genome transcriptomic studies have identified the landscape of transcriptome of MM, however, they failed to pinpoint these changes are the drivers of disease or the consequences of plasma cell transformation. Here, we propose to define the SE landscape in MM and discover their cognate genes that are common for MM or subtype-specific. Such approaches would help to identify those true driver genes whose expression must be sustained to transform of plasma cells into malignant state. We will conduct ChlP-seq (H3K27Ac3, BRD4, MED1, POLII) in selected MM patient samples and cell lines, representing major subtypes of MM disease, followed by analysing occupancy of SEs and their associated genes (AIM 1). Then, we will study the role of selected SE-associated genes in MM cell survival, proliferation, and tumor formation in both in vitro and in vivo settings by gain-of and loss-of –function approaches. Biomarkers and novel targets for anti-MM therapy could be unveiled (AIM 2). Last, we will define SE constituent, transcription factor occupancy and SE interactions in a 3D chromatin structure by TF ChIP-seq, dCas9-KRAB and 4C-seq (AIM 3). In conclusion, we believe our study will lead to a greater understanding of the SE features that define the malignant state of MM cells, the identification bona fide driver genes and the development of novel therapeutics for MM.
kw: multiple myeloma, super-enhancer, epigenetics, biomarkers, targeted therapy

title: Landscape of transcriptionally active chromatin in brain health and malignancies
abs: Human brain demonstrates incredible complexity in gene expression programs. However, little is known about architectures of active cis-regulatory elements (AREs) and regulatory circuitries differentiating cell identities between normal and diseased brains. In an effort to build a comprehensive compendium of brain- and brain cancer/glioma-associated AREs, we have charted the H3K27ac-inferred active regulatory landscapes of 12 normal brain tissues, 1 oligoastrocytoma, and 49 glioblastoma/GBM. Analysis of differentially regulated AREs uncovered a strong enrichment of transcription factors and druggable targets in GBM tissues. Functional studies demonstrated critical roles of previously unrecognized super-enhancer-driven genes in GBM. Moreover, ARE-centric classification scheme uncovered transcriptionally active chromatin as a new informative layer that is interconnected to GBM microenvironment, genomic abnormalities, core TF networks, and transcriptional subclasses. Therefore, we hypothesize that active chromatin structures in normal and diseased brain tissues will provide clinically relevant insights into brain homeostasis, pathobiology, and therapeutics. This proposed study will elaborate topographies of transcriptionally active chromatin in both normal brain tissues and glioma biopsies, and explore ARE-centric mechanisms dictating cell identity, as well as core oncogenic dependency. Specific Aim 1 will chart the chromatin and transcriptomic landscape of normal and tumor brain tissues. Chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing and RNA sequencing will be performed in homogenized normal/glioma tissues. Specific Aim 2 seeks to develop integrative molecular classification scheme of brain tissues and construct subtype-associated core transcriptional regulatory circuitries. Specific Aim 3 will explore clinical and functional relevance of super-enhancer-driven genes in glioma. Leading candidates of super-enhancer-driven glioma-promoting genes will be examined for their prognostic potentials and biologic functions. Together, our integrative study will generate a blueprint of disease/glioma-specific ARE atlas in human brain and provide profound insights into both glioma pathobiology and therapeutics. Moreover, our study will establish a framework for exploration of epigenetic dysregulation in other neurological and/or malignant diseases.
kw: Chromatin modification; Core transcriptional regulatory circuitry; Enhancer dysregulation; Epigenetics; Glioma; Glioblastoma

title: DAP3 Reshapes the Cancer Transcriptome as a Master Regulator of RNA Processing: Mechanistic Understanding and Therapeutic Potential
abs: The processing of precursor messenger RNAs including 5’ capping, 3’ polyadenylation and cleavage, splicing and editing of nucleotide sequences is critical to generate diverse and functional mature messenger RNAs. RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) are the key players in RNA processing pathways by directly interact with RNAs in a sequence or structure dependent manner. Dysregulations of RBPs are frequently observed in numerous cancers and drive the tumor initiation and progression. Recently, I discovered a novel RBP, called DAP3, was overexpressed in many cancer types including esophageal and liver cancer, and required for tumorigenesis in in vitro assay and in vivo xenograft model. Transcriptome-wide profiling of DAP3-bound RNA sites by eCLIP revealed DAP3 bound ubiquitously to exonic and intronic regions of RNA transcripts. Strand-specific RNA-seq in DAP3 stable knockdown Huh7 and SNU398 liver cancer cells, as well as KYSE180 and EC109 esophageal cancer cells showed depletion of DAP3 significantly affect on the cancer transcriptome, including gene expression, A-to-I RNA editing, splicing and polyadenylation. By combining our eCLIP data with RNA-seq data, we observed DAP3-regulated splicing and polyadenylation involved direct binding of DAP3 to the splicing and polyadenylation sites and identified splicing and polyadenylation factors SFPQ, NONO and NUDT21 as novel DAP3-interactor. Therefore, we hypothesize overexpression of death-associated protein 3 (DAP3) in cancer dysregulates multiple RNA processing steps including adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) RNA editing, RNA splicing and polyadenylation, which reshapes the cancer transcriptome and drives carcinogenesis. In this study we aim to investigate the role of DAP3 in carcinogenesis in conditional knockout mice model. We also aim to elucidate the molecular mechanisms of how DAP3 reshapes the cancer transcriptome via regulating different RNA processing steps. Last, we aim to Identify DAP3-regulated RNA processing events critical for carcinogenesis and explore the therapeutic potential of targeting these events for cancer treatment.
kw: Cancer, RNA processing, DAP3

title: Role of GASC1-ROCK2 axis in the regulation of liver metabolism under pathological conditions
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a devastating malignancy without targeted therapeutic options. Our preliminary studies revealed that the histone demethylase GASC1 expression was elevated in HCC. GASC1 silencing led to diminished HCC cell proliferation and tumor growth. We also found a positive correlation between GASC1 expression and the protein level of Rho-kinase ROCK2. Mechanistically, GASC1 represses the transcription of FBXO42, a ROCK2 interacting ubiquitinase, through epigenetic demethylation of H3K36me3. GASC1 activity ensured ROCK2 protein stability by blocking its poly-ubiquitination by FBXO42. Treatment with the GASC1 inhibitor SD70 impaired the growth of both HCC cell lines and xenografts in mice, sensitizing them to standard-care chemotherapy. Our work identifies GASC1 as a malignant-cell-selective target in HCC, and GASC1-targeting therapeutics represent promising candidate for novel treatment option to control this malignancy. We also showed that GASC1 depletion led to compromised metabolic flexibility in liver cancer stem cells (CSCs), and significantly reduced expression of key regulators of glucose uptake and glycolytic activity in differentiated non-CSCs. Given that ROCK2 is highly expressed in several models of Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD), we believe the GASC1-ROCK2 axis plays a role in the pathogenesis of NAFLD. We hypothesize that GASC1-ROCK2 axis plays a key role in the regulation of both mitochondrial and glycolytic metabolism in liver under pathological conditions. Specifically, we will investigate the epigenetic regulation of mitochondrial and glycolytic metabolism by GASC1 in both liver CSCs and differentiated non-CSCs (Aim 1); we will also investigate the role of GASC1-ROCK2 axis in the pathogenesis of fatty liver diseases (Aim 2). Accomplishing these studies will allow us to gain significant insights into the role of GASC1-ROCK2 axis in the liver metabolism under pathological conditions. The knowledge obtained from this project will provide us with novel drug targets and open new avenues for anti- HCC and NAFLD therapy.
kw: Liver metabolism; Histone demethylase; Glycolytic activity; Mitochondrial oxidation; Obesity

title: A Biomechanical Sensing Model of Scleral Remodeling in High Myopia
abs: High myopia (HM) and glaucoma are among the most common blinding diseases worldwide. Links between these two conditions have long been reported. Changes in scleral biomechanical properties may play a key role in both diseases. HM is due to excessive eye elongation, which results in scleral biomechanical weakening, allowing focal outpouchings called staphyloma, which immediately precede vision-threatening changes of pathologic myopia (PM). Glaucoma, an optic neuropathy leading to visual field loss, is often associated with elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) and changes in scleral biomechanical properties in the peripapillary (PP) area adjacent to the optic nerve. Although many studies have explored palliative therapies for the vision-threatening changes in PM and glaucoma, the causal mechanism underlying pathologic changes remains unclear. Only a fundamental understanding of the underlying scleral biomechanical alterations will allow the development of preventive therapies. We now have a guinea pig myopia model that can rapidly and readily develop HM with PP staphyloma, and a validated microbead protocol that readily produces glaucomatous animals. Moreover, we have novel imaging modalities that can track changes in vivo in eye shape and biomechanical properties, and assess ex vivo biomechanical properties at a 7-micron resolution. We are therefore well-equipped to test our hypothesize that scleral biomechanical changes in HM are a reaction to stress-induced changes on the PP sclera, facilitated by scleral fibroblast activity, which ultimately leads to pathological changes. Thus, altering fibroblast activity and IOP may slow this progression and explain the link between glaucoma and HM. Specifically, we aim to: 1) elucidate the sequence and location of biomechanical events that underlie PP scleral remodeling in HM, 2) determine the importance and specific changes in PP scleral fibroblast activity to scleral remodeling during HM progression and 3) determine if IOP stress induced by glaucoma fast tracks biomechanical remodeling and associated factors in HM.
kw: Ultrasound; Acoustic Microscopy; fibroblasts; Pathologic; Glaucoma; Myopia

title: Cilia and airway disease: Genes, mechanisms and therapeutic strategy
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Our airways are populated by multiciliated cells (MCCs), a specialised cell-type characterised by hundreds of motile cilia on their apical surface. These cilia beat to generate mechanical force for clearing pathogen- and pollutant-laden mucus, and constitute an essential line of defence for the respiratory system. MCC abnormalities are causative of an expanding spectrum of airway disorders. We use cell biological and genetic analysis in model vertebrates and human cells to study the mechanisms that drive MCC formation and function. Recently, we and others have identified important transcription factors, Gmnc and its paralogue Mcidas (Mci), as central regulators of MCC development. However, large gaps remain in our understanding of MCC formation, especially regarding how they generate hundreds of basal bodies for multiciliation, the relevance of GMNC and MCI in airway disease and interventional strategies to restore cilia function in disease. Here, we describe experiments that will allow us to address these issues. First, we will use CRISPR/Cas9 mediated gene editing in a human embryonic stem cell line and then differentiate them into airway epithelium to assess the roles of GMNC, MCI and associated transcriptional regulators in human MCCs. Next, using transcriptome analysis in airway cells from Mci mutant mice as well as exploration of a novel cytoplasmic localization of Mci indicative of a basal body production nucleating centre, we will unravel the mechanism by which Mci induces basal body biogenesis for multiciliation. Finally, we will examine the feasibility of gene therapy in airway disease by utilizing transgene-mediated rescue of a ciliary gene mutant in the zebrafish and lentivirus mediated gene transduction for mutations of ciliary genes in cultured human airway cells. The knowledge we will derive from this exercise will be of significance in the detection, diagnosis, counselling and the possible development of therapeutic interventions for a variety of respiratory disorders.
kw: Cilia; Multiciliated cell, Mucociliary clearance; Airway disease; Basal bodies; Gene therapy;

title: Autologous neutrophil-infused PCL-TCP scaffold for bone tissue engineering: therapeutic efficacy in a clinically relevant rabbit mandibular model and molecular mechanism
abs: Background: Reconstruction of bone defects due to trauma, tumors or congenital deformities remains a major challenge in modern medicine. The current gold standard of using autologous bone has significant limitations including limited quantity and donor-site morbidity. Modulation of early inflammatory phase is a plausible therapeutic strategy to promote tissue regeneration. Previously we discovered the neutrophil-mediated angiogenic and osteogenic potential in vitro using a triple-cell co-culture model. Subsequently we demonstrated in vivo vascularization and bone regeneration ability of autologous neutrophils using a rabbit calvarial-defect model. The next essential step is to examine this hypothesis using a clinically-relevant large in vivo model, using autologous neutrophils in combination with a scaffold. Additionally, we aim to obtain an insight of the mechanism of action. Objective: The present study aims to evaluate the in vivo efficacy of autologous neutrophils-infused PCL-TCP scaffold on bone regeneration using a rabbit mandibular defect model. Moreover, molecular mechanism pertaining to the angiogenic/osteogenic effects of neutrophils will also be investigated. Methods: Thirty-six rabbits, each with surgically-created two bicortical mandibular defects will be randomly divided into three groups: 1) PCL-TCP with 15×106 neutrophils vs PCL-TCP scaffold alone, 2) PCL-TCP with 30×106 neutrophils vs PCL-TCP scaffold alone, 3) Autologous bone graft vs sham control. Animals will be sacrificed and specimens will be evaluated by micro-CT and histological analyses at 6 and 12 weeks postoperatively. Molecular mechanism of neutrophil-mediated neovascularization will be investigated under normoxic and hypoxic conditions. Neutrophil induced HIF1-alpha signaling pathways will be comprehensively examined by antibody array, Western blot, blocking assays and gene expression analysis. Significance: The proposed study will fulfill essential preclinical stage of this novel approach towards bone bioengineering for craniomaxillofacial bone defects. The success will have considerable clinical impact benefiting patients requiring bone reconstruction, as the need to harvest bone from a donor site could potentially be avoided.
kw: Neutrophils, PCL-TCP scaffold, vascularization, bone regeneration, mandibular defect

title: Regulation of mitochondrial dynamics and function by O-GlcNAc transferase (OGT) in brown adipose tissue
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Obesity poses a significant risk for serious metabolic diseases, such as diabetes mellitus, cardiovascular diseases, and cancer. While white fat is known to accumulate fat as energy storage, two types of fat cells – brown adipocytes and beige adipocytes - conduct non-shivering thermogenesis (NT) via uncoupling of respiration from ATP synthesis in the mitochondria to enable survival under cold conditions. Studies in mice have revealed that brown adipose tissue (BAT) activation promotes energy expenditure and protects against obesity[. Adult humans also possess functional BAT which can produce heat under cold conditions, thus BAT activation has been suggested as a potential therapy for tackling human obesity. However, the full molecular mechanisms remain elusive. O-GlcNAcylation is a nutrient-sensing post-translational modification with altered O-GlcNAc levels implicated in several pathophysiological conditions such as cancer and diabetes. Recent studies have shown that dysregulation of O-GlcNAc modification is also observed in adipocytes of obese rodents and humans. In addition, O-GlcNAc transferase (Ogt) deletion in BAT results in “whitening” of BAT and severe cold intolerance. Our preliminary results further indicate that inducible deletion of Ogt in BAT leads to mitochondrial hyper-fragmentation and compromised mitochondrial functions. Changes in mitochondrial morphology and function are associated with physiological and pathophysiological consequences. The molecular mechanisms governing the mitochondrial morphology of BAT during NT remains unclear. Building on these genetic and biochemical evidence, we hypothesize that OGT plays a key role in regulating BAT mitochondrial structure and function to support the utilization of substrates during non-shivering thermogenesis. This proposal will link OGT to mitochondrial dynamics in BAT and facilitate therapeutic target identification to treat obesity and other metabolic disorders. Here, we propose to (1) examine the role of OGT on mitochondrial morphology and function in BAT and (2) establish the mechanisms of how OGT affects mitochondrial dynamics and BAT thermogenesis.

title: Distilling the bio-signatures and mechanisms underlying severe viral induced acute respiratory distress syndrome
abs: Pediatric acute respiratory distress syndrome (PARDS) is a clinical syndrome characterized by oxygenation failure with significant morbidity and mortality. The pathogenesis of PARDS is complex, involving diverse innate and adaptive immune cell subsets that mediate the propagation of lung injury. A viral etiology is common and is associated with greater hypoxemia in critically ill children with severe pneumonia. To address the complexity of viral-induced PARDS, we will identify pathognomonic immune signatures within the diseased pulmonary microenvironment using multiple high throughput technological platforms (transcriptome and secretome). Specifically, the pulmonary microenvironment transcriptomic profiles will be determined using probe-based NanoString technology with subsequent single-cell RNA sequencing to distill the immune cell heterogeneity and track their trajectories in a well-characterized longitudinal PARDS cohort. Differential gene expression (DGE) analysis will be done to identify differences between mild and severe viral induced PARDS to determine the key mechanisms responsible for disease progression. The pulmonary inflammatory secretome (pro-inflammatory, anti-inflammatory, chemokines, cytokines and growth factors) will be determined concurrently using multiplex luminex technology. Cross-platform data integration between transcriptomic and secretomic profiles will ensure robustness of the identified immune-signatures. After identifying the pathognomonic pulmonary immune signatures, we will seek to identify the peripheral blood immune profile complementary to the pulmonary microenvironment with a dual translational potential for disease monitoring and therapeutic manipulation.
kw: acute respiratory distress syndrome; acute lung injury; pneumonia; virus; pediatrics; intensive care unit

title: Engineering probiotic to fight obesity: Modulating gut hormone level and increasing butyrate production to reduce appetite
abs: The prevalence of obesity has increased tremendously over the last few decades. This poses a huge global public health problem. Increasing evidences are supporting that appetite is regulated by the gut-brain axis via gut peptides like Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), Peptide YY (PYY) and Oxyntomodulin (OXM). Butyrate may also play a part in preventing and treating obesity by promoting fatty acid oxidation, inhibiting fat accumulation and stimulating gut peptides secretion. Modulating gut hormone level and increasing butyrate production are promising therapies against obesity and diabetes mellitus. The hypothesis of this study is to use bioengineered probiotic gut microbe as a non-invasive in-situ delivery of gut hormones (i.e. GLP-1, OXM and PYY), and to increase the production of butyrate, which can act synergistically to reduce food intake and body weight. In this study, I aim to develop and validate the bioengineered probiotic in three phases. First, a bacterial system that can express and secrete recombinant gut peptides will be constructed and characterized. The system will be optimized to produce concentration that is comparable to therapeutic dose. Second, the functional activity of these recombinant gut peptides will be evaluated on neuronal cell lines for its ability to promote satiety signalling. Last, the bioengineered probiotics that are secreting functional gut peptides and increasing butyrate production will be tested on an obese mice model to evaluate the efficacy in reducing apetite and weight. In addition, changes in plasma level of gut peptides, plasma lipids and tolerance to insulin and glucose will be thoroughly assessed. The outcome of this research will serve an important foundation of using bioengineered probiotics to modulate hormonal and butyrate level to mitigate obesity, which is fast becoming a huge global health crisis.
kw: Obesity; synthetic biology; gut peptides; butyrate; probiotics

title: Portable SERS-based Breathalyzer for Rapid and Online COVID-19 Detection and Surveillance
abs: Breath volatile organic compounds (BVOCs) in human breath have shown promise for the detection of biomarkers for the diagnosis of COVID-19 and other illness. However, existing breathalyzers are not portable and not able to perform on-site screening. Our team has developed a breathalyzer using surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) platform for multiplex metabolite and molecular detection. This proposal focuses on achieving instant and direct SERS readout of multiplex BVOCs-related to COVID-19 at the point-of-need. The major goal of this proposal is to use our SERS-based breathalyzer to perform a case-control study involving 100 COVID-positive and non-COVID-19 subjects. We will measure the SERS profiles of these subjects and develop a machine-learning-driven prediction model to differentiate the COVID-positive and negative populations in a rapid and automated manner. Our SERS-based breathalyzer system aims to achieve a non-invasive and rapid diagnosis of COVID-19 in less than 15 minutes. The successful prototyping and deployment of our SERS-breathalyzer will address the current lack of rapid COVID-19 screening kit for high-throughput and routine screening, which is of utmost importance if countries want to return human activities to normalcy. Additionally, the development of our system also gives rise to the potential of bypassing the swabbing tests for surveillance testing, which cause high discomfort and requires trained professionals for sampling. The test results also can be significantly shortened which can increase our capacity for testing. We emphasize that there are presently no SERS-based COVID-19 diagnostic kit in the market or at the trial stages. Our SERS breathalyzer is well-positioned to fill the technological gap and provide the ideal solution to address the limitations present in current emerging technologies. NTU’s SERS spin-off company, Silver Factory Technology (SFT), is working to ensure seamless translation of this SERS-based research towards commercialization and manufacturing with ISO13485 medical standard for eventual HSA and FDA approval.

title: Characterisation of longitudinal tumour transcriptomic and immune microenvironment changes to predict response to targeted radionuclide therapy in metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma
abs: Distant metastatic recurrence predominates in nasopharyngeal carcinoma patients who recur following definitive treatment. In this unfavourable subgroup of patients, conventional chemotherapy with gemcitabine and cisplatin represents the standard of care for first-line therapy, but response to this doublet chemotherapy is often short-lived. We have shown that somatostatin receptor 2 (SSTR2) is upregulated in recurrent/metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma. As a result, we have proposed a single-arm prospective phase II clinical trial to investigate the objective response rate (ORR) of 177Lu-DOTATATE, which is tumour-specific radionuclide therapy that binds to SSTR2, in recurrent/metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma patients who have progressed following first-line chemotherapy. The mechanism of action with this radionuclide agent is primarily through DNA damage induced by direct ionising radiation effects on the tumour cells. Nonetheless, there is now emerging evidence supporting the effects of ionising radiation on the tumour immune environment, whereby radiation can induce tumour cell killing through a parallel immune cell death mechanism. The radiation immune response is however widely heterogeneous between patients, which can be explained by the interplay between host- and tumour-specific factors that cooperate to modulate the systemic and local immune contextures. In this study, we propose to investigate the changes in the tumour microenvironment by profiling for expression of immune- and inflammatory-related genes following treatment with 177Lu-DOTATATE. We further hypothesise that these responses are correlated to tumour responses with this radionuclide therapy; clinical responders will demonstrate an activated and inflamed tumour, with further upregulation of these pathways following treatment. In contrast, non-responders will demonstrate a “cold” immune environment at baseline that remains unstimulated post-targeted radiation. The longitudinal surveillance of the immune environment in response to treatment provides for a comprehensive analysis to determine the baseline and early treatment-related correlates of response to 177Lu-DOTATATE.
kw: nasopharyngeal cancer, radiotherapy, theragnostics, immunology, radionuclide therapy

title: Identification of novel pathways involved in the genesis of carpal tunnel syndrome- Fibrosis, mast cells and more
abs: The Carpal Tunnel Syndrome (CTS) is the most common entrapment neuropathy of the upper limbs encountered in primary care and is the result of the compression of the median nerve within the wrist while it passes through the carpal tunnel. It leads to numbness and paresthesia with potential pain and in more severe cases muscles weakness and nerve damage. The most efficient treatment is a surgical intervention to release the carpal tunnel through transection of the transverse carpal ligament (TCL). No pharmacological solution currently exists to treat CTS besides corticosteroids injections which relieve the symptoms but do not prevent the progression of the disease. The most common histological finding in CTS is that of fibrosis of the subsynovial connective tissue (SSCT) and currently represents a promising therapeutic target to investigate in order to develop new pharmacological avenues aimed at CTS treatment. Abnormal mast cells activation has been reported to be involved in other joints conditions and injuries in which fibrosis development has been associated. We hypothesised that unusual mast cells activation may play a role in CTS development and that the use of a mast cell stabilizer such as ketotifen could represents a new therapeutic strategy in CTS treatment. Therefore using tissue samples collected from CTS patients and control tissues obtained from cadavers and non-CTS patients requiring wrist surgery we aim to investigate the fibrotic pathways involved in CTS related to mast cell activation. We also aim to establish metabolic, proteomic and redox profiles of both TCL and SSCT to explore the progression mechanism of CTS and potentially identify new pharmacological ways to treat it.
kw: Carpal tunnel syndrome, fibrosis, mast cells

title: Single cell Profiling to Evaluate Genetic and Epigenetic Abnormalities of p53 in Multiple Myeloma
abs: Background Multiple myeloma (MM) is an incurable plasma cell malignancy with an incidence of 100 patients per year in Singapore. TP53 is a key tumour suppressor gene inactivated in many cancers. Loss of p53 through chromosome 17p deletion or mutation is associated with a poor prognosis in MM and is more frequent at disease progression. It is possible that the remaining p53 allele may be inactivated through epigenetic mechanisms but this cannot be detected through standard diagnostic tests. Similarly, clonal heterogeneity of p53 abnormalities in MM and their evolution over time have not been described. The impact of p53 deregulation through different mechanisms on clinical outcomes is also not known. We propose using the single cell genotype, expression, methylation (sc-GEM) assay to study p53 abnormalities in MM. sc-GEM is a technique which allows single cell analysis of mutational profile, gene expression and DNA methylation status in a single high throughput microfluidics platform. This technique has been used successfully in primary lung cancer specimens. Hypothesis scGEM can unravel the spatial and temporal heterogeneity of p53 pathway abnormalities in MM at the single cell level. Methods We will apply sc-GEM to study patient bone marrow samples from our myeloma cell bank. SC-GEM will be used to profile the remaining p53 allele in patients with 17p deletion or p53 mutations. We will also study p53 abnormalities in patients with monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) as well as smouldering myeloma to determine how p53 abnormalities change with disease evolution. Finally, we will correlate p53 abnormalities defined by sc-GEM with clinical outcomes. Proposed Statistical Analysis We will be conducting the final analysis through the scripted SINGuLAR analysis toolet ( Fluidigm) software. sc-GEM data will be correlated back to patient’s clinical information to look for associations with known prognostic factors.

title: An Artificial Intelligence-powered Approach to Precision Immunotherapy of Human Arthritis
abs: Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) is the epitome and the most common of autoimmune diseases. There is no cure for RA. The combination of partial efficacy of available, expensive treatments, and the chronic burden on patients and Society makes an effective transformational intervention a priority. A safe and affordable therapeutic approach reliant on the true restoration of immunological balance via the induction of tolerance is still an unfulfilled promise. The incomplete understanding of the mechanisms of immune tolerance leads to the lack of a therapeutic immune intervention truly capable of restoring immune balance safely, effectively clinically and financially and, perhaps, permanently. We developed programs of high translational value which will be advanced here to address the following specific objectives, which are comprised in the overarching goal: To identify and dissect mechanisms of induction of immune tolerance in RA patients in response to immune therapy with dnaJP1, a microbiome-derived peptide. dnaJP1 is an E.coli derived peptide which has been developed for immune tolerance. In previous work, we have treated for six months a total of 96 RA patients with clear safety, biological and clinical effects, and have generated mechanistic hypotheses, and the tools to address them. The specific aims of the project are: Specific aim 1) Can we discern how RA perturbates the architecture of the healthy Immunome, and distil mechanisms and cell subsets which are clinically and pathogenically relevant?; Specific Aim 2a) Is the increase in PD1 Treg the pivot for clinically relevant immune tolerization? Specific Aim 3) As dnaJP1 is a microbiome peptide, how does the interface between microbiome and immunity affect tolerization? This project integrates AI in immune therapy, with the potential to directly benefit patients by developing an effective, safe and financially viable cure for the most common autoimmune disease.
kw: Immunome; Artificial Intelligence (AI); Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)

title: Precision medicine using single cell genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics and lipidomics in fluid biopsies to diagnose and manage primary vitreoretinal lymphoma
abs: Primary vitreoretinal (VRL) is predominantly a diffuse large B cell lymphoma (DLBCL). It is a subset of primary central nervous system (CNS) lymphoma and both are increasing in incidence worldwide. VRL leads to vision loss but its associated CNS involvement (50-85%) results in loss of neurological function and even death. We recently published improved MYD88 mutation detection in VRL by using single cell technology. Our preliminary data also suggests that proteomic and lipidomic analysis can elucidate protein and lipid signatures from lymphoma B cells that represent treatment response. VRL management is currently hampered by low diagnostic rates and limited drugs for ocular treatment especially in refractory or relapsed disease. This study aims to use single cell technology to overcome these limitations. We hypothesize that single cell genomic mutation testing will improve current diagnostic sensitivity, specificity and predictive values (Hypothesis 1). We will determine the diagnostic role of single cell next generation sequencing of MYD99, CD79B mutations and chromosomal copy number aberrations compared to diagnostic cytology and cytokine ratios of IL10 and IL6 (Aim 1) as means to improve our current diagnostic rates. To address the limitation in therapeutics, we hypothesize that MYD88 and CD79B mutations result in upregulation of molecular and proteins related to B cell receptor signalling and NFKB pathways that may correlate with treatment response. Additionally, treatment-resistant lymphoma cells show upregulation of lipid regulatory pathways (Hypothesis 2). We will determine the molecular, proteomic and lipidomic signatures of treatment-resistant and responsive B lymphoma cells in lymphoma cell lines with MYD88 and CD79B mutations after treatment with current and new VRL therapies (Aim 2). These signature will be correlated with patient samples and outcomes to determine the clinical relevance for use as precision medicine in VRL and CNS lymphoma theragnostics (Aim 2) in order to improve our therapeutic management.

title: Deeply Subwavenghth Superoscillatory Imaging (DSSI)
abs: Resolution of conventional far-field microscopy does not go beyond a half of the wavelength of light, preventing imaging of sub-wavelength features of the sample, while sophisticated and powerful super resolution techniques such as STED and STORM require labelling of samples with luminescent material that is not acceptable for many biomedical and nanotechnology applications. We have recently developed a new principle of super-resolution imaging that exploits advances of singularity optics and artificial intelligence. Our pump-priming modelling studies and pump-priming experiments show that our Deeply Subwavelength Superoscillatory Imaging can reveal the fine structure of a physical object through its far-field scattering pattern under illumination with topologically structured light that contains optical singularities. The image is reconstructed from intensity profiles of scattered light by a convolutional neural network trained on a large number of scattering events. We have shown that this approach offers resolution orders of magnitude beyond the conventional “diffraction limit”. The main objective of the Programme is to build a practical Deeply Subwavelength Superoscillatory Imaging instrument, investigate limitations of the technology and demonstrate a variety of imaging modalities including 1D, 2D and 3D imaging aiming at never previously achieved far-field unlabelled sample resolution exceeding wavelength/100. Imaging modalities for applications for nanotechnology and biology will be developed and tested on silicon chips, nanomechanical devices, carbon nanostructures, 2D material devices and DNA origami structures.
kw: Super-resolution imaging, Nano-Photonics, Artificial Intelligence

title: Sources, impacts and solutions for plastics in South East Asia coastal environments.
abs: Marine coastal environments provide an abundance of natural resources, which sustain economies and societies that are under increasing pressure because of different sources of pollution. The South East (SE) Asian region is facing one of the most important marine plastic pollution crises on the planet, threatening the biodiversity of marine ecosystems and environmental resources, on which depends the economic growth. Plastics are persistent in the marine environment and are mainly degraded by mechanical abrasion, which leads to smaller plastic particles and fibres < 5mm, defined as microplastics (MP) that are of increasing concern. At the organism level, the impact of MPs has been described for many taxa, including plankton, invertebrates, fish, sea turtles, and marine mammals. At the cellular level, MPs can alter digestive enzymes activities such as lipase, esterase, trypsin, amylase, or alkaline phosphatase in several organisms. MPs can also induce oxidative stress through the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), when plastics are recognised as foreign particles by inflammatory cells. Although studies have investigated which species are more susceptible to the plastic uptake within the marine foodwebs, their effects on the ecosystem functioning are not fully understood or quantified at the molecular level. This proposal will describe the threat of different types of marine plastics (MPs), including source and fate in the marine environment (trophic mobility) by monitoring their distributions and abundance in marine compartments (horizontal and vertical distribution and assessing their ecological effects at both organisms and molecular levels to understand their implications for food safety issue, fisheries and human health.

title: Solution-Processed Perovskite Materials for Next-Generation Integrated X-Ray Sensors
abs: X-ray machines are widely used in medical diagnostics, airport security, baggage screening, and industrial non-destructive inspection. However, current X-ray detection technologies involving conventional or flat-panel detectors are not suitable for 3D imaging of curved objects such as conformal electronics, because the fabrication of large-area, flexible, silicon-based photodetectors on highly curved optical surfaces remains a challenge. In addition, traditional scintillators, which are key components of X-ray detectors, generally require high-temperature processing. In this proposal, we aim to design a series of perovskite nanocrystals and investigate their radioluminescent properties. We also plan to develop spectroscopic and microscopic techniques that allow us to correlate radioluminescence dynamics in the local structure of perovskite nanocrystals at a single-particle level. In addition, quantum simulation based on density functional theory (DFT) and time-dependent DFT will be employed as a complementary tool to probe the electron exchange process in terms of the spatial distribution of excited-state wave-functions for low-dimensional perovskites. The results will provide a better understanding of X-ray energy conversion and mechanisms through perovskite-based scintillators. A central theme of this proposal is to evaluate the solution processability of these nanomaterials for thin-film fabrication and its utility as high-sensitivity detectors for X-ray imaging applications. We propose to design and construct ultrasensitive, flat-panel X-ray detectors, fast CT scanners and flexible radiographic imagers for medical imaging and non-destructive electronics inspection, and also to benchmark the detector prototypes against existing commercial detectors. In conclusion, this proposal presents a conceptual advance in the implementation of low-dimensional perovskites as scintillators that could open new avenues to the construction of ultrasensitive X-ray detectors and flexible radiographic platforms. Our proposed solution is novel in terms of material synthesis, scintillation performance, fabrication cost, and radiographic technology.

title: Smart antifouling polymer composites
abs: Widespread adoption of composites as alternatives to metal, steel and wood in many applications are occurring due to their low cost to weight savings, versatility, improved life cycle, good mechanical properties and corrosion resistance. As a result, composites find themselves being increasingly used in fouling environments. With their growing use in sectors such as building and construction, marine, aquaculture and urban farming as well as oil and gas industries in and around Singapore, the need for robust and sustainable antifouling solutions for composites become increasingly important. However, the present antifouling methods predominantly involve the use of biocides which are harmful to the environment or coating solutions which lack mechanical strength and long-term stability. The key objective of this project is to develop polymer composites for direct deployment in fouling environments without the use of coatings or biocides, thereby offering a long-term solution, and are sustainable and environmentally benign. In our non-coating solution to combat fouling, nanoscale dispersion of hybrid fillers such as graphene oxide and titanium dioxide would be incorporated directly into polymeric matrices via processing methods, such as vacuum forming and molding, to create composites with tunable and smart characteristics such as antifouling, antistatic and self-cleaning functions. The performance of the resulting composites would be benchmarked against commercially available antifouling coating products. It is to be noted that the product developed under this proposal will be evaluated by Jonite Pte Ltd (Collaborator and end-user) and used for their existing range of products and applications. In addition, the dispersion of hybrid nano-fillers is also of potential interest to Lubrizol Southeast Asia Pte Ltd (Collaborator and team member). The proposed project will built upon an earlier intellectual property (IP) developed by this research team from Republic Polytechnic (RP) on bulk polymer composites exhibiting self-cleaning properties without the use of coatings, of which Jonite Pte Ltd is currently in the process of finalizing the commercial license agreement with RP for this IP.
kw: smart; antifouling; polymer; composites

title: Hypernutritious crop through nutrient recipe formulation and controlled stress induction
abs: Singapore has been looking at ways to improve food security, and the “30 by 30” is an ambitious goal towards that direction. It is expected that many more indoor farms will be built over the years as the agricultural industry becomes more promising. To support this rapid growth, the agricultural technology sector has to innovate and develop. Growing indoor using under controlled environment agriculture (CEA) system, plant growth can be optimized to maximize yield. Due to the fierce competition and high running cost, there is a need to be more resource efficient and/or to produce better produce. One of the ways is to reformulate the hydroponics nutrient solution such that nutrient update by the crops are in ratio, such that it will not become imbalanced when residual nutrient accumulates. Current practice is to discharge the imbalanced nutrient solution after a few growth cycles, and this poses a waste to the farm and an environmental risk of eutrophication. On the other hand, increasing the value of the crop can be done by increasing the phytonutrient of plant. Plant produces many metabolites and some of them are inducible by stress to combat the internal ROS. Some of these metabolites, such as phenolics, flavonoids, carotenoids, have antioxidant properties and confer health benefits when consumed. This project is thus setup in a 2-prong approach: 1) better nutrient solution recipe for better growth and reduced wastage, and 2) improved plant phytonutrient via specific stress treatment regime.
kw: Plant; Nutrient; Stress; Phytonutrient; Development

title: 3D Monitoring-Tracking System to Inspect Inaccessible Internal Aerostructure
abs: Aviation market in Southeast Asia is one of the fastest expending markets in the world, and it is expected to become the world’s largest in the next 20 years. Powered by rapid economic growth and increasing popularity of budget carriers, there is increasing passenger traffic and aircraft demand– around 40% of the global deliveries of new aircrafts (42,000 planes) will come from the Asia-Pacific region from 2018-2037. The consequent need for maintenance as well as the technological upgrades of existing fleet is set to promote the role of Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul (MRO) services in assuring aircraft safety and airworthiness. In this regard, Singapore has made itself as one of the world’s leading and Asia’s largest MRO hubs, and is already recognised as the “Aerospace City of the Future”. The MRO sector in Singapore is growing at a healthy 8.6%, accounting for over 25% of Asia’s MRO revenues and up to 10% of the global output. Major aerospace leaders such as Rolls Royce and Airbus have a long-term and significant footmark in Singapore. Local bigwigs such as SIA Engineering Company and ST Engineering (world’s largest MRO provider) continue to expand their operations. With over 130 aerospace players operating in the market, Singapore hosts a large and diverse ecosystem which caters to engines, components and avionics for comprehensive nose-to-tail services. In aircraft MRO service, borescopes is an important tool to inspect inaccessible regions of objects. For example, when inspecting the internal structure of a jet engine for cracks or fatigue, small openings from the outside allow the borescope to be snaked into the engine without having to drop the engine from the plane. During the process, it is often difficult for operator to know the exact borescope tip location within the engine, making it tough to identify the location of new cracks found or to return to previously identified trouble spots. When a crack is found, the operator must measure its size and location which is puzzling if the borescope’s pose is unknown. Traditional techniques for tracking an object do not work well within the environment a borescope typically encounters. Electromagnetic fields are corrupted by the surrounding presence of metal. Acoustic techniques are susceptible to ringing caused by metal parts and convoluted passages, and any technique that relies on a clear line of sight is by definition implausible in the borescope inspection environment. The only option is tracking based on the borescope images themselves or any embedded sensors which has minimum impact. In this context, we propose an enhanced borescope imaging system that utilizes 3D imaging technology, Artificial Intelligence (AI), simultaneous localization and mapping(SLAM) , Image/Signal Processing and pattern recognition technology to address the issue of pose estimation of borescope. title: A Cross-Platform, Smart Drone Control Framework
abs: ACADEMIC SIGNIFICANCE: Sustained productivity is critical for economic growth and the productivity push has become a national agenda with the Singapore government introducing a slew of initiatives. As part of RIE2020’s strategic goals, there is a call to tap on autonomous technologies and innovative digital applications to enhance urban mobility and service productivity [18]. In the Land Transport [13] and Air Transport [2] Industry Transformation Maps, there are similar calls for exploitation of innovative drone technologies to enhance productivity and improve processes. With multiple drones increasingly deployed in missions, support for autonomous teamwork is essential. Currently, autonomous teamwork in a group of drones can be achieved with customised, on-board firmware. Such drones are costly, for special missions and not available commercially. For example, the Perdix drones developed for surveillance in a US$20 million programme [15], and the US$29.7 million LOCUST programme for military operations [14]. Commercial programmable drones like TelloEdu or the AR Parrot Drone, however, can only be flight controlled via pre-defined code blocks that do not support autonomous teamwork. Some commercial drones have been equipped with AI to help make sense of image data [4]. To-date, there is no reported initiative for enabling autonomous teamwork for drones based on mission intelligence. We propose a cross-platform, mission-focused machine learning framework to support real-time autonomous teamwork for multiple deployed drones. The framework can support different missions flexibly without excessive re-programming. It can be implemented on drone controller platforms e.g. mobile phones, tablets or Raspberry-PIs, removing the need to customise IP-protected drone firmware. The current move by major platform enterprises, like Microsoft and Enterprise Ethereum Alliance, towards cross-platform development strengthens the commercial basis and significance of this approach. A range of specified applications can be supported via a plug-and-play design enabling a best-mix of commercial drones to be deployed with reduced dependency on human pilots. For airspace-limited Singapore, this proposal offers a commercially-viable solution for enhancing productivity and work-related safety. Under the framework of Singapore’s first broad university-industry partnership, the Association of Small and Medium Enterprises and the Singapore Institute of Technology (SIT) will collaborate to build industry capability for local SMEs. Our project’s outputs will create value by directly contributing to knowledge and technology innovation as well as enterprise development of SMEs.
