title: SINGAPORE ANGLE CLOSURE GLAUCOMA PROGRAM: FROM GENETICS TO PRECISION MEDICINE AND THERAPY
abs: Glaucoma is the leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide, with primary angle closure glaucoma (PACG) a major form of glaucoma in Singapore and Asia. For the past decade, my research program has made substantial contributions to the understanding of the epidemiology, risk factors, genetics, imaging features, clinical phenotype and management of PACG. However, we have almost no data to inform clinical practice about which individuals are at greatest risk for developing advanced PACG and blindness. While we have made advances via genome wide association studies and have identified common genetic variants that increase risk for PACG, there is a need to identify and evaluate more genetic factors for PACG via whole exome sequencing in order to uncover new genetic risk factors, pathways/mechanisms and thus potentially new treatments to prevent blindness. We hope to integrate novel genetic and ocular biomarkers of PACG using a multimodal artificial intelligence approach in order to identify individuals with highest risk of advanced visual loss so as to develop and enhance personalized management strategies for PACG. We will then validate this new algorithm for the prediction of advanced PACG using prospectively ascertained clinic-based cohorts. Finally, with the identification of new genes with deleterious rare variants conferring large effect sizes from whole exome sequencing, we need to understand better the biological impact and physiological relevance of new gene(s) and their role in the PACG disease process. Such genetic findings have the potential to illuminate therapeutic targets. This program will capitalize on the multi-disciplinary team of clinician-scientists and researchers with unique access to clinical data and DNA that we have collected over a decade from on-going studies in Singapore. Furthermore, we have a network of international collaborators with access to global PACG data, and have demonstrated our ability to lead and utilize these datasets for important findings.
kw: Primary angle closure glaucoma; exome sequencing; Ophthalmic genetics; imaging, gene function, risk prediction

title: Using Novel imaging biomarkers to predict Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor inhibitor retreatment load for neovascular Age related Macular Degeneration
abs: Current treatment for neovascular age related macular degeneration (nAMD) requires frequent injections of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) inhibitors. Retreatment strategies are dependent on disease activity assessed at every visit which is defined as a combination of clinical signs and fluid detected in the different compartments of the retina by optical coherence tomography (OCT). This strategy results in large variability of retreatment (4-12 injections per year) and it is currently unknown as to which patients may have higher or lower retreatment requirements. This study aims to use disease features on OCT in the early treatment phase (baseline to month 3) to predict which patient may require low or high retreatment. A “severity score” will be derived by the associations of OCT features detected at baseline and changes of these features at month 3 (assessed by trained graders and with a novel machine-learning (ML) algorithm) with patients with optimal outcomes that have either required high retreatment (≥6 treatments/year) or low retreatment (<6 treatments/year) over 12 and 36 months. This will be a retrospective analysis using data from a comprehensive AMD registry. (2)This score will be validated using a prospective cohort study with patients divided into high/low retreatment groups based on the severity score and treated with standard of care. Primary outcome will be to compare number of injections required over 1 year between groups. Early stratification of patients can help identify those that may require closer monitoring and may have potentially the most benefit from switch in drug. A comprehensive dataset from the validation study can be used to further inform retreatment interval at each visit allowing for even more individualized treatment. Overall these results may change current clinical practice by providing more precision in retreatment decision individualizing management for each patient from visit to visit.
kw: Imaging Biomarkers; AMD; Anti VEGF

title: Decoding Protein–Protein Interactions in Single Dendritic Spines
abs: One of the greatest challenges in neuroscience is to decipher molecular mechanisms of brain plasticity and its impact on diseases. Changes in the strength of neuronal connections, a process known as synaptic plasticity, is believed to underlie learning and memory formation. Defects in synaptic plasticity are commonly implicated in the pathogenesis of neurodevelopmental disorders such as autism and fragile X syndrome (FXS). Various forms of synaptic plasticity are mediated by dynamic biochemical signaling through protein–protein interactions (PPIs) in dendritic spines, which are small postsynaptic compartments of neurons. Despite intensive studies in the past decades, the dynamic mechanisms regulating synaptic plasticity remain poorly understood partly due to the lack of techniques to precisely probe PPIs in dendritic spines. In this proposal, we will develop an innovative strategy to image PPIs with unprecedented accuracy and detail, and elucidate mechanisms of PPIs underlying synaptic plasticity in healthy and diseased states. In our preliminary studies, we have successfully imaged endogenous PPIs at a single spine resolution by combining a cutting-edge protein labeling technology with an advanced imaging system. In this study, we will further expand this strategy and establish a generic platform for probing various endogenous PPIs in living neurons (Aim1). We will then elucidate the mechanisms of PPIs underlying spine actin remodeling (Aim2) and investigate the spatiotemporal dynamics of PPIs implicated in FXS (Aim3). Because PPIs regulate almost all neurobiological processes, the proposed strategy will be broadly applicable to many fields in neuroscience. Further, we expect to elucidate when, where, and how PPIs regulate synaptic plasticity and how they are disrupted in FXS. This may provide significant insights into the molecular basis of synaptic dysfunction commonly observed in various neurodevelopmental disorders of unknown origin.

title: Engineering Personalized Cancer Vaccines Using Pluripotent Stem Cells-Derived Red Blood Cells As Artificial Antigen Presenting Cells
abs: Immunotherapies that boost the ability of T cells to eradicate cancer cells have achieved remarkable clinical efficacy in a range of human malignancies. Despite their revolutionary success, there are still limitations in the immunotherapy approaches. For example, CAR T-cells target tumor-associated antigens that are also expressed in normal tissues potentially leading to tissue damage. Furthermore, solid tumors are less susceptible to CAR-T therapies. On the other hand, checkpoint inhibitors have demonstrated efficacy in several cancer types, including solid tumors, but are ineffective in tumors with low tumor mutation burden and low T-cells infiltration (“cold” tumors). These limitations thus underscore the need to develop alternative strategies. Solid tumors constitute an immune privilege microenvironment that restricts access of T-cells and their ability to detect mutated antigens. Enhancing tumor-specific antigen recognition through vaccination would be an attractive therapeutic strategy for such tumors. In particular, neoantigens arising from tumor-specific mutations are not present in normal tissues and hence present excellent immune targets for vaccine immunotherapy. Indeed, neoantigen-specific T-cells are postulated to be the most potent immune cells in tumor rejection. Advancement in sequencing technologies and computation prediction tools have made it possible to identify and predict patient-specific neoantigens. Recent clinical trials with neoantigen vaccines have demonstrated potent T-cell responses and anti-tumor effects in patients, including those with ‘’cold tumors’’. Despite the tremendous therapeutic potential of neoantigen vaccines, including the promise of personalized treatment, significant challenges remain. These include: 1) the lack of an effective delivery strategy that targets the vaccine to the dendritic cells (DC) and 2) the ability to accurately predict immunogenic neoantigens. Notably, current vaccination methods using RNA and peptides require multiple boosters over an extended period of time, potentially due to inadequate delivery to DC – the professional antigen presenting cells (APC) in the body. Because current in silico prediction programs are suboptimal, only a very small proportion of predicted neoantigens actually elicit anti-tumor response in the patients. These challenges call for a need for a reliable, rapid, and high-throughput method for empirical validation of predicted neoantigens. In this proposal, I aim to address both issues through the engineering of an artificial antigen presenting cell (aAPC). Firstly, to address 1) the lack of an effective cancer vaccine delivery approach, I propose to engineer red blood cells (RBC) to present antigens for activating endogenous CD8+ T-cells. RBC present as an attractive alternative aAPC candidate for in vivo vaccination given the lack of genetic material and endogenous MHC complex. title: Development of Novel Electric Machine Systems with Gearless Structure for Emerging Applications
abs: The broad objective of the proposed research is to develop novel electric machine systems with gearless structures. The proposed electric machine systems consist of very high potential to be employed in areas of emerging applications, including electric vehicles, electric ships and wind power generations. The proposed gearless machine systems can enjoy definite merits of high efficiency, high power density, high torque density, maintenance-free and compact structure. All the mentioned emerging applications share similar features of high-torque low-speed characteristics and differential features. To provide sufficient torque-speed level and differential feature for standard operations, a mechanical gearbox has to be installed together with high-speed electric machines. This undesirable mechanical gearbox not only suffers from mechanical loss and maintenance issue, but also heavy weight and bulky size. Additional loss and weight from gearbox definitely deteriorates operating range, which is a major concern for most of the emerging applications. In this project, novel machine concepts, i.e., magnetic gearing and magnetic differential, will be proposed and developed. The proposed electric machines can be inbuilt with gearing and differential features to provide same operations from mechanical gearbox. The undesirable gearbox can then be eliminated for gearless operations. New design equations and analytical models of the proposed electric machines will be developed for machine optimizations. An experimental prototype will be established for concept verifications. The technical performances and market values of the proposed machine systems in various applications will be evaluated. In conclusion, this proposed research will explore a new direction for electric machines.
kw: electric machine; electric vehicle; electric ship; wind power generation

title: Develop an innovative flow reactor system for green and cost-effective spent battery materials recycling
abs: With the retirement of massive amount of end-of-life lithium ion batteries (LIBs), proper disposal of the hazardous wastes and cost-effective valorization of useful materials have become increasingly pressing and attracted extensive attention worldwide. The state-of-the-art recycling technologies, which are generally based on chemical leaching methods, have critical issues of enormous chemicals consumption, secondary pollution and tedious procedures. Here, we propose to develop an innovative technology, based on the proof-of-concept study and ground IP of our collaborator, for the recycling of spent LiFePO4. LiFePO4 is readily broken down into FePO4 and Li+ via the redox-targeting reaction between the redox mediator and material, with a recylcing efficiency for lithium removal up to 99.80% at room temperature. The reacted redox species are instantaneously regenerated on the electrode for subsequent round of reaction while Li+ is separated from the counter electrode compartment. Consequently, chemicals consumption is drastically minimized and secondary pollutions are eliminated. By virtue of the new process, high purity LiOH (99.90%) and FePO4 (99.97%) have been obtained. We envisage that this cost-effective and environment-friendly approach can be extended to other materials and promote the sustainability of LIB technologies.

title: A Scalable and Intelligent Tutoring System for Air Traffic Control Training
abs: In this research, we introduce an immersive and collaborative VR training platform that is scalable and cost-effective to the traditional method of training Air Traffic Controller (ATC) in a physical mockup of a 360-degree air control tower simulator. The use of immersive VR technology through Head Mounted Display (HMD) would not only solve the space constraints but also immerse users in their tasks while supporting better management and analysis of the complex data produced during training. The data captured can be used to profile the learned skill levels of the trainee to infer his/her strength and weakness. The performance model is then used to drive the intelligent tutoring system in providing personalized instruction and content to allow for self-paced learning. Specific aims include: • Design and develop a scalable air traffic control simulation engine that supports dynamic configuration of training procedures and scenarios that leads to individualized learning. • Design and develop a multi-model training system that supports instructor guided multi-player training and self-paced independent learning. • Design and implement an Intelligent Tutoring System (ITS) that supports analytical performance models to provide an objective assessment of learned skills. On-the-job-training alone is one model that does not fit well with air traffic control training. Instead, the use of advanced simulation devices and set up in a controlled environment is required and utilized in every phase of air traffic control training programs. The use of immersive virtual reality technology is significant in that it bridges the need for a simulation platform that provides an immersive and visual environment which closely emulates the on-site control tower facility and yet support a scalable architecture. The project will be managed and led by SIT in collaboration with DigiPen and in consultation with our industry collaborator, the Air Force Training Command (AFTC), through regular meetings, project updates, and reviews. The proposed work will be structured into four work packages, WP1 to WP4, that are aligned with our objectives stated earlier. The four work packages are: • WP1: A scalable and composable air traffic control tower simulation engine. • WP2: A multi-model training system that supports instructor guided training and, self-paced and independent learning. • WP3: An Intelligent Tutoring System (ITS). • WP4: Final Integration and Evaluation of Framework Prototype. The feasibility of the project was demonstrated through the implementation of a prototype that we developed in collaboration with Air Force Command Training. Although the implementation was simplified in terms of the 3D models and scenarios being simulated, it was sufficient to validate the impact of VR and its effectiveness in providing high fidelity and immersive training of ATC. title: Developing Durable Economical Membrane Electrode Assemblies (MEA) with Hybrid Technique
abs: Major advanced countries are actively exploring hydrogen economy, Singapore cannot risk being left behind this value chain. The high quality manpower and R&D enable Singapore to play a big role in the high value domains, especially, in crucial materials & components development and manufacture. Membrane Electrode Assembly (MEA) is the core part of electrolyzers & proton exchange membrane (PEM) fuel cell stacks (FCs) and accounts majority cost of them. The market value of MEA has huge potential with the increasing usage of FC technology. Successful integration of PEM FC technology into automobile and stationary power applications requires significant reduction of the overall stack cost, which is mainly attributed to the expensive platinum group metal (PGM) catalysts needed for the pertinent electrochemical reactions. To reduce the cost, PGM-free MEA, which means MEA with other catalyst, has been intensively studied for decades but is still far from practical application due to the poor durability. The MEA degraded quickly after several hours’ operation, far below the target set by the U. S. Department of Energy (DOE). Reducing the loading level of PGM on the MEA is a relative practical approach. Continuously efforts have been undertaken, especially through improving the active areas of the supporting carbon black and the distribution of catalyst nano particles. However, the efforts encounter a bottleneck, that is, poor durability appears again when the PGM loading level is reduced to certain level. So far, the PGM catalyst still accounts 70% of the MEA cost. The high stack cost retarded widely adoption of fuel cell technology, and is the one of the biggest challenge in hydrogen economy. The objectives of this project are realizing and commercializing a durable economical MEA through hybrid technique, which is from a concept combining IP & knowhow from our clean energy research center (CERC) and research publications from Universities. In this MEA, hybrid technique is used to tackle the durability problem. Firstly, reinforced proton exchange membrane with net structure on the surface will be used which restricts the expansion of the MEA and thus enhancing the adhesive condition of the catalyst layers and reducing the degradation of membrane itself. Secondly, a Pt/graphene oxide and Pt/C hybrid catalyst will be developed to solve the problems of catalyst agglomeration and supporting mattress oxidation. The durability of the MEA can be enhanced by 2--3 folds due to a synergistic effect when the 2-D graphene and 3-D carbon black mattress are combined. Consequently, the usage and cost of the precious metals can be cut down more than 40%. The economical MEA will be highly competitive in the market due to low cost and long service. There will be good space for commercialization, we can spin-off as key components provider, and license out the processing technology.
kw: Membrane Electrode Assembly (MEA), platinum group metal (PGM) catalysts, graphene oxide, durability, hybrid technique

title: Identification and characterisation of the regulatory elements of muscle stem cells in reference to sarcopenia in patients with colorectal cancer
abs: Aims Age-related sarcopenia is a multi-organ process that lead to a loss of skeletal muscle mass resulting in the decline in physical functions. This negatively affect surgical outcomes of the patients, resulting in increased complication rates and a higher propensity of delay to return to baseline. These naturally would result in higher healthcare costs. Even though nutrition and resistant training have shown positive effects on sarcopenia, the process and regulatory mechanisms of sarcopenia are poorly understood. There has been great amount of research on sarcopenia, but none of these studies triangulated the muscle epigenetics, serum biomarkers and clinical outcome. The primary aim is to evaluate the effects of sarcopenia on short-term surgical outcomes. Secondary aims include an exploratory study to triangulate the regulatory elements of muscle stem cells, serum biomarkers and surgical outcomes in relation to sarcopenia for patients who will be undergoing elective colorectal surgery. We would also be validating the use of MuscleSound for the assessment of muscle quality for sarcopenia. Hypotheses: 1. There will be significant differences in the epigenetic regulation of muscle stem cells between the patients with sarcopenia. 2. A combination of inflammation-related, growth-related and protein-turnover-related biomarkers can predict for poor surgical outcomes. 3. Ultrasonographic assessment of muscle quality would play an important role in assessment for sarcopenia Methodology We will conduct an interventional cohort study recruiting patients who requires elective colorectal surgeries. Patients would be separated into those with and without sarcopenia. They would have their functional, nutritional and muscle quality (ultrasonographically) assessed after enrollment. Patients would have skeletal muscle harvested during surgery evaluated for its composition, mRNA and protein expression. Of focus will be to analyse the epigenetic characteristics for the identification of regulatory mechanisms in sarcopenia. Serum obtained prior to surgery, would be tested for biomarkers which correlate with subsequent clinical outcomes.
kw: Sarcopenia; Frailty; Surgery; Colorectal; Biomarkers; Prehabilitation

title: Healthy Early Life Moments in Singapore (HELMS): Metabolic health and lifestyle intervention for overweight and obese women during preconception and pregnancy
abs: The rapidly increasing rate of obesity has contributed to the burden of multiple non-communicable diseases (NCDs) in Singapore and worldwide. A pro-food culture and low awareness on health literacy leads to lifestyle choices that results in overweight and obesity, with adverse consequence on maternal health and pregnancy outcomes. We propose a novel primary prevention model of care (MOC) - Healthy Early Life Moments in Singapore (HELMS), commencing at preconception, and followed through pregnancy, culminating in enhanced intergenerational health of the family. HELMS leverages on building a healthy mental model of nutrition through preconception to postnatal life. We hypothesised that lifestyle interventions targeting overweight and obese woman in preconception will (i) establish healthy behaviour in the journey of preparing for a successful pregnancy; (ii) enhance reproductive potential and fertility; and during pregnancy, will (i) promote optimal gestational weight gain; (ii) improve pregnancy and birth outcomes; and (iii) establish healthy behaviour in the journey of preparing for a healthy live birth. We aim to recruit 300 overweight and obese women (body mass index ≥25 kg/m2) attempting to conceive, implement the designated interventions during preconception, and those who get pregnant within a year of recruitment will be followed-up throughout pregnancy. Components of intervention is based on the 6P mental model (Portion, Proportion, Pleasure, Phase, Physicality, Psychology). Primary outcome is pregnancy rate and fecundability, as compared with an observational preconception cohort (S-PRESTO). Secondary outcomes include dietary behaviour and physical activity changes, metabolic profiles, gestational weight gain, pregnancy complications and birth outcomes, before and after the intervention. Through the application of lifestyle interventions initiated during the preconception phase and continuing through pregnancy, there is great potential to enhance maternal health in overweight and obese women during pregnancy, shaping a healthy environment in which the fetus will develop with consequently improved pregnancy and birth outcomes.
kw: Obesity; preconception; pregnancy; gestational weight gain; lifestyle intervention

title: EVALUATION OF CHANGES IN POST-TRABECULAR AQUEOUS OUTFLOW PATHWAYS USING HIGH RESOLUTION MULTIMODAL IMAGING PLATFORMS
abs: Research Project Title: Efficacy and safety of direct selective laser trabeculoplasty (DSLT) in patients with primary angle closure (PAC) and primary angle closure glaucoma (PACG) Aims: To evaluate the efficacy and safety of trans-limbal direct selective laser trabeculoplasty (DSLT) in reducing intraocular pressure (IOP) in subjects with primary angle closure (PAC) and primary angle closure glaucoma (PACG). Hypothesis: Direct selective laser trabeculoplasty (DSLT) therapy is efficacious and safe in reducing IOP in PAC and PACG. Methodology and Approach: Thirty subjects diagnosed as PAC & PACG and uncontrolled intraocular pressures will be enrolled in this prospective, single arm trial designed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of DSLT to reduce IOP. All subjects will be screened for eligibility on pre-defined inclusion and exclusion criteria and will be treated with a novel DSLT delivered using a novel device [External Automatic Glaucoma Laser (EAGLE)] designed to deliver laser to the trabecular meshwork area of the eye without the use of a gonioscopy lens. Subjects will be followed up at week 1, Months 2,4 and 6 and a comprehensive clinical evaluation will be done to determine efficacy and safety of DSLT. Novel imaging technology ( Optical Coherence Angiography Tomography) will be used to evaluate and understand changes in the POST-TRABECULAR aqueous outflow patterns post-intervention.

title: The Search for Pathophysiology of Small Fiber Neuropathy, with a focus on immunological and genetic mechanisms and interactions.
abs: Small fibre neuropathy (SFN) is a heterogeneous neurological disease caused by exclusive damage to the small unmyelinated nerve fibers. After exclusion of the secondary causes of SFN, such as vitamin B12 deficiency, sarcoidosis, diabetes mellitus, amyloidosis and other toxic substances, the cause of SFN may not be found in up to 50% of cases. This project aims to elucidate the pathophysiology of SFN, with a main focus on autoimmune and genetic mechanisms. The first hypothesis is that idiopathic SFN is autoimmune in nature. A sample size of 80 patients and 20 controls is targeted. Initial stages of this study will look for autoantibodies towards sodium channels, potassium channels, Trpv and Trpa channels in the patients' sera via cell based assays. The second stage involves an unbiased proteomic approach to search for other potential antibodies, immunoprecipitation with IgG from patients' sera, followed by gel electrophoresis and Western blotting, and finally with mass spectrometry to identify the antigenic proteins. Stage 3 will engage mass spectrometry to screen patients' sera for soluble immune compounds. All three stages will occur in parallel. If any of the stages are positive, further independent validation studies, pathogenicity tests, tissue binding and expression, and further clinical characterization of patients with positive antibodies or immune compounds will be performed. The second hypothesis is that idiopathic SFN may have a genetic inheritance in our locale. Mutations towards sodium channel (Nav 1.7, 1.8 and 1.9) will be investigated by Sanger sequencing. Whole exome sequencing will be performed to search for other possible genetic mutations. Finally, the autoimmune and genetic interactions will be analyzed and clinically subtyped.
kw: small fibre neuropathy, antibody, immunology, genetics, sodium channels

title: New MHC technologies to identify and analyze SARS-CoV-2-specific CD8+ T cells
abs: The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic has had a devastating impact on public health and the global economy. Development of effective COVID-19 vaccines and therapeutics is critically dependent on better understanding the human immune response to SARS-CoV-2, the causal agent of COVID-19. CD8+ T cells are critical for anti-viral defense, as they have a unique ability to recognize and kill virus-infected cells. However, the role of CD8+ T cells in COVID-19 protection and/or pathology is currently unknown. This is mainly due to lack on information CD8+ T cell specificity during COVID-19, and lack of reagents to identify and characterize SARS-CoV-2-specific CD8+ T cells. We will use new MHC class I technologies to identify SARS-CoV-2 peptides presented on MHC (HLA in human) class I variants common in the Singaporean population, generating tetramers to identify and characterize the phenotype, signaling and function of SARS-CoV-2-specific CD8+ T cells from recovered patients, and to expand SARS-CoV-2-specific CD8+ T cells for potential use in immunotherapy. We will use UV-cleavable conditional MHC-I technology to test SARS-CoV-2-derived peptides for binding to HLA class I variants common in Singapore. We developed a new MHC technology using soluble single chain dimers of HLA heavy chain and 2-microglobulin, expressed in mammalian cells. This is simple to implement, offering a way to generate MHC molecules with intact glycosylation. We will use this technology to identify SARS-CoV-2-specific CD8+ T cells, and to analyze their phenotype, function and signaling. We will use HLA class I presenting SARS-CoV-2-derived peptides expressed as covalently linked single chain trimers, shown before to be more stable and immunogenic than conventional MHC, to expand SARS-CoV-2-specific CD8+ T cells. Our work will generate a critical set of reagents to identify, analyze and expand SARS-CoV-2-specific CD8+ T cells, with special relevance to the Singapore population.
kw: Covid-19, CD8+ T cell, vaccine, T cell response, MHC class I, peptide

title: Targeting Endothelial Dysfunction to Ameliorate Cytokine Storm in COVID-19
abs: To date, clinical findings indicate unequivocably that the single largest predisposing factor for COVID-19 related mortality underlying cardiovascular and metabolic disease, namely hypertension, diabetes and obesity. The unifying pathology underlying these conditions is endothelial dysfunction. Furthermore, very recent findings implicate inappropriate and excessive endothelial activation as a primary cause for morbidity and mortality in COVID-19 patients, manifested in the form of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), thrombosis and endothelitis in adults, and Kawasaki-like endothelial-centric pro-inflammatory autoimmune disease in children. These findings squarely implicate the endothelial compartment as a key player in the pathogenesis of COVID-19. We hypothesize that the endothelium can be effectively targeted to suppress COVID-19 associated hyper-inflammation to ameliorate disease pathology. Our team has recently discovered a mitochondrial program in endothelial cells that is activated during viral inflammation to promote resolution and to prevent hyper-cytokinemia, which underlies fatal cytokine storm in CAP (community acquired pneumonia). In this proposal, we seek to investigate the utility of our anti-inflammatory mitochondrial program in suppressing COVID-19 associated hyper-cytokinemia.
kw: Endothelium; IL-6; cytokine storm; inflammation; immuno-metabolism; mitochondria

title: Direct detection of COVID-19: integrating molecular switches with automated microfluidics
abs: SARS-CoV-2 is a new RNA virus identified as the cause of the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic. Its deadly nature warrants immediate efforts to diagnose and contain the spread. Detection of viral nucleic acids can distinguish the novel coronavirus from other viruses; however, current viral testing is almost exclusively performed through polymerase chain reaction (PCR), in centralized laboratories, due to its high complexity and lengthy processing (6–12 hours). These limitations have resulted in delayed diagnoses and a global shortage of supplies. For accessible and prompt detection, assay platforms that can bypass PCR and bring the testing to the patient level are urgently needed, to improve disease surveillance and health outcomes. We have recently developed a molecular nanotechnology for sensitive detection of viral nucleic acids. The technology utilizes enzyme-DNA nanocomplexes, which function as independent recognition and signaling elements, to form a molecular switch. The switch activates through direct target hybridization and generates exponential electrical signal. The platform is thus well-suited for clinical applications: (1) it requires minimal sample preparation, operates at room temperature, is fast (<30 mins) and sensitive (<100 copies); (2) its modularity facilitates programmable assay design and rapid translation. When tested with patient RNA samples, the technology demonstrated highly accurate detection of COVID-19. To address the current challenges, we propose to advance the technology through integrative engineering of molecular switches and microfluidics, to achieve direct detection of COVID-19 in native biological samples. We hypothesize that the advanced integration can improve assay performance against a complex biological background. This hypothesis stems from our recent work in developing enzyme-DNA nanocomplexes and chip-based detection platforms. The approach will not only enable robust testing, thereby reducing our dependence on conventional assays and safeguarding our national ability amidst a global shortage, but also empower rapid technology translation, in community clinics and resource-limited settings.
kw: Molecular switches; automated microfluidics; direct RNA detection; native clinical samples; COVID-19

title: Nanoparticle-based Serological Assays for COVID-19 using Linear B-Cell Epitopes from Spike and Nucleocapsid Proteins from SARS-CoV-2
inst: IMRE - Institute of Materials Research and Engineering
abs: The ongoing SARS-CoV-2 pandemic demands rapid development of serological detection tools. Sensitive and specific immunoassays that can determine SARS-CoV-2 exposure could serve as sero-epidemiological surveillance tools that would greatly help to control virus transmission. In this proposal, we aim to use the optical nanoparticle sensing technology to develop peptide-based rapid serological tests as Point of Care Tests (PoCTs) to identify individuals with exposure to SARS-CoV-2 with better accuracy and efficiency. Inorganic nanoparticles (particularly metal nanoparticle) with unique optical properties are versatile sensing materials for design one-step “mix-and-measure” assays for antibodies, which is less tedious than traditional ELISA assays. They also provide quantitative results rather than yes/no result in lateral flow assays. In our assay development, instead of using recombinant SARS-CoV-2 proteins (as used in most existing serological tests), we will use immunodominant anti-SARS-CoV-2 specific linear B-cell epitopes on the SARS-CoV-2 spike (S) and nucleocapsid (N) viral proteins as the affinity ligand. We have proved that these peptides have higher specificity and sensitivity to detect COVID-19 patients than the recombinant S and/or N proteins. The proposed assays combine nanoparticle sensors’ robustness and rapid attribute with the peptides’ higher specificity and sensitivity, for more efficient and accurate identification of COVID-19 exposure. These assays are rapid, enzyme-free, using less reagent and thus are more suitable for POC applications. They can be performed in 96 well plate measured using a standard plate reader in hospital. They can also be operated in single tube in community, measured using a handheld color detector. They will be important serological tools for efficient immunosurveillance in population to identify individuals with recent or past exposure to SARS-CoV-2 and mitigate transmission.
kw: SARS CoV-2 Serological Assay; Inorganic Nanoparticle; Linear B-Cell Epitopes; Spike and Nucleocapsid Proteins; Point of Care Test

title: Mathematical modelling for assessment and optimal deployment of COVID-19 vaccination in Singapore
abs: Currently, there is no vaccine for COVID-19 and control has relied on non-pharmaceutical interventions including contact tracing and quarantine, social distancing and lockdowns. Much of the hope for future of COVID-19 control has been focused on vaccination, and the premise of most countries’ responses has been to prolong the epidemic until a vaccine— and therefore a safe route to herd immunity—becomes available. Many vaccines are in development, and will need to tested safely and efficiently in the population. Once a vaccine is available there will most likely be limited supply and so decisions about allocation of vaccine will need to be made. The study will use mathematical modeling techniques and health economic evaluation to assess how best to evaluate and to use COVID-19 vaccinations in Singapore. Firstly, we will use modelling to explore trial designs for the optimal testing of Phase 3 trials in Singapore, given the past infections. We will assess the optimal use of vaccinations with different target product profiles as developed by the WHO and provide a mathematical modeling framework for use in the decision making process about optimal deployment of COVID-19 vaccinations in Singapore. This framework will be therefore ready for use when the actual vaccination becomes available. The modelling work will also be used to support the design of post-licensure studies to determine waning of immunity as well as any disease enhancement.
kw: COVID-19, vaccination

title: Mitigating SARS-CoV-2 transmission through expiratory droplet control and environmental intervention
abs: A three-component study involving expiratory droplet characterization and infectivity, evaluating the efficacy of facial (surgical) masks to contain expiratory droplet release from common oral activities, and technological mitigation by ventilation with pressurization, is undertaken to provide new data to inform effective measures for mitigating SARS-CoV-2 transmission in the community. This enhances the development of strategies and innovations to improve health across a spectrum, from facility design and operation to event organization, quarantine and recovery (including home) practice, and individual behavior. A Gesundheit-II machine, a recent innovation capable of efficiently capturing exhaled and coughed droplets separated by size ( >5 μm and ≤5 μm), is used to evaluate COVID-19 patient viral emission and intensity, and to assess the efficacy of wearing surgical masks to contain viruses emitted by breathing, talking and singing. Recent variants seem to be more infectious, and this is explored within a carefully designed and operated perspex enclosure simulating air change rate and airflow approximating exposures in an indoor environment. This is achieved by controlling the air change rate and preventing contamination by positioning an infected subject to contribute aerosols via talking into the perspex enclosure. An aerosol-sized differentiated (( >5 μm and ≤5 μm) sampling technique are applied to deposit aerosols onto VERO E6 TMPRSS2 cell cuture plates within the enclosure. Cytopathic effect (CPE) indicates transmissibility by expirated emissions, with CPE achieved by fine (≤5 μm) aerosols indicative of airborne transmission. Since October 2021 when Home recovery was introduced as the default for qualifying infected cases, as well as exposed cases who may be potentially infected, the risk of transmission in the home has elevated. Studies have reinforced airborne transmission as the dominant mode, and hence the movement of viral-laden air within the home is an under-studied factor that impacts community transmission. In the pre-symptomatic phase, viral shedding is also known to be the highest. Simulated dispersion and movement of tracer gas and fine particles provide an indication of the viral dispersion within the home, and the reduction of such dispersion into the non-isolation areas through feasible options of exhaust and/or pressurization fans. This data would be useful for understanding the concerns, and effectiveness of simple fan solutions, associated with Home Recovery. Whilst envisaged to be informative for understanding and developing solutions for quarantine and isolation facilities (including hotels), these efforts would not be pursued due to time and budget constraints. The findings would seed a separate grant application.

title: Phase 1 dose-finding study of Irinotecan to reduce systemic inflammation in COVID-19
abs: Mortality in coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) infections occurs due to a systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS). The underlying pathophysiology of COVID-19 SIRS is a macrophage activation syndrome, with release of inflammatory cytokines including IL6, IL1 and TNF-a. Multiple strategies to blunt this hyperactive immune response are being tested globally; including anti-IL6 blocking antibodies, steroids and etoposide chemotherapy (a component of secondary haemophagocytic lymphohistocytosis (HLH) treatment). At present, Remdesivir and Dexamethasone are considered standard of care treatment for COVID-19. In this proposal, we hope to evaluate a chemotherapeutic agent- Irinotecan, on the basis of strong pre-clinical evidence for its efficacy in viral hyperinflammation. The target of irinotecan, topoisomerase-1 (Top1), is a critical regulator of inflammatory gene expression, as described by our collaborators in Science (2016). In-vitro and in-vivo preclinical models demonstrate that inhibition of Top1 suppresses microbe-induced inflammation and lethality. We propose a phase 1-2 trial of Irinotecan in combination with remdesivir and dexamethasone in cancer patients with moderate COVID-19, who as a group are at higher risk of COVID related mortality and morbidity. In the phase 1 dose-finding trial, we will evaluate 3 fixed sub-cytotoxic doses of Irinotecan (20, 40, 60mg). These doses are well below typical chemotherapy levels and not expected to cause myelosuppression or diarrhea. The objective of the phase 1 component is to establish the lowest single dose of irinotecan that yields adequate plasma levels of topoisomerase inhibition, and is safe in combination with dexamethasone and remdesivir. We expect to enroll a maximum of 18 patients using a standard 3+3 dose escalation design. In the randomized phase 2 component, we aim to compare irinotecan in combination with dexamethasone + remdesivir (Arm A n=50) with standard of care treatment of dexamethasone + remdesivir (Arm B n=50) in cancer patients with moderate COVID-19. The sample size is calculated based on a power calculation of 0.9 for a 5 fold drop in inflammatory markers (IL6, Ferritin and CRP) 10 days after administration. Secondary objectives include evaluating the impact on ICU admission, ventilation and mortality. This may represent a practical option for patients in low-middle income countries, where access to expensive novel agents is limited. Given the current numbers of cases in Singapore, we propose to lead this study through a multicentre effort across academic cancer centres in India.

title: A Point-of-care Rapid Antigen Test Kit for the Detection of SARS-Cov-2 Infection
abs: The current gold standard for COVID-19 testing is via the RT-PCR test. While highly sensitive, it requires extensive sample preparation steps to extract the SARS-CoV-2 RNAs enclosed within the virus within a laboratory. As such, this test cannot be performed onsite nor easily scaled up for rapid mass testing. An alternative is a rapid antigen test which looks for viral surface proteins without the need for extraction and amplification. We aim to develop a point-of-care (POC) disposable dipstick sensor test kit to detect SARS-CoV-2 Spike (S) glycoproteins expressed on the surface of the virus directly from nasopharyngeal, nasal swabs and saliva samples obtained from patients. This is based on a patent pending POC dipstick immunosensor technology that the PI has developed to test for inflammatory cytokines from bodily fluids. This test kit comprises an electrochemical aptamer based sensor that can be directly dipped into the sample to provide rapid (15min) and quantitative readout of the S glycoproteins. As this protein is found on the viral surface, no sample preparation step is needed to lyse the virus. In terms of scalability, our POC rapid antigen test kit can be easily mass produced as the aptamer sensors can be mass produced cheaply through chemical synthesis. This can enable rapid commercialization of the test kit for regulatory approval and eventual clinical use. Moving forward, we can also develop this into a high-throughput format either in the form of a 96-well plate or with a reader that can read and analyze multiple samples all in one go for onsite testing in locations such as workplaces, clinics, schools, airports, etc. This will enable quick and early detection of viral spread within the community as well as to identify any asymptomatic cases for better outbreak control and management.

title: Digital technology solutions to improve the vision-specific quality of life and social engagement in the visual impaired older population- a pilot study
abs: Purpose: To develop and validate five performance-based activities of daily living task tests (ADLTT), evaluating the effects of visual impairment (VI) associated with age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Methods: A multi-disciplinary team developed 5 ADLTTs for validation:1) reading test(RT); 2) facial expression(FE) recognition; 3) item search(IS) task; 4) money counting(MC) task; and 5) making a drink(MD), using both binocular and monocular vision. A prospective observational cohort study of 36 cases of patients with VI (visual acuity (VA) ≤6/15) in at least one eye caused by AMD compared to 36 healthy control subjects without VI was used to test criterion, convergent, divergent validity, and test-retest reliability. Results: Compared to controls, patients with VI from AMD had a slower reading speed (-77.41 words/min; P< 0.001); took longer to complete MC using monocular worse eye and binocular vision (difference 15.13 sec and 4.06 sec, respectively; both P< 0.001); and MD using monocular worse eye vision (9.37 sec; P=0.033), demonstrating criterion validity. RT and MC demonstrated convergent validity, showing moderate to strong correlations with VA, contrast sensitivity, and microperimetry testing. The other ADLTT showed no significant convergent validity. Divergent validity when correlated with race and gender, was observed in most ADLTT except for FE. Moderate to good test-retest reliability was observed for MC and MD (ICC=0.55 and 0.77;p< 0.001) using monocular worse eye vision; but not for the other tests. Conclusions: Real-world visual functioning associated with AMD can be assessed with our ADLTTs, which demonstrated promising validity and reliability metrics overall, particularly MC and MD.

title: RESILIENCE UNDER FIRE:  ROBUST KIT COMPONENTS FOR COVID-19 DETECTION DEVELOPED AND MADE IN SINGAPORE
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: The current gold standard diagnostic for COVID-19 is the RT-PCR assay. This test utilises specialised proteins known as enzymes that first identify viral genetic material and then act as molecular photocopiers to boost its amount to readily detectible levels. The enzymes currently being used in kits being deployed across Singapore are produced and shipped from overseas. This poses key challenges to our national interest. What would happen if production or transport issues arising from widespread illness and/or foreign political mandates restricted availability? Resilience is preparedness. Therefore, we are proposing to develop improved versions of the key enzyme components in the RT-PCR assay as “drop-in” reagents for kits currently being used. These improved enzymes will belong to Singapore. The development process will also address scalable domestic production concerns to meet the increasing demand for population-wide screening in the absence of a vaccine or therapy.

title: Chimeric Antigen Receptor-Natural Kill Cell Therapy to Ameliorate Macrophage Activation Syndrome in Severe COVID-19
abs: Patients with severe COVID-19 pneumonia exhibit features of the macrophage activation syndrome (MAS). Macrophages are the greatest cytokine factory in the body and, once aberrantly activated, can produce large amounts of pro-inflammatory cytokines, leading to “cytokine storm”. The cytokine storm often triggers the acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), the most common indication for transferring COVID-19 patients to ICU and the leading cause of patient death in severe COVID-19. Post-mortem examination of this patient population has revealed macrophages/monocytes as the major infiltrated immune cells in the lungs. We propose here to develop natural killer (NK) cell-based cellular therapeutics modified with two different RNA chimeric antigen receptors (CARs) to target both sides of the virus-host interaction in COVID-19, namely pro-inflammatory macrophages that play a key pathogenic role in cytokine storms and virally infected cells. Cord blood mononuclear cells will be used as a source of third-party, virus-free NK cells and an RNA CAR approach allows high-level expression of CAR genes for effective but short-term action to eliminate the target cells. Two CARs are selected for NK cell modification: One targeting a cell surface protein that is significantly upregulated on activated macrophages, and another targeting NKG2D ligands that are upregulated upon coronavirus infection. CAR-mediated specific elimination of pro-inflammatory macrophages will serve as a host-directed therapy to combat pathological overreactions of the immune system that result in MAS/ARDS in patients with severe COVID-19, whereas the NKG2D CAR will significantly enhance the NK cell ability to destroy virally infected cells, providing a viable antiviral solution for fast virus clearance. The deliverable of the project is to file a patent application through NUS for this novel therapy approach, based on the proof of concept in vitro study with human macrophages and in vivo study in a murine MAS model completed within 12 months.

title: Non-invasive liquid biopsies for monitoring Covid-19 infection, co-infections and host response
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Covid-19 poses a significant challenge to patients and healthcare system. The most vulnerable people are the elderly and those who have weakened immune systems such as patients undergoing chemotherapy. A retrospective study of Chinese Covid-19 patients showed that half of non-survivors experienced a secondary infection. Protecting these patients in the hospital through good hygiene is critical but hospital acquired infections is still prevalent in our acute-care hospitals. There is a need to quickly identify the relevant pathogen so that the appropriate therapy can be administered. Our first objective is to apply our clinical metagenomics platform that we have established with NUH to monitor Covid-19 infection and co-infections in high-risk Covid-19 patients. The ability to quickly identify the cause of the underlying co-infection will guide treatment of the patient as well as help establish the underlying cause of sepsis. Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is associated with significant morbidity and mortality and caused by damage to blood vessels in the lungs. Early detection and prevention of ARDS is important as progression is rapid and treatment options are not effective. Clinicians need an early surrogate of disease severity. Cell death is a common outcome of viral infection. Early identification of ARDS will allow for timely intervention to arrest disease progression. Our second objective is the deployment of a sensitive, non-invasive liquid-biopsy assay we have developed to quantify tissue specific injury, particularly the lungs and liver during the course of Covid-19 infection. We achieve this by quantifying lung and liver specific RNA levels in the plasma and using these measurements to inform us on the extent of tissue specific injury brought about during the course of Covid-19 infection. Understanding the extent and dynamics of tissue injury will open up new treatment windows for clinical management.

title: Study of vascular complications in patients with rheumatoid arthritis
abs: This study is to establish a composite of vascular consequences in patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA), including radial artery maximum distensibility index (RA-MDI), aortic artery stiffness and carotid artery intima-media thickness (CIMT). Explore their correlations with traditional cardiovascular risk factors and characteristics of disease. Our hypothesis is the composite of vascular consequences are good potential surrogate markers of cardiovascular risk in patients with RA, and it may correlate with traditional cardiovascular risk factors and characteristics of disease. Measurements of RA-MDI by EndoPAT, aortic artery stiffness using SphygmoCorAortic pulse wave velocity (PWV), and CIMT by carotid ultrasonography are well established in our collaborator Dr Rinkoo Dalan’s vascular laboratory. Patient data will be collected during the study visits with a standard form and HbA1c, fasting glucose and lipid panel will be measured. We have an annotated set of patient information collected prospectively over the past 15 years by specialist Rheumatologists from the Department of Rheumatology, Allergy and Immunology, Tan Tock Seng Hospital. We aim to establish a composite of vascular consequences for RA patients in our RA registry patients. In the long run, we aim to develop a good prediction model for cardiovascular risk in RA patients by combining the composite of vascular consequences and traditional cardiovascular risks in our large and long term follow up RA registry. If the results of our study support the thinking that inflammation of RA promotes atherosclerosis, then better disease control not only improves the joint disease but potentially reduces cardiovascular complications in our patients, which will reduce the morbidity and mortality of RA patients.

title: Large area synthesis and applications of atomically thin amorphous materials
abs: arrangement remains an open issue. They are generally believed to be Zachariasen continuous random networks (Z-CRNs), but recent experimental evidence favours the competing crystallite model in the case of amorphous silicon. Corresponding questions in 2D materials are wide open. But a fundamental understanding is urgently needed to overcome limitation of material synthesis. Existing methods do not allow the growth of atomically thin amorphous materials. We have very recently succeeded in the synthesis of amorphous carbon films, which are only one atom thick. By atomic resolution imaging we were able to directly confirm the complete absence of long-range periodicity. A threefold-coordinated structure with a wide distribution in bond lengths, bond angles, and 5-, 6-, 7-, and 8-member rings is observed. Transport measurements confirm that in 2d amorphous films behave very different from both their 2D crystalline and 3D bulk amorphous counterpart. This proposal aims at clarifying the exact nature of amorphous materials and at developing new synthesis routes for atomically thin amorphous films. The importance of such films will be demonstrated for four specific applications. We will show that atomically thin amorphous films represent a new class of materials. By leveraging on a patented laser-based chemical vapour deposition (LCVD) process and in close collaboration with a group of industry collaborators, we will demonstrate that this new class of material can specifically boost the performance of semiconductors, magnetic hard discs and batteries and has commercial value.

title: Towards Carbon-Neutral Plastic Bio-Upcycling
abs: Natural plastic degradation takes hundreds of years and plastic waste is reduced or recycled through physical and chemical methods which are not sustainable. Our proposed programme aims to reduce poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET) waste (7.4% of the world’s plastic demand) by engineering enzymes and microbes that convert PET into compounds of industrial value (up-cycling). This programme will therefore be the first to provide a carbon-neutral bio-upcycling solution for plastic waste management by converting PET into a range of value-added molecules. PET-degrading microbes isolated from environmental samples degrade PET by excreting the enzyme, PETase. However, genetic tools for engineering these environmental isolates are unavailable, and attempts at engineering the native PET-degrading enzymes (e.g. PETase and cutinase) to increase the catalytic efficiency have so far been met with limited success. Our goal is to convert PET to value-added molecules. We will accomplish this by engineering both enzymes and microbial hosts for improved PET degradation into feedstock and conversion to value-added molecules. Through directed evolution and mutagenesis methods to improve PETase and cutinase catalytic efficiency and a novel high-throughput screening, the ten candidates with the highest activity will be characterized for efficiency of degrading PET to MHET to terephthalate (TPA) and ethylene glycol (EG). TPA and EG will be then used as feedstocks for production of value-added compounds (e.g. L-DOPA, free fatty acids, cellulose, polyunsaturated fatty acid). PET utilization modules (PUMs) will be designed and integrated to three industrially relevant microbes: a recently isolated, highly productive Singaporean (photosynthetic) cyanobacterium, a cellulose-producing bacteria, and tractable yeast strains. These strains were selected for their carbon sequestration, cellulose production and lipid accumulation capabilities, respectively. The integration of the carbon-fixing cyanobacterium in the process allows carbon dioxide (CO2) produced by growth of the other two microbes to be captured, thus upcycling PET in a carbon-neutral and sustainable way.

title:
Additive manufacturing of resilient, strong and functional
composites through bio-inspired microstructures.
abs: (Major goal 1) Synthetic building blocks, organic and inorganic, will be synthesised in large quantities their self- and directed-assembly via magnetic fields into bio-inspired microstructures studied, in particular concentric plywood patterns, aligned structures and gradients. Strategies to tune the densification of these microstructures by solvent removal and crosslinking will be investigated to reach compositions yielding satisfying strength, toughness and other functional properties. Microstructural and compositional characterisation will be done by imaging and spectroscopy with deep understanding of the processes and mechanisms involved. The hypotheses behind this aim are (i) that the choice of the building blocks chemistry and dimensions will determine self- or directed-assembly methods as well as some of the final properties; and (2) that their assembly in dilute phase can artificially reproduce bio-inspired microstructures whereas their densification will lead to the mechanical and functional properties. (Major goal 2) These assembly methods will be implemented into an AM set-up based on direct-ink-writing where a liquid or a paste is extruded through a nozzle, to enable the automated local tuning of the chemical composition, the microstructure and the density within a 3D macroscopic part. Building on the characterisation of the set architectures using mechanical testing and functional properties measurements such as resistivity or thermal conduction, the arrangement of multiple microstructures in the structure will be optimised to achieve target local and global properties. Focus will be first on graded composites binding soft to hard dissimilar materials to be used as flexible joints in orthopaedics, robotics and aerospace. The hypothesis is that the additive manufacturing platform will provide local microstructural control in a 3D structure in an automated, fast and scalable way to allow the fabrication and testing if single microstructures. These data will be used as inputs for computational modelling and simulation to further design and optimise complex arrangements of multiple microstructures within one larger macroscopic structure. Preliminary results demonstrate the feasibility to obtain controlled microstructures using combinations of self- and directed assembly methods in highly concentrated amounts of ceramic reinforcements. Densification via solvent removal and crosslinking has also been demonstrated prior to this proposed research by the PI, to generate high strength and toughness. Collaborators in Singapore have been identified and approached to provide the facilities and expertise required for the research. The research will provide further understanding on relationships microstructure-properties in structural composites and address practical needs. The application and interest of the proposed research have been discussed with many actors in Singapore, including the National Dental Hospital for resilient bone implants, A*ST

title: Beyond MOORE – Negative Capacitance Field-effect Transistor for Ultra-low-power Electronics
abs: The scaling of MOSFET to a smaller physical dimension has been the primary driving force behind its unprecedented prosperity. However, the voltage scaling almost stopped around 2005 due to the non-scalability of the subthreshold swing (SS) to below 60 mV/decade arising from Boltzmann statistics that governs the operation of conventional MOSFETs. Apart from this, dimension scaling seems extremely challenging beyond 5 nm gate length owing to fundamental material limitations and short channel effects. So it is not too far when all aspects of MOSFET scaling will completely stop, marking the end of the Si MOSFET era. In this program, we are aiming to develop the two-dimensional (2D) negative capacitance field-effect transistor (NCFET) device architecture, combining the superior scalability of atom-thin materials with negative capacitance mechanism, for boosting the full scaling beyond MOSFET. The envisioned outcomes are (i) to synthesize atom-thin semiconductor and room-temperature van der Waals ferroelectric; (ii) to develop a machine learning methodology to accelerate the material synthesis and analysis for wafer-scale production; and (iii) to build NCFET with the atom-thin semiconductor and van der Waals ferroelectric and integrate the NCFET with CMOS process for ultra-low power computing. The proposed NCFET with atom-thin semiconductor as the channel can provide superior immunity to short channel effects and enable aggressive miniaturization of transistors to sub-5 nm. Most importantly, negative capacitance of ferroelectric insulator in NCFET can provide a potential amplification for gate voltage and realize SS beyond the fundamental limit to boost the voltage scaling. Moreover, the facile wafer-scale growth and transfer of two-dimensional semiconductors promise lower cost and high performance and reliability (due to the atomically sharp and chemically clean van der Waals interface) than the ones built up by traditional semiconductors and ferroelectrics, implying the great economic potential in modern mobile computing (including wearables and Internet-of-Things) markets.

title: Designing resilient and inclusive cities in Asia-Pacific
abs: Current research in urban resilience highlights the role of ecosystem-based management, i.e. approaches that aim to sustainably manage natural or modified ecosystems to respond to future pressures. Despite recent advances in this field, researchers and practitioners consistently raise two challenges: the difficulty to scale ecosystem-based management to the level required to address sustainability issues, and the geographical bias toward Western countries, making it difficult to apply research insights to other geographies. The proposed research pushes the frontiers on these two issues by increasing the evidence base on the role of natural infrastructure for urban resilience and climate adaptation in Asia-Pacific, and informing policy and practice to create more resilient and inclusive cities. Natural infrastructure comprises a broad range of assets, from urban or peri-urban forest to single trees or green roofs. Building on my extensive experience in urban water management and ecosystem services science, I will assess the potential of natural infrastructure to deliver hydrologic services (water purification, flood mitigation) in Asia-Pacific cities using integrated environmental modeling at the city and regional scales. Next, I will study the role of natural infrastructure in the context of climate justice by exploring how ecosystem-based adaptation strategies affect differently a range of vulnerable groups. The third pillar of the research aims to develop effective strategies to distill knowledge to society – both to inform urban management processes and to educate the new generation of urban leaders. This research plan reflects my strong commitment to action-oriented research and belief in the role that universities will play in building a sustainable world.

title: Moiré scale engineering of atomically thin materials to achieve higher-temperature superconductivity
abs: Numerical studies predict that there are more than 1000 different layered materials that can be exfoliated down to a single layer, and to date only a small fraction of these have been fabricated experimentally. These atomically thin two-dimensional crystals can then be restacked using different material combinations and with different relative twist angles to generate millions of possible distinct electronic materials that are collectively referred to as moiré van der Waals heterostructures. Only recently has it become clear that the two-dimensional constituent layers are not rigid, but that the atoms within the moiré superlattice shift by about 0.01 nm in the out-of-plane direction and by about 0.001 nm in the in-plane direction due to the large strains caused by the van der Waals attraction between adjacent layers, especially at small twist angles. These shifts in turn strongly modify the electronic structure. This opens up a pathway, that we call moiré engineering, that allows for the tailoring of electronic band structure specific to particular applications. Our goal is to use moiré engineering to design a higher temperature superconductor. The first milestone is to develop a general theory of moiré engineering that would enable us to obtain accurate band structures, Wannier orbitals and electron-phonon matrix elements in much the same way that ab initio techniques like density functional theory currently provide this information for non-moiré heterostructures (the large superlattice unit cell and the corrugations and strains makes these traditional methods prohibitive for moiré van der Waals heterostructures). The second milestone concerns some specific theoretical results for both conventional and unconventional superconductivity including using spectral weight to identify which moiré-engineered band structures are likely to have a higher Tc, using the Wannier orbitals to determine the Hubbard U of moiré heterostructures, and using functional renormalization group to identify the optimal value of Hubbard U for a higher Tc superconductivity. We will also explore the interplay between membrane elasticity and the electron-phonon matrix element to determine the ideal conditions for conventional superconductivity. Armed with these theoretical results, for the third and final milestone we will do a large-scale materials screening to identify the optimal candidate material combinations and twist angles for higher temperature superconductivity. While our approach does not guarantee a room temperature superconductor, it does guarantee that we will identify from these millions of possible material combinations, those, that within this theoretical framework, support the highest value of the superconducting transition temperature.

title: Understanding and targeting the Interleukin 1 Receptor Associated Kinase 1 (IRAK1) pathway in solid tumors
abs: Background: Patients with refractory solid tumors have poor prognosis and often lack effective treatment options. The interleukin-1 receptor-associated kinases (IRAKs) mediate toll-like receptor (TLR) and interleukin-1 receptor (IL-1R) signaling, influencing downstream processes including inflammation and apoptosis. Our previous studies have indicated that chromosome 1q21.3 copy number amplification is observed in patients with recurrent and advanced stage solid tumors and can be detected from cell-free DNA (cfDNA) using blood samples. Using breast cancer as a study model, we have shown that chromosome 1q21.3 copy number amplification leads to over-expression of IRAK1, causing increased tumor growth. Inhibition of IRAK1 through knockdown and use of a IRAK1 inhibitor pacritinib decreased tumor growth. We propose a clinical study using pacritinib to treat patients with refractory solid tumors harboring chromosome 1q21.3 copy number amplification. We have included several translational components to investigate potential biomarkers for identification and monitoring of response, and also to study how pacritinib affects immune modulation. Hypothesis and aims: IRAK1 is effective in disease control in patients with refractory solid tumors harboring 1q21.3 amplification. Plasma cfDNA monitoring of 1q21.3 may be a potential biomarker for patient selection and response. Treatment with IRAK1 causes immune modulation that affect the tumor microenviroment and interact with tumorigenesis. Methodology and approach: A phase II study with single agent pacritinib will be conducted in patients with solid refractory tumors harboring 1q21.3 amplification. Patients will be treated with oral pacritinib twice daily and observed for therapeutic efficacy in terms of improvement in progression-free survival (primary endpoint) and response rate (secondary endpoint). Serial blood sampling will be carried out to identify and monitor changes in both 1q21.3 copy numbers and immune markers, and correlated to treatment outcome. Paired biopsies will be carried out for further interrogation of changes in tumor microenvironment and findings will be investigated in pre-clinical models.

title: SMART SERIOUS GAME ANALYTICS ENGINE TO IMPROVE LEARNER’S SKILLS AND PERFORMANCE
abs: Background and Hypotheses: Serious game has been introduced as an interactive educational tool for teaching specific knowledge. It serves as a pedagogical tool with a learning purpose, moving beyond entertainment to deliver engaging interactive media to support learning. It is designed to distil specific and complex learning concepts while maintaining the entertainment factors through the learner’s engagement and interaction with information, tools, materials, other learners as well as the lecturer/facilitator within the game. Previous studies have identified the benefits of using game-based learning to support teaching and learning. It includes enhancing engagement and encouraging curiosity, motivation, self-directed learning, self-monitoring, self-assessment, problem-solving and decision making. It promotes active participation and interaction as a centre of experience to advance the students’ understanding. In spite of numerous studies and engines proposed by academia and experts to design, evaluating the serious game effectiveness and learner’s improvement are not easy. Two main questions that need to be answered are: (1) how to understand the learner’s skill and performance improvement and (2) how to capture and analyse the data (i.e. data from gameplay session or other data). These questions need to be answered and incorporated in the game from the beginning (i.e. game design stage) and not only in the game evaluation stage. To date, there is limited engines that can help to evaluate the serious game’s effectiveness on improving the learner’s skills and performance. Most of the available engines merely focus on improving the game entertainment experience rather than improving the learner’s skills and performance. This project aims to develop a novel serious game engine to improve learner’s skills and performance based on the intended learning outcomes of the game. Based on the intended learning outcomes, the engine would be able to gather relevant gameplay data (i.e. learner’s in-game actions and decisions) and turn it into valuable analytics (or actionable intelligence) for performance measurement, assessment and improvement. Leveraging on AI algorithms and technologies (such as Collaborative Filtering, Deep Learning and Gradient Boosting), this engine would identify learner’s behaviour patterns and recommend a personalized learning strategy to seamlessly and continuously improve the learner’s skills and performance throughout the gameplay session. Specific Aims: The specific aims of this project is to develop a smart serious game engine for improving learner’s skills and performance. It can be further elaborated to the following objectives: • Develop a serious game design framework to identify the required gameplay data based on the specific intended learning outcomes. Not all the gameplay data is useful. This framework would be able to help identifying the important data and removing the irrelevant data. • Develop data collection engine

title: Wireless Miniaturised GonioPEN for irido-corneal imaging
abs: Glaucoma is a condition that will affect more than 76 million people by 2020 and majority will be in Asia. This is an irreversible blinding condition which needs early diagnosis. One of the unmet needs is an inexpensive device that can image the front portion of the eye which drains the nutritive fluid of the eye (aqueous humor) called the angle. This area is closed in angle closure disease and the clinician has to identify it early to diagnose the condition. Currently, there is no availability of “inexpensive” devices for imaging the iridocorneal angle. EyeCam and anterior segment optical coherence tomography are the main competing instruments, both of which are bulky and expensive (between 25,000 to 120,000 USD). We have developed a simple device and provided proof of concept clinical trials earlier. This phase of the project will refine this miniaturized probe prototype developed by us (GonioPEN), into a wireless handheld probe with integrated software to automatically diagnose angle closure. The imaging probe will have a basic camera with LEDs with power source to image the angle of the eye with minimal contact at limbus. Preliminary clinical trials show an AUC of 0.96 for angle closure diagnosis in comparison to gonioscopy (n=35 eyes). The probe can be stand-alone (to be used by a technician/nurse) or to be integrated with slit lamp (to be used by a clinician). The device is slated for primary, secondary or tertiary care use along with visual acuity examination as a replacement for gonioscopy and the cost is meant to be relatively inexpensive ( < SGD 7000). Additional images that can be taken include external, anterior segment and fundus images. Future projects can look into integrating hardware and software refinements, to document intraoperative images (during glaucoma surgeries and Minimally Invasive Glaucoma Surgeries) and wide-field fundus images.

title: Reducing anti-microbial resistance in intensive care units – a regional randomised strategy trial
abs:
In healthcare settings, antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is driven by excessive antimicrobial exposure while transmission is affected by infection control standards. Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) is the most common nosocomial infection in ICU patients globally. In a survey of 1,417 ICUs worldwide, the prevalence of respiratory tract infection in patients with nosocomial infections, was 64%. VAP prolongs the length of mechanical ventilation, hospitalization and inpatient cost. The high prevalence and antibiotic usage makes VAP a key driver of AMR in ICUs. We would like to propose a three-pronged approach to combat AMR.
  
The first focus is a RCT where the intervention is to shorten the antibiotic treatment of VAP to 3 or 5 days, challenging the current standard treatment (up to 14 days). REGARD-VAP emphasises individualised treatment, unlike previous studies with strict 8 days of antibiotics treatment. Fitness to stop antibiotics is dependent on objective clinical criteria of defervescence and hemodynamic stability, making the protocol reproducible and cost effective. This study will investigate the treatment of VAP in ICUs for the first time in Asia.

title: Asian Diabetes Outcome Prevention Trial (ADOPT)
abs:
Rationale: Cardiovascular events are the leading cause of death among patients with diabetes. Early identification of high risk diabetic (DM) patients for intensification of preventive therapy may prevent cardiovascular events.

Aims: Among biomarker (N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide, NT-proBNP)-identified high risk type 2 DM patients without pre-existing cardiovascular disease

Design: Prospective multinational randomized open-label, parallel group, active-controlled, two-arm, long-term morbidity and mortality trial involving 5 countries (Singapore, Malaysia, China, Taiwan, India; estimated 6 sites each) with patients followed for 2 years.

Population: Adults with type 2 DM without cardiac disease* and with NT-proBNP > 125 pg/mL (*defined as known coronary stenosis >70%, reduced left ventricular ejection fraction <40%, or a history of myocardial infarction/ coronary revascularization/ heart failure hospitalization/ ischemic stroke/ prior lower limb amputation or angioplasty)

Randomization: 1:1 randomization to either
 (1) Intensive Treatment group (high dose of RAASi and beta-blockers as well as SGLT2i) on top of standard therapy; or
 (2) Control group (standard therapy where the use of SGLT2i at randomization is not allowed but RAASi and beta-blockers, with the exception of maximal dosage, are allowed). Every attempt is made to use other blood pressure lowering drugs than RAASi or beta-blockers, as well as other anti-DM agents, in the control group.
 Primary endpoint: Combined endpoint based on the first occurrence of cardiovascular death and major cardiovascular event (ischemic stroke/myocardial infarction/heart failure events)
