title: Use of a wirelessly-powered intracranially implanted near-infrared light delivery device for neuro-protection in rodent model of Parkinson's Disease
abs: Hypothesis We hypothesize that a wirelessly powered intracranially implanted near infrared light (NIR) delivery device prevents alpha synucleopathy progression and its related deficits in an alpha synuclein preformed-fibril induced Parkinsonian rodent model. This is aimed at being a proof of concept study with the aim of translating this technology for use in human Parkinson's Disease (PD) patients. Specific Aim 1 To generate a rodent model of Parkinson’s disease by stereotaxic injection of human alpha synuclein pre-formed fibrils into the mouse striatum. Specific Aim 2 To create a wirelessly powered miniature NIR delivery device that can be safely implanted into the mouse brain and allow consistent delivery of NIR light. Specific Aim 3 To test the efficacy of the wirelessly powered NIR delivery device by stereotaxic implantation into the mouse striatum, followed by delivery of NIR therapy over several months to see if alpha synuclein pathology can be mitigated. Specific Aim 4 To determine the cellular mechanisms through which alpha synuclein achieves its neuroprotective effects using an in-vitro cell culture PD model. Methodology and Approach We aim to generate a rodent model of PD using stereotaxic injection of alpha synuclein PFF into the mouse striatum. Alpha synuclein PFF are known to induce lewy body pathology both in in-vitro and in-vivo. Subsequent implantation of an NIR delivery device into the mouse striatum with delivery of pulsed NIR is aimed at retarding the progression of alpha synucleopathy. The purpose of selecting this model is because it recapitulates the gradual degeneration of neurons and slow progression of lewy body pathology over time. It also allows us to test our ultimate intent of neuroprotection in early Parkinson's disease in human patients in a mouse model. We have shown in primary neuronal culture PD models that NIR therapy is effective at rescue from PD-toxin mediated neuronal death. We also have engineering expertise that have successfully produced miniature wirelessly powered implants in the mouse. Coupled with our expertise at generating Parkinsonian mouse models, this project is likely to be feasible.

title: The next-generation non-volatile memory: towards THz operation
abs: The expensive CMOS based memories (SRAM and DRAM) which are currently operational in gigahertz will fail to accommodate this expanding demand due to their small capacity and power-hungry behaviors. Therefore, in order to meet the ever increasing demands, the computing and memory speed need to evolve from the gigahertz (GHz) to terahertz (THz) regime. The science of low dimensional magnetics or spintronics devices which exploit the spin degree of freedom of electrons is one of central growing fields in modern science and technology, some of which have already had enormous technological impact such as magnetic sensors and magnetic random access memory (MRAM). Here, we propose the use of optics and spintronics elements to realize the THz speed operation for non-volatile magnetic memories. So far, ferromagnetic spintronics has been a main focus as it offers non-volatile memory through current-induced switching effects. However, as the cell size reduces, it becomes extremely difficult to meet the required thermal stability and low enough switching current using conventional ferromagnet based spintronics. Therefore, there must be a fundamental game changer in terms of materials and structures. Further, the inherent speed limit of the electrical control of spintronics can be only overcome by using materials with the resonance frequency at THz and their integration with optical components as there are no electrical means to measure this kind of speed. Optical techniques have been proven to be able to handle spin dynamics in the THz range and beyond. One could open new avenues in operation speeds by combining ultrafast photonics with spintronics. Our proposed novel material based spintronics elements will push the speed to THz regime. Further, our proposed integration of optics with spintronics enables the use of THz optics elements to read and write the THz memory device. The reach of THz spintronics elements can be further extended to IoTs and other peripheral short-range devices to create an ultrafast computing and storage environment operating in the THz range.
kw: non-volatile memory, magnetic random access memory, THz

title: A protein biophysical strategy for discovering and targeting key protein nodes in cancer
abs: Proteins are key players in most cellular processes and targets for nearly all drugs. However, studies of functional aspects of proteins in their physiological environment have been challenging. Mass-spectrometry (MS)-based proteomics have made significant advances in recent decades. In addition to assessing protein levels and post-translational modifications in cells, several different functional proteomics techniques have yielded critical information on protein interactions with biomolecules at the proteome level. Unfortunately, most of these techniques depend on engineered cells and/or chemical probes and/or analysis of samples equilibrated in cell lysates before measuring interactions, and hence, only partially reflect the situation in unperturbed cells. This is particularly problematic for cancer research and anti-cancer drug development, when cancer cells are evolving rapidly, dramatically changing functional and organizational aspects of their proteomes upon progression and drug treatment. Hitherto, however, no direct, comprehensive and interactive proteome-wide approaches have been available for studies of functional modulations of the human proteome in intact cells and tissues. Here, we will further develop and apply the novel, high-resolution MS-CETSA platform to shed new light on biological processes underpinning cancer progression, focusing on the challenges of cancer resistance and metastasis, and as a result, identify new, potentially important molecular processes and protein nodes that can be targeted pharmacologically or can serve as biomarkers for critical events in patient samples. Crucially, this platform can be applied directly towards interrogating freshly resected human tumors to gain insights into the drug-target interactions and essential downstream effects, and therefore reveal mechanisms of resistance that cannot be otherwise probed in situ. Focusing on breast and lung cancers, the Specific Themes for this project are: (i) Applying MS-CETSA for deep mechanistic studies on the action of cellular proteomes in cancer processes; (ii) To provide in-depth mechanistic understanding of drug action and resistance to current and emerging cytotoxic cancer drugs and immune activating drugs, thereby generating novel biomarkers and drug targets for improved cancer therapies; (iii) Phenotypic screening of CRISPR/Cas9 and compound libraries to identify hits overcoming resistance and compounds which serve as starting points for drug development; and (iv) Further development of CETSA integration with other less direct proteomics techniques to support CETSA data interpretation and provide complementary functional information.
kw: Biophysics, CETSA, Cancer, Drug resistance

title: Geometric Interface Optics: A Synthetic Platform for High-capacity & Low-dimensional Metaphotonics
abs: The proposed project aims at developing functionalized and unprecedented low-dimensional photonic devices by hybridizing multi-physical geometric effects at flat-profile configurations, thereby achieving full manipulation of photons and excitons with higher efficiency, reconfigurable flexibility, and nanometer-precision control of polarization/phase/amplitude. To empower next-generation integrated circuits and nanophotonics, the geometric effects are probably one out of the very limited options yet usually neglected factor which may actually dominate the material properties and device performances. The research will be dedicated to the fundamental physics investigation for a series of cooperating geometry-induced effects, including excitonic-photonic interplay, intrinsic spin Hall materials, transformation-optic quantum effect, and size-dependent tunability. Novel phenomena and applications will be demonstrated consequently. On the other hand, geometric designs for meta-structures provide a sophisticated means to manipulate photons, plasmons, electrons, and excitons and make them addressable at nanometer scale right on the interface. We will establish a synergetic photonic framework: geometric interface optics, on which novel geometric effects and materials are to be leveraged and used to transform conventional bulk devices into low-dimensional interfaces with versatile high-capacity functionalities.

title: Using GM-CSF as a Host Directed Therapeutic against COVID-19 - A Phase 2 Investigator Initiated Trial
abs: The coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) has rapidly become a pandemic. COVID-19 poses a mortality risk of 3-7%, rising to 20% in older patients with co-morbidities. Of all infected patients, 15-20% will develop severe respiratory symptoms necessitating hospital admission. Around 5% of patients will require invasive mechanical ventilation, and up to 50% will die. Evidence in severe COVID-19 suggests that these patients experience cytokine storm and progressed rapidly with acute respiratory distress syndrome and eventual multi-organ failure. Early identification and immediate treatment of hyperinflammation is thus recommended to reduce mortality. Granulocyte Macrophage Colony Stimulating Factor (GM-CSF) has been shown to be a myelopoietic growth factor that has pleiotropic effects in promoting the differentiation of immature precursors into polymorphonuclear neutrophils, monocytes/ macrophages and dendritic cells, and also in controlling the function of fully mature myeloid cells. It plays an important role in priming monocytes for production of proinflammatory cytokines under TLR and NLR stimulation. It has a broad impact on the processes driving DC differentiation and affects DC effector function at the mature state. Importantly, GM-CSF plays a critical role in host defense and stimulating antiviral immunity. Detailed studies have also shown that GM-CSF is necessary for the maturation of alveolar macrophages from foetal monocytes and the maintenance of these cells in adulthood. The known toxicology, pharmacologic and safety data also support the use of Leukine® in hypoxic respiratory failure and ARDS due to COVID-19. This study aims to recruit patients with evidence of pneumonia and hypoxia who have increased risk for severe disease and need for mechanical ventilation. The overall hypothesis is that GM-CSF has antiviral immunity, can provide the stimulus to restore immune homeostasis in the lung with acute lung injury from COVID-19, and can promote lung repair mechanisms, which would lead to improvement in lung oxygenation parameters.

title: The SARS-CoV-2 Antibody Initiative
abs: There are significant ongoing efforts in both NUS and A*STAR to develop antibody-based tests, diagnostics and biologic countermeasures for COVID-19. To reduce unnecessary overlap/competition and accelerate out-put, teams of Immunologists and Virologists from both organizations have formulated a plan for how they can coordinate their research activities with clinical colleagues at NCID and NUH. This represents an aggregation of most of the leading antibody engineers and viral Immunologists in Singapore and all are committed to working as a team to develop solutions for COVID-19. Because antibodies form the principal raw materials for Point-of-Care tests (POCT) and can also be exploited as direct prophylactic /therapeutic agents, we are in a strong position to make a direct impact on this disease in the immediate to mid- term. This is based upon access to well-characterized convalescent COVID-19 patients (from our clinical colleagues) combined with our collective expertise in advanced Antibody (HuMab) technologies and the human Immunology of COVID-19.

title: Media communication, online falsehoods and population responses surrounding the novel coronavirus disease crisis (COVID-19) in Singapore
abs: The recent outbreak of the novel coronavirus disease (COVID-19) has had a large impact on Singapore which is an Asian travel, finance and education hub. A fundamental determinant of successful management of the infectious disease outbreak crisis is to ensure that health preparedness messaging can educate and engage the public in preventative health behaviors before and during community transmission. This not only requires strategic communication of health messaging but also the containment of falsehoods and fake news surrounding the outbreak. In this research project, the research team aims to investigate how mainstream media and social media have played a role in contributing to public preparedness versus paranoia during infectious disease outbreaks, particularly from the perspective of health messaging and online falsehoods. First, the team will access, chronicle, and analyse both the mainstream media coverage of the crisis of the novel coronavirus (SARS-COV-2), its disease (COVID-19) and the way news has been circulated in Singapore. Special attention will be paid to how mainstream media and the government have tackled various online falsehoods, including common misinformation, deliberate fake news, disinformation, and rumours about the disease and the resulting effects. Second, the study plans to examine the Singapore public's attitudinal and behavioural reactions to online falsehoods and health messaging surrounding the COVID-19 crisis by monitoring social media posts and responses. Lastly, the study aims to examine and further provide scientific evidence on public reactions towards false media content via online risk communication experiments and a nation-wide survey. This proposed project will extend our understanding of the effects of current risk communication strategies, in particular, in relation to online falsehoods on population behaviors both online and offline. The research findings would make important contributions to global crisis response, better health communication strategies and public health policy.

title:
Coronavirus disease-19: A seroepidemiology study among healthcare workers in Singapore 
(the COVSEP study)
abs: The 2019 outbreak of the novel coronavirus (SARS-CoV-2) has spread to a growing number of countries worldwide. Accumulating data indicate that a majority of patients develop point to a predominantly mild and self-limiting illness, despite initial concerns that SARS-CoV-2 would inevitably lead to severe respiratory failure in most infected patients. As healthcare workers harbour an increased risk of nosocomial transmission, we propose a prospective seroepidemiology study to examine the hypothesis that younger and healthier healthcare workers develop fewer or no symptoms should they develop Covid-19 infection compared with older individuals and those with medical comorbidities. A detailed study on the full spectrum of Covid-19 is necessary to understand the proportion of individuals who develop interval seroconversion with minimal or no symptoms, and the reasons why these individuals do not manifest apparent clinical symptoms. Between 24 February 2020 and 6 March 2020, 643 healthcare workers (mean age 36 years, 80% women) who work in clinical environments at either the Emergency Room, medical intensive care unit, isolation wards, general medical wards and hospital/research laboratories, were prospectively recruited using an approved ethics protocol (DSRB 2020/00166). These subjects will be closely followed for the development of clinical features of infection and fatigue; Covid-19 serology will be assayed at baseline and at 3 months later to diagnose interval seroconversion to Covid-19. Biomarkers of inflammation, oxidative damage and endothelial damage will be measured to explore potential reasons why some patients develop more symptoms than others. The study team comprises senior clinician scientists and infectious disease specialists with extensive experience in translational clinical research. title: Investigating airway cell tropism, responses and entry receptor of COVID-19 virus (SARS-CoV-2) in elucidating its transmission and pathogenesis in the airway
abs: The emergence of the novel coronavirus (SARS-CoV-2) has resulted in an outbreak that affected its country of origin greatly and is threatening to escalate into a pandemic. In comparison to SARS, which infected ~8000 people in 6-8 months, SARS-CoV-2 has exceeded the numbers in one months’ time. While the rapid spread may be attributed to the increased transport capabilities and population density, there may also exist fundamental virologic difference between SARS-CoV-2 and its severe disease-causing counterparts, SARS-CoV and MERS-CoV. Initial reports suggested that SARS-CoV-2 are likely to utilize the ACE2 receptor for their entry into the airway like SARS-CoV, their rapid transmission may also suggest a differential tropism compared to SARS-CoV, possibly in the affinity to the upper airway. The usage of air-liquid interface (ALI) differentiated airway epithelial cells of the upper and lower airway was shown to be pivotal in the study of emerging respiratory viral diseases. Here we proposed the use of human and bat nasal epithelial culture to study the upper airway interaction of SARS-CoV-2 infection; followed by comparing the interaction with lower airway ALI-culture models, where its establishment is imperative for current and future outbreak response related studies in Singapore. By establishing the infection biology of SARS-CoV-2 in human and bat airway cells, we can elucidate the pathogenesis of the virus leading to severe diseases as well as identify the mechanism of inter-species transmission. We will also further apply bioinformatics and proteomics analysis to further identify the entry receptor of SARS-CoV-2 as a target for treatment and vaccination. The findings from this study will not only further the understanding on how SARS-CoV-2 transmit and cause severe disease; the pipeline established for this study can also be applied to CoV and other respiratory viruses, including emerging zoonotic viruses yet to make an interspecies jump.

title: Lung Organoids: A tool of the fourth industrial revolution to study COVID-19 pathogenesis
abs: In December 2019, healthcare facilities in Wuhan, Hubei Province, China reported a cluster of severe pneumonia, complicated by acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) in patients linked to an animal wholesale market. Routine microbiology could not identify a causative agent, and, ensuing viral cultures, coupled to genomic sequencing of specimens from affected patients revealed a novel coronavirus of potential zoonotic origin, now termed SARS-CoV-2 (severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2). Since the early reports from Wuhan, the numbers of COVID-19 cases globally have exponentially increased with a reported 95,483 cases and 3,286 deaths in 84 countries (including Singapore) as of 5th March 2020. Therefore, an urgent unmet clinical need exists to better expound pathogenic mechanisms of SARS-CoV-2 airway infection, which, will be leveraged to identify early biomarkers predictive of severe infection. Studying this necessitates a relevant model system that recapitulates the in-vivo airway microenvironment, one provided by lung organoids. Lung organoids are optimal physiological and clinically relevant model systems resembling intimately the airway microenvironment allowing detailed study of the complex, multi-faceted interplay between host and pathogen. Organoids derived from patient or donor cells retain an individual’s genetic and biological characteristics attesting for relevance in applying precision medicine to infectious diseases. Using innovative approaches reinforced by strong preliminary data, the PI and his team have established 3D lung organoid primary cell culture systems that demonstrate susceptibility to viral infection, and, offer significant advantages over traditional air-liquid interface (ALI) and ex-vivo explant systems. Here, we propose extending our studies to focus on SARS-CoV-2 infection in lung organoids to dissect out pathogenic mechanisms, and, better understand why some patients become critically ill. By employing a multi-omics and systems biology approach with a multi-disciplinary investigating team that demonstrate complementary expertise, we aim to identify potential biomarkers predictive of progression to severe infection for clinical translation.

title: Covid-19 Virtual Disease health System Outcomes model for Singapore (CoViD- SOS)
abs: As the COVID-19 outbreak unfolds it will lead to health system-wide consequences. These can be direct consequences experienced by COVID-19 patients; and indirect ones faced by non-COVID-19 patients due to downstream effects of policy responses, particularly due to re-prioritization of existing services and opportunity costs. Therefore, our overall aim is to minimize impact of the evolving COVID-19 disease outbreak on Singapore health systems’ outcomes by advising policy through whole-system modeling using existing data and novel modelling methods leading to measured policy responses. Building upon local data, preliminary studies and prior experience of the investigators, we have set three specific aims: 1) Build computer simulation models to: a) evaluate impact of policies on health systems estimating overall mortality, morbidity and service utilization; b) understand high infectious disease dynamics at higher resolution for more precise policy decisions. 2) Assess actual health services utilization attributable to COVID-19 and non-COVID-19 conditions through analyzing disease registries. Qualitative data from patients and other stakeholders will enrich this data. Costs of care will also be assessed capitalizing on routine data sources. 3) Evaluate policy experiments, through conventional and probabilistic sensitivity analyses in three potential scenarios i.e. a)COVID-19 remains under control; b)difficult to control with local clusters and c)full-blown local epidemic. If successful, this proposal will use sophisticated simulation modelling and analyses to inform current and future policy decisions optimizing resource allocation and reducing business interruptions in such situations locally and even globally. The virtual outbreak model can be further developed to address different disease outbreak scenarios in the future, and will also enhance our national response to future epidemics.

title: Environmental SARS-CoV-2 surveillance in Singapore built environment
abs: The recent outbreak of the novel coronavirus SARS-CoV-2 has resulted in a large number of infections and significant mortality in more than 100 countries globally. Spreading of SARS-CoV-2 infections is currently monitored by testing individuals with respiratory and other symptoms on a case-by-case basis, often multiple times. This results in substantial costs and efforts and is not suited in instances where large groups of people in mass gatherings have to be assessed on a short time scale. We therefore propose to establish the limits of detection for SARS-CoV-2 nucleic acids, collected by high volumetric flowrate air samplers in indoor settings. The approach is based on an ultra-low biomass analysis pipeline that was established within an MOE Tier 3 programme on the sources, function and ecology of urban air microbiomes. Using a sampling regime within NUH isolation wards, the team aims to demonstrate in principle that detection of SARS-CoV-2 in air samples is possible. Our ongoing collaborative efforts between NUS, NUH and NEA during the COVID-19 outbreak have established experimental procedures in NUH isolation wards that can now serve as test beds for the proposed population-scale testing. Using the airflow in NUH isolation rooms for pilot studies, we will sample airborne biomass both in-room and the exhaust air, thereby testing the feasibility of RT-PCR detection of viral nucleic acids in large volumes of air. The knowledge gained from these pilot studies can then be extended to other settings in the Singapore built environment. This potentially will enable continuous monitoring of schools, religious gathering places, shopping centres, airports, and various forms of mass transport. The development of air sample-based environmental surveys can proceed instantly using an experienced team of investigators and an existing fleet of 47 air samplers at SCELSE and 20 units at NEA.

title: Rapid Cellulose-Based Serological and Diagnostic Tests for COVID-19
inst: CREATE - Singapore-MIT Alliance for Research and Technology (CREATE-SMART)
abs: The alarming spread of the corona virus, SARS-CoV-2, has raised emergency public health concern, globally. With no treatment and vaccine available, the best control is to rapidly diagnose infected individuals and apply quarantine period to prevent further viral transmission. However the symptoms caused by SARS-CoV-2 infections may be mild or unnoticeable. Patients may not know they have been infected and may have spread the disease unknowingly. Current diagnostic tests depend largely on the detection of a viral genomic profile using RT-PCR. However this method often lacks accuracy for patients with mild or no symptoms. Serological test for detection of antibodies against SARS-CoV-2 virus is preferred for diagnosis of mild symptomatic or asymptomatic patients. Although RT-PCR and serological tests provide satisfy results, they require up to 5 days of turn-around-time. Furthermore, they demand skilled personnel and special laboratory facilities to run the tests, thereby restricting the tests only to hospitals and laboratories. Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) that can be operated outside of hospitals are urgently desired to screen as many people as possible to timely triage SARS-CoV-2 infected cases and prevent the virus from spreading. We propose development of two types of paper-based RDTs that requires only 10 minutes operation time and can be operated outside of hospitals. (i) Serological test to detect antibodies against SARS-CoV-2 and (ii) RDTs to detect SARS-CoV-2 biomarkers. Protein engineering technologies will be used to (i) immobilize high densities of fragments of SARS-CoV-2 S protein within a cellulose matrix to capture SARS-CoV-2 antibodies and (ii) to create new binder proteins to capture the SARS-CoV-2 biomarkers, N and S proteins. With our technologies, the tests will be more robust than standard serological and antibody-based tests and therefore can be deployed for field applications without the need for temperature controlled facilities, facilitating a larger scale of disease screening.
kw: Diagnosis; rapid diagnostic test; protein engineering; biomarkers; protein detection; antibodies

title: Establishment of COVID-2019 animal infection models
abs: The 2019 novel coronavirus outbreak (COVID-19) is a major challenge for public health globally. Infection with severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) has been associated with serious respiratory distress in a large number of patients and hospitalization in intensive care settings is required. Conversely, the vast majority of infected people experience a mild illness. However, the dynamics of viral infection, replication and shedding are poorly understood. A better understanding of viral pathogenesis and infection dynamics will shed light on the COVID-19 disease and provide valuable information for patient management. We will assess four animal models to determine susceptibility to infection by SARS-CoV-2. The animal species that we will test are cynomolgus macaques, marmoset, and mice. We hypothesize that NHP and mice possessing the human ACE2 receptor will be susceptible to infection with SARS-CoV-2 and will develop hallmarks of COVID-19 disease. As SARS-CoV-2 does not readily infect mice, we will develop and test humanized mice and ACE2 mice. Establishment of a small animal model and non-human primate model provides a valuable platform to study SARS-CoV-2 pathogenesis and to evaluate vaccines and therapeutics.

title: Enabling Scalable Quantum Computation via a Programmable Quantum Router
abs: Scaling up a quantum system without sacrificing the performance of its individual elements is currently one of the most significant challenges towards realising robust universal quantum computing (QC). One promising strategy to tackle this challenge is via a modular architecture, where small quantum modules, each consisting of several error-corrected logical elements, are wired together via coherent quantum communication channels to form a complex network capable of large-scale information processing and computation. This is akin to putting together simple Lego bricks to construct more complex structures, with enhanced isolation between the constituent parts, robustness against local errors, and full system reconfigurability. Recent experimental progress has enabled the realisation of many crucial building blocks of a modular quantum computer using microwave circuits, a powerful and versatile platform favoured for its robustness, simplicity, and engineerability. One of the most critical elements needed to enhance the computational power of a modular system is a quantum router that can provide deterministic and all-to-all connectivity on demand across multiple isolated modules. While direct state transfer between two modules has recently been demonstrated using microwave circuits, the realisation of a programmable quantum multimode router remains a challenge due to the complexity in achieving robust integration and control across multiple quantum elements. The overall goal of this project is to engineer such a programmable quantum router using superconducting circuits to enable scalable QC. This will build upon my prior works on the realisation of robust logic gates, which were recently published in renowned journals such as \textit{Nature} and mark a significant breakthrough in our ability to effectively engineer programmable interactions between bosonic quantum memory modules. Through this research programme, I aim to first establish the state-of-the-art infrastructure in Singapore to robustly design, fabricate, and characterise these circuit elements. With these capabilities, we will construct the router using an array of superconducting resonators interacting through frequency-converting elements based on Josephson junctions. We will then demonstrate its ability to coherently transfer quantum signals across multiple different modules on the fly. Additionally, using the same hardware, we plan to design and implement an efficient protocol for on-demand generation of multimode entangled states, which are valuable resources for quantum computing and quantum communication. This research programme, together with my expertise, provides a valuable avenue to develop the technical capabilities and talent pool in superconducting microwave circuits, which are currently absent in the Singapore quantum computing ecosystem. The device and techniques developed through this project are indispensable ingredients for robust and scalable QC in a modular architect

title: Multi-omic, multi-platform profiling of the tumor immune microenvironment in colorectal cancers.
abs: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the 3rd most common cancer globally with >1.5 million new cases diagnosed annually. Colorectal cancer have generally been refractory to current ICB therapy. The majority of CRCs are microsatellite stable (MSS), where objective response rates to checkpoint inhibition have been near zero. A thorough evaluation of the complexity of tumor-host immune-drug interactions is required to understand mechanisms of immune evasion across patients and tumours and enable optimal therapy development & deployment. Few studies have evaluated immunotherapy in early stage surgically resectable cancers. Compared to late stage cancers, in early stage disease, immunotherapy may work through different mechanisms. Pre-operative (or neoadjuvant) treatment of early stage cancers may leverage primary tumour as antigen source for expansion and activation of tumour-specfic T cells and systemic surveillance of micrometastases. Singhealth has set up an academic-industry collaboration with Merck Sharp & Dohme (MSD) to address the unmet medical need of the immuno-refractory state of colorectal cancer, by establishing a multi-platform multi-omic programme comprehensively cataloguing tumour-immune interactions in colorectal cancer to empower the discovery, development and more precise deployment of effective immunotherapy regimens to be deployed in colorectal cancer. Our programme is distinguished by simultaneous profiling of different immune-biology properties with multiple leading-edge high throughput technologies in the same tumours to enable an unparalleled comprehensive catalogue and analysis of tumor-host immune-drug interactions. We will focus on multi-omic profiling of two patient groups: 1) 50 early stage colorectal cancer tumours to define the native immune biology of colorectal cancer, and 2) 50 early stage colorectal cancer tumours from patients pre-treated with two doses of Pembrolizumab (anti-PD-1) to understand how PD-1 blockade alters the immune biology of colorectal cancer. Depending on the site (colon or rectum) and local extent of disease, pembrolizumab will be administered with chemotherapy or radiotherapy in the pre-operative setting.

title: Singapore lYMPHoma translatiONal styudY (SYMPHONY)
abs: Diagnosis of lymphoma is difficult, lacks reproducibility and often requires an extensive and costly array of immunohistochemistry (IHC) stains. Leveraging on the advancement of artificial intelligence / machine learning field and emerging technologies such as microRNA (miRNA) expression profiling, we aim to combine extracted tissue biomarker features from multiple sources, including computer-aided digital image analysis, to maximise the amount of biological information derived from individual patient samples to unlock diagnostic, prognostic and potential theranostic information. Advances in this field have made it possible to analyse conventional haematoxylin and eosin stained slides and provide a list of broad differential diagnoses in a given case. Our preliminary work has shown that it is possible to utilize ML strategies on annotated digital pathology images to generate a list of differential diagnoses. However, further histological subtyping often requires the integration of a wide panel of IHC stains and additional cytogenetic/molecular investigations. The limitations of IHC have driven a growing need for an alternative diagnostic tool that is tissue-saving, cost-effective and clinically practical. With the advent of low-cost qPCR machines, detection of miRNA is now economical and technically within reach of many laboratories. Combining data from clinical history and other laboratory investigations, we aim to develop novel, cost-efficient morpho-molecular lymphoma diagnostics that will overcome the lack of haematopathologist expertise in developing nations and enhance the productivity of experienced pathologists in first-world nations. This effort will be supported by industry collaborations with MiRXES and Qritive.

title: Using A Robotic Endoscope to Perform Appendicectomy
abs: Background Although laparoscopic surgery is minimally invasive, its problems are the limited degrees of freedom of the rigid instruments. Robotic laparoscopic surgery overcomes this with multiple degrees of freedom of robotic wrists. However, robotic surgery is costly, and has not been shown to be cost-effective compared with conventional surgery. Natural orifice transluminal endoscopic surgery (NOTES) aims to overcome this limitation with “scarless” surgeries, decreased postoperative pain and faster recovery. However, effective triangulation is challenging in a pure NOTES platform using rigid instruments. Recently, robotic flexible endoscopy was introduced for complex procedures. The efficacy of robotic endoscopy in intraabdominal surgery has yet to be tested. Aims and hypotheses We aim to perform an appendicectomy using the robotic endoscope in a pilot animal study. We hypothesize that robotic endoscopes can perform intraabdominal surgeries through an anterior abdominal wall incision or via NOTES. Methodology As pigs do not have an appendix, a right salphingo-oophorectomy in a female pig will be performed instead to simulate an appendicectomy. Traditional steps of an appendicectomy will be modified to perform surgery using a robotic endoscope. Instead of laparoscopic hem-o-loks, the artery will be secured with endoscopic Resolution clips. The base of the fallopian tube will be tied with endoscopic endoloops. Endoscopic Roth Net will be used to retrieve the specimen, instead of laparoscopic specimen retrieval bags. Primary outcomes assessed are successful completion of each surgical step. Secondary outcomes include total operative time, equipment failures and intraoperative complications. Health technology assessment will be done. Feasibility Technically, we have performed prior animal studies which demonstrated the feasibility and safety of using the robotic endoscope to perform complex therapeutic endoscopic procedures. We have also demonstrated the feasibility of performing suturing using the existing robotic endoscope in animal trials. Logistically, the study team comprises of engineers from Nanyang Technological University (NTU), a surgeon and a gastroenterologist from National University Hospital (NUH). Together with inputs from the surgical team, the engineering team will make improvements to the existing robotic endoscope prototype. The surgical team will conduct the animal study and perform the appendicectomy using the improved robotic endoscope. Clinical significance With robotic flexible endoscopes performing intraabdominal surgeries, there is effective instrument triangulation. With its compact size, robotic endoscope is cheaper, occupies smaller space, and has a much shorter set-up time, thus will be more cost-effective. The success of this study will radically change intraabdominal surgical approaches.

title: Advancing precision medicine for cardiovascular disease and diabetes in Asian populations
abs: Identification of the mechanisms underlying the increased risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) and diabetes in Asian populations, and developing affordable, effective and scalable strategies for risk stratification and prevention of these major diseases, are urgent national and global public health priorities. To address these challenges, we first create a longitudinal population study of >100,000 Singaporeans (“SG100K”) comprising comprehensive phenotypic characterisation, high quality biological samples, and linkage to national electronic health records. In partnership with the National Precision Medicine programme, we will exploit SG100K to determine the behavioural (including nutrition and physical activity), environmental, genetic and other molecular factors that underpin CVD and diabetes in the multi-ethnic Asian population of Singapore. We will use the knowledge generated to develop and validate algorithms for accurate identification of Asian men and women at risk of CVD and diabetes, taking polygenic information into account, and to identify people with monogenic metabolic defects that may cause early-onset disease. We will strengthen tools for communication of cardiovascular and metabolic risk, taking into account non-genetic and genetic information, and develop personalised approaches to behaviour change for health promotion, that are tailored to social, cultural and environmental context, and delivered by scalable digital platforms. We will evaluate the impact of our risk stratification, communication and behavioural support platforms on engagement with health promotion, and quantify efficacy and cost-effectiveness for prevention of CVD and T2D in community and primary care settings. We will thus advance population and precision health for CVD and diabetes, the leading causes of death and disability in Singapore. In addition, we will deliver SG100K as a unique platform for state-of-the-art epidemiological, translational and precision medicine research, in the genetically distinct and culturally diverse Asian populations of Singapore, which will impact management of a wide range of chronic disease, at national, regional and international scale.

title:
DYNAMO: Diabetes studY on Nephropathy And Microvascular cOmplications
Theme Title: Identification and Validation of Biomarkers to develop predictive models for the onset and progression of DN
abs: Diabetic nephropathy (DN) is a devastating complication of diabetes causing significant morbidity, mortality and human suffering. In Singapore, the incidence of DN as a cause of end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) is among the highest in the world. Despite the substantial public health burden associated with DN, its molecular pathogenesis is poorly understood and no new drugs for DN have been introduced in nearly 20 years. Within the population of diabetics, only a subset develops DN indicating a strong familial contribution to this risk. Nonetheless, identification of genetic variants controlling DN susceptibility has been difficult. Furthermore, no reliable biomarkers exist to stratify high-risk patients before the onset of clinically apparent diabetic kidney disease. Capitalizing on a confluence of world-class expertise in research on diabetes and its complications in Singapore, the Diabetes studY of Nephropathy And other Microvascular cOmplications (DYNAMO) plans to employ multiple experimental approaches to identify new mechanistic pathways in DN, discover and validate new targets for DN treatment, and define novel biomarkers and strategies to stratify DN risk within the T2D population. These approaches include human genetics, targeted and non-targeted metabolomics, animal modeling, and urinary exosomes studies. DYNAMO also takes advantage of several established, well-characterized Singaporean patient cohorts, consisting of nearly 30,000 individuals with stored serum, genetic samples, urine, and retinal photographs for analyses. When sample sizes are limited, DYNAMO has assembled an international collaborative network to allow for the integration of data with the largest human genetics studies ongoing in the world. The strategic focus of our LCG incorporates cutting edge technologies to take a systems biology approach to target and biomarker discovery and validation. The work is based on world class science, substantial track record and prior work of the participating investigators, and a clear focus on unmet needs for DN in Singapore and globally.

title: Singapore Lymphoma Translational Study Symphony
abs: 1. Predictive analytics to enhance pathological diagnosis Using digital pathology and machine learning, we intend to develop artificial intelligence (AI)-enhanced diagnostic solutions to enhance the quality of pathology diagnosis. Advances in this field have made it possible to analyze conventional hematoxylin and eosin (H/E) stained slides and provide a list of most likely differential diagnoses in a given case. Our preliminary work has shown that it is possible to utilize machine learning strategies on annotated digital pathology images to generate accurate differential diagnoses. Combining data from clinical history and other laboratory investigations, we aim to develop a solution that will overcome the lack of pathologist expertise in developing nations and enhance the productivity of experienced pathologists in first-world nations. 2. MicroRNA profiling as a more affordable platform for lymphoma classification Accurate histological classification often requires the integration of a wide panel of immunohistochemical stains and additional cytogenetic/molecular genetic investigations. However, the limitations of immunohistochemistry and the constraints of small tissue samples derived from needle-biopsy procedures have driven a growing need for an alternative diagnostic tool that is tissue-saving, cost-effective and clinically practical. With the advent of low-cost qPCR machines, detection of miRNA is now economical and technically within reach of many laboratories. In preliminary studies, we have shown that a 5-miRNA signature is able to separate reactive lymphoid proliferations from indolent B-cell lymphomas with an AUC of >0.95 and using a 7-gene miRNA signature, we could subclassify the 4 main types of low grade B-cell lymphomas with an accuracy of more than 90%. We plan to validate our findings in a larger study to develop miRNA-based diagnostic biomarkers for the diagnosis of indolent B-cell neoplasms.

title: Robust prediction of disinfectant degradation in drinking water distribution systems integrating water quality sensing and digital twin technologies. (Note: Changed from "The utilization of a water quality sensing network for the development of surrogate models for chemical disinfection in drinking water distribution systems.")
inst: Xylem Water Solutions Singapore Pte. Ltd.
abs: Effective treatment and disinfection of source waters and the safe delivery of potable water to customers requires a comprehensive understanding of water quality changes from source-to-tap. Variations in source water quality, treatment and supply operations, and water demand present significant challenges to maintaining consistent water quality across the system, and can lead to areas that suffer from low residual, nitrification episodes, and chemical or microbial water quality violations. The proposed project for the Competitive Research Program combines real-time water quality sensing with data-integrated hydraulic and chemical reaction models, as the basis for predicting disinfectant residual throughout a portion of the PUB distribution system. The approach will test different water quality sensing approaches, from relatively simple configurations of total residual chlorine (TRC) sensors, to more complex (but more informative) designs that add optical spectroscopy in the UV through visible range. The intention of the research is to identify the simplest sensing package that will provide meaningful information about natural organic matter (NOM) variability in treated source water, as NOM is a key determinant of TRC decay rates. By incorporating the variability of source natural organic matter, along with operational actions and water demands, the proposed approach seeks to address a long standing research challenge to develop high fidelity and robust water quality predictions – well suited to providing operational decision support for optimized distribution system management.

title: Interplay between Geometry and Topology: Effective Theories and Novel Manipulations in Low-dimensional Strongly Correlated Topological Materials
abs: One of the most important examples of strongly correlated topological system is the fractional quantum Hall effect (FQHE) in two-dimensional electron gas systems (2DES), where one can observe anyonic or non-Abelian statistics very useful for topological quantum computing. Theoretical understanding on the stability of such topological materials, as well as the experimental realization from various platforms, are challenging due to the strong interaction that needs to be delicately tuned. Recent development shows that quantum geometry plays a fundamental role in the robustness of the topological phases. Systematic exploitation of the emergent geometric degrees of freedom can potentially lead to novel experimental tuning and manipulation methodologies, for realizing exotic systems with both rich physics and practical applications for next generation quantum devices. This proposal aims to develop theoretical tools, and applications of such tools both in theoretical and experimental studies, for understanding low-dimensional strongly correlated topological systems with non-trivial geometric structures. Such tools allow for the first time systematic characterization of anisotropic interactions commonly found in experimental systems. Theoretically, this allows us to construct effective models capturing the mechanisms of the phase transitions driven by anisotropy, as well as the competition between different energies scales arising from the boundary and disorder effects. Experimentally, we can now introduce anisotropy as additional “experimental knobs" for probing and stabilizing topological systems, based on the generalised pseudopotential formalism we developed. While a major part of this proposal focuses on non-Abelian properties of the FQHE, I will also generalise the methodologies and concepts from FQHE to other novel condensed matter systems, including and not limited to fractional Chern insulators, genuinely 2D materials such as graphene and phosphorene, as well as cold atom systems and related driven floquet systems.
kw: Topological materials; novel quantum devices; exotic low-dimensional systems; fractional statistics; topological quantum computing

title: A Chemical Biology Approach to Investigate the Structures and Functions of Blood Peptidoglycan-ome in Human
abs: The human (and animal) serum ubiquitously contains a collection of soluble peptidoglycan fragments that are originated from the gut microbiota. Peptidoglycan is an essential constituent of the bacterial cell wall, which triggers host defense mechanisms during infections. However, the natural presence of these microbiota-derived molecules in the host circulatory system affords them broad-reaching impact beyond infections. Recent studies have shown that modulations of serum peptidoglycan levels can enhance systemic innate immunity and avert autoimmune diseases in mouse models, raising potential therapeutic implications. The emergent roles of systemic peptidoglycan warrant further investigations. Unfortunately, current understanding of peptidoglycan in host-pathogen interactions has largely relied on two surrogate substrates: muramyl dipeptide and iGlu-mDAP, which cannot represent the whole of systemic peptidoglycan in host. Our knowledge on the structures and mechanisms of systemic peptidoglycan is much in the infancy. In this proposal, I will leverage my expertise in bacterial peptidoglycan biosynthetic enzymes to develop novel chemical biology strategies for peptidoglycan-omics studies. Specifically, I seek to elucidate the structures of natural peptidoglycan molecules in serum, identify their cognate protein targets in host, and investigate their roles in a panel of functional testing. The proposed study represents an unprecedented effort to address blood peptidoglycan-omics using ‘bottom-up’ approaches. Understanding of fundamental questions regarding systemic peptidoglycan will have great impact on development of diagnostics and therapeutics.

title: SLADE : Smart Learning Analytics for Digital crimE
abs: 1. Aim The SLADE project aims to address and overcome several limitations in existing incident response and investigation tools / systems with a proposed new system (SLADE) at TRL 7 which will be deployed and validated at the end user’s site. SLADE will be built to deal with the following challenges: a) Large volume of security data to deal with during digital investigation. Due to significant and rapid evolution of IT systems, evidence in the digital crime domain (logs, images) have grown in size and complexity. Such data is not designed or intended for direct human analysis. Although, there are existing log management and analytic tools to support log analysis, there is heavy reliance on human effort to convert it into meaningful outputs. On the contrary, specialised forensic tools are available to ease the generation of usable output from disk/memory images. b) No/minimal analytical and learning capability in existing investigation tool/system. There is hardly any known tool to-date which focuses on applying relevant analytical models to deliver operational and anticipatory learning capability for the investigation of digital crimes. There is an urgent need for a new system with the capability for seamless interaction with the investigation team and to identify and capture important inputs for progressive and on-the-fly learning. Such learning will allow forecast of potential crime scenarios for look-ahead risk management and pre-emptive security defence. c) No tool/system which incorporate both technical data and contextual data for investigation. Existing forensic investigation tools are very focused on technical artifacts (e.g. operational log files and disk/memory images) and are typically not sufficient to generate complete evidential information for crime resolution. For example, a perpetrator’s motivation for attacking a target could be for monetary gain, revenge or as a warning. Existing tools cannot capture or deduce such abstract intelligence directly. This will only be possible if we have a system which has technical data that is analyzed in conjunction with other data such as logged activities in cyberspace, past criminal records including perhaps a psychological profile composed from the suspect’s social and professional networks. d) Need for suitably designed system which can improve collaboration and better support the investigation process. Existing investigation tools do not support effective real-time collaboration and seldom present complicated findings that is readily ingested by human investigators. There is potential to design a new system with a suitably designed man-machine interface which can improve collaboration and minimise/avoid the need to deal with system-specific syntax (e.g. switching to query-based command language). title: Highly efficient electrochemical kinetic energy harvesting using nanomaterials
abs: Energy harvesting is currently a topic of intense interest as a result of the growing energy demands of society and as a means to create autonomous and self-powered systems. In particular, kinetic energy harvesting system has large potential to supply power to various applications, such as wearable device, bio-implantable device, Internet of Things (IoTs), remote power for sensors and etc. In spite of extensive study of piezoelectric and triboelectric systems for kinetic energy harvesting, there are still inherent difficulties of them such as large impedance in MΩ range, demand of high frequency mechanical vibration to supply quasi-continuous current, and degradation of the materials. Recently, we have developed new electrochemical system for kinetic energy harvesting using selective ion sweeping by hydrodynamic flow of electrolyte. The hybrid electrochemical cell consists of ion-hosting battery electrode and supercapacitor electrode. The flow of electrolyte induces inequal sweeping of ions in each electrode and results voltage change. Then, the periodic flow can generate ulternating current as a kinetic energy harvesting. In the proposed study, we propose to utilize the nanomaterials to enhance the output current and voltage from the kinetic energy and to understand the relationship between ion sweeping behavior and the shear rate of the flow. There are three key components in the hybrid cell for electrochemical kinetic energy harvesting using selective ion sweeping. Task1 will study the EDLC electrode to enhance the ion sweeping efficiency by replacing the ion to charged molecules and nanomaterials. Task2 will study how to reduce the contribution of ion sweeping in the ion-hosting battery electrode (PBA in here) to maximize the output voltage of the hybrid cell under the flow. Task3 will study the relationship between the ion sweeping behavior and shear rate of the flow using shear flow tomography using rare earth doped nanorods in the microfluidic channel. The proposed electrochemical system never has been reported and our preliminary study has proven the concept. I believe that this is great opportunity to lead the field of kinetic energy harvesting using the electrochemistry with various applications. Furthermore, we have advantage of intellectual property for the future commercialization. In addition to the engineering matter, the proposed study will bring many scientific interests of electrochemistry, surface chemistry, and even fluidic dynamics.

title: Provable Mitigation of Side Channel through Parametric Verification
abs: The Spectre vulnerability was recently reported in 2018 which caused a big fuss as it affects most modern processors. The idea is that attackers can extract information about the private data through a side channel. It is an example of the many kinds of side channel attacks, where secure information flows through channels like timing and cache state unintentionally. How to systematically mitigate such attacks is an important and yet challenging research problem. We propose to automatically synthesize mitigation of side channel attacks, in particular timing side channel, using well-developed verification techniques. The idea is to reduce this problem to the parameter synthesis problem of certain formal models (for instance, parametric timed automata). Given a program/system with design parameters which can be tuned to mitigate side channel attacks, our approach will automatically generate provably *secure* valuations of the parameters. We plan to deliver a toolkit which can be automatically applied to real-world systems including those in the DARPA challenge.
kw: Cyber-security, privacy, formal methods, side channel, model checking

title: ALIAS - Adaptive Learning for Interactive Agents and Systems
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: A critical challenge in the current digital era is the need for real-time decision-making in complex systems, often based on data that arrive at very high volumes: traffic routing in packet-switched networks, online matching markets (taxi-hailing apps, micro-labor markets, etc.), generative adversarial networks in machine learning, and malware/fraud detection systems are just some of the hallmark examples where real-time decision-making plays a major role. Techniques based on adaptive learning have met with prolific success in addressing these challenges by exploiting a simple feedback loop: first, the agent interfaces with their environment (a computer network, other agents, etc.) by selecting an action (e.g., a synaptic weight configuration in a neural network or a client/provider matching in an online assignment market); subsequently, the agent receives some feedback based on the quality of the action and the state of the environment, and the process repeats. While this simple online process has had big successes in many applications, several fundamental challenges remain: A. Does adaptive learning lead to stable outcomes in multi-agent systems? B. What types of behavior can be expected otherwise, and how far are they from optimality? We intend to approach these questions with a blend of techniques from game theory, machine learning, online optimization and dynamical systems, our ultimate aim being to circumvent – or, at worst, predict – the failures and successes of online learning in multi-agent systems. In more detail, we intend to structure our work along two synergistic theory thrusts that target a distinction which is commonly neglected in the literature: 1. Prescriptive multi-agent learning: Here the features of the underlying game are known in advance and the aim is to calculate an optimal action profile. The computation process does not need to be rationally justifiable or otherwise provide good interim payoffs – the only desideratum is to return an optimum (or near-optimum) conﬁguration. Accordingly, the main goal is the design of convergent learning algorithms for complex multi-agent interactions. 2. Predictive multi-agent learning: at the other end of the spectrum, if the game is not known in advance (or it evolves over time), the agents' most sensible choice is to implement a simple online algorithm with reasonable worst-case guarantees – such as the minimization of the agents' regret. In this case, the overriding goal is to predict the outcome of an adaptive multi-agent learning process and to contrast it to the solution of the underlying game. These overarching goals dovetail to provide a uniﬁed answer to the question of stability in multi-agent systems: for systems that can be controlled (such as programmable machine learning models), prescriptive learning algorithms can steer the system towards an optimum conﬁguration; for systems that cannot (e.g., online assignment markets), a predictive learning analysis can determine wheth

title: Towards Building Trustworthy and Robust Intelligent Systems and its Application on Human Brain
abs: Over the past decade, artificial intelligence (AI) has achieved tremendous success in many cutting-edge intelligent applications, such as image processing, speech recognition, natural language processing, and autonomous driving. However, just like traditional software, AI system could still have defects. The importance of quality and security assurance of AI system starts to draw attention, especially for those applied in safety- and mission-critical scenarios. Currently, a lot of techniques including adversarial attack and defense techniques have been proposed. However, such techniques are ad-hoc and available on specific models. In this project, we aim to develop systematic analysis and verification techniques for building trustworthy and robust AI system. We mainly focus on the machine learning based system (MLS) which is a general data-driven model and trained from a large mount of data. From an even more exciting aspect, we find that human brain could also be a data-driven learning-based model, our techniques will be further applied on human brain analysis.
kw: Deep Learning Security; Security and Robustness of Artificial Intelligence

title: Nanostructured Materials for Advanced Na Solid-Sate Batteries
abs: Limiting global warming requires paradigm-shift discoveries in energy storage, leading to rechargeable batteries that give electric cars the desired 800-km range. The complementary use of synthesis and advanced characterization techniques in synergy with modelling have enabled the discovery of materials by design, which we apply here. We will discover nanomaterials and nanocomposites for long-lasting and inexpensive Sodium-ion batteries. We will combine computation with experiments to develop novel, inexpensive, NA-Super-Ionic-CONductor (NASICON) solid-electrolytes, NazZr2-yMySixP3-xO12, for safe solid-state batteries (SSB). By optimizing the composition and nanostructure of NaSICONs, we will decrease the operation temperatures of existing SSB from 200°C to ambient temperature. This synergistic approach is possible by bringing together the expertise of the PIs : NUS : high-throughput density functional theory; Softbond potentials for screening ion-transport, solid-state NMR. LRCS : synthesis, crystallography and electrochemistry; impedance spectroscopy and SSB manufacturing.

title: Designing Functional Interfaces of Batteries Using Theory and Computation
abs: Today’s energy supply relies heavily on finite fossil fuel resources, which raises concerns about CO2 emissions, global warming and the depletion of natural resources. While photovoltaics and wind technologies can efficiently harvest intermittent clean energy, one of the notable challenges is storing large quantities of energy for powering vehicles. To that end, we need to develop energy-dense, safe and inexpensive energy storage devices is a key scientific and societal challenges of the century. Notably, current Li-ion batteries fail to meet the demanding requirements of novel energy storage applications in transportation (hybrid- and pure-electric cars, trains and ships), and stationary support for a sustainable grid infrastructure. One strategy to “boost” the energy density of commercial batteries is to replace the conventional graphite anode with dense alkali metals, such as Li metal. However, Li-metal anodes are unstable when in contact with commercial flammable non-aqueous electrolytes triggering short circuits, leading to overheating and catastrophic fires. Short circuits are caused by the inhomogeneous deposition of Li as filament-like structures, commonly known as dendrites which grow through the porous separator and bridge the electrodes. As even the charging of small-scale lithium-ion batteries for personal mobility devices’ batteries, e.g. scooters, has become a significant fire hazard in Singapore and globally, safer alternatives are imperative for more energy dense and larger-scale systems. Advanced batteries with improved energy density and safety, longer cycling life and lower cost require alternative battery architectures. Designs incorporating a non-flammable inorganic solid as their electrolyte, termed as solid-state batteries, show strong potential to address the aforementioned challenges. Nevertheless, the solid-state battery technology faces three pressing challenges: i) finding solid electrolytes that are electrochemically stable against electrodes, ii) maintaining physical contact between components over many Li deposition/stripping cycles, and iii) suppressing Li-dendrite formation. In particular, the composition and reactivity of “buried” interfaces between solid-electrolyte and the electrodes, as those in solid-state batteries, are difficult to probe by typical characterisation techniques (X-ray photoemission and Auger spectroscopies, microscopies etc.), hence curbing our ability to optimise the properties and the degradation of devices. While computational studies tend to focus mostly on bulk properties, neglecting the importance of interfacial effects, modern computational materials science and the availability of computer power now allow us to tackle large systems (more than 500 atoms), including interfaces. These aspects become even more pressing when interfaces and devices are critical to push the development of green energy technologies. title: Long-Term Environmental Behaviour for Treated Incineration Bottom Ash
abs: The prevalent thermal treatment of municipal solid waste (MSW) in Singapore is incineration, which produces incineration bottom ash (IBA) as the treatment residue. The residue can potentially be used as aggregate substitute for construction applications. However, IBA has to be treated before safe usage. Long-term environmental behaviour of treated IBA (IBA-T) has not been monitored in local applications. This study serves to investigate such an application along Tanah Merah Coast Road where IBA-T will be used in the road base and sub-base layers. The trial road will consist of three 50-m long sections built with IBA-T from different suppliers. A series of groundwater monitoring wells will be installed on the trial site to monitor and study the long-term environmental behaviour of the residue. Meanwhile, laboratory testing and modelling will be conducted to improve the overall understanding of the performance of the residue in actual operating environments. Specific emphasis will be placed on constructing a framework for the modelling and management of the residue. The specific tasks are: 1) establishment of a conceptual site model with risk assessment; 2) baseline site investigation; 3) groundwater and environmental monitoring for the trial site; and 4) laboratory tests. Based on the different activities introduced by the project, we aim to build a full spectrum of testing, monitoring, and modelling capabilities related to IBA-T applications in Singapore.

title: Integrating environmental, virological and population approaches to understand the transmission of COVID-19
abs: Much is still unknown about the way the novel coronavirus (2019-nCoV) is transmitted between individuals and causes coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19). This study applies the epidemiological triad of environment, agent and host framework for understanding transmission and facilitating the challenging task of identifying links between cases and transmission clusters in outbreak investigations as well as determining the most vulnerable groups. (1) We will identify the specific environmental sources of viral contamination in (a) immediate hospital environment (isolation room) of infected patients and areas of PPE worn by healthcare workers (HCWs) in close contact with infected patients (26 sites), (b) outbreak environments, including inadvertent healthcare exposures outside isolation rooms and community settings of large transmission clusters (e.g. workplaces, dormitories, cruise ships, as and when the opportunity presents) (sites similar to healthcare environment studies). (2) We will use next generation sequencing to investigate virus adaptation and transmission bottlenecks by studying samples from positive environmental samples and clinical specimens serially collected from COVID-19 patients (primary and secondary cases). (3) We will use epidemiological data, serological testing and transmission modelling to assess source and risk of infection in key populations including (a) transmission clusters, to retrospectively identify possible sources of infection for index cases with unclear epidemiological links, and assess extent of asymptomatic and undiagnosed infection, (b) HCWs with different levels of occupational risk including front line hospital areas, other administrative areas and primary care, (c) children of HCWs as sentinel population as well as paediatric seroepidemiology using residual sera, and (d) general population completing online symptom reviews who will subsequently be recalled for serological assays.

title: Serological investigation of 2019-CoV infection
abs: The emergence of a novel betacoronavirus in Nov/Dec 2019 (2019-nCoV) has raised a public health emergency. This virus has caused more than 42,000 confirmed infections with more than 1,000 deaths, surpassing the 2002-3 SARS outbreak in both accounts. The number of infected cases in Singapore is likewise increasing with 45 cases reported thus far, with proven local transmission. With no clear sign of infection dropping in China as well as the other parts of the world, despite containment efforts through case detection and isolation, there is an urgent need for improved diagnosis and surveillance tools and medical countermeasures against this newly emerged virus. Current diagnosis and screening of 2019-nCoV is solely relying on PCR testing. There is currently no serological test available, but there is an urgent need to apply serological testing in the context of contact tracing, high risk group monitoring and community cohort studies to examine the possibility of asymptomatic or mild infection missed in the current surveillance systems being applied. Antibody-based therapeutics and vaccines against 2019-nCoV are now under development by various international bodies and research groups. Coronaviruses have been associated with antibody-enhanced infection in experimental models. Any antibody-based therapeutics and vaccines must thus also be tested for the potential for 2019-nCoV infection enhancement to ensure safety. We thus propose here a study that is directed at serologic investigation involving both technology development and filling knowledge gaps. This collaborative effort will develop serological assays for epidemiological and immunological investigations. It will also adapt well established assays from antibody-enhanced infection for dengue virus for use to determine the potential for such infection enhancement with 2019-nCoV. Finally, we will explore if pooled sera from subjects who have recovered from SARS-CoV infection in 2003, could be developed into intravenous immunoglobulin therapy against 2019-nCoV.

title: Modelling and analytics for the outbreak of the novel coronavirus in Singapore
abs: A rapidly evolving body of literature on COVID-19 is beginning to emerge, but much is still unknown, especially on the infection dynamics within Singapore, potential for local transmission and how best to respond. Preliminary research suggest a high level of virulence exists with cough and fever being primary symptoms; while there appears to be a low fatality rate especially among healthy adults and children, the high proportion of asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic individuals may make the virus hard to control and hence increase the number of fatalities, which has already exceeded the global toll of SARS-CoV. Lessons from the two most recent coronaviruses of concern (SARS-CoV and MERS-CoV) suggest that these case definitions and epidemiological characteristics may vary as the outbreak evolves. Few treatment options are available, though therapeutics are being tested as a matter of urgency. The exact level of transmissibility and virulence for SARS-CoV-2 has yet to be determined with a high level of uncertainty in the potential size of outbreaks in mainland Chinese cities. Estimates of the basic reproduction number straddle a wide but high range between 1.9 and ~4, requiring modelling efforts to determine the appropriate response for epidemic aversion and nationwide treatment response once community-wide local transmission begins in earnest. The models will altogether examine the efficacy of surveillance, importation risk, potential size of outbreaks and interventions to mitigate SARS-CoV-2 spread. Each study is expected to develop new understanding in the transmissibility of SARS-CoV-2 in Southeast Asia with long reaching relevance to many countries with risk of case importation. For Singapore, this multi-model study is expected to provide valuable information for current surveillance efforts and interventional approaches to avert the potential risk of sustained community transmission and respond effectively should it occur. Aim 1: Literature review of current developments in COVID-19 epidemiology and modelling Aim 2: Reviewing and optimizing COVID-19 and SARS-CoV-2 surveillance in Singapore Aim 3: Forecasting and nowcasting the COVID-19 epidemic Aim 4: Modelling intervention measures for COVID-19 Aim 5: Outbreak analytics – modelling clusters, transmission chains, risk factors Aim 6: Phylogeodynamic model of SARS-CoV-2 Aim 7: Implementation of community based syndromic surveillance system

title: A Multicenter, Adaptive, Randomized Blinded Controlled Trial of the Safety and Efficacy of Investigational Therapeutics for the Treatment of COVID-19 in Hospitalized Adults
abs: COVID-19 is a respiratory disease caused by a novel coronavirus (SARS-CoV-2) and causes substantial morbidity and mortality. There is currently no vaccine to prevent infection with SARS-CoV-2 or therapeutic agent to treat COVID-19. Remdesivir (GS-5734) is a broad-spectrum nucleotide prodrug that inhibits RNA-dependent RNA polymerase activity among a diverse group of RNA viruses including filoviruses, paramyxoviruses and pathogenic coronaviruses. Nonclinical in vitro and in vivo data suggests that remdesivir might be useful for the treatment of COVID-19 for which no medical countermeasures are currently approved and support testing the efficacy of remdesivir treatment among hospitalized adults with COVID-19. This study is an adaptive, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial to evaluate the safety and efficacy of novel therapeutic agents in hospitalized 394 adult patients diagnosed with COVID-19. The study is a multicenter trial that will be conducted in up to 50 sites globally. All subjects will undergo a series of efficacy, safety, and laboratory assessments. Blood samples and oropharyngeal (OP) swabs will be obtained on Day 1; 3, 5, 8, 11; and Day 15 and 29. The proposed primary outcome, a 7-point ordinal scale at Day 15, will be defined based on blinded review of data from the first 100 subjects. This study utilizes an adaptive design that maximizes our efficiency in identifying a safe and efficacious therapeutic agent for COVID-19 during the current outbreak. As the a multicenter, multinational randomized controlled study, we will be able to acquire rigorous data about the safety and efficacy of investigational therapeutic agents for COVID-19 that will lead to generalizable evidence. Last, collecting clinical and virologic data using a standardized timeline and collection instruments should provide valuable information about the clinical course of and morbidities associated with severe COVID-19 in a diverse group of hospitalized adult patients.
kw: Coronavirus Infectious, Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome, Viral Pneumonia, RNA Virus Infections, Remdesivir, Nidovirales Infections

title: Personalizing Sleep Recommendations Across the Lifespan Using Large Scale Device Data
abs: Many Asians have poor sleep habits that impact health, wellbeing and productivity. This can be transformed by; 1. Developing and integrating smartphone and wearable based technologies to unobtrusively obtain long-term measurements of sleep patterns and cognition. 2. Collecting data using the aforementioned platform to characterize sleep patterns across the lifespan and from there uncover their associations with outcome variables relevant to cognition, mood, cardiometabolic health and ageing. 3. Using the above knowledge to personalize age-specific sleep recommendations in a manner relevant to Asians. Existing cohorts of adolescents, young adults and old adults will be assessed for sleep habits, physical activity and cognitive performance continuously over at least 2 months, using human smartphone interactions, ecological momentary assessment and consumer health wearables to yield population-level characterization of sleep habits.
