title: HUMAN UMBILICAL CORD-LINING DERIVED INDUCED PLURIPOTENT STEM CELLS (CLIPS) AS A UNIVERSAL SOURCE OF CELLS FOR REGENERATIVE THERAPY FOR NEUROSENSORY DISORDERS
abs: Neurological and Sense Disorders (NSDs) exact a huge socio-economic impact globally particularly in countries with rapidly aging populations like Singapore. Current treatments for NSDs are largely symptomatic, which offer little prospects for improving prognosis for these diseases. Given that NSDs are characterized principally by the loss of selected cellular populations, cell-based therapies represent an intuitive therapeutic approach. However, a major obstacle is the issue of immune compatibility, which concerns all types of donor cells including induced pluripotent stem cells (iPS). What we need is a source of iPS that is hypo-immunogenic that can serve as universal donor cells for cell therapy. Specific Aims: Given that the maternal-fetal interface are widely considered to be immunoprivileged. we hypothesize that umbilical cord lining-derived iPS are endowed with immunoprivilege properties and could serve as an ideal source of cells for regenerative medicine. Accordingly, the objective of this proposal is to develop a safe, stable and renewable source of hypo-immunogenic iPS from human umbilical cord lining cells and demonstrate that their utility for allogeneic transplantation in 2 important model NSDs: Parkinson’s disease (PD) and Adult Macular Degeneration (AMD), which are recognized by the Neurosensory Taskforce as diseases of national priority. Methodology: We will develop a safe, stable and renewable source of hypo-immunogenic iPS from human umbilical cord lining cells (designated CLiPS) that is suitable for use as universal donor cells for allogeneic transplantation. By using our established rodent and non-human primate models of PD and AMD, we will transplant CLiPS-derived neural progenitors into these animals to provide preclinical validation of their therapeutic potential. By means of transcriptomic and epigenomic analyses, we also aim to elucidate the mechanism underlying the hypo-immunogenicity of CLiPS. Finally, we will establish a pipeline to manufacture clinical grade (cGMP-compliant) cord lining iPS that will be ready for human trials. The development of such an ideal cell source will be of huge impact and will represent a game changer to regenerative medicine.
kw: Stem Cells; Parkinson's disease; Adult Macular Degeneration; Cell therapy, Regenerative Medicine, Immunoprivilege

title: Smart Water Grid Anomaly Detection and Localisation
abs: With an increasing adoption of Advanced Meter Infrastructure (AMI), smart sensors, and temporary and/or permanent data loggers, it is imperative to develop data analytics and couple the results with hydraulic modeling to improve the quality and efficiency of water service. One important task is to timely detect and localize anomaly events, which may include, but not be limited to, pipe bursts and unauthorized water usages. In this project, a comprehensive solution method is proposed for anomaly detection and localization by formulating and integrating the data analytics methods with the Pressure Dependent Leakage Detection (PDLD) that has been developed by the PI. Data analysis for anomaly detection proceeds in multiple steps including (1) a data-preprocess to eliminate and correct erroroneous data records, (2) decomposition of time series data to ensure stationarity, (3) outlier detection by statistical process control methods and the Deep Learning with Extended Kalman Filter (DL-EKF), (4) anomaly event classification per sensor, so-called sensor event, and finally (5) system anomaly classification by correlation analysis of multiple sensor events. Classified system anomalies are localized by the PDLD method via hydraulic model calibration. The integrated solution software will be developed as a user-friendly and effective tool for PUB, tested and validated on the selected target areas. The results will be rigorously evaluated according to the predefined key performance index for detecting and localizing anomaly hotspots. The proposed approach represents a holistic solution for analyzing large monitoring datasets, detecting and localizing where the newly occurred anomalies and long-lasting leaks are hidden underground before causing significant sinkholes or water service interruptions.
kw: Smart water, data analytics, machine learning, hydraulic model calibration, anomaly detection, and localization

title: Provably Verified and Explainable Probabilistic Reasoning
abs: The unprecedented advances in the machine learning techniques have led to a proliferation of Artificial Intelligence(AI)-based devices in our day to day life. The AI-based tools are increasingly employed to make consequential decisions for human subjects, in areas such as credit lending, policing, criminal justice, and medicine. Decisions made by these AI-based predictive models often have a long-lasting impact on people's lives. This, combined with the black-box nature of modern AI-systems, has propelled the issues of explainable and verification of AI systems to be the central challenges of AI research today. The issue of explainable and verified AI systems is not restricted to just research community but has captured the attention of the general public as evidenced by articles in popular news media. Over the past few years, overwhelming evidence has demonstrated that minor changes in the environment can lead to AI systems behaving arbitrarily and dangerously. The widespread consensus among researchers and technologists is that {\em the current process of design of AI systems lacks a methodological approach to verification and explainability}. \\ The objective of my proposal is thus: “ the development of a rigorous mathematical framework for provably verified, correct-by-construction, explainable probabilistic reasoning systems building on recent breakthroughs in formal methods and symbolic reasoning; and deployment of our algorithmic framework in the real world including applications in reliability estimation of critical infrastructure and computational sustainability. “ To achieve this goal, we will: • Develop computational paradigm to achieve provably correct-by-construction probabilistic reasoning. • Develop a mathematically rigorous framework for the functional verification and testing of probabilistic reasoning systems. • Develop a scalable framework to generate interpretable classification rules with rigorous formal guarantees for the tradeoff between interpretability and accuracy. Probabilistic reasoning is prevalent in virtually all modern practical AI systems. As a result, this project addresses a critical concern regarding the adoption of AI techniques and the underlying framework combines symbolic and probabilistic reasoning and has the potential to impact the design of AI systems with rigorous guarantees significantly. The planned deployment of proposed models for predicting the location of the fire in Indonesia is direct relevance to human health and economy of Singapore. The PI will benefit from his strong track record of prior research in formal methods and artificial intelligence.
kw: Probabilistic Reasoning; Formal Methods; SAT

title: Development of novel smart sensor for reverse osmosis fouling detection
abs: The Electrical Impedance Spectroscopy (EIS) technology developed by the Project Team has been proven to be a sensitive and reliable technique compared to conventional pressure drop (∆P) method or salt rejection to detect the onset of reverse osmosis (RO) fouling. Early fouling detection is critical for water treatment plant operators to optimize the timing to implement mitigation measures, such that the RO fouling can be controlled within an acceptable level, excess chemical consumption can be avoided and frequency of cleaning-in-place (CIP) can be reduced significantly. However, the current EIS system is based on side-stream canary cell, EIS-canary, which is expensive as it requires proper process control to mimic the hydrodynamic conditions in the actual spiral wound module (SWM). To reduce the product cost, a newly designed SWM with EIS, known as EIS-module, is proposed where the electrodes and electronics are directly embedded in the SWM. The EIS-module can simply replace one of the standard elements in the pressure vessel in a RO train, as such no modification to existing infrastructure is required and the filtration process is not interupted while membrane fouling information can be obtained directly. The EIS-module has a great market potential as there is no competing fouling sensor that give direct fouling information of SWM. In this project, 3 main tasks will be performed: a) design, fabrication and assembly of EIS-module, b) validation of EIS-module signals, c) field testing of EIS-module. While the EIS-module concept is promising, it requires the collection of field data for reference. The EIS-module data will be correlated with the EIS-canary data collected in previous work. Therefore, this CRP grant serves as an important resource avenue to support evaluation works for the EIS-module and facilitate the commercialisation of EIS technology to the market.
kw: electrical impedance spectroscopy, fouling, reverse osmosis, sensors monitoring

title: Integrated optofluidic system for single E. coli fast detection
abs: Drinking water contamination worldwide, caused by waterborne bacteriological outbreaks, has an important impact on public health, increase perceived risk and decrease acceptance for the drinking water. Rapid detection and identification of bacteria such as Escherichia coli (E. coli) are important to prevent waterborne bacteriological outbreaks. Current methods for E. coli detection such as cell culture, metabolized enzyme detection and conventional PRC have the limit of long incubation time, high cost and poor accuracy. In this proposal, a novel optofluidic system is proposed with (1) an ultra-fast pre-concentration system to directly concentrate tap water sample from 1 L to 100 µL. This system has two steps which use the mechanical membrane filter and microfluidic filtration accordingly; (2) an optofluidic chip with picoliter well arrays is used to trap the single E. coli inside and enhance detecting signal. The two systems will be integrated a novel prototype demonstrated for a high-sensitivity, real time, low cost and fast enzyme detection of single E. coli in drinking water according to USA EPA standard 1604.
kw: optofluidics, E. coli

title: Efficient Algorithms with Provable Guarantees for Causal Inference
abs: A causal model at its heart is a way of encoding a collection of joint distributions {D_A} over a set of variables V, where A ranges over all possible ways to act on V. Even when the number of variables is 2, properly defining a useful notion of a causal model is a challenging problem and was addressed by the fathers of modern statistics. In modern scenarios, V is a large set, consisting of thousands of features, some observable while others not, and the set of actions could also be quite complicated depending on the application domain. Our research agenda can be roughly classified as falling into three areas: * Predict: We give provable guarantees for efficient estimation of causal effects under the presence of latent variables, selection bias, and finite sample complexity. * Prescribe: We develop efficient algorithms to learn causal models for collections of variables, allowing us to design policies to achieve desired effects. * Transfer: We design methods to transfer causal knowledge from one model to another with minimal loss. Our eventual goal is to develop a {\em Never-Ending Causal Model Building} (NECauMB) machine (inspired by the Never-Ending Language Learning (NELL) project) that takes in a feed of performed experiments and tunes its model by comparing the observed outcome against its own prediction. For example in the context of economics, the goal of the NECauMB machine would be to construct a complex econometric model that can predict the outcome of implementing a particular policy (such as increasing the interest rate) given a particular context (e.g., current oil price, exchange rate, GDP, etc.).
kw: causality; statistics; inference; hypothesis testing; algorithms; complexity; bias

title: Engineering Build and Commercialization of Advanced Low-Pressure Hollow Fiber Nanofiltration Membrane for Domestic and Industrial Water Application
inst: Century Water Systems & Technologies Pte. Ltd.
abs: Currently, spiral-wound NF membranes from several companies, e.g. Dow, GE, etc. are dominating in the market. These membranes are all made of thin film polyimide composite (TFC) using interfacial polymerization method. However, they have many disadvantages, such as, high cost, lower fouling resistance, lower oxidant/chlorine resistance and limited cleaning methods. We, at Century Water, developed two next-generation NF membranes, NanoPureTMLPNF01 and NanoPureTMLPNF02, with many extraordinary features: high fouling/scaling resistance, high chlorine resistance, and high water flux and separation efficiency. For example, the chlorine resistance of the NanoPure membranes is up to 250,000 ppmh which is 500 times higher than the TFC NF products. In addition, the excellent fouling/scaling resistance is due to the smooth surface with determined charges so that foulants are neither chemically attached nor physically trapped. Thus, limited pre-treatment measures are required. Besides, the membranes are back-washable. Last but not least, water flux of these two products is typically 2-3 times higher than their counterparts. With all these features, our NF products will replace the current TFC NF membranes in both domestic and industrial applications. The targets of this project are to (1) fully scale up current pilot-scale product to industry scale manufacturing standard for 8 inch module with professional engineering design, (2)set up an industrial-scale testing system with capacity of 10m3/h which will be positioned at one of PUB plant to test the performance of organic removal for both NEWater RO concentrate and SWRO pre-treatment, and (3) maturate the two products in respective markets. At the end of the project, the novel hollow fiber NF membrane products will be fully commercialized for domestic water market; it will also compete with Spiral-wound NF in industrial water applications.
kw: NF membrane, Hollow fiber, Water softening, RO pre-treatment, higher flux, wastewater treatment

title: Data Science as a Service (DaaS) to Improve Waterworks Operation Efficiency and Event Detection – A Smart SCADA
abs: Our proposal will focus on four main parameters: pH, conductivity, turbidity and free chlorine levels. In consultation with the plant manager of Choa Chu Kang Water Works (CCKWW), these four parameters are identified as useful indicators when determining the health and status of the operational processes. Breaching of thresholds in these four indicators currently point towards potential anomalies or decline in water quality that is affected by performance objectives of Pulsators, Filters, Membranes, Ozone and Biological Activated Carbon (BAC), and/or Chlorine Contact Tank (CCT). The modelling process starts with conductivity and free chlorine levels, whereby free chlorine levels indicate the integrity of disinfection process and affected by presence of undesired compounds such as ammonia. Subsequently, we extend the models to pH and turbidity, and perform correlation analysis sequentially and for all parameters for a complete analysis. We will use the Cross-industry Standard Process for Data Mining (CRISP-DM) methodology to build machine learning models and draw correlations, pick up new patterns and relationships, and perform predictions on future events. Several machine learning models will be trained and ensembled, including Regression, Decision Trees, Bayesian Networks, Neural Networks, etc. Models will then be validated, tested, optimized and selected based on performance. A data visualisation dashboard will be developed with integration of the final model(s), displaying vital information such as prediction outputs and health indicators of the plant processes. This interactive dashboard will serve as an Artificially Intelligence (AI) tool to assist operators in making decisions and necessary actions to take during event detections. In daily operations, operators can also perform self-help analytics such as visualisation drilldowns to see specific data indicators at different areas of the plant.
kw: scada, smart, data science, data analytics, machine learning, artificial intelligence

title: Employing Novel In-vivo/Ex-vivo Models of Advanced Gastric Cancer to Identify Potential Therapeutic Targets for Tumour-Resident Lgr5+ Stem Cells
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Gastric cancer is the fifth most common cancer globally (>1 million new cases) and second highest cause of cancer related deaths (>780000 deaths. In Singapore 2500+ new cases are diagnosed, annually, and 300+ deaths are caused due to gastric cancers. This emphasises the need to identify novel therapies that can help improve the treatment and management of the disease. In this study, I propose to use our novel CLDN18-IRES-Cre-ERT2 mouse line that accurately recapitulates human gastric cancer exclusively in the gastric epithelium, from early onset of disease to invasion and ultimately allows for the formation of metastasis. Using this model, I have successfully identified mutational combinations that give rise to metastatic gastric cancer. Lgr5 has previously been shown to mark a population of therapy-resistant cancer stem cells within intestinal tumours. Lgr5+ cells also exist within gastric cancers and I hypothesise that these are functioning as cancer stem cells to drive cancer progression towards invasion and metastasis. Here, I propose to establish the cancer stem cell identity of the tumour-resident Lgr5+ cells. I shall isolate these tumour-resident Lgr5+ cells from tumours and via transcriptomic profiling at early, invasive and metastatic stages to gain novel mechanistic insight into dysregulated pathways in this population. The targets will undergo a series of q-PCR, ISH and IHC validation on mouse and human samples before being taken further for more rigorous functional validation. Targets will be functionally validated in mouse and human organoids to assess the survival, proliferative and invasive advantage these bestow upon the cultures. Targets that show a significant change in the disease initiation and progression capacity of the organoids will further be validated for their ability to generate metastatic lesions in an orthotopic transplantation model. Eventually, I hope the targets can be developed further as novel therapeutics for gastric cancer treatment.
kw: Cancer, Stem cells, Cancer stem cells, Lgr5, Claudin18, Gastric cancer

title: WeeCare - Bringing personalised care to patients with lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) into community
abs: The Urology Department at Singapore General Hospital sees 25000 patients with lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) annually, representing around 50% of the clinic visits. This number will grow with an ageing population. The clinical evaluation of patients with LUTS and, in particular, males with benign prostate enlargement (BPE) involves history taking, clinical examination and investigations including uroflometry (measuring peak urine flow rate, among other parameters), both at the time of initial diagnosis and subsequent follow up visits. LUTS form the bulk of referrals from primary care physicians to tertiary urology centres. These referrals are usually made with reference to patients' subjective complaints of voiding and storage symptoms, without any objective clinical parameters, This is mainly due to the lack of affordable and available equipment (i.e. clinic setting uroflometry machines). We aim to develop a portable device which can empower the primary care physician in the assessment and monitoring of patients with benign prostate enlargement (BPE), a chronic condition prevalent in the ageing population of Singapore. The primary physician can use this device easily to follow up these patients.
kw: Benign prostate enlargement, primary care, lower urinry tract symptoms

title: Identification of innate T-cell activation signatures in influenza infection in contact free system of epithelial-immune cell co-culture
abs: Annually, influenza virus infection causes a large number of vaccine-preventable deaths worldwide. This is due to the severe nature of the infections and highly limited measures against influenza infections. Innate responses against influenza is an important event during infection in that it limits the viral load and thus modulates the subsequent adaptive immune responses, preventing major inflammatory damages leading to severe infections and complications. Therefore, there is an urgent need to enhance our understanding of influenza innate responses as means to devise containment strategies against severe influenza infections. Recently, we have developed a co-culture model that contains human nasal epithelial cells (hNECs) and immune cells (PBMCs) derived from healthy subjects. We used the model to elucidate the cross-talk between the nasal epithelium and PBMCs during influenza infection. We found that influenza infection exerted strong innate T-cells activation response through factors released from infected hNECs. Additionally, we also found that the hNECs are a key source of exosomes, which serves to transduce signals in the nasal mucosa. Therefore, we hypothesized influenza infected nasal epithelium secretes both soluble and exosomic factors that is crucial in activating innate immune T-cells. We will use our established co-culture system to generate innate T-cells activated by influenza infected hNECs, and delineate their activation using flow cytometry and cell killing assays. Further, by utilizing our previous studies of influenza responses by the hNECs, we will identify factors that are involved in the activation of innate T-cells. Finally, we will then detect activation factors in exosomes to establish their significance of signal transduction in the infected nasal mucosa. The findings from the study can fill the gap of early innate responses in curbing influenza transmission and potentially be utilized as prognosis markers and control measures to prevent the development of severe influenza infections, particularly for emerging influenza strains.
kw: Influenza; Innate T-cell; human nasal epithelial cells; cytokines; exosome

title: Meningeal macrophage and its role in meningeal lymphatics development
abs: Neurodegenerative diseases such as dementia has affected at least 50 million people worldwide and the number is expected to rise. One of the common types of dementia is Alzheimer's disease (AD), which is characterised by early and marked cognitive impairment. One of the hallmarks of AD is the deposition of amyloid plaques in the brain. Recently, meningeal lymphatics were rediscovered and were shown to be involved in the initiation and progression of AD. However, the mechanistic control of tissue-resident macrophages in the regulation and development of meningeal lymphatics vasculature, and how dysfunctional lymphatic vasculature affects neurodegenerative diseases remains unclear. In this proposal, we intend to comprehend the role of meningeal macrophages in the regulation and development of meningeal lymphatic vessels, and also investigate how dysfunctional lymphatic vasculature can affect brain development, and development of neurodegenerative diseases. We hypothesise the meningeal macrophages maintain and regulate the integrity of meningeal lymphatics. Hence, dysfunctional meningeal lymphatics will exacerbate neurodegenerative diseases. To address these questions, we will utilise a variety of techniques such as flow cytometry, microscopy, transcriptomics, as well as the use of conditional genetic mouse models to comprehend the functional role of meningeal macrophages in lymphangiogenesis in the meninges. We believe that this integrated approach will unravel the physiological role of meningeal macrophages in the meninges, thereby enabling us to better comprehend how meningeal immunity can affect brain physiology and its dysregualation. This will also allow us to identify novel mechanistic pathways that can serve as potential therapeutics for neurodegenerative diseases.
kw: neurodegenerative diseases; meninges; macrophages; lymphatics; infection

title: Understanding and Targeting the Non-Canonical Oncogenic Function of EZH2 for Therapeutic Intervention in Cancers
abs: The dysregulation of euchromatic regions by epigenetic writers such as PRC2 is a fundamental hallmark of cancers. EZH2 maintains the repressive mark through PRC2-dependent H3K27 trimethylation. However, in the highly refractory cancers of NKTL, TNBC and castrate–resistant prostate cancer, EZH2 can functionally switch from a transcriptional repressor to activator thereby stimulating oncogenic pathways that cannot be overcome by EZH2 methyltransferase inhibitors. Our preliminary studies show that Jak3-mediated phosphorylation can lead to dissociation of EZH2 from PRC2 and subsequent binding to Pol2, culminating in upregulation of genes involved in proliferation and invasion. It is our hypotheses that targeted degradation of EZH2 protein and elucidation of oncogenic factors driving addiction to non-canonical EZH2 signalling will produce novel and meaningful therapeutic outcomes for these aggressive cancer subtypes. We further hypothesize that concordant expression of EZH2 and non-canonical oncotargets will generate unique gene signatures and biomarkers for classification and treatment of these patients. In this study, we aim to perform transcriptomics analysis on CRISPR-Cas9 engineered models of EZH2 WT, KO and catalytically-dead mutants in conjunction with a targeted loss-of-function screen to identify and validate transcriptionally activated oncogenic targets of EZH2. From the oncogenes identified in Aim1, we intend to develop a non-canonical EZH2 gene signature which will be tested and validated on public datasets and new patient samples using the sensitive and robust NanoString platform to accelerate clinical translation. Finally, we aim to generate a novel series of therapeutic compounds which target the proteolytic degradation of EZH2 via two strategies 1) Inhibition of USP36 which deubiquitinates and stabilises EZH2 protein and b) Syntheses of cutting-edge EZH2-PROTAC probes which specifically tags EZH2 for proteasomal-mediated degradation through targeted ubiquitination. Taken together, this study will enhance our understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying aggressive non-canonical EZH2 cancer phenotypes, with direct applications in diagnostics, therapeutics and prognostication.
kw: PRC2-independent EZH2; Therapeutics; Non-Canonical; NKTL; Cancer; PROTAC																																				PRC2-independent EZH2; Therapeutics; Non-Canonical; NKTL; Cancer; PROTAC

title: A pre-clinical study of zone-specific MSC-derived chondrogenic cells pre-differentiated on a nano- topographic platform for functionally superior cartilage repair
abs: Articular cartilage has a zonal architecture and biphasic mechanical properties. The recapitulation of surface lubrication properties together with high compressibility of the deeper layers of native cartilage during cartilage regeneration is essential in achieving longevity of the repaired cartilage. Current clinical approaches for cartilage repair, especially with the use of mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) or chondrocytes, have yet to restore the hierarchically organized architecture of normal articular cartilage. The main reason for this may be the use of a single delivery of heterogeneous mixture of cells. We hypothesize that MSCs differentiated on substrates with specific nano-topographic patterns can provide phenotypically stable and defined chondrocytes, and when delivered as a stratified hydrogel construct, will facilitate the formation of hierarchically organized cartilage tissue. We have previously established that phenotypically stable zone specific chondrogenic cells can be derived from MSCs differentiated on distinct nano-patterned surfaces. In a proof-of-concept rabbit osteochondral defect study, we further demonstrated the potential of delivering these MSC-derived cells as a bilayered hydrogel construct, generating cartilage tissue with superior mechanical properties. In this proposal, our objective is to establish a scale-up production of nano-patterned surfaces using a nano-injection molding method that can support mass generation of MSC-derived pre-differentiated chondrocytes; and to further validate our approach for cartilage regeneration in a load-bearing large animal chondral defect model, with the aim for clinical translation. This proposal will build upon our previous collaborative study, and further the development of a scalable manufacturing strategy for mass production of nano-patterned substrates. The approach will provide a relatively straightforward method of obtaining large quantities of zonal-specific chondrocytes to engineer a stratified cartilage construct. The outcome of this pre-clinical study on an anatomically relevant porcine cartilage model will advance the translational application of engineering zonally stratified cartilage constructs for functional repair of critical size cartilage defects.
kw: articular cartilage repair; zone-specific chondrocytes; mesenchymal stem cells; nano-topographic platform

title: Bayesian Machine Learning Approach to Identify Markers of Progression in Primary Angle Closure Glaucoma
abs: Glaucoma is the leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide, with primary angle-closure glaucoma (PACG) a major form of glaucoma in Singapore and Asia. While we have made considerable advances in understanding the epidemiology, risk factors including genetic susceptibility, and clinical phenotypes of PACG, one of the greatest challenge and unmet clinical need is in identifying which individuals are at the highest risk of progression and development of advanced disease/blindness. The current strategies for patient risk assessment in PACG are inadequate and non-specific. There is lack of long-term clinical data and knowledge of specific determinants for PACG progression. We recently identified some clinical markers for rapid progression; however, the major limitations of our study was that clinical parameters were evaluated in only those subjects who showed progression and not for all who were assessed. Additionally, the possible contributions of PACG-related imaging parameters and genetic markers were not investigated. It is thus not known if there are specific genetic variants and clinical features that predisposes to disease progression and development of advanced PACG/blindness. In this proposal, we hypothesize that disease progression in PACG varies greatly among individuals; and biometric, imaging, and genetic factors contribute to an individuals’ variations. By combining clinical and genetic markers in a Bayesian machine-learning platform, we will develop a clinical tool that will predict the probability/rate of disease progression. To address our hypothesis, we will collect comprehensive clinical and imaging data of patients in whom genome-wide association (GWAS) genetics data is already available; and develop a risk prediction algorithm (Aim 1). Next, we aim to validate the risk algorithm in a separate PACG cohort (Aim 2). It is hoped that this project will give rise to resources that will lead towards precision medicine approaches, which will allow clinicians to stratify patients for more effective customized treatments and management.
kw: Primary angle closure glaucoma; risk prediction; anterior segment optical coherence tomography;  Ophthalmic genetics; imaging; Bayesian machine-learning

title: Pre-clinical development of brain-penetrant MNK inhibitors for glioblastoma therapy
abs: Adult glioblastoma (GBM) is the deadliest form of brain cancer with fewer than 5% of patients surviving five years, and most succumbing to therapy-resistant disease. To overcome multiple resistance mechanisms, several groups advocate targeting the process of aberrant mRNA translation in GBM, since altered translation represents a final common pathway mediating glioma stem cell (GSC) persistence and therapy resistance. In particular, inhibition of the MAPK-interacting kinase-eFI4E (MNK-eIF4E) axis abrogates translation of resistance-conferring mRNAs in GBM. However, to date, brain-penetrant MNK inhibitors (MNKi) have not been described, an indispensable requirement for effective anti-GBM drugs. Accordingly, we have developed a potent and specific brain-penetrant MNKi, ETC-501, that overcomes temozolomide (TMZ) resistance in a panel of MNK-expressing GSCs. Given that approximately 50% of patients have TMZ-resistant disease, MNKis may have utility in a significant proportion of GBM patients. Our preliminary data indicate that MNKis act via three inter-related mechanisms: (i) augmenting the ability of TMZ to induce DNA double-strand breaks; (ii) synergistically enhancing the senescence-inducing activity of TMZ, while simultaneously inhibiting the pro-tumourigenic ‘senescence associated secretory phenotype’ produced by DNA damaging agents (DDA); and (iii) inhibiting the expression of established GSC drivers, e.g. TGM2. Based on these findings, we hypothesise that MNK-eIF4E-dependent mRNAs contribute to GBM persistence and drug resistance. Our Specific Aims are: 1. To establish efficacy of MNKi and DDA combinations in GBM, 2. To determine the mechanism of action of MNKis in GBM, and 3. To establish efficacy of novel MNKi combinations in GBM. In completing these Aims, we will increase our mechanistic understanding of MNKi activity in GBM, discover novel MNKi combinations effective against GSCs, and identify functional biomarkers for testing in clinical trials. Our work will support and guide the design of MNKi clinical trials, and satisfy a major unmet need in the management of patients with GBM.
kw: Glioblastoma, MAPK-interacting kinase (MNK) inhibitors, drug resistance, pre-clinical drug development.

title: The role of epistatically interacting mutations in maintaining the fitness of influenza B virus in humans
abs: Acute respiratory tract infection is a major cause of death in children under 5 years of age, accounting for almost 20% of childhood deaths globally each year. In Singapore, there are about 900,000 visits annually to public clinics and hospital emergency departments for acute respiratory infection, with 3,500 cases requiring hospital admission. Influenza virus is one of the major causes of upper respiratory infection in humans. In Singapore, influenza viruses circulate year-round with two peaks in April–June and November–January, corresponding to influenza seasons in the Southern and Northern Hemispheres. An estimated 20% of the Singapore’s population is infected with influenza each year and the mortality rates (14.8 per 100,000 person-years) are comparable to those in the United States. According to the Singapore Ministry of Health, ~41–52% of all cases of influenza-like illnesses are caused by influenza viruses every year. Of these, ~18–48% are influenza B cases. In this proposal, we aim to understand the evolutionary mechanisms contributing to the occurrence of epidemics and changes in the biology of influenza B viruses. Specifically, we will test the hypothesis that the influenza B virus evolution is subject to genetically interacting mutations that affect the survival of one virus group over another, and how this may influence the emergence of epidemic strains in the human population. Knowing which mutations contribute to virus survival will provide a basis for predicting future successful influenza B viruses, and this information can be used to help decide which viruses should be included in the WHO recommended influenza vaccines. Improving the match between circulating influenza viruses and the vaccine components would lead to a direct improvement in vaccine efficacy and reduce influenza related illness and death.
kw: Evolution, epistasis, viral fitness, epidemic, vaccine

title: Elucidating the immunobiology of nasopharyngeal carcinoma
abs: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) is endemic in Southern China/South-east Asia. Few disease models exist for NPC and existing cell lines are unreliable. Treatment of NPC with PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors show limited tumor response despite high levels of PD-L1 expression, suggesting checkpoint blockade is not the only driver for immune dysregulation. We propose to investigate the immunobiology of NPC using clinical biopsies (tumor/blood) and humanized mouse patient-derived xenograft models in the following manner: Specific Aim 1: To elucidate the pathobiology of NPC and drug response through extended analysis of paired NPC samples. Integrated molecular analyses of biopsy samples from patients will be done to extensively curate datasets of tumor and blood. These samples are paired and within the context of NPC clinical trials or from patients undergoing standard of care therapy. Clinical data and treatment outcomes for correlative analyses are collected. Specific Aim 2: To establish and expand patient-derived xenografts (PDX) to elucidate the immunobiology of NPC. Fresh tumor biopsies are implanted in NOD SCID mice. Established PDX are compared with primary tumor biopsies for fidelity and EBV status, and expanded in mice with humanized immune background. Successful humanized PDX are studied to understand immune dysregulation using flow cytometry of tumor immune infiltrate, tumor/immune cell checkpoint gene expression, tumor and circulating cytokine levels. Specific Aim 3: To understand the mechanistic basis for response/resistance to immunotherapy/novel therapeutics using the above models. Drug treatment of the NPC humanized PDX will be done. Immunomodulation in the tumor and in mouse circulation are studied using flow cytometry and circulating and intratumoral cytokines. Untreated/treated PDX are interrogated with multicolor immunohistochemistry to investigate changes in tumor microenvironment. Mouse PDX data will be correlated with paired human clinical data where available. This project will establish an inestimable resource of NPC data and human PDX for scientific use and drug testing.
kw: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma; immunotherapy; integrated molecular profiling; mouse models; patient-derived xenografts

title: Diseases as perturbations of the human Immunome: A high dimensionality approach to Translational Medicine in silica
abs: The project proposal entitled “Studying the tolerance-inflammation balance of the human immune rheostat using a deep immunophenotyping approach” aims to address unmet translational clinical needs for comprehensive analyses of clinically well characterised, focussed disease datasets that can be compared against that of robust, age-matched healthy state samples. The study also aims to establish human disease datasets that are hallmarks of opposing ends of pathological immune perturbation represented by autoimmunity on one end and patho-tolerance on the other. We propose to use representative sample sets from various rheumatological diseases to study autoimmunity and to contrast, samples from cancer samples of viral and non-viral etiology to study a state of path-tolerance. The premise being, given sufficient sample sizes and keeping constant several comparator parameters like the baseline healthy cohorts to test against, CyTOF panels that span broad immune cell categories and harmonised experimental protocol, functional and molecular mechanisms that are correct hallmarks of autoimmunity and patho-tolerance as immune perturbances of human disease can be better understood. The proposed development of high dimensional disease datasets through this bid aims to address the unmet needs by: Utilising sufficient sample size to make a clinical inference of autoimmune and patho-tolerance disease states Studying tissue microenvironment of autoimmunity and patho-tolerance to understand correlates with peripheral circulation Deploying an in-depth immune phenotyping approach to generate dense datasets of high quality and low variability by the purposeful of clinical parameters Develop machine learning approaches to enable the datasets for future health applications such as training datasets for AI An eminent clinician-researcher team that is already collaborating will be driving the study through their expertise, and collective strengths of being able to access well defined clinical cohorts and to study them using cutting edge technologies and analyses approaches.
kw: Immunomics; Disease datasets; Standardised clinical samples

title: TCF20 rs932376 genotype-directed dosing of tamoxifen in Asian estrogen-receptor positive breast cancer patients
abs: Tamoxifen is a selective estrogen receptor modulator effective against estrogen-receptor positive breast cancer. Tamoxifen’s therapeutic activity is mainly due to its principal active metabolite endoxifen, which is formed from tamoxifen mostly (>90%) via CYP2D6 mediated metabolism. It is thus hypothesized that low resultant serum endoxifen levels are a harbinger of increased cancer recurrence and poor outcome. Should this be true, it suggests that a critical endoxifen concentration for oncologists to aim for could exist. As preliminary data, we conducted the first genome-wide association study on steady-state endoxifen levels in 154 Singaporean Chinese breast cancer patients, with replication analysis in 290 Germans and 70 Lebanese breast cancer patients. Strong evidence of association was observed between a TCF20 genetic marker and serum endoxifen levels (effect size = -11.15 mmol per-copy of the minor allele; P = 1.19 x 10-40) with no evidence of heterogeneity across collections. Analysis compensating for the canonical CYP2D6 metabolizer genotypes still showed TCF20 to be strongly genome-wide significant over and above CYP2D6, retaining consistent evidence of association across the patient collections. Carriers and individuals homozygous for the minor allele of TCF20 showed poorer clinical outcome (N = 2091 women with 257 events) compared to wild-type individuals (Hazard ratio per-allele = 1.24; P = 0.015; I2 index for heterogeneity=0%). These low-pass GWAS findings herald the presence of genetic variants of higher penetrance and stronger effect with regards to control of endoxifen pharmacokinetics as well as clinical outcome of breast cancer patients following treatment with tamoxifen. The objective of this proposal is to now build on the Singaporean GWAS finding and conduct a prospective TCF20 genotype-based dosing of tamoxifen in Singaporean hormone receptor positive breast cancer patients.
kw: Tamoxifen; Genotype-directed dosing; TCF20 rs932376; CYP2D6; ER-positive breast cancer

title: Pharmacological activation of TEAD activity for potential use in regenerative medicine
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: The transcriptional co-regulators YAP and TAZ are the downstream effectors of the Hippo signaling pathway that control various physiological and pathological processes. YAP and TAZ pair with the TEAD family of transcription factors to initiate transcription. YAP/TAZ activity is increased during tissue regeneration and enhancing it using pharmacological tools is proposed to be a viable option for regenerative medicine. We previously identified a tractable pocket in TEADs that could be leveraged to modulate YAP/TAZ activity; the pocket is physiologically shown to bind palmitate. A medium throughput TEAD-Palmitate AlphaScreen was developed to select small molecules occupying the palmitate-binding pocket (PBP) of TEADs. Quinolinol compounds were identified as TEAD-binding compounds that augment YAP/TAZ-TEAD activity, which was verified using TEAD reporter assay, RT-qPCR and RNA-Seq analyses. In this grant proposal we lay out a plan to do a high-throughput screen, to generate tool compounds, and to test the hypothesis whether pharmacological activation of TEADs will have utility in regenerative medicine. Various quinolinol analogs will also be generated to investigate whether a tool compound could be developed using this scaffold. The generation and validation bona fide YAP/TAZ-TEAD activating tool compounds are described in three major specific aims (i) high throughput screen (ii) generation of tool compounds and (iii) validation of tool compounds. PBP is exploited to inhibit TEAD activity but leveraging it to activate TEADs is a novel concept, which we will explore in-depth in this grant. Apart from the drug discovery aspects, we are also very interested in TEAD biology. In specific aim 4, plans are outlined to understand TEAD regulation through post-translational modifications and to understand the mechanism behind the specificity in TEAD-dependent gene expression.
kw: Hippo signalling, YAP, TAZ, regenerative medicine, TEAD

title: Determine the role of circular RNAs in adipocyte development and metabolism
abs: The upsurge of obesity and metabolic syndrome has elicited an explosion of interest in adipocyte biology over the last two decades. A frontier research topic in the battle with obesity and its associated diseases is to understand the detailed molecular mechanism underlying adipocyte development and metabolism. In the preliminary study, we discovered thousands of circular RNAs (circRNAs) expressed in mouse and human adipose tissues, profiled their dynamic regulation during adipogenesis and obesity, and demonstrated that a circRNA, circArhgap2, was required for adipocyte differentiation and mature adipocyte program. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first systemic study to determine circRNAs’ function in adipocytes. Here, we hypothesize that circArhgap2 is a novel non-coding regulator in adipocyte metabolism, and will test our hypothesis by (aim 1) determining the function of circArhgap5-2 on adipocyte metabolism and (aim 2) by determining the mechanism used by circArhgap5-2 to exert its function in adipocytes. The proposed study will leverage on cutting-edge RNA technology, innovative algorithms and functional genetic studies in an integrative project. Outcomes of these proposed studies will shed lights on the function and mechanism of a new class of non-coding RNAs in adipocytes. The knowledge gained will lay down cornerstones to understanding how circRNA-mediated pathways are altered in metabolic diseases and point to potential strategies for modulating these pathways to improve metabolic health.
kw: adipocyte, obesity, adipose, non-coding RNA

title: Interrogating the RNA interactome to discover key regulators of colorectal cancer
abs: Aberrant changes in post-transcriptional regulation can contribute to tumorigenesis by regulating the expression of key genes. Two large classes of post-transcriptional regulators are RNA binding proteins (RBPs) and microRNAs (miRNAs). As RBPs often exhibit context-specific expression patterns, it is likely that the current RBP census based on profiling in specific cell lines, literature curation and RNA binding domain prediction only represents a subset of the RBPs present in any given cell type. Secondly, although several studies have described RBP:miRNA crosstalk, these reports have mostly focused on particular transcripts of interest. As both RBPs and miRNAs often regulate hundreds or thousands of targets, a large-scale analysis is of critical importance to unravel the interplay between these facets of post-transcriptional regulation. We hypothesize that RBPs are key regulators of tumorigenesis and will study this in colorectal cancer (CRC), which is the most common cancer in Singapore and one of the most common cancers worldwide. We will investigate this through the following specific aims: (1) Interrogation of global changes in RBP expression, (2) Examination of the functional role of candidate RBPs in tumorigenesis, and (3) Exploration of the interplay between RNA:protein and RNA:RNA interactions in CRC. We have assembled a team of world-leading experts with complementary expertise to address this unmet research need. Our main PI, Yvonne Tay, is an expert in various aspects of RNA biology and post-transcriptional regulation. Our team also comprises experts in RBPs (Gene Yeo), quantitative proteomics (Dennis Kappei), CRC (Ker Kan Tan), and patient-derived CRC models (Wai Leong Tam). A systematic interrogation of the RBP atlas and RBP:miRNA crosstalk will represent a paradigm shift in the roadmap to studying RBP function and lead to novel insights into CRC tumorigenesis, the discovery of novel oncogenes and/or tumor suppressors and potential diagnostic, prognostic and therapeutic targets for future clinical applications.
kw: RNA, RNA binding protein, microRNA, competing endogenous RNA, cancer, colon

title: Aquaporin-5 (AQP5) is a functional membrane marker of gastric cancer stem cell populations driving tumour growth and metastasis in mice and humans
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Gastric cancer is a leading cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide, particularly in Asia. Therapeutic options for gastric cancer patients are limited to conventional treatments targeting tumour bulk, and there is a pressing need to devise novel therapies to improve patient survival. We have recently discovered that Aquaporin-5 (Aqp5) marks stem cells of the distal pyloric stomach in mice and humans and serve as the cell-of-origin of gastric cancer. Furthermore, we have isolated functional normal human pyloric stem cells for the first time using anti-AQP5 antibodies. Preliminary evidence in mouse cancer models suggest that Aqp5+ cells in gastric tumours behave as cancer stem cells. Cancer stem cells are thought to drive the incessant growth of the tumour, thus targeting them would halt tumour progression. We hypothesize that AQP5+ tumour cells in mouse and humans are cancer stem cells. We will prove this functionally with a combination of in vivo mouse models, ex vivo organoid culture, and transplants. We will also test the effects of ablating AQP5+ cancer cells in gastric cancer as a pre-clinical evaluation of adopting this strategy for therapeutic use in the clinic. In parallel, we will identify other novel gastric cancer stem cell-specific candidates that have therapeutic potential for selective targeting of the population through transcriptome and proteome profiling of the AQP5+ cancer stem cells from mouse and human tumours. Furthermore, we plan to investigate the functional role of AQP5 in mouse and human cancer cells through a combination of knockout and overexpression assays in organoid cultures and transplants. Taken together, our proposed study aims to functionally establish AQP5+ cancer cells as cancer stem cells, provide a holistic understanding of how these cells contribute to tumourigenesis during tumour initiation, progression and metastasis, and facilitate future development of new, improved gastric cancer therapies to augment current treatment regimens.
kw: gastric cancer; stem cells; stomach

title: Determining the molecular and structural basis for inflammasome activation in human
abs: The inflammasome complex consists receptors and sensors that regulate the activation of caspase-1 and induce inflammation in response to infectious microbes and molecules derived from host proteins. The overarching goal of this proposal is to investigate the molecular details of how human NOD-like receptors (NLRs) recognize their pathogenic substrate, and subsequently how such molecular recognition leads to activation of the inflammasome complex involving ASC and Caspase-1 in human. Our central hypothesis is that such molecular knowledge of the human inflammasome provides us better models to develop novel regulators of human innate immune responses, and eventually facilitating targeted immunotherapy or suppressing autoimmune diseases. Our preliminary data include several new complex structures at moderate resolution demonstrating how different NLRs signaling converged into ASC activation. Furthermore, the reconstituted biochemical platforms we developed along the structural investigation are conveniently available for screening of immune-regulators for human inflammasome. The rationale behind our specific aims and the corresponding approaches are described as follows.
kw: Autoimmune Disease; Innate Immune Responses; NOD-like Receptors; Cryo-EM; Pathogen-Host Interactions

title: Immune-based Therapeutic Small Molecule Discovery to Enhance Neutrophil Anti-fungal Response
abs: Opportunistic fungal infections constitute a major health threat, especially among immunocompromised patients. Currently, licensed treatments for fungal infections are limited to four classes of antifungal drugs, all with adverse side effects to patients, and are increasingly failing as frontline therapies. This situation is worsened by the emergence of multidrug-resistant pathogenic fungi such as Candida Auris. To counter the problem, one should reduce the reliance on currently available fungicides and develop a broad range of therapeutic strategies to combat fungal diseases. At the molecular level, fungi infection leads to the activation of C-type lectin receptors such as Dectin-1 and its signalling pathway in immune cells such as macrophages and neutrophils, and results in the production of effector molecules for fungal clearance. Critical to the host anti-fungal response is the adaptor Card9 whose deficiency in human is characterized by spontaneous fungal infections across multiple tissues and organs. Our preliminary data show that loss of another signalling adaptor, Downstream of Kinase (Dok)-3, protects mice from lethal systemic infection with Candida albicans. Dok3-deficient neutrophils exhibit enhanced killing of Candida in-vitro. We subsequently show that Dok3 negatively regulates antifungal immunity in neutrophils by recruiting Protein Phosphatase 1 to de-phosphorylate Card9, thereby attenuating downstream antifungal responses. Here, we propose to study in detail Dok3-Card9 binding to identify motifs involved in their interaction using overexpression and co-immunoprecipitation and western blot analyses. Concurrently, we plan to implement a “humanized” yeast-based drug screen for lead compounds to disrupt Dok3-Card9 interaction. These lead compounds will be tested in cell assays to examine their effects in enhancing neutrophil-mediated clearance of fungi, and in preclinical mouse models for their efficacy as prophylactic and treatment in systemic yeast infection. This study will yield drug candidate for clinical development and hopefully, represents a new immune-based approach to develop drugs to fight opportunistic yeast infection.
kw: Candida, Drug Screening, Innate Immunity, Fungus, Signaling, Infection

title: Rapid Automated Peripheral non-Invasive Diagnostic (RAPID) optical measurement of blood parameters
abs: Cancer is the 2nd highest cause of total disease and injury burden in Singapore in 2010. Chemotherapy is the mainstay of treatment and chemotherapy-induced febrile neutropenic illness is a life-threatening emergency complicating the treatment of many cancer patients. Close monitoring of cancer patients’ white cell count can help early detection of infection and tailor more effective chemotherapy treatments. However, current monitoring methods involves frequent blood taking via venipuncture which is painful and requires very frequent visits to the hospital. These result in a poor quality of life for cancer patients and increase use of hospital resources. A non-invasive portable white blood cell monitoring device can allow patients to monitor their counts at home thereby allowing patients to spend more time out of hospital and optimize their chemotherapy regimens. We will develop and validate non-invasive optical microscopic techniques for counting white blood cells (WBC) and monitor blood total haemoglobin concentration (SpHb) in human subjects. Specifically, we will develop an ultrahigh-resolution and ultrahigh-speed micro-optical coherence tomography (μOCT) system with an oral cavity probe for visualization and counting of WBC at the labial mucosa; We will also add a visible spectroscopic imaging channel to the μOCT device for point measurement of hemoglobin concentrations in blood vessels of the labial mucosa. The proposed methods will be fully established by validating them against the clinical gold standard - full blood count (FBC) in human. An open label single group of patients will be examined by both methods (at first using RAPID and then by conventional blood sampling) to obtain haematological parameters (total white cell count and differential count and haemoglobin). Based on this preliminary data we will optimize the blood monitoring system for use at home or a community health center.
kw: White blood cell count; total hemoglobin ; noninvasive measurement; optical coherence tomography

title: Regulation of monocyte / macrophages metabolism and anti-TB responses by histone deacetylase SIRT1
abs: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the causative agent of tuberculosis (TB), persist within infected cells by hijacking several immune We recently demonstrated that active TB patients have reduced sirtuin 1 (SIRT1) mechanisms. expression and activating SIRT1 by resveratrol induces autophagy and inhibits Mtb growth in mice TB model. SIRT1 is a histone deacetylase and is involved in a range of cellular metabolic and epigenetic processes. Our study indicates the potential of developing SIRT1 activators as an effective and clinically relevant host-directed therapies (HDTs) for TB. We hypothesize that – (i) Mtb mediated reduction in SIRT1 expression result’s in the induction of aerobic glycolysis and perturbation of macrophage metabolism, and (ii) that activating SIRT1 will result in metabolic and epigenetic reprograming, thus negatively regulating TB pathogenesis by suppressing Mtb-induced aerobic glycolysis via targeting mTOR-HIF1 signaling. This will lead to SIRT1-mediated (i) increased innate anti-microbicidal pathways such as autophagy, (ii) dampening of TB pathology, and (iii) increased host-fitness (i.e ability to restrict the growth of bacteria) against pathogen. In this project, we will take parallel and complementary approaches to elucidate the mechanism behind SIRT1-mediated modulation of macrophage metabolism / aerobic glycolysis during Mtb infection. We will perform epigenetic (histone acetylation), transcriptomic and metabolic studies in Mtb-infected human monocytes/macrophages to test whether SIRT1 activation rewires mTOR-HIF1 pathway. Outcome will be validated in mice with targeted disruption of key elements in the proposed pathway. We also hypothesize that the reduced SIRT1 expression seen in TB patients could be linked with SIRT1 gene polymorphisms. Therefore, to understand the role of host genotype on SIRT1-mediated protection against TB we will investigate SIRT1 SNPs (Single Nucleotide polymorphisms) in a Chinese TB cohort. These integrative approaches will help us to identify precise mode of action contributing to SIRT1-mediated enhancement of immunity against Mtb-infection.
kw: Tuberculosis; host-fitness; sirtuin; monocyte; metabolism; epigenetics

title: Regulators of viral inflammation in the bat and their application for health.
abs: To target inflammation and its implications for human health we must change our approach to the problem. Using natural, robust, animal models such as bats, we can gain insight into effective measures to control disease. We hypothesize that bats are naturally resistant to excessive inflammation from many pathogens due to unique regulators of immunity and this can be applied to human biology to help alleviate the burden of infectious diseases. We will dissect the immune tolerance mechanisms of bats during viral infection of Melaka Virus or MERS-CoV in vivo in our colony animals to identify novel regulatory mechanisms that may control inflammation, post-infection. We will utilize un-biased deep sequencing by RNASeq, proteomics, secretome analysis and examine immune cell subsets and single-cell heterogeneity to identify regulatory pathways affecting inflammation in response to these viruses. The activated/suppressed pathways will be analysed relative to untreated controls and also inter-species comparisons with data from infected mice and humans. We will then trigger intervention of these pathways in bats to validate their suitability as anti-inflammatory targets. Next, we will apply regulation of these inflammatory control mechanisms in infection of other mammals such as mice and macaque to examine potential therapeutic value in alleviating the burden of disease. We strongly believe that the tolerance in bats, a natural model immune to the side-effects of excessive inflammation, can provide unique opportunities for discovering new mechanisms to alleviate disease burden and unveil new pathways for drug discovery and design. As inflammation also plays a key role in many other human diseases, the findings from this study can later be extended to other biomedical disciplines.
kw: infectious disease; virus; inflammation; bat; immunity; immune regulator

title: Rifampicin resistance, transcriptional efficiency and  bacterial fitness in Mycobacterium tuberculosis
abs: Selected rifampicin-resistance mutations in the rpoB subunit in Mtb have been correlated to enhanced bacterial fitness in the presence or absence of putative compensatory mutation. As such, it is hypothesized that some rifampicin-resistance mutations, in the presence or absence of putative compensatory mutations, may enhance the spread of tuberculosis; while others may have detrimental impact on bacterial fitness, virulence and host-response. Given that rifampicin-resistance is associated with mutations of the DNA directed RNA polymerase rpoB subunit, we hypothesize that fitness is directly correlated to transcriptional efficiency. We question how different mutations on the rpoB disrupt transcriptional efficiency and whether additional mutations within the rpoB or putative compensatory mutations stabilize the transcriptional process. We wonder whether transcriptional disruption is homogeneous, affecting all transcription of genes proportionally, or uneven, affecting the expression of particular genes more than others, in the presence or absence of putative compensatory mutations. We plan to address these questions by engineering a collection of isogenic rifampicin-resistant rpoB mutants and rpoB compensatory mutants for the determination of transcriptional efficiency analysis and impact on overall bacterial physiology and fitness. It is puzzling to note that some rifampicin-resistant rpoB mutations with enhance fitness reported in the literature are not found in clinical samples in the absence of rifampicin treatment, as would be expected in an evolutionary context, suggesting plausible other fitness factors at play. Understanding resistance-fitness dynamics would help in defining genetic markers in strains prone to dissemination or destine to die within a patient and human population. Identifying fit versus unfit drug-resistant mutants would lead to better preparedness for patient treatment, management and infection control. In this proposal, we aim to address some of the questions regarding resistance-fitness dynamics experimentally by engineering isogenic resistant strains and determining their impact on cell physiology, host-response and fitness.
kw: Mycobacterium tuberculosis, rifampicin, resistance, bacterial fitness, transcription efficiency, digital drop PCR

title: Modulation of p53 splicing as an approach to improve cancer therapy
abs: Chemo- and radio-therapies are the mainstay of current cancer treatment. Yet, significant side-effects and toxicities are associated with them. Enhancing their therapeutic efficacy will benefit patients tremendously and improve their quality of life. p53 is one of the most-important tumor-suppressers that is activated by, and is required for, the effects of these therapies. Hence, 50% of all patients whose cancers have p53 mutations generally do not respond well to these treatments. Nonetheless, p53 can be activated in the other half of patients with cancers without p53 mutations, to enhance the therapeutic response. In this context, we have recently uncovered that expression of p47, an amino-terminal-truncated isoform of p53, can sensitize cancer cells to cell death in response to cancer drug treatment, due to p47’s ability to selectively transactivate the expression of some apoptotic target genes. p47 is naturally expressed from an alternate p53 mRNA transcript that retains the intron 2 of p53, which represents about 5-10% of all p53 transcripts. Thus, our hypothesis is that inducible retention of p53 intron 2 would lead to enhanced p47 expression in tumor cells and can be a strategy to improve the therapeutic index of standard cancer therapies, especially in cancers with an unmutated p53. Our preliminary results demonstrate an interplay of splicing factors that regulate p53 intron 2 retention. Moreover, based on an initial bio-modelling screen, we have identified several anti-sense oligonucleotides (AONs) that are capable of inducing p53 intron 2 retention. Hence, this proposal aims to perform a comprehensive analysis to characterize the mechanistic basis of p53 intron 2 retention, and to understand its relevance in vivo. Finally, our aim is to exploit the initial findings to evaluate the therapeutic effects of AONs in promoting p53 intron 2 retention, especially in response to therapeutic treatment and tumor growth in vivo.
kw: cancer, intron, p53, splicing, targeting

title: Small Molecule Fluorescent Probe Development for Human Liver Stem Cells with High Differentiation Capability into Hepatocyte Lineage
abs: The chronic liver disease involves loss of functional hepatocytes and irreversible scarring of the liver, leading to end-stage liver disease. Although liver transplantation is the curative treatment, the amount of donor organ is limited and alternative strategies, therefore, are needed. A number of studies have shown that human hepatic stem cells are capable of propagating in vitro, can be differentiated into hepatocyte-like cells. Hence, the transplantation of patient-derived hepatic stem cells (PdHSCs) or PdHSC-derived hepatocytes has been offered as an ideal therapeutic option for the treatment of liver disease. However, isolated HSCs seem to come in two flavors. One is more hepatocyte lineage committed, whereas the other is more prone to go in the direction of cholangiocytes. So far the “flavor” can only be determined by costly and time-consuming works. In the current absence of a specific marker for HSCs, especially “flavor” specific a fast translation is limited. Thus, the specific identification and isolation of HSCs from patient tissue would contribute significantly to the effective clinical application of PdHSCs. Development of bio-imaging probes using synthetic small molecules has been explored for a biologically safe and highly sophisticated way to visualize the specific type of cells. Diversity-Oriented Fluorescence Library Approach (DOFLA), which includes a high throughput screening (HTS) step of the synthetic fluorescent compound libraries, have demonstrated various cell type-selective probes through unbiased phenotypic screenings. While DOFLA would be a promising approach for the HSC probe development, unbiased screening requires a reliably established cell model for the HTS step. Fortunately, we have established a PdHSC platform by various patients. Our goal is to identify specific probes for human HSCs using the DOFLA and PdHSCs platform. This study would provide an enormous advance in the field and for the application of HSCs in regenerative medicine for the treatment of chronic liver disease.
kw: Metabolic liver disease; Cell therapy; Liver stem cells; Fluorescent probe; High-throughput screening

title: Modulating Endoplasmic Reticulum Stress as a prophylactic approach against symptomatic viral infection.
abs: Zoonotic pathogens continue to emerge to threaten human health at an even quicker pace since the turn of this century but vaccines and drugs development lag behind these outbreaks. Therefore it is imperative that we advance our understanding of the molecular basis of host-viral interaction that define clinical outcome to gain insights into how such epidemics can be effectively managed. Using the live-attenuated yellow fever 17D vaccine to induce a mild acute viral illness, we have now shown in two separate studies that baseline adaptive endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress and compensatory reduced tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle activity increased susceptibility to symptomatic infection: Infection in such individuals triggered maladaptive ER stress response with production of reactive oxygen species (ROS). ROS in turn triggered downstream innate immune and pro-inflammatory responses that correlated with symptomatic infection. Metformin, a widely used anti-diabetic drug has recently been shown to act on multiple pathways in the cell, in addition to its anti-glycemia function. One of its functions is ER stress modulation. Our preliminary data also showed that metformin reduced the expression of key intermediates in the ER-stress induced apoptotic pathway, suggesting its potential to reduce maladaptive ER stress and subsequent cell death. The goal of this proposal is thus to show proof-of-concept that modulating ER stress alone with metformin, can reduce the rate of symptomatic viral infection. We will employ a placebo-controlled experimental medicine approach to test the utility and efficacy of metformin as a ER stress modulator to reduce the likelihood of symptomatic YF17D infection, complemented with comprehensive omics-level analyses to define how metformin modulates the host response to YF17D infection and thus alter symptomatic outcome. If successful, this study would clarify a poorly understood but clinically important aspect of host-viral interaction and show a therapeutic pathway to minimize the impact of emerging viral epidemics.
kw: Metformin; endoplasmic reticulum stress; YF17D infection; symptomatic; metabolic; immunometabolism

title: Understanding, influencing and empowering the spouses of colorectal cancer patients
abs: The aims of this study are to determine: 1. The quality of life of colorectal cancer (CRC) patients and their spouses in the first year from curative surgery and to ascertain the differences between the patients and their spouses. 2. If tailored interventions would overcome previously identified barriers to improve CRC screening rates of the spouses via a randomized controlled trial (RCT). 3. If spouses of CRC patients are willing to be advocates for CRC screening to their loved ones. The hypotheses include: 1. Quality of Life (QoL) of Spouses are also impaired and will recover to pre-operative level within 12 months from the index operation. 3. Tailored Interventions will improve screening rates amongst the spouses of CRC patients. 4. Spouses can be mobilized to be advocates for CRC amongst their loved ones and those who are current with screening will be more likely successful advocates for screening. Methodology Patients with CRC who are scheduled for elective surgery and their spouses will be recruited to participate in the study. Validated QoL instruments will be applied to the couple through the first year of the cancer journey. At the same time, a RCT comparing a targeted intervention programme in which issues related to a lack of education and inconvenience are addressed, against the current standard of care. The primary outcome will be the number of spouses who underwent FIT. Lastly, we will explore if these spouses could be empowered to become advocates for CRC screening amongst their family and friends with the necessary resources. Clinical significance This study will seek to understand the impact of CRC of the patients onto the spouses and then determine if tailored interventions could get these spouses to undergo screening and if empowering the spouses could mobilise them as advocates for CRC screening in the community.
kw: Spouses; Colorectal Cancer; Screening; Advocacy; Quality of Life; Intervention

title: Transforming patient care through development of non-invasive, in-vivo bedside skin imaging tools for diagnosis, classification and delineation of skin cancer.
abs: Currently, diagnosis of skin cancer is done through skin biopsy, which involves an invasive surgical procedure, a waiting time of 2 weeks and results in unsightly scars. When diagnosed, current treatment involves complete surgical excision with wide margins to ensure clearance. Wide excision usually requires extensive surgery which inevitably results in poor cosmetic effects. Therefore, the aim of this translational research proposal is to transform patient care though the development of novel non-invasive, in-vivo skin imaging tools that can be used in the clinics to instantly and automatically diagnose and stratify Non-Melanoma Skin cancers (NMSC), doing away with the need for traditional biopsies, while improving surgical management by precisely mapping the tumor before surgery allowing for individualized surgery. This will be achieved by:- • Specific Aim 1. Automated detection, diagnosis and stratification of NMSC through AI. We will develop image analysis algorithms to automatically detect, diagnose and stratify NMSC lesions in acquired in-vivo confocal images. • Specific Aim 2. Developing in-vivo 3D imaging of NMSC. Currently, we have good preliminary results on in-vivo 3D mapping of pigmented Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC) through photo-acoustics imaging (PAI) systems. In this specific aim, we will further develop our PAI system by addressing shortcomings identified in our preliminary studies through an iterative clinical-pathological-imaging correlation process to achieve a sensitivity and specificity of 95%. • Specific Aim 3. Validation of systems developed in Specific Aim 1 and 2. We will validate the automated detection, stratificaiton and diagnosis algorithm as well as the 3D mapping system for Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC) through a prospective clinical study. We are confident that an integrated team approach of clinicians, biophotonic and imaging experts from SBIC and image processing expertise from NTU and TUM, we will be able to automate diagnosis of NMSC and then to map out that skin cancer in-vivo.
kw: Basal cell carcinoma, non-invasive, in-vivo imaging, AI

title: Precision Medicine in Systemic Sclerosis Gastrointestinal Disease: Evaluating Imaging and Stool Biomarkers for Differentiating Disease Stages and Treatment Responses
abs: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) has one of the highest mortalities among autoimmune diseases (66% 10-year survival), with SSc-associated gastrointestinal disease (SSc-GI) the second highest cause. Intestinal failure leading to malabsorption necessitates costly long-term parenteral nutrition. Although one of the earliest manifestations of disease, SSc-GI is often diagnosed late after fibrosis has occurred. Unmet needs in SSc-GI management are non-invasive biomarkers for (i) early diagnosis (ii) differentiation of SSc-GI stages and (iii) treatment response. We hypothesize that SSc-GI fibrosis is preceded by an early inflammatory stage that represents a window of opportunity for immunosuppressive treatment. Aim 1: Determine if imaging biomarkers differentiate patients with early SSc from those with late SSc. Stool markers will be used as secondary biomarkers supporting inflammation. Aim 2: Evaluate imaging biomarker change over a 6- and 12-month treatment period with mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) in patients with early SSc. Stool markers will be used as secondary biomarkers supporting inflammation. Exploratory aim: To map imaging and stool biomarkers over one year in untreated patients with early SSc Methods: We will use combined 18F-Fluorodeoxyglucose-positron emission tomography and magnetic resonance imaging T1-MOLLI mapping as a novel tool to distinguish inflammation from fibrosis as the predominant pathological process in the bowel wall. Stool biomarkers indicative of an inflammatory state, will be derived using metagenomic analysis of the microbiota, metabolomics and faecal-calprotectin. In a cross-sectional study (Aim 1), we will compare biomarkers between patients with early [pre-scleroderma stage of “Very early diagnosis of SSc” or ≤3 years onset; (n=40)] and late SSc (>5 years onset; n=20). In symptomatic early SSc patients (n=25), we will determine change in biomarkers after 6 and 12 months of MMF (Aim 2). Significance: Non-invasive biomarkers that enable stratification of SSc-GI disease stages and treatment response will greatly advance the field in SSc by enhancing evaluation of SSc-GI.
kw: systemic sclerosis; gastrointestinal; imaging; stool; microbiota; biomarker

title: Novel palliative care model for advanced cancer patients: A randomized controlled trial study
abs: Cancer is the leading cause of death in Singapore, accounting for 30% of deaths in 2017. Advanced cancer patients have poor quality of life and high utilisation of acute healthcare services. When provided alongside standard oncology care, early access to palliative care improves quality of life of patients with advanced cancers and their caregivers, as well as reduces acute healthcare utilisation and costs by these patients. Yet, in Singapore and elsewhere around the world, palliative care is delivered to a minority of advanced cancer patients shortly before death, with a median time from first consult to death of only 30 days. We propose to conduct a randomized controlled trial of the ‘Supportive and Palliative care Review Kit in Locations Everywhere’ (SPARKLE) intervention, an outpatient-based model of early palliative care. The SPARKLE intervention comprises regular symptom monitoring using questionnaires, early identification and prompt treatment of problems identified. Proactive screening for problems facilitates earlier palliative care interventions for advanced cancer patients, whenever needs arise. The SPARKLE intervention extends palliative care to a larger number of advanced cancer patients and delivers palliative care before terminal phase of life, whenever patients have physical, psychological or social needs. We hypothesize that the SPARKLE care model results in a) improved quality of life of both advanced cancer patients and their caregivers, and b) reduced acute healthcare utilization and costs by these patients.
kw: Cancer; Palliative; Quality of Life; Patient Reported Outcome Measures

title: The Immunostimulatory Effects of Gentamicin: Translating Aminoglycoside Antibiotics into Antiviral Therapeutics for Pandemic Response
abs: Viral epidemics continually threaten global health. In the last 5 years alone, we have witnessed outbreaks of Ebola, Zika and yellow fever viruses. These infections universally have no effective treatments, and development of new therapeutics cannot keep pace with outbreak emergence. A potential solution is thus to exploit licensed drugs that exhibit potentially useful off-target antiviral properties. Such drugs could be used as a first-line pharmacological response during viral outbreaks. One such class of drugs are aminoglycoside antibiotics.
