Aminoglycosides are antibacterial drugs with well-established safety and pharmacokinetic profiles. In mouse models of mucosal infection, topical aminoglycosides exerted antiviral effects against respiratory and genital tract infections by stimulating toll-like receptors to induce interferon-simulated gene (ISG) expression: ISGs effect antiviral responses in cells. In this proposed study, my goal is to show proof-of-concept that parenterally administered gentamicin, an aminoglycoside, can generate a systemic level antiviral state. Such an approach has the added advantage of preventing secondary Gram-negative bacterial sepsis that often complicates the clinical outcome of viral infections. Critically, parenteral aminoglycosides do not enter the gastrointestinal tract to disrupt the gut microbiome and hence pose minimal risk for antibiotic resistant bacterial selection. The specific aims of my study thus are to: 1) Define ex vivo the effects of gentamicin on the innate immune transcriptional response in different subsets of peripheral blood mononuclear cells; 2) define the optimal dose of intramuscular (IM) gentamicin required to elicit an innate immune transcriptional response in whole blood of healthy adults and; 3) determine the efficacy of prophylactic intramuscular gentamicin in reducing live attenuated yellow fever virus (YF17D) infection in a placebo-controlled trial. If successful, this study would not only demonstrate the impact of gentamicin on systemic-level antiviral response, it would also pave the way to translate a pharmacological approach as an emergency response to viral outbreaks.
kw: aminoglycoside; gentamicin; innate immune system; antiviral; viral infections

title: Development and Validation of a Myopia-Specific Item Bank Administered using Computerized Adaptive Testing: The MyoCAT Study
abs: Myopia imposes a massive public health burden, with almost 85% of young adults having this disease. People with myopia not only suffer from impaired vision, but also experience side-effects from corrective therapies and are at increased risk of developing sight-threatening complications such as pathologic myopia (PM). Therefore, understanding the impact of un- or under-corrected myopia, PM and the effectiveness of myopia corrective therapies from the patient’s perspective is becoming increasingly important, with many governing authorities mandating the use patient-reported outcomes data to guide and improve clinical management, support medical decision-making, and inform policy decisions in healthcare measures and resource allocation. While several questionnaires exist to measure myopia-related quality of life (QoL), there are serious psychometric short-comings with these instruments with issues related to conceptualization, generalizability, validity and responsiveness. Moreover, current myopia-specific questionnaires are paper-pencil based, and are therefore static, inflexible and burdensome to administer and answer. Evidently, a culturally valid instrument that allows a rapid, accurate and comprehensive assessment of the impact of myopia and its associated complications and corrective therapies from the patient’s perspective in Asia is urgently required. Fortunately, these problems can be overcome by using item banking (IB) and computerized adaptive testing (CAT). An IB is a large pool of questions calibrated for difficulty based on participant response and the use of modern psychometric techniques. IBs are operationalized by CAT, which is ‘smart’ technology that adapts the items asked based on participants’ responses to previous items, enabling a precise and reliable assessment while minimizing measurement error and reducing test length. The main objective of this project is to develop, validate and evaluate the clinical applicability of a novel IB and CAT system for myopia (MyoCAT) that is able to comprehensively assess the QoL impact of un/under-correction, PM and the different corrective therapies, in a multi-ethnic Singaporean population.
kw: Myopia; Quality of Life measurement; patient-reported outcomes; questionnaire; psychometrics; impact

title: Guided transposition bisulfite sequencing as a novel approach to efficiently assess DNA methylation states in heterogeneous cell population.
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: The dysregulation of the epigenome is implicated in a myriad of disorders. DNA methylation (5mC) is the best studied epigenetic mechanism to date and has been found play major roles in transcriptional regulation, particularly in the silencing of repetitive elements, X-chromosome inactivation and genome imprinting during organismal development. Aberrant 5mC profiles has been described many forms of cancers and more recently in neurological disorders. Therefore, there is a great interest on the potential use of DNA methylation states as diagnostic biomarkers to discriminate between diseases states and gain insights into the underlying disease biology. For such studies, single cell based bisulfite sequencing (SCBS) is required because 5mC differences at potential biomarkers are concealed by bulk signals in conventional sequencing approaches. However, present SCBS are suboptimal and costly, prompting a need to develop new methodology. Herein, this proposal describes a droplet-based single cell bisulfite sequencing termed guided transposition bisulfite sequencing (GTBS). In GTBS, 5mC immunoprecipitation is immediately coupled to a Tn5 mediated transposition which simultaneously fragment genomic DNA and inserts sequencing adapter in a single droplet reaction. This method enriches for CG sites which reduces the required sequencing depth and thus cost savings, and libraries are immediately amplified with a set of universal primers which can reduce and prevent PCR amplification biases. I anticipate that GTBS may potentially overcome limitations of current SCBS, and can be applied to assess 5mC states in a wide variety of heterogeneous samples
kw: Sequencing, Epigenetics

title: Assessment of tricuspiD regurgitation with 4D flow cardioVAscular magNetic resonanCe for clinical dEcision-Making and trEatmeNT planning (ADVANCEMENT)
abs: Tricuspid regurgitation (TR) is the one of the most common types of valvular heart disease with estimated incidence 1.2% to 1.5% in the general population. TR is frequently associated with significant morbidity and mortality, and its surgical treatment is still the object of debate in terms of timing and surgical techniques. The new guidelines state that surgical intervention should be considered in patients with severe TR after left-sided valve surgery if signs of progressive right ventricular (RV) dilation or dysfunction are detected—even in asymptomatic patients. On the other hand, delaying surgery would result in irreversible RV damage, failure and poorer outcome. Previous studies suggest that systemic measurement of TR severity, accurate sizing of the tricuspid annulus (TA) and some degree of tricuspid leaflet tethering is essential in planning tricuspid annuloplasty and for implantation of new percutaneous tricuspid devices. Advances in medical imaging techniques have made it possible to study the mechanism of valvular regurgitation and treatment strategies at a patient-specific level. This proposed study will provide detailed information on the effects of TA, tricuspid leaflets and trabecular muscle on TR, as well as how they together with TR severity affect RV remodeling and dysfunction during follow up (with vs without TR treatment). The specific aims of this project are: 1) Quantification of TA dimension (TA surface area) and deformation (TA displacement and velocities), tricuspid valve leaflet length, trabecular muscle function (displacement and velocities) by radial cine cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) and feature tracking technique, and TR severity by 4D flow CMR; 2) Agreement of TV regurgitation severity grade by 4D flow CMR and echocardiography; 3) Association of TA dimension, leaflet length and trabecular muscle on TR and RV remodeling and dysfunction; 4) Identification of predictors of risk for RV remodeling and exercise intolerance during the 1-year follow up.
kw: Tricuspid regurgitation; 4D flow CMR; TEE; tricuspid valve repair/replace; tricuspid annulus dimension and deformation; radial CMR scan

title: Interferon beta modulation for therapeutic outcomes in disease management
abs: Previously in our lab, we have demonstrated G3BP1 as a positive regulator of IFN-β production, by bridging TBK1 and IRF3 interaction. USP10 is a known binding partner of G3BP1 and have an opposing regulatory role in the p53 pathway. Our preliminary data identified USP10 as a novel negative regulator of IFN-β production as USP10-/- MEFs exhibited 10 fold increase in the IFN-β production as compared to the wildtype MEFs upon poly(I:C) stimulation. Our biochemical data showed that this negative regulation required the deubiquitination of ifn-b transcription factor IRF3 by USP10. Scientifically, this is a novel finding since phosphorylation has been the hallmark of IRF3 activation. Our research proposes four main aims. First, dissect molecular mechanism in which USP10 down regulate IRF3, this includes identifying ubiquitin modified lysine residue on IRF3 that is targeted by USP10. Secondly, we aim to prove further that USP10 could downregulate IFN-β by exploring a viral infection model. We hypothesize that animal model lacking USP10 may exhibit an up-regulated IFN-β response and improved sufficient viral clearance. Thirdly, USP10-/- mice have a propensity to secrete high level of IFN-β production that would predispose USP10-/- to succumb to lupus or other type-I IFN-related autoimmune diseases. Therefore we will subject wild-type and USP10 knock-out mice to pristane-induced lupus, to observe whether USP10-/- develops more severe lupus phenotype. Finally, we aim to propose a natural small molecule called resveratrol (RES) as an immunomodulatory drug that can dampen the production of IFN-β production.
kw: Type-I Interferon, anti-viral signaling, autoimmunity and systemic lupus erythematosus

title: Management of Atypical Infections and Altered Immunity: Novel Diagnoses and Immune-targeted Therapy
abs: ‘Targeting the pathogen with antimicrobials’ has long been the central tenet in the practice of infectious diseases. The ‘host’ and appropriateness of the host response to infection is only now being better appreciated as the other vital arm in determining outcome. Our hypothesis is that susceptibility and response to atypical infections, namely Mycobacteria and invasive fungal diseases are determined by either immune dysregulation or latent host immune traits mediated genetically. Adjunctive therapy against identified immune targets in conjunction with conventional antimicrobials may further optimize outcomes. In patients with (a) severe / recurrent Mycobacteria infections (b) invasive fungal diseases (IFD), we aim to: [1] Investigate the role of immune dysregulation predisposing to such infections in patients with anti-cytokine auto-antibodies For the patients with above infections and detected to have auto-antibodies, we will perform immunophenotyping, assess the functional immune response of these patients to various ligands and pathogens and investigate the hypothesis if the underlying mechanism of this new condition may be attributed (i) regulatory B cell dysfunction (ii) immune anergy (iii) alternative autoantibodies through immunoprotein screening (iv) immunogenetics [2] Elucidate novel or latent immune modulating genetic traits conferring susceptibility to atypical infections in our yet-to-be-characterized Asian population In patients who do not have anti-cytokine autoantibodies, we will look for occult immune genetic defects using state-of-art whole exome or genome sequencing coupled with functional immune assays probing candidate variants/pathways of interest and validation through cloning/transfection methodologies. [3] Explore immunotherapeutic options targeting the identified immune defects, for treatment in conjunction with conventional antimicrobials Against the identified target immune dysfunction, we will explore usage of immunotherapeutic agents in conjunction with conventional antimicrobials for treatment. We will also investigate the use of checkpoint inhibitors anti-PD1 and anti-CTLA4 as adjuncts in treating opportunistic invasive fungal infections.
kw: opportunistic infections; immunodeficiency; auto-antibodies; whole exome sequencing; immunotherapy

title: Immunosequencing and Deep Profiling of T-Cells in Children with Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (IMPACT)
abs: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is the most common cancer in childhood. Treatment is fraught with life-threatening complications such as infections. A significant proportion of children with this aggressive cancer still succumb to relapsed leukemia, of which a large proportion remain unexplained. There is growing evidence in solid tumors and stem-cell transplantation that host T-cell immune response correlates with treatment outcomes. However, T-cell profiles in the context of contemporary regimens have not yet been systematically examined in ALL. This study aims to systematically and longitudinally examine the T-cell profile in paediatric patients with ALL during chemotherapy, and elucidate its role in outcome and toxicities. We hypothesize that T-cell populations and diversity changes dynamically during chemotherapy in response to alteration in leukemic burden and immunosuppressive effects of cytotoxic agents. This profile reflects immune surveillance against residual leukemia and infective agents, and immune-mediated allergies. This will be a large scale retrospective profiling study involving all patients <21 years of age who have completed treatment for ALL in 5 centres accross 3 countries (n=1000). Patients have banked bone marrow or peripheral blood samples taken at diagnosis and during the course of ALL therapy – diagnosis, induction, re-induction, maintenance and at end of treatment. Cell sorting will be performed to separate various T-cell populations, followed by quantitative analysis of subpopulations via flow cytometry. From each T-cell population at each time-point, genomic DNA will be extracted for high-throughput T-cell receptor (TCR) sequencing, from which TCR repertoire diversity and TCR clonality scores will be calculated. This data will be compared against the patients’ risk group, clinical profile, treatment response, and toxicities. Elucidating T-cell profiles allows us to understand the potential role of host immunity in both treatment and complications of childhood ALL, enabling us to study means of modulating these responses to improve survival and minimise toxicity.
kw: leukemia; lymphoblastic; children; immunosequencing; T-cell; receptor

title: Investigating the functional roles of human-specific liver metabolic regulators using a humanized mouse liver model to tackle liver metabolic disease
abs: The upsurge of the prevalence of metabolic liver diseases such as non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) over the past decades has raised a global public health alarm. Despite advances made in deciphering the molecular pathogenesis underlying NAFLD, treatment strategies remain limited. This is largely attributed to a lack of a representative animal model to recapitulate the key features of hepatocyte biology in human. Significant cross-species barrier has made it a difficult task to transfer findings from rodent studies to human. To address this issue, we made used of a humanized mouse model reconstituted with human hepatocytes to delineate the transcriptome profiles for human hepatocytes. Our preliminary data has demonstrated that transcriptome of human-origin hepatocytes in humanized mice resembles that from human liver and exhibits proper catabolic program changes upon fasting challenge, indicating that the humanized liver is metabolically functional. Interestingly, we identified a set of human-specific genes such as MOGAT3 and GBP1, which are significantly regulated during energy stress. We hypothesize that these human-specific genes in hepatocytes are novel regulators in liver metabolism. To test this, we will determine the functions of these genes by AAV-mediated gain- and loss- of function both in vitro and in vivo (Aim 1). Next, we will also examine the functional role of these genes in simple steatosis by performing the gain- and loss-of-function for the candidates in response to diet induced fatty liver (Aim 2). This work aims to establish the functions of a set of novel human-specific regulators in liver metabolism under different pathophysiological conditions by harnessing the humanized liver mouse model. We strongly believe that in long term, this line of research will reveal new mechanistic insights for many aspects of liver metabolism in human with the ultimate aim of providing novel therapeutic targets for NAFLD and other metabolic liver diseases.
kw: Liver metabolism, humanized liver mouse, type 2 diabetes, obesity

title: Targeting chondroitin sulphate synthase I for prevention and treatment of pathological vascular remodelling
abs: A major pathology underlying cardiovascular disease (CVD) is arterial vasculopathy, including vascular fibrosis, arterial stiffening and atherosclerotic plaque formation. The extracellular matrix (ECM) plays a significant role in both arterial stiffening and plaque formation. A polysaccharide component of ECM, chondroitin sulfate (CS), accumulates in the myocardium and arterial walls in human end-stage cardiomyopathy. CS accumulation is found to be associated with coronary artery hyperplasia in a rare condition of systemic CS degradation inefficiency. We recently made an unexpected finding that loss of one of the CS synthase genes, Chsy1, abolished all signs of myocardial arterial remodeling in a mouse model of arterial fibrosis. Human individuals with CHSY1 exhibit no major abnormalities, suggesting low safety risk in targeting the gene. We therefore hypothesize that inhibition of Chsy1 expression prevents, or even reverses the progression of arterial hyperplasia and atherosclerotic plaque formation. We propose in this application to tested the efficacy of Chsy1 knockdown in reducing arterial fibrosis and myocardial tissue perfusion in a mouse model, and the effect of Chsy1 knockdown in preventing/reverting plaque formation in the Ldlr-/- mouse model of atherosclerosis. Successful development of the project could open up a new direction of novel treatment options for preventing/reversing CVDs caused by arterial pathology.
kw: coronary artery, fibrosis, stiffening, atherosclerosis, smooth muscle cells, extracellular matrix, chondroitin sulfate

title: Combinatorial drug screening for novel appetite and metabolic pathway discovery
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Appetite dysfunction underlies obesity, eating disorders and metabolic disease, yet few pharmacological treatments are available. My colleagues and I have recently shown that the larval zebrafish is an ideal vertebrate model not only for the study of appetite-control brain circuits, but also for high-throughput screening of factors that regulate both appetite and metabolic pathways, which can be reliably translated to mammals. Here I propose a novel screening platform for the discovery of of appetite-modulating compounds and pathways in zebrafish, that will improve upon conventional phenotypic screening methods in two ways: 1) Adopt a machine learning-based combinatorial screening approach to identify synergistic or antagonistic effects of drugs on appetite; 2) Use supervised machine learning for detailed behavioral validation of drug effects on food-seeking, consumption and other locomotor behaviors. These approaches combined should not only lead to the discovery of potentially translatable drugs and drug combinations, but also to a more detailed understanding of their biological pathways than currently possible with a conventional drug screen. Further, the establishment of a fine-tuned combinatorial strategy and algorithm will be valuable in numerous phenotypic screening contexts beyond this study.
kw: Drug screening, Appetite, Obesity, Metabolic Disease, Zebrafish, Machine Learning

title: Diet and lifestyle intervention strategies to treat β-cell dysfunction and insulin resistance in Asian Indians
inst: IHDP - Institute for Human Development and Potential
abs: Compared to other races, Asian Indians have a greater risk of developing type 2 diabetes (T2D), increased insulin resistance(IR) and more rapid decline in β-cell function, highlighting the urgency and importance of early intervention strategies for improving insulin sensitivity and preserving/improving β-cell function to prevent T2D and mitigate against the increased vascular disease risk. Preliminary findings show a reduction in glycemic load selectively depletes visceral and ectopic lipid and improves insulin sensitivity and β-cell function in non-diabetic adults. The proposed research will investigate if the phenotypic features increasing T2D risk in individuals of Indian ancestry (IR and impaired β-cell function) can be favorably modified by a low glycaemic (LG) intervention, and if the increased IR is attributable to genetic factors regulating adipocyte differentiation and function. These research objectives will be achieved through a 24-week randomised controlled trial comparing isocaloric LG versus control diets in Indians with prediabetes. Compared to individuals in the control group, those on the LG diet are expected to have greater ectopic (pancreas, liver, visceral and intramyocellular) fat depletion assessed with MRI/MRS, and improvements in first phase insulin secretion and insulin sensitivity assessed with the C-peptide model and oral minimal model, respectively during an OGTT. Reductions in hepatic and pancreatic lipids will be associated with improvements in first-phase β-cell response. Individuals with a greater number of risk alleles from a 53-SNP IR genetic score will have lower insulin sensitivity and leg fat, supporting the notion that impaired adipocyte differentiation leading to limited peripheral adipose expansion capacity is an important etiological factor underpinning IR cardiometabolic disease in Indians. The results will broaden the evidence base for effective prevention strategies in this high risk population by investigating the effect of the proposed diet intervention on underlying physiological and molecular mechanisms implicated in the pathophysiology of T2D in Indians.
kw: Diet, β-cell function, insulin resistance, Asian Indians

title: Functional role of increased coupling between task-negative and task-positive brain networks in cognitively normal older adults
abs: Managing cognitive decline in normative and pathological ageing is a worldwide challenge. Cognitive control diminishes considerably in ageing, but its neural correlates remain to be elucidated. In the ageing brain, there is a significant increase in functional coupling between the default mode network (DMN) and task-positive networks (TPN), especially the executive control network. Few studies have attempted to make a direct association between these two major features in neurocognitive ageing. To this end, we propose to unravel their potential link by examining the performance of healthy young (aged 22-30) and older adults (aged 55-75) in two cognitive tasks that tax cognitive control using magnetic resonance imaging. If identified, this link could serve as a 'signature' for cognitive training and monitoring. Furthermore, we will investigate if white matter microstructure moderates the degree of network coupling, leading to individual differences in cognitive control. Identification of this association will provide further insights regarding risk factors such as cerebrovascular health. First, we will examine age-related changes in performance and brain networks when young and old participants perform a fade-out procedure, which is a modified task-switching paradigm and sensitive to group differences in cognitive control. We aim to establish the brain-cognition association between DMN-TPN coupling and response time disadvantage in older adults. We will then extend this investigation to a timing paradigm, in which older adults were shown to be influenced by explicit and implicit temporal information differently than young adults. We aim to establish an association between DMN-TPN coupling and use of temporal information, as well as timing ability per se, a relatively understudied aspect in neurocognitive ageing. Second, we will associate white matter microstructure properties with network coupling that modulates task performance. Our results will enrich ageing theories, and provide insights into the critical elements for effective intervention and training.
kw: Healthy ageing; magnetic resonance imaging; inter-network functional connectivity; brain-cognition association; cognitive control

title: Uncovering the Role of Nuclear Import Protein KPNA1 in Inflammasome Regulation and Disease
abs: The inflammasome is an essential arm of the innate immune system in host defence against pathogens. It is a multi-protein complex that induces inflammatory cell death in response to specific pathogenic molecular patterns and physiological stresses. As potent as its activity in pathogen clearance, its dysfunction causes auto-inflammatory diseases and cancers. In our search for novel inflammasome regulators to develop new therapeutic approaches, we identified the nuclear import protein, KPNA1. I found that KPNA1 binds to the inflammasome sensor NLRP1 and mediates inflammasome-induced cell death. I further demonstrated that the expression of a de novo KPNA1 mutant variant alone is sufficient to aberrantly trigger inflammasome activity and account for the pathology of a patient with a skin tumour condition called multiple keratoacanthoma centrifugum marginatum (KCM). Based on these findings, and the established role of KPNA1 in shuttling proteins into the nucleus, I hypothesize that changes in the localization and protein interactions of KPNA1 alter its regulation of inflammasome activity. To test this, I will delineate the inflammasome regulatory mechanism of KPNA1 in healthy, inflammatory and diseased states by 1) mapping the changes in nuclear/cytoplasmic localization of KPNA1 and in turn NLRP1; 2) elucidating the domains of KPNA1 that are critical to its inflammasome regulatory function; and 3) identifying changes in binding partners and cargo proteins of KPNA1. These findings will uncover not only the molecular underpinnings of KPNA1’s role in inflammasome regulation, but also new avenues for the treatment of inflammasome-associated disorders and cancers.
kw: Inflammasome; NLRP1; nuclear import; KPNA1; inflammation; cancer

title: Development of Hybrid Phase Change Materials (PCMs) and PCM-Integration Technology for Indoor Passive-Cooling
inst: IMRE - Institute of Materials Research and Engineering
abs: Many different kinds of PCMs including organic, inorganic and eutectic materials can be incorporated into buildings, and each class of PCMs have its own pros and cons. The first objective is to identify and then select suitable PCMs (base PCM) that possess an appropriate phase-transition temperature range, specific latent capacity and thermal conductivity, and integrate them into building materials, which target for new and existing buildings. The suitability of the PCM would also include its insulation capabilities in the fluid phase (thermal conductivity studies in Phase 1), as it will determine how efficient a PCM is throughout its temperature cycle. For each PCM material, we will be measuring the thermal conductivity of them at both solid and liquid phases. If the thermal conductivity for the liquid phase is smaller than the solid phase, the liquid phase can also perform as a better insulator. During the incorporation of PCMs into building materials, two main issues have to be addressed: the safety of the building structure and the containment of PCM. While incorporating PCMs into the buildings, it must ensure that the building material and structural integrity still conform to the safety standards (eg. compression strength, elasticity, bending tensile strength, fire resistant etc). Equally importantly, the PCMs added have to be contained such that there are no odours, leakage of the toxic substance in the long run. Thus our second objective would be: 1) Study all the side-effects (toxicity, odour, leakage, chemical and thermal resistance, flammability, etc.) which can potentially hinder PCM applications in buildings. 2) Formulate, design and fabricate PCMs or PCM-incorporated structures so that the detrimental side-effects could be eliminated or mitigated to an acceptable level. 3) Investigate PCM-based building envelope structures from the perspective of engineering. All in all the project aims to introduce a PCM-based/integrated system that insulates buildings from solar heat and does not interfere with the safety aspect of the buildings. It aims to improve indoor thermal comfort and reduce energy consumption due to cooling needs. Moreover, it will neither produce harmful effects nor discomfort to residents.
kw: Phase Change Materials

title: Rigorous AI using Game Theory and Statistics
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: The broad objective of the proposed research is to address the need of satisfactory understanding of Artificial Intelligence by building empirically relevant theoretical foundations of deep learning. The effort of such understanding involves not only optimization, computer science and statistics communities but also researchers from areas such as physics, neuroscience, healthcare etc. The last five years we have witnessed the entering of AI (one main reason of its recent success is deep learning) in our daily lives, some aspects of which are sensitive (like autonomous driving, healthcare), and thus there is a need to develop computationally efficient and robust algorithms with theoretical (provable) guarantees (e.g., self-driving cars trained so that provably they will not misclassify objects, i.e., the used classification algorithms will not be based mainly on ”heuristics”). Our goal is to develop computationally efficient, robust, (a) optimization and (b) statistical methods with provable guarantees for the purpose of training deep models and for regression models respectively. (a) Training neural networks typically boils down to the task of optimizing an objective function (with strange landscape) and our understanding about the behavior of current optimization methods is very limited without enough theoretical guarantees. Nevertheless, techniques from online learning algorithms, that mainly appear in Game Theory for predicting the behavior of rational players in complex games (systems), have been recently used to improve our understanding of optimizing objective functions with difficult landscapes. We will first exploit these recent developments on the intersection of Game Theory and Online Optimization. (b) Typical regression models (e.g., linear, logistic etc) assume that the response variables are independent, but share the same linear relationship to their corresponding vectors of covariates. However, examples abound in financial and meteorological applications where correlations naturally arise in social networks through peer effects. We would like to develop new tools/methods in statistics to analyze regression models with correlated or even censored/truncated observations (important question that has many applications in Econometrics as well). Last but not least, while our research proposal mainly focuses on the theoretical foundations of AI, we will would like to apply our findings to real world data, especially for estimating models that combine peer and individual effects to predict behaviour. We firmly believe that a combination of Game Theory and Statistics is the key to get deep understanding and build the theoretical foundations of deep learning and AI.
kw: Deep Learning; Gradient Descent; Regression; Optimization; Online Learning; Game Theory

title: Development and verification of prototype real-time and online monitoring system for metal ions in water systems by ions-imprinted polymers
abs: Metals are present everywhere in living species, water bodies, and soil. Some metals, e.g. iron, copper, zinc, are essential for innumerable biological processes and enzymatic reactions that occur in human body. But, presence of some of them, like cadmium, lead, mercury etc., in the environment can cause health risks and hazards. Currently used techniques for metal analysis are expensive and lab-based while requiring experienced analysts for performing the analysis. Consequently, there is a huge demand for developing rapid, real-time, online, economical, and highly sensitive techniques for analysis of metals in the global markets. In Singapore, PUB has guidelines on metal ions in drinking water, and NEA has regulations on metal ions in trade effluent discharged to the public sewers. In the past 4 years, we worked on a project (1301-IRIS-21) entitled “Water Safety Monitoring and Risk Assessment: Real-time Sensors for Threat Agents Detection” with NRF funding administered by PUB, and have developed 4 patented molecularly imprinted polymer (MIP) technologies to prepare sensors for various analytes, including metal ions, pesticides, chemical threat agents, biotoxins, proteins, cholesterol, etc. In this proposal, we aim to further translate the ions-imprinted polymer (IIP) technology into commercialization. The objectives include: 1. To automate the prototype sensor platform based on quartz crystal microbalance (QCM) developed from our previous project; 2. To validate the conditions for IIP production and commercialization, including stability, calibration, repeatability, reproducibility, and storage conditions; 3. To debug software for automated sample handling, data collection and data processing; 4. To conduct operational testing of standalone real-time sensing devices and online sensing devices in simulated operation environments; 5. To test prototype products in relevant on-site and real-time operational environment; and 6. To set up pilot scale manufacturing and to commercialize both the sensor platform and sensor devices.
kw: real-time; online monitoring; metal ions: ions-imprinted polymers

title: Design and Evaluation of Novel Bioretention Systems for Applications in the Tropics
abs: The continued infrastructure development of cities in recent decades with addition of impervious surfaces, caused by urbanization, is responsible for multiple issues affecting the sustainability of urban water resources. For example, in urban areas with a wide range of buildings and roads, rainwater infiltration decreases. This results in increased runoff rates and volumes, reduced infiltration, and baseflow to urban streams. The generation of pollutants by urban land surfaces and human activities degrades water quality. In general, this degradation can be attributed to increased mobilization and transport of pollutants contained in surface runoff. Urban stormwater includes numerous pollutants such as suspended solids, nutrients, organic compounds, pathogenic bacteria, heavy metals, debris, and floatable materials. Mitigating the consequences of urbanization on urban stormwater hydrology and quality is the key to addressing environmental sustainability-related issues. This has led to the development and adoption of stormwater best management practices (BMPs) or low-impact development (LID) practices to treat storm flows from urban areas. In Singapore, these best practices are promoted under the ABC (Active, Beautiful and Clean) Waters program, and a key practice is bioretention”, i.e. retention and cleansing of stormwater. Bioretention systems are widely used to capture stormwater runoff from external impervious catchments to reduce runoff volume, peak flow rates and pollutant loads (Davis et al., 2009). Systematic field studies have been carried out in various climatic conditions around the world to evaluate the effectiveness of bioretention systems in enhancing management of runoff and in improving surface water quality. However, the performance of bioretention systems in the tropics is poorly understood due to lack of fundamental investigations and field research studies. A recent field study conducted by Wang et al (2017) monitored 96 storms in the first bioretention basin in Singapore. This study analyzed flow measurements during 80 events and 15 water quality parameters (including nitrogen and phosphorus species, total suspended solids, and chemical oxygen demand) during 6 events. The mean removal rates were 25%, 46%, and 53% for total nitrogen, total phosphorus, and total suspended solids, respectively. Specifically, low pollutant removal efficiency was observed during high rainfall-depth events, which was attributed to a lack of storage capacity and resulting high overflow. In many counties, garden potting media such as mulch are generally employed as filter media in bioretention systems. During high storm events, the filter media may not perform satisfactorily, which often results in flash flood and poor drainage. In addition, filter media may not be effective in terms of affinity towards various organic and inorganic pollutants in stormwater runoff, and thus often results in mediocre removal efficiency. title: Effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of noninvasive fractional flow reserve for physiological assessment in suspected coronary artery disease (ECONOMY)
abs: Chest pain due to coronary artery disease (CAD) is a main driver of healthcare costs, including invasive coronary angiography (ICA) for diagnosis and revascularization. ICA, guided by invasive fractional flow reserve (FFR) assessment of coronary physiology improves clinical outcomes. FFR measurement requires insertion of a pressure wire through the coronary stenosis invasively. Non-invasive FFR - FFRCT, pioneered by Heartflow« company - using full computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulation of anatomic models derived from coronary computed tomographic angiography (CCTA) approximates invasive FFR values, and significantly improves diagnostic accuracy when added to anatomical information provided by CCTA alone. We developed a rapid simplified method to determine non-invasive FFR using reduced-order CFD and novel steady-state assumptions - FFRb - that compares favourably with full-CFD FFRCT in preliminary studies involving CAD patients. There is need to study the impact of implementing FFRb in a real-world setting for decision-making in suspected CAD, especially in Asia, which does not have access to expensive commercial Heartflow« FFRCT. We shall study the clinical effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of FFRb when added to CCTA in the management of patients with suspected CAD. Specific Aim 1: To compare the diagnostic accuracy, clinical effectiveness and safety outcomes, and quality of life of using novel FFRb on top of CCTA for diagnosis and treatment planning of suspected coronary artery disease (CAD) subjects, versus standard of care (CCTA) in Singapore;. Specific Aim 2: To compare the agreement of test results obtained from novel reduced order CFD-derived non-invasive FFRb and full CFD-derived FFRCT technique (that is similar to Heartflow«); andSpecific Aim 3: To measure health care resource utilization and assess cost-effectiveness of adopting FFRb or FFRCT on top of CCTA to support decision making in managing patients with suspected CAD. This new non-invasive method, FFRb, will help reduce the need for ICA in patients with suspected CAD.

title: Predicting Survival in End Stage Organ Disease: Developing and Validating Prognostic Models
abs: With population growth and global aging, death secondary to chronic diseases such as kidney, cardiac and pulmonary failure is rising. Despite the significant contribution to worldwide mortality from non-cancer illnesses, patients dying with end stage organ diseases do not commonly receive palliative care although evidence shows that their needs are comparable with those dying from cancer. There is differential access to palliative care in non- cancer advanced illness, a significant barrier being the difficulty in prognostication. It is arguably more challenging to prognosticate in end stage organ diseases where the pattern of decline is characterized by “entry-re-entry” death trajectories characterized by acute exacerbations, hospitalizations, and stabilization in the midst of steady decline. Referral to palliative care is all the more difficult compared with cancer in the midst of such clinical uncertainty, particularly in the context of current available technology and treatment. The consequence of lack of accurate prognostication is patients being referred too late in their illness trajectory, and for many, not at all. Simple, well validated prognostic models with easily accessible predictive variables are urgently needed to objectively identify patients and their caregivers who would benefit from an interdisciplinary collaboration with palliative care. The primary aim of this study is to develop and validate prognostic models in end stage renal, cardiac and pulmonary disease to identify patients with a life expectancy of less than 1 year. Predictive variables identified a priori through a scoping literature review will be studied in tertiary care institutions through medical chart review, and multivariate models will be developed and internally validated. The models will subsequently be externally validated on another cohort of patients bearing similar clinical characteristics. The development and validation of these models will follow guidelines developed by the TRIPOD (Transparent Reporting of a multivariable prediction model for Individual Prognosis or Diagnosis) statement.
kw: End Stage Organ Disease; Development; Validation; Prognostic Models

title: Demonstration of cost-effective PV Recycling Solutions
abs: Crystalline silicon photovoltaic (PV) modules have an expected lifetime of 20-25 years, and they are backed by a warranty from the manufacturer in most cases. However, not all modules last that long. Some will be damaged during production, transportation, handling or installation, and some will even stop functioning after a while. Hence, there will be a massive market for the reclaim of PV modules. Other than that, there is another noticeable market which is usually overlooked by the recyclers, and that is the market for the factory-reject modules. Due to the exponential growth of the PV industry over the past 30 years, and the long lifetime of PV modules in the field, we are currently facing a somewhat strange situation whereby the number of factory-reject modules (which account for approximately 1% of today’s production) is far greater (approximately 50 times more) than the number of actual end-of-life modules that are currently available. The amount of discarded PV modules in need of reclaim has already reached a significant volume of several thousand metric tonnes per year. The European industry association PV Cycle has collected more than 15,000 metric tonnes of end-of-life modules in 2016, and this represents only 0.06% of all the PV modules installed in 2016. Therefore, over the next 5-15 years, we can expect a similar growth rate of the end-of-life modules as we saw for PV installations from 2001 to 2016. By the end of 2011, take-back and recycling of PV modules was made mandatory by the European Union. Hence, we foresee similar actions from the other leading PV regions, such as Asia and North America. Recently, it was reported that the first solar panel recycling plant opened in Europe and achieved recycling rate of 95% for silicon based PV modules. However, they only reclaimed the pure glass cullets and aluminium frames, and left the most valuable materials in the form of a combination of EVA laminate, silicon-based semiconductors and metals, which is not able to be reused directly. It is necessary to develop a new, more sophisticated and sustainable recycling process. During the preliminary study, the batch pilot scale recycling process has been developed by the team at the Advanced Materials Technology Centre, Singapore Polytechnic (SP-AMTC), and trial runs of recycling over 10 pieces of PV modules have been performed, in order to determine the feasibility of separating the various constituent module materials using mechanical, thermal and chemical means. The results of these batch pilot-scale experiments were fed into the calculation of the cost of reclaiming the various module materials. Over 90% of the materials were successfully reclaimed from the PV modules and could be reused for the fabrication of new PV modules. These materials include the silicon wafers, silver, copper, aluminium, glass, and back sheet. title: On-site Pilot Trial Using Anaerobic Digestion of Food Waste for Energy and Resource Recovery at East Coast Lagoon Food Village (ECLFV)
abs: Food waste is a burgeoning issue in Singapore, with an ever-increasing amount of it being produced year on year, but with persistently low recycling rates. The current food waste management system, where food waste is incinerated, results in ash being sent to the Semakau Landfill. The current model is not an optimal one as the burning efficiency of wet food waste is poor and the Semakau Landfill will eventually run out of space. The on-site food waste treatment pilot at East Coast Lagoon Food Village (ECLFV) aims to reduce waste being incinerated. This is to be achieved by encouraging food waste reduction, sorting, and recycling into resources such as electricity and fertiliser. Waste generated from ECLFV can be sorted into organic and inorganic fractions. The organic fractions which are typically food waste, can be treated via anaerobic digestion, with multi-faceted benefits such as reducing the amount of waste transported to the incineration plants, recovering energy in the form of biogas and the production of a nutrient-rich digestate which can be converted for use as fertiliser for cultivating plants. The remaining inorganic fraction will then be burnt at incineration plants. The on-site food waste treatment pilot study at ECLFV serves as an initial point to demonstrate a new sustainable model for food waste management. A multi-disciplinary approach is required in order to realise the full potential of the environmental and economic benefits. In this project, three parallel tasks will be undertaken simultaneously, in order to tackle the issue of food waste by 1) treating food waste using onsite anaerobic digestion for the generation of electricity and fertiliser, 2) educating and influencing behavioural change on the separation of food waste by the stall holders and cleaners, as well as the return of trays and separation of food waste by diners, and 3) conducting life cycle and cost benefit analyses to determine the environmental impacts and economic viability. The successful implementation of the above objectives would result in ECLFV being a model for the rest of Singapore to learn from and emulate in order to achieve the vision of a Zero Waste Nation.

title: Efficient Modeling and Learning for Video Understanding
abs: Video is the next frontier to be conquered in artificial visual intelligence. Automatic interpretation of video reflects the ability for intelligent systems to visually perceive and understand the world over time. There are now unprecedented amounts of video data coming from CCTV, internet video platforms and robotics, creating an urgent need for efficient and intelligent video understanding algorithms. Yet currently, almost all computer vision algorithms treat video simply as a collection of image frames. State- of-the-art methods often directly and naively apply models designed for images on a frame-wise basis. This adds complexity to the problem with little gain in performance. As such, progress in video understanding has been incremental and we’ve yet to see the same transformative impact of deep learning as in image understanding. This project aims to rethink and redefine the way video is being represented, modeled, and proposes new methods of learning for video understanding by • analyzing and developing novel efficient multi-scale representations and models for spatio-temporal data, • exploring methods for learning from large-scale video collections using guidance from auxiliary signals and multimodal data, • and advancing the interpretation of physical, semantic and human information from video data to learn high-level common sense knowledge for intelligent systems. Even though this project focuses on fundamental research, the results will serve as the basis for technological advances in many high-impact applications which will change our everyday lives. Examples include autonomous vehicles, home assistance robots, improved surveillance, content-based video indexing and retrieval, and other intelligent visual systems.
kw: computer vision, machine learning, video understanding,

title: Unlocking the secrets of microbially influenced corrosion:  From detection to control mechanisms
abs: Increasingly, the Oil and Gas industry, as well as other marine dependent industries, are exploring the deep sea for resources as well as deploying critical infrastructure. Oil rigs, telecommunication cables and other metallic infrastructures in the marine environment are subject to corrosion, in which microbially influenced corrosion (MIC) constitutes a key, and poorly understood, aspect. Further, MIC under conditions relevant to deep-sea infrastructure (e.g., high hydrostatic pressure and low temperature) is poorly understood, due to a knowledge gap in high pressure microbiology and difficulty of sampling these poorly accessible environments. Using novel high hydrostaticpressure (HHP) bioreactor systems, coupled with the ability to measure bioelectrochemistry and MIC s under HHP conditions, we will study the mechanisms by which pressure adapted microorganisms drive the corrosion process and the actual MIC rates for metals relevant to deep-sea infrastructure. This project will reveal new insights into the metabolic and genetic capacities of deep sea microbial communities, how they utilize metals for growth and ultimately will develop predictive models for MIC and overall corrosion at HHP conditions. This knowledge will be vital for Industries operating in marine and deep sea environments to manage critical and sensitive infrastructure and has the potential to develop tools for monitoring MIC in the deep sea.

title: Recovery and microbial synthesis of high-value aquaculture feed additives from food-processing wastewater
abs: By 2050 the World’s population is expected to reach 9 billion, which combined with improving diets will increase demand for animal protein; hence, crop production will have to increase by 60% to feed livestock and aquaculture. This highlights the need for a fundamental reorientation of the food supply chain towards greater resource efficiency. Developing more sustainable animal feed sources, and advanced resource recycling technologies, is key to decoupling economic growth from the overuse of natural resources, ensuring food security and mitigating the environmental impact of waste streams. Our goal is to develop an integrated sustainability approach in the food industry through advanced resource recycling of food-processing wastewaters to produce high-quality aquaculture feed. This multidisciplinary proposal brings together industrial knowhow and research expertise in the fields of environmental biotechnology, biochemical engineering, biosynthesis, food quality and animal nutrition in Singapore. In the first stage, wastewaters from key breweries, soy sauce and soy milk industries in Singapore will be screened. Their potential will be evaluated by analysing their chemical and microbial properties, and the most valuable stream selected for advanced resource recovery. This will entail a stepwise approach: 1) initial separation of valuable products; 2) production of feed-grade microbial products from the wastewater, 3) formulation of high-value feed additives; and, 4) aquaculture trials using these products and/or additives. Additionally, the absence of pathogens, antimicrobial resistance genes, and toxins will be assessed to ensure the health of the animals, and the resulting effluent treated to recycle energy and water. The sustainability and economic feasibility of the integrated process will be evaluated by comparing it with conventional treatment and feed production, using life cycle analysis and life cycle cost. The methodology developed in this study offers a roadmap toward sustainable resource management, and a case study for other food processing industries and animal feed producers.
kw: Integrated resource recovery; bio-waste recycling; microbiome biosynthesis; feed product; high-quality aquaculture feed; nutritional quality assessment

title: An Integrative Cardiac Rehabilitation Employing Smartphone Technology (i-CREST) for patients with post-myocardial infarction: A randomized controlled trial
abs: Aims and Hypotheses: This study aims to develop and evaluate an integrated home-based mHealth cardiac rehabilitation programme (CRP), entitled Integrative Cardiac Rehabilitation Employing Smartphone Technology (i-CREST), on uptake, adherence, and completion rates of the CRP, cardiac self-efficacy, exercise capacity, health-related quality of life (HRQoL), anxiety and depressive symptoms, and cardiac risk factors for patients with post-myocardial infarction (post-MI). It is hypothesised that compared with participants allocated in a traditional centre-based CRP (TCRP) group, participants in the i-CREST group will: 1. Have significantly higher uptake, adherence and completion rates of the CR programme; 2. Have higher levels of cardiac self-efficacy; 3. Demonstrate equivalent exercise capacity (i.e. six-minute walking test), HRQoL, anxiety and depression symptoms and cardiac risk factors; and 4. Have significantly lower cost to patients and hospitals. Methodology and Approach: There are two phases to the proposed study: (a) development and field testing of the i-CREST system and (b) evaluation of the effectiveness of the i-CREST via a randomized controlled trial. The i-CREST is designed as a 6-week home-based phase II CR programme supported by a multi-disciplinary cardiac rehabilitation team through the use of various technologies. A single-blinded randomised controlled trial using between groups repeated measures will be adopted. A convenience sample of 124 post-MI patients will be recruited from National University Hospital. They will be randomly assigned to the i-CREST group or TCRP group. Outcomes will be assessed at baseline, 6 weeks immediately after the intervention, and at 3 and 6 months from the baseline. At the end of the programme, a process evaluation will be conducted to assess the acceptability, compatibility, complexity and observability of the i-CREST based on participants’ verbal feedbacks. All quantitative data will be analysed using SPSS 25.0, and content analysis will be used for qualitative datasets.
kw: cardiac rehabilitation, post myocardial infarction, mobile health, home-based

title: Preventing cardiovascular disease by uncoupling nuclear-cytoskeletal interactions
abs: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) accounted for 30.7% of deaths in Singapore in 2017. Although age is a major contributory factor to CVD, there is increasing evidence that the onset of CVD occurs earlier, and in a more severe form in Singapore. To address these issues, we study the premature ageing disease, Hutchinson-Gilford Progeria (HGPS) as a reproducible model of CVD. HGPS is caused by the mutant LaminA protein -Progerin and children with HGPS die in their mid-teens from CVD. We will 1) produce microfluidic 3-D organ-on-a-chip reconstructions of human vasculature using HGPS (and isogenic controls) iPS stem cell derived vascular smooth muscle and endothelial cells that are assembled into a vascular system. This will function to model human atherosclerosis and CVD in vitro. 2) We identified 2 proteins of relevance to CVD, SUN1 and CISD2. SUN1’s expression is increased by Progerin whereas CISD2 preferentially binds to Progerin, as mice deficient in CISD2 develop diabetes and age prematurely. 3) We will determine whether disrupting CISD2 leads to vascular degeneration, as we hypothesize that Progerin sequesters CISD2 from the ER, so it can no longer regulate ER-mitochondrial Ca2+homeostasis. As a potential therapeutic, we will increase CSID2 levels to determine if this ameliorates atherosclerosis in our microfluidic model. A second therapeutic avenue is that functional disruption of SUN1 prevents lamin induced cardiomyopathy and significantly extends longevity of HGPS mice. We will determine if disrupting SUN1 in the vasculature prevents CVD. This will be performed in our mouse model of HGPS and in our microfluidic system. 4) We will determine if pre-laminA accumulation, which may cause age related vascular degeneration, similar to Progerin, is both a biomarker and contributory factor to vascular ageing. Overall our goal is to identify pathways that both suppress HGPS and be effective to treating CVD in the wider population
kw: Cardiovascular disease; progeria; ageing; lamins; vasculature, CISD2, Sun1

title: Precision oncology approach to identification and expansion of tumor-targeting cytotoxic T-lymphocytes in head and neck squamous cell cancer
abs: Given the limited efficacy of targeted therapy, there is tremendous interest in the role of immunotherapy in treating patients with head and neck squamous-cell carcinoma(HNSCC). Despite the presence of tumor-infiltrating T-cells(TILs), most tumors evade the immune system, suggesting these are dysfunctional. Drugs inhibiting immune-checkpoint receptors(ICB) are intended to reverse this, but are effective in less than 20% of patients. Conventional therapy further depletes effective cytotoxic T-cell(CTL) populations, which is evident in trials where neo-adjuvant ICB therapy appears to be more effective than the adjuvant setting. Undoubtedly, there is a need to reconfigure treatment strategies such that ICBs are instituted when effective CTL-populations are more prevalent. Therefore, we hypothesize that untreated tumors contain the most effective source of CTLs capable of targeting more heterogenous populations of cancer cells. We will utilize a number of unbiased and marker-based strategies to identify tumor-targeting T-cells in untreated primary/metastatic lymph-nodes, and matched tumor recurrences using single-cell analysis and high-dimensional flow cytometry. Functional efficacy of specific subpopulations will be tested by expanding these in TIL-cultures, and tested in cytotoxicity assays against matched, patient-derived tumor culture. Markers for tumor-targeting CTLs will also be validated in independent cohorts of treatment-naïve and ICB-treated tumors. Our secondary hypothesis posits that exhaustion status vary between(requiring individualization), and within patients(primary versus metastatic versus recurrent tumors), hence require different strategies to re-invigorate CTL-based cytotoxicity. To address this, we will compare drivers of exhaustion across tumors to identify differences amenable to specific ICB-therapy. Alternatively, we will set up medium-throughput screens to identify drugs that enhance CTL-based killing of matched tumor-cells, to uncover actionable differences between T-cell reactivation in these states. The eventual aim is to identify the best source and CTL sub-population with the ability to maximize tumor kill, either through immunomodulation with drugs, or to effect cellular therapy with expanded, bio-banked CTL populations.
kw: Immuno-oncology; CTL; cytotoxicity assay; Immunotherapy; CD8; T-cell receptor

title: Re-invigorating cytolytic tissue resident memory T cells (cTRM T cells) for treating recurrent/relapsed nasopharyngeal cancer
abs: Epstein Barr Virus (EBV) driven nasopharyngeal cancer (NPC) is highly endemic in Southern China, Southeast Asia and Singapore. Up to 80 new cases per 100,000 persons are reported annually in these regions. Despite a relatively good clinical outcome (five-year overall survival of 75-80%), a significant number (~20%) of NPC develops loco-regional failure or distant relapse following definitive treatment. Therefore, newer and more effective treatment options are needed to manage NPCs with recurrences/relapses. Our preliminary study showed that when tumour infiltrating lymphocytic (TIL) T cells were primed with a pool of EBV peptides, they increased tumour specificity and incrementally killed EBV-positive NPC cells by nearly three-fold. We have further identified a specific clone of cytolytic CD8+CD69+CD103+ T cells, termed cytolytic tissue resident memory T cells (cTRM T cells), in approximately 50-60% of our expanded TIL T cell populations. Based on these findings, we hypothesize that our expanded EBV primed cTRM T cells are novel, cellular therapy candidates that can be used either alone or in combination with other immunotherapies, such PD1 monoclonal antibody, to increase treatment efficacy in recurrent/relapsed NPC cases. We will test our hypothesis with the following specific aims: 1) Compare the cytotoxicity levels and functional immune activity of EBV primed cTRM T cells versus EBV primed peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) derived cytolytic T cells (CTLS) against NPC in vitro. 2) Compare the treatment effect between EBV primed cTRM T cells and EBV primed CTLS against NPC in vivo using patient derived xenograft (PDX) models; and 3) Determine if combination of EBV primed cTRM T cells with programmed cell death protein (PD1) monoclonal antibody enhances the anti-NPC efficacy using humanized NPC PDX models. Results from this study will establish the fundamental role for cTRM T cells and their potential therapeutic utility to treat NPCs with recurrence/relapse.
kw: T cell therapy, Nasopharyngeal cancer, cell therapy,

title: Patients with gout - their journeys from symptoms to management: implications for health care in Singapore
abs: Gout is a common form of arthritis, more prevalent in older populations. Its incidence is rising, with a significant burden for patients in terms of increased morbidity and mortality, and for healthcare systems. Many patients present and are managed in primary care. With early intervention, gout can be cured/go into remission by urate-lowering therapy and dietary modification. There is widespread global evidence that gout is inadequately treated and that adherence to therapy is low. There is a small literature suggesting reluctance among patients to seek care and advice because of negative beliefs, a lack of understanding of the condition, and social stigma. Only one, UK-based, study has looked at patients’ experiences from initial onset of symptoms to diagnosis. Aim: To explore patient experiences, perceptions and expectations from initial symptoms to diagnosis and management, in order to identify strategies to support early access to care and optimize outcomes, taking into account cultural differences in a Singaporean context. Recruitment and sampling. A wide range of recruitment strategies will be used, including posters and leaflets in polyclinics, private solo and group GP practices, rheumatology clinics and media statements/interviews. Sampling will be across Chinese, Malay and Indian communities. Methods will be mixed-method individual patient semi-structured interviews (n≤60): the CASP-19 (quality of life) and the HL-SF12 (health literacy) will be administered, alongside a qualitative topic guide exploring barriers and facilitators to care and management. Quantitative data will be integrated into the qualitative analysis, and findings compared across individuals and groups. Data collection and analysis will be iterative from first data collection across all 3 groups concurrently. Findings will be disseminated through conferences, peer-reviewed journals and public media. If this methodology for identifying patient-acceptable, effective strategies to ensure early intervention is successful we intend applying it to other chronic conditions managed in primary care.
kw: Singapore; Family Medicine; Gout; Patient Experiences; Qualitative and Quantitative Methods; Health Outcomes

title: Surveillance of Hospital Environmental Microbiome for Healthcare Associated Infection (HAI) Outbreaks
abs: Healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) are associated with significant morbidity and mortality. Despite strict adherence to national infection prevention and control guidelines and excellent hand hygiene compliance, Singapore General Hospital (SGH) continues encountering HAIs. Although one can surmise from empirical experience that the current infection control practices may transiently contain an outbreak of HAIs, gaps in our understanding and management of HAI transmission exist since HAI outbreaks continue to occur periodically. There is an urgent need for a surveillance system within hospitals to prevent and fortify the control of such periodical outbreaks. Existing literature has attributed a significant number of HAI outbreaks to hospital sinks, taps and drains. We hypothesize that the hospital drainage system harbors HAI pathogens and are sources of HAIs. These microbial communities present in the drainage interacts with ward occupants and reflect HAI transmission risks. Environmental samples and remnant clinical samples will be collected together with relevant clinical and environmental data. These samples will be analyzed using shotgun metagenomics, ITS and 16S rRNA sequencing. We will develop customized bioinformatics pipelines to correlate drainage microbiome changes with the occurrence of a HAI outbreak. The signature microbiome changes can then be exploited for HAI risk prediction. HAIs are preventable. Despite the current best practice, vulnerable patients continue to suffer from the harms associated with HAIs. Insightful understanding of the HAI pathogen sources and novel solutions are necessary to mitigate the risk posed by increasingly drug-resistant HAI pathogens. As treatment options for multidrug-resistant HAI pathogens dwindle, HAI prevention becomes ever more important. If findings from this study confirm our hypotheses, novel strategies for HAI surveillance and prevention may be developed and implemented in SGH and other hospitals, aiming at improving health care quality and patient outcomes, as well as cost saving from caring for HAI-related adverse outcomes.
kw: Hospital microbiome; Healthcare associated infection; Outbreak; Infection control; Surveillance

title: Optimizing the robotic endoscope for clinical application
abs: A medical innovation is only useful if it can be utilized in clinical practice. The aim is for the medical innovation to improve, modify or replace current gold standard equipments and practices. Similarly, a robotic endoscope is only useful if it can be used in clinical practice to benefit patients and procedurists. Our preliminary studies thus far have focused on the use of the robotic endoscope in conventional endoscopic procedures such as the endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD). We now aim to extend the clinical reach of the robotic endoscope beyond traditional endoscopy. Hypothesis Our hypothesis is that the robotic endoscope can be used in various clinical settings to modify current gold standard practices. Our sub-aims are - Aim #1: To perform suturing of a full-thickness perforation using the robotic endoscope and support structure Aim #2: To perform pure transrectal natural orifice transluminal endoscopic surgery (NOTES) appendicectomy using a robotic endoscope Aim #3: To provide haptic feedback by attaching an electronic skin to the end-effectors of the robotic endoscope Approach i. Subproject #1: Performing Suturing Of A Full-thickness Perforation Using The Robotic Endoscope And Support Structure We will design a robotic suturing device and a support structure to maintain the lumen of the gastrointestinal tract after a full-thickness perforation is created. Suturing of the full-thickness perforation will then be performed on an anesthetized live pig. ii. Subproject #2: Performing Pure Transrectal NOTES Appendicectomy Using A Robotic Endoscope As there is no appendix in pigs, we will use the right fallopian tube as a substitute for the appendix. The right fallopian tube and appendix share similar anatomies. Each procedure step of the laparoscopic appendicectomy procedure will be modified to allow the use of the robotic endoscope for NOTES. For comparison of the outcomes of pure transrectal NOTES appendicectomy using a robotic endoscope, we will perform laparoscopic appendicectomy on the pig as the gold standard procedure. iii. Subproject #3: Providing haptic feedback by attaching an electronic skin to the end-effectors of the robotic endoscope We will attach an electronic skin to the end-effectors of the robotic endoscope to allow haptic feedback for users. Feasibility Our proposed study is feasible on multiple levels. Firstly, our multidisciplinary research group provides both technical and medical expertise for this hybrid research topic. Secondly, we have access to an engineering laboratory and a vivarium to perform ex-vivo experiments and animal trials.
kw: Robotics; Innovation; Endoscopy

title: Diabetic foot ulcers among patients with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: lifelong cost, risk prediction and cost effectiveness of risk tailored diabetic foot screening in Singapore
abs: Specific aims: 1) to quantify the lifelong cost attributable to diabetic foot ulcers in Singapore; 2) to stratify Type 2 DM patients according to their risk of developing diabetic foot ulcers. A patient level prediction model will be developed and validated using diabetic foot screening data, and data collected from enterprise data warehouse. The developed model will be implemented using R shiny for real time risk prediction & risk tailored intervention for individual patient; 3) to determine the tailored DF screening (DFS) strategy for diabetic patients with different risk level for cost effective intervention & prevention. There is no specific statistical hypothesis to test as this is a modeling and simulation study. Methodology Aim 1: Incidence based approaches will be applied to estimate the lifelong cost attributable to diabetic foot complications. Cost will be analyzed from societal perspective. Both direct and indirect cost will be included. A Markov model will be developed to mimic the lifetime disease progression and management. Aim 2: Patients screened for DFU in NHGP in 2013-5 will be included as study cohort and followed up for 3 years. Patient data will be obtained from NHG administrative databases and the B.R.A.I.N. Cox regression will be used to determine the important risk predictors and to predict the time to developing DFU. Aim 3: The Markov disease transition and microsimulation models developed in Aim 1 will be used to estimate the cost and quality adjusted life years (QALYs) for various screening strategies; and to identify the most cost effective screening strategy. Importance of the research This research will aid in predicting individual diabetic patient’ risk of developing ulcers (and eventual amputation) and help target risk tailored intervention for early prevention. This will lead to improved outcomes for the patients, and lower healthcare utilization for the society.
kw: Diabetic Foot Screening; Risk prediction and intervention; Attributable cost of illness; Cost Effectiveness Analysis

title: Novel genetic and non-genetic risk factors for endothelial dysfunction and diabetic micro-angiopathies - meeting future challenges
inst: Khoo Teck Puat Hospital Pte Ltd
abs: Background Supported by previous NMRC grants, the in-depth phenotyping and serial follow-up of 2,100 multi-ethnic individuals with type 2 diabetes (T2DM) from 2011-2017 have made major contributions to diabetes research (https://www.ktph.com.sg/cru/section_page/494). The cohort also provided rich data and bio-repository to support the operations of national diabetes research consortium. Contemporary epidemiology has informed future unmet needs: (1) increase in longevity related disability e.g. cognitive dysfunction; (2) Amputation due to diabetic foot syndrome (DFS) remains unabated. In this region, our cohort is the only one focusing on these issues. Nonetheless, important gaps in phenotyping remain in our cohort. Thus, we aim to systematically recall all participants from the study-base over ~3 years for re-assessment (including blood and urine collection). Hypothesis Traditional and novel risk factors (RFs) (including genetics), collected at baseline and reassessed serially (to derive their variability), will predict long-term changes in vascular (endothelial) function and incident diabetic complications (including cognitive dysfunction). Methods We will include exposures critical to chronic metabolic disorders: (1) dietary assessment (using the newly-developed web-based platform evolved from the GUSTO cohort, suitable for non-pregnant adults) and (2) physical activities (by tri-axial accelerometer). We will focus on important but under addressed outcomes such as cognitive dysfunction (assessment as employed by the SLAS cohort), and diabetic foot syndrome (DFS) which are in-part attributable to vascular (endothelial) dysfunction. Therefore, our enhanced plan will investigate the long-term relationship between (i) traditional (e.g. hyperglycemia) & novel RFs (e.g. haptoglobinuria) and their variability over time, (ii) endothelial function, (iii) intermediate phenotype (e.g. arterial stiffness) and (iv) extended spectrum of final phenotype i.e. cognitive function, DFS, nephropathy and retinopathy. Significance Collaborating with other major local cohorts (GUSTO & SLAS), we will meet the needs of providing high-quality culturally sensitive local exposures (e.g. nutrition) and outcomes data and biorepository dedicated to T2DM.

title: Extracellular vesicle based biomarker discovery in mouse models of Alzheimer's disease utilizing proximity-based protein labeling (BioID)
abs: Liquid biopsies” have emerged as an exciting new technique in the field of biomarker discovery. These non-invasive techniques, utilizing plasma derived extracellular vesicles (EVs), are especially promising in diagnosing dementia and neurodegeneration where brain biopsies are not practical. Neuron-derived EVs have been reported to contain proteins and miRNAs that may represent potential Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) biomarkers which can be useful in the context of AD diagnosis and treatment, such as the Amyloid-beta peptide (Abeta) whose accumulation in extracellular plaques is the hallmark characteristic of AD. However, the isolation of neuron derived EVs is particular challenging because of their low abundance in patient blood plasma and the lack of unequivocal neuron-specific surface markers that can be used for purification. Importantly, definitive evidence of their brain and neuronal origin or specificity in published reports is still lacking. Hence, there is an unmet need for alternative strategies that can provide more definitive support for brain derived neuron-specific EV-based biomarkers. We hypothesize that brain-specific expression of a biotin ligase BirA-CD63-fusion protein will generate biotin-tagged protein markers which can be recovered from extracellular fluids or plasma and provide unequivocal identification of their neuronal origin. Further, the profile of these biotin-tagged proteins may represent biomarker signatures of ongoing brain dysfunction or disease. Accordingly, we have developed and tested (preliminary data) a versatile lentivirus-based toolkit termed “ExoBioID” that will allow us to recover and identify biotin conjugated EV proteins that are of brain origins. We will apply this system to in vitro and in vivo models that are relevant for AD to identify AD-related biomarkers. If successful, this strategy is applicable to any neurodegenerative animal model to provide cell type-specific biomarker discovery from plasma derived EVs. If funded this project has the great potential to advance the field of biomarker discovery and to be utilized for commercialization.
