title: Therapeutic Repositioning and Development of Phase I/II Drug OTSSP167 to Target 4 Molecular Subtypes of Medulloblastoma
abs: PROJECT BACKGROUND: Pediatric brain cancer is the leading cause of death in childhood cancer. Medulloblastoma (MB) is the most common malignant brain tumor in children globally. Genomics era has robustly classified pediatric MB into 4 molecular subtypes: sonic-hedgehog-activated MB, Wingless-activated, and less-characterized, more aggressive Group 3 and 4 subtypes. Recurrent MB is invariably fatal. Our drug discovery platform identifies Phase I/II drug OTSSP167, used in adult cancers, as a compelling therapeutic agent against 4 MB-subtypes, including recurrent/disseminated MB. SPECIFIC AIMS: The goal of this proposal is to therapeutically reposition Phase I/II drug OTSSP167 to target 4 MB-subtypes, and establish a new therapy for aggressive subtypes and recurrent tumors refractory to current regimens. Specifically, we will evaluate in-vivo therapeutic efficacy of OTSSP167 against a panel of well-characterized, patient-derived orthotopic xenograft (PDOX) Models of 4 MB-subtypes and a pair of primary/recurrent PDOX Models which we have successfully established, to further identify new secondary targets of OTSSP167 for co-determinants of drug response. This will uncover new molecular mechanisms within aggressive Group 3/4 MBs, and treatment resistance in recurrent MB/SHH-MBs. HYPOTHESES: Based on our preliminary data, our working hypothesis is that there exist new secondary targets of OTSSP167, effective against Group 3/4 MBs, and treatment-resistant tumors. METHODOLOGY/APPROACH: Our established subtype-specific PDOX MB Models represent the most complete, patient-relevant MB disease spectrum in the field of neurooncology, that can serve as an excellent preclinical screening platform to evaluate therapeutic efficacy of OTSSP167. FEASIBILITY: Our preliminary studies support that this approach will be effective in predicting clinical trial drug response of OTSSP167 against lethal and treatment-resistant MB. IMPORTANCE: Our PDOX Models provide immediate, clinically-relevant in-vivo models for preclinical drug positioning and downstream translation to clinical trials for MB within large international collaborative groups, which will serve an urgent unmet need for the global pediatric neurooncology community.
kw: Therapeutic Respositioning; Medulloblastoma Subtypes; Phase I/II Dug; OTSSP167; Brain Tumors

title:
Cardiovascular Clinical Trials in Asia:
Asian Diabetes Outcomes Prevention Trial (ADOPT)
abs:
Rationale: Cardiovascular events are the leading cause of death among patients with diabetes. Early identification of high risk diabetic (DM) patients for intensification of preventive therapy may prevent cardiovascular events.

Aims: Among biomarker (N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide, NT-proBNP)-identified high risk type 2 DM patients without pre-existing cardiac disease, to test if intensive preventive therapy (high dose renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system inhibitors [RAASi], beta-blockade, sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 inhibitors [SGLT2i]) may be associated with reduced cardiovascular events compared to standard of care.

Design: Prospective multinational randomized open-label, parallel group, active-controlled, two-arm, long-term morbidity and mortality trial involving 5 countries (Singapore, Malaysia, China, Taiwan, India; estimated 6 sites each) with patients followed for 2 years.

Population: Adults with type 2 DM without cardiac disease* and with NT-proBNP > 125 pg/mL (*defined as history of coronary heart disease [prior myocardial infarction of significant coronary artery disease] or heart failure [reduced ejection fraction or hospitalization for heart failure])

Randomization: 1:1 randomization to either
(1) Intensive Treatment group (high dose of RAASi and beta-blockers as well as SGLT2i) on top of standard therapy; or
(2) Control group (standard therapy where the use of SGLT2i at randomization is not allowed but RAASi and beta-blockers, with the exception of maximal dosage, are allowed). Every attempt is made to use other blood pressure lowering drugs than RAASi or beta-blockers, as well as other anti-DM agents, in the control group.

Primary endpoint: Combined endpoint based on the first occurrence of cardiovascular death and cardiovascular hospitalization
kw: clinical trials; cardiometabolic disease; biomarkers; heart failure; prevention

title: Novel Effective Breast Cancer Therapeutics Utilising Non-invasive Pulsed Electromagnetic Field
abs: Breast cancer, as the most prevalent cancer among women worldwide, is detrimental to the intention and ability of women to live well for longer. In Singapore alone, the incidence of breast cancer continues to rise. Current treatment standards involve combinations of surgery, chemotherapy, radiotherapy and hormonal therapy. While effective, these lead to adverse effects that could be life threatening. Treatment resistance and intolerance in some patients also lead to suboptimal oncological outcomes which render them prone to recurrence. Our novel anticancer platform based on low intensity pulsed electromagnetic fields (PEMFs) is highly selective in killing breast cancer cells without implicating normal tissues. In our in vitro, ex vivo and in vivo models, significant breast cancer cell apoptosis was achieved by direct PEMFs application to the cancer. Normal cells exposed to this fields are not adversely affected. Anticancer effect can also be demonstrated indirectly, when skeletal muscles are stimulated by PEMF at a specific muscle stimulating amplitude. At such setting, PEMF stimulates myogenesis in muscles and induce secretion of myokines with anticancer properties. PEMF is a promising novel breast cancer treatment modality which may enhance oncological and clinical outcome as well as overall survival. It may revolutionise breast cancer management and benefit millions of patients worldwide. Further understanding of the underlying pathway is essential to set the stage for the translation of this technology to clinics and benefit millions of patients worldwide.
kw: breast cancer, electromagnetism, myokines, conditioned media, apoptosis

title: Mapping the trajectory and prognosis of patients with mild-moderate traumatic brain injury – The NEurodegeneration & Understanding of Risk Overlay in Neuroimaging Study (NEURON) 2
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI) will soon be a leading cause of global death and disability; the greatest rise is in the elderly. TBI consequences may be devastating, including physical, cognitive and psycho-behaviours. TBI is now known as a major risk factor for lifelong neurological disorders, including Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s diseases, and other dementias. Although some patients successfully recover and some adapt despite deficits, others continuously decline. Currently, it is not possible to differentiate cohorts as they progress towards either good or poor prognoses. We are unable to characterize the spectrum of processes favouring decline, termed “Chronic Brain Injury” (CBI). Longitudinal data on CBI are severely lacking worldwide. My previous work in normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH), supported by an NMRC TA award, provides proof-of-concept that different cohorts of disease exist with differing degrees of responsiveness to treatments. NPH is one end-point of TBI. Thus, I hypothesize that post-TBI, different cohorts exist, with differing degrees of adaptation to injury. It is possible to find markers and milestones to differentiate such cohorts, and thus manage them appropriately and individually. Modelling such trajectories requires knowledge of the spectrum of reversible to irreversible brain injury. There are no comprehensive data in this regard. To address such gaps, we propose NEURON 2, the first study to confirm CBI, and discover post-TBI markers correlated with good vs. poor prognoses. We aim to explore whether it is possible, prior to any clinical manifestations, to distinguish patients within 3 years of mild-moderate TBI, who will recover from those who will deteriorate from CBI. We shall examine whether advanced brain tissue imaging signatures reflect structural adaptation to injury vs. decline, particularly in those with higher risk of CBI. An experienced team spanning expertise in NPH, TBI and neurodegenerative diseases, and established exemplar datasets, make us well-positioned to deliver NEURON 2.
kw: Traumatic Brain Injury; Chronic brain injury; Magnetic Resonance Imaging; Diffusion Tensor Imaging; Biomarkers

title: Primary Care Based Integrated Community Care Team to meet the needs of the complex  patient
abs: In the last decade, several definitions of the complex patient have emerged in literature. However, no one clear definition has emerged. The definition goes beyond the concept of multi-morbidity and builds upon the concept of the social determinants of health. Peek et al introduced the concept of care delivery complexity where there are person specific factors that interfere with the delivery of usual care. These patients are also more vulnerable to fragmented care and poor outcome as a result of inherent factors of low literacy, or health systems factors such as having to interface with various care teams through their health care journey. It is thus important to identify the complex patient for early intervention. Locally, there is limited data on the definition of a complex patient, hence the challenge, especially during the busy consultation. With the shift in focus from hospital to the community, various care models are also emerging. The integrated community care team (ICCT) is a novel concept, bringing together the 3 main care providers in the community, each with it’s unique roles. Primary Care, the medical anchor; Community Social Care Providers, the social anchor; and the Regional Health System’s Community Nurses, who play a role in patient engagement and empowerment. There is no study locally, to determine the effectiveness if the ICCT in the outcome of the complex patient. This will be a mixed-method study, to understand the perspectives of the various stakeholders on what is the definition of the complex patient in primary care, their care needs and the care objectives. This will allow better identification of the complex patient. Through a randomized control methodology, the study will determine the impact on clinical outcome of the complex diabetic patient. The study will also generate knowledge that facilitates the successful implementation of ICCT in the community.
kw: complex patient ; integrated care;  community ;  primary care

title: Investigating the Genetic and Phenotypic Architecture of Advanced Primary Angle Closure Glaucoma for Stratified Disease Management
abs: Glaucoma is the leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide, with primary angle closure glaucoma (PACG) a major form of glaucoma in Singapore and Asia. While we have made considerable advances in understanding the epidemiology, risk factors, imaging features, and clinical phenotypes of PACG, one of the key unanswered questions is who is at greatest risk for developing advanced PACG/blindness. Current strategies for patient stratification are inadequate to identify those who progress to advanced disease. Our recent work has demonstrated that angle closure exhibits substantial clinically heterogeneity. However, such approaches are inadequate in their abilities to stratify patients as they do not account for both within-disease and across-disease heterogeneity. Our group have also identified eight genetic loci associated with PACG; however, they have all been identified using a broad categorization of PACG. It is thus not known if there are specific genetic variants that confer susceptibility to development of advanced PACG. In this proposal, we hypothesize that specific anatomical features and rare variants of moderate-large effect sizes confer susceptibility to the development of advanced PACG. To address our hypothesis, we will perform comprehensive phenotyping of advanced PACG to identify specific factors associated with severe disease (Aim1). Next, we aim to identify genetic variants that confer susceptibility to advanced disease/blindness by performing targeted sequencing of the known PACG-loci in these subjects (Aim 2). Finally, we aim to build a multimodal artificial-intelligence driven patient stratification model to identify earlier those individuals at risk of developing advanced PACG disease (Aim 3). It is hoped that this project will lead to improved disease stratification of PACG and facilitate early administration of prophylactic treatments to those at the greatest risk of developing advanced disease.
kw: Primary angle closure glaucoma; patient stratification; anterior segment optical coherence tomography;  Ophthalmic genetics; imaging; artificial intelligence

title: Study into the role of Cerebrovascular Disease and Amyloid Pathology on Progression of Cognitive Impairment among Patients with Young Onset Mild Cognitive Impairment (SYNC-Longitudinal)
abs: While cerebral fibrillary beta- amyloid is the pathological hallmark of Alzheimer ’s disease (AD), there is evidence that small vessel cerebrovascular disease (svCVD) co-exists and accelerates the amyloid cascade. Existing studies evaluating the interaction between beta-amyloid and svCVD have been limited to older cohorts with multiple cerebral pathologies, thus not allowing for analyses of the specific contribution of svCVD to beta-amylid pathology. Studies focused on a younger cohort will allow for elucidation of the specific pathophysiological contributions of svCD to cerebral beta-amyloid and AD. Published data from our group has demonstrated that 30-40% of Southeast Asian patients with AD to have a severe burden of svCVD. Thus unravelling the contribution of svCVD to beta-amyloid pathology is of high clinical importance to the Southeast Asian population. In this proposal we will evaluate the interaction between beta-amyloid and svCVD in 250 young subjects (<65 years) with amnestic mild cognitive impairment (a-MCI). This will be a follow-up study to our cross-sectional Singapore Young Onset Dementia Study (SYNC). We will evaluate the interaction between svCVD and beta-amyloid pathology on specific cognitive measures (global cognition, episodic memory, executive function), incident svCVD lesions and integrity of specific functional networks (executive control network, default mode network). As hypertension is a leading mechanism for svCVD, we will carry-out proof of mechanism trial to study the risk-benefit of intensive blood pressure control (<120/80mm Hg) on reducing cognitive decline and reducing svCVD lesions among a-MCI subjects having both svCVD and beta-amyloid pathology. This study will provide novel data on the magnitude of contribution of svCVD to accumulation of beta-amyloid, cognitive decline and functional network integrity. The data would be used to plan randomized clinical trials targeting svCVD for the prevention of AD dementia and to develop novel commercializable softwares to quantify svCVD and to track cognitive performance.
kw: Young Onset Mild Cognitive Impairment, Cerebrovascular Disease, Amyloid, Cognitive Impairment, Mild Cognitive Impairment

title: Tracking circulating tumour cells and microRNAs in high-risk breast cancer
abs: Circulating nucleic acids and circulating tumour cells (CTCs) may potentially be useful for decision-making in breast cancer (BC). Unlike standard tissue-based biopsies, these blood-based biomarkers are non-invasive, and may provide real-time assessment of the evolution of disease biology with changing disease burden better than radiological imaging and other commercial assays. We hypothesize that dynamic changes in CTCs and microRNA expression reflect the tumour burden in BC, and provide insights into mechanisms of resistance. Aim 1: To determine the potential of serial CTC counts with the microfluidic ClearCell® FX platform for monitoring response and surveillance in high-risk BC patients requiring neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Aim 2: To characterize the CTCs with the 2-gene MMP signature which has prognostic value in various tumours Aim 3: To identify changes in circulating microRNA signatures with treatment for breast cancer, and correlation with relapse status. Over 1 year, 60 breast cancer patients undergoing neoadjuvant chemotherapy at 2 centres will be recruited. For Aims 1-3, blood will be performed at baseline, after 6 months of chemotherapy before surgery, within 1 month after surgery, then at 1 year and 2 years after initial diagnosis. For Aim 1, CTCs will be enumerated using the microfluidic platform. For Aims 2 and 3, expression of MMP1 and MMP12 will be evaluated with RNA extracted from single CTCs, and microRNA will be extracted from serum for profiling using the MiRXES IDEALTM miRNA qPCR assays. The sensitivity of the circulating markers at the different timepoints and the correlation with disease relapse status will be compared using the appropriate statistics. These promising blood-based biomarkers may serve as surrogates for not only tumour response, but more importantly, residual disease burden status, and predict risk of relapse. By refining the risk stratification, BC patients at high risk of relapse can potentially be identified for escalation of adjuvant therapies while patients at low risk of relapse after standard treatments may be spared from unnecessary toxic treatments.
kw: circulating tumour cells, microRNA, breast cancer

title: Oral capsule-administered faecal microbiota transplantation for intestinal carbapenemase-producing Enterobacteriaceae decolonization
abs: Introduction: Carbapenemase-producing Enterobacteriaceae (CPE) are a global, antibiotic-resistant “superbug” threat with up to 80% mortality. Despite standard-of-care infection prevention, CPE numbers increase in Singapore and many parts of the world. CPE-intestinal colonization, the main human reservoir, is a source for ongoing transmission and progression to invasive disease. Available data supports antibiotic-induced gut microbiota dysbiosis as a leading mechanism predisposing to CPE-intestinal colonization. There are no standard-of-care regimens for CPE-intestinal decolonization. Faecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) by capsule is a safe, proven therapy for recurrent C. difficile infection. Limited data from single-arm uncontrolled studies suggests FMT can restore normal gut microbial diversity and decolonize CPE-intestinal carriage. Hypothesis: Oral capsule-administered FMT significantly increases the proportion of CPE-intestinal decolonization of CPE-intestinal colonized adult subjects at 2 weeks following FMT administration, compared with placebo. Methods: We plan to conduct a double-blind, randomized controlled trial in 3 sites (SGH, NUH and TTSH) where CPE-intestinal colonization positive adults will be randomized 1:1 to FMT by capsule compared with placebo. The primary endpoint measured 2-weeks post-capsule administration will be CPE-intestinal decolonization (defined as two rectal swabs negative by culture-based detection on consecutive days and a rectal swab negative by direct-PCR-based detection). Subjects will be followed-up for 48 weeks post-FMT to determine long-term CPE-intestinal decolonization rates. The two secondary aims are to determine microbiome correlates of CPE-intestinal decolonization using metagenomic sequencing (Secondary aim 1) and to use a mouse-model to undertake mechanistic studies of CPE-intestinal colonization (Secondary aim 2). The two secondary studies would use samples collected as part of the primary randomized controlled trial. Clinical significance: The primary study would help determine if FMT is an effective and safe intervention for CPE-intestinal decolonization. The secondary studies would provide data to understand the mechanistic pathways by which FMT impacts CPE-intestinal colonization.
kw: Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae; Randomized-controlled trial; Antimicrobial resistance; Oral Capsule; Fecal microbiota transplantation; Intestinal decolonization

title: Ma-Spore ALL-Seq 2020: RNA-Seq and IgH/TCR-Seq to improve risk assignment in childhood, adolescent and young adult acute lymphoblastic leukaemia
abs: Minimal residual disease (MRD) and genetic factors allowed us to better risk stratify patients for treatment of ALL. However, they are still constrained by the limited resolution of RQ-PCR, cytogenetics and RT-PCR. Majority of patients who relapse lacks high risk MRD or genetic features. Next generation sequencing provides both exceedingly high read depths and sequence resolution at nucleotide level. Using a combination of whole genome transcriptomic sequencing, (RNA-Seq) and targeted sequencing of IgH/TCR (IgH/TCR-Seq) we hope to test whether improved resolutions of both MRD and genetic stratification will help us improve treatment outcome for children, adolescents and young adults (AYA) treated on Ma-Spore ALL-Seq 2020 study. “B-others” lack identifiable genetic factors (hyperdiploidy>50, ETV6-RUNX1, TCF3-PBX1, BCR-ABL1 or MLL-AF4) forms the largest group accounting for 56% of Ma-Spore ALL patients. We will RNA-Seq ~280 B-others patients out of 500 patients on Ma-Spore ALL to find any genetic risk. We hypothesise that we can better genetic stratify ~40% of total patients to either standard or high risk genetic group which have clinically significant hazard ratio ≥ 4. We will use IgH/TCR-Seq to determine whether an improved MRD depth by at least 10 fold to 1 x 10-5 can better predict the risk of relapse. As IgH/TCR-Seq also provide a snapshot of the immune repertoire, we aim to correlate if a limited diversity of IgH/TCR repertoire is associated with increased risk of severe infections. Ma-Spore ALL-Seq 2020 hope to use the improved NGS depth and single nucleotide level resolution to improve risk assignment for ALL, allowing safe deceleration of therapy in a larger group of genetic/MRD standard risk patients and early intensification of therapy in a smaller group of genetic/MRD high risk patients. Taken together this will help us further improve the overall treatment outcome of ALL in Malaysia and Singapore.
kw: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia; RNA-Seq; Next generation sequencing; clinical trial; minimal residual disease; genetic risk

title: Targeting transcription factor pathways in liver cancer
abs: My long-term goal is to translate our knowledge on cancer and transcription factors into clinical applications and therapies. Our overall hypothesis is that it will take a combination of targeted therapies, including those aimed at transcription factors, in order to effectively treat cancer. For this STaR application, I propose to focus on two transcription factors, the oncofetal protein SALL4, and the tumor suppressor CEBPA, for selectively targeted therapies in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), a disease of importance in Singapore with dismal prognosis and no effective drug therapies. SALL4 is not expressed in most normal adult tissues and expressed in approximately 30% of cancers, including HCC. Specifically, I propose the following aims: (1) In order to develop small molecules targeting SALL4 in liver cancer, we will optimize and further develop SALL4 inhibitor compound leads using structure based drug discovery, develop SALL4 degraders, and define the mechanism(s) of the inhibitor and degraders in SALL4-mediated HCC. (2) We will also develop novel RNA based therapies targeting the transcriptional network of SALL4 and CEBPA in HCC, by investigating the mechanism of CEBPA short activating RNA (saRNA) therapeutics in HCC, defining the therapeutic effects of SALL4 siRNA in HCC and compare with small molecule inhibitors and degraders, and defining the therapeutic effects of combination therapy of CEBPA activating RNA and SALL4 siRNA (sasi) as well as CRISPR-based novel RNA therapeutics in HCC. This proposal will involve interactions with basic scientists, clinicians at the National University Hospital, and well as industry partners, and if successful will lead to novel therapeutics targeting pathways not engaged by other therapeutic approaches.
kw: cancer, tumor suppressor, gene regulation, oncofetal protein, liver, HCC

title: Clinical evaluation of a novel 20-gene signature as a biomarker and metabolic target in breast cancer stem cells
abs: There is much work on developing strategies to target breast cancer stem cells (CSCs), which exhibit intrinsic resistance to conventional treatments. We have recently identified a novel gene signature comprising of 20 genes related to oxidative phosphorylation from functional CSC assays using patient-derived tumourspheres. We hypothesise that this signature is a more sensitive CSC marker than existing ones and may predict tumour sensitivity to oxidative phosphorylation inhibitors such as metformin. We also found metformin to be effective in chemo-resistant cells. Primary objectives are to evaluate this 20-gene signature as an indicator of CSC subpopulation size and to determine the effect of metformin on CSCs. Secondary objective is to establish patient-derived xenografts for future characterisation. The 20-gene signature will be evaluated in non-diabetic women prior to and after completing neoadjuvant chemotherapy in combination with metformin, and will be correlated with known CSC markers using NanoString technology, and with proliferative and apoptotic markers using immunohistochemistry. The association with pathological response will also be examined. Analyses will be stratified according to tumour subtype, to account for variations in chemotherapy regimen. A similar evaluation will be carried out in diabetic women undergoing neoadjuvant chemotherapy, stratified according to whether they receive metformin for diabetic treatment or otherwise. The correlation with CSCs will be further validated in 2 cohorts known for CSC enrichment: pre- and post-chemotherapy pairs and primary and matched recurrent tumour pairs. To validate the association with prognosis, recurrent tumours from the cohort will be compared with matched controls consisting of tumours from women who did not relapse; controls will be matched in terms of disease stage, tumour subtype, histological classification, treatments received. Findings will provide insight into the potential of the 20-gene signature as a CSC marker and as a therapeutic target.
kw: breast cancer stem cells; oxidative phosphorylation

title: PASSIvation of Vulnerable plaques with Alirocumab in acuTE coronary syndrome (PASSIVATE)
abs: Acute myocardial infarction (AMI), which is caused by thrombotic occlusion of a destabilized coronary atherosclerotic plaque, is one of the top four rapidly-growing diseases in Singapore. Worryingly, mortality at 30 days after AMI in Singapore is ~1.5-2-fold greater than in other high-income countries. We aim to investigate whether a potent cholesterol-lowering monoclonal antibody, alirocumab, can stabilize vulnerable coronary plaques in patients and how treatment with alirocumab modifies the circulating lipidome and proteome. The methodology will be that of a randomized controlled trial in which patients recently hospitalized for AMI at 3 hospitals will be randomly assigned to 14 months of alirocumab (N=100) or placebo (N=100) and will undergo hybrid 18F-NaF position emission tomography-computed tomographic coronary angiography at baseline, 14 months and 28 months, paralleled by measurement of the circulating lipidome and proteome at the same timepoints. We hypothesize that initiation of alirocumab early in the post-MI period is safe and that alirocumab will be superior to placebo in stabilizing coronary plaques (efficacy effect). We further hypothesize that when alirocumab is withdrawn after 14 months of treatment, its protective effect in coronary plaque stabilization will persist in the subsequent 14 months (legacy effect). We anticipate that alirocumab will modify the circulating lipidome differentially from statins alone, including a reduction in newer atherogenic lipid species such as ceramides, while serial plasma proteomic analysis may offer new insights into potential pleiotropic and off-target effects of treatment with alirocumab. Weaving together state-of-the-art cardiovascular imaging and 'omic' capabilities positions Singapore as a hub for innovative clinical trials incorporating deep biological phenotyping. By studying the ‘legacy effect’ of alirocumab, we will be investigating an new strategy to employ powerful but expensive biologics in a sustainable manner.
kw: PCSK9 inhibitor, acute myocardial infarction, PET-CT, lipidomics and proteomics

title: Community-based Screening for Pathological Visual Impairment among Elderly Residents using Artificial-Intelligence Integrated Retinal Imaging
abs: Visual impairment (VI) is a major public health problem, associated with reduced quality of life, and increased frailty risk. Globally, 400 million suffer from VI. Among them, pathological VI (poor vision due to eye diseases not refractive error) accounts for 60%. In Singapore, 12% of individuals aged ≥60 (~90,000) suffer from pathological VI. This number will increase as Singapore population ages. Most causes of pathological VI such as cataract, diabetic retinopathy, when detected early, can be treated and halted from worsening to severe visual/functional loss. Hence, screening for pathological VI is crucial for healthy ageing and productive longevity. Currently, as part of the MOH-initiated functional screening program, community vision screenings are conducted among elderly Singaporeans. The screening model includes 2-tier screening procedures conducted at different days and sites, involves multiple tests and requires skilled manpower, substantial time, to identify pathological VI cases. These factors limit the capacity and coverage of current model. Thus, it is challenging for the current model to operate sustainably to meet the demand of nation-wide annual vision screening for elderly, in the long run. Hence, a simpler, more efficient modality for screening pathological VI is critically needed in Singapore. Artificial intelligence (AI) technology offers unique opportunities to revolutionize current screening model. We propose a novel vision screening modality integrating retinal photography and AI-based algorithm to detect pathological VI. In this proposed project, we will refine, validate this newly developed modality, and pilot its implementation and performance in a ‘real-world’ community outreach screening setting for elderly Singaporeans. This model provides a ‘one-stop shop’ screening using only one objective test, and is time-, labor-efficient and cost-saving. Importantly, this is in line with MOH’s long-term focus of preventive care among Singapore’s elderly (beyond healthcare to health), while adopting a streamlined and sustainable model (beyond quality to value).
kw: Community screening; Visual Impairment; Retinal imaging; Artificial intelligence

title: The Skin Microbiome in Early Childhood Atopic Dermatitis
abs: Background: Atopic dermatitis (AD) is an chronic, incurable skin disease afflicting 20% of children in Singapore and is associated with allergic rhinitis, asthma and food allergy. Studies suggest that prophylactic administration of emollients from birth in infants with a family history of atopy might prevent AD development in a small proportion. It is, however, not known if there are predictive non-invasive skin biomarkers of AD present in early life which could more precisely identify infants at risk of AD and the atopic march, for whom preventive interventions might be specifically tailored towards. Aims: Primary Aim 1) To identify unique characteristics of the newborn’s skin microbiome at 7 days of life which predict development of AD and its severity, allergen sensitization and allergic rhinitis by 18 months in comparison to healthy controls. Secondary Aims 1) To elucidate the relationship between the newborn’s skin microbiomes in relation to the mode of delivery and to correlate this with the development of AD by 18 months of age. 2) To define the maturation patterns of the healthy infant skin microbiome with age by tracking the skin microbiome signatures of healthy infants longitudinally from birth to 18 months of age. Methods: Clinical data collection, skin tape stripping, AD examination and skin prick tests will be performed for mother-offspring dyads in the ongoing Singapore PREconception STudy of maternal and child Outcomes (S-PRESTO) cohort at multiple time-points from birth to 18 months. Whole metagenome sequencing and bioinformatics analysis will be carried out for skin microbiome analysis. Clinical significance Identification of predictive skin biomarkers in the pre-disease phase will identify at-risk infants who would benefit from implementation of early interventions, such as prophylactic emollients from birth in high-risk infants or modification of the skin microbiome for the primary or secondary prevention of atopic dermatitis and its associated co-morbidities.
kw: atopic dermatitis; skin microbiome; allergy; childhood; developmental origins

title: Neurocognitive development and human capital: The influence of digital media consumption on young children in Singapore
abs: Aims and hypotheses: This study aims to define the timing and extent to which young children are most vulnerable to digital media consumption and to gain clarity on the neural mechanisms. We hypothesize that the brain is most sensitive to digital media before 12 months. During this early age, we anticipate that processes underlying the maturation of the brain networks are impaired. Methodology: We will use the Singapore population-based GUSTO (Growing Up in Singapore Towards healthy Outcome) birth cohort to examine the trajectories of digital media use in children from 0-36 months. We will then determine the relationships of media exposure at 4 time points (12, 18, 24, and 36 months) with neurocognitive developmental outcomes, including intelligence, school readiness, and social-emotional skills. Group differences in outcomes between children with excessive use and those without will be quantified with effect sizes. Using autoregressive time series models, the bidirectional effects between media exposure and cognitive characteristics of children will be explored. The raw, pre-processed neurophysiology data (i.e., eye tracking, EEG with event-related potential) from infancy will be cleaned and carefully interpreted. We will employ mixed model, repeated-measure analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) to examine 1) the main effects and 2) the interactions between age and degrees of media exposure on the brain waveform and networks. Greenhouse-Geisser correction will be applied. Clinical significance: This will be one of the first studies to capture longitudinal developmental profiles and neurobiological mechanisms occurring in young children after early introduction of digital media. The scientific evidence has the potential to be translated into public policy for the entire paediatric population.

title: Evaluate the reliability of MRI brain sequence across different MRI scanners
abs: Aim: In KK Women’s and Children’s Hospital, we are keen to leverage on new technology that can have advantages in our paediatric patients. Some of the new MRI technologies includes fast sequences that allows MRI brain scans to be done in 5 minutes as well as arterial spin labelling (ASL), a method of assessing cerebral perfusion without need for an intravenous injection of exogenous contrast. As patient recruitment can be a rate limiting step, multicenter studies can help to achieve sample size required, yet the MRI scanners across the SingHealth hospitals come from different vendors. The aim of this proposal is to evaluate the reliability of MRI brain sequences across different MRI scanners in SingHealth which can determine the feasibility of carrying out multi-center studies. Hypothesis: MRI brain sequences (T1, T2, FLAIR, SWI, DWI/ADC, DTI, ASL, myelin water fraction) of same human volunteer on different MRI machines will give similar quantitative values. MRI brain sequences of same human volunteer done at least 1 week apart will give similar quantitative values. Methodology: Data Acquisition Single human volunteer will be scanned twice, 1 week apart, on the MRI scanners in KK Women’s and Children’s Hospital (KKH)- 3T Siemens,1.5T General Electric Singapore General Hospital (SGH) – 3T Siemens, 3T Philips National Neuroscience Institute (NNI) – 3T Philips Sengkang Hospital (SKH) - 3T General Electric, 1.5T Siemens Parameters for the MRI brain sequences will be standardized with similar field of views, slice thickness and slice selection. Scans obtained at baseline and follow up will be compared across all scanners. Paired t test will be used to test for statistical significance between data obtained at baseline and that obtained 1 week later. Approach of this research: Approval from IRB will be sought for this prospective study.

title: Tracking circulating tumour cells and microRNAs in high-risk breast cancer
abs: Circulating nucleic acids and circulating tumour cells (CTCs) may potentially be useful for decision-making in breast cancer (BC). Unlike standard tissue-based biopsies, these blood-based biomarkers are non-invasive, and may provide real-time assessment of the evolution of disease biology with changing disease burden better than radiological imaging and other commercial assays. We hypothesize that dynamic changes in CTCs and microRNA expression reflect the tumour burden in BC, and provide insights into mechanisms of resistance. Aim 1: To determine the potential of serial CTC counts with the microfluidic ClearCell® FX platform for monitoring response and surveillance in high-risk BC patients requiring neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Aim 2: To characterize the CTCs with the 2-gene MMP signature which has prognostic value in various tumours Aim 3: To identify changes in circulating microRNA signatures with treatment for BC, and correlation with relapse status. Over 1 year, 60 BC patients undergoing neoadjuvant chemotherapy at 2 centres will be recruited. For Aims 1-3, blood will be performed at baseline, after 6 months of chemotherapy before surgery, within 1 month after surgery, then at 1 year and 2 years after initial diagnosis. For Aim 1, CTCs will be enumerated using the microfluidic platform. For Aims 2 and 3, expression of MMP1 and MMP12 will be evaluated with RNA extracted from single CTCs, and microRNA will be extracted from serum for profiling using the MiRXES IDEALTM miRNA qPCR assays. These biomarkers may serve as surrogates for not only tumour response, but more importantly, residual disease burden status, and predict risk of relapse. By refining the risk stratification, BC patients at high risk of relapse can potentially be identified for escalation of adjuvant therapies while patients at low risk of relapse after standard treatments may be spared from unnecessary toxic treatments.

title: Oral capsule-administered faecal microbiota transplantation for intestinal carbapenemase-producing Enterobacteriaceae decolonization
abs: Introduction: Carbapenemase-producing Enterobacteriaceae (CPE) are a global, antibiotic-resistant “superbug” threat with up to 80% mortality. Despite standard-of-care infection prevention, CPE numbers increase in Singapore and many parts of the world. CPE-intestinal colonization, the main human reservoir, is a source for ongoing transmission and progression to invasive disease. Available data supports antibiotic-induced gut microbiota dysbiosis as a leading mechanism predisposing to CPE-intestinal colonization. There are no standard-of-care regimens for CPE-intestinal decolonization. Faecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) by capsule is a safe, proven therapy for recurrent C. difficile infection. Limited data from single-arm uncontrolled studies suggests FMT can restore normal gut microbial diversity and decolonize CPE-intestinal carriage. Hypothesis: Oral capsule-administered FMT significantly increases the proportion of CPE-intestinal decolonization of CPE-intestinal colonized adult subjects at 2 weeks following FMT administration, compared with placebo. Methods: We plan to conduct a double-blind, randomized controlled trial in 3 sites (SGH, NUH and TTSH) where CPE-intestinal colonization positive adults will be randomized 1:1 to FMT by capsule compared with placebo. The primary endpoint measured 2-weeks post-capsule administration will be CPE-intestinal decolonization (defined as two rectal swabs negative by culture-based detection on consecutive days and a rectal swab negative by direct-PCR-based detection). Subjects will be followed-up for 48 weeks post-FMT to determine long-term CPE-intestinal decolonization rates. The two secondary aims are to determine microbiome correlates of CPE-intestinal decolonization using metagenomic sequencing (Secondary aim 1) and to use a mouse-model to undertake mechanistic studies of CPE-intestinal colonization (Secondary aim 2). The two secondary studies would use samples collected as part of the primary randomized controlled trial. Clinical significance: The primary study would help determine if FMT is an effective and safe intervention for CPE-intestinal decolonization. The secondary studies would provide data to understand the mechanistic pathways by which FMT impacts CPE-intestinal colonization.

title: Cardiovascular Clinical Trials in Asia: Asian Diabetes Outcomes Prevention Trial (ADOPT)
abs:
Rationale: Cardiovascular events are the leading cause of death among patients with diabetes. Early identification of high risk diabetic (DM) patients for intensification of preventive therapy may prevent cardiovascular events.
Aims: Among biomarker (N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide, NT-proBNP)-identified high risk type 2 DM patients without pre-existing cardiac disease, to test if intensive preventive therapy (high dose renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system inhibitors [RAASi], beta-blockade, sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 inhibitors [SGLT2i]) may be associated with reduced cardiovascular events compared to standard of care.
Design: Prospective multinational randomized open-label, parallel group, active-controlled, two-arm, long-term morbidity and mortality trial involving 5 countries (Singapore, Malaysia, China, Taiwan, India; estimated 6 sites each) with patients followed for 2 years.
Population: Adults with type 2 DM without cardiac disease* and with NT-proBNP > 125 pg/mL (*defined as history of coronary heart disease [prior myocardial infarction of significant coronary artery disease] or heart failure [reduced ejection fraction or hospitalization for heart failure])
Randomization: 1:1 randomization to either
(1) Intensive Treatment group (high dose of RAASi and beta-blockers as well as SGLT2i) on top of standard therapy; or
(2) Control group (standard therapy where the use of SGLT2i at randomization is not allowed but RAASi and beta-blockers, with the exception of maximal dosage, are allowed). Every attempt is made to use other blood pressure lowering drugs than RAASi or beta-blockers, as well as other anti-DM agents, in the control group.
Primary endpoint: Combined endpoint based on the first occurrence of cardiovascular death and cardiovascular hospitalization

title: Development of a system comprising digital exhaled-breath carbon monoxide self-monitoring device linked to virtual smoking cessation coaching and virtual network of quit-supporters via social media
abs: Specific aims Cigarette smoking is the leading cause of preventable death and a major public health threat. Current smoking cessation approaches have suboptimal quit rate, accessibility and scalability. We postulate that smokers with access to a personal device for self-monitoring of quit effort and linking them to a virtual smoking cessation coaching program and virtual network of quit-supporters via social media will increase the quit rate. The proposed innovation aims to 1. develop a system comprising a digital exhaled-breath carbon monoxide self-monitoring device (STEADES-2) which is integrated to a virtual smoking cessation coaching program and a virtual network of trained quit supporters, 2. conduct a feasibility study of STEADES-2 using mix research method to gather feedbacks and to assess acceptability and utility by users Method: The investigators had developed a prototype device to measure exhaled breath carbon monoxide (eCO) with comparable accuracy to a commercial instrument. The second version (STEADES-2) will include facial and individual recognition functionality to reduce fraudulent usage. The accompanying STEADES mobile application will allow transmission of eCO data via social media to virtual smoking cessation coaching program and a virtual network of quit supporters. The virtual system will be developed concurrently with the device, with reference to existing programs from HPB and polyclinics. The entire STEADES system will be assessed for utility and acceptability by the users in a feasibility study involving 20 smokers, 10 coaches and 10 virtual quit-supporters. The participants will provide feedbacks using questionnaire, individual and group interviews. The quantitative and qualitative results will be used to enhance the STEADES’ system and to design a randomized controlled trial protocol to determine the proof of value of the system in the next development phase.

title: Household transmission of carbapenemase-producing Enterobacteriaceae Singapore: A cohort study
abs: Specific aim: To estimate and device ways to prevent the community spread of carbapenemase-producing Enterobacteriaceae (CPE) by studying the secondary household transmission from a recently hospitalised index family member. Primary hypothesis: We hypothesise that acquisition of CPE is higher among household members of recently hospitalised index subjects with CPE. Methodology: We will conduct a case-ascertained cohort study where we will recruit the household members of CPE-positive and CPE-negative index patients and their immediate neighbours in the community for 1 year. We will test for the presence of carbapenemase genes by direct polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and culture CPE isolates. We will leverage upon the precision of WGS to establish intrahousehold transmission of carbapenemase genes. We will conduct shotgun metagenomics approach, combining Illumina and Nanopore sequencing, to characterise microbial community dynamics in the gut associated with CPE acquisition and continuous carriage. We will calculate the hazard ratio of household transmission by comparing the CPE acquisition rate between CPE-positive and CPE-negative index subjects. We will study the clinical and gut microbiome related risk factors for CPE acquisition among family members and prolonged CPE carriage among index subjects. Approach: Index cases meeting the inclusion criteria, who are still hospitalised will be recruited. Household members will be recruited and a baseline stool sample will be collected. All study subjects will be visited at their residences at weeks 1, 2, 3, 12, 24, 36, and 48 (1 year). At every visit, we will collect stool samples, socio-demographic information, healthcare contact information, travel history, antibiotics exposure history, and dietary history. Importance to science: The potential for household transmission of CPE has never been studied anywhere in the world at the moment. Singapore is in a unique position to study this as we have co-circulation of multiple carbapenemase genes and a contained waste management system.

title: The Brain and Optic Nerve Study using Artificial Intelligence (BONSAI)
abs: Optic disc swelling is one of the most important signs in patients presenting to the emergency department (ED), prompting rapid and accurate detection, because they can signal presence of an underlying vision or life-threatening condition. Brain conditions causing raised intracranial pressure are typically associated with optic disc swelling (papilledema), which is not necessarily visually symptomatic, explaining why patients with other non-specific symptoms (headache, nausea, tinnitus), can initially present to non-ophthalmic departments, including emergency departments (ED). Diagnosing optic disc abnormalities with ophthalmoscopy is difficult outside ophthalmic departments, when ophthalmologists are not immediately available. Retinal imaging has been shown as useful in EDs, but interpretation of disc images by non-ophthalmologists is still a challenge, exposing patients and healthcare actors to errors. Image recognition by artificial intelligence may bring a solution to this problem. In a preliminary study, we have developed a deep-learning system (DLS) based on training and testing in 6443 fundus images (3563 abnormal disc images in 1776 patients). The algorithm had excellent performance distinguishing papilledema from normal optic discs(AUC, 0.98),anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (AUC, 0.95) and pseudo-papilledema (AUC, 0.94). The main aim of this proposal is further refine and validate this DLS in a large dataset (30.000 images from twenty countries), for identification of optic disc swelling, aiming to detect and classify vision or life-threatening conditions affecting the optic nerves and/or the brain. The algorithm will subsequently be applied for evaluation of papilledema severity in a prospective study in Singapore and Atlanta, including 300 patients with known intracranial abnormalities (idiopathic intracranial hypertension, brain tumours). If effective, such an algorithm may translate into a practical solution for a clinical need, i.e. improved detection and streamlining in the ER of patients with suspected brain and/or optic nerve disease, when ophthalmologists are not immediately available.

title: Neural network reorganzation associated with upper limb motor recovery in stroke patients- establishing a prognostic model and tailoring neuromodulation for rehabilitation
abs: To date, neural network reorganization in stroke recovery process is still not fully understood. Currently there is lack of biomarkers to inform rehabilitation with regards to predicting outcomes and measuring and predicting responses to treatment. Prognostic models that are clinically feasible are being explored recently and have not been validated in the local population. Neural network changes associated with motor recovery appear to differ according to lesion and individual characteristics, suggesting that neuromodulatory interventions such as noninvasive brain stimulation should be tailored to individual stroke patients according to predicted patterns of neural reorganization to achieve the best motor outcomes. We will aim at upper limb (UL) motor recovery in this study as loss of UL function remains a significant cause of disability following stroke. This will be a multicentre study comprising 2 sub-studies. Study 1 will be an observational study to investigate the patterns of neural network reorganization in stroke patients with moderate to severe UL motor function impairment, and its correlation with motor function recovery. The integrity and excitability of the corticospinal tract will be measured by transcranial magnetic stimulation, high density electroencephalogram and functional magnetic resonance imaging , from within 1 month to 1 year post-stroke. UL motor function will be measured at the same time point. A model for predicting motor outcomes will be elicited. Study 2 will be a randomized trial to investigate which transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) strategy best facilitates UL motor recovery and the determinants of response. 2 excitatory tDCS strategies with different stimulating sites will be compared. This study is significant in that the result will help to stratify patients and tailor treatment, not just for neuromodulation, but also other treatment modalities in post-stroke rehabilitation. Knowledge of neural network reorganization will help in the future design of targeted treatment in stroke rehabilitation.

title: Singapore Gastric Cancer Consortium - Bringing Discoveries to Patients
abs: Gastric cancer (GC) is the 5th leading cause of cancer mortality globally. While GC age-adjusted incidence is declining, the absolute number of GC cases is expected to increase due to overall population growth and aging. GC is prevalent in Asian countries and in Singapore, GCs represent the 4th/5th highest causes of cancer death in males/females respectively. The Singapore Gastric Cancer Consortium (SGCC) is an integrative multidisciplinary national research program, which over the past decade has established Singapore as a global leader in GC research and treatment, establishing unique population cohorts, novel GC molecular classifications, insights into GC carcinogenesis, and innovative investigator-initiated clinical trials. In this renewal, we seek to take these discoveries back to patients, through five investigational themes in precision prevention, precision therapy and data-driven target identification. First, as early diagnosis is a major factor to improving GC outcomes, we have developed and will be validating novel methods for early detection and risk stratification in high-risk patients, with implications for population screening. Second, for advanced GC patients, we will combine information from molecular biomarkers, organoid platforms, and artificial intelligence to guide the rational and data-driven selection of optimal combination therapies and dosing. Third, we will deeply study the clinical challenge of GC peritoneal carcinomatosis, representing the deadliest and most treatment-refractory presentation of this malignancy. Fourth, using lineage-tracing technologies, we will probe potential GC cells-of-origin (“cancer stem cells”) to identify new therapeutic targets. Fifth, as intra-tumour heterogeneity (ITH) is a major barrier to successful GC treatment, we will apply single-cell technologies to comprehensively demarcate ITH evolution through distinct stages of gastric carcinogenesis and across different intra-tumour cell types. Findings from these themes will apply directly to GC patients, maintain Singapore’s leadership role in the GC field, form a rich training ground for new researchers/clinician scientists, and opportunities for industry partnerships.

title: Overcoming Resistance to Radioactive Iodine (RAI) Therapy in RAI-Refractory Advanced Thyroid Carcinoma
abs: The survival and remission outcome is poor in locally advanced or metastatic thyroid cancers that become refractory to RAI therapy. MAPK is the predominant signaling pathway in majority of thyroid cancers. A common mutation in thyroid cancer, BRAFV600E mutation, is associated with downregulation of sodium-iodide symporter (NIS), a key transporter in the uptake of RAI. System therapy with BRAF inhibitor or MEK inhibitor had been shown to improve clinical efficacy of RAI in RAI-refractory thyroid cancers via the upregulation of NIS expression. However, resistance often arise after prolonged pharmacological inhibition of BRAF through feedback mechanisms involving HER signaling, which in turn suppressed NIS expression and concomitantly reduced iodine uptake. This dysregulation of the MAPK-NIS-HER axis, if successfully dissected, would be an exciting approach in improving the treatment outcome of thyroid cancer patients. The preliminary data on multiple thyroid cancer cell lines with BRAF activating mutation (V600E) have demonstrated strong sensitivity to inhibitors of MAPK signaling, such as selumetinib (MEK inhibitor) and vemurafenib (BRAF inhibitor). By building on the stance that re-differentiation effect of systemic therapy in thyroid cancer cell lines could be achieved by BRAF/MEK inhibition, and that HER signaling may negatively regulate this mechanism by NIS upregulation, we hypothesize that sustained BRAF or MEK inhibition reduces iodine uptake of thyroid cancer cells by increased HER signaling. Combination therapy of BRAF inhibitor or MEK inhibitor with pan-HER inhibitor, afatinib will potentially enable sustained blockade of MAPK signaling & upregulation of sodium-iodide symporter. This will consequently increase iodine uptake in thyroid cancer cell lines. We aim to investigate this in vitro, with an eventual goal of a clinical trial using FDA-approved agents. Moreover, we provide evidence that the mechanism of HER upregulation (ErbB2, ErbB3) may be dependent on the histological class of thyroid cancer. By curating the relevant study models and clinical specimens, we aim to delineate this and potentially design targeted therapies that may benefit thyroid cancer patients with different cancer subtypes.

title: Singapore Parkinson’s disease Translational Clinical Programme (SPARK, Phase  II)
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Background: Parkinson’s disease (PD) with a prevalence of 3:1000 (>50 years) in Singapore will significantly increase as 20% of our population will be > 65 years old by 2030. Objectives: We will develop an integrated clinical, biochemical, and genetic profile identified in several clinical longitudinal cohorts of patients that we have initiated in Phase I so as to develop a model to better manage, prevent development and reduce PD progression. 2. We aim to create cutting edge human brain models, validate new drug targets that we have identified, and unravel key disease mechanisms so as to develop individualized drug and cellular replacement therapies. Methodology Epidemiology/Health Services: To develop an integrated clinical, biochemical, and genetic models to better manage, prevent development and reduce PD progression and identify factors that influence disease progression and drive healthcare costs, so as to improve quality of life in PD. Pathophysiology: To further elucidate the molecular pathways underlying common gene related PD, so as to investigate potential therapeutic interventions through the selection of viable targets using non-human primate and small animal models. Brain Organoids: To develop the next generation human brain organoid model system for innovative and translational research to facilitate screening and validating therapeutic molecules identified in other themes. Regenerative Medicine: To identify and investigate intrinsic and extrinsic factors which would affect the therapeutic efficacy of cell transplant in PD using both non human primate and small animal models. Novel Therapeutics: To conduct a placebo controlled clinical trial in PD involving a propriety compound, to validate the positive autoantibodies identified in PD patients and to conduct experimental therapeutics based on new drug targets. Conclusions: The novelty, international competitiveness and industrial commitment in this Phase II proposal build on our scientific discoveries and achievements in Phase I.

title: Oncogenic roles and molecular functions of ARID5B in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia
abs: Genetic mutations or aberrant expressions of the genes that encode chromatin modifiers are commonly found in cancers. One example is the AT-rich interactive domain (ARID) proteins, which can directly or indirectly regulate the chromatin and epigenetic status. We recently identified ARID5B as a critical downstream target of the TAL1 oncogene in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL). Our study indicated that many of ARID5B-bound regions are associated with active histone marks. ARID5B transcriptionally activates TAL1, its regulatory partners and the MYC oncogene. ARID5B is required for the survival of T-ALL cells, and forced expression of ARID5B in immature thymocytes results in thymus retention, radio-resistance and tumor formation in a zebrafish model. These results indicated that ARID5B plays a pro-oncogenic role in T-ALL. We hypothesize that abnormal expression of ARID5B leads to changes in chromatin status, which sustain or reinforce the oncogenic transcriptional program. It is also noteworthy that ARID5B is normally expressed in hematopoietic stem cells and mature T-cells. Hence, we further hypothesize that ARID5B may contribute to the self-renewal and/or long-term survival capability of malignant T-cells. The overall purpose of this project is to clarify the roles of ARID5B in T-cell leukemogenesis. In Aim 1, we will analyze the involvement of ARID5B in epigenetic and chromatin regulations in T-ALL cells. We will also identify interacting proteins of ARID5B. In Aim 2, we will analyze physiological activity of the ARID5B enhancer and function of ARID5B in normal development using animal models. We will analyze genetic abnormalities that induce aberrant expression of ARID5B in human T-ALL. In Aim 3, we will analyze the roles of ARID5B in tumor development using zebrafish models. Lastly, we will evaluate the effect of anti-sense oligonucleotides targeting ARID5B. Success in this project will not only elucidate molecular mechanisms but also provide a novel therapeutic strategy for T-ALL.
kw: ARID5B; T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia; TAL1; zebrafish; hematopoiesis

title: Therapeutic targeting IL-11 signaling to treat NASH and phenotypic dissection of fibro-inflammatory liver disease in Singaporeans
abs: Hepatic fibrosis is common in liver diseases and leads to cirrhosis and liver failure. There are no approved therapies for treating liver fibrosis, which represents an unmet clinical need. In Singapore, and Asia more generally, non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) is common. In Singapore, it has been suggested that a ‘lean or low BMI NASH’ phenotype may exist that occurs at lower body mass indices than in Caucasians, similar to type 2 diabetes: ‘lean diabetes’. While liver fibrosis can be reversed as seen after the use of antiviral therapies in hepatitis, the reversal of liver fibrosis in NASH and other liver conditions is not possible. Liver fibrosis is driven by the transformation of hepatic stellate cells (HSCs) into fibrogenic, pro-inflammatory myofibroblasts and HSC activation is a defining pathology underlying NASH. In recent studies we discovered that HSC transformation is centrally dependent upon the autocrine activity of the Interleukin-11 (IL-11) cytokine, that IL-11 is upregulated in many fibrotic human liver diseases and that IL11RA deleted mice are protected from liver fibrosis and methionine choline deficient diet-induced NASH. This novel finding follows on from our breakthrough discovery published in Nature in 2017 where we showed IL-11 was centrally important for cardiac fibrosis. In the project described here we will build on our very strong preliminary data and use newly developed therapeutic antibodies and human disease relevant murine models of fibro-inflammatory liver diseases (Specific Aim 1), apply advanced molecular techniques in our recently generated reporter mice strains (Specific Aim 2) and study liver steatosis, fibrosis and inflammation using elegant MRI techniques in a deeply phenotyped Singaporean cohort (Specific Aim 3). These complementary Aims will help us develop a better understanding of fibro-inflammatory hepatic dysfunction in a local Singaporean context and to explore IL-11 as novel therapeutic target and paradigm for fibro-inflammatory liver diseases.
kw: NASH, liver, fibrosis, IL-11, biological, therapy

title: Head-of-Bed positioning in large artery acute ischemic stroke
abs: Background and aims- Positioning of the patient with hyperacute large artery ischemic stroke (IS) is an important, yet understudied aspect of care that could impact the course of treatment and ultimately clinical outcome. Positioning with the head of bed (HOB) at 0-degree has been shown in small studies to increase cerebral blood flow across arterial occlusion in hyperacute large artery IS, leading to clinical improvement in stroke symptoms. However, this position is believed to increase the risk of aspiration pneumonia. In this randomised clinical trial we aim to evaluate whether use of 0-degree HOB positioning is associated with clinical stability in hyperacute IS. We hypothesise that patients with large artery occlusions placed in a 0-degree HOB position will experience less early neurologic deterioration within the first 24 hours, than those in the 30-degree or more HOB elevation group. The study aims to confirm the safety of 0-degree-HOB positioning in a large, generalizable sample of hyperacute large artery IS patients. Material and Methods- In this randomised trial, patients presenting to our tertiary care hospital and eligible for intravenous thrombolysis, with (if presenting within 4.5 hours of symptom-onset) or without (presenting between 4.5 to 16 hours of symptom-onset) mechanical thrombectomy. Eligible patients would be randomised to either a zero-degree HOB or an HOB of 30-degree or more. Impact of HOB position on neurological status would be evaluated with serial NIHSS scores. Cerebral hemodynamics would be monitored by transcranial Doppler ultrasonography. Validated criteria would be used to diagnose pneumonia. Functional outcome would be measured by modified Rankin scale. SPSS version 20 would be used to analyse the data. Results and conclusion- The trial would provide clinical and hemodynamic data to determine the optimal HOB position in patients with large artery acute ischemic stroke.
kw: acute ischemic stroke; thrombolysis; large artery occlusion; mechanical thromectomy; head of bed position; cerebral hypoperfusion; aspiration pneumonia

title: Development of Cell Therapy for Parkinson's Disease
abs: Parkinson’s disease (PD) results from degeneration of dopamine (DA) neurons in the midbrain. Current therapies, including the use of L-Dopa and deep brain stimulation, treat symptoms but do not stop disease progression. The advent of human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs) opens a promising possibility to develop disease-modifying therapeutics for PD by generating DA neurons for cell therapy. Remarkable progress has been made to guide hPSCs to regionally and functionally specialized neural types, including midbrain dopamine (mDA) neurons. These human mDA neurons, following transplantation into the brain, appear to correct the motor deficits in rodent and nonhuman primate (NHP) models of PD. To translate the recent development in laboratory research, we aim to develop a technology to expand the midbrain dopamine neural progenitors by at least 1000 times so that a large quantity of dopamine neurons is produced in a consistent manner for clinical application. Following transplantation, the grafted mDA neurons need to functionally integrate into the host neural circuits in order to contribute to therapeutics. What inputs the grafted mDA neurons receive and how the activity of the transplanted neurons is regulated remain largely unknown. We will use sophisticated rabiesvirus-based circuit tracing and electrophysiological recording to reveal the anatomical and function inputs the grafted mDA neurons receive. The technology developed and the information gained from this study will prepare us for clinical translation.
