Singapore is in a unique position to study this as we have co-circulation of multiple carbapenemase genes and a contained waste management system.
kw: carbapenemase-producing Enterobacteriaceae, antimicrobial resistance, household transmission control

title: Deciphering the Role of ADARs-interacting RNA Helicases in Modulating RNA Editome in Cancer
abs: In the past decade, adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) RNA editing, catalyzed by ADARs (Adenosine DeAminase that act on RNAs), has been proven to be implicated in cancer development. However, it remains elusive how cancer cells disrupt the RNA editome balance to acquire malignant properties for their survival advantage. Structure of editing substrates and their recognition by ADARs have been described as key factors for A-to-I editing. By performing ADARs immunoprecipitation followed by mass spectrometry analysis (ADAR IP-MS), we identified 23 RNA helicases, a family of enzymes modulating RNA structures, RNA-RNA and protein-RNA interactions, may therefore play pivotal regulatory roles in A-to-I editing. Recently, 5 of them, including DDX5, DDX21, DDX3X, DDX6 and DDX17, were validated as ADARs-interacting RNA helicases. Our preliminary analysis suggested these ADARs-interacting RNA helicases are most likely to play distinct roles in reshaping A-to-I RNA editome in cancer. We hypothesize that these ADARs-interacting RNA helicases can precisely modulate the editing efficiency and substrate selectivity of ADARs, which in turn reshapes A-to-I RNA editome ultimately driving cancer development. In this research, we will be delineating regulatory roles of DDX5, DDX21, DDX3X, DDX6 and DDX17 and deciphering how they work in tandem to shape the global A-to-I editome profile and the underlying regulatory mechanisms adopted by each helicase. Our long-term goal is to understand whether disrupting cancer-driven (“hotspot”) editing events which are frequently regulated by different RNA helicases could block cancer progression.
kw: ADARs, RNA helicases, A-to-I RNA editing, Cancer

title: VALIDATION OF MOLECULAR TARGETS AND VULNERABILITIES IN NASOPHARYNGEAL CARCINOMA
abs: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is a common EBV-associated epithelial malignancy in Southern China and Southeast Asia, ranking as the third most common cancer among middle-aged Chinese males in Singapore. Patients are treated uniformly with radiotherapy and chemotherapy, with the majority of patients experiencing radiation-associated long-term side effects, such as dysphagia and xerostomia. Unfortunately, 35% of patients will also develop recurrent disease, for which treatment options are limited. As NPC biopsies are small and have significant stromal infiltrate, obtaining pure epithelial cells for gene expression profiling is a major challenge. In this proposal, we apply Smart-3SEQ, a novel microdissected paraffin-based RNA-seq approach, to overcome challenges with tumor purity in NPC. We will identify top molecular candidates differentially expressed in recurrent tumors, confirm them on immunohistochemistry, and model them in-vivo. We will also evaluate gene expression profiles from the tumor microenvironment to identify specific cell types and markers contributing to disease recurrence. We will leverage on our molecular understanding of the biology of NPC tumors, together with novel insights from gene expression profiles, in order to validate molecular therapies specific to DNA-repair vulnerabilities in NPC. We will establish in-vivo preclinical data that will serve as a foundation for clinical trials for de-escalation of radiotherapy in combination with targeted molecular therapies in primary NPC tumors, with the goal of reducing radiation-associated side effects. This study will provide critical information about heterogeneity between tumors, gene expression signatures for risk-stratification, correlation with the tumor microenvironment, as well as disease markers validated in-vivo and in histology. In particular, the systematic testing of DNA-repair vulnerabilities in-vivo and in patient-derived xenografts will provide an important basis for clinical translation in clinical trials, paving the way for the targeted treatment of NPC.
kw: Nasopharyngeal cancer; gene expression profiling; molecular vulnerabilities

title: Neural network reorganzation associated with upper limb motor recovery in stroke patients- establishing a prognostic model and tailoring neuromodulation for rehabilitation
abs: Todate, neural network reorganization in stroke recovery process is still not fully understood. Currently there is lack of biomarkers to inform rehabilitation with regards to predicting outcomes and measuring and predicting responses to treatment. Prognostic models that are clinically feasible are being explored more recently and have not been validated in the local population. Neural network changes associated with motor recovery appear to differ according to lesion and individual characteristics, suggesting that neuromodulatory interventions such as noninvasive brain stimulation should be tailored to individual stroke patients according to predicted patterns of neural reorganization to achieve the best motor outcomes. We will aim at upper limb (UL) motor recovery in this study as loss of UL function remains a significant cause of disability following stroke. This will be a multicentre study comprising 2 sub-studies. Study 1 will be an observational study to investigate the patterns of neural network reorganization in stroke patients with moderate to severe UL motor function impairment, and its correlation with motor function recovery. The integrity and excitability of the corticospinal tract will be measured by transcranial magnetic stimulation, high density electroencephalogram and functional magnetic resonance imaging , from within 1 month to 1 year post-stroke. UL motor function will be measured at the same time point. A model for predicting motor outcomes will be elicited. Study 2 will be a randomized trial to investigate which transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) strategy best facilitates UL motor recovery and the determinants of response. 2 excitatory tDCS strategies with different stimulating sites will be compared. This study is significant in that the result will help to stratify patients and tailor treatment, not just for neuromodulation, but also other treatment modalities in post-stroke rehabilitation. Knowledge of neural network reorganization will help in the future design of targeted treatment in stroke rehabilitation.
kw: Stroke, Motor recovery, Neuroplasticity, Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation, Transcranial direct current stimulation

title: Lipid Mediators of Brain Growth and Function
abs: The insulating myelin sheath surrounding axons is vital for optimal computational function of the brain. Demyelination is a hallmark of multiple sclerosis, brain injury, and normal aging. One of the barriers to developing treatments for demyelinating diseases is a limited understanding of the intrinsic factors that regulate oligodendrocyte differentiation and myelination, representing a major unmet medical need. Here we leverage our clinical data, mouse and cell models, and biochemical studies that deficiency of Mfsd2a, an omega-3 fatty acid lysolipid (LPC) transporter, in mice and humans resulted in microcephaly and severe hypomyelination. Remarkably, Mfsd2a is expressed in oligodendrocyte precursors (OPC) and specific deficiency of Mfsd2a in this precursor pool resulted in hypomyelination, indicating that LPC transport by OPC might regulate their proliferation and/or differentiation. Our long-term goal is the development of LPC-based therapeutics for brain health. The objective here, which builds upon our expertise of the Mfsd2a/LPC pathway, is to determine the mechanism by which LPCs regulate myelination. The central hypothesis is that LPC transport into OPCs via Mfsd2a is essential for OPC proliferation and differentiation. The rationale for our proposed studies is that determination of a mechanism of action for LPCs in myelination and demonstration of efficacy in enhancing myelination would catalyse clinical development of LPC-based nutritionals for aging and demyelinating disorders. Guided by strong preliminary data, the goal of this application will be achieved by two specific aims: (1) To determine the biochemical mechanism by which LPC transport via Mfsd2a functions to regulate myelination; (2) To determine if dietary LPC treatment can enhance myelination. The approach is innovative because it is designed to determine a biochemical function of LPCs in myelination. The proposed research is significant because it will provide key experimental information for the clinical development of LPC-based agents to enhance myelination in aging and demyelinating diseases.
kw: brain, lipid, polyunsaturated fatty acids, docosahexaenoic acid, transporters, metabolism

title: Mechanistic insights into kindlin-3 regulation and their roles in leukemia
abs: A major challenge in treating leukemia is the development of drug resistance. Cell adhesion mediated drug resistance (CAM-DR) protects leukemic cells from apoptosis induced by cytotoxic drugs and gamma irradiation. Defining key signaling nodes in CAM-DR will facilitate the development of new therapeutic strategies. Kindlins are cytoplasmic proteins that promote cell adhesion and migration. Kindlin-3 is expressed primarily in hematopoietic lineage cells. Deregulated expression of kindlin-3 has been reported in different cancers. We have shown that kindlin-3 regulates the proliferation of chronic myeloid leukemia cells. In this study, we will define the mechanism of kindlin-3 regulation. In our preliminary studies, we resolved the first structure of human full-length kindlin-3, demonstrated the presence of kindlin-3 monomer and trimer, and identified two phosphorylation sites in kindlin-3. Our central hypothesis posits kindlin-3 trimer in an auto-inhibited state. Dissociation of the trimer into monomers, and phosphorylation are required to promote kindlin-3 function. These post-translational modifications in kindlin-3 can have important roles in CAM-DR of leukemic cells. The specific aims of this research proposal are as follows. S.A. #1 To determine the function of kindlin-3 oligomerization. S.A. #2 To determine the function of kindlin-3 phosphorylation sites. S.A. #3 To analyze the structural and dynamical properties of kindlin-3 with interacting partner(s). S.A. #4 To examine the contributions of kindlin-3 oligomerization and phosphorylation in cell adhesion mediated drug resistance (CAM-DR), and to examine the phosphorylation status of kindlin-3 in leukemia patient samples. In this study, we will make use of different techniques and approaches that are direct and feasible. The team comprises basic scientists and a clinician with expertise in cell and molecular biology, X-ray and NMR structural biology, mass spectrometry proteomics, and leukemia drug-resistance.
kw: cell adhesion; cell signaling; cell migration

title: Single-cell histone modification analysis to study epigenetic heterogeneity and plasticity as a mechanism of tumor chemoresistance
abs: Understanding the underlying epigenetic mechanisms that drive drug resistance is crucial to identifying ways of circumventing resistance in cancer patients. Current bulk epigenetic assays, however, cannot dissect the intratumor heterogeneity and diversity of epigenetic response that lead to acquisition of drug resistance. We propose the novel Single Cell CUT&RUN (sc-CUT&RUN) method, which allows sensitive profiling of histone modifications in single cells, as a tool to investigate the selection and adaptation processes that lead to fixation of drug resistant epigenetic states in heterogeneous tumors. In Aim 1, we will establish sc-CUT&RUN for sensitive histone modification profiling in single cells. sc-CUT&RUN introduces in situ antibody-targeted endonuclease cleavage to solve the key bottleneck of inefficient immunoprecipitation and library preparation steps in chromatin immunoprecipitation. Development of sc-CUT&RUN will set a new paradigm for robust, high throughput measurement of epigenetic heterogeneity in various biological contexts. A further sub-aim is to combine sc-CUT&RUN with single-nuclei RNA-sequencing (sn-RNAseq) in the same cell to enable epigenomic-transcriptomic correlation. In Aim 2, we will investigate the epigenetic selection and adaptation of tumor cells that lead to acquired drug resistance. We will perform sc-CUT&RUN on patient-derived tumor cells before, during and after drug treatment, to evaluate pre-existing intra-tumor heterogeneity, as well as epigenetic response of individual cells that lead chemoresistance. Insights into trajectory of epigenetic response to cancer drugs will shed light on the multistep fixation of drug resistant epigenetic states. Finally, in Aim 3, we will test novel strategies to prevent the development of drug resistance by targeting the epigenetic landscape. Resistance promoting epigenetic changes identified from Aim 2 will be genetically or pharmacologically targeted to prevent drug resistance. Pre-empting these epigenetic changes early in disease progression may be an effective treatment strategy to circumvent resistance and improve survival of cancer patients.
kw: single cell analysis, histone, chromatin immunoprecipitation, drug resistance, epigenetics, tumor heterogeneity

title: Investigation of flavivirus immunity on the vertical transmission of Zika virus
abs: Zika virus (ZIKV) belongs to the family Flaviviridae, which includes globally relevant pathogens such as dengue virus (DENV), yellow fever and Japanese encephalitis. Although originally isolated in 1947, ZIKV is considered an emerging pathogen due to the recent wider spread and the more severe complications, such as ZIKV congenital syndrome (ZCS) that has been observed during recent outbreaks in the South Pacific and Latin America. The mechanism by which ZIKV crosses the placenta to establish an infection in the developing fetus is not well understood. Once established however, the potential options for therapeutic intervention become significantly narrowed. ZIKV transmission to fetuses is likely to depend on factors such as maternal viral load, local intrauterine viral persistence as determined by maternal antiviral antibodies and pre-existing immunity. Reduction in intrauterine viral load and persistence represents an important point of therapeutic intervention in the vertical transmission from mother to child. We have observed that maternal DENV immunity can enhance embryonic neural complications in mice and therefore hypothesise that immunity against flaviviruses prior to pregnancy facilitates vertical transmission of ZIKV leading to more severe manifestations of ZCS in primates and humans. In this proposal, we aim to test our hypothesis in cynomolgus macaques (Macaca fascicularis). This animal model is essential for understanding ZIKV transmission and pathogenesis, and for evaluating candidate vaccines and therapeutics. Furthermore, building upon preliminary data showing efficacy in the mouse model, we will test a candidate therapeutic monoclonal antibody for the prevention of fetal infection and severe ZCS. The results of this proposal have the potential to identify novel risk factors for ZCS and bring a candidate therapeutic through early pre-clinical testing.
kw: Zika virus; pathogenesis; pregnancy; macaque; transmission; microcephaly

title: Role of Semaphorin3e-Plexind1 signaling in left ventricular noncompaction (LVNC)
abs: Left ventricular noncompaction (LVNC) is one of the most common forms of genetic cardiomyopathy characterized by excessive trabeculation and impaired myocardial compaction during fetal development. In patients with primary cardiomyopathy of all types, LVNC is the third most common cardiomyopathy after dilated and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. LVNC has been associated with various forms of congenital and adult heart diseases and contributes to cardiac dysfunction. The LVNC phenotype may occur in isolation (22.6%) or associated with other cardiomyopathies such as dilated (58.7%) or hypertrophic (11%) cardiomyopathy. Patients with LVNC are at higher risk of developing systolic and diastolic dysfunction leading to heart failure, arrhythmias, and sudden cardiac death. While key regulators for cardiac chamber development are well studied, the role of Semaphorin-Plexin signaling in this process remains poorly understood. In this study, we propose to use Plxnd1 knockout, endothelium-specific Plxnd1 knockout, transgenic mice overexpressing Plxnd1 in endothelium and Sema3e knockout mice to determine the role of the Sema3e-Plxnd1 signaling pathway in ventricular trabeculation and compaction. Preliminary results demonstrate that genetic deletion of Plexind1 (Plxnd1), a class 3 semaphorin receptor in endothelial cells, leads to severe cardiac chamber defects, as characterized by excessive trabeculation and non-compaction similar to LVNC patients. To further establish the role of Semaphorin-Plexin signaling in ventricular noncompaction, we are doing gain-of-function experiment by generating transgenic mice overexpressing Plxnd1 in endothelial cells. Furthermore, for the first time, we demonstrate that Semaphorin 3e (Sema3e), one of Plxnd1’s ligands is expressed in the developing heart and may be required for myocardial compaction. Collectively, our results demonstrate that the Sema3e-Plxnd1 pathway is essential for myocardial trabeculation and compaction.
kw: LVNC, Semaphorin; Sema3e; Plxnd1; Myocardial trabeculation; Myocardial non-compaction

title: Target RAF Complex for Cancer Therapy
abs: Hyperactive Ras/RAF/MEK/ERK signaling has well-defined role in cancer development, which exists in over 85% cancers and plays a functional role in disease progression. Genetic studies have revealed that the aberrant activation of this signaling pathway mainly arises from the alterations of RAF, Ras, and Ras upstream regulators. In contrast to other components of this pathway, RAF and MEK have been thought as ideal targets for developing anti-cancer drugs, and indeed two RAF inhibitors (Vemurafenib and Dabrafenib) and one MEK inhibitor (Trametinib) have been generated and applied to clinic cancer treatment. However, these drugs have on efficacy to cancers with active Ras and only a short-term efficacy to BRAF(V600E)-mutated cancers. Mechanistic studies have shown that in cancers with active Ras, RAF, MEK and other molecules form a super complex that leads to the inhibitor resistance. The goal of this study is to understand how the RAF complex is assembled and thereby develop approaches to disrupt this complex for achieving better therapeutic efficacy. To reach this goal, we will employ advanced molecular biology, biochemistry, cancer biology and pharmacology methods to explore the compositions of RAF complex and its dynamic characteristics under variable pathological conditions and to construct effective approaches to block the hyperactive Ras/RAF/MEK/ERK singling by disrupting the RAF complex for cancer treatment. We believe the execution of this study will provide us more effective approaches/drugs for the treatment of cancers driven by hyperactive Ras/RAF/MEK/ERK singling, especially Ras-mutated cancers and drug-resistant BRAF(V600E) cancers.
kw: Oncogenic Protein kinases, Cancer, Cellular Signaling, Ras/RAF/MEK/ERK signalling, Protein kinase inhibitors, and drug resistance

title: The regulation of mTOR signaling in skeletal muscle growth and sarcopenia
abs: Sarcopenia is defined as a reduction of muscle mass and strength. Current clinical trials show that nutrient supplements have positive effects on muscle mass, but not on muscle function and strength. This demonstrates our limited understanding of the molecular events involved in the aging muscle. Disturbed protein homeostasis is implicated in the development of sarcopenia. The mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) is a conserved serine/threonine protein kinase that regulates protein homeostasis. Increased mTOR signaling, above basal level, causes a loss of sensitivity to nutrient availability in the elderly. Moreover, dysfunctions of muscle and adipose tissue often progress in parallel. Increased incidence of sarcopenia is also often seen in obese elderly and cachexic cancer patients, suggesting a complex systemic interplay between muscle and fat tissues. We hypothesize that uncontrolled mTOR activity, insensitive to nutrition, mediates age-related sarcopenia. Constitutive activation of mTOR in mice leads to premature aging in skeletal muscle and recapitulates many key features of human sarcopenia progression. In these mice enhanced protein synthesis and restricted autophagy leads to increased ER stress. Conversely, reduced mTOR signaling through activation of 4E-BP1 (eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4E–binding protein 1), a downstream effector, enhances protein quality by increasing autophagy activities and protects mice from aging-associated sarcopenia. These data underscore the importance of mTORC1 in the regulation of muscle homeostasis during aging. The proposed work seeks to identify (1) the mechanism(s) underlying sarcopenia upon mTOR activation in skeletal muscle and (2) the regulatory signaling between muscle and adipose tissue. We aim to examine the functional interplay at the organismal level and the effect of mTOR in muscle and adipose tissues. Identification of the mechanistic links between mTOR, sarcopenia and systemic metabolism will provide novel therapeutic strategies for sarcopenia and age-induced metabolic decline.
kw: sarcopenia; aging; mTOR; metabolism; protein homeostasis;

title: A novel chemical-biology approach to identify small-molecule modulators of death receptor p75NTR signaling and activity
abs: Ligand binding to transmembrane receptors triggers conformational re-arrangement of intracellular domains mediated by relative movement of transmembrane domains (TMDs) in receptor complexes. The main hypothesis of this proposal is that small molecules targeting the molecular interphases of TMDs in receptor complexes may perturb TMD movements that underlie ligand-mediated receptor activation and hence constitute useful chemical probes for acute and reversible modulation of transmembrane receptor activity. The p75 neurotrophin receptor (p75NTR) is a prototypic “death receptor” and a member of the Tumor Necrosis Factor Receptor Superfamily (TNFRSF). A highly conserved Cys residue in the p75NTR TMD is required for ligand-mediated receptor activation by mediating a scissor-like movement of TMDs that leads to transient separation of intracellular domains, allowing the binding of intracellular effectors. In addition to its activities in the nervous system, p75NTR has been shown to control the survival and invasiveness of melanoma tumors, as well as other canncers. The crucial role played by the p75NTR TMDs prompted us to investigate whether small molecules capable of binding to the p75NTR TMD can affect receptor function. Applying this concept in a screening assay, we have identified a compound targeting the TMD of p75NTR which induced profound conformational changes leading to receptor activity, melanoma cell death, and inhibition of tumor growth. We propose to use our discovery pipeline to identify novel small molecules to modify the activity profile of p75NTR. The specific aims of this proposal include: 1. Identification of novel chemical probes targeting the TMD of p75NTR 2. Molecular and structural studies of identified compounds 3. Optimization of lead compounds by medicinal chemistry 4. Characterization of in vitro and in vivo activities in relevant biological systems: cell signaling and biological assays, pharmacokinetics and toxicology, in vivo assays The new compounds identified will have applications in the development of novel cancer therapeutics.
kw: drug discovery, transmembrane receptor, p75ntr, melanoma, glioma

title: Molecular mechanisms of synaptic depression: Roles of synapsin-synapsin interactions
abs: Synapses are the target of many, and perhaps most, brain disorders. Repeated activity causes synapses to weaken over time, a type of plasticity known as synaptic depression. Synaptic depression is involved in numerous higher-order brain functions, with alterations in depression associated with a variety of neurological and psychiatric disorders, including epilepsy, neurodegenerative disorders, schizophrenia and other brain disorders. The goal of this project is to refine our understanding of the molecular mechanisms of depression. Specifically, we will focus on synapsins, a family of presynaptic proteins implicated in synaptic depression. Synapsins bind to synaptic vesicles (SVs), membrane-bound organelles involved in neurotransmitter storage and release. We will advance understanding of the function of synapsins in depression at excitatory synapses by testing four novel hypotheses motivated by the well-known ability of synapsins to bind to other synapsins (oligomerization). First, we will consider the possibility that synapsin IIa cross-links SVs to create a “reserve pool” of SVs. Second, we will test the hypothesis that another isoform, synapsin Ia, makes cross-linked SVs sensitive to synaptic activity via a calcium-calmodulin-dependent protein kinase. Third, we will determine whether another synapsin isoform, synapsin Ib, serves as an endogenous dominant-negative regulator of synaptic depression. Finally, we will examine the functional consequences of a schizophrenia-associated mutation in a fourth isoform, synapsin IIIa. To test these hypotheses, we will use both in vitro reconstitution assays and electrophysiological and imaging experiments in living hippocampal neurons. Our experiments will clarify molecular mechanisms involved in regulation of synaptic depression, a widespread and important form of synaptic plasticity. Our results also will improve our understanding of SV trafficking mechanisms and yield novel insights into the numerous neurological and psychiatric disorders that result from defects in synaptic depression and/or defects in synapsins.
kw: synaptic transmission; synaptic plasticity; membrane trafficking; synapsins; neuroscience

title: Understanding the Paradigm of Elderly and Middle-Age Onset of Diabetes
abs: Aims: 1. To understand the age-related pathophysiology of glucose intolerance, in terms of body composition, insulin resistance and β-cell dysfunction. 2. To investigate how this pathophysiology drives diabetic complications, against the backdrop of evolving (non-diabetes specific) aging-related loss of organs function. Hypotheses: 1. Individuals with elderly-onset diabetes (>=65 years old) are more likely to have excessive adiposity and lower skeletal muscle mass than those with middle-age-onset diabetes (40-64 years old) 2. Excessive adiposity and sarcopenia (uncommon among the young) are associated with IR, β-cell dysfunction, which contribute to glucose intolerance in the elderly. 3. Sarcopenic obesity, IR and hyperglycemia (secondary to β-cell dysfunction) are associated with vascular dysfunction (e.g. arterial stiffness & other intermediate phenotype) in those with elderly-onset diabetes. 4. Sarcopenic obesity, IR and hyperglycemia are associated with geriatric syndrome (e.g. frailty) and end organ injury (e.g. chronic kidney disease) Methodology and Approach Cross-sectional phase (for hypotheses 1-4): This will involve 300 individuals in three groups: (1) aged ≥65 years old and diagnosed with diabetes within 1 year from study entry (n=100); (2) aged 40-64 years old and diagnosed with diabetes within 1 year from studty entry (n=100) ; and (3) no diabetes (n=100). The following will be assessed: body composition, insulin resistance, β-cell function (HOMA2b) and β-cell reserve; arterial stiffness and inflammation, and frailty using FRAIL questionnaire and Reported Edmonton Frail Scale. Prospective phase (for hypotheses 3-4): This involves 2,100 individuals with type 2 diabetes in SMART2D cohort recruited from NMRC-funded PPG KTPH and primary care polyclinics in 2011-2013 and then followed up till 2017 had measurements collected at baseline and follow-up including body composition, insulin, glycemic control, pulse wave velocity, footscreen and renal function). These patients will be recalled again for prospective assessment of body composition, insulin resistance, β-cell function, vascular function, diabetes complications and frailty. Clinical Significance 1. Understanding the body composition in the elderly-onset diabetes vs. middle-age-onset diabetes will justify experiments which help to (a) quantify body composition in increasing details / resolution; (b) better understand adipocytes physiology (e.g. measuring adipokines, inflammatory markers) and muscle function (e.g. measuring myokines, muscle strength etc.) 2. Understanding IR in elderly-onset diabetes vs. middle-age-onset diabetes will lay the foundation for intervention i.e. to reduce (visceral) adiposity or to increase muscle mass or both. 3. The findings on the roles of IR and hyperglycemia in the pathophysiology of diabetic complications will help identify potential points of intervention to delay or prevent diabetic complications 4. The study offers a precious opportunity to obser
