title: Dissecting the Spatio-temporal Dynamics of Chromatin Remodeling in Single Human Cells in Health and Cancer
abs: In human cells, the packing of genomic DNA into nucleosomes poses a topological challenge when genome access is required. Such constraint is alleviated via chromatin remodeling mediated by remodeler proteins, and misregulation of chromatin remodeling has been associated with a wide range of human diseases, including cancer. To date, our knowledge of the remodeling process is mainly limited to its genetics and biochemistry; on the other hand, how this process takes place in both time and space within individual human cell remains poorly understood. We hypothesize that the spatio-temporal organization and dynamics of chromatin remodeling plays an equally, if not more critical role in dictating the modes of remodeler-DNA interaction, and the aberrant regulation of such organizational dynamics may lead to unintended genome access and expression, and thus constitute a driving force that underlies tumorigenesis. Leveraging on a set of powerful imaging-based approaches we have previously developed (specifically reflected light-sheet super-resolution microscopy and photoactivatable fluorescence correlation spectroscopy), this proposal aims to elucidate the spatial organization and temporal dynamics of chromatin remodeling in both healthy and cancerous cells, and quantitatively dissect the role of such organizational dynamics in tumorigenesis. Using the SWI/SNF family of remodelers as model system, we will: 1: Directly visualize the temporal DNA-binding dynamics of remodeler proteins in single human cells; 2: Elucidate the spatial distribution of remodeler binding “hotspots” within the cell nucleus; 3: Reveal quantitative changes in such spatio-temporal organization and dynamics associated with cancer. Overall, this study promises to reveal first-of-its-kind insights into the hierarchical landscape regulating chromatin remodeling at the single-cell level, and provide a novel framework for understanding the molecular and physical origins of cancer. Such insights could potentially transform our ability to detect and diagnose cancer, as well as aid the development of more efficacious therapeutic strategies.
kw: Chromatin remodeling; tumorigenesis; single-cell imaging; molecular genomics; origins of cancer

title: Roles of the MYCN enhancer and its associated enhancer RNA in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia and hematopoiesis
abs: Dysregulation of transcription factor genes is a hallmark of T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL), a hematological malignancy arisen from immature thymocytes. Oncogenic transcription factors are often abnormally expressed or activated in this disease and induce an aberrant transcriptional network by regulating downstream targets including protein-coding genes and non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs). I recently conducted a comprehensive profiling of long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) activated by the oncogene TAL1 in T-ALL. I identified a novel lncRNA, named encMYCN, that was expressed from a putative enhancer controlling the MYCN oncogene. A significant positive correlation between MYCN and encMYCN expressions were observed in primary T-ALL cases. Importantly, the MYCN enhancer was directly activated by the TAL1 transcriptional complex. Repression of this element resulted in inhibition of both MYCN and encMYCN expressions. MYCN expression was required for the survival of T-ALL cells. These findings led to my central hypothesis: ectopic expression of TAL1 ‘hijacks’ the MYCN enhancer and re-activates this locus that is normally silenced in immature T-cells, thereby aberrantly inducing the MYCN oncogene. encMYCN may serve as an enhancer RNA (eRNA) to activate the enhancer in cis to promote the expression of MYCN during T-cell leukemogenesis. Notably, the MYCN enhancer and encMYCN are normally expressed in hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells. Hence, I further hypothesize that the MYCN enhancer and encMYCN may be essential for normal hematopoiesis. The overall purpose of this study is to clarify the roles of the MYCN enhancer and encMYCN in hematopoiesis and T-cell leukemogenesis. In Aim1, I will analyze molecular mechanisms of how encMYCN activates MYCN enhancer to promote MYCN expression. In Aim 2, I will analyze whether the conserved Mycn enhancer affects normal hematopoiesis or/and T-cell leukemogenesis using mouse models. Results from this study will provide both molecular insights into eRNA functions and also novel therapeutic strategy for T-ALL.
kw: T-Cell Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia; non-coding RNAs; Enhancer; Oncogene; MYCN; Hematopoiesis

title: Post-transcriptional mechanisms shape the fibrotic response in NASH
abs: Numerous common and rare diseases have a fibrotic component, which either drives or modulates disease. Liver fibrosis due to indications such as NASH is prevalent in Singapore. We will focus on a key hepatic cell type, the hepatic stellate cell (HSC), and profile the genome-wide translatome using Ribo-seq during the pathogenic activation of HSCs through TGFB1. This will reveal the molecular mechanisms underlying this pathogenic cellular transition and lead to the identification of key downstream therapeutic targets for the treatment of human liver disease. We will then perform sophisticated bioinformatic analyses to prioritize key pathogenic hubs, either post-transcriptional regulators such as RNA-binding proteins or extracellular signalling molecules that are amenable to therapeutic targeting. Integration of additional public and in-house datasets will reveal central downstream molecules that are required for the fibrogenic TGFB1 effect. As a final step, identified drivers of disease will be verified using established in-house in vitro and in vivo preclinical models of disease. This preclinical data package will be the basis for further diagnostic and therapeutic developments beyond this project.
kw: Fibrosis; NASH; Post-transcriptional regulation; Therapeutic target discovery

title: Light-Activatable Theranostic Nanoparticles to Improve the Delivery and Cardioprotective Efficacy of Cytoprotective Peptides in Acute Myocardial Infarction.
abs: Recently clinical studies have failed to demonstrate beneficial effects with different cardioprotective agents in patients with acute myocardial infarction (AMI). This outcome may have, in part, been due to reduced bioavailability and failure to deliver the agent to ischaemic cardiomyocytes within the first few minutes of reperfusion. The goal of this proposal is to develop a theranostic nanosystem that is able to provide fast and on-demand timed delivery of a cardioprotective agent for reducing infarct size together with simultaneous imaging of the ischaemic myocardium. We will load the nanosystem with a novel multi-target cytoprotective peptide, ND-13 (a mimic of the mitochondrial protein, DJ-1), which has been shown to reduce myocardial infarct (MI) size in an ex vivo AMI Langendorff model, but was compromised in an in vivo AMI rodent model due to low systemic bioavailability. Hypothesis: Novel PEGylated multi-functional nanoparticles, which are near-infrared (NIR) light-activatable, and which contain cardiac-homing peptide, will improve the delivery of ND-13 peptide to the ischaemic myocardium, and increase the efficacy of ND-13 in reducing infarct size, when compared to ND-13 alone or conventional nanoparticles. Aims of the proposal: By exploring a theranostic strategy with targeting nanosystems in a AMI murine model, we aim: (1) To achieve a “Burst” drug release upon NIR irradiation localised to the ischaemic area-at-risk; (2) To facilitate AMI imaging and monitor the delivery by targeting the heart ; (3) To achieve superior pharmacological efficacy in reducing MI size via timed/targeted delivering ND-13 into cardiomyocytes. The overarching goal of this project is to develop novel smart nanoparticles for improved drug delivery to reduce MI size, prevent heart failure and improve clinical outcomes in patients with AMI.
kw: Theranostic Nanoparticles, Targeting, Smart Drug Delivery, Peptide, CT, Acute Myocardium Infarction

title: Assessing the Effect of Flaviviral Pre-immunity on Yellow Fever Vaccine-induced Humoral Responses Using A Systems Serology Approach
abs: Mosquito-borne flaviviruses are significant public health concerns to Singapore and many other tropical and subtropical nations. Licensed vaccines for human use currently exist against three flaviviruses, namely Yellow Fever virus (YFV), Japanese Encephalitis virus (JEV), and Dengue virus (DENV). Unfortunately, the most recently licensed vaccine for DENV (i.e. Dengvaxia) had low efficacy in flavivirus-naïve individuals despite generating neutralizing antibodies. Interestingly, this vaccine elicited high protective efficacy in flavivirus-immune individuals. To date, the effect of flavivirus pre-immunity on the immune response to a subsequent unrelated flavivirus has not been well characterized. This proposal investigates the effect of pre-existing cross-reactive flaviviral antibodies on the humoral response to a subsequent flavivirus vaccine. We utilized samples from a recently completed study in our group, where healthy flavivirus-naïve individuals were either given JEV vaccine followed by YFV vaccination (i.e. the pre-immune group) or only the YFV vaccine (i.e. the naïve group). Preliminary data show that the pre-immune group had higher YFV-specific binding antibodies, but lower YFV neutralization as compared to the naïve group. This indicates differences in the antigen-recognition properties of the YFV-specific polyclonal antibodies. Furthermore, we observed that the pre-immune group had significantly lower ratio of YFV-specific IgG3 to total IgG, implying a possible difference in antibody effector functions between pre-immune and naïve groups. Taking our preliminary results into account, we hypothesize that the presence of preexisting flavivirus antibodies can shape both the antigen-recognition and effector-mediated human antibody response following subsequent vaccination with an unrelated flavivirus. We will investigate this hypothesis using a cutting edge approach called Systems Serology, which allows the bioinformatic integration of experimentally measured antigen-recognition and effector features of the humoral response. As the first Systems Serology platform in Singapore, it will serve to stimulate future collaborations with academia and industry in evaluating current vaccines and designing new protective vaccines.
kw: Vaccination; Flavivirus; Antibody response; Systems serology; Bio-computational analysis; Yellow Fever virus

title: A mechanistic study of epigenetic regulation by PBRM1 towards targeted therapy in clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC)
abs: An in-depth knowledge of the epigenetic mechanisms that drive cancer initiation, development and progression can enhance our understanding of tumorigenesis and provide opportunities for better diagnosis and novel therapy. We previously found that polybromo-1 (PBRM1), an accessory subunit of the SWItch/Sucrose-Non-Fermentable (SWI/SNF) nucleosome remodeling complex, is the second most commonly mutated gene in clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC, 40%) (Varela, Nature). Additionally, we demonstrated that the loss of PBRM1 is indispensable for ccRCC initiation in genetic mouse models (Nargund, Cell Reports). Despite its importance, the epigenetic function of PBRM1 remains largely obscure, due to the lack of genome-wide PBRM1-binding profiles and detailed profiling of chromatin changes upon PBRM1 loss. Here, we seek to elucidate how PBRM1 regulates the chromatin with the hypothesis that tumorigenic genes are liberated epigenetically upon PBRM1 inactivation (Aim 1). Consequently, we like to understand how the downstream targets of PBRM1 affect ccRCC development and initiation (Aim 2). Finally, with the deciphered mechanisms we may be able to pinpoint new druggable targets that are synthetically lethal with the loss of PBRM1 (Aim 3). Mechanistic understanding of driver mutations can identify vulnerabilities specific to cancer. CcRCC has two main drivers – VHL and PBRM1. Recent study by our team has showed that the first driver event, VHL loss, epigenetically triggers master regulators of ccRCC through enhancer activation and paved the technical groundwork for this study (Yao, Cancer Discovery). Characterizing the second driver PBRM1 will complete a major milestone in understanding epigenetic malfunction of ccRCC. Our study is also applicable to other cancer types, as the loss of PBRM1 is also one of the top drivers for them. Importantly, we hope that findings from our study can lead to targeted and effective treatment for patients harboring these driver mutations, and translate into better patient survival and life quality.
kw: ccRCC, epigenomics, PBRM1, drugs

title:
Modelling the immune suppressive solid tumor microenvironment
for immunotherapy optimization
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Immunotherapy aims to redirect the patient’s immune system to fight against a specific pathology and holds great promise as a novel cancer treatment. While the investment in research and pharma is at an all-time high in the immunotherapy and cell therapy sector, these new strategies are more likely to fail in a solid tumor context during clinical trials. The critical role of the tumor microenvironment (TME) in adoptive cell-mediated cancer immunotherapy is now recognized in the research and clinical community. However, our understanding of the relationship between the TME components and the immune system is limited. 3D microfluidic multicellular assays with real-time imaging and precise control over spatiotemporal parameters are poised to help elucidate the roles played by each cell type involved in this complex domain. Therefore, we propose a multidisciplinary strategy to model solid human liver cancer microenvironment in vitro. The final goal is to reach the clinical trial stage with a higher percentage of successful treatment to reduce the cost of research and drug development process. In particular, we’ll focus on the investigation of engineered tumor-specific T cell combined with immune checkpoint inhibitors in a TME microfluidic model which has a remarkable feature of monitoring cell-cell interactions and dynamics. The model could represent an efficient preclinical tool to be potentially used during clinical trials to match the optimal drug and technique to individual cancer patients. Indeed, proposed here is a novel approach by using primary human tumors to investigate patient-specific responses and use the assay as a preclinical tool. Since there are currently no validated methodologies to study immunotherapy response in patient-derived cancer specimens, this proposal has the potential to provide a state-of-the-art technology with wide ranging implications and have the potential to be clinically and economically impactful.
kw: immunotherapy, tumor microenvironment, liver tumor, T cell therapy, 3D cell culture, microfluidic

title: Point-of-Care diagnosis of pathogen nucleic acids using DNA nanostructure enzyme complexes for amplification and visual readout
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: By constructing multiple DNA-enzyme molecular complexes, I can leverage on the ability of DNA to specifically recognize nucleic acid sequences and the enzymes' ability to amplify the signal and convert it into a colour output. This system works at room temperature and uses inexpensive components, allowing a Point-of-Care disease test to be performed at under a dollar. It can also be redesigned to recognise different sequences by changing just a single component, a DNA strand. To expand ability of the sequence to detect single base pair mutations, which are associated with many diseases and may change the treatment, I will use chemically modified bases and secondary structures which have been successfully used to detect single nucleotide mutations in other assay systems. By trying various chemical and enzymatic lysis conditions, I will optimise a simple nucleic acid extraction protocol from cells in various biological fluids at room temperature. The preliminary results show promising yields, and success will enable Point-of-Care sample to result tests. I will incorporate these advances into a new prototype microfluidic chip to create a foolproof diagnostic chip. I will design tests that detect respiratory viruses and bacteria which cause pneumonia. This will be validated in biological samples and a proof-of-concept will be shown with collected clinical samples.
kw: Diagnostic, Infectious Disease, Point-of-Care

title: Exploiting Chromosomal Translocations and Fusion Genes in Multiple Myeloma for Targeted Therapy
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Multiple Myeloma (MM) is a plasma cell malignancy characterised by marked molecular heterogeniety including varying ploidy status and chromosomal translocations. The t(14;16) translocation occurs in about 4% of MM patients and is associated with poor prognosis and resistance to proteosome inhibitor (PI) therapy. Recently, a study of a cohort of MM cases suggested that patients with the t(14;16) translocation tended to aberrantly activate kinase domains via formation of fusion genes. For example, the EML4-ALK (Echinoderm microtubule-associated protein-like 4-anaplastic lymphoma kinase) fusion gene that is prevalent in lung adenocarcinomas, was also present in these t(14;16) MM patients. While various ALK fusion genes have been reported in various maglinancies, how ALK contributes to poor prognosis and PI therapy resistance in t(14;16) MM is not known. Additionally, a recent compound screen carried out in our lab identified ALK inhibitors as selectively killing MM cell lines that carry the t(14;16) translocation, further supporting a role for ALK in MM and ALK inhibitors as a possible form of disease intervention. In addition, several gene fusions with the NF-κB-inducing kinase (NIK) was also reported. While the overexpression of NIK due to mutations in TNF receptor associated factor 3 (TRAF3) in MM is well-studied, stabilisation of NIK in t(14;16) has not been previously described. Since there is an on-going project in the lab developing novel inhibitors to NIK, it will be interesting to investigate the use of NIK inhibitors in t(14;16) MM. In view of this, we aim identify the prevalence of the kinase fusion genes in t(14;16) primary patient and immortalised MM cell lines. We will then elucidate the roles that these kinase fusion proteins play in MM and investigate the use of kinase inhibitors in t(14;16) MM, demonstrating the importance of stratifying patients according to both their translocation and fusion gene status.
kw: multiple myeloma; targeted therapy; drug discovery; gene fusions

title: Detecting Early Changes in Kidney Function in Preadolescents with Poor Fetal Growth Using Functional MRI
inst: IHDP - Institute for Human Development and Potential
abs: Singapore has a high prevalence (12.8%) of chronic kidney disease (CKD), with the prevalence projected to increase to 25% by 2035. Progression of CKD to end stage renal disease represents a significant burden on the local healthcare infrastructure due to the intensive management required. There is compelling evidence that poor fetal growth and the resulting deficits in nephron endowment can increase susceptibility for CKD and hypertension. Our preliminary work in the GUSTO birth-cohort indicated that children with poor fetal growth (25.9% incidence) had elevated blood pressure as early as 6 years, but it was not clear if this was associated with altered kidney function. Low nephron endowment and compensatory renal growth have been linked to an increased single nephron glomerular filtration rate and increased sodium reabsorption. Poor fetal growth can also increase kidney sodium reabsorption through pathways not related to nephron deficits, particularly developmentally programmed elevations in glucocorticoid and sympathetic activity. We hypothesize that the above maladaptive changes in the kidney can be noninvasively imaged using functional kidney MRI techniques. Specifically, in 10-year-old children recruited from the GUSTO cohort, we aim to evaluate the effect of poor fetal growth on functional MRI based markers of kidney perfusion, diffusion and oxygenation. We also plan to assess if these markers are associated with estimated GFR (by plasma creatinine), glucocorticoid activity (by salivary cortisol), sympathetic activity (by salivary α-amylase), urine concentrating defects (by urine osmolality) and serum metabolic profile (by NMR metabolomics). The feasibility of the proposed MRI techniques has been already evaluated in adult volunteers. An improved understanding of the early changes in kidney function in children with poor fetal growth can better inform the timing and nature of the specific dietary, lifestyle or pharmacological interventions that can halt the progression of kidney disease at a very early stage.
kw: Chronic Kidney Disease, Poor Fetal Growth, Nephron Endowment, Hypertension, MRI

title: Critical re-evaluation of APP trafficking and Aβ production models in neurons in concert with development of microimmunoelectrode sensors for real-time Aβ measurements in culture
abs: The amyloid precursor protein (APP) and its proteolytic derivative amyloid-beta (Aβ) are critically implicated in Alzheimer’s disease (AD), the most common dementia. APP trafficking pathways and their effects on Aβ production and secretion are well described in non-neural cell lines, and clathrin-/dynamin-dependent APP endocytosis is proposed to be a key step in Aβ production. However, direct evidence for this hypothesis is lacking in neurons, and significant knowledge gaps concerning the underlying mechanisms remain. We developed an assay to quantify APP endocytosis in cells using the previously characterized bungarotoxin-ligand system. Unexpectedly, the dynamin inhibitor Dyngo4A did not block APP endocytosis in the somatodendritic compartment of mouse hippocampal neurons, even though Dyngo4A profoundly inhibited APP endocytosis in Hela cells. Surface biotinylation experiments likewise revealed no decrease in endogenous APP endocytosis in mouse cortical neurons pre-incubated with Dyngo4A. These exciting preliminary findings, if confirmed and expanded, would transform our understanding of APP trafficking in neurons. In this proposal, our first aim is to study APP endocytosis in axonal compartments, primarily through the use of microfluidic chambers. Given that dynamin inhibitors decrease secreted Aβ in transgenic AD mice in vivo, our working hypothesis is that neurons utilize different endocytic mechanisms to internalize axonal and somatodendritic surface APP pools – a remarkable example of neuronal compartment-specific regulation. Concurrently, we aim to develop an in vitro microimmunoelectrode (MIE) system capable of measuring Aβ concentrations in real time. By measuring the effect of Dyngo4A on Aβ secretion in neuronal cultures, we will be able to correlate compartment-specific (axonal versus somatodendritic) APP endocytosis with Aβ secretion. Together, these observations will help provide answers to the longstanding question regarding the subcellular location(s) of Aβ production and secretion. In addition, the institutional collaborations fostered through this proposal should provide rich opportunities for future scientific and clinical inquiry.
kw: Alzheimer's disease; Amyloid Precursor Protein; Amyloid-beta; Protein trafficking; Real-time sensors; Primary Neurons

title: Unraveling the evolutionary origin of low vaccine efficacy                                       in the H3N2 influenza virus
abs: Influenza H3N2 virus is the predominant form of seasonal influenza virus. It infects 5-15% of the total population and leads to an estimated half a million deaths annually. Vaccination against influenza viruses is the primary strategy for prevention and control of influenza outbreaks. Despite many years of efforts, there has been an alarming decrease in the efficacy of the H3N2 vaccine in recent years. Both antigenic drift and passage adaptation (substitutions accumulated during vaccine production in embryonated eggs) can result in mismatches between the vaccine and circulating strains, leading to low vaccine efficacy. In our two earlier studies, we observed a strong negative correlation between egg passage adaptation and vaccine efficacy. Accordingly, we plan to employ approaches from evolutionary genetics and computational biologic to achieve the following goals: 1) Characterize the temporal dynamics of passage adaptation across the years and pinpoint major codon positions responsible for low vaccine efficacy, 2)Experimentally validate adaptive alleles through viral culturing and functional studies, 3) Study passage adaptation in other genes and explore the evolutionary link to vaccine efficacy, 4) Develop a computational package guiding vaccine production and link it to the public server (FluSurver) for real-time surveillance, and 5) Construct a computational package for analyzing adaptive evolution over large phylogenies.
kw: H3N2 influenza virus, Vaccine efficacy, Passage adaptation, Mutational mapping

title: Mapping Cellular and Molecular Pathology in Autism Spectrum Disorders using Human Brain Organoids and Spatial Transcriptomics
abs: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is the top disease burden among children in Singapore and across developed world. Patients struggle with social communication, display repetitive behaviors and have restricted interests. These behavioral hallmarks manifest early in childhood but persist for life, costing society >USD260 billion per year. To date, no drugs target the above core symptoms- existing drugs only alleviate co-morbidities like seizures and hyperactivity, while behavioral interventions provide limited relief. A major roadblock has been a poor understanding of pathology at a cellular and tissue level. Our objective is to define neuropathological substrates in autistic brains and surrogate models, with a long-term goal of developing molecular therapeutics that target core symptoms of ASD. We hypothesize that specific changes in organization, morphology and interactions of particular cell types underlie ASD. Since these cellular features are three-dimensional, we will model ASD in human brain organoids and analyze these features within their tissue architecture. We will first verify patient-derived organoid models against bulk transcriptomes and gross anatomy of postmortem ASD brains (Aim 1). Next, we will identify cell types with altered gene expression in ASD organoid models using single-cell RNAseq (Aim 2). Then, we will determine abnormal arrangement and morphology of cell types in ASD organoids using protein markers and a novel, high-throughput RNA-imaging technology called Multiplexed, Error-robust Fluorescence In Situ Hybridization (MERFISH) (Aim 3). I have tested eight brain organoid protocols and identified the optimal method for reproducible generation of brain organoids. Since application of MERFISH to brain organoids is novel, I optimized sample preparation and performed single-molecule FISH as a proxy for MERFISH, with success. The cellular cartography of autistic brains and ‘mini-brains’ will unveil ASD pathology and identify potential drug targets that can be directly tested on our organoid platform.
kw: Autism; Pathology; Organoids; Human Brain; Transcriptomics

title: Single-cell RNA-seq in combination with CRISPR screening to Identify mode of Immunoresistance in Metastatic Breast Cancers
abs: Tumors are the complex ecosystem of various cell populations ranging from malignant cells to immune cells. Outcome of this interplay results in either elimination or colonization of tumor cells at primary and secondary metastatic sites (1). The first layer of immune defense is effected by Natural killer (NK) cells of the innate immune system, and the second layer by T cells of the adaptive immune system (2). While exciting advances have been made in T cell-mediated cancer therapies, the comparative lack of understanding of how NK cells can better control cancer has kept this promising therapeutic avenue relatively unexplored (3). Furthermore, a common immune evasion mechanism in cancer cells relies on downregulation of the antigen presentation complex, which prevents T-cell recognition, but conversely increases the targeting efficacy of Nk-cells. However, the variation within tumor cells i.e. Intra-Tumor Heterogeneity (ITH), allows tumor cells to escape adaptive immune clearance (4). Moreover, it is believed given their motile nature and ability to survive in hostile environments, metastatic cells are more prone to immune escape (5). Therefore, this proposal focuses on investigating the mechanisms of Nk-mediated immune evasion, employed by metastatic cancer cells. I will further optimize our existing technologies that enable expansion of patient-derived Nk cells and tumor cells, and use these paired models to mimic immune-tumor interaction for both noninvasive and metastatic breast cancer (Aim 1). I will probe at the single-cell resolution whether and how variation among tumor cells might impact Nk-mediated killing of metastatic cells (Aim 2). Finally, I will interrogate the genetic dependencies underlying tumor-Nk interaction with single-cell CRISPR-screens to uncover the mechanism of immune sensitivity and resistance (Aim 3). Our goal is to identify biomarkers of NK-cell-mediated immunotherapy response for better patient stratification, and to identify targetable vulnerabilities that can be exploited for immunotherapy.
kw: Breast Cancer, Nk cells, Immunoresistance, Metastasis, Single cell genomics, CRISPR

title: Investigation of RETO, A Novel Endogenous Peptide Inhibitor of chemokine receptors CCR7 and CCR9.
abs: We have identified a novel gene, RETO that is enriched in the skin and downregulated in several conditions associated with skin inflammation. The RETO gene encodes for a secreted peptide. By carrying out a high throughput screen for putative receptors, we found that RETO inhibits chemokine receptors CCR7 and CCR9, both of which have established roles in regulating the immune system. In particular, the CCR7 receptor is required for the migration of skin immune cells to the lymph nodes under steady state and inflammation. Congruent with our screening results, we found that Reto knockout mice have exacerbated inflammatory responses upon exposure to the Hapten DNFB (2,4-dinitro-1-fluorobenzene), supporting our hypothesis that one of the physiological functions of this novel peptide is to regulate skin immunity. Using biochemical and functional assays, we will carry out in depth characterisation of this novel receptor-ligand pair and identify residues critical for the interaction. To gain insights to the physiological function of Reto, we will carry out immune profiling of Reto knockout mice in order to identify changes in the skin immune population under steady state and during DNFB induced inflammation. The characterisation of RETO may open new paradigms for understanding how the immune system is regulated, and pave the way for the discovery of other endogenous antagonists of the immune system. Both targets of RETO are well established chemokine receptors and are recognised as potential drug targets for several clinical indications including Crohn’s disease, chronic graft vs. host disease and cancer. In the long term, as an endogenous peptide for these receptors, RETO may serve as a potential lead molecule for the development of biologic agents targeting CCR7 and CCR9.
kw: Novel peptide, chemokine receptor antagonist

title: The role of LINC complex-mediated nuclear migration in striated muscle development and laminopathies
abs: The proposal will investigate 2 aspects of LINC complex-mediated nuclear migration in striated muscle relevant to muscular dystrophy and dilated cardiomyopathy. First, we will use live fluorescence microscopy of mNeonGreen-labeled nuclei in differentiating C2C12 myotubes to study nuclear centration, the first stage of muscle fiber formation, where the nuclei of myoblasts fusing with myotubes migrate to the centre of the myotube. To facilitate determination of nuclear centration speed, we are developing computational image analysis tools. We will determine the role of the LINC complex, specifically the KASH domain proteins Nesprin-1 and Nesprin-2, and their potential or known microtubule-associated interactors, dynein, Pericentrin and Akap450, in the speed of nuclear centration. We will use siRNA depletion, chemical inhibition, or dominant negative disruption of these proteins to assess their role in nuclear centration. We will validate potential physical interactions between the Nesprins and the microtubule-associated proteins by co-immunoprecpitation. Second, we will use myotubes as an in vitro model to investigate the role of Sun1 mutations in ameliorating physiological defects associated with lamin A/C (Lmna) mutations in mice. Recent evidence suggests that Sun1-containing LINC complexes preferentially interact with microtubule cytoskeleton proteins to drive nuclear damage in Lmna mutant myotubes, leading to pathology. We propose to dissect the role of Sun1 in this system by Sun1 complementation experiments using constructs with mutations affecting Sun1 tertiary structure and domain swaps with the paralogous Sun2. We will test, via Sun1-dependent recruitment of Pericentrin to the nuclear envelope of myotubes, whether these mutations interfere with Sun1 LINC interactions with microtubule cytoskeleton proteins. We will then test how these mutations influence nuclear damage in Lmna mutant myotubes using established indicators of nuclear rupture (cGAS accumulation) and DNA damage (gH2AX). These studies will enable us to understand both fundamental mechanisms of muscular dystrophy and related cardiomyopathy caused by Lmna mutations.
kw: muscle development; LINC complex; nuclear migration; laminopathies

title: Investigating mechanisms and potential treatment regimes of diabetes in the non-obese adult through the usage of the lipodystrophic diabetic seipin mouse model.
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Diabetes is highly prevalent in today’s society, and carries serious health consequences. Obesity is well-characterized as a major risk factor for type 2 diabetes, where prolonged excess calorie intake causes adipocytes to expand beyond their capacity, causing fibrosis and inflammation, resulting in ectopic lipid accumulation, insulin resistance and eventually diabetes. Interestingly, lipodystrophic individuals with scarce adipose tissue present with many clinical symptoms similar to that of obese individuals, e.g. ectopic fat accumulation leading to dyslipidemia and insulin resistance. This demonstrates the importance of functional adipose tissue in human health. The recent recognition of diabetes in lean adults highlights a gap in current knowledge regarding the mechanisms of diabetes in non-obese adults. As ectopic fat accumulation is a hallmark of both obese and lean individuals suffering from insulin resistance and diabetes, we wish to examine the pathogenic mechanisms underpinning diabetes in the non-obese using a lipodystrophy mouse model (BSCL2/seipin knockout or SKO), to investigate if fat or stromal cell transplantation could alleviate diabetic symptoms in these mice. In addition, we wish to characterize the differences in adipose tissue-derived secreted factors between control and non-obese diabetic mice, and investigate if increasing levels of certain factors is sufficient to improve diabetic symptoms in these mice. Through this project, we aim to gain insights into the mechanistic differences between insulin resistance and diabetes in the lean and the obese. As the SKO mice exhibit many metabolic phenotypes resembling that of lean diabetic adults, the results obtained from this study will provide valuable insights into the pathogenesis of diabetes in non-obese individuals and potentially be developed into a treatment regime to improve metabolic function and insulin sensitivity in these adults. In addition, the results from this proposal may be relevant in developing possible treatments for individuals suffering from generalized lipodystrophy and lipoatrophy.
kw: Diabetes; non-obese; seipin; insulin resistance; adipokines; secretome

title: Investigating CHCHD2 as genetic risk factors for familial Parkinson’s Disease (PD) using zebrafish
inst: TLGM - Translational Laboratory in Genetic Medicine
abs: Although defective mitochondria are an early hallmark of several neurodegenerative disorders, their causal link is poorly understood. We have identified a novel mitochondrial protein, CHCHD2, whose expression is upregulated in the context of neurodegeneration. Interestingly, loss of function mutations in human CHCHD2 have been linked to an increased incidence of Parkinson’s disease, a neurological disorder characterized by cellular, motor, and cognitive deficits. To understand the function of CHCHD2 in the vertebrate nervous system, we have generated a zebrafish model that is deficient in CHCHD2 to study the following: 1. Evaluate the impact of CHCHD2 deficiency on mitochondrial health and function in zebrafish, 2. Investigate the impact of CHCHD2 deficiency on dopaminergic neurons under basal and mitochondrial stress conditions, and 3. Examine the effect of loss of CHCHD2 on viability, neurological functions, and behaviour in zebrafish under basal and stress conditions. Through this study, we hope to understand how mitochondrial dysfunction contribute to Parkinson’s disease specifically, or to other neurological disorders in general. Besides understanding the basic mitochondrial biology in these disorders, we hope to identify potentially viable genes and pathways for therapeutic interventions.
kw: Mitochondria, Parkinson's disease, zebrafish, genetic

title: Advancing precision medicine for cardiovascular disease and diabetes in Asian populations
abs: Identification of the mechanisms underlying the increased risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) and diabetes in Asian populations, and developing affordable, effective and scalable strategies for risk stratification and prevention of these major diseases, are urgent national and global public health priorities. To address these challenges, we first create a longitudinal population study of >100,000 Singaporeans (“SG100K”) comprising comprehensive phenotypic characterisation, high quality biological samples, and linkage to national electronic health records. In partnership with the National Precision Medicine programme, we will exploit SG100K to determine the behavioural (including nutrition and physical activity), environmental, genetic and other molecular factors that underpin CVD and diabetes in the multi-ethnic Asian population of Singapore. We will use the knowledge generated to develop and validate algorithms for accurate identification of Asian men and women at risk of CVD and diabetes, taking polygenic information into account, and to identify people with monogenic metabolic defects that may cause early-onset disease. We will strengthen tools for communication of cardiovascular and metabolic risk, taking into account non-genetic and genetic information, and develop personalised approaches to behaviour change for health promotion, that are tailored to social, cultural and environmental context, and delivered by scalable digital platforms. We will evaluate the impact of our risk stratification, communication and behavioural support platforms on engagement with health promotion, and quantify efficacy and cost-effectiveness for prevention of CVD and T2D in community and primary care settings. We will thus advance population and precision health for CVD and diabetes, the leading causes of death and disability in Singapore. In addition, we will deliver SG100K as a unique platform for state-of-the-art epidemiological, translational and precision medicine research, in the genetically distinct and culturally diverse Asian populations of Singapore, which will impact management of a wide range of chronic disease, at national, regional and international scale.
kw: precision; medicine; longitudinal; population; personalized; healthcare

title: MAP3K6 Expression in Recurrent Glioblastoma (GBM): A Marker for Poor Survival with Potential as a Therapeutic Target
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common primary malignant brain tumour in adults. Despite standard of care, median survival remains poor at 15 months, necessitating better treatment strategies. Numerous clinical trials of targeted therapies in GBM have failed, in part due to mis-identified molecular targets, inadequate patient stratification methods and poorly understood treatment-resistant pathways. To address these gaps, we established a novel analytical, computational pipeline that identified up-regulated, biochemically active kinases from STAT3-perturbed patient-derived glioma cells, and these kinases correlated with patient prognostic outcome. We identified mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase kinase 6 (MAP3K6) as a potential druggable candidate, and aim to evaluate the role of MAP3K6 and its pathway inhibitors in the pathogenesis and treatment of recurrent GBM. Our specific aims in this preclinical study are 1) to evaluate the role of MAP3K6 in GBM cells and primary tumours, and 2) to examine the effect of MAP3K5/6 inhibitor on MAP3K6-stratified orthotopic mouse xenograft model. Firstly, patient-derived glioma cells, both proneural and mesenchymal subtypes, will each be treated with clinical stage small molecules targeting MAP3K6. We will evaluate cell viability, proliferation and self-renewal capacity. We will also verify specificity where over-expression of MAP3K6 rescues the drug treatment effect and utilize the MAP3K6 knockdown to characterize the biological phenotype. Next, we will test the effect of MAP3K6 knockdown and efficacy of MAPK5/6 inhibitor in orthotopic mouse xenograft models. These tumours will be created from MAP3K6-stratified glioma-progenitor cells. We will evaluate for time to neurological deficit development and survival outcome. Our overall hypothesis is that MAP3K6 expression level is a significant determinant of GBM survival, and inhibition of MAP3K5/6 will mitigate tumour growth. The long-term goal of this research is to develop drugs that will successfully target the MAP3K6 pathway in stratified patient cohorts, hence present new therapeutic options for patients with GBM.
kw: Glioblastoma; Cancer; Mitogen-Activated Protein Kinase Kinase Kinase; Targeted Therapy

title: Therapeutic exploration of pro-oxidant and mitophagy-related strategies for Parkinson's disease with Asian-related LRRK2 risk variants
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Studies on Parkinson’s disease (PD) causative genes, including Parkin and LRRK2, and related factors, such as reactive oxygen species (ROS) provide invaluable clues for the understanding and treatment of the disease. Defective Parkin-dependent mitophagy is linked to the pathogenesis of PD, whereas boosting mitophagy may provide beneficial effect to PD patients. Our previous study demonstrates that ROS contribute to initiating mitophagy by recruiting Parkin translocation to mitochondria, and additionally drive mitophagy progression thereafter, suggesting ROS modulation as a potential therapeutic strategy for neurodegeneration. LRRK2 G2019S mutation, linked to PD in Caucasian population, causes mitochondrial abnormalities which may be attenuated by Parkin. We have identified that patients who carry the LRRK2 haplotype, constituting of S1647T, R1628P and G2385R variants, developed PD significantly earlier than non-carriers in Asia population. The LRRK2 haplotype may be utilized to establish the first Asian relevant PD model. The interaction between mitophagy and PD caused by this haplotype is a novel pursuit in the scientific community, providing substantial room for therapeutic discoveries. We hypothesize that mitophagy may provide beneficial effects on Asian-related PD. We aim to establish in vitro and in vivo PD models carrying Asian-related LRRK2 haplotype and study the effects of ROS on mitophagy and its related neurodegeneration in such models to test therapeutic potential of stimulating mitophagy in PD. The knowledge gained from patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), utilizing a wide range of research methods including confocal microscopy, flow cytometry and electronic microscopy, will be brought to in vivo models for pathological and behavioural study in attempt to identify potential drug compounds that may interfere with the pathophysiological events implicated in PD. Together, our study outcomes would clarify the role of ROS-mitophagy axis in the pathogenesis of PD and yield potential chemical candidates to halt or slow PD progression in a local setting.
kw: Parkinson's disease; LRRK2; risk variants; mitophagy; pro-oxidant

title: Using the Multiphase Optimization Strategy to Improve Diet Quality (MOSTDQ)
abs: A key focus of the ‘Health Promotion’ theme is the development of interventions that can cost-effectively decrease the onset of non-communicable diseases (NCDs). Poor diet quality is a well-established risk factor for numerous NCDs. As a result, Singapore is looking for strategies to improve diet quality. Possible strategies include price manipulations, food labelling, targeted messaging, and behavioral nudges. Each strategy can be implemented using multiple approaches and in combination with the others. Yet to date, no studies have addressed how different interventions can be combined across these domains in efforts to cost effectively improve diet quality. That is the focus of this effort. Specifically, we propose to apply the Multiphase Optimization Strategy (MOST) framework and our fully functional web-based grocery store (NUSMart), containing over 4,000 products, to design a multicomponent intervention aimed to cost effectively improve diet quality. We will then conduct a 2-arm randomized controlled trial to test whether the assembled multicomponent intervention has a sustained positive effect on diet quality over repeated purchases. This study is the first to propose to systematically combine select components of an evidence-based multi-component intervention in efforts to improve diet quality of consumers in Singapore. Given rising rates of obesity, diabetes, and other chronic diseases, and the government’s interest in using food policy to improve diet quality, this study is both timely and has high potential to have a significant public health impact in Singapore and beyond.
kw: diet quality; behavioral intervention; multiphase optimization strategy; MOST; online grocery store; nutrition

title: Collaborative Model of Care between Orthopaedics and Allied Healthcare Professionals Trial (CONNACT)
abs: With a rapidly aging population, osteoarthritis is expected to become the 4th leading cause of global disability by 2020. Established guidelines for knee osteoarthritis strongly advocate lifestyle changes such exercises and weight loss as first line treatment reserving surgery as the last resort. Our current model of care is doctor-centric and inefficient leading to suboptimal use of allied health intervention for effective lifestyle and behaviour changes resulting in unnecessary surgery. Redesigning the model of care by moving away from costly surgical treatment through the optimization and synergizing of proven non-surgical treatments is key to deliver value-based care. The study is designed using an effectiveness-implementation hybrid study design utilizing a mixed methods approach. The hybrid study has dual aims. The primary aim is to evaluate the clinical effectiveness (pain, function and quality of life) of a 12-week multidisciplinary (Orthopaedics, Physiotherapy, Dietetics, Psychology) personalized, community-based program for patients with knee osteoarthritis through a pragmatic randomized patient preference trial. The secondary aim is to obtain data that will inform the context for implementation and guide future wider scale application. We hypothesize that this multidisciplinary program is clinically more effective in the treatment of knee osteoarthritis at 12 months compared to standard care. The primary outcome is the Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS). Secondary outcomes include quality of life (QOL) scoring, functional and psychological assessments. An economic evaluation using Markov modelling will be undertaken to evaluate both the short and long-term cost effectiveness. A qualitative component through interviews and focus group discussions with patients, healthcare providers and stakeholders will evaluate the acceptability, feasibility and scalability of this program for further refinement and large-scale implementation. Long term follow-up evaluating the incidence and outcomes for knee arthroplasty post intervention will be undertaken to evaluate long-term impact.
kw: Osteoarthritis; Model of Care; Multidisciplinary

title: A novel murine model of atherosclerotic plaque vulnerability and rupture for testing new plaque-stabilising therapies
abs: Cardiovascular diseases are the leading causes of death and disability in Singapore and worldwide. Rupture of vulnerable atherosclerotic plaque leads to luminal thrombosis causing acute myocardial infarction, stroke and sudden death. Although inflammation plays a key role in plaque rupture, the causes of plaque progression from stable to vulnerable are not completely understood. Visceral obesity increases the risk of cardiac events, and the increased volume and inflammation of epicardial adipose tissue (AT) are associated with vulnerability of coronary plaques. Inflammation in pericoronary AT likely implies local chemokine effects to the adjacent artery and contributes to plaque progression and vulnerability. Currently, there is no available murine model that consistently develops high-risk plaques and plaque rupture with thrombus. The signs of unstable plaques, such as thin fibrous cap, necrotic core and intraplaque haemorrhage, are rarely present in mice and only occur after long-term high-fat diet feeding (25-60 weeks), or following a severe surgical/mechanical intervention to the vessel itself. Thus, novel models are needed to study the mechanism of plaque rupture and preventive therapies. We have shown that visceral AT transplanted adjacent to carotid artery in mice induces local high-risk lesions displaying necrotic core, intraplaque haemorrhage and thrombosis after a short time period (8 weeks). This murine model recapitulates the pathophysiological effects of inflamed AT onto arterial wall, where the transplanted AT mimics obesity-induced macrophage infiltration found in epicardial AT in patients with unstable plaques. In this proposal, we will characterise the plaque progression from stable to unstable in our novel murine model of plaque rupture, and use our model to evaluate two novel plaque-stabilising therapies targeting mitochondrial metabolism and interleukin-11, which are implicated in apoptosis, oxidative stress and inflammation. Based on our pilot data, these two novel therapeutical approaches lead to reduction in neointimal plaque size in a wire-injury model of restenosis.
kw: atherosclerosis; coronary artery disease; atherosclerotic plaque rupture; myocardial infarction; plaque-stabilising therapies; inflammation

title: Improved Detection of Glaucomatous Structural Damage using Wide-Field Optical Coherence Tomography
abs: Glaucoma is the leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide. Diagnosis of early glaucoma remains challenging. By the time the current method of visual field testing detects glaucoma, at least 25% of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) are lost. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) imaging is commonly used to aid glaucoma diagnosis in clinics but its diagnostic ability for detecting early glaucoma remains inadequate due to the considerable overlap of retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) thickness measurements between normal and glaucoma eyes. Some of this overlap is partly due to the variations in ocular anatomical parameters such as optic disc size, and shape, and the anatomy of the retinal vascular tree, which are important sources of measurement error. We propose a method to mitigate the influence of anatomical ocular parameters on OCT-derived measurements. We have already shown that this anatomy-based compensation method narrowed the variability in RNFL measurements in healthy subjects and reclassified half of eyes in the 1% high-risk category (with very thin RNFL) to the normal category. The main objective of this proposal is to compare wide-field optical coherence tomography (WF-OCT) combined with compensation for anatomical parameters (termed as WF-OCT plus) and standard OCT in terms of detecting early glaucomatous structural damage and progression in a clinical setting. We hypothesize that WF-OCT plus will significantly improve diagnostic performance in early detection of glaucomatous damages and optimize the role that OCT imaging plays in glaucoma management. Early glaucoma diagnosis is essential to improving patient outcomes, as earlier treatment can prevent or slow the disease progression, and thus preserve patients’ visual function. Given that glaucomatous damage irreversibly leads to blindness at late stages, the outcome of this study, a novel method to advance glaucoma diagnosis, will confer a great impact on the prevention of blindness, not only in Singapore but worldwide.
kw: Glaucoma; Wide-Field Optical Coherence Tomography

title: Investigating the role of the primary angle closure glaucoma (PACG) susceptibility gene, PLEKHA7 in Plekha7-/- mutant rats.
abs: Glaucoma is characterized by retinal ganglion cell and optic nerve axonal loss resulting in glaucomatous optic neuropathy. Primary angle closure glaucoma (PACG), a major form of glaucoma and visual loss in Singapore and Asia, is defined by the presence of iris-angle contact. Iris-angle contact can cause aqueous outflow obstruction and intraocular pressure (IOP) elevation progressing to PACG. The molecular effects underlying this progression is unknown and represents the current gap in knowledge. PLEKHA7, a recently identified PACG-susceptibility gene, encodes a pleckstrin homology domain containing GTPase-activating protein that is functionally related to cellular adhesion and extracellular matrix (ECM) remodelling. In normal eyes, PLEKHA7 expression is present in PACG-related structures: iris, non-pigmented ciliary epithelium (NPCE), trabecular meshwork (TM), and choroid. In tissues (iris and lens capsule) obtained from PACG eyes, a significant downregulation of PLEKHA7 mRNA expression is present when compared to controls, suggesting that reduced levels of PLEKHA7 may contribute to PACG pathophysiology. Furthermore, we found that in vitro silencing of PLEKHA7 expression led to decreased cellular adhesion in NPCE cells and reduced contractility of TM cells. In our colony of homozygous (Plekha7-/-), heterozygous (Plekha7-/+) and wild type (WT) rats which have ablated and normal expression of Plekha7 respectively, young Plekha7-/- rats compared to WT littermates have a phenotype related to PACG risk—shallower anterior chambers, narrower angles and elevated IOP. Based on these findings, we aim to use Plekha7 mutant rats as an in vivo system to study the ocular effects of PLEKHA7 downregulation. We will study the Plekha7 ocular phenotype, particularly, degree of iris-angle contact with age and provocation (Aims 1 & 2); as well as altered cellular adhesion and ECM remodelling pathways (Aim 3) in PACG tissues specifically related to choroidal thickness and loss of barrier integrity in order to determine the role of PLEKHA7 in PACG

title: Blood-based measurement of brain amyloid plaque deposition
abs: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is the most common form of dementia and leads to debilitating loss of mental functions. However, long before full-blown symptoms appear, AD molecular hallmarks (e.g., amyloid) may manifest and advance. Early detection and intervention are thus thought to be essential to the success of disease-modifying therapies. Current AD diagnostic technologies, however, are either subjective and late-stage or invasive and expensive. There is thus an intense interest and urgent need to develop blood-based AD measurements. Exosomes have recently emerged as an attractive circulating biomarker for AD. Exosomes are nanoscale extracellular vesicles. They are robust and abundant in blood. Recent studies have identified that exosomes preferentially associate with pathological AD proteins and are implicated in their prion-spread. Capturing this exchange of exosome information could present a transformative, blood-based approach to molecularly characterize the disease. Despite such clinical potential, exosome detection remains challenging, primarily due to the vesicles’ nanoscale dimension. We aim to address this technology challenge and evaluate the clinical potential of exosomes for AD molecular characterization. Using amyloid as a model system, we will test the hypothesis that circulating exosome contents can be correlated to brain amyloid plaque load. This hypothesis stems from our growing understanding of exosome composition but has yet to be validated, due to a lack of compatible technologies. The goal of this proposal is thus two-fold. First, platform development. Through integrative sensor engineering and assay development, we will advance our recently developed exosome nanosensor to significantly improve its analytical capabilities. Second, clinical validation. Employing the developed platform, we will perform a translational study to profile exosomes derived from patient blood samples and correlate the measurements with amyloid PET imaging. These advances will significantly expand our understanding and clinical applications of circulating exosomes for characterizing AD pathology.
kw: Nanoplasmonic sensor; Blood measurement; Exosome; Amyloid; PET imaging; Alzheimer’s disease

title: In vivo 2C-BioID, a new platform technology for interactome analysis
abs: The human genome comprises about 20,000 genes. However, the protein repertoire encoded by these may run to more than a million. Proteins rarely function in isolation since their activities are invariably tightly regulated. It follows, therefore, that how proteins interact with each other in response to both internal and external cues affects every aspect of normal cell physiology and behavior. Because of this, defining protein interactomes has now become an important adjunct of genomics and transcriptomics. Furthermore, it has become clear that the mapping of protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks in a variety of human diseases, from schizophrenia to muscular dystrophy has the potential to identify novel therapeutic targets. While advances in mass spectrometry have revolutionized protein identification, experimental methods to map PPIs, even in cultured cells, are quite limited. Defining PPIs within tissues in vivo containing multiple cell types is even more challenging. We have recently developed an advanced two-component proximity labelling method, 2C-BioID, that can be used to identify PPIs in an unbiased manner. The method takes advantage of a promiscuous biotin-protein ligase (BioID2) that is delivered to a protein of interest by rapamycin-dependent heterodimerization of FKBP and FRB protein domains. While we have validated this method in cell culture systems, there is every reason to believe that it can be adapted to work in vivo. Moreover, since expression of the FKBP-BioID2 component can be rendered inducible in a tissue-specific manner, this raises the prospect of performing tissue-specific interactome analyses. The goal of this proposal is to develop in vivo 2C-BioID as a platform technology. We will validate and refine our protocols on an analysis of a multifunctional nuclear pore complex protein, Nup133, defects in which are associated with Galloway-Mowat syndrome, a rare disease affecting primarily the central nervous system and kidneys.
kw: Proteomics; interactome; BioID; Nuclear pore complex;

title: Non-invasive photoacoustic mesoscopy imaging of clinical skin inflammatory disorders coupled with AI-assisted scoring to evaluate disease prognosis and associated metabolic co-morbidities
abs: Chronic inflammatory skin diseases affect more than 25% of our population and there is strong evidence linking them to metabolic syndrome; putting patients with such dermatoses at risk of cardiovascular events. While metabolic diseases have objective measures to reflect disease severity, chronic inflammatory skin disorders lack such scoring measures and is scored based on clinical questionnaires and are subjected to intra- and inter-observer variations. Non-invasive imaging techniques for assessing the skin vascular structures could potentially serve as objective indicators for these diseases to characterize its severity and understand how inflammation plays a role systemic metabolic co-morbidities. For the first time, we aim to employ photoacoustic (PA) technique- Raster scanning-Optoacoustic Mesoscopy (RSOM) as surrogate clinical measures to objectively characterize the severity of atopic dermatitis and psoriasis. We also aim to automate the classification of disease severity through machine learning and explore vascular features of systemic complications in these inflammatory disorders. Next, we will develop a multiple wavelength-RSOM (Multispectral Optoacoustic Mesoscopy-MSOM) technique to evaluate the saturated oxygen changes in the remodelled vascular networks of the inflammatory skin. To assess and classify these changes and to predict related metabolic co-morbidities, we will be working on the following sub-aims:- 1. Develop customized PAI system, Raster Scanning-Optoacoustic Mesoscopy (RSOM) with optimized transducer frequency for imaging inflammatory skin diseases. 2. Develop quantitative new specific RSOM imaging metrics for disease’s severity and correlate it with the standard clinical scores. 3. Develop Multispectral Optoacoustic Mesoscopy (MSOM) system to evaluate microvascular saturated oxygenation parameters. 4. Develop an artificial-intelligence (AI) approach for accurate and objective classification of ISD from pattern-recognition of MSOM images by using initial RSOM images as training sets. 5. Correlating skin microvasculature and saturation oxygen pattern changes with associated diabetes mellitus using AI to extract disease-specific visual features, which may be used for a downstream classification.
kw: Inflammatory skin diseases, Metabolic co-morbidities, In vivo imaging, Photoacoustic imaging, Raster scanning-Optoacoustic Mesoscopy, Multispectral Optoacoustic Mesoscopy, Artificial-intelligence, Machine Learning, Atopic Dermatitis, Psoriasis, Photoacoustic Mesoscopy

title: Mapping hematopoietic lineages of healthy and high-risk acute myeloid leukemia patients with FLT3-ITD mutations using single-cell omics
abs: In this project, we aim to map hematopoietic lineages of healthy and high-risk acute myeloid leukemia patients with FLT3-ITD mutations using single-cell omics. We will profile hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) from the bone marrow using single cell genomics, single cell transcriptomics and mass cytometry (CyTOF) techniques. Such integrative analysis of single cell genome landscape, trancriptome and protein expression will allow us to fully characterize cellular heterogeneity at the phenotypic and functional level. We will compare the single-cell landscape of HSPCs in AML with that of healthy donors to identify which cell populations are perturbed and which genes/proteins are dysregulated in patients. Moreover, we will construct cell lineages as well as gene regulatory network to better characterize hematopoiesis in healthy individuals and AML patients. Altogether, such unprecedented knowledge at the single cell level will allow us to evaluate AML heterogeneity and find new populations, new molecules and pathways involved in AML immunopathogenesis. Dissecting AML biology at the single cell level may lead to the improvement of AML diagnosis, monitoring, as well as the development of new treatment strategies. Meanwhile, we will build a single-cell artificial intelligent (AI) platform based on deep learning framework, which will be readily applicable to other single cell studies.
kw: single-cell RNA-seq, CyTOF, Acute Myeloid Leukemia, hematopoiesis, cellular differentiation

title: Improving acute myocardial infarction outcomes by reducing myocardial infarct size and preventing adverse cardiac remodelling through the use of pharmacological and telemedicine strategies.
abs: Acute myocardial infarction (AMI) and the heart failure (HF) that often follows are among the leading causes of death and disability in Singapore and worldwide. Here, we investigate three different strategies for preventing HF post-AMI. Aim 1: Platelet Inhibition to Target Reperfusion Injury (PITRI trial) Objective: To investigate the effect of intravenous P2Y12 platelet inhibitor, Cangrelor, on myocardial infarct (MI) size in ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) patients. Hypothesis: Administration of Cangrelor prior to reperfusion will reduce MI size. Methodology: In the ongoing PITRI multi-centre trial, 210 STEMI patients will be randomised to receive either placebo or Cangrelor, prior to PPCI. Primary outcome is MI size on CMR at day 4 post-AMI. Aim 2: Platelet STEMI study Objective: To investigate the effects of high blood glucose at time of STEMI admission on platelet activation and coronary microvascular injury. Hypothesis: Hyperglycaemia at time of STEMI will induce platelet activation via reactive oxygen species (ROS)-NF-kB and upregulation of P2Y12 expression resulting in larger MI size and microvascular obstruction (MVO). Methodology: 50 STEMI patients with either high (>11mmol/L) or low (<8mmol/L) blood glucose will have blood samples taken within 24 hours of admission for platelet ROS, NF-kB, P2Y12 expression, and CMR at 4 days post-AMI for MI size and MVO. Aim 3: Improving reModelling in Acute myoCardial infarction Using Live and Asynchronous Telemedicine (IMMACULATE trial) Objective: To investigate the effect of telemedicine-guided management for maintaining compliance and dose-uptitration of post-AMI medication for preventing post-AMI adverse LV remodelling. Hypothesis: Maintaining compliance and dose-uptitration of post-AMI drugs using a telemedicine-guided management will prevent post-AMI adverse LV remodelling. Methodology: In the ongoing IMMACULATE multi-centre trial, 300 AMI patients at risk of HF will be randomised to receive standard post-AMI care or post-AMI telemedicine-guided management. Primary outcome is post-AMI adverse LV remodelling on CMR at 6 months.
kw: Myocardial infarction; Infarct size; Remodelling; Cangrelor; Telemedicine; Platelet activation

title: Evaluate the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of ‘Supportive Parenting App’ a mobile based application on parental and newborn outcomes: A multi-center randomized controlled trial
abs: Aims: The aims of the study are to: (1) develop theory-based supportive parenting App (SPA) based educational intervention for both first-time and experienced parents across the perinatal period; (2) examine its effectiveness on parental outcomes: including maternal depression at 12 months postpartum (primary outcome), paternal depression, parental anxiety, parenting self-efficacy, help - seeking behavior (social support), parental bonding and parenting satisfaction (secondary outcomes); new-born outcomes: physical, social and emotional developments (secondary outcomes); (3) evaluate SPA’s cost-effectiveness as compared to standard perinatal care; and (4) examine the experiences of parents in receiving this intervention. Hypotheses: When compared with those in the control group receiving standard care: 1. parents receiving SPA intervention will have better - emotional well-being (Reduced depression and anxiety); - parenting self-efficacy; - social support; - bonding and satisfaction. 2. new-borns of parents receiving SPA will have better; - physical development; - social development; and - emotional development. 3. It will be more cost-effective to provide SPA than the standard care Methodology: A multi-centered randomized controlled two-group pre-test and repeated post-test experimental design will be used. Parents (n = 200) recruited from a tertiary hospital will be randomly assigned into the two groups. Data will be collected by questionnaire surveys using locally validated and reliable instruments, semi-structured face-to-face interviews and telephone interviews. Data will be analyzed using SPSS25.0 and thematic analysis. Significance of the study: This study will identify a clinically useful and potentially effective and cost-effective SPA intervention to improve parental and new-born outcomes. The widely accessed M-Health App will be used to prevent postpartum depression, one of the debilitating condition that influence parents, their children and the overall family dynamics. Receiving evidence-based timely support, may eventually lead to more positive parenting experiences which may then influence psychosocial well-being of both parents and their new-borns.
kw: Postpartum depression, Mobile-based Application, Parents, Perinatal period, Newborns

title: Forecasting the burden and long-term impact of poor mental health on healthcare utilisation and cost in the community versus secondary/tertiary care setting
abs: Worldwide, it is estimated that 20% of elders aged 60 and above suffer from a mental or neurological disorder, attributing to 6.6% of all disability. In Singapore, about one in five elderly persons aged 75 and above showed signs of depression, while the proportion of elders among those who take their lives has risen from 23% in 2000 to 30% in 2014. Yet, little is known about the distribution of care for mental disorder within the community versus secondary/tertiary sector, and if these care models are sustainable in light of our rapidly ageing population. Such questions are of critical relevance to the provision of sustainable end-to-end care, as they contribute to the identification of policy gaps, the potential for capacity development in the community, and the projection of future mental health burden attributable to ageing. To answer these questions, we propose to construct a Future Elderly Model (FEM) for mental health, a dynamic Markov micro-simulation model that predicts future mental health status and healthcare costs for the elderly population of Singapore up to 2050. Forecasting future mental health status for the elderly in the presence of multiple related co-morbidities is highly challenging. Estimating health care expenditure is even more difficult, as utilisation and cost are a function of many factors including health status, age, gender, diseases and insurance coverage. We will estimate the mental health states and associated outcomes for the FEM model using existing population cohorts, prevalence studies and administrative data on medical claims. In the long-term, we will also model the impact of various policies or interventions on population mental health. The FEM-mental health thus offers the potential to answer pressing questions regarding the long-term impact of mental disorders on health and economic outcomes for Singapore.
kw: Mental Health; Healthcare cost; Economics; Simulation; Projections; Ageing

title: Developing the Application of T regulatory and CD62L-depleted T cells in Adoptive Cellular Therapy
abs: The overarching goal is to cure relapsed refractory (r/r) B-lineage leukaemia with minimal long-term complications using dual-targeting CAR-T cell therapy. In parallel, the broad translational goal is to develop a safe and effective allogeneic CAR-T without graft-versus-host disease (GvHD) potential to replace the need for autologous CAR-T manufacturing. Specific Aim 1: Phase I Clinical Trial of Autologous Anti-CD22/CD19 CAR-T (CART2219.1) for relapsed/refractory B-lineage leukaemia (R/R B-ALL) The current standard of treatment for R/R B-ALL requires bridging towards a total body irradiation-based transplantation or CD19-directed CAR-T. The former results in significant long-term toxicities, and the latter is limited by CD19-negative relapses (antigen escape). In SA1, a novel dual-targeting tandem CAR-T(CART2219.1) will be investigated for safety and efficacy in a phase I and dose expansion trial for relapsed/refractory adult and pediatric B-ALL, with a goal to replace transplantation and irradiation. The hypothesis is that CART2219.1 is safe and effective in eradicating R/R B-ALL as a definitive treatment. Simultaneous targeting of CD22 and C19 can overcome antigen escape as loss of both antigens is highly unlikely to occur. Specific Aim 2: Development of chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-modified memory T cells (memory CAR-T) for the treatment of post-HSCT relapse. Patients who relapse soon after transplant have limited success with conventional donor lymphocyte infusions at the expense of severe graft-versus-host disease (GvHD). These patients have poor T cell quantity and quality for autologous CAR-T manufacturing. CD45RA-depleted allogeneic central memory cells have low GvHD potential and can be redirected by CAR against relapsed leukaemia cells. SA 2.1 Phase 1 Clinical Trial of Central Memory CAR-T We will validate the product specifications of allogeneic CD19-directed central memory CAR-T using CD45RA depletion to enrich for central memory T cells in place of CD4 and CD8 selection. Safety and efficacy will be studied in a phase I clinical trial for post-transplant relapsed B-ALL. The hypothesis is that allogeneic CD45RA-depleted CAR-T will be safe and effective in post-transplant relapses. SA2.2 Preclinical development of an alternative memory subset by CD62L depletion We will characterize the properties of CD62L-negative memory T cells on research-scale depletions and explore its potential as a novel allogeneic CAR-T cell in a series of preclinical studies. The hypothesis is that T effector memory cells are effective for T cell immune reconstitution post-HSCT without the risk of GVHD and may be exploited as a non-alloreactive CAR-T in the allogeneic setting. Collectively, this research addresses the need for less toxic cures for R/R B-ALL patients, the unmet need for overcoming antigen-negative relapse after conventional CAR-T and an allogeneic CAR-T with no GvHD potential for post-transplant relapses.
kw: T-regulatory; CD62L-depletion; T-memory; Chimeric Antigen Receptor; Adoptive Cell Therapy

title: Utilizing Machine Learning and Natural Language Processing methods on real-world Electronic Medical Record data for automated surgical complications prediction and detection
abs: The measurement of surgical outcomes allows hospitals to provide patients with accurate risk estimates to make informed choices about their care; surgeons and hospital administrators with knowledge for quality improvement; and policymakers with data when making funding decisions. However, most healthcare institutions do not have systematic surgical outcomes measurement procedure. Hence, healthcare systems have started to utilize a “clinical database”, where clinically trained coders systematically record information from clinical sources and documents. However, this process is labor-intensive, expensive, and often suffers from bias due to lack of blinding, objectivity and consistency across the coders. The implementation of electronic medical records (EMR) in Singapore hospitals creates an opportunity to automate this chart review process. EMR data are present in different modalities, such as unstructured text, semi-structured text, and structured tabular data. These can be analyzed with a robust machine learning (ML) and Natural Language Processing (NLP) platform and significantly reduce the workload and manpower costs while improving the quality of data abstraction. The best ML framework for this purpose is currently unknown. The overarching aim of this project is to improve the surgical patients’ outcome by developing and validating an automated and cost-effective ML/NLP framework which can accurately predict the occurrence of complications and identify the modifiable risk factors. Surgical site infection (SSI) will be used as the use case. We hypothesize that the performance of this newly developed model will be similar to the manual data collection done by the ACS-NSQIP SCRs, with Jaccard Similarity Coefficient of at least 0.7; and the predictive model would achieve good accuracy with an AUROC of > 0.8 and Negative Predictive Value > 98%. Furthermore, we will aim to assess the impact of the model's deployment on patient outcomes in terms of reducing the rate of SSI.
kw: Data Science; Artificial Intelligence; Electronic Health Records; postoperative complications
