title: Characterization of immune evasion in NK/T-Cell Lymphoma
abs: Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma (NKTL) is an aggressive EBV-associated neoplasm more prevalent in South East Asians than in other populations. It is commonly refractory to conventional chemotherapy, and new treatment approaches are urgently required. Immune checkpoint inhibitors affecting the Programmed Death 1 (PD1) pathway show promise in early clinical trials for NKTL, suggesting an important role for the immune system in modulating these tumours. However, PD1 is only one of many pathways employed in cancer immune evasion and new immunotherapy approaches are being tested in various cancers. The interplay between these different immune evasion pathways as well as the role of EBV in immune regulation is not understood in NKTL. This information will be relevant to the incorporation of immunotherapy into NKTL treatment. In this grant, we aim to study immune evasion in NKTL in 2 sections. Section 1 is a pathological characterization of immune evasion markers in clinical NKTL samples. Our previous gene expression studies on NKTL revealed elevated expression of immune modulatory genes. We will validate the protein expression of these transcripts, and study their relationship to Programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1), as well as novel immuno-oncology targets such as TIM3 and VISTA. We have established a multispectral imaging assay to quantify these molecular markers in tumour and immune cells in the microenvironment of NKTL, to identify appropriate immuno-oncology trial strategies. In Section 2, we will decipher the role of EBV in immune evasion in NKTL by modulating the expression of EBV proteins and miRNA in NKTL cell lines, and analyzing their effects on immune evasion molecules of therapeutic interest. Overall, this grant will help clarify the clinical relevance of immune evasion pathways in NKTL and identify pertinent immune regulatory targets for future clinical trials.
kw: Natural Killer / T-cell lymphoma, EBV, immune evasion

title: Alpha-synuclein Gene Promoter (Rep1) Polymorphism and Cognitive Decline in Parkinson’s Disease
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by cytoplasmic alpha-synuclein aggregates in the substantia nigra. The alpha-synuclein gene (SNCA) is implicated in familial PD; while polymorphism of the SNCA promoter region (Rep1) i.e. variation in Rep1 allele length, is associated with increased PD risk in multiple studies. The frequencies of Rep1 genotypes in our PD population are ~30% for the shortest allele (allele 0), and ~40% and ~30% for the longer alleles (alleles 1 and 2 respectively). Increased risk of PD may occur via variation in transcriptional regulation of SNCA expression, with longer Rep1 allele lengths displaying increased SNCA expression in both mouse and human brain tissue. Furthermore, clinical studies have shown that longer Rep1 allele carriers show greater motor decline and neuropsychiatric complications compared to shorter allele carriers. However, the association of Rep1 with cognition remains unknown. To address this gap, our primary aim is to investigate the association of Rep1 allele-lengths with cognitive decline in mild- to moderate-stage PD (Hoehn & Yahr score ≤3). We hypothesize that longer Rep1 allele carriers (alleles 1, 2) will show greater decline in cognition based on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) test over 2 years, compared to shorter Rep1 allele carriers. A secondary aim is to determine if peripheral SNCA expression levels at baseline are associated with cognitive decline in longer Rep1 allele carriers. An exploratory aim is to study longitudinal changes in brain structure (grey matter volumes, cortical thickness, and white matter microstructure) and functional connectivity in longer vs shorter allele carriers. We hypothesize that longer allele carriers will show greater decrease in these measures over a 2-year period compared to shorter allele carriers. These will add evidence to the link between Rep1 polymorphism and cognitive dysfunction in PD, identifying Rep1 as a novel therapeutic target for neurodegeneration in PD.
kw: Parkinson's disease; cognition; genetics; synuclein

title: Wnt pathway in synovial sarcoma: Implications for therapy
abs: Sarcomas are difficult to treat due to a lack of efficacy in conventional chemotherapy drugs. Drugs that target specific tumorigenic pathways offer the potential of having less patient morbidity and more therapeutic efficacy. Our preliminary work has demonstrated synovial sarcoma(SS) may be dependent on the Wnt signaling pathway for survival and growth. In other sarcomas, the Wnt pathway may have an inhibitory effect on angiogenesis. My mentor’s lab has developed an upstream Wnt Inhibitor (ETC159) that is currently in clinical trials. Understanding the role of the Wnt pathway in in these sarcomas will allow us to bring this new drug to clinical use in more cancers. Hypothesis and Aims Our hypothesis is that SS is driven by an upstream Wnt pathway mutation and can be inhibited by an upstream Wnt inhibitor (ETC159). ETC159 inhibits SS by direct inhibition of tumour cell viability as well as disrupting the tumour’s angiogenic potential. We aim to: 1. investigate how SSX-SS18 upregulates the Wnt pathway in SS 2. demonstrate the efficacy of ETC 159 in the treatment of synovial sarcoma 3. investigate the effects of Wnt modulation on angiogenesis in sarcomas Methodology Co- immunoprecipitation of SSX-SS18 will identify the key Wnt proteins, which bind to SSX-SS18. Over expression/ knock down of these proteins will allow us investigate the Wnt signaling pathway in SS. Treatment of synovial sarcoma murine xenografts with ETC159 will allow us to investigate the effects of Wnt modulation on the tumor phenotype as well as transcriptional changes. We will also investigate the effects of ETC 159 on angiogenesis by immunohistochemistry analysis of the treated tumor specimens, as well as chicken chorioallantoic membrane angiogenic model. Clinical Significance Understanding the role of the Wnt signaling pathway in driving sarcomas will allow us to develop a new, locally developed treatment modality for these cancers.
kw: Synovial sarcoma, Wnt pathway, therapy

title: Expansion of hematopoietic stem cells by the modulation of mitochondrial metabolism
abs: Our ongoing studies conducted under the STaR project (2013-2018) have discovered that the microenvironment directly alters HSC metabolism and their fate – either to self-renew or to differentiate into mature cells. Our data suggest that appropriate regulations of the metabolic state of HSCs may allow HSCs to self-renew and expand. For the STaR proposal renewal (2019-2024), we therefore propose to build upon our existing findings, and expand towards the following areas that will have impactful clinical implications in terms of HSC expansion for application in disease settings. The difficulty in recapitulating HSC self-renewal in vitro is mainly due to the difficulty of inhibiting their differentiation under normoxic culture conditions containing growth factors. This suggests that, unlike embryonic stem (ES) cells and induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells, HSCs cannot be expanded in vitro by self-renewal divisions. Our novel and innovative approach differs from the cytokine-based culture and can complement the previous approach. This project will focus on the metabolic regulation of HSCs and optimize the environment surrounding the stem cells for efficient self-renewal. We wish to cultivate the most advantageous system for the ex vivo expansion of HSCs.
kw: Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs); cancer stem cells; stem cell niche; stem cell expansion; mitochondria regulation

title: Patient, Physician, and Organizational Factors Influencing Decision-Making for Antibiotic Use, and N-of-1 Trials of Interventions to Improve the Decision-Making
abs: Upper respiratory tract infection (URTI) is a commonly-cited reason for antibiotic use, although antibiotics are not clinically indicated for the majority. Antibiotic misuse drives antimicrobial resistance. Antibiotic prescribing for URTIs at emergency departments (EDs) is complex and influenced by many patient-, physician-, and organizational-level factors. The proposed research will be conducted over 2 phases in 4 adult EDs that provide Singapore-wide coverage. Phase 1 will involve mixed methods studies on physicians and patients that include questionnaire surveys and in-depth interviews to better understand the multi-level psychosocial, cultural, and systemic determinants of antibiotic prescribing. Based on findings from Phase 1, a multicenter stepped-wedge cluster randomized trial will be conducted in Phase 2 to evaluate the effectiveness of tailored interventions targeting at: 1) patient- (patient education via tailored information leaflets that address local knowledge gaps and misconceptions), 2) physician- (senior physician education through active outreach efforts), and 3) organizational- (clinical decision support tool via mobile or desktop app, based on local epidemiology) levels, in reducing unnecessary antibiotic use. The N-of-1 trials study design will be used to gain a deeper understanding of prescribing practices at the individual physician level in response to the interventions. Unlike conventional methods that evaluate intervention effectiveness for an average physician practicing in an adult ED, the N-of-1 trials will enable the assessment of the interventions that work for individual physicians and allow the design of personalized interventions. With Singapore’s rapidly ageing population, who are more prone to infections and exposure to antibiotics, tailored-interventions after elucidation of root causes for unnecessary antibiotic use that target patient-, physician-, and organizational-level factors in EDs, are necessary to curb the rising tide of antimicrobial resistance amidst the background of a dwindling antibiotic pipeline. This research study will contribute to the limited international understanding of the determinants for antibiotic prescribing in EDs.
kw: Antimicrobial stewardship, Antimicrobial resistance, Antibiotic prescribing, Antibiotic use, Upper respiratory tract infection, Emergency department

title: Scleral Biomechanical Properties in Pathologic Myopia and Myopic Glaucoma
abs: High myopia (HM), or extreme near-sightedness, is a leading cause of blindness worldwide and affects 1 in 12 Singaporeans. By 2050, it is estimated that a billion people will have HM. HM is due to progressive and extreme eye elongation with subsequent eye wall (sclera) thinning, which may allow for focal, ectatic outpouchings called staphyloma. Staphyloma development often occurs immediately before or together with myopic macular degeneration (MMD) and the irreversible vision loss of “pathologic” myopia (PM). The main threats to vision in HM patients are the development of MMD, staphyloma and/or myopic glaucoma. Glaucoma is the most common cause of blindness worldwide, affecting greater than 79.6 million people by 2020, with half being of East Asian origin. Glaucoma is an optic neuropathy with unknown pathogenesis that is related to intraocular pressure, and therefore scleral biomechanical properties. A link between myopia and glaucoma has long been reported. Although scleral changes are believed to underlie both glaucomatous changes and staphyloma development, there are no biomechanical tests available to detect early changes in myopic scleral stiffness and/or reveal whether HM-related biomechanical changes may lead to myopic glaucoma. A fundamental understanding of the biomechanical alterations in scleral tissue may provide a link between pathological pathways in glaucoma and myopia and allow for future therapeutic approaches. We now have imaging technology to assess the eye wall in vivo, providing unprecedented insight into scleral biomechanical properties and allowing us to map regional stiffness. As such, we propose to conduct cross-sectional studies on 200 existing low myopia, HM and PM patients. Scleral biomechanical properties will be compared across cohorts, which allow us to identify and localize scleral regions susceptible to myopia-related remodeling and determine if localized biomechanical weakness in HM is associated with localized functional changes, as well as identify scleral biomechanical changes in myopic glaucoma.
kw: biomarker, myopia, progression, pathologic, staphyloma, sclera

title: The IFIT Family in Breast Cancer: Evaluation of Expression Patterns, Functional Roles and Potential Use as Prognostic Indicators
abs: Breast carcinoma is the commonest cancer in women worldwide, and a leading cause of malignancy-related deaths. In Singapore, its incidence has tripled over the past 40 years, while its mortality rate has remained relatively unchanged for the past 25 years. This underlines the importance of a deeper understanding of breast cancer, and to discover better markers for patient prognostication. The interferon induced protein with tetratricopeptide repeats (IFIT) family consists of four members. Previous studies have mainly focussed on their roles in immune response to viral infections. In our preliminary experiments, we found that silencing IFIT1 or IFIT3 in human breast cancer cells decreased tumour cell migration and invasion through Matrigel. Further, elevated IFIT1 or IFIT3 in breast cancer tissue was associated with reduced patient survival and increased risk of tumour recurrence. Contrastingly, knocking down IFIT5 increased the migratory and invasive characteristics of breast cancer cells. Thus, this project aims to determine the differential biological roles of IFITs in breast cancer, identify candidate downstream signalling mechanisms, and evaluate the potential use of IFITs as prognostic indicators in breast cancer patient survival and disease relapse. Knockdown/knockout and overexpression of IFIT members will be performed to investigate their functional roles in vitro using human breast carcinoma cells and in vivo using a SCID mouse model. Transcriptomic and proteomic studies will be performed using microarrays and mass spectrometry analyses to identify candidate downstream pathways, which will then be selected for experimental verification. Expression of IFITs in breast cancer tissue samples will be examined and analysed for associations with clinicopathological features. Survival analysis will evaluate the potential use of IFITs to predict patient survival and breast cancer recurrence. Together, the study will deepen our knowledge on IFITs in breast cancer as well as assess the potential use of IFITs in prognostication for breast cancer patients.
kw: Breast cancer; IFIT1; IFIT2; IFIT3; IFIT5; prognostic markers

title: TO-ChERIsH: Trajectory of Cardiovascular Ageing, Its Determinants and Impact on Health
abs: Background: Cardiovascular (CV) ageing is a heterogeneous process that exhibits great variation with advancing age among individuals. Some individuals develop ageing-related deteriorations in CV structure and function resulting in CV disease (CVD) (unhealthy CV ageing) while others have relatively preserved CV health with chronological ageing (healthy CV ageing). Determinants of either CV ageing trajectories remain unknown. We hypothesize that investigations of CV ageing trajectories will unravel determinants of unhealthy and healthy CV ageing. Our hypothesis is based on data (2014-2017) from a community-based cohort of elderly individuals with CV imaging and bio-specimens that showed a spectrum of CV functions ranging from preserved to unhealthy measurements, that correlated with lifestyle (physical activity), systemic conditions (diabetes mellitus) and circulating metabolites (such as amino acids and acyl-carnitines). Traditional risk factors such as diabetes mellitus and physical activity, could not fully account for the extent of CV ageing observed. Specific Aims: (i) To determine rates of change in CV ageing over time via CV imaging markers; (ii) To assess if circulating metabolites markers present in archived blood samples (2000-2004) are associated with CV ageing 15 years later (2014-2017) and rates of CV ageing progression (2018-2021) and how these differences vary by gender, physical activity and diabetes mellitus; (iii) To determine impact of CV ageing on development of clinical CVD and overall physical, cognitive and functional health outcomes. Methodology: Participants from 2014-2017 will return in this proposal (2018-2021) for repeat biodata, CV imaging markers, and bio-specimen collection. Baseline and change in CV imaging and metabolite markers will be analysed from archived (2000-2004, 2014-2017) and fresh bio-specimens, adjusting for longitudinal covariates. Significance: Distinguishing trajectories of healthy versus unhealthy CV ageing will reveal determinants and impact of CV ageing. Targeting CV ageing may therefore improve burden of CVD and important ageing-related health outcomes among ageing populations.
kw: cardiovascular; ageing; cardiovascular imaging

title: A Cardiosleep Research Program on Obstructive Sleep Apnea, Blood Pressure Control and Maladaptive Myocardial Remodeling
abs:
The objective of this proposal is to evaluate whether mandibular advancement device (MAD) is non-inferior to continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) in the treatment of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) and blood pressure reduction. OSA and hypertension are highly prevalent disorders with profound impacts on health. Apart from improving quality of-life, an effective OSA treatment could improve cardiovascular risk partly through blood pressure reduction, particularly in patients with high cardiovascular risk in whom blood pressure control is often suboptimal. Although CPAP is useful, the high non-adherence precludes its widespread use. 

East Asians have a restrictive craniofacial phenotype that predisposes them to OSA and the associated cardiovascular stress. CPAP has failed to improve cardiovascular outcomes in randomized trials till date because it is poorly tolerated. MADs are oral appliances that correct the restrictive craniofacial phenotype present in East Asians by protruding the lower jaw to reduce upper airway collapsibility. MADs are better tolerated than CPAP, and this may be an important determinant of the overall effectiveness in treating OSA, and thus ameliorating the downstream adverse health outcomes. We hypothesize that MADs are non-inferior to CPAP in treating OSA and reducing cardiovascular risk by blood pressure reduction in East Asians.

We will recruit East Asian subjects with hypertension and high cardiovascular risk for polysomnography. Patients diagnosed with OSA (n=220) will be randomized to MAD or CPAP groups in a 1:1 ratio for a treatment

title: Innovative Tele-monitored Home-Based Program for Post Total Knee Replacement Rehabilitation: A Noninferiority Randomized Controlled Trial
abs: Background and Aims With an ageing population and an increasing prevalence of obesity and knee osteoarthritis, the number of total knee replacement (TKR) surgery will increase with time. In Singapore, although hospital-based outpatient rehabilitation is standard-of-care for patients post TKR, outpatient rehabilitation is costly and inconvenient for patients and their caregivers. A monitored home-based exercise program provides the best access to care and is an alternative for patients who do not require intensive "hands-on" rehabilitation. We have developed a tele-monitored home-based rehabilitation program and aim to compare the clinical- and cost-effectiveness of this innovative program with that of standard hospital-based rehabilitation among post-TKR patients in a randomized controlled trial (RCT). Hypotheses We hypothesize that an 8-week home-based exercise program, combined with tele-monitoring, will not be clinically inferior to an 8-week hospital-based rehabilitation program at 6 months post TKR, in terms of improving physical functional outcomes, and that the home-based program will be more cost-effective than the hospital-based rehabilitation program. Methods This will be a single assessor-blinded, parallel design, RCT. One hundred thirty patients with TKR will be randomly assigned to either an 8-week hospital-based, physiotherapist-supervised rehabilitation program or an 8-week tele-monitored home-based program. To monitor patients’ functional recovery, the home-based program will use rehabilitation tools and monitoring devices that have been validated for use by patients after TKR. Outcome measures will be collected preoperatively and at 1, 3, and 6 months post TKR. The primary outcome will be physical function. Secondary outcomes include healthcare costs, knee pain intensity, knee impairments, and quality of life. Significance This study is the first in Singapore to examine an innovative and affordable solution for delivering post-TKR rehabilitation services. If successful, the home-based program has the potential to serve as a model for managing knee osteoarthritis and other costly, chronic musculoskeletal conditions to which exercise therapy is beneficial.
kw: Osteoarthritis; Total knee replacement; Home-based exercise program; Tele-monitoring

title: Study into the association between brain amyloid deposition and diabetes mellitus in amnestic mild cognitive impairment
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: The prevalence of Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) are increasing rapidly and both diseases are acknowledged as major public health concerns in Singapore and worldwide. While various epidemiological studies found a link between T2DM and AD, the underlying pathophysiology of this association remains unclear. Amyloid-beta, a core AD histopathological feature, develops early in the AD continuum, including mild cognitive impairment (MCI) stage. Insulin resistance and chronic compensatory hyperinsulinemia, which characterizes T2DM, may also affect amyloid metabolism leading to increased amyloid plaque formation. Therefore, cerebral amyloid deposition may be the pathophysiology underlying the increased risk of AD among T2DM individuals. In this cross-sectional pilot study of 160 amnestic MCI (aMCI) subjects with biomarker evidence of neurodegeneration (80 with T2DM and 80 without T2DM), we will study the association of T2DM with cerebral amyloid deposition and the influence of cerebral amyloid deposition and T2DM on cognitive performance among aMCI subjects. All subjects will undergo a comprehensive neuropsychological assessment and blood test for the measurement of oligomeric amyloid-β. We hypothesise that aMCI subjects with T2DM will have higher levels of oligomeric amyloid-β in the blood compared to aMCI subjects without T2DM. We further hypothesise that the levels of oligomeric amyloid-β in the blood in aMCI subjects with T2DM will be associated with greater impairment in domains of episodic memory and executive function than aMCI patients without T2DM. This pilot study will provide insight into the underlying pathophysiology linking T2DM and the AD process so as to support a personalized and precise approach to prevent or treat AD in patients with T2DM by targeting the specific biological dysfunction. Preliminary data obtained from this study will support subsequent grant applications for future longitudinal studies with a larger sample size.
kw: Mild Cognitive Impairment, Amyloid, Diabetes Mellitus

title: Studies in Chronic Myeloid Leukaemia
abs: CML is caused by the fusion gene, BCR-ABL1, which transforms normal haematopoietic stem cells into their leukaemic counterparts. While inhibitors of the ABL1 tyrosine kinase (TKI) have turned CML into a chronic condition, several important clinical issues remain. These include the inability of TKIs to eradicate leukaemia stem/progenitor cells (SPC) and cure chronic phase (CP) patients, accurately identify CP patients at risk of transforming into a terminal blast crisis (BC) stage, and the lack of effective BC therapy. To understand the mechanisms mediating SPC TKI resistance, and identify risk factors for BC transformation, we undertook a comprehensive evaluation of the CP to BC progression genome, epigenome, and transcriptome. In CP we identified an RNA binding protein, SRSF1, to mediate cytokine-dependent TKI resistance. We also observed a CML-specific DNA methylation signature, which when analyzed together with transcriptional events, identified a set of methylation-silenced genes predicting aggressive behaviour in CP. In BC, PRC pathway and RUNX mutations occurred in a mutually exclusive manner in 70% of BC genomes, suggesting that either class of mutation is sufficient for BC transformation. Additionally, EZH2, a component of PRC2, marked genes in CP for hypermethylation in BC, while DNA methylation cooperated with activation of the PRC1 complex to silence BC tumour suppressor genes. Together, our studies suggest a model in which a limited set of genetic mutations induce BC transformation through reprogramming of the CP epigenome. Our Specific Aims are: 1. To determine the role of SRSF1 in CP CML, 2. To evaluate epigenetic reprogramming of CP SPCs and identify therapeutic targets, and 3. To determine if recurrent BC mutations contribute to BC transformation. The completion of our Aims has the potential to uncover mechanisms of SPC persistence, identify biomarkers to predict BC transformation, and provide insights into new therapies for both stages of CML.
kw: Chronic myeloid leukaemia; Drug resistance; Genetic studies; Leukaemia stem cell

title: An Integrated System to Produce Recycled Mixed Plastic Ingredients and Composites for Infrastructural Applications
abs: This project aims to deliver new products and processes for infrastructural applications, by transforming municipal solid waste (MSW) mixed plastics into raw ingredients (e.g. fibers, aggregates and polymer modifiers) via an integrated system. MSW mixed plastics are incorporated into bituminous mixtures as partial replacement of aggregate and fiber reinforcement (dry process) and as a polymer modifier (wet process). Due to the high cost of sorting, issues to non-homogeneity of the feedstock, and limitation to the usage of recycled plastics, global recycling rates of plastics are currently very low. The majority of waste plastics will have to be disposed of either through landfilling or incineration. In this study, an integrated system will be developed to process MSW mixed plastics into suitable and consistent feedstock; converting them into raw ingredients; and incorporating these ingredients into finished products. This would significantly reduce waste plastics to be discarded in the landfill or through incineration, thus reducing Singapore’s carbon footprint and closing the waste loop. Utilization of MSW mixed plastics could offer enhanced resilience, thermal insulation, noise reduction, corrosion resistance and impact resistance properties in bituminous mixtures. The outcome has high commercial impact: transformation of MSW mixed plastics into value-added raw ingredients for infrastructure, involving environmental-friendly processes with comparable to more superior products performance at estimated cost savings of at least 20%. Hence, this project creates a win-win situation in promoting an eco-friendly Singapore and also in meeting real industry needs with huge market potential.
kw: Integrated System; Recycled Mixed Plastics; Raw Ingredients; Composite Finished Products; Infrastructure

title: A Scalable and Sustainable Process for Transforming Incineration Bottom Ash into Green Aggregates to Significantly Reduce Semakau Landfill Waste Handling
abs: The project aims to develop an integrated, scalable, sustainable and cost-effective granulation process for the production of green incineration bottom ash (IBA) aggregates. To circumvent the challenges associated with the use of IBA in concrete namely, (1) heavy metal leaching & (2) low mechanical strength, this proposal outlines the process wherein a slurry comprising of a mixture of Ground Granulated Blastfurnace Slag (GGBS), and Ordinary Portland cement (OPC) is used to produce GGBS-OPC-coated IBA (as “Go-IBA”) aggregates. Through this project, the different liquid-to-solid ratio of GGBS-OPC liquid binders will also be formulated and optimised to produce high performance, low-cost and marketable aggregates. This innovative product will have the potential to address the rising demands for high-quality aggregates, which are currently dominated by costly and depleting natural aggregates. The project is in collaboration with EnGro Corporation Limited (EnGro) for pilot scale test-bedding and validation. EnGro has expressed their commitment to scale-up and commercialise the technology, as well as the product. This R&D project will not only benefit the local construction industry per se but has worldwide benefits through valorisation of municipal solid waste (MSW) incineration bottom ash (IBA) into aggregate substitutes at a significant volume. As such, the project approach will be expected to result in not only reducing the dependence on natural aggregates but also conserving landfill space and thus prolonging Semakau Landfill (SL) lifespan.
kw: Go-IBA; aggregates; granulation; GGBS-OPC; immobilisation; heavy-metals

title: Catalytic active catalyst support using incineration ash
abs: It has become a major concern to the management of large amounts of ashes being generated after waste incineration in Singapore. With the constantly increasing ash volumes, the burden of Semakau Landfill - the offshore landfill in Singapore is getting heavier. Currently, the reuse of incineration ash (IA) are very limited and restricted due to their potential environmental concerns (mainly heavy metal release with rainwater). Here, we propose a new concept/technique to develop IA as catalytically active ceramic catalyst/substrates. The product is aimed to replace the inactive ceramic support made from cordierite (2MgO-2Al2O3-5SiO2), which has been widely used in the auto-vehicles three-way catalytic converters (TWCC) and other stationary air filter facilities. IA will be modified via a simple physical-chemical method and processed into ceramic catalyst blocks with moldable shapes. Physical-chemical properties and catalytic activities of the developed prototypes will be tested in the laboratory and by industrial partners. Through this cost-effective, functionally efficient and safe solution, approximately 20-25% of the IA produced in Singapore can be consumed annually and converted into valuable feedstock resources as exporting products. The landfill burden is expected to be relieved. Additionally, approximately 2 billion SGD profit is expected to be created each year through this waste-to-resource technique.
kw: waste-to-resource; ash; catalyst; support; ceramic

title: Recycling of Polyethylene- and Polyethylene Terephthalate  Containing Multilayer Packaging Materials
inst: ISCE2 - Institute of Sustainability for Chemicals, Energy and Environment
abs: Multilayer films (MLF) are abundantly used in flexible packaging of consumer goods. Recycling of MLF poses a significant challenge due to the complex composition of the films. While simple mechanical recycling results in inferior materials, separation of the layers can ideally recycle the individual polymers into high value pure components. However, the separation is not easily achieved. A few processes have been developed for selective extraction and recycling of polymers, but can address only selected materials like polyolefins, without catching the full potential of recycling. This proposal aims to develop a chemical process to recycle the polyethylene (PE) and polyethylene terephthalate (PET) commonly found in MLFs by selective extraction and glycolysis, and deliver a high quality PE recyclate, as well as highly pure (ideally food-grade quality) raw material for repolymerization to PET. The process must be able to remove impurities like colors from printing, additives and other soluble polymers. The methodology relies on developing a suitable extraction process for PE extraction, and developing highly active depolymerization catalysts that allow the glycolysis to be run at mild conditions, and adsorbents that can selectively remove the impurities from PET oligomers.
kw: PE, PET, Recycling

title: Scale-up the fabrication of high performance aquaporin (AQP)-based biomimetic flat-sheet membranes for seawater desalination
abs: State-of-the-art reverse osmosis (RO) membranes are able to desalinate seawater with much less energy demand. However, the energy usage is still 1.5-2.0 times of the theoretical minimum dictated by thermodynamics [1]. There remains room for the membrane improvement driven by economy and energy. Among various new concepts, AQP-based biomimetic membrane (ABM) has attracted considerable interests over the recent 10 years. The SMTC/NEWRI team has been working on this area with EWI and PUB funding supports since 2009. A newly invented flat-sheet AQP-based composite membrane showed superior performance compared with commercial BWRO membranes. However, the selectivity of current ABMs shall be further increased for seawater desalination. There is need to further tighten the selective skin without too much sacrificing the water flux by adopting new formula for thin film formation. On the other hand, the flat-sheet ABMs can be used for practical applications if a large-scale production can be realised. As a continuation of our efforts, this proposed research aims to further increase the selectivity of the current flat-sheet ABMs via improved interfacial polymerization formula and better controlled substrate casting. In addition, the biomimetic membrane will be fabricated in commercial level via the collaboration with industry (START and Hyflux) and tested in pilot scale setup to target 10 m3/day permeate using seawater feed. The main tasks include: (1) inventing new formula for AQP-embedded polyamide thin film synthesis on a flat-sheet substrate using three types of AQPs (AQP-Z, fish AQP or mangrove AQP); (2) confirming the feasibility of spray method for AQP embedment (i.e., spraying proteoliposomes on membrane substrate prior to IP layer formation) in both lab-scale and industrial scale; (3) Fabrication of flat-sheet ABMs in large scale and assembly into 2.5-inch and 4-inch spiral wound modules; and (4) Membrane module performance/stability testing in pilot-scale setup.
kw: Aquaporin, Biomimetic membrane, Flat-sheet, Scale-up production, Seawater desalination

title: Exploiting capsule synthesis pathway in Streptococcus pneumoniae to identify new antimicrobial compounds.
abs: Streptococcus pneumoniae is an important respiratory pathogen that causes more than two million deaths worldwide annually. Similar to other pathogenic bacteria, S. pneumoniae encases its cell envelope with capsular polysaccharide (CPS) which protects itself from opsonophagocytosis and mucus clearance. Because of its importance in pathogenesis, all clinically relevant vaccines against S. pneumoniae target the CPS. There are over 98 serotypes identified in S. pneumoniae. The structural variance in CPS produced is problematic and hinders the efficacy of our current vaccines. This variance is attributed to the extreme diversity of glycosyltransferases (GTs), flippases, and polymerases located in the cps locus. Although these enzymes were identified decades ago, little is known about the molecular mechanisms governing their specificity, regulation, and function. Therefore, the long-term goal of this project is to address this knowledge gap by investigating how specificity is determined by the CPS enzymes. This proposal is based on the wealth of structural information available for pneumococcal CPS, genetic approaches enabled by the conditional essentiality of the CPS pathway, and strong unpublished data on the related cell wall synthesis pathway in E. coli. Aim 1 and 2 will elucidate how specificity is determined by the CPS flippases and GTs as well as define the essential residues required for their function. Aim 3 will identify small molecules that inhibit different steps of the CPS pathway. Understanding how CPSs are synthesized in S. pneumoniae is critical to improving our current antimicrobial and vaccine strategies. Results from this study will also have a broad impact on our understanding of related polysaccharide pathways such as O-antigen biosynthesis, O-linked and N-linked glycosylation, and exopolysaccharides synthesis. Finally, enzyme variants isolated from this work with relaxed or altered substrate specificity will provide valuable tools for synthetic biology and glycoengineering.
kw: Antibiotic resistance; Streptococcus pneumoniae; Capsule biosynthesis; Bacterial pathogenesis; Infectious disease

title: Enhancing Cyber Resilience of Deep Learning Models against Adversarial Cyber Attacks
abs: Over the last decade, deep learning has become an integral part of artificial intelligence. It has enabled great leaps of progress in the domains of computer vision, robotics, finance, medicine, and more. In the domain of cybersecurity, deep learning has been widely used to detect malware, intrusions, data leakage, theft, fraud, vulnerabilities, and so on. Given their ability to deal with complex problems and massive amounts of data, deep neural networks have often exceeded the capabilities of humans. However, these models are often trained and executed without considering the possibility of a malicious actor. Such an actor can abuse this powerful tool at any point of its life cycle. For example, the attacker may evade detection, force a system to cause damage, or even reveal confidential information contained within its training data. As a result, researchers have been exploring the domain of adversarial machine learning, to understand and mitigate this threat. Although multiple defence techniques exist, they either apply to computer vision problems, or can be evaded by countering the countermeasures. Therefore, to better secure deep neural networks, we must develop the necessary tools to form a proactive arms-race. In this way, we can safely rely on deep neural networks to perform sensitive tasks and behave as expected. By implementing these tools, we will be able to fully utilize deep learning to further improve our quality of life. The proposed research will focus on developing new methods how to measure a deep neural network’s resilience to all possible attacks with or without knowledge about the model structure and training set. The research will also focus on exploring the resilience of deep learning algorithms to compromised hardware that is used for accelerating their performance. During the research we will provide insights how to compare different deep learning algorithms from resilience point of view and how to improve the resilience of existing models. In the proposed project, there will be two teams: one from Ben-Gurion University, Israel (BGU) and another from Nanyang Technological University, Singapore (NTU). Together, they will cooperate to investigate and develop the tools necessary for protecting the deep learning development cycle; from the beginning to the end.
kw: Deep Learning Security; Security and Robustness of Artificial Intelligence

title: Framework for Practical Quantum Communication with Untrustworthy Devices
abs: As our modern world becomes more and more connected through the Internet and smart mobile devices, the pace of cybercrime and disruptions also quickens. Emerging technologies like artificial intelligence, the Internet of Things, and quantum technologies are also threatening to outpace current cybersecurity practices. This is especially the case for quantum technologies—quantum computers capable of breaking today’s most prevalent cryptosystems such as RSA and ECC are becoming a reality. It has been recently highlighted in a Nature news article that Google, Microsoft, and IBM are now very close to implementing a working quantum computer. Crucially, this means that we have to migrate to a quantum-proof platform quickly, for otherwise our critical information infrastructures will soon lose their ability to secure trade secrets and confidential documents. To achieve a quantum-proof platform, it is necessary to develop communication techniques that are provably-secure. These techniques should not only be secure against quantum computing threats, but also against any other technological advances. The only known method that achieves these is quantum communication: its security is based solely on the established laws of quantum physics and not on how powerful the attackers could be. Importantly, this implies that messages and data secured using quantum communication techniques are mathematically unbreakable. For this reason, quantum communication is widely regarded as the best solution for long-term information security. On the economic side of things, the global quantum communication industry is projected to grow to USD $24 billion by 2025. At present, there are however still challenges that have to be resolved before quantum communication technology can be made truly practical and cost-effective. One major challenge is that near perfect components and devices are needed for current quantum communication technology to be effective. Clearly, this requirement is unrealistic and expensive: real devices are bound to have flaws (however minor) and alignment of components can never be perfect. Consequently, this creates a dangerous gap between the theory and practice of quantum communication. In fact, it has been repeatedly demonstrated that this gap can lead to serious security loopholes. One famous example is the insecurity of quantum detection units: researchers have found an unrepairable loophole in single-photon detectors which can allow attackers to remotely control the behavior of quantum devices from the open channel. Currently, the only known (abstract) solution is to use nonlocal correlations and Bell inequalities to certify the security of untrusted devices. However, this approach is highly unrealistic and overly conservative: it leads to sub-optimal communication rates. The broad objective of this proposal is to devise a novel quantum information framework that enables practical and efficient quantum communication using untrusted or imperfect devic
kw: Quantum Information; Quantum Technologies; Quantum Cryptography; Quantum Information Theory; Quantum Key Distribution; Quantum Random Number Generation

title: Satellite of Excellence in Design Science and Technology for Secure Critical Infrastructure [Satellite DeST-SCI]
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: In the context of DeST-SCI, the primary goal of design science research is to develop knowledge that professionals in cyber security can use to design solutions that when transformed into usable technology, and deployed, would enhance the resilience of CI to cyber-physical attacks. This knowledge comes in several forms such as algorithms, attacker models, impact of attacks, and design principles. Tools to aid a designer in ensuring resilient infrastructure support these forms. The algorithms and tools together constitute what we refer to as “technologies.” During the initial phase, iTrust has successfully created knowledge that has potential applications in the design of new critical infrastructure as well as in legacy systems. However, there remain several challenges to be addressed before the knowledge generated can be put to use in commercial plants. These challenges can be broadly categorized into the following types: resilience, scalability, assessment, analysis, and generality as explained next. Resilience Resilience of a CI refers to its ability to continue operations, possibly with diminished output, when under a cyber-physical attack. While the design of resilient systems has been a widely researched topic in the area of fault diagnosis and tolerance, much work remains to be done in the cyber security domain. Several key challenges must be overcome in the design of systems, particularly CI, that are resilient to cyber-physical attacks. First, the attack space is potentially infinite. Attackers devise new attacks while researchers devise new techniques to detect such attacks. Thus, a major challenge is to design prevention, detection, and other defense mechanisms that can perform well under an exceptionally broad class of attack scenarios. Another challenge is in the design of defense mechanisms that are scalable. The distributed attack detection mechanisms based on invariants is not scalable unless tools are available to accurately generate a complete set of invariants. Similarly, state estimation methods for large power networks either fail to produce accurate estimates in real time or lead to approximate results that result in false alarms. A third key challenge is in the detection of malicious commands and preventing them from arriving at the actuators such as generators, circuit breakers and pumps. Design of highly resilient CI requires technological solutions that address the above as well as several other challenges. Scalability Attack detection in a critical infrastructure is generally formulated as an anomaly detection problem. An anomaly is said to exist in a process when that process deviates from its expected, or “normal” behavior. Anomalies could be in network traffic as well as in process behavior, i.e. in an individual state or in state transitions. Anomalies could be due to faults -- temporary or permanent -- or cyber and physical attacks. In either case, one needs to either specify, or learn, the normal behavior of the pl

title: National Satellite of Excellence in Mobile Systems Security and Cloud Security
abs: The research scope of the programme is as follows: - Mobile platform security. Today’s mobile platforms are some of the most complex and capable computing devices ever created. They share many of the same security threats as traditional desktop computers and are exposed to more threats brought about by their mobility, complexity, and additional sensors. Attacks directed at mobile platforms are much more damaging than attacks at the application level and hence, it is paramount to secure mobile platforms so that they can be effective in protecting both user privacy and ensuring execution of critical functions. - Automatic and continuous user authentication. Real time monitoring/decision systems such as the elderly monitoring system present many demanding problems for users in authenticating themselves to various devices and systems. Traditional authentication methods like passwords are not suitable for elderly and may disrupt workflow and interfere with the primary mission of elderly care. New authentication techniques must blend into the monitoring space seamlessly. - Mobile app security. Mobile apps allow users to access various sensors built into their mobile devices, access files stored locally, and communicate with other users, systems and cloud services. As a result, vulnerable or maliciously infected mobile apps can be very costly to both individual users and organizations. - Mobile cloud security. Data records in real time monitoring systems may contain sensitive information, hence measures must be in place to protect data security and privacy when they are outsourced to the cloud. In particular, access control and privacy-preserving computation over the outsourced records are essential to prohibit leakage of private information to unauthorized parties, including the cloud operators. Data records provide a basis for decision making. Access to and computation on data should be accountable, which means measures must be in place to monitor buggy or inappropriate behaviour of the virtual machines or applications in the cloud.
kw: Mobile platform security; user authentication; mobile app security; mobile cloud security

title: Substitution of Natural Sand with Granite Dust in Concrete Production
abs: There has not been any in-depth research done on the long-term durability of concrete produced with granite dust based on local conditions. Thus, the engineering study is to demonstrate that it is technically feasible to replace natural sand with granite dust in concrete. This would address the industry’s concerns on the higher adoption rate of granite dust in concrete production and provide the confidence to the industry to drive towards higher substitution rate, which will eventually reduce the reliance on natural sand. Useful findings from this engineering study may be incorporated as an Annex into SS 544 for Singapore practice. The skills and technical know-hows learned from this project will be invaluable in the commercialization of this technology. The manpower trained in this project will very likely take the lead in the further development of this technology in Singapore. There are huge potential for this technology to be implemented in the region and beyond, due to the continuous shrinking availability of natural sands and growing concern on environmental protection of natural environment around the globe.

title: Highly permeable, superior anti-fouling thin film nanocomposite hollow fiber membranes for energy-efficient desalination
abs: Insufficient water permeance / selectivity and fouling are the two major obstacles that hinder the improvement in energy efficiency of membrane desalination. Nanomaterials such as polyhedral oligomeric silsesquioxane (POSS) serve as ideal water channels that allow the fast passage of water while rejecting salt ions. By integrating POSS into the selective layer through chemical bonding, the thin fim nanocomposite (TFN) hollow fiber membranes has shown simultaneous increment in the water permeability and salt rejection. Furthermore, with a fast one-step grafting modification, the membrane surface is covered with a zwiterionc polymer layer to combate fouling. In the lab-scale tests, the resultant membrane has not only shown a high water permeability of 6.5 LMH/bar, NaCl rejection of 98.1%, but also superior antifouing properties. At the initial water flux of 35 LMH, no significant fouling is observed for 5 days when NEWater retentate was used as the feed. This proposal aims to bring together the joint expertise between research institute and companies to translate the new technology into commercializable products. Long-term performance of the antifouling TFN membranes in realistic environment will be firstly demonstrated in the lab scale. 1-inch and 4-inch modules with a water permeability of 6 LMH/bar, 98% NaCl rejection and good anti-fouling properties will be fabricated, by unique process and equipment design to overcome the technical bottleneck currently encountered in upscaling thin film composite (TFC) hollwo fiber membranes. The modules will be intergrated into a pilot-scale reverse osmosis (RO) system to produce NEWater at 103 / day and energy saving of 0.2 kWh m-3. The proposed project will lead to further understanding in synthetic water channels and anti-fouling strategies, innovations in membrane and module fabrications, and a novel anti-fouling TFN technology that is close to commercialization.
kw: Hollow fiber membrane; Thin film nanocompoiste; Anti-fouling; Desalination;      Wastewater

title: Rapid Triage for Serious Infections in Infants Younger than 3 Months using A Novel Heart Rate Variability Tool
abs: Febrile infants <3 months present a diagnostic dilemma to paediatricians and emergency physicians. Tension remains between the need for early aggressive intervention among patients with suspected sepsis and the global phenomena of increasing antibiotic resistance. Current triage tools are insufficient. A non-invasive triage tool to detect infants at risk of serious infections (SI) would reduce unnecessary investigations and unwarranted interventions. We aim to develop a novel artificial intelligence (AI) triage tool including heart rate variability (HRV), and evaluate its utility in predicting serious infection (SI) among febrile infants aged <3 months in KK Women’s and Children’s Hospital (KKH) Emergency Department (ED). We hypothesize that HRV provides incremental diagnostic information and a novel triage tool incorporating HRV is superior to current triage tools in discriminating infants with SI from those without. This is a prospective observational study to be conducted in KKH, ED. We will include infants <3 months presenting with a rectal temperature >38oC between Jan 2019 and Dec 2020. SI includes sepsis (including bacteremia), meningitis, lobar pneumonia (confirmed radiologically), osteomyelitis, abscess and urinary tract infection. HRV will be monitored for 5 minutes using a single-lead electrocardiogram (ECG). The ECG signal will be extracted and processed to obtain HRV data. Performance indicators are the area under receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive values, which will be compared between the novel and current existing triage tools. If successful, including HRV information will improve triage precision for febrile infants with SI, allowing resources be focused on the sickest infants.
kw: Serious infections; Sepsis; Triage

title: Effectiveness of diabetes education and medication adjustment with telemonitoring intervention in reducing diabetes complications during Ramadan fasting – a randomized control trial
abs: Aim Investigate the effectiveness of focused diabetes education and medication adjustment with telemonitoring to reduce diabetes complications during Ramadan fasting and assess the cost-effectiveness for Muslims with diabetes in Singapore. Hypotheses Focused diabetes education and medication adjustment with tele-monitoring of blood glucose levels using a standardized mobile device during the month reduces the 30-day incidence rate of diabetes complications when compared to standard care, with increased cost effectiveness compared to increased cost for the intervention. Methodology In a parallel group randomized controlled trial, recruit 100 adults with diabetes who fast at least 15 days in Ramadan, randomized to intervention group comprising of focused diabetes education, medication adjustment and telemonitoring, and control group receiving standard care. outcome is the first incidence of hypoglycemia in Ramadan. The secondary outcomes are (i) first incidence of other diabetes complications in Ramadan episodes including hyperglycemia, episodes of acute infections, attendances in clinic and emergency department and that of hospital admission, (ii) health-related quality of life and (iii) cost-effectiveness of the intervention. Feasibility of the study There are potential difficulties in recruiting. The high drop-out rate has been considered in the sample size estimation. We plan to recruit through primary care in collaboration with their primary care physicians with frequent reminder daytime phone calls when less religious rituals are performed to reduce the loss to follow-up. With the rigor of fasting that encourages discipline, we hope that the patients will be motivated to participate. If needed, other Singhealth polyclinics will be approached to increase patient recruitment. Clinical Significance The study enables us to evaluate focused pre-Ramadan diabetes education and medication adjustment with tele-monitoring as a means to reduce the markedly increased risk of diabetes complications for a large population during the fasting month, with potential for increased cost-effectiveness through reducing unscheduled attendances at clinic and hospital.
kw: Diabetes; Health education; Diabetes complications; Fasting; Cost-benefit analysis; Telemedicine

title: Exploring the Therapeutic Potential of Narciclasine in Treating Metabolic Disorders
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Many countries, including Singapore, are facing a surge of metabolic disorders due to sedentary lifestyle and high-calorie food consumption. As such, there is an urgent need for effective therapeutic approaches for the treatment of these diseases. Recently, we discovered a novel pharmacological strategy in which a natural compound, narciclasine, ameliorates diet-induced obesity (DIO) in mice by promoting energy expenditure. Moreover, narciclasine promotes fat clearance from peripheral metabolic tissues, improves blood metabolic parameters in DIO mice and protects these mice from reduced voluntary physical activity. Further investigation suggested that narciclasine achieves these beneficial effects by promoting a shift from glycolytic to oxidative muscle fibers thereby enhancing mitochondrial respiration and fatty acid oxidation (FAO) in the skeletal muscle. Mechanistically, narciclasine stimulates FAO likely through activating the AMPK signaling pathway. Finally, the beneficial effects of narciclasine treatment in fat clearance and AMPK activation were faithfully reproduced in vitro in cultured murine and human primary myotubes, suggesting its potential use in treating human metabolic diseases. We hypothesize that narciclasine can be developed into efficient therapeutics in treating various metabolic disorders associated with obesity. Moreover, we have synthesized 90 narciclasine analogues and identified one analogue (Ncls-A22) that out-performs ncls in promoting mitochondrial respiration, oxidative metabolism gene expression and AMPK activation. Ncls-A22 also demonstrated stronger anti-obesity activity than ncls. In this study, we propose to fully characterize the beneficial metabolic effects of narciclasine (Aim 1) and decipher the molecular mechanism underlying narciclasine function (Aim 2). We will also explore the therapeutic potential of narciclasine and Ncls-A22 in treating metabolic disorders (Aim 3). Given narciclasine’s distinct chemical structure as compared with other existing metabolic drugs, accomplishing the above proposed studies may lead to the development of a novel class of metabolic drugs for the prevention and treatment of obesity, diabetes, and other metabolic disorders.
kw: Narciclasine, Obesity, diabetes, energy expenditure, fatty acid oxidation, AMPK signaling pathway

title: Enabling a molecular approach to live attenuated flaviviral vaccine development
abs: The recent emergence of Zika virus (ZIKV) as a threat to fetal development, the re-emergence of yellow fever in Brazil and Central Africa and recurrent cyclical dengue epidemics throughout the tropics demand for more effective control measures. Vaccines are one of the most effective tools for controlling disease. However, deriving safe and effective vaccines against flaviviruses such as dengue virus (DENV) has proven challenging. It is further complicated by the need for vaccines to elicit long-term immunity to prevent waning of immunity to levels that paradoxically enhance infection. Among the various vaccine constructs, the live attenuated vaccine (LAV) has been the most successful in eliciting long-term immunity. However, LAV development is more an art instead of science due to deficient understanding of the molecular attributes of LAVs. We have begun to address this knowledge gap and have found that successful flaviviral LAVs balance viral replicative fitness with host antiviral responses; replicative fitness ensures adequate antigen expression while host antiviral responses limit antigenic burden and interrupt pathogenesis. This proposal thus aims to extend upon our findings to establish a molecular approach to flaviviral LAV development, focusing firstly on DENV and ZIKV. Our overall goal is to define the virus-host interaction that characterizes flaviviral attenuation. A unique feature of this study is the elucidation of virus-host interaction in cells with diploid instead of aneuploidic genomes, which are unstable and confounded by abnormal gene copy numbers. We will also elucidate the virus-diploid host interactions that distinguish successfully attenuated from over- or under-attenuated DENVs. Finally, we will explore an interesting attenuating mutation in the ZIKV DN-2 strain, which we recently derived and which suggests the intriguing possibility that viral lipid membrane is a determinant of attenuation. If successful, this study could pave the way for a rational approach to LAV development.
kw: Dengue, Zika, flavivirus, live attenuated vaccine

title: DEVELOPING PATIENT-SPECIFIC HEPATOCELLULAR CARCINOMA (HCC) ORGANOIDS WITH STROMA (PDO+S) FOR DRUG SCREENING AND PERSONALIZED MEDICINE
abs: Recently developed patient-derived organoid (PDO) technologies hold tremendous potential for personalized cancer therapy, particularly for preclinical drug development and predicting patient drug response. However, PDO remain a model system exclusively composed of cancer cells and devoid of other cell types (tumor stroma) present in the tumor microenvironment. This is a major limitation as the tumor stroma (vasculature, immune cells etc.) may significantly influence drug efficacy. As such, PDO models may have limited predictive power for drug screening particularly for cancer drugs that work by targeting the tumor stroma. Indeed, a seminal clinical trial (Science, 2018) recently showed that PDO models were incapable of identifying an anti-angiogenic drug as effective in a PDO-based drug screen. Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is one of the leading causes of cancer death worldwide and is the fourth most common cancer in men in Singapore. Most approved and experimental drugs in HCC target the tumor microenvironment. We hypothesize that it is necessary to tailor HCC PDO to compositionally reflect the unique patient tumor stroma for organoids to be truly predictive of drug response in HCC patients. We will characterize the stromal composition of 10 HCC tumors and develop corresponding PDO that incorporate stromal cells (PDO+Stroma or PDO+S) using tissue engineering technologies (Aim 1). We will then validate these engineered PDO+S by comparing their genomic and transcriptomic profiles against that of the original patient tumor (Aim 2) using next generation sequencing. Lastly, we will subject both PDO and PDO+S to a drug screen and validate observed differences by comparing against the drug response of PDO grown as xenografts in vivo (Aim 3). Elucidating the effect of including stroma in HCC PDO will greatly impact the field as it will radically change how HCC PDO are used for drug development and personalized drug testing.
kw: organoids, personalized medicine, cancer, tumor stroma, drug testing

title: Role of T-cells in the pathogenesis of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS): Identification of a unique immunologic signature
abs: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS), the most common glomerulopathy resulting in end stage kidney failure in children, is a heterogeneous disease. Current protocols tend to treat FSGS as a single entity, and this may explain the lack of response to treatment with subsequent progression of the disease. We have recently reported a subgroup of FSGS patients with a specific immunological profile of T-cell exhaustion which could account for their favourable response to rituximab (anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody) therapy. This was further supported by significant downregulation of CD8 memory T-cells in FSGS patients with steroid dependent nephrotic syndrome (SDNS) compared to minimal change disease (MCD) and healthy controls. Moreover, our preliminary results showed higher expression of CXCR5 T follicular helper (Tfh) cells in FSGS compared to MCD and controls. We therefore hypothesized that T-cell activation plays a role in the pathogenesis of immune-mediated FSGS associated with increased expression of CXCR5 Tfh-cells and subsequent T-cell exhaustion, characterized by decreased expression of memory T-cells and downregulation of stimulated CD154 and IFNγ. Activation of T-cells could produce circulating metabolites that increase podocyte permeability and hence proteinuria. The primary aim of this study is to elucidate the T-cell events of this immune-mediated subset of FSGS patients by firstly, investigating the nature of the dysregulated T-cell activation, and in particular the co-stimulatory pathways involved in upregulation of CXCR5 by analysis of upstream transcription factors, cytokine profile, and T-cell subsets. The secondary aim is to identify the circulating metabolites with subsequent in-vitro validation using albumin permeability assay and podocyte injury assay. Delineating the immunological mechanism underpinning this difficult disease in this subgroup of FSGS patients will allow us to stratify the patients according to their specific immunological signature and the corresponding treatment regimes.
kw: T-cell activation; Primary nephrotic syndrome; Circulating metabolites

title: HOXC10 Maintains White Adipose Tissue Identity and its loss via Proteasomal Activity Leads to Enhanced Browning of White Adipose Tissues
abs: Browning of subcutaneous white adipose tissue (WAT) promotes energy expenditure and improves glucose homeostasis in humans, and hence is a promising avenue to treat obesity and metabolic diseases. However, the underlying mechanisms regulating this process are incompletely understood. The homeobox-containing transcription factor HOXC10 was initially identified as a regulator of forelimb specifications in mammals. Subsequent studies revealed that perturbations in HOXC10 protein stability play a key role in the progression of several cancers, indicating that HOXC10 regulate a wide array of processes through distinct mechanisms. We show that HOXC10 is selectively expressed in subcutaneous WAT. In cultured adipocytes, ectopic expression of HOXC10 suppressed thermogenic brown genes, while knockdown of HOXC10 drives thermogenesis and converts subcutaneous WAT to brown-like adipocytes. In cold-exposed mice, the abundance of HOXC10 protein levels inversely correlates with thermogenic genes in subcutaneous WAT, suggesting that HOXC10 is post-translationally regulated upon activation of β3-adrenergic signaling. These results highlight that HOXC10 as a dominant regulator in remodelling WAT browning. It is therefore of great clinical relevance to investigate the molecular mechanisms of HOXC10 governing the process of subcutaneous WAT browning. We proposed that cold adaptation requires enhanced proteasome activity to regulate the turnover of HOXC10, thus converting white adipocytes into thermogenic brown-like adipocytes, and increasing energy expenditure. Moreover, we aim to identify novel downstream effectors that stimulates HOXC10 degradation and its impact on energy expenditure. These studies will provide mechanistic understanding of proteolytic control of HOXC10 and may provide a potential therapeutic target for obesity and metabolic diseases.
kw: HOXC10, Obesity, Browning, White adipose tissue, Thermogenesis, energy expenditure, cold challenge

title: Modulating branched-chain amino acid availability as a new paradigm in treatment of hepatocellular carcinoma
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Cancer is currently the leading cause of death in Singapore, with liver cancer accounting for almost 10% of all cancer deaths, and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) being the most predominant liver cancer subtype. Despite the attention paid to elucidating the signaling pathways involved in HCC, there are still limited therapeutic options available, especially for advanced stages of HCC, and the rate of recurrence in patients is high. Thus, there is a need to find novel pathways and therapeutic targets for patients with advanced stage and diffuse tumors, and to limit cancer recurrence in patients after treatment. Our lab had recently identified that there is a progressive loss of branched-chain amino acid (BCAA) catabolism, and a corresponding accumulation of intracellular BCAAs in HCC tumors. BCAAs are a class of essential amino acids that cannot be synthesized by human cells and are thus required within our diet. They are important for protein synthesis, and serve as major nitrogen donors for alanine and glutamine synthesis. Moreover, BCAAs, in particular Leucine, activate the mTOR pathway in the presence of active growth signaling to promote protein synthesis and cell proliferation. We have found that decreasing the amount of intracellular BCAA in tumor cells by restricting dietary BCAA intake can significantly decrease tumor burden and improve overall survival in vivo (unpublished data). Since nutrient transport into cells is a downstream limiting factor in BCAA availability, we hypothesize that modulating the transport of BCAAs into cancer cells will be a more direct and effective method for controlling intracellular BCAA levels and cancer progression compared to dietary control, and thus be a potential therapeutic target. We propose to 1) establish the viability of reducing BCAA uptake and tumor proliferation by inhibiting BCAA transporters in HCC, and 2) develop compounds specific for BCAA transporters based on rational design and evaluate their effectiveness.
kw: branched chain amino acids; hepatocellular carcinoma; L-type amino acid transporters; liver cancer; small molecule inhibitors

title: Actin cytoskeleton driven intrinsic chirality – a role in collective cell migration and in tissue engineering application
abs: Consistent left-right patterning (or chirality) is a biomedically important morphogenesis process during embryonic development. Left-right characteristics are evident at the level of cell collectives, and even at the level of individual cells. Development of cellular left-right asymmetry is thought to involve the activities of the cytoskeleton, a dynamic system of intracellular filaments. However, the specific cytoskeletal mechanism(s) responsible for such left-right symmetry-breaking remains unknown. Furthermore, the link between single cell asymmetry and asymmetric morphogenesis of tissue or organism is missing. Based on our recent discovery of a chiral organization of the actin cytoskeleton in cells confined to isotropic circular adhesive islands, and our previous theoretical study of formin-driven actin polymerization, we proposed a model showing how asymmetric interaction of actin filaments with formins could generate chirality of entire actin cytoskeleton in isotropic cell. A role for formins in determining organismal level left-right patterning was later confirmed in genetic studies, in which formins control the direction of snail shell coils and asymmetric positioning of frog heart. Taken together, one envisions that single cell chirality orchestrated by the actin cytoskeleton potentially underlies the asymmetric development of tissue and organism. Here, the main hypothesis proposed that helical asymmetry of actin filament is translated with the aid of actin-associated proteins, in particular formins, to cellular-scale chirality which drives chiral cell locomotion, and may serve as the primary asymmetric signal in tissue morphogenesis. We plan to employ single-molecule studies to investigate how interplay of proteins at actin filament barbed-end influences actin filament assembly to control cellular-scale chirality. Next, we will investigate how the characteristic of intrinsic chirality of individual cell leads to the emergence of left-right asymmetric collective cell migration on micropatterns. Finally, we ask if the phenomenon of L-R asymmetry observed in cardiomyocytes could be useful as an endpoint for screening putative cardiotoxic compounds.
kw: Actin cytoskeleton; Left-right asymmetry; Micropatterning; Collective cell migration; Phenomics; Drug testing

title: Bedside to bench and back again: evaluating Neisseria spp. as novel respiratory pathobionts using systems biology
abs: Chronic respiratory disease is a major health and economic burden to individuals and societies. These diseases, including asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and bronchiectasis are challenging to diagnose and treat; due to clinical heterogeneity, multiple endo-phenotypes and their overlap. Consequently, a personalised approach accounting for microbiomes requires exploration particularly in bronchiectasis: a chronic and irreversible heterogeneous airway disease of high Asian prevalence. In work performed by the PI, we have identified an Asian-bronchiectasis phenotype whose microbiome is dominated by the bacterial taxa Neisseria. This phenotype associates with poorer clinical outcome compared to Pseudomonas, a well-established bronchiectasis pathogen. Neisseria is best known as a cause of meningitis and gonorrhoea and only limited case reports suggest it as an airway pathogen. Using clinical isolates derived from airway specimens of Asian bronchiectasis patients demonstrating our deleterious clinical phenotype, we have established an animal model of Neisseria lung infection that demonstrates significant inflammation and tissue destruction. In this proposal, we extend our studies to address three key issues related to Neisseria airway pathogenesis. First, we will elucidate mechanisms by which Neisseria establishes airway infection using our animal model and systems biology illustrating it as a novel respiratory pathogen. Next, we will determine its role in the development of bronchiectasis using an animal model at high risk of disease: a Multicilin (Mci) mouse mutant, deficient in airway cilia, a key risk factor for bronchiectasis. Finally, we will validate our animal findings in human cohorts and translate discovered biomarkers and mechanisms of Neisseria lung pathogenesis including a prospective assessment of its immunological consequence. The novel mechanisms elucidated and new approaches developed will permit improved patient stratification and a deeper understanding of Asian phenotypes of pulmonary disease: an understudied field with significant implications for patient care and clinical outcome.
kw: Bronchiectasis; Microbiome; Pathobiont; Endophenotype; Precision medicine.

title: Functional implication of cytoplasmic EZH2 in cancer stem cells
abs: We reported that the histone methyltransferase, EZH2, controls leukocyte migration through interaction with the cytoskeleton remodeling effector, VAV, and direct methylation of the cytoskeletal regulatory protein, Talin. It remains unclear, whether this regulatory mechanism is relevance for tumorigenesis. Our recent study revealed that cytosolic EZH2 was enriched in breast cancer stem cells and overexpression of EZH2 promoted adhesion turnover and tumorigenesis in a VAV interaction-, Talin1-methylation-dependent manner. We were able to abolish the transformation and tumor growth by targeted disruption of EZH2 interaction with VAV. To further investigate the relevance of our finding in human cancers and determine the mechanisms controlling the cytosolic localization of EZH2 in breast cancer stem cells, and develop novel therapeutic strategies for cancer by targeting cytosolic EZH2, we propose 3 complementary specific aims, which will make use of cell-biological, structural, biochemical and proteomic approaches, in vitro culture systems and in vivo mouse models. Specific Aim 1: To establish the relevance of cytoplasmic EZH2 in primary cancer stem cells We showed an enrichment of cytosolic EZH2 in triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) cell line and will investigate cytosolic EZH2 in primary human cancer stem cells. Cytosolic EZH2 during cancer progression will be studied in a TNBC mouse model. Specific Aim 2: To determine the molecular mechanisms governing subcellular localization and functions of EZH2 in breast cancer stem cells The molecular mechanisms regulating cytosolic localization and cellular functions of EZH2 in breast cancer stem cells (CSCs) will be determined. Single cell RNA-seq will be used to identify novel surface markers to isolate live cells with cytosolic EZH2 for functional characterizations. Specific Aim 3: Targeted disruption of VAV interaction-dependent oncogenic activity of EZH2 We showed reduced cellular transformation and tumor growth by genetically disrupting EZH2-VAV interaction. We will establish strategies to effectively disrupt endogenous EZH2-VAV interaction in vivo.
kw: Cancer; Ezh2; lysine methylation; cancer stem cells

title: Novel Intrinsic mechanisms promoting neural stem cell reactivation
abs: Neural stem cells have the potential to regenerate and repair brain damage. However, in the mammalian adult brain, the majority of neural stem cells (NSCs) are in a mitotically inactive, quiescent state with little regenerative ability. Interestingly, in response to extrinsic stimuli, these quiescent NSCs can exit from quiescence and resume proliferation (reactivation) to generate new neurons. However, failure in NSC reactivation may result in the neurodevelopmental disorders. The quiescence state of NSCs is also associated with aging brain. Despite these abundant evidence, how NSCs switch between quiescence and proliferation remains poorly understood. Our work supported by NMRC (July 2015-Jan 2019) showed that the spindle matrix complex, as a key nuclear factor, intrinsically promotes NSC reactivation. Here, we have identified Cullin 4 (Cul4)-RING ubiquitin ligase complex (CRL4) as a new intrinsic factor promoting reactivation of Drosophila NSCs. In addition, mutations in Cul4B, which encodes a subunit of CRL4 E3 ligase, are reported to cause neurodevelopmental disorders including mental retardation syndrome and malformations of cortical development. Given that the Hippo pathway maintains the quiescence (or inhibits the proliferation) of NSCs in both Drosophila and mammalian brains, we hypothesize that CRL4 promotes ubiquitination of Warts, a key Hippo pathway component, to stimulate NSC reactivation. We will investigate the role of both Drosophila and mammalian CRL4 complex in NSCs proliferation/reactivation (Aim 1). We will directly test our hypothesis that CRL4 complex promotes the ubiquitination of Warts, a key component of the Hippo pathway (Aim 2). We will establish the link between CRL4 and Wts biochemically and genetically in Drosophila models. Given the association of human Cullin 4B mutations with neurodevelopmental disorders, the outcomes from this application will provide important novel insight into intrinsic mechanisms that promote NSC proliferation and will ultimately contribute to our understanding on brain development, associated neurological disorders and aging.
kw: Drosophila, neural stem cells, quiescence, proliferation, reactivation, neuroblasts

title: Mechanisms of enhancer alterations in etiologically-distinct CCAs and their clinical implications
abs: Cholangiocarcinoma (CCA) is a dismal, heterogeneous malignancy with a need for new therapeutic strategies. Enhancers are distal regulatory regions implicated in tumorigenesis, and their studies have generated novel therapeutic targets in various cancers. Our recent study uncovered two CCA subtypes associated with different etiologies and mutations in epigenetic modifiers (liver-fluke-infected CCAs, versus BAP1-mutant fluke-negative CCAs), and subsequent analysis suggested divergent enhancer alterations as well. Since inflammatory signaling leads to enhancer alterations, and biliary tract inflammation is a risk factor for CCA (particularly for liver-fluke-infected cases), inflammatory response may therefore play a role in CCA enhancer dysregulation. The histone deubiquitinase BAP1 has been shown to regulate enhancer activity, thus BAP1 loss may also play a role in enhancer dysregulation.
