We therefore hypothesize that divergent enhancer dysregulation in fluke-positive and BAP1-mutant fluke-negative CCAs drive distinct oncogenic regulatory circuits and transcriptional programs. Inflammatory response (predominantly in fluke-positive CCA) and BAP1 mutations (predominantly in fluke-negative CCA) play mechanistic roles in enhancer dysregulation, and may underlie divergence in enhancer landscapes. To investigate this hypothesis, we will profile and compare the enhancer landscapes, regulatory circuits, and transcriptional programs, in these CCA subtypes (Aim 1). We will investigate the effect of inflammatory signaling on enhancer dysregulation, and the development of enhancer dysregulation during chronic inflammation (Aim 2). We will investigate the effect of BAP1 loss on enhancer dysregulation, and discover drugs synthetically-lethal with BAP1 mutations (Aim 3). This study will elucidate mechanisms of enhancer alterations in etiologically-distinct CCAs, and allow the identification of regulators of tumor-promoting enhancers as potential therapeutic targets tailored to specific CCA subtypes.
kw: Cholangiocarcinoma, Enhancer, BAP1

title: Elucidating molecular mechanisms of the OmpC-Mla system in bacterial lipid transport and virulence
abs: Gram-negative bacteria depend for their survival on having an intact outer membrane (OM), which functions as a permeability barrier against toxic molecules including antibiotics. The OM is an asymmetric lipid bilayer in which the outer leaflet is comprised of lipopolysaccharides (LPS) and the inner leaflet of phospholipids (PLs). Lipid asymmetry in the OM is required for its barrier function, but building and maintaining this asymmetric bilayer is a challenge. Maintenance of lipid asymmetry is believed to be mediated by the OmpC-Mla system. This system is proposed to remove PLs that are mislocalized in the outer leaflet of the OM, and transport them back to the inner membrane (IM). The OmpC-Mla system is the first PL-trafficking system reported in Gram-negative bacteria, and is also directly involved in the virulence of several pathogens. Despite its fundamental and clinical importance, however, the molecular mechanisms responsible for OmpC-Mla activity are unknown. This proposal outlines experiments to characterize the protein complexes of the OmpC-Mla system, the molecular mechanisms of PL transport, and the role of the system during Gram-negative infection. We will characterize the structure and function of the OmpC-MlaA complex to elucidate the mechanism of PL extraction from the OM. We will also reconstitute PL transfer reactions from OmpC-MlaA to MlaC, and subsequently to the MlaFEDB complex, and characterize how MlaC interacts with these other OmpC-Mla components during PL transfer. Finally, we will use a mouse model of urinary tract infection to understand the role of the OmpC-Mla system in virulence, which is independent of its function in OM lipid asymmetry. Given the role of OM lipid asymmetry in intrinsic Gram-negative antibiotic resistance and in pathogenesis, this proposal will provide a key foundation for future studies into small molecule OmpC-Mla inhibitors that may function as novel antibiotics or as adjuvants to existing antibiotics.
kw: lipid asymmetry, phospholipid binding and transport, protein-protein interactions, phospholipid

title: Development of SGLT2 inhibitors as a novel targeted therapy for EGFR-WT and LKB1-mutant human non-small cell lung cancer
abs: Lung cancer is one of the leading cancers worldwide including Singapore. Approximately 85% lung cancers histopathologically are non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). At present, specific inhibitors against epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) have been successfully developed as a targeted therapy applicable for those NSCLC patients with EGFR mutation (approximately in 40% Asian and 15% Caucasian NSCLC patients). However, the EGFR inhibitors are not applicable to majority of the NSCLC patients wild-type (WT)-EGFR and therefore there is an urgent need to develop a new targeted therapy covering this group of lung cancer patients. On the other hand, liver kinase B1 (LKB1) (also called STK11) is an important tumor suppressor and its loss-of-function mutation is frequently observed in NSCLC. The ongoing work in our laboratory has obtained two key preliminary findings: (i) EGFR mutation and LKB1 mutation are mutually exclusive in NSCLC; (ii) NSCLC cells with WT-EGFR and mutant-LKB1 are hypersensitive to cell death induced by glucose starvation and by a specific sodium-glucose linked transporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor canagliflozin. We thus hypothesize that (a) NSCLC cells with WT-EGFR and mutant-LKB1 are highly susceptible to cell death induced by glucose starvation due to impaired AMPK activation and defective autophagy induction; (b) SGLT2 inhibitors possess selective therapeutic efficacy on EGFR-WT and LKB1-mutant NSCLC cells. The main objective of this study is to develop SGLT2 inhibitors as a novel targeted therapy for a specific group of NSCLC patients with WT-EGFR and mutant-LKB1. This project is highly translational as SGLT2 inhibitors are FDA-approved first line anti-diabetic drugs. Our project will repurpose SGLT2 inhibitors as a new class of therapeutic agents targeting a significant percentage of NSCLC patients with WT-EGFR and mutant-LKB1 (ranging from 7-34%, on average in about 10% Asian and 30% Caucasian NSCLC patients), thus filling a big gap in treatment of lung cancer.
kw: non-small cell lung cancer, targeted therapy, LKB1, AMPK, SGLT2, EGFR

title: Harnessing and enhancing immunotherapy against nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC)
abs: EBV associated nasopharyngeal cancer is the commonest head and neck cancer in Singapore, and is common in South East Asia. The disease is often diagnosed late, carries a high risk of recurrent and metastatic potential, and novel therapy is an urgent need. Despite the strong EBV etiology, prior immunotherapy strategies targeting EBV antigens have largely been ineffective. Immune check point inhibitors are currently being investigated in NPC, but current data shows modest efficacy for undefined reasons. Nonetheless, NPC shows an “inflamed T cell phenotype” with rich lymphocytic infiltrate, and our hypothesis is that the tumour microenvironment is characterised by strong immunosuppressive cells (Treg, myeloid derived suppressor cells) and cytokines, including VEGF, TGF􀀀􀀃and IDO, which limit efficacy of antiPD1 treatment. Based on our preliminary data that VEGF inhibition is able to enhance immune infiltration, we propose a randomised phase II study aimed at: 1. evaluating the efficacy of antiPD1 pembrolizumab therapy with or without bevacizumab. 2. Evaluating the anti EBV immune response with antiPD1 treatment. 3. Genomic sequencing analysis of tumour and both tumour and peripheral blood T cells of clinically responding and non-responding patients for T cell neo-epitopes that are predicted to incite T cell activation. To our best knowledge this is a unique effort and will potentially provide unprecedented insights to immunotherapy for NPC, through elucidating 1. The role of anti-VEGF therapy in combination with pembrolizumab 2. the contribution of EBV antigens in the immune response in NPC 3. biomarkers for predicting clinical benefit from antiPD1 therapy and 4. potential tumour neoantigens, shared and individual, which may be used in future work to design individualised vaccines against NPC.
kw: nasopharyngeal cancer, Epstein Barr virus, anti-PD1, immunotherapy, tumour neoantigens

title: Determining the Function of Live-Attenuated Vaccine Induced Pro-Inflammatory Responses in Eliciting Vaccine-Associated Adverse Events and Immunogenicity.
abs: Vaccination to prevent infectious diseases has been hailed as the greatest public health achievement in the 20th century. Increasingly, vaccines are being used to prevent chronic infections and cancers. Moreover, World Health Organisation (WHO) has advocated for vaccines to be used as countermeasures to prevent antimicrobial resistance. Despite these successes, however, there is growing public concern on vaccine safety. Although no causal link has been established between vaccination and conditions such as autism, segments of the public have reduced vaccine uptake, resulting in re-emergence of what were once well-controlled infections, such as measles and mumps. Such mistrust in vaccines stems, at least in part, from the lack of detailed understanding of the molecular basis of vaccine safety. Such understanding is needed for an evidence-based approach to public education. It would also form the molecular basis for the development of vaccines with fewer adverse events. We propose that such understanding is now possible due to recent findings from our group. We have shown that the molecular correlates of vaccine-induced immunity are distinctly separated from the correlates of adverse events (AEs) by the time in which the innate immune and pro-inflammatory responses are induced. Herein, we propose a study that demonstrates the functional relationship between an early innate immune and pro-inflammatory response with AEs. We will use an experimental medicine approach with detailed molecular investigations to demonstrate the functional specificity of our molecular correlates of AEs. We will test the hypothesis that inhibition of the molecular correlates of AEs, which are expressed in the first 24 hours post-vaccination, will reduce the rate of vaccine-associated AEs by 50%. We will also show that AE suppression will not impact the molecular determinants of robust vaccine-induced immunity. If successful, this study will fill a major gap in knowledge on the determinants of vaccine safety.
kw: Vaccine; Live attenuated; NSAIDs; Randomised; Single-blinded

title: Novel genetic and non-genetic risk factors for endothelial dysfunction and diabetic micro-angiopathies – meeting future challenges
inst: Khoo Teck Puat Hospital Pte Ltd
abs: Background Supported by previous NMRC grants, the in-depth phenotyping and serial follow-up of 2,100 multi-ethnic individuals with type 2 diabetes (T2DM) from 2011-2017 have made major contributions to diabetes research (https://www.ktph.com.sg/cru/section_page/494). The cohort also provided rich data and bio-repository to support the operations of national diabetes research consortium. Contemporary epidemiology has informed future unmet needs: (1) increase in longevity related disability e.g. cognitive dysfunction; (2) Amputation due to diabetic foot syndrome (DFS) remains unabated. In this region, our cohort is the only one focusing on these issues. Nonetheless, important gaps in phenotyping remain in our cohort. Thus, we aim to systematically recall all participants from the study-base over ~3 years for re-assessment (including blood and urine collection). Hypothesis Traditional and novel risk factors (RFs) (including genetics), collected at baseline and reassessed serially (to derive their variability), will predict long-term changes in vascular (endothelial) function and incident diabetic complications (including cognitive dysfunction). Methods We will include exposures critical to chronic metabolic disorders: (1) dietary assessment (using the newly-developed web-based platform evolved from the GUSTO cohort, suitable for non-pregnant adults) and (2) physical activities (by tri-axial accelerometer). We will focus on important but under addressed outcomes such as cognitive dysfunction (assessment as employed by the SLAS cohort), and diabetic foot syndrome (DFS) which are in-part attributable to vascular (endothelial) dysfunction. Therefore, our enhanced plan will investigate the long-term relationship between (i) traditional (e.g. hyperglycemia) & novel RFs (e.g. haptoglobinuria) and their variability over time, (ii) endothelial function, (iii) intermediate phenotype (e.g. arterial stiffness) and (iv) extended spectrum of final phenotype i.e. cognitive function, DFS, nephropathy and retinopathy. Significance Collaborating with other major local cohorts (GUSTO & SLAS), we will meet the needs of providing high-quality culturally sensitive local exposures (e.g. nutrition) and outcomes data and biorepository dedicated to T2DM.
kw: Type 2 diabetes; Microvascular complications; Endothelial function; Biomarkers; Cognitive function; Lifestyle

title: Comprehensive interrogation of the epigenetics promoter and enhancer landscape in HCC to identify aberrant regulatory mechanisms associated with HCC.
abs: Overall survival in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains exceedingly poor due to the dearth of efficacious systemic therapies for this complex malignancy. There are still no validated biomarkers to date and this translated to the inadequacy of extant investigative approaches. Additional and more comprehensive exploration of HCC is therefore required to address this urgent unmet clinical need. The epigenetics enhancer and promoter landscape as well as chromatin organization remain unexplored in HCC. We aim to conduct a comprehensive interrogation of the promoter and enhancer landscape to elucidate deregulated regulatory mechanisms associated with HCC at the epigenetics level. We hypothesize that aberrations in these key regulatory elements are significant drivers in HCC tumorigenesis and will help us identify critical pathways and biomarkers directly impacting on the clinical trajectory of HCC. Specifically, we will perform global epigenomics profiles of primary HCC to identify key promoters and enhancers involved in driving HCC, elucidate aberrant promoter-enhancer interactions and interrogate the chromatin organization in non-viral and Hep B-driven HCC. In addition, we will investigate the co-dependence between phylogenetic and phyloepigenetic trees responsible for the intra-tumoral heterogeneity in HCC evolution. We will adopt ChIP-seq technology (both modified histone marks and CTCF) and Hi-C chromosomal conformation techniques to pursue the aims of this study. Pipelines for these epigenetic techniques have been established and successfully applied in our lab. Through comprehensive analysis of the global epigenetic promoter and enhancer landscape, we seek to unravel novel biomarkers and therapeutic approaches for HCC. Importantly, this epigenomics study leverages on the comprehensive multi–omics platform in HCC already established by our NMRC TCR National Flagship Program in Liver Cancer. Our prospective multi-disciplinary and multi-institution translational-clinical program collects multi-region samples from resected HCC in a surgical cohort and interrogates the genomics, immunomics and metabolomics of HCC to guide Precision Medicine strategies.
kw: epigenetics; chromatin organization; promoters; enhancers; hepatocellular carcioma; genetics

title: Discovering novel regulators of gene expression by CRISPR dCas9-ORFeome fusion screen
abs: Gene expression is the fundamental of life. Dysregulation of gene expression underlies the pathology of a myriad of diseases, including developmental disorders and cancers. Multiple cis and trans players, including promoter, transcription factors, and chromatin modifiers, participate in this tightly regulated process. The human genome encodes for about 23,000 genes, of which the functions of many remain elusive. Furthermore, many proteins are multifunctional, but the various functions of these proteins are not well established. To illuminate this dark matter of the genome, we will engineer fusions of the human ORFeome with the catalytically inactive Type II CRISPR-associated protein, dCas9, to screen for novel gene expression regulators. We will use a clinically relevant multidrug transporter, ABCG2, as readout for high throughput screen in the human chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML) cell line, K562. ABCG2 is implicated in multidrug resistance, and upregulation of ABCG2 in K562 cells is known to confer drug resistance to imatinib, a BCR/ABL tyrosine kinase inhibitor. In cancers, genetic mutations often cause expression change and mislocalization of proteins. The dCas9-ORF fusions simulate mislocalization of cytoplasmic and membranous proteins into the nucleus, acting as a tool to dissect the functional roles of mislocalized proteins in disease states. Furthermore, using the same system, we are also screening for effective dCas9-activator to improvise current CRISPR activation (CRISPRa) system and as candidate for gene therapy. In summary, the dCas9 fusion system that we are constructing is a powerful tool for many downstream applications. Our genome-wide CRISPR-based functional screen can comprehensively identify novel gene expression regulators that will be of value for disease targeting and drug discovery.
kw: CRISPR, dCas9, gene expression regulators, ORF, transcription factors, chromatin modifiers

title: Therapeutic targeting of oncogenic transcriptional dependency by protein degraders
abs: Extensive genomic sequencing has enriched cancer research and precision medicine, yet unfortunately the oncological targets pursued by pharmaceutical companies have not expanded as rapidly. Many desirable oncoproteins especially transcription factors and epigenetic regulators remain intractable. To address these challenges, we and others have investigated a novel class of Proteolysis Targeting Chimeras which redirect the ubiquitin proteasome pathway to degrade oncoproteins. Importantly, degraders targeting BET bromodomain proteins and CDK9 show superior activities to abolish the core oncogenic transcriptional programs. Therefore, we hypothesize that protein degraders can be implemented to interrogate and target transcriptional addictions of human cancers. This proposed study will elaborate the druggability of oncoprotein dependency and its mechanistic connections to the aberrant core transcriptional programs in soft-tissue sarcomas. Specific Aim 1 will chart the enhancer landscape and identify core transcriptional programs governed by disease-specific oncoproteins. Core transcriptional regulatory circuitry will be reconstructed based on H3K27ac ChIP-seq analysis, followed by experimental verification and functional investigation. Specific Aim 2 will examine the vulnerability of core transcriptional programs to newly developed protein degraders against BET bromodomain proteins and CDK9. Both chemical biology and genetic approaches will be applied to explore oncoprotein dependency in both cell line and animal models. Specific Aim 3 seeks to identify biomarkers associated with responsiveness to protein degraders and develop favourable schemes of combination therapy. Predictive markers which can guide patient stratification and combination therapy, will be verified by integrative transcriptomic and functional analysis. Together, our data will improve substantially current understanding of the molecular mechanisms driving sarcomagenesis, and guide the therapeutic targeting of transcriptional addictions in cancer. This study will also nurture the development of protein-degrading modality for cancer treatment and provide insights into both preclinical optimization and clinical translation of protein degraders.
kw: BET bromodomain protein; CDK9; Core transcriptional regulatory circuitry; Proteolysis targeting chimera; Soft-tissue sarcoma

title: INTERROGATING THE ROLE OF FATTY ACID METABOLISM IN INDUCING MESENCHYMAL-TO-EPITHELIAL TRANSITION IN TRIPLE NEGATIVE BREAST CANCER
abs: Triple negative breast cancers (TNBCs) represent a subtype often prone to metastasis and refractory to standard of care. Their resistance to chemotherapy may be attributed to cancer stem cells (CSCs) found within tumors. The activation of epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) has been demonstrated to promote the dedifferentiation of cancer cells to gain CSC status. Thus, we hypothesized that induction of the reverse process of EMT, also known as MET, would convert mesenchymal cells into a chemosensitive epithelial state. Preliminary results show proof-of-concept that upon retinoid-induced MET in mesenchymal cells, there was a stark decrease in mammosphere forming capacity (reflecting a decrease in stemness), accompanied by an increased sensitivity to chemotherapeutic drugs and a significant reduction in tumor burden in NSG mice. Probing deeper into the mechanism of retinoid-induced MET by ChIP-Seq and RNA-Seq techniques reveal perturbations in lipid metabolic pathways, specifically in lipid storage. These indicate that rewiring of lipid metabolism may be crucial during breast cancer cell state transitions. We aim to elucidate how lipid metabolic pathways are altered during induction of MET by lipidomic mass spectrometry and investigate if the changes in lipid profiles are consistent during cell state transitions. This will lead to the defining of a unique lipid signature that can distinguish between breast tumor cell states and potentially predict breast cancer progression. We propose to use various cell line models as well as clinical samples from patients with different subtypes to investigate the possible correlation between dependency on lipid metabolism and breast cancer progression. In addition, we propose to interrogate the intermediate steps involved in lipid synthesis and fatty acid oxidation by genetic manipulation to identify key enzymes or metabolites that drive MET or are crucial in maintenance of CSC status. This would reveal novel therapeutic targets and more efficacious combinational regimens in the treatment of TNBC.
kw: breast cancer stem cells; epithelial mesenchymal transitions; lipid metabolism

title: Establishing the role of STARD10 in pancreatic islet development and function to identify novel mechanisms in diabetes predisposition in humans
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Diabetes is characterised by absolute or relative lack of insulin due to pancreatic beta cell dysfunction, leading to hyperglycaemia and severe complications over time. Most patients require escalated therapies and use of insulin over time due to progressive beta cell failure, resulting in increased cost and risk of hypoglycaemia. Therefore, new treatments are needed to target the root cause of diabetes – beta cell dysfunction. Many genetic loci have been implicated in type 2 diabetes (T2D) risk, including the STARD10 gene which encodes a lipid-transfer protein associated with insulin processing and secretion based on human genetic studies and mouse models, though the precise underlying mechanisms remain unclear. We hypothesise that STARD10 regulates beta cell maturation and function, and therefore dysregulation of STARD10 can contribute to the pathogenesis of T2D. We first aim to evaluate the impact of STARD10 perturbation on human pancreatic beta cell development using human embryonic stem cell (hESCs)-derived cells with CRISPR/Cas9-mediated STARD10 knockout. STARD10 knockout beta-like cells have significantly increased expression of SCG2 and PIRT, which encode a secretory protein and phosphoinositide-interacting protein respectively. Other global transcriptomic changes and the role of these specific proteins in the human beta cell will need to be investigated. We further elucidate the molecular mechanisms through which STARD10, a phospholipid-binding protein, may regulate beta cell lipid profiles, proinsulin processing and insulin secretion. Both hESCs and the human beta cell line EndoC-βH1 will be used for genetic manipulation studies and functional assays. Through studying STARD10 we seek to highlight novel regulators of beta cell function that may translate into potentially druggable targets for modulating beta cell function. The identification of actionable targets or lipid-related interventions will be valuable given the need for improved and more targeted strategies to tackle human beta cell dysfunction, which is relevant not just to T2D but also prediabetes.
kw: Type 2 diabetes; beta cell function; STARD10; lipid transfer; human embryonic stem cells; SCG2

title: Enhancing adoptive T cell therapy through tumour-responsive immune checkpoint inhibitory nanogels
inst: IBN - Institute of Bioengineering and Nanotechnology
abs: In adoptive T cell therapy (ACT), tumour-specific T cells are obtained from patients, expanded ex vivo, and then injected back into the patients to have the advantage of numbers. Recent advances in ACT have led to striking durable complete responses in patients with leukaemias and melanoma. Despite its success, the efficacy of ACT for solid tumours such as lung cancer is still mediocre. The immunosuppressive tumour microenvironment (TME) remains one of the major challenges to ACT treatment. Tumour infiltrating ACT T cells are subjected to immunosuppression and lose function before tumour eradication. In addition to exogenously prepared ACT, immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) targeting PD-1 and CTLA-4 pathways have been successfully applied to bolster patients’ endogenous anti-tumor immunity. However, the benefits of immune checkpoint blockade are only limited to a subset of patients and survival rates are still not satisfactory. Here we propose to synergize the two most promising cancer treatments nowadays by protecting ACT T cells from intratumoral immunosuppression with ICIs. We aim to design tumour-responsive nanogels (NGs) which can target ACT T cells in vivo and only release ICI drug cargo in TME, thus augmenting the therapeutic efficacy of ACT while minimizing systemic side effects. Specifically, we aim to 1. Synthesize NGs by reversibly crosslinking monoclonal antibodies that block immune checkpoint pathways such as PD-1 and CTLA-4. 2. Functionalize immune checkpoint inhibitory NGs with targeting ligands for repeatedly reloading of ACT T cells in vivo. 3. Enhance the functional persistence and proliferation of ACT T cells in vivo with targeting NGs. 4. Improve the therapeutic efficacy of ACT with immunosuppression-blocking NGs in murine lung cancer model. This approach can be generalized to treat other frequent solid tumours such as colon and breast cancer. It can also be a complimentary solution to any existing ACT, particularly CAR-T therapies.
kw: cancer immunotherapy; adoptive T cell therapy; immune checkpoint blockade; PD-1 / CTLA4; lung cancer;

title: INVESTIGATING THE ROLES OF NON-CODING RNAs IN INFLAMMATION
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Inflammation is a physiological response, normally triggered by infection, tissue-injury, senescence or stress. However, when left unchecked, chronic inflammation is the underlying cause of many diseases including autoimmune disorders, type-2 diabetes and cancer. Despite advances in understanding the roles of many enzymes and other proteins that regulate inflammation, the roles of non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) in both acute and chronic inflammatory conditions remain poorly explored. These ncRNAs include long non-coding RNAs (lnc-RNAs) which are emerging as important regulators of development and homeostasis. Indeed dysregulation of lncRNAs has been reported in various diseases including cancers. Given the importance of ncRNAs, we hypothesize these non-coding RNAs may also play an important role in the initiation and regulation of the inflammatory responses. Recently, we found that initiation of inflammation by TNF-alpha activates the transcription of Gm16685 (Human homologue: loc105375914), a novel lncRNA, and genetic loss of this lncRNA specifically reduces inflammation through dampened activation of p38 stress kinase pathway without affecting other TNF-alpha induced signalling cascades. This suggests that Gm16685 / loc105375914 might be the missing link that orchestrates the well-known cross talk between NFκB and p38, which has been implicated in sustained inflammatory response through the maintenance of TNF-alpha transcript stability. In this project, we aim to mechanistically delineate how Gm16685 / loc105375914 is involved in the inflammatory response, investigate the in-vivo functions of Gm16685 lnc-RNA. Functional analysis of lnc-RNA Gm16685 / loc105375914 and other novel ncRNAs will lead to better biomarkers and understand the roles of such RNAs in inflammatory ailments.
kw: inflammation, non-coding RNA, NFkB signalling

title: INVESTIGATING DIVERSIFIED BIFUNCTIONAL MACROCYCLES BY PHAGE DISPLAY AS A NOVEL TECHNOLOGY PLATFORM
abs: Recent studies from our lab and others have shown that small molecules and macrocycles are much more versatile at eliciting specific ligand induced molecular recognition than previously thought of. These “molecular glues” elicit their effect by strongly binding to target protein surface then the resulting complex can interact with other proteins. Cyclosporine, sanglifehrin, FK506 and rapamycin, which are immunosuppressive compounds, represent the few privileged naturally occurring molecules with such characteristics. These molecules can enter cells to form a complex with ubiquitously expressed immunophilins such as FKBP or cyclophilins. The resulting macrocycle-immunophilin binary complex is now a neo-substrate for novel target proteins, resulting in their inhibition and subsequent antagonization of their signalling pathways. Sanglifehrin operates by a mechanism similar to cyclosporine, except that it targets inosine-monophosphate dehydrogenase 2 (IMPDH2). These findings highlight the plasticity and permissivity of cyclophilins, as well as FKBPs, to varied spatial orientation and presentations of diverse ligands to neo-substrates. Such drug-immunophilin complexes can modulate large, flat, undruggable surfaces typical of protein-protein interactions (PPIs). Many of such PPIs, like the p53-Mdm2 interaction, go awry in cancers like acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and thus have been attractive targets for therapeutic intervention. Unfortunately, such interfaces are largely intractable by current small molecule therapies due to the lack of binding pockets. Based on these principles, we hypothesize that a library of novel bifunctional macrocycles generated through a novel cyclophilin-biased phage display technology can exploit this unique mechanism to address “undruggable” protein-protein interactions. Specifically a diverse cyclophilin-biased libraries can be harnessed as a portable and robust platform to quickly identify bifunctional molecules capable of modulating protein targets of interests and then be optimized as lead compounds. A combination of this approach coupled to phage has not been achieved previously and offers a unique opportunity to position us as pioneers in this area.
kw: drug discovery platform; cancer; protein-protein interactions; phage display; macrocycles; acute myeloid leukemia

title: Structural and functional studies of GABPA/GABPB in complex with mutant TERT promoter DNA and druggable p52/ETS1 and ETS1/DNA complexes
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Levels of catalytic subunit of telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT) are limiting in reconstituting telomerase activity in normal somatic cells. However, cells from 95% of human cancers transcriptionally reactivate TERT and this is necessary for cancer progression. How the WT TERT promoter is shut off in normal cell and how it is reactivated are the most fundamental questions in cancer biology. Highly Recurrent -146C>T and -124C>T TERT promoter mutations have been shown to drive upregulation of TERT in multiple cancers. Since both these hotspot mutations create a binding motif for E-twenty-six (ETS) transcription factors, ETS1/2 and GABPA have been shown to be involved in reactivation of these two mutant TERT promotors. ETS1/2 synergize with non-canonical NF-κB signalling through interaction with p52 to activate -146C>T TERT promoter while GABPA forms a heterotetramer with GABPB to drive the reactivation of both -146C>T and -124C>T mutations. However, the underlying mechanism of this process remains unclear. Built upon the successful structure determination of p52/ETS1 in compex with the -146C>T TERT DNA, we aim to solve the crystal structure of GABPA/GABPB in complex with the mutant TERT promoter DNA for elucidating the mechanism governing the activation of -146C>T and -124C>T mutant TERT promoters. The structures and subsequent functional assays will reveal whether p52/ETS1 and GABPA/GABPB share a unifying mechanism for the activation of -146C>T and -124C>T mutants. Since reactivation of -146C>T and -124C>T mutant TERT promoters only occurs in cancer cells rather than in normal and stem cells, We are interested in identifying small molecular compounds that specifically block TERT synthesis through inhibiting the reactivation of these two TERT mutations. As aberrant proto-oncoprotein ETS1 overexpression have been implicated in various tumours. We are also interested in identifying a small molecule that can disrupt ETS1/DNA interaction. Such a compound may act as a broad spectrum anticancer agent.
kw: TERT reactivation;p52/EST1 interaction;TERT mutation;GABPA/GABPB;ETS1/DNA interaction

title: Investigating the Role of HtrA Protease in Antimicrobial-Resistant Gram-Positive Infections
abs: Enterococci and Pneumococci are pathogenic members of the lactic acid bacteria order that are a significant threat to global public health. Enterococci are a leading cause of hospital-associated infections, where they are frequent opportunistic pathogens of the urinary tract, wounds, and the bloodstream. Pneumococcal infections are a major threat to human health, causing about 11% of all deaths among young children; moreover, pneumonia is 2nd leading cause of death in Singapore. Pneumococcal secondary infection following influenza A virus can render a mild influenza infection more severe or even fatal. The rise of both Pneumococcus and Enterococcus strains resistant to “last resort” antimicrobials creates the possibility of untreatable infections and has led to the listing of both bacteria on the WHO’s list of priority pathogens for which new antibiotics are most urgently needed. Therefore, identifying new therapeutic targets against Enterococci and Pneumococci is crucial for our ability to treat these infections in the future. We have discovered that the conserved HtrA protein is necessary for Enterococcus faecalis to persist within chronically infected wounds and is also necessary for S. pneumonia secondary infections of the lower respiratory tract following influenza virus infection. Our goal for this proposal is to the understand host-pathogen interactions following E. faecalis and S. pneumonia infection, particularly those that are enabled by HtrA. We hypothesize HtrA participates in the ability of E. faecalis and S. pneumonia to adapt to an inflammatory environment characterized by oxidative and other stresses encountered during infection. To address these hypotheses, our specific aims are to: 1) Determine the role of HtrA in E. faecalis virulence in wounds, 2) Define the role of S. pneumoniae HtrA during influenza-associated polymicrobial pneumonia, and 3) Determine the structure-function parameters of HtrA for the future design of inhibitors as antivirulence therapies.
kw: bacterial pathogenesis; gram positive pathogen; wound infection; influenza coinfection; antimicrobial resistance

title: Functional and structural analysis of flaviviral NS5 protein and its impact on pathogenesis
abs: Mosquito-borne flaviviruses such as dengue (DENV) and Zika viruses (ZIKV) are a major global health threat. Their non-structural protein 5 (NS5) plays a critical enzymatic role in virus replication and modulating the host response to virus infection. While there are four serotypes of DENV, most of the studies of DENV NS proteins have been performed on DENV2. But we and others have identified differences among the NS5 proteins from the various DENV serotypes and ZIKV, including subcellular localization, phosphorylation sites and conformational differences. In this grant, we will focus on examining the NS5 across the DENV serotypes and ZIKV, in particular its subcellular localization via the manipulation of its nuclear localization signal (NLS). Extensive use of reverse genetics will be employed to introduce mutations in NS5 using cDNA clones of DENV1-4 or ZIKV to interrogate the impact on viral replication, NS5 sub-cellular localization and NS5 modulation of the host response. We will use molecular virology and classical virology approaches but will also assess the impact of selected changes in vivo in robustly established mouse models in our laboratory. In addition, we will employ proteomic and transcriptomic analysis to identify and compare host proteins and pathways that interact with either one or multiple flavivirus NS5. Together with structural elucidation of the surfaces of NS5 involved in protein interaction, the outcome of this grant will uncover important insights that can instruct the long term development of direct acting antiviral drugs. In the short term, the clinical significance of the fundamental project we undertake here is to provide evidence of the differences that exist in the non-enzymatic role of NS5 that can impact on flavivirus pathogenesis. Our research is of high priority because there are no safe preventative vaccines or antiviral treatment available for dengue or zika infections.
kw: Dengue virus; Zika virus; NS5 protein; Reverse genetics; Proteomics; Flaviviral Pathogenesis

title: Role of glycosylation in Dengue virus fitness and virulence
abs: In many infectious diseases caused by either viruses or bacteria, pathogen glycoproteins play important roles during the infection cycle, from entry to successful intracellular replication and host immune evasion. Dengue (DEN) is no exception. Dengue virus (DENV) envelope glycoprotein E is critical for the virus entry while non-structural glycoprotein NS1 has been involved in DEN pathogenesis via several mechanisms. Both proteins are popular sub-unit vaccine candidates. However, despite their critical role in disease and protection, the glycosylated variants of these two proteins and their biological importance have been largely overlooked. In this project, using cutting-edge glycomics and glycoproteomics technologies we propose to carry out the in-depth analysis and characterization of the glycan structures present on E protein of prototype DENV2 D2Y98P strain when produced in relevant host cell types, and when purified from infected mosquitoes’ salivary glands or from various organs in infected mice. This approach will allow investigate the correlation between glycan structures at the virion surface and species/tissue tropism, hence virulence of DENV. In addition, de-glycosylated (on E or NS1) D2Y98P viruses will be generated to study the role and importance of the glycan structures in the virus in vitro and in vivo fitness. The contribution of glycosylation in NS1’s ability to increase vascular permeability will also be addressed. Furthermore, the role and importance of DENV glycosylation in viral clearance mediated by the mannose binding lectin (MBL) complement pathway will be studied. Finally, using functional assays and structural approaches, we will investigate the role of DENV glycan structures in influencing and interfering with the host antibody response, with possible consequences on virus neutralization and enhancing efficacy. Overall, the findings from this project will provide further insights into the contribution of glycosylation in DENV pathogenesis with important implications for the development of effective therapeutic antibodies and vaccine candidates.
kw: dengue; glycosylation; glycoproteomics;

title:
To decipher the molecular mechanisms regulating Protein Regulator of Cytokinesis 1 (PRC1) protein and Wnt signaling to tackle early recurrent human hepatocellular
carcinoma disease.
abs: The early identification of human hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) recurrence is of paramount importance as unlike other cancers, curative treatment is still possible for many of these recurrences if detected early enough and highlights the necessity of developing new therapeutic strategies targeting at tumor recurrence and metastases in HCC. Unfortunately, the variations in prognosis following treatments differ substantially and cannot be ascertained by surrogate clinicopathologic features. While tremendous progress has been made in recent years regarding hepatocarcinogenesis, the underlying molecular mechanisms for early recurrent HCC disease remains largely unknown. Previously, we demonstrated that elevated PRC1 expression correlated with poor overall survival and PRC1 interacts with the Wnt signaling pathway to mediate early HCC recurrence. Coupling with these early observations, we propose to decipher the architecture of the PRC1-Wnt/beta-catenin interactome and how transcriptomic variations contribute to early HCC recurrence using SILAC (Stable isotope labeling by amino acids in cell culture) analysis (Aim 1). Using 330 archival HCC tumor tissue samples with known early (<2 years) and non-recurrent (>5 years) disease and designing a prospective study of 150 HCC patients who has undergone partial hepatectomy to evaluate the clinical value of PRC1 for predicting the risk of early HCC recurrence (Aim 2). Employing yeast as a simple and inexpensive heterologous system for the screening of chemical libraries against PRC1 in a eukaryotic cellular environment (Aim 3). Importantly, as we have demonstrated the functional role of PRC1 in early recurrent HCC disease, insights from the present proposal can be used to enhance our understanding of the detailed underlying molecular mechanisms of how the canonical Wnt signaling function in regulating the level of the transcriptional co-activator 􀈕􀀐catenin in the cytoplasm and nucleus, thereby controlling key developmental gene expression programs, which has wide implications in disease modelling, prediction of early disease, and drug discovery.
kw: Protein regulator of cytokinesis 1 (PRC1); Hepatocellular carcinoma; Early recurrence; Stable isotope labeling by amino acids in cell culture (SILAC) analysis; Wingless (Wnt) signaling cascade; Small molecule inhibitors.

title: A Computational Microscope to Decipher the Tumor Microenvironment and Its Role in Immune Checkpoint Blockade Therapy
abs: The field of cancer therapy is currently experiencing a paradigm shift. Rather than attempting to kill cancer cells with cytotoxic drugs, new breakthrough treatments are instead directly activating and unleashing the patient’s own immune system on the cancer cells. One key class of treatments do this through immune checkpoint blockade/inhibition (ICI). Such treatments are currently producing remarkable improvements in disease outcome across a wide range of cancer types, in some cases completely curing patients from cancer. However, ICI is not effective in most cancer patients and it is challenging to predict which patients will benefit from therapy. Importantly, tumors are heterogeneous masses of malignant cancer cells, non-malignant stromal and immune cells, as well as intercellular connective structures. Heterogeneity of this environment can negatively confound cancer treatments. Here we hypothesize that the tumor microenvironment (TME) modulates and dictates the response to immunotherapy. We propose to develop a data-driven algorithm, an unbiased and systematic computational “microscope”, that can tease apart the molecular signatures of both malignant and non-malignant cells in the patient TME. We will use this approach to mine thousands of patient tumor molecular profiles as well as rich data from ongoing clinical trials of ICI, aiming to decipher the role of TME in ICI treatment response. This will allow development of new TME biomarkers to improve the cost-effectiveness of ICI treatment, and inform the design of the next-generation of ICI treatments.
kw: Cancer; Immuno therapy; Computational Biology

title:
Investigation of the role of polyamines as critical
regulators of wound healing
abs: Singapore has a rapidly aging population and the second highest incidence of diabetes globally. Wound healing is compromised with age and diabetic foot ulcers are a significant healthcare problem in diabetic patients. Current treatments to increase the rate of healing in these patients are limited. Understanding the process of wound healing is essential to enable insights into clinically slow-to-heal or non-healing wounds, and to enable the development of therapeutics that will promote healing. We have recently discovered that a group of metabolites called polyamines are critical regulators of wound healing and propose that mis-regulation of polyamines at the wound edge results in a failure or delay in healing which can lead to a chronic non-healing wound. Understanding the cause of and consequence of the changes in polyamine ratios in wound edge cells is essential for their utilization as a therapeutic. This proposal aims to identify the mechanisms by which the polyamines drive wound closure. Polyamines exist largely bound to RNA within the cell so we will determine the molecular targets using genome wide technologies including RNA structural probing, transcriptional and translation profiling. These polyamine targets will then be characterized for their role in cell migration and wound healing. The final aim focuses on determining if the polyamine shift we have shown to be essential for wounding is mis-regulated in chronic wounds. We propose to use a combination of diabetic rat models, human ex vivo wounds and human chronic wound samples to determine if mis-regulation of polyamines is seen in non-healing wounds and if modulation of these levels can promote wound closure. This grant brings together a unique combination of expertise to enable us to examine wound healing in the context of polyamine regulation and RNA biology. This team is ideally positioned to successfully address the unique and challenging questions posed.
kw: Diabetes, Chronic wounds, Polyamines, RNA structure, Gene regulation, Therapeutic targets

title: Pre-empting renal injury ensuing drugs by elucidating microRNA and proteomics of renal tubular dysfunction at its earliest (PRE-EMPTII study)
abs: Drug-induced acute kidney injury (AKI) develops in 13% of patients on nephrotoxic therapy and predisposes to chronic kidney disease. AKI is diagnosed by serial increase in serum creatinine, itself a late biomarker of renal dysfunction. Our preliminary studies demonstrate that urinary KIM1, clusterin, ß2-microglobulin, MCP1, and more recently, select urinary microRNAs, are elevated in days prior to AKI onset in patients versus non-AKI controls, while receiving aminoglycosides or vancomycin. We want to further advance our research by refining the biomarker panel that intercepts drug-induced renal tubular dysfunction at its earliest, well before AKI is evident. First, we will perform exosome analysis of above identified protein biomarkers, to determine if the distinction in levels between cases and controls could be exemplified at >3 days prior to drug-induced AKI, using our biobank urine samples. Next, the selected microRNAs we discovered will be correlated to inducible injury microRNAs in vitro to examine for reproducibility, using a microfluidic human renal proximal tubule cell-model with nephrotoxic insult from antimicrobials, calcineurin-inhibitors, and anti-cancer drugs. The area under receiver operating characteristic curve of these more selective protein and microRNA biomarkers or their combination for AKI prediction at its earliest, will be determined in our current 130 patient-cohort, to derive few better performing biomarkers. Concurrently, we will recruit 150 patients over 1.5 years, prescribed with similar drugs; We will collect urine samples at intervals guided by known AKI trajectory from commencement of respective drugs. Their samples will be batch-analyzed, and the refined biomarker panel for AKI prediction will be validated. The refined biomarker panel would be implemented for real-time analysis to allow fluidity of detecting patients at highest risk of AKI during nephrotoxic therapy. It will be examined in a clinical trial to triage patients for pre-emptive drug cessation or dose reduction to effectively prevent drug-induced AKI.
kw: Drug induced acute kidney injury; urinary biomarkers; exosome proteomics; microfluidic model; microRNA; nephrotoxicity;

title: Role of collagen signalling via YAP in self-renewal of human multipotent pancreatic progenitor cells
abs: The purpose of this proposal is to identify niche signals required for self-renewal of multipotent progenitor cells (MPC) during pancreatic organogenesis. We hypothesise that collagen signalling through integrin receptors and the transcriptional coactivator YAP is essential for self-renewal of pancreatic MPC. We recently published culture conditions that enable long-term self-renewal of human cultured pancreatic progenitor (cPP) cells, which will be used as a model system to test our hypothesis. The three major aims of this proposal are to: (1) identify collagen ligands capable of maintaining self-renewal, (2) assess the role of integrin signalling upstream of YAP mediated activation of gene expression, and (3) determine whether these pathways are active in developing embryos. Understanding the pathways that control growth during development will be useful for designing more efficient protocols for the generation of adult pancreatic cell types from pluripotent stem cells. Furthermore, the same pathways are often used to regulate growth in different organs, and pathways required for growth in the embryo are often involved in organ homeostasis and recovery from injury in the adult. Therefore, these studies will have implications for our understanding of organogenesis, tissue regeneration and cancer in various organs.
kw: human pancreas development; stem cell niche; multipotent progenitor cells; self-renewal; extracellular matrix; YAP/TAZ signalling

title: Identifying new cell surface receptor(s) for the WNT enhancer R-SPONDINS ligands
abs: The canonical WNT signaling pathway plays crucial roles during embryonic development and cancer. The R-spondin family of secreted ligands (RSPO1-RSPO4) act as WNT enhancers by preventing WNT receptor degradation mediated by the RNF43/ZNRF3 E3 Ubiquitin ligases. Up until now, the R-spondins were believed to exclusively act via their obligate LGR4/5/6 cognate receptors, which together would interact with the RNF43/ZNRF3 ligases to prevent them from ubiquitinating WNT receptors for degradation. However, we recently discovered that the LGR4/5/6 receptors are surprisingly dispensable for RSPO2 and RSPO3 functions during vascular, limb and lung development, suggesting that R-spondins can signal through hitherto unknown receptor(s). In this proposal, we aim to (1) identify these unknown R-spondin receptor(s) using two distinct approaches that will make use of LGR4/5/6 triple-knockout and RNF43/ZNRF3 double-knockout mouse cell lines, and (2) characterize them in vivo, through loss- and gain-of-function studies. Firstly, we will perform a CRISPR-Cas9 screen using the SUPERTOPFLASH luciferase system as a direct readout for WNT signaling, and look for genetic mutations that impact the ability of exogenous RSPO2/RSPO3 to potentiate WNT signaling. In parallel, we will use the Proximity Labeling with Ascorbate Peroxidase (APEX) technique to label and identity the R-spondin receptors. RSPO2/3-APEX fusion proteins will be incubated on LGR4/5/6 triple-knockout and RNF43/ZNRF3 double-knockout mouse cell lines, allowing the identification and quantification of interactions between these ligands and their receptors at the cell surface. These two independent and complementary approaches are expected to lead to the discovery of new R-spondin receptor(s), which in turn will shed fundamental insights on WNT signaling by deciphering R-spondins functions and modes of action. This research will have immediate translational implications in cell biology, development and oncology, and carries the patent potential for identifying new targets for innovative therapies against WNT-associated diseases and cancers such as, but not limited to, colorectal cancer.
kw: R-SPONDINS, LGR, RNF43/ZNRF3, WNT signaling, Development, Colorectal cancer.

title: Neural basis of energy homeostasis dysregulation in Huntington’s disease.
abs: Huntington’s Disease (HD) is a debilitating hereditary motor syndrome resulting from the expansion of trinucleotide CAG repeats in the huntingtin (htt) gene. Less well characterized and largely unexplained are metabolic dysfunctions that affect patients’ quality of life. Presymptomatic HD patients show distinct changes in their metabolic profile similar to Type I diabetes and may represent early stages of the disease. Interestingly, MRI of early stage HD and autopsy brain samples of HD patients show atrophy in the tuberal nucleus (TN), a region of the brain we have recently identified to be involved in feeding regulation. Considering the role of these neurons in feeding regulation and the pathological change in human HD patients, we hypothesize that mutant htt causes abnormal activation of TN neurons in early stage HD that leads to increased appetite and body weight gain; and that chronic over-activation of TN neurons leads to cell death and ultimately loss of appetite and decreased body weight. We will test these hypotheses by using mouse models of HD and measure cellular and electrophysiological readouts of neuronal activity of TN neurons and correlate this with expression of mutant htt and metabolic parameters (Aim 1). To determine causality, we will overexpress mutant htt specifically in TN neurons using viral-mediated delivery in mouse brain (Aim 2) to recapitulate disease phenotypes observed in mouse models of HD. Lastly, we will perform transcriptome analysis of TN neurons using RNA sequencing at various stages of disease progression to identify potential molecular targets and pathways resulting in abnormal activation and subsequent degeneration of these neurons (Aim 3).
kw: Huntington's disease; Neurobiology; metabolism;

title: Smart, wearable electrical stimulation device to improve lower limb venous return
abs: Retrograde neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) via the posterior tibial nerve is able to safely, comfortably and effectively improve lower limb venous return via stimulation of the superficial and deep posterior calf muscles. Photoplethysmography (PPG) is a non-invasive optical technique that measures local blood flow. This technique has been validated in multiple studies against invasive methods and is considered to be the best non-invasive measurement of local blood flow. Our hypothesis proposes that smart, mobile user driven input can be guided by photoplethysmography feedback while under neuromuscular electrical stimulation for lower limb venous return. Our study specific aims are: 1) Develop a prototype NMES device with PPG sensor feedback suitable for augmentation of lower limb venous return 2) Develop a smart, wireless mobile application capable of capturing NMES data via PPG 3) Develop an algorithm to guide user experience in improving lower limb venous return Methodology Bench top prototyping and fabrication of a wearable NMES system will be performed by Intellectual Property Translation and Engineering Centre (iPtec). Tender will be called for development of a smart, wireless mobile application to capture device data. Bench top prototype testing will be performed at Singapore Stanford Biodesign Office. Significance Current wired neuromuscular electrical stimulation devices activate the calf muscles to promote venous return from a fixed platform. Our proposed design is intended to improve venous return in a smart, wearable, easy to comply device. The device is also the first to incorporate feedback via the PPG sensor to enable informed user input. Our proposed device will be suitable for chronic venous insufficiency patients. Current preventative therapy is the compression stocking, which suffers from poor compliance. This results in ulcer formation and recurrence. Our device looks to improve preventative treatment compliance in order to reduce morbidity and healthcare costs.
kw: Neuromuscular; Electrical Stimulation; Vascular; Venous Insufficiency

title: Dissecting the role of long noncoding RNA product SGHRT and targeting it for heart failure
abs: Cardiac regeneration involving limited proliferation of pre-existing cardiomyocytes (CMs) holds the promise for novel and game-changing therapeutic strategies for heart disease. While current therapy only delays disease progression, regenerative therapy promises instead to reverse the course of disease. In neonatal mouse CMs that retain their proliferative potential, there is effective regeneration and repair response to injury up to post-natal D7. Much still remains to be discovered for the regulation of dedifferentiation and proliferation of post-natal adult CMs. We previously performed single RNA-seq in failing and non-failing adult CMs and identified lincRNA Sghrt as a nodal gene within co-regulatory gene networks. Sghrt knockdown increased marker expression of dedifferentiation and cell cycle entry in post-natal CMs in vitro. Similarly, Sghrt knockdown increased dedifferentiation markers in neonatal mouse CMs in vivo; and Sghrt knockdown improved cardiac function in an adult mouse model of disease, together with evidence of CM dedifferentiation. In human ES-derived CMs, we now find that SGHRT deletion also results increased CM dedifferentiation. Together, these results point to a role for SGHRT in regulating CM dedifferentiation. Here, we aim to further characterize the role of mouse Sghrt in CM dedifferentiation and proliferation using (a) a conditional knockout and (b) a humanized mouse models that we have now generated. In assessing their response to myocardial stress by pressure-overload and myocardial infraction, we aim to determine the therapeutic value of targeting SGHRT in human cardiac diseases. Furthermore, we will characterize the role of human SGHRT in hES-derived cardiomyocytes and Engineering Heart Tissue (EHT) in response to oxidative stress. Finally, we aim to dissect the mechanism of SGHRT as a novel mitochondrial micropeptide in the regulation of cardiomyocyte dedifferentiation. Understanding the biology of how SGHRT regulates CM dedifferentiation and proliferation will allow us to develop a rationale approach to target SGHRT for human HF.
kw: Heart Failure, Epigenetics, Regeneration, Repair, Long noncoding RNA

title: Laminin-based Human Embryonic Stem Cell Differentiation and Cell Therapy Approaches for Diabetic Complications
abs: The goals of the project are to develop novel stem cell based therapies for type 1 diabetes, myocardiac infarction and Age-related Macular Degeneration using pluripotent hESC-derived cells differentiated on specific laminin matrices that drive differentiation specifically to pancreatic islet cells, cardiomyocyte progenitors and retina photoreceptors. The mechanisms of respective cell differentiation from hESCs and their proliferation are studied using transcriptome and single cell RNAseq analyses of the cells studied, state-of-the-art bioinformatics and inhibition studies. The methods that are being or have been developed in our Duke-NUS lab have been successfully used to generate endothelial cells, cardiomyocytes, photoreceptors and skin keratinocyte cells. The pluripotent hESC derived islet cells will be characterized and used to develop artificial islets that will be transplanted into diabetic animals. We are entering a phase 1 clinical trial for burn wound treatments with our novel method keratinocyte culture method. Using whole transcriptome and single-cell RNAseq, we will decipher the expression signatures and pathways of proliferating islet cells to identify which genes are needed to turn on cell proliferation. This can facilitate identification of drugs that increase islet cell mass. We have already demonstrated that different laminins induce and maintain stable differentiation of hESCs endothelial cells, cardiomyocytes, retina RPE and photoreceptors as well as keratinocyte stem cells without feeder cells that has not been possible before. We are convinced that our fully human and defined, highly reproducible differentiation methods will allow new tools for regenerative medicine. We have successfully attracted major pharmaceutical companies to test our differentiation methods for development of novel cellular therapeutics. This project is novel, innovative and well feasible, and it may strengthen Singapore´s position in diabetes care and regenerative medicine, in general.
kw: Stem cell differentiation; cell therapy; Diabetes complications; Pancreatic islets; RNA sequencing; Regenerative medicine

title: Probing the Immunometabolic Factors of Influenza Vaccine Immune Response in Singapore Elderly
abs: Novel, effective influenza vaccination strategies are needed in the elderly who have the highest rate of influenza-related morbidity and mortality. Unfortunately, vaccine effectiveness in this segment of the population is greatly reduced due to immunosenescence and/or, inflamm-aging. The escalating incidence of metabolic syndrome, diabetes mellitus are factors that potentially contribute to immune dys-regulation, and we hypothesise vaccine response may be associated with key metabolic parameters. The increased severity of influenza in the elderly, decreased influenza vaccine performance and prevention of severe influenza in these populations are important knowledge gaps that need to be addressed. The DYNAMIC trial (funded by NHG CSCS) has just recruited a cohort of 220 community dwelling elderly with the aim to evaluate metabolic predictors (specifically diabetes mellitus and 25-OH D) of influenza-vaccine humoral immune response, as measured by haemagglutination inhibition (HAI) titer. Baseline and Day 28 post-vaccination serum and peripheral blood mononuclear cell samples are available for this multi-ethnic cohort. All study participants have received trivalent inactivated influenza vaccine (IIV3). Data on subjects’ food history and physical activity habits are available. Our novel approach in the current proposal is to probe the various immunometabolic factors (including clinical metabolic phenotype) associated with collective cellular and humoral influenza vaccine-immune response. Assays will be performed on stored samples. These include metabolic markers (leptin, adiponectin), and pro-inflammatory cytokines at baseline. We will also determine associations between leptin-related gene and VDR (vitamin D receptor) gene variants with immune response as an exploratory aim in Chinese elderly, and validate in another comparable local cohort. This study has several translational applications, including developing targeted vaccine strategies such as using differing dose of vaccine, adjuvants in vaccine non-responders to improve vaccine immunogenicity and prevention of influenza-related complications in these populations.
kw: Metabolic, Leptin, Influenza Vaccine, Immune Response, Elderly

title: Mild Behavioral Impairment: Structural-Connectivity Patterns and Influence on Cognition in amnestic Mild Cognitive Impairment
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Neuropsychiatric symptoms (NPS) are common in mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and are associated with poorer cognitive outcomes. Mild behavioural impairment (MBI) is a diagnostic construct which identifies individuals with persistent late-life NPS (≥6 months) and there is an emerging conceptual framework which support MBI as an early non-cognitive manifestation of Alzheimer’s disease (AD). However, the prevalence of MBI and its pathophysiology and influence on cognition in MCI remains unclear. MBI could potentially be used to identify pre-dementia patients who are at risk for AD. In a cross-sectional cohort, we will study the local prevalence and characteristics of MBI among MCI (amnestic and non-amnestic) patients seen consecutively in our memory clinic over 1-year. All subjects will undergo neuropsychological assessments (NPA) at baseline and 6-month time points for the diagnosis of MBI. In a prospective longitudinal cohort, we will study the pathophysiology of MBI and its influence on cognition over 1-year in only amnestic MCI (aMCI) subjects. 150 aMCI subjects (75 with MBI (aMCI+MBI), 75 without MBI (aMCI-MBI)) with structural and resting-state functional-MRI within a 6-month window will be recruited from 3 ongoing studies. We will enrich this cohort with 40 aMCI subjects with known cerebrospinal fluid amyloid (CSF Aβ1-42). All subjects will undergo NPA at baseline and 1-year follow-up. We hypothesize that MBI is prevalent among MCI subjects locally, aMCI+MBI subjects have greater grey matter atrophy and functional disconnectivity in limbic and AD-related regions and lower CSF Aβ1-42 at baseline and poorer cognitive performances at 1-year follow-up, compared to aMCI-MBI. Characterizing the behavioural and cognitive profiles of MBI and understanding its role in determining cognitive decline will enable prompt detection of aMCI+MBI patients. This will facilitate timely targeted cognitive and behavioural interventions to treat NPS, improve quality of life and stabilize cognitive decline.
kw: Alzheimer’s disease; Mild behavioral impairment; Neuropsychiatric symptoms; Mild cognitive impairment; Magnetic resonance imaging; Functional connectivity

title: Next-Generation Clinical Trials and Integrative Research for Fighting Lung Cancer
abs: Lung cancer is the most lethal disease in Singapore, but unlike in the West, lung cancer in Asia is far more likely to be driven by mutation of EGFR (epidermal growth factor receptor) and to occur in patients who have never smoked. Many patients respond initially to kinase inhibitor drugs, only to relapse with drug-resistant disease. Our 5-theme proposal harnesses genomics and informatics to predict and direct appropriate interventions, to reduce lung cancer mortality in Singapore. Theme 1 centres around 4 investigator-initiated trials (IIT), 23 pharma-sponsored trials, and observation of non-trial patients, to generate a unique and comprehensive body of clinical data and serial biospecimens for the remaining themes. We have procured substantial industry support for our IITs, including a novel adaptive clinical trial (BESPOKE) which uses genomic profiling to adjust treatments and track response dynamically. Theme 2 clarifies the risks and benefits of immuno-oncology in EGFR-mutant(EGFRm) and EGFR-wildtype(EGFRwt) non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) by interrogating serial biospecimens (blood and tumor) from patients treated with PD-1-related combinations (nivolumab with ipilimumab or metronomic vinorelbine), looking to identify determinants or biomarkers for patient response and toxicity outcomes. Theme 3 provides data processing and analytics for patient-derived data, and performs virtual dissection of tumor heterogeneity to identify molecular changes associated with response and resistance. Statistical methods will identify biomarkers and a clinical decision-support system will cater to the adaptive clinical trial. Theme 4 employs NSCLC-derived model systems for seeking novel therapeutic targets based on stemness and cancer metabolism; for pursuing long-term drug development efforts; and for assessing how combination treatments affect the evolution of drug-resistance. Theme 5 addresses present-day needs in the broader population by testing the feasibility, cost-effectiveness, and psychological burdens of screening people who have never smoked, and by studying environmental exposures in our population.
kw: Not applicable

title: Rapid Triage for Serious Infections in Infants Younger than 3 Months using A Novel Heart Rate Variability Tool
abs: Febrile infants <3 months present a diagnostic dilemma to paediatricians and emergency physicians. Tension remains between the need for early aggressive intervention among patients with suspected sepsis and the global phenomena of increasing antibiotic resistance. Current triage tools are insufficient. A non-invasive triage tool to detect infants at risk of serious infections (SI) would reduce unnecessary investigations and unwarranted interventions. We aim to develop a novel artificial intelligence (AI) triage tool including heart rate variability (HRV), and evaluate its utility in predicting serious infection (SI) among febrile infants aged <3 months in KK Women’s and Children’s Hospital (KKH) Emergency Department (ED). We hypothesize that HRV provides incremental diagnostic information and a novel triage tool incorporating HRV is superior to current triage tools in discriminating infants with SI from those without. This is a prospective observational study to be conducted in KKH, ED. We will include infants <3 months presenting with a rectal temperature >38oC between Jan 2019 and Dec 2020. SI includes sepsis (including bacteremia), meningitis, lobar pneumonia (confirmed radiologically), osteomyelitis, abscess and urinary tract infection. HRV will be monitored for 5 minutes using a single-lead electrocardiogram (ECG). The ECG signal will be extracted and processed to obtain HRV data. Performance indicators are the area under receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive values, which will be compared between the novel and current existing triage tools. If successful, including HRV information will improve triage precision for febrile infants with SI, allowing resources be focused on the sickest infants.

title: Next-Generation Clinical Trials and Integrative Research for Fighting Lung Cancer
abs: Lung cancer is the most lethal disease in Singapore, but unlike in the West, lung cancer in Asia is far more likely to be driven by mutation of EGFR (epidermal growth factor receptor) and to occur in patients who have never smoked. Many patients respond initially to kinase inhibitor drugs, only to relapse with drug-resistant disease. Our 5-theme proposal harnesses genomics and informatics to predict and direct appropriate interventions, to reduce lung cancer mortality in Singapore. Theme 1 centres around 4 investigator-initiated trials (IIT), 23 pharma-sponsored trials, and observation of non-trial patients, to generate a unique and comprehensive body of clinical data and serial biospecimens for the remaining themes. We have procured substantial industry support for our IITs, including a novel adaptive clinical trial (BESPOKE) which uses genomic profiling to adjust treatments and track response dynamically. Theme 2 clarifies the risks and benefits of immuno-oncology in EGFR-mutant(EGFRm) and EGFR-wildtype(EGFRwt) non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) by interrogating serial biospecimens (blood and tumor) from patients treated with PD-1-related combinations (nivolumab with ipilimumab or metronomic vinorelbine), looking to identify determinants or biomarkers for patient response and toxicity outcomes. Theme 3 provides data processing and analytics for patient-derived data, and performs virtual dissection of tumor heterogeneity to identify molecular changes associated with response and resistance. Statistical methods will identify biomarkers and a clinical decision-support system will cater to the adaptive clinical trial. Theme 4 employs NSCLC-derived model systems for seeking novel therapeutic targets based on stemness and cancer metabolism; for pursuing long-term drug development efforts; and for assessing how combination treatments affect the evolution of drug-resistance. Theme 5 addresses present-day needs in the broader population by testing the feasibility, cost-effectiveness, and psychological burdens of screening people who have never smoked, and by studying environmental exposures in our population.

title: Enhancing PUB Plant’s operational efficiency through early prediction, diagnosis and/or recommendation for equipment faults and alarms sequencing and improving knowledge management process through advanced digitisation and artificial intelligence
abs: Project 1: Early Fault Detection and Diagnostics (EFDD) of Critical Equipment through Failure Pattern Modeling Non-linear, Self-learning and Dynamic modelling: The novelty will be the development of self-learning and dynamic data based models for continuous monitoring of critical equipment (like Rotating Equipment, Membranes, RO, Valves, etc) for the early detection and diagnosis of failures. Self-learning and dynamic data based models can be built using Kernel principal component analysis method which not only capture the linear features but also capture the non-linear features in the data and update itself along with the variations in equipment behaviour. Self-learning of data based models can be improved by learning about frequently occurring problematic signatures from trend data and quantify different clusters of problematic “fingerprints” in rotating equipment with the application of machine learning tools (such as neural networks, genetic programming, and pattern recognition), time series analysis (such as ARX modeling, State Space modeling) and Vibration analysis (such as Fourier transform methods). As a whole, for given rotating equipment, this method will alert maintenance engineers.Project 2: Work Process Automation & Optimization (WPAO) using text and video analytics The novelty of the research proposal lies in the development of analytical framework that aims to uncover the global patterns hidden in a variety of the data sources that are currently being stored separately (“siloize” systems) and in a variety of formats (like texts, images, structured & unstructured, etc). The core of the framework would consist of state-of-the-art text and video analytics engine based on word embedding, bag-of-words and deep learning approaches like layer-wise fine-tuning of Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to analyse the maintenance logs and work orders in conjunction with process & machine data, CCTV images, etc., to identify patterns that would further streamline the work flow, and ultimately lead to automation of the whole work flow: from generating the work order to closing the work order and all the in-between steps in the most optimal way that would result in increased plant efficiency and decreased downtime. The innovation of this project lies in the adaption of the natural language processing techniques and image analysis techniques for industrial application specifically water treatment plants of PUB. Because of the manual entry as well as lack of documentation guidelines, it is expected that the entries will contain industry specific jargons, spelling and grammatical errors, as well as non-standard usages. title: CogniVision – Energy-autonomous always-on cognitive and attentive cameras for distributed real-time vision with milliwatt power consumption
abs: Untethering cameras with nearly-perpetual lifetime for massively distributed visual sensing is currently an unfulfilled challenge, due to the impractically large power consumption and wireless data volume in state-of-the-art cameras. Wireless transmission and video compression currently require several tens or hundreds of mWs and several Mbps, largely exceeding the milliWatt power budget available in miniaturized sensor nodes with energy harvesting (e.g., centimetre-scale thin-foil solar cell). CogniVision aims to enable cognitive cameras with mW power by embedding ultralow-power on-chip scene sensemaking (e.g., object classification), leveraging the recent impetuous advances in deep learning. Accordingly, CogniVision cameras transmit only short aggregate data rather than long raw video streams, and can hence be untethered, always-on, nearly-perpetual, miniaturized (<100 mm3), inexpensive ($ range). CogniVision cameras are also attentive as they can constantly listen to commands from the cloud monitoring the global scene via novel ultralow-power radios, adapting to the visual task or operating condition required by the overall scene (e.g., unusually large crowd, drastic lighting change). CogniVision is an inter-disciplinary program cutting across the areas of ultra-low power image sensors, circuits/architectures for video processing and wireless communications, and machine learning algorithms for scene sensemaking. The ambitious mW-level power target is pursued through true system design, bringing innovation into three dimensions: 1) innovative approximate digital architecture and power-aware neural networks for deep learning with 10-20X improved energy/area 2) always-on components with the unprecedented ability to skip irrelevant frame activity and hence reduce power (imager with near-pixel processing, low-activity SRAM, ultra-low power wakeup radio) 3) innovative architecture embedding energy-quality scaling to exploit the robustness of vision against approximations. CogniVision is now timely, leveraging the convergence of advances in deep learning, smart image sensors and energy-quality scalable circuits in the last few years.
