title: Beyond surviving colorectal cancer: how cancer survivors can influence the attitudes of their family members towards screening and play a role to support those with cancer
abs: AIMS To determine: 1. Screening rates and barriers amongst the first degree relatives (FDRs) and spouses of patients with colorectal cancer (CRC) and if tailored intervention could increase their adoption of screening modalities 2. Quality of life (QoL) of CRC patients through the first 18 months following their diagnosis 3. Feasibility of a survivorship program for CRC survivors to support new CRC patients in their initial stages of treatment to improve their QoL. HYPOTHESES 1. Screening rates amongst the FDRs and spouses of patients with CRC are suboptimal and tailored interventions can improve their screening rates. 2. Patients with CRC have poor QoL in the earlier stages of their treatment, and their QOL would worsen with additional treatment 3. A survivorship program is feasible and may improve the QoL of new CRC patients. METHODOLOGY The study will be conducted at the various hospitals across Singapore with a recruitment target of 300 patients, 150 spouses and 100 FDRs. All patients with CRC will be approached upon diagnosis and the QoL instruments would be administered at various timepoints over the subsequent 18 months. A randomized trial to contact the FDRs would be performed while spouses would be recruited during the patients’ appointments with oncologists. Barriers towards screening will be ascertained and a randomized trial to determine if tailored interventions targeting cost, and/or logistical barriers would improve their adoption of screening modalities will be performed. Once the QoL of the CRC patients has reached pre-operative levels, they would be invited to join a survivorship program to assist and guide new CRC patients to cope with treatment during the initial phases. SIGNIFICANCE OF THE STUDY This study will determine what interventions could improve the screening rates amongst the FDRs and Spouses and if CRC survivors could improve the QoL of new CRC patients.

title: The VICTORY (Virus-Induced Cancers: Translational Oncology Research & immunologY) Consortium
abs: The Virus-Induced Cancers: Translational Oncology Research and immunologY consortium (VICTORY) is a national translational team of leading key opinion leaders combining synergistic expertise to optimise immunotherapeutic strategy against virally-driven cancers (VDCs). This will be accomplished by examining host and viral interactions in the tumour microenvironment – specifically how VDCs induce immunosuppression, target discovery and validation, and experimental therapeutics. Major VDCs will be examined, Epstein-Barr virus-driven cancers such as nasopharyngeal cancer (NPC), Human papilloma virus-driven oropharyngeal and cervical cancers, and Hepatitis B-driven hepatocellular carcinoma. The VICTORY team has a proven track record: • 30 joint publications • 9 joint grant applications • >34 clinical trials • >400 recruited patients Virus-induced cancers in Asia account for over 60% of global VDCs, and still expected to increase. The VICTORY consortium harnesses unique, competitive capabilities and resources across academic institutions with industry to establish: 1) The world’s largest collection of functionally, clinically annotated VDC biospecimens. The VDC Biobank forms a centrepiece for the consortium for systematic comprehensive analytics, 2) Deep immunophenotyping and broad omics capability to complete comprehensive characterisation of VDC immune microenvironment including molecular, functional and mechanistic assessment of VDC immune suppression, 3) novel humanised mouse models of VDCs able to host both human solid cancers and a recapitulated human immune system, and shown to harbour oncogenic virus infection, 4) Strong interdisciplinary team of world class clinician-scientists, immunologists, virologists, molecular biologists and metabolism experts, and 5) Robust collaborations with pharmaceutical and biotech companies locally and internationally and with the non-profit Parker Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy. The enhanced understanding of VDCs and underlying immune/metabolic drivers of disease that will result from the VICTORY consortium forms the basis of novel, next generation immunotherapies and discovery of biomarkers informing therapy. The VICTORY consortium creates an unprecedented, coordinated, leading global centre of VDC excellence embracing the biomedical, academic healthcare, and industry sectors.

title: Life Trajectory of Older Major Blunt Trauma Survivors with Risk Factors for Long-Term Post-Discharge Mortality: Perspectives of Patients and their Caregivers – A Mixed Methods Study
abs: End-of-life perspectives in cancer patients have been well studied. Studies on end-of-life care in trauma currently focus on care at the index hospitalization for injury, for example end-of-life support in the intensive care unit for un-survivable head injury. There is increasing interest in the factors affecting increased long-term mortality for survivors of severe injury (age, fall, chronic disease, function at discharge); however, there are no published studies on the end-of-life trajectory for these patients, including: the effect of surviving severe injury on patients’ and caregivers’ perspectives and attitudes towards the reduced quality of life or disability post-injury, and specific concerns trauma survivors and their caregivers may have with regard to the potential imminent end-of-life trajectory after surviving major blunt trauma. Our recent retrospective study of blunt trauma survivors, using Singapore National Trauma Registry Data, showed overall 7.2% 1-year mortality and 16.7% 3-year mortality for adult survivors of blunt trauma. However,for patients aged over 55 with at least one major risk factor (high Charlson score, low fall, head and neck Abbreviated Injury Scale of 3 and above), 3-year mortality exceeded 25%, reaching 50% for patients with two major risk factors. The majority of these deaths (60%) occurred in the acute hospital. With the increasing awareness of end-of-life issues in our population, it is timely to study high-risk patients and their caregivers after surviving injury. We will study quality of life post-injury at 3-months, 6-months, 12-months, 18-months, 24-months, 30-months, and 36-months post-injury. For the patients who pass away during the study period, their caregivers will be given the Quality of Death and Dying questionnaire, and semistructured interviews used to explore their concerns and needs not addressed in the questionnaire.

title: Neurorestoration after Spinal Cord Contusion with Cocktail Cell Transplant Therapy
abs: In human, spinal cord injuries (SCI) are mostly contusive and highly debilitating. The disruption of ascending and descending tracks in the spinal cord following injury results in sensory and motor dysfunctions. Unfortunately, nerve tracks in the adult central nervous system (CNS) lack the capacity to regenerate. Transplantation of glial cells capable of providing a pathway for regenerating axons is one of the most promising current approaches for neurorestoration after spinal cord injury. Our previous studies have shown that transplantation of olfactory ensheathing cells (OECs) to treat spinl cord injury in both experimental rat models and clinical applications can be a promising strategy. OECs can be obtained from the olfactory mucosa in the nose and the olfactory bulbs in the cranium. Functional restoration of long-tract injuries has been demonstrated in various rat studies by reinstating forepaw grasping, supra-spinal control of breathingor proprioceptive function on a climbing task.(Ibrahim et al. 2009a; Keyvan-Fouladi et al. 2003; Li et al. 2003; Li et al. 1997; Lu et al. 2002; Ramon-Cueto et al. 2000). Clinical trials of transplantation of autologous OECs into spinal cord injuries have been carried out (Lima et al. 2010; Lima et al. 2006; Tabakow, aisman et al. 2014).However, the challenge is limited amount of OEC cells that can be obtained fromone biopsy. In order to solve this problem, we have been testing novel mixture cell transplant therapy. Preliminary study has been performed. The study demostated that mixure of he OECs with a collagen gel are able to maximize the usage of the limited number of human OECs from olfactory bulb biopsy. We tested functions of the OEC-collagen scaffold in vivo by transplanting it into a rat model of brachial plexus injury. This cellular scaffold occupied the cavity caused by injury and gave structural integrity to support cell transplants spanning the lesion to partially reinstate proprioception in the rats.However, repair of spinal cord injuries requires not only reconnect the severed nerve fibres, but also replace the loss of the local cells such motor neurons, astrocytes. OECs transplantation is kwown to repair the neural pathway and facilitate nerve reconnection. It is also known that tranplantation of neural stem and precursor cells (NSCs/NPCs) reconstitutes the local loss. In the present proposal we would like to further test a novel cocktail cell transplant therapy. This is to determine whether combinations of OECs, neural stem cells and collagen scaffolds would be able to induce axonal regeneraition and to repair injuries in a rat contutive spinal cord injury model.

title: validaTing biomARkers of myocardial fibrosis and investiGating thErapies To regress FIBROSIS (TARGET-FIBROSIS)
abs: Heart failure is a global pandemic. Despite recent treatment advances, the burden of heart failure remains a leading cause of death worldwide. Myocardial fibrosis is a common pathologic manifestation in heart failure, regardless of etiology. Despite its potential clinical value, there are currently no specific treatment approaches targeted at regression myocardial fibrosis. This clinical gap reflects a lack of well-validated biomarkers of myocardial fibrosis to monitor disease progression, risk stratify and assess treatment response in heart failure. Our previous research had identified novel biomarkers (clinical, imaging and circulating) of myocardial fibrosis in aortic stenosis and hypertensive heart disease, both are common causes of heart failure in the adult population. The Clinician Scientist Award proposal extends our previous research and aims to systematically address these critical knowledge gaps. Accordingly, we will determine the association between biomarkers and progression of myocardial fibrosis in a pre-heart failure cardiac condition. In hypertensive cardiac disease, we hypothesize that biomarkers of fibrosis at baseline can predict progression of fibrosis at 3 years (Aim 1). In addition, we will establish and clinically validate a panel of biomarkers (clinical, biochemical and routine clinical investigations) of myocardial fibrosis diagnosed on cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) in patients with heart failure. We hypothesize an integrated panel of clinical markers that diagnoses focal fibrosis also predicts all-cause mortality in heart failure, regardless of underlying etiology (Aim 2). The anti-fibrotic potential of a novel treatment agent (valsartan/sacubitril) will be evaluated in a pilot Phase II randomized controlled trial using CMR to assess treatment response. We hypothesize valsartan/sacubitril is associated with greater regression in myocardial fibrosis volume compared to valsartan after 12 months of treatment in hypertensive patients with left ventricular hypertrophy (Aim 3). Results from these studies will support the role of personalized risk profiling and preventive treatment strategies to improve patient outcomes and reduce the burden of heart failure.

title: A Randomised Controlled Trial Evaluating a Novel Individualised Treatment Strategy for Carbapenem-Resistant Gram-Negative Bacteria Infections
abs: Carbapenem (a potent last-line high therapeutic index antibiotic)-resistant gram-negative bacilli (CRGNB) is resistant to all beta-lactam antibiotics, and likely extensively/pan-drug resistant. Against a background of dwindling antibiotic pipeline effective against these infections, using antibiotic combinations is one of the few viable options left to clinicians. However, evidence for the use of antibiotics is controversial because the mortality reduction associated with antibiotic combination therapy was not consistently observed in all studies. One main reason for this could be the strain-specific effectiveness of different antibiotic combinations. This also underscores the limitation of on-going randomised clinical trials in Europe and the USA, comparing one fixed antibiotic monotherapy against one fixed antibiotic combination. An investigator-initiated, prospective, open-label, randomised controlled clinical trial will be conducted to evaluate a new treatment strategy for CRGNB infections. Termed ôguided antibiotic combination therapyö, the study arm will receive the most effective (synergistic and bactericidal) antibiotics combination derived from in vitro antibiotic combination testing (iACT). The comparator arm will receive standard therapy of either antibiotic monotherapy or unguided combination therapy, depending on treating physicians' clinical judgment. The primary hypothesis is that when compared to standard therapy, guided combination of antibiotics following iACT reduces 30-day mortality by 10% in patients with CRGNB infections. The mechanisms of resistance in CRGNB, and patientsÆ adverse drug reactions will be described. iACT will be performed for all trial patients although test information will be withheld for comparator arm. Instead, results from the iACT will be used to explore the 30-day all-cause mortality rates between patients whose treatments are matched with the iACT result, versus those whose treatments are not matched, within the standard therapy arm. We hypothesize that the mortality rate is 10% lower in the standard therapy arm among patients whose therapies matched with the iACT results than those whose therapies did not match.

title: Characterization of immune evasion in NK/T-Cell Lymphoma
abs: Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma (NKTL) is an aggressive EBV-associated neoplasm more prevalent in South East Asians than in other populations. It is commonly refractory to conventional chemotherapy, and new treatment approaches are urgently required. Immune checkpoint inhibitors affecting the Programmed Death 1 (PD1) pathway show promise in early clinical trials for NKTL, suggesting an important role for the immune system in modulating these tumours. However, PD1 is only one of many pathways employed in cancer immune evasion and new immunotherapy approaches are being tested in various cancers. The interplay between these different immune evasion pathways as well as the role of EBV in immune regulation is not understood in NKTL. This information will be relevant to the incorporation of immunotherapy into NKTL treatment. In this grant, we aim to study immune evasion in NKTL in 2 sections. Section 1 is a pathological characterization of immune evasion markers in clinical NKTL samples. Our previous gene expression studies on NKTL revealed elevated expression of immune modulatory genes. We will validate the protein expression of these transcripts, and study their relationship to Programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1), as well as novel immuno-oncology targets such as TIM3 and VISTA. We have established a multispectral imaging assay to quantify these molecular markers in tumour and immune cells in the microenvironment of NKTL, to identify appropriate immuno-oncology trial strategies. In Section 2, we will decipher the role of EBV in immune evasion in NKTL by modulating the expression of EBV proteins and miRNA in NKTL cell lines, and analyzing their effects on immune evasion molecules of therapeutic interest. Overall, this grant will help clarify the clinical relevance of immune evasion pathways in NKTL and identify pertinent immune regulatory targets for future clinical trials.

title: Applications and development of a thermostable protein nanoparticle
abs: Protein-based nanoparticles with unique materials qualities are being sought as therapeutic delivery systems. The field of biologics, namely protein-based therapeutics, has become a central tool for precision medicine. Biologics that go beyond antibody-based platforms represent an open opportunity for disease treatment. Recent work from our group, published in Nature Communications, engineered a gene from the hyperthermophilic halophile, Archaeoglobus fulgidus (Afu), as a thermostable exoshell (tES) for expressing and folding proteins within its hollow internal surface. The shell can be then disassembled at pH 5.8 to release the expressed protein. We also discovered the tES are highly protective of internalized substrates, protecting them against 0.4% trypsin, a variety of organic solvents and thermal denaturations. This CSA will fund the next iteration of data and publications, focusing on an initial in vivo application of the tES and a new application of tES to encapsulate and deliver nucleic acid based substrates, both DNA and RNA. This proposal will also fund scale up studies in order to produce gram quantities of tES and encapsulated substrates suitable for expanded in vivo applications.

title: Synergistic genetic lesions in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma tumour tissue and peripheral blood.
abs: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) is globally the most common aggressive lymphoma. Approximately 50% of cases are cured with RCHOP chemotherapy. The remainder will relapse or will be treated palliatively to avoid toxicity. It is therefore vital to develop less toxic targeted therapies and to identify patients who will respond poorly to RCHOP so that alternative treatments may be offered. The aim of this project is to investigate the prognostic impact of combinations of genetic lesions in DLBCL and to evaluate the beta-catenin pathway as a potential target. TP53 and MYD88 mutations are associated with a poor prognosis, as is the non-germinal centre cell of origin (COO) subtype. The co-occurrence of MYC and BCL2 or BCL6 translocations (“double-hit” lymphoma (DHL)) defines a subgroup with an aggressive disease course. Recent studies suggest that TP53 mutations combined with MYC translocations also result in a poor prognosis. However, these studies have either included too few DHL cases or were prone to selection bias. Pilot data indicates that mutations in the beta-catenin regulator DDX3X are found in ~40% of relapsed/refractory DLBCL but only ~3% of unselected cases. 4/5 DDX3X lesions co-occurred with a translocation indicating possible synergy. A large study to investigate TP53, MYD88 and DDX3X mutations in combination with MYC translocations is therefore required. The SGH DLBCL archive has >400 cases with FFPE material and known translocation status and COO subtype. We propose to sequence MYD88, TP53, and DDX3X in this cohort using the Fluidigm platform and correlate the combination of genetic lesions with COO and clinical outcomes. The effect of DDX3X mutations on proliferation, apoptosis, and beta-catenin activity will be investigated in lymphoma cell lines using standard assays. Finally, sequencing of cell-free tumour DNA from stored patient plasma will be explored as a novel method of identifying these mutations in blood samples.

title: Programmed-cell death 1 (PD1) inhibitor therapy on the immune system in the treatment of Natural-Killer/T-Cell lymphoma
abs: Background: Natural-killer/T-cell lymphoma (NKTL) is an EBV-associated non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma (NHL) more commonly found in Asia. Treatment outcomes for advanced-stage (AS) and relapsed/refractory (R/R) NKTL are dismal with 5-year overall survival (OS) of less than 10%. Recent retrospective data suggests that programmed cell death protein 1 (PD1)-inhibitors are active in NKTL. However, there are no prospective clinical trials or established biomarkers of response. Hypothesis and specific aims: We hypothesize that PD1 inhibitors are active in a subgroup of NKTL patients and there are immune and genomic biomarkers of response to identify these patients. Methods: We will recruit 20 AS and R/R NKTL patients into a pilot study comprising 3 phases. In the first phase, all patients will be treated with 4 doses of nivolumab 240mg given every 2 weeks afterwhich a PET/CT will be performed. In the second phase, patients who obtain a complete response (CR) or good partial response (PR) will continue on single agent nivolumab until disease progression. Patients who obtain less than a good PR will be treated with nivolumab 360mg, gemcitabine 800mg/m2 day 1 and 8, cisplatin 20mg/m2 days 1 to 4, dexamethasone 10mg days 1 to 4 and l-asparaginase 6000units/m2 days 2-8 (GDP/L-aspa) every 3 weekly for up to 6 cycles. In the third phase, patients who have not progressed on treatment may receive maintenance nivolumab. The primary and secondary objectives are to estimate the best overall response rate (ORR) after 6months and rates of grades 3-5 adverse effects of this treatment strategy respectively. We will perform multiplex immunohistochemical staining on pre-treatment tumours and correlate the intensity of PD-ligand 1 (PDL1) staining with treatment responses. Whole exome sequencing (WES) on pre-treatment fresh tumour will be done to identify recurrent somatic aberrations and correlate the presence of PDL1 structural rearrangements (SR) and JAK3 mutations with treatment responses.
kw: Lymphoma, T-cell, selinexor, novel therapeutics, phase I, phase II

title: Diet-derived metabolites and the risk of colorectal cancer: a nested case-control study in a population-based cohort, the Singapore Chinese Health Study
abs: Background: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the most common cancer and one of the leading cause of cancer-related deaths in Singapore. To date, no previous study has evaluated the association between diet-derived metabolites and the risk of CRC in the context of Asian diet, microbiota composition, and anatomical subsite in the local population. Aims and Hypothesis:1) Compare pre-diagnostic plasma levels of diet-derived metabolites (short chain fatty acids, amino acids, Trimethylamine-N-Oxide (TMAO) and its precursors, secondary bile acids and glycolytic metabolites) among 500 CRC cases and their matched controls nested within the Singapore Chinese Health Study (SCHS). We hypothesize that cases will have elevated plasma levels of pro-carcinogenic metabolites such as TMAO and reduced levels of anti-carcinogenic metabolites such as butyrate compared with control subjects. 2) Examine the association of diet-derived metabolites with CRC risk by anatomical subsite (colon versus rectum). Given differences in embryological origin, genetic and molecular signatures, and microbiome composition between anatomical subsites, we hypothesize that the associations between diet-derived metabolites and CRC risk will be more pronounced in colon cancers compared to rectal cancers.3) Evaluate if pre-diagnostic blood metabolites modulate histopathological and molecular characteristics of incident CRC tumors. We hypothesize that tumors from cases with different levels of pro- or anti-carcinogenic metabolites implicated in CRC will differ in histopathological and molecular characteristics.Methodology: This is a nested case-control study of 500 incident CRC cases and 500 matched controls within the SCHS. The metabolites will be measured using mass-spectrometry approaches. Measurement of gene expression in tumours will be performed using Nanostring expression assay and targeted sequencing with a 216-gene cancer panel. Clinical Significance: This project informs putative molecular pathways mediated by diet-derived metabolites in CRC carcinogenesis. This enables the identification of tumors of particular molecular profiles with targetable metabolic dependencies, and may enable stratified development of metabolic therapeutics.
kw: Colorectal cancer risk, diet, metabolites

title: Caregiving Transitions among Family Caregivers of Elderly Singaporeans (TraCE)
abs: Family members play an essential role in caregiving for elderly in Singapore, given a strong sense of filial piety and its accompanying social expectations and relevant government policies. However, comprehensive investigations on family caregivers – central to developing evidence-based programs and policies for family caregivers of elderly Singaporeans – are lacking. Existing studies are mostly based on cross-sectional data, largely investigate negative caregiving outcomes, focus on caregivers of elderly with one particular disease, and include only already-caregivers at baseline – thus, precluding a holistic understanding. We address these limitations through an unprecedented longitudinal dyadic study of family caregivers of elderly (aged ?75) Singaporeans with functional limitations. Together, an index-elderly care recipient/potential care recipient and his/her caregiver/potential caregiver will form the participant dyad. Over 1.5 years, we will interview 869 dyads from existing cohort studies of elderly Singaporeans, every 6 months (4 interviews maximum). Using group-based trajectory modelling, we will delineate trajectories of health (healthcare use; stress; depressive symptoms; quality of life), work, and caregiving-related (disrupted health, schedule; lack of family support; lack of finances; esteem; self-affirmation; outlook on life) outcomes among caregivers. We will identify predictors of these trajectories, and variables that shift each trajectory upward or downward. This will enable a deeper understanding of the variability in longitudinal pattern in caregiver outcomes, which can be duly considered in designing/implementing targeted caregiver interventions. We will also provide national estimates of the quantity and cost of caregiving time using the proxy good method. Finally, we will examine the impact of transition into caregiving on the ‘new’ caregivers’ health and assess grief among caregivers and potential caregivers of decedents. Through the scope of its caregiver population, overall methodology and expected findings, TraCE will fill crucial research gaps in context of family caregiving for elderly Singaporeans and inform evidence-based programs and policies for family caregivers.
kw: family caregivers, elderly, longitudinal study, trajectory analysis, group based trajectory modeling, cost of caregiving time

title: Life Trajectory of Older Major Blunt Trauma Survivors with Risk Factors for Long-Term Post-Discharge Mortality: Perspectives of Patients and their Caregivers – A Mixed Methods Study
abs: Major injury is a life-changing event. For older survivors of moderate and severe injury (aged 55 and above), some of these survivors are at increased risk of long-term death, either due to other chronic diseases they have at the time of injury, frailty, or the disability from injury. Our recent study of major trauma survivors, using Singapore National Trauma Registry Data, showed a 7.2% 1-year mortality and a 16.7% 3-year mortality for adult survivors of blunt trauma. Major risk factors for long-term mortality included: low fall, Charlson comorbidity score of 2 or more, and head injury. The majority of these deaths (almost 60% for both the 1-year and 3-year mortality) occurred in the acute hospital. Another study showed a 1-year readmission risk of more than 40%, increased for patients with the same risk factors for increased mortality.However, not much is known about the unmet clinical, social or psychological needs for this group of patients, for example, the effect of the hospitalization and recovery from injury on quality of life, and resulting end-of-life trajectory, for these high-risk patients and their caregivers. We plan to study survivors of injury at higher risk of long-term mortality (due to head injury, low fall, age or other chronic diseases) and their caregivers to understand their quality of life post-injury, trend their quality of life for the 3 years post-injury, and study the end-of-life trajectory for those who die during the study period. We will study their quality of life at 3-month intervals for 3 years post-injury, and interview patients and care-givers in-depth after emergency department visits or unplanned hospital readmission. We will also conduct in-depth interviews to explore their concerns that may not be addressed in the questionnaire.
kw: Quality of Life, End of Life, Trauma, Injury, Caregiver

title: A united airway approach in patients with asthma and chronic rhinosinusitis: identifying inflammatory endotypes to aid personalised management.
abs: Background: Asthma and chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS) with or without nasal polyps (NP) affects more than 300 million people worldwide. Their prevalence is rising, along with significant disease burden and costs. Data suggest that there is significant interaction between the two diseases, leading to increased disease burden. Asian patients with CRS have more T1-driven neutrophilic inflammation compared to Caucasians. Hence we need to study the immunopathologic mechanisms of severe airway disease in Asians, to identify new disease targets and treatment options. Specific aims: We will adopt a ôunited airway endotyping approachö to (1) determine the true prevalence of patients with uncontrolled, co-existing asthma with CRS, (2) identify specific inflammatory endotypes across the different disease combinations and severity, (3) to use the inflammatory endotype to guide personalised treatment, and assess the impact of this approach on clinical and healthcare utilization outcomes.Approach: A prospective prevalence study. We will screen for and target 4 groups with uncontrolled combined airway disease (a) severe asthma (SA) with CRSwNP (b) SA with mild/moderate CRS (c) mild/moderate asthma with CRSwNP (d) mild/moderate asthma and CRS. Disease control and severity is based on validated scores. Inflammatory endotypes are quantified by nasal and sputum eosinophil/ neutrophil cell counts, immunofluorescence for ciliary dysfunction and T2/T1/T17 cytokines measurements. Patients will be followed up longitudinally over 1 year to assess the impact of endotype-guided treatment compared to a historical control (case-matched) on clinical outcomes (asthma control, quality of life, exacerbations) and healthcare utilization (medication usage, clinic visits, sick leave, hospitalization, treatment costs).Significance/ Strengths: Our multidisciplinary team will identify specific inflammatory endotypes in Asians, that can be used to guide targeted treatment. This might lead to discovery and development of new predictive biomarkers and disease targets. This might guide and change workflow practice, leading to better clinical outcomes and cost savings.
kw: asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, endotypes, airway inflammation, ciliary dysfunction, biomarker

title: Healthy Older People Everyday (HOPE) – Role of High Protein Diet on Muscle and Bone Health
abs: Sarcopenia and frailty is associated with many negative outcomes including poor quality of life, falls, fractures, increased healthcare resource utilization, increased caregiver burden and mortality. Prevalence of pre-frailty in our community dwelling older adult is 37% and frailty 6.2%. Frailty prevalence in diabetics is 12% and those attending medical outpatient clinics 27%. Frailty is reversible in up to 20% of older adults and various small scale studies incorporating nutrition and exercise interventions have shown improvement in function. An adequate intake of dietary proteins is vital to maintaining muscle mass and stimulating protein synthesis and the current recommended dietary allowance for protein (0.8 g/kg/day) might not be sufficient for preserving muscle mass and quality in old age. We aim to develop local delicacies enhanced with protein content, and evaluate its effect on muscle strength, function and quality of life with or without physical activity. The first phase of the study will include development of protein enriched food prototypes that are culturally relevant for the various ethnic groups in Singapore which can deliver an effective dosage of protein and acceptable to the local older population. Older adults in the community will be screened for frailty and sarcopenia using the FRAIL scale and Sarc-F. Those screened positive will be randomized to control (n=250), nutrition intervention (n=250), nutrition and exercise (n=250), and exercise (n=250) only. Intervention phase will last 24 weeks , and participants will be followed up for total of 48 weeks. Outcomes measurements will include balance, functional status, gait speed, falls, quality of life and use of healthcare services within the same cluster. In addition, the results from this study will provide the basis and baseline for a review of the current recommended dietary allowance for protein, especially among older adults.
kw: Frailty; sarcopenia; high protein diet

title: Timely Identification of Developmental and Behaviour problems In Toddlers (TIDBIT)
abs: Timely identification and early intervention for developmental problems have good promise for better outcomes in children. The Health Booklet (HB) – a parent-held child health record, is Singapore’s main tool for developmental surveillance. This study aims to determine the clinical utility of the HB checklists to support primary care monitoring of developmental issues in young children in Singapore, and to compare its detection rates with other overseas-developed parent-filled developmental screening tools when used in the Singapore context. It also aims to determine the frequency and intensity of temper tantrums in the sample of toddlers, and examine the associations with the children’s developmental profile and other family factors. Parents and their children who are within 15 to 30 months old will be invited to participate. Parents will complete the HB checklists, two overseas-developed general developmental screening tools – ASQ and PEDS/PEDS:DM, an autism-specific screening tool – M-CHAT-R/F, and questionnaires about their children’s tantrums and their own stress levels, when their children are 18-months-old and/or 30-months-old. The children will undergo usual care at well-child check-ups with primary care doctors and nurses, and data on the outcome of the check-up will be collected. Children who are identified as “at-risk” by usual care, and the research screening tools, will complete standardized assessments for development and adaptive behaviour, within 1-3 months of the screening. Parents who attend the assessment with their children will complete another autism-specific screening tool – the ASDetect app. Target sample sizes for each screening time-point was approximately 800. Due to challenges with recruitment and data collection amidst the current COVID-19 pandemic, it is hoped that data from 200-250 participants or more will be achieved for each screening time-point. We are confident that due the large set of data being collected from each participant, the results of the study will still yield clinically meaningful results.
kw: Child Development, Screening, Surveillance, Developmental delay, Autism Spectrum Disorder

title: End-of-Life Management Protocol Offered Within Emergency Room : a multicentre study (EMPOWER)
abs: End-of-life (EOL) care has garnered increasing recognition and acceptance in the field of emergency medicine. Some emergency departments (EDs) in Singapore have instituted or plan to institute EOL care as part of their workflow. However, the EOL protocols are not standardised across all these EDs. The adherence to and quality of EOL care have not been formally measured in all institutions. Hence, gaps to improve the quality of care have yet to be determined.The aims are to systematically measure the current quality of EOL care in three Singapore hospital EDs and identify the quality gaps; formulate interventions to address these gaps and implement the improved EOL care; and measure the improvement post-implementation. We hypothesise that the current quality of EOL care in three EDs is suboptimal and the interventions planned will improve the quality of care provided.We plan to conduct an interrupted time series study to detect whether the interventions have an effect significantly greater than any underlying trend over time. The quality of care indicators to be measured are timely identification of patients who require EOL care, adequacy of symptom control based on compliance to prescriptions, opportunities to discuss and develop an individualised care plan, perceived quality of care by healthcare providers and next-of-kin, and cost effectiveness. Planned interventions include refining the protocol with collaboration of content experts in palliative care, education and training of healthcare providers, and addressing specific gaps identified to improve cost effectiveness. The results of this study will form the standardisation and foundation for establishing the national benchmark for quality of EOL care in Singapore EDs.(263 words)
kw: palliative care; emergency medical services ; end-of-life ;quality of care; cost effectiveness

title: Cost containment in pharmacogenomic testing, identifying obstacles to implementation of pharmacogenomics and impact on anticonvulsant prescription patterns
abs: Background: Pharmacogenomics and precision medicine are driving forces in biomedical research today. The HLA-B*1502 biomarker for severe adverse cutaneous drug reactions to carbamazepine has led to national-level legislation internationally. However implementation at the clinical front-line is highly variable, with resultant increased health system costs.We will employ a staged approach of validating a rapid HLA-B*15:02 testing system , then evaluate cost savings and reduced number of consultations from adopting this system and patient preferences for anticonvulsants and the factors which affect their decision-making process. This will improve and guide cost-effective implementation of pharmacogenomic testing in healthcare systems.Overall aim:a.) Improve speed and reduce cost of point-of-care pharmacogenomic testing, and b.) Identify and resolve factors impeding pharmacogenomics implementation to HLA-B*1502 and carbamazepine allergic reactions and apply findings to manage healthcare system costs.Primary aim: Clinically validate a rapid HLA-B*1502 testing system Primary hypothesis:Rapid HLA-B*1502 testing has 99% specificity and 99% sensitivity compared to the current gold standard.Secondary aim 1: Reduce the cost of pharmacogenomic testing for HLA-B*1502Secondary hypothesis 1:Rapid HLA-B*1502 testing can be performed at 33% of the cost of current pharmacogenomic testing methods.Secondary aim 2: Reduce consultations prior to anticonvulsant initiationSecondary hypothesis 2:Rapid HLA-B*1502 testing reduces medical consultation from pharmacogenomic testing to initiation of anticonvulsant treatment by 50%.Exploratory aim: Characterize the impact of focused rapid pharmacogenomic testing on anticonvulsant prescription patterns to identify obstacles and solutions and guide future national pharmacogenomic testing strategies.We will explore the impact of pharmacogenomic testing on anticonvulsant prescription patterns in the past, with implementation of rapid testing and the factors which affect individual anticonvulsant choices by patients and caregivers.Clinical significance. This project can reduce pharmacogenomic test costs and consultation numbers and characterize the impact of focused rapid pharmacogenomic testing to guide future national strategies in pharmacogenomic testing.
kw: Pharmacogenomics, anticonvulsant, prescription, cost containment, point-of-care

title: Understanding female health professionals' decisions to remain, return to, or exit the professional workforce
abs: This study will investigate the opportunities and challenges that female health professionals face when balancing their careers with their responsibilities as mothers and caregivers, and how these influence their decision to remain, return to or to exit the workforce. The increasing chronic disease burden of an ageing population requires more health professionals. This need can be achieved most cost effectively by increasing the numbers trained whilst simultaneously introducing initiatives that promote retention in the workforce. We hypothesized that women are less likely to stay in the health profession if they have greater family responsibilities imposed on them. Women are likely to be expected to sacrifice their working hours for the family. They are more likely than men to reduce their working hours after having a child or even leave the workforce to care for their children. Gender inequality in income and promotion, and the lack of female mentors may also act as the factors that caused women to consider working part-time or to leave the jobs. The proposed study will use a mixture of methodologies (structured literature review, one to one interviews, focus groups, survey questionnaire). The study involves the collection of data beyond the women themselves; in the focus group discussions each woman will be invited to contribute with the individual she had identified as having had a strong influence on her career decisions. In the final phase the observations generated from non-probability sampling will be tested for frequency and generalizability in a questionnaire survey of a large random sample of female health professionals. This enables the assessment of the relative importance of the different challenges and experiences identified within the female health professional workforce. The data will be interpreted with the help of our Study Advisory Panel and reports generated for different target audiences (ministries, employees, professional bodies). (word counts: 300)
kw: health professionals, women, workforce, retention, qualitative, important others

title: Preventing obesity-related diseases from young: Evaluating the longitudinal impact of multimedia intervention in promoting self-regulation of calorie consumption in children.
abs: Governments around the world have recognized that the improvement of public health is dependent on two major health behaviors: exercise and healthy consumption. Locally, initiatives have been launched to promote healthier food choices and protect young people from unhealthy eating habits. This is in line with PM Lee Hsien Loong’s 2009 National Day Rally Speech, which emphasized promotion of a healthy lifestyle among Singaporeans as one of the key areas for the nation. Specifically, the PM urged Singaporeans to maintain a healthy lifestyle by maintaining a nutritional diet, exercising regularly, and keeping their weight down. An increasing number of nations have implemented campaigns battling unhealthy diets and obesity. However, many of these prevention campaigns have tended to concentrate on (a) providing only information or (b) utilizing only a single medium of mainly traditional media.With edutainment theorists proposing that psychosocial factors such as self-efficacy and reflected appraisal are the keys for successful long-term programs for preventing obesity, intervention methods which enhance participation, fun and interaction appear particularly promising especially when targeting the young.We propose that digital technology offers a number of possible approaches to battling obesity. Advantages of using interactive media in the intervention include (1) the interactive nature of digital technology that creates more engagement from users; (2) the ability to personalize, or “tailor”, health messages and interventions to specific audience groups; and (3) the ability to synthesize entertainment with educational tasks. We propose to study the efficacy of an integrated, interactive health messaging intervention for health promotion and the prevention of obesity. In particular we aim to promote knowledge of the consequences of obesity (e.g. diabetes) and cultivate habits on how to choose foods lower in calories and sugar content among young people in Singapore. Our findings will have implications for health communication strategies and policies.
kw: Health Promotion, Digital Technology, Diabetes Prevention, Obesity, Health Messaging

title: Malnutrition and Frailty: Integrated Community-based and Clinic-supported Screening and Lifestyle Interventions
abs: One third of older Singaporeans are at moderate to high risk of malnutrition and one half of older Singaporeans are either pre-frail (45%) or frail (4.5%).The major cause of frailty is malnutrition: 66% of frail individuals and 40% of pre-frail individuals are at risk or malnourished. Nearly all (91%) of malnourished older people are frail (27%) or pre-frail (64%). We will develop and evaluate simple, effective and generically appropriate algorithms and protocols to screen and assess, prevent and treat malnutrition and frailty for use in an integrated care model in both community and clinic settings. 1.Community-based screening and interventions based in senior activity centers (SAC) performed by non-healthcare professionals trained to use simple ‘pen-and paper’ tools will identify low-moderate nutrition risk and pre-frail older persons for nutritional and physical exercise lifestyle interventions. Community-based lifestyle interventions will employ NCSS-inspired Our Kitchen Programme (OKP) and KTPH Share-a-Pot Programme communality approach for dietitian-guided shared food resourcing, preparation and meal participation to empower and enable frail older persons to improve the quality and quantity of protein and calorie and micronutrient intake, in conjunction with physical exercise intervention using key elements of high velocity resistance training (power training) and dual tasking. 2.Clinic-based program. High risk (malnourished) and frail individuals identified from SAC screening above will be referred to a designated geriatric outpatient service unit in one community hospital providing clinic-based programs for stepped-up clinical assessment, intensive nutritional and physical therapy, and management of multi-morbidity and polypharmacy. A 3-month randomized controlled trial will determine whether the community-based and clinic-supported integrated multi-sector service model to screen and treat malnutrition and frailty will improve nutritional status, physical and functional status, quality of life, and reduce falls risk, hospitalization and need for long-term care.
kw: Frailty, Malnutrition, Elderly, Lifestyle intervention, Integrated care and service

title: Improving recruitment, retention and re-engagement of doctors within general practice and family medicine
abs: Singapore recognizes that caring for an ageing population with multiple chronic conditions will require more doctors with generic clinical skills, and doctors whose style of practice has a whole patient and family focus, characteristics found in General Practitioners and Family Physicians. An increase in workforce can be achieved by increasing the numbers of doctors trained, an example being the recent scheme to increase the number of Family Physicians in training by 30%. We hypothesised that in parallel to recruitment, there is a need to have initiatives that focused on retention of doctors in the primary care workforce, together with schemes to facilitate re-entry of doctors taking a career break. We also hypothesized that the trend of health care needs and/or career opportunities in General Practice/Family Medicine may potentially affect the choice in career path for medical students and, affect currently working physicians to make a decision on whether to leave or to stay in the General Practice/Family Medicine workforce. Plans to boost recruitment, retention and re-entry need to be informed by an understanding of the experiences, perceptions and career aspirations of the workforce. We have planned a series of sequential studies involving medical students, doctors working in General Practice/Family Medicine and those who have left this field of work. The research will use qualitative (in-depth interviews and focus groups) and quantitative methods (online surveys), and the findings generated will help inform interventions to boost recruitment, minimize attrition and optimise the contribution of appropriately qualified doctors to the general practice workforce. (250 words)
kw: General Practice/Family Medicine, doctors, labour or workforce, retention, attrition, return

title: Investigating the roles of gelsolin, a cytoskeletal protein, in regulating autophagy that contributes to the survival of colorectal cancer cells.
abs: Colorectal cancer is one of the commonest cancers worldwide, and a leading cause of cancer death. During colorectal cancer development and therapeutic treatment, cancer cells encounter various stresses from the tumour microenvironment, including nutrient insufficiency, and cytotoxic effects from chemotherapeutic agents. The ability of cancer cells to survive against stresses not only affects the disease outcome, but also impedes the effectiveness of therapy. Therefore, understanding molecular mechanisms underlying cancer cell survival under stress conditions is crucial for designing and achieving effective therapy. Gelsolin, an important cytoskeletal regulator, has been demonstrated to contribute to the survival of several types of cancer cells. Our preliminary studies have shown that gelsolin contributes to resistance to cancer cell death induced by nutrient starvation and 5-fluorouracil, via regulating autophagy, a cytoprotective machinery. Interestingly, autophagy has been shown to contribute to cell death resistance to nutrient deprivation and chemotherapeutic drugs in colorectal cancer. Preliminary analysis shows that co-expression of gelsolin and the autophagy-related proteins, cathepsins, correlates with poorer disease-free survival of colorectal cancer patients. We hypothesize that gelsolin affects cancer cell survival against stresses, including chemotherapy, by modulating autophagy. In this study, we propose to evaluate the molecular mechanisms by which gelsolin regulates autophagy and the clinical relevance of gelsolin and autophagy in prognosis of patients. We aim to 1) investigate the pro-survival and autophagy-regulating roles of gelsolin in cancer cell survival to stresses; 2) investigate the underlying mechanisms on how gelsolin regulates autophagy and lysosomal functions; 3) ascertain the clinical implications of the interactions between gelsolin and autophagy pathways in colorectal cancer, 4) investigate the effects of gelsolin on autophagy in modulating tumor growth and chemotherapeutic responses using in vivo mouse models. Our study will provide new insights into cancer recurrence and drug resistance, with aims to develop more effective strategies to treat colorectal cancer.
kw: Gelsolin, autophagy,cancer survival,colorectal cancer

title: Identification of super-enhancer-associated cancer genes and master transcription factors in adult T-cell leukemia
abs: Mapping mutational landscapes has paid large dividends in terms of the discovery of causative genetic abnormalities. Development of intensive chemotherapy has also resulted in a remarkable improvement in the prognosis for many hematological malignancies. However, such benefits have not been recognized in adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATL), a highly aggressive lymphoproliferative disorder arising from the mature T-lymphocytes. A genomics study has demonstrated the large mutational prevalence and the high heterogeneity in ATL. Hence, further advances in treatment outcome will require an improved knowledge for functionally-important genes. Interestingly, a number of studies have recently demonstrated the importance of “super-enhancers” in cancer. Super-enhancers are often enriched at cancer genes in various malignancies. “Master transcription factors” that establish super-enhancers also play central roles in the pathogenesis. We hypothesized that the identification of such super-enhancers would pinpoint critical cancer genes in genetically-complicated cancers such as ATL. To test idea, we have performed super-enhancer profiling combined with gene expression analysis in ATL cells. We discovered several genes that are activated under super-enhancers specifically in ATL cells. This included CCR4, which has been previously implicated in ATL. Additionally, we identified a previously-uncharacterized gene, TIAM2, that is required for ATL cell survival. Discovery of these genes places us in an ideal position to understand how abnormal activation of super-enhancers contributes to the ATL pathogenesis. The objective of this project is to elucidate the oncogenic role of TIAM2 and identify the mechanism of activation of super-enhancers in ATL. In the final aim, we will identify master transcription factors in ATL, thus expanding the repertoire beyond these two genes. We will employ a powerful approach through combining bioinformatics with functional analyses using cell culture and zebrafish systems we established. Our study will lead to further understanding of ATL and also give us multiple options for the development of therapeutic strategy.
kw: Adult T-cell leukemia, Super-enhancer, Transcription factor, TIAM2, CCR4, Zebrafish

title: Unravelling pathway addiction to the long non-coding RNA EGFR-AS1: a basket trial strategy
abs: Squamous-cell cancers (SCCs) represent one of the commonest lethal malignancy worldwide, arising from a range of sites. Despite evidence demonstrating that majority are addicted to Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR)-signaling, targeting with monoclonal antibodies or tyrosine-kinase inhibitors (TKIs) has been met with limited success. We recently published our findings showing that TKI-sensitivity is modulated by the expression of a long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) situated in the antisense strand of EGFR (EGFR-AS1). Mutations in EGFR-AS1 (A/A genotype) and changing lncRNA expression affected TKI-response in patient-derived models and a small patient cohort. Importantly, modest knockdown showed profound effects on TKI sensitivity. Based on our mechanistic insights, we hypothesize that patient-response to EGFR inhibitors is contingent on establishing a comprehensive suite of inter-related biomarkers. To address this, we aim to conduct a proof-of-concept “basket” trial of EGFR-TKI for EGFR-driven solid tumours harbouring the A/A genotype, profiling the entire pathway. Given that these responses can be attenuated due to disruption at each level, analysis of pre-treatment tumour biopsies will provide further insights to the determinants of drug sensitivity. Therefore, our second aim is to identify and validate mechanisms of primary/secondary resistance to EGFR-TKI. This will be done by unbiased profiling of pre- and post-treatment biopsies in trial patients, and understanding these mechanisms in pre-clinical models. Our secondary hypothesis relates to tumors which demonstrate addiction to EGFR-AS1, where effective knock-down of the lncRNA augments therapeutic vulnerability to EGFR-TKIs. The third aim is to target EGFR-AS1 in this cohort, for optimal knock-down in vitro and in vitro. This would be based on medium-throughput in vitro RNA-interference screens along the EGFR-AS1 molecule, in patient-derived lines, with in vivo validation in patient-derived xenografts. Through this grant, we intend to extend this strategy, which started as a clinical observation, into a bona fide therapeutic strategy with widespread clinical ramifications.
kw: LncRNA, Basket trial, Tyrosine kinase inhibitors, Synonymous mutation, TKI resistance, Epigenetics

title: Validation of the World Health Organization Disability Assessment Schedule 2.0 among those with mental and physical illness in Singapore
abs: Disability has increasingly become an important indicator of disease burden and for evaluating the effectiveness of health interventions. With the significant increase in healthcare treatment and community mental health care programmes across the country, there is an urgent need to evaluate the effectiveness of these programmes using reliable and accurate measures that are able to capture all aspects of patientsÆ functioning and disability that are comparable not only across health conditions, but also across treatments and programmes of care. The current study aims to validate the WHODAS 2.0 in patients diagnosed with schizophrenia spectrum, depression, anxiety disorders and diabetes, to assess the divergent, concurrent and known-group validity of the WHODAS 2.0 against disease-specific and other known measures, to examine test-retest reliability and agreement between three modes of administrations (self-report, rater-administered, and proxy-administered), to develop and evaluate a crosswalk conversion algorithm between WHODAS 2.0 and the Global Assessment Functioning scales and mapping the relationship between the WHODAS 2.0 and the EQ-5D utility scores, and to compare the responsiveness to change of the WHODAS 2.0 against disease-specific and other known measures over 1-year follow-up. A cross-sectional study will be conducted among outpatients at the Institute of Mental Health and National Healthcare Group Polyclinic. Data on WHODAS 2.0, generic and disease-specific measures, socio-demographic characteristics, clinical history and service utilization will be collected. Findings from this study will provide evidence to clinicians and researchers about the psychometric properties of the WHODAS 2.0 that can be used to assess disability of patients with mental and physical conditions in an Asian patient population. This measure also will allow comparisons of burden of disease and quality adjusted life years in Singapore in future.
kw: WHODAS, disability, schizophrenia, depression, anxiety, diabetes

title: Autologous PKD iPSC-derived kidney organoids: a novel platform for personalized drug screening
abs: Polycystic Kidney Disease (PKD) is one of the most common life threatening genetic disorders caused by single gene mutations. Autosomal dominant PKD (ADPKD) is an adult-onset form of PKD, while autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD) is an early-onset form of PKD that affects mainly infants and young children. There are currently no effective drug treatments and preventive strategies that could specifically target PKD associated renal cyst formation. The high genetic and phenotypic variability in PKD patients requires the establishment of a more precise approach to study the genotype-phenotype correlation, which will ultimately lead to the development of personalized clinical intervention.We have successfully developed a patient iPSC (induced pluripotent stem cell)-based kidney organoid platform that allows us to mimic PKD cyst formation in a dish. In this proposed project, we aim to use this novel platform to perform PKD drug screening in a patient specific manner. The rationale behind this project is patient iPSC-derived kidney organoids faithfully recapitulate renal cyst formation in a patient-specific manner. To realize our goal, we will employ a wide spectrum of experimental approaches, including next generation sequencing, iPSC reprogramming, organoid differentiation, high resolution mass spectrometry, molecular and cell biology, and biochemistry. Singapore has world’s 4th highest incidence of kidney failure, and 2nd highest incidence of diabetes induced kidney failure, incurring a heavy burden onto the national health care system. This proposed project emphasizes on the correlation between clinical studies and basic research. The success of this project will greatly advance our understanding of PKD pathogenesis, and propose novel and safer therapeutic approaches. More importantly, this iPSC-based kidney organoid platform can be further implemented and generalized to accommodate any genetic kidney disease.

title: Exploring the dynamic processes of psychological resilience and physical function recovery of elderly hip fracture patients in Singapore
abs: This proposal aims to investigate recovery trajectories of physical function after a hip fracture among the elderly in Singapore and to explore the factors associated with different recovery trajectories, guided by a conceptual model of functional loss and recovery developed by the Duke-NUS Medical School using the system dynamics methodology.The specific aims are to:Aim 1: Assess the relationship between psychological resilience and physical function recovery following a hip fracture.Aim 2: Determine the relationship between psychological resilience and trajectory of recovery following a hip fracture.Aim 3: Test empirically key feedback relationships among physical function, frequency of stressors, expectation of recovery and uptake of rehabilitation services hypothesised in our conceptual model on the dynamics of functional loss and recovery.Hypothesis: Resilient patients are more likely to recover physical function following a hip fracture, and the trajectory of resilient patients is significantly different from their non-resilient counterparts. It is also hypothesised that medically versus surgically treated patients have different outcomes.Methodology: A longitudinal survey of surgically and medically treated hip fracture patients will be conducted over a year to assess hip fracture outcome. A simulation model will also be developed with hip fracture stakeholders to delineate the processes and mechanisms that support or hinder recovery.Importance: As Singapore’s population continues to age, a larger number of older adults are at increased risk of hip fracture due to osteoporosis and falls, which can result in reduced mobility and disabilities. Thus it is of import to understand the determinants of recovery from hip fracture and similar stressors over the life course to develop interventions that promote a resilient pattern of recovery. Given its substantial burden, hip fractures can potentially serve as a model to explore the factors associated with different recovery trajectories from major health stressors among the elderly in Singapore.
kw: resilience, recovery, hip fracture, longitudinal survey, systems modelling

title: Development of immune-modulatory RNAs to regulate RIG-I mediated antiviral immune response for therapy and vaccination
abs: As the “first responder” to infection, human innate immune receptor RIG-I is able to survey and fight infections by most pathogenic RNA viruses. Therefore, the development of immune-activating and immune-modulating strategies targeting RIG-I is a very attractive research direction with profound clinical implications in antiviral and vaccine development. This proposal focuses on discovering and developing functional RNA-based antiviral bullets (RIG-I agonists) that modulate the cellular innate response via the cytosolic RIG-I. By targeting RIG-I, these unique immune-modulatory RNAs (immRNA) can stimulate the host immune system, boost the antiviral state, and override virus countermeasures - to stimulate, restore, and enhance innate antiviral immunity against pathogenic viruses like dengue, influenza, chikungunya and hepatitis D viruses (co-infection with hepatitis B viruses). The immunogenic antiviral identified in this project can also serve as novel vaccine adjuvants to boost immune response. The aims of this project are to design and synthesize a targeted library of novel, patentable immRNAs for the identification of potent lead candidates, to further characterize and optimize the lead immRNAs and to perform proof of concept studies of the immune-activating activity of the lead immRNAs and to assess the vaccine adjuvants efficacy and anti-viral efficacy. We hope to deliver one lead immRNA with novel drug-or-adjuvant-like properties, which can be further evaluated in clinical settings to uncover its full therapeutic potential in fighting against infectious diseases. These highly selective immRNAs are valuable research tools to study host-pathogen interactions and immunological diseases related to RIG-I mediated immune responses. Through this study, we can also gain better understanding on how the immune system specifically senses different forms of RNA and how it differentiates between danger- and non-danger signals at the molecular, cellular and systemic level.

title: Targeted Inhibition of Ceramide Production in Acute Myocardial Infarction
abs: Acute myocardial infarction (AMI) remains the most common cause of death in cardiovascular disease. In Singapore, there are more than 8000 hospital admissions per year for AMI. Onset of heart failure and mortality after AMI are mainly determined by myocardial infarct size and adverse left ventricular (LV) remodeling. However, we lack effective pharmaceutical therapy to inhibit ischaemia reperfusion injury and subsequent adverse LV remodeling. Dosing with current medications is also often limited by intolerance and/or side effects from systemically administered drugs. Targeted delivery of drugs specifically to the cardiac lesion is therefore highly desirable. In this project, we will test a recently developed nano-drug delivery system, polymeric micelles (for poorly water soluble drugs), to deliver a promising drug candidate, myriocin, to improve MI treatment. Myriocin is chosen mainly relies on three observations: (i) several species of ceramides are positively associated with adverse LV remodeling in a post-AMI cohort and in both human and rodent failing hearts; (ii) Myriocin, a specific inhibitor of de novo synthesis of ceramides, reduced infarct size in a non-survival ischemia reperfusion injury model and (iii) Myriocin attenuated LV remodeling and cardiac dysfunction in a model of chronic myocardial ischemia. Given the extremely poor water-solubility and concerns regarding toxicity upon systemic administration of myriocin, we will use nano drug delivery systems to achieve our goal. We have obtained some preliminary finding that micelles promptly target and accumulate specifically in the injured myocardium and are retained there over several days. These findings allow delivery of our drug candidate specifically to the insulted myocardium for a more efficient inhibition of ceramide production. We expect to improve cardiac function by limiting infarct size (Aim 1) and attenuating LV remodeling (Aim 2). This research will facilitate the translation of myriocin towards clinical application in the setting of AMI.

title: Role of secreted exosomes from mesenchymal stem cells in growth plate repair following injury
abs: Growth plate injuries have the propensity to cause shortening and angular deformities due to intramembranous ossification, which results in bone bridge formation. Intramembranous ossification begins with the inflammatory phase, where there is a neutrophil dominant inflammatory cell infiltration, resulting in upregulation in production of inflammatory cytokines including interleukin (IL)-1? and tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-?. Pharmacological inhibitions of IL-1? and TNF-? have been shown to be effective in overcoming bone bridge formation, however, complete growth plate regeneration was not achieved. Owing to their immunomodulatory and regenerative capacities, mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) have been previously reported to demonstrate therapeutic efficacy in repair and regeneration of growth plate defects. Increasingly, this therapeutic efficacy of MSCs is attributed to its secretion of exosomes, which are small membrane vesicles that protect cells from injury and promote tissue repair. Our prior study found that MSC exosomes promoted repair and regeneration of osteochondral defects in immunocompetent rats at least partly through mediating regenerative macrophage infiltration and suppression of pro-inflammatory synovial cytokines including IL-1? and TNF-?. We therefore hypothesize that MSC exosome could replicate the therapeutic efficacy of MSCs to attenuate inflammation and prevent/overcome bone bridge formation, and in doing so, promote growth plate repair and regeneration in growth plate injuries. In this proposed study, we aim 1) to investigate the effects of MSC exosomes at different treatment doses in the bony repair of injured growth plate in rats, and 2) to decipher the cellular processes and associated mechanisms modulated by MSC exosomes in repair and regeneration of growth plate defects.
kw: exosome; stem cell; growth plate injury; growth plate repair

title: Mesenchymal stem cell exosomes in combination with hyaluronic acid for treatment of knee osteoarthritis in rabbits
abs: Osteoarthritis (OA) has a heavy global socioeconomic impact on both personal and societal levels, with rates expected to rise in the coming decades in tandem with an aging population. Currently, there is no effective treatment for OA, and joint replacement surgery is the end-stage surgical option. The limited longevity of current prostheses however, generally limits its use to patients above 50 years old. Cell-based therapies utilizing mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) have obtained promising results, but still require cell isolation and as a result lack off-the-shelf availability. Increasingly, the therapeutic efficacy of MSCs has been attributed to the secretion of extracellular vesicles, particularly the exosomes. In our prior work, we showed that weekly intraarticular injections of human MSC exosomes effectively repair the osteochondral defects and alleviate pain and degeneration in immunocompetent rat models of osteochondral defect and surgically-induced OA models respectively. To circumvent the need for multiple injections for better clinical translation and to further improve the therapeutic efficacy of MSC exosomes, we aim to develop a combination therapy based on MSC exosomes and clinically used hyaluronic acid (HA) carrier that could be injected in a minimally-invasive manner in a single-stage procedure. Given that HA is commonly used as viscosupplementation and carriers for cells, we hypothesise that an exosome-HA combination therapy would be able to exert synergistic anti-inflammatory and regenerative effects to attenuate OA progression and promote cartilage regeneration. In this proposed study, we aim 1) to investigate the combined effects of MSC exosomes and HA on chondrocytes in vitro; and 2) to evaluate the in vivo therapeutic efficacy of exosome-HA combination therapy in an immunocompetent rabbit model of knee OA. Our long-term goal is to develop human MSC exosomes as a safe, off-the-shelf and patient-friendly therapy for OA treatment in patients.
kw: osteoarthritis, mesenchymal stem cells, therapeutics, hyaluronic acid, exosomes

title: Cancer Cell Metabolism and the Development of Oxidative Phosphorylation Inhibitors as Cancer Therapy
abs: The development of therapies targeting cancer metabolism is novel and highly promising. In a paradigm shift from the Warburg theory, it has emerged that certain tumors are metabolically re-programmed to depend on oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) for cellular metabolism and survival, representing an AchillesÆ heel of cancer. Our existing clinical and preclinical data indicate that oncogene-addicted cancers which have acquired resistance to primary pharmacologic inhibition are critically dependent on OXPHOS upregulation for survival. Therefore, our central hypothesis is that a subset of oncogene-addicted cancers develop a metabolic switch towards the OXPHOS pathway as a mechanism of secondary resistance. This represents a therapeutic niche for OXPHOS inhibition, either alone or in combination with inhibitors of activated co-operative signaling pathways. We will leverage on our promising preliminary data and unique access to a novel OXPHOS inhibitor to achieve our aims of establishing proof-of-concept for OXPHOS inhibition as anti-cancer therapy and identifying predictive biomarkers. In our preclinical program, we will evaluate molecular profiles of sensitivity/resistance to OXPHOS inhibition in a broad range of oncogene-addicted cancer cells, and delineate the precise mechanisms by which OXPHOS inhibitors mediate cytotoxicity. Furthermore, we aim to prove the synthetic lethality of OXPHOS inhibition in combination with inhibitors of activated co-operative signaling pathways. Our clinical program will be anchored by an ongoing investigator-initiated phase IIa dose-expansion study of an OXPHOS inhibitor in an enriched patient population with oncogene-addicted tumors and tumors which over-express OXPHOS markers. As resistance to primary pharmacologic inhibition is inevitable in all advanced cancers, we expect this novel class of agents to have immense therapeutic potential and diverse clinical applications. The robust translational program and proof-of-concept early-phase clinical trial outlined in this proposal will enhance SingaporeÆs reputation as the preferred Asian site for early-phase clinical trials in cancer.
kw: Cancer cell metabolism, Oxidative phosphorylation, Oncogene-addicted cancers, Acquired resistance

title: The application of Terahertz scanning system on the evaluation of corneal opacities
abs: Corneal opacity affects 146 million people worldwide and is a priority eye disease as defined by the WHO. However, there is a gap in existing clinical practice, as the evaluation of a corneal opacity is purely by subjective grading. There is a need to develop an objective tool for evaluation of corneal opacities to monitor disease progression better as well as to aid in the decision-making of surgical intervention. Our preliminary work has shown that the Terahertz scanning system is promising in differentiating the severity of corneal edema in an ex-vivo models and corneal fibrosis in an in-vitro model. Hence, we hypothesize that Terahertz scanning has the capacity to provide quantitative information on corneal opacities. In this proposal, we aim to study the feasibility and accuracy of the use of Terahertz scanning system as a quantitative method in the evaluation of corneal opacities. We will use an in-vitro corneal opacity model as well as two rabbit models (acute and chronic) by inducing corneal opacities using chemical burns and excimer laser. The Terahertz signals generated, including the signal intensity and area under curve, will be analyzed and correlated with the results of clinical grading, optical transmittance, reflectivity in in-vivo confocal microscopy, and immunohistochemical staining, to evaluate the accuracy of quantification. This study has the potential to open a new avenue for clinicians to more precisely approach patients with corneal opacities, and to help in the development of a specific tool in early detection, monitoring, and decision-making of the managements of corneal opacities. It may be also helpful in the research related to corneal opacities, such as the evaluation of efficacy of topical eye drops or cell-based therapy on ameliorating opacities, as the severity can be more objectively investigated.
