title: Elucidation the molecular mechanism of STAG2 in conferring sorafenib resistance in hepatocellular carcinoma OFYIRG17nov009
abs: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the sixth most common cancer and the second leading cause of cancer related deaths worldwide. Sorafenib is the only FDA-approved systemic first-line chemotherapy drug for advance stage HCC. Unfortunately, sorafenib is very costly and associated with very low tumor response rate and significant side-effect. Therefore, there is an urgent clinical need to understand the mechanism of sorafenib resistance in HCC so that precision medicine can be practiced in prescribing sorafenib to the right group of patients. To identify the genetic factors responsible for sorafenib resistance in HCC, we performed genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 functional knockout screens on sorafenib resistant HCC cell lines and found Stromal Antigen 2 (STAG2) as one of the promising hits associated with sorafenib resistance. Further experimental validation showed that siRNA/shRNA mediated knock-down of STAG2 in the sorafenib resistant cells did not significantly alter the tumor cell growth in vitro and in vivo when compared to mock knockdown control cells under normal growth condition. However, when upon sorafenib treatment, STAG2 knocked-down cells showed significantly reduced tumor cell growth both in vitro and in vivo, compared to mock knockdown cells. In addition, STAG2 expression was found to be significantly higher in sorafenib resistant cell lines compared to the sensitive cell lines. Moreover, high STAG2 level is associated with poorer patient survival. These data demonstrated that STAG2 plays an important role in mediating sorafenib resistance in HCC cells. In this study, we aim to identify the gene regulatory network through which STAG2 mediate sorafenib resistance using RNA-Seq, elucidate molecular mechanism of STAG2-dependent sorafenib resistance through functional assays and evaluate STAG2 and its associated genes as prognostic biomarkers to predict sorafenib response in HCC.

title: The associations of maternal night-eating pattern with glucose tolerance during pregnancy
abs: A novel line of research has emerged, suggesting that synchronizing the timing of food intake with body’s circadian rhythms or day-night cycle has metabolic implications. Eating at the inappropriate time can disrupt circadian system which might induce metabolic perturbations, including glucose abnormalities. Recent evidence showed that circadian timing of eating was associated with glucose regulation in pregnant women. However, little is known about night-eating pattern during pregnancy, particularly the influence of night-eating snack on glycaemic control. The general objective of this study is to assess the association of both timing and amount of meal and snack intake on glucose tolerance at midpregnancy. We hypothesize that small meal and less frequent snack intake at night is associated with better glucose tolerance at 24-28 weeks’ gestation. Our specific aims are i) to examine the association of maternal night-eating pattern with glucose tolerance at mid-pregnancy; ii) and to examine the associations of behavioural and environmental factors with night-eating pattern at mid-pregnancy. Our secondary aim is to assess the feasibility and validity of using food record mobile app to digitally capture dietary intakes in pregnant women. We will recruit 400 pregnant women at 18-21 weeks’ gestation from the KK Women’s and Children’s Hospital. Dietary intake will be recorded using 4-day food diarywith both paper-based and mobile-based methods; while 24-hour activity-rest pattern and light-dark exposure over 10-day will be captured using actigraphy monitors. We will measure maternal plasma glucose and insulin levels at 24-28 weeks’ gestation. This study will help to understand the importance of food timing, which is a modifiable behavior, in glycemic control during pregnancy, and to provide evidence for the development of nutritional guidelines which can ameliorate metabolic health for mother and child.

title: Lysosomal Calcium Channels in Neurodegeneration and Cancer Therapeutics
abs: Introduction The role of lysosomal calcium channels in neurodegeneration and cancer is poorly understood and have not been investigated before. This will be the first study to characterize the redox regulation of lysosomal calcium channels via lipid metabolism modulation, and its effects on cancer and neurodegeneration. Aims The overarching aim is to investigate the role of lysosomal calcium channels in neurodegeneration and gastric cancer by characterizing the role of NO and mTOR in mediating lysosomal and autophagic dysfunction via modulation of lysosomal calcium channels, and its implications in neurodegeneration and gastric cancer. Hypotheses I predict that lysosomal calcium channels are redox-regulated, and dysfunction in lysosomal calcium channels contribute to the pathogenesis of neurodegeneration and lysosomal storage disease, and to chemo-resistance in gastric cancer. Methodology and Approach Using both in vitro and patient-derived fibroblasts with lysosomal storage disease or Alzheimer’s Disease as models of lysosomal and autophagic dysfunction, the effects of NO will be characterized using a panel of lysosomal enzymatic and substrate assays, in the presence of siRNA knockdown of lysosomal calcium channels. Furthermore, using a drug screening high-throughput automated microscopy platform, the effects of these lysosomal calcium channels on DNA-damage response induced by drug library of chemotherapy drugs will be identified and teased out on both induced-neuron systems derived from these fibroblast models, and gastric cancer patient-derived xenografts. Finally, we will seek to validate these identified lysosomal calcium channels in tissue micro-arrays in a larger cohort of gastric tumours and correlate with clinical outcomes.
kw: Lysosomes, Calcium Channel, Autophagy, Neurodegeneration, Cancer

title: Obesity-Related Glycine Deficiency: Investigating A Longstanding Metabolic Paradox Using Bench and Bedside Approaches
abs: Obesity leads to broad-spectrum dysfunction in nutrient homeostasis. We have shown that obesity is associated with increased concentrations of multiple amino acids but a paradoxical decrease in glycine. Glycine is required for the synthesis of critically important biomolecules including the principal intracellular antioxidant, glutathione (GSH). GSH is essential to protect against obesity-induced oxidative damage, a common etiology for obesity-associated metabolic complications. Presently, the mechanisms, and consequences, of obesity-related glycine deficiency remain unknown. Further, there are no specific treatments against obesity-induced oxidative damage. By investigating the metabolic etiologies of glycine deficiency in morbid obesity, we may discover novel therapeutic targets for obesity management. We hypothesize that (1) Low glycine concentration in morbid obesity is due to an increase in glycine utilization to support GSH synthesis; (2) GSH concentration is significantly low in morbid obesity because of elevated oxidative stress. These abnormalities would resolve following weight loss after bariatric surgery. Our specific aims are to: (1) Compare the rates of glycine synthesis and clearance between morbidly obese patients and lean healthy controls prior to and 6-months following bariatric surgery, and examine the changes in glycine and GSH concentration in cultured human myoblasts following experimental induction of oxidative stress ; (2) Quantify GSH and oxidative stress levels in the same groups of subjects, and in human myoblasts following induction of oxidative stress under glycine-enriched vs. -deprived conditions. We will recruit 20 morbidly obese subjects scheduled for bariatric surgery and 20 matched lean controls. Through the infusion of multiple stable-isotope tracers, 1,2-[13C2]-Glycine, 2,3,3,-[2H3]-Serine and Ring-[2H5]- Phenylalanine, we will examine pathways of glycine influx and clearance that determine circulatory glycine concentration. To validate human kinetic findings, we will measure glycine, GSH and oxidative stress levels in human myoblasts following experimental induction of oxidative stress with H2O2, and in cells incubated under glycine-enriched and -deprived conditions.
kw: obesity, glycine deficiency, bariatric surgery, stable-isotope tracers,glutathione, oxidative stress

title: Somatostatin receptor theragnostics in Nasopharyngeal cancer
abs: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) is the eight most common cancer among men, with an age standardized rate of 8.8 per 100,000 per year (1). Unfortunately most patients present with advanced disease and treatment options for NPC generally involve radiation therapy and/or chemotherapy. Recently, there have been reports of the expression of somatostatin receptors in nasopharyngeal cancer. Somatostatin is a peptide that functions as a neurotransmitter in the central nervous system and acts as a regulator of endocrine and gastrointestinal functions. Somatostatin receptors are not only found in normal tissues, but are over expressed in certain tumour tissues such as neuroendocrine tumours. Interestingly, NPC has been found to have moderate to high expression of somatostatin-receptor-2 (SSTR2) in about 75% of patients (2). We have also found increased expression of SSTR2 in another Ebstein Barr Virus (EBV) related cancer, Lymphoepithelialoma like lung carcinoma (LELC), and there are reports that EBV viral proteins, latent membrane protein-1 (LMP1) and Ebstein barr nuclear antigen-2 (EBNA2) are able to increase expression of SSTR2 (3,4). This opens up potential theranostic applications for radionuclide therapy in EBV related cancers. The aim of our initial study is to first describe the utility of Gallium68-DOTATATE PET in the locally advanced, metastatic and locally recurrent setting and to determine the proportion of patients with high somatostatin receptor density that may benefit from somatostatin receptor targeted therapeutic trials planned. Patients will be followed up clinically to determine the prognostic value of the scan. Gene expression profiling will be done on SSTR2 high and SSTR2 low samples to better understand pathways involved. Correlation will also be done between EBV viral proteins and SSTR2 expression. The second aim is to test the therapeutic efficacy of Lutetium177-DOTATATE and Actinum225-DOTATATE. Biopsies from NPC patients will be used to establish a NPC Patient Derived Xenograft (NPC-PDX) model. SSTR2 positive NPC PDX models will be used to test Lu177-DOTATATE and Ac225-DOTATATE. Results of this will help guide the third aim of the study which is the test the safety and efficacy of somatostatin receptor targeted radionuclide therapy in a phase II metastatic NPC cohort.
kw: theranostics, NPC, EBV, immunology, imaging,

title: Cost containment in pharmacogenomic testing, identifying obstacles to implementation of pharmacogenomics and impact on anticonvulsant prescription patterns
abs: Background: Pharmacogenomics and precision medicine are driving forces in biomedical research today. The HLA-B*1502 biomarker for severe adverse cutaneous drug reactions to carbamazepine has led to national-level legislation internationally. However implementation at the clinical front-line is highly variable, with resultant increased health system costs. We will employ a staged approach of validating a rapid HLA-B*15:02 testing system , then evaluate cost savings and reduced number of consultations from adopting this system and patient preferences for anticonvulsants and the factors which affect their decision-making process. This will improve and guide cost-effective implementation of pharmacogenomic testing in healthcare systems. Overall aim: a.) Improve speed and reduce cost of point-of-care pharmacogenomic testing, and b.) Identify and resolve factors impeding pharmacogenomics implementation to HLA-B*1502 and carbamazepine allergic reactions and apply findings to manage healthcare system costs. Primary aim: Clinically validate a rapid HLA-B*1502 testing system Primary hypothesis:Rapid HLA-B*1502 testing has 99% specificity and 99% sensitivity compared to the current gold standard. Secondary aim 1: Reduce the cost of pharmacogenomic testing for HLAB*1502 Secondary hypothesis 1:Rapid HLA-B*1502 testing can be performed at 33% of the cost of current pharmacogenomic testing methods. Secondary aim 2: Reduce consultations prior to anticonvulsant initiation Secondary hypothesis 2:Rapid HLA-B*1502 testing reduces medical consultation from pharmacogenomic testing to initiation of anticonvulsant treatment by 50%. Exploratory aim: Characterize the impact of focused rapid pharmacogenomic testing on anticonvulsant prescription patterns to identify obstacles and solutions and guide future national pharmacogenomic testing strategies. We will explore the impact of pharmacogenomic testing on anticonvulsant prescription patterns in the past, with implementation of rapid testing and the factors which affect individual anticonvulsant choices by patients and caregivers. Clinical significance. This project can reduce pharmacogenomic test costs and consultation numbers and characterize the impact of focused rapid pharmacogenomic testing to guide future national strategies in pharmacogenomic testing.

title: Life Trajectory of Older Major Blunt Trauma Survivors with Risk Factors for Long-Term Post-Discharge Mortality: Perspectives of Patients and their Caregivers – A Mixed Methods Study
abs: End-of-life perspectives in cancer patients have been well studied. Studies on end-of-life care in trauma currently focus on care at the index hospitalization for injury, for example end-of-life support in the intensive care unit for un-survivable head injury. There is increasing interest in the factors affecting increased long-term mortality for survivors of severe injury (age, fall, chronic disease, function at discharge); however, there are no published studies on the end-of-life trajectory for these patients, including: the effect of surviving severe injury on patients’ and caregivers’ perspectives and attitudes towards the reduced quality of life or disability post-injury, and specific concerns trauma survivors and their caregivers may have with regard to the potential imminent end-of-life trajectory after surviving major blunt trauma. Our recent retrospective study of blunt trauma survivors, using Singapore National Trauma Registry Data, showed overall 7.2% 1-year mortality and 16.7% 3-year mortality for adult survivors of blunt trauma. However, for patients aged over 55 with at least one major risk factor (high Charlson score, low fall, head and neck Abbreviated Injury Scale of 3 and above), 3-year mortality exceeded 25%, reaching 50% for patients with two major risk factors. The majority of these deaths (60%) occurred in the acute hospital. With the increasing awareness of end-of-life issues in our population, it is timely to study high-risk patients and their caregivers after surviving injury. We will study quality of life post-injury at 3-months, 6-months, 12-months, 18-months, 24-months, 30-months, and 36-months post-injury. For the patients who pass away during the study period, their caregivers will be given the Quality of Death and Dying questionnaire, and semistructured interviews used to explore their concerns and needs not addressed in the questionnaire.

title: The VICTORY (Virus-Induced Cancer: Translational Oncology Research & immunologY) Consortium
abs: The Virus-Induced Cancers: Translational Oncology Research and immunologY consortium (VICTORY) is a national translational team of leading key opinion leaders combining synergistic expertise to optimise immunotherapeutic strategy against virally-driven cancers (VDCs). This will be accomplished by examining host and viral interactions in the tumour microenvironment – specifically how VDCs induce immunosuppression, target discovery and validation, and experimental therapeutics. Major VDCs will be examined, Epstein-Barr virus-driven cancers such as nasopharyngeal cancer (NPC), Human papilloma virus-driven oropharyngeal and cervical cancers, and Hepatitis B-driven hepatocellular carcinoma. The VICTORY team has a proven track record: • 30 joint publications • 9 joint grant applications • >34 clinical trials • >400 recruited patients Virus-induced cancers in Asia account for over 60% of global VDCs, and still expected to increase. The VICTORY consortium harnesses unique, competitive capabilities and resources across academic institutions with industry to establish: 1) The world’s largest collection of functionally, clinically annotated VDC biospecimens. The VDC Biobank forms a centrepiece for the consortium for systematic comprehensive analytics, 2) Deep immunophenotyping and broad omics capability to complete comprehensive characterisation of VDC immune microenvironment including molecular, functional and mechanistic assessment of VDC immune suppression, 3) Novel humanised mouse models of VDCs able to host both human solid cancers and a recapitulated human immune system, and shown to harbour oncogenic virus infection, 4) Strong interdisciplinary team of world class clinician-scientists, immunologists, virologists, molecular biologists and metabolism experts, and 5) Robust collaborations with pharmaceutical and biotech companies locally and internationally and with the non-profit Parker Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy. The enhanced understanding of VDCs and underlying immune/metabolic drivers of disease that will result from the VICTORY consortium forms the basis of novel, next generation immunotherapies and discovery of biomarkers informing therapy. The VICTORY consortium creates an unprecedented, coordinated, leading global centre of VDC excellence embracing the biomedical, academic healthcare, and industry sectors.

title: Life Trajectory of Older Major Blunt Trauma Survivors with Risk Factors for Long-Term Post-Discharge Mortality: Perspectives of Patients and their Caregivers – A Mixed Methods Study
abs: Major injury is a life-changing event. For older survivors of moderate and severe injury (aged 55 and above), some of these survivors are at increased risk of long-term death, either due to other chronic diseases they have at the time of injury, frailty, or the disability from injury. Our recent study of major trauma survivors, using Singapore National Trauma Registry Data, showed a 7.2% 1-year mortality and a 16.7% 3-year mortality for adult survivors of blunt trauma. Major risk factors for long-term mortality included: low fall, Charlson comorbidity score of 2 or more, and head injury. The majority of these deaths (almost 60% for both the 1-year and 3-year mortality) occurred in the acute hospital. Another study showed a 1-year readmission risk of more than 40%, increased for patients with the same risk factors for increased mortality. However, not much is known about the unmet clinical, social or psychological needs for this group of patients, for example, the effect of the hospitalization and recovery from injury on quality of life, and resulting end-of-life trajectory, for these high-risk patients and their caregivers. We plan to study survivors of injury at higher risk of long-term mortality (due to head injury, low fall, age or other chronic diseases) and their caregivers to understand their quality of life post-injury, trend their quality of life for the 3 years post-injury, and study the end-of-life trajectory for those who die during the study period. We will study their quality of life at 3-month intervals for 3 years post-injury, and interview patients and care-givers in-depth after emergency department visits or unplanned hospital readmission. We will also conduct in-depth interviews to explore their concerns that may not be addressed in the questionnaire.

title: Timely Identification of Developmental and Behaviour problems In Toddlers (TIDBIT)
abs: Timely identification and early intervention for developmental problems have good promise for better outcomes in children. The Health Booklet (HB) – a parent-held child health record, is Singapore’s main tool for developmental surveillance. It contains developmental milestone checklists for parents to complete at different age intervals from 0 to 6 years old, which aids primary care professionals to conduct routine developmental surveillance at well-child checkups, and determine if a child is at risk of developmental problems. The study aims to examine the effectiveness of the routine developmental surveillance process for identifying children at risk of developmental problems at 18-months-old. It explores the use of the HB checklists as a screening tool, and the use of overseas-developed parent-filled developmental screening tools in the Singapore context. A longitudinal within-subjects study design will be used. Children who are 18-months-old will be recruited from the primary care setting (Target N=1050). Parents will be asked to complete the HB checklists, two overseas-developed general developmental screening tools – ASQ and PEDS/PEDS:DM, and an autism-specific screening tool – M-CHAT-R/F, before their child’s well-child check-up. The children will go through usual care at well-child check-ups with primary care doctors and nurses, and data on the outcome of the check-up will be collected. Children who are identified as “at-risk” by usual care, HB checklists, ASQ, PEDS/PEDS:DM or M-CHAT-R/F, will be invited to complete standardized assessments for development and adaptive behaviour, within 1-3 months of the screening. At 30 months old, all children will be screened with the same tools, and children identified as “at-risk”, will be invited to complete the same standardized assessments. The detection rates of usual care, HB checklists, ASQ, PEDS/PEDS:DM, and the M-CHAT-R/F for children at risk of developmental problems or autism will be compared. The acceptability by parents for completing the parent-filled screening tools independently will be compared.

title: Physiological Role of Dok3 in Candidiasis
abs: Invasive fungal infection is a serious health threat with high morbidity and mortality, and Candida species are the most prevalent causative agents of such infection. However, current antifungal drugs only demonstrate partial success in improving prognosis. Together with the rapid emergence of drug resistance among Candida species, there is a pressing need to develop novel antifungal therapies to improve clinical outcomes. Understanding the mechanistic interaction between host immune system and fungal pathogens holds the key for uncovering novel immune-based treatments to combat candidaemia. Our preliminary study suggests that Dok3, an adaptor protein involved in immune receptor signaling, acts as a negative regulator of antifungal immunity in neutrophils. As such, we aim to elucidate the underlying mechanisms of Dok3 in antifungal immune response by determining their role in the regulation of neutrophilic antifungal effector functions, which include phagocytosis, secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines, production of reactive oxygen species, release of neutrophil extracellular traps, and the formation of neutrophil granules. In addition, the signaling pathway of Dok3 during antifungal immune response will be examined through microarray, mass spectrometry and biochemical approaches. By dissecting the mechanistic role of Dok3 in antifungal immunity, we will be able to propose the potential utility of Dok3 inhibitors as novel therapies and prophylaxis for invasive candidiasis. Such immune-based approach could act as an adjunctive therapy to current antifungal drugs for further improvement of outcomes in fungal-infected patients. As such, our proposed research will not only extend our understanding about the mechanisms regulating host antifungal immune response, but may also have translationally relevant implications for the development of novel antifungal drugs and infection control.
kw: Infectious diseases, immunology

title: Elucidation the molecular mechanism of STAG2 in conferring sorafenib resistance in hepatocellular carcinoma
abs: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the sixth most common cancer and the second leading cause of cancer related deaths worldwide. Sorafenib is the only FDA-approved systemic first-line chemotherapy drug for advance stage HCC. Unfortunately, sorafenib is very costly and associated with very low tumor response rate and significant side-effect. Therefore, there is an urgent clinical need to understand the mechanism of sorafenib resistance in HCC so that precision medicine can be practiced in prescribing sorafenib to the right group of patients. To identify the genetic factors responsible for sorafenib resistance in HCC, we performed genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 functional knockout screens on sorafenib resistant HCC cell lines and found Stromal Antigen 2 (STAG2) as one of the promising hits associated with sorafenib resistance. Further experimental validation showed that siRNA/shRNA mediated knock-down of STAG2 in the sorafenib resistant cells did not significantly alter the tumor cell growth in vitro and in vivo when compared to mock knockdown control cells under normal growth condition. However, when upon sorafenib treatment, STAG2 knocked-down cells showed significantly reduced tumor cell growth both in vitro and in vivo, compared to mock knockdown cells. In addition, STAG2 expression was found to be significantly higher in sorafenib resistant cell lines compared to the sensitive cell lines. Moreover, high STAG2 level is associated with poorer patient survival. These data demonstrated that STAG2 plays an important role in mediating sorafenib resistance in HCC cells. In this study, we aim to identify the gene regulatory network through which STAG2 mediate sorafenib resistance using RNA-Seq, elucidate molecular mechanism of STAG2-dependent sorafenib resistance through functional assays and evaluate STAG2 and its associated genes as prognostic biomarkers to predict sorafenib response in HCC.
kw: sorafenib resistance, hepatocellular carcinoma, STAG2

title: Role of novel covalent homocysteine modification of the autophagy protein, Syntaxin 17, in regulating non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) progression
abs: Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) currently is a pandemic and affects an estimated 40% of Singaporean adults. It represents a spectrum progressing from hepatosteatosis to steatohepatitis (NASH) and cirrhosis. Whereas hepatosteatosis is thought to be benign and reversible, the inflammation and fibrosis of NASH causes chronic hepatic damage that can lead to liver failure. There currently are no pharmacological treatments for NASH; thus, finding effective therapies that prevent or retard its onset and progression is of paramount importance.Hyperhomocysteinemia (HHcy) has been strongly associated with NAFLD in several clinical studies. Using different dietary mouse models of HHcy and NAFLD, we recently found that HHcy and NAFLD inhibited autophagy and surprisingly increased homocysteinylation of several proteins in liver, including Syntaxin17 (Stx17) that regulates autophagosome/lysosome fusion in autophagy. HHcy and NAFLD mice also had decreased hepatic mitochondrial function, increased lipid content, and higher expression of inflammatory/fibrosis markers. Accordingly, we hypothesize that homocysteinylation of hepatic proteins occurs in NAFLD that causes autophagy inhibition and mitochondrial dysfunction leading to hepatic inflammation and fibrosis which accelerates NAFLD progression. We further hypothesize that reduction of homocysteine levels by vitamin therapy can reduce hepatic inflammation and fibrosis. We thus propose the following Specific Aims; Specific Aim 1: To characterize Stx17 homocysteinylation and its role(s) in steatosis and NASH. Specific Aim 2: To investigate therapeutic efficacy of homocysteine-reducing vitamins (B12 and folate) in steatosis and NASH.Specific Aim 3: To investigate global protein homocysteinylation during steatosis and NASH.This study will provide insight into the novel molecular consequences of protein homocysteinylation, during HHcy and NASH. Also, the information obtained might be useful to prevent or delay progression of NASH. The findings from this study may help establish that a novel and inexpensive vitamin therapy for NAFLD, a condition for which there currently is no pharmacological therapy.
kw: Homocysteinylation, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), Protein Modification, Autophagy, Syntaxin17

title: Mitofusin 2 as a novel therapeutic target to prevent adverse post-myocardial infarction remodelling
abs: BackgroundHeart failure (HF) following an acute myocardial infarction (AMI) is one of the leading causes of patient disability in Singapore and worldwide, exerting enormous burdens on healthcare/economic resources. Therefore, we aim to identify Mfn2 as a novel therapeutic target for preventing adverse post-AMI LV remodelling, reducing HF, and improving health outcomes in AMI patients. Disturbances in mitochondrial function and impaired autophagy flux have been demonstrated to contribute to the development of post-AMI HF. The mitochondrial fusion protein, Mitofusin 2 (Mfn2) has been shown to be downregulated in heart failure, impacts on cellular metabolism, and plays an essential role in both autophagy and mitophagy. However, whether changes in myocardial Mfn2 levels contribute to adverse post-AMI LV remodelling by inhibiting autophagy/mitophagy is not known, and is investigated in this research proposal.HypothesisA reduction in myocardial Mitofusin 2 (Mfn2) levels following acute myocardial infarction (AMI) induces adverse left ventricular (LV) remodelling by inhibiting autophagy/mitophagy flux.Specific Aims1)To investigate whether myocardial Mfn2 levels are reduced, and autophagy/mitophagy flux is inhibited following AMI.2)To investigate whether pharmacological upregulation of Mfn2 and activation of autophagy/mitophagy flux following AMI can prevent adverse LV remodelling.3)To investigate the effects of Mfn2-deficiency in human iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes on autophagy/mitophagy flux and the response to cellular stress.ImplicationsNew treatments are required to prevent adverse post-AMI LV remodelling to prevent HF following AMI. In this research proposal, we aim to demonstrate Mfn2 to be a novel therapeutic target for preventing adverse post-AMI LV remodelling, and this should result in novel therapies for preventing HF following AMI and improving health outcomes for the Singaporean population.
kw: Heart failure, acute myocardial infarction, mitofusin 2, autophagy, mitophagy, mitochondria

title: Understanding ciliopathy: disease modeling with Rab23 mutations in mouse and human iPSCs
abs: The non-motile primary cilium functions as an “antenna’’ on nearly every cell that serve as a hub for transducing growth signals from factors such as Sonic Hedgehog (Shh) and Wnt through GPCR signaling pathways. Defective cilia lead to ciliopathies, an expanding spectrum of at least 35 diseases involving multiple genes 1. Resolving the intricate regulatory networks for cilia biogenesis and signaling is critical for the understanding of disease pathogenesis.RAB23 is a small GTPase. The mutations of RAB23 in humans underlie Carpenter Syndrome (CS). Given the significant clinical resemblance between CS and ciliopathies, including craniofacial defects, polysyndactyly, hydrocephaly, eye defect, obesity, and intellectual disability 1-6. I hypothesize that CS patients’ phenotypes stem from primary cilia impairment, and that RAB23 mutation causes cilia dysfunction. This study aims to validate RAB23 as a causative gene for ciliopathy using mouse and human disease models of CS. Mice with global or conditional knock-out (CKO) of Rab23 in the brain have been generated. These animals exhibit CS/ciliopathy-associated defects that phenocopy some of the clinical features of CS patients. Brain-specific Nestin-CKO of Rab23 exhibited reduced ciliation and neurological impairments. This is the first in vivo evidence implicating Rab23 in ciliogenesis and neurophysiology. A human disease model of CS is established from CS patient-derived induced-pluripotent stem cells (iPSC). Mutant iPSCs-derived neurons also showed reduced ciliation, thus suggesting a relationship between CS and ciliopathies. To validate RAB23 as a new causative gene for ciliopathy, the human RAB23 L145X allele mutation will be corrected by CRISPR-cas9 technology to rescue the phenotypes. Disease mechanism underpinning RAB23-mediated ciliopathy will be probed by neuronal tissues specific characterization of interacting partners and signaling pathways. The proposed study will shed new lights on the role of Rab23 in ciliogenesis and brain development, and potentially uncover novel therapeutic targets for CS and ciliopathy.
kw: Rab23, Primary cilia, Ciliopathy, Neurological disorders, Neurodevelopment, iPSC

title: Determine the role of a conserved lncRNA, lnc-dPrdm16, in brown fat
abs: As the population of obesity is rising, there is an upsurge of the interest in brown adipocyte biology because of its unique energy expenditure feature and the recent discovery of brown adipose tissue (BAT) in human adults. Recent findings from other and our groups have revealed long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) as novel regulators in adipocyte lineage-specific development, but the role of lncRNA in human BAT development remain largely unknown and the function of lncRNAs in BAT in vivo has yet to be established. In our preliminary study, we have constructed a de novo human adipose tissue lncRNA catalogue and identified a set of lncRNAs conserved between human and mouse. One of the top candidates is divergently transcribed from Prdm16 promoter and is referred as lnc-dPrdm16. Loss-of-function study using primary adipocyte culture revealed an essential role of this lncRNA in brown adipogenesis. We hypothesize that lnc-PRDM16 is an essential regulator during brown adipocyte development. To test this hypothesis, we have generated a lnc-dPRDM16 mouse by inserting a transcription stop cassette to inactivate lnc-dPRDM16’s transcription. We aim to determine the role of lnc-dPRDM16 in BAT function and WAT browning in vivo, establish the influence of lnc-dPRDM16 inactivation on whole body metabolic homeostasis, and determine the molecular mechanism used by lnc-dPRDM16 to regulate gene expression. Moreover, we will also test lnc-dPRDM16’s human relevance by charactering its role in human brown adipocyte differentiation. Accomplishing the proposed experiments will shed a light on the lncRNA-mediated regulation of brown adipocyte development in vivo. Knowledge gained may lead to new approaches to manipulate adipose tissue energy homeostasis and new therapeutic strategies for obesity and its related diseases.
kw: Brown fat, Brown Adipocyte, RNA, Diabetes, metabolic diseases

title: A novel way of neuroprotection for extracranial carotid stenosis.
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Extracranial carotid stenosis (ECS) is a narrowing of the lumen of the carotid artery. Severe stenosis increases the risk of stroke and chronic hypoperfusion may lead to cognitive impairment. Besides surgical intervention, there is a lack of neuroprotective treatment for ECS. In this study, we propose a novel way of neuroprotection in managing ECS by targeting an ion channel TRPM4. TRPM4 is a monovalent cation channel and our preliminary study has shown that TRPM4 was upregulated in neurons under chronic hypoxia. Importantly, blocking TRPM4 could ameliorate glutamate induced calcium influx in hypoxic neurons and improved learning and memory in ECS animal models and human tissues. Therefore, we propose that TRPM4 can be a novel target for neuroprotection in ECS, and blocking TRPM4 may provide a novel approach in managing ECS. In this proposal, we will examine the expression of TRPM4 under chronic hypoxia conditions using in vitro cultured neurons and in vivo ECS animal model. The functions of TRPM4 are examined by electrophysiological studies and calcium imaging method. We also seek to understand the potential mechanism of blocking TRPM4 by studying the functional interaction between TRPM4 channel and NMDA receptors. Importantly, a patented antibody M4P which has been developed in our lab will be examined in this study to evaluate its therapeutic potential. By completing this study, we hope to identify the therapeutic potential of blocking TRPM4, and provide a novel way of managing cognitive impairment in ECS.
kw: cerebral hypoxia, neuroprotection

title: Self-propelling upconversion Janus nanoparticles for overcoming light and diffusion limited penetration of drugs in solid tumors
abs: Photodynamic therapy (PDT) is an alternative cancer therapeutic option that involves the administration of light-sensitive photosensitizer drugs. As the drug preferentially accumulates in the tumor through the enhanced permeability and retention effect (EPR) owing to its leaky vasculature, light shone at it activates the drug to release reactive oxygen species, thus leading to tumor eradication. PDT at present relies on the use of low tissue penetrating visible light for activating the photosensitizer drug, which limits its application to surface and endoscopically accessible tumors. In addition, solid tumors are poorly vascularized in their interior, leading to poor distribution of the drug to these regions. Here, we aim to develop near-infrared (NIR) light propelled Janus nanoparticles for active diffusion of the photosensitizer drug throughout the solid tumor, thereby overcoming drug delivery barriers for an enhanced PDT. These particles consist of two distinct parts - an upconversion fluorescent nanoparticle (UCNP) core to carry and activate photosensitizers in response to 980 nm light and a partial gold nanocluster shell for propulsion through thermophoresis in response to its surface plasmon resonance (SPR) wavelength (in the NIR light range). Besides ensuring even distribution of the drug throughout the solid tumor, these particles by virtue of their upconversion property would also allow the use of NIR light instead of visible light for activating the photosensitizer drug, thus affording greater tissue penetration depths and allowing larger tumors to be treated. We hypothesize that these new NIR propelled upconverting Janus nanoparticles will help overcome drug delivery barriers in solid tumors, allow the use of deep penetrating NIR light instead of visible light for PDT and thereby enable PDT application to be extended for the treatment of large, solid deep-seated tumors as opposed to just surface and endoscopically accessible tumor masses.
kw: Self-propelling; Janus nanoparticles; upconversion; photodynamic therapy; barriers to drug delivery in solid tumors

title: Identification and elucidation of antifungal resistance mechanisms in the human fungal pathogen Candida albicans
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Invasive fungal infections kill ~1.5 million people worldwide annually, and one of the leading causative agents is the fungus Candida albicans. Despite the availability of several classes of antifungal drugs, therapies often fail. Two primary reasons are: (1) many fungal cells are either intrinsically resistant to antifungal agents or evolve resistance after exposure to them, and (2) fungi can form biofilms that possess properties conferring remarkable resistance to most antifungal drugs. Resistant strains are routinely isolated in hospitals worldwide, and biofilm formation is commonly associated with the use of medical implants. Antifungal resistance greatly compromises our ability to treat fungal infections, representing a major public health threat. Thus, it is imperative to identify and understand the molecular mechanisms governing antifungal resistance. Current understanding of resistance mechanisms remains incomplete. Here, we propose to apply our newly developed technology platform to identify genes and cellular processes important for antifungal resistance and biofilm formation. We have successfully introduced the piggyBac transposon system into haploid C. albicans. This platform can create random insertional mutations throughout the genome and allows rapid identification of mutated genes. This technology is revolutionary because it, for the first time, enables large-scale, genome-wide genetic screens in C. albicans. Once the mutations have been identified and phenotypes confirmed, the genes affected and cellular processes involved will be characterized in detail by using a combination of genetics, molecular biology, biochemistry, imaging, and mass spectrometry tools and mouse infection models. We will investigate the clinical relevance of the mutations by examining a large collection of drug-resistant clinical isolates of Candida. Knowledge gained in this study is crucial for achieving a deep understanding of the causes of antifungal resistance and will provide valuable information for designing future strategies for effective prevention and treatment of invasive fungal infections.
kw: Candida albicans invasive infection, Antifungal resistance, Antifungal drugs, Biofilm, Genome-wide genetic screen, Virulence

title: Role of G9a in embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma
abs: Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (ERMS) is the most prevalent subtype of soft tissue sarcoma in children. While significant advances have been made in understanding underlying molecular and genetic alterations, metastatic disease remains a clinical challenge as drugs that target differentiation and self-renewal of tumors cells have not been identified.Our preliminary data provide strong evidence that the chromatin modifier G9a plays a central role in controlling growth and differentiation in ERMS through regulation of Wnt signaling. Interestingly, ERMS is characterized by down regulation of Wnt signaling that is required for myogenic differentiation and to suppress growth and self-renewal of tumor cells. We therefore hypothesize that overexpression of G9a in ERMS inhibits Wnt signaling resulting in the inability of tumor cells to undergo myogenic differentiation. In this proposal, we will examine the mechanisms by which G9a impacts proliferation, differentiation and self-renewal of tumorcells in vitro and in vivo. The molecular mechanisms by which it regulates Wnt signaling will be examined.Comprehensive analysis of human cancers has revealed pervasive deregulation of epigenetic writers, readers and erasers. Our studies demonstrating overexpression of G9a in ERMS and its impact on the Wnt-b catenin axis provide compelling rationale to target G9a as atherapeutic approach for this deadly cancer. Development of such targeted therapies in combination with conventional therapy could reduce adverse side effects in young survivors and lead to a decline in long-term morbidity.
kw: Cancer, epigenetics, rhabdomyosarcoma, histone methyltransferase, Wnt

title: Linking APP and LRRK2 to Pinpoint the Cause of Dopaminergic Neurodegeneration in Parkinson’s disease
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disease in Singapore. Leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) mutations are the most common genetic cause of PD. The G2019S mutation has been shown to elevate LRRK2 kinase activity andinduce dopaminergic neuron loss. Although the role of LRRK2 in PD has been intensively researched, only a handful of LRRK2 substrates have been elucidated that have illuminated the disease pathways involved. Here, we have identified the Alzheimer’s disease (AD)-related Amyloid Precursor Protein (APP) as a novel target of LRRK2. We found that LRRK2 interacts with and phosphorylates APP at threonine-668 (T668). This in turn stimulates the production of the APP intracellular domain (AICD).Hypothesis: APP is a potential downstream target of LRRK2-mediated neurodegeneration in PD, and that targeting APP pathway may provide a novel therapeutic strategy for PD.Objectives: We seek to elucidate the role of LRRK2-mediated APP phosphorylation in association with LRRK2-related PD, and evaluate if the inhibition of APP phosphorylation and processing can rescue LRRK2 G2019S-induced neurotoxicity.Methodology: Engaging LRRK2 G2019S’siPSCs-derived human dopaminergic neurons,post-mortem tissue, mouse dopaminergic neurons, and mice, we aim to 1) elucidate the mechanism on how APP phosphorylation at T668 contributes to LRRK2-mediated neurotoxicity in PD, 2) evaluate if inhibition of APP processing rescues LRRK2 G2019S-mediated loss-of dopaminergic neurons. Using CRISPR/Cas9 system, we will create constitutivelyphosphorylated form of APP T668E and phospho-mutant T668A mice to explore physiological contribution of APP phosphorylation at T668 in LRRK2-mediated neurotoxicity in PD.Scientific/Clinical Impact: We identify APP as a novel substrate of LRRK2 and highlights LRRK2-mediated neuronal loss in PD. It links LRRK2 and APP, and providesa crucial understanding on the pathways connecting the two most common neurodegenerative diseases. The identification of APP as target holds promises to provide a new therapeutic approach for LRRK2-related PD patients.
kw: APP, Neurotoxicity, Phosphorylation, LRRK2, Parkinson's disease, Amyloid Precursor Protein Intracellular Domain (AICD)

title: The Role of the Endothelial Glycocalyx, Mast Cells and Vascular Nitric Oxide in the Pathogenesis of Dengue
abs: The primary objective of the proposed project is to investigate the involvement of endothelial glycocalyx, vascular nitric oxide and mast cells, as part of microvascular health, in the pathogenesis of dengue. While plasma leakage is well known to occur in dengue, the reasons and how it occurs remains obscure and results from previous studies are not conclusive. Secondary aims include looking at cardiac function and fluids administered, so as to examine the interplay between microvascular and macrovascular health and their correlation with clinical outcomes. We will also investigate the relationship between co-morbidities, medication usage, the cytokine profile and microvascular health, and whether these factors influence severe dengue. Our hypothesis is that dengue disease has a direct effect on microvasculature via virulence factors or immune mediated effect via cytokines. The involvement of microvasculature can be quantified or identified by measuring glycocalyx thickness, vascular nitric oxide and mast cell activity. The health of the microvasculature in turn affects clinical outcomes. Baseline microvascular health itself is affected by other factors which may be protective or predictive of severe dengue. These factors include co-morbidities such as diabetes, as well as medications such as statins and metformin, which have been shown to be associated with severe dengue in previous retrospective observational studies. Cardiac dysfunction may also play a role in disease severity in dengue, but has not been systematically evaluated in the adult populationA prospective observational study of dengue in adults (with and without) co-morbidities with serial measurements of clinical indexes, EndoPAT, bedside sublingual video-microscopy, transthoracic echocardiograms, vascular nitric oxide, cytokines and outcomes will deepen our understanding of dengue pathogenesis. The knowledge gained may also assist in developing better prognostic markers, advance evidence-based targeted interventions, and refine current treatment strategies.
kw: Dengue, Glycocalyx, Nitric oxide, Mast cell

title: Primary Aldosteronism in Singapore: a Curable Cause of Hypertension
abs: Although majority of patients have essential (unexplained) hypertension, 10% are estimated to have a curable condition, primary aldosteronism (PA). Left untreated, PA leads to difficult-to-control hypertension and cardiovascular complications. PA is due to excess aldosterone hormone release from the adrenal glands, and is treatable with medications. In half of these cases, only one adrenal gland is diseased and surgical removal cures PA, and improves/cures hypertension. While appropriate diagnosis and treatment may prevent complications, accurate diagnosis of patients remains challenging.My hypothesis is that a significant proportion of hypertensive patients in Singapore have unilateral PA, curable with surgery. My first aim is to assess the prevalence of PA in stroke patients. If PA is common in hypertensive patients, and hypertension is the most important risk factor for stroke, then PA is likely common in stroke patients. To achieve this, we have funding to screen 300 consecutive patients admitted to an acute stroke unit for PA. Demonstrating a high prevalence of PA in stroke patients will emphasize the need for early diagnosis.My second aim is to identify unilateral PA using a novel functional imaging, 11C-metomidate PET/CT. Adrenal vein sampling (AVS), the current reference method, is invasive and technically challenging, failing to diagnose ~50% of patients. We have funding (provisional approval) to recruit 25 patients with PA in a multi-centre trial. We hope to demonstrate that 11C-metomidate PET/CT can be as accurate as AVS in correctly identifying unilateral, surgically-curable PA, and this may potentially replace current diagnostic tests.My third aim is to evaluate clinical response after therapy. To achieve this, we have funding to prospectively assess the post-treatment effects in 50 patients treated for PA: blood pressure, cardiovascular, renal, metabolic outcomes, and quality of life. For patients who underwent surgery, we will re-evaluate for cure of PA and hypertension.
kw: Secondary hypertension; Resistant hypertension; Adrenal endocrinology; Renin; Adrenal vein sampling

title: Investigating the role of epigenomic alternative promoter isoforms in modulating the immunogenicity of gastric cancer
abs: BackgroundA recent study published in Cancer Discovery from our lab highlighted the role of epigenomic alternative promoters (EAP) in immunomodulation of gastric cancer. The reversible nature of epigenetic modifications makes them an attractive therapeutic strategy. Further studies are warranted on identification and validation of epigenetically driven mechanisms of immunoediting in gastric cancer for development of rational immuno-combination therapies. AimsWe propose to achieve the following aims in our study1)Analyze EAP expression in gastric cancer treated with immunotherapy and correlate with response and survival data to identify predictive EAP biomarkers. 2)Investigate the immunogenicity of EAP associated N-terminal peptides being depleted in gastric cancer as possible targets of epigenetic exploitation.3)Identify novel EAP associated immunogenic peptides overexpressed in gastric cancer as potential tumor antigens for peptide-vaccination strategies HypothesisAlternative promoters influence the immunogenicity of gastric cancers via depletion of N-terminal peptides, and epigenetic strategies can be deployed to increase anti-tumoral T cell reactivityMethodologyAim (1)We have data from a cohort of 50 patients with advanced gastric cancer treated with pembrolizumab (an anti-PD-1 monoclonal antibody immune checkpoint inhibitor). RNA-seq will be performed on the pre-and post-immunotherapy treated biopsy samples. EAP usage in pre-and post-treated samples will be correlated with response and survival to identify biomarkers of response and resistance. Aim (2)EAP depleted N-terminal peptides will be tested for in silico immunogenicity. Peptide-MHC class I complexes will be generated for identified high-affinity binders. T cell responses will be measured in healthy volunteer and gastric cancer patient samples via Cytof assays. Aim (3)Proteomic data for multiple gastric cancer cell lines will be generated via mass spectrometry. Data will be queried for expression of predicted novel N-terminal peptides generated via usage of EAP and further queried for immunogenicity in silico and in vitro.
kw: Epigenetics; gastric cancer; immunology

title: Interactions between Insulin Resistance, Osteocalcin and Skeletal Muscle in Older Chinese Males with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
abs: Background and Clinical SignificanceType 2 diabetes mellitus (T2D) accelerates sarcopenia, an independent predictor for functional impairment, physical disability, falls and fractures. Animal studies suggest osteocalcin (OCN) may reverse sarcopenia and enhance exercise capacity. A better understanding of how osteocalcin affects muscle strength and function in T2D may potentially help clinicians stratify these patients’ sarcopenia risk. It may also lead to development of novel preventive and therapeutic strategies for sarcopenia, and improve their cardiorespiratory fitness and quality of life. Aims(1) Determine the longitudinal association between total OCN (tOCN), undercarboxylated OCN (unOCN) and carboxylated OCN (cOCN) with sarcopenia in Chinese males aged ? 50 with T2D for 5 or more years. (2) Assess the effects of chronic hyperglycaemia and insulin resistance (IR) on sarcopenia. (3) Evaluate how the interactions between osteocalcin and hyperglycaemia / IR affect skeletal muscle. Hypotheses(1) Sarcopenia is negatively correlated with unOCN, but positively correlated with IR and HbA1c.(2) The detrimental effects of hyperglycaemia / IR on skeletal muscle are attenuated by unOCN. ApproachThis is a single-centre prospective observational study of 80 T2D individuals with HbA1c ? 9.5%, 80 T2D individuals with HbA1c ? 7.5%, and 80 controls with normal glucose tolerance. These subjects will be reviewed upon recruitment and annually thereafter for 2 years. During each review, muscle mass, strength and function and trabecular bone score will be assessed. Fasting blood samples will be drawn for determination of tOCN, unOCN, cOCN, other bone turnover markers and indices of glycaemia and IR. Frequency of falls and fractures during the preceding 1 year will be ascertained, and self-reported physical activity level, functional capability and nutritional status determined. Baseline characteristics of the 3 groups will be described using descriptive statistics. The linear mixed model will be used to compare the outcome variables among the 3 groups.
kw: Insulin Resistance, Osteocalcin, Muscle, Diabetes

title: Genomic and Epigenomic Correlates of Radioresistance in Nasopharynx and Prostate Cancers
abs: Precision radiotherapy (RT) has advanced cure rates of nasopharynx (NPC) and prostate cancers. However, 20-30% of patients still recur locally despite high dose RT. In these individuals, therapeutic options for salvage are limited, highlighting the need for improved clinical stratification and novel therapeutics to improve therapeutic ratio of RT. In keeping with the conventional model of clonal selection as the dominant mechanism for radioresistance, we and others have shown that recurrence following RT is driven by selection of a small population of radioresistant clones, followed by clonal expansion that is associated with an increased mutational burden. It was also reported that RT exposure can leave a genomic fingerprint that is comprised of large insertion-deletion mutants. Here, we propose to investigate the genomic and epigenomic correlates of the RT-response in NPC; a disease primarily treated by RT and is endemic in this part of the world. We will first analyse and compare the genomic, epigenomic, and transcriptomic profiles of pre-RT and post-RT tumour-pairs from a cohort of radioresistant NPC cases. The hypothesis under test in this pairwise analysis is that mutational indices associated with radioresistance will be common and enriched between the lesions, while RT-induced genomic and epigenomic signatures will be exclusive in the post-RT tumours. Next, to validate our observations, we will conduct a matched case-control study comparing the differential molecular profiles between pre-RT samples from the radioresistant cohort against pre-RT samples of a cohort without relapse that is matched for prognostic clinical indices. The controls will be selected from a published Singapore NPC dataset and a 600-sample unpublished dataset from SYSUCC. Additionally, we will investigate for commonalities in molecular profiles between our radioresistant NPC and prostate cancer cohorts. Finally, we will utilise in-house derived radioresistant tumour cell lines to perform functional validation experiments and investigate for novel “druggable” targets.
kw: Cancer, Radiotherapy, Genomics, Biomarkers, Radiosensitivity, Nasopharynx Cancer

title: Allergy to the prebiotic galacto-oligosaccharide – molecular evaluation of primary sensitizer and IgE epitopes
abs: Background and Aims: Allergy to the prebiotic, galactooligosaccharide (GOS), is a unique allergy to a pure carbohydrate and likely to result from an IgE-induced cross reactive allergen(s). Based on preliminary studies, we hypothesize that the cross-reactive allergen(s) is an unidentified glycoprotein(s) derived from the house dust mite, Blomia tropicalis, and that the cross-reactive IgE molecules bind to several epitopes on the oligosaccharide and hence cause GOS allergy. The aims are: (1) To identify the cross reactive dust mite glycoprotein allergen responsible for GOS allergy (primary sensitizer); (2) To understand the mechanism of GOS allergy and identify IgE epitopes in GOS.Methods: Using sera of GOS allergic subjects, IgE immunoblots and liquid chromatography tandem-mass spectrometry identification will be employed to identify the primary sensitizer glycoprotein of dust mite, Blomia tropicalis. Peripheral blood mononuclear cells of GOS allergic subjects will be used to construct ScFv phage display expression of VH and VL of IgE and identify clones that bind GOS. Production of these GOS specific antibodies would then be used for the identification IgE epitopes on GOS. This would lead to further work on the molecular characterization by matrix assisted laser desorption/ionization(MALDI-TOP)-mass spectrometry, nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, surface plasmon resonance.Benefits: This research into the sensitizing agent and the IgE epitope(s) will greatly expand our knowledge of carbohydrate allergy, which till now has been largely considered to be without clinical signficance. Given how common GOS is in food products and its beneficial effects on the gut microbiome, this proposal will provide the scientific strategies to develop GOS prebiotics that are ‘non-allergenic’ and therefore enable safe global consumption of such carbohydrates in food.
kw: Galacto-oligosaccharide, Primary sensitizer, IgE epitopes, glycoallergens

title: The Singapore Epidemiology of Eye Diseases (SEED) Study 3: Prospective multi-ethnic cohort study of 12-year incidence, risk factors, and impact of major age-related eye diseases
abs: There is a disproportionate burden of age-related eye diseases in Asians. Specifically, Asia accounts for 30% of diabetic retinopathy (DR) and 60% of glaucoma cases worldwide. There are ethnic variations in the prevalence of major eye diseases in both Singapore and Asia. These observations highlight the need for in-depth evaluation on the long-term incidence and progression of age-related eye diseases in Asians. However, long-term cohort data are still extremely limited in Asia. In 2004-11, we completed the baseline Singapore Epidemiology of Eye Diseases Study (SEED-1), a population-based multi-ethnic study on 10,033 participants (75.5% response rate) of Malays, Indians and Chinese. Subsequently, in 2011-17 we successfully completed the 6-year follow-up examination (SEED-2) in 6,762 baseline participants (78.7% response rate). Data collected from SEED have been used widely by national and international agencies and in clinical guidelines. SEED-3 will re-examine this multi-ethnic cohort 12 years after the baseline examination. We will 1) determine the 12-year incidence and progression of visual impairment (VI) and major eye diseases; 2) employ state-of-art ocular imaging technology; 3) link VI with cardiovascular outcomes via nationwide electronic medical record database; 4) discover new metabolite biomarkers; and 5) evaluate the health impact of major blinding eye diseases in Singaporean adults. The major strengths of SEED-3 include a well-established and characterized cohort at baseline and 6-year visit, an experienced international team of clinician-scientists and epidemiologists, and the highest-quality baseline ocular/systemic data, including high-resolution images of retina and optic nerve, stored serum/blood/urine, and existing genome-wide genotype data. The ultimate completion of 12-year follow-up visits in SEED-3 will provide unprecedentedly comprehensive information on the development of major eye diseases in Asians, covering the 3 major ethnicities in the region. These data will be critical for the planning of public health strategies to reduce visual loss not only in Singapore but across Asia.
kw: population-based study, incidence, progression, glaucoma, age-related macular degeneration

title: TRAnslational pig models and Clinical cohorts to seeK FIbrotic BiomaRkers: biOdiScovery and valIdation Study (TRACK FIBROSIS)
abs: Heart failure (HF), the final common pathway of many cardiovascular disorders, has a mortality rate rivalling many cancers. Cardiac fibrosis is common to the pathophysiology underpinning the majority of cardiovascular conditions impinging adversely on cardiac structure and function through increased ventricular stiffness, impaired diastolic and systolic function, reduced coronary flow reserve, and propensity to arrhythmia. These changes foster progression to HF with associated severe morbidity and mortality. Reliable circulating biomarkers for myocardial fibrosis would provide a tool for diagnosis, surveillance and the testing of novel therapies including specific anti-fibrotic agents. Currently no candidate marker has crossed the threshold for routine clinical application. This background defines a clear unmet need to rigorously validate existing candidates and extend the search for novel markers of cardiac fibrosis. Any new biomarker must be validated against the “gold standard” of histological assessment of fibrosis. Accordingly, we will use histologically defined fibrosis measured in cardiac biopsies and entire hearts to validate both cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMRI) markers of fibrosis plus existing (but non-validated) and novel candidate circulating biomarkers in two established pig models of cardiac disease (i) post-myocardial infarction (MI) HF and (ii) pressure overload induced by thoracic aortic constriction (Aim 1). In addition, unbiased screening by mass spectrometry will be deployed to discover novel candidate biomarkers (Aim 2). In parallel to pre-clinical studies, we will interrogate our post-MI clinical cohorts (IMMACULATE and PITRI) and hypertensive (REMODEL) cohort with state-of-the-art CMRI and longitudinal profiling of candidate circulating biomarkers (Aim 3). Results from these combined pre-clinical and patient cohort studies will provide histologically proven circulating biomarkers of fibrosis and advance validation of CMRI markers of fibrosis. Implementation of these biomarkers into standard clinical practice will improve diagnosis, risk stratification and eventually survival and quality of life for patients with developing and chronic heart disease.
kw: heart failure, fibrosis, biomarker, CMRI, myocardial infarction, animal model

title: Obesity-Related Glycine Deficiency: Investigating A Longstanding Metabolic Paradox Using Bench and Bedside Approaches
abs: Obesity leads to broad-spectrum dysfunction in nutrient homeostasis. We have shown that obesity is associated with increased concentrations of multiple amino acids but a paradoxical decrease in glycine. Glycine is required for the synthesis of critically important biomolecules including the principal intracellular antioxidant, glutathione (GSH). GSH is essential to protect against obesity-induced oxidative damage, a common etiology for obesity-associated metabolic complications. Presently, the mechanisms, and consequences, of obesity-related glycine deficiency remain unknown. Further, there are no specific treatments against obesity-induced oxidative damage. By investigating the metabolic etiologies of glycine deficiency in morbid obesity, we may discover novel therapeutic targets for obesity management.We hypothesize that (1) Low glycine concentration in morbid obesity is due to an increase in glycine utilization to support GSH synthesis; (2) GSH concentration is significantly low in morbid obesity because of elevated oxidative stress. These abnormalities would resolve following weight loss after bariatric surgery. Our specific aims are to: (1) Compare the rates of glycine synthesis and clearance between morbidly obese patients and lean healthy controls prior to and 6-months following bariatric surgery, and examine the changes in glycine and GSH concentration in cultured human myoblasts following experimental induction of oxidative stress ; (2) Quantify GSH and oxidative stress levels in the same groups of subjects, and in human myoblasts following induction of oxidative stress under glycine-enriched vs. -deprived conditionsWe will recruit 20 morbidly obese subjects scheduled for bariatric surgery and 20 matched lean controls. Through the infusion of multiple stable-isotope tracers, 1,2-[13C2]-Glycine, 2,3,3,-[2H3]-Serine and Ring-[2H5]-Phenylalanine, we will examine pathways of glycine influx and clearance that determine circulatory glycine concentration. To validate human kinetic findings, we will measure glycine, GSH and oxidative stress levels in human myoblasts following experimental induction of oxidative stress with H2O2, and in cells incubated under glycine-enriched and -deprived conditions.

title: Role of Mesenchymal Stem Cell Exosomes in Periodontal Complex Regeneration
abs: Periodontitis is a chronic inflammatory disease that results in the degradation of the supporting tissues around teeth, which if left untreated, can lead to tooth loss. Currently, guided tissue regeneration is considered the main surgical technique used to regenerate intrabony defects caused by periodontitis. However, the technique has poor predictability in treatment outcome and is associated with complications from exposure of the barrier membrane leading to infection and graft loss. To improve the technique, mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) have been supplemented as adjuvant therapy to enhance periodontal regeneration. However, this therapeutic efficacy of MSCs is increasingly attributed to its secretion of exosomes, which are nano-sized vesicles that protect cells from injury and promote tissue repair. Our previous studies revealed that MSC exosomes contain a complex cargo of proteins and miRNAs that contributes to its wide-ranging therapeutic efficacies for repair and regeneration of complex tissues such as the osteochondral defects. We, therefore hypothesize that MSC exosomes could exert a multi-faceted mechanism to activate multiple cell types (macrophages, endothelial cells, periodontal ligament cells, osteoblasts) at the defect site to attenuate inflammation and promote well-coordinated processes of angiogenesis, osteogenesis, cementogenesis, and insertion of periodontal ligament fibers to bring about periodontal complex regeneration. Here, we aim 1) to investigate the effects of MSC exosomes at different doses for periodontal complex regeneration in a rat intrabony defect model; and 2) to investigate the cellular processes and associated mechanisms modulated by MSC exosomes in periodontal regeneration. Our goal is to develop MSC exosomes as a standardized and ready-to-use therapeutic for treatment of intrabony defects in patients. If successful, this approach of supplementing MSC exosomes to bone substitutes could potentially improve the current technique to regenerate intrabony defects, by removing the need for barrier membrane, thereby improving predictability in treatment outcomes and reducing risks of associated complications.
