title: An Integrative Approach to Build a Microbial Alkaloid Production Platform for Biotechnology
inst: SIFBI - Singapore Institute of Food and Biotechnology Innovation
abs: Alkaloids are a diverse set of nitrogen-containing molecules with unique biological activities that are valuable to the pharmaceutical and agrochemical industries. For example, opioids such as morphine and codeine are psychoactive benzylisoquinoline alkaloids used clinically for pain management. Terpenoid indole alkaloids, vinblastine and vincristine, are used in anticancer and immunosuppressive therapies. Currently, plants are the main source of medicinal alkaloids but the low quantities produced in plants and rising demand have spurred development of microbial platforms for producing plant alkaloids from simple carbon sources. Nonetheless, there are still major bottlenecks in identifying uncharacterized plant biosynthetic pathways and functionally reconstituting them in yeast or bacteria, greatly hindering the development and optimization of these heterologous production platforms. Alkaloid biosynthesis in bacteria is increasingly recognized with advances in mass spectrometry and genomics. Besides being an underexplored source of non-plant alkaloids, bacteria offer potentially more efficient biosynthetic routes and enzymes to produce natural and non-natural alkaloids. In this proposal, we leverage on a unique Singapore resource, one of the world’s most comprehensive and diverse microbial collections (NPL), together with a multidisciplinary team composed of chemists, biologists, bioinformaticians and engineers to build a microbial alkaloid production platform for biotechnology applications (e.g. agriculture and medicine). It is envisioned that the pipeline of outputs (novel drug leads, enzymes-based or whole-cell biocatalysts and propriety strains) may serve to seed collaborations with other Singapore research entities (e.g. BioTrans, SynCTI, NUS Medical School, and TLL). Overall, this platform fits well into the larger Singapore research strategy by providing the foundation on which existing programs to develop biotransformation and bioprocess technologies for high value products can be built upon.
kw: Bacterial alkaloid;Pathway discovery;Pathway characterization;Genetic engineering;Scaffold diversification;Production Platform

title: Promoting Rational Use of preemptive pharmacogenotyping through developing a multicriteria DEcisioN analysis framework and conducting Cost-Effectiveness analysis (PRUDENCE).
abs: We seek to answer three overarching questions related to preemptive pharmacogenotyping (PGx). First, how should we frame our decision on whether to reimburse preemptive PGx? While clinical utility is clearly an important decision attribute, there are other attributes such as cost-effectiveness, privacy and equity to consider. Furthermore, what is the relative importance of these decision attributes? We seek to develop a reimbursement decision framework based on multicriteria decision analysis. We shall elicit the attributes and levels of the decision framework through face-to-face interviews involving participants across different ethnicities, age group, educational level, language and health status (healthy versus patients with known conditions). Second, who should be tested? Should we test everyone aged 40 years old or should testing be limited to those at high risk of receiving a drug with known PGx association within a given time frame (e.g. 5 years)? Third, what is the optimal composition of a multiplex gene panel? It is clear that testing has moved from single gene testing to multiplex gene testing. Should we include all genes that are clinically actionable? Should we include only genes where the rate of reduction in ADR due to PGx test (i.e. efficacy) exceeds a certain threshold level? If so, what is that threshold level? Should we include only high penetrance genes (i.e. rare variants that confer high risk)? The composition of the gene panel will determine the type of patients to test. Patient characteristics such as ethnicity may also influence the composition of the gene panel. The second and third overarching questions are thus related. Hence, we shall develop a computer simulation model to address the role of patient selection criteria and gene panel composition on outcomes (i.e. quality-adjusted life years). The simulation will be used to examine the cost-effectiveness of various algorithms for using preemptive PGx.
kw: Pharmacogenetics, Multicriteria decision analysis, Cost-effectiveness analysis, Discrete choice experiment, Adverse drug reactions

title: Dissection of the interaction between stem cell and niche by high-resolution imaging
abs: In this project, we will approach the stem cell/niche interaction by two-photon microscopy. We have observed that niche cells are remodeled around a single hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) after HSC homing to the bone marrow (BM) niche (cuddling). However, how HSCs interact functionally with niche cells is not well understood. HSC and cancer stem cell (CSC) behavior shows some similarity in the niche dependency and quiescence in cell cycle, resulting in CSC chemoresistance. We hypothesize that HSC and CSC functions are spatiotemporally and metabolically controlled by niche cells. We aim for identification of the role of the functional interaction of HSCs and leukemia/myeloma cells with niche cells. For this aim, we have done the preliminary studies regarding; (1) establishing in vivo imaging of the BM with subcellular resolution; (2) motile HSCs keeping direct contact with niche cells; (3) cuddling of non-motile HSCs by niche cells; (4) protrusion including mitochondria from HSCs; and (5) establishing the xenograft model of human myeloma cells in immunodeficient mice. To elucidate the role of the interaction in HSC functions through thrombopoietin (TPO), we will transplant HSCs from mice in which mitochondria are labelled by Dendra2, a photoswitchable fluorescent protein into TPO- or control mice. Then, we will compare HSC motility, adhesion, and mitochondrial metabolism by in vivo time-lapse imaging. To comprehensively compare the localization of HSC adhesion, we will conduct whole-bone imaging after bone clearing in situ. We will examine the ROS level, mitochondrial membrane potential, and cell cycle of HSCs in the presence or absence of niche cells. Finally, to identify the interaction between leukemia/myeloma and niche cells, we will perform the transplantation of human leukemia/myeloma cells into immunodeficient mice and examine the CSC behavior. Our proposal will lead to find novel targets for niche-therapy to block the interaction between leukemia/myeloma and niche cells.
kw: hematopoietic stem cells, cancer stem cells, niche, leukemia, myeloma, in vivo imaging

title: Therapeutic efficacy of exosome-infused PCL-TCP scaffold for repair and regeneration of critical-size mandibular defects
abs: The current bone grafting techniques have significant limitations including the limited availability and donor site morbidity of autografts, the reduced healing potential and risk of pathogen transmission of allografts, and the inferior healing rate and lack of remodeling capacity associated with use of synthetic grafts. Thus, there is an unmet clinical need for alternative therapies. Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) have emerged as a promising cell-based therapy for bone repair. However, as with all cell-based therapies, there are inherent challenges associated with cell isolation, storage and delivery. Increasingly, the therapeutic efficacy of MSCs is attributed to the secretion of extracellular vesicles, particularly the exosomes. Our preliminary findings show that MSC exosomes exhibit potent capacity in enhancing osteogenic differentiation of human MSCs, and in promoting cartilage and subchondral bone regeneration of critical-sized osteochondral defects in immunocompetent rats. Furthermore, these exosomes can be supplemented to scaffolds such as the collagen membrane and still retain the comparable integrity and bioactivity as the fresh exosomes. Among the bone graft materials, PCL(polycaprolactone)-TCP(tri-calcium phosphate) scaffold have demonstrated good biocompatibility, biodegradability and mechanical properties for bone healing. We postulate that exosomes could be loaded into PCL-TCP scaffold and this combination device would not only provide the structural support but also enable a sustained high local concentration of exosomes to facilitate bone regeneration through activation of multiple cell types (osteoblasts, endothelial cells and MSCs) and associated cellular processes including proliferation, angiogenesis and osteogenesis. Therefore, we aim to 1) optimize the development of a novel off-the-shelf exosome-infused PCL-TCP scaffold, and 2) evaluate the in vivo host response and therapeutic efficacy of exosome-infused PCL-TCP scaffold device in an immunocompetent rabbit mandibular defect model. The long-term goal of this study is to develop an off-the-shelf exosome-infused PCL-TCP scaffold that could be applied in clinics for bone repair in a single-stage procedure.
kw: Bone regeneration, MSC exosomes, osteogenesis, mandibular defect model, PCL-TCP scaffold

title: Focal Therapy for Prostate Cancer: Personalized Therapy to Maximize Functional Outcomes while achieving Oncological Success
abs: Prostate cancer is the third most frequent male cancer and the seventh most frequent cause of death in Singapore. The gold standard curative treatment of localized prostate cancer is whole-gland therapy with radical prostatectomy (surgical removal of the prostate gland) or radiotherapy. These methods are effective at curing cancer but result in collateral damage to adjacent structures resulting in impaired urinary continence and erectile dysfunction. In patients with cancer localized to one area of the prostate gland, focal therapy of just the dangerous cancer focus may allow a patient to maintain continence and erectile function and avoid the side-effects of radical treatment while achieving cure. We aim to evaluate the degree of preservation of continence and erectile function and early oncological outcomes in patients treated with focal cryoablation of the prostate.This is a phase II study of men with localized prostate cancer. Consenting men will undergo multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) and targeted biopsy of suspicious lesions to select only those with: (1) mpMRI cancer focus < 3 ml in size, (2) involvement limited to one anatomic region (left, right or anterior gland), (3) localized cancer on mpMRI, (4) target lesion Gleason ?4+4 and (5) no outfield Gleason?3+3 cancer, to undergo focal cryoablation. The primary outcome, post-treatment functional status, will be tracked with standardized questionnaires performed at 0, 1, 3, 6 and 12 months. The secondary outcome, oncological success, will be assessed at 1 year with repeat biopsy and mpMRI. To demonstrate no significant deterioration in post-treatment functional outcome, we will recruit 27 men for this study.Our findings will establish the safety of focal cryoablation and be the basis of further research into the utility of this technique in achieving cure while preserving function in men with prostate cancer.
kw: Prostate Cancer, Focal Therapy, MRI, Saturation Biopsy, Robotic Biopsy, Targeted Therapy

title: Factors affecting patient, caregiver and physician preferences for treatment of myeloma and indolent lymphoma.
abs: Myeloma and lymphoma are being transformed into chronic diseases. Numerous treatment options are available, with little high-quality evidence to guide choice. Decisions are made by various stakeholders (patients, caregivers and physicians) based on a variety of clinical and non-clinical factors. Decision-makers vary in involvement and how they weigh trade-offs. Aims:1.Examine patient, caregiver and physician preferences for treatment characteristics2.Determine if these are influenced by clinical and non-clinical factors3.Determine perceived and preferred levels of participation in decision-makingMethodsThis will be a multi-centre, cross-sectional, mixed-methods study of patients with myeloma and indolent lymphoma. Caregivers and physicians will be included. The first phase will be a qualitative exploratory analysis. Subjects will be interviewed separately about values, the decision-making process, perceived and desired degrees of control, and barriers to communication of preferences and adherence to a treatment plan. Responses will be coded and used to design the second phase, a quantitative survey.For the second stage, we aim to recruit 400 patients and caregivers. The survey will have four modules: 1.Demographics 2.Discrete choice experiment (DCE) to assess the relative importance and interplay of factors identified in the qualitative phase 3.Perceived and desired levels of control via the control preference scale; agreement with barriers to communication of preferences assessed via a Likert scale4.Quality-of-life based on EQ-5D Data will be analysed using multinomial logit regression; willingness-to-pay will be estimated via the cost attribute of the DCE. Responses will be stratified by treatment length and socioeconomic status to determine if these influence preferences.ImpactKnowledge of preferences can guide shared decision-making, improving outcomes, costs and satisfaction. It influences resource allocation and improves utilisation. The long-term goal is a decision aid which integrates insights from this study with cost and efficacy data to guide tailored, efficient treatment.
kw: decision-making, willingness-to-pay

title: An evaluation of the introduction of peer support services in a large mental health hospital
abs: Peer specialist services are recognized as integral to the implementation of recovery-oriented care systems. Peers, or people with lived experience of mental illness, can be effective sources of hope, information, and guidance. When paired with clinical teams, peer specialists services can have beneficial impacts on the recovery of people with mental illness, by improving their community function, and may ultimately lead to reduced hospitalization. In the Asian context, the role or peer specialist services has not been explored. We propose a quasi-experimental observational study with 12-month follow-up. The proposed study seeks to evaluate the impact of a newly implemented peer specialist services on 1) the health of service users (with comparison group) 2) the health of the peer specialists and 3) the opinion of staff towards people with mental illness. Because of the nascent status of the program, observational comparison rather than experimental control groups will be used. Service users and peers will complete questionnaires to assess health outcomes. Staff will complete questionnaires on opinion of people with mental illness. Administrative data of service users will be use to quantify the impact of peers on service use outcomes. We hypothesize that the introduction of peer specialists will increase service user working alliance and engagement with service providers, self-esteem, positive mental health, quality of life, and reduce hospital admissions to mental health services and reduce length of stay, compared to baseline and comparison group levels. Subset analysis will be conducted to determine if a particular type of service user benefits most from receiving peer support.We hypothesize that people placed into the role of peer specialists will experience better community involvement, increased positive mental health, greater self-esteem, and reduced hospital admissions to mental health services and reduced length of stay, compared to baseline levels.
kw: Peer Support Services; Mental Health Services; Quasi-experimental; Administrative data

title: Neurophysiological and neuropathological function of Mfsd7c transporter
abs: Blood brain barrier (BBB) is particularly important for development and homeostasis of central nervous system (CNS). Tight junction and minimal transcytosis of vascular endothelial cells (EC) on BBB protect CNS from invasion of almost all cellular and non-cellular contents in circulation system. However, to maintain homeostasis of CNS neurovascular EC develops a multiple substrate transporter system to deliver nutrients and essential compounds into brain and expel toxic products from brain to blood stream. Dysfunction of this transport system impairs the BBB function and that could to lead several neurological disorders and complex neurodegenerative diseases such as Multiple Sclerosis, Alzheimer and brain cancer. In this study, we aim to characterize the molecular and physiological roles of an orphan transporter belonging to Major Facilitator Superfamily Domain, MFSD7c. The mutation of MFSD7c has been genetically linked with Proliferative Vasculopathy and Hydranencephaly-Hydrocephaly syndrome (PVHH) or Fowler’s disease. However, the molecular and pathological functions of Mfsd7c in PVHH remain unknown. We showed the MFSD7c is expressed on the plasma membrane of nerovascular endothelial cells. Analysis of a genetic Mfsd7c knockout mouse model showed that loss of Mfsd7c caused brain blood vessel defects and embryonic lethality. Therefore, we hypothesize that MFSD7c is expressed on BBB and transport an important ligand necessary for BBB and brain function. To test our hypothesis, firstly we use a candidate approach and metabolomics analysis to identify the endogenous ligand(s) of MFSD7c. Secondly, we use the Mfsd7c KO mice model to characterize neurological and pathological phenotype caused by loss of Mfsd7c. These studies will reveal the molecular and physiological details of a new transporter and its ligand on BBB which can be translated into a novel pharmaceuticals development exploiting the endogenous barrier component for drug delivery and deposition to the brain.
kw: Blood Brain Barrier, membrane transporter, brain development

title: Achieving robust cancer-specific lethality by dual blockade of the lipid kinase PIP4K and mitotic pathways in Ras-activated/mutated cancers
abs: The Ras/Raf/MEK/ERK and PI3K/Akt/mTOR signaling pathways play a fundamental role in human cancer. However, crosstalk between these two pathways results in de novo drug resistance, limiting the effective development of anti-Ras strategies. Identifying targets that mediate resistance/crosstalk between Ras-PI3K pathways is critical to developing novel agents that may prolong therapeutic response.We have identified a compound with dual-inhibitory properties, named a131, that selectively kills Ras-activated/mutated cancers, while protecting normal cells, and identified the PIP4K lipid kinases as the target of a131 (Nat. Commun., accepted). Notably, PIP4Ks inhibition by a131 causes reversible growth arrest in normal cells by transcriptionally up-regulating PIK3IP1 that suppresses the PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway. Strikingly, Ras-activation overrides a131-induced PIK3IP1 up-regulation and cross-activates the PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway. Consequently, Ras-transformed cells override a131-induced growth arrest and enter mitosis where a131’s ability to de-cluster supernumerary centrosomes in Ras-activated/mutated cancers eliminates them through mitotic catastrophe. PIP4Ks has been implicated in tumorigenesis. Therefore, together with a131’s ability to inhibit PIP4Ks, its potent anticancer efficacy via cancer-selective mitotic catastrophe may provide novel pharmacological strategies against Ras-activated/mutated cancers. Moreover, our discovery on new cross-activation mechanism for Ras-PI3K pathways promises further insight into the role of the Ras?PIK3IP1?PI3K signaling network in crosstalk driving de novo resistance to clinically relevant targeted therapies. Together, we aim to delineate the underlying mechanism of Ras-PI3K pathways cross-activation via Ras?PIK3IP1?PI3K signaling network in carcinogenesis (Aims 1 & 2), new roles for PIP4Ks in controlling PI3K pathway and drug development targeting PIP4Ks (Aim 3), and identifying the oncogenic Ras-dependent mitotic target(s) of a131 (Aim 4). These will delineate cancer-specific signalling networks thereby providing a deeper understanding of this novel mechanism underlying de novo resistance, which arises in clinically relevant Ras-PI3K pathway-targeted therapies. Our long-term aim is to understand how to target the Ras?PIK3IP1?PI3K signaling network as unique complement to the treatment of Ras-dependent cancers.
kw: Ras-PI3K, Signal-crosstalk, mitosis, lipid-kinases, synthetic-lethality, chemoprotection

title: Exploiting the relationship between cancer cell intrinsic respiratory properties and sensitivity to electron transport chain (ETC) inhibitors to enhance therapeutic targeting
abs: Adequate mitochondria respiration is indispensable for cancer cell proliferation and survival. For this reason, existing and novel anti-mitochondria compounds are under development. Metformin, an electron transport chain (ETC) inhibitor, has been extensively studied for its anti-cancer potential. Meta-analyses of the vast database of type II diabetes patients revealed a significant reduction of cancer occurrence in patients taking metformin. However, numerous subsequent phase II cancer trials, which set no patient stratification criteria based on the molecular mechanism of action of metformin, have been inconclusive. In our recent effort to identify patient stratification markers, we have characterized a broad range of human cancer cell lines of diverse tissue origin. We discovered that respiratory capacity and respiratory reserve, two related ETC properties indicating the ability of a cell to adapt to energy stress, strongly correlate to the cell’s sensitivity to metformin. In this proposal, we delineate plans to explore the potential of using tumor cell respiratory capacity to predict its sensitivity to ETC inhibitors and to design drug combinations. To do this, we will: (1) establish the causative link between cancer cell respiratory capacity/reserve and metformin sensitivity, (2) develop a method to measure respiratory capacity using fresh surgical samples from cancer patients, and further validate the predictive value of respiratory capacity for cancer metformin sensitivity using patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models, (3) evaluate the roles of AMPK activation and autophagy induction in cancer cells’ response to metformin treatment, and explore synergistic efficacies of combining metformin with either an AMPK or autophagy inhibitor, and (4) systematically evaluate the impact of malignant transformation by different oncogenic pathways on cellular respiratory properties and their susceptibility to ETC inhibitors. Completion of these studies would define a mechanism-based patient stratification strategy and establish the method to enhance the evaluation of clinical efficacy of ETC inhibitors.
kw: mitochondria, metformin, cancer cell metabolism, clinical trials, patient stratification, AMPK

title: Mechanisms of decline in vascular cognitive impairment
abs: Aims : To leverage upon human cohort studies conducted by the Memory Aging & Cognition Centre (MACC) as well as the technical and analytical capacity of the Centre for Imaging Research (A*Star-NUS) and Cardiovascular Research Institute (CVRI), to address the problem of Vascular Cognitive Impairment a common chronic illness which constitutes a major clinical and economic burden world-wide. Methods and Approach : To develop biomarkers by characterizing neuropsychological patterns, exploring mechanisms, in particular vascular processes (cerebrovascular lesions, cardiac and vascular), accounting for cognitive decline in these individuals, so as to develop therapeutic interventions to prevent cognitive decline in high risk patients. Hypotheses : High risk groups will show characteristic neuropsychological trajectories and be associated with brain, cardiac and vascular markers of disease. Specifically, a) brain MRI and cardiovascular markers will provide prognostic information on cognitive decline; b) circulating biomarkers of proven diagnostic and/or prognostic importance in heart failure and acute coronary disease will be useful in identification and risk stratification in patients with early and advanced cognitive impairment in that plasma concentrations of one or more of these markers will correlate with (i) measures of cognitive function and/or (ii) brain MRI changes. Moreover, both baseline and serial change in, one or more of these biomarkers, will add additional predictive information on progression.We aim to improve understanding of Vascular Cognitive Impairment

title: Deubiquitinating enzymes of the Hippo Pathway and their potentials as cancer diagnostic markers and therapeutic targets
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: The turnover of many cellular proteins is regulated via ubiquitination pathway which selectively targets proteins for degradation in the proteasome. The substrate specificity of protein ubiquitination is mediated by ubiquitinating enzymes, but the process is reversible by deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs) which remove ubiquitin from the ubiquitinated proteins. The Hippo pathway is an emerging tumor suppressor pathway and dysregulation of this pathway results in tissue overgrowth and cancer development. Although Hippo components are regulated by protein phosphorylation, recent studies suggest that Hippo components are also destabilized by ubiqutination-dependent proteasome degradation, and several ubiquitinating enzymes were identified to target Hippo components. However, not much work on DUBs has been shown to regulate Hippo components. Several recent studies have revealed a few deubiquitinating enzymes regulating Hippo pathway components, including USP9X identified in our lab. The research on deubiquitination of Hippo pathway components is still nascent but represents an exciting new area of the Hippo pathway. To identify DUBs for the Hippo pathway, we searched our protein interacting network of the Hippo pathway constructed in the lab through proteomic analysis. Several DUBs (USP9X, USP15 and USP22) were identified as high confident interacting proteins of the Hippo pathway and we have published recently USP9X as a tumor suppressor stabilizing LATS kinases and other upstream Hippo components to suppress tumor growth. Since deubiquitinating enzymes play important roles and are potential drug targets for various diseases including cancers, this proposal aims to study the hypothesis that these DUBs regulate the Hippo pathway to control cell proliferation and tumor growth, offering novel opportunities for alterative targets for cancer treatment and new diagnostic methods.
kw: Hippo Pathway, USP9X, USP15, USP22, MST1/2, Cancer

title: Molecular mechanisms of Plasmodium vivax malaria parasite invasion in reticulocytes
abs: Plasmodium vivax is the most prevalent malaria parasite in South East Asia. Despite its high burden and increasing morbidity and mortality, no vaccine candidates have reached phase II/III so far. Studies on P. vivax have been hampered because there is no continuous culture of its blood stage. The Duffy antigen (CD234) is the only erythrocyte receptor known to mediate invasion of P. vivax into reticulocytes. However, CD234 is expressed on both mature erythrocytes and reticulocytes and as P. vivax specifically invades reticulocytes it is likely that there is (are) co receptor (s) other than CD234. We previously developed a robust invasion assay for P. vivax merozoites in vitro with cord blood reticulocytes and demonstrated that P. vivax merozoites invades only CD71+ reticulocytes. Using a differential proteomic approach, we identified proteins only expressed in CD71+ but not CD71- reticulocytes. Using antibodies in inhibition of invasion assay, we have obtained evidence that CD98 is receptor for P. vivax. Using a P. vivax antigen library, we showed that CD98 is recognised by the reticulocyte-binding protein 2a (PvRBP2a). This is the first evidence of a specific receptor-ligand interaction for P. vivax selective invasion of reticulocytes and we also obtained data showing that antibodies that block PvRBP2a-CD98 interaction inhibit P. vivax invasion. These findings provide the basis for the development of vaccine against P. vivax. Our HYPOTHESIS is that PvRBP2a binding to CD98 allows P. vivax to invade reticulocytes and that antibodies that block this interaction will be effective in inhibiting P. vivax invasion. The specific AIMS of this project are: Aim 1. Further characterised the role of CD98 as a reticulocyte-specific receptor for P. vivax Aim 2. Further characterize PvRBP2a interaction with CD98 Aim 3. Identify conserved protective epitopes that impart global strain-transcending protection against P. vivax
kw: Malaria,Plasmodium vivax,invasion,reticulocytes,vaccine

title: Mechanisms of sphingosine-1-phosphate signaling in vascular health and disease
abs: Sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) is a signaling lipid that is essential for blood vessel development and functions. S1P exerts its roles by being a potent ligand for 5 different S1P receptors. Much effort has been made to understand the receptor-mediated signaling mechanisms and S1P synthesis. One major gap of knowledge is how S1P is released for its extracellular signaling. S1P is synthesized from sphingosine by phosphorylation by two sphingosine kinases (SphK1/2). It must be exported out of cells for signaling roles. Blood cells and endothelial cells and are proposed as the main sources for plasma S1P. Nevertheless, the transporters responsible for S1P release were not identified until recently. Spinster homolog protein 2 (Spns2) was cloned by two laboratories as the endothelial S1P exporter which contributes ~25% plasma S1P. My laboratory has recently identified Mfsd2b as the S1P exporter in blood cells and showed that red blood cells (RBC) and platelets contribute ~50% plasma S1P via Mfsd2b (Vu et al., Nature 2017). It is unclear how plasma S1P contributed by blood and endothelial cells for maintenance of blood vessel functions. Here, we plan to determine the mechanisms for S1P release and the molecular roles of plasma S1P for vascular functions. Aim 1: determination of mechanisms for plasma S1P production during development and in postnatal life. Aim 2: determination of mechanisms for physiological roles of plasma S1P in vasculature in normal and pathological conditions. Our central hypothesis is that plasma S1P is a critical factor to regulate blood vessel functions and disruption of its release process will affect vascular functions. The rationale for the proposed research is that the fundamental knowledge obtained will establish the foundation for development of S1P-based therapeutics for treatment of vascular diseases.

title: Rho-regulated Protein Kinases: Unraveling the biochemical & spatial regulation of the cellular acto-myosin network in cell movement and axonal outgrowth.
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Protein kinases (PKs) are a very important class of drug target and for many years represent ~ 25% of spending in pharmaceutical sector. In very few cases (eg. receptor tyrosine kinases) do we have a good understanding individual PK targets and function. By-and-large much of the human 'kinome' is under-investigated, and tends to be approached 'one substrate at a time'. We wish to apply a number of new technologies to over come this bottleneck. Starting with the serine/threonine PKs acting downstream of the Rho proteins termed PAK1, PAK4, ROCK2, MRCK-beta and PKN2 (several discovered by our group). This analysis will start with a BioID approach, which can identify the local protein-protein interaction (PPI) network extending ~20 nm in the vicinity of each of these PKs in order to find new adaptor proteins. We will apply mass-spectrometry (MS) using several complementary approaches to identify the in vivo substrates for these PKs. In cultured cells we can investigate how these PKs affect the architecture of the acto-myosin network in migrating cells using super-resolution microscopy and live imaging. These studies will be extended to primary neurons grown in culture, to test the hypothesis that the axonal growth cone is regulated by Rho proteins via these various PK in a similar manner. Finally we will identify the best candidate sites and generate high quality phospho-specific antibodies to probe the sites of substrate phosphorylation in these cells. An important goal of our work will be to validate these antibodies to allow accurate tracking of Rho-associated kinase activity, including in the context of tissue samples.
kw: Protein kinase, phospho-proteomics, acto-myosin, myosin II organization, cell movement, growth cone

title: Manipulating mTOR’s nutrient-sensing function for cancer therapeutic intervention
abs: While mTOR is known to play a central role in cell growth and proliferation, little is known about the regulation and subcellular localization of the nutrient-sensing complexes in adult tissues and cancer cells. Our recent results suggest that cancer cells manipulate the nutrient-sensing arm of mTOR by regulating the abundance of specific nutrients, and that this may be exploited for therapeutic purposes. Therefore, the major aims of the project will be: 1) To characterize the subcellular localization of mTOR-related nutrient-sensing complexes in normal and cancerous liver cells. 2) To determine the efficacy of manipulating nutrient-sensing mechanisms to regulate cancer cell proliferation in vitro and tumor formation in vivo. The results of the proposed studies will not only lead to a more comprehensive understanding of this critical cell signaling pathway, but could unveil novel chemotherapeutic approaches that specifically target cancer cells.
kw: cancer, molecular biology, metabolic regulation

title: Targeting Agrin as a therapy for Hepatocellular carcinoma
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is one of the leading causes of cancer-related deaths with a high mortality rate globally. Despite offering a poor survival of HCC patients, sorafenib (broad spectrum receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor) is the best known therapeutic offered at present for HCC. As such, there is a clinical urgency to identify the suitable target(s) and create additional therapeutic avenue(s) to control liver cancer. We have previously elucidated a critical role of proteoglycan Agrin in mediating liver oncogenesis through maintaining the integrity of focal adhesions. Agrin also acts a stiffness and mechanical signal for promoting the activity of YAP/TAZ oncogenes and thereby HCC development. In this grant proposal, we aim to target Agrin in liver cancer via antibody therapy. Accordingly, our specific aims include generation and extensive characterization of function-blocking antibodies against Agrin. More importantly, we plan to perform pre-clinical efficacy and mechanistic studies of Agrin antibody therapy in animal models of HCC, therefore, laying a solid foundation for future clinical relevance. In addition, we plan to stratify HCC patients with higher expression of secretory and tumor tissue Agrin for an effective therapeutic response. Hence, Agrin antibody therapy offers the possibility of new treatment strategies and additionally may be combined with the present-standard-of-treatments for HCC. Taken together, the successful development of Agrin antibody therapy may serve to appropriately screen patients and significantly improve HCC treatment strategies.
kw: Agrin, HCC, Antibody therapy, Hippo pathway, YAP/TAZ

title: Development of a multivalent, live-attenuated vaccine candidate against HFMD
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Hand, Foot and Mouth disease has as a public health threat in recent years with outbreaks occurring globally, particularly so for countries in the Asia-Pacific Region. The disease can result from infections by a plethora of enteroviruses of Enterovirus A and Enterovirus B species, with Coxsackievirus A16 (CV-A16) and Enterovirus 71 (EV-A71) being the predominant serotypes worldwide. There is no effective antiviral against HFMD available for treatment and vaccines against EV-A71 had only been recently approved for use in China. Although, with more EV-A71 vaccine candidates undergoing phase 3 trials, licensure of an EV-A71 vaccine for the prevention of severe disease in most countries is expected to happen soon, all of them are formalin-inactivated virus vaccines which offer no protection against CV-A16, the most common HFMD-associated serotype globally. In addition, the shifting trends of both endemic and epidemic serotypes can diminish the effectiveness of an EV-A71 vaccine against HFMD on general. Hence, far from being the much-needed panacea for HFMD, a vaccine effective against EV-A71 only is, without a doubt, insufficient to eliminate HFMD as a public health threat. Much focus had been placed on the development of bi- and tri-valent inactivated whole virus vaccines for HFMD, research on live-attenuated vaccines has been largely neglected, despite its offer of a superior protection. In view of the challenges to a vaccine against HFMD and the benefits of a live-attenuated vaccine, this proposal aims to develop a platform to generate live-attenuated vaccine candidates for use in multivalent formulations effective against HFMD.
kw: vaccine, HFMD, live-attenuated vaccine, multivalent

title: Rosetting as a possible protective shield for Plasmodium falciparum late stages against artemisinin.
abs: The wide-spreading artemisinin resistance in Plasmodium falciparum is the current healthcare emergency to mankind. As artemisinin is the current last line of defense against malaria, a prompt strategy is needed to tackle this issue with currently available resources. The current understanding of artemisinin resistance revolves around the higher anti-oxidative capacity and dormancy triggering by the early ring forms of the K13 mutant parasites. The more mature stages of the mutant parasites are believed to remain susceptible to artemisinin. However, the picture may be incomplete as few earlier studies reported contradictory findings. A complete understanding on the mechanism of artemisinin resistance development by the parasites is essential to decide the best way forward to tackle this problem in clinical setting while waiting for the arrival of the next new antimalarial agent. This project intends to investigate the immediate rheological changes of erythrocytes infected with P. falciparum late stages (the most vulnerable stages of malaria parasites to artemisinin) upon brief artemisinin exposure (in line with the short in vivo half-life of the drug), the impact of such changes on the parasite survival, and how the parasites respond to such alteration, in an attempt to decipher the complete mechanistic picture of artemisinin resistance development by P. falciparum. The knowledge garnered from this project will contribute towards a better understanding, hence better preparation in handling and combating artemisinin-resistant malaria in clinical setting.
kw: malaria, artemisinin resistance, rheology, rosetting

title: Validation of molecular targets for novel treatment directions in allergic rhinitis
abs: Allergic Rhinitis (AR) is a common chronic disease of the upper airways which results from a dysregulated immune response associated to allergen exposure. The AR phenotype is characterised by an inflammatory immune profile and an altered nasal epithelial barrier. The highest prevalence is in kids with nearly 40-50% of kids in Singapore having AR symptoms. Unfortunately, the prevalence of AR has also been steadily increasing in the recent years and thus would pose a significant burden on healthcare both locally in Singapore and internationally. Thus we need effective treatment and potentially prevention strategies to control this problem. Studies using Gene expression as a tool serve to help understand disease pathogenesis and also provide molecular targets for potential intervention and treatment. In a large transcriptional association study, I identified statistically significant association of genes to AR. I then replicated the top hits in an independent AR cohort in Sweden which identified 11 significantly associated candidates for AR in both Singpore and Swedish cohorts. In this proposal, I want to evaluate the relevance of these significant genes in eosinophils from whole blood along with nasal cells to determine their relevance in the disease tissue (nose). In addition, I also plan to perform an in vitro assay using the primary nasal cells under house dust mite stimulation to get the gene expression in context of an activated environment. Taken together, these results would help prioritise genes among the selected candidates for future screening assays and/or humanised mouse models. Additionally, we also have international collaborators from Sweden and Netherlands who would be able to replicate our findings in their cohorts to determine the context in their respective environments. This proposal thus provides potential targets for novel treatment directions in AR both locally and internationally.
kw: allergic rhinitis, gene targets, treatment, singapore, therapy

title: INVESTIGATING LEUKEMOGENESIS FROM THE BONE MARROW (BM) STROMA PERSPECTIVE
abs: All cancer is driven by the accumulation of phenotype altering genetic mutations. In leukemogenesis, the acquisition of cancerous mutations in hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) can occur with considerable assistance from mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs), given that these cells make up an essential cellular component of the hematopoiesis supporting stromal niches in bone marrow (BM) tissue. As MSC-derived factors have been shown to affect HSC self-renewal and differentiation, dysfunctional MSCs, such as those in disease sates can induce significant changes to the BM stroma that triggers malignant transformation of HSCs.The overarching goal of this proposal is to investigate stromal-driven leukemogenesis with a focus on: 1) the de novo conversion of healthy HSCs to a pre-leukemic state, and 2) the evolution from pre-leukemic disorders (myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS)) to acute myeloid leukemia (AML). These investigations will utilize available patient repository samples, both hematopoietic and mesenchymal, that have been well characterized and show leukemia stage-dependent engraftment in mice and different capabilities for supporting hematopoietic differentiation (impaired with high-risk MDS-MSCs, etc), respectively. A significant effort of this investigation will be to compare the kinetics of acquisition of epigenetic or genetic alterations in HSCs after exposure to different stroma conditions produced in an in vivo implanted artificial BM niche. Mechanistic studies on the means by which stromal cells affect HSCs in the context of leukemia, such as through inflammatory signaling or exosome transfer of small RNAs will carried our as a secondary aim.Many of the anticipated outcomes of this work will have meaningful clinical impact on the manner in which we view and characterize leukemia; this knowledge, together with information from mechanistic studies of the cancer-stroma communication could also provide the basis for the introduction of new cancer drugs that target the stromal microenvironment. (292 words)

title: Study of Mitochondrial Maladaptation in Metabolic Inflexibility of Heart Failure
abs: Background: Heart failure (HF) is one of the leading causes of death globally. HF has been shown to present at least 15 years earlier in Southeast Asian patients, in comparison to their Western counterparts, thereby forecasting a significant socio-economic burden in the years ahead. Among HF cases, HFpEF (HF with preserved ejection fraction) with its characteristic diastolic dysfunction account for 50% of HF patients, and is steadily on the rise, projecting it to be the dominant form of HF. Specific aims: Recent clinical trials have implicated left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) as a prognostic marker for HFpEF, yet it is unclear as to how LVH results in diastolic dysfunction and HFpEF. Hypotheses: Cytosolic calcium overload (a feature of LVH) perturbs mitochondrial functionality, resulting in metabolic inflexibility in hypertrophied cardiomyocytes. Dysfunctional mitochondria together with loss in substrate selectivity between glucose and fatty acids would aggravate reactive oxygen species (ROS) formation and lipotoxic compound build-up contributing to increased sarcomere stiffness that culminate in diastolic dysfunction. Approach: Using induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) technology, due to its characteristic hypertrophic phenotype I plan to model LVH from patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Using this platform, I hope to gain insights into signalling pathways regulating mitochondrial dynamics and metabolic flexibility as well as identify molecular targets for therapeutic intervention. Understanding diastolic dysfunction of HFpEF, in context to LVH would help offer meaningful insights of this complicated disorder which is becoming more prevalent in rapidly ageing societies such as Singapore.

title: Validation of the World Health Organization Disability Assessment Schedule 2.0 among those with mental and physical illness in Singapore
abs: Disability has increasingly become an important indicator of disease burden and for evaluating the effectiveness of health interventions. With the significant increase in healthcare treatment and community mental health care programmes across the country, there is an urgent need to evaluate the effectiveness of these programmes using reliable and accurate measures that are able to capture all aspects of patients’ functioning and disability that are comparable not only across health conditions, but also across treatments and programmes of care. The current study aims to validate the WHODAS 2.0 in patients diagnosed with schizophrenia spectrum, depression, anxiety disorders and diabetes, to assess the divergent, concurrent and known-group validity of the WHODAS 2.0 against disease-specific and other known measures, to examine test-retest reliability and agreement between three modes of administrations (self-report, rater-administered, and proxy-administered), to develop and evaluate a crosswalk conversion algorithm between WHODAS 2.0 and the Global Assessment Functioning scales and mapping the relationship between the WHODAS 2.0 and the EQ-5D utility scores, and to compare the responsiveness to change of the WHODAS 2.0 against disease-specific and other known measures over 1 -year follow-up. A cross-sectional study will be conducted among outpatients at the Institute of Mental Health and National Healthcare Group Polyclinic. Data on WHODAS 2.0, generic and disease-specific measures, socio-demographic characteristics, clinical history and service utilization will be collected. Findings from this study will provide evidence to clinicians and researchers about the psychometric properties of the WHODAS 2.0 that can be used to assess disability of patients with mental and physical conditions in an Asian patient population. This measure also will allow comparisons of burden of disease and quality adjusted life years in Singapore in future.

title: Focal Therapy for Prostate Cancer: Personalized Therapy to Maximize Functional Outcomes while achieving Oncological Success (CNIG17nov018)
abs: Prostate cancer is the third most frequent male cancer and the seventh most frequent cause of death in Singapore. The gold standard curative treatment of localized prostate cancer is whole-gland therapy with radical prostatectomy (surgical removal of the prostate gland) or radiotherapy. These methods are effective at curing cancer but result in collateral damage to adjacent structures resulting in impaired urinary continence and erectile dysfunction. In patients with cancer localized to one area of the prostate gland, focal therapy of just the dangerous cancer focus may allow a patient to maintain continence and erectile function and avoid the side-effects of radical treatment while achieving cure. We aim to evaluate the degree of preservation of continence and erectile function and early oncological outcomes in patients treated with focal cryoablation of the prostate.This is a phase II study of men with localized prostate cancer. Consenting men will undergo multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) and targeted biopsy of suspicious lesions to select only those with: (1) mpMRI cancer focus < 3 ml in size, (2) involvement limited to one anatomic region (left, right or anterior gland), (3) localized cancer on mpMRI, (4) target lesion Gleason ?4+4 and (5) no outfield Gleason?3+3 cancer, to undergo focal cryoablation. The primary outcome, post-treatment functional status, will be tracked with standardized questionnaires performed at 0, 1, 3, 6 and 12 months. The secondary outcome, oncological success, will be assessed at 1 year with repeat biopsy and mpMRI. To demonstrate no significant deterioration in post-treatment functional outcome, we will recruit 27 men for this study.Our findings will establish the safety of focal cryoablation and be the basis of further research into the utility of this technique in achieving cure while preserving function in men with prostate cancer.

title: Germanium-Based Materials for Silicon-compatible Near-IR and Mid-IR Light Source
abs: Although researchers have succeeded in integrating most of the necessary components such as waveguide, phase tuner, grating, and photodetector on a silicon chip, they could not achieve an on-chip light source. Therefore, the ability to realize a fully integrated photonics chip requires an on-chip laser source on silicon. Thus, making a practical silicon-compatible laser is the “Holy Grail”. However, efforts to create a practical on-chip laser using silicon-compatible materials (e.g. group-IV silicon, germanium) have been in vain. Fundamentally, silicon-compatible materials are indirect band-gap semiconductors (as opposed to III-V materials which are direct band-gap). Consequently, the light emission from these materials is highly inefficient, if any. We propose to realize a fully integrated photonics chip by using germanium-on-insulator (GOI) on silicon platform. To tackle the most challenging problem, which is the realization of a silicon-compatible light source, we propose to use highly strained germanium as the primary approach. Other components such as waveguides, photodetectors, and grating can also be realized on the same GOI platform readily. GOI is highly viable as the peripheral electronics components can be built on the silicon substrate, making it a platform of choice for a truly monolithic integration approach for heterogeneous components such as photonics chip. In addition, pushing operation wavelength to ~2µm with strained-Ge is also advantageous compared to working at 1.55 µm in terms of lesser atmosphere scattering and absorption losses.

title: Singapore Initiative in Next Generation T-cell Decoding for Immunotherapy (SiT-Decode)
abs: Our goal is to generate paradigm-shifting fundamental Next Generation understanding of the role of every annotated human gene in the regulation of T-cell functioning, and develop novel anticancer immunotherapeutic T-cell targets, focusing on hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and lymphoma. Current understanding of the role of every annotated human gene in regulating these functions of T-cells is minimal, severely limiting knowledge on both the mechanisms regulating T-cell functioning and novel drug targets for T-cell immunotherapy. Our study will eliminate this critical knowledge bottleneck in T-cell field, by interrogating the hypothesis that identification of previously unrecognized T-cell regulatory genes will reveal powerful novel T-cell immunotherapeutic targets. We will discover novel genes regulating T-cell functioning through genome-wide functional reverse genetic screening in human/mouse T-cells using cutting edge CRISPR-technology, wherein we will ablate the expression all 18000 protein coding genes individually to assess their role in T-cell activities. After discovering key novel genes/signaling modules regulating T-cells, we will characterize novel T-cell regulation mechanisms, and develop selected new genes as novel druggable T-cell immunotherapeutic targets using a solid tumour, hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and lymphoma as model systems, using in vitro and in vivo preclinical models. We will also evaluate existing drugs targeting our novel targets for their therapeutic efficacy against HCC and lymphoma in model systems. In addition, we will develop partnerships with Singapore-based drug discovery leaders and initiate the discovery of new therapeutic drugs (e.g., antibody) targeting our newly-discovered immunotherapeutic T-cell targets. This study will identify novel immunotherapy targets, and will expand immunotherapeutic intellectual property space. The proposed research programme will be accomplished through four individual interlinked projects: Project-1: T-cell activation and Immune Checkpoint Regulator Gene Discovery. Project-2: CD8+ T-cell Cytotoxic Effector Function Regulator Gene Discovery. Project-3: Treg Suppressor Function Regulator Gene Discovery. Project-4: Pre-clinical evaluation of novel targets for cancer immunotherapy.

title: Algorithmic Prediction and Practical Control of Large Scale Population Dynamics
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: Our goal is to develop novel algorithmic tools for understanding and controlling phenomena that arise from the networked interaction between individuals in large populations. The evolution of these systems is typically captured by dynamical systems that are both high dimensional and nonlinear and thus raise formidable analytical obstacles. Our research plan is two-fold: First, we will utilize the latest developments from the intersection of computer science, and mathematics to understand and formalize the limits of predictability of such systems. Which features of the system behaviour can be systematically predicted and which are effectively random? This requires studying questions that lie on intersection of two differences sources of complexity, chaos, i.e. the unpredictability of (even low dimensional) dynamics due to sensitive dependence on initial conditions (butterfly effect) and computational complexity, i.e. the inability to perform a computation within a reasonable time horizon due to a large number of involved variables. Secondly, we aim to explore novel and efficient ways to control such systems. Such small changes made to the parameter values can cause abrupt 'qualitative' changes to its behavior, known as bifurcations. Exploring how to best introduce minor behavioral tweaks so out to maximize their positive effects requires bringing together elements of bifurcation theory with mechanism design and decision/game theory. Finally, while the main focus on this proposal is the underlying theory, we intend to complement our work with large scale experiments and data analytics that will allow us to couch our work in the reality of human decision making and Singapore in particular.
kw: Computer Science;Algorithmic Game Theory;Dynamical Systems;Mechanism Design;Chaos;Bifurcation Theory

title: Nanostructured Bactericidal Metal Oxides for Consumer Care and Self-Disinfecting Surface Applications
inst: ISCE2 - Institute of Sustainability for Chemicals, Energy and Environment
abs: About 80% of infectious diseases are contracted from contact with surfaces. Killing bacteria on frequently touched surfaces is an effective way to avoid cross-infection. Currently, small molecular antimicrobial agents are commonly used in consumer care products as disinfectants. To overcome the toxicity and resistance issues of small molecular antimicrobial agents, we propose two innovative approaches targeting different applications: (1) metal oxide nanopattern coating technology for self-disinfecting surfaces, and (2) non-photoactive bactericidal nanostructured metal/metal oxide composite materials for consumer care and general disinfection applications. The bio-mimicking metal oxide nanopatterned surface can kill bacteria by physically rupturing microbial cell membranes. The nanopatterned surface will be developed via “bottom-up” coating approach. This approach is simple, inexpensive and scalable. Surface nanopatterns will be evaluated with both in vitro and in vivo models against various bacteria and fungi. We will systematically study the interactions between the cell and the nanopatterned surface to achieve a highly active and selective microbicidal surface by modifying surface physical properties, such as surface charge and structural morphology. The durability, anti-contamination property, cytotoxicity and biocompatibility of surface structures will also be studied. Metal oxide semiconductors have been widely used as photoactive antimicrobial materials as they are able to release reactive oxygen species (ROS). However, photo-irradiation is energy-consuming, has low efficiency and also has apparent limitations in the applications. We will develop novel nanostructured metal oxides (with metal junction) which could generate non-photoactive radicals. We will screen potential metal/metal oxide combinations that have matched energy levels to release radicals spontaneously. We will systematically study the composition-structure-property relationship and their bacteria killing and surface disinfection activities. The application protocols of this type of new materials will also be developed, especially on surface coating and consumer care products.
kw: disinfection;antimicrobial;nanostructure;metal oxide;non-photoactive;surface

title: Epitope Dynamics during Flaviviral Entry for Targeted Antibody Discovery
abs: Singapore faces a continual threat from multiple flaviviruses, ranging from the endemic dengue virus and emergent zika and yellow fever (YF). Vaccination success has been variable with a vaccine available solely against YF but none against zika and only trials underway for dengue. Despite the success of empirically developed vaccines such as the live-attenuated virus for YF, the efficacy has not been established. The lack of success in the rational design of vaccines has its roots in our lack of understanding of how binding of neutralizing antibodies to specific surfaces of different flaviviruses impairs the intrinsic viral flexibility and how this interferes with their ability to infect human host. Although high resolution structures of multiple flaviviruses and in complex with antibodies are available, they do not offer insights into how the virus enters the cell or how it elicits an immune response. Flaviviruses are dynamic entities that ‘sense’ their entry into human hosts by differentially altering their structures to mediate entry into the host cell. Based on recent results from members of our team, we hypothesize that neutralizing antibodies impair viral entry into host cells by blocking the dynamics of viral particles. The goal of this proposal is to accelerate vaccine development by mapping dynamics of multiple epitopes during the critical process of viral host entry. This will be combined to generate a map of epitope sites from known neutralizing antibodies to computationally model a pan-flaviviral epitope landscape. This will provide enormous insights into the vulnerable hotspots on flaviviral structures and will be used to develop targeted antibodies against multiple flaviviruses. These antibodies will be tested in animal models. This will also accelerate targeted monoclonal antibody discovery and vaccine design against multiple flaviviruses through a dynamics-driven description of the efficacy of the YF vaccine.

title: Clinical and Translational Research in Movement Disorders
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Essential Tremor (ET) and Parkinson’s disease (PD) are two of the most common movement disorders and have underlying genetic etiologies. Identification of disease pathogenic variants, followed by studies of these variants in in vivo and in vitro models will shed light on the key molecular mechanisms/pathways and help identify new therapeutic targets. We aim to establish a resource containing prospective clinical and genetic data for different subsets of ET patients from our Asian population. Samples will include those from familial ET, sporadic ET, coexistent ET and PD (those who presented initially as ET but later developed PD), healthy controls and disease controls (enhanced physiological tremor). We will generate induced pleuripotent stem cell (IPSC) derived neurons (Purkinje cells, GABA neurons, serotonergic neurons and dopaminergic neurons) from these subjects, and also transgenic Drosophila models expressing novel and known ET gene mutations (such as FUS and TENM4 etc) and using these iPSC and isogenic lines and transgenic Drosophila models, to conduct RNA-seq and ribosomal profiling to identify potential therapeutic targets. In addition, we will develop cerebellum and midbrain organoids from different subsets of ET patients to uncover any potential deficits in Purkinje neurons and their neural networks, and to investigate any potential degeneration in the midbrain.Separately, we aim to conduct a prospective clinical study to evaluate motor and non motor clinical progression in PD patients who are carriers of the LRRK2 protective variants, compared to LRRK2 risk variants and those carrying both the risk and the protective variants and to conduct RNA-seq of newly synthesized mRNA from dopaminergic neurons in the different groups of transgenic Drosophila expressing these variants and validate the top genes/targets that have been identified using cell based assays, post-mortem specimens from human LRRK2 carriers, human IPSC-derived neurons, transgenic LRRK2 mice and Drosophila.

title: Integrated Molecular Analysis of Cancers in Gynaecologic Oncology (IMAC-GO)
abs: Background: Genetic and molecular heterogeneity in cancer underpins the observed variations in patient outcomes. Hence, the ability to characterise the unique genetic and molecular features of each patient’s tumour will be a critical step to identifying the optimal therapeutic strategy for the individual. Aims: To provide and evaluate the impact of molecular profiling information on patients with gynaecological cancers by setting up and maintaining a platform for integrated molecular analysis of cancers in gynaecologic oncology (IMAC-GO) in patients who are candidates for molecular-targeted therapy/ biomarker-driven clinical trials, in order to identify potentially actionable mutations/ activated molecular pathways and mechanisms of drug resistance in gynaecological cancers. Hypothesis: • Molecular profiling will improve the outcome of novel targeted-agent treatment in clinical trials • Molecular profiling of paired samples (primary/recurrent and primary/metastatic) will provide new insights into mechanisms underlying drug resistance and metastasis in gynaecological cancers. Methodology: Patients who consent to participate in this study will have their tumour specimens, blood, and pleural or ascitic fluid collected. Molecular profiling of tumour cells will be performed using Next- Generation Sequencing (NGS), quantitative-PCR, fluorescent or chromogenic-in-situ-hybridisation (FISH/CISH), immunohistochemistry and/or other relevant techniques. Primary, metastatic and recurrent tumours will be profiled and compared to identify mechanisms of metastasis and drug-resistance. Clinical data to be collected include baseline patient and tumor characteristics, treatment regimen(s) administered, time on treatment(s), and survival. Progression free survival (PFS) and overall response rates (ORR) on matched targeted therapy based on molecular profiling will be used to assess the clinical impact of molecular profiling in these patients. Research significance: Characterising the genetic mechanisms and molecular pathways driving oncogenesis and tumour progression in different primary/ recurrent gynaecological cancers will enable differences in tumour behavior and optimisation of therapy to be addressed earlier, rather than a 'one size fits all' treatment approach, thus fulfilling the promise of personalised cancer medicine.

title: Application and Evaluation of an Artificial Intelligence Deep Learning System to Detect Referable and Sight-threatening Retinal Diseases in the Singapore Integrated Diabetic Retinopathy Screening Programme (SiDRP): Screening Performance and Cost-effectiveness Analysis
abs: Screening for diabetic retinopathy (DR), a leading cause of visual loss, is a widely recommended strategy. In Singapore, patients with diabetes undergo DR screening via the Singapore Integrated DR Programme (SiDRP). In 2016, SiDRP screened nearly 80,000 people using a system of >20 professional technicians covering 18 polyclinics. With rising diabetes prevalence, SiDRP is projected to screen 200-250,000 people in the next decade and is thus challenged by issues related to availability of manpower and financial sustainability. Deep learning system (DLS) is a novel machine learning technology that utilizes artificial intelligence to detect not only referable DR, but also glaucoma suspect (GS) and age-related macular degeneration (AMD). We have trained a DLS to detect all 3 conditions, validated it using an independent sample of another 220,494 images, and found optimal diagnostic performance. However, whether this DLS can replace current DR screening model in SiDRP based on human/manual grading remains unknown. We hypothesize that the DLS will have similar or superior diagnostic performance, and enhance screening efficiency and productivity, ultimately saving cost and manpower. In this project we aim to evaluate 1) DLS diagnostic performance in detection of referable DR, GS, AMD via comparing referral accuracy of two new screening models (fully automated DLS, semi-automated DLS combined with manual grading) vs. current manual assessment of retinal images; and 2) cost-effectiveness of the two new models vs. current manual model. We will recruit 13,000 patients with diabetes over 3 years under SiDRP. All patients will undergo 2-field retinal photography (optic disc, macula fields), transmitted into a cloud-based system and assessed by two models of DLS (fully automated and semi-automated) as well as professional graders (current system) and retinal specialists (reference standard). We will compare diagnostic performance and costeffectiveness of the two new models to the current manual model.

title: Phase II study of Intravenous Vinorelbine in Patients with Relapsed Platinum Resistant or Refractory C5 High Grade Serous, Endometrioid, or Undifferentiated Primary Peritoneum, Fallopian Tube or Ovarian Cancer (VIP)
abs: Background: It has been difficult to progress beyond platinum-based therapy for the treatment of ovarian cancer (OC) because OC is still largely treated as a single entity. A number of sub-classifications of the most common OC histiotype – high-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSC) suggest that more specific therapeutic approaches may be useful. Four molecular subtypes of HGSC – C1, C2, C4 and C5 which correlate with clinical outcome have been validated. The C5 subtype, comprises about 20% of HGSC, is associated with a poor outcome and potential oncogenic drivers have been identified. Recent preclinical experiments demonstrated vinorelbine targeted C5 subtype more effectively compared to the other subtypes. Several phase II trials of vinorelbine in recurrent OC have shown variable response rates of 3 – 29%, however, previous studies have involved “allcomers” and there has never been a trial involving patient selection based on pure HGSC and biomarkers of response. Specific Aims: Our aim is to determine if targeting treatment based on the C5 molecular subtype with oral vinorelbine improves response rates and progression free survival. This open label phase II trial is a collaboration between Singapore and Australia for patients with platinum resistant or refractory C5 high-grade serous, high grade endometrioid or undifferentiated ovarian, primary peritoneal and fallopian tube cancer. Methodology: A total of 36 patients with confirmed C5 HGSC based on the molecular classifier developed by the NATA accredited Bowtel Lab will be recruited and treated with 60mg/m2 oral vinorelbine until the appearance of significant treatment-related toxicity or disease progression. Dose modifications will be made based on a proforma. Simon’s Optimal two-stage design will be employed with a null hypothesis of response rate <10% based on historical data; and the alternative hypothesis of response rates ≥30% in patients with C5 HGSC following treatment with vinorelbine.

title: Clinical and translational research in movement disorders
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Essential Tremor (ET) and Parkinson’s disease (PD) are two of the most common movement disorders and have underlying genetic etiologies. Identification of disease pathogenic variants, followed by studies of these variants in in vivo and in vitro models will shed light on the key molecular mechanisms/pathways and help identify new therapeutic targets. We aim to establish a resource containing prospective clinical and genetic data for different subsets of ET patients from our Asian population. Samples will include those from familial ET, sporadic ET, coexistent ET and PD (those who presented initially as ET but later developed PD), healthy controls and disease controls (enhanced physiological tremor). We will generate induced pluripotent stem cell (IPSC) derived neurons (Purkinje cells, GABA neurons, serotonergic neurons and dopaminergic neurons) from these subjects, and also transgenic Drosophila models expressing novel and known ET gene mutations (such as FUS and TENM4 etc) and using these iPSC and isogenic lines and transgenic Drosophila models, to conduct RNA-seq and ribosomal profiling to identify potential therapeutic targets. In addition, we will develop cerebellum and midbrain organoids from different subsets of ET patients to uncover any potential deficits in Purkinje neurons and their neural networks, and to investigate any potential degeneration in the midbrain. Separately, we aim to conduct a prospective clinical study to evaluate motor and non motor clinical progression in PD patients who are carriers of the LRRK2 protective variants, compared to LRRK2 risk variants and those carrying both the risk and the protective variants and to conduct RNA-seq of newly synthesized mRNA from dopaminergic neurons in the different groups of transgenic Drosophila expressing these variants and validate the top genes/targets that have been identified using cell based assays, post-mortem specimens from human LRRK2 carriers, human IPSC-derived neurons, transgenic LRRK2 mice and Drosophila.

title: Singapore Programme of Research to Investigate New approaches – to drug discovery and clinical translation – to deliver improved treatments for Tuberculosis (SPRINT)
abs: Tuberculosis (TB) is the ninth leading cause of death worldwide, with an estimated 1.6 million TB deaths in 2016. The standard antibiotic treatment regimen for TB lasts between 6-9 months, with patient adherence and development of antibiotic resistance being major issues that can lead to failed treatment or disease relapse. As such, a shortened, effective course of TB therapy is essential for the successful treatment of TB. The SPRINT program aims to tackle this issue from multiple angles, with a drug discovery team delving into new generations of drugs more effective in controlling Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) and overcoming drug resistance, to multiple clinical teams examining novel methods of TB detection, and treatment shortening trials. Projects also employ cutting edge technologies, such as high throughput sequencing for the transcriptomics study as a predictor of TB disease development in TB contacts, and developed a modern app as an aid to increasing patient adherence to TB medications. The program is strengthened through its numerous collaborations with local and international institutions and organizations. Through its multi-pronged bench-to-bedside approach, the program aims to improve the treatment and disease outcome of TB patients.

title: NUS Master of Clinical Investigator (MCI) RIE2020
A mechanistic study of the role of Paired Box Protein 6 / Munc18 interaction in pancreatic beta-cell compensation and decompensation throughout type 2 diabetes development
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Diabetes is a major public health threat and is reaching epidemic levels. In Singapore, diabetes and its complications become the major cause of hospitalization and death among the ageing population where type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) accounts for >90% of diabetes. The escalating prevalence and the limitation of effective therapeutic options highlight the need for a more complete understanding of T2DM pathogenesis. The pre-diabetic state represents an extremely critical phase in which the beta-cell compensatory capacity determines the disease progression. Deciphering the mechanism regulating beta-cell compensation and decompensation would help pave the way for generation of innovative anti-diabetic therapy. In this regard, the transcription factor Paired Box Protein 6 (PAX6), which plays crucial roles in the development of pancreas, has emerged as a potential target. In this study, we hypothesize that PAX6 modulates insulin secretion by regulating the expression of the exocytotic protein Munc18; in which this pathway may determine the compensatory capacity during transition from pre-diabetes to overt diabetes. To test our hypothesis, various biochemical assays are performed to examine the regulation of PAX6 on Munc18 expression and insulin secretion in human beta-cell line EndoC-bH1. We also examine the in vivo association between PAX6-Munc18 axis and beta-cell function throughout T2DM pathogenesis using different type 2 diabetic mouse models. The exact roles of PAX6-Munc18 axis in beta-cell compensation and decompensation are also investigated by in vivo PAX6 knockdown and overexpression.If the hypothesis is confirmed, this project will provide mechanistic evidence to identify PAX6-Munc18 axis as a novel mechanism that underlies the progression of beta-cell compensation to decompensation which culminates in frank T2DM. Moreover, this study also provides new insights and scientific basis on the development of anti-diabetic therapy by targeting PAX6-Munc18 axis. Overall, this proposed study may be translated into better management strategies of T2DM in future.

title: Molecular characterisation of the host response during antibody-enhanced dengue virus infection
abs: Dengue is the most prevalent arthropod-borne viral disease. Heterotypic secondary dengue virus (DENV) infection is the greatest risk factor for the severe form of the disease, and is characterised by hypovolemic shock from vascular leakage, internal haemorrhage and multi-organ failure. Antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE) posits that non-neutralising or subneutralising antibody levels can opsonise DENV infection in Fc-gamma-receptor bearing myeloid cells, increasing systemic viral burden and pro-inflammatory responses. Indeed, the clinical relevance of ADE is recently supported by our clinical trial and prospective observations from a long-term pediatric cohort in Nicaragua, where we both show that a limited range of cross-reactive antibodies is linked to severe dengue. Elucidating the mechanisms that enable ADE will hence lead to targeted interventions to prevent severe dengue. Besides augmenting viral entry, we found that ADE-mediated DENV infection results in differential virus compartmentalisation compared to direct viral infection that increases viral fusion and replication. Moreover, this entry pathway appears to affect downstream host responses, where transcriptomic differences related to RNA splicing, pro-inflammatory responses and apoptosis between ADE and direct virus infection were observed, despite controlling for virus load within the cells. To systematically unravel the host responses engendered by ADE-mediated DENV infection, we propose in this study to characterise the host responses following ADE-mediated infection in a full spectrum of antigenic loads. This characterisation will include transcriptomic and lipidomic analyses as both host gene expression and lipid re-modification have been shown to play important roles in viral replication. Moreover, this study will examine how ADE affects the host cell antiviral responses through induction of alternative splicing. The specific aims thus include defining the transcriptomic changes in cells that collectively represent the full spectrum of infection intensity following ADE infection, characterisation of the lipid composition of DENV-containing compartments and evaluating how alternative splicing influence ADE-mediated DENV infection.
