title: The interplay of platelets and Toll-like receptors in neutrophil extracellular trap formation and its role in premature cardiovascular disease in systemic lupus erythematosus
abs: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is an autoimmune disease with abnormalities in both the innate and adaptive arms of the immune system. Low-density neurophils (LDNs) present in SLE-derived peripheral blood mononuclear cell fraction readily form neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs), a phenomenon that promotes externalization of modified proteins to trigger loss of immune tolerance and induce endothelial dysfunction. Patients with SLE are at much higher risk of coronary heart disease (CHD) than age- and gender-matched controls, with traditional risk factors underestimating the risk of CHD in SLE patients. It has been shown that ribonucleoprotein-containing immune complexes can induce NET formation in a FcgammaRIIa- and Toll-like receptor 7 (TLR7)-dependent manner. However, resting mature neutrophils do not express TLR7 while platelets have functional TLR7. It has demonstrated by different groups that platelet-TLR7 stimulation mediates formation of platelet-neutrophil aggregates and activated platelets stimulates NET formation. Our preliminary data indicate that LDNs, compared to high-density neutrophils (HDNs), have higher percentage of platelet-neutrophil aggregates and form NETs preferentially to TLR7 stimulation. Overall, these results raise the hypothesis that NET formation in SLE patients is mediated by platelet-TLR7 and neutrophil cross-talk. In this proposal, to more clearly define the pathogenic potential of LDNs in SLE, we will perform cell surface marker and intracellular TLR7 messenger ribonucleic acid analyses of LDNs, lupus and control HDNs. We will also examine the role of platelet-TLR7 on NET formation in TLR7 knockout mice, murine and human SLE. Lastly, we will explore the contribution of LDNs to endothelial dysfunction through assessment of flow-mediated dilation in SLE patients. The mechanisms driving the enhanced capacity of LDNs to generate NETs and the clinical significance of LDNs remain unclear. Through the experiments outlined in this proposal, we will study if TLR7-dependent platelet-neutrophil interactions might lead to increased formation of NETs and premature CHD in SLE.
kw: Systemic lupus erythematosus, Platelets, Toll-like receptors, Neutrophil extracellular traps, Biomarkers, Cardiovascular diseases

title: Understanding the genetic basis of variability associated with CYP3A4/5 enzymatic activity: A pilot study
abs: Over 60% of current prescription drugs are metabolized by the CYP3A4/5 subfamily of enzymes whereby observed interindividual variability in drug effects may be as high as 4- to 13-fold. The high degree of genetic variation at the CYP3A4/5 locus is mainly responsible for the observed interindividual variability. The probe drug, midazolam, has often been employed to determine CYP3A4/5 enzymatic activity. However, the practical use of the midazolam probe test is deterred by the need for repeated blood withdrawals, inconsistency of sampling time points that correlate with CYP3A4/5 activity and lack in reproducibility in ethnically diverse populations. Although several genetic variants in the CYP3A locus have been purported to predict CYP3A4/5 activity, they remain impractical in the Asian context due to clear differences in CYP3A4/5 variant penetrance amongst different ethnicities. This study proposes the use of an unbiased, comprehensive and global approach such as genome-wide association study (GWAS) to uncover germline marker(s) that may be predictive of CYP3A4/5 enzymatic activity. Blood samples will be taken at 1h and 3.5h from a pilot cohort of healthy volunteers (N=150) receiving a single low dose of midazolam. A GWAS analysis will be performed and correlated with midazolam concentrations taken at these time points. Midazolam concentrations determined at these time points were previously shown to significantly correlate with midazolam clearance in the local population. The functional impact of the genomic positive hits on CYP3A4/5 expression will be further assessed using human liver and intestinal tissues. The robustness of these novel marker(s) will also be validated in a pilot cohort of Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML) patients (N=100) who had previously taken imatinib, a putative CYP3A4/5 drug substrate. Ultimately, this study may provide a deeper insight into the genetic factors involved in mediating CYP3A4/5 activity and thereby improve our ability to better predict drug response.
kw: Midazolam, CYP3A4/5, GWAS

title: The functional role of a highly abundant cardiac circular RNA (circRNA) and artificial circRNAs for therapy
abs: Advanced sequencing technology now highlights an abundant and ubiquitous, but previously less known, species of non-coding RNA: circular RNA (circRNA). CircRNAs are single-stranded RNA formed by a covalent closed looped structure generated during gene transcription and largely proposed to control gene expression via sponging of another non-coding RNA species known as microRNA (miRNA). In our genome-wide analysis of circRNA expression in both human and mouse hearts we have identified a highly expressed circRNA named here as circHeart. Because of its specific abundance in cardiomyocytes we hypothesize an important role for circHeart in cardiomyocyte physiology and homeostasis.We have thus far performed fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) to confirm the existence and localization of circHeart. AAV9-mediated RNAi knockdown and overexpression of circHeart in vivo in mice produces a cardiac phenotype requiring further validation. Moreover, disease relevance for circHeart was also tested with the pathological pressure-overload mouse model of transverse aortic constriction. Online tools predict multiple potential miRNA binding sites on circHeart including cardiac-enriched miRNAs. We have assessed for the effect of modulating circHeart on these miRNAs by luciferase reporters and pull-down assays. Our data so far supports an important role for circHeart in cardiomyocyte physiology. We propose to perform follow up experiments to test if and how circHeart functions as an endogenous sponge for cardiac miRNA. Its precise mechanism of action will be delineated. Additionally, we will generate artificial circRNA designed to specifically neutralize pathological disease-relevant miRNAs and test their in vivo therapeutic potential. Newly described circRNA represents a novel avenue for cardiovascular research and holds a real potential for using non-coding RNA as therapeutic targets or novel therapeutic approaches.
kw: Circular RNAs; Cardiovascular diseases; heart failure; microRNAs; non-coding RNAs; therapy

title: Unravelling differences between SMCHD1 mutations for potential therapy development in Facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD)
abs: SMCHD1 is an epigenetic regulator involved in gene repression. We have recently found that mutations in SMCHD1 cause two distinct diseases: facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD) and Bosma arhinia and microphthalmia syndrome (BAMS). FSHD is an adult onset degenerative disease affecting skeletal muscles while BAMS is a rare disease of embryological origins that affects craniofacial development. Patients of one disease do not show symptoms of the other. As an epigenetic factor, SMCHD1 can potentially regulate the expression of hundreds of genes. In this grant, I propose to study the different mutations in FSHD versus BAMS in terms of their biochemical effects on the protein and the downstream targets. Understanding the mechanism of action of these mutations can help us understand these diseases, and importantly, develop potential treatments. Our preliminary results have suggested that FSHD mutations are loss of function whereas BAMS mutations are gain of function. In particular, I propose that the gain of function mutations in BAMS may be used as a means to increase SMCHD1 activity in FSHD patients.
kw: SMCHD1, epigenetics, FSHD, BAMS, craniofacial, muscular dystrophy

title: Unravelling the functional dynamics of monocytes at the maternal-fetal interface of the placenta and its consequences during gestational diabetes
abs: Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM) is defined as a state of glucose intolerance with onset during pregnancy that predisposes towards adverse perinatal outcomes. Recent evidence have documented the placenta, which supports the growth and development of the fetus, to be structurally and functionally altered during GDM. However mechanisms that exacerbate these alterations remain unclear. It is increasingly recognized that diabetes is not a sole metabolic and endocrine disorder, and that a dysregulation in the function of immune cells such as monocytes, which are important for the maintenance of tissue homeostasis and vascular integrity, play a pivotal role in the exacerbation of the disease. Nevertheless, their cellular behavior and homeostatic role in the placental circulation remains unclear. In this proposal, we intend to comprehend the functional dynamics of monocytes in the maternal-fetal interface of the placenta and their role in GDM. We hypothesize that maternal monocytes drive vascular and structural abnormalities in the placenta that result in undesired fetal outcomes during GDM. Furthermore, we propose that the placental environment during GDM functionally programs monocytes to alter their trafficking patterns that exacerbates disease progression. To address these questions, we intend to utilize a combination of transcriptomics, intravital imaging, multicolour flow cytometry, functional assays and genetic modified mice models that target specific subsets of monocytes to comprehend their functional role in the placenta during healthy versus GDM-complicated pregnancies. By providing a strong expertise in immunology and state-of-the-art experimental technologies into the largely unexplored field of pregnancy and GDM, we believe that this integrated approach will unravel novel mechanistic pathways that will pave the way towards potential identification of monocyte associated biomarkers and a better comprehension of the dysregulations that occur during pregnancy and GDM.
kw: Monocytes; Macrophages; Placenta; Trafficking; Gestational Diabetes

title: Translational study of recurrence related oncogenic kinases for potential precision treatment of liver cancer
abs: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the most common type of primary liver cancer and is the second leading cause of cancer-related death worldwide. Once diagnosed with HCC, only 30% of patients are eligible for curative treatments. Even after curative resection in patients with early-stage disease, tumor recurrence is estimated to occur in 70% of patients. Hence, there is an unmet need for understanding of hepatocarcinogenesis and development promising targeted therapy. Kinases have emerged as one of the most intensively pursued targets in cancer pharmacological research. Based on our comprehensive whole genome expression database of HCC patients’ samples, we have identified a panel of HCC overexpressed oncogenic kinases. The hypothesis of this application is to identify and functional characterization of recurrence related oncogenic kinases for effective precision treatment of HCC. Our aims are to understand the role of recurrence related oncogenic kinases in hepatocarcinogenesis and investigate whether targeting these oncogenic kinases could provide effective precision treatment of advanced HCC. Among the panel of HCC overexpressed oncogenic kinases, the expression of MELK, PBK and NEK2 is significantly associated with recurrence and patients’ survival. Interestingly, MELK, PBK and NEK2 are not expressed in most of adult normal tissues, which indicate as a promising therapeutic target of HCC. In this application, we will investigate the role and mechanism of MELK, PBK and NEK2 in different HCC cells and animal models using shRNA knockdown and CRISPR/Cas9 knockout assay. The therapeutic effects of small molecules targeting these recurrence related oncogenic kinases and their combination will also be investigated using in vitro HCC cells and in vivo orthotopic mice models or patient-perived xenografts (PDXs). The results from these proposed studies will understand the important role of recurrence related oncogenic kinases in hepatocarcinogenesis and develop kinase inhibitors as personalized targeted therapeutic strategies for advanced HCC.
kw: Translational study, Recurrence, Oncogenic kinase, Precision medicine, Liver cancer

title: Investigating the functional role and mechanism of action of MBNL1 in cancer.
abs: Post-transcriptional gene expression is regulated via multiple mRNA-processing mechanisms, such as alternative splicing, polyadenylation, transcript stability or localization. Deregulation of any such mechanism may lead to cancer. Muscleblind like-1 (MBNL1) is an mRNA-processing factor that binds target mRNAs and regulates alternative splicing, polyadenylation, stabilization and localization. In our recent transcriptomic study in gastric cancer and in several other published studies in other cancer types MBNL1 has been identified as a tumor-specific splice regulator. We also observed from our dataset and other publicly available data that mRNA levels of MBNL1 is down-regulated relative to normal tissue in gastric, lung and colorectal cancer. The down-regulation of MBNL1 is correlated with poor overall-survival in gastric and lung cancer patients. Furthermore, exon5+ transcripts of MBNL1 is preferentially expressed in tumors, whereas exon5- transcripts are found in normal tissue. While MBNL1 has been linked to cancer in several studies, none have investigated the functional role and mechanism of action of MBNL1 in cancer. In this proposal we hypothesize that: a) down-regulation of MBNL1 expression contributes to tumor progression; b) MBNL1 exon5+ isoform expressed in tumors functions antagonistically to MBNL1 exon5- isoform expressed in normal tissue and contributes to tumor progression; and c) that down-regulation of MBNL1 expression as well as expression of exon5+ MBNL1 transcripts leads to tumor progression by regulating changes in mRNA-processing (splicing, polyadenylation and or stability) of its downstream target mRNAs. To this end we aim to i) investigate the role of MBNL1 down-regulation in gastric, colorectal and lung cancer, ii) investigate the function of exon5+ MBNL1 tumor associated isoform and iii) elucidate the molecular mechanism of MBNL1 function in cancer. This proposal will establish the functional role and molecular mechanism of MBNL1 in cancer; the findings from this work will be utilized for designing therapeutic strategies in subsequent studies.
kw: MBNL1, mRNA-processing, alternative splicing, gastric cancer, colorectal cancer, lung cancer

title: Determining the Regulatory Role of RNA-binding Protein in Energy Homeostasis of Brown and White Adipose Tissues
abs: As the population prevalence of obesity is rising, there is an upsurge of interest in adipocyte biology. An attractive therapeutic target for obesity is brown adipose tissue (BAT), because of its high-energy expenditure capability and the recent discovery of BAT in human adults. My long-term goal is to determine the regulatory mechanism governing BAT development. Recent findings from other and our groups have shown that RNA binding proteins (RBPs) are emerging as novel regulators in adipose biology by targeting a set of mRNA transcripts and controlling their posttranscriptional processing, but our understanding of RBPs in adipose tissue is still at its infancy. Using high-throughput profiling across different mouse adipose tissues, we have identified Y-box-binding protein 2, Ybx2, as a novel post-transcriptional regulator in BAT. Loss-of-Ybx2 resulted in impaired BAT-selective program in vitro and in vivo, while its overexpression promotes BAT markers in white adipocyte cultures. We have shown that Ybx2 preferentially interacts with a set of genes enriched in mitochondria, and the majority of these targets are down-regulated in the absence of Ybx2, suggesting a mRNA-stabilizing function of Ybx2. Based on these observations, we hypothesize that Ybx2 regulates BAT function by enhancing the stability of its mRNA targets. To test this hypothesis, we will determine the function of Ybx2 in BAT development and function (Aim1), white fat browning in vivo (Aim2) and the detailed molecular mechanisms of how Ybx2 functions (Aim3). Understanding the mechanism underlying BAT development and function is no doubt an important frontier in the battle against obesity. The proposed experiments, through studying the central post-transcriptional regulator Ybx2, will advance our understanding of fat biology; the knowledge gained may expand our potential strategies to manipulate adipose energy homeostasis and improve human metabolic health.
kw: Brown fat, brown adipose tissue, adipocyte, brown adipocyte

title: Genome wide in vivo functional genetic screen for modulators of NAFLD
abs: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is the chronic liver disease of the 21st century, with already about 1 billion people suffering from it. It is estimated that it will soon be the number 1 reason for liver transplantation worldwide. NAFLD includes a variety of histopathological findings ranging from simple steatosis to non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) to cirrhosis. Despite its seemingly unstoppable rise, the mechanism behind disease manifestation and progression remains unclear and so far no therapeutic options rather than lifestyle modifications are available. Furthermore correct diagnosis and staging relies on invasive liver biopsy. Therefore, there is an urgent need to understand the underlying pathogenic mechanisms in order to develop new innovative therapies and new non-invasive diagnostic approaches. We will use a functional genetic approach to unravel NAFLD development and progression. A genome wide RNAi screen with inducible expression of the hairpins in the western diet mouse model, complete in vivo will pinpoint pathways involved in NAFLD. This approach holds also the promise to identify points for therapeutic intervention. In addition we will investigate the potential of exosome derived RNA signatures for diagnosing and staging NAFLD. Finally our results will be validated for application to the human situation, using humanized mice.
kw: NAFLD, RNAi, mouse, exosome

title: Exploiting the metabolic vulnerabilities of lung cancer stem cells for therapeutic interventions
abs: Cellular metabolism is increasingly recognized as a key driving force for the phenotypic adaptations of tumor cells. Recent landmark studies have characterized the metabolic alterations between normal and neoplastic cells, particularly the Warburg effect for sustaining proliferation, energy and redox balance. Some cancers also exhibit strong requirements for certain amino acids such as glutamine and serine. Tumors are, however, highly heterogeneous. The metabolic differences between phenotypically distinct carcinoma cells within tumors remain unexplored. Cancer stem cells (CSCs), which initiate tumor growth and promote resistance, may have metabolic requirements and adaptations that are substantially different from bulk differentiated cells. They are likely to bear metabolic alterations which contribute towards tumor-initiation and resistance to front-line therapies. Focusing on lung cancer, to unravel the metabolic complexities of heterogeneous tumor cell populations, we employ advanced metabolomics, fluxome, and genome engineering technologies to accurately quantify and trace metabolites to uncover metabolic modules which are distinct to CSCs. We will investigate the mechanistic manner by which they produce and utilize metabolites, and understand the functional consequences of these metabolic pathway activities. In particular, we first focus on the role of the one-carbon pathway and branched-chain amino acid metabolism which we identified as key regulators of tumor-initiation. To further uncover new essential metabolic processes in CSCs, we will employ CRISPR-based knockout screens for targeting over 1600 metabolic genes. This will reveal clinically relevant metabolic targets for which we will test with currently available small molecule inhibitors. In the long-term, we aim to develop novel clinically-viable pharmacologic agents for disrupting their activity. This proposal will help create the first comprehensive blueprints for functional metabolic modules in CSCs and connect metabolic reprogramming to disease progression. Uncovering metabolic dependencies of CSCs will unlock novel avenues for exploiting their therapeutic vulnerabilities, discovering new classes of pharmacologic agents, and improve disease outcome.
kw: lung cancer; cancer stem cells; metabolism

title: Simultaneous Profiling of Circulating Tumor Cells and Tumor in relation to Immunotherapeutic Response in Cancer
abs: Immune checkpoint inhibitors are promising in cancer patients but responses are difficult to predict. Tumor re-biopsies are limited by tissue and access issues. Peripheral blood immunophenotyping is limited to only peripheral immune cells (PIC) given the paucity of circulating tumour cells (CTC). This proposal seeks to integrate analysis of CTC and tumor to predict outcomes from immunotherapy treatment underpinned by a clinical study: CTC-IMMUNITY.Specific Aim 1: Simultaneous Profiling of PIC, CTC and CTC clusters in relation to Response and Prognosis. Using label free enrichment methods for CTC from blood, we hypothesize that the relative expression of cancer and immunologic proteins in CTC, CTC clusters and PICs can be profiled, and are relevant to clinical outcomes. In patients undergoing immunotherapy, blood samples will be enriched for CTCs, CTC clusters and PICs and subjected to RNA expression analysis. Differential RNA expression from each component and relevant relationships will be assessed in relation to data from CTC-IMMUNITY (immunotherapy response). Specific Aim 2: Assessment of Germline Polymorphisms that Contribute to Immunotherapy Resistance and Prognosis. Germline polymorphisms have been described to contribute to drug resistance. We hypothesize that germline polymorphisms contribute to immunotherapeutic resistance as well. From the same blood draw for CTC enrichment during PDL-1/PD1 therapy, we will also extract germline DNA to sequence for BIM del polymorphism and polymorphic variants of PDL-1/PD-1 that may contribute to resistance. This will be correlated to tumor response to PDL-1/PD-1 inhibitors treatment in CTC-IMMUNITY. The 2 studies above will build on the prior CSA that has successfully contributed to bringing to market a local CTC isolation platform. They will allow the testing of additional applications for the CTC platform and the development of novel CTC assays for cancer applications. This effort will leverage on Singapore’s strengths in medical engineering and biology.
kw: Cancer, Biomarkers

title: Wnt signalling pathway biomarker for diagnosis and therapy of soft tissue tumours.
abs: Misregulation of Wnt signaling leads to a variety of disease including diverse cancers. Recent studies have identified many tumor types that have over-expression of Wnts. Therefore, targeting the production and secretion of Wnts may have therapeutic benefit. Consequently, new agents targeting the upstream component of the Wnt pathway have been developed collaboratively in our lab. Despite these developments, there is still a paucity of reliable tools or biomarkers to identify and better characterize Wnt driven tumors. Expanding on recent preliminary findings that identified WLS high expression in certain subsets of bone tumors, through the utility of the novel biomarker YJ5, this proposal intends to fill significant deficits in our understanding of the upstream mechanism in soft tissue tumors. Here we wish to extend this study by addressing a number of issues and questions. Firstly, confirming and validating the presence of aberrant Wnt expression in soft tissue tumors using both genomic analysis of functional Wnt mutations as well as novel antibodies for immunohistochemical analysis. Secondly, studying if this aberration in Wnt signaling affects cancer biology by correlating this data with clinical data (i.e. chemo response, percentage necrosis, metastasis, survival rates). Thirdly, investigating the response of these selected tumours to novel Wnt inhibitors in the murine model both in isolation and in combination with conventional drug therapy.
kw: Wnt, YJ5, Sarcoma

title: Improving Outcomes for Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest through a National, Living, Learning, Pre-hospital Emergency Care Laboratory
abs: BackgroundSingapore has a single provider Pre-hospital Emergency Care (PEC) system with more than 1800 Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrests (OHCA)/year. The current CSA funding allowed us to conduct implementation research that has increased OHCA survival from 2.5% (2001) to 11.0% currently, with potential for further improvements.ObjectivesOur overall aim is to increase survival for OHCA. The specific aims of the study are to develop and evaluate the effectiveness of a bundle of ambulance-based interventions which include: manual defibrillation by intermediate life-support providers, high performance team cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), impedance threshold device (ITD), and intravenous amiodarone. HypothesisWe hypothesize that this ambulance-based implementation bundle will result in an increase in pre-hospital return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) from 5% currently to 10% in intervention sites (ambulance divisions) over 4 years, compared to concurrent controls. We also hypothesize that the survival rate for the intervention sites will increase by 5% compared to controls (witnessed, shockable arrest). Methodology and ApproachThis will be a stepped-wedge, adaptive design, prospective, ambulance-based implementation trial of 4 ambulance intervention strategies with concurrent controls. The research design entails a stepped-wedge implementation of interventions randomised to the 4 SCDF Divisions in Singapore. A multiple adaptive design will incorporate the use of a combination of adaptive group sequential design and drop-the-losers design. A clinical trial simulation will be conducted to evaluate the performance of the resultant multiple adaptive design at the planning stage. A decision algorithm will be applied to decide the intervention bundle to be implemented at each 12-month wedge in the trial. The controls will entail concurrent SCDF divisions not receiving the same intervention. We will compare any incremental improvement in ROSC and survival between intervention and controls in multiple interim analyses.
kw: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, Stepped wedge design, prehospital emergency care, Data model

title: FAILURE OF PODOCYTE REGENERATION UNDERLIES DIABETIC KIDNEY DISEASE
abs: Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) is the leading cause of chronic kidney disease worldwide. A hallmark of DKD is a decrease in glomerular podocyte number. Hyperglycemia causes podocyte loss. Neither Angiotensin-converting-enzyme inhibitors (ACE-i) nor Angiotensin-II receptor blockers (ARB) increase podocyte numbers in DKD. Parietal epithelial cells (PEC) and cells of renin lineage (CoRL) are sources of local adult podocyte stem/progenitor cells. In podocyte-depleted states, PEC and CoRL have been shown to transdifferentiate into podocytes in vitro and in vivo. However, in DKD mouse models, our preliminary data suggest PEC and CoRL readiness to increase podocyte number are blunted.Our first hypothesis: in a diabetic environment, the initial loss of podocytes remains depleted because hyperglycemia impairs podocyte progenitors transdifferentiation to replace them. Firstly, we aim to show PEC and CoRL fail to replace lost podocytes in DKD in 2 different dual reporter mice. Each mouse simultaneously fate maps 2 different individual cell types in the same kidney (PEC-Podo and CoRL-Podo reporter mice). Hyperglycemia is induced in both strains with streptozotocin. Secondly, we aim to show PEC and CoRL do not respond to ACE-inhibition in DKD, by administering Enalapril (or Hydralazine as control) to diabetic PEC-Podo and CoRL-Podo reporter mice after 20 weeks of hyperglycemia when podocyte loss occurs. The response of labeled PEC and CoRL to transdifferentiate to a podocyte fate will be evaluated. Our second hypothesis: hyperglycemia limits transdifferentiation of cultured PEC and CoRL towards a podocyte fate. We aim to demonstrate, following podocyte loss induced by hyperglycemia, cultured mouse PEC and CoRL fail to transdifferentiate into podocytes via separate novel 3D microphysiological systems (MPS). Glucose concentration in the media will be increased to induce podocyte loss, followed by addition of labeled PEC or CoRL progenitors to 3D MPS and then measure their stemness towards podocyte fate under normal/high glucose concentrations.
kw: DIABETES MELLITUS, DIABETIC NEPHROPATHY, STEM CELLS, PODOCYTES, REGENERATION, GLOMERULUS

title: Rational Therapeutic Combinations for Wnt Driven Cancers
abs: Pathologic activation of Wnt signaling is found in cancers, fibrosis and other diseases; hence there is considerable interest in blocking Wnt signaling to achieve therapeutic benefit. There are 19 Wnts that couple to different receptors, to activate multiple downstream pathways. At Duke-NUS we have pursued a novel strategy to block all (canonical and non-canonical) Wnt dependent pathways concomitantly by preventing the secretion of all Wnts. In collaboration with Experimental Therapeutics Centre, A*Star we have developed novel, highly potent small molecules that inhibit porcupine, a key enzyme required for secretion of all 19 Wnts. One of these small molecules, ETC-159 has shown remarkable efficacy in pre-clinical models with genetically defined lesions. ETC-159 is Singapore’s first anti-cancer drug to advance to Phase I Clinical Trial. To expand the utility of ETC-159 and other Wnt pathway inhibitors, I propose to pursue the following three Aims: 1) I propose to identify pathways that cooperate with Wnt signaling to drive tumor growth and hence develop rational therapeutic combinations for Wnt pathway inhibitors. 2) While the ?-catenin pathway is well studied, understanding of the “non-canonical” Wnts, their specific signaling pathways remains elusive. Exploiting the pan-Wnt activity of ETC-159, I will elucidate ?-catenin independent transcriptional networks. This will identify novel markers and provide novel targets for tumors and other diseases with activated non-canonical Wnt signaling. 3) Activation of Wnt/?-catenin signaling pathway is implicated as a key mechanism of resistance in platinum resistant cancers. Given the key role of Wnt signaling in maintenance of stem cells, I will test if inhibition of Wnt signaling can reverse resistance to platinum based therapies. Successful completion of these studies will advance our basic understanding of how Wnt signaling drives cancers, and benefit Singapore’s drug development efforts by expanding the therapeutic applications of ETC-159 and identifying novel targets for future drug development.
kw: Wnt singaling, Cancer Therapeutics

title: Heart Repair through Direct Cardiac Reprogramming
abs: Direct reprogramming of human fibroblasts into induced cardiomyocytes (iCMs) offers a great therapeutic approach for cardiovascular disease. Inefficiency of human iCMs generation is one of the main hurdles to translate direct cardiac reprogramming into clinical application. To address this gap in knowledge, we have now established a platform for direct cardiac reprogramming of human fibroblasts into functional iCM. We propose to apply this platform to develop an efficient approach for the generation of functional human iCMs through a systemic screen of both signaling pathway modulators and reprogramming promoting factors. We will define a chemically defined medium and dissect signaling pathways supporting direct cardiac reprogramming (Aim 1). In addition, novel cardiac reprogramming factors identified (Aim 2) will be consolidated with signaling pathway modulates to develop an optimal cardiac reprogramming approach which will be assessed a myocardial infarction (MI) animal model for heart repair in vivo(Aim3). Collectively, these studies will expand our knowledge of how signaling pathways and cardiac reprogramming factors impact on cardiac cell fate transition. Our aims will: 1) develop a simple and low-cost recipe of chemically defined medium; 2) identify novel small molecules and cardiac reprogramming factors that modulate direct cardiac reprogramming; 3) implicate a novel approach for cardiac regenerative medicine.
kw: cardiomyocyte, direct reprogramming, transcription factor, regeneration

title: Characterization of the functions of Tjp1 and Tjp2 in the heart
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: The mammalian heart loses its regenerative capacity shortly after birth. While adult cardiomyocytes (CMs) have long been thought to be unable to regenerate, recent work has revealed a limited regenerative potential, which, however, is inadequate to cope with a massive loss of CMs seen after myocardial infarct (MI). Current treatment in survival patients is limited at managing the consequences of CM loss, although a few regenerative approaches are in clinical trials. We recently found that CM specific inducible deletion of Tjp1 activates the cell cycle in non-CMs and CMs, whereas inactivation of Tjp2 only activates non-CMs. We hypothesize that Tjp1 and Tjp2 supress cell activation by inhibiting ErbB4 signalling. While Erk, Stat3 and Akt are activated in both Tjp1 and Tjp2 deficient heart, Wnt signalling is only activated in the absence of Tjp1. Inactivation of Tjp1 following MI shows beneficial effects on heart function. Here, we propose to confirm these preliminary findings and characterize the role of Tjp1 and Tjp2 in the heart and the underlying molecular mechanisms resulting in the observed phenotypes. If inactivation of Tjp1 is required or even sufficient to promote regeneration and improve heart function after injury, Adeno-associated virus (AVV) mediated silencing of Tjp1 could provide novel therapeutic approaches for MI and heart failure (HF).Our aims are to i) confirm the activation of the cell cycle in adult CMs in response to Tjp1 deletion and determine if this leads to CM proliferation, ii) characterize the mechanisms by which Tjp1 and not Tjp2 suppresses CM activation and iii) confirm the stabilization of heart function by inactivating Tjp1 after MI, and analyze the effect of Tjp1 and Tjp2 deficiency on excitation contraction coupling, heart development and activated non-CMs.
kw: heart regeneration, heart remodeling, cardiomyoctye, myocadial infract, intercalated disc

title: A comprehensive survey of the interactome inside the cytoplasm of red blood cell infected by Plasmodium parasite
abs: Plasmodium have a complex life cycle and all the symptoms of malaria are caused when they develop within the human erythrocytes. The parasite must refurbish its host-cell in order to stabilize the host-cell cytoskeleton, to acquire nutrients and to ultimately promote virulence. For this, Plasmodium export proteins in the host-cell cytosol which form an interaction network involving parasite and host proteins. Using export motif identified in silico,increasing data provided partial information on the identity of the malaria proteins exported in the host and highlighted that exported proteins are mostly unique to Plasmodium with no further functional annotation. To date, only a few exported proteins have been characterized and were proposed to be involved in functions that promote parasite virulence. Importantly, knock-out experiments reported that these proteins are mostly not essential for parasite development in vitro. The role of the remaining exported proteins is unknown but it is likely that a fraction of the exportome is involved in parasite survival via a complex network of functional interactions. Using proteomic approach, we have mapped the proteome of five Plasmodium species, revealing its exportome. Here, using these results, we propose to identify 1) the subset of exported proteins conserved across the genus and essential for the parasite development, 2) the interaction networks of these proteins with parasite and host proteins and 3) identify the interactions essential for parasite survival. Reaching a fine understanding of the interactome in the host cell could provide new therapeutic avenues less prone to the resistance that has rendered current antimalarial treatment ineffective. Indeed, the blockage of essential interactions between Plasmodium and the host proteins with strategies that target the host protein could be the downfall of the parasite with a lower likelihood to develop resistance than approaches that would target parasite molecules.
kw: Malaria, Pathogenesis, Host cell remodeling, Exported proteins, Protein interactions

title: DUSP4 regulates STING-mediated type I interferon production in infection and cancer
abs: Microbial DNA or DNA derived from cancer cells in the cytosol induces potent innate immune responses by inducing the expression of type I interferons (IFNs) and the transcription of type I IFNs is regarded as the dominant response upon the detection of cytosolic DNA. Activation of STING leads to phosphorylation of IRF3 by TBK1 for the production of type I IFNs. Therefore, the STING-TBK1-IRF3 signaling is central for the induction of type I IFNs in response to cytosolic DNA of pathogen- and self-origin. Elucidating the mechanisms that govern the activation and inactivation of this pathway is essential for understanding host-virus interaction, the initiation of anti-tumor innate and adaptive immunity and for targeting this pathway to develop strategies to treat human diseases including viral infection, cancer, as well as autoimmune diseases that are caused by aberrant type I IFN response. However, how this pathway is negatively regulated is unclear. Our preliminary study on a molecule known as DUSP4 demonstrates that this molecule may negatively regulates STING-mediate type I IFN response by inhibiting the activation of both TBK1-IRF3 and ERK. We hypothesize that DUSP4 inhibits STING-mediated signaling including TBK1-IRF3 and ERK to suppress the expression of type I IFNs in response to cytosolic DNA derived from microbial pathogens or cancer cells, thereby playing important roles in anti-microbial and anti-tumor immune responses. In this project, we will address the regulatory roles of DUSP4 in microbial infection and in anti-tumor immune response. Knowledge gained from this study will shed new light on physiological function of DUSP4 in immune response to viral infection and in cancer immunology, which will help for the development of DUSP4-targeted novel therapeutic methods for treatment of human disease such as cancer.
kw: DUSP, STING, type I interferon, ERK, DNA virus, cancer

title: A Novel Centrifugal Blood Pump with Low Blood Damage
abs: The centrifugal pump is widely used as implantable (LVADs) and extracorporeal (ECMO and heart-lung machine) blood pumps. Blood damage occurs to a substantial number of pump recipients, with serious consequences, due to 2 mechanisms. Firstly, fast moving pump impellers impose high fluid stresses to cause hemolysis and thrombosis. Secondly, foreign surfaces causes protein adsorption, which leads to coagulation cascades. Blood damage can lead systemic inflammation and organ damage, and thromboembolic events that include stroke, and clot-associated device failure. As a clinical example, severe hemolysis occur to 7% of ECMO patients, and causes 6x increase in mortality rate.Superhydrophobic (SHP) surfaces can resolve blood damage due to both mechanisms. SHP is achieved with nano-structures on hydrophobic material, and is an enhanced repelling of water, such that blood can slip past the SHP surface with little stress, thus reducing hemolysis. SHP traps a layer of air that is thermodynamically difficult to remove, and reduces the surface area of structures in contact with blood, thus reducing protein adsorption. Our strategy of coating the tips of the nano-structures with anti-adsorption material can further reduce protein, while maintaining the trapped air layer. We recently pioneered the idea of using SHP surfaces to reduce blood damage, and now propose to apply this concept to the ECMO blood pump. We may be able to apply the concept to LVADs as well through the process. The use of SHP will drastically alter the way centrifugal pumps function, and thus require careful re-designing. We will perform computational flow simulations to obtain an optimal design, before fabricating and bench-testing the pump. Efforts to develop the SHP pump head as well as a magnetic levitated pump driver system are proposed. Finally, animal studies will be performed. The ultimate goal is the commercialization of the pump to bring the benefit to patients.
kw: Centrifugal Blood Pump, Thrombosis, Hemolysis, Protein Adsorption, Superhydrophobicity, Anti-adosorption Surface

title: Drop-Screen: A functional screening platform to investigate mechanisms of innate resistance, and metastasis for personalised therapeutic intervention
abs: Background: Successful implementation of precision oncology requires treatment individualization not only taking into account patient and tumor factors, but also tumor heterogeneity and evolution over time. Recent studies have demonstrated the existence of intra-tumor heterogeneity (ITH) in various cancers. These studies uncover the genetic and epigenetic heterogeneity at clonal and sub-clonal levels within tumors that have been suggested to drive treatment resistance and metastasis.Hypothesis: Treatment failure in cancer stems from ITH, where the different sub-clonal populations respond differently to chemotherapeutic or even targeted drugs. This is likely to be based on their inherent heterogeneity in their molecular signatures that define their response to treatment. Novel, comprehensive approaches are therefore required to identify and functionally characterize ITH at the single cell level, and to rapidly screen for patient-optimized drugs.Specific Aims: 1) Design and develop a novel, rapid droplet-based highthroughput single cell screening (HTS) platform (“Drop-Screen”); 2) Isolate and characterize individual clonal populations of treatment resistant, and metastatic OSCC and CRC cells; 3) Investigate and functionally validate gene signatures, biomarkers identified in resistant or metastatic clonesStudy design: An integrated microfluidic platform (Drop-Screen) for high throughput single cell drug screening will be developed to rapidly screen for cancer drugs, individually tailored for on-time personalized therapy. With continuous flow real time analysis, this system will be able to determine single cell drug response with efficiency ~1000 cells per second. This system will therefore be capable to predict optimized drugs or combinations based on individual patient’s tumor profile and heterogeneity. Importantly the Drop-Screen method allows for the isolation and comprehensive functional and genomic characterization of rare populations of tumor cells that are innately resistant to therapy or prone to metastatic transformation. Drop-Screen will also aid in the identification of biomarkers, and the underlying molecular, mechanisms that drive treatment failure and metastasis.
kw: Personalized theraputics, Single cell analysis, Real time drug screening, Systems Engineering, Precision medicine, Integrative Microfluidics

title: The therapeutic potential of IL11 monoclonal antibody in treating renal fibrosis
abs: The common manifestation of chronic kidney diseases (CKD) is renal fibrosis. Despite the serious hazard and high prevalence of CKD, the existing therapies are ineffective and cause serious side effects. Thus, there is an unmet medical need for new therapeutic approaches to treat renal fibrosis. We recently discovered that 1) interleukin-11 (IL11) is a point of signalling convergence of major pro-fibrotic factors; 2) IL11 induces renal fibrosis both in vitro and in vivo, and 3) IL11 signalling is required for key pro-fibrotic factors to exert its fibrotic phenotype. These findings suggest the potential therapeutic strategy of IL11 inhibition in treating renal fibrosis. The long term goal is to develop new IL11 antibody-based drug that can be both effective and safe in treating renal fibrosis and improve renal function in CKD patients. The objective here is to investigate the therapeutic potential of IL11 monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) in treating renal fibrosis in mouse disease models. Our central hypothesis is that IL11 is a crucial pro-fibrotic factor in the CKD pathogenesis and that IL11 is amenable to therapeutic targeting for CKD management. Guided by our preliminary data, the goal of this application will be achieved by three specific aims: 1) To screen and validate IL11 mAbs in vitro; 2) To study the pharmacokinetics and efficacy of lead IL11 mAbs in mouse disease models; and 3) To elucidate the transcriptional and translational regulations involved in renal fibrosis progression and the ability of IL11 mAbs to modulate these regulations. The proposed research is both innovative and significant because the knowledge obtained from the successful investigation of both the regulation of the renal fibrosis progression and the efficacy of IL11 mAbs in treating renal fibrosis could potentially be translated into development of an effective and safer IL11 antibody-based drug in the future.

title: Characterization of the translational regulation of dengue antiviral response by G3BP1, G3BP2 and CAPRIN1
abs: One third of the world population is at risk of dengue and millions of dengue cases are reported worldwide every year. Efficacious therapeutics to treat dengue infection are not available. One promising avenue for therapeutic development is to revitalise the host innate immune system that dengue virus (DENV) has evolved to inhibit. For this goal, our group utilized RNA chromatography combined with quantitative mass spectrometry and discovered that DENV subgenomic flaviviral RNA (sfRNA) binds to host G3BP1, G3BP2, and CAPRIN1 proteins. This sequestration results in the impairment of anti-viral interferon (IFN) stimulated mRNA translation. In this proposal, we seek to understand the mechanism for the translational regulation by G3BP1, G3BP2, and CAPRIN1 in host anti-viral IFN response. In order to achieve this understanding, we will accomplish each of the following aims. The specific aims are I) to characterize the mechanisms by which G3BP1, G3BP2, and CAPRIN1 promote IFN stimulated mRNA translation II) to perform structure-function analysis of G3BP1, G3BP2, and CAPRIN1 in IFN stimulated mRNA translation and III) to identify drug candidates that disrupt sfRNA-protein interactions. In the first aim, we will perform RNA sequencing and ribosome profiling to identify cellular factors and cis-acting elements that are regulated by G3BP1, G3BP2, and CAPRIN1 with or without IFN stimulation. In the second aim, we will generate several plasmids encoding various G3BP1, G3BP2, and CAPRIN1 wild type and mutant proteins. These proteins will be expressed in siRNA mediated G3BP1, G3BP2, and CAPRIN1 knocked down cells and their roles in IFN stimulated mRNA translation will be characterized. Finally, we will employ time-resolved fluorescence resonance energy transfer (TR-FRET) assay to screen compounds that disrupt sfRNA-protein interactions and thus develop novel tools to combat DENV infection. We envision that the pharmacological disruption of sfRNA-protein interactions will restore host immune response and restrict viral replication.
kw: Dengue virus, molecular virology, innate immunity, RNA biology, protein biochemistry

title: Digital Real-Time PCR (dqPCR) – A New Paradigm for Telomere Length Measurement
abs: Telomere length (TL) is emerging as a useful integrated biomarker for age-associated disease and cancer, but so far TL measurement methods are laborious, requires large amounts of material and not amenable to high-throughput studies. We propose the novel digital real-time PCR (dqPCR) method, which allows simple, rapid, measurements of TL distributions in multiple samples. In Specific Aim 1: Develop the dqPCR method for telomere length distribution measurement, we will make use of limited dilution to confine individual (digital) telomere in nanoliter chambers within a microfluidic device. Next, qPCR will be conducted to measure the telomeric repeats within each telomere, which translates to TL of each chromosome when compared to a calibration standard. Development of dqPCR will set a new paradigm for simple, rapid, and accurate measurement of TL distribution as a biomarker in disease and population-wide studies.In Specific Aim 2: Diagnose Alternative Lengthening of Telomeres (ALT) in cancer cells with dqPCR, we hypothesize that the broad distribution of telomere lengths and presence of extrachromosomal telomeric repeats (ECTR) are specific biomarkers of ALT mechanism in cancer cells. dqPCR will be used to measure variances in TL and presence of ECTR in cancer cells. A set of criteria will be established to diagnose ALT from non-ALT status in samples based on dqPCR results. This simple ALT diagnosis method could be used to stratify patients for telomere-based drug treatments.In Specific Aim 3: Perform drug screening to target ALT using dqPCR, we hypothesize that dqPCR can be used to monitor the molecular symptoms of ALT during drug treatment. dqPCR will be used to measure TL distribution in cancer cells that are cultured with candidate ALT drugs, to evaluate the efficacy of these drugs in inhibiting ALT. This platform could be used to screen for ALT drugs that are not widely available today.
kw: telomere, microfluidics, cancer, digital PCR, aging, biotechnology

title: Establishing new single cell microfluidic assay to dissect the evolutionary genomics and transcriptomics changes in pancreatic cancer during disease progression
abs: Pancreatic cancer has unique molecular phenotype in Asian populations. Metastatic spread and resistance to therapy are the leading causes of pancreatic cancer death. Targeted therapy was selected for individual patient after analyzing the primary tumor for the expression or genomic status of a specific molecular target. However, this is often hampered by resistance to therapy that is driven by the tumor heterogeneity and emergence of tumor subclone after selection pressure of a therapy. Due to the complex heterogeneity, bulk tumor cell analysis failed to provide detailed insights on the evolving genomics and transcriptomics changes during disease progression. To address this, we hypothesize that the co-measurement of both genomic and transcriptional signatures at the single cell level is needed to accurately assess transcriptional and phenotypic consequences of genomic changes in cancer. We envisage that by dissecting the evolving mutation and expression changes of individual cancer cell during disease progression, it allows us to identify potential new biomarker and therapeutic targets for pancreatic cancer. Though recent advances in single-cell sequencing have created new possibilities to characterize intra-tumor heterogeneity and dissect clonal diversity during cancer progression, existing technology is hampered by incremental cost, low throughput and laborious procedures.We aim to achieve the followings:1) Establishing a new microfluidic assay for concurrent evaluation of transcriptomic and genomic analysis of the same single cell.2) Applying the established assay on single cells isolated from pancreatic tumor and circulating tumor cells collected at different treatment cycles and disease progression stages to delineate the evolving tumor genomics diversity and transcriptomic changes under the selection pressure of therapy and cancer progression; Our work integrates innovative new technology development and provides novel biological insights for new biomarker and drug discovery in pancreatic cancer. Our technology and discovery carry the great promise to extend into various commercialization programs.
kw: Microfluidic assay, Single cell, Concurrent genomics and transcriptomics evaluation, Evolutionary cancer changes, Pancreatic cancer

title: Translating circulating extracellular RNA into noninvasive measurements of pancreatic health during diabetes progression
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: We propose to develop a quantitative molecular assay to identify the prevalence and changes in levels of pancreas specific circulating RNA during the pathogenesis of metabolic diseases, specifically diabetes. Circulating nucleic acids found in plasma have been shown to originate from apoptotic and necrotic cells, and relates directly to cellular turnover rates. While circulating cell-free DNA (cfDNA) levels, especially those of tumor origin, have found uses in the form of liquid biopsy for cancer patients; circulating RNA remains largely a class of under-explored and under-utilized biomarkers. RNA, which, unlike DNA, are expressed at levels that differs from organ to organ in the body, and can thus be used to target specific organs of interest. In our previous work, we showed that genes whose expression is highly specific to tissue types can be detected in circulating RNA via high throughput sequencing. Using a combination of tissue specific amplification strategy and a molecular barcoding approach to label single RNA molecules means that a diverse range of desired pancreatic specific transcripts can be screened simultaneously from a single plasma sample. Quantitative measurements of pancreatic transcripts in plasma has the potential to quickly and reliably indicate turnover of alpha and beta cell types, and can double up as a rapid way of monitoring treatment impacts down to the cellular level. Evaluation of circulating tissue specific RNA in diabetes will be a stepping stone towards finding potential application in a wider variety of metabolic linked diseases.
kw: Extracellular RNA

title: Aversive learning and memory under stress: a neuroimaging study
abs: In rapidly urbanizing societies, individuals are increasingly exposed to chronic and acute psychosocial stress. Associations learned during extreme stress may result in debilitating emotional responses in posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), yet the mechanisms by which this occurs are unclear. One possibility is that fear memories that are derived from aversive experiences may also be applied to nonhazardous situations in PTSD patients. In this proposal, we seek to investigate the neuropsychological mechanisms underlying aversive learning under stress using a neuroimaging approach combined with a novel learning and memory task. We predict that stress augments aversive but not appetitive learning and facilitates the overgeneralization of aversive memories. Based on the stress induced deliberation-to-intuition (SIDI) model Dr. Yu proposed, we further predict that stress modulates the emotion responses in subcortical regions and deliberative processes in the prefrontal cortex. We will further examine how stress modulates brain network during resting state and how it predicts subsequent performance. Humans inevitably have to perform in situations when the stakes are extremely high, for example in emergency rooms. Thus, enhancing individuals’ resistance to stress is an impressing issue. Stressful situations may ultimately lead to increased threat-related associations in healthy and pathologically anxious individuals. The present work aims to precisely delineate the impact of stress upon aversive and appetitive conditioning and the underlying neural mechanisms. Given the enormous and growing psychological, social, and economic impact of stress-related disorders, our work is of clear value in helping researchers tackle stress-related diseases, including PTSD, anxiety disorder, and schizophrenia.
kw: stress, Decision Making, learning, memory, fmri

title: Hybrid PET-MRI imaging of cardiovascular system from vulnerable plaques to infarct tissue for improved care of STEMI patients
abs: Acute myocardial infarction (AMI), a leading cause of death and disability worldwide, occurs when rupture or erosion of a coronary atheromata leads to thrombus formation and sudden occlusion of a major epicardial coronary artery. Mere identification of atheromatous plaques is insufficient as many atheromatous plaques are stable and not prone to rupture or erosion. Tools are needed to better identify vulnerable plaques as the presence of these plaques may indicate an increased risk of AMI, therefore prompting escalation of medical treatment or targeted mechanical stabilization of vulnerable plaques by selective coronary stenting. However, present modalities to identify vulnerable coronary plaques are mostly invasive, requiring the insertion of physical devices directly into a patient’s coronary arteries, thereby risking coronary artery injury. Non-invasive imaging methods to assess plaque vulnerability are therefore a major unmet need. Recently, 18F-NaF PET-CT has shown its potential to detect active coronary atheromata, while phase-contrast MRI (PC-MRI) techniques have shown potential in measuring the functional severity of coronary stenosis as a surrogate to invasive fractional flow reserve (FFR). In this study we intend to recruit 40 STEMI patients and will combine 18F-NaF PET/MR imaging and PC-MRI FFR imaging at two time points to bring new understandings of plaque rupture mechanism and coronary lesions evolution. Additionally, recent findings indicate that 18F-NaF targets the myocardial infarct as well as the vulnerable plaques. We will therefore analyze the 18F-NaF uptake in the myocardium and compare with MRI structural sequences (T1 delayed enhancement for infarct, T2 map for edema) at both time points to evaluate the power of these imaging methods to predict scar extent evolution. Such hybrid cardiac imaging protocols will allow clinicians to answer multiple questions with a single scan.
kw: Coronary lesions; 18F-NaF PET/MRI; myocardial scar; PC-MRA

title: Simultaneous profiling of circulating tumor cells and tumor in relation to immunotherapeutic response in cancer
abs: Immune checkpoint inhibitors are promising in cancer patients but responses are difficult to predict. Tumor re-biopsies are limited by tissue and access issues. Peripheral blood immunophenotyping is limited to only peripheral immune cells (PIC) given the paucity of circulating tumour cells (CTC). This proposal seeks to integrate analysis of CTC and tumor to predict outcomes from immunotherapy treatment underpinned by a clinical study: CTC-IMMUNITY. Specific Aim 1: Simultaneous Profiling of PIC, CTC and CTC clusters in relation to Response and Prognosis. Using label free enrichment methods for CTC from blood, we hypothesize that the relative expression of cancer and immunologic proteins in CTC, CTC clusters and PICs can be profiled, and are relevant to clinical outcomes. In patients undergoing immunotherapy, blood samples will be enriched for CTCs, CTC clusters and PICs and subjected to RNA expression analysis. Differential RNA expression from each component and relevant relationships will be assessed in relation to data from CTC-IMMUNITY (immunotherapy response). Specific Aim 2: Assessment of Germline Polymorphisms that Contribute to Immunotherapy Resistance and Prognosis. Germline polymorphisms have been described to contribute to drug resistance. We hypothesize that germline polymorphisms contribute to immunotherapeutic resistance as well. From the same blood draw for CTC enrichment during PDL-1/PD1 therapy, we will also extract germline DNA to sequence for BIM del polymorphism and polymorphic variants of PDL-1/PD-1 that may contribute to resistance. This will be correlated to tumor response to PDL-1/PD-1 inhibitors treatment in CTC-IMMUNITY. The 2 studies above will build on the prior CSA that has successfully contributed to bringing to market a local CTC isolation platform. They will allow the testing of additional applications for the CTC platform and the development of novel CTC assays for cancer applications. This effort will leverage on Singapore’s strengths in medical engineering and biology.

title: A phase I Investigator Sponsored Trial of Selinexor (KPT-330), a Selective Inhibitor of Nuclear Export / SINE™ Compound and ifosfamide, carboplatin, etoposide (ICE) in patients with relapsed or refractory peripheral T-cell lymphoma
abs: Treatment outcomes for patients with peripheral T-cell lymphoma (PTCL) are poor with conventional chemotherapy regimens. Second line regimens such as ICE (ifosfamide, carboplatin, etoposide) are administered with the goal of cytoreduction occasionally prior to stem cell transplantation (SCT) however many patients do not achieve a response. Novel therapeutic strategies are needed. Selinexor is a selective inhibitor of nuclear export which has shown pre-clinical activity in T-cell lymphomas and has been shows in vitro to sensitise cells to topoisomerase II inhibitors such as etoposide. We hypothesize that the combination of selinexor and ICE will be safe and effective in inducing responses in patients with relapsed/refractory (R/R) PTCL. We propose a phase I study with the primary objective to determine the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) of selinexor when given in combination with ICE in patients with R/R PTCL. Secondary objectives include assessing response rates, progression-free survival, overall survival and feasibility of stem cell collection after selinexor-ICE. This will be a single centre, phase I study with a standard “3+3” design. Selinexor will be orally administered on days 3, 5 and 7 of each chemotherapy cycle and ICE will be administered on days 1-3. Three dose levels (DL) of selinexor will be tested; 40mg, 60mg and 80mg. Three patients will be recruited onto DL1 and if no cycle 1 dose-limiting toxicities (DLT) are observed, dose escalation will continue to the next higher DL. If 1/3 DLT is observed then 3 additional patients will be enrolled in the same DL. If no DLT is observed from the additional 3 patients, then dose escalation will continue. If any DLT is observed from the additional 3 patients, then the previous lower dose will be chosen as the MTD. Patients will receive 2 to 6 cycles of selinexor and ICE and SCT if eligible.
kw: lymphoma, chemotherapy, phase I

title: Exploring the inflammatory signatures underlying progression of knee osteoarthritis: A prospective study
abs: Background. Knee osteoarthritis (OA) is a leading cause of disability; however, treatment is palliative. No drugs have demonstrated adequate symptoms and disease modification due to two main reasons: 1) poor understanding of the pathogenesis; 2) failure to consider OA as a heterogeneous disease. Inflammation plays important roles in the pathogenesis of OA, and patients with an inflammatory phenotype of knee OA may have better response to anti-inflammatory treatments. Further unravelling the mechanistic pathways underlying the inflammation in OA will inform of how to phenotype. Aim. We aim to build on the longitudinal follow-up of an existing cohort of patients with early knee OA to recognize and differentiate inflammatory phenotypes of OA, who are at faster rate of structural progression. Methods. To follow-up at a 4-year time point, on 139 patients with frequent knee pain who have given detailed symptoms, and knee imaging (radiography, and magnetic resonance imaging) at baseline. Live peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs), serum, urine and synovial fluid at baseline were collected. At follow-up, patients will be invited for clinical data, biological samples, radiographs and MRI. Structural progression will be defined by validated radiographic and MRI criteria. We will evaluate the association of pro-inflammatory biomarkers with structural progression. We will explore the immunological signatures in defining inflammatory phenotypes of knee OA that may lead to progression. We will use an agnostic approach starting with RNA sequencing of the cell pellet from synovial aspirate, followed by targeted single cell mass cytometry in peripheral blood, and comparison on immune cell subsets on individual basis. Clinical Significance. This project will provide insight knowledge of knee OA in terms of underlying inflammatory pathological processes, associated biomarkers, and potential targeted therapies. New knowledge may offer individualized therapeutic approach for success in clinical trial to treat subgroups of OA patients with specific inflammatory markers.

title: Understanding the genetic basis of variability associated with CYP3A4/5 enzymatic activity: A pilot study
abs: Over 60% of current prescription drugs are metabolized by the CYP3A4/5 subfamily of enzymes whereby observed interindividual variability in drug effects may be as high as 4- to 13-fold. The high degree of genetic variation at the CYP3A4/5 locus is mainly responsible for the observed interindividual variability. The probe drug, midazolam, has often been employed to determine CYP3A4/5 enzymatic activity. However, the practical use of the midazolam probe test is deterred by the need for repeated blood withdrawals, inconsistency of sampling time points that correlate with CYP3A4/5 activity and lack in reproducibility in ethnically diverse populations. Although several genetic variants in the CYP3A locus have been purported to predict CYP3A4/5 activity, they remain impractical in the Asian context due to clear differences in CYP3A4/5 variant penetrance amongst different ethnicities. This study proposes the use of an unbiased, comprehensive and global approach such as genome-wide association study (GWAS) to uncover germline marker(s) that may be predictive of CYP3A4/5 enzymatic activity. Blood samples will be taken at 1h and 3.5h from a pilot cohort of healthy volunteers (N=150) receiving a single low dose of midazolam. A GWAS analysis will be performed and correlated with midazolam concentrations taken at these time points. Midazolam concentrations determined at these time points were previously shown to significantly correlate with midazolam clearance in the local population. The functional impact of the genomic positive hits on CYP3A4/5 expression will be further assessed using human liver and intestinal tissues. The robustness of these novel marker(s) will also be validated in a pilot cohort of Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML) patients (N=100) who had previously taken imatinib, a putative CYP3A4/5 drug substrate. Ultimately, this study may provide a deeper insight into the genetic factors involved in mediating CYP3A4/5 activity and thereby improve our ability to better predict drug response.

title: A randomized trial on the impact of External Counterpulsation therapy on cerebral hemodynamic parameters in patients with symptomatic and severe steno-occlusive disease of intracranial internal carotid or middle cerebral artery and impaired cerebral vasodilatory reserve.
abs: Primary aim- To evaluate whether Enhanced External Counter-Pulsation (EECP) therapy would lead to an improvement in cerebral vasodilatory reserve (CVR) in patients with severe and symptomatic stenosis of intracranial carotid (ICA) or middle cerebral artery (MCA). We hypothesize that EECP therapy would lead to at least 4-points improvement in CVR as compared to best medical therapy and reduce the risk of cerebral ischemic events by at least 10%.. Secondary aims- 1. To evaluate the impact of EECP on reducing recurrent cerebral ischemic event in the study population. 2. To evaluate the impact of EECP on neurocognitive performance in the study population. Background and hypothesis- Intracranial stenosis is widely prevalent among ischemic stroke patients in Singapore (seen in upto 50% patients). Despite a high risk of cerebral ischemic events, management of severe intracranial stenosis remains suboptimal and controversial. Intracranial stenting and surgical revascularization are associated with high early peri-procedural risks. EECP therapy appears to be a possible adjuvant therapeutic option for patients with severe intracranial stenosis. Methods- Patients with recently symptomatic severe stenosis of intracranial ICA or MCA with impaired CVR on transcranial Doppler (TCD) would be evaluated with acetazolamide- challenged single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT). Patients with impaired CVR would be randomized to receive best medical therapy (plus sham EECP) alone or best medical therapy plus EECP for 7 weeks. Detailed clinical, imaging and neuropsychological assessments would be performed by blinded assessors at 4 months. This project intends to generate the physiological and clinical data related to the changes in cerebral hemodynamic parameters, short-term reduction in stroke/TIA risk and changes in neurocognitive performance in patients treated with adjuvant EECP therapy. Our findings will lead to a larger well planned phase-3 efficacy study and open a new therapeutic option for patients at very high risk of cerebral ischemic events.

title: Improving Outcomes for Out-Of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest through a National, Living, Learning, Pre-hospital Emergency Care Laboratory
abs: This project aims to increase the survival rate for Out-Of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest (OHCA) in Singapore. The current survival rate is low, about 4%, but been improving slowly with ongoing efforts. We hypothesize that in patients with OHCA in Singapore, a series of community and ambulance based intervention bundles will significantly increase bystander CPR and survival to discharge compared to historical and contemporary community controls. The methodologies will include (1) dynamic simulation models of the prehospital emergency care system and mathematical programming models with multi-criteria decision support systems to optimise ambulance response times, (2) a community implementation bundle that includes public education, community response apps, CPR feedback cards, and public access defibrillation to increase bystander CPR rates, (3) an ambulance based Advanced Life Support treatment bundle that includes impedance threshold devices, high performance team CPR, manual defibrillation by EMS personnel and prehospital administration of amiodarone, to increase prehospital return of spontaneous circulation amongst cardiac arrest patients. The project builds on ongoing efforts via multiple agencies, including the Unit for Prehospital Emergency Care, Singapore Civil Defence Force, and various community partners.

title: Layerwise microstructure scanner: A new technology for online materials assessment in additive manufacturing
abs: Additive manufacturing (AM) provides the unique capability of making parts with complex 3-D geometries by assembling the material at the micrometer scale, layer after layer. Because of this bottom-up manufacturing process—which spans over six orders of magnitude in length scale—difficult-to-assess microstructural heterogeneities and defects are prone to be incorporated across the build volume. This material variability has significant effects on the behavior of 3-D printed components and creates uncertainty around their performance and lifetime, limiting the employment of AM materials in most engineering applications. The goal of the proposed research is to develop a new AM-compatible technology for online characterization of 3-D printed metallic materials to assess their variability as they are formed. The technology will leverage the layerwise nature of AM to rapidly “scan” the surface—and assess the microstructure—of each consolidated layer of material using advanced optical microscopy techniques. This non-destructive characterization method will allow mapping the character and distribution of crystal grains, phases, and defects across the volume of 3-D printed metal parts. Since this microstructural information will be directly available upon manufacturing, it will be possible to accurately predict and even “engineer” the mechanical performance and lifetime of the 3-D printed components without the need for costly post-production quality assessments or additional materials processing. Because of its simplicity, versatility, and low-cost, the layerwise microstructure scanning technology (LMS) to be developed has the potential to be widely adopted in the AM industry to collect microstructure data for different AM technologies. In the long term, this information may also be used to create standards for AM and to guide the design of materials with spatially-controlled microstructures and tailored properties. Additionally, the optical-based techniques at the core of LMS may be used offline as inexpensive and rapid microstructure characterization methods for academic research.

title: Designing Novel Quantum Materials at the Microscopic Level with Ultracold Molecules
abs: The goal of the proposed research is to study transport dynamics in materials at the microscopic level to impact the development of next-generation electronics that are lighter, faster, cheaper and flexible, and future technology like powerful quantum computers. Designer quantum materials, of which properties like electrical conductivity and photovoltaic coefficients can be precisely engineered, offer a potential breakthrough in the electronics industry. Yet, a detailed understanding of such dynamical properties in strongly-interacting matter remains elusive due to limits on computational power. Quantum simulators, which are isolated but tunable quantum nanomachines, offer an attractive path that promises to be more powerful than classical supercomputers: due to their inherent quantum nature, they can be easily set up to mimic various models that describe quantum phenomena, and the dynamics can be obtained by empirically observing the time-dependent results. To realize quantum simulators, we will develop a bottom-up approach for assembling and manipulating arrays of ultracold Rydberg atoms, which form the building blocks for synthesizing and simulating strongly-correlated quantum matter. This laser-based approach will allow full programmable control of the internal and external quantum states, atom number, doping fraction, disordered potentials, and array dimensionality. We will then use the atom-simulator array to explore the spin models that can be applied to a range of materials including high-temperature superconductors, organic semiconductors, and topological materials. Such studies can only be realized in a well-isolated system such as ultracold atoms, and will benefit future technologies in quantum information processing.
