title: Investigating Altered Metabolic Pathways in Neurodegeneration using Organoids
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS), is an age-onset neurodegenerative disorder that causes death of motor neurons that control voluntary muscles. Approximately half a million people worldwide suffers from ALS and in aging societies including Singapore, the incidence of ALS will increase. Unfortunately, there is no cure for ALS. The only FDA-approved drug for ALS, Riluzole, was approved in 1995 and prolongs lifespan of sufferers by an average of three months. There has been no better drug for ALS for more than 10 years since Riluzole, in part because the mechanisms of ALS pathogenesis and progression are still unclear. Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) have become invaluable tools for modeling ALS. However, the challenge for using iPSCs to model ALS is that iPSC-derived motor neurons rarely mature fully, and late phenotypes of ALS such as formation of intraneuronal aggregates or inclusion bodies are rarely observed. This suggests that many late pathological events in ALS motor neurons are also likely masked. In addition, astrocytes are important players in the development of many neurodegenerative diseases including ALS. Current directed differentiation strategies generally exclude this important glial population, making it an unrealistic and inaccurate disease model. Overcoming these hurdles is critical for precise and accurate modeling of ALS to advance therapeutic discovery. Our preliminary evidence indicates that three-dimensional organoid cultures contain both neurons and astrocytes, and promote neuronal maturation, an important aspect of modeling late-onset disorders. Using spinal organoids as a more accurate model of ALS, we aim to establish gene expression and metabolic signatures of ALS motor neurons and astrocytes – two key players in ALS pathogenesis. Our preliminary evidence suggests that ALS motor neurons exhibit changes in energy metabolism. Therefore, we aim to investigate the mechanisms underlying these changes, and whether re-establishment of energy homeostasis will restore motor neuron health.
kw: Induced pluripotent stem cells;Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis;Spinal organoids;Energy metabolism;Motor neurons

title: Multimodal Characterization of the Impact of Sleep Disturbances on Traumatic Brain Injury Outcomes
abs: In Singapore, stroke is the fourth most common cause of death in 2019 and the third highest in terms of disease burden, also being one of the top five leading causes of combined death and disability. A single-centre study done in Singapore that examined hospitalized patients with acute ischemic stroke over a period one year found that overall, 3.7% of patients deceased during the hospitalization. For longer-term mortality outcomes in Singapore, a multi-site retrospective cohort study showed that 41.7% of all-cause stroke patients had died by 5 years of follow-up, and that haemorrhagic stroke had higher early mortality than ischemic stroke. Another common outcome measure of stroke is functional independence, based on independence in activities of daily living (ADLs). The single-centre Singapore study showed that 46.3%% of their stroke sample were not ADL-independent at the time of hospital discharge. There is relatively less literature about the non-motor neuropsychiatric outcomes of stroke, as research was mainly directed at developing new treatments for acute stroke to improve survival and functional outcomes. However, now that these new treatments have been shown to improve survival and at least short-term functional outcomes, there is an even stronger imperative to examine the non-traditional outcomes that potentially have an even greater impact on long-term outcomes and quality-of-life. For example, a recent study showed that post-stroke depression was associated with higher rates of death and disability at three and twelve months after stroke, independent of other post-stroke neuropsychiatric conditions. Disappointingly, in a review of 190 published trials of acute ischemic stroke treatment, only 7 included a specific measure of neuropsychiatric outcome, and even then it was a single brief measure of cognition or mood. These non-traditional outcomes of stroke are mainly of the behavioral, psychological and cognitive domains, such as mood and anxiety disorders, apathy, psychosis, personality change, sleep disturbances and cognitive impairments. Not surprisingly, there is a paucity of research on these subject matter in our local context. This thesis will be a detailed exploration of three specific non-motor outcomes of stroke, namely post-stroke depression (PSD), post-stroke cognitive impairment (PSCI) and post-stroke sleep disturbances, as well as their inter-relationships and impact on recovery outcomes.
kw: sleep, traumatic brain injury, neurcognitive, biomarkers

title: Developing chromosomal 1q21.3 amplification as a circulating biomarker and actionable target for monitoring and treating breast cancer recurrence
abs: Despite advances in therapies for breast cancer, many patients still develop recurrence and die of metastasis years after treatment. Distant recurrence is often diagnosed late when symptoms arise, by which time the disease is no longer curable. There is a pressing unmet clinic need to develop non invasive diagnostics such as cell free DNA assay to monitor disease status so that tumor recurrence can be detected and treated earlier to improve the patient’s survival outcomes. Increasing evidence has demonstrated that treatment resistance and metastasis are attributed to the distinct and rare, aggressive subpopulation of cancer cells, known as tumor-initiating cells (TICs). Using an integrated genomics approach, we have identified a chromosomal region, chr1q21.3, to be amplified in patient’s breast tumor sphere populations and this gene amplification event is highly enriched inup to 75% of recurrent tumors, in both ER positive and ER negative tumors. We have designed a plasma cell free DNA assay to detect the chr1q21.3 amplification using digital PCR and this cfDNA assay is able to identify the breast tumor chr1q21.3 amplification with high sensitivity and specificity, and is able to predict relapse in patients with both early and late stage tumors. Importantly, we show that ch1q21.3 consists of important genes linked to signaling pathways crucial for metastasis, chemoresistance and tumor recurrence. In this proposal, we aim to develop further our cfDNA assay to increase the sensitivity for detecting disease recurrence and pursue more clinical validation in both retrospective and prospective studies. Also, we seek to investigate the functional role of chr1q21.3 amplication in tumor recurrence and chemoresistance and to develop a therapeutic strategy to targetchr1q21.3-amplified tumors. Our ultimate goal is to develop both diagnostic and therapeutic solutions to target tumor recurrence, which we hope will provide a true clinical benefit to improve patients’ survival.
kw: Breast cancer, liquid biopsy, gene amplification, cell free DNA, tumor recurrence, therapeutics

title: Uncoupling Thrombosis and Haemostasis in Patients Needing Combination Antiplatelet and Anticoagulant Therapy
abs: Patients with cardiovascular disease frequently require combination antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy in the acute care setting. Ten per cent of these patients require combination therapy beyond hospital discharge (chronic care setting). Combination therapy is necessary to prevent thrombosis but carries a high risk of bleeding, so new strategies to reduce thrombotic risk while preserving haemostasis are a major unmet need with combination therapy. Over the last three years, we have expanded our pipeline of anticoagulant peptides targeting factor IIa (thrombin) and factor XIa. Our lead direct thrombin inhibitor is variegin, a 32-amino acid peptide that has a nine-fold greater affinity for thrombin than bivalirudin (Ki = 0.3 nM compared with 2.9 nM for bivalirudin). We have shown that variegin delivers superior antithrombotic efficacy with less bleeding than reference thrombin inhibitors like bivalirudin, when combined with antiplatelet therapy. Our lead direct factor XIa inhibitor is rFasxiatorN17R,L19E, which inhibits FXIa with a Ki of 0.86 nM and has 170-fold selectivity towards FXIa compared with other plasma serine proteases. FXIa is an interesting target as it tapers but does not abolish thrombin generation; genetic deficiency of FXI in humans rarely leads to spontaneous bleeding but protects from ischaemic stroke and venous thrombosis. We seek to uncouple the balance between thrombosis and haemostasis in patients requiring combination antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy. We hypothesize that, combined with antiplatelet therapy, low dose variegin will have greater efficacy and better safety than other acute care anticoagulants in a first-in-human trial incorporating novel ex vivo stent thrombosis and venous bleeding endpoints. We will prolong the half-life of rFasxiatorN17R,L19E using biodegradable thermogelling copolymers to enable weekly injections in the chronic care setting and test this nanoparticle modification in an ovine atrial fibrillation model of thromboembolic stroke. Finally, we will examine cardioprotective and neuroprotective properties of our two lead compounds.
kw: thrombin, factor XIa,

title: HALT-NUCS: Halting Nucleoside Analogue Therapy
abs: Chronic Hepatitis B (CHB) affects over 250 million persons and is considered one of the major causes of mortality and morbidity globally. Standard treatment consists of nucleos(t)ide analogues (NA) or peginterferon (PEG). Most patients are on NA long term, but this leads to HBsAg loss (defined as functional cure) of only 2% at 6 years. A recent finding that 39% of patients on long term adefovir after stopping therapy, developed viral relapse then viral remission, reduction in quantitative HBsAg (qHBsAg) leading to HBsAg loss was novel. Further studies confirm that HBsAg loss is achievable to varying degrees when stopping long term NA therapy especially in patients with low qHBsAg. Consequently, the objective of the study is not only to determine the proportion of patients able to achieve HBsAg loss in those with qHBsAg?100IU/ml, but also to examine the virological and immunological features associated with HBsAg loss, since this is poorly understood. This will be performed through intensive immune and virologic monitoring after stopping NA to dissect these mechanisms. Our hypothesis is that low qHBsAg levels lead to a state of relative relief from immune cell exhaustion and the viral relapse seen after stopping NA allows immune recognition and HBsAg seroclearance. The study design is that of a randomized control trial of 150 HBeAg negative CHB patients with qHBsAg?100 IU/ml, undetectable HBV DNA, on NA?1 year, excluding cirrhosis. Patients will be randomized 1:2 to continue NA(tenofovir alafenamide, TAF) or stop NA. Study drugs will be provided by Gilead Sciences. Subjects who have significant reactivation will be started on TAF. This study may lead to a significant advance in being able to stop NA therapy as a therapeutic procedure to induce HBsAg loss, of which the immunological and virological features would provide a major insight into the mechanism of HBsAg seroclearance.

title: MSC exosomes: the next-generation MSC therapy for treatment of cartilage injuries
abs: Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) are the most widely used stem cells in clinical trials for many disease indications, including treatment of cartilage injuries and osteoarthritis (OA). However, the mechanism of action for the therapeutic efficacy of MSCs has undergone a dramatic paradigm shift in the last decade. Instead of differentiating to form new cells to replace dead or injured cells, transplanted MSCs have been increasingly reported to secrete small lipid vesicles known as exosomes to protect cells from injury and promote tissue repair. Unlike cell-based therapies, exosome-based therapeutics are advantageous in that they are small, not viable and could be mass produced from a clonal immortalized cell source. These features eliminate the permanence of a cell therapy, and batch variability, respectively. The use of exosome-based therapeutics also overcomes the logistical and operational costs and challenges of a cell-based therapy which include shipping constraints, storage and proper handling of cells needed to maintain the cell viability and vitality for transplantation. This proposal seeks to develop the requisite preclinical proofs of concept for clinical testing of MSC exosomes as the next-generation MSC therapeutic for treatment of cartilage injuries. Our previous study has demonstrated that weekly intra-articular injections of MSC exosomes can repair osteochondral defects in the rat model. To overcome the challenges of a cell-based therapy and to improve patience compliance, we propose the development of novel, off-the-shelf exosome-coupled biomaterial scaffold. We hypothesize that an exosome-coupled biomaterial scaffold would be able to sustain high local concentration of exosomes in the synovial joint to reproducibly replicate the osteochondral repair efficacy of MSCs in a clinically relevant pig model. Accordingly, we will develop exosome-coupled biomaterial scaffolds for cartilage repair, determine the optimal exosome-scaffold therapeutic strategy and exemplify the in vivo efficacy in rat and pig models of cartilage defects.
kw: exosome, mesenchymal stem cells, cartilage, osteoarthritis, ready-to-use, tissue repair

title: Targeting telomere maintenance for therapeutic intervention in human cancer and aging
abs: The ends of human chromosomes are capped by telomeres. The telomeres are synthesized by the enzyme telomerase. The balance of telomere elongation and telomere attrition controls the telomere length homeostasis that is implicated in both human cancer and aging. On one hand, telomerase is up-regulated in more than 85-90% of human cancers underlying the telomere maintenance that supports continuous proliferation of cancer cells. On the other hand, accelerated telomere shortening in tissue progenitor/stem cells due to mutations in telomere- and telomerase-associated genes lead to various diseases, termed telomere syndromes or telomeropathies. These patients display premature aging and increased risk of cancer. Therefore, understanding the underlying mechanisms and identification of new factors controlling telomere length homeostasis are necessary for therapeutic intervention of human cancer and aging. A recent clinical study has shown that Danazol treatment in telomere syndrome patients led to telomerase activation and telomere elongation. We have identified the nuclear receptor NR4A1 as a potential target of Danazol that negatively regulates hTERT expression. We will further investigate the potential roles of NR4A1 in Danazol-induced telomerase activation in human cells. Additionally, to gain further insights into the regulation of telomere length homeostasis, we conducted a genetic screen that identified a number of known and novel telomere maintenance factors (termed TMFs). Modulation of TMF17 expression alone, which encodes a histone chaperone-NAP1L1, resets steady-state telomere length. Rare and recurrent NAP1L1-MLLT10 translocations have been identified in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL), indicating the possible role of NAP1L1-MLLT10 in cancer initiation by promoting telomere elongation by telomerase. We propose to further determine the functions of NAP1L1 and NAP1L1-MLLT10 in telomere maintenance. Identification of novel cellular factors controlling telomerase activity and telomere length homeostasis can provide potential druggable targets for therapeutic intervention of human cancer and aging.?
kw: Telomere, telomerase, cancer and aging

title: Development of a palliative care intervention to support advanced cancer patients and their caregivers
abs: Palliative care improves physical symptom burden, quality of life and overall survival in advanced cancer patients, particularly when provided earlier in the patient’s illness journey. However, the current form of a multidisciplinary and comprehensive palliative care service delivered by specialist trained personnel is resource intensive and not feasible for widespread implementation. Therefore, new models of palliative care need to be developed and tested for effectiveness. A recent pilot study of an outpatient nurse-led palliative care intervention showed that these nurse education sessions were feasible and acceptable in our local context. However, the content was too narrow in scope and needs to be expanded. The overall aim of this proposed study to understand the illness experience of advanced cancer patients and their caregivers, so as to further develop the palliative care intervention that can support patients and caregivers, thereby improving their health outcomes. Semi-structured interviews will be conducted with a purposive sample of advanced cancer patients and caregivers in order to explore i) their needs and challenges, ii) their healthcare decision making experiences and iii) their views on the content and form of the palliative care intervention. Interviews will be audio-recorded and transcribed verbatim. The framework method will be used for data analysis. The results from this study will inform the further development of a palliative care intervention which can in future be piloted and evaluated for effectiveness in improving health outcomes. The overarching goal is to develop a health service model that can extend the benefits of palliative care to more advanced cancer patients.
kw: Palliative Care, Supportive Care, Oncology Nursing, Neoplasms, Health Services Research

title: Harnessing LOXL1 as a therapeutic candidate for exfoliation syndrome and exfoliation glaucoma
abs: Exfoliation syndrome (XFS) is a disorder of aging that affects the extracellular matrix (ECM). In the eye, XFS results in obstruction of the trabecular outflow, causing raised intraocular pressure, glaucoma, and subsequent blindness. Although XFS is a major cause of blindness worldwide, it is notable that the prevalence of XFS is low in Chinese people. Genetic studies have shown that common LOXL1 gene variants are strongly associated with XFS. However, the mechanism by which common LOXL1 variants convey differential risk of XFS is unknown. Recently, we sequenced LOXL1 in 5,566 XFS cases and 6,279 controls from nine non-Chinese populations, identifying 63 naturally occurring rare amino acid substitutions. These LOXL1 variants were significantly enriched in normal controls compared to XFS cases, amongst all populations, suggesting a strong protective effect against XFS (Aung T et al., Nature Genetics 2017). We now propose to perform deep sequencing of the LOXL1 locus in Chinese XFS patients and compare them to Chinese controls to define the genetic architecture which could be responsible for the higher degree of protection in the Chinese. We next aim to perform comprehensive functional characterization of all naturally occurring rare genetic variants across the LOXL1 locus. This will first be done by assessing the impact of LOXL1 genetic variants on LOXL1 enzymatic action using a LOXL1 oxidase assay and how it affects downstream ECM components such as elastin, fibrillin, and collagen. We will follow this up with further assessing the manner in which these LOXL1 protective genetic variants affect physiological cell-cell adhesion in human eye tissue cell lines as a direct consequence of altered ECM metabolism. Our proposal will help elucidate the mechanisms by which LOXL1 are involved in XFS biology with the long term aim of designing therapy to halt the disease process and prevent blindness.
kw: LOXL1 genetic, Exfoliation Syndrome, Glaucoma, Biochemistry

title: Characterization and application of spiral micro-channel-sorted chondrocytes for cartilage regeneration
abs: Current clinical approaches for articular cartilage repair have not been able to restore the joint surface with hyaline cartilage with its hierarchically organized architecture, and its normal biomechanical function. Although mimicking the zonal organization of articular cartilage in neo-tissue by the use of zonal chondrocyte subpopulations could enhance the functionality of the graft, engineering of stratified tissue has not yet been realized using zonal chondrocytes due to the lack of specific zonal chondrocyte isolating protocols and limited amounts of donor tissue to yield adequate viable zonal cells. We have established a protocol of segregating zone-specific chondrocytes based on the principle of inertial focusing of cells with different sizes in spiral micro-channels, and demonstrated the potential of these size-sorted cells to regenerate a functionally superior cartilage in a rodent cartilage defect. We hypothesise that chondrocytes of specific zonal characteristics isolated from full thickness cartilage based on cell size using spiral microfluidic-channels and expanded under specific condition(s), when delivered in a bi-layered stratified hydrogel construct at cartilage defect site, will facilitate the formation of hierarchically organized, functionally superior, cartilage tissue in vivo.The proposed study consists of two Parts. Part (A): the establishment of specific culture conditions for the expansion of zonal chondrocytes that maximize the retention of their phenotypic properties. Part (B): in vivo validation of the efficacy of delivering the expanded zonal chondrocytes in a bi-layered construct for cartilage regeneration in a porcine chondral defect model. This approach provides a straightforward and rapid method of obtaining zone-specific chondrocytes for the engineering of stratified cartilage. Delivery of the chondrocyte subpopulations in a sequential injectable approach can cater to defects of variable shapes and sizes, and can be easily adopted for clinical application. The outcome of this study will contribute to the development of functional repair of critical size cartilage defects.
kw: Cartilage repair, Zone-specific chondrocytes, inertial focusing cell sorting

title: Evaluation of a hepatitis B virus minichromosome disruption strategy using CRISPR/dCas9-FokI nuclease delivered by modified polyethyleneimine polymers, in combination with nucleotide analogue therapy
abs: There is no cure for chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection to date. The failure to clear HBV minichromosome remains the major obstacle to curing the infection. Our preliminary work demonstrated that functionalized carbonate mitigated the toxicity of polyethylenimine (PEI) polymers, and provide broad-spectrum activity against a number of DNA and RNA viruses, including HBV. These polymers can also be complexed with nucleic acids into nanoparticles for DNA and RNA delivery. We hypothesize that the combination of CRISPR/Cas9 disruption of the HBV minichromosomes, targeting multiple steps of HBV replication pathway simultaneously, including viral entry and reverse transcription, will accelerate the kinetics of HBV minichromosome and HBsAg loss to less than 1 year. The aims of the study are 1. To optimize the delivery of HBV minichromosome-targeting CRISPR/ dCas9-FokI nuclease by modified PEI polymer and adeno-associated virus, 2. To synthesize galactose-, mannose- and PEG-functionalized PEI polymers at various levels to optimize their anti-HBV property, and characterize their mechanisms of action, and 3. To study the kinetics of HBsAg and HBV minichromosome decline with repeated CRISPR/ dCas-FokI therapy in HBV-infected HepG1-hNTCP cells, human hepatocytes, and humanized mice model, with and without concurrent nucleotide analogue therapy. Methodology: hNTCP-HepG2 cell infection system will be used for in vitro testing of the system before the conduct of HBV-infected humanized mouse model studies. Indices of viral replication (HBV DNA/RNA, viral protein production) and direct measurements of HBV minichromosome using qPCR and Southern blot will be performed. The pharmacokinetics and toxicity of the PEI polymers and the DNA-based therapies will be monitored. The PEI polymers will be continually modified and tested, aiming for optimal efficient delivery and antiviral efficacy. Our long-term goal is to develop a finite therapy that results in permanent HBsAg loss and normalization of liver function in all chronic HBV patients.
kw: Hepatitis B virus, CRISPR/dCas9-FokI, polyethyleneimine polymer, HBV minichromosome, viral entry inhibitor

title: A Single-Round Infectious Particle approach to a Zika vaccine
abs: The mosquito-borne Zika virus (ZIKV) is a flavivirus that, in just a few years, has emerged across the globe, causing epidemics in the Americas and sporadic outbreaks in Asia. ZIKV does not only causes an acute febrile disease, but is also associated with congenital defects such as microcephaly when infection occurs during pregnancy. This makes ZIKV a significant threat to human health worldwide, and tools to combat this infection either by vaccination or antiviral drugs are urgently needed. In this proposal we explore a strategy that combines the safety of inactivated/subunit vaccines with the immunogenicity of live attenuated vaccines by using a single-round infectious particle (SRIP) approach.The SRIP contains the non-infectious genetic material coding for ZIKV non-structural proteins, packaged inside a Zika virus-like particle. This packaging ensures uptake of the vaccine by ZIKV susceptible cells, while the SRIP core containing the non-structural genes are self-replicating when delivered to the target cells. The non-structural proteins in them selves are not capable of creating new infectious particles; hence the infection is limited to SRIP-infected cells. We recently showed that immunization with ZIKV-SRIP (zSRIP) protects against ZIKV infection in vivo. In this proposed study we will further evaluate the feasibility of zSRIP as a vaccine candidate using a well-established mouse model. We will find optimal dose for protection to severe disease and examine protection efficacy of zSRIP to fetal ZIKV infection. We will also study CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell activation, proliferation and memory formation elicited by zSRIP. In addition, we will evaluate the capacity of the zSRIP to mimic live attenuated vaccines by examine zSRIP-induced expression of molecular correlates to immunogenicity ex vivo.If successful, this zSRIP strategy could be a safe and rapid approach to ZIKV vaccine development.
kw: Vaccine, Virology, Immunology, Infection, Flavivirus, Zika virus

title: Deciphering the role of NS1-PB as a novel target for neuronal ageing in humans
abs: Neurological disorders are the third largest health concern worldwide after cancer and cardiovascular diseases. In 2010, neurological diseases contributed to 14% of the Singapore’s national disease burden (www.moh.gov.sg). Since the world is ageing rapidly and the number of people aged above 60 years old will represent 22% of the total global population in 2050 (WHO, 2015), ageing-related illness such as dementia, stroke and neurodegenerative diseases will take a larger burden on healthcare. It is therefore urgent to gain a deeper knowledge of the nervous system to find innovative therapeutic intervention points. We recently identified a novel premature ageing syndrome characterized by progressive and degenerative neuropathy together with skin atrophy and dramatic hair whitening. Through whole-exome sequencing, we identified the cause of this disease to be a germline mutation in the NS1-BP gene. NS1-BP encodes an evolutionary conserved protein believed to serve as an E3 ubiquitin ligase adaptor. Previous studies showed that the ubiquitin-mediated proteasome pathway is an essential cellular machinery often linked to neurological diseases. We therefore hypothesize that NS1-BP controls neuronal proteostasis and protects cells from the degenerative effects of ageing. Our first aim will be to characterize the underlying mechanisms by which mutation in NS1-BP cause neurodegeneration using in vitro and in vivo model systems. Our second aim will be to identify the substrates of NS1-BP to delineate novel intervention points for the treatment of more common neurodegenerative disorders. This research will bring novel fundamental knowledge on how NS1-BP regulates ubiquitin-mediated proteasome and how its loss specifically affects neuronal lineages in humans. We anticipate that it will bring translational insights into more common ageing-related disorders and potentially allow the identification of new targets for these diseases.
kw: neurological disorders, ageing, NS1-BP, neuropathy, proteostasis

title: The Nuclear Envelope and Microtubule Organization in Myogenesis: Disease Mechanisms in Cardiomyopathy and Muscular Dystrophy
inst: SRIS - Skin Research Institute of Singapore
abs: Microtubule distribution in many cell types is defined by a centrosome or microtubule-organizing centre (MTOC) that behaves as a focus for microtubule minus ends. The MTOC is typically formed about a pair of centrioles, often in a juxta-nuclear location. Differentiation of both cardiac and skeletal muscle, however, features a unique relocation of centrosomal proteins to the nuclear envelope (NE). In this way, the NE itself is coopted as a new MTOC with concomitant changes in the global distribution of microtubules. Dissemination of the MTOC to the NE in this way is thought to be required for appropriate nuclear positioning in muscle cells. Indeed, mutations in the genes encoding several centrosomal components, including PCNT and ALMS1, are associated in part with life-threatening cardiomyopathy. Similarly, taxol a well-characterized microtubule stabilizing drug, used in the treatment of certain cancers, is associated with significant cardiac toxicity. The goal of this proposal is to elucidate the molecular mechanisms that underlie the reorganization of the MTOC during myogenesis. It will take advantage of a proteomic method known as BioID, which was developed in the PI’s laboratory, to map protein interactions at the nuclear periphery. This will reveal the identities of proteins at the nuclear surface that might function as adaptors for centrosomal components. Preliminary BioID data, as well as RNAi studies combined with both conventional and super-resolution microscopy, strongly suggests that this adaptor role is taken by LINC complexes containing the outer nuclear membrane protein Nesprin 1. These investigations should shed new light on the role of microtubules and MTOC rearrangements in myogenesis. Furthermore these studies will provide a foundation for our understanding of disorders affecting myoblast remodelling and potentially identify novel therapeutic targets.
kw: Muscular dystrophy, cardiomyopathy, LINC complex, nuclear envelope, microtubule, Nesprin

title: Rtl1, a neofunctionalized retrotransposon, a novel factor regulating myogenesis
abs: The muscular dystrophies (MD) are a heterogeneous group of genetic diseases characterized by progressive weakness and degeneration of the skeletal musculature and in some, heart function is also affected. Extensive muscle wasting is also a frequent consequence of other more common diseases such as cancer and diabetes. We identified the paternally expressed retrotransposon-like 1 (Rtl1) gene, as being essential for efficient muscle regeneration and is expressed in murine models of muscular dystrophy, including Duchenne’s (DMD) and Emery-Dreifuss (AD-EDMD). In patient biopsies with AD-EDMD RTL1 regulation is disrupted. We have derived a mouse line carrying a conditional allele of Rtl1 for in vivo studies. These mice will be crossed with inducible Cre lines to either delete or overexpress RTL1 tissue specifically and determine loss/gain of function of RTL1 on muscle rowth and regeneration.The biochemical functions of RTL1 are unknown except that RTL1 overexpression causes muscle hypertrophy in sheep and mice. We will characterize RTL1s’ function with respect to myogenesis during the complex process of muscle regeneration. This will be performed in muscle killed by cardiotoxin injection, and in congenital muscle diseases, namelly DMD and the AD-EDMD. We use murine and human muscle cell lines to determine RTL1’s biochemical functions, defining RTL1’s subcellular localization and by identifying RTL1’s protein interaction partners. Preliminary evidence localized RTL1 to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). RTL1 expression is induced in primary myoblast cultures by treating the cells with a proteosome inhibitor, indicating that RTL1 maybe involved in the ERstress/Unfolded Protein Response Pathways. We have generated antibodies to human RTL1 to validate RTL1 expression in human myogenesis, and in archived muscle biopsy from patients with congenital human muscle disease. These antibodies will be used in determining the molecular function(s) of RTL1 and potentially for diagnostic purposes. Understanding RTL1’s function may provide novel approaches to ameliorating muscle atrophy, and other myopathic diseases.
kw: Muscle growth, regeneration, muscular dystrophy, RTL1, ER Stress,

title: A Prospective Study to develop a Genomics-Phenomics Platform Approach for Precision Medicine in Hepatocellular Carcinoma
abs: Tumor heterogeneity (both inter- and intra-tumor heterogeneity) is important for tumor evolution, disease progression, and treatment response. Previous unsupported assumptions of intra-tumor homogeneity have hindered the development of efficacious systemic therapeutics for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). In our recently published study, we confirmed that significant intra-tumor heterogeneity is found in HCC. Such heterogeneity may be elucidated at the level of genome/epigenome/transcriptome, as well as at the metabolome and clinical phenotype levels, where interaction between the genes and the environment is played out. We hypothesize that an integration of genomic heterogeneity with multiple downstream layers/datasets (e.g. epigenetics, transcriptomic, immunomics, metabolomics and clinical phenotypes) will allow a more coherent understanding of molecular pathways, tumor evolution and disease progression. Additional insights can be expected if such vertical integration is carried out in the context of a prospective study that follows the clinical trajectory of the disease, thus allowing for longitudinal integration of datasets as well, and mitigating the significant impact of inter-patient variability. To achieve this, we propose to leverage on the current NMRC TCR Flagship Program in Liver Cancer, which is a multi-center prospective genomic-immunomic study that follows a surgical cohort of patients from resection of HCC to cancer recurrence. From this program, sequential tissue and humoral samples will be collected for targeted and untargeted serum, urine and tissue metabolomics. In addition, mass spectrometry imaging will also be performed on tissue sections to quantify micron-scale metabolic heterogeneity. This proposal adds metabolomics to the program, as this will give information closer to the tissue phenotype. A systems-based approach will be applied to integrate metabolomics data with the other datasets in order to identify critical pathways in HCC and to discover metabolic biomarkers that are predictive of disease outcomes.
kw: Hepatocellular carcinoma, immunomics, metabolomics, genomics

title: PRL-3 Basic and Translational Researches
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: In 1998, we identified PRL-3 intracellular protein phosphatase. In 2001, Professor Vogelstein’s team from Johns Hopkins first found that PRL-3 was upregulated in colorectal cancer metastasis. In 2003, we further demonstrated that PRL-3 promotes cancer metastasis. Since then, we and others have been working on the role and mechanism of PRL-3 in various cancers as well as developing potential therapeutics, leading to the development of a vibrant PRL-3 research community. Intracellular PRL-3 oncoprotein normally will be targeted with small chemical drugs that are derived from culture dishes (In vitro), where the conditions are oversimplified from tumor microenvironments (in vivo). Since 2008, we proposed a new concept of using antibodies to target PRL-1 and PRL-3 intracellular oncoproteins in multiple animal models: tail vein, xenograft tumor, spontaneous tumor models, orthotopic ‘seed & soil’ tumor models, such animal models are more clinical relevant and have therapeutic impacts for future clinical trials to demonstrate that antibodies can be used to target intracellular oncoproteins as unconventional immunotherapies that offer enormous opportunities for novel cancer treatments. In this proposal, our objectives are to further study in this forefront area by focusing on 3 specific aims: 1. To understand the role of PRL-3-induced polyploid giant cancer cells (PGCCs) in cancer metastasis and tumor relapse. This novel property of PRL-3 has not been investigated and its underlying mechanism and role in cancer are yet to be established; 2. To target PRL-3 positive tumors and weed out PRL-3 positive “stem cell”-like PGCC with PRL3-zumab as a novel targeted cancer immunotherapy and as a prevention for cancer relapse. 3. To elucidate the mechanism of action (MOA) of how tumors are under inflammation, tissue necrosis/lysis, leaking intracellular PRL-3 antigen into the tumor microenvironment. PRL3-zumab and ‘externalized PRL-3’ antigens result in recruitment of immune effectors and/or classical ADCC- and/or ADCP-mediated tumor clearance.
kw: PRL-3, clinical useful animal models, new cancer therapies

title: Development of Allosteric Inhibitors of Eya2
abs: The Eye absent (Eya) proteins are a class of proteins which possess tyrosine phosphatase activity. Their C-terminal regions contain a conserved ED domain comprised of approximately 270 residues that possess enzymatic activity and are involved in protein-protein interactions. Their interaction with Six1 is essential for the functional activity of Six1 in cell survival and invasion. Six1 and Eya proteins are essential developmental genes but are not expressed in normal adult tissues. However, they are over-expressed in many tumors including those of the breast. As Six1 and Eya phosphatase activity is thought to drive the proliferation and survival of cancer cells, inhibitors disrupting the Six1-Eya interactions, or inhibiting the Eya phosphatase activity can potentially be developed into therapeutic agents. Working with our collaborators at the University of Colorado, we propose the following activities. Aim 1, Characterize and map the binding interface of Six1 and Eya2. Aim 3, Perform structural studies on Eya2 in complex with identified hit compounds from screening. Aim 3, Optimize the identified Eya2 allosteric hit compounds and further develop them into more potent lead phosphatase inhibitors. Aim 4, Characterize the in vivo activity of optimized compounds in relevant animal models.

title: Drugging an epigenomically modulated master regulator of clear cell renal cell carcinoma
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Advanced clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) represents an unmet clinical need due to its chemo-radio-resistant nature and rapid emergence of resistance against targeted therapies including angiogenesis blockade and mTOR inhibitors. There is an urgent need to identify new actionable targets to expand current treatment options and improve patient outcome.Over 90% of ccRCC tumors acquire insufficiency of the von Hippel Lindau (VHL) tumor suppressor but restoration of VHL is not a viable therapeutic strategy. In our most recent work (Yao et al, under revision at Cancer Discovery), we utilized chromatin profiling of VHL-deficient primary normal-tumor pairs and isogenic cell lines to examine epigenomic malfunctions directly driven by VHL loss. This led us to discover ZNF395 as novel master regulator of ccRCC tumorigenesis -- its depletion caused near-complete tumor elimination in vitro and in vivo. Rarely mutated or amplified by chromosome gain, ZNF395 is epigenomically regulated by an active super-enhancer of high histone 3 lysine 27 acetylation (H3K27ac) signals that is bound by HIF2?-HIF1? heterodimer and P300, a histone acetyltransferase.We propose that epigenomic inhibition of ZNF395 represents a new therapeutic strategy for ccRCC. Firstly, elucidation of its direct targets will inform its mechanism of action, and reveal new disease vulnerabilities for ccRCC. We will perform whole-genome binding profiles of ZNF395 and transcriptomics analysis to pinpoint ZNF395’s oncogenic pathways. Second, since ZNF395 is epigenomically regulated, pharmacological attenuation of its active chromatin state will likely dampen its transcription, and by association, the proliferation of ccRCC. We will screen small-molecule epigenomic modulators that will induce downregulation of ZNF395 through chromatin remodeling in VHL-deficient ccRCC cell lines.Mostly importantly, if funded, this work will establish a pipeline that bridges epigenomics-guided target discovery to proof-of-concept epigenetic therapy, and may be applicable to other mutation-defined cancer types.

title: Role of the Hedgehog Signaling Pathway in Obesity-induced Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD) and Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC)
abs: Obesity is a risk factor for many malignancies, including hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). However, the mechanism by which non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) progresses to cirrhosis and ultimately to HCC is poorly understood. In this project, we propose to investigate the role of the oncogenic Hedgehog (Hh) signaling pathway in the development of hepatic injury and HCC in the context of an obese setting, with the goal of identifying Hh effectors that serve as potential therapeutic targets for intervention in patients with chronic fatty livers and liver cancers. We hypothesize that excess fat deposits in the liver trigger an injury response leading to up-regulated Hh signaling in NAFLD that subsequently contributes to the formation of HCC. We first developed a mouse model of obesity-induced HCC in which only mice fed a high-fat diet and injected the chemical carcinogen diethylnitrosamine (DEN) develop HCC. Using this model, we aim to identify the hepatic cell populations that secrete, and respond to Hh ligands at different stages in the transition from NAFLD to HCC. Subsequently using various mouse lines with conditional genetic abrogation of the Hh pathway in targeted cell populations, we then seek to establish the functional significance of Hh signaling. Finally, we aim to elucidate the mechanism by which hepatic Hh signaling regulates liver injury and HCC by identifying Hh transcriptional targets critical for these processes. Owing to the promiscuous roles that Hh signaling plays in various developmental and homeostatic processes, we believe that these candidates, upon further pre-clinical validation, would potentially serve as novel drug targets for more targeted and personalized treatment of fatty liver disease and HCC.

title: Designing unconventional inhibitors for BCR-ABL protein kinase
abs: Mitogen-activated protein (MAP) kinase-interacting kinases (Mnk) 1/2 are involved in the phosphorylation of eukaryotic initiation factor 4E (eIF4E), a protein that is overexpressed in many cancer cell lines. ETC has been interested in developing novel small molecule drugs for treatment of blast crisis CML, prompting us to identify ATP-competitive inhibitors for Mnk1/2. Due to the highly conserved nature of the ATP-binding site in protein kinases, achieving high selectivity is very challenging and a lack of selectivity may lead to toxicity. Allosteric inhibition of protein kinases has recently emerged as an alternative strategy in search for novel kinase inhibitors. Instead of competing with ATP, allosteric kinase inhibitors disrupt the protein-substrate interaction by binding to a separate site, which changes the conformational dynamics of the protein. Such conformational changes can also affect the way protein kinases interact with other proteins, potentially leading to modulation of downstream signaling. The comparatively low sequence homology of allosteric binding sites affords unique opportunities for improved selectivity and reduced off-target pharmacology. Another advantage of allosteric inhibitors is the ability to overcome mutation associated drug resistance, in particular, mutations in the ATP-binding site. Mnk1/2 being a novel target for cancer-drug discovery serves as an excellent target for developing inhibitors with unique modes of action. We propose to use chemical biology techniques to identify novel and potent allosteric inhibitors of Mnk1/2 and this approach would expand BMRC’s portfolio of clinically useful Mnk inhibitors for emerging indications such as obesity.

title: Development a patient centered-approach to improving outcomes of patients with multi-morbidity in primary care
abs: The rising burden of chronic medical conditions has generated a new clinical challenge: the management of large numbers of patients with multi-morbidity. Traditional disease-focused methods of chronic disease management may hinder rather than help patients. A more patient-centered approach is required, but current evidence on effective patient-centered interventions for patients with multi-morbidity is very limited.Aims To develop and pilot a patient-centered intervention with the aim of improving patient-oriented and disease-specific outcomes in adult patients with multi-morbidity.HypothesesOne of the hypothesized consequences of patient-centered care is that patients will be empowered to achieve better health outcomes through behavior change; with increasing accountability being placed on the patient to choose to make changes in their health behavior on their terms. This requires a change in how care is delivered; the patient is seen as an equal member of the healthcare team, actively collaborating with healthcare providers for a feasible care plan, leading to the best outcomes. The patient is also enabled to better understand, manage and communicate their healthcare issues with their healthcare providers. The implementation of such an intervention will likely improve patients’ quality of life, self-efficacy and disease-related outcomes.Methodology Initially a systematic review on interventions for improving outcomes in patients with multi-morbidity in primary care will be conducted. This will be followed by a qualitative study to better understand patients’ experiences and perspectives of patient-centered care and their ideas on how it can be improved. Lessons learned from the review and the qualitative study will guide the development of patient-centered intervention, which will be based on the UK Medical Research Council guidance on developing and evaluating complex interventions. A protocol for the evaluation of the intervention will be designed, followed by conducting a pilot study to evaluate the outcomes of the patient centered intervention.

title: A nationwide knowledge, attitudes and practice (KAP) survey on diabetes in Singapore’s general population
abs: This proposal for a nationwide study aims to (i) conduct a survey to examine the knowledge, attitudes and protective practices (KAP) pertaining to diabetes among Singapore’s general population, supplemented with a diabetic patient population from polyclinic (primary care) and specialized diabetes (tertiary care) clinic; (ii) identify the knowledge gaps and behavioural patterns that may hamper diabetes prevention and control; (iii) identify socio-demographic correlates of knowledge gaps, to enable targeted diabetes education programmes; (iv) examine diabetes related stigma from the perspective of those with and without diabetes and (v) conduct a qualitative study to elucidate and understand the major themes that facilitate adoption of healthy lifestyle. We hypothesise that certain socio-demographic groups such as older adults, those with less than university education, lower income and those without diabetes (versus those with diabetes) will have poorer KAP. We also hypothesise that those with diabetes will report significant self stigma which will be associated with poorer KAP and lower quality of life. This study which will be the first of its kind in Singapore is proposed as a nationwide, cross-sectional study of Singapore residents aged 18 years and above, belonging to the four major ethnic groups. A disproportionate stratified sampling approach will be used; 3000 respondents will be recruited from the population supplemented by a clinical sample of diabetes patients (about 330 diagnosed patients). A vignette based approach will be used to examine the recognition of diabetes. Data on KAPs as well as stigma towards diabetes will be collected using relevant questionnaires. Other data collected will include socio-demographic information, quality of life as well as details of chronic conditions among respondents. Focus group discussions will be conducted with patients with diabetes and those without to compare and contrast themes related to health lifestyle with those that emerge from the surveys.

title: The Impact of Dynamic and Static Distraction in Disc Regeneration – A Longitudinal Study using Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) in Rabbit Model
abs: Intervertebral disc (IVD) degeneration can result in low back pain which is a disabling condition. It imposes an enormous clinical and socioeconomic burden on society. Surgical decompression and/or fusion of vertebral bodies is commonly employed to treat patients with disabling symptoms from IVD degeneration. However, surgery can only provide symptom relief at the expense of disrupting spinal mechanics, leading to accelerated degeneration of adjacent spinal levels. IVD regeneration strategies are ideal goals aiming to provide a better solution. Unfortunately, lack of nutrient supply reduces the efficiency of stem cell and growth factor therapy in degenerated human IVD. Our previous study has proven that regeneration occurs with tensile loading of degenerated IVD as evidenced by improved nutrient flow, increased cell survival rate and more abundant disc extracellular matrix up to 1-month.However, no longitudinal data exists to show the possibility of sustained impact of static and dynamic tensile loading under physiological conditions over a longer time frame (up to 3 months). Since IVD is a relatively avascular tissue with low regenerative potential, a longer-term longitudinal and physiological study is crucial to determine whether sustained disc regeneration could be achieved by dynamic and static tensile loading. Development of an MRI-compatible distraction device will fill this information gap and provide valuable longitudinal data such as disc height, hydration level and nutrition flow over the whole regeneration process.Rabbits will be divided into 4 groups - no treatment, static distraction, dynamic distraction and naïve. Disc degeneration in groups 1-3 will be induced by needle stabbing method. Disc height, degree of hydration and nutrient diffusion will be measured by MRI at baseline, 1st , 2nd and 3rd month after treatment. Post sacrifice analysis using microCT and histological tests will also be conducted. This promising study will advance regeneration strategy for patients with IVD degeneration.

title: Identifying Curable Unilateral Disease using 11C-Metomidate PET-CT in Primary Aldosteronism (CURE_PA)
abs: Hypertension afflicts 1 in 4 Singaporeans, of which 10% have the treatable condition – primary aldosteronism. Primary aldosteronism is caused by either bilateral adrenal disease (~40%), managed with life-long medications; or unilateral disease (~60%), cured with laparoscopic surgery (adrenalectomy). Unfortunately, many patients with curable hypertension remain undiagnosed and consequently develop cardiac disease and strokes. The difficulty with identifying curable unilateral disease is due to adrenal vein sampling (AVS): an invasive, and technically-difficult procedure, with inconclusive results in 50% of patients. An alternative novel imaging, 11C-metomidate PET-CT, can detect adrenal tumors, and concurrently confirm their over-activity. It is non-invasive, non-operator-dependent, and can identify more patients with curable hypertension.We hypothesize that 11C-metomidate PET-CT can accurately identify patients with surgically-curable unilateral adrenal disease among hypertensive Asians with primary aldosteronism.Our aims are:1.To determine the accuracy of 11C-metomidate PET-CT and AVS in identifying unilateral primary aldosteronism, as established by cure post-surgery (primary aim); 2.and as established by clinical diagnosis (secondary aim);3.To evaluate the cost-effectiveness of 11C-metomidate PET-CT, versus AVS, in diagnosing patients with unilateral disease (secondary aim).To achieve this, our multi-centre collaboration will recruit 25 patients nationwide with primary aldosteronism. All patients will undergo standard-of-care diagnostic tests (CT imaging and AVS) and the research procedure (11C-metomidate PET-CT). All results will be evaluated to determine the clinical diagnosis (unilateral or bilateral) at a multi-disciplinary meeting. Management (surgery or medication) will be decided by the managing clinician in consult with the patient. Patients who undergo surgery will be reassessed six months post-surgery for cure of primary aldosteronism (primary outcome).11C-metomidate PET-CT has potential to replace current standards. Leveraging on our team’s technical expertise, we aim to demonstrate that 11C-metomidate PET-CT can accurately identify patients with curable hypertension, and establish Singapore as a world-leading centre in primary aldosteronism and hypertension.

title: Development of a real-time machine learning approach to improve surgical outcomes during deep brain stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus in Parkinson disease
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Aim: We aim to use a machine-learning approach to automate target localisation during deep brain stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus (STN DBS) in patients with Parkinson disease (PD).Background: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is a safe and effective established surgical treatment for advanced PD, but good clinical outcomes are highly dependent on the placement of the electrodes accurately and precisely in the relatively small subthalamic nucleus (STN). Microelectrode recording (MER) by detecting the specific pattern of neuronal firing characteristic of the STN is the gold-standard method used during DBS surgery to refine targeting of the STN intra-operatively. However, the method requires significant expertise of the neurosurgeon and neurophysiologist, and can therefore be operator dependent, costly and time consuming.Method: Machine learning classification procedures will be used to identify optimal features in the MER (such as neuronal firing patterns with beta oscillations and spectral power analysis of local field potentials) which can discriminate the STN from white matter tracts and neighbouring structures. A 3D neurophysiological map will be constructed with the extracted features at multiple depths and trajectories. A probability index will be derived to indicate the return probability of the electrode proximity to the optimal target within the STN.Significance: We aim to improve the targeting of STN DBS by providing a novel automatic, reliable, objective and real-time method to locate the STN during DBS surgery based on neurophysiological monitoring of MER. This will translate into improved clinical efficacy of neuromodulation and reduce side effects from incorrect bioelectric stimulation. The short-term benefits include performing DBS faster and safer by eliminating human error and integrating complex data leading to improved clinical outcomes. In the long term, this will be a cost-effective solution as it eliminates the need for a dedicated neurophysiologist whose services are either expensive or may not be readily available.

title: Targeting Interleukin-1 receptor-associated kinase 1 (IRAK1) in breast cancer through single agent and combination strategies
abs: Background: Breast cancer is a leading cause of cancer and second leading cause of cancer death in women. The interleukin-1 receptor-associated kinases (IRAKs) mediate toll-like receptor (TLR) and interleukin-1 receptor (IL-1R) signaling, influencing downstream processes including inflammation and apoptosis. While the role of IRAK in inflammatory diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis is relatively well studied, its role in cancer is less well elucidated. Our group has found that IRAK1 is overexpressed in a proportion of breast cancers, and knockdown of IRAK1 decreased tumor growth and improved survival in mice model. Hypothesis and aims: IRAK1 as a potential therapeutic target driving metastasis and treatment resistance in breast cancer. Inhibition with novel compounds with reported IRAK1 activity (PF06650833 and thymoquinone), either as a single agent or in combination with chemotherapy, will lead to cell killing and decrease tumor growth in preclinical models. Methodology and approach: Breast cancer cell lines will be cultured and MTT assays performed to look for differential cell viability between cell lines that have high and low IRAK1 expression levels. Drug assays will be carried out to determine IC50, and functional assays will be performed on cell line derived tumorspheres to study apoptotic effects. Western blot analysis will be completed to confirm target inhibition of IRAK1 through downregulation of pIRAK1. Results will be validated in patient derived cell lines and patient derived xenograft (PDX) tumorspheres. In vivo studies utilizing PDX tumors with IRAK1 upregulation engrafted into mice will then be conducted to confirm in vitro findings. Mice will be euthanized as per ethical guidelines, and tumors will be harvested for further characterisation of pIRAK1 expression levels using IHC or RT-PCR techniques. The most promising single agent compound will then be combined with paclitaxel chemotherapy to test for potential additive or synergistic effects both in vitro and in vivo.
kw: IRAK1, breast cancer, therapy

title: Establishment of 3D Expansion of Cervical Circulating Tumor Cells as a Prognostic Tool for Chemoradiotherapy Response
abs: Circulating Tumour Cells (CTCs) are rare cells shed from tumours into the bloodstream (Pantel et al. 2007). In vitro expansion of CTCs allows better characterization of cancer as compared to tumour biopsies. However, current CTC enrichment techniques are limited in sensitivity, and present an underestimate of total CTCs. This study aims to develop a procedure for the label-free expansion of CTC clusters from serial blood samples of patients. The CTC Cluster Assay, a novel microfluidic assay for CTC expansion (Khoo et al. 2016) which mimics tumour microenvironment in vitro is utilised. This is a single-step procedure that does not require pre-enrichment, minimizing loss of cells and viability. Efficiency of cluster formation has been demonstrated previously in patients with breast cancer (>70% in pre-treatment samples) (Khoo et al. 2016, Khoo et al. 2015). In the absence of tapered microwells (i.e. flat substrates), clusters do not form. Cluster phenotype correlates with patient prognosis. We demonstrate the assay’s applicability to samples from patients with stage 2-4 cervical cancer undergoing chemoradiation or palliative chemotherapy. We have recruited eight subjects to date, seven of whom have completed the trial after four blood sample collections each. Samples were processed for device optimisation or culture. Clusters were detected in samples from patients with more advanced stages of cervical cancer. CD45-putative CTC population varies from 10-50%. For one positive sample, about 40% of the putative CTC population was EpCAM+. The ability to enrich CTCs from blood liquid biopsy is a minimally invasive method which can be carried out routinely. This allows personalized evaluation of cancer-immune cell interactions throughout treatment which translate to high applicability in cases where the tumor cannot be biopsied, allowing us to utilise the cultures for biomarker discoveries.

title: Translational program in ocular surface and dry eye
abs: Ocular surface inflammatory disease (OSID) is a heterogeneous group of conditions that affects approximately 300 million people globally. Corneal blindness, a result of end stage OSID, is the second leading cause of blindness worldwide. The commonest cause of OSID is dry eye, which affects up to a third of the adults in Asian countries. In the ongoing CSA which will end in late 2017, important findings such as tear and meibum lipids have been characterized, and novel tools such as automated analysis of meibography and thermography-based tear-evaporimetry have been evaluated. Research publications have propelled the Singapore group to one of the top three most frequently published groups internationally in the dry eye domain. Reputation has increased, resulting in an invitation to participate in an international expert consensus panel (Dry Eye Workshop 2), frequent overseas invited lectures by the industry, and invitation to join the Asia Dry Eye Society council. To further improve patients’ lives, dry eye cannot be addressed by improving tear stability alone, and the inflammatory process will need to be treated. Current treatment of inflammation is unsatisfactory (has adverse effects, lack efficacy or uncomfortable). We aim to build on the existing achievements in the current CSA and focus on investigating the basis of inflammation in dry eye, the immune-regulatory environment of the ocular surface; and translating molecules already identified to real therapy for dry eye patients. Specifically, we will investigate the immunology of graft-vs-host disease, a group of patients with very severe, sight- threatening OSID, elucidate small lipid molecules and role of microbes in dry eye, chart levels of inflammatory mediators after commencement of therapy, and survey for patient preferences in topical anti-inflammatory drugs. The proposed CSA will critically facilitate all existing translational efforts and grant projects by supporting the research team trained over the years.

title: Characterizing Zika virus transmission to inform vector management
abs: Singapore is currently hit by a Zika outbreak that caused devastating long term neurological effects throughout the world. In absence of vaccine and therapeutics, the only available tool to immediately alleviate Zika burden on public health is vector management. However, while Singapore vector control program for dengue is one of the best in the world, further understanding of Zika virus transmission under local context will facilitate efficient use of existing infrastructures to stop the Zika outbreak. Here, we propose to undertake a thorough and comprehensive exploratory study of the entomological, virological and environmental factors that determine Zika virus transmission. This work will directly inform the on-going vector control efforts. As indicated by the speed at which the Zika epidemic has spread to all continents and as confirmed by our preliminary data showing a high infectivity of Zika virus for mosquito vectors collected in Singapore, the high transmission efficiency is a key driver of the alarming situation of the pandemic, further emphasizing the importance to target transmission. Our specific aims include identification of all the mosquito vectors responsible for the Singaporean outbreak using field and laboratory experiments, and characterization of the impact of mosquito and virus genetics, infectious viral dose, temperature and gonotrophic cycle on horizontal and vertical transmission. Fast production of results will be ensured by transferring methods and infrastructures available to study dengue virus. By synergizing the academic expertise of a major player in the field of flavivirus research, Duke-NUS, and the operational strength of the government arm to vector management, the Environment Health Institute, we believe to have gathered the best expertise in Singapore to reach our goals. This new collaborative dynamics will not only place Singapore at the forefront of the research on Zika virus transmission but also result in real-time translation of our data into policies.

title: Characterizing the epigenome of human heart failure and functional validation for disease- related variants
abs: Heart failure (HF) is a major cause of morbidity and mortality and looks to be a rapidly worsening heathcare burden as our world population ages. In Singapore, Cardiovascular Disease is named one of 5 key diseases areas in our national research focus. The identity of regulatory genetic variants for human disease has proven benefit for yielding genetic biomarkers, and also highlighting the full spectrum of molecular mechanisms of disease. It has however been difficult to identify causal variants for HF from genome-wide association studies alone, partly because large cohort sizes are required for statistically significant power, HF disease heterogeneity can be difficult to overcome, and also because it is difficult to assign cis-regulatory functions of implicated candidate loci. Motivated by our collaborator’s success with identifying >2,000 regulatory loci (haQTL), leveraging tissue-specific epigenetic signatures simply from small sample sizes of human brains, we propose to undertake the same approach using human hearts. Gene expression changes are a hallmark of HF, and cardiac epigenetics is an important underlying mechanism of disease. However, whether and how epigenetic changes are linked to variants in regulatory regions remains unestablished. Here, (Aim 1) we will map genome-wide Enhancers for human HF and identify causal regulatory variants by haQTL. (Aim 2) We will map genome-wide Enhancer-Promoter Interaction for HF by Hi-C, integrate haQTL from Aim 1 and assign their role to the regulation of their corresponding gene expression. (Aim 3) We will verify the functionality of HF Enhancers and validate haQTL variants in their role with regulating gene expression in a cardiac-organoid system. Collectively, these studies aims to expand our knowledge on the role that variants in regulatory regions play in the pathophysiology of HF and whether experimental targeting of regulatory regions would improve clinical features of HF.

title: Development of a platform to bridge genomic information with phenotypic information for healthcare and healthcare research.
abs: A key enabling tool in precision healthcare is the integration of molecular data with associated clinical and phenotypic data. Unprecedented volumes of genomic data is being generated through –omic studies of human diseases, particularly cancer. This molecular information is derived from patient samples, each with unique phenotypes and clinical course. A key gap is the correlation of this information to learn more about the determinants of the clinical course of human diseases or indeed to influence and improve the management of human diseases.Achieving this will require a rich data-science platform that enables integration of genomic information with phenotypic information. Cancer forms a template disease for personalized –omic informed medicine leverage on in depth omics analysis of patient material combined with detailed phenotypic information of disease parameters and longitudinal effects of treatment. In collaboration with Systems, Applications & Products in Data Processing (SAP), a large German multinational software corporation that designs and maintains enterprise software, we seek to apply and build upon their existing healthcare platforms to customize and optimize a data science solution to integrate omic and phenotypic data, specifically focused on three domains: (1) integrating genomic information with phenotypic and longitudinal patient efficacy and toxicity outcomes (2) integrating genomic information with constantly accumulating biological knowledge from the biomedical literature. (3) integrating genomic information with global databases of ongoing clinical trials evaluating hypothesis of drugs with therapeutic selectivity in specific molecular subtypes. By developing platforms that integrate genomic information with these 3 layers of information platforms, it is envisaged that we can develop a comprehensive research and clinical decision aid tools that pools these “big data” sources together for transformative research and clinical care.

title: Markers of macrophage activation syndrome, Natural Killer cell (NK) function and associated genetic polymorphisms in the pathogenesis of severe dengue
inst: CREATE - Singapore-MIT Alliance for Research and Technology (CREATE-SMART)
abs: Dengue can present with different clinical phenotypes, with severe disease being characterized by vascular leakage, organ dysfunction and coagulopathy. Severe dengue shares many features with macrophage activation syndrome (MAS)/ reactive haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (rHLH). MAS is a recognised complication of many autoimmune and infectious diseases, particularly viral infections. Mechanistically, genetic polymorphisms in the natural killer (NK) cytolytic pathways underlie MAS: NK cell dysfunction result in uncontrolled macrophage activation, and hyper-inflammation causing organ damage. Although there is emerging evidence that MAS may occur in dengue, with high levels of ferritin and sCD163 documented in dengue patients, neither the NK functional phenotype nor associated NK genetic polymorphisms have been studied; demonstration of which are major criteria for MAS diagnosis. We therefore plan to determine if the underlying mechanisms and genetic associations of MAS can be found in a well characterized cohort of Vietnamese patients. Our hypothesis is that markers of MAS are associated with dengue severity and are linked to decreased NK cytolytic function and polymorphisms in NK genes. Our approach is to perform a nested case-control study uisng clinical data and samples already collected in Vietnam. This cohort includes 88 severe cases which we will compare to 120 mild cases as controls. Firstly we will measure the plasma markers of MAS including ferritin, sCD25, sCD163, fibrinogen and triglycerides at serial time-points. Secondly, we will measure the cytolytic activity of NK cells at the same time-points and correlate with the MAS biomarkers. Finally, we will investigate the polymorphisms in the NK cell cytolytic genes and correlate these with NK cell functional phenotype, MAS biomarkers and clinical outcome. The results from this study will deliver definitive evidence of dengue-associated MAS, which would provide the biological rationale for immediate translation of existing biologic therapeutics currently used in patients with MAS, for treatment of severe dengue.

title: Role of skin-based T cell immunity during Dengue virus infection
abs: Dengue virus (DENV) infection is spreading at alarming rates worldwide. The lack of a clear definition of the correlates of protective immunity for DENV and in particular, the poor understanding of the role of T cells, represent a major hurdle for the design of a fully protective vaccine. We have shown that acute DENV infection elicits DENV-specific T cells that express the skin-homing marker cutaneous lymphocyte-associated antigen (CLA) and which are found at highest frequencies in the skin tissue as compared to peripheral blood. “Bystander” activation of T cells that are specific for unrelated antigens such as human-cytomegalovirus (HCMV) also occurs, but these cells do not express similar skin-homing phenotypes. The aim of this proposal is to define the role of DENV-specific T cells present in the skin of dengue patients and understand their relationship with those present in peripheral blood. We hypothesize that DENV-specific tissue-resident T cells are established in the skin during acute dengue infection and these cells provide superior anti-viral capacity as compared to their blood counterparts. In contrast, “bystander-activated” T cells, which represent a large proportion of activated T cells present in circulation during acute DENV infection, may play a detrimental role by contributing to the inflammatory process which underlies the increase in vascular permeability. An in-depth characterization of the phenotypic, functional and transcriptional profiles of antigen-specific T cells present in the skin and blood of adult dengue patients will be performed. We hypothesis that “bystander-activated” rather than DENV-specific T cells drive the T cell gene expression profiles which were shown to correlate with the development of DHF. This study will provide an improved definition of the correlates of protective immunity for DENV and will demonstrate for the first time in humans the impact of skin-based T cells for protection against viral infection.

title: Channelopathy Pathogenesis in a Human Stem Cell Model of Angelman Syndrome.
abs: Angelman syndrome (AS) is a genetic disorder characterized by developmental delay, severe epilepsy, intellectual disability, and abnormal social interactions. AS is caused by mutations in or deletion of UBE3A gene, which encodes an E3 ubiquitin ligase UBE3A. Although deficits in both excitatory glutamatergic and inhibitory GABAergic synaptic signaling and plasticity underlie behavioral dysfunction in a mouse model of AS, the exact functional role of UBE3A in the pathogenesis of AS is still elusive, largely due to the inaccessibility to examine the functional properties of neurons in AS affected individuals. To determine how neuronal UBE3A loss-of-function contributes to AS, we have generated isogenic UBE3A Knockout (UBE3A KO) hESC clones using CRISPR/Cas9 mediated genome editing. In parallel, we recently reprogramed dermal fibroblasts from AS patients and controls into induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs). Most importantly, we could differentiate these UBE3A KO hESCs and AS iPSCs into either glutamatergic excitatory neurons or GABAergic inhibitory neurons efficiently by expressing selected transcription factors. Intriguingly, only induced excitatory, not inhibitory, neurons from UBE3A KO hESC exhibited enhanced amplitude of afterhyperpolarization (AHP) currents, indicating potential changes in ion channels in excitatory neurons derived from UBE3A KO hESC. Our objective is to determine epilepsy and intellectual disability mechanisms of UBE3A-linked AS in humans. We will test the central hypothesis that the loss of UBE3A leads to paradoxical increase in AHP currents, as well as alterations in synaptic and network changes that underlie neuronal and network hyperexcitability in AS by combining stem cell biology, electrophysiology, and in vivo multi-photon imaging of transplanted human neuron in mouse cortex. The successful completion of this work will provide new insights into the molecular and cellular mechanisms of UBE3A in the pathophysiology of AS and related neurological disorders including epilepsy and autism.

title: Eradication of Chronic Hepatitis B
abs: The Singapore Hepatitis B Consortium (SHBC) is a national translational group of 29 researchers and scientists who have been working collaboratively, now plan to focus on the eradication of Chronic Hepatitis B (CHB), through a comprehensive approach via three integrated themes of examining host/viral interactions, target discovery with validation, and experimental therapeutics. The SHBC has a proven track record as follows:ò33 joint publicationsò5 joint grant applicationsCHB has been considered difficult but not impossible to eradicate with current therapies. The SHBC plans to tackle this successfully by exploiting its joint expertise and strong working relationships using its unique capabilities and resources:òA 1458 patient cohort of long-term followup (mean 6.7years) CHB patients (DSRB standing database ref: NUH-2004-0016) with 17,154 stored serums and 2,815 PBMC linked to laboratory and clinical outcomes. òA novel humanised mouse model of hepatitis B that is able to host both human liver cells and immune cells, and shown to harbour HBV infection, which now can be fully exploited for hypothesis testing, target validation and experimental therapeutics. òA state of the art cytometry by time-of-flight (CyTOF) machine that is capable of simultaneously and sensitively probe >100 antigen specificities all in a single human blood sampleòStrong expertise in intra-hepatic immunologyòEstablished collaborations with many pharmaceutical companiesIn this proposal, we initially plan to discover host genes/SNPs that contribute to viral eradication and explore the immune mileau by which this occurs through state of the art CyTOF assay and interrogating intrahepatic immune cells and innate immunity. Concurrently, discovery of new targets for intrahepatic viral replication will be explored through multiple technologies and validated in the humanised mouse model, which we plan to establish as a standard model for CHB research. Finally, clinical trials as proof of principle studies, will address specific strategies to optimise HBV eradication.
