title: Understanding the Psychosocial, Cultural, and Systemic Determinants of Antibiotic Use and Utilizing a multilevel Approach to Address Inappropriate Antibiotic Use
abs: The rapid emergence and unimpeded increase in antimicrobial resistance has raised serious concerns about the threat of a postantibiotic era. One major contributing factor is inappropriate antibiotic use. The decision to use antibiotics is complex, involving not only a physician’s propensity to prescribe antibiotics but also the interplay of psychosocial, cultural, and systemic factors among the patient, caregiver, clinical care team, and physician. Antimicrobial resistance, which increases with age, can result in a decreased quality of life, higher morbidity and mortality risks, and increased healthcare expenditure. It is preventable through a successful antimicrobial stewardship program. Most studies on antibiotic use and antimicrobial stewardship have been conducted in developed Western countries, where healthcare provision is a patient-centered model. A relationship-centered model could be the framework for optimal care and antibiotic prescribing in Singapore. However, to date, there is no study evaluating antimicrobial stewardship comprehensively at multiple levels throughout the continuum of care. Through a series of mixed-methods studies involving sequential qualitative and quantitative phases carried out in the community, public and private primary care clinics, and the three largest hospitals in Singapore, the research proposal aims to explore the views and opinions of diverse stakeholders (general public, patients, caregivers, healthcare providers) to gain insights into the multi-dimensional determinants of antibiotic use and prescribing practices. The understanding will guide an evidence-based multi-level intervention that will align the goals of all stakeholders towards a synchronized national antimicrobial stewardship program to reduce inappropriate antibiotic use, prevent antimicrobial resistance, and decrease healthcare costs in Singapore. With a rapidly ageing population, who are more prone to infections and inappropriate exposure to antibiotics due to atypical symptomatic presentations, such an approach is necessary to curb the rising tide of antimicrobial resistance and prevent antibiotic-resistant infections amidst the background of a dwindling antibiotic pipeline and limited healthcare resources.

title: Earlier Assessment of RheumatoLogical diseases to ImprovE Recognition and outcomes (EARLIER)) Study
abs: Background: Connective tissue diseases (CTDs) have a disproportionately large disease burden despite their low prevalence. Rheumatoid arthritis and “other musculoskeletal diseases” account for 55 and 410 per 100,000 years lost to disability (YLD) worldwide. Taken together their disease burden exceeds that of asthma, ischemic heart disease, tuberculosis, or HIV/AIDS. Despite this heavy disease burden, the diagnosis and treatment of CTDs have not received as much attention as other disabling conditions. This may partly be due to the low prevalence of CTDs, and the protean manifestations that make them difficult to diagnose. This is unfortunate as early diagnosis, which leads to early treatment within a “window of opportunity” in the first months of symptom onset, has been shown to improve outcomes in patients with CTDs. To address this gap, this study aims to: 1. Cross-culturally adapt 2 validated questionnaires that screen for CTDs: • The “Connective Tissue Disease Screening Questionnaire” (CSQ) which screens for the following CTDs: Rheumatoid Arthritis, Systemic Lupus Erythematosus, Systemic Sclerosis, Sjogren’s Syndrome, Myositis, and Mixed Connective Tissue Diseases • The “Patient Self-Reported Screening Questionnaire for Axial Spondyloarthropathy” which screens for spondyloarthritis (SpA) - henceforth referred to as the Hamilton SpA questionnaire 2. Test the diagnostic accuracy of the adapted questionnaires in Singapore 3. Develop a shorter questionnaires based on the CSQ and Hamilton SpA questionnaires for use in general population surveys Methods: We will adapt the 2 screening questionnaires for use in Singapore by carrying out a rigorous process of forward and backward translation, expert panel review, and patient cognitive debriefings. We will test the diagnostic accuracy by prospectively administering the crossculturally adapted questionnaire to patients referred from primary care to the Singapore General Hospital for evaluation of possible CTD(n=1,300). We will then develop shorter versions of these questionnaires to be used in the general population.

title: Adolescent and young adult cancer patients: Cognitive Toxicity on Survivorship (ACTS)
abs: Background: As the cure rates for adolescent and young adult (AYA) cancers continue to improve and survivors live longer, survivorship issues in this group of patients are becoming increasingly relevant, and more in-depth research is needed. Among these undesirable toxicities, cognitive toxicity remains inadequately studied in the AYA population. Enhancing the understanding of cognitive toxicity will facilitate the development of effective interventions for AYA cancer survivors to better cope with their daily lives. Aim, Hypothesis and Objectives: In the ACTS study, we aim to elucidate the prevalence, mechanism and survivorship impact of cognitive toxicity among adolescent and young adult (AYA) patients diagnosed with curable cancers. We hypothesize that cognitive impairment is clinically significant among AYA cancer patients treated with chemotherapy. We also hypothesize that structural and functional changes in the brain are detectable in AYA cancer patients treated with chemotherapy. Hence, the primary objective is to compare the prevalence of cognitive impairment at 6 months from baseline, in AYA cancer patients and healthy AYA controls. The secondary objectives are to describe the trajectory of cognitive impairment, and to correlate cognitive impairment with (i) work/education status, (ii) physical symptoms and psychological distress, (iii) cytokines, and (iv) neuroimaging. Methodology/Approach: This will be a multicenter, prospective, longitudinal, observational study. The study participants will comprise two groups, a group of 15 to 39-year-old patients newly diagnosed with breast cancer, lymphoma and germ cell tumors being treated with curative intent and a group of healthy control. Assessment tools and blood draws (standardized timing) will be serially conducted at baseline, 3-, 6-, 9- and 12-months from baseline. Neuroimaging will be conducted at baseline and 6-months after baseline, in patients who are not contraindicated for MRI.

title: Precision Medicine in Liver Cancer across an Asia-Pacific Network _
abs: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the 6th most common cancer in the world but the 2nd most important cause of cancer death. Because of its highly heterogeneous nature, the current approach to identifying druggable targets have not delivered efficacious therapies in HCC and is a main reason for the high case fatality. Even when surgical resection is potentially curative in early disease, tumor recurrence remains high and long term survival poor because of the absence of useful adjuvant therapy. To address these unmet needs, we bring together internationally recognized scientists from genomics and immunology and established clinician investigators in a synergistic team. This TCR capitalizes on recent collaborative advances made by the PIs in the consortium. We have shown through multi-region sampling of freshly resected HCC and phylogenetic analysis, that significant intra-tumoral heterogeneity exists and have identified the specific positions of known clonal drivers. Simultaneously we have analyzed the immune landscape of the tumor microenvironment with deep immune-phenotyping and found unique inter-patient immune landscapes predictive of clinical trajectory. In this TCR, Phase I is a prospective study that samples resected HCC from multi-ethnic sites within the established Asia-Pacific Hepatocellular Carcinoma (AHCC) Trials Group, which has enrolled approximately 1000 patients through 6 multi-center trials in 35 centers in the region. Clinical trajectories are tracked and genomic and immunological studies are repeated when tumors recur, to confirm clonally dominant driver mutations and immunological processes that are targetable. In Phase II these patients with recurrent tumors are enrolled in a proof-of-principle clinical trial using therapeutics selected or developed on the basis of discoveries in this study. Concurrently, representative pre-clinical models will be developed from the tissues sampled. We aim to combine these approaches to overcome the challenges posed by genomic heterogeneity and to guide the development of therapeutics and precision medicine in HCC.

title: Design and analysis methods for the evaluation of the effectiveness of vaccines and chemoprevention against infectious diseases
abs: Vaccines and chemoprevention are major means to fight infectious diseases. The technical demands for the evaluation are changing as many interventions currently under investigation concern diseases that can occur multiple times and offer only moderate levels of protection, unlike many earlier products that concern diseases that offer lifetime immunity after one single disease episode and are highly efficacious. One obvious example of the challenges is that typical statistical analysis of time to single event will not be sufficient. In the context of real-life conditions that are changing constantly and are insufficiently represented by the evidence from controlled clinical trials, there are needs to (a) assess the level of time-varying protection and the effect of booster doses, (b) differentiate the primary effect of interventions on repeatable disease episodes from secondary effect due to variation in disease history that has been affected by the interventions and evaluate how they contribute to waning of protection, and (c) assess the impact of interventions on the joint profile of severe and non-severe disease episodes and mortality. These are important aims in post-licensure effectiveness studies, often using case-control study designs or disease surveillance systems. Nonetheless, the statistical methods for the design and analysis of such effectiveness studies are not yet sufficiently developed or evaluated. We will (i) develop novel methods for the design and analysis of effectiveness studies of vaccines and chemoprevention, (ii) evaluate their properties by simulation, (iii) demonstrate their usefulness with data on pneumococcal conjugate vaccine and malaria chemoprevention and elucidate the effectiveness profile of these two important public health interventions, and (iv) develop computer macros for implementing the methods.

title: Targeting Oxidative Phosphorylation for the Rational Development of Sterilising Drug Combination for Drug-resistant Tuberculosis
abs: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the causative agent of tuberculosis (TB), kills more people than any other bacterium. TB control is threatened by the continued spread of drug resistance; multi-drug and extensively drug resistant Mtb require longer, more costly, treatment with multiple drugs causing worse side effects and have a lower likelihood of treatment success. The urgent need for better treatment options for drug resistant Mtb has led the World Health Organization to prioritize development of not only new individual antitubercular agents, but also new drug regimens. Mtb is an obligate aerobe, requiring the use of its branched electron transport chain (ETC) for energy production via oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS). Even during hypoxic non-replicating persistence, Mtb uses its ETC to maintain its proton motive force (PMF). OXPHOS catalyzed by cyt-bd-, cyt-bcc-aa3 and F-ATP synthase lies at the heart of bacterial bioenergetics. Our team has unraveled • Nature’s paradigms for securing energy inside mycobacteria by identifying that three subunits of Mtb F-ATP synthase contribute to the suppression of OXPHOS and PMF-maintenance, • discovered novel targets inside these subunits. • Identified a new compound against the drug epitope of one Mtb F-ATP synthase subunit. • Unraveled that cyt-bd will be one cornerstone of a sterilizing drug regimen for multi-drug resistant tuberculosis. • Discovered the first cell-active small-molecules targeting the cyt-bd. The proposal describes a research program that will combine understanding and translation of oxidative phosphorylation operation by forming a network of experts, whose overall goals are: • To archive novel structural information about domains of Mtb F-ATP synthase and cyt-bd, which together with own developed compounds will pave the way to identify new leads. • To deliver a preclinical development candidate. • To develop diarylquinolines (BDQ) analogues with improved properties. • To archive synergistic efficacy of multi-drug combination.

title: Low Cost, Low Power, Multi-wavelength WDM Sources Leveraging Highly Nonlinear Ultra-silicon-rich Nitride Devices
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: Within the burgeoning industry of active optical cables (AOCs) and transceivers for short and long haul data center communications, silicon photonics-based technologies have shown themselves to be highly competitive in cost and bandwidth scaling with industry roadmaps. AOCs/transceivers are fundamental components enabling ultrafast transmission of laser-driven optical data over fiber for transatlantic data transmission (internet), and optical data transmission between servers, network nodes etc. in a data center. Today's silicon photonics-based transceivers are operating nowhere near their full cost and bandwidth potential – A problem in silicon photonics is its indirect band gap and therefore, inability to generate lasing. This problem has impacted transceiver costs (and concomitantly data costs) significantly, because the transceiver lasers are implemented non–monolithically, creating a significant cost burden. Consequently increasing the number of channels for higher capacities becomes prohibitive because of the multiple lasers required (one laser per channel). We propose a method to scale up the number of data channels with a negligible cost increase. Our approach involves utilizing a single laser to generate coherent light at multiple wavelengths using state of the art, monolithic parametric wavelength conversion on a highly nonlinear, CMOS compatible platform with one of the largest nonlinear figures of merit to date. This platform has been demonstrated for broadband ultra–low power parametric wavelength conversion, and can enable at least 10X lower power levels for multi-wavelength generation compared to competing platforms. The proposed multi-wavelength source, generated with a single laser will be combined with an appropriately designed wavelength division multiplexer (WDM) to realize a WDM transmitter with 4, 8 and potentially up to 100 channels. The proposed technology can be integrated with any transceiver system’s laser to enable drastic reductions in data costs per bit by a factor similar to the number of channels implemented using the WDM transmitter.

title: Panel study Investigating Status of Cognitively impaired Elderly in Singapore (PISCES)
abs: Dementia is a growing epidemic affecting 10% of elderly in Singapore. Caring for patients dying with severe dementia (PDSD) during end of life (EOL) is a medical and economic challenge for the health system and primary informal caregivers. However, to date there is a lack of systematic information regarding EOL care received by community dwelling PDSD, their EOL direct and indirect costs and caregiver burden. This lack of data impedes development and evaluation of interventions to support PDSD and their caregivers. We aim to address this information gap by conducting a first-of-its-kind prospective cohort study of 312 primary informal caregivers of PDSD in collaboration with leading public hospitals and home care foundations caring for PDSD in Singapore. We will assess the EOL care received by community dwelling PDSD and their caregivers, EOL medical and social care costs of severe dementia and caregiver burden; and will develop a risk score to predict 6-month mortality for PDSD. We will survey primary informal caregivers (n=312) every 4 months for 2 years, or until patient death and then 6 weeks and 6 months thereafter. Presence of severe dementia will be established using the Quick Dementia Rating System. At study completion we will extract and match patient medical and billing data with study survey data for comprehensive assessment of care costs. The study will provide data for improved early decision making by caregivers and physicians regarding EOL care. It will also provide a better understanding of EOL care for PDSD and their caregivers that will lead to cross-sector collaborations to improve delivery of palliative care to PDSD. In the long term this study will improve clinical and public health policy and has the potential to be the foundation for future initiatives for dementia care and improved social and medical infrastructure planning.

title: A Randomized Trial to Slow the Progression of Diabetes (The TRIPOD Study)
abs: A primary focus of the ‘Diabetes’ theme is to identify new models to arrest the rate of deterioration and reduce acute episodes for those with diabetes, and to do so in a cost-effective manner while incorporating elements of secondary and tertiary care aligned with primary prevention efforts. This proposal is highly responsive to those objectives. We will conduct a three arm randomized controlled trial to test whether a low cost mobile diabetes management package (DMP), with or without an incentive program (M-POWER rewards), can improve blood sugar levels at 12 months as measured by HbA1c levels (primary) among those with type 2 diabetes. We hypothesize that the greatest improvements will occur for those exposed to both interventions (DMP+M-POWER). Similar hypotheses will be tested for secondary outcomes, including HbA1c at 6 months, proportion of participants initiating insulin, weight, blood pressure, and self-reported weight monitoring, physical activity, blood glucose monitoring, medication adherence and quality of life measures. All outcomes will be tested at baseline, 6, and 12 months. We will also quantify the incremental cost-effectiveness of DMP+M-POWER and the net cost implications of both from a third party payer’s perspective. We hypothesize that despite its higher cost, effectiveness will be greater and net costs will be lower for DMP+M-POWER relative to control due to the reduction in medical expenditures that comes through improved blood sugar control. Given the rising health and cost implications of diabetes in Singapore, this application is timely and offers an innovative and scalable model to address Singapore’s diabetes epidemic.

title: Tailoring Health Communication Materials to Improve Decision Making of Elderly ESRD Patients
abs: Literature suggests that dialysis prolongs survival for younger and healthier patients but for elderly patients with comorbidities, dialysis may offer little to no survival benefits compared with conservative management (CM), which focuses on pharmacological management of symptoms, dietary control and supportive care. Dialysis is also associated with greater costs, greater rates of hospitalization, and lower quality of life. Given these findings, one might expect CM to be the preferred treatment for elderly end stage renal disease (ESRD) patients, yet in Singapore most undergo dialysis. We believe this results because current counselling materials convey little information on CM as a viable alternative and does not adequately convey the pros and cons of dialysis treatment. The goal of this proposal is to address these gaps. Aim 1 proposes to conduct a qualitative study of ESRD patients to explore factors that were influential in their decision to choose a form of dialysis or CM, information that they would have liked to know, their treatment experiences, and whether and to what extent they may have experienced decision regret. Aim 2 uses the results of Aim 1 to develop a new set of counselling material, including printed material and a video with patient testimonials, to be used as patient decision aids, specifically for elderly ESRD patients. Aim 3 evaluates the patient decision aids from Aim 2 in a Phase II trial, using stated choice (primary) and revealed choice (secondary). If the results from Aim 3 suggest the new information is superior, they will be further tested in a longer term study that focuses on real, as opposed to stated, choices. Ultimately all patients should be choosing their treatments after being presented with complete, comprehensive and unbiased information about the available options. This application will help ensure that this goal is achieved.

title: Heart-Brain Connection: Cognitive Impairment in Patients with Heart Failure
abs: Vascular cognitive impairment (VCI) is increasingly recognized in patients with heart failure (HF). Data from our preliminary studies indicate a high burden of VCI among HF patients and that existing cognitive tests can be simplified to expeditiously screen patients for VCI. We hypothesize that VCI is prevalent among HF patients and is correlated with cerebral vascular pathology. The primary objective of this study is to determine the burden of VCI among HF patients and to evaluate a novel method of screening VCI in this high-risk population. The secondary objective of the study is to examine the value and feasibility of an intervention that centers on lifestyle changes and cognitive training for HF patients with mild cognitive impairment (MCI).We propose a two-stage study to achieve these objectives: •In stage one, we propose a cross-sectional study involving 300 HF patients who will be screened for VCI using a standardized brief cognitive test and a detailed formal neuropsychological assessment. One hundred patients who consent to an MRI brain will be followed up for a year to assess for the development of cognitive impairment. Additional vascular investigations will be performed to assess for the risk of cardiac arrhythmia and structural cardiac diseases. •In stage two, we propose a randomized control trial design to examine the feasibility of a multi-domain intervention trial in a smaller cohort of 60 MCI patients who will be randomized to receive intervention and control (no intervention) in a 1:1 ratio. Cost-benefit analyses of cognitive screening and intervention in HF patients will be performed.Outcome of this study will provide important insights on the actual burden of VCI among HF patients and risk factors that contribute towards its development. The feasibility of a multi-domain interventional trial incorporating cognitive training will be addressed in this study.

title: Nano-enabled Electrochemical Deposition (NEED) for anti-infective dental implants
abs: The predictability of osseointegration in dental implant therapy has led to the routine use of dental implants in oral rehabilitation of the edentulous patients. Globally, an estimated one million implants were performed annually. Increasingly, these are placed using non-submerged surgical protocols with transmucosal abutments. Systemic antibiotics is often prescribed following surgery to prevent post-operative infections. Maintenance of stability and function of load-bearing implant is dependent on a well-functioning barrier mechanism established at the transmucosal passage of implant. In recent years, an increasing number of implants and patients affected with peri-implant diseases have been identified. These biofilm-mediated inflammatory conditions are responsible for soft tissue destruction and may lead to pathological bone loss. Currently, there are no established predictable concepts for treatment of peri-implant diseases. Disease management hinges on the prevention of peri-implant mucositis as it is reversible when treated but can potentially progress into peri-implantitis if left untreated. Management of peri-implantitis often requires surgical intervention and in severe cases, explantation, which may compromise function and negatively affect quality of life. With increased emergence of antibiotic-resistant microorganisms, alternative strategies to the use of antibiotics to prevent peri-implant infections are necessary. The overall vision of the proposal is to develop a ‘proof-of-concept’ durable anti-infective and biocompatible coating for implants to decrease the risk of development of biofilm-mediated peri-implant infections. The strategy involves utilising a rapid, inexpensive and easily scalable technique, electrodeposition, to produce a durable protective coating infiltrated with antimicrobial polyphenols that can inhibit biofilm formation and microbial colonisation. Specific aims to achieve this include (i) optimisation of electrochemical coating conditions for selected aromatic polyphenols and characterisation of adherent coatings by surface chemical methods, (ii) in vitro assessment of antimicrobial activity, cytotoxicity and durability of the adherent nanocoatings and (iii) assessment of oral soft tissue response to antimicrobial implant nanocoating in a rabbit model.
kw: Dental implants, anti-infective surfaces, biocompatibility, electrodeposition, surface nanocoating, aromatic polyols

title: Safety and Efficacy of Tissue Engineered Endothelial Keratoplasty (TE-EK)
abs: The specific aim of this clinical trial is to assess the clinical efficacy and safety outcomes of patients receiving Tissue-Engineered Endothelial keratoplasty (TE-EK) graft material generated from human corneal endothelial cells (HCEnCs) propagated in a regulatory-approved dual media approach. We hypothesize that these functional TE-EK graft material prepared expanded primary HCEnCs is able to reverse corneal blindness caused by the dysfunction of the corneal endothelium layer, and alleviate the heavy reliance of donor cornea graft material. This study is a prospective clinical study. Thirty patients who require Descemet’s Stripping Endothelial Keratoplasty (DSEK) surgery for the treatment of their corneal diseases such as Fuchs’ endothelial dystrophy and pseudophakic bullous keratopathy will be selectively recruited. They will each receive a TE-EK graft, which will be prepared within a GMP certified facility. Generation of a TE-EK graft material will involve the expansion of HCEnCs from one donor, and the devitalizaton of a thin stromal scaffold carrier, with an intact Descemet’s Membrane, obtained from a separate donor. Once the HCEnCs have been expanded to the second passage, the cells will be seeded at a physiological cellular density of 3000 cell/mm^2 onto the devitalised carrier, and incubated for at least 5 days before transplantation. All TE-EK surgical procedure will be performed by the Principal Investigator of this study Associate Professor Jodhbir Mehta, whom has performed over 300 EK surgeries, using the EndoGlide DSEK insertion technique. Post-operative follow-ups and visits will follow current EK protocols of Singapore National Eye Centre. Clinical assessments include postoperative visual acuity, intraocular pressure, keratometric astigmatism, spherical equivalent, endothelial cell density, anterior segment optical coherence tomography (ASOCT), contrast sensitivity, as well as any postoperative complications such as graft dislocation or primary graft failure.
kw: Human corneal endothelium; Tissue engineered; Keratoplasty

title: Prospective Study for the Evaluation of Dengue Prognostic Biomarkers in Singapore (PrognosDen)
abs: Annually, 100 million individuals are infected with Dengue and manifest clinical symptoms. One in every 200 proceeds to develop potentially fatal Dengue hemorrhagic fever (DHF) and/or shock syndrome (DSS), and requires hospitalization. If left untreated, 20% to 50% of DHF/DSS patients may succumb to the disease, but this is significantly reduced to 3.5% with timely fluid replacement. To minimize fatality, approximately half of all Dengue patients in Singapore are hospitalized although only less than 1 in 4 eventually develops DHF/DSS. This results in considerable health resource wastage, especially during Dengue epidemics. We have identified three biomarkers that can accurately identify Dengue patients who will develop severe Dengue complications prior to them doing so. By utilizing these biomarkers, we hypothesize that triage and clinical management of Dengue patients can be significantly improved. Patients who will only develop Dengue fever can be accurately identified and managed as outpatients, and hospitalization costs and health resource wastage minimized. Physicians can also better focus their medical attention on Dengue patients who will proceed to develop severe complications. Through this project, we aim to perform (1) a prospective clinical feasibility study to further evaluate the Dengue prognostic biomarkers, and (2) a cost-effectiveness analysis to better understand how utilization of these biomarkers can help save healthcare costs using the socioeconomic data collected. Serum concentrations of the biomarkers in Dengue subjects will be measured, and patients with biomarker concentrations above a specific threshold will be identified as at high risk of developing severe complications. This project is important to better understand the effectiveness of the prognostic biomarkers, and the potential health economics contributions in Dengue endemic countries.
kw: Dengue, prognosis, biomarkers, severe Dengue

title: Psychosis and Apathy in Parkinson’s Disease: A Holistic Approach
abs: This project focuses on neuropsychiatric evaluation of Parkinson’s disease (PD), with emphasis on psychosis and apathy. Data collected is intended to encompass three aspects – scale development, clinical evaluation, and intervention. A case-control study and a clinical cohort study will be performed. In 2007, an international workgroup redefined the landscape of PD psychosis into a continuum of severity, leading to the rapid expansion of literature focusing on clinical aspects, mechanisms, and treatment (Ravina, B. et. al 2007). Evolving literature (de Maindreville et. al, 2005; Diederich et al. 2009; Fenelon et al. 2002;2003;2006;2011; Frei et. al 2017; Graham et. al, 1997) highlights the importance of identifying and treating PD psychosis, and understanding its role as a clinical biomarker of disease stage, distribution, and future progression (ffytch et al. 2017). Apathy is one of the most under recognised, underdiagnosed and poorly managed aspects of Parkinson's disease(Aarsland et. al, 2015). Depending on methodological approach of the study, its prevalence is estimated to be between 17 and 76% (Starkstein et al. 1992). Apathy can be dissociated from depression (Kirsch-Darrow L et al. 2006), and may herald cognitive decline and dementia in PD (Dujardin K et al 2009). In a Singaporean sample population of patients with PD, 45.7% suffered from apathy (Wee et al 2016). So far, there is a lack of randomized controlled studies for the treatment of apathy in Parkinson’s disease. Both psychosis and apathy have significant negative impact on quality of life in PD patients, with associations to greater cognitive decline (ffytch et. al 2017; Guillard et al., 1991) and increased nursing-home placement (Aarsland et al, 2000; Factor et al, 2003). Given the range of deleterious effects from both psychosis and apathy, as well as the current increased emphasis on the non-motor symptoms of PD, there is a compelling need for a standard approach to neuropsychiatric assessment in collaborative PD research. The evidence in support of identification and management of both psychosis and apathy has been challenged by variable definitions, the lack of a validated effective and efficient harmonious core screening battery for both which limits comparisons across studies, and by the absence of robust treatment for both neuropsychiatric symptoms. This represents a significant unmet need. The King’s Parkinson’s International Centre of Excellence (web address: http://parkinsons-london.co.uk) is an ideal place for such a study in scale development and validation as King’s is a world leader in non-motor symptoms research in Parkinson’s disease. title: Preventing emergence of antimicrobial resistance in intensive care units
abs: Background: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is prevalent in Southeast Asia (SEA) including Singapore, especially in intensive care units (ICUs), where antibiotics consumption is high. Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) is the commonest hospital-acquired infection (HAI) in ICUs and is associated with high morbidity and mortality in these vulnerable patients despite antibiotic therapy. title: Effect of vitamin D deficiency on host susceptibility to invasive fungal infections
abs: Vitamin D has emerged as an important regulator of host responses against infections. Vitamin D deficient states have shown increased susceptibility to infections like tuberculosis, bacterial sepsis, viral infections, etc. Patients with chronic ailments are especially prone to dietary vitamin D deficiency. The emergence and rise of invasive fungal infections (IFI) caused mostly by Candida and Aspergillus is of major global concern in critically ill and immunocompromised patients. Candidemia is the fourth most common blood stream infection in hospitals worldwide. Invasive aspergillosis is of major concern in immunocompromised patients, with high mortality rate of 50-60% despite treatment. The relevance of the role played by vitamin D in IFI is slowly emerging and needs to be explored further. One of our recent studies implicated a role for vitamin D in Candida infections. We showed that candidemic patients had significantly lower serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels compared to healthy volunteers. Vitamin D was also shown to induce pro-inflammatory cytokines. This led us to hypothesize that vitamin D deficiency would increase host susceptibility to IFI.In this study, we aim to examine the immune effects and susceptibility to IFI in the vitamin D deficient state. The effects of vitamin D supplementation to the deficient host will also be studied. We propose to achieve our goals by in-vivo studies, whereby animals on normal diet and vitamin D deficient diet will be compared. Differences in the fungal burden, cytokine levels and transcriptomics between the two groups following infection will be determined. We also propose to do gut microbiome analysis in the control and vitamin D deficient hosts. These studies will help us to augment patient care by indicating how vitamin D deficiency can affect host defense mechanisms against IFI. It will also aid in determining the utility of vitamin D supplementation in vitamin D deficient immune-susceptible patients.

title: Improving Outcomes for Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest through a National, Living, Learning, Pre-hospital Emergency Care Laboratory: Bundle of Ambulance-based Interventions
abs: BackgroundSingapore has a single provider Pre-hospital Emergency Care (PEC) system with more than 1800 Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrests (OHCA)/year. The current CSA funding allowed us to conduct implementation research that has increased OHCA survival from 2.5% (2001) to 11.0% currently, with potential for further improvements.ObjectivesOur overall aim is to increase survival for OHCA. We will establish a national, living, and learning PEC laboratory, which will inform policy and clinical efficacy for OHCA interventions.DesignSpecific aims:1.Build dynamic data model that will integrate information from dispatch, first responders, ambulance, emergency department and hospital medical records, to feed into a simulation model of the PEC system to optimize ambulance deployment and evaluate implementation of aims 2 and 3.2.Develop and evaluate the effectiveness of community based interventions which include mass, simplified cardio-pulmonary resuscitation (CPR) training, installation of automated external defibrillators (AEDs) in residential blocks, a first responder app and a novel CPR Card.3.Develop and evaluate the effectiveness of a bundle of ambulance based interventions which include the Impedance Threshold Device (ITD), manual defibrillation by intermediate life-support providers, intravenous amiodarone and high performance team CPR.SignificanceThis is an opportunity to build a world-class, dynamic, living PEC laboratory on a national scale. MethodsSpecific aim 1 will create an Incremental Build Case Record (IBCR) for every PEC patient, with an added layer of data analytics and simulation modelling capability. Specific aim 2 will be achieved by a 3 year mixed-methods, prospective interventional, community-based implementation trial involving 50,000 people in 6 pre-selected constituencies as the intervention cohort with the controls being the balance of the country not receiving this bundled intervention. Specific aim 3 will be achieved by a 4 year prospective, stepped-wedge interventional trial using an adaptive design to test a bundle of ambulance interventions.

title: Nano-enabled Electrochemical Deposition (NEED) for anti-infective dental implants
abs: The predictability of osseointegration in dental implant therapy has led to the routine use of dental implants in oral rehabilitation of the edentulous patients. Globally, an estimated one million implants were performed annually. Increasingly, these are placed using non-submerged surgical protocols with transmucosal abutments. Systemic antibiotics is often prescribed following surgery to prevent post-operative infections. Maintenance of stability and function of load-bearing implant is dependent on a well-functioning barrier mechanism established at the transmucosal passage of implant. In recent years, an increasing number of implants and patients affected with peri-implant diseases have been identified. These biofilm-mediated inflammatory conditions are responsible for soft tissue destruction and may lead to pathological bone loss. Currently, there are no established predictable concepts for treatment of peri-implant diseases. Disease management hinges on the prevention of peri-implant mucositis as it is reversible when treated but can potentially progress into peri-implantitis if left untreated. Management of peri-implantitis often requires surgical intervention and in severe cases, explantation, which may compromise function and negatively affect quality of life. With increased emergence of antibiotic-resistant microorganisms, alternative strategies to the use of antibiotics to prevent peri-implant infections are necessary. The overall vision of the proposal is to develop a ‘proof-of-concept’ durable anti-infective and biocompatible coating for implants to decrease the risk of development of biofilm-mediated peri-implant infections. The strategy involves utilising a rapid, inexpensive and easily scalable technique, electrodeposition, to produce a durable protective coating infiltrated with antimicrobial polyphenols that can inhibit biofilm formation and microbial colonisation. Specific aims to achieve this include (i) optimisation of electrochemical coating conditions for selected aromatic polyphenols and characterisation of adherent coatings by surface chemical methods, (ii) in vitro assessment of antimicrobial activity, cytotoxicity and durability of the adherent nanocoatings and (iii) assessment of oral soft tissue response to antimicrobial implant nanocoating in a rabbit model.

title: Concomitant limb cryocompression and scalp cooling to reduce paclitaxel-induced neuropathy and alopecia
abs: Paclitaxel is a key chemotherapeutic agent used in the management of common cancers, such as breast cancer. Chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN) due to paclitaxel is a common dose-limiting toxicity with no effective prevention or treatment. Limb cryocompression is currently being developed as a method to reduce CIPN. Another common toxicity of paclitaxel is chemotherapy induced alopecia (CIA), for which scalp-cooling is currently an approved therapy to reduce the incidence of this adverse effect. As scalp cooling use in day-to-day clinical practice increases, future studies involving hypothermia to treat neuropathy must factor this into the treatment algorithm, lest patients be denied or are required to trade-off one treatment for the other. However, there is concern of causing core hypothermia and/or general intolerance to concomitant therapy. Both scalp-cooling and cryocompression individually have not shown to cause this, but simultaneous use has not been studied previously. Clinical safety studies, in healthy subjects and cancer patients would need to be conducted first, before larger efficacy studies are performed. We propose that we can deliver scalp-cooling and limb cryocompression with a single treatment modality to prevent two toxicities of paclitaxel – CIA and CIPN. This study will consist of two parts:A) Healthy subjects: To assess safety and tolerability of scalp and limb cryocompression, as well as to determine the optimal temperature and pressure to be used, that will contribute to the cryocompression protocol. The occurrence of core hypothermia or intolerance will be closely monitoredB) Cancer patients: Once the optimal cryocompression protocol is established in healthy patients, a group of cancer patients will undergo concomitant limb cryocompression and scalp cooling over multiple cycles of chemotherapy to establish safety and tolerability of repeated therapy. Early clinical efficacy signal data will also be collected, to prepare for the subsequent larger randomized efficacy study.

title: Next Generation Broadband, Compact, Ultra-sensitive, Real-time, Tunable Laser Spectroscopy Analyzer
abs: Laser spectroscopy in the mid-infrared (MIR) region (~ 3-14 micrometer) is an emerging technique, for quantitative analysis of multiple trace gaseous chemicals, because this region is the so-called “finger-print” region where gas molecules have unique and strong absorption features and coherent lasers have ultra-narrow linewidth and high power spectral density. However, there are still several challenges. The tuning range, size, cost, accuracy, and data acquisition and signal process speed all hinder the widespread application of these otherwise highly promising mid-infrared laser spectroscopy techniques. We will address the limitations of the aforementioned current MIR laser spectroscopy technology in this program. Particularly, we will investigate fundamentally ground-breaking solution of MIR semiconductor laser frequency comb generation through radically scientific breakthrough of understanding and designing highly nonlinear many-body solid-state quantum systems. Such artificial semiconductor-based quantum system demonstrates highly complex interplays among physical phenomena such as the instabilities, four wave mixing, strong photon-photon interactions, and the fast gain recovery. Strikingly, one can design the parameters of such systems through resonant tunneling, LO phonon transition, nonlinearity design through intersubband transitions, and dispersion management to manipulate the properties of such dynamic lasing systems. The complete understanding of such highly nonlinear complexity system through e.g. ultrafast pump-probe, bandstructure design and verification, step-scan characterization of photo- & electroluminescence etc, will significantly advance the developments of many other types of optoelectronic devices too. We will implement the following FIVE main focused projects: Project 1: Mid-IR broadband quantum cascade lasers (QCLs) Project 2: Mid-IR broadband room temperature photodetectors Project 3: Mid-IR spectroscopy with broadly tunable laser and frequency comb Project 4: Development of advanced signal processing techniques for real-time data analysis Project 5: Packaging and Test Trial Applications Our preliminary results already showed the potential of the above approach for achieving broadband high sensitive mid-infrared laser spectroscopy analyzers.
kw: mid-infrared photonics;quantum cascade laser;laser spectroscopy;gas analysis;broadband photodetection;breath analysis

title: Adolescent and young adult cancer patients: Cognitive Toxicity on Survivorship (ACTS)
abs: Background: As the cure rates for adolescent and young adult (AYA) cancers continue to improve and survivors live longer, survivorship issues in this group of patients are becoming increasingly relevant, and more in-depth research is needed. Among these undesirable toxicities, cognitive toxicity remains inadequately studied in the AYA population. Enhancing the understanding of cognitive toxicity will facilitate the development of effective interventions for AYA cancer survivors to better cope with their daily lives.Aim, Hypothesis and Objectives: In the ACTS study, we aim to elucidate the prevalence, mechanism and survivorship impact of cognitive toxicity among adolescent and young adult (AYA) patients diagnosed with curable cancers. We hypothesize that cognitive impairment is clinically significant among AYA cancer patients treated with chemotherapy. We also hypothesize that structural and functional changes in the brain are detectable in AYA cancer patients treated with chemotherapy. Hence, the primary objective is to compare the prevalence of cognitive impairment at 6 months from baseline, in AYA cancer patients and healthy AYA controls. The secondary objectives are to describe the trajectory of cognitive impairment, and to correlate cognitive impairment with (i) work/education status, (ii) physical symptoms and psychological distress, (iii) cytokines, and (iv) neuroimaging.Methodology/Approach: This will be a multicenter, prospective, longitudinal, observational study. The study participants will comprise two groups, a group of 15 to 39-year-old patients newly diagnosed with breast cancer, lymphoma and germ cell tumors being treated with curative intent and a group of healthy control. Assessment tools and blood draws (standardized timing) will be serially conducted at baseline, 3-, 6-, 9- and 12-months from baseline. Neuroimaging will be conducted at baseline and 6-months after baseline, in patients who are not contraindicated for MRI.

title: Mineralocorticoid Antagonism to Stop Progression of Atrial Fibrillation (MONITOR-AF) Study
abs: The rising global prevalence of atrial fibrillation (AF), with its associated increases in morbidity and mortality, has significant health and socio-economic consequences. Being a progressive disease, each year 15% of patients with early stage paroxysmal AF will progress to more established, persistent AF. This change is driven by a process of atrial remodelling and culminates in worsening heart failure, reduced quality of life, more strokes and greater healthcare expenditures. To date, anti-arrhythmic agents have limited success in preventing AF and there exists a need for new therapeutic strategies that can modulate atrial remodelling and prevent AF progression. Mineralocorticoid activity plays an important role in many processes implicated in pathogenesis of AF and atrial remodelling. Mineralocorticoid antagonism (MRA) has proven benefits in patients with heart failure. Hence we propose a dual country, double-blind randomized controlled trial to test the hypothesis that MRA can prevent AF progression and reduce AF burden in patients with paroxysmal AF. Unlike previous studies, primary endpoints will be accurately quantified by recruiting patients with pacemakers, capable of monitoring atrial arrhythmias. Secondary endpoints will evaluate the mechanistic effects of MRA on cardiac remodelling and validated cardiac and systemic biomarkers of stretch, inflammation and fibrosis. 334 patients (150 recruited at Christchurch Hospital, New Zealand with approved funding from the Health Research Council New Zealand and 184 patients to be recruited at National University Hospital for which funding is currently sought for in this application) will be randomized to either 50mg of spironolactone or placebo daily for 18 months. Both patients and clinicians will be blinded to treatment allocation. Patients will be reviewed regularly for repeated clinical assessment of efficacy and safety endpoints, pacemaker interrogations, echocardiography, ECGs and blood taking for biomarkers and serum electrolytes. If successful, MRA will represent a novel, non-arrhythmic and cost-effective strategy to prevent AF.

title: Clinical trial of rosuvastatin as an adjunct to standard treatment for drug-sensitive tuberculosis
abs: New approaches are needed to shorten treatment for tuberculosis (TB). Treatments working on host targets represent an important new approach. We hypothesize that rosuvastatin, a cholesterol-lowering drug, may be of value as an adjunct to standard TB treatment by disrupting essential lipid metabolism pathways and/or modulating the host immune response to therapy to enhance bacterial killing.We will conduct a phase II proof-of-concept trial enrolling 110 patients with confirmed drug-sensitive pulmonary TB who have received less than 7 days of standard TB treatment. title: Investigating mercaptopurine dose intensity and pharmacogenomics in Asian children and adults with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia
abs: Mercaptopurine (MP) is integral in the treatment of acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) in children and adults. Asians are inherently more sensitive to MP due to inherited variants in NUDT15 and less frequently, TPMT. Our work based on Singapore data contributed to the discovery and naming of 4 out of the 5 deleterious variants. We have genotyped 485 children treated in the Ma-Spore ALL 2003 study and found that 2% have genetic score of 2 which makes them exquisitely sensitive to MP. These patients tolerate only 10% of the regular MP dose. An addition of 22.5% have a genetic score of 1 which require a modest dose reduction of 20%. We propose the first prospective polygenic pharmacogenetic guided study for MP dosing based on NUDT15/TPMT variant genotype score in 498 children and 60 adults with ALL. Patients’ germline DNA will be typed for NUDT15 *1 to *6 and TPMT*3A,*3C and *6. Patients with variant NUDT15 and/or TPMT will start with reduced MP doses; wild type (WT) patients will receive full dose. The MP doses are then adjusted to maintain ANC 1-2. Daily MP dose will be collected prospectively. Thioguanine metabolites and WBC DNA-TG will be measured by LCMS-MS at 3 and 6 months of MP treatment. We hope to derive the optimal tolerated mean MP dose for patients with each genetic score to guide future treatment. Overall, we aim to develop a polygenic NUDT15 and TPMT-based MP guided dosing for Asians. The high frequency of 2% Singaporeans who are severely sensitive to MP necessitate a rationally designed dosing similar to TPMT testing mandated by FDA. 264 words.

title: Targeting hypoxia specific calcium channels for ischemic stroke
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: In ischemic stroke, vasodilators such as calcium channel blockers (CCBs) fail to improve stroke outcome in many clinical trials. The major side effect is the relaxation of blood vessels outside ischemic area, causing systemic hypotension and possible steal phenomenon by shunting blood to non-ischemic region.CCBs block voltage-gated calcium channel Cav1.2 in vascular smooth muscles and reduce muscle contraction. In the past decade, we have been studying the structures and functions of Cav1.2 channels in physiology and diseases, focusing on alternative splicing which can generate electrophysiologically and pharmacologically different Cav1.2 isoforms. In our recent preliminary studies, we found that the exonal patterns of vascular Cav1.2 channels were altered by hypoxia, in particular at the sites of exons 9* and 33, generating hypoxia-specific Cav1.2 channels. Using an antibody targeting exon 9* peptide, exon 9* was found in cerebral blood vessels in human patients after stroke. Importantly, preliminary results from a stroke animal model showed that inhibition of exon 9* reduced infarction following stroke reperfusion. Therefore, we hypothesize that these hypoxia-induced splice variants could be better targets for stroke.In this proposal, we will investigate the in vivo functions of exons 9* and 33 in a rat stroke model using in vivo antisense oligonucleotides and siRNA. We will further compare the blocking effect of various CCBs on the hypoxia-specific Cav1.2 channel, and their potential roles in stroke. Additionally, neuronal Cav1.2 channels will be examined for their alternative splicing patterns.After investigating the functions of alternatively spliced Cav1.2 in stroke as well as their interactions with various CCBs, we will understand whether blocking stroke specific Cav1.2 channel would improve stroke outcome and whether certain CCBs that have not been tested in stroke would be effective to ameliorate stroke injury.
kw: calcium channel, ischemic stroke, alternative splicing, calcium blockers

title: Tumor-microenvironment interaction and its impact on drug response in advanced pancreatic adenocarcinoma (PDAC)
abs: The underutilization of pre-clinical models incorporating tumor-stroma interactions may explain the lack of clinical translation. Construct of a clinically relevant pre-clinical model may bridge this disconnect. The mechanism of resistance to MEK inhibitors in KRAS mutant (MT) pancreatic adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is mediated via JAK1/2-STAT pathway in preclinical studies. Combined MEK and JAK inhibition demonstrated significant in vivo anti-tumor activity. Both MEK and JAK inhibition is expected to modulate tumor microenvironment. We hypothesize that combination trametinib (MEK inhibitor) and ruxolitinib (JAK inhibitor) is safe and demonstrates preliminary activity in a proportion of patients with KRAS MT PDAC. We aim to determine feasibility of this combination by determining its maximum tolerated dose (MTD)/recommended phase II dose (RP2D), safety, tolerability and preliminary activity in a phase I study in patients with advanced KRAS MT PDAC. Pharmacokinetics would be evaluated. Modulation of gene expression and predictive biomarkers relevant to the MAPK and JAK/STAT pathway would be perused from pre-treatment and on-treatment tumor biopsies. We hypothesize that generation of patient-derived tumor cell models from pancreatic tumor biopsy with distinct tumor and stroma compartment is feasible and represents a more clinically relevant approach. We aim to evaluate feasibility of generating patient-derived tumor cells and organoids (epithelial and stellate cell co-culture) from tumor biopsy. The genetic characterization and anti-tumor activity of this treatment in co-culture organoids would be compared with trial subjects in parallel. We aim to study interaction between pancreatic epithelial and stellate cells created and explore other therapeutic vulnerabilities which would inform construct and patient selection of subsequent trials. The ability to generate patient-derived pancreatic tumor and associated stromal cells through tumor biopsies is novel and paradigm shifting providing expedient personalized ex vivo therapeutic screening.
kw: RAS mutant, Tumor micro-environment, pancreatic adenocarcinoma, organoid model

title: The applications of Terahertz scanning system on corneas
abs: Corneal opacity affects 146 million people worldwide and is a priority eye disease as stated by WHO. However, there is a gap in existing clinical practice as there are no devices to directly and objectively evaluate the severity of corneal edema and corneal scars, two disease entities of corneal opacity. Our preliminary work has shown that the Terahertz scanning system is promising in differentiating the severity of corneal edema and monitoring corneal hydrodynamics in porcine eyes. It also successfully quantified the severity of collagen fibrosis in an in-vitro model. Hence, we hypothesize that Terahertz scanning has the capacity to measure water content in different corneal conditions and to objectively quantify corneal scars. We aim to 1. Evaluate the accuracy of corneal hydration profiles obtained by the Terahertz scanning system in different corneal conditions 2. Evaluate the feasibility and accuracy of using the Terahertz scanning system as a quantitative method for corneal scarring. In Aim 1, we will use human cadaveric corneas, two rat corneal bullous edema models, and two rabbit refractive surgery models. The hydration profiles obtained by the Terahertz system will be correlated with corneal thickness assessed by the anterior segment optical coherence tomography to evaluate the scanning accuracy. In Aim 2, in-vitro corneal fibrosis and rabbit corneal scarring models will be used. Clinical evaluation with slit lamp biomicroscopy and specular microscopy evaluation, as well as histological and immunohistochemistry analyses will be also performed to evaluate the accuracy of the measurements and safety profiles of the Terahertz scanning.This study has great potential in the development of a specific tool in early detection and decision-making of the managements of corneal edema and corneal scars. It may also be helpful in the tear film analysis in dry eye patients and in the adjustments of laser ablation parameters during refractive surgery.
kw: Cornea, corneal edema, corneal scar

title: Using patient-derived colorectal cancer models for personalized prediction of drug response, study of drug resistance mechanisms and identification of treatments to mitigate resistance
abs: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the commonest cancer in Singapore. Various standard chemotherapies and drug combinations are used in the treatment of advanced CRC but each patient’s response to a treatment regimen is highly variable and drug resistance inevitable. There is currently no reliable way to accurately predict an individual’s response to the different drugs/drug combinations and treatment sequencing in the clinics is largely empiric. We hypothesize that we can generate and utilize patient-derived 3D (PD-3D) in vitro models to accurately reflect a patient’s clinical response to standard of care therapies. In addition, drug screening performed on these in vitro models and in vivo modeling of drug response can inform potential drugs and treatment strategies that may overcome intrinsic and acquired resistance. We aim to first evaluate the feasibility of using PD-3D models to predict objective response to a panel of chemotherapy drugs and determine their accuracy in relation to a patient’s clinical response. Next, we seek to generate drug-resistant in vivo patient-derived xenograft (PDX) and PD-3D models, employing the in vitro models to perform high throughput screen of anti-cancer drug libraries. Drug hit(s) and potential novel drug combinations identified in these resistant models that can potentially pre-empt or overcome drug resistance will be validated in the in vivo PDX models. Transcriptomic profiling of relevant tumors will also be performed; as will the continued accumulation of tumor samples stored in a viable ‘living biobank’ as an invaluable tumor tissue repository for subsequent validation of results obtained from this study and downstream work. In so doing, we seek to perform drug screening and evaluate drug resistance in a personalized manner, to better tailor and inform effective therapies for the individual patient. This will reduce unnecessary exposure as well as minimize unwanted side effects from ineffective therapies and reduce delays to effective treatment.
kw: Colorectal cancer, drug screening, drug resistance, patient derived models

title: Interrogation of Childhood Onset Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Immunome for the Elucidation of Disease Mechanisms
abs: The pathogenesis of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) involves multiple derangements that perturb the fine balance between immunity and regulation. Traditional investigational approaches focusing on the pathogenic or protective role of individual cell type or molecule independently are inadequate for the study of a complex, multifactorial disease like SLE. The lack of a holistic understanding of the lupus immunome is a critical unmet need. Simultaneously, there are other important knowledge gaps pertaining to the role of B regulatory cells in SLE where there is a lack of specific cell surface and transcriptional factor markers akin to the forkhead box protein P3 (Foxp3) found in T regulatory cells. The over-arching hypothesis is that abnormalities in multiple components of the immune system contribute to lupus pathogenesis. Specifically, we hypothesise that the immune regulatory component is dysfunctional (both quantitatively and qualitatively) during lupus flare. To address such unmet needs, we aim to use a high dimensional approach using mass cytometry to unravel the contribution of the regulatory and inflammatory immunome to lupus pathogenesis simultaneously. This will be achieved with the characterisation of 37 immune markers at the single cell level using mass cytometry, followed by an unbiased and unsupervised analysis with a machine learning custom software based on dimensional reductions followed by automated cells classification and clustering. Subsequently, hierarchical prioritisation of the cell populations based on its strength of association with disease activity for downstream mechanistic characterisation with fluorescence based flow cytometry sorting of the target cells of interest for full transcriptome analysis and in-vitro functional study will be done.This approach has the immediate dual translational potential of identifying immune cell subsets relevant for clinical prognostication and the elucidation of disease mechanisms which will subsequently provide important information for the development of a multi-pronged immunotherapeutic strategy against SLE.
kw: Paediatric, Systemic Lupus Erythematosus, Immunome

abs: The underutilization of pre-clinical models incorporating tumor-stroma interactions may explain the lack of clinical translation. Construct of a clinically relevant pre-clinical model may bridge this disconnect. The mechanism of resistance to MEK inhibitors in KRAS mutant (MT)pancreatic adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is mediated via JAK1/2-STAT pathway in preclinical studies. Combined MEK and JAK inhibition demonstrated significant in vivo anti-tumor activity. Both MEK and JAK inhibition is expected to modulate tumor microenvironment.We hypothesize that combination trametinib (MEK inhibitor) and ruxolitinib (JAK inhibitor) is safe and demonstrates preliminary activity in a proportion of patients with KRAS MT PDAC. We aim to determine feasibility of this combination by determining its maximum tolerated dose(MTD)/recommended phase II dose (RP2D), safety, tolerability and preliminary activity in a phase I study in patients with advanced KRASMT PDAC. Pharmacokinetics would be evaluated. Modulation of gene expression and predictive biomarkers relevant to the MAPK andJAK/STAT pathway would be perused from pre-treatment and on treatment tumor biopsies. We hypothesize that generation of patient-derived tumor cell models from pancreatic tumor biopsy with distinct tumor and stroma compartment is feasible and represents a more clinically relevant approach. We aim to evaluate feasibility of generating patient-derived tumor cells and organoids (epithelial and stellate cell co-culture) from tumor biopsy. The genetic characterization and anti-tumor activity of this treatment in coculture organoids would be compared with trial subjects in parallel. We aim to study interaction between pancreatic epithelial and stellate cells created and explore other therapeutic vulnerabilities which would inform construct and patient selection of subsequent trials. The ability to generate patient-derived pancreatic tumor and associated stromal cells through tumor biopsies is novel and paradigm shifting providing expedient personalized ex vivo therapeutic screening.
kw: RAS mutant, Tumor micro-environment, pancreatic adenocarcinoma, organoid model

title: Interrogation of Childhood Onset Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Immunome for the Elucidation of Disease Mechanisms
abs: The pathogenesis of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) involves multiple derangements that perturb the fine balance between immunity and regulation. Traditional investigational approaches focusing on the pathogenic or protective role of individual cell type or molecule independently are inadequate for the study of a complex, multifactorial disease like SLE. The lack of a holistic understanding of the lupus immunome is a critical unmet need. Simultaneously, there are other important knowledge gaps pertaining to the role of B regulatory cells in SLE where there is a lack of specific cell surface and transcriptional factor markers akin to the forkhead box protein P3 (Foxp3) found in T regulatory cells. The over-arching hypothesis is that abnormalities in multiple components of the immune system contribute to lupus pathogenesis. Specifically, we hypothesise that the immune regulatory component is dysfunctional (both quantitatively and qualitatively) during lupus flare. To address such unmet needs, we aim to use a high dimensional approach using mass cytometry to unravel the contribution of the regulatory and inflammatory immunome to lupus pathogenesis simultaneously. This will be achieved with the characterisation of 37 immune markers at the single cell level using mass cytometry, followed by an unbiased and unsupervised analysis with a machine learning custom software based on dimensional reductions followed by automated cells classification and clustering. Subsequently, hierarchical prioritisation of the cell populations based on its strength of association with disease activity for downstream mechanistic characterisation with fluorescence based flow cytometry sorting of the target cells of interest for full transcriptome analysis and in-vitro functional study will be done. This approach has the immediate dual translational potential of identifying immune cell subsets relevant for clinical prognostication and the elucidation of disease mechanisms which will subsequently provide important information for the development of a multi-pronged immunotherapeutic strategy against SLE.
kw: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus, Immunome, Mechanism of disease

title: Elucidating the determinants and therapeutic vulnerabilities of primary tyrosine kinase inhibitor-resistant EGFR mutation positive NSCLC
abs: Activating EGFR mutations are the commonest oncogenic driver in non-small cell lung cancer, and occurs in up to 60% of cases in Singapore. While EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) are associated with high response rates, 20-30% of patients do not exhibit significant tumour shrinkage – referred to as primary resistance. While secondary or acquired resistance to EGFR TKI has been well characterized and include mechanisms such as T790M and c-MET alterations, the determinants of primary resistance are poorly understood. Recently, through multi-sector exome sequencing, we have identified co-existing driver alterations (such as PTEN loss) as potential mediators for suboptimal response, and this was validated in combination therapy from candidates arising from a high content drug screen. In a separate primary TKI resistant patient-derived model, we unexpectedly show potential antagonism in dual targeting of co-drivers (in this instance c-MET and EGFR L858R), suggesting that a more nuanced approach is required to unravel the context of genomic alterations to address primary resistance. In this grant, I plan to use a combination of techniques including the use of integrative genomics (including transcriptomics), establishment of patient-derived models and high content drug screens to identify novel therapeutic approaches.
kw: EGFR TKI Resistance, Biomarkers, Omics

title: Preclinical evidence for STAT3 inhibition therapy in recurrent malignant glioma (MG) patients: Use of ruxolitinib
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Scientific AbstractBackgroundSTAT3 signaling promotes tumorigenesis in various cancers, including myelofibrosis (MF), polycythemia vera (PV) and glioblastoma. STAT3 is phosphorylated by upstream JAK; ruxolitinib, a JAK1/2-inhibitor, is currently FDA-approved for the treatment of MF and PV. In MG, STAT3 activation contributes to drug resistance and tumor recurrence. Our preclinical study in MG demonstrated a unique STAT3-Gene Signature that is prognostic and predictive of response to JAK1/2 inhibition. We showed a 15-fold greater median survival difference in mice bearing STAT3-high tumors compared to mice bearing STAT3-low tumors. Importantly, we identified unique somatic mutations corresponding to STAT3-stratified subgroups. Moving forward, we will test mouse models established from recurrent GBM tissue as this represents the actual clinical scenario for patient selection and treatment. HypothesisWe propose that STAT3-stratified patients respond favorably to STAT3 inhibition therapy. Since recurrent patients can potentially be subjected to the treatment, we will provide preclinical evidence to test the response of mouse xenografts established from recurrent GBM tissue to ruxolitinib, an anti-JAK1/2 small molecule currently in clinical trial. Specific Aims1.To identify recurrent patient GBM tissue for creation of orthotopic mouse xenograft tumors.2.To test response of mouse model towards ruxolitinib. 3.To establish clinical and molecular criteria for identification of STAT3-responsive cohort. Approach / MethodsWe established transcriptomic and exome-sequencing data from our national NNI brain tumor resource, thereby facilitating identification of STAT3-stratified subgroups. Mouse models will be established from STAT3-high recurrent tissue and tested for their response to ruxolitinib. Kaplan-Meier survival curves will be analysed in conjunction with mouse models established from tumors at first diagnosis. Significance of ProposalOur study demonstrates that STAT3 signaling contributes to the molecular heterogeneity of glioma tumors. The transcriptomic and mutation profile identifies patients most likely to respond to STAT3 inhibitory small molecule treatment. This will lay the groundwork for clinical trials using JAK/STAT inhibitors for malignant glioma.
kw: Glioblastoma, Connectivity Map, Precision Medicine, JAK/STAT, Patient-Derived Xenograft (PDX) mouse model

title: Case Control Nigrosome-1 and Connectivity MRI Study in Parkinson’s-Linked Asian LRRK2 Gene Carriers
abs: BackgroundParkinson’s disease (PD) patients show dopaminergic denervation in the substantia nigra (SN), with maximum cell depletion in nigrosome-1. There is growing evidence of excellent diagnostic accuracy of 3D high-resolution susceptibility-weighted MR imaging (HRSWI) at 3T in radiologically delineating the healthy nigrosome-1. Recent functional connectivity studies (rsfMRI) show abnormalities in preclinical PD stages. We have previously identified common Asian-specific leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) gene risk variants in Chinese PD patients, with accelerated motor progression compared to non-carrier patients, suggesting that these genetic risk variants may facilitate neurodegeneration. Specific AimsUtilizing a case control methodology, we will establish clinical utility of 3T nigrosome-1 HRSWI in a large PD cohort compared to controls, and evaluate if quantitative grading of nigrosome-1 signal intensity correlate with motor scores and connectivity abnormalities, and differentiate asymptomatic Asian genetic carriers of LRRK2 variants from non-carriers.HypothesesWe hypothesize that loss of nigrosome-1 will accurately differentiate PD from controls, correlate with motor grading and connectivity abnormalities, and differentiate asymptomatic Asian genetic carriers of LRRK2 variants from non-carriers. Methodology & Approach300 subjects will be screened and 200 subjects (100 PD, 100 controls) recruited. All subjects will have genotyping for Asian specific LRRK 2 gene variants, clinical evaluation with the Hoehn and Yahr and Unified Parkinson Disease Rating Scale, and undergo HRSWI optimized for nigrosome-1 detection in the midbrain and rsfMRI. Two blinded neuroradiologists will visually grade the nigrosome-1, and inter-rater agreement assessed. Loss of nigrosome-1 signal intensity against other parts of the SN will be quantified through voxel intensity ratio from regions-of-interests measurements. Functional motor neural network modulations will be extracted from rsfMRI.Clinical SignificanceNigrosome-1 imaging is an attractive, practical radiological biomarker for PD, with potential utility as a surrogate quantitative biomarker in disease progression, preclinical/prodromal genetic carriers and in correlation with abnormalities on functional connectivity
kw: Parkinson disease; Gene Carriers; Neuroimaging; MRI; Brain

title: Oligodendroglia contribution in TDP-43-mediated neurodegeneration
abs: The landmark discovery of TDP-43 (TAR-DNA binding protein-43 KDa) as the defining pathological hallmark for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) coupled with ALS/FTD-causing mutations in TDP-43 indicate that TDP-43 dysfunctions incur damages to the motor and cognitive system. Furthermore, TDP-43 pathologies are present in Alzheimer’s disease and hippocampal sclerosis patients, and correlate with poor cognitive performance. In diseases associated with TDP-43 proteinopathies, TDP-43 aggregates are found in neurons, astrocytes and oligodendrocytes, indicating that TDP-43-mediated damage could occur in non-neuronal cells, thereby forming a potential feed-forward loop to drive disease pathogenesis. Intriguingly, recent genetic analysis identified MOBP (myelin-associated oligodendrocyte basic protein) as a risk factor for ALS and FTD, highlighting the critical involvement of oligodendrocytes. Therefore, we hypothesize that TDP-43-mediated damages within oligodendrocytes may contribute to the impairment of the motor and cognitive system. To test this, we generated and characterized two mouse models exploiting conditional TDP-43 allele and transgene expressing a dominant disease-linked TDP-43 mutation. Mice with TDP-43 deleted in oligodendrocytes developed progressive motor phenotypes leading to early lethality accompanied by reduced myelination and altered oligodendrocyte biogenesis in the spinal cord. Strikingly, myelination deficits and altered oligodendrogenesis were also observed in TDP-43 mutant mice. Furthermore, TDP-43 mutant mice displayed deteriorating cognition accompanied by reduced spine density and altered electrophysiological properties in the hippocampus. Here, we propose to comprehensively analyze these two sets of mice and investigate how TDP-43-medaited oligodendroglial dysfunctions may lead to motor and cognitive impairment using a combination of mouse genetics, viral gene transfer, neuron-oligodendrocyte co-culture and genomic methods. Moreover, we will delineate the mechanisms by which loss of TDP-43 and mutant TDP-43 expression in oligodendrocytes contribute to myelination, oligodendrogenesis and neurodegeneration. The mechanisms underlying TDP-43 dysfunctions in oligodendrocytes will provide novel insights into disease mechanisms and therapeutic avenues for ALS, FTD and cognitive impairment.
kw: amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), frontotemporal dementia (FTD), TDP-43, oligodendrocyte, mouse genetics

title: Synaptic excitation and inhibition in the primary auditory cortex during deep brain or vagus nerve stimulation for generating targeted plasticity
abs: The neocortex is a complex network of excitatory and inhibitory neurons that is plastic and changeable by experience. Plasticity may be harnessed to remediate disorders due to aberrant neural circuitry. To optimize plasticity for clinical application, we must understand still poorly understood rules of plasticity, and how they play out in complex circuits. We shall build on advances in two related paradigms for targeting plasticity to restricted groups of synapses in living animals. The first paradigm employs nucleus basalis stimulation (NBS), and was shown to change post-synaptic inhibition, an important discovery because many mechanisms altering inhibition had been observed in brain slices, but their occurrence in vivo was obscure. The second paradigm employs vagus nerve stimulation (VNS), which was shown to resemble NBS in generating targeted plasticity, a discovery which enabled clinical exploration of targeted plasticity for tinnitus and stroke rehabilitation, because the peripheral vagus nerve is more accessible than the nucleus basalis. Investigation of the synaptic mechanisms in these paradigms has been restricted to NBS paired with a single tone, whereas clinical explorations use more complex pairings. Here we test the hypotheses that the changes in synaptic excitation and inhibition caused by pairing NBS with a single tone generalize to pairing NBS or VNS with multiple tones. To do so, we will perform in vivo whole-cell measurements of the changes in net synaptic input, synaptic excitation and inhibition caused by pairing NBS or VNS with two tone frequencies. Our work will illuminate the excitatory-inhibitory dynamics supporting learning, and help harness plasticity to treat central nervous system disorders such as tinnitus and stroke. Our focus is on targeted plasticity, but the results may be relevant to epilepsy, for which VNS is an established treatment with poorly understood mechanism; and potentially to Alzheimer'sdisease, which NBS is being explored to treat.
kw: cortex, auditory, in vivo whole-cell, targeted plasticity, nucleus basalis, vagus nerve

title: Endogenous Retroviruses in Cancer: Driver Genes and Targets for Immunotherapy
abs: ERVs are highly repetitive and often fragmented copies of retroviral genes that once copied and pasted their DNA in the human genome. While most ERVs are under tight epigenetic control or inactivated through mutations, a subset of ERVs can still be transcribed. These ERVs generate RNAs whose expression is critical to early embryonic development, and recent reports have found an association of ERV expression with key cancer properties and cancer immunotherapy. However, unlike protein coding genes, ERVs are highly repetitive, making it much harder to identify their expression. Therefore, despite their importance, RNAs that are generated from ERVs in the human genome are still largely unknown, and the contribution of ERVs to cancer biology and immunity remains largely unexplored.Here we propose to identify and quantify expressed ERVs across 18,000 samples from 30 cancer types and matched normal tissue and integrate this information with clinical data (Aim 1), probe the function of candidate ERVs in patient-derived models (Aim 2), and test their influence on tumor immune interaction (Aim 3).This proposal is based on previous work and preliminary data demonstrating that ERVs can be essential to cell identity and that they are frequently deregulated in cancer. The 2 key pillars that enable this research are the integration of ultra-large, publicly available datasets with internal data sets and existing research infrastructure, and an interdisciplinary team with complementary expertise in computational biology, personalized oncology, and tumor immune interactions.
