Successful identification of cancer-associated ERVs, their role as driver genes in tumor development, and their contribution to response to immunotherapy will be breakthrough with a significant impact on cancer research and on the biomedical landscape in Singapore and worldwide.
kw: Cancer, Endogenous Retrovirus, Personalised oncology,Immunotherapy, Transcriptomics, Computational Biology

title: Engineering of novel and synthetic cellular states for applications in regenerative medicine
abs: Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) are highly regarded for their promise in regenerative medicine, but their realization has been hampered by technical issues; amongst others, iPSCs derived from current protocols show an epigenetic memory resembling the cell-of-origin, thereby limiting their potency. During development, pluripotency is established from cells that underwent a complete erasure of epigenetic memory to establish a state of maximal cell potency between the 4-cell and morula stages. This suggests that induction of such a cell state with expanded potency in vitro has the potential to overcome the inherent limitations of iPSCs. We recently described a method that converts ESCs to a state resembling aspects of pre-implantation blastocyst cells, demonstrating the possibility of in vitro modelling of earlier embryonic cells. Coupling this with stage-specific synthetic reporters that we designed based on endogenous retroviruses, we devise a systematic strategy to isolate cellular states resembling early embryonic human cells (Aim 1). Using high-throughput genomics technology, we will then study the key processes required for establishment of cellular potency (Aim 2). By combining insights generated from large-scale data analysis with genome-wide loss-of-function screens, we will rationally engineer and fine-tune enhanced cellular states that have the ability to advance the potential application of iPSCs in regenerative medicine (Aim 3). Only very few laboratories world-wide have the capability to work on alternative states of pluripotency. The outcomes of this project will therefore further strengthen Singapore’s scientific reputation for excellence in stem cell research. In addition, the cell engineering technologies and synthetic reporter cell lines established in the process could potentially be commercialized, which will bring about economic impact. Most importantly, being able to rationally engineer cellular states will be a breakthrough that has the promise to overcome limitations of current iPSC models, providing opportunities that are of outstanding interest for future clinical applications.
kw: Induced pluripotent stem cells, Reprogramming, Cellular potency, Synthetic reporters, In vitro modeling, Endogenous retrovirus

title: Development of optoelectrical bimodal monitoring technique for neuronal activity in live brain: an application to the investigation of neural circuit functions
abs: Electrical recording and optical imaging are conventional methods for recording single-neuron activity in freely behaving animals. However, each of them has its own major shortfall. Electrical recording allows for the detection of individual neuronal firings at high temporal precision. However, spatial and cell-type information about the source of recorded activity cannot be obtained. In contrast, although optical imaging can provide spatial and cell-type information, its temporal resolution is poor. These shortfalls of conventional recording methods have made it difficult to understand how neural circuits work for cognition and behavior. To address this technical limitations, we will develop a flexible, bimodal fiber probe device which is capable of simultaneously detecting electrical and optical signals of neuronal activity, and performing optogenetic control of neurons under recording. A preform-to-fiber fabrication method is proposed with constructing a macroscopic version of the desired structure and subsequently scaling it down to the microscopic dimensions by thermal drawing. The resulting devices contain axially and radially uniform, and globally oriented optical waveguides and metallic wire arrays inside a thin and flexible fiber. The bimodal recording through this fiber probes is validated using a transgenic mouse expressing a Ca2+ sensor, G-CaMP7. Electrical and optical signals are monitored simultaneously, and temporally compared to match spatial information of optical signals and temporally precise electrical signals. Once validated,this optoelectrical bimodal recording is applied to investigate neural circuit functions in the dentate gyrus, a hippocampal subregion deep inside the brain. We characterize how different neuronal cell types in the dentate gyrus works during spatial exploration. The successful development, optimization and application of the optoelectrical bimodal recording of neuronal activity would facilitate our understanding of brain functions, and dysfunctions related to neurological diseases and mental illness, by providing a novel tool essential for dissecting neural circuit functions.
kw: optical imaging, electrophysiology, optogenetics, hippocampus, neurogenesis

title: Consequences and Therapeutic Implications of a Defective Molecular Switch in Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma:
inst: SRIS - Skin Research Institute of Singapore
abs: Epithelial carcinomas are known to activate a prolonged wound-healing program that promotes malignant transformation. In an attempt to explore parallel molecular mechanisms involved in wound healing and progressive squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), we sought to investigate the role of the wound-healing switch in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC). We identified a dual-state molecular switch in which a single transcript can make either a microRNA or a protein and reversibly shift between these two stable states. This molecular switch is essential for normal wound healing and orchestrates wound re-epithelialization. In normal skin, expression of anti-migratory microRNA-198 (miR-198) from the 3’-untranslated region of follistatin-like-1 (FSTL1) mRNA, switches to pro-migratory FSTL1 protein expression upon wounding. Temporal cell migration is enhanced, facilitating re-epithelialization. Investigation of the wound healing switch in HNSCC revealed a defect in the switch, which shuts off miR-198 expression in favour of sustained FSTL1 production. A prolonged ‘wound healing’ phase is maintained which may contribute to uncontrolled cell migration and metastasis. We hypothesize that carcinoma cells may hijack the wound-healing switch to enhance invasion and metastasis.Here we propose to characterize the physiological role of the defective switch in HNSCC and investigate its potential therapeutic implications. Our primary objectives are to: 1) Investigate the consequence of the defective molecular switch in HNSCC. 2) Elucidate the molecular mechanism underlying the defective regulatory switch in HNSCC. 3) Modulate the defective switch and identify a novel therapeutic strategy to treat HNSCC. This study will have a significant scientific impact on our understanding of the molecular mechanisms behind HNSCC, and also holds promise for the development of novel, targeted therapies with better patient outcomes.
kw: epithelial carcinoma, head and neck cancer, molecular switch, high throughput screening

title: Targeting skin microbial proteases as novel therapeutic for common skin disorders
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Skin diseases account for some of the most prevalent human diseases worldwide, with Singapore experiencing one of the highest non-fatal skin disease burden per capita. Skin diseases have significant negative impacts on patients’ quality of life and an estimated $300 million USD alone are spent yearly on scalp conditions. Malassezia is a genus of lipophilic fungi that is the major skin-residing fungi on human skin. Although Malassezia is generally thought to be commensal, several species have been strongly implicated as the etiologic agents of skin disorders such as seborrhoeic dermatitis and pityriasis versicolor. Intriguingly, genomics and proteomics analyses indicate that Malassezia globosa secretes aspartyl proteases that are highly similar to those produced by the pathogenic yeast Candida albicans, which utilize aspartyl proteases as major virulence factors. We hypothesize that skin microbial secreted proteases have crucial roles in host-microbial interactions especially during skin disease pathogenesis and that pharmacologic agents that specifically target these proteases can be used as novel skin disease therapeutics. In this proposed project, we will first identify the major proteases secreted by clinically relevant Malassezia species. We will then define their human skin-associated substrates to explore the roles of the secreted proteases during skin disease pathogenesis. To determine the functional relevance of Malassezia secreted proteases in skin diseases, we will perform metagenomics of skin swab samples obtained from healthy and diseased human volunteers to assess the expression levels of the fungal secreted proteases. Finally, we will design and synthesize novel peptidomimetic inhibitors that can selectively target these fungal secreted proteases without cross reactivity with human skin proteases. Taken together, this project aims to establish skin microbial secreted proteases as novel targets for intervention of human skin diseases.
kw: drug discovery, skin microbiome, skin disease, anti-microbials

title: Generation of Clinically Safe and Functional Human Embryonic Stem Cell-derived Photoreceptors
abs: Aged Macular Degeneration (AMD) and Retinitis Pigmentosa (RP) cause blindness in more than 10 million people worldwide. It is a result from the loss of photoreceptors and the underlying retina pigmented epithelium (RPE), both of which govern the visual system. Human retina lacks the ability to regenerate when lost due to disease or injury. To date, there is no effective treatment to restore central vision from these forms of retina degeneration. There is currently no clinical trial for photoreceptor therapy and the existing protocols do not produce clinically safe and transplantable competent hESC-derived photoreceptors. The major challenge is to develop a robust method for differentiating hESCs to photoreceptor cells in a chemically defined and xeno-free culture environment with the prospect of transplanting clinically safe photoreceptors into patients. Currently I have successfully developed a robust chemically defined LN-521-dependent protocol for generating photoreceptor precursors that express biomarkers, Chx10 and Crx. I have also generated cell lines that produce human recombinant retina-specific LN-523 and LN-323 that have not been available before but have the potential to promote the differentiation of hESCs to photoreceptors. The next paramount step is to isolate the staged specific photoreceptor progenitors required for transplantation studies. This is critical because the existing protocols results in high cell batch variabilities. The first aim of the research proposal makes use of the expressed selective cell surface biomarkers to isolate staged specific photoreceptor progenitors. Second aim will determine the retina specific LN isoforms necessary for the support of photoreceptor progenitors and further maturation. The third aim will test for the in-vivo functional roles of the photoreceptor progenitors in the animal model for visual restoration. I anticipate that results from this study will form the body of evidence that advances the application of these hESC-derived photoreceptors in visually impaired patients in the long run.
kw: Photoreceptors, human embryonic stem cells, Aged Macular Degeneration, Retinitis Pigmentosa, Laminin Isoforms, Magnetic Cell Sorting

title: Understanding the Role of Endoplasmic Reticulum Stress in Liver Fibrosis
abs: Chronic liver disease is increasingly a major health burden to society worldwide. Liver fibrosis is the scarring process that represents the liver’s intrinsic response to injury. It may develop as a consequence of viral hepatitis, chronic alcoholism, drug use, diabetes or obesity. This gradual scarring of the liver puts people at risk to develop liver cirrhosis and liver cancer. We have identified several patients with chronic liver fibrosis that is caused by homozygous loss of function mutations in a Protein Disulfide Isomerase, PDIA6. Protein Disulfide Isomerases (PDIs) are residents of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and are important for the proper folding of proteins. Loss of PDI activity results in protein misfolding. Accumulation of misfolded proteins activates the ER stress mechanism which aims to restore ER homeostasis or initiate cell death. Previous studies have implicated ER stress in contributing to fibrosis, however, the cause and effect relationship between fibrosis and ER stress has remained elusive. We hypothesize that loss of PDIA6 activity increased ER stress and this contributes to the initiation and progression of liver fibrosis. In this proposal, we aim to investigate the underpinning molecular mechanism by which PDIA6 maintains ER homeostasis in the liver and understand how its loss drives fibrosis. We will use patients’ cells, induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) and liver cell lines to investigate how loss of PDIA6 affects ER stress. In addition, using CRISPR technology we will generate an in vivo PDIA6 knockout liver fibrosis zebrafish model to study the development and progression of liver fibrosis. Finally, we will use biochemical techniques to identify downstream substrates of PDIA6 that may mediate liver fibrotic mechanisms. This research is expected to have fundamental implications in liver biology and carries the potential for identifying targets to develop antifibrotic therapies.
kw: Liver Fibrosis, Endoplasmic Reticulum Stress

title: THE ROLE OF AMINO ACID ONCOMETABOLITES IN TUMOR INITIATING CELLS
abs: Tumor-initiating cells (TICs) are rare cells in a tumor mass that are resistant to chemotherapy. Persistent TICs give rise to tumor relapse and eventually terminal metastasis. This suggests a need to specifically target TICs in a tumor mass. Cancer cells remodel their metabolism to maximize proliferation and adapt to the tumor microenvironment. On top of these known functions, we hypothesized that specific metabolic fluxes might also confer tumor re-initiating abilities to TICs, and therefore represent a eminently druggeable vulnerability. As proof of concept, we recently found lung adenocarcinoma TICs to be highly dependent on methionine cycle flux and consequently, pharmacological inhibition of MAT2A, the rate-limiting enzyme of the methionine cycle, leads to a dramatic abrogation of TIC tumor initiating abilities. This now implies that downstream epigenetic methylation pathways are critical for conferring tumor-initiating abilities to TICs. We propose to tease out these methylation pathways and elucidate their mechanism of action in order to uncover novel epigenetic drug targets. This would allow us to connect unique TIC metabolism to downstream epigenetic vulnerabilities. In addition, we also found that alanine, an amino acid previously thought to be non-essential as it could be synthesized from the oncometabolite glutamine, was required by TICs to grow. Metabolic profiling of alanine-starved TICs revealed that alanine exerts a unique and widespread influence in TIC metabolic fluxes. Intriguing, alanine could directly influence the rate of glutamine catabolism, and/or also control cellular acetylation pathways. These could also represent another potential metabolic vulnerability that could directly influence TIC epigenetic programs. We propose to investigate and elucidate the mechanisms of action in order to uncover more metabolic drug targets. Both aims will drive the development of TIC-directed pharmaceuticals, improving chemotherapy response outcomes in the long term.
kw: cancer metabolism; tumor initiating cell/cancer stem cells; drug targets

title: Characterizing the function of a novel immune sensor NLRP1 in skin infection and inflammation
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Bacterial infection of the skin represents a significant clinical problem in Southeast Asia and world-wide, particularly those caused by antibiotic resistant bacterial strains such as methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). We have recently identified Nod-like Receptor Protein-1, NLRP1 as an orphan inflammasome protein specifically involved in skin immunity. Here we propose that wild-type NLRP1 is a bona fide sensor for Gram positive bacteria including MRSA. We aim to identify the cognate ligand molecule recognized by NLRP1 and determine its function in inflammasome signaling and S. aureus infection. This work will lead to better understanding of a fundamental question in innate immunity, i.e. how human cells sense pathogens, and provide new opportunities to develop better treatment for persistent bacterial skin infections. Aim 1 will determine the role of NLRP1 in inflammasome activation during Staphylococcus aureus skin infection.Aim 2 will identify the cognate NLRP1 ligand and determine its function in inflammasome activation.
kw: Skin, inflammation, pathogen sensing, inflammasome

title: Characterizing antigen-specific and global immune cell responses in chronic HBV-infected children
abs: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection is a major public health problem, particularly in Asia, where two third of the 300 million people with chronic infection lives, and where virus transmission from mother-to-child is the primary cause of infection. Despite the development of an effective preventive HBV vaccine, about 10-15% of children born to HBV+ mothers still develop chronic infection. HBV infection in infants or young children is thought to induce a state of “immunotolerance”, whose existence is however controversial, since it is mainly supported by data from HBV transgenic mice that do not fully recapitulate the natural course of HBV infection. This immunotolerance hypothesis is also at odds with several epidemiological and experimental evidences, and to our recent findings that 1) chronic HBV-infected adolescents labeled as immunotolerant harbor HBV-specific T cells that were functionally better than their adult counterparts, and 2) HBV-exposure in utero induces a state of trained immunity in newborns of chronic HBV-infected mothers. Since there is limited information on the immunological events occurring during the early phases of chronic HBV infection in children, this study aims to gain an understanding of the key components of the immune response to hepatitis B (antigen-specific and non-specific) present in HBV-infected or resolved pediatric patients using a systemic approach comprising flow cytometry, gene expression, and protein analyses of the immune cell populations at both the protein and mRNA levels. In particular, we would like to test whether children with persistent or resolved HBV infection harbor HBV-specific immune responses and whether such responses trigger liver inflammation, as seen in chronic HBV-infected adults. The characterization of the immune responses in chronic HBV-infected children could provide invaluable information on the ability of HBV to establish persistent infection in this young population and may have an impact on treatment strategies.
kw: Hepatitis B virus, immune response, pediatric, immune tolerance, infectious disease, HBV-specific T cells

title: Identification of DNA methylation biomarkers associated with longitudinal weight change in a Chinese population
abs: The rates of obesity and type 2 diabetes (T2D) are increasing in Singapore and worldwide. Ageing, obesity, dietary influences and reduced physical activities are major risk factors that increase susceptibility to T2D. Obesity is an important but imperfect predictor of T2D risk. Among obese individuals, there is heterogeneity in their overall risk of developing T2D. In recent years, emerging biomarkers such as C-reactive protein, amino acids, and genetic risk scores have seen less utility due to the lack of a consistent discriminatory evidence. There is growing literature and data on the role of epigenetic markers in the complex interplay between genes and the environment. A recent large-scale epigenome-wide association study demonstrated the potential of aggregated epigenetic markers associated with weight change as an independent risk predictor of incident T2D in Europeans and South Asian Indians. The epigenetic risk score also showed improved discriminatory power to distinguish the highest quartile of obese individuals at risk of T2D. Such improved understanding of molecular mechanisms linking obesity and T2D can support risk stratification of high-risk individuals, and development of therapeutic targets to mediate disease progression. The same epigenetic patterns may not be completely relevant to other populations due to significant differences in genetic and lifestyle patterns. In this proposal, we propose to (1) identify novel epigenetic biomarkers associated with weight change in a Chinese population; and (2) identify plausible downstream obesity-related biological pathways such as dyslipidemia, inflammatory, insulin resistance that are affected by the epigenetic mechanisms. We implement a longitudinal approach to account for intra-individual variability, and eliminate reverse causality. This effort will contribute to improved understanding of physiological changes during the progression of obesity to T2D in a Chinese population, and has the potential to provide clues to new methods of modifiable prevention and treatment measures.
kw: Obesity; DNA methylation; Type 2 Diabetes; Longitudinal

title: Quantification of blood flow based on OCT-angiography
abs: Vascular risk factors play a role in a wide variety of blinding eye diseases such as diabetic retinopathy, glaucoma, age-related macular degeneration and vascular occlusive disease. The introduction of optical coherence tomography (OCT), a medical imaging technique has revolutionized the diagnosis and clinical care of eye diseases. Standard OCT is, however, not clinically optimized to visualize the anatomy of blood vessels or quantify blood flow, making it essentially challenging to identify the onset/progression of ischemia/hypoxia, which is a major underlying factor for retinal vascular diseases and glaucoma. In the present grant, our central hypothesis is that it is possible to better quantify retinal and optic nerve head microvascular blood flow using swept source (SS) OCT angiography. To achieve this aim, we propose a collaborative approach that will harness the expertise of biomedical engineers, computer engineers, pre-clinical scientists as well as clinicians. Specifically, we aim to establish a state of the art imaging prototype SS-OCT system based on an akinetic light source that will allow the measurement of blood flow in the neurosensory retina and optic nerve non-invasively. Mathematical modeling will allow the quantification of perfusion rate at tissue level. Validation of the technology will be done against histology as well as invasive gold standard technology for measuring blood flow in non-human primates. A small pilot study in patients with glaucoma is finally scheduled as a proof of concept of the clinical applicability of this approach. Early detection of ischemia/hypoxia is crucial for identifying those who are at risk from visual debilitating eye diseases such as diabetic retinopathy, age-related macular degeneration and glaucoma and for allowing optimized treatment monitoring. Quantification of blood flow using SS-OCT angiography will be thus a major advancement in the management of patients in the future and will help reduce the burden of blindness from these diseases.
kw: Eye, Blood flow, Optical coherence tomography (OCT), Glaucoma

title: Molecular dissection and therapeutic targeting of cardiac fibrosis
abs: Fibrosis is an essential physiological process that is a central to wound healing. However, excessive fibrosis causes disease and is recognized as the final common pathway of cardiac damage. We recently undertook a large genomic discovery program in cardiac fibrosis using RNA-sequencing of primary human atrial fibroblasts stimulated with transforming growth factor beta (TGFB) and observed that TGFB most strongly upregulates interleukin 11 (IL11, >10-fold). The true physiological function of IL11 is unknown and we tested the hypothesis that IL11 may act as an autocrine factor in fibroblasts. We found that IL11 is a very potent pro-fibrotic factor and that the action of TGFB, and other pro-fibrotic factors, depends on IL11 activity. This finding is very exciting as it not only reveals new biology but identifies a secreted cytokine, the preferred target for antibody-based therapeutics, as a critical determinant of fibroblast activation. In this study we will leverage our newly created biological reagents that include tissue-specific loss- and gain-of-function mice that will be applied to study the effects of IL11 in fibroblasts in vivo by crossing to a Col1a2-CreER line. We will examine the molecular mechanisms underlying cis- and trans IL11 signaling in fibroblasts and dissect the relative contributions of the JAK/STAT and MAPK signaling pathways. We will test the hypothesis that inhibiting IL11 signaling with either anti-IL11 or anti-IL11RA antibodies that we have generated can prevent, arrest or reverse cardiac fibrosis. In molecular imaging and biomarker studies we will examine IL11 detection methodologies as a means of revealing active fibrosis in rodents and humans. These studies will open a new avenue of research in fibrosis, define new biology and explore the possibility of blocking IL11 signaling, directed by biomarker stratification, as a therapeutic approach for inhibiting maladaptive fibrosis, which is an area of unmet clinical need.
kw: heart, fibrosis, cytokine

title: Development of Novel Exosome Infused Bioactive Collagen Sponge for Effective Cartilage Regeneration in Rabbit Model of Osteochondral Lesion
abs: Articular cartilage lesion repair remains to be challenging in musculoskeletal medicine due to the poor intrinsic regenerative capacity of this tissue. In our prior work, we showed that exosomes are the principal mediator underlying the biological effects of human mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) for cartilage repair in an osteochondral defect model in immunocompetent rats. Importantly, no adverse tissue reaction or immune rejection was observed in all animals treated with MSC exosomes. This study demonstrates for the first time the efficacy of human MSC exosomes in cartilage repair and the utility of MSC exosomes as a ready-to-use and cell-free therapeutic alternative to cell-based MSC therapy. However, weekly intra-articular injection of exosomes was performed for 12 weeks in a rodent model, which might not be practical for clinical translation. To improve the feasibility of MSC exosome as a ready-to-use and cell-free clinical therapeutics for cartilage repair, it would be pivotal to develop a one-step, bioactive scaffold-based approach that would circumvent the need for weekly injections. Collagen sponge has excellent biocompatibility and biodegradability, and has been widely used in orthopaedic procedures. We hypothesize that a collagen sponge infused with therapeutic MSC exosomes represents a novel bioactive scaffold for effective cartilage regeneration. In this proposed study, we aim to optimize the development of exosome infused collagen sponge, and to evaluate the in vivo host response and therapeutic efficacy of exosome infused collagen scaffold in an immunocompetent rabbit osteochondral defect model. Our long-term goal of this study is to develop a one-step therapeutic approach toward physiological regeneration of a functional articular hyaline cartilage to improve clinical outcome.
kw: Cartilage regeneration, exosomes, tissue engineering, rabbit model, osteochondral lesion

title: LCP1/L-plastin inhibition as a novel actionable target in multiple myeloma
abs: The aims of this research are to investigate the mechanism of LCP1/L-plastin directed NIK-RelB:NF?B2 activation and to develop and characterize LCP1/L-plastin inhibitors as novel anti-cancer agents. We hypothesize that LCP1/L- plastin over-expression drives NIK:NF-?B cellular motility and its proteasome inhibitor resistance through two mechanisms: (1) Calcium binding and (2) Actin-binding. We plan to evaluate the molecular mechanism of LCP1/L-plastin directed NIK-RelB:NF?B2 activation by identifying its functional motifs and the proteins that interact with LCP1. We also plan to evaluate the calcium buffering and actin-bundling function of LCP1 and LCP1 mediated MM cell migration. We also would look at the effect of LCP1 on tumourgenesis by injecting mice with transduced cells. Transcription factor NF-?B is known to be aberrantly activated in many human cancers causing apoptosis inhibition and cancer cell proliferation. TNF receptor associated factor 3 (TRAF3) plays a pivotal role as a negative regulator in the non-canonical NF-?B pathway by mediating TNFRs signalling to induce immune responses and limit B-cell survival. TRAF3 mutation is implicated in B cell tumourgenesis and in MM, loss-of-function of TRAF3 is a high-risk factor associated with poor prognosis due to proteasome inhibitor resistance. Recently, a study of genetic heterogeneity of 203 MM patients in tumour-normal pairs revealed 5% of patients presented with mutations in TRAF3. Our preliminary study demonstrated that LCP1 is one of the most differentially highly expressed genes in TRAF3 mutant MM cell lines. Using an LCP1 inhibitor, we can overcome proteasome inhibitor resistance and the bad prognostic marker of TRAF3 mutation. On a broader scope, LCP1 is also known to enhance metastasis in CLL, breast and colorectal cancer. As NF-?B activation is present in many tumour types, the findings in this study would be translatable to the cancer community at large leading to novel therapeutics.(293 words)
kw: Multiple myeloma, LCP1/L-plastin, NF-kB inducing kinase, proteasome inhibitor, TRAF3

title: Exosome-induced Primary Repair of the Anterior Cruciate Ligament: A Revolutionary Biological Technique
abs: The primary repair of anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) has not been able to achieve the required clinical outcomes, and as a result, has to resort to surgical reconstructive procedure using tendon autografts or allografts, with issues of donor site morbidity and risk of disease transmission. Therefore, there is an unmet need to devise a viable tissue engineering (TE) approach to repair and regenerate the torn ACL. Current TE approaches utilizing biomaterial scaffold combined with mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) or platelet-rich-plasma (PRP) have obtained promising results, but still require cell/plasma isolation and as a result lacked off-the-shelf availability. Increasingly, the therapeutic efficacy of MSCs has been attributed to the secretion of small nano-sized vesicles known as the exosomes. Previously, we have developed a silk-nanohydroxyapatite scaffold for ACL repair. The objective of this study is to create a novel off-the-shelf exosome-impregnated implantable biological silk scaffold to promote primary healing of the ACL by demonstrating its effectiveness in a rabbit model. We hypothesize that an exosome-impregnated silk scaffold would not only provide the critical structural support, but also sustain high local concentration of MSC exosomes to stimulate natural ligamentous healing through activation of multiple signaling pathways, namely PDGF, TGF-?, VEGF and FGF pathways that are important for angiogenesis, proliferation and extracellular matrix synthesis to bring about complete ACL regeneration in a one-step procedure. Accordingly, we will develop exosome-impregnated silk scaffold, optimize the dosing and loading strategies, determine the bioactivity and effects in vitro and exemplify the in vivo efficacy in rabbit model of ACL injury.
kw: Exosome, Secretome, Anterior cruciate ligament, silk scaffold, bioscaffold

title: Preoperative anemia among the elderly undergoing major abdominal surgery: Impact on healthcare outcomes
abs: Preoperative anemia is a known risk factor for morbidity, mortality and increased healthcare resource utilisation. The PI’s previous study demonstrated the rate of any preoperative anemia in Singapore General Hospital (SGH) to be at 26.6%. The rate is highest in the elderly group which stands at 49.9%. The main objective of this study is to investigate the perioperative morbidity and mortality, blood transfusion rate, healthcare outcomes and patient-centric outcomes among anemic elderly patients undergoing major surgery. We hypothesize that elderly patients who undergoes major abdominal surgery with preoperative anemia will have higher composite morbidity and mortality rates (primary outcome), longer length of hospital stay, higher blood transfusion requirements and lower health-related quality of life (HRQoL) at 1, 3 and 6 months (secondary outcomes) when compared to elderly patients without preoperative anemia. We will conduct a prospective observational study of 450 consecutive patients above 65 years, who are undergoing elective major open abdominal surgery in SGH over 12 months. Baseline clinical assessment, including iron studies for anemic patients, will be done within 14 days prior to surgery. To determine the primary outcome, patients will be followed up prospectively for 30 days from the day of surgery. This will be done via a mixture of medical records review and phone interview. For secondary outcomes, the length of hospital stay and readmissions for any reason within 3 and 6 months will be recorded. HRQoL questionnaires will be self-administered during preoperative consults and again via returned mail at 1, 3 and 6 months. Findings from this study will hopefully fill the knowledge gaps such as how anemia impacts elderly people in terms of perioperative morbidity, mortality, post-surgical quality of life and their eventual return to the community as well as providing local data on the healthcare resource utilisation in this group.
kw: anemia, preoperative care, outcome assessment, surgery, blood transfusion; aged

title: The Feasibility and Acceptability of A Psychosocial Intervention for Advanced Colorectal Cancer Patients
abs: Cancer is the leading cause of death in Singapore and colorectal cancer is the most frequently diagnosed cancer in males and second most frequently diagnosed cancer in females. Between 2009 – 2013, approximately 25% of colorectal cancer cases in Singapore were at the advanced stage. Patients with advanced colorectal cancer can face unique challenges that are stoma- or bowel-related in addition to other symptoms burden such as pain, fatigue, and existential distress that have deleterious consequences on their psychological and social functioning. Psychosocial care is increasingly recognized as an important part of supportive/palliative treatment for this population at such a vulnerable time. Psycho-behavioural interventions (PBIs) that are based on cognitive-behavioural frameworks can meet the needs of these patients by targeting and modifying their maladaptive thoughts and behaviours associated with cancer-related suffering. The aim of the current pilot study is to determine the feasibility and acceptability of a PBI program based on cognitive-behavioural framework for advanced colorectal cancer patients that incorporates culturally-appropriate topics. We also aim to obtain an initial estimate of the efficacy of the 4 session-intervention, with the primary outcome being change in psychological distress. It is hypothesized that the intervention will be feasible and acceptable to patients. We also hypothesize that there will be a decrease in depression and anxiety scores for the intervention group compared to the waitlist control group during the same time period. The findings will provide preliminary data for and determine the worthiness of a phase III confirmatory study of such a PBI and its scalability for advanced-staged cancer patients in Singapore. The proposed PBI is potentially able to provide an often overlooked need of advanced cancer patients seeking health services.
kw: Psychological treatment, Colorectal cancer, Depression, Anxiety, Supportive/palliative care, Health service

title: Optimising influenza vaccination uptake and timing among the elderly in Singapore: a modelling study
abs: The aim of this project is to understand how influenza vaccination of the elderly in Singapore can be improved in terms of uptake and deployment. The specific objectives are to:•Assess price sensitivity to vaccination,•Assess cost-effectiveness of subsidized vaccine in reducing hospitalization rates,•Investigate whether respondent-driven referrals can improve vaccine uptake rates,•Assess how influenza vaccination among the elderly should be timed to optimize protection.These objectives will be met using a mixture of health economic and mathematical modelling. The first three objectives fall under subproject 1, while the latter falls under subproject 2. To evaluate price sensitivity to vaccination costs among the elderly, we will conduct two randomized trials of incentive structure and quantum among the elderly. These will compare straightforward compensation for vaccination receipt, to two more complex compensation schemes involving respondent driven referrals and perceived scarcity of compensation. To evaluate the optimal timing of influenza vaccination, we will build upon previous work on the antibody response following infection or vaccination, the protection conferred by varying antibody levels, and the social contacts of the elderly, by developing a simulation model that allows the outcome of a given vaccination schedule to be assessed.
kw: Influenza, Vaccination, Modelling, Economics, Public Health, Elderly

title: Genetic origin of adverse drug reactions in Singaporean breast cancer patients
abs: More than 90% of breast cancer patients receive systemic therapy and adverse reactions caused by such treatment are not uncommon. Occurrence and severity vary greatly among individuals and clinically validated biomarker for adverse reactions is not yet available. The proposed project aims to identify genetic variants that influence susceptibility to aromatase inhibitor-induced bone density loss and taxane-induced febrile neutropenia among breast cancer patients in Singapore.Breast cancer patients are recruited from six public hospitals in Singapore as part of the ongoing Singapore Breast Cancer Cohort Project. Participants are asked to donate blood or saliva sample and DNA are extracted and stored at a central laboratory. Socio-demographic data, lifestyle and reproductive risk factor are collected using a structured questionnaire and clinical data such as tumor characteristics and treatment can be retrieved from hospital-based breast cancer registry. For patients treated with aromatase inhibitor, baseline and follow-up measurements of bone mineral density will be retrieved from medical record. A text mining algorithm for electronic medical record will be developed using the surgical data systems directorate database at National University Hospital. With this tool, occurrence of neutropenia among patients receiving taxane will be identified from discharge summary and accompanied laboratory results. With a cohort of 10,000 patients in the next two years, we propose to 1) identify rare variants that can distinguish patients who may suffer from extremely severe ADRs in 500 Chinese patients treated with aromatase inhibitor and 500 Chinese patients treated with taxane-based chemotherapy using whole exome sequencing technology and 2) complement the rare coding variants with information from common and typically low risk genetic variants through whole genome array with customized coding, known genetic loci fine mapping and pharmacogenomics loci imputed to local population reference panels.
kw: breast cancer; adverse drug reactions

title: Characterisation of B cells during Hepatitis B seroclearance
abs: Chronic hepatitis B (CHB) affects 300 million globally and commonly causes liver disease. A recently awarded NMRC TCR(TCR13dec008) grant is to examine mechanisms for eradication of CHB, and examines adaptive immunity (T cells), innate immunity and Hepatitis B Virus (HBV) in the clearance of CHB, it does not examine B cell responses. Clinical evidence of the importance of B cells in protecton from CHB is the finding that anti-HBs post-HBV vaccination are protective. Two important events, HBeAg and HBsAg seroconversion, show that B cells play an important role in CHB. We hypothesize that there is increasing B cell activity in the progression of CHB towards HBV clearance, and that this is related to the development of new B cell epitopes, that lead to seroconversion or are neutralising. Thus, the aim of theme 1 is to identify B cell epitopes following HBeAg seroconversion and HBsAg seroclearance, by phage display and antibody repertoires from vaccinated or recovered HBV patients using established techniques, then fine mapping them employing peptide ELISA and cyroelectron microscopy. Using a neutralising assay for HBV, we can identify neutralising epitopes. Theme 2, will focus on the role of B cells in clinical studies (treated and untreated), where patients have evolved to achieve HBeAg and HBsAg seroconversion. We will examine evidence for B cell activity by phenotyping and functional studies such as ELISPOT assays for anti-HBs secreting B cells, cytokine/chemokine profiling and TLR expression. Using archived serum we can examine historical viral quasispecies and determine if isolated B cells secrete antibodies that recognise them and match previously identified neutralising epitopes. Finally in theme 3 we will examine the crucial issue of T cell help for B cell function through identifying frequency of CD4+CXCR5+ICOS+ cells, isolate them and perform functional studies to determine if they are dysfunctional in CHB.
kw: antibody responses, HBsAg loss, adaptive immunity, immunoglobulin, epitopes

title: Unsupervised Machine Learning of Mental Disorder Factors From Magnetic Resonance Imaging
abs: The U.S. National Institute of Mental Health has developed a major initiative to “develop … new ways of classifying mental disorders based on behavioral dimensions and neurobiological measures”. The initiative addresses the fundamental problem that current mental disorder categories are based on symptom checklists and not carving nature by its joints. Indeed, subtypes within disorders (e.g., ADHD) and overlaps across disorders (e.g., co-occurrence of autism and ADHD in the same individuals) suggest the existence of shared neurobiological factors across disorders. We propose to develop unsupervised machine learning algorithms to discover these unobserved disorder factors from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). For example, the algorithms might find a factor associated with temporal lobe atrophy; patients exhibiting this factor might suffer from memory loss regardless of traditional disorder diagnosis. Unsupervised machine learning seeks to uncover hidden structures in data, and is therefore ideal for discovering unobserved factors. We will exploit an advanced class of unsupervised machine learning algorithms – mixed-membership Bayesian models. The mixed-membership models would account for patients exhibiting multiple disorder factors to different degrees, in contrast with traditional unsupervised learning algorithms that would constrain a datapoint (patient) to associate with a single category (factor). This is necessary to reconcile the phenomena of heterogeneity within disorders and overlaps across disorders. Since the goal is to potentially reshape diagnostic categories with MRI-derived neurobiological factors, an important requisite for this project is large-scale MRI datasets across multiple disorders that have only become available in the past five years. While the factors will be discovered from large-scale international datasets, the Bayesian modeling allows us to automatically estimate the factor decomposition of new patients in Singapore cohorts, which will then be used to predict the unique behavioral symptoms of individual patients. The personalized factor diagnosis might also be useful for individual-level prognosis and customized therapies.
kw: Human Brain Mapping;Brain Imaging;Unsupervised Machine Learning;Mental Disorders;Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI);Probabilistic Graphical Models

title: Targeting NF1-associated glioma invasion and therapeutic resistance for improved clinical outcome
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Glioblastoma multiforme is incurable with an average survival of less than 1.5 years. Underlying such dismal prognosis is the heterogeneity of the glioma cells, which heightens radio-chemoresistance and promotes tumor infiltration that underpin disease recurrence commonly observed in GBM patients. Our results implicate the loss of the tumor suppressor gene, neurofibromin (NF1), in the transition of proneural GBM to an aggressive mesenchymal state with enhanced invasion and treatment resistance. Since NF1 inactivating mutations or loss of expression is found in 23% of GBM, targeting NF1-loss associated signaling is relevant to glioma therapy. Accordingly, we hypothesize that loss of NF1 promotes mesenchymal transition of gliomas, which results in tumor recurrence and radiochemo-resistance. Our data indicate the leucine rich domain (LRD) functions to suppress motility and invasion in glioma. Thus, our first aim is to investigate whether NF1-loss or mutation confers therapeutic resistance in mesenchymal GBM. We will characterize the somatic mutations identified in GBM patients found in the LRD region and will assess whether they play a role in mesenchymal transition. As a separate, but complementary aim, we will test whether other domains of NF1 mediate mesenchymal regression to a less invasive proneural state to serve as surrogate therapeutic targets. We will investigate whether LRD or other domains of NF1 regulate NF1-loss associated downstream molecules that mediate GPM invasion. We found that loss of NF1 upregulates expression of angiogenic and cell motility related genes, angiopoietin-like (ANGPTL)-4 and ephrinB2 (EFNB2). Accordingly, our third aim is to elucidate how activation of ANGPTL4 and EFNB2 mediate glioma invasion and self-renewal. Results obtained from this proposal will allow us to establish crucial downstream pathways that are required for NF1-loss mediated mesenchymal transition of human GBM that in turn will facilitate the development of novel treatment strategies to target these specific effector for glioma therapy.
kw: glioma, glioblastoma multiforme, neuro-oncology, neurofibromin (NF1), therapeutic resistance,

title: Understanding of artemisinin resistance in malaria parasites
abs: Resistance of human malaria to artemisinin, the main chemotherapeutic agent, is now spreading through Southeast Asia and it is threatening all malaria control programs around the world. Mutations in the PfK13 gene, have been associated with artemisinin resistance and are presently the main molecular markers for monitoring. However, recently, we showed that artemisinin resistance is mediated by the unfolded protein response (UPR) pathway in conjunction with deceleration of the Plasmodium falciparum intraerythrocytic developmental cycle (IDC). Here we propose to carry out a series of experiments to establish mechanistic links between K13 polymorphisms and the newly discovered cellular physiological features of resistances. First, we will generate transgenic parasite lines with candidate genes involved in artemisinin resistance as key regulatory factors. These studies are aimed to identify the primary mechanisms that drive the emergence and spread of artemisinin resistance. Second, we will carry out functional genomics studies with P. falciparum strains carrying multiple K13 genotypes to establish their mechanistic links with artemisinin resistance. These studies will be carried out with in vitro transgenic lines and with newly collected field isolates. Third we will investigate the potential and mechanisms of K13-independent pathways of artemisinin resistance by studying in vitro derived parasite lines as well as field isolates. Finally we will employ a proteomics based approach termed Cellular Thermal Shift Assay (CETSA) that has the ability to study artemisinin resistance in a direct context of the drug mode of action. The main goal will be to identify direct targets of artemisinin and their role in resistance. These results will be crucial for the future understanding of emergence of drug resistance in the future and will have direct impact on monitoring and controlling the spreading artemisinin resistance in the world.
kw: drug resistance, malaria, artemisinin, infectious diseases, genomics, proteomics

title: Study the mechanism of mitophagy associated execution of mutant KRAS addicted cancer cells via its hyper-activation
abs: RAS proto-oncogenes are frequently mutated in 30% human of cancers making them the most abundant oncogenic mutations involved in tumorigenesis. Currently the main strategies against mutant RAS driven cancers is by blocking/inhibiting effectors of RAS signaling or by designing strategies to directly inhibit GTP loading of RAS. We recently demonstrated the feasibility to use an opposite strategy, whereas overactivation rather than inhibition of mutant KRAS by a small molecule compound (C1) resulted in mitochondrial ROS-dependent execution of RAS driven colon carcinoma cell lines, pancreatic cancer cells and in an in vivo murine xenograft. In the proposed study we aim to investigate the mechanism underlying the hyper-activation of mutant KRAS. Additionally, the association of mutant KRAS and downstream AKT phosphorylation and their translocation to the mitochondria with mitochondrial morphology changes and redox driven execution will be studied. Intrigued by our preliminary findings, we also aim to decipher the mechanism and involvement of the upregulated mitochondrial VDAC, in the activation of mitochondrial fission and mitophagy downstream of activated mutant KRAS. To that end, we will be investigating the changes in phosphorylation of Drp-1 and the processing of OPA-1, proteins that counteract each other’s activity in inducing mitochondrial morphology changes (fission vs fusion). Finally, we aim to employ a computational strategy for screening existing FDA approved drugs to identify agents with similar anti-cancer activity involving mutant KRAS activation. Taken together, these studies will provide a novel insight into the potential therapeutic relevance of leveraging on cancer cells’ Achilles heel-addiction to KRAS.
kw: mutant KRAS driven tumors, selective targeting, ROS, mitochondria, drugs repurposing

title: Evaluating the efficacy of exosomes derived from human mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) in promoting osteochondral regeneration for osteoarthritis
abs: Osteoarthritis (OA) of the knee is a significant cause of pain and morbidity. For the elderly patients, joint replacement surgery is the definitive treatment. For middle-aged patients suffering from early OA, but enjoy an active sporting lifestyle, current therapies available include cell-based therapies such as autologous chondrocyte implantation and mesenchymal stem cell (MSC) therapy. However, there are challenges, such as limited cellular capacity for self-renewal, proliferation and differentiation with older patients, logistic and operational challenges associated with proper handling and cell storage to maintain cell viability and vitality. There is increasing evidence that MSC therapy is neither dependent on engraftment of cells at the site of injury nor the differentiation capability of transplanted MSC. Instead, the mechanism of repair is based on paracrine factors secreted by MSCs, suggesting a paradigm shift from a cell-based MSC therapy to a cell-free MSC therapy. In recent years, MSC conditioned medium has been characterized to elucidate the MSC secretome and to better elucidate the paracrine factors underlying the reparative/regenerative functions of MSCs. Of late, the most promising therapeutic candidate in MSC secretome is extracellular vesicles (EVs), namely microvesicles and exosomes. Exosomes are a specific class of EVs with a diameter of 40-100nm, with an endosomal origin, and possess characteristic exosomal markers such as ALIX, tumor susceptibility 101 (TSG101) and tetraspanins (CD9, CD63 and CD81). It is increasingly demonstrated and accepted that MSC exosome is the principal mediator underlying the biological effects of MSCs in tissue repair. The aim of the study is to evaluate the efficacy of exosomes derived from human MSCs in promoting osteochondral regeneration for OA in a rat model. The hypothesis is that exosomes derived from human MSCs can be a new treatment modality to promote osteochondral regeneration in a rat model of anterior cruciate ligament transection model of OA.
kw: osteoarthritis, tissue engineering, cartilage, exosomes

title: Modeling of the Kidney Filter Using Biologically Relevant Laminin Matrix
abs: Despite two-thirds of kidney disease cases originating from damage to the glomeruli (the kidney filtering unit), most of their pathomechanisms are still understudied. The lack of a functional in vitro model makes it difficult to dissect molecular mechanisms of the glomerular sieving process and limits the development of therapeutic treatments. The objective of this proposal is to develop a functional 3D glomerular filtration barrier (GFB) model by co-culturing fenestrated endothelial cells (ECs) and podocytes – two main cell types of the GFB – derived from human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) on relevant extracellular matrices (ECM). My long-term goal is to apply this tool to address molecular mechanisms of genetic kidney diseases together with animal disease models. Based on my published work to derive ECs from hESCs on relevant ECM protein Laminin, and my collaborator’s computational algorithm to predict transcription factors (TFs) inducing cell-type conversions, my central hypothesis is that proper ECM substrates and specific sets of TFs are required for the differentiation of ECs and podocytes, and to maintain their phenotypes in vitro. The rationale is that successful generation of this model offers a platform to test novel drugs for their nephrotoxicity and facilitates a better understanding of pathophysiologic mechanisms of renal injuries. The goal of this application will be achieved by three specific aims: 1) Identify TFs to induce hESC-podocyte differentiation on relevant Laminin matrices, 2) Determine the mechanism of fenestrae formation in ECs, and 3) Develop a 3D human GFB model using a flow-cell system. The approach is innovative because it utilizes, for the first time, kidney-specific ECM components together with computational tools to create highly differentiated unique cell types of the GFB. The proposed research is significant because it promises to provide a functional platform for analyzing drug clearance and toxicity, and for studying molecular mechanisms of glomerular diseases.
kw: kidney, glomerular filtration barrier, laminin, podocyte, glomerular endothelial cell, human embryonic stem cell

title: Treating Atherosclerosis with Remote Implantation of Bioresorbable Drug Eluting Particles
abs: Atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory disease that results in the narrowing of arteries. These lesions develop into plaques that rupture to form emboli that cause acute myocardial infarction and stroke. Despite significant advances in healthcare, atherosclerosis and other cardiovascular diseases result in several of the leading causes of death in Singapore. It is for this reason that HBMS has indicated that treating cardiovascular disease is a priority. The key challenge in treating atherosclerosis is that most drugs do not address the inflammatory feedback loop. Additionally, systemic treatments rely on the passive diffusion of the drug molecule from blood into the diseased tissue, despite evidence that diffusion alone is inadequate for applications with poor circulation and in blood vessels dominated by convective mass transport (as is the case for atherosclerosis). As a result, elevated dosages are necessary to improve efficacy, but result in damaging off target side effects. Therefore, developing a minimally invasive targeted drug delivery strategy that minimises drug dose and maximises its distribution is one of the greatest challenges facing current medicine. We propose the use of ultrasound in conjunction with bioresorbable drug-loaded cavitation agents to generate cavitation-induced microstreaming. These acoustically tunable microstreams enhance endothelial permeability and propel the drug-loaded particles into the atherosclerotic lesion. In this proposal, we outline the necessary key performance indicators that must be accomplished in order to enable this technology. This proposal is divided into two Work Projects. Work Project 1 focuses on developing the novel drug-loaded cavitation agent. Work Project 2 seeks to develop in vitro and ex vivo atherosclerotic models to test the efficacy of the cavitation agents developed. This will enable an optimisation of drug delivery whilst minimizing potential vascular damage. Upon completion, this project will satisfy the vision of HBMS by improving Singaporean wellness and enabling economically valuable technologies.
kw: Atherosclerosis, Cardiovascular Disease, Ultrasound, Drug Delivery, Cavitation

title: Deciphering highly recurrent non-coding insertions in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia
abs: The advent of novel DNA sequencing technologies has led to the description of an unprecedented number of somatic mutations in all types of cancer. Yet despite the identification of highly recurrent non-coding DNA mutations, their functional contribution to carcinogenesis is largely unexplored. The study of protein binders to these mutated sites is an attractive entry point to examine their function. Here, we want to unravel the mechanism underlying one of the best documented non-coding somatic cancer mutation: Insertions of a few nucleotides upstream of the TAL1 gene locus have recently been described in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (T-ALL) to create a super-enhancer that is bound by the MYB transcription factor. This change in epigenetic organisation leads to upregulation of TAL1 expression, which in return is a master oncogenic transcription factor governing a “core” transcriptional regulatory circuit causatively contributing to the formation of T-ALL. In this project, we aim to identify proteins differentially binding between the wild-type sequence and its cancer-mutated variant upstream of the TAL1 locus using state-of-the-art quantitative mass spectrometry. This will allow us to comprehensively investigate how the presence and/or absence of insertion-specific protein factors beyond MYB leads to transcriptional dysregulation of TAL1. Transcriptional changes both in reporter gene assays and in endogenous TAL1 expression will be examined upon depletion and overexpression of the differential binding proteins. Furthermore, we will test whether the formation of the super enhancer upstream of TAL1 is dependent on the differential binding factors. Ultimately, we will analyze whether the depletion/overexpression of the insertion-specific binding proteins impacts on features of tumorigenic potential such as cellular proliferation, survival and in vivo models. This work will serve as a blueprint to de-orphanise non-coding mutations in cancer, providing both a mechanistic understanding of these alterations and a potential route towards novel therapeutic targets.
kw: Cancer, non-coding mutations, mass spectrometry, T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, transcription, epigenetics

title: Investigating the role of H2S in resistance and persistence mechanisms in mycobacteria
abs: The goal of the proposed studies is to characterize the role of the gasotransmitter hydrogen sulfide (H2S) in the drug resistance and persistence of tuberculosis (TB). M. tuberculosis (Mtb), the causative agent of TB, remains the greatest bacterial killer, responsible for nearly 2 million deaths annually. The stresses of infection, such as oxygen and nutrient deprivation, cause Mtb and other mycobacteria to enter a programmed non-replicative or dormant state characterized by broad antibiotic resistance and persistence. This phenotypic or reversible form of drug resistance necessitates a prolonged 6-month treatment regimen of rifampicin, isoniazid, ethambutol and pyrazinamide, with genetically-acquired resistance further complicating treatment. Gasotransmitters such as oxygen, carbon monoxide, and nitric oxide are known to regulate the induction of the dormancy genetic program in mycobacteria and are increasingly recognized as important regulators of Mtb pathophysiology. H2S was recently shown to cause antibiotic resistance by a variety of mechanisms in other bacterial pathogens, in which H2S production arises from two pathways: 3-mercaptopyruvate sulfur-transferase, or cystathionine-?-synthase and cystathionine-?-lyase. Underlying the proposed studies, we found that mycobacteria possess homologs of the three enzymes and we detected H2S production in M. bovis, M. abscessus and M. smegmatis, with H2S generation inhibited by known chemical inhibitors of these pathways. Here we address the role of H2S in mycobacterial persistence and drug resistance in three Aims. In Aim 1, we employ genetic recombineering and chemical genetic tools to characterize this undescribed mycobacterial H2S biosynthetic pathway and then prepare mutant strains lacking the enzymes. In Aims 2 and 3, we define the role of H2S in antibiotic resistance and persister formation. Such findings would shed light on an unexplored aspect of mycobacterial physiology and offer novel targets for adjuvant TB therapies.
kw: Antimicrobial resistance, Persistence, Tuberculosis, Combination Therapy, Gasotransmitters

title: Mapping the chromatin interactome of non-canonical NF-?B pathway in multiple myeloma and the identification of new therapeutic targets.
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: The 3D chromatin architecture of the human genome has fundamental roles in regulating transcriptional programs of cancer cells and is a major determinant for their malignant transformation. Enhancer-promoter chromatin interactions form the basis of this spatial organization and are modulated by genetic alterations as well as dysregulated driver pathways during cancer progression. Functional enhancers were recently discovered to serve as transcription units that produce non-coding enhancer RNAs (eRNAs). While studies have implicated the role of eRNAs in gene activation, their relevance in cancer development and function in enhancer-promoter looping during malignant transformation remain unexplored. This proposal aims to investigate the role of eRNAs and cancer-activating chromatin interactions specifically in multiple myeloma (MM) progression. MM is a B-cell malignancy that is currently incurable and well-known for its complex genetic heterogeneity which hampers efficient treatment of the disease. The non-canonical NF-?B and RAS-ERK pathways are frequently deregulated due to recurrent somatic mutations in key signalling components and their aberrant activation are known to drive MM malignancy. Here, we hypothesize that these pathways mediate critical chromatin interactions driving malignant transformation of cancer cells and focus on the role of non-canonical NF-?B activation in MM progression. We aim to use NF-?B2 p52 ChIP-seq as a novel strategy to identify an eRNA signature that is induced during malignant progression of MM patients and can serve as prognostic biomarkers of MM. We will also investigate the pathological significance of this eRNA signature and their associated enhancer-promoter chromatin loops in MM development. The key chromatin regulators, target promoters and eRNAs which we identify in this study will provide valuable insights for the future design of drug targets in the precision therapy of MM.

title: Molecular Mechanisms Underlying Soft Tissue Sarcoma Predisposition
abs: In developed countries, the 2 largest contributors to premature mortality are behavior (40%) and genetics (35%), in contrast to access, which accounts for 10%, although we suspect that the former two may impact the latter. Patients at genetic risk of cancer are an important subset for several clinically relevant reasons. Importantly, appropriate testing for many of these high-penetrance genes leading to cancer predisposition have clear clinical validity, clinical utility and actionability. The long-term goal of this project is to elucidate hereditary genetic defects leading to soft tissue sarcomas (STS) to develop better therapies for our patients, and generate knowledge that could be applicable to other conditions. Using next-generation sequencing of patients with familial, multiple and/or rare cancers, our group has successfully characterized the frequency of germline mutations in known tumor predisposition genes in different cancer subtypes. In a pilot study, we recently identified that a significant proportion (22%) of patients with apparently sporadic STS harbor pathogenic germline mutations in known cancer predisposition genes, suggesting that a subset of STS may have a previously not recognized underlying genetic predisposition. We have also identified novel cancer predisposition genes such as the CDNK2A and DNA damage repair (DDR) pathway genes, through studying families with a strong history of sarcomas. In the next three years, we would like to continue the identification of new genetic defects in STS using both clinical and biochemical phenotyping alongside next generation sequencing and related technologies, in addition to classic genetic approaches; elucidate further the role CDNK2A and the DDR pathway plays in soft tissue sarcoma tumorigenesis and utilize cells engineered to be sensitive to CDNK2A and DDR pathway defects for in-vitro drug screening. This approach is expected to lead to the discovery of molecules that may be used therapeutically for STS.

title: Next Generation Sequencing and Mechanistic Understanding for the Diagnosis and Management of Primary Glomerular Disease in Asia
abs: Primary glomerulopathy can cause renal failure. Almost all genetic glomerulopathy involves podocyte genes. While there have been consortiums in America and Europe, there have been no such initiatives in Asian, which is an under-studied group, especially Malays. We have set up “Deciphering Diversities: Renal Asian Genetics Network (DRAGoN)” with 20 Asian centres to date. We hypothesize genetic variants in Asians are different from those in Caucasians. Part A of this study aims to establish comprehensive genotype and longitudinal phenotype databases of Asian patients with likely genetic glomerular diseases using genome-wide association studies, next-generation sequencing. We expect 650 patients over 3 years.Our preliminary work has identified a mutation in angiomotin (AMOT) in a family with X-linked recessive nephropathy. AMOT gene occurs in sex chromosome and is expressed in podocytes. Amot knockout HEK293 cells have altered cell cycles. All male rats with an AMOT mutation corresponding to the human mutation, developed proteinuria and podocyte foot process effacement by 6 months. Mutant females were healthy. AMOT knockout rats survived into adulthood, unlike knockout zebrafish and mice, and had only isolated proteinuria. RNA-seq suggested altered pathways in glomerular injury, renal necrosis, and nephritis. AMOT may exert its function in podocytes in 3 pathways: Rich1/Gap complex affecting RhoGTPase activation; interactions with slit diaphragm; Hippo/Yap signalling and apoptosis. We hypothesize an absent or mutated AMOT affects slit diaphragm signaling and Rich1/GAP interactions causing inappropriate activation of RhoGTPases. Part B of this study aims to study the pathomechanism of podocytopathy via AMOT in rat models, particularly the expression, (co)localization and interactions of AMOT downstream molecules. We will also study tight junction function and migration of ex vivo podocytes and effects of RhoGTPase inhibitors.Part A can help stratify glomerular disease and direct management strategies. Part B may potentially identify novel therapeutic targets.

title: The trajectory of pre-death grief in dementia family caregivers and its effect on caregiving
abs: The demand for nursing home in Singapore has increased steadily in recent years, especially from persons with dementia (PWD). This can be a cause for concern considering that dementia already has a 10% prevalence in Singapore and with dementia being an age-related disease, its absolute numbers are expected to soar with our rapidly ageing population. To avoid the escalating societal cost associated with building more nursing homes, we need to better support the emotional needs of family caregivers so that they can maintain PWD in the community for a longer time.In this proposal, we wish to uncover an unmet emotional need of dementia caregivers (pre-death grief, PDG) that may adversely affect caregiving. We define PDG as the emotional responses as caregivers mourn the psychological death of PWD. Based on the hypothesis that persistently high PDG can have greater impact on caregiving, we aimed to assess how the trajectory of PDG affects the risk of major depression in caregivers (using mixed-effect logistic regression) and nursing home placement of PWD (using Cox regression). Additionally, we will test, using mixed-effect linear regression, whether PDG improves with currently available social interventions (such as day-care attendance or assistance from foreign domestic helper). We hypothesize that PDG, unlike caregiver burden, may worsen with these interventions. To achieve the study aims, we will recruit 200 caregivers to complete self-administered questionnaires at 0, 6 and 12 months. By showing how PDG can lead to caregiver depression and premature nursing home placement of PWD, the results of this study will provide the groundwork to guide our approach to better support the emotional needs of caregivers in current services, to implement strategies for early detection and intervention for caregivers at high risk of adverse outcomes, and to conduct future research on the efficacy of grief counselling.

title: Predicting responders to electroconvulsive therapy across schizophrenia and depression: a prospective study.
abs: The overall aim of this study is to determine the prognostic values ofcombinatorial neuroanatomical-genetics-cognitive biomarkers inpredicting electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) response in treatmentrefractoryschizophrenia and major depressive disorder (MDD).Unlike patients in US or western Europe—where ECT is used as a potentand fast-acting treatment for treatment-refractory depression—patientswith schizophrenia form the majority of patients receiving ECT inSingapore and Asia. Although our hospital records indicate increasingnumbers of patients receiving ECT, only 40% of the depressed patientsand 20% of the schizophrenia patients respond favourably to ECT. Giventhe cost and length of this stigma-bound treatment, there is an urgentneed to identify the subtype of patients receptive to ECT beforetreatment prescription.First, we aim to determine neuroanatomical signatures of ECT responsein schizophrenia and MDD using non-invasive magnetic resonanceimaging (MRI). We hypothesize that a subpopulation of treatmentrefractoryschizophrenia and MDD patients share abnormal hippocampalstructure and frontolimbic regions; and that ECT works by restoring theabnormalities in hippocampal structural and frontolimbic connectivity. Wehypothesize the plasticity of the postulated neurocircuitries correlate withECT-related symptomatic and cognitive response.Second, we aim to determine peripheral brain-derived neurotrophic factor(BDNF)-related signatures of ECT response, by extracting blood DNA,RNA and serum. We hypothesize that a sub-population of treatmentrefractorypatients share common BDNF gene variants, promotermethylation status, and expression that make them more receptive toECT. We will also examine common gene variants, epigenetic status andexpression of proteins along converging signaling pathways with BDNFknown to enhance neuroplasticity.Third, we aim to combine the neuroanatomical and biosignatures of highpredictive values (identified from the first and second aims) together withcognitive and clinical data, to construct a combinatorial signature that canpredict ECT response on a single-subject level.
kw: ECT, Electroconvulsive therapy

title: Phase 0 trial of 18F-3-Fluoro-5-[(pyridin-3-yl)ethynyl] benzonitrile ([18F] FPEB), a PET imaging tracer for quantifying the cerebral distribution of Metabotropic Glutamate 5 receptors(mGluR5): To study radiochemical safety, biodistribution, tracer kinetics, and radiation dosimetry in the Asian population.
abs: BACKGROUND Glutamate is a major excitatory neurotransmitter found to be implicated in several neurodegenerative disorders. Signalling of glutamate is mediated by G protein-coupled metabotropic receptors (mGluRs) that are predominantly expressed in the brain. The binding of glutamate to mGluR activates intracellular messenger systems and thus regulates neuronal excitability.There are eight subtypes of mGluR (mGluR1 to mGluR8). In this study, we focus on mGluR5. mGluR5 is linked with neurological disorders such as Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s disease and multiple sclerosis. [18F] FPEB is a Position Emission Tomography (PET) tracer which is highly selective for mGluR5. In preclinical and clinical studies, they show a regional uptake pattern consistent with known distribution of mGluR5 in the brain.AIMS In an Asian population, (1) evaluate the safety of [18F]FPEB positron emitting radiotracer administered intravenously, for potential use as a PET tracer for mGluR5, and (2) assess the ability of [18F] FPEB (radiotracer) to image and quantify mGluR5 in the brain regions by PET imaging.METHODOLOGY The study will consist of two parts. The first cohort will receive a single dose of [18F] FPEB. A whole body scan, with venous sampling will be performed to calculate radiation exposure. The second cohort of patients will receive two separate doses of [18F]-FPEB. Dynamic PET brain and arterial blood samples will be performed to analyze pharmacokinetics of [18F]-FPEB and validate its utility for quantifying mGluR5 in brain. Test-retest reliability of the method will be performed by repeating the PET scan on the same subjects at a different time points.SIGNIFICANCE Quantification of mGluR5 binding in vivo could help to elucidate the role of glutamate in physiological and pathological conditions.No potential benefit is expected. The potential risks will be radiation exposure to the subjects, which will be kept to a minimum by selection of as low dose as possible.

title: Visually-disabling pathologic myopia in the SEED and SCORM high myopia cohorts: Longitudinal changes, novel biomarkers and impact on health-related quality of life
abs: Singapore has one of the highest prevalence rates of myopia and myopia is a significant public health problem worldwide. Adults with high myopia (SE worse than -5.0 D) may have pathologic myopia (PM) complications including myopic macular degeneration and PM is a leading cause of visual impairment in Asia. Unlike other blinding eye diseases such as cataract or glaucoma, there are gaps in our knowledge of the clinical course and predictors of PM in myopic adults. The aims are to determine the 10-year changes in PM and effects on visual function and health related quality of life in adults with in the SEED and SCORM high myopia cohorts. The SEED older adult cohort comprises 992 highly myopicadults from 4 Singapore studies: SP2, SIMES, SINDI, and SCES while there are 300 from the SCORM young adult cohort. The adults will be recalled to the SERI clinic at 10 years and fundus photographs/OCT graded for all PM lesions. The visual impairment, visual function, quality of life, mobility and depression in high myopes with and without PM, and emmetropic controls will be compared. We will also assess eye shape, choroidal thickness and choroidal vasculature using novel SS-OCT Triton Angiogram imaging approaches and scleral rigidity with a novel adaption of the Quantal B scan machine to compare high myopes with and without PM. Our proposal offers a new means of characterizing disease phenotypes in PM, detailed evaluations of the impact on quality of life and new knowledge on imaging biomarkers that will provide baseline data for the development of new clinical treatments including scleral reinforcement surgery and collagen cross-linking. This would further position Singapore as a world-leading research center for myopia.

title: Elucidating the determinants and therapeutic vulnerabilities of primary tryosine kinase inhibitor-resistant EGFR mutation positive NSCLC
abs: Activating EGFR mutations are the commonest oncogenic driver in non-small cell lung cancer, and occurs in up to 60% of cases in Singapore. While EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) are associated with high response rates, 20-30% of patients do not exhibit significant tumour shrinkage – referred to as primary resistance. While secondary or acquired resistance to EGFR TKI has been well characterized and include mechanisms such as T790M and c-MET alterations, the determinants of primary resistance are poorly understood. Recently, through multi-sector exome sequencing, we have identified co-existing driver alterations (such as PTEN loss) as potential mediators for suboptimal response, and this was validated in combination therapy from candidates arising from a high content drug screen. In a separate primary TKI resistant patient-derived model, we unexpectedly show potential antagonism in dual targeting of co-drivers (in this instance c-MET and EGFR L858R), suggesting that a more nuanced approach is required to unravel the context of genomic alterations to address primary resistance. In this grant, I plan to use a combination of techniques including the use of integrative genomics (including transcriptomics), establishment of patient-derived models and high content drug screens to identify novel therapeutic approaches.
