title: Preoperative anemia among the elderly: impact on healthcare outcomes
abs: Preoperative anemia is a known risk factor for morbidity, mortality and increased healthcare resource utilization. The PI’s previous study demonstrated the rate of any preoperative anemia in Singapore General Hospital (SGH) to be at 26.6%. The rate is highest in the elderly group which stands at 49.9%. The main objective of this study is to investigate the perioperative morbidity and mortality, healthcare outcomes, patient-centered impact and economic impact of anemia in elderly patients undergoing major surgery. We hypothesize that elderly patients who undergoes major abdominal surgery with preoperative anemia will have higher composite morbidity and mortality rates (primary outcome), longer length of hospital stay, poorer recovery post-surgery, lower health-related quality of life (HRQoL) at 3 and 6 months and increased healthcare costs (secondary outcomes) when compared to elderly patients without preoperative anemia, controlled for other important comorbidities. We will conduct a prospective observational study of all patients above 65 years, who are undergoing elective major open abdominal surgery in SGH over 12 months. Baseline clinical assessment will be done within 14 days prior to surgery. To determine the primary outcome, patients will be followed up prospectively for 30 days from the day of surgery. This will be done via a mixture of medical records review and phone interview. For secondary outcomes, the length of index hospital stay and readmissions for any reason within 3 and 6 months will be recorded. HRQoL questionnaires will be administered during preoperative consults and again via a telephone interview at 3 and 6 months. Findings from this study will hopefully fill the knowledge gaps such as how anemia impacts elderly people in terms of perioperative morbidity, mortality, post-surgical quality of life and their eventual return to the community as well as providing local data on the healthcare resource utilization in this group.

title: Single-cell omics and mouse models to understand cellular heterogeneity and therapeutic resistance in chronic myeloid leukaemia
abs: Chronic myeloid leukaemia is caused by the acquisition of the BCR-ABL1 oncokinase in haematopoietic stem cells (HSC). Dysregulated BCRABL1 kinase activity transforms HSCs into leukaemic stem cells (LSC), giving rise to a myeloproliferative disease. BCR-ABL1 kinase can be targeted by tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) to control the chronic phase (CP) of the disease, and in most cases prevents progression to the preterminal blast crisis (BC) stage. However, despite the success of TKIs, only 5-10% of patients can discontinue TKI treatment without disease recurrence. The inability to isolate rare but persistent CML LSCs from patients, as well as the lack of suitable mouse models, are significant barriers to understanding how CML LSCs resist TKIs. In addition, clinical responses to TKIs remain heterogeneous, and current biomarkers cannot reliably predict which patients will transform to BC, require life-long TKI therapy, or enjoy long-term treatment free remission. The mechanisms responsible for clinical heterogeneity are incompletely understood, but likely reflect an underlying intra- and inter-patient heterogeneity among leukaemia cells as well as the immune cells capable of targeting them. In this work, we will leverage novel single cells approaches to correlate LSC and immune cell heterogeneity with clinical responses, develop our ability to facilitate long-term engraftment of CML LSCs in mice with humanized bone marrow (hBM) compartments, and isolate and analyze CP LSCs which are capable of evading TKI therapy. Our Specific Aims are: 1. To use innovative single cell approaches to identify biomarkers that predict clinical outcomes; 2. To establish a hBM mouse model for long-term engraftment of CP LSCs; and 3. To combine single cell approaches and the hBM mouse to discover mechanisms underlying CML LSC persistence. The completion of our Aims will increase our understanding of CP TKI response heterogeneity, identify biomarkers for improved prognostication, and uncover mechanisms of LSC persistence.
kw: Leukaemia, Biomarker, Leukaemia stem cell, Mouse model, Drug resistance

title: Metagenomic discovery and clinical characterization of HHV-7 in human angiosarcoma
abs: Background. Certain soft tissue sarcomas have been known to occur more frequently in immunocompromised individuals, inducing suspicion of an oncoviral etiology. In particular, proof of an oncoviral etiology for angiosarcoma, a type of aggressive soft-tissue tumor has remained elusive. The advent of next generation sequencing may overcome this hurdle in search of putative oncoviruses.Hypothesis & Aims. We hypothesize that an oncogenic virus is responsible for, or at least contribute to, the development of angiosarcoma. Specifically, we aim to examine the tissue tropism and specificity of our candidate oncovirus (HHV-7) in human angiosarcoma. In addition, we will examine if HHV-7 is genomically-integrated in angiosarcoma, and explore potential mechanisms by which HHV-7 contribute to its pathogenesis. Finally, the clinical significance of HHV-7 in angiosarcoma as a prognostic biomarker will be explored.Methodology & Approach. To survey the metagenomic landscape, whole genome sequencing will be applied to survey pairs of well-annotated angiosarcomas with their matched normal tissue. Specifically, the presence of viral genomes will be examined via computational subtraction. Corroborative evidence will be obtained from a validation cohort of archival or prospectively obtained angiosarcoma tissue as well as cell lines, through several independent methods, including polymerase chain reaction, immunohistochemistry, in-situ hybridization and transmission electron microscopy. Manual dissection of tumor samples with adjacent normal tissue, in addition to examination of non-angiosarcoma tumors, will allow the evaluation of tissue specificity as well as biological gradients. Clinical relevance of the virus detected will be explored through in vitro experiments on angiosarcoma cell lines, and via statistical correlations with patient data.Clinical Significance. The discovery of an angiosarcoma-causing virus will not only represent a scientific breakthrough but more importantly, may unlock diagnostic, prognostic and therapeutic options for this otherwise dismal disease.

title: A Framework for the development, evaluation and implementation of M-Health Psychological Interventions for Persons with Addiction Disorders
abs: There has been massive advances in M-Health recently, allowing individuals to use M-Health applications as interventional tools. However, prior reviews have demonstrated the lack of evidence base of these applications, and there are concerns about data collation and security of data collation. Prior reviews have suggested ways to improve the evidence base of current applications, but there remains a lack of research looking into the domain of M-Health data collation. The aim of the current research is to systematically review existing M-Health data collation strategies for post-natal depression, and to evaluate user preferences and lastly to integrate these findings with recommendations of healthcare professionals and any existing evidence base. In doing so, we aim to test the feasibility of using this framework approach for the collation of data for Postnatal depression. We will test the same framework for other medical and psychiatric applications, to determine if our proposed framework works. We hypothesize that with the implementation of the above framework, there will be better M-Health data collation and better M-Health based interventions. In order to fulfill the aims, we intend to perform a systematic review and content analysis of existing applications. This will be coupled with a crowdsourced cross-sectional study of user preferences, followed by a workshop to gather healthcare professionals' opinions. Lastly, proof of concept testing will be conducted.

title: Linking Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease Clinical Phenotypes to Endotypes for possible disease-modifying targets in Asia
abs: COPD is a common respiratory condition resulting in significant morbidity, mortality and socioeconomic burden. World Health Organization estimates suggest that by 2030, COPD will become the 4th leading cause of death worldwide and is currently the 10th leading cause of death in Singapore. COPD is a heterogeneous disease with a large inter-individual variation in disease progression and treatment responses. Differences in risk factor exposure, cultural and genetic background across Asia likely results in distinct COPD characteristics conferring variable responses to current guideline directed treatment. Therefore, a need to better define the Asian COPD phenotype is required. We hypothesize that Asian COPD has a unique phenotype. This has potential implications for clinical management. Our objective is to determine if inflammatory, microbiological or immune differences exist relative to western cohorts. This is important as it has the potential to uncover avenues amenable to precision medicine approaches specific to Singaporean patients. We will determine the airway and systemic inflammatory, immune and microbiological phenotype in early, advanced and at acute exacerbations of COPD, three critical and well defined disease states impacting on disease pathogenesis and progression.A prospective study of 180 patients with COPD will be undertaken. Of this cohort, 60 patients will have early COPD, 60 established severe COPD (GOLD score = III/IV) and 60 acute exacerbations of COPD (necessitating hospital admission). We will assess cytokine and chemokine levels and the phagocytic activity of alveolar and monocytes derived macrophages (MDM). The airway microbiome will also be determined for the first time in Asian COPD patients. This work will significantly enhance our understanding of the Asian COPD phenotype and in turn offer potential novel diagnostic and/or therapeutic approaches specific to our population. This, in turn may permit more targeted precision medicine approaches to COPD management in the Asia-pacific region.

title: Concomitant limb cryocompression and scalp cooling to reduce paclitaxel-induced neuropathy and alopecia
abs: Paclitaxel is a key chemotherapeutic agent used in the management of common cancers, such as breast cancer. Chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN) due to paclitaxel is a common dose-limiting toxicity with no effective prevention or treatment. Limb cryocompression is currently being developed as a method to reduce CIPN. Another common toxicity of paclitaxel is chemotherapy induced alopecia (CIA), for which scalp-cooling is currently an approved therapy to reduce the incidence of this adverse effect. As scalp cooling use in day-to-day clinical practice increases, future studies involving hypothermia to treat neuropathy must factor this into the treatment algorithm, lest patients be mdenied or are required to trade-off one treatment for the other. However, there is concern of causing core hypothermia and/or general intolerance to concomitant therapy. Both scalp-cooling and cryocompression individually have not shown to cause this, but simultaneous use has not been studied previously. Clinical safety studies, in healthy subjects and cancer patients would need to be conducted first, before larger efficacy studies are performed. We propose that we can deliver scalp-cooling and limb cryocompression with a single treatment modality to prevent two toxicities of paclitaxel û CIA and CIPN. This study will consist of two parts:A) Healthy subjects: To assess safety and tolerability of scalp and limb cryocompression, as well as to determine the optimal temperature and pressure to be used, that will contribute to the cryocompression protocol. The occurrence of core hypothermia or intolerance will be closely monitoredB) Cancer patients: Once the optimal cryocompression protocol is established in healthy patients, a group of cancer patients will undergoconcomitant limb cryocompression and scalp cooling over multiple cycles of chemotherapy to establish safety and tolerability of repeated therapy. Early clinical efficacy signal data will also be collected, to prepare for the subsequent larger randomized efficacy study.
kw: Cryocompression, hypothermia, alopecia, neuropathy, paclitaxel chemotherapy, scalp-cooling

title: Regulation of Circadian Rhythms
abs: The circadian clock is an ~24 hr intrinsic biological clock that regulates critical physiological functions such as sleep-wake cycles, feeding-fasting pattern, hormonal and body temperature regulations. Circadian disruptions due to shift work, inadequate sleep, weekend time shifts and jet lag are an increasingly common feature of Singaporean and international culture. Circadian stresses lead to increased risk for diseases like diabetes, obesity, cancer and mood disorders. A deeper understanding of the mechanisms of circadian clock can provide significant insights into these pathological conditions. In addition, since circadian rhythms are controlled by phosphorylation/degradation cycles, they are amenable to therapeutic interventions by specific kinase inhibitors. Finally, targeted mutations in mice provide excellent model systems to study the effects of circadian disruption on health. In this proposal, we build on our recent insights (Zhou et al., Mol Cell, 2015) into the molecular basis of circadian rhythmicity including temperature compensation. We have now generated novel mice with a single amino acid mutation at the predicted kinase regulated degradation site of Per2, in both a PER2-luc reporter and wildtype background. This study will be the first in vivo test of the phosphoswitch model. As the circadian clock and many disease states interact, we will compare mice with opposing circadian behavior, Per2-mutant mice with longer, and tau mice with shorter period, examining if chronotype regulates disease susceptibility. Finally, we will test a key prediction of our model, that a currently unidentified priming kinase is responsible for phosphorylating the PER2 FASP site. Identification of the priming kinase will help us to further understand the mechanisms of FASPS and will provide a novel therapeutic target for circadian related disorders.

title: Optimizing local immunomodulation therapy for reducing the health and economic burden of surgical site infections
abs: Surgical site infections (SSIs) are the most common healthcare infection, adding billions to healthcare costs, increasing morbidity, and contributing to rising antibiotic resistance. Amazingly, modern health care still struggles with SSIs despite knowing exactly which patients are at risk and when and where the infection will occur. Simultaneously, immunomodulatory therapy is steadily revolutionizing the effectiveness of cancer therapy. Leveraging the immune system is a natural alternative to antibiotics for treating infection as well. We propose to combine the unique features of SSI with immunomodulation to develop a new therapy for SSIs, taking it through proof of concept and initial preclinical validation. Our strategy involves immunomodulatory drugs targeted at locally resident mast cells that coordinate initial infection responses. We have already identified a set of 79 drug-like immunomodulatory drugs targeting mast cells, and have preliminary data showing that known mast cell activators decrease bacterial infection burden and accelerate wound healing. This effect was enhanced when the mast cell activator was delivered with a microparticle delivery system. We will use both in vitro cell models and in vivo infection models to verify the specificity of our new candidate mast cell activators; to optimize the delivery of these activators in a time scale that matches the risk window of SSIs; and to validate that these provide benefit in reducing bacterial infection and promote wound healing in an animal model of SSI. The end goal of this translational research is to exploit the unique knowledge of when and where SSIs are going to occur to develop a convenient, single dose, preventative local that is ready for initial human clinical trials. There is high commercial potential with protectable intellectual property based on our development of the delivery system and a large target market for cost savings and improvement of health outcomes.

To establish a hBM mouse model for long-term engraftment of CP LSCs; and 3. To combine single cell approaches and the hBM mouse to discover mechanisms underlying CML LSC persistence. The completion of our Aims will increase our understanding of CP TKI response heterogeneity, identify biomarkers for improved prognostication, and uncover mechanisms of LSC persistence.
kw: Leukaemia; Biomarker; Leukaemia stem cell; Mouse model; Drug resistance

title: Investigating INPP4B loss in hepatocellular carcinoma for precision drug targeting
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Recent studies from our lab have shown that Inositol polyphosphate 4-phosphatase (INPP4B) loss in the context of PTEN deficiency causes tumour progression and metastasis in follicular thyroid cancer. Loss of INPP4B was shown to increase signalling through the PI3K/AKT pathway, and thereby increasing anchorage independent proliferation, invasion and metastasis. The PI3K-AKT signalling axis has been found to be aberrantly activated in HCC. PTEN, which antagonizes AKT signalling, is mutated in 5% of HCC, is frequently deleted, and downregulated in half of all HCC patients, thereby hyperactivating PI3K-AKT-mTOR signalling. In addition, in advanced HCC, resistance to Sorafenib has been found to be mediated through the activation of the PI3K pathway. Given the importance of INPP4B in regulating PI3K-AKT pathway, we hypothesize that INPP4B loss is the potential second hit that it required for progression of HCC to advanced, metastatic lesions. This presents exciting potential for the identification of a novel biomarker in HCC, which can be used to stratify patients according to disease prognosis and therapeutic intervention, which is critical for the success of patient treatment outcome. We aim to answer two important questions in the field: 1) Does INPP4B act as a tumour suppressor or oncogene in advanced, metastatic HCC? 2) Can INPP4B be used as a biomarker for patient stratification for the purpose of prognosis and therapeutic intervention? We aim to investigate the clinical correlation of INPP4B loss in stratified HCC patient samples through performing western blotting, immunohistochemistry and sequencing on FFPE patient samples from SGH. We will also determine the functional significance of INPP4B loss in the context of liver cancer cells through CRISPR knockdown and subsequent functional assays. Lastly, we want to establish a patient-derived xenograft (PDX) model of metastatic HCC with INPP4B loss, through which we can test for synthetic lethality and effective PI3K/AKT inhibitors.
kw: INPP4B, Hepatocellular Carcinoma, Precision drug targeting

title: Integrated Molecular Analysis of Cancers in Gynaecologic Oncology (IMAC-GO)
abs: Background: Genetic and molecular heterogeneity in cancer underpins the observed variations in patient outcomes. Hence, the ability to characterise the unique genetic and molecular features of each patient’s tumour will be a critical step to identifying the optimal therapeutic strategy for the individual. Aims: To provide and evaluate the impact of molecular profiling information on patients with gynaecological cancers by setting up and maintaining a platform for integrated molecular analysis of cancers in gynaecologic oncology (IMAC-GO) in patients who are candidates for molecular-targeted therapy/ biomarker-driven clinical trials, in order to identify potentially actionable mutations/ activated molecular pathways and mechanisms of drug resistance in gynaecological cancers.Hypothesis: •Molecular profiling will improve the outcome of novel targeted-agent treatment in clinical trials •Molecular profiling of paired samples (primary/recurrent and primary/metastatic) will provide new insights into mechanisms underlying drug resistance and metastasis in gynaecological cancers.Methodology: Patients who consent to participate in this study will have their tumour specimens, blood, and pleural or ascitic fluid collected. Molecular profiling of tumour cells will be performed using Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS), quantitative-PCR, fluorescent or chromogenic-in-situ-hybridisation (FISH/CISH), immunohistochemistry and/or other relevant techniques. Primary, metastatic and recurrent tumours will be profiled and compared to identify mechanisms of metastasis and drug-resistance. Clinical data to be collected include baseline patient and tumor characteristics, treatment regimen(s) administered, time on treatment(s), and survival. Progression free survival (PFS) and overall response rates (ORR) on matched targeted therapy based on molecular profiling will be used to assess the clinical impact of molecular profiling in these patients.Research significance: Characterising the genetic mechanisms and molecular pathways driving oncogenesis and tumour progression in different primary/ recurrent gynaecological cancers will enable differences in tumour behavior and optimisation of therapy to be addressed earlier, rather than a 'one size fits all' treatment approach, thus fulfilling the promise of personalised cancer medicine.
kw: Gynaecological, cancer

title: Novel therapeutic interventions to target GATA4-related pathways in hepatocellular carcinoma
abs: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the third commonest cause of cancer mortality worldwide. In 2007, the multi-targeting tyrosine kinase inhibitor sorafenib became the first FDA-approved systemic therapy for advanced HCC with modest overall survival (OS) benefit. This year (2017), regorefenib was reported to improve OS in sorafenib-treated advanced HCC. All other drugs tested have failed to improve on survival results in the past 10 years. HCC is partly caused by impaired terminal differentiation of hepatocyte in liver. We have identified a highly deleted candidate tumour suppressor gene GATA4 in HCC (68% deletion in TCGA and 44% in Singapore cohort), making GATA4 deletion more frequent than TP53 deletion and mutations. By time-of-flight cytometry (CyTOF), we confirmed an immunosuppressive microenvironment in GATA4-deficient HCC, including an abundance of CD4+ Foxp3+ Treg, M2-like macrophages, and exhausted CD8+ T cell. Our functional studies showed that GATA4 overexpression significantly downregulated CCL20 expression, normally highly upregulated in HCC. Tumoural GATA4 expression is also positively correlated with CEBPA and HNF4A. Functional analyses including CRISPR-mediated knockout prove that GATA4 acts upstream of CEBPA and HNF4A. We aim to 1) develop a novel spontaneous GATA4-deficiency HCC models and humanised HCC models to recapitulate GATA4-deficiency in human HCC, 2) test the combination of anti-CCL20 antibody and immune checkpoint inhibitors in the novel preclinical GATA4-deficient mouse models, followed by the mechanistic studies and biomarker studies of treatment responses, 3) testing the efficacy and investigate potential biomarkers and therapeutic outcome of MTL-CEBPA and MTL-HNF4A alone and in combination with checkpoint inhibitors in in vitro and novel in vivo models. Our key strategy is to elucidate mechanistic interactions in GATA4-deficient HCC within the ‘seed’ and with the ‘soil’ and how to therapeutically intervene to retard HCC oncogenesis by targeting the HCC or its microenvironment but likely by combination synergistic targeting of both.

title: Role of non-canonical activation of ?-catenin by PRL-3 phosphatase in Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML)
abs: The Wnt/?-catenin signaling pathway is aberrantly activated in leukemic stem cells (LSCs) and AML cells. However, the mechanistic basis for the dysregulation of ?-catenin is unclear. PRL-3 is an important mediator of leukemogenesis through its oncogenic phosphatase activity. Interestingly, in PRL3-overexpressing cells, we observed the nuclear accumulation of ?-catenin and transcription of downstream target genes, c-myc and cyclin-D1, both hallmarks of ?-catenin activation. Through SILAC-based phosphoproteomics, we identified Leo1 as a key substrate of PRL-3. Interestingly, Leo1 was reported as an interacting partner of ?-catenin. Based on these compelling evidence, we hypothesize a PRL3-Leo1-?-catenin regulatory axis in AML, which can possibly account for the observed activation of ?-catenin in a certain subset of AML patients. In the current proposal, we plan to perform an in-depth analysis of the PRL3-modulated Leo1 phosphosites. Through knowledge of the critical phosphosites, we will generate and characterize the Leo1 phospho-mutants. These mutants will be used in functional assays to assess their contribution towards PRL3-mediated oncogenesis. We also seek to determine whether these phosphosites played a role in the direct interaction between Leo1 and ?-catenin, and determine the mechanism of how the interaction activates the ?-catenin signalling pathway, for example, through the retention of ?-catenin in the nucleus, or prolonging the half-life of ?-catenin protein. Despite about 50% of AML primary samples displayed PRL-3 overexpression, therapeutics targeting PRL-3 has been a major hurdle. Therefore, if the PRL3-overexpressing cells depended on the aberrant signaling of ?-catenin to confer survival advantage, these cells can be selectively targeted through the inhibition of ?-catenin. Furthermore, ?-catenin is a promising drug target, with several small molecule inhibitors currently in clinical trials. Through the completion of this project, we will unravel a critical signaling pathway consisting of PRL3-Leo1-?-catenin, as well as propose clinical biomarkers and new avenues for targeted therapy in AML.
kw: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML), beta-catenin, PRL-3 phosphatase, SILAC phosphoproteomics, PAF1 complex, Leukemic stem cells (LSCs)

title: Functional characterization of ADAR1-mediated-RNA editing events in multiple myeloma (MM)
abs: Despite the emergence of novel therapies, the prognosis of multiple myeloma (MM) patients in the high-risk groups remains unfavourable. One of the high-risk features is the gain of chromosome 1q21 (1q21(amp)). RNA editing abnormalities have been implicated in various cancers, however, its significance in MM has never been studied. ADAR1 gene, encoding for the key enzyme for A-to-I RNA editing, is located within 1q21 locus. Herein, we hypothesize that ADAR1 is a potential critically deregulated gene in 1q21(amp) cases, conferring aberrant RNA editing activities. Our preliminary analyses on patient datasets revealed a close correlation between 1q21(amp) with ADAR1 expression level, with a gradual up-regulation of ADAR1 along the disease progression route. Importantly, high ADAR1 expression was found to be associated with a poorer overall survival in the patients. In vitro analyses revealed that ADAR1 harbours critical editing functions, manifested by the change in the A-to-I editing frequencies upon ADAR1 knockdown and overexpression. These interesting data sets the stage for further characterization of direct mechanisms of ADAR1 and RNA editing in MM. In this proposal, we aim to define the RNA editome landscape of MM and to delineate the critical function of a disrupted RNA editing phenomenon in driving myelomagenesis. We will utilize the availability of primary patient samples and human myeloma cell lines in our MM-cell bank to fulfil the proposed aims. RNA sequencing will be performed to characterize the RNA editome in patient samples and cell lines and to identify the critical ADAR1 targets in MM. Utilizing the in vitro and in vivo methods, we aim to study the oncogenic properties of ADAR1 and its specific edited target. We believe this study would help provide better insights into the poorly-defined molecular mechanism of this aggressive MM-subgroup and unveil novel therapeutic targets that potentially have broader relevance to other cancers.
kw: Multiple myeloma, RNA editing, ADAR, 1q21(amp), epigenetic

title: Investigating the in vivo dynamics of colorectal cancer dormancy and metastasis
abs: Cancer is the leading cause of death in Singapore, with colorectal cancer (CRC) being the most common cancer diagnosed in men and breast cancer most commonly diagnosed in women. For both CRC and breast cancers, a significant number of patients suffer from metastatic recurrence of the cancer many years even after surgical resection of the primary tumor and adjuvant chemotherapy. Recurrent metastatic disease can arise from dormant cancer cells that were disseminated to metastatic sites such as the liver and lungs are subsequently highly refractory to therapy, resulting in cancer-related mortality. The molecular mechanisms involved in tumor dormancy and disseminated cancer cells’ transition from dormancy to metastatic organ colonization are not well understood. We propose to 1) establish genetically barcoded, fluorescent-labeled patient-derived cancer cell populations and use them to 2) study the in vivo dynamics of cancer dormancy and metastasis using patient-derived xenograft (PDx) models of CRC metastasis. A barcoded cell-population in which individual cells are labeled with a unique DNA barcode will allow lineage tracing of disseminated cells and their progeny. 3) Using next- generating sequencing methods, genomic and transcriptomic profiles from lineages of disseminated cells, micro- and macro- metastases will be established and computational analysis performed to identify endogenous pathways that are activated during the natural progression of cancer metastasis from different disseminated cells in vivo. 4) Finally, we will shortlist pathways that can potentially be targeted to investigate proof-of-principle therapeutic intervention in preventing metastatic progression in our PDx models.
kw: cancer, metastasis, heterogeneity, xenograft, dormancy

title: Two is better than one – Her2 in combination with WBP2 improves anti-Her2 precision medicine in breast cancer
abs: Targeted therapies are beneficial in managing breast cancer (BC) heterogeneity. Her2-positive BC are treated routinely with trastuzumab(Herceptin). In the neo-adjuvant setting, anti-Her2 therapies produced complete pathological responses in only 30-40% of the patients. This reveals a critical gap: Her2 is the only approved biomarker for anti-Her2 therapy but alone, it is insufficient for achieving good response rate. Additional critical determinants of drug response are required for better stratification of patients for better response rate. Preliminary in vitro and in vivo data support WBP2 as one such determinant. Discovered in Lim’s lab as a novel BC oncogene, WBP2 has been shown to be a phosphorylation substrate of EGF/EGFR signaling, participate in ER and Wnt signaling. More recently, analysis of >200 clinical samples showed that high WBP2 expression in Her2-positive BC has worse prognosis than either alone – suggesting interaction between these 2 molecules. Coupled to the knowledge that Her2 heterodimerizes with EGFR, we will test the hypotheses that WBP2 is within the Her2 signaling network and aberrant WBP2 expression influences the response of Her2+ BC cells to anti-Her2 drugs including trastuzumab/Herceptin, lapatinib and pertuzumab through gain/loss-of-function studies using in vitro, xenograft, PDX models and clinical samples. We will also elucidate how WBP2 regulates response to trastuzumab at the molecular and cellular level to understand and overcome clinical resistance. WBP2 is indeed downstream of Her2 signaling. Overexpression of WBP2 sensitized BC cells to trastuzumab in vitro (2 times) and in xenografts (7 times). Our PDX model also supports the notion that WBP2 enhanced cellular response to trastuzumab. The study will impact precision medicine by establishing that WBP2 in combination with Her2 is a more powerful companion diagnostics for anti-Her2 neo-adjuvant therapy. In turn this will create value through an innovative immunodiagnostic product and accelerating commercialization that builds economy and improve clinical oncology performance.
kw: Her2, breast cancer, precision medicine, companion diagnostics, targeted therapeutics, WBP2 oncogene

title: Non-Hodgkin’s Lymphoma – Translating Discoveries in Genomic into Clinical Applications
abs: Non-Hodgkin’s Lymphoma (NHL) is a group of very heterogeneous lymphomas consist of both the B and T-cell subtypes. Precision medicine enabled through next-generation sequencing is gaining pace, but hampered by downstream validations (preclinical and clinical trial). To date, several subtypes of lymphoma have been sequenced and key driver genes have been identified. We have recently characterized the Monomorphic Epitheliotropic Intestinal T-cell lymphoma (MEITL), which is an aggressive intestinal disease with poor prognosis (Leukemia, 2016). Using whole-exome sequencing and gene expression data, we have discovered frequent alterations of the JAK-STAT and MEK-ERK signaling in MEITL and further demonstrated that primary MEITL cells are sensitive to inhibitors of both pathways. In addition, we have also found frequent dysregulation of histone modifier, especially functional loss of CREBBP in all 4 samples in our discovery cohort. Mutational loss of this gene has also been reported in the more common B-cell subtype. Excitingly, the synthetic lethal partner of CREBBP, EP300 was recently discovered and is targetable by small molecules. With the convincing preliminary data, we propose to: (1) determine the feasibility of targeting these oncogenic pathways in MEITL using the in vivo model that we have developed, (2) determine the efficacy and viability of targeting NHL harboring loss of function mutation in CREBBP and (3) determine the heterogeneity and decipher the mechanisms of drug resistant in NHL which will help us to strategize or tailor treatment, especially developing combinatorial treatment. This proposal will lead to potential novel strategy to treat MEITL which could quickly be implemented in clinical trial. The second aim open up novel therapeutic strategy which is at early stage of development targeting several subtypes of NHLs. Finally, understanding the heterogeneity of various NHLs might shed light on the mechanism of drug resistant.
kw: Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, JAK-STAT pathway, MEK-ERK pathway, Drug resistant, EP300, CREBBP

title: The Hypoxisome in Neuronal Resilience and Cell Death in Stroke
abs: Stroke is a major cause of morbidity and mortality. We have recently identified that hypoxia and cerebral ischemia activate five prominent signaling pathways (Notch-1, Pin1, NF-?B, HIF-1? and p53) that converge on a conserved DNA-associated nuclear multi-protein complex, the ‘hypoxisome’, which controls the expression and/or activation of genes that can determine the fate of neurons. We first identified Notch-1 as a novel and potent therapeutic target for the treatment of stroke. Notch-1 signaling is known to be involved in regulating NF-?B and HIF-1? activities. In 2011, we demonstrated that Notch-1 signaling endangers neurons after ischemic stroke by modulating the NF-?B, pro-death BH3-only protein, Bcl-2-interacting mediator of cell death (Bim), and caspase pathways. More recently, in 2013, we identified that Notch-1 and HIF-1? collaborate to engage pro-inflammatory and apoptotic signaling pathways in stroke. In 2015, we discovered that Pin1 regulates Notch stability and worsens brain damage in stroke. Our preliminary data shows that a Notch/p53 interaction is involved in transcriptional regulation of genes downstream of p53 and Notch to modify stroke severity. Our over-arching hypothesis is that the hypoxisome plays an important role following stroke. Specifically, (i) when ischemic injury is severe, the hypoxisome upregulates proteins that trigger and execute a neuronal death program, and (ii) during remodeling following ischemic stroke, the hypoxisome up-regulates adaptive stress response genes that promotes neuronal survival. The aims of the project are to:Aim 1: Identify the mechanism(s) responsible for hypoxisome-dependent activation of the cell death program, and understand how the hypoxisome directs inflammation and neuronal apoptosis in ischemic stroke. Aim 2. Elucidate the mechanism(s) underlying hypoxisome-dependent up-regulation of adaptive stress response genes encoding proteins that promotes neuronal survival during remodeling following stroke. Aim 3: Characterise hypoxisome involvement in the etiology of human stroke.
kw: Ischemic stroke, neuroprotection, cerebral ischemia, reperfusion, infarct, neurological deficit

title: Hippocampal networks as a target of, and remedy for, juvenile stress
abs: Exposure to stress in childhood (juvenile Stress, JS) is considered a major risk factor for developing psychopathologies later in life. Juvenile stress compromises the ability to establish hippocampus-dependent memory and has long-lasting effects on the ability to induce long-term synaptic potentiation (LTP) in the hippocampus. LTP is a sustained, activity-dependent enhancement in synaptic transmission that is thought to be a mechanism responsible for memory storage. Dysregulation of epigenetic mechanisms has been implicated in stress-related synaptic plasticity and memory impairment. Our preliminary data indicate that associative plasticity mechanisms such as synaptic tagging and capture (STC), substance P (SP) induced plasticity in CA2 hippocampal region and behavioural tagging are impaired in JS animals. In this context, we ask, 1) whether epigenetic mechanisms can regulate and re-establish plasticity and memory in juvenile stressed animals 2) To determine whether activating regulating metaplastic mechanisms via optogenetic tools can overcome the consequences of JS. We will use multi-electrode long-term electrophysiology, optogenetic, molecular biology and behavioural approaches to study the electrophysiological, biochemical and behavioural changes occurring in the hippocampus of JS animals. Our research may help clinicians for finding appropriate therapeutic targets to improve memory or at least prevent memory impairments that occur due to juvenile stress.
kw: Metaplasticity, Synaptic tagging and capture, PKMzeta, LTP, LTD

title: Unraveling PI3K p110 delta signaling plasticity towards next-generation anti-leukemia strategy
abs: One of the major breakthroughs in the treatment of leukemia is the development of Idelalisib, a small molecule inhibitor for Phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) p110 delta. In 2014, it was approved globally as a treatment for chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL), a disease previously deemed incurable. It is the first-in-class (PI3K inhibitor) that has been approved after more than a decade’s preclinical and clinical studies. Despite its exciting clinical success, there are still major caveats of Idelalisib-based treatment, including toxicity, high risk and adverse effects when used as first-line option or part of the combinatory therapy. Critically, CLL patients do not express mutations or display abnormal expression pattern in p110 delta, making it challenging to identify target patient through genetic means. In the proposed work here, we will try to fill an important knowledge gap in understanding the cellular mechanisms that could tune the PI3K activity independent of any mutation or overexpression of PI3K. Our hypothesis is that in immune cells that highly express p110 delta, there are unknown cellular mechanisms and factors that could specifically control and sense the level of p110 delta activation. Their identification could serve as novel nodes of intervention, reliable biomarkers to screen for potential p110 delta inhibitor-sensitive CLL patient, minimize the risk of drug resistance or adverse side effects as well as guide safer, targeted, combinatory cancer therapy. We propose that the unique oscillatory dynamics of p110 delta, which we are the first to discover in 2016, provides a novel platform to elucidate the feedback control in p110 delta activation. The experimental strategy combining frequency-dependent translation and ribosome profiling adds a critically missing cell and systems biology perspective to the current drug discovery workflow, which could have general implications in combating human diseases with poorly defined genetic basis.

title: Development of multiple serological platforms for differentiation of Zika and dengue virus infecctions
abs: Although it is not a totally new virus, the recent outbreaks and rapidglobal spread of Zika virus (ZIKV) has caught the internationalcommunity by surprise. There are many challenges in the response tothe ZIKV outbreaks internationally, and more recently in Singapore. Oneof them is the lack of a reliable serological diagnostic method. This ishighly important for ZIKV infection because most infected individualsdon’t develop clinical symptoms, hence will likely miss the narrow windowof laboratory diagnosis based on virus detection, and there is significantantibody cross reactivity between ZIKV and other flaviviruses, especiallydengue virus (DENV). With the increasing evidence linking ZIKV infectionand neurological disorders such as microcephaly and Guillain-BarreSyndrome (GBS), there is an urgent need for serodiagnosis of ZIKVinfection, especially among pregnant women. Traditional serologicaltests, mostly ELISA based, using various ZIKV antigens haveencountered major problem of cross reactivity with antibodies from otherflavivirus infection. Here we proposed to address this major gap andurgent need using multiple new technology platforms which address themain cross reactivity issue by replacing the conventional one-antigenone-reading antibody test format with a multiplex format which will givecomparative readings on multiple antigens. For this study, we will focuson our development of differentiation serological tests for ZIKV andDENV specifically, but the same strategy and technological platforms canbe extended to other viruses in future. One of the approaches employedin this proposal will target ZIKV infection-specific anti-host antibodieswhich will not only serve as novel biomarkers for serological diagnosis,but may also shed new light to better understanding of ZIKVpathogenesis.

title: Precision Rheumatology International Platform (PRIP)
abs: Unmet needs:• Lack of a Translational Rheumatology platform where Molecular Immunologic and Functional Genomicsare seamlessly integrated with Clinical Studies.• Precision Rheumatology should inform early clinical development by identifying predictors andsurrogates of efficacy and toxicity.• Precision Rheumatology should provide the foundation for stratifying current therapeutic approaches.• Precision Rheumatology should be the catalyzer for target identification, lead development and first-inmantesting.Hypotheses:The immune microenvironment: a) determines pathogenic pathways where damage occurs; b) acts as aninterface with the systemic immune compartments, shaping pathogenically relevant immune responses.Understanding of this interface will provide the necessary knowledge to meet the unmet needs.Components and Objectives:A translational immunology and a translational clinical component, organized in an international network(Duke-NUS/SingHealth/KKH/A*STAR (Singapore), Queen Mary University (London), University MedicalCenter (Utrecht), which will share the same clinical research protocols and will integrate technologies into acogent platform.1: To develop a Standardized Cytometry Platform suitable for clinical studies in humans by: a) optimizationof barcoding multiplexing capabilities; b) standardization of assessment of true signal intensity vsbackground by use of appropriate isotope controls; c) design, development and validation of CyTOF andFACS panels; d) development of a database of Cytometry data from a cohort of healthy controls, includingPediatrics; e) development of CyTOF tools to define Class I and Class II restricted antigen-speciifc T cells; f)harmonization of the procedures into an automated work flow governed by an ad-hoc algorithm.2: To optimize and standardize the Immunomics work flow (from multidimensional signatures to single cellmolecular analyses, exploitation of multidimensional big data). To synchronize the technologies within theNetwork.3: To integrate into a cogent Network translational clinical research capabilities at the various sites.4: To perform a validation study.

title: DYNAMO: Diabetes studY in Nephropathy And other Microvascular cOmplications
abs: Diabetic nephropathy (DN) is a devastating complication of diabetes causing significant morbidity, mortality and human suffering. In Singapore, the incidence of DN as a cause of end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) is among the highest in the world. Despite the substantial public health burden associated with DN, its molecular pathogenesis is poorly understood and no new drugs for DN have been introduced in nearly 20 years. Within the population of diabetics, only a subset develops DN indicating a strong familial contribution to this risk. Nonetheless, identification of genetic variants controlling DN susceptibility has been difficult. Furthermore, no reliable biomarkers exist to stratify high-risk patients before the onset of clinically apparent diabetic kidney disease.Capitalizing on a confluence of world-class expertise in research on diabetes and its complications in Singapore, the Diabetes studY of Nephropathy And other Microvascular cOmplications (DYNAMO) plans to employ multiple experimental approaches to identify new mechanistic pathways in DN, discover and validate new targets for DN treatment, and define novel biomarkers and strategies to stratify DN risk within the T2D population. These approaches include human genetics, targeted and non-targeted metabolomics, animal modeling, and urinary exosomes studies.DYNAMO also takes advantage of several established, well-characterized Singaporean patient cohorts, consisting of nearly 30,000 individuals with stored serum, genetic samples, urine, and retinal photographs for analyses. When sample sizes are limited, DYNAMO has assembled an international collaborative network to allow for the integration of data with the largest human genetics studies ongoing in the world.The strategic focus of our LCG incorporates cutting edge technologies to take a systems biology approach to target and biomarker discovery and validation. The work is based on world class science, substantial track record and prior work of the participating investigators, and a clear focus on unmet needs for DN in Singapore and globally.

title: Finding Gems in Disguise: Novel Peptides and Hormones from Long Non-Coding RNAs Significance, Utility and Therapeutic Potential
abs: As the frontier of genomic research advances, deep sequencing and new annotation techniques are rapidly expanding the size of the “functional genome”. While the 20,000 known protein coding genes account for only 2% of the genome, current evidence suggest that up to as much as 70% of the genome is actively transcribed. What was traditionally thought as “junk” intergenic DNA has now been shown to code for thousands of RNA molecules with diverse functions, of which long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) make up the majority. However, “non-coding” might in fact a misnomer for some lncRNAs. Using a technique known as ribosome footprinting, which detects regions of the transcriptome undergoing active translation, lncRNAs in multiple species appear to contain small open reading frames (lsORFs) that encode short peptides (<100 amino acids). Although lsORF translation might not generally apply to all lncRNAs, nor always result in functional protein, recent validated examples of bona fide lncRNA-encoded peptides demonstrate that in some cases productive lncRNA translation does occur. For instance, we recently discovered a secreted peptide hormone ELABELA (ELA) encoded by a lsORF that is required for embryonic development, pluripotency, pregnancy and blood pressure control. LncRNAs are therefore a potentially rich and unexplored repository of new peptides and peptide hormones with diagnostic and therapeutic utility. Using a combination of ribosome profiling, RNA-seq and peptidomics, I aim to mine the lncRNA transcriptome for bona fide lncRNA-encoded peptides and peptide hormones that are associated with human disease. I will also address the fundamental question of whether lncRNAs with lsORFs toggle between coding and non-coding functions, and elucidate the specific mechanisms governing the switch between these alternate states. lsORF peptides, when found, will expand the size of the functional proteome, provide new hormones as therapeutic targets, and uncover new modes of genome regulation.

title: Translating ‘omics' into a stratified approach for prevention of type 2 diabetes: TOAST-T2D
abs: Type-2 diabetes (T2D) is a major public health problem, driven by a global epidemic of overweight and obesity. My recent studies identify DNA methylation, a key epigenetic regulator of genomic function, as a novel, independent predictor of future T2D. DNA methylation improves prediction of T2D compared to conventional approaches, and in particular enables identification of normoglycaemic individuals at high risk of T2D. I will build on these state-of-the-art observations to determine whether DNA methylation and other molecular biomarkers can be translated to clinical benefit, to inform stratified approaches for pharmacologic intervention and / or lifestyle modification for prevention of T2D in Singapore. I will first replicate and extend knowledge of the relationship of DNA methylation with T2D amongst Singapore Chinese (N=1000, 500 with incident T2D). This will include fine-mapping the epigenetic association signals at the identified genetic loci, to determine the set of methylation markers that best predict T2D. I will develop and validate molecular risk scores comprising DNA methylation and/or molecular measures for prediction of T2D, amongst independent samples from Singapore, South Asia and Europe (N=6,000, 3,000 with incident T2D). Using a randomised clinical trial, I will then determine whether pharmacologic intervention and intensive lifestyle modification reduce risk of diabetes amongst individuals (N=1,500) who are normoglycaemic, but predicted to be at high risk of T2D (>10% per annum) based on molecular risk score. I will use the data generated to assess the incremental value, and health economic implications of the molecular approach to T2D risk stratification and prevention, compared to conventional strategies. Results of this research will determine whether molecular information can be exploited by the health sector, and by the pharmaceutical and medical diagnostic industries, for personalised strategies to promote health, and reduce the clinical and economic burden of T2D in Singapore and elsewhere in the world.

title: Increasing the Uptake of Influenza and Pneumococcal Vaccines among Chronic Disease Patients through General Practitioner Clinics
abs: Influenza and pneumococcal disease contribute considerably to hospitalisation and mortality in the elderly, especially those with chronic diseases such as diabetes mellitus, cardiovascular and respiratory diseases. While recommended vaccines can reduce disease burden, vaccine uptake remains very low in Singapore, with less than 10% of elderly appropriately vaccinated for either disease.Improving vaccine uptake rates requires robust health promotion strategies to address barriers to vaccination, and an effective means of delivering these to the community. This could be effected through private sector primary care clinics, which are highly accessible in Singapore. An intervention bundle we piloted in one clinic comprised physician reminders and patient-targeted posters and brochures. Influenza and pneumococcal vaccine rates both increased by >30% over the baseline, although half of eligible patients remained unvaccinated. There is thus scope to devise a more effective intervention bundle and demonstrate its efficacy through a more robust and generalisable study design.Our study aims to evaluate the efficacy of an intervention bundle deployed in general practice clinics to promote influenza and pneumococcal vaccine uptake among elderly chronic disease patients. The intervention bundle components will be based off previous qualitative research findings amongst community-dwelling elderly on vaccinations (by the PI, study already completed), as well as our previous pilot programme. It will include visual cues, reminder slips for attending physicians, financial incentives for patients, and vaccine counselling by a trained healthcare staff. The intervention will be implemented in a two-arm cluster randomised crossover trial in up to 30 primary care clinics. Control arm clinics will receive no interventions. Clinics will be randomised into either of the two arms for a period of 3 months, followed by a washout of 1 month before a crossover is performed. We will subsequently compare vaccination rates during intervention and control periods to provide evidence for efficacy.

title: Forecasting the health and medical expenditure of the future elderly – A Future Elderly Model for Singapore
abs: Policymakers in Singapore are facing one of the fastest aging populations in the world, as well as an increasing burden of chronic diseases as lifestyles change. Healthcare use and cost is affected not only by these factors but multiple others as well, including the expansion of financial support under Medishield Life and the Pioneer Generation Package (for the eligible cohort). How will these trends and other potentially still unforeseen economic, technological, demographic and social changes affect the burden of care, financing needs and optimal resource allocation in the future? To answer these questions, we propose to construct a Future Elderly Model (FEM) ,a dynamic Markov micro-simulation model that predicts future health status and medical costs elderly population of Singapore up to 2050. FEM-Singapore will simulate individual health states and associated expenditures that evolve over time, accounting for Singapore-specific trends in background drivers such as aging, obesity, diseases and disability. We will estimate the health transition matrix and associated outcomes for the FEM model for the Singapore context using existing population cohorts matched to administrative data on medical claims, and then forecast the future health and medical spending of Singapore’s population aged 55+ up to 2050 under a baseline scenario assuming the persistence of current trends . We will also model and evaluate additional different policy-relevant hypothetical scenarios including emergence of new technologies, increase in smoking cessation, reduction in obesity and reduction of disability trends, and draw comparisons with a range of other international dynamic micro-simulation models e.g. for Japan and Taiwan that are compatible with FEM and relevant to Singapore. FEM-Singapore thus offers the potential to answer pressing questions for Singapore’s health system as well as to make a significant wider contribution to the study of aging in developed Asia.
kw: Elderly, Costs, Economics, Simulation, Modeling, Technology

title: Radiobiology Investigations into Cancer Therapy using High Energy Protons
abs: Proton beam therapy is a new form of cancer therapy, where a high energy proton beam is used to target cancerous tumours with high accuracy, thereby minimizing damage to surrounding healthy tissue. However, little is known about the interaction between high energy protons and cancer cells at the cellular, subcellular and molecular level, or the fundamental differences between proton therapy and conventional X-ray radiotherapy. Our aim therefore is to study the physical interactions of high energy protons with biological cells as compared with X-ray therapy, and investigate the resulting changes in gene expression and signaling responses in both single cells and small animal tumours. We hypothesize that the mechanism of cellular and molecular damage caused by protons would be different from X-rays and therefore the knowledge gained by carrying out this research will be used to improve the efficacy of cancer therapy using protons. The proton/cell interactions will be carried out using the new proton microbeam radiobiology facility in the Centre for Ion Beam Applications (CIBA), Dept of Physics, NUS, and the resulting biological and signaling responses will be investigated by research groups in the National Cancer Centre of Singapore (NCCS), Duke-NUS Medical School, the Dept of Pharmacology, NUS. We also aim to investigate translational benefits: For example; (a) it is known that the hypoxic environment found in the centre of tumours render cancer cells radio-resistant: Is targeting hypoxic cells more efficient when using protons? (b) Is the damage induced in radio-resistant tumour-initiating cells (eg cancer stem cells (CSCs), known to be responsible for metastatic cancer as well as cancer recurrence) more efficient when using protons? (c) Can we increase radio-sensitivity to protons in cancer cells using known drug compounds (eg HDAC inhibitors etc.) and nanoparticles? (d) Are such sensitizers also effective in augmenting proton beam therapy in small animal models?

title: Development of Mosquito-Borne Infectious Disease Diagnostic Devices with New Antibody Alternatives
inst: IBB - Institute of Bioengineering and Bioimaging
abs: Simple and rapid diagnostics are highly desired for effective management of infectious diseases. However, existing rapid diagnostic platforms are complicated by the high cost, low stability, and low specificity of antibodies that are used as the binding agent to recognize the pathogen targets. Nucleic acids-based aptamer is a preferred antibody alternative that can overcome the drawbacks of antibodies. Aptamers have high specificity and low immunogenicity, and they can be chemically synthesized and modified in large scale with low cost. However, conventional DNA/RNA aptamers have relatively low binding affinity. In this study, we propose to incorporate our unnatural bases into the aptamers. The unnatural bases are hydrophobic, which gives rise to aptamers with extremely higher binding affinity and specificity. We will generate unnatural base aptamers using the SELEX process and a customized library of DNA oligonucleotides with unnatural bases. We also propose several novel approaches to generate new types of hybrid ligands by combining the improved SELEX method (DL-SELEX) and high-throughput peptide aptamer generation developed at IBN. By doing so, we would be able to increase the success rate of finding unnatural base aptamers or hybrid aptamers targeting proteins/antigens and antibodies for dengue, Zika and Chikungunya. The selected aptamers will be used as the binding agent for both paper-based rapid diagnostics and PCR-based molecular diagnostics. The focus will be placed on rapid paper-based assay, whereby a pair of aptamers will be used to recognize the target antigens such as dengue and Zika NS1 proteins or the IgM and IgG antibodies derived from patients infected with dengue, Zika and Chikungunya. One aptamer will be immobilized on the lateral flow test strip, and the other aptamer will be conjugated to gold nanoparticles. In the presence of the target, the two aptamers will form a sandwich structure and generate a colorimetric readout. For PCR-based molecular diagnostics, the aptamer will be conjugated to magnetic particles and capture, isolate and concentrate pathogens for improved detection sensitivity.

title: Integration of Electrically Driven Plasmonic Components in High Speed Electronics
abs: The microelectronics industry is moving to new technologies (e.g., system-on-chips, 2.5D and 3D Si integrated circuits, SFQ circuits, or quantum) for which energy efficient interconnects with a broad bandwidth are needed. Traditional interconnects are too slow and photonic interconnects are too large. Plasmonics, unlike photonics, makes it possible to confine and manipulate light (in the form of plasmons) at the metal-dielectric interfaces well below the diffraction limit. Thus, plasmons have in principle the best of both worlds: plasmonic interconnects are small but have the speed of optical elements. For applications in electronics it is a prerequisite to excite and detect plasmons by electrical means, and to demonstrate efficient plasmonic waveguiding. Over the last 4 years, under the CRP program which ends in 2016, we have demonstrated prototype devices that efficiently excite and detect propagating surface plasmon polaritons in plasmonic interconnects. These devices are based on tunnelling junctions where tunnelling charge carriers excite plasmons in one of the electrodes that simultaneously functions as a plasmonic wave guide. These tunnelling junctions convert an electrical signal directly into a plasmonic signal (i.e., so-called plasmonic-electronic transducers) without the need for intermediate steps involving photon generation/detection. The major objective of the current proposal is to integrate the plasmonic-electronic transducers with CMOS (in collaboration with IMEC) and SFQ (in collaboration with Hypres, Inc.) based technologies. We aim to replace global/intermediate interconnects that are currently the bottle-necks in information processing and limit data transport speeds such as I/O pins or interconnects that connect processors in system-on-chip or 3D integrated circuits. A second objective is to expand our tool-box and develop active plasmonic-electronic components including an electrically driven plasmonic signal amplifier, or introduce gain media, to compensate for plasmonic losses. We also propose strategies to improve our devices from a materials science perspective and investigate the plasmonic properties of industry grade metal oxides and ceramics to find the best balance between plasmon confinement and propagation.

title: Engineering the Next Generation Ceramic Membranes for Water and Wastewater Treatment
abs: Ceramic membranes for water and wastewater treatment have been demonstrated to outperform the polymeric counterparts in mechanical, chemical and thermal stability, and therefore able to achieve much longer life at reduced maintenance and overall cost while producing high quality water. They are becoming the main competitor for the commonly used polymeric membranes. In Singapore, for example, part of the water treatment system in the Choa Chu Kang Water Works is being upgraded with ceramic membranes, which will have a daily capacity of 40 million gallons when completed in 2018. To make ceramic membranes the game changer, we will develop the next generation ceramic membranes by addressing the bottleneck issues, including the membrane flux, selectivity, antifouling and reduction in production cost. For this objective, we will establish a newly engineered mesoporous gradient configuration and conical-shaped pores, in contrast to the widely used asymmetric structure with discrete double/triple layers. This will be achieved by successfully developing a novel fabrication technique of effectively combing nano-particles and templated sol-gel processes, which will offer a lowered production cost because some of the expensive chemical precursors will be replaced by the less expensive nanoparticles. The combination of mesoporous gradient and conical-shaped pores will deliver high flux, make the internal mesopores fouling-resistant, and achieve effective backflow operation for de-fouling. The elimination of the unwanted interfaces in the asymmetric membrane will improve the key mechanical properties and therefore life expectance. To further mitigate the surface fouling of ceramic membranes, we will investigate a surface micro-patterning approach, which has been demonstrated successful for polymeric membranes. To ensure the success of this program, we will take a holistic approach, experimental works complemented by simulation studies, by a highly multidisciplinary team consisting of top experts in ceramic fabrication, water and wastewater treatment and dynamic modeling, in close collaboration with industry partner.

title: Understanding TERT Promoter Reactivation: Key for Making Cancer Cell Specific Telomerase Inhibitors
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Since the enzyme telomerase (TERT) is activated and essential for growth of almost all human cancers, blocking its enzymatic function has been attempted by many academic labs and pharmaceutical companies as this might cure most human malignancies. Inhibitors of TERT indeed are the elusive magic bullet in cancer therapy. But none of the inhibitors designed to inhibit TERT enzymatic activity have been successful in making it to the clinic because 1) these direct enzymatic inhibitors of TERT or its partners are not effective in completely inhibiting cancer promoting effects of TERT because the TERT protein has non-enzymatic functions that also promote cancer and the enzymatic inhibitors do not block these non-canonical roles of TERT, 2) they also inhibit TERT activity in stem cells, which require continued high levels of TERT enzyme, causing severe toxicity. Hence, while TERT is recognized as a key target, some inhibitors despite having strong drug potential in terms of efficacy are unsuccessful in the clinic. Imeltestat, touted as the blockbuster telomerase inhibitor from a major pharma called Geron, showed promising results in the laboratory but failed to progress beyond early phase clinical trials in 2015. This is the end of the road for telomerase “enzymatic” inhibitors. We propose a disruptive technology based on new evidence generated in the last 2 years that TERT synthesis in cancer-cells (unlike in stem cells) is mediated by 2 cancer-specifc mutations in its promoter. This allows blocking TERT synthesis specifically in cancer cells and, by blocking its synthesis, we can target both the enzymatic/non-enzymatic cancer promoting functions of TERT. The objective of this research proposal is to comprehensively • identify key molecules and signalling pathways that specifically synthesize TERT in cancer-cells and not in normal stem cells. • develop chemical inhibitors that selectively target cancer-cell specific activators of TERT identified via these assays.

title: Green and Sustainable Pharmaceutical Manufacturing via Biocatalysis
abs: Biocatalysis is a useful tool for green and sustainable pharmaceutical manufacturing. In this project we aim to develop a multidisciplinary and integrated program on biocatalysis to promote and speed up biocatalysis application in pharmaceutical industry. Together with our industrial partners (GSK, Pfizer, Lonza), we will tackle several key challenges in biocatalysis development, directly address the industries’ needs, and actively explore commercialization possibility. We plan to develop fast enzyme evolution methods to engineer new enzymes with desired properties for target reactions. Our methods are based on microfluidics with generic high-throughput activity and selectivity screening assays, complemented with in silico prediction. The developed methods will significantly speed up enzyme development in both industries and academia. We plan to develop new enzymes with diverse substrate scope and desired selectivity for green oxidations and enantioselective reductive aminations which are two key reaction types in pharmaceutical manufacturing that are used but need better and greener methods. By using conventional and, late on, our newly developed fast evolution methods, we will be able to obtain new enzymes with diverse substrate scope, high activity, and desired selectivity for green oxidations and reductive aminations, to provide with better and greener technologies to replace the existing toxic chemical methods in pharmaceutical manufacturing and develop new syntheses. This program will also develop research capability and train workforce in biocatalysis for Singapore’s pharmaceutical industry, which could help meet future manufacturing challenges and bring Singapore to a leading position in green manufacturing.

title: Beyond surviving colorectal cancer: how cancer survivors can influence the attitudes of their family members towards screening and play a role to support those with cancer
abs: AIMS To determine: 1. Screening rates and barriers amongst the first degree relatives (FDRs) and spouses of patients with colorectal cancer (CRC) and if tailored intervention could increase their adoption of screening modalities 2. Quality of life (QoL) of CRC patients through the first 18 months following their diagnosis 3. Feasibility of a survivorship program for CRC survivors to support new CRC patients in their initial stages of treatment to improve their QoL. HYPOTHESES 1. Screening rates amongst the FDRs and spouses of patients with CRC are suboptimal and tailored interventions can improve their screening rates. 2. Patients with CRC have poor QoL in the earlier stages of their treatment, and their QOL would worsen with additional treatment 3. A survivorship program is feasible and may improve the QoL of new CRC patients. METHODOLOGY The study will be conducted at the various hospitals across Singapore with a recruitment target of 300 patients, 150 spouses and 100 FDRs. All patients with CRC will be approached upon diagnosis and the QoL instruments would be administered at various timepoints over the subsequent 18 months. A randomized trial to contact the FDRs would be performed while spouses would be recruited during the patientsÆ appointments with oncologists. Barriers towards screening will be ascertained and a randomized trial to determine if tailored interventions targeting cost, and/or logistical barriers would improve their adoption of screening modalities will be performed. Once the QoL of the CRC patients has reached pre-operative levels, they would be invited to join a survivorship program to assist and guide new CRC patients to cope with treatment during the initial phases. SIGNIFICANCE OF THE STUDY This study will determine what interventions could improve the screening rates amongst the FDRs and Spouses and if CRC survivors could improve the QoL of new CRC patients.

title: Assessing Progression to Type 2 Diabetes (APT-2D): A Prospective Cohort Study Expanded from BRITE-SPOT (Biobank and Registry for StratIfication and Targeted IntErventions in the SPectrum Of Type 2 Diabetes)
abs: The Bio-bank and Registry for StratIfication and Targeted intErventionsin the Spectrum Of Type 2 Diabetes (BRITE-SPOT) aims to build a majorresource that can support a diverse range of research intended toimprove the prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of T2D. We hypothesize that there are distinctbiomarkers in circulation that reflect the underlying mechanistic pathwaysspecific to disease stage and reflect different trajectories in T2Dprogression. Characterization of subgroup-specific markers will facilitateefforts towards more targeted, effective interventions to improveoutcomes for people with, and at risk for, T2D.

title: Development of a quality of life scale in English and Chinese for family caregivers of patients with advanced cancers in Singapore
abs: “If you don’t measure it, you can’t improve it”, said an Institute ofMedicine report on caring for patients with life-threatening illnesses andtheir families. Assessment of quality of life of caregivers is an importantpart of care for patients with advanced cancers. Yet, its practice is limitedin Singapore and Asia. Our recent qualitative research in Singaporedemonstrated substantial differences in quality of life concerns betweenSingaporean caregivers of patients with advanced cancers and theircounterparts in western societies. There is a shortage of validated qualityof life assessment scales for caregivers in Singapore.This study aims to develop and validate English and Chinese versions ofa user-friendly quality of life measurement scale for assessment of familycaregivers of patients with advanced cancers. A secondary aim is toestablish the measurement equivalence between the English andChinese versions.In phase 1 of this study we will develop an initial version of ameasurement scale (in English and Chinese) based on the findings fromour recent qualitative study in Singapore. This will ensure that the scalecontents are locally relevant. We will conduct cognitive interviews toensure clarity and usability and to refine the initial scale. In phase 2, wewill conduct a survey of caregivers to quantitatively assess the individualand collective characteristics of the scale items, including factor structureand measurement equivalence between the English and Chinese items.The scales will be modified according to the results, including theremoval of items with limited or overlapping information contents, so asto keep the scales as short and user-friendly as possible. Phases 1 and 2will involve 24 and 300 family caregivers, respectively.The proposed research will facilitate quality improvement programs andresearch on effectiveness of interventions to improve health careoutcomes among family caregivers.

title: Developmental pathways to health and disease: metabolic, neurodevelopmental and related outcomes
abs: The TCR flagship programme in metabolic disease, awarded in 2008, focuses on developmental pathways that affect health outcomes across the population. In this renewal, we address developmental components of obesity, metabolic disease, and neurodevelopment that have major public health and economic importance in Asia and globally.We have to date:•Established the GUSTO birth cohort investigating how conditions of early life induce epigenetic changes that, in turn, associate with specific developmental outcomes. This cohort leveraged substantial nutritional industry co-funding and energized Singapore’s thrust in nutritional sciences.•Established a non-human primate (NHP) platform for related studies.• Deeply phenotyped adult males at risk of insulin resistance. This platform has now leveraged national and industry co-funding to become an independent programme outside this renewal. •Developed extensive capacity in translational and applied.epigeneticsGUSTO is, globally, one of the most intensively studied perinatal cohorts and is unique in its repeated DNA sampling of infants, permitting analysis of the human epigenome longitudinally from birth. This allows an assessment of how the perinatal environment affects subsequent metabolic, neurodevelopmental and other phenotypes. Over the next 5 years, more sophisticated analyses of epigenotype–phenotype relationships become possible as the children age. Because it is now evident that the early embryonic period is a critical time for epigenetic reprogramming in response to maternal signals, we plan a new preconception cohort, GUSTO-Mum, based on our extant infrastructure, to investigate this potentially important clinical window. Proof-of-concept studies that inform potential clinical interventions will continue in our NHP platform. These studies build on our established position as leaders in understanding the biology of developmental programming of non-communicable diseases and its translational implications. The programme is designed to develop public health, clinical and commercially-valuable interventions within the context of expanding commercial partnerships and building multidisciplinary translational research capacity in Singapore.

title: Phase II study of Intravenous Vinorelbine in Patients with Relapsed Platinum Resistant or Refractory C5 High Grade Serous, Endometrioid, or Undifferentiated Primary Peritoneum, Fallopian Tube or Ovarian Cancer (VIP)
abs: It has been difficult to progress beyond platinum-based therapy for the treatment of ovarian cancer (OC) because OC is still largely treated as a single entity. A number of sub-classifications of the most common OC histiotype – high-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSC) suggest that more specific therapeutic approaches may be useful. Four molecular subtypes of HGSC – C1, C2, C4 and C5 which correlate with clinical outcome have been validated. The C5 subtype, comprises about 20% of HGSC, is associated with a poor outcome and potential oncogenic drivers have been identified. Recent preclinical experiments demonstrated vinorelbine targeted C5 subtype more effectively compared to the other subtypes. Several phase II trials of vinorelbine in recurrent OC have shown variable response rates of 3 – 29%, however, previous studies have involved “allcomers” and there has never been a trial involving patient selection based on pure HGSC and biomarkers of response. Our aim is to determine if targeting treatment based on the C5 molecular subtype with oral vinorelbine improves response rates and progression free survival. This open label phase II trial is a collaboration between Singapore and Australia for patients with platinum resistant or refractory C5 high-grade serous, high grade endometrioid or undifferentiated ovarian, primary peritoneal and fallopian tube cancer. A total of 36 patients with confirmed C5 HGSC based on the molecular classifier developed by the NATA accredited Bowtel Lab will be recruited and treated with 60mg/m2 oral vinorelbine until the appearance of significant treatment-related toxicity ordisease progression. Dose modifications will be made based on a proforma. Simon’s Optimal two-stage design will be employed with a hypothesis of response rate <10% based on historical data; and the alternative hypothesis of response rate ?30% in patients with C5 HGSC following treatment with vinorelbine.

title: Zika Virus in Pregnancy in Singapore - A Multi-Centre Prospective National Longitudinal Study
abs: Zika virus (ZIKV) infection has recently been named as a public health emergency by the World Health Organisation in light of its possible association with fetal central nervous system malformations as well as possible association with Guillain-Barre syndrome. At current, further evidence is still needed to establish a definite causal link between these associations. Evidence on serology testing for Zika infection in the local population of Singapore is also lacking. In addition, there are currently no drugs to treat nor vaccines to prevent acquisition of the Zika virus. This study thus aims to study the immune response to the virus infection to better understand the interplay between the virus and the pregnant host immune system. This might give rise to vaccine or therapeutic strategies to prevent or fight an outbreak in Singapore and to better specific treatments for infected people. The study will also allow us to evaluate the impact of Zika infection on pregnancies in terms of fetal malformations by following these pregnancies up antenatally and in the neonatal period. Knowledge from this study will therefore help to add to the existing limited amount of information in the literature, and further help to establish the presence or absence of a link between ZIKV and fetal CNS malformations.
