title: The Economics of Childhood Obesity
abs: Specific Aims & HypothesisChildhood obesity is a rising global epidemic – since the past decade, with few exceptions the prevalence of childhood overweight and obesity has been rising in almost all countries for which data is available (Wang et al 2006). This proposal will focus on the relationship between childhood obesity and the economic environment in Singapore, with the following specific aims: Aim 1: Assess lifetime economic costs attributable to childhood obesity for a Singaporean child•We hypothesize that over a lifetime, estimates of both medical and nonmedical economic costs are significantly different for obese children, when compared to children of normal weight. Aim 2: Project the likely burden of childhood obesity in Singapore in the future adult population under various scenarios, using an existing micro-simulation demographic model of Singapore, DEMOS. •We hypothesize that at the population level, given existing trends in childhood obesity, the macroeconomic impact of childhood obesity will be significant and increasing over time. Aim 3: Evaluate the contribution of economic factors to childhood obesity by combining existing longitudinal data on children and families from a unique ongoing birth cohort study from Singapore with a new and innovative data collection effort focused on socioeconomic factors to investigate the economic drivers of childhood obesity.•We hypothesize that, controlling for confounding factors, low socioeconomic status is a significant risk factor for childhood obesity. •We further hypothesize that economic resource constraints have direct negative effects on childhood obesity due to differences in the availability of healthy foods and facilities for physical activity, as well as indirect negative effects on childhood obesity due to increased maternal stress, parental attention and childcare arrangements
kw: childhood obesity, economics, cost-effectiveness, socioeconomic determinants

title: Delineating novel targets for direct megakaryocyte lineage priming in healthy and malignant hematopoietic stem cells
abs: A balanced generation of platelets and mature megakaryocytes (Mk) from bone marrow (BM) hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPC) is crucial for healthy hemostasis. Generation of platelets/Mks must also meet demands during stress hematopoietic states which efficiency determines the clinical outcomes of BM transplantation, chemotherapy and inflammatory diseases. Recently, single cell-based analysis on cell heterogeneity in HSPCs has re-defined the classical hematopoietic hierarchy through the identification of early and direct pathways of Mk-lineage commitment. Nonetheless, the physiological significance of such de-novo lineage commitment pathway, along with the precise combination of surface markers to identify Mk-lineage committed HSPCs is still not well understood. While the close relationship of hematopoietic stem cells (HSC) and Mks renders difficulty to distinguish these two cell populations, such relation also suggests that HSCs may be manipulated with ease towards Mk lineage. Studying the mechanism of Mk-lineage priming will thus provide insights into enhancing the production of Mks from HSCs for the treatment of thrombocytopenia. Investigating direct Mk-lineage priming in acute megakaryoblastic leukemia (AMKL) leukemic stem cells may delineate the pathophysiology of the disease and serve as a treatment target for differentiation induction therapy. Using classic experimental hematology methods (flow cytometric analysis, BM transplantation assay, immunohisto-/cyto- chemistry) along with novel single cell based genomic and proteomic approaches, we plan to investigate the mechanism and the physiological relevance of early Mk-lineage priming in HSCs. Our research aims to (1) identify the mechanism of how HSCs are directly primed to Mk-lineage differentiation and (2) identify novel molecules involved in the transformation of HSCs into AMKL leukemic clones. Outcomes of our research will provide cues that will accelerate ex vivo and in vivo production of Mks for the treatment of thrombocytopenia and related diseases along with the identification of novel targets for the treatment of AMKL
kw: hematopoiesis, stem cell, megakaryocyte, acute megakaryoblastic leukemia

title: Singapore Young Dementia Cohort Study (SYNC): Longitudinal evaluation of clinical and neuroimaging markers in Frontotemporal Dementia (SYNC-FTD)
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Worldwide, frontotemporal dementia (FTD) is the second most common cause of young-onset dementia (dementia occurring before the age of 65). FTD has 3 clinical variants – behavioural variant (bvFTD) in two-thirds of subjects presenting with behavioural and personality change, and two language variants known as semantic variant primary progressive aphasia (svPPA) and non-fluent variant primary progressive aphasia (nfvPPA). Behavioural symptoms are frequently diagnosed as mid-life schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, as memory impairment is absent in early stages of bvFTD. This highlights the need for improved awareness of bvFTD amongst the public, healthcare professionals, and researchers in this region. This study will be looking primarily at the behavioural variant of FTD in a longitudinal manner. We aim to perform detailed clinical characterization, neuropsychological and socio-emotional testing, as well as advanced neuroimaging (including diffusion tensor imaging and functional studies) to understand anatomical-functional connectivity patterns in bvFTD and investigate its utility as a potential biomarker. The longitudinal changes in clinical and neuroimaging patterns will be correlated with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) findings to provide insight into the pathophysiology of bvFTD. Subjects will be grouped according to those who fulfill international criteria for possible (fulfills clinical syndrome) or probable bvFTD (clinical syndrome plus brain atrophy), with comparisons made to analyze differences in rate of clinical progression according to cognitive and functional scores. Imaging data will be compared between both groups, but also with age-matched longitudinal healthy control data to determine differences in rate of brain atrophy. Many patients without atrophy on MRI only satisfy criteria for possible bvFTD and remain in this category for years. Some of these patients are described as “phenocopy” cases. Identifying possible bvFTD cases that will evolve to probable disease, and at what time point remains difficult. This longitudinal study is ideal to address these issues and explore these outcomes.
kw: Frontotemporal dementia, young-onset dementia, neuroimaging

title: Neural Structural and Functional Features of Mood Disturbances in Parkinson’s Disease: A Multi-Modal Neuroimaging Approach
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Background: Depression, anxiety, and apathy are prevalent in Parkinson’s disease (PD) and associated with disability and caregiver burden. Neuroimaging techniques can elucidate the neuropathologies of these mood disturbances in PD. Most previous neuroimaging studies, however, failed to employ standardized diagnostic criteria to ensure the diagnoses of mood disturbances and did not comprehensively investigate their neuropathological alterations.Specific aims:• To comprehensively examine the neural structural and functional features of depression, anxiety, and apathy in PD• To determine the impact of the severity of depression, anxiety, and apathy on neural structural and functional alterations in PDHypotheses: • Compared with healthy controls and PD patients without any of the mood disturbances, PD patients with depression, anxiety, or apathy will show less brain volumes and diminished structural and functional connectivities.• Greater neural structural and functional alterations will be associated with severer mood disturbances in PD. Approach/ Methodology: • Participants: A total of 100 participants will be recruited comprising a PD group without depression, anxiety, and apathy; a PD group with depression alone; a PD group with anxiety alone; a PD group with apathy alone; a healthy control (HC) group (20 participants per group). • Mood assessments: Established standardized diagnostic criteria and clinimetrically validated scales will be employed to ensure the presence/ absence and severity of these mood disturbances.• Neuroimaging: T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), resting state functional MRI, diffusion tensor imaging, and fluid-attenuating inverse recovery (FLAIR) imaging will be acquired. Whole-brain voxel-wise analyses will be performed to unbiasedly examine the neural structural and functional substrates of these mood disturbances in PD.Significance of the proposal: The proposed study will improve the current understanding of the neuropathologies of mood disturbances in PD and facilitate future development of disease-modifying interventions that target the specific neuroimaging markers of these mood disturbances in PD.
kw: Parkinson's disease, depression , anxiety, apathy, neuorimaging

title: Effects of household environmental microbiome in early life on development of allergic diseases in children
inst: IHDP - Institute for Human Development and Potential
abs: There is strong evidence that the surrounding microbial environment we are exposed to, has an influential role in shaping our predisposition to developing allergy. However there are no studies on the effect of environmental microbiome in early life: preconception, pregnancy and early infancy on the development of allergy in the child. In addition, the mechanism of how environmental microbiome affects subsequent allergy risk is not well established. The Developmental Origins of Health and Disease (DOHaD) hypothesis postulates that early environmental stimuli may contribute to the early onset of allergic diseases, hence we propose to determine the contribution of the environmental microbiome to the development of allergic diseases in the pre-conception birth cohort “S-PRESTO”. We hypothesized that in Singapore households that there is a different and distinct environmental microbiome profile between homes of allergic and non-allergic subjects which may be influenced by lifestyle and that the environmental microbiome profile can serve as a predictor for allergic disease development. In addition, we hypothesized that a possible mechanism in which the environmental microbiome regulates immunity and allergy risk is through influencing the composition of the gut microbiome. To study this, we aim to determine any association between household environmental microbiome and eczema onset/ allergen sensitization in infants by the first year of age as well as the correlation between household environmental microbiome and maternal as well as infant’s gut microbiome. We will be analyzing household dust microbiome by 16sRNA sequencing from dust collected at 3 timepoints: preconception, pregnancy and postnatally. Families will be asked to complete questionnaires regarding lifestyle, smoking habits, pets, time spent indoors and household cleaning methods. Household dust microbiome will be correlated to gut microbiome and lifestyle. We hope to provide recommendations to modify our environmental microbial exposure in order to decrease the prevalence of allergic diseases.
kw: environmental microbiome, allergic diseases

title: INVESTIGATING ACCELERATED DISEASE PHENOTYPES IN NEURAL ORGANOID CULTURES FOR MODELING PARKINSON’S DISEASE
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: The accumulation of ?-synuclein (a-syn) aggregates in Lewy bodies is the hallmark of synucleinopathies, a group of neurodegenerative diseases including Parkinson’s disease (PD). It has been suggested that a-syn aggregates may be taken up and propagated between cells in a prion-like manner. Supporting the prion-like spreading hypothesis, recent in vivo studies report Lewy body formation in grafted fetal dopaminergic neurons within the striatum of PD patients. However, modeling synucleinopathies in human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neurons has proven to be challenging because even with elevated toxic a-syn levels, robust demonstration of a-syn aggregation is rarely observed. Overcoming these hurdles is critical for precise and accurate modeling of PD to advance therapeutic discovery, and to this end, we propose to culture dopaminergic neurons in three-dimensional brain organoids to provide a niche microenvironment for neuronal maturation for accumulation of a-syn aggregates in diseased neurons. We have preliminary evidence suggesting that a-syn aggregate formation is accelerated in organoids and to test our hypothesis that these aggregates spread from diseased to healthy neurons, we have 1) established that midbrain organoids can be derived from both wild-type and PD iPSCs and that accumulation of a-syn aggregates are observed only in PD organoids, 2) generated mixed or chimeric brain organoids by co-culturing wild-type GFP-reporter neurons and PD neurons. In this novel co-culture system, we aim to visualize spread of a-syn aggregates from PD neuron to wild-type GFP+ neuron and measure changes at the genomic level, Eventually, we will conduct small proof-of-concept study to demonstrate that small molecule therapeutics can be applied to brain organoids for subsequent small molecule screening efforts. We expect results from this study would provide insight into an under-explored topic in PD pathogenesis and this in vitro model would be critical as a platform for the eventual discovery of therapeutics.
kw: Brain organoids, Parkinson's disease, Disease modeling, Intraneuronal aggregates, Alpha synuclein, Three-dimensional cell culture

title: Understanding the mechanisms underlying developmental and ageing processes of cardiomyocyte using a dual-color metabolic reporter
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Energy metabolism of cardiomyocytes changes during development, differentiation and maturation, and ageing 1. Human pluripotent stem cell (hPSC) derived cardiomyocytes are fetal-like in nature and derive energy mainly from glycolysis while mature cardiomyocytes primarily utilize beta-oxidation for energy production. Interestingly, if hypertrophic stress is placed on the adult heart (a typical ageing-related phenotype), cardiac energy metabolism switches back to a more fetal phenotype, which includes an increase in glycolysis and decrease in mitochondrial fatty acid beta-oxidation. It is therefore of paramount importance to understand how cardiomyocytes mature and undergoes ageing, and understand the underlying molecular mechanisms associated with the metabolic shifts during these physiological changes. As such, we propose in this study to generate hPSCs that harbor a dual-color metabolic reporter (DMR) system encoding for metabolic genes important for glycolysis (hexokinase) and ?-oxidation (acyl-coA dehydrogenase) using CRISPR technology. This DMR system would allow us to track the physiological status of the cardiomyocytes (fetal-like, mature, or undergoing hypertrophic stress) by quantitating the usage of different metabolic pathways based on colorimetric analysis, thereby answering fundamental questions in genetic regulation of metabolism in cardiomyocytes during cellular maturation or when then cell undergoes cardiac hypertrophy. In addition, this system is also particularly useful for the conduct of the following pilot screens: (1) Targeted siRNA to identify transcription factors that are highly expressed in fetal-like or ageing cardiomyocytes since glycolysis is the main energy source for both physiological state (2) Compounds that either enhances cardiomyocyte maturation or prevent/slow down the ageing heart from cardiac hypertrophy.
kw: Cardiomyocytes, Metabolism, CRISPR, Genome profiling, Maturation, Cardiac Hypertrophy

title: Mechanistic insights into the role of HNF4A to human pancreatic ? cell dysfunction using HNF4A mutation as an experimental model
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Diabetes is a complex disease which results in widespread healthcare burden. Whilst mutations and gene variants are postulated to contribute to human pancreatic ? cell dysfunction in diabetic patients, their specific mechanism and contribution remain unclear. HNF4A mutations result in MODY1 that is associated with a progressive loss in human pancreatic ? cell function. Gene variants associated with type 2 diabetes (T2D) have also been found to reside near or in the HNF4A gene. Therefore, we hypothesize that the pancreatic cells in subjects with a HNF4A mutation/variant exhibit developmental defects, alterations in pancreatic transcriptional network and display functional abnormalities in ? cells. To investigate the role of HNF4A in human pancreatic ? cell development and function, hiPSCs will be derived from MODY1 and control subjects. These hiPSCs will be differentiated into pancreatic progenitors and pancreatic ?-like cells, and characterized extensively to determine the effects of HNF4A mutation. The effect of MODY1 mutation on the transcriptional regulatory function of HNF4A will be assessed via the examination of downstream target genes, ChIP and luciferase assays. Transcriptional and proteomics profiling will also be performed to evaluate genome-wide perturbations due to the HNF4A mutation. Subsequently, MODY1-hiPSC-derived pancreatic ?-like cells will be subjected to functional assays such as glucose-stimulated insulin secretion and C-peptide ELISAs. Electron microscopy will also be performed to evaluate the morphology of insulin and glucagon granules. Overall, our proposed research will provide mechanistic insights into the cause of HNF4A-attributed pancreatic defects in both MODY1 and T2D. This will help stratify diabetic patients with and without HNF4A variant/mutation so that targeted pharmacological approaches can be applied for diabetes disease prevention and treatment.
kw: stem cells, hiPSCs, type 2 diabetes, HNF4A, pancreas, beta cells

title: Identifying potential antiviral targets for human enterovirus-71 infection through high-throughput analysis of host:viral translational interactions and ribosome heterogeneity
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Hand, foot and mouth disease (HFMD) is endemic to Singapore; the annual epidemics it causes results in much physical discomfort for young children and substantial losses in opportunity costs for parents. In particular, HFMD caused by human enterovirus-71 (EV71) can lead to severe neurological symptoms and death. EV71 has caused outbreaks in Singapore and globally. It is thus of paramount importance that antivirals be developed for EV71 infections, for which there is currently no effective vaccine, or available antiviral treatment. Because the small genome of EV71 has limited coding capacity, the virus is highly dependent on host factors for essential viral functions. We thus hypothesize that a high-throughput approach can identify host factors whose continued translation is imperative for viral survival, that ribosome heterogeneity is a mechanism employed by viruses to subvert host translation, and that both of these aspects have functional consequences that can yield potential targets for antiviral development. To test this hypothesis, we will 1) use ribosome profiling to identify candidate host factors whose translation is preserved upon infection, 2) probe the functional significance of identified candidate host factors to viral fitness; 3) determine, proteomically, whether viral RNA-translating ribosomes have different ribosomal protein composition compared to host ribosomes, and 4) probe the functional significance of heterogeneous ribosomes to viral fitness. This multi-prong approach will provide a comprehensive strategy to study host:viral translational interactions, greatly enhancing our current aetiological understanding of EV71-HFMD. Our functional assays will also facilitate the selection of candidate host targets whose downregulation exert maximum viral-specific impact, with minimal side effects to the host. Moreover, because host factors are slower-evolving, emergence of acquired resistance will be less likely. An effective antiviral will bring substantial medical and economic benefits to Singapore, and give Singapore a head start in EV71 antiviral development for the global market.
kw: Hand, foot and mouth disease; Enterovirus 71; Ribosome profiling; Ribosome heterogeneity; Host:viral interactions; Antiviral targets

title: Mitofusins as novel therapeutic targets for preventing post-infarction cardiac arrhythmias
abs: Cardiac arrhythmias following ischaemia and reperfusion (IR) are a major cause of morbidity and mortality in acute myocardial infarction (MI) patients. Mitochondrial dysfunction induced by IR is known to reduce energy production, increase oxidative stress, and impair calcium handling in the heart, thereby disturbing ionic flux and energy homeostasis, the result of which is an increased susceptibility to arrhythmias. Changes in mitochondrial morphology by fusion and fission can affect mitochondrial shape and function. Our preliminary data suggests that murine hearts deficient in the mitochondrial fusion proteins, Mitofusins 1/2 (Mfn1/Mfn2), have impaired mitochondrial respiratory function, altered electrical conductivity, and an increased susceptibility to post-MI arrhythmias. In this research proposal, we characterize the arrhythmogenic substrate in adult hearts deficient in Mfn1/Mfn2, and we investigate the mechanisms underlying this arrhythmogenic effect. The findings from this research proposal will hopefully identify Mfn1/Mfn2 as novel therapeutic targets for preventing post-MI arrhythmias.
kw: Cardiac arrhythmias, Mfn1, Mfn2, ischemia-reperfusion, mitochondria

title: A predictive computational framework to identify novel transcriptional and epigenetic regulators of cell conversion
abs: One of the greatest promises of regenerative medicine lies in the possibility to reprogram any cell of the body to any other by altering transcription factor networks. Despite the great potential of this technology for both cell therapies and modelling diseases, only one paradigm has been explored; cell conversions are currently achieved by overexpression of factors. Furthermore, there are no standard means with which to assess the success of a cell conversion. This proposal will address this by combining the rapidly increasing volume of publically available data on gene expression, epigenetics and regulatory networks with cutting-edge computational biology techniques. We will implement and validate a systematic means with which to identify drugs, transcription factors and epigenetic remodelers that can induce a cell conversion between any two human cell types.To do this we will initially collect, curate and QC public data on gene expression, epigenetics and regulatory networks on a massive scale. This data will allow us to create a metric with which to assess cell conversions but also to expand a framework we recently published [Nature Genetics 2016]. This will involve the development of a number of new algorithms specifically designed to predict each different type of regulator. Following this we will demonstrate that these predictions are both correct and have the ability to treat disease by both (A) predicting and validating novel factors to convert patient-derived cells myofibroblasts and fibroblasts and (B) converting an in vitro model of schizophrenic neurons in order to correct their synaptic functionality back to that seen in their healthy counterparts.This proposal is at the cutting edge of the field of cell reprogramming; by successfully combining computational techniques with clinical and experimental expertise it will rapidly advance the transition to the clinic, as well as making Singapore a world-leader in this field.
kw: Transdifferentiation, Cell conversion, network biology, systems biology

title: MiMIC (Migration and Metastasis in a Chip): A microfluidic platform for the biological capture of functionally metastatic tumour cells
abs: Bone metastasis is often observed in late stage cancers of the breast, lung and prostate, and is associated with severe morbidity and mortality. Recent studies suggest that mesenchymal stem cells play major roles in the chemoattraction of circulating tumour cells to the metastatic niche, where ensuing interactions between cancer cells and bone microenvironment lead to a cascade of events, resulting in metastatic activation. Efforts to study these interactions, however, are curtailed by the lack of adequate experimental models to represent these early events in metastasis. We have recently demonstrated the utility of tissue engineered bone for the recruitment of human prostate cancer cells in a humanised mouse model of bone metastasis. We hypothesise that engineered bone tissues replicate features of the haemopoietic niche, thus providing the necessary conditions for the attraction and proliferation of bone-metastatic prostate cancer cells. To test this hypothesis, we have developed the following:Specific Aim #1: Engineer bone-tissue-on-chip as an in vitro model of prostate cancer metastasis to bone Specific Aim #2: Study on-chip interactions of engineered bone with prostate cancer cell linesSpecific Aim #3: Study the capture of prostate cancer cells from model mixturesThe key innovations of this approach lie in the use of engineered tissue and microfluidic devices to create vascularised micro tissue comprising major compartments of the bone marrow niche. If successful, this platform will have major applications as a device to capture functionally metastatic cancer cells and as an experimental tool to study early events in cancer metastasis.
kw: Bone metastasis, Disease model, Bone tissue engineering, Prostate cancer, Microfluidic device

title: Targeting ceramide kinase and ceramide-1-phosphate in limiting endometriosis lesion vascularization and development
inst: CREATE - Singapore-MIT Alliance for Research and Technology (CREATE-SMART)
abs: Background: Endometriosis, characterized by vascularized endometrial lesions outside of the uterine cavity, affects up to 12% of women with significant morbidity of severe chronic pelvic pain and infertility among other complications. Symptom relief and hormonal suppression are the primary goals of existing treatment options, but with significant side effects and do not address disease recurrence. Hence, novel, non-hormonal therapies are urgently needed. Endometriotic lesions must stay within a strict vasculature radius to ensure continued growth. We found significantly elevated ceramide-1-phosphate (C1P) in the peritoneal fluids of endometriotic women and in activated macrophages. Ceramide kinase (CerK), the central enzyme in generating C1P, is known to be angiogenic/vasculogenic, hence providing an excellent target for suppressing endometriotic lesion vascularization and growth. NVP-231 is a recently developed competitive CerK inhibitor that specifically keeps C1P levels low. Hypothesis: Thus, disruption of lesion vasculature via abrogation of ceramide phosphorylation by NVP-231 may present as an attractive non-hormonal strategy to controlling endometriosis. Aims: (I) Identify and characterize peritoneal macrophage phenotypes in ectopic sites and peritoneal fluids in endometriosis.(II) Dissect the mechanisms and molecular collaborations between macrophages and endothelial cells played by CerK and C1P in network stabilization. Understanding the key determinants of CerK inhibition on vasculostabilization via NVP-231 will shed light on a critical aspect of controlling lesion growth and development.Approach: Lesion vasculature destabilization can be studied by using human endothelial cells grown in 3D cultures exposed to C1P, NVP-231 and other treatment conditions, and together with macrophages. Our preliminary studies identified C1P as a potent inducer of endothelial cell vascular stabilization. Investigations on known and novel targets of vasculostabilization identified through transcriptomics will be conducted to understand their spatial localization, activity and regulation with CerK suppression. If successful, results from this proposal will facilitate the development of a novel drug candidate for endometriosis management.
kw: Endometriosis, macrophages, ceramide kinase, ceramide-1-phosphate, vascular network

title: Development of computational 3D wrist model for the interactive analysis of synovial fluid dynamics and ligament injury
abs: The study of wrist kinematics is crucial to the development of a new treatment for ligament injury, wrist instability and, eventually, Carpal Tunnel Syndrome which is commonly referred as a neurological disorder. However, soft-tissue interaction in the wrist for in vivo study increases the difficulty tremendously, due to the small size of the carpal bones and the complex geometry of cartilage, ligaments, and synovial fluid. To overcome this challenge, computational 3D modeling of biomechanical systems provides an efficient tool for investigating the ligament injury.In the study of synovial fluid dynamics and its influence on wrist kinematics (Grant No. SHF-FG564P-2014) using computational 3D modeling, several evidences had been found. Pressure in the synovial fluid is generated due to synovial fluid dynamics. It was shown that this pressure repeatedly appears at the osseous junction. title: Targeting factor XIa for the development of safer anticoagulants
abs: Cardiovascular diseases is one of the largest causes of morbidity and mortality, worldwide and in Singapore. Thrombosis, the pathological formation of blood clots, plays major roles in many of these diseases. The cornerstone therapeutics in the treatment and prophylaxis of thrombotic diseases are anticoagulants. The ‘ideal anticogulant’ should have good efficacy in preventing thrombosis and minimal risks for unintended bleeding. However, all anticoagulants in the market have major drawbacks, mainly due to difficulties in striking the balance between efficacy and safety. Recently, coagulation factor XIa (FXIa) becomes a highly pursued target for anticoagulation. Strong evidences based on human genetic and animal data have emerged that FXIa plays an important role in thrombosis but not in haemostasis. We have identified and characterized two novel FXIa inhibitors from snake venom (rFasxiatorN17R,L19E) and tick saliva (P1456KD1) with nanomolar affinity for human FXIa. rFasxiatorN17R,L19E has at least 170-fold selectivity for FXIa over other serine proteases. We showed that rFasxiatorN17R,L19E effectively prevented occlusion of carotid artery in rat without increasing the risk of bleeding. In contrast, unfractionated heparin, the parenteral anticoagulant of choice, bleeding was increased by more than 10-fold at doses that achieve the same efficacy as rFasxiatorN17R,L19E. Here, we propose to perform in vitro optimizations of P1456KD1 for potency and selectivity by yeast surface displays. Subsequently, we will fully evaluate the efficacy, safety and pharmacokinetics of rFasxiatorN17R,L19E (lead molecules) and the optimized P1456KD1 (2nd molecule) in clinically relevant murine models. We hypothesize that our FXIa inhibitors have high efficacy-to-safety index as anticoagulants and fill a major unmet need in anticoagulation therapy. Our goal is to establish the therapeutic potential of two locally-developed anticoagulants. In vivo data in small animals will inform dose selection in large animal models and toxicology studies in the future to complete all preclinical testing required before the first-in-human trials.
kw: anticoagulants, structure-function relationships, factor XIa, thrombosis, drug discovery and development, animal models

title: Evaluating XAF1 as a bonafide tumor suppressor in neuroblastoma
abs: Neuroblastoma, the most common and aggressive childhood extracranial solid tumor, is characterized by segmental chromosome changes and deletion of 1p36 in 25-35% of cases. Along 1p36 resides a gene called KIF1B and loss of KIF1B beta isoform through 1p36 deletion or loss-of-function mutations is frequently associated with Type 2B late-stage neuroblastomas with 5-year survival at 25%. Loss of KIF1B? expression in neuroblastoma patients leads to 20% overall survival compared to 80% in KIF1B?-positive patients. Recently, we showed that loss of KIF1B? abrogates a key apoptotic protein XAF1. Indeed, TMA analysis revealed that approximately 30% of neuroblastoma cases display complete loss of XAF1 expression. In addition, low or complete loss of XAF1 expression leads to poor survival outcome in overall and post-treatment patients. Our in vitro and in vivo studies also show that XAF1 is necessary and sufficient for apoptosis in neuroblastoma tumor suppression. Given that much of paediatric solid tumor therapy is still dependent on conventional cytotoxics, we hypothesize that XAF1 may be a potential tumor suppressor for high-risk neuroblastomas and understanding the biology may enable more personalized treatment and better disease stratification. To address this, we aim to determine the precise apoptotic mechanism mediated by XAF1 in neuroblastoma, assess XAF1 therapeutic value and evaluate treatment strategies that aim to recapitulate XAF1-mediated apoptosis pathway. In order to meet these aims, we will employ molecular techniques to map XAF1 domains and residues to its precise function, knockout/transgenic mouse models to ascertain XAF1 bonafide tumor suppressor status, in vitro assays to determine XAF1 therapeutic potential and patient-derived xenograft mouse models to examine the efficacies of investigational chemotherapeutics currently not used to treat neuroblastoma. These are targeted at recapitulating XAF1-mediated apoptosis pathway. In the long-term, our findings may be useful for other paediatric solid tumors with similar origin such as paraganglioma and pheochromocytoma.
kw: XAF1, neuroblastoma, tumor suppressor, XIAP inhibitors

title: Advancing non-viral mRNA delivery with nature inspired anti-viral counterschemes
abs: Perpetual mRNA transfection regimes employed during stem cell reprogramming are inefficient and toxic due to anti-viral response against mRNA molecules. An existing solution uses mRNA transcribed with modified nucleotides followed by HPLC purification, which is too costly to scale and threatens broad translation of mRNA therapeutics. In this proposal, we aim to achieve performance of modified mRNA at the cost of unmodified mRNA by investigating effects of influenza A virus (IAVs) derived non-structural protein 1 (NS1) on mRNA transfection. NS1 is a nature inspired molecule evolved by IAVs to overcome delivery barriers posed by host's anti-viral responses and promote the translation of non-host mRNA. The objective of this proposal is to demonstrate that anti-viral counter schemes mediated by NS1 enhances non-viral delivery of mRNA. The central hypothesis is that NS1 mutes type I interferon responses by actively suppressing all known immune triggers against mRNA, leading to improved cell viability and transfection efficiency. Specific aims to test the hypothesis are (1) Evaluate the impact on toxicity and transfection efficiency mediated by different IAV derived NS1, (2) Investigate mechanism of NS1 enhancement of mRNA transfection, (3) Evaluate impact of co-delivering NS1 in perpetual mRNA transfection regimes. We will develop in vitro models for transfection and toxicity evaluations. Mechanisms of enhancement will identified by using mutant NS1. NS1 will be evaluated for enhancement of both normal and modified mRNA transfection. This proposal will improve performance, reduce cost and develop a permanent upgrade of all mRNA transcription templates by incorporating NS1 as part of the standard mRNA template design.
kw: mRNA delivery, non structural protein 1, mRNA therapeutics, type I interferon, transfection efficiency, cell reprogramming

title: Phenotypic Interrogation of pathogenic and protective LRRK2 variants using functionally mature human induced midbrain dopamine neurons
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Parkinson’s disease (PD) is a leading cause of neurodegenerative disease that is characterized by the selective loss of dopaminergic neurons of the midbrain. Modeling PD using human patient derived cells represent an attractive means to advance our mechanistic understanding of the neuropathological processes that cause the disease; yet progress has been limited so far, largely due to 1) confounding phenotypic variations coming from the polymorphism in genetic backgrounds of individuals 2) the immature function of the human neuronal cells used for modeling. To overcome these issues, we have recently developed a novel and efficient method that could generate large numbers of functionally mature dopaminergic neurons. Here we wish to apply this method to study the effects of an Asian-specific pathogenic LRRK2 variant, G2385R, along with a protective variant R1398H. To eliminate the possible effects from background polymorphism, we have created a triad of isogenic hESC lines that differ exclusively at the specific mutation site. Using a combination of genetic, molecular and biochemical techniques, we aim to perform a detailed cellular and morphological characterization of the induced neurons, and to document any alternations observed among the isogenic traid, under both basal and stressed conditions. In addition, we will evaluate various electrophysiological parameters of the cells to uncover possible effect of the LRRK2 mutations on the function of dopamine neurons. Outcome from study will likely shed light on the how pathogenic LRRK2 mutation contribute to (and how protective LRRK2 variant protect against) PD phenotype, and define a phenotypic framework that future PD modeling studies could build on.
kw: PD, Stem cells, disease modeling

title: A sensitive microRNA detection system for disease diagnostics based on a self-cleaving ribozyme
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: The molecular revolution has allowed scientists to pinpoint the genetic defects underlying many diseases. Scientists and clinicians are employing disease biomarkers to improve disease diagnosis and prognosis, and to predict the responses of individuals to treatment. One important emerging class of biomarkers are microRNAs, short, 19-25 nucleotide single-stranded RNAs that bind to target mRNAs to regulate their expression. Distinct microRNAs are dysregulated in many human diseases, and microRNA signatures may aid in patient diagnosis, staging, prognosis and response to clinical therapies. Importantly, microRNAs are found circulating in the blood, allowing for their detection with minimally invasive procedures. In 2008, circulating microRNAs were described for patients with diffuse large B cell lymphoma, and since then, circulating microRNA signatures have been reported for many diseases, including cancer and neurodegenerative disease.Sensitive methods to detect disease-specific microRNA signatures will be key for clinical application of biomarker analysis; however, current methods require complex biochemical processing, are expensive, time consuming and/or require specialized skill sets for analysis. We previously developed and patented Pandan, a Spinach RNA-based microRNA sensor that fluoresces by sequence-complementary binding to its target microRNA. In this proposal, we will use a similar principle to alter a ribozyme into a microRNA detector that works in conjunction with Pandan, to produce a sensor system with amplified fluorescence changes many orders of magnitude larger than can obtained with Pandan alone. We will then explore the application of this sensor system for microRNA disease biomarker diagnostics. With our clinical collaborator, we will shortlist strongly validated microRNA biomarkers, design and optimize their corresponding Pandan-ribozyme sensors, and determine binding parameters in vitro. We will then determine the ability of the sensor system to detect microRNAs of interest in patient samples, either in RNA purified from serum or directly in serum.
kw: Disease biomarkers, Diagnostics, microRNAs, Biosensors, Synthetic biology

title: Determining Downstream of Kinase (DOK)-3 as Candidate Gene for Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD)
abs: Inflammatory Bowel Diseases (IBD) are chronic debilitating gastrointestinal autoimmune diseases that include Ulcerative Colitis (UC) and Crohn’s Disease (CD). They are incurable and current treatments include invasive surgery to remove inflamed colon parts and the administration of anti-inflammatory steroids which have adverse side-effects. Novel therapeutic is therefore needed for the treatment of IBD but this is hindered by a lack of understanding of its etiology and the role of the immune system in its pathogenesis. A recent GWAS study (Nature 491: 119-124 (2012)) implicated an 18 gene-chromosomal region as associated with IBD. This chromosome region comprises several immune related genes and amongst them, the Downstream of Kinase (DOK)-3 gene that encodes an adaptor protein previously shown to be involved in several immune receptor signaling. So far, DOK-3 has not been shown to be involved in any inflammatory diseases. In this proposal, we hypothesize that DOK-3 is a novel candidate gene for IBD and aim to study its role in the maintenance of intestinal homeostasis. To achieve this objective, we aim to (1) establish unequivocably if DOK-3 plays a role in IBD by examining the response of DOK3-deficient mice in a dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-mediated colitis model, (2) determine if DOK-3-deficiency would perturb the composition of commensal gut microbiome by performing microbial16S rDNA next-generation sequencing, (3) elucidate the DOK3-associated immune signaling pathway(s) critical for the prevention of colitis and finally (4) validate the significance of the results from our animal models and in-vitro studies in the human IBD cohorts by examining histopathological analysis staining of DOK-3 protein expression of all UC, CD or normal human samples obtained from colonoscopy. This proposal will yield critical insights to the pathogenesis of IBD, yield potential target for therapeutic intervention and more importantly, identify DOK3 as a novel IBD candidate gene.
kw: immunity, inflammation, colitis, gastrointestinal

title: Rapid Identification of Stem Cell Donors
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Adult mesenchymal stem cell (MSC) therapies are a rapidly evolving pillar of clinical medicine for treating conditions where body tissue needs to be replaced, repaired, or regenerated. These stem cells typically reside in our tissues and are administered to patients in the form of cellular infusions or incorporated into cellular grafts. Because of their small numbers in body tissues, MSCs are usually surgically isolated from patients or prospective donors and further processed to achieve the quantities needed for therapeutic use or cell banking. These processes are time-intensive and extremely costly with no guarantee that, if needed, the stem cells will be capable of sufficient ex vivo growth or remain efficacious after their extensive processing. Our proposal seeks to address this problem by leveraging pioneering work recently filed for patent protection at A*STAR that has identified a novel biomarker found in the blood of patients or prospective donors. Screening blood samples for this biomarker predicts the likely growth capacity and regenerative ability of the stem cells before they are isolated. This proposal aims to produce, and then validate, a simple kit that would allow hospitals, medical clinics, stem cell companies and related industries to screen patients or prospective donors for this biomarker before deciding whether to harvest the stem cells or tissues. In doing so, this proposal aims for Singapore to take the lead in generating the world’s first validated stem cell quality kit, and for this kit to be ready for immediate commercialisation.

title: Arc and Alzheimer's disease: a novel perspective
abs: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a devastating neurodegenerative disease characterized by the progressive loss of both synaptic function andmemory, for which no effective therapy exists. Arc is a “master regulator” of synaptic plasticity and is required for memory consolidation. Recentstudies have already implicated Arc in the pathophysiology of AD, but unpublished data from the VanDongen laboratory have considerablystrengthened this link by demonstrating that Arc epigenetically regulates the transcription of hundreds of activity-dependent genes involved in awide range of neuronal functions critical to memory. More importantly, Arc knock-down alters the expression level of 15 AD susceptibility genes.Taken together, these results have prompted us to formulate the following hypothesis: Arc expression and molecular function are criticaldeterminants of the pathophysiology of Alzheimer’s disease. This hypothesis will be tested by experiments organized in 3 Specific Aims:Aim 1. Investigate the mechanisms by which Arc affects AD pathophysiologyAim 2. Manipulate Arc levels to examine its effects on AD pathology in a mouse modelAim 3. Develop novel epigenetic therapeutics targeting Arc to slow down AD progressionThe experiments propose here will employ the AD models: 1) postmortem brain samples from AD patients and age-matched non-dementedcontrol subjects, 2) induced Pluripotent Stem Cell-derived neurons generated from sporadic and familial AD patient and controls, and 3) a widely-used triple mutant mouse model and wild-type controls. The results from these experiments will provide a critical test of ourhypothesis and is expected to provide a new avenue for developing novel therapeutics to treating AD.
kw: Alzheimer's disease; Therapeutics; Aging; Memory decline; Epigenetics

title: Interplay between Mevalonate and Hippo Pathways Regulates DDX20 Transcription via YAP-TEAD Complex in Triple Negative Breast Cancer
abs: Statins, used for the treatment of hypercholesterolemia, inhibit the rate-limiting enzyme of the mevalonate pathway, HMGCR. Cancer cells are dependent on the sustained availability of this pathway. Our group previously reported a metastasis-promoting oncogene, DDX20 in invasive breast cancer cells and in patients. Here, we assessed correlation between mevalonate pathway genes and expression of DDX20 in cohorts of breast cancer patients. Amongst the genes evaluated, positive correlation with DDX20 expression was observed with eight of them, HMGCR being the most significant. In vitro experiments showed exposure of invasive breast cancer cells to statins led to a Rho-dependent decrease in the expression of DDX20 resulting in decreased proliferation in a mevalonate pathway-dependent manner. A similar observation was also observed in a mouse model, where simvastatin-treated mice showed significant decreased DDX20 expression and lung metastases. We also show decreased expression of DDX20 in primary breast cancer patients who received simvastatin daily in a retrospective trial. Interestingly, studies have suggested that potential metastasis-initiating cells might be present within small cancer stem cells (CSC) populations, largely responsible for drug resistance and cancer recurrence. Our preliminary data proposes the identification of DDX20 a novel CSC-promoting oncogene, thus presenting itself as a targetable molecule for eradication of these cells and significantly improving clinical outcomes.Herein, the aims of this proposal:Aim 1: Immunohistochemical analysis of HMGCR and YAP-TEAD expression in breast cancer patients’ specimens and marker correlation to DDX20 expression.Aim 2: To further elucidate the consequences of gain and loss of function of DDX20 on simvastatin sensitivity.Aim 3: Elucidating the role of DDX20 in inducing cancer stem cell phenotype and sensitivity to statins.Aim 4: Determine if DDX20 gene is a novel YAP-TEAD target. Aim 5: To decipher the mechanism by which DDX20 possibly regulates YAP-TEAD signaling
kw: DEAD-box RNA Helicase DDX20, Rho-GTPases,YAP-TEAD Complex, Simvastatin, Triple Negative Breast Cancer, Cancer Stem Cells

title: An axis comprising of nerve growth factor and septohippocampal cholinergic neurons mediates experimental neuropathic pain and co-morbidity
abs: Chronic pain is associated with an enormous health care cost to the society and for many individuals it leads to a reduced quality of life, in part due to co-morbid affective changes. At present, our understanding of the mechanism of chronic pain and its treatment is not as comprehensive as that for physiological pain. In order to understand the basis of chronic pain, we have pursued a path wherein we have investigated the role of the forebrain septo-hippocampal network, a region traditionally linked with cognition and affect-motivation, in experimental pain. Our findings so far have indicated that the network, especially the medial septum (MS) plays a nodal role in the mediation of ongoing nociceptive behaviors and affect in experimental persistent pain. The present proposal will advance our understanding of the neurochemical and neuro-circuit basis of the role of MS in ‘chronic pain’ by testing the hypothesis that the neurotrophin, nerve growth factor (NGF), and the septal cholinergic neurons mediate peripheral hypersensitivity (PH) and cognitive and affective changes co-morbid in experimental neuropathic pain. The hypothesis is based on our preliminary findings that intraseptal NGF and partial destruction of cholinergic neurons attenuate PH in chronic constriction injury model of neuropathic pain. To test the hypothesis, we plan experiments using established (electrophysiological, drug microinjection, molecular biology/cell biology) and innovative (optogenetic) techniques in anaesthetized and behaving rat/mice to investigate whether (a) intraseptal NGF mediates behavioral and cellular changes in experimental neuropathic pain, (b) septal NGF mediates nociception via increased activity of septal cholinergic projection to hippocampus, including ventral hippocampus, and (c) NGF and cholinergic hyperactivity modulate co-morbidity in experimental neuropathy. On successful conclusion, the study will provide a neural basis for the role NGF in experimental chronic pain and highlight novel neural and chemical target(s) in central nervous system for pursuing translational investigations.
kw: Neuropathic Pain, Nerve Growth Factor, Medial Septum, Hippocampus, Co-morbidity, Cholinergic Neurons

title: Analysis of immune mechanisms supporting Hodgkin lymphoma, and development of novel therapeutics
abs: Hodgkin Lymphoma (HL) is a haematological malignancy that affects people already in their young adulthood. Recently, we demonstrated ectopic expression of the cytokine receptor CD137 (TNFRSF9, 4-1BB) on Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg (HRS) cells, the malignant cells that cause HL. We discovered that CD137 aids HL in escaping immune surveillance. Further, the ectopic CD137 expression provides additional growth advantages, the induction of IL-3 and hepaCAM expression, which regulate HL growth and the organization of the extended HL tumor stroma, and which are to be investigated in this proposal. We aim to identify inducers of CD137 expression on HRS cells (Aim 1), a prime candidate of which is Epstein-Barr Virus. The signal transduction leading to CD137 expression will also be identified. CD137 signaling into HRS cells induces the secretion of IL-13, a potent growth factor for HRS cells. Aim 2 will investigate the role of CD137-induced IL-13 on HRS cell proliferation, survival, and the ability of HL to skew immune responses. CD137 signaling also induces the expression of hepaCAM, an adhesion molecule that regulates cell adhesion and migration. We aim to verify data indicating that hepaCAM is involved in the generation of the extended tumor stroma that is essential for HL pathogenesis (Aim 3). Our goal is to translate knowledge gained from this research to a therapeutic application by generating a bispecific antibody that is selective for the malignant HRS cells. Coexpression of CD137, hepaCAM and CD30 on HRS cells and leukocytes will be determined (Aim 4). Based on these results we will generate an antibody specific for 2 of the 3 antigens, and test it in vitro and in a murine xenograft model (Aim 5). These studies have the potential to identify hitherto unknown molecular mechanisms underlying the pathology of HL, and to develop novel therapeutics for HL.
kw: Hodgkin lymphoma, IL-13, CD137 HepaCAM, immune escape, immunotherapy

title: Innovative epigenetic solutions to overcome acquired resistance to targeted therapies: mechanisms, biomarkers and therapeutic approaches
abs: Although genetic events leading to aberrant activation of HER2, PI3K or CDK4/6 in breast cancer have indicated the clinical benefits for targeted therapies, patients inevitably develop resistance and relapse after treatment. This unmet clinical need highlights a pressing need to seek alternative approaches to resolve it. Although genetic or signalling events are the current major focuses for understanding the resistance mechanisms, epigenetic mechanisms which have received much less attention, might be equally important in contributing to drug resistance. In this proposal, we plan to investigate systematically the unique and common epigenetic mechanisms in acquisition of resistance to targeted therapies in breast cancers which has not been previously studied. Rather than developing therapeutic approaches to reverse already acquired drug resistance which is unrealistic for advanced patients, we seek to develop an epigenetic upfront co-targeting approach with an aim to prevent the clinical development of resistance to targeted therapies. This proposal is based on our long-term accumulation of epigenetic expertise and strong preliminary proof of concept findings in relation to PI3K or HER2 signaling. In particular, we have obtained preclinical evidence that breast cancer cells upon acquisition of resistance may employ epigenetic reprogramming to confer survival advantage. We hypothesis that the epigenetic alterations in particular the gain of histone bivalency at some of the key tumor suppressor gene loci contribute to the development of drug resistance which can be therapeutically targeted by epigenetic combination approach patented in my lab. Specifically, this project aims to: 1) systematically identify the epigenetic reprogramming events contributes to the acquisition of resistance to targeted therapies such as anti-PI3K/HER2/CDK4/6 therapies; 2) develop upfront epigenetic co-targeting strategies to delay or even prevent the onset of drug resistance; 3) Functional and clinical validation of the epigenetic determinants that can be exploited as potential biomarkers to predict the therapeutic outcomes of targeted therapies.
kw: breast cancer, taregeted therapy, resistance, epigenetic, histone methylation

title: Structural and functional studies of the core kinase Mst-WW45 complex and druggable YAP/TAZ-TEAD complex in the Hippo pathway
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Hippo signaling pathway is a tumor suppressor pathway implicated in the regulation of organ size. Proteins in the pathway are grouped into three components: upstream regulatory factors, kinase core, and downstream transcriptional machinery. The aim of this project is to study the structures and functions of protein complexes, in order to elucidate the molecular mechanism of the pathway. In particular, we are focusing on the kinase core, which contains Mst kinase, its binding partner WW45, Lats kinase, and its binding partner Mob. The functional role of WW45 in the Mst-WW45 complex, and the interactions between the four proteins remain unclear. Based on our preliminary X-ray diffraction data, we hypothesize that WW45 may be a regulator of Mst, rather than a scaffolding protein to bring Lats close to Mst. Structural information of the protein complexes in different activation states, together with results from cell-based studies, will give us a better understanding of how the kinases are regulated to control cell proliferation. Downstream of the kinase core is the transcriptional machinery, consisting of YAP, TAZ (transcription coactivators) and TEAD (transcription factor). The YAP/TAZ-TEAD complex presents a validated target in the development of cancer therapeutics. We have solved the structure of TAZ-TEAD complex, which reveals a novel binding mode, not seen in YAP-TEAD. Hence, we hypothesize that different transcription coactivators may influence DNA target selectivity of a transcription factor. Thus, we aim to determine genes that are specifically regulated by TAZ and YAP. In addition, we have screened a fragment library and identified a hit compound. We have also solved the structure of TEAD in complex with the compound, which showed that the latter may disrupt YAP/TAZ-TEAD interactions. Subsequently, we plan to use computational modeling to grow the hit into a lead compound, that is capable of inhibiting tumorigenesis and tumour progression.
kw: Hippo pathway, Mst-WW45, YAP, TAZ, TEAD, drug design

title: Managing gut microbiota and the use of ?-lactam antibiotics as novel strategies combating invasive Candida albicans infection
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: According to the World Health Organization, the damaging consequences of the misuse of antibiotics have become one of the most important threats to public health. In addition to the emergence and spread of antibiotic-resistant bacteria, antibiotic disruption of the human microbiota is associated with increased risk for a variety of diseases including susceptibility to infections by other pathogens. One prominent example is the life-threatening invasive infection caused by the commensal fungus Candida albicans. However, the mechanism remains unknown, significantly hindering risk management. Our recent revelation that bacterial peptidoglycan subunits can potently drive the invasive hyphal growth of C. albicans offers reasonable explanations. As ?-lactam antibiotics inhibit peptidoglycan synthesis leading to its degradation into subunits, we hypothesize that the sudden release of large quantities of peptidoglycan subunits by the trillions of bacterial cells in our body following antibiotic treatment will strongly promote C. albicans invasive growth, leading to increased invasion of the host. Currently, no literature has reported tests of any natural peptidoglycan subunits for the promotion of C. albicans hyphal growth, which bacteria produce such activity, and which antibiotics potently enhance its production and release. Here, we propose to screen human commensal bacteria for their ability to release the hyphal-inducing peptidoglycan subunits and compare the effect of the high and low peptidoglycan producers on C. albicans growth and host invasion using mouse models of gastrointestinal colonization and infection. We’ll also examine the impact of different antibiotics on the release of peptidoglycan subunits by various bacteria and C. albicans growth in the gastrointestinal tract in correlation to changes in the gut bacterial composition. Knowledge gained in this study is crucial for achieving a thorough understanding of the causes of C. albicans infection and developing new strategies for the prevention, management, and treatment of the disease.
kw: Candida albicans invasive infection, Antifungal strategies, microbiota, peptidoglycan, beta-lactam antibiotics, risk management

title: Towards Stable Peptide-Based Therapeutics for Adjunctive Treatment of Tuberculosis
abs: This multidisciplinary collaborative project aims to provide a detailed understanding of the role and mechanism of action of synthetic antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) and analogues as a novel arsenal of defense against Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) infection. Our team has previously developed synthetic AMPs effective against drug-susceptible and –resistant Mtb strains and clinical isolates via a rational approach and demonstrated their potential to evade drug resistance when applied as adjunct treatments. The bacterial membrane lytic action of these AMPs was well established, although mounting research suggests that their immunomodulatory functions may play just as an important role. To advance our molecules towards clinical development, the overall goal of this study is therefore towards stable AMP and analogues via novel modification strategies for adjunctive use with first-line antitubercular drugs, in parallel with a detailed understanding of their mechanism of action at the bacterial interface as well as at the level of the host cell. By using state-of-the-art tools and technology, we seek to understand strain susceptibility to AMP and analogue treatment and possible facilitation of cross-talk with host immune cells. Specifically, we aim to: (1) Optimize lead molecules via peptoid modification and cholesterol conjugation to develop stable and potent preclinical candidates; (2) Evaluate the in vitro and in vivo anti-mycobacterial activity and stability of lead molecules; and (3) Elucidate the detailed mechanism of action by profiling mycobacterial lipid changes and global host cell responses to our lead molecules. These fundamentally-linked aims will help us understand how AMPs and analogues impact, exploit or affect Mtb and host cell functions for Mtb removal and allow us to adopt the knowledge for successful drug design. Such a knowledge-driven approach will significantly accelerate the development of novel peptide therapeutics for counteracting pressing issues of tuberculosis drug resistance.
kw: Antimicrobial peptides, multidrug resistance, tuberculosis, treatment, infections

title: Towards a molecular understanding of pathway dysfunction in Fragile-X syndrome
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Fragile-X Syndrome (FXS) is a genetic disease inherited through a single locus, and the most common cause of intellectual disability. It is also strongly linked to autism spectrum disorder (ASD). The lack of the FMRP protein in affected individuals is considered the primary defect in FXS, and this leads to defects in synaptic architecture and neurotransmission. We and others have shown that PAK kinases can interact with, and are important for the function of fragile-X proteins.This project seeks to examine in detail the protein environment in which FMRP functions and the way in which the brain-enriched kinase PAK1 contributes to FMRP function. It is known that inhibiting PAKs can ameliorate several defects associated with FXS. We will take advantage of cutting edge mass-spectrometry combined with so-called BioID technology using cell lines that express FMRP 'probes' to examine the local protein complexes in a bottom-up approach. We will first characterize proteins that lie within an ~15 nm radius around FMRP in vivo to validate that a sub-set of these do biochemically interact. After defining the types of protein/RNA complexes where FMRP operates, we will build a 'map' of the local interactions and combine with optical microscopy to confirm their co-localization. In the next step the function of the proteins that directly bind FMRP will be probed by looking at their ability to genetically interact or 'rescue' FXS in a Drosophila model. We have confirmed this approach for Lingerer, a protein identified in our preliminary studies. Finally, by looking in depth at different cells lacking FMRP we will test hypotheses regarding how the lack of FMRP impacts cellular outputs such as protein translation. Our project will likely yield several new insights into the deficiencies in FXS, and in turn novel functional information on the etiology of related disorders such as ASD.
kw: mental retardation, protein translation, PAK1, proteomics

title: Isoform of Fyn tyrosine kinase as a novel potential therapeutic target for Alzheimer’s disease
abs: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the leading cause of dementia in old age. Fyn tyrosine kinase has been suggested to have a pathogenic role in AD, as an essential mediator between ?-amyloid (A?) and tau. One would assume that the brain-predominant FynB is involved in the disease. Instead, we observed selective up-regulation of FynT in AD neocortex which was closely associated with neurofibrillary tangle formation and reactive astrogliosis. Consistently, our preliminary data showed that 3xTg-AD mice exhibited increased FynT to FynB ratio, and double positive staining of FynT and hyperphosphorylated tau, suggesting that FynT could be the pathogenic isoform of Fyn in AD. Furthermore, cell-based assay revealed that FynT kinase activity may facilitate TNF?-induced pro-inflammatory signaling. We therefore hypothesize that dysregulation of alternative splicing machinery in AD brain may favor FynT expression during neurofibrillary degeneration and neuroinflammation; and targeted depletion of FynT may have protective effects on disease progression of AD. Here we propose a multimodal study using rodent models, cell-based assays and postmortem brains to test our hypothesis. Specifically, we aim to: (1) study the critical role of FynT in neurofibrillary degeneration and neuroinflammation using P301S transgenic model crossing with FynT knockout; (2) elucidate the mechanism of splicing switch from FynB to FynT in AD and identify the specific role of FynT induction in association with tau pathology, synaptotoxicity and neuroinflammation using cell-based assays; (3) study the association between FynT induction and neuropathological hallmarks in AD and non-AD neurodegenerative dementias; (4) assess the utility of antisense oligonucleotides as potential therapeutics via specific repression of FynT expression through splice-switching or RNA interference. In addition to providing further insight into the pathogenic role of FynT in AD, successful identification of FynT as a novel target will drive therapeutic approaches which specifically target FynT to potentially improve drug efficacy and reduce off-target effects.
kw: Fyn tyrosine kinase, alternative splicing, Alzheimer's disease, neurofibrillary tangle, neuroinflammation, tau

title: Structural mechanisms of retinoic acid receptor alpha mutations in breast fibroepithelial tumors and drug discovery
abs: Fibroepithelial tumor of the breast is a group of lesions consisting of the benign fibroadenoma, which is highly common in young women, and the relatively rare but potentially aggressive phyllodes tumors. We have recently demarcated the genetic landscapes of breast fibroepithelial tumors, (Lim et al., Nature Genet., 2014; Tan et al., Nature Genet., 2015), with the discovery of MED12 and RARA mutations as the two most common somatic genetic alterations in all classes of these tumors. RARA encodes for RAR?, a member of the nuclear hormone receptors, which are well-known to be successful drug targets. While previously known RARA mutations found in acute promyelocytic leukemia are translocations resulting in the fusion with other genes such as PML, this has been the first report of tumor-associated frequent point mutations in RARA. Our in vitro assays revealed a set of functionally distinct properties displayed by mutant RAR? compared to the wild type, which include marked enhanced interactions with transcriptional corepressors. Preliminary analyses based on the published crystal structure of wild type RAR? showed that the majority of the mutations occur at residues that are not directly in contact with ligand or corepressor, suggesting that the mutations may have induced novel structural changes to elicit the altered functions. We have also established isogenic cell lines from patient samples and showed that RAR? agonists inhibit the viability of cells expressing wild-type but not mutant RAR?, justifying the specific targeting of latter cells. These lines of evidence supports that mutant RAR? differ structurally from the wild-type protein and require mutant-specific agonists to promote their transcriptional activity and growth inhibitory effects. We therefore propose to 1) determine the crystal structures of mutant RAR? to elucidate their structural mechanisms and 2) implement computational and biochemical screening to discover potential mutant-specific ligands to be further developed as therapeutics.
kw: Breast fibroadenoma, Breast phyllodes tumors, Retinoic acid receptor mutations, Crystallography, Structural studies, Novel mechanisms

title: Myocardial regeneration of neonatal pig
abs: Heart failure resulted from ischemic heart disease is one of the leading causes of morbidity and mortality in the world as well as in Singapore. It is well-known that the mammalian heart does not have the capacity for cardiac regeneration throughout life. More recently, studies demonstrated transient regenerative capability of cardiomyocytes in neonatal mice: hearts of 1-day-old neonatal mice can regenerate after partial surgical resection, but this capacity is lost by 7 days of age. This suggests that hearts of small mammalian animals, such as mice, retain regenerative capacity during early life after birth. However, it is unknown whether hearts of large mammalian animals have this capacity and when it is switched off early after birth. Our preliminary study suggests that the hearts of 2-day-old neonatal piglets can almost fully repair with minimal fibrosis after myocardial infarction, but this capacity is lost by 3 days of age. In the current proposal, we will further validate this finding and explore the mechanism. The central hypothesis of the proposal is that cardiomyocyte regeneration (proliferation), stimulated by IL-6 from cardiac macrophages, is the major mechanism of cardiac repair in 2-day-old piglets after myocardial infarction. An in-depth cellular and molecular analysis will be carried out to determine whether cardiomyocyte regeneration stimulated by IL-6 from cardiac macrophages is the major mechanism of cardiac repair in hearts of 2-day-old piglets. The findings of the study can identify novel genes, cytokines, or signaling pathways that may have important implications in regenerative medicine for the treatment of human cardiac diseases. It will advance our knowledge of whether large mammalian animal hearts have regenerative capacity after birth and understanding the mechanism how immune response after injury triggers the regenerative process. It has broad scientific and translational impact to move forward regenerative medicine for cardiac regeneration.
kw: Myocardial regeneration, mammalian animal, Heart

title: Renewable platform to model achondroplasia growth plate defects and enhance chondrocyte growth
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Patients born with disproportionately short stature frequently have achondroplasia (ACH), an oft-neglected disease caused by growth defects in the growth plate chondrocytes. ACH is caused by a mutation in FGFR3 (1-5), affecting ~1/10,000 births, and remains incurable today like many other cartilage diseases, including osteoarthritis. A critical barrier to the development of targeted therapies has been the lack of scalable human cartilage models for high-throughput screens.Here, we propose that mature chondrocytes generated from patient-specific induced pluripotent stem cell-derived mesenchymal stem cells (iPS-MSCs) could represent a self-renewable platform to model ACH pathogenesis and normal chondrocyte growth. Our group had been establishing this iPS-chondrocyte platform to recapitulate ACH patients’ growth plate chondrocyte defects in vitro. Moving forward, we aim to (1) Optimize our generation of mature chondrocytes from iPS- MSCs to recapitulate normal cartilage; (2) Firmly establish our model of ACH growth plate chondrocytes; (3) Identify therapeutic targets for treating ACH and enhancing normal chondrocyte growth, by setting up high- throughput drug and genetic screens.Our research on this well-defined monogenic disease model, could lead to therapeutic targets for treating ACH children and normalizing short stature. Moreover, in the process, our research could illuminate and lead to new therapies for stimulating normal chondrocyte growth, differentiation and regeneration. This will have important implications for other cartilage diseases as well as degenerative diseases of aging, including the devastatingly painful cartilage degeneration widely observed in osteoarthritis.
