title: Muscle Imaging and Genomic Subtyping of Paediatric Neuromuscular Diseases
abs: Neuromuscular diseases (NMDs) are a genetically and phenotypically heterogeneous group of more than 200 disorders with a combined prevalence of 1:3000. They are characterized by progressive muscle weakness, which leads to motor, respiratory, and swallowing difficulties. Advances in treatment options have been challenging as the molecular causes and hence disease pathways remain known in at least 50% of these patients. Elucidating the molecular cause would be the first step to finding a potential cure for these patients. In the last 2 decades, the application of molecular genetic strategies has led to a delineation of clinically indistinguishable neuromuscular disorders and disclosed marked disease overlap 2. The expanding number of molecular defined NMDs requires new strategies to classifying overlapping and clinical indistinguishable phenotypes. Next generation sequencing (NGS) has been successfully employed to identify causative gene(s) in patients with neuromuscular disorders. In addition, there has been increasing evidence that MRI can be a valuable tool in the diagnosis of the different NMDs, aiding the clinical in selecting appropriate genetic and biochemical diagnostic investigations, as well as which muscle to target for muscle biopsy.We hypothesize that a combination of next generation sequencing and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the limb musculature would significantly improve diagnostics in paediatric neuromuscular disorders. This will also allow us to study and understand the disease mechanisms for NMD. We aim to study the utility of (a) next generation sequencing and (b) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the limb muscles in establishing diagnosis in paediatric neuromuscular disorders (n=50). Understanding the genetics of NMDs in the contact of our local patients will enable us to reach a molecular diagnosis. It will also be a stepping stone towards understanding the mechanism of this heterogeneous group of disorders, with eventual discovery of a treatment for these patients.
kw: muscle, MRI, genetic analysis

title: Exploring the CNS Toxicity of Dexamethasone in the Treatment of Paediatric ALL: A Multi-faceted fMRI/MRS Study including Innovative Use of Fitbit Trackers in Children
abs: Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) is the most common childhood cancer, with cure rates approaching 90%. Dexamethasone is a steroid which is the cornerstone of ALL therapy, however it causes significant side effects such as mood changes and disturbed sleep -adding significantly to the family's stress of managing a child with cancer and can even put a child at risk of suicide. Little is known about how and why Dexamethasone causes all these side effects. Our study aims to use resting state functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging(MRI) and spectroscopy as a non-invasive way to discover the parts of the brain which are affected and changes in neurotransmitters caused by Dexamethasone, in relation to neuropsychiatric tests and the use of Fitbit for sleep tracking. We will recruit 100 children with ALL who are treated on the same protocol from 2 institutions over 24months. This will consist of 3 main time points, before, during and after completion of specific blocks of Dexamethasone. At each time point, children aged 4 to 16 will complete an MRI scan as well as neuropsychiatric testing. A study pilot involving 3 children with ALL aged 4 to 10 has been successfully implemented. A healthy control arm involving 20 adult subjects who voluntarily received 12mg of oral Dexamethasone for 5 days was also completed. Preliminary analysis revealed significant decrease in total brain volume and specifically the hippocampus, cerebellum and grey matter at drug peak -all of which were reversed on wash out scans. Functional MRI revealed significant decrease in functional connectivity in the frontal cortex and specifically between the cerebellum, hippocampus and thalamus. In addition, spectroscopy showed significant decrease in the GABA concentrations in the hippocampus from baseline to peak scan with reversal at washout. We hypothesize that similar changes and more will be seen in same study in children.
kw: Dexamethasone, Pediatric Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia

title: Integrative Profiling to refine risk assignment in childhood acute lymphoblastic leukaemia
abs: Contemporary high throughput methodologies like global gene expression profiling and targeted nextgeneration sequencing are now sufficiently affordable for clinical use. We aim to use these new platforms to characterize genetic alterations that are clinically significant in children with ALL of Asian ancestry and develop a highly personalized and practical treatment regimen for these children based on algorithms incorporating minimal residual disease (MRD), genetic features of the leukemic cells and host genetic variants in the context of the Ma-Spore 2010 protocol. Early response to treatment as determined by MRD quantitative strategies – ability to detect submicroscopic leukaemia - is the most critical adverse prognostic in ALL. However, current allele specific MRD quantitation using real-time quantitative PCR has limited sensitivity of only 0.01% and unable to accurately pick out patients who relapsed but cleared their MRD to <0.01% within 5 weeks of remission induction therapy. In addition, clonal evolution where the PCR MRD marker is lost may occur, risking relapse. Massively paralleling technologies are now sufficiently affordable for clinical use. We will use sequence-based, instead of allele-specific, MRD quantitation strategies centered on next generation sequencing Roche 454 platform with at least another 10-fold improvement in sensitivity and specificity to risk assign children (<18 years old) with newly diagnosed ALL in the multi-centre Ma-Spore ALL 2010. Clonal evolution of markers is minimized as all rearrangements are surveyed without bias. In addition to the current IgH/TCR/IgK receptor antigen rearrangements, we will develop new MRD markers using recently described somatic alterations in Ikaros, CDKN2A/B, JAK2, CRLF2 and p53 genes. To this end, every patient will have at least one MRD marker of 10 fold increase in sensitivity without compromise in specificity (<0.001%) for risk assignment compared to ~90% currently so that risk assignment and hence treatment intensity and outcome can be optimized for every patient.
kw: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, Children, Next generation sequencing, Gene expression profiling, Minimal residual disease, Stratified medicine

title: Singapore Young Dementia Cohort Study (SYNC): Longitudinal evaluation of clinical and neuroimaging markers in Frontotemporal Dementia (SYNC-FTD)
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Worldwide, frontotemporal dementia (FTD) is the second most common cause of young-onset dementia (dementia occurring before the age of 65). FTD has 3 clinical variants – behavioural variant (bvFTD) in two-thirds of subjects presenting with behavioural and personality change, and two language variants known as semantic variant primary progressive aphasia (svPPA) and non-fluent variant primary progressive aphasia (nfvPPA). Behavioural symptoms are frequently diagnosed as mid-life schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, as memory impairment is absent in early stages of bvFTD. This highlights the need for improved awareness of bvFTD amongst the public, healthcare professionals, and researchers in this region. This study will be looking primarily at the behavioural variant of FTD in a longitudinal manner. We aim to perform detailed clinical characterization, neuropsychological and socio-emotional testing, as well as advanced neuroimaging (including diffusion tensor imaging and functional studies) to understand anatomical-functional connectivity patterns in bvFTD and investigate its utility as a potential biomarker. The longitudinal changes in clinical and neuroimaging patterns will be correlated with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) findings to provide insight into the pathophysiology of bvFTD. Subjects will be grouped according to those who fulfill international criteria for possible (fulfills clinical syndrome) or probable bvFTD (clinical syndrome plus brain atrophy), with comparisons made to analyze differences in rate of clinical progression according to cognitive and functional scores. Imaging data will be compared between both groups, but also with age-matched longitudinal healthy control data to determine differences in rate of brain atrophy. Many patients without atrophy on MRI only satisfycriteria for possible bvFTD and remain in this category for years. Some of these patients are described as “phenocopy” cases. Identifying possible bvFTD cases that will evolve to probable disease, and at what time point remains difficult. This longitudinal study is ideal to address these issues and explore these outcomes.
kw: Dementia, biomarkers, longitudinal study

title: Injury in the Over 55: Risk Factors and Determinants for Increased Healthcare Utilization Post-Injury
abs: Specific AimsThe primary objective of this proposal is to identify modifiable factors that drive healthcare utilization following moderate and severe injury in older Singaporeans. The secondary objective is to quantify the societal and economic impact after injury. To this end, we propose the first prospective cohort study of older Singaporeans hospitalized for injuryrelated to the most common mechanisms of injury in Singapore: falls and motor vehicle injuries.Hypothesis1. In the over-55, the risk of increased healthcare utilization (both outpatient visits and in-patient hospitalization) and re-hospitalization within 12 months of moderate (injury severity score ISS 9-15) and severe (ISS >15) injury is increased by certain pre-existing medical (co-morbid) conditions, specific injury types, poor functional outcome at discharge,reduced compliance with rehabilitation, lack of social support, and postinjury caregiver burden.2. The effect of injury on patients’ lifestyle interacts with pre-injury health, socio-demographic and caregiver arrangements to determine post-injury lifestyle, caregiver burden and compliance with rehabilitation.SignificanceMore than 4000 patients with moderate or severe injuries are admitted to hospital annually, with approximately half aged over 55 years.In Singapore, the all-cause readmission rate within six months of injury, as captured by the National Trauma Registry (NTR), is higher for the more severely injured (ISS>15, 10.0%), compared to the moderately injured (ISS 9-15, 5.6%), for older patients (age over 55, 7.5%), compared to younger patients (age below 55, 5.9%), and for patientswith multiple co-morbidities (11.1% in patients aged over 55 with Charlson scores of 2 or more).MethodologyCohort study of older patients admitted to a public hospital after moderate (injury severity score of 9 to 15) or severe (injury severity score of 16 or more) injury. Two surveys (PHASE questionnaire and modified caregiver reaction assessment) that have been used in older patients in Singapore will be administered.
kw: Ageing Rehabilitation Risk Factors Community Prevention Healthcare Utilization Injury Trauma Care Co-ordination

title: Developing phosphorylated IRAK1 (p-IRAK1) as targeted treatment for triple negative breast cancer
abs: Background. Prognosis of triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) remains poor. Chemotherapy is the only available systemic modality, and there are no approved targeted therapies. We have identified the phosphorylated form of IRAK1 (p-IRAK1) as a novel biomarker that predicts recurrence and identifies paclitaxel-resistant TNBCs that benefit from alternate treatments. Hypothesis. Tumours overexpressing p-IRAK1 while resistant to paclitaxel, respond to alternate non-cross resistant agents (cisplatin, gemcitabine) and IRAK1 inhibitor pacritinib. Objectives. We aim to validate the correlation of p-IRAK1 with outcome and pathological response (an indicator of chemo-sensitivity), and to evaluate the efficacy of cisplatin, gemcitabine and a paclitaxel/pacritinib combination in p-IRAK1-overexpressing (paclitaxel-resistant) tumours. Methodology. p-IRAK1 expression in tumours treated with taxanes will be evaluated with immunohistochemistry and correlated with clinical outcome and pathological response. Two independent cohorts will be evaluated. Efficacy studies of cisplatin, gemcitabine and paclitaxel/pacritinib combination will be performed in TNBC lines, first exposed to paclitaxel to induce resistance. Drug doses will be optimised and response (cell viability) stratified according to p-IRAK1 levels. The role of p-IRAK1 in acquired paclitaxel resistance will be verified by shRNA knockdown of IRAK1 and simultaneous re-introduction of a phosphorylation-resistant IRAK1 mutant. Efficacy studies will be repeated in MDA231 and SUM159 xenografts, and finally in patient derived xenografts generated from fresh TNBC samples. MDA231 and SUM159 xenografts and PDX from treatment naïve TNBC will first be exposed to paclitaxel to induce resistance before efficacy studies; this being unnecessary for PDX from post-taxane treated residual tumours, which are presumably already paclitaxel-resistant. Tumour response and complete regression will be correlated with p-IRAK1 levels. Xenografts will be characterised to identify other potential biomarkers. This study demonstrates several clinically useful applications of p-IRAK1 in TNBC: as a prognostic marker, predictor of paclitaxel resistance, predictor of response to alternate non-cross resistant agents, and as a novel therapeutic target.
kw: pIRAK1, triple negative breast cancer, alternate non-cross resistant agents, pacritinib

title: Educating maternal immunity to improve donor cell engraftment: The kinetics of maternal immune cell trafficking and a novel therapeutic strategy in a murine.
abs: Intrauterine haemopoietic stem cell transplantation (IUHSCT) has the potential to cure inherited genetic diseases before the onset of irreversible pathology, and can be applied to a variety of congenital disorders, with the fetus’ relative immune-nai?vete? being a critical advantage. However, the challenge remains of achieving significant engraftment following IUHSCT in the context of competent fetal immunity. While much is known about individual maternal and fetal responses to transplacentally-trafficked antigens, the gaps in knowledge concern the maternal immune system’s influence on fetal alloresponsiveness, and how this affects donor cell engraftment following IUHSCT. A persistent maternal immune presence in the recipient fetus may influence rejection of donor cells over time. This is an important mechanism to understand considering the broad applicability of IUHSCT. While our long-term objective is successful IUHSCT for major thalassaemias, our short-term objective is to probe the relationship between trafficked maternal immune cells and donor cell engraftment. We propose that trafficked maternal immune cells influence donor cell engraftment following allogeneic IUHSCT, and that blocking maternal antigen presenting cells (APC) will educate maternal T cells to become tolerant to donor cells and in transplanted fetuses. Our specific aims will elucidate the kinetics of trafficked maternal cells in a semi-allogeneic fetus, first in an uninterrupted pregnancy, then following allogeneic IUHSCT, alone and with maternal APC depletion using a transgenic B6/CD11c.DTR model. Donor cell chimerism will be examined after IUHSCT and postnatal re-transplantation, as will fetal immune response to the latter. If this strategy enhances engraftment, we will use it to demonstrate proof of cure in a knockout mouse model of thalassaemia major in future work. This research may uncover new knowledge into mechanisms underlying maternal-fetal immune tolerance and long-term transplant engraftment, and create opportunities for novel therapeutic strategies to fulfil the potential of IUHSCT.

title: An Immunological Study on the effects of radioembolization in combination with anti-PD1 therapy in hepatocellular carcinoma
abs: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the sixth most common form of malignancy worldwide and the second most common cause of cancer- related mortality. It has especially high prevalence in Southeast Asia, due to the high rates of viral hepatitis, including chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV). Escape from immune control is a critical hallmark of cancer that has recently come under intense scrutiny with the dramatic yet unpredictable successes of cancer immunotherapies, such as Merck’s Pembrolizumab (anti-PD1). Here, leveraging our current clinical practices, permitting us to perform a small clinical trial in collaboration with Merck, and our unique capacity to deeply probe antigen-specific T cell responses, we will investigate relationships between the antigen- specific T cell response to HCC and HBV in the context of transarterial radiombolization with Yittrium-90 microspheres and in combination with Pembrolizumab. In the process, a number of immunological mechanisms will be explored as we test the hypothesis that liver-localized radioembolization will stimulate tumour and/or HBV specific T cell responses that are associated with favourable patient outcomes and that can be boosted using anti-PD1 immunotherapy. In aim 1, we will use existing tools to evaluate T cell responses to known HBV, HCC tumour and other unrelated antigens in the blood before, during and after radioembolization treatment. In aim 2, we will use blood and liver tissues obtained from HCC tumour resection patients to compare profiles of antigen-specific T cells of patients with or without chronic HBV infection. This will allow us to validate strategies for identifying individualized blood- derived tumour-specific T cells used in aim 3. Finally, in aim 3, a clinical trial with deep exploratory analysis will be performed to assess the benefit of using Pembrolizumab in combination with radioembolization therapy. This study will help lead the way to the broader more effective usage of immunotherapy for cancer patients in Singapore.
kw: Hepatocellular carcinoma, Radioembolization, Anti-PD1, Immunology, Immunotherapy, Immune checkpoint bloackade

title: Evaluation of predictive factors for outcomes for knee replacement surgery in osteoarthritis in a multi-ethnic Asian country
abs: Background. The demand for total knee replacement (TKR) has been increasing worldwide, and the need for surgery is projected to rise by over 600% by 2030. There are 15-30% of patients who report little or no improvement after TKR for knee osteoarthritis (KOA). Traditional socio-demographic and clinical factors do not fully explain why some patients do not respond to surgery. Hypothesis. There are some biological and psychological factors, like pain sensitization, widespread pain, pain catastrophizing, and mood symptoms that may better explain knee replacement outcome. Aim. We aim to evaluate factors that better predict outcomes for TKR for knee osteoarthritis. We also aim to identify patients who may not respond to surgery and provide alternative intervention before or in place of surgery.Methods. We will prospectively assess 1500 consecutive patients enlisted for TKR at Singapore General Hospital. Assessment will include demographics, knee symptoms, widespread pain, neuropathic pain, pain catetrophizing and mood symptoms before surgery. Pressure pain thresholds at the knee and a distant body part will be measured using digital pressure algometry. Patients will then undergo similar assessments at 6 months, 1 year and 2 years after surgery. Poor outcome will be defined as reporting “somewhat dissatisfied” with the overall result of surgery. Clinical Significance. Identifying factors associated with poor outcomes to TKR is the first step in optimizing utilization of TKR. Patients could then be offered alternative therapies, like physiotherapy, bracing, and medications for surgery or even in place of TKR.
kw: prediction, knee replacement surgery, osteoarthritis

title: Platelet inhibition to target reperfusion injury: The PITRI trial
abs: Clinical need: There remains a clinical need to improve health outcomes in patients with ischemic heart disease (IHD) the leading cause of death and disability in Singapore and worldwide. One neglected therapeutic target is ‘myocardial reperfusion injury’ in ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) patients treated by primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PPCI). This results in microvascular obstruction (MVO) and cardiomyocyte death and contributes upto 50% of the final myocardial infarct (MI) size. Cangrelor, a potent intravenous platelet P2Y12 inhibitor with rapid onset and offset of action, has been demonstrated in experimental animal studies to reduce MI size when administered prior to reperfusion. Whether Cangrelor is effective in STEMI patients treated by PPCI is not known and is investigated in the Platelet Inhibition to Target Reperfusion Injury (PITRI) trial.Specific aim: To investigate whether Cangrelor administered prior to PPCI, can prevent MVO and reduce MI size in STEMI patients.Hypothesis: Cangrelor administered prior to PPCI will prevent MVO and reduce MI size in STEMI patients.Methodology: The PITRI proof-of-concept clinical trial will randomise 250 STEMI patients to receive either Cangrelor (single intravenous bolus followed by a 120-minute infusion) or matching normal/saline placebo, initiated prior to PPCI. The primary endpoint will be MI size at 6 months (measured by cardiac MRI). Secondary endpoints will include incidence and extent of MVO (cardiac MRI); and left ventricular size and ejection fraction (measured by cardiac MRI at 6 months).Expected outcome: If Cangrelor is shown to prevent MVO and reduce MI size, there is the potential to perform a large phase 3 clinical trial to determine whether it can improve clinical outcomes at one year (cardiac death and hospitalisation for heart failure), thereby demonstrating a real impact on health outcomes for IHD patients in Singapore and worldwide.
kw: Cangrelor; ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction; Primary percutaneous coronary intervention; Myocardial reperfusion injury; Microvascular obstruction; Cardioprotection

title: Carbohydrate (Chondroitin 6) Sulfotransferase-3 in Breast Cancer: Expression and Functional Studies and Evaluation of Potential Clinical Use in Patient Prognosis and Therapeutics
abs: Breast cancer is the commonest malignancy and top cause of cancer deaths in women globally. Locally, breast cancer incidence has tripled over the past four decades. Thus, there is an important need for better patient prognostication and therapeutic options. Carbohydrate (chondroitin 6) sulfotransferase-3 (CHST3) catalyses the addition of sulfate groups to chondroitin. Our preliminary study of breast cancer samples showed that reduced CHST3 expression was significantly associated with late stage tumours, leading to our hypothesis that CHST3 may suppress cancerous behaviour. Silencing CHST3 expression in poorly-invasive breast cancer cells resulted in doubling of their invasive capacity. The opposite was seen after overexpressing CHST3 in highly invasive MDA-MB-231 cells. Chondroitin monomers bearing 6-O-sulfate groups reduced cancer cell viability and invasion, and augmented the cytotoxicity of chemotherapeutic agents in cancer cells but not in non-tumourigenic breast epithelial cells. Hence, this project aims to determine if CHST3 can be used for patient prognostication, understand the mechanisms by which CHST3 regulates breast cancer behaviour, and explore if it can be exploited for therapeutic purposes. The expression pattern of CHST3 will be examined in breast cancer tissue samples, and analysed for associations with clinicopathological features. Survival analysis will evaluate if CHST3 can predict patient survival and cancer recurrence. Knockdown/knockout and overexpression of CHST3 will be carried out to determine its biological functions both in vitro and in vivo using a SCID mouse model. Candidate CHST3 signalling pathways will be identified through transcriptomic and proteomic studies using microarrays and mass spectrometry respectively, and selected pathways experimentally verified. Chondroitin oligosaccharides with specific sulfation patterns will be designed and tested for optimal augmentation of chemotherapeutic drug cytotoxicity in cancer cells with minimal side effects. Together, the study will lead to a better understanding of CHST3 in breast cancer, with potential improvements in patient prognostication and therapeutic options.
kw: Breast cancer, chondroitin sulfate, carbohydrate (chondroitin 6) sulfotransferase-3, biomarker, prognostic indicator, therapeutic target

title: Epigenetics of Psychotic Disorders: investigating the impact of early-life adversities on DNA methylation, white matter connectivity and symptoms severity.
abs: Although generally accepted that both genetic and environmental factors contribute to the risk of psychosis, there is still a lack of understanding on the precise biological mechanism that serve as a substrate for this interaction and may trigger the emergence of symptoms. A growing body of evidence documents the higher prevalence of trauma and disrupted parenting in psychiatric populations. Trauma experienced during childhood can affect DNA methylation of genes involved in synaptogenesis and cell signaling and contribute to the emergence of psychosis in adult life. The specific aims for this study are (i) to demonstrate higher prevalence of early-life trauma in adolescents with prodromal symptoms of psychosis (UHR), first-episode (FE) and chronic schizophrenia (CSZ) patients, (ii) to demonstrate altered methylation of the RELN, NR3C1, FKBP5, BDNF, 5HTR1A and GAD1 gene promoters in UHR, FE and CSZ (iii) to show impaired white-matter integrity at the Superior Longitudinal, Inferior Longitudinal, Uncinate Fasciculi level in UHR, FE and CSZ (iv) to demonstrate that trauma-triggered epigenetic abnormalities mediate between impaired white-matter integrity and severity of both psychotic and non-psychotic comorbid symptoms. Four groups of participants will be studied: (1) a group of 93 UHR participants, (2) a group of 50 FE patients, (3) a group of 100 CSZ patients and (4) a group of 148 healthy controls (HC). Methylation percentage differences across the four groups will be tested for each of the six gene promoters by repeated measures MANCOVA with five covariates (age, gender, BMI, medication and ethnicity). Regression analyses will probe the association between severity of trauma, methylation percentage, white matter integrity as measured by Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) and symptoms severity.
kw: Schizophrenia, DNA Methylation, Diffusion Tensor Imaging, Disconnection Hypothesis, Trauma

title: Response of the myocardium to hypertrophic conditions in the adult population
abs: Calcific aortic stenosis and hypertensive heart disease are leading causes of adult heart failure. In response to the increased afterload, myocardial hypertrophy is initially compensatory to maintain cardiac function. Due to progressive myocyte death and myocardial fibrosis, ventricular decompensation and heart failure ultimately occur.Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) techniques and high-sensitivity cardiac troponin I are novel markers of myocardial fibrosis. Therefore, they hold potential of identifying patients at risk of heart failure. We hypothesize myocardial fibrosis is associated with impaired ventricular function recovery after valve replacement in patients with small aortic valve area low transvalvular gradient (small-area low-gradient) aortic stenosis and impaired systolic ejection fraction; and it is associated with increased left ventricular mass and reduced cardiac performance in patients with essential hypertension. The specific study aims are to:(1) Establish reference ranges of cardiac morphology in an Asian population Current CMR reference ranges were developed in Caucasian populations. We will establish reference ranges of cardiac morphology in 240 healthy adults using 3T CMR, in order to develop new paradigms for assessing myocardial disease in Singapore.(2) Validate markers of myocardial fibrosis in predicting functional recovery after aortic valve replacementContemporary approach of dobutamine stress echocardiography is limited in predicting myocardial function recovery after valve replacement in patients with small-area low-gradient aortic stenosis and impaired ejection fraction. In 50 patients with small-area low-gradient aortic stenosis and impaired ejection fraction, we will investigate novel imaging and circulating markers of fibrosis in predicting myocardial function recovery after valve replacement.(3) Assess determinants associated with myocardial fibrosis in patients with essential hypertensionThe significance of myocardial fibrosis in hypertensive heart disease is currently not well characterized, underscoring a critical knowledge gap. We will determine the association of left ventricular mass, measures of cardiac performance and peripheral blood pressure with myocardial fibrosis in 500 patients with essential hypertension.
kw: cardiovascular magnetic resonance imaging; aortic stenosis; hypertensive heart disease; left ventricular hypertrophy; myocardial fibrosis

title: Research and Development Platform for medical technologies at NHCS: The Medtech elab
abs: AIMSThis proposal is to support the set-up at NHCS of a Med-Tech portal called the eLAB. The eLAB is designed to provide expertise for training and preclinical evaluation of novel cardiovascular technologies and serve as platform for both NHCS clinical investigators led projects as well as partnership with industry.BACKGROUNDNHCS has developed and cultivated a number of collaborations with industrial partners, typically at the time point of clinical trials of new devices/therapeutics. NHCS has the largest flow of patients with cardiovascular diseases in Singapore with over 100,000 cardiovascular outpatient visits and over 3000 operations every year. Medical Technologies play a large role in diagnostic, monitoring and rehabilitation of our patients. PROPOSALWe will set-up eLAB around 4 translational core research capabilities:Focus 1 : Visual Heart Lab / In-vitro Medtech experimentationAnatomical heart models, lab instruments, pulse replication pumps, training tools and 3D visual heart imaging capabilities Focus 2 : Digital-Heart Lab: Sensors/Analytics Sensors, monitoring, Clinical Data AnalyticsFocus 3 : Pre-clinical In-vivo Models In-vivo preclinical disease models, device safety testing.Focus 4 : Virtual Heart Lab Computer models of heart diseases/treatment simulation. Proposal includes manpower and equipment for establishing eLAB and initiate pilot research projects, with high potential of attracting industry co-funding or commercialization. eLAB will be integrated into our National Heart Research Institute Singapore (NHRIS) structure and serve as platform for NHCS clinical investigators led projects as well as partnership with industry and institutional collaborators. IMPACTIn practice, currently no cardiovascular research institute in Singapore has a platform dedicated and designed specifically for medical device research. During tenure of this grant, we will specifically target to grow collaborations between clinical P.I.s, scientists and industry partners based on our 4 described focus areas. We believe that this platform will increase the opportunities and avenues for NHCS-Industry collaboration.

title: Targeting Ceramide Kinase and Ceramide-1-Phosphate in Limiting Endometriosis Lesion Vascularization and Development
abs: Endometriosis, characterized by vascularized endometrial lesions outside of the uterine cavity, affects up to 12% of women with significant morbidity of severe chronic pelvic pain and infertility among other complications. Symptom relief and hormonal suppression are the primary goals of existing treatment options, but with significant side effects and do not address disease recurrence. Hence, novel, nonhormonal therapies are urgently needed. Endometriotic lesions must stay within a strict vasculature radius to ensure continued growth. We found significantly elevated ceramide-1-phosphate (C1P) in the peritoneal fluids of endometriotic women and in activated macrophages. Ceramide kinase (CerK), the central enzyme in generating C1P, is known to be angiogenic/vasculogenic, hence providing an excellent target for suppressing endometriotic lesion vascularization and growth. NVP-231 is a recently developed competitive CerK inhibitor that specifically keeps C1P levels low. Hypothesis: Thus, disruption of lesion vasculature via abrogation of ceramide phosphorylation by NVP-231 may present as an attractive nonhormonal strategy to controlling endometriosis. Aims: (I) Identify and characterize peritoneal macrophage phenotypes in ectopic sites and peritoneal fluids in endometriosis. (II) Dissect the mechanisms and molecular collaborations between macrophages and endothelial cells played by CerK and C1P in network stabilization. Understanding the key determinants of CerK inhibition on vasculostabilization via NVP-231 will shed light on a critical aspect of controlling lesion growth and development. Approach: Lesion vasculature destabilization can be studied by using human endothelial cells grown in 3D cultures exposed to C1P, NVP-231 and other treatment conditions, and together with macrophages. Our preliminary studies identified C1P as a potent inducer of endothelial cell vascular stabilization. Investigations on known and novel targets of vasculostabilization identified through transcriptomics will be conducted to understand their spatial localization, activity and regulation with CerK suppression. If successful, results from this proposal will facilitate the development of a novel drug candidate for endometriosis management.
kw: Endometriosis, macrophages, ceramide kinase, ceramide-1-phosphate, vascular network

title: Characterizing the Role of Iris Surface Features in Iris Sponginess and their relevance to Angle-Closure Glaucoma
abs: Primary angle-closure glaucoma (PACG) is common and visually destructive, particularly in Asia. About 10% of adults have narrow angles, the anatomical trait predisposing to PACG. Laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI) has been commonly used as a prophylactic procedure for people with narrow-angles to prevent acute primary angle closure (APAC). However, evidence is lacking as to its efficacy in preventing the progression to PACG, as only 1 in 10 narrow-angle persons would develop PACG if untreated. Established anatomic parameters do not sufficiently explain why many people with small eyes never develop glaucoma. LPI, while relatively safe, has potential adverse consequences. Therefore, there is a need for clinicians to accurately identify those who are at greatest risk for progression to glaucoma and/or development of an APAC attack, and thus really need LPI. Our objective is to develop a novel approach using easily observable iris surface features (crypts, furrows and color) to effectively identify the “at risk” patients. Altered dynamic iris response has been proposed as a contributing factor for PACG. Patients whose irises retain aqueous humor on dilation are the most likely to develop APAC attack, because the iris remains thick and blocks the angle. We hypothesized that eyes with less iris crypts and more furrows have poorer iris “sponginess”, i.e., poorer aqueous humor conductivity between iris stroma and anterior chamber. We propose a comprehensive study, integrating clinical and imaging investigations to characterize iris surface features and elucidate their associations with 1) dynamic iris response, 2) the progression of angle closure, and 3) the risk of APAC in narrow-angle eyes. We will developan automated program to quantify the iris surface features and ascertain these associations. The findings of this study may provide a useful clinical LPI treatment guideline for angle-closure disease not only in Singapore but have a major clinical impact worldwide.
kw: Primary angle closure glaucoma, Iris, Laser peripheral iridotomy, Risk prediction, Optical coherence tomography, Automated iris detection

title: The Use of Atropine 0.01% in the Prevention and Progression of Myopia: ATOM 3
abs: Epidemiological data shows that 80% of 18 year old Singaporeans will become myopic (SE<-0.5D), and 15% will have high myopia (SE<-5.0D)1-3. High myopia is associated with ocular morbidity (eg. macular degeneration, glaucoma and retinal detachment) later in life4. Ways of tackling this problem include delaying the onset of myopia and preventing children from developing high myopia. The aim of this study is to evaluate the use of atropine 0.01% in premyopic and low-myopic children. Previous Atropine Treatment of Myopia (ATOM) studies suggest that atropine 0.01% daily slowedmyopia progression by 58% over 2 years in children aged 6-12 years5, with less side effects (pupil dilation and near blur) compared to higher doses. We hypothesise that atropine 0.01% will also be effective in preventing the onset and progression of myopia in young Singaporean children at greater risk of developing high myopia (ie. with family history). We also hope to determine efficacy of lower frequencies of atropine. In this study, we hope to recruit 470 pre-myopic children (SE +1.00 to -0.49D) and 150 low myopic children (SE -0.50 to 1.25D). Pre-myopic children will be randomized to atropine 0.01% daily or placebo, while low myopic children will be randomized to either atropine 0.01% daily, every alternate day or placebo. Included will be children aged 5-9 years old, preferably with 2 myopic parents (each with at least -1.00D of myopia). Children will be followed every 6 months for 2.5 years with a final (washout) visit at 3 years. Outcome measures in pre-myopic children will be the proportion of children developing myopia (SE <-0.50D) or low myopia (-0.50 to -1.50D) and in low-myopic children, outcomes measures will be a mean change in SE, and proportion ofchildren with myopia (>1.50D) at 3 years.
kw: Atropine 0.01%, myopia, progression, prevention

title: Whole-genome Sequencing to Assess Effectiveness of Control Strategies Combating Carbapenemase-producing Enterobacteriaceae in Singapore from 2010 to 2015: the Carbapenemase-Producing Enterobacteriaceae (CaPES) Study Group
abs: Introduction:Carbapenemase-producing Enterobacteriaceae (CPE) are a global, antibiotic-resistant “superbug” threat with 40 to 80% mortality. Without safe, efficacious anti-CPE antimicrobials, infection control remains the main practical intervention to reduce CPE morbidity and mortality. Infection control is hindered by inability to accurately determine transmission pathways. Standard-of-care infection control practices are based on the dogma of the detected CPE-carrier as the main source of CPE transmission, despite lack of population evidence to support this assertion and known alternate sources of transmission (e.g. inanimate objects). CPE numbers in Singapore increase despite international standard-of-care infection control practices.A recent seminal publication on another nosocomial gastrointestinal pathogen, C. difficile highlighted whole-genome sequencing combined with a regional (multi-centered; 4 hospitals; combined 1,600 beds providing 90% of hospital services) approach as game-changing inunderstanding C. difficile transmission and evaluating infection control interventions. We adopt a similar design in our current proposal on CPE.Aims and Methods:Our current proposal aims to apply whole-genome sequencing on all CPE isolates detected from all acute-care Singapore government hospitals (7 hospitals; combined 7,161 beds covering 80% of the country’s inpatient admissions) from the onset of the Singapore CPE epidemic in September 2010 to April 2015 (~5 years) to understand CPE transmission and evaluate infection control interventions.Our specific aims are to:1. title: Integrated computational modelling of right heart mechanics and blood flow dynamics in congenital heart disease
abs: Advances in paediatric cardiology and cardiac surgery have enabled the survival of most patients born with congenital heart disease (CHD) into adulthood. Many CHD patients have undergone palliative or reparative surgery earlier in life. As patients survive into adulthood, they may need intervention or surgery for residual haemodynamic lesions. This is because they are at risk of arrhythmias secondary to structure heart disease and are susceptible to acquired heart disease. In these patients, pre-operative and post-operative evaluation of right ventricular (RV) structure (shape and volume) and function is an essential component of clinical management.Advances have been made in cardiac imaging so that accurate assessment of the right heart chamber in terms of its structure, function and physiology is possible. However, this technology has as yet never been applied in an effort to comprehensively assess RV structure, function and physiology. CMR will be used in this comprehensive assessment of structure and function. Multiple RV parameters will be characterized: RV structure (volume and curvedness in a 15-segment RV model), RV function (EF, Regional area strain in a 15-segment RV model) and RV physiology (RV vortex size). Thus, this research will allow development of a comprehensive integrated biomedical engineering (BME) R&D platform for in-depth study and clinical diagnosis of the RV structure-function relationship and physiology and its association with exercise capacity.Specific Aim #1 (Primary aim): Establish a prospective clinical and image registry of paediatric and adult CHD patients with reference control subjects. Specific Aim #2 (Secondary Aim): Study intra-cardiac blood flow using computational fluid dynamics (CFD) to quantitate RV vortex surface area in CHD vs. healthy control subjects.Specific Aim #3 (Exploratory aim): Generate CMR-derived RV pressurevolume loop for quantitation of RV wall stiffness and contractility and ventricular-arterial coupling in patients with pulmonary hypertension (PH) These new findings will enable clinicians to recognize RV dysfunction promptly and optimize individual patient management in preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative interventions.

title: Clinician Scientist/ Clinician Investigator Salary Support Programme
abs: In Singapore, diabetes constitutes 10% of disease burden and 25% of pregnancies are complicated by gestational diabetes (GDM), which is linked with fetal macrosomia, adverse obstetric outcomes and future offspring risk of obesity and type 2 diabetes. Preliminary studies suggest that myoinositol supplementation reduces the rate of GDM but its mechanism of effect in pregnancy is not understood. The placenta is a focal point of GDM pathophysiology, with placental lipid flux postulated to be the main driver of fetal adiposity. Our overarching hypothesis is that dysregulated placental lipid flux is a major determinant of fetal fat accretion in GDM, and that this pathophysiology is amenable to correction by myoinositol supplementation to reduce the risk of fetal macrosomia. This proposal aims to (i) characterise the specific changes in placental lipid flux associated with placental myoinositol status, (ii) assess the effects of in vitro myoinositol treatment on placental uptake and metabolism of stable isotope-labelled fatty acids, (iii) determine if these effects are mediated by disruptions in second messenger signalling, PPAR activity, secretion of signalling agents, and expression of proteins involved in lipid transport and metabolism, (iv) investigate if in vivo myoinositol supplementation in the NiPPeR randomised controlled trial, regulates placental lipid flux thus reducing fetal fat accretion and macrosomia risk in GDM. This innovative, integrated series of experiments ranging from in vitro to in vivo studies, employing advanced LC-MS lipidomics, utilising perinatal samples from the three Singaporean birth cohorts with extensive phenotypic data, provide an unprecedented opportunity to investigate the mechanistic effects of myoinositol in pregnancy. The evidence gained from this proposal will provide critical scientific underpinning for on-going clinical trials and would greatly strengthen support for widespread implementation of a potentially effective and first ever supplementation strategy for GDM prevention with substantial public health impact worldwide.

title: Phase II study of Intravenous Vinorelbine in Patients with Relapsed Platinum Resistant or Refractory C5 High Grade Serous, Endometrioid, or Undifferentiated Primary Peritoneum, Fallopian Tube or Ovarian Cancer (VIP)
abs: It has been difficult to progress beyond platinum-based therapy for the treatment of ovarian cancer (OC) because OC is still largely treated as a single entity. A number of sub-classifications of the most common OC histiotype – high-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSOC) suggest that more specific therapeutic approaches may be useful. Four molecular subtypes of HGSOC – C1, C2, C4 and C5 which correlate with clinical outcome have been validated. The C5 subtype, comprises about 15- 20% of HGSOC, is associated with a poor outcome and potential oncogenic drivers have been identified. Recent preclinical experiments demonstrated vinca alkaloids targeted C5 subtype more effectively compared to the other subtypes. Several phase II trials of vinorelbine in recurrent OC have shown variable response rates of 3 – 29%, however, previous studies have involved “all comers” and there has never been a trial involving patient selection based on pure HGSOC and biomarkers of response. Our aim is to determine if targeting treatment based on the C5 molecular subtype with vinorelbine improves response rates and progression free survival.This open label phase II trial is a collaboration between Singapore and Australia for patients with platinum resistant or refractory C5 high-grade serous, high grade endometrioid or undifferentiated ovarian, primary peritoneal and fallopian tube cancer. A total of 36 patients with confirmed C5 HGSC based on the molecular classifier developed by the NATA accredited Bowtel Lab will be recruited and treated with 25mg/m2 intravenous vinorelbine until the appearance of significant treatment-related toxicity or disease progression. Dose modifications will be made based on a proforma. Simon’s Optimal two-stage design will be employed with a hypothesis of response rate <10% based on historical data; and the alternative hypothesis of response rates ?30% in patients with C5 HGSC following treatment with vinorelbine.

title: Developing Experimental Therapeutics and Understanding Mechanisms of Drug Resistance in Asian Breast Cancer
abs: Systemic treatment remains the cornerstone for breast cancer therapy, but intra-patient tumor heterogeneity and tumor evolution following drug treatment are major challenges to effective therapy. Funded by the NMRC Senior Clinician Scientist Award over the last five years, we have developed an internationally recognized breast cancer program comprising of a clinical trial program to test novel treatment strategies along with a breast tissue biobank and pharmacogenetic DNA bank for discovery of tumor and host predictive biomarkers of treatment response and toxicity. In parallel, we have established a translational laboratory to analyze drug pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic effects, and a pilot study to enrich circulating tumor cells (CTCs) with culture to increase their detection limit. In the next five years, we will expand the program by: (1) continuing to design and execute clinical trials in the refractory/metastatic, neoadjuvant, or window-of-opportunity settings, focusing on optimizing combination strategies between novel biological agents and the backbone chemotherapy or endocrine therapy of breast cancer. In addition, we will evaluate immunotherapy in breast cancer using a patented technology to expand and activate autologous natural killer cells to enhance antibody-directed cell cytotoxicity mediated by therapeutic monoclonal antibodies such as trastuzumab; (2) expand our collection of resistant tumors post-systemic therapy for deep molecular characterization and to generate patient-derived cell lines for in vitro drug sensitivity studies to understand mechanisms of resistance and uncover potential therapeutic targets to inform the selection of drugs in clinical trials; and (3) develop a reliable liquid biopsy protocol for ex vivo drug sensitivity testing using enriched CTCs and test its utility in guiding therapy and tracking progress in the clinic. This breast cancer experimental therapeutics program will address the challenges of tumor heterogeneity, tumor evolution and drug resistance, with the ultimate goal of applying the findings in routine clinical practice and improving patient outcome.
kw: Breast cancer, Drug resistance, Developmental therapeutics, Circulating tumor cells, Predictive biomarkers, Clinical trials

title: Whole-genome Sequencing to Assess Effectiveness of Control Strategies Combating Carbapenemase-producing Enterobacteriaceae in Singapore from 2010 to 2015: the Carbapenemase-Producing Enterobacteriaceae (CaPES) Study Group.
abs: Introduction: Carbapenemase-producing Enterobacteriaceae (CPE) are a global, antibiotic-resistant “superbug” threat with 40 to 80% mortality. Without safe, efficacious anti-CPE antimicrobials, infection control remains the main practical intervention to reduce CPE morbidity and mortality. Infection control is hindered by inability to accurately determine transmission pathways. Standard-of-care infection control practices are based on the dogma of the detected CPE-carrier as the main source of CPE transmission, despite lack of population evidence to support this assertion and known alternate sources of transmission (e.g. inanimate objects). CPE numbers in Singapore increase despite international standard-of-care infection control practices. A recent seminal publication on another nosocomial gastrointestinal pathogen, C. difficile highlighted whole-genome sequencing combined with a regional (multi-centered; 4 hospitals; combined 1,600 beds providing 90% of hospital services) approach as game-changing in understanding C. difficile transmission and evaluating infection control interventions. We adopt a similar design in our current proposal on CPE.Aims and Methods: Our current proposal aims to apply whole-genome sequencing on all CPE isolates detected from all acute-care Singapore government hospitals (7 hospitals; combined 7,161 beds covering 80% of the country’s inpatient admissions) from the onset of the Singapore CPE epidemic in September 2010 to April 2015 (~5 years) to understand CPE transmission and evaluate infection control interventions. Our specific aims are to:1.Estimate the prevalence of genetically-linked CPE transmissions in Singapore government hospitals attributable to unknown sources over a five-year period (2010 to 2015);2.Evaluate effectiveness of hospital-based infection control strategies in Singapore government hospitals over a five-year period by determining the rate of change over time of proportion of new cases due to genetically-linked transmissions (2010 to 2015).Clinical significance:1. This study would provide “real-world” data for uncovering sources of CPE transmission. 2. This study would enable population-level assessment of effectiveness of interventions targeting CPE transmission and disease. Word count: 299

title: Developing phosphorylated IRAK1 (p-IRAK1) as targeted treatment in triple negative breast cancer
abs: Background. Prognosis of triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) remains poor. Chemotherapy is the only available systemic modality, and there are no approved targeted therapies. We have identified the phosphorylated form of IRAK1 (p-IRAK1) as a novel biomarker that predicts recurrence and identifies paclitaxel-resistant TNBCs that benefit from alternate treatments. Hypothesis. Tumours overexpressing p-IRAK1 while resistant to paclitaxel, respond to alternate non-cross resistant agents (cisplatin, gemcitabine) and IRAK1 inhibitor pacritinib. Objectives. We aim to validate the correlation of p-IRAK1 with outcome and pathological response (an indicator of chemo-sensitivity), and to evaluate the efficacy of cisplatin, gemcitabine and a paclitaxel/pacritinib combination in p-IRAK1-overexpressing (paclitaxel-resistant) tumours. Methodology. p-IRAK1 expression in tumours treated with taxanes will be evaluated with immunohistochemistry and correlated with clinical outcome and pathological response. Two independent cohorts will be evaluated. Efficacy studies of cisplatin, gemcitabine and paclitaxel/pacritinib combination will be performed in TNBC lines, first exposed to paclitaxel to induce resistance. Drug doses will be optimised and response (cell viability) stratified according to p-IRAK1 levels. The role of p-IRAK1 in acquired paclitaxel resistance will be verified by shRNA knockdown of IRAK1 and simultaneous re-introduction of a phosphorylation-resistant IRAK1 mutant. Efficacy studies will be repeated in MDA231 and SUM159 xenografts, and finally in patient derived xenografts generated from fresh TNBC samples. MDA231 and SUM159 xenografts and PDX from treatment naïve TNBC will first be exposed to paclitaxel to induce resistance before efficacy studies; this being unnecessary for PDX from post-taxane treated residual tumours, which are presumably already paclitaxel-resistant. Tumour response and complete regression will be correlated with p-IRAK1 levels. Xenografts will be characterised to identify other potential biomarkers. This study demonstrates several clinically useful applications of p-IRAK1 in TNBC: as a prognostic marker, predictor of paclitaxel resistance, predictor of response to alternate non-cross resistant agents, and as a novel therapeutic target.
kw: pIRAK1, triple negative breast cancer, alternate non-cross resistant agents, pacritinib

title: Evaluation of comparative in vitro and in vivo nephrotoxicity of novel antifungal agents
abs: Candida albicans is a major fungal pathogen of humans, affecting millions and killing hundreds of thousands annually. Emerging drug resistance and undesirable properties of existing antifungal agents are major problems in managing C. albicans infections. We recently discovered a novel molecule, SM21 with promising antifungal properties. Subsequently through a NMRC-CIRG grant, we identified glucan 1,3-beta-glucosidase, an important component of C. albicans cell wall, as the potential drug target. Further development of SM21 into an antifungal drug requires pre-clinical toxicological studies of SM21 and its analogue CID2147408.The present study aims to evaluate the comparative nephrotoxicity of novel antifungal candidates with established antifungal agents by using a novel in vitro model and a standard in vivo murine model. We will examine the nephrotoxicity of SM21 and CID2147408 in comparison with the common antifungal agents, amphotericin B, liposomal amphotericin B, caspofungin and voriconazole in a newly established renal proximal tubular cell model that has a higher predictive value of human nephrotoxicity. This model includes high-throughput imaging, phenotypic profiling and machine learning. The murine model will include dose-dependent administration with control and tested compounds followed by histological evaluations (i.e. TUNEL assay, annexin V and trypan blue staining) and serum analyses (i.e. potassium, sodium, urea nitrogen, and creatinine levels). Foregoing studies will provide a vital dataset to comparatively evaluate potential human nephrotoxicity of established and novel antifungal agents. As a secondary objective, these data can also be used to evaluate our novel in vitro model vs. standard in vivo model in predicting human nephrotoxicity of antifungals. Hence, the present study will fulfil an essential aspect of SM21, safety before commencing human trials. If proven to be safe, the study will lead to a new class of antifungal agents. Therefore, the success of the project is clinically and commercially valuable and impactful.
kw: Candida albicans, antifungals, nephrotoxicity

title: Genome-Wide Environment-Interaction Study of Chronic Diseases and Ageing Outcomes in a Prospective Cohort of 30,000 Chinese in Singapore - The Singapore Chinese Health Study
abs: Precision public health is an emerging approach for disease prevention in the general population that takes into account individual variability in genes, environment and lifestyle for targeted preventive strategies. Understanding how genes and environment interact can help identify high-risk populations and devise precise behavioral and environmental modifications, thus leading to effective disease prevention. Recently, investigations on gene-environment interactions have been performed in Western populations. However, these results cannot be generalized easily to Asians, which remain a vastly understudied population. This proposal aims to conduct gene-environment interaction analyses between genome-wide DNA sequence variants and environmental exposures, including lifestyle and diet factors, in association with ageing outcomes and common diseases of public health importance in Singapore and globally. The study will be conducted on 30,000 participants who have donated blood in the on-going Singapore Chinese Health Study (SCHS), a population-based prospective cohort of middle-aged and elderly men and women assembled during 1993 to 1998, and continuously followed for incident morbidities and mortality via follow-up interviews and linkage with nationwide disease and death registries. The DNA has been extracted for genetic analysis. Data on lifestyle, dietary and environmental factors were collected at baseline recruitment (1993-1998), and selected factors were updated during follow-up 1 (1999-2004), follow-up 2 (2006-2010) and follow-up 3 (2014-2016) interviews. In addition, about 11,000 have also been assessed for cognitive, physical and functional status of ageing during follow-up 3. Significant interaction results, using SCHS as the discovery cohort, will be replicated for validation in other Asian cohorts, who have committed to collaborate in this effort. We have assembled a team of experienced collaborators with expertise in epidemiology, genomics and biostatistics. This extremely cost-efficient proposal will enable us to more accurately quantify genetic and environmental modifiers of health outcomes, thus empowering efforts at primary prevention and health systems research in Singapore.

title: Thyroid hormone regulation of hepatic mitochondrial turnover: Implications for NAFLD
abs: Thyroid hormone (TH) plays a key role in both hepatic gluconeogenesis and lipid metabolism. Previously, we found that thyroid hormone (TH, T3), stimulates hepatic autophagy. In particular, we observed that lipids from fat droplets are incorporated into autophagosomes that fuse with lysosomes (lipophagy) whereupon triglycerides are hydrolyzed into fatty acids that undergo -oxidation in mitochondria. We also showed that mitophagy and increased mitochondrial synthesis are coupled with increased TH-mediated lipophagy. Moreover, this increase in mitochondrial turnover is absolutely necessary to maintain quality control of mitochondria and efficient oxidative phosphorylation. Our preliminary studies also have shown that decreased intrahepatic TH concentration may contribute to progression of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) as lipotoxicity from over-accumulation of lipids in the liver may induce mitochondrial dysfunction, cell death, and fibrosis, Additionally, SIRT1 plays an essential role in TH-mediated autophagy since siRNA knockdown of SIRT1 completely blocked autophagy induced by T3. Currently, the mechanism(s) for TH regulation of mitochondrial turnover and the role of SIRT1 in this process is not well understood. We hypothesize that TH and SIRT1 play important roles in the regulation of TH-mediated mitochondrial turnover in normal physiological conditions and in NAFLD and propose:Specific Aim 1: To determine the mechanisms for TH-mediated mitochondrial turnover by mitophagy and mitochondrial biogenesis. Specific Aim 2. To examine the role of SIRT1 on basal and TH-mediated mitochondrial turnover.Specific Aim 3. To examine the effects of TH in mitochondrial turnover in obesity and NAFLD.Understanding these mechanisms may lead to better hormonal/pharmacological management of NAFLD and other metabolic disorders
kw: mitophagy, Fatty acid, mitochondria, Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, autophagy, Thyroid hormone

title: A reproducible model for Influenza virus infection and co-infections of human nasal epithelial cells: towards transcriptomic signatures of susceptibility and severity
abs: Influenza virus infections are one of the most common infectious diseases worldwide. Our recent study (supported by NMRC CIRG 12nov033) has demonstrated the successful establishment of in vitro viral infection models of rhinovirus (RV16), H3N2 influenza virus and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) using human nasal epithelial cells (hNECs). Hence, we intend to further utilize the hNECs model to: (1) conduct repeated controlled influenza infection to obtain the post infection transcriptomic data of hNECs from each individual. Since the genetic information of the individual is retained in these cells, we aim to establish a repository that provide a reference transcriptome library and platform for further population level studies and surveillance of influenza infections with a greatly reduced number of subjects. Through this library platform we can (1a) identify possible gene susceptibility and severity signatures that affect viral replication kinetics in the nasal epithelium; (1b) monitor and predict the extent and severity of emerging strains with reference to existing strain; and (1c) utilize hNECs as an in vitro platform of pre-clinical testing of topical drugs. Additionally, secondary infection by other pathogens and commensals constitute a large number of morbidity and mortality post influenza infection, thus with the hNECs we will (2) conduct a similar cohort studies (as in aim 1) to obtain co-infection transcriptome signatures of co-infection of influenza virus with Rhinovirus, Streptococcus pneumoniae and Staphylococcus aureus. The development of this library platform will provide a reference for transcriptome patterns following Influenza Virus infection and its subsequent secondary infections, allowing for the further study and surveillance to effectively assess and predict the severity of an influenza outbreak, as well as identifying the appropriate measures against any emerging influenza strain.

title: Long term outcomes of AAV directed human Factor IX and X Intrauterine Gene Transfer in Non Human Primates
abs: Inherited monogenic diseases affect one-percent of births, many of which causes irreversible pathology in-utero or perinatally. Intrauterine therapy is an evolving strategy with several advantages over post-natal approaches, especially in diseases where irreversible pathology occurs pre-natally. Even in diseases with a perinatal onset, unique ontological opportunities that exist only during fetal life such as ability to induce tolerance and avoid immune rejection argues for its broader implementation. To translate promising findings in the mouse models into a clinically relevant model, we have established a macaque-based non-human primate (NHP) model for intrauterine gene transfer (IUGT) over the past eight years. The NHP recapitulates human fetal development both physiologically and immunologically, along with a similar placentation and are thus an accurate reproductive model for translation into human studies. Moreover, the longevity of macaques allows crucial long-term safety and efficacy data to be derived, which is not possible with mouse models. We have previously demonstrated long-term transgene expression (human factor IX) after late-gestation IUGT up to 22 months of age. Our objective here is to map out the long-term outcomes of Adeno-Associated Virus (AAV)-directed IUGT in both early and late gestation macaques (n=15) till sexual maturity and adulthood. Specifically, we will:1.Investigate transgene expression in relation to vector integration and cellular / humoural immune responses.2.Derive safety parameters for vector integration, germ-line transmission, and establish state-of-the-art immuno-monitoring and immunogenomic monitoring approaches3.Test the ability of androgen driven vector re-infusion in enhancing transgene expression levels in female low responders.Defining the efficacy and in particular the safety parameters in these macaques will set the stage for IUGT not only for the perinatally lethal conditions such as Factor X deficiency, but other single gene enzyme deficiency disorders such as neuropathic Gaucher and others where there are no curative or satisfactory post-natal treatments.

title: Investigating the roles of transcription factor GATA4 in HCC and its tumour microenvironment
abs: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the 3rd leading global cause of cancer death and the 5th commonest cancer worldwide. The only FDA-approved multi-kinase inhibitor, sorafenib, only marginally extends survival by several months. A crucially different scientific strategy targeting the tumour and tumour microenvironment is needed. Recently, we discovered previously undescribed somatic deletion and germline mutation of GATA4. Genomic, transcriptomic, and proteomic profiling followed by bioinformatics analysis reveals the potential roles of GATA4 in liver differentiation, EMT, and metabolism in HCC. Functional characterisation with CRISPR technology further showed that GATA4 regulates key liver differentiation and EMT genes in HCC. Liver-specific conditional Gata4-knockout mouse showed a fatty liver phenotype and enhanced liver cell proliferation, suggesting that Gata4 is essential to terminal differentiation and fatty acid metabolism in liver. Furthermore, we have discovered a prognostic gene signature of inflammatory microenvironment, which could be regulated by NF?B pathway. Recent literatures also linked GATA4 to NF?B pathway activation and that protective inflammatory NF?B pathway is important in HCC-genesis. Taken together, we hypothesise that GATA4 is a key differentiation driver, metabolic regulator, and key microenvironment modulator in HCC. Its loss or mutation result in de-differentiation, EMT, impaired fatty acid metabolism, and microenvironment changes. We postulate that targeting GATA4 and inter-related pathways can potentially accelerate HCC in a transgenic mouse model. In this proposal, we aim to 1) delineate the molecular mechanisms by which GATA4 mutation and deletions in hepatocellular cancer (HCC) confer clonal advantage, 2) develop improved transgenic mouse models that recapitulate GATA4 deletion-driven HCC-genesis, and 3) interrogate the changes of microenvironment and immune infiltration in GATA4-deleted livers and tumours. Our overarching objective is to generate novel scientific approaches to guide rational therapeutic intervention against HCC focusing on our observations with GATA4 deletion/mutation and its attendant functional sequelae both in the ‘seed’ and in the ‘soil’.

title: Repair of Osteochondral Defects using a Combination Stem Cell and Heparan Sulfate Device
abs: Damage to knee cartilage exposes underlying bone tissue, so causing significant pain and inflammation, often leading to osteoarthritis, one of five main causes of disability in Singapore. Worldwide, osteoarthritis incurs an estimated global expenditure of USD$18.5 billion annually, a figure growing rapidly. Current standard-of-care focuses on surgically drilling into the exposed bone tissue to create micro-fractures, which in turn release cells and growth factors to promote heading of the cartilage and subchondral bone. Unfortunately the success of this procedure is limited due to a complex mix of surgeon- and patient-related variables. An emerging treatment option involves transplantation of the patients’ own stem cells into the osteochondral lesion site after the micro-fracture procedure. Although autologous treatments of this type are considered safe, efficacy is reliant on the quantity and quality of the patients’ stem cells. These important parameters are largely dependent on the age and health status of the patient, as well as the method used to prepare and administer the cells. This proposal seeks to utilize a sugar therapeutic that can greatly augment and sustain the pro-healing effects of such a stem cell therapy, with a view to providing surgeons with a novel treatment for osteochondral injuries. This should translate into improved health outcomes for a quickly growing patient cohort with only restricted therapeutic options.

abs: Globally, long-term care (LTC) insurance coverage rates are low and, for those who are enrolled, only part of their potential future LTC expenses are covered. title: Telehealth Assessment of Persons with Aphasia
abs: Aphasia is a language disorder affecting one third of patients after stroke. While treatment can improve the ability to communicate, access to therapy is limited in Singapore due to barriers such as accessing transport to attend therapy. Telehealth offers a solution however current videoconferencing technology is not appropriate for those who need additional assistance to communicate. To address this, our team developed a novel iPad application, Access2Aphasia, that integrates videoconferencing, collaborative whiteboarding, flashcard stimulus and a database to record responses. This enables speech therapists (STs) to use supported conversation techniques to facilitate assessment and treatment for the person with aphasia (PwA). It is critical to ensure that assessment via telehealth is equivalent to a face-to-face (FTF) assessment. This study therefore aims to determine the reliability of telehealth aphasia assessment in the home environment using Access2Aphasia.35 PwAs and 2 speech therapists will be randomized to an online or FTF group. Assessment will evaluate language impairments of PwA and the impact of these on their daily life. In the online group, each PwA will be assessed in their own home remotely by an online ST using Access2Aphasia while another ST sits near the participant and scores silently. The same assessment will be conducted in the FTF group. Video recordings will be conducted for both groups. Scores obtained by the 2 STs in the online group will be analyzed for agreement. Inter and intra-rater reliability for the FTF and online assessments will be conducted and compared. Once reliability has been determined, Access2Aphasia will be further developed to include other aphasia tests and adapted for use for aphasia intervention. The study has the potential to improve outcomes of PwA through maximizing access to speech therapy services. It is envisioned that telehealth aphasia assessment will save time and cost to patients and their families having to travel to therapy sessions.

title: A Randomized Controlled Trial to Improve the Uptake of and Adherence to Outpatient Rehabilitation Services among Stroke Patients
abs: Background: Stroke is the leading cause of long-term disability in Singapore, and studies have found that intensive specialized stroke rehabilitation can improve post-stroke functional outcomes for a substantial proportion of stroke patients. However, despite the benefits associated with adherence to prescribed rehabilitation, the uptake rate of outpatient rehabilitation services (ORS) in Singapore is only 33%. According to local longitudinal studies, the financial burden of out-of-pocket service costs and the inconvenient transportation from home to rehabilitation centres are important barriers to access to ORS.Objective: To examine the effect and cost-effectiveness of providing incentives for ORS to improve the uptake of ORS compared to usual care (control) with no incentivesHypothesis: An evidence-based program to test the effectiveness of providing incentives to alleviate the financial burden as well as inconvenience of transportation for ORS will improve the uptake of and adherence to ORS among stroke patients.Methodology: This study is an individual randomized controlled trial (RCT) of 270 stroke patients recruited from SingHealth National Neuroscience Institute (NNI) and CGH. They will be randomized to one of three study arms (education only, free transportation, and free services and transportation) and interviewed at the time of recruitment and at 4 months. Participants’ health conditions, socioeconomic situation, health & medical services utilization, stroke-related disability measures, quality of life, and reasons for take up/rejection/withdraw from the services will be collected.Significance: As the first study in Singapore to test innovative ways to increase the stroke ORS uptake rates, it will provide evidence for future policy changes in financing outpatient rehabilitation and other long-term care services in Singapore. It will also provide important empirical parameter estimates for Systems Dynamics modeling of the demand and supply of ORS in Singapore.
kw: stroke, health services delivery, outpatient rehabilitation

title: Evaluation of Robotic-assisted Treadmill Therapy and Nutritional Optimisation on Gait Performance in Adolescents with Cerebral Palsy
abs: Cerebral palsy (CP) is the most common physical disability in children following damage to the developing brain. The brain injury results in muscle weakness, spasticity and musculoskeletal deformities causing lifelong, progressive motor impairment. Consequently, CP children have reduced mobility and quality of life. Unfortunately, there is no cure for CP and treatment is limited to supportive physical therapies. Robotic-assisted treadmill therapy, a new technology, provides individualized, high-intensity, physiological gait training, although there is currently limited evidence for its use in neurologically-impaired children. In Singapore, we have piloted adolescents with CP on Lokomat, a robotic gait-trainer, and shown clinically significant gait improvements. We postulate that in a targeted group of adolescents with CP of moderate functional impairment and adequate nutritional intake in terms of calories and proteins, intensive robotic-assisted treadmill therapy combined with conventional physiotherapy will improve their gait from baseline, more than conventional physiotherapy alone. We propose a randomized, 2-phase, single-blinded interventional study to recruit 32 adolescents with CP: Phase 1a (8 weeks) will evaluate the nutritional optimization alone (n=16), with a control group (n=16) on the primary outcomes of walking endurance (6-min walk test) and speed (10-metre walk test). The control group will sequentially undergo the same dietary interventions in Phase 1b to ensure all 32 adolescents are nutritional optimized for intensive physiotherapy in Phase 2. Phase 2 (4 weeks) will examine the effects of Lokomat- conventional physiotherapy combination (n=16) with conventional physiotherapy alone (n=16), on the same outcomes. Secondary outcomes include changes in body composition of fat, lean muscle mass and bone mineral density, resting metabolic rate, balance and trunk control, gait kinematics and health-related quality of life measures. With limited treatment options in CP, research in nutritional supplementation and robotic therapy can provide novel management strategies to improve the function of these disabled children.

title: Injury in the Over 55: Risk Factors and Determinants for Increased Healthcare Utilization Post-Injury
abs: Specific AimsThe primary objective of this proposal is to identify modifiable factors that drive healthcare utilization following moderate and severe injury in older Singaporeans. The secondary objective is to quantify the societal and economic impact after injury. To this end, we propose the first prospective cohort study of older Singaporeans hospitalized for injury related to the most common mechanisms of injury in Singapore: falls and motor vehicle injuries. Hypothesis1. In the over-55, the risk of increased healthcare utilization (both outpatient visits and in-patient hospitalization) and re-hospitalization within 12 months of moderate (injury severity score ISS 9-15) and severe (ISS >15) injury is increased by certain pre-existing medical (co-morbid) conditions, specific injury types, poor functional outcome at discharge, reduced compliance with rehabilitation, lack of social support, and post-injury caregiver burden.2. The effect of injury on patients’ lifestyle interacts with pre-injury health, socio-demographic and caregiver arrangements to determine post-injury lifestyle, caregiver burden and compliance with rehabilitation. SignificanceMore than 4000 patients with moderate or severe injuries are admitted to hospital annually, with approximately half aged over 55 years. In Singapore, the all-cause readmission rate within six months of injury, as captured by the National Trauma Registry (NTR), is higher for the more severely injured (ISS>15, 10.0%), compared to the moderately injured (ISS 9-15, 5.6%), for older patients (age over 55, 7.5%), compared to younger patients (age below 55, 5.9%), and for patients with multiple co-morbidities (11.1% in patients aged over 55 with Charlson scores of 2 or more). MethodologyCohort study of older patients admitted to a public hospital after moderate (injury severity score of 9 to 15) or severe (injury severity score of 16 or more) injury. Two surveys (PHASE questionnaire and modified caregiver reaction assessment) that have been used in older patients in Singapore will be administered.
