title: Bystander CPR and survival in six regions of Singapore saturated with trained and equipped volunteers with AED access
abs: BACKGROUND: In 2013, there were more than 1800 out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) deaths. Only 20% of those cases involved bystander CPR. For many years in Singapore the bystander CPR rates hovered around that 20%. Recent studies show that implementation of dispatcher assisted CPR has resulted in the bystander CPR rates in Singapore to double to 42%, and survival rates to increase to 3.2% from 1.6%. Still only about 1% of victims are defibrillated using a public Automated External Defibrillators (AED). Based on the experience of other countries and cities around the world, Singapore can achieve another 15-20% in the bystander CPR rate with training and attitude change. Over 70% of Singapore’s OHCA occur in residential areas. Most OHCA events are witnessed by friends or family members. Significant barriers to bystander CPR persist and translate into critical delays. Barriers include timely recognition of a cardiac arrest, waiting for someone else to act first, lack of skill or confidence, and fear of performing CPR incorrectly. The DARE programme and this study will increase the number of people who are better informed and prepared to cooperate with dispatchers during an emergency event until an ambulance arrives. AIM: We aim to study whether there is significant uptake of a simplified chest compression only CPR training programme including instruction on AED use; and whether that in turn will lead to an increase in the rate of bystander CPR in six constituencies. METHODS: 50,000 Singaporeans will be trained in the DARE programme. Rates of bystander CPR during and after the study period will be compared to historical data. OHCA survival rates during and after the study will also be compared with historical data. Knowledge gain and attitude change will be measured using surveys to be administered during training day in 2% (1,000) of those trained.
kw: Sudden cardiac arrest, cardiopulmonary resuscitation, bystander, automated external defibrillator

title: Tuberculosis in the resident and migrant population in Singapore: a mixed-method study
abs: Singapore has intermediate tuberculosis (TB) incidence rates that have been rising in both the resident population and foreign migrants, who now constitute almost a third of Singapore’s overall population. Meanwhile, rapid aging has been linked to the rise in TB cases among the resident population, coupled with a substantial projected rise in the burden of diabetes, a major risk factor for TB. This project has four goals structured around these trends:(1) Projecting the future burden of TB among Singapore’s resident population;(2) and her non-resident population;(3) understanding the experience of newly diagnosed TB cases in both groups; and(4) what is the cost and projected cost to the health system of TB in Singapore.The study will use mixed-methods to answer these questions, combining computational and statistical modelling, in-depth interviews, and health economics. In particular, for project (1) we will build upon an existing individual based modelling framework to forecast the aging population to 2050, combining this with (i) the age specific incidence of TB and (ii) historical TB incidence that may surface as reactivated TB in the future. For project (2), we will perform a meta-analysis of incidence of TB in the nine main source countries that Singapore receives migrants with TB, including the incidence of drug-resistant and multi drug-resistant TB. This will be related to incidence of TB in Singapore among foreign workers by nationality, and used to create projections of the future incidence of TB, and the risk of drug-resistant TB, among migrant workers to Singapore. For project (3), we will conduct in-depth interviews (IDIs) of TB patients (locals, foreign construction workers, foreign domestic helpers) with qualitative analysis using NVivo. For project (4), we will combine projects (1) and (2) with a health economic analysis to determine the societal costs of TB in Singapore.
kw: Tuberculosis, Modelling, Health systems, Mixed-methods, Global health, Migration

title: A Prospective Study to Evaluate the Safety and Efficacy of Transfusing Intraoperative Salvaged Blood in Metastatic Musculoskeletal Tumour Surgery
abs: Specific aims:To investigate the effect of reinfusion of ‘Intraoperative Cell Salvage in combination with Leucocyte Depletion Filter’ (IOCS-LDF) processed blood on ‘allogeneic blood transfusion’ (ABT) rate, clinical outcomes and survival in patients undergoing ‘Metastatic Musculoskeletal Tumour Surgery’ (MMTS).Hypothesis IOCS-LDF blood transfusion reduces the need for blood transfusion and does not affect clinical outcomes and survival. Methods/ApproachThis is a prospective study in adult patients with known epithelial primary tumours and musculoskeletal metastases undergoing MMTS. 60 patients will divided into two arms; a study group will receive IOCS-LDF blood while the control group will not. Both groups will receive allogenic blood depending on clinical requirements. All the patients will be followed up at the respective outpatient clinics at 2 weeks, 6 weeks, 3 months, 6 months, till their demise or till the end of the study period. In order to investigate the clinical outcomes of our study, which are tumour progression and/or new metastasis, all the patients will have CT (chest, abdomen, pelvis), MRI (whole spine) and bone scan at the 6-month follow-up. This will be compared with pre-operative investigations (baseline investigation). SignificanceIn the past the use of intraoperative cell salvage blood was considered to be contraindicated in tumour surgery due to the theoretical risk of contamination with malignant cells. A review of the literature and our preliminary studies have shown this to be untrue. This will be the first study to attempt the reinfusion of (IOCS-LDF) processed blood, if successful it may lead to a change in clinical practice, and lead to the use of autologous blood transfusion in MMTS surgery. This will reduce the dependence on scarce allogenic blood resources and reduce the risks associated with transfusion.
kw: Musculoskeletal Metastases, cell saver, autogenic transfusion, allogenic transfusion, leukocyte depletion filter

title: Wnt signalling pathway biomarker for diagnosis and therapy of soft tissue tumours
abs: Misregulation of Wnt signaling leads to a variety of disease including diverse cancers. Recent studies have identified many tumor types that have over-expression of Wnts. Therefore, targeting the production and secretion of Wnts may have therapeutic benefit. Consequently, new agents targeting the upstream component of the Wnt pathway have been developed collaboratively in our lab. Despite these developments, there is still a paucity of reliable tools or biomarkers to identify and better characterize Wnt driven tumors. Expanding on recent preliminary findings that identified WLS high expression in certain subsets of bone tumors, through the utility of the novel biomarker YJ5, this proposal intends to fill significant deficits in our understanding of the upstream mechanism in soft tissue tumors. Here we wish to extend this study by addressing a number of issues and questions. Firstly, confirming and validating the presence of aberrant Wnt expression in soft tissue tumors using both genomic analysis of functional Wnt mutations as well as novel antibodies for immunohistochemical analysis. Secondly, studying if this aberration in Wnt signaling affects cancer biology by correlating this data with clinical data (i.e. chemo response, percentage necrosis, metastasis, survival rates). Thirdly, investigating the response of these selected tumours to novel Wnt inhibitors in the murine model both in isolation and in combination with conventional drug therapy.
kw: Wnt signalling Soft tissue tumours

title: The Effectiveness of Pharmacist-involved Collaborative Care Model in the Management of Patients with Diabetes Mellitus in Singapore
abs: In September 2012, a 6-month prospective, randomized controlled study supported by the Ministry of Health (HSRG11MAY016) was conducted in three government-owned primary care institutions and one outpatient clinic in a tertiary hospital in Singapore. This was the first study conducted in Singapore to assess the effectiveness of a pharmacist-involved collaborative care model (intervention) versus usual care in managing patients with uncontrolled type 2 diabetes. Based on a preliminary analysis performed from September 2012 to April 2014, statistically significant clinical outcomes comparable to those reported in the literature were observed in the intervention arm throughout the 6-month period. Positive trends in humanistic outcomes, particularly in patients’ emotional functioning and treatment satisfaction, were also observed in the intervention arm. Finally, compared to the usual care, the total diabetes-related direct outpatient gross cost incurred by the health care system per patient over the 6-month period was S$149 less in the intervention arm.Given the promising outcomes observed in our 6-month data, the primary objective of this renewal proposal is to implement the same study design over a 12-month period to assess the long-term clinical, humanistic and economic outcomes of such a collaborative care model compared with usual care. This proposal also suggests extending the study into the community setting by conducting a similar care model in family medicine clinics and local community pharmacies to assess the effectiveness of a community pharmacist-involved collaborative care model in caring for patients with uncontrolled type 2 diabetes over a 12-month period. It is hoped that through this long-term study, an effective and sustainable chronic disease care model can be assured and delivered to all tertiary and primary health care settings and throughout the community to improve the overall outcomes of the top chronic disease states in Singapore.
kw: Collaborative Care, Diabetes Mellitus, Health Care Professionals, Chronic diseases, Pharmacists, Pharmaceutical Care

title: High Performance Ceramic Materials and Components by Innovative One-step Forming-Sintering Process
abs: In the present manufacturing industry, almost all ceramic components are manufactured by multi-steps, including powder preparation, consolidation into a powdered shape before densification at high temperatures, as it is almost impossible to machine them in the same way as for polymers and metallic materials, as they are among the strongest, hardest and yet very brittle materials. One step near-net-shape forming has been a dream for ceramists, in delivering the desired component shape and structural integrity by one step. Additive manufacturing has been well developed for polymeric and metallic materials. For high-performance ceramic components, the direct laser sintering would be an ideal one-step fabrication technique. In order to develop the designed the structures with precision, high laser absorption rate especially with short wavelength laser source (with wavelength near 1 μm) should be required. However, most oxide ceramics have poor fibre laser absorption rate. Therefore, one of the key challenges of fabricating high performance ceramics by the selective laser sintering is to enhance laser absorption rate significantly. Commercially available selective laser melting systems are basically designed for metallic materials. It is therefore absolutely necessary to develop a new system suitable for ceramic materials. Recently, our research has resulted in a significant breakthrough – enhance the fibre laser absorption rate for oxide ceramic powders greatly. This achievement allows us to develop a new laser sintering strategy for one-step fabrication of ceramics with refined structures. Besides, we have also conducted preliminary investigations into several other key factors for laser sintering of ceramics such as new powder delivery mechanism for high packing density and reduction in thermal shock. Encouraged by these very interesting results, in this programme, we propose to develop a one-step forming-sintering technique for ceramic components, including key laser printable materials aspects, and a brand new laser sintering system suitable for ceramics.

title: Novel Integrated Agrotechnologies, Plant Nutrients and Microbials for Improved Production of Green Leafy Vegetables in Singapore
abs: In order to meet food security targets in Singapore, a nation with limited natural resources, we aim to develop and utilize novel technologies in food production, specifically for Asian Green Leafy Vegetables. Current practices of urban vegetable production are not suitable as they rely on extensive land usage, intensive inputs of water and chemicals, and there is scarce knowledge of their nutritional benefits, or nutrient- and water- use efficiency. Current practices do not exploit the synergistic microbes that aid nutrition, growth and plant resistance to pests and diseases, to reduce the input costs and yet be ecologically friendly bypassing transgenic technologies. Finally, reliance on land and soil has limitations of land availability, nutrient leaching and soil-borne pathogens. To overcome these limitations, our overall goal here is to develop integrated solutions tailored specifically for urban crop production by developing breakthrough technologies that utilize the synergy between plant traits, their associated microbes and physico-chemical traits of soil substratum and light. The three interrelated themes are (i) Growth, Nutrients and Nutraceuticals in Vegetables – involving selection of Asian vegetables, with high nutritional values and biomass growth properties; (ii) Effective Microbial Solutions – involving microbial communities of above vegetables and developing their beneficial microbial consortia to improve plant nutrients and defense against urban pests and diseases, thereby increasing yields and reducing chemical inputs with relying on transgenic technologies; (iii) Cost-effective Agrotechnologies – involving development of Nutrigels, novel soil supplements based on low-cost soya waste okara to retain water and release nutrients slowly, and wavelength-controlled LED lighting systems to improve growth, resilience and freshness of urban leafy vegetables. As these components are highly interdependent, they will be integrated from half-way point in the project; first, at laboratory scale followed by test-bedding in partnership with the largest agrotechnology farm in Singapore.
kw: Green Leafy Vegetables;Urban Agrotechnology;Plant Nutrition;Food Security;Microbiomes;Waste Utilization

title: Image-enabled Development for 3D Microelectronics Nanofabrication
abs: The microelectronics industry demands denser and more energy efficient components than before. As a result, we are now challenged to fabricate tall and thin, three-dimensional (3D) nanoscale semiconductor transistors of feature sizes that are fewer than a hundred atoms across. New techniques have to be invented to reliably and affordably fabricate billions of such 3D nanoscale transistors on each of the hundreds of millions of electronic chips produced annually. Unfortunately, we do not yet have a good understanding of the underlying nanoscale mechanisms needed to rationally design new fabrication techniques. Furthermore, simply extending today’s nanofabrication techniques to obtain smaller, taller and denser chip components often lead to catastrophic functional and structural failures. In this proposal, we aim to use disruptive in-situ dynamic electron microscopy developed in our just-completed Interfacial Water CRP to diagnose these failure modes and innovate wet-etching techniques for the next-generation transistors. Our team has the twin advantage of being pioneers in developing such imaging capabilities, and the only ones in the world to have mass fabricated realistic 3D nanostructures compatible with these imaging techniques. By imaging the intermediate stages of wet-etching in these nanostructures, we will determine conditions necessary for selective and anistropic etching of high aspect-ratio features in semiconductors. Using in-situ imaging and chemical mapping of wet-etching processes we hope to accelerate the discovery of surface and solution chemistry modifications that drive new nanofabrication techniques. Our team will translate knowledge gained here to our industry partners into practical processing techniques ready for the next generations of microelectronics.
kw: in situ electron microscopy;spectroscopy and elemental analysis;Interfacial processes;3D device fabrication failure modes;nanofabrication process prototyping;semiconductor surface chemistry

title: The Role of Tumor Heterogeneity in Lymph Node Metastasis in Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma(OSCC): A Precision Medicine Approach
abs: Development of lymph node metastasis is the strongest prognostic factor in oral squamous cell carcinoma(OSCC), predicting the development of treatment failure and distant metastasis. Previous data show that the potential for metastasis, is present a priori in the primary tumor, and clonal diversity of the primary tumor generates sub-populations with the metastatic phenotype. There are two models to explain this process: linear- and parallel-progression models. The former is where metastasis occurs systematically in a stepwise manner through successive(and organised) metastatic echelons, and the latter proposes that sub-populations within the primary tumor converge on the metastatic phenotype and each metastatic deposit represents each of these subclones. In this study, we hypothesize that heterogeneity within primary tumors drives metastasis through either a linear-progression or parallel-progression model that is specific to the individual tumor, with consequent implications on therapeutic approach. Our aims are therefore: 1.To understand clonal evolution, thereby determine major pathways and progression-models in tumor metastasis in the context of tumor heterogeneity, and 2.To determine specific vulnerabilities in individual tumor models through targeting metastatic drivers or drivers of heterogeneity.To answer the first aim, we will utilize carefully dissected tissue from tumor and metastases, and perform single-cell genomics to determine the extent of heterogeneity and clonal evolution during metastasis. These will combined with bulk analysis data to confirm or refute our hypothesis. Bulk analyses would also include chromatin sequencing to determine whether epigenetic alterations play a critical role in the diversity of metastasis. For the second aim, we will establish ex vivo models using the same material, and undertake functional screens to identify specific vulnerabilities of metastases, including using chromatin modifies to target epigenetic drivers of the process.Through these experiments, we intend to utilise a precision medicine (non-reductionist) approach to understand and target the metastatic process in OSCC.
kw: oral cancer, head and neck cancer, single-cell genomics, high-throughput screens, therapeutics, individualized treatment

title: Building the Kidney Confidence Program. A study to identify factors associated with suboptimal initiation of dialysis
abs: Suboptimal initiation of dialysis is very common in chronic kidney disease patients referred early or late. The benefits of early referral are lost if dialysis is initiated sub-optimally. This is also associated with worse clinical outcomes and increased health care costs. There is however a paucity of data on reasons for suboptimal initiation despite early referral. Patient delay is show to be a key contributor but it is not well understood. Patient perceptual barriers (illness or treatment beliefs) and capability (health literacy, mood, or planning ability) may drive delay in initiating access but evidence from CKD patient is lacking. The proposed study will seek out to explore the associations between these potentially modifiable barriers and facilitators with suboptimal dialysis initiation in local context so as to guide the future ‘kidney confidence’ intervention. Design: mixed method observational study. First, a representative sample of 60 comprising CKD Stage 4-5 patients, new on dialysis patients (with and without access) and their family members will be interviewed to explore the process and experience of decision making and planning around dialysis. Data were thematically analyzed to identify main drivers of dialysis initiation and planning based on patients and family members perspectives.Building on the interviews a sample of 150 CKD patients will be surveyed using standardised self-report measures of health literacy illness and treatment beliefs, decisional conflict, mood and quality of life. Outcomes related to dialysis decision, initiation and/or access will be collected through medical records in the ensuring 12 months. Analyses will model the effect of these predictors onto dialysis initiation outcomes (optimal/ suboptimal)
kw: chronic kidney disease, decicion making, access, suboptimal initiaion

title: The effect of a behaviour-based lifestyle change program using combined face and remote sessions on weight, diet intake and physical activity level in people at-risk of diabetes: a randomised control trial.
abs: Background: The important role of healthy lifestyle choices in promoting health is increasingly being recognised. Adverse lifestyle factors are directly linked with the risks of developing many of the major chronic diseases including type 2 diabetes. Studies have demonstrated that factors such as weight reduction are linked with positive outcomes; however, lasting compliance with these programmes is difficult with correspondingly diminished healthcare benefits.   Despite MOH recommendations for the provision of healthy lifestyle programmes targeting lifestyle factors in reducing diabetes risk, there is a paucity of research on such programs in Singapore. JurongHealth Lifestyle Intervention Program is developed to address the need for a Regional Health System to deliver an effective and affordable service for people with pre-diabetes. The program delivers diet and physical activity strategies grounded on an established behavioural framework using a unique model of mixed delivery modes. Aims: To compare the immediate (6 months) and short-term effects (12 months) of the JurongHealth Lifestyle Intervention Program with usual care on weight loss, physical activity level and dietary calorie intake in persons with pre-diabetes within a primary care setting.Methods: An assessor-blinded, randomized  controlled clinical trial comparing the lifestyle intervention programme with usual care. title: Singapore cohort of patients with advanced heart failure (SCOPAH)
abs: Specific aims: Congestive heart failure (CHF) is one of the leading causes of death in Singapore. Although anecdotal data suggests that end-of-life (EOL) care that patients with advanced CHF receive is sub-optimal, limited data is available that assesses the EOL experience of patients and that can be used to identify specific areas for improvement. Further, advance care planning, a promising intervention recently introduced in Singapore to enable patients with life limiting illnesses, including those with advanced CHF, to receive EOL treatments according to their own preferences, has not been systematically evaluated. This project thus aims to (1) enroll a cohort of patients with advanced CHF (n=250) to assess their EOL experience and to identify specific areas for improvement; and to (2) conduct a 2-arm randomized controlled trial of patients with advanced CHF (n=250) to assess whether patients receiving ACP are more likely to receive EOL care consistent with their preferences and to compare health care expenditures, patient’s quality of life, understanding of their own illness and participation in decision making between ACP and control arm.Methodology: Patients will be recruited from National Heart Centre and Singapore General Hospital. Patients for the RCT will be randomized to receive the intervention (ACP arm; N=125) or usual care (control arm; N=125). All patients will be followed for one year or till death, whichever is earlier and interviewed every 4 months during the study

title: Evaluation of predictive factors for outcomes for knee replacement surgery in osteoarthritis in a multi-ethnic Asian country
abs: Background. The demand for total knee replacement (TKR) has been increasing worldwide, and the need for surgery is projected to rise by over 600% by 2030. There are 15-30% of patients who report little or no improvement after TKR for knee osteoarthritis (KOA). Traditional socio-demographic and clinical factors do not fully explain why some patients do not respond to surgery. Hypothesis. There are some biological and psychological factors, like pain sensitization, widespread pain, pain catastrophizing, and mood symptoms that may better explain knee replacement outcome. Aim. We aim to evaluate factors that better predict outcomes for TKR for knee osteoarthritis. We also aim to identify patients who may not respond to surgery and provide alternative intervention before or in place of surgery.Methods. We will prospectively assess 1500 consecutive patients enlisted for TKR at Singapore General Hospital. Assessment will include demographics, knee symptoms, widespread pain, neuropathic pain, pain catetrophizing and mood symptoms before surgery. Pressure pain thresholds at the knee and a distant body part will be measured using digital pressure algometry. Patients will then undergo similar assessments at 6 months, 1 year and 2 years after surgery. Poor outcome will be defined as reporting “somewhat dissatisfied” with the overall result of surgery. Clinical Significance. Identifying factors associated with poor outcomes to TKR is the first step in optimizing utilization of TKR. Patients could then be offered alternative therapies, like physiotherapy, bracing, and medications for surgery or even in place of TKR.

title: Statistical Methods for Process Evaluation in Randomised Clinical Trials
abs: Background:Interventions in health services often comprise multiple components, interacting to produce a therapeutic effect. A logic model is often used to describe the relationships between the intended activities with intermediate and long-term outcomes. Thus the logic model forms the theoretical underpinnings describing for whom the intervention will work, under which conditions and how the interventions are thought to work. Evaluations of health services typically focuses on outcomes evaluation to answer the question: “Is the treatment effective?”. Increasingly, there is recognition of the value of process evaluations (PE) in understanding aspects of how complex interventions work, answering the question: “How does the intervention work?”. However, there is currently a lack of principled methods of analysis in the assessment of the theories implied by the logic model. This research aims to utilise methodological developments in the field of causal inference to fill this gap.Aim:The aim of this research project is to provide statistical design and analysis guidelines for quantitative process evaluation in trials of complex interventions.Methodology:The research would proceed in 3 phases. In the first phase, a systematic review would be conducted on the current types of process indicators and their associated analytical methods. This would form the foundation on which to either refine existing methods or to develop new ones with the focus on providing causal inferences on why the treatment works. In the second phase, principled methods would be refined or developed for the analysis of PE. Simulations of typical trials will be used to assess these methods and software will be developed to use these methods. The third phase focuses on using the methods on real trials to determine their applicability to real research scenarios and to outline possible problems with the developed methods.
kw: process evaluation, causal inference, structural equations model

title: Synergistic genetic lesions in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma tumour tissue and peripheral blood.
abs: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) is globally the most common aggressive lymphoma. Approximately 50% of cases are cured with R-CHOP chemotherapy. The remainder will relapse or will be treated palliatively to avoid toxicity. It is therefore vital to develop less toxic targeted therapies and to identify patients who will respond poorly to R-CHOP so that alternative treatments may be offered. The aim of this project is to investigate the prognostic impact of combinations of genetic lesions in DLBCL and to evaluate the ?-catenin pathway as a potential target.TP53 and MYD88 mutations are associated with a poor prognosis, as is the non-germinal centre cell of origin (COO) subtype. The co-occurrence of MYC and BCL2 or BCL6 translocations (“double-hit” lymphoma (DHL)) defines a subgroup with an aggressive disease course. Recent studies suggest that TP53 mutations combined with MYC translocations also result in a poor prognosis. However, these studies have either included too few DHL cases or were prone to selection bias. Pilot data indicates that mutations in the ?-catenin regulator DDX3X are found in ~40% of relapsed/refractory DLBCL but only ~3% of unselected cases. 4/5 DDX3X lesions co-occurred with a translocation indicating possible synergy. A large study to investigate TP53, MYD88 and DDX3X mutations in combination with MYC translocations is therefore required.The SGH DLBCL archive has >400 cases with FFPE material and known translocation status and COO subtype. We propose to sequence MYD88, TP53, and DDX3X in this cohort using the Fluidigm platform and correlate the combination of genetic lesions with COO and clinical outcomes. The effect of DDX3X mutations on proliferation, apoptosis, and ?-catenin activity will be investigated in lymphoma cell lines using standard assays. Finally, sequencing of cell-free tumour DNA from stored patient plasma will be explored as a novel method of identifying these mutations in blood samples.

title: Two-dimensional Covalent Organic Framework: Synthesis and Applications
abs: Covalent organic frameworks (COFs) are a class of highly porous, purely organic crystalline polymers, in which the molecular components are organized into a periodic network linked by covalent bonds.The attraction of COFs as a material platform arises from its vast variety of possible material combinations and crystal structures, which give rise to a diverse range of tunable chemical and physical properties. The successful realization of COFs through molecular building blocks would provide lightweight materials that could be specifically optimized for gas storage, electronic, photonic, catalytic applications and more. In contrast to 2D inorganic materials which are often derived from a thermodynamically stable, bulk phase found in nature (examples are graphite, or bulk MoS2), 2D organic materials are fully synthetic and thus afford greater structural diversity, chemical stability and tunability. The large scale synthesis of 2D-COFs with useful technological application is now recognized as an important challenge. This proposal addresses the following challenges: 1. Design and synthesis: Currently, most 2D-COFs are built from reversible reactions which are chemically unstable even in ambient conditions. Typically, the flake size of 2D-COF is in the sub-micron range, which is too small for many applications. Here, we present a range of novel synthesis approaches to target the synthesis of large sized 2-D COF crystals. 2. Scalable synthesis: Methods to exfoliate bulk 3D-COF into 2D-COF have not been fully developed. Control over key parameters such as crystallinity and porosity has been elusive, and techniques to develop 2D-COFs into multifunctional ultra-thin membranes are currently lacking. We aim to address these challenges in this proposal using both wet and dry synthesis methods. 3. Fundamental physics: The physics of 2D-COFs have not been studied as well as their inorganic analogs, even from a theoretical viewpoint. However, this means that it presents a rich intellectual playground for research. We have assembled a team of theoreticians and experimentalists to work on this aspect. 4. We will study the application of these materials in technological applications such as in ion transport membranes, molecular sieving and energy storage.

title: CMOS Terahertz Interconnect towards Tera-scale Personalised Cloud Server
abs: We aim developing a scalable data link to support future personalized cloud server with low cost and low power. Conventional data-server data links are normally realized by Giga-scale electronic back-plane PCB traces, which have limited bandwidth as well as undesired EM-crosstalk, We will demonstrate the Terahertz meta-devices including sources and transmission lines all in CMOS technology, which can be directly integrated with data server. The main specifications to achieve include: energy efficiency at 0.01pJ/bit/mm, crosstalk ratio at -21dB/mm and output power at 5dBm for sub-Terahertz communication (>45Gbps) per channel in CMOS. The scientific breakthrough is the development of CMOS-based Terahertz meta-devices: metamaterials, spoof surface-plasmon-polariton, and metasurfaces. Judiciously designed sub-wavelength building blocks such as periodic metallic groove can support spoof surface-plasmon (SSP), which can be properly confined at the surface of metal/dielectric in CMOS process. This property offers a possible route to reduce the crosstalk as well as to scale down the power and size of the devices. By further controlling the phase of SSP using planar zero-phase coupler, one can design a coherent signal source with sufficient output power for Terahertz communication on chip in CMOS.

title: Towards Personalised Medicine for Type 2 Diabetes mellitus: Validation of Circulating microRNAs as Biomarkers of Pancreatic ?-Cell Function.
abs: Type 2 diabetes is a heterogeneous disease with regard to its clinical presentations and pathogenesis, but most patients are treated as if they are the same. Progressive ?-cell dysfunction is the key pathophysiology leading to failure of oral hypoglycaemic agents and poor glycaemic control. Therapies that improve ?-cell function are being developed, and the ability to measure ?-cell function in response to these therapies is important. However, it is difficult to measure ?-cell function in a clinical setting. MicroRNAs are negative regulators of gene expression and has been shown to regulate ?-cell function. This proposal is a continuation of a pilot study which explored the role of circulating microRNAs as biomarkers of ?-cell function. In the pilot study, we demonstrated that 33 plasma microRNAs differentiates between those with low and high ?-cell function (determined by intravenous glucose tolerance test). This proposal aims to 1) validate the aforementioned circulating microRNAs in a validation cohort (n=100) to ensure its robustness as biomarkers for a range of ?-cell function; 2) examine the expression levels of these microRNAs in response to a hyperglycaemic clamp. The ability to response to a hyperglycaemic stimulus will help us to focus on the microRNAs that have physiological relevance in ?-cell function. For this, we will select 20 healthy individuals to undergo a 3-hour hyperglycaemic clamp. Baseline, 0.5-hour and 3-hour plasma will be obtained for microRNAs analysis. A sample size of 20 will provide at least an anticipated effect size of 1.1, with a power of 0.8 and ?=0.001. We will quantify the microRNA expression levels using the qRT-PCR MiRXES miR ? assays. The findings of this study will be used to advance the development of microRNAs as biomarkers of ?-cell function to promote personalised medicine in Type 2 diabetes and as potential therapeutic targets for ?-cell function.

title: Identification of hematopoietic stem cell enhancers associated with normal and leukemic stem cells
abs: Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) possess unique ability to produce progenitor cells (differentiation) as well as additional stem cells (self-renewal) and are responsible for producing and replenishing all blood cells throughout our life. On the other hand, leukemic stem cells (LSCs), which are considered to evolve from HSCs or progenitor cells, can initiate and sustain leukemia. HSCs and LSCs share several functional characteristics to keep their “stem cell” ability, but the underlying mechanism remains unclear. Gene expression is regulated by a network of transcription factors that bind to cis-regulatory sequences including promoters and enhancers, and their diversity is now considered to be central to distinct expression of each gene. We hypothesize that HSC-specific enhancers are also actively utilized by LSCs and that their genetic, and subsequent functional, alternations can cause leukemia.Our primary aim is to identify cis-regulatory elements of HSC genes that are required for survival, proliferation and function of those cells. Firstly, we will select several candidate elements by in silico screening, i.e., combining publicly available data including comparative genomics, histone marks, and chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP)-based sequencing data. Then we will use candidate enhancer-linked eGFP reporter transgenic zebrafish and mice as an in vivo validation animal model to verify HSC-specific activities. After the discovery of HSC-specific cis-regulatory elements, we will clarify how these HSC-enhancers work in normal HSC physiology, with in vivo and in vitro functional analyses. Further, we will elucidate the pathophysiology of these enhancers in leukemogenesis, especially LSCs. Finally, we plan to detect disease-causative alternations in these enhancers using clinical genome samples to verify our hypothesis.Our proposal will lead to substantial contributions towards HSC biology as well as our understanding of how deregulation of genetic programs will cause leukemia, which is the key step to establish a new therapeutic concept.

title: A novel tissue engineered scaffold-free cartilage graft for temporomandibular condylar repair in rabbit models: a factorial study of decellularization and recellularization of chondrocytes and chondroprogenitors
abs: The articular cartilage is a well-organized tissue for smooth and friction-free joint movement in animals and humans. Adult articular cartilage has a very low self-regeneration capacity due to its avascular nature. Osteoarthritis (OA) is a common disease causing joint pain, joint deformity, and functional disability. Temporomandibular joint (TMJ) is the joint that connects the mandible to the temporal bone and temporomandibular joint disorders (TMD) may develop due to trauma or OA. This disorder often leads to a lifetime of pain and restricted motion of the jaw, greatly affecting patients’ life quality. Although various joint resurfacing procedures in experimental articular cartilage defects have been developed, no standardized clinical protocol has yet been established. The emerging cartilage tissue engineering strategies to regenerate or reconstruct condylar cartilage have gained increasing attention and are promising as new therapeutic approaches. This research proposal aims to develop a tissue engineered ‘scaffold-free’ graft to repair the TMJ condylar cartilage in rabbit models. The xenogenic synthetic scaffold-free construct with hyaline quality, termed living hyaline cartilaginous graft (LhCG) will be applied for treating cartilage lesions in 28 rabbit models in 4 groups. The study will compare between the negative control (empty defect), grafting with decellularized–LhCG, recellularized –LhCG with allogenic bone marrow stromal stem cells (BMSCs) or allogenic chondrocytes. The assessment will be on macroscopic and microscopic inspection on the restoration of cartilage thickness, promotion of integration with surrounding native cartilage, cartilage-specific matrix molecules, and re-establishing an intact superficial tangential zone. The outcome of this pioneering work would be to repair damaged TMJ cartilage using tissue engineering approach and is especially relevant in our ageing population where rising number of joint degenerative disorders are expected.

title: Evaluation of Mobile Interactive Supervised Therapy (MIST)
abs: Specific Aims: further develop a smartphone based system for monitoring and supporting adherence to medication; compare treatment adherence with MIST compared to standard of care in TB participants; compare MIST and standard of care on quality of life, costs, participant satisfaction and clinical outcomes.Hypotheses: MIST is a feasible approach to support and monitor medication adherence in selected participant populations;MIST is associated with non-inferior levels of treatment adherence compared to standard DOT in participants with TB; MIST improves quality of life, costs and participant satisfaction compared to standard DOT without compromising clinical outcomes Methodology: We wish to expand the MIST system to enhance its capabilities. 10 TB patients will be recruited and simply asked to take pills at a fixed time for the first month. For the second 2 months the MIST system would send notification reminders to the participants’ phone before their allocated pill times. At their allocated pill time the participant would be notified to open the MIST app and record themselves taking their pill. This video would then be uploaded to the server. A healthcare worker would then review all uploaded videos daily to assess if they are of acceptable quality and confirm pill ingestion. Adherence will be assessed by MEMScaps. title: Educating Maternal Immunity to Improve Donor Cell Engraftment: The Kinetics of Maternal Immune Cell Trafficking and A Novel Therapeutic Strategy in a Murine Model of Allogeneic Intrauterine Haemopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation
abs: Intrauterine haemopoietic stem cell transplantation (IUHSCT) has the potential to cure inherited genetic diseases before the onset of irreversible pathology, and can be applied to a variety of congenital disorders, with the fetus’ relative immune-naïveté being a critical advantage. However, the challenge remains of achieving significant engraftment following IUHSCT in the context of competent fetal immunity. While much is known about individual maternal and fetal responses to transplacentally-trafficked antigens, the gaps in knowledge concern the maternal immune system’s influence on fetal alloresponsiveness, and how this affects donor cell engraftment following IUHSCT. A persistent maternal immune presence in the recipient fetus may influence rejection of donor cells over time. This is an important mechanism to understand considering the broad applicability of IUHSCT. While our long-term objective is successful IUHSCT for major thalassaemias, our short-term objective is to probe the relationship between trafficked maternal immune cells and donor cell engraftment. We propose that trafficked maternal immune cells influence donor cell engraftment following allogeneic IUHSCT, and that blocking maternal antigen presenting cells (APC) will educate maternal T cells to become tolerant to donor cells and in transplanted fetuses. Our specific aims will elucidate the kinetics of trafficked maternal cells in a semi-allogeneic fetus, first in an uninterrupted pregnancy, then following allogeneic IUHSCT, alone and with maternal APC depletion using a transgenic B6/CD11c.DTR model. Donor cell chimerism will be examined after IUHSCT and postnatal re-transplantation, as will fetal immune response to the latter. If this strategy enhances engraftment, we will use it to demonstrate proof of cure in a knockout mouse model of thalassaemia major in future work. This research may uncover new knowledge into mechanisms underlying maternal-fetal immune tolerance and long-term transplant engraftment, and create opportunities for novel therapeutic strategies to fulfil the potential of IUHSCT.
kw: Intrauterine Haemopoietic stem cell transplantation; Bidirectional immune trafficking; Antigen presenting cells; Immune cell education; Thalassaemia

title: Vitreoretinal Interface Abnormalities as detected on Optical Coherence Tomography: Epidemiology and association with Distance Vision and Health Related Quality of Life.
abs: In this study we aim to describe the overall prevalence and specific racial prevalence of vitreoretinal interface abnormalities (VIA) and its associated conditions, in a large multi-ethnic populations; the (Singapore Epidemiology Eye Disease [SEED] cohort) and the Blue Mountain Eye Study (BMES) through the use of optical coherence tomography (OCT). The secondary aim is to explore the relationship between individual conditions of VIA such as epiretinal membranes (ERM), vitreomacular traction (VMT) lamellar holes (LMH) and full thickness macular holes (FTMH) with vision and health related quality of life measures (HRQoL).We hypothesize that prevalence of VIA based on OCT may be lower than VIA diagnosed by retinal photography. In addition, we postulate that Prelance of VIA based on OCT is highest between asian population versus caucasian population and the difference is contributed by myopia and increased axial length as these have been shown to be a risk factor for ERM.Lastly, specific abnormalities detected on OCT correlate with visual impairment as they represent a structural disruption that adversely affects retinal physiology. Despite good visual acuity, patients may suffer from other visual disturbances that could adversely affect HRQoL. OCT images from both cohorts (SEED n=7187, SEED cohort which had subjects with OCT measurements consist of the Singapore Chinese eye study 1 (SCES1), Singapore Indian Eye Stydy 2 (SINDI2) and the Singapore malay eye study 2 (SIMES2). and BMES n=929) will graded by 2 trained graders for associated conditions of VIA and structural changes and adjudicated by a retinal specialist if necessary. Overall prevalence, and racial prevalence will be compared and factors that may influence results will be examined. Anatomical findings on OCT will be compared against visual outcomes including HRQoL scores.
kw: Epidemiology, Vitreoretinal Interface Abnormalities, Epiretinal Membrane, optical coherence tomography

title: The pulmonary mycobiome in health and disease
abs: Research focus on the bacterial microbiome inevitably neglects the fungal mycobiome despite key roles in respiratory diseases such as bronchiectasis, a permanent irreversible airway dilatation of high prevalence in Singapore. This proposal studies the presence and clinical impact of Aspergillus fumigatus in bronchiectasis; the commonest filamentous fungi within an archetype for anatomical lung damage, as a proof-of-concept model which builds on my existing work in fungal detection for pulmonary disease. Anatomically distorted airways are at high risk of fungal acquisition, colonization and disease. Fungal exposure is a fact of daily human life where >50,000 fungal spores/m3 are detectable in inhaled air. While spore exposure is universal, clinical consequences are not. Aspergillus lung disease is difficult to identify and treat because of non-specific symptoms, delayed diagnosis and emerging anti-fungal resistance. Aspergillus lacks dedicated study in bronchiectasis despite documented effects in asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. We hypothesize that occurrence of Aspergillus and its clinical states are highly prevalent and going undetected in bronchiectasis. To study this, we employ culture and molecular biology for its detection. We next identify clinical states of sensitization, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis and chronic pulmonary aspergillosis even when subclinical. Following comprehensive assessment of immune responses to Aspergillus, next generation pyrosequencing is applied to define the airway mycobiome. Utilizing an unbiased untargeted metabolomics approach, we aim to uncover novel Aspergillus derived small molecules from blood, sputum and airway secretions with the potential to represent novel biomarkers for diagnostic use. This work generates a detailed understanding of the mycobiome in bronchiectasis with the intention of influencing paradigm shift, leading to international recommended guideline change for bronchiectasis management in the short-term and promoting development of novel diagnostics in this field with international impact over the long-term.

title: Development of Preclinical Drug Screening Strategies to Target Unmet Therapeutic Needs in a Treatment-Resistant Aggressive Model of Pediatric Germinoma
abs: PROJECT BACKGROUND: Pediatric brain cancer is the leading cause of death in childhood cancer. Intracranial germ cell tumor (ICGT) has an incidence five-to-eightfold greater in Asia/East-Asian regions than Western countries. ICGTs are classified as germinomas (50-70%) and non-germinomatous germ cell tumors. Although majority of children with germinomas are long-term survivors following chemo-radiotherapy, there is an aggressive biological subset of germinoma which are universally lethal, and these tumors occur in infants and very young children. Moreover, 10-15% of all germinomas remain refractory to multimodal therapy. HYPOTHESIS/AIM: Our central hypothesis is that there exist FDA-approved anti-cancer drugs (single agent/combination), which can effectively target treatment-resistant cell populations in germinoma. The specific aim of the proposal being: To determine in-vitro and in-vivo drug sensitivity pattern, and molecular effects of a shortlisted of FDA-approved drug candidates, selected based on their mechanisms of action, against a patient-derived biologically aggressive germinoma model established in our laboratory. RATIONALE AND METHODS: The cell line and patient-derived orthotopic xenograft model derived from a patient with highly aggressive, disseminated, and chemo-resistant germinoma, to be employed in this study, have previously been demonstrated by us that they represent biologically aggressive variants of germinoma and can serve as excellent platforms for the identification of novel compounds to target resistant subpopulations of germinoma. This is the first cell line and mouse xenograft model available for germinoma in the neurooncology field that accurately recapitulates the biological and histological characteristics of the original patient tumor. The panel of selected FDA-approved drug candidates will be screened initially using this cell line and then validated by the xenograft model. CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE: Our study is highly significant since it will formulate a pioneer therapeutic blue-print for treating resistant germinoma and will enable the rapid translation of the validated drug candidates into bedside clinical trials directly relevant to Asia.

title: A biomaterials approach for endodontic (dental pulp) regeneration
abs: Dental caries and trauma to a tooth affects the pulp and leads to pulpitis, which is most often irreversible. Currently, root canal treatment is the golden standard for irreversible pulpitis and involves removal of the entire pulp and replacing it with gutta-percha. There is currently no effective treatment to repair the infected or injured pulp tissue besides complete amputation. Endodontic treatment leads to substantial loss of dental structures, with the risk of microleakage and reinfection leading to fracture. Hence, there is great interest in the regeneration of dental pulp and dentin via delivery of dental pulp stem cells (dPSC). Recently, dental pulp derived stem cells have been successfully used to fill and regenerate dental pulp and dentinal tissue in animal models using growth factors and hydrogels. This strategy has serious limitations for clinical implementation as it makes use of expensive chemical inducers such as growth factors. Recently, micro- and nano- technologies have provided avenues for surface functionalization of biomaterials with precision. These physical surface modification approaches such as surface topographies demonstrate trophic effects on cell behavior similar to that of growth factors. We propose to use this physical surface functionalization approach on existing set of biomaterials for pulp regeneration. Using our Cellompic chip high throughput-screening platform we shall identify optimal topography that promote homing of progenitor cells from periapical region into the pulp chamber as well as one that favors subsequent endothelial and neuronal differentiation of dPSC’s. A biodegradable polymeric material such as polylactic acid based cones with identified topographies shall then be fabricated and will be used for filling the root canal in a primate model. The function of the regenerated tissue will be determined with histology and immunohistochemistry. The success of this project would represent a potential breakthrough in clinical endodontics using physical functionalization of biomaterials.
kw: Dental Materials, Endodontics, Surface topography, high throughput screening

title: Oncogenic determinants of Homologous Recombination (HR) DNA Repair Deficiency in tumours
abs: Impaired DNA repair by homologous recombination (HR) sensitizes cells to platinum chemotherapeutics and targeted small molecule inhibition of the repair enzyme Poly-ADP Ribose Polymerase 1 (PARP-1). However, identifying the right patient population for PARP inhibitor therapy remains a major hurdle in sporadic cancers, since traditional cellular markers of the HR tumour suppressor pathway are technically challenging in histological material. Interestingly, in-vitro data suggests that overexpression of certain oncogenes is associated with suppression of specific DNA repair pathways. Aberrant overexpression of the mitotic kinases AURORA Kinase-A (AURKA) and Polo-like Kinase 1 (PLK1) has been shown to suppress HR, and therefore may help identify sporadic epithelial cancers that are sensitive to platinum treatment and PARP inhibition. The major aim of this study will be to evaluate the relationship between AURKA/ PLK1 overexpression and PARPi/ platinum response, using patient derived xenografts and clinical samples of ovarian cancer, to establish a novel predictive assay for HR deficiency. We will use an automated multispectral microscopy system (Vectra2) to quantitatively assay for mitotic kinase expression in formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) samples. We will then correlate our kinase expression assay with clinical responses to PARP inhibition in PDX samples, and in archival material from clinical data sets and trials of platinum treatment in ovarian cancer. Concurrently, we also aim to conduct an exploratory in-vitro lentiviral expression screen, to identify other potential oncogenes that may confer PARPi/Platinum sensitivity through suppression of HR. Since high expression is preferable to loss of expression for immunohistochemical biomarkers, we will focus on transcripts that have been enriched in an analysis for good platinum response when overexpressed. This segment of the proposal will help yield novel FFPE biomarkers for HR deficiency, towards refining the selection of patients for future clinical trials involving platinum compounds and PARP inhibitors.

title: Diet and cognitive health in ageing: a community-based prospective cohort study
abs: We propose a prospective cohort study to identify dietary factors that are associated with better cognitive health in late life, to investigate their partial mediating role in reducing oxidative damage and inflammation, and to examine the interaction between diet and APOE genotype in influencing cognitive function. We hypothesized that (1) the consumption of certain foods and beverages and the adherence to certain dietary patterns can delay cognitive decline and reduce the incidence of neurocognitive disorders; (2) the cognitive benefits of dietary factors can be explained by various nutrients and compounds from diet and are mediated partially by reduced oxidative damage and systemic chronic inflammation; (3) carriers of certain allelic polymorphisms of APOE gene may benefit more or less from brain healthy diets. Information on diet and cognition has been collected from the Diet and Healthy Ageing Study. In this study, we will conduct follow-up assessments of 900 participants aged 60+ at baseline. We will use standard cognitive tests and clinical tools to assess cognitive functioning and obtain consensus diagnoses of mild and major neurocognitive disorders based on DSM 5 criteria. We will measure APOE genotype, oxidative damage, pro-inflammatory cytokines, ergothioneine, L-theanine, catechins, curcumin and other nutritional biomarkers using archived blood specimens and blood and urine specimens that we will collect at follow-up. We will repeat food frequency questionnaire (FFQ) and related measures to detect diet changes over time. Hypothesis-driven analysis will be conducted using appropriate statistical techniques. The proposed study will be the first that rigorously examines the relationships between Asian diets and cognitive function in late life. It will identify dietary targets to guide prevention initiatives. Translation of the research findings into clinical and public health practices may potentially lead to an enormous impact on health care savings.

title: The Role of the Endothelial Glycocalyx, Mast Cells and Vascular Nitric Oxide in the Pathogenesis of Dengue
abs: Dengue is the most common arboviral infection in the world and is spreading globally. Dengue infection is mostly asymptomatic or an acute self-limiting febrile illness, but in some cases can be fatal. The hallmark of severe dengue is plasma leakage resulting in decreased intravascular volume, hypotension and shock, but the pathogenic mechanism remains unclear. The endothelial glycocalyx and microvascular flow play major roles in regulating vascular permeability and plasma shift into the interstitium. Animal models of dengue have shown mast cells mediators (MCM) also play a role in plasma leakage, but it is unclear if MCM such as tryptase act to breakdown the glycocalyx in dengue. The roles of the glycocalyx, microvascular flow and MCM have not been studied in adult dengue.In a prospective observational study, we aim to measure in dengue patients in the febrile, critical and recovery phases the, i) glycocalyx thickness of sublingual capillaries in real time using a sidestream darkfield spectroscope and glycocalyx breakdown products ii) microvascular flow using a near infrared resonance spectroscope, and iii) mast cell mediators. We will determine if glycocalyx breakdown leading to decreased thickness, increased MCM, and increased microvascular flow are associated with disease severity. We hypothesize that1.Endothelial glycocalyx thickness will be decreased in the febrile and critical phase of dengue and will be associated with disease severity and plasma leakage. 2.Mast cell mediators will be increased in the febrile and critical phase of dengue and will be associated with glycocalyx breakdown, disease severity, and plasma leakage.3.Microvascular flow will be increased in the critical phase of dengue and be associated with disease severity and plasma leakage.Delineation of the pathogenic roles of the glycocalyx, microvascular flow and MCM in dengue plasma leakage will identify new therapeutic targets to treat the major pathogenic mechanism of dengue.

title: Placental lipid flux in gestational diabetes and the effects of myoinositol
abs: In Singapore, diabetes constitutes 10% of disease burden and 25% of pregnancies are complicated by gestational diabetes (GDM), which is linked with fetal macrosomia, adverse obstetric outcomes and future offspring risk of obesity and type 2 diabetes. Preliminary studies suggest that myoinositol supplementation reduces the rate of GDM but its mechanism of effect in pregnancy is not understood. The placenta is a focal point of GDM pathophysiology, with placental lipid flux postulated to be the main driver of fetal adiposity. Our overarching hypothesis is that dysregulated placental lipid flux is a major determinant of fetal fat accretion in GDM, and that this pathophysiology is amenable to correction by myoinositol supplementation to reduce the risk of fetal macrosomia. This proposal aims to (i) characterise the specific changes in placental lipid flux associated with placental myoinositol status, (ii) assess the effects of in vitro myoinositol treatment on placental uptake and metabolism of stable isotope-labelled fatty acids, (iii) determine if these effects are mediated by disruptions in second messenger signalling, PPAR activity, secretion of signalling agents, and expression of proteins involved in lipid transport and metabolism, (iv) investigate if in vivo myoinositol supplementation in the NiPPeR randomised controlled trial, regulates placental lipid flux thus reducing fetal fat accretion and macrosomia risk in GDM. This innovative, integrated series of experiments ranging from in vitro to in vivo studies, employing advanced LC-MS lipidomics, utilising perinatal samples from the three Singaporean birth cohorts with extensive phenotypic data, provide an unprecedented opportunity to investigate the mechanistic effects of myoinositol in pregnancy. The evidence gained from this proposal will provide critical scientific underpinning for on-going clinical trials and would greatly strengthen support for widespread implementation of a potentially effective and first ever supplementation strategy for GDM prevention with substantial public health impact worldwide.

title: Determination of microRNA signatures in FUS/TLS-mediated neurodegeneration
abs: Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) represent two ends of the same disease spectrum of adult-onset neurodegenerative diseases that affect the neocortex and spinal cord. Multiple common genetic loci such as FUS/TLS (fused-in-sarcoma/translocated-in-sarcoma) were recently identified to have a role in ALS and FTD aetiology. Furthermore, intracellular FUS/TLS protein aggregates are present in the brain and spinal cord tissue of ALS/FTD patients regardless of FUS/TLS gene mutation status. Such gene-pathology connections are commonly seen in neurodegenerative diseases, which implies that distinct initiating events might be funneled into a pathogenic pathway leading to the same endpoint for the disease. We postulate that there is a pathogenic cascade for FUS/TLS-mediated neurotoxicity, with dysfunctional FUS/TLS contributing to differential effects on the cognitive and motor systems. Furthermore, we hypothesise that additional specific molecular underpinnings are layered onto the core cascade to give rise to region-specific outcomes. Molecularly, FUS is known to participate in biogenesis of cellular RNAs, including mRNAs and microRNAs (miRNAs). Each miRNA species can modulate multiple mRNAs that function in a certain biological pathway, and changes of cellular states are often associated with characteristic changes of miRNA expression profiles. We hypothesize that a small number of miRNA genes govern the core and region-specific responses to FUS/TLS dysfunction, and the analysis of miRNA expression profiles will provide a simple means of investigating molecular mechanisms underlying cognitive and motor dysfunction. We will test this hypotheseses by using mouse disease models and elucidating how the affected miRNAs contribute to neuronal and synaptic dysfunction.

title: Evaluation of the Antibacterial and Osteogenic Potency of Co-Substituted Apatite during Bone Remodeling Process under Three In-Vitro Contamination Models
abs: Hydroxyapatite (HA) is a favourable biomaterial for bone regeneration and remodelling, but stoichiometric HA lacks antibacterial and osteogenic potency against pre-operative or post-operative contamination. Co-substitution of silver and silicon into apatite (Ag,Si-HA) will overcome the challenges of implant-related infection and lack of native tissue integration, since Ag is an antibacterial agent and Si is a bone promoter. It is hypothesised that the Ag component (either surface-bound or local release) of Ag,Si-HA actively inhibits the growth of both gram-positive and gram-negative microbes, thus preventing biofilm formation, whilst the Si component allows for mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) attachment, proliferation and osteogenic differentiation in a bacteria-contaminated environment. This research will investigate the antibacterial and osteogenic potency of Ag,Si-HA on bacteria and cells under three in-vitro contamination models, which simulate surgical site infection (Model 1), failure of sterilisation (Model 2), and haematogenous seeding of bacteria from a bacteraemic patient (Model 3). Model 1 is applied to co-culturing of Ag,Si-HA with Pseudomonas aeruginosa (P. aeruginosa) and MSCs simultaneously, to evaluate the responses of Ag,Si-HA in mediating bacteria-cell competition. Model 2 is applied to co-culturing of Ag,Si-HA firstly with P. aeruginosa, followed by the introduction of MSCs, in which Ag,Si-HA is able to maintain a surface viable for MSC attachment and growth even after prolonged exposure to bacteria. Lastly, Model 3 is applied to co-culturing of Ag,Si-HA firstly with MSCs followed by the introduction of Propionibacterium acnes (P. acnes), to further ascertain its antibacterial performance. Furthermore, the mechanistic route undertaken by the Ag+ ions of Ag,Si-HA in exhibiting its antibacterial action when cells layers are attached on Ag,Si-HA will be investigated. On the whole, this work will demonstrate the antibacterial and osteogenic potency of Ag,Si-HA towards clinical implant-related infection challenges, and further serve as a strong support in translating Ag,Si-HA from bench to bedside.

title: Study Early Asymptomatic Molecular Pathology Of Neurodegeneration In Dementia: Proteomic Identification Of Priority Drug Targets
abs: There are 47.5 million people worldwide affected by dementia, and the social and economic costs of this disorder surpassed those attributed to cancer and heart disease. Despite World Health Organization declarations that dementia now represents a public health priority, disease pathogenesis remains poorly understood and there are still no effective treatments for this disorder. Accordingly, the number of dementia patients is projected to triple by 2050, and there is an urgent need to identify key mechanisms of dementia pathogenesis for subsequent therapeutic targeting.Human dementia is regarded as a ‘proteinopathy’ in which changes in brain protein structure and function promote neurodegeneration. Our laboratory is therefore focused on uncovering the complex molecular pathology of this disorder using proteomics; an unbiased, discovery-driven approach that can identify pathological changes in protein structure and function in human cells and tissues.Over the past 10 years, we have focused on proteomic studies of hypoxic-ischemic brain injury, degenerative protein modifications (DPMs) and aggregation. We discovered for the first time a ‘vicious cycle’ of brain tissue damage induced by hypoxic-ischemic brain injury that critically dysregulated key enzymes mediating protein degradation and repair in the affected tissues, leading to accumulation of DPMs damaged proteins and subsequent protein misfolding and aggregation, resulting in neurodegeneration and dementia. We now propose to conduct a longitudinal proteomic study of dementia pathogenesis in an animal model of inducible vascular dementia. We will monitor dementia progression from the asymptomatic stages to the advanced stages, assess whether active lifestyle and mental activity can modify disease course, and validate potential drug targets by analyzing post-mortem brain tissues from dementia patients and age-matched controls. Taken together, these approaches will generate vital new data on the molecular pathology of early, asymptomatic dementia, and will critically support drug discovery efforts aiming to tackle this major public health problem.

title: Integrating germline risk variants into a clinically testable predictor for sporadic colorectal carcinomas likely to metastasize
abs: Colorectal Cancer (CRC) is one of the highest incidence cancers and leading cause of cancer mortality in the developed world.1 Majority of mortality is attributable to metastasis to distant organs. Late or stage IV CRC patients have distant metastasis by definition. Up to 25% of early-stage CRC (Stage I and II) and 50% of stage III patients, however, succumb to distant metastasis. We are developing a metastasis predictor in CRC based on genome-wide expression profiling.2 Recent evidences indicate that germline predisposition also contributes to metastasis.3-4 We aim to identify the germline genetic variants associated with metastasis risk and integrate these to the expression-based predictor to improve its predictive values. Association test performed on 437 metastasis-negative (stage I/II) vs 185 metastasis-positive (stage IV and I/II that succumb to metastasis) patients from a previously generated genome-wide genotyping dataset5 identify several potential risk regions, each with 10 or more single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). The highest risk SNP is at chromosome 22 (–log10 p-value = 5.6); and this encompasses an interesting gene in the Wnt/?-catenin signalling pathway. Preliminary findings thus suggest the feasibility of finding such germline variants.In the study proposed here, we will perform genome-wide genotyping on another 2000 CRC patients with detailed clinicopathological documentation from the same center to increase the power to identify more SNPs and structural variants. These variants will be validated on an independent replication panel. Validated loci will be integrated into the expression-based predictor by bioinformatics analysis to further improve the predictive values of such a signature which has not been previously performed. Finally, we will validate the integrated predictor in an additional independent cohort of patient samples. The ultimate goal is the development of an accurate biomarker-based predictor for metastasis that can subsequently be made widely available to improve clinical outcomes.

title: Low-cost, portable, real-time pulsed laser diode photoacoustic tomography (PLD-PAT) system for brain tumor imaging, and monitoring of photothermal therapy in small animal model
abs: Malignant brain tumor diagnosis and treatment is of significant impact to our society. They are hard to treat as it is highly vascularized with abnormal architecture; therefore there is a need for better therapeutic options, tissue characterization and diagnosis using reliable noninvasive imaging technology. Photoacoustic tomography (PAT) is a relatively new hybrid imaging modality combining optics and ultrasound for deep tissue in vivo imaging of intrinsic optical absorption distribution. Blood being a strong optical absorber, PAT is capable of imaging brain vasculature noninvasively. However, translating PAT into clinic has been a great challenge due to its cost, bulky size and inability to do real-time imaging. Here, we propose to build a portable, low-cost, and real time pulse laser diode photoacoustic tomography (PLD-PAT) system for imaging brain tumor in small animal model. Use of PLD will address all the three challenges PAT is facing at present to translate it into clinical practice. Together with targeted organic nanoparticles contrast agents and photothermal therapy (PTT), PLD-PAT system will be used for early tumor detection and therapy treatment monitoring. The treatment response will be monitored using our PLD-PAT system on a C6 glioma brain tumor model in small animal.
kw: photoacoustic tomography, low cost imaging, brain imaging, photothermal therapy

title: Targeting a novel Ca2+-PP2A-RIPK1-dependent cell death pathway in cancer metabolism
abs: Unlike normal cells, many cancer cells generate energy and anabolic building blocks by glycolysis in the presence of oxygen (aerobic glycolysis or the Warburg effect) and are more dependent on glucose for survival than normal cells. Glycolysis inhibitors predicted to selectively eliminate cancer cells have been investigated, but the response is mild and varied. We investigated how glucose deprivation affected different cancer cell lines, and discovered a previously unappreciated cell death pathway. After glucose removal, intracellular glucose levels become critically low in glucose-dependent cancer, but not normal, cells. Intracellular glucose depletion was accompanied by calcium influx, activation of CAMK1, demethylation of the phosphatase PP2Ac, phosphorylation of RIPK1, and cell death. Unexpectedly, PP2Ac demethylation and cell death were rescued with a glucose analog that inhibits glycolysis. These findings reveal a novel requirement for glucose independent of glycolysis, suggest an entirely new therapeutic avenue and question the therapeutic potential of glycolysis inhibition. We hypothesize that glucose acts as a signaling molecule to suppress activation of this cell death pathway. In Aim 1 we will elucidate the molecular mechanisms of this novel pathway through biochemistry and molecular biology. We further hypothesize that unique combination therapies targeting different components of this pathway will selectively eliminate cancer cells. We will investigate new therapeutic strategies in Aim 2 by molecular biology, cell culture, and mouse xenograft cancer models. Successful completion of this proposal will reveal how glucose withdrawal induces calcium influx, PP2Ac demethylation, RIPK1 activation, and cell death, providing a useful information to target this pathway for cancer therapy. We will also develop strategies to specifically kill cancer cells by combination drug therapies which block glucose transport and elevate cytosolic calcium levels. These unique combination treatments could translate quickly to the clinic and represent an original therapy emerging from Singapore.
kw: calcium, cancer, glucose, PP2A, RIPK1, metabolism

title: Muscle Pressure Ulcers and a Potential Drug Therapy
abs: Pressure ulcers (PrU) are painful, chronic wounds that arise in the skin and muscle of people who have lost mobility, particularly in the frail elderly. PrU are extremely common (18% prevalence in one Singapore study) and highly disruptive to quality of life. Desferoxamine (DFO) is a clinically-approved iron-chelating drug currently used for treating iron-overload syndromes. In animals, local application of DFO has also been extremely effective for accelerating wound healing in PrU of skin. How DFO aids wound healing is unclear, and its efficacy for treating severe PrU, which involve muscle, is also unknown. Our primary goal (Aim 1) is to evaluate the efficacy of DFO in a murine model of muscle PrU. This information will be crucial for designing DFO clinical trials in PrU patients. We will also evaluate the role of myoglobin (Mb) in PrU development and in DFO therapy. Mb is an abundant iron-containing protein that, when released during muscle trauma, can cause endothelial dysfunction and oxidative stress. The contribution of Mb toward PrU injury and healing is unknown, so we will observe muscle PrU in Mb-knockout mice. This experiment will also determine whether the therapeutic benefits of DFO are mediated by Mb. Aim 2 will employ microscopic imaging in live mice to analyse myocyte and capillary dynamics during PrU progression and DFO therapy. Aim 3 will use an in vitro mimic of muscle PrU, myocyte mechanical deformation, to explore the causes and consequences of deformation injury, and will perform low-throughput testing of candidate therapeutic compounds, other than DFO. In summary, the proposed research will provide a wealth of information about PrU pathophysiology. Its impact will be to develop DFO toward clinical trials and to further elucidate the aetiology of muscle PrU.
kw: Wound healing, Bioimaging, Muscle regeneration, Iron chelator, Myoglobin, Image analysis

title: Investigating the dynamic genomic and antigenic landscapes that govern the adaptive evolution of human influenza viruses in Singapore
abs: Human influenza virus circulates globally to cause significant morbidity and mortality. Influenza viruses are subject to continuous evolutionary selection, referred to as “antigenic drift”, leading to the emergence of new variants with reduced host immune protection. The pandemic A/H1N1 (H1N1/2009) virus that emerged from pigs in 2009 is now established as a seasonal influenza virus along with A/H3N2 and influenza B viruses, and is included as a component in the bi-annual WHO influenza vaccine strain recommendations. Most genomic studies have primarily focused on A/H3N2 virus with comparisons made to the now extinct seasonal H1N1 virus (i.e. prior to 2009), but less attention has been given to the current circulating H1N1/2009 virus. However the PI and some Co-Is recently characterized H1N1/2009 virus evolution from 2009–2014, highlighting the transition from host adaptation to evolution driven primarily by immunological escape. In this proposal, we aim to extend this work to provide further characterization of H1N1/2009 evolution as a seasonal virus and to experimentally investigate antigenic evolution and epistatic interactions affecting virus replicative fitness. The specific project objectives are:(1) To elucidate how epidemiological and spatial processes interact to drive the evolution of human influenza A virus in Singapore(2) To characterize the patterns of phenotypic variation of influenza A virus in shaping antigenic dynamics(3) To investigate the effect of epistatic mutations on replicative fitness of human influenza virus using bioinformatic and experimental approachesThis study will generate new genomic data to allow us to characterize population dynamics and intra-host variation of influenza viruses circulating in Singapore. We will identify emerging antigenic variants associated with increased disease severity. More profoundly, our research findings will ultimately contribute a wealth of up-to-date data for improving health control strategies to reduce risks of influenza spread and infection.
kw: Seasonal influenza, natural selection, antigenic evolution, spatial transmission, monoclonal antibody, next-generation sequencing

title: Enabling sexual genetics in bacteria to study the evolution of virulence and antibiotic resistance
abs: Sexual genetics combined with linkage analysis is a powerful and scalable approach for mapping phenotypes to genotypes, underlying decades of discovery in human Mendelian diseases and basic biology in yeast and other organisms. Two key phenotypes of fundamental and immediate practical importance are the ability of some bacteria to cause disease and antibiotic resistance. Typically, two random clinical isolates of disease-causing bacteria of the same species may differ by up to hundreds of thousands of sequence differences. Sexual genetics and linkage analysis provide a ready solution to systematically assaying all of these differences, a task that is intractable using other current bacterial techniques. Unfortunately, sexual genetics is not available for bacteria such as Escherichia coli that are not naturally competent.
