We have developed a stringent negative selection system for pathogenic clinical isolates of E. coli and have demonstrated its feasibility for allelic exchange at a single locus (sexual recombination at a targeted locus, which we term generalized allelic exchange (GAE)). In this proposal, we aim to extend these initial results to create the first general system for hybridizing arbitrary strains of E. coli, thereby enabling the use of sexual genetics to systematically analyze the thousands of gene differences and tens of thousands of single nucleotide polymorphisms that differentiate unrelated E. coli strains. Such a strategy (which we term mass allelic exchange (MAE)) would enable genomic studies of virulence, providing insight into pathogen evolution and novel therapeutic targets. We will also apply this to rapidly profile the full complement of polymorphisms that impact quantitative differences in antibiotic resistance. Other applications in synthetic biology and extension other bacteria are also possible with potential benefits for basic knowledge as well as biotechnology.
kw: Antibiotic resistance; bacterial infection; bacterial genetics

title: Elucidating the novel role of cytosolic PINK1 in mitochondrial quality control and its relevance to Parkinson’s disease
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Mutations in PINK1, a serine/threonine kinase, are responsible for recessive forms of Parkinson’s disease (PD). Recent studies have revealed that PINK1 collaborates with another PD-linked gene Parkin (encoding a ubiquitin ligase) to regulate the clearance of damaged mitochondria via mitophagy, suggesting that mitophagic defects may promote the pathogenesis of the disease. However, PINK1 exists in two major forms: full length and a cleaved form that resides in the cytosol (albeit typically fleetingly). The potential cellular function of the 53 kDa cytosolic form of PINK1 (PINK1-53) is often overlooked due to its rapid degradation by the proteasome upon its production. Although a number of recent studies have suggested various roles for PINK1-53 (including being a neuroprotectant), how this labile PINK1 species attain an adequate expression level to fulfil these roles remains unclear. Whether disease-associated mutations residing on PINK1-53 are relevant to PD pathogenesis is also unclear. In an exciting development, we have recently found that PINK1-53 may be stabilized via the NF-kB pathway and promotes non-selective mitophagy (Lim et al., 2015 JBC). In this proposal, we seek to characterize the physiological role of PINK1-53 and potential pathophysiological role of its mutations more comprehensively. Accordingly, our objectives are to 1) elucidate the novel mechanism underlying PINK1-53-mediated mitophagy, 2) elucidate the physiological role of PINK1-53 in vivo (by generating a unique PINK1-53 mouse model alongside the Drosophila model), and 3) elucidate the potential role of PINK1-53 in PD pathogenesis. The outcomes of this study are expected to lead to an important paradigm shift in the mechanistic model of PINK1 function that will feature altered PINK1-53 function as a novel player in PD pathogenesis. Obviously, these clarifications not only have significant scientific impact but also hold promise for the development of novel PD therapeutics targeted at (the hitherto poorly characterized) PINK1-53 function.
kw: Parkinson's disease; neurodegeneration; mitochondria; PINK1; Parkin

title: Understanding the physiological and pathological roles of MOAP-1 in regulating the Fas-Bid mitochondrial apoptosis signalling system in liver
abs: Mitochondria play central role in regulating mammalian apoptosis. MOAP-1 (Modulator of apoptosis-1) is a Bax-binding protein residing at the outer mitochondrial membrane. Apoptotic stimuli stabilize MOAP-1 and promote its interaction with Bax. Earlier work showed that levels of MOAP-1 protein can regulate sensitivity of tumor cells to chemotherapeutic drugs.Preliminary work in characterizing the MOAP-1 knockout (KO) mice showed they were resistant to the hepatic injury and lethality triggered by activation of the Fas signaling. An essential step in activating apoptosis in hepatocytes by Fas is the generation of the cleaved (activated) form of Bid, t-Bid, by activated caspase-8. Mitochondrial targeting of t-Bid is necessary and it has recently been reported that it is mediated by binding to its mitochondrial receptor, MTCH2. In MOAP-1 KO mice, mitochondrial targeting rather than production of t-Bid was found to be affected. MOAP-1 associates with MTCH2 rather than t-Bid. Interestingly, MOAP-1 is required for effecting binding of t-Bid to MTCH2. Fas-mediated apoptosis is implicated in a broad spectrum of liver diseases. Surprisingly, in the diethylnitrosamine (DEN)-mediated liver cancer model, while tumor development was retarded in the Bid KO mice, significant enhancement of tumor burden was observed in the MOAP-1 KO mice, raising the possibility that MOAP-1 may act as tumor suppressor in liver. We hypothesize that MOAP-1 regulates liver physiology and pathology via the Fas-Bid mitochondrial apoptosis signaling system. The proposed project aims to use genetic mouse models and primary hepatocytes for investigating the roles of MOAP-1 in regulating the Fas-Bid-Bax signaling axis, liver carcinogenesis and fulminant hepatitis. MOAP-1 is regulated by the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) which makes it potentially druggable. It is anticipated that the proposed study will advance our understanding of the physiological and pathological roles of MOAP-1 in liver to permit exploration of MOAP-1 as drug targets for certain liver diseases.
kw: Cell Death, MOAP- 1, Fas, Bid, Fulminant Hepatitis, Liver Cancer

title: ZO-1 and ZO-2 in liver development, regeneration and cancer
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: The liver has an amazing capacity for regeneration, being the largest organ responsible for metabolism and bile production. Hepatocytes make up ?80% of the liver but bile duct cells are important too. Besides forming canaliculi between hepatocytes and sealing off the lumen of bile ducts, tight junctions also mediate signal transduction. ZO-1 and ZO-2 connect transmembrane tight junction proteins such as claudins and occludin to the cytoskeleton, and are essential for assembly and maintenance of tight junctions. When deleting ZO-1 and ZO-2 simultaneously in hepatoblasts (ZO-1flox/flox ZO-2flox/flox Alb-Cre mice), we observed a disturbed organization of the hepatic plate and complete lack of bile ducts in postnatal livers. We intend to assess the functions of ZO-1 and ZO-2 during liver development by focusing on the processes implicated in the differentiation of hepatoblasts into biliary cells as well as morphogenesis of the intrahepatic biliary system. In addition, livers lacking ZO-1 and ZO-2 show enhanced cell proliferation. To identify a role for ZO-1 and ZO-2 during hepatocyte-driven regeneration and wound healing response, control and KO livers will undergo partial hepatectomy or CCl4 injections, respectively. The liver progenitor cell (LPC) compartment will be activated by CDE diet administration, upon which expansion of LPC and accompanying microenvironment will be studied for alterations induced by the lack of ZO-1 and ZO-2. As tight junctions are also intimately associated with carcinogenesis, we will induce liver cancer in KO mice by using DEN injections or by crossing with p53 deficient or Yap/Taz KO mice and evaluate the initiation, progression and invasiveness of the induced tumors. Elucidation of the role of ZO-1 and ZO-2 in the regulation of liver development, homeostasis, regeneration and cancer induction should not only advance our understanding of the pathophysiology of the liver but also help to provide new clues for potential novel intervention.
kw: Liver depvelopment, bile duct, liver progenitor cell, tight juncitons, heptocellular charcinoma, liver regeneration

title: Investigation of the nucleolus as a novel target for complement C1q binding and a source of novel substrate for C1q-associated proteases C1r/C1s
abs: C1q-mediated complement activation was historically defined as the bacteriolytic arm of antibody effectors. C1q binding to antigen-congregated IgM or IgG antibodies activates C1q-associated C1r/C1s proteases so as to trigger complement activation, a well-studied pathway. Another striking feature of C1q, C1r and C1s is that their deficiencies cause systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). This is poorly understood but a valuable interface to understand SLE pathogenesis. Besides antibodies, C1q also binds to DNA and this has been used to precipitate C1q from the serum for its purification. Intriguingly, DNA is also a key target of autoantibodies in SLE patients. Furthermore, immune complexes formed between these autoantibodies and DNA released from apoptotic cells are pro-inflammatory and pathogenic. C1q binds to apoptotic cells but the dominant cellular ligand(s) remains elusive. Whether nuclear DNA inside apoptotic debris are C1q ligand is apparently relevant but not studied. With this question, we generated apoptotic HeLa cells by UV irradiation and examined C1q binding to these apoptotic cells. At 1-3 hr, C1q bound punctuate and peripheral sites. By 6 hr, it bound predominantly to the nucleolus, a core nuclear body containing many autoantigens. C1q also bound isolated nucleoli and, with C1r/C1s, caused degradation of the nucleolar protein nucleophosmin 1 (NPM1). In these experiments, we also discovered anti-C1s autoantibody in SLE patient sera.This led us to the following questions: 1) What are the nucleolus component(s) that C1q binds to? 2) Does this form of binding modulate phagocyte responses to apoptotic debris? 3) Does C1q binding to nucleolus cause C1r/C1s proteolytic degradation of nucleolus antigens that may otherwise induce autoantibodies and do the newly identified anti-C1s autoantibodies in SLE patients impair C1 degradation of nucleolar antigens?Answers to these questions can provide major new insights into the causative relationship between C1q and C1r/C1s deficiency and SLE pathogenesis.
kw: Complement C1q, C1s, SLE, nucleolus, apoptotic cells

title: Whole exome sequencing to identify actionable mutations causative of exfoliation syndrome and exfoliation glaucoma.
abs: Caused by Exfoliation syndrome (XFS), exfoliation glaucoma is the most prevalent, distinctive, and easily identified secondary form of open angle glaucoma, which affects an estimated 80 million people worldwide, but has been markedly underdiagnosed, under investigated, and largely ignored by researchers until recently. This year, we reported a genome-wide association study (GWAS) of XFS comprising 1,484 cases and 1,188 controls (Aung T et al. Nature Genetics 2015; 47:387-392) identifying CACNA1A (and confirming LOXL1) as associated genes. We recently followed up the initial GWAS with additional GWAS of 8,238 XFS cases and 97,605 controls. This effort identified a further four new XFS loci robustly surpassing genome-wide significance (unpublished). Collectively, all six XFS loci identified to date implicate members of the Calcium signaling pathway (CACNA1A), connective tissue biogenesis (LOXL1), ephrin receptor signaling pathway (EPHA7), antigen presentation (HLA-DRB5), cell and transmembrane signaling (TMEM136), and proteasome mediated proteolysis (POMP). Many XFS patients show positive evidence of familial clustering, leading us to the hypothesis that rare protein-changing mutations of higher penetrance could also underlie XFS. Our targeted deep re-sequencing experiment of CACNA1A revealed strong enrichment of rare non-synonymous genetic mutations in XFS cases compared to controls (Figure 4, Preliminary data). We now propose to perform whole exome sequencing in up to 2000 XFS cases, matched to 3,000 non-XFS controls. This application of whole exome sequencing has identified a wealth of rare mutations of higher penetrance in other complex diseases such as breast cancer, Alzheimer’s disease, and coronary artery disease. If successfully conducted, our proposal will revolutionize the field of XFS research, and may lead to the development of genetic tests for high-risk adults who will benefit from interventions to slow the rate of progression of XFS to glaucoma and blindness. The identification of loss-of-function mutations may also lead to the identification of therapeutic targets.
kw: Exfoliation glaucoma. Whole exome sequencing.

title: Deciphering the Non-Coding Cancer Genome: New Biomarkers and Therapeutic Targets for Gastric Cancer Precision Medicine
abs: Due to reasons of research focus and cost, the search for cancer-causing (driver) mutations has so far been confined to the 2% of our DNA that codes for proteins. The remaining 98% of our genome, the non-coding DNA (ncDNA), make up regulatory circuits critical for many essential cancer processes but is largely ignored in cancer research today. However, the falling cost of unbiased whole genome sequencing is today generating a unique opportunity to systematically probe this dark matter of the cancer genome. Gastric cancer (GC) is one of the world's deadliest cancers, and we hypothesize that alterations in ncDNA develop alongside protein-coding alterations to promote and sustain malignant transformation of GC. Accordingly, we will design and execute a high-throughput experimental/computational screening approach to systematically both identify and functionally characterize non-coding driver alterations in GC. The approach will consist of three components: a) design of a novel data-driven computational algorithm, GCdriver, with increased accuracy for inference of non-coding driver alterations in GC, the algorithm will integrate diverse functional data and leverage new powerful machine learning techniques from computer science to accurately separate driver regions from randomly altered regions, b) assemble the largest cohort of GC genomes to date using public and in-house data, and apply GCdriver on this cohort to generate an unprecedented atlas of non-coding driver mutations and structural alterations in GC, c) generate a detailed functional genomics map of GC using a focused cohort of GC tumors and cell lines, allowing high-throughput functional characterization of driver candidates in epigenetic, transcriptional, and translational regulation. We anticipate that a subset of these non-coding driver regions will have direct translational impact as new biomarkers and novel therapeutic targets in GC, ultimately enabling us to leverage the entire human genome for next-generation precision medicine.
kw: cancer, cancer genomics, gastric cancer, biomarkers, computational biology, precision medicine

title: Modelling metabolic diseases using human pluripotent stem cell-derived liver organoids
abs: Metabolic liver diseases are currently impinging a growing burden in Singapore. Management of liver diseases remains inadequate due to a shortage of liver donors and an incomplete understanding of the underlying mechanisms of disease pathology. While research on metabolic liver diseases is crucial in tackling this issue, this is hindered by the lack of faithful models for metabolic liver diseases. Here, we propose to generate hepatic organoid cultures from human induced pluripotent stem cells as a model for metabolic liver diseases, with the hypothesis that complex cellular systems such as organoid cultures derived from human cells provide better disease models that reflect the in vivo state. We plan to achieve this by first, utilizing self-renewing multipotent endoderm progenitors which serve as a more robust and practical source of terminally differentiated cells compared to pluripotent stem cells. Particularly, we can derive liver organoids from these progenitors, which show closer resemblance to the mature human liver in both structure and function. Moreover, the process of deriving these hepatic units provides an in vitro model for human liver organogenesis. Finally, by combining genome editing and organoid technology, we plan to produce liver organoid units that recapitulate human metabolic diseases, which will be utilized for disease modelling, therapeutic drug discovery and hepatotoxicity screening. These technologies would not only accelerate research on metabolic disease pathogenesis and treatment, but might also offer regenerative therapeutic potential as a source of transplantable tissue. This development will also be valuable to the pharmaceutical industries by providing a scalable in vitro model for human liver function and injury for high-throughput screening purposes.
kw: Embryonic stem cell, Disease modelling, Organoid, Metabolic disease, Liver, Induced pluripotent stem cell

title: Investigating the functions of RNA-binding proteins during neuronal differentiation of human pluripotent stem cells
abs: RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) have emerged as important regulators of gene expression, especially in the nervous system, but only a small percentage of them have been functionally characterized so far. Hence, our overarching goal in this project is to dissect the roles that RBPs play during neural fate specification. First, we aim to perform genetic screens to identify RBPs that regulate the specification, maintenance, or differentiation of neural stem/ progenitor cells. We have developed a novel inducible CRISPR-Cas9 system that will allow us to perform genetic screens in ways that are previously difficult to achieve. By controlling when the Cas9 enzyme is active, we will be able to identify the RBPs that are involved in different aspects of neural stem cell biology. Second, we aim to characterize the functions of one particular family of RBPs, the ADAR enzymes, during neural differentiation. The enzymes catalyse adenosine (A)-to-inosine (I) RNA editing, a widespread regulatory mechanism that diversifies the transcriptome. There are three ADARs encoded in the human genome. We have generated ADAR1-/-, ADAR2-/-, and ADAR3-/- human embryonic stem cells and plan to characterize these knockout cell lines by differentiating them into motor neurons or dopaminergic neurons, identifying abnormal phenotypes, and performing a detailed transcriptome analysis at multiple timepoints during the differentiation process. Third, we aim to investigate the regulation of A-to-I RNA editing in Parkinson’s disease. We have recently discovered a novel editing regulator, AIMP2, which has been implicated in the disease. Overproduction of AIMP2 causes loss of dopaminergic neurons in the brain. Here, we plan to characterize in detail the interaction between AIMP2 and the editing enzymes and to understand how AIMP2 contributes to Parkinson’s disease through RNA editing. Our research will contribute to the understanding of debilitating neurodegenerative disorders and has important implications for human disease modelling.
kw: RNA-binding proteins, A-to-I RNA editing, ADAR enzymes, CRISPR-Cas, motor neuron diseases, Parkinson's disease

title: Integrated computational modelling of right heart mechanics and blood flow dynamics in congenital heart disease
abs: Advances in treatment enable survival of most patients born with congenital heart disease (CHD) into adulthood. Many CHD patients have undergone palliative or reparative surgery earlier in life. Adult survivors may need intervention or surgery for residual hemodynamically significant lesions. The latter predispose patients to increased risk of cardiac arrhythmia, including sudden premature death. In these patients, pre- and post-operative evaluation of right ventricular (RV) structure (shape and volume) and function constitutes an essential component of clinical management. Accurate reproducible assessment of the RV in terms of its structure, function and flow is imperative. Despite advances in cardiac imaging, technology has yet to make significant inroads into comprehensive quantitative assessment of the RV. We aim to develop methods for automated quantitative assessment of the RV in CHD using cardiac magnetic resonance images. Multiple RV parameters, including exploratory indices, will be investigated: RV structure (volume and regional curvedness in a 15-segment RV model), function (regional strain and ejection fraction) and physiology (RV vortex size). These parameters will be correlated with clinical status and objectively-assessed exercise capacity. This research allows development of a “one-stop-shop” integrated biomedical engineering R&D platform for in-depth study and clinical diagnosis of RV structure-function relationship in diverse diseases. (200 words)Specific Aim #1 (Primary aim): Establish a prospective clinical and image registry of paediatric and adult CHD patients with reference control subjects. Specific Aim #2 (Secondary Aim): Study intra-cardiac blood flow using computational fluid dynamics (CFD) to quantitate RV vortex surface area in CHD vs. healthy control subjects. Specific Aim #3 (Exploratory aim): Generate CMR-derived RV pressure-volume loop for quantitation of RV wall stiffness and contractility and ventricular-arterial coupling in patients with pulmonary hypertension These new findings will enable clinicians to recognize RV dysfunction promptly and optimize individual patient management in preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative interventions.
kw: Right ventricle, structure-function relationship, congenital heart disease, ventricular mechanics and stiffness, hemodynamics, computational fluid dynamics

title: Novel approaches for better BCG vaccines against tuberculosis
abs: Tuberculosis (TB) remains a major health threat killing 1.5 million humans annually. Vaccines are the most cost-effective means to control infectious diseases. The only TB vaccine in clinical use, Bacillus Calmette–Guérin (BCG), provides insufficient protection against pulmonary tuberculosis, the most common form of the disease accounting for 9.6 million new clinical cases worldwide in 2014 of which 58% were in South-East Asia and the Western Pacific region. The NADH dehydrogenase 1 subunit G (nuoG) gene of the TB pathogen Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) was reported to prevent apoptosis of host cells during infection, which is a normal defense mechanism in response to bacterial intruders. In an attempt to improve the immunogenicity of BCG, we have deleted the nuoG gene to introduce a pro-apoptotic phenotype. Our preliminary data shows that mice vaccinated with BCG ?nuoG were better protected from Mtb infection than animals receiving canonical BCG. In contrast to Mtb, deletion of nuoG in BCG did not increase apoptosis of host cells suggesting that improved pre-clinical efficacy of BCG ?nuoG has a new underlying mechanism which we want to investigate. To further improve our new vaccine candidate BCG ?nuoG, we will focus on 3 strategies: (1) stimulation of T cells by immunogenic epitopes of mycobacteria, (2) secretion of the human cytokine B cell activating factor (BAFF), and (3) overexpression of mycobacterial antigens related to latent TB infection. The efficacy and immunogenicity of the newly generated BCG ?nuoG derivatives will subsequently be evaluated in BALB/c mice and more importantly in humanized mice that maybe more predictive of the clinical outcome. The proposal aims to deliver a new recombinant BCG vaccine candidate with a novel mechanism of action and improved pre-clinical efficacy over BCG, allowing to acquire funding for further development including first in man studies.
kw: Recombinant BCG, tuberculosis, latency antigen, T cell, B cell, human cytokine

title: SIRT1 regulation of fatty acid synthase (FASN) acetylation in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD)
abs: Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) represents a spectrum of conditions ranging from fatty liver to early and late steatohepatitis (NASH) to cirrhosis. This disorder is due to an imbalance between hepatic synthesis and breakdown of fats, leading to fat accumulation in the liver. However, its pathogenesis remains poorly understood and therapeutic options for NAFLD currently are limited. We recently showed that the histone deacetylase, SIRT1, participates in the regulation of hepatic glucose and lipid metabolism by inducing transcriptional and post-translational changes in proteins. Moreover, dysregulation of these pathways contribute to development of hepatosteatosis in NAFLD. However, SIRT1’s effect on the acetylation state of hepatic proteome is not known in NAFLD. Using the SIRT1 acetylome as a comprehensive and unbiased method to detect changes in global protein acetylation, we found that fatty acid synthase (FASN), an enzyme that is critical for regulating de novo fatty acid synthesis, is a novel direct target of SIRT1. Interestingly, we also found increased FASN acetylation and decreased SIRT1 expression in the mouse livers during steatosis. Therefore, we hypothesized that dysregulation of SIRT1-dependent FASN deacetylation contributes to the development and progression of NAFLD. To examine this issue, we plan to investigate the role of role of SIRT1 in the regulation of FASN acetylation and lipogenesis in hepatic cells, livers from a NAFLD mouse models (Specific Aim 1) as well as in acetylation mutant FASN transgenic mice (Specific Aim 2). Furthermore, we will also analyze SIRT1 and other SIRTs expression and changes in global protein acetylation (acetylome) in mouse livers exhibiting steatosis and steatohepatitis; and liver tissues from NAFLD patients (Specific Aim 3). Our findings should lead to a better understanding of SIRT1 regulation of fatty acid synthesis and NAFLD progression, and may lead to development of therapeutic interventions based upon SIRT1 activation.
kw: NAFLD, NASH, SIRT1, Acetylome, Fatty acid synthsae, Lipid metabolism

title: Use of positron emission tomography–computed tomography (PET-CT) for the non-invasive study of dengue virus infection in mice
abs: The study of dengue pathogenesis is hampered by the lack of clear mapping of target tissues involved in virus replication during the acute infection phase. The aim of this study is to assess the utility of positron emission tomography–computed tomography (PET-CT) for the non-invasive study of dengue virus (DENV) infection for better understanding of DENV pathogenesis in vivo. Recently, the PI group showed that high mortality was induced in DENV-infected AG129 mice (lacking IFN receptors) by the increase in TNF-induced vascular permeability specifically in small intestine. This novel finding suggests that dengue disease severity is regulated in a tissue-dependent manner. We hypothesize that PET biomarker imaging with radioactive probes can serve to noninvasively identify sites of inflammation and vascular leakage caused by DENV infection and examine the mechanism(s) underlying the dengue disease severity in preclinical models. Notably, our preliminary data of PET imaging in lethally DENV-infected AG129 mice showed a strong correlation with the data of tissue cytokine profile obtained by the PI’s group in a previous study. We will pursue the following specific aims to test our central hypothesis: (1) to systematically identify sites that exhibit abnormal FDG probe accumulation during the progression of acute dengue diseases in mouse models of DENV1 and DENV2 by using 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG), a probe for glucose metabolism and a surrogate marker of inflammation, and (2) to explore the role of DENV non-structural protein 1 (NS1) in DENV pathogenesis by using 125/124I-labeled NS1 protein and FDG.
kw: dengue virus, PET imaging, tissue inflamation, vascular leakage, mouse model

title: Targeting the Mitochondrial Calcium Uniporter Regulator 1 in neuronal ischemia-reperfusion injury
abs: The Singapore Burden of Disease Study recently reported that stroke as the second highest cause of premature mortality and the eighth highest cause of disability burden in Singapore. Reperfusion of the brain after ischemic stroke initiates pathologic intracellular cascades that contribute to post-ischemic neuronal cell death. The paradox of reperfusion injury after brain ischemia remains mechanistically unresolved and clinically untreated. Aligned with NMRC’s mission, our long-term goal is to identify a molecular target for drug development to improve the outcomes of patients who undergo brain reperfusion during the treatment of stroke. While mitochondrial Ca2+ overload is largely implicated in stroke, attempts to prevent [Ca2+]m overload remain unsuccessful. We recently identified MCUR1 as a regulatory subunit of mitochondrial Ca2+ uniporter. Our central hypothesis is that neuronal reperfusion injury is caused by MCUR1-mediated mitochondrial matrix Ca2+ overload. We will test this hypothesis by silencing MCUR1 and measuring the effects in progressively translational models of neuronal reperfusion injury. Thus, the overall objective of this application is to elucidate the role of MCUR1 mediated mitochondrial Ca2+ overload and the downstream mechanisms of neuronal reperfusion injury and to validate whether MCUR1 targeting offers protection to neurons from reperfusion injury. In Specific Aim 1, we will determine the role of MCUR1 in neuronal mitochondrial Ca2+ homeostasis, redox signaling and bioenergetics. In Specific Aim 2, we will determine the in vivo efficacy of silencing MCUR1 in preventing neuronal reperfusion injury in a well-established mice model of stroke. Taken together, our proposed studies will advance the field by elucidating a key mechanism of mitochondrial mediated neuronal reperfusion injury, and by identifying a novel molecular target to prevent neuronal reperfusion injury after stroke. Furthermore, this work will provide the foundation and tools for future research examining the role of mitochondrial Ca2+ uniporter in other acute and chronic neurodegenerative diseases.
kw: mitochondria, stroke, ischemia-reperfusion, uniporter, ion channel

title: Microfluidic Assay for Routine Evaluation of Anti-Cancer Drug Therapy on Clinical Human Circulating Tumor Cells
inst: CREATE - Singapore-MIT Alliance for Research and Technology (CREATE-SMART)
abs: Progression of anti-cancer drug development into actual clinical utility remains hindered by the inherent heterogeneity of the disease, as well as limitations of in vitro screening systems. Clinicians are often also provided a short window of opportunity to make decisions for treatment, based on the information generated from tumor imaging and sample profiling. In this proposal, we describe the development of a rapid and convenient microfluidic anti-cancer drug assay for clinicians to carry out screening and evaluation. Routine sampling of cancer cells from each patient can be achieved via serial withdrawals of small volumes of blood from patients, making it a promising strategy for early-stage cancer detection and monitoring of treatment efficacy. Cancer cells from blood are termed as circulating tumor cells (CTCs), and comprise of subpopulations with self-renewal, high plasticity or adaptive capabilities. The presence of CTCs negatively correlates with patient survival, and are associated with heightened drug resistance or tolerance traits. The microfluidic assay combines a gradient generator with a microwell culture platform optimized for the development of clinical human CTCs-containing clusters. Clinical utility of the assay will be evaluated with both cancer cell lines and primary cells from blood of cancer patients. Data of prognostic value can be obtained within two weeks. The assay will allow rapid and efficient screening of anti-cancer drugs on primary CTCs, through the exposure of drugs at different concentrations to primary CTCs of an individual patient obtained at various time points of treatment. A robust protocol to expedite repeated sampling of CTCs from patients may enable clinicians to more accurately detect relapse or predict treatment efficacy for each individual patient, facilitating personalized treatment. This non-invasive and inexpensive assessment of drug response can potentially guide drug discovery development and provides therapeutic choices for personalized treatment.
kw: Cancer, Circulating Tumor Cell, Microfluidics, Drug Response, Combinational Therapy, Prognostic assay

title: Identifying novel human drug targets for anti-dengue therapeutics through a systems analysis of human host factors and pathways engaged by the dengue virus NS4B protein
abs: The dengue virus (DV) NS4B protein is a small integral membrane protein that is essential for virus replication and suppresses the host innate immune response. However, it is undetermined mechanistically how NS4B is involved in these processes. Despite this, the identification of mutations in NS4B that result in the development of resistance to specific virus replication inhibitors has pinpointed it as the target of those inhibitors and made it a prime focus for drug development. But it is currently unclear whether these inhibitors directly target NS4B or unknown host factor(s) that interacts with NS4B. In addition, it is undefined how these mutations mediate resistance to these inhibitors. We hypothesize that NS4B-interacting host factors and pathways play a crucial role in promoting virus replication. Host factors and pathways have now emerged as effective targets for antivirals, as in the case of Maraviroc for HIV. Current methods to identify antivirals rely on inefficient large-scale screens. In this research proposal, we will take a guided two-pronged systems approach to directly identify NS4B-interacting host factors and pathways that are critical for dengue infection. We will then select the most significant top candidates from each proteomic and genomic analyses, with a focus on host factors and pathways that are scored as significant in multiple proteomic and/or genomic analyses. Next, we will validate and determine the functional significance of the interaction between these host factor hits and NS4B using molecular approaches, and evaluate their roles in DV replication by genetic and chemical approaches. The successful completion of this research project will provide clear understanding of NS4B’s function and the mechanism of action of the DV inhibitors, thus achieving the overall goal of opening new avenues to direct the development of novel, rationally designed antivirals.
kw: Dengue; Virus; Virus-Host Interactions; Systems Biology; Proteomics; Genomics

title: Investigating the molecular mechanisms and intrinsic stem cell heterogeneity driving epithelial homeostasis and cancer in the stomach
abs: Gastric cancer is highly prevalent worldwide, especially in Asia, where it is among the cancers with the highest mortality rates. While we are now able to identify and purify stem cells of the pyloric antrum using the Lgr5 marker, we only have rudimentary basic knowledge about the molecular mechanisms underpinning normal gastric stem cell biology, identity of the cancer-initiating cell, gastric carcinogenesis and invasion. We propose to elucidate the signaling mechanisms responsible for maintaining healthy gastric epithelium in mouse and human pyloric stomachs based on candidate pathways identified through a recently completed transcriptome analysis. We will then employ mouse models and in vitro organoid culture technologies to investigate how dysregulation of these pathways contribute to cancer initiation and progression in the stomach. From the transcriptome profiles and RNA in situ hybridization, we found that Wnt/ß-catenin, Notch, Hedgehog and Hippo pathways are active in the pylorus. To further our studies, we will employ genetic mouse models and human organoids to investigate their individual roles. In particular, expression of the receptor tyrosine kinase Ror2 is enriched in the stem cells relative to the other populations in the pylorus, suggesting that non-canonical Wnt signaling activity is also present in the stem cell population. As Ror2 expression has been associated with cell motility and poorly differentiated cancers, we will also probe its role in gastric homeostasis, tumorigenesis and invasion in mouse and human systems. Given earlier successes of receptor tyrosine kinases as drug targets, Ror2 could be a drug target candidate for gastric cancer if it does drive gastric cancer and tumour invasion. The mechanistic insight gained from correlating homeostatic and cancer states in the stomach is expected to reveal novel opportunities for developing rational approaches to effectively diagnose and treat gastric cancer with minimal impact on normal gastric homeostasis.
kw: Gastric stem cells, cancer, niche, signaling

title: Evaluation of Lgr5-expressing chief cells as gastric stem cells of the corpus epithelium and a cellular origin of gastric cancer.
abs: The glandular stomach is divided into pyloric and corpus epithelium. Due to constant exposure to mechanical stress and hostile contents within the stomach lumen, highly specialized cell types must be constantly replaced to maintain a functional stomach epithelium. Limited reservoirs of adult stem cells residing within numerous tubular glands are believed to fuel the process of repetitive tissue renewal.The seminal identification of Lgr5-expressing stem cells in organs such as the intestine and pyloric stomach has driven major advances in our understanding of stem cell biology during tissue homeostasis and disease and has fuelled the development of culture methods to harness the regenerative capacity of stem cells for clinical applications.Using a highly sensitive in-situ hybridization technique, we detected endogenous expression of Lgr5 at the gland base throughout the epithelium of the main body of the stomach (the corpus domain). Our preliminary lineage tracing data identified Lgr5-expressing corpus cells to contribute to long-term epithelial maintenance in the corpus region. Tissue damage significantly amplified the process of Lgr5-driven tissue renewal. Here, we aim to characterize the role of Lgr5-expressing corpus cells during adult homeostasis, injury repair and cancer. We propose that adult Lgr5-expressing corpus cells function as stem cells during adult tissue homeostasis and regeneration and also serve as a major cell-of-origin of gastric cancer following mutation.Identification of corpus stem cells would represent a major breakthrough in our understanding of the basic stem cell biology of the stomach body. Analyzing the homoeostatic behavior of such stem cells represents a valuable benchmark for identifying altered stem cell behavior during disease and epithelial injury. Characterizing a novel population of gastric cancer initiating cells has also important translational applications for the development of novel targeted stomach cancer therapeutics.
kw: adult stem cells, gastric cancer, Lgr5, Organoid technology

title: Single-cell analysis of crosstalk between tumor, immune cells and pathogens in gastric cancer
abs: With the emergence of single-cell RNA-sequencing technologies, increasing number of single-cell analyses measuring only tumor or immune cells have revealed previously underappreciated heterogeneity in both compartments. However, while there are existing studies on tumor-immune interactions at the bulk tissue level, the crosstalk between tumor and immune cells at single-cell level remains unstudied. Within a tumor different individual or groups of tumor cells could develop specific mechanisms to escape and even suppress anti-tumor immune responses. A similar situation exists in the study of pathogen-host interactions, in which there is evidence indicating that pathogen cell-to-cell variability can drive heterogeneity in host immune response. Again pathogen-host interactions are poorly studied at single cell level. In this project, we will perform the first single-cell analysis of crosstalk between tumor, immune cells and pathogens in pathogen-associated cancer. Gastric cancer is known to be associated with pathogens and a sizable subgroup (9%) are Epstein-Barr virus(EBV)-associated. We will isolate and sequence individual tumor cells and CD45+ immune cells from 10 EBV+ gastric cancers, wherein viral transcriptomes and cellular transcriptomes are measured simultaneously. We aim to identify viral transcriptomes within individual cells, to investigate what effects different viral transcriptomes have on the host cells; if and how EBV modulates immune cell infiltration, activation and functions. By examining cellular transcriptomes of individual tumor and CD45+ immune cells, we aim to identify heterogeneity and segregate sub-populations of tumor cells; delineate tumor-infiltrating immune cell composition, activation status and functions; and identify the connections between tumor and immune variability. Furthermore, we will devise novel computational algorithms to infer cell-cell interactions between tumor and various subtypes of immune cells. Via single-cell analysis of crosstalk between tumor, immune cells and pathogens, we hope to identify cell-specific mechanisms of tumor immune escape especially virus-related immune evasion mechanism, and discover new markers for anti-tumor immune rescue.
kw: Single-cell analysis, Immune, Cancer, EBV, Host-pathogen interaction, Immune-cancer interaction

title: Characterization of MMSET I and REIIBP Roles in T(4;14) Multiple Myeloma
abs: Multiple myeloma (MM) is characterized by recurrent chromosomal translocations. The translocation t(4;14)(p16;q32) is one of the most common translocation in MMs, affecting 15% of patients, and is associated with very poor prognosis. The histone methyltransferase (HMTase) MMSET is universally overexpressed in t(4;14) MM as a result of the t(4;14) chromosomal translocation. Different MMSET transcripts are produced by alternative splicing and alternative transcription initiation events. The full-length isoform MMSET II and short isoforms REIIBP and MMSET I are three major isoforms. In cancer associated genes, splicing has important roles in tumor initiation, progression and metastasis. Therefore, alternative spliced variants are potential biomarkers for the cancer diagnosis and prognosis and may be the targets for cancer therapy based on specific isoform treatments. MMSET II has been suggested to plan an important tumorigenic role in t(4;14) MM, but little is yet known about whether and how the MMSET short isoforms contribute to tumorigenesis. In this study, we will knock down MMSET I or REIIBP expression through shRNAs to explore their oncogenic roles in t(4;14) MM cells. Gene expression arrays will be used to analyze downstream targets of MMSET I or REIIBP and signaling pathways will be formulated based on identified targets. Then we will test biological importance of the identified targets in t(4;14) MM cells. Furthermore, we will explore the drug combinations in vitro and in vivo for t(4;14) MM based on the downstream targets and signaling pathways identified in this study. Currently MM is not curable and t(4;14) MM is associated with very poor prognosis. This study will provide a functional characterization of MMSET I and REIIBP in t(4;14) MM. Hopefully the novel potential molecular targets will be provided for t(4;14) MM therapy.
kw: Multiple myeloma, MMSET, isoform, ShRNA, oncogene

title: Development of transcriptome imaging technology for cellular mapping of the tumor microenvironment
abs: The aim of this proposal is to develop a transcriptome imaging method for tissue samples, with the scientific goal of spatially mapping the molecular and cellular tumor microenvironment of lung cancer. Recent applications of single cell transcriptomics has demonstrated that clustering of gene expression can be used for unbiased reconstruction of cell types. However, RNA sequencing methods cannot provide the spatial locations of the measured transcripts or cell types. We have recently developed Multiplexed Error Robust Fluorescence in situ Hybridization (MERFISH) to overcome this barrier. We demonstrated its ability to accurately characterize both the copy number and spatial distribution of a thousand RNA species in single cells, representing a major breakthrough for spatially resolved transcriptomics. We aim to further develop this technology for 3D transcriptome imaging and in situ cell type identification of tumors, which will allow us to generate the first transcriptomic map of an intact tumor. Such map may contain important information on the roles of tumor microenvironment, immune responses, spatial patterns that better classify tumors, and new pathways that could be therapeutically targeted. Further analysis of inter-tumor microenvironment variability may identify key structural differences between benign and malignant tumors. Importantly, our technology can be the basis for future translation into a highly sensitive, transcriptomics-based clinical pathology platform. Current tools to diagnose cancers have low predictive power and high false positive rates. Our highly sensitive in situ transcriptome imaging platform will transform clinical histology by allowing clinicians to precisely locate the relevant cancer markers and their heterogeneity within tumors in an unbiased fashion. This ability to pinpoint the location and molecular origin of cancer in patient biopsies will redefine cancer diagnostics and precision medicine.
kw: spatial transcriptomics, single cell technology, RNA imaging, tumor microenvironment, lung cancer, cell type mapping

title: Predicting Responders to Electroconvulsive Therapy Across Schizophrenia and Depression: A Prospective Study
abs: The overall aim of this study is to determine the prognostic values of combinatorial neuroanatomical-genetics-cognitive biomarkers in predicting electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) response in treatment-refractory schizophrenia and major depressive disorder (MDD). Unlike patients in US or western Europe—where ECT is used as a potent and fast-acting treatment for treatment-refractory depression—patients with schizophrenia form the majority of patients receiving ECT in Singapore and Asia. Although our hospital records indicate increasing numbers of patients receiving ECT, only 40% of the depressed patients and 20% of the schizophrenia patients respond favourably to ECT. Given the cost and length of this stigma-bound treatment, there is an urgent need to identify the subtype of patients receptive to ECT before treatment prescription.First, we aim to determine neuroanatomical signatures of ECT response in schizophrenia and MDD using non-invasive magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). We hypothesize that a subpopulation of treatment-refractory schizophrenia and MDD patients share abnormal hippocampal structure and frontolimbic regions; and that ECT works by restoring the abnormalities in hippocampal structural and frontolimbic connectivity. We hypothesize the plasticity of the postulated neurocircuitries correlate with ECT-related symptomatic and cognitive response. Second, we aim to determine peripheral brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF)-related signatures of ECT response, by extracting blood DNA, RNA and serum. We hypothesize that a sub-population of treatment-refractory patients share common BDNF gene variants, promoter methylation status, and expression that make them more receptive to ECT. We will also examine common gene variants, epigenetic status and expression of proteins along converging signaling pathways with BDNF known to enhance neuroplasticity.Third, we aim to combine the neuroanatomical and biosignatures of high predictive values (identified from the first and second aims) together with cognitive and clinical data, to construct a combinatorial signature that can predict ECT response on a single-subject level.
kw: Electroconvulsive therapy; Clinical Outcomes; Schizophrenia; Depression; MRI; Epigenetics

title: Aberrant activation of the GIMAP onco-enhancer in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia
abs: Our long-term goal is to improve cancer cure rates by developing novel therapeutics through combining cancer genomics with functional genetics and bioinformatics. To meet this challenge, we have been studying T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL), a malignant disorder resulting from the leukemic transformation of thymic T-cell precursors. The most frequent molecular abnormality in T-ALL is the dysregulation of transcription factors. We previously reported that the oncogenic transcription factor TAL1 and its regulatory partners form a stem cell-like transcriptional circuitry. A recent study demonstrated that these factors are regulated by large cluster of enhancers (“super-enhancers”) in T-ALL cells. Additionally, a somatic mutation near the TAL1 gene loci generates a super-enhancer capable of driving leukemogenesis. These implicate oncogenic roles of enhancers in tumorigenesis. Importantly, TAL1 is normally expressed in hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) but is silenced in immature T-cells. Hence, we hypothesize that TAL1 may reactivate HSC genes in malignant T-cells, contributing to leukemogenesis. To test this hypothesis, we identified enhancer elements regulated by TAL1 in T-ALL cells. We found a super-enhancer within the GIMAP gene cluster. This enhancer is activated in HSCs and is repressed in immature T-cells but is aberrantly activated in T-ALL cells. Ectopic expression of GIMAP genes in thymus caused T-ALL in zebrafish. Discovery of these findings places us in an ideal position to understand how abnormal activation of oncogenic enhancers contributes to T-ALL. The overall purpose of this project is to elucidate the mechanism of activation and oncogenic roles of the GIMAP enhancer in T-ALL. First, we will elucidate the mechanism by which the TAL1 complex induces aberrant activation of the GIMAP enhancer in T-ALL cells. Second, we will clarify the mechanism by which GIMAP proteins promote cell survival of T-ALL cells. Third, we will analyze tumorigenic ability of GIMAP genes in vivo using zebrafish model.
kw: T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, enhancer, TAL1, GIMAP, zebrafish

title: Generation of inhibitors to trefoil factor-3 for preclinical development in oncology
abs: Trefoil factor-3 (TFF3) is a secreted protein with an established oncogenic function and a highly significant association with clinical progression of various human carcinomas. Specifically, TFF3 expression is absent or relatively low in normal tissues but elevated in various human malignancies; and in both univariate and multivariate analyses is a poor prognostic indicator of outcome for patients with mammary, hepatocellular and gastric carcinoma amongst others. Functionally, TFF3 is an extremely potent promoter of cancer cell survival and dissemination, concordant with the observed clinicopathologic associations. In addition, TFF3 predicts and is functionally involved in acquired resistance to specific therapeutics such as Tamoxifen in ER+ breast cancer. Hence, it is apparent that inhibition of TFF3 function in cancer warrants consideration as a therapeutic approach. Commercial efforts to develop inhibitors to TFF3, with intellectual property arising from my previous laboratory, have therefore focused on a monoclonal antibody approach (www.perseis.co.nz) and have garnered much interest from large pharmaceutical companies. Whilst fully human function inhibiting antibodies have been developed, and licensed, there are critical production issues which have impeded further preclinical development and progression to the clinic. Despite the technical issues involved in production, monoclonal antibodies to TFF3 are potent inhibitors of cancer cell survival. There remains a need to develop effective, yet commercially viable, first in clinic inhibitors to TFF3. Efficacy and ease and cost of production are clearly factors of importance for any lead compound to progress past the preclinical stage. With these considerations in mind we wish to initially determine an optimal approach to inhibit TFF3. In addition, the specific approach must be able to harness an intellectual property position such that commercial-, and consequently clinical- development can proceed. Therefore, the aims of this project are to determine an optimal inhibitory approach to TFF3 that will be of utility.
kw: Trefoil factor, breast cancer, oncogene, inhibitor, metastasis

title: Global circulation patterns and phenotypic characterisation of human parainfluenza viruses
abs: Human parainfluenza viruses (HPIVs) are an important cause of acute respiratory infection (ARI), accounting for 16% of the 545,000 ARI hospitalizations annually in the United States. Although the epidemiological profiles and temporal distributions of HPIVs are generally well characterized, relatively little is known about global virus circulation patterns or the genetic basis of virus traits relevant to population level transmission and clinical disease. Genetic material from more than 400 HPIV positive clinical specimens and virus isolates collected over 10 years (2001-2011) from Australia, the Netherlands, Singapore and Vietnam are currently being sequenced in the PI’s laboratory. Here, we propose to expand this collection by including viruses from more regions collected between 2012-2018 to examine the relationship of HPIV viruses from diverse geographic locations. We will sequence the haemagglutinin-neuraminidase (HN) gene of 2,000 viruses and conduct whole genome sequencing on a subset of 400 viruses. This data will be used to characterize the population dynamics of HPIV, including global transmission patterns, using advanced Bayesian phylogenetic methods. Furthermore, we will examine the antigenic relationships within and between HPIV types, by using ferret post-infection antisera and generating antigenic maps. We will then determine cellular tropism and replicative fitness of different HPIV types and isolates in hNESPC-derived ciliated respiratory epithelium tissues grown at an air-liquid interface. In addition, clinical data is available from Singapore and will be used to stratify disease (mild, moderate and severe disease). Replicative fitness in hNESPCs, antigenic characterization and genetic make-up of viruses from each of theses groups will be compared. This study will provide the first comprehensive analysis of parainfluenza evolution, spatial transmission and phenotypic characterization of all four types. More profoundly, our research findings will ultimately contribute a wealth of up-to-date data for improving health control strategies to reduce risks of parainfluenza spread and infection.
kw: evolution, epidemiology, clinical severity, antigenic characterisation, virus replication

title: Etiology of Cortical Cerebral Microinfarcts and Impact on Brain Function and Long Term Outcomes
abs: Aims : To leverage upon human cohort studies conducted by the Memory Aging & Cognition Centre (NUHS) and the technical and analytical capacity of the Centre for Imaging Research (A*Star-NUS), Multimodal Imaging Laboratory (Duke-NUS) and Brain Centre Rudolf Magnus Institute (Utrecht) to address the problem of Vascular Cognitive Impairment (VCI), a common chronic illness which constitutes a major clinical and economic burden world-wide, focusing on cortical cerebral microinfarcts (CMIs), a novel and important MRI biomarker for VCI. We aim to demonstrate the association of CMIs with brain and blood biomarkers at baseline and subsequently associate CMIs with ischemic events, cognitive decline and MRI changes on longtitudinal follow up.Hypotheses : We hypothesize that a) CMIs as detected by MRI will be associated with decreased brain structural and functional connectivity compared to subjects without CMIs; b) that CMIs at baseline predict worse cognitive functioning on a detailed neuropsychological testing on follow up visits as well as fatal and non-fatal recurrent cardiovascular events and cerebrovascular lesions on MRI; c) that presence of CMIs will be associated with decreased brain perfusion and that these perfusion deficits will be observed in regions with abundance of CMIs compared to regions without CMIs; d) that biomarkers such as Troponin T, Brain Natriuretic Peptide, and Growth Differentiation Factor-15 will be associated with the presence and incidence of CMIs.Methods and Approach : To determine the impact of CMIs on brain function and long term outcomes and unravel the etiology of CMIs by characterizing neuropsychological patterns, exploring mechanisms, in particular cerebrovascular processes (structural, connectivity, perfusion) accounting for cognitive decline in these individuals, so as to eventually develop therapeutic interventions to prevent cognitive decline in high risk patients.This study may enable intervention to delay progression of cognitive decline, translating research into clinical practice and preventing dementia.
kw: Cortical cerebral microinfarcts, Cerebrovascular diseases, Cognitive impairment, Dementia, Magnetic Resonance Imaging

title: Immunological profiling of paediatric patients with focal segmental glomerulosclerosis responsive to rituximab therapy: Linking the synapses and defining the key players
abs: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) is a devastating kidney disease with rapid progression to end-stage kidney failure. There is conflicting evidence as to the exact pathogenesis of this disease, that is, the role of the immune system acting on podocytes versus direct podocyte damage, partly because FSGS is probably a heterogenous disease. Our preliminary data demonstrated a hyporesponsive T-cell phenotype corresponding to a favourable response to rituximab therapy, an anti-CD20-monoclonal antibody, highlighting the possible role of B-T interactions in this subgroup of patients with FSGS. This was accompanied by significantly reduced T-cell production of the ‘inhibitory’ cytokines in FSGS rituximab responders in contrast to non-responders and controls where no immunological signature was apparent. This ‘disinhibited’ T-cell phenotype may possibly result in decreased inhibition of monocyte production of potential permeability factors. We therefore hypothesized that in a subgroup of immune-mediated FSGS, T-cells are important in the immune regulation of a cascade leading to production of a permeability factor ultimately resulting in proteinuria. This study aims to further characterize the subgroup of immune-mediated FSGS with T-cell hyporesponsiveness to activation (HT phenotype) by phenotyping the T- and B-cell subsets, and investigating the interplay of B-T interactions through T- and B-cell co-culture. In addition, we will study the defective regulation of T-cells on monocyte/macrophage production of putative permeability factor(s) in order to elucidate both the upstream and downstream immune effectors involved in pathogenesis of proteinuria in this subgroup of FSGS. We will subsequently validate the putative permeability factor(s) both in human podocyte cell cultures as well as an animal model of FSGS. The significance of this work lies in delineating, in detail, the dysregulated B-T-monocyte immunological axis in the subgroup of immune-mediated FSGS in order to identify unique immunological signatures to which targeted novel therapies can be developed, for patients with this difficult-to-treat disease.
kw: Rituximab, B-cells, Hyporesponsive T-cells, permeability factors

title: Targeted Drug Delivery for Non-muscle invasive Bladder Cancer
abs: Bladder cancer is one of the costliest cancers to treat because of its high recurrence rate and intensive bladder surveillance program by frequent follow-up cystoscopy. Intravesical chemotherapy is highly promising for reducing recurrence rate in the short-term, but fails in the long-term, due to the short residence time and low penetration of the drug within the bladder. Cytotoxicity associated with administered chemotherapeutic agents limits higher doses for increased efficacy. Thus, it is a challenge to achieve an ideal intravesical agent that can target and penetrate into tumor cells and be highly effective with minimal toxicity. The proposed work aims to develop targeting strategies with different drug formulations for more effective drug delivery to bladder tumors. We propose to design peptides to target fibroblast growth receptor 3 (FGFR3), epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) and CD47 on human bladder tumor cells. Screening experiments will be first carried out by evaluating the ability of the proposed peptide to bind two or more cell lines which overexpress FGFR3, EGFR or CD47. At the same time, a number of intravesical drug delivery systems such as prodrugs and drug-nanoparticulate formulations will be developed. Since chemotherapeutic drugs have a wide range of solubility and diverse properties, we will design three types of nanoparticulate drug carriers: native proteins, protein-based nanoparticles and amphiphilic polymeric micelles. Lastly, the drug-containing nanoparticles will be conjugated with tumor-targeting peptides to achieve effective targeting of bladder tumors. The targeted penetration in tumor cells and the corresponding therapeutic efficacy of the drug-nanoparticulate formulations conjugated with/without targeting peptides will be further evaluated in vitro and in a mouse orthotopic model. The use of fluorescence tagged peptide conjugated carriers as possible bladder cancer diagnostic tool will also be evaluated ex vivo with tumor biopsy samples and cell pellets from patients’ urine.
kw: Bladder cancer, Nanoperticulate drug carriers, Murine model, Tumour-targeting peptides, Chemotherapy

title: Exploring Frizzled-7 (FZD7)-mediated non-canonical Wnt-Planar Cell Polarity (PCP) signaling as a novel molecular driver for a specific ovarian cancer subtype which harbors stem-cell property.
abs: Ovarian cancer (OC) is highly heterogeneous with five distinct molecular subtypes, Epi-A, Epi-B, Mes, Stem-A and Stem-B. For the poor-prognosis Stem-A subtype, the Wnt receptor Frizzled-7 (FZD7) has been shown to be overexpressed and is crucial for its aggressiveness. Loss of FZD7 in Stem-A OC induces decrease in cell proliferation and cell cycle arrest. Loss of FZD7 also increases epithelialization and decreases anchorage independency via a subset of gene involved in the non-canonical Wnt-planar cell polarity (PCP) pathway. The hypothesis of this project is that the FZD7-PCP pathway drives the aggressiveness of the Stem-A-subtyped OC and can be utilized as a therapeutic target for Stem-A OC. Our preliminary work has shown that Stem-A OC cells with high FZD7 expression are sensitive to cytotoxic effect initiated by a monoclonal antibody (mAb) against FZD7. Pre-clinical testing of the therapeutic effect of this anti-FZD7 mAb on Stem-A patient derived xenografts (PDXs) will be performed. Secondly, FZD7 is crucial in maintaining stemness in embryonic, adult, and cancer stem cells. We also hypothesize that FZD7 has a tumor-initiating role in OC. We will utilize immortalized ovarian surface epithelium (OSE) and fallopian tubal epithelium (FTE) to study its role upon overexpression. Finally, our preliminary work has demonstrated that transient silencing of PCP pathway genes, CELSR3, PRICKLE4, PTK7, gave rise to similar functional phenotypes as silencing FZD7. Knock-out (KO) clones of FZD7, CELSR3, PRICKLE4, PTK7, by using the Crispr-Cas9 system in the Stem-A OC cells will be established. These FZD7-PCP pathway KO clones will be tested for their in vitro and in vivo functions. In conclusion, molecularly stratifying OC patients and targeting the Stem-A subtype with therapeutics against FZD7-PCP pathway would be a landmark treatment innovation for OC.
kw: FZD7, planar cell polarity, ovarian cancer

title: Dissecting triggers and defining treatments for cardiac dysfunction associated with titin gene mutations
abs: Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) has a prevalence of up 1:250 and remains a progressive disease despite optimal medical management. DCM is the commonest indication for heart transplantation with significant associated health care costs. We have shown that Titin truncating variants (TTNtvs) commonly cause DCM but that these mutations are incompletely penetrant for reasons that are unclear. Indeed, putative disease-causing TTNtv occur in ~1% the general population in the absence of an overt cardiac phenotype. Hence we hypothesize that an additional myocardial stress, a ‘second hit’, is required to reveal the effect of a TTNtv and cause cardiac dysfunction. In our preliminary human studies, we have observed an association between hypertension and alcohol intake and TTNtv-related DCM. In our rodent studies we recently documented a metabolic shift and impaired autophagy in the myocardium secondary to TTNtvs. Building on these preliminary observations, we propose to specifically test the hypotheses that dietary, alcohol and/or hypertension are environmental triggers for cardiac dysfunction in the presence of a TTNt. In parallel experiments, we use the mechanistic insights from our initial studies to trial drugs to promote autophagy and fatty acid oxidation to see whether these interventions prevent/improve cardiac function in the context of a TTNtv. We are hopeful that these studies this will lead to new ways to prevent and to treat DCM using dietary, environmental and new therapeutic approaches as a stratified medicine advance.
kw: Heart failure; repurposing; titin; alcohol; diet; cardiomyopathy

title: Novel heart failure treatment with arylsulfatase B: targeting chondroitin sulfate glycosaminoglycans in pathological cardiac remodelling
abs: Heart failure (HF) remains a leading cause of death and morbidity worldwide. Patients with HF have a high 5-year mortality rate of up to 50%. The ever-increasing burden of HF underlies an urgent need for novel therapeutics.Drugs in routine use now include angiotensin receptor blockers, ACE-inhibitors, diuretics and beta-blockers. These have strong evidence-base for improving symptoms, decreasing hospitalization and reducing mortality. However, these drugs target hormonal pathways, and do not suppress every component of the extracellular matrix (ECM) that may contribute to pathological cardiac remodelling. In particular, we have been investigating the role of myocardial glycosaminoglycans (GAG): the carbohydrate component of ECM comprising of chondroitin sulfate (CS) and dermatan sulfate (DS). Deregulated GAG degradation occurs in the serious congenital disease Mucopolysaccharidosis VI (MPS VI), which is caused by mutation in the ARSB gene that encodes for the enzyme arylsulfatase B, responsible for CS and DS degradation. Children with MPS VI develop GAG accumulation, manifesting as growth retardation, multiple organ failure including myocardial fibrosis, and acute heart failure. We therefore set out to study the role of GAGs in non-MPS VI related HF. In preliminary work we observe that: (1) GAG deposition is significantly increased in the myocardium of HF patients, and also in the rat pressure-overload model of HF; (2) In the rat, targeting GAGs with recombinant ARSB (FDA-approved therapy for MPS VI) led to significant reduction of cardiac fibrosis and rescued contractility.Based on these, we now aim to (1) elucidate the mechanism of how CSs affect contractile function and fibrosis; and (2) further test the feasibility of recombinant ARSB for treatment of full-blown HF again using the rat model of disease.We believe that this proposal presents a truly novel approach of drug repurposing in HF and opens a new avenue of GAG research in cardiovascular disease.
kw: extracellular matrix, heart failure, therapeutics

title: Dissecting the molecular and clinical role of RUNX in the Fanconi anemia pathway of DNA repair
abs: DNA interstrand crosslinks (ICL) are highly mutagenic DNA damaging lesions. Left unrepaired, they dramatically increase cancer predisposition. The Fanconi anemia (FA) pathway of DNA repair is dedicated to the repair of DNA-ICLs. Monoubiquitination and recruitment of DNA repair protein FANCD2 to damage sites is the central event of this pathway.We have recently identified a novel non-transcriptional role for the RUNX proteins in the FA pathway. RUNX knockout-mice exhibit FA manifestations like crosslinker sensitivity, bone marrow failure and leukemic predisposition (1). RUNX proteins physically interact with the FANCI/FANCD2 heterodimer and enable FANCD2 recruitment to DNA damage sites. Here, we will precisely dissect the biochemical and clinical role of RUNX in the FA pathway and translate our findings to the clinic. To gain better molecular insights, RUNX co-immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry studies will be done under DNA damaging conditions. Structural studies with purified RUNX, Fanconi anemia proteins (FANCI and FANCD2) and DNA repair intermediates FANCD2 will be done. To study the clinical implication of RUNX involvement in the FA pathway, mouse knockouts RUNX1 and SOD1, representing a genomic deletion in two unclassified FA patients will be made to recapitulate FA phenotypes. Since RUNX1 and RUNX3 defects are widespread in human cancer, we will ask if cancer-associated RUNX mutants disrupt the FA pathway. Lastly, we will test the use of DNA damaging agents and PARP inhibitors as combination-therapies to target RUNX-fusion expressing acute myeloid leukemias and mechanistically validate the basis for PARP inhibition.Based on the precise role of RUNX in the FA pathway, novel intervention strategies to eliminate RUNX-deficient cancers will be conceived. If RUNX defects are indeed identified in FA patients, it would be considered as a major breakthrough. We anticipate the proposed research to generate exciting basic and clinical findings translatable across the FA, RUNX and DNA repair fields.
kw: DNA repair, DNA damage, FANCONI ANEMIA, RUNX, CANCER

title: The Singapore diabetes complications study: closing the screening-referral uptake loop for diabetic retinopathy, nephropathy, and foot complications
abs: The prevalence of diabetes-related complications, namely retinopathy (DR), nephropathy (DN), and diabetic foot complications (DFC) are estimated to range between 25% and 40% in Singapore. In Singapore, screening for these complications is performed mostly at the 18 government polyclinics within the SingHealth and NHG clusters. Data from the NHG cluster however suggest differential and high rates of non-adherence to screening for DR, DN and DFC i.e., 58%, 30%, and 43%, respectively. However, currently there are almost no prospective data on the magnitude; predictors; and clinical and economic impact of non-adherence to the MoH diabetes complication screening guidelines in Singapore. Moreover, barriers and facilitators to adherence to DR, DN, and DFC screening have never been explored either qualitatively or quantitatively in Singapore which compromises our ability to provide effective recommendations to MoH and implement effective evidence-based interventions to improve adherence. Therefore, the main objective of this study is to prospectively investigate, using a mixed method approach, the magnitude; independent predictors (primary outcome); the clinical; and economic impact of non-adherence to diabetic complications screening in polyclinic patients with type 2 diabetes. We hypothesize that the rate of non-adherence to complications screening is high but varies across complications; polyclinic clusters; patient characteristics and ethnicity; and our mixed methods approach will yield a range of barriers consisting of predisposing, enabling, and reinforcing factors; and facilitators associated with adherence to complications screening. This will be a prospective, multi-centred, and clinic-based study of patients with diabetes attending DR, DN, DFC screening, respectively, who will be followed at the next screening appointment. The study findings will have important implications for Singapore’s public health and healthcare as they will inform the design of evidence-based interventions addressing modifiable risk factors to reduce non-adherence to diabetes complications screening at the system, provider, and patient levels in the public sector.
kw: Diabetes, Diabetic Retinopathy, Diabetic Nephropathy, Foot complications, Screening, Adherence

title: An Immunological Study on the effects of radioembolization in combination with anti-PD1 therapy in hepatocellular carcinoma
abs: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the sixth most common form of malignancy worldwide and the second most common cause of cancer-related mortality. It has especially high prevalence in Southeast Asia, due to the high rates of viral hepatitis, including chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV). Escape from immune control is a critical hallmark of cancer that has recently come under intense scrutiny with the dramatic yet unpredictable successes of cancer immunotherapies, such as Merck’s Pembrolizumab (anti-PD1). Here, leveraging our current clinical practices, permitting us to perform a small clinical trial in collaboration with Merck, and our unique capacity to deeply probe antigen-specific T cell responses, we will investigate relationships between the antigen-specific T cell response to HCC and HBV in the context of transarterial radiombolization with Yittrium-90 microspheres and in combination with Pembrolizumab. In the process, a number of immunological mechanisms will be explored as we test the hypothesis that liver-localized radioembolization will stimulate tumour and/or HBV specific T cell responses that are associated with favourable patient outcomes and that can be boosted using anti-PD1 immunotherapy. title: A novel tissue engineered scaffold-free cartilage graft for temporomandibular condylar repair in rabbit models: a factorial study of decellularization and recellularization of chondrocytes and chondroprogenitors
abs: The articular cartilage is a well-organized tissue for smooth and friction-free joint movement in animals and humans. Adult articular cartilage has a very low self-regeneration capacity due to its avascular nature. Osteoarthritis (OA) is a common disease causing joint pain, joint deformity, and functional disability. Temporomandibular joint (TMJ) is the joint that connects the mandible to the temporal bone and temporomandibular joint disorders (TMD) may develop due to trauma or OA. This disorder often leads to a lifetime of pain and restricted motion of the jaw, greatly affecting patients’ life quality. Although various joint resurfacing procedures in experimental articular cartilage defects have been developed, no standardized clinical protocol has yet been established. The emerging cartilage tissue engineering strategies to regenerate or reconstruct condylar cartilage have gained increasing attention and are promising as new therapeutic approaches. This research proposal aims to develop a tissue engineered ‘scaffold-free’ graft to repair the TMJ condylar cartilage in rabbit models. The xenogenic synthetic scaffold-free construct with hyaline quality, termed living hyaline cartilaginous graft (LhCG) will be applied for treating cartilage lesions in 28 rabbit models in 4 groups. The study will compare between the negative control (empty defect), grafting with decellularized–LhCG, recellularized –LhCG with allogenic bone marrow stromal stem cells (BMSCs) or allogenic chondrocytes. The assessment will be on macroscopic and microscopic inspection on the restoration of cartilage thickness, promotion of integration with surrounding native cartilage, cartilage-specific matrix molecules, and re-establishing an intact superficial tangential zone. The outcome of this pioneering work would be to repair damaged TMJ cartilage using tissue engineering approach and is especially relevant in our ageing population where rising number of joint degenerative disorders are expected.

title: Targeted Drug Delivery for Non-Muscle Invasive Bladder Cancer
abs: Bladder cancer is one of the costliest cancers to treat because of its high recurrence rate and intensive bladder surveillance program by frequent follow-up cystoscopy. Intravesical chemotherapy is highly promising for reducing recurrence rate in the short-term, but fails in the long-term, due to the short residence time and low penetration of the drug within the bladder. Cytotoxicity associated with administered chemotherapeutic agents limits higher doses for increased efficacy. Thus, it is a challenge to achieve an ideal intravesical agent that can target and penetrate into tumor cells and be highly effective with minimal toxicity. The proposed work aims to develop targeting strategies with different drug formulations for more effective drug delivery to bladder tumors. We propose to design peptides to target fibroblast growth receptor 3 (FGFR3), epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) and CD47 on human bladder tumor cells. Screening experiments will be first carried out by evaluating the ability of the proposed peptide to bind two or more cell lines which overexpress FGFR3, EGFR or CD47. At the same time, a number of intravesical drug delivery systems such as prodrugs and drug-nanoparticulate formulations will be developed. Since chemotherapeutic drugs have a wide range of solubility and diverse properties, we will design three types of nanoparticulate drug carriers: native proteins, protein-based nanoparticles and amphiphilic polymeric micelles. Lastly, the drug-containing nanoparticles will be conjugated with tumor-targeting peptides to achieve effective targeting of bladder tumors. The targeted penetration in tumor cells and the corresponding therapeutic efficacy of the drug-nanoparticulate formulations conjugated with/without targeting peptides will be further evaluated in vitro and in a mouse orthotopic model. The use of fluorescence tagged peptide conjugated carriers as possible bladder cancer diagnostic tool will also be evaluated ex vivo with tumor biopsy samples and cell pellets from patients’ urine.
