title: Effect of Tocotrienols, a Class of Therapeutically-Active Vitamin E, on Biotransformation and Toxicity of Secondary Bile Acids
abs: ?-Tocotrienol, ?-tocotrienol, ?-tocotrienol, and ?-tocotrienol, which are members of the vitamin E family, have multiple biological actions, including anti-inflammatory, chemopreventive, anti-angiogenic, and neuroprotective activities. Pregnane X receptor (PXR), which belongs to the superfamily of nuclear receptors, regulates the expression of genes [e.g. cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4) and uridine diphosphate glucuronyltransferase 1A3 (UGT1A3)] involved in biotransformation of drugs and other chemicals. Previously, it was reported that ?-tocotrienol, ?-tocotrienol, ?-tocotrienol, and ?-tocotrienol activate human PXR (hPXR) and increase hPXR target gene expression [CYP3A4, CYP3A5, UGT1A1, and multi-drug resistance protein-1 (MDR-1; ABCB1)]. However, the pharmacological, toxicological, and therapeutic consequences of hPXR activation by tocotrienols are not known. Bile acids play essential physiological roles, including intestinal absorption of dietary fats, fat-soluble vitamins, and drugs, and their concentration may be increased in a high fat diet or diseases. Excessive accumulation of toxic bile acids, such as lithocholic acid and deoxycholic acid, in the gastrointestinal tract is a risk factor for colorectal cancer. Given that lithocholic acid is detoxified by CYP3A4 and UGT1A3, my hypothesis is that tocotrienols (?-tocotrienol, ?-tocotrienol, ?-tocotrienol, and ?-tocotrienol) will increase hPXR-mediated detoxification of lithocholic acid, thereby decreasing lithocholic acid-induced toxicity. The specific aims are to determine 1) whether tocotrienols modulate the biotransformation of lithocholic acid and deoxycholic acid, and 2) the impact of tocotrienols on the cytotoxicity and apoptotic effect of lithocholic acid and deoxycholic acid. The experiments will involve gene expression assays, UPLC-MS quantification of bile acid metabolites, and cell-based toxicity/apoptosis assays in human cell culture models. Overall, the findings will indicate the impact of tocotrienols on bile acid biotransformation and toxicity and provide a metabolic basis for further investigation of tocotrienols as chemopreventive agents for colorectal cancer. The findings will also provide a rationale for exploring the pharmacological and therapeutic consequences of the concurrent ingestion of tocotrienols and drugs.

title: CELL THERAPY OF CANCER
abs: The overall objective of our research is to harness the power and specificity of immune cells to treat cancer. Results of recent trials have provided unequivocal evidence of the clinical potential of cell-based therapy, showing that immune cells can succeed when all other available treatment has failed. This STaR Investigator Award renewal application builds on encouraging progress made by our laboratory during the first funding cycle. Studies in Specific Aim 1 focus on chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-directed T cell therapies and are designed to significantly improve CAR technology as well as to develop methods that would allow the use of CAR-modified allogeneic T cells, thus creating an off-the-shelf living drug. To this end, we have made exciting advances towards developing practical new ways to downregulate expression of the endogenous T-cell receptor and deprive T cells of the capacity to recognize antigens, except the one recognized by the CAR. Studies in Specific Aim 2 focus on natural killer (NK) cells and are based on a unique portfolio of techniques developed in our laboratory to expand and genetically engineer them. Preliminary findings point to more effective expansion techniques and to ways to convert inhibitory signals into stimulatory signals; we have also gained insights on possible new molecular regulators of NK cell cytotoxicity. In Specific Aim 3 we propose to complete the 5 immune cell-based clinical studies for patients with hematologic malignancies and solid tumors that we initiated in the last 2 years, as well as to begin new ones targeting hepatocellular carcinoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma. Our infrastructure and expertise should also allow the rapid translation of the most promising discoveries emerging from research in Aims 1 and 2 into clinical applications. Success in the comprehensive translational research program proposed should lead to new and better therapies for patients with cancer.
kw: T lymphocytes, Natural killer cells, Immunotherapy, Chimeric antigen receptor

title: Augmentation and Modulation of Host Immune Response for Optimized Management of Invasive Fungal Diseases
abs: In the context of the increasing numbers of immunocompromised patients seen in haematology, oncology, transplantation and critical care units, mortality rates from invasive fungal diseases (IFD) have remained high, approaching 50% despite treatment. This is attributable to the immunosuppressed host’s altered capacity to respond appropriately to the infection and treatment. We aim to optimize the treatment paradigm by addressing the other arm of the conundrum – the Host. We hypothesize that susceptibility to IFD or sustaining an eventual adverse outcome from the disease is either due to (i) impaired effective host immune response at the onset of infection OR/AND(ii) unnecessarily prolonged or exaggerated proinflammatory response post-infection which induce collateral host injury at the tissue/organ level. We propose to improve outcomes by optimising the immune milieu for host response to the fungi using the following novel biologics:(a) muramyl dipeptide (MDP), a natural peptidoglycan which we have found to have potent propensity to enhance immune response at the onset of infection(b)anti-interleukin 6 (Tocilizumab) which is currently in use for inflammatory conditions like rheumatoid arthritis, to curb the post-infective inflammatory flare Extending the findings from our preliminary work, we will investigate use of MDP and anti-IL6 using immunocompetent and immunosuppressed mice models of invasive candidiasis and invasive aspergillosis at different phases of infection. Primary outcome measures include survival and fungal burden in tissues. To obtain a thorough picture, including at the tissue/cellular level, we will also study the mechanistic sequelae resulting from such immunomoduatory manipulation at the molecular and epigenetic levels. These findings will be further validated in human cells, using immune cells from patients with acute leukemia or undergoing allogenic stem cell transplantation. With success, we envisage that the findings will be translated to the bedside for use of these adjunctive agents together with conventional anti-fungal agents for IFD.

title: Enhancing axon regeneration by nanofiber-mediated microRNA delivery for spinal cord injury treatment
abs: Traumatic nerve injuries (TNI) in the central nervous system, such as spinal cord injuries, (SCI), present enormous healthcare burden due to early loss of function in patients who are mostly young and healthy. Axon loss and its lack of regeneration is one of the hallmarks of TNI. Both neuron-intrinsic growth ability and the extracellular environment control the process of nerve regeneration. Unfortunately, current treatments mainly focus on the latter and the results remain sub-optimal. An alternative is to recognize that the diminished intrinsic regenerative capacity of neurons is a major cause of regeneration failure. Additionally, instead of focusing only on delivering inductive factors to stimulate nerve regeneration, an alternative may be to silence critical genes involved in axon regeneration by RNA-interference (RNAi). Therefore, we will like to propose a novel approach to enhance nerve regeneration after TNI – to modulate neuron-intrinsic growth ability by controlling local protein synthesis in severed axons through scaffold-mediated RNAi. We hypothesize that controlling neuron-intrinsic growth ability in the injured nerve is critical to nerve regeneration and functional recovery, and may be achieved through directing local protein translation in severed axons using a scaffold-mediated non-viral gene-silencing approach. We propose to develop a scaffold-mediated microRNA-dependent gene-silencing method to modulate neuron-intrinsic growth to direct axon regeneration in vitro and in vivo after SCI. We propose to pursue the following specific aims: 1) Establish a robust platform to provide reproducible and effective delivery of microRNAs for axon regeneration; 2) Investigate the functions and mechanisms of microRNA-incorporated nanofiber scaffolds on axon regeneration in vitro; 3) Evaluate the potential of microRNA-incorporated nanofiber scaffolds in enhancing axon regeneration and function recovery in SCI treatment.

title: T cell activity in development of Type II Diabetes
abs: Type II diabetes (T2D) is a major health problem worldwide, with special relevance to South East Asia. The disease is associated with chronic inflammation, caused by interplay of immune system and adipose tissue. Perturbed functions of different T cell subsets are important in causing the inflammation in adipose tissue leading to development of T2D. We have discovered that mice deficient in Themis, a newly-discovered protein with critical role in T cell developmental selection, show enhanced development of age and obesity-induced T2D. Themis is only expressed in the T cell lineage, and our laboratory has recently identified Themis as a negative regulator of T cell receptor signal strength through its interaction with tyrosine phosphatase Shp1. The role of Themis in the development of diabetes is novel, and suggests that Themis-deficient mice are a useful model to investigate T cell mediated aspects of T2D induction. We will fully characterize pre-T2D metabolic syndrome and T2D in Themis deficient mice, with detailed investigation of phenotype and cytokine profile of T cell subsets present in visceral adipose tissue from aged and high fat diet fed Themis-deficient mice. We will use adoptive cell transfer to identify T cells involved in the enhanced development of T2D in Themis-deficient mice, and we will analyze expression levels of Themis in T cells in lean and obese adipose tissue. We will characterize phenotype and cytokine profile of Themis-deficient regulatory CD4+ T cell subsets from lymph nodes and adipose tissue, and determine role of gut microbiota in development of Treg functions in metabolic syndrome. As Themis binding partner Shp1 is a critical negative regulator of insulin signalling, we will test T cell intrinsic effects of insulin signalling on Themis-deficient T cell functions. The project will have important implications understanding the role of T cells in development of metabolic syndrome and T2D.

title: Novel in vivo and ex vivo models to investigate the molecular mechanisms involved in Enterovirus 71 neurovirulence.
abs: The increasing incidence of Hand, Foot and Mouth Disease (HFMD) outbreaks and epidemics due to enterovirus 71 (EV71) infection in South East Asia, and the propensity of EV71 strains to cause severe neurological complications in young children underscore the need to further our knowledge and understanding of the mechanisms involved in EV71 neuropathogenesis. However, progresses have been limited by the lack of relevant in vivo and ex vivo models.The major route proposed for EV71 to invade the central nervous system (CNS) is the retrograde axonal transport whereby the virus gains entry into the CNS at the neuromuscular junctions in the limbs, infecting motor neurons to reach the spine and eventually accumulate into the brainstem. However, the molecular mechanisms remain to be deciphered, and the viral and host players have not been identified. Using a mouse model previously established in our laboratory which supports the retrograde axonal transport, we have identified EV71 isolates that display either myotropism or neurotropism. To understand the differential in vivo tropism observed with these EV71 strains, we have established a novel ex vivo platform using the motorneuron cell line NSC34. We showed that NSC34 cells are permissive to EV71 strains, and observed a direct correlation between replication efficacy in these cells and neurotropism in vivo. Furthermore, productive infection did not lead to cytopathic effect, thus uncovering for the first time a nonlytic infection mode for EV71. In this project, we propose to fully characterize the EV71 infection cycle in NSC34. Furthermore, transcriptomics and proteomics approaches will be carried out to profile the cell responses to EV71 infection. In addition, a siRNA-based high throughput screen will be performed to study the role of host factors during EV71 infection of NSC34. Finally, using a site-directed mutagenesis approach, we propose to identify the viral determinants involved in neurotropism.

title: Enhancing memory by modifying plasticity in hippocampal CA2-CA1 synapses via metaplasticity and optogenetics: implications in ageing and Alzheimer’s disease
abs: Memory loss such as in dementia with advanced aging or in neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a major concern in elderly populations and needs immediate attention in Singapore. Intensive research is going on in various disciplines to address the causes of age related memory loss but less attention has been paid for the causes of impairment of long-term memory consolidation at the neural network level. Synaptic plasticity impairments such as absence of late-long-term potentiation (late-LTP) is observed in the hippocampus of aged or AD models. In light of the previous and preliminary data, we hypothesize that an imbalance of synaptic co-operation and competition in CA2-CA1 pyramidal neurons contributes to the time-dependent memory loss that occurs in advanced aging and in AD. We predict that balancing plasticity in CA2 and CA1 area is critical for the consolidation of long-term memory at the hippocampal neural networks. We further predict that one of the hallmarks of aging and AD is the loss in neurons the ability to change the rules of plasticity, i.e. these neurons lose the ability to implement the rules of metaplasticity by themselves. Metaplasticity is a mechanism, by which, due to the history of the neuron, the rules of plasticity are changed. We intend to use pharmacological substances like ryanodine, Substance P or mGluR agonists to regulate plasticity or optogenetical activation and inactivation of CA2-CA1 synapses. Activating metaplastic mechanisms by employing pharmacological or optogenetical tools might strengthen the storage capacity of neurons, or in other words, reduce the threshold of certain synaptic units/clusters to be plastic in order to store information in aged and AD neural networks. Our research may help clinicians for finding appropriate therapeutic agents to improve memory or at least prevent memory loss that occur in aging and AD.
kw: Metaplasticity, hippocampal CA2 region, Synaptic tagging and Capture, PKMzeta, LTP, LTD

title: Advanced nonlinear optical microscopy for in vivo imaging of whole mouse brain
abs: Specific aims:1. To develop advanced nonlinear light microscope methods for in vivo visualization of neuronal connections in the entire brain of mouse models.2. To demonstrate an imaging depth 2-4 mm in brain tissue and a spatial resolution better than 2 microns.3. To conduct initial animal imaging experiments to assess the imaging performance of developed new methods and the new opportunities for neuroscience research.Hypotheses:1. Nonlinear excitation can be combined with focal modulation to dramatically improve the signal to background ratio in deep tissue imaging. A 2-3 fold improvement in imaging depth can be achieved.2. Deep tissue imaging coupled with appropriate animal model can open new windows to basic neuroscience research.How our minds emerge from our flock of neurons remains deeply mysterious. It’s the kind of question that neuroscience has been ill equipped to answer. Some neuroscientists dedicate their careers to the workings of individual neurons. Others choose to look at how the hippocampus, a cluster of millions of neurons, encodes memories. Others might look at the brain at an even higher scale, observing all the regions that become active when we perform a particular task, such as reading or feeling fear. Conventional light microscopes only allow visualization of neurons ex vivo or in top cortical layers in vivo. We propose to develop two-photon and three-photon microscopes that can provide high-resolution images of neuronal morphology and connection in the entire brain of mouse models. This will help neuroscientists to better understand how brain works. Such a platform technology can be readily utilized to find the mechanisms of neurodegenerative diseases, and to screen and evaluate the drugs for treatment.
kw: Brain imaging, Multi-photon microscopy, Focal modulation microscopy, Penetration depth, Spatial resolution, Mouse model

title: Function of lnc-BATE1 in brown adipose tissue in vivo
abs: Obesity is a major risk factor for several diseases such as type2 diabetes, stroke and certain cancers. An attractive therapeutic target for obesity is brown adipose tissue (BAT), which possesses a unique energy expenditure feature and contributes to the regulation of whole body energy homeostasis. Our long-term goal is to determine the regulatory mechanisms governing BAT development, thereby facilitating the development of new strategies for obesity therapies. Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNA) are emerging as a novel class of regulators in many biological processes. The recent studies from our and other groups are revealing important function of lncRNA in brown fat development. In our preliminary study, we performed massively parallel sequencing of poly-A selected RNA from brown and white adipose, reconstructed de novo transcriptomes and identified 1,500 lncRNAs, including 127 BAT-enriched lncRNAs, one of which, lnc-BATE1, is necessary for brown adipocyte differentiation. Inhibition of lnc-BATE1 impairs concurrent activation of brown fat and repression of white fat genes. To determine the role of lnc-BATE1 in BAT development and function in vivo, we have generated a knockout mouse model and will perform comprehensive phenotyping caused by lnc-BATE1 knockout (Aim1). Moreover, we will conduct detailed mechanistic studies to determine the functional interactions between lnc-BATE1 and one of its protein partners, hnRNPU (heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein U) and identify other protein partners of lnc-BATE1 using RNA pull-down approach (Aim2). These studies will fully establish the role of lncBATE1 in BAT development and provide important insights into the mechanism of how lnc-BATE1 function. The knowledge and methods developed in this research will advance our understanding of brown fat biology, which will contribute the development of BAT-based therapy for obesity and its related diseases.
kw: brown fat, long non-coding RNA, non-coding RNA, adipose, adipogenesis

title: Uncovering the Mechanisms of Sterile Neuroinflammation
abs: The sterile neuroinflammation associated with stroke is thought to be a major driver of tissue loss and consequent functional incapacity. However, the mechanisms behind the initiation of sterile neuroinflammation are poorly understood. The Macrophage inducible C-type Lectin (Mincle) belongs to a family of myeloid receptors with important roles in innate immunity, and with an emerging role in sterile inflammation. Mincle-induced signaling cascades lead to the activation of nuclear factor kappa B (NF-?B) and mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPKs) through the spleen tyrosine kinase (Syk)- and Caspase recruitment domain-containing protein 9 (CARD9)-dependent pathway(s) and induces an inflammatory responses. Activation of intracellular NF-?B and MAPK signaling pathways results in increased production of multi-protein complexes called inflammasomes. Inflammasomes have recently been identified and shown to contribute to cell death in tissue injury. The proposed research is the first exploration of Macrophage Inducible C-type Lectin (Mincle)-mediated activation of NLRP inflammasome in neuronal cells. Our preliminary data shows that Mincle is a central driver of neuronal loss during ischemic stroke, an observation that surprisingly does not require Mincle activation in peripheral blood immune cells. Our over-arching hypothesis is that Mincle plays a role in dictating the clinical severity of cerebral ischemic injury. Specifically, that (i) Mincle recognises a self-ligand in neurons undergoing metabolic stress, to activate NLRP inflammasomes and caspase-3 to initiate cell death and that (ii) blocking Mincle-Syk pathway attenuates the initiation and amplitude of a recruited inflammatory cell response, thereby improving functional outcomes after ischemic injuries caused by blood-vessel occlusion in the brain. The study will provide important insights into the mechanisms of neuronal cell loss under ischemic injury and provide the rationale and strategy for targeting specific molecular events to limit injury resulting from sterile neuroinflammation.
kw: Neuroinflammation, Ischemic stroke, Mincle, SYK, Inflammasome, Neuronal cell death

title: Targeting dengue non structural protein 3 and its essential interactions with small molecules
abs: The non-structural (NS) proteins of Dengue virus (DENV) are essential for viral RNA replication, and our previous studies elucidated the x-ray structures of the full-length proteins of NS3 and NS5, and also identified critical residues involved in their interaction. Major gaps still remain in the structural and mechanistic events within the membrane-tethered replication complex (RC) where NS3 and NS5 carry out their function. So our long-term goal is to gain a clear mechanistic understanding of the events in the RC so that the knowledge can be exploited for the development of antiviral therapeutics for dengue. The objective of this renewal grant is to obtain structures of full-length NS3 protein together with the NS2B cofactor bound to substrates in the protease as well as helicase domains to in order to gain new insights on how the coordinated activities may occur within the RC and identify and validate the small molecule inhibitors that block the function. The specific aims for this renewal grant are firstly to obtain new crystal structures of NS2B-NS3 that can support rational drug design. Secondly we will mimic the membrane environment by assembling NS2B and NS3 within lipid containing nanoparticles called nanodiscs to measure its enzymatic functions and reconstitute the interactions with other viral and host proteins. To continue to maintain a translational connect in keeping with our long-term goal we will examine the impact of small molecule compounds arising from our studies in a mouse model of infection. More specifically we will monitor dengue pathophysiology in a mouse model using Positron Emission Tomography (PET) imaging and correlate these with dengue infection and protection by new and established tool compounds already in hand. Our research addresses a high priority disease in Singapore (22,318 cases of dengue in 2013) and the collective outcome will support urgently needed interventional studies.
kw: Dengue NS5 protein, Dengue NS3 protein, Chemical Biology, Protein interactions, Drug Discovery, Reverse Genetics

title: Alternative splicing networks in gastric cancer
abs: Gastric cancer, (GC) is the fourth most common cancer worldwide and is prevalent in Asia with a five-year survival rate of less than 20%. Improvement in GC survival has been achieved with the use of anti-Her2 MAb therapy for Her+ GC patients. However, the paucity of effective precision medicines for this disease is evidence of the need for still greater delineation of GC-specific oncogenic driver events. We recently completed a transcriptome-wide analysis of alternative splicing events (ASEs) in GC and identified 340 ASEs in 198 genes associated with pathways implicated in cancer (cell adhesion, growth factor and cellular signaling, metabolism and proliferation). We seek to develop an alternative splicing network model for human gastric cancer. Alternative splicing activates oncogenes in a variety of tumor types, but a splicing network model describing pathway specific molecular changes in tumor cells has yet to be described. More specifically, the Splicing Regulatory Proteins (SRPs) that control splicing networks in GC has not been explored, nor has the functional relevance of such networks been ascertained. Our data indicates a novel set of simultaneous splicing events within the ligand-binding domains of cell surface proteins, and likely in other pathways. We hypothesize these coordinated events are regulated by a set of SRPs. Derivation of a splicing network model will enable experimental study of the function of coordinated splicing. To develop a GC-specific alternative splicing network model, we first intend to identify the SRPs which regulate the ASEs we have identified using western blot analysis and HITS-CLIP. Second, through deletion and/or ectopic expression of SRPs, we will assess whether the ASE patterns discerned in GC are coordinately regulated, and if so, by which SRPs. We will determine if splicing networks impact cell survival, growth or metastatic properties of GC cells.
kw: Alternative Splicing, Gastric Cancer

title: Identifying novel epigenetic regulators for targeted therapy in the treatment of rhabdomyosarcoma
abs: Rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS) is the most common soft-tissue sarcoma in children. Current standard of care involves chemotherapy and radiation. However these broadly cytotoxic treatment regimes are ineffective against metastatic/aggressive forms of RMS, in particular against Alveolar Rhabdomyosarcomas (ARMS), which is characterized by the aberrant fusion of transcription factors Pax3 and Foxo1 (Pax3-FKHR). While Pax3-FKHR is an attractive therapeutic target, current treatments are not capable of blocking its oncogenic activity. Moreover traditional non-targeted therapeutics in young children increases the risk of developmental impairment and incidence of secondary tumors. Epigenetic de-regulation is a hallmark of cancer, and while the role of chromatin regulators is well established in the regulation of myogenesis, little is known about their role in RMS. Our preliminary data provide compelling evidence that chromatin modifiers play critical roles in ARMS tumorigenesis. Thus understanding the epigenetic landscape in ARMS will provide critical drug targets. To this end, we performed a siRNA screen to identify chromatin regulators that are deregulated in ARMS. To identify key operational regulatory circuits that drive ARMS, we will perform transcriptomic and chromatin profiling and elucidate binding partners and substrates. We expect that our studies will establish the identified targets as high value novel drug targets in ARMS.
kw: Rhabdomyosarcoma, epigenetics, myopathies, skeletal muscle, differentiation, cell cycle

title: Characterizing the E3 ubiquitin protein ligase WWP2 as a new selective gene target for cardiac fibrosis
abs: Cardiac fibrosis is characterized by the increased deposition of extracellular matrix (ECM) components and proliferation of interstitial fibroblasts, resulting in increased myocardial stiffness, ventricular dysfunction and ultimately heart failure. Activation of the TGF?-Smads axis in fibroblasts serves as a main “fibrotic-switch”, but since this pathway is required for the normal regulation of tissue regeneration and inflammation, anti-fibrotic strategies that completely inhibit TGF?-Smad signaling often cause significant toxicity and adverse side effects. To overcome these limitations, we have focused on the identification of new gene targets for cardiac fibrosis, to modulate pro-fibrotic agents downstream of TGF?-signaling. Combining genetics and transcriptomics analysis in dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) patients and by comparative-genomics in a rat model of cardiovascular disease, we have identified a cross-species conserved network of ECM-genes that are strongly co-expressed and TGF?-activated in cardiac fibroblasts. In the DCM heart, we found this ECM-gene network to be regulated by genetic sequence variation at the WWP2 gene (a E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase). Subsequent genetic and in vitro studies suggested a specific isoform (WWP2-N terminal) as a positive, trans-acting genetic regulator of ECM and type I collagen in DCM-associated cardiac fibrosis. Here we propose to characterize and ultimately identify WWP2 as a new druggable gene target that can be modulated to reduce cardiac fibrosis. To this aim we will (1) define the detailed regulatory functions of WWP2 in TGF?-stimulated human cardiac fibroblasts by RNA-seq, (2) determine the pathophysiological role of WWP2 in cardiac fibrosis in vivo and (3) translate our findings to human hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) patients (characterized by excessive cardiac fibrosis) by identifying WWP2 variant(s) regulating fibrosis and with prognostic value for disease progression and cardiovascular outcome. The characterization of WWP2 as a modulator of cardiac fibrosis will provide a proof of concept for the development of novel and specific anti-fibrotic treatments in heart disease.
kw: Cardiac Fibrosis, Systems-Genetics, Gene Target, Cardiomiopathy, TGFb-signaling pathway, Antifibrotic therapies

title: Control of fat accumulation and energy expenditure by activin receptors
abs: ALK4 and ALK7 are receptors for a subset of TGF-? superfamily ligands, including activins and GDF-3. Recent results from our group show that ALK7 functions cell-autonomously and homeostatically in adult adipocytes to regulate catecholamine sensitivity in response to the diet. The central hypothesis of this proposal is that targeting ALK4 and ALK7 signaling may limit fat accumulation and improve energy balance in obesity. This hypothesis will be tested by pursuing the following specific aims:1: To elucidate the role of ALK4 signaling in adipogenesis and adult adipose tissue homeostasis. We will test the hypothesis that paracrine interactions mediated by ALK4 are necessary for adipogenesis and adipose tissue remodeling through regulation of the expression of critical master genes in preadipocytes. 2: To elucidate the role of ALK7 signaling in the control of diet-induced fat deposition and obesity. We will elucidate the molecular mechanisms by which ALK7 regulates diet-induced catecholamine resistance in adipose tissue, testing the hypothesis that ALK7 mediates diet-induced repression of beta-adrenoreceptor expression and beta-adrenergic signaling in adipocytes through specific signaling pathways. We will also assess the metabolic effects of acute inhibition of ALK7 signaling in adult mice, testing whether acute inhibition of ALK7 can reverse diet-induced fat accumulation in already obese aimals, a proof-of-concept for the development of anti-ALK7 therapies to combat human obesity.3: To elucidate the relevance of ALK7 signaling for human adipocyte function and human obesity. We will investigate the role of ALK7 signaling in human adipocytes, and determine whether human ALK7 controls fat accumulation by regulating diet-induced catecholamine resistance. We will also investigate the relationship between polymorphisms in ALK7 and fat accumulation in the human population. Using data from the GUSTO cohort, we will assess whether polymorphisms that reduce or attenuate ALK7 function ameliorate fat accumulation and obesity in the human population.
kw: obesity, adipogenesis, TGFbeta

title: To decipher the cellular and metabolic pathways lead to alterations in the uptake of glucose in human hepatocellular carcinoma.
abs: The concept of cancer as a genetic disease has been supported by numerous studies documenting genetic mutations that are consistently found in specific signaling pathways in tumor cells. However, there is now a renewed emphasis on cancer as a disease of altered metabolism. Compelling evidence suggests that deregulated metabolism such as the well-described Warburg effect (aerobic glycolysis) is a hallmark of many cancers including human hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Positron emission tomography (PET) using 18F-fluoro-2-deoxy-D-glucose (18F-FDG), FDG-PET, is a reliable diagnostic imaging tool for various kinds of malignancy, allowing for the functional assessment of tumour. Increased glucose uptake is found in malignant tumours resulting from the increase of both glucose transporters and intracellular enzymes such as hexokinase and phosphofructokinase that promote glycolysis. The standardized uptake value (SUV) is often used as a simple semi-quantitative analysis of the cellular concentration of 18F-FDG, representing the overall glycolytic activity of viable tumour cells when evaluating FDG-PET images. FDG-PET is most commonly used in brain, lung, breast, lymphoma and colon cancers. Unfortunately, the detection of early-stage primary HCC was less successful with FDG-PET because of the high background uptake of 18F-FDG by HCC cells. We have studied HCC patient samples that gave high (SUV high) or low (SUV low) glucose uptake when imaged with FDG-PET and have identified differentially expressed genes that can stratify HCC patient samples with high and low glucose uptake. In this application, we propose to uncover molecular mechanism(s) that lead to the reprogramming of metabolic pathways resulting in the alterations of glucose uptake in HCC cells. An understanding of the functional integration of cellular signalling pathways associated with the alterations in cellular metabolism relevant to HCC will enable the development of new concepts and approaches for the more accurate diagnosis and evaluation of treatment outcome in HCC.
kw: Hepatocellular Carcinoma; Positron emission tomography (PET); Glucose uptake; Transcriptome map; Metabolomics analysis; Orthotopic HCC mouse tumor model

title: Periodontal Health and Its Impact on Diabetes
abs: Periodontitis is a complication of diabetes mellitus but is less appreciated compared to other diabetic complications such as neuropathy, nephropathy, retinopathy and cardiovascular disease. Studies suggest that the relationship between diabetes and periodontal disease is bidirectional; diabetes has been shown to be a risk factor for periodontal disease, and the severity of periodontal disease has been associated with glycemic control and the development of diabetic complications. However, the periodontal health status and its impact in our local diabetic patients are largely unknown. Thus, the specific aims are to: (1) Determine the prevalence and severity of periodontitis in local diabetic patients, (2) Evaluate the clinical impact of non-surgical periodontal treatment in diabetic patients, and (3) Screen periodontal patients for undiagnosed and pre-diabetes during dental visits. We hypothesize that a significant proportion of our diabetic patients has undiagnosed periodontal disease and periodontal treatment should improve their diabetic status. Similarly, with the increasing prevalence of diabetes in Singapore, we postulate that there are unknown/undiagnosed diabetics among our periodontal patients and early detection will reduce clinical complications. We believe the proposed studies will be important because optimal periodontal health may improve diabetic control and reduce clinical complications. In turn, this should reduce disease burden, leading to lower overall healthcare costs. Identification of undiagnosed diabetes among periodontal patients is equally important because it enables early intervention and treatment, thereby reducing morbidity. Lastly, the findings from our study may change diabetes care management by incorporating oral health care as an integral component of diabetic care.
kw: Periodontitis,Oral inflammation, Non-surgical periodontal treatment, Diabetes Mellitus, Early disease detection, Diabetic Complications

title: Optogenetic control of an epigenetic regulator, PRMT8, in inhibitory interneurons to reactivate visual cortical plasticity and recovery of visual acuity.
abs: Neuronal circuits that process sensory information are shaped by patterns of cellular activity during early brain development called critical periods. The term ‘critical period’ refers to a specific developmental window during which target systems are sensitive to a specific environmental input. There are several known critical periods across several systems in the brain but the best-described case is the role of light on the development of the visual system. Visual cortical circuits exhibit maximal plasticity during the critical period and this plasticity is lost by adulthood. This loss of this extraordinary plasticity may reflect sequential locks placed on a molecular pathway as it consolidates into a structurally elaborated circuitry. Recently, the critical period in mouse visual cortex has been linked to a specific molecular logic of gene regulation and we propose that epigenetics help to fine-tune gene activity and their expression essential for defining plasticity. Our proposal takes advantage of recent technical developments merging novel optical approaches, novel candidate genes discovery and wireless technology. Brain circuitry can be precisely controlled with optogenetic probes, which can turned on or off with pulses of light. The goal of this project is to apply optogenetic approaches to study epigenetic changes affected in neurological diseases, using the intact circuitry of visual system as a model. We use the mouse brain, as this organism is genetically tractable yet, has a level of complexity that makes it an appropriate model for the sophisticated circuitry of the human brain. We hypothesize that the chromatin modifying enzyme, PRMT8 is activity-dependent and using electrical activity, PRMT8 can be controlled in cortical interneurons and inhibitory synaptic circuitry. Our hypothesis also predicts that the activity-dependent regulation of PRMT8 levels enhances cortical inhibitory circuits and the critical period in visual system can be reactivated.
kw: critical period, plasticity, excitatory inhibitory balance, epigenetics, optical control

title: Investigating the Prevalence and Impact of Vision Impairment, Hearing Loss and Dual Sensory Impairment in Residential Care Facilities in Singapore
abs: Due to the rapidly aging population, visual impairment (VI) and hearing loss (HL) are becoming more common in Singapore. Previous research has shown that both these conditions are associated with depression, poor functioning, frailty, reduced quality of life (QoL) and increased mortality; with the concurrent incidence of VI and HL (dual sensory impairment [DSI]) being associated with significantly poorer QoL and higher mortality rates then either VI or HL alone. Although previous epidemiological and clinical data have demonstrated the prevalence and impact of VI and HL in the Singaporean community, no study has ever evaluated the prevalence of VI, HL and DSI and their patient-centred and health-related impact in adults living in residential care (nursing home) facilities in Singapore.Studies outside Singapore have established that the residential care population is at greater risk of these conditions compared to those in the community. Our recent pilot data in a Singaporean residential care home corroborates these findings, with a disproportionately large number of adults ? 40y presenting with VI (81%). The lack of data on the prevalence and impact of VI, HL and DSI can critically impact on health care planning, resource allocation, public health initiatives, and policy for the residential care population. We therefore propose to address this knowledge gap by investigating the prevalence of VI and associated eye diseases (including cataract, refractive errors, diabetic retinopathy, glaucoma, and age-related macular degeneration); HL and DSI; and the impact of these conditions on daily functioning, QoL, frailty, and depression, in a population of 236 adults (? 40y) living in six different residential care homes in Singapore. The outcomes of this proposed study will provide evidence-based data to inform strategies for improving VL and HL, prevent blindness and deafness, and improve QoL for adults living in residential care in Singapore.
kw: Residential care homes, Elderly, Aging, Hearing loss, Vision impairment, Dual sensory impairment

title: Epigenetics of Psychotic Disorders: investigating the impact of early-life adversities on DNA methylation, white-matter connectivity and symptoms severity.
abs: Although generally accepted that both genetic and environmental factors contribute to the risk of psychosis, there is still a lack of understanding on the precise biological mechanism that serve as a substrate for this interaction and may trigger the emergence of symptoms. A growing body of evidence documents the higher prevalence of trauma and disrupted parenting in psychiatric populations. Trauma experienced during childhood can affect DNA methylation of genes involved in synaptogenesis and cell signaling and contribute to the emergence of psychosis in adult life.The specific aims for this study are (i) to demonstrate higher prevalence of early-life trauma in adolescents with prodromal symptoms of psychosis (UHR), first-episode (FE) and chronic schizophrenia (CSZ) patients, (ii) to demonstrate altered methylation of the RELN, NR3C1, FKBP5, BDNF, 5HTR1A and GAD1 gene promoters in UHR, FE and CSZ (iii) to show impaired white-matter integrity at the Superior Longitudinal, Inferior Longitudinal, Uncinate Fasciculi level in UHR, FE and CSZ (iv) to demonstrate that trauma-triggered epigenetic abnormalities mediate between impaired white-matter integrity and severity of both psychotic and non-psychotic comorbid symptoms.Four groups of participants will be studied: (1) a group of 93 UHR participants, (2) a group of 50 FE patients, (3) a group of 100 CSZ patients and (4) a group of 148 healthy controls (HC). Methylation percentage differences across the four groups will be tested for each of the six gene promoters by repeated measures MANCOVA with five covariates (age, gender, BMI, medication and ethnicity). Regression analyses will probe the association between severity of trauma, methylation percentage, white matter integrity as measured by Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) and symptoms severity.
kw: Schizophrenia; DNA Methylation; Diffusion Tensor Imaging; Disconnection Hypothesis; Trauma.

title: Validation of Candidate Biomarkers in Plasma for Diagnosis and Prognosis of Lung Cancer
abs: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer mortality worldwide. Most of the current lung cancer biomarkers show limited diagnostic value due to their low sensitivity while low-dose computed tomography has been found to have high false positive rate. There is thus an urgent need for identification of novel biomarkers that have high specificity and sensitivity for diagnosis and prognosis of lung cancer.This study aims to evaluate the clinical utility of a panel of biomarker candidates derived from in vitro study using exosomes from non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cells, by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay and immunohistochemistry for their diagnostic and prognostic roles. Our in vitro proteomic analysis conducted using exosomes from NSCLC cells revealed significant number of exosome-specific proteins for each cell line (n>1400). The top 20 proteins that have the highest fold-change (cancer cell/normal lung fibroblast) and the pool of 158 proteins that were present only in the cancer cells were analyzed based on several factors such as subcellular localization, functional relevance and association with cancer. A panel of 17 proteins (8 out of the top 20 proteins - YWHAE, ANXA4, RPS9, HSP1A1, PSME3, Radixin, FAM3C and RPLP1; and 9 novel proteins - RALA, CIB1, AGRIN, CDCP1, MAL2, PTPRF, EPHB3, DSG2 and SCRIB were identified from the 158 proteins present in cancer cells only) were selected and will then be subjected to validation studies in an independent cohort of patient plasma samples (n=300) to interrogate their diagnostic and prognostic values for lung cancer. Plasma samples from healthy individuals (n=150) and patients with benign lung diseases (n=150) will be used as control groups for comparison. This validation study will confirm if the panel of biomarker candidates has better diagnostic and prognostic roles for NSCLC than the current standard biomarkers.
kw: Plasma, Biomarker, Diagnosis, Prognosis, Lung Cancer

title: Enhancing the Efficiency of Modelling and Simulating Complex Systems via Quantum Mechanics
abs: What are the signatures of impending economic turmoil or meteorological disasters? Many pressing problems in science and society necessitate day to day predictions on systems of immense complexity. This motivated the search for systematic methods to infer patterns of behaviour from observational data – and in doing so, build predictive models that isolate key indicators of future behaviour to make statistical predictions. Complexity theorists studied this problem extensively in the field of computational mechanics, resulting in sophisticated techniques for inferring predictive models from observational data. Yet inexplicably, even provably optimal constructions are inefficient – they track information which is statistically uncorrelated with the future behaviour. Computer simulations based on such models are forced to waste resources storing this information, and in turn incur unavoidable energetic cost. This project aims to harness quantum mechanics to reduce this inherent waste beyond classical limits. I will design systematic methods to build more efficient quantum models of complex phenomena directly from time-series data of their observed behaviour – and tailor these methods for implementation via available quantum technology. This will be supported by an extensive investigation of the practical and foundational benefits of such models, both in reducing memory and energetic waste, and in unveiling how quantum information may change our view of what is complex. In doing so, we will determine and demonstrate the power, practicality and consequences of using quantum information to understand the complex phenomena that permeate everyday life. This research has the potential to impact much of quantitative science. The tools of computational mechanics are applicable to almost all systems that output observational data, and have contributed to understanding complex systems of remarkable diversity, from neural networks to atmospheric turbulence. Our research thus motivates the adoption of quantum technology in disciplines that traditionally never considered the immediate benefits that such technology can bring.
kw: Quantum Information;Quantum Technology;Complex Systems;Computational Mechanics;Quantum Computing;Information Theory

title: Genetic and genomic approaches to unlock the secrets of neurological diseases
abs: The aim of my research is to define heritable genetic variation which underlies neurological diseases in the Singaporean and Asian populations. I hypothesize that such genetic variants are “experiments of nature” that provide insights into direct causal relationships between genotype and phenotype. A genetics platform focused on identifying naturally-occurring gene disruptions will lead to the identification of new drug targets, and contribute to our understanding of the differences in disease susceptibility between individuals. My research will focus on Parkinson’s disease, a common yet poorly-understood age-related disease in collaboration with the National Neuroscience Institute. I plan to perform a rigorous interrogation of the entire protein coding regions of the human genome by whole-exome sequencing of at least 1000 patients and 3000 controls, to identify genes that are recurrently disrupted by germline variants in disease cases but not in controls. I plan to validate the findings in large sample collections from other research groups across East Asia. In parallel, I will investigate the roles of somatic mutations in post-mortem diseased brain tissue using the single-cell whole-exome sequencing, thus exploring an alternative mechanism through which protein-disrupting mutations may underlie a disease. Newly-identified genes and variants will be followed up; both epidemiologically in patients to better understand their utility for risk prediction and stratified medicine, and functionally in cell and animal models to dissect the molecular mechanisms underlying disease. These approaches will be extended to other genetically-tractable neurological diseases as new collaborations are established. Apart from adult-onset common diseases, my research will be complemented by studies on rare recessive childhood neurological disorders, which make up another major class of neurological diseases. This study will start on a large collection of consanguineous pedigrees from Pakistan. Any novel gene will be functionalized in vitro and in vivo, and screened for a possible role in common diseases.

title: GNA13 induction of stemness and resistance to chemo- and radiotherapy in breast and head and neck cancers
abs: Despite advancement in cancer therapy, the ability of cancer cells to evade therapy often leads to tumor recurrence and distant metastasis, and ultimately to the death of the patient. Increasing evidence shows that these properties of recurrence can be attributed to a small population of cells within the tumor termed cancer stem cells (CSCs). Understanding the mechanisms that support the growth of CSCs could provide new tools to target these cells and improve therapeutic outcomes. G12 proteins, comprised of G?12 (GNA12) and G?13 (GNA13) are mediators of G protein coupled receptor (GPCR) signaling. These proteins are highly expressed in several cancers, and blocking their signaling can significantly inhibit cancer cell invasion and metastasis. Recently, we have shown that loss of GNA13 alone can suppress invasion of breast and prostate cancer cells. Moreover, we have recently obtained evidence that enhanced expression of GNA13 is capable of inducing a stem cell phenotype in cancer cells. Specifically, enforced expression of GNA13 in cancer cells containing low levels of GNA13 protein significantly induced CSC population as shown by increased aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH1) activity, increased CD44+/CD24- cells, and enhancement of tumor sphere formation. In contrast, in cancer cells that express high levels of GNA13, knockdown of GNA13 suppressed ALDH1 activity, the CD44+/CD24- cell population, and the formation of spheres. We therefore hypothesize that GNA13 plays a pivotal role in the induction of CSCs, and the suppression of GNA13 activity may provide therapeutic advantage to cancer therapy. Using in vitro and in vivo models of breast cancer and head & neck cancer (HNSC), this proposal aims to (1) elucidate the role of GNA13 in inducing CSCs, (2) identify signaling pathways induced by GNA13 that are important for inducing CSC phenotype, and (3) assess the potential of GNA13 expression level as a marker for resistance to therapy.
kw: GNA13, Cancer Stem cells, Drug resistance, Tumor development, G12 proteins, GPCR signaling

title: A novel organelle-wide RNAi screening for the identification of mitochondrial matrix Ca2+ sensors.
abs: Studies for the past five decades identified many different physiological roles of mitochondrial Ca2+, and in more recent years the identification of major Calcium entry and exit pathways spurred the research on mitochondrial physiology. Interestingly, our discoveries of MCUR1, as the regulatory subunit of mitochondrial calcium uniporter (MCU) and MICU1 as a gatekeeper of MCU contributed substantially on elevating the knowledge on mitochondrial ca2+ homeostasis. Discovery of MICU1 as the gatekeeper closed the three decade quest for the molecular identity of the regulatory mechanism that evades Ca2+ uptake under resting physiological conditions. However the regulation of matrix calcium is controlled by the components in the mitochondrial matrix. To our surprise MICU1 is localized in the inter-membrane space and lacks the capacity of sensing mitochondrial matrix calcium. Our central hypothesis is that MICU1 controls MCU channel activity by its inherent cytosolic Ca2+ sensing coupled with the signals transmitted by a Ca2+ sensing matrix counterpart. The proposed study is aimed at identifying the molecular components that sense matrix calcium to regulate the gatekeeping of the uniporter. RNA interference methodologies have evolved in recent years as an important tool in discovery research. We ourselves have tested the power of RNAi screening approach and successfully identified MCUR1. In this proposal we will use a siRNA based screening approach, coupled with an advanced strategy of employing exclusively mitochondrial targeted siRNA library. The proposed studies will elucidate the unresolved mystery of matrix Ca2+ sensing components of the gatekeepers of the MCU. Understanding the complete molecular components of the uniporter complex will help us to target these components and design therapeutic intervention in a variety of diseases where detrimental mitochondrial Ca2+ overload is implicated.
kw: mitochondria, calcium signaling, uniporter, RNAi, gatekeeper

title: Blood vessel-on-a-chip: A biomimetic model to study the immunomodulatory effects of vitamin D in atherosclerosis
abs: Atherosclerosis is the leading cause of cardiovascular disease (CVD) in Singapore and globally. While vitamin D deficiency affects ~50% of the population worldwide and has been associated with dyslipidemia, CVD and endothelial dysfunction, its role in atherosclerosis remains incompletely understood.SPECIFIC AIMSThe overarching goal is to develop novel microfluidic strategies to investigate how vitamin D influences vascular inflammation, recruitment/differentiation of monocytes in the pathobiology of atherosclerosis and its potential as an immunomodulator to mitigate atherogenesis.HYPOTHESISWe hypothesize that vitamin D deficiency can down regulate nuclear vitamin D receptors (VDR) on endothelial cells and monocytes, leading to pro-atherogenic phenotypes and increased foam cell formation. Vitamin D supplementation can reverse these atherogenic processes for therapeutic intervention.METHODOLOGYWe will develop “organ-on-a-chip” microfluidics technologies to characterize the effects of vitamin D on monocyte-endothelial interactions in vitro. Peripheral monocytes isolated from patients with vitamin D deficiency would be assessed for macrophage cholesterol metabolism and pro-atherogenic phenotypes using microfluidics, flow cytometry and molecular biology.APPROACHWe will develop a new inertial microfluidics-based cell sorting strategy to purify monocytes from whole blood in a label-free manner. We propose to create a biomimetic microsystem to model atherosclerotic vessel microenvironment in vitro using co-culture of aortic endothelial and smooth muscle cells with low density lipoprotein (LDL) insudation for on-chip dynamic characterization of vascular permeability, monocyte-endothelial interactions (rolling, adhesion and migration), as well as the effects of vitamin D supplementation. We aim to clinically validate our cell-based microdevice by testing peripheral monocytes isolated from patients with vitamin D deficiency (25OH(D)<10ng/mL) and healthy controls. The DFF-sorted monocytes would be further characterized for macrophage cholesterol homeostasis with and without vitamin D supplementation (foam cell formation, modified LDL binding/uptake), VDR expression and macrophage M1/M2 membrane markers (M1: CCR7 and CD86; M2: CD163 and MR) using flow cytometry and RT-PCR.
kw: Microfluidics, Atherosclerosis, Vitamin D, Endothelial dysfunction, Inflammation

title: Imaging through Dynamic Scattering Media, a Pilot Study toward Non-Invasive Biomedical Imaging by Light
abs: A laser beam passing through our finger tips creates a bright halo with speckle patterns which do not seem to contain any information. In this proposal, we aim to study an exciting and challenging technology that allows taking optical images through dynamic scattering media. The technology will utilize the statistical properties of speckle patterns in a novel imaging modality where both optical imaging configurations and image recovering algorithms play crucial roles. As is now well understood, the speckles have a “short memory” about the direction of the incoming laser beam. Therefore, the autocorrelation of speckle intensity at different angles resemble the object autocorrelation from which the hidden object can be recovered by phase retrieval algorithms. Thick dynamic scattering media limit the memory effects and require fast imaging. These create challenges for image recovering algorithms because of the limited information that can be collected and the low signal-to-noise ratio. Fortunately, very much is known about the statistical properties of the images of biological tissues and statistical Bayesian techniques can give principled ways of combining prior statistical knowledge of the structure with the information brought from the speckle patterns in order to recover the images of structures lying deep with biological tissues. In our preliminary studies we successfully recovered biological images with a tenfold increase in the level noise and a tenfold decrease in memory effect angle in comparison with conventional techniques. Our methods will be further developed to tackle more ambitious and realistic situations. A young and yet established team comprised of an optical physicist and an applied statistician will lead the project to success.
kw: laser speckle, scattering media, phase retrieve, non-invasive, auto-correlation, optical physics

title: Intrauterine Reduction in Growth Velocity As A Predictor of Poor Perinatal Outcome In Term Appropriately Grown Fetuses
abs: Background- Current research on intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) has focused on the poorer outcome of fetuses with an estimated fetal weight (EFW) of less than 10% and abnormal Doppler measurements. However, there are still babies born with birthweights of more than 10% whose postnatal outcome is poor but unexplained. Hypothesis- We postulate that fetuses who start the 2nd trimester on a normal EFW but reach the third trimester on a lower than expected EFW and with a birth weight that is within normal range represent a group of IUGR fetuses which could potentially remain undetected but are at risk of poor perinatal outcome. The placenta may play a role in this.Aims- To identify term ‘appropriately-grown’ fetuses with an intrauterine reduction in growth velocity and correlate them to their perinatal outcome. To correlate outcomes with maternal angiogenic factors and placenta histopathology.Methods- Singleton fetuses with an EFW of more than 25 % at the 2nd trimester and a reduction in the EFW of more than 15 % between the 2nd and 3rd trimester will be recruited. Pregnancies will be dated by first trimester crown–rump length measurements. The EFW will be calculated using the Hadlock formula. Only cases of cephalic presentation without contraindications for a vaginal delivery will be considered. Umbilical, uterine and middle cerebral arteries blood flow Doppler will be evaluated. Maternal angiogenic factors will be collected. The placenta will be examined histopathologically for evidence of placental under-perfusion. Perinatal outcome data (emergency delivery for non-reassuring fetal status and neonatal metabolic acidosis) will be recorded. Significance- This will be the first ever study that looks at the intrauterine reduction in growth velocity as a possible risk factor of poor perinatal outcome. This may revolutionize our understanding of IUGR and help improve the identification of fetuses at risk.
kw: PlGF, Growth Velocity, Acidosis, IUGR, Umbilical artery, Perinatal

title: Medically Actionable and Pathogenic Incidental Findings in Genomic Sequencing of Singaporeans
abs: Background: While genomic sequencing aims to improve patient care by delivering precision medicine tailored to the individual’s genome, it also presents the risk of incidental findings (IFs), referring to variants in genes that are unrelated to patient’s primary condition. Some of these IFs are important because they are medically actionable (e.g. BRCA1 in breast cancer), hence leading the American College of Medical Genetics initially to recommend the wholesale return of IF results to patients. The additional burden that management of IFs creates on the healthcare system could thus be a significant concern. In individuals of European and African descent, the cumulative incidence of IFs is reportedly 1.7% and 1.0%, respectively. However, the prevalence and types of IFs in Asian populations have never been explored. Hypothesis and aims: We hypothesize that the prevalence of IFs in our multi-ethnic Singaporean population will be comparable to that reported in the Western population. We aim to study the prevalence of medically actionable IFs in individuals of (a) Chinese descent (n=2,700), (b) Malay ancestry (n=1,400) and (c) Indian ancestry (n=1,000), in Singapore by bioinformatically identifying pathogenic variants in the genomic data of individuals recruited through a wide spectrum of co-funded genomic sequencing research projects. We will analyse the precise distribution of IFs, class of genes, related medical conditions, potential clinical impact and implication for subsequent clinical management.Clinical significance: The work proposed in this grant is urgently needed in Singapore before clinical genomics can be effectively implemented for a genomics-based practice of precision medicine. The results of our analysis will be unique to Singaporean genomes, forming a resource and building towards ongoing experience of interpreting our own Singaporean genomes. Our analysis will benefit national policymakers as well as medical bodies as they move towards discussing, debating and formulating recommendations for clinical genomic sequencing in Singapore.
kw: Genomic sequencing, Incidental findings, precision medicine

title: Muscle imaging and genomic subtyping of paediatric neuromuscular diseases
abs: BackgroundNeuromuscular diseases (NMDs) are a genetically and phenotypically heterogeneous group of more than 200 disorders with a combined prevalence of 1:3000. They are characterized by progressive muscle weakness, which leads to motor, respiratory and swallowing difficulties. Advances in treatment options have been challenging as the molecular causes and hence disease pathways remain unknown in at least 50% of these patients. Elucidating the molecular cause would be the first step to finding a potential cure for these patients. In the last 2 decades, the application of molecular genetic strategies has led to a delineation of clinically indistinguishable neuromuscular disorders and disclosed marked disease overlap2. The expanding number of molecular defined NMDs requires new strategies to classify overlapping and clinical indistinguishable phenotypes. Next generation sequencing (NGS) has been successfully employed to identify causative gene(s) in patients with neuromuscular disorders. In addition, there has been increasing evidence that MRI can be a valuable tool in the diagnosis of the different NMDs, aiding the clinician in selecting appropriate genetic and biochemical diagnostic investigations, as well as which muscle to target for muscle biopsy.Aims and hypothesisWe hypothesize that a combination of next generation sequencing and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the limb musculature would significantly improve diagnostics in paediatric neuromuscular disorders. This will also allow us to study and understand the disease mechanisms for NMD. We aim to study the utility of (a) next generation sequencing and (b) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the limb muscles in establishing diagnosis in paediatric neuromuscular disorders (n=50).Clinical significanceUnderstanding the genetics of NMDs in the context of our local patients will enable us to reach a molecular diagnosis. It will also be a stepping stone towards understanding the mechanism of this heterogeneous group of disorders, with eventual discovery of a treatment for these patients.
kw: Muscle MRI, genotype-penotype correlation, paediatric neuromuscular diseases, whole exome sequencing

title: Development of novel targeted therapy in the RAS-RAF-MEK pathway in advanced solid tumours.
abs: Phase I clinical trials are a fundamental component in the process of translating preclinical scientific data of a drug in the laboratory into clinical utilisation for cancer patients. In addition to assessing toxicity and tolerability, phase I trials have now assumed the “gate-keeper” role in drug development, and are a crucial first-step in the bench to bedside translational drug development process.The RAS-RAF-MEK pathway has been targeted in anticancer drug development over the last two decades with differing degrees of success. BRAF inhibitors have recently enjoyed success in the treatment of melanoma, yet treatment is not curative and responses are finite. While BRAF inhibitors are successful in treating BRAF mutant cancers, they are not effective in BRAF wild type cancers. Biologically, MEK inhibitors have the advantage of targeting multiple downstream kinases that drive cancer such as RAS and RAF. The Drug Development Unit (DDU), at The Institute of Cancer Research (ICR) and The Royal Marsden (RM), London has been developing methods to target this pathway, by creating multi-kinase inhibitors, including a novel dual RAF-MEK inhibitor (RO5126766) which inhibits BRAF, CRAF and MEK. The aim of this project is to be the lead fellow in a phase 1 study, understand the pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic characteristics of a novel multikinase inhibitor and understand the role of novel imaging modalities as predictive imaging biomarkers of response. The DDU at The ICR/RM is a well-established and world renowned unit, specialising in phase 1 studies, with about 30-40 studies on-going at any point in time. The aim of this fellowship is to acquire skills in translational science of drug development, gain experience in designing and writing clinical trial protocols, develop a phase 1 study protocol to study a novel therapeutic agent and establish a strong relationship between the ICR/RM and Singapore for future collaborations and projects.
kw: drug development, novel therapy, advanced solid tumours, RAS, RAF, MEK

title: Altered inflammation in response to pathogens via Inflammasome signalling pathways in the fruit bat.
abs: Natural reservoir hosts are capable of low-level infection without succumbing to disease. Several bat species are known to be zoonotic hosts of viruses such as Ebola, SARS and Hendra Virus causing mass-inflammation in animals and humans while remaining asymptomatic in the bat. The inflammasome is a rapidly growing area of research that covers the cross-talk between innate immunity and activation of the adaptive immune system. The mass inflammation triggered and the subsequent recruitment of adapter molecules such as NLRP3 and Asc1, effector molecules such as Caspase-1 and cleavage of functional cytokines like IL-1? all converge to a rapid and effective recruitment or maturation of immune cells. In addition to pathogens, these pathways have been implicated in inflammatory auto-immune diseases such as Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA), Hereditary Periodic Fever (HPF) and Cryoporin Associated Periodic Syndrome (CAPS). We hypothesise inflammasome signalling may be altered in bats as part of their restricted inflammatory response to pathogens. We aim to characterise the activation of the inflammasome in response to pathogens and artificial ligands and evaluate downstream recruitment of caspase activation and cytokine output to gain insight into this control. By investigating how sensing and inflammasome activation is altered, we can understand mechanisms for controlling excess inflammation and disease in humans. Our data so far suggests that while bats mount sufficient, yet altered, induction of the IFN pathway and NF?B signaling, most ligands do not result in activation of the inflammasome complexes. Interrogation of inflammasome pathways reveals poor Asc-recruitment and low induction of caspase-activation in response to natural and synthetic ligands. Initial observations show several key mutations, altered kinetics and decreased sensitivity of induction all appear to be involved. This natural inhibition of systemic inflammation may be a key feature for the bats ability to withstand virus infection.
kw: inflammation, virus, bat, immunity, inflammasome, signalling

title: Non-clonal transposon libraries with saturating genome-wide coverage for mapping phage-mediated horizontal gene transfer.
abs: In recent decades, the shadow of multidrug-resistant bacteria has grown and now threatens to unravel modern medicine on a global scale. Of the superbugs, the notorious pathogen Staphylococcus aureus has emerged as a leading cause of life-threatening infection in both hospitals and the community. Faced with rapidly evolving environmental challenges and antibiotics, S. aureus has become progressively more contagious, more virulent, and more resistant to antibiotics. This ability to evolve dynamically reflects a remarkable level of genomic plasticity, most probably maintained by horizontal gene transfer. Because nearly all gene transfer in S. aureus is mediated by bacteriophages, the hypothesis proposed herein is that phage-mediated horizontal gene transfer drives S. aureus rapid adaptation by preferentially transferring a subset of the genome that includes genes important for pathogenicity. Accordingly, the overarching aim of this study is to define the genes preferentially transferred by the phages of S. aureus. To achieve this aim, we will use transposon sequencing (Tn-seq), which combines classical transposon insertional mutagenesis with massively parallel sequencing. More specifically, we will first develop the genetic tools necessary for generating high-density non-clonal transposon insertion pools in S. aureus. Once these insertion libraries are assembled, we will utilize high-throughput, parallel-sequencing methods for analyzing phage-mediated gene transfer of the transposons to recipient strains, en masse. The positions of the transposon insertions and the relative frequencies of transfer will reveal the precise regions of the S. aureus genome that are preferentially transferred by specific phages. Therefore, determining the genes that are preferentially exchanged by phages will elucidate the evolutionary “game plan” of this pathogen, and will assist in predicting the emergence of new virulent strains and will highlight specific determinants to be targeted for the development of therapeutics.

title: KidCard Study: Kidney Kids with Cardiovascular Disease Study
abs: Background: Children with chronic kidney disease (CKD) suffer from tremendous burden of cardiovascular disease (CVD). Recognising the need to effectively predict and agressively prevent early CVD, our centre initiated a prospective cohort KiDCarD study in 2010. During phase1 of study,110 paediatric patients with various stages of CKD and 110 controls (children with minor structural abnormalities unlikely to progress) were recruited and baseline arteriopathy scans, echocardiography and ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) obtained to determine the burden of CVD in our patients. Blood and urine samples were taken and novel biomarkers known to predict CVD including GDF-15, ST2, NT-proBNP and hsTNT were analysed and found to be predictors of early CVD. Specific Aims and hypothesis: During the phase 2 of the study we will continue the longitudinal follow-up of the existing patient cohort and further evaluate several new biomarkers implicated in CVD based on our preliminary findings. These include biomarkers of volume overload (mid region pro-adrenomedullin, c type natriuretic peptide), and CKD-mineral bone disease (fibroblast growth factor-23, Klotho, and osteoprotegerin).
