title: Investigating the Role of Inflammation in Primary Angle Closure Glaucoma
abs: Glaucoma is the leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide, with primary angle closure glaucoma (PACG) a major form of glaucoma in Singapore and Asia. Angle closure disease covers a spectrum that starts with the primary angle closure suspects (PACS) stage, followed by the primary angle closure (PAC) and culminates in PACG. One of the features of PAC/PACG eyes is the presence of permanent scarring of the angle structures called peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS). Evidence suggests that the pathogenesis of PACG is complex with multiple contributory mechanisms. However there are still significant lacunae in the area of PACG etiology, and the reasons for development of disease, and progression from early stages to blindness are not known. PAS formation is typically associated with uveitis and inflammation within the eye, where disruption of the blood aqueous barrier allows the inflammatory cells and their cytotoxic/proinflammatory agents infiltrate the trabecular meshwork. Since PAS is also present in PAC/PACG eyes (although of a lesser magnitude than in uveitis), we hypothesize that an underlying low-grade inflammation is present in these eyes, and is responsible for the development and progression of the condition. To address our hypothesis, we will assess the biochemical evidence of inflammation in the aqueous, lens capsule and iris tissues (through the measurement of specific markers of inflammation via well-established proteomics, cytokines and gene expression techniques) obtained from the entire spectrum of angle closure eyes; and will also correlate with in-vivo assessment of inflammation and extent of PAS. An evaluation of inflammation-related markers may help in early recognition of subjects at-risk for development and/or progression of PAS, and thereby aid in targeted treatment to this group of at-risk individuals.
kw: Primary angle closure glaucoma, inflammation, peripheral anterior synechiea, aqueous humour cytokines

title: Topological electronics and opto-electronics: van der Waals heterostructures as a platform for new valley, spin, energy, and charge manipulation in devices
abs: Charge carriers in materials are often described as quasiparticles similar to free electrons. This description, however, fails to fully explain the physics of topological materials. For instance, valley-polarized electrons in certain van der Waals’ (vdW) materials such as transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs, e.g. MoS2, WSe2) and heterostructures (e.g. G/h-BN, bilayer graphene) experience an anomalous Hall effect even in the absence of an applied magnetic field. My goal is to understand and utilize electron topology in vdW heterostructures, and exploit its interaction with light to devise new schemes for manipulating valley, spin, charge, and energy degrees of freedom. Because wavefunction topology fundamentally affects electronic properties, I expect that a range of elementary responses of vdW heterostructures can be altered and engineered. With the emergence of synthesis techniques for 2D materials and their heterostructures, this topological behavior can be readily accessed and exploited. Specifically, my goal is to unveil electronic, and opto-electronic properties that include new photocurrent generation mechanisms of valley electrons, the collective/interaction behavior of valley electrons, how guided modes such as plasmon polaritons are affected by the unusual electron topology of vdWs, low dissipation valley transport for information processing, edge state motion for novel transistor action, and how vdW superlattices can give rise to large boosts in intrinsic optical absorption. These will provide the building blocks of new kinds of electronic device concepts that rely on electron topology.
kw: van der Waals heterostructures;Topological currents;Opto-electronics;Berry curvature;Valleytronics;Transition metal dichalcogenides

title: Phase III, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of post-operative adjuvant concurrent chemo-radiotherapy with or without nimotuzumab for stage III/IV head and neck squamous cell cancer
abs: Two large randomized studies (RTOG & EORTC) were reported recently that show that adjuvant CTRT improves DFS in patients with locally advanced HNSCC as compared to adjuvant RT alone. Nimotuzumab is a recombinant humanized murine antibody IgG subtype 1 kappa. It recognizes the EGF receptor(EGFR) and also blocks EGF and TGF binding, thereby effecting an antagonistic biological activity. Clinical trials performed to date demonstrated efficacy with low toxicity with nimotuzumab. We would like to explore the role of nimotuzumab in combination with cisplatin/RT in the adjuvant setting for locally advanced Stage III/IV HNSCC. For concurrent cisplatin and radiotherapy (combined therapy arm) Bernier et al (2004, Figure 1) reported 2 year DFS as around 65% while Cooper et al (2004, Figure 2) reported 2 year DFS as around 55%. We assume that the average 2 year DFS for this cohort of patients would be about 60%, and that the addition of nimotuzumab to CDDP/RT will improve 2 year DFS by 10% to 70%. To detect a 10% difference at a 5% two-sided significance level and 90% power, 355 subjects would be required in each group for a period of 3-years accruement. This is a Phase III, double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized trialStratified according to treatment centre, primary site (oral cavity versus others), nodal status (positive versus negative) and presence or absence of any of the following adverse features (extracapsular spread or microscopic margins). The control arm is adjuvant cisplatin with concurrent radiotherapy plus placebo and the study arm is RT and cisplatin as above plus Nimotuzumab 200 mg weekly for 8 weeks beginning on first week of radiotherapy.
kw: nimotuzumab; head/neck squamous cell carcinoma, adjuvant, phase 3

title: Development and characterization of novel inhibitors of the KCa3.1 potassium channel for use as therapeutics for fibrovascular disorders
abs: Background: The calcium-activated KCa3.1 potassium channel is of immense physiological significance and medical importance. It regulates calcium signaling, cell proliferation and migration in lymphocytes, endothelial cells, epithelia, glial cells, and fibroblasts and myofibroblasts. TRAM-34, a selective KCa3.1 inhibitor we developed, is effective in rodent and pig models of vasculoproliferative disorders (atherosclerosis, vascular stenosis), fibrosis (liver, kidney, lung, heart), immunological diseases (colitis, graft rejection), neuroinflammation (microglia-induced inflammation), and cancer (glioma, non-small cell lung cancer). TRAM-34 is safe in rodents and monkeys. However, TRAM-34 has high lipophilicity, poor oral bioavailability and short circulating half-life. NS6180, another KCa3.1 inhibitor developed by NeuroSearch, also has poor pharmacokinetic properties. Objective: Develop novel KCa3.1 inhibitors with improved oral bioavailability and pharmacokinetic properties for all the clinical indications described above. Aim 1: Starting with a molecular model of KCa3.1, we will in silico-screen three compound libraries including a TRAM-34+NS6180-focused library (~270,000 compounds) to identify novel binders and scaffolds. Promising compounds (~300) will be tested for blockade of KCa3.1 by automated patch clamp and structure-activity-relationships determined.Aim 2: Guided by in silico approaches, we will synthesize 150 analogs of the most potent blockers discovered in Aim 1. We will select analogs that potently block KCa3.1 and exhibit KCa3.1 specificity, drug-likeness, optimized ADME properties, and represent novel intellectual property. Aim 3: We will assess oral bioavailability and pharmacokinetic properties of leads and determine their mean tolerated dose. As proof-of-concept, the best lead will be tested in a humanized mouse model of hepatitis C virus-induced liver fibrosis. Expected outcomes: (a) Selective KCa3.1 blocker as platform therapeutic for diverse clinical indications. (b) Training of a PhD student and 2 postdoctoral researchers in drug discovery. (c) High impact publications. (d) Commercialization of intellectual property.
kw: Potassium channel, Fibrosis, Cancer, Immunomodulator, Therapeutic, Vasculoproliferative

title: Whole exome sequencing to identify actionable mutations causative of primary angle closure glaucoma
abs: Glaucoma is the leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide, with primary angle closure glaucoma (PACG) a major form of glaucoma in Singapore and Asia. In 2012, we reported the world’s first successful genome-wide association study (GWAS) of PACG comprising 2,000 cases and 9,600 controls (Vithana et al. Nature Genetics 2012) identifying 3 novel disease loci. We recently followed up the initial GWAS with additional GWAS of 3,500 PACG cases and 6,615 controls. This effort identified a further four new PACG loci robustly surpassing genome-wide significance (unpublished). Collectively, these loci implicate members of the collagen family (COL11A1), cell-to-cell barrier and adhesion (PLEKHA7, DPM2, EPDR1), amino acid transport (SLC38A11), and acetylcholine metabolism (CHAT) related genes. However, the role of these genes underlying PACG susceptibility still remains unclear. As we observed that many PACG patients show positive evidence of familial clustering, we hypothesize that rare protein-changing genetic variations of higher penetrance could be significant contributors to PACG susceptibility. We now propose to perform whole exome sequencing in up to 2000 PACG cases, matched to 2,000 non-PACG controls, which have been exome-sequenced in Singapore (available as a national resource). The 2000 PACG cases will comprise 100 familial cases, and 1900 sporadic cases. This effort will also allow us to assess the spectrum of continuity and generalizability between alleles contributing to familial and sporadic forms of PACG. This concept has shed much light in other complex diseases such as breast cancer, Alzheimer’s disease, and coronary artery disease, amongst others. The identification of protein-changing mutations of higher penetrance will revolutionize the field of PACG research, and may lead to the development of genetic tests for high-risk adults who will benefit from interventions to slow the rate of progression of disease. The identification of loss-of-function mutations may also provide in-vivo validation of potential therapeutic targets.
kw: PACG, mutations, whole-exome sequencing, actionable molecular genetic markers of PACG

title: Towards Reprogramming of the Blast Crisis Chronic Myeloid Leukaemia Transcriptome
abs: The use of tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) in chronic phase (CP) chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML) has led to remarkable and enduring responses, but does not control blast crisis (BC) CML. Currently, a critical barrier to effective control of BC is the lack of information regarding the genetic or epigenetic drivers of BC. By employing multiparameter ‘omics’ to study a rare collection of 13 paired progression samples, we find that BC progression is characterized by genome-wide DNA hypermethylation occurring on the background of a stable genome (<5 coding mutations/pair). Our data also demonstrate a functional association between methylation and expression signatures in both CP and BC, and that even partial reversal of BC hypermethylation is associated with reexpression of silenced transcription factors (TFs) controlling myeloid differentiation. Accordingly, we hypothesize that epigenetic events are the major driver of BC transformation. In this application, we will refine our understanding of the epigenetic changes underpinning BC transformation, and devise pharmacologic and genetic approaches to reprogramme the BC transcriptome. We will also employ a novel computational network-based framework (Mogrify) to aid the identification of core pathways, genes, and TFs responsible for BC transformation, and target these for modulation by epigenetic modifier drugs and CRISPR/Cas9-based genetic manipulations. Our Specific Aims are: 1. To define the genetic and epigenetic events that characterize BC progression, 2. To determine the functional role of specific gene expression changes found in BC, and 3. To use pharmacologic and genetic approaches to reprogramme the BC transcriptome. The completion of our Aims will provide a comprehensive map of the BC genome and epigenome, identify the core regulatory elements underpinning the BC transcriptome, and evaluate novel therapies designed to reverse the BC phenotype. Our approach to reprogramme BC may also be applied to modulate the transcriptome of other epigenetically-driven human cancers.
kw: Leukaemia, therapy, genetics, epigenetics

title: Importance of TFEB acetylation in determination of cancer therapeutic efficacy of HDACIs via regulation of lysosomal function and autophagy
abs: Nuclear transcription factor EB (TFEB) has been well-established as a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis, function and autophagy. The transcriptional activity of TFEB is mainly controlled by its post-translational modification (PTM) via phosphorylation. Protein acetylation is one important form of PTM mediated by both histone acetyltransferases (HATs) and histone deacetylases (HDACs). Preliminary data from our laboratory suggest that TFEB acetylation is associated with its nuclear translocation and transcriptional activity in human cancer cells treated with histone deacetylases inhibitors (HDACIs). Therefore, we hypothesize that TFEB acetylation is an important form of PTM in determination of cancer therapeutic efficacy of HDACIs via regulation of lysosomal function and autophagy. This hypothesis will be tested via the following specific aims:(1)To measure TFEB acetylation in different cancer cells under treatment with various HDACIs (2)To study the molecular mechanisms controlling TFEB acetylation by identifying (i) the site(s) of acetylation, (ii) the HDACs involved; and (iii) the HATs involved(3)To explore the role of TFEB acetylation in control of its transcriptional activity by studying (i) its nuclear translocation, (ii) its DNA binding, and (iii) transcriptional activation of its target genes(4)To examine the importance of TFEB acetylation in regulation of lysosomal functions and autophagy in HDACIs-treated cancer cells (5)To test whether TFEB acetylation would affect the therapeutic efficacy of HDACIs both in cultured cancer cells in vitro and in a nude mice xenograft model in vivo.At present, HDACIs are important group of cancer therapeutic agents. Data from this proposed study will not only reveal novel insights into the molecular mechanisms controlling the function of TFEB, a master regulator of lysosomal function and autophagy, but also provide new opportunities for developing more effective therapeutic strategies by regulating TFEB acetylation and TFEB-mediated lysosomal and autophagy in cancers treated with HDACIs.
kw: HDACIs, lysosome, autophagy, acetylation, TFEB

title: Dissecting regulatory pathways in dilated cardiomyopathy and experimental targeting for heart failure
abs: Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM), defined by a weakened thinned left ventricle (LV), is a common form of heart failure (HF), contributes significantly to worldwide morbidity and mortality, and is a rapidly worsening healthcare burden as our world population ages. Apart from HF, DCM patients are also at high risk of arrhythmias, thromboembolism and sudden death. DCM may result from non-genetic factors (e.g. diet, smoking) which are themselves risk factors for ischaemic heart disease, but mutations in genes including titin, lamin A/C, cardiac actin and myosin heavy chain also predispose to DCM. Recently, our collaborators discovered that truncating mutations in the titin gene (TTN) account for ~25% of DCM patients [4]. Gene expression changes are a hallmark of HF. However, whether and how titin gene mutations affects gene regulatory pathways to produce HF remains uncertain. To address this, (Aim 1) we have established and will characterise novel DCM mouse models by modulating Ttn expression using the powerful adeno-associated virus (AAV) platform. This will be done in collaboration with the team who published on TTN truncation mutations in man [4,5]. (Aim 2) We propose to use these models to analyze for regulatory pathways mediating DCM, before and after the onset of echo-visible signs of disease. Transcriptomics will be analysed for candidate genes in DCM regulatory pathways. (Aim 3) We will validate candidate genes by applying AAV to modulate candidate gene expression and perform detailed cardiac analyses. Collectively, these studies will expand our knowledge of how deregulated pathways impact on DCM and whether experimental targeting of regulatory genes would improve clinical features of DCM. Our aims will: 1) Establish novel DCM disease models using the powerful AAV platform targeting cardiac expression for the first time in Singapore; 2) Identify and dissect regulatory pathways that mediate DCM; 3) Implicate candidates for future HF drug development.
kw: dilated cardiomyopathy, heart failure, gene regulatory networks

title: DR-region of Na+/K+ ATPase is a new target to treat stroke
abs: Stroke is a major cause of disability and death worldwide. Unfortunately, few effective drugs is available to treat this disease. Therefore the discovery of new treatment target and development of new drugs are urgently needed.Na+/K+ATPase (NKA) is responsible for maintaining the electrochemical gradient, and hence the cell membrane potential. Malfunction of this protein causes cell injury. However, its activity is suppressed in oxidative stress and excitotoxicity, two main mechanisms responsible for brain injury during ischemia/stroke. Therefore, stimulation of NKA may be a novel approach to protect neurons against ischemic injury. We developed an antibody against the DR region of NKA (DR-Ab). It was found that DR-Ab not only stimulated NKA activity, but also protected neurons against cell death in ischemia. In the transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (tMCAO) mice, both pre- and post-stroke treatment with DR-Ab significantly decreased the infarction volume. More importantly, systemic administration of DR-Ab successfully penetrated blood–brain barrier (BBB) and produced significant therapeutic effects. We therefore hypothesize that DR-region of NKA is a new target to treat ischemic brain diseases and activation of NKA with DR-Ab may be useful to treat stroke. This proposal is therefore designed to study the underlying mechanisms for the therapeutic effect of DR-Ab. The underlying mechanisms to be studied include anti-apoptosis, membrane NKA stabilization, and anti-excitotoxicity. Since platelet NKA activity correlates well with the severity and outcome of stroke, we also endeavor to develop a marker to reflect stroke severity and predict its outcome.
kw: Na+/K+ ATPase, antibody, stroke, therapy

title: Simultaneous activation of NFkB and degradation of p53 via Superoxide dependent modulation of B56gamma subunit of PP2A
abs: The tumor suppressor p53 and the cancer promoting NF-kB reciprocally regulate each other with opposing functional outcomes. Therefore, identifying cellular networks that simultaneously activate one and suppress the other has potential clinical relevance. The stability and biological activity of these transcriptional factors are a function of phosphorylation events at specific residues; phosphorylation of IKK?/? at serine 177/181 results in the phosphorylation/degradation of IkB?, thereby permitting NF-kB activation. Similarly, specific phosphorylation of threonine 55 of p53 signals for its proteasomal degradation. Notably, both these phosphorylation events are regulated by the same substrate-binding sub-unit (B56?) of the phosphatase, PP2A. We recently reported that the pro-survival activity of intracellular superoxide anion was linked to redox modification of the B56? sub-unit, which prevented its recruitment to the PP2A core sub-units (A-C). This resulted in the sustained serine 70 phosphorylation of Bcl-2, thereby stabilizing its anti-apoptotic activity. Interestingly, the specific tyrosine residue within B56? that is amenable to redox modification is highly conserved within the B56 family, including B56?. Intrigued by these observations and our preliminary data linking an increase in intracellular superoxide to simultaneous degradation of p53 and activation of NF-kB, we hypothesize that superoxide anion promotes carcinogenesis and its progression via inhibition of B56?-mediated simultaneous regulation of T55 phosphorylation of p53 and serine 177/181 of IKK?/?. Therefore, we propose to decipher the underlying mechanism of the redox modification using (a) established in vitro model systems, (b) an in vivo xenograft model and (c) tissue microarrays generated from patient derived biopsies. As the reciprocal regulation of these transcription factors is observed in human cancers, these investigations will not only enhance our understanding of how a pro-oxidant milieu promotes carcinogenesis and its progression, but also have potential implications for identifying specific signatures for stratifying cancers and novel targets for developing specific therapeutic strategies.
kw: Cancer cells, PP2A, Chemoresistance, pT55 p53, pS177/181 IKK, Metastasis

title: Real-time modeling of tumor progression, metastasis, and chemo/radiosusceptibility of oral squamous cell carcinomas (OSCCs)
abs: Precision medicine requires treatment individualization not only taking into account patient and tumor factors, but tumor evolution through time. The use of pre-established ex vivo surrogate models often lack the desired effect on management as they may not be available in real time nor represent the tumor being treated. Oral squamous cell cancer(OSCC) is endemic to the Asian context and often presents with locally advanced disease with lymph node metastasis. Despite treatment with curative intent, 60% will develop treatment failure presenting with locoregional recurrence or distant metastasis. We hypothesize that ‘real- and accelerated-time’ individualized ex vivo models of tumor metastasis and resistance, are likely to closely mirror the same processes in OSCC patients who develop distant and locoregional recurrence, respectively.Therefore, our aims are to:1.Derive 2D/3D cell line/microtumors and patient-derived xenografts from patients with OSCC and develop ‘accelerated-time’ models using established protocols to promote chemo-resistance and distant metastasis. 2.Characterize PDX and patient-derived primary 2D/3D cell line/microtumor models by: a.Molecular profiling to identify candidate driver mutations and molecular/cancer pathway signatures to generate hypotheses b.Functional screens of genes and pathways using 3D microtumor-based high-throughput screening (HTS) platform to validate the clinical genomics-driven hypotheses with knock-down(RNAi) and over-expression(ORF) libraries 3.Test for hypothesis-driven combinatorial therapeutic approaches that may provide the rationale for inclusion of novel therapeutic targets and re-positioning of existing drugs into the individual patients studied here and developing subsequent treatment protocols for recurrent OSCC. As the screens will all be done in ‘real time’ while the patient is in remission, if treatment failure were to occur, these data will also be used to determine a treatment plan in the individual patients under the IMPACT study. The experiments proposed will also be used to generate and validate “sequence-informed” algorithms for key mediators of drug-resistance and tumor metastasis.
kw: Precision medicine, targeted therapy, HNSCC, oral cancer, squamous cell, therapeutics

title: A new design of bileaflet valve reconstruction for right ventricular outflow tract to prevent pulmonary regurgitation during growth
abs: Specific aimsPaediatric patients who require ventricular outflow tract reconstruction usually need valve reconstruction to prevent valvular regurgitation. They would face problems like lack of suitable, affordable conduits and the need to undergo several operations in their lifetime due to the short lifespan of existing valves. Their natural growth and development are also of concern, even if they manage to receive suitable conduits. Current prosthesis including homografts, bioprosthetic valves, mechanical valves, and bovine jugular veins either do not have long-term durability or the ability to adapt to the growth of such patients. HypothesesWe have developed a new design of bileaflet valve based on the previous version of our bileaflet valves. This new technique accommodates patients’ annular size growth while maintaining valvular patency. We hypothesise that this new valve is durable and its improved valvular patency is achieved even when the dimension of the annulus is expanded to simulate a patient’s growth. MethodologyAn appropriate valve shape will be analysed with in-vitro experiments with finite element analysis, particle image velocimetry and cardiac simulator to visualise flow and current around the valve, and to perform haemodynamic assessment. The newly designed valve will be implanted, using conventional methods, into goat models assisted by cardiopulmonary bypass and kept for approximately 6 months to simulate patients’ growth. Valve function will be assessed with transoesophageal echocardiogram and necropsy will also be performed to assess the clinical events on the valve. Clinical SignificanceWith the proposed novel design of the bileaflet valve, it could prove to be more durable and effective in minimising requirements for valvular re-intervention, thus reducing the frequency of reoperations in the lifetime of paediatric patients.
kw: Bileaflet valve, right ventricular outflow tract , patch augmentation, growth

title: Carbohydrate (Chondroitin 6) Sulfotransferase-3 in Breast Cancer: Expression and Functional Studies and Evaluation of Potential Clinical Use in Patient Prognosis and Therapeutics
abs: Breast cancer is the commonest malignancy and top cause of cancer deaths in women globally. Locally, breast cancer incidence has tripled over the past four decades. Thus, there is an important need for better patient prognostication and therapeutic options. Carbohydrate (chondroitin 6) sulfotransferase-3 (CHST3) catalyses the addition of sulfate groups to chondroitin. Our preliminary study of breast cancer samples showed that reduced CHST3 expression was significantly associated with late stage tumours, leading to our hypothesis that CHST3 may suppress cancerous behaviour. Silencing CHST3 expression in poorly-invasive breast cancer cells resulted in doubling of their invasive capacity. The opposite was seen after overexpressing CHST3 in highly invasive MDA-MB-231 cells. Chondroitin monomers bearing 6-O-sulfate groups reduced cancer cell viability and invasion, and augmented the cytotoxicity of chemotherapeutic agents in cancer cells but not in non-tumourigenic breast epithelial cells. Hence, this project aims to determine if CHST3 can be used for patient prognostication, understand the mechanisms by which CHST3 regulates breast cancer behaviour, and explore if it can be exploited for therapeutic purposes. The expression pattern of CHST3 will be examined in breast cancer tissue samples, and analysed for associations with clinicopathological features. Survival analysis will evaluate if CHST3 can predict patient survival and cancer recurrence. Knockdown/knockout and overexpression of CHST3 will be carried out to determine its biological functions both in vitro and in vivo using a SCID mouse model. Candidate CHST3 signalling pathways will be identified through transcriptomic and proteomic studies using microarrays and mass spectrometry respectively, and selected pathways experimentally verified. Chondroitin oligosaccharides with specific sulfation patterns will be designed and tested for optimal augmentation of chemotherapeutic drug cytotoxicity in cancer cells with minimal side effects. Together, the study will lead to a better understanding of CHST3 in breast cancer, with potential improvements in patient prognostication and therapeutic options.
kw: Breast cancer, chondroitin sulfate, carbohydrate (chondroitin 6) sulfotransferase-3, biomarker, prognostic indicator, therapeutic target

title: Synergy between Thymosin ?4 and cardiomyocytes for cardiac protection, regeneration, and metabolism
abs: Ischemia results in the death of cardiomyocytes (CMs) and severely reduced energetic capacity in the infarct myocardium. Though endogenous cardiac progenitor cells hold promise for cardiac repair, their ability to proliferate, differentiate and regenerate damaged heart structure and restore heart function is far from enough. The discovery of human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs), one of the most significant achievements in modern science, has shed further insights into the regenerative capacity of stem cells and allow for using patients’ own cells for CM (hiPSC-CMs) regeneration. Poor engraftment and diminished survival of stem cells or their CM derivatives is a barrier harnessing the full benefits of cardiac regenerative medicine. In this study, the PI proposes to use hiPSC-CMs in combination with sustained-release of thymosin ?4 (T?4) from gelatin microspheres for cardiac repair and regeneration. The main hypothesis is that synergy between T?4 and hiPSC-CMs transplantation is a safe therapeutic approach which will enhance hiPSC-CMs engraftment, inhibit myocardial apoptosis, promote cardiogenesis, and improve metabolism after myocardial infarction (MI) in an established clinically relevant large animal model. An in-depth cellular and molecular analysis will be carried out to determine the efficacy, mechanism and safety of this treatment strategy in vitro and in vivo. This proposal has major implication for developing a clinically relevant and promising new therapeutic strategy for reversing deleterious cardiac remodeling following MI. One remarkable feature of the strategy is that gelatin has been used widely as a food ingredient while T?4 is a naturally occurring peptide in the body. Combined with autologous hiPSC-CMs, a safe and effective patient specific cardiac cell therapy will be developed.
kw: Stem Cell, Cardiac Repair, Regeneration

title: Understanding pathogenic and protective cellular mechanisms of Alzheimer’s dementia by studying its most common genetic form
abs: Alzheimer’s Dementia (AD) prevalence in Singapore is doubling every decade, presenting an increasing health, social and economic burden. Down Syndrome (DS) (trisomy-21) represents the most common genetically-defined form of AD. All people with DS develop hallmarks of AD (amyloid plaques) by age 35, but <70% develop clinical dementia in their fifties. The cause is triplication of chromosome21-gene for amyloid-precursor-protein (APP). Non-DS people with triplication of APP-gene (but not the rest of chromosome21) develop 100% penetrant early dementia in their 40s-50s. Comparing the DS +/- early AD could therefore lead to (i) understanding AD-modulatory/triggering/protective mechanisms, and (ii) detection of early biomarkers predictive of overt clinical dementia, applicable to general population AD.Hypotheses:i) mechanisms modulating rate of onset of clinical dementia are caused by an overdose of (unknown) genes on human chromosome 21, other than APP. ii) as fibrillar insoluble amyloid deposition does not correlate with dementia, we hypothesize that generation and/or clearance of soluble toxic A?-oligomeric and non-canonical forms could be AD-severity modulatory/triggering mechanism. iii) as DS immune system malfunctions, we hypothesize the ability to launch an inflammatory response by macrophages/microglia against own amyloid aggregates and/or damaged neurons could be an additional AD-severity triggering/modulatory mechanism.Approach/team:Starting with brain cells derived from P.I.’s internationally-leading collection of human-induced-pluripotent-stem-cells (hiPSC) from clinically contrasting DS (+/- early AD), isogenic DS, and non-DS DupAPP, we propose to use new Singapore-lead technological breakthroughs forming a unique set of cellular tools, to investigate the determinants of AD pathogenesis: (i) Co-I C.Cheung with new assay for the clearance of pathological A? peptide in brain blood vessels (ii) Co-I F.Ginhoux, with novel proprietary protocols for derivation of microglia from iPSCs, (iii) Co-I Chang Young-Tae with original A?-oligomer specific fluorescent probes, (iv) collaborators E.Koo and Hong Wanjin with expertise and reagents for quantitation of APP-processing, and synaptic protein trafficking.
kw: Down Syndrome, aneuploidy, chromosome 21, trisomy 21, Alzheimer's disease

title: Identifying genetic dependencies and therapeutic vulnerabilities of metastasis in patient-derived colorectal cancer models
abs: Metastasis is the major cause of death for patients with colorectal cancer (CRC). Chemotherapy administered after surgery (adjuvant chemotherapy) prevents metastasis from developing in some patients, increasing cure rates in CRC. However, besides 5-Fluorouracil and Oxaliplatin, there has been no progress in finding new drug targets or treatments that prevent clinical metastasis. There is an urgent need to develop better pre-clinical models to understand the genetic dependencies and therapeutic vulnerabilities of metastasis. We have established several in vitro patient-derived micro-tumor (PDmT)/organoid and in vivo mouse “avatar or patient-derived xenograft (PDX)” models of CRC. We hypothesize that experimental recapitulation of the metastatic dissemination of distant organs with patient-derived tumor models will enable us to identify genetic dependencies and therapeutic vulnerabilities of metastasis in CRC. We will functionally characterize metastatic phenotypes across 20 patient-derived CRC models by measuring invasion, migration and epithelial mesenchymal transition in our PDmTs and observing metastasis in our PDXs following orthotopic implantation, surgical resection and adjuvant therapy. We will correlate these metastatic phenotypes with molecular profiles of these tumors and the patient’s clinical outcomes. Next, we will perform in vitro and in vivo genome-wide shRNA/siRNA screens in highly-metastatic PDmTs and PDXs to identify genetic dependencies of metastasis. We will also perform high throughput chemical/compound screens to identify therapeutic opportunities to abrogate metastasis in our PDmTs and PDXs. We will intersect information from the metastatic potential of our patient-derived models, their molecular profiles, genome-wide shRNA screens and compound screens from PDmTs and PDXs from several patients. These complimentary analyses will enable us to prioritize follow-on validation and mechanistic studies to unravel patient-specific or generalized genetic dependencies and therapeutic vulnerabilities of metastasis as well as to evaluate candidate predictive biomarkers leading to rationale design of anti-metastatic therapy in CRC.
kw: Colorectal Cancer, Metastasis, Adjuvant Therapy, Patient derived Xenografts

title: The Clinical And Economic Effectiveness Of Extending Diabetic Eye Screening In Singapore.
abs: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is the most common microvascular complication of diabetes and in Singapore, 30% of those with diabetes have DR and 10% have vision-threatening DR. The burden of DR is staggeringly high. The Singapore Ministry of Health guidelines recommend that people with diabetes are screened annually for diabetic eye diseases, or referred for tertiary care for those with evidence of the disease. In 2010, the Singapore integrated Diabetic Retinopathy Programme (SiDRP) was implemented as an innovative telemedicine model to optimize screening for DR at the primary care level (i.e. polyclinics). When we retrospectively examined the data from SiDRP, we found that 96.6% and 98.7% of patients still had non-referable DR and DME (diabetic macular edema) at 24 and 36 months, respectively. We also found that of those who progressed to referable status, 65.4% and 66.6% had non-referable mild DR at visits 3 and 4, respectively. We found relatively smaller rates of progression in those with no DR (~33%). Overall these data suggest that almost all patients with diabetes have non-referable DR or DME after 2 or 3 years of follow-up; and progression rates to referable status appear to be smaller in those with no non-referable DR compared to mild non-referable level. We therefore propose a novel and important prospective study to solve this problem. Our objective is to risk stratify patients attending the SiDRP (N=9,000) from annual to a two-yearly and three-yearly rescreen by developing and validating a DR/DME grading- and risk factor-specific algorithm; and estimate the associated potential economic benefits of biennial and triennial screening models. This proposal will improve the efficiency of our primary care system, provide better outcomes for people with diabetes, and demonstrate cost savings to patients and society. We aim to translate our findings into policy, once confirmed.
kw: Eye

title: Epigenomic manipulation to facilitate a ROS-based strategy for Precision Medicine in Glioblastoma
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Glioblastoma is among cancers with the worst prognosis, despite surgery with chemo/radio-therapy. Clearly, better treatment strategies are needed to eradicate the infiltrative and recurrent nature of the disease. Our lab previously demonstrated that glioma cell chemoresistance is governed by a balance between two reactive oxygen species (ROS), superoxide, O2- and hydrogen peroxide, H2O2. An elevated O2-:H2O2 ratio (ROS Index) confers enhanced resistance to common chemotherapeutic drugs. By inference, pharmacologic reduction of this Index can present a novel therapeutic strategy. We developed a ROS gene signature that quantified this ratio, and stratified patient survival, independent of current clinical indicators. Using Gene Ontology, we identified SLC1A2 as a plausible determinant of ROS-mediated chemoresistance. We showed that SLC1A2 has tumor-suppressive properties. As SLC1A2 displays no changes in copy number or presence of somatic aberrations, we explored epigenetic regulation. Using patient tumor molecular information with global H3K27me3 methylation profile of glioma cells, we identified EZH2 as a possible regulator. We found that EZH2 binds to and represses SLC1A2 expression, thereby elevating the ROS Index and promoting tumor cell survival. We hypothesize that patient stratification can identify individuals most likely to receive treatment benefit from EZH2 inhibition.In this study, we will decipher the mechanism of EZH2 regulation of SLC1A2. We will use EZH2 loss- and gain-of-function mutants, as well as pharmacologic agents to determine its domain mediating SLC1A2 binding. We will measure effects on ROS Index, cell viability and self-renewal, invasion and glutamate metabolism. We will further establish proof-of-concept that ROS gene signature-stratified patient cells display differential responses to EZH2 pharmacologic inhibitors. Finally, we will create orthotopic patient-derived xenografts in mice to test if EZH2 inhibition enhances tumor cell sensitivity to temozolomide with radiation treatment.Our work is important as we demonstrate epigenomic manipulation to facilitate a ROS-based strategy for precision medicine in glioblastoma.
kw: glioblastoma, precision medicine, neuro-oncology, epigenome, EZH2, SLC1A2

title: Characterizing the Role of Iris Surface Features in Iris Sponginess and their relevance to Angle-Closure Glaucoma
abs: Primary angle-closure glaucoma (PACG) is common and visually destructive, particularly in Asia. About 10% of adults have narrow angles, the anatomical trait predisposing to PACG. Laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI) has been commonly used as a prophylactic procedure for people with narrow-angles to prevent acute primary angle closure (APAC). However, evidence is lacking as to its efficacy in preventing the progression to PACG, as only 1 in 10 narrow-angle persons would develop PACG if untreated. Established anatomic parameters do not sufficiently explain why many people with small eyes never develop glaucoma. LPI, while relatively safe, has potential adverse consequences. Therefore, there is a need for clinicians to accurately identify those who are at greatest risk for progression to glaucoma and/or development of an APAC attack, and thus really need LPI.Our objective is to develop a novel approach using easily observable iris surface features (crypts, furrows and color) to effectively identify the “at risk” patients. Altered dynamic iris response has been proposed as a contributing factor for PACG. Patients whose irises retain aqueous humor on dilation are the most likely to develop APAC attack, because the iris remains thick and blocks the angle. We hypothesized that eyes with less iris crypts and more furrows have poorer iris “sponginess”, i.e., poorer aqueous humor conductivity between iris stroma and anterior chamber. We propose a comprehensive study, integrating clinical and imaging investigations to characterize iris surface features and elucidate their associations with 1) dynamic iris response, 2) the progression of angle closure, and 3) the risk of APAC in narrow-angle eyes. We will develop an automated program to quantify the iris surface features and ascertain these associations. The findings of this study may provide a useful clinical LPI treatment guideline for angle-closure disease not only in Singapore but have a major clinical impact worldwide.
kw: Primary angle closure glaucoma, Iris, Laser peripheral iridotomy, Risk prediction, Optical coherence tomography, Automated iris detection

title: New ophthalmic antifungal, DE-109
abs: Infections of the cornea, infectious keratitis, are common in Asia and a leading cause of blindness according to the World Health Organization which has stated that 4-5 million people in Asia are affected by “corneal blindness”. Moreover, Asia differs from the West in that about 40% of eye infections are due to fungus while bacteria infections are more common in the West. However, there is only one approved antifungal medication for ophthalmology, natamycin which has received a great deal of concern due inconsistent action against Candida, Aspergillus and Fusarium. Sirolimus, originally found to be very active against fungus was until recently pursued for its use in inflammation and graft rejection will be tested against clinical strains from Asia and also in a rabbit model of corneal fungal infection. It is hypothesized that a 40?l depot of sirolimus in a sub-conjunctival pocket will act as a slow release anti-fungal to effectively eradicate corneal fungal infections. Corneal PK/PD studies will be carried out for dosing details, basic microbiology of Asian strains, and the in vivo activity will be tested in a rabbit model of fungal keratitis using ATCC strains of fungus and yeast. Finally, MICs will be established for a panel of clinical strains of these organisms from various sites in Asia. An excellent working relationship between SERI, and Santen Pharmaceuticals from Japan will take advantage of the complimentary expertise to develop a data package for IND filing of sirolimus for clinical use. Importantly, Santen has obtained approval from the European Medicine Agency for use of sirolimus as an ocular anti-inflammatory and shown that it has a favorable toxicity profile. Thus, the experiments to be undertaken here have an excellent outlook for success and as the toxicology profile has been established, the track to an IND should be very positive.

title: DNA topological and epigenetic regulation in neurodevelopment and disease
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: The rapidly expanding repertoire of chromatin related mutations implicated in neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders underscores a need to evaluate the role of epigenetic processes in the maintenance or deregulation of mental health. DNA topology represents an unexplored facet of epigenetic regulation, largely due to the lack of appropriate experimental tools. Yet, accruing evidence points to a pervasive role of DNA topology in neuronal gene regulation, where mutations in DNA topoisomerases have specifically been identified in patients with autism spectrum disorders (ASD). The overarching goal of this proposal is to investigate how DNA topology impacts gene regulation through epigenetic mechanisms, framed within the context of neurological disorders. First, I will employ innovative high-throughput genomic methodologies to probe for the dynamic changes in DNA topology (supercoiling and non-B DNA) during neural differentiation (AIM 1.1). This represents the first effort to integrate DNA torsion states with chromatin features, in a genome-wide fashion. Second, I propose to investigate a role of DNA topology in the patterning and inheritance of gene expression programs, the findings of which may lead to better strategies for cell fate manipulation and cancer therapy (AIM 1.2). Third, I will explore a paradoxical role of non-B DNA structures in driving genomic instability causal for many neurodegenerative disorders, and to develop human embryonic stem cell (hESC) - based screens to identify potential therapeutic agents (AIM 2). These efforts will help set the stage for determining how impaired epigenetic mechanisms may lead to neurological disorders. Leveraging on the host of chromatin mutations identified in ASD, I will use hESCs as an investigative platform to dissect the causality of sequence variants in mental health disorders (AIM 3). I anticipate that this ‘chromatin-centric’ perspective will provide novel molecular insights into neurological disease etiologies, inspiring the use of epigenetic-based therapies for these devastating disorders.
kw: Epigenetics;chromatin regulation;cancer;disease modeling;neuroscience;DNA topology

title: Role of Hippo Signalling in the epicardium: Expanding the outer limit of heart repair
abs: Congenital and adult heart diseases are the leading causes of mortality worldwide. According to World Health Organization (WHO), by 2030, more than 23 million people will die annually from cardiovascular disorders. In recent years, there has been a significant increase in the number of people suffering from heart diseases and every third death in Singapore is due to cardiovascular disorders. Heart failure is strongly associated with aging and represents the most common cause of hospitalization for patients older than 65 years. Cardiac fibrosis after myocardial infarction has been identified as one of the key factor in the development of heart failure. Singapore is now facing an unprecedented age shift. As the number of people over age 65 in Singapore is expected to triple over the next 10 years, the burden of cardiovascular diseases in the elderly will markedly increase. Therefore, it is urgent to develop new strategies to treat cardiovascular diseases. The broad objective of the proposed research is to identify novel regulators of cardiac fibrosis after myocardial infarction. Our goal is to identify direct drug targets or reveal druggable signaling pathways to modulate cardiac repair/regenerative response after myocardial infarction. In this application, we have proposed to determine role of Hippo signaling pathway in the epicardium during cardiac development and disease. We would like to explore the therapeutic potential of Hippo signaling targeting for better cardiac repair/regenerative response. We are taking multidisciplinary approach to investigate role of hippo signaling in cardiac fibrosis and also to identify small molecules that can block Hippo signaling after heart failure to reduce fibrosis and increase cardiac regeneration. Our preliminary results demonstrate that in the adult heart Hippo signaling is activated in the epicardium-derived fibroblasts after myocardial infarction and modulates inflammatory and fibrotic response, indicating that Hippo signaling inhibition could be therapeutic.

title: Profiling and Monitoring of Risk Factors For the Development of Post-Transplant Lymphoproliferative Disorder in Pediatric Renal Transplant Recipients
abs: Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD) is a well-known complication post-transplant and contributes significantly to the morbidity and mortality seen in transplant recipients. A key risk factor in the pathogenesis of PTLD is chronic Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infections. Chronic EBV infection may potentially lead to uncontrolled B cell proliferation in patients with decreased EBV-specific T-cell function. The predisposition towards EBV infection/reactivation maybe consequent to over-immunosuppression in transplant recipients. Not all transplant recipients with chronic EBV infection, however, develop PTLD nor all PTLDs are associated with EBV infection, thus suggesting an underlying genetic predisposition towards PTLD development, in addition to known viral pathogenic and host immunological factors. Additionally, the incidence of PTLD in our pediatric renal transplant population is higher as compared to the West. We therefore hypothesize that there may exist a unique immunologic or genetic signature in our Asian pediatric renal transplant population, predisposing to PTLD development. Hence, the primary aim of this study is to comprehensively identify and evaluate risk factors for the development of PTLD via: 1) Immunological subset (T-, B- and natural killer (NK) cells) and cytokine profiling; 2) Performance of functional cytotoxic cell assays on CD4+ and CD8+ T-cells and NK cells; 3) Profiling of EBV-specific antibodies (anti-EBV VCA-IgA, IgG, IgM, anti-EBV early antigen IgG, and anti-EBNA1); 4) Elucidation of molecular gene alterations, including polymorphisms, microsatellite instability, and aberrant somatic hypermutation using next-generation sequencing. The secondary aim of this study is to evaluate the diagnostic utility of immunoglobulin/T-cell receptor gene rearrangements, as a tool for the early detection and monitoring of PTLD in our Asian pediatric renal transplant recipients. The study results will assist in identifying individuals at risk of EBV infection and PTLD development and also possibly provide a guide towards individualized immunosuppressant dosage use in a bid to prevent the development of this dreaded disease.

title: Particle characterization and cytokine expression in failed joint replacements – early and individualized detection of molecular biomarkers to predict adverse tissue responses and early prosthesis loosening
abs: With aging populations across nations, increasing life expectancy and younger patients asking for joint replacements, the demand for these surgeries has increased substantially over the last decade. The ideal joint replacement should last for the lifetime of the patient. The average prosthesis currently lasts 15-20 years. In the quest to increase implant longevity, 2 issues need to be considered: improvement of biomaterials, and biology (periprosthetic tissue responses to wear debris and interindividual variations in threshold to response). The end point of these biological pathways is prosthesis loosening (early osteolysis). When patients do develop adverse tissue responses to wear particles from joint replacements, there is a need for early detection so as to decide if they require an early revision surgery, which is much easier to perform than a late revision with huge amounts of bone loss. The aims of this research proposal are to (i) understand the manner in which periprosthetic tissues react to wear debris of different materials and sizes(ii) identify at risk patients for adverse tissue reactions to implants (iii) develop molecular biomarkers for predictive and diagnostic test kits which would allow early detection of adverse tissue responses and early intervention, resulting in huge cost savings to both patient and the health system. A sensitive and specific biomarker can potentially function analgous to a tumour marker.These aims are in line with the HypOrth project, a 7.1 million Euro multi-centre study headed by Professor Christoph Lohmann and his laboratory in Magdeburg, Germany (collaborator). A collaboration with Professor Christoph Lohmann will enable the P.I. to study how research of this nature is designed and conducted and thereafter establish a fruitful collaboration between Singapore and Germany/Europe along the similar theme, addressing also the differences in disease patterns as well as anatomical make up of Asian and European populations.

title: The interplay of platelets and Toll-like receptors in neutrophil extracellular trap formation and its role in premature cardiovascular disease in systemic lupus erythematosus
abs: Cognitive dysfunction is a prevalent manifestation of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and negatively impacts on mortality, health-related quality of life and employment rates. Anti-N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor subunit NR2A/B antibodies appear to be a convincing candidate to mediate cognitive dysfunction in SLE patients. However, earlier results of serum anti-NR2A/B antibodies have been controversial.We hypothesize that this disease model requires two hits: (i) presence of anti-NR2A/B antibodies and (ii) a breach in blood-brain barrier (BBB) integrity mediated by abnormal endothelial cell-immune cell interactions. In this proposal, we aim to elucidate the mechanisms of anti-NR2A/B antibodies mediating cognitive dysfunction in SLE through basic science, neuroimaging and clinical approaches. We will examine the effects of anti-NR2A/B antibodies on NMDA receptors in hippocampal neurons, spiral ganglion neurons in the cochlear and mitral cells in the olfactory bulb. The role of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) expressing matrix metalloproteinase-9 (MMP-9) in mediating spontaneous endothelial dysfunction will be studied. Serum MMP-9 and dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging will assess the integrity of the BBB. Finally, we will correlate serum anti-NR2A/B antibodies and MMP-9 with cognitive dysfunction, sensorinueral hearing loss (SNHL) and olfactory dysfunction to demonstrate that (i) hippocampal neurons (shielded by the BBB) and spiral ganglion neurons (shielded by the blood-labyrinthine barrier) are dependent on a barrier breach to mediate cognitive dysfunction and SNHL, respectively, whereas (ii) mitral cells (not shielded by any barrier) are readily accessible by anti-NR2A/B antibodies to mediate olfactory dysfunction and serve as an internal control.To date, there is no method that can reliably and conveniently diagnose and monitor cognitive dysfunction in SLE. This proposal, if successful, will promote the use of a multimarker panel including anti-NR2A/B antibodies, NETs and MMP-9 to diagnose cognitive dysfunction and the potential association of cognitive dysfunction and SNHL might open a new diagnostic and monitoring paradigm.

title: 3D Printed Scaffold Device for Ridge Preservation after Tooth Extraction - A Randomised Controlled Clinical Trial
abs: Following tooth extraction, the socket heals naturally with bone in 1 to 2 months. This healing process occurs with substantial reduction of the original height and width of the alveolar ridge. In a significantly resorbed ridge, bone augmentation procedures are necessary before dental implant placement. Autogenous bone is the gold standard for this purpose but the harvesting procedure results in additional morbidities and expenses. Ridge preservation techniques have been introduced, using xenografts, allografts or synthetic materials to fill the tooth socket immediately after extraction. While the current materials used have improved ridge dimensions to various extents, their osteoconductivity is suboptimal and unpredictable. They do not reduce vertical resorption of the bony walls and often interfered with the normal healing process. Polycaprolactone – tricalcium phosphate (PCL-TCP) is a bioactive, bioresorbable composite polymer that is non-toxic and tissue-compatible. This study aims to test the use of a novel 3D printed PCL-TCP device for ridge preservation, leveraging on its 3D shape that fits snugly in the tooth socket, high porosity and bioactivity to promote osteogenesis and reduce resorption. The hypothesis is that the insertion of a PCL-TCP scaffold in extraction sockets allows normal bone healing and better maintenance of ridge dimensions after 6 months compared to extraction sockets without a space filler. This will be a prospective, randomised controlled clinical trial in patients who require single tooth extraction and replacement with a dental implant. The study will compare the ridge dimensions and the quality and quantity of bone formed in tooth sockets, using histology and microcomputed tomography, in both groups after 6 months. The PCL-TCP scaffold to be used in this study will be fabricated by a local company, Osteopore International Pte Ltd. The market potential for this device is tremendous due to a growing demand for tooth replacement from an ageing population worldwide.
kw: 3D printing, bioresorbable, scaffold, polycaprolactone-tricalcium phosphate, ridge preservation, bone bioengineering

title: Application of an expanded whole blood bactericidal activity platform to evaluate pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamics relationships of novel anti-tuberculosis drugs and combination regimens
abs: Tuberculosis remains a major health problem in Singapore, Asia and globally. There is an urgent need to improve anti-tuberculosis therapy.We aim to determine whether co-trimoxazole and rosuvastatin possess anti-tuberculosis activity alone and in combination with rifampicin. We also aim to determine the incremental anti-tuberculosis activity of combination regimens using higher doses of rifampicin.The whole blood bactericidal activity (WBA) platform is a method to determine the summated activity of anti-tuberculosis drugs. It may offer greater precision, is simpler to conduct than standard methods for early evaluation of TB drugs, and allow us to study the synergistic effects of the immune system and immunomodulatory drugs. The WBA platform has been used to test anti-tuberculosis regimens, but we have modified it to allow the detection of effects of drugs against different strains and provide better indications of sterilising activity.We plan to conduct four clinical trials. In the first trial, we will study the pharmacokinetics and WBA of co-trimoxazole alone and in combination with rifampicin. In the second trial, we will study rosuvastatin in the same way. A third trial will study combinations of linezolid with high dose rifampicin. These trials will be conducted in Asian healthy volunteers. A fourth trial will confirm these results in tuberculosis patients.The results may have a major impact on the treatment of both drug-resistant and drug-sensitive tuberculosis and potentially benefit the millions of patients who are prescribed these therapies and combinations.The research capitalizes on some unique advantages in Singapore: a multi-ethnic Asian population representing almost half of the global population, a position in a region with over half the global TB burden, and a dynamic TB research programme that offers state-of-the-art clinical trials and laboratory infrastructure.
kw: Tuberculosis, Clinical pharmacology, Pharmacokinetics/Pharmacodynamics, Statin, Whole blood bactericidal activity

title: An Open Label, Non-Randomized Phase I Dose Escalation Study to Characterize Safety, Tolerability, Pharmacokinetics and Maximum Tolerated Dose of BAY1163877 in Subjects with Refractory, Locally Advanced or Metastatic Solid Tumors
abs: The FGF/FGFR signaling pathways play fundamental roles in several cellular pathways, e.g. proliferation, differentiation, adhesion, migration, survival and transformation. Dysregulation of FGFR expression and its activity is considered oncogenic. This affects all four FGFR subtypes and has been associated with various human cancers, including sarcoma, multiple myeloma, breast, bladder, prostate, gastric or endometrium cancer. Besides activating mutations, gene amplifications, chromosomal translocations and fusion genes as well as alterations in the autocrine and paracrine signalling have been described for various human malignancies including bladder and lung cancer.BAY 1163877 is a novel small molecule kinase inhibitor which selectively inhibits FGFR1, 2 and 3 and showed efficacy in monotherapy in various preclinical cancer models. Additive to synergistic effects with broad range kinase inhibitors, targeted agents or conventional chemotherapeutics were also demonstrated in lung and bladder cancer animal models. BAY 1163877 showed superior activity in models with overexpression of FGFR1, 2 or 3 mRNA or in models with pathway activation due to mutations in FGFR3. These results indicate that the clinical development of BAY 1163877 could result in an improved and more effective alternative compared to current treatment and patient stratification options.To date, BAY 1163877’s safety and maximum tolerated dose has been clinically evaluated at other sites. This proposal aims to conduct the next phase of this global first-in-man clinical trial with the aims of studying (1) pharmacokinetics and (2) biomarker status, pharmacodynamic (PD) parameters, and tumor response of BAY 1163877. Results of this study will determine decision on whether to advance to Phase 2 studies and its recommended dose.

title: Sphingolipids as serial biomarkers of disease progression in acute myocardial infarction
abs: Background: Acute myocardial infarction (AMI), the unstable and often unexpected expression of coronary heart disease, is a major global cause of death. Biomarkers of disease progression may presage a second AMI and prompt pre-emptive coronary angiography and treatment escalation. Sphingolipids are a class of lipids containing a backbone of sphingoid bases, which are set of aliphatic amino alcohols that includes sphingosine. Ceramides, key intermediates in the synthesis of sphingolipids, are implicated in the progression of atherosclerosis. Conversely, sphingosine-1-phosphate, a phosphorylated form of sphingosine, may be cardioprotective. Preliminary data: We have found sphingolipids measured in human aortic biopsies to strongly discriminate patients with recent AMI from patients with stable coronary heart disease; the most strongly discriminatory sphingolipids were the ceramides, lactosyl-ceramides and shingomyelin. In an independent cohort of 1124 patients with AMI, plasma ceramides, dihyrosphingomyelin and lactosylceramides were predictive of 12-month cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction and stroke. Conversely, higher S1P levels were associated with better survival. Aims: We aim to: first, determine the reference change values (RCV) of sphingolipids in healthy individuals at multiple time points, so as to identify biomarkers suitable for serial testing; second, measure sphingolipids longitudinally in patients with recent AMI to assess whether changes in sphingolipids exceeding the RCVs are predictive of recurrent AMI and third, measure these sphingolipids in asymptomatic ‘at-risk’ individuals undergoing screening with quantitative coronary calcium scoring. Methods: We will measure sphingolipids quantitatively using targeted multiple reaction monitoring of ceramide species and ‘deep profiling’ of S1P with an enhanced phospho-monoester capture and derivatization workflow. Hypothesis: We hypothesize that changes in ceramide and S1P levels over time presage recurrent AMI and sphingolipid levels quantitatively reflect underlying atherosclerotic disease risk in asymptomatic individuals. Approach: Our downstream approach seeks to optimise sphingolipids as biomarkers of disease progression in AMI and potentially presymptomatic biomarkers of coronary heart disease.
kw: Sphingolipids, biomarkers, acute myocardial infarction, biological variability

title: Analysis of oxidative stress in cultured and diseased human corneal endothelial cells
abs: Corneal transplantation is the commonest allogeneic transplanted tissue. With an ageing population, the number of corneal transplant proceduresis increasing. The leading indication for corneal transplantation is corneal endothelial disease. The only treatment is tissue replacement i.e. corneal transplant. Any transplantation procedure is reliant on a supply of donor tissue (for which there is a worldwide shortage). The project aims to investigate the mechanisms involved in corneal endothelial cell survival in an oxidative stressful environment. We aim to(i) Elucidate the effect of oxidative stress on the proliferative capacity of cultured CEC and investigate the role of oxidative stress in maintaining the quiescent state of CEC (ii) Elucidate the role and expression levels of the antioxidant proteins perioxiredoxins (PRDXs) in the corneal endothelium (iii) Investigate the role of oxidative stress in the pathogenesis of corneal diseases such as Fuchs’ corneal endothelial dystrophy (FECD)We hypothesize that a targeted medical therapy to improve endothelial cell survival will focus on the prevention of oxidative stress that is a known key mediator of endothelial cell loss. We will use several methods to assess oxidative stress including probes in combination with fluorescence microscopy and fluorescence activated cell sorting. Oxidative stress will be measured in both cultured and primary CEC and verified by Western Blot and quantitative real-time PCR. To manipulate the expression of PRDX we will use siRNA reagents and examine the role antioxidants play in regulating cell division and cell growth. To model the role of oxidative stress in Fuch’s (FECD) we will use a mouse model of FECD. Using CEC isolated from these mice we will assess the expression of PRDX proteins by qPCR and western blot and compare to wild type CEC before and after treatment with H2O2. Any candidate PRDX proteins will be cloned and rescue experiments attempted.

title: Feeding-related Bowel Ischemia in Necrotizing Enterocolitis
abs: Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is a major cause of mortality in premature infants. However, the pathophysiology of NEC remains elusive. Our previous study has revealed that ischemia is the key pathogenesis factor of NEC. Prematurity and feeding are two major risk factors of NEC. It has been found that both intestinal oxygen consumption and blood flow increase after feeding. However, the postprandial mesentery blood supply is inadequate in premature infants. Hence we hypothesize that feeding increases oxygen consumption in the intestine, which is barely met by the limited intestinal blood supply in premature infants. Aggressive feeding and additional hypoxia stress will tilt the balance of oxygen consumption and supply and result in ischemia and NEC. Aims: •To evaluate the role of feeding in triggering intestinal ischemia and subsequent NEC in a newborn mouse model. •To evaluate the role of a modified feeding regime (avoiding feeding during hypoxia events) in the prevention of NEC.•To investigate the effect of mesenteric vasodilators in prevention of intestinal ischemia and NEC. Methodology: •NEC will be induced in established mouse/rat model by the combination of formula gavage with hypoxia/cold stress. The intestinal oxygen consumption, ischemia marker expression and histological severity of NEC will be compared between the pups with formula feeding and those fed with saline to determine role of feeding in bowel ischemia and NEC. •Two feeding regimes (bolus feeding concurrent and non-concurrent during hypoxia exposure) will be compared in the NEC mouse model for the capability of inducing bowel ischemic and NEC.•In the above NEC mouse model, various mesenteric vasodilators (L-arginine, sodium nitrate, Endothelin-1 inhibitors) will be added into the feeds and compared with controls for their protective effect on intestinal ischemia and NEC.

title: Synergising targeted therapy by combination use – addition of novel PI3K inhibitor pictilisib to CDK4/6 inhibitor palbociclib in treatment of solid tumours
abs: Increasing knowledge of molecular pathways in carcinogenesis has ushered in an era of targeted therapy as an alternate option to conventional cytotoxic chemotherapy, offering a more precise method of cell killing with better tolerability for patients. However, a major limitation of targeted therapy has been the development of tumor resistance due to activation of alternative pathways to bypass inhibition from treatment. As such, combination of various drug targets has been pursued to explore possible synergism and also to overcome such resistance. The phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)-AKT signaling pathway regulates cell metabolism, growth, and survival, and its hyperactivation has been shown to drive tumour progression. Additionally, aberrant control of the cell cycle is a key hallmark of cancer, and disruption of restriction points through loss of RB1 function making them refractory to the effects of CDK4/6 inhibition. Both the PI3K and CDK4/6 pathways are well recognized in carcinogenesis, and targeting either pathway have been shown to be effective in inhibiting tumor growth. In vivo studies of combination of PI3K inhibitor pictilisib and CDK4/6 inhibitor palbociclib has shown promising results with improved apoptosis in clonogenic assays.The Royal Marsden Hospital Drug Development Unit (RMH/DDU) is a well-established unit with a focus on early phase I clinical drug development studies. In view of promising results from in vivo studies with combination treatment of pictilisib and palbociclib, a phase I study has been developed to further test the hypothesis in patients with refractory solid tumors. The aim of the research fellowship is 2 fold – the scientific objective being to study the combination of pictilisib and palbociclib in refractory solid tumors; and the manpower development objective to develop skills in phase I trial design and conduct in a high volume phase I drug development centre, and forge relationships for future collaborations between RMH and Singapore.
