title: Mast cell-driven T cell responses during acute viral infection
abs: Mast cells (MCs) are granulated cells that are crucial for pathogen immunosurveillance at the host-environment interface. In the skin, they are abundant throughout the dermis and, as such, are some of the first immune players to encounter pathogens, including during cutaneous viral infection. Although MC responses to pathogens are highly varied, recent evidence has shown that MCs promote clearance of the arboviral pathogen, dengue virus (DENV), which is injected into the skin by mosquitos during natural-route infection. During DENV-induced activation, MCs degranulate nearly instantaneously, releasing a broad panel of pre-synthesized pro-inflammatory and vasoactive mediators from intracellular stores. MCs also bridge innate and adaptive responses. For example, MCs are required for draining lymph node swelling, a process that promotes efficient T cell immunity. MC-dependent endothelial activation during DENV infection is also protective by promoting recruitment of cytotoxic cells. Aside from the of the preliminary observations that DENV activation of MCs promotes T cell recruitment, little is known about the role of MCs in promoting functional T cell responses. Here, we propose to define the contributions of MCs to functional T cell responses during acute viral infection of the skin, in terms of cellular activation and recruitment to sites of infection. Conducted as a comparative study examining responses to three clinically significant arboviral challenges: DENV, Chikungunya virus (CHIKV), and the Yellow Fever vaccine (YF17D), this will allow us to compare the anti-viral responses of MCs to two viral pathogens with unique life cycles to the responses elicited by YF17D, which is arguably the most effective vaccine on the market thus far. These studies will provide valuable insight into how optimal T cell immunity is achieved during cutaneous viral infection and inform our design of vaccines to capitalize on or recapitulate the immune-modulatory capacity of MCs.
kw: mast cell, T cell, cellular recruitment, arbovirus, inflammation

title: Bacterial hijacking of host iron acquisition pathways
abs: Recurrent urinary tract infections (UTIs) caused by uropathogenic E. coli (UPEC) are common and morbid infectious diseases with very limited therapeutic options. Previous studies have demonstrated that persistent intracellular infection of bladder epithelial cells (BEC) by UPEC contributes to chronic or recurrent UTI that are refractory to antibiotic treatments. How UPEC hijack host cellular pathways to survive intracellularly within the acidic endocytic vacuole is a key knowledge gap and understanding of this process shall provide the most direct, rational path towards novel therapeutics for recurrent/chronic UTI. We hypothesized that UPEC may exploit host vesicular trafficking proteins for intracellular survival and identified a major role for the small GTPase Rab35 in facilitating UPEC survival within UPEC-containing vacuoles (UCV) in BEC. Rab35 regulates the trafficking of transferrin receptor (TfR), which is required for the uptake of iron in host cells. We found that UPEC modulates the expression and recruitment of Rab35 and TfR to the UCV, which provide UPEC with the essential nutrient iron for survival. In the absence of Rab35, UPEC is preferentially trafficked to degradative lysosomes and killed. We propose a model in which UPEC subverts two different steps in endocytic vesicular trafficking (endosomal recycling and degradative lysosomal fusion) through their control of host Rab35, thereby simultaneously enhancing iron acquisition and avoiding lysosomal degradation of the UCV. This proposal seeks to extend our observations to further characterize these molecular pathways in detail. We will use a combination of in vitro cell culture, in vivo mouse model of UTI pathogenesis, bacterial genetics, and cell biology approaches to understand the mechanism of UCV biogenesis and intracellular survival mechanisms of UPEC in UCVs through Rab35 and iron transport. Using recurrent UTI patient samples, we will also explore the feasibility of developing iron and iron homeostasis proteins as potential susceptibility biomarkers for recurrent UTI.
kw: Uropathogenic E. coli, iron, Rab GTPase, recurrent urinary tract infection

title: Mechanisms of Group A Streptococcus Biofilm Formation on Mammalian Cells
abs: Group A Streptococcus (GAS) causes a wide range of infections, from pharyngitis to necrotizing fasciitis, and has a global disease burden of more than 18 million people. The means by which GAS causes so many different types of infections is incompletely understood, but is thought to involve differential regulation of virulence factors in response to host niche. It is well-accepted that bacterial biofilms, dense communities of bacteria that are phenotypically different than their free-swimming counterparts, are associated with the vast majority of infectious diseases. Despite this, very little is known about the role of GAS biofilms in infection. Current approaches to study biofilms, for GAS and for most bacteria, are based on growing biofilms on abiotic surfaces as an approximation of growth on mammalian tissues. This approach is inadequate, however, as biofilms on abiotic surfaces and biofilms formed in vivo during infection have different molecular and architectural properties.We aim to surmount these limitations by developing and characterizing a more physiologically relevant in vitro model in which to study biofilms formed by pathogens during infection. We will leverage existing advanced sequencing and imaging platforms in Singapore, and combine molecular genetics with infection biology, to define the role of GAS biofilm in infection. We will characterize the transcriptional differences between GAS biofilms grown on mammalian cells in vitro and within mammalian hosts, using immortalized cell lines, murine and piscine infection models, and 3-D organotypic tissue models. We will integrate bacterial and host transcriptional profiles with spatial mapping of the bacterial expression data onto the biofilm architecture, to identify unique signatures of biofilm-associated infection throughout the biofilm and infection life-cycle. Biofilm-specific signatures will provide the foundation for mechanistic studies leading to novel diagnostics, biomarkers, and therapeutics for GAS disease.
kw: Group A Streptococcus, biofilm, tissue models, animal models, transcriptomics, infection biology

title: Novel Non-invasive Biomarkers for the Early Detection of Breast Cancer among Women with Abnormal Mammograms
abs: NOVEL NON-INVASIVE BIOMARKERS FOR THE EARLY DETECTION OF BREAST CANCER AMONG WOMEN WITH ABNORMAL MAMMOGRAMSBACKGROUNDMammography is the current gold-standard for breast cancer screening however false-positive mammograms are common resulting in unnecessary investigations and increased healthcare costs. Of the ~1,500 women with abnormal mammograms referred each year to the National Cancer Centre, Singapore, only ~110 women are diagnosed with breast cancer.HYPOTHESISOur hypothesis is that serum-derived microRNA species are differentially expressed in patients with breast cancer, as compared to healthy women with abnormal mammograms. AIMS Aim 1: Discovery Phase:To perform microRNA profiling on serum samples from women with abnormal mammograms who are either (a) diagnosed with breast cancer (n=100) or (b) found to have no evidence of cancer by biopsy (n=200).Aim 2: Validation PhaseTo validate the microRNA signatures derived in Aim 1 in serum samples from an independent cohort of women with abnormal mammograms who are referred for biopsy (n=200).NOVELTYFirstly, there are no previous studies utilizing microRNA profiling for women with abnormal mammograms to discriminate between women with breast cancer versus those proven not to have breast cancer.Secondly, our team will utilize a novel microRNA profiling platform that is both reliable and sensitive to identify robust microRNA signatures. CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCEIn the short-term, development of a non-invasive blood test used in conjunction with mammography may reduce the false-positive rate of mammography and improve the accuracy of screening. If found to have a high sensitivity and specificity, this test could help circumvent problems associated with false-positive mammograms, e.g. expensive specialist scans, painful procedures and psychological distress.In the long-term, an understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying the microRNA signatures associated with breast cancer could potentially result in the development of novel strategies for disease prevention and therapy.
kw: Breast cancer, circulating microRNAs, biomarkers, early detection, screening mammography

title: Characterizing dynamic functional connectivity in the adult and developing brain using concurrent fMRI-EEG
abs: The structure and function of the human brain undergo dramatic changes during development. Functional connectivity derived from functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) maps large-scale neural network function and dysfunction. Recent studies by our group and others found distinct functional connectivity changes in both task-negative and task-positive networks in patients with neuropsychiatric disorders. Nevertheless, emerging work suggested that the assumption of static brain state over time is insufficient to understand brain connectivity. It remains unclear how these regions interact dynamically and support cognition during neurodevelopment. Moreover, the underlying neural mechanism of functional connectivity remains largely unknown. We propose to employ concurrent fMRI and electroencephalography (EEG) techniques to examine functional connectivity and its underlying neural oscillations in the adult and developing brain. Two hundred healthy individuals (aged 12-26) will be recruited to undergo task-free concurrent fMRI-EEG experiments. In contrast to static functional connectivity approaches that assume constant connections over time, we will develop novel dynamic functional connectivity (DFC) approaches based on hidden Markov models to interrogate the temporally varying coordination and competition among different neural systems. We will test the stability and reliability of the new methods compared to existing methods based on repeat scans of 40 adults within one month. Cross-sectionally, we hypothesize that (1) DFC metrics would outperform static functional connectivity scores in detecting age-related changes underlying cognitive performance; (2) EEG-fMRI correlation and modulation between low- and high-frequency oscillations would strengthen with age. Furthermore, we will investigate the changes in functional connectivity and neural oscillations in a subset of 35 healthy adolescents at 18 months follow-up. This study will provide novel insights on how dynamic interactions between brain regions mature with age to support brain functions. It will lay the foundation for future studies to detect aberrant dysconnectivity in neurodevelopmental disorders, leading to noninvasive neuroimaging-based biomarkers for prognosis and diagnosis.
kw: Development, functional magnetic resonance imaging, dynamic functional connectivity, electroencephalography, neural oscillations, neurodevelopmental disorders

title: Combinatorial high-throughput screening of physical micro niches supporting stem cell derived hepatic and cardiac cell maturation
abs: Hepatotoxicity is a major cause for attrition of drugs from the market. Inadequate in vivo or in vitro drug testing methods, which rely either on animals, human cell lines or primary human cells, fail to identify toxic effects of some drugs. Human pluripotent stem cells (hPSC: ES and iPSC) generated enormous promises for prospective role in better disease modeling and drug safety testing. However, these differentiated cells from hPSC’s were not mature and failed to mimic adult disease processes. Inspired by high throughput screening in industry and the recent success in identifying chemical molecules that improve cell maturation, we propose to systematically investigate by a combinatorial screening approach the hypothesis that micro-environmental physical cues are critical for cell maturation. We have recently developed a TopoSphero Chip platform with 7200 physical microenvironments comprising combinations of 3D topography, and stiffness on which we can grow cells with variable cell densities. Human stem cells will be induced into hepatocytes by chemical inducers, to grow on the Chip. Different meteorologically defined surface features and stiffness of the chip will result in differential cell aggregation with diverse cell-cell and cell-substrate interactions. Combinations that yield the most mature cells will be identified and scaled up to fully study the responses of cells with a plethora of assays such as qPCR, DNA microarrays as well as functional assays. Role of mechanical parameters leading to maturation of cells will be dissected with bioinformatics to understand their gene expression repertoire. We will then validate the maturity and application of mature cells with paradigm compounds used in drug safety testing assays such as IC50 measurement and CYP induction relevant for the real-life drug development process. On completion, the project aims to provide patentable robust and mature cells as well as cell culture substrates that favor maturation.
kw: topography, stem cell, mechanobiology, lab on chip, drug safety testing

title: Human apolipoprotein E isoforms and intranasal insulin effects on cognition.
abs: Intranasal insulin can improve cognition. But, it is unclear why this has little effect in non-demented subjects inheriting the human apolipoprotein E4 (ApoE4) allele. ApoE is genetically linked to cognitive function and ApoE4 accelerates memory decline during ageing. This could be due to impaired neuronal insulin signaling we have observed in ApoE4 mice. Our preliminary study using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) also showed lower cerebral flow blood (CBF) in ApoE4 mice. Put together, our data lead us to hypothesize that intranasal insulin enhances cognition by up-regulating brain insulin signaling in ApoE dependent manner. Here, we will test this hypothesis via the following specific aims, Aim 1: To compare the effects of intranasal insulin on neuronal insulin signaling protein expression and activation, and cognitive function in ApoE3 and ApoE4 mice. Aim 2: To determine the influence of intranasal insulin on CBF and cognitive network, especially the hippocampal network and default mode network in the brain of ApoE3 and ApoE4 mice using advanced MRI. This will enable us to connect insulin signaling with brain function and the corresponding behavior. Aim 3: To examine if intranasal insulin effects on insulin signaling is modulated by ApoE expression in primary hippocampal neurons. This proposal serves to decipher the mechanisms underlining this therapeutic option for age- and Alzheimer-related cognitive decline.
kw: Insulin signaling, apolipoprotein E, cognition.

title: The interplay of phosphorylation and dephosphorylation regulates accurate chromosome segregation and the spindle assembly checkpoint
abs: Mitosis is one of the most basic and essential processes in living organisms. Mitotic defects inevitably generate chromosome alterations that fuels tumorigenesis and many genetic disorders. It also has a direct clinical relevance since the anti-microtubule drug Taxol is one of the most successful anti-cancer drugs, which disrupts chromosome segregation and promotes cancer cell death. We aim to uncover new mitotic signaling pathways for proper chromosome segregation that could be exploited to implement the appropriate defense to chromosome instability and tumorigenesis.We study the recently identified mitotic-specific kinase Greatwall/Mastl that inhibits the phosphatase PP2A, which reverses the phosphorylation of substrates by the mitotic kinase Cdk1. We have generated conditional knockout mice for Mastl. Loss of Mastl leads to lethality at any stage of development, indicating that Mastl is an essential gene. When Mastl is deleted, cells exit from mitosis with massively mis-segregated chromosomes, which become unraveled. We will determine the molecular mechanism that underlies this defect, which is likely due to the alterations in chromosome architecture regulated by the phosphorylation of chromosome scaffolding proteins, which include condensin, cohesion, and topoisomerase-II. Erroneous kinetochore-microtubule attachment causes mitotic arrest by activating the spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC). Defects in SAC signaling also cause chromosome mis-segregation. We found that when Mastl is deleted, SAC is weakened and prematurely silenced before kinetochore-microtubule attachment is properly established. Using a mass spectrometry screen, we have identified proteins whose phosphorylation decreases in the absence of Mastl, which includes MPS1, an essential kinase for SAC signaling. We will study in detail how Mastl (through PP2A) regulates the SAC and whether changes in MPS1 phosphorylation are important for this regulation.We aim to decipher the new signaling pathways for chromosome segregation and SAC regulation. Specific pharmaceutical targeting of such signaling pathways will be a valuable strategy for anti-cancer therapy in clinic.
kw: Cell Cycle; Mitosis; Spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC); Kinase - Phosphatase; Chromosome segregation; Chromosome condensation

title: Develop and apply four novel experimental tools to study the Xist RNA and human iPS cells
abs: Synthetic Biology defines the approaches to re-organize and combine different biological components to achieve engineering purposes. Here, taking the synthetic biology approach, we propose to develop the following new experimental methods: (1) “Crisp-Pad” (an efficient genetic screening tool for mammalian cells with low off-target effect and no unnecessary genetic perturbing); (2) “RNA Foot-print” (a method of high-resolution mapping of protein binding sites along a candidate RNA); (3) “Tracer” (a re-engineered CRISPR/Cas9 system for live-cell imaging of RNA); (4) “FLAG-out” (a re-engineered CRISPR/Cas9 system for identifying binding proteins of a candidate RNA). All the established methods will be applied to study the Xist RNA, a prototype and mysterious long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) and human iPS cells.
kw: Xist, lncRNA, CRISPR/Cas9, epigenetic, Human iPS cells, Padlock sequencing

title: Investigating the role of Npac in epigenetic regulation of ES cell identity and reprogramming
abs: Embryonic stem (ES) cells are pluripotent and are capable of giving rise to many cell types. Recently, a tremendous amount of work has focused on deciphering how ES cell identity is epigenetically regulated. It has been shown that different histone modifications play crucial roles in ES cells. In particular, histone H3K36 methylation has been discovered to be correlated with transcriptional activation and be located in the 3' coding region of heavily transcribed genes. However, not many studies have been conducted to dissect the regulatory mechanism of histone H3K36 methylation in ES cell identity. We have identified Npac/Glyr, a nuclear protein, to be an essential pluripotency factor since loss of Npac results in ES cell differentiation. Our Npac ChIP-seq results showed that Npac co-localizes with histone H3K36me3 in a large number of genomic sites in mouse ES cells. We also found that Npac can interact with several RNA-binding proteins such as L1td1 and Nucleolin which are essential for ES cell pluripotency. Interestingly, Npac not only contains a PWWP domain which can recognize H3K36 methylation but also harbors an AT-hook domain (which can bind to DNA) and a NAD-binding domain (which is involved in redox reaction and can bind to RNA). Taken together, we hypothesize that Npac plays multiple functions which are related to gene transcription and RNA metabolism. Therefore, we aim to address how Npac is involved in epigenetic regulation of ES cell identity. We propose to perform functional analysis in order to decode the role of Npac in histone H3K36me3-associated functions. We plan to identify RNA targets which Npac or Npac interacting proteins may bind to. Lastly, we aim to expand our knowledge to human NPAC in human ES cells and reprogramming. Our research is expected to provide new insights into epigenetics and stem cell biology.
kw: Npac; ES cell identity; Epigenetics, Histone modification; RNA metabolism; Reprogramming

title: Understanding disease pathology and mechanisms for Rett Syndrome and other Autism Spectrum Disorders
abs: The genetics of ASD is complex and hundreds of genes have been linked to increased risk of ASD. Rett syndrome (RTT) is a rare form of ASD that has an unusually strong genetic component. Sporadic mutations in methyl-CpG binding protein 2 (MeCP2) have been detected in more than 80-90% of RTT patients. Rodent animal models with various Mecp2 mutations and deletions exhibited RTT-like behavioral phenotypes, such as impaired learning and memory and social avoidance. Neurons in Mecp2 mice can survive until adulthood but show defects in neuronal development and circuitry. These findings suggest the possibility of reversing the neurological phenotypes of RTT by appropriate therapeutic interventions. Impairments in both neuronal structure and synaptic function have been implicated in the brain function defects associated found in RTT animal models. Signaling via the A-type ?-aminobutyric acid receptor (GABAAR) has been implicated in the defects in excitatory neurotransmission MeCP2 deficiency-mediated and is a process that is essential for neuronal development and synaptic transmission, potentially providing the underlying mechanism for the defective neuronal structure and synaptic function associated with RTT. Therefore, we hypothesize that (1) GABAAR signaling plays an important role in the defects associated with MeCP2 deficiency and (2) modulators of GABA signaling are potential therapeutics that could alleviate the symptoms and/or delay the onset of RTT. The proposed experiments will use in vitro neuronal culture systems, animal studies and induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSC) derived from human RTT patients to compare causal relationships between genetic, cellular, circuitry and behavioral defects in RTT, with a focus on GABAAR signaling. These results will aid in developing a 3-D culture microfluidic system suitable for high throughput drug screening and finding potential therapeutics that can reverse RTT phenotypes.
kw: autism spectrum disorder, Rett syndrome, Channelrhopsin, microfluidics, neuronal development

title: Comprehensive characterization of the HBV and host transcripts and HBV proteins in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) patients
abs: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is amongst the deadliest cancer due to its late diagnosis and limited treatment options. Although ~80% of HCC patients are chronically infected with HBV, the association between chronic HBV-infection and HCC remains unclear. A significant feature is the integration of HBV-DNA into host-genome, playing ‘cis’ and/or ‘trans’ roles in hepatocarcinogenesis. Long-read sequencing of HBV-DNA from HCC patients revealed preferential integration of HBV into tumor gene promoters. Notably, integration into chromosome 10 was significantly associated with poorly differentiated tumors. In addition, the 3’-end of the HBx gene is the preferred site of integration as well as viral structural alterations (deletions/insertions). Upon integration, the 3’-end of the HBx is often deleted and/or fused to host sequences forming truncated or viral-host chimeric transcripts. Interestingly, recent reports suggest that 3’-truncated [1] and HBX-Human chimeric transcripts [2] are associated with tumorigenesis and progression. Hence, it is worthwhile to comprehensively characterize HBV at the transcript/protein level in HCC patients using ultra-high-throughput sequencing to understand the role mutated/truncated or HBV-chimeric transcripts play in tumorigenesis as well as associate the various HBV forms with clinical characteristics and prognosis of the patients.To elucidate the transcript form(s) that play important role in hepatocarcinogenesis, we aim to functionally characterize the different forms of the different HBV/chimeric transcript as observed in cells of the patients. The elucidation of the characteristics of the HBV transcripts in HCC patients may serve as potential prognostic tools guiding doctors in recommending treatment options. Understanding the roles they play in HCC can also facilitate the design of therapy for HBV-associated-HCC treatment.
kw: Hepatitis B Virus, Hepatocellular Carcinoma, Next Generation Sequencing, HBV-Human chimeric transcripts

title: The Singapore Chinese Eye Study 2 (SCES-2): Prospective cohort study of 6-year incidence, risk factors, and impact of major age-related eye diseases
abs: There is a disproportionate burden of age-related eye diseases in Asians. Specifically, Asia accounts for 35% of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and 60% of glaucoma cases worldwide. Amongst the 3 ethnic groups (Chinese, Indians, Malays) in Singapore, Chinese have the highest AMD prevalence, and have higher glaucoma prevalence. These observations highlight the need for in-depth evaluation on the incidence and progression of AMD, glaucoma, and other age-related eye diseases in Chinese. Currently, such data are not present in Singapore, and extremely limited in Asia. In 2009-11, we conducted the baseline Singapore Chinese Eye Study (SCES-1), a population-based study on 3,353 (72.8% response rate) Chinese. We have completed prospective follow-up of eye disease studies in Malays in the Singapore Malay Eye Study-2 (SiMES-2) in 2013, and will complete the prospective study of Indians in the Singapore Indian Eye study-2 (SINDI-2) by 2015. The proposed SCES-2 study will re-examine the Chinese cohort 6 years after the baseline examination. We will determine the 6-year incidence and progression of AMD and glaucoma; discover novel biomarkers, genetic variants, imaging parameters, modifiable risk factors; and evaluate the impact of major blinding eye diseases in Singaporean Chinese. With the completion of SCES-2, we will have the unique longitudinal data from SCES-2, SiMES-2 and SINDI-2, covering the 3 major ethnicities in Asia. The major strengths of SCES-2 include a well-established and characterized cohort at baseline, an experienced international team of clinician-scientists and epidemiologists, and the highest-quality baseline ocular/systemic data, including high-resolution images of retina and optic nerve, frozen serum/blood, and existing genome-wide genotype data. Coupled with SIMES-2 and SINDI-2, SCES-2 will provide critical information on the incidence and progression of major eye diseases in Asians. These data will be critical for the planning of public health strategies to reduce visual loss not only in Singapore but across Asia.
kw: population-based study, incidence, progression, glaucoma, age-related macular degeneration

title: Characterizing the role of CACNA1 in Exfoliation Syndrome and Glaucoma
abs: Exfoliation syndrome (XFS) is an age-related systemic disease with important manifestations in the eye, where the accumulation of deposits of exfoliation material damages the trabecular meshwork, resulting in raised intraocular pressure and eventually glaucoma, a progressive blinding disease. XFS is the commonest identifiable cause of glaucoma.In 2007, common variants in the LOXL1 gene were found to be associated with XFS, albeit with inconsistent directions of effect depending on ethnicity. When we recently performed a genome-wide association study on >8,000 cases and 21,000 controls from 17 countries, we discovered a novel association between the CACNA1A polymorphism rs4926244a?g and susceptibility to XFS (Odds ratio=1.16, P<1x10-10) and also confirmed the LOXL1 association. The identification of CACNA1A as a gene for XFS opens up new avenues of research as the gene encodes a voltage-dependent calcium (Cav2.1) channel. Previous electron microscopy studies on human XFS eyes showed the presence of high calcium concentration in association with aggregating XFS fibrils. In addition, it is known from in-vitro studies that fibrillin utilizes calcium to form stable aggregates. Thus, we hypothesize that altered function of a calcium channel could lead to alterations of calcium concentrations that may facilitate the formation of XFS material and subsequent glaucoma. This potential mechanism involving ion transport signalling in XFS pathogenesis warrants further investigation as it may be amenable to therapeutic intervention.This proposal aims to characterize the molecular genetics of CACNA1A in human cells and tissues relevant to XFS. We aim to identify the causal XFS mutations in CACNA1A via targeted re-sequencing in XFS cases and controls and characterize these identified variants with respect to CACNA1A biology and function in human eye tissue. Information from this study on XFS pathogenesis could lead to identification of potential therapeutic targets and eventual treatments to ameliorate XFS disease and ultimately reduce glaucoma blindness.
kw: molecular genetics, genome-wide association study, calcium channel, Exfoliation syndrome (XFS), XFS pathogenesis, glaucoma

title: Percutaneous Approach to Valved Stent Implantation at Vena Cava – Atrial Junctions to Mitigate effects of Severe Tricuspid Regurgitation
abs: Severe tricuspid valve regurgitation (TR) is a common condition that results in right heart failure, liver and renal dysfunction and death if left untreated. Currently, the only available treatment is open heart surgery. Unfortunately, many cannot undertake such high risk surgery. We have previously developed a bench tested unidirectional stent valve that can be implanted in the vena cava. We hypothesize that this valve can be implanted safely and effectively in the superior and inferior vena cava percutaneously and may shield end organs from the harmful effects of regurgitation. The first aim would be to demonstrate the safety and feasibility of percutaneous implantation of the valve stent in 6 pigs. The second aim would be to develop a TR model and test the efficacy of the valve stent. Thirty pigs would first be used to develop a tricupid regurgitation model by percutaneously inducing valve dysfunction by a biotome. These pigs would be assessed for signs of right heart failure. Imaging (cardiac MRI, echocardiography), invasive assessment of hemodynamics and biochemistry would be performed at baseline and 1 month after percutaneously inducing TR. Following this, 15 pigs would be used as controls and 15 pigs would undergo percutaneous implantation of the caval valves. Repeat imaging, invasive and biochemical tests would be performed after 1 month of valve implantation. Both groups of pigs would be sacrificed and pathohistological assessment of the myocardium, liver and renal structures as well as stent endothelization and potential degeneration of the valve leaflets (using electron micrography) would be assessed. This project aims to develop a novel technique to treat severe TR. There is currently no commercially available percutaneous technique to treat TR. This may allow very sick patients to be treated percutaneously and address a large unmet clinical need to reduce of heart failure, re-hospitalization and potentially mortality.
kw: Tricuspid Valve Regurgitation, Percutaneous Heart Valve, Heart Failure, Transcatheter Technologies, Interventional Cardiology

title: An Investigator Sponsored Phase I Study of the Safety, Pharmacokinetics and Pharmacodynamics of Escalating Doses followed by Dose Expansion of the Selective Inhibitor of Nuclear Export (SINE) Selinexor (KPT-330) in Asian Patients with Advanced or Metastatic Solid Tumor Malignancies.
abs: Aim: To establish the safety, pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of escalating doses followed by dose expansion of Selinexor (KPT-330), a selective inhibitor of the nuclear export protein (XPO-1), in Asian Patients with advanced or metastatic solid tumor malignanciesMethods: An investigator initiated open-label, dose-escalation (Phase 1a) and expansion (Phase 1b) study to evaluate the safety and tolerability of KPT-330 and determine the recommended phase 2 dose (RP2D) in patients with solid tumor malignancies.Importance of research: Tight regulation of tumour suppressor proteins (TSPs) and growth regulatory proteins (GRP) is required within cells to prevent neoplastic transformation. Tumour cells can inactivate critical TSPs/GRPs by increasing the levels of nuclear export proteins like XPO1. First-in-class selective inhibitors of nuclear export (SINE) such as Selinexor (KPT-330) have been developed which can inhibit XPO1, resulting in the nuclear retention of key TSP/GRPs and forced reactivation of their function. Consistent with its mechanism as an activator of the major TSPs/GRPs including p53, pRB, BRCA1, and others, KPT-330 has shown broad and durable anti-tumor activity as a single agent, even at low doses in ongoing phase I studies in North America. Durable (> 3 months) disease stabilization and responses have been observed in haematological and heavily pretreated solid tumours. However, this compound has not been extensively tested in Asian patients or Asian type tumours and hence the need to evaluate its safety and tolerability in our Singaporean patient population.
kw: Selinexor, Pharmacokinetics, Pharmacodynamics, Solid, Metastatic, Tumor

title: SingValve – The First Mitral Valve Prosthesis in the World with a Natural Design
abs: Mitral valve disease is still a common heart disease, with 2/3 of patients require mitral valve replacement (MVR) as a definite treatment. For the last 40 years, mitral valve prostheses for MVR have been invariably built in an unnatural, circular shaped fashion, and mostly consisting of rigid materials, featuring two or three symmetric leaflets which are unnatural as compared to the normal anatomy of the mitral valve. Therefore, the heart muscle does not recover well from surgery. Also, those prostheses do not last long (7-10 years), causing patients to need a second or third high-risk surgery during their life span. Moreover, they are associated with serious complications, such as bleeding, thrombosis and embolization, stroke, and prosthetic valve infections. In this surgical project, we propose to prove the feasibility to build a naturally-shaped artificial mitral valve for MVR. Furthermore, this valve should be entirely manufacturable in Singapore, as to be identified as the “The SingValve”. The novel prosthetic valve will be built in absolute resemblance of the natural mitral valve, which can be a custom-made prosthesis specific to a patient, using simple preoperative echocardiographic data. MVR with this valve is expected to produces good short- and middle term hemodynamic effects, similar to those of heart valve repair, with the long term perspective being subject to a second series of funding and experimentation/clinical trial. We will also ex fashion this natural valve from autologous pericardium and explore feasibility of an intraoperative, same session autologous production along with the mitral valve procedure. This project will serve to develop a biological heart valve of Singapore, contributing to the development of a valve manufacture hub in our country. It will save millions of patients with MVR the need for long-term anticoagulation, prevent repeated operations, and promote a better and faster heart muscle recovery.
kw: Mitral Valve, Implantation, Replacement, Prosthesis, Natural design, Physiological Valve

title: Systems for assessing mutation signatures in-vitro and discovering mutagenic exposures in tumors
abs: Mutagenesis is a major cause of cancer, and cancer genomes are affected by mutations as part of oncogenesis. There are unmet needs for improved mutagenicity testing (i.e., safety testing) and for improved assessment of the roles that specific mutagens play in causing cancer. The advent of inexpensive genome sequencing has created novel opportunities to meet these unmet needs with (1) improved in-vitro testing of compounds’ mutagenicity and safety and determination of their characteristic mutation signatures and (2) vastly improved understanding of the roles of mutagens in causing cancer. This project builds on our recent work on aristolochic acid, a carcinogen found in some natural remedies. The in-vitro mutation signatures of aristolochic acid occur in some liver tumors and several types of urological tumors, thus implicating it in these tumors' etiology. This work constitutes a proof of concept that (1) the approach in this project can identify mutation signatures in cell-culture systems and (2) we can detect these signatures in the somatic mutations of tumors and thereby infer hitherto unexpected carcinogenic exposures. The mutation signatures will be important tools for understanding the causes of cancer. This project will create a robust in-vitro platform for assessing mutagenicity and determining the characteristic extended mutation signatures of mutagens, i.e. patterns of DNA mutations in their larger sequence contexts. We will apply this platform to known and suspected carcinogenic mutagens. Novelty stems not only from development of the platform, but also from new knowledge of the extended mutation signatures of mutagens. In addition, this project will develop and apply new computational tools to identify known mutation signatures in worldwide databases of somatic mutations from >12,000 tumors, thereby revealing hitherto unknown mutagenic exposures that cause cancer. The results of this project will offer new opportunities for cancer prevention through reduction in mutagenic exposures.
kw: carcinogen, genotoxicity mutagen, chemical safety, molecular epidemiology of cancer, mutation signature

title: The genetic basis of endoxifen pharmacokinetics with the purpose of tamoxifen dosage optimization to prevent breast cancer recurrence/progression
abs: Tamoxifen is a selective estrogen receptor modulator effective against estrogen-receptor positive breast cancer. Tamoxifen’s therapeutic activity is mainly due to its principal active metabolite endoxifen, which is formed from tamoxifen mostly (>90%) via CYP2D6 mediated metabolism. It is thus hypothesized that low resultant serum endoxifen levels are a harbinger of increased cancer recurrence and poor outcome. Should this be true, it suggests that a critical tamoxifen concentration for oncologists to aim for could exist.As preliminary data, we conducted the first genome-wide association study on steady-state endoxifen levels in 154 Singaporean Chinese breast cancer patients, with replication analysis in 290 Germans and 70 Lebanese breast cancer patients. Strong evidence of association was observed between a TCF20 genetic marker and serum endoxifen levels (effect size = -11.15 mmol per-copy of the minor allele; P = 7.42 x 10-30) with no evidence of heterogeneity across collections. Analysis compensating for the canonical CYP2D6 metabolizer genotypes still showed TCF20 to be strongly genome-wide significant over and above CYP2D6, retaining consistent evidence of association across the patient collections. Carriers and individuals homozygous for the minor allele of TCF20 showed poorer clinical outcome (N = 778 women with 160 events) compared to wild-type individuals (Hazard ratio per-allele = 1.4, P = 0.0027). These low-pass GWAS findings herald the presence of genetic variants of higher penetrance and stronger effect with regards to control of endoxifen pharmacokinetics as well as clinical outcome of breast cancer patients following treatment with tamoxifen. The objective of this proposal is to now build on the unexpected Singaporean GWAS finding and conduct more detailed whole-genome sequencing of Singapore breast cancer patients who have been prescribed tamoxifen chemotherapy at a fixed dose. Information thus gleaned can be correlated to clinical outcome and endoxifen pharmacokinetics in prospectively enrolled Singaporean breast cancer cases.
kw: tamoxifen, endoxifen, pharmacogenomics, pharmacokinetics, whole genome sequencing, breast cancer

title: Understanding rheumatoid arthritis through whole-exome sequencing and epigenetics
abs: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic inflammatory joint disease characterized by progressive bone and cartilage destruction. The contribution of genetic and environmental factors to RA pathogenesis is evident but their complex interaction remains elusive. A better understanding of the pathogenic mechanisms will aid in the development of preventive intervention and rationale therapies. This proposal therefore aims to dissect the multifactorial nature of RA and discover novel determinants for preventive, early and curative treatments by employing an integrative omics approach including genomic, epigenomic, RNA expression analyses and clinical evaluation. Whole exome seqencing will be performed in 600 anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody-positive (anti-CCP) Chinese patients compared with healthy controls. This endeavour has been aided by the attainment of large and well-characterized collections of samples from patients in Tan Tock Seng Hospital (TTSH) and the exome sequence database of healthy Chinese Singaporeans in Genome Institute of Singapore. Samples will be sequenced on high coverage (30x) on the illumina Hiseq and variant calling will be performed with the Genome Analysis Toolkit (GATK) pipeline. Given that the genetic architecture of RA differs substantially among major ethnic groups, whole-exome investigations in large cohorts will identify genetic risks and rare variants associated with local population. The candidate genes will be validated in an independent cohort of 800 patients and 600 controls. To understand how these genetic variants translate into pathogenic mechanisms and ultimately into phenotypes, mRNA expression and epigenomic profiling studies in synovial fluid and T-lymphocytes will be performed by RNA sequencing and Assay for Transposase Accessible Chromatin sequencing (ATAC-seq). The outcome of this proposed research will facilitate the development of test panel for preventive intervention in susceptible individuals as well as predic¬tions of disease outcome and treatment response in patients, thus paving the way for personalized medicine and more efficient patient care.
kw: Rheumatoid arthritis; Exome sequencing; RNA sequencing; Chinese; Epigenetics; Personalized medicine

title: A novel mechanism of hypertension-induced cerebral damage
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Hypertension is one of the most important risk factor for prevention of a first stroke. Sustained uncontrolled hypertension usually causes cerebral damage, including small vessel stroke. Although the pathogenesis of hypertension-induced stroke is complex, blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption is believed to be a major cause for vasogenic edema and subsequent stroke. A major question relating with BBB damage remains unclear, which is why edema formation starts from a few loci, rather than from multiple sites.Stroke-prone spontaneously hypertensive rats (SHRSP) are widely used to study hypertension-related cerebral injury. Our preliminary studies identified robust angiogenesis in brains of SHRSP. Interestingly, only few newly generated capillaries express transient receptor potential subfamily melastatin 4 (TRPM4) channel which is a nonselective cation channel, conducting monovalent ions. Our most recent data further identified TRPM4 in the vascular endothelium in human brain samples with hypertension. Upregulation of TRPM4 in spinal cord injury and stroke causes oncotic cell death of the capillary endothelium and secondary hemorrhage. Therefore, TRPM4 may be involved in the hypertension-induced BBB damage. We postulate that those newly generated blood vessels with de novo TRPM4 expression may be vulnerable to be damaged after sustained hypertension.We have successfully used in vivo siRNA to suppress TRPM4 expression in a rat stroke model. Furthermore, a novel polyclonal antibody has been generated in our lab that can inhibit TRPM4. In this proposal, we will use various biochemical, functional, imaging, and behavioral approaches to evaluate the effect of inhibiting TRPM4 in the BBB damage in SHRSP.Understanding the mechanism of BBB damage during uncontrolled hypertension can help to develop new therapies to delay or prevent cerebral damage, including stroke. This novel angioprotective strategy will undoubtedly improve our current stroke management.
kw: hypertension, stroke, cerebral edema, ion channel

title: A Psychosocial Intervention Program for Adolescents and Young Adults (AYA) Cancer Patients at National Cancer Centre Singapore (NCCS) – A Pilot Study
abs: Background: Adolescents and young adults (AYA) with cancer, defined as patients between 16 and 39 years old, constitute a vulnerable group with unmet needs. In contradistinction to children and older adults with cancer, their clinical outcomes have not improved significantly in recent times. The physical, financial and psychological toxicities of disease and treatment are compounded by the significant changes and life events attendant to this age group, including sexual coming of age, economic independence, and establishing a family. These factors add substantively to the challenges and distress of cancer treatment and negatively impact health related quality of life (HRQOL). Objective: We aim to undertake a pilot study evaluating the effectiveness of a psychosocial intervention program in a subset of AYA cancer patients with lymphoma, sarcoma and germ cell tumour. In addition, we aim to determine the level of psychosocial distress and cost burden amongst AYA patients. Methodology: This is a single centre, prospective, longitudinal, pre-post interventional study at the National Cancer Centre Singapore. All patients will undergo an orientation program and be screened for psychosocial distress. Patients at high risk for distress will receive monthly multidisciplinary input and two psychosocial intervention modules. All patients will be assessed using instruments evaluating psychological health, symptom burden and cognitive function at 1, 3, 6, 9 and 12 months to determine the changes in their HRQOL. Direct and indirect costs of disease and treatment will be determined through health records, bills and questionnaires.Significance: This study will provide data on psychosocial and cost burden of cancer care amongst AYA patients, as well as feasibility and efficacy of risk-adapted interventions for these patients. This can form the base from which prospective randomised interventional studies are conducted to realise the goal of enhancing care for this often neglected subset of cancer sufferers.
kw: Adolescent Young Adults, Cancer, Psychosocial Intervention

title: Mendalian randomization study of adiponectin and colorectal cancer survival
abs: Background: Adiponectin is a hormone secreted by adipose tissue and has been shown to be inversely associated with the risk of colorectal cancer (CRC). However, its influence on survival is not fully elucidated. We recently demonstrated that prediagnostic adiponectin is associated with increased CRC-specific and overall mortality among 621 CRC cases within the Nurses Health Study (NHS) and Health Professional Follow up Study (HPFS) (unpublished data). However, the causal nature of this association is unclear, given the paucity of studies. Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified genetic variants known as single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) that influence circulating adiponectin levels and CRC development. The relationship between these SNPs and CRC prognosis remains to be determined. Aims: As an extension of our previous study, we aim to investigate the causal nature of association between circulating adiponectin and CRC survival using a mendalian randomization approach.Hypothesis: We hypothesize that circulating adiponectin is causal for increased risk of CRC and overall mortality.Methodology and approach: Participants from the Genetics and Epidemiology of Colorectal Cancer Consortium (GECCO) with detailed epidemiologic and genetic data will be included. We will genotype the patients for common and putative SNPs associated with circulating adiponectin and CRC. Cox proportional hazards models will be used to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence interval (CI) for CRC-specific and overall mortality. We will adjust for putative and established risk factors for CRC mortality (age, gender, BMI, physical activity, smoking, alcohol, regular use of aspirin or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, stage, grade and tumor site). Analyses by subgroups defined by age, BMI, stage, grade and tumor site will be performed. We will derive a multi-SNP genotypic risk score based on “at-risk” genotypes to better estimate the hazard of death. We will conduct separate analyses for each study and subsequently pool the results for meta-analyses.
kw: adiponectin, colorectal cancer, survival

title: Developing Experimental Therapeutics and Understanding Mechanisms of Drug Resistance in Asian Breast Cancer
abs: Systemic treatment remains the cornerstone for breast cancer therapy, but intra-patient tumor heterogeneity and tumor evolution following drug treatment are major challenges to effective therapy. Funded by the NMRC Senior Clinician Scientist Award over the last five years, we have developed an internationally recognized breast cancer program comprising of a clinical trial program to test novel treatment strategies along with a breast tissue biobank and pharmacogenetic DNA bank for discovery of tumor and host predictive biomarkers of treatment response and toxicity. In parallel, we have established a translational laboratory to analyze drug pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic effects, and a pilot study to enrich circulating tumor cells (CTCs) with culture to increase their detection limit. In the next five years, we will expand the program by: (1) continuing to design and execute clinical trials in the refractory/metastatic, neoadjuvant, or window-of-opportunity settings, focusing on optimizing combination strategies between novel biological agents and the backbone chemotherapy or endocrine therapy of breast cancer. In addition, we will evaluate immunotherapy in breast cancer using a patented technology to expand and activate autologous natural killer cells to enhance antibody-directed cell cytotoxicity mediated by therapeutic monoclonal antibodies such as trastuzumab; (2) expand our collection of resistant tumors post-systemic therapy for deep molecular characterization and to generate patient-derived cell lines for in vitro drug sensitivity studies to understand mechanisms of resistance and uncover potential therapeutic targets to inform the selection of drugs in clinical trials; and (3) develop a reliable liquid biopsy protocol for ex vivo drug sensitivity testing using enriched CTCs and test its utility in guiding therapy and tracking progress in the clinic. This breast cancer experimental therapeutics program will address the challenges of tumor heterogeneity, tumor evolution and drug resistance, with the ultimate goal of applying the findings in routine clinical practice and improving patient outcome.

title: Randomized control trial to improve hypertension outcomes using wireless home blood pressure monitoring with automatic outcome-based feedback and financial incentives
abs: Hypertension is a major risk factor for cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. Despite the risks of hypertension and availability of effective treatment, a substantial number of patients have uncontrolled blood pressure in Singapore and around the world. Systematic reviews have shown that home blood pressure monitoring (HBPM) produces only modest improvements in blood pressure control. These systematic reviews also reveal that HBPM yields greater benefits when combined with other interventions such as remote titration change or adherence-enhancing strategies.Our strategy to improve the effectiveness of HBPM to reduce blood pressure is to use the full potential of new wireless and mobile technology. Our comprehensive intervention consists of regular and automatic monitoring of the patient’s adherence to blood pressure monitoring and of her blood pressure readings accompanied by an appropriate response. The response of the clinic will include remote titration change, automated and personalized hypertension management advice based on blood pressure results, automatic reminders for blood pressure monitoring, behavioral advice in terms of physical activity and diet, positive reinforcement of good outcomes as well as use of the assistance of a person that is trusted by the patient (e.g. care giver, family member, friend) to reinforce treatment adherence and cut the response time in case of emergency. Flagging of patients that are non-adherent to blood pressure monitoring as well as those with blood pressure readings that are consistently outside of healthy ranges will further improve the effectiveness of our intervention.We propose a 6-month randomized controlled trial with 228 hypertensive patients with uncontrolled blood pressure from the Singhealth Polyclinic in Bedok, Singapore. The proposed trial will have three equal sized and parallel study arms in order to measure the incremental effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of an intervention with wireless HBPM and automatic outcome-based feedback with and without financial incentives compared to HBPM alone.
kw: Hypertension, home blood pressure monitoring, tele-monitoring, tele-medicine, RCT, incentives

title: Identifying Highly Cost-Effective Strategies for Mammography SCREENing in Singapore (ICE SCREEN Study)
abs: Breast cancer is the most common cancer among women worldwide and in Singapore, thus posing a significant disease burden. Cost-effectiveness analyses are increasingly performed to inform optimal healthcare resource allocation. Several issues cast doubt on whether mammography screening strategies applied overseas are cost-effective in Singapore. Compared to Western populations, (i) incidence of breast cancer in Singapore is lower, hence the cost per case detected may be higher in Singapore, (ii) Singaporean women tend to have smaller and denser breasts, which limits the usefulness of film mammography screening, (iii) the age of onset for breast cancer is younger in Singaporean women, suggesting that screening should begin at a younger age. In this proposal, organized as three sub-studies, we seek to identify highly cost-effective mammography screening strategies for screening-age women in Singapore. Sub-study 1: We aim to calibrate and validate the Erasmus MC MISCAN Breast Cancer Model for use in Singapore. Sub-study 2: In a survey of women undergoing screening, we will evaluate the impact of mammography screening on health-related quality of life (HRQoL) and psychosocial distress. This will inform future studies to reduce screen-related distress, thus improving adherence to and cost-effectiveness of mammography screening. Sub-study 3: We aim to determine the preferences and willingness to pay (WTP) for a hypothetical tailored screening programme based on risk stratification in Singaporean women aged 40 and over. This will provide information on the expected participation rates, which is required to capture the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio fully and inform health policy. This study will analyze preference heterogeneity and provide elicited preferences for risk stratified subgroups, which will inform implementation of screening in these subgroups. The impact of screening on HRQoL (sub-study 2) will be incorporated into the MISCAN model and the WTP threshold (sub-study 3) will be applied to identify highly cost-effective mammography screening strategies for Singapore.
kw: breast cancer, cancer screening, cost-effectiveness analyses, psychological stress, adherence

title: The effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of web-based and home-based postnatal psychoeducational interventions for first-time mothers: A randomized controlled trial
abs: Aims The aims of the study are to: (1) develop a web-based postnatal psychoeducational programme for first-time mothers; (2) examine its effectiveness on maternal self-efficacy in newborn care (primary outcome), as well as social support, psychological well-being and maternal satisfaction with the postnatal support (secondary outcomes); and (3) evaluate its cost-effectiveness as compared to home-based psychoeducational programme and routine postnatal care. HypothesesThe hypotheses are: 1.When compared with those in the control group receiving routine care, first-time mothers in both web-based and home-based psychoeducational intervention groups will report a significantly-higher level of self-efficacy in newborn care;-higher level of social support received; -lower level of anxiety and depression; and-higher level of satisfaction with postnatal services.2.When compared with those in the home-based psychoeducational intervention group, mothers in the web-based psychoeducational intervention group will not report significantly poorer aforementioned maternal outcomes.3.It is more cost-effective to provide web-based psychoeducational intervention than home-based intervention and routine care. MethodologyA randomized controlled three-group pretest and repeated posttest, experimental design will be used. First-time mothers (n = 204) recruited from a tertiary hospital will be randomly assigned into the three groups. Data will be collected by questionnaire surveys using locally validated and reliable instruments, medical reviews, diaries, semi-structured face-to-face interviews and telephone interviews. Data will be analysed using SPSS20.0 and thematic analysis. Significance of the studyThis study will identify a clinically useful and potentially effective and cost-effective web-based postnatal psychoeducational programme to improve first-time mothers’ self-efficacy in newborn care, which will then improve their social-support seeking behaviours, psychological well-being and the satisfaction with postnatal services. The provision of widely accessed web-based postnatal psychoeducational programme will eventually lead to more positive postnatal experiences for first-time mothers and positively influence their future birth plans.
kw: First-time mother, Home-based, Postnatal, Psychoeducational intervention, Randomized controlled trial, Web-based

title: Development of a layer by layer nanoparticle sustained delivery system for nucleic acid therapeutics
abs: Successful delivery of RNAi-based therapeutics is a fast-moving field of research and major scientific and commercial interest. The prospect of using RNAi as a potent and highly specific small molecule inhibitor to any gene of choice opens the doors to therapy for many intractable disorders. RNAi has the potential to be highly specific. An increased understanding of the molecular events underlying the pathogenesis has implicated specific gene products for which suppression is anticipated to lead to a therapeutic benefit. This is precisely the scenario in which RNAi should be explored as a potential treatment strategy. A major challenge of siRNA therapeutics however, is in vivo delivery of siRNAs, since they are not easily penetrable into the targeted cells. Moreover, stable and sustained expression of the siRNA is desirable in therapeutic application as opposed to transient expression, which is usually sufficient as an in vitro research tool. In an attempt to solve these problems, we have designed and developed nanoparticles specifically for sustained siRNA delivery. Wound healing is a highly orchestrated event involving several spatiotemporal cues. Anti-fibrotic therapy ideally targets the early and late stages of wound healing for best clinical outcome. It is proposed in this study that by using an animal model of post surgical fibrosis, a one time local application of the siRNA delivery system containing 2 different siRNAs to attenuate 2 critical stages of wound healing, releasing sequentially into the target tissue, will provide an improved and novel therapeutic approach to treating fibrosis. We propose to use the LbL nanoparticle nucleic acid delivery system to test this hypothesis.
kw: siRNA, sustained drug delivery, nanoparticles, fibrosis

title: The Role of Circulating Pathogenic-Like CD4+ T Cells in Early Rheumatoid Arthritis.
abs: TitleThe Role of Circulating Pathogenic-Like CD4+ T Cells in Early Rheumatoid Arthritis. AuthorsChin-Teck Ng1, Costantino Pitzalis2, Julian Thumboo1,4, Salvatore Albani3,4Affiliation1 Department of Rheumatology and Immunology, Singapore General Hospital, Singapore.2 Queen Mary University of London, United Kingdom. 3 SingHealth Translational Immunology and Inflammation Centre, Singapore.4 Duke-NUS Medical School, Singapore.HypothesesCirculating pathogenic-like CD4+ cells play a significant role in the pathogenesis of early rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and can be used to stratify therapeutic response in RA. Specific Aims1.To characterize CPLs in detail using CyTOF (Cytometry by Time-Of-Fligh)2.To dissect and understand the phenotypical and functional changes of circulating pathogenic-like lymphocytes (CPLs) in peripheral blood and in synovium, before and after treatment in early RA3.To correlate the findings of CPLs in peripheral blood and synovium to disease activity and therapeutic response4.To validate and compare the findings of CPLs between PEAC and SGH Early Arthritis CohortsMethodologySamples from two cohorts of early RA (PEAC and SGH-EAC) are analyzed in this study. Both cohorts have similar standardized recruitment, treatment, data collection and biological sample collection protocols. Identification of circulating pathogenic-like CD4+ T cells (CPLs) is performed in peripheral blood mononuclear cells and synovium by flow-cytometry. In order to prove the correspondence between CPLs and T cells in the synovium next generation sequencing of TCR? CDR3 regions is performed. Deep immuno-phenotyping CPLs is performed using CyTOF and transcriptomics are analyzed by Nanostring.The laboratory data are correlated with disease activity and therapeutic response. Clinical SignificanceExamining the role of CPLs in early RA will further our knowledge of the immunological mechanisms of this chronic disease. CPLs have the potential to stratify therapeutic response and revolutionized the treatment strategy in early RA.
kw: Rheumatoid Arthritis, Early Arthritis, T cells

title: Non-invasive Optical Coherence Tomography Angiography for Deep Phenotyping and Diagnosis of Polypoidal Choroidal Vasculopathy
abs: Background: Polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy (PCV) is a variant of age-related macular degeneration, which is one of the commonest causes of visual loss in the world. PCV is of particular importance to Singapore as it occurs more commonly in Asians. The diagnosis of PCV requires indocyanine green angiography (ICGA), which is an invasive investigation that carries risks to the patient. The study team has described a new classification system using ICGA which differentiates PCV into 3 subtypes. These subtypes manifest with clear differences in long-term clinical outcomes. Objectives: This study aims to assess the sensitivity of novel non-invasive optical coherence tomography (OCT) angiography in diagnosing PCV and to perform detailed phenotyping of its abnormal vacular channels in order to differentiate its subtypes. We hypothesise that OCT angiography is a sensitive method of identifying PCV lesions, and is comparable to ICGA, which is the current gold standard. Furthermore, we hypothesize that there is a high concordance between OCT angiography and ICGA in classifying PCV into its individual subtypes, and that these subtypes will manifest with differences in clinical outcomes. Methods: In a prospective, longitudinal study, a cohort of patients diagnosed with PCV will undergo detailed systemic history, clinical and ophthalmic examination, as well as ocular imaging using ICGA and OCT angiography. The ICGA images will be used to diagnose and classify PCV into its subtypes. The OCT angiograms will be graded by masked graders and the findings will be correlated with the ICGA to determine its concordance. Significance: This study will achieve greater understanding of the characteristics of PCV and its subtypes and explore the role of a novel, non-invasive imaging technology to diagnose and characterise this important condition.

title: Study of interactions between immune response and Hypoxia-related genes in triple negative breast cancer and potential role in prognosis in a Singaporean patient population
abs: Background: Increased expression of certain immune response pathways genes are associated with reduced risk of breast cancer recurrence, supporting the view that cancer-immune cell interactions may limit the biological growth of breast cancer. The functions of infiltrating immune cells are influenced by hypoxia mediated by hypoxia-inducible factors (HIF), the main molecular transcriptional mediator in the hypoxia response. Overall, the immune cell response to hypoxia, or lack thereof, may be a factor that contributes to immunosuppression in the tumor microenvironment. Identification of a subset of effective immune responders under hypoxic conditions has prognostic significance in triple negative breast cancer (TNBC). Objective: We intend to study the protein expression and gene signatures of immune and hypoxia response in local Singaporean population of TNBC by supervised analysis of an integrated dataset of 352 TNBC expression profiles, and the association between gene expression and survival outcome. The secondary aim is to identify any potential interaction between the two gene signatures and the effect of a combined gene signature on patient outcome.Materials and methods: The following techniques will be employed in the proposed study: (a) Immunohistochemistry to assess the immunophenotypic expression of various immune response-specific biomarkers, transcription factors and other related proteins (b) High-throughput mRNA hybridization (Nanostring technology) to assess transcription levels of these molecules and identification of genetic signatures. (c) Statistical and biocomputational analyses to (i) test the association of the gene expression with clinicopathologic parameters and survival outcomes using Kaplan-Meier curves, log-rank and Cox proportional hazard regressions. (ii) identify the gene signature with optimal predictive power.
kw: Breast Cancer, Triple Negative Breast Cancer, Immune Response

title: Combination studies to enhance the activities of active targeted agents: LEE001, BGJ398, RAD001 Compound X and Compound Y.
abs: Hepatocellular cancer (HCC) is the fifth most common malignancy worldwide with 660,000 deaths annually. The unsuccessful treatment of HCC is, at least in part, due to the various, diverse molecular alterations present in the individual tumor and on the abnormal activation of multiple signaling transduction pathways controlling cell proliferation, apoptosis, and angiogenesis. Thus, there is a pressing need to identify new drugs and effective treatments of this fatal disease. HCC is highly dependent on angiogenesis for growth and metastasis. Several critical molecular signaling pathways such as Raf/MEK/ERK, PI3K/Akt/mTOR, FGFR, JAK/Stat pathways as well as cell cycle regulators are aberrant in HCC. Their activation contributes to tumor development, progression and metastasis. A considerable crosstalk and redundancy in signaling pathways are also observed in HCC. Hence targeting single molecule or signaling pathway may have a limited efficacy. In the future, targeted agents will likely be combined with cytotoxic drugs or growth factor receptor inhibitors or intracellular kinase inhibitors to effectively control advanced HCC. This multi-target approach can be accomplished by using either combinations of selective agents or agents that interfere with various targets. In this proposal we propose to evaluate the efficacy of combination therapies for HCC treatment. Understanding the mechanisms of action of these therapeutic agents and methods of combining these drugs may help to increase their efficacy, reduce toxicity, and improve overall survival and quality of life in patients of patients with HCC.
kw: targeted agents, combination studies, HCC

title: Targeting tumors harboring high incidence loss-of-function mutations in epigenetic modulators
abs: Recent whole-genome and whole-exome sequencing efforts have revealed that proteins involved in epigenetic modulation are among the most frequently mutated gene class in both solid and hematological malignancies. Members of this gene class include modifiers of DNA or histones, readers of epigenetic marks, and even histones themselves. While there are a few examples of gain-of-function (GOF) mutations/translocations (e.g. EZH2, DOT1L, MMSET, BRD1, 3 & 4), the incidence of loss-of-function (LOF) mutations in epigenetic targets is significantly greater (e.g. PBRM1, KDM6A, ARID1A, MLL2, MLL3, SETD2, SMARCA4, CREBBP, EZH2). Unlike GOF mutations that can be targeted directly with small molecules, the very nature of LOF mutations precludes this approach. Although targeting another component of the LOF pathway may be an effective strategy to inhibit tumors with these LOF mutations, in many cases there is insufficient understanding of the mechanistic consequences of these LOF mutations due to the novelty of this area.We propose to conduct shRNA screens of the druggable-genome in a panel of tumor cell lines to identify protein targets whose knockdown selectively inhibits the growth of cells bearing LOF mutations in the KDM6A. This gene is frequently mutated in at least 12 tumor types including 30% of bladder TCC.Overall, this study aims to identify potential therapeutic targets by sequencing (phase 1) and secondary sequencing or hit triaging (phase 2.1). Upon completion of this collaboration, both parties will discuss further validation.
kw: Tumor, Mutations, LOF, Epigenetics, Sequencing

title: Study on the prevalence of Fibroblast Growth Factor Receptor 1-3 (FGFR1-3) expression in squamous lung carcinoma and Asian endemic cancers
abs: We plan to interrogate several groups of cancers (with a focus on Asian endemic cancers) for mRNA expression levels of FGFR1-3: 1. Squamous non-small cell lung cancer (sqNSCLC)2. Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC)FGFR1-3 mRNA expression levels will be evaluated using two different methods, RNAscope and Nanostring technology1. Studying the prevalence of FGFR1-3 in TMAs from diverse cancers by RNA in situ hybdridization using RNAscope technology [Investigators: Tan Soo Yong (AMPL, NCCS), Daniel Tan (NCCS)]We will initially plan to stain existing TMAs with a positive control (PPIB) and negative control (dapB). If these TMAs are suitable, we will then proceed with staining for FGFR1, FGFR2 or FGFR3 respectively, on sqNSCLC (n=87) and HNSCC (n=40) TMAs. If not, we will proceed with staining for FGFR1, FGFR2 or FGFR3 respectively, on sqNSCLC (n=48) and HNSCC (n=18) tissue sections.2. Feasibility of evaluating FGFR1-3 expression levels using Nanostring technology [Investigators: Alexander Lezhava (GIS), Tan Soo Yong (AMPL), Daniel Tan (NCCS)]This will be performed in a staged manner. We will initially cut paraffin slides for 12 samples from the sqNSCLC blocks to pilot the feasibility on stored archival tissue. Blocks of various ages will be selected for these initial samples. RNA will be extracted from FFPE using standard established protocols. Should the initial 12 samples be successful, we will proceed to cut and extract remaining sqNSCLC and HNSCC tumors (same set of samples used in RNAscope) to complete the dataset. Slides will be cut at AMPL and sent to Dr Lezhava at GIS for extraction, QC and running of nanostring customized nCounter Human Cancer Reference Kit (230 genes).

title: Neuroprotective pentapeptide improves outcome after ischemic stroke
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Background: Apolipoprotein E has direct neuroprotective properties in a cell culture paradigm of glutamate excitotoxicity. It down regulates glial activation and reduces secondary neuronal injury in an in vivo model of CNS inflammation. A apoE mimetic pentapeptide, VR55, has been identified to retain anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective effects of the intact holoprotein, is well tolerated, and effectively crosses the blood brain barrier. Aim: to define the therapeutic window for neuroprotection in murine model of ischemic stroke and determine whether administration of apoE mimetic peptide improves long-term functional outcomes following stroke. Methods: Using a validated murine model of cerebral ischemia, middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO), we will establish the maximal latency for the first i.v. injection of VR55 (0.05mg/kg) following MCAO in which the peptide still confers benefit. Once we establish this maximal therapeutic latency following single dosing, we will test the hypothesis that repeat dosing might allow an increase in therapeutic latency. We will assess long-term functional outcomes for 7 consecutive days after ischemia/reperfusion, weekly for the following 3 weeks, then every other week for 2 months (total assessment time: 3 months). This data will help to inform the design of a pilot clinical trial in stroke injury.

title: Next Generation High Performance Transparent Conductors for Flexible Interactive Touch Devices
abs: The objective of the programme is to develop next generation high performance transparent conductors (TCs) based on low cost solution processing methods. We aim to integrate novel TCs into emerging interactive touch devices such as active matrix touch sensors and thin film transistors, interactive haptics and electrochromics for flexible touch screens. Current indium tin oxide (ITO) transparent conductors used in touch screens are brittle, rigid, costly, highly reflective, tinted yellow and require high vacuum fabrication procedures. It is facing severe challenges in meeting the demand of scalable touch electronics and emerging flexible devices. The proposed research thrusts focus on the materials strategies and basic understanding in developing novel flexible TCs, investigate the printability and integration of multifunctional touch devices with TCs. We propose the preparation of transparent conductors (TCs) using innovative materials made of metallic-nanocellulose conductive network. This new transparent conducting nanopaper is flexible, foldable and stretchable, making it a key enabler in wearable or flexible interactive touch electronics in the field of digital signage, commercial retail, gaming and hospitality. Our proposed flexible TCs offer high optical transmittance (above 80%) with lower sheet resistance than ITO substrates, with cost advantages and printability prospects. The presence of surface functional groups on the nanocellulosic hybrid network promotes an effective chemical coupling with the subsequent overlay active layers for device fabrication, ensuing effective electrons conduction and charge distribution while maintaining strong physical properties. Our proposed studies on the intricate interactions of TC with functional coatings will lead us to address basic scientific understanding on the electronic and ionic conductance under strain, stretch or flexural states. The envisioned outcome of this programme is to deliver solution processible TCs integrated into interactive touch-based devices to overcome the technological problems encountered with the use of ITO. The market for interactive devices such as touchscreens has a compound annual growth rate of 25% with 3 billion units by 2018 giving $32 billion in revenue.
