title: Metformin as an adjuvant anticancer therapy in the treatment of high grade glioma
abs: The prognosis of high grade glioma remains dismal despite the standard treatment with temozolomide (TMZ) and irradiation (IR). Therefore, new therapeutic strategies are needed. Studies have suggested that metformin exerts an anti-proliferative activity on glioma. This is supported by our preliminary results that demonstrated increased cell death with the combined treatment of metformin and TMZ in-vitro. We thus hypothesize that metformin will have a synergistic effect when combined with TMZ and irradiation. Preclinical studies involving glioma cell lines and xenografts will be performed to explore our study hypothesis.Cancer stem cell (CSC) theory proposes that a subpopulation of cells known as tumour initiating cells (TICs) is responsible for the therapeutic failure in glioma. We will evaluate the efficacy of metformin alone and in combination with TMZ and IR on TICs. We will also ascertain if the anti-tumour efficacy of metformin is dependent on adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase (AMPK). To further correlate our findings, we will evaluate metformin’s effects on clinical glioma samples via molecular interrogation. We will examine the EGFR status, AMPK activation pathway and selected CSC markers on these tumour samples. There has been emerging evidence to suggest the co-existence of wild-type EGFR and mutant EGFR which drives glioma progression. The mutant EGFRvIII, a common genetic aberration in gliomagenesis, may also be more sensitive to metformin due to higher glycolytic activity. We will examine the correlation between the proportion of wild-type EGFR and mutant EGFRvIII and responsiveness to metformin.The favorable safety profile and well established pharmacodynamics of metformin makes it an attractive adjuvant anticancer drug. The results from this study will enable us to validate the efficacy of metformin, explore the mechanisms by which metformin exert its tumouricidal effects and also allows us to identify potential predictive biomarkers that can be studied further in future clinical trials.
kw: Glioma, Metformin, Temozolomide, Irradiation

title: Lipid Mediators of Brain Growth and Function
abs: Low birth weight and extremely low birth weight preterm newborns are unable to obtain adequate nutrition via the GI tract require parenteral nutrition (PN) support. While PN is a life-saving intervention, infants on PN have been shown to have major negative outcomes later in life on physical and intellectual development, and increased risk for cardiovascular and metabolic disorders. It is becoming widely accepted that PN is inadequate. Importantly, the optimal composition of nutrients in PN remains unknown. We recently identified Mfsd2a as the transporter for docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) uptake by the brain. Moreover, we identify lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC) linked DHA as the physiological carrier lipid in blood for delivery of DHA to the growing brain, and show that LPCs are required for normal brain growth and function. The long-term goal is to develop LPC-based nutritionals to enhance neonatal brain development in preterm infants. The objective here, which is the next step in meeting this long-term goal, is to determine the mechanism by which LPC-DHA regulates brain growth and function. Our central hypothesis is that Mfsd2a-transported LPC-DHA is essential for neuroprogenitor cell proliferation during fetal and neonatal development. The rationale for the proposed research is that the fundamental knowledge obtained from the successful completion of this proposal will facilitate the development of nutritional formulations to improve neurocognitive outcomes of babies on PN. Guided by strong preliminary data, the goal of this application will be achieved by two specific aims: 1) To determine the function of Mfsd2a during fetal and postnatal development and in adults; 2) To determine the mechanism by which LPCs and Mfsd2a regulate brain growth. The approach is innovative because it uncovers the function of LPCs in brain growth and function. The proposed research is significant because it will provide key information for the clinical development of LPC-based PN.
kw: Blood-brain Barrier,neurogenesis, Omega-3 fatty acids, microcephaly, transporter, nutrition

title: Investigating the Autocrine Regulatory Roles of Adipokines on Adipose Tissue Browning and the Implications in Metabolic Diseases
abs: Accumulation of excess white adipose tissue (WAT) has notorious effects on the development of metabolic disorders, such as diabetes and cardiovascular diseases. On the other hand, adipose tissue is not only a passive depot for storage of excess energy as fat but also the largest endocrine organ which secretes a variety of bioactive factors called adipokines. These adipokines play essential roles in regulating energy metabolism and also influence the adipose tissue’s own remodeling and functions. We hypothesize that adipokines (e.g., apelin) locally secreted by white adipose tissue (WAT) can critically regulate the development and thermogenic activity of brown adipose tissue (BAT) and the beige transformation in WAT (collectively called as adipose tissue browning). It is also hypothesized that stimulated browning is a novel route to combat obesity and associated metabolic diseases. We aim to reveal the molecular mechanisms underlying the currently-elusive autocrine regulations of adipokines on adipose browning based on various cell and animal models, using integrative and interdisciplinary approaches.
kw: Adipose tissue, Adipokine, Brown adipocyte, Thermogenesis, Obesity, Metabolic diseases

title: Advancement of 11C Radiolabeling and Microfluidic Technologies for PET Imaging
abs: Clinicians today utilize a wide range of tools and information to help treatment, diagnosis and evaluation of a disease. One of such informative tools is positron emission tomography (PET) which can provide visualization and quantitative measurements of metabolic, biochemical and physiological function in vivo in real time using short-lived positron-emitting molecular probes (radiotracers). However, there are limited number of radioligands available for clinical studies or research todate due to the stringent criteria required of a radiotracer and the relatively complex preparation process of the radiotracer. In this project, through the collaborative expertise of a team of engineer, chemist and radiochemists, we aim to develop a technological platform (through chemical methodology and instrumentation engineering) to advance radiolabeling efficiency and expedite the development of new or existing PET imaging probes. Specifically, a versatile [11C]CO2 fixation strategy based on guanidine bases would be developed to advance the [11C]CO2 labeling technologies, expanding the scope of molecules that can be radiolabeled and increasing the portfolio of radiotracers available for PET studies. Furthermore, a versatile and tunable device platform based on the cutting-edge lab-on-chip and droplet microfluidic technology would further enhance radiolabeling efficiency and contribute to advance the transition of basic research to translational research, as well as to facilitate scientific discoveries from bench to industry. Together, it is envisioned that advancement made from this research would further fuel the developments of PET imaging as an indispensible tool in clinical and basic research, greatly impact clinical practices, and improve patients' disease outcome and their quality of lives.
kw: Positron Emission Tomography, Radiochemistry, Carbon-11, Microfluidic, Molecular Imaging, Carbon Dioxide

title: Understanding the function of the Tol-Pal complex in outer membrane biogenesis in Gram-negative bacteria
abs: Gram-negative bacteria depend for their survival on having an intact outer membrane (OM), which functions as a permeability barrier against toxic molecules, including antibiotics and detergents. The OM is an asymmetric lipid bilayer in which the outer leaflet is composed of lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and the inner leaflet of phospholipids (PLs). Proper biogenesis of the OM is achieved via the transport of beta-barrel proteins, lipoproteins, LPS and PLs from the IM, across the aqueous periplasm, and assembly into the OM. Of all these processes, PL transport is the least understood; while it is known that PL transport is bidirectional and requires the proton motive force (pmf), no protein factor that mediates either anterograde (IM-to-OM) or retrograde (OM-to-IM) transport has been identified. This proposal outlines experiments to define and characterize the function of a highly-conserved protein complex in OM biogenesis, specifically in retrograde PL transport. The Tol-Pal complex comprises five proteins (TolQRAB/Pal) that form a physical bridge connecting the membranes in the presence of the pmf. Cells lacking the Tol-Pal complex exhibit OM permeability defects and increased OM vesiculation, suggesting its importance in maintaining OM structure. We will provide molecular understanding of the OM defects observed in the absence of the Tol-Pal complex and establish a basis for the hypervesiculation phenotype. In addition, we will demonstrate a specific role of the Tol-Pal complex in retrograde PL transport using cell-based PL transport assays and in vitro activity reconstitution experiments. Our findings will answer an important fundamental question in bacteria physiology and pave the way for the discovery of new PL transport systems. Furthermore, given the role of the OM in intrinsic Gram-negative antibiotic resistance, this proposal will provide a key foundation for future studies into small molecule Tol-Pal inhibitors that may function as novel antibiotics or as adjuvants to existing antibiotics.
kw: Tol-Pal, outer membrane biogenesis, phospholipid transport, phospholipid binding

title: Dissecting the flavivirus replication complex for the discovery of antiviral inhibitors.
abs: Flaviviruses constitute major public-health problem with increasing cases of the severe hemorrhagic form every year and a large proportion of the world population at risk. No specific drug is currently available to treat dengue nor any diseases caused by flaviviruses, including West-Nile virus and Japanese encephalitis virus. In the absence of a vaccine conferring protection against the four dengue virus (DENV) serotypes, outbreak control and patient care has to rely on symptomatic treatment and specific antivirals. Plus-strand RNA virus replication occurs in association with cytoplasmic host-cell membranes, where both viral and cellular host factors cooperate within organelle-like structures called replication complex (RC). A major impediment in developing drugs targeting the DENV RC is that both its morphology and composition, the interplay between its molecular constituents as well as the precise molecular mechanisms for viral RNA replication are still elusive. Individual protein components of the RC were characterized both at the functional and structural level and several human and insect proteins putatively linked to DENV replication have been identified. However a main challenge lying ahead is a better understanding of the entire flavirus RC. The study proposed here combines biochemical, structural and virology approaches to reveal key interactions at the core of the DENV RC that will inform and accelerate drug discovery. We will determine novel crystal structures for non-structural proteins NS2B-NS3, NS4B and NS5 as multi-proteins assemblies and bound to RNA, to capture various stages of viral replication. The work will capitalize on recent progress on the NS4B and NS5 protein for which we obtained crystals, and whose network of interactions with NS2B-NS3 will be addressed. Inhibitors targeting the viral RC will serve as probes to further our understanding of its structure. The most promising inhibitors will be developed into drug candidates.
kw: flavivirus, replication complex, viral non structural proteins, lead compound

title: Characterization of innate immune disruption by flaviviral subgenomic RNA (sfRNA)
abs: Disruption of the innate immune response is a common mechanism for viral immune evasion, but few studies describe immune disruption by viral RNAs[1]. Subgenomic flaviviral RNA (sfRNA) was shown to disrupt the innate immune response during West Nile Virus (WNV) and Japanese Encephalitis Virus (JEV) infection[2, 3] and our laboratory uncovered the first mechanism of sfRNA action with Dengue virus (DENV) (Bidet et al., submitted). SfRNA results from incomplete degradation of the genomic RNA of flaviviruses and is made during infection by mosquito- and tick-borne flaviviruses, but not pestiviruses and hepaciviruses[4, 5]. We hypothesize sfRNA-mediated disruption of the innate immune response is a common feature of flavivirus infection and a potential target for antiviral therapies. We performed RNA chromatography and quantitative mass spectrometry to identify cellular proteins that interact with DENV and Yellow Fever virus (YFV) sequences found in the sfRNA and identified PRKRA, which activates PKR and RIG-I during stress or infection[6, 7]. In Specific Aim I, we will determine if PRKRA-sfRNA interaction disrupts the innate immune response to DENV or YFV infection, map interaction sites for PRKRA and sfRNA and define the role of PRKRA-sfRNA interaction in modulating the innate immune response. In Specific Aim II, we will identify cellular proteins that bind sfRNA sequences from several flaviviruses, particularly focusing on clinical isolates of DENV-1-4, to determine if sfRNA-mediated disruption of the innate immune response occurs through a common set of cellular proteins for all four DENV serotypes, or a diverse group of serotype-specific cellular proteins. In Specific Aim III, we will perform a screen for pharmacological inhibitors of protein-sfRNA interactions to identify compounds that reconstitute the innate immune response DENV infection. The specific aims of this proposal will identify novel targets for therapeutics and develop alternative approaches for treating flavivirus infections and significantly impact antiviral research.
kw: Dengue, Antiviral therapies, Innate immunity,RNA, Host-virus interactions, Host cell proteins

title: The Role of Cadherin-13 (CDH13) in the Development and Function of the Brain Circuitry and Its Implication for Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASDs).
abs: Autism spectrum disorders (ASDs) constitute complex, heritable, neuropsychiatric disorders. Recent genomics studies have been identified a number of susceptibility genes, but how these genes cause ASDs is largely unknown. Our proposal focuses on a neural cell adhesion molecule, cadherin-13 (CDH13), that we have independently identified in a genetic screen of 500 ASD patients. The identification of CDH13 as having the highest number of missense/nonsense mutations out of 700 ASD candidate genes provides strong support for an involvement of CDH13 in synaptic formation/plasticity, which may underlie the etiology of ASDs. Therefore, we aim: 1) to establish the link between our identified ASD mutations in CDH13 and the assembly and maintenance of central synapses; 2) to develop a CDH13 mouse model to explore the roles of CDH13 in synaptic plasticity, learning and memory, and ASD related behaviors. For the first aim, we will examine whether and how ASD variants of CDH13 affect excitatory and inhibitory synapse density, synapse morphology, synaptic transmission using dissociated cortical neurons and organotypic cortical slices. Specifically, we will test whether the expression of ASD variants of CDH13 can restore the structural and functional synaptic impairments caused by CDH13 knockdown. For the second aim, we will generate mice with specific deletion of CDH13 in the forebrain using newly generated CDH13-floxed mice. Using these mouse lines, we will evaluate the role of CDH13 on two forms of long-lasting changes in synaptic efficacy. Additionally, we will subject these mice to a battery of spatial and associative learning and memory tasks and will evaluate autism-like behaviors such as repetitive movements, vocal communications, and social behavior paradigms on these mice. Together, our studies may reveal insights how ASD susceptibility gene affect synapse formation, neuronal network, and animal behavior and help us to develop diagnostic and/or therapeutic strategies for ASD patients
kw: Autism, Synaptic plasticity, Cell-adhesion protein, Behavior, CDH13

title: Characterization of Annexin A1 as a Clinically Useful Biomarker of Responsiveness to PPARG Ligand Therapy in Triple Negative Breast Cancer
abs: The basal-like breast cancer subtype is predominantly lacking estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, and C-erb B2 receptor, aptly named triple negative breast cancer (TNBC). TNBC lacks defined targeted therapies, aggressive behavior, distinct patterns of metastasis and, thereby, a poor clinical outcome. Thus, identifying markers for targeted therapy in TNBC is of pressing need. Breast cancers are often associated with dysregulated expression of growth factors, growth factor receptors as well as kinases in the growth factor signaling pathways, including Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARG), which belongs to the nuclear hormone receptor superfamily of ligand-activated transcription factors. Our preliminary findings established basal and claudin-low subtypes of breast cancer (TNBC types) express significantly higher levels of Annexin A1 (ANXA1). Using model cell lines of TNBC we show that expression of ANXA1 mediates chemosensitivity to PPARG ligands via interaction with the “death-switch” RIP-1 and initiation of apoptosis cascade. This proposal is designed not only to provide evidence for ANXA1 as a clinically useful biomarker but also to provide preclinical evaluation on an in-house PPARG drug, CN-1 and use of a Phase II-completed PPARG drug, CS7017. Herein, we propose:1) To better define the prognostic value of ANXA1 expression in breast cancer patients.2) To elucidate the consequences of gain and loss of function of ANXA1 to our in-house PPARG ligand, CN-1 and CS7017.3) Assess the mechanism(s) involved in the upregulation of ANXA1 gene expression by CN-1 and CS7017 in MDA-MB-231 and BT549 cells.4) Elucidate mechanism of deubiqutination of RIP-1 by CN-1 and CS7017.5) Pharmacokinetic and nude mouse xenograft studies for CN-1.Since biomarker measurements have become an essential component of oncology drug development, particularly so in this era of targeted therapies, this study would demonstrate the suitability of using baseline expressions of PPARG and ANXA1 stratifying TNBC patients for PPARG ligand therapy.
kw: Triple Negative Breast Cancer, Therapeutic biomarker, Novel PPARG ligands, RIP-1 mediated cell death, Annexin A-1

title: Alternative splicing and RNA editing of CaV1.3 channels: implications on neuronal function and neurological disorders
abs: Mutations in the CaV1.3 channel are associated with hearing loss, slow heart rate, adenomas and anxiety-like behaviours. Alternative splicing and RNA editing of the CaV1.3 channels calibrate Ca2+ concentration within the neuron. Any imbalance in availability of Ca2+ is likely to negatively affect various neurological functions.We therefore hypothesize that sustained alterations in alternative splicing and RNA editing of CaV1.3 channels can impair neuronal and neurological functions by disrupting Ca2+ homeostasis leading to (i) altered neuronal excitability and behaviour or (ii) lysosomal stress that will result in neuronal death.The specific aims are:(1) To characterize the CaV1.3 ECS-/- mice and determine the physiological role of RNA editing in the IQ-domain of CaV1.3 channels in relation to neurological defects such as anxiety, circadian rhythm or motoric disorders. (2) To determine the role of RNA binding splicing factors in tissue-specific repression of ADAR2-mediated CaV1.3 IQ-domain editing and changes in global editing due to lack of these repressors. (3) To determine the mechanism by which various C-terminal alternatively spliced variants and edited channels influence lysosomal function through modulating the acidification process. From a previous BMRC grant, we have generated ECS-/- mice that express unedited IQ-domain of the CaV1.3 channels and we have identified SRSF9 splicing factor that repressed IQ-domain editing. This proposal will test the significance of RNA editing in behavioural studies of the ECS knock-out mice and to understand the mechanism through which SRSF9 inhibits IQ-domain editing. By RNAseq we aim to add depth into investigating global changes in gene transcription and identify other editing sites inhibited by SRSF9. We will investigate how in a CaV1.3 splice-variant selective manner, Ca2+ influx triggers NO production and affect ATP13A2 activity to lead to reduction in lysosomal function. This proposal will provide a different angle to understanding of Parkinson’s disease, circadian rhythm and anxiety.
kw: Alternative Splicing; RNA Editing; L-type Calcium Channel; Lysosomal function; neurological disorder

title: Blood banking-induced impairment of transfusion efficacy for hemorrhagic shock: Effects on hemodynamics and gas transport
abs: Red blood cell (RBC) transfusion is a common clinical intervention for acute blood loss (hemorrhage). Although the clinical outcome of the RBC transfusion is generally positive, the efficacy of using ‘Aged’ RBCs to achieve successful clinical outcomes from the transfusion is still under debate. In particular, the prolonged storage causes biochemical and biomechanical changes in RBCs which thereby reduces the viability and functionality of the cells (the RBC ‘storage lesions’). Despite the potential detrimental effects of using stored RBCs, information on how the RBC storage lesion influences the hemodynamics and gas transport in the microvascular network is currently limited. Therefore, this research proposal aims to highlight the mechanism on how stored RBCs modulate the capability of microvascular perfusion. The efficacy of using stored RBCs in the transfusion for maintaining the microcirculatory tissue perfusion will be evaluated in accordance with the following specific aims. Firstly, the alterations in biochemical and biomechanical properties of the stored RBCs will be quantified in vitro, and their effects on hemodynamics will be examined through an in vitro artificial microvascular network. Secondly, this research proposes to investigate the partitioning behavior of stored RBCs in a rat cremaster muscle arteriolar network with the consideration of RBC redistribution and gas transport, in order to further elucidate the dynamics of stored RBCs in vivo. Lastly, a computational model for the prediction of multi-cell dynamics with gas transport will be developed to highlight the underlying mechanism of the storage-induced RBC impairments on the microcirculatory tissue perfusion. The scientific findings from this proposed research will provide firm evidence to unveil the detailed mechanism in explaining the effects of storage-induced RBC lesion on microvascular tissue perfusion. This can also provide possible insights beyond the current knowledge of transfusion medicine with regards to the efficacy and usage of stored blood for transfusion.
kw: Blood transfusion, Blood storage lesion, Microcirculation, Blood rheology, Hemodynamics, Gas transport

title: Origin and Mechanisms of Pluripotency Regulated by STAT3
abs: Aims are to fully understand a STAT3 initiated remodeling events that may have essential roles for regulation of pluripotency. Critically shown that regulatory circuitry, including Oct4 and Nanog during early embryogenesis, is directly regulated by STAT3 in vivo during early embryonic development. STAT3 is essential for the formation of the inner cell mass (ICM), source of embryonic stem cells (ESCs) during embryo development. STAT3 is highly expressed in mouse oocytes and becomes phosphorylated and translocates to the nucleus in the 4-cell and later stage embryos. Using genetically modified mouse strains to eliminate Stat3 in oocytes and embryos, we establish that STAT3 is essential for maintenance of ICM lineages but not for trophectoderm (TE) formation. We further show that STAT3 directly binds to the Oct4 (Pou5F1) and Nanog distal enhancers, modulating their expression to maintain pluripotency of mouse embryonic and induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells. These results provide a novel model of cell-fate determination operating through STAT3 in the preimplantation embryo and in pluripotent stem cells in vivo. With this application, we will further investigate the molecular mechanism of pluripotency regulated by STAT3. Using Inducible Pluripotent Stem Cells (iPS) as a model system to reveal possible reprogram mechanisms initiated or maintained by STAT3. Determine a novel pathway from STAT3 to NuRD complex and its key roles in iPS cell induction. Our findings should significantly contribute to a better understanding of iPS cells and their applications in therapies in regenerative medicine.
kw: Pluripotency, iPSc, STAT3, Gene Regulation, Stem Cells, DNA methylation

title: Development of Xanthone-Derived Antibiotics as Therapeutics for Multidrug-Resistant Gram-Positive Pathogen Infections
abs: Antibiotic resistance is a critical global healthcare problem and described by clinicians as a “perfect storm”. Antimicrobials which selectively interfere with prokaryotic membrane physiology are attractive agents for combating the rapidly increasing antibiotic resistance. Membrane-active antimicrobials are promising antibiotics due to their advantages of rapid bactericidal action and minimal tendency to develop resistance. Recently, we have carried out studies of structure-activity relationships of a new family of membrane-active antimicrobials derived from xanthone/?-mangostin. Two lead compounds AM-052 and AM-218 were identified which showed potent in vitro antimicrobial activity, especially against multidrug-resistant (MDR) Gram-positive bacteria, e.g., methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium (VRE). Using microbiological, biophysical and in silico approaches, we have determined that coupling a cationic residue/amines with high pKa values to the hydrophobic xanthone is a key determinant of membrane selectivity. The overall hypothesis of this proposal is that the hydrophobic xanthone core promotes membrane interactions leading to disruption and bacteria death, but that the structures can be modified at certain sites for increased biocompatibility. This study will use three specific aims to identify the best characteristics for lead compounds: Structural parameters of AM-218 and AM-052 will be optimized by synthesizing specific analogues to enhance their biocompatibility and selectivity. Coupling cationic residues (Arg) with high pKa value will form a series of peptidomimetics with a sequence of (Arg)n-Xan-(Arg)n (n=1-3) by mimicking the amphiphilic conformation of cationic antimicrobial peptides. Then pharmacological properties of the four most potent compounds will be studied. The pharmacokinetic (PK) characteristics will be evaluated to determine their doses. Finally, we will evaluate the in vivo efficacy of two best compounds in an animal model of infective endocarditis using MRSA and VRE. The outcome of this work will highlight a new drug for Phase I clinical trials and a new approach for developing antibiotics.
kw: Xanthone, membrane-targeting, antibiotics, lead optimization, pharmacokinetic (PK), infective endocarditis (IE)

title: Characterization of a novel non-coding RNA mediated signaling mechanism through which Myostatin regulates postnatal muscle growth and wasting
abs: Myostatin (Mstn), a TGF-? superfamily member, is a secreted growth factor and well-characterized negative regulator of myogenesis. Given that inactivation of Mstn leads to increased muscle growth and enhanced insulin sensitivity, there is a huge interest in identifying the mediators of Mstn function and developing Mstn-based therapies. Although Mstn function in muscle growth and metabolism is well known, its downstream effector molecules are not fully elucidated. Our recent molecular search identified that miR-34a expression is positively regulated by Mstn. Molecular analysis further established that over expression of miR-34a in myoblasts completely phenocopies Mstn over expression effects, and as such inhibits myogenesis. Much like Mstn, over expression of miR-34a also resulted in increased insulin resistance. In addition, we find elevated Mstn and miR-34a expression in aged muscles that are undergoing sarcopenia, an aging-related form of muscle wasting. Based on these compelling data we hypothesize that Mstn induces muscle wasting and insulin resistance by promoting the up regulation of miR-34a expression. To prove this hypothesis, we will first identify the mechanism through which Mstn induces miR-34a expression using a miR-34a enhancer-reporter system in myoblasts. Secondly, we will determine whether or not miR-34a is required for Mstn-mediated inhibition of myogenesis, by assessing if Mstn can negatively regulate myogenesis in miR-34a-/- muscles and myoblasts. Since lack of Mstn increases insulin sensitivity and alleviates sarcopenia, we will further investigate if miR-34a-/- mice have increased muscle mass, reduced sarcopenia, enhanced insulin sensitivity and are resistant to diet-induced obesity. Collectively, these data will further advance the field by identifying an important non-coding RNA signaling intermediate for Mstn. Earlier research has clearly established that prolonged absence of Mstn alleviates sarcopenia and overcomes insulin resistance and therefore, identifying a critical downstream mediator of Mstn function will help in drug discovery in metabolic medicine.
kw: myostatin, miR-34, sarcopenia, muscle wasting, myogenesis

title: Lipid-based Pro-drug Development for Glioblastoma
abs: Malignant gliomas are the most frequent cancers originating from the central nervous system. Glioblastoma (GBM) (World Health Organization (WHO) grade IV glioma) is the most common and biologically aggressive subtype. GBM is also the most common malignant primary central nervous system tumor in Singapore, accounting for up to 48% of intracranial glioma. It is a highly aggressive tumor with a dismal prognosis. One of the factors that limit the efficacy of chemotherapeutic agents is the presence of the blood-brain barrier (BBB) that impairs the delivery of cytotoxic agents to the brain tumor. A lack of strategies to drug delivery across the BBB is a major barrier to developing therapeutic treatments for GBM. We recently identified the previously orphaned transporter Mfsd2a to be exclusively expressed in endothelium of the blood-brain barrier of micro-vessels, as the major transporter for DHA uptake into brain. Cell-based and in vivo studies indicated that Mfsd2a transported DHA in the form of lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC). Moreover, we have identified a minimum chemical scaffold based on the LPC structure for transport via Mfsd2a to the brain. Our central goal is to develop pro-drugs using the LPC scaffold (i.e. pharmacophore) that have efficacy against GBM tumors. The rationale for the proposed research is that LPC chemistry can be exploited for drug delivery across the BBB via Mfsd2a. The goal of this application will be achieved by two specific aims: 1) To identify and synthesize LPC-based pro-drugs for treating GBM; and 2) To determine the efficacy of LPC-based pro-drugs in a pre-clinical mouse model. The approach is innovative because it develops technology for the delivery of therapeutics to the brain that will utilize Mfsd2a and novel LPC chemistry. The proposed research is significant because it is expected to result in the development of novel LPC-based therapeutics to treat GBM.
kw: Blood-brain Barrier, glioblastoma, lysolipids, Pro-drug, transporter, High-throughput screen

title: Generation of zone-specific chondrocytes from mesenchymal stem cells with a nanotopographic platform for injectable delivery of bilayered construct for cartilage repair.
abs: Current clinical approaches for cartilage repair have not been able to restore the hierarchically organized architecture of normal articular cartilage. Although mimicking the zonal organization of articular cartilage in neo-tissue by the use of zonal chondrocyte subpopulations could enhance the functionality of the graft, the engineering of stratified functional tissue has not yet been realized due to the lack of specific zonal chondrocyte isolation protocols and limited amounts of donor tissue to yield adequate numbers of viable zonal cells. We have successful derived zone-specific cartilage phenotypes by subjecting mesenchymal stem cell (MSC) differentiation on specific nano-topographic surfaces. We hypothesise that MSCs differentiated on specific nano-topographic patterns can provide phenotypically stable and defined chondrocytes, and when delivered as bilayered hydrogel construct at cartilage defect site, will facilitate the formation of hierarchically organized cartilage tissue in vivo. Our strategy is to subject MSC chondrogenic differentiation on 2D nano-patterned surfaces to derive superficial zone and middle/deep zone like chondrocytes. After enzymatic release, these pre-differentiated cells will be delivered sequentially, as injectable bilayered hydrogel construct at the site of cartilage defect. The proposal will entail (1) optimisation of MSC differentiation on 2D nano-patterned surfaces to produce stable, zone-specific chondrocytes in 3D hydrogel culture; (2) in vitro characterisation of the bilayered hydrogel construct, and (3) In vivo study on the efficacy of injectable delivery of bilayered phenotypically distinct chondrogenic cells for generation of zonally organized cartilage tissue in a rabbit defect model.This approach provides a straight forward method of obtaining large quantities of zone-specific chondrocytes. Delivery of the chondrocyte subpopulations in a sequential injectable approach can cater to defects of variable shape and size, and easily adopted for clinical application. The outcome of this study will contribute to the development of engineering zonally stratified cartilage constructs for functional repair of critical size cartilage defects.
kw: Cartilage repair, Mesenchymal stem cells, Zone-specific chondrocytes, Nano-topography, Injectable hydrogel

title: The Role of Physiologic Hypoxia in the Pathogenesis of Chronic Myeloid Leukaemia
abs: Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) targeting the oncogenic BCR-ABL1 kinase have led to remarkable responses in patients with chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML), but do not eliminate the leukaemia stem cells (LSC) that are thought to initiate and maintain the condition. Accordingly, even in patients with long-term complete molecular responses, recrudescent disease frequently occurs upon TKI cessation. As a result, most patients will require life-long TKI therapy to prevent outgrowth of CML progenitors from LSCs. Given the high cost of TKI therapy and the increasing prevalence of CML, this situation presents a serious financial challenge to patients as well as national healthcare systems. We recently indentified physiologic hypoxia as a critical microenvironmental factor maintaining CML LSC function and impairing TKI-induced apoptosis. Specifically, we found that hypoxia induced a HIF-dependent, but BCR-ABL1-independent, transcriptional programme that could be genetically disabled to impair LSC function. Because we also observed changes in pre-mRNA splicing regulators in hypoxia, and find that an oncogenic splicing factor, SRSF1, is regulated by BCR-ABL1 in CML cells, we will explore the contribution of hypoxia and BCR-ABL1 toward modulating alternative splicing (AS) in CML. By understanding how physiologic hypoxia enables CML LSCs to evade therapy through HIF-dependent mechanisms as well as through AS, we will facilitate the development of novel strategies to eradicate CML LSCs. In Aim 1, we will elucidate the role of HIF2-alpha in CML. In Aim 2 we will determine the role of hypoxia-induced genes in CML LSC maintenance and TKI-resistance. In Aim 3, we will determine the contribution of altered pre-mRNA splicing to CML LSC function and TKI resistance. Because the prevalence of CML is increasing across the world, and TKIs are non-curative, this project will address a major health problem for patients in Singapore and globally.
kw: Leukaemia stem cell, Drug resistance, Alternative splicing , Hypoxia, Microenvironment

title: Evaluation of plaque characteristics, plaque inflammation and embolic potential with high resolution cerebrovascular ultrasonography, high resolution magnetic resonance imaging and Positron Emission Tomography imaging in ischemic stroke patients with symptomatic carotid stenosis
abs: Background and hypothesis- Ischemic stroke is a leading cause of death and long-term disability in Singapore. Carotid atherosclerosis accounts for about 20% of ischemic stroke. The risk of recurrent stroke in carotid disease has traditionally been estimated on the degree of stenosis. It does not take into account the plaque morphology, plaque inflammation and its embolic potential. Accumulating evidence indicates that inflammation is of key importance in plaque destabilisation, local thrombosis, cerebral embolization and stroke. Carotid plaque inflammation can be evaluated with high resolution magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and positron emission tomography (PET) while its embolic potential may be determined with transcranial Doppler (TCD) for developing a model for risk stratification. We hypothesise that plaque inflammation (with MRI and PET) in recently-symptomatic ischemic stroke patients with carotid stenosis (>50% diameter reduction), combined with positive TCD-emboli monitoring will be associated with increased risk of recurrent stroke at 90 days, after adjusting for degree of lumen stenosis and other co-variates.Methods- It is a prospective cohort study. Ambulatory patients with ischemic stroke or TIA (within 7 days of clinical presentation) and carotid stenosis (>50%) will be identified, have baseline procedures (clinical assessments, high sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP) measurement, carotid high resolution MRI, PET/CT, and cervical duplex ultrasonography) and followed for recurrent stroke for 90 days. All patients will receive medical and carotid revascularisation treatment in accordance with current guidelines as standard of care. Primary outcome will be assessed for ischemic event within 90 days not related to revascularisation. Secondary outcome will be any recurrent stroke, Myocardial infarction or death due to vascular events and modified Rankin Scale at 3 months.Conclusion: Advanced imaging of carotid plaque inflammation and assessment of embolic potential in patients with symptomatic carotid stenosis will help in improved risk stratification in patients presenting with recent cerebrovascular ischemia.
kw: acute ischemic stroke; carotid stenosis; plaque inflammation; PET; ultrasonography; transcranial Doppler

title: Reprogramming of Colorectal Cancer Cells: Up-regulation of Cancer Stem Cell Markers for Immune Intervention
abs: Aim: We aim at (1) understanding the transcriptional regulation of the CD24 gene that encodes a cancer stem cell (CSC) marker and (2) establishing the translation of the findings into a dendritic cell (DC) therapy protocol to target CSCs. Hypothesis: Our preliminary findings have shown that in human colorectal cancer (CRC) cells the ectopic expression of a set of reprogramming factors, named as OSKM factors, promotes CSC tumorsphere formation. We identified CD24 to be the consistently up-regulated marker in the modified cells. Based on these findings and considering the bioinformatics analysis of the CD24 core promoter and intron regions, we hypothesize that two of the OSKM factors, Sox2 and Klf4, might function as the major upstream regulatory molecules for CD24 expression and can in turn control the CSC phenotype of CRC cells. Furthermore, since cancer immunotherapy via DCs, also known as DC vaccination, has been explored as a possible adjuvant treatment for CRC, we envision that tumorspheres derived from the reprogrammed CRC cell lines can be used as a readily accessible, generic source to provide CSC-related antigens for DC vaccination. Methodology: In seeking the evidence supporting the hypotheses, the OSKM genes are inserted into CRC cell genome using zinc-finger nuclease technology to induce cancer cell reprogramming. CSC-like cells are then enriched from the OSKM-expressing CRC cells under a tumorsphere forming culture condition for studies addressing the above two specific aims. Clinical Significance: Colorectal CSCs are considered to be responsible for tumorigenesis, cancer recurrence, metastasis, and the failure of CRC treatment. Given the significant gap in our current knowledge on the transcriptional regulation of CSC markers and the technical gap in large-scale production of CSCs for DC vaccination, the success of this project will advance our understanding of CSC biology and suggest the feasibility of a novel adjuvant therapy for CRC.
kw: Colorectal cancer, Cancer stem cell, Cell re-programming, Transcriptional regulation, Dendritic cell, Cancer immunotherapy

title: Whole-exome sequencing to identify genetic variants associated with severe childhood obesity, and tracking the changing prevalence of obesity related complications
abs: Susceptibility variants contributing to obesity are being uncovered by candidate gene approach, genome wide linkage studies, and genome wide association studies (GWAS), but the collective effect is small and does not explain most of the BMI heritability. We propose a whole exome sequencing (WES) approach to systematically interrogate coding variants and to identify novel obesity loci in 130 Chinese subjects from our existing cohort of Singaporean severe early-onset obese subjects, and an additional ~200 subjects will be recruited to augment this. Sequencing will be performed at high coverage (50X) on the Illumina-HiSeq platform. Statistical association tests will be performed for identified variants (single-variant analysis and gene-based mutational load test) using normal, lean (BMI between 18.5 and 23 kg/m2) adult Singaporean Chinese individuals as controls (N=500). A stringent approach will be undertaken to identify and prioritize novel obesity variants, including checks with genotype data, through bioinformatics tools for predicting functional effects and by re-sequencing and/or de novo genotyping of top hits. We will replicate top hits by targeted sequencing in 96 (out of 200 subjects) extreme obese Chinese children and through de novo genotyping in additional Chinese children with extreme BMI from childhood datasets from Singapore and China. We will study the in-vitro functions of the aberrant proteins of novel variants. Our secondary aim is to assess the change in prevalence of obesity related complications over 15 years by recruiting 350 severely obese children and compare against the complications prevalence data obtained from an NMRC funded childhood obesity study in 2001-2004. The identification of novel genes for extreme early-onset obesity can provide novel insights into human weight regulation mechanisms and new therapeutic targets for drug development, and also identification of high-risk children so that potential intervention measures can be implemented at an early stage of life.
kw: Obesity, childhood obesity, genetics, exome sequencing, functional validation

title: Deciphering the mechanism of action of a novel antifungal agent with the use of Candida albicans haploids
abs: Candida albicans is a major fungal pathogen of humans, affecting millions and killing hundreds of thousands annually. Emerging drug resistance and undesirable properties of existing antifungal agents are major problems in managing C. albicans infections. We recently discovered a novel antifungal compound SM21 with high potency and low toxicity. However, the mechanism of action (MoA) remains unknown, hindering its further development into antifungal drugs. This proposal aims to decipher the MoA of SM21.We will use the newly discovered C. albicans haploids in a genetic screen to first identify mutations that cause SM21 resistance. By sequentially exposing C. albicans haploids to increasing concentrations of SM21, we have isolated resistant mutants (SM21-Rs). We hypothesize that mutations disrupting the SM21 target(s) or its uptake underlie the resistance. Therefore, we will perform Next Generation Sequencing on SM21-R and identify the common mutations by comparative genomics. To verify SM21 target(s), we will introduce the identified mutations into or delete the candidate genes individually in wild-type haploid and diploid C. albicans before testing for SM21 resistance. Next, we will use a combination of genetic, molecular-biological, and biochemical approaches to functionally characterize the SM21 resistance gene(s) and its encoded protein. Current antifungal agents often target the plasma membrane or cell wall. Our preliminary results suggest that SM21 damages the cell surface. Thus, we will investigate this possibility by pulse-labelling C. albicans cells with radioactive precursors of cell wall and membrane components and tracing their cellular distributions. Moreover, we will use a mass spectrometry-based approach to investigate proteome changes in SM21-treated cells, focusing on cell wall and cytosolic fractions. This study is expected to provide key information on the MoA of SM21 required for developing it into antifungal drugs, and serve as a proof-of-principle for using C. albicans haploids as an effective tool in drug discovery.
kw: Candida albicans, antifungal, haploid

title: Psychosocial, lifestyle, behavioural, biological and genetic determinants of healthy ageing in the Singapore Longitudinal Ageing Studies
abs: The aims are to explore psychosocial, lifestyle, behavioural, biological and genetic determinants of healthy and successful ageing (HSA) in the Singapore Longitudinal Ageing Studies (SLAS). The general hypothesis is that HSA is a complex and multidimensional trait, and its several phenotypic presentations are determined by many genetic and environmental factors. Specific hypotheses will test the independent associations and predictions of HSA by (1) health-related behaviors and lifestyles, their personality and social behavioural determinants, (2) novel vascular and endothelial function, and immune ageing and inflammation biomarkers, (3) gene variants associated with biological pathways involved in ageing, age-related diseases and functional declines, and personality/behavioural traits (4) gene-gene, gene-environmental interactions and epigenetic marks. The PI started the SLAS in 2004, a population-based cohort study of ageing and health among Singaporeans aged 55 and over (N?6,000).The subjects will be recruited from continued follow up of SLAS1 and SLAS2 cohorts for additional 3 or more years and from a new multi-ethnic cohort of octogenarians (SLAS3).The study will define biological phenotypes of biological ageing (quantitative trait variable), healthy ageing (categorical state variable) and a bio-psycho-socio-behavioural phenotype (successful ageing) for comparison with their counterparts (controls). Exploration of psychobiological, vascular and immune factors will involve measures of personality and social behavioural traits (conscientiousness, harm avoidance, agreeableness, openness to experience, and altruism) associated with positive social, emotional and cognitive behaviours and healthy lifestyles; cellular and molecular biomarkers of immunosenescence (e.g. CD8+CD28-CD27+) and ‘inflammageing’ cytokines biomarkers, physiological and molecular biomarkers of vascular and endothelial functions (NTproBNP,GDF15, Galectin 3, etc), and their associated genetic and epigenetic markers. The research advances understanding of biological ageing and facilitates the identification of individuals for more effective biological, behavioural or environmental interventions to extend healthy and productive lifespan, impacting on public health and clinical interventions to promote healthy ageing and quality of life.
kw: Healthy Ageing, Biological Ageing, Lifestyle, Nutrition, Genetic, Immune Ageing

title: Identification of novel components of lipid signaling pathways as therapeutic targets for inflammatory pain
abs: Orofacial pain is a family of nociceptive pathologies and includes dental pain, temporomandibular disorders, neurovascular disorders and migraine, and a number of idiopathic conditions. It is one of the most common forms of nociceptive disability, affecting an estimated 26% of the general population. Currently, no effective therapies are available for chronic orofacial pain, creating a significant unmet medical need. Lysolipids and sphingolipids are known to be important bioactive molecules that regulate neurological processes, but their involvement in pain is poorly understood. Our group, though a series of published studies, has demonstrated that bioactive lipids are essential components orofacial pain. Surprisingly, we found that these lipids are unlikely to belong to the eicosanoid family of inflammatory lipids, but instead appear to be lysolipids. We hypothesize that specific lysolipid/sphingolipid signaling events mediate orofacial pain sensitivity, and represent novel, druggable targets for analgesic therapy.The proposed project will identify specific bioactive lipids that mediate orofacial pain, and will characterize this signaling pathway. This will be done by inducing controlled derangements of lipid profiles both genetically (with knockout mice) and pharmacologically (with intracranial injection of enzyme inhibitors) that are characterized by advanced lipidomic analyses. The animals will then be evaluated in our fully-validated model for orofacial pain to correlate specific lipid species with pain sensitivity. Subsequent molecular and functional studies will be performed to identify druggable targets and lead drug compounds. The research team combines expertise in neurobiology and pain models (A/Prof. Ong), with lysolipid/sphingolipid metabolism and signaling (Dr. Herr). All methodologies are validated in numerous high-impact publications, but will be applied in a novel, creative context. It has been over 50 years since the development of new class of analgesics. Development of a drug with a novel mechanism of action would represent a major breakthrough.
kw: Orofacial pain, lipids, inflammation

title: Characterization of a novel leukemia gene MLL5 as a partner of the hematopoietic master regulator RUNX1
abs: Runt-related transcription factor 1 (RUNX1) is essential for hematopoiesis and among the most documented leukemia genes. Mixed Lineage Leukemia 5 (MLL5) has been suspected to be a leukemia gene located within one of the most frequently deleted chromosomal region, 7q22, in human myeloid leukemia, and is a family gene of the most characterized leukemia gene, MLL1. However, how MLL5 involves in both normal hematopoiesis and leukemogenesis remains poorly understood.Our preliminary studies suggest that MLL5 shares remarkable similarities with RUNX1 in their functions to maintain hematopoietic stem cell integrity. Notably, we found that MLL5 physically and functionally interacts with RUNX1. Clinical observation clearly shows that low MLL5 expression are associated with poorer prognosis in acute myeloid leukemia (AML), in particular in subtypes with RUNX1 related genetic abnormalities. We hence hypothesize that MLL5 may function in collaboration with RUNX1 in normal hematopoiesis and any defects in these two molecules contribute to leukemogenesis. In this proposal, we aim to validate whether MLL5 is a novel myeloid leukemia gene using conditional knockout mouse strategy and targeted deep sequencing of human leukemia samples. Subsequently, we intensively examine the precise molecular mechanism mediated by MLL5 and RUNX1 in normal and pathological hematopoiesis, by employing assays to capture defects in transcription, DNA repair, chromosomal stability, protein stability, and subcellular localization. Lastly, we test the combinatorial treatment of PARP inhibitor and BET inhibitor which are expected to target abnormalities in RUNX and MLL respectively, using in vitro assay and in vivo xenograft models. We believe the knowledge generated from this study will not only shed light on the currently unknown role of MLL5 in leukemogenesis but also contribute to drug development for RUNX-related leukemia and other cancers.
kw: leukemia, mouse model, Runx, MLL5, DNA repair

title: RNA editing: a novel major contributor to gastric cancer and clinical implications
abs: Gastric cancer (Gastric adenocarcinoma) is one of the most common and deadly types of cancer worldwide with few effective treatment options available and it is particularly prevalent in Asian countries. Up to now, most cancer scientists have focused on studying DNA mutations which convey irreversible changes in the genome. However, discoveries in last decade completely changed our views on RNA and the enormous diversity that can be generated at the RNA level. RNA editing may lead to tumor-specific “RNA mutation”, exceeding the number of genomic mutations. In humans, the most frequent type of editing is the conversion of adenosine to inosine (A-to-I), which is catalyzed by the double-stranded RNA (dsRNA)-specific ADAR (Adenosine DeAminase that act on RNA) family of protein. In this proposed research, we will be the first group worldwide to exploit “RNA editing/mutation” across the Gastric cancer transcriptome, in the light of our previous studies 1) identifying the widespread frequency of editing across human liver cancer transcriptome, and 2) highlighting links between RNA editing imbalance and tumorigenesis in two types of gastrointestinal (GI) cancers, liver cancer and esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC). Our preliminary data also suggested that A-to-I RNA editing is dysregulated in Gastric cancer. The broad objective is to further characterize the RNA editing enzyme ADARs and A-to-I RNA editome of Gastric cancer, uncover key editing targets for better classifying and diagnosing Gastric cancer, and investigate the biological importance of RNA editing events within coding and non-coding regions. A final aim is reserved for more exploratory studies to develop feasible therapeutic approaches for targeting this epigenetic process.
kw: Gastric cancer, ADARs, Adenosine-to-Inosine, RNA editing, epigenetics, therapeutics

title: The microtubule dynamics regulated by TUBGCP4 and NAT10 in the Stem-A molecular subtype of epithelial ovarian cancer and the clinical implication in cancer therapy.
abs: Epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC) is highly heterogeneous with five distinct subgroups, Epi-A, Epi-B, Mes, Stem-A and Stem-B. For the poor-prognosis Stem-A subtype, two genes involved in microtubule (MT) processing, TUBGCP4 and NAT10, were found essential for cell growth. The Stem-A cells were more sensitive to MT plus-end polymerization inhibitors, vincristine/vinorelbine. There was no difference in the sensitivities to MT stabilizers, paclitaxel/docetaxel. We hypothesize that the differences of plus-end MT dynamics contribute to the intrinsic sensitivity of anti-MT agents within the molecularly heterogeneous EOC. TUBGCP4 and NAT10 might also affect the MT functions in Stem-A cells and render them more sensitive to vinca-agents. Pilot results reveal that one Stem-A line PA1 has slower MT plus-end growth and faster catastrophe rate than the non-Stem-A HeyA8 line. Loss of TUBGCP4 causes cell-cycle arrest at G0/1 phase which might lead to lethality in PA1. Loss of TUBGCP4 has no significant growth perturbation for HeyA8. The loss of NAT10, a protein with acethyltransferase activity, causes paradoxical effects on cell-cycle progression in PA1 and HeyA8 cells. Loss of NAT10 causes significant increases in S phase in HeyA8 versus a trend in decreasing S phase events in PA1. In this proposal, we aim to explore the mechanisms of the differential sensitivity to MT-targeted drugs in expanded panel of Stem-A/non-Stem-A lines and test the MT dynamics and functions in TUBGCP4 and NAT10 knockdown cells. This study aims to provide mechanism behind the differential chemo-sensitivity in Stem-A cells to guide future therapeutic innovations. Molecularly stratifying EOC patients and targeting Stem-A patients with anti-MT plus-end agents or compounds targeting TUBGCP4 or NAT10 would be novel options in EOC management.
kw: ovarian cancer, microtubule, vinca-binders

title: The influence of gut microbiota composition (metagenome, metatranscriptome and metabolome) and its development/maturation on the development of eczema in Singaporean infants and toddlers in the well-defined multi-ethnic GUSTO (Growing Up in Singapore Towards Healthy Outcomes) birth cohort
abs: Eczema is the most common chronic inflammatory skin disorder of childhood, and is the earliest manifestation of the atopic march. Perturbation of the maturation of the stool microbiome in early life has been shown to influence the development of childhood eczema, but its mechanism is unknown. This study aims to leverage on the largest and clinically well-defined GUSTO birth cohort in Singapore to investigate and monitor the compositional structure and functional microbial genes catalogue (metagenome and metatranscriptomes) and fecal metabolites (metabolome). Serial stool samples of 30 matched cases and controls that have been archived over 4 times points over the first year of life will provide valuable insights into (1) the factors that drive/influence the maturation of the gut microbiota in early life, and (2) the dynamic host-gut microbiota metabolic interactions that predispose or prevent allergic inflammation and eczema. The metagenomic DNA and metatranscriptomics RNA genes sequencing will be performed to obtain the functional/phylogenetic profiles of microbiome. Targeted profiling of fecal SCFAs will be performed using LC/MS/MS. A global GC/TOFMS metabolomics profiling will also be conducted to profile other potentially perturbed metabolic pathways to better elucidate the disease etiology and mechanism related to eczema. We envision that the wealth of metagenomic, metatranscriptomics and metabolomic data generated from this study will provide critical information for the conceptualization of strategies for early life nutritional intervention to optimize the influential role of the maturing gut microbiota on the programming of the immune system and the prevention of eczema.
kw: Gut microbiome, eczema, infant, metagenome, metabolome, metatranscriptome

title: Differentiation of human embryonic stem cells into retinal pigment epithelial cells using retina-specific laminins for treatment of age-related macular degeneration
abs: Age related Macular Degeneration (AMD) is the commonest cause of irreversible blindness in the elderly but clinical cell therapy using stem cell derived retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells is hindered by their inefficient differentiation into functional RPE and dependence on animal products in vitro. Here we propose a novel approach to efficient xenogen free derivation of clinical grade RPE from human embryonic stem (hES) cells using niche specific basement membrane (BM) extracellular matrix proteins as culture substrates. Adhesion protein Laminin (LN) is a critical component of most BMs, which lie in close proximity to plasma membranes of organized cells such as epithelia, endothelia, muscle and neuronal cells. LN exists in 16 different isoforms, each of which is highly cell type specific, and important for cellular differentiation and phenotype specificity. We have recently shown that niche specific recombinant LN isoforms allow efficient isolation and generation of hES cells lines in a xenogen free manner. They further promote differentiation of such hES cells into specialized cell types such as cardiomyocytes and endothelial cells. LN isoforms specific to the BM of RPE (Bruch's membrane and External Limiting Membrane) have now been identified and we hypothesize that functional RPE can be derived from hES in an efficient and completely xenogen free manner using RPE specific laminin isoforms as culture substrates. We intend to culture hES cell lines on RPE BM specific LN isoforms using chemically defined xenogen free media to achieve RPE differentiation. RPE thus generated will be analyzed for their functionality in vitro; as well as their ability to rescue lost photoreceptor function in vivo in mouse and primate models of AMD. If successful, this work could lead to the first fully defined xeno-free protocol for generation of functional RPE, paving the way for clinical use of these cells in treatment of AMD.
kw: Macular degeneration, retinal pigment epithelial cells, hES cells, cell differentiation, laminin

title: Effective antimicrobial stewardship strategies: A comparison of 2 different methodologies
abs: Antibiotic resistance is a major global and regional public health concern as it can lead to increased mortality and higher healthcare cost. There are increasing rates of multi-drug resistant (MDR) bacteria in Singapore and in the region. Antimicrobial stewardship limits inappropriate use and optimizes antimicrobial use to maximize clinical cure, while limiting the emergence of resistance, adverse drug events, and cost. There is limited evidence of direct comparisons of the efficacies of different interventions. Prospective review and feedback by a dedicated antimicrobial stewardship team is effective but resource intensive. Clinical decision support system (CDSS) has been found to be effective and could be a cost-effective alternative. Our hypothesis is that prospective review and feedback by a dedicated antimicrobial stewardship team is comparable to clinical decision support systems in achieving antimicrobial utilization, clinical and microbiological outcomes. We propose to conduct a cluster randomized study. Wards will be randomized to 2 study groups with different ASP strategies. Hospital guidelines, pre-authorization of selected antibiotics and regular quality monitoring reports are common to both groups. Study group A consists of active auto-triggering of clinical decision support system for all broad-spectrum antibiotics while group B consists of a dedicated ASP team providing prospective review and feedback The primary outcome is 30-day mortality from antibiotic prescribing. Secondary outcome are 14-day re-infection rates, 14-day readmission rates, 6 month incidence of MDR organisms, antimicrobial usage, hospitalization costs, appropriateness of antibiotic use and antibiotic adverse effects. A time series analysis will be conducted to compare the effect of the 2 different ASP strategies on the antibiotic utilisation, clinical and microbiological outcomes. Identifying the most effective ASP strategy can direct limited resources, contribute to improved patient outcomes and combat antibiotic resistance.
kw: Antimicrobial stewardship, Antimicrobial prescribing, Prospective review and feedback, Bacterial Resistance, Clinical decision support, Hospital

title: Expanded Natural Killer (NK) Cells : Immunotherapeutics against Aspergillosis
abs: Background: Invasive aspergillosis (IA) is an opportunistic fungal infection afflicting patients with compromised immune systems. The current anti-fungal treatment options are limited and despite treatment, IA causes significant morbidity and mortality rates in excess of 50%. Given so, it is imperative to look into adjunctive therapeutic options, one of which is immunotherapy. Natural killer (NK) cells are innate cells that possess potent cytotoxic activity against microbes. However the interaction between fungus and NK cells is not well understood. Aim: The aim of the study is to compare antifungal activity of activated, expanded NK cells with primary NK cells and PBMCs both in vivo and in vitro experiments. We aim to explore cross-talk between NK cells other immune cells in synergizing and modulating anti-fungal effects of each other. We also aim to obtain further insights into the involvement of cell surface receptors in fungal recognition by NK cells. The knowledge gained from this study will be translated and tailored as immunotherapeutics in clinical management of invasive Aspergillosis.Methodology: The activity of highly purified activated NK cells against Aspergillus will be studied. . XTT assay will be performed to assess fungal damage. Cytokine production will be assessed by ELISA. Involvement of cell surface receptors will be assessed by blocking assays and inhibition experiments. Contact mediated versus soluble factor mediated killing will be determined by use of permeable transmembrane inserts. In vitro findings will be translated to in vivo studies using IA infection mice model. Conclusion: This study will approach IA treatment from immunological point of view using expanded NK cells so that future IA patients with poor response to conventional treatment will have option of immunotherapy.
kw: Invasive Aspergillosis; Anti-fungal; Monocytes; Interferon-gamma

title: Mechanistic characterization of Mfsd2b, a homolog of the DHA transporter protein Mfsd2a/NLS1
abs: Essential fatty acids such as DHA play important physiological functions such as neuroprotection and neurosignaling roles. The tissue distributions of these fatty acids (FAs) are unique and regulated by active transportation mechanisms. We recently discovered that brain accumulation of DHA is mainly regulated by Mfsd2a/NLS1 transporter that is expressed in the microvessels of the blood-brain barrier. NLS1 transports DHA in the form of lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC) which is found abundantly in plasma. Importantly, NLS1 also transports plasma LPC containing other FAs such as oleate and palmitate into brain, indicating the needs for not only essential FAs but also non-essential FAs for brain metabolism. This discovery of a secondary transporter for long chain FAs indicates that distribution of FAs to tissues indeed requires active transport mechanism. Using blast search with NLS1, we found that NLS1 shared a high sequence homology to an uncharacterized protein, namely Mfsd2b. We cloned and sequenced Mfsd2b cDNA and found that murine Mfsd2b shares 58% protein sequence similarity with murine NLS1. Structural analysis showed that Mfsd2b has also 12 transmembrane domains and belongs to the major facilitator superfamily domain. Mfsd2b retains conserved residues that we have found to play essential roles in activity of NLS1. Mfsd2b expression is found in liver, spleen, and bone marrow. Our long-term goal is to identify the physiological functions of Mfsd2b, which will provide a fundamental understanding of the roles of this newly identified transporter family. Facilitated by the discovery of NLS1 functions and by strong preliminary data on Mfsd2b, we hypothesize that Mfsd2b functions as a facilitative transporter that transports FAs (e.g. glycerolipids). The primary goal of this application is to identify the physiological ligand of Mfsd2b. This will be achieved through two independent approaches using and a candidate ligand approach, and using floxed Mfsd2b-knockout mice and targeted mass spectrometry.
kw: DHA, Lipid transporters, lipid mediators, Platelets, Membrane transporters

title: AGO and Associated Small RNAs Regulate Alternative Splicing Events That Cause Drug Resistance to MK2206
abs: The EGFR/Akt signalling is an important contributor to the occurrence of breast cancer. A novel inhibitor of Akt, MK2206, is being tested in the Phase II clinical trials. Although it has achieved considerable success in clinical application, MK2206 meets with resistance in some breast cancer cells. Therefore, we propose to investigate the underlying mechanism from a novel aspect, the alternative splicing of pre-mRNAs. Our previous research has discovered that SRPKs and SR proteins are important splicing regulators for Akt signalling and that human AGO proteins, recently shown to interact with SR proteins, can associate with a new type of small RNAs to regulate teratocarcinoma cell proliferation. Hence, we aim to: 1) Study whether MK2206 regulates the activation of SRPKs and formation of AGO/SR protein complex by biochemistry experiments, cell survival assays and loss-of-function assays; 2) Examine whether MK2206 triggers the expression of AGO-associated small RNAs and modulate the formation of AGO/SR protein complex by the Northern blot, qPCR, RNA immunoprecipitation, immunocytochemistry and deep sequencing; 3) To profile the MK2206-induced alternative splicing events guided by the AGO-associated small RNAs with the genome-wide sequencing and Exon array; 4) To show in the animals that resistant xenografts can become sensitive to MK2206 after disrupting the small RNA-guided AGO/SR protein-dependent alternative splicing. The study will have profound implications in both the scientific advancement and clinical application. It will elucidate the role of AGO and the associated small RNAs in regulating pre-mRNA alternative splicing and provide a comprehensive profile of splicing events that could cause resistance to MK2206. In addition, the new pre-mRNA splicing mechanism can be targeted to improve the efficacy of this new drug. Furthermore, the MK2206-induced pre-mRNA splicing profile and proteomic signatures can be developed as a suitable indicator or biomarker to stratify breast cancer patients and to predict the efficacy.
kw: Argonaute, Small RNA, DNA repeat, Alternative splicing, Breast cancer, Drug resistance

title: Evaluation of Vaccibodies® as a novel dendritic cell targeting strategy to protect against Hepatitis B virus
abs: More than 350 million people are chronically infected by Hepatitis B virus (HBV) in the world with more than 75% of them being in Asia. HBV chronic infection can lead to cirrhosis, liver fibrosis and Hepatocellular carcinoma, the third leading cause of cancer death worldwide. Although prophylactic vaccination is efficient in most individuals, treatment of chronic HBV infection remains a great challenge since available antiviral drugs efficiently decrease serum viral load in most patients but fail to eradicate the virus. This could be achieved by stimulating cytotoxic CD8+ T cells responses against HBV-infected hepatocytes, which are the viral reservoir during chronic infection. Such stimulation requires an optimal cross-presentation of antigens derived from HBV-infected cells to CD8+ T cells, function in which XCR1+ dendritic cells (DC) are specialized.The proposed study aims at evaluating a new antibody-based therapeutic strategy (Vaccibodies®) that targets vaccine specifically to human cross-presenting CD141+XCR1+ DCs for the induction of anti-HBV CD8+ T cell responses in ‘HIL” humanized mice. HIL mice, that have both human liver and immune system, can be efficiently chronically infected by HBV. We hypothesize that the delivery HBV peptides specifically to these DCs will restore strong anti-viral CD8+ T cell responses, which otherwise are compromised during chronic HBV infection.A more fundamental aim will be to demonstrate that, like mouse CD8?+XCR1+ DCs, human XCR1+ DCs are specialized in CD8+ T cells cross-priming in vivo. We hypothesize that the “in vivo” environment will allow maximizing human XCR1+ DC’s advantage to cross-present antigens as compared to the other DCs, and thus induce strong cytotoxic CD8+ T cell responsesThe success of this study will pave the way for pre-clinical evaluation of Vaccibodies® in macaques and will have a high impact in the field of human DCs.
kw: Humanized Mice, Dendritic Cells, Vaccine Delivery, Hepatitis B, Chronic Infection

title: Adoption of prophylactic cranial irradiation for extensive stage small cell lung cancer: A population based outcomes study
abs: Specific aimsOur aims are to describe the adoption of prophylactic cranial irradiation (PCI) and to evaluate its impact on the outcome of extensive stage small cell lung cancer (ES-SCLC) at population level in Singapore. HypothesesThere will be an increase in the adoption of PCI following the publication of the EORTC 08993-22993 trial in 2007 which reported that PCI improved overall survival in non-Asian patients with ES-SCLC who had a favorable response to chemotherapy. The adoption of PCI is associated with a significant improvement in overall survival at the population level, demonstrating that the results of the EORTC trial are generalizable to our local patients. MethodologyWe will employ a retrospective population based cohort study design to answer this research question. We will identify patients diagnosed with ES-SCLC and no brain metastases between 2003 and 2010 from the National University Cancer Institute, Singapore and National Cancer Centre Singapore pathology registries. We will link the treatment records of the included patients to the National Death Registry. We will describe the time trends in the use of PCI and compare the survival of all patients before and after the widespread adoption of PCI. Clinical significanceThis study is essential to identify whether our practice has changed appropriately following the publication of the EORTC trial and to determine whether our patients are achieving the expected outcomes. If this study finds an improvement in survival outcome that commensurate with the results of the EORTC trial, it will support the use of PCI. If it does not, the value of PCI must be questioned. Recently, a Japanese phase III trial reported that PCI was associated with survival detriment in Asian patients with ES-SCLC. Hence it is crucial that we validate the findings of the EORTC trial in our patients.
kw: Radiotherapy, small cell lung cancer, chemotherapy

title: Investigating The Inflammatory Response at The Early Phase Of Growth Plate Injury and Anti-Cytokine Approaches To Restore Growth
abs: Background: Bone bridge formation following growth plate trauma is a significant cause of deformity in children. Inflammatory cytokines including IL-1? and TNF-?‘s surge at the early stages of the growth plate trauma, triggering the osteogenic differentiation by both attracting the bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BM-MSCs) from and stimulating ossification at the injury site. However these cytokines are also required for regulation of endochondral ossification, a developmental process in growth plate. Hypothesis: We hypothesise that by transient inhibition of IL-1? and/or TNF-? levels at the early period following the growth plate injury, it will be effective in overcoming the bony bridge formation by controlling the inflammatory infiltration, recruitment of stem cells from bone marrow and subsequent bone bridge formation without further growth disturbance.Aim: Phase I of study aims to identify the optimum dosage of anti- IL-1? and TNF-? antibodies, and MSCs, that are required for effective inhibition of inflammatory cells infiltration at the early phase of growth plate injury. With the optimum dose of antibodies and MSCs identified, Phase II of study will investigate the effect of administrating anti-IL-1? and TNF-? antibodies, or MSC, towards inflammatory infiltration, bone bridge formation and cartilage regeneration at the growth plate defect site.Approach: Using a rat epiphyseal defect model, our objective is to investigate the effects of IL-1? and TNF-? neutralizing monoclonal antibodies and BM-MSCs on modulating inflammatory response after the growth plate injury, and study the role of pro-inflammatory cytokines in regulating the initiation of bone bridge formation and growth plate arrest. Importance: This study aims to translate the growth plate injury research into a possible treatment modality to overcome bone bridge formation, and prevent partial or complete growth arrest following growth plate injury, leading to significant improvements in quality of life of paediatric patients with growth plate injuries.

title: The Singapore Colour Pupillometry Evaluation (SCOPE): A novel detection test for glaucoma
abs: Background. Glaucoma, one of the leading causes of blindness worldwide, remains typically asymptomatic until advanced stages. Its early detection, allowing early treatment, remains challenging, since current methods of screening have poor sensitivity and specificity. In preliminary studies, we have shown that patients with glaucoma have reduced pupillary constriction in response to high irradiance blue light, as compared to healthy controls.Hypothesis and Aims. Our hypothesis is that the study of the pupillary light reflex, mediated by the melanopsin expressing cells (also called intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells or ipRGCs), could be a reliable strategy for glaucoma detection. The aim of our research is to develop a novel colour pupillometry-based protocol (SCoPE – Singapore Colour Pupillometry Evaluation) for identifying patients with glaucoma. The novelty of our strategy, in comparison with the few previous pupillometric studies in glaucoma, consists in the use of a novel light exposure protocol addressing specifically the ipRGCs, which are affected in glaucoma.Methods. We will first assess the classification accuracy of SCoPE for discriminating glaucoma patients (n=200), from controls (n=200). Next, we will compare the diagnostic performance of SCoPE with an alternative commercially available method, i.e. RAPDx, which, from preliminary studies, seems to have a poorer accuracy. We will then use SCoPE prospectively in a population study in Singapore, screening 1000 consecutive patients for glaucoma. These studies will set the ground for patenting subsequently a small, affordable, reliable pupillograph that can be used for glaucoma detection at community levels in Singapore.Clinical significance: These studies could lead to a novel cost-effective approach for reliably detecting glaucoma. If successful, our research could lead to the development of a commercializable pupillometry-based method and/or device that can be used for early detection of glaucoma in community-based screening programs, hence reducing the burden of blindness in Singapore.
