title: Study of leukemic niche by human bone marrow model
abs: Leukemic stem cells (LSCs) reside in a biochemically distinct (e.g. low pH, hypoxic) niche in the bone marrow and are surrounded by non-leukemic cells. Accumulating evidence have shown that this niche environment is important in supporting LSCs functions, including therapeutic resistance and disease relapse. In chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML), we have shown that individual niche factors (hypoxia and stroma) confers primary LSC drug resistance as well as maintenance in vitro. Remarkably, hypoxia upregulates genes involving in cell-cell interaction and communication, suggesting that there is an extensive interplay between local hypoxia and intercellular interaction in the niche. We hypothesize that these interactions represent LSC specific therapeutic targets. However, further in vivo testing is difficult to carry out because of inefficient LSC engraftment in the commonly used immunodeficient mouse xenograft model. Recent studies demonstrated that human bone marrow could be feasibly reconstituted in immunodeficient mouse, which provides a novel platform for human niche study. Here, we will test the role hypoxia-driven genes in intercellular communications using this new in vivo bone (IVB) model. To prepare for large scale experiment and potentially drug screening, firstly we will optimize the IVB (Aim 1). Secondly, we will engraft human LSCs and normal hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) in the optimized IVB (Aim 2). It is expected that LSCs/HSCs engraftment will be significantly enhanced with human-derived niche in the IVB. In addition, the niche components (including LSCs and HSCs) can be genetically manipulated in the IVB model, which allows further analysis and validation of LSCs-specific genes (Aim3, in long term). The IVB applies not only to CML but in general to all bone marrow related hematological malignancies (e.g. Acute Myeloid Leukemia and Multiple Myeloma). This would also facilitate clinical translation by providing local community a human relevant drug testing platform.
kw: Leukemia, Stem Cell, Bone Marrow Niche, Stroma and Hypoxia, Drug Resistance, Mouse Xenograft

title: Rational design of synthetic mimics of antimicrobial peptides: from in silico to in vivo
abs: Bacterial resistance to current antibiotics has become a global health problem noted recently at the G8 Summit and by the Center for Disease Control. The excessive use of antibiotics is often cited as the major contributing factor for the evolution of bacterial resistance. Moreover, the available antibiotics target specific intracellular pathways, which can be easily mutated by the pathogens. As next generation antibiotics, membrane-active antimicrobials such as synthetic mimics of antimicrobial peptides (SMAMPs) offer a potential solution to this problem because these molecules interfere with membrane function, an essential component of bacterial survival. However, the development of SMAMPs is largely by trial and error due to poor understanding of mechanism of action and paucity of design principles. Using fragment-based approach, we propose a pharmacophore model consisting of five key fragments that could discriminate between eukaryotic and prokaryotic membranes. We hypothesize that this simple pharmacophore model possesses the key structural elements of a membrane-active molecule and can be used as a template for the design of new class of SMAMPs. Recently, we have reported a derivative of the pharmacophore model (AM016), which displayed potent antimicrobial activity. Building on these preliminary studies, the overall objective of this proposal is to decipher the mechanism of action and obtain key biophysical parameters for the design of new SMAMPs with enhanced activity and biocompatibility. To this end, we propose a multi-disciplinary approach that involves (i) identify key parameters underlying the antimicrobial activity, (ii) dissect the molecular details of toxicity, (iii) design, synthesize and validate new SMAMPs using in vitro and in vivo models. The translation of fundamental knowledge of detailed molecular interactions to antibiotic development will greatly accelerate the drug discovery process, providing cost saving measures, as well as the basis for a continued developmental process to meet new challenges presented by pathogens.
kw: Antibiotic resistance, synthetic mimics of antimicrobial peptides, molecular dynamics, structure-activity relationship, pharmacophore model

title: Role of Mesenchymal Stem Cell Secretome in Cartilage Regeneration and Potential for Development of Novel Cell-Free Therapeutics
abs: Articular cartilage has a very poor intrinsic regenerative capacity and responds poorly to trauma as a result of sports injuries or degenerative conditions such as in osteoarthritis. Although cell-based therapy with autologous chondrocytes has shown some early success, long-term results show cartilage degeneration. Recently, mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) have shown superior results to chondrocytes, but the repair is not always optimal. This is very much due to the lack of understanding of how the MSCs help in the cartilage repair. The long term goal of this study is to elucidate the role of MSCs in cartilage repair for development of new therapeutics to overcome the current limitations/difficulties of a cell-based therapy. In prior work, we have demonstrated the abilities of MSCs and progenitor cells to repair articular cartilage injuries. As inflammation is a major player mediating the progression of cartilage injuries to degenerative joint diseases such as osteoarthritis, and MSCs are generally immunomodulatory, a possible mechanism for MSC-mediated cartilage regeneration is an immune-based mechanism that attenuates the pro-inflammatory condition present in injured/diseased joints to halt disease progression and facilitate tissue regeneration. Indeed, the efficacy of many MSC-based therapies has been increasingly attributed to paracrine secretion of signaling molecules, trophic factors and microvesicles (exosomes). We therefore hypothesize that MSCs mediate cartilage regeneration by paracrine secretion of factors to attenuate inflammation, promote chondrogenesis and halt overall disease progression. To test this hypothesis, three specific aims are to: 1.Investigate if MSCs can modulate the pro-inflammatory condition present in injured/diseased joints by adaptive alteration of their secretome. 2.Investigate if MSC exosomes are active components within the secretome that underpins the chondrogenic and immunomodulatory properties of MSCs. 3.Identify and characterize prospective cartilage-protective exosomes and testing the efficacy of this novel cell-free therapeutic in the cartilage repair and regeneration in animal model.
kw: Mesenchymal Stem Cells, Exosomes, Cartilage, Regeneration, Immune Modulation, Chondrogenesis

title: Neurosteroids as novel therapeutic agents for Schizophrenia
abs: Neurosteroids are endogenously synthesised from cholesterol and are involved in many physiological functions. For example, pregnenolone levels are abnormal in certain areas of postmortem brain tissue from schizophrenic patients. Furthermore, recent preclinical trials have shown that pregnenolone is effective in reducing the negative symptoms and cognitive deficits of schizophrenic patients. These evidences suggest that pregnenolone, and likely its downstream metabolites, are involved in the neurological underpinnings of schizophrenia, and are thus strong candidates as novel treatments for schizophrenia.Specific Aim 1 involves characterising the behavioral effects of a neurosteroid, pregnenolone sulfate, on symptoms of schizophrenia that are mirrored by the dopamine transporter knockout (DAT-KO) mouse model. Specific Aim 2 involves quantifying the levels of pregnenolone and its metabolites in mouse brain tissue following pregnenolone administration. Specific Aim 3 involves elucidating the pharmacological mechanisms of pregnenolone, pregnenolone sulfate and their downstream metabolites to uncover novel potential targets for the treatment of schizophrenia.Methods: We will perform behavioral studies to examine the effects of neurosteroids, such as pregnenolone sulfate, on hyperactivity, impaired sensorimotor gating and deficient working memory in DAT-KO mice. Gas chromatography/mass spectrometry (GC/MS) will be used to determine the concentration of pregnenolone and its metabolites in tissues following pregnenolone administration. Pharmacological manipulations and electrophysiological recordings will be used to determine the molecular mechanisms that are important for the efficacy of these neurosteroids.Clinical significance: Schizophrenia is a debilitating, chronic neuropsychiatric disorder that affects approximately 1% of the world’s population. Currently available antipsychotic treatments are efficacious in treating positive symptoms, but are only modestly effective in treating the negative symptoms and cognitive deficits, which are the major contributing factors to the incapacitating nature of schizophrenia. Thus, there is a need to develop novel treatment options that are effective against the negative symptoms and cognitive deficits, and are well tolerated by patients.

title: BPGAP1 as an active scaffold for Vav1/Rac1 activation in cancer cell invasion
abs: Cancer metastasis is a multi-step process of malignant cells undergoing infiltration, invasion and colonization to new sites. It involves Rho GTPases to regulate active remodelling for morphological changes, force generation and cell adhesion. Although much has been learned about Rho regulation by their activators guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEFs) and inactivators GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs), the precise timing and locales of these checkpoints remains unclear. We previously identified BPGAP1 as a multi-functional RhoGAP that inactivates RhoA and promotes cell motility. While its expression is up-regulated in tumors and invasive cancers, the underlying mechanism for its pro-metastasis potential remains unknown. Here, we show that BPGAP1 also binds to another GTPase, Rac and its RacGEF, Vav, leading to active lammellipodia formation and increased cell invasion. We therefore hypothesize that BPGAP1 could act as an important scaffold that mediates Vav1/Rac activation in cancer cell invasion. To confirm this, we aim to: 1)elucidate how BPGAP1 links Rac and Vav in cancer cell invasion. This will be investigated using specific mutants and knockdown of BPGAP1, Vav and Rac to define their binding profiles and impact on (i) Rac activation, (ii) lamellipodia formation, (iii) transendothelial migration and (iv) invasion through collagen matrix;2)examine the impact of BPGAP1/Vav/Rac signaling as described in Aim 1 under EGF stimulation by using the phospho-mimicry and phospho-dead mutants for BPGAP1, and3)correlate the expression and activity of BPGAP1/Vav/Rac complex in different stages of breast cancer development by screening the expression of BPGAP1 and Vav1 in different stages and types of breast cancer using tissue and DNA microarrays.A clear understanding on the action and regulation of this BPGAP1-Vav-Rac signaling complex in normal and disease states would provide new insights to cancer metastasis and offers novel and alternative targets for therapeutic intervention.
kw: Cancer metastasis, Rho, Rac, Lamellipodia, Cell invasion, Scaffold protein

title: Human Foetal Cardiovascular Fluid Mechanics in Relation to Congenital Malformations - Preparations for Foetal Surgery
abs: We envision that in the near future, foetal surgery will replace post-natal surgery as the therapy of choice for congenital cardiovascular malformations, since foetal surgery has the potential of tapping into the regenerative ability of foetuses, which is lost at birth, and the potential of arresting the mal-development process before it is complete at birth. Currently, foetal cardiovascular surgery is in its infancy (only limited institutions worldwide can perform this, and there are limited medical devices), and there is currently no such expertise in Singapore, both R&D and clinical. We propose to take the first step to establish local foundational expertise, through establishing methods for quantifying human foetal cardiovascular mechanical force environment, and then studying how abnormal pre-natal hemodynamic mechanical forces can cause congenital malformations. Our proposed methodology is as follows: through our 5 clinical collaborators, we will obtain 3D ultrasound scans of foetal cardiovascular organs. We will reconstruct 3D organ geometries through image processing and segmentation techniques, and perform computational fluid dynamics simulations to compute the mechanical force environments. We will compare hemodynamic force patterns in normal foetuses and foetuses who will be born with malformations, to understand force patterns that may be causing the malformation.With improved understanding of foetal hemodynamic mechanics, we will enable a host of highly translational research, including (1) design of catheter- and stent- based medical devices; (2) devising new strategies for surgery; (3) developing ultrasound diagnostic techniques to predict foetal predisposition towards malformations; and (4) development of large animal models of congenital malformations for training surgeons in foetal surgery. We envision that Singapore will become a leading center in foetal cardiovascular surgery, where scientific research, commercialization of medical devices by startups, and clinical practice will be conducted, leading the way in this new paradigm for congenital cardiovascular malformation treatment.
kw: Congenital Cardiovascular Malformation, Foetal Cardiovascular Fluid Mechanics, Foetal Cardiovascular Surgery

title: Role of JAK3 in modulating EZH2 function in natural killer/T-cell lymphoma
abs: Nasal-type natural killer/T-cell lymphoma (NKTL) is an aggressive lymphoid malignancy associated with very poor survival outcomes. Although more effective therapy is now available, treatment is still completely reliant on radiotherapy and combinations of chemotherapy. A better understanding of the molecular abnormalities underlying this disease will provide important insights into the therapeutic approach to challenging clinical entities. JAK3 is a non-receptor tyrosine kinase mediating signals initiated by cytokines and growth factor receptors. Recent data indicate that persistent activation of JAK3 due to activating mutations is involved in several haematologic malignancies, including acute megakaryoblastic leukemia, cutaneous T cell lymphoma, and myeloproliferative diseases and NKTL. Notably, JAK3 deregulation by activating mutations confers invasive growth advantage in NKTL. The best-understood mechanism by which EZH2 exerts its oncogenic function is to induce gene repression through its effect on chromatin via its histone methyltransferase activity. However, there is rapidly accumulating evidence to suggest that EZH2 may switch its function from a PcG repressor to a transcriptional co?activator. We previously showed that EZH2 enhances proliferation of malignant NK cells without requiring its enzyme activity. In this proposed study, we further explore the mechanisms leading to this non-canonical function of EZH2 in NKTL. We found that JAK3 protein interacts with EZH2 in NK malignant cells and affect H3K27me3 levels. Therefore, the proposed research aims to uncover the role of JAK3 in modulating EZH2 function in NKTL. The study would provide insight in the pathogenesis and tumor biology of NK-cell malignancies, and would be informative to the development of targeted therapy for this disease.
kw: Natural killer/T-cell lymphoma; EZH2; JAK3; H3K27me3

title: Next Generation Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) for the Cornea and Anterior Segments of the Eye
abs: Background: Corneal diseases are the second most common cause of irreversible blindness, with more than 180 million people worldwide suffering from corneal scarring. The depth of the corneal pathology is important in determining the treatment modality. However, imaging of the cornea using current optical coherence tomography (OCT) technology is unable to clearly distinguish corneal layers or detect cells in the cornea. Aims: To develop a novel high-resolution OCT system by combining a new micro-OCT (?OCT) real-time imaging system (1?m resolution) with a compatible image enhancement software. Hypothesis: We hypothesize that a) the images from this new ?OCT will be superior to existing OCT; and b) these in vivo images of the ?OCT will not be inferior to ex vivo histology images. Methodology and Approach: We have already completed pilot studies to demonstrate the use of the ?OCT system and software enhancement. This proposed study aims to demonstrate targeted identification of corneal pathology using the ?OCT system, enhanced by our software to obtain ‘histology-like’ resolution images. Three animal models will we be used to show that the utility of ?OCT system to image various pathologies in each layer of the cornea: (1) Innermost layer: Slc4a11 knockout mouse model which exhibit endothelial cell damage (2) Middle layer: Rat corneal transplant model with serial images of corneal stromal layers (3) Outermost layer: Mouse model for superficial corneal scars. All serial ?OCT images will be compared to current OCT (hypothesis a) and histology images (hypothesis b). Future development: If successful, this study can be further developed into a larger project to study the use of this novel ?OCT for clinical use in vivo human studies for the cornea, as well as other parts of the eye such as the optic nerve and retina.
kw: Cornea, Optical Coherence Tomography

title: Circulating tumor cells (CTCs)-specific microRNA expression and DNA methylation as markers of resistance to systemic and targeted therapies in metastatic colorectal cancer.
abs: Chemotherapy resistance is a major problem in the treatment of patients with colorectal cancer (CRC), with at least half of patients developing resistance during therapy. Circulating tumor cells (CTCs) are shed from solid organ tumors into the blood on their way to metastatic sites. Serial profiling of CTCs permits repetitive, non-invasive monitoring for emergence of chemoresistance during therapy and a real-time indication of clinical response. However, the use of CTC-specific microRNA and methylation profiles to indicate in real-time the emergence of resistance to systemic chemotherapy has not yet been published. We propose to study the microRNA expression and DNA methylation profiles of CTCs isolated from metastatic CRC patients undergoing chemotherapy and bevacizumab. We hypothesize that specific microRNAs and epigenetic DNA changes directly regulate resistance to chemotherapeutic agents. Knockdown of the microRNA expression and increased expression of the specific DNA will thus result in eradication of chemo-resistant CTCs and prevent cancer relapse.Using the microsieve device we patented, we will isolate CTCs from 30 metastatic CRC patients undergoing chemotherapy and targeted therapy with bevacizumab. CTC enumeration will be performed prior to each chemotherapy session. DNA and microRNA will be extracted from the CTCs. Quantitative real-time PCR will be used to characterize the microRNA expression of the CTCs. Methylation-specific PCR will be used to characterize the methylation status of specific genes from the CTCs. Frequently and highly expressed microRNAs as well as methylated and silenced DNAs will be selected for functional characterization using in vitro models of colorectal cell lines and in vivo models of mice xenografts. These functional studies will validate the involvement of identified microRNAs and methylated DNAs in signaling pathways underlying chemotherapy resistance. Our long-term goal is to develop practical non-invasive cancer diagnostic solutions based on CTCs, to guide selection and application of targeted cancer therapies.
kw: Colorectal adenocarcinoma, Chemotherapy resistance, Circulating tumor cells, MicroRNA, DNA methylation

title: Doxycyline and the modulation of tissue destruction in human pulmonary tuberculosis: A pilot study
abs: Background: Pulmonary cavitation, a hallmark of tuberculosis (TB), is the site of high mycobacterial burden leading to disease transmission. The cause of tissue destruction leading to cavitation in TB is primarily due to the host inflammatory response. A matrix degrading phenotype develops in TB, in which the activity of host proteolytic enzymes, specifically matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) is unopposed by their specific inhibitors (TIMPs), thus driving tissue destruction and cavitation in TB. MMP inhibition with doxycycline has shown to improve lung function in patients with chronic lung diseases but its use in TB is unclear.Hypothesis: We hypothesise that the MMP inhibitor doxycycline will modulate tissue destruction in human pulmonary tuberculosis.Specific aims: •To investigate the effects doxycyline has on biological markers of tissue destruction in TB patients•To assess the tolerability and side effects of doxycline with concurrent standard TB therapyMethodology and approach:In this proof-of-principle study, doxycycline or placebo shall be given to 10 TB patients in each arm for 2 weeks, with recruitment done at the National University Health System. All TB patients are to keep to their standard anti-tuberculous treatment. A standardized questionnaire of symptoms, side-effects and weight shall be recorded. Induced sputum and plasma samples from all TB patients shall be analysed for MMPs and TIMPs before and after the administration of doxycycline. In addition, human neutrophils shall be harvested at week 0 and 2 from TB patients and these shall be stimulated with live, virulent H37Rv M. tuberculosis in a Biosafety Level 3 laboratory. The supernatants from these cells shall be analysed for MMPs and TIMPs. This pilot study will evaluate if doxycycline can decrease the host inflammatory response in TB and will be a springboard to a large randomized control trial to examine if doxycycline inhibits tissue destruction in human TB.
kw: Tuberculosis, tissue destruction, cavity, matrix metalloproteinases

title: SERIAL QUANTIFICATION OF URINARY BIOMARKERS IN PREDICTING AMINOGLYCOSIDE-INDUCED ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY
abs: Specific AimsTo examine serial changes in urinary renal biomarkers during course of aminoglycoside therapy, and determine their predictive ability for aminoglycoside-induced acute kidney injury (AG-AKI).Hypotheses1.Elevation of AKI biomarkers (in response to AG-nephrotoxicity) will precede and predict clinically evident AG-AKI.2.AG therapy and renal tubular stress will induce selective elevation of tubular-damage biomarkers, versus markers of glomerular filtration.3.Baseline AKI biomarker levels will be higher with pre-existing chronic kidney disease versus normal baseline renal function.4.Biomarker elevation will return to baseline after cessation of AG therapy, in absence of AKI.Methodology and ApproachProspective, observational study, of hospitalized adults initiated on AG for infections and projected therapy

title: CD4+ T-cell epitopes and cytokine responses to Blo t 5 allergen in patients with allergic rhinitis
abs: Sensitization to dust mite Blomia tropicalis is a main triggering factor for allergic diseases in tropical, subtropical and certain temperate regions. It was reported that approximately 1 billion people were sensitized to Blomia tropicalis worldwide. In Singapore, 60-70% of patients with allergic asthma, allergic rhinitis or eczema are sensitized by Blomia tropicalis allergens, particularly in young allergic children. Blo t 5 protein has been identified as a predominant major allergen of Blomia tropicalis, with T helper (Th)2 sensitization rates of up to 90% in Blomia tropicalis allergic patients. The allergen-specific Th phenotypes in non-allergic subjects are less studied as compared to allergic subjects. This proposal aims to evaluate frequencies and Th cytokine profiles of Blo t 5 epitope-specific CD4+ T cells from allergic and non-allergic subjects. The hypothesis is that Blo t 5 specific-epitopes are differentially recognized and induced different Th effector CD4+ T cells in allergic and non-allergic subjects. The T cell epitope mapping will be performed with a series of overlapping synthetic peptides that cover the whole Blo t 5 protein sequence. The readouts will be T cell proliferation and cytokine production to each peptide. The Blo t 5 epitopes that elicit Th2 responses in allergic subjects will provide information on the candidate peptides for potential peptide-based immunotherapy for dust mite allergy. These peptides will also facilitate the design of altered peptides to improve the safety issue. The T epitope-specific cytokine profiles from non-allergic subjects will provide information on the Th phenotypes of health subjects and can be used as the benchmark for monitoring the progress of immunotherapy for allergic subjects in the future. Allergen-specific Immunotherapy is the only disease modifying treatment for allergic asthma and rhinitis. The information obtained from this study will pave the road for the next generation of allergen-specific immunotherapy.
kw: T cell epitope, Allergic rhinitis, Atopy, House dust mite, Blomia tropicalis, Blo t 5

title: Effect of anti-HLA antibodies in long surviving Asian kidney transplant recipients
abs: Kidney transplantation is the best treatment for end-stage kidney disease. It also offers significant cost savings compared to dialysis. While 1-year graft survival has improved significantly over the years, long-term graft survival has not seen similar advancement. Chronic allograft rejection is the leading cause of late renal allograft loss and anti-human leukocyte antigen (HLA) antibodies have been implicated in the pathogenesis. Transplant recipients who develop de novo anti-HLA antibodies, especially donor-specific antibodies (DSA), have significantly higher allograft loss rates compared to their anti-HLA antibody negative counterparts. A unique characteristic of transplant recipients in the National University Hospital (NUH) is their long graft survival beyond 20 years, as compared to that of 5-8 years described in the Western population. This cross-sectional study will examine the prevalence of anti-HLA antibodies in kidney transplant recipients on follow-up at NUH with further characterization of these antibodies into preformed vs. de novo DSA and non-DSA. Sera will be examined for anti-HLA antibodies at least one year after the transplant. Patients will be grouped according to their anti-HLA antibody response, ie. anti-HLA antibody positive vs. anti-HLA antibody negative. The utility of anti-HLA antibodies as a prognostic biomarker of graft function and survival will be investigated. Patient and clinical characteristics will be compared between the groups and according to their time post-transplant to determine whether there is an association between the presence of anti-HLA antibodies and graft function or survival. This study will serve as a platform for future studies to dissect antibody characteristics that render graft acceptance (or damage), which can subsequently be used to develop diagnostics and therapeutics to optimize success in transplantation. Reasons for the differences in the magnitude of immune response will also be evaluated in later studies.
kw: Kidney, transplant, survival, HLA antibodies

title: Extensive A-to-I RNA editing in 3’UTR and its involvement in hepatocellualr carcinoma development
abs: The broad objective of this proposal is to fully understand the biological importance of RNA editing events in 3’ untranslational regions (3’UTRs) during human hepatocelluar carcinoma (HCC) initiation and progression. RNA editing, one of the aberrant post-transcriptional modifications, may lead to tumor-specific transcriptome diversity. As a relatively novel epigenetic mechanism, RNA editing introduces changes in the RNA sequences encoded by the genome. Discoveries in the last decade completely changed our view on RNA. Because RNA can be more easily modified than DNA, it also suggests potential therapeutic approaches. In humans, the most frequent type of editing is the conversion of adenosine to inosine (A-to-I), which is catalyzed by the double-stranded RNA (dsRNA)-specific ADAR (Adenosine DeAminase that act on RNA) family of protein. However, the biological significance of widespread global A-to-I RNA editing of non-coding, repetitive sequences remains largely a mystery. Our recent RNA-Seq analysis of clinical HCC and matched non-tumor liver specimens revealed that more than 90% of A-to-I RNA editing occurs to non-coding regions with the highest enrichment in 3’UTRs and HCC displays a distinct RNA editing profiles in 3’UTR. We therefore hypothesize the A-to-I RNA editing dysregulation in 3’UTRs could be an essential driver event in HCC. In this proposed project, we will select candidate genes with multiple editing sites within 3’UTRs for further investigation on the regulatory mechanisms (e.g. altered RNA stability, altered microRNA targeting and nulear retention of the edited transcript) of 3’UTR RNA editing on target gene expression. In addition, the functional roles of these candidate genes during HCC initiation and progression will be investigated in cancer cells and mice models. The knowledge gleaned from this project could fully understand the interplay between the 3’UTR editing dysregulation and HCC initiation and progression, which could result in new therapeutic approaches for HCC.
kw: A-to-I RNA editing; ADARs; 3'UTR; HCC

title: A prospective randomized study to examine mechanisms of diabetes remission between sleeve gastrectomy and RYGB surgery
abs: Sleeve gastrectomy (SG) and Roux-en-Y gastric bypass surgery (RYGB) are the choice of bariatric procedures to facilitate weight loss in obese type 2 diabetic patients. Both procedures results in significant weight loss and cause remission in diabetes, the mechanisms underlying the diabetes remission in particular for SG are not clear. Changes in the key pathophysiologies of diabetes, insulin secretion and insulin sensitivity are flawed by non-gold standard methodologies. In addition, molecular pathways that lead to diabetes remission for SG and RYGB are not systematically explored. This study aims to systematically examine the molecular mechanisms of diabetes remission especially common and differential pathways for these procedures, and to determine the changes in insulin secretion and insulin sensitivity using gold standard measures. We will randomize 30 obese (BMI>32 kg/m2) diabetic patients to either RYGB or SG. They will undergo mixed meal tolerance test, intravenous glucose tolerance test, and hyperinsulinemic euglycemic clamp for the assessment of nutrients appearance and clearance, insulin secretion and insulin sensitivity respectively. All clinical measurements will be collected before surgery, at 3-month and 6-month post-surgery. Subcutaneous adipose and skeletal muscle tissues will be collected at pre-surgery and 6 months post-surgery for gene and protein expressions related to macronutrients (glucose, fat and protein) metabolism. Key intermediate metabolites will be examined in the peripheral blood and target tissues to examine the changes in nutrient metabolism. Linear mixed models will be used to determine the effect of time or/and surgical procedures on the aforementioned parameters. The molecular and physiological insights on these bariatric procedures will spur research on new therapeutic targets and potentially provide a none invasive substitute to weight loss and to diabetes treatment. In addition, the information from this study will be clinically relevant in stratifying bariatric procedure for patients toward remission of diabetes.
kw: RYGB surgery, sleeve gastrectomy, insulin secretion, insulin sensitivity, adipose tissue, skeletal muscle

title: Understanding and targeting liver fibrosis through the characterization of the novel functional interaction between c-Jun and the Hedgehog pathway
abs: The liver’s response to injury is to initiate a fibrotic process, which results in scarring. In chronic situations, severe scarring can lead to serious complications of the liver, including portal hypertension, liver failure and liver cancer. Hepatitis infections, as well as alcohol consumption and fatty liver disease, have been shown to result in fibrosis and severe liver damage. While the basic mechanistic details of liver fibrosis have been worked out, many questions remain, and effective treatment is still not on the horizon. In our efforts to uncover the role of c-Jun - a member of the AP-1 family transcription factors involved in liver cancer development - in the fibrotic process, we noted that absence of c-Jun in embryonic livers led to activation of heptatic stellate cells, indicative of liver fibrosis, concomitant to increased hedgehog (HH) signaling, which has recently emerged as a crucial driver of liver fibrosis. These data has prompted us to hypothesize the existence of functional crosstalk between these signaling pathways, exploration of which may potentially provide essential nodal points for therapeutic intervention of fibrosis. Given that c-Jun-/- embryos are lethal at mid-gestation, we propose here to perform a systematic analysis to understand the role of c-Jun in the 3 major cell types that are involved in liver fibrosis: hepatic stellate cells, Kupffer cells and hepatocytes, using the conditional knockout strategy. In addition, molecular analysis in specific cell types will be carried out to delineate the signaling among them with respect to the c-Jun/HH signaling axis. Finally, the clinical relevance of these findings will be evaluated using clinical material of various etiologies such as hepatitis and alcohol. Thus, the goal of the proposed research is to comprehensively tackle the unanswered questions, so as to obtain essential information that could be translated to clinical utility in the near future.
kw: c-Jun, hedgehog, liver fibrosis, mouse models

title: Olympics for gingival fibroblasts: towards soft tissue integration of dental implants
abs: Dental implant research over the years has been focused on Osseointegration. However, inadequate soft tissue integration poses a major hurdle for the success of implant surgery. Presently about 7-26% of dental implants fail due to lack of soft tissue integration. It is known that, surface topography of an implant can dictate the behavior of cells surrounding it, without the need for expensive growth factors. Altering the surface topography would therefore offer a cost-effective straightforward strategy for the development of bioactive dental implants capable of integrating with soft tissue surrounding it. However, selection of the best topography from a myriad of geometric combinations is a time consuming, inefficient and daunting task. In this proposal, we introduce Cellompic chips, which allow us to study the role of surface topographies on cell behavior. A Cellompic chip is a 3 cm diameter circular chip, which allows us to study cell migration, adhesion, proliferation and differentiation amongst others, in short, ‘Olympics for cells’ and hence the name. This chip is comprised of 160 mathematically designed random topographies. We hypothesize that optimal topography favoring soft tissue integration of dental implants can be identified by adapting a high throughput screening approach using the Cellompic chip. Our proposal is specifically aimed at developing fabrication of Cellompic chips using biomaterials that are routinely used in dentistry. We plan to study the morphology, adhesion markers, migration and expression of inflammatory mediators by gingival fibroblasts in the context of these exotic topographies. Using this interdisciplinary approach we shall identify and validate hit topographies on larger surface areas. These hits shall then be translated to abutment surfaces for in vivo testing in a canine model.
kw: Dental implants, Biomaterials, High throughput screening, Soft tissue regeneration, Surface topography

title: Ezh2-regulated dendritic cell functions in health and disease
abs: Polycomb group protein Ezh2, one of the key epigenetic regulators, is involved in various important biological and pathogenic processes. Ezh2 overexpression or somatic mutations are known to associate with several aggressive human cancers including prostate, breast cancers, lymphomas and leukemias, however the functional importance of Ezh2 in immune responses is poorly understood. We demonstrated previously that Ezh2 is required for the development and activation of lymphocytes. Our recent data further reveals critical roles of Ezh2 in dendritic cells (DCs). DCs, the most potent antigen-presenting cells, are known to be recruited to the infection sites or inflamed tissues, propagating local inflammation and disease progression. In this proposal we will further determine the molecular mechanisms, by which Ezh2 regulates dendritic cell functions in health and pathogenic inflammation. We propose three complementary aims utilizing a conditional DC-specific Ezh2-deficient mouse model, candida infection, allergic contact dermatitis, experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) model for multiple sclerosis (MS), in vitro DC-culture system and biochemical approaches. Accomplishing these Aims, we will gain better understanding of the Ezh2 function in immune responses and may be able to develop alternative therapies for immune disorders regulated by DCs.Aim 1) We have identified talin1 as the first cytosolic substrate of Ezh2 and the preliminary data suggests critical roles for Ezh2-mediated talin methylation in cell adhesion and migration. Functional significance of these methylation sites will be determined. Aim 2) We will determine the molecular mechanisms underlying the defective emigration of Ezh2-deficeint Langerhans cells (LCs) from epidermis in steady state and under inflammatory conditions. Whether Ezh2-regulated DC function is critical for skin immunity will be examined using mouse models. Aim 3) The reduced EAE disease progression in mice with Ezh2-deficient dendritic cells is probably partially regulated by defective DC migration. Additional factors contributing to the overall progress of the disease will be determined.
kw: Ezh2, Langerhans Cells, Dendritic cells, inflammation

title: Leucine rich alpha-2-glycoprotein 1 as a novel therapeutic target in ischemic cardiovascular diseases
abs: Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) caused by atherosclerotic plaque formation are the leading cause of death in Singapore and worldwide. Conventional revascularization methods could relieve the symptom but offer no cure. In addition, not all patients are suitable for or benefit from these treatments. The non-surgical therapeutic angiogenesis has been shown to improve tissue perfusion and function in animal models but none of the tested pro-angiogenic factors fulfilled the promise of clinical benefits. Therefore, there remains a significant unmet clinical need. My recent study led to the identification of a novel angiogenic factor LRG1, which promotes vessel formation either on its own or in combination with VEGF-A. Preliminary data show that LRG1 regulates the signalling in different types of vascular cells suggesting a multifunctional role of LRG1 in angiogenesis. In this proposal, we will test the hypothesis that LRG1 promotes the functional vasculature formation, and enhances ischemic tissue perfusion and function. As comorbidities such as diabetes can strongly affect the result of angiogenic therapies, we will study the impact of diabetes on LRG1 regulated angiogenesis. Cells and organ explants from diabetic mice will also be used in a wide range of angiogenesis assays. Finally, heart ischemia will be induced in diabetic mice to evaluate the therapeutic potential of LRG1 in CVDs. The sustained LRG1 expression will be achieve by adenovirus mediated gene transfer technology. In summary, we proposed a comprehensive analysis of LRG1’s function in angiogenesis under normal and diabetic condition. The mechanistic information extracted from this work will make a major contribution to our understanding of the molecular and cellular mechanisms of angiogenesis, aid the on-going development of Lrg1 therapeutics, and facilitate the treatment of ischemic vascular complications. If LRG1 increases tissue perfusion and function in our mouse model we will extend this study in large animals and eventually in human.
kw: LRG1, angiogenesis, TGFbeta, diabetes, cardiovascular diseases, ischemia

title: DEVELOPMENT OF A CHIMERIC MULTIVALENT VACCINE AGAINST HAND, FOOT AND MOUTH DISEASE
abs: Hand, foot and mouth disease (HFMD) is emerging as a significant threat to public health, particularly in the Asia-Pacific region. Large scale outbreaks at epidemic levels have been associated with social and economic consequences, with the disruption of daily activities of children and adults alike. No approved specific anti-viral therapy or vaccine exists for HFMD while only a handful of whole-inactivated vaccine candidates based on HEV71 are undergoing clinical trials. The disease can result from infection by human enteroviruses, over 25 serotypes of which, spanning over the three species, human enterovirus A (HEV-A), B (HEV-B) and C (HEV-C). Based on the well-documented success of poliovirus eradication, a HEV-C enterovirus, increasing herd immunity of the general population at risk, in the form of a rigorous vaccination program, would likely be the best way to control HFMD effectively. However, due to the large genetic diversity of enteroviruses implicated as etiologic agents of HFMD, a monovalent vaccine against HEV71 may not be the best solution for HFMD. The aim of this investigation is to develop a broad-spectrum, multivalent vaccine candidate, able to confer protection against all three species of HEVs that can cause HFMD. We describe the intended development of the multivalent vaccine candidate for HFMD using two approaches: the construction of chimeric viruses based on the poliovirus vaccine strain, Sabin 1 and the production of virus-like particles (VLPs) with cocktail formulations. The genetic stability, immunogenicity and protective efficacy of the multivalent vaccine will be evaluated in a suitable murine model in this study. Most importantly, the development of a multivalent vaccine against HFMD will enable the translational development of an effective anti-viral strategy against these human viral pathogens with increasing medical importance.
kw: Hand, foot and mouth disease (HFMD), human enteroviruses, Chimeric technology, vaccine development

title: Genetic dissection of p75 neurotrophin receptor function in health and disease
abs: Injury and degeneration in the adult nervous system often results in re-activation of signaling pathways that are normally only active during development. The p75 neurotrophin receptor (p75NTR) is one such signaling molecule whose expression increases markedly after neural injury and neurodegeneration. p75NTR signaling actively contributes to neuronal and glial cell damage, axonal degeneration and synaptic dysfunction, hence there is a good rationale for inhibiting p75NTR in neural injury and neurodegeneration. However, p75NTR has been a difficult receptor to study; the mechanisms by which p75NTR couples to downstream pathways and how these contribute to p75NTR function remain outstanding questions in the field. Moreover, the signaling pathways regulated by p75NTR in human neurons and their relevance to human nervous system diseases remain unexplored. Recent discoveries from our laboratory have provided new insights into the underlying logic of p75NTR signaling, paving the way for a genetic dissection of p75NTR function and physiology and a better understanding of the role of p75NTR in nervous system injury and degeneration. The overall objective of this proposal is to elucidate the physiological relevance of the different signaling pathways regulated by p75NTR in health and diseases of the nervous system. This will be achieved through studies in genetically modified mice carrying pathway-specific mutations in the p75ntr gene, which uncouple distinct downstream pathways, and in human neurons derived by differentiation from human embryonic stem (ES) cells and induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells from patients and controls, focusing on Alzheimer’s disease (AD). Our hypothesis is that alterations in p75NTR signaling in diseased neurons and glial cells activate pro-apoptotic and neurodegenerative pathways which amplify neuropathology. Closing this knowledge gap will give us a better understanding of disease mechanisms and open new opportunities to develop neuroprotective strategies to improve disease outcome.
kw: neurotrophins; p75NTR; neuron survival; neurodegeneration, Alzheimer's disease; amyotrophic lateral sclerosis

title: Annexin-A1: a host factor modulating influenza virus replication
abs: Influenza virus infects millions of people each year and can result in severe or even fatal complications. Understanding virus recognition and host responses to influenza infection will enable the future development of more effective anti-viral therapies The host immune system recognizes viral RNA via specific toll-like receptors (TLRs), and intracellular sensors that directly activate anti-viral immune responses. Previous research has revealed diverse yet important roles for Annexin family of proteins in modulating the course of influenza infection. However, the role of Annexin-A1 (ANXA1) in influenza virus infection has not been addressed. Our published and preliminary data demonstrate key involvement of ANXA1 in innate viral receptor pathways in macrophages. ANXA1 is upregulated in nasal swab samples obtained from influenza infected patients and mice. ANXA1 enhances influenza virus replication in vitro and in vivo, and presence of ANXA1 is detrimental during infection in vivo. We hypothesize that ANXA1 is a host response protein which may be critical in host anti-viral responses and that modulation of the ANXA1 pathway by virus may represent a new mechanism of virus-mediated regulation of the host immune response. To test this hypothesis, we combine our expertise in ANXA1 biology, transgenic mouse generation, influenza infection and innate immune signaling to : (1) Assess how ANXA1 expression and activation in different cell types can influence the immune response to influenza in vivo. (2) Determine the role played by ANXA1 in the innate immune response to influenza; (3) Examine the molecular mechanisms by which ANXA1 modulates the viral receptor response.The investigations we propose will clearly define the role played by ANXA1 in influenza infection. If modulating ANXA1 can functionally regulate virus replication, novel therapeutic avenues can be created. These data will enhance our understanding of disease pathogenesis and may lead to the identification of novel targets for anti-viral therapies.
kw: Virus infection, host factor, host-pathogen interaction, toll-like receptor, innate immunity, inflammasome

title: Development of anticancer therapeutics from a lead proapoptotic peptide targeting cell-surface GRP78
abs: Cancer is characterized by uncontrollable cell proliferation and massive angiogenesis. Both proapoptotic and antiangiogenic agents have been developed as anticancer drugs. However, current cancer drugs tend to present severe side effects due to unintended targeting of normal cells. Hence, there is a pressing need for therapeutics that specifically target and kill cancer cells while sparing normal cells. One emerging target is glucose regulated protein 78 kDa (GRP78), which is preferentially expressed on the surface of cancer cells and tumor endothelial cells, and promotes tumor cell survival and metastasis. It is a major stress response protein residing in the ER lumen of normal cells. To adapt to the stressful cancer microenvironment of hypoxia, acidity and metabolic toxicity, cancerous cells overexpress GRP78 and translocate a subpopulation of this protein to cell surface. Isthmin (ISM) is a novel secreted 60 kDa anticancer protein discovered by us. Intravenous delivery of recombinant ISM potently suppressed tumor growth in mice by inducing apoptosis in cancerous cells. Significantly, ISM induces apoptosis by targeting cell-surface GRP78.We have further designed a cyclic pentapeptide, ISM-Pep1, which binds GRP78 with single-digit nanomolar affinity and potently induced apoptosis and suppressed tumor growth in mice. Based on this, we hypothesize that ISM-Pep1 can serve as a lead compound to be optimized into a drug candidate for cancer.In this proposal, we aim to:1.Synthesize a library of ISM-Pep1 analogs for structure-activity relationship studies to optimize bioactivity, specificity and drug-like properties. 2.Elucidate the mechanism of action of ligand-induced cancerous cell apoptosis.This proposal is based on protected IP originated from Singapore. The optimized drug candidate could potentially result in a first-in-class oncology drug and possibly the first oncology drug developed by a collaboration of Singapore-based academic institutions. It would make a significant contribution in translating basic research for better human health.
kw: GRP78, Isthmin, angiogenesis, cancer, peptide, peptidomimetic

title: An integrated approach to identify therapeutic targets for skeletal muscle disorders
abs: De-regulation of epigenetic control is increasingly apparent in many human pathologies including cancer. Small molecule inhibitors of chromatin modifying proteins have shown great promise in preclinical trials, validating druggability of epigenetic modulators. In muscle cells, proliferation and differentiation are mutually exclusive events that are regulated by chromatin-associated proteins. Among these, lysine methyltransferases that mediate methylation of histone and non-histone proteins play a central role in maintaining this equilibrium. We have recently shown that the lysine methyltransferase G9a inhibits differentiation of muscle precursor cells. Interestingly, G9a not only mediates repressive histone H3 lysine 9, chromatin marks on differentiation specific muscle promoters, but also methylates MyoD, a key transcription factor required for differentiation. Our preliminary studies show for the first time that besides regulating differentiation, G9a concomitantly controls proliferation via regulation of cell cycle genes. This proposal is based on the hypothesis that G9a-mediated methylation of both histone and non-histone proteins, is a central regulator of muscle growth and differentiation. G9a therefore presents a potentially important therapeutic target. We will systematically dissect mechanisms underlying G9a involvement in muscle tissue homeostasis. Mechanisms by which G9a regulates cell cycle control by repressing some genes, while activating others, will be analyzed. In addition, protein methylome profiling will be performed to identify non-histone substrates of G9a. Effector proteins that interact with methylated residues will be identified using SILAC technology. These studies will for the first time, provide an integrated global view of the interplay between proliferation and differentiation of muscle precursor cells by G9a. This is an essential first step to identify and develop novel druggable targets in the context of muscle dysfunction (e.g rhabdomyosarcomas). Our cutting-edge research capability in this field is combined with a unique collection of reagents and backed by a solid body of prior work.
kw: skeletal muscle, methylation, epigenetics, chromatin, differentiation

title: Co-agonists in human T cell activation
abs: The proportion of MHC molecules on an antigen-presenting cell that present antigenic peptide to a responding T-cell is small compared to those presenting non-stimulatory self peptides – the T-cell must find the antigenic “needle in the haystack” of seemingly irrelevant MHC molecules. T-cell responses are enhanced by the presence of seemingly irrelevant endogenous pMHC, a phenomenon termed co-agonism. Non-stimulatory pMHC complexes have not yet been studied in clinically relevant settings. Here we determine the requirements of human hepatitis B virus (HBV)-specific T-cells for recognition of co-agonists. TCR-like monoclonal antibodies, recognizing the MHC-peptide complex, will enable determination of the amount of antigen displayed on the surface of the APC in relation to other non-stimulatory MHC class-I molecules. T-cells from a patient can be “engineered” to express a TCR recognizing HBV, which can then be transferred back into the patient for therapy. We will determine the role of co-agonists in activation of such engineered T-cells. We will use single chain pMHCI molecules to determine the molecular requirements for human T cell recognition of co-agonists, separating CD8 binding to agonist and co-agonist, determining the strength of interaction between CD8 and non-stimulatory MHCI required for effective co-agonism. We will analyze the role of co-agonists in MHCI-restricted CD4+ T-cells (particularly useful in T-cell therapy) which may have very different co-agonist requirements from normal MHCI-restricted T-cells. We will use advanced imaging techniques (TIRF and FRET microscopy) to investigate signalling parameters during co-agonist-aided T-cell activation at the immunological synapse. We will investigate the recruitment of Lck, and its activation, along with the phosphorylation of TCR/CD3 ITAMS. Combinations of transduced fluorescent molecules for live imaging, and of antibodies for fixed cell imaging will be used to identify the role of co-agonists in the formation of TCR signaling microclusters during formation of the immunological synapse.
kw: T cell activation, CD8+ T cells, co-agonist, immunological synapse

title: Characterization of a novel mouse model of severe dengue mediated by maternally acquired dengue specific antibodies
abs: Dengue represents the most serious arthropod-borne viral disease. Dengue clinical manifestations range from mild febrile illness to life-threatening haemorrhage and vascular leakage. The development of a relevant animal model of dengue has long been recognized as one of the major roadblocks in understanding dengue pathogenesis and validating therapeutic and prophylactic strategies.Epidemiological studies indicate that most of the severe dengue cases arise from a secondary infection with a heterologous serotype of dengue virus (DENV) or upon primary infection of infants born to dengue immune mothers. From these observations emerged the hypothesis of antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE) of disease severity whereby sub-neutralizing levels of anti-DENV antibodies cross-react but fail to neutralize DENV. Mechanistically the antibody-mediated virus entry into Fc receptor-bearing cells eventually results in high virus output and massive inflammatory response that correlate with increased disease severity. So far the ADE hypothesis has been supported experimentally by the passive administration in adult mice of sub-neutralizing concentrations of DENV specific antibodies prior to DENV infection. We have generated a novel mouse model of severe dengue mediated by maternally acquired DENV specific antibodies. We showed that DENV2 infection of young mice born to DENV1-immune mothers resulted in increased disease severity as assessed by survival rate, viremia and vascular leakage, compared to DENV2-infected mice born to dengue naïve dams. This work represents a landmark in the development of a relevant mouse model of severe dengue. The first aim of this project is to fully characterize this novel mouse model of ADE. This includes the virus kinetic profile and cell tropism, the role of breast milk antibodies, and the age windows of disease protection versus susceptibility. In the second aim, we will study the mechanisms that are involved in the disease severity. The role of selected soluble mediators, complement proteins and mast cells will be determined.
kw: antibody-dependent enhancement; maternal antibodies; AG129; mouse model; vascular leakage; severe dengue

title: Characterizing novel mechanisms of neuroinflammation in Experimental Autoimmune Encephalomyelitis and Multiple Sclerosis
abs: CD137 (4-1BB, TNFRSF9), a member of the tumor necrosis factor (TNF) receptor family, is a potent T cell costimulatory molecule that is expressed on activated T cells and vascular endothelial cells. CD137 ligand (CD137L) is expressed by antigen presenting cells (APC) as a transmembrane protein on the cell surface. CD137L not only crosslinks CD137 on T cells but also transmits signals into APC. This reverse CD137L signaling is activating for APC. In monocytes and macrophages it induces adherence, secretion of proinflammatory cytokines and migration. Our recent work demonstrates that CD137L signaling also activates microglia, the resident APC in the central nervous system. Microglia is intimately involved in the process of neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration. Employing experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE), a commonly used murine model for human Multiple Sclerosis (MS), we found that gene-modified mice lacking CD137L are protected from this disease. In this project we propose to clarify why CD137L-/- mice are protected from EAE. Specifically, we will determine the effects that the absence of CD137L has on leukocyte infiltration, T cell costimulation, and the activation of APC and microglia (aim 1). We just discovered that CD137 can also be expressed by neurons under certain conditions. We will characterize induction and expression pattern of CD137 on neurons, and test whether CD137 on neurons can activate microglia, leading to oligodendrocyte death (aim 2). Further, we will determine the expression of CD137 and CD137L in human MS brain tissue, and whether activation of human microglia by CD137L signalling will lead to oligodendrocyte death as we have observed in the murine system (aim 3). In MS myelin glycolipid-specific T cells have been found with high frequency. We will investigate the importance of CD137 and CD137L engagement for the stimulation of human glycolipid-specific T cells, with the aim of exploiting possible immunomodulatory interventions (aim 4).
kw: Microglia, neurodegeneration, inflammation, CD137, Experimental Autoimmune Encephalomyelitis, Multiple Sclerosis

title: Roles of DAP3 in mitochondrial dynamics and neurodegeneration
abs: Mitochondria are organelles with dynamic properties, which constantly fuse and divide. Moreover, mitochondrial dynamics plays critical roles in regulating cell death and dysfunction which may cause many human diseases such neurodegenerative diseases, cardiac disorders and cancers. Death associated protein 3 (DAP3) is a novel GTP binding mitochondrial protein which was identified as a mediator in TNF-alpha induced apoptosis. Some results suggested that DAP3 played a promoting role in extrinsic apoptosis pathways and loss of DAP3 could result in protection for extrinsic stimuli induced apoptosis. On the other hand, controversial results argue that DAP3 indeed has a protecting role in cell death. These results suggested that characterization of DAP3’s bio-physiological function is critical. Our preliminary results show that loss of DAP3 could break down the homeostasis of mitochondrial dynamics, which leads to mitochondrial fragmentation and induces cell death, indicating that DAP3 plays a vital role in maintaining mitochondrial dynamics and is essential for mitochondrial quality control. We therefore hypothesize that DAP3 plays an important role in mediating mitochondria dynamics, which directly entails the function of DAP3 in cell death. Hence, we will be dissecting the central molecular mechanisms of how DAP3 mediates mitochondrial dynamics and the role of DAP3 in cell death. To extend our understanding on these aspects, we will generate a DAP3 knockout model in Drosophila and investigate its role in mitochondrial biogenesis and neurodegeneration. Thus, our specific aims are: 1) To investigate the role of DAP3 in mediating mitochondria dynamics. 2) To dissect the role of DAP3 in cell death. 3) To study the role of DAP3 in vivo using Drosophila as a model. A better understanding of the molecular mechanisms of DAP3 in regulating mitochondrial functions will lead to novel therapeutic strategies for neurodegenerative disorders in the future.
kw: Parkinson, Mitochondria, neurodegeneration, cell death, cell biology

title: Near-infrared-to-ultraviolet photon upconversion for highly penetrating photodynamic therapy of solid and deep seated cancers
abs: Photodynamic therapy (PDT) is an alternative cancer therapeutic option that involves the administration of light-sensitive photosensitizer drugs. As the drug preferentially accumulate in tumor cells, light shone at it activates the drug to release reactive oxygen species, thus leading to tumor eradication. As most photosensitizers are activated by visible light which cannot pass through a thick tissue, conventional PDT is limited to flat, superficial tumors or tumors that are accessible to endoscopes, whereas solid organ tumors are at a thickness much greater than that possible with current technology. The use of near-infrared (NIR) light in PDT can afford greater tissue penetration depths than that of visible light because the absorbance for most biomolecules reaches a minimum in the NIR window. Here, we aim to develop a new NIR-PDT technique using titanium dioxide (TiO2)-coated upconversion fluorescent nanoparticles (UCN) at a new excitation wavelength of 800nm. The UCN core act as a light transducer to ‘harness’ energy from the deeply penetrating NIR light and converts it to higher energy visible and ultraviolet (UV) light that can excite the coated TiO2 photosensitizer for synergistic imaging and photodynamic treatment of large and deep-seated tumors. As the UCN would be neodymium-doped, a shift in its excitation wavelength from classical 980nm to 800nm can be expected. Since the main constituent of biological tissue – water - absorbs strongly in the 980nm region, this shift in excitation to 800nm is expected to improve the light tissue penetration depth and alleviate overheating effect associated with the use of conventional 980nm light. Toxicity and efficacy of the newly developed NIR-PDT will be studied in cells and animals. We hypothesize that the new NIR-PDT will help overcome the limitations of conventional PDT by offering a higher penetration depth of NIR light and upconversion of nanoparticles to convert NIR to UV/Visible light.
kw: Photodynamic therapy, Near-infrared, Upconversion, Titanium dioxide, Cancer therapy, Deep penetration

title: Evaluation of Magnetic Resonance Image (MRI)-Based Novel 3-Dimensional (3-D) Printed Scaffold Meniscus to Replicate and Replace Native Meniscus in an Ovine Model: In Vivo Studies of Morphology, Function, Viability and Response
abs: The knee menisci are fibro-cartilaginous crescent-shaped wedges that are essential to knee joints in load bearing, shock absorption and joint stability. Their morphology and internal structure are crucial to their normal functioning. Meniscal injuries are common in both younger individuals (sports injuries) as well as older patients (degenerative tears), and increase the risk of post-traumatic knee osteoarthritis. Current treatment modalities (meniscectomy, repair) are often suboptimal due to poor healing potential and disruption of normal structure, while allograft transplantation is limited by mismatch and availability issues.This clinical need has prompted research in new scaffold technologies for meniscal replacement, but current techniques do not recreate the internal microstructure crucial to meniscal function. Our group has developed a novel patented 3-D printing process using drop-on-demand micro-dispensing technology that can create multi-material meniscal scaffolds with morphology and microstructural patterns similar to native menisci. We believe this specific advantage in being able to replicate internal microstructural orientations is a breakthrough in bioscaffold technology that will enhance the chances of long-term bio-implant success. Our 3-D printed cell-laden polymer/collagen meniscal scaffolds have been characterized in vitro for material and biomechanical properties and biological responses, with promising results. The proposed present investigation aims to develop this technology further, using an in vivo ovine model; we aim to validate the customized 3-D replication of meniscal morphology by MRI-based scaffold printing in a large animal model. The meniscal scaffolds (without and with autogenous cell seeding) will be surgically implanted in the sheep or goat knees, and assays performed for knee function and complications, biocompatibility and inflammatory response (with sham surgery and meniscectomy controls). After euthanasia and knee harvesting at time intervals, further evaluations will be made for biomechanical function and histological, cellular and molecular changes.This project aims to support the downstream development of customized meniscal implants in clinical applications.
kw: 3-dimensional (3D) printing; Knee Meniscus; Tissue Engineered Scaffold; Animal models; Magnetic Resonance imaging (MRI); Inflammation biomarkers

title: Metabolic control by the TGF-beta superfamily receptor ALK: A novel regulator of insulin secretion, fat accumulation and energy balance
abs: The aim of this proposal is to understand the functions of a novel regulatory network controlling insulin secretion, fat accumulation and energy balance centred around selected components of the transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-beta) signaling system, including the type I receptor ALK7 and its ligands activin B and GDF-3. We have shown that these molecules are part of paracrine signaling networks that control important functions in pancreatic islets and adipose tissue through feedback inhibition and feed-forward regulatory mechanisms. These discoveries open up a new area of research with important basic and clinical implications for the understanding and treatment of metabolic diseases, such as diabetes and obesity. In this project, we propose to use conditional knock-out mouse models, human adipocytes, samples from a human cohort with impaired insulin secretory capacity controlled for insulin sensitivity, and a novel chemical-genetic approach to elucidate tissue-specific and acute homeostatic functions of the ALK7 signaling network in the control of insulin secretion, glucose homeostasis, adipose tissue accumulation and energy balance. The results of the proposed work may pave the way for the development of improved anti-diabetic drugs capable of enhancing insulin secretion, limiting fat accumulation and ameliorating diet-induced obesity by targeting components of the ALK7 signaling network.
kw: Insulin, pancreas, adipose, diabetes, obesity, glycemia

title: Bridging Discovery to Development of a Novel Direct Thrombin Inhibitor
abs: Thrombosis, encompassing cardiovascular, cerebrovascular and venous thromboembolism, is the commonest cause of mortality worldwide. Antithrombotic therapy remains the primary therapy in these conditions with global sales of anticoagulants exceeding S$6 billion annually. Our team has successfully identified and clinically tested several anticoagulant leads targeting specific procoagulant serine proteases, including factor IIa (thrombin), factor IXa and factor Xa. We have isolated variegin, a novel direct thrombin inhibitor (DTI) with enhanced structural-activity relationships compared with the market-leading reference compound, hirulog-1 (bivalirudin). Variegin potently inhibits thrombin (Ki of 0.318 ± 0.020 nM) 10-fold more potently than hirulog-1 (Ki of 2.94 ± 0.12 nM). Unlike hirulog-1, which must be given as a continuous infusion because of its short half-life of 25 minutes, variegin, through sustained inhibition of thrombin exosite-1 via a unique cleavage by-product, MH22, has a terminal half-life of 117 minutes. We expect variegin will achieve sustained anticoagulation during the majority of percutaneous coronary intervention procedures, which typically last 60-90 minutes. We propose to refine bioanalytic assays of our locally discovered lead compound, variegin, targeting sensitivity levels sufficient for microdosing studies, and investigate variegin’s in vitro and in vivo stability, reversibility, nonclinical toxicity and efficacy using human blood and disease-specific animal models. We hypothesize that variegin will show better preclinical efficacy (anticoagulant intensity) and safety (bleeding risk) compared with 2 reference compounds, hirulog-1 and heparin, and that calibrated bioanalytic assays can measure the anticoagulant effect of variegin with high sensitivity. Our ultimate goal is to develop variegin, a locally discovered DTI, into a single anticoagulant that can be used interchangeably for intravenous and subcutaneous clinical applications, coupled with the parallel development of a calibrated bioanalytic assay for treatment monitoring. The lead clinical application will be anticoagulation during percutaneous coronary intervention, which is performed on more than 2 million patients annually around the world.

title: Hybrid Quantum Technologies
abs: We propose to create hybrids between two pairs of quantum systems: Atomic degrees of freedom, which provide a number of ways to store and process information, and optical and microwave photons, respectively. Optical photon are suited for long-range transport, microwave photons allow to couple to many different physical systems, be it atoms, flux qubits, or nuclear spins in solid state defects. For the atom-optical hybrid system, we capitalize on two recent developments in the participating teams. The CQED system at CQT hosts up to a million atoms in a cavity in a super-lattice. The large number of atoms enhances atom-cavity interaction by almost 3 orders of magnitude, and provides resonant optical depths on the order of 1000. This lattice also enables photons entering the cavity sideways to scatter super-radiantly into the cavity mode. We have also reduced the bandwidth of entangled photon pairs by about 4 orders of magnitude, suitable for absorption by an atomic system. We now can efficiently scatter these photons into the cavity, mapping the photonic qubit state to the atomic ensemble in the process and forming Dicke qubits. Dicke qubits can be manipulated using two-photon Raman transitions with a high efficiency, and state detection can be achieved via the excellent single atom detection capability of the cavity. For the atom-microwave hybrid, R. Dumke had demonstrated the controlled interaction of ultra cold matter with the vortices on type-II superconductors, providing a bridge between coherent atomic states and solid-state quantum devices. Building on this idea, he will employ coplanar waveguide resonators to couple atomic quantum states to superconducting quantum systems. For this, much lower temperatures have to be reached, which a recently set up dilution refrigeration system will provide. This will enable an information exchange between the atomic states and superconducting structures.

title: Development of a Clinical Assay of Homologous Recombination (HR) DNA Repair Deficiency in Gynaecological Cancers
abs: Aims: To develop a clinical assay of homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) in gynaecological tumours that correlates with functional HRD.Background: The HR DNA repair pathway mediated by proteins like BRCA1/2 is required for the repair of DNA double-strand breaks arising from DNA-damaging chemotherapeutic agents (e.g. platinum salts), as well as DNA single-strand breaks that are generated by Poly(ADP-ribose) Polymerase inhibitors (PARPis). Cancer cells lacking HR are exquisitely sensitive to PARPis and platinum salts. There is, however, currently no validated clinical biomarker of functional HRD that can predict response to PARPi or DNA-damaging agents. Cytoplasmic mislocalisation of the key HR related-protein RAD51 has been observed in cancers with germline BRCA1/2 mutations and after downregulation of HR-related proteins in vitro, thus suggesting that this may be a marker for HRD. Methods: Using immunofluorescence, we will assess the prevalence of cytoplasmic mislocalisation of RAD51 in gynaecological tumours, and patient-derived xenograft and cell line models of ovarian, uterine and cervical cancer. The relative intensity score of RAD51 staining in the nucleus and cytoplasm (i.e. a nuclear-cytoplasmic or NC-ratio) will be calculated using automated microscopy and correlated with the presence of underlying mutations/ downregulation of HR or HR-related proteins in tumours and cell lines by whole exome/ genome sequencing. The functional relevance of the NC-ratio will also be assessed in vitro and in vivo by evaluating the effect of PARPi and platinum treatment in cell lines and xenografts respectively across the spectrum of NC-ratios. We will thus assess if low NC-ratios (i.e. less than 1 = higher staining in cytoplasm versus the nucleus) are likely to predict HR deficiency and hence PARPi/ platinum sensitivity. Further evaluation of this biomarker will be performed by correlating the NC-ratio of tumour tissue from patients with mutations in HR-pathway genes and outcome/ response following chemotherapy or treatment with PARPis.

title: Novel genetic and non-genetic risk factors for endothelial dysfunction and diabetic micro-angiopathies – a follow-up prospective study.
inst: Khoo Teck Puat Hospital Pte Ltd
abs: BackgroundPathogenesis of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) and micro-vascular complications is highly complex and incompletely understood. Key pathogenic factors (e.g. hyperglycemia & excess adiposity associated pro-inflammatory milieu) converge upon the vascular endothelium resulting in systemic endothelial dysfunction. Our NMRC-funded program project grant (PPG) recruited ~2,100 T2DM for cross-sectional endothelial function & arterial stiffness assessment in-vivo and detailed phenotyping of foot & kidney complications. Blood and urine samples were also bio-banked for biomarkers discovery. We have made several interesting preliminary observations (details below). However, given the limitation of cross-sectional study, the present proposal aims to recall these subjects for prospective assessment of vascular function and incident diabetic complications. HypothesisWe hypothesize that baseline traditional risk factors and novel biomarkers (including genetics) predict changes in vascular function and incident diabetic complications prospectively. MethodsAll ~2,100 PPG participants will be systematically recalled over 2-3 years for re-assessment (including blood and urine collection) using the same protocol as baseline visit. Furthermore, bi-ocular single-field fundophotography and detailed cognitive assessment will be obtained for additional phenotyping. We plan to prospectively study the relationship between (i) traditional (e.g. hyperglycemia) and novel risk factors (RFs) (both non-genetic and genetic), (ii) endothelial function, (iii) intermediate phenotype (e.g. arterial stiffness) and (iii) final phenotype i.e. diabetic foot syndrome and nephropathy (refer to figure).SignificanceDiabetic complications are common and confer considerable morbidities and mortalities. There is ethnic disparity in susceptibility to diabetic complications e.g. nephropathy is more common among Asians. Hence, Asian data are needed. Uncovering novel RFs can help improve risk stratification. Some of these RFs may be amenable to therapeutic interventions. The large amount of data and bio-banked samples collected from carefully phenotyped T2DM subjects will be an invaluable resource for future research, to groom the next-generation investigators and to forge industry-academic or international collaborations.
