title: RNA Helicase DP103: Characterization of a novel modulator of Wnt/?-catenin signaling in Triple Negative Breast Cancers
abs: Breast cancer is a diverse malignancy; and is a principle cause of death in women globally. Understanding the molecular mechanisms driving tumor progression is important, as it will facilitate development of targeted therapies. Amongst the various subtypes of breast cancers, Triple negative breast cancers (TNBCs) are a subtype of breast cancers that are highly invasive, and have poorer prognosis compared to other breast cancer subtypes. Due to its lack of hormone receptor expression, treatment available for TNBCs are limited and prognosis of this subtype of cancer is also worse compared to other subtypes of breast cancers. De-regulation of the wingless and integration site growth factor (Wnt) signaling pathway via mutations in APC and Axin, proteins that target ?-catenin for destruction; have been linked to various types of human cancer. Although Wnt inhibitors are in early clinical development, it is unclear whether they will be of therapeutic benefit to breast cancer patients, and subsequently, to which ones. Recent studies show that TNBCs are more Wnt-responsive compared to other breast cancer subtypes. We recently uncovered a new role for a DEAD-box RNA helicase, DP103 to define the metastatic potential of TNBCs. Given the correlative expression of Wnt activity and higher DP103 levels in TNBC, we sought to explore if there is a link between DP103 and Wnt activity. Indeed our preliminary data presents DP103 as a novel modulator of Wnt signaling in TNBCs. The specific aims of this proposal are to:1) Determine clinical correlation between DP103 and Wnt-associated genes in patients’ tissue specimens. 2) Elucidate the consequences of gain and loss of function of DP103 on Wnt/?-catenin signaling. 3) Determine if DP103 gene is a novel Wnt target. 4) Decipher the mechanism(s) by which DP103 regulates Wnt/?-catenin activity.5) Demonstrate the role of DP103 in modulating Wnt/?-catenin activity in vivo.
kw: DEAD-box RNA Helicase; novel modulator of Wnt Signaling; Triple Negative Breast Cancer; New binding partner of TCF/beta catenin; therapeutic target

title: The role of human fetal antigen presenting cells in tolerance and immunity
abs: Intra-uterine stem cell transplantation and gene therapy are potentially curative treatments for a number of disorders such as immune defects, metabolic disorders and osteogenesis imperfecta. In this setting, transplantation is performed without the need for preparative conditioning or post-transplant immunosuppression due to the general state of immune-tolerance within the developing fetus. However, poor engraftment and rejection still present significant barriers to successful prenatal transplantation. A key challenge in intra-uterine transplantation is to determine an optimum window of opportunity for treatment that will ensure graft tolerance. This window is intimately linked with the development of the fetal immune system and its functional competence. Dendritic cells and macrophages, collectively known as antigen presenting cells (APC), are critical regulators of immune system. These cells are responsible for self-tolerance but can activate potent immune responses upon challenge from pathogens, vaccines and foreign non-self proteins. We hypothesise that fetal APCs exert a critical role in mediating immunological tolerance during early development. The aim of our study is to precisely map the development of APCs in the human fetus and to establish their functional properties. State-of-the-art multi-parameter flow-cytometry and microscopy will be used to characterize the different populations of APCs and to determine their anatomical localization in fetal tissues. This will be complemented by gene expression analysis to identify novel markers, cytokine and growth factor requirements which will predict their functional specializations. In vitro studies to determine their activatory or suppressive properties and precursor potential will also be performed.Detailed understanding of how APCs exert tolerogenic and immunogenic effects in the human fetus will allow us to develop better strategies for prenatal transplantation therapy. It will also provide insights into the mechanisms underlying fetal susceptibility to intra-uterine infections and feto-maternal tolerance. In addition, these findings will form the basic foundation for any future APC-based immunotherapy programmes.

title: Designing and evaluating syndromic surveillance in context: utility and performance for detection of outbreaks in Singapore
abs: Syndromic data are increasingly used for surveillance, and can be used to detect outbreaks of known infectious diseases, and potentially novel infections and bioterrorist attacks. However, more work is needed to understand the optimal ways of using such surveillance systems, their ability to detect different types of outbreaks, and how such data sources compare with and can be integrated with “traditional surveillance” activities.Singapore is an island-state vulnerable to emerging and re-emerging infectious disease threats, with Nipah, SARS, Chikungunya, dengue and pandemic influenza having caused serious outbreaks in the last 15 years. We propose to design and evaluate syndromic surveillance systems for Singapore, spanning the clinical disease spectrum for a range of pathogens, including potential agents of bioterrorism. Leveraging on our expertise in surveillance and outbreak related studies, and with partners from statistical and computing sciences and contacts with local healthcare institutions and relevant government ministries, we aim to:- set up processes for collecting syndromic data as well as confirmed outbreaks- field surveys to collect data to simulate how outbreaks may present- development of appropriate processing algorithms including natural language processing algorithms on electronic medical record data from primary care and emergency departments- validation of algorithms to detect outbreaks - produce analytic tools and software applications to integrate syndromic and traditional data sourcesKey hypotheses to test are whether syndromic surveillance can detect signals of known outbreaks earlier, how it performs in simulated outbreak scenarios of different characteristics, and how much improvement in system performance is possible by adding syndromic data to traditional surveillance. By answering the above questions, we will be able to rationalize when and what types of syndromic surveillance systems are useful, and significantly increase the options for infectious disease surveillance available to public health practitioners and policy makers in Singapore and elsewhere.

title: Evaluation of a Novel Preferential Covered Stent Capability of Emboli Prevention and Side Branch Flow Preservation using Swine Model
abs: Stroke is the fourth leading cause of death in US, Singapore and many developed countries. It is also the leading cause of disabilities resulting in huge socio-economic burden. This project aims to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of a new stent invented by our team targeted to prevent stroke. Carotid artery stenosis, usually over the bifurcation, is a major cause of stroke and is treatable. It causes stroke by athero-embolization, where loose fragments of atherosclerotic plaque dislodge and go into the brain circulation. Minimally invasive carotid stenting is appealing and well received by the publics and the clinicians. However, the peri-procedural stroke rate with carotid stenting is still higher than open surgery. The main reason is the bare metal stents currently used are not designed to treat athero-embolic disease. Targeting this clinical demand, we invented a new device – preferential covered stent. The prototype of this novel stent was shown to significantly reduce emboli releasing from the vessel wall and yet able to maintain side branch blood flow in mechanical flow loop experiment. We aim to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of this novel device using swine model with induced carotid atherosclerosis. We hypothesize 1) the preferential covered stent is able to reduce 50% or more of emboli going into the brain circulation compare to bare metal stent; 2) novel stent is capable of maintaining ?70% of the original side branch blood flow. Our project translates a new invention generated locally targeting unmet clinical need to a potential medical device through the experiments in large animal diseased model. The success of this research project will help prevent stroke, promote medical innovation and bring along economic benefit to our society.

title: Prevalence, severity and determinants of cancer-related fatigue (CRF) in Asian breast cancer patients
abs: There is a paucity of studies that focus on the symptom burden of cancer patients in Singapore, particularly the clinical effects of cancer-related fatigue (CRF). Knowing that early-stage breast cancer is curable, it is of paramount importance to evaluate the clinical and biological determinants of lingering symptoms in breast cancer survivors so that appropriate psychosocial interventions can be formulated. We hypothesize that variations in clinical and biological determinants contribute to different severities of CRF among Asian breast cancer patients. Through this study, we aim to evaluate the prevalence and severity of CRF among Asian breast cancer patients, and to identify the biological and clinical determinants of CRF among these patients. This will be a multicenter, prospective, longitudinal, observational study conducted at the National Cancer Centre Singapore and KK Women’s and Children’s Hospital. Informed consent will be obtained from participants before we proceed with data collection. The study participants will comprise two groups: a patient group and a matched healthy control group. They will be assessed at relevant time points. Biological determinants and symptoms associated with CRF will be assessed. The associations between changes in CRF, plasma cytokines levels, serum cortisol levels, and other clinical determinants will be elucidated. The study represents potentially landmark translational research addressing the clinical and biological determinants of CRF in breast cancer patients. On the basis of the data that will be obtained, interventional studies to alleviate symptoms of CRF can be designed to help cancer survivors better cope with their daily lives through continued symptom monitoring and management. The results of this study will clarify further research directions within the arena of cancer supportive care, survivorship, and psychosocial disciplines.

title: Molecular mechanism and treatment of acute megakaryoblastic leukemia in Singapore
abs: Singapore-Malaysia populations show high incidence of acute megakaryoblastic leukemia (AMKL); a quarter of local childhood acute myeloid leukemia (AML) patients suffer from AMKL. It is also known that AMKL develops frequently in patients of Down’s syndrome (DS), a most common congenital disease. The prognosis of AMKL is poor. Despite such a worldwide healthcare issue, the mechanistic basis for this disease remains not fully understood. Novel therapeutic approaches that are more effective and less toxic are clearly needed. In the proposed study, we aim to identify currently unknown genetic alterations, and also aim to develop a new treatment.In the preliminary study, we generated a mouse model of AMKL by combining genetically engineered mouse and retroviral insertional mutagensis (RIM). The mice developed AMKL-like disease and identified Jak/Stat and Notch pathways as AMKL-related key mechanism. Subsequent exome sequencing of primary AMKL patient cells exhibited that genes involved in Jak/Stat and Notch pathways were indeed frequently mutated. Furthermore, Jak/Stat inhibitors and Notch activator (but not inhibitor) both potently inhibited cell proliferation and induced apoptosis in AMKL cell lines. In the proposed study, we will further validate the Jak/Stat and Notch pathways as drug targets. Gene mutation status will be examined in a bigger cohort as the prevalence study employing targeted deep sequencing. Detailed molecular analysis as to how such genetic mutations contribute to leukemogenesis will be carried out, employing in vitro and in vivo hematological studies. Drug efficacy is further confirmed using in vivo xenograft model and its mechanism will also be precisely investigated. Interestingly, the Notch activator proved useful for AMKL treatment is a natural product, abundant in edible cruciferous vegetables such as broccoli. More intake of kai-lan (Chinese broccoli) could help reduce the high incidence of AMKL and other tumors caused by Notch inactivation in Malay-Singapore.

title: Examining the functions of gelsolin, a cytoskeletal protein, in regulating oxidative mechanisms that contribute to cancer cell behaviour
abs: Cancer cell invasion is a critical step in cancer progression and involve complex mechanisms. Gelsolin, which regulates cytoskeletal dynamics, has recently emerged as a player in several key aspects of tumour biology, leading to invasion, resistance to apoptosis, oncogenic signaling and control of gene transcription. We published that gelsolin is highly expressed at invasive edges of metastatic colon cancers, and promotes cancer cell invasion by enhancing extracellular matrix degradation. We have now discovered that gelsolin also promotes pro-oxidant states in colon cancer cells – it increases reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels and this confers heightened invasiveness. This is consistent with previous observations of increased ROS in cancer cells exhibiting enhanced invasion. Gelsolin also appears to alter antioxidant levels and activities. We propose that gelsolin potentially functions in regulating ROS levels, promoting redox disequilibrium that result in aggressive cancer cell behaviour. We aim to investigate the interactions of gelsolin with ROS, by examining the influence of gelsolin on ROS levels, as well as on expression and activities of ROS-regulating enzymes (antioxidants and ROS-producing enzymes). Gelsolin expression will be modulated in cancer cells using overexpression and siRNA-knockdown. ROS levels will be measured by assays to determine changes in superoxide (O2-) and other ROS species, eg. by Lucigenin assay and CM2-DCFDA. The mRNA and protein levels of ROS-regulating enzymes will be determined by real-time PCR and Western blotting. Changes in enzymatic activities will be assayed using enzyme-specific activity assays. The mechanisms by which gelsolin alters enzymatic activities will be studied to ascertain if gelsolin binds to and inhibits (or activates) enzymes at specific interaction sites. Techniques employed include computational modelling to predict protein interaction sites, co-immunoprecipitation, site mutagenesis and crystallography. The clinical relevance of gelsolin and its associations with ROS-regulating enzymes will be investigated by correlating their expression in human tumours with clinico-pathological outcomes.
kw: oxidative mechanisms, cytoskeleton, cancer

title: Identification and validation of hypoxia-dependent gene-regulatory mechanisms and von Hippel-Lindau tumor suppressor-dependent pathways for regulation of tumor growth and metastasis
abs: It has become increasingly clear the hypoxic microenvironment of tumours promotes oncogenic adaptation. The overall aim of this project is to understand hypoxia-dependent regulatory mechanisms that ultimately promote a more aggressive tumour phenotype. We will use an integrated, multidisciplinary approach, combining genomic and proteomic analysis, high-throughput functional screening, state-of-the art preclinical cancer models and clinical patient data with the specific aims:1. To systematically identify novel hypoxia-induced isoforms on a transcriptome-wide basis in cancer cells. In preliminary studies we have observed that hypoxia alters splicing mechanisms to generate novel RNA and protein products. This observation opens up new areas of exploration on the diversity of oncogenic mechanisms and addresses a currently unmet need in cancer therapeutic strategies as these mechanisms produce abundant and diverse mRNA and protein derivatives from genes that play poorly understood roles in oncogenesis.2. To investigate the epigenetic landscape in hypoxic tumour cells and hypoxia-dependent epigenetic regulatory mechanisms in tumours with the ultimate aim to understand their function in oncogenesis.3. Systematic sequencing of renal carcinoma has revealed co-mutation of the von Hippel Lindau tumour suppressor protein (VHL) with epigenetically regulatory histone modifying genes. Our studies on epigenetic changes in hypoxia will therefore also be important to understand VHL function. We will also use a protein affinity screen to identify novel substrates for VHL. It acts as an E3 ubiquitin ligase to mediate degradation of HIF proteins in normoxia but its other functions have remained enigmatic. Our preliminary data suggest that important metabolic regulators may be targeted by VHL as an E3 ubiquitin ligase. These novel regulatory mechanisms will now be explored in translational studies to investigate their importance in establishing tumour-specific changes in metabolism.Taken together these studies aim to develop new strategies for therapeutic intervention in cancer medicine.
kw: Hypoxia, Splicing, Gene regulation, tumor growth, epigenetics, tumor metastasis

title: In-depth exploration of the neuropathophysiology of cognitive dysfunction in systemic lupus erythematosus by combining resting-state and task-related functional magnetic resonance brain imaging
abs: Aim 1: To further unravel the functional neuropathology of cognitive dysfunction in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) by combining the use of resting-state and task-related functional magnetic resonance imaging of the brain (fMRI). We hypothesize that during resting state, connectivity would be dysfunctional (particularly in the default mode, salience and executive control networks) in SLE patients with cognitive dysfunction as compared to lupus patients without cognitive dysfunction and healthy subjects, and hypothetically such connectivity dysfunction would be correlated with the disruption of functional neural circuits gauged by task-related fMRI. Aim 2: To rationalize the clinical use of fMRI by addressing whether baseline abnormality of fMRI brain signals can predict cognitive decline in SLE patients. We hypothesize that dysfunctional connectivity and/or disruption of functional neural circuit may predict decline in lupus-related cognitive function. Methodology & approach: This proposal comprises both cross-sectional and prospective parts. Sixty-nine SLE patients and 69 demographically- and intelligence quotient-matched healthy subjects will undergo a formal computer-based neuropsychological test based on the Automated Neuropsychological Assessment Matrix (ANAM) for identifying cognitive dysfunction. The subjects will then undergo structural MRI brain scans, followed by an 8-minute resting-state fMRI to assess connectivity, and subsequently another 25-minute task-related fMRI scans to probe functional neural circuit, using a 3-Tesler MRI scanner. We will employ voxel-based general linear models to detect group-difference in functional connectivity metrics, and the two-sample t-test to compare the connectivity metrics between SLE patients with and without cognitive deficits against healthy controls. Whole-brain regression models will be built to examine the correlations between clinical variables, cognitive scores and metrics of connectivity and functional neural circuit, which will be analyzed in R and MATLAB statistical toolbox. Prospectively, patients with and without baseline fMRI abnormalities will be assessed yearly for cognitive decline using ANAM and emergence of clinically-overt neuropsychiatric symptoms for 5 years.
kw: systemic lupus erythematosus, cognitive dysfunction, functional brain imaging

title: Toll-like receptor 2 as a therapeutic target in heart failure
abs: Heart failure (HF) is a major global public health problem. HF is a clinical syndrome where the heart fails to supply adequate peripheral oxygen delivery to meet the requirements of the body. HF is the most rapidly growing cardiovascular syndrome worldwide (US, EU, Asia) with the highest health system costs per patient.HF was traditionally assumed to be synonymous with pump failure, where ejection fraction (EF, the fraction of blood pumped from the heart with each heart beat) is reduced – so called HF with reduced EF (HFREF) but HF can also exist with preserved EF (HFPEF). HFPEF and HFREF have high mortality that rivals most cancers. There is an urgent need to improve outcomes in HF, and particularly HFPEF where there is, to date, no proven effective therapies. Evidence is accumulating that inflammation is an important mechanism in both HFREF and HFPEF. Toll-like receptors (TLRs) recognize exogenous microorganisms but also endogenous danger signals that mediate repair mechanisms of injured tissue including the heart. We showed that TLR2 is involved in HFREF after myocardial infarction and TLR2 deficiency reduce stiffening of the left ventricle in HFPEF. Moreover, we showed that a blocking TLR2 antibody works in a mouse and pig myocardial infarction model providing us with a clinical grade therapeutic. TLR2 blockage as therapy for HF has not been explored.In this proposal, we hypothesize that TLR2 is a target for HF with a blocking TLR2 antibody as therapy.To investigate the therapeutic potential and mechanism of TLR2 blocking in HF, we will use mouse and pig models of both HFPEF and HFREF.This proposal will identify TLR2 as a therapeutic target for heart failure and will provide basic understanding as well as timing and dosage in clinically relevant animal models necessary for the first clinical study in HF patients.
kw: heart failure, toll-like receptor, mouse, pig, innate immunity, blocking antibody

title: Experimental heart failure therapy by targeting 8-oxoGuanine DNA repair enzyme OGG1
abs: Heart failure (HF), a syndrome resulting from different possible initiating causes, remains a major problem of mortality and morbidity worldwide, and is set to worsen as the world population rapidly ages. Novel therapeutic targets for the drug discovery pipeline are urgently needed. Oxidative stress is a well-known component of heart failure. During oxidative stress, reactive oxygen species (ROS) attack different components of the cell. This grant proposal seeks to fill a gap in knowledge where it remains unclear whether and how ROS-induced DNA damage lesions, predominantly 8-oxoG, predispose to HF onset or progression. We have previously found evidence of extensive 8-oxoG damage in the nuclei of failing human hearts and failing hearts of mouse models of disease. 8-oxoG accumulation was in part due to the lack of DNA repair with the loss of base repair enzyme OGG1. Recombinant OGG1 completely restored base excision repair activity in an ex vivo assay, implicating its potential role as an important limiting factor. Here, we propose to generate 2 genetic mouse models. One, a cardiac-specific Ogg1 knockout mouse, to investigate the sufficiency of OGG1 loss in producing 8-oxoG damage, and consequent accelerated cardiomyopathy, with or without treatment with surgical Transverse Aortic Constriction. Next, we will generate an inducible cardiac-specific overexpression of Ogg1, so that we may investigate the beneficial effect of restoring OGG1 following disease onset with surgical TAC and Myocardial Infarction. If current experimental therapies treat only by reducing oxidative stress or ROS, the lack of DNA repair in HF still means that critical accumulation of 8-oxoG lesions will be left unattended. This set of experiments will conclusively elucidate the role of 8-oxoG DNA lesions in the heart and potentially contribute to an important novel area of HF therapeutics.
kw: oxidative 8-oxoG DNA damage, heart failure, cardiac genome, transcriptional mutagenesis

title: Discovery and validation of oncogenic splice variants as drug targets in gastrointestinal cancers
abs: Gastrointestinal cancers impose major public health burdens worldwide, with gastric cancer and colorectal cancer being the second and fourth leading causes of cancer death, respectively. Colorectal cancer is the most common cancer and second leading cause of cancer death in Singapore. Our overall goal is to identify and validate new therapeutic targets and biomarkers for treatment of gastric and colorectal cancers. Although there are instances in which alternative splicing is associated with specific oncogenes, the possibility of targeting oncogenic spliceforms, particularly in gastric and colorectal cancer, has not been systematically explored. To identify oncogenic spliceforms that are potential drug targets, we will carry out a transcriptome-wide search for druggable spliceforms that are cancer-specific or cancer-enriched. To identify these spliceforms, we will use next-generation RNA sequencing to capture the sequences of all transcribed RNA in malignant gastric and colorectal cancer cell lines as well as in the respective tumors and non-malignant tissue controls. We will then develop and use bioinformatics pipelines to discover alternative splicing in each of the sequenced transcriptomes. Cancer-enriched or specific spliceforms will be identified through a comparative analysis of alternative splicing across cancer cell lines, tumors, and normal tissuesWe will prioritize these candidate oncogenic spliceforms using the following criteria: potential as therapeutic targets; the predicted effect of alternative splicing on protein function,, the prevalence of the cancer-enriched spliceforms in tumor tissue, and level of enrichment in tumors. We will experimentally test the oncogenicity of the highest-priority candidate spliceforms using knockdown by RNA interference techniques, or, where possible, by pharmacological intervention. The results will provide a foundation for future in-depth biological validation of select spliceforms as therapeutic targets, and, hence, for subsequent drug development efforts utilizing either small-molecule or biologics-based approaches.
kw: Colorectal Cancer, Gastric Cancer, Stomach Cancer, Alternative Splicing, RNA-seq, Drug target

title: Mesenchymal Stromal Cell (MSC) Approaches for the Study and Treatment of Myelodysplastic Syndrome (MDS)
abs: Bone marrow (BM) failure syndromes such as myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) are increasingly common with our aging population. Although MDS characteristically manifests as dysfunctional hematopoiesis with perturbations of hematopoietic progenitors, recent evidence suggests a pathogenic link to underlying micro-environmental changes induced by defective BM mesenchymal stromal cell (MSC) populations that exist within the hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) niches. Molecular and functional deficits of these MSCs, which are normally involved with regulating HSC activity, could contribute to the dysfunctional hematopoietic system in MDS patients. Treatment options for reversing this phenomenon in BM niches could therefore correct the hematopoietic defects in MDS patients. Our overarching goal is thus to explore potential strategies for MSC replacement therapy as a therapeutic option for MDS through strategies to extract, expand in vitro, and re-implant additional numbers of healthy MSCs, such that they aid in regeneration by supplanting damaged cells or by stimulating endogenous repair mechanisms. Investigation of this proposed therapy is guided by our recent work on how MSCs support HSC expansion as well as work on the BM tissue regeneration showing that different MSC subpopulations constitute different functional environments. These studies indicate the opportunity for utilizing subpopulations of culture expanded MSCs in an optimized transplant strategy to foster healthy BM tissue environments for restoring normal function to MDS derived hematopoietic cells. In light of new evidence demonstrating the biological relevance of MSCs to the pathogenesis of MDS, it is possible that existing hematopoietic-centric methodologies for diagnosis and treatment (e.g. chemotherapy or hematopietic growth factors) may not be addressing some of the underlying causes associated with defects in MSC and their subpopulations in BM niches and a MSC-based approach to therapy could have significant clinical impact for patients.
kw: Myelodysplastic Syndrome (MDS); Mesenchymal Stromal Cells (MSC); Bone Marrow Failure; Tissue Regeneration; In Vivo Mouse Model; Bone Marrow Microenvironment

title: Identifying Host Response in Antibody-Dependent Dengue Infection
abs: Pneumonia is one of the most important infectious complications in the immunocompromised host with high morbidity and mortality, and identification of the causative pathogen is important for making therapeutic decisions. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is an ubiquitous betaherpesvirus that can reactivate from latent infection, and occasionally cause severe pneumonia during periods of increased immunosuppression. However, differentiating CMV replication without disease from true CMV pneumonia and other aetiologies is often difficult based on clinical history and current diagnostic tests. It is generally known that viruses have the ability to induce direct cellular damage or alter of host factors at the genetic level, particularly but not exclusively the immune response, in its own favour for successful infection. At present, the global pathological changes in host gene expression associated with CMV pneumonia are not well characterised. This study hypothesise that CMV, in the absence of other co-infections, will elicit unique transcriptional responses that could serve as potential biomarkers that differentiates true CMV pneumonia from mere viral shedding without disease. The advent of next generation sequencing (NGS) has revolutionised the study of infectious diseases by enabling the detection and characterisation of pathogens, host responses and pathogenesis at the genome level even without prior knowledge of the targets. This study will use NGS to first characterise the host gene expression profiles of CMV-infected cells in vitro. Subsequently, results will be compared with host transcriptome profile in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) collected from a carefully selected group of immunocompromised patients with CMV pneumonia, and compare that with patients without. Concurrently, NGS will be used to detect other infective aetiologies that cannot be identified by routine laboratory investigations. Collectively, this work could contribute significantly to improving the management of pneumonia in the immunocompromised patients.

title: Defining the early molecular interactions in antibody-dependent dengue
abs: The lack of sustainable preventative measures, especially a licensed vaccine, has enabled dengue virus (DENV) to be firmly entrenched throughout the tropics. Vaccine development has been hampered by the incomplete understanding of immunity and pathogenesis, both of which are mediated by antibodies against DENV. Indeed, result of a recent phase 2b vaccine trial showed poor efficacy, indicating that the empirical approaches taken for vaccine development and surrogate measures of immunity need to be urgently replaced with mechanistically sound methods. Our goal is thus to understand how antibody-dependent neutralization or infection occur molecularly. We have shown with the previous CSA funding that in addition to blocking DENV binding or fusion, antibodies can also aggregate DENV to form immune complexes that co-ligates the inhibitory Fc gamma receptor IIB (Fc?RIIB) that blocks phagocytosis and hence entry. Although this mechanism could be applied to distinguish serotype-specific from cross-reactive antibodies more accurately, it questions the mechanistic plausibility of the most widely accepted model for the pathogenesis of severe dengue: antibody-dependent enhancement of DENV infection. Without Fc?RIIB signaling, activating Fc?Rs would signal to induce type-I interferon-stimulated gene (ISG) expression. Entry through activating Fc?R would thus place DENV in an antiviral intracellular environment. To escape this antiviral response, we have recently found that antibody-opsonized DENV co-ligates leukocyte immunoglobulin-like receptor-B1 (LILRB1) on plasma membrane. This immunoreceptor tyrosine-based inhibition motif (ITIM)-bearing receptor recruits Src homology phosphatase-1 (SHP-1) to dephosphorylate spleen tyrosine kinase (Syk), a key intermediate of Fc?R signaling needed to activate ISG expression. LILRB1 co-ligation hence inhibits early ISG expression for enhanced DENV replication. This proposed renewal of the CSA thus aims to determine how DENV binds LILRB1, the downstream consequences of this interaction on host gene expression and phagosomal compartmentalization. This study may further define the molecular requirements for any candidate dengue vaccine.
kw: Dengue, antibody-depedent, Fc gamma receptor, leukocyte immunoglobulin-like receptor B1 (LILRB1), host response, phagosomal trafficking

title: Harvest of Myelodysplastic Syndrome (MDS) Deep Sequencing: BCOR and ZRSR2
abs: Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) are clonal hematopoietic disorders with limited therapeutic options after progressing to acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Our whole exome and candidate gene sequencing of 1,400 MDS samples identified frequent driver mutations including BCOR and ZRSR2. Both are located on the X chromosome and have nonsense mutations in 5-10% of MDS patients with MDS. BCOR is an epigenetic repressor and ZRSR2 is a spliceosome protein; neither gene has been studied in detail in MDS/AML. Specific Aim 1: BCOR. BCOR is expressed in early hematopoietic stem cells (HSC) and preliminary experiments using a BCOR conditional knockout (KO) mice model suggests that BCOR is associated with quiescence. We will first use this conditional BCOR KO murine model to study role of BCOR in hematopoiesis including proliferation and differentiation as well as identifying its target genes and binding partners. Second, similar studies will be done with both MDS samples having nonsense BCOR mutation and normal human CD34+ cells with silencing (shRNA) of BCOR. Third, we will develop an in vivo AML model to investigate the effect of loss of BCOR on leukemogenesis. Specific Aim 2 will study the biology of mutant and normal ZRSR2. Preliminary experiments using mini-genes, endogenous genes, and RNA sequencing in normal and ZRSR2 deficient cells, found severe alterations in splicing occurred with silencing of ZRSR2. First, we will perform and analyze RNA sequencing of human MDS samples with ZRSR2 nonsense mutations. Second, hematopoietic specific ZRSR2 knockout male mice will provide a model system to study alterations of the hematopoietic compartment by enumerating hematopoietic subpopulations, evaluating HSC’s ability to reconstitute different cell linages in a competitive repopulation assay, performing limiting dilution transplant assays and also analyzing expression of hematopoiesis-related genes. An alternative approach is offered using ZRSR2 shRNA vector in murine HSC. Third, we will study proliferation and differentiation potential of human hematopoietic stem cells having loss of expression of ZRSR2 (shRNA). Fourth, the range and magnitude of splicing defects will be determined in ZRSR2 mutant MDS samples using RNA seq. Fifth, because our whole exome sequencing data discovered that TET2 and ZRSR2 are often co-mutated in MDS samples; we will perform in vitro and in vivo experiments to investigate the growth advantage caused by loss of function of both genes. In summary, our studies of BCOR and ZRSR2 will provide a better understanding of normal and MDS-associated hematopoiesis which may provide new therapeutic targets for MDS and AML patients.
kw: MDS, AML, BCOR, ZRSR2, Spliceosome genes

title: IMproving outcomes in acute MyocArdial infarCtion throUgh reversal of early and LATe cardiac rEmodeling. (IMMACULATE study)
abs: IMMACULATESIGNIFICANCE: Outcomes, including death and heart failure (HF), following acute myocardial infarction (AMI) are OECD benchmark measures of healthcare quality. Evidence-based acute management for AMI is rigorously applied in Singapore yet 28-day case-fatality rates exceed the OECD average by more than 60%. Death and readmission are frequent in the year following AMI, the leading cause being HF. Post-MI left ventricular (LV) remodeling is a key mechanism through which infarct expansion and LV dilation occur, leading to increased haemodynamic stress, symptomatic HF and death.AIMS: To improve prediction of post-MI ventricular remodeling, to minimize post-MI HF and death and to progress a new candidate pharmacotherapy. METHODS: 1. Cardiac imaging and longitudinal profiling of candidate circulating biomarkers will be undertaken to identify predictors of post-infarct ventricular remodeling in consecutive AMI patients (Bioregistry)Hypothesis: Hybrid magnetic resonance-positron emission tomographic (MR/PET) imaging will identify regional myocardial metabolic patterns (inefficiency) predictive of post-MI myocardial structural remodeling and HF. Hypothesis: Peripheral blood peptides, cytokines and lipid metabolite signatures predict post-MI ventricular remodeling. 2. In a registry-based randomized controlled trial (RRCT), the efficacy of a biomarker-determined intervention incorporating risk stratification, telemedicine and multi-facetted intensified management (systems approach) will be compared with usual care. Hypothesis: Our systems approach to post-discharge management will have salutary benefits upon Plasma NTproBNP, ventricular remodeling and on cardiovascular risk at 6 months which will presage clinically significant reductions (~30%) in death and unplanned all-cause rehospitalization at 2 years post-MI. 3. We will undertake a dose-escalating randomized pre-clinical trial (RPCT) of a first-in-class slow-release H2S donor in ameliorating adverse ventricular remodeling. Hypothesis: GYY4137 will dose-dependently reduce infarct size and ventricular remodeling in rat and porcine models of AMI. This integrated programme will:- (a) identify new biomarkers and imaging indicators predictive of post-MI ventricular remodeling (b) trial an innovative model of care to transform long-term outcomes of this highly-prevalent disease; and position Singapore’s healthcare system as a leader in the field, and (c) bridge a promising novel drug class (H2S donor agents) from discovery to development.Word Count = 300

title: SINGAPORE ANGLE CLOSURE GLAUCOMA PROGRAM: CHARACTERIZATION, PREVENTION AND MANAGEMENT
abs: Glaucoma is the leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide, with primary angle closure glaucoma (PACG) a major form of glaucoma in Singapore and Asia. The unifying theme for this application is to aim to provide a ‘patient-centric’ customized management for PACG by utilizing an integrative approach incorporating epidemiological studies, novel risk factor biomarker discovery, Bayesian modelling of patient-based risk prediction, and evidence-based treatment guidelines.In this program, we will determine the incidence, progression, and risk of blindness among persons with asymptomatic angle closure using prospective data from the three major Asian ethnic groups (Chinese, Indians, Malays) in Singapore. Building on these baseline determinants, we further aim to identify novel systemic and ocular biomarkers of PACG using advanced genomics, biomechanics and imaging studies. We will follow this up by attempting development of a novel risk-prediction algorithm based on quantitative anatomical features, novel biomarkers and prospective clinical data to identify those high-risk cases that are most likely to progress.To create a national resource for the long term study of PACG, we will also establish a laboratory-based biobank for the collection, processing, storage, and tracking of PACG related biospecimens, which are critical components of biomarker-related studies. Lastly, we plan to conduct comprehensive meta-analyses of all available data garnered by us and world-wide collaborating partners to develop evidence-based guidelines for the screening and systematic management of angle closure disease.For the past decade, our group has made substantial contributions to the understanding of the epidemiology, risk factors, imaging features, clinical phenotype, genetics and management of PACG. We have established and are currently leading a world-wide PACG genetics consortium comprising >7500 PACG cases and 26,000 controls from 14 different countries.

title: Neuroglobin in a Primate Experimental Model of Glaucoma: A novel Neuroprotectant in Glaucoma
abs: Neuroglobin (Ngb) is a 17kDa heme protein with specific oxygen binding properties and redox activities found predominantly in neurons. In the eye, it is expressed in the retina, schlemm’s canal (SC) and trabecular meshwork (TM). Using an ocular ischemia-reperfusion model using neuroglobin (Ngb)-overexpressing transgenic mice, we recently demonstrated that Ngb protects the retina against apoptosis during ischemia. Although there is a transient upregulation of Ngb occurred during the initial ischemic insult, the failure to achieve persistent elevations of Ngb resulted in apoptosis and retinal damage in WT-mice. Neuroglobin expression is increased in human retinas with end-stage glaucoma suggesting that a chronic IOP stimulus may induce its expression. The role of neuroglobin in glaucoma and methods for its endogenous upregulation is unknown. The presence of Ngb in the anterior chamber structures suggests a potential role in the oxidative stress mediated damage during glaucoma. Our latest data shows that intravitreal delivery of Ngb does not result in adverse clinical effects. Neuroglobin is neuroprotective in chronically raised IOP glaucoma and plays a role against the oxidative stresses within the SC, TM, retina and optic nerve in glaucoma.To support our hypotheses, we aim to use a primate model of chronically raised IOP to study the role of Ngb.Our specific aim is:To determine the neuroprotective role of Ngb in chronically raised IOP (using the microbead primate model of glaucoma) on the SC, TM, retina and optic nerve by studying the structural, proteomic and gene expression profile of Ngb and markers of oxidative stress such as superoxide dismutase (SOD), glutamine synthase (GS), nitric oxide synthase (NOS) and apoptosis (activated caspase 3 and TUNEL assay) in primate globes subjected to an IOP of more than 30mmHg (high IOP non-treated eyes), in comparison to the high IOP Ngb-treated eyes and the untreated normal pressure control eye.

title: Assessing placental perfusion and fetal growth by examining maternal retina during pregnancy
abs: Uteroplacental blood flow is vital for fetal growth and development. Decreased uterine blood flow may reduce placental perfusion and lead to fetal growth restriction. A body of evidence has shown that smaller placental size is associated with fetal growth and predicts risk of intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) during pregnancy. Mammal models have shown changes in the histomorphology of the placental microvessels, leading to the hypothesis that smaller placental size during normal gestation might involve placental vascular and angiogenesis dysfunction which affects placental transport capacity and blood flow. However, the role of placental vasculature in vivo is still unclear, because placental function is difficult to assess by ultrasonography due to its low inter/intra-rater reliability. The eye is a “window” to the human circulation. The retinal blood vessels can now be captured and visualized non-invasively by advances in retinal imaging, which offers an exceptional opportunity for advanced imaging techonology to document, monitor and study human disease. Recent epidemiological and clinical studies have implicated that retinal vasculature mirrors systemic microvasculature in vivo. Hence, we hypothesized that maternal retinal vasculature can reflect the placental circulation and fetal growth pattern in very early pregnancy. This prospectively-designed cohort study will be the first group worldwide to evaluate utero-placental circulation by assessing retinal vascular parameters throughout the whole gestation. We will firstly investigate whether retinal microvascular parameters are associated with placental perfusion and fetal growth, and secondly study the additional value of retinal imaging in assessment of fetal growth in-utero and placenta perfusion beyond conventional examinations such as traditional imaging (US) and serum bio-markers (e.g. placental growth factor). This study can potentially help researchers better understand the possible morphology of placental microvasculature through retinal vascular imaging, and how changes in maternal microvasculature in vivo may reflect fetal growth (e.g. slow fetal growth) during pregnancy.
kw: Retinal vasculature, pregnancy, placental perfusion, fetal growth, intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR)

title: Imaging kidney function and fibrosis.
abs: Renal fibrosis is the final common pathway of renal injury (including diabetic nephropathy) that results in loss of renal function. Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors (ACE-I) have been demonstrated to retard the process of renal fibrosis. The Roche-Singapore Translational Medicine Hub has an interest to explore an imaging biomarker for the process of renal fibrosis. Such a biomarker would aid development of agents that retard or reverse renal fibrosis. We hope to undertake an initial validation experiment, comparing known biomarkers of renal fibrosis (Diffusion weighted imaging (DWI), Diffusion Tensor imaging(DTI)) as well as novel biomarkers of renal fibrosis (Dynamic Contrast Enhanced MRI (DCE MRI) and Fine model, Magnetization Transfer Ratio (MTR)) in mice with renal fibrosis induced by unilateral ureteric obstruction. Once the biomarker efficacy is established, we would then undertake the same experiment in mice with diabetes induced by Streptozocin untreated and treated with ACE-I to determine if the biomarker can pick up the retardation of fibrosis. The validated imaging biomarkers can be readily translated to humans by MRI (DWI, DTI, MTR) or nuclear medicine techniques (Technetium DTPA dynamic renal studies for DCE MRI findings as gadolinium is contraindicated in renal failure).
kw: MicroMRI, imaging biomarker, renal fibrosis, renal function

title: Testing Bayer compounds in hepatocellular carcinoma
abs: Hepatocellular cancer (HCC) is the fifth most common malignancy worldwide with 660,000 deaths annually. HCC is highly dependent on angiogenesis for growth and metastasis. Several critical molecular signaling pathways such as fibroblast growth factor (FGF)/FGF receptor, vascular endothelial growth factor (VFGF)/VEGF receptor, Raf/MEK/ERK, Ang/Tie2, PI3K/Akt/mTOR, Wnt/?-catenin, JAK/Stat pathways are aberrant in HCC. A considerable crosstalk and redundancy in signaling pathways are also observed in HCC. Hence targeting single molecule or signaling pathway may have a limited efficacy. To be effective in HCC therapies, new agents and novel therapeutic strategies must target various key signaling pathways. In this proposal we propose to evaluate the efficacy of PI3K inhibitors (BAY 1236, BAY 2439), MEK inhibitor (BAY 9766), AKT inhibitor (BAY 5976), and WNT inhibitors (BAY 6167, BAY 6071) in preclinical models of HCC. In addition, combination of PI3K inhibitor (BAY 2439) and Sorafenib with different dosing schedules is also tested. Understanding the mechanisms of action of these therapeutic agents and methods of combining these drugs may help to increase their efficacy, reduce toxicity, and improve overall survival and quality of life in patients with HCC.

title: PD biomarker analysis of FGFR2 mAb in FGFR2-overexpressing gastric cancer PDX models (GC10-0608, GC08-0212, GC12-0811)
abs: Gastric cancer (GC) is the second most common cause of cancer-related deaths. The FGFR signalling pathway is involved in regulation of cell proliferation, survival, differentiation, angiogenesis and tissue regeneration. Somatic FGFR2 mutations have been reported in GC. Amplification of the FGFR-2 gene was identified in a subset of patients with gastric cancer. FGFR-2 activation is required for growth and gastric cancer carrying FGFR2 gene amplification in vivo and it might play a role in chemotherapy resistance, suggesting that inhibition of FGFR2 may have therapeutic potential. In this study, we aim to investigate the efficacy and to identify pharmacodynamics biomarker for FGFR-2 antibody (BAY 1179470) in preclinical models of gastric cancer.

abs: Ovarian cancer is the leading cause of death from gynaecological cancer. Clear ovarian cancer is extremely common in Singapore and Asia and may be considered a predominantly Asian disease. title: Doped Contacts and Heterostructures for Solution-Processable Plastic Electronics
abs: While the performance of organic semiconductor materials and their devices have improved tremendously over the last 5 years, fundamental knowledge of their contacts to electrodes and their heterostructures has remained rather limited. To take the performance of these materials and devices to the next level, it is now crucial to develop a concerted effort to understand these topics, in particular to find new ways to generate the desired interfaces in a practical manufacturable way. In this Grant Application, we propose to develop solution-processable doped injection layers (of both signs: electrons and holes) to achieve ohmic contacts to the organic semiconductor, and quality heterostructures leveraging on the “general-purpose” crosslinking methodology we have recently developed. Both these issues are related. The key challenges for the doped contacts are related to present lack of knowledge in this space, and perceived difficulties related to stability of the doped states (particularly at extreme values), and counter-ion migration. In this project, we intend to overcome these by developing new doped injection layer concepts based on self-doped polyelectrolytes which are generated in situ within the device. This will be supported by a fundamental research programme to uncover the factors which determine work function, stability and ohmicity, in organic semiconductor devices. Using the crosslinking methodology, it has recently become possible to generate high-quality abrupt interfaces between a polymer semiconductor and a polymer dielectric which would have dissolved in the same solvents, and to generate robust crosslinked donor–acceptor network heterostructures. In this project, we will also exploit these new opportunities to develop practical organic field-effect transistor architectures, and a new concept in scalable polymer donor–polymer acceptor solar cells. To achieve these broad aims, we have put together an integrated programme of research that covers device physics and chemistry, synthetic chemistry, computational quantum chemistry and surface science. Its success will likely lead to advancement in fundamental understanding and a step-improvement in the performance and stability of organic light-emitting diode (OLED), and transparent high-performance displays and lighting, bandwidth in organic field-effect transistors (OTFTs), and power conversion efficiencies of polymer solar cells, even with the active semiconductor materials that are already presently available.

title: TOWARDS THE REALITY OF 3D IMAGING AND DISPLAY: Development of the World's First Viable Glasses-free Television System
abs: An autostereoscopic display operates in two fundamental ways; it can produce images whose appearance is fixed at any particular position in the viewing field, or the images can follow the positions of the viewers’ eyes. Examples of the first type are multi-view and light field displays, and the second type is head tracked where images dynamically follow the viewers’ eye positions so the viewers are always located in ‘sweet spots’. Examples of both types have their particular advantages and disadvantages and the suitability of a particular type in the future is likely to be determined by the enabling technologies available at the time. The non-head tracked displays include a light field display that employs the 4D plenoptic function in order to faithfully reconstruct the original scene with the use of multiple transparent layers, and super multiview (SMV) where a large number of discrete views are presented across the viewing field in order to provide the continuous motion parallax as observed in real-world scenes. Head tracked displays function by producing regions referred to as exit pupils where a left image or a right image is observed across the complete area of the screen. The exit pupils follow the positions of the viewers’ eyes under the control of a non-intrusive multi-user head tracker. title: Controlling Cell-cell Signaling Using Synthetic Biomimetic Interfaces
abs: The vast majority of all cell culture-based experiments occur in the presence of undefined integrin-mediated cell-matrix adhesion and the absence of other adhesion junctions or signaling junctions. This fact contributes substantially to the notoriously different behavior of cells in culture and in tissue, and seriously limits the utility of cell culture technology in both academics and industry. In the US$1.02 trillion global pharmaceutical industry, this cuts heavily into profits by requiring extensive animal studies to be done on molecules that ultimately fail for reasons that could have been identified earlier if a good enough cell culture-based assay existed. We propose to develop a materials-based device platform to establish molecular level control of living cells. Our overarching strategy builds off the success of the hybrid live cell-supported membrane interfaces, which have led to a series of major discoveries in cell-cell signaling. The key to this success is the incorporation of actual biological signaling ligands into synthetic membrane surfaces. We will greatly extend this concept by simultaneously defining the biochemistry, geometry, and mechanics of ligands displayed to cells within an integrated format. By engaging the cell’s natural signaling machinery, these structures will enable a variety of quantitative cell-based assays and diagnostic tools. We will develop these technologies into a scalable format, which can bridge the gap between academic usage and industrial applications. Specifically, personalized medicine (a growing aspect of the pharmaceuticals industry) is heavily reliant on efficient and informative screening and diagnostic tools—precisely the unmet need our technology platform addresses. We bring experience in the commercialization of academic inventions and we see an opportunity to develop this type of technology industry locally in Singapore.
