title: Clinical trials on des-aspartate-angiotensin I
abs: Introduction: Des-aspartate-angiotensin I (DAA-I) is a lead compound of our current R&D on the Development of a New Class of Cardiovascular Drugs. The R&D was based on our earlier discovery of aminopeptidase X in the aorta and hypothalamus of the rat (1, 2). Aminopeptidase X converts angiotensin I to des-aspartate-angiotensin I (DAA-I), a nine amino acid peptide that is able to antagonise the deleterious effects of angiotensin II in the cardiovascular and renal systems and in diabetes. Subsequent pharmacological studies show that DAA-I has potential therapeutic actions in animal models of cardiovascular, renal and metabolic diseases. With data from these studies, DAA-I has been patented by NUS for five disease states, namely: cardiac hypertrophy (3), restenosis and arteriosclerosis (4), glomerulosclerosis and renal failure (5), post-infarction cardiac injuries (6), viral infection and type 2 diabetes (7). The preclinical toxicological studies on DAA-I have been performed at Quintile/Edinburgh, a GLP-accredited contract research organisation. DAA-I shows a favourable toxicological profile and an Investigator Drug Brochure has been written to support the Phase 1 clinical trial study.Clinical Trials: Phase I clinical trial is an important first step in opening up DAA-I for efficacy study in human. On completion of the Phase I study, Phase IIA clinical study to establish efficacy of DAA-I for each of the indications could be carried out in 18 to 24 patients at NUH. This offers a rare opportunity for local clinicians to pioneer efficacy testing of a novel lead, and good chances to publish the findings in NEJM and Lancet. Completion of the Phase I and IIA study would also provide the flexibility for NUS to prospect for more comprehensive Phase II study with venture capital companies. NUS (ILO) has encountered companies that cited the absence of Phase I clinical trial as a major reason for postponement of collaborative development of DAA-I. In addition, most multi-national pharmaceutical companies would only be interested in leads that show efficacy in Phase IIA clinical trial*,#. Hence, this application seeks funding to support the phase 1 clinical trail on DAA-I, which would pave the way for phase II studies of its efficacy in diabetes, cardiovascular and renal diseases.*NUS has signed an option agreement with Panorama Research Inc (an US incubator) to prospect for funds. However, the absence of Phase I trial data i.e. the safety dose range for DAA-I in human, attracted small amount of money sufficient only for confirmatory efficacy tests in animals. Panorama Research Inc has confirmed the efficacy of DAA-I in infarcted rat heart i.e. DAA-I is able to significantly reduce the infarct size. Due to lack of funding, the option agreement had lapsed.#NUS has also licensed the right to develop DAA-I as a stent-incorporated drug to Medlogics Device Corporation for the treatment or prevention of restenosis and other abnormal lumina
kw: Des-aspartate-angiotensin I, Phase 1 clinical trial, Angiotensin peptides, Novel hypoglycemic agent

title: Investigation of LGR5 as a bona fide retinal stem cell marker
abs: Retinal diseases are amongst the leading causes of irreversible blindness worldwide resulting in almost 6 million blind and 37 million with low vision. Stem cell therapy to replace damaged retinal neurons has been investigated as a potential solution to this problem. Amongst the various sources of stem cells, a recently identified population of stem cells within the adult human retina shows therapeutic promise. Early studies in animal models of retinal disease have shown successful engraftment of these cells with functional restoration. These findings raise the possibility of harvesting autologous retinal stem cells from the patient's own retina. However the complex retinal cellular composition and sparse distribution of these stem cells within the human retina makes it difficult to selectively isolate them in clinically useful quantities. Leucine rich-repeat containing G protein coupled receptor 5 (LGR5) is a stem cell marker expressed in regenerating adult tissues. We have preliminary data that shows previously unreported expression of this cell surface receptor in the retina. This proposal aims to characterize LGR5 within the adult mammalian retina, with the dual purpose of investigating its potential as an adult retinal stem cell marker and promoting our understanding of the adult mammalian retinal stem cell niche. A transgenic mouse model with a GFP reporter for LGR5 will be used to identify the nature and distribution of retinal cells expressing this protein. LGR5 positive cells will be assessed for their stem cell behavior with regards to proliferation, clonal expansion, differentiation and response to injury.If LGR5 can be validated as a bona fide retinal stem cell marker, it could potentially be developed into the first biomarker to enable efficient isolation of adult retinal stem cells from autologous retinal biopsies, paving the way for clinical translation of stem cell therapy for irreversible retinal disease.
kw: stem cell marker, stem cell isolation

title: Clinical Evaluation of Intraosseous and Intravenous for Cardiac Arrest Treatment in Singapore Emergency Ambulance
abs: Aim:In adult and paediatric patients with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest in Singapore, we aim to evaluate the incremental benefit of introducing a resuscitation protocol including the use of intravenous (IV) access and/or intraosseous (IO) vascular access compared to protocols with only IV access by SCDF paramedics in the pre-hospital setting on the return of spontaneous circulation rates. Hypothesis:The hypothesis is that low vascular access rates could be due to difficulty of setting IV cannulas in the field due to certain factors like poor lighting or space constraints. Thus, by introducing a protocol including IO access for difficult IV cases, success rates for vascular access will be higher and this might lead to a higher ROSC and survival rates.Methodology:This is a prospective, parallel-group, cluster-randomized study comparing ‘IV+IO’ and ‘IV alone’ protocols in patients with cardiac arrest managed by SCDF emergency ambulance service. The trial will recruit 200 patients over 1 year. Each of the 34 SCDF ambulances will provide both ‘IV+IO’ and ‘IV alone’ treatments in 2 consecutive phases of 6-months in order to allow for all ambulance crew a chance to be trained on usage of EZ-IO. As the size of the fire station, namely the number of ambulances within that fire station is a factor that may confound the order of randomisation, stratified randomisation with 4 strata was carried out. The 1st, 2nd, 3rd and 4th stratum consist of ambulances coming from fire stations or fire posts equipped with 1 ambulance, 2 ambulances, 3 ambulances and 4 ambulances respectively. Block randomisation within each stratum will be carried out to randomise the ambulances to administer ‘IV+IO’ or ‘IV alone’ in the first 6 months of study. In the 2nd phase of the study (next 6 months), each ambulance will then administer the other treatment.
kw: Intraosseous; Intravenous; Cardiac Arrest; Return of spontaneous circulation

title: The new haploid state of Candida albicans on biofilm formation, drug resistance, mucosal infections and transcription regulators
abs: Background: Candida albicans is the major fungal pathogen of humans capable of causing both mucosal and systemic mycoses, and a leading cause of hospital-acquired infections. Haploid state of C. albicans was discovered very recently (Nature, 2013), disproving the hitherto common belief of its “obligate diploid” state. This important discovery has opened up a new avenue for functional genetic analysis of pathogenesis of C. albicans. Key issue: Biofilms (surface-attached communities) of C. albicans are highly resistant to antifungals and directly associated with therapeutic failure. C. albicans produce filamentous appendages termed “hyphae” that facilitate penetration of mucosal surfaces. There are no studies in the literature that has examined the inter-connection of aforementioned virulence traits of C. albicans in haploid state. Aims: Present study aims to investigate the role of newly discovered haploid state of C. albicans in comparison to its previously known diploid state focusing on the biofilm formation, mucosal tissue invasion and drug resistance using in vitro and in vivo models. In addition, functional analysis of key transcription factors that are associated with biofilm formation will be performed using haploid state mutants. Approach: Role of C. albicans haploid state on biofilm formation and antifungal susceptibility will be examined in in vitro denture-stomatitis model using parent haploid isolates and its auxotrophic transcription factor mutants in comparison to diploid cells. Mucosal infections of Candida strains will be investigated using ex-vivo and in vivo oral candidiasis models. Expression of beta-defensins from oral epithelia in response to Candida invasion will also be investigated using standard methodology. Finally, proteomics will be employed to unravel entangled protein network of C. albicans haploid and diploid biofilm cells. Significance: Success of the project would yield much needed information on haploid state of C. albicans pathogenicity, leading to novel therapeutics for this recalcitrant fungal pathogen and clinical benefits for patients.
kw: Candida albicans, Haploid state, Biofilms, Drug Resistance, Tissue invasion

title: Neuropathic pain generator visualization study on rodent model with Metalloproteinase-12 activatable MRI probe
abs: Neuropathic pain is a chronic pain condition resulting from nerves injury costing 40 billion annually in USA. One of the common clinical causes is spinal nerve root compression due to intervertebral disc extrusion. Even though MRI can show radiological changes in multiple prolapsed discs, it fails to localize pain generator. Selective diagnostic nerve root block is common clinical practice to sort out pain generators. However it is far from satisfactory due to diffusion problem, which may lead to misdiagnosis and wrong level surgery. Pain persists postoperatively even following “successful” surgical decompression. From our previous rodent neuropathic pain study, MMP-12 is significant up-regulated in affected dorsal root ganglion. MPP-12 is also up-regulated in neuroinflammation, spinal cord injury model. Matrix Metalloproteinase 12 (MMP-12) is highly regulated enzyme secreted by infiltrated macrophages in pain generating dorsal root ganglion (DRG). Aim of this study is to develop an MMP-12 specific activatable probe to visualize pain under MRI. Proposed probe consists of three parts 1) acidic peptide cap, 2) MMP-12 selective peptide linker 3) cell penetrating functionalized iron oxide. Once the probe contacts with MMP-12, cell penetrating peptide functionalized iron oxide will be uptake by the cell and shown in MRI.Our hypothesis is pain generating dorsal root ganglion express MMP-12, will activate MMP-12 probe and increase tissue uptake, while in the normal side, inactive probe will be washed out by blood circulation. The difference of probe quantity will be shown in MRI T2 image. Proposed project we will evaluate MMP-12 probe efficiency in visualizing pain generator via following parts 1) in vitro uptake study 2) MMP-12 quantification of DRG on spinal nerve ligation (SNL) rodent model 3) Probe uptake evaluation of SNL rodent model with MRI T2 imaging. This study will provide foundation for clinical translatable pain diagnostic probes development for neuropathic pain patient.
kw: Neuropathic pain, matrix metalloproteinase, nerve root compression

title: Systemic T-cell Immunity defects in Immunocompetent Individuals with Cytomegalovirus Infection: New Modalities for the Detection and Surveillance for Viral Reactivation
abs: Up to 90% of adults in the community carries cytomegalovirus (CMV) in their body. Although CMV is usually kept inactive by the immune system in health, in some presumed immunocompetent individuals without HIV infection (particularly among Asians), recurrent viral activation occurs in their eyes from unknown mechanisms, resulting in progressive corneal swelling and glaucoma. Corneal transplants and glaucoma surgeries are ultimately needed in these working adults to preserve vision. However, viral reactivation remains a cause of recurrent corneal transplant failure.The diagnosis of CMV eye infection in these patients is difficult, as it depends on viral DNA detection in the eye fluid drawn using fine needles. The need for repeated eye fluid sampling carries risks of blindness from devastating bacterial infection or accidental eye damage from the needles. Unlike CMV infection in canonically immunocompromised individuals, CMV remains undetectable in the blood of our patients. There is also no objective endpoint currently to guide the cessation of expensive antiviral treatment without reactivation. We clearly need to develop new non-eye-invasive methods to diagnose and guide therapy.Studies on CMV infection in immunocompromised patients have demonstrated the ability of enzyme-linked immunospot (ELISPOT) assays and flow cytometry in the prediction of CMV activation and clinical disease. As the control of CMV replication largely depends on CMV-specific T-cell immunity in health, we hypothesize that undiscovered cellular immunity defects are the underlying reasons for CMV disease in immunocompetent individuals. The novel application of ELISPOT assays and multi-dimensional cytokine flow cytometry using blood samples from our ocular CMV patients will allow a new level of immunity characterization and surveillance, and less risky ways to better manage our patients with recurrent CMV reactivation. If our hypothesis is proven, immunity surveillance will potentially change our future practice and improve our clinical management of CMV ophthalmic and systemic infection.
kw: Cytomegalovirus, uveitis, endotheliitis, immunocompetent, cellular immunity

title: Gestational Diabetes Mellitus and Risk of Postpartum Metabolic Syndrome
abs: Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), defined as glucose intolerance with onset or first recognition in pregnancy, is an increasingly common condition that affects approximately 14% of pregnancies each year. There is increasing recognition women with history of GDM are at risk of obesity, dyslipdemia and insulin resistance – central attributes of the metabolic syndrome (MetS) and even type 2 diabete, which might be due to systemic inflammation and vascular dysfunction. However, there is no study to date that directly has examined the postpartum microvascular changes in women with a history of GDM, and whether these changes are correlated with the development of MetS. In this proposed study, we hypothesize that structural and functional changes of retinal microvascular parameters, reflecting systemic inflammation and endothelial dysfunction, are associated with risk of postpartum MetS among women with a history of GDM. Also, we hypothesize that quantitative assessment of retinal microvascular dynamic and structural parameters can contribute additional values in identifying a subset of subjects at risk of metabolic syndrome, aside from conventional examinations. Our main objective is to evaluate the risk of postpartum MetS among women with a history of GDM and suboptimal dynamic and structural retinal signs pre- and post-delivery. A total of 400 women with history of GDM and also recruited from a local birth cohort study (Growing Up in Singapore Towards Healthy Outcome, GUSTO) will be recruited in our study. Among these 400 women, 200 are with a history of GDM while the other 200 are healthy nested-control matched with age, ethnicity and comorbidity from the same cohort. Retinal photography and dynamic vessel analysis will be performed according to standard protocols. Blood tests, blood pressure and anthropometric measurement to evaluate metabolic condition will be performed on all participants. Multiple regression models and Cox proportional hazards model will be used for statistical analyses.
kw: Gestational diabetes mellitus, Metabolic syndrome, retinal vascular morphology, Retinal vascular dynamic function

title: Are sST2 and IL-33 useful prognostic biomarkers of stroke outcome? A prospective cohort study
abs: Biomarkers that play important roles in guiding treatment decisions are lacking in stroke. Accumulating evidence implicates the immune system in stroke pathogenesis. Among putative immune mediators, the ST2-IL33 signaling pathway has emerged as potential immune biomarkers in cardiovascular heart diseases. It is unknown whether soluble ST2 and IL-33 can reliably identify stroke patients at risk for future vascular events and how these biomarkers correlate with key clinical endpoints. As the ST2-IL33 pathway is associated with cardiovascular heart diseases, we hypothesize that the levels of soluble ST2 and IL-33 are significantly altered in ischemic stroke patients and the extent of change in their levels predicts future stroke recurrence and cardiovascular events.In a preliminary study, we demonstrated the feasibility of accurately measuring soluble ST2 and IL-33 in sera of stroke patients and highlight significant differences in their levels compared with non-stroke controls. The levels of soluble ST2, in particular, were found to correlate positively with stroke severity, suggesting its potential clinical utility to identify high-risk stroke patients. By including more subjects and time-points, we propose to generate more compelling data to understand the variation of these markers in stroke patients and how these correlate with long-term vascular outcomes.Our primary objective is to investigate the relationships between soluble ST2 and IL-33 in ischemic stroke patients and vascular outcomes. The secondary objective of this study is to investigate the association between soluble ST2 and IL-33 with key pathological processes and clinical endpoints of ischemic stroke.Findings from this study are pivotal to the successful translation of advances in immune biology to individualize the risk and management of cardiovascular complications in stroke patients.
kw: Ischemic stroke, immune, inflammation, biomarkers

title: Understanding the role of JAK-STAT pathway in NK/T Lymphoma radiosensitivity
abs: T-cell lymphomas are more common in Asia with NK/T Cell Lymphoma (NKTL) occurring almost exclusively in Asia and South America; the incidence of nasal NKTL is over 4-fold higher amongst Asian compared to Western countries. The 5-year overall survival for early-staged disease is around 50% whilst most with advanced disease succumb. This has led to strategies to intensifying treatment with multi-agent chemotherapy and radiotherapy.Radiotherapy is fundamental in the treatment algorithm of nasal NKTL. Although lymphomas are generally radiosensitive, high doses of at least 50Gy are necessary to be effective in nasal NKTL causing significant toxicity. Receptor signalling cascades have been postulated to be involved in tumour radio-resistance; this aspect however has not been investigated in NKTL. There is therefore a need and potential for a more targeted approach.Recent gene expression profiling (GEP) studies have revealed various activated oncogenic pathways in NKTL. Our group, through whole-exome sequencing, recently identified Janus Kinase 3 (JAK3) activating mutations in NKTL, highlighting the potential importance of the JAK-STAT signalling pathway in NKTL (Koo GC et al, Cancer Discovery 2012). We hypothesise that abrogating the JAK-STAT pathway will enhance the efficacy of radiotherapy induced cell kill in NKTL; this should lead to a novel targeted approach allowing translation into improved clinical outcomes. Our specific aims are: 1) to understand the mechanisms of the JAK-STAT signalling cascade with regards to radiation induced cell death in NKTL cells and 2) to validate these findings in JAK knockdown and overexpression models as well as in vivo on an animal model previously developed by our group. This will create the necessary platform for translation into clinical trial investigation.
kw: JAK-STAT pathway, Radiation, NK/T Lymphoma

title: Targeting a potential means to risk stratify heart failure
abs: Heart failure remains a major cause of morbidity and mortality. Current treatment is empirical and step-wise: each medication is added one after another, titrated only according to drug response or if side-effects emerge. Device therapy is also expensive, lacking in clear risk stratification strategies. Heart failure patients will therefore benefit significantly from biomarkers for risk stratification and/or personalized therapy. This proposal takes a two-prong approach to establishing means for risk stratifying heart failure, based on the premise that disease manifestation is influenced by genetic predisposition. Our previous unique genome-wide study has demonstrated the significant contribution of genetic diversity to heart disease, and yielded candidate genes; some are well-established players in cardiac regulation and others novel. It was performed using the hybrid mouse diversity panel (HMDP) where genetically diverse strains of mice developed differential degrees of pathological responses to a constant pathological stressor. One of our most significant finding is the potential biomarker Lgals3. Galectin-3 encoded by Lgals3 is a cell surface molecule important for inflammatory response and has been proposed as a human heart failure biomarker. Here, we will set out to identify genetic determinants that regulate Lgals3 expression. We will prove whether early detection of Galectin-3 predict disease severity by using the strains of HMDP that we previously found gave the most and least response to stress. Genetic determinants and the causal function of Lgals3 will be validated by in vitro gain- or loss-of-function approaches. Galactin-3 levels may represent disease progression but the genetic basis for Lgals3 expression will give us the real opportunity for tackling genetic susceptibility and risk stratification in patients with heart failure. In our second aim, we will extend our systems analysis of HMDP to uncover epigenetic modules that predict disease severity. We will further analyze genetic determinants that regulate the epigenetic response. All together these powerful approaches promise not only to validate a biomarker for heart failure management but also uncover genetic and epigenetic susceptibility so that heart failure patients may have ways to be treated with stratified medicine.
kw: risk stratification, heart failure, biomarker, novel therapeutics

title: Noninvasive Brain Stimulation and Brain-Computer Interface-Assisted Motor Imagery for Rehabilitation of Mobility After Stroke
abs: Non-invasive brain stimulation (NIBS) techniques have emerged as effective techniques of neuromodulation to augment motor outcomes of stroke patients. Studies thus far have focussed on upper limb recovery. Few have examined lower limb recovery. Our studies in brain-computer interface-assisted motor imagery (MI-BCI) have also demonstrated efficacy for upper limb recovery post-stroke. The specific aim of this study is to 1. Compare the efficacy of the 2 NIBS techniques (repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation [rTMS] and transcranial direct currentstimulation [tDCS]) to determine the most effective and appropriate neuromodulatory technique to augment motor outcomes in the lower limbs in stroke subjects.2. Determine the efficacy of lower limb MI-BCI training for rehabilitation of lower limb function following stroke.3. Examine the interaction of combining NIBS and MI-BCI training.4. Investigate the neurophysiological correlates to clinical outcomes of lower limb rehabilitation using MRI and TMS. 5. Investigate the role of brain-derived neurotropic factor (BDNF) polymorphism in motor recovery and response to the above neuromodulatory techniques. We hypothesize that 1) NIBS will improve gait and mobility outcomes ofstroke survivors, when combined with conventional gait training; 2) NIBS will modulate excitability of the motor cortical representation of the lower limbs; 3) MI-BCI training will improve functional gait parameters in stroke survivors with gait impairment; 4) combined NIBS and MI-BCI will be more effective than conventional rehabilitation therapies to improve functional outcomes. 5) BDNF polymorphism is associated with response to the above neuromodulatory techniques.Methodology: 1) a randomised sham-controlled trial on 2 NIBS protocols combined with standardised conventional gait training. 2) We will further develop the MI-BCI protocol that has been demonstrated in our pilot study to be effective for healthy subjects, for MI training in stroke subjects, and perform a randomised trial comparing MI-BCI with conventional gait training vs conventional gait training alone. 3) We will combine the above 2 modalities to explore the interaction between NIBS and MI-BCI for lower limb gait training.
kw: noninvasive brain stimulation, stroke, neurorehabilitation, motor imagery, brain-computer interface

title: Validation study on serum methylation markers for early detection of colorectal cancer in Chinese
abs: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the most common cancer in Singapore. In our phase I project on Chinese CRC patients, we have demonstrated a capability to develop serum markers which address common and urgent clinical concerns including a panel of methylation markers for early diagnosis of CRC and another panel for recurrence detection. In this proposed validation study for early diagnosis of CRC in Chinese, we seek to validate previously identified serum methylation markers through a larger and independent set of stage I CRC and age-matched endoscope-verified healthy controls. We’ll also extend these activities and expand study scope to adenoma cases with the hope to find serum markers for detecting pre-cancerous lesions. Two independent case-control sets for advanced adenomas (training and validation sets) will serve this purpose. A more sensitive assay (digital quantitative PCR) will be employed in this phase II study as compared to the MethyLight assay used in the phase I project. With over 1000 samples to be examined in this study, the final validated serum markers might improve the early diagnosis of CRC or even better, enhance the current CRC screening armamentarium applicable to asymptomatic populations. All these benefits would perhaps ultimately reduce the mortality from colorectal cancer.
kw: Colorectal cancer, Serum marker, Methylation, Early detection, Adenoma

title: Bone regeneration using NELL-1, a non BMP-2 osteoinductive growth factor, delivered by novel carriers in a lumbar interbody spinal fusion model
abs: Osteobiologics are increasing important in spinal fusion field. Although BMP-2 has gained clinical success in spinal fusion rate, it has been reported to associate with severe complications. NELL-1 is a new osteoinductive growth factor for bone regeneration. The aim of the current study is to assess the safety and feasibility of NELL-1 when delivered by polyelectrolyte complex (PEC) and Bioactive nano-particle based putty (BNPP) and to evaluate the bone regeneration capacity of these two formulations in both small and large animal spinal fusion model. We hypothesize that the therapeutic efficiency of NELL-1 will be enhanced by polyelectrolyte complex (PEC) and bioactive nano-particle based putty (BNPP). Loading capacity and releasing kinetics of NELL-1 will be evaluated when delivered by new carriers. In vitro bioactivity and safety of NELL-1 will also be assessed after its release from carriers. The bone formation capacity of NELL-1 delivered by new carriers will be evaluated in a rabbit interbody fusion model. The rate and quality of fusion will be evaluated using histology and computed tomography. Following testing in the rabbit experiments, we will next utilize a porcine interbody fusion model designed to evaluate the rate and quality of fusion in a more challenge dynamic-load-bearing large animal model to facilitate clinical translation. If successful, a new generation of non-BMP based bone graft substitute consistingof NELL-1 matched with an optimal carrier will significantly improve the clinical outcome of spinal fusion procedure.
kw: bone regeneration, growth factors, control release, osteoinduction, ageing

title: Critical roles of caveolin-1 and lipid rafts in modulation of autophagy and therapeutic responses in human breast cancer cells
abs: At present, autophagy is generally considered as a pro-survival mechanism and thus suppression of autophagy becomes an important cancer therapeutic approach. Caveolin-1 is one of the key membrane-bound scaffolding proteins, and together with lipid rafts, plays crucial roles in various important cellular processes. Moreover, caveolin-1 has been shown to exert tumor suppressor function in human breast cancer. Based on our preliminary data, we hypothesize that caveolin-1 and lipid rafts play a critical role in determining cell stress responses in human breast cancer cells via modulation of autophagy, and those breast cancer cells with deficient caveolin-1 are more susceptible to autophagy suppression as a therapeutic approach. We attempt to address these hypotheses with the following specific aims: 1. To examine the regulatory function of caveolin-1 and lipid rafts in both basal and inducible autophagy in human breast cancer cells2. To study the molecular mechanisms underlying the regulatory role of caveolin-1 and lipid rafts in early stage of autophagy by focusing on autophagosome precursor membrane formation3. To identify the molecular mechanisms underlying the regulatory role of caveolin-1 and lipid rafts in late stage of autophagy by focusing on lysosomal function 4. To investigate the role of autophagy mediated by caveolin-1 and lipid rafts in cellular responses to stress in human breast cancer cells5. To test whether knockdown of caveolin-1 in breast cancer cell (MDA-MB-231) will enhance the susceptibility to autophagy inhibition in a nude mice xenograft model6. To establish the association between the expression level of caveolin-1 and autophagy markers in human breast cancer tissues.Results from this study will reveal the novel function of caveolin-1 and lipid rafts in autophagy regulation. More importantly, this study will help establish caveolin-1 expression level in breast cancers as a potential selection criterion for autophagy inhibition as a novel cancer therapeutic approach.
kw: caveolin-1, lipid rafts, autophagy, lysosome, cell death, breast cancer

title: Defining the role of 3’ untranslated region of the dengue virus genome in determining viral fitness and epidemic dengue
abs: The global spread of all four serotypes of dengue virus (DENV-1 to -4) results in 400 million infections annually. Disease prevention relies solely on vector control guided by surveillance, as neither a licensed vaccine nor antiviral drug is available. However, surveillance for changes in DENV serotype prevalence is not adequately sensitive, as introduction of new genetic strains has resulted in several epidemics without any detectable change in serotype prevalence. Sequencing genomes of circulating DENV could thus improve surveillance but only if how genomic differences result in fitter and more virulent DENV is understood mechanistically. This is critical to distinguish noise from random mutations to those that are functionally relevant. We have recently examined DENV-2 isolated during the 1994 epidemic in Puerto Rico. We identified nucleotide changes in the 3’ untranslated region (3’UTR) that altered production of subgenomic flavivirus RNA (sfRNA) and showed that this sfRNA inhibits interferon (IFN) expression for improved DENV fitness. Intriguingly, this same mechanism may also explain another DENV-2 epidemic in Nicaragua, suggesting a surveillance application for such knowledge. We hence propose to develop a greater understanding of DENV sfRNA and how it inhibits IFN expression for epidemic transmission. Specifically, we will characterize the different species of sfRNA present in infected cells and identify the host proteins sfRNA interacts with to inhibit IFN expression. We will achieve these aims using the latest technologies, such as quantitative RNA sequencing and RNA affinity chromatography methodology coupled to stable isotopic labeling in cell culture (SILAC), on epidemiologically informative DENV strains. We will also explore if similar mechanisms apply to all four DENV serotypes and potentially explain the emergence of another outbreak in Sri Lanka. Collectively, we envisage that the studies proposed here will serve as a beginning for the translation of molecular virology into mechanisms-based, DENV surveillance applications.
kw: Dengue; Epidemic emergence;Subgenomic flavivirus RNA (sfRNA); Viral factors; 3’ untranslated region

title: Effects of a BCAA (branched chain amino acids)-supplemented hypocaloric diet versus a standard hypocaloric diet on weight loss, lean mass preservation and improvement of insulin sensitivity, and its benefits over a high-protein hypocaloric diet.
abs: In obesity treatment, high-protein diets have shown to be more effective than conventional low-fat, diets in increasing lean mass preservation, but are costly and have potential health risks. Lean mass preservation is crucial for sustaining high basal energy expenditure for greater initial weight loss, mitigating weight regain and improving insulin sensitivity. Branched-chain amino acids (BCAA) supplements are known to stimulate protein synthesis and preserve lean mass but their effects during weight loss have not been investigated. We propose to investigate if a BCAA-supplemented hypocaloric diet when compared to a standard, moderate-protein hypocaloric diet will result in greater lean mass retention and improvement in insulin sensitivity. Additionally, we investigate if the BCAA-supplemented diet has added advantage to a high-protein hypocaloric diet by leading to less detrimental effects on bone mineral density and renal function. Using a 16-week weight loss intervention, combined with 8 weeks of weight maintenance, overweight and obese men and women will be randomized to one of three diets: a hypocaloric diet with BCAA supplements, a standard hypocaloric diet (as control) or a high-protein hypocaloric diet with placebo supplements. Participants’ compliance to the diet versus supplements will be compared. Body composition and bone mineral density (by DEXA), resting and diet-induced energy expenditure (by indirect calorimetry and test meals) and insulin sensitivity (by HOMA) will be measured before and after weight loss. Blood and urine samples will be analyzed for biochemical parameters and renal function. Body composition and bloods will also be measured at the end of weight maintenance. The effect of the diet intervention will be assessed by using repeated-measures ANOVA. Findings of this study will provide novel insight on the use of BCAA-supplementation during energy restriction and may offer an alternative cost-effective strategy for weight loss and maintenance, without the adverse health effects of a high-protein load.
kw: Branched-chain amino acids; High-protein diet; Weight loss; Lean mass preservation; Weight maintenance; Insulin sensitivity

title: Role of Soluble Urokinase Plasminogen Activator Receptor (suPAR) in Pathogenicity of Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS)
abs: Immune-mediated focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) is the most common cause of acquired end-stage renal disease in children worldwide. Studies on the pathogenetic mechanism suggested a plausible role for induction of urokinase plasminogen activator receptor (uPAR) signaling with increase in circulating soluble uPAR. Several questions, however, remained unanswered: i) High suPAR levels are also found in non-proteinuric diseases (eg. sepsis); ii) Is the whole suPAR molecule or one of its subunits, the elusive proteinuric-inducing circulating factor; iii) Are immune cells the only possible source of suPAR in FSGS? Our preliminary studies demonstrated increased suPAR production in monocyte supernatant and injured podocytes. We therefore hypothesized that:1.Secreted suPAR from podocytes promotes podocyte migration, contributing to elevated circulating suPAR levels in FSGS patients;2.A specific isoform of suPAR may be responsible for podocye foot process effacement;3.Filtration of suPAR into urine in the presence of podocyte damage may explain the discrepant suPAR levels observed in FSGS patients, and the elevated suPAR levels in the presence of decreased glomerular filtration rate.Thus, the primary aims are to:1.Demonstrate suPAR production by injured podocytes and its role in promoting podocyte migration, 2.Identify the suPAR isoform responsible for foot process effacement, 3.Identify the upstream mediators leading to increased uPAR expression in podocytes and monocytes/immune cells.The secondary aim is to validate the above findings in both wild type and Plaur-/- (CD87-/-) mice via introduction of these upstream mediators, to determine if uPAR is increased on the mouse podocytes resulting in FSGS. The tertiary aim is to assess the clinical utility of suPAR (plasma+urine) as an early biomarker of podocyte injury.Understanding the role of suPAR and its isoforms in podocyte injury will facilitate the design of novel targeted therapies for this disease, as well as provide a potential biomarker.
kw: suPAR; FSGS; Podocyte Injury; Biomarker

title: FIT (Fat Storage Inducing Transmembrane Proteins), Skeletal Muscle and Metabolic Disease: Understanding Mechanisms to Develop Novel Therapeutic Strategies
abs: Excessive amounts of triglyceride stored in lipid droplets (LDs) in skeletal muscle is highly associated with type 2 diabetes. There is a fundamental gap in understanding the mechanisms that mediate the formation of LDs. This lack of information is a significant barrier in developing therapeutic interventions to directly modulate tissue triglyceride levels to treat type 2 diabetes. Fat storage-InducingTransmembrane protein 1 and 2 (FIT1/FITM1 & FIT2/FITM2) are phylogenetically conserved endoplasmic reticulum membrane proteins that mediate LD formation. The long-term goal is to determine how LDs form in order to devise therapeutic strategies for regulating triglyceride storage in tissues. The objective in this particular application, which is the next step in meeting this goal, is to determine the physiological function of FIT1 and FIT2 in skeletal muscle, a tissue critical in the pathogenesis of type 2 diabetes. Our central hypothesis is that FIT1 and FIT2 play distinct roles in muscle, with FIT1 associating with mitochondria to drive fatty acid oxidation, and FIT2 generating LDs not coupled to mitochondria. Guided by strong preliminary data, the hypothesis will be tested via two specific aims.Specific Aim 1 will involve determining the physiological role of FIT1 and FIT2 using a) mouse models of FIT deficiency in skeletal muscle, and b) primary human muscle cell lines as experimental models. Specific Aim 2 will involve identifying the mitochondria targeting sequence of FIT1 and role in mediating fatty acid oxidation. The approach is innovative because it represents a new and substantive effort to determine the physiological function of FIT1 and FIT2 in skeletal muscle. The proposed research is significant because it represents the first step in a continuum of research that is expected to result in the future development of novel therapeutic strategies to regulate skeletal muscle triglyceride in metabolic disease.
kw: muscle, metabolic disease, fat

title: High-throughput and high-dimensional assessment of the relationship between the antigen-specific T cell response and Hepatitis B viral escape during viral control and viral reactivation
abs: Despite the success of vaccine programs, there remains a large pool of chronically infected patients (~ 350 million) who are at risk of premature death from liver disease complications. We plan to build upon our unique and well-characterized studies of HBV quasispecies evolution in phenotypes of chronic hepatitis B patients undergoing HBeAg-seroconversion, and combine this with several new cutting-edge approaches to interrogate adaptive and innate immune responses established by the Singapore Immunology Network. Several lines of evidence strongly suggest that the HBV-specific T-cell response varies over the course of infection and, in general, the frequencies, phenotypes and range of epitopes targeted by T-cells are highly indicative of the status of any cellular immune response. Thus, we hypothesize that changes in the specificity and phenotypes of antigen-specific T-cells will correlate with the occurrence and severity of HBV reactivation events related to altered viral evolution and diversity. We will take advantage of several major breakthroughs in our ability to probe the antigen-specific T-cell response as well as the composition of the viral quasispecies longitudinally using stored samples. First, we will use high throughput DNA sequencing of HBV viral genomes to more accurately identify quasispecies that occur during HBeAg-seroconversion and HBeAg-negative reactivation. Concurrently, we will use high throughput ‘epimax’ T-cell proliferation assays to broadly assess the sum of the active HBV-specific T-cell response. Also, taking full advantage of new generation single-cell mass spectrometry-based flow cytometry (CyTOF) that provides an unprecedented number of independent cellular measures (currently 49), we will simultaneously screen T-cell populations for HBV epitope usage (with multiplexing), and deeply phenotype and functionally delineate these antigen-specific cells. Lastly, we will use cutting-edge immune monitoring to assess the nature and extent of innate-immune response during reactivation. Ultimately, these may lead to understanding pathogenesis through which, better diagnostics and therapeutic approaches can be initiated.

title: Development of Super-resolution and High-sensitivity Optical Nanoscopes
abs: Optical microcopy is extensively applied in our daily lives as well as our industries and researches. Different from the imaging techniques with a collimated electron or ion beam, optical approaches can acquire the images in ambient air at a fast speed, and especially the molecules behaviors can be studied in vivo. Optical diffraction limit is an inherent property in the nature of light. A lot of research efforts are being focused on how to increase the optical imaging resolution, such as light behaviors controlled by meta-materials, near-field signals captured by using near-field scanning optical microscopy (NSOM) and saturated optical nonlinearity in stimulated emission depletion (STED) system. Though these super-resolution methods can achieve the resolving capability down to sub-50 nm, each of them has its own technical obstacles, such as high energy loss in materials, weak optical signals and high requirement of specific dyes to label molecule samples, which limit their extensive applications. In this research programme, we will carry out novel scientific research to further our current research activities in Active meta-materials, Near-field energy enhancement through particle lens and Nonlinear plasmonic effect excited by a ultrafast laser. Through these feasible approaches, 20 nm spatial resolution in optical images can be obtained as the specimen are placed in ambient air. Secondly, advanced image processing and fast computing algorithms will be developed and coupled into the optical super-resolution apparatus to obtain images at 10 nm spatial resolution. Finally industrial cooperation will be established to integrate the optical nanoscopes and prototype instruments for technical commercialization with high economic impacts. These super-resolution nanoscopes being accomplished in ambient air not only act as an investigation tool to observe the molecular or electromagnetic interactions at 10 nm scale, but also provide a promising access to lively manipulate, locate nano-objects and make novel functional nano-devices.

title: Peripheral Nerve Prostheses - A Paradigm Shift in Restoring Dexterous Limb Function
abs: Peripheral nerve injury due to accident or disease afflicts a large and disproportionately young segment of the population at a great cost to society and those individuals' quality of life. Regenerative and reparative solutions are highly experimental and do not address the fundamental challenges of long regeneration times and loss of muscle function. Our central hypothesis is that a bio-electronic (or “bionic”) interface linking the injured nerve to the peripheral muscles controlling limb function will serve as a functional neuroprosthesis to sustain muscle capabilities, and restore hitherto unattainable dexterous hand functions. Our overarching aims are to research neural interfacing and prosthetics, create intellectual property, and demonstrate feasibility of what we call a “Bionic Link" technology. We will develop a novel nerve to electrode bionic interface, and test it, first in a non-human primate model, and subsequently in human patients, to demonstrate, for the first time, a completely implanted dexterous hand control. The innovation of this work lies in the technological advancements of implantable circuitry, including microelecronics, power sources, antennas, novel low-power on-chip neural decoding algorithms, and packaging of the integrated system. Important experimental results will stem from this model system to set the stage for preclinical but translational medical technology. These experiments will also allow further study of peripheral nerve signals and their neuromuscular representation and the training of decoding models. The clinical impact of this proposal lies in the restoration of dexterous limb function, thus restoring quality of life at the individual level and mitigating the aggregate cost to society of treatment and productivity decline of affected individuals.

title: New Approach to Low Power Information Storage: Electric-Field Controlled Magnetic Memories
abs: In this collaborative program, we aim to develop the new generation low power magnetic memories which will be controlled by electric fields through an applied voltage rather than current. Five possible approaches will be used to achieve the electric field controlled magnetic memories: (1) the control of magnetism through a control of the carrier concentration by an electric field in diluted magnetic semiconductor, where the magnetism is caused by carrier-mediation; (2) modulation of the number of electrons in d orbital of a metallic ferromagnet with an electric field resulting in the change of the magnetic properties (3) Modulation of the spin polarization of ferromagnets by the interaction between ferroelectric and ferromagnetic layers arising from the switching of ferroelectric polarization by an electric field. (4) Interfacial magnetic exchange-coupling between antiferromagnetic ferroelectric and ferromagnetic where the antiferromagnetic ferroelectric is a magnetoelectric multiferroic. (5) Strain-mediated control of spin ordering and charge ordering in ferromagnetic/piezoelectric heterostructure. These approaches require the synthesis and characterization of high quality ultra-thin ferroelectric films and magnetic films, and the control of interface in atomic scale. Furthermore, the fundamental investigation of the mutual coupling coupling between the ferroelectric and ferromagnetic properties, spin and charge under magnetic field and electric field will be conducted. In order for final technique transfer and commercialization, investigations on technology aspects such as large scale deposition techniques of high quality ferroelectric and ferromagnetic oxide films, lithography technique of such special materials and device fabrication and characterization will also be the focus of the project.

title: The Singapore Indian Eye Study 2 (SINDI-2) – Prospective cohort study of 6-year incidence, risk factors, and impact of retinal and other major eye diseases
abs: Asian Indians account for one sixth of the world’s population, with a global estimate of >1 billion persons. Due to an aging population and a higher prevalence of diabetes/cardiovascular risk factors, retinal diseases such as diabetic retinopathy (DR) and age-related macular degeneration (AMD) are considered to be of major public health consequences in Indians. There is thus a need for accurate population-based data on the incidence of DR, AMD and other eye diseases in Indians and to discover specific modifiable risk factors for these conditions. Such data are currently extremely limited worldwide. We conducted the Singapore Indian Eye Study (SINDI), a population-based study of 3,400 (75.6% response rate) Indian adults aged 40-80 years, in 2007-09. SINDI-1 collected and provided new data and resulted in a significant understanding of the prevalence and impact of DR, AMD and other eye diseases. In the current proposal, we will re-examine this cohort 6 years after the baseline examination in 2013-15. This new study, SINDI-2, will examine the 6-year incidence and progression of DR, AMD and other major eye diseases, discover novel lifestyle and clinical factors, including dietary factors and new retinal imaging measures, and study the impact of these diseases on vision-related quality of life and socio-economic cost of vision impairment. Major strengths of the SINDI-2 include a well-established and characterized cohort at baseline, an experienced international team of clinician-scientists and epidemiologists, and the highest-quality baseline data including digital retinal images, frozen serum/DNA. SINDI-2 will be the first comprehensive prospective cohort study of eye diseases in Asian Indians, and will provide critical information on gaps in our understanding of vision disorders, in particular DR and AMD, from which to plan broad public health strategies to reduce visual loss in Indians in Singapore and globally.

title: Atmospheric Organic Aerosol in the Changing Environment of Southeast Asia
abs: Accurate estimations of the global and local environments in the future, including air pollution, water pollution, and increase in the global surface temperature, are necessary for policy development as well as for effective investment on public infrastructure. Aerosol particles, those are defined as solid or liquid materials suspended in the air, play important roles in the environment. The research in the last decade clarified that biogenic organic materials account for a significant portion of atmospheric aerosol particles. However, reactivity, formation processes, and physicochemical properties of those particles are not sufficiently understood to predict the impacts on the climate and human health. The research proposed in this document is developed to understand the following specific topics: (1) chemical aging of organic aerosol particles emitted from biomass burning, (2) formation mechanism of organic aerosol particles from biogenic volatile compounds, and (3) water uptake by organic aerosol particles. Those topics will be experimentally addressed, incorporating detailed data analysis using numerical models. A flow tube aerosol reactor will be developed to conduct precise kinetic experiments on chemical aging as well as on aerosol formation. Peat burning particles will be injected for aging experiments, while seed particles will be continuously supplied for organic aerosol formation experiments. Reactive gas species will also be injected. Variables for the experiments will include size, phase, and chemical composition of original particles. Mean residence time of particles in the reactor will also be controlled. Size distribution, chemical composition, and water uptake by organic aerosol particles will be simultaneously monitored. Detailed numerical models will be developed for quantitative data analysis. Simplification of those detailed models will be attempted in order to facilitate implementation of those processes in three-dimensional chemical transport models.

title: Pure Spin Current and Spin Wave Devices
abs: Devices which make use of the spin degree of freedom of electrons, or spintronics, have the potential to offer more than Moore of the CMOS technology. Although so far the interest in spintronics has been fuelled mainly by the application of spin-valves and magnetic tunnel junctions in magnetic data storage, these devices are primarily based on spin polarized current which comprised of both charge and spin current. In order to fully make use of the spin degree of freedom of electrons for next-generation high-frequency and low-power spintronics applications, there is an urgent need to develop technologies that are based solely on the generation, manipulation and detection of flow of the spin angular momentum of electrons. To this end, recently intensive efforts have been focused on two hottest frontiers in spintronics: spin waves in magnetic nanostructures and generation and detection of spin current in non-magnetic materials. In this proposal, a systematic investigation of the dynamic behaviour of magnetic nanostructures will be conducted using broadband ferromagnetic resonance spectroscopy and correlated with spin dependent transport properties. Focusing on materials with long-spin diffusion length such as graphene, ZnO, and Si, systematic studies will be carried out to improve the efficiency of spin current generation and detection in these materials. Different spin current sources will be explored such as magnon, magnetization precession, spin Hall effect, etc. Efforts will also be extended to exotic materials such as topological insulators in which a more robust spin current can be created at either the edges or surface of the material. We also aim to demonstrate reconfigurable magnonic based logic devices using magnonic crystals. Prototypes of pure spin current based devices such as field-effect transistors and spin caloritronic devices will be fabricated and their performances will be studied and compared with similar but non-spin based devices.

title: Patient-primary tumor specific circulating tumor Nucleic acids (pps-ctNAs) as personalized surveillance biomarkers for early detection of recurrent colorectal cancer
abs: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the 3rd most common cancer worldwide and commonest cancer in Singapore. Initially, many patients have intermediate stage (stage 2B to 3C) cancer without distant metastases. However, 30-50% of these patients will develop cancer recurrence with metastatic disease appearing, typically within 3 years after surgery. Major oncology guidelines recommend patients undergo surveillance with annual CT scans and regular carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) blood tests. When recurrence is detected early, curative-intent secondary surgery that removes the metastases is more often possible. Meta-analyses suggest intensive surveillance improves overall survival outcomes. However, CEA has limited sensitivity of 65% and specificity of 90% for detecting CRC recurrence. By the time CEA is elevated, cancers are often large. There is an urgent unmet need to develop better surveillance biomarkers.Previous studies observed tumor derived nucleic acids in the circulation of cancer patients, and our preliminary studies suggest that paired metastatic CRCs harbor mutations vastly similar to their corresponding primary tumors. Additionally, we have developed ability to detect plasma circulating nucleic acids (ctNAs) at very low concentrations. Intersecting these complementary developments, we propose a personalized approach for early detection of CRC recurrence: first, we will sequence each patient's primary tumor to identify an individual complement of patient primary-tumor specific (pps) mutations (viz. a molecular thumbprint); next, we will assay for this thumbprint in the patient’s plasma samples during follow-up [patient primary-tumor specific circulating tumor nucleic acids (pps-ctNAs)]. We hypothesize that in each patient, presence of pps-ctNA correlates with presence of tumors and that pps-ctNAs can detect CRC recurrence with lower technical limits of detection and higher sensitivity and specificity to enable earlier diagnosis of CRC recurrence than currently possible. Using pps-ctNAs as personalized surveillance biomarkers, curative-intent secondary surgery may become possible for more patients and cure rates in this common cancer could improve.

title: Peroxiredoxin III as a prognostic marker and therapeutic applications in breast cancer
abs: The Peroxiredoxin (Prx) family comprise of six thiol-specific antioxidant enzymes which catalyze the reduction of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2). Prxs confer protection against oxidative stress and regulate cell signaling associated with H2O2 as a secondary messenger, thereby influencing cell differentiation, proliferation and apoptosis. Our previous studies have shown that silencing the PRDX3 gene (which encodes the Prx III protein) enhanced cell proliferation and metastatic potential in breast cancer in vitro. The hypothesis in this study is that Peroxiredoxin III is involved in breast carcinogenesis and could be a potential prognostic biomarker and molecular target for cancer therapy. We will analyze the functional significance of Prx III and its downstream target, serglycin which was selected from an Affymetrix screen after silencing the PRDX 3 gene. Chemosensitivity to therapeutic drugs following depletion of the Prx III and serglycin will also be evaluated. Advanced quantitative mass-spectrometry-based SILAC (Stable isotope labeling Amino Acids in Culture) will be used for pathway and network analysis. A metastatic mouse model for human breast cancer will be utilized to further verify the definitive association of Prx III with cancer progression and understand the molecular effects of Prx III in the in vivo system. In addition, a panel of microRNAs will be analyzed to identify upstream microRNAs which regulate the PRDX 3 gene. We will also determine the utility of Prx III and serglycin as prognostic markers of breast cancer by correlating Prx III and serglycin immunostaining with clinico-pathological parameters such as histological grade, AJCC staging, tumor stage, lymph node status, metastasis, recurrence and survival in 300 archived breast cancer specimens. Identification of biomarkers which can predict aggressive tumors would facilitate the selection of appropriate treatment regimes for breast cancer patients and the development of novel and more effective molecular targets for therapy.

title: Learning from Bats: From Genomics to Controlling Viral Infection and Combating Cancer
abs: Bats are one of the most abundant, diverse and geographically dispersed mammals on earth, representing almost a quarter of all the known living mammals in the world. They display several unique but poorly characterized biological features with great significance to human health, such as longevity, low rate tumourigenesis and co-existence with different viruses without showing clinical diseases. Our overarching hypothesis is that studies on these bat-specific evolutionary adaptations will offer unprecedented opportunities in understanding human health problems, with profound medical implications. This study will focus on two major aspects of the unique bat biology. (1) To uncover novel principles of immune control of deadly human viruses. Bats are the reservoirs for many zoonotic viruses highly lethal to humans, including SARS, Ebola, Nipah and Hendra viruses. Two of them, SARS and Nipah, hit Singapore the hardest and caused substantial economic loss in the region. Yet, these viruses are totally harmless to bats, despite bats themselves are mammals. (2) To gain insights into the underlying mechanisms of aging and tumourigenesis. Most bat species have very long lifespan, as high as 41 years. Bats also seem to have a lower rate of tumourigenesis than other mammals, and indeed our preliminary genome analysis revealed that there are unique sequence variations in the bat homologues of key human tumour suppressor genes. Up to date, there has been little research conducted into these unique bat biological features due to the lack of genome information and research tools. The proposed program aims to bridge this knowledge gap, and exploit bat biology to find solutions for human health problems. This will be achieved in four integrated projects using cutting-edge technologies covering genomics, bioinformatics, infection studies under highest biocontainment, immunology, cancer biology and structural biology.

title: Artificial Liver Platform for Next Generation Drug Discovery and Development
abs: The critical importance of the human liver for metabolism and detoxification has generated tremendous interest among scientists and clinicians to study liver biology and pathology. Unfortunately, current models of human liver are: 1) unable to prospectively predict human drug metabolism, including hepatotoxicity; 2) poor representations to understand the mechanisms of liver diseases such as hepatitis C virus (HCV) and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC); and 3) not suitable for generating artificial liver tissues to treat end-stage liver disease. In light of these challenges, we seek to develop improved models of human liver and change the current paradigm for studying liver biology and pathology, developing new drugs, and treating liver diseases. To date, we have discovered that polymer hydrogels represent an excellent scaffold to maintain the phenotype of encapsulated hepatocytes, and thus hold great potential for creating improved models of the human liver. Towards this goal, our key hypotheses are: 1) mimicking the liver microenvironment can foster the maintenance and acquisition of hepatic morphology and function among various cell types; 2) employing artificial liver platforms which mimic critical features of the liver microenvironment under different disease conditions can improve our understanding of treatment strategies; and 3) humanized mouse models can provide a transformative approach to study infectious liver diseases with clinically relevant endpoints. To test these hypotheses, we seek to achieve the following specific aims: Aim 1. To design a hydrogel-based, three-dimensional artificial liver platform for hosting different types of liver cells. Aim 2. To perform modeling of liver diseases, including viral hepatitis and hepatocellular carcinoma, with application to drug development. Aim 3. To engineer a mouse model with a humanized liver for in vivo liver disease studies. Taken together, this research programme will build upon cutting-edge advances in engineering technology to produce transformative solutions for treating infectious liver diseases and liver cancer.

title: Synthesis, Characterizations and Performance of Novel Two-dimensional Atomic Layers: Hexagonal Boron Nitride (h-BN) and Molybdenum Disulfide (MoS₂)
abs: The proposal builds on my past research in the investigations of 2D crystals and the relevant devices. As miniaturization of silicon-based electronics reaches its fundamental physical limits, atomic layers of graphene, h-BN and MoS₂ have been proposed as a potential complementary material. Since the technology have been developed for synthesizing single-layered graphene, a remaining challenge in the realization of these applications lies in the high-quality, large-area synthesis of h-BN and MOS₂ . The aims of this proposed research consist of three parts. The first part will be to a systematic investigation of scalable and flexible synthesis of the h-BN and MOS₂ in high quality and atomic layered thicknesses and their derived/hybridized structures as well, based on an optimized chemical vapor deposition. Some alternative approaches such as micro/nano-fabrication, hydrothermal method, chemical exfoliation and template-based method will be also involved. The second part will be comprehensive characterizations of the above materials and structures, evaluating their quality and investigating their atomic structures, by various characterizing tools, revealing their possible unique properties in electronics, chemistry and mechanics. The third part will be an elaborated and sustainable research to the engineer/fabricate functional devices built on the understanding of the properties of these novel materials. Functional prototype devices will be developed as a possible fundamental component used in the next generation semiconducting and optical areas, and following a scalable production for their potential large applications in industry such as high-performance coating and composites.

title: Using biophysics to probe the mechanisms of scaling and robustness in development
abs: Successful embryogenesis requires both scaling (correction for size variations) and robustness (reliable decision-making in the presence of noise). My research addresses two major questions: (1) How does scaling of morphological and genetic boundaries occur in vivo? (2) How do genetic networks, cell-cell communication and interactions between tissues correct for changes in environmental conditions and protein number fluctuations to ensure robust development? Using multiview lightsheet microscopy and Drosophila melanogaster as a model organism, I will construct in vivo fate maps of development in embryos of different lengths, and uncover how cell division, cell dynamics and apoptosis contribute to scaling. By imaging key genetic factors in vivo and through cell lineage tracing, I will probe the roles played by tissue mechanics and genetics in the positional scaling of boundaries. In particular, I will investigate whether the response to embryo length variations is approximately uniform across the embryo or whether specific regions respond differently. A system’s response to fluctuations provides valuable insight into its underlying biological mechanisms. Temporal variations in embryogenesis processes – whether between embryos or in the relative timing of internal processes – have received little attention despite their important role in development. I will probe how the embryo corrects for heterochronicity, focusing on whether interactions between tissues compensate for temporal fluctuations. Moreover, I intend to probe heterochronicity due to temperature changes inside single embryos and between embryos at different temperatures, to further understanding of how embryogenesis adapts to environmental variation. Finally, although organogenesis is vital to development, it has been subject to limited robustness analysis. I will investigate the Drosophila cardiogenesis gene network to explore how it ensures reliable cardioblast specification. Overall, I bring a multi-level spatial and temporal approach to studying scaling and robustness in development, considering not only processes inside cells, but also how those cells contribute to tissue formation and how the tissues themselves interact.

title: Quantum query complexity, communication complexity, and semidefinite programming: exploring the limits of efficient computation
abs: My research will focus on three topics: quantum query complxity, communication complexity, and semidefinite programming. In query complexity one wants to compute a function---say determining if a graph contains a triangle---but can only access the input through queries, is there an edge between vertex i and vertex j? Quantum query complexity is an extremely successful model for studying the power of quantum computing, leading both to interesting algorithms and understanding of their limitations. We will develop new quantum query algorithms using the beautiful learning graph framework of Belovs. We used this model to give the best algorithm for determining if a graph contains a triangle (and more generally a constant sized subgraph) and the first non-trivial algorithm to tell if a binary operation is associative. I wish to use learning graphs to show that every disjunction of polynomially many clauses has sublinear complexity. Communication complexity studies how much two parties need to communicate to compute a function when each party has only partial knowledge of the input. Communication complexity has many applications for example to circuit lower bounds, proof complexity, and streaming algorithms. A long standing open question is if for total functions (those which are defined for every input) quantum messages can offer substantial savings over classical ones. I will investigate this question by developing new lower bound techniques for quantum communication based on the adversary lower bound for query complexity. Linear and semidefinite programming are powerful algorithmic paradigms widely used in practice. Recently, super-polynomial lower bounds were shown on the size of linear programming formulations of the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP). However, TSP could still have a small size positive semidefinite programming formulation. Showing this is not the case amounts to analyzing a fascinating new quantity known as positive semidefinite rank. No one knows how to prove good lower bounds on positive semidefinite rank and I hope to develop techniques to do this.

title: Multimorbidity in primary care and its association with Depression, Anxiety and Quality of Life (MDAQ)
abs: Multimorbidity is common in primary care but it has not been studied in Singapore to date. Self-management of chronic condition, especially multiple conditions, is very important. This is especially so in Singapore with an increasing aging population and a society that is adapting to a decreasing working adult to elderly ratio. For patients with poorly-controlled chronic conditions, reduced self-management may be due to comorbid psychological distress like depression and anxiety more than outright non-adherence to dietary and prescribed pharmaceutical compliance. Several studies have demonstrated the association of chronic diseases to depression. This is a cross-sectional study on the prevalence and severity of psychological distress and the quality of life experienced by patients with multimorbidity in the primary care setting in Singapore. Patients with the three commonest chronic conditions – Diabetes, Hypertension and Dyslipidaemia are randomly selected for the study. The PHQ9, GAD7 and EQ5D will be administered by a trained research assistant. Demographics and the social economic status will also be captured during the interview. Our research hypothesis is with increased level of severity of multimorbidity, patients would experience a higher level of psychological distress and lower quality of life. We hope to highlight the interdependency of mental and physical health for patients with multimorbidity. This will enable better services to be developed and provide insights to adapt the current consultation model to a more suitable one for such patients. The specific aims are:1. To measure the prevalence of depression and/or anxiety amongst patients with multimorbidity in a primary care setting2. To study the association between multimorbidity and the psychological distress (depression and anxiety), quality of life and socio-economic status 3. To measure the quality of life of patients and to determine severity of disease burden with multimorbidity in a primary care setting.

title: Quantum sensor using guided matter waves in optical fibers
abs: Precision measurements and quantum sensors based on matter waves require precise control of matter wave packets. In theory, this can be accomplished using atom-photon interactions. In practice, however, the diffractive nature of light means that high accuracy requires large, bulky and inflexible setups. The broad objective of the proposed research is to use optically guided matter waves inside a hollow-core photonic bandgap fiber to mitigate these problems. Such hollow-core fibers have the advantage of low speckle and bending loss over the conventional total internal reflection fibers. Ultra-cold atoms loaded into the hollow core of the fiber will be guided by an optical dipole trap to prevent collision with the fiber wall. This research will have a broad impact on the field of precision measurements with a wide range of applications. I will use this system to develop mobile gravimeter/accelerometers and gravity gradiometers for use in inertial navigation, mineral exploration, and remote sensing of civil and military targets; high spatial resolution magnetometers for biomedical science. In addition to these applications, the methods proposed here will also be useful in fundamental research. I will measure the Newtonian gravitational constant G, study large momentum transfer matter wave beam splitter, and test charge neutrality of atoms.

title: Molecular mechanisms that dictate cell fate following treatment with anti-mitotic drugs
abs: Anti-mitotic drugs, such as microtubule toxins, are used extensively during chemotherapy. These exert their anti-neoplastic effects via activation of the spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC), culminating in a prolonged mitotic arrest which usually leads to mitotic cell death. Although prolonged mitotic arrest is a necessary prerequisite for drug-induced death, little is known about the molecular mechanisms and pathways that link the SAC to mitotic cell death. Moreover, it is poorly understood why some tumour cells are susceptible to these anti-mitotic drugs while others are not. Thus, the main objective of my research proposal is to decipher the regulatory interface between the SAC, mitotic machinery and mitotic cell death. Better understanding of the molecular mechanisms that trigger cell death can promote sensitivity to current anti-mitotic drug treatments if these drugs are then used in combination with the modulated apoptotic pathways. Both non-transformed and tumour cell lines will be used to study how these drugs can trigger death of tumour cells with little detrimental effect to normal cells. Since inter- and intra cell line variability in cell response to anti-mitotic drug treatment exists, methodologies such as live-cell imaging coupled with quantitative approaches and high-content imaging will be utilized. Differences between a normal mitosis and prolonged mitotic arrest will be characterized to gain clues to why an extended arrest is central to drug-induced cell death. Cells can also escape mitosis and progress to G1 without cytokinesis via “mitotic slippage”, rendering them aneuploid (harbouring abnormal number of chromsomes). Aneuploidy activates p53-dependent pathways that result in cell arrest or death. However, aneuploid cells can also bypass these surveillance mechanisms and proliferate, reflecting resistance to chemotherapy. Hence, this proposal also aims to elucidate the molecular circuitries that underlie the SAC, mitotic slippage and death, arrest or proliferation. Using network–based analysis, quantitative immunofluorescence microscopy, time-lapse imaging and high-content imaging to characterize these pathways will provide insights into improving efficacy of existing drugs and suppressing chemoresistance. Additionally, cells that slip into G1 often contain multiple micronuclei, structures commonly found in cancer cells and not normal cells. Micronuclei will thus be studied as a possible tumour-specific strategy and could also serve as a possible biomarker for patients that are susceptible to anti-mitotic drugs.

title: Spin Transport across Interfaces in Emerging Materials - Towards Materials Design for Next Generation Data Storage Applications
abs: The main focus of the research proposed here is to predict the electronic structure and spin transport properties of emerging materials of potential interest for achieving higher density, higher speed, higher endurance, lower power and even flexible disks for next generation data storage applications. Spintronics, the use of electron spin to control charge flow, is fundamental to many non-volatile memory applications, which store data in the form of microscopic regions of the material that are magnetized in different directions. As we approach the limits of Moore’s law, technical challenges faced in further miniaturization of bit size can only be overcome by a paradigm shift in storage materials, and by a fundamental, systematic understanding of charge and spin transport at the nanoscale. First principles calculations (i.e. calculations with no empirical parameters) have played a key role in the prediction of novel electronic and spin transport properties. In the proposed work, we will apply state-of-the-art first principles calculations to compute the magnetoresistance, resistance-area products and spin transfer torques in two classes of carefully chosen emerging materials systems – two-dimensional chalcogenides and organic spintronics systems. The magnetoresistance, resistance-area products and spin transfer torques are important spin transport properties for data storage applications. We will compute these quantities using non-equilibrium transport and many-electron quasiparticle theory in addition to density functional theory, and work closely with experimentalists to verify our predictions. The expected outcome of this work is the prediction of the electronic structure and spin transport properties in the chosen exciting, emerging nanoscale materials and an identification of useful materials for next generation high density, high speed, high endurance, lower power, and possibly mechanically flexible, data storage applications.
kw: spintronics and data storage;nanoscience;first principles electronic structure calculations;charge and spin transport;two-dimensional chalcogenides;organic-metal interfaces

title: Long-term clinical outcomes, cost-of-care, quality-of-care and re-admission rates in patients with coronary artery disease or congestive heart failure in Singapore (SingCLOUD): Proof of Concept
abs: Coronary artery disease (CAD) and congestive heart failure (CHF) are the leading causes of death in developed countries including Singapore. CHF may occur as a consequence of CAD or other causes. CAD and CHF are responsible for significant health care costs as patients have reduced functional status, may have repeat hospital admissions and ultimately result in working hours lost. The aim of this study is to examine the short and long term cost-of-care, clinical outcomes and measures of quality-of-care (eg. physician adherence to guideline recommended therapy) in patients who are admitted with CAD or CHFThe SingCLOUD project is a retrospective observational, multicentre study which will harness (1) the clinical data collected by the Singapore Cardiac Data Bank, (2) clinical, pharmacy, financial data; and (3) administrative data from participating institutions. These will eventually include all restructured hospitals and polyclinics. This current grant application is to fund a proof-of-concept study to perform data integration across the NHCS and NUHC databases. The data from these sources will be anonymized, merged and analyzed to provide information on the 1-year major adverse clinical events such as death, heart attacks, strokes, heart failure admissions and repeat revascularization procedures in these patients. Frequency and predictors of readmission would be analyzed. Overall cost of follow-up care over this
