title: How much do doctors and patients in Singapore differ in their perspectives on patient care, what are the causes, and how do they affect healthcare outcomes?
abs: AimsResearch in Western countries shows that there are systematic differences between what patients want and what doctors think they need. These differences are rarely negotiated openly in clinical encounters but have serious implications for healthcare outcomes. We hypothesize that such general differences also exist in Singapore and aim to determine how large they are, to what extent they are perceived by doctors and patients, how they vary, and what impact they have on healthcare outcomes. MethodsThis is a cross-sectional observational study focusing on Type 2 Diabetes and Rheumatoid Arthritis. The treatment need or want is conceptualized into three categories: treatment goals, information, and strategies. We will first develop a list of items representing both doctors’ and patients’ viewpoints through focus group discussions with patients and consultation with endocrinologists and rheumatologists. A random sample of 894 patients (Half with each disease) and all their doctors (24 by current count) will be asked to choose three most important items in each of the three categories on the list. In addition to demographics, we will also collect data on health status, disease characteristics, patient satisfaction, adherence and clinical outcomes from patients and practice characteristics from doctors. Descriptive analyses will be performed to determine the differences between doctors and patients and their perceptions of them. Regression analyses via path model and structural equation model will be performed to determine factors accounting for these differences and their impact on treatment outcomes.SignificanceThis is the first systematic study of general differences between doctors’ and patients’ perspectives in Singapore. The study results help identify unmet needs in doctor-patient communication and patient education. They form an essential basis for development of more effective programs to bridge these gaps. They will also lead to experimental studies to test the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of these new programs.
kw: Patient-doctor communication, patient education, patient satisfaction, medication adherence, chronic disease management

title: Simulation Modelling and Optimization of Pre-hospital Emergency Care in Singapore
abs: Pre-hospital Emergency Care (PEC) is the initial medical care given to an ill/injured patient before transfer to an appropriate healthcare facility. PEC has a major impact on time-sensitive acute medical conditions, such as Out-of-hospital Cardiac Arrests (OHCA), ST elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), stroke and severe trauma. Inefficiency in the PEC system can have major downstream effects, resulting in problems such as Emergency Department (ED) overcrowding, delays in treatment and hospital gridlock. The aims of the project are to: (1) utilize discrete event simulation (DES) to mathematically model the PEC system of Singapore which is supported by the Emergency Medical Services (EMS) and hospital EDs; (2) develop a simulation-based approximate dynamic programming approach for dynamic operations planning to support the optimal allocation of ambulances and zoning of hospital catchment, and; (3) develop a multi-objectives decision aid to assist policy decisions on the delivery of pre-hospital care for major emergency cases, such as OHCA, STEMI, stroke and severe trauma. Data and insights derived from the Cardiac Arrest and Resuscitation Epidemiology (CARE) study (Ong, Ng et al. 2009) will be expanded and utilized to develop the high resolution DES model and simulation optimization framework for realizing a cost-effective and efficacious PEC system in order to improve the health outcomes of patients.
kw: Ambulance Redeployment; Emergency Medical Services; Discrete Event Simulation; Process Optimization; Approximate Dynamic Programming; Operations Research

title: Tools to improve panic screening in the Emergency Department (TIPS-ED)
abs: Background: The overall aim of this Phase I study is to develop a time efficient screening method to detect Panic Disorder (PD) among emergency department (ED) patients in Singapore. PD is a disabling anxiety disorder characterized by somatic symptoms that mimic those of common medical conditions. Approximately 20-35% of North American ED patients with chest pain meet criteria for PD, but only 2% of these cases are diagnosed due to limited time. Unrecognized PD has a chronic course and is associated with high rates of repeat ED visits and unnecessary hospital admissions. Early detection is essential to improve clinical management and reduce unnecessary medical costs, but the optimal method for identifying PD patients in ED settings is unknown. Method: We will enroll a sample of 309 patients presenting to the Singapore General Hospital Department of Emergency Medicine with PD-like somatic complaints (i.e., palpitations, tachycardia, chest pain, dizziness, difficulty in breathing). Adult men and women of all racial/ethnic groups will be included. Participants will be recruited by clinical research coordinators and asked to complete a clinical report form. Diagnosis of PD will be made using the PD module of the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-IV (SCID). PD symptoms will be assessed using the PD modules of the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ) and the Psychiatric Diagnostic Screening Questionnaire (PDSQ). We will compare receiver operating characteristics, sensitivity, specificity, and positive/negative predictive values for the different measures. The study will be conducted over a two-year period.Clinical and healthcare significance: The high costs and poor patient outcomes associated with unrecognized PD point to a need for improvements in screening and intervention for this population. An effective screening method will increase identification of PD patients who can then be referred to appropriate psychiatric interventions, thereby reducing unnecessary ED visits, investigations, and hospitalizations.
kw: Panic disorder, Emergency Department, Screening

title: Improving physical and psychological symptoms in inpatients with acute myocardial infarction through the symptom self-management programme: A pilot randomized controlled trial.
abs: Specific Aims: To develop and evaluate the symptom self-management programme that can help patients with acute myocardial infarction (AMI) self-manage their physical and psychological symptoms. Hypotheses: 1) Comparing with the symptom self-management programme delivered through a face-to-face method (IManage-FF) and standard care, participants who attend the symptom self-management programme delivered through virtual reality device (IManage-VR) will report significantly:- lower levels of chest pain, stress, anxiety, depression, the number of re-hospitalization and emergency visit, and health care cost, and - greater levels of perceived relaxation and cardiac self-efficacy 2) Participants in the IManage-VR, IManage-FF, and control groups will identify strengths, weaknesses, usefulness, areas for improvement, and undesirable effects of the programmes. Methodology: This study will use randomized, single-blinded, controlled trial. A convenience sample of 90 will be recruited. Eligible participants will be adults patients with AMI hospitalized at a tertiary hospital in Singapore. Participants will be randomly assigned to one of the three groups: IManage-VR plus standard care (n=30), IManage-FF plus standard care (n=30), and standard care alone (n=30). Data will be collected by self-reported questionnaires, physiological measures, and open-ended questions. Quantitative data will be analysed by descriptive statistics, T-Test, and repeated measures analyses of variance and open-ended questions will analysed by content analysis. Significance of this study: This study will identify a potentially effective and cost-effective symptom self-management programme for patients with AMI. If the effectiveness has been shown, the programme can be integrated into hospital services to improve patient care. A new teaching method (virtual reality-based teaching) and new teaching materials (Virtual reality VCDs and Audio Relaxation CDs) derived from this study can be offered to patients. Future research (i.e., RCT) with larger samples and multi-centres can be undertaken to further test the interventions.

title: A Randomized Controlled Trial to Increase Glaucoma Medication Adherence using Value Pricing
abs: By reducing intraocular pressure, glaucoma topical eye medications are effective at controlling disease progression for the majority of patients. Yet evidence shows that many glaucoma patients have incomplete adherence to medications, resulting in significant personal costs in terms of disease progression and visual field loss. The cost to the health system from poor adherence is also substantial as glaucoma surgery is more costly than treatment with topical medication. Behavioural economics theory suggests that adherence rates can be improved by providing a clearer link between non-adherence and the resulting costs thereof. In the proposed study, this link is made by granting subsidies to adherent patients for their medications and physician visits, whereas those who are not sufficiently adherent would not receive the subsidy and thus pay a higher rate for their treatment. These subsidies provide a financial incentive for patients to take their medicines as prescribed, and because prescription refills and visits occur regularly, also provide a tangible and near-term cost resulting from non-adherence. We refer to this approach as value pricing as subsidies are allocated to medications that have not only been shown to be clinically effective but that are also effectively used by the patient. In efforts to increase adherence among glaucoma patients in Singapore, we propose to conduct a 6-month proof-of-concept randomized controlled trial among 150 participants from the Singapore National Eye Centre (SNEC) to test the extent to which value pricing can improve medication adherence. As Singapore’s population continues to age and a larger share of the population requires daily medications to treat chronic diseases, such innovative solutions are needed to ensure not only that patients take their medications as prescribed and receive the full benefit of their treatment but also that Government subsidies are allocated effectively so that to ensure the sustainability of the health system.
kw: glaucoma, behavioral economics, medicine adherence, cost-effectiveness, value pricing

title: Developing tools for risk assessment of bat-borne viruses in bats in Singapore
abs: A majority of outbreak responses to EIDs are reactionary, which tend to be costlier than proactive responses. Until we understand how pathogens emerge and spread, our approaches will always be behind the epidemic curve. Rapid ascertainment of circulating viruses and host exposure will greatly facilitate surveillance and prevention programs. Furthermore, these findings could also improve our ability to identify potential zoonotic viruses by targeted surveillance, and better prepare for the possible emergence of novel pathogens. The involvement of bats in the maintenance and transmission of several medically important viruses is well established. The continued marginalization of native ecosystems and encroachment of human habitats has increased interactions between humans and bats, increasing the likelihood of virus spillover, seen with both Nipah and Melaka viruses. In order to asses the diversity of viruses, and the risk they pose, circulating in bats in Singapore we propose developing a novel MassTag PCR diagnostic for bat-borne viruses, establishing existing bat cell lines and creating new lines from species endemic to Singapore, and assisting in the testing of a novel serological assay currently under development. The characterization of virus sequences from multiple virus families detected with these assays will help fill the gaps in evolutionary history, which in turn will assist in understanding virus natural ecology and the potential for cross-species transmission. Additionally, this study will help frame future questions regarding virus dynamics over time and help establishing the role of specific bat species as virus reservoirs. This project will aid in protecting human health through active surveillance, outbreak detection, and molecular epidemiology by providing a robust diagnostic panel for bat-borne viruses.
kw: Bat-borne pathogens, diagnostic development

title: Determining the repertoire of MMSET-interacting proteins in cancer cells by quantitative proteomic analysis
abs: MMSET (WHSC1/NSD2) gene is expressed ubiquitously in early development. Recent studies showed that MMSET is highly expressed in a large number of different types of tumors. Furthermore, MMSET mRNA levels are associated with tumor aggressiveness or prognosis in several of these tumors. MMSET is a SET domain-containing histone methyltransferase. It has been proposed to generate numerous different histone marks, including of H3 at lysines K4 (H3K4Me2), K27 (H3K27Me1/Me2/Me3) and K36 (H3K36Me1/Me2/Me3), H4 at lysine 20 (H4K20Me1/Me2/Me3). Although recent data have shown that MMSET expression is essential for growth of t(4;14) MM cells in vitro and in vivo, the detailed molecular mechanism or signaling pathways describing how deregulation of MMSET contributes to cancer cell growth and survival is still uncertain. A preliminary step in understanding protein structure and function is to determine which proteins interact with each other, thereby identifying the relevant biological pathways. In this study, we will use quantitative immunoprecipitation combined with knockdown (QUICK) methodology to determine the repertoire of MMSET-interacting proteins in cancer cells. In QUICK, the stable isotopic amino acids in cell culture labeling (SILAC) approach is used to differentially label proteins in two cell populations. Then the differentially labeled proteins in the immunoprecipitation are identified by mass spectrometry. MMSET interactor network will be extracted from the STRING database based on the identified interacting proteins. The high potential MMSET-interacting proteins will be selected for verification by immunoprecipitation assay. Then we will knock down MMSET interacting protein expression with shRNAs to test biological significance of the interactors in cancer cells. Information about these protein-protein interactions (PPIs) will improve understanding MMSET functions in cancers. Furthermore, currently there are no drugs targeting MMSET proteins directly. PPIs that will emerge from this study are expected to reveal a multitude of targets for novel therapeutics in cancers overexpressing MMSET.
kw: MMSET, Cancer, Proteomics, interacting proteins

title: Development of Tissue Engineered Bone as a Model for the Study of Cancer Metastasis
abs: Metastasis, as seen in late stage cancers, often develop as secondary tumours in the bone, leading to significant issues, including pain, aberrant skeletal remodeling and cancer remission following treatment. Prostate cancer, in particular shows almost exclusive tropism to bony tissue, where reciprocal interaction between the cancer and bone cells result in extensive skeletal remodeling and tumour growth. Current experimental models to study bone metastasis are limited by lack of human bone models, difficulties in monitoring cancer progression and / or inability to recapitulate extravasation. We have previously demonstrated the generation of human tissue engineered bone (TEB) with high osteogenicity and vascularity, when implanted subcutaneously in a rat model. We hypothesize that a novel nude-rat humanized TEB model will recapitulate the events of tumor cell extravasation, colonisation and skeletal remodeling in bone metastasis. Specifically, we aim to:1./ Develop TEB with an osteogenic gene reporter system as a reproducible and representative of human prostate cancer metastasis, and compared to the existing bone chip model in a nude rat2./ Examine homing and function of CaP cells to the tissue engineered human bone microenvironment using luciferase expressing cells in the above in vivo model, correlated with osteogenic reporter lines and microCT imaging.We will utilise multimodal imaging techniques to track and evaluate the cellular and molecular events of CaP metastasis to human bone, and correlate this to skeletal remodeling and changes in mineral composition. The development of this model will provide the basis for developing strategies to prevent or diminish their occurrence and associated complications. Additionally, this model may be useful for reclinical drug testing applications.

title: Fat Hope- Innovative Strategy Towards Small Molecule Probe of FTO as Potential Treatment for Obesity
abs: Obesity is one of the world’s most serious health problems. It predisposes the individual to serious co-morbidities, and imposing a crushing burden on healthcare. Currently, there is no safe and effective treatment for the disease. A series of landmark studies have identified FTO (fat mass and obesity associated) gene to be strongly linked with an increase risk of obesity. Importantly, inactivation of FTO protein was found to protect against obesity, hence suggesting that FTO inhibition may be a promising, novel therapeutic strategy for obesity. Before any therapeutic targeting of FTO can be considered, the mechanistic link between FTO and obesity needs to be clarified. This research seeks to explore whether FTO is a probable therapeutic target for obesity, through the discovery of chemical probes of FTO. To date, there is no report of selective inhibitor for FTO. However, our recent studies has shown that AlkB and, by inference, the structurally related FTO is amenable to small molecule inhibition. High-throughput screen of an in-house library of compounds later identified several compounds as potential FTO inhibitors. In the proposed research, we will apply an innovative drug discovery platform that we have developed, called Dynamic Combinatorial Mass-Spectrometry (DCMS), to the rapid identification of FTO probes. These probes will be analysed through a combination of biophysical, biochemical, protein crystallographic, computational and cell-based methods. The proposed approach takes advantage of our promising preliminary results our well-established experience and competency in all the above methodologies. It is expected to lead to potent and selective FTO probe, which will enable us to explore the functional link between FTO and obesity, hence providing valuable insights into the pathogenesis of obesity. They could also pave the way for novel anti-obesity drugs, in keeping with our larger vision to translate this research into promising treatment for obesity.

title: Understanding the role of XAF1 during developmental apoptosis of the sympathetic nervous system and its implication in the suppression of neural crest-derived tumors
abs: Developmental apoptosis of neuronal precursors is crucial in determining the final number of terminally differentiated cells. During development of the neural crest, cells undergo apoptosis as growth factors such as Nerve Growth Factor (NGF) becomes limiting. Abnormal NGF signaling leading to aberrant developmental apoptosis is implicated in pediatric nervous system tumors. Several genes act upon a developmental apoptotic pathway that is activated when NGF becomes limiting, which requires KIF1B?. KIF1B? is necessary and sufficient for neuronal apoptosis during NGF withdrawal. KIF1B? maps to 1p36.22, a region that is frequently deleted in neural crest-derived tumors including neuroblastoma and melanoma. Recently, we identified a transcriptional pathway for KIF1B?-induced apoptosis during NGF withdrawal and in neuroblastoma, which requires KIF1B?-mediated nuclear translocation and accumulation of RNA helicase A (DHX9), leading to the transcription of apoptotic target gene XAF1 (XIAP-associated factor 1). XAF1 antagonizes the anti-caspase activity of XIAP and other IAPs, and degrades Survivin, a key negative prognostic marker of neuroblastoma. XAF1 has been described as a potential tumor suppressor through its ability to overcome apoptotic resistance in tumor cells. More importantly, we observed KIF1B?/DHX9-dependent up-regulation of XAF1 in neuroblastoma cells and upon NGF withdrawal in differentiated PC12 cells. Knockdown of XAF1 is able to protect neuroblastoma cells from KIF1B? whereas over-expression of XAF1 is sufficient to induce apoptosis to similar extent as KIF1B? in neuroblastoma and melanoma cells. Furthering these findings, this project aims to validate XAF1 role during developmental apoptosis of the mouse sympathetic nervous system upon competition for NGF and evaluate its potential as a bonafide tumor suppressor in neuroblastoma and melanoma using cell lines, mouse xenografts and analysis of patient samples, with the long-term aim of developing compounds that could mimic XAF1 or turn on its expression in patients with tumors that lack XAF1 or defective in KIF1B? signaling pathway.
kw: Neural crest, Neuroblastoma, Developmental apoptosis, Tumor suppressor, XAF1, KIF1B?

title: Antigenic characterization of pandemic H1N1/2009 influenza viruses using novel monoclonal antibodies: Insights into influenza antigenic drift in tropical countries
abs: Influenza A is a major respiratory infection of humans that causes annual seasonal epidemics in the winters of Northern and Southern temperate regions while more variable seasonal patterns are observed in tropical and subtropical zones. Two hypotheses of influenza epidemics have been proposed. The source-sink model suggests that influenza viruses persist year-round in the tropics (the source) where it seeds annual temperate epidemics (the sink). The alternative meta-population model posits that influenza virus persists through migration of spatially separated populations consisting of a series of temporally overlapping epidemics, with global transmission occurring between large flight-connected cities. The source-sink model therefore predicts that influenza viruses in the tropics will exhibit higher diversity compared to temperate epidemics, while the meta-population model predicts that influenza virus populations across global centers are connected thereby resulting in a stochastic distribution of influenza virus genetic and antigenic diversity. Furthermore, if the source-sink model is correct, vaccination targeting source populations offers the hope of controlling influenza, while the meta-population model suggests region-specific strategies are needed. While these models have been tested using genetic data, little is known about the fine-scale antigenic evolution of influenza viruses in tropical regions. Influenza antigenic evolution is typically measured with hemagglutinin inhibition assays using polyclonal animal antisera. More accurate evaluation can be assessed by monoclonal antibodies, of which only limited numbers are produced. Here we propose to develop tools to test whether pandemic H1N1 (pH1N1) influenza viruses in Singapore exhibit higher antigenic diversity than viruses from temperate epidemics. This project will provide crucial information for understanding the antigenic evolution of influenza viruses and has important implications for vaccination strategy.The specific aims of this project are:(1) To generate novel monoclonal antibodies against the hemagglutinin gene of pH1N1 viruses for the characterization of influenza antigenic diversity.(2) To test the source-sink and meta-population models by quantifying relative rates of antigenic variation of pH1N1 influenza viruses in Singapore.
kw: antigenic variation, monoclonal antibody, influenza virus, pandemic, H1N1, hemagglutinin gene

title: Elucidating the novel role of MAO-B in LRRK2-induced parkinsonism through the use of MAOU1 - a new generation MAO-B-specific probe
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Although the mechanism underlying selective dopaminergic neuronal death in Parkinson’s disease (PD) remains to be fully elucidated, the neurotransmitter dopamine itself is thought to be a key culprit because of its ability to generate reactive oxygen species (ROS) after oxidative deamination by monoamine oxidases (MAO), particularly MAO-B. The resultant production of ROS can contribute to progressive redox imbalance, eventually leading to neuronal demise. Notably, MAO-B expression increases with age and its activity is particularly enhanced in affected regions of the PD brain, suggesting that increased MAO-B levels can promote disease pathogenesis. Intuitively, one would propose that MAO-B inhibition could produce beneficial outcomes. Indeed, this is precisely the mechanism underlying the action of rasagiline, a recently available PD drug. Given the important relationship between MAO-B and PD, there is significant interest in the development of sensitive methods to monitor its activity. Here, we have developed a unique MAO-B probe that is not only highly specific but allow visualization cellular MAO-B-associated events in great detail via 2-photon detection. In parallel, we have made a novel discovery that PD-associated LRRK2 mutations significantly enhance MAO-B expression/activity. Accordingly, the proposal seeks to: 1) characterize the utility of our MAO-B-specific probe in detecting MAO-B expression/activity changes in various PD models, including patient-derived samples and 2) exploit the MAO-B-specific probe in understanding the novel relationship between LRRK2 and MAO-B. We will address these questions by means of different model systems, including Drosophila, primary mouse neuronal cultures and iPS-derived human dopaminergic neurons from control and PD individuals. Clearly, the outcomes of the characterization of our in-house developed probe holds promise for its future use as a preclinical or diagnostic biomarker for PD. Moreover, the clarification of the role of MAO-B in LRRK2-associated neurotoxicity also promises to shed novel insights into the mechanisms underlying PD pathogenesis.
kw: Parkinson's Disease, LRRK2, Monoamine Oxidase, Neurodegeneration, Oxidative Stress

title: Targeting Hepatic Cancer Stem Cells with Nanotechnology
abs: Primary liver cancer is a particularly deadly disease as the third deadliest cancer in the world with the highest incidence occurring in Asia. Determining the key fundamental mechanisms of hepatic cancer initiation is important to developing better therapeutic options. Recently, populations of cells, identified as cancer stem cells (CSCs), have been demonstrated to be required for cancer initiation and progression in multiple hepatic cancer models. CSCs appear to share properties of self-renewal and differentiation with normal stem cells as well as have other characteristics such as chemoresistance. Hepatic CSCs have been previously identified by a number of different external and internal markers in hepatic cancer cell lines and primary human hepatic tumor samples. Preliminary work in our laboratory, however, suggests that specific oncogenes may determine the identifiable characteristics of hepatic CSCs. These oncogenes may also mediate different mechanisms of CSC formation and maintenance that can be exploited when developing therapeutics. In this project, we will utilize oncogene-specific hepatic tumor mouse models to identify hepatic CSC markers that associate with specific oncogenes, as well as the key mechanisms by which MYC drives CSC formation. A major goal of this project is to develop better cancer treatment options through the development of CSC-specific imaging and therapeutic reagents. As such, we will also develop a CSC-targeted nanodiamond drug-delivery platform for the diagnostics and treatment of oncogene-specific hepatic cancers. Previous work in our laboratory has shown that nanodiamonds can be potent drug-delivery reagents to enhance the efficacy of existing drugs while lowering their systemic drug toxicity. The work proposed here should provide the basis of a fundamental understanding of the mechanisms behind hepatic CSC mediated tumorigenesis as well as the development of a personalized nanomedical approach to treating hepatic cancer based on the targeting of oncogene-specific hepatic CSCs.
kw: Hepatic Cancer, Nanotechnology, Drug Delivery, Cancer Stem Cells

title: The integration of nutrient-sensing network and autophagy in exercise-induced skeletal muscle adaptations
abs: The benefits of exercise for the prevention and improvement of metabolic diseases are well-recognized. Exercise-induced adaptations such as enhanced skeletal muscle glucose uptake and oxidative metabolism are associated with amelioration of type 2 diabetes and obesity. The capacity of skeletal muscle to sense the metabolic changes during exercise and to induce the corresponding adaptations is critical for exercise-induced adaptations. However, the cellular events that drive these exercise benefits are largely unknown. Skeletal muscle AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK, an energy-sensor) and autophagy (a lysosome-mediated degradation of cellular components) are activated in response to exercise. In this proposal, we hypothesize that AMPK and autophagy are critical for skeletal muscle metabolism, and they are critical for exercise-mediated adaptations. The specific aims are: (1) to evaluate the role of AMPK and autophagy in amino acids balance of myotubes, and (2) to study the role of AMPK in exercise-induced skeletal muscle autophagy in vivo.For aim 1, C2C12 myotubes will be utilized as an in vitro model to assess the role of AMPK and autophagy in amino acids and energy homeostasis. The myotubes will be subjected to various metabolic stress conditions to activate AMPK and autophagy, and the ensued metabolic adaptations will be determined. The specific role of AMPK and autophagy will be assessed by transfection of a dominant-negative form of AMPK and pharmacological inhibition of autophagy. For aim 2, AMPK?2 knockout and control mice will be subjected to acute or long-term exercise training to determine the role of AMPK in exercise-induced skeletal muscle autophagy. The role of autophagy in exercise-mediated adaptations will be characterized by subjecting the mice to exercise in the presence or absence of pharmacological inhibition of autophagy. Exercise adaptations in the mouse models including glucose tolerance, mitochondria biogenesis and oxidative metabolism will be determined.
kw: AMP-activated protein kinase, autophagy, exercise, skeletal muscle, metabolism

title: Dental and oral - systemic cell differentiation potential of induced pluripotent stem cell from oral sources
abs: The differentiation of systemic osteoblast and oral odontoblast from induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSC) of oral tissue can allow the development of human specific oral and systemic diseases models such as periodontitis, osteoporosis and osteoarthritis. The objective is to reprogram human oral epithelial cells (OE) and dental pulp stem cells (DPSC) into iPSC and test their potential toward osteogenic and odontoblastic differentiation. The hypothesis to be tested is that OE and DPSC can be reprogrammed into IPSC and differentiate into osteoblast (in vitro) and odontoblast (in vitro and in vivo). OE and DPSC will be reprogrammed according to the Protocol of Ohnuki et al. and tested for embryoid body formation and in vivo differentiation. iPSC from OE (OE-iPSC) and DPSC (DP-iPSC) will be induced for osteoblastic and osteogenic differentiation using induction medium. Differentiation will be investigated using RT-PCR for osteoblast and odontoblastic differentiation markers after 0, 3 and 7 days. Alkaline phosphatase, Von Kossa and Alizarin R staining will be carried out to investigate mineralization processes. Odontoblastic differentiation will be further investigated using tooth slice model. OE, DPSC, OE-iPSC and DP-iPSC will be mixed with PLLA scaffold within dentin slice and kept in minimum essential medium for 28 days. Proliferation assay using WST-1 reagent and RT-PCR for odontoblastic differentiation will be performed every 7 days. To evaluate the ability of cells to differentiate towards odontoblast and form a human dental pulp in vivo, cells will be seeded in the dentin disks and implanted in the subcutaneous tissue dorsum of immunodeficient mice for 28 days. After 14 and 28 days from implantation the implants will be retrieved. RT-PCR will be performed for odontoblastic differentiation. Histological and immunohistochemestry (Factor VIII, PCNA and TUNEL) analysis will be performed. New dentin deposition will be assessed by tetracycline staining.
kw: Induced pluripotent stem cell, osteoblast, odontoblast, oral epithelial cells

title: Prospective study on the utility of 18F-Fluorocholine PET/CT in documenting metabolic response to y90 and Sorafenib therapy in locally advanced hepatocellular carcinoma
abs: AimsTo evaluate if there is a correlation between changes in tumoural size and/or enhancement with the metabolic activity (detected on 18F-Fluorocholine PET/CT) of hepatocellular carcinomas (HCC). Secondly, to evaluate if this change in metabolic activity is a better assessment of response to treatment of HCC in terms of overall survival and progression-free survival.HypothesesPrimary Hypothesis ():There is no correlation between change in HCC tumor metabolic activity (18F-Fluorocholine PET/CT) and reduction in viable or vascularized tumour burden (mRECIST criteria). Secondary Hypotheses ():1. There is no correlation between change in HCC metabolic activity and percent change in tumour size (RECIST criteria). 2. Change in HCC tumor metabolic activity in response to HCC treatment is not a predictor of overall survival (OS) or progression-free survival (PFS).MethodologyAt the pre-treatment stage, patients will undergo a supplementary 18F-fluorocholine PET/CT scan in addition to the dynamic CT/MRI scan that will be performed as part of the SirveNIB trial. Data from this stage will determine what percentage of HCC tumours detected on dynamic CT/MRI scans also display positivity on the PET/CT scan. Patients who have a lesion that is positive on PET/CT and also displays classical imaging features of HCC on dynamic CT/MRI will be recruited into the study. Patients will have two further 18F-fluorocholine PET/CT scans, at 12 and 24 weeks post-treatment. The percent change in SUV of the radiotracer for the lesion under study will be compared with the percent change in the size of its enhanced areas (as per mRECIST criteria). This will enable an assessment of the correlation between the two. The percentage change in SUV will also be compared against the overall survival and progression-free survival to see if it is a predictor of survival.
kw: Fluorocholine, y90 therapy, sorafenib, hepatocellular carcinoma

title: Computer-assisted quantification of intracranial collateral flow in acute ischemic stroke
abs: Aims- To develop a model for computer-assisted quantification of collateral flow patterns in acute ischemic stroke (AIS).Hypothesis- It is generally accepted that good collateral circulation leads to a larger area of salvageable ischemic penumbra and better outcomes whereas poor collaterals often lead to worse outcomes and higher risk of hemorrhage. However, due to the tortuosity and variability of the collaterals seen in CT-A, it is difficult to differentiate between ‘good’ and the ‘poor’ intracranial collaterals. Currently employed methods for the assessment of collaterals are indirect, arbitrary, qualitative and highly observer dependent. A computer-based automated software would be able to quantify the collateral patterns and help in prognostication as well as therapeutic decision making in the early phase in AIS.Methods- AIS patients treated with intravenous thrombolysis with tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) undergo CT-A before initiating the treatment. Most of the patients at our institution are evaluated for the arterial patency by CT-A on day 2. AIS patients with pre-tPA as well as follow up CT-A on day 2 would be included in this study. We seek to develop a computer-based stroke analysis software to analyse and quantify the CT-A images using medical image analysis method and build a 3-dimensional view of the collateral circulation. This model would evaluate the temporal behaviour of intracranial collaterals, evaluate the side-to-side difference as well as quantify the collaterals (volume and intensity) for an objective measurement of the individual cerebral hemispheres. Significance-Our computer based model would enable us to define various profiles like ‘good’, ‘poor’, and ‘failed’ intracranial collateral flow patterns. Our model would aid in predicting the functional outcomes as well as decision making for appropriate therapeutic measures during the early phase of AIS. It would enable us to ultimately improve patient selection for treatment with improved outcomes and reduce complications and mortality.
kw: intracranial collaterals, computer-assisted assessment, ischemic stroke, quantification

title: Antibiotics for Klebsiella Liver Abscess (A-KLASS)
abs: Background: Klebsiella pneumoniae liver abscess (KLA) is the most common etiology of liver abscess in Singapore and its incidence is increasing worldwide. Appropriate management includes prolonged intravenous antibiotic therapy but there are no practice guidelines addressing the efficacy of early step-down to oral antibiotics. Aim: Our primary aim is to compare the efficacy of 4 weeks of intravenous antibiotics to early step-down to oral antibiotics in patients with KLA.Hypothesis: The hypothesis for our trial is that the degree of inferiority of our intervention (early step-down to oral antibiotics) to our active control (continued intravenous antibiotics) is no greater than 10%.Methods: Multi-centre randomised open-label active comparator-controlled non-inferiority trial. Clinical Significance: Our results would help inform local and international practice guidelines regarding the optimal antibiotic management of KLA. A finding on non-inferiority may translate to the wider adoption of a more cost-effective strategy that reduces hospital length of stay and improves patient-centered outcomes and satisfaction.
kw: klebsiella, live abscess, antibiotic therapy

title: Pharmacogenomics of Cisplatin-Induced Deafness in Singaporean Patients with Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma
abs: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) is one of the most common forms of cancer in Singapore, and is treated with a combination of radiation therapy and cisplatin-based chemotherapy. While overall survival rates are very good, many patients suffer from permanent hearing loss as a consequence of their treatment which is due to effects of the tumor itself, damaging effects of radiation, and importantly, ototoxicity of cisplatin. Severe hearing loss occurs commonly in patients treated with cisplatin plus radiation, but few patients treated with radiation alone, suggesting that this is predominantly attributable to cisplatin. Very recently, genetic variants in two genes, TPMT and COMT, were identified as being key markers for cisplatin-induced hearing loss in children, but the role of these variants has not been investigated in adult populations or in patients with NPC. The major hypothesis of this proposal is that specific genetic variants will be highly associated with and predictive of cisplatin-induced deafness in NPC patients in Singapore. We will perform genetic studies in two populations of patients with NPC: patients with a new diagnosis of NPC invited to participate at the time of their initial assessment at NUH and a retrospective cohort of patients. A blood sample will be collected for DNA isolation. Patients will undergo serial hearing tests before and after treatment. All patients will be genotyped for ~4500 DNA variants known to impact drug metabolism, with allele frequencies compared between cases (severe hearing loss) and controls (normal hearing). Ultimately these studies are aimed at identifying important genetic biomarkers that predict hearing loss in response to treatment for NPC. The availability of such a predictive test would allow identification of patients at highest risk for this toxicity, thus enabling appropriate counseling, monitoring, otoprotectant use or dose-modification to make treatment safer and more efficacious.
kw: Genetics, pharmacogenomics, cancer, deafness

title: Is ciliary dysfunction a feature of the frequent-exacerbation phenotype of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD)?
abs: Background: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD), the most common chronic respiratory condition in adults, is characterized by progressive airflow limitation and airway inflammation. A subgroup of COPD patients suffer from frequent exacerbations, which is associated with increased morbidity, mortality and high economic and social burden. COPD exacerbations are mostly triggered by infections. In health, the efficacy of mucociliary clearance provided by the ciliated epithelium that lines the respiratory tract, protects the lungs from infections. Therefore, the frequent exacerbation phenotype of COPD patients might be associated with impaired mucociliary clearance due to impaired ciliary function, resulting in airway bacterial colonisation and increased risk of infections.The primary hypothesis is that there is ciliary dysfunction in COPD patients with the frequent-exacerbation phenotype, compared to those with infrequent-exacerbation phenotype and healthy controls. Aim: To determine if COPD patients with the frequent-exacerbation phenotype have ciliary dysfunction (in terms of reduced ciliary beat frequency and increased dyskinesia [abnormal beat pattern]), compared to those with infrequent-exacerbation phenotype and healthy controls. Methods: In this cross sectional study, 24 subjects with COPD (12 with frequent and 12 with infrequent exacerbations) and 12 healthy subjects will be recruited. The subject’s phenotype will be characterised using clinical details, imaging and lung function tests. Ciliated epithelium obtained by bronchoscopic bronchial brushing will be studied using high speed digital videomicroscopy, to assess ciliary function. As exploratory studies, bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) will be obtained for extensive microbiological investigations to study the relationship between ciliary function and airway microbial colonisation. Cytokines, chemokines, growth factors and proteases profile in the BAL will be measured, to study its relationship to ciliary function.Implications: The results of this study may help us understand the role of ciliary dysfunction in the pathogenesis of frequent-exacerbation phenotype of COPD, and thereby offer potential novel therapeutic targets and provoke further research.
kw: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease, COPD, Cilia, Respiratory epithelium, COPD exacerbation, Respiratory

title: Prospective study of UDP-gluconoryltransferase (UGT) 2B17 and other exemestane pathway genetic polymorphisms as predictive biomarkers of exemestane pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics in Asian women with hormone receptor-positive advanced breast cancer
abs: Exemestane is one of three widely used aromatase inhibitors (AIs) in the endocrine treatment of hormone receptor-positive advanced breast cancer. To date, there are no predictive biomarkers of AI efficacy and tolerability and the challenge of prioritizing endocrine therapy for individual patients still remains. We aim to conduct a prospective biomarker study to identify predictors of exemestane pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics, focusing on the pharmacogenetics of UGT2B17 (a metabolizing enzyme), and including a comprehensive analysis of other exemestane pathway target and metabolizing enzymes. The UGT2B17*2/*2 deletion genotype has been selected as the gene variant of interest because it is associated with markedly reduced in-vitro glucuronidation of the active metabolite, 17-dihydroexemestane, and is seven times more common in Asians than Caucasians (60-70% vs less than 10%). While we have recently demonstrated that this genotype correlated with improved clinical outcomes in Asian breast cancer patients receiving vorinostat (a UGT2B17 substrate), in-vivo studies of exemestane are lacking.We propose a prospective clinical study of exemestane in a cohort of Asian advanced breast cancer patients, with pre-specified analysis according to UGT2B17 genotype and a target accrual of 110 patients. Genotype will be correlated with exemestane clinical benefit rate, pharmacokinetics, musculoskeletal toxicities, progression-free and overall survival. Secondary biomarker endpoints include a comprehensive interrogation of other exemestane pathway gene variants for potential biomarkers of exemestane pharmacokinetics/ pharmacodynamics, as well as the development of a population pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic model as the potential basis of genotype-guided dosing. This study also aims to delineate the in-vivo metabolism of exemestane, which is currently ill-defined. If our hypothesis is proven, the practical implications include the genotype-guided selection of exemestane as frontline therapy over the other AIs as well as exploration of genotype-based exemestane dosing in future studies.
kw: Breast cancer, pharmacogenetics, UGT2B17, aromatase inhibitors, exemestane

title: The Use of Umbilical Cord Derived Cells To Enhance Wound Healing in Burns
abs: Aim: Our primary objective is to demonstrate the wound-healing efficacy of a novel bi-layered skin substitute developed from umbilical cord lining-derived epithelial (CLEC) and mesenchymal cells (CLMC) in a porcine excisional wound model. Our secondary objective is to study the use of CLMC when transfused as an adjunct therapy in the same wound model.Hypothesis:1. A novel bi-layered skin substitute developed from umbilical cord lining cell lineages may function as an effective transplantable skin allograft.2. Systemic infusion of cord-derived mesenchymal cells may serve as an effective adjunct therapy for wound healing in patients with massive burn injuriesBackground: The healing of extensive wounds in massive burn injuries remains a challenging clinical problem. There is a lack of available autologous, resulting in wound sepsis from chronic wound exposure. The extensive wounds and the increased metabolic demands for skin healing also increases the demands for marrow-derived cells, leading to marrow exhaustion. Many types of synthetic or biological skin substitutes are available for temporary cover. Fresh cadaveric allografts are considered the gold standard but their use is severely impeded by their inadequate availability and rejection. Therefore, patients have to undergo multiple operations to replace cadaveric grafts. Considerable progress has been made in the culture of human keratinocytes but this process requires at least 3–4 weeks. Therefore, there is a need to develop a durable immunopriviledged and transplantable allotypic skin substitute that can be applied immediately after early excision of the burn wounds.Methods:Human umbilical cord derived epithelial and mesenchymal cells will be co-cultured to produce a novel bi-layered skin substitute which will be evaluated in a porcine excisional wound model and compared against human cadaveric allografts. The use of CLMCs as an infusional adjunct therapy in wound healing in burns will also be studied concurrently.
kw: Umbilical Cord Derived Mesenchymal Stem Cells, Cord Lining Epithelial Cells, Burns

title: Fronto-extracephalic transcranial direct current stimulation for depression: a pilot study
abs: This study aims to determine whether fronto-extracephalic tDCS would reduce depression symptom severity scores more than bifrontal tDCS in patients with major depressive disorder. We hypothesise this stimulation technique may have greater efficacy in reducing the severity of depressive symptoms compared to the bifrontal stimulation technique, as deeper dysfunctional brain circuits could be stimulated. In this double-blind, parallel-group study, participants with major depressive disorder will be randomized into either the fronto-extracephalic or bifrontal tDCS group. Participants will receive active tDCS treatment for 20 sessions conducted on consecutive weekdays over 4 weeks. Participants, who continue to improve at the end of 4 weeks, will be offered a further 2- week extension using the same treatment. The primary outcome measure will be the change in Montgomery Asberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS) scores. Observer ratings will be conducted at baseline, after treatment sessions 10 and 20, and at 1 week, 1 month and 3 months after the end of treatment. Self-ratings will be done at baseline, after treatment sessions 5, 10, 15 and 20, and at the 1 month and 3 month follow-ups. tDCS is emerging as an effective treatment for depression. This study will add to the existing knowledge base about tDCS. It is likely that research in this new technique will have meaningful translation into better clinical outcomes for patients. tDCS can potentially be developed into a user-friendly, cost-effective and portable device, providing treatment for depressed patients who may not benefit from other forms of treatment or have exhausted various treatment options. The delivery of healthcare may be significantly altered and improved as physical treatment for depression can be administered at home by patients using tDCS. Effective treatment will lead to better quality-of-life for affected patients and reduce healthcare costs associated with depression

title: Genetic and pharmacological intervention of mitochondrial impairment in Drosophila models of Parkinson’s disease
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Parkinson’s disease (PD) is the most common neurodegenerative movement disorder due the progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substania nigra compacta. Mitochondrial dysfunction is an important aetiological feature of PD. Consistent with this, in vivo studies using various genetic models reveal that dopaminergic (DA) neurons are highly susceptible to oxidative stress and also exhibit at least one form of mitochondrial dysfunction, such as impairment in fission/fusion, dysregulation in mitophagy or abnormal mitochondrial biogenesis. Although the mitochondria is an important target for the treatment of PD, little is known of how to protect DA neurons from mitochondrial insults. Thus it is of clinical importance to understand the mechanisms governing mitochondrial homeostasis so that we could develop mitochondrial-specific drugs as a new therapeutic strategy for PD. Previously, we had characterized two genetic models of PD, Parkin-deficient and LRRK2 G2019S transgenic flies, and found that they recapitulate the pathology of the human condition including DA neuronal loss, reduction in dopamine content and mitochondrial dysfunction. Therefore to further our findings, we aimed to (1) conduct a comprehensive study on how mitochondrial dynamics could affect dopaminergic neuronal survival and (2) exploit our established methods to screen for potential mitochondrial drugs that could mitigate PD-linked mitochondrial impairments. We had taken the initial steps to treat these mutant flies with drugs that stimulate genetic pathways that could either activate autophagy, fission or mitochondrial biogenesis. Our preliminary results demonstrate that these pathways are important for restoration of impaired mitochondria in our models, leading to improvement in survival of DA neurons. We anticipate that this study will inevitably be applicable in finding a treatment for PD.

title: Identifying genes associated with breast cancer susceptibility in an Asian population
abs: BACKGROUNDThe BRCA1, BRCA2 and other high-, moderate- or low- penetrance genes known to be associated with familial breast cancer, account for less than 50% of familial clustering of breast cancer, suggesting that additional genes remain to be discovered.HYPOTHESIS We hypothesize that rare variants exist in familial breast cancer which can be identified using next generation sequencing of families with a strong family history of breast cancer, but who are BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutation-negative.OVERALL AIMTo identify candidate genes associated with breast cancer susceptibility in Asian patients with familial breast cancer who are BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutation-negative.AIM 1: To perform exome sequencing on DNA from matched tumor and blood samples of familial breast cancer patients who are BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutation-negative. Our multi-disciplinary team has established a registry of breast cancer families with DNA specimens, and has experience in exome sequencing.AIM 2: To validate the sequence variants detected in Aim 1 by performing PCR and Sanger sequencing on the same samples, first-degree family members of the breast cancer patients and independent series of familial and early-onset breast cancer cases. In addition, we will also screen sporadic breast tumors and healthy controls.AIM 3: To perform functional analysis of the candidate genes. If the candidate gene is thought to have a tumor suppressor function, assays such as cell proliferation or wound healing assays in breast cancer cell lines with enforced expression of the candidate gene will be done. CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCEThe discovery of new candidate genes associated with susceptibility to breast cancer may have significant impact on disease screening and breast cancer management. In the long term, knowledge gained on the biology of these genes and their effect on breast cancer may result in the development of novel treatment strategies for breast cancer patients.
kw: Breast cancer, exome sequencing, rare variant discovery, cancer susceptibility, hereditary cancer

title: Elucidation of Stathmin-1’s anti-metastatic and chemosensitising effect on colorectal cancer
abs: Colorectal carcinoma (CRC) is the second leading cause of cancer deaths in the world. Locally, CRC is the most prevalent cancer, where metastatic spread accounts for deaths in 30-50% of CRC patients within 5 years. Due to unique circulatory pattern of the portal vein system, liver-specific metastasis of CRC is common, yet existing treatment options are largely ineffective against metastatic CRC. Hence it follows that lowering CRC mortality should involve inhibition of hepatic dissemination and chemosensitisation.Comparative proteome analysis of HCT116 colon carcinoma and its hepato-metastatic variant identified a prominent up-regulation of Stathmin-1 (STMN1) with metastasis. Clinical validation revealed that high STMN1 was predictive of poor prognosis, and stable over-expression of STMN1 also induced a strong metastatic phenotype in vitro. These evidence support a functional role for STMN1 in CRC metastasis, and raise the possibility of metastatic prevention by STMN1 silencing. Hence, the effect of STMN1 depletion was systematically evaluated by quantitative proteomics. Indeed, stable STMN1 silencing suppressed the expression of numerous metastatic proteins with simultaneous induction of metastatic inhibitors. Moreover, proteome changes following STMN1 silencing also recapitulated apoptotic sensitization, with reduction in apoptotic defense and up-regulations in apoptotic machinery including Caspase 6. Together, these evidence support further investigations into the mechanism of metastatic inhibition and chemosensitisation by STMN1 silencing. Herein, we aim to (i) assess the contribution of specific STMN1 phosphorylation(s) to metastatic induction, (ii) validate expression changes by MRM, (iii) determine if STMN1 silencing-induced changes are transcriptional, and (iv) visualise the strengthening of cell junctions after STMN1 knockdown. In addition, we also attempt to (v) investigate chemosensitising effect of STMN1 depletion, and (vi) test if STMN1 silencing can inhibit the EMT process in primary CRC cells. The outcome of these investigations could potentially establish STMN1 as a therapeutic target against CRC metastasis, and justify development of phospho-STMN1 inhibitors.
kw: Colorectal Cancer Metastasis, Stathmin-1, Phosphorylation, Proteomics, Chemosensitisation, Epithelial-mesenchymal Transition

title: In vivo histology by Micro-Optical Coherence Tomography (?OCT) for early detection of intraepithelial neoplasia in gastrointestinal tracts
abs: Colorectal, stomach, and esophageal cancer are the most diagnosed cancers in Singapore and worldwide. Missed diagnosis are common and the risk of complications after the endoscopic intervention is not negligible due to inability of the standard-of-care tools for obtaining histology-grade images of the gastrointestinal (GI) mucosa in situ and in vivo. The standard-of-care procedures are also costly and associated with complications, placing substantial burden to the patients and the healthcare system. Micro-Optical Coherence Tomography (?OCT) is a novel, clinically viable, endomicroscopic tool for visualizing biological tissue microstructures at the cellular and sub-cellular level. We hypothesize that ?OCT can capture many key morphological features of intraepithelial neoplasia with resolution equivalent to medium-power histology, and provide important diagnostic information complementary to existing clinical endoscopic tools. The goal of this proposal is to validate ?OCT as an in vivo histology tool for detection of intraepithelial neoplasia in animals. Towards this goal, we will construct a ?OCT transendoscopic imaging system suitable for clinical use (Aim 1), conduct ex vivo animal studies to validate the feasibility of µOCT for detection of early neoplastic changes (Aim 2), and validate the safety of the µOCT transendoscopic imaging device (Aim 3). The proposed research opens up an opportunity to alter the clinical practice for screening/surveillance, diagnosis, and treatment of cancers in GI tracts. µOCT endoscopy has the potential to change the paradigm of cancer screening/surveillance by implementing 3-dimensional histology in vivo. Morphological biomarkers of intraepithelial neoplasia established in this project may allow targeted removal of small polyps with neoplastic changes, and thereby, reduce risk of complications and attendant cost. The outcome of the project will also facilitate future clinical trials to determine the diagnostic yield. The results of this project may additionally be useful for other types of cancer and biomedical applications.
kw: Gastrointestinal cancer, Early detection, Micro-optical coherence tomography, In vivo histology, Endoscopy

title: Insights into the mechanisms and structure of the key coupling subunits ? and ? of the Mycobacterium tuberculosis F1FO ATP synthase, and their potential as novel TB drug target
abs: Tuberculosis is in focus of interest due to the emergence of multi- and extensive drug-resistant TB strains. The Mycobacterium tuberculosis F-ATP synthase is one of the essential enzymes in energy requirement of both proliferating aerobic and hypoxic dormant stage of mycobacterium life cycle. The MtF-ATP synthase, which does not show detectable ATP hydrolysis activity, consists of an FO domain with the subunits a:b:b’:c9-12 and an F1 part (?3:?3:?:?:?:). Subunit ? plays an important role in coupling, whereas subunit ? is also proposed to be responsible for the suppression of hydrolytic activity, preventing excess ATP consumption under low oxygen tensions. Stimulation of latent ATP hydrolysis activity would lead to depleted cellular ATP levels during dormancy and decrease the bacteria’s viability. In our effort to understand the biological role of this, we will (i) determine the NMR structure of M. tuberculosis subunit ? (MT?) using our recombinant MT?, (ii) to see the effect(s) of our generated and ATPase-active Mt?3:?3:?-complex in the presence of the proposed regulator MT? and its truncated forms, and (iii) to identify critical C-terminal residues of MT? in vivo. In addition, we described a key role of MT? and subunit c in the interaction of the TB drug candidate TMC207, which we aim to further understand in vivo. Furthermore, we revealed a low resolution structure of subunit ? of the MtF-ATP synthase and the unique loop of ?165-178, representing a novel TB drug target. We aim to determine the 3D structure of this subunit by NMR spectroscopy, which will be essential to describe the arrangement of the loop inside Mt?1-204 and its interaction with the H+-pumping c-ring. To assess the functional role of Mt?165-178 during catalysis, we mutagenize Mt? in the entire F-ATP synthase by deleting the loop or substitution specific residues, present in the loop of pathogenic forms.

title: Systematic Profiling of Benzodiazepines as Potential Bromodomain-Targeting Therapeutic Agents
abs: ?-N-acetylation of lysine residues (KAc) is one of the most frequently occurring posttranslational modifications in proteins associated with epigenetics. Lysine acetylation is abundant in macromolecular complexes that function in chromatin remodeling, DNA damage, and cell-cycle control. Regulation of the cellular histone acetylation is controlled by histone acetyltransferases, histone deacetylases and bromodomain (BRD)-containing proteins which bind to acetylated proteins via protein-protein interaction (PPI). There is growing evidence linking the dysfunction of BCPs with diseases including cancer and autoimmune/inflammatory diseases. BRDs therefore represent novel therapeutic targets. Two recent reports showed some benzodiazepine compounds are potent inhibitors of BRD4 (one of the 61 BRDs known in human). A lack of suitable high-throughput screening (HTS) platforms and strategically diversified benzodiazepines has however rendered it difficult to identify new inhibitors against other BRDs. In this proposal, we aim to (1) design and synthesize diverse chemical libraries based on the benzodiazepine pharmacophore; (2) develop a small molecule microarray (SMM) platform suitable for HTS of benzodiazepine-BRD interactions, and identification of potent and specific candidate hits for most human BRDs; (3) carry out cell-based proteome and expression profiling for identification of potential cellular targets of selected hits using the corresponding AfBP with quantitative proteomics; (4) perform small molecule bioimaging experiments with live cells/tissues to delineate the cellular uptake and subcellular distribution of selected compounds; and (5) validate selected candidate compounds and investigation of their potential biological/therapeutic implications in disease models (e.g. cancer). This proposal rides on the world-pioneering expertise of the PI in the application of SMM for discovery of small molecule PPI inhibitors as potential therapeutics for cancer and other diseases. It strives to make significant contributions to basic knowledge in chemical epigenetics, and will facilitate the translation of this knowledge into better health and economic outcomes for Singapore and elsewhere.
kw: Epigenetics, Bromodomain, cancer, Inhibitor, Protein-protein interaction, Chemical Biology

title: Do Maternal Anxiety, Depression, and Associated Parenting Practices Impact Infant Prefrontal Structure & Function?
abs: Poor maternal mood is prevalent, with far-reaching, adverse effects on parents and children. Unfortunately, however, until recently, the effects of antenatal and postnatal mood on very young children have been overlooked. Recent work has begun suggesting maternal mood contributes to infant prefrontal functioning, which is essential to cognitive and emotional regulation, therefore influencing optimal abilities at school age and adulthood. However, past research is “small-scale,” Western biased, and limited to comparisons of infants of mothers with versus without psychopathology, via non-task specific assessments. We propose a unique “large-scale” longitudinal study of continuously measured maternal depression and anxiety and prefrontal anatomy and function in the first three years of Asian infants’ life, utilizing developmentally appropriate in-depth neuroanatomical, neurocognitive, and parent-child assessments. Specifically, we willl explore the existing database of an on-going cohort study (Growing Up in Singapore towards Healthy Outcomes, GUSTO) to determine 1) the effects of antenatal maternal mood upon the prefrontal cortex (PFC) at multiple stages of infants’ early life, using multi-modal neuroimaging (MRI and event-related potential) and eye-tracking techniques; 2) the relation between current maternal mood and its past variability upon infants’ PFC development; 3) whether the parent-child relationship mediates the aforementioned postnatal associations. We expect that (1) maternal mood influences upon infants’ PFC can be seen at birth; (2) long-lasting poor postnatal maternal mood can further impair infants’ PFC in early life; (3) the parent-child relationship will mediate postnatal relations.We expect this methodologically rigorous prospective large-scale study will greatly advance our understanding of individual differences in early life development of a brain region essential to cognitive and emotional regulation. By repeatedly measuring mothers, infants, and their interactions with one another during early stages of life, we will be well positioned to assist clinicians deciding upon when (e.g., antenatally) and how (e.g., via parenting interventions) to intervene.
kw: maternal anxiety, maternal depression, structural magnetic resonance imaging, diffusion tensor imaging, event-related potential, mother and child interaction

title: Synapses in recession: Investigation of a new phase of long-term memory through synaptic competition and its relevance for Alzheimer’s disease
abs: How consolidated memories in a neural network erases with time is a central question in neuroscience. Memory loss such as in dementia or in neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a major concern in elderly populations and needs immediate attention in Singapore. Intensive research is going on in various disciplines to address the causes of age related memory loss but less attention has been paid for the causes of impairment of long-term memory consolidation at the neural network level. By using synaptic tagging and capture (STC) as a model we are planning to investigate how associative memory formation from single spine to behavioral level is impaired especially in a state of ‘synaptic competition’. We hypothesize that, in addition to the short and long-term phases, memory consists of a transition stage, that we call ‘competition phase’ or ‘distribution phase’. If a synaptic population is able to overcome the synaptic competition successfully it will have a better capacity to store long-term memory, otherwise the memory formed in these synaptic networks will erase with time. Our aims are to prevent the synaptic competition through the processes of metaplasticity. Metaplasticity is a mechasnism, by which due to the history of the neuron, the rules of plasticity are changed and can be investigated by activating specific receptors. In our studies we will use ryanodine receptor or metabotropic receptor mediated metaplasticity and analyzes the role of metaplasticity induced protein PKMzeta for preventing synaptic competition. Understanding the phase and properties of competition of memory will provide new insight into the onset of age related dementia and AD. In addition, we will explore the possibility of using metaplasticity mechanisms as a therapeutic target for improving memory at synaptic level. We will use cutting edge technologies that range from glutamate uncaging at single spine to animal fMRI.
