title: Pathomechanistic Characterization of Fe2+ and Mn2+ Uptake by Divalent Metal-Ion Transporter 1 (DMT1) in Neurotoxicity
abs: Iron, manganese, copper and zinc are essential trace elements for proper brain function. Excessive levels are detrimental as unliganded metal ions contribute to protein aggregation and free radical generation. Notably, increased iron deposition has been found in the aging brain and a correlation between upregulation of the divalent metal transporter (DMT1) and iron accumulation in the substantia nigra of Parkinson’s disease patients was reported. The substantia nigral region has the highest density of microglia, and with age more activated microglia. We have generated transgenic mice over-expressing DMT1 in the brain to determine the significance of our in vitro results that showed that Fe2+ was able to rescue Mn2+ toxicity. Additionally, we found that nitric oxide S-nitrosylate DMT1 to increase its transport activity.We hypothesize that the interplay between signaling pathways upon entry of iron and manganese via DMT1 influences manganese neurotoxicity and that nitric oxide mediated modification of DMT1 enhances its deleterious effect.To test this hypothesis, we aim:1)To clarify the interplay between iron and manganese upon uptake into the brain via DMT12)To identify the molecular mechanism underlying the alteration of DMT1 activity by S-nitrosylationThis proposal aims to examine the effect of Fe2+ supplementation on Mn2+ toxicity and to determine the signaling pathways and cell-death mechanism. Additionally, it will examine how S-nitrosylation of DMT1 will increase Fe2+ or Mn2+ transport and will determine the cysteine residue involved. This novel finding will lead, long-term, to the investigation of how activated microglia production of NO may activate DMT1 to contribute to the selective neuronal vulnerability of the substantia nigral neurons.This proposal may have implications for dietary iron supplementation in groups at risk of manganese toxicity, such as the estimated 2 billion people suffering from iron deficiency, or involved in industries such welding, mining or battery manufacture.
kw: DMT1 transporter; nitric oxide; patch clamp electrophysiology, transgenic mice, manganese

title: Proof of Concept of the Transient Drug as Applied to Therapeutic Intervention in Oncology
abs: This research proposal aims to show Proof of Concept for the Transient Drug (TD); a medicine that dynamically interacts with multiple targets. The concept will be evaluated on key disease relevant protein targets in oncology. Study of the oncoproteins JAK2 kinase, histone deacetylase (HDAC) and the chaperone HSP90 will be undertaken with a focus on less potent inhibitory intervention. We hypothesize that milder inhibition of several targets in synergy will provide graduated and efficient pharmacological intervention without the side effects usually seen with highly potent ‘on-off’ therapies. Transient lead candidates will be evaluated for potency in biological assays including pharmacodynamic effects on selected tumor cells as well as inhibition of cell proliferation. As transient drugs are characterized by relatively weak binding to the target in the range of µM or less of affinity, technology that can sensitively detect such binding events will be applied. In addition to established techniques such as Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) and Surface Plasmon Resonance (SPR), we have recently introduced a powerful screening technology based on weak affinity chromatography in combination with mass spectroscopy (WAC; weak affinity LC/MS) to enable much faster (high throughput) and quantification of binding events, discovery of novel binding ligands and appreciation of selectivity of binding to several targets in parallel. In a second aspect to this research, development of new tools for the assessment of metabolism and distribution properties will be undertaken. We will develop a facile new P450 enzyme and serum albumin binding assay. Application of WAC will enable quantification of ligand interactions with important metabolizing enzymes, the cytochrome P450s, and serum albumin will be assessed for the first time with this approach. (273 words)
kw: transient drug, weak affinity chromatography, oncology

title: G Protein Signaling in Oncogenesis and Metastasis
abs: Members of the G12 subfamily of G proteins play important roles in development, and have also been implicated in oncogenesis. Two members of this subfamily, GNA12 and GNA13, are upregulated as prostate and breast cancers progress to an aggressive phenotype, and signaling through these G proteins promotes cancer cell invasion and metastasis. GNA13 function is also required for the tumorigenic behavior of at least one type of breast cancer cells. We have recently identified the mechanism for upregulation of GNA13 expression in cancer cells to involve specific microRNAs (miRNAs), and shown that GNA13 signaling can be controlled through manipulation of miRNA function. Our hypothesis is that GNA12/13 signaling can be important regulator of oncogenesis on the one hand, and cancer cell invasion and metastasis on the other, and that a critical element of its dysregulation in cancer involves miRNA function. In this application, we detail a series of experimental approaches to rigorously test this important hypothesis. With numerous direct binding partners of G12 proteins now identified, the key will be to dissect the signaling pathways controlled by GNA12/13 and to determine which of these pathways contribute to specific cell biologic and pathophysiologic processes. We have developed a unique set of reagents to facilitate these studies and allow precise determination of specific molecular interactions involved. In Aim 1 we will dissect the signaling mechanisms contributing to G12-mediated tumorigenesis and cancer cell invasion. In Aim 2, we will elucidate the importance of microRNA function in controlling expression of GNA13, and the potential dysregulation of this process in prostate cancer progression. Identification of the precise events that contribute to these processes would open avenues to the use of targeted strategies to interdict pathophysiologies arising from deregulation of GNA12/13 signaling, such as that recently identified for GNA13 in Burkitt lymphoma.
kw: G proteins, G protein-coupled receptors, Cell invasion, Metastasis, MicroRNA, Tumorigenesis

title: Characterization and Development of the potential diagnostic and therapeutic utilities of LYVE-1 expressing macrophages for vascular diseases
abs: Research over the past decade has provided unprecedented insights into the mechanisms of new blood vessel formation. However, the challenge is now to generate a network of blood vessels that is functionally and structurally mature, and thus stable and durable. This knowledge will benefit regenerative medicine and treatment of various vascular diseases. Although lymphatic vessel endothelial hyaluronic acid receptor-1 (LYVE-1) is considered as a specific marker for lymphatic vessels, it is also expressed by some tissue macrophages. Our recent data contained herein demonstrate that LYVE-1 expressing macrophages present in the adventitia of arteries are required to maintain smooth muscle cells in the media and vascular stability. In the present proposal, we will follow-up on these findings by investigating the mechanisms by which LYVE-1+ cell stabilize blood vessels and by addressing the potential diagnostic properties of this population of macrophages in experimental and clinical aortic aneurysm. Finally, we propose to develop an alternative approach to the current insufficient angiogenic therapies for ischemic heart disease resulting from myocardial infarction based on the unique property of LYVE-1+ macrophages. This novel strategy will ameliorate cardiac dysfunction by enhancing the heart’s intrinsic regenerative capabilities and improving vessel stabilization and arteriogenesis of the ischemic myocardium. Altogether, this collaborative, innovative and multi-disciplinary project will offer opportunities for the development of new diagnosis for aortic aneurysms which remains a clinical challenge as aortic aneurysms are generally asymptomatic, and alternative therapeutic strategies for ischemic diseases, the leading cause of death in the developed world.
kw: macrophage, vessel stabilization, aneurysm, myocardial infarction, smooth muscle cell, tissue engineering

title: In vivo models for Spinal Muscular Atrophy: Insight into the molecular mechanisms of motor neuron degeneration
abs: Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is a common neuromuscular disorder characterized by degeneration of a-motor neurons in the spinal cord. SMA patients carry mutations in the Survival of Motor Neuron (SMN) protein, which is expressed ubiquitously and critical for general snRNP (small nuclear ribonucleoprotein) assembly. Additional motor neuron-specific functions have been proposed to explain the motor neuron specific disease phenotype. However, studies from several laboratories, including our own, provide evidence that deficiencies in snRNP assembly and consequently pre-mRNA splicing are responsible for the observed motor neuron degeneration. Notably, most of the aberrantly spliced transcripts remain unknown. We propose that reduced efficiency of the splicing machinery after SMN knock-down leads to splicing defects in a subset of pre-mRNAs required for the functional maintenance and survival of motor neurons. We hypothesize that this affects transcripts that are expressed in motor neurons as well as other cell types required for motor neuron activity.Objective 1 therefore is to identify aberrantly spliced pre-mRNA transcripts in the zebrafish SMA model by RNA deep sequencing (with S. Mathavan, GIS). Objective 2 is to characterize the endogenous roles of identified candidates for motor neuron activity and survival in vivo in zebrafish and mouse SMA models (with M. Sendtner, Univ. of Wuerzburg). Objective 3 is the analysis of motor neuron excitability by live calcium imaging in the zebrafish SMA model after knock-down of candidate SMN targets. This includes Neurexin2, which we have identified as novel SMN target in a preliminary zebrafish microarray study. We show that Neurexin2 is also affected in the mouse SMA model. This demonstrates that zebrafish can be used to identify factors with physiological relevance for SMA research. The identified aberrantly spliced transcripts represent excellent new targets for therapeutic strategies that might aim to restore motor neuron functionality rather than motor neuron survival in SMA patients.
kw: Spinal Muscular Atrophy; neurodegeneration; snRNP assembly; motor neurons; RNA splicing diseases; zebrafish and mouse models

title: Vivax Malaria Invasion Target: New vaccine candidates against blood stage Plasmodium vivax
abs: The continued spread of drug resistant vivax malaria is one of the major threats to public health in Asia. Despite its importance, this form of malaria has remained largely neglected, due in part to the complex biology of its causative agent; Plasmodium vivax. The Duffy antigen (CD234) is the only erythrocyte receptor known to mediate the invasion of P. vivax into reticulocytes. However CD234 is expressed on both mature erythrocytes and reticulocytes and as P. vivax specifically invades reticulocytes it is likely that CD234 is only a co-receptor. The specific aim of this study is to discover the primary reticulocyte invasion receptor for P. vivax. We will also investigate whether this yet to be discovered receptor specifically binds to any of the reticulocyte binding proteins (Pvrbp 1a, b & 2a, b, c) expressed at the apical end of the P. vivax merozoite. To achieve these aims we will utilize a reliable P. vivax ex vivo invasion assay and FACS-sorted cord blood reticulocytes to specifically identify which subset (s) is (are) invaded (Heilmeyer Reticulocyte Stage I, II, III or IV). A detailed immunophenotyping of the preferred reticulocyte target will help create a short list of reticulocyte receptors for antibody inhibition assays followed by confirmatory reticulocyte knock down invasion assays (using in vitro cultivated reticulocytes). To determine if any of the Pvrbps specifically interact with the reticulocyte receptor(s) identified in the step above we will produce tagged Pvrpbs proteins on the surface of HEK293 cells. Rosetting assays with in vitro produced knocked-out reticulocytes and Pvrbp -HEK293 cells and interaction screening by AVEXIS will be used to discover the primary receptor-Pvrbp ligand pair. The discovery of the primary receptor for P.vivax invasion will provided a much needed target for vaccines against the blood stages of P. vivax.
kw: Vivax Malaria, Plasmodium vivax, Retriculocyte invasion, Cord Blood, Invasion receptors, Vaccines

title: Multivalent Tetrabranched Peptides for Topical Fungal Infections: From Design to Delivery
abs: Superficial fungal infections disrupt critical structural components of innate immunity such as skin, eye, nail, buccal cavity and vagina, exposing the underlying tissues to more invasive secondary infections. Fungal infections of the eye are leading cause of corneal blindness in South East Asia. Effective management of fungal infections is hampered by the limited number of antifungals available, their narrow spectrum of activity, poor tissue penetration, toxic side effects, fungistatic (rather than fungicidal) nature and increased emergence of drug resistance. The multivalent peptide (B4010) developed by our group showed excellent biocompatibility and antifungal properties such as low MIC (0.4-1.4 ?M), rapid fungicidal action, and significant retention of activity in tear fluid and avoid fungal resistance. We hypothesize that optimizing the sequence of B4010 by rational design and encapsulating the most potent peptides into nanofibre/nanoparticles may over come several limitations of current antifungals and antifungal peptides. The approach will use a database filtration method to investigate the structural parameters that are critical for antifungal action in silico. Applying these principles, we will synthesize a series of peptides containing proteinogenic or non-proteinogenic amino acids. The toxicity and stability of peptides will be assessed and their antifungal properties are investigated in complex biological environments. Using S. cerevisiae phenotype screening, we will identify the cell wall/membrane targets of the most potent peptides. Finally, we will encapsulate the peptide into nanofibre/nanoparticles and assess their efficacy by FDA approved tests for contact lens solutions, mouse model of cornea fungal infection and an ex vivo skin infection model. The interdisciplinary team has experience, expertise and a strong track record in science, engineering and medicine. This project will advance the basic knowledge in design and delivery of bioactive peptides and provide an opportunity to expand a general program in fungal disease management.
kw: Multivalent peptides, Fungal infections, Antifungals, Membrane Targeting, Phenotype screening, Electrospinning

title: Elucidating the role of Parkin-AF6-AMPK axis in mitochondrial quality control and its relevance to Parkinson’s disease
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Parkinson’s disease (PD) is a prevalent neurodegenerative disease characterized pathologically by the progressive loss of substantia nigra dopaminergic neurons and the presence of intra-neuronal protein aggregates known as Lewy bodies. Although the etiology of PD remains unclear, aberrant mitochondrial homeostasis is widely regarded as a key pathogenic contributor. Supporting this, recent discoveries have identified parkin, whose mutations cause recessive PD, as a critical regulator of mitochondrial quality control (QC). Towards the development of PD therapeutics centered on improving neuronal mitochondrial function, we have recently discovered that the activation of AMPK, a key cellular energy sensor, protects against mitochondrial and dopaminergic dysfunction in Drosophila models of PD. Further, in an exciting development in collaboration with scientists at Technion-Israel, we have identified AF6 (an F-actin binding protein) as a novel parkin interactor and demonstrated a previously unreported role for AF6 in mitochondrial QC. Interestingly, AF6 is a substrate of AMPK. Importantly, we found that AF6 is sequestered within Lewy bodies and that its levels are strikingly decreased in PD brain samples. Taken together, our results demonstrate a novel role for AF6 in mitochondrial homeostasis and suggest that AF6 deficiency might contribute to PD pathogenesis. Mechanistically how AF6 regulates mitochondrial QC and whether it can be exploited to provide neuroprotection for the PD patient are obvious and important questions to pursue, which the current proposal seeks to accomplish. Because mitochondrial QC is inherently linked to its transport, we are also interested to examine whether AF6 influences axonal mitochondrial trafficking and associated synaptic dynamics, and whether its deficiency would impair the nigro-striatal circuitry. We will address these questions by means of different model systems, including Drosophila, primary mouse neuronal cultures and iPS-derived human dopaminergic neurons from control and PD individuals, the outcomes of which have obvious clinical implications for the PD patient.
kw: Parkinson's disease; Mitophagy, Parkin, LRRK2, Neurodegeneration

title: A role for medial septum cholinergic neurons in chronic pain?
abs: The proposal will test the hypothesis that the cholinergic neurons of the forebrain medial septum (MS) facilitate chronic pain. The peripheral hypersensitivity (PH) and secondary affect of chronic pain are harbinger of negative effect on lifestyle. In this regard, both clinical and pre-clinical investigations indicate that chronic pain-induced peripheral hypersensitivity is co-morbid with cognitive decline and depression. Based on our findings and preliminary trends we suggest that the MS cholinergic neurons and associated network underpin, at least in part, tissue injury-induced motivated behaviors and PH. Indeed, the MS cholinergic neurons are upstream to the hippocampus and cingulate cortex, both of whom are associated with pain. To determine the neural basis of the MS role in chronic pain we plan the following experiments in anaesthetized and behaving rat: one, to determine whether manipulating cholinergic neurons of the medial septum affect tissue- and nerve damage-induced behaviors, PH and affective changes; two, to investigate whether peptidergic and glutamatergic neurotransmission in MS mediate pain; three, to investigate whether MS cholinergic neurons facilitate pain through the hippocampus and cingulate cortex. These investigations will use cell biology techniques, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), optogenetics and electrophysiology that will be coupled with drug microinjection and behavioral investigations. On successful conclusion, the study will provide a neurochemical basis for the role MS in chronic pain that will, on one hand, strengthen the credentials that MS is a viable target for manipulations to relieve pain and additionally provide neural and chemical target(s) for pursuing translational investigations.
kw: Chronic pain, medial septum, cholinergic neurons, hippocampus and cingulate cortex, intraseptal microinjection, glutamate and substance P

title: TRPV4 Calcium Permeable Channel, A Novel Breast Cancer Metastasis Effector
abs: Phosphoproteomics of an isogenic model of breast cancer metastasis revealed TRPV4 Ca2+ permeable channel to be a novel breast cancer metastasis-associated protein. We aim to i) elucidate how TRPV4 exerts its effect on metastatic processes such as intra/extravasation through the regulation of cancer cell plasticity & signaling cascades involving intracellular calcium, migration/invasion-associated regulators such as AKT, FAK, Twist and E-cadherin via pharmacological, knock down and overexpression approaches, ii) investigate the role of TRPV4 mutants, its pharmacological inhibitor & novel downstream target in metastasis via in vitro cell-based assays & mouse model with survival outcome analysis and iii) evaluate it as a predictive marker for metastasis by performing retrospective study of TRPV4 expression in clinical samples and statistically correlating them with clinical data such as disease free survival and nodal status. Analysis of >400 clinical samples demonstrated that TRPV4 is overexpressed in breast cancer. Its expression correlated significantly with dissemination to the lymph nodes. We showed that TRPV4 is required for cancer cell plasticity, invasion, transendothelial migration and metastasis possibly via the Ca2+-dependent activation of AKT, FAK and dowregulation of E-cad cell adhesion proteins. A key deliverable of the proposed work is the insights into the mechanisms through which TRPV4 contributes to breast cancer metastasis. Our data supports the notion of TRPV4 as a biomarker for predicting metastasis that would be useful in stratifying patients for adjuvant therapy as well as presents a feasible option of TRPV4 target-directed therapeutics for metastatic breast cancers (MBC) thus leading to a lower healthcare cost, more rational management and better quality of life for patients. A patent application for TRPV4 as a biomarker and drug target has been filed in 2011. Under a Commercialization Of Technology (COT) funding, we are developing monoclonal antibodies against a portfolio of candidates including TRPV4 for molecular diagnostics and therapy.
kw: TRPV4, Breast Cancer, Metastasis, Signaling, Therapy, Biomarker

title: Sensing of host signals by the two component regulatory system VirA/VirG to activate Type VI secretion system in Burkholderia pseudomallei
abs: Type VI Secretion Systems (T6SSs) are important for the virulence of many Gram-negative bacterial pathogens. In Burkholderia pseudomallei, the causative agent of melioidosis, one of its T6SSs (T6SS1) is critical for bacterial pathogenesis in mammalian hosts. T6SS1 is upregulated only inside host cells through the action of the two component histidine sensor kinase VirA and its cognate response regulator VirG. Together, they affect the transcription of almost all T6SS1 genes. We have identified cysteine and glutathione as signals sensed by VirA in our preliminary data. These signals could represent authentic signals derived from the host cells that are sensed by intracellular bacteria during infection. Since they are low molecular weight thiols with reducing power, our hypothesis is that these thiols are sensed either through disulphide bond reduction or S-thionylation on the cysteine residues in VirA. This results in a conformational change, altering the phosphorylation state of the cytoplasmic domain of VirA, leading to activation of VirG. Furthermore, there may be unidentified negative modulators of VirA to maintain it in its “off” or oxidized state normally. Our aims include determining which cellular compartment the signals for VirAG emanate and the relevance of these in vitro identified signals to cellular infection models; identification of the chemical modifications induced by these signals on VirA; examining the mechanism of signal transduction from VirA to the response regulator VirG via hydrogen/deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDXMS); and identification of novel modulators of VirAG signalling by screening a transposon saturation mutagenesis library for mutants with constitutive activation of T6SS1 genes. Since two component systems in bacteria are attractive drug targets as they are not found in metazoans, and T6SS1 is critical for virulence of B. pseudomallei, our work will pave the way for developing novel therapeutics against this difficult-to-treat disease endemic in Singapore and surrounding regions.
kw: two component system, histidine kinase, Type VI Secretion Systems, Burkholderia pseudomallei, VirA

title: The Role of Sphingolipids in the Pancreatic beta-Cell
abs: Type 1 and 2 diabetes result from inadequate postprandial secretion of insulin, a peptide hormone that promotes the uptake and storage of nutrients in skeletal muscle and fat. Pancreatic ?-cells secrete insulin when blood glucose reaches a critical, threshold level. Recent studies suggest that sphingolipids generated by inflammatory cytokines or nutrient oversupply may have important regulatory roles on the survival and function of pancreatic ?-cells. The sphingolipid precursor ceramide has been shown to induce ?-cell apoptosis and inhibit insulin secretion. Moreover, gangliosides, which are glycosylated forms of ceramide, are putative autoantigens involved in the induction of insulitis and type 1 diabetes. To investigate the therapeutic potential of manipulating this pathway as a means of improving ?-cell homeostasis, we treated rodent models of type 1 and type 2 diabetes with myriocin, an inhibitor of serine palmityoltransferase, which catalyzes the initial and rate-limiting step in sphingolipid biosynthesis. As shown in the preliminary data section, this compound prevented the onset of both forms of the disease. To investigate the role of sphingoolipids further, we will use novel lines of conditional knockout mice to evaluate the role of specific genes controlling ceramide biosynthesis (i.e. Sptlc2 and Des1) in diabetes and to delineate the mechanisms accounting for the profound pharmacological benefits of sphingolipid depletion. Ultimately these studies will help reveal whether modulating ?-cell sphingolipid levels is a useful strategy for blocking ?-cell death during transplantation or preventing the onset of type 1 or type 2 diabetes.
kw: Diabetes, Pancreatic b-Cell, Ceramide, Insulin, Sphingolipids, Apoptosis

title: Decipher the RACGAP-1-linked molecular mechanisms leading to the early recurrence of human hepatocellular carcinoma.
abs: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is one of the most common fatal cancers worldwide. Surgery currently offers the only possibility of prolonged survival for HCC patients. Unfortunately, recurrence occurs in more than two-thirds of these patients despite initial curative intent and converts the situation to a dismal prognosis. The variations in prognosis following surgery differ substantially and such large variation is mostly unexplained. Various surrogate clinicopathologic features such as lymphovascular invasion, capsular invasion, satellite lesions, and tumour numbers are often used but give varying degree of reliability. Previously, we have reported a 57-member gene signature for identifying HCC patients who are at higher risk of having early recurrent disease with high degree of accuracy. When the prognostic significance of individual members of the 57-member gene signature was studied using multivariate and log-rank test, RacGTPase-activating protein 1 (RACGAP1) gave the best ability to predict early recurrent HCC disease and survival outcome. RACGAP1 is a component of the central spindlin complex that has been implicated in cytokinesis initiation and plays key roles in controlling cell growth and differentiation. We hypothesize that deciphering the gene networks associated with RACGAP1 will help to understand the molecular mechanisms underlying the development of early recurrent disease in HCC. Furthermore, dissecting the RACGAP1-associated gene network will lead to the identification of potential novel diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers associated with early HCC recurrence. Despite the extensive application of sorafenib, the prognosis for patients with advanced HCC remains poor and the identification of diagnostic and prognostic bioamrkers with clearly defined molecular and cellular networks is currently an unmet clinical need for HCC. The successful development of these biomarkers will enable the development of targeted therapeutic strategies and to appropriately select patients for more aggressive treatments to be monitored more closely.
kw: ECT2, Metastasis and recurrence, PRC1, Hepatocellular carcinoma, Personalized medicine,RACGAP1

title: Defining transcription synergy factors which upregulate IL12b gene expression in infection
abs: Cytokines such as interleukins and interferons secreted by immune response cells during an infection, immunomodulate intercellular communications. In addition to immediate innate immune defense, macrophages secrete cytokines that initiate inflammatory responses and facilitate the development of antibody-based acquired immunity. Therefore, the timely and appropriate level of production of cytokines is crucial for survival. Under- or over- production of cytokines manifests autoimmune diseases and sepsis syndrome. Thus, investigation into the regulation of the anti- or pro- inflammatory cytokine production has been a key subject of biomedical research. Knowledge gained from such research has important implications on our understanding of the mechanisms of diseases and in guiding the development of specific therapeutics. Our recent investigation on the interaction between distinct immune signal transduction pathways in macrophages has revealed synergy at the transcriptional level of critical cytokine gene expression, prompting us to hypothesize that “transcription synergy factors” regulate and facilitate immune signaling crosstalk. Thus, we aim to: (1) compare the proteomes of nuclear extracts from macrophages challenged by various regimes of stimulation, to define transcription synergy factors which regulate downstream events of TLR signaling pathways in global settings and networks, (2) examine a gene-specific transcription apparatus of the critical pro-inflammatory cytokine gene, IL12b, by developing a novel proteomics approach and (3) functionally validate the identified synergy factors involved in crosstalk of distinct signal transduction pathways. We will use cultured cells and mouse models for gene knockdown and knockout studies to ascertain our biochemical, cellular and molecular findings. Our proposed novel proteomics approach will demonstrate real-time and direct biological events in an infection. It has the advantage of revealing infection-mediated post-translational modifications and intracellular translocation of gene regulatory proteins. Our findings will provide fundamental knowledge and innovation of new methodology, leading to the development of novel therapeutics for clinical control of the cytokine level.
kw: infection; innate immunity; immune signaling crosstalk; regulation of cytokine gene expression; transcription synergy factors; pro-inflammatory cytokine gene (IL12b)

title: Yap-ping at the Achilles Heel of Cancer: Genetically Defined Models of Oncogenic Transformation in Fly and Man Uncover Collaborations between Ras and Hippo/YAP Pathways
abs: Cancer genomics reveals that tumors contain a complex mixture of driver mutations in different pathways. The combination of mutations and their possible synergistic interactions impacts the tumor phenotype, but predicting this is difficult on tumor data alone. It is therefore important to be able to assign mutations to pathways and be able to asses their effects in a genetically defined system. Loss of p53 and pRB, and expression of hTERT, oncogenic Ras and the viral oncoprotein SV40 small t has been shown to cause oncogenic transformation of primary cells. We identified the tumor suppressive Hippo pathway as the crucial target of small t. Both the Hippo and Ras pathways have been implicated in tumor proliferation, migration and metastasis, and our preliminary data and literature shows that these pathways can intersect at multiple levels. Our findings now allow us to systematically investigate the cooperative interactions between perturbations in these pathways. We will identify the components of the Hippo pathway that are relevant to suppress or activate growth under tumorigenic conditions in the oncogenic transformation model in primary human cells. We will identify genes that cooperate with loss of Hippo in a Drosophila model of epithelial neoplasia and metastasis, and verify these cooperative interactions in human cells in vitro and in vivo. We expect to identify new tumor suppressors in the Hippo and Ras pathways that show cooperative effects. This will help interpret personal genomics data and guide interventions. Moreover, we will identify candidate drug targets in the Hippo pathway, whose inhiition can restore or hyper-activate the growth suppressive effect of Hippo. Investigating this pathway in a relevant model of oncogensisi is attractive since it has been relatively less studied, but therapies based on this pathway are likely to act synergistic with existing drugs targeting the Ras/MAPK/ERK pathways.
kw: Cancer, Hippo, YAP, Ras, transformation, biomarker

title: Characterization of PLEKHA7 role in Primary Angle Closure Glaucoma Pathogenesis
abs: Glaucoma is the leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide, with primary angle closure glaucoma (PACG) a major form of glaucoma in Singapore and Asia. We recently identified significant association at three genetic loci for PACG (Vithana et al, Nature Genetics, 2012). One of the susceptibility genes, PLEKHA7 encodes a plekstrin homology domain containing protein, proposed to regulate apical junctional complexes (AJCs). As AJCs control epithelial and endothelial paracellular permeability, we speculate that PLEKHA7 may be involved in the patho-physiology of angle closure related to aberrant fluid dynamics. Apart from anatomical risk factors, physiological or dynamic factors, such as differences in iris volume with pupil dilation, and choroidal expansion, may have a significant role in PACG pathogenesis. We hypothesize that these dynamic changes observed in the iris and/or choroid of angle closure eyes result from the suboptimal functioning of AJCs in the said tissues, due to either aberrant levels of PLEKHA7 or gain/loss of function PLEKHA7 variants at the junctional complexes. The dynamic mechanisms of PACG warrant further investigation as they may be amenable to modulation and therapeutic intervention unlike the anatomical risk factors of angle closure, which cannot be altered.This proposal aims to characterize the function of PLEKHA7, in cells and tissues relevant to PACG in a disease specific context to improve our understanding of disease etiology. To this end we will identify the causal variants in PLEKHA7 via targeted resequencing in PACG cases and controls and characterize the identified variants with respect to PLEKHA7 function. New information obtained from this study on PACG pathogenesis in the form of involved signaling pathways or key molecules could identify potential drug targets that may lead to effective therapies to ameliorate or prevent angle closure glaucoma in the future.
kw: Primary angle closure glaucoma, PLEKHA7, causal variants, apical junctional complexes, blood aqueous barrier, paracellular permeability

title: Metabolite signatures and risk of type 2 diabetes in Singapore adults
abs: The etiology of type 2 diabetes (T2D) is multifactorial and involves a complex interplay among genetic, metabolism and environmental factors. The recent advances in metabolite profiling techniques (metabolomics) have offered a unique approach for measuring a full profile of small-molecular metabolites, providing a comprehensive picture of an individual’s metabolic status. Although some studies suggest that blood amino acid and lipid profiling predicts T2D, these existing studies are limited in scope and did not adequately consider the role of diet, lifestyle and genetic factors. Moreover, studies have been mainly conducted in western populations, and no prospective data on circulating metabolite signatures and risk of T2D are available in Asian population.We will therefore evaluate the associations of circulating metabolite signatures with risk of incident T2D in a large nested case-control study of 800 incident cases and 800 matched controls within the Singapore Chinese Health Study. The aims of this project are: 1) To examine individual metabolites and metabolomic patterns associated with T2D in Singapore Chinese through a combination of non-targeted and candidate approaches;2) To explore whether the clinical standard and novel biomarkers for T2D mediate the relationships between metabolomic signatures and T2D risk; 3) To identify genetic loci associated with individual metabolites and metabolomic patterns implicated in T2D, and estimate the causal effects of the metabolites on T2D using SNPs that are robustly associated with the metabolites as instrumental variables;4) To examine whether the T2D-metabotypes mediate the relationships between specific dietary and lifestyle factors and T2D risk.This project utilizes data from a well-established cohort with high-throughput assessment of novel metabolite signatures to study an important public health problem. The results can directly advance our understanding of the pathophysiology of T2D, and the development of measures to reduce the burden of T2D in Asia.
kw: Metabolomics, Type 2 diabetes, Biomarker, Epidemiology

title: Reprogramming and screening of easily accessible somatic cells into insulin-producing cells for diabetes therapy
abs: Dysfunction and loss of islet ?-cells leads to clinical diabetes. ~10% of 284 million diabetic patients worldwide are insulin-dependent and suffer costly and debilitating diabetes-related complications. Transplantation of pancreata or isolated islets is the only effective therapy to cure insulin-dependent diabetes, but the shortage in donor tissues and extremely poor ability of ?-cells to replicate have limited its application. Alternative approaches to generate surrogate ?-cells for replacement therapy through differentiation of stem cells and trans-differentiation of somatic cells have remained inefficient and have not produced sufficient functional surrogate ?-cells to support replacement therapy. We have been exploring the feasibility of reprogramming somatic cells into insulin-producing surrogates. To facilitate the identification and isolation of reprogrammed insulin-producing surrogates, we used easily accessible and expansible GFP-negative somatic cells such as adipose-derived stem cells and fibroblasts from transgenic mice expressing GFP under insulin promoter. In preliminary studies to develop and optimize reprogramming, we were able to generate GFP-positive insulin-producing cells from the GFP-negative somatic cells using a novel reprogramming strategy. The general aim of this proposal is to develop a clinically relevant protocol eventually to reprogram human somatic cells into insulin-producing surrogates for cell therapy. Our specific aims are to 1) optimize the robustness of reprogramming protocol by selecting and testing different permutations of transcription factors, growth factors/cytokines, small molecules and chemicals. The use of insulin promoter-GFP hybrid gene will facilitate the dynamic and quantitative effect of these different permutations on the efficacy of reprogramming; 2) translate the reprogramming protocol from mouse to human somatic cells; 3) comprehensively in vitro characterize the insulin-producing cells; 4) transplant reprogrammed insulin-producing cells into large type 1 diabetic animals to assess their hyperglycemia-correcting capacity for preclinical applications. This proposal could facilitate robust generation of patient-specific surrogate human ?-cells from accessible somatic cells for cell replacement therapy for diabetes.
kw: Diabetes; Re-programming; Cell replacement therapy; Insulin-producing cells; Transplantation; Somatic cells

title: Repurposing existing cAMP modulators for the treatment of urinary tract infection
abs: Urinary tract infection (UTI) is one of the most common infectious diseases in humans, predominantly affecting women. UTI is the second leading reason for antibiotic therapy, thus contributing to rising antibiotic resistance. Particularly troubling is recurrent UTI, which is managed but not cured by antibiotics. Most (80-90%) UTI is caused by Escherichia coli, thus the term uropathogenic E. coli (UPEC). Recent work in mouse and in vitro cell culture models has demonstrated that UPEC and other uropathogens are able to establish intracellular infection within bladder epithelial cells. Intracellular infection accounts for resistance to host immune responses and antibiotic therapy, thus contributing to persistence and recurrence. The mechanism of bacterial intracellular invasion is through normal fusiform vesicle cycling, which in turn is regulated by cAMP levels. Modulation of host cAMP levels is thus a rational potential strategy for UTI therapy that may synergize with traditional antibiotics. Because several cAMP modulators are already in use for other diseases in humans, we will preclinical cell culture and animal models to evaluate existing cAMP modulators for efficacy in preventing intracellular infection, host immune activation, and overall UTI by UPEC and other uropathogens. We will also evaluate synergy with standard antibiotic treatment. This work is a direct expansion of previous work showing that forskolin, a cAMP elevating agent, reduces intracellular infection by UPEC and that small molecule inhibitors that prevent intracellular infection synergize with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole treatment in mouse models of UTI. This study aims to collect sufficient preclinical data to allow future human studies aimed at repurposing promising existing approved cAMP modulators for use in UTI prevention and therapy.
kw: cAMP, urinary tract infection, repurposing

title: Isolation and molecular characterization of intracellular bacteria relevant for recurrent urinary tract infection
abs: Urinary tract infection (UTI) is an exceedingly common infectious disease in humans and clinically notable for its propensity to recur. Current diagnosis and treatment is based on an ascending model of infection, but animal studies and microbiological data indicate that chronic tissue infection of the bladder may be responsible for some recurrent infections. The applicability of mouse studies of UTI has been disputed, and ongoing efforts to develop vaccines and UTI therapeutics therefore ignore the possibility of latent tissue infection. This results in inadequate treatment of recurrent infections (affecting 15-20% of all women), excessive and inappropriate use of antibiotics, and heightened risk for complicated UTIs that may require hospitalization. Previous efforts at studying intracellular tissue infection have been hampered by experimental limitations in humans and small bacterial quantities. We aim to surmount these difficulties using a combination of technologies and resources that is unique to Singapore, applying three different expression profiling technologies and a custom microfluidic device to prove that chronic intracellular infection occurs in humans and causes recurrent UTI. We will characterize the transcriptional differences between intracellular and extracellular bacterial populations in mouse urine and tissue samples and assess concordance with bacteria from human urine samples. We will also mine for signature transcriptional changes that are unique to the intracellular state; these signatures provide a necessary foundation data for mechanistic studies, novel therapeutic approaches, and dedicated diagnostic tests for UTI. Completion of the work proposed will provide a sound rationale for the targeted search for new prognostic and therapeutic strategies for recurrent UTI; a rapid and cost-effective platform for UTI research and clinical diagnostics; and a validated chain of model systems to enable development and evaluation of UTI management strategies.
kw: Urinary tract infection, Escherichia coli, Dielectrophoresis force, Microfluidics, Point of care diagnostics

title: Transatrial, Catheter-based Valve Implantation on the beating heart.
abs: Recently, catheter-based heart valve implantation technologies have conquered the clinical field, bringing about new applications, a tremendous industry drive, new devices and operation theatres, and affect the way heart specialists train and practice [1-4]. However, a large number of these procedures are performed transapically, i.e. through the tip of the heart, directly through the full thickness of the heart muscle, to reach the aortic and mitral valves [5]. This technique is traumatic, and often results in hemorrhage, intraoperative conversion to open sternotomy, cardiopulmonary bypass, and mortality. Of note, the apex of the heart and the left heart chamber constitute the high-pressure system in the circulation, with wall tensions reaching 300mmHg in systole. In the present project, we introduce a novel minimally invasive approach from the side of the torso for the implantation of commercially available expandable valves. We will enter the heart from the side of the chest, through the atria, which constitute a low-pressure system (4-30mmHg), hence, less risk for hemorrhage and complications. Multiple procedures can be performed. While the transapical procedure addresses the aortic and mitral valves, we will address the mitral valve and the tricuspid valve, in minimally invasive, single small incision approach. This way we will cover a large portion of the heart surgery portfolio with minimal risk, address diseases, which are very prevalent on a global scale – particularly in Asia, and provide a platform for a disruptive surgical methodology that may shift practice in the field.
kw: Transatrial, Transapical, Catheter-based, Expandable valves, Mitral valve, Tricuspid valve

title: Studies on the role of the MULE in intestinal homeostasis and colorectal cancer.
abs: As the most commonly diagnosed cancer in Singapore, improvements in colorectal cancer (CRC) prognosis and treatment have disproportionate benefits based on the number of patients affected. Toward improving CRC patient outcomes, this project uses clinical capabilities of the NCCS and SGH as well as a novel mouse model to probe how MULE, a gene product commonly overexpressed in tumor cells, worsens the disease. Although MULE is known to impact a number of gene products involved in cancer biology, the pathways/factors through which this oncogene functions are inadequately characterized. In this study, we plan to use a superior pathological assay for MULE that we have recently developed to elucidate the clinical importance of MULE expression and hopefully provide a prognostic assay for future patients.We have also generated a mouse with a deletion of MULE specifically in the tissue that becomes cancerous in CRC. Surprisingly, this tissue remains normal in unstressed mice, thereby allowing us to probe the molecular and physiological outcomes of specific cancerous stimuli. We are particularly interested in pursuing our recent finding that MULE might function in positively regulating anti-oxidant response through NRF2, since we have found these gene targets to be reduced upon MULE loss-of-function. We hypothesize that MULE promotes survival in transformed intestinal epithelia by enhancing the anti-oxidant response pathway(s) in order to counteract excessive reactive oxygen species generated in tumor cells. Identifying how and where MULE might function in tumor promotion could, in short order, lead to improved therapy. True hope for patients requires expansion of our repertoire of treatments and better prognostics to improve the efficacy of the existing therapies. MULE shows promise in both respects, particularly in regard of its newly discovered role in controlling NRF2, a common regulator of therapeutic efficacy.
kw: prognostic assay, anti-oxidant, drug resistance, ubiquitin ligase, HUWE1, ARFBP1

title: Harnessing the tumor suppressor function of Parkin in adult malignant glioma for improved clinical prognosis and therapy
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) represents the most advanced and prevalent primary adult malignant brain tumor with dismal prognosis despite surgical intervention and chemo- and radiation therapies. The mean survival period is 15 months upon diagnosis. Temozolomide, the current drug-of-choice, is at best able to prolong survival by 3-6 months. There is thus a clear, unmet need for better medicines to target the highly infiltrative and recurrent nature of the disease. In 2010, The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) effort demonstrated that histologically similar GBM tumors are molecularly distinct, with each subclass having unique gene expression, genomic aberrations and clinical profile. These data indicate that gene expression drives disease progression and survival outcome. Importantly, it highlights the limitation of relying solely on morphology-based histological methods to diagnose and subsequently treat patients. The TCGA data also revealed that frequent focal alterations are detected in the PARK2 gene (coding for Parkin protein), frequently implicated in Parkinson’s disease but with an as yet unexplored role in tumorigenesis. Consistent with this, we and others have shown that Parkin functions as a tumor suppressor in GBM, likely via PI3K/AKT downregulation. Importantly, we showed that Parkin pathway activation correlated inversely with survival outcome and tumor grade. Recognizing that our initial U87MG-based cell line model cannot recapitulate the patient heterogeneity suggested by our clinical database analysis, moving forward, we seek to: (i) Understand what signaling mechanisms distinguish Parkin+/- patient cohorts, characterized by molecular subgrouping, and test those predictions in primary patient-derived GBM cells; (ii) Identify small molecule candidates that offer treatment benefit to Parkin- patients; and (iii) Develop the Parkin signature as a prognostic and predictive biomarker. Collectively, we will define the role of Parkin in glioma by utilizing a patient-centric approach, and provide strong evidence that patient genome-directed therapeutic strategies are viable.
kw: glioma, connectivity map, Parkin

title: Quantitative assessment of the virulence of rhinoviruses, influenza viruses and respiratory syncytial viruses and host defense mechanisms of human nasal epithelium in vitro
abs: The viral upper respiratory infections (URIs), including common cold, influenza and acute rhinosinusitis, are very common disease, affecting millions of people annually. They can be caused by any of the more than 200 different strains of viruses, such as rhinovirus, coronavirus, respiratory syncytial viruses (RSV), influenza, parainfluenza and adenoviruses. With the SARS pandemic of 2003 and that of H1N1 in 2009, global concerns was raised, stemming from virulent new strains of viruses such as corona virus (or SARS virus), H1N1, H5N1, which appear to be more promiscuous and circulate in several species and are endemic in humans, birds and pigs. In addition to continuous efforts in surveillance of naturally occurring viruses in humans and domestic animal hosts, experimental studies elucidating susceptibilities to respiratory viruses and response to infection by human nasal epithelium, which is the primary target site for common cold and influenza viruses, are required. In this study, we aim to develop an in vitro model for screening and quantitative assessment of the virulence of common cold and influenza viruses, and the host defense mechanisms of human nasal epithelium using our newly developed in vitro experimental models of human nasal epithelial stem/progenitor cells (hNESPCs) and differentiated epithelial cells derived from hNESPCs in an air-liquid interface (ALI) culture. In addition, we will investigate the host defense functions including viral fusion and uncoating, transport of viral ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes from nucleus, replication, transcription and translation of the viral genome, export of viral RNP complexes from the nucleus, viral assembly and budding, and potential drug targets, which will provide us with a useful reference for public health risk assessment, interventions, disease control and prognosis for viral upper respiratory infections. This information is particularly useful in preparation for eventual pandemics or outbreak of viral infection.
kw: Viral infection, human nasal epithelial stem/progenitor cells (hNESPCs), rhinoviruses, influenza viruses, respiratory syncytial viruses, host defense

title: Targeting Na+/K+ ATPase to treat osteoporosis-Evidence from the protective effects of DR-Ab against osteoblast injury through activation Na+/K+ ATPase
abs: Osteoporosis is a disease of bones that leads to an increased risk of fracture. It affects more than 20% women and 6% men above 50 years old. However, the treatment of osteoporosis has been problematic, warranting more studies to understand the pathophysiology of osteoporosis. Na+-K+-ATPase (NKA), an important ion transporting protein, has recently been found to be a signaling protein relaying extracellular signals to intracellular compartments in cardiovascular system. The role of NKA in bone physiology and pathology, however, is still unknown. In our preliminary experiments, we found that membrane expression of NKA was largely decreased during oxidative stress. We developed a rat NKA DR region specific antibody (DR-Ab) and found that stimulation of NKA with DR-Ab stabilized NKA on the membrane and promoted osteoblast differentiation under pathological conditions. More importantly, DR-Ab stimulated bone formation and reduced bone resorption in ovariectomized rats, a well accepted osteroposis animal model. We, therefore, hypothesize that NKA may play an important role in bone growth and impairment of NKA may accompany osteoporosis. This proposal is therefore designed to: 1. Investigate the therapeutic effect of DR-Ab against osteoporosis in the rat ovariectomy surgery model. Specifically, serum level of bone-specific alkaline phophatase (BALP), osteocalcin procollagen type 1 N-terminal propeptide (P1NP), tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase 5b (TRACP5b), C-telopeptide of type I collagen (CTX-1) will be assessed using commercially available kits. Bone microarchitecture and mechanical properties and bone mineral density (BMD) will be studied with a desktop micro computed tomography (µCT) system, a peripheral quantitative computed tomography (pQCT) and atomic force microscope (AFM) nanoindentation. 2. Examine the mechanisms for the therapeutic effect of DR-Ab on osteoporosis. Specifically, mechanisms for membrane NKA stabilization, anti-oxidative stress and proliferative effects of DR-Ab will be investigated. Involvement of PP2A, PKC, PI3K/Akt, MAPK, GSK-3? and glutathionylation will be studied.
kw: Na+/K+ ATPase, osteoporosis, bone, oxidative stress, proliferation

title: Immunogenic cell death induced by chemoradiotherapy against upper GI cancer
abs: Specific AimsStep-1; To evaluate tumor antigen-specific T cell responses in patients with esophageal cancer (EC) and gastric cancer (GC) receiving chemoradiotherapyStep-2; To evaluate the expression of alarmin-related molecules (HMGB1, calreticulin, galectin-9, TIM3, and RAGE) in tumor-microenvironment of GC and ECHypothesesIt has been shown in murine models that chemoradiotherapy may induce immunogenic cell death, which could trigger T-cell immunity through interaction between alarmin HMGB1 and DCs. On the other hand, TIM3 on tumor-infiltrating DCs is reported to acts as a negative receptor for HMGB1 and attenuate anti-tumor immunity. There is no previous report to clarify this discrepancy in a clinical setting, due to the lack of appropriate assay to detect tumor-specific T cell responses. Since we have successfully established an assay system to evaluate tumor antigen-specific T cell responses against EC and GC, it is currently possible to clarify the discrepancy.Methodology and approachStep-1; We will evaluate antigen-specific T cell responses against 6 Cancer-Testis antigens employing our unique ELISPOT system before and after neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy in EC and GC patients (n=25). Then, we will evaluate a correlation between tumor-antigen specific immunity and expression of alarmin-related molecules in resected tumor samples.Step-2;Expression of alarmin-related molecules within tumor-microenvironment of EC (n=100) will be evaluated in resected samples with and without preoperative chemoradiotherapy. Then, we will investigate the expression patterns of HMGB1, calreticulin, TIM3, galectin-9 and RAGE in relation to chemoradiation and patient`s survival. Moreover, HMGB1 and calreticulin expression will be measured in in vitro treatments with chemoradiation against EC and GC cell lines.Clinical significanceIf we could clarify whether chemoradiotherapy induces tumor-antigen specific T cell responses, we will be able to predict the clinical responses of chemoradiotherapy by parameters including alarmin-related molecules, and to improve efficacy of chemoradiotherapy by enhancing the specific T cell-immunity.
kw: gastric cancer, esophageal cancer, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, immunogenic cell death, antigen-specific CTLs

title: Effectiveness of a Peer-led Self-Management Programme (PLSMP) for people with Schizophrenia: A randomised controlled trial
abs: Introduction Self-management programmes have been developed to empower patients with severe mental illness in achieving recovery. Literature suggested that Peer-Led Self-Management programmes (PLSMP) have positive impacts on patient recovery. However, the evidence is inconclusive due to lack of credible RCT and longer-term follow-up assessment.Aims 1.To examine the effectiveness of the designed PLSMP for people with schizophrenia in reducing psychotic symptom severity, hospital readmission and psychiatric consultation, and in enhancing cognition, empowerment, functioning level, medication adherence, perceived recovery, quality of life, and social support compared with the control group. 2.To explore perspectives of the trainers’ experience in leading PLSMP, and the perspectives of the participants experienced in the PLSMP and the standard rehabilitation programme.Method A stratified randomised controlled trial will be conducted at six community psychiatric rehabilitation centres. A total sample of 242 (121 in each group with power of 82%, 80%, and 82% to test between, within, and interaction factors with a 5% significance level and an effect size of 0.32, 0.29, and 0.30, respectively, and estimated dropout rate of 30%) will be recruited. A PLSMP will be implemented in the intervention group and standard rehabilitation programme for the control group. Outcomes will be measured at baseline, immediately after the programme, six-month and 12-month follow-up: cognition, empowerment, functioning level, medication adherence, perceived recovery, quality of life, social support, symptom severity, hospital readmission and psychiatric consultation. Repeated measure MANCOVA will be used to analyse results. Semi-structured interview will be conducted to explore peer trainers’ (n=9) perspectives in leading PLSMP, and to explore participants’ perspectives (n=30) on the programmes. Thematic analysis will be conducted for the interviews. SignificanceThis study will provide evidence on the effectiveness of the PLSMP. The designed PLSMP can be adopted as routine care to promote patients’ recovery, self-management ability, community remission and to reduce hospital readmission, healthcare cost, and disease burden.
kw: Schizophrenia, self-management, peer led, community, empowerment, recovery

title: Investigating the oncogenic role of a small tyrosine phosphatase, PRL-3 in acute myeloid leukemia and its potential therapeutic intervention
abs: Protein tyrosine kinases (PTKs) transfer a phosphate group from ATP to a target protein, while protein tyrosine phosphatases (PTPs) reverse this process. Phosphatase of regenerating liver (PRL)-3 (also known as PTP4A3) is a dual-specificity PTP. PRL-3 has been identified as a critical player in cancer cell metastasis, migration, and angiogenesis. While widely studied in solid tumors, its potential oncogenic role in leukemia is unknown. In our previous studies, we identified PRL-3 as an important molecule mediating the synergistic anti-leukemic effect of the combination of a FLT3 inhibitor and a HDAC inhibitor, thus for the first time implicating PRL-3 in drug resistance and leukemia biology. We also showed that PRL-3 in aberrantly expressed in AML and is an independent negative prognostic factor. Over-expression of PRL-3 in AML cell lines confer cytokine independence and enable greater colony forming ability and xenograft tumor generation. These oncogenic properties are related to the induction of a stem-cell self renewal transcriptional program. These studies established the functional and clinical relevance of PRL-3 in AML. In the current proposal, we will study the contribution of functional domains of PRL-3 to its oncogenic function. We will also examine the role of PRL-3 in the transformation of leukemia stem cells (LSCs) by using a genetically engineered (transgenic,Tg) mouse model specifically expressing PRL-3 in hematopoietic stem cells that we have generated. We will develop a genome-wide RNAi screen to identify gene or pathways that will either attenuate PRL-3 expression or are critically dependent upon by cells with high PRL-3 expression. Using novel tools uniquely available to us and cutting edge technologies, we believe our study will yield important new understanding on the oncogenic role played by PRL-3 in AML particularly through its impact on stem cells and identify new therapeutic strategies to target AML with aberrant PRL-3 expression.
kw: acute myeloid leukemia, PRL-3, targeted therapy, synthetic lethality, whole genome shRNA screen, leukemia stem cells

title: Intravesical Immunotherapy of Bladder Cancer with Baculoviral Vectors
abs: Aim: The objective of the study is to investigate the feasibility of using intravesical instillation of insect baculoviurus to treat bladder cancer in preclinical animal models. The information collected will be used to determine the clinical potential for the approach to be used as an intravesical salvage option for bladder cancer patients who fail bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) therapy or who are intolerant of BCG therapy. Hypothesis: Viral vector-based gene therapy has been explored as a possible adjuvant treatment for bladder cancer. We hypothesize that baculoviral vectors may offer an unprecedented advantage over other viral vectors and BCG, given their efficient cell transduction capacity and intrinsic potent immunostimulatory property. Methodology: In seeking the evidence supporting the hypothesis, we believe it is especially important to understand the immune mechanism possibly involved. We will use both normal mice and a syngeneic orthotopic murine model of bladder cancer to analyze the cytokine response profiles and immune cell infiltrates associated with intravesical instillation of baculoviruses, and compare the changes with those induced by BCG instillation. To investigate the possibility of using baculovirus as a new intravesical agent for bladder cancer therapy with a dual function of therapeutic vaccination and therapeutic gene delivery, we will further examine whether the immune stimulatory effects of empty baculoviral vector can be improved by the use of cytokine-expressing baculoviral vectors. Clinical Significance: Intravesical BCG therapy remains the most effective adjuvant treatment for non–muscle-invasive bladder cancer, but up to 40% of the patients will fail the therapy. There is still no gold standard for salvage therapy after BCG failure. Our studies on the combinatorial approach that harnesses the power of immunotherapy and gene therapy in a baculoviral vector will suggest the feasibility of a novel adjuvant treatment that can be placed intravesically to treat bladder cancer.
kw: Bladder Cancer, Immunotherapy, Baculovirus, bacillus Calmette-Guérin failure

title: An evaluation of a unique IgE-mediated allergy/anaphylaxis to galacto-oligosaccharide, a commercial prebiotic.
abs: Background: Galactooligosaccharide (GOS) is a commercially manufactured prebiotic that has been conferred GRAS (generally regarded as safe) status and used as a functional food. We, however, recently reported a series of Singaporean patients with IgE-mediated anaphylactic reactions to GOS supplemented milk formula. Unlike conventional glycoprotein allergens, GOS is a small molecule and a pure carbohydrate.Aims: (1) To determine the extent of this potential allergy by conducting a GOS sensitization survey of our atopic population and setup an active surveillance system for anaphylaxis in Emergency Departments in Singapore, (2) To evaluate the IgE epitope on GOS, and (3) To screen using sera of sensitized patients for the primary sensitizer(s) as we hypothesize that GOS acts as a hapten, and GOS-specific IgE is induced by a primary sensitizer in our environmentMethodology: The GOS sensitization survey will screen 500 atopics for sensitization to GOS via skin prick and basophil activation tests. Non-exposed sensitized patients will be offered oral GOS challenge testing to ascertain clinical allergy. The hospital anaphylaxis survey would potentially identify new patients. Sera from these subjects would provide the ‘reagents’ to discover the IgE epitope specific to GOS by using human IgE immunocolumns. The bound GOS components will be investigated using monosaccharide and linkage analysis (gas-liquid chromatography-electron impact mass spectrometry), matrix-assisted laser-desorption-ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry, and nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy. Inhibition studies used to screen a panel of crude extracts of potential primary sensitizers will be used to identify the putative primary sensitizer.Benefits: This study will delineate the extent of GOS allergy in our population. This will have direct implications on patient counseling, and labeling of food products containing GOS in Singapore. It will provide crucial information for the production of GOS lacking the IgE epitope (non-allergenic) and prevent exposure of an at risk population to this ‘hidden’ allergen.

title: Whole Plasmodium exportome: Identification of survival and virulence factors
abs: Despite recent encouraging results, malaria remains one of the main health problems globally. Most of malaria associated mortality and morbidity in humans is caused by Plasmodium falciparum the deadliest species know to infect humans. In addition P. vivax poses a considerable public health burden in S.E. Asia and is the most difficult to cure. To date, progress in our understanding of parasite biology and pathogenicity is slow, and there is an urgent need to expand the number of new molecular targets for intervention if elimination of human malaria is to be achieved. After invasion, parasites extensively modify and remodel the red-blood-cell to ensure their survival and promote virulence. Underlying these modifications are parasite proteins exported into the red-blood-cell cytoplasma. To date, the nature of these molecules remains elusive and could prove its downfall, providing new avenues for anti-disease/parasite intervention. The goal of this proposal is to determine the repertoire of exported proteins conserved across Plasmodium genus that are essential for parasite survival/virulence. We have recently identified an export signal named PLASMED in P. yoelii and used it to predict an expanded exportome; we now aim to extend our studies to P. falciparum and P. vivax. For this, The PLASMED exportome of both species will be predicted and refined using machine learning method. Conversely to in silico prediction, proteomic analysis will be used to identify the plasmodial proteins localised in the host cell-cytoplasma. Merging these exportomes will define a repertoire of conserved exported proteins which will be validated and functionally characterized using gene knockout and tagging. Phenotypes of genetically modified parasites will be assessed for biological as well as biomechanical changes. The data obtained here will not only address fundamental questions regarding host-cell remodelling, but will also provide new therapeutic targets able to block the parasite development/virulence.
kw: Plasmodium, virulence factors, multigene families, host cell remodeling, pathology, exported protein

title: The control of gene expression in the protozoan parasite Plasmodium falciparum
abs: Forty-eight hours after being invaded by the protozoan parasite Plasmodium falciparum, a red blood cell ruptures to release several progeny ready for a new round of invasion. During these 48 h of the intraerythrocytic developmental cycle (IDC), 80% of the parasite genome is expressed in a finely graded cascade of mRNA appearance and disappearance. To understand the relative contribution of transcriptional initiation versus post-initiation events in controlling mRNA flux in P falciparum, we have raised and used antibodies against the most fundamental component of the parasite’s transcriptional machinery, the large subunit of RNA polymerase II (RNAPII). We have used these antibodies in so-called ChIP-on-chip experiments to map the distribution of RNAPII, especially the enzymatically active form of the polymerase, across the entire parasite genome over the course of the IDC. We have brought to light two novel findings. First, the distribution of transcriptionally active RNAPII reveals a highly simplified pattern, with most genes falling into one of two groups: early binders that recruit RNAPII for the first 32 hours post invasion, and late binders that recruit RNAPII for the last 12 hours. Second, for a large group of genes, the binding of transcriptionally active RNAPII is strongly negatively correlated with peak mRNA levels. This proposal first seeks to understand the mechanisms by which genes recruit RNAPII either early or late in the IDC. The second goal is to identify post-initiation mechanisms that must temporally displace the peak of mRNA accumulation from the peak of transcription for many genes.Specific Aim 1Identification of cis-acting sequences directing RNAPII recruitment early or late in the IDC.Specific Aim 2Use of ChIP-seq to finely map RNAPII distribution across the genome and the IDC.Specific Aim 3Investigation of the Mediator and CCR4-NOT1 complexes in regulating transcriptional initiation and post-initiation events.
kw: malaria, transcription, mRNA, microarray, gene expression, chromatin

title: Angiopoietin-like 4 as a Biomarker and Therapy Target for Acute Lung Damage in Influenza and Secondary Bacterial Infection.
abs: Influenza infections and associated secondary bacterial infections threaten the lives of millions of people every year. However, designing effective vaccines and treatment options has proven difficult because the influenza virus evolves rapidly. Therefore, it may be beneficial to identify host proteins that are associated with influenza infection. One effective therapeutic option is to accelerate lung repair and recovery following influenza infection. However, although many individual aspects of these host-pathogen interactions during the course of influenza infection have been studied, there is little information on the host’s response during the repair stage of the infection. In our preliminary study, we identified the host protein angiopoietin-like 4 (ANGPTL4) as a potential biomarker of acute lung damage and a therapy target to facilitate lung repair. We demonstrated that ANGPTL4 expression was increased during influenza infection and that treatment with neutralizing antibodies against ANGPTL4 significantly improved lung recovery. However, the role of ANGPTL4 and its underlying mechanism remain unclear. In this proposal, we will first identify the stimuli and the cell types responsible for the increased expression of ANGPTL4 by performing in situ hybridization, dual immunofluorescence and in vitro culture. Next, using in vivo imaging, multiple analyte detection and laser capture microdissection coupled to microarrays we will investigate the in vivo effects of ANGPTL4 during influenza infection. Finally, we will examine the expression of ANGPTL4 and the effect of anti-ANGPTL4 during both influenza virus infections and influenza virus-bacterial super-infection. To underscore the biological relevance of ANGPTL4, we will examine its expression in clinical samples of pneumococcal infection and in lung resections from various inflammatory and infectious diseases. Our study will represent the first demonstration of the novel role of ANGPTL4 in influenza lung infection and will therefore advance our understanding of influenza pathogenesis and promote the development of new diagnostic and therapeutic strategies.
kw: angiopoietin-like 4, influenza virus infection,secondary pneumococcal infection, acute lung damage

title: Understanding mammalian microRNA biology in health and disease
abs: Precise regulation of gene expression is essential for normal organism development and function and errors in this process often lead to disease. microRNAs (miRNAs) are endogenously encoded ~22 nucleotide-long regulatory RNAs that coordinate outputs of extensive sets of genes by altering translational efficiency and stability of their mRNA transcripts. miRNAs often contribute to establishment and maintenance of cell-specific gene expression programs and the nervous system-enriched miRNA miR-124 provides a functionally important example of this category. Several lines of evidence have previously uncovered possible links of miR-124 with neurological diseases. However, the mechanisms underlying normal neuronal functions of this miRNA and pathological consequences of its dysregulation in mammalian systems are poorly understood. To this end, we propose to examine three interrelated aspects of miR-124 biogenesis and function. First, we will use a combination of molecular approaches to elucidate novel post-transcriptional mechanisms that control the expression of miR-124 and other intron-encoded miRNAs. Second, we will use conditional miR-124 knockout mouse lines to address the biological role of this miRNA in the nervous system. Finally, we will examine the repertoire of neuronal miR-124 targets and will further use the miR-124-controlled network to tackle several fundamental problems of miRNA biology. This research program will expand our general understanding of disease mechanisms, establish new mouse models for neurological disorders including epilepsy, depression and Alzheimer’s disease and develop innovative strategies for modulating gene expression in biomedically relevant contexts. This should ultimately facilitate development of future knowledge-based therapies and novel diagnostic tools and lead to substantial healthcare improvements.
kw: MicroRNA biogenesis and function; Mammalian miR-124; Nervous system; Molecular mechanisms of disease; Epilepsy; Depression; Alzheimer's disease; Cancer

title: Silicon as a Platform for Ultra-High-Speed Photonic-Electronic Integration
abs: The field of silicon photonics is concerned with making use of the multi-billion dollar infrastructure that has been developed for manufacturing integrated microelectronics, and repurposing it to make chips that can manipulate photons as well as electrons. The field has advanced to the point where there are now products shipping millions of units, and projections suggest that this will be a multi-billion-dollar industry within a few years. The PI of this proposal, Prof. Hochberg, is in the process of starting a group at NUS, while running a national institute called OpSIS in the US dedicated to advancing this field, and he is one of the co-founders of Luxtera, the company that is widely regarded as the technology leader in the field. In this proposal, we propose an effort aimed at leveraging, for the first time, truly advanced CMOS and BiCMOS microelectronics and integrating these chips with the photonic circuits being developed at IME, through the use of 3D integration. We will demonstrate the first silicon transmitters and receiver subsystems operating at speeds of 100 GHz (a factor of 2-3 faster than the state of the art for CMOS-compatible photonic systems), and we will demonstrate photonic core-to-core interconnects that are compatible with a 28nm or smaller CMOS node, operating at aggregate multi-terabit on-chip bandwidths, for the first time. To date, nearly all of the work in silicon photonics has leveraged trailing edge electronics, due to both the high costs of leading-edge microelectronics and to the risks of using immature silicon photonic platforms: With the relatively mature platform that we have been developing with IME, we can make the first practical silicon photonic-electronic systems with truly leading edge electronics and photonics as part of the same integrated chip stack.

title: Predicting, Modeling, and Engineering New Topological Materials for Spintronics and Nanoelectronics Application
abs: The broad objective of the proposed research is to develop and deploy critically needed ab initio electronic structure calculations to search for new topological phases in real materials and demonstrate novel design principles for using these topological materials in spintronics and nanoelectronics devices. Recent development of topological band theory combined with the predictive power of ab initio calculations has led to discovery of new states of quantum matter as well as their material realization. These topological materials are distinguished by unique physical properties. The Z2 topological insulators host back-scattering-free spin-polarized surface states that enables viable applications in spintronics. Topological superconductors offer the opportunity to observe Majorana fermions and their non-Abelian statistics, which is a first step towards fault-tolerant quantum computation. Topological materials are interesting from both a fundamental physics and a practical applications point of view. While Z2 topological insulators have been realized experimentally, there is no material realization of many other distinct topological phases that have been predicted by topological band theory. In this proposal, we will develop algorithms in ab initio calculations to identify topological phases in real materials. In order to capture many exotic interesting properties of topological surface states, surface simulations will be performed with an emphasis on the modeling of the surface spectroscopy, enabling direct comparisons between theoretical predictions and experimental measurements. A bottom-up theoretical approach of quantum transport will be carried out to simulate spintronics and nanoelectronics devices that are engineered on the atomic scale, allowing development of design principles based on the physics of the topological insulators. This proposed research emphasizes the material aspects of applying topological band theory. Automatic computer routines will enable the search to cover the entire collection of known crystalline materials. A materials database of electronic structures will be built during this process. This materials database will also be useful for materials, chemical, and energy sciences.
