title: Physics-Based and Data-Driven Predictive modelling of the Earthquake Cycle in Sumatra
abs: The goal of this research is to build a much improved understanding of seismic hazard in Sumatra using physical models of fault behaviour tuned to geophysical, geological and laboratory observations. The Sunda subduction zone, located only a few hundred kilometers southwest of Singapore, generated some of the deadliest earthquakes and tsunamis in recent history, killing more than 200,000 people since 2004. These tectonic events are not only responsible for local hazards, but also have farther-reaching impacts, such as regional-scale change in sea level and economic setback or loss of opportunity for neighbouring countries, including Singapore. Much can be done to significantly improve theoretical and practical understanding of the seismic cycle in this region. In fact, the presence of a large plate boundary in Singapore's backyard represents a unique opportunity of observation and analysis. Significant efforts will be directed towards monitoring the kinematics of the region with the required accuracy to inform the physical modelling. This will be accomplished by the installation of 20 additional geodetic stations in islands offshore Sumatra, and by carrying out temporary GPS surveys around the Sumatran Fault. These data and other available observations will form the basis of physical models of fault slip that can simulate long sequences of earthquakes. These calculations account for all phases leading to earthquakes, including slow slip, earthquake initiation and rupture, and the propagation of seismic waves. An exploration of models with different physical properties of rocks will produce a range of plausible scenarios of future seismicity that will improve seismic hazard mitigation. The proposed research plan represents a timely opportunity for Singapore to promote earthquake preparedness and resilience and have a profound impact on people's lives in neighbouring nations.

title: Harnessing the Power of Next-Generation DNA Sequencing: Characterization of Human Transcriptomes and Transcriptome Regulation Mechanisms in Gastric Cancer
abs: My goal is to understand transcription and transcription regulation in a genome-wide manner in cancer. Cancer is a leading cause of mortality in the world today, and gastric cancer is a poorly understood, highly lethal cancer that is common in Asia. I propose to use next-generation sequencing-based methods to characterize major oncogenic transcription factor binding sites and chromatin interactions, non-coding and coding transcriptomes in cancer, and functionally characterize their relevance to cancer: (1) Characterize the binding sites and chromatin interactions of c-MYC, an oncogenic transcription factor, in gastric cancer. I propose to perform ChIP-exo and ChIA-PET on c-MYC to identify high-resolution binding sites and chromatin intractions, in AZ521 gastric cancer, and comparison with other cell lines such as K562 leukemia, and GM12878 lymphoblastoid cell lines. RNAi, overexpression and bromodomain inhibitors of c-MYC will be used to examine effects of c-MYC dysregulation on transcription. (2) Characterize the developmental and tissue specificities of normal human non-coding and coding transcriptomes. Non-coding RNA is poorly understood. I propose to conduct ribosomal RNA-depleted RNA-Seq in stomach tissues as well as a wide range of other normal adult and fetal tissues, to dissect differences in development and tissue specificity in human transcriptomes, with validations by Reverse Transcriptase Polymerase Chain Reaction (RT-PCR) and Sanger sequencing. (3) Characterize the relevance of novel non-coding RNAs to gastric cancer. I will perform RNA-Seq on gastric cancer cell lines, and combine RNA interference and overexpression using novel RNA with cancer assays, such as cell proliferation, cell mobility and anchorage-dependent growth, in gastric cancer cell lines. I will intersect the data from Aim 1 with other epigenomic and transcriptomic datasets, to understand modes of transcriptional regulation of non-coding RNAs. Taken together, these aims will generate a large resource of functional DNA elements with relevance to cancer.

title: Assessing seismic hazards in Southeast Asia by characterizing the geometries and slip histories of active faults
abs: I propose to study the 3D geometries and slip histories of active faults in Southeast Asia in order to assess seismic hazards and mitigate the impacts of future earthquakes. I will use a variety of datasets to constrain active faults, including industry seismic reflection data, well data, geological maps, fault maps, seismicity, historical earthquakes, and published cross-sections. I will also purchase and deploy an IVI EnviroVibe with a 240-channel seismograph to acquire high-resolution, shallow seismic data across the tips of active fault systems in order to constrain their slip rates and recent earthquake histories. These data will serve as the basis for improved forecasts of the magnitudes and frequencies of future earthquakes. Data that constrain active faults will be integrated into a 3D CAD environment to construct large-scale, regional 3D fault models that will be available to, and vetted by, scientists and emergency response planners. Such 3D “community” fault models have proven highly successful in fostering improved seismic hazards assessment in Southern California, and my goal is to implement them for areas of Southeast Asia. Initial study areas will include (1) the Intraplate Deformation Zone, Myanmar, (2) the Chittagong-Tripura fold belt, Bangladesh, (3) the Dauki and Naga thrusts, northeastern India, (4) the Main Frontal Thrust of the Himalaya, and (5) the Sumatran fault zone, Indonesia. These models will be used for improved probabilistic seismic hazard assessment, which is the primary mechanism used to establish building codes and insurance rates in many parts of the world. They will also allow us to simulate earthquakes on fault systems and generate movies and maps that provide quantitative predictions of the specific levels of groundshaking or other hazards. These hazard forecasts will serve to improve building codes, tsunami protection systems, and emergency response plans, which will save lives and protect property in future earthquakes.

title: Methods for Verifying Quantum Computation
inst: Singapore University of Technology and Design
abs: This project aims to develop techniques for ensuring that the output of a quantum computer is correct. Existing fault-tolerance techniques cannot be used to rule out systematic or malicious errors, or errors introduced by correlated noise. In order to ensure that the results of a computation are indeed correct, I intend to formulate the problem as an interactive proof system. Thus a main aim of the project is to settle the question of whether or not the complexity class BQP admits an interactive proof where the power of the prover is bounded to BQP. The project will be split into three phases. In the first phase, two verification scenarios will be considered. In the first setting, a purely classical user will be considered, while in the second the second the user is augmented with limited quantum capabilities. The aim of this phase is to determine if an interactive proof is possible in the first setting by attempting to construct a precursor protocol based on blind quantum computation. In parallel, work will be done to exploit existing blind computation protocols to address the second setting. The outcome of the first phase will determine which setting to focus on in the second phase, with preference for the first setting, where the aim will be to refine the results. In the final phase of the project the protocols developed in earlier stages will be tailored to specific physical systems with a view to experimental implementation. This research should support the development of quantum technologies in the near to medium term by providing efficient means to determine if the device is functioning correctly, and provide an objective means for proving that a device is indeed a fully functional quantum computer, without any need to reveal the architecture of the device itself.
kw: quantum computation;verification;interactive proofs;cryptography;physics;computer science

title: Novel Therapeutics Targeting the Core Regulatory Circuits in Human T-cell Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia
abs: Cancer is one of the leading causes of death worldwide, both in children and adults. Now that the technologies needed to precisely assess cancer-related genetic changes are at hand, one can identify specific oncogenic proteins and signal transduction pathways that are crucial for the sustained growth and survival of cancer cells and therefore offer attractive targets for molecular therapy. Using several of these innovative technologies, I recently identified the “core” transcriptional regulatory circuits controlled by the oncogenic transcription factor TAL1 in human T-cell lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) – a malignancy with a paucity of molecular targeted therapies. This discovery is significant because it showed, for the first time, that cancer/leukemia cells possess the same general transcriptional network motifs that control the pluripotency and self-renewal of embryonic stem (ES) cells. This observation led to the current application and its central hypothesis: those transcriptional circuits analogous to those in ES cells drive the initiation and maintenance of T-ALL and likely other types of leukemia/cancer as well. Thus, I propose to test the concept that disruption of this essential transcriptional machinery will provide more effective and less toxic cancer treatment than is currently available. The broad objective of this research is to exploit two potential T-ALL oncogenes that I recently discovered by RNA interference screens, TRIB2 and TYK2, to demonstrate the feasibility of this proposed strategy. A final aim is reserved for more exploratory studies to identify additional candidate drug targets, thus expanding the repertoire beyond TRIB2 and TYK2. Success in this project will not only validate the therapeutic approach outlined above, but should also generate a series of highly effective, first-in-class small-molecule inhibitors for future clinical testing. The knowledge gleaned from this work could well extend to other leukemia/cancer in which an oncogenic transcription factor controls the core transcriptional machinery.

title: Study to elucidate the influence of Cerebral White Matter Disease in the pathogenesis of Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease Dementia with combined Structural-Functional Imaging
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Dementia, a major public health problem in Singapore and worldwide is a result of .neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and Parkinson’s disease (PD). Cerebrovascular disease (CVD) may have a role in the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative diseases. This is of high significance to Asians, as the prevalence of small vessel CVD is high among Asians. Data from National Neuroscience Institute (NNI) has demonstrated that 70% of patients with AD and 60% of patients with PD have significant small vessel CVD. This small vessel CVD appears as white matter hyperintensity (WMH) on MRI scans.In this proposal we will investigate the longitudinal increase in WMH among patients with AD and PD and study how the increase in WMH burden influences cognitive performance and progression to dementia. We will also use diffusion tensor imaging to investigate microstructural changes to cerebral white matter tracts in relation to areas of WMH. With the use of resting state functional MRI, we will study the influence of WMH and microstructural changes in white matter tracts on the “Default Mode Network (DMN)” and “Executive Control Network (ECN)” in patients with AD and PD. DMN and ECN are two networks that correlate with cognitive status and disease progression in AD and PD. We hypothesize that over a 3 year period; there will be an increase in WMH volume with related microstructural changes to white matter tracts, which than will result in disconnectivity to the DMN and ECN. Findings on how white matter microstructural changes correlate to WMH volume and their influence on DMN and ECN will provide important insights into the pathogenesis of both AD and PD. Further clinical trials with novel treatment strategies can then be planned to reduce the burden of WMH. This will provide an opportunity to reduce the onset and progression of dementia.

title: Image and model-based human-robot collaborative system for large liver tumor ablation
abs: Hepatocellular Carcinoma is the sixth most common cancer and liver is the common site of metastatic diseases for intra-abdominal malignancies. Surgical resection of the metastatic hepatic tumor is the gold standard for treatment. Surgical treatment using the open procedure is an option for a small percentage of patients due to other co-morbid conditions like old age or other related diseases like uncontrolled diabetes or high blood pressure. Patients who are not candidates for the open procedure can gain benefit from an alternative procedure called radiofrequency ablation (RFA). RFA is a treatment technique which denaturizes the tumor cells with heat created from ionic agitation generated by a needle electrode. A limitation of RFA is the ablation volume coverage. In spite of the availability of medical devices for multiple needle ablations, they have not been proven to be successful when the diameter of the tumor is greater than 30 mm. A promising approach is to take advantage of medical imaging, computational models and robotic technologies to construct an integrated surgical navigation and medical robotic system with advanced human-robot interface for precise overlapping insertion-ablation of large tumors. --The engineering and clinicial investigators in Singapore and China will collaboratively research and develop a clinically viable system for animal experiments in 3 years. The tasks include:--(1) Design and implement a novel manipulator for radiofrequency ablation of large liver tumor. This is a continuation of the development of a patent pending robotic system. --(2) Design and implement a set of tools for optimization of ablation planning, including segmentation of liver parenchyma, hepatic vessels and lesions, simulation of the deformation of the liver during intervention, and stochastic finite element analysis for ablation prediction.--(3) Develop a prototype system by integrating the manipulator and the tools. A series of novel human-computer interaction methods will also be integrated in the prototype system to facilitate the execution of the surgical procedures. --(4) Evaluate the performance of the prototype system with animal experiments.--(5) Develop a deep understanding of the underlying bio-physics in thermal ablation therapy.If successful, the proposed solution could help save the lives of many patients, particularly those suffering from large liver tumors.

title: Structural basis and molecular mechanisms of isthmin-induced apoptosis toward anticancer therapy development
abs: Structural basis and molecular mechanisms of isthmin-induced apoptosis toward anticancer therapy development--A cancer is a complex organ whose behavior is influenced not only by genetic and epigenetic changes in cancer cells but also by stromal cells, local extracellular matrix and specific tissue architecture. The fast proliferation of cancer cells resulting from oncogene activation/tumor suppressor inactivation quickly lead to a cancer microenvironment that is hypoxic, acidic, starved of nutrients, rich in proteinases, growth factors/cytokines with altered metabolites. This unique cancer microenvironment leads to not only highly proliferative cancer cells, but also highly stressed cancer cells and activated blood vessel endothelial cells (ECs). ECs are the major type of stromal cells in cancer and cancer growth, survival and metastasis depend on the cancer vasculature to provide oxygen and nutrients as well as removing metabolic waste. Thus angiogenesis, the formation of new blood vessels, is a key target for anticancer therapy. --A major challenge of anticancer drug development is the severe side effects due to off-target toxicity and the shortage of cancer cell-surface specific target molecules that are absent in normal cells. Glucose regulated protein 78 kDa (GRP78) is one such protein whose presence on cell-surface is restricted only in cancer cells and activated ECs such as cancer ECs. In particular, the level of cell-surface GRP78 increases as cancer progresses to advanced stages and become highly metastatic. GRP78 promotes tumor proliferation, survival, angiogenesis, metastasis and resistance to chemotherapeutic agents. In normal cells, GRP78 is a major endoplasmic reticulum chaperone that functions as a master regulator of the unfolded protein response, facilitating protein folding and protecting cells from ER stress. However, in cancer, altered glucose metabolism (glucose starvation), impaired blood flow and hypoxia lead to GRP78 overexpression and translocation to cell-surfaces of both cancer cells and blood vessel ECs. Thus, targeting GRP78 has great potential for anticancer/antiangiogenic drug development. --We have identified that Isthmin (ISM) is a novel antiangiogenic/anticancer protein. Overexpression of ISM suppressed mouse tumor growth by inhibiting angiogenesis and inducing tumor cell apoptosis. Recently, we uncovered that cell-surface GRP78 is the high affinity receptor of ISM (Kd = 8 nM) and ISM-GRP78 interaction induces potent apoptosis in both ECs and cancer cells (unpublished). Significantly, ISM induces apoptosis more potently in highly metastatic cancer cells correlating with GRP78 up-regulation. Thus, we hypothesize that ISM or its derivatives have great potential to be developed into powerful dual targeting anticancer agents targeting both cancer cells and ECs. --In this proposal, we aim to determine the structural basis and molecular mechanisms of ISM-GRP78 interaction and apoptosis induction through X-ray crystall

title: Diagnostic and therapeutic application of functional secreted proteins in breast cancer
inst: IMCB - Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology
abs: Breast cancer is the most common malignancy in women. Although many breast cancer oncogenes have been identified, the causes for breast cancer development and recurrence are not clear yet. Our previous studies demonstrated that secreted proteins may play important roles in breast cancer; combinatory expression of several secreted proteins can promote transformation of breast epithelial cell. In addition, we hypothesize that secreted proteins are not only the regulators for breast cancer but also serve as biomarkers for breast cancer development and progression. Therefore, we aim to investigate systematically the roles of secreted proteins (alone or in combination) in breast cancer, and develop in vitro diagnostic assay for breast cancer based on detection of secreted proteins in the circulation. The achievements of this study will provide novel insight into the molecular mechanism of breast cancer development and offer novel diagnostic and therapeutic targets.

title: The Regulation and Function of Tumour Suppressor p53 and its isoform, delta113p53/delta133p53.
abs: Cancer, a leading cause of death, is a diverse group of diseases characterized by hyperplasia and metastasis. 50% of cancers possess a mutation in Tp53, a key tumour suppressor gene. It encodes a transcription factor that activates a large number of genes in response to cellular stress, and is activated by a number of biological processes, such as DNA damage, oncogene activation, heat shock, hypoxia, ribosomal stress, and metabolic stress leading to cell cycle arrest or apoptosis. --DNA Double stranded breaks (DSB) are the most catastrophic forms of genotoxic insult a cell can encounter. Improper repair of such damage results in genomic instability which predisposes an organism to immunodeficiency, neurological damage and cancer. As such, organisms have evolved three efficient systems to repair such damage. They are Homologous Recombination (HR), Non-Homologous End Joining (NHEJ) and Single Strand Annealing (SSA) pathways. Our preliminary data suggests that delta113p53 in the zebrafish may play a role in DSB repair following gamma-irradiation. First, we seek to develop assay systems that will allow the quantification of DNA repair by the aforementioned repair systems. This would allow us to investigate the role of delta113p53 (and delta133p53, the mammalian equivalent) in promoting DSB repair using zebrafish and mammalian tissue culture systems. --p53 levels are tightly regulated, primarily through a feedback loop, where it is targeted for degradation by one of its transcriptional targets, Mdm2, a ubiquitin E3 ligase, which targets p53 for degradation by the 26S proteosome. The interaction between p53 and Mdm2 is mediated through the N-terminus of p53. We have shown that the N-terminal truncated delta113p53 is not degraded via the Mdm2-26S proteosome pathway. --We have previously the identified the Digestive organ Enriched Factor (Def) in the zebrafish and described its crucial role in the development of organs of the digestive system. Our observation that Def promotes the degradation of both p53 and delta113p53 lead us to hypothesize that Def-mediated degradation of p53 and delta113p53 is ubiquitination independent. title: Toward Commercialization of Graphene Technologies
abs: The progress of CVD growth of graphene on metal substrates has been impressive. It seemed it would quickly enable graphene commercialization. Unfortunately, such graphene films have three critical drawbacks. First, such production methods are not scalable. Second, such grown graphene consists of many small domains, which are stitched together by forming defective domain boundaries. Such polycrystalline graphene films are in almost all relevant material parameters far inferior to that of single crystal graphene. In particular when strained, domain boundaries not only increase their electrical resistance, but also make them brittle and porous. In the short term, the sheet resistance of polycrystalline graphene is too high (~300 ohm per square). More importantly, such films cannot provide in the long term highly sought after flexible, transparent, conductive electrodes and/or gas barrier films. Since graphene’s uniqueness and its ultimate market advantage reside in its multi-functionalities, ITO replacement with polycrystalline graphene films is doubtful. However, even if it were possible to produce perfect CVD graphene, two fundamental obstacles remain. First, graphene grown on a conducting metal substrate needs to be transferred to a (transparent) non-conducting substrates. Current methods rely on a roll-to-roll process, which has been optimized for the transfer of conventional (flexible) thin films, but their mechanical and thermal properties differ fundamentally from that of atomically thin graphene film. Second, and equally important, intrinsically, graphene is highly resistive. Only after heavy doping does it become sufficiently conducting. Existing approaches both damage graphene during transfer and provide insufficient doping. The goal of this proposal is to develop the manufacturing technology for the production of commercial grade graphene. We will in particular establish a new multi-step, high-quality 2D graphene film growth process and a new large-volume, 3D graphene foam production process. Finally we will also develop a new transfer and doping process based on ferroelectric polymer coating.

title: Research and Development of Novel Interfacial Water Technologies
abs: In fluid mechanics the boundary conditions determine the flow on every length scale. Yet, the working hypothesis of free-slip and no-slip interfaces are largely unexplored experimentally. This region is mostly studied using simulations or by experiment which however do not resolve the last few molecules at the interface. Our proposal bridges this knowledge gap using high resolution environmental TEM for water flows on the nanoscale. Currently our group has the strategic advantage to be the only one able to create and observe liquid flows on the nanoscale. The proposal explores the spreading of flows and nanodroplets on chemically decorated surfaces. We'll study how nature resolved the singularity of a moving contact line and how nanobubbles are formed and test for their dynamic stability. The experiments will be supported by MD simulations and newly developed analytical models of this interfacial water. Our proposal aims to deliver knowledge on an largely unexplored length scale in fluid mechanics to tackle critical problems Singapore industry experiences: nanofiltration of water and ultraclean processing of silicon wafers, and filtration/membrane technologies

title: Non-volatile Magnetic Logic and Memory Integrated Circuit Devices
abs: The manipulation of magnetic domain wall in nanostructures promises potential technological applications in the field of sensors, logic and memory devices. Such magnetic memory device exploits the movement of magnetic domain wall that driven by pulsed electrical current along a ferromagnetic nanowire. In this research program we aim to confirm our unique design experimentally and develop that technology into non-volatile integrated circuit devices. The first project involves the design and fabrication of magnetic logic gate device that based on domain wall motion. When a domain wall propagates along a nanostructure, the wall spin direction can be controlled as either pointing upward (bit ‘1’), or pointing downward (bit ‘0’). Using a splitting geometrical design the manipulation of the wall spin direction is made possible, hence the realization of the magnetic logical operation. The second project involves the design and implementation of new magnetic memory architecture. This memory structure utilizes the movement of DW, which is fast and involves no movement of atom, hence the proposed memory device is high speed and has unlimited writing endurance. Our design is based on our modeling result that no applied electrical current is needed to flow through the memory storage element. Instead, the DW movement in the storage element can be driven via magnetic field coupling with adjacent DW.

title: Fundamental Limits and Applications of the Atomic Level Ion Source: (Angstrom Level Imaging and Quantum Foundry)
abs: Recent technological breakthroughs have enabled researchers to push imaging technology into the deep sub-nanometer regime. The Atomic Level Ion Source (ALIS) is at the heart of this revolutionary new capability, and the first instruments utilizing it are able to resolve features on solid samples with an edge resolution of a mere 2.5 Angstroms (0.25nm). The same properties that enable this phenomenal imaging capability promise to push pattern fidelity to a single nanometer so that a range of impossibly small and complex quantum devices are now realizable. While this capability is still in its infancy, the extraordinary resolving and patterning capability has been recognized as one of the most significant advances in nanotechnology in recent decades. Major programs have been launched in the USA and Europe to expand these capabilities, the most recent initiative is a $23M USD grant awarded to our development partner Zeiss-USA to explore semiconductor applications. Our research program is complementary to Zeiss’, and will initiate a series of research activities to explore opportunities of a more fundamental nature. A core element of our program is to establish a “Quantum Foundry”, dedicated to the realization of “impossible” devices, and to use these devices to perform experiments at dimensions previously accessible only to theoretical and simulation studies. These experiments can in-turn drive our fundamental understanding and contribute to new theories and new device concepts. Our investigations will concentrate on frontier fields rich with opportunities for discovery, such as plasmonics, spin-wave propagation and magnonics. The second core element is to improve the imaging performance of the ALIS to sub-Angstrom dimensions. This improvement, combined with the ability to image insulating samples and a novel approach to 3D reconstruction of sequential slices of biological specimens will open a whole new range of scientific problems that can be solved much rapidly, without artifacts.

title: Modeling and Simulation for Solid-State Dewetting Problems
abs: Funds are requested to carry out research on mathematical modeling, asymptotic and multiscale analysis, and efficiently numerical computation for studying numerically and theoretically solid-state dewetting problems and the morphological evolution of patterned holes/patches on a substrate with application in microelectronic processing, catalysts for the growth of carbon nanotubes and semiconductor nanowires, and the formation of nanocrystals for optical and magnetic devices. In fact, solid thin films are usually metastable or unstable in the as-deposited state, and they will dewet to form islands when heated to sufficiently high temperatures. The process is driven by surface energy minimization and can occur via surface diffusion well below a film's melting temperature. Although the problems are highly nonlinear, most existing theoretical approaches use linearized models and treat the problem in highly simplified geometries. Recent experiments demonstrate that such approaches miss important phenomena that are of highly scientific and potential technological interest, such as corner-induced instabilities, faceting, and break-up into patterns of islands. In this project, we propose to build new mathematical models based on the Chan-Hilliard equation with isotropic/anisotropic surface tension and variable mobility, design highly efficient and accurate numerical methods based on phase field approaches, establish mathematical theory for the models via asymptotic and multiscale analyasis, design efficient and accurate numerical methods for the models, implement the algorithms in parallel computing and/or three dimensions, and compare and predict new experiments related to solid-state dewetting problems. The results from this project will improve our understanding on solid-state dewetting of thin films and thus potentially help to guide in making arrays of nanoscale particle for electronic and photonic devices and for catalyzing the growth of nanotubes and nanowires.

title: High-magnetization ferrite films via a novel green-fabrication technique
abs: Soft magnetic materials are widely used in our life, from motor, generator of electric energy and transformer to small-sized electronic devices including recording head, antenna, inductor, microwave absorber/shielding and energy harvester. Applications of softmagnets usually require high magnetic flux (high saturation magnetization) and/or high magnetic permeability (dependent on the particular application). Frequently, high electric resistivity is required because of eddy-current loss particularly for high-frequency use. Oxide-based softmagnets (magnetic ferrites such as MFe2O4 with M = Mn, Ni, Zn or their mixture) form an important class of engineering softmagnets, due to their obvious advantages, such as low loss due to their high resistivity, chemical stability and low cost. However, magnetization of ferrites (in the order of 0.5 Tesla) is much lower than those of metal-based softmagnets (such as 2-2.5 Tesla for Fe-Co and ~ 1 Tesla for permalloy).Recently, our research has achieved a significant breakthrough. Using the simple chemical route - thermal decomposition, the obtained ferrite thick films (in order of mm) have exhibited high saturation magnetization over 1 Tesla. Our preliminary calculation results have shown that through a careful selection of doping (substitution), significant enhancement of saturation magnetization can be achieved.In this project, we will carry out a systematic study to develop novel ferrite magnet with high magnetization. We will develop a silicon-technology compatible fabrication process, so that high-quality ferrite films can be patterned into different nano- or micro-structure for device fabrication. We will explore commercial applications, such as recording head and soft-magnetic layer in high-density recording media in collaboration with DSI. Furthermore, we will also explore the potential in other applications, such as energy harvester (mobile power generation during moving - for example walking or under water), inductor-on-chip for power efficiency, electromagnetic shielding for IT (such as hand phone).

title: Unraveling the chemistry of catecholic building blocks: Biomimetic approaches to new materials
abs: Biomaterials, especially biopolymers containing catechol functionalities are abundantly found in nature. There is continuing, significant interest in being able to mimic the structures and functions of catechol containing biopolymers. This is, in part, due to the amazing range of properties that such biopolymers can display -from strong impenetrable and water repellent polymers (insect cuticle) to adhesives that can set and function under water (mussel glue). One critical factor impeding progress in this field is the need for better understanding of the chemistry that governs this class of compounds, the catechols. Specifically, nature mainly uses L-3,4-dihydroxy-phenylalanine (L-DOPA) and related compounds as building blocks in the biosynthesis of these polymers and yet the chemistry that underpins the polymerization reactions are not well-studied. As this knowledge is critical for further progress in biomimetic materials engineering, we aim to provide an understanding of the chemistry of these systems for potential manipulation of its reactivities and selectivities. Synthetic routes to novel DOPA and Dopamine (DA) analogues will be developed and a repertoire of these building blocks will be available. We will explore the structure-property relationships of two biomimetic systems incorporating these catechols as proof of concept of their potential applications in the specialty chemical industries e.g. in biomedical devices, in food packaging, coatings for fouling prevention and so on.

title: Modeling and Simulation of Moving Contact Lines in Complex Fluids
abs: A lot of efforts have gone into modifying the hydrodynamics model in order to remove or weaken the stress singularity at the moving contact line. These modified models either postulate slip occurs near the contact line or diffusion occurs across the fluid interface. While these models do succeed in weakening the stress singularity, they are often quite ad hoc and it is not clear whether they have anything to do with the real physics near the contact line. In one of the PI's recent work, a first-principle continuum model was derived for moving contact lines in Newtonian fluids. In this project, these results will be extended to complex fluids. A continuum model will be derived based on thermodynamics principles and molecular dynamics simulations. Macroscopic thermodynamic principles are used to place constraints on the form of the boundary conditions. This information is then used to set up molecular dynamics, from which the detailed constitutive relations in the boundary conditions are computed. Novel numerical methods will be developed for the contact line model. In the numerical methods, the fluid interface is tracked using the level set method; the capillary force on the fluid interface and the unbalanced Young stress at the contact line are treated as body forces and are included in the momentum equation and the slip boundary condition, respectively. In recent experiments, it was observed that even a small amount of polymers can strongly alter the dynamics contact angle and change the contact line speed. In this project, molecular dynamics and simulations at the continuum level will be carried out to understand the interaction between the flow field and the polymers, with particular attention to the influence of the polymers on the macroscale contact line dynamics. The simulation results will be compared with the experimental data.

title: Olefin-Heterofunctionalization via triple-relay catalyst system – Toward Formation of C-O and C-N bonds
abs: Olefin (C=C double bond compound) functionalization has been the study of many organic and organometallic chemists since the beginning of 20th century. Olefins are plentiful from either cracking of crude oil or biodiesel. Conversion of these inexpensive raw materials to higher-value chemicals using low production cost methods that also have low impact on the environment would have high economic returns on top of the scientific advancements brought on by the development. Single-step catalytic Anti-Markonikov olefin hetero-functionalization for the formation of terminal C-N bonds such as in intermolecular hydroamination, C-O bond formation in hydration and hydroalkoxylation or C-X bond formation in hydrohalogenation has been a long-standing challenge for both organic and organometallic chemists. At present, other than the Wacker oxidation process, there are no known, reproducible catalysts that can carry out single-step anti-Markonikov addition to produce primary-functionality (addition of heteroatom to less hindered carbon), which is often preferred for its higher reactivity compared to secondary functionality from Markonikov addition. In this proposal, we aim to develop catalytic systems that are able to heterofunctionalize olefins at the terminal position to yield linear alcohols/glycols and amines, all of which are important precursors for bulk/fine chemical, pharmaceutical and material industries. Multi-relay catalyst systems would be explored where a combination of several inter-compatible catalysts are combined in a single system to produce the desired conversions. Anti-Markonikov olefin hydration and hydroamination, the process to add a molecule of water or amine across an olefin to produce linear alcohols or amines, have been listed as one of the Top ten challenges of catalysis since 1993. Once successful, this development will bring immeasurable benefits to the scientific community as well as industry. Apart from using the multi-relay catalyst system for studying anti-Markonikov olefin heterofunctionalization, we can also adopt it for asymmetric hydration to produce chiral alcohols, selectively.

title: LogBase: A Scalable Log-Structured Distributed Data Platform
abs: Write-ahead-logging is a common approach for providing recovery capability while allowing no-force buffer management and improving performance in most storage systems, ranging from traditional DBMSes to the emerging cloud storage systems, a.k.a distributed key-value stores such as HBase and Cassandra. Nevertheless, the separation of log and application data in this approach incurs potential write overheads observed in write-heavy applications and therefore adversely affects the write throughput and recovery time in the system.--In this project, we propose to build LogBase - a scalable distributed log-structured database system that adopts log-only storage for removing the write bottleneck and supporting fast system recovery. LogBase is designed to be dynamically deployed in commodity environments to take advantage of elastic scaling property. LogBase will provide efficient multiversion indexes for supporting efficient access to data maintained in the log and efficient query processing. LogBase will also support transactions that bundle read and write operations spanning across multiple records.

title: Fabrication of Tissue-Engineered Tendon for Enhanced Healing Capability via E-Jetting Technique
abs: Clinical need in musculoskeletal tissue engineering, in particularly for tendon, has prompted the emergence of new bioscaffolding technologies since damaged or injured tendon rarely regain its normal biomechanical and biological properties. Existing scaffolds for tendon applications, even with cell augmentation, have yet to provide sustained, reliable long-term results. This is so because the internal microstructure is normally not recreated in the existing scaffolds. As such, the development of an engineered tendon graft implant that will allow cells to orientate and form matrix in specific microstructural architecture identical to that found in normal tendon, will be a breakthrough in bioscaffold technology and at the same time, a major step in the treatment of such injury, obviating donor site morbidity with autografts and tissue incompatibility with allografts. The proposed technology in this project - Electrohydrodynamic jetting (or known as E-jetting), has the ability to fabricate a 3-dimensional (3D) biocomposite scaffold that not only mimics the structure of native tendon, but also the structural orientation, thereby possessing the biomechanical competency required for tissue regeneration. The team also aims to immobilize appropriate growth factors on these scaffolds to enhance implant integration at the tendon-muscle interface. Biological testing will then be performed in vitro. While both the Principal Investigator (PI) and Clinical Co-PI have been very productive in their respective areas of research, this collaboration is a new joint venture that seeks to apply an engineering technology to meet a significant clinical need, which is of paramount significance in the fields of sport medicine and occupational injury. As this is a novel application of E-jetting technology to this special clinical need, the chance of interest from industry is envisaged to be high as the project is need-driven and technology-orientated. The project also incorporates novel aspects of scaffold precision engineering with advanced surface modification technique.

title: Dynamic Vision in the Sparse Way
abs: Our proposal comprises of complementary threads of research. The mathematical theories and the numerical algorithms are common across all applications. We aim to find better and faster numerical algorithms that can deal with the realistic conditions in various video-analytic problems. Specifically, a more general proximal-point based framework will be used as a template to solve nonsmooth convex problems with more complex constraint (e.g. inequality constraints, joint sparsity constraint) required to harness the specific structures of the problems. In terms of vision applications, we investigate problems crucial to a video analytic system: subspace clustering for motion segmentation, foreground /background classification for change detection, and feature/object tracking with higher-level interaction. For the motion segmentation problem, we seek to better capture the global structures of data than current sparse techniques and to better estimate the number of motion clusters, and to better handle the conditions where missing data, noise, and outliers are prevalent, and when the motions are partially dependent. For change detection, we aim to substantially improve the results achieved by conventional approaches in realistic sequences, by both exploiting the low dimensional structure of the background and the spatial connectedness of the foreground, and to dynamically adapt to the scale of the foreground objects. For feature/object matching under difficult conditions such as severe background clutter, we avoid a purely bottom-up approach but instead incorporate higher-level interaction. The feature set is augmented to include proto-object-like features whose appearance can be sparsely represented by a set of target templates. Together with outlier modelling, robust tracking can then be achieved by L1 minimization. We also carry out extensive study of suitable feature set for various problem including activity representation. Many theoretical and algorithmic issues are common to all these problems -that of linear inverse recovery of data with low dimensional structures.

title: Cyber Remote Control of Biological Legged Machine:   insect-machine hybrid walking system integrated with wireless neuromuscular stimulator
abs: The broad objective of the proposed research is to create a wireless biological machine, which is the fusion of a living organism and a man-made machine through neuromuscular stimulators. The stimulators are integrated with a radio built-in microprocessor unit (MPU) and implanted into the living organism. --Even state-of-the-art miniature ground robots have not matched yet with insect walking system in terms of power consumption, range, mobility despite many of them were inspired by insect system. What if we could remotely control the insect walking system itself with wireless stimulator? Compared with 1000 mW order of the power consumption in man-made machine, such an insect-machine hybrid walking system would save power down to 0.01 mW as electrical stimulation consumes power of just 0.01 mW. Such a hybrid system would not need complicated algorithm and control, which is necessary for man-made machine to transverse obstacles on ground, but just let the insect physically overcome the obstacles by itself. --We, the PI's research team, should have the most potential to realize such a hybrid system as we have developed a miniature neuromuscular stimulator and achieved radio control of insect flight in air. We map out the leg muscle configurations through anatomical investigation and conduct varieties of electrical stimulation to induce our desired leg motion. Insect walking gait will be elucidated through motion tracking by high speed camera and leg muscle potentials will be measured to find out which muscles are activated at which timing. We then have integrated stimulation protocols (what electrical stimulation signals are applied to which leg muscles at which timings) to induce our desired walking gait--The success of the research provides a miniature wireless biological legged machine, which extremely saves power, eliminates complicated manufacturing process and simplifies control algorithms compared with man-made legged machine.

title: Effectively Simultaneous Localized Manipulation of Multiple Magnetic Particles
abs: This proposed research aims to develop an engineering solution that enables simultaneous manipulation of multiple magnetic particles and to demonstrate its effectiveness and potential as a scientific instrument in a proof-of-concept application. --The proposed approach is to control the movement of a specially design magnetic needle to apply a magnetic force on the beads such that (i) the magnetic force thus applied on a given bead is localized and does not significantly affect other beads (if any) near by, and (ii) the application of the magnetic forces on the individual beads in an ensemble is to occur at a sufficiently high frequency to achieve effectively simultaneous localized manipulation of the beads.--The effectiveness and the potential for meaningful application of the developed solution will be demonstrated in the context of mechanical manipulation of ECM stiffness in real-time. This demonstration involves first embedding magnetic beads in the ECM via bio-conjugation such that the beads are firmly attached to the collagen fibers in the ECM, and then applying an external magnetic field to anchor the beads individually so as keep them in their nominal locations even under the influence of traction forces due to cell migration. This form of real-time anchoring of the beads creates resistance to the movement of the beads (and thus impeding the movement of the fibers), resulting in a change of apparent stiffness of the ECM as it is sensed by the migrating cells. The migration behavior of endothelial cells under the influence of such stiffness manipulation will be investigated, and the possibility of controlling angiogenesis by direct manipulation of the ECM stiffness will be explored.--Achieving this aim will confirm the developed solution as a pioneering technique for simultaneous and localized manipulation of multiple magnetic particles.

title: Magnetofluidic spreading: the roles of magnetoviscous effect, bulk magnetic force, magnetophoresis and convective transport
abs: The proposed project aims at the fundamental investigation of magnetofluidic spreading in microchannels. The use of magnetism provides a wireless and heat-free actuation concept for microfluidics. Micro magnetofluidics, the combination of magnetism and microfluidics, offers fundamentally new capabilities for the manipulation of heat-sensitive and pH-sensitive bioparticles such as bacteria, viruses and cells. In a preliminary study, we discovered the spreading phenomenon of the magnetic fluid core in a three-stream flow system under a uniform magnetic field. We called this phenomenon magnetofluidic spreading. We hypothesise that the four factors contributing to this phenomenon are: (i) the magnetoviscous effect, or the increase in viscosity of the magnetic fluid under an applied magnetic field, (ii) the magnetic force due to a gradient in magnetic properties, (iii) magnetophoresis and (iv) convective transport.--We will use a solution of dispersed magnetic particles as the magnetic fluid. We will experimentally investigate the role of magnetoviscous effect by varying the field strength, the size and the concentration of magnetic particles, as well as varying the relative orientation of the flow. We will investigate the role of magnetic force caused by the magnetic susceptibility gradient using ferrofluids, which show a negligible magnetoviscous effect. Magnetic force may induce secondary flow and instability that will be tested and confirmed experimentally. We will investigate how magnetic force acting on individual magnetic particles causes magnetophoresis. We will vary the flow rate to test the impact of convective transport on magnetofluidic spreading. We will formulate numerical models to gain more insights into the physics of this phenomenon. The results of this project will provide novel wireless technologies for important microfluidic applications such as micromixers, cytometers, cell sorters and tuneable optofludics. We intend to introduce these technologies into products and processes of the microfluidics foundry at SIMTech, A*STAR.

title: Luminescent Materials as Spectral Converters for Enhancing the Power Conversion Efficiency of Solar Cells
abs: One of the major problems in currently solar cells is the large range of wavelengths over which energy conversion has to take place. Due to the photovoltaic effect, low-energy photons are not absorbed at all by the solar cells, whereas high-energy photons are not used efficiently. This so-called spectral mismatch between solar cells and incident solar spectrum induces major energy losses in solar cells, leading to low energy conversion efficiencies of solar cells. To make full use of the solar spectrum, lanthanide (Ln3+)-doped up-conversion and quantum-cutting luminescent materials were proposed as potential spectral converters to reduce the spectral mismatch losses and, as a consequence, boost the efficiency of solar cells. Our proposed approach utilizes novel Ln3+-doped up-converting nanoparticle systems that can generate either tunable or single-band up-conversion emissions under near-infrared (NIR) irradiation that allows the output emissions match well with the external quantum efficiency of solar cells. On the other hand, we also aim at developing a common methodology to realize efficient visible-to-NIR quantum-cutting luminescence in Ln3+-doped nanoparticles. The main challenges of our proposal lie in the design of efficient energy-transfer host/activator systems and the integration of the as-prepared nanoparticles with solar cell devices.

title: Multiscale, high dimensional, stochastic mathematics and computation of composites and metamaterials
abs: Mathematically, classical methods are unsuitable for solving the equations of physical processes in composites whose properties vary with microscales, as these scales are much smaller than the macroscales of the domains, and require small discretizing mesh to capture, leading to prohibitive complexity. The equivalent effective equations describing macroscopic homogeneous behaviour of the materials are expensive to establish, and do not provide any microscale information. -The project formulates and justifies novel numerical methods that compute the macroscopic and microscopic information with high accuracy and minimum complexity by solving a macroscale equation in high dimensions whose solution contains all the information. We overcome the difficulty of high dimensions completely by developing a sparse finite element method that achieves equal accuracy to that for solving a macroscale equation in the low dimension of the physical domain, and requires only equal complexity. -We concentrate on Maxwell equations of electromagnetism but the research can be extended to other multiscale equations. The methods are especially advantageous for metamaterials. The coefficients of the high dimensional equation are those of the composites' components and are known. Whereas computing the effective coefficients and the microscale information is highly complex by standard routines due to the more complicated composite structures of metamaterials.-We also analyze and develop an optimal method for solving stochastic multiscale equations in composites whose properties are only known probabilistically. This is the case of metamaterials whose resonators are subject to manufacturing imprecision. -For metamaterials in the electromagnetic context, we study the scattering properties of the composites of negative effective electric permittivity and magnetic permeability. We perform mathematical analysis and propose novel numerical methods. -The project produces mathematically justified optimal numerical methods for solving complex multiscale problems in composites and metamaterials. It sheds lights into the unusual properties of metamaterials that cannot be found in natural ones.

title: Studies on the controllable inert carbon-carbon and related bonding cleavage through a selective oxidation-activation process
abs: Over the past decades, significant efforts were devoted to the synthesis of new chemical compounds and materials for different purposes such as medicines and plastics. Thus, scientific communities target mainly on how to make bonding between various atoms in order to construct functional molecules. A major focus is the formation of carbon-carbon bonding; this is an essential tool in various areas such as pharmaceutical industry, material science, and biomedical researches. --In a sharp contrast, the studies on inert bond breaking are sporadic. In many cases, breakings of inert carbon-carbon bond, and the related systems including carbon-oxygen and carbon-nitrogen bonds, are high energy processes; typically harsh conditions are required and the outcomes are uncontrollable.--In this proposal, we aim on the study of activation such kinds of inert carbon-carbon and related bonds through a selective oxidation process. The activation will facilitate a facile and mild carbon bonding cleavage. Our main objective is to develop a novel oxidation protocol which can selectively oxidize inert carbon-carbon and related bonds. Such oxidation can activate the inert carbon-X bonds (X = carbon, oxygen, nitrogen) which can facilitate the inert bond breaking under a mild condition. Potentially, such method can be applied to stable polymer and biomaterial degradation under mild conditions. The products after degradation can potentially be useful, for example adipic acid, which is widely utilized in chemical industry and is commonly synthesized from KA oil.--Currently, many research activities in ASTAR-SERC institutes such as ICES, SimTech, and IMRE are focusing on constructing novel compounds and materials. Many of these products contain inert carbon-carbon and related bonds. However, in most circumstances breaking such inert bonding are not investigated. This technology is a complementary effort to the current research focuses, which can open a new direction in the inert bond activation/breaking and subsequent structure modification.

title: Solvent Free Fabrication of Synthetic Porous Membranes for Engineering Three Dimensional Organized Tissues
abs: A novel discovery in our laboratory revealed that the heating and subsequent cooling of a layer of fine polycaprolactone particles on a water surface is capable of generating a thin, porous biodegradable membrane. However, the exact physical mechanism of membranization is unclear. Some qualitative understanding has been obtained, but a quantitative understanding on how these fluid particles coalesce on a liquid substrate to form a porous membrane is lacking. Moreover, the fabricated membranes may offer a myriad of potential applications that remain unexploited due to the novelty of the process. This research aims to model and simulate the phenomenon for quantitative understanding as well as to optimize the fabrication process for quality production, and then followed by a systematic characterization of the membrane in comparison with other membrane fabrication methods. This research also aims to develop a bio-patterned membrane , in which bioactive molecules and several cell types are controllably deposited on the surface of the membrane via a robotic dispenser to create a patterned cellularized surface. The bio-patterned membrane will be rolled up to create blood vessel like tubes and also stacked in a bioreactor allowing the cultivation of a three dimensional organized tissue, to replicate the 3D organization of native tissues and organs . This research will impact multiple disciplines. The mathematical model will contribute to physical sciences on understanding of a new natural phenomenon, which has the potential of leading to the development of new membrane technologies, while the bio-patterned membrane will advance tissue engineering and make a transformative progress towards organ engineering, which promises to bring immense medical benefits to the society.

title: Attosecond x-ray metrology of valence electron dynamics in nanoscale functional materials
abs: The recent advent of attosecond time-resolved spectroscopy has enabled the real-time tracking of electron dynamics in atoms and small molecules. The investigation of electron motion in complex molecules and materials, however, remains unexplored. The aim of the proposed research program is to develop new approaches to attosecond x-ray metrology and to apply them to observe electron motion in functional nanomaterials with attosecond time resolution. Nanoscale materials that will specifically be examined in the proposed work are nanoelectronic junctions and artificial light harvesting arrays. In the case of nanoelectronic junctions, attosecond spectroscopy will allow the observation of real-time charge transport across nanowires or single-molecules embedded in these junctions. In the case of artificial light harvesting arrays, the proposed research seeks to elucidate the effect of coherent electron motion on the quantum efficiencies of photovoltaic devices. From a fundamental standpoint, the above studies will shed some of the earliest insight into the physics of electron-phonon coupling and quantum decoherence involving nonstationary electronic states. Moreover a detailed understanding of the electron dynamics in nanoelectronics and photovoltaics gained from these studies will likely lead to the emergence of new guiding principles for enhancing the functionalities of these materials. To achieve this scientific goal, a tabletop experimental apparatus with attosecond x-ray spectroscopic capabilities will be designed and constructed. New measurement schemes that utilize a few-cycle optical pulse to initiate coherent electron motion and either attosecond x-ray absorption or Auger electron emission to probe the ensuing electron dynamics will enable the study of complex functional materials with attosecond time resolution. The new approaches to attosecond metrology that will be developed here can be further extended to allow the freeze-frame capture of other fundamental quantum dynamical processes that are relevant to physics, chemistry, biology, and materials science.

title: Experimental and computational investigations of topological electronic states in Sb-based thin films and nanostructures
abs: To make Sb ultra-thin films and nanostructures topological insulators (TI), a bandgap must be opened taking advantage of quantum confinement effect, whereas the topological surface states (TSS) need to be preserved. The latter requires the coupling between the TSS from different surfaces of the thin films or nanostructures to be relatively weak. In addition, a relative simple dispersion relation for the TSS is desirable for various application purposes. But the dispersion of TSS on (bulk) Sb(111) surface is strongly distorted from an ideal Dirac cone, therefore we will try different ways to modify the TSS dispersion. Specifically, We will carry out these research works: 1) Search for proper procedure to grow Sb thin films and nanostructures, and examine the bulk (interior), surface and edge states of these Sb structures to verify if they can be three-dimensional (3D) or 2D TIs, using ultrahigh vacuum low-temperature scanning tunnelling microscopy and spectroscopy (UHV LT-STM/STS) and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES); 2) Density functional theory (DFT) computational studies, effective Hamiltonian and tight-binding numerical modelling of the electronic states of these ultrathin films and nanostructures; 3) Modification of the properties of these TIs using doping, adsorption, alloying, strain effect and interfacing with other materials; 4) For thin film and nanostructural TIs, the coupling of the boundary states from different surfaces must be considered. We will characterize such coupling in our Sb-based samples and examine their effects on electronic and spintronic transport properties related to their device applications. We have already carried out preliminary experimental studies on the synthesis of Sb(111) and Sb(110) ultrathin films, and computational studies of the electronic structures of Sb(111) ultrathin films. The encouraging results of these preliminary works provide us with great confidence to pursue this exploration of Sb-based TIs.

title: A fast micro-Raman system for  high-resolution chemical imaging in biomedicine
abs: Raman spectroscopy has been widely adopted as a powerful tool to study cells and tissues in biology and medicine. The major advantages of this labeling free technique includes its high chemical specificity and non-invasiveness, which makes it particularly attractive in the biochemical analysis of biological samples. In contrast, the major disadvantage of Raman spectroscopy is the weak Raman signal coming out of most biological samples. As a result, Raman imaging of a biological sample with a reasonable spatial/spectral resolution is extremely time consuming, which is typically on the order of minutes to hours. This disadvantage has prevented Raman spectroscopy from being used to monitor the dynamic biochemical changes in cells. --We propose to develop a fast Raman imaging technique to enable the non-destructive and label-free chemical analysis of biological (or non-biological) samples in nearly real time, based on a special color camera and a compressive sensing method. While the color camera will capture all required narrow-band Raman images at once, the compressive sensing method will rapidly reconstruct the full Raman spectrum at each pixel from narrow-band measurements. The accuracy of the new Raman imaging system will be evaluated and the advantage of fast Raman imaging will be demonstrated in the visualization of drug diffusion in cells.--This new technique is expected to improve the speed of Raman imaging by a few orders of magnitude to be nearly in real time. This system will make it possible to use Raman spectroscopy to assess the dynamic biochemical changes in cells or tissues in fields such as pharmacology, biological science, tissue engineering and biomaterials. This technique can be also used to inspect non-biological samples in applications such as quality control in pharmaceutical industry, composition assessment in nanomaterials, or water quality monitoring in environmental science.

title: Role of Thymosin-?4 in enhancing function and survival of endothelial progenitor cells in diabetes mellitus
abs: Endothelial dysfunction plays a primary role in the development of vascular complications in diabetes mellitus (DM). It is known that high glucose level increases endothelial progenitor cells (EPC) apoptosis by inhibiting the PI3-kinase/Akt pathway. DM, with its associated dyslipidemia, inhibit EPC proliferation, reduce EPC numbers, inhibit migratory activity and in vitro angiogenesis. Improvement in the capacity of proliferation, migration and angiogenesis of EPC is a key factor in the success of therapeutic angiogenesis in DM.Thymosin-ß4 (Thy-ß4) possesses angiogenic activity and promotes endothelial cell migration, adhesion, tubule formation, and angiogenesis. Thy-ß4 promotes wound-healing and tissue-repair by inhibiting apoptosis and inflammation. However, the effects of Thy-ß4 on EPC derived from diabetic subjects are not known. The current study aims to investigate the effects of Thy-ß4 on function and survival of EPC derived from diabetic rat.EPCs isolated from Zucker Diabetic Fatty (ZDF) rat and treated with recombinant Thy-ß4 protein, will be assessed in vitro, in terms of apoptosis, survival, proliferation, migration, and tubular formation. Then, Thy-ß4 pre-treated EPCs will be assessed for therapeutic angiogenesis in a diabetic rat heart model of myocardial infarction. Echocardiography and microsphere injection will be performed to assess heart function and perfusion respectively, after which, the heart will be harvested for immunohistochemistry.We aim to provide new insights on the protective effects of Thy-ß4 on diabetes EPC, which has significant impact on endothelial function and regeneration of diabetic subjects. It will provide the scientific basis for which Thy-ß4 can be use to promote or rescue EPC function and survival in a diabetic environment. The enhanced endothelial function should reduce the incidence of macro- and microvascular diseases, which, in turn reduce morbidity and mortality in patients with diabetes mellitus. There is potential for future projects as a new therapeutic modality for treatment of endothelial dysfunction in diabetic patients.

title: In vivo Control of Muscular Motor-Reaction by Electrical Stimulation for Wireless Bio-Machine Hybrid System
abs: In order to fine tune the wireless bio-machine hybrid system, we will bridge the gap between the electrical stimulation from a man-made machine and computer, and the motor reactions and behaviors of a living organism. The flight muscle of Mecynorrhina torquata, a live beetle, is selected as a model system. The remote radio control of insect flight has been demonstrated by the Singapore principal investigator (PI). Based on the strong background of the Japan PI on the muscle physiology and the florescence microscopy, this collaborative research is now developing a new in vivo microscopy system to observe the Ca2+ dynamics in single flight muscle fibers in a live beetle. We will then compare the microscopic analyses between the measurements in natural turn in tethered flight and the one in electrically stimulated turn by the electrode implanted into the flight muscles in tethered flight. The electrical stimulation protocol is to be improved to induce arbitrary turns during the flight. Finally, the improved stimulation protocol will be examined in the free flight (no tethering) through the wireless communication. The research activities will be mainly held in Nanyang Technological University and Waseda Bioscience Research Institute in Singapore managed by Waseda University of Japan, both of which are located in Singapore. The current insect-machine hybrid system, often referred to as Cyborg Beetle, will advance the understanding of neuromuscular physiology as well as the more detailed mechanics of insect flight muscles and the flight itself. Potential applications include a micro flyer with thermo sensors, for example, which would help rescue missions especially in disaster areas. It can navigate into tiny spaces and locate missing people. The methodology developed here would be used clinically in future for a therapy of human paralyzed patient by wirelessly communicating with the brain machine interface.

title: Development of wearable micro blood flow sensors for livestock breeding
abs: The commercial wearable blood flow sensors can only be used at well-controlled occasions such as hospitals. Prof. Sawada, PI, successfully developed a laser Doppler blood flow microsensor which was used to monitor the blood flow of chickens and collect information for preventing avian influenza infection. To develop a generic micro-blood-flow-sensor ( microBFS) used in various applications, the grand challenges are location and method of attaching the microBFS to skin of animals and/or humans. For example, the loose contact between microBFS and skin leads to weak signals, while the optimal measurable skin depth varies from one animal to another. By combining optical MEMS and ultrasonic MEMS, a novel integrated microBFS will be developed with capability of measuring blood flow in wide range of skin depth. More clearly, optical- microBFS gives high resolution in a shallow part near the skin and ultrasonic-mBFS may detect the blood flow in a deeper part from the skin. The ultrasonic- microBFS deploys piezoelectric suspended membrane and phononic-crystals-based acoustic lens to generate focused ultrasonic wave propagating to much deeper region. Meanwhile, this microBFS can also detect the contact pressure in order to make sure the tight contact between skin and microBFS in vitro animal testing and can make the livestock insensible to the existence of the sensor and reduce the mental stress in mounting. It has been reported that blood flow of cows increases in estrous period. We will further apply this microBFS to the detection of estrus insemination timing by monitoring the blood flow of cows so as to enable efficiently artificial insemination. By leveraging research outcome developed in this project, we can further explore applications of this microBFS to various livestock and humans at the end of this project, leading to the formation of Asian bio-industrial infrastructure centered at Singapore and Japan.

title: A ferritin-based DNA sequencer via nanoimprint technology
inst: IMRE - Institute of Materials Research and Engineering
abs: This proposal seeks to develop a technique of reading DNA sequences using an electrical method. Nanoimprint and biomineralization technology will be jointly used for arraying metal nanoparticles (NP). Homogenous metal NPs ranging from 3 nm to 8 nm will be synthesized and enclosed inside cage-shaped protein molecule, ferritin or Dps (DNA binding protein from Listeria Innocua), and delivered to specific positions designated by nanoimprint technology. Selective elimination of the protein shell yields metal NP array, to which probe-DNA single strands will be attached, resulting in their precise high density ordering. The density of array and each DNA position are nanometrically controlled so that maximum hybridization efficiency and lower errors are realized. These DNA arrays will be connected to electrodes for the electronic detection of DNA hybridization. This involves the principle of charge transfer through double stranded DNA using electron donor-labeled oligonucleotides. The ability to detect DNA hybridization events with an electrical output will be a technological advance in the development of DNA chips. Furthermore, with this novel method of sequencing through hybridization, DNA sequences can be converted to bar-coded token sequences. Realization of this goal will be directly useful in many current DNA array applications such as DNA microarray diagnostic chips, single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) detection, and especially, 'Token DNA Sequencing'.

title: Insulin Resistance and Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) in Older Adults with Pre-Diabetes andDiabetes: Cognitive Effects of Lifestyle Intervention and Metformin Treatment in a RandomizedControlled Trial
abs: "Vascular-related risk factors are now widely recognized to play hugely important roles in the etiology of both Alzheimer’s disease and vascular dementia. Experimental and clinical studies amply support the pervasive role of insulin resistance in increasing the risks of rapid cognitive decline and dementia in diabetic and non-diabetic individuals. The strategy of lowering insulin resistance is thus highly promising. Recent failed trials of rosiglitazone, an insulin sensitizer with adverse cardiovascular effects were disappointing, because they were conducted in patients with established Alzheimer’s disease. Secondary prevention studies of selected populations with high risk of cognitive decline and dementia such as prediabetic and early diabetic patients with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) may be more fruitful. We propose a 24 month randomized controlled study among over-weight or obese, pre-diabetes or untreated diabetes individuals with amnestic MCI or non-amnestic multidomain MCI, to test the hypothesis that: the lowering of insulin resistance (as indexed by the homeostasis model assessment (HOMA-IR) with exercise and dietary modification with or without metformin as appropriate would be associated with: (1) relative increase in regional cerebral glucose metabolic rate (CMRglu) as measured by fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG PET) in areas known to be associated with increased risk of Alzheimer disease (AD) and vascular dementia (VaD), and (2) decreased rate and relative risk of cognitive decline on domains characteristically associated with AD and VaD using a battery of sensitive neurocognitive tests. This research will provide pivotal findings for evidence-based management of prediabetic and diabetic patients for the prevention of cognitive impairment and dementia, and for public health strategies for dementia prevention using targeted population lifestyle interventions."

title: PEG INTERFERON IN NUCLEOS(T)IDE TREATED PATIENTS RANDOMISED TOCONTINUE NUCLEOS(T)IDES, ADD-ON OR SWITCH THERAPY (INITIATE TRIAL)
abs: Chronic Hepatitis B afflicts 400 million people worldwide, causing significant morbidity and mortality. Nucleoside analogues (NAs) can rescue patients with significant risk of disease progression, but most require long-term therapy as HBsAg-seroclearance was uncommon, and stopping therapy was associated with relapse and hepatitis B flares. Pegylatedinterferons therapy showed an increased HBeAg-seroconversion rate compared to NAs but the combination has no advantage compared to pegylated-interferon monotherapy. However, it is unclear whether the combination of pegylated interferon and nucleosideanalogue therapy was optimized. Small studies with adefovir and pegylated-interferon showed a surprising high rate of HBsAg-seroclearance but this may be peculiar to certain genotypes. There is an unmet need for the large number of patients on long-term NAs therapy who have not achieved HBeAg-seroconversion (HBeAg-positive CHB) and those who have not achieved HBsAg-seroclearance (HBeAg-negative CHB). An exploration of add-on or switch to pegylated-interferon is an attractive option but this has not been studied. We propose to take advantage of the hundreds of patients in this category to examine if addon or switch to pegylated-interferon can improve endpoints. Patients fulfilling inclusion and exclusion criteria will be randomized to add-on pegylated-interferon, switch to pegylated interferon or remain on NA therapy (2:2:1 ratio). The primary endpoint will be a composite endpoint of HBeAg loss (for HBeAg-positive patients) or qHBsAg reduction of >1log (for HBeAg-negative patients) at week 72. Reduction in qHBsAg>1log is a strong indicator of subsequent HBsAg-seroclearance. Estimated sample size is 310 patients randomized to add-on pegylated-interferon, or switch to pegylated-interferon or continued NA in 2:2:1 ratio (124:124:62 patients) stratified by HBeAg status and fibroscan score. Pegylated-interferon treatment will be 1.5?g/kg weekly for 48 weeks, with a further 24 weeks of follow-up (total study duration 72 weeks). Multivariate analysis will be performed on baseline and ontreatment factors that predict the primary outcomes.

title: Gene Polymorphisms and Response to Bacillus Calmette-Guerin Therapy for Bladder Cancer
abs: Bacillus Calmette-Guerin (BCG) is the gold standard immunotherapy for non-muscle invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC). We had previously showed that NRAMP1 gene polymorphisms correlate with BCG response in Asian NMIBC patients. We seek to validate our results in a larger patient cohort, and hypothesize that NRAMP1 gene polymorphisms may predict cancer recurrence and response to BCG therapy in a more heterogenous population. We also seek to compare its predictive value with other known gene polymorphisms that have been suggested to predict for BCG response or bladder cancer risk. We aim to 1) determine if NRAMP1 gene polymorphisms can predict the clinical outcome of Asian and Caucasian NMIBC patients who have undergone BCG therapy, 2) compare and evaluate the NRAMP1 gene polymorphisms’ predictive values in Asian and Caucasian NMIBC patients, 3) compare its predictive value and possible synergism with other known gene polymorphisms. A multicentre study in Singapore, Hong Kong and Switzerland will be conducted. NMIBC patients (n=300) who had transurethral resection (TUR) and received at least a minimum 6 once-weekly plus 3 once-aweek intravesical BCG for EORTC intermediate or high risk disease, will be retrospectively recruited. Peripheral blood samples (10ml) of NMIBC patients and controls from each centre will be collected, stored and transported in -20 oC. Genomic DNA will be isolated from the frozen blood. Genotyping assays (Goldengate Genotyping Assay, Illumina) and mutation screening using high resolution melting (HRM) analysis will be used to assay for sequence variations. Patient demographic, initial disease characteristics, vaccination status, intravesical BCG therapy details, and clinical outcome data will be collected and analyzed using multivariate and Kaplan–Meier analyses. Our proposed work may help to determine the relative importance of gene polymorphisms (including NRAMP1 and other genes), and providing insight on ethnic differences, and their possible synergistic value in predicting BCG response for NMIBC patients.
