title: Molecular, cellular, and metabolic regulation of thyroid hormone-mediated hepatic lipophagy
abs: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is a progressive disorder that commences with hepatosteatosis, progresses to fibrosis, and can lead to cirrhosis (1). It is commonly associated with obesity and diabetes, and its incidence is increasing dramatically worldwide, including Asia (2). Currently, there is no effective drug therapy for NAFLD. Recently, we found that thyroid hormone (TH, T3) surprisingly stimulates autophagy, a catabolic process that promotes cell survival during starvation and metabolic stress, in human hepatic cells in vitro and in mouse liver in vivo (3). Moreover, T3–mediated hepatic autophagy involves incorporation of lipids from fat droplets into autophagosmes that fuse with lysosomes (lipophagy). This process leads to hydrolysis of triglycerides and generation of fatty acids that undergo ? oxidation within mitochondria. Thus, T3 stimulation of hepatic lipophagy is tightly coupled with induction of fatty acid metabolism. Our findings demonstrated a critical role for T3-mediated autophagy in normal lipid homeostasis as well as suggested that defects in TH-mediated hepatic autophagy may be responsible for the hepatosteatosis observed in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). In this proposal, we plan to characterize the mechanisms and physiological role of T3-regulated autophagy within the liver. Thus, we will pursue the following Specific Aims: 1) Determine the molecular, cellular, and metabolic mechanisms involved in T3-mediated hepatic autophagy and fatty acid ? oxidation. 2) Determine the nutritional and endocrine mechanisms that regulate T3-mediated hepatic autophagy in vivo and their dysregulation in hepatosteatosis. It is expected that better understanding of T3 regulation of lipophagy will help identify novel drug and hormonal targets that can be used for the treatment of NAFLD, a condition for which there currently is no proven effective drug therapy. Additionally, insight into T3 regulation of autophagy may improve the clinical management for the most prevalent endocrine maladies-diabetes and thyroid disease.

title: Whole exome sequencing to identify genes for extreme myopia in Asian populations
abs: "There is an epidemic of myopia in urban Asian cities such as Singapore. Extreme myopia is associated with visually disabling ocular pathologic lesions and is likely to be enriched with heritable predispositions in contrast to common low myopia, a disorder largely attributed to environmental factors. We propose to launch a whole exome sequencing approach to interrogate rare variants and identify novel genes for extreme myopia in a homogenous Singapore Chinese population with replication in several Chinese and Japanese populations. Whole exome sequencing will be performed using the Nimblegen SeqCap EZ exome kits in 700 cases of extreme myopia defined as SE at least - 10.0 D and 700 non-myopic controls with SE > -0.5 D in Singapore Chinese. Each sample will be sequenced to high coverage (50X) on the Illumina HiSeq 1000 platform using 101bp paired end sequencing. Variant detection and filtering will be performed using the Genome Analysis Toolkit (GATK) pipeline. The top genes (p<10-4) identified by mutational load-based analysis (burden test) with the strongest associations with extreme myopia from the discovery study will be validated in an independent case-control in Sichuan, China with readily available exome sequencing data. Furthermore, an estimated 1-2 genes in the Sichuan collection with a Bonferonni corrected p < 0.05 will be replicated by deep re-sequencing in 2 Chinese (Hong Kong; Wenzhou, China) populations and further confirmed in 1 Japanese population (Kyoto). Ocular tissue gene expression profiles of extreme myopia genes confirmed by replication studies will be characterized in human fetal and adult, as well as mouse myopia models. The identification of novel genes for myopia will lead to the development of gene tests for high risk children who may benefit most from interventions to slow the rate of progression of myopia and prevent the development of extreme myopia when the child reaches adulthood."

title: EZH2 Deregulation in Natural killer/T-cell lymphoma (NKTL)
abs: "Extranodal natural killer/T-cell lymphoma (NKTL) is among the most aggressive lymphoid neoplasms with very poor prognosis. We found that EZH2 is aberrantly over-expressed in NKTL in comparison to normal NK cells1. EZH2 is the catalytic component of the polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2), which methylates lysine 27 of histone H3 to epigenetically silence genes. EZH2 expression is an independent prognostic marker that is correlated with the aggressiveness of prostate, breast and endometrial cancers. The potential of EZH2 as an oncogene is supported by the findings that suppression of EZH2 by RNAi significantly decreased tumor growth in breast and prostate tumor xenograft models and overexpression of EZH2 confers invasiveness and immortalized benign mammary epithelial cells. By contrast, the most recent discoveries reported identification of recurrent somatic EZH2 mutations in lymphoma2, myelodysplastic syndromes and myelodysplastic / myeloproliferative neoplasms3, 4, and indicate that inactivation of EZH2 contributes to the pathogenesis of myeloid malignancies. Considering the fact that EZH2 acts as an oncogene in certain cellular contexts and as a tumor suppressor in others, there is a pressing need to dissect the potential role of EZH2 in NKTL and decipher mechanistic consequences of EZH2 overabundance in NKTL. We will carry out a series of analyses and experiments as outlined in this proposal aiming to 1) study the functional and molecular consequences of EZH2 overexpression in NKTL through knockdown studies using RNAi as well as genome-wide techniques, including microarray and chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing; 2) study the mechanism of EZH2 over-expression in NKTL with particular focus on regulation by miRNAs; 3) therapeutic targeting of EZH2 in NKTL using PRC2 inhibitors. The study would provide insight in the pathogenesis and tumor biology of NK-cell malignancies, and would be informative to the development of targeted therapy for this disease."
kw: Natural killer/T-cell lymphoma (NKTL), EZH2, Overexpression, Therapy

title: Persistent rhinitis and wheezing in early childhood - Its relationship with upper airway microbes
abs: Background: The Allergy sub-study of the GUSTO (Growing up in Singapore towards Healthy Outcomes) birth cohort has been ongoing since 2009. Its focus on early childhood persistent rhinitis has shown that it is relatively common (10.6% at 12mths) and is associated with wheeze and maternal atopy. In this proposal, we hypothesize that persistent rhinitis (>4weeks) and recurrent wheeze at the age of 5years is not only influenced by the presence of atopy (IgE sensitization), but this risk is amplified by the presence of certain upper respiratory microbes (and their diversity) in early life. Specific Aims: (1)To evaluate the clinical phenotypes of persistent rhinitis and allergic disorders in the first 5years of life of the GUSTO cohort (n=1283), including IgE sensitization to common food and environmental allergens, (2)To detect respiratory viruses, mycoplasma pneumoniae and common bacteria colonizers using molecular techniques, and analyze commensal bacterial diversity from archived nasal swabs taken at regular intervals in the first 18months, (3)To correlate the results on microbes with the clinical outcomes of persistent rhinitis and wheeze/asthma at age 5years. Methods: This study will continue follow-up of this cohort from age 15 till 60months by active screening for rhinitis/wheeze/eczema, compilation of environmental data via home/clinic visits and structured questionnaires. Nasal swabs which were obtained at 7time points will be subjected to realtime PCR for the detection of respiratory microbes and viruses. IgE sensitization will be assessed by skin prick test to common allergens at 18, 36, and 60months. Data will be stored in a web-based dataset, and analyzed to determine the clinical characteristics of rhinitis and correlate microbiological studies. Benefits: This large scale population-based prospective birth cohort study will fill current knowledge gaps of early life persistent rhinitis, especially regarding the role of respiratory microbes. These results may translate to rationale strategies on prevention and management.

title: Targeting autophagy for cancer prevention and cancer therapy using anoncogene-driven hepatocellular carcinoma model in zebrafish
abs: "At present the involvement of autophagy in cancer remains a highly controversial and debatable topic. One common understanding is that autophagy suppresses tumorigenesis at the initiation stage, but promotes tumor growth at the promotion and progression stage. So far, most of the evidence supporting such a notion is from in vitro cell culture or cancer cell xenograft models, with very limited information in animal models with primary tumor. The zebrafish is now a well established model system in cancer research and we have established a zebrafish hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) model by inducible expression of xmrk oncogene, an epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) homologue in Xiphophorus (platyfish). Therefore, the zebrafish cancer model provides an excellent opportunity to evaluate the role of autophagy in tumorigenesis in vivo. The main objective of the proposed study is to understand the role of autophagy in oncogene-driven tumorigenesis, based on the hypothesis that autophagy has a dual function in tumor development: suppressing the tumor initiation and fostering the tumor promotion-progression. The specific aims of the study include: 1) To trace the changes of autophagic flux in zebrafish liver in liver tumorigenesis process induced by transgenic expression of xmrk, 2) To investigate the function of autophagy on xmrk-driven tumorigenesis in zebrafish liver by induction of autophagy using target of rapamycin (TOR) inhibitors, 3) To investigate the function of autophagy on xmrk-driven tumorigenesis in zebrafish liver by inhibition of autophagy using a chemical inhibitor chloroquine (CQ), 4) To establish and characterize a mifepristone-inducible liver-specific dominant negative (DN) Atg5K130R transgenic zebrafish, 5) To investigate the function of autophagy on xmrk-driven tumorigenesis by suppression of autophagy through inducible over-expression of DN-Atg5K130R in zebrafish liver, 6) To test the therapeutic potential of autophagy suppression in xmrk-driven hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) in zebrafish, by using chloroquine (CQ) in combination with EGFR inhibitors."

title: Building Oral Microbiome to Identify Novel Biomarkers/Modulators for EarlyChildhood Caries and Oral-Systemic Link
abs: Dental caries is a diet-related chronic infectious disease with approximately 5 billion people suffering it worldwide. Despite the great progress in caries control, early childhood caries (ECC) remains the most common chronic childhood disease. A skewed distribution of caries has been observed in many developed countries, with 25% of children bearing 75-80% disease burden. Recently, caries resurgence has been documented in many developed countries. In spite of 100% water fluoridation coverage in Singapore, 40% caries prevalence and 43.7% incidence rates were revealed in our recent population-based study, posing a great need to search for novel preventive strategies/therapies. Furthermore, the oral cavity is a unique bacterial reservoir with at least 35% unknown species in diverse ecological niches. Although periodontal diseases have been associated with cardiovascular and other systemic diseases among adults, little is known regarding pediatric oral-systemic link(s). Using a microarray technology, oral microbiota was recently linked to pediatric inflammatory bowel disease. Utilizing an arguably leading technology (Rapid Multiplexed 16s Barcode Sequencing) to understand how oral microbiome exerts influence on oral/general health, this prospective study aims to identify novel caries risk markers/modulators and oral-systemic links, with comprehensive pre-, peri-, and post-natal data collected from 1,200 participants of the GUSTO cohort; through prospective questionnaires, clinical examinations, and biofilm sampling. Both the traditional statistical methods and unconventional computational programs with artificial intelligence will be employed to unravel dynamic complex interactions between microbiota, diet, and biopsychosocial factors pertinent to ECC and oral-systemic link(s). With multidisciplinary teamwork and comprehensive longitudinal data collection, this study is positioned to generate new knowledge/insights to tackle major chronic childhood diseases and to explore the largely unknown pediatric oral-systemic link. If successful, this project may help healthcare professionals and policy makers to develop cost-effective diagnostic, therapeutic, and preventive measures/strategies for better quality of life of children in Singapore and beyond.

title: Singapore INfra-Genicular Angioplasty with PAclitaxel-eluting balloon for Critical Limb Ischaemia (SINGA-PACLI) Trial
abs: "Background: In patients with critical limb ischaemia (CLI), the infragenicular arteries are often involved. Without revascularisation, amputation often is imperative. There is a high technical success rate of endovascular revascularisation of infragenicular arteries with percutaneous transluminal angioplasty (PTA), but mid- and long-term results are disappointing as restenosis frequently occurs. Drug-eluting balloon (DEB) PTA has been shown to improve patency rates after PTA of coronary arteries. Aim: To study the results of DEB PTA compared to conventional balloon (CB) PTA for the treatment of infragenicular lesions in patients with CLI. Hypothesis: DEB PTA results in improved patency rates compared to CB PTA for treatment of infragenicular arterial lesions in patients with CLI. Methodology: Multi-center, prospective, randomised parallel-group trial. Patients are eligible for enrolment if they have CLI and at least one infragenicular lesion with a maximal total lesion length of 20cm. Randomisation will be performed on a 1:1 ratio to either DEB PTA or CB PTA. Patients will be assessed prior and directly after the intervention, at 3, 6 and 12 months by Rutherford classification, ankle-brachial index, toe pressure and adverse events. Duplex will be performed at 3 months. Angiography will be performed before and directly after PTA and at 6 months. Primary end-point will be primary patency of the treated lesions at 6 months after intervention on angiography (defined as <50% stenosis, without re-intervention in the interim). Secondary end-points are limb salvage at 3, 6 and 12 months, primary patency of the treated lesion on Duplex at 3 months (defined as patency of the treated artery with peak systolic velocity (PSV) ?2.0 m/sec) and Rutherford classification, minor and major amputation, infrapopliteal endovascular re-intervention, patency of treated femoropopliteal sites (if applicable), infrapopliteal surgical bypass, peri-procedural complications and death at 3, 6 and 12 months."

title: Phase I trial of OXIRI [oxaliplatin (O), xeloda (X) and irinotecan (I)] as first line treatment in patients with advanced and/or metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma
abs: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is one of the most aggressive cancer in humans with a poor 5-year survival rate of less than 5%. Several deregulated biological pathways coupled with limited means of early detection and presentation at advanced stages of disease partly contributes to the poor survival rates. The choice of treatment with chemotherapeutic agents is dismal and chemoresistance to treatment is a common phenomena. The majority of chemotherapeutic agents employed in the treatment of PDAC have demonstrated little or no activity in phase II studies. Gemcitabine has been the only agent used to date in the treatment of PDAC following the pivotal trial by Burris et al [37] which demonstrated its clinical benefit over 5-flurouracil (5-FU). Gemcitabine was shown to improve median survival by 5.6 months and the response rate was 5%. Several doublet and triplet agent trials have since been designed and tested with gemcitabine as the backbone of these trials in an attempt to further improve the survival and overall outcome but the results have not been promising. Recently, the FOLFIRINOX regimen, a gemcitabine-free regimen was shown to be superior to gemcitabine with a significant improvement in median survival from 6.8 months to 11.1 months, albeit at a cost of higher toxicity. Thus the current treatment status of pancreatic cancer is inadequate and necessitates the need for more effective regimens that are also less toxic. The aim of this exploratory Phase I study is to assess the safety and efficacy of the OXIRI regimen [oxaliplatin (O), xeloda (X) and Irinotecan (I)], a gemcitabine-free regimen in patients with advanced and/or metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma. We hypothesize that 2 of 3 weekly doses of oxaliplatin and irinotecan in combination with xeloda administered in a continuous chronomodulated fashion will be more tolerable than the FOLFIRINOX regimen with improvement in response rate.

title: Protein Aggregation Diseases: Clinical Manifestations to Biochemical Characterization for the Intervention of TGFBI-associated Corneal Dystrophies
abs: "In recent years, there has been a significant number of publications, especially in Asia, in the number of reported cases of stromal corneal dystrophies (CDs). CDs are characterized as a group of bilateral, heterogeneous inherited disorders. The majority of these CDs in the stromal layer of the cornea have been attributed to mutations found on the TGFBI gene coding for a 683-amino acid transforming growth factor induced protein (TGF?Ip). Defects in this gene lead to progressive accumulation of protein aggregates in the cornea that can result in loss of corneal transparency and hence vision. At present, 63 distinct pathogenic mutations have been identified in TGFBI that are associated with different clinical phenotypes. Though TGF?Ip is present in various other tissues, only cornea-specific aggregation is triggered by the occurrence of these mutations. Current treatment relies on laser/ surgical intervention, which often involves high recurrence rates. Since there are no effective medical treatments of TGFBI-associated CDs, this research project aims to develop viable therapeutic strategies to treat these dystrophies. Following genetic analysis and clinical characterization of patients with TGFBI-associated CD mutants, clinically significant proteolytic mutants will be recombinantly expressed and examined. The biophysical and biochemical aspects of the mutations will be analyzed. The present study will involve the development of in vitro models of protein aggregation and evaluating the role of pharmacological chaperones (PCs) capable of inhibiting or dissolving the aggregates. This will allow us to develop a novel therapy for these stromal dystrophies. Expanding the relevance of this study is the report that the age-dependent accumulation of structurally aberrant, aggregation-prone proteins has been implicated in the pathogenesis of over 30 heritable disorders including Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and Huntington's. Hence the development of PC to dissolve aggregates can have more widespread medical indications. "

title: Developing paclitaxel-loaded poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) particles as a treatment modality in breast cancer
abs: Background. Chemotherapy is an important modality in the treatment of breast cancer. However, it is limited by significant systemic toxicity and poor drug penetration of the tumour mass. Drug-loaded particles administered directly to the tumour produced a more marked and sustained therapeutic effect compared to the free drug in preclinical studies. Aims. In this study, we focus on 3 primary objectives that will bring this technology closer to clinical trials. We aim to optimise the distribution of paclitaxel-loaded poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) particles within the tumour, to evaluate the effect on regional nodal disease and the effect on adjacent normal tissue. Secondary objectives of this study are to evaluate our proposed strategy for therapeutic screening, and to determine whether response to paclitaxel-PLGA is influenced by tumour subtype. Methods. Paclitaxel-PLGA particles will be designed and tested in in vitro cell monolayers, multicellular tumour spheroids, then in NOD/SCID mice implanted with tumour spheroids generated from MDA-MD-231 breast carcinoma cells and finally in patient-derived xenograft models. Indocyanine green loaded onto PLGA particles and visualised with near-infrared imaging will be used to evaluate drug distribution and track the diffusion to the regional nodes. These will be correlated with treatment efficacy, assessed in terms of tumour mass, necrosis and proliferative index. Changes in the extent of nodal disease following paclitaxel-PLGA treatment will be assessed through bioluminenscence in MDA-MB-231-luc-D3H1 mice. The intensity of the inflammatory response and extent of necrosis in the normal tissue adjacent to the tumour will be evaluated by histological analysis. Clinical significance. Paclitaxel-PLGA can potentially enhance tumour response and improve treatment outcomes in breast cancer. This study addresses 3 aspects that are of importance prior to clinical trials. The proposed strategy for therapeutic screening is a more reliable and efficient method that ensures better screening and optimisation of novel therapeutics for clinical trials.

title: Targeted therapy by combining photodynamic therapy with anti-angiogenic Nimotuzumab for improving the outcome of cancer treatment
abs: Cancer is a major healthcare burden. The conventional treatment options, surgery, radiotherapy and chemotherapy, each have known limitations. Therefore new therapeutic approaches are needed. Photodynamic therapy (PDT) is a promising cancer treatment modality that involves the interaction of a photosensitizer, molecular oxygen and light to destroy tumors. However, tumor recurrence due to inflammation, neoangiogenesis or incomplete eradication of tumor cells is a problem. The aim of this project is to combine nimotuzumab, a monoclonal antibody against epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) with Chlorin e6-PDT to prevent tumor recurrence. EGFR is highly expressed in most epithelial cancers. We hypothesize that following PDT there is an upregulation of EGFR in the residual tumor cells that repopulate to form recurrence and by using EGFR inhibitor this upregulation and tumor recurrence can be prevented. Our preliminary results using PDT and Erbitux (an EGFR antibody) have shown increased tumor suppression. In this study we plan to use nimotuzumab due to its intrinsic property of selective bivalent binding to moderate and high EGFR expressing cells. Our specific aims and methodology include: (i) To understand the expression profile of EGFR in oral squamous carcinoma (OSCC) cells pre- and post-Ce6 PDT. (ii) To understand the treatment efficacy of nimotuzumab with and/or without PDT in an oral carcinoma xenograft model. Tumor regression, proliferation, angiogenesis and apoptosis will be assessed to determine the effectiveness of the combination therapy. (iii) To investigate the molecular mechanism involved in EGFR-signaling by studying the gene expressions in the pathway. (iv) To conduct a pilot study of PDT and nimotuzumab combination therapy in cancer patients with squamous cell carcinoma based on preclinical results. We propose that exploring new targeted therapeutic agents that can be combined with PDT and understanding the molecular basis of oral cancer can provide a strong rationale for clinical applications.

title: Harnessing Interacting Dirac Fermions for Future Technology
abs: Dirac fermion surface states exist in both graphene and topological insulators. The exposed surface allows for controllable tuning of its properties, such as the strength of disorder and electron-electron interaction as well as being accessible to both electronic transport and surface scanning probes. In particular, the presence of accidental or intentional impurities implies that close to charge neutrality, the energy landscape will be highly inhomogeneous, forming a sea of electron-like and hole-like states, which determine the electronic properties at low carrier density. The characteristics of these puddles depend crucially on strength of the electron-electron interactions. We focus on four ways to controllably modify the interaction strength: (a) Encapsulating in a dielectric medium, (b) Coupling to a second, twisted layer; (c) Introducing curvature or strain fields; (d) Applying a strong magnetic field. While each of these methods controllably changes the interaction strength, they also introduce additional features that influence the properties of the electron-hole puddles (whose effects continue to persist at larger carrier densities, well away from the charge neutrality point). The objective of the proposed research is to use the Random Phase Approximation (RPA) to calculate the effect of changing electron-electron interaction using each of the methods outlined above. While the RPA is valid when the interaction strength is weak, it necessarily fails close to a quantum phase transition. Numerical methods like Quantum Monte Carlo and Renormalization group will be used to benchmark the range of validity of the RPA, and to understand the evolution to a strongly interacting state. Strong emphasis will be given to calculating theoretically the anticipated experimental signatures in both transport and scanning probe measurements. These results will illuminate the feasibility and performance characteristics of proposed beyond CMOS graphene devices including the ballistic graphene field-effect transistors and the bilayer pseudo-spin field effect transistors.

title: Design and Development of a Comprehensive Information Technology Infrastructure for Data-Intensive Applications and Analysis
abs: A major trend today is the "Big Data" revolution. Massive amount of data are being generated by man and machines at a rate much faster than what can be consumed/processed. Thus, it becomes imperative to build large-scale IT infrastructures to store, retrieve, and analyze massive amounts of data. The proposal aims to conduct research on future generation cloud computing infrastructures which can enable societal, scientific and cyber-physical system applications processing large volumes of data. The research is divided into three tightly integrated programmes. The first programme will develop novel DBMS architectures that are cloud-enabled. It will investigate a new paradigm called database virtualization to support multi-tenancy in DBMS. New technolgoies for efficient access and query processing will be studied. The second program further broadens the capabilities of the DBMS for large-scale data analytics. We will extend the MapReduce framework for more complex analysis, e.g., for processing very large graphs in the context of social interaction data. The third program explores novel technologies for a secure cloud-enabled DBMS that is privacy-preserving. In addition, cloud-based infrastructure has to operate in a predictable manner and is fault tolerant. We will also develop algorithms and evaluation metrics for cloud computing systems that account for the notion of affordability. The project will be led by PI Ooi, and assisted by six co-PIs, all from the National Unviersity of Singapore. Three international research collaborators who are experts in the field have agreed to participate in the project. HP Labs Singapore is the industry partner. Technically, the project will advance science to deal with the "Big Data" revolution as parallelism is the future of computing. The indirect impact will come from the infrastructures and technologies that will be developed. This will result in lowered barriers for Singapore-based small and medium sized enterprizes to move from enterprise setting to the cloud.

title: Self-Powered Body Sensor Network for Disease Management and Prevention Oriented Healthcare
abs: Advances in electronics, communications and physiological sensing technologies have spurred considerable interest in wireless health monitoring systems which can be realised by wireless body sensor networks (WBSNs). An integrated WBSN and telemedicine system can facilitate the continuous monitoring of biomedical signals and data for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes, optimal maintenance of chronic conditions or remote healthcare provisioning. Current state-of-the-art WBSNs however are neither lightweight, flexible nor small enough to be truly wearable. The primary reason is the need for batteries as the power source. The proposed program aims at developing a truly wearable WBSN with wireless biomedical sensors that are self-powered and suitable for packaging in small, flexible, stretchable form factors such as a patch(plaster) or embedded in undershirt. To do this, research into techniques for self-powered wireless transceivers, ultra low-power biomedical sensors, energy harvesting, lightweight (in terms of compute power) communications and networking protocols, cloud computing, and human trials needs to be pursued. title: Graphene nanopore platform for single-molecule DNA analysis and physical DNA sequencing
abs: Nanopore-bases devices are used to detect and analyze individual biopolymers, and they offer a prospect for inexpensive and rapid DNA sequencing. In such device, a long DNA molecule is electrophoretically threaded – in linear fashion – through a nanometer size pore fabricated in a freestanding membrane separating two ionic solutions. As the DNA molecule partially blocks the ionic current from passing through the nanopore, this leads to transient “ionic blockade” signal. During the translocation, nucleobases can be interrogated as they enter the highly confined space of the nanopore (using ionic-current, electrical, optical or the other detection method), in the succession that corresponds to their native genetic sequence. Here we propose to develop and implement a new DNA sequencing method based on graphene nanopores – a new class of nanopores with the superior molecular sensing properties, which we have developed recently. Several important challenges for implementing the nanopore sequencing method will be tackled within this project: (i) achieving a spatial resolution sufficient to distinguish the neighboring nucleobases; (ii) achieving sufficient contrast in signal to distinguish between different types of nucleotides, and (iii) slowing down and controlling the DNA translocation through the nanopore. We have demonstrated previously that the graphene nanopores is in principle capable of discerning between adjacent nucleotides. Our preliminary data and modeling indicate that graphene nanopores could also achieve sufficient nucleotide contrast, even with using the ionic-blockade measurements. Excellent electrical sensitivity of the graphene opens up an alternative possibility to use graphene as an electrical sensor to detect nucleotides. The final goal of the project is to demonstrate a proof-of-principle sequencing device capable of reading 1kB long DNA stretches, within 1 second, and with 90% accuracy. The commercially viable device will be subsequently developed with an industrial partner.

title: Identifying novel genes underlying tumorigenesis in retinoblastoma beyond loss of RB1
abs: Retinoblastoma (RB) is a pediatric eye tumor arising from inactivation of the RB1 gene. RB has been the classic model for Knudson’s two-hit hypothesis of tumorigenesis involving tumor suppressor genes. Genetic lesions in RB1 or its pathway have been identified in most, if not all, cancers. It is known that biallelic loss of RB1 genes initiates RB. However, evidence from various studies now suggests that beyond loss of RB1, additional genetic events are required for full malignant transformation of retinal cells to tumors. HYPOTHESIS: RB cells harbor multiple abnormalities driving tumor progression which can be detected by exome sequencing.OVERALL GOAL: To annotate global single nucleotide alterations and identify novel genes underlying tumorigenesis in RB. SPECIFIC AIMS:1. Characterize a discovery data-set of 20 tumor-lymphocyte pairs from sporadic unilateral RBs by exome sequencing,2. Identify novel candidate genes from somatic point mutations in coding regions, and 3. Validate implicated genes by targeted sequencing of an additional cohort of 60 RB tumors METHODOLOGY: We will use state-of-art deep sequencing methods and bioinformatics pipelines to identify cancer-associated genes to better understand tumorigenesis in RB. SIGNIFICANCE: We propose to collect and analyze the first ever whole exome sequence data in RB which has not been attempted before. This project leverages on access to our collection of RB tumors as well as our diagnostic laboratory and clinical experience in the management of RB patients in SE Asia for the past 15-20 years. Identification of candidate genes and pathways has clinical significance as novel therapeutic targets for treatment of RB patients involving less radical therapy or avoiding enucleation in preserving vision and life. Improved prognostication and management will also reduce overall costs to families and society. The findings will provide unique insights not only to RB disease pathogenesis but also to other cancers in general.

title: Novel antagonists of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors and understanding of specific pharmacophores
abs: Neurological and neuromuscular diseases are on the rise in developed and developing countries with the increase in aging population. Acetylcholine receptors (AChRs) are the main targets for the development of therapeutic strategies for the prevention and treatment of these diseases that will improve the quality of life of the elderly. Historically, alpha-bungarotoxin, a postsynaptic neurotoxin was instrumental in the identification and isolation of nicotinic AChRs (nAChRs). Since then several snake venom toxins have contributed to better basic understanding of mechanisms of normal human physiology and provided impetus in the search for pharmaceutical drugs. Recently, we isolated and characterized a number of novel antagonists of nAChRs. They differ from classical neurotoxins in their receptor-specificity, species-specificity and reversibility. The main objectives of this project are to determine the structure-function relationships of these novel antagonists and identify specific pharmacophores. The specific aims are: 1.Recombinant expression of wild type and mutant toxins2.Pharmacological characterization of wild type and mutant toxins3.Biophysical interaction between toxins and their receptors4.Determination of structural details of interaction We will examine the pharmacological properties of recombinant toxins and the mutants in organ bath experiments on the neuromuscular junctions and on various nAChRs using electrophysiology (voltage clamp) studies. The activities of the mutants will be compared with the wild type toxins to determine the role of specific residues. We will examine their interaction with the receptor proteins using surface plasmon resonance and isothermal titration calorimetry. We will also determine the 3D structure of toxins and their complexes with nAChRs. These studies will help us to understand the receptor-specificity (peripheral vs. Neuronal), species-specificity (avian vs. Mammalian) and reversibility, and to identify the pharmacophores that distinguish various nAChRs that are important for the development of specific and potential drug leads for human neuropathy therapy.

title: Redox Flow Lithium Batteries as a New Concept and Implementable Solution for Large Scale Energy Storage
abs: Based upon the encouraging initial results from our preliminary study on redox targeting of insulating battery materials, this program introduces a conceptually new and implementable solution to address the critical challenges confronted by the state-of-the-art power sources for large-scale energy storage. The approach of this program is inspired by our discovery that without being attached to the current collector, active electrode material can be charged/ discharged via redox targeting reactions with suitable redox shuttle molecules dissolved in the electrolyte. The exchange of electrons between the active material and the electrode is mediated by the diffusion of redox shuttle molecules through the electrolyte. The application of redox targeting to both cathode and anode leads to a novel energy storage device—the Redox-Flow Lithium Battery. This novel device combines the fast rechargeability and the decoupling of power and energy densities of the flow battery system with the high energy density of lithium ion batteries. In the program, three interconnected projects are proposed to address the various challenges and critical issues, ranged from the development of redox-flow lithium battery single cells to the prototyping of large battery system. At the end of the program, a 1 kWh redox-flow lithium battery pack will be prototyped, demonstrated and extensively evaluated. We are confident that once fully developed, the redox-flow lithium batteries will provide a potentially disruptive solution to redraw the technology landscape for both large-scale stationary and automotive energy storage.

title: Herbalomic: Novel Approach for Fingerprinting and Authentication of Herbal Products
abs: Herbal medicines are gaining recognition worldwide due to their long historical usage and relatively low risk. A major hurdle in developing herbal products is their uncontrollable quality which poses serious safety issues and a bottleneck for their modernization. The proposed herbalomic program aims to overcome this bottleneck. It focuses to develop novel approaches and modern analytical methods in determining the full-spectrum composition of herbal products, involving biologic-, metabolite-, pharmaco-fingerprintings and herbal informatic. Whereas metabolite fingerprinting of herbal products involving organic molecules is well established, biologic fingerprinting of peptides and proteins in herbal products is novel. Plant synthesizes 24 families of cysteine-rich peptides (1-8kDa), which are relatively unexplored because of the misconception that they are susceptible to heat during the decoction preparation, enzymatic and acidic hydrolysis after ingestion, and poorly absorbed through the gastrointestinal tract. However, cysteine-rich peptides are exceptionally stable with diverse pharmacological activities, due to their chemical structures resulting from cross bracing by multiple disulfur bonds. The objectives of this program are: 1. develop novel approaches of biologic fingerprinting, 2. validate biologic fingerprinting by correlation with metabolite fingerprinting, 3. determine the pharmacologic fingerprints of selected herbal products, and 4. establish informatics and resource library of herbal products. The program also focuses on developing new methodology and high-throughput strategy for detailing herbal compositions through chemical and biologic profiling, standardization and authentication. The use of biologics as chemical markers will provide a new standard to the authentication and standardization of herbal products and complement current quality control methods based exclusively on metabolites. The development of high throughput assays for interpreting the multi-component and multi-targets of herbal components can generate valuable information for the selection and evaluation of TCM prescription for vital and chronic diseases and in turn, provide feedback on the herbal products to be analyzed.

title: Control of Exotic Quantum Phenomena at Strategic Interfaces and Surfaces for Novel Functionality by in-situ Synchrotron Radiation
abs: Quantum phenomena at interfaces and surfaces are important and exciting to both fundamental sciences as well as modern device technologists as device dimensions shrink to the nano scale. The interface/surface is becoming a dominant part of device performance in many technologies such as logic and memory, e.g. oxide layers in CMOS transistors or tunnel barriers in magnetic tunnel junction are only three atomic layers thick, and the read head in today’s laptop utilizes a three unit cell MgO barrier which imparts a twenty fold improvement in device sensitivity over prior technology. At small dimensions the interfaces between dissimilar materials become dynamic and generate new, exotic quantum properties, e.g. the interface of two band insulators LaAlO3/SrTiO3 generate an unconventional quasi two dimensional electron gas with high mobility above room temperature, exhibiting unusual magnetic properties. Such phenomena at the interface/surface are driven by the interplay of electronic, orbital, magnetic and lattice degrees of freedom. Their study presents a real challenge, as they are just a monolayer thick, easily contaminated and, especially for interfaces, buried. The grand challenge faced now is how to measure and control these degrees of freedom at clean interfaces/surfaces using non-destructive, direct techniques ? With better understanding and control of such quantum phenomena we aim to fabricate novel interface-based devices and concepts. We will address this by developing and using new experimental methods, combining atomically controlled layer-bylayer growth and in-situ synchrotron-based techniques of resonant soft X-ray magnetic scattering and ultravioletvacuum ultraviolet magneto-optical ellipsometry. We will directly measure and control electronic, orbital, magnetic and lattice degrees of freedom of several strategic interfaces/surfaces, based on complex oxides and grapheme, fully supported by theoretical calculations. The outcome of these experiments will be deployed into the design and testing of novel device concepts, placing Singapore at this research frontier.

title: Plasmonic-Electronics: New Generation of Devices to Bypass Fundamental Limitations
abs: 1) To integrate plasmons in current-day technology, one must be able to generate plasmons on single chips electrically. Currently, plasmons are generate in nanostructures by using external exitation, i.e., external light sources (for instance lasers), high voltage electron beams, or scanning tunneling microscopes (STMs). We propose to use tunneling junctions, integrated on chips, to generate plasmons on a chip electrically. This so-called plasmonic-electronic transducer will be coupled to plasmonic interconnects, such as, silver nanobeam/wires, a long which these plasmons can propagate over tens of micrometers -- enough for most applications. At the other end of the plasmonic interconnect, we position a second tunneling that functions as a plasmonic-electronic transducer. It converts the plasmonic signal to an electrical signal by exploiting plasmon assisted tunneling. 2) The efficiency of solar cells are limited by one trade off of the worst kind. Thick films (>100 nm) of photo-active material absorbs all light, but the diffusion length of the exciton (<10 nm) is too short and recombination of charge occurs before they can reach the electrodes. Thin films (<100 nm) solves this problem, but these thin films can not absorb all light. Plasmons can interact strongly with both excitons and charge carriers, and light. This interaction can increase the diffusion lengths of excitons, and increase the efficiency of thin films to absorb sunlight increasing the solar cells efficiency while keeping the cost low.
kw: plasmonics;solar cells;nanoelectronics;graphene;fabrication;devices

title: Regulation of Brown Fat Development by Non-coding RNAs
abs: The broad objective of my research is to identify novel drug targets for the development of therapeutics that can be used to combat obesity. Obesity is a major source of morbidity and mortality, and its prevalence is rising in many areas of the world. However, available treatments for obesity are limited. Brown adipose tissue (BAT) is an attractive target for obesity treatment. Mammals have two principal types of fat. White adipose tissue (WAT) primarily serves to store extra energy as triglycerides, while BAT is specialized to burn lipids for heat generation and energy expenditure. In humans, the activity of BAT negatively correlates with body mass index (BMI). Ablation of BAT in mice reduces energy expenditure, resulting in obesity development. Conversely, augmentation of BAT’s activity and prevalence often prevents obesity. In light of the anti-obesity feature of BAT, the interest in understanding the mechanisms underlying BAT development is increasing. Although multiple protein factors have been identified as regulators in BAT development, roles of non-coding genes in this process are unknown. Here, I propose to investigate the roles of non-coding RNAs including microRNAs and lincRNAs (large intergenic non-coding RNAs) in BAT development. Specifically, I will use an adipose tissue-specific knockout mouse model to determine the roles of miR-193b-365 in brown fat development in vivo (Aim 1). I will combine biochemical methods and computational prediction to identify the repertories of targets for miR-193b-365 (Aim 2). In addition, I will employ next generation RNA-sequencing genome-wide profiling and cellular biology methods to determine the roles of lincRNAs in brown fat development and corresponding mechanisms (Aim 3). Successful accomplishment of my proposed research will shed new light on the regulation of brown fat development and provide direct drug targets or reveal druggable pathways for the development of anti-obesity therapies.

title: Targeting proteome homeostasis: a new approach to antimycobacterial drug discovery
abs: We demonstrated essentiality of the caseinolytic protease ClpP1/2 for viability of Mycobacterium tuberculosis in vitro and in vivo, and showed that the protease is required for protein quality control under aminoglycoside-induced translational stress. In other bacteria, ClpP protease is part of complex machines which include ATPases required for substrate recognition and unfolding, as well as adaptor proteins and cofactors involved in substrate selection. Clp degradation machines play roles not only in proteome housekeeping, but also in regulation of cellular physiology, stress adaptation and virulence. In mycobacteria, the components, functions and regulation of the Clp machine remain largely undefined. Here we will carry out a mechanism-based whole cell screen to identify small molecule modulators of ClpP1/2 activity. The modulators will be employed as chemical probes for the functional dissection of the Clp complex. Clp-specific degradation of SsrA-tagged substrates was exploited to construct M. smegmatis reporter strains capable of detecting tool compounds that either inhibit or activate ClpP1/2 protease activity. Genetic and biochemical means will be employed to deconvolute their targets and mechanisms of action. Genetic methods include selection of spontaneous resistant mutants and whole genome sequencing, followed by confirmation of the mechanism of resistance via introducing the detected polymorphisms into wild type background, and over- and under-expression as well as protein depletion of candidate targets. Furthermore, whole cell ClpP1/2 modulators will be tested in a biochemical ClpP1/2 protease assay to identify direct hits of the core protease. Taken together, this work represents a chemical genetic approach to the dissection of the mycobacterial Clp degradation machinery and information networks feeding into it. The program will result in the identification of new factors and mechanisms involved in the regulation of mycobacterial proteome homeostasis. The tool compounds will deliver chemically validated targets with cidal potential and chemical starting points for antimycobacterial drug discovery programs.

title: Development of novel fluorescent probes for detection and isolation of human lung cancer stem cells and for in vivo cancer imaging
abs: The central goal of this grant is to identify novel fluorescent probes for the isolation, characterization and bioimaging of lung cancer stem cells (CSCs) also known as Tumor Initiating cells (TICS). Such probes when precisely characterized will be extremely useful in supporting the diagnostic stratification and prognostic management of patients and for imaging cancer cells in vivo thereby allowing tracking of treatment response and relapse of disease. Lung cancer is the most common cancer causing more than a million deaths worldwide each year. A growing body of evidence suggests that cancers are driven by subpopulations of TICs responsible for the initiation, propagation, and metastasis of tumors. A preferential resistance of these TICs to cancer drugs is thought to be one of the major reasons for relapse and treatment failure. Therefore understanding and learning how to target TICs is currently an important question in clinical oncology. Compared to other common cancers such as in breast and colon, lung cancer TICs remain poorly characterized. We have recently shown that the surface marker CD166 can be used to sort for TICs in lung cancer. However, many CD166+ cells are not TICs. Our goal is to identify even more specific probes for TICs. The key technology to achieve this is our Diversity Oriented Fluorescence Library Approach (DOFLA), which provide thousands of highly versatile fluorescent small molecules. Our immediate goal is to discover novel fluorescent probes for detecting TICs in tumors and apply them for in vivo tumor imaging in animal cancer model. Our long term goal is to develop these probes for the detection and imaging in patients of a subpopulation of cells responsible for driving cancers in patients. This capability will provide an enormous advance in our treatment and care of cancer patients while generating novel approaches to develop better drugs against cancer.
kw: Cancer stem cell, DOFLA, Fluorescent probe, High-throughput screening, in vivo optical imaging, Lung cancer

title: Novel Drug Targets for Gastric Cancer Therapy
abs: Gastric cancer is a leading cause of cancer deaths. Target-directed therapeutics has gained popularity for its lower side effects and potential impact on personalized medicine. However, gastric cancer is a heterogeneous disease with clinical targets like c-Met and Her2 limited to subsets of gastric cancers. Identification of drug targets with higher penetrance than current goal standards is the key goal of this proposal. Many signaling molecules possess enzymatic activities, are critical regulators of cancer biology and therefore attractive drug targets. Majority of them are also regulated by phosphorylation. Hence, we conducted phosphoproteomics and profiled the phosphorylation levels of >1000 proteins across 14 gastric cancer cell lines and ranked them according to their amplitude and frequency of aberrant phosphorylation. The overall top hit is PLC-?2 while DDR1 is the top hit within the tyrosine kinase category. We aim to: i) conduct a retrospective study to determine the relevance of DDR1 and PLC-?2 to clinical gastric cancer through immunohistochemistry and statistical correlation of experimental data with clinical information and ii) elucidate the function and mechanism of DDR1 and PLC-?2 through gain- and loss-of-function studies using in vitro cell-based and animal model studies. DDR1 and PLC-?2, which have not been previously implicated in gastric cancer, are interesting because they were ranked higher than c-Met and Her2 in our phosphoproteomics screen. Immunohistochemistry and aCGH also revealed them to be aberrantly expressed in about 60-85% of >100 clinical samples analyzed as opposed to 20-30% reported for c-Met and Her2. We have also demonstrated DDR1 to be important for gastric cancer cellular processes. The proposed works will validate DDR1 and PLC-?2 as genes critical/fundamental to gastric cancer and as viable drug targets, following which drug discovery efforts can ensue as a separate project. The data may also support first-in-man trial for gastric cancer therapy.
kw: Gastric Cancer, Molecular Etiology, Phosphoproteomics, DDR1 receptor tyrosine kinase, PLC-?2, Target-directed therapeutics

title: Blood flow in the microcirculation: Influences of hemorheological disorders
abs: Many clinical studies have reported that abnormal alteration of blood properties can be a radical cause of physiological malfunctions in hemorheological disorders including hear diseases, diabetes mellitus, and malaria. In these pathological conditions, intensified red blood cell (RBC) aggregability, rigidified RBC and anomalous hematocrit levels are commonly found. However, despite of the clinically significant findings, information on how such rheological changes of blood influence hemodynamics and gas transport in the microcirculation is currently very limited. Thus, this study aims to provide such information by performing in vivo experiments and computational simulations. Since cell-free layer (CFL) formation in microvessels has been of great interest as an important hemodynamic parameter in understanding the microcirculatory response to physiological changes, our proposed approaches will focus on revealing physiological and pathophysiological roles of the CFL in the microcirculation. To ascertain its roles, detailed quantitative information on the CFL characteristics in the presence of hemorheological abnormalities will be acquired by pursuing the following specific aims. Firstly, in vivo CFL data will be obtained from small arterioles in the rat cremaster muscle at pathophysiological levels of RBC aggregability, deformability and hematocrit. In addition, with use of microsensors developed here, oxygen and nitric oxide levels in the tissue will be measured under the physiological and pathophysiological conditions. Finally, numerical models for hemodynamics and gas transport in the arterioles will be developed to better understand the pathophysiological role of CFL in microcirlculatory functions. The scientific findings obtained in this research will pave the way for a more detailed exploration of blood disorders, possibly leading to development of better diagnostic tools.
kw: Cell-free layer, NO/O2 diffusion, Microcirculation, Computational simulation of red cell flow

title: The Mechanisms of Breaking Cellular Symmetry in Metazoan Development
abs: Cell polarity is necessary for diverse processes in development. A hallmark of polarized cells is the segregation of the PAR proteins into asymmetric domains at the cell cortex, but the mechanisms that initiate to polarize the PAR domains are not understood. The goal of this project is to uncover “the mechanisms for breaking cellular symmetry” with the use of two complementary models, C. elegans zygotes and rodent neurons. Specific Aim I (SA1) will use C. elegans to focus on the identity of the symmetry-breaking cue from sperm centrosome and the nature of the signaling from cue to asymmetric segregation of PAR proteins. This aim will uncover how centrosomal kinase Aurora-A triggers asymmetric contraction of actomyosin cytoskeleton. SA2 will focus on the mechanism that determines “size” and “pattern” of the asymmetric PAR proteins. This aim will challenge in vitro reconstition of PAR protein segregation in heterologous cells and phospholipid liposome, and use C. elegans zygotes to verify the findings highlighted from in vitro reconstitution. SA3 will use cultured rodent neurons to focus on the nature of the symmetry-breaking cue that initiates and guarantees the specification of a single axon from multiple neurites. This aim will illustrate the initial landmark signaling to remodel cytoskeletons and reinforce the axon fate in live neurons undergoing symmetry breaking. This project will use a combination of biochemical, genetic, and microscopy approaches to test each of these hypotheses, and identify the biochemical interactions involved. Unlike other polarity models, the proposed systems do not rely on pre-localized determinants to generate asymmetry, and thus gives me the unique opportunity to explore the mechanisms that directly trigger cellular asymmetry. By taking advantage of these simple systems, this project will illuminate the mechanisms that build and maintain the architecture of many cell types and prevent tumor formation.
kw: Cell polarity;Symmetry breaking;PAR protein;Cytoskeleton;C. elegans;Neuron

title: Green factories for Essential Oil Production - Develop Plant System and Microbial Systems for the Sustainable Production of Valuable Chemicals from Plants
abs: Terpenes are plant secondary metabolites that find wide usage in flavours and fragrances, cosmetics and pharmaceutical industries. Mint is the source of the best known monoterpene - menthol which is produced in specialized organs called glandular trichomes. This proposal plans to study the regulation of terpene and trichome production in mint to enable metabolic engineering of the pathway and increase yield. Mint is suitable for this since extensive research in mint has led to the identification of the entire complement of genes and enzymes involved in the menthol pathway. We propose to identify key genes and transcription factors involved in this process by comparative transcriptomics and promoter cloning approach. Additionally, genes involved in Jasmonic acid induced terpene synthesis will also be determined by microarray analysis. To analyse the function of candidate genes, we will set up a VIGS (Virus induced gene silencing system) and an over expression system in mint. Once we get the handle on key genes, we plan to engineer novel terpenes or different terpenes production in mint glandular trichomes by over expressing heterologous terpene synthase from other aromatic plants (e.g. sandalwood) with and without blocking its native menthol production pathway at various steps. This will enable us to explore the terpene chemical space in mint and see what molecules the plant can synthesize when presented with different substrates and enzymes. The knowledge gained from these studies will be extrapolated to engineer large scale production of terpenes in fermentable organisms such as red yeast (Rhodosporidium toruloides). This has been shown in budding yeast and E.coli but the key advantage of using R. toruloides lies in its inherent high fermentation density (> 5-fold higher than budding yeast), strong metabolic flux to fatty acid synthesis and high oil content. This research will help us to build plant and microbial platforms for the sustainable production of high value terpenes.
kw: Terpene biosynthesis;Mint;Red yeast;Transcription factors;Trichomes;Sustainable production platforms

title: New Generation HVAC Systems - Total Energy Efficiency Solutions
abs: An HVAC system essentially consists of the water side and air side component systems with complex interactions and interconnections at several levels. The much more complicated air side system components offer great potentials for scientific breakthroughs and technology innovations that can revolutionize fresh air treatment, room air ventilation, comfort measurement and controls to optimize the system's operation. In turn, the improved air side energy performance will reduce the cooling load demand and lift the chilled water supply temperature on the water side system, thereby improving the overall system's energy efficiency. This research program leverages on fundamental sciences to address challenges in low grade energy based cooling and dehumidification, active chilled beam, cooperative sensing and real-time control and optimization, indoor environmental quality analysis, data and information aggregation methodology, and visual analytics so as to realize energy efficient new generation HVAC systems. The key objectives are to achieve an overall 50% energy savings and to simultaneously optimize human comfort thereby improving productivity. The whole program involves intensive research into the following seven inter-related projects and their inter-connections: Project 1 - Renewable Energy based Cooling Systems Project 2 - A Novel Energy Efficient Desiccant Dehumidification System Project 3 - Active Chilled Beam for HVAC Systems Project 4 - Networked Sensing and Actuation System for Energy Efficiency and Human Comfort Project 5 - Real-time Integrated Dynamic Optimization and Control for HVAC Systems Project 6 - Indoor Environmental Quality of New Generation HVAC Systems Project 7 - HVAC Visual Analytics for Overall Performance Evaluation Through our hierarchy of approaches, with each of the above contributing towards the overall objectives, we are able to realize more than 50% of energy saving and significant improvements in IEQ because of real-time control and sensor feedbacks.
kw: HVAC systems;Energy efficiency;Renewable energy;Dehumidification systems;Sensor network;Visual analytics

title: Understanding the relevance of p73 regulation by hypoxia
abs: p73, the homologue of the tumor-suppressor p53, exists as 2 major forms: the transactivation (TA) proficient TAp73 form or the TA-deficient deltaN(DN) form. TAp73 is endowed with growth inhibitory properties, whereas DNp73 opposes the inhibitory properties of both TAp73 and p53. Consistently, a variety of cellular stress stimuli lead to the upregulation of TAp73 with the concomitant down-regulation of DNp73, so that apoptosis can ensue. However, clinical data suggest that unlike p53, both TAp73 and DNp73 are not mutated, but are overexpressed in cancers, implying that TAp73 may have other roles in carcinogenesis. Analysis of mice specifically lacking the TAp73 form showed that they are susceptible to tumors, but less frequently and with a longer latency than p53-/- mice, indicating that TAp73 may be a weak tumor-suppressor. Exploration of TAp73’s non tumor-suppressive functions by us and others has revealed that TAp73 can indeed support cellular growth in a context-dependent manner, highlighting that TAp73 is capable of positively regulating cellular growth. Consistently, our preliminary data demonstrates that hypoxia, a condition prevalent in tumors and that promotes cellular survival, leads to the upregulation of both TAp73 and DNp73 (unlike other stimuli), in a HIF-1a-dependent manner. Importantly, loss of p73 expression leads to reduced blood vessel density in hypoxic tumors. These data therefore suggests that hypoxia-mediated p73 upregulation provides cellular survival signals to promote tumor formation. The proposed experiments are therefore aimed at understanding the mechanistic basis of these observations, with the hypothesis that molecular regulators of hypoxia-induced p73 stability and p73-dependent angiogenesis would be amenable for therapeutic intervention to reduce tumorigenesis. The proposed work would therefore lead not only to generation of new knowledge that would be of paramount importance in understanding p73 biology, but also provide molecular regulators operative to promote tumorigenesis, which could be nodal points for future therapeutic intervention.
kw: cancer, p73, HIF, targets, hypoxia

title: Functional analysis of the c-Jun-N-terminal kinase 1 (JNK1)-SIRT1 interaction – directly or indirectly through the novel JNK1/deleted in breast cancer-1 (DBC1) interaction – from molecular characterization to pre-clinical testing
abs: The c-Jun-amino terminal kinases (JNKs) - JNK1, 2 and 3, have overlapping and specific roles in regulating apoptosis, proliferation and other cellular processes. Not surprisingly, they have been targets for therapeutic intervention, though selectivity issues have hampered progress. We therefore embarked on identifying specific JNK-interacting partners that may provide specificity for targeting specific cellular processes. Our efforts have identified deleted-in-breast-cancer-1 (DBC1) as one such candidate that selectively interacts only with JNK1. DBC1 was initially found to be deleted in breast cancers, and shown to possess tumor-suppressive functions by activation of p53 and FOXO3, primarily through inhibition of SIRT1 – a protein that regulates metabolic processes involved in cancer and aging. However, recent data have also demonstrated direct regulation of SIRT1 by JNK1-mediated phosphorylation. Our preliminary data, and data from JNK1-/- and DBC1-/- mice, reveal two major scenarios of JNK1-mediated SIRT1 regulation: JNK1 and DBC1 have opposite effects on SIRT1 activity, in the context of cellular survival/proliferation, with SIRT inactivation and increased p53 acetylation when JNK1 is silenced or DBC1 is overexpressed; or on the contrary, both JNK1 and DBC1 have similar roles in regulating SIRT1 activity, as noted in DBC1-/- or JNK1-/- mice which have increased SIRT1 activity and are resistant to hepatosteatosis. These data suggest a complex crosstalk between JNK1, DBC1 and SIRT1, depending on the cellular context.Since general modulation of JNK1/SIRT1 activity would have pleotrophic effects, this proposal hypothesizes that delineating the specific role of JNK1 in regulating SIRT1 activity, either directly or indirectly through DBC1, will uncover nodal points for molecular intervention. Cellular processes of proliferation/survival and hepatosteotosis will be interrogated to investigate the effect of inhibiting JNK1/DBC1 or JNK1/SIRT1 interactions using peptide inhibitors, both in cell-lines and in pre-clinical models, which will provide new knowledge and open up possibilities for selective JNK1/DBC1 or JNK1/SIRT1 therapeutic targeting

title: Applications of Semiparametric Regression Models in Prospective Cohort Studies
abs: Semiparametric model has become attractive in recent years for modeling longitudinal data in prospective cohort studies. In many situations, the relationship between the response variable and the independent variable is not a constant. Instead, a functional regression coefficient may be more flexible and provide more insight to the underlying relationship. The model studied in this project has been recently applied in two medical studies in the US: the first is a population based data analysis to examine the temporal relationship between systolic blood pressure and urinary albumin excretion for diabetes patients; the second is a recent multi-center two-armed clinical trial for Scleroderma patients. In both studies, using varying-coefficient model leads to more meaningful results. In this project we are particularly motivated by the study of dependence of stroke on the retinal vascular caliber. Previously six cohort studies were carried out in different countries to examine their association. We intend to combine previous evidence and also use the data from Singapore Malay Eye Study and Singapore Prospective Cohort. We will analyze the longitudinal data collected in these studies with our proposed new semiparametric regression models and provide a meaningful answer on the association between stroke and retinal vessel caliber. The research findings will be used to predict the stroke outcome in clinical practice with higher accuracy and thus facilitate disease prevention and timely medical care.
kw: Cohort study, Longitudinal data, Simulation and computation, Statistical model, Semiparametric regression, Retinal vascular measure
