title: Interaction between Galectin-1 and L-type CaV1.2 Calcium Channel Splice Variants: Implications in Vascular Hypertension
abs: L-type CaV1.2 channels have a dominant role in arterial smooth muscle contraction and its dysregulation is therefore important in hypertension. Recently, our group identified that galectin-1 (Gal-1) binds directly to the CaV1.2 I-II loop in a splice variant specific manner. Functionally, Gal-1 decreases the surface expression of CaV1.2??9? But not CaV1.29?9? Channels by possibly masking the ER export signal found on exon 9. We hypothesize that altered expression of Gal-1 and CaV1.29* channel variant is an adaptive response in hypertension; and that mechanistically the dibasic residues of the ER export signal in the I-II loop are important for interaction with Gal-1 or exon 9* to reduce surface expression of CaV1.2 channels. To test our hypothesis, we propose 3 specific aims:1)To characterize the critical residues within Galectin-1 (Gal-1) or exon 9* that will interact with the I-II loop ER export signal and vice versa;2)To identify the mechanisms for understanding how Gal-1 binds to CaV1.2 I-II loop in a splice variant specific manner;3)To examine the mechanistic link between expression of Gal-1 and CaV1.2 splice variations to hypertension.To address these aims, we will generate or acquire 3 rat models of hypertension, begin a pilot project on human hypertension and conduct physiological experiments to uncover the mechanistic link between Gal-1 expression and CaV1.2 splice variations to hypertension. Our working model is that Gal-1 either masks the ER export signal or competes out ?-subunit binding at the I-II loop. We will determine the crystal structure and also use patch-clamp electrophysiological technique to understand this interaction and the mechanism for splice-variant specific Gal-1 inhibition of CaV1.2 channels.In the long-term, we will design peptidergic Gal-1 mimetics to mask the CaV1.2 ER export signal to selectively downregulate CaV1.2 channels to offer a new approach to the management of hypertension.
kw: L type calcium channel, Galectin 1, vascular smooth muscle cell, vasotone, hypertension, electrophysiology

title: The zebrafish liver cancer models for rapid in vivo testing of cancer gene potency and anti-cancer drug discovery
abs: The zebrafish has been well recognized as a new animal model for human disease studies as it offers several unique advantages, e.g. easy availability of a large number, accessibility of all embryonic stages, feasibility of live imaging of fluorescently labeled internal organs in the near-transparent body, economy of maintaining, etc. We earlier demonstrated that zebrafish and human liver cancers share significant transcriptomic similarity in both cancer hallmarks and progression. Recently we found that high-level expression of a single oncogene can cause liver cancers in transgenic zebrafish. In particular, we developed two inducible transgenic systems to allow dose-dependent high-level induction of oncogene expression for liver tumorigenesis. We hypothesize that our inducible transgenic systems can be used to develop a rapid, in vivo assay to test oncogenic potential of candidate cancer genes identified from large-scale genomic and bioinformatic analyses. We further envision that the tumor transgenic zebrafish we developed will be useful for screening of small molecules for discovery of new anticancer drugs. In this project, we will focus on three areas. First, we will develop rapid F0 transgenic zebrafish assays for functional validation of at least 70 human oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes for their potential roles in hepatocarcinogenesis. Potential tumor phenotype will be monitored in fluorescence-labeled cells in semi-transparent zebrafish fry/adults. Second, we will generate liver tumor metastasis models by transgenic manipulation of multiple genes affecting both oncogenesis and metastasis. Third, we will develop proof-of-concept assays using our available liver cancer transgenic zebrafish for anti-cancer drug screening from selected chemical inhibitors and a library of 640 FDA-approved drugs. While the first two parts will be important for understanding various molecular mechanisms of hepatocarcinogensis and identification of therapeutic targets, the last part will be directly applicable for discovery of new drug to benefit cancer patients.
kw: Hepatocellular carcinoma, Oncogene, Tumor suppressor, Drug screening, Liver cancer, Metastasis

title: Establishing the feasibility of targeting the non-structural protein 1 of influenza A virus for the development of a novel and broad-spectrum antibody-based immunotherapy
abs: Recent studies have shown that monoclonal antibody (mAb)-based passive immunotherapy is a promising new approach to combat the influenza A virus. With the availability of mAbs that target and inhibit different viral proteins, combination therapy can be developed to minimize the emergence of escape viruses. Thus far, it is not known if any of the non-structural viral proteins can be targeted for passive immunotherapy. This proposal tests the hypothesis that mAbs targeting the non-structural protein 1 (NS1) can be developed into a novel class of antiviral therapeutic agents. We specifically aim to: (i) Generate and characterize a panel of NS1 mAbs that bind different functional important domains in NS1.(ii) Determine the abilities of the NS1 mAbs to inhibit viral replication in vitro and examine potential synergism between different mAbs.(iii) Determine if the virus can escape inhibition by the NS1 mAbs when they are used individually or in combination. (iv) Determine the abilities of the NS1 mAbs to inhibit viral replication and/or pathogenesis in mouse infection models.To target the intracellular NS1, which binds RNA and host proteins, a multi-disciplinary approach will be used to generate and characterize a panel of mAbs that can bind important domains in NS1. The mechanisms of inhibition will be determined, so will the ability of the virus to mutate in order to escape inhibition. The abilities of these mAbs to inhibit the functions of NS1 and reduce viral pathogenesis will be determined by using appropriate mouse infection models. Establishing a proof-of-concept for targeting and inhibiting the function of NS1 with mAb(s) will be highly novel and significant because NS1 is essential for viral replication and an important virulence factor. Hence, this project will yield knowledge that is important for the development mAb-based passive immunotherapy and may provide some reagents for future antiviral development.
kw: Monoclonal antibody (mAb), Non-structural protein 1 (NS1), Influenza A virus, Broad-spectrum immunotherapy, Combination therapy, Single chain variable fragment (scFv)

title: Elucidating the role of Zfp553 in ES cell Identity and reprogramming
abs: Mouse Zfp553, has been found to be located predominantly in the pluripotent inner cell mass (ICM) of early mouse embryos. However, the function of Zfp553 in early embryos and stem cells has been poorly studied. Interestingly, our preliminary experiments have demonstrated that Zfp553 depletion significantly down-regulates the expression of pluripotency genes in mouse embryonic stem (ES) cells. In addition, loss of Zfp553 directs ES cells towards differentiation. Moreover, our chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) results indicate that Zfp553 binds to not only the “hotspot” of the Oct4 distal enhancer, but also the proximal promoter of Nanog, suggesting that Zfp553 probably regulates Oct4 and Nanog transcription in ES cells. Together, these suggest that Zfp553 plays an essential role in ES cell pluripotency and self-renewal by regulating the master pluripotency factors Oct4 and Nanog. We will intensively study the functions of Zfp553 in ES cells. We will utilize ChIP-seq to map the genome-wide Zfp553 binding sites in the mouse ES genome and also combine the ChIP-seq results with expression microarray data of Zfp553 RNAi. We plan to identify Zfp553 interacting proteins by co-immunoprecipitation in combination with mass spectrometry. We aim to unravel the molecular mechanism underlying the functions of Zfp553 in ES cells. Lastly, we will extend our investigation to the role of Zfp553 in reprogramming. Our research will contribute greatly to the knowledge of pluripotency and will be significant in regenerative medicine
kw: Zfp553, Differentiation, ES cell identity, Reprogramming

title: Role of G9a in skeletal myogenesis and muscular dystrophy
abs: Growth and differentiation of muscle precursor cells is essential for the development and regeneration of muscle tissue. In adult, these processes rely on resident muscle stem cells. Defects in proliferation, differentiation and the regenerative response underlie muscle diseases such as muscular dystrophies, rhabdomyosarcomas, and the ageing related decline of muscle regenerative capacity.Recent findings from my laboratory have identified lysine methyltransferase G9a as a critical regulator of muscle differentiation. Our preliminary data demonstrates dysregulated G9a expression in muscular dystrophy. G9a is a novel, and hitherto unreported, inhibitor of skeletal muscle differentiation. As G9a deficiency in mice is embryonic lethal, the mechanisms through which it functions are largely uncharacterized. A thorough understanding of G9a function in skeletal myogenesis provides basis for development of new therapeutic strategies to address muscle repair or growth in a variety of human pathologic states. This proposal brings together complementary capabilities of two well-established research groups. We will test the hypothesis that G9a activity is required for muscle fiber development or repair, and as a therapeutic target for muscular dystrophy. This hypothesis will be tested by characterizing the role of G9a in skeletal muscle development and regeneration in vivo. Proof of principle will be established initially in zebrafish embryos, with complementary experiments in conditional G9a knockout mice. Mouse models of dystrophy will be used to determine the role of G9a in muscle repair and regeneration. The successful completion of the proposed aims will establish G9a as a new molecular target that could be used to combat muscle degenerative disorders.
kw: Skeletal muscle, Muscular dystrophy, epigenetics, regeneration, differentiation, methylation

title: Development of Andrographolide As Novel Therapy for Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease
abs: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is the fourth leading cause of death worldwide, and is projected to become the third leading cause of death by 2020. COPD affects over 5% of the adult population with increasing prevalence in an ageing population. COPD is characterized by airflow obstruction, mucus hypersecretion, and emphysema. Cigarette smoking is the major risk factor forCOPD. Corticosteroids are not effective for COPD, and the phosphodiesterase inhibitor roflumilast suffers from dose-limiting side effects. Currently, there are no satisfactory treatments to slow the inflammatory and destructive processes in COPD. There is an unmet medical need to discover novel anti-inflammatory agents for COPD. We have reported broad-spectrum anti-inflammatory effects of andrographolide, a bioactive molecule isolated from a herbal plant Andrographis paniculata, in mouse asthma model. Recently, we have preliminary data showing anti-inflammatory effects of andrographolide in both acute and chronic cigarette smoke-induced lung injury mouse models. We hypothesize that andrographolide may be effective for the treatment of COPD. The specific aims of this proposal are to investigate (1) anti-inflammatory effects of andrographolide in both acute andchronic models of cigarette smoke-induced lung injury, (2) anti-inflammatory effects of andrographolide in steroid-resistant models of airway inflammation, (3) metabolomics of COPD with and without andrographolide treatments, and (4) inhibitory mechanisms of action of andrographolide using image-based multivariate profiling technology. The proposal will fulfill the mission and vision of NMRC by, in the short term, enhancing translational knowledge of the efficacy and the mechanisms of action of andrographolide in the treatment of COPD, and, in the long term, leading to clinical trial of andrographolide for COPD and promoting better health care for COPD patients. This multi-disciplinary collaboration ensures that the proposed aims can be accomplished within the granting period, and high impact and clinically-relevant research work will be produced.
kw: Cigarette smoke, Mouse model, Inflammation, Drug targets, Metabolomics, Lung

title: Regulatory mechanisms of MAPK phosphatase 5 in metabolic disorders
abs: Type 2 diabetes stems from the failure of the body to respond appropriately to insulin which is known as insulin resistance (IR). IR is the key primary defect underlying the development of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease. IR is closely associated with obesity and inflammation. Adipose tissues secrete various inflammatory mediators to regulate metabolic and inflammatory responses. On the other hand, proinflammatory activation of adipose tissue macrophages (ATMs) is both necessary and sufficient for the development of insulin resistance. However, the cellular and molecular mechanisms through which IR is initiated have not been well understood. MAPK signaling pathways play important roles in inflammation and metabolic homeostasis. Members of MAPK phosphatase (MKP) protein family are the major negative regulators of MAPKs. Our study on MKP5 showed that this protein inhibits the production of inflammatory cytokines by macrophages. In another study utilizing MKP5 knockout (KO) mice, we demonstrated that MKP5 KO mice develops IR and glucose intolerance, visceral obesity, enhanced p38 activation and enhanced adipokine gene expression in the VAT. For this proposal, we hypothesize that by controlling adipocyte function and adipose tissue macrophage infiltration and activation, MKP5 regulates systemic metabolic homeostasis. In this project, the regulation of MAPK activation and adipokine production within adipocytes and the regulation of ATM activation by MKP5 will be determined. The contributions of different VAT cellular compartments in the development of IR in MKP5 KO mice will be elucidated. The function of MKP5 in human adipose tissue will also be examined. Knowledge gained from this study will help us understand the mechanisms underlying the development of metabolic disorders in MKP5 deficient mice and will pave the way for targeting MKP5 in developing therapeutic interventions for the prevention and treatment of metabolic diseases such as type 2 diabetes.
kw: Insulin resistance, MAPK phosphatase, Inflammation, adipocyte, macrophage, type 2 diabetes

title: Quantitative Proteomic Analysis of Gastric Fluid for Biomarker Discovery and Development of Multiple Reaction Monitoring Assays for Clinical Applications
abs: Gastric cancer is a significant public health burden, being the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide. Its lethality is mainly due to the lack of reliable and clinically acceptable techniques for diagnosing early-stage gastric cancer, for which 5-year survival rates are >90%. Hence, early detection can significantly reduce mortality and improve outcomes for gastric cancer patients. However, there are currently no biomarkers of acceptable sensitivity and specificity for gastric cancer. The goal of our proposed project is to identify informative biomarkers for gastric cancer and to develop them for clinical applications. We have identified fasting gastric fluid to be an excellent source for seeking sensitive biomarkers for gastric cancer because it is produced at the site of the disease. Using SELDI-TOF mass spectrometry, we recently identified numerous distinctive proteomic features in gastric fluids of gastric cancer patients compared to non-cancer controls. We hypothesize that the composition and concentration of proteins in gastric fluids reflect the functional state of the stomach. The specific aims of our project therefore are to (1) use a quantitative proteomics approach (iTRAQTM) to analyze proteins in gastric fluids of gastric cancer patients and non-cancer controls for biomarker discovery, (2) validate and evaluate the clinical utility of candidate biomarkers and (3) develop multiple reaction monitoring (MRM) assays of candidate biomarkers for clinical applications. The proposed studies are new and there are no reports of similar work in the literature. We believe these studies will be important because identification of early-stage disease will enable early clinical intervention, leading to reduced mortality and better outcomes for patients. In addition, targeted quantitative assays of gastric fluid proteins by MRM could be a useful adjunct to clinical gastroscopic evaluation to enhance diagnostic accuracy. Lastly, the newly identified biomarkers may provide new leads to investigate the molecular mechanism in gastric oncogenesis.
kw: Gastric Juice (or Gastric Fluid), Biomarker, Quantitative Proteomics, Gastroenterology, Multiple Reaction Monitoring (MRM), Gastric Cancer

title: Tissue Engineering of the Intervertebral Disc - Regenerating the Annulus Fibrosus with Electrospinning and Physiologically Mimetic Culture.
abs: Tissue engineering a functional intervertebral disc (IVD) replacement offers a promising new treatment modality over current treatment options like spinal fusion and artificial disc replacement. Majority of tissue engineering studies on the IVD today focused on the nucleus pulposus (NP) rather than the annulus fibrosus (AF). However, without a proper strategy to regenerate a functional AF, NP replacement strategies would have limited clinical success. Function and form are intimately related, and hence materials that can mimic the anatomical form of the native tissue are often desirable and of great interest. The AF is a multi lamellar construct, and has been a particularly challenging area to reproduce because of its complex architecture and organization. The objective of this project is to develop a novel tissue engineering strategy to regenerate the AF using a combination of topographical cues and mechanical stimulus. Electrospun silk nanofibres will be used to mimic the native AF extracellular matrix and biomimetic culture of tissue engineered AF like lamellae will be carried out under physiological like forces. Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) from bone marrow and adipose tissue will be studied. Cell-sheet engineering will be assessed for its suitability in combination with the nanofibrous mats in creating a native AF like (NAFL) construct, which will subsequently be cultured in a bioreactor that will be developed to assess the biomechanical response of the NAFL construct under dynamic culture conditions. Clinical implications deriving from the success of this study include the use of NAFL technology as part of a minimally invasive off-the-shelf total disc replacement strategy. Conservative discectomy can be carried out to debride a severely degenerated disc, leaving behind the outermost AF to act as a “shell”. After which regenerated AF lamellae and nucleus pulposus cells can be inserted into the debrided space to form the new functional IVD.
kw: Tissue Engineering, Intervertebral Disc, Adipose Derived Stem Cells, Annulus Fibrosus, Cell-Sheet, Bone Marrow Derived Stem Cells

title: Development of Therapeutic Microbes for Prevention and Treatment of Infectious Disease
abs: Current antibiotic treatments against human pathogens are frequently ineffective due to the rapid emergence of multi-drug resistant superbugs. Furthermore, as antibiotics are wide spectrum antimicrobials, antibiotic treatments kill beneficial microbiota that promote a healthy human immune system together in addition to target pathogens. Among multi-drug resistant pathogens, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a leading cause of hospital-acquired infection, is known to be a major risk factor in the recovery of immuno-compromised patients such as those suffering from cancers and surgical transplants, and the aging population. In this light, we have recently developed a novel engineered Escherichia coli strain that can specifically sense and kill P. Aeruginosa, not harming other microbial species. In this proposed research, we aim to advance this novel sensing and killing E. Coli strain into a more clinically relevant, next-generation form with key therapeutic functionalities in probiotic microbes. In particular, we will further develop probiotic microbes that swim towards P. Aeruginosa upon sensing and disrupt biofilm, and exert strong antimicrobial activity against gastrointestinal infections in animal models. Towards this aim, the proposed research entails the development of the following three objectives: (1) identification and characterization of biological parts that enable directed bacteria motility and biofilm disruption; (2) Integration of genetic circuits that regulate bacterial motility and biofilm disruption into the sensing and killing microbes; and (3) In vivo characterization and safety assessment of the therapeutic probiotic microbes for infection prevention and treatment in animal models. We envision that our novel therapeutic microbes will provide an effective means to prevent and treat P. Aeruginosa infection in the gastrointestinal tract. In the long term, the framework developed in this study could be readily applied to the treatment of other infectious diseases, and ultimately lead us towards the development of probiotic microbes that are able to diagnose and treat multiple infections.

title: Validating candidate biomarkers in plasma microvesicles for the diagnosis and prognosis of lacunar infarction
abs: Lacunar infarction (LACI) is a subtype of acute ischemic stroke affecting around 25% of all ischemic stroke cases. The prevalence of LACI is higher than other stroke subtypes such as large vessel disease or cardioembolic in Singapore and in South Asia compared to western countries. However, inadequacies of the imaging tools to reliably examine small cerebral arteries and arterioles lead to the potential misclassification of ischemic stroke subtypes for diagnosis, treatment, prognostication, research into pathogenesis or patient recruitment for clinical trials. Hence, blood-based biomarkers could be a complementary diagnostic, prognostic and research tool. Our preliminary quantitative proteomics-guided discovery approach; 1) by profiling the microvesicles in pooled plasma of three groups of LACI patients (n=46) (divided by clinical outcomes following LACI) and age-matched control (n=17) with iTRAQ-2D-LC-MS/MS, and 2) by comparing the LACI-plasma proteome with previously generated datasets from ischemic rodent and human brain samples helped to shortlist 20 proteins for validation. Our hypothesis is that plasma microvesicles’ proteins such as Zyxin, Integrin-linked protein kinase, and other proteins targeting different aspects of the pathology of LACI (e.g., endothelium dysfunction or blood brain barrier abnormality) are differentially present in patients’ plasma microvesicles compared to healthy controls. This dysregulation may be associated with the recurrence of vascular events or decline in cognitive functions.Here, we propose to validate the panel of 20 selected candidates by a dual strategy of Multiplex Luminex Technology and mass spectrometric multiple reaction monitoring-based targeted proteomic approach in a large (n=200) prospectively studied cohort of LACI and control (healthy and large vessel disease) patients. The specificity of each of these candidates to differentiate among the various outcomes following LACI (e.g., recurrent vascular event or incident cognitive decline) will also be evaluated. Our study will deliver specific signature of plasma proteins to diagnose LACI and to predict the long-term outcome.
kw: Ischemic stroke, Biomarker, Validation, Lacunar infarction, Proteomics, LC-MS/MS

title: Targeting Assembly and Function of Hepatitis C Virus Replicase
abs: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) affects over 170 million people worldwide, and current treatment options are inadequate. Development of more effective treatments requires identification of new structural and functional targets, and understanding of the molecular basis of drug-resistant mutants. Like other positive-strand RNA viruses, HCV genome replication is characterized by the formation of a membrane-associated replicase complex, which is composed of viral proteins and replicating RNA. Given its critical role in the HCV life cycle, inhibiting replicase activity is an attractive therapeutic strategy. However, optimal targeting of the HCV replicase is limited by a technology gap that precludes study of replicase assembly and function in the membrane-associated state. To target these steps, we hypothesize that model membrane sensing platforms can support in situ reconstitution of the multi-protein replicase. We will first determine if biologically relevant model membranes can host full-length NS5B polymerase—the core enzyme of the HCV replicase. Based on successful membrane association of NS5B, we additionally hypothesize that engineering approaches will enable detailed study of replicase assembly and function. We will determine template RNA requirements for activation of membrane-associated NS5B, and develop a quantitative method to measure polymerase activity. Further, we will investigate how additional HCV nonstructural proteins interact with membrane-associated NS5B, and modulate replicase function. To demonstrate the platform’s utility for accelerating HCV drug development, we will also determine the specific mechanism of action of promising drug candidates that target replicase assembly and function. Taken together, the proposed studies will lead to the establishment of a technology platform that uniquely supports functional studies of membrane-associated HCV replicase. Importantly, this technology will help deliver the best possible treatment regimens by enabling development of pharmaceuticals that precisely target specific steps in replicase assembly and function, and by determining the molecular basis of drug-resistant mutations which arise within individual replicase components.
kw: Antiviral medicine, Biosensor, Hepatitis C, Model membrane, Viral replication, Drug development

title: Comprehensive chromosome-wide allele-specific analyses of X chromosome inactivation
abs: X chromosome inactivation (XCI) occurs in mammals. Each female cell transcriptionally inactivates one of the two Xs to balance X-linked gene dosage between males and females. Although a few critical genes involved in XCI are identified, the chromosome-wide gene silencing mechanism remains poorly understood. A crucial missing link in XCI research is a method, which can comprehensively examine allele-specific expression pattern of all genes along the entire chromosome. Although deep-sequencing has made comprehensive allele-specific gene expression profiling possible, several new methods, for example the padlock-captured SNPs method, were developed to concentrate the sequencing power onto a selected pool of valuable DNA targets to achieve more quantitative analyses and higher mapping resolutions. These methods fit perfectly for XCI studies. Here, I propose to apply these methods, especially the padlock-captured SNPs method, to study XCI in genetically defined mouse cell lines. We will generate several global views on different aspects of XCI. For example, how gene silencing spreads out along the X chromosome at the onset of XCI? Are there any DNA sequences functioning as “way-stations” to facilitate the gene silencing? The gene silencing status of Xi, once established in ES cells, is tightly maintained in somatic cells. Conditional deletion of a key XCI gene in fibroblast cell only caused reactivation of few individual genes. Gene reactivation is believed to occur in a “sporadic” manner. Such a view was based on allele-specific RT-PCR results on a small sampling of genes. How many genes are reactivated along the entire X chromosome? Does the gene reactivation truly occur in a sporadic manner? Can any consensus DNA motif be recognized within the reactivated genes? Meanwhile, we will also study on allele-specific DNA methylation and transcriptional regulation networks. The proposed study will generate unprecedentedly comprehensive and quantitative analyses on all these questions.
kw: Epigenetics, Padlock probes, Digital RNA allelotyping, X chromosome inactivation, Embryonic Stem Cell, Deep-sequencing

title: Membrane trafficking in mTOR signaling and autophagy - the roles of Golgi localized ARF-like GTPases
abs: mTOR and autophagy signaling pathways play important roles in regulating cellular homeostasis and the malfunction of them has been connected to numerous human diseases. Autophagy is controlled by mTOR signaling pathway and it requires membrane trafficking for the biogenesis of autophagosomes and autolysosmes. However, it is still unclear how the three signaling pathways, mTOR, autophagy and membrane trafficking, are integrated and regulated in response to nutrient. We propose here that, a Golgi localized ARF like small GTPase, Arl5b, could provide us a novel insight of these fundamental cellular processes. Our preliminary data indicated that 1) Arl5b could interact with the Regulator complex, which has been known to regulate mTOR signaling; 2) AP4 heterotetrameric protein complex could be the effector of Arl5b; 3) Arl5b translocates between TGN (trans-Golgi network) and late endosome/lysosome in a nutrient dependent manner, similar to mAtg9, which is essential for the biogenesis of autophagosomes; and 4) Arl5b is specifically required for late endosome-to-TGN trafficking. Our hypothesis is that Arl5b participates and coordinates TGN-endosome trafficking, mTOR and autophagy signaling. We propose here to further explore our findings to elucidate these newly discovered roles of Arl5b. We also propose to study other Golgi localized ARF like small GTPases for their novel functions in both membrane trafficking and autophagy. Our study will expand our knowledge by making novel connections among the three signaling pathways — mTOR, autophagy and membrane trafficking and will eventually contribute to the improvement of human health.
kw: ARF like GTPase, mTOR signaling, autophagy, Golgi, endosome, membrane trafficking

title: Development of Therapeutic Microbes for Prevention and Treatment of Infectious Disease
abs: Current antibiotic treatments against human pathogens are frequently ineffective due to the rapid emergence of multi-drug resistant superbugs. Furthermore, as antibiotics are wide spectrum antimicrobials, antibiotic treatments kill beneficial microbiota that promote a healthy human immune system together in addition to target pathogens. Among multi-drug resistant pathogens, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a leading cause of hospital-acquired infection, is known to be a major risk factor in the recovery of immuno-compromised patients such as those suffering from cancers and surgical transplants, and the aging population. In this light, we have recently developed a novel engineered Escherichia coli strain that can specifically sense and kill P. Aeruginosa, not harming other microbial species. In this proposed research, we aim to advance this novel sensing and killing E. Coli strain into a more clinically relevant, next-generation form with key therapeutic functionalities in probiotic microbes. In particular, we will further develop probiotic microbes that swim towards P. Aeruginosa upon sensing and disrupt biofilm, and exert strong antimicrobial activity against gastrointestinal infections in animal models. Towards this aim, the proposed research entails the development of the following three objectives: (1) identification and characterization of biological parts that enable directed bacteria motility and biofilm disruption; (2) Integration of genetic circuits that regulate bacterial motility and biofilm disruption into the sensing and killing microbes; and (3) In vivo characterization and safety assessment of the therapeutic probiotic microbes for infection prevention and treatment in animal models. We envision that our novel therapeutic microbes will provide an effective means to prevent and treat P. Aeruginosa infection in the gastrointestinal tract. In the long term, the framework developed in this study could be readily applied to the treatment of other infectious diseases, and ultimately lead us towards the development of probiotic microbes that are able to diagnose and treat multiple infections.
kw: Infectious disease, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Therapeutic microbes, Infection prevention, Probiotic microbes, Antimicrobials

title: Single cell genomics, a new window into malaria parasite physiology and pathogenicity.
abs: Non-genetic Cell-to-cell Gene Expression Variability (NCGEV) in clonal populations is a widespread phenomenon that occurs in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic organisms. In this project we will carry out single cell transcriptome analyses (SCTA) of human malaria parasites, P. falciparum and P. vivax, in order to understand the overall variability of these pathogens with respect to their physiology and pathogenicity. First, we will characterize intrinsic NCGEVs in several developmental stages of the P. falciparum intra-erythrocytic developmental cycle (IDC) in vitro. Subsequently we will analyze extrinsic NCGEVs of both the P. falciparum and P. vivax in the natural infections. Finally, we will characterize the stochastic gene expression profiles during the P. falciparum programmed cell death (PCD) that is induced by malaria drugs. The main objective of the SCTA studies of the Plasmodium in-vitro and in-vivo will be to identify genes or gene families that undergo stochastic gene expression and may contribute to variable nature of host-parasite interactions during malaria infection. We will carry out a series of functional analyses with several newly identified candidates that exhibit these properties in order to understand their role in host-parasite interaction. In addition, the SCTA of P. falciparum PCD is aimed at identifying molecular mechanisms associated with this process. Here we will focus on molecular factors of intracellular signaling and assess their role in PDC. The overall goal of this study is to use the cutting edge genomic approach involving single cell analyses in order to understand phenotypic variability of malaria parasites during infection and identify molecular factors associated with their adaptation to its host. Such factors are likely candidates as targets for development of new and/or improvement of existing malaria intervention strategies
kw: single-cell genomics, transcriptomics, Plasmodium falciparum, malaria, infectious diseases, Plasmodium vivax

title: Scaffold-mediated RNA interference to enhance remyelination and nerve regeneration in traumatic nerve injuries
abs: Traumatic nerve injuries (TNI) in the central nervous system (CNS) presents tremendoushealthcare burden due to early loss of function in patients who are mostly young and healthy.Unfortunately, effective clinical treatment is lacking. Pre-clinical tissue-engineering approaches havealso adopted restricted methods by focusing on directing nerve regeneration with inductive factorsand neutralizing growth inhibitory factors in the CNS. The results have been suboptimal and suggest aneed for alternatives. Remyelination, while important to nerve regeneration, has not been adequatelyintroduced in tissue engineer scaffolding approaches for TNI. Furthermore, instead of focusing ondelivering inductive factors to stimulate tissue regeneration, the opposite of silencing critical genesinvolved in the process of CNS regeneration may be considered using RNA interference (RNAi).Accordingly, the overall objective of this project is to develop a scaffold-mediated genesilencing approach to direct remyelination and nerve regeneration in TNI in the CNS. We willfocus on enhancing remyelination, nerve regeneration and functional recovery in an injured spinalcord using RNAi via microRNA delivery. We believe that the incorporation of microRNA withinbiomimicking nanofibers will provide a combinatorial approach to enhance CNS regeneration. Wehypothesize that remyelination of the injured nerve is critical to nerve regeneration and functionalrecovery and may be achieved through a scaffold-mediated gene silencing approach. We propose topursue the following specific aims: 1) Synthesize and characterize gene-silencing nanofiberscaffolds for spinal cord injury (SCI) treatment 2) Evaluate the potential of gene-silencingnanofiber scaffolds in enhancing in vivo remyelination, axonal growth and functional recoveryin SCI treatment. Results from this study will contribute to the knowledge required for translationalworks on CNS remyelination and can potentially be extended to treat other pathological conditionsrequiring remyelination. It will also demonstrate the feasibility of using scaffold-mediated genesilencingfor prolonged gene knockdown in vivo.

title: Role of tight junction proteins in adaptive and innate immunity
abs: Tight junction (TJ) proteins contribute crucially to stability and integrity of epithelial and endothelial cell layers whose barrier function is essential for life. Recently it has become clear that the cells of adaptive and innate immunity that locate themselves in epithelia express tight junction proteins, probably as an adaptation for their epithelial environment. These cells are the peripheral sentinels that will alarm the rest of the immune system about potentially harmful invaders be they in gut, airway, urogenital or skin epithelia.Here we propose to study if the absence of important TJ proteins, the Zonula occludens family, in immune cells has pathophysiological consequences. We will exploit our new mouse strains that allow conditional, Cre mediated, ablation of ZO-1 or ZO-2 genes in target cells that are already ZO-3 deficient. More specifically we will inactivate ZO genes in dendritic cells (DC) or T lymphocytes by crossing ZO-1 or ZO-2 mice (that are ZO-3 deficient) with relevant Cre transgenic mice. We will then monitor histologically as well as through flow cytometry if the distribution of DC in different types of epithelia like in skin, gut and lung are disturbed when DC cells cannot express ZO-1,3 or ZO-2,3. Similarly in different sets of mice we will study if intraepithelial localization of ZO-1,3 or ZO-2,3 deficient ?? and ?? T lymphocytes changes. In addition we want to study the importance of ZO-1,3 or ZO-2,3 in T cells when they form tight and intimate contacts with antigen presenting cells during T cell development in the thymus as well as during conventional immune activation.Finally we want to test if the mice can mount normal immune responses to invading pathogens and mucosal antigens when either their innate or adaptive immune cells are deprived of ZO-1,3 or ZO-2,3 proteins.

title: Effects of different light qualities on skin and their use in photodynamic therapy in cosmetics and skin disorders
abs: As skin is the most exterior organ of the body, it is exposed almost constantly to light. Daylight has positive (e.g. Vitamin D production) and negative effects (e.g. skin cancers), and while much is known about UV exposure, very little is known about effects of visible and infrared light. Until recently light sources for in-vitro work are used mostly for fluorescence imaging and are not precisely wavelength specific, emit variable intensity of light, are bulky, produce unwanted heat and are energy inefficient. Recent advances in LED and semiconductor laser diode technology address these issues, and provide great opportunities for photobiological investigations and treatment strategies. Our preliminary work clearly indicates that skin cells, amongst others, acutely react to specific light stimuli, however it is necessary to investigate this novel phenomenon further to find the specific mechanisms involved. There is also a requirement to study how light signals from the skin are transduced into the nervous system - in essence, can the skin 'see'?--The proposal will allow interrogation of the acute and long-term exposure of different wavelengths of light, or combinations thereof, through controlled exposure of in-vitro tissue preparations to light generated from bespoke LED or semiconductor laser light sources. From this we will develop novel devices for use in wound healing or treatment of various skin conditions. We will also develop LED lamps to improve patient or user well-being through controlled light exposure and for beauty applications for the general public. Most significantly these investigations will develop novel photodynamic therapy (PDT) treatments, and will address the intense burning sensations experienced by patients during this therapy. The impact of PDT will be widened by developing melanocortin ligands as cell-selective photosensitizers to target melanocytes (for skin whitening and pigmented skin lesion therapy), with longer-term prospects of targeting different skin cells and cancers.--

title: ENABLING TECHNOLOGIES TO ADVANCE RADIOCHEMISTRY FOR MOLECULAR IMAGING
inst: ISCE2 - Institute of Sustainability for Chemicals, Energy and Environment
abs: Successful advancement of PET to support imaging efforts in drug discovery, biomarker validation and clinical development relies primarily on the ability to radiolabel any radioligand with high efficiency whilst cost effective and reproducible. Additionally, the discovery of new radioligands is hampered by the development of ligands that are target-specific and will give useful information. The proposed research will address specific chemical and analytical hurdles that currently hinder the effective incorporation of a radioisotope, enable potential discovery of radioligands and the development of technologies that will allow the synthesis and then, validation of the radiotracer as imaging agent in vivo. The development of improved detection limits necessary to translate normal chemistry to radiochemistry will be investigated by combining an analytical algorithm developed around Band-Target Entropy Minimization (BTEM) with Surface Enhanced Raman Spectroscopy (SERS). Application of this technology to a known radiotracer synthesis will demonstrate the enhanced analytical capability and the relevancy of this analytical insight for radiotracer synthesis. Furthermore, new organometallic methodology relevant to both existing and potential radiotracers will be investigated, and then coupled with the improved analytics capability. Discovery of new radioligands will be attempted by a Diversity Oriented Fluorescence Library Approach (DOFLA) approach which will obviate the need for known probe-receptor recognition information. Introduction of a stable isotope directly into the design of the library ensures that replacement of the stable isotope with a radioisotope will not change the activity of the ligand and will be introduced by the methodology described above. Collaboration with IMRE to develop large scale integrated (LSI) microfluidics for the synthesis of radiotracers provides a competitive radiochemical platform to optimize conditions for the development of novel PET tracers. All successful radiotracers will be used in pre-clincal evaluation studies in relevant in vivo models for translation to clinical applications.

title: Biochemical Mechanisms of Triglyceride Droplet Formation
abs: Excessive amounts of triglyceride stored in lipid droplets (LDs) in adipose tissue, skeletal muscle andliver are highly associated with diseases such as type 2 diabetes, and the metabolic syndrome. Thereis a fundamental gap in understanding the mechanisms that mediate the formation of LDs. This lackof information is a significant barrier in developing therapeutic interventions to directly modulate tissuetriglyceride levels to treat obesity-associated diseases. Fat storage-Inducing Transmembrane proteins1 and 2 (FIT1/FITM1 & FIT2/FITM2) are the first endoplasmic reticulum membrane proteins identifiedthat mediate LD formation, with FIT2 being the only FIT protein expressed in adipose tissue, a tissuecentral to the pathobiology of obesity-associated diseases. The long-term goal is to determine howLDs form in order to devise therapeutic strategies for regulating triglyceride storage in tissues. Theobjective in this particular application, which is the next step in meeting this goal, is to determine thebiochemical mechanism by which FIT2 mediates LD formation in adipose tissue. Our centralhypothesis is that FIT2 is physiologically important for LD formation in adipose, and mechanisticallyfunctions by binding triglyceride to create a driving force to partition triglyceride out of the ERmembrane. Guided by strong preliminary data, the goal of this application will be achieved by twospecific aims: 1) To determine the physiological role of FIT2 using a mouse model of FIT2 deficiency;2) To determine the mechanism by which FIT2 mediates LD formation by reconstituting FIT2 functionusing a novel in vitro assay. The approach is innovative because it represents a new and substantiveeffort to determine a biochemical mechanism for LD formation. The proposed research is significantbecause it represents the first step in a continuum of research that is expected to result in thedevelopment of novel therapeutic strategies to regulate triglyceride storage in tissues.

title: Investigation of a Novel Stress Repressor, CReP in Human Renal Cell Carcinomas
abs: Kidney cancers are the deadliest urological malignancy, and renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is the mostfrequent type of kidney cancers. RCCs are facing limited treatment options as they are resistant tochemotherapy and radiotherapy. Cancer cells are facing high level of cellular stress due to theirunique growth conditions. To this regard, inhibitors of stress repressor, which boost cellular stresslevel, will selectively kill cancer cells. Our preliminary data shows, CReP, a stress repressor isupregulated in human kidney cancers by RT-qPCR and ectopically expression of CReP promotescancer cell proliferation. Based on this, we hypothesize CReP, an eIF2a phosphatase, is able topromote cancer cell proliferation and tumorigenesis. We propose to investigate this with multiple invitro and in vivo RCC models, as well as confirm its potential oncogenic role in human RCC samples.Moreover, we will investigate the molecular mechanisms of how CReP promotes cell proliferation. AsCReP is an attractive anti-cancer drug target, we foresee, this study will be vital to design CRePspecificinhibitors as novel targeted therapies for human tumors.

title: Defining the function of ERI3 in DENV replication and selection of RNA aptamers that inhibit ERI3 activity
abs: Dengue virus (DENV) is a rapidly re-emerging infectious RNA virus endemic to tropical areas of the worldand of particular concern in Southeast Asia. The tools to prevent or treat DENV infection have yet to bedeveloped. One promising avenue for the discovery of therapeutic targets is to identify host cell proteinsrequired for DENV replication. We utilized genome-wide siRNA screens and proteomics-based RNAaffinity chromatography to identify a putative 3’-5’ exonuclease, ERI3, that is required for DENVreplication and that binds to DENV RNA. The specific aims of this proposal are to i) define the bindingsite for ERI3 in DENV RNA and identify the protein domains required for RNA binding and exonucleaseactivity, ii) to characterize the function of ERI3 in DENV replication, and iii) to perform SystematicEvolution of Ligands by EXponential enrichment (SELEX) in order to select an RNA aptamer capable ofinhibiting ERI3 activity. We hypothesize that ERI3 is required for proper 3’ end formation of the DENVRNA and that ERI3 activity is required for production of infectious DENV RNA. To investigate thishypothesis, we will utilize RNA affinity chromatography and in vitro binding assays to define the minimalbinding site for ERI3 in DENV RNA and define amino acid residues in ERI3 required for RNA binding orexonuclease activity. We will perform siRNA-mediated knockdown of ERI3 and DENV-2 infection toprecisely define the effect on DENV-2 RNA and protein expression, as well as on infectious virusproduction. We will analyze whether ERI3 knockdown results in sequence changes at the 3’ end ofDENV-2 RNA and identify proteins that associate with ERI3 during infection by immunoprecipitation andquantitative mass spectrometry. Finally, we will utilize SELEX to identify RNA aptamers capable ofinhibiting ERI3 activity, thus developing new tools to combat DENV infection.
kw: Dengue Virus, RNA, Proteomics, Host Cell proteins, RNA aptamers

title: Brugada Syndrome: An in vitro humanized disease modeling with iPSC approach
abs: The ability to generated disease specific cardiomyocytes from induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) has enormous potential for applications in disease modeling and drug screening. In the current proposal, we propose to differentiate cardiomyocytes from viral free iPSCs generated from patient suffering from Brugada Syndrome for the first time. Generated cardiomyocytes would provide a unique in vitro model to study both the diseases. Evaluation of short and long-term exposure of current clinical used drugs either in monotherapy or their combination in these diseased cardiomyocytes would provide better understanding of channelopathies and mechanistic insight in electrical remodeling in arrhythmia. Quantitative gene expression analysis of ion channel coupled with electrophysiology and multi-electrode array (MEA) would provide significant insight into hitherto unknown molecular interactions of drug and ion channels and their disease manifestations. Our proposed study aims to form the basis to prognosticate safe therapeutic regimes which could be administered clinically for an evidence-based arrhythmic disease management.

title: Birth parameters, early life course factors, and associations with myopia in young children [GUSTO-EYE].
abs: Aims: To determine the effect of early life course factors on spherical equivalent refraction in young childrenHypothesis: Early life course factors such as maternal characteristics including first born children, advanced maternal age, poor antenatal health with consequent poor fetal growth and small birth size, as well as non breast-feeding, may be associated with refractive errors (myopia) in 3 year old children.Methodology: Participants will be recruited from 1,200 mothers as part of the GUSTO study in their early antenatal period. Family size, birth order, age of mother at delivery, antenatal health including smoking, exercise, alcohol intake, birth size, breastfeeding status every 3 months during infancy will be investigated. At 36 months, cycloplegic autorefraction would be performed to determine the spherical equivalent refraction and axial length will be measured.Importance: Myopia is a major public health problem, especially in Singapore where the prevalence is estimated to be as high as 53.1% in 9-year olds based on the Singapore Cohort Study of Risk Factors for Myopia (SCORM). The average age of onset of myopia is 8.5 years. Hence, the aim of the study is to identify novel early life course factors and provide a prospective documentation of these factors to develop primary prevention health programs to prevent the development of refractive errors and poor visual acuity in early childhood.

title: Studying the mechanisms of Negative Pressure Wound Therapy (NPWT) in aiding wound healing and its possible link towards cancer progression
abs: Negative Pressure Wound Therapy (NPWT) is widely used in the management of many different types of wounds from diabetic ulcers and infections to traumatic injuries. Surgical removal of solid tumors is frequently performed in cancer patients and in certain cases; the wounds are deep or wide and require assistance in wound closure. Although this technology has been around for over a decade, the underlying molecular mechanisms have not been studied in detail.Anecdotally, we have observed rapid local recurrence or growth of sarcomas in three patients when NPWT dressings were applied for wound management following tumor resection. In addition, we have preliminary data on biopsy specimens from NPWT treated patients with non-cancerous wounds having increased expression of HIF-1a, AKT, angiopoietin 1 and anti-oxidative enzymes implicating activation of proliferative and survival mechanisms. On the backdrop of these clinical observations and preliminary clinical data, we hypothesize that negative pressure wound therapy could have a role in tumorigenesis through modulation of the intracellular redox milieu, regulation of prosurvival factors involving Hypoxia inducible factor-1 alpha (HIF-1a) responsive genes, PI3K-AKT pathway and promotion of angiogenesis. Here we propose to study the molecular mechanisms of NPWT in patients with traumatic wounds, and the functional relevance and the clinical significance of NPWT use in cancer patients. Using two models, human patients and rodent-injury system, we propose to study: (i) the upregulation of oncogenic pathways such as HIF-1a and AKT, (ii) angiogenesis with the upregulation of VEGF and angiopoietins (iii) assessing oxidative stress by checking the status of anti-oxidative enzymes such as copper zinc superoxide dismutase and manganese superoxide dismutase. These bed-to-bench side studies will enable us to identify potential targets during NPWT that would help unravel the undefined molecular mechanisms of negative pressure therapy in wound healing and its possible role in the promotion for cancer progression.
kw: Negative pressure wound therapy, Mechanism of action, Cancer growth, angiogenesis, Wound healing, proliferation

title: The prevalence and natural history of cow milk and hen’s egg allergy in an Asian population - impact of component resolved diagnostic tests in predicting severity and natural history
abs: Background: Food allergy is considered the next global allergy epidemic. Cow’s milk (CM) and hen’s egg (HE) are the most common food allergens in early childhood.Aims and Hypothesis: (1) To carry out the first population-based prevalence of CM and HE allergy in young children in Singapore and assess the demographic and clinical risk factors; (2) To follow up a cohort of CM and HE allergic children to determine its natural history in our population (3) To measure specific IgE levels to CM and HE using component resolved (natural component proteins) diagnostic (CRD) testing and allergen-specific T-cell cytokine responses and correlate these with clinical severity and persistence of the food allergy. We hypothesize that CRD testing and T cell immune markers are useful tools in predicting clinical severity and natural history of the allergy. CRD would differentiate IgE sensitization to clinically important major allergens,and identify cross reactive allergens which may not evoke clinical symptoms, whilst immune responses measure markers of immune tolerance.Subjects and Methods: Six thousand children, aged 11-30 months, will be recruited from several childhood vaccination centres. Using a food allergy questionnaire survey, those with convincing symptoms of IgE-mediated CM and/or HE allergy will undergo skin prick testing and, if consented, a food challenge to confirm the diagnosis. Blood (1ml) will be collected by finger prick method for CRD testing and allergen-specific T cell cytokine profiling. In order to have sufficient sample size in the follow cohort, additional allergic children will be recruited from specialist allergy clinics.Significance: The epidemiological data derived is important for public health planning and the formulation of management guidelines. The evaluation of CRD as a diagnostic tool CM and HE allergy could add a relatively non-invasive means in improving our capabilities in CM and HE allergy evaluation and management

title: Development of Biomarkers for Contrast Enhanced Endoscopy in Gastric Cancer
abs: Early detection of gastric cancers confers a significant mortality benefit, but remains a diagnostic challenge. We hope to identify and develop novel biomarkers to improve the efficiency of detection by endoscopy. Our multidisciplinary research proposal has two major themes- the identification of novel antigens on the cell surface that are compatible with endoscopy, and the optimization of existing reagents to enable ‘multiplexed’ analysis in-vivo.Traditional approaches for surface biomarker discovery compare ‘normal’ and ‘malignant’ cell surfaces, but are prone to artifacts of cell line derivation and evolution. Our proposed strategy exploits the observation that a majority of gastric cancers are initiated by Helicobacter Pylori, through injection of the CAG-A oncoprotein into the host gastric epithelium. We therefore propose to use mass spectrometry to screen for changes that occur on the surface of gastric epithelial cells after induced CAG-A expression. Overexpressed molecules on the surface of CAG-A positive cells will be validated in a second ‘virtual’ bioinformatic screen, using microarray databases to select for candidates that are retained in cancer specimens. This dual screening strategy is expected to yield relevant hits that advance our understanding of gastric cancer pathogenesis, and are compatible with endoscopic screening of gastric cancer. Existing reagents and approaches to endoscopic detection of cancers also fall short due to technical limitations in antibody performance and poor quality of in-vivo fluorescence imaging. Concurrent to the screen, we will optimize existing cancer-specific antibodies for a luminescent imaging assay, by conjugation to novel bright fluorescent nanoparticles. We expect this to prepare the pipeline for future development of a multiplexed assay, with a significant improvement in imaging quality. Collectively, these approaches will help generate a set of optimized reagents and techniques, in preparation for clinical trials using biomarker guided endoscopy for early, standardized detection of gastric cancer.
kw: Gastric Cancer, Early diagnosis, Biomarkers, Upconversion Nanoparticles, Endoscopy, Helicobacter Pylori

title: Novel cellular substrate for complement protease C1s: implications in the pathogenesis of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE
abs: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a complex autoimmune disease of unknown aetiology. It has a strong genetic component involving more than 30 genes. C1q, C1r, C1s and C4 deficiencies are the strongest, specific SLE risk factors. Limited experimental documentation regarding how C1q and C4 deficiencies contribute to SLE autoimmunity is available. However, there is no data how deficiency of C1r or C1s causes autoimmunity. The classic functions of C1r and C1s originate from their protease activities – both being known as highly specific serine proteases that cleave the complement proteins C4 and C2. However, this long-held view might need to be modified as a recent study showed that many intracellular proteins contained potential C1s cleavage sites. From the perspective of the complement system, the fact that C1s is a secreted serum protease discounts the relevance of its potential cleavage of intracellular proteins as they are inaccessible to C1s in live cells. However, these cellular proteins will become accessible to the extracellular C1s in apoptotic cells which present intracellular proteins in apoptotic blebs. Accumulation of apoptotic cells can lead to its necrosis which becomes pro-inflammatory and is known to contribute to autoimmunity. If C1s cleaves some of these pro-inflammatory proteins or autoantigens, it renders C1s a role in host tolerance to self-autoantigens and explains its deficiency being causative of SLE. One intracellular protein that bears a potential C1s cleavage site is high mobility group box-1 (HMGB1). It is a `danger-associated molecular pattern (DAMP)’ released by late apoptotic cells which can cause SLE-like phenotype in mice. Our preliminary data showed that C1s indeed cleaved HMGB1 which inactivated its pro-inflammatory activity. Here we propose to examine whether C1s also cleaves other DAMPs and autoantigens and the results can fundamentally enrich our understanding of SLE pathogenesis and improve our perspective of new therapy
kw: Complement C1s, Lupus, Danger associated molecular patterns, Autoantigens, Macrophage, Substrate

title: Understanding Role and Molecular Mechanism of LIN28B-Let-7 microRNA Regulatory Axis in Leukemia Stem Cell
abs: One of the most significant scientific breakthroughs in the past a few years is induced pluripotent stem cells (iPS cells), which was pioneered by Shinya Yamanaka1 and James Thomson.2 The Thomson factors include SOX2, OCT3, NANOG and LIN28.2 LIN28 (LIN28A) was originally identified as a regulator of developmental timing in C.elegans. Lin-28 homolog B (LIN28B) is closely related to LIN28, sharing high similarity in nucleotide sequence and protein domain structure.3 LIN28/LIN28B is evolutionarily conserved RNA-binding protein (RBP), binding terminal loop of let-7 microRNA (miRNA) family precursors and blocking them processing into mature miRNAs.4 Let-7 is undetectable in embryonic stem cells and elevated level of let-7 promotes cell differentiation.5,6 Recently, there has been considerable interesting in the role of LIN28B in solid tumors and cancer stem cells (CSCs).6,7 Deregulation of LIN28B/let-7 expression has been documented in colon cancer,8 ovarian cancer,9,10 prostate cancer11 and hepatocellular carcinoma.12 However, the potential role of LIN28B/let-7 miRNA is largely unknown in hematological malignancies. Our preliminary data indicate that LIN28B is markedly increased in CD34+CD38- TF-1a cells than the parental TF-1 cells, which are CD34+CD38+. Our experiments suggest that this more immature and aggressive phenotype of TF-1a cells with enriched LSC-like characteristics arise from increased LIN28 expression. In this proposal, we will set to delineate LIN28B/let-7 regulatory axis in leukemogensis and LSC. We will quantify the expression of LIN28B and family of let-7 miRNAs in a large number of AML patients and examine the correlation with patients’ overall survival and molecular abnormalities. We will manipulate LIN28B expression in hematopoietic cells and then determine their functional consequences. We will undertake a detailed investigation of what are the coordinating factors in this transformation signalling. We believe the success of implementation of this study could provide an advanced knowledge of LIN28B/let-7 axis malignant hematopoiesis, as well as CSCs
kw: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML), LIN28B, microRNA, Leukemia stem cell (LSC), RNA binding protein (RBP), Biomarker

title: Using a HAT (histone acetyltransferase) to pull a trick on cancer
abs: TIP60 (Tat-interacting protein 60 kDa) is a tumor suppressor with histone acetyltransferase (HAT) activity (1). TIP60 not only acetylates histones but also non-histone proteins like p53 and ATM (ataxia telangiectasia mutated) (2-4) that are master regulators of cell’s surveillance pathways. In addition to this, a novel feature of TIP60 in virus induced cancers is my recent finding which shows that human TIP60 is destabilized by human papillomavirus (HPV) E6 oncoprotein (5). By doing so the virus attenuates the activation of TIP60 dependent apoptotic and transcriptional networks of cells. Furthermore, this destabilization is proteasome dependent and E6AP independent. This is very interesting as no ligase, other that E6AP has been identified that cooperates with E6 to regulate other cellular proteins (6). This also opens up a new avenue and leads to the hypothesis of my grant proposal: Can identifying the HPV E6 dependent ligase involved in destabilization of TIP60 be used as a therapeutic target for virus induced cancers? To test this, I plan to (i) To identify the ubiquitin ligase involved in destabilization of TIP60, (ii) Develop biochemical assays that will use TIP60’s destabilization by E6 as a read out and (iii) Develop a high-throughput screen to identify inhibitors of HPV E6. In order to achieve these aims I will adopt two different strategies. The first approach involves identification of HPV E6 interacting proteins by mass spectrometry analysis, while the second utilizes the genome-wide siRNA screen. Once the ligase is identified, both in vitro and in vivo assays will be developed to screen molecules that inhibit E6 function. Long term goal of these studies is to identify inhibitors of HPV E6 function. Keeping in mind that the currently available vaccines have only preventive function, these studies hold a great promise for treatment of cancer.
kw: Tumor Suppressor, Human Papillomavirus, Histone Acetyltransferase, Cancer, Small Molecule Inhibitor, Therapeutics

title: Role of phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase signaling pathway in cell proliferation during radiotherapy: a mechanistic study on lung cancer and normal cell repopulation
abs: Lung cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer and a leading cause of cancer death globally (Jemal et al. 2011). In Singapore, lung cancer is the second frequent common cancer in men and third in among women (Singapore Cancer Registry Report, 2011). Along with surgery and chemotherapy, radiotherapy (RT) continues to be an important therapeutic modality for the lung cancer treatment. However, repopulation or relapse of cancer after RT is a serious clinical problem.Radiation damages both normal and tumour/target tissues microenvironment. Prime goal of RT is to deprive cancer cells multiplication potential and eventually kill cells. However, cells develop radioresistance is a major issue in cancer cure. It has been shown that phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase (PI3K)/protein kinase B (AKT) signal pathway is a key pathway in war on cancer (Markman et al. 2010), involved in cell survival and repopulation through multiple downstream targets that mediates several cellular processes like cell growth, proliferation, survival and motility.In light of information about PI3K on cell proliferation, we hypothesize that PI3K pathway has a major role on radioresistance and relapse of human lung cancer cells after RT treatment. We additionally hypothesize that this pathway can be inhibited by molecular targeted drugs and therefore affecting only on the fast doubling cancer cell repopulation during or after fractionated RT treatment.To execute the above novel hypotheses, human normal lung and cancer cells will be used. Using monolayer and spheroid (ex vivo) cell culture methods the differential mechanisms involved in repopulation of lung cancer and normal cells will be studied.Thus, identifying the differential mechanisms involved in repopulation of cancer (radioresistance) and normal cells protection after RT will shed light in lung cancer treatments by RT alone or in combination therapy. Therefore, understanding how cancer cells attain radioresistance can provide clues for designing new therapeutic strategies.
kw: Lung cancer, Radioresistance, Repopulation, Dose Fractions, PI3K pathway, Survival inhibition

title: Modulation of Ras-induced autophagy via genetic and pharmacological targeting of CK1?: a novel anti-cancer strategy.
abs: Cancer is the leading cause of death in Singapore, with a total number of 47,579 new incident casesdiagnosed among the resident population during the period 2004-2008. In 20-25% of all human tumors andup to 90% in specific tumor types, activating mutations in the RAS oncogene together with frequentinactivation of tumor suppressors like p53 and the retinoblastoma protein (pRB) have been documented.Recent reports suggest that the activation of oncogenic Ras alone can promote tumorigenesis as well as celldeath, both of which are associated with features of autophagy. Autophagy is an evolutionarily conservedand highly regulated catabolic process that enhances cell survival in response to a threatening host of stresscues by enabling programs to recycle biosynthetic intermediates from misfolded proteins and dysfunctionalorganelles. Since it remains an open question whether one should promote or inhibit autophagy to improvethe efficacy of our existing anti-cancer regimens, ongoing research effort is required to fully understand themolecular clockworks of Ras-induced autophagy.We recently discovered the involvement of Casein Kinase 1 alpha (CK1a), a ubiquitously expressedserine/threonine kinase, in the regulation of Ras-induced autophagy. In this study, we plan to furtherinvestigate how oncogenic Ras regulates CK1a and determine the precise role of CK1a in the modulation ofRas-induced autophagy. Importantly, using in vitro cultured human cancer cells and xenograft and/orgenetically engineered mouse models of human cancer, we will study whether the modulation of autophagyby specific genetic or pharmacological (as a single agent or in combination with other standard-of-care anticancerdrugs) targeting of CK1a would improve therapeutic outcomes. If successful, this study will uncover anew pathway that could be exploited to treat Ras-driven cancers and improve the outcome of combinatorialcancer therapy in humans, via specific pharmacological targeting of key nodes of tumorigenesis-dependentbasal autophagy.
kw: CK1?, Ras, Autophagy, Anti-cancer therapy, RNAi, Small molecule inhibitors/activators

title: Survey of human host factors modulating the activity of HIV integration complex using a newly developed high-throughput protein screening system
abs: Viruses are responsible for numerous acute and chronic diseases in humans. The humanimmunodeficiency virus (HIV) is the causative agent of acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS),one of the leading causes of infectious-diseases related mortality in the world. Although currentantiviral treatments successfully suppress HIV in patients by inhibiting the viral enzymes, the majorconcern now is to give rise to the drug-resistant viruses. Therefore, it is necessary to develop novelanti-HIV drugs that exhibit entirely distinct mechanisms of action.Integration, one of the hallmarks of HIV infection, is required for efficient gene expression andensures the equal segregation of genetic material to daughter cells upon division. In virus-infectedcells, this process is mediated by a cytoplasmic nucleoprotein complex containing viral DNA, calledthe preintegration complex (PIC). Importantly, PICs isolated from infected cells are able to reproducean authentic integration reaction in vitro, indicating that PIC-based assays allow a reliable assessmentof HIV integration in vitro. In our research, we aim to develop an in vitro assay monitoring PICintegration in a high-throughput setting. In combination with human protein libraries produced by thewheat germ cell-free protein synthesis system, this assay will allow identification of novel cellularproteins involved in HIV integration. Once candidate proteins are identified by the in vitro screening,the functional roles of these factors in viral replication will be elucidated by biochemical and cell-basedapproaches.Increasing evidence indicates that host factors clearly play an essential role in HIV replication.Hence, understanding the molecular aspects of virus-host interactions in the integration step shouldprovide new insights into alternative strategies for treatment of HIV infection by targeting cellularfactors, which can act synergistically with existing drugs. Since the new drug target is a host factor, it s unlikely that the resistant viral strains will arise.
kw: HIV, Cellular proteins, Wheat germ cell-free protein production, Integration complex, In vitro high-throughput assay

title: Genetic regulation of dopamine neuron integrity, Drosophila and human studies.
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Specific Aims: We will use the powerful genetics of the fruit fly (Drosophila melanogaster) to screen for novel genes involved in dopamine (DA) neuron development and integrity, followed by investigation of these novel genes in PD pathogenesis. In addition, we will also screen blood samples of human PD patients for modifications of DNA sequences and mRNA expression of human homologues of these novel genes.Hypotheses: As our pilot screen has identified 2 novel genes in DA differentiation pathway, our large scale screen should identify more novel genes in this pathway. Genes identified from this screen are likely to show genetic interactions with existing genes in the pathway as well as with transgenic flies carrying human disease genes. We also expect to see modifications in DNA sequences and mRNA expression of the identified genes in some human PD samples.Methodology: Available mutant strains in the form of deficiency and P-element insertion lines will be screened for deviation from wild type tyrosine hydroxylase expression (which marks DA neurons) as well as enhancement or suppression of an adult Parkinsonian phenotype. The obtained novel genes from the screens will be characterized for their roles in DA differentiation and PD pathogenesis through some genetic interaction studies. Validation will also be carried out by genetic epidemiology screening of peripheral blood of 1,000 human PD patients and 1,000 control individuals.Importance to furtherance of medical science: Our research proposal will provide novel insights in DA neuron differentiation and integrity. This knowledge is applicable towards generation of improved cell replacement and drug therapies. Identification of differentially expressed bio-markers will also contribute to better management of the disease, i.e. more accurate identification and earlier detection of the disease.
kw: Parkinson’s disease, dopamine neuron, genetic screen, Drosophila PD model, disease management, cell replacement and drug therapies

title: Neural Causes of Cognitive Decision Making
abs: Impaired decision-making is a common feature of many neurodegenerative diseases, such as Alzheimer disease, frontotemporal dementia, Parkinson disease and Huntington disease. Identifying the essential brain areas of decision-making will be the first step toward future medical treatments. Here we propose an approach that localizes the essential parts of the brain that are causally involved in human decision-making. We focus on the “neural causes” of decision-making by searching for neural antecedents that occur before and predict human decisions. Our approach goes beyond conventional paradigms that only look for the “neural correlates” of decision-making, and will grant us the ability to localize the candidate brain areas that are the “neural causes” of decision-making but not merely “neural correlates” or “neural consequences”. Specifically, we investigate whether pre-stimulus brain states (i.e. baseline brain states right before stimulus presentation and decision-making) can affect evaluative decisions and their locations/means of exerting an influence if one exists. Our preliminary date show that evaluative decisions can be predicted by human subjects’ pattern of fMRI signals across a widely distributed network of regions in the frontal lobes before the stimuli are presented. Further examining the underlying neural basis could provide valuable information about decision-making in normal brain processing as well as how it can break in neurodegenerative diseases.
kw: fMRI, Consciousness, Decision-making

title: A human ocular surface disease constituted in mouse, from molecular targets to priming of human pterygium derived cells.
abs: Pterygium is a common ocular surface disease characterized by abnormal epithelial and fibrovascularproliferation, invasion, and matrix remodeling. The lesion leads to visual disturbances and has nomedical treatment apart from surgical resection. The mechanism of pterygium formation remainsambiguous, however, evidences from epidemiology and histopathology studies supporting theconcept that pterygium develops from ultraviolet irradiation damaged limbal progenitor cells.Lack of appropriate animal model delayed the development of new drugs or evolution of new surgicalmethod for treatment of pterygium. The specific aim of this proposal is to exploit previously evaluatedmolecular targets to constitute mouse model of pterygium, using human cultured cells derived fromsurgically excised human pterygium tissue. Previous studies implicated the involvement or activationof NF-kB pathway and the transcription co-regulator WBP2. We hypothesize that activating thesepathways will push cells towards a more ‘pterygium-like’ phenotype, and increase the likelihood oftransforming into a pterygium when injected into mice in-vivo.Cells cultured from human surgical specimens will be immortalized by a collaborator (SW). Variouschemicals will be used to push cells towards a more pterygium like behavior, eg, LTB, TNF-alpha, or EGF.We will use state-of-the-art technology to evaluate cellular and molecular markers associated withpterygium and check for enhanced cell proliferation and migration before injecting them into the ocularsurface of immune-compromised mice that will not reject the allogeneic cells.If pterygium-like phenotype is observed, we can use this tool to test the effect of potential drugs thatmay be used in humans. This can be used in pterygia that are not severe enough to warrant surgery,or be used together with surgery to prevent post surgical recurrence. This may also save costs forsociety because earlier pterygium can be successfully treated and reducing the number of cases thatrequire surgery.
