title: Phosphatases as potential regulators of LRRK2-induced neurotoxicity
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Parkinson’s disease (PD) is the most common neurodegenerative movement disorder affecting millions of elderly individuals worldwide. Despite intensive research, the etiology of sporadic PD remains poorly understood. Most PD cases are sporadic with no known cause. A small percentage of PD cases are inherited in a Mendelian manner, and several disease-causing genes have been identified. Although most of the familial cases are of early onset, mutations in leucine-rich repeat kinase 2(LRRK2) gene have been identified in patients with late-onset autosomal-dominant PD. Genetic studies have revealed that LRRK2 is the most common PD-causing gene. LRRK2 encodes a large multidomain protein including protein-protein interaction domains as well as a GTPase and kinase domain. Although the cellular role of LRRK2 is not yet fully elucidated, recent studies point to the importance of increased LRRK2 kinase activity which is believed to play a major role in the etiology of PD. Consequently, disease progression is likely mediated by phosphorylation-dependent LRRK2 substrate pathways. We therefore generated a transgenic Drosophila model of PD by overexpressing a kinase domain G2019S mutant of human LRRK2, under the control of the UAS-Gal4 system. These flies display a typical parkinsonian phenotype: loss of dopaminergic neurons, locomotor deficits, and increased susceptibility to rotenone( Ng et al, 2009 J.Neurosci.). We propose here to use this fly PD model to pursue the following objectives: 1) to screen for potential phosphatases which regulate the phosphorylation and dephosphorylation of LRRK2-substrate pathways that might contribute to LRRK2-induced neurotoxicity. 2) to screen for novel LRRK2 interactors(suppressor/enhancer). We believe that identification of potential phosphatases and novel LRRK2 interactors will help improve our understanding of LRRK2 function and uncover pathways that may be important to PD pathology.
kw: LRRK2, Parkinson's Disease, Phosphatase, Neurotoxicity

title: Evaluation of the significance and clinical utility of soluble CD137 and soluble CD137 ligand in monitoring and treating rheumatoid arthritis
abs: BackgroundCD137 and CD137 ligand (CD137L) are potent activators of immune cells. Their soluble isoforms (sCD137 and sCD137L) are of potential diagnostic significance as they indicate the activation status of the immune system, and of potential therapeutic value as they are inhibit immune responses. Murine models of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) demonstrate a contribution of CD137 and CD137 ligand to RA pathogenesis. However, their significance as biomarkers of disease activity, and their potential as therapeutics for human patients have not been evaluated.Objectives1. Evaluate the relationships of sCD137 and sCD137L with disease activity in RA at a clinical, ultrasonographic and radiographic level in longitudinal assessments.2. Evaluate how sCD137 and sCD137L influence the activities of peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) from RA patients.Methods1. In a non-randomized, prospective, longitudinal study of 72 RA patients, matched to 36 healthy controls, clinical, laboratory and ultrasonographic disease activity measures and X-rays will be collected at 0, 6, 12 and 24 months. Serum concentrations of sCD137, sCD137L and cytokines will be determined, and correlated to each other and to disease activity measures and radiographic progression.2. The effects of sCD137 and sCD137L on PBMC from RA patients and healthy controls will be evaluated by (1) depletion, and (2) addition of sCD137 or sCD137L to PBMC. Cytokine secretion, proliferation and apoptosis rates will be determined.SignificanceBy correlating levels of sCD137 and sCD137L with RA disease activity and tissue damage over time this research will enable us to understand the value of these molecules as disease activity surrogates, and predictors of worsening or improving disease. Testing the functional effects of sCD137 and sCD137L on PBMC from RA patients is a step towards the evaluation of CD137 and CD137L as targets for treatment of RA.

title: Identification and functional characterization of novel microRNAs associated with liver cancer epithelial-mesenchymal transition, recurrence, metastasis and chemoresistance
abs: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the most common type of primary liver cancer and is the fifth most common cancer in the world. The postsurgical recurrence, intrahepatic metastasis and extreme chemoresistance are major obstacles to improve the prognosis of HCC. Epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) has been identified as a key step in cancer metastasis and has also been implicated with drug resistance. Therefore, the aims of this application are to identify and characterize novel microRNAs associated with the EMT, recurrence, metastasis and chemoresistance of HCC. We have analyzed the genome-wide microRNA expression profile of thirty cases of human HCC tissue samples, including 10 recurrence, 10 non-recurrence and 10 match normal samples. A panel of significant differentially expressed microRNAs were selected for further confirmation and functional characterization. Among them, the miR-216a/217 cluster is of particularly informative. The miR-216a/217 cluster was significant upregulated in HCC tissues with recurrence compared with non-recurrence or match normal tissue samples. The miR-216a/217 cluster was also significant upregulated in a panel of HCC cell lines compared with normal liver tissues. More significantly, the expression of miR-216a/217 cluster was relatively higher in HCC cell lines (such as SK-HEP-1 and HLE) of mesenchymal phenotype compared to HCC cell lines (such as HepG2 and PCL/PRF/5) of epithelial phenotype. Expression of the miR-216a/217 cluster has been demonstrated to increase in the TGF-beta induced EMT model of HCC cell lines. In this application, we hypothesize to investigate the effects of miR-216a/217 on HCC carcinogenesis and EMT, invasion and chemoresistance in vitro, its role in the tumorigenicity and metastasis of HCC cells in vivo using the xenografts model. We also propose to identify the functional downstream targets and signal regulation networks mediated by miR-216a/217 cluster. The results from this proposed study will provide novel prognostic predictors and/or therapeutic targets for miRNA-based therapy against HCC.
kw: microRNAs, liver cancer, epithelial-mesenchymal transition, recurrence, metastasis, chemoresistance

title: Elucidating the role of Phosphodiesterase 4D (PDE4D) inhibitors in cancer
abs: AimConfirm the in vitro efficacy of Phosphodiesterase 4D (PDE4D) inhibitors in the treatment of melanoma, triple negative breast, lung, endometrial and ovarian cancers in vivo and that it is due to an ‘on-target’ effect.Confirm the prevalence of PDE4D protein overexpression in a cancer tissue array and also correlate expression level with clinical outcomes.HypothesisWe have found PDE4D copy number changes and protein over-expression in the above cancers compared to the non-neoplastic normal tissue. We have also shown that three PDE4D inhibitors [from the National Institutes of Health Center for Translational Therapeutics] possess potent in vitro activity against A375, M229 (melanoma), MB231, MB157 (triple negative breast cancer), H460, A549 (lung cancer), AN3CA, Ishikawa (endometrial cancer), C13, Caov2 (ovarian cancer) cell lines (i.e. elevation of cAMP levels, inhibition of the MAPK pathway and apoptosis).We hypothesize that these inhibitors would also have potent in vivo activity and that this is due to inhibition of PDE4D and its downstream pathway.We further hypothesize that PDE4D protein expression levels are correlated with clinical outcomes in the above cancers.MethodsThe project will be supervised by Prof Chng We Joo and will be conducted at the Cancer Science Institute, NUS in the laboratory of Prof HP Koeffler:1.Assess the activity of the PDE4D inhibitors against the above cancer cell lines in vivo (using xenografts in athymic nude mice).2.Verify the ‘on-target’ effect of these inhibitors by assaying the downstream pathway of PDE4D (e.g. cyclic AMP levels, CREB, PKA, and MITF protein expression levels).3.Perform a PDE4D immunohistochemistry tissue array using archived paraffin blocks of the above cancers from the Department of Pathology, National University Hospital and correlate expression levels with clinical outcomes.Clinical significancePDE4D inhibitors and PDE4D could potentially be a new class of anti-neoplastic agents and biomarker respectively in cancer.
kw: Phosphodiesterase 4D Inhibitors, Cancer

title: Randomized clinical trial of Epstein-Barr virus-specific autologous cytotoxic T lymphocytes for the treatment of advanced nasopharyngeal carcinoma patients
abs: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) is endemic in Asia with no new standard systemic treatment for advanced stage/recurrent/metastatic disease. While it is a chemosensitive disease, the median overall survival for recurrent,/ metastatic NPC still remains only about one year. Our recent Phase 2 clinical trial has shown that autologous EBV-specific T-cell therapy following gemcitabine and carboplatin is a very promising approach. These T cells are activated, expanded ex-vivo and adoptively transferred as an immunotherapeutic strategy against EBV-transformed cancers such as post-transplant lymphoproliferative disease and NPC. We have successfully shown in 38 advanced NPC patients that combined use of upfront chemotherapy and autologous EBV-specific cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) yields a median survival of 29.9 months, and a 2-year overall survival rate of 65.6%, and CTL infusions were safe and well tolerated. A recent Phase 2 study of paclitaxel/gemcitabine/carboplatin at our same centre reported a median survival of 18.6 months and a 2-year survival rate of 35%. Hence our results warrant further evaluation in an open-label randomized Phase 3 clinical trial. Our randomized trial will randomly assign advanced recurrent/metastatic NPC patients to GC followed by infusions of autologous EBV-specific CTLs (experimental arm) or GC alone with and potential salvage treatment upon progression of disease based on the attending physician’s decision. High-throughput systems biology and the latest immune monitoring platforms will be employed to interrogate NPC tumor, sera and the immune compartment respectively to evaluate specific immune responses, and to execute biomarker discovery as correlation with outcomes.To our knowledge, this will be the first randomized trial in the world for any therapeutic intervention in advanced recurrent/metastatic NPC and the first randomized trial of adoptive T cell therapy in any cancer. This study has the potential to significantly improve the outcome overall survival for advanced recurrent/metastatic NPC and to have a major impact on the field of cell therapy for human cancer

title: Potential role of Branched Chain Amino Acids in the development of insulin resistance and involvement of lifestyle, anthropometric and genetic factors
abs: BackgroundBranched-chain amino acids (BCAA) may play a role in the pathogenesis of insulin resistance (IR), subsequent development of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) and coronary artery disease (CAD), both increasingly prevalent diseases associated with premature death and significant co-morbidity. Little research has been done to understand the lifestyle, genetic and anthropometric factors that may be associated with BCAA levels.Aims1. To prospectively examine the relationship between plasma BCAA levels and changes in IR2. To examine the association between lifestyle factors, namely dietary protein intake and physical/sedentary activity, and plasma BCAA levels3. To examine whether genetic variants at the BCAT/BCKDH loci (BCAA catabolic enzymes) are associated with plasma BCAA levels and IR4. To examine the relationship between lean and fat body mass and plasma BCAA levelsMethodologyThis study will be based on 3137 Chinese participants who were examined between 2004-2007 as part of the Singapore Prospective Study Program and the Singapore Cardiovascular Cohort Study. Of these 1000 healthy participants are being re-examined in 2010-2011. Data collected includes medical history, diet, physical activity, anthropometric measures, blood pressure, fasting lipids, glucose and insulin (and DXA scans in 1000 participants as part of the follow up examination only). BCAA levels will be determined by MS-based metabolic profiling. Genotyping for variants of the BCAT and BCKDH loci will be done. Data analysis includes simple descriptive analysis, multivariate linear regression modeling to assess the effect of lifestyle and genetic covariates, and gene-gene interactions on BCAA levels and IR. Clinical SignificanceEvidence of the role of BCAA on IR and understanding how BCAA levels may be modified could serve to identify pathways and strategies to regulate it. This may lead to better intervention strategies or therapeutic targets that may result in novel treatments for prevention and treatment of T2DM and CAD

title: Nitric oxide synthase inhibition in cancer patients: phase I trial of L-NNA and biomarker devlopment
abs: BackgroundNitric oxide (NO) is an important signalling compound that is synthesised during the conversion of Larginineto citrulline, catalysed by the nitric oxide synthase (NOS) enzymes. The effects of NO on thetumour vasculature has been widely investigated in pre-clinical studies, and NO has been implicated intumour angiogenesis, as well as maintaining the vasodilator tone of tumour blood vessels. More recently,endothelial NOS (eNOS) was shown to be activated by oncogenic Ras signalling to promote cancer. KRasis mutated to remain in the active GTP-bound oncogenic state in many cancers. Tumour cells becomeaddicted to the expression of initiating oncogenes like Ras, such that loss of oncogene expression inestablished tumours leads to tumour regression.

title: To define the role of phosphatidic acid-preferred phospholipase A1 in glucosestimulated insulin secretion in pancreatic beta-cells
abs: Diabetes became the epidemic metabolic disease affecting 284 million patients worldwide.Dysfunction and loss of islet ß-cells play key roles in the development of diabetes. Insulin secretionfrom ß-cells is under the control of a complex signaling network which remains to be elucidated.Phospholipids and hydrolyzed derivatives by phospholipases are involved in insulin secretion andother functions in ß-cells. Lysophospholipids constitute a group of important lipid mediators, amongwhich lysophosphatidic acid (LPA) exhibits multiple biological functions. LPA may evoke its effectsthrough G-protein-coupled receptors followed by activation of various signaling pathways. We foundfor the first time that islets and a ß-cell line (INS-1) specifically express a PA-preferred phospholipaseA1 (PA-PLA1). Knockdown of PA-PLA1 in INS-1 cells by small RNA interference abolished theproduction of LPA and markedly reduced glucose-stimulated insulin secretion by >75%, with aseverer inhibition on the late phase secretion, suggesting an important role PA-PLA1 in regulatinginsulin secretion of ß-cells. The objective of this proposal is to understand this novel signalingpathway in ß-cells and define the molecular events underlying the defected glucose-induced insulinrelease after PA-PLA1 knockdown. We will investigate the signal cascade implicated in glucoseinducedinsulin secretion in both ß-cell line and isolated pancreatic islets after PA-PLA1 knockdown,including glucose metabolism, membrane potential depolarization, and cytosolic free Ca2+ levels. Thedownstream molecular signal pathways including cAMP, PI-3-kinase/Akt, and ERK that might beinvolved in the PA-PLA1 and LPA action will be also assessed. We will over-express PA-PLA1 to seeif up-regulation of its activity could enhance glucose-stimulated insulin-secretion in ß-cells, a potentialtarget for drug discovery. These proposed studies will substantiate the novel mechanism maintainingphysiological function of ß-cells and may also provide better knowledge to facilitate developing newstrategy for diabetes therapy.

title: A study to determine whether cytokine gene therapy can improve the efficacy and toxicity of Bacillus Calmette Guerin (BCG) immunotherapy for bladder cancer

This will be evaluated in a novel syngeneic, orthotopic murine model of bladder cancer. title: Study the mechanisms underlying the pro-survival effect of Bcl-2-Rac1 interaction in cancer cells and primary tissue from clinical lymphomas and to elucidate the role of STAT3 in this signaling network
abs: We previously demonstrated a novel mechanism of Bcl-2-induced cancer progression by linking the death inhibitory activity of Bcl-2 to an increase in intracellular pro-oxidant state. Recent findings provide evidence that this new biological activity of Bcl-2 is a function of a physical interaction between Bcl-2 and the small GTPase Rac1, involved in the assembly and activation of NADPH oxidase (Nox). Of note, the interaction was specifically detected in primary tissues from malignant lymphomas, and disruption of the interaction sensitized Bcl-2 expressing cells to chemotherapy-induced apoptosis. Stimulated by these findings, we propose to unravel the functional biology of this interaction, particularly focusing on, (i) identifying the interacting domains within Bcl-2 and Rac1, (ii) investigating the downstream mediator(s) of the pro-survival effect of Bcl-1-Rac1 interaction, and (iii) studying the clinical relevance of this interaction using clinical material derived from lymphoma patients. In this regard, our preliminary findings support involvement of the unstructured loop region within Bcl-2, which contains a number of phosphorylation-sensitive residues, as well as active GTP bound Rac1. To identify downstream mediators of this novel interaction, we made use of an in silico computer simulation driven model based on the protein dynamic network (Cellworks Inc.). The analysis implicated the onco-protein STAT3; STAT3 activation was observed in Bcl-2 overexpressing cells in Rac1 dependent manner. Based on that, we propose to investigate the interplay between these three oncogenic proteins in established cancer cell lines as well as in primary cells from patients with B cell lymphomas. Using primary cells and tissue arrays, we will look at Bcl-2 overexpression, Rac1 activation, and STAT3 phosphorylation and attempt to correlate these to disease severity and chemoresistance. The overall objective would then be to come up with an algorithm for stratifying B cell lymphomas, which could have tremendous prognostic and therapeutic implications.
kw: Cancer cells, Redox, Bbl-2, Lymphoma, GTPase Rac1, Stat 3

title: Translating the Role of Aspergillus Galactomannan in Pathogenesis and Optimization of Diagnostic Capability in Invasive Fungal Infection
abs: On the background of ever increasing numbers of immunocompromised patients seen in haemato-oncology, transplantation and intensive care units, invasive aspergillosis (IA) is the most common opportunistic mould infection fraught with diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. As susceptible patients cannot mount an appropriate immune response during infection, disease presentation is usually atypical. Diagnosis is difficult as the fungus cannot be routinely isolated from conventional microbiological cultures. There is only one commercial Aspergillus galactomannan-based (Platelia) immunoassay but its accuracy is variable. Current anti-fungal drug targets are also dismally limited. On the background of compromised host immune response, mortality rates from IA have remained high at 50%. From the front of diagnostics, the current Platelia assay was developed using rat-based antibodies which may account for its variable performance. We aim to develop much-needed new antibodies against Aspergillus galactomannan using a novel method involving phage display screening of recombinant libraries. The candidate antibody will undergo subsequent clinical validation for potential development as rapid diagnostic kit in IA.With the aim of identifying new targets for anti-fungal drugs and in immunotherapy, we will investigate the role of Aspergillus cell wall galactomannan in host immune response and as a virulence factor during infection. Our hypothesis is that galactomannan serves as a pathogen-associated molecular pattern involved in immune recognition and seek to identify its corresponding pattern recognition receptor. This is through use of Gal-negative strains, purifed galactommanan in immunoassays and knockout animals/immune cell lines and in animal infection models. In contrast to fungal beta-glucan which has been extensively studied and from which a new class of anti-fungal has been developed (the ecchinocandins), knowledge on the role of Aspergillus galactomannan in disease is nominal. Our focus on Aspergillus galactomannan aims to improve the diagnostic capability and provide insights for development of novel therapeutic modalities against this difficult-to-treat disease
kw: Invasive aspergillosis, Diagnostic assay, Immunocompromised host, Pattern recognition receptors, Pathogen associated molecular patterns

title: Image-guided simultaneous fingerprint and high wavenumber Raman spectroscopy for improving in vivo diagnosis and detection of nasopharyngeal and laryngeal cancer during clinical endoscopy
abs: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma and laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma in the head and neck (H&N) are the sixth most common malignancies worldwide. Early diagnosis and localization of H&N malignancy is clinically challenging even for the experienced otolaryngologists with the aid of conventional diagnostic techniques (e.g., white-light endoscope).The specific aims of this project are: (i) to develop a novel simultaneous fingerprint (800-1800cm-1) and high wavenumber (2800-3800cm-1) Raman spectroscopy technique for improving in vivo diagnosis and characterization in nasopharynx and larynx at molecular level; (ii) to develop an integrated pointwise diffuse reflectance spectroscopy and narrowband imaging technique for quantifying the vascular changes of pathologic tissues in nasopharynx and larynx; (iii) to assess efficacy of the radio-therapeutic treatment of patients with nasopharyngeal/laryngeal cancer using multimodal spectroscopy and imaging techniques developed; (iv) to develop robust on-line diagnostic algorithms for realizing real-time, in vivo diagnosis of early cancer and cancer in H&N at endoscopy.Our hypotheses are that the integrated fingerprint and high wavenember Raman spectroscopy are complementary; the combination of Raman/diffuse reflectance spectroscopy with narrowband imaging technique can be used to completely characterize the changes of biochemical/biomolecular structures and compositions, morphological architectures, vascular structures and blood supply associated with pathologic tissues; and these changes can be exploited and quantified for differentiating early cancer and cancer from normal tissue in H&N.The clinical significance of this research are that the simultaneous fingerprint and high wavenumber Raman spectroscopy combined with diffuse reflectance spectroscopy under narrowband imaging guidance can be a clinically powerful tool for improving in vivo diagnosis of early cancer and cancer in H&N. The ability to accurately detect, classify, and stage the H&N neoplasia as well as to assess the treatment efficacy using the advanced imaging and Raman/diffuse reflectance spectroscopy techniques developed will allow substantial improvements in the health care and outcomes of H&N patients.
kw: Tissue Raman spectroscopy, Narrowband imaging, Laryngeal cancer, In vivo optical diagnosis, Nasopharyngeal carcinoma

title: Development of therapeutic approaches to overcome drug resistance conferred by a novel BIM deletion polymorphism in chronic myelogenous leukemia and EGFR-mutated non-small-cell lung cancer
abs: The use of tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) to target oncogenic kinases has led to remarkableresponses in patients with chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) and EGFR-mutated non-small cell lungcancer (EGFR NSCLC). However, significant numbers of patients experience suboptimal responsesdespite adequate kinase inhibition, suggesting the existence of intrinsic TKI-resistance mechanisms.We recently discovered a resistance-conferring germline deletion polymorphism in the BIM gene. BIMis a pro-apoptotic member of the BCL2 family of proteins, and its upregulation is required for TKIs toinduce apoptosis in CML and EGFR NSCLC. The polymorphism switches BIM splicing from exon 4 toexon 3, encoding for a BIM protein missing the critical ‘BH3 domain’ required for BIM apoptoticfunction. Introduction of the polymorphism into TKI-sensitive CML and EGFR NSCLC cell lines issufficient to confer intrinsic TKI resistance through impaired apoptotic signaling, while polymorphismpositivepatients experience significantly inferior TKI responses compared to those without. Here, wewill develop strategies to overcome resistance conferred by the polymorphism, and enablepersonalized therapy to overcome TKI resistance. In Aim 1, we will precisely map cis-acting elementscontrolling BIM exon 3 splicing. In Aim 2 we will: (i) use information from Aim 1 to identify spliceswitchingantisense oligonucleotides that restore exon 4 splicing; and (ii) determine if BH3 mimeticdrugs can overcome polymorphism-mediated resistance in cell lines and tumour xenografts. In Aim 3,we will generate mice with a humanized Bim gene to recapitulate the splicing changes induced by thedeletion polymorphism. These mice will eventually be crossed into other cancer strains, includingthose modeling CML and EGFR NSCLC. Such animals will be critical for evaluating therapies toovercome polymorphism-mediated TKI resistance. Because the polymorphism is exclusive to East-Asians, and represents 15,000 new cancer patients/year, this project will address a major healthproblem for East-Asians in Singapore and worldwide.
kw: Drug-resistance, Pre-mRNA splicing, Anti-sense oligonucleotides, Personalised therapy, Chronic myelogenous leukaemia, EGFR-mutated non-small cell lung

title: Pyrosequencing assay for early detection of hepatitis B virus (HBV) drug resistant mutants in chronic HBV patients on antiviral therapy
abs: Hepatitis B (HBV) drug resistance is an important cause of treatment failure. At present, drug resistance mutation can only be detected after virologic breakthrough. We hypothesize, and have supporting preliminary data, that the HBV drug resistant mutants emerge early and can be detected using a highly sensitive pyrosequencing assay within the first year of antiviral therapy, before they are detectable using currently available assays.The aims of the study are as follows:1.To determine the incidence of HBV drug resistant mutants within the first 12 months of nucleoside/nucleotide analogue therapy.2.Validation of the pyrosequencing assay protocol for the detection of HBV drug resistance mutations against a commercial reverse hybridization assay and cloning-sequencing by Sanger’s method.3.To determine the impact of early detection of drug resistant mutants on predicting the emergence of clinical resistance in a case-control study.4.To optimize and validate the performance of a prototype point-of-care pyrosequencing device.Methodology:The study will be conducted using a case-control design. 150 patients with known drug resistance will be recruited as cases and 150 patients with no clinical resistance after 3 years of treatment as controls. The stored sera of these patients collected in the first year of their treatment will be retrieved and analyzed with pyrosequencing (Qiagen Pyromark Q96 ID and a prototype DNA analyzer) for the presence of drug resistant mutants. The commercial reverse hybridization assay and traditional cloning-sequencing will be used to validate the results. Outcome measures:The emergence of HBV drug resistant mutants at 3, 6 and 12 months after antiviral therapy will be evaluated. The sensitivity, specificity and predictive values of early drug resistance assay in risk stratification of subsequent clinical resistance development can be determined. The impact of the therapy change based on the specific mutation profile will be evaluated.
kw: Hepatitis B, Early detection, Drug Resistance, Polymerase mutation, Pyrosequencing

title: Identification of Drugs for Targeted Treatment of PTEN-Deficient Tumors
abs: PTEN is one of the most frequently dysregulated tumor suppressor genes in human cancers, and loss of PTEN function is associated with advanced cancers and metastases. Nevertheless, the therapeutic vulnerabilities of PTEN-deficient cells have not been systematically and comprehensively explored. We will use a two-stage approach to meet this challenge. The first stage consists of a high-throughput RNA interference screen of 7,000 genes in the druggable genome and additional confirmatory experiments to identify and confirm druggable genes that are synthetic lethal to PTEN. The second stage consists of (i) identifying small-molecule (drug) inhibitors of the confirmed PTEN-synthetic-lethal genes and (ii) validating the generality of their effects in a panel of ~20 cancer cell lines that lack PTEN function and, to show specificity, ~20 cell lines with intact PTEN function.In preliminary studies we have optimized the siRNA screen conditions and shown that we can identify candidate PTEN-synthetic lethal genes and drugs that inhibit them. These preliminary studies are based on a pilot siRNA screen of ~900 kinases, phosphatases, and related genes in a pair of isogenic human cell lines that differ primarily with respect to PTEN functionality. This enabled a follow-up focused screen using 65 small-molecule inhibitors, which identified three candidate PTEN-synthetic-lethal drugs. At least one of these significantly reduces cell viability in multiple PTEN-mutant cells without affecting cell viability in PTEN wild-type cells. The proposed project will expand these preliminary studies to include the remaining druggable genes in the human genome (~7,000 genes), and will include identification of drugs that preferentially inhibit growth of multiple cell lines lacking functional PTEN while sparing cells with intact PTEN function. Drugs identified in this study will have immediate translational potential as they are commercially available and their molecular targets are known.
kw: Cancer, PTEN, Drug screen, Synthetic Lethal, siRNA screen, Personalized cancer treatment

title: PBRM1, a novel therapeutic target for kidney cancer – from drug discovery to mouse model.
abs: We have recently identified PBRM1 (Valera et al., Nature 2011), a member of the SWI-SNF complex, as the second most frequently mutated gene in clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC), after the VHL gene. The VHL/HIF/VEGF pathway, through VHL mutations, contributes primarily to angiogenesis/hypervascularization in ccRCC, forming the molecular basis for the approved anti-angiogenic therapy which unfortunately gives rise to frequent resistance. We hypothesize that PBRM1, previously associated with cell cycle and genomic instability, on the other hand, plays a more important role in cancer cell rather than endothelial cell biology. Therefore, a new class of therapeutic agents targeting specifically ccRCC cancer cells will be beneficial and, when combined with anti-angiogenic therapy, may achieve a long-lasting therapeutic effect. We propose to perform synthetic-lethality studies using the kinases inhibitors library provided by GSK to identify targets that are synthetic lethal to PBRM1-mutations ccRCC cell lines we generated. Along the same line, we hypothesize that, a combined conditional knock-out model of VHL (which itself did not yield a tumor phenotype) and PBRM1, will lead to a ccRCC phenotype which not only can serve as an effective drug testing tool, but will also shed lights on their functions and their cooperative roles in ccRCC tumorigenesis. Finally, we propose to understand the downstream landscape of PBRM-target genes by performing chip-sequencing and subsequent functional validation studies. We are confident in achieving these goals: 1) the team is a leading group in RCC research with varied expertise from molecular studies to mouse genetics; 2) strong GSK collaboration on synthetic lethality kinase inhibitors screening and subsequent drug development; and 3) the tremendous resources related to RCC including a large tissue bank with well annotated clinic-pathological information, database of over 1000 ccRCC gene expression profiles and 30 ccRCC next-generation sequencing to date, and strong collaborations with RCC clinicians.
kw: Renal Cell Carcinorma, Kinase Inhibitors, Polybromo 1, Synthetic Lethal Screening, von Hippel Lindau, Transgenic Mouse Model

title: Hematopoietic stem cell-specific imaging, transgenesis and gene targeting
abs: There has been considerable interest in identifying a cis-regulatory element that targets gene expression to stem cells. Such an element, so called stem cell enhancer, holds the promise of providing important insights into the transcriptional programs responsible for “stemness”, and also serves as a molecular handle for stem cell-specific marking, transgenesis and gene targeting, and consequently become an invaluable powerful tool for research on stem cell biology. A series of candidate enhancers have been identified for hematopoietic stem cells (HSC). However, none of them have met the stringent requirements as a HSC enhancer. We recently succeeded in identifying an intronic enhancer in the Runx1 gene which is essential for the generation of HSC and critical for the maintenance of HSC integrity. The element, named Runx1 +24mCNE, was discovered through a combinatorial in silico approach and subsequent in vivo verification using zebrafish and mouse transgenic models. Runx1 +24mCNE is active specifically in HSC and hence the most ideal bona fide HSC enhancer. To further exploit this enhancer, we will generate Runx1 +24mCNE-CreERT2 transgenic (Tg) mice which allow for a tamoxifen-inducible HSC-specific gene targeting. In addition, Runx1 +24mCNE-(loxP-stop-LoxP)-(gene of interest)-Tg mice will be generated as a system to enable an inducible HSC-specific marking and transgenesis. The Runx1 HSC enhancer also marks hemogenic endothelial cells (EC), the immediate precursor of HSC. The precise detection of hemogenic EC would help to better understand the developmental machinery of HSC generation and facilitate the development of method to produce HSC from embryonic stem (ES) cells.The Runx1 HSC enhancer is likely to be active in leukemia stem cells (LSC). Because of their rarity, LSC is difficult to detect using currently available methods. If LSC marking system is developed using the Runx1 HSC enhancer, it would serve as a powerful tool for cancer research and drug development.
kw: hematopoietic stem cell, hemogenic endothelium, cancer stem cell, mouse model

title: AN IMMUNIZATION STRATEGY TO PREVENT HEPATOCELLULAR CARCINOMA
abs: Human hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the third most common cause of death from cancer world-wide, resulting in over 600,000 deaths a year. A very high-risk population is clearly defined because recurrence of HCC after potentially curative resection is common, and the prognosis is not favorable. We hypothesize that the generation of a potent immune response in post-surgery patients could prevent HCC. Our research has been focused on the identification and characterization of HCC-specific biomarkers. Among these, glypican-3 (GPC3) has been identified to be HCC-specific. GPC3 is a foetal protein that is not detected in adult tissues but is re-activated in around 80% of HCC. Recently, our colleague Dr. Sabapathy has established a mouse model to induce liver-specific mouse HCC by treating albumin promoter driven-HBSAg cell surface antigen bearing transgenic mice (TG) with aflatoxin. This project will be built on the earlier immunological studies of our collaborators at the King’s College London whom have demonstrated the generation of potent, functional T cell responses against tumour-specific antigens. Their strategy has been termed CASAC. The primary objectives of the present proposal are to determine whether immunization with recombinant HCC-specific tumor proteins such as GPC3 protein using the CASAC strategy can prevent the development of liver tumours in TG mice treated with aflatoxin whilst not causing autoimmune injury in normal or regenerating liver. We will determine the phenotypes and function of the circulating and tumour infiltrating GPC3-specific T cell immune responses, over time. It is anticipated that the data obtained from these murine studies will provide the basis for exploring this immunization strategy for secondary prophylaxis in patients who have undergone potentially curative loco-regional therapy for HCC. An immunization strategy that could prevent the development of HCC in patients at very high-risk of this cancer would be a significant contribution to world health.
kw: Human Hepatocellular Carcinoma, Glypican-3, Immunization strategy, Potent T cells responses, Molecular adjuvant, T regulatory cells

title: ST3Gal1 sialyltransferase mediates invasiveness and tumorigenicity in gliomapropagating cells and associates with patient survival outcome and disease progression
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Gliomas have poor prognosis despite advanced surgical intervention with adjuvant radiationand chemotherapy. Temozolomide, the drug-of-choice in the clinic, at best extends survival by 15months following diagnosis. Clearly, better therapies are needed to eradicate the highly infiltrative andrecurrent nature of the disease. Glioma-propagating cells (GPCs) are candidates of tumor recurrencebecause of their extensive self-renewal characteristics. Our study identifies the gene responsible forconferring the invasive profile of GPCs attributed to extensive sialylation. Our preliminary dataimplicated ST3Gal1 as a mediator of a2,3-sialylation. High ST3GAL1 expression portends poorprognosis. Importantly, depletion of ST3Gal1 by pharmacological and lentiviral knockdownapproaches attenuated cell surface sialylation with concomitant loss of GPC frequency, viability andinvasiveness. These data suggest that ST3Gal1 mediates GPC survival and the invasive phenotype.We hypothesize that ST3Gal1 sialyltransferase represents a novel prognostic marker andtherapeutic target in gliomas. We will define ST3Gal1 mechanism in mediating cell adhesion andmotility since these pathways emerged from our analysis of differentially expressed genes uponST3GAL1 perturbation. Specifically, we will determine integrin activation and subsequent focaladhesion kinase (FAK) activity by immunoblot analyses. A hyperactivated FAK mutant will be utilizedto genetically implicate the mechanism. Cell motility will be studied by time-lapse microscopy. We willdetermine the tumorigenicity of ST3GAL1-knocked down GPCs in an orthotopic mouse model. Finally,we will interrogate our gene signature in public patient databases using a rank-based, patternmatchingmethod to assess patient relatedness to ST3GAL1 pathway activation, thus potentiallyidentifying patient sub-groups likely to demonstrate favorable response to anti-ST3Gal1 inhibitiontherapies.Our study will identify ST3Gal1 as a novel prognostic marker and therapeutic target ingliomas. Importantly, we will develop capability to associate our in vitro findings with clinicalinformation. Our work will justify the development of anti-ST3Gal1 inhibitors.

title: Prophylactic laser iridotomy for eyes with narrow drainage angles: A randomized controlled trial
abs: Glaucoma is the leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide. With ageing of the population, glaucoma morbidity will rise, causing increased health care costs and economic burden for a condition in which visual loss, once established, cannot be reversed. In contrast to western countries, primary angle closure glaucoma (PACG) is a major form of glaucoma in Asia. In a recent population based survey in Singapore, the prevalence of glaucoma was 3.2% in Chinese people over 40. Glaucoma was the leading cause of blindness, with PACG the most blinding form of the disease. It was estimated that 10% of the population have narrow angles (NA), the anatomical trait predisposing to PACG. Laser iridotomy (LI) is a proven treatment for established angle closure. In eyes with NA, LI performed prophylactically can arrest angle-closure, and prevent acute attacks of angle closure from developing. However, as the natural history of NA is not established, data are limited on who should have prophylactic therapy or remain untreated, and it is not known if performing LI for all eyes with NA is cost effective.This is an ongoing randomized controlled trial that aims to compare LI versus no treatment in 482 subjects with NA in order to assess the effectiveness of LI in the prevention of PACG. One eye of each subject was randomized to undergo LI, and the other eye left untreated as an internal control. Subjects will be followed up once a year for 5 years. The outcome criteria are the development of peripheral anterior synechiae and/or raised intraocular pressure. NMRC has twice funded this trial over the last 6 years. This study will address the question of whether prophylactic LI can arrest the progressive blinding course for which PACG is renowned. The study findings will have great relevance for the prevention of blindness worldwide.
kw: Glaucoma, Angle Closure, Blindness, Visual Impairment, Elderly, Prevention

title: Zinc finger nuclease-mediated transgenesis for autologous cell therapy of hemophilia A
abs: AimWe aim to develop autologous cell therapy for hemophilia A by integrating a highly secreted, B domain-deleted hybrid human/porcine factor VIII (BDD-FVIII) in the genome of primary cord-lining epithelial cells (CLEC) and bone marrow stromal cells (BMSC).BackgroundFVIII replacement products are so costly due to complex and inefficient manufacturing processes that few persons with hemophilia A can afford optimal therapy. Clinical trials of FVIII gene/cell therapy have not met with the same success as in animal models probably because of transgene silencing and immune reactions directed at gene transfer vectors. Approach/MethodsOur approach uses cell-type expression promoters and safe genomic harbors that are transcriptionally permissive for integrating hybrid BDD-FVIII cDNA in primary CLEC and BMSC to achieve durable and efficacious expression. This makes FVIII replacement potentially accessible to every child and adult patient. BDD-FVIII cDNA will be integrated in primary human CLEC and BMSC ex vivo using zinc finger nuclease (ZFN) technology. Single cell-derived clonal cultures of FVIII-secreting CLEC and BMSC will be characterized by whole genome sequencing to assess potential genotoxicity and by transcriptome profiling. Building on work already done, we propose to improve the efficiency and accuracy of transgene integration into the AAVS1 locus of CLEC by synchronizing ZFN action to cell cycle phases. We will investigate and optimize ZFN-mediated integration of fibronectin promoter/BDD-FVIII cDNA into the CCR5 locus of human and canine BMSC. The latter is preparatory to future pre-clinical in vivo autologous BMSC therapy in FVIII-deficient dogs. Clinical significanceEfficacious and safe autologous cell therapy will greatly reduce the prohibitive cost of FVIII replacement. Our approach is relatively inexpensive, scalable and could significantly improve the mortality and morbidity of under- or untreated hemophilia. This can be expected to reduce healthcare costs, improve personal health and social integration, and mitigate economic unproductivity through higher employment.
kw: Autologous cell therapy, Cord-lining cells, Bone marrow stromal cells, Factor VIII, Zinc finger nuclease, Genotoxicity

title: A Brain-Computer Interface Based Intervention versus Sham Intervention for the Treatment of ADHD - a Double-Blind Randomized Controlled Trial
abs: IntroductionAttention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is the most common child psychiatric condition, with the majority of patients experiencing significant impairment in attention. Medications are often declined by their parents because of concerns about side effects and costs. We have locally developed an electroencephalogram (EEG)-based brain computer interface (BCI) system as a treatment to improve attention and behavior. We have conducted two pilot trials that strongly suggest this training programme would improve inattentive symptoms of ADHD in children. We aim to confirm its efficacy versus a sham intervention in a double-blind randomized controlled trial.AimsWe aim to confirm whether treatment with our BCI-based programme can improve inattentive symptoms in ADHD children compared to controls.MethodWe will enroll 160 drug naïve children aged 6 to 12 years who have been diagnosed with ADHD through a structured interview (Computerized Diagnostic Interview Schedule for Children, 4th edition). They will be randomized to either the intervention or control group. Subjects in the intervention group will receive 24 sessions of BCI-based therapy over an 8-week period, followed by monthly 'booster' sessions over the subsequent 3 months. Those in the control group will receive a sham intervention matching the intervention schedule of the intervention group. Parents and teachers of all subjects will complete the ADHD Rating Scale (ADHD-RS) and other questionnaires at baseline, during and after intervention. The children will also undergo neurocognitive testing. The primary outcome is the improvement in the inattentive score on the ADHD-RS as rated by blinded clinicians.SignificanceIf shown to be effective and safe, this newly-developed intervention involving the use of BCI technology has the potential to be an alternative mode of treatment for patients who are unable or unwilling to be on medication for ADHD. This may eventually be employed in conjunction with medications and psychosocial interventions.
kw: Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder, Neurotherapy, Inattention, EEG, Brain-Computer Interface

title: Safety and efficacy of blocking IL-4 in patients receiving standard combination therapy for pulmonary tuberculosis (TB): a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, proof-of-concept clinical trial
abs: New approaches are needed to achieve more rapid elimination of dormant mycobacteria and thereby shorten treatment for drug-sensitive and drug-resistant TB. Dormant mycobacteria are relatively resistant to antibacterial drugs and approaches that enhance immune clearance have the potential to be more effective. Interleukin-4 (IL-4) is a key cytokine in the immune response to TB that may impair the clearance of mycobacteria. We hypothesize that pascolizumab, an anti-IL-4 monoclonal antibody, might be of value as an adjunct to standard treatment. This proof-of-concept trial aims to evaluate the safety and efficacy of pascolizumab. Patients with smear-positive, drug-sensitive pulmonary TB who have received less than 14 days of standard TB drug therapy will be randomized to receive pascolizumab (dose increasing with successive cohorts) or placebo in addition to normal treatment. This will initially be administered as a single intravenous dose, repeated after 1 month in the later cohorts. Safety will be evaluated by assessment of symptoms, physical examination and by routine safety blood tests. Preliminary evidence of efficacy will be sought on a range of parameters including bacterial clearance in sputum (measured by time to detection of growth in liquid culture, decline in serial colony counts on solid media, serial counts with resuscitation promotion factors), changes in bacterial and host transcriptome patterns, host immune response and lung imaging by PET/MRI. The trial has the potential to identify a new approach to TB therapy that might merit subsequent evaluation in large-scale clinical trials and that might ultimately improve clinical outcomes. The trial also presents a unique opportunity to intervene against a specific component of the immune response and has the potential to generate a wealth of scientific data that could lead to improved understanding of the host immune response to TB

title: Novel statistical methods for analysis of complex clinical, serological and biological data in vaccine research
abs: Singapore, along with the rest of South-East Asia, has experienced a substantial burden of infectious diseases. Research on vaccines and vaccination strategies are vital for protecting the people and their livelihood. Statistical analysis of clinical, serological and biological data is an important part of this research. Such data often suffer two problems: complex censoring (including detection limit) and data clumping at zero. Some commonly-used laboratory and statistical approaches to handle such problems give rise to bias in estimates of mean concentration, prevalence of true negative and association between exposure and response, as well as poor type I error control and power. Regulatory and academic researchers have raised their concerns and called for improvements in statistical methods. This project aims to develop novel statistical methods that can improve the analysis of serological and biological data. I propose to develop three sets of models for handling data with: •undefined “fold increase” endpoints due to complex censoring in measurements at one or two time-points, •clumps of zeros, and •combination of censoring (detection limits) and clumps of zeros. The development of these models will follow the principles of mixture models and (censored) time-to-event analysis. Advanced algorithms will be proposed for the estimation. We will mathematically/theoretically assess their properties, and compare their performance versus that of existing methods by simulation. We will also develop and validate computer macros for implementing these methods. These novel methods will improve the accuracy of estimates and inference of important parameters needed for the evaluation of vaccines and vaccination strategies. The gain in statistical precision/power will also speed up the research process. Although this research is mainly motivated by vaccine and vaccination studies, the methodological problems are general. The results will benefit other medical research, such as studies of censored and/or zero-inflated medical expenditure data and chemical contaminant data.

title: The Oceanographic Perspective: Reconstructing seasonal climate variations in the Indo-Pacific using coral geochemical records
abs: Reconstructing the past several hundred years of climate change is fundamentally important to our understanding of natural climate variability, as they include a period of pro-longed cooling following a period of prolonged warming. Faced with the challenges of predicting precipitation and temperature variation in a world of climate change, we are realizing just how limited our knowledge of the natural climate system is. Tropical and subtropical Southeast Asia, with its low lying, heavily populated deltas, high demand for limited water resources, and exposure to a significant typhoon season is increasingly dependent on climate predictions to protect its human, natural and economic resources. Research has shown that the region is one of the most complex climate systems in the world. Modeling the regional climate system in the face of such complexity is also inhibited by limited instrumental observations and thus poorly constrained by physical equations. I propose to build a research team that uses coral skeletons to reconstruct climate and oceanographic behavior in the tropical indo-Pacific in areas important for 1) the flow of the Kuroshio Current into the South China Sea, 2) the impact of El Nino on the South China Sea, 3) the interaction of the El Nino and the Asian Monsoon and 4) the changing behavior of the Indonesian Trough-flow. These four sites of study have been chosen as they are known to host long-lived corals exposed to distinct but interrelated climate and ocean conditions. As corals grow they form seasonal growth bands allowing for high resolution sampling. From such material, I will reconstruct seasonal changes in sea surface temperature, salinity and ocean circulation and then connect these changes to improve regional climate and oceanographic models including those that examine the interactions of El Nino, the monsoon, and larger scale circulation in and around the South China Sea.

title: Silicon Biophotonics Program for cancer biomarker detection
abs: The objective of this proposal is to develop a biophotonics program specifically targeted for cancer diagnostics to address a major challenge in global health. The proposed programme is a collaborative effort between IME and IMCB designed to develop cost-effective and reliable point-of-care (POC) diagnostic systems based on silicon biophotonic devices for bladder cancer biomarker detection by leveraging on IME's advanced silicon micro- and nano-fabrication technologies as well as molecular diagnostic device capability and IMCB's expertise on cancer research.--Toward this goal, we aim to develop an integrated device with high multiplexing detection capabilities for a panel of different classes of biomarkers -proteins and DNAs to address complexity of cancer disease. The main sensing component, silicon biophotonics sensor, is highly sensitive label-free sensor and fabricated by the standard CMOS technology, which ensures low-cost and scale-up capability of the sensor fabrication. In addition, IME's innovative approach enables the use of an inexpensive LED, which provides means to develop inexpensive and portable device for POC applications. The proposed device is integrated with a customized Lab-on-a-Chip system to process the urine samples to bypass centralized and expensive laboratory instruments. In this project, we plan to identify bladder cancer biomarkers in urine by taking multiple approaches via collaboration with clinicians at NUH and incorporate them to the panel of biomarkers. Toward the end of the project, we will build a prototype device and test for cancer biomarkers detection in urine from healthy controls and bladder cancer patients. The sensitivity and specificity of the device will be obtained to determine the accuracy of the diagnostic test. --The successful outcome of this proposal would have multiple applications including screening of high-risk individuals for early cancer detection, monitoring of cancer recurrence and assessing effects of cancer therapy. This provides tremendous opportunities for the commercialization of biophotonic diagnostic assays.--

title: Engineering Plasmonic Nanocrystal Super-lattices for Emerging Optical Properties and Sensing Applications
abs: The nanomater scaled plasmonic nanocrystals are able to control and manipulate light at the larger sub-micrometer length scale. Just like molecules, which are formed by different combination and configuration of atoms to create the entire substances in the universe, we intend to use plasmonic nanocrystals as artificial atoms to create a diverse range of artificial molecules and crystals. The main interest is to impart structure-to-function properties on the resultant super-lattice, to study and manipulate the plasmonic coupling between these metallic nanocrystals, and their incorporation for environmental toxin sensing. I introduce a two-step strategy to achieve hierarchical complex nanocrystal structures with anisotropy, tunable porosity and modularity. Firstly, shaped-controlled plasmonic nanocrystals will be engineered into unique spatial arrangement of 2 – 6 fold symmetrical nanocrystal structures that mimic molecules configuration. Secondly, the nanocrystal structures will be self-assembled into complex hierarchical 2D and 3D super-lattices with non-close packing, anisotropy and heterogeneous porosity. These super-lattices are anticipated to display intriguing optical properties with frequency-selective response at visible light and near infra-red region. Emerging properties such as fano resonances, frustrated opto-magnetic properties, and enhanced light transmission are predicted to arise from the spatial arrangement of the nanocrystal super-lattices. Our plasmonic super-lattices can be readily used as the portable and disposable SERS sensor chips for various environmental toxins in environmental laboratory and field measurements. Our plasmonic super-lattice sensors will allow identification and quantification of probe molecules at low volume and low concentration. Our target environmental toxins are arsenic, mercury, lead, and cadmium. These target compounds are listed by Singapore National Environmental Agency (NEA) as the top hazardous species. This project is of significance because of it provides innovative ideas – two-step strategy towards anisotropic super-lattices to create new materials with emerging properties. Important fundamental information will be gained to improve the environmental sensors’ sensitivity and reliability, making Singapore a safer place to live.

title: Analysis and Conception of Symmetric Key Cryptography Primitives
abs: The first goal of this research proposal is to study the security of current block ciphers and cryptographic hash functions. The second phase will consist in designing new secure cryptographic components and eventually building new block cipher and hash function proposals. Concerning the analysis part: - block ciphers: we will look for improvements over the best known attacks on high profile block ciphers such as AES, the current worldwide standard and by far the most widely deployed algorithm in the industry. In particular, we will study and generalize the recent splice-and-cut methods and related-key attacks. - hash functions: based on preliminary analysis, we will search for an attack on RIPEMD-128 and RIPEMD-160, two unbroken standardized hash functions that are used in many crucial security protocols. Then, we will improve the collision attack on SHA-1, currently the most utilized hash function in the world. Finally, we will analyze the security of the candidates and the future winner of the ongoing SHA-3 competition organized by the NIST that will output in 2012 the next hash function standard. Concerning the conception part: - block ciphers: we will concentrate our efforts on finding a design strategy to resist related-key attacks thanks to computer aided proofs. More precisely, we will design a key-schedule function with enough structure such that all possible related-key differential paths can be analyzed by a computer. This work will be concluded by the specification of a secure and efficient block cipher. - hash functions: we will continue the recent work done on hash functions for lightweight applications (such as RFIDs). We will especially generalize the lightweight diffusion matrices currently used and this work will be concluded by the specification of a secure hash function with a good efficiency profile for any application.

title: Enhancement of optical absorption in coherent photonic structures
abs: When light is incident on a photonic structure containing an optically absorptive material, some of the energy will be absorbed rather than scattered. Coherent wave interference within the structure plays a large role in determining the degree of absorption, and it is possible to design the structure and/or the incident waveform so that nearly all the incident energy is absorbed and hence converted into heat, current, or fluorescent light. This phenomenon occurs as a result of the self-interference of a light wave propagating in an absorptive medium, and can occur even when the underlying medium is only weakly absorbing in the bulk. Photonic systems in which optical absorption can be thus manipulated include: (i) coherent perfect absorbers, "anti-laser'" cavities that act as the time-reversed counterparts of laser cavities; (ii) optically-absorbing random scattering media, such as doped foams or tissues, subjected to specially optimized incident waveforms; and (iii) "PT-symmetric'" optical cavities designed to incorporate both gain and loss, in which some incident waveforms can be nearly perfectly absorbed while other waveforms are reflected with amplification. This research proposal lays out plans for a range of theoretical investigations into the design principles, performance limits, and applications of these structures. The enhancement of optical absorption has a broad range of potential applications involving delivery of electromagnetic energy into a material, including optical modulators, detectors, and switches.

title: Mechanisms of miRNA biogenesis: Substrate recognition by the miRNA processing enzymes and regulation of miRNA stability
abs: microRNAs (miRNAs) play central roles in post-transcriptional gene regulation in higher animals. Hundreds of miRNA genes have been identified in humans, and their malfunction often leads to diseases including cancers. Furthermore, the miRNA pathway is used for artificial gene knockdown via RNA interference (RNAi) technologies. However, the mechanism by which miRNA hairpins are specifically selected from many plausible hairpins is unknown, and it is currently not feasible to predict miRNA genes solely from genomic sequences. Moreover, this renders the effects of single nucleotide variations in miRNA hairpins on their processing efficiency impossible to predict. In addition, although the levels of miRNA expression are determined by the rates of their production and turnover, regulation of miRNA turnover is poorly understood. The overall aim of this proposal is to understand how miRNAs are generated and how their stability is regulated in cells. Our strategy combines well-established tools in Drosophila genetics, genomics and biochemistry to understand 1) how 5’ ends of miRNAs are precisely determined, 2) how the miRNA pathway selects specific miRNA hairpins and 3) how miRNA stability is regulated. Drosophila genetics will also allow us to delineate the biological roles for the regulatory mechanisms identified through this study. The knowledge obtained from the biochemical studies will be used to develop computational methods to predict processing efficiency and cleavage positions by the miRNA processing enzymes, enabling us to efficiently interpret mutations in miRNA hairpins. In addition, the proposed genome-wide studies will likely identify non-miRNA substrates for the processing enzymes, revealing their previously unknown roles. Generality of the findings made with Drosophila materials will be tested using mammalian systems. Taken together, the proposed studies should provide a framework for better understanding of miRNA mediated gene regulation in animals. Furthermore, this information could lead to improvement of RNAi methods and possibly have clinical application.

title: Novel Strategies to Develop Elite and Improved Varieties for Sustainable Rice Production
abs: Rice is the most important staple food in Singapore and feeds over half of the world population. Rice production is affected by abiotic (temperature, water) and biotic (fungal, bacterial diseases) stresses. Thus, the accomplishment of producing more rice becomes increasingly challenging in the face of global environmental changes. Moreover, the crop is subject to major losses in yield due to fungal and bacterial diseases. Ensuring rice yield stability under adverse growing conditions, while using less water, fertilizers and pesticides is crucial. New technologies with a multifaceted strategy must be developed to go beyond the yield gains made from the Green Revolution of the 1960s and meet growing food needs of the expanding population in the future. To achieve these goals, we propose to initiate an integrated research project to 1) develop tester lines of new-generation rice varieties with improved yield stability under adverse soil conditions and climatic effects; 2) develop novel strategies to increase crop yield with minimal environmental damage by targeting rice root architecture as key to a second green revolution; 3) identify the molecular mechanism of resistance to key fungal and bacterial diseases; 4) identify genes controlling flowering time in male-sterile lines and restorer lines that will help to develop a strategy for synchronization of the parent lines for hybrid seed production; 5) generate transgenic plants with better architecture and disease resistance that can be made available for field evaluation and future breeding plans. Therefore, the findings from this study will contribute towards sustainable rice production and enhanced food security.

title: Development of Virus-Controlling Biotechnologies for Cost-Efficient & Sustainable Aquaculture
abs: Food demand increases steadily worldwide. Innovative technologies are urgently needed to meet future food demands. With a 6.9% annual growth from 1970-2007, aquaculture has been the fastest growing animal food production sector. Singapore is well-known for seafood including fish. This program aims to develop biotechnologies for cost-efficient and sustainable aquaculture. We propose to target viral diseases, a major aquaculture challenge causing massive loss and currently lacking effective intervention. We will identify and disrupt viral infection-related (VIR) host factors to produce virus resistant medaka cells and fish as a model, and develop novel biotechnologies to disrupt viral susceptibility in food fish of aquaculture importance. We will study host responses to viral infection and host-virus interactions. In parallel, we will identify potential antiviral agents by a small molecule screen. Host factor identification is made possible via a haploid mutagenesis genetic screen by using the haploid embryonic stem cells we have recently generated from medaka fish. Normal cells will die of viral infection. Upon genome-wide mutagenesis and virus inoculation, many cells will die, but few cells will survive through the loss of viral susceptibility by a mutation in the VIR gene(s), thus enabling mutant cells’ expansion and identification of mutated VIR genes. This mutagenesis genetic screen is practical only in haploid cells (one gene set), due to the clear phenotype of a single gene mutation, namely the survivability upon viral infection via the loss of viral susceptibility. However, this approach is impractical in diploid cells (two gene sets), as simultaneous mutation occurs at an exceedingly low frequency in both copies of a VIR gene necessary to confer survivability. Our program features (1) unique ability, (2) innovative multidisciplinary strategy, (3) basic & applied aquaculture research, (4) prototype of novel and achievable R&D research from infectious biology to aquaculture intervention, and (5) strong research team.

title: 3D Wafer Stacking with Considerations on Low Thermo-mechanical Stress and Efficient Heat Dissipation
abs: 3D integration has emerged as a critical performance enabler for integrated circuits, at a time when the microelectronics industry is faced with unprecedented scaling barriers, which have arisen due to fundamental physics and economic constraints. 3D integration provides a mechanism for space transformation of the traditional planar implementation of integrated circuits into three-dimensional space. It therefore provides a pathway to augment geometrical scaling for further performance enhancement ( More Moore ), as well as enables functional diversification ( More than Moore ) to improve higher-level system operation. At its core, 3D integration is simply the process of vertically stacking of circuits and forming electrical connections between them. Despite this seemingly simple concept, however, 3D integration involves significant development of many new technologies, from the basic processes and materials issues, to new approaches to system architectures. This proposal specifically aims to develop, refine and integrate two core technologies, i.e. Cu-Cu bonding and through silicon via (TSV) to realize a robust 3D platform that enables a wide range of future applications in a smarter planet.The scope spans several aspects of materials, process, devices, interconnect and packaging. One of such effort is on fine-pitch (<10 mm) Cu-Cu bond formation with precision alignment and low temperature formation. This approach promises to increase the interconnection density between stacked chips close to 1M/unit area hence offering high bandwidth between the chips. The other important aspect of the research is on through silicon via (TSV). The ultimate goal is to develop highly robust and manufacturing worthy enabling technology for 3D IC. This 3D platform is designed with important considerations in mind to curb thermo-mechanical stress and enhance heat removal efficiency. Both are identified as major roadblocks for successful implementation of 3D integration. These goals are attained by careful selection of carbon-based material with favorable properties and compatible integration flow.

title: Design and Implementation of a New Recording Architecture for Future High-Density, Long-Term BMI Experiments
abs: Neural recording technology is greatly demanded for building closed-loop neural implants to treat neurological diseases and conduct neuroscience research. Over the past 50 years, progresses in recording tools have allowed the number of recorded neurons to double every 7.4 years. Current systems allow simultaneous data acquisition from about 100 channels, equivalently up to 200 neurons in total, which is small in number compared with a natural system. Under the current system architecture, it is difficult to support a further exponential increase in recording density due to multifold constraints of the application. Another challenge is to support long-term experiments, because electrode impedance tends to increase due to the elicited adverse tissue response, which results in electrical isolation from target neurons. From recording perspectives, acquired neural data become noisy and distorted.--This project focuses on a new system architecture allowing higher recording density and more tolerance to interface degeneration and artifacts. Compared with its conventional counterpart, the proposed architecture has a frequency dependent gain stage that inherently rejects DC-offset and attenuates low frequency interference. In the digital domain, frequency compensation is used to restore the signals seen by an electrode. Powered by a switched-capacitor design, the proposed architecture leads to major improvements on system performance metrics. --In simulations with different electrode sizes and degeneration levels, the architecture obtains >10dB SNDR over the full data spectrum; while the conventional architecture has much degenerated SNDR for recording spikes. Moreover, the proposed architecture offers 4-bit improved tolerance to data fluctuation. The incurred cost is 2-3 times increased circuit noise which contributes to less than 15% of the total noise. We argue the proposed architecture is more suitable for future long-term, high-density recording applications; as a replacement to better support a mimicked Moore's Law on recording density in next decades.

title: Modifying Redox Active Vitamins and Coenzymes for Improved Efficiency
abs: The exact biological function of many vitamins remains a highly contentious area of research. For example, vitamin E is one of the most widely studied vitamins but uncertainties in its true biological function have increased in the new millennium. One reason for the controversy is because many of the supposed benefits of a diet enriched in vitamin E have not been realized in clinical trials. Since free radical damage has been linked to aging, it has been argued that vitamin E should have significant health benefits (by preventing free radical damage) if taken as a dietary supplement.-Medical trials on the health effects of vitamin E and other antioxidants (such as vitamin C) have often resulted in contradictory findings, with no definitive study that proves vitamin E, or other antioxidants, are beneficial when consumed in doses above what is present naturally in a well-balanced diet. Furthermore, while vitamin E certainly has antioxidant properties in the laboratory, there is scanty evidence that these antioxidant properties are important in real biological systems. Therefore, vitamin E's role as an antioxidant has become more controversial or uncertain as more research is conducted. -In this proposal, voltammetric and spectroscopic (EPR, UV-vis, FTIR) techniques will be used to examine the electrochemical (redox) properties of vitamins (A, B, C, D, E, K) and low molecular mass coenzymes. The compounds will be examined in aqueous and non-aqueous solvents, and the liposoluble compounds will also be examined inside artificial bilayer membranes. New compounds will be synthesised to test whether the electron transfer properties can be improved via small changes to the natural structure. The results of the study could lead to the development of new improved forms of vitamins with significant health benefits that are potentially marketable within the multibillion dollar health supplement industry.

title: Scalable Timing Analysis Methods for Embedded Software
abs: Real-time embedded software are ubiquitious and control the functionality of many devices used in our everyday lives. The focus of the proposed project will be on compositional timing analysis methods which efficiently derive Worst Case Execution Time (WCET) estimates of large real-life embedded software. WCET analysis usually involves program path analysis as well as micro-architectural analysis. We will aim for achieving compositionality both at the program level, as well in the construction of timing models for the underlying micro-architecture. At the program level, we plan to generate timing summaries of the individual program fragments such as functions / procedures. Consequently, if a library or a small part of a program is changed - we do not need to re-do the entire analysis. --At the micro-architecture level, our focus will be on building timing models to capture the timing effects of multi-cores. Processor manufacturers have increasingly moved towards multi-cores, and this has impacted the embedded processor market as well. However, when we build a software timing analyzer for multi-core platforms, we want the analyzer to be configurable with respect to small changes, such as changes in the number of cores. Such configurability may be achieved by compositional analysis of the timing effects of the individual cores, that is, we want to analyze the timing effects of each processor core individually and compose them to get the timing effects of a multi-core platform. This removes the need to re-do the complete analysis in case of small changes in the platform.-The main deliverable of the project is a scalable WCET analysis tool that can generate tight execution time bounds for software (possibly running via a real-time operating system RTOS) on multi-core platforms. This will validate the utility of the compositional timing analysis methods proposed in the project.

title: Antimicrobial materials against drug-resistant bacteria: design, spectroscopic characterization and computational modeling
abs: Currently, increased resistance of bacterial infections to antibiotic treatment has been extensively documented and is recognized to be a health threat to the community. One promising alternative for the inactivation of bacteria is the photodynamic antimicrobial chemotherapy (PACT), which involves the efficient uptake of a photosensitizer (PS) by the bacteria and the activation of the PS by visible light which may then produce cytotoxic singlet oxygen species to subsequently destroy the microbes. Despite the initial success of PACT in relieving the symptoms of bacterial infections, PACT continues to suffer from limitations which have hindered its progress toward being a universal treatment for pathogen related diseases. The major challenges facing PACT today are the lack of: 1) stable photosensitizers that targets specific sites at the subcellular level, 2) multifunctional strategies for combining PACT treatments and real-time molecular imaging of therapy intervention, and 3) fundamental understanding of the exact nature of the interaction between the PS and specific site of action. To systematically address these challenges, this project will focus on the development of novel and low toxicity glycopeptide antibiotic (to target Gram (+) bacteria), bacterial targeting peptides and lipopolysaccharide (to target Gram (-) bacteria) affinity ligands conjugated porphyrin, perylenediimide and terrylenediimide PS analogs that exhibit increased PACT efficacy in the treatment of drug resistant pathogen related diseases. The polyvalent/multivalent properties of the photostable and long wavelength activated affinity ligand conjugated photosensitizers will be exploited in order to significantly increase their binding affinity towards the sites of action in bacteria. The knowledge and innovation derived from this project will allow the Nanyang Technological University to eventually set-up a center dedicated to PACT and related research and will further boost the pharmaceutical and health care industries in Singapore and globally.
