title: QDOT colour-converting TV-LEDs
abs: For television (TV) and other displays, conventional cathode ray tubes (CRTs) do not offer deeply saturated red or green hues found in nature towards the edge of CIE 1931 chromaticity diagram (colour space of human perception). Flat panel displays including plasma displays and liquid crystal displays (LCDs) lit with fluorescent lamps fall even shorter of that ideal colour space (down to 75% of the National Television System Committee (NTSC) standard). LED-TVs that have been developed more recently use solid state lighting LEDs instead of fluorescent lamps for their back-lit (or edge-lit) LCD displays. These LED-TVs use III-nitride LEDs integrated with conventional phosphors that are developed for general lighting purpose and not optimized at all for LCD displays. As a result, the challenge of offering the richest possible viewing experience in an energy-efficient way remains a fundamental problem for TVs and displays today due to the limitation of the existing technologies. In this project, to offer solutions to these problems, we propose to develop and demonstrate high-quality, high-efficiency TV-LEDs that integrate semiconductor quantum dot nanophosphors on single chips for superior colour definition with >100% coverage of NTSC colour space. --These QDOT colour-converting TV-LEDs will deliver the properties of -1.) high colour purity (with full-width-at-half-maximum of 30-50 nm for colour saturation) to match the spectral filters as desired, --2.) precise spectral tunability and control across the entire visible spectrum of human perception (420 to 650 nm if desired), --3.) multi-colour components (3, 4, or more if desired), --4.) Forster-type resonance energy transfer (FRET) based colour-conversion to provide further enhancement in efficiency, and --5.) high luminous efficiency across the full emission spectra including the green gap (>40 lm/W). --Therefore, these QDOT colour-converting TV-LEDs will provide several competitive advantages over the existing conventional LEDs and offer important benefits in TV and display technologies.

title: Evaporation-induced self-assembly of nanoparticles in drying nanofluids
abs: The evaporation-induced self-assembly of nanoparticles is an easy way to produce miniature devises, which could benefit a wide breadth of research and technology areas. Mastering the process of nanoparticle aggregation into prescribed structures will provide great opportunities in more effective and energy-saving manufacturing. The process driving the fractal-like structures formation can be described by the lattice-gas kinetic Monte Carlo (KMC) model. Monte Carlo simulation results are proving the possibility of fractal aggregation in residual thin film during the final drying process. These simulation results were confirmed in the series of experiments with nanometer copper or graphite nanoparticles dispersed in the deionized water in the preliminary experiments. However, the self-assembly process is a complex process. Until now it is not well understood how the various factors are affecting the aggregate formation during drying nanofluids. Extensive simulation in a circle open domain and experimental work should be performed to generate a unique and universal approach to produce the nanoparticle self-assemblies with the prescribed geometry and properties. The modeling and simulation will be performed simultaneously. In the modeling, the present two-dimensional KMC model will be developed further by conducting the parameter study. Statistical data analysis will be made. Alternatively, the two-dimensional KMC model will be incorporated with the Diffusion Limited Aggregation theory; the three-dimensional model will be further developed. In the experiments, the drying patterns will be investigated from nanofluids with different sizes and species by monitoring the temperature by an infrared camera and pressure in an evaporating chamber to be designed. All the processes of the droplet drying and fractal formation will be recorded in real-time, and images of the final structures will be captured by SEM or AFM. The coupling of the experiment and modeling will be mainly conducted by a research fellow in an aid of the principle investigator.

title: Developing Nanoscale Laser for Imaging and Sensing
abs: A recent discovery (Nature, 2009, 460, 1110) showed that surface plasmons on metal nanoparticles can be amplified with the help of the surrounding gain materials to give off laser. Simulation by Boris Luk'yanchuk (DSI, A*Star) has shown that anisotropic metal nanorods with dendritic branches will give off much improved laser signals. Such improved signals are critical for improving the sensitivity in both detection and imaging. Recently, works from our team demonstrated the synthesis of dendritic metal nanostructures, which is similar to that proposed by theories. We will start from this sweet spot to explore various directions for improving nanolaser.--The PI, Chen Hongyu, is specialized in synthesizing complex nanostructures particularly core-shell nanostructures, whereas the Co-PI Li Shuzhou is specialized in theoretic simulations. Thus, our team will form ideal collaboration to carry out the proposed works. We will be guided by theoretic predictions to explore different nanostructures and different materials. The key aspect is to coat dendritic metal nanostructure with a uniform layer of gain materials, which is well within our demonstrated synthetic capabilities. We will further explore the edge of lasing to develop very sensitive sensing schemes.

title: One Step Multicomponent Self-assembly of Highly Ordered Mesoporous Carbon-Transition Metal Oxide Nanocomposites for Supercapacitors
abs: Supercapacitors offer a very high power density, which is inevitably required by a number of energy storage applications. However, their energy storage density at the moment is too low, which dramatically hinders their applications. In a timely response to break this big technological bottleneck, we propose to develop a new one step multicomponent self-assembly strategy for highly ordered 3D mesoporous carbon-transitional metal oxide nanocomposites, aiming at developing a class of supercapacitors of much improved performance approaching to the theoretically predicted. --In formulating this proposal, we have carefully considered the key operating parameters that are largely determining the performance of supercapacitors, including the requirement for a highly ordered 3D mesoporous structure, and the presence of nanoparticles of transition metal oxides, notably MnO2 nanoparticles, which will enable the dual storage mechanisms of pseudocapacitance. -The objectives of research proposed in this project are summarized as follows:--1) To develop a class of highly ordered 3D mesoporous carbon-transition metal oxide (MnO2) nanocomposites in thin film form for supercapacitors of much improved performance approaching to the theoretically predicted, by properly establishing the new one step multicomponent self-assembly strategy, where copolymers will be employed as soft templates;--2) To establish the highly ordered mesoporous carbon structure of different configurations including hexagonal, cubical, and vesicle morphologies, which will provide the wanted ultrahigh specific area to accommodate the electrolyte, offer high electrical conductivity, and at the same time to provide structural support for transition metal oxide nanoparticles formed in-situ in the one step multicomponent self-assembly;--3) To establish the electrochemical behavior of these highly ordered mesoporous carbon-transition metal oxide nanocomposites for their performance in supercapacitors, aiming at significantly increasing their energy density and improving the overall performance, where several of the key structural, surface and interface parameters will be thoroughly investigated and made understood.

title: Optical Dynamic Manipulation of Multiple Groups of Cells
abs: The research and development of robotics and automation technology in the past few decades has fundamentally revolutionized the modern manufacturing industries. However, rapid advances in biological sciences and nanotechnology have led to the demand of robotics automation at micro and nano scales, thus opening up new challenges to the understanding robotic manipulation of cells or nanoparticles.-The ability to manipulate cells and biological molecules automatically and efficienctly is crucial towards automation in micro and nano scales. Robotic manipulation has shown to be a key technology driver in factory automation, but the study of cell manipulation introduces new research problems that are non-existence in the traditional robotic manipulation tasks. --This research aims to bridge the gap between traditional robotic manipulation techniques and optical manipulation techniques of cells. We proposed to develop a robotic manipulation technique for optical tweezers that integrates automatic trapping and manipulation of cell into a unified approach. The dynamics of the cells and the manipulator will be taken into consideration in the design technique. The dynamic interactions between the manipulators and cells will be analyzed to provide insight into the dynamic manipulation problem using optical tweezers. --Considering different groups of cells as a whole during manipulation will limit the manipulation tasks and make achieving the adaptation to the environment very difficult. Decomposition of different cells into different groups gives flexibility in tasks and remarkably increases environmental adjustability. We propose to develop a multi-group manipulation technique for coordination of multiple groups of cells. Independent control of each group of cells enhances manipulation of group interactions among different types of cells or between bacterial and cells. The development of robotic group manipulation of biological cells will open up a new dimension in robotics that will significantly impact the automation of clinical processes.

title: Power-Efficient Multicore Scalable System for Cloud Computing Using Emerging Technologies
abs: Multicore system has been widely used in embedded system, server, graphics processors, etc., to satisfy the increasing demands for computing capacity. With the emergence of cloud computing, it can be expected the system scale will continue increasing from tens of cores to hundreds, even thousands of cores. In such large-scale system, bandwidth and power efficiency are two fundamental requirements. Researches have shown that memory system and on-chip communication have significant impacts on the system performance and power efficiency, hence, large-scale multicore machines will push the limits of on-chip communication and memory architecture in terms of capacity, power, and performance. Emerging technologies provide a promising solution to address the problems. For example, photonic interconnection network can greatly enlarge the communication bandwidth among the cores and cores to memory with the same power budget. This also provides an opportunity to flatten the memory hierarchy and reduce the overhead for deep memory hierarchy on area, power, design cost of complicated coherence protocol. The emerging of high-density, low-power, non-volatile nano memories enables the possibility of increasing the cache capacity with little area and power penalty. Dynamic power management can be performed to gate the idle processing cores and corresponding caches for leakage power saving due to the cache non-volatility. 3-dimensional (3D) integration enables the integration different technologies on one chip. How to apply the promising new technologies in multicore system will play an important role for future multicore system development. In this proposal, we seek to optimize multicore system design using the emerging technologies through hardware software co-design targeting high performance and low power. A new hardware platform using nano memory based cache hierarchy and photonic network will be built. Software mapping which optimizes benchmark implementation on the hardware platform will also be developed to best facility the design space exploration and system optimization.

title: Formal Verification Systems for Simulink and Stateflow
abs: A Simulink diagram is formed by connecting blocks with wires, and represents a set of mathematical relationships which model system behavior over time. Simulink adopts continuous-time semantics to support dynamic systems such as hybrid control systems. Its simulation facility allows system behavior to be visually observed for specific parameter values over specific simulation periods. However, simulations are deficient in checking system behavior for infinite parameter values or over infinite simulation periods. In addition, open systems whose exact input functions are usually unknown are un-analyzable in Simulink because simulations are inapplicable to these systems. Moreover, Simulink lacks timing analysis which becomes necessary due to an increasing usage of embedded systems in real-time safety-critical domain. In our recent research work, we applied Timed Interval Calculus (TIC) to construct semantic models for the major Simulink library blocks and developed a prototype for automatically transforming Simulink diagrams into TIC models. We have also developed a semantic model and proof theories of TIC in a generic theorem prover, Prototype Verification System (PVS). With these research results, we are in position to develop a full mechanical formal verification system for Simulink. Stateflow extends Simulink with event based notations for modeling state machines and flow charts. MathWorks only provided a simulation tool for Stateflow and is lacking verification tool. In this project, our second major goal is develop a model checking system for Stateflow based on our recent developed model checker framework PAT (http://www.comp.nus.edu.sg/~pat/). Note that PAT is a self-contained extensible framework for composing, simulating and reasoning of concurrent, real-time systems and other possible domains. It implements various model checking techniques catering for different properties such as deadlock-freeness, divergence-freeness, reachability, LTL properties with fairness assumptions, refinement checking and probabilistic model checking. So far, PAT has 1300 registered users from 290 organizations in 35 countries and regions.

title: A radical reaction approach for site-specific protein acylation
abs: Post-translational modification (PTM) is a fundamental cellular mechanism for modulating protein function. However, a great challenge in the structural and functional analysis of PTMs lies with the tremendous difficulties in isolating homogeneously modified proteins from the natural source. Chemical modification of proteins provides a powerful approach to preparing site-specifically modified proteins, provided that the reaction used targets the amino acid residue of interest only. --The sidechain e-amine of lysine provides a platform for several important PTMs such as methylation, acetylation and ubiquitination/sumoylation. Both lysine acetylation and ubiquitination can be characterized as a biochemical acylation reaction in which an acyl group (acetyl or ubiquitinyl) is transferred to the lysine side-chain amine. In addition, propionylation and butyrylation have also been identified recently as novel acylation-type PTMs on lysine. It is now known that lysine acetylation and ubiquitination play key roles in regulating a diverse range of cell functions. As common to most PTMs, the biochemical processes of lysine acetylation and ubiquitination are tightly controlled, and dysfunction of these processes is implicated in many human diseases. At present, the biology of protein lysine acetylation and ubiquitination is the subject of intensive research which is bound to uncover novel drug targets for the treatment of cancer, neurological disorders and other human diseases. --In the proposed project, we aim to discover and develop a convenient method for the site-specific introduction of acyl groups (such as acetyl and ubiquitinyl) into recombinant proteins. We propose to use a previously unexplored free radical addition reaction to modify the thiol group of cysteine residues in recombinant proteins to generate close isosteric mimics of acyl-lysines. We envision that our method can be easily adopted by a non-chemistry trained researcher and will be able to provide large quantities of site-selectively modified proteins for structural and biochemical studies.

title: Advanced Energy Devices Using Carbon Nanotube Aerogels
abs: Vehicles drivelines utilize electric motors and electrical energy storage to supplement the output of fuel cell during vehicle acceleration/cruise and for energy recovery during braking. In fuel cell vehicles, supercapacitors have a higher recovery of energy from braking than batteries, have a longer economic life, and are more environmentally friendly in their manufacture and disposal. When paired with fuel cells in stop-and-go mobility applications like forklifts, supercapacitors provide burst power for lifting and acceleration and enable regenerative braking; in backup power applications, they provide instantly available short-term bridge power. They also buffer power demand peaks, allowing our scalable fuel cell systems to be optimized for size and low cost. CNT aerogels can be ideal for hydrogen and electrical energy storage because of their unique structure and advanced properties. The CNT aerogels have low-density, conductive, and transparent. The new CNT aerogel also combines the strength and ultra-light, heat-insulating properties of aerogels with the electrical conductivity of CNTs. The CNT aerogel responds to applied voltages by expanding 220% in a few milliseconds, operating in temperatures from 80-1900oK. In this proposal, aerogels made out of CNTs is chosen as it is an inexpensive manufacturing method that can be used on an industrial scale. Their electrical conductivity is found to depend on several factors, including CNT (chiarity, type, volume fraction, orientations), and the drying process (temperature, time). The flexibility afforded by the developed process enables us to control CNT concentration, to utilize optimized CNT dispersion processes to reinforce the networks with. --The proposal consists of: (1) Developing advanced aerogels using CNTs having controlled morphology through manufacturing condition optimization, and (2) Developing advanced supercapacitors and fuel cells using the developed CNT aerogels. The developed CNT aerogels can be also used in thermal insulator, energy storage, wasted water and air pollution treatment.-

title: Applications of Spectral Imaging for Consumer Cameras
abs: This project aims to investigate the advantages that spectral imaging offers consumer-based digital photography. In particular, we are interested in exploring how spectroscopy can be used to enhance photo-finishing in ways that are currently not possible with conventional digital cameras. To this end, our project has three main objectives:--Objective 1 is focused on methods that exploit the visible spectra (i.e. wavelengths between ~380nm to 720nm) to assist in photo-finishing. Specifically, we are interested in exploiting the discriminating ability offered by spectral data to identify scene content to allow selective scene enhancement (e.g. skin detected in the scene is rendered using portrait-mode colors, while foliage and sky can be rendered in landscape-mode, producing vivid greens and blues). This objective will focus on both fully automated methods, as well as methods that incorporate user preferences and manipulation.--Objective 2 is focused on ways non-visible spectra (e.g. ultra-violet and near infrared) can be exploited in the photo-finishing process to enhance the perceptual saliency of a captured scene. Specifically, we will examine how perceptually salient information in the non-visible bands can be integrated into various stages in the photo-finishing pipeline to produce more desirable output. --Objective 3 focuses on ways to leverage findings from objective 1 and 2 to develop hybrid methods that use only a few selected spectral bands combined with conventional RGB imaging to provide a subset of features targeted in objectives 1 & 2. Such hybrid methods can prove more viable for short-term adoption of spectral imaging by camera manufacturers.

title: A next-generation rare-cells isolation device for single-cell analysis and on-chip cell culture
abs: Circulating tumour cells (CTCs) quantified in cancer patients' blood can predict disease outcome and response to therapy. However, a major problem in the field has been the lack of sensitive and efficient methods to capture and process CTCs for swift bedside diagnosis and prognosis. In preliminary work, we developed a microfluidic MEMS device based on a high-throughput size-exclusion filtration method and validated its practical application with blood samples from consenting breast cancer patients. We aim to introduce innovative features to enable single-cell analytical capabilities and on-site cell culture for pharmacokinetic studies. Apart from the microsieve used for CTC isolation from the patients' blood, a PDMS microwell array will be integrated into the microdevice to enable segregation of captured CTCs into single cell entities for downstream molecular processing. Incorporation of the microwell array offers the dual advantages of (1) complete separation of CTCs from contaminating blood cells which will complicate post-capture analysis, and (2) separation of the heterogeneous CTC population into discrete space-confined units, for single-cell transcriptome, mutation and proteome analyses. Notably, the ability to perform single-cell assays will permit identification of rare malignant CTCs (such as metastatic and cancer stem cells) from among the general CTC population captured, providing accurate risk stratification for better treatment decisions. Also, a built-in microheater will afford desirable on-chip CTC culture capability, permitting high-throughput drug screening with live-patient material to select the best treatment option with maximal cancer cell killing and minimal chemoresistance. The inclusion of the microwell arrays and microheater into a CTC capture system is unprecedented, and will vastly increase the number of diagnostic modalities that can be performed on our automated bedside device. These innovations are expected to generate powerful post-capture processing capabilities in CTC-integrated diagnostic platforms to yield more comprehensive disease information and paving the way to personalised cancer treatment.

title: Cost-Benefit Analysis for Smart Grid in Singapore
abs: The project is proposed to conduct research on the cost-benefit analysis and business case model for the integration of smart grid in Singapore. The project will provide critical information on the technical, economical and societal benefits and justification of adopting the smart grid in Singapore including detailed analysis on investment costs, annual savings and payback years. The methodology for the cost-benefit analysis of the smart grid technologies/applications centers on the use of computer models that simulate the specific characteristics and behaviors of the Singapore power grid, with and without certain smart grid technologies being applied. The impacts of the external factors are also included in the simulations. The project will identify the economic parameters in which the smart grid will be cost-effective, define the different smart grid capabilities and benefits associated with each capability, illustrate cost and environmental effectiveness over optimal deployment timeline to optimal customer segment, and develop a reusable business case model to quantify the unique value of smart grid in delivering new capabilities. The project will be conducted in the Laboratory for Clean Energy Research (LaCER) at Nanyang Technological University. This laboratory is dedicated to support research projects in the grid integration of clean energy systems from renewable energy sources such as solar and wind. The various simulator and hardware systems especially for the renewable energy sources that are available in the laboratory can be used to obtain accurate data for the cost-benefit analysis of the smart grid system. The project will strive to exploit new technologies and innovation to achieve a competitive edge in providing cost-competitive and effective solutions to utilities and consumers. The manpower capabilities developed will strengthen our technical know-how and contribute in building up good and secured R&D infrastructures for sustainable energy solutions that can be transformed to the Singapore power grid.

title: AQMARINOME2016: Increasing Singapore’s Food Fish Production Through Aquaculture Genomics R&D
abs: The current culture of Asian seabass (Lates calcarifer) and Mozambique tilapia (Oreochromis mossambicus) is based mostly on classical techniques. We propose to improve their production by introducing genomic and marker-assisted selection using platforms developed through the application of high throughput genomic tools. We will sequence and analyze the transcriptome of both species as well as the genome of the seabass and use the information acquired for the development of advanced genomic platforms, e.g. mass genotyping of a large number of SNPs or transcriptomics using expression microarrays. Together with fast growth, we will focus on disease resistance (seabass) and salt tolerance (tilapia). We will perform genome-wide association studies on these traits through genotyping with >20,000 SNPs covering the whole genome. SNPs significantly associated with the above traits will be identified and used to select elite brooders. The mechanisms underlying the phenotypic differences will be studied using genomic tools. Hybrids of lines with increased growth-rate, disease-resistance and/or salt-tolerance will be generated and offered for commercial production. We will also perform nutritional and nutrigenomic studies to reveal the effects of different kinds of feeds, feed additives, and feeding conditions on the growth rate and/or meat quality of the fish. Data from these experiments will indicate the type of feed and additives that will be suitable for the fish and conditions used at our facilities. The approaches described will allow us to perform faster and more efficient selection for the above-mentioned traits and produce hybrids with superior traits for commercial culture.

title: Genomic-Based Diagnosis, Classification and Targeted Treatment of Multiple Myeloma
abs: Multiple myeloma is an incurable bone marrow cancer characterized by an abnormal expansion of plasma cells that secretes monoclonal immunoglobulin. Over the years, the molecular and genetic heterogeneity of the disease have been dissected. With the maturation of technologies, the time is ripe now to apply genomics to diagnose, classify, risk-stratify and prognosticate myeloma in the clinical setting and use this information to guide current treatment. We hypothesize that the use of gene expression profiling as a single test will be more economical, efficient and accurate compared to the current standard panel of tests done at diagnosis. We also hypothesize that we can use predictive markers to identify prospectively patients who will respond to Velcade and that with more effective treatment, ability to measure depth of response beyond conventional complete response become important since more patients are achieving conventionally determined complete response. Using a cohort of patients treated on a standard treatment protocol based on Velcade-based induction treatment followed by consolidation and maintenance treatment, we will study specifically the feasibility and accuracy of gene expression diagnostics, the predictive power of our pre-defined predictive markers and the clinical utility of minimal residual disease measurement in myeloma. At the same time, the use of genomics facilitated the identification of novel therapeutic target and biomakers that can be translated. We will study sphingosine kinase and PIM1 as novel therapeutic targets in myeloma using pre-clinical in vitro and in vivo model. We will also study the use of AKT/MTOR inhibitors using FAIM as the predictive biomarker and the use of a natural inhibitor of STAT3 and NFKB Celastrol in phase I/II clinical trial setting. These studies could lead to significant paradigm shift both now and in the future of myeloma treatment and will have highly significant impact on myeloma patients.

title: Translational Research in Dementia : Mechanisms of Disease, Pathophysiology and Biomarker Discovery
abs: The theme of this CSA renewal application is to further develop translational research in dementia which combines the applicant’s research interests in dementia and stroke.The goal is to discover mechanisms of disease, pathogenesis and candidate biomarkers by comprehensively characterizing neurochemical, proteomic and lipidomic alterations in a group of longitudinally assessed patients with non-Alzheimer’s disease (AD) neurodegenerative dementias, namely, subcortical ischemic vascular dementia (SIVD), mixed dementia (MIX), dementia with Lewy Bodies (DLB), Parkinson’s disease dementia (PDD). Using postmortem brain tissues from prospectively studied cohorts, we aim to: 1.Study G-protein uncoupling to muscarinic M1, serotonergic 5-HT1A, and cannabinoid CB1 receptors in AD, SIVD, MIX and Lewy Body dementia (PDD and DLB) as a potential mechanism for their differential response to neurotransmitter replacement therapies;2.Uncover proteomic and lipidomic changes in PDD and DLB as a basis for differences in clinical features;3.Uncover proteomic and lipidomic changes in AD, SIVD and MIX to elucidate the pathogenic factors and contributing disease processes in MIX for the purpose of correlating neurochemical changes with clinical and neuropathological changes. Subsequently, the findings are expected to 1) add further insight into the pathogenesis and classification of these diseases; 2) suggest neurochemical, proteonomic or lipodomic correlates of clinical features; and 3) suggest potential targets and markers for therapeutic strategies.

title: Targeting the purine binding sites, and understanding the protein interactions of the multifunctional dengue virus proteins NS3 and NS5 for discovery and development of novel antivirals.
abs: Dengue virus (DENV) non-structural proteins NS3 and NS5 are multifunctional enzymes that are essential for viral RNA replication and proven antiviral targets. Although reasonably well studied, there is still a dearth of knowledge on how the NS proteins function as a replication machine to carry out the viral replication cycle. Our goal is to uncover the details of functionally relevant protein interactions and test them biochemically or by reverse genetics so that they can be exploited for therapeutic intervention. Using recombinant proteins expressed in bacteria, insect cell baculovirus expression system or cell-free expression system, we aim to develop biochemically tractable interaction assays that can be quantified in a high throughput manner. Peptide phage display technology will be used to screen strong binders of NS3 and NS5 to obtain the footprint and identity of binding partners. Chemical cross-linking, reverse genetics or siRNA gene knockdown strategies will be employed to pin-point the binding partners and provide insights into how they might contribute to dengue pathogenesis. By using the purinome mining chemical-biology approach, which has been demonstrated to pull-down NS3 and NS5 from complex infected cell extracts, an entirely new platform for discovering novel small molecule inhibitors from diverse chemical libraries will be accessed. Early leads will be tested in cell-based infections assays and mouse model for dengue virus infection for efficacy. DENV infection causes a spectrum of clinical illnesses in nearly 50 million people annually and of these nearly 500000 cases are severe dengue cases that can be lethal. Dengue is a major health concern and threat to Singapore’s economy during epidemics. This research is of high priority as there are no safe preventative vaccines or antiviral treatment currently available for dengue.

title: Elucidating the mechanistic role of lipid and protein metabolism on the pathophysiology of insulin resistance towards nutritional intervention to prevent Type 2 diabetes mellitus
abs: Greater understanding of insulin resistance is crucial in designing effective prevention and treatment strategies fortype 2 diabetes mellitus. Emerging evidence suggests abnormal accumulation of lipid- and protein-related metabolitesimpair insulin signaling leading to insulin resistance. These metabolites include partially oxidized acylcarnitines (frommitochondrial overload), ceramides and branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs). Pharmacological agents that reducethese metabolites improve insulin sensitivity. However, the relevance of these metabolites in the pathogenesis ofinsulin resistance in humans is not clear. Herein, we propose a study to elucidate the mechanistic role of thesemetabolites on the pathophysiology of insulin resistance in humans. Using controlled feeding protocol, we willrandomize normoglycemic male individuals to high-fat, high-fat with BCAAs and usual-mixed diet for 2 weeks

title: Identification of disease related cis-regulatory elements in the RUNX3 gene
abs: The Runx3 gene is frequently involved in a variety of cancers and immunological diseases. Despite its frequent association with human diseases, the transcriptional regulation of Runx3 remains elusive. To identify functional cis-regulatory elements in Runx3, we employed a novel in silico approach that combines comparative genomics and retroviral integration site (RIS) mapping, and selected 14 distinct candidate elements. In vivo functionality of 14 elements was subsequently assessed in zebrafish. One element, CNE-L, displayed specific activity in hematopoietic tissues, coinciding with known sites of endogenous runx3 expression. This hematopoieisis-specific enhancer activity was further confirmed in mice by generating Runx3 mCNE-L-EGFP transgenic (Tg) mouse. Based on our further analyses, we propose the working hypothesis: Runx3 hematopoiesis-specific enhancer CNE-L positively regulates Runx3 expression, predominantly in thymic CD8 T cells, in response to a potent immune suppressor glucocorticoid (GC). GC-induced Runx3 expression in turn regulates the differentiation of anti-inflammatory regulatory T cells (Treg), particularly a subset of CD8 Treg cells which is responsible for immunological homeostasis in the intestine. Runx3 CNE-L consists of 3 Runx binding sites and a glucocorticoid response element (GRE). Intriguingly, a single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) falls within the GRE in human. Our preliminary data suggest that this SNP is likely to abrogate Runx3 expression and result in the loss and/or functional defect of CD8 Treg cells, consequently causing chronic inflammation and subsequent tumorigenesis in the intestine. Such chronic intestinal inflammation and subsequent colorectal cancer (CRC) are reminiscent of human inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).In this poposal, we examine the relationship between CNE-L and IBD using immunological assays, SNP study using IBD patient samples, and CNE-L knockout mice. The results would provide deeper insights into the pathogenesis of IBD and may lead to the development of novel diagnostic and therapeutic methods.

title: Synergistic cancer treatment using chitosan-p53 nanoparticles and doxorubicin loaded double-walled microspheres
abs: Cancer is a leading cause of death and has become the number one killer in many countries. Despite several attempts in the development of new anti-cancer drugs, drug combinations or treatment regimens, the progress in traditional cancer therapy is still relatively unsatisfactory. This research proposal aims to develop a novel synergistic therapy strategy for cancer treatment on the basis of combining chemotherapy and gene therapy using double-walled microparticles as delivery carriers for controlled and sustained release. When a therapeutic gene is administered, certain anti-cancer drugs can be delivered to the cancer cells simultaneously with the aim to keep targeted cells sensitive to the drug during the entire treatment period.It is hypothesized that coaxial double-walled microparticles, which consist of encapsulated doxorubicin (anti-cancer drug encapsulated in poly(D,L-lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) core) and chitosan-p53 nanoparticles (nanoparticles encapsulated in poly(D,L-lactic acid)/poly(L-lactic acid) (PDLLA/PLLA) shell) developed via acoustic excitation and coaxial electrospraying/electrospinning techniques, will provide a promising synergistic treatment for liver cancer. The effective restoration of the tumor suppressor gene p53 function allows reestablishment of normal cell growth control and restores appropriate response to chemotherapeutic drug. Furthermore, by selectively loading the agents into the core and shell phases respectively, and by adjusting the shell thickness, it is possible to control the drug release schedule, optimize the drug device formulation and enhance the drug efficacy.In this proposal, we will show the synergistic effect in inhibiting HepG2 (wt-p53) cell growth by systemic administration of chitosan-p53 nanoparticles and doxorubicin simultaneously. In vitro experiments will be performed to determine the efficacy of the chitosan-p53 nanoparticles and doxorubicin loaded double-walled microparticles. In vivo experiments will be performed to test for clinical applications. Evaluation of the proposed delivery devices both in vitro and in vivo will provide qualitative and quantitative insights for the development of optimal controlled release devices.

title: Translating Drug-Induced Cell Death into Novel Anti-Malarial Strategies
abs: Malaria is the most prevailing parasitic disease in the world, causing around 200-500 million cases each year and between 1-2 million deaths. Approximately half of the world’s population is at risk of malaria infections. The continual resurgence of the disease is chiefly attributed to resistance of the malaria parasite to nearly all of the clinically used drugs today. There is, therefore, a real urgency in the search for new anti-malarials, new drug combinations, and new screening platforms. Our laboratory has identified a cell death pathway in both drug resistant and sensitive strains of the malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum. We found this pathway to involve mitochondrial permeabilization, proteases and nuclear DNA loss (Ch’ng et al. 2010). Importantly, cell death is associated with disruption of the lysosome-like digestive vacuole (DV) and cysteine protease activity. Our current proposal seeks to identify the key mediator proteases and establish a high-content (drug library) screening platform for DV-disrupting anti-malarial leads. We have already shown the use and potential of lysosomotropic fluorescent-labeled chloroquine (CQ-CM) in the determination of drug resistance on the basis of differential DV-accumulation between drug resistant parasites (low accumulation/ fluorescence) to drug sensitive parasites (high accumulation/ fluorescence). Herein, we shall employ conventional plate readers in parallel with the DV-accumulator CQ-CM and potential chemoreversal agents. This novel high-content assay will thus detect the restoration of drug DV-accumulation in drug resistant parasites, as evidenced by high fluorescence readings. We therefore aim to exploit this convenient method for screening drug libraries in order to quickly identify clinically useful chemoreversal agents. The clinical importance of our proposal is further strengthened with the current interest in the re-introduction of CQ as a cheap, well tolerated and potentially effective anti-malarial, especially if chemoreversal agents are co-administered or chemically conjugated with the drug leads, as we propose herein.

title: Importance of distinct myeloid cell subsets in protection and pathology to malaria parasite
abs: Plasmodium spp. infections trigger strong innate and acquired immune responses, which are oftenassociated with severe pathology like in the case of cerebral malaria. Dendritic cells (DC) andmacrophages (Mphi) constitute the most important myeloid lineages that orchestrate the host immuneresponse against the parasite. However, due to the cellular complexity of the innate (myeloid) immunesystem the contribution of its different components has remained elusive. In order to entangle theroles of different myeloid cell subsets in protection against Plasmodium parasites and in parasiteinduced pathology we have recently generated five independent mouse strains that allow us to ablate(delete) in vivo different subsets of DC and Mphi (Siglec H-, Clec9a-, Clec4a4, CD11b- and CD169DTR mice). Our aim is to study the consequences of the absent myeloid subtypes in experimentalmurine malaria model. In addition this setup allows us, after identification of critical subsets, to fill thecreated “vacuums” with genetically modified counterparts in order to enhance the protection or toalleviate the pathology. This allows us to gain deeper understanding of the mechanisms involved. Ourunique set of transgenic mouse strains makes our proposal internationally highly competitive andprovides realistic opportunities to advance our knowledge about the cellular mechanisms controllingmalaria immunity and pathology. Understanding the complex cellular interactions between differentsubsets of DCs and Mphi is crucial to the development of effective vaccines as well as novelimmunotherapies.

title: Targeting STAT3 signaling pathway in hepatocellular carcinoma using small molecule inhibitors of a key epigenetic modification, histone acetylation
abs: Despite advances in earlier detection and therapy for HCC, it still remains the fifth most common cancer and causes more than 600,000 deaths annually worldwide. Existing drugs lack efficacy and yet are highly toxic. Thus, finding an agent that is both pharmacologically safe and efficacious is needed. Increasing evidence from studies examining tumor cells in culture and clinical samples suggest that signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3) is a critical mediator of oncogenic signaling in HCC. Hence, targeted inhibition of STAT3 signaling could be a potential therapeutic strategy for the HCC, especially at the advanced stages. Since hyperacetylation of histones is almost a kind of hallmark of HCC and acetylation of a single amino acid residue, (K685) has been reported to be essential for STAT3 to activate transcription, we propose a study to investigate the effects of small molecule inhibitors of histone acetyltransferase (HAT) on STAT3 signaling cascade using HCC cell lines and mice model. The specific aims of this proposal are:(1) Potential effect(s) of small molecule inhibitors of HATs on STAT3 activation pathway in HCC cell lines. Three different HAT inhibitors: Garcinol, Isogarcinol, and LTK14 will be used in these studies.(2) To identify the mechanism(s) by which HAT inhibitors alter gene expression that ultimately leads to STAT3 inhibition in HCC.(3) To determine the effect(S) of small molecule inhibitors of HAT on HCC growth and STAT3 activation in vivo in ectopic xenografts SCID mice model.The proposed study will generate novel information on potential effect(s) of small molecule inhibitors of HAT on deregulated STAT3 signaling and may lead to identification of potential therapeutic scaffolds for HCC. HAT inhibitors targeted to STAT3 signaling may also be use to design combinatorial drugs with the existing antinepoplastic therapeutics.

title: Investigation of the physiological roles of MOAP-1 in mitochondrial apoptosis signaling pathway
abs: Mitochondria play central role in energy production, reactive oxygen species (ROS) biology and apoptosis. Apoptosis is a physiological process by which unwanted, damage or infected cells are to be eliminated from multi-cellular organisms. Deregulation of mitochondrial function including apoptosis signalling has been linked to a plethora of major human ailments facing the ageing population worldwide, ranging from neurodegenerative diseases to cancers.MOAP-1 (Modulator of apoptosis-1) was initially identified as a binding partner of Bax, which is a member of Bcl-2 family that acts as an executioner of apoptosis mediating the release of apoptogenic factors from mitochondria. Knocking down MOAP-1 in tumor cells inhibits release of cytochrome c from intact cells and isolated mitochondria. MOAP-1 is a short-lived protein and apoptotic stimuli upregulate its protein levels by uncoupling its regulation from the ubiquitin-proteasome system.Based on our current understanding of MOAP-1 from studies conducted primarily in human tumor cell lines, MOAP-1 appears to be a critical regulator of apoptosis signaling in mitochondria and can potentially be targeted by small molecular weight compounds. The proposed project aims to investigate the physiological role of MOAP-1 in apoptosis and possibly other function using MOAP-1deficient animals as well as primary cells and isolated mitochondria derived from the knockout mice.Preliminary data showed that mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) from the MOAP-1 knockout mice are less sensitive to apoptotic stimuli than MEFs from the wild-type littermates. Remarkably, MOAP-1 knockout mice injected with the Fas antibody, Jo-2, survive, whereas wild-type mice die from massive hepatocellular apoptosis, revealing that MOAP-1 is essential for the Fas-mediated mitochondrial apoptosis signalling in liver.It is anticipated that the proposed study will advance our understanding of the function of MOAP-1 in intact animals significantly to support the development of MOAP-1 as drug target for the treatment of cancers and possibly other diseases.

title: Pathophysiological significance of PTEN and IQGAP1 in aggressive cancer and biological impact of their interaction during migration
abs: This proposal aims to decipher how PTEN suppresses cancerous dissemination by analyzing a new interaction between PTEN and IQ-domain GTPase-activation protein 1 (IQGAP1). The ultimate goal is to identify the pathophysiological significance of prognosis and potential therapeutic targets for cancer treatment.Most cancer deaths are caused by metastatsis. Malignant cancers show a diffuse phenotype, and tumor invasion is a highly complex process. The mechanisms regulating cell migration may indicate key elements of the invasive cascade. Thus, it is important to study how cells migrate and acquire an invasive phenotype.PTEN’s mutation and epigenetic silencing have been implicated in the malignant progression in a veriety of cancers. PTEN is a phosphatase that negatively regulates the phosphatidyl-insitol-3-kinase (pI3k) pathway and regulates migration, is a novel interactor of PTEN by using Tandem Affinity Purification (TAP) and mass spectrometry. In our preliminary observations, we validated the PTEN/IQGAP1 interaction under physiological conditions.IQGAP1 is an evolutionary conserved modular protein and highly expressed in some cancer tissues. In several cancer types prognosis was poor in patients with high IQGAP1 expression. IQGAP1, an effector of Rac1 and Cdc42, is an integral protein of the cytoskeletal organization and also exhibits properties of a scaffold protein in epithelial and endothelial intercellular junctions. IQGAP1 accumulates at the leading edges of migrating cells and cross-links actin filaments, thereby contributing to cell migration. Moreover, we will ascertain whether the expression patterns of PTEN and IQGAP1 correlate with the clinically relevant parameters in cancer patients to understand the pathophysiological significance.Uncovering such a novel mechanism and clinical relevance of PTEN/IQGAP1-mediated function will aid the development of rationally designed cancer therapeutics and provide prognosis markers for malignant cancer.

title: Paired pre and post treatment whole genome gene expression profiling of bone marrow as a diagnostic and novel prognostic tool for treatment of childhood acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – a Malaysia-Singapore study proposal
abs: In patients with acute leukemia, accurate identification of prognostically distinct leukaemia subtypes is essential to avoid under- and over-treatment. The former increases the risk of relapse, which is often fatal, while the latter carries the risk of serious toxicities. Current risk stratification relies on presenting clinical, biologic and genetic features, as well as on early response to therapy as determined by minimal residual disease (MRD) measurements.We devised a novel and robust risk stratification platform that relies on changes in whole genome gene expression profiles during early treatment of acute lymphoblastic leukaemia. We propose to validate this new promising platform in our Malaysia-Singapore (Ma-Spore) ALL 2010 and AML 2006 studies. This will becompared against traditional classification schemas including PCR-MRD in ALL and flow–MRD in AML. We plan to construct Internet-based computer software to process raw gene expression results to both diagnose the subtype of acute leukaemia and predict the risk of relapse, thereby developing this into a clinically valuable, patentable platform. This single platform when fully realized will simplify process of diagnosis and risk stratification of acute leukaemias, enhancing translating our biological knowledge into clinical management.

title: An investigation into the immunomodulatory properties of Blomia tropicalis and thedevelopment of a better asthma model
abs: People are exposed to a wide range of inhaled substances yet they become allergic to only a few. This suggests that there is something different about allergens that cause diseases such as asthma. To treat allergic disease more effectively it is necessary to understand what it is about allergens that make them allergenic. Wind pollinated plants, cockroaches, mites and animal danders account for the majority of airborne allergens. By contrast, exposure to cereal and other organic dust produce little or no allergies. Studies of the house dust mite, Dermatophagoides pteronyssinus, have identified enzymes that can modify the respiratory epithelium, enzymes that cleave immune cell surface ligands, as well as proteins that stimulate the TLR4 signaling pathway. Blomia tropicalis is a tropical allergen to which over 2 billion people are exposed. We have developed a mouse asthma model using B. tropicalis that induces up to 80% lung eosinophilia, airway hyperresponsiveness and IgE antibodies following inhalation in the absence of adjuvant. Preliminary investigation of B. tropicalis extract demonstrate that it can inhibit LPS induced dendritic cell maturation and is sensitive to protein digestion. Fractionation on a Superdex G75 column indicates a particularly potent high molecular weight component that induces IL-4 in IL-4-IRES-eGFP (4get) mice. The goal of this project is to determine what makes B. tropicalis such a potent allergen and to use this knowledge to develop a more physiological mouse model of asthma. Specifically we aim: (i) to identify the substance(s) that account for B. tropicalis allergenicity using size exclusion chromatography, charge and other physicochemical methods, (ii) to identify to which allergens in B. tropicalis mice become sensitized, (iii) using chronic exposure to B. tropicalis extract to induce airway re-modeling and other features of asthma. Such a model will be useful for testing new drugs and treatments.

title: Molecular Targeting and Mechanism of Action of Ruthenium Anticancer Agents
abs: The primary role of chromatin structure in genomic regulation together with the profound epigeneticdistinctions between normal and cancer cells render the nucleosome a unique therapeutic target.Platinum-based drugs are chromatin-binding agents that achieve therapeutic efficacy by forming DNAlesions. However, these drugs are associated with severe toxicity and resistance effects, promptingmuch interest in developing anticancer agents based on alternative metals. Two promising rutheniumcompound families have demonstrated great therapeutic potential by displaying specific anticanceractivities, while showing low toxicity and favourable clearance properties; two agents are in phase 2clinical trials. Nonetheless, the binding site selectivity and cellular mechanisms of action for theruthenium compounds are not established. Recently we found that a ruthenium antimetastasis agent,RAPTA-C, associates with chromatin in cancer cells and forms stable adducts in the nucleosomecore at specific histone protein sites. This has illuminated the general macromolecular bindingproperties of ruthenium compounds and notably revealed novel possibilities for site-selectivechromatin targeting, leading us to hypothesize that RAPTA-C may in fact operate by interfering withchromatin function. We propose to determine, for a variety of ruthenium drugs and candidate agents,nucleosomal site specificity and adduct structure, effect of adducts on chromatin conformation andcompaction, as well as intracellular distribution of compounds following uptake. We will utilize a novelnucleosomal drug characterization platform that can yield high resolution structural, kinetic (‘timelapseX-ray crystallography’), site selectivity and dynamics data and a new model system forunderstanding DNA binding behaviour and reactivity relationships. In this regard, we can establishlinks between site preference, localization and effects on chromatin to shed light on mode oftherapeutic action. In parallel, the information gained on histone protein and DNA binding activitieswill aid in the directed design of novel compounds to test principles of selective nucleosome targetingfor anticancer therapy.

title: Circadian Disruption in Prostate Cancer
abs: Circadian rhythms play fundamental roles in a wide range of physiological processes. Consequently, disruption of circadian regulation has the potential to influence various disease-related pathways including those involved in tumorigenesis. Prostate cancer (PC) is the most common malignancy diagnosed worldwide and its incidence in Singapore is markedly increasing. We were one of first to discover that the core circadian genes, Per 1 and Per 2, can act as potent tumor suppressor genes. Their forced expression blunts cancer growth, and their silencing stimulates cancer growth. We found that Per-1 and -2 are often silenced in a variety of cancers. Also, we identified Per1 as a novel androgen-inducible gene which in turn behaves in a negative feedback manner to down-regulate function of the androgen receptor (AR). Thus, dysregulation of Per may lead to dysregulation of AR providing a proliferative advantage for PC cells. Our proposed study is among the first to address a possible molecular link between circadian dysregulation and PC. Our goal is to obtain a comprehensive understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying circadian regulation in PC cells, by investigating a wide range of clock functions using engineered mice and tumor cell lines and tissue. We believe that the cancer-clock connection is an emerging new field which holds great promise for the development of new therapeutic strategies, as well as to discover ways to optimize current therapies that could greatly benefit patients suffering from PC.Specific Aim 1. Uncover the molecular mechanisms underlying deregulation of clock genes in prostate cancer.Specific Aim 2. Study the functional significance of Per1 in prostate cancer cell growth in vitro, and examine whether loss of Per1 plays a role in prostate tumorigenesis in vivo.Specific Aim 3. Examine the relationship between Per1 as well as other clock genes with the androgen receptor signaling pathway.
kw: circadian, androgen receptor, prostate cancer

title: FUNCTIONAL GENOME-WIDE ANALYSIS OF HOST AND VIRAL FACTORS IN MEDIATING THECLINICAL PATHOGENESIS OF HUMAN ENTEROVIRUS 71 INFECTION: AN IMPLICATION FOR BIOMARKER(S) DISCOVERY.
abs: Little is currently known about the replication biology, neurotropism and clinical pathogenesis of human enterovirus 71 (HEV71). There is no approved antiviral or vaccine available for HEV71. Furthermore, the number of clinical cases and complications associated with HEV71 infection is increasing at an explosive rate worldwide. As such, there is indeed scientific and clinical priority to identify the biological and clinical importance of the human host determinant(s) that may contribute to the virulence, neurotropism and clinical pathogenesis of HEV71. In this study, we will first attempt to establish a highly versatile high throughput HEV71 infection screening platform for the identification of cellular factor(s) essential for the replication biology and clinical pathogenesis of HEV71 via a human genome-wide small interference RNA (siRNA) profiling. The functional role of the identified cellular factor(s) responsible for the replication, virulence and pathogenesis of HEV71 infection will be further analyzed and confirmed using molecular reverse genetics, proteome profiler arrays and specific gene-knockout murine models. As a proof-of-concept on the importance of the identified cellular factors that could be identified by the siRNA genome-wide profiling platform on the pathogenesis of HEV71 infection. We will also focus on the elucidation of the potential mechanism(s) of identified neuropathogenesis-specific cellular kinases (MAP4K2 & PIK3) in mediating the replication of HEV71 and neuroinvasion in the murine model. Most importantly, the novel clinical and scientific knowledge gained from this study will definitely accelerate the path towards discovery of functional biomarker(s) for the rapid diagnosis and in detecting the viral disease progression hence allows for better clinical management of patients. In addition, data generated will enable the rationale and translational development of anti-viral therapeutic strategies against this human viral pathogen with increasing medical importance.
kw: Clinical pathogenesis, Enterovirus 71, Human Genome-wide Analysis, Virulence determinants, Small interference RNA, Anti-viral Strategies

title: A Phase Ib Trial of Gefitinib (EGFR Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitor, Iressa™) in combination with BKM120, an oral pan-class I PI3K inhibitor in patients with Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer, with enrichment for patients whose tumours harbour molecular alterations of PI3K pathway and known to overexpress EGFR
abs: The emergence of multiple molecular subtypes of lung cancer has led to the early successes of targeted therapeutic approaches such as the use of epidermal growth factor receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors and anaplastic lymphoma kinase inhibitors. However, despite seemingly molecularly homogeneous cohorts, drug resistance invariably ensues with median progression free survival of 9-10 months. Improved understanding of the mechanisms contributing to EGFR resistance – as well as new strategies to circumvent them – are urgently needed. This first part of this study aims to explore the therapeutic potential of targeting the PI3 kinase pathway, a key downstream cellular survival pathway, in overcoming resistance to EGFR TKI. Patients accrued onto this clinical trial must meet the clinical definition of EGFR resistance. Patients with primary or acquired resistance to EGFR TKI will receive escalating doses of BKM120 and gefitinib. The continuous reassessment method (CRM) will be adopted for dose escalation. Once a recommended phase II dose is attained, up to 30 patients will be enrolled into an expansion cohort. In addition, up to 10 patients will be recruited into a pathway driven cohort, where patients will sequentially receive BKM120 followed by gefitinib. The second part of the study involves comprehensive proteomic, transcriptomic, and genomic interrogation of tumour specimens. All patients accrued on this trial are required to undergo tumour biopsies. Depending on patient cohort, pre-treatment or on-treatment biopsies may be obtained under stringent collection procedures and subsequently stored in paraffin embedded blocks or frozen in liquid nitrogen. These tissues, together with matched patient plasma and circulating DNA from circulating tumour cells, will be archived for future analysis with immunohistochemistry and mutational and gene expression and copy number profiling.
kw: EGFR TKI resistance, Phase Ib clinical trial, Non small cell lung cancer, Mutational Profiling, Biomarker development, Circulating Tumour Cells

title: Ad-sig-hMUC-1/ecdCD40L vector vaccine for immunotherapy of epithelial cancers.
abs: MUC-1 (mucin) is a O-glycosylated transmembrane protein with tandem repeated mucin domains. It is normally expressed at low levels in epithelial cells and overexpressed in over 90% of epithelial cancers including breast, ovary, colon, prostate, and lung. MUC-1 is highly immunogenic in both the murine and human clinical models and is hypoglycosylated in these cancers, providing itself a cancer-specific antigen for immunization. CD40L (also known as CD154) is a strong adjuvant, binding to dendritic cells and inducing cytokine production, tumoricidal activity and proliferation of activated T-cells. This vector vaccine encodes a secretory sequence (sig) attached to a portion of the extracellular domain (ecd) of MUC-1 (subunit I) that is attached to the ecd of CD40L. Thus, vector transduced cells will secrete MUC-1/ecdCD40L fusion protein. Tang et al showed in murine models that the Ad-sig-hMUC-1/ecdCD40L vaccine activates dendritic cells and induces a potent CD8+ tumor suppressive immune response against hMUC-1 antigen, breaking tolerance in old mice where anergy exists to these antigens, circumventing the need for cytokine adjuvants. We will test if such responses are induced in human subjects by performing a phase I dose escalation trial (approved by FDA) of subcutaneous Ad-sig-hMUC-1/ecdCD40L replication incompetent adenoviral vector vaccine in patients with metastatic or recurrent cancers of lung, breast, colon, ovary, or prostate who have elevated serum MUC-1 at accrual. Emphasis of this first-in-human clinical trial is safety and tolerability. Serum MUC-1 levels and immuno-monitoring will evaluate MUC-1-specific immune responses. If the vaccine is safe, a subsequent trial will test a vector prime and protein boost strategy. Confirmation of our hypothesis has wide implications for immunotherapy against epithelial cancers and will allow us to further develop human capital, technology platforms and infrastructure for novel immunotherapeutic therapies in Singapore.
kw: MUC-1, Adenoviral vector, Cancers

title: Role of FAT10 in inflammation-induced tumorigenesis
abs: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is amongst the commonest cancers which occur ina background of chronic inflammation. However, the molecular and cellular mechanisms ofinflammation-induced tumorigenesis remains incompletely understood. We previously foundthat FAT10 is over-expressed in the tumors of HCC patients(22) and its expression is cellcycleregulated(25) and negatively-regulated by p53(56). Significantly, we demonstratedthat FAT10 interacts with the spindle checkpoint protein, MAD2, during the mitotic phase ofthe cell-cycle and high levels of FAT10 protein leads to increased mitotic non-dysjunctionand chromosome instability (CIN)(39). We have unpublished evidence that Tumor NecrosisFactor-alpha (TNFalpha) induced FAT10 expression through the TNF Receptor-1 and the NFkBpathway. Notably, we found that chronic TNFalpha treatment leads to CIN which is mediated byFAT10. Hence, our data suggests that FAT10 may play a role in TNFalpha-induced CIN. In thisproposal, cell- and mice-models will be utilized to test the hypothesis that FAT10 plays a rolein TNFalpha-induced cellular transformation/tumorigenesis and delineate the region within theFAT10 molecule that may be responsible for CIN/cellular-transformation/tumorigenesis.We believe that our proposal have important potential clinical/medical applications.Currently, anti-TNFalpha therapy has clinical applicability, but targeting this important pleiotropiccytokine may have unwanted serious side effects. We hypothesize that targeting FAT10,further downstream in the TNFalpha pathway and more directly associated with tumorigenesis,may be a better choice for a therapeutic target to treat inflammation-associated-cancers(HCC) as this will result in lesser side-effects. Although FAT10 may be involved in othercellular processes, it may be possible to dissect only the region in FAT10 responsible forCIN/tumorigenesis by capitalizing on the differences in the interaction between FAT10 andits target to facilitate the design of specific therapy targeting regions crucial to thetumorigenesis function without affecting other regions of FAT10 that may facilitate othercellular processes to reduce unintended side effects.
kw: FAT10, chromosome instability, inflammation, tumorigenesis

title: Elucidating a novel ARF-ANT2 pathway in mitochondria and targeting ANT2 with small ARF peptides to overcome apoptosis resistance in cancer
abs: One aspect of cancer’s lethal nature stems from its resistance to apoptosis induced by chemotherapy and radiotherapy; however, the underlying mechanisms of this resistance are largely unknown. Because mitochondria play a key role in the regulation of apoptosis, increasing our understanding of mitochondrial metabolism is important for identifying a way to sensitize cancer cells to apoptosis. Recently, we showed that a subset of the tumor suppressor protein ARF, which is mutated in 40% of cancers, is localized in mitochondria and sensitizes cells to apoptosis. Our preliminary results suggest that mitochondrial ARF reduces oxidative phosphorylation and mitochondrial membrane potential. During a search for proteins responsible for ARF functions, we isolated ANT2 as a novel ARF-binding partner. ANT2 is a transporter that exchanges ADP and ATP to support oxidative phosphorylation and the mitochondrial membrane potential, and an essential component of the permeability transition pore complex that is regulated by Bax and Bcl-2. We hypothesize that ARF reduces oxidative phosphorylation and the mitochondrial membrane potential, and sensitizes cells to apoptosis by inhibiting ANT2. Therefore, inhibiting ANT2 using small ARF peptides will be an effective therapy against cancer.To test this hypothesis, we will identify the role of ANT2 in ARF-mediated reduction of oxidative phosphorylation and the membrane potential and sensitization to apoptosis. Based on the nature of binding between ARF and ANT2, we will develop small ARF peptides that specifically inhibit ANT2 to sensitize cancer cells to apoptosis.Through understanding the mechanism by which ARF sensitizes cells to apoptosis, we can provide a novel mitochondrial therapeutic target, ANT2, which is overexpressed in many cancer types. Consistent with such an approach, we will screen ARF peptides that specifically target ANT2 and validate their effect against cancer. If successful, we will conduct clinical trials in collaboration with clinicians and pharmaceutical companies as a long-term goal.
kw: ARF, apoptosis, mitochondria, peptides therapy, p53, Adenine Nucleotide Translocator

title: Signaling during Plasmodium falciparum merozoite invasion.
abs: Malaria remains a huge global health burden, affecting hundreds of millions of people each year.While progress has been made in controlling the disease in some parts of the world significantchallenges remain. Of particular concern is the appearance of parasite resistance to artemesininhighlighting the urgent need for new effective drugs. Currently most antimalarial drugs targetprocesses during the maturation of the parasite in the erythrocyte with no drug targeting the merozoiteor merozoite invasion. Recent work showed that in Plasmodium falciparum Calcium-signaling in themerozoite are important during invasion while studies carried out mainly in the 1980’s have indicatedthat specific phosphorylation of erythrocyte proteins are important for invasion. Neither merozoitesignaling nor the signaling events that lead to phosphorylation of erythrocyte proteins are understoodin any detail though they could potentially serve as a new set of targets against the blood stage of theparasite. In the proposal here we aim to gain more insight into the different signaling steps that occurboth in the merozoite as well as the host erythrocyte early on during the invasion process. Using arange of inhibitors that arrest merozoites at different stages of the invasion process along with uniquefluorescent sensor molecules we aim to study changes in Ca2+, Na+, K+ and pH in both the merozoiteas well as erythrocyte during the invasion. In addition, we will complement these studies with adetailed identification and analysis of the changes in the phosphorylation pattern of merozoite anderythrocyte proteins during invasion. Molecules identified to play a role in signaling will be studied inmore detail to understand their mode of action. Together this will provide us a first glimpse of thesignaling mechanisms important in merozoite invasion and how these processes might be a newtarget for malaria intervention.

title: Role of cathepsins in pathogensis of Burkholderia pseudomallei infection
abs: Melioidosis, a potentially fatal disease with a wide spectrum of disease manifestations, is caused by the Gram-negative bacterium Burkholderia pseudomallei. Treatment of melioidosis is particularly difficult as the bacterium is resistant to many conventional antibiotics and requires extended treatment modalities. It is thus imperative that novel therapeutic interventions be developed for effective control of the disease. B. pseudomallei is equipped with the Type VI secretion system (T6SS). We have recently shown that the T6SS5 is essential for bacterial virulence in mice and multinucleated giant cell (MNGC) formation in RAW 264.7 murine macrophages. We found that expression of T6SS5 genes is exclusively activated inside host cells; a cathepsin inhibitor is able to suppress the expression of T6SS5 when bacteria are intracellular and human cathepsin B activates the expression of B. pseudomallei T6SS5 in culture medium. Thus, we hypothesize that cathepsin activity provides the host signal that is relayed to the bacterial T6SS5 transcriptional regulator to activate T6SS5 expression. Our specific aims include identifying the specific cathepsin that is responsible for activating T6SS5 expression during infection of macrophages through the use of specific cathepsin inhibitors and siRNA targeted against murine cathepsin genes. We will also determine how cathepsin is activating T6SS5 gene expression by identifying which regulators are necessary and whether cathepsin is acting on bacterial surface components which then relay the signal or is acting on the sensor-regulator directly. Our specific aims would allow us to lay the foundation for the future evaluation of cathepsin inhibitors as therapeutics for the treatment of melioidosis. This potential therapeutic is attractive since it could target intracellular bacteria where many conventional antibiotics cannot, and many cathepsin inhibitors are already in various clinical stages of development for the treatment of other diseases such as osteoporosis and autoimmune conditions, which would significantly shorten the drug development timeline.

title: Elucidating the genetic and clinical heterogeneity of neuromuscular disorders (NMDs)
abs: Neuromuscular disorders (NMDs) are disorders affecting the muscles and the peripheral nervous system such as the nerve-muscle (neuromuscular) junction, peripheral nerves in the limbs, and the motor-nerve cells in the spinal cord. More than 400 types of inherited NMDs are known, eg. muscular dystrophies, myopathies and neuropathies. Among the inherited NMDs, there is considerable clinical and genotype heterogeneity making definite diagnosis difficult when phenotypes overlap. Patients within each disease group often have wide ranging clinical features. Some disorders are caused by more than one gene. Conversely, mutations in a single gene can lead to different diseases. In a number of other diseases, the causative genes are still unknown. Diagnosis and clinical management is thus difficult and challenging in NMDs. The overall goal of this proposal is to comprehensively uncover novel genes underlying the clinical heterogeneity of inherited NMDs. This will be the first attempt to interrogate the whole exomes (~18,000 genes) of NMD phenotypes using a recently emerging approach. As an exploratory project, a small cohort of ten selected patients with clinical presentations of inherited NMDs will be analyzed by whole exome sequencing to identify candidate disease-associated genes. We hypothesize that NMD patients harbor genetic aberrations in the coding regions of these genes. The results will have direct clinical benefits in providing improved diagnosis, effective clinical management and therapeutic options for patients. Gene discovery will solve diagnostic dilemmas and help provide improved diagnostic strategies for NMDs in general. Identification of new disease entities and genes will help future patients avoid invasive muscle biopsies, or provide a definite diagnosis for those with ambiguous biopsy results. Besides identification of primary disease-causing genes, uncovering novel candidate genes involved in muscle pathology or mediating disease phenotype can lead to future therapeutic interventions using new drug targets and pathways.
