title: Comparative evaluation of the bacterial gene composition of stool mircobiota in infants with or without eczema
abs: Eczema is common chronic inflammatory skin disorder with significant impact on child health, and its prevalence is increasing worldwide. It is known that the interaction between gut microbes and the host immune system influences early life development of the immune system. We and others have shown that the composition of the stool microbiota signatures differ between eczema and healthy controls in infancy. We hypothesize that the immune dysregulation associated with childhood eczema is influenced at least in part, by the products of certain gut bacterial structural and functional genes e.g. (i) virulence genes and (ii) genes involved in carbohydrate metabolism. We aim to assess the structural and functional gene composition of stool microbiota of 10 infants with eczema and their matched (for age, gender, mode of delivery, feeding) controls at the age of 3 months. The scope of work will include the identification of functional and structural gene composition present in the stools of infants with and without eczema by comparative metagenomics. Bacterial genomic DNA will be extracted from fecal samples and prepared for 454 Shotgun pyrosequencing. Data analysis such as sequence quality check, contigs assembly and gene annotation will be carried out for the DNA sequences obtained from 454 pyrosequencing. Differences of bacterial structural and functional genes between infants with and without eczema will be determined by statistical analysis. The proposed study will provide the initial steps towards a comprehensive evaluation of the bacterial gene composition in stool microbiota in relation to development of eczema. The anticipated findings will facilitate the future mechanistic studies on the interaction of host immunity and gut microbiota in driving the development of eczema. The information could be exploited to devise early intervention therapeutic strategies for eczema.
kw: bacterial gene, gut microbiota, infant, eczema

title: Interaction between LRRK2 genetic variants and caffeine in Parkinson’s disease
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Background: We have developed an in vivo model that showed an interaction between a LRRK2 risk variant and environmental toxin. Our previous cross sectional and prospective cohort studies reveal that caffeine from coffee and tea protects against PD. The interaction between caffeine intake and LRRK2 variants has not been examined.Objectives: In a collaborative study with our Chinese and Taiwanese colleagues, we aim to study the interaction between caffeine from coffee and tea, and LRRK2 variants in ethnic Chinese using a case control methodology.Methods: A total of 6000 study subjects (3000 PD and 3000 controls) will be recruited from centers in Singapore, Guangzhou, China and Taipei, Taiwan. PD patients will be diagnosed using widely accepted clinical criteria. Information on caffeine intake from coffee and tea drinking will be assessed using in-person interview and previously validated questionnaire, and interview of caregivers. We will utilize the allelic discrimination method to detect the various LRRK2 variants and confirmation with direct sequencing. The subjects will be grouped into caffeine and non-caffeine takers, analysis will be also carried out based on quantification of caffeine intake. Based on the estimated OR of 2 to 3 for the genetic variants and OR of 0.5-0.6 for caffeine exposure and an interaction OR of 1.5 to 2.0, our study has >80% power at alpha=0.05.Conclusions: Our research proposal is novel and as carriers of many of these LRRK2 variants are found only in Chinese, our research is internationally competitive. Demonstration of an interaction between LRRK2 variants and caffeine intake has potential clinical impact because this would assist screening for drugs/small molecule compounds in LRRK2 genetic models. Our application can be further expanded into an IRG, through validation and further studies in multi-centre consortium in Asia, and prospective population based study in Singapore.
kw: Parkinson's disease, LRRK2, caffeine

title: Iris and Choroidal Characteristics in Asian Eyes: Elucidating the Mechanism of Primary Angle Closure Glaucoma
abs: Primary angle closure glaucoma (PACG) is common and visually destructive, particularly in Southeast Asia. The mechanism of PACG has not been fully understood. Our hypothesis is that iris features, choroidal thickness, and their physiological changes in persons with narrow anterior chamber angle may confer significant risk to the development of PACG. First, we aim to develop a new grading scheme for qualitative iris surface features specifically for Asian eyes. We will conduct a case-control study of 200 patients with angle closure disease and 200 normal controls to compare their difference in iris surface features. Second, we aim to use high-resolution spectral-domain optical coherence tomography, with recently developed enhance depth imaging technique, to measure and compare static iris and choroidal parameters between the two groups. Furthermore, we will perform two physiological stress tests, Valsalva maneuver and the water drinking test, in 40 patients with angle closure disease and 40 normal controls to investigate the dynamic changes in iris volume and choroid thickness. Our study will provide the first knowledge on iris surface features in angle closure patients, and will result in significant progress in our understanding of the mechanisms of PACG, which is one of the leading causes of blindness worldwide.
kw: Angle closure glaucoma, Iris, Choroid, Physiological stress, Optical coherence tomography

title: A STUDY OF THE BIODYNAMIC, BIOMECHANICAL AND MOLECULAR PROPERTIES OF THE IRIS IN ANGLE CLOSURE DISEASE
abs: Angle closure and angle closure glaucoma (ACG) occur more commonly in eyes with shorter axial length (AL), shallower anterior chamber (AC), and a relatively larger lens. However, anatomic risk factors for ACG do not adequately explain why many people with small eyes and narrow angles never develop the disease. Static measurements ignore how profoundly the internal structures of the eye such as the iris change from moment to moment, and these changes strongly determine the status of the angle from attaining a narrow, closed or open configuration. Anterior segment optical coherence tomography (ASOCT) is a non-contact biomicroscopic device system that uses low-coherence interferometry to capture the dynamic iris responses to illumination. This technology has provided us a strong platform to image the iris and study its unique characteristics in vivo. The iris in eyes with ACG could vary from those without disease and could have differences in their biomechanical properties because essentially the iris is predominantly composed of collagen, extracellular matrix proteins and smooth muscle fibers. Apart from the anatomical structure, the characteristics of the iris could also be influenced by its molecular and proteomic composition. The integral relationship between the physical, biomechanical and molecular properties of the iris has not been understood or been evaluated in detail. This proposal is being designed to specifically evaluate and understand the biodynamic and biomechanical properties of the iris that could be involved in the pathogenesis of ACG and also to find a molecular basis that may be responsible for the variations in iris behavior. An in-depth evaluation of these properties may provide us with significant insights into the pathogenesis and management of angle closure disease.
kw: Iris, Biomechanics, Proteomics, Angle closure

title: Novel Retinal Imaging as a “Biomarker” to Identify Acute Coronary Syndrome in Low-risk Chest Pain Patients Presenting to the Emergency Department
abs: Chest pain is one of the most common symptoms presented to hospitals’ emergency departments (EDs). However, many of these patients do not warrant further action and often undergo unnecessary hospitalization and extensive evaluation to rule out acute coronary syndrome (ACS). This is a major burden to the existing hospital care system. Rapid and accurate diagnostic tools in the management of these patients are required to identify patients not at further risk of developing immediate ACS to facilitate early discharge and retinal imaging is a potential tool. The retinal vasculature is a window into the coronary circulation. Recent multiple large epidemiologic studies have showed retinal microvascular abnormalities are associated with the risk of coronary heart disease (CHD) event and mortality, suggesting that evaluation of retinal vasculature may act as an easy and non-invasive surrogate measurement for coronary circulation. We have now developed advanced computer-based programs to measure novel quantitative retinal vascular parameters, which are more indicative of the overall “optimal state” of the retina and may parallel dysfunction of the coronary circulation.We hypothesize that changes in retinal vasculature, measured quantitatively from retinal images, can become “cardiac biomarkers” of ACS/CHD in patients with chest pain, allowing us to better stratify the level of risk in these patients. We will prospectively recruit 820 low-risk patients with chest pain presenting to the ED, National University Hospital, Singapore. All patients will be followed-up after the initial ED visit. Advanced retinal imaging analysis and explore whether retinal microvascular signs can assist in identification of ACS, leading to safer and more efficient management of patients with chest pain presenting to EDs. This study may provide better risk stratification of low-risk chest pain patients in EDs, and improve patient care and the cost-efficiency of hospital’s ED, not only in Singapore but also around the world.
kw: Retinal Imaging, Chest Pain, Acute Coronary Syndrome, Retinal vascular changes, Biomarker, Emergency Department

title: An Expanded Polytetrafluoroethylene Trileaflet Valve for Ventricular Outflow Tract Reconstruction involving Semilunar Valves
abs: Background: Paediatric patients who require ventricular outflow tract reconstruction usually need valve reconstruction to prevent valvular regurgitation. They would face problems like lack of suitable, affordable conduits and the need to undergo several operations in their lifetime due to the short lifespan of existing valves and/or patient’s growth, even if they manage to receive a suitable conduit. Current prosthesis include homograft, bioprosthetic valve, mechanical valve, bovine jugular vein and expanded polytetrafluoroethylene (ePTFE) monocusp, bicusp, and trileaflet valves. The trileaflet ePTFE valve may prove to be durable and haemodynamically satisfying. Hypotheses: We hypothesise that the ePTFE trileaflet valve modified with deep coaptation is durable and capable of performing similarly to the native valve, enabling a more uniform stress distribution compared to conventional ePTFE trileaflet valves. Specifically, we aim to compare the performance of the ePTFE trileaflet valve with deep coaptation against the conventional unmodified trileaflet and the pericardial valves.Methodology: An appropriate shape will be heat-molded to produce an ePTFE trileaflet valve with deep coaptation. In-vitro experimentation with Particle Image Velocimetry will be applied to quantify and visualize flow and current around the valve for haemodynamic assessment. Leaflet coaptation area and stress distribution can be computed to verify valve performance. Finite Element Model will be used to study structural mechanics. The ePTFE valve with deep coaptation will be compared to conventional ePTFE and pericardial valve as a baseline. Thereafter, the ePTFE trileaflet valve with/without deep coaptation will be implanted in porcine models using cardiopulmonary bypass. Valve function will be assessed with echocardiogram and necropsy will also be performed for the valves.Clinical Significance: With the proposed trileaflet valve, it could prove to be superior, durable, effective and physiological so that there is minimal requirement for new valve implantation, thus reducing the frequency of re-operations in the lifetime of paediatric patients.
kw: Polytetrafluoroethylene, Trileaflet valve, Ventricular outflow tract reconstruction

title: Evaluation of a new positron emission mammography (PEM) scanner: a preliminary study
abs: Treatment of breast cancer by breast conservation surgery (BCS) has shown similar survival to patients treated with mastectomy, with improved psychosocial outcomes. Successful BCS depends on an accurate pre-operative evaluation of the total disease burden. Breast MRI which is highly sensitive but has a lower specificity has been used widely in this capacity, leading to a significant number of false positive findings. Positron emission mammography (PEM) has been shown in early studies to accurately depict breast cancer. This preliminary pioneer study explores the clinical use of an A*STAR designed and built PEM scanner. The two specific aims are to evaluate the feasibility of performing a good diagnostic PEM study and performing a safe and accurate PEM-guided breast biopsy, with the hypotheses that it is able to do both.Patients with a newly diagnosed invasive breast cancer who desire BCS will be identified by the attending breast surgeons and referred for the study. If agreeable, patients will undergo a breast MRI study followed by the PEM study within a week. Technical parameters for the PEM study will be recorded. For the index tumour, detectability, tumour size and type of MRI/PEM finding will be recorded. For any additional tumour focus/foci, if there is a correlative MRI/PEM finding or if there is a MRI-only finding, the patient will undergo a second look ultrasound. If there is a sonographic correlate, she will undergo a US-guided biopsy. If there is none, she will undergo a MRI-guided breast biopsy. If there is a PEM-only finding, the patient will be offered a PEM-guided biopsy. Technical parameters, patient comfort and accuracy will be documented. If the patient is not keen for any biopsy, she may require more extensive surgery or mastectomy. All PEM findings will be compared to MRI findings with histopathology as a gold standard.
kw: breast cancer, functional imaging, positron emission mammography, MRI

title: Telomere-dependent and -independent functions of telomerase in cellular response to cisplatin treatment
abs: Cisplatin and its analogues are widely used chemotherapeutic drugs in the treatment of human cancers, including testicular cancer, bladder cancer, lung cancer and ovarian cancer. However, most cancer develops resistance to cisplatin and patients succumb to their disease. Therefore, new modalities are necessary for the treatment of human cancers, especially the cancers that have become resistant to the existing chemotherapeutic strategy. Up-regulation of telomerase has been observed in 85%-90% of human cancers. Such up-regulation of telomerase is necessary for telomere maintenance in cancer cells and underlies the ability of cancer cells to divide continuously. Therefore, telomerase is an attractive target for cancer therapy. Recent results suggest that there are telomere-independent functions of telomerase contributing to cancer cells’ proliferation and progression, including the potential function of telomerase in sustaining the proliferation of cancer stem cells/cancer initiation cells, which have been implicated as determinant of tumors’ resistance to chemotherapy.Our preliminary data indicate that inhibition of telomerase in cisplatin-resistant ovarian cancer cells resensitizes these cells to cisplatin treatment. Further insights into the potential mechanisms underlying the synergistic suppression of cancer cell growth by inhibition of telomerase and cisplatin treatment both in vitro and in vivo may provide a new therapeutic modality for treatment of ovarian cancer, especially for the vast majority of patients who develop resistance to cisplatin.

title: CARE- Cord-stem cell Application for Regeneration Enhancement
abs: Aims We investigate the efficacy of hepatic-like cloned Cord Lining Epithelial Cells (CLEC) in liver regeneration, using a porcine animal model. Hypothesis1. Proof of concept that hepatic-like cloned CLEC can enhance liver regeneration 2. Delivery of these CLEC directly into the portal vein is an effective way of delivering CLEC to the liverMethodologyHepatic-like cloned CLEC will be prepared using the Co-I’s proprietary technique.75% hepatectomy will be performed on 12 pigs.These animals are then randomized into three groups, with 4 pigs in each group1.Control Group – Four pigs to receive Porta Cath implantation and infusion of medium without hepatic-like CLEC 2.Experimental Group 1 – Four pigs to receive Daily Injection of hepatic like CLEC into the portal vein, via Porta Cath3.Experimental Group 2 – Four pigs to receive a single Infusion of hepatic-like CLEC into portal vein, via Porta Cath immediately after liver resection.The pigs will undergo investigations such as LFT (liver function test), CRP (C-reactive protein), CBC (complete blood test) and PT/INR (prothrombin time/ international normalized ratio) daily for 3 weeks together with CT (computed tomography) scan immediately after surgery, at one week and two weeks post operation. The results of the 3 groups will help determine the effects of CLEC infusion on liver function as well as the rate and volume of hypertrophy of remnant liver.Importance to medicineLiver failure is on the rise worldwide but the shortage of liver organs has limited the rates of liver transplantation which is the only cure.Cellular transplantation is an attractive alternative to whole organ transplantation since it is now possible to culture hepatocytes from cord lining epithelial cells.This research investigates a novel method of accelerating liver regeneration in a liver failing porcine model using cord lining epithelial cells.

title: A multidimensional study of IDH1-overexpressing cancer cells
abs: Signature mutations of IDH1 and IDH2 genes, recently discovered in gliomas and acute myeloid leukemias (AML), have revealed a new class of cancer genes. Mutated IDH1 and IDH2 are neomorphic enzymes that catalyze the conversion of a-ketoglutarate (aKG) to 2-hydroxyglutarate (2HG). High intracellular 2HG levels appear to alter the epigenome through methylation of genomic DNA. Gliomas and AML with high 2HG levels exhibit distinctive patterns of promoter hypermethylation and unique epigenetic signatures comprising hypermethylated genes. We have observed IDH1 overexpression in nine of 10 human gastric cancer cell lines (p=0.003, binomial test). Gene Expression Atlas, a large database of human cancer cell lines, confirms high IDH1 expression in some malignancies (including gastric cancer), though not in all. As IDH1 and IDH2 mutations are restricted largely to gliomas and AML (being rare or absent in other malignancies), we postulate that overexpression of native IDH1 itself may be oncogenic by generating high intracellular aKG levels. Dioxygenases have an absolute requirement for aKG as co-substrate. Among their varied roles, dioxygenases affect methylation of genomic DNA and histones. We postulate that neomorphic IDH1 and overexpressed native IDH1 have opposite effects (hyper- and hypomethylation, respectively) on the cancer epigenome – effects that are mediated by small metabolites. Either state of epigenetic imbalance could alter gene expression and/or chromatin structure to sustain oncogenesis. We propose to downregulate IDH1 expression by shRNA in gastric cancer cell lines that overexpress IDH1. The project will characterize isogenic pairs of cell lines with low or high IDH1 expression by targeted and discovery metabolomics, genome-wide DNA methylation, ChIPSeq for methylated histone genome association sites and transcriptome profiling. Integrated analysis of these datasets could reveal links between cancer cell metabolism and transcription. This exploratory study in gastric cancer cells could justify future investigations in other common cancers that also overexpress IDH1.
kw: isocitrate dehydrogenase, metabolite profiling, genome methylation, histone methylation, transcriptome, pathway analysis

title: TLR-3 ligand as an immune adjuvant in cetuximab based therapy in Head and Neck Cancer
abs: Cetuximab based immunotherapy is clinically effective in a subset of head and neck cancer (HNC) patients. This difference in clinical efficacy among patients can be attributed to individual patient’s immune responses and highlights the importance of testing novel immune adjuvant to overcome the inherent immune suppression seen in some patients with advanced HNC. Our preliminary study demonstrated enhancement of HNC tumor cell lysis treated with a TLR-3 ligand (poly I:C) in the antibody dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity assay (ADCC) in an EGFR specific fashion.HypothesisThe anti-tumor efficacy of cetuximab-based immunotherapy can be enhanced by the concurrent use of poly I:C as an immune adjuvantAims:I: To determine the extent of enhancement in antitumor efficacy of poly I:C treated PBMC in cetuximab-mediated ADCC, using a panel of EGFR+ HNC cell lines and correlate these results with FcR genotype of NK cells and monocytes in healthy donors and HNC patientsII: To determine the signaling pathway(s) activated and tumor cell survival of poly-I:C treatment of TLR-3+ HNC cells in vitro MethodsThe extent of immune enhancement of poly I:C with cetuximab will be tested using PBMC derived from both HNC patients and healthy donors via ADCC assays. The degree of immune enhancement will be correlated with the FcRIIIa genotypes expressed by NK cells . Furthermore, we will test the direct killing effects of poly I:C on HNC cell lines using cell proliferation assays and apoptosis assays. :These information will contribute to (i) our understanding of utilizing TLR3 ligand as an immune adjuvant in cetuximab mediated immunotherapy in HNC patients; (ii) the optimization of strategies for enhancing the clinical efficacy of poly I:C and cetuximab in combination and (iii) future selection of patients with advanced HNC who are most likely to benefit from combination immunotherapy with cetuximab and poly I:C.
kw: Immune adjuvant, Cetuximab, Head and Neck cancer, TLR-3 ligand

title: HIV-Associated Osteoporosis in Singapore: Prevalence and Risk Factors
abs: Osteoporosis is a systemic skeletal disease characterized by low bone mass and microarchitectural deterioration of bone tissue with a consequent increase in bone fragility and susceptibility to fracture. Its increasing prevalence is underpinned by ageing of populations worldwide. In Singapore, osteoporosis is an important public health problem as the population ages. The incidence of hip fracture has increased 1.5 times in men and 5 times in women since the 1960s. The prevalence of HIV in Singapore is 0.1%, approximately 5,000 in total. A large number of HIV-positive persons remain undiagnosed and the true number may be 2-3 fold higher. Effective antiretroviral therapy has changed HIV infection from a fatal condition to a chronic, but manageable disease. The emphasis of HIV medicine now is in the consequences of life-long treatment and associated toxicities, including osteoporosis. The silent epidemic of HIV-associated osteoporosis and fragility fracture remain underdiagnosed and contributes to significant economic and health burden. This is particularly relevant in Singapore as the HIV population here have two very significant risk factors: older age demographics and advanced HIV disease in comparison to other US and European HIV cohorts. There is currently no data available on HIV-associated osteoporosis in Singapore; there is also paucity in data for Asian HIV cohorts.To test the hypothesis that HIV-associated osteoporosis and fragility fractures are highly prevalent and under-diagnosed in Singapore, I will conduct a propective, cross-sectional study on 350 HIV-positive patients attending two large tertiary referral, restructured hospitals in Singapore.Specific aims:1. To examine the prevalence of HIV-associated osteoporosis and related fragility fractures in Singapore.2. To investigate both HIV and non-HIV associated risk factors for osteopenia and osteoporosis and related fragility fractures in Singapore.3. To examine the cost-effectiveness of mass screening by bone densitometry followed by therapy for Singaporeans living with HIV.
kw: Bone, Demineralisation, Fracture, HIV, Cost effectiveness, Osteoporosis

title: Emergency Department management of sepsis patients: A Goal-Oriented Non-Invasive Sepsis Trial (AGONIST)
abs: Annually, 100 patients are admitted to our intensive care units for severe sepsis. Mortality rates approach 40% despite the current best practice of early goal-directed therapy (EGDT). EGDT involves a 6-hour protocol requiring an invasive approach to achieve haemodynamic goals. The landmark EGDT study by Rivers and colleagues achieved 16% absolute mortality reduction compared to our modest experience of 8%, which mirrored other studies. Currently, only 10% of our severe sepsis patients received the EGDT in its entirety. We hypothesize that a 3-hour non-invasive haemodynamic optimization protocol in managing patients with sepsis in the emergency department (ED) will result in faster lactate clearance, translating to lower mortality compared to current best practice. The ease of application of non-invasive devices will enable a more efficient and accurate fluid resuscitation strategy compared to the current invasive and time-consuming central venous and intra-arterial catheter insertions. This prospective randomized clinical study also aims to determine if the 3-hour protocol results in expedited attainment of resuscitation endpoints measured by lactate clearance as a surrogate and if resource consumption is reduced. This study will enroll patients in the ED who meet sepsis criteria and serum lactate of =3mmol/L. The control group will be treated according to the managing clinician’s discretion in line with current best practice. The intervention group will be managed using a step-wise resuscitation approach to optimize haemodynamics, thus improving global organ perfusion. A predefined protocol utilizing the Cheetah Non-Invasive Cardiac Output Monitor and passive leg raise manoeuvre will be used to assess fluid responsiveness leading to a more accurate management regime with intravenous fluids and vasoactive agents. The primary endpoint is lactate clearance >20% at 3 hours. A non-invasive approach would herald a paradigm shift towards standardization of care, improved efficiency and sustainability in mortality reduction of septic patients presenting to the ED.
kw: Sepsis, Non-invasive, Haemodynamic, Emergency Department, Fluid responsiveness, Lactate clearance

title: RACGAP1 and HCC metastasis
abs: Human hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is among the most lethal and prevalent human cancers. In Singapore, it is ranked the fourth most common cancer in the males and the third cancer with the highest mortality. Surgery provides the best option of cure for patients with early-stage HCC, however long-term disease-free survival remains unsatisfactory and advanced HCC remains incurable. The high mortality rate of HCC is mainly related to tumor metastasis, which is also one of the major causes of tumor recurrence in more than two thirds of HCC patients after tumor resection. Hence, identification and characterization of novel metastasis-associated genes are indispensable for development of effective treatment of HCC patients. Previously, we reported a 57-member gene signature for selecting HCC patients who are at higher risk of having recurrent disease following curative partial hepatectomy. We recently found that Rac GTPase-activating protein 1 (RACGAP1), a member of this gene set, gave the best ability to predict early recurrent disease and survival outcome. Following transient transfection of RACGAP1-siRNA, endogenous RACGAP1 in metastatic HCC cells was suppressed, and the cell migratory and invasiveness were significantly decreased. Given the reported roles of RACGAP1 in cytokinesis and cell survival, as well as its function as nuclear chaperone and mediator in STATs activation, we hypothesize that repressing RACGAP1 could inhibits HCC progression and metastasis, possibly through various important oncogenic signalling molecules/pathways. We therefore propose to investigate the role of RACGAP1 in HCC tumorigenecity and metastasis in pre-clinical orthotopic metastatic nude mouse model using short hairpin RNA (shRNA). cDNA microarray gene profiling of primary and metastatic tumors derived from mouse model will be analyzed to identify RACGAP1-regulated genes/pathways. The signature derived could be useful to evaluate the importance of RACGAP1-regulated gene expression signature in human HCC pathogenesis and to characterize HCC subgroup with aggressive/metastatic traits and poor prognosis.

title: Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging Investigation of the Effects of Brain-Computer Interfaced Based Training on Selective Attention and Response Inhibition in Children with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)
abs: IntroductionAttention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is one of the commonest child psychiatric conditions worldwide. In Singapore, it ranks as the condition with third highest burden among youth aged 14 and below. With the Multimodal Treatment Study of ADHD (MTA) showing little difference in longer-term outcomes between medication management, combination treatment and community care groups, there is a need for novel treatment approaches. We developed a novel computer-based training programme involving an electroencephalogram-based brain computer interface (Brainpal®) which has shown to improve inattentive symptoms of ADHD in our pilot study. We aim to study the neural processes explaining the behavioural improvement observed.AimsWe aim to determine whether brain structure/function is a mechanism of action underlying the treatment effects observed with Brainpal® training, and to determine if initial indices of brain structure/function can predict treatment outcomes.MethodThis pilot study will enroll 30 un-medicated children aged 6 to 12 years diagnosed with ADHD using a structured interview (Diagnostic Interview Schedule for Children). After baseline assessment, they will receive Brainpal® intervention at week 8. The initial intensive training schedule will be thrice per week for 8 weeks (24 sessions), followed by one-monthly booster training for 3 months. Brain imaging will be performed at week 0, week 8 (start of Brainpal® training), week 16 (end of intesnive training) and week 28 (end of booster training). Clinician, parent and teacher ratings on ADHD-rating scale will be collected at these time points.SignificanceUnderstanding how Brainpal® training affects the brain will help us understand the mechanisms by which it works and also contribute towards the understanding of the neurobiology of ADHD. This study is essential in the development of Brainpal® as a potential mode of treatment for ADHD.
kw: Attention, Brain-Computer Interface, Brain imaging

title: Development of an autologous gamma-delta T cell immunotherapy platform for Nasopharyngeal carcinoma
abs: All distinct histological subtypes of NPC (WHO type I-III) are universally associated with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), one promising approach is immunotherapy that targets the EBV antigens EBNA1, LMP1 and LMP2 expressed by the tumor cells of NPC. Adoptive transfer of autologous EBV-specific cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) has shown promising results and without any significant toxicity in past Phase I/II clinical studies. However, this strategy is limited by the lengthy production process and by the dominance within the resulting CTL lines, which are largely specific for immunodominant EBV antigens not found in these cancers. Therefore, we identified a need for a new protocol to enhance the NPC specificity of these CTL lines in order to improve the efficacy.Gamma-delta T cells are involved in host defense against microbial infection and tumours. Unlike gamma-delta T cells, antigen binding by gamma-delta TCRs are not MHC-restricted and detects non-peptide antigens. Vgamma9Vdelta2 T cells represent the major subset of gamma-delta T cells. Upon stimulation by phosphoantigens such as isopentenyl pyrophosphate (IPP) or zoledronate, they undergo rapid proliferation and activation of effector functions. Recently, they are found to also capable of functioning as potent antigen-presenting cells that activate antigen-specific CTL responses. These properties make gamma-delta T cells potential candidate as new cancer immunotherapy platform.We hypothesize that by employing EBV LMP antigen-pulsed gamma-delta T cells as stimulating cells, we can generate CTL lines more specific against NPC for adoptive transfer treatment in these cancer patients, leading to improved efficacy. We also hypothesize that these antigen-pulsed gamma-delta T cells could be used effectively as a dual function LMP-targetting vaccine that also possesses cytolytic ability.
kw: gamma-delta T cells, Nasopharyngeal carcinoma, immunotherapy, LMP, adoptive transfer

title: Design and development of an artificial graft to replace airway cartilage in laryngo-tracheal reconstruction
abs: BackgroundResection of airway cartilage may be necessary in cases of laryngeal or tracheal stenosis, or for cancer. Such resections can cause airway compromise from collapse of the airway, and difficulty clearing secretions from loss of ciliated mucosal lining.HypothesisWe hypothesise that a biocompatible artificial implant can be customized for different patients, and effectively serve as a cartilage framework substitute that provides mechanical stability, and recruits cells to re-epithelialise.Aims1. Create replicas of airway framework cartilages (focusing on trachea) with the same mechanical properties, using biocompatible material.2. Assess ability to form functioning ciliated mucosa on the graft surface, i.e one that: (a) is confirmed on microscopy and (b) demonstrates ability to transport mucous.3. Demonstrate ability of the implant to replace resected cartilage in-vivo in an animal model.MethodWe start by analyzing mechanical properties of airway cartilage using an animal model. The implant is developed using simulation based design, with images obtained by computed-tomography scanning. The main implant material studied is Poly-E-caprolactone (PCL), or PCL-tricalcium-phosphate blend (PCL-TCP) which increases yield and tensile strength. The porous structure is manufactured using fused deposition modeling. Extra-cellular matrix coating can promote vascular and connective tissue in-growth. Cell culture techniques will be used to evaluate in-growth of connective tissue and epithelialisation in grafts of differing porosity and surface characteristics.Finally, animal experiments are used to study the clinical viability of our solution. Using a porcine model, predetermined sections of trachea and/or cricoid cartilage are resected and are replaced with artificial graft. Bio-integration of graft material, including shape retention, mucosalisation, and inflammatory reaction are studied macroscopically and microscopically.Clinical SignificanceThe proposed implant will be the first clinically viable customizable implant to replace airway cartilage for laryngo-tracheal reconstruction. Biocompatible artificial material is currently unavailable in the surgical armamentarium for this purpose.
kw: Laryngotracheal reconstruction, Airway cartilage, Graft, Implant, Artificial

title: The clinical utility of rapid ATP (adenosine triphosphate) bioluminescence-based time-kill methodology to guide antimicrobial combination in pan-drug resistant gram-negative bacteria
abs: The evolution of resistance to all, or almost all, antibiotics among Pseudomonas. aeruginosa, Acinetobacter baumannii and Enterobactericeae isolates has made necessary the use of antibiotic combinations consisting of one or more agents to which the organism may be resistant, in our last desperate attempt to save lives. Carbapenem resistance in gram-negative bacilli infections, is the highest in Singapore in Asia Pacific region. Antibiotic combinations for empiric use are often selected using synergy testing methods, e.g. time-kill assay. They are time-consuming and labour intensive. A rapid turnaround method is needed to elucidate effective antimicrobial combinations for appropriate treatment at the bedside.This study aims to produce and validate a reliable, fast turnaround methodology of using a biomarker-based ATP bioluminescence immunoassay to identify the optimal antibiotic combination to treat patients with carbapenem-resistant gram-negative bacilli infections, which is on the rise. This method is novel as no one has adopted the use of a biomarker to quantify bacteria counts so as to identify optimal antimicrobial combinations. Time-kill analysis will be performed with maximally achievable clinical, unbound concentration of antibiotics alone and in combinations against 10 P. aeruginosa, 10 A. baumannii and 30 enterobactericeae isolates, which are carbapenem-resistant, using customized microtiter assays. Quantification of bacterial burden will be carried out using an Adenosine-Triphosphate (ATP) bioluminescence-based assay. The concordance between the results of the ATP-based assay and the conventional time-kill methods will be evaluatedIf successfully validated, this method can potentially provide clinicians with effective antibiotic combinations for treating carbapenem-resistant infections within 24 hours post availability of the culture and susceptibility result. This is also necessary as a final safety net, should there be a breach in infection control processes, where clonal spreading of pan-drug resistant infections has resulted.
kw: Antimicrobial, combination, resistant, gram-negative, infection, ATP-bioluminescence-based

title: The Immunomodulatory Role of Sphingosine Kinase in T cell/Neutrophil Interactions
abs: Immune-target therapies are of demonstrable clinical efficacy in many chronic inflammatory diseases. Discovery of safe, novel immunomodulators will be of considerable importance. Sphingolipids are potent second messengers modulating biochemical intracellular events and acting as ligands to medicate extracellular systems. Sphingosine kinase (SphK) is the enzyme that phosphorylates sphingosine into sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P). Immune cell activities including cytokine production, proliferation, differentiation, motility and survival have shown to be modulated by the dynamic balance between sphingosine and S1P. Influx of inflammatory cells in the target tissue is a common features in chronic inflammatory diseases such as Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA), and frequently with destruction and remodelling of the extracellular matrix. Tissue destruction is ruled by proteases such as MMPs and is controlled by many factors including cytokines, and direct cell-cell contact. However, the therapeutic potential of SphK blockade in human cell-cell contact system has not been explored. The present project represents a series of novel studies to dissect the functional role of SphK1/2 in human HL-60 cells, and more importantly, RA PB neutrophils by addressing the following questions: (1) Can SphK1/2 blockade through either specific chemical inhibitors or siRNA approach modulate neutrophil function? (2) Which component of SphK1/2 is active in regulating inflammation, and (3) potential distinct role in pro- vs anti-inflammatory responses? (4) The signalling pathways underlying the effects of SphK1/2 inhibition as described above? As the development of therapeutic strategies involving targeting SphKs needs to have their roles in the pathologic process defined, this study is required.
kw: Rheumatoid Arthritis, T cells, Neutrophils, Sphingosine Kinase, Cytokines

title: A study to investigate the relationship between epicardial adipose tissue and coronary artery calcification in Chinese and Indian men with type 2 diabetes.
abs: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) represents a major global public health threat and patients with T2D are at increased risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) due to atherosclerosis. However, the mechanisms of CVD in T2D remain poorly defined. Abdominal visceral obesity is reported to play an important role in the development of accelerated diabetic cardiovascular atherosclerosis. While much of the interest has focused on abdominal visceral adipose tissue (aVAT), some extra-abdominal visceral fat deposits such as epicardial adipose tissue (EAT), the visceral fat around the heart, have only recently been studied. Recent evidence suggest that EAT may be potentially relevant for the development of coronary atherosclerosis via a paracrine effect due to its proximity to the coronary tree. However, the factor(s) responsible for the initiation of proatherogenic effects of EAT is currently unknown. We aim to conduct a cross-sectional study in Chinese and Indian males (age =40 years) with T2D to investigate the association of EAT with other measures of obesity and metabolic risk factors as well as the relationship between EAT and coronary artery calcification (CAC), through cardiac and abdominal CT imaging. We hypothesize that EAT is associated with CAC independent of the effect of aVAT. We will also evaluate for ethnic differences between Chinese and Indians, testing the hypothesis that ethnicity is an important modifier of this relationship. Lastly, we will test the hypothesis that that the relationship between EAT and CAC is modified by the presence or absence of systemic inflammation in patients with T2D. We hypothesize that EAT is associated with CAC only in the presence of systemic inflammation. By investigating this novel link between EAT and coronary atherosclerosis, as assessed by CAC, we will be able to more precisely determine the role of obesity, particularly of fat distribution, on the risk of CAD in patients with T2D.

title: Angiotensin II receptors on adipocytes: study of the physiological functions and therapeutic potentials for metabolic diseases
abs: We hypothesize that angiotensin II regulates adipokine secretion, lipid metabolism, adipogenesis through distinct signaling pathways in adipocytes mediated by angiotensin type 1 receptor (AT1) and type 2 receptor (AT2). The dominance of AT1 and AT2 signaling depends on the AngII level and the expression ratio of AT1 and AT2 receptors, which alter in pathological conditions and different adipocytic stages. Considering the increasingly recognized central roles of adipocytes in metabolism and the multifaceted influences on AngII on adipocyte functions, we also hypothesize that angiotensin receptors on adipocytes may serve as novel therapeutic targets for metabolic diseases (e.g., obesity or diabetes mellitus). In this EDG project, we aim to investigate the physiological functions and therapeutic potentials of AT1 and AT2 receptors on adipocytes.

title: Design and Study of Non-invasive Transdermal Electrical and Magnetic Stimulators for Acute and Chronic Pain Management
abs: The project aims at designing and investigating a non-invasive transdermal pulsed RF and magnetic stimulator (TP-RFMS) capable of peripheral nerve stimulation leading to pain relief. The stimulator is a novel stimulator which can be configured as a transdermal pulsed radio-frequency stimulator (TPRFS) as well as a transdermal pulsed magnetic stimulator (TPMS) with seamless integrated circuits and antenna. Earlier studies have reported the use of transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) or repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) for stimulation. They have certain limitations and their efficiency for pain relieve are not perfect performed. The proposed TP-RFMS, evolving from TENS and rTMS, has the potential to surpass the performance of them. Another aim of developing the stimulator is for performing clinical trials which will help determining the stimulation strategy and optimum settings in relieving pain. Through the project, the effects of TPRFS and TPMS can be monitored, and a preferable dosage, frequency,

title: Towards Hybrid MRI Contrast Agent / Metal-based Drug Carrier with Minimal Adverse Effects
abs: Early detection of cancer allows possibility of curative surgical resection/ chemotherapy/ chemoembolization thereby improving overall prognosis. Limitation of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in the detection of cancerous lesion can be overcome by the use of contrast agent. Self-assembling protein nanocapsule (PNC) has been shown as either a potential drug carrier or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) contrast agent. One aspect of the PNC that is relatively unexplored is its potential as a multifunctional delivery system that allows both diagnosis and therapy of HCC. In this proposal, our goal is to develop multi-cargo PNC derived from Archaeglobus fulgidus (AfPNC) for therapeutic and diagnostic (theranostic) applications with minimal adverse effects. We hypothesize that the PNC cargo carrying ability is expandable beyond the formation of iron nanocore by concurrent loading of therapeutic agents. However, due to its non-human nature, the AfPNC may cause some unwanted responses in vivo. Minimization of the adverse effects is possible by functionalization of the external surface of the PNC. The specific aims of the project are:(1)Co-encapsulation optimization of iron (Fe) and metal-based small molecule drug (e.g. cis-platin (CDDP)) within the AfPNC through modulation of the AfPNC self-assembly property and assessment on the effect of the co-encapsulation on drug delivery/ image enhancement capabilities.(2)Improvement of the effectiveness, undesired side effects, shelf-life, and patient compliance by functionalization of the AfPNC external surface (e.g. poly-ethylene glycol (PEG)) and assessment on its half inhibitory concentration in vitro.(3)Investigation on cellular uptake in vitro and immunological properties of the AfPNC by testing for inflammatory response, circulatory half-life, and clearance rate as well as evaluation of contrast enhancement in vivo.Significance. The proposed work will provide an insight in the development of multifunctionalprotein-based delivery system which will allow advance diagnosis and therapy for HCC patients.

title: Perioperative Analgesic and Anxiolytic Effect of Melatonin in Patients Undergoing Third Molar Teeth Extraction - A Randomized Controlled Trial
inst: Khoo Teck Puat Hospital Pte Ltd
abs: The aim of the study is to investigate the effect of preoperative melatonin on postoperative pain and perioperative anxiety in patients undergoing elective wisdom teeth extractions. Hypothesis:1)Patients scheduled for elective wisdom teeth extractions experience considerable levels of anxiety and pain.2)Melatonin has analgesic, anxiolytic, anti-inflammatory, antioxidative, and chronobiotic effects, making it a useful drug for premedication before general anaesthesia.3)Melatonin has the potential of reducing preoperative anxiety and ameliorating postoperative pain. A qualitative systematic review of the literature concerning the perioperative use of melatonin as an anxiolytic or analgesic in adult patients was recently published by the principle investigator. The conclusion of the review indicated that melatonin was useful in ameliorating perioperative anxiety. However, its analgesic effects remain controversial in the perioperative period and more studies need to be carried out. Each year, a large number of wisdom teeth extraction surgeries are performed in Singapore under general anaesthesia. Khoo Teck Puat Hospital handles approximately 800 cases a year. Pain from the procedure can be moderately severe. The patients are young and have high anxiety levels. Study Design: Prospective placebo-controlled randomized trial.Participants: Adult patients undergoing all four wisdom teeth extraction under general anaesthesia.Intervention/Control: Oral melatonin 6mg administered 90 minutes prior to surgery vs placebo.Main Outcome: The primary outcome is the patient's visual analogue pain scores postoperatively. Secondary outcomes are anxiety scores, postoperative nausea and vomiting, patient satisfaction scores and quality of sleep after surgery.Melatonin’s analgesic and anxiolytic properties, coupled with a favourable side effect profile, potentially make it an ideal premedication. Through this randomized controlled trial, we would be able to ascertain the usefulness and feasibility of melatonin as a premedication for painful wisdom teeth extraction operations in young anxious patient. Melatonin could prove to be a useful adjunct adding to the armamentarium of multimodal analgesics.
kw: Analgesia, Anxiolytic, Melatonin, Perioperative, Third Molar Teeth

title: The host protein determinants of UPEC infection persistence as biomarkers and therapeutic targets
abs: Urinary tract infections (UTIs) account for the second most common bacterial infections in man. Most of these infections are caused by Uropathogenic E.coli (UPEC) which gains entry into highly impregnable superficial epithelium of the bladder. Once in their intracellular niche, these bacteria become immune to flushing actions of urine, host’s immune defenses as well as antimicrobial agents, therefore are extremely difficult to eradicate resulting in persistent infection.Interestingly, it has been observed that infected bladder epithelial cells (BECs) have a powerful and largely overlooked innate capacity to exocytose most of the infecting UPEC without loss of cellular viability. Within 24 hours of infection, over 80% of infecting bacteria were successfully expelled by a novel host mechanism; however, a small fraction of internalized bacteria escapes expulsion, stays in special vesicles and forms the major source for recurring and persistent antibiotic resistant UTIs. We hypothesize that by elucidating the underlying molecular mechanism of UPEC exocytosis, it may be possible to boost BEC defense mechanisms for therapeutic purposes. To accomplish this goal, we propose to comprehensively identify novel human cellular genes/pathways involved in UPEC expulsion and infection, though a human genome-wide gene silencing screen. We have developed and validated a genome-wide RNAi screen UPEC infection assay of human BECs. We also performed a proof-of-principle pilot screen by silencing 300 human genes and identified several new genes that impact on UPEC infection. We anticipate that this study will significantly enhance our understanding of mechanisms behind UPEC expulsion and infection of human cells, and open novel therapeutic avenues. Specific aims are: (1). Identify and validate genes required for expulsion of UPEC employing a recently developed genome-wide RNAi gene-silencing screen assay of human bladder epithelial cells. (2). Define the role of 1 to 2 newly identified human genes or pathways that specifically regulate expulsion of UPEC.

title: A Non-invasive Microwave Acoustic Imaging Apparatus for Breast Cancer Scanning and Diagnosis
abs: Our focus of this proposal is directed towards non-invasive imaging diagnosis. The main limitation of current readily available anatomic imaging modalities, namely ultrasound, computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging, is the relative lack of ability in distinguishing between benign and malignant tissues. In addition, existing imaging modalities have difficulty in achieving satisfactory contrast in diagnose of specific disease in some cases.There is currently no simple and efficient imaging method that can accurately distinguish between benign and malignant disease in diagnostic imaging. By investigating a radically different dielectric properties of ex vivo and in vivo tissues, the microwave-based imaging technology potentially allows for characterization of tissues, based on the fact that malignant tissues have different tissue-packing density, cellular, water content, the amount of extracellular fluid, and the membrane proteins. In this project, combining the correlated backscattered microwave and induced thermoacoustic signals, we will develop a novel non-invasive imaging technique, named Microwave Acoustic Imaging (MAI), to offer both high contrast and high resolution by utilizing the dielectric properties of human tissues. This system can potentially differentiate between the normal, benign and malignant tissues for cancer diagnosis in some organs, specifically for early-stage breast cancer detection, and will greatly help the clinician in treatment planning. The novelty aspect of the proposal study is: utilizing the proposed MAI modality, along with the proposed correlated super-resolution imaging algorithm, we expect to achieve high resolution and high contrast imaging. Potentially the proposed MAI technique can be employed as an alternative diagnostic tool for earlier cancer detection, with the underlying capability to characterize the benign and malignant tissues. We also hope to extend our imaging modality to a wider application (such as lymph node, thyroid module and liver fibrosis/cirrhosis) in the next stage (e.g. IRG project), bringing it to various clinical diagnosis and even homecare.

title: Modeling brain tumors in vivo---Identification and analysis of negative regulators of serine-threonine kinase AKT
abs: Glioblastomas are the most common adult malignant brain tumors. Serine-threonine kinase AKT, an essential mediator of the PTEN / PI3K pathway, is deregulated in glioblastomas. To date, little is known about how AKT is attenuated by its negative regulators, which would be crucial for the targeting of Akt signaling in brain tumor therapies. Given that Drosophila is a powerful genetic system, we propose to model AKT dysfunction in vivo to identify novel negative regulators of AKT1 in flies and validate their potential functions in human brain tumor samples. Our preliminary finding that hyperactivated AKT signaling results in neuroblast (neural stem cell) hyperproliferation in the Drosophila system, analogous to the human brain tumors, strengthens the basis for using the fly model to mimic this disease pattern. We will test whether known brain tumor suppressors (such as PP2A, Brat, etc.) interact genetically with AKT1 and perform modifier screens to further identify novel negative regulators of AKT1 that upon overexpression suppress neuroblast overgrowth caused by hyperactivation of AKT1. We will validate the significance of negative regulators of Akt in human brain tumor samples by ranking gene signatures from both public glioma databases and brain glioblastoma tissue microarray. We will further characterize novel negative regulators of AKT in fly model in vivo to understand how they regulate asymmetric division of neuroblasts and prevent neuroblasts overgrowth or tumor formation. Our proposed project will significantly contribute to our understanding of brain tumors formation and ultimately lead to advanced brain tumor therapy strategies.

title: Development of Diagnostic Assay and Biomarker Discovery for Renal Allograft Dysfunction
abs: Although advances in anti-rejection therapy on kidney transplants have resulted in a decrease in acute rejection rates, this has not been successfully translated into increased allograft survival due to the lack of information on the associated causes, i.e., immune and non-immune factors. The goal of this proposal is therefore (1) to develop a new approach for highly sensitive biomolecule detection by polymeric passivating coating that increases biomolecule detection sensitivity, and (2) to discover a list of biomarkers that show complementary indications on the renal allograft dysfunction. Here, we describe research that will allow us tailoring morphology, composition and surface chemistry of pOEGMA polymer brush for the application in diagnostic assay that offers high sensitivity and selectivity against the selected biomarkers. This proposed study will provide important information that will reveal combinations of materials chemistry and microstructure that are important in creating high performance diagnostic biosensors and understandings on the both immune and non-immune renal dysfunction. To date, there has been no attempt to utilize the combination of biomarkers for renal dysfunction. In this proposed research the specific aims are to: (1) design and synthesize pOEGMA polymer brush, (2) investigate biomolecular detection on pOEGMA-coated substrates (3) develop a diagnostic assay for renal allograft dysfunction. These aims will be achieved by employing an interdisciplinary approach including organic chemistry, polymer engineering and clinical evaluation. The outcome of this proposed research may provide insight into the design of biosensors that are clinically useful for the diagnosis of acute and chronic renal diseases.

title: Localized Virulence Factor Assembly in Gram Positive Bacteria: Mechanism of Formation, Coordination and Therapeutic Targeting
abs: Localized assembly of surface-exposed proteins appears to be a general strategy among Gram-positive pathogens and is strongly associated with microbial virulence and disease progression. I hypothesize that a macromolecular protein complex is intentionally assembled at specific sub-cellular loci in Gram positive cocci; that the assembly is hierarchically organized, with primary proteins directing the assembly of additional proteins in the complex; that localization of this machinery serves to coordinate virulence factor secretion, assembly and processing for optimal expression; and that this localized machinery is specifically targeted by antimicrobial agents to reduce virulence. My research aims to clarify the details and implications of this hypothesis for Gram-positive infection and therapy using two complementary approaches. First, I will determine the molecular components that guide focal localization and retention at single domains using classical and chemical genetic methods to manipulate localization patterns of secretion and sorting proteins, coupled with biochemical assays for focal interactions. Second, I will assess the functional consequence of perturbing focal localization for virulence factor assembly read out at the single cell level, the bacterial population level, and in models of disease. The virulence factor and model organism ] for these studies is the sortase-assembled pilus of E. faecalis because of its outstanding clinical importance and important roles in biofilm formation and endocarditis. The accessibility of localized sites of Enterococcal secretion and sorting to the extracellular environment and its critical role in processing and secreting virulence factors make it a likely site for both localized interaction between the bacterium and the host (thus supporting virulence) and for targeting by antivirulence and antimicrobial agents (thus representing a vulnerable target). Therefore, this research program has relevance not only for fundamental bacterial processes but also for host-pathogen interactions and therapy of an important disease agent as well as difficult-to-treat Gram-positive pathogens in general.

title: Novel Electronic and Opto-electronic Materials from Solution-based Assembly of Two-Dimensional Layered Transition-Metal Dichalcogenide Nanosheets
abs: The ability to obtain atomically thin two-dimensional (2D) sheets from layered parent structures has enabled observation of intriguing physical phenomena while also opening up new perspectives on potential applications. Layered transition-metal dichalcogenides (LTMD) represent a family of materials that can be exfoliated to atomically thin layers due to weak inter-layer van der Waals forces. Type VIB LTMDs such as MoS2 and WS2 are semiconductors with interesting electrical and optical properties. These materials exhibit superior electronic transport properties and strong absorption of solar spectrum and therefore have attracted substantial interest. Recently, LTMD monolayers were found to exhibit electronic properties that are distinctly different from those of their bulk counterparts and have emerged as potentially new fundamental building blocks for electronic devices. The overall objective of the proposed research is to translate the unusual properties of atomically thin LTMDs into novel functional devices. A challenge for device integration of atomically thin LTMD sheets is the absence of robust and technologically viable methodology for preparation, processing, and deposition. The proposed research will address this seminal hurdle by developing a novel solution-based processing scheme which enables rapid synthesis, deposition, and integration of chemically exfoliated LTMD sheets. The exfoliation procedure will involve intercalation chemistry to produce monolayer sheets in solution. It is hypothesized that the chemically exfoliated LTMDs will possess dramatically different electronic properties. The proposed research will explore the fundamental electrical and optical properties of these materials and will open up exciting new possibilities for fundamental and technological research.

title: Mechanotransduction by Integrin-mediated Cell Adhesions
abs: Mechanical force is an important physical factor that profoundly influences many biological processes from the subcellular to the organism levels. Mechanotransduction, the ability of cells to sense and respond to force, is thus a fundamentally important biological phenomenon. The integrin-mediated cell-matrix adhesions together with the actin cytoskeleton are cellular machineries that mediate important mechanosensitive functions including migration and differentiation, and whose aberrations are involved in cancer and other diseases. Recent studies have implicated mechanotransduction by these machineries in mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) differentiation. However, our understanding of the molecular mechanism underlying such processes remains elusive. In the proposed research, I will focus on developing novel imaging methods to study mechanotransduction at the molecular level in living cells, and on studying how these processes regulate migration and differentiation in MSCs. The aim of the imaging method development is to simultaneously measure force and nanoscale protein structural changes within living cells. This ability to directly visualize mechanosensing processes will be instrumental in dissecting mechanotransduction pathways. This approach will be based on a recent 3-D superresolution fluorescence microscopy, capable of sub-10 nm localization uncertainty, to detect nanoscale structural changes, in combination with fluorescence speckle microscopy which enables force mapping in the actin cytoskeleton of living cells. Since cell migration is a major mechanosensitive process regulated by the integrin and actin machineries and which play important roles in MSCs biology as well as its therapeutic applications, I will apply this approach as well as other state-of-the-art imaging, RNAi, and bioengineering tools to study the relationship between migration and differentiation in MSCs, with the aim of dissecting the signaling pathways controlling these processes. Insights gained not only will serve to elucidate the fundamental mechanism of mechanotransduction but will also be instructive for ongoing efforts in applying MSCs in tissue engineering or regenerative medicine.

title: Regulation of Endocytosis by Curvature-Generating Proteins and the Actin Cytoskeleton
abs: Endocytosis is the process used by eukaryotic cells to internalize extracellular materials and a small portion of the plasma membrane via their sorting to vesicular carriers. It is a fundamentally important process for many aspects of cellular activity, including nutrient uptake, receptor signaling, cell growth and proliferation; misregulation of the process has been implicated in many human diseases. The fidelity of this process is ensured by the concerted action of over a hundred cytosolic proteins. While many of these components have been identified and biochemically characterized, information regarding their integration into functional machinery is still largely lacking. In particular, the mechanisms underlying curvature generation and actin cytoskeleton regulation remain the most mysterious. Understanding these complex and fleeting processes has been hampered by the lack of a cell-free assay that reliably recapitulates the endocytic process. As a postdoctoral researcher I have developed a cell-free system that reconstitutes vesicle budding and fission reactions from plasma membrane sheets. This system serves as a valuable experimental tool that allows 1) decomposition of the complex endocytic reaction into multiple sub-reactions, 2) dynamics of each sub-reaction to be visualized at single vesicle resolution, 3) the molecular anatomy of endocytic intermediates to be determined at nanometer resolution and 4) acute manipulation of cytosolic content. Together with high resolution imaging techniques, quantitative analytic methods and nanofabrication, I will use this cell-free system to advance knowledge of the molecular mechanisms of membrane traffic and cytoskeleton regulation. I will test the hypothesis that curvature-generating proteins and their regulation of the actin cytoskeleton are key variables underlying the versatility of the endocytic machinery. The innovative approaches of the proposed research capitalize on my unique interdisciplinary training in areas spanning the physical sciences, cell biology, and engineering and will fundamentally impact biology and have medical implications.

title: General Theory of Quantum Sensors: Estimation, Control, and Fundamental Limits
abs: The proposed research program has three specific aims: 1. To establish a general quantum Bayesian estimation theory and devise efficient estimation techniques suitable for quantum sensing. 2. To devise control techniques that optimize the performance and efficiency of quantum sensors. 3. To discover fundamental limits to sensing accuracy imposed by quantum mechanics. The accuracy and resolution of any sensor are ultimately limited by the inherent uncertainties imposed by the laws of quantum mechanics. Such quantum noise is now routinely observed in many different systems, including atoms, electromagnetic fields at optical and microwave frequencies, and even micromechanical oscillators. For future sensing applications, including optomechanical force sensors, gravitational wave detection, magnetometry, and optical imaging, one must properly take into account quantum mechanics to achieve optimal performance. Prior work on the theory of quantum sensing focuses mainly on foundations and toy models; much work remains to be done to generalize the toy models to more realistic situations. Applying "battle-tested" engineering methodologies, such as Bayesian estimation and optimal control, to quantum sensing allows one to anticipate and solve real-life issues in future quantum sensors. Although the proposed program will be primarily theoretical, collaborations with experimentalists are currently ongoing and will be actively sought to demonstrate the feasibility of the theoretical work. The importance of this project to science is twofold: 1. Quantum noise is expected to become a major source of noise for many sensing applications in the near future, so a new quantum paradigm of engineering that allows one to optimize the design of quantum sensors is urgently needed. 2. Sensing and metrology technology is a prerequisite to most scientific advances, which will demand increasingly precise knowledge and control of space, time, and energy. Given the fundamental nature of quantum noise, a general theory of quantum sensors will be indispensable to future science.

title: New Catalysis Concepts and Methods for More Efficient and Economical Chemical Synthesis and Improvement of Chemistry Tools for Biological Labeling
abs: This project is aimed at the identification of efficient silica-supported chiral catalysts to catalyze one key step towards a facile synthesis of Tamiflu, one of the two drugs currently used to treat influenza viruses. Immobilization of chiral catalysts is highly preferred since it provides practical advantages including simplified reaction workup, product purification and catalyst recovery. The proposed catalyst motifs will be attached to silica and optimized on the solid support. This approach of chiral catalyst development takes advantage of the steric environment of silica and is directly applicable to flow chemistry. Mesoporous silica functionalized with an appropriate linker will be directly prepared by co-condensing controlled amounts of the organo-trialkoxysilanes with tetraethoxy-orthosilicate. Silica prepared in this way has well-ordered structures and uniform pore sizes. The chiral motifs that are designed for asymmetric catalysis will then be attached through the linker onto silica. Libraries of these silica-supported chiral compounds will be prepared and tested against the key reaction. Once an effective and selective catalyst is identified, this silica-supported catalyst will be packed into a column. Stoichiometric amounts of the reactants at a certain concentration in a given solvent will be transferred into the packed silica in a disposable pipette and allowed to pass through at a certain rate. In an ideal scenario, the desired product of the reaction will be collected after removal of solvent in perfect yield and purity. This compound will be converted to the target, Tamiflu in another short sequence of three or four steps. This method will not only result in a facile preparation of important drugs like Tamiflu, but also have significant impacts in the development of heterogeneous catalysis. It is believed this optimization approach will find wide use in catalyst development.

title: Pathophysiology of HBeAg negative Chronic Hepatitis B
abs: Chronic hepatitis B (CHB) afflicts 350million persons and a phenotype that is increasingly common is HBeAg-negative CHB, characterized by increased levels of HBVDNA and alanine aminotransferase(ALT), which may be severe (hepatitis B flare). We have shown previously that viral quasispecies evolution and diversity may play a pathogenic role in development of HBeAg seroconversion(1), an important clinicopathological endpoint. However, the role of viral quasispecies in pathophysiology of HBeAg-negative CHB is uncertain. In our proposed study, we plan to examine clones of full-length viral genomes and assess their diversity and evolution over time as well as within genome diversity by comparing diversity in the different open reading frames. This may provide insights into the relation between the liver damage, viral load and viral evolution/diversity. Initiation of HBeAg-negative CHB starts with a low baseline viral load followed by spontaneous increases in HBVDNA. By selecting such patients, we can examine whether viral mutated sequences bind more precisely to nuclear proteins (using the ChIP assay), which have been shown to be important in replication control(2). Recently we showed that hepatitis B flares are related to a rise in the chemokines CXCL8, 9 and 10(3), which have an important role in liver damage in chronic hepatitis C but not yet examined in CHB. By using in-situ hybridization and cell cultures we hope to gain insights into the mechanism of liver damage of these chemokines and their related products. This study will be hypothesis driven – whether viral polymorphisms can lead to a super virus with high levels of viral replication and liver damage though stimulation of innate immunity and a chemokine pathway. Furthermore, what is the role of viral diversity since high diversity may lead to error catastrophe and loss of viral fitness?

title: Detection of minimal residual disease in acute myeloid leukemia
abs: Approximately half of patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML) eventually succumb to their disease. The long-term objective of the proposed research is to improve their clinical management (and hence their outcome) through sensitive identification of minimal residual disease (MRD) and tracking of leukemia stem cells. We developed a flow cytometric method for MRD detection in AML which we applied in a multicentric study to guide intensity of therapy, demonstrating the clinical benefits of this approach. Our overall objective is to develop a highly sensitive, practical and universal approach for MRD detection in AML. Aim 1 is to extend sensitive MRD monitoring (i.e., 1 AML cell in 10,000 or more normal cells) to all children with AML by identifying novel leukemic cell markers. This research relies on the results of a comparison of gene expression profiles of AML cells (157 cases) with those of normal immature myeloid counterparts, which identified several genes differentially expressed in AML. Taking advantage of these new markers, we propose to define immunophenotypic signatures of AML composed of combinations of 6-8 markers, using commercial and newly developed antibodies. Aim 2 will determine whether the immunophenotypic signatures and methods developed under Aim 1 allow sensitive and reliable MRD testing in adult AML. There is evidence that AML arises from a subset of immature cells with leukemia-reconstituting capacity, the so-called AML stem cells. Aim 3 is to determine whether the signatures identified in Aims 1 and 2 extend to leukemia stem cells and, if so, whether they can be used to assess leukemia stem cell responses to chemotherapy. The studies proposed should establish a novel, reliable, widely applicable and cost-effective way to measure treatment response in patients with AML. In turn, this should lead to improvements in risk classification and refine the selection criteria for hematopoietic stem cell transplant.

title: A novel isoform of human Mixed Lineage Leukemia 5 (MLL5) in the development of HPV16/18-associated cervical cancer: a potential new diagnostic marker and therapeutic target
abs: Cervical cancer is the second most common cause of death from cancer in women worldwide. Over 99% of cervical cancers are caused by infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV). A common feature among cervical cancers is the selective up-regulation of two HPV oncogenes, E6 and E7, which encode multifunctional proteins that are known for their abilities to inactivate cellular tumor suppressors, p53 and pRb. We have recently cloned a novel isoform of Mixed Lineage Leukemia 5, designated as MLL5B, and demonstrated that knockdown of MLL5B led to down-regulation of both E6 and E7 transcripts, resulting in the restoration of p53 and pRb functions. We hence hypothesize that MLL5B may play a regulatory role in the E6 and E7 transcription. Indeed, over-expression of MLL5B enhances the promoter activity of bicistronic transcription of E6-E7 oncogenes. Importantly, MLL5B appears to be present in HPV16/18-containing cell lines and absent from HPV-negative and primary cell lines. Taken together, MLL5B is a potential new marker for the progression of the HPV-associated cervical neoplasia and may be a new host target for cervical therapeutic. In this proposal, we aim to examine the correlation of MLL5B with different stages of dysplasia, and to assess the occurrence of MLL5B with the subtypes and physical status (integration/episome) of HPV using patients’ cervical samples. In addition, we aim to elucidate the molecular mechanism of MLL5B’s regulatory role in the transcription of E6-E7 oncogenes by identifying the associated transcriptional factor and examining the changes in the promoter activity through chromatin modification activity of MLL5B Lastly, we will evaluate the anti-tumor growth property of silencing MLL5B by cellular studies and xenograft nude mouse models. The knowledge gained here will have a great potential in discovering a new biomarker for progression of HPV-associated cervical dysplasia and a novel cellular therapeutic target for cervical cancer treatment.

title: Enabling Technologies for Large-scale Urban Subterranean Space Exploitation in Soft Soil Conditions
abs: The scope of the project covers the following aspects: (a) Development of new ground improvement technologies with far better control, predictability, uniformity and reliability. While soil improvement technologies for soft soils are available, they do not have the required reliability to be used as a support system for heavy loading as the strength of the improved soil varies tremendously from point to point. Because of this high degree of heterogeneity, designers often have to use the lower bound strength to be safe. In large-scale subterranean construction, using such low strengths will render the system practically unbuildable. By enhancing the uniformity of the improved ground, much higher design strengths will be available. This will require a significant amount of fundamental and scientific studies into the process of mixing in the ground. Most existing ground mixing and grouting technologies are still not rigorously underpinned by fundamental scientific understanding of the cutting and mixing processes of multi-phase non-Newtonian fluids and solids in a deep cavity wherein gravity can play a significant role. At the same time, researcher will also be conducted into new materials which will help to improve strength and ductility. The overall aim in this part is to bring ground improvement technologies to a level whereby the improved ground mass has the necessary degree of uniformity, strength, ductility and reliability for it to be used as a critical underground support element during and even after construction. (b) Development of non-vertical and “around-the-corner” improvement technologies with directional control will need to be developed, along the lines of the "geosteering" technology used in petroleum production. However, there are some important differences in requirements, notably the much smaller radii of turn and larger diameter cutting tools which are often encountered in ground improvement processes. The overall aim in this part is to develop the technologies to enable ground below existing infrastructures to be improved and for the configuration of the improved ground mass to be accurately and reliably controlled. (c) Developing the science and technology needed for compartmentalized excavation. As opposed to the sequential approaches which are currently used in long tunnels, compartmentalized construction sub-divides the underground construction into compartments, each of which is then excavated and constructed, but not necessarily in a sequential fashion. Although it is more complex than sequential methods, compartmentalized construction has the potential to minimize disturbance and movements to surrounding ground and structures. More importantly, it may well be more suitable for large cavern-type constructions, which does not have a long run with a constant cross-section. (d) Development of new design methodologies will also be needed since current design methodologies are largely tailored towards a sequential construction
