In this study we propose to recruit 100 patients with PD and follow them up for 18 months to comprehensively investigate the influence of small vessel CVD on cognition in PD. We will investigate the influence of white matter hyperintensity on executive function, visuomotor speed and episodic memory. Both the volume of white matter disease at baseline and the longitudinal increase in white matter disease volume will be quantified and its correlation to specific cognitive domains will be studied. We will also study the utility of measuring CSF tau as a biomarker for predicting cognitive impairment and its relationship to cerebral white matter disease.APOE4 which can potentially influence cerebrovascular pathology will be additionally studied with regards to its impact on white matter disease, cognition and CSF tau levels. Clarifying the role of small vessel CVD in the pathopysiology of PD dementia has important treatment implications. Strategies to treat cerebrovascular disease including use of anti-platelets and optimization of vascular risk factors can potentially reduce the incidence of cognitive impairment in PD.
kw: Parkinson’s Disease, Cognitive Impairment, White Matter Hyperintensity, CSF Tau, Apolipoprotein, Biomarkers

title: AMPK (AMP-activated protein kinase) - A novel neuroprotective target for Parkinson’s disease?
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Dopaminergic neurons harboring mutations in Parkinson’s disease (PD)-linked genes such as Parkin, DJ-1, PINK1 and LRRK2 are more prone to mitochondrial dysfunction and protein aggregation, which may explain their susceptibility towards degeneration. Consistent with this, genetic fly models of PD including Parkin flies and LRRK2-G2019S transgenic flies exhibit neuronal degeneration that is accompanied by mitochondrial dysfunction and aberrant protein homeostasis. Interestingly, recent studies suggest that deregulation in the activity of 4E-BP-1, an inhibitor of protein translation, may be a pathogenic mechanism that gives rise to these parkinsonian phenotypes. An important upstream regulator of 4E-BP-1 is mTOR. Not surprisingly, pharmacological inhibition of mTOR via rapamycin treatment could arrest degeneration in fly PD models, possibly via its downstream effects on 4E-BP-1. Although mTOR is currently under clinical trials for cancers, its undesirable side effects as an immunosuppressant are well established. Here, we have found an alternative approach to modulate the phosphorylation of 4E-BP-1, i.e. anti-oxidant (-)-epigallocatechin-3-gallate (EGCG), the main catechin of green tea, could apparently reduce 4E-BP-1 phosphorylation and concomitantly prevents the loss of dopaminergic neurons in our fly models. There are evidences to suggest that EGCG acts on AMPK, a master energy sensor that links the cellular energy status to metabolism. Supporting this, a number of studies have demonstrated that enhanced AMPK activity could provide neuroprotection, although its role in PD is unclear. Accordingly, we propose to examine the potential role of AMPK in mediating protection against dopaminergic neurodegeneration in vivo using our Drosophila models of PD. Alongside this, we also seek to examine the neuroprotective properties of candidate AMPK-activating compounds. We anticipate that the outcomes of our proposed project would shed insights into molecular pathways involved in PD neuroprotection, which will invariably provide directions for the development of new therapeutic approach to fight against dopaminergic neuronal degeneration in PD.
kw: AMPK, Parkin, LRRK2, Parkinson's disease, Drug discovery

title: Colorful Genetics To Illuminate Stem Cell Dynamics In The Mammary Gland
abs: Recent data suggest that the developmental state of the cancer cell of origin dictates the aggressiveness of the eventual cancer. Elucidation of processes that are specific to the cell of origin and that affect tumor behavior could yield novel therapeutic targets to complement those based on oncogenic mutations. Tissue stem cells have therefore received considerable attention as likely cells of origin for most tumors. Accumulating evidence however suggests that certain types of breast cancer may instead derive from developmentally-restricted progenitor cells. To determine the relevant characteristics of stem and progenitor cells that impact on tumor behavior, we need to accurately measure their activity. Unfortunately, the current gold standard limiting dilution assay to quantify mammary stem cells may also detect progenitor cell activity. We plan to use a novel mouse model to stochastically color-code mammary epithelial cells by genetic recombination. This allows us for the first time to visualize mammary stem cell activity in situ, which is a critical step to start investigating the control of stem cell identity and proliferation by their immediate environment. Moreover, color-coding will demonstrate the relative contribution of stem and progenitor cells in gold standard assays and reveal the rate of cellular turnover. Comparing cellular dynamics in the mammary gland with tissues like the intestine is important because disparate demands on stem cell and progenitor activity may result in different cells of origin whose distinct capabilities ultimately direct the aggressiveness of the tumor. Finally, exploring the use of genetic color-coding in the mammary gland will set the stage for future studies addressing tumor heterogeneity and therapy resistance.
kw: stem cell, breast cancer, mouse model, tumor cell of origin, heterogeneity

title: Multifunctional folic acid-tagged nano-core-shells for targeting and treatment of epithelial ovarian cancer
abs: Ovarian cancer is the leading cause of mortality among the gynaecological malignancies. Human alpha-folate receptor (hFRa) is upregulated in ovarian serous adenocarcinoma (OSA) cells. Serous histology and hFRa-overexpression are associated with poor prognosis. Interestingly, hFRa-overexpression provides the opportunity for specifically targeting these cells with labels that allow their identification and delivery of anti-cancer drugs.We recently developed a novel biosynthetic type of multifunctional nanoparticles with the unique nano-core–shell–shell structure, where tiny magnetite (Fe3O4) nanocrystals and conjugated fluorescent polymers are encapsulated by a thin silica shell and polyethylene oxide (PEO). The free PEO chains on the exterior can be functionalized with several different agents, including folic acid through an -CONH- interaction. Folic acid is a high-affinity ligand that would enhance the differential specificity of these nano-core-shells by targeting hFRa-positive cancer cells. The nano-core can be loaded with (i) superparamagnetic nanocrystals for magnetic resonance imaging, (ii) fluorescence tags for optical visualisation, and (iii) anti-cancer drug moieties that could deliver the therapeutic agent directly into the ovarian cancer cell. We hypothesize that folate-coated nano-core-shells will: (1) preferentially enter hFRa-overexpressing OSA cells, (2) in themselves are not cytotoxic, and (3) allow labelling with magnetite/fluorescence tags, and (4) if loaded with a cytotoxic agent will lead to selective cell kill of OSA cells. We propose in vitro cell biology experiments that would allow characterisation and understanding of folic acid-coated nano-core-shell behaviour in an OSA cell line. We will determine uptake advantages conferred by folic acid ligands, cell viability, growth, and cell kill by selective targeting of SKOV-3 by ligand-coated nano-core-shells. We believe their selective entry into hFRa-overexpressed cells offers concentrated drug delivery and an improved therapeutic window. Pilot data from this grant will facilitate an IRG submission to test these multifunctional nano-core-shells in vivo in an orhtotopic, xenograft, murine-SCID ovarian cancer model.
kw: Ovarian Cancer, Mulitfunctional nano-core-shells, Folate targeting, In vitro

title: The putative mammalian siderophore – a potential novel therapeutic target for neuroinflammation and neurodegenerative disease
abs: Acutely following injury or infection, neuroinflammation is protective but, chronically, it is implicated as a common mechanism of cell death in various neurodegenerative diseases. One component of the acute immune response to bacterial infection is release of lipocalin-2 (LCN2). Bacteria require iron for growth. To obtain iron they secrete siderophore proteins. These proteins bind to iron to form a siderophore-iron complex that is captured by receptors expressed by the bacteria. LCN2 has a bacteriostatic action because it deprives bacteria of iron by binding to the bacterial siderophore-iron complex, which is then captured by mammalian host cells expressing receptors for LCN2. However, in the absence of bacterial siderophore, LCN2 is internalized and leads to reduction of free intracellular iron triggering expression of Bim and apoptosis. Thus, in the absence of an acute bacterial infection, release of LCN2 can contribute to host cell death. It has been proposed that the reduction in intracellular iron is mediated by an endogenous mammalian siderophore that complexes with iron and binds to LCN2. Our preliminary data has confirmed that LCN2 is expressed in the mammalian brain in situ and that LCN2 expression is elevated in models of neuroinflammatory injury. These data suggest the possibility that the putative endogenous mammalian siderophore could be a novel therapeutic target for the amelioration of neuroinflammation. In this proposal, we aim to test the hypothesis that the putative endogenous mammalian siderophore is required to explain LCN2-mediated triggering of Bim expression. If the putative mammalian siderophore exists, we aim to identify it by proteomic analysis of co-immunoprecipitation and pull-down fractions from cellular lysates following neuroinflammatory injury or treatment with LCN2 in the absence of bacterial infection.
kw: neuroinflammation, neurodegeneration, siderophore, lipocalin-2, iron, Bim

title: Identification of Cancer-Associated Sequence Variations in Ultra-Conserved Genes
abs: Cancer, like other diseases, has a clear genetic component. GWAS has however yielded only few small sequence variants conferring a strong relative risk. Moreover, when searching for mutations in tumors, few samples can be analyzed due to the cost of sequencing. We propose a pooled-capture-sequencing approach that makes it economical to use high throughput sequencing to identify novel sequence variants in hundreds of genes while comparing hundreds of samples. To evaluate this approach we use a best-case scenario by studying a novel class of 481 ultra-conserved genes (UCGs) that encode for non-coding RNA. These genes are highly conserved and therefore contain very few variations in the population and have a low mutation frequency in tumors. Nevertheless they are an excellent case to search for cancer predisposing genes, since a pilot study tested 28 UCGs by conventional sequencing in 254 tumor and control samples, and found 6 with variations specifically in cancer patients, of which at least three were germline variants. Moreover, we have tested three of these cancer variants and have shown them to have oncogenic and tumorigenic capacities in a model system of oncogenic transformation.We will leverage recent advances in genomic capture technology and high throughput sequencing to interrogate 481 UCGs captured from pools of genomic DNA of 50 cancer patients and matched DNA of their tumors to identify germ line or somatic mutations. We will use 150 matched controls to filter cancer-unrelated variants. The identified cancer variants will be verified by Sanger sequencing and then functionally validated in our transformation model. We anticipate to identify new cancer related genes that predispose to cancer or contribute to tumor development, and moreover to validate our approach and uncover its potential for discovering other candidate cancer genes that naturally show more variations, and which have been elusive to current approaches.
kw: non-coding RNAs, cancer, tumor suppressors, SNPs, Deep sequencing, cancer predisposition

title: Quorum-Based Technology: Developing Anti-Virulence Therapeutics Targeting Gram-Positive Bacterial Pathogens.
abs: The virulence of Gram-positive bacterial pathogens is mediated by quorum signaling pathways. An attenuation of this pathway, in the form of degradation of the quorum molecule, would be an effective way of attenuating the pathogenecity of these bacterial pathogens. In Gram-positive microbes, such as the multidrug-resistant Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), quorum signaling is mediated by auto-inducing peptides. However, there are currently no known effective disrupters for Gram-positive microbial quorum-signaling, nor are there known enzymes that will degrade the auto-inducing peptides.We seek to create Auto-Inducing Peptidases (AIPases) for use in the biomedical industry, and understand the structure-function relationships of these biomolecules so that we can translate our studies toward the development of a new class of therapeutic biomolecules against infectious diseases that are caused by Gram-positive bacterial pathogens.We will develop anti-virulence Gram-positive “antimicrobials” by specifically targeting the quorum-sensing pathways of these pathogenic microbes. Due to the anti-virulence nature of the mode of disruption, this strategy does not present the selective pressure that always results in the development of resistance in microbes.Using a novel directed evolution platform that recreates Gram-positive quorum-signaling in a Gram-negative host system, we will evolve AIPase activity into amenable enzymes that possess the (beta/alpha)8-barrel scaffold to achieve this significant breakthrough in anti-virulence therapeutic development. Our work will provide anti-virulence therapy to many nosocomial infectious diseases, limiting drug resistance and providing essential and required treatment. We envision that, in combination with our previously developed Gram-negative quorum-quenching lactonases, the work detailed in this proposal will generate template biomolecules for future translational studies, and be of tremendous biomedical use in various clinical settings in Singapore, such as in replacement surgeries to prevent opportunistic infections arising from prosthetic implants.
kw: Quorum-Based Technology, Directed Evolution, Therapeutic Biomolecules, Anti-Virulence, Gram-Positive Pathogens, Anti-Biofilms

title: A biomaterial strategy to prevent Acinetobacter biofilm formation
abs: Bacterial biofilms, comprising a multicellular community encased within a self-produced exopolymeric coat which adheres to abiotic and biotic surface, have been associated with persistent and sometimes untreatable infections because of poor response to antibiotics. The closely-related Acinetobacter spp (A. baumannii, A. genomospecies 3 and A. genomospecies 13TU) rank among the top five organisms causing nosocomial infections of the pulmonary system, bloodstream, urinary tract, surgical site and soft tissue, and are associated with high morbidity and mortality rates in hospitals in Singapore and worldwide. Acinetobacter can form biofilm on medical devices such as catheters and shunts in patients in intensive care units. Formation and development of biofilms are dependent on the bacterial quorum sensing (QS) mechanism. We aim to inhibit biofilm formation using acyl homoserine lactone (AHL) analogues that inhibit the synthesis of QS signals. These QS antagonists compete with endogenous AHLs for binding to the AHL synthase transcriptional regulator. Even if biofilm formation is not completely inhibited, we expect biofilms formed by QS-deficient bacteria to be significantly less resistant to antimicrobial agents. This is because QS controls the differentiation of bacteria into the more antibiotic-resistant swarmer cells which enable the bacteria to adhere and spread over a surface, such as during initiation of a biofilm. We will identify AHLs produced by the Acinetobacter spp. using LC-MS/MS and construct reporter plasmids to screen for QS antagonists (AHL analogues) which we will synthesize. We will design a hydrogel to entrap the novel QS antagonists for slow release and evaluate the anti-biofilm properties of the hydrogel in vitro using single-time point assays and time-course monitoring using confocal laser scanning microscopy. If successful, the hydrogel can be applied as a coating on medical devices and be used to entrap other types of small molecules with known antimicrobial properties (e.g. AI-2 inhibitors, furanones, etc).
kw: Acinetobacter, biofilm, quorum sensing, antagonists, biomaterial, acyl homoserine lactones

title: Basic characterization of a panel of neutralizing monoclonal antibodies targeting the hemagglutinin (HA) of the H5N1 influenza A virus: assessment of the potential for development as reagents for passive immunotherapy.
abs: The highly pathogenic H5N1 avian influenza A virus has been transmitted to humans and resulted in a fatality rate of 59%. The objective of this study is to characterize a panel of five neutralizing monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) targeting the hemagglutinin (HA) protein of H5N1. Two of the mAbs have been shown to not only neutralize the homologous clade 1 virus but also cross-neutralize viruses of clades of 2.1 and 2.2. This implies that these mAbs do not bind to the known antigenic sites on HA, which are known to undergo antigenic drift, but rather bind to well-conserved neutralizing epitopes. Specifically, we will (i) determine the epitopes in HA that are targeted by these new neutralizing mAbs, (ii) determine whether these mAbs block the binding of HA to host receptors or prevent the membrane fusion activity of HA, (iii) generate recombinant mAbs and compare their abilities to interact with HA and prevent viral entry and (iv) determine if these mAbs have the ability to neutralize other subtypes of influenza A virus. Besides the current strategies against influenza, like vaccination and antiviral drug treatment, passive immunotherapy could play an important role in combating highly pathogenic influenza A viruses in the future. Importantly, a diversified collection of potent neutralizing mAbs will be needed for use in combination therapy, which is highly recommended to minimize the development of escape viruses, and this will increase our chances of stopping a future H5N1 pandemic. After characterizing our panel of neutralizing mAbs, we can choose the promising mAbs for further studies, including structural and animal experiments, to ascertain if they can be developed as reagents for passive immunotherapy. In addition, this pilot study may lead to the identification of previously uncharacterized neutralizing epitopes which is important for the design and development of an effective vaccine against H5N1.
kw: H5N1 influenza A virus, Passive immunotherapy, Neutralizing epitope, Monoclonal antibody (mAb), Pandemic, Hemagglutinin (HA)

title: Design and synthesis of small molecules that target nuclear co-repressor (N-CoR) protein in acute promyelocytic leukemia
abs: Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) resulting from the fusion of the promyelocytic leukemia (PML) protein and the retinoic acid receptor (RAR) is a subtype of acute myelogenous leukemia. In APL cells, the nuclear PML oncogenic domains (POD) are detected as microspeckles in the nucleus and cytoplasm. A reorganization of microspeckles to dots is observed on treatment with retinoic acid, the current standard for APL therapy. This transition which precedes the retinoic acid-induced differentiation of APL cells is attributed to the dissociation of the nuclear co-repressor (N-CoR) protein from the PML-RAR complex. It has been shown that PML-RAR- accumulates N-CoR in its misfolded state in APL cells and that the misfolded N-CoR triggers endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress and the unfolded protein response (UPR). As a result, APL-cell specific proteases are induced leading to cleavage of the misfolded protein and protection of APL cells from UPR-induced cell death. These findings propose a possible direct link between N-CoR misfolding and differentiation arrest of APL cells and accordingly, a role for targeting the mechanisms underlying the balance between natively folded – misfolded N-CoR as a therapeutic strategy for APL. In support of this hypothesis, genistein and curcumin were found to induce differentiation of APL by shifting the equilibrium towards natively-folded N-CoR (genistein) or the misfolded protein (curcumin). We have on hand several curcuminoids that are more potent or more selective than curcumin on APL cells. Here, we aim to provide proof of concept that the targeting of N-CoR conformation is involved in the anti-APL effects of these compounds. Detergent solubility assays and thermal shift analysis will be employed in this regard. We will also work towards using appropriate medicinal chemistry approaches to expand our panel of compounds and obtain novel /patentable curcuminoids with greater potencies and selectivities for APL.
kw: acute myelocytic leukemia, curcuminoids, medicinal chemistry, nuclear co-repressor protein, conformation of N-CoR

title: Human Induced Pluripotent Stem Cell-Derived Functional Cardiomyocytes as a Novel Cellular Model for Electrophysiological Cardiac Drug Testing and Potential Personalized Medicine
abs: There is an increasing need to thoroughly evaluate the safety and efficacy of cardiac drugs particularly antiarrhythmic drugs in patients. Human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) can differentiate to functional cardiomyocytes (hiPSC-CMs). We hypothesized that such CMs can serve as a novel and ideal cellular model for effective and efficient cardiac drug testing. Moreover, patient-specific hiPSC-CMs could be adopted in developing personalized medicine. Aims:1. To establish hiPSC-CMs as a novel cellular model for electrophysiological cardiac drug testing2. To evaluate the feasibility and clinical significance of personalized medicine by observing the response of patient-specific hiPSC-CMs to common arrhythmia prevention drugs for LQT syndrome.Procedures:Human iPSCs from 3 normal control subjects and 3 unrelated Type I or II LQT syndrome patients will be obtained from NHC laboratories.1. To derive functional (contracting) iPSC-CMs from control and patient iPSCs by cardiomyogenic differentiation via embryoid body (EB) formation followed by guided cardiomyogenic differentiated by a p38-MAPK inhibitor (SB203580) 2. To electrophysiologically characterize the normal and disease phenotypes of control and patients hiPSC-CMs by a combination of microelectrode array (MEA) mapping for the field potential
kw: Induced pluripotent stem cells, long QT syndrome, cardiomyocytes, Personalized medicine, Electrophysiology, Drug testing

title: Project to study the potential use of emodin (1, 3, 8-trihydroxy-6-methylanthraquinone) for the treatment of hepatocellular carcinoma in vitro and in vivo
abs: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the fifth most common malignancy worldwide and the third cause of global cancer mortality. More than 80% of HCC patients present at advanced disease stages where surgery is not possible, and in cases where surgical resections are performed the two year recurrence rate is high as much as 50%. Although several chemotherapeutic agents have been used in treatment of HCC no single or combination chemotherapy regimens have been shown to be particularly effective. Thus, a great challenge lies in identifying novel agents to treat HCC. Increasing evidence from studies examining tumor cells in culture and clinical samples suggest that signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3) is a critical mediator of oncogenic signaling in HCC. STAT3 is constitutively activated in HCC and regulates the expression of various genes that play a major role in cellular transformation, suppression of apoptosis, promotion of cellular proliferation, invasion and angiogenesis. Hence, targeted inhibition of STAT3 signaling could lead to a potential novel therapy for advanced HCC. Our preliminary experiments suggest that emodin can suppress constitutive and inducible STAT3 signaling pathway in HCC cells. Based on this, we propose a study to explore the mechanism(s) of inhibitory effects of emodin on STAT3 signaling cascade using HCC cell lines and orthotopic nude mice model. The specific aims of this proposal are to investigate:(1)Elucidate the mechanism(s) by which emodin modulates constitutive and inducible STAT3 activation pathway in HCC cell lines.(2)Determine the mechanism(s) by which emodin-induced STAT3 inhibition can mediate apoptosis of HCC cells.(3)Effect of emodin on tumor growth in orthotopic HCC nude mice model using bioluminescent imaging. The proposed study will generate novel information on potential effect(s) of emodin on deregulated STAT3 signaling and may form the basis of novel therapy for HCC.
kw: Hepatocellular carcinoma, STAT3, Apoptosis, Emodin, Proliferation, Orthotopic mice model

title: An Exploratory Randomized Controlled Trial of a Novel Family-Based Intervention to increase Outdoor Time for the Prevention of Myopia and Increase Physical Activity among Singapore Youth
abs: Myopia and physical inactivity are huge public health problems in Singapore and worldwide. Recent studies suggest that outdoor physical activity may be protective against myopia. Increased activity would also reduce the incidence of obesity and other chronic diseases. We aim to develop, implement, and evaluate a novel incentive-based family intervention to increase time spent outdoors and increase physical activity among children aged 6 to 10 years in a 1-year exploratory randomized controlled trial. 450 children from an expected 360 families will be randomized to either a family-based intervention or basic intervention. The family-based intervention comprises structured weekend outdoor activities and provides incentives for children to increase their daily steps, as measured via pedometers. Families who meet their monthly step and outdoor activity goals will receive a range of prizes. The control arm will receive brochures from the National Myopia Prevention Program (NMPP) and information on the health benefits of physical activity. The success of the intervention will be evaluated through pedometer steps, 24 hour weekday, weekend diaries and the WHO Myopia Risk Factor questionnaire documenting outdoor time, and CHAMPS Physical Activity questionnaires. Secondary outcomes include body mass index and cycloplegic refraction. The sustainability to the intervention will be tested over the 1-year period and the cost-effectiveness ratio of the intervention will be assessed in terms of costs per increase in outdoor time or physical activity. Our proposal to develop and evaluate an evidence-based, novel, and cost-effective family-based intervention to increase outdoor time and physical activity will lead to the submission of an IRG for a large-scale 3-year RCT with a sample size of > 2,000 children aged 6 to 10 years to evaluate the efficacy of this new intervention to change behavior and prevent the incidence of myopia, reduce shifts of refraction towards myopia, increase physical activity, and prevent obesity.
kw: Myopia, Obesity, Randomized Controlled Trial, Behavior modification, Physical activity, Pedometer studies

title: Functional characterization of aberrantly spliced Cav1.2 channels during cardiovascular development
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: L-type voltage-gated Cav1.2 calcium channels are important for heart and blood vessel functions. Molecular changes of Cav1.2 channels generated by alternative splicing could diversify their electrophysiological and pharmacological properties. Altered splicing was found in many cardiovascular disorders. However, the alternative splicing of Cav1.2 channels during cardiovascular development has not been investigated in detail. Our preliminary study has revealed an upregulation of aberrantly spliced channels in neonatal heart and blood vessels at multiple splice loci. Electrophysiological study uncovered a dominant negative effect. However, the functions of aberrant channels in native tissues are unclear.We hypothesize that these aberrant Cav1.2 channels could exhibit functions rather than simply being non-conducting channels in native tissues. They may participate in pathophysiology of cardiovascular disorders. We aim to identify these aberrant channels to test their functions. As our preliminary findings are mainly at the mRNA transcript level, we will generate specific antibodies to detect the expression and trafficking of these aberrant channels during cardiovascular development. We will characterize the functions of the aberrant channels by electrophysiological studies and by using siRNA to knock down the aberrant channels in cultured cardiomyocytes or vascular smooth muscle cells. Furthermore, we will test whether the expression of the aberrant channels will be altered under pathological conditions such as in ischemia.The study of Cav1.2 channels during development is of clinical importance. Molecules expressed at the fetal stage could re-emerge in diseases such as heart failure. For example, a fetal splice variant of Cav1.2 channels was upregulated in human heart failure. Identification of the expression and functions of the aberrant channels during development will help to understand the pathophysiology of diseases. In the future, we will test whether these aberrant channels are altered in human diseases. Furthermore, the aberrant channels have the potential to serve as targets for treating cardiovascular disorders.
kw: Development, Calcium channel, Heart, Blood vessel, Aberrant splicing

title: Identification of Frizzled-7 (FZD7) as a novel molecular driver for a specific ovarian cancer subtype which harbors stem-cell property.
abs: Epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC) is the most fatal cancer of the female reproductive tract and its incidence in on the rise in Singapore. EOC is a heterogeneous entity which comprises different histological and biological subtypes. Regardless of different subtypes, the current standard treatment is surgical debulking followed by taxane/platinum-based chemotherapy in high risk patients. The process of molecular oncogenesis of different subtypes of EOC has not been clarified due to high levels of genomic instability and complex genetic alterations. This complexity has hindered the development of novel targeted therapeutics specific to disease subtypes thus the treatment outcome of EOC has not improved significantly. Therefore, the calling for better translational approach focusing on EOC progression geared towards the personalized therapeutic options is mandatory. This project will focus on frizzled-7 (FZD7), a known receptor for Wnt ligands, to investigate its role in EOC. We propose that FZD7 can be utilized as a marker to identify a subgroup of EOC patient with poorer prognosis which might harbor stem-cell property. From our preliminary work, a comprehensive in silico subtyping of EOC has been established. This proposal will extend the preliminary in silico work to correlate FZD7 expression with the subtypes identified from archived ovarian carcinoma tissue samples. Functional studies in pre-clinical models will be utilized to investigate the biological role of FZD7 in conferring stem-cell property in ovarian cancer. This proposal is intended to provide convincing evidence that one EOC subtype with stem-cell property can be robustly identified by a novel marker, FZD7, and the pathway could be targeted by specific inhibitors.
kw: ovarian cancer, frizzled-7, personalized medicine

title: Identification of “stemness” genes and signaling pathway activated in the hematopoietic stem cell generation
abs: Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) generated from embryonic stem (ES) cells in vitro could be alternative source for therapeutically transplantable HSCs to patients like leukemia. Although many cytokines and stromal cells have been tested for their ability to induce hematopoietic lineages from ES cells, derivation of multilineage long-term repopulating HSCs from unmanipulated ES or iPS cells has not been achieved, owing in part, to the lack of information on HSC formation in the embryo. Given that HSCs are autonomously generated within the normal physiology of the embryo, detailed analysis of HSC formation in the embryo will aid in the identification of factors leading to their growth and could be useful in the derivation of HSC from ES/iPS cells. In this project, we will compare the gene expression signature between pre-HSC and HSC isolated from mouse embryos to identify HSC specification genes and signals. To this end, we use single cell microarray technique, which is suitable for the analysis of developing embryo.
kw: hematopoietic stem cell, development, stemness, embryonic stem cell, single cell microarray, Ips

title: Preferences for care at the end-of-life among middle-aged and older Singaporeans
abs: Background and Aims: Understanding preferences for care at the end-of-life is important for planning and improving services that provide such care. However, the nature and extent of these preferences among Singaporeans remains unknown. This study aims to understand:1. Preferences for care at the end-of-life among Singaporeans aged 50 years and over.2. Whether preferences for care at the end-of-life vary by demographic and socio-economic characteristics.Methodology: A stated preference conjoint survey, using a nationally representative sample of 1500 community dwelling Singaporeans aged 50 years and over, will be conducted. This age cohort of Singaporeans has been chosen as they are more likely to access services providing care at the EOL in the coming decade. Information on socio-economic characteristics, health status, attributes of a ‘good death’, preferences for life prolonging/ sustaining technology, decision making, diagnostic and prognostic disclosure, advance care planning, and advance medical directives will be elicited. Preferences and trade-offs for what constitutes good care at the end-of-life for Singaporeans will be determined using conjoint analysis.Significance: This will be the first nationally representative study from Singapore to examine preferences for care at the end-of-life. The study will provide policy makers and health professionals an insight into Singaporeans’ preferences for care at the end-of-life, and clarify any stereotypes and misconceptions, so that ultimate decisions made and care given at the end-of-life are relevant to and consistent with wishes of Singaporeans. The findings will also help deliver services to meet the end-of-life preferences of Singaporeans and prudent medical resource allocation for palliative care.
kw: End-of-life care, Good death, Advance care planning, Conjoint analysis

title: Augmentation of liver regeneration and liver support in extended liver resections and small for size liver.
abs: Success of Liver resection and transplantation with partial liver grafts either from living donor or from splitting a cadaveric graft is dependent on liver regeneration. The maximum extent of resection compatible with safe postoperative outcomes remains unknown, but it is believed that the risk for liver failure increases when the remnant liver volume is too small (<25%). Successful regeneration following resection and transplantation leads to normal liver function without sequelae, whereas failed regeneration results in death. The rate of regeneration increases with the extent of liver resection but the tipping point when the regeneration fails is poorly understood. Heptaocyte transplantation to treat liver insufficiency in acute and chronic liver failure has shown only limited short term efficacy to date. The important reasons for failure include low engraftment rate in liver due to lack of a potential space for transplanted cells to engraft as well as hostile environment in the liver during liver injury. Hepatocyte function is insufficient from the 5% mass of transplanted hepatocytes. The liver insufficiency model due to small for size results from liver volume below threshold and thus has a better chance of being augmented by hepatocyte transplantation. The spleen is an important but non-critical organ and offers a natural reservoir for in-vivo siting of transplanted hepatocytes to support the liver when it is in the critical stage of regeneration. The natural anatomy of the spleen allows its easy modification to reattach to the portal vascular system to simulate an accessory liver. We propose to use the spleen to transplant encapsulated hepatocytes following an extended resection in a porcine model.The aim of this study is to support Liver regeneration following extended resection (80%) with (i) Transplantation of encapsulated hepatocytes in porcine spleen in vivo (ii) Transplantation of encapsulated hepatocytes in decellularized spleen ex vivo with reimplantation.
kw: Liver, Hepatocyte transplant, Allograft, Liver Regeneration

title: Mechanisms of pattern recognition and immune response in invasive aspergillosis
abs: Invasive fungal infections remain a major cause of mortality and morbidity in immunocompromised patients, of which invasive aspergillosis (IA) is emerging as the most common IFI. The overall aim of this proposal is to study the mechanisms through which cells of the immune system recognize Aspergillus fumigatus to initiate effective host immune response and understanding the pathophysiology of IA. This information will be used to optimize management of patients with the disease and for development of new immunotherapeutic strategies given the limited options in currently available anti-fungal drugs. Several key objectives will be pursued:(1) To systematically characterize the interaction between pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) of A.fumigatus and pattern recognition receptor (PRRs) on host immune cells. To date, beta-glucan in the Aspergillus cell wall is the only characterized PAMP. We want to investigate the role of the other polysaccharide cell wall components of Aspergillus, in particular, galactomannan; and to identify the corresponding candidate PRRs. We postulate that the macrophage mannose receptor and galactose C-type lectin receptor are candidate PRRs. Purified cell wall polysaccharides and A.fumigatus mutant strains will be used to decipher the PAMP-PRR interaction (2) To study the dynamics of the immune response to A.fumigatus in hematological patients during the course of treatment: either post- chemotherapy or stem-cell transplantation through whole blood stimulation assays in-vitro.(3) To investigate the functional role and clinical relevance of known PRRs (Dectin-1, Toll-like receptor 4 and 9) against Aspergillus in susceptible patients. We will study if patients with functional single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) for the above PRRs have an increased susceptibility to the disease. Knowledge obtained from the above studies will enable risk stratification of at-risk patients and individualized optimization of anti-fungal therapy. This will be a major step forward towards reducing morbidity and mortality in IFI.
kw: Aspergillus fumigatus, Pattern recognition receptors, Pathogen-associated molecular patterns, Leukocytes, Cytokine

title: Adaptation and divergence of H1N1/2009 influenza A virus under controlled experimental conditions
abs: Evolution of influenza A viruses are marked by random drift (antigenic and genetic) and reassortment that necessitates frequent vaccine updates. Relatively little is known about how the fitness of a virus lineage (or population) may change over time or how changes in fitness are affected by genetic variation. Furthermore, the underlying causes of variation in fitness have not been systematically studied in controlled experiments. The lack of this empirical evidence remains a crucial gap in our knowledge of influenza virus behavior and adaptation. In this proposal we will establish an experimental protocol to study long-term evolution of influenza A virus and generate preliminary data that addresses these questions. Here we propose three scenarios for in vitro transmission experiments. In the first, we will examine the affect of serial transmission bottlenecks on viral replication fitness of a population. Theory predicts that this will result if reduced fitness. Second we will simulate the role of diversity pools on the overall evolution and fitness of a virus population. The prediction from this experiment is that if genetic diversity is constant over time then environmental conditions will select for viruses with increased replication fitness. The third experiment incorporates changes in the host immune status overtime. In this scenario it is predicted that changes in fitness will occur in a stepwise manner in concert with changes in genetic diversity. This initial study will be restricted to pandemic H1N1 virus, but it is intended that future studies will include human H3N2 and influenza B viruses. Understanding factors that influence influenza A virus fitness will allow us to assess assumptions that underlie mathematical models that are frequently used in formulating public health policy. These experiments would also provide a platform to test anti-virals against influenza to failure, thereby providing information on strategies for anti-viral use.
kw: Evolution, Epidemiology, Fitness, Influenza A, pandemic H1N1

title: A study to delineate the relationship between obesity and bone mass/architecture.
abs: Ageing and increasing urbanization have contributed to the rising incidence of “lifestyle diseases” such as osteoporosis and obesity. Osteoporotic hip fracture incidence rate in Singapore is now among the highest in Asia and approaching that of Caucasian populations (1). Concurrently, the prevalence of obesity is also increasing (2). Recent evidence suggests that adipose tissue may have a negative impact on bone health (3), challenging the traditional paradigm that increased body mass, through mechanical loading is beneficial to the skeletal system. Therefore, the coexistence of both morbid conditions in the population, and particularly within the same individual may be more detrimental than expected. The primary aim of our study is to investigate the role of body composition in skeletal health. We hypothesize that it is primarily the visceral compartment of body fat that is detrimental to bone metabolism, resulting in impairment of bone mineral density as well bone architecture. Thus we propose a cross sectional study to phenotype healthy overweight (BMI>25kg/m2) young (<50 years of age) Chinese males through CT quantification of body fat compartments (visceral vs. subcutaneous) as well as bone marrow adipose tissue and QCT acquisition of volumetric bone mineral density (vBMD) and bone geometry, to test the hypothesis that VAT is negatively correlated with these important bone parameters, independent of body weight. We will also evaluate for differences in this relationship between Chinese and Caucasians, testing the hypothesis that ethnicity is an important modifier of the relationship. By investigating this novel link between fat and bone, there will be potential opportunities to identify new biomarkers of osteoporosis risk. In addition, our study will also have important clinical relevance for health preventive strategies and drug discovery and design in osteoporosis and obesity.
kw: Obesity, Osteoporosis, Visceral adipose tissue, Bone density, architecture, Bone quality, Bone marrow adipose tissue

title: Development of novel anti-HIV-1/AIDS drugs targeting host-viral protein interactions based on a unique high-throughput screening platform using the cell-free protein synthesis system
abs: Specific aims: Highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) has contributed enormously to the prolongation of life and increase of quality in HIV-1-infected individuals. Nevertheless it is not clear how long clinical benefit will last given the emergence of multiple drug-resistant viral strains. To solve this problem, we intend to develop novel AIDS drugs interfering with virus-host protein interaction as new anti-HIV targets, based on our unique cell-free protein synthesis system using wheat germ.Hypothesis: Current treatment of HIV/AIDS consists of a combination of drugs targeting different viral proteins and aims to suppress viral replication below detectable levels. Most antiviral drugs attempt to interfere with viral replication. However several steps of the viral life cycle remain incompletely characterized, and therefore cannot be effectively exploited in antiviral strategies. Our recent data together with others strongly suggest that cellular factors and their interaction with viral proteins can be useful targets for near-future antiviral therapy. We believe that if we fully exploit our cell-free protein synthesis system, it is possible to discover inhibitors and elucidate the weak points of viruses so as to develop potent drugs useful for combating this highly mutation-prone HIV infection.Methodology and Approach: Based on our results, the following studies will be conducted to develop new class of anti-HIV-1 drugs with less-frequent association with drug-resistance. They include; 1) Studies on the molecular mechanism of virus-host interaction in the HIV life cycle. 2) Drug discovery with high-throughput drug screening system by the cell-free protein synthesis/AlphaScreenTM system from chemical libraries. The following HIV-1 and host protein interactions will be targeted in this pilot study; Vif-APOBEC3G, IN-Huwe1 and Vpr-protein kinases. 3) Pre-clinical evaluation of candidate compounds through in vitro and in vivo mouse assays using hematopoietic as well as stem cells.
kw: HIV-1/AIDS, Antiviral drugs, Resistance, Host factor, Wheat-germ cell-free protein synthesis, AlphaScreen

title: Stimulation of cardiac Na+/K+ ATPase with its antibody - A novel approach to treat chronic heart failure
abs: Chronic heart failure (CHF) is becoming the leading cause for death in aged people. Glycosides are commonly used to treat CHF. Glycosides bind to Na+/K+ ATPase (NKA) and produce positive inotropic effect. However, this group of drugs produces positive inotripic action but with severe toxic effects. The toxic effects and narrow therapeutic range of cardiac glycosides limit their clinical uses and warrants development of new drugs to treat CHF. We developed r-DRSAb, a rat NKA RD region specific antibody. In our preliminary study, we found that r-DRSAb stimulated heart contractility and, more importantly, induced cardioprotection against ischemic injury. This proposal is therefore designed to: 1)investigate the signaling mechanism for the positive inotropic effect of r-DRSAb. Specifically, we will examine its regulatory effect on Ca2+ handling proteins and study the involvement of protein kinase C (PKC), mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPKs), Src, phosphoinositide-3 kinase (PI3K/Akt). 2)Investigate the signaling mechanisms underlying r-DRSAb induced cardioprotection. Specifically, we will measure myocardial infarction size, cell viability, myocyte contractile function and examine the involvement of ATP-sensitive K+ channels (KATP), PKC, MAPKs, Src, PI3K/Akt. 3)Investigate the therapeutic effect of r-DRSAb in both myocardial infarction- and isoproterenol-induced CHF rat models.
kw: Na+/K+ ATPase, Chronic heart failure, cardioprotection, heart, antibody

title: Dietary fatty acids, oxylipins, and risk of coronary heart disease in Singapore Chinese
abs: The incidence of coronary heart disease (CHD) is increasing rapidly in many Asian countries in parallel with changes in diet. Dietary fatty acids have been implicated in the aetiology of CHD, but the biological effects of specific fatty acids (e.g. n-3 vs. n-6 fatty acids, marine vs. plant n-3 fatty acids) are markedly different and many uncertainties remain about optimal intakes for the prevention of CHD. Oxylipins (e.g. eicosanoids) are fatty acid-derived signaling molecules that have been identified as key mediators of the effects of dietary fatty acids on inflammation and blood pressure regulation in experimental studies. However, epidemiological studies of oxylipins in relation to CHD risk are sparse. Also, research on diet and risk of CHD has predominantly been conducted in western populations that have a variation in intake that is different than in Asian populations. We will therefore evaluate the role of dietary fatty acids, potential biological intermediates, and risk of CHD in a large nested case-control study of 750 incident cases and 750 matched controls within the Singapore Chinese Health Study. The aims of this project are to evaluate: 1). How fatty acid intakes, their food sources, and plasma fatty acid biomarkers (>25 fatty acids) are related to risk of CHD in Singapore Chinese.2). How oxylipin concentrations are related to chronic inflammation, blood pressure, and risk of CHD. 3). To what extent associations between dietary fatty acids and CHD are mediated by oxylipins, circulating lipoproteins, blood pressure and chronic inflammation. This project combines a large prospective nested case-control study with the high-throughput assessment of novel biomarkers to increase insight into an important public health problem. Greater knowledge on the effects of specific dietary fatty acid can directly improve dietary recommendations as well as the production of healthier foods to reduce the burden of CHD in Asia.
kw: Nutrition, Fatty acids, Biomarkers, Coronary Heart Disease, Oxylipins, Eicosanoids

title: Defining the mechanism of Y-glutamyl transpeptidase-mediated pathogenesis in Helicobacter pylori-associated severe gastric diseases and the development of a potential diagnostic marker for the disease.
abs: The indelible link between Helicobacter pylori and gastroduodenal diseases, exacerbated by the high prevalence of gastric cancer and the emergence of multiple-antibiotic-resistant strains in Singapore, poses a major public health concern. Amongst the known pathogenic factors of H. pylori, y-glutamyl transpeptidase (GGT) has been reported to be a colonizing and apoptosis-inducing factor. However, the GGT-mediated pathogenic mechanism as well as the regulatory system(s) responsible for its expression remain unclear.Our earlier study (Gong et al., 2010. Gastroenterology), found that H. pylori strains possessing high GGT activity proliferate more aggressively in culture and display a close association with peptic ulcer disease (p<0.001). Furthermore, purified native GGT generates H2O2 in gastric epithelial cells resulting in oxidative DNA damage and upregulation of IL-8, suggesting firm inflammatory response. Apart from generating H2O2, GGT also hydrolyses glutamine to produce ammonia, an important contributor to vacuolation induced by H. pylori vacuolating cytotoxin (VacA). To test our hypothesis, isogenic mutants, inhibitors of GGT activity and complementation studies will be utilized. By using co-immunoprecipitation, Western blot, 2D-gel electrophoresis and/or microarray, we will also seek potential interacting partners of H. pylori GGT. Regulation of GGT expression will be investigated by comparing sequences of ggt promoter regions from strains with different GGT activity. RT-PCR and deletion mutants of the potential regulators involved will also be performed. Seroanalysis of sera from patients with gastroduodenal diseases will help to confirm the effectiveness of GGT as a diagnostic marker for H. pylori infections. It is conceivable that our study will provide insights into how H. pylori GGT induces gastric epithelial cell damage during host-pathogen interaction. Defining the mechanisms regulating GGT activity will provide useful information for the development of potential therapeutics and may lead to changes in the outlook and clinical management of H. pylori-associated severe gastroduodenal diseases.
kw: Helicobacter pylori, Gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase, Vacuolating cytotoxin A (VacA), Vacuolation, Regulation, Diagnostic marker

title: Linking BRAF/KRAS mutations and the CpG island methylation phenotype by methylome sequencing
abs: Much interest in KRAS and BRAF mutations in colorectal cancer (CRC) has been generated because of their strong links to cetuximab resistance. The CpG island methylator phenotype (CIMP) is also strongly linked to BRAF mutations, and more controversially, KRAS mutations. However, the mechanisms involved in this prominent association of mutation and methylation events have remained elusive, with a major source of ambiguity being the biased and inconsistent markers used to assess methylation. We recently developed methods to sequence methylation on a genome-wide scale (methylome) by next-generation sequencing (NGS), a capability demonstrated by only a few centres worldwide. The specific aims of this study are (1) To characterize DNA methylation events occurring in colorectal cell lines and tumours with KRAS, BRAF and no KRAS/BRAF mutations using NGS (2) To assess the potential of using selected CpG markers identified by NGS for early detection of CRC (3) To functionally investigate the mechanistic links between unique DNA methylation events in each CRC mutation subtype and their respective mutation status. Methylome NGS will be applied to well-defined groups of cell lines and clinical samples to characterize common and unique methylation events associated with the different mutation subtypes. The common events, more likely to occur early before subtype diversification, will be investigated in normal tissue from CRC and non-cancer subjects for the potential as early detection markers for CRC. The methylation events unique to each subtype will be validated in larger independent series of CRCs, and tested for their involvement with the respective kinase mutations using shRNA technology and relevant assays based on candidate gene function. The results of this study are anticipated to provide greater insight into the events underlying and linking the three distinctive and clinically relevant CRC subtypes, potentially highlighting novel diagnostic tools and mechanisms for more intelligent therapeutic intervention.
kw: CpG island methylator phenotype (CIMP), BRAF mutation, KRAS mutation, Colorectal cancer, Methylome sequencing

title: Reduction in hemorrhagic transformation by RNA interference from microRNAs upon tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) treatment of ischemic stroke
abs: Cerebral hemorrhage is a dreaded complication following treatment with recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (rtPA) in acute ischemic stroke. Although distortion of the blood-brain-barrier has been implicated, much of the pathogenesis of cerebral hemorrhage has been poorly understood. In this proposal, we propose to evaluate the involvement of microRNA in hemorrhagic complications following rtPA therapy. In our previous study, we have identified several proteins, mRNAs and microRNAs that are dysregulated during cerebral ischemia in rat models for stroke as well as in human stroke patients. From these studies, we have identified some genes (such as MMP-9, TIMP3, AQP, VCAM1 and VEGF) whose expression can be regulated to reduce the extent of intracranial hemorrhage as well as to improve the efficacy of tPA treatment. We propose to use RNA interference such as a) anti-microRNAs (to down-regulate the selected highly expressed miRNAs) and b) pre-miRNAs (to up-regulate the selected poorly expressed miRNAs) in rat stroke models subjected to embolic stroke (middle cerebral artery occlusion). We will assess the effect of modulating endogenous microRNA levels on the expression of functionally related genes that are involved in cerebral ischemia with respect to infarct volumes and functional stroke outcomes. The selected microRNAs will also be tested in combination with rtPA to optimize the therapeutic benefits of rtPA. This study aims to translate state-of-art advances in molecular biology to address an important therapeutic gap in clinical practice. This proposal has been amended and resubmitted according to the reviewers’ and NMRC-LRP panel members’ comments as attached.
kw: stroke, hemorrhagic, embolic, microRNA, Cerebral ischemia, tPA

title: The quantification and physiological function of ergothioneine in vivo
abs: The naturally occurring amino acid ergothioneine can only be synthesized by fungi and certain bacteria. However despite this, ergothioneine accumulates in tissues of animals and humans at up to millimolar concentrations. This degree of uptake and conservation in tissues together with the recent identification of a highly specific transporter responsible for ergothioneine uptake into cells, is highly suggestive of an important physiological role in the human body. Mutations of the ergothioneine specific transporter may also be linked to several chronic inflammatory conditions. Earlier studies by us and others indicate that ergothioneine has potent antioxidant properties in vitro with some reports claiming it to be up to 7000 times more effective than Vitamin E. Some groups have also shown that inhibition of the ergothioneine uptake in cells results in increased susceptibility to oxidative damage. The function of ergothioneine, however, has eluded researchers for nearly a century. Furthermore, non-specific analytical methods have led to conflicting reports of ergothioneine levels in foods and tissues.This project specifically aims to:1.Use highly specific and sensitive analytical techniques to standardize a method for the accurate quantification of ergothioneine in foods, animal tissues/body fluids and cell culture media2.Directly test the hypothesis that ergothioneine has antioxidant properties in vivo (animal model and humans)3.Establish the relevance of ergothioneine in relation to oxidative and inflammatory-linked disorders and its potential as a therapeutic agent.On completion of these aims, we anticipate to gain a better understanding of the functional role of ergothioneine in vivo, the purpose of its high abundance in the body and its potential antioxidant and therapeutic applications in humans.
kw: Ergothioneine, Antioxidant, Oxidative stress, Organic cation transporter 1, Thiol, Dietary supplementation

title: Identification and characterization of dengue virus receptors
abs: Dengue virus (DENV) infects approximately 100 million people worldwide each year and threatens almost one half of the globe’s population, including those living in Singapore. Even after concerted campaigns against dengue, including the one initiated in Singapore by NEA in 2005, there are to date, no effective vaccines or therapeutics for DENV. In order to facilitate the development of safe dengue vaccines and therapeutics, it is important to understand how DENV infects cells. The overall goal of this project is to characterize host cell receptors or co-receptors important for DENV entry into the host cell, and to understand their interactions with DENV. Preliminary results from our siRNA studies have provided receptor protein candidates that may be involved in DENV propagation. To achieve this goal, the following specific aims will be pursued:Specific aim 1: Validation of candidate receptors or co-receptors for DENV infection.Specific aim 2: Determination of the ability of the validated candidate receptors to bind directly to the surface proteins of DENV and mapping of the interacting interface on the host cell receptor and DENV envelope (E) protein.Specific aim 3: Determination of the atomic structure of receptors complexed with DENV surface protein E using a combination of x-ray crystallography and cryoEM image reconstruction techniques.Significance: The results generated from these studies will provide insights into the mechanisms of DENV entry and form the basis for rational structure-based drug design that can interfere with DENV binding to target cells. In addition, the epitopes on DENV, that are important for interactions with the receptors or co-receptors, can be incorporated into a vaccine. Presumably, antibodies elicited against the DENV receptor(s) binding sites should neutralize DENV infection.
kw: dengue, receptor, structure, SiRNA, host factor, E protein

title: Role of stress granule components in Dengue virus propagation
abs: Dengue viruses (DENV) are locally and globally important human pathogens that currently cannot be prevented due to lack of approved vaccines and cannot be treated owing to the absence of specific antiviral drugs. These deficiencies underscore the need for a more complete understanding of the molecular mechanisms used by DENV to productively infect human cells, which requires the discovery and characterization of host proteins that interact with the viral RNA genome. To characterize DENV-2 RNA binding proteins, we purified and identified a set of proteins that specifically associate with a DENV-2 RNA genome and are components of RNA granules. Here, we propose to characterize these proteins, which are known RNA binding proteins found in stress granules where they are believed to regulate mRNA metabolism. At the conclusion of the three-year funding period we expect to understand the role these proteins play in the DENV lifecycle. In order to achieve this we propose the following specific aims: (1) To elucidate the role of the DEAD-box protein, DDX6, in the DENV viral life cycle. We propose to characterize the molecular details of the DDX6-DENV-2 RNA interaction and to ascertain the step in the viral life cycle that requires DDX6. We will test the hypothesis that late in infection DDX6 is used by the virus to sort viral RNAs away from replication and translation in order to package these genomes into infectious virions. (2) To elucidate the mechanism of DENV inhibition of stress granule formation. We propose to identify the viral product responsible for this effect. While we propose a comprehensive approach, we will test our preferred hypothesis that stress granules are inhibited by expression of a sub-genomic DENV RNA. These experiments will set the stage to understand the importance of inhibiting this stress response for productive DENV infection.
kw: Dengue, Host factors, Stress granule components

title: Role of Th2 cytokines in dysregulation of cholesterol metabolism in nephrotic syndrome: Modulation of SREBP and OSM-mediated pathways in an IL-13 overexpression model of minimal change nephropathy
abs: Hypercholesterolemia is a major risk factor for atherosclerotic heart disease in children with long-standing minimal change nephrotic syndrome (MCNS). In non-MCNS experimental rat models of nephrotic syndrome, hypercholesterolemia is thought to be secondary to massive proteinuria. However, in our IL-13 gene over-expression rat model of MCNS, a Th2-cytokine model similar to that in human disease, hypercholesterolemia correlated significantly with serum IL-13 levels, and in some even preceded the development of proteinuria. This was associated with significant changes in expression of genes involved in cholesterol metabolism (HMG-CoAR, CYP7A1, ACAT2, LDLR). Microarray studies on liver tissue showed downregulation of Oncostatin M (OSM) (regulator of LDLR), downregulation of ABGC5 and ABCA1 (molecules involved in cholesterol excretion into bile), and increased expression of SREBP (regulatory protein binding to promoter regions of HMG-CoAR and LDLR). In MCNS, despite the presence of severe hypercholesterolemia, upregulation of HMG-CoAR and concomitant downregulation of LDLR have been demonstrated.We therefore hypothesized that in MCNS relapses, hypercholesterolemia is due to dysregulation of cholesterol homeostasis, mediated by the direct action of Th2 cytokines like IL-13, on pathways regulating SREBP-mediated cholesterol regulation and OSM regulation of LDLR, and not secondary to proteinuria or hypoalbuminemia. The specific aim of this project is to establish the role of Th2 cytokines in regulating cholesterol homeostasis both in the IL-13 overexpression rat model of MCNS, and a rat hepatocyte cell culture system by:i.Profiling the genes and proteins involved in the SREBP-mediated cholesterol regulation pathways and OSM mediated downregulation of LDLR.ii.Using siRNA-transfected rat hepatocyte cells to study the inhibitory effects on the downstream molecules of cholesterol metabolic pathways following IL-13 stimulationSubsequently we will validate this pathway in an IL-13 stimulated human hepatocyte cell culture system. Understanding the mechanisms that contribute to hypercholesterolemia of this disease should open up new therapeutic avenues.
kw: Minimal Change Nephrotic Syndrome (MCNS), Hypercholesterolemia, Interleukin-13 (IL-13), Sterol responsive element binding protein (SREBP), Low density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR), Oncostatin M (OSM)

title: Promoting effective lymphatic drainage of the arteries as a new therapeutic intervention for atherosclerosis
abs: Atherosclerosis is the leading cause of industrialized countries throughout the world despite the great success of statin drugs for lowering LDL cholesterol. Formation of atherosclerotic plaque results from the continuous accumulation of lipids, cells of the immune system and fibrous elements in the large arteries. Our recent published work, and preliminary evidence contained herein together with existing literature, leads us to propose the active promotion of lymphatic drainage as a key process to reduce atherosclerosis by returning proteins, lipoproteins and cholesterol that enter the artery walls back to the blood circulation.Specifically, we will investigate in mouse models of atherosclerosis and clinical biopsies whether the poor lymphatic drainage associated with atherosclerosis results from alterations in lymphatic vessels and/or imbalance in the growth of lymphatic versus blood vessels (aim 1). We will then examine the involvement of vascular endothelial growth factor-C (VEGF-C) in promoting the remodeling of blood and lymphatic vessels in human and mice arteries affected by atherosclerosis. Furthermore, we will evaluate whether circulating levels of VEGF-C in humans may serve as a predictor of cardiovascular events (aim 2). Finally, preclinical studies in mice will be used to examine the synergistic effect of manipulating VEGF-C/VEGFR-3 pathway and cholesterol-lowering drugs, including ezetimibe and statins, on lymphatic drainage and atherosclerosis incidence. In an attempt to validate the clinical translation of promoting lymphatic drainage to reduce atherogenesis in humans, we will assess whether the growth of lymphatic vessels can be induced ex vivo from human arteries (aim 3).This collaborative project will involve a multi-disciplinary team consisting of basic scientists in biology and imaging and clinical disciplines. In summary, this innovative project will help to optimize the current therapeutic strategies in cardiovascular diseases and the identification of novel cardiovascular risk factors.
kw: atherosclerosis, inflammation, lymphatic drainage, (lymph)angiogenesis

title: Inflammation and effect of statins on retinal microvascular structure in TNF-alpha induced and spontaneous diabetic mouse model - novel understanding and treatment for diabetic retinopathy
abs: The prevalence of diabetes has reached epidemic proportions worldwide. Persons with diabetes are at risk for developing diabetic retinopathy (DR). In later stage, it can lead to sight-threatening form of the disease. People with diabetes are 25 times more likely to lose vision than those who are not diabetic. There is increasing evidence that diabetes causes a range of metabolic and physiologic abnormalities in retinal vessels, and that inflammation plays a substantial role in the development of DR. The concept of localized inflammatory processes that play a role in the development of DR is relatively new, but evidence that supports the hypothesis is accumulating rapidly. This hypothesis offers new insight into the pathogenesis of DR, and offers novel targets to inhibit DR. Animal model studies shows that as compared to normal, TNF-a levels are significantly greater in the diabetic retinal vessels. Our pilot study exhibited TNF-a induced retinal inflammatory responses and it modulated the retinal microvascular changes (with arteriolar dilation and venular constriction). The retinal arteriolar dilation has been proposed as a physiological indicator of diabetes-related retinal microvascular-dysfunction. In humans, retinal arteriolar dilatation predicts the development of DR. Arteriolar dilation and venular constriction was reversed in control groups in fluvastatin treated mice retinal vessels.In this grant, we propose to (i) investigate retinal microvascular caliber changes in TNF-a induced inflammatory process (ii) determine these complications in diabetic mouse and (iii) determine the protective effect of fluvastatin as a potential preventive treatment for retinal microvascular-dysfunction in early stages of DR. We hypothesize that inflammatory processes contribute to the development of DR. However, there is no preventive treatment to reduce the retinal microvascular-dysfunction in the development of DR in patients. This study would enable us to investigate novel pharmacological intervention in the prevention of microvascular changes in diabetic induced retinal vascular inflammation.
kw: Diabetes, Microvascular, TNF alpha, Retina, Inflammation, Fluvastatin

title: Elucidation of the role of microRNA in the pathogenesis of atopic dermatitis
abs: Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a common, chronic and relapsing inflammatory skin disease that affects about 10% of the population. AD is associated with high morbidity with significant adverse impact on the patient’s quality of life and healthcare costs. Current evidence suggests that the primary dysregulation of genes encoding epidermal proteins play a critical role in the development of AD. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) have been recently emerged as key regulators in the differentiation and development of the skin. A study has identified a specific epidermal miRNA that play role in the development of psoriasis. However, there is so far no such a study to identify specific epidermal miRNA that may play role in AD. We hypothesize that miRNAs play a vital pathogenic role in the abnormal expression of epidermal proteins that contribute to altered skin barrier function and initiation of dendritic cell maturation in AD. The role of miRNAs in the regulation of epidermal proteins that have altered expressed in AD will be investigated in our proposed study. To achieve this aim, we will first perform microarray analysis to compare the expression profiles of miRNAs in the epidermis isolated from lesional and non-lesional skin of AD patients, and the epidermis of healthy controls to identify AD-associated miRNA candidates. After validation using qPCR and Northern blot analyses, the identified AD-associated miRNAs will be used to search for their putative mRNA targets using bioinformatics approach. Subsequently, functional study will be performed to elucidate the direct regulatory effect of each ‘miRNA–mRNA target’. The results of this study will provide novel insights into the molecular mechanisms of AD pathogenesis by miRNAs. Furthermore, the identification of AD-associated miRNAs may further guide development of novel, specific molecular targeted therapeutic strategy for AD.

title: A Randomised Controlled Trial of Cabergoline Prophylaxis for Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome in IVF Cycles and Derivation of Biomarkers for OHSS.
abs: Severe ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) occurs in 2% of in-vitro fertilisation (IVF) cycles as a consequence of controlled ovarian hyper-stimulation (COH), which is caused by the release of vaso-active cytokines with consequential increased vascular permeability (VP). Affected patients develop ascites, pleural and pericardial effusions, resulting in haemo-concentration which in turn can be complicated by thromboembolism, organ hypoperfusion, renal and respiratory failure. There are neither reliable strategies for predicting the occurence of OHSS nor any good strategies to prevent it currently. Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) has been implicated in the pathogenesis of OHSS, with small RCTs showing a benefit of cabergoline in reducing the incidence of OHSS. However, these trials are underpowered to detect any benefit in severe OHSS. In addition, the incidence of overstimulation in KKIVF is higher than those reported in publicly-funded cycles and it is likely that ethnic differences will account for differences in responses to cabergoline treatment. Hence, we propose to conduct an adequately-powered double-blind placebo-controlled RCT for prophylaxis of severe OHSS in KKIVF centre, and to derive serum and follicular fluid biomarkers for the risk of developing OHSS. Five hundred and forty at-risk women (>20 oocytes retrieved at oocyte-pickup) will be randomised to cabergoline or placebo treatment, with the occurrence of OHSS being the primary end-point. Secondary end-points include the need for abdominal or pleural tap, other complications of OHSS, implantation and pregnancy rates, miscarriage and ongoing pregnancy rates.Serum and follicular fluid collected with be assayed for VEGF and other vaso-active cytokines (Interleukins 2 and 6, soluble Flt ligand), and sensitivity/specificity estimates derived for the prediction of OHSS and its severity.The reduction in incidence and severity of OHSS with cabergoline treatment and derivation of biomarkers here should reduce the morbidity, hospitalisation and costs associated with the development of moderate-severe OHSS.
kw: Cabergoline, Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome, Vasoactive cytokines, Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor, In vitro fertilisation, Biomarkers

title: Generation of highly osteogenic bone tissue-engineered graft for treatment of fracture non-union – A Pre-Clinical to Phase I Study.
abs: Fracture injuries represent a significant clinical burden, with up to 14,000 cases occurring in Singapore annually, and are complicated by non-union in 10% of cases. Current methods for treatment with autografts have been fraught with multiple short-comings, leading to an urgent and unmet need for alternative approaches such as bone tissue-engineering (BTE).Successful BTE approaches require adequate numbers of osteogenic cells, dynamically cultured with osteo-conductive macroporous scaffolds. We have recently demonstrated superior proliferative and osteogenic potential of human fetal mesenchymal stem cells (hfMSC) over perinatal and post-natal MSC for BTE applications, and its utility for the generation of a tissue-engineered bone graft (TEBG) through dynamic culture and osteogenic-priming in a bi-axial rotating bioreactor. Transplantation of this hfMSC-mediated TEBG resulted in the healing of a rat critical-sized femoral defect through the induction of neo-vasculogenesis, raising the prospect of its use for healing atrophic fracture non-union. However, optimal scale up techniques and the adequacy of osteogenic priming of TEBG is not known.We aim to (i) optimise bioreactor-cultured microcarrier-based scale-up technology for optimal expansion of cGMP hfMSC and (ii) define the optimal

title: Transcriptional Regulation of Ezh2 Expression in Immune Cells and Lymphoma
abs: Polycomb group protein Ezh2 is implicated as a master regulator that is involved in various important biological and pathogenic processes, such as cell fate determination, proliferation and cancer progression. Given its important role in diverse biological processes, the expression of Ezh2 has to be tightly regulated. High levels of Ezh2 mRNA are found in several cancer cells, including breast cancer, prostate cancer and Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma. However, little is known about its transcriptional regulation. Here, we propose three complementary Specific Aims, which make use of in vitro and in vivo systems to uncover the positive and negative regulators of Ezh2 expression at the transcriptional level. Identification of the upstream regulators of Ezh2 will help us to understand the origin of pathogenic expression of Ezh2 in cancer cells and aid in the design of novel strategies to either counteract the disorders or re-direct the development of the diseased cells. Specific Aim1: To determine chromatin structure and regulatory regions of Ezh2 locusTo understand the regulation of Ezh2 expression pattern, chromatin configuration of the Ezh2 locus will be first examined. Subsequently, the regulatory regions of Ezh2 locus are determined by DNase I hypersensitivity assay and other in vitro systems. Specific Aim2: To determine the positive and negative Ezh2 regulators Upon the identification of the regulatory regions on Ezh2 locus, transcriptional regulators of Ezh2 will be first determined using methods based on protein-DNA binding or DNA sequence analysis. To identify the Ezh2 regulators, which bind to DNA indirectly, or require an intact chromatin structure for locus specific binding, a cDNA screening strategy will be employed. Specific Aim3: To determine the physiological significance of Ezh2 regulators in vivo The physiological relevance of the identified Ezh2 regulators in developing and activated lymphocytes will be further studied and monitored in Ezh2-GFP reporter mice.
kw: Ezh2, transcriptional regulation, Lymphoma, lymphocyte development, chromatin

title: Functional genomic analyses of human malaria parasite resistance to artemisinin
abs: Human malaria is one of the most dangerous infectious diseases in the world, affecting over 250 million and killing close to 1million people each year. Artemisinin combination therapies (ACTs) are the most important presently available medical interventions against malaria. More importantly, the ACTs have a pivotal importance for to the global malaria eradication programs that are presently ongoing in all malaria endemic regions. Unfortunately, first signs of resistance of the malaria parasites, Plasmodium falciparum, to artemisinin have emerged in several sites in Southeast Asia. There is a great need for diagnostic tools that could help to understand the spread of artemisinin resistance and allow to derive the most optimal intervention strategies. Here we propose to carry out transcriptional profiling of P. falciparum field isolates that exhibit the artemisinin treatments delayed clearance phenotype (ATDCP). These isolates will be collected from the sites in western Cambodia and northwestern Thailand where this phenotype was first identified. Assessing the differential gene expression in these isolates, we will search for genes whose differential expression can be linked with ATDCP. Subsequently we will carry out functional analyses of the identified candidate genes using P. falciparum transfection approaches. These functional analyses will allow us to solidify the roles of the candidate genes in P. falciparum artemisinin resistance and help to characterize the molecular mechanisms underlining ATDCP. Based on these results we will explore genomic sequence of the ATDCP parasites with the goal of identifying the causative polymorphisms that could be used for diagnostic purposes.
