title: Effect of topical application of encapsulated PPARbeta/delta agonist GW501516 microparticles, with two release kinetics, on cutaneous wound healing in diabetic mice -a preclinical animal study.
abs: Wound complications in diabetic patients present therapeutic problems of increasing clinical importance. Despite the compelling evidence for a role of PPARß/d in wound healing, using PPARß/d agonists as pharmacological agents in the treatment of diabetic wound healing remain to be justified. Using the genetically and high-fat diet-induced diabetic mice as a model of impaired wound healing, we will perform a preclinical study of the effect of topical application of PPARß/d agonist GW501516 on the healing of full-thickness wounds. We will chemically synthesize and encapsulate GW501516 into single- and double-walled spherical microparticles to achieve early and sustained release, respectively. This method of drug delivery is novel with respect to PPARß/d research, and it allows the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of the drug to be controlled more effectively and selectively. Topical application of encapsulated agonists was chosen as the method of delivery because of its clinical practicability. This delivery method results in non-systemic exposure to the drug and thereby establishes a more favorable safety profile of the drug. At various days post-treatment, detail wound healing review that includes inflammatory response, rate of re-epithelialization, scarring and angiogenesis assessment will be performed. A focused real-time PCR array of the wound biopsies will also be performed to provide holistic perspective on the effect of the various treatments. To adopt an evidence-based wound care practice, it is imperative to obtain information pertaining to changes in gene expression during the healing of human acute wound. Although such information would validate our current findings, more importantly, it will provide the pertinent information for future human wound care management. The findings from this project will enable the further advancement and development of novel therapeutic options for patients with chronic diabetic wounds. This study will lead to future clinical advancement and development of novel drug delivery systems.
kw: PPARbeta/delta, Diabetic wound, microencapsulation, preclinical trial

title: Improving Radiotherapy using 4D Magnetic Resonance Imaging and Visualization
abs: The overall objective of this proposal is to significantly improve the efficacy and efficiency of high precision radiotherapy for the treatment of pulmonary tumors. In radiotherapy of lung cancer patients, a major challenge to overcome is the motion of pulmonary tumor. If the motion of the tumor can be accurately visualized and quantified, higher radiation dose could potentially be applied to the target volume while causing only minimal damage to the surrounding normal tissue. The proposal proposed the use of advanced dynamic 4D magnetic resonance imaging MRI (which enables high spatial and temporal volumetric images to be acquired with excellent soft tissue contrast and without the use of radiation) to perform visualization and quantitative analysis of lung tumor mobility. Specific aim is to demonstrate that our new MRI based system which enables the dynamic motion of the lung and lung tumor to be visualized in 4D (3D + time) allows improved derivation of clinical parameters for radiotherapy of lung tumor as compared to the current standard practice which uses 3D/4D CT. The hypothesis is that there will be no significant different in the clinical parameters used for radiotherapy derived using our MR based method as compared to current standard method which uses CT. The aim of the proposal will be achieved by imaging a cohort of lung cancer patients using MRI, processing of 4D MR images, and comparing the clinical parameters derived using MRI with that derived the current practice that uses CT. The clinical significance is that if the aim is achieved then use of the system will facilitate more effective radiotherapy of lung cancer patients with improved tumor delineation and lung tumor motion visualization without excess exposure to radiation during imaging for treatment planning, delivery and follow-ups. This new method could serve as an alternative/complement to CT.
kw: 4D MRI, Radiotherapy, Lung Imaging, Medical Image Processing, Lung Cancer, Medical Visualization

title: Handheld depth-selective Raman probe for optimizing and evaluating laser treatment of pigmentary disorders
abs: Pigmentary disorders constitute a highly prevalent dermatological problem in Asians. Laser treatment has emerged as a promising therapy for managing pigmentary disorders. To optimize laser treatment and evaluate the outcome of laser treatment, the depth and size of pigmented lesions and depth dependent photothermal damage need to be measured. Unfortunately such a method is not clinically available yet. Raman spectroscopy has demonstrated great potential for skin examination but traditional Raman measurements lack the capability of depth selective measurements. Confocal Raman spectroscopy has the capability of optical sectioning but the working depth range is too small.Our objective is to develop a handheld Raman probe and a progressive estimation method to achieve depth selective measurements in the skin. The method will be used to derive the depth and composition of pigmented lesions buried in the epidermis and dermis for optimal laser treatment. Our hypotheses are:Hypothesis 1. Depth selective Raman measurements can be achieved by steering the angles of light illumination and Raman detection and a progressive estimation method.Hypothesis 2. This technique can be used to estimate the depth of pigmented lesions and evaluate the outcome of laser therapy.The following aims will be pursued:Aim 1. Develop a handheld Raman probe for depth selective measurements.Aim 2. Characterize the effectiveness of the technique in skin tissue phantoms.Aim 3. Investigate the efficacy of the technique for estimating the depth of pigmented lesions in an in vivo human study and evaluating the treatment outcome in ex vivo skin samples.The depth dependent chemical composition will be obtained in both the epidermis and dermis non-destructively if successful. This unique information will assist dermatologists optimize laser parameters in laser therapy and evaluating treatment outcome. This technique may reduce the number of unwarranted skin biopsies and improve the management of pigmentary disorders.

title: Novel Evolutionary Approaches to Studying Host-Pathogen Interactions and Infectious Diseases
abs: Infectious disease is a major health burden and in great need of additional research. Advances in sequencing technology and genomic techniques provide the raw material and promise for accelerating discovery in all of biology, but methods to translate large data sets into specific knowledge of disease mechanisms are still few. My research applies molecular evolution and population genetics methods to large sequence data sets to understand mechanisms of pathogenesis and host-pathogen interactions. A key feature of my work is a close marriage between theory and experiment, so that in silico algorithms may be calibrated to generate relevant, specific hypotheses about in vivo processes. I use a mouse model of urinary tract infection (UTI) caused by uropathogenic Escherichia coli (UPEC) for these hybrid computational/experimental studies. Using a known UPEC virulence factor (FimH), I have shown that in silico analysis of positive selection is powerful and accurate enough to identify individual amino acids that are functional during in vivo infection. Furthermore, this analysis identifies mutations that are missed by other genetic, biochemical, epidemiological, and structural analyses. In the next 5-7 years, I will (i) prove the utility of my approach by elucidating the molecular mechanism of a novel FimH function discovered using positive selection analysis and by characterizing additional novel virulence factors for UTI; and (ii) complete a suite of methods that can be used to analyze evolutionary pressures on all parts of the genome including coding and non-coding sequences. My long term goal is to develop a complete, integrated, evolutionary analysis framework for translating sequence information into candidate therapeutic targets for UTI and other infectious diseases. A validated in silico framework that can identify key proteins and amino acids relevant to in vivo host-pathogen interactions will be especially valuable for emerging infectious diseases where experimental systems may be immature or nonexistent.

title: Glucose-evoked renal cell death and underlying molecular mechanisms: in relevance to the development of diabetic nephropathy
abs: Nephropathy which his one of the microvascular complications in types 1 and 2 diabetes is now the leading cause of end stage renal disease. It casts a great social economic burden on societies. Poor glycemic control, hypertension, dyslipidemia and genetic determinants are amongst the recognized risk factors. Possible interplays between environmental (metabolic and societal) factors and genetic components are also implicated. Despite the consensus on the major risk factors, very little is known about the ideology of diabetic nephropathy. More recently, apoptotic death of renal cells is increasingly recognized in the development of diabetic nephropathy. However, many critical issues remain to be addressed for a better understanding the roles of renal cell apoptosis in pathogenesis of nephropathy in diabetes. In the proposed pilot study, we aim to: 1. establish cell line models of renal cell (mesangial and proximal tubular cells) apoptosis evoked by high concentration of glucose, for investigations of the underlying molecular mechanisms. In this group of experiments, the sensitivity of the two renal cell lines towards glucose toxicity will be determined and compared. These can be achieved by determining cell survival assay rate and percentage of sub-G1 cells, using XTT and flow cytometry assays respectively; 2. investigate whether the polyol pathway (i.e., aldose reductase) and oxidative stress play their roles in the glucose-mediated renal cell apoptosis, aldose reductase inhibition, quantification and modification of reactive oxygen species; and 3. document globally candidate protein signal mediators involving in the glucose-triggered renal cell apoptotic death, through proteomic analysis. All the required techniques are established in my laboratory. Expected outcomes would demonstrate and compare sensitivities of mesangial and proximal tubular cells towards glucose-evoked apoptosis. Molecular analyses would assess roughly possible involvement of redox regulation, and identify some signal transduction proteins in the renal cell apoptosis. Thus, the pilot study would produce a phathophysiology-relevant experimental model for further IRG-based study of renal cell apoptosis and underlying molecular mechanisms, which might identify molecular probes for diagnostic and/or therapeutic development.
kw: Diabetic nephropathy, Glucose toxicity, Apoptosis, Functional proteomics, Cell signal transduction, Redox

title: Cell Therapy of Cancer
abs: Natural killer (NK) cell therapy of cancer has been limited by difficulty in obtaining sufficient numbers of NK cells, and by their weak cytotoxicity against certain tumors. My laboratory developed a method that allows the long-term expansion of human NK cells. We also developed methods for their genetic modification, thus enhancing their anti-cancer capacity. These methods have been adapted to large-scale conditions suitable for clinical cell therapy, leading to Phase I clinical trials currently open to patient accrual. Specific Aim 1 is to establish these methods in Singapore. We will then test the hypothesis that the anti-leukemic capacity of NK cells can be significantly enhanced through cellular engineering. We will determine whether suppression of inhibitory signals with RNA interference improves their cytotoxicity (Specific Aim 2), assess the effect of enforcing the expression of activating and co-stimulatory receptors (Specific Aim 3), and test the effect of transducing the IL-2 and IL-15 genes on NK cell survival and function in vivo (Specific Aim 4). Our long-term objective is to translate the most promising findings of this research into clinical trials. We intend to initiate these trials in Singapore within this funding cycle. The studies will rely on our unique and robust methods for NK cell expansion and transduction. Gains in specific NK cell cytotoxicity will be measured using established in vitro and in vivo models of leukemia and solid tumors. Approval by the US Food and Drug Administration of our methods, preliminary results demonstrating the feasibility of large-scale electroporation of NK, and our proven expertise in cell therapy trials lend credibility to this plan. If the proposed aims are met, there will be a better understanding of the mechanisms that regulate NK cell cytotoxicity, and new ways to enhance the efficacy of cell therapy of cancer.
kw: natural killer cells, acute myeloid leukemia, acute lymphoblastic leukemia, sarcoma, cellular engineering, gene therapy

title: Association of placental syncytiotrophoblast membrane micro-particles with maternal immune response in recurrent pregnancy loss.
abs: Recurrent pregnancy loss (RPL) is a perplexing clinical problem that affects approximately 2% of pregnancies and not only has a significant psychological impact on couples but also societal implications, particularly in Singapore with its declining birthrate. Although multiple etiologies for this devastating condition have been described, over one-half of the cases remain unexplained. Immunopathological studies of the placental bed in RPL have demonstrated decidual inflammation, perivillous and decidual fibrin deposition and thromboembolism in decidual vessels. While it is clear that inflammatory and thrombotic processes at the maternofetal interface are the final pathologic assault in most cases, the exact immunopathogenic mechanisms preceding this remain unclear. In normal pregnancy, trophoblast cells and syncytiotrophoblast membrane microparticles (STBMs) are spontaneously released from the placenta as a sign of normal placental physiologic turnover. Shedding of placental microparticles has been associated with systemic inflammatory response in pregnancy. However, specific changes with regard to its composition and function in adverse pregnancies associated with placental pathologies have not yet been reported.Cell-derived microparticles may represent novel pathways in short or long-distance paracrine transcellular signaling in vascular environment. There is mounting evidence to suggest that STBMs are potential contributors to altered systemic inflammatory responsiveness in normal and adverse pregnancies. However, to date, few studies have compared the inflammatory potential of placenta-derived purified STBMs generated from placentas of normal and adverse pregnancy outcomes.In this proposal, we aim to evaluate the cohort of women with RPL using a standardized protocol to characterise them into two main subgroups: (i) Autoimmune RPL (ii) Unexplained RPL (2) study the immunopathogenic role of STBMs in these women compared to normal pregnancies. We hypothesize that STBMs in RPL are capable of more robust immunomodulation compared to normal, healthy pregnancies. This knowledge may allow for novel diagnostic or interventional approaches.
kw: Recurrent Pregnancy Loss, Microparticle, Placenta, Immunomodulation

title: Statistical Methods for Secondary Analysis of Nested Case-Control Data
abs: Nested case-control design is very popular epidemiological studies. Unlike cohort studies, exposure measurements are only needed for a subset of controls. This makes this design very attractive when exposure is expensive. However, sampling for nested case-control design is conditional on time of disease onsets. The conditional sampling means that once collected under one disease as main disease of interest, nested case-control data cannot be used to analyze other diseases, even if information for other diseases are available (see BACKGROUND). This is a major drawback since often researchers cannot afford to 'waste' the time and budget resources they allocated to measure the expensive exposure and this is when the ability to reuse is very important. Salim et al (2009) showed that is is possibl to reuse nested case-control data for secondary analysis of another outcome. Their approach, based on weighted likelihood, was demostrated using stimulated and real datasets. Although this method opens exciting avenue, a lot of practical questions on whether reusing nested case-control data is feasible, remains. Questions such as: Can we predict the study power and statistical efficiency when reusing old nested case-control data? Do we need to collect additional new data at all? need to be answered. If we can identify factors under which efficiency/power gain will be good, then researchers can use these criteria before deciding on reanalyzing the old data. Also, it is still possible to develop a novel semiparametric approach that promises much greater statistical effeciency than method in Salim et al (2009). These more efficient methods will give more powerful options to researchers when reusing nested case-control data. Finally, these methods need to be made available as use-friendly software that will be freely available to researchers worldwide. We have started preliminary works that show promising signs. Funding is requested to continue this work.
kw: Novel statistical methods, Study power, Study design, Open-source software, Cost-efficiency, Collateral breast cancer

title: Phase II Trial of Oxaliplatin/ Adriamycin/ 5 Fluorouracil in Continuous Infusion/ Interferon ?-2b (OXAFI) combination as Neo-Adjuvant Therapy in Metastatic and Locally Advanced Unresectable Hepatocellular Carcinoma. AHCC0 protocol 08
abs: Aim: The specific primary aim of this phase II trial is to assess the response rate of the combination oxaliplatin/adriamycin/5 fluorouracil continuous infusion/interferon a-2b (OXAFI) in metastatic and unresectable non-metastatic hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Hypothesis: Conventional chemotherapeutic agents when administered at their maximum tolerated dose (MTD) levels may allow restarting of angiogenesis due to the rest commonly introduced between successive conventional cycles to allow marrow recovery. We hypothesized that the response rate of patients with HCC can be optimized by the administration of a combination of cytotoxics and immunotherapy in a metronomic fashion to enhance anti-angiogenic effect with minimal toxicities.Methodology: Patients with unresectable HCC will be treated with intravenous oxaliplatin (30mg/m2) and doxorubicin (20mg/m2) given on days 1, 8 and 15 in a 28-day cycle, a daily continuous infusion of fluorouracil (200mg/m2) and subcutaneous interferon alfa-2b 5 MU administered thrice weekly. Surgery for non-metastatic tumors will be contemplated after every 2 cycles based on radiological evaluation of response. Treatment is administered up to a maximum of 6 cycles in total. Preliminary results and study approach: In our pilot experience involving 19 patients, the best response was 1 complete pathologic response, 6 partial responses with 4 conversions to resectability after OXAFI. The median follow-up was 14 months (range 2-23 months). Median survival has not been reached yet. In view of this favorable experience, we have decided to initiate this multicentre study with the inclusion of 2 overseas centers under the auspices of the Asia Pacific Hepatocellular Carcinoma Trials Group (AHCC 08) with multicentre trial management by SCRI to help achieve accrual target of 54 patients. Clinical significance: Use of OXAFI guided by tumour genomic analysis and angiogenesis factors profiling will be a major advancement in HCC management in the individualization of a potentially highly efficacious therapy.
kw: Hepatocellular carcinoma, Phase II, Interferon, Metronomic, Angiogenesis, Multicentre trial

title: Deciphering the interaction between dengue immune complex and monocytes in antibody-mediated immunity and disease enhancement.
abs: The global spread of the dengue virus (DENV) has put nearly 3 billion people at risk of potentially life-threateninginfections annually. The presence of four antigenically distinct serotypes complicates vaccine development.Furthermore, the risk of severe dengue increases with waning levels of maternal antibodies in infants. Theseindicate that both antibody specificity and concentration are important determinants of immunity. Recent structuralstudies have demonstrated the stoichiometric requirements for virus neutralization with different monoclonalantibodies. However, how immune complexes interact with monocytes, whether in neutralizing or enhancingquantities of antibody are poorly understood. Using an in vitro model with a mouse-human chimeric antibody andTHP-1 cells, we demonstrated in our preliminary studies that antibody concentration has important effects on Fcreceptor (FcR) function. High antibody concentration inhibited FcR-mediated uptake, while immune complexesformed with lower antibody concentration were rapidly trafficked into the LAMP-1 compartments, preferentially viaFcRI instead of FcRII. Moreover, convalescent sera obtained following DENV infection neutralized the homologousserotypes at concentrations that permitted FcR-mediated uptake but heterologous serotypes only at concentrationsthat inhibited FcR-mediated uptake. This proposal thus aims to extend our preliminary work and (1) elucidate themechanism in which immune complexes with high antibody concentration inhibit FcR function, (2) identifysusceptibility or co-factors of antibody-dependent enhancement of dengue infection as only a small subset of THP-1 cells take up the immune complex even with enhancing antibodies, (3) determine the pathways taken by immunecomplexes formed with either neutralizing or enhancing antibodies and finally, (4) validate the clinical utility of ourobservation as a surrogate marker for immunity. We envisage that by using a triad of antibodies, virus andmonocytes, all of which play key roles in DENV infection, new light on dengue immunity and pathogenesis will beshed that boosts vaccine development and improved case management.
kw: dengue, neutralization, immune complex, monocytes, FC receptors, antibody-dependent enhancement

title: Clinical Phenotypes of Persistent Rhinitis in Young Children (0-5years) and the Role of Respiratory Viral Infections– A Prospective Evaluation of a Birth Cohort
abs: Background: Persistent rhinitis in young children (<5 years old) is a poorly defined but a common clinical problem. Based on population surveys in Singapore, a significant proportion of young children below 6 years of age (up to 42%) suffer from rhinitis that is not related to a cold. Although likely heterogenous in etiology, often times they have been labeled with allergic rhinitis and may therefore betreated inappropriately.Hypothesis and Aim: We hypothesize that persistent rhinitis in young children has a heterogeneousetiology with a varied clinical outcome, and that respiratory virus infections in early life influence theclinical outcome of rhinitis in those predisposed. The aims of this study are to define the phenotypes of early childhood rhinitis, understand the natural history, and identify risk factors (including viral infectionsin early life) and co-morbidities associated with this common problem.Methods: The Singapore population-based GUSTO birth cohort (1,200 newborns) will be employed forthis rhinitis cohort study. To define the phenotypes of persistent early childhood rhinitis, subjects withsignificant problems of rhinitis will be actively identified prospectively using a simple questionnairesurvey at each home visit (6 times in first year and twice yearly subsequently), as well as through atelephone hotline and email provided to parents. These subjects would be followed with a detailedsurvey by a team of nurses and in the clinic by the paediatrician, and if indicated, the otolaryngologist.Nasal swabs for cytology and molecular studies for respiratory viruses (first 2 years) will be taken atclinic visits. Allergy skin prick testing to relevant inhalant allergens will be carried out at 18 m and 3years. To evaluate the role of early life viral infections, all 1200 subjects (rhinitis group and controlgroup) will undergo scheduled nasal swabs for respiratory viruses at 3weeks, and at 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 and18 months. The data will be collated into a web-based database for data acquisition and analyzedstatistically for prevalence, etiology, risk factors and outcome.Clinical Significance: This will be the first large scale prospective population-based birth cohort studyon the early predictors of persistent rhinitis in young children. It will fill the chasm in our knowledge onrhinitis in children below 5 years of age and impact on its evidence based management, which iscurrently lacking.
kw: Rhinitis, Allergy, Respiratory viruses, Childhood, Hygiene hypothesis, Clinical phenotypes

title: Development and application of sustained drug release technology for the delivery of nucleic acid molecules for the prevention of post-operative scarring in glaucoma.
abs: Glaucoma is the commonest cause of irreversible blindness worldwide. The number of people affectedwith glaucoma is predicted to be 79.6 million by 2020, of which over 8 million will suffer from bilateralblindness. Elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) is the most important modifiable risk factor for thedevelopment and progression of glaucomatous optic neuropathy resulting in blindness. Filteringsurgery is reserved for cases poorly controlled on topical medications. The post-operative scarringresponse remains the final barrier to achieving long-term surgical success. Current anti-fibrotics in useare not ideal. They are associated with a life-long risk of blinding complications.The project aims to investigate the therapeutic ocular delivery of small interfering (si)-RNA by use ofsustained release technology for inhibiting post-operative scarring following glaucoma surgery.We hypothesize that a therapeutically effective approach to reduce post-operative subconjunctivalscarring is to firstly target the action of the effector cell (fibroblast), by silencing a key gene(s)responsible for the development of fibrosis. Secondly, delivery of such a molecule(s) will requiresophisticated delivery technology, for which the application of non-viral delivery platforms to deliversuch molecules in vivo will be applied. Sustained release is mandatory to provide a continual release ofthe inhibitor molecule to effectively attenuate the post-operative wound healing response which canpersist several weeks to months.Subconjunctival delivery of siRNA will be evaluated using specific vectors to determine the most effective one for such route of delivery. The gene silencing capability and delivery efficiency will beestablished in vitro as well as in vivo by using established animal models of glaucoma filtration surgery.The identification and development of a sustained delivery system to inhibit post-operativesubconjunctival scarring in vivo will not only demonstrated the potential application of siRNAtechnology as a therapeutic agent in glaucoma, but also contribute major advances in sustained ocular drug delivery research.
kw: glaucoma, wound healing, liposomes, siRNA, polyelectrolyte capsules, SPARC

title: Determining The Relative Importance of Modifiable Factors Affecting Survival From Out-Of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest In Singapore And The Cost-Effectiveness Of Strategies To Improve Outcomes.
abs: BackgroundOut of Hospital Cardiac Arrest (OHCA) is a global health concern. Survival rates in Singapore are low (2%) compared to USA or Europe (up to 40%). DesignA prospective, international, multi-center cohort study of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest in Singapore and across the Asia-Pacific. The cost-effectiveness analysis for this study will be focused on Singapore’s Emergency Medical Services (EMS) system. ObjectivesWe aim to identify the relative importance of modifiable factors affecting survival from OHCA. We will then derive the most cost-effective strategy to improve survival from OHCA in Singapore. This will be based on a comparison of 5 competing (although not exclusive) strategies targeting major systemic and modifiable factors for OHCA survival. The large sample size and international nature of the study provides a unique opportunity for analysis of preventable risk factors for OHCA and systemic predictors of survival. Identifying the relative incremental cost-effectiveness of modifiable factors for OHCA survival will allow prioritization and selection of 5 pre-identified competing interventional strategies (namely: increasing bystander cardio-pulmonary resuscitation (CPR), public access defibrillation, decreasing EMS response times, developing advanced EMS life support, specialized Cardiac Arrest Centers).MethodsData will be collected from emergency dispatch records, ambulance patient case notes, Emergency Department (ED) and in-hospital records. All completed data will then be collected and sent to the Study Co-ordination Center (Singapore) for data management using Electronic Data Capture (EDC).Our required sample size for the study is 13,447 OHCA patients and Singapore will contribute 1,000 cases. The relative effectiveness of the interventions associated with each of the 5 strategies will be determined. A cost analysis for the various strategies will be conducted to determine the incremental cost-effectiveness in Singapore for each strategy. EligibilityAll OHCA patients presenting to EMS ‘995’ or Emergency Departments during the study period as confirmed by the absence of pulse, unresponsiveness and apnea.
kw: emergency medical services, out of hospital, cardiac arrest, cost of effectiveness, resuscitation

title: The Role of Immune Monitoring in Predicting Acute and Chronic Complications Among Renal Transplant Recipients
abs: Renal transplantation is the best treatment option for end stage renal disease patients. Significant advances have been made resulting in the reduction of early acute allograft rejection rates. However, the inability to accurately gauge the level of immunosuppression post transplantation or to detect ongoing subclinical allograft injury has resulted in late allograft losses due to opportunistic infections, malignancies and chronic rejections. This may account for the lack of improvement in long-term allograft survival in spite of the initial success. In multiple retrospective studies in the transplant literature, it has been shown that patients who experience recurrent acute rejections and have shorter allograft survival time demonstrate enhanced donor specific alloreactivity on ex vivo assays, either in the form of increased interferon gamma (IFN gamma) producing cells on ELISPOT assay or increase circulating donor specific anti HLA antibodies. Hypothesis: We hypothesize that prospective immune monitoring of post transplant patients will allow the identification of patients at risk for acute or chronic complications prior to the onset of clinical manifestation. Specific Aims: We will prospectively monitor the cellular and humoral immune status of transplant patients using the ELISPOT assay to detect IFN gamma producing alloreactive cells and the ELISA assays to detect donor specific anti HLA antibodies at pre-specified time interval post transplantation. Specific Aim 1: Cellular and humoral profiles of patients with acute complications will be compared to that of stable transplant patients. Specifc Aim 2: Cellular and humoral profiles of patients with chronic complications will be compared to that of stable transplant patients.Conclusion and Clinical Significance: The ability to prospectively identify and correct over/under immunosuppressed states prior to the onset of complications and permanent end organ damage may result in improved long-term patient and organ allograft survival.
kw: Renal Transplantation, Acute Allograft Rejection, Immune Monitoring, Chronic Allograft Nephropathy

title: Immunology and immunopathology of influenza A infection
abs: In early 2009, a novel variant of influenza A (influenza A/California/7/2009) emerged in southern California that was of swine flu origin (S-OIV). This strain of was identified as the cause of an epidemic of respiratory disease in Mexico that has since spread worldwide and is now a pandemic. Mortality to is greater than with previously circulating seasonal Influenza and appears to particularly target asthmatics. Understanding the pathological processes induced by this virus and its relationship to other influenza viruses is important for the successful management of influenza with this strain of flu and other emerging influenzas. To this end, we propose to adapt our current in vivo model for influenza A infection that employs the H1N1/PR8/34 virus to include influenza A/CALIFORNIA/7/2009 and recent Singapore H1N1 isolates from 2008. We will focus on the dendritic cells that take up and present the virus and the CD8/CD4 T cell response they elicit. Our preliminary data suggest that lung DCs have a dichotomy of function. Both CD11c+CD11b-CD103+ and CD11c+CD11b+CD103- DCs take up DiD labelled influenza, but the former migrates to the draining LN and initiates CD8 T cell expansion while the latter remains in the lung. We have optimized lethal and non-lethal in vivo infection models employing 1,1’-dioctadecyl-3,3,3’,3’-tetramethylindodicarbocyanine (DiD) labelled and unlabelled influenza A/H1N1/PR8/34 virus in C57BL6 and BALB/c mice. In this project we propose to: (i) compare the immune response to sub-lethal and lethal infection with influenza A/H1N1/PR8/34, Singapore 2008 H1N1 and A/CALIFORNIA/7/2009; (ii) investigate influenza uptake and presentation by lung dendritic cells and the cellular and molecular events associated with the delivery, processing and presentation of influenza antigens; (iii) determine the response to the different strains of influenza in normal and asthmatic mice; (iv) determine the potential of immunomodulatory drugs and in-house novel monoclonal antibodies as potential therapeutics for influenza infection.
kw: Influenza A, Immunopathology, Asthma, Cytopathology, Pandemic, Immune regulation

title: A phase II trial of preoperative concurrent chemotherapy and intensity modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) in locally advanced rectal cancer
abs: INTRODUCTIONFor locally advanced rectal cancer, preoperative chemoradiotherapy followed by surgery has been shown to have an improvement in local control, decreased acute treatment toxicity and increase rates of sphincter preservation compared with postoperative chemoradiotherapy.A complete pathological response (pCR) after preoperative treatment for rectal cancers is associated with an improved outcomeResults from Phase II studies show that radiotherapy dose escalation correlates with increased pCR in locally advanced rectal cancers treated with preoperative chemoradiotherapyIntensity Modulated Radiotherapy (IMRT) is a highly conformal radiotherapy technique that has the potential to deliver a higher radiation dose to the primary tumour whilst sparing the critical structures such as the femoral heads, bladder and bowel.AIMThe aim is to improve the rates of pCR, and hence local control and overall survival by the use of dose escalated chemoIMRT in patients with locally advanced rectal cancer.HYPOTHESISThe hypothesis is that dose escalated IMRT to a dose of 55Gy in 25# to primary tumour concurrent with oral capecitabine results in an improved pCR from 8% (German rectal cancer trial) to 25%. METHODOLOGYThe patients from both the NUH and TTSH would be enrolled.Planned sample size would be 53 patients. Patients will be treated with preoperative concurrent chemoIMRT - Radiotherapy to a dose of 55 Gy/25 Fractions concurrent with oral Capecitabine. TME will be performed 8 weeks later.ENDPOINTSPrimary - pCR ratesSecondary - Treatment Toxicity, Downstaging rate, Sphincter preservation rate, DFS at 2 yrs.SIGNIFICANCEIf the study shows radiotherapy dose escalation improves pathological response rates with acceptable toxicties, then there is a potential for improvement of clinical outcome.This is potentially practice changing and can be a nidus for further research at improving pCR rates including preoperative chemoradiotherapy with combination chemotherapy or high dose rate brachytherapy boost.
kw: Intensity Modulated Radiotherapy, Dose escalation, Rectal cancer, Locally advanced

title: Suppression of AMPK as a novel cancer chemotherapeutic strategy via inhibition of autophagy
abs: At present, modulation of autophagy becomes an attractive strategy in cancer prevention and therapy. Suppression of autophagy has been found to sensitize cancer cells to cell death induced by cancer therapeutics. AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) is one of the key molecules responsive to cellular energy status and activation of AMPK leads to suppression of mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) and then induction of autophagy. Moreover, DNA alkylating agents are an important group of cancer chemotherapeutics and autophagy has been implicated in their therapeutic effects. Therefore, the main objective of this proposed study is to establish AMPK as the molecular target for modulation of autophagy and cell death induced by DNA alkylating agents, based on the hypothesis that inhibition of AMPK would sensitizes DNA alkylating agents-induced cell death in human cancer cells via suppression of autophagy. The specific aims of this study include:1.To determine the role of the AMPK-mTOR pathway in autophagy induced by DNA alkylating agents in human cancers 2.To evaluate the pro-survival function of autophagy in cell death induced by DNA alkylating agents3.To synthesize specific activity-based probes (ABPs) for detecting AMPK enzymatic activity in situ, as well as chemical inhibitors as novel autophagy suppressors4.To test the sensitization effect of AMPK inhibitors on cell death induced by DNA alkylating agents on both short-term cell viability assay and long term colony formation assay5.To test the efficacy the combined therapy in a nude mouse xenograft modelThis is a typical cross-disciplinary research project combining the strength of two research groups in biology and chemistry, respectively. Data from this proposed study will not only advance the understanding of AMPK in modulation of autophagy and cell death, but also help develop novel AMPK inhibitors as chemosensitizers to overcome the resistance, in particularly in those cancers with a deficient apoptosis machinery, to DNA alkylating agents.
kw: Autophagy, AMPK, DNA Alkylating Agents, Cancer, Chemotherapy, Sensitization

title: The purification and use of FGF-2-binding heparan sulfate to increase the healing of critical-sized bone defects
abs: Although millions of fractures occur annually, and the majority heals satisfactorily, 10-15% go on to either delayed union or nonunion. For such cases, a bioactive agent to stimulate bone formation, not only for the treatment of fracture healing, but also for other osteolytic diseases that result in substantial bone loss is needed. Importantly however, the use of growth factors is currently hindered by 1) their cost, 2) their rapid clearance rate and 3) their susceptibility to proteolytic degradation. It is possible to increase the half-life and thus sustain the bioactivity of growth factors through their association with heparan sulfate (HS) glycosaminoglycan sugars. Moreover, HS variants that strongly bind specific growth factors can be purified using well-established chromatographic techniques, so creating growth factor-binding HS variants. Thus we propose to induce bone repair in rat calvarial bone defects by delivering FGF-2-binding HS to the bone injury site. By doing so, we aim to protect endogenous FGF-2 from extracellular proteases, as well as from pH and thermal changes, so enhancing its activity and downstream signaling, and ultimately stimulating local bone progenitor cells to grow and repair the defect. We also postulate that an FGF2-specific HS variant will also significantly reduce the dose of growth factors required to repair the bone, as heparan sulfates have been shown to enhance FGF-2 signaling.This research is particularly important, as it will reduce fracture-healing times and improve healing success rates and significantly lower health care costs, whilst providing a better quality of life for patients due to the reduced length of hospitalization and/or on-going treatment.
kw: MSCs, Bone, Heparan Sulfate, Osteogenesis, FGF-2, Fracture repair

title: Evaluation of the anti-cancer function of autophagy in a zebrafish liver cancer model
abs: Autophagy refers to an evolutionarily conserved process in which intracellular proteins and organelles are sequestered in autophagosomes and subsequently degraded by lysosomal enzymes. At present, there is accumulating evidence supporting the notion that autophagy serves as an anti-cancer mechanism in the process of tumorigenesis. However, the anti-cancer function of autophagy has not been tested in a primary cancer model. On the other hand, zebrafish has gained its popularity as a model organism in cancer research. The Co-Investigator’s lab has recently established a zebrafish liver cancer model by inducible overexpression of Xmrk, an EGFR orthologue in zebrafish. Therefore, the main objective of this study is to test the hypothesis that autophagy plays an anti-cancer function and activation of autophagy will suppress and inhibition of autophagy will promote cancer development in Xmrk transgenic zebrafish. The specific aims of the study include: 1.To create a double transgenic line with liver-specific EGFP-LC3 expression in the Xmrk-expressing transgenic fish2.To examine the autophagy flux level in zebrafish liver in the tumorigenesis process induced by over-expression of Xmrk, an EGFR orthologue in zebrafish liver 3.To investigate the effect of autophagy induction on liver cancer in the Xmrk zebrafish liver cancer model4.To investigate the effect of autophagy suppression on liver cancer in the Xmrk zebrafish liver cancer modelData from the above proposed experiments will provide evidence for the first time showing the anti-cancer function of autophagy in a primary cancer model in vivo. Such finding will not only significantly advance our understanding about the anti-cancer function of autophagy, also lay a solid function for further studies on the role of autophagy in cancer development in humans.
kw: autophagy, Liver cancer, Xmrk, zebrafish, rapamycin, TOR

title: Identifying Potential Biomarkers Functionally Linked to t(4;14) Multiple Myeloma Using Plasma Membrane Proteomics
abs: Multiple myeloma (MM) is the second most common haematological malignancy in adults and is currently incurable. It is characterized by recurrent chromosomal translocations. Patients with t(4;14)(p16;q32) have the worst prognosis, although the basis for this poor prognosis is unknown. MMSET, identified by its fusion to the IgH locus in t(4;14)-associated MM, is universally overexpressed in t(4;14) MM. Knockdown studies demonstrated that MM cells rely on MMSET expression forclonogenic growth and tumorigenicity in vivo. The plasma membrane is of particular interest as a source of novel biomarkers, as it may present targets for small molecule or antibody based therapies and may act as a source of circulating markers shed into the general circulation. The aim of this study is to identify potential cell surface biomarkers functionally linked to t(4;14)-associated MM. We will knock down MMSET expression with MMSET shRNA and generate a cell line pair from KMS11, a t(4;14) MM cell line. Using stable isotope labelling by amino acids in cell culture (SILAC) followed by enrichment of plasma membrane proteins by cell surface biotinylation/avidin-affinity chromatography and quantitative analysis by GeLC-MS/MS, MMSET associated differences in plasma membrane proteins will be analysed. The potential biomarkers will be verified in t(4:14) MM cell linesand MMSET transfected cell line by western-blot. Then, we will validate the potential biomarkers in clinical samples of t(4;14)-associated MM by western-blot and immunohistochemistry (IHC). Last, the role of these proteins in clonogenic growth, tumor invasion and formation will be determined by knockdown studies. This study may discovery novel diagnostic or therapeutic targets for t(4;14) MM.
kw: MMSET, Multiple Myeloma, Proteomics, SILAC

title: Structure and functional interactions of translational factors with ribosome by X-ray crystallography
abs: The ribosome is the large molecular machine that uses an mRNA template to synthesize proteins, in a process referred to as translation. Rapid protein synthesis in bacteria requires the four GTPase factors: initiation factor IF2, elongation factor EF-Tu and EF-G, and peptide release factor RF3. These factors catalyze all major steps of mRNA translation in a GTP-dependent manner. Little is understood about their molecular interactions with the ribosome, and what they actually do to help the ribosome through the translation cycle, due to lacking structural details of factors bound the ribosome. In all previously reported crystal forms of the ribosome (both E. coli and T. thermophilus), a lattice contact with ribosomal protein L9 from a neighboring molecule would result in a steric clash with a bound GTPase factor. Very recently, I discovered a new crystal form of the 70S ribosome by use of a L9-deletion ribosome that eliminates the steric clash excluding GTPase factors in all previously published crystal forms. Compared to a huge ribosome, small change of the GTPase factors has little influence on crystallization, discovery of this new crystal form being compatible with GTPase factors binding is a big breakthrough. Using this new crystal form, the structures of EF-G and EF-Tu bound to ribosome for the first were determined (publication list 3 & 4). Based on these results, further understanding of EF-G function in translation, including its structure in complex with the ribosome in the hybrid state, prior to GTP hydrolysis and translocation as well as in post-termination complex with ribosome recycling factor, will be performed by X-ray crystallography. Using this crystal form, try to determine the structures of IF2, RF3, and elongation factor SelB bound to ribosome is also the topic in the proposed research.
kw: structure;function;ribosome;tranlational factor;protein synthesis;fusidic acid

title: The Mechanisms of Chromosomal Instability in Human Cancers and Development of Novel Anti-Mitotic Cancer Therapies
abs: First observed over 110 years ago, abnormal chromosome content, also known as aneuploidy, is the most common characteristic of human solid tumors. Indeed, in contrast to normal cells, various cancer cell lines show frequent gain and loss of whole chromosomes, known as chromosomal instability (CIN). The mitotic phase of the cell cycle is the period for equal segregation of replicated sister chromatids and cytokinesis to generate two genetically identical daughter cells. Although the mechanisms how human cancer cells establish such an altered chromosomal state remains unknown, an error in a mitotic process is considered as a direct cause of aneuploidy and CIN. Therefore, to ensure error-free chromosome segregation, cells have evolved complex regulatory networks called the mitotic spindle checkpoint. However, the molecular mechanisms how this checkpoint maintains chromosome stability in normal cells and whether its deregulation is a cause of tumorigenesis remain unclear. Thus, together with our recent findings that the essential components in the mitotic checkpoint are also important for regulating cytokinesis, this proposal is designed to study the molecular mechanisms how this checkpoint machinery coordinates the mitotic checkpoint with cytokinesis and to determine the effects of its deregulation on CIN and tumorigenesis. For anti-cancer therapeutics, interrupting a mitotic progress of tumor cells using anti-microtubule toxins (e. g. taxol) is one of the most successful strategies to treat human cancers. Furthermore, the advance in molecularly targeted drug discovery has facilitated the identification of a new generation of anti-mitotic therapy that targets proteins with specific function in mitosis. In this study, we propose a novel anti-mitotic target in order to improve the efficacy of current anti-mitotic therapeutics in clinic. We will explore the mechanisms of which inhibition of the mitotic target proposed in this study induces a synergistic mitotic cell death of human cancers in combination with current anti-mitotic drugs in clinic. Thus, we believe that this proposal is aimed not only to improve our academic knowledge basis, but also to provide significant economic potential.
kw: Mitosis;Chromosome instability;Mitotic Checkpoint;Anti-Mitotic Cancer Therapy;Mitotic Cell Death;Mitotic Kinesin

title: Light- and pH-Operated Mechanized Nanoparticles as Controllable Drug Delivery Systems
abs: Mechanized nanoparticles consisting of supramolecular machines attached to the surfaces of mesoporous silica nanoparticles will be prepared to store drug molecules and release them controllably upon light irradiation or pH activation. Two supramolecular machines will be fabricated, i.e., (1) alpha-cyclodextrin rings will be threaded onto the trans-azobenzene-containing stalks on the surfaces of the nanoparticles to form the [2]rotaxanes, thus the trans-cis photoisomerization of the azobenzene units will lead to the association/dissociation of the cyclodextrin rings with the azobenzene units, resulting in controllable storage and release of the drug molecules upon photoirradiation, and (2) cucurbit[6]uril rings will encircle tethered triammonium stalks on the surfaces of the nanoparticles to form the [2]rotaxanes, and the position of the rings can be tuned to respond under specific pH conditions through chemical modification of the stalks, thus the mechanized nanoparticles will be able to contain drug molecules within nanopores at neutral pH levels and then release them once the pH is lowered. Furthermore, such mechanized nanoparticles will be used to explore their applications as drug delivery vehicles in biological systems, in order to transport therapeutic anticancer drugs into various types of human cancer cells under a controllable manner.

title: Involvement of the forebrain theta network of structures in acute and chronic pain
abs: The proposal will test the hypothesis that attenuation of synaptic transmission with manipulation of GABAA- and nicotinic-receptor mechanisms in the medial septum (MS) and the supramammillary (SuM) nucleus, respectively, modulates pain behaviors, associated hippocampal activity and spinal plasticity in acute and chronic rat models of pain. The spinal plasticity is proposed to be a basis of persistent/chronic pain. While, the MS and SuM comprise part of the neural network that mediate theta wave activity that reflects rhythmic oscillations of hippocampal CA1 neurons in processing of noxious information. Theta wave activity is affected by GABAergic- and cholinergic-receptor mechanisms in the MS and SuM, respectively, though the role of the regions in pain is unclear. The present proposal will investigate the following in behaving rat: One, change in pain-induced hippocampal activity, behaviors and spinal plasticity following microinjection of GABAA receptor agonist/allosteric modulator into MS. Two, effects of microinjection of the GABAA receptor antagonist, bicuculline, and the nicotinic receptor antagonist, mecamylamine, into MS and SuM, respectively, on animal behaviors and spinal molecular plasticity in models of pain.Additionally, the proposal will examine whether nicotinic receptor mechanisms in SuM modulate the transfer of noxious information to the septal-hippocampus and, moreover, modulate spinal nociceptive transmission through these structures. In this context the proposal will investigate the following: Three, effect of intra-SuM mecamylamine on hippocampal nociceptive information processing. Four, effect of attenuation of theta generation with inactivation of MS on the modulation of spinal nociceptive reflexes by activation of the SuM with microinjection of the nicotinic agonist, nicotine. On successful conclusion, the study will show that the theta-network structures in the forebrain are a basis of both acute and chronic pain. Furthermore, the evidence will suggest a forebrain basis for the analgesic role of drugs that affect GABAergic and cholinergic receptor mechanisms

title: Novel Approaches to Promote Vascular Regeneration and Tissue Healing in Orthopaedic Surgery Via Biomaterial Functionalization
abs: One challenging aspect of musculoskeletal healing and regeneration is the engineering of implants that can incorporate the ability to enhance revascularization around a region with poor blood supply, in order to enhance healing potential. Implant success and tissue integration is highly dependent on the crucial role of blood supply in driving bone and tissue repair. Therapeutic application by delivery of angiogenic growth factors to localized sites is a promising approach in treating avascular conditions, which are commonly encountered in ageing and trauma. Using chemical modification techniques, we aim to functionalize metal substrates and biodegradable polymeric suture materials with proangiogenic (vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF)) and promaturing (angiopoietin-1 (ANG1) and angiopoietin-2 (ANG2)) factors, to achieve consistent and constant localized activity of growth factors. These functionalized materials would accelerate tissue regeneration crucial to the healing process in conditions like avascular necrosis and poor fracture healing. Such a strategy would have advantages over other approaches that utilize angiogenic growth factor adsorption or entrapment in matrices, which may have problems with factor retention.Both in vitro and in vivo models will be used to access the biological activities of the immobilized growth factors. We will assay these modified materials using both in vitro and in vivo models for angiogenetic biological activity. Assays will include cell adhesion, proliferation, and in vitro angiogenesis models, as well as in vivo rabbit models of vascular formation. Chemical composition and surface topographies of the substrates will be investigated. This project incorporates novel aspects of research, investigating the synergistic effects of combinations of VEGF, ANG1 and ANG2 on angiogenesis and vascularization as applied to functionalized biomaterials. In addition, we will also explore novel approaches to the functionalization of bioabsorbable materials, such as sutures, that do not compromise their mechanical integrity while allowing targeted delivery of bioactive molecules to surgical sites.
kw: Biomaterials, Vascularization, Orthopaedic Implant, Regeneration, Functionalization, VEGF

title: Identification of cell-associated and soluble mediators that modulate the inflammatory microenvironment in classical Hodgkin Lymphoma
abs: Classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) is a unique malignant lymphoma of B-cell origin in which the malignant Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg (HRS) cells form only a very small minority of the cells in the involved lymph nodes (LN). The majority of the lesional tissue is composed of inflammatory cells of many different types. The disease arises in a single LN and spreads to adjacent nodes, probably via lymphatics. Associated with the disease are a variety of systemic symptoms similar to those present in other benign inflammatory conditions. The extent of LN involvement and the presence (or absence) of such systemic symptoms are both of prognostic importance. CHL offers a unique possibility of studying the pathogenesis of inflammation, both locally and systemically. Although we know that the malignant cells must be responsible for causing the inflammatory infiltrate and the systemic symptoms, the mechanisms by which the malignant cells cause these changes are not well understood. In this proposal entitled “Identification of cell-associated and soluble mediators that modulate the inflammatory microenvironment in classical Hodgkin Lymphoma”, we propose to (1) examine the role of VEGF in endothelial cell activation and its contribution to the recruitment of the inflammatory infiltrate in cHL; and (2) identify the costimulatory or coinhibitory molecules found on HRS cells that may be involved in the differentiation of Tregs incHL. Our working hypothesis is that HRS cells express growth factors (e.g. VEGF) and costimulatory molecules (ICOSL and CD137) to regulate the phenotypes of the cells present in the lesion to provide a conducive microenvironment for their survival in cHL. Understanding the mediators produced by HRS cells and the mechanisms involved will allow us to design and produce new medications that will be helpful in alleviating inflammation, both locally and systemically.
kw: Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma, immunomodulation, Regulatory T cells, Adhesion molecules, VEGF, Endothelial cells

title: Identification of Prognostic Biomarkers for Hepatocellular Carcinoma
abs: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the most common primary cancer of the liver, responsible for approximately one million deaths each year. In Singapore, HCC ranks as the 4th most common malignancy in males, and is the 2nd leading cause of cancer deaths.Prognosis determination and indication for treatment are critical in the clinical management of HCC patients. There is no information that reliably stratifies HCC patients into groups with respect to prognosis. This information is crucial because the natural course of early HCC is unknown and its progression to intermediate and advanced HCC can be quite diverse. Some early stage HCC patients enjoy disease-free survival whilst others suffer aggressive tumours relapse to Stage 4 metastatic cancer within a year. Biomarkers with the ability to identify early stage HCC patients who are at higher risk of recurrence are thus urgently needed to guide surgical and chemotherapeutic treatment decisions. In this study, we will be applying high throughput, state-of-the-art proteomics technologies for the discovery of these prognostic markers for HCC.Proteomics profiling of HCC tumour tissues and autologous sera will be carried out to identify proteins that can distinguish between 2 groups of Stage 1 HCC patients with non-aggressive and aggressive tumours that lead to either disease-free survival or rapid progression of disease, respectively. Proteins that are found differentially expressed represent prognostic biomarkers that can aid clinicians in identifying early stage HCC patients at high risk of recurrence, predicting patient’s survival and stratifying them for prospective treatments. Our preliminary results showed that aggressive tumours of relapse HCC patients exhibited a more enhanced “Warburg effect” as compared to non-relapse patients. Following subsequent clinicopathological validation, further insights into the roles of these prognostic biomarkers in determining tumour aggressiveness will lead to the development of new drugs / therapies to halt HCC progression.
kw: Liver Cancer, Recurrence, Biomarkers, Prognosis, HCC Progression, Proteomics

title: Linking cell-cell adhesion with the actin cytoskeleton: Combining genetics and mechano-manipulations to discover novel adaptors in cadherin-based adhesion.
abs: Cell adhesion is at the heart of being multicellular. Mechanical links between cells and with the matrix are critical for cells to change shape and move, fundamental processes underlying embryonic morphogenesis, wound healing and cancer metastasis. Interactions with the extracellular matrix and with other cells are mediated by integrin and cadherin receptors, respectively. On the inside of the cell these receptors connect, via a network of adaptor proteins, to the actin cytoskeleton. Very little is known about the adaptor network of cadherin mediated adhesion beyond alpha- and beta- catenin. The goal of this proposal is to expand the number of cell-cell adhesion adaptors studied and to acquire sufficient information about each component to build a model of the adaptor network. The approach taken in this proposal combines the best of model organism genetics and tissue culture studies. We will use the nematode C. elegans as a discovery and validation tool, making use of RNA interference to knockdown candidate genes. We will start by looking at paralogs of proteins identified by a collaborator in biochemically purified junctions from mouse cells. Rapid screening for adhesion related phenotypes will be followed by GFP tagging and expression to identify proteins with cell junctional localization. A subset of these novel components will be analyzed in cultured mammalian cells, using state-of-the-art microscopy and micromanipulation techniques. Following the spatiotemporal dynamics of each protein in response to varying forces will help elucidate their function. Ultimately, we will combine the knowledge about each protein with protein interaction data to build a model of the adhesion network, make predictions and test them in-vivo in the nematode. The knowledge gained by this research will deepen our understanding of the pivotal role of adaptors in cell-cell adhesion and may offer better diagnostics and/or therapy for common birth defects, wound healing and possibly treatment of some cancers.
kw: Mechanotransduction;Microscopy;Cell-cell adhesion;Tissue morphogenesis;Cytoskeleton;Systems biology

title: Novel targeting of central growth regulation in malignant gliomas
abs: Background: Deregulated cell growth underpins oncogenicity. Receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK)/mTOR pathway and its coupled tumour specific metabolism (aerobic glycolysis) play a central role in glioma malignancy. In our preliminary study, we identified ECT2 oncoprotein as a novel and significant member in the central growth regulation pathway of glioma. We hypothesize that targeting ECT2 associated, tumour specific signaling suppresses glioma growth, and sensitize temozolomidechemotherapy.In this study, we aim to 1) define the role of ECT2 in glioma central growth regulation; 2) validate ECT2 as a synergistic therapeutic target by combined ECT2, RTK/mTOR and glycolysis inhibition; 3) sensitize TMZ-induced autophagic cell death with growth inhibition.Methodology: The effect of ECT2 on tumour cell growth will be studied in multiple glioma cell lines by manipulating ECT2 cellular levels (siRNA, cDNA over-expression). Cell growth will be analyzed by verifying the effect of ECT2 expression and specific inhibition of glycolysis and RTK/mTOR activity on proliferation, cell volume, RNA content, cell cycle progression, ribosome RNA synthesis, ribosomeexport and mTOR activity. Autophagy will be analyzed by LC3-II quantification, acidic vesicular organelle staining and GFP-LC3-II distribution. Synergistic effect will be analyzed by combination index (CI)–isobologram method. Results will be verified in multiple glioma primary cell cultures established in our lab.Significance: 1) Novel oncogenic mechanism: Our study will provide key information on ECT2 oncogenicity through dissecting its position in glycolysis and mTOR pathway; 2) Novel biological targeting: For the first time, central growth regulation, including glycolytic metabolism and RTK/mTOR signaling, will be targeted together with the suppression of a core downstream protein, ECT2; 3) Build on existing limited efficacy of glioma chemotherapy: Current glioma chemotherapy has very limited success. Our approach to simultaneously target proliferation and cell growth through inducing autophagic cell death may significantly reduce glioma chemoresistance.
kw: glioma, cell growth, mTOR, autophagy, temozolomide, ECT2

title: Streptococcus bovis: incidental or opportunistic pathogen in colon cancer
abs: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is now the most common form of cancer for Singaporeans. It is estimated that one in 20 people will be diagnosed with CRC within their lifetime. The patient outcome of this disease, however, can be significantly improved by developing better screening techniques as early detection can greatly impact patient survival rates.The gut epithelium that is the origin of CRC is constantly exposed to a barrage of intestinal microflora attempting to get a selective advantage in the host. These can contribute to inflammatory host defenses being activated that can eventually contribute to the carcinogenesis process. In this context, we are interested in how specific species of gut microflora may initiate or exacerbate CRC.As early as 1974, a correlation has been suggested between Streptococcus bovis and CRC. Although many case studies have followed the original investigation, there has never been a rigorous examination of the potential of S. bovis as a potential cause or contributing factor in CRC development.As described in this proposal, we have designed a two-pronged approach for elucidating the relationship between S. bovis and CRC. We propose to apply genetic identification of clinical samples, integrating the now-recognized distinction of different subtypes of S.bovis. Using an available repository of S.bovis isolates, we propose to generate models through which we can probe the host-microbial interactions. We also propose to develop a novel screen for S. bovis from clinical samples, in order to test the hypothesis that increased S. bovis microbial load correlates to known risk-factors for CRC as well as for diagnosis of the disease.We firmly believe that patient outcomes could be greatly impacted by such a screen and that future therapies, designed to target S.bovis infections in the gut, could be a reasonable outcome.
kw: Streptococcus bovis, Colorectal cancer, Infection, Inflammation, Diagnostics

title: The molecular epidemiology of influenza in a tropical country
abs: Specific aims: To track and better understand how seasonal influenza viruses from a tropical region (Singapore) spread globally and potentially contribute to the seasonality of influenza in northern and southern hemispheres (within the framework of the recently proposed ‘source-sink’ hypothesis for influenza virus migration).Hypothesis: The well-recognized seasonality of influenza in northern and southern hemispheres is less well-defined in tropical regions. Global movements of different influenza strains can now be effectively tracked via full-genome sequencing and in-depth phylogenetic analysis. Previous studies of this kind (mainly using influenza genomes from the USA and Australasia) suggested that some influenza viruses migrate annually between northern and southern hemispheres, resulting in slightly different viruses populating the two different hemispheres. However, some influenza viruses may, instead, over-winter and persist in some populations, perhaps remaining sub-clinical, to re-emerge the following season with relatively little genetic drift. Both mechanisms (migration and persistence) may contribute to influenza seasonality to different extents in different countries. Tropical regions may be ‘cross-over points’ for such north-south migrating influenza viruses. Hence, the analysis of influenza viruses from Singapore (one of these potential tropical ‘cross-over’ points) will help to further elucidate the north-south seasonal migration patterns of seasonal influenza viruses.Methodology: Full-genome sequencing and in-depth phylogenetic analysis of influenza isolates from Singapore, archived during 2005-2013.Clinical significance: Although influenza vaccination has been shown to be effective in reducing the incidence of influenza infection, its uptake each year is very low. Findings from this study also have the potential to improve the timeliness and accuracy of seasonal influenza vaccine composition recommendations. A better understanding of the mechanisms underlying influenza seasonality is also important for healthcare planning because influenza-related infections and exacerbations of chronic diseases (e.g. asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, diabetes, heart and renal disease) cause annual surges in hospital admissions and outpatient consultations.
kw: Influenza, Epidemiology, Molecular, Sequencing, Phylogenetics, Evolution

title: Surveillance of More Virulent and Drug-Resistant Influenza A Strands in Singapore by High-Throughput Mass Spectrometry
abs: The current pandemic 2009 influenza A/H1N1 virus has spread rapidly around the globe through human-to-human transmission and has caused more than 6000 deaths (WHO, 13 Nov. 2009) in the past 7 months. Although severity of the viral infection is still considered as mild, past pandemic patterns have raised concerns that the virus will mutate or reassort with other subtypes of influenza A virus, causing another wave of more severe infection and possibly resistant to prevailing drug treatment. Actually, 52 oseltamivir-resistant pandemic H1N1 influenza viruses have been detected worldwide so far, all of them showing the same H275Y mutation in the N1 gene (WHO, 13 Nov. 2009). These concerns call for more vigilant surveillance of sequence changes in the viral genome. We propose to adopt an established method based on high-throughput comparative sequencing by mass spectrometry to track those changes - both point mutations and reassortments. The generated sequence data will be used to construct phylogenetic trees, which will allow us to elucidate the evolutionary relationship among the viruses. The protocols and bioinformatic skills establish in this proposed project will enable us to provide the same standard of genomic analyses as the WHO reference centers. The results will provide a continuous source of bio-surveillance information, and allow the surveillance capabilities established in the proposed project to be part of the national plan to fight the current and future influenza pandemics.
kw: H1N1, Influenza virus, surveillance, virulence, drug resistance, mass spectrometry

title: Understanding Molecular Mechanism of Supradamal, a Novel Adamantanyl-Based Antimalarial Drug
abs: Malaria still remains one of major human diseases. About 40 % of the world’s population lives in areas where malaria is transmitted. Human malaria is caused by infection with one of the four related parasitic protozoan species. P. falciparum and P. vivax are main pathogens among the four species of Plasmodium and have developed resistance to many drugs currently in use. Malaria vaccines are an area of intensive research. Unfortunately, a high degree of antigenic variation and complex biology of the parasite is hindering the introduction of malarial vaccines. This leaves antimalarial drugs still primary weapons to control malaria. So far, malaria control has been heavily dependent on a restricted number of chemically related drugs belonging to either the quinoline or the antifolate and artemisinintype compounds. However, the recent emergence and spread of drug-resistant malaria parasites have been concerns, prompting a search for novel compounds with mechanisms of action that are different from the traditionally used drugs to combat malaria.PfFKBP35 and PvFKBP35 are the molecular targets of the immunosuppressant FK506 in P.falciparum and P. vivax. FK506 and its analogues with no immunosuppressive activities show antimalarial activities, prompting us to design new class of antagonists that specifically target the parasite enzymes. To this end, recently we have determined three-dimensional structures of the isomerase domains of PfFKBP35 and PvFKBP35 in the absence of FK506 and also in complex with FK506. The outcomes of the structural studies led us to perform structure-guided drug screening and identified novel adamantanyl-based-antimalarial compounds named Supradamal (SRA) and its derivatives that not only bind to the parasite chaperones but also inhibit growth of Plasmodium falciparum cultured in human erythrocytes. In this proposal we aim to fully characterize the underlying mechanism of the novel antimalarial compounds and evaluate their efficacy on the life cycle of Plasmodium parasites.
kw: Malaria, Plasmodium falciparum, Plasmodium vivax, Antimalarial drugs, FK506, FK506 binding proteins

title: Role of macrophage and dendritic cell lineages in immunity against Mycobacterium tuberculosis
abs: Myeloid cells, especially macrophages (Mo) and dendritic cells (DCs), are crucial for successful first line defense against foreign invaders since they decide what kind of an adaptive immune action should be taken in order to restore the normal homeostasis.Here we propose an approach that allows us to study the roles of different myeloid cell lineages in immune defense against Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb). To do this we want to generate mouse strains where we can ablate subsets of Mo and DCs in order to study the consepquences of their absence in Mtb pathology and where we can then complement the ablations with a transfer of normal or genetically modified cells. More specifically genetic loci active in different subsets of myeloid cells will be replaced in corresponding BAC clones with the expression cassette coding a diphereria toxin receptor (DTR) and the bright red fluorescent protein. Modified BACs are introduced in the C57BI/6 embryonic stem (ES) cells and the mice are then derived from these ES cells. Understanding the functional roles of different types of myeloid cells in Mtb infection allows us to decipher the underlying mechanisms how the immune system tries to clear the infection. Ultimately the increased knowledge can be channeled into new and more specific anti-microbial therapies.
kw: Dendritic cells, Tuberculosis, Macrophages, Infection, Diphtheria toxin receptor transgenic

title: Evolutionary genomics of the 2009 swine-origin H1N1 influenza A pandemic virus
abs: During March and early April 2009, an H1N1 virus lineage previously undetected in humans emerged in Mexico and the United States. This novel virus was sufficiently antigenically divergent from seasonal H1N1 that the human population was immunologically naïve. Subsequently this virus spread rapidly via human-to-human transmission, developing into the first influenza pandemic in 40 years. Currently this novel virus co-circulates with the existing seasonal H1N1 and H3N2 viruses in several regions around the world. Reassortment between influenza viruses circulating in humans has occurred previously: In 2000 - 2002, H3N2 and H1N1 viruses reassorted to generate H1N2 viruses that subsequently co-circulated with H1N1 viruses. The pandemic H1N1 virus has also transmitted from humans to pigs in at least 7 countries further increasing the possibility for the emergence of novel reassortant viruses. The consequence of any potential reassortment is currently unknown.Using a variety of sequencing techniques and genetic analyses we seek to understand the interaction of the pandemic strain with seasonal and swine influenza viruses, and possibly avian influenza viruses that are endemic in the region. Analyses will also assess mutation rates and antigenic drift of A/H1N1 pandemicinfluenza viruses as they adapt to their newly acquired human hosts which is critical to assess the threat these viruses pose to human health in Singapore and worldwide. The sequences and information generated from this study will contribute directly to global efforts tracking the evolution and mutation of the pandemic viruses.The specific objectives of this project are:(1) To assess the adaptive pressure acting on this new virus in the human population(2) To detect reassortment of pandemic H1N1 with seasonal H1N1 and H3N2 viruses(3) To assess the effects of the new H1N1 virus on the population dynamics, including competitive interactions, of the human influenza gene pool
