title: Understanding the specific roles of p53 and p44(p47) in regulating tumorigenesis
abs: p53 is probably the most studied tumor-suppressor, by virtue of its functional inactivation in most human cancers. Astoundingly however, further in-depth exploration is still required to really understand its functions. One aspect that has not received sufficient attention is the function of the various forms of p53. At least 3 amino-terminal p53 variants exist: the full-length p53, p47 and a delta(D)133 - the latter two lacks the amino-terminal transactivation domain. The exact in vivo roles ofthe p47 and D133 are not clearly understood, except that they can affect full-length p53’s function when co-expressed. However, p47’s expression has been noted to be upregulated in many human cancer cells and in erythroleukemia-virus transformed mouse cells. Moreover, p47 is generated by several mechanisms, including through internal translation sites and by an alternate mRNA transcript,suggesting an important functional role. p53 mutations are often found in its DNA-binding domain - common to all p53 isoforms - raising the possibility that they may not only affect the function of full-length p53, but also that of p47 and D133. Hence, understanding the specific roles of these proteins would have immense implications in the way we understand carcinogenesis and treat cancer. We thus aim to initiate a systematic analysis of the specific physiological functions of p53 and p44 (human p47) in detail, by generatingknock-in mice that will either express only the p53 form (without p44), or that which will express only the p44 form (without p53), as current models do not discriminate between both. This will reveal the in vivo relevance of these proteins individually, and by crossing these mice together, in a compound manner. These studies will not only provide new knowledge in this old field, but will set the stage for subsequent studies to understand the effects of mutations on these variants.
kw: apoptosis, p44 (p47), isoforms, p53, Mouse models, Tumorigenesis

title: Identification of novel tumor suppressors in the p53 pathway by combining hypothesis-driven statistical analysis of genomic tumor data with functional loss of function screens.
abs: The advent of shRNA technology to specifically inhibit gene expression has boosted the search for unknown tumor suppressors. Large shRNA screens sufferfrom several problems however, including noise in screens that rely on enrichment ofactive clones, and off-target effects. Nonetheless I identified a novel tumorsuppressor gene, Brd7, required for full activity of p53. Brd7 loss, like loss of p53,facilitates the full transformation of primary cells genetically poised to become tumorlike cells that can grow anchorage independently. Biochemical and genetic evidence suggests no selective advantage to Brd7 loss in p53-mutant tumors. Indeed, the expression of Brd7 was found to be specifically compromised in subsets of tumors that had retained wild type p53, but not in p53 mutant tumors.I propose a novel approach which selects novel tumor suppressor candidatesfrom genomic data of genetically characterized tumor samples, followed by afunctional loss of function assay. First we select genes that are only compromised ina subset of p53 wild type, but not p53 mutant tumor samples, like Brd7. Secondly, tofilter out false positives, we will individually test the 100 most significant candidates,from both a gastric and a breast cancer data set, in a loss of function screen using atransformation assay of primary fibroblasts and epithelial cells. This assay is sensitive and robust enough to identify genes whose loss gives a subtle phenotype in the p53 pathway, or only affects p53-dependent apoptosis or arrest.Using a small but unbiased shRNA library, this project should yield previouslyunrecognized tumor suppressors in the p53 pathway that may have prognostic valuefor disease progression. Moreover, by identifying tumor suppressors with a lesspenetrant phenotype but combinatorial potential, this approach generates candidates to be tested in multi-gene familiar cancer studies or genome wide association studies.
kw: p53, gastric cancer, shRNA, breast cancer, tumor suppressor

title: Mesenchymal stem cell therapy for acute lung injury
abs: Acute lung injury (ALI), such as that arising from smoke inhalation, can be complicated with the development of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), brought about by aggressive inflammatory responses in the alveolar system. Current treatment for ALI/ARDS has been limited to symptomatic management. However, mortality rates of up to 40% remain, even with pharmacological intervention, necessitating alternative treatment modalities. Injected mesenchymal stem cells (MSC) accumulate in the pulmonary circulation and have also been shown to attenuate immune responses, suggesting potential use in ALI/ARDS therapy. We hypothesise that a clinically relevant ALI model may be generated through exposure to environmental toxins, which may be ameliorated through the delivery of fetal MSC (fMSC). Our hypothesis is based on the following observations. First, fMSC demonstrate greater immunomodulation compared to their adult counterparts. Secondly, ongoing clinical trials show fMSC to be safe and suitable for allogeneic applications. Finally, murine MSC applied in chemically-induced murine models of ALI result in reduced lung injury, inflammation and mortality. We have developed the following specific aims to test this hypothesis. First, we will establish a murine model of smoke inhalation-induced ALI. This will be validated with histology and physiological assessments. Subsequently, we aim to evaluate and optimise the administration of fMSC for the treatment of smoke-injured mice. This will allow us to demonstrate the ability of fMSC in ameliorating ALI. Furthermore, through cell fate and microarray expression analyses, we will study and suggest possible mechanisms for the therapeutic effects of fMSC.We have assembled a multi-disciplinary team of clinicians, biologists and bioengineers to achieve these aims. Our competitive strengths lie in the use of a novel stem cell source in a clinically relevant model of smoke-induced ALI. If successful, the work will demonstrate the efficacy of fMSC for the treatment of immunological disorders
kw: Mesenchymal stem cells, Acute Lung Injury, NOD/SCID Mice, Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome

title: A novel closed-loop, double-vasopressor infusion system for strict control of arterial pressure to improve perioperative outcome and to predict the risks of developing abnormal blood pressure due to adrenoreceptor genetic polymorphisms during anaesthesia.
abs: Perioperative fluctuations of arterial blood pressure (BP) are common and may be associated with adverse outcome. In caesarean section, severely low BP is difficult to predict and occurs in excess of 50% of the cases during anaesthesia. Vasopressors are drugs commonly used to maintain BP but could lead to significant side effects if used inappropriately. Aim: To individualize therapy and closely maintain arterial pressure, we propose a novel clinical algorithm that integrates data from non-invasive continuous BP monitoring to effect and command a 'closed-loop' dual-pump automated system ( CLDPAS) to infuse vasopressors. CLDPAS continuously analyzes and adjusts the infusions of vasopressors according to the real-time, beat- to-beat changes in the patients ' BP. Hypothesis: We hypothesize that our novel system could reduce the incidence of abnormal maternal BP during anaesthesia vis-à-vis the current (control) method of infusing a predetermined dose of a vasopressor when needed.Secondarily, we hypothesize the inter-individual variability in BP and requirement for vasopressors are associated with genetic polymorphisms of a1 and B2 adreno-receptors. Methods: We will randomize 200 healthly subjects scheduled for caesarean to receive and validate CLDPAS with two vasopressors, namely phenylephrine (a1 agonist) and ephedrine ( mixed a and Bagonist) or the control therapy with phenylphrine. Differences in BP ( primary outcome), heart rate, amount of vasopressors used, neonatal and maternal morbidities will be compared. Blood samples will be used for genotyping of a1 and B2 adreno-receptors. Clinical significance: The development of CLDPAS to tightly control arterial pressure could reduce maternal-fetal morbility due to haemodynamic instability and improve clinical outcome in the perioperative and critical care setting without the need for invasive monitoring. The association of genetic polymorphisms of adreno-receptors with the data generated by CLDPAS could be predictive of the risks of unstable BP and adverse events related to the cardiovascular system during anaesthesia and surgery.
kw: Monitor-noninvasive, Closed -Loop, Blood Pressure, Adreno-receptors, Caesarean Section, Anaesthesia

title: Development of a novel mouse model of Enterovirus 71 infection
abs: Enterovirus 71 (EV71) is one of the most virulent agents responsible for Hand, Foot and Mouth Disease (HFMD) which has been consistently associated with severe, life-threatening complications in infants and children during outbreaks in the Asia Pacific region.Progress in understanding EV71 pathogenesis and in developing effective treatments has been greatly hampered by the lack of a suitable animal model. Monkeys and neonate mice are susceptible to EV71 infection but obvious limitations make both animal models unsatisfactory. Alternatively, mouse-adaptation of EV71 strains has the disadvantage to bias the tissue tropism of the virus, challenging the relevance of this model. In this project, we propose to develop a novel mouse model of EV71 infection. The known role of interferons (IFNs) in controlling EV71 infection prompted us to consider the immunocompromised AG129 mouse background as a potential model for EV71 infection. AG129 mice lack both IFNa/B- and y-receptors, and have been shown to be permissive to a number of medically important viruses such as dengue and lymphocytic choriomeningitis viruses. We have generated preliminary data which indicate that AG129 mice are susceptible to EV71 infection, exhibit relevant disease symptoms (paralysis) and eventually succumb to the infection. In this project, we will determine the optimal mouse age group, infectious dose and route of inoculation of the virus. Subsequently, virus titers will be measured in the blood and tissues over time. Histopathology and cytokine profiles will be carried out to further characterize the infection. Finally, anti-EV71 drug and vaccine prototypes will be tested in this model. We believe that, despite impaired IFN signaling pathways, the development of AG129 mice as an animal model of EV71 infection will contribute to further decipher some of the aspects involved in EV71 pathogenesis and will provide a better platform for the evaluation of drug and vaccine candidates.
kw: Enterovirus 71, Hand, Foot and Mouth Disease, AG129, Mouse model

title: Epigenetic regulation of muscle differentiation
abs: Differentiation of skeletal muscle from precursor cells requires the activity of muscle specific transcription factors as well as chromatin modifying enzymes. The genetic regulation of myogenesis has been extensively examined. However, much remains to be determined how epigenetic regulators control muscle differentiation. Elucidating the function of epigenetic regulators during muscle differentiation will provide a new foundation for the development of novel therapeutic drugs for muscle diseases and ageing. Work from our laboratory has determined the function of the transcription factor Sharp-1 as a genetic regulator of muscle differentiation. Interestingly, in humans, Sharp-1 overexpression is associated with muscle pathologies such as inclusion body myositis, and rhabdomyosarcomas that are linked to defective differentiation. Together, these studies strongly suggest that dysregulation of Sharp-1 expression is important in the pathogenesis of specific myopathies. However, the molecular mechanism by which Sharp-1 regulates differentiation of muscle cells has been poorly characterized. Our preliminary data demonstrates that Sharp-1 interacts with the histone methyltransferase G9a, suggesting that Sharp-1 may recruit chromatin modifying factors to epigenetically control the differentiation state of muscle cells. The focus of this proposal is to elucidate the mechanisms involving G9a in differentiation of muscle precursor cells centered around Sharp-1 recruitment of G9a to inhibit skeletal muscle differentiation. Modulation of epigenetic regulators has already proven clinically useful: Understanding how such regulators function in the muscle context will contribute to the design of therapeutic strategies for the treatment of muscle pathologies, and ageing-related decline in muscle regenerative potential.
kw: Epigenetic, Methylation, Differentiation, Skeletal Muscle

title: A striatal synaptic dysfunction hypothesis for repetitive behaviors in autism evaluated by re-sequencing of candidate genes
abs: Autism spectrum disorders (ASD) are characterized by a triad of behavioral abnormalities: impaired social interaction, deficits in communication, and restrictive and/or repetitive interests and behaviors. ASD has a strong genetic component. Recent results show that rare variants at multiple genetic lociconfer risk of ASD and suggest the existence of other, undiscovered risk loci. The neurobiological bases for ASD’s three core symptoms are unknown. Our collaborator on this proposal, Dr. Feng, recently identified a novel mechanism underlying compulsive/repetitive behaviors. These mechanisms center on SAPAP3, a key glutamatergic postsynaptic protein that is highly expressed in the striatum, a brain region implicated in compulsive/repetitive behaviors. Deletion of Sapap3 leads to compulsive/repetitive behaviors in mice, and SAPAP3 mutations can cause these behaviors in humans. SAPAP3 interacts directly with SHANK3, a gene in which variants can cause ASD in humans. Thus, we hypothesize that rare mutations in other genes in related neurological pathways can cause compulsive/repetitive behaviors in ASD. To test this hypothesis, we propose to resequence, in each of 500 ASD patients, 200 candidate genes that are enriched in striatal synapses.For this we will employ hybridization-based exon capture followed by massively parallel nextgeneration sequencing. After mapping the sequence reads to the reference human genome, we will exclude from consideration common variants contained in public databases. Subsequently, we will prioritize rare variants using computational predictions of functional consequences. We will then confirm that high-priority candidates are not low-prevalence polymorphisms by targeted enotyping in unaffected controls. Finally, using other funding, Dr. Feng will functionally characterize confirmed extremely rare, high-priority variants by experimental studies in mice and/or cultured neurons. If successful, this study will substantially contribute to the understanding of genetic causes of ASD andwill open new avenues for experimental dissection of the molecular and cellular mechanisms that cause it.
kw: autism spectrum disorders, human genetics, synapse, next generation sequencing, striatum, repetitive behaviors

title: Implantation of autologous gene-modified bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stromal cells in pigs: Pre-clinical development of insulin-secreting bioimplants for diabetes therapy.
abs: In previous work, we demonstrated that transplantation of gene-modified autologous primary hepatocytes ameliorated dysmetabolism and target organ injury in diabetic swine. Primary bone marrow mesenchymal stromal cells (BMMSC) are an alternative and less invasively procured cell type for this approach. We have shown that EGR1 expression in BMMSC is rapidly and reversibly stimulated by high glucose. Transfection of primary BMMSC of Yorkshire-Landrace pigs with a nonviral vector expressing human insulin from the EGR1 promoter induced insulin secretion with near-physiological dynamics and reduced hyperglycemia in xenotransplanted diabetic NOD-SCID mice. We propose to extend this proof of concept to diabetic swine. We hypothesize that autologous gene-modified primary BMMSC can be developed as bioimplants for insulin-deficient diabetes. The project comprises 2 phases. Phase 1 We will optimize conditions to scale up expansion of primary porcine BMMSC ex vivo. Primary porcine BMMSC, serially passaged to obtain clinically meaningful cell numbers, will be evaluated for genomic instability by karyotyping and tumorigenicity by implantation in NSG mice. Four implantation sites – subcutaneous, omental, renal subcapsular and intrahepatic - will be evaluated for best engraftment of autologously transplanted green fluorescent protein (GFP)-tagged BMMSC in Yorkshire-Landrace pigs. Engraftment will be compared by quantitative GFP assays in tissues excised from each implantation site. Engrafted BMMSC will be examined for evidence of in vivo proliferation, differentiation and genomic alterations.Phase 2 Primary porcine BMMSC will be electroporated with a nonviral episomal vector co-expressing EGR1 promoter-human insulin cDNA, GFP and the scaffold/matrix attachment region. Human C-peptide radioimmunoassay will determine insulin secretory capacity of GFP-selected gene-modified BMMSC expanded ex vivo. Outcomes of autologous BMMSC transplantation in streptozotocin-diabetic pigs will be investigated by regularly monitoring plasma C-peptide, clinical, biochemical and metabolic indices. Tissues affected by diabetes-associated complications will also be histologically and transcriptionally evaluated in treated diabetic pigs, untreated diabetic and healthy control animals.
kw: bone marrow mesenchymal stromal cells, biosafety, diabetes mellitus, autologous cell therapy, engraftment and efficacy, pre-clinical model

title: The Singapore Malay Eye Study 2 (SiMES-2) - Propective cohort study of 6-year incidence, risk factors, and impact of major Asian Eye Diseases
abs: The major eye diseases threatening vision in Singapore include age-related macular degeneration, diabetic retinopathy, cataract, glaucoma, and refractive errors. The challenge posed by these conditions highlights the need for accurate data, not only on the epidemiology, but also on specific modifiable risk factors and key pathogenic mechanisms for these conditions in Asia. Such data are currently quite limited. In 2004-2006, we conducted the Singapore Malay Eye Study (SiMES-1), which examined 3,280 (78.7% response) Malays aged 40-80 years. SiMES-1 was strategically designed using the same standardized protocols as the Blue Mountains Eye Study in white Australians, so that direct comparison and data pooling could be achieved. Since 2007, SiMES-1 has become a landmark cross-sectional assessment of the prevalence, risk factors, and impacts of major eye diseases, producing >50 peer-reviewed publications, and generated a set of new hypothesis for the pathogenesis of eye diseases in Asians. This proposal describes the 6-year follow-up of the cohort (SiMES-2), to be conducted from 2010-2013. It aims to assess the incidence, progression, risk factors and impacts of major eye diseases as well as access to eye care by Asian Malays. As the first truly comprehensive cohort study of eye disease in older Singaporeans, SiMES-2 will provide a unique opportunity to address clinically-relevant hypotheses/questions on the contribution of new risk factors for major eye diseases and will link baseline serum biomarkers and environmental factors with incident eye outcomes. Strengths of the SiMES-2 include a well-established and characterized cohort, an experienced international team of clinician-epidemiologists, with the highest-quality baseline data including digital images, frozen serum, DNA and data collected on the widest range of baseline risk factors. SiMES-2 will provide critical information on the major eye disease that is currently unavailable, from which to plan strategies that will lead to reduction of visual loss in Singapore and Asia.
kw: blindness, age related macular degeneration, cataract, diabetic retinopathy, glaucoma, epidemiology

title: GADD34 in Insulin Synthesis and Beta-Cell Survival
abs: Diabetes currently affects nearly 1 in 10 individuals worldwide and is anticipated to double in countries like singapore in the next 30 years. The fundamental defect that triggers disease in the inability of pancreatic B-cells to keep up with increasing demands for insulin. This is particularly serious in obese individuals, whose tissues develop insulin resistance, requiring more and more insulin to manage their blood sugar levels. Emerging points to the high demand of insulin placing B-cells in considerable danger as they work to synthesize, fold and secrete adequate insulin. This stress in the endoplasmic reticulum stops synthesis of most proteins including insulin as the cell attempts to avoid serious buildup of misfolded proteins.This also gives B-cells an opportunity to synthesize stress proteins that correct or clear the backlog of proteins awaiting processing in the ER. As proteins control critical cell functions, B-cells tolerate the shutdown of general protein synthesis for only a short time. Indeed, unless protein synthesis resumes, cells suffer irreparable damage and are actively eliminated. Our research focuses on understanding how B-cells control a specific stress protein, GADD34, which allows effective recovery from day to day perturbations in protein folding. Having resolved protein misfolding, GADD34 must be actively destroyed as its persistence also overloads cells with newly synthesized proteins and triggers cell death. Frequent ER stress means that B-cells must also develop some resistance to protein misfolding. We hypothesize that B-cells modify GADD34's activity as they adapt to regular demands for insulin. We will analyse B-cells and mice with altered GADD34 activity to gain new insights into GADD34'S ability to protect B-cells from metabolic stress. Information gained from these studies will enable the design of novel therapeutic strategies to maintain B-cell function and viability, providing for more effective management of diabetes and reducing organ failure.
kw: GADD34, elF2alpha, ER stress, Protein Phosphatase-1, Beta-cell, Insulin

title: Engineering Biology for Valuable Fuels
abs: The aim of this program is to convert inexpensive carbon sources into a new class of valuable fuels, which can be easily accepted by existing mode of transportation. The entire program consists of 5 projects. In project 1, we will use ionic liquid to deconstruct the lignocellulosic biomass to glucose and xylose. In project 2, we will engineer yeast to increase uptake of xylose by using xylose specific transporter and metabolize it. In project 3, we will express heterologous pantothenate kinase gene and pyruvate dehydrogenase gene to increase the acetyl-CoA level in yeast and delete appropriate genes to increase the flux to precursor acetyl-CoA. In Project 4, we will express plant KAS IV and thoesterases in yeast to optimize the production of medium chain fatty acids. In project 5, we will express fatty acyl-CoA reductase and decarbonylase in yeast to convert fatty acids to alkanes. The proposed work will be done exclusively in the well-known eukaryotic yeast host Saccharomyces cerevisiae. The use of this host will allow us to take advantage of genetic tools that are readily available for engineering its metabolism and to make rapid strides in engineering the intracellular chemistry. Saccharomyces cerevisiae has already been used in industrial production of bioethanol, thus the yeast we engineer can be easily used in the upscale production of alkanes. The similar synthetic biology techniques can also be used in other eukaryotic yeast cells by moving the modular systems created here into other organisms.
kw: Synthetic biology;Medium chain hydrocarbons;Medium chain fatty acids;Yeast S. cerevisiae;Microbial engineering;Engineering biology

title: Gene expression profile of solute carrier (SLC) transporters and their roles in the uptake of antiretroviral drugs across human T4 lymphocytes
abs: The current treatment for HIV infection interrupts the viral lifecycle, at the HIV reverse transcriptase, HIV protease, and HIV integrase steps. Therefore, antiretroviral drugs have to enter T4 lymphocytes to inhibit viral replication. The intracellular concentrations of antiretroviral drugs are a composite of both influx and efflux processes. Thus far, antiretroviral research has primarily focused on drug efflux transporters; carrier-mediated drug uptake is relatively unexplored in comparison to drug efflux transport systems, possibly due to traditional concept of passive drug transport. Detection of SLC transporter gene expression in the human T4 lymphocytes is a necessary first step in the identification of candidate SLC transporter proteins involved in intracellular penetration of antiretroviral. This study will be the first exploratory study to identify all known SLC transporters (43 gene families; 298 transporter genes) that are expressed in T4 lymphocytes. In addition, Phytohemagglutinin (PHA) is a commonly used mitogen in HIV research, but anti-CD3/anti-CD28 provides a more physiologically relevant mechanism of activating T cells than PHA. We find it necessary to explore differential expression of SLC transporters between PHA activated T4 lymphocytes and anti-CD3/anti-CD28 activated T4 lymphocytes. Therefore, the objectives of this study are 1) to investigate the gene expression profile of all known human solute carrier (SLC) transporter (43 gene families; 298 transporter genes) in T4 lymphocytes (non-activated, PHA activated, and anti-CD3/anti-CD28 activated T4 lymphocytes), 2) to investigate whether top 5 most highly expressed SLC transporters in T4 lymphocytes play an important role in intracellular penetration of representatives from different classes of antiretroviral drugs (HIV integrase inhibitor raltegravir, nucleotide analogue reverse transcriptase inhibitor tenofovir, and nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor emtricitabine).
kw: SLC transporters, cellular uptake, T4 lymphocytes, antiretroviral drugs, intracellular accumulation

title: Evaluation and screening of scorpion sodium channel toxins for potential antitumor activity.
abs: Toxins are known to induce cytotoxicity in human cancer cell lines and ion channel modulators from venoms have been shown to impede cancer progression in animal models. Hence, the proposed project aims to screen the anti-cancer activity of peptides isolated and purified from venoms. The primary objective of this study is to verify the hypothesis that scorpion VGSC ( voltage-gated sodium channel) peptides are potential anti-cancer therapeutic agents, and may possibly yield a useful and effective lead peptide suitable for cancer drug development. The outline of the study design includes isolation and purification of peptides from commercially available crude scorpion venom using standard chromatographic techniques, pharmacological and structural characterization of selected peptides, followed b in vitro screening of cytotoxicity in cell-based assays and in an animal model. The anti-carcinogenic effects of two commercially available VGSC blocking peptides will also be included in the study. Established cancer cell lines derived from breast prostate gastric and nasopharyngeal cancers will be used for in vitro cytotoxicity screening. A comparison of the effects of the VGSC blocking peptides will also be performed on the side population of stem-cell like CD44+/CD24- cancer initiatingMDA-MB231 breast cancer cells( which are known to be more chemoresistant) as compared to the general population of MDA-MB-231cells. The most promising VGSC blocking peptide with maximal anti-cancer activity observed in vitro will be tested in SCID mice inoculated with MDA-MB231 breast cancer cells to assess its potential for cancer intervention therapy. This could ultimately lead to solving the toxicity-related health problems associated with current chemotherapeutic drugs and radiation therapy. The data generated will lead to development of and IRG proposal for detailed mechanistic and efficacy studies to advance the cancer drug discovery process from concept to clinic.
kw: Cancer therapeutics, Voltage-gated Na+ channel (VGSC) blocking peptide, Anti-tumor activity, Breast Cancer, Animal model, Apoptosis

title: Conducting Polymer Scaffold and Interface for Electrically Stimulated Osteogenesis
abs: Laboratory and clinical evidence has shown that electrical stimulation can be an effective tool to promote bone healing. Thus, combining this technique with the great capacity of human mesenchymal stem cells (hMSCs) for self-renewal and potential for differentiation into cells of various types of tissues can be potentially promising for regenerative medicine. The proposed project intends to develop conducting polymer scaffolds and interfaces for use as supporting substrate for hMSCs and concomitantly facilitate the application of electrical stimulation to these cells. With the polymer serving as the electrode as well as cell support substrate, no additional conductive coating material is needed, and it also eliminates the need for additional surgery to retrieve the implanted electrode when used in vivo. Furthermore, the conductive polymer can be designed and fabricated to possess porosity for enhanced cell interaction and functional groups for subsequent conjugation with growth factors to direct the differentiation of stem cells. The polypyrrole family of conducting polymer will be investigated in this project since it possesses high electrical conductivity and is biocompatible. Porous scaffolds comprising conducting polymer with and without a second polymer will be fabricated using different techniques. The suitability of these scaffolds for osteoblasts and hMSCs seeding and growth will be assessed in the absence and presence of electrical simulation. Conducting polymer coatings will also be deposited on commercially available metal and non-metal implant materials and similar tests will be carried out. The relative advantages and limitations of each type of conducting polymer system in enhancing and supporting the growth, development and osteogenic differentiation of hMSCs will be established. The possible synergistic combination of conducting polymer and electrical stimulation may also be used to direct the differentiation of hMSCs into other cell types for application in regenerative medicine.
kw: conducting polymer, electrical stimulation, stem cells, implant materials, osteogenic differentiation, regenerative medicine

title: Bioengineering Hybrid Antifungal Molecules Based on Naturally Occurring Carbazoles for Eye Infection
abs: Fungal infections in the eye lead to devastating visual loss and do not have satisfactory treatment currently. Recently, we developed a series of branched cationic peptides (e.g., V2-dimer and V2-tetramer), which showed potent antifungal/antiyeast activity, also displayed broad-spectrum antibacterial activity without toxicity to host cells and without the formation of resistance. However, the peptide-based molecules represents less than an ideal drug candidate compared small organic molecule drug, namely because of uncertain bioavailability, short half time due to enzymatic degradation, potential immunogenicity and high production costs. The use of new approach of peptidomimetics to overcome these limitations inherent to peptides is becoming an important and promising approach for translating the therapeutic potential of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs). Carbazole and carbazole alkaloid (antibiotic murrayanine from Murraya Koenigii Spreng) were natural products with less toxicity. [1-3] In India, the leaves of this small tree (known as currypatta or curry-leave tree) was used in curry. Carbazole derivatives are well known for their various pharmacological activity, including antibacterial, antifungal, anti-HIV and anticancer activities. [4-6]In this proposal, we use carbazole as double functionalized units of a pharmcophore group of typically antifungal carbazoles and fluorescent (a typical blue-light emission) hydrophobic moiety for peptidomimetics of antifungal peptides. This proposal focuses on engineering of a novel family of hybrid antifungal molecules based on cationic carbazole derivatives by a new approach of peptidomimetics of antifungal peptides. These hybrid antifungal molecules consist of structural characteristics of both typically antifungal carbazoles and antifungal peptides, thus have a combination advantages of two types of antifungal molecules, they are expected to have increased fungicidal activity and maintain low cytotoxicity to host cells. In addition, these hybrid molecules have a remarkable set of advantageous properties ranging from ease synthesis/low cost, low drug resistance of fungi, to stability and rapid killing.
kw: Carbazole derivatives, peptidomimetics, fungicidal, candia species, structure-activity relationship (SAR), eye infection

title: Autologous cord blood cells for brain injury in term newborns
abs: With an incidence of 0.5-1.0 per 1,000 livebirths (20-40 infants annually in Singapore), neonatal hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) accounts for over 20% of neonatal deaths worldwide and thousands of cerebral palsy (CP) cases annually. Recent multicentre trials demonstrate that hypothermia after HIE reduces death and impairment, but 40-50% of cooled infants died or survived impaired. Clearly, other therapies for HIE are needed. In HIE animal models, umbilical cord blood (UCB) cell infusion reduces brain injury and improves outcomes (Meier 2006). In infants with genetic neurologic diseases, transplanted allogenic UCB cells migrate to and engraft in brain, prolonging life and improving outcomes. (Prasad 2008). We hypothesise that infusion of autologous UCB cells shortly after birth will facilitate cellular repair of HIE brain injury and reduce incidence and severity of CP. This is a phase I study. Our aims are to: 1) demonstrate safety and feasibility of collection, preparation, and infusion of autologous UCB cells in infants with HIE, and 2) assess neuroimaging and neurodevelopmental outcomes. Neuroimaging analyses include a novel diffusion tensor MRI sequence to distinguish myelin from axonal injury. We will conduct an open label pilot study of autologous UCB cells in 10 infants > 36 weeks gestation with moderate to severe HIE. All eligible patients will receive moderate hypothermia according to established protocols. Cord blood cells will be volume-reduced following standard procedures. A maximum of four low-volume aliquots containing 5 x 107 cells per kg birth weight will be infused within 72 postnatal hours. Infants will be assessed for neurodevelopmental outcome prior to discharge, at 1 month post-discharge and at 4 -6, 9-12 and 18-24 months of age. MRI scans will be performed at 7 - 28 days to quantify initial injury and repeated at 4- 6 months to assess evolution of injury.
kw: Hypoxic, Encephalopathy, Cord, Ischemic, Autologous, Blood

title: Derivation of induced pluripotent stem cells from the reprogramming of human adipose-derived mesenchymal stem cells
abs: Induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells have been derived from the reprogramming of human dermal fibrobalsts (hDFs) (1,2) through ectopic expression of transcription factors. A limitation to the use of dermal fibroblasts as the starting population for reprogramming is that it usually takes weeks for expansion from a single biopsy to obtain sufficient cells, and the induction efficiency has been reported to be very low at 0.01% (1).In contrast, adipose tissue enjoys the advantage of being easily accessible in large quantity from subcutaneous depots and generates millions of adipose-derived mesenchymal stem cells (Ad-MSCs) without the need for significant culture-expansion (3-5).The aim of this study is to evaluate the efficacy of using Ad-MSCs, as the initiating cell source, for reprogramming into iPS cells through the ectopic expression of transcription factors.Ad-MSCs will be derived from human adipose tissue as previously described by our group (3), following the method of Zuk et al (5). Ad-MSCs will be transduced with viruses containing Oct4, Sox2, Klf4 and c-Myc and repeated two days later to increase the infection efficiency. These induced pluripotent human stem cells will be characterized for their ability to express cell surface markers (SSEA4, TRA1-60) and genes (OCT4, NANOG, SOX2), and also for their ability to maintain the developmental potential to differentiate into derivatives of all three primary germ layers: endoderm, mesoderm and ectoderm. Clonal lines of fully characterized human iPS cells from different adipose tissue donors will be generated and expanded.The successful reprogramming of Ad-MSCs into iPS cells may provide a robust autologous source of cells for generating patient-specific iPS cells. Patient-specific iPS cells will facilitate our basic understanding of specific disease mechanisms. More importantly, the generation of patient-specific and disease-specific iPS cells has the potential to greatly impact the regenerative medicine industry, and facilitate drug and vaccine development.
kw: Induced pluripotent stem cells, Human adipose stem cells, Mesenchymal stem cells, Reprogramming, pluripotency, self-renewal

title: Exploring repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation to improve gait disorder in Vascular Parkinsonism.
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: This research proposal aims to evaluate the efficacy of applying 5Hz repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (rTMS) of the motor cortical area to improve gait dysfunction in Vascular Parkinsonism (VP) patients. Early studies on healthy volunteers demonstrated that regularly repeated rTMS to the primary motor cortex (M1) can induce a lasting change in cortico-motor excitability. Several investigators have found that rTMS of the cerebral cortex leads to clinical improvement of bradykinesia and UPDRS motor subscores in PD patients. In VP, as in PD there is dysfunction in the subcortical circuits (pathologically and radiologically demonstrable lacunes in the basal ganglia and/or diffuse subcortical white matter disease). Because the basal ganglia output is via the motor cortex, modulation of cortical excitabitity to facilitate cortico-spinal pathways is likely to be effective when applied to VP patients. In this pilot study, patients will be selected according to prespecified criteria for vascular parkinsonism. A total of 50 patients will be randomized into a treatment arm consisting of 5 consecutive sessions of rTMS at 5Hz , and a placebo arm using sham rTMS. All patients will receive 1000 stimuli on each side of the leg motor cortex. They are evaluated at baseline, post-treatment on day5 , and at 2 weeks, 4 weeks and 6 weeks respectively from treatment start. The primary outcome measures is the timed 10m walk. The secondary measures are UPDRS III, number of freezing, Global Impression of Change (patient self assessment and physician assessment), Visual Analogue Scale of severity 0 to 100 (patient self assessment and physician assessment). This novel approach may become an effective and simple treatment modality for patients who develop VP after cerebral vascular events. It may potentially be used to treat other neurodegenerative gait disorders as well.
kw: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation, Motor cortex, Vascular Parkinsonism

title: Does a mutation at the KCNQ1 locus that confers susceptibility to type 2 diabetes mellitus also cause QT abnormalities in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus?
abs: People with long QT interval syndrome are at risk of malignant arrhythmia and sudden cardiac death. Recently, a single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) at the KCNQ1 locus was found to be a strong candidate for conferring susceptibility to type 2 diabetes (T2DM) in the Singapore population. KCNQ1 is also expressed in the heart and rare variants are known to cause hereditary long QT syndrome. However, the common polymorphisms that are associated with T2DM and QT interval are at different ends of the gene, and do not seem to be in linkage disequilibrium. It is not known whether the same polymorphism that confers increased risk of T2DM is also associated with QT abnormalities. We will examine the association of KCNQ1 SNP (rs2237897) and QT abnormalities in adult T2DM patients. We aim to recruit 500 consecutive T2DM patients, age >21 years. Exclusion criteria are history of ischemic heart disease, arrhythmia and on medications that prolong QT interval. Medical history, blood for HbA1C, electrolytes, calcium and magnesium and DNA extraction for genetic analysis will be collected. Genotyping for rs2237897 will be carried out using a validated Taqman assay. ECG will be performed and QT interval will be calculated using Bazett formula. Association between the QT interval and KCNQ1 mutations will be examined using ANCOVA under an additive model of inheritance. We will first perform univariate analysis. Subsequently, multivariate analysis will be carried out adjusting for age, gender, HbA1C, and other CVD risk factors with QT interval as dependent variable. The presence of genetic variants that confer susceptibility to both T2DM and QT abnormalities may explain the greater risk of sudden cardiac death in diabetics with ischemic heart disease. It may be that individuals who carry these mutations should undergo more detailed testing for underlying cardiac ischemia and avoid situations that may further prolong QT interval.
kw: TYPE 2 DIABETES MELLITUS, KCNQ1 POLYMORPHISM, QT INTERVALS, CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE, SUDDEN DEATH, ARRHYTHMIAS

title: Dual-compartmental growth factor delivery to achieve periodontal tissue regeneration
abs: Periodontitis, which refers to the destruction of the dentoalveolar complex causing chewing inability, has become one of the major health hazards since the last decade. Current treatments still cannot achieve predictable results. Growth factor-based controlled-release tissue engineering approach appears to be the promising approach for regenerating the loss of periodontal tissue. However, most of the designs focus on single periodontal compartment and are difficult for clinical manipulation. Our hypothesis is that periodontal tissue regeneration could be optimized and predictable with the consideration of diversity of components within the periodontal complex in a clinically-accessible way. We propose to deliver two engineered biologics loading specific biomolecules respectively in order to reconstruct the soft (periodontal ligament, PDL) and hard (alveolar bone) components of the periodontal complex in vivo. For the ease of manipulation, the layer of PDL will be reconstructed using a coaxial-designed biodegradable composite micro-sheet loading PDL-related growth factor, such as enamel matrix derivatives (EMD) or platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF). The segment of alveolar bone will be filled with PLGA-based microspheres containing bone morphogenetic protein (BMP). Both biologics will be designed to control growth factor release following the biological cascade of the periodontal wound repair. In vitro releasing profile and cell viability test will be examined before in vivo implantation. The outcome of regeneration will be qualitatively and quantitatively evaluated through site-specific gene expression, histological examination, micro-computed tomography, and immunohistochemical staining. The specific aims of this study are,1. To fabricate the micro-sheet and microspheres with desirable controlled release characteristics. 2. To characterize and optimize the regenerative effect from different formulations of growth factor in this dual-compartmental delivery approach.Accomplishing these specific aims will provide better understanding of dual-compartmental growth factor delivery in periodontal regeneration and establish a solid fundamental for considering this application as a future clinical treatment modality.
