title: Study to unravel the functional biology of a novel interaction between the anti-apoptotic protein, Bcl-2, and mitochondrial cytochrome C oxidase subunit Va in vitro and in primary cells derived from lymphoma patients.
abs: Recent evidence indicates that dergulation of normal metabolic pathways linked to the maintenance of homeostatic growth is a critical underlying mechanism during carcinogenesis. A central player in the regulation of cellular metabolism is the mitochondiron, which utilizes fatty acid oxidation and oxidative phosphorylation for the generation of ATP. In the regard, our work over the years has highlighted the critical involvement of superoxide anion in cancer cell survival and inhibition of apoptitic signaling. Of particular note, we linked the anti-apoptotic activity of the oncogene Bcl-2 to its ability to increase intracellular superoxide anion in cancer cells and demonstrated this effect to be a function of increases in mitochondrial oxygen consumption and activity of the terminal complex of the electron transport chain, cytochrome C oxidase (COX or complex IV). On the backdrop of that and our prelimary data supporting interaction between Bcl-2 and COX subunit VA, we hypothesize that the effect of Bcl-2 on COX could be mediated cia a direct protein-protein interaction between Bcl-2 and Va subunit of the COX enzyme complex, and that this interaction could be critical in endowing Bcl-2 expressing cancer cells a survival advantage. Therefore, we propose to study the molecular aspects of this interaction, its functional relevance and clinical significance in the wake of the anti-apoptotic activity of Bcl-2. Using a variety of model systems, such as stable and transient over-expression of Bcl-2, cell lines with difference constitutive levels of Bcl-2, siRNA mediated gene knockdown of Bcl-2, MEF cells from Bcl-2 transgenic as well as Bcl-2 knock out mice, and primary cells from patients with lymphomas, we propose to study: (i) the sub-cellular localization of this interaction, (ii) identify the domain(s) within Bcl-2 involved in this interaction, (iii) assess the effects of physiological stress states (hypoxia, glucose withdrawal) on this interaction, and (iv) the effects of this interaction on the death inhibitory activity of Bcl-2 to assess the clinical significance of this novel observation.These studies will not only enhance our understanding of theis hitherto undefined biology of Bcl-2, but also promise to unravel novel target(s) for potential therapeutic intervention in cancers where Bcl-2 over-expression is a major hurdle in the management of the disease.
kw: Cancer cells, mitochondria, apoptosis, Bcl-2, cytochrome C oxidase, ROS

title: Investigating the roles of gelsolin, a cytoskeletal protein, in mechanisms that contribute to tumour dissemination.
abs: Gelsolin is a cytoskeletal protein which participates in actin turnover during cell migration. Gelsolin appears to have complex functions in tumour formation and progression. Whilst the initiation of tumour formation from normal cells may be associated with loss of gelsolin, there is evidence that gelsolin also participates in tumour recurrence and metastasis. Overexpression of gelsolin and proteins involved in its signalling predict tumour recurrence in certain tumour types. In particular, tumours harbouring foci of gelsolin overexpression have been found to recur more frequently and have higher capacity to disseminate. Much focus has been placed on the role of gelsolin as a tumour suppressor, but little is known about its antagonistic role as a candidate protein in tumour dissemination.We postulate that gelsolin adopts different functions during the malignant progression of tumours and may contribute to local and distant tumour dissemination. In agreement with previous studies, we found that gelsolin enhances the invasion and scattering of tumour cells. We have also found that increased levels of gelsolin in tumour cells are associated with changes in the expression of genes which affect invasion and transcription. Furthermore, we observed that the expression of gelsolin is upregulated at the invasive edges of human metastatic colorectal tumours. These observations suggest that gelsolin may have tumour-disseminating roles and possibly interacts with other proteins to induce tumour progression.We aim to determine the mechanisms by which gelsolin promotes tumour dissemination. The invasive and scattering potential of tumour cells is crucial for tumour spread, both locally and to distant metastatic sites. We will use in vitro and in vivo models to investigate if changes in gelsolin levels and its interacting molecular partners affect invasion and metastasis. As cytoskeletal changes are key events in malignant progression, our investigations can potentially identify new approaches to understanding and inhibiting metastatic behaviour.
kw: gelsolin, invasion, metastasis, actin, tumour, colorectal

title: Halting p25/Cdk5 induced neuroinflammation in an Alzheimers disease paradigm
abs: Neuroinflammation is thought to be a major contributing factor to the pathogenesis of Alzheimer's disease (AD) . In a mouse model that develops the pathological hallmarks of the disease, neuroinflammation is robustly found at an early time point. The model function through the inducible expression of the aberrantly formed hyperactivator of Cyclin dependent kinase 5 (Cdk5), p25. This proposal seeks to determine how important the early onset of neuroinflammation found during p25 expression,is to the development of the pathological lesions and cognitive decline in these mice. We will determine levels of astrogliosis and chemokine production in brain of mice from 1-4 wwks of induction. We will also use a synthetic oleanane triterpenoid CDDO (2-cyano-3, 12-dioxoolean-1, 9-dien-28-oic acid) which has been used as a potent anti-inflammatory. We will treat the mice at early time points as well as to the point when we have found the formation of the hallmarks of hyperphosphorylated tau and amyloid accumlation. Since members of the peripheral circulation have been found at AD lesion sites, we will also determine the activation profiles of peripheral blood lymphocytes(PBL) harvested from p25 trangenic mice that have been treated with CDDO as well as AD patients and their matched controls by virtue of measuring the activated peripheral immune cells by cytokine production surface marker analysis. We will then test if CDDO can modify the activation profiles of these PBL and whether CDDO-mediated inhibition of inflammation would afford btter survival of the neurons. The data from these experiments will open avenues of research into inhibiting neuroinflammation in the AD paradigm which is of obvious clinical significane in Singapore, dementias , especially Alzheimer's disease, is a rapidly growning problem.
kw: Alzheimer's disease, neuroinflammation, neurodegeneration, p25/Cdk5

title: Optimising local management of global pandemics – a modelling approach
abs: Emerging infectious diseases have the potential to cause global pandemics which directly impact Singapore, as evidenced by the outbreaks of Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome in 2003 [1] and the history of influenza pandemics [2]. The novel H1N1 influenza strain recently detected in Mexico and the United States [3] has raised concerns that a new virus with the capability to cause a pandemic has emerged [4].A historical review we conducted previously showed that the influenza pandemics of 1957 and 1968 caused epidemics in Singapore earlier than in most Northern hemisphere countries. Moreover, the pandemic of 1918 caused two waves of infection, the second being more severe than the first [5]. The last time a novel strain of influenza emerged and spread around the world was in 1977, and that virus also caused a major epidemic in Singapore with evidence of second wave about 1 year later [6]. However, there was little data collected in previous pandemic events to characterize spread of infection or effectiveness of interventions.With the lead-time prior to community transmission of the new H1N1 virus in Singapore, studies have been planned to collect data about the spread of the new virus (see Annex A on list of epidemiological studies proposed located after the reference section). In addition, there are several existing projects led by parties on this grant application to model the spread of pandemic influenza in different settings within Singapore, as well as community perceptions of the impact of various health outcomes and policy options. The data collected during the epidemic and the different modeling approaches already in progress need to be analyzed and synthesized into a set of results that can produce recommendations for action. In addition, should be translated into cost-effectiveness/cost-benefit assessments to help policy-makers prioritize different strategies according to different policy objectives.
kw: Influenza, Pandemic, Epidemiology, Intervention effectiveness, Cost-effectiveness, Modeling

title: A NEW AND PRECISE METHOD FOR CONTINUOUS BEDSIDE MONITORING OF CARDIAC OUTPUT IN THE INTENSIVE CARE UNIT
abs: Cardiac output (CO), rather than blood pressure (BP), determines final oxygen delivery to vital organs. Detecting low CO states in the intensive care unit (ICU) well before low BP occurs will allow early treatment to prevent organ failure, resulting in better outcomes for the patient. 1 Intra-arterial, real-time BP monitoring is the standard of care in ICUs. However in contrast, there has not been a similar device to easily, accurately and continuously measure systemic blood flow (a reflection of CO). Available techniques (dilution, direct Fick, echocardiography, arterial waveform contour) are all handicapped by the inability to provide continuous and accurate readings which at the same time is also user-friendly as well as independent of user expertise, all of which are features critical for ICU treatment decisions. Our proposed application uses a known, but rarely used technology (intravascular Doppler probe) for measuring blood flow. We have tested this probe in a rabbit, and were able to obtain excellent physiologic aortic blood flow waveforms and velocities in the abdominal aorta of the rabbit (3mm diameter). The probe is thin enough to be inserted through even the smallest intra-arterial catheter (24G) and umbilical arterial catheter (3.5F) meant for extremely premature babies who weigh less than 1 kg. We plan to test the intravascular Doppler further in piglets and validate its accuracy with a perivascular Doppler flow probe (the laboratory gold standard, which cannot be used practically in a patient because it requires surgery for placement). Once proven to be accurate we plan to obtain normative data of cardiac output in sick preterm babies at a later stage as well as to develop a device prototype which allows real-time display of volumetric flow. With this novel application, we envisage that it will be used as the standard method for hemodynamic monitoring in all ICUs.
kw: cardiac output, continuous, bedside, Doppler, precise

title: Role of fatty acids in colorectal carcinogenesis – a case-control study nested within the Singapore Chinese Health Study
abs: In Singapore, an increasing influence of Western dietary and lifestyle factors contributes to the doubling colorectal cancer incidence since 1968. Epidemiologic studies, in general, support a positive association between saturated fat and colorectal cancer, but are equivocal with respect to the association of n-6 and marine n-3 PUFAs. We have reported a positive association with marine n-3 PUFA intake and advanced colorectal cancer among those with =5 years of follow-up, suggesting that the mechanism by which fatty acids increase colorectal cancer risk may depend on the type of fatty acid and timing of exposure. The lack of a coherent etiologic picture of the relationship between PUFAs and colorectal cancer is due in part to the inadequate measurement of dietary fat inherent with the use of self-reported diet histories in epidemiologic studies. The overall goal of the proposed project is to measure fatty acids in pre-diagnostic blood samples among 658 incident colorectal cancer cases and 1,316 matched controls nested within the prospective Singapore Chinese Health Study, and to provide definitive results for the effects of fatty acids on colorectal cancer risk. This goal are accomplished with the following specific aims: (1) Determine baseline plasma levels of 25 fatty acids among cases and matched controls; (2) Examine the associations between fatty acid subgroups and colorectal cancer. The investigation of dietary fats and their possible role in preventing and promoting colorectal carcinogenesis has major public health implications. As Singaporeans are a population in transition and becoming increasingly more westernized, the population in this Chinese Cohort is unique in possessing a wide range of exposures in diet for an efficient examination of their effects on disease risk. By using a biomarker approach, we will be able to provide key information for advancing our knowledge of the underlying mechanisms for fatty acids and colorectal cancer.
kw: Diet, Colorectal Cancer, Fatty Acid, Prevention, Epidemiology, Public Health

title: Evaluation of HepaCAM activities in leukocyte biology and immune regulation
abs: HepaCAM is a novel cell adhesion molecule that was indentified and cloned by Dr. Shali Shen (Co-PI). HepaCAM, a member of the Immunoglobulin superfamily, is a glycoprotein localized predominantly on the cytoplasmic membrane. The gene was originally isolated from liver and subsequently found to be widely expressed in normal human solid tissues. The expression of hepaCAM is frequently downregulated in a variety of cancers, including hepatocellular carcinoma. Reexpression of hepaCAM in hepaCAM-deficient cancer cells inhibits colony formation and delays cell growth suggesting a role of hepaCAM in tumor suppression. Furthermore, hepaCAM is capable of enhancing cell-extracellular matrix interactions such as cell adhesion and migration through direct interaction with f-actin. Our recent data demonstrate that hepaCAM is also expressed in human leukocytes. However, nothing is known about the role of hepaCAM in leukocyte biology and the regulation of immune responses. In this exploratory project we propose to characterize hepaCAM expression on leukocytes and its regulation by cellular activation (aim 1). Also, we intend to test how stimulation and neutralization of hepaCAM influences activities of leukocytes and leukocyte subsets (aim 2). Lastly, we propose to produce a recombinant hepaCAM protein to identify the hitherto unknown ligand of hepaCAM, and to investigate its expression on leukocytes (aim 3). Data from this project are expected to clarify whether hepaCAM influences leukocyte activities and immune responses, and to yield an initial characterization of the nature of this influence. If hepaCAM and its ligand are involved in the regulation of immune functions their activities will be characterized in more detail in subsequent projects which will also evaluate the potential of hepaCAM and its ligand as therapeutic targets.
kw: hepaCAM, Immune regulation, leukocytes, Cell adhesion

title: Measuring optic disc tilt objectively with a new software with the scanning laser ophthalmoscope, Heidelberg Retinal Tomograph
abs: Glaucoma is a major cause of blindness 1. Optic disc morphology is an important aspect of diagnosis and monitoring the progression of glaucoma. The scanning laser ophthalmoscope (SLO) in the form of the Heidelberg Retinal Tomograph (HRT) is now a main means to study the morphology of the disc 2, 3,4,5. Tilted optic discs are one of the variations in the morphology of the disc and can affect up to 40% of the population, especially in young myopes in Asia 6. Myopia and astigmatism are increasing in prevalence, and there is a correlation of the two with glaucoma. Studies have shown that optic disc tilt affects HRT measurements significantly3. Until now, disc tilt has not been properly measured objectively. Disc tilt affects our assessment of glaucoma.The PI and Co-PI (Dr Paul Healey) have now developed a new software which allows the standard HRT version III software to calculate the amount of disc tilt. We firstly aim to compare and correlate the results we have using this new method with an older subjective method which we have identified the disc tilt6. Using HRT scans derived from this study 6, in which we have identified 32 cases with optic disc tilt. We show that the new software is able to assess the cases with tilt quantitatively and accurately, and the results correlate well with those identified using the older methods. We are now able to assess disc tilt.With the same methodology, we intend to study HRT data on 18 000 eyes from the Chinese, Malay and Indian local population based studies. We intend to analyse the HRT scans of these cases, define and classify tilt, then look for risk factors and association with disc tilt. This will improve our diagnosis and monitor of glaucoma and myopia in the presence of disc tilt.
kw: Heidelberg Retinal Tomograph, optic disc tilt, glaucoma, disc tilt

title: STAT3 mediated regulation of Innate Immune responses of cardiomyocytes
abs: Cytokines and inflammation have emerged as one of the most important factors involved in the development of chronic congestive heart failure (CHF). However, the molecular mechanisms by which inflammation contributes and leads to pathogenesis of CHF are not well understood. We have created novel strains of mice that can serve as models for studies of inflammation and CHF. we have found that signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3) is a critical regulator in expressing the inflammatory cytokines. Furthermore, we have shown that cardiomyocyte-restricted deletion of STAT3 may be participating in enhanced expression of inflammatory cytokine and heart failure with aging. Intriguingly, STAT3 appears to have a critical role in protecting heart against damages that are induced either through inflammatory cytokines or reduced cytoprotection. STAT3 knock-out (KO) mice treated with lipopolysaccharide (LPS) has demonstrated a significant increase in apoptosis than their wild-type counterparts. At the cellular level, STAT3 deleted cardiomyocytes secrete significantly more TNF-a in response to LPS than those in wild-type. This may be the cause for dramatic increase in cardiac fibrosis in aged mice despite having no overt signs of heart failure in young STAT3 deficient mice. Thus, based on the preliminary results, we propose that STAT3 might have dual functions in regulating the innate response of cardiomyocytes by generating inflammatory cytokines as well as providing cytoprotection against apoptosis. The loss of STAT3 in cardiac myocytes leads to pathogenesis of age-related heart failure. In this approach, we will investigate the role of STAT3 in regulating the expression of inflammatory cytokines in cardiac restricted tissues, and to reveal molecular mechanisms of innate response to LPS/endotoxin during pathogenesis of CHF; In particular we will investigate the molecular basis of apoptosis induction in STAT3 deficient cardiomyocytes, and whether STAT1 also plays a more active role in activating apoptotic genes in the absence of STAT3.
kw: STAT 3, Cardiomyocyte, Apoptosis, TNF-?, Inflammation

title: Frontiers in Magnetic Recording Research: Vision for 10 Terabits per square inch
abs: Ten Terabits per square inch require dimensions beyond our process capabilities of today. Basic research projects will need to be put in place for understanding basic physics of magnetism of small structures (~2-4nm), processing of small structures such as bit pattern media, read sensors of the order of 5-7nm, reading and writing of the these small structures would be a key challenge. In addition to the magnetoresistance phenomena, we will investigate the nonmagnetic originated reading schemes such as the quantum hall effect. Not only does one have to have the small structures but they have to be placed with accuracy of atomic distances over large areas. The magnetic spacing of 2nm dictates we have overcoat-less media & heads. Surfaces have to have smoothness of the order of 0.5A rms and extremely low micro-waviness. New tribological materials have to be developed either in the form of monolayer (graphene, BCN etc.) or some sort of atomic mixing at the interface would be required to over come some of the tribological challenges. A lube molecule will have to be developed to get the required tribological properties and at the same time be corrosion inhibitor. In the servo area we have to be able to place the head on a data track to within 3A (1 sigma). This will require a whole new PZT materials development effort to even come close to what is required. Once this material is developed this will have to be integrated into the slider fabrication and maybe used as second stage MEMS device for positioning the head on data track.
kw: Hard Disk drive;read heads;Bit Pattern Magnetic Media;tribology;Lithography;novel materials

title: Combined transcranial direct current stimulation and motor imagery-based robotic arm training for stroke rehabilitation - a feasibility study.
abs: Stroke is the most common cause of adult disability. Current treatments for functional loss of the upper extremity post-stroke remain limited in efficacy, particularly for those with moderate to severe impairment. Previous studies have demonstrated the efficacy of transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) for motor recovery post-stroke, a technique of neuromodulation. Motor imagery is effective to enhance motor recovery, with activation of neural pathways similar to that of motor execution. This treatment is accessible to more severely impaired stroke survivors. Our previous studies have demonstrated feasibility and efficacy of motor imagery-based brain computer interface (MI-BCI) for post-stroke motor impairment, in which motor imagery is detected by surface EEG and translated to execution of the target movement with the aid of an arm robot (MIT-Manus). In this study, we investigate the feasibility of combining robot-assisted MI-BCI training, with tDCS to facilitate post-stroke motor recovery in moderate to severe impairment of upper extremity function. We hypothesise that both tDCS-BCI and sham-BCI will improve motor function in the stroke-affected arm; but that tDCS-BCI will be more effective than sham-BCI. Our secondary aim is to gain insight into the neurophysiological mechanism by comparing the cortical excitability changes following sham-BCI vs tDCS-BCI, using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS).We will conduct a randomized, double-blind sham-controlled crossover study of MI-BCI combined with tDCS (tDCS-BCI) vs MI-BCI with sham-tDCS (sham-BCI). Subjects will undergo 10 sessions of tDCS each lasting 20 minutes, followed by 40 minutes of robot-assisted MI-BCI training at each session. Primary outcome will be functional ability measured by upper extremity component of the Fugl-Meyer Assessment. Secondary outcome measures will be the Box & Block Test, Modified Ashworth Score (measuring spasticity), grip strength and TMS measures of cortical excitability. This study will be important to develop a new and effective treatment (tDCS-BCI) for post-stroke motor impairment.
kw: Transcranial direct current stimulation, Stroke, Motor imagery, Brain-computer interface, Motor recovery, Robotics

title: Role of drug transporters in anthracycline-induced cardiotoxicity – Development of in vitro screening tool for rapid identification of potential cardioprotective agents in cancer therapy
abs: Specific Aims The primary goals of this study are to: (1) examine the role of drug transporters in mediating anthracycline-induced cardiotoxicity; (2) identify potential cardiac transporters responsible for the uptake and efflux of adriamycin, daunomycin and idamycin; (3) identify potential inhibitors (phytochemicals in plant foods and herbs) of the solute carrier transporters for concomitant or sequential administration with anthracyclines in cancer therapy. Hypotheses We hypothesize that a) uptake transporters that are expressed abundantly in the heart play a role in anthracycline-induced cardiotoxicity; and (b) the inhibition of the uptake transporters confers a cardioprotective function. Methodology This pilot project proposes to systematically screen for inhibitors of uptake transporters as cardioprotective agents for mitigating anthracycline-induced cardiotoxicity. Cardiomyocyte cell line is chosen as the in vitro model for rapid screening of inhibitors of drug transporters expressed in the human heart. Cells will be cultured and harvested, and RNA extracted for reverse-transcriptase PCR analysis for measurement of transporter mRNA. The drug transporters found to be expressed abundantly in the cardiomyocyte cell line from the RT-PCR analysis will be examined for protein expression using Western blot analysis. The initial uptake assay for screening of inhibitors will be done using untransfected cardiomyocyte cell line (representative in vitro model of the human heart), and subsequently studied in specific transporters expressed in transfected HEK293 cell line. This will involve incubating the cells with radiolabeled [14C]anthracyclines in the absence or presence of non-radiolabeled test compounds, and measuring the radioactivities of the cell lysates. To ensure that the efficacious effect at the target site is not attenuated in the presence of the inhibitor, drug sensitivity assay will be performed to assess their anti-proliferative activity. Conclusion The identification of candidate compounds as solute carrier transporter inhibitors may ultimately lead to the development of cardioprotective agents against anthracycline-induced cardiotoxicity.
kw: Drug transporters, Anthracyclines, Cancer therapy, Inhibitors, Cardiotoxicity, Cardioprotection

title: An investigation into the efficiency, precision and safety of gene targeting in primary human umbilical cord-lining cells using zinc finger nucleases
abs: Hypothesis By integrating therapeutic transgenes precisely into pre-selected sites, zinc finger nucleases may advance cell therapy towards clinical care.Background Gene therapy is not yet standard of clinical care. The inability of current vectors to target transgenes into safe genomic sites has been associated with oncogenic mutations and fatal leukemias in clinical trials. Zinc-finger nucleases (ZFN) are an elegant approach for achieving highly precise genome modifications. Each ZFN monomer is composed of 3 or 4 zinc fingers in tandem, C-terminally fused to the Fok1 nuclease domain. Finger arrays are tailored to bind DNA sequences at pre-selected sites. Thus ZFN dimers generate a double-stranded DNA break (DSDB) at a unique genomic locus of choice and facilitate transgene integration by homologous recombination. Specific aims We will integrate a construct co-expressing human clotting factor VIII and GFP into the VEGFA locus (upstream of transcription initiation) of primary human umbilical cord-lining epithelial cells (CLEC). Methodology Detailed information on the design of ZFN for this locus is in the public domain and can be reconstructed from non-proprietary reagents. We will evaluate the (a) efficiency; (b) targeting precision; and (c) genotoxic potential of ZFN-mediated transgene integration in CLEC. Efficiency will be assayed by flow cytometric analysis of GFP+ cells in ZFN-modified cultures compared to control unmodified cultures. Targeting accuracy will be determined by sequencing cloned DNA fragments that span the junctions between transgene construct and genome integration sites. Genotoxic potential will be evaluated using biomarkers of DSDB (phosphorylated H2AX), non-homologous end joining (53BP1), in vitro clonogenicity and karyotyping for rearranged chromosomes. Clinical significance If ZFN-mediated transgene integration is accurate and of low genotoxic risk, secretion of factor VIII antigen and procoagulant activity will be assayed. This will set the stage for future testing of ex vivo-modified primary cells as in vivo bioimplants for haemophilia A treatment.
kw: cellular therapy, integration sites, umbilical cord-lining cells, zinc finger nuclease, homologous recombination, haemophilia

title: INTRAUTERINE GENE THERAPY FOR FACTOR X DEFICIENCY IN NON HUMAN PRIMATE
abs: Monogeneic diseases such as lysosomal enzyme deficiency, urea-cycle disorders, alpha-thalassaemia and inherited bleeding disorders including Factor VII and X deficiency, have a perinatal or fetal onset of pathology / end-organ damage. In order to avert this, therapeutic strategies must be directed to the developing fetus through gene transfer or stem cell mediated approaches. Intrauterine gene transfer (IUGT) results in long term production of the defective/absent protein, and capitalises on the ontological advantages of a high vector-to-cell ratio, unique access to fetal stem cell compartments, and predisposes the individual to immunological tolerance of the introduced protein. We have previously demonstrated lifelong correction of Factor IX deficiency in murine models through IUGT, and now seek funding to test this out in a pre-clinical non-human primate (NHP) model, which shares similar immune and haematological ontogeny, as well as a haemochorial placenta to humans. Using congenital factor X deficiency (CFXD) as a model of a perinatally-lethal monogenic disease, we hypothesise that a single IUGT of self-complementary Adeno-Associated Virus (scAAV) will lead to safe long term expression of Factor X at therapeutic levels in a clinically relevant NHP model of human reproduction. Fetal macaques will be transduced systemically with scAAV-hFX at either 0.9 or 0.4 gestation through the intrahepatic vein, and delivered by Caesarean section. The transgene expression (FX), immune response and biodistribution of the vector will be sought longitudinally in both treated offspring and dam. In addition, the phenomenon of trans-placental passage of vectors, transduction of maternal tissue and gonads will allow several questions regarding the safety of IUGT to be answered.This work evaluates a novel strategy of IUGT for a perinatally-lethal disease in a clinically relevant model which will be of importance to other disorders that will benefit from IUGT to avert permanent organ damage or infant death.

title: TRPC6 and Its Interactions in Genetic and Immune-mediated Focal and Segmental Glomerulosclerosis
abs: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) causes chronic kidney disease and renal failure, and occurs due to podocyte injury. Mutations in Transient Receptor Potential Cation Channel 6 (TRPC6), a calcium channel, were identified to cause hereditary FSGS. So far, only seven mutations have been reported. Four of these cause alterations in calcium influx, while others do not. The exact FSGS pathomechanism by TRPC6 mutation is unknown. In our preliminary studies, we found one Chinese family carrying a novel TRPC6 R68W missense mutation which causes alterations of calcium influx when transfected into human embryonic kidney(HEK) cells, suggesting a gain of function. There is variable penetrance which may be explained by concomitant nephrin and podocin polymorphisms. We hypothesize mutant TRPC6 and concomitant nephrin/podocin polymorphisms alter interactions and signaling at podocyte slit diaphragms, and that cytokines in immune FSGS cause upregulation or increased function of TRPC6. The specific objectives are to:1.Co-transfect podocin/nephrin polymorphisms with wild-type/mutant TRPC6R68W into HEK293 cells and examine TRPC6 function by whole-cell patch-clamp technique, and to perform co-immunoprecipitation of TRPC6 with FLAG-tagged nephrin/podocin.2.Obtain podocyte cultures from TRPC6-/- mice, transfect them with mutant TRPC6R68W, and analyse them using patch clamp system and molecular studies.3.Generate a transgenic mouse with podocyte-specific expression of TRPC6R68W. This will be crossed with TRPC6-/- mouse. Phenotypic and molecular analysis, including quantitative PCR and gene expression profiling, of kidneys and glomeruli will be performed. 4.Study the effect of Th1 and Th2 cytokines on wildtype TRPC6 function in podocytes using whole cell patch clamp. This study aims to study if nephrin/podocin polymorphisms can explain the variable penetrance of TRPC6 mutations. This allows the nephrologist to identify at-risk patients. We attempt to identify pathomechanisms by which TRPC6 mutations cause FSGS. This allows for identification of potential therapeutic targets of TRPC6-associated and other forms of FSGS.
kw: TRPC6, glomerulosclerosis, nephrotic syndrome, podocin, nephrin, patch-clamp electrophysiology

title: Study to provide evidence for tumor-specific repression of Mn-superoxide dismutase by PPAR? in human breast carcinoma cells – a new method to eliminate cancer cells directly via induction of apoptosis or indirectly by sensitization to chemo-based therapies.
abs: Recent experimental evidence linking siRNA-suppression of mitochondrial manganese-dependent superoxide dismutase (MnSOD) expression to decrease in breast cancer cells’ invasive property and sensitization to anti-cancer drugs, together with our preliminary results showing targeted silencing of MnSOD decreased breast cancer cells’ ability to form colonies and increased cells’ sensitization to cisplatin, this proposal attempts to present MnSOD repression as a novel target for intervention.Incidentally, increased expression of peroxisome proliferator-activated gamma (PPAR) has also been reported in a variety of cancer cells, including breast cancers, and ligand-induced activation inhibits proliferation in a variety of cancer cells in vitro and in vivo. The present proposal provides an interesting association between these two proteins by identifying potential PPAR binding sites in the promoter region of MnSOD gene. Ligand-induced activation of PPAR resulted in downregulation of MnSOD mRNA and protein levels in breast cancer cell lines expressing high levels of PPAR, but not in non-cancerous cells expressing low levels of PPAR. As preliminary proof of concept, we also show a marked decrease in MnSOD expression in tissues obtained from PPAR ligand treated mice.Therefore, in this project we propose to confirm the effects of 15dPGJ2 and synthetic PPAR ligands on MnSOD gene expression in a wider panel of breast cell lines, patients’ tissue samples and mouse breast xenograft models. We will also assess the mechanism(s) involved in the repression of MnSOD gene expression by PPAR in ERa-negative cells. We provide evidence in ERa-positive cells, ERa switches out PPAR activity on MnSOD expression and its anti-tumor effect. Hence, we will determine if activated ER interacts with PPAR to antagonize its repressive activity at MnSOD promoter. As proof of concept, we will question if MnSOD repression is an effector mechanism in tumor cell growth arrest upon PPAR activation and if PPAR-induced repression of MnSOD increases breast cancer cells’ sensitivity to anti-cancer drugs in cell lines and breast carcinoma xenografts in nude mice.
kw: PPAR? and MnSOD regulation, Breast cancer treatment, ER? and PPAR? crosstalk, Anti-tumor action, Anti-estrogens, Breast xenograft model

title: Studies on the anticancer effects of Human Wharton’s Jelly Stem Cells (hWJSCs)
abs: It was recently reported that human Wharton’s jelly stem cells (hWJSCs) completely abolished mammary adenocarcinomas in immunodeficient mice when injected intratumourally and intravenously compared to sham-transplanted controls. In pilot studies we observed that hWJSCs and its conditioned medium (hWJSC-CM) induced apoptosis in breast, colorectal and liver cancer cells in two dimensional (2D) coculture. In a three dimensional (3D) anchorage independent in vitro system we observed that hWJSCs and hWJSC-CM ablated green fluorescence protein tagged hepatocarcinoma (GFP-HepG2) cells growing in 60-day old hESC-derived embryoid bodies when microinjected into them. When we studied several hWJSC lines we noted that their behaviour was influenced by culture conditions. Furthermore, their transcriptome profiles showed several proapoptotic and tumour suppressor genes that were highly expressed and it is unclear how this translates to the anticancer effect observed. The hWJSC appears to be a unique stem cell in that it does not induce tumorigenesis in immunodeficient mice and at the same time has the propensity to bring about apoptosis in proliferating cancer cells. The central question that remains unanswered is whether this anticancer behaviour is in fact the true intrinsic property of this novel stem cell type (direct contact or cytokine mediated), or if this is an artifact from the different culture conditions used in these experiments to date. The influence of the derivation protocol and culture conditions, and specificity of anticancer effects of hWJSCs to certain cancer types have not been studied in depth and the mechanisms behind the homing signals and anticancer behaviour have not yet been identified. We propose to examine if hWJSCs and hWJSC-CM exhibit bona fide anticancer properties in a stepwise translational manner in two in vitro systems (2D and 3D) and in vivo in the SCID mouse model, and elucidate the mechanisms underlying this anticancer effect using genomics and proteomics tools.
kw: Wharton’s jelly stem cells, Anticancer effects, Mechanism, Conditioned medium, Tumourigenesis, Cell based therapies

title: Molecular and functional characterization of hydrogen sulphide effects in the area of sexual medicine
abs: Hydrogen sulphide (H2S) has been identified as the third endogenous gasotransmitter similar to carbon monoxide and nitric oxide (NO) with physiological roles as neuromediator and smooth muscle relaxant. In our earlier studies conducted in male and female animal models, H2S displayed significant vasodilatory and smooth muscle relaxant effects suggestive of an endogenous functional role in sexual function (Srilatha B, Adaikan PG, Hu L, Li L, Moore PK, 2006; 2007; 2009). These physiopharmacological effects were mediated through cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP), NO- cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) and adenosine triphosphate-sensitive potassium (K+ATP) channels. Furthermore, H2S was found to be endogenously formed in these tissues through the presence and activity of two H2S generating enzymes, cystathionine gamma-lyase (CSE) and cystathionine beta-synthase (CBS). Based on these observations, we believe that the H2S pathway is capable of playing a positive role in the male and female sexual responses and our next step would be to explore its exact molecular mechanisms and interactions at relevant cellular pathways for an extensive comprehension and identification of possible therapeutic targets.In this proposal, using tissues from male and female treatment groups, we aim to quantify and compare the respective H2S effects at isoforms of nitric oxide synthases. In addition, the possible interactions of H2S pathway with cAMP and cGMP binding protein kinases, phosphodiesterases and vasorelaxant kallikrein-kinins and vascular endothelial growth factor will be evaluated. Further information will be obtained through the estimations of enzyme(s) and by-products of L-cysteine metabolism and likely conversion of H2S to nitrosothiol in the presence of nitric oxide. In view of the promising pioneering results of sulphide’s role in sexual function, we are attempting to completely unravel its molecular and cellular mechanistic effects from the standpoint of therapeutic exploitation. With this understanding of the H2S and NO synthase interactions and the metabolic reactions of H2S, we can achieve our therapeutic aim through possible endogenous manipulation at any level of its physiological pathway.

title: Development of Bordetella pertussis as a live attenuated pertussis vaccine and vaccine delivery system
abs: Despite high vaccination coverage, pertussis or whooping cough remains endemic and reports of increasing incidence worldwide have been accumulating for the past twenty years. The waning and/or sub-optimal efficacy of the current pertussis vaccines in adults have been proposed to account for resurgence. Antigenic shift and adaptation of the circulating strains to the vaccines may also be involved, thus calling for the development of a new generation of pertussis vaccines.Live attenuated vaccines have been successfully used in humans against various diseases. Natural infection with B. pertussis is known to induce strong and long-lasting immunity that wanes later than vaccine-induced immunity. A live attenuated B. pertussis vaccine might therefore represent an interesting alternative or complement to the current acellular pertussis vaccines. Moreover, the potential of live attenuated B. pertussis as a nasal delivery system of heterologous vaccines has been explored and represents a promising approach for targeting respiratory diseases.A highly attenuated B. pertussis strain, named BPZE1, has recently been described in which three toxins have been inactivated. However, BPZE1 bacteria still produce the adenylate cyclase (AC), one of the major toxins responsible for the cytotoxic activity of the pathogen. The use of live BPZE1 bacteria in neonates or immunocompromised individuals may thus not meet the necessary safety criteria. Here we propose to further attenuate the BPZE1 strain upon deletion of the AC-encoding gene. The adherence/invasion properties, cytotoxic activity and ability to induce cell apoptosis will be determined in this attenuated strain. Bacterial lung colonization efficacy will be evaluated in the mouse model. Lung inflammation will be examined by histopathology and cytokines measurement. Furthermore, the safety profile of the bacteria will be addressed in immuno-compromised animals. Finally the immunogenicity and protective efficacy of this newly attenuated B. pertussis strain will be assessed and compared to the current acellular pertussis vaccines

title: Evaluation of a skin patch functionalized with anti-inflammatory peptide embedded micro-emulsion carrier for arthritis treatment: a translational study for therapeutic intervention
abs: The anti-inflammatory peptide that we have developed inhibits proinflammatory molecules, and suppressed inflammation and bone erosion more effectively than existing antirheumatic drugs. We aim to confirm the hypothesis that this novel peptide when combined with the microemulsion gel (MEG) drug carrier can be targeted to inflamed sites most effectively and with less irritation to experimentally induced arthritic rats via transdermal application. This will open up interesting perspectives for targeting of a peptide drug to arthritic tissues with reduced toxicity and side effects, thus creating the new knowledge that can be translated into clinical use. Our approach includes (1) Functionalization of the transdermal system to obtain desired characteristics of the formulation for optimal delivery; (2) Ex vivo skin permeation studies for evaluation of skin patch delivery and release of peptide from the formulation to the target (synovial fibroblasts); (3) Selection of non-cytotoxic peptide concentration for subsequent use in animal studies by means of cytotoxicity/proliferation assays on cultured human and animal arthritis rheumatoid arthritis synovial fibroblasts after drug exposure; (4) Evaluation of the effectiveness of varying doses (10-30 mg/kg) and treatment schedules of the formulation patch, topically applied on the inflamed joints of animals to moderate the arthritis progression of adjuvant-induced arthritic rats; (5) Assessment of treatment effects on synovial inflammation, bone erosion and cartilage destruction on the basis of clinical and histological scorings, articular cartilage integrity and osteoclast formation; (6) measurement of changes in the disease activity, and plasma levels of disease markers and biomarkers for cartilage degradation in blood and/or urine to achieve a better evaluation of the response of the animals. The preclinical data from this project may generate important scientific knowledge which can lead to drug discovery and as tools for biomedical research with a short term clinical impact possibly evident within the next 3-5 years.
kw: Anti-inflammatory peptide, Microemulsion gel (MEG), Rheumatoid arthritis (RA), Skin patch, Transdermal application, Adjuvant induced arthritis model

title: The role of sphingolipids in the pancreatic beta cell
abs: Recent studies suggest that sphingolipids may have important regulatory roles in the survival and function of pancreatic beta-cells. Ceramides, which are produced in response to inflammatory cytokines (e.g. tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-alpha), interleukin 1, etc.), have been shown to induce beta-cell apoptosis and inhibit insulin secretion. Gangliosides, which are glycosylated forms of ceramide, are putative autoantigens involved in the induction of insulitis and type 1 diabetes. And, sphingosine 1-phosphate, a derivative of ceramide produced by various growth factors, has been shown to promote beta-cell survival and growth, perhaps by opposing effects of its precursor, ceramide. Despite these isolated studies, the importance of sphingolipids as regulators of beta-cell growth, proliferation, and function has not been studied in detail, either in isolated cells or in intact animals. Herein we propose to initiate studies investigating the role of sphingolipids in beta-cell function. First, using pharmacological inhibitors and novel knockout mice that are incapable of making ceramides, we will determine the consequence of modulating sphingolipid levels on beta cell function in rodents. Second, we will investigate the molecular mechanisms through which ceramide and sphingosine 1-phosphate divergently regulate cell survival, while evaluating the role of either as a modulator of cytokine or free fatty acid-induced cell death. Ultimately these studies will help reveal whether modulating beta-cell sphingolipid levels is beneficial for blocking beta-cell death during transplantation or preventing the onset of type 1 or type 2 diabetes.
kw: Insulin, Beta cell, Sphingolipid, Diabetes, Ceramide, Lipotoxicity

title: Characterization of the Hepatitis B virus (HBV) in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) patients
abs: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) ranks amongst the top ten fatal cancers in Singapore due to its high frequency and limited treatment options. In Singapore, it is the 3rd most frequent cancer and 2nd leading cause of cancer deaths. Here, ~80% of all HCCs occur in HBV-infected individuals. Chronic-HBV infection is epidemiologically linked to HCC where these individuals carry 20-100-fold increased risk for developing HCC compared to uninfected persons. However, the association between chronic HBV infection and HCC remains poorly understood. A significant feature of chronic HBV infection is the integration of HBV DNA fragments into different locations within the host DNA which was implicated to play ‘cis’ and/or ‘trans’ roles in hepatocarcinogenesis either via insertional-mutagenesis or the retention/expression of the original/ modified HBV proteins that interfere with cellular processes leading to tumorigenesis. Chimeric human-HBV related transcripts/proteins have been identified. Due to technological limitations, it was previously not feasible to fully/comprehensively characterize all possible HBV integrants/transcripts in 100s of HCC patients reasonably which was why previous reports identify/characterize only the most common HBV integrant(s) in only few patients. The advent of the next-generation, massively-parallel, ultra-high-throughput genome-sequencer make it possible to attempt to fully/comprehensively characterize all the possible HBV integrants/transcripts (including chimeric transcripts) in a large number of HCC patients simultaneously and within reasonable period/cost which is the primary aim of this proposal. This proposal also aims to functionally characterize selected interesting chimeric transcripts to delineate their role in tumorigenesis. Fully characterizing the HBV DNA, integrants and transcript in Singaporean HBV-associated HCC patients will enable one to identify HBV chimeras/variants that may be associated with poor prognosis and help us elucidate their role in tumorigenesis. This may serve as a potential prognostic tool that may guide doctors in recommending treatment options. It can also facilitate the design of therapy for treatment of HBV-associated-HCC.

title: A new biodegradable, sustained-release drug delivery system in a rabbit model – betamethasone, prednisolone acetate and ganciclovir drug delivery trial
abs: AimsTo develop a new, self-bending, biodegradable microfilm for ocular drug delivery over 12 months– using 3 drugs separately: ganciclovir, betamethasone and prednisolone acetate for the treatment of ocular inflammation and infectionsHypotheses Multilayered biodegradable microfilms are able to deliver a steady, sustained concentration of drugs, which may be superior to single-layered films. Intrascleral insertion of this film may allow better penetration of drugs into the eye. A special surgical technique may facilitate removal in adverse events or re-insertion of a new film if required. Methodology The study is divided into two phases: The in-vitro study involves producing the films using PLLA, PLGA and PCL, with the various drug dispersed separately in each film. These films spontaneously bend to the curvature of eyes when exposed to body temperatures. Drug release profiles are studied for 12 months. The in-vivo study involves intra-scleral insertion of the drug-loaded films into 30 rabbits and monitored over 24 weeks. Rabbits are sacrificed and their eyes are analyzed to produce drug release profiles in various parts of the eye. Approach and clinical significance Sustained ocular drug delivery is the ‘holy grail’ of ocular therapeutics. Corticosteroids are used to control ocular inflammation in patients post-operatively, post-trauma; and in patients with severe ocular infections and uveitis. Inflammation is also believed to play in a part in age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and ocular vascular disease. Corticosteroids thus plays major role in reducing ocular morbidity and blindness. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is an emerging infection that causes blindness through corneal decompensation, glaucoma and retinitis. Treatment requires long, sustained therapeutic levels of ganciclovir. The development of a new slow-release biodegradable microfilm will allow long-term treatment of the above-mentioned diseases that cause ocular inflammation leading to blindness. This microfilm may also deliver other drugs to treat glaucoma, ocular infections or diabetic retinopathy in future.
kw: Ocular inflammation, Biodegradable drug delivery system, Steroids

title: The role of SCF E3 ubiquitin ligases in cancer
abs: F-box proteins are important substrate receptor proteins of Cullin1-based E3 ubiquitin ligases. They are known to recruit many substrates related to cell signalling, transcription and the cell cycle to the E3 ligase complex, leading to their ubiquitination and subsequent degradation by the 26S proteasome. F-box protein mediated ubiquitination is thus of great importance for the normal function of the cell. Three F-box proteins, Skp2, Fbxw7 and TrCP, are known to play a major role in cancer. Altered expression or activity of these F-box proteins causes or promotes the formation of different cancers by increasing or decreasing the stability of its specific protein substrates. The role that the additional approximately 70 members of the F-box protein family play in cancer is currently not well characterized. We therefore plan to compare the mRNA expression of candidate F-box proteins in normal and cancer tissue. We hypothesize that altered expression of F-box proteins can promote tumorigenesis via changes in the stability of substrate proteins. Therefore, we are planning to complement these studies by efforts to identify substrates of F-box proteins with altered expression in cancer, using a number of different approaches. In future research, we will then validate these substrates, determine the mechamisms through which they are targeted for F-box protein dependent ubiquitination and characterize the role they play in cancer. Given the emerging role of the ubiquitin-proteasome system as an important target for cancer therapy, we believe that our studies would help to identify and validate novel drug targets.
kw: cancer, drug targets, ubiquitin, proteomics

title: Characterization of a novel non-canonical Lys-tRNA synthetase (LysRS) pathway that links extracellular signals to activate MITF and gene transcription in dendritic cells (DC)
abs: Microphthalmia-associated transcription factor (MITF) is a major regulator of Melanocyte and Osteoclast development. MITF-deficient (mi/mi) mice are also mast cell deficient and NK cell impaired but nothing is known about the function of MITF in other immune cells. MITF deficient mice, in common with Microphthalmia patients, have small eyes and are susceptible to infection and cardiac hypertrophy. In mast cells, a novel non-canonical Lys-tRNA synthetase (LysRS) pathway responds to extracellular signals to activate MITF and subsequent gene transcription. LysRS production of a diadenosine phosphate (Ap4A) co-messenger releases MITF from inhibition by the histidine triad nucleotide-binding protein-1 (Hint1). We hypothesize that the LysRS signalling pathway is conserved in other immune cells such as dendritic cells (DC) and T cells, and that it regulates DC function. In preliminary experiments we observed that Ap4A and MITF were expressed in CD4 and CD8 T cells and DC, and that it was expressed at the highest levels in DC. The aim of this project is to investigate the LysRS signalling pathway in DC using primary DC from normal and MITF deficient mice and DC cell lines. TRACP5 will be studied as a reporter gene as it is under the direct control of MITF and has been reported to have important effects on DC function. Our aims are: (i) to characterize the LysRS pathway in DC, (ii) to identify the different stimuli that activate this pathway in DC; (iii) to elucidate the regulatory roles of Ap4A hydrolase and Hint1 in the DC LysRS signalling; (iv) and to determine the consequences of LysRS signalling on DC function. The development of effective intervention strategies that regulate this pathway may lead to the development of novel treatment for immune disorders.
kw: MITF, Dendritic cell, Hint1, TRACP5, Ap4A, interleukin-12

title: Epigenetic control of fibrosis – molecular and preclinical characterization of the recently discovered effects of the histone deacetylase inhibitor suberoylanilide hydroxamic acid (SAHA)
abs: Fibrosis of organs and around implants poses a substantial disease burden globally and in SE Asia. Histopathologically, fibrosis is an excessive accumulation of collagen affected by myofibroblasts and this can occur in any tissue which is exposed to acute injury or chronic insult. The biosynthesis of collagen and its posttranslational modifications are well characterized, and so are the growth factor pathways (most prominent: TGFb1) that fuel fibrosis. Yet, no effective antifibrotic drug is in the market, the urgent clinical need for fibrosis treatment remains unmet. In an indication discovery approach we have firstly described (Wang et al 2009) the potential antifibrotic effects of suberoylanilide hydroxamic acid (SAHA): SAHA abrogates TGFb1 effects in normal and pathological fibroblast lines. It prevents their transition into myofibroblasts, normalizes collagen deposition without inducing apoptosis, inhibits fibroblast proliferation, and downregulates inflammatory cytokine. As SAHA is a broad spectrum inhibitor of histone deacetylases we want to single out enzymes that are responsible for the SAHA effects, and exactly where SAHA interferes with the TGFb signaling cascade, and in which time window SAHA is most effective in inhibiting fibroblast-myofibroblast and epithelial-mesenchymal transition. As SAHA leads to hyperacetylaton of a-tubulin, a cytoskeletal component in fibroblasts, we will investigate mechanical and locomotional properties of SAHA-treated myofibroblasts as this might reveal an additional therapeutic facet to fibrosis treatment. In a bid to augment SAHA’s effects we will investigate its combination with FDA-approved DNA methyltransferase inhibitors. The obtained results will be fed into an international collaborative preclinical study in a mouse model of heterotypic trachea transplantation. This model emulates a local fibrotic state without the need to induce pathology with toxic chemicals. Because SAHA is an FDA-approved cancer drug, we would expect that the data derived from this study can be translated faster from the bench to the bedside.
kw: epigenetics, histone deacetylases inhibitors, SAHA, fibrosis

title: The effects of Thymosin-?4 on skeletal myoblast migration, proliferation, and survival
abs: Thymosin-ß4 is an important mediator of cell survival, migration, and proliferation. It is the most abundant member of the ß-thymosin family in mammalian tissue and is regarded as the main G-actin sequestering peptide. Studies have shown that Thy- ß4 is up-regulated in regenerating muscle fibers after an injury. However, the effects of Thy-ß4 on skeletal myoblast (SkM) are yet known. The current study aims to investigate the effects of Thy-ß4 on SkM proliferation, migration, and survival. This has significant impact on SkM transplantation. It is a known fact that massive early cell death associated with poor donor cell survival is a limiting factor in the success of SkM transplantation. Most donor SkMs die within 48 hours after implantation. The accelerated death of SkMs is related to maladaptation or anoxic conditions and inflammatory response at the site of cell injection. Thus, improving donor cell survival is a key factor in the success of SkM therapy. We hypothesize that Thy-ß4 can enhance SkM proliferation, migration, and survival, and thus lead to the success of SkM therapy. Upon completion of the project, we hope to provide new insights to the effects of Thy-ß4 on SkM survival, proliferation and migration, which can improve the efficacy of skeletal muscle repair and regeneration. It will also provide the scientific basis for which Thy-ß4 can be use as an agent to promote proliferation, migration, and survival of transplanted SkM. The enhancement of these three parameters will improve the efficacy of SkM therapy and lead to successful muscle repair and generation. This will have more widespread applications and potential for commercialization as a new therapeutic modality for treatment of skeletal muscle disease.
kw: Skeletal myoblast, Cell survival, Muscle repair/regeneration, Cell migration, Cell proliferation

title: Application of RNA interference (RNAi) technology in novel controlled release gene/drug delivery systems for synergetic therapy of glioma
abs: This research proposal aims to demonstrate the promising application of DNA vector-based RNA interference (RNAi) technology in developing innovative therapeutic agents, together with controlled release strategy, to evaluate the synergetic therapeutic effects for glioma treatment. Combination of chemotherapy, anti-invasive therapy and anti-angiogenic therapy in a synergetic fashion is a highly challenging field to be explored in tumor therapy. RNAi technique, with its inherent supreme specificity in downregulating endogenous genes, is proposed in this study as new concept gene therapy, to ensure the curative efficacy. While utilizing controlled release systems, the therapeutic effects are expected to be sustainable for an extended period.A variety of implantable, biodegradable and biocompatible gene/drug delivery devices in the form of micro-/nanofibers, core/shell microparticles, and co-axial microparticles, will be fabricated using techniques such as electrospinning, co-axial Electohydrodynamic Atomization (EHDA) and co-axial electrospray. The dosage forms will then be characterized both in vitro and in vivo. Their efficacy will be evaluated in view of the objective function in loading multiple agents of different hydrophilicity and engineering the favorable release profile to achieve better therapy.Evaluation of the therapeutic systems both in vitro and in vivo, would provide qualitative and quantitative insight for the development of optimal controlled release devices. In vitro test applied in cultured cells will be the initial phase before animal experiments. In vivo study, with the proposed intracranial animal model for glioma treatment, will utilize the state-of-the-art in vivo bioluminescence imaging (BLI) system to better monitor tumor regression with the treatment in living animals in real time. Synergetic therapeutic effects will be investigated and compared with individual therapy and control, from the aspects of survivability, tumor volume, gene/drug penetration, together with the additional real-time vasculature imaging study. These studies altogether, will allow the rationale gene/drug delivery system design in the end of this project.
kw: Gene therapy, Glioma, Drug delivery, In vivo, RNA interference, Synergetic therapy

title: Platelet Gene Expression Profiling of Patients with Poor Response to P2Y12 Receptor Inhibition
abs: Clopidogrel, a platelet P2Y12 receptor inhibitor, is universally administered to patients with myocardial infarction and to patients undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention. However, 25-30 percent of patients fail to achieve adequate platelet inhibition, termed high post-treatment platelet reactivity (HPPR). Recent data showed a strong association between HPPR and downstream adverse events, confirming its importance as a pharmacologic phenotype. Apart from a loss of function (LOF) polymorphism of the hepatic CYP2C19 enzyme system, which accounts for only 20% of the variability in platelet inhibition, biological factors influencing clopidogrel response heterogeneity remain largely unidentified. The ability of gene expression profiling to accurately predict the chemotherapeutic response in hematological malignancies is proof-of-concept for the broader application of this technology to the study of platelet pharmacobiology. Traditional pharmacodynamic measures quantify treatment response in a linear uni-dimensional fashion while CYP2C19 genotyping estimates the treatment response in a more limited categorical fashion, but these lack the power and multidimensionality of expression profiling. We will compare the platelet transcriptome among 25 patients with HPPR and 25 without HPPR receiving clopidogrel prior to elective angiography at 2 levels: a targeted analysis comparing differential expression between classes, informed by previously annotated platelet-specific mRNA sequences, and an unbiased analysis identifying platelet mRNA signatures predicting class membership. Individual genes identified in the targeted analysis will be biochemically validated with quantitative polymerase chain reaction, while RNA signatures from the unbiased analysis will be statistically validated with leave-one-out cross validation. We hypothesise that patients with HPPR express a unique set of platelet mRNA transcripts, compared to patients without HPPR, and that platelet gene expression signatures discriminate HPPR with high fidelity. This proposal presents a novel means of investigating platelet factors regulating treatment response and identifying unique RNA signatures to inform future risk prediction studies and the investigation of personalised antiplatelet strategies.
kw: Platelets, Clopidogrel, Case-control, Gene expression, Platelet function tests, Bioinformatics

title: Phenotyping Asian Macular Diseases – a prospective functional and angiographic study of the clinical course of three common acquired retinal conditions in an Asian population
abs: Acquired macular diseases, including age-related macular degeneration (AMD), polypoidal choroidalvasculopathy (PCV) and central serous chorioretinopathy (CSCR), are common causes of vision lossworldwide. There is accumulating evidence that their phenotype differs between Asians and Caucasians.PCV, for example, is a more frequent presentation of exudative maculopathy than neovascular AMD inAsians, to the extent PCV is often referred to as the “Asian form of AMD”. CSCR is also more frequentwith more visually damaging sequelae in Asians. In Caucasian populations, certain genetic andcardiovascular risk factors have been associated with AMD and macular disease, although such riskfactors have not been studied in detail in Asian populations. Few data exist on the clinical characteristicsand course of Asian macular conditions, hampering development of treatment strategies.This proposal will be the first to prospectively investigate clinical characteristics (presentation, clinicalfeatures, environmental and genetic risk factors and clinical course) of three inter-related conditions in anAsian population. We will recruit 300 cases (100 AMD, 100 PCV and 100 CSCR) using standardprotocols to obtain clinical characteristics and standardized fluorescein/indocyanine green angiographicsigns. We will determine associations between a comprehensive range of risk factors (including smoking,cardiovascular risk factors, socio-economic status, metabolic disease, body mass index) of theseconditions with 900 age-matched population-based controls in Singapore (Singapore Epidemiology ofEye Diseases [SEED]) and 900 controls from Australia (Blue Mountains Eye Study [BMES]). This study isalso the first to use questionnaires on functioning and quality of life, validated using Rasch analysis, andmodern psychometric parameters in an Asian population. Blood specimens will be collected to establisha serum and DNA biobank for future biomarker and genetic studies (later funding applications).This study will fill existing knowledge gaps regarding the phenotype, risk factors and impacts of threecommon acquired macular diseases in Asians.
kw: Age-related macular degeneration, Central serous chorioretinopathy, Angiography, Polypoidal Choroidal Vasculopathy, Natural history, Quality of Life

title: G Protein Signaling in Oncogenesis and Metastasis
abs: Members of the G12 subfamily of heterotrimeric G proteins play important roles in cell proliferativeand developmental pathways, and have also been implicated in oncogenic transformation. We havefound that G12 proteins are upregulated as prostate and breast cancers progress to an aggressivephenotype, and that G12 signaling specifically promotes cancer cell invasion and metastasis both invitro and in vivo. Our hypothesis is that G12 signaling contributes to aberrant proliferation and is animportant regulator of cancer cell invasion and metastasis. In this application, we detail a series ofexperimental approaches to rigorously test this important hypothesis. With numerous direct bindingpartners of G12 proteins now identified, the key to elucidating the mechanisms involved in their abilityto control proliferation and metastasis will be to dissect the signaling pathways controlled by G12 andto determine which of these pathways contribute to specific cell biologic and pathophysiologicprocesses. We have developed a unique set of reagents and experimental systems to facilitateapproaching this problem in a comprehensive way; one that should allow precise determination ofspecific molecular interactions involved. In Aim 1, we will dissect the signaling mechanismscontributing to G12-mediated tumorigenesis and cancer cell invasion in cell-based systems. In Aim 2,we will investigate the mode of tumor cell invasion induced by G12 signaling. In Aim 3, we will employmouse models to elucidate the specific G12-mediated signaling axes that contribute to cancer cellinvasion and metastasis in vivo. Identification of the precise signaling events that contribute to theseprocesses would then enable the targeted inhibition of specific G12 signaling pathways as a rigoroustest of their importance in a particular process, and open avenues to the use of such targetedstrategies to interdict pathophysiologies dependent on aberrant G12 signaling.
kw: G protein, Rho GTPase, Metastasis, G protein-coupled receptors, Cell invasion, Xenograft models

title: Bioactive Scaffold with Sustained Release of Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor for Vascular Tissue Engineering in Peripheral Arterial Disease
abs: Lower limb peripheral arterial disease (PAD) caused by the obstruction of arteries can lead to death of tissue and even amputation. Surgical bypass is the most common treatment but with limitations. We hypothesize that a biocompatible hydrophilic tissue engineering scaffolds with sustained release of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), promoting arteriogenesis to treat both macro- and micro-circulation occlusion can improve the recovery of lower limb PAD. Many PAD patients have both macro- and micro-vascular disease. We will study two bioactive scaffolds with sustained delivery of VEGF for PAD treatments. Hydrophilic polymers to be used in our study, polysaccharides and poly (vinyl-alcohol), are advantageous in the design of vascular prosthesis because of their non-antigenicity and non-immunogenicity. The poly(vinyl alcohol) tubular graft can serve as a bypass for macro-circulation occlusion, while presenting both sustained release of VEGF for the recovery of the micro-occlusion and nanotopography to enhance endothelialisation of the graft. A second bioactive graft will be an injectable polysaccharide scaffold that can sustained deliver VEGF in a minimally invasive procedure. In this exploratory project, we aim to verify our hypothesis that sustained delivery of growth factors can improve the recovery of PAD caused by macro- and micro-circulation occlusion in a rat model, and also to explore the therapeutic potentials of the two scaffolds. Our preliminary studies have demonstrated the feasibility and potentials of the bioactive scaffolds. As we aspire to identify a better treatment to improve the healing of PAD, any improvement observed in the ischemia observed in this exploratory study could help us further improve the bioactive scaffold for therapeutic delivery. This study will enable us to develop the study into a larger animal model in future, and eventually assessed in a clinical trial, to be developed into a pharmaceutical product for patients.
