title: Panning for gold: identification of novel stem-cell specific microRNAs
abs: Panning for gold: identification of novel stem-cell specific microRNAs MicroRNAs play an important role in the regulation of cellular processes, including differentiation and cell fate determination. The premise of this project is that currently known microRNAs were expressed in relative abundance in the cell lines and whole tissues they were cloned from. We hypothesize that many microRNAs have therefore eluded identification, especially those with an expression restricted to a rare cell type like tissue stem cells. The combination of our expertise in stem cell isolation and validation, microRNA-bioinformatics and microRNA-biology puts us in a unique position to sieve out stem-cell specific microRNAs. The frequency of stem cells in the mouse mammary gland is approximately 1 in 2000, and we propose to enrich this stem cell population a 100-fold by FACS sorting and subsequently sequence the small RNA fraction. To increase our chances of identifying (novel) microRNAs, we will examine whether these sequences contain one or more of ~44,000 potential microRNA precursors that have previously been predicted by a pattern recognition-based algorithm. The top 10 of potential microRNA loci that show the highest enrichment in the stem cell fraction compared to the bulk of mammary epithelial cells will be functionally validated. To that end we will clone the predicted precursor sequences and test them for proper processing and microRNA function in reporter assays. The expression of bona-fide microRNAs will be analyzed in young mammary glands and glands depleted for stem cells to confirm their exclusive expression in stem cells in vivo. A stem cell-specific microRNA would provide an invaluable tool, both to mark stem cells by using the stem-cell specific microRNA promoter and to study the role of the microRNA in regulating stemness of normal and tumor cells.
kw: microRNA, In silico discovery, In vivo assays, Tissue stem cells, Mammary gland

title: Lumbar spinal canal stenosis: Expression and functional investigations on a library of different chondroitin sulphate molecules in normal and hypertrophic ligamentum flavum
abs: Low back pain is one of the commonest orthopaedic conditions in Singapore and worldwide, and can be severely disabling. An important pathology in low back pain is lumbar spinal canal stenosis, and its primary cause is ligamentum flavum hypertrophy. Chondroitin sulphate is a long, highly anionic glycosaminoglycan with differential sulphation of its disaccharide subunits, made up of glucuronate and N-acetylgalactosamine residues. In addition to a structural role, chondroitin sulphate regulates cellular behaviour and modulates the production of extracellular matrix molecules and signalling factors. It is present in the ligamentum flavum, and increases with advancing age. Our previously published studies have shown that different chondroitin sulphate species can have diametrically opposite actions on cellular behaviour. Thus, the aims of this project are to compare the expression patterns of a library of different chondroitin sulphate molecules in lumbar spinal canal stenosis patients with and without ligamentum flavum hypertrophy, and to determine the biological effects of various chondroitin sulphate species on the ligamentum flavum. These aims will be achieved through immunohistochemical studies of clinical samples, as well as in vitro cultures of ligamentum flavum cells. The results will be correlated with clinical parameters of disease severity and disability. The project will exploit cross-disciplinary expertise, capitalising on the collaboration between scientists and clinicians to ensure clinical relevance and to promote bench to bedside research. The overall goal of this project is to discover important markers of disease severity that can be applied towards patient care in the clinics, and develop novel therapeutic targets that may be used to prevent or treat ligamentum flavum hypertrophy.
kw: Lumbar spinal canal stenosis, Ligamentum flavum, Functional studies, Chondroitin sulphate, Expression analysis, Biomarker

title: Investigating role of electrical subthalamic and pallidal stimulation of the brain on the expression of GDNF family of ligands and GFR? receptor splice isoform and neurogenesis
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is an established therapy for Parkinson’s Disease. Established targets include the sunthalamic nucleus (STN) and globus pallidus interna (GPi) and emerging targets include the pedunculopontine nucleus (PPN). Glial Cell Line Derived Factor (GDNF) family of ligands have been shown to confer neuroprotective effects on dopaminergic neurons and putaminal infusion of GDNF have been investigated in patients with Parkinson’s Disease with promising results. The presence of multiple closely related GNDF ligands and splice isoforms of GFRa receptors with overlapping and differing functions raises questions on the interaction between the various factors involved. We aim to study the effects of DBS on GDNF family of ligand and related splice isoform receptor expression and investigate putative signaling pathways by targeting and stimulating the STN and GPi in a rodent model with similar parameters used in humans. It is hypothesized that differential expression levels of splice isoform receptor expression arises from electrical stimulation and can activate different signaling pathways. As Parkinson’s Disease results in loss of dopaminergic neurons, we are also investigating the effects of electrical stimulation on hippocampal neurogenesis by examining the labeling of bromodeoxyuridine (BrdU) in the dentate gyrus with stereology microscopy and determine the lineage of the cells with immunohistochemistry staining. Elucidating the interaction between DBS and GDNF signaling has important clinical implications in determining target selection for DBS, investigating potential new targets for stimulation and also providing valuable information for future clinical trails utilising GDNF family of ligands.
kw: GDNF, Parkinson’s Disease, DBS, Deep Brain Stimulation, Electrical Stimulation

title: Pharmacogenomics of efflux transporters and their impact on the disposition of doxorubicin in Asian breast cancer patients.
abs: Objectives Pharmacogenetic causes of variability in the pharmacokinetics(PK) and pharmacodynamics(PD) of doxorubicin is not well characterized. It is hypothesized that single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in candidate genes involved in the disposition pathway of doxorubicin in breast cancer patients receiving doxorubicin/cyclophosphamide regimen may affect its PK/PD and influence therapeutic outcome. Recent novel findings from our laboratory have shown that functional polymorphisms in pregnane xenobiotic receptor gene, PXR, SLC22A16 (influx transporter gene), ABCB1 and ABCG2 (efflux transporter genes) and carbonyl reductase genes (CBR1 and CBR2; drug metabolizing enzymes catalyzing the conversion of doxorubicin to doxorubicinol) are important in influencing the PK of doxorubicin. Besides the abovementioned polymorphic genes influencing the disposition pathway of doxorubicin, we hypothesize that polymorphic variants in the ABCB5, ABCB8, ABCC5 and RLIP76 genes that are associated with efflux transport functions also participate in regulating the PK/PD of doxorubicin. The objective of this grant proposal is to characterize the pharmacogenetics of these efflux transporters and understand the mechanistic basis of the variability in doxorubicin’s PK resulting from the polygenic interaction of SNPs in the various candidate genes affecting the PK/PD of doxorubicin in Asian breast cancer patients. Methodology Sixty patients with histologically confirmed breast cancer starting on chemotherapy with doxorubicin (60mg/m2) and cyclophosphamide (600mg/m2) will be accrued. Serial blood samples will be drawn at 0, 5, 15, 30 minutes and 1, 4, 8 and 24 hours after the administration of chemotherapy for PK study. A single draw of 10 mls of blood will be taken to extract germ-line DNA for SNP analysis of the following efflux transporter genes: ABCB5, ABCB8, ABCC5, and RLIP76. The nadir neutrophil counts and incidence of febrile neutropenia in these patients will be correlated with the PK of doxorubicin and the SNP profile of the studied genes in the patients.
kw: transporters, pharmacogenomics, Breast cancer, pharmacokinetics

title: A Phase 1 Study of Oral Vinorelbine in Combination with Erlotinib in Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer (NSCLC) using Two Different Schedules
abs: Non-small cell lung cancer is the commonest cause of cancer mortality in Singapore. Conventional palliative chemotherapy has reached a plateau in survival benefit and there is a need for novel agents for treatment of this disease. New approaches are needed for metastatic NSCLC patients as all “classical” cytotoxic or targeted drugs provide the same poor range of efficacy in the salvage setting. Erlotinib is currently approved for use in the salvage setting as monotherapy for non-small cell lung carcinoma. Adding an established oral cytotoxic such as oral vinorelbine is attractive due to the oral route of administration. Using this approach combines the convenience and cost-savings of oral therapy with the potential of increasing response rates. Additive or supradditive activity of an EGFR TKI with vinorelbine has been demonstrated in-vitro. Clinical synergism is described between gefitinib and vinorelbine in NSCLC. Preclinical studies show that by using cytotoxics in a low-dose protracted manner, endothelial cells are preferentially affected via inhibition of proliferation and induction of apoptosis. In addition to this anti-angiogenic mechanism, an anti-vasculogenic process may also be involved that acts by reducing circulating endothelial progenitor mobilization and viability. We hypothesize that the combination of a EGFR-TKI and metronomic doses of chemotherapy may overcome acquired resistance to cytotoxics. This phase I study combines erlotinib and oral vinorelbine on two different schedules. The conventional schedule vinorelbine (CSV) to determine the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) of conventional schedule of oral vinorelbine given on days 1 and 8 every 21 days plus daily erlotinib and the metronomic schedule vinorelbine (MSV) to determine the optimal metronomic dose of vinorelbine given 3 times a week plus daily erlotinib. The objectives are:a) To assess whether combination of oral vinorelbine and erlotinib is safe and feasibleb) To determine dosing of oral vinorelbine on a metronomic schedule leading to anti-angiogenesis as demonstrated by circulating endothelial cell/progenitor assays
kw: Metronomic chemotherapy, EGFR, Tyrosine kinase inhibitors, Phase 1, Pharmacokinetics

title: A Sero-Epidemiology Cohort for studying Infection rates and Host Immune Responses to the 2009-H1N1 Influenza A virus
abs: Sero-epidemiological studies have been proposed by leading experts as part of pandemic surveillance efforts to understand the virulence, severity and clinical manifestation of the new virus, as well as the effectiveness of various interventions. For the 2009-H1N1 pandemic, the most accurate way to do so will be to use paired serology since cross-reactive antibodies exist in a significant segment of at-risk populations.Historically, influenza epidemics have caused more intense transmission in some sub-populations, particularly in institutional settings. There are also vulnerable groups such as elderly persons, residents of long-term care facilities and pregnant women for which attack rates and complication rates should be assessed, with a view to better management of future epidemics. Seroepidemiological studies can also assess the effect of interventions like oseltamivir prophylaxis, and the effectiveness of personal precautions and social distancing measures adopted at the individual level. In addition, should the vaccine become available before the epidemic peaks, baseline serological samples can help us target the use of vaccination, and host antibody and T-cell immune response before and after infection can shed light on immune mechanisms relevant to vaccine development.We have launched a multi-site seroepidemiology study to compare infection and complication rates for 2009-H1N1 in several subpopulations of interest, including:1. community dwelling adults2. pregnant women3. healthcare workers4. residents of long-term care facilities5. military personnelBaseline samples for some cohorts (1, 3, and 5) have already been taken. Nested within the larger cohort is also a group of vaccinated and unvaccinated individuals for whom detailed antibody and T-cell immune responses will be studied.The above study can facilitate management of the current epidemic by answering key questions such as how to use prophylaxis and vaccines (if they become available before the epidemic ends), as well as advise on future epidemic management.
kw: Influenza, Pandemic, Attack rate, intervention effectiveness, sero-epidemiology, antibodies

title: Telomere length and attrition rate in intrauterine growth restriction
abs: Intrauterine growth restriction or retardation (IUGR) occurs in approximately 3-10% of pregnancies. Thefoetuses are pathological small for gestational age; usually due to placental insufficiency or variousmaternal or foetal genetic factors. There is high risk of foetal death, still birth and neonatal mortality andmorbidity. Long-term consequences for IUGR children who survive into adulthood include higher risk ofcardiovascular and metabolic disorders.We aim to investigate the telomere length of 200 normal weight and 100 IUGR newborns at birth to testthe hypothesis that IUGR babies have shorter telomeres compared to their peers due to intrauterinestress. For the latter group, telomeres will be measured again at 12 months as there might be catch-upgrowth and frequent infections during the first year of life leading to rapid loss. Rapid telomere loss canbe caused by stress, oxidative damage, inflammation and rapid cell division. Additional telomereshortening due to increased turnover of cells during postnatal somatic growth and repair may explain theearlier senescence of cells and the observed higher incidence of cardiovascular disorders.There is as yet no longitudinal study or direct data on the rate of telomere loss in man. The currentknowledge of rate of telomere loss is extrapolated from cross-sectional studies to be between 25-200basepairs/year but it may be as high as 2-3 kilobasepairs during the first year of life. Our results willprovide data on telomere attrition rate for high-risk infants after the first 12 months of life, and crosssectionaldata on telomeres in our newborns of different birth weights and gestational periods. Forinfants with history of infection events, it will also be tested whether the rate of telomere loss is a usefulbiomarker for infection history.There is no data on telomere lengths in the children from our population. Our results will provide data ontelomeres in our newborns with normal and very low birthweight and different gestational periods. Ouruse of serial samples on IUGR cases will also yield prospective data on telomere attrition rate over thefirst year of life, reported to be the period of highest loss. No data is available for this critical period orany other period as there had not been any study investigating serial samples from the same individuals.We will also generate some data on whether the rate of telomere loss is a useful biomarker for infectionhistory as IUGR neonates are at increased risk of infection and inflammation and hence oxidative stress,which are known to be related to telomere shortening.

title: Aspirin for Dukes C and High Risk Dukes B Colorectal Cancers - An International, Multi-centre, Double Blind, Randomised Placebo Controlled Phase III Trial (ASCOLT)
abs: The utility of Aspirin and NSAIDs in preventing cancer, especially colon cancer is the subject of intense pre-clinical and clinical interest and investigation. Whereas high quality evidence (randomized controlled studies) indicates that aspirin is effective in reducing colorectal adenomatous polyps; and numerous studies point towards an ability to prevent colorectal cancer; the role of Aspirin as an adjuvant agent in patients with established cancers remains to be defined. Recently it was noted within an adjuvant chemotherapy trial, that patients who had been on Aspirin or cox-2 inhibitors had half the rate of cancer relapses and death. Although this data is supportive of Aspirin’s biological activity in this disease and possible role in adjuvant therapy, it still needs to be confirmed in a randomized prospective trial. Two large randomized cox-2 inhibitor studies have also been undertaken to answer the same question, but had to be suspended prematurely, due to the emergence of data concerning cardiovascular toxicity. In contrast, Aspirin is cardio-protective and is one of the most widely used drugs with a well established safety profile. We hypothesize through this randomized, placebo-controlled adjuvant study, that Aspirin in patients with dukes C or high risk dukes B colorectal cancer (ASCOLT) can improve survival in this patient population over placebo control. If indeed found to be beneficial, because aspirin is cheap and easy to administer, it will positively impact the lives of many individuals in Asia and globally. The recent failure of the anti-VEGF monoclonal antibody bevacizumab in the adjuvant treatment of colon cancer reminds us about what we still do not understand about this disease and makes the search for effect agents even more urgent.
kw: Colon, Rectal, Cancer, Aspirin, Adjuvant

title: A Phase 1/2 Study of AZD6244 in Combination with Sorafenib in Advanced Hepatocellular Carcinoma
abs: The Raf/MEK/ERK pathway is one of the most critical signaling cascades for liver tumorigenesis and can be activated by HBV or HCV infection or mitogenic growth factors. Sorafenib, a multi-kinase inhibitor of Raf/VEGF/PDGF, as a single agent has been shown to improve overall survival in advanced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and is now considered a standard of care. AZD6244 (Astra Zeneca) is a potent, selective, adenosine triphosphate-uncompetitive inhibitor of MEK1/2. In our study on human HCC xenografts, we found that inhibition of tumor growth and angiogenesis by sorafenib resulted in upregulation of IGF-IR, which is in part responsible for elevated phospho-ERK, which is inhibited by Mek inhibitor, AZD6244. We found that combinational inhibition of angiogenesis and the ERK signaling pathway using sorafenib with AZD6244 was highly effective for inhibition of tumor growth and induction of apoptosis in vivo compared to either agent alone. (in press) This will be a phase I/II clinical trial testing the combination of sorafenib and AZD6244 in advanced hepatocellular carcinoma with Childs A liver cirrhosis. The aim of the phase I portion is to determine the maximally tolerated dose (MTD) and pharmacokinetics of this drug combination. The phase 2 study will look at clinical efficacy and safety of this combination in advanced HCC patients. The hypothesis is that the addition of AZD6244 enhances the efficacy of sorafenib in advanced HCC. . A standard “3+3” dose escalation method will be employed in phase1. When a MTD is determined, patients will be accrued onto the phase II part of the study.The benefit of sorafenib alone in advanced HCC has been significant but modest -improved overall survival of about 2.5 months over placebo and response rates of < 3%. It would be a clinical breakthrough if we can show that AZD6244 further enhances the efficacy of sorafenib without compromising safety in advanced HCC patients.
kw: Hepatocellular carcinoma, sorafenib, Mek inhibitor, AZD6244, Liver cancer

title: Understanding Asian Lung Cancer through genomic profiling under the Lung Cancer Consortium, Singapore (LCCS)
abs: Our recent study has shown that the epidemiology of non-small cell lung (NSCLC) cancer here differs significantly from that seen in the West. In particular, never-smokers with this condition are rather prevalent in Singapore comprising nearly a third of all NSCLC. The recent explosion of studies exploring the cancer genome primarily aim to 1) further the understanding of cancer pathogenesis and behaviour, 2) develop better biomarkers for improved diagnosis, classification, and prognostication of patients and 3) discover novel oncogenes and tumour suppressor genes that may lead to new therapeutic targets. Several reports and in particular the recent report from Dukes University showed the usefulness of using gene expression profile to predict survival outcome of patients with NSCLC who underwent resection. However, these studies include patients who are mainly smokers. The never-smoking subset in these Western studies is relatively low in numbers. The Lung Cancer Consortium, Singapore (LCCS) was set up in 2007 under Singapore Cancer Syndicate grant to kick-start the prospective collection of tissues, blood, and life-style epidemiologic, and clinical data of lung cancer patients. This study involves major institutions in Singapore including NCC/SGH, CGH, and TTSH. To date, we have collected 1469 tumour tissues, 492 blood samples, and 355 filled life-style questionnaire forms. The web-enabled database was started and the clinical data/epidemiologic life-style data are entered prospectively. Preliminary analyses of the gene-expression profiles showed significant difference between never-smokers and ever-smokers and the pathways specific to never-smokers are undergoing further analyses. This application is to obtain funding to continue this rich resource of Asian lung cancer that can generate data/hypotheses and support future clinical trials that require biological correlates and these can potentially enable us understand the biology of this disease better. Hopefully, this can translate to better therapeutic strategies for future patients. Our hypothesis is that the maintenance of this Lung Cancer Consortium will facilitate and enhance quality translational research in lung cancer in Asia.

title: Clinical Validation of a Microfluidic Device for Isolation and Molecular Characterization of Circulating Tumor Cells (CTC)
abs: We hypothesize that isolating circulating tumor cells (CTC) and characterizing them in cancer patients is a potentially useful tool to adapt therapy and prognosticate disease.Potential applications include:•‘Real-time’ treatment adaptation: Multiple redundant pathways and tumor resistance evolves within malignancies in temporal relation to tumor growth and treatment. Increasing numbers of drugs are signal transduction pathway specific and it is important to develop technologies that may allow us a glimpse of the tumor in ‘real-time’ so as to guide our hand in targeting treatment. It also potentially allows us to understand how the tumors evolve biologically with time.•Prediction of risk of relapse or recurrence: Current actuarial methods give only a statistical prediction of risk of relapse or recurrence. Quantification of CTC could potentially allow the early detection of relapse/recurrence or guide the

title: MicroRNA based diagnosis and prognosis of H1N1 and related viral diseases
abs: In June 2009, World Health Organization declared that flu due to a new strain of virus, H1N1-2009 has become pandemic. Singapore has been taking every precaution to contain the spread of the virus while making measures to treat the patients more effectively and efficiently. Despite all the efforts, the virus is now known to remain endemic in Singapore and many other countries. Although there are methods available to detect the presence of the virus in patients infected with H1N1, there has been no detailed molecular studies aimed at understanding the mechanisms by which the virus overcome the host’s defense machinery. Usually the viruses employ a set of small RNA molecules (microRNAs) to invade and negate the important cellular processes including the immune system of the host cells. The primary aim of this project is to identify these viral microRNAs that are responsible for infection and transmission/propagation of the H1N1 virus. This study will also enable us to develop methods for easy diagnosis of the H1N1 pathogenesis as well as to follow up the progression of the disease (prognosis) when the patients are subjected to specific viral treatments/ hospital management. We are also hoping to develop a microRNA based chips that can speed up the diagnosis and prognosis of H1N1 flu.

title: Does Vascular Endothelial Cell Function aid in Prediction of Diabetic Retinopathy Progression?
abs: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is a leading cause of blindness in Singapore and worldwide. Vascularendothelial dysfunction occurs early in diabetes, but its relationship to the presence and severity of DR isnot known.This study will investigate and quantify the role of ocular and systemic vascular endothelial dysfunction inDR. Ocular vascular endothelial function will be quantified by dynamic and static retinal vascular changesand systemic endothelial function assessed in the peripheral vasculature using the EndoPAT. Ocular endothelial function will be assessed by the Dynamic Vessel Analyser (DVA) whichmeasures retinal vascular dilatation in response to diffuse illuminance flicker. Additionally, staticfeatures of the retinal vascular system (diameter, tortuosity, branching angles, junctional exponents,and fractal dimensions) will be measured using computer software; and Systemic endothelial function will be measured by the EndoPAT, a computerized plethysomographthat quantifies the vascular endothelial response to a temporary period of vascular deprivation in thearm.The aims are to determine the relationship of1. Dynamic and static retinal vascular parameters with presence and severity of DR;2. EndoPat measures with presence and severity of DR;3. Dynamic/static retinal vascular parameters and EndoPAT measures to the 1 year progression ofearly to vision threatening DR and the need for laser treatment.To achieve these aims, we will recruit a cohort of 300 individuals with diabetes: 150 with diabetes with noDR, and 150 with varying severity of DR (likely 75 with mild DR, 50 with moderate DR, 25 with severeDR). Participants will undergo a standardised examination including dynamic/static retinal measurementsand EndoPAT.The study will provide new insights into the contribution of vascular endothelial dysfunction in thepathogenesis of DR. It is possible that these novel measurements may improve risk stratification of DR toallow for early intervention and management.

title: Improving the efficacy of light therapy: A comparative study to determine whether exposure to intermittent light enhances circadian, neuroendocrine,and alerting responses relative to exposure to continuous light
abs: Background: Appropriately-timed exposure to light, termed 'light therapy', accelerates adaptation to shift work and jet-lag, improves sleep quality in patients with circadian rhythm sleep disorders, and alleviates depressive symptoms in patients with Seasonal Affective Disorder. Also, acute exposure to light at night suppresses the sleep-promoting hormone melatonin and enhances levels of alertness. Preliminary studies suggest that the three-cone visual system, which is most sensitive to 555nm green light, ontributes substaintially to circadian photoreception. However, the relative contribution of cones to 'non-visual' light responses decreases across time in continuous light. Hypothesis and Aims: We hypothesize that intermittent light therapy will prevent the decay in cone-driven responses by providing for sustained activation and dark adaptation of cone photoreceptors. We therefore predict that intermittent green light will elicit stronger circadian phase shifts, increase melatonin supression, and enhance levels of alertness and performance relativeto exposure to constant green light. Methods: Healthy subjects ages 18-24 from the general population will be recruited to take place in a 6 day laboratory study. In a between subjects design, participants will be randomly assigned to receive either 6.5 h of intermittent (n= 10, 2Hz) or continuous (n=10) green light during the night (555nm, 12 log photons cm2s1). Using standard procedures in chronobiology, we will measure supression of melatonin and body/skin temperature rhythms. Also, during the light exposure we will measure suppression of melatonin, and alertness will be assessed using standardized sleepiness scales, suditory reaction time, and the electroencephalogram. Clinical significance: these studies could lead o the development of better light therapy regimens and devices for sleep and psychiatric disorders. Also, our finding will help elaborate the role of cone photoreceptors in human non-visual responses, and may demonstrate that even dim light can be therapeutically effective if intermittent light protocols are used.
kw: Photoreception, Circadian, sleep, performance, melatonin, alertness

title: Exploring Mesenchymal Stem Cell-derived Conditioned Medium As Hepatoprotective Agents Against Drug-induced liver injuries
abs: Acute liver injury is a major clinical problem arising from both diseases and therapeutic misadventures. This issue not only translates into significant morbidities worldwide, but also causes the repercussions of drug removal from market and socio-economic burden. Management of drug-induced liver injuries is often limited to cessation of drug use and support therapy as there are no therapeutically proven hepatoprotective agents. To address this unmet need, we propose using paracrine secretion from human mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) as a protective biologic for drug-induced liver toxicity. The underlying rationale for this proposal originated from our observations that human MSC-conditioned medium (MSC-CM) exhibit significant cardioprotection in a porcine myocardial infarction model, and computational analysis of the proteome of the MSC-CM predicted a hepatoprotective role. Our overarching aim is to determine if MSC-CM is hepatoprotective in both cell and animal models of hepatotoxicity. The specific aims are to:1.To establish in vitro evidence of hepatoprotective effect of MSC-CM a.Determine the effects MSC-CM on hepatocytes treated with various hepatotoxicants known to have different mechanism of toxicityb.Determine effect of prophylactic vs. post-exposure to MSC-CM2.To determine cytoprotective effect of MSC-CM in vivo models of drug-induced liver injury (carbon tetrachloride)3.To explore potential target pathway of cytoprotection.As a new lab with limited resources, this small focused proposal seeks to create the proof-of-concept study to form the basis for a subsequent IRG application. This study could potentially offer a biological alternative to xenobiotics and chemicals for hepatoprotection, and may provide an insight into the key molecular pathways underlying drug-induced liver injury and repair. As this study will be using MSC secretion of human origin, it may lead to direct clinical applications.
kw: Liver injury, Hepatoprotection, Conditioned medium, Hepatotoxicity, Mesenchymal stem cell

title: Bone-targeting Nanomedicine for Treating Osteomyelitis
abs: Osteomyelitis, or bone infection, is treated through systemic delivery of antibiotics over a period of time.The current treatment strategy has many setbacks, which include over-dosing of patients and may resultin an increase in drug resistance by the bacteria. Inadequately treated acute osteomyelitis may also leadto chronic osteomyelitis where prognosis is often poor. As such, our approach is to utilize nanoparticlesas drug carriers to delivery therapeutic agents to targeted infected-bone tissues, thereby increasingefficacy and reducing drug dosage. Till date, targeted delivery to bones using nanoparticles is currentlystill not well studied. If successful, this approach will lead to better patient compliance and perhapsimprove prognosis. In this study, it is hypothesized that the delivery of drugs through bone-targetingnanoparticles will improve treatment efficacy of osteomyelitis, over current systemic treatment. The aimsof this proposal are therefore: 1) to develop three different drug delivery systems to target bone sitesinfected with osteomyelitis, and 2) to investigate the treatment efficacy for each of these bone-targetingdrug delivery systems over conventional systemic treatment. In the final outcome of this study, thetreatment efficacy for osteomyelitis using the best delivery system will be validated and proposed. Themethodology in this study to achieve the specific can be summarized into the following four projectobjectives/milestones:1. Establish synthesis of drug-containing bisphosphonate-tagged nanoparticles.2. In vitro investigation of drug release from nanoparticles and their anti-bacterial effects onStaphylococcus aureus.3. In vitro targeting efficiency of nanoparticles onto bone samples.4. Comparison of treatment efficacy of targeted delivery systems against systemic administrationof antibiotics through in vivo models.
kw: Osteomyelitis, Polymeric micelles, Liposomes, Bisphosphonates, Calcium phosphate, Nanoparticles

title: Precision in the assessment of health-related quality of life in breast cancer patients
abs: Presently, disease-specific health-related quality of life (HRQoL) measurement scales for use in cancer patients are ordinal in nature. They do not provide a utility score, which is needed in cost-utility and quality-adjusted life-years analyses. The EQ-5D is a generic HRQoL measure that provides a utility score and is the instrument recommended by the National Institute for Clinical Excellence, UK, for eliciting health utility values. Moreover, it is short and easy to complete and therefore imposes little burden on the respondents. Nevertheless, oncologists often use disease-specific HRQoL instruments that are lengthier and have no utility interpretation. These instruments are supposed to have better precision when applied to their target disease groups. In our recent study in Singapore, however, we have found that the EQ-5D and the Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy – General (FACT-G) have comparable precision and discriminative power in cancer patients with heterogeneous diagnosis. It may be argued that the FACT-G did not out-perform the EQ-5D because it is not disease-specific enough. Incidentally, the EQ-5D’s 3-level response descriptors are currently being changed to 5-level, which is expected to increase precision. We propose to conduct a study of breast cancer patients to compare the relative performance of FACT-Breast, a disease-specific instrument, and the (5-level) EQ-5D. We hypothesize that the EQ-5D is non-inferior to FACT-Breast in discriminative ability and test-retest reliability. Two hundred and eighty breast cancer patients will be recruited from the NCC outpatient clinics and SGH oncology ward. They will fill in a questionnaire package that includes the FACT-Breast and the EQ-5D. Performance status and other clinical variables will be recorded by oncologists. Two weeks later the same questionnaire package will be posted to the patients for a second assessment. Statistical analysis comparing the measurement performance of the two instruments will be conducted and interpreted according to pre-specified non-inferiority margins.
kw: Health-related quality of life, EQ-5D, Utility, Breast cancer, Precision

title: Prevalence and Clinical Impact of Adverse Drug-Drug Interactions in Cancer Patients
abs: Study objectives: (1) Examine the prevalence of the co-prescription of potentially interacting drugcombinations involving oral anticancer drugs (OAAs) in the two largest cancer centers in Singapore, and(2) Quantify the risk of drug-drug interaction (DDI)-associated adverse clinical outcomes after adjustingfor potential confounders.Methods: Thirty-seven clinically important and potentially interacting drug combinations involving anOAA and a non-anticancer drug were identified at the preceding stage of this proposed study throughprimary and tertiary literature reviews. The prevalence of the co-prescription of these 37 drugcombinations between the years 2007 and 2009 will be assessed by a retrospective analysis of thepharmacy electronic records databases of the National Cancer Center and the NUH cancer center,where all prescription records are computerized. For each commonly prescribed drug combination, 400patients with a co-prescription (i.e., exposure cohort) will be identified using the pharmacy databasesand then individually matched on a 1:1 basis with a control cohort according to age, gender, cancer type,index date, and the object drug. Pertinent information will be extracted from patients’ medical chartrecords, and a Cox proportional hazard model will be developed to compare the relative risk of theadverse clinical outcome associated with the DDI between the two cohorts while adjusting for potentialconfounders.Contribution: This proposed study will be the first in Singapore and one of the few in the world toinvestigate the existence and extent of clinically important DDIs in cancer patients. The findings canadvance our understanding of the presence and likelihood of clinical consequences resulting from DDIs,which could help physicians in weighing the benefits and risks of prescribing these drug pairs.Furthermore, the evidence established can be used to develop or refine prescribing guidelines orelectronic drug alerts, with the ultimate goal of eliminating DDI-associated harm.
kw: drug interactions, drug safety, prevalence, drug utilization review, oncology, pharmacoepidemiology

title: Effect of fibrin glue (Tissel) on human Endothelial cell morphology for harvesting of Descemet’smembrane/endothelium for transplantation
abs: The aims of the study are to examine the effects of fibrin glue on human endothelial cell function andmorphology and to subsequently examine the morphological effects following stripping of Descemetmembrane (DM). We hypothesize that fibrin glue if applied to the DM before stripping will provide a rigidplatform to make peeling easier with minimal damage to the endothelial cells and thus will have nosevere effects on endothelial morphology and function. We aim to prove this by first examining theeffects on fibrin glue on human corneas kept perfused by using an air-interface organ culture techniqueon an AC (Anterior chamber) maintainer. Corneas with good endothelial function will be assigned andcoated with fibrin glue or no glue (control) before placement on the AC maintainer. Physiological functionwill be assessed by daily cornea pachymetry with anterior segment optical coherence tomography.Following 2 weeks of perfusion the fibrin glue will be dissolved by perfusion with r-TPA (Tissueplasminogen activator). Corneas will then be removed and endothelial viability assessed by live dead cellassay and Scanning electron microscopy (SEM). Histology and TUNEL assay will be performed toassess apoptosis. Corneas will then be assigned to undergo descemets stripping with and without fibringlue spray on the endothelium. Endothelial cell damage comparing the 2 techniques will be assessedusing live dead cell assay and SEM. The clinical significance of this project is to combat the majordifficulties related to transplantation and handling of 10 µm DM/endothelial complex. Moreover, there is asignificant endothelial damage during harvesting of the DM/endothelial complex and subsequenttransplantation. The addition of fibrin glue will provide rigidity to this complex which may allow easierstripping without significant endothelial cell loss. This will aid tissue handling and transplantation of pureDM/endothelium much easier and successful.

title: In vitro Hair Follicular Unit Reconstitution with Natural Appearance and Functions by Tissue Engineering Method
abs: In vitro Hair Follicular Unit Reconstitution with Natural Appearance and Functions byTissue Engineering MethodAims: To engineer hair follicles in vitro, we will:Aim 1: Fabricate an array of microstructured molds with biocompatible polymers that mimic the hairfollicle micro architecture.Aim 2: Seed keratinocytes and dermal papilla (DP) cells onto the micromold at designated locations andculture the scaffold in vitroAim 3: Study the anatomy and function of engineered hair folliclesThe novelty of this project is to create three dimensional (3D) biomimetic microstructures similar to thoseof the actual human hair follicles. Epithelial cells (keratinocytes) and mesenchymal (DP) cells wereimmobilized inside the microstructures at designated locations for hair to develop. At the end of theproject we will have a method to engineer human hair follicles, which can be used to generateengineered hair follicles in a high throughput manner.Background: There is a shortage of human hair follicles for surgical transplantation. So far no methodsare available to obtain human hair follicles except from human donors. Tissue engineering may providean approach to generate human hair follicles in large quantity to meet the clinical needs. Hair folliclesresult from epithelial–mesenchymal cell interactions. Using homospecific mouse or rat cells, normalappearinghairs can be reconstituted in vitro. Heterospecific mouse–rat combinations are also good.However, homospecific human cells did not work and cannot grow into normal hair follicles. So far, theclosest human hair follicle–like structures can be obtained using cell mixtures derived from human androdent epidermis and dermal papillae. The failure to form better differentiated and organized follicles isbelieved to be the lack of communication between the mesenchymal and epithelial cells. Somemolecular signals may be able to crosstalk to conserved receptors while others may not, leading to animbalanced morphogenesis. To solve this problem, we aim to fabricate microstructured biomaterials toimprove the communication between different cell species and grow human hairs with naturalappearance and functions.Technical Approach: For Aim 1, an array of micro-molds will be fabricated by photolithography.Hydrogels based on photocrosslinkable polymers such as hyaluronic acid (HA)-collagen will be used formaking mold prototypes. The design of the mold includes a microwell and an islet located in the centerof the microwell to mimic the physiological topology of hair follicles. Such micromold will be fabricated inthe format of array with density similar to that of the normal hair on the skin. The microstructure of theHA-collagen hydrogel will be studied using microscopic methods. The mechanical properties of themicromold will be tested to make sure that it can retain its microstructure for extended exposure to cellculture media. For Aim 2, DP cells will be encapsulated insi

title: Novel stress-based left ventricular contractility index for diagnosis of heart failure with normal and reduced left ventricular ejection fraction
abs: Background Heart failure (HF) is a major health care burden. It can occur with either normal or reduced LV ejection fraction (EF), depending on different degrees of ventricular remodeling. We recently published a novel LV contractility index, d(sigma)*/dtmax (maximal change rate of pressure-normalized wall stress) that correlates well with dP/dtmax and end-systolic elastance, Ees(SB)7. We have also reported the diagnostic utility of d(sigma)*/dtmax in various cardiac diseases8-10. We now propose to prospectively assess d(sigma)*/dtmax for diagnosis of heart failure with normal ejection fraction (HFNEF) and with reduced ejection fraction (HFREF), and examine the correlation between d(sigma)*/dtmax and N-terminal pro B-type natriuretic peptide (NTproBNP) as a marker of heart failure. AimsPrimary aim: Determine the sensitivity, specificity and accuracy of d(sigma)*/dtmax for diagnosis of HFNEF and HFREFSecondary aim: Evaluate the utility of d(sigma)*/dtmax and NTproBNP, alone and in combination, for the diagnosis of HFNEF and HFREFExploratory aim:Evaluate the utility of d(sigma)*/dtmax compared with LV diastolic indices (E/A ratio, mitral deceleration time (DT), septal and lateral E/Eprime, pulmonary venous flow (S/D ratio)) for diagnosis of HFNEFMethodology60 HFNEF, 60 HFREF, and 60 age- and sex- matched normal controls will be recruited. All subjects will undergo echocardiography. All HF patients (based on clinical diagnosis) will also undergo blood sample collection for NTproBNP at the time of presentation of HF in the wards or emergency department prior to starting anti-failure treatment. D(sigma)*/dtmax and NTproBNP will be determined and compared in all groups.Clinical Significance d(sigma)*/dtmax is easily measured noninvasively, sensitive to LV inotropic changes and preload and afterload independent. We hope to demonstrate the utility of the d(sigma)*/dtmax index in diagnosis of heart failure. We expect that d(sigma)*/dtmax can significantly contribute to diagnostic precision, and hence be useful in triage and management of HF patients.

title: The role of Ras and RUNX2 in cancer metastasis
abs: Oncogenic Ras mutations are prevalent in metastatic cancer diseases for example in colorectal cancer. It is known that the oncogenic Ras acts through the extracellular growth factor receptor pathway resulting in uncontrolled proliferation that leads to tumorigenesis. However, the role that oncogenic Ras plays in the arena of metastasis is not as well characterized. Because Ras mutation status affects the outcome of current anti-metastasis drug regime, there is a need to study the oncogenic Ras pathway’s pro-metastatic effect. Conventional cell culture systems use a tumor derived cell line approach. This is plagued with unknown inherent mutations in these cells, thus confounding the conclusions. This project proposes to use a more genetically defined fibroblasts system as an initial cell system before venturing into the tumor tissue specific cell lines and clinical samples validation. Using this novel approach, our preliminary data showed RUNX2 to have a pro-migratory after oncogenic Ras activation. This project proposes to study how RUNX2 features in oncogenic Ras associated metastasis within the novel cell culture system. With this understanding, we seek to use RUNX2 as a potential biomarker for the metastatic disease and to devise more mechanistic driven strategies to counteract metastasis.
kw: Metastasis, Ras, RUNX2

title: Developing Functional Scaffolds for Blood Vessel Engineering using Human Hair Proteins.
abs: Given that every human is a hair producing factory, human hair is readily available and abundant. By processing human hair into useful forms we have the possibility to recycle a largely untapped and free natural biomaterial. Human hair is an attractive biomaterial because it is made up primarily of keratins, which are biocompatible, have superior mechanical strength and contains specific cell adhesion motifs. Therefore it is proposed in this study to extract keratins from human hair for biomedical applications. Specifically, the procedure to efficiently extract and process human hair proteins will first be established. Subsequently extracted hair proteins will be fabricated into scaffolds for tissue engineering blood vessels, using the technique of electrospinning.Electrospinning of nano-scale fibers have been shown to be an attractive way of fabricating think layers of substrates from various natural and synthetic biodegradable polymers. However, the greatest drawback of electrospinning is the poor mechanical properties of the substrates produced. It is hypothesized that using proteins extracted from human hair for electrospinning can produce scaffolds with more superior mechanical properties compared with conventional natural materials, thereby offering new possibilities for application. In this study, keratins extracted from human hair will be electrospun into small-diameter tubular scaffolds and extracted for blood vessel tissue engineering. These scaffolds will be characterized for their physical, thermal and mechanical properties. In vitro biocompatibility will also be evaluated using endothelial cells. The novelty of the proposed study is in the use of extracted human hair protein in an electrospun form as a platform scaffold for tissue engineering blood vessels. This will enable human hair as a huge and natural resource of choice for clinically viable tissue engineering and regenerative medicine applications.

title: Seroproteome analysis of Enterovirus 71
abs: Enterovirus 71 (EV71) has been recognised as the main etiologic agent of Hand, Foot and Mouth Disease (HFMD), a childhood disease characterized by fever, multiple ulcers in the mouth and vesicles on the limbs and buttocks. However, EV71 has been widely associated with neurological complications such as aseptic meningitis, brainstem encaphilitis, and have resulted in fatalities in the recent outbreaks in the Asia Pacific region. In 2008, more than 21,000 HFMD cases were reported in Singapore and nearly half of the cases were caused by EV71, including 2 fatalities. At present, there is no vaccine available and treatments are limited to symptomatic treatment. The lack of knowledge in the pathogenesis of EV71 has greatly hampered the effective epidemic control of HFMD outbreak.In this project, we sought to characterize EV71 by seroproteomic analysis. The approach will allow us to better understand the pathways leading to the pathogenesis of the EV71-induced HFMD, as well as the host- and virus-mediated cellular responses. We reasoned that proteomic analysis will elucidate the potential candidates suitable for development as vaccines against EV71. Moreover, we hypothesize that active enzymatic components essential for EV71 virulence, including proteases are necessary for cleaving host cellular protein precursors during the virus infection. Identification of these active proteases will potentially allow us to develop assay which could be used to screen for small chemical inhibitors that can antagonize the viral infection processes. The knowledge gained from our proteomic analysis of the EV71 will be critical for the ultimate aim of developing vaccines and treatments necessary for the epidemic and therapeutic intervention of HFMD outbreaks.

title: The CHloroquine for Influenza Prevention (CHIP) Trial. A randomised, double-blind, placebo controlled trial of chloroquine in the prevention of influenza: evaluation of its clinical pharmacology and relationship between drug levels and protective efficacy
abs: Clinical significance and aimsThere are no measures currently available for widespread use in the prevention of H1N1 influenza in the general population. Chloroquine (CQ) has activity against influenza virus (including H1N1 and H3N2 strains) in vitro at clinically-achievable concentrations. CQ is well-tolerated, widely available and inexpensive and would be an ideal candidate for community pre-exposure prophylaxis against influenza. The primary aim of this study is to determine the efficacy of CQ for this indication. We also aim to establish a comprehensive high quality database of community influenza H1N1 infection for conducting additional translational research studies. MethodsThe study aims will be addressed through a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. We will recruit 1500 healthy participants aged 18-65 from the community rapidly, predominantly using a web-based recruitment and screening approach. Participants will be randomized to take CQ 300mg (of base) or matching placebo once daily for one week, and then once-weekly until they complete the intervention period of 12 weeks. Participants will self-complete a daily symptom diary (using, in most cases, a web-based data entry platform), and will be trained to take nasal swabs in the event of illness that will be preserved and used for later PCR diagnosis of acute influenza. There will be two clinic visits, at baseline and at the end of the 12 week intervention period at which additional clinical, demographic and epidemiological information will be obtained and blood will be drawn for paired serological testing for influenza infection, and for typing into H1N1 versus seasonal influenza virus infection. The primary endpoint will be laboratory-confirmed influenza-like illness defined as the combination of influenza symptoms (recorded in the diary) and laboratory confirmation by four-fold rise in serology or positive PCR on nasal swab or other documented laboratory diagnosis made in the community.

title: Development of Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) specific T cell therapy for Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma.
abs: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) is endemic in Asia. NPC expresses Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)-related proteins eliciting weak T-lymphocyte responses, causing immune evasion. AutologousEBV-antigen specific cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTL) can be activated, expanded and adoptivelytransferred as an immunotherapeutic strategy against virally-transformed cancers. We propose todevelop an improved adoptive cell therapy strategy of autologous EBV-specific CTLs for advancedNPC patients.We aim to perform a first-in-man Phase I-II clinical study of EBV-targeted cell therapy by ex vivoexpansion of EBV-specific CTLs stimulated with a novel construct (nontoxic LMP1 mutant (Nterminaldeletion mutant DLMP1) and full-length LMP-2) transfected into dendritic cells (DC) via anFDA-approved replication-deficient adenoviral vector (Ad5f35). Previous studies focusedexclusively on LMP1 or LMP2 stimulated CTLs. Our proposed study is first to generate combinedDLMP1 and LMP-2 stimulated CTL against NPC. Pre-clinical studies (Gottschalk S, personalcommunication) show high LMP1 expression levels in human DCs with little toxicity using AD5f35containing the fusion construct (Ad5f35DLMP1-LMP2). Ad5f35DLMP1-LMP2 is transduced intoDCs and co-cultured with patient’s peripheral blood mononuclear cells elicit significant LMP-specificCTL compared with LMP-1 or LMP-2 alone. High-throughput genomics and immune monitoring willbe employed to analyse NPC tumor and specific immunity respectively to correlate response totherapy.Straathof K et al showed EBV-specific CTL lines were used to treat advanced NPC patients withstabilization of disease and minimal toxicity. Comoli P et al also employed EBV-targeted (LMP2)autologous CTL with specific immune response and demonstrate tolerability in NPC patients.Confirmation of our hypothesis has wide implications for immunotherapy especially against virallytransformedtumors. Our institution, in partnership with the Center for Cell and Gene Therapy, isfurther developing human capital, technology platform and infrastructure (Class 1000 GMP isavailable at National Cancer Centre) for T-cell therapy capability to initiate a quality-controlled highthroughput clinical Cell Therapy facility.

title: DEVELOPMENT OF PREDICTIVE BIOMARKERS AND NOVEL APPROACHES TO THERAPY IN BREAST CANCER
abs: Breast cancer is a common malignancy with rising trends of incidence. Systemic treatment is an important treatment modality, although choice of therapy is still empirical. Development of predictive markers to guide treatment choice is critical to avoid futile therapies. In addition, there is pressing need for novel treatments to improve outcomes. The main themes of the breast cancer program are (1) to develop biomarkers to predict response and toxicity to anti-cancer agents, and (2) to develop novel approaches to therapy. The backbone of the program is to design and conduct clinical trials, along with systematic collection of biological samples. Clinical trials will be designed for three groups of patients to fulfill different research goals: (1) Identification of biomarkers that predict treatment response (genomics, proteomics) using the neoadjuvant therapy model in patients with locally advanced/metastatic breast cancers; (2) Studying biological changes of novel anti-cancer compounds using the window-of-opportunity studies model in the pre-operative setting for patients with early stage breast cancers prior to definitive surgery; (3) Evaluation of novel approaches to therapy in refractory/metastatic breast cancers. 2-3 new clinical trials in each category will be initiated over a 5-year period. Predictive panels will be developed through germline pharmacogenetics studies, tumor and peripheral blood mononuclear cell genomics analysis, tumor and plasma proteomics analysis, and drug pharmacokinetics studies. In addition, cutting edge technologies will be applied in sample analysis, including genome-wide association studies and proteomics analysis using LC-MS/MS. In the development of novel approaches to therapies, we intend to distinguish our program from others internationally through development of relatively less expensive therapies that focus on highly academic drug development in areas of non-commercial interest to pharmaceutical companies. The program will leverage on established basic laboratory discovery programs and industry drug discovery programs, and amalgamate existing resources to evaluate these in the clinic.

title: Assessing the capacity of H1N1-2009 to development oseltamivir resistance bymutation and reasort with influenza A subtypes circulating in Singapore.
abs: Although the current H1N1-2009 can cause severe infection in certain high risk groups (e.g.immunosuporessed) it is currently associated with relatively low levels of severe infection in healthyadults. The virus has developed efficient human to human transmission which is of major concern,and which is largely responsible for the current pandemic. The virus is resistant to amantadine baseddrugs, but although isolated cases of H1N1-2009 resistance have been reported (Promed mail 78, 83,and 84), it remains largely treatable with the available neuraminidase inhibitors. However, if the virus isable to gain drug resistance either by mutation or resortment with other circulating viruses inSingapore, this may have implications for the control of infection in Singapore. Reasortment is animportant process in influenza virus evolution, and the H1N1-2009 virus recently arose byreassortment event involving avian, human and swine viruses (Shinde et al., 2009). However, manyinfluenza virus isolates are unable to reasort to produce viable progeny virus; presumably due toincompatibility of the properties of proteins that are encoded by these segments. Therefore thecapacity of H1N1-2009 to acquire drug resistance either by mutation or by gene reasortment with othercirculating drug resistance viruses in Singapore is unknown. This project will assess the capacity ofH1N1-2009 to acquire drug-resistance either by mutation, or by reasortment with other humanadapted influenza viruses that are circulating in Singapore (e.g. seasonal H1N1 and H3N2).This likely will have important clinical implications in Singapore, and the data obtained shouldalso help assist in policy decisions should the H1N1-2009 infected patients start to exhibit a highermortality and morbidity rates as the pandemic continues.

title: Molecules in pterygium : from cell dysfunction to ocular surface pathology
abs: Pterygium is a common ocular surface disease that results in redness, irritation and visual disturbances due to tear instability, astigmatism and occlusion of the visual axis. Currently the only viable treatment is surgical resection, this being the most common ophthalmic surgery performed in Singapore, after cataract and corneal refractive surgeries. The cause of this condition is essentially unknown and this investigator has found, over the last few years, that a few molecules play an important role in the disease: the S100 proteins, the phospholipase (PL)D and the transglutaminase (TGM)-2.The cellular dysfunction in pterygium involves epithelial to fibroblastic transformation, abnormal matrix remodeling, abnormal cell migration and adhesion, increased angiogenesis as well as increased chronic inflammatory process. To varying extent, the S100, PLD and TGM-2 proteins have been implicated in these processes. Since an animal model of pterygium is not available, we intend to study the functional role of these proteins in cultured cells by genetic over expression or deletion. The cell phenotypes will be investigated by microscopy, cell proliferation and migration assays, expression of matrix proteases and inflammatory cytokines, and immunohistochemistry for focal adhesion and cytoskeletal changes. For selected proteins such as TGM-2, the in-vivo function will be evaluated by experiments on homozygous TGM-2 deleted mice available at the investigator’s center. Many tear proteins such as S100 proteins are markers of inflammation. A clinical component of this project involves finding out if any of these proteins can predict the recurrence of pterygium after excision.Since the various cellular processes evaluated here are relevant to other ocular surface diseases, the findings will not only suggest new modalities of treatment to pterygium or adjunctive treatment to surgical resection, but likely also shed light on other inflammatory conditions such as dry eye, allergies, infections, persistent corneal epithelial defects and other ocular surface epitheliopathies.

title: To win the war against H1N1 influenza A: breaking through the limitations of significant sideeffects and resistance of current anti-flu drugs
abs: Influenza, a common and highly infectious disease, kills hundreds of thousands annually and millionsduring its outbreaks. At this writing, the recent outbreak of 2009 H1N1 influenza A (swine flu) is rapidlyevolving into a global pandemic (125 countries affected as of 4 July 2009) and creating great panicworldwide as SARS and bird flu did a few years ago.In the limited drug arsenal against influenza, neuraminidase (or sialidase) inhibitors, specifically,Tamiflu (oseltamivir phosphate) excel as the effective weapons to combat various strains of influenzaby preventing virus replication. Despite of its wide use, there are great concerns relating to Tamiflu:side effects on the human nervous system and the emergence of resistant influenza virus. Urgentsolutions are needed to overcome those limitationsIn this proposal, first we will continue our efforts in the past two years in elucidating the molecularmechanism underlying the mysterious neurological side-effects of Tamiflu and tackle this problemusing combined approaches of synthetic chemistry, molecular biology and cell biology. Second, we willcontinue our efforts in the past two years in developing economical synthetic routes to Tamiflu and itsanalogues based on the cheap and abundantly available starting materials (e.g., D-glucose) andreagents to combat 2009 H1N1 influenza A and tamiflu-resistant subtypes. Third, new neuraminidaseinhibitors with enhanced efficacy for H1N1/A and other strains of influenza will be discovered.Our short-term (3 years) aim is to break through the limitations of significant side effects andresistance of current anti-flu drugs and to develop next generation of new inhibitors for neuraminidaseof new influenza virus strains. Potential small molecule neuraminidase inhibitors will offer opportunityto develop the novel therapeutics against the flu pandemic.

title: Overcoming Drug Resistance in Cancer Targeted Therapy by Combining Genomics and Molecular studies
abs: The discovery of targeted therapy drugs, whether designed to cripple a major cancer pathway or cancer-related angiogenesis, constitutes a major milestone in the fight against cancer. Many more of these drugs are expected to make their way to the clinic in the near future. However, an emerging problem that concerns cancer patients, their treating clinicians and pharmaceuticals alike is drug resistance which can arise at any stage in the course of treatment. The goals of this proposal are to identify the underlying molecular mechanisms of targeted cancer drug resistance, to find molecular solutions to these problems, and to identify biomarkers that can predict resistance. Our general approach is to combine high-throughput genomic studies (third-generation sequencing, microarray gene expression and SNP profiling etc) on assorted clinical material with in vitro and in vivo studies (including generation of in vivo models that mimic drug resistance in patients), to discover and validate novel drug resistance targets, and to further develop them into predictive markers and therapeutic agents for clinical use. As an example, we describe below proposed drug-resistance studies of a key cancer targeted therapy, i.e., sunitinib (2007 sale: 650 million USD) in kidney cancer. Our preliminary studies were funded by three grants including two from Pfizer and have resulted in one provisional patent filing. However, follow-up studies are warranted to develop them into clinical application as proposed below. We want to emphasize that our strategy is to adopt the same general approach to study drug resistance in other major and novel cancer drugs (e.g., mTOR inhibitors, CDK inhibitors) in Singapore especially in relation to Asian patients.Metastatic kidney cancer or clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCCs) has a very poor prognosis. Recently, promising new targeted therapies have been approved for this cancer and sunitinib is currently considered the standard of care as first line therapy. However, development of resistance to sunitinib treatment is a major clinical problem. In our preliminary studies, we have identified the pro-angiogenic chemokine interleukin-8 (IL-8) as a potential mediator of sunitinib resistance in ccRCC. We generated xenograft mouse models that mimic the development of clinical resistance to sunitinib treatment seen in human ccRCC. Resistant tumors showed elevated levels of IL-8 and were able to re-establish angiogenesis. Treatment of these sunitinib-resistant xenografts with an inhibitory antibody against IL-8 re-sensitized tumors to sunitinib, resulting in decreased tumor size and associated angiogenesis. Moreover, we found that IL-8 expression levels were elevated in a limited number (5 responsive vs. 5 resistant cases) of human ccRCC samples unresponsive to sunitinib treatment. We hypothesize that IL-8 upregulation in ccRCC activates pro-angiogenic pathways that allow the tumor to circumvent the anti-angiogenic effects of sunitinib treat

title: Tailoring Oxide Electronics by Atomic Control
abs: This CRP aims to set up a series of research activities around the theme of tailoring oxide electronics by atomic control, with an impact in such areas as next generation electronics; novel sensors; optics and lighting; and the development of new materials with exceptional properties with future potential. It will enable us to lead at the cutting edge of this scientific field, publish in world class journals whilst developing technology for the future, leading to patents and spin off companies. In the following, five projects will be introduced under two broad categories: transparent electronic materials and novel routes to creating new functionalities in oxide materials. 1 Transparent Oxide electronic materials: While silicon is irreplaceable for conventional electronics, when it comes to transparent electronics, which is a growing industry, oxides are the materials of choice. The low carrier mobility, the bane of oxides has been dramatically overcome recently by the discovery of oxide based conducting superlattices of insulators. The key challenge left is to make oxide based pn junctions. 1.1 Atomically Controlled Oxide Heterostructures for Novel Functionality: Here we will use the PLD/MBE process to fabricate atomic superlattices of alternating layers of different oxides to creat new functionalities. 1.2 Transparent oxide based pn-junctions: We have identified thin films of TiO₂ as the right host to work along with a nano wire approach to ZnO. 2 Novel routes to creating new functionalities in oxide materials: While the previous section dealt with nanostructuring and doping of established materials to get new device functionalities, in this part of the program we will try radically new approaches to create new material properties by control of cationic vacancies and by introducing dopants that will produce midgap bands (super-hydrogenic dopants) . 2.1 Cation vacancy-induced conductivity and magnetism: Defect mediated magnetism is today a hot theoretical topic with sparse experimental data. We hope to make a significant impact here. 2.2 Super-Hydrogenic Dopants: This is a high risk, but unique experimental work with potential high payoff in terms of discovering new materials with valuable functionality. 2.3. Nanometer scale imaging and structuring in Oxides: We are going to take two approaches; by the use of an atomic force microscopy and by the use of a unique helium ion microscope. This section will make our work more visible to application.

title: Adult and Induced Pluripotent Stem Cells for Neurological Disorders and CNS Repair
abs: Transplantation of stem cells is a potentially valuable therapeutic treatment for many neurological disorders. Stem/progenitor cells also have been found to occur naturally in different regions of the adult central nervous system (CNS). However, there is still very little understanding of how well newborn neurons that are formed from stem cells integrate into the existing circuitry of the CNS. Our studies will make use of the recently developed channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2) photostimulation technique to define the functional integration of transplanted neuronal precursor cells into the brain. Many factors that enhance neurogenesis, such as physical exercise and enriched environment, are potential targets for novel treatments for these disorders. Therefore we also will determine how these factors affect integration of transplanted neuronal precursor cells into brain circuitry. Finally, altered neurogenesis has been found in many brain disorders, including Parkinson’s diseases (PD), epilepsy and stroke. By deriving induced pluripotent stem cells from patients with CNS diseases such as PD, we will for the first time be able to study the cellular functions of these affected cells in vitro, ex vivo and in vivo. Our studies will provide basic understanding of these debilitating neurological diseases. Most importantly, our work will shed light on potential treatments for such diseases and evaluate various novel therapeutic strategies, including autologous transplantation.

title: Membrane Protein Sciences – Tools for Rational Discovery of Novel Therapeutics and Diagnostic Targeting Integral Membrane Proteins
abs: Integral membrane proteins (IMPs) constitute a third of prokaryotic and eukaryotic proteomes and are involved in almost every cellular process. IMP malfunction results in a range of diseases, and activity modulation of IMPs is one of the main therapeutic strategies available. The importance of IMPs in drug discovery and diagnostic applications is immense, but the knowledge of IMPs structure and mechanism is rudimentary, and technologies for in vitro studies of IMPs, which can accelerate drug design programs, are highly underdeveloped. The present proposal addresses these problems by (i) establishing a core facility for IMP production, (ii) developing innovative technologies for IMP production and stabilisation, (iii) performing mechanistic studies of IMP families of high therapeutic and diagnostic importance and (iv) developing generic strategies for in vitro selection of IMP directed ligands or binding proteins for diagnostic and therapeutic use. New library technologies for IMP production, combined with parallel platforms for screening expression parameters will be developed. These will be complemented by structure-function studies of IMPs, facilitated by new crystallisation methods of IMPs and NMR methods of structure determination specific to IMPs. Novel IMP ligand-binding paradigms will be investigated by NMR and other biophysical approaches. Another aim of this proposal is the identification of proteins that bind IMPs and the generation of specific antibodies, to be used as diagnostic or therapeutics, which will be facilitated with the availability of purified IMPs. Direct collaboration with the Novartis Tropical Institute is expected, and it is also anticipated that the funding of a leading Membrane Protein Sciences project in Singapore will attract the interest of other Pharmaceutical companies to collaborate.

title: Interface Science and Technology
abs: Digital synthesis of heterostructures with atomically sharp interfaces will be developed to create new functionalities emerging at the interface but absent in the bulk. The quality of materials to be developed will enable the construction of charged quantum bits at the interface of magnetic oxides such as the manganites, with high mobility charges, thus allowing high temperature operation. We will employ ultra-short light pulses to control conduction properties and to transmit information through the disturbance of an electron orbital. The dynamic response of the orbital to an external field is 1000 times faster than the spin precession frequency used today in magnetic-disk-drives, magnetic-sensors and magnetic random access memories. This fact alone opens opportunities for breakthroughs in the energy performance of these systems in nano-sized low dimensional interface devices. We will use linearly and circularly polarized light to manipulate the spin dynamics of antiferromagnetic materials at the sub-picosecond to picosecond timescale - this is orders of magnitude faster than switching speeds in the read-write heads of hard drives. We will tune, study and utilize the coupling between intrinsic order parameters, address the mechanism leading to the observed interfacial electronic states of oxide transistors, including the mechanism of oxide resistance switching memory and consequent search for electric-field-induced exotic phases. The almost limitless variation in these systems may outperform commonly used structures and bring about a similar burst to the science and application of semiconductors. With the implementation of this project we anticipate the introduction of ultimate resistance-change devices, aiming at future electronics where not only spin, but also electric pulse control on spin, charge, and orbital degrees of freedom drive novel functionalities.

title: Enrichment of epsilon-globin-positive fetal primitive erythroblasts and amplification of the fetal genome for array comparative genomic hybridization
abs: Invasive fetal testing for aneuploidy and monogenic disorders is associated with a small but significant risk of miscarriage. Non-invasive prenatal diagnosis is the Holy Grail that would eliminate this risk of miscarriage that often limits uptake of prenatal diagnostic procedures, and always causes considerable parental anxiety. The advantage of enriching fetal cells over fetal DNA is that once these cells are enriched, they could be used to diagnose a wide range of chromosomal and genetic disorders. We have shown previously that epsilon-globin is the ideal marker for fetal erythroblasts enriched from maternal blood, and that these cells are suitable for fluorescence in situ hybridization. We have shown that conventional nucleated red blood cell markers enrich maternal cells, but are not effective for enriching epsilon-globin positive fetal erythroblasts. We have also developed the ideal in vivo model for studying fetal cells enriched from maternal blood for non-invasive prenatal diagnosis. This project is proposed in context as an extension of our earlier work.We hypothesize here that we can enrich and expand adequate numbers of epsilon-globin positive fetal nucleated red blood cells harvested from maternal blood so as to obtain sufficient quantities of pure fetal DNA to perform molecular karyotyping by array CGH. In model mixtures and in clinical samples we will explore the usefulness of the novel surface antigens we have discovered to date and the novel microfluidic device we have developed. We will attempt to culture fetal erythroblasts in human embryonic stem cell culture systems to expand their numbers, and prevent their enucleation. We will determine the ideal number of fetal cells enriched from maternal blood that are needed for an accurate fetal genetic diagnosis, and determine the fidelity of whole genome amplification of DNA obtained from these cells for singleplex and multiplex PCR, and molecular karyotyping by array CGH.

title: Establishing a practical and theoretical foundation for comprehensive and integrated community, policy and academic efforts to improve dementia care in Singapore.
abs: Specific Aims: This application aims to establish a laboratory in Singapore for health systems modeling, focusing on the theory and methods of System Dynamics (SD). To achieve this programmatic aim, we will complete a series of integrated research projects to identify and implement solutions for addressing a serious and growing problem in Singapore and internationally: how to find and care for older individuals with cognitive impairment (CI) in a way that is effective, humane, and sustainable. The specific aims are organized in 3 phases: I.Establish the contextual and methodological foundation for approaching CI in Singapore using SD and engage a broadly representative team of SD specialists, epidemiologists, biostatisticians, sociologists, economists, policy makers, practitioners, community health workers and NGOs.II.Develop and validate a computer simulation model representing a common understanding of CI and the potential impact of interventions.III.Develop, implement, and evaluate new implementation approaches, influence concrete clinical and public health policies, and build local and regional research capacity.Hypothesis: SD provides an approach to addressing complex health issues that is both compelling (attractive to participants) and effective (leads to successful interventions).Methodology: The key methodology is the set of tools classified as SD. These methods, developed primarily in industrial and business settings will be tailored to address CI.Importance: Issues such as CI are exceedingly challenging because of the complexity of the health system and breadth of health care needs. To effect positive change, research must: take a systems perspective; engage all stakeholders in the first instance to promote insight to and ownership of solutions; and establish a scholarly foundation which serves to efficiently guide advances in the field of health services and systems improvement. SD provides a basis for systematic scenario planning that offers an innovative and promising approach to the challenges of rapid growth of Singapore’s aged population and the concomitant rise in dementia prevalence and its impact on the family, health sector, and the economy.
