title: (i) A genome-wide association study for cardiovascular and metabolic risk factors in Singaporean Chinese & (ii) High density lipoprotein associated protein variants and their association with diabetes mellitus and cholesterol efflux
abs: In two projects we willa) Identify genetic variants associated with blood lipids, obesity, c-reactive protein, retinal vascular caliber and blood pressure in 3300 Chinese participants of a large cross-sectional population that has been collected from 2003-2007. After genotyping using Illimina 610s Infinium Beadchips, statistical analysis will be conducted to identify single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) associated with each trait. The credibility of each association will further be tested by meta-analysis using data from 3000 Malay individuals, for which the same genotype and phenotype information is available. This study may identify novel loci involved in the pathogenesis of cardiovascular disease (CVD), facilitating the development of novel therapies for the prevention of CVD. SNPs identified may also be incorporated into predictive algorithms for identifying individuals at high risk of CVD so that appropriate preventive measures can be taken.b) Identify novel protein variants associated with high density lipoprotein (HDL). HDLcholesterol levels are inversely associated with the risk of CVD. However, HDL-cholesterol provides little information on the ability of the HDL in plasma to promote cholesterol efflux, a critical role of HDL. HDL contains several proteins that affect its metabolism and function. Mass Spectrometric Immunoassay (MSIA) has been used to show that several of these proteins are present as multiple variants resulting from genetic variation, transcriptional editing, or post-translational modification. The functional effects of these protein variations on HDL function are unknown. We will study 125 Chinese with type 2 diabetes mellitus and 125 controls to describe and compare the protein variants present on HDL in these 2 groups. We will also identify the determinants of the concentrations of each protein variant and the effect of this concentration on the ability of HDL to support cholesterol efflux. These protein variants could become biomarkers for HDL function, providing greater precision for assessing CVD risk.

title: Nanonets: New Materials, Devices for Integrated Energy Harnessing & Storage "Nanonets" comprising networks of electrically interconnected nanowires is exploited for its inventive, high-performance and fault-tolerant properties in electronics, green energy harnessing and storage applications
abs: Electronic materials occur in different shapes and forms, which lead to diverse application opportunities. For example, silicon exists as single crystal, polycrystalline, and amorphous; with all three forms yielding distinct properties and radically different applications. Similar analogies can be drawn up for zinc oxide (and a host of other materials) where nanowires, will lead to exciting opportunities which are yet to be exploited from its single crystal, polycrystalline, and amorphous forms. A “Nanonet,” comprising a planar network of electrically interconnected nanowires, that promises a revolution in the world of electronics with low-cost, inventive, and fault-tolerant properties that will stimulate opportunities in energy harnessing and storage systems. The program will focus on developing nanonetworks of semiconducting oxides and hybrid materials to fabricate integrated solar cells and charge storage devices. Rather than focus on the oft studied ZnO and TiO₂ as used in dye sensitized solar cells, this program will exploit the little studied, but promising properties of Fe, Cu, and Sn oxides and sulphides. So far most studies on Fe, Cu, and Sn have focused on their thin film forms and although sulphides of these materials showed excellent absorption in the visible spectrum, problems with recombination and effective charge collection have hampered progress. The nanonet device designs proposed in this program will enable exploitation of their superior absorption and tunable transport properties in high efficiency solar cells. Furthermore, the same materials would also be effectively employed in charge storage devices. In addition to the exciting device possibilities, this research will be driven by the fundamental properties of nano networks that remain to be explored: photogeneration and separation of charges in 2D & 3D multijunction nanonets, charge transfer (& transport) between different nanoscale species, and electrochemical reactions at interfaces in interpenetrating networks and heterophases.

title: Novel Studies in Leukemia: Pax5 and Other Transcription Factors
abs: Pax5 is one of the key transcription factors mediating differentiation of B-lymphocytes. We examined by SNP chip 633 acute lymphocytic leukemia (ALL) samples and found at least 27% samples had Pax5 genomic abnormalities including 26 Pax5 fusions to other genes. Specific Aim 1. Explore novel function of Pax5 fusion proteins, as well as other oncogenic fusion products. We have made a novel discovery which may be applicable to a large number of fusion products from a variety of cancers that involve transcription factors that behave in a dominant negative (DN) fashion. We discovered that Pax5 fusions, unlike wild-type Pax5, are immobile in the nuclei of living cells. Using fluorescent recovery after photobleaching (FRAP), fluorescent residence energy transfer (FRET) and a variety of other cellular and molecular biology techniques, the mechanism and overall range and frequency of this nuclear immobility of DN fusion proteins will be determined. Specific Aim 2. Identify proteins interacting with Pax5 fusion products. Using two hybrid selections, we will determine if the fusion protein acquires protein partners that can repress the normal transactivation mediated by Pax5. Specific Aim 3. Determine the secondary events that cooperate with allelic deletion of Pax5 to induce leukemia, utilizing retroviral insertional mutagenesis. About 25% of cases of ALL and 80% of Ph1+ ALL have deletion of 1 allele of Pax5. Paradoxically, Pax5 +/- deletional mice do not develop leukemia. Therefore, a logical conclusion is additional mutations are required to cause ALL. We will discover these additional genomic changes using retrovirus mutagenesis analysis. Specific Aim 4. Discover and study novel fusion proteins in hematopoietic malignancies (Pilot Project). Using SNP Chips, we have discovered that novel fusion partners can be identified in cancers with unbalanced translocations. This new approach should lead to identifying exciting new fusion genes in various cancers. Overall, these studies will foster our understanding of the pathogenesis of ALL and should offer new therapeutic targets for ALL and other malignancies.

title: To define the mechanisms thereby knockdown of p21-activated kinase (PAK1) reduces glucotoxicity-induced apoptosis of insulin-secreting cells
abs: Both type 1 and type 2 diabetes involve a loss of islet ß-cell mass. It is well knownthat high glucose is toxic to islet ß-cells (glucotoxicity) that plays a key role in thedevelopment of type 2 diabetes, but the underlying mechanisms remain to be fullyunderstood. P21-activated kinase (PAK), a downstream effector of the small Gproteins(Rac and CDC42), functions as a regulator of cytoskeleton and may be alsoimplicated in apoptotic signaling pathways. We found that exposure of insulinsecretingINS-1 cells to high glucose culture induced marked apoptotic death peakedat 96 h, an event after significant activation of caspase-8, caspase-9 at 12-24 h andcaspase-3 peaked at 48 h. Such glucotoxicity-induced cell death was significantlyreduced by a general caspase inhibitor. Glucotoxicity also activated stress-inducedsignaling pathways implicated in activation of p42/44MAPK and p38MAPK. When aPAK isozyme (PAK1) was knocked down in INS-1 ß-cells by RNA interferencetechnique, both glucotoxicity-induced caspase-3 activation and cell death weresignificantly suppressed, demonstrating that PAK1 may play an important role inglucotoxicity-induced apoptotic death of insulin-secreting cells. This researchproposal aims to further explore the signaling pathways implicated in glucotoxicityinducedcaspase activation and ß-cell death and to define the mechanisms how PAK1knockdown prevents ß-cells from glucotoxicity-induced death. One focus will be onexamining the events/pathways possibly involved in glucotoxicity induced caspaseactivation during ß-cell damage, including oxidative stress, FAS expression,inflammatory cytokine production, and mitochondrial damage. Another focus will beon assessing the possible involvement of PAK1 in the association of glucotoxicityinducedcell death with stress-activated signaling pathways (p38MAPK, p42/44MAPK,JNK). In addition, some key findings will be confirmed in isolated islets. The findingsfrom these studies will improve our understanding how glucotoxicity causes damageto islet ß-cells and help formulate a novel strategy to prevent and/or treatglucotoxicity for diabetes therapy.

title: Information Theoretical Security for Wireless Communications
abs: We propose a mathematical approach to security for wireless communication via information theory through different approaches. Using tools from algebraic coding theory, we plan to investigate the existence of wiretap codes and to propose practical schemes to implement cryptographic primitives such as bit commitment and oblivious transfer over noisy continuous channels. We also consider the generalization of existing adversary models which mainly consider eavesdropping to take into account active adversaries. We aim at bringing both new mathematical results and theoretical means to evaluate the potential practical application of information theoretical security to wireless communication.
kw: information theoretical security;algebraic codes;wireless communication;wiretap codes

title: Algorithmic Aspects of Coalitional Games
abs: Algorithmic game theory is an exciting new research area at the border of economics and computer science. It studies algorithmic aspects of game-theoretic concepts and is important for evaluating the practical applicability of these concepts. In this project, I plan to study algorithmic complexity issues that arise in cooperative game theory, the subfield of game theory that models cooperation and teamwork. My proposed research can be broken down into four main themes. First, I would like to study cooperative games with non-transferable utility. My goal is to develop expressive yet compact formalisms for such games, and investigate the possibility of designing efficient algorithms to answer natural questions about these games under this representation. Second, I plan to study settings where agents can belong to more than one coalition simultaneously, using the framework introduced in a recent paper of mine (WINE'08). I intend to extend this framework, apply it to games that model resource allocation and provision of network connectivity, and study the algorithmic properties of various notions of stability in such games. Third, I intend to design new algorithms for computing and approximating the nucleolus of coalitional games, building on the new ideas that I and my NTU colleague Dr. Dmitrii Pasechnik introduced in our upcoming SODA paper (SODA'09). The nucleolus is the payoff vector that corresponds to the ``most stable'' outcome of the game, and therefore its computational properties are of great practical interest. Finally, I would like to study the loss of efficiency in coalition formation that is caused by stability considerations, thus generalizing the notion of the price of anarchy to cooperative games.
kw: game theory;coalitional games;computational complexity;representation complexity;algorithms

title: Nanostructured White LEDs of Nanocrystal Quantum Dot Emitters for High Quality Mesopic Solid State Lighting
abs: Today lighting consumes 20% of electrical energy worldwide. Solid state lighting is expected to reduce the energy consumption of lighting by 50%, corresponding to a significant energy saving of 10% in the overall global energy consumption and a substantial reduction in the annual carbon emission by 300 million tons per year. Commercial white light emitting diodes (WLEDs), however, typically suffer from “cool” white appearance with low color rendering indices (CRI), typically around 70, preventing their wide-scale use in domestic applications for photon-adapted (day time) photopic vision. Also, commercial phosphors integrated WLEDs currently exhibit low scotopic/photopic (S/P) ratios, below a barrier of 2.5, also preventing their efficient use for dark-adapted (night time) scotopic vision. As a result, also in mesopic vision as the transition region between the photopic and scotopic regimes, these WLEDs provide undesirably low optical quality. This research work proposes to overcome these limitations in photometric performance that commercially available WLEDs currently face, offering a new class of mesopic WLEDs that use semiconductor nanocrystal quantum dots with high CRI (around 80) and high S/P ratio (above 2.5). In this proposal, the custom design combinations of such nanocrystal emitters enable the ability to achieve precise tuning and engineering of the photometric properties for spectrally improved mesopic vision. This is the first proposal of such a new class of mesopic WLEDs with high S/P-ratio and high CRI.

title: Clinical Validation of Stathmin as a Biomarker for Colorectal Cancer Metastasis Using Tissue Microarrays
abs: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the third most common malignancy and the second leading cause of cancer deaths in developed countries. In Singapore, CRC has overtaken lung cancer to be the most common malignancy. About 30%-50% of patients with CRC die within 5 years after diagnosis. The high mortality is largely due to extensive metastatic spread of the disease, with secondary hepatic tumours being the most common occurrence. Patient survival will greatly benefit from earlier recognition (and intervention) of metastasis but as yet, proper markers indicating metastases are not available. E1 is a highly metastatic variant of HCT-116 (human colon cancer cell line derived from the primary tumour) that was generated using a liver colonization model. Proteomics profiling of HCT-116 versus E1 showed 3 isoforms of stathmin to be up-regulated in metastatic E1 as compared to HCT-116. This is the first finding of stathmin up-regulation in colorectal cancer metastasis. We subsequently also confirmed stathmin expression to correlate strongly with increasing metastatic potential in other paradigms/cell lines of colorectal metastasis examined. Most importantly, RNA interference assays showed that knockdown of stathmin in E1 significantly decreased cell migration by 41% in an in vitro assay. In this proposal, we aim to carry out large scale clinical validation of stathmin as a potential biomarker for colorectal cancer metastasis using tissue microarrays (TMA). A pilot study will be carried out using immunohistochemistry (IHC) to examine stathmin expression in a small set of CRC samples (n=20), each comprising of adjacent normal colonic mucosa, primary tumour, lymph node metastasis and secondary tumours of the same patient. Subsequently, we will be expanding the validation numbers to 1000 patients using TMA to study the subcellular and tissue localization of stathmin, as well as its correlation to various tumour clinicopathological characteristics. These will determine if stathmin expression contributes to cancer progression/prognosis in clinical samples, and validate stathmin as a potential biomarker and a therapeutic target for CRC metastasis.

title: Fabrication of Tissue-Engineered Intervertebral Disc using both non-or pre-Tensioned Human Annulus Fibrosus and Nucleus Pulposus Cells and PNmPh Nanofibrous Scaffford in vivo
abs: Low back pain (LBP) is the second most common reason for absence of work in the economically productive population. Degenerative disc disease is the single most common cause of chronic back pain. The current treatment modalities involve conservative management or surgical intervention e.g. fusion or disc replacement. The use of biological solutions e.g. tissue engineering presents the opportunity to restore the function of the IVD.Increasing evidence showed that micromechanical stimuli modulate the biological response of the IVD cells and play a critical role in determining the fate of individual IVD cells. We have shown that equibiaxial cyclic tensioned (ECT) was capable of increasing collagen and proteoglycan synthesis, and therefore improving the proliferation of pre-compressed AF and NP cells. In this study, human AF cells and NP cells from adolescent spines undergoing scoliosis surgery will be isolated and cultured separately without ECT, or pre-tensioned with ECT. IVD cells will be seeded onto Poly[bis(methylphenoxy)phosphazene] nanofibrous scaffolds(PNmPh NFSs). The PNmPh NFSs created by AF cells will be seeded onto the side of scaffold. This will be followed by injection of cell and hyaluronic acid (HA) slurry into the center of the NFS. The assembled tissue-engineered IVD constructs will be implanted subcutaneously into the dorsum of athymic mice and harvested at 4, 8, and 12 weeks. The quantity of glycosaminoglycan, hydroxyproline, DNA content, collagen type I, II, and histology will be analyzed.This study aims to create a composite IVD with non-tensioned or pre-tensioned human AF and NP cells and PNmPh NFSs for potential future clinical applications. It maybe a prelude to the development of a “disc bank” where disc cells can be cultured and transplanted back into patients for therapeutic purposes.

title: The Singapore H1N1 Influenza Study (SHINE)
abs: The advent of the first influenza pandemic of this century was announced by the World Health Organisation in June 2009. This novel influenza A H1N1 (2009-H1N1) resulted from triple genetic re-assortment with genes from human, swine and avian influenza. As at end of June 2009, the virus was in six continents, with 60,000+ laboratory confirmed cases and 263 deaths. The first 2009-influenza A H1N1 case was detected in Singapore on 26th May 2009 in a young returning traveler from North America. At the time of writing, Singapore has confirmed more than 600 cases with no fatalities, but infections are anticipated to increase exponentially, and fatalities will surface as it rages through the community.Critical questions remain: Is 2009-H1N1 clinically different from other influenza, given reports of severe cases in younger ages? Can we clinically distinguish 2009-H1N1 from other influenza/non-influenza respiratory illnesses? Are there early prognostic makers for severe cases? Will the virus acquire resistance mutations and/or mutate into more severe forms (as with H1N1 in 1918)? Will it displace H3N2/pre-2009 H1N1 strains?We propose a multi-centre study involving five public hospitals and other research institutes, allowing comprehensive study of participants across all ages. Retrospective and prospective designs are used to study confirmed 2009-H1N1, seasonal influenza, and a sample of influenza PCR negative patients. Nested within a prospective study are targeted studies on viral shedding and host immune response. The combined approach will shed light on multiple facets of 2009-H1N1infection, while adding knowledge on seasonal influenza and other respiratory illnesses posing significant disease burden in public hospitals, while monitoring for changes in 2009-H1N1 which might portent mutations to more severe forms.The study is time-sensitive and essential for gathering new knowledge on the novel virus, and enabling application of scientific and clinical information on disease management, outbreak response and mitigation strategies.

title: Inhibition of renin production: evidence for hydrogen sulfide as a novel and powerful anti-hypertensive drug
abs: Hypertension is the most common chronic disease. It is the major contributor to cardiovascular diseases, which are the leading cause of death. Hydrogen sulfide is a new biological gas, which is endogenously generated from cysteine in a reaction catalyzed by cystathionine-B-synthase (CBS) and cystathionine-y-lyase (CSE). We recently reported that H2S produces protective effects in both cardiovascular and central nervous systems.Blood pressure is controlled by renin-angiotensin system. Renin is an enzyme acting on the rate-limiting step to produce angiotensin II, a powerful vasopressor and a stimulator of aldosterone secretion. Thus, renin release could be an important therapeutic target for the treatment of hypertension. In our preliminary data, we found that H2S significantly attenuated the elevated blood pressure and suppressed renin and angiotensin II levels in 2-kidney-1-clip (2K1C) renovascular hypertensive rats. We therefore hypothesize that H2S may be a potential anti-hypertensive drug. The present proposal is designed to investigate the action mechanisms for the effect of H2S on renin secretion. The therapeutic effects of H2S on renovascular hypertension, cardiac hypertrophy and vascular injury will also be investigated.
kw: Hydrogen sulfide, hypertension, hypertrophy, renin, Angiotensin II

title: Control of Burkholderia pseudomallei’s virulence through the regulation of Type III and Type VI Secretion Systems – identifying novel targets for therapeutic intervention in melioidosis
abs: Melioidosis is a potentially fatal disease caused by the Gram-negative bacterium Burkholderia pseudomallei. Melioidosis is endemic in Singapore with an average annual case fatality rate of 27.4%. Treatment is particularly difficult as the bacterium is resistant to many conventional antibiotics and require extended treatment modalities. Currently there are no vaccines available. B. pseudomallei is equipped with the Bsa Type III secretion system (T3SS) that is required for virulence in murine models of melioidosis. The bacterium also possesses six Type VI secretion systems (T6SS) and T6SS has been shown to be important for virulence in other pathogens. We have previously identified a mutant which shows greatly downregulated expression of bsaT3SS and T6SS5. We hypothesize that the disrupted gene in this mutant, which we name bviR, is a specific regulator of virulence in B. pseudomallei by controlling the expression of bsaT3SS and T6SS5 genes. We aim to determine the mechanism of bviR regulation and whether it is directly or indirectly regulating the secretion systems via intermediate regulators. This is accomplished through determining gene expression in various mutants, and examining the effect of expressing putative regulators in trans in the relevant mutant backgrounds and/or in an E. coli heterologous system on transcriptional activation of the T3SS and T6SS genes. We will determine if cofactors are necessary for BviR to work and distinguish between the possibilities that BviR is derepressing a repressor or acting as a positive regulator. We will also examine how secretion of bacterial effectors is coupled to gene expression and how the loss of the bsaT3SS or T6SS5 or both impact pathogenesis in the acute and chronic models of murine melioidosis. Understanding how BviR controls virulence and pathogenesis presents an opportunity for us to formulate a novel approach to treatment with anti-virulence drugs to counter the development of antibiotic-resistance.

title: Isolation and characterization of gastrointestinal stem cells and their potential for liver and pancreatic differentiation
abs: Gastrointestinal stem cells (SC) are the perfect stem cells in that they are self-replicative with seemingly unlimited regenerative capability. Yet, human upper gastro-intestinal stem cells have never been identified or isolated. Hypothesis:Upper gastrointestinal stem cells would be identifiable using current markers for endodermal stem cells and would allow isolation by magnetic or fluorescent flow sorting. Culture of these cells with co-culture technique will sustain these cells and manipulation by external environment can differentiate these cells into gastrointestinal epithelium as well as hepatocytic and pancreatic lineages. Aims: 1. To isolate gastrointestinal stem cells and culture them in in-vitro cultures2. To characterize and prove stem cell features via in vitro and in-vivo techniques.3. To test ability to differentiate these cells into pancreatic and hepatocytic lineages.Methodology:SC are obtained from clinical biopsies obtained from volunteers during clinical endoscopies. Tissue is dissociated with trypsin and SC are isolated by magnetic sorting for EPCAM and Cd44 antibodies by magnetic flow sorting. They are then expanded and cultured in co-culture systems with myofibroblast feeder layers. Confirmation of SC is checked for self-regenerative capability, asymmetric division, gene expression and in-vitro differentiation into specialized cell type. Cells are labeled with GFP lentivirus and injected into rat model of ulcer injury to look for regeneration of gastroduodenal glands by human cells. Approach: Gastric and duodenal SC are derived from the endoderm during development. As such, they would likely share markers with liver progenitor cells, allowing dual-label isolation and culture using co-culture techniques we have developed for liver SC. These cells would provide an invaluable opportunity to study stem cell biology and niche maintenance by epithelial-mesenchymal interaction. Their ability to differentiate into hepatic or pancreatic cells, ready availability and potential for autologous transplant is huge for islet cells and liver cells transplantation.
kw: Gastrointestinal Stem Cell, Pancreatic Stem Cell, Liver Stem Cell

title: Transcriptional Regulation of cFLIP in Glucose Deprivation-induced Sensitization of Bcl-2 Overexpressing Cancer Cells to Death Receptor-mediated Apoptosis
abs: Resistance to apoptosis and an altered cell metabolism are essential hallmarks of cancer. Evidence supporting this is the insatiable appetite of cancer cells for glucose and the associated upregulation of anti-apoptotic proteins, such as Bcl-2 and cFLIP. We recently provided evidence to link the antiapoptotic activity of Bcl-2 to an increase in mitochondrial metabolic activity and intracellular superoxide generation. Decreasing intracellular superoxide sensitized Bcl-2 overexpressing cells to death receptor-induced apoptosis via activation of the upstream caspase, caspase 8, however the mechanisms of caspase 8 activation remained elusive. A critical regulator of caspase 8 activation is the apoptosis inhibitory protein, cFLIP, which blocks capase 8 recrutiment to the death receptor complex. Interestingly, glucose deprivation of Bcl-2 over-expressing cancer cells resulted in sensitization to death receptor-induced apoptosis via a decrease in intracellular superoxide and downregulation of cFLIP. As cFLIP is a critical player in immune evasion as well as resistance to death receptor-induced apoptosis, here we propose to invstigate the link between Bcl-2 over-expression and redox regulation of cFLIP using glucose deprivation as a physiological model for manipulating metabolic activity. Our preliminary data indicate increased cFLIP gene promoter activity upon overexpression of Bcl-2, and furthermore that the regulation of cFLIP expression by superoxide is at the transcriptional level. To that end, a recent report demonstrated that the cFLIP promoter region contained the transcription factor CREB binding motif. Intrigued by this, we will investigate the effect of Bcl-2 expression on CREB activation and its downstream transcriptional activity, in particular its three target genes, cFLIPL, Bcl-2, and MKP1. We hypothesize that superoxide-dependent activation of protein kinase A (PKA) leads to CREB phosphorylation and activation of cFLIPL, MKP1 and Bcl-2; cFLIPL could inhibit death receptor-induced signal via blocking caspase 8 activation as well as by inhibiting JNK activation, MKP1 could inactivate JNK via its phosphatase activity, and Bcl-2 could function as a positive feedback loop to further increase intracellular superoxide and CREB activationin addition to blocking mitochondrial-mediated apoptosis. This work could have tremendous clinical implications due to the heightened interest in the use of death receptor ligands such as TRAIL in the clinical settings and will provide novel insights into the mechanism of redox-dependent regulation of cFLIP (and its relationship to Bcl-2 expression) with potential for novel anti-cancer drug design.
kw: Warburg effect, ROS, cFLIP, MAPK, CREB, Apoptotic signaling

title: The significance of C/EBPalpha up-regulation in human hepatocellular carcinoma and its implications for treatment
abs: C/EBPalpha is a well-established tumor suppressor in acute myeloid leukemia. However, its function in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) has yet to be defined. We had previously reported that C/EBPalpha may prevent liver cancer in a knock-in mouse model with one allele of alpha-fetoprotein replaced with C/EBPalpha. Unexpectedly, recent results from our laboratory demonstrated that both C/EBPalpha mRNA and protein expression were up-regulated in a subset (about 60%) of human HCCs; 30% showed no change and 10% a decrease in expression compared to adjacent non-tumor tissues. There was a trend for C/EBPalpha expression to be higher in the higher stage tumors. Expression of C/EBPalpha in HCC cell lines recapitulated the pattern of expression in HCC tumors, with Hep3B and Huh7 expressing high, PLC/PRF/5 intermediate and HepG2 low levels of C/EBPalpha. The high expression of C/EBPalpha in HepG2 and Huh7 cells was dependent on HDAC activity. Inhibition of HDAC with either pharmacological inhibitors (TSA or PXD101) or specific siRNA decreased C/EBPalpha expression. The functional significance of C/EBPalpha up-regulation was evidenced by the reduction in colony formation when C/EBPalpha expression was decreased by specific siRNA or HDAC inhibitor treatment. We hypothesize that HDAC-mediated C/EBPalpha up-regulation promotes tumor growth in a subset of HCCs which over-express C/EBPalpha. The specific aims of the project are to determine: (1) the expression of C/EBPalpha (mRNA by qRT-PCR and protein by immunohistochemistry) in additional samples of human HCC relative to adjacent liver tissue; (2) the correlation of C/EBPalpha expression to HCC clinicopathological characteristics; and (3) the effect of knocking-down C/EBPalpha, either genetically through siRNA or pharmacologically by targeting HDAC pathway, on cell growth and sensitivity to chemotherapy in vitro and in vivo. Our findings that C/EBPalpha is up-regulated and that it may have growth-promoting activities are novel. A better understanding of the role of C/EBPalpha in liver cancer cell growth has important implications towards designing treatment strategies for HCC. It is envisaged that lowering C/EBPalpha levels in a subset of HCCs, either alone or in combination with existing chemotherapy can be a potentially new effective treatment strategy for liver cancer.
kw: C/Ebpalpha, hepatocellular carcinoma, tumor suppressor, cancer, chemotherapy, gene regulation

title: Inhibition of telomerase and DNA repair by a natural plant product in human cancer cells
abs: A major concern of cancer chemotherapy is the side effects brought about the non-specific targeting of both normal and cancerous cells by therapeutic drugs. This has been a major problem for radiotherapy as well as treatment with cytotoxic drugs. Much emphasis, recently, has been placed on discovering new compounds which target tumour cells more efficiently and selectively (affecting signalling pathways) while having minimal toxic effects on normal cells. In this proposal, we plan to study a natural plant product, Thymoquinone on its anti-cancer properties specifically on telomerase and DNA repair pathways with the following objectives:a)To understand the mechanism of telomerase inhibition and telomere shortening by natural products such as thymoquinone (obtained Black Seed)b)To determine possible interaction of thymoquinone with the telomeric (DNA and associated proteins such as TRF1, TRF2 and POT1) complex or DNA repair proteins known to have function in telomere maintenance (e.g. PARP-1, ATM, DNA-PKcs).c)To inhibit DNA repair pathway and other signalling pathways in combination with telomerase inhibition to facilitate efficient anti-cancer strategy.Our preliminary studies show that thymoquinone affects the telomerase pathway by inhibiting telomerase in telomerase positive cancer cells. Telomerase inhibition is an attractive anti-cancer strategy as more than 90% human cancers express variable levels of telomerase. The compound, thymoquinone (derived from black seed oil), we are testing will have a potential use in chemoprevention and/or anticancer therapy as it is an ingredient used in Asian food (Indian and Malay). The outcome of the proposed study would provide a better understanding on the molecular mechanism of anticancer properties of thymoquinone and will help in the use of thymoquinone in combinatorial approach to facilitate efficient cancer cell killing.
kw: Natural Plant Products, Telomerase, Experimental Therapeutics, Thymoquinone, Telomeres

title: New Organic Catalysis and Applications
abs: The controlled chemical modification of proteins is of crucial importance in basic biological research and protein-based pharmaceutical application development. The major challenge in this field is to achieve site-specificity. This project seeks to develop biocompatible chemical methods for the site-specific modification of proteins via cooperative organic catalysis. A working hypothesis is to use the distinct local environment surrounding the target residue to achieve site-specificity. For example, functional groups (such as acid groups from glutamic and aspartic residues) present in the protein will be used as catalytic or cocatalytic moieties to direct the modification reaction to a target residue. Selective modification of the target residue will be achieved through its close proximity and proper orientation with these directing groups. As an important step to realize site-specific protein modifications, the first stage of this program involves the development of new synthetic methodology for the functionalization of the side chains of natural amino acids under mild aqueous conditions. Carboxylic acid and hydrogen bond-donor catalysts that resemble the directing groups in proteins will be used as catalysts or cocatalysts in these model reactions. Subsequent research will apply these reactions to develop site-specific methods for in vitro chemical modification of proteins. Further research will use the protein modification methods as crucial tools in addressing challenges in chemical biology and developing protein-based pharmaceutical agents. An immediate impact of this research lies in the use of these methods to produce protein conjugates (such as protein-polymer conjugate) to extend circulatory half-life and reduce immunogenicity of protein therapeutics. Meanwhile, these methods will be used to elucidate important biological processes (such as cancer-relevant protein-protein interactions), leading to medicines of the next generation. Apart from its impact in chemical biology, this research should improve fundamental understanding of catalysis involving complicated systems, and therefore likely stimulating new strategies in catalysis and synthesis.
kw: catalysis and organic chemistry;Protein modification and biomolecule labeling;chemical biology;biological imaging;health science;medicine and pharmaceutical application

title: Nanostructured-Biomaterial Hybrid Systems for Bioelectronics
abs: Nanoscience and nanotechnology-based approaches are poised to give new insight into the nature of biological processes (e.g. sensing and signaling) at the nanoscale. Recently, there have been revolutionary advances in the utilization of synthetic nanomaterials to probe important biological processes, but the manipulation of such processes at the nanoscale is still in its infancy. This research proposal aims to combine three complementary methodologies – nanofabrication, electronics, and cell biology – with the goal of addressing how to monitor, manipulate, and mimic biological processes at the single molecule and/or cell level. We propose an aggresive three-year research program aimed at developing integrated nanostructure-biomaterial hybrid systems for bioelectronics and probing biological processes at the nanoscale. Furthermore, such work can lead to the development of nanobioelectronic tools and devices that regulate cellular functions by controlling the architecture at the interface between nanostructures and biomolecules, which would then allow the modulation of chemical and electronic signals through the interface. The specific research thrusts will be: 1) to fabricate protein transport junctions within nanogaps in order to understand charge transport through proteins and explore the functional nanodevices based on them; 2) to develop and evaluate bio-inspired synthesis and assembly at the nanoscale in order to exploit the nanocircuit based on biomolecules, mimic the biological sensing and signaling pathways, and improve the ability to study subcellular structure; and 3) to develop new integrated and complex nano-platforms to interface between nanoelectronic devices and cells in order to create new tools for monitoring and regulating cellular activities. Many important fundamental scientific issues such as the nature of charge transport through proteins, interfacial biological processes, and inter-/intra-cellular communications will be addressed in the proposed research. Ultimately, based on these specific thrusts, two-way communication of nanoelectronic devices with cells or cellular networks will be explored with the aim of developing future portable and implantable clinical nanodevices. This interdisciplinary project will create a knowledge base and technical platform for understanding and exploring interfacial biological processes and will also make valuable contributions to the fields of biology and medicine. Additionally, this research proposal may promote the development of cellular electronics and organic bioelectronics.
kw: nanofabrication;nanodevices;surface engineering;electrochemistry;bioelectronics;bio-inspiration

title: Development of Cooperative Transition Metal Catalysis for Carbon-Carbon Bond Formation
abs: The development of sustainable, efficient, and selective catalysis is one of the fundamental research goals in chemistry. During the last decades, a large number of transition metal catalysts especially based on precious metals such as palladium, rhodium, iridium and ruthenium have proven to be effective for various applications to the production of bulk and fine chemicals. However, the limited availability of these metals and their considerable toxicity makes it desirable to search for more economical and environmentally friendly alternatives. Our long-term goal is to develop powerful and selective catalysis based on first row transition metals, which are much less expensive and in some cases nontoxic. The specific hypothesis behind the proposed research is that synergism of transition metal and main group metal is the key to promote otherwise difficult molecular transformations, which has been cultivated through our previous studies on nickel and iron catalyses of Grignard reagents (Ni/Mg and Fe/Mg cooperation). Based on these experiences, the experimental focus of this proposal is on the development of highly efficient and selective carbon-carbon bond formation reactions catalyzed by appropriately designed combinations of first row transition metals, main group metal reagents, ligands, and other catalytic components. Specific aims include the development of highly efficient and selective catalysts for cross-coupling of unreactive aryl electrophiles (Specific Aim #1-A), multi-component coupling of unsaturated compounds (Specific Aim #1-B), and direct functionalization of C-H bonds (Specific Aim #2). Accomplishing these specific aims will offer an inexpensive way to fine chemicals including pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals and materials for organic electronics, and renovate the present catalytic processes that rely on the use of precious transition metal catalysts. Significant scientific contributions to synthetic and physical organic chemistry, organometallic chemistry and theoretical chemistry are also expected.
kw: homogeneous catalysis;transition metal complex;organometallic chemistry;green chemistry;asymmetric catalysis

title: Myeloid derived suppressor cells in Helicobacter pylori associated gastritis, pre-malignant and malignant gastric lesions
abs: Gastric cancer is a common cancer in Singapore. 90% of gastric cancers are Helicobacter pylori associated and chronic gastritis is thought to play a role in its pathogenesis. Evidence from animal and human studies show that tumours may modify the host immune response and subvert tumour immunity by inducing suppressor cells eg regulatory T cells. MDSCs are a heterogenous group of suppressive cells which have not previously been examined in gastric cancer. Murine MDSCs have been shown to be induced by prostaglandin E2(PGE2) and IL1beta, both of which are found in the H. pylori infected stomach. They express S100A8/9, a protein which has previously been demonstrated in gastric cancer. This study will examine the number and phenotype of MDSC in the tissue and the peripheral blood of patients with premalignant and malignant gastric tissue before and after surgery. We shall also examine the level of IL1beta, COX2, PGE2, S100A9 in patients with premalignant and malignant gastric lesions and correlate the number of MDSCs with tumour stage and patient prognosis. Finally, we shall investigate the mechanistic relationship between Helicobacter pylori, induction of MDSCs and the different T lymphocyte subsets. If MDSC numbers correlate with tumour burden and with the level of COX2 and PGE2 expression in the tumour, then the size of the MDSC population could be used to differentiate patients withearly vs late stage disease, and therefore patients who may benefit from adjuvant chemotherapy. It will also form the basis of future studies to determine the potential impact on patient outcome of strategies to reduce MDSC numbers by COX2 inhibitors which reduce PGE2 production.
kw: gastric cancer, inflammation, myeoid derived suppressor cells, Helicobacter pylori

title: Profiling of membrane lipids of adult and fetal red blood cells using mass spectrometry to identify novel surface marker for enrichment of fetal nucleated red blood cells (FNRBCs) from maternal blood for first trimester non-invasive prenatal diagnosis
abs: Without prenatal diagnosis, 1 in 50 babies are born with serious physical or mental handicap (Harper, 1998). One in five pregnant women in Singapore is above the age of 35 (Lai et al., 2002), and are offered to undergo an invasive procedure such as amniocentesis, chorionic villus sampling or fetal blood sampling to exclude chromosomal abnormalities in their fetus. These procedures, however, carry small but finite risks of miscarriage. Fetal cells, enriched from maternal blood, can facilitate non-invasive prenatal diagnosis. This is the Holy Grail of prenatal diagnosis as it eliminates the need for invasive fetal testing. Of the fetal cells that enter maternal circulation, fetal nucleated red blood cells (FNRBCs) are considered ideal for non-invasive prenatal diagnosis. But rarity of these cells in maternal circulation have hampered most efforts of enrichment (Bianchi, 1999) and an antibody specific to FNRBC membrane alone is yet to be available for immuno-cell-sorting. In this proposal, we aim to explore and study the membrane lipids of FNRBCs employing mass spectrometric technology to compare with that of adult red blood cells (RBCs) and identify a unique lipid class/specie(s). Antibody of the potential lipid class/specie(s) would serve as candidate(s) for use in enrichment. We hypothesize that identification of unique membrane lipids in FNRBCs is possible and can be pursued for development of antibody for immune-cell-sorting. This would enhance the enrichment of these rare cells from maternal blood.Our preliminary study indicates that there is differential expression of lipid class/specie(s) in these cells and a database for lipid species could be developed. However we require more samples to arrive at a more robust database, which could be achieved with lipid profiles generated by the proposed study. To our knowledge, there is no official database available in public domain on membrane lipids for either adult RBCs or FNRBCs.
kw: non-invasive, enrichment, surface marker, prenatal diagnosis, FNRBCs, membrane lipids

title: Effect of oxidative stress on dysbindin-1 expression in the rat hippocampus
abs: Significance The hippocampus is a brain region particularly vulnerable to ischemic damage and oxidative stress. Recently, a SNP in dysbindin-1 has been shown to interact with serious obstetric complications to dramatically increase risk for schizophrenia (Nicodemus et al. 2008). This supports the notion that changes in dysbindin-1 could interact with the effect of ischemic injury or oxidative stress to increase brain vulnerability to schizophrenia. Hypothesis to be tested Accordingly, we propose to investigate a possible role of the promoter of dysbindin-1 in response to oxidative stress, in view of significant associations between schizophrenia and genetic variation in intronic and / or promoter regions of the dysbindin-1 gene (Hall et al. 2004; Williams et al. 2005). Notably, the C-terminal PEST (proline-glutamic acid-serine-threonine) domain of IKK plays an important role in degradation of the protein after oxidative stress (Schoonbroodt et al. 2000). The dysbindin-1 protein, which also has a PEST sequence at its C-terminal is therefore suspected to play a similar role in the response of dysbindin-1 to oxidative stress. Our preliminary studies also showed that oxidative stress induced by intracerebroventricular ferrous ammonium citrate injection or kainate injection led to rapid dysbindin-1 degradation in hippocampal neurons similar to findings in human subjects. Therefore studies will also be carried test if oxidative stress could induce downregulation of dysbindin-1 expression in vivo, and if so, whether the effect could be reversed by antioxidant treatment.Methodology Human SH-SY5Y cells will be transfected with wildtype dysbindin-1 or dysbindin-1 with deleted or mutated PEST sequence. The cells will be exposed to oxidative stress, and degradation of dysbindin-1 in these cells evaluated by Western blots. The possible importance of the promoter of dysbindin-1 will also be evaluated, by promoter luciferase assay after exposure to oxidative stress. We will clone the sequence upstream of dysbindin-1 transcriptional start site into the promoter-less pGL3-Basic vector and assess the promoter activity in untreated transfected cells and in cells exposed to oxidative stressors. Mild or severe oxidative stress will be induced by i.c.v. injection of ferrous ammonium citrate or kainate in rats, and lipid peroxidation and dysbindin-1 levels in the hippocampal formation quantified with GC/MS and quantitative immunofluorescence. We will also attempt to reverse any oxidative stress-induced downregulation of dysbindin-1 expression by intraperitoneal injection of a blood-brain-barrier permeable antioxidant, gamma-glutamyl cysteine ethyl ester.Impact This set of experiments will investigate the neurobiologic effects of oxidative stress and specific promoter changes in dysbindin in terms of their effects on dysbindin expression levels. Further, these findings will be taken to the in-vivo level in murine hippocampus. By explicitly investigating the

title: Improving stem cell-derived insulin-producing cells for type 1 diabetes therapy by enhancement of MafA
abs: A loss of pancreatic islet ß-cell mass plays a critical role in the development of both type 1 and type2 diabetes. Type 1 diabetics need multiple daily insulin injections because their ß-cells are nolonger secreting enough the hormone. Such treatment has some limitations, e.g. hard to manage bythe young children, hypoglycemic risk, and impossible to achieve the physiological insulin releasepattern. An ideal therapy would be the replacement of the lost ß-cells by transplantation. However,the shortage of organ donors has limited the application of such treatment. Derivation of surrogateß-cells from stem cells may solve the problem. We have successfully achieved highly pure insulinproducingcell lines by differentiating mouse embryonic stem and progenitor cells (see 2publications below). These cells can secrete insulin in response to stimulation by glucose in vitroand reverse hyperglycemia in diabetic mice after transplantation. However, further characterizationrevealed that these cells seem immature and less physiologically functional compared to theprimary ß-cells, since they exhibit higher basal insulin release, lower amount of insulin secretionupon glucose stimulation and mitotic growth after transplantation. It is known that MafA is anessential master transcription factor involved in development and differentiation of ß-cells and inmaintenance of normal ß-cell function. The expression of MafA is much lower in our insulinproducingcells compared to that in islets. We hypothesize that such deficiency of MafA mightcontribute to the immaturity and less physiological function of our cells, whereas an enhancement ofMafA could bring the cells to normality. We will use a lentivirus-based system to overexpress MafAin our insulin-producing cells. Subsequently, we will examine insulin production, basal insulinrelease, secretory response to insulin stimulation, proliferation rate, and in vivo function in theMafA-elevated cells. The knowledge from this project will facilitate the derivation of physiologicallyfunctional insulin-producing cells for type 1 diabetes therapy.
kw: Diabetes, MafA, Insulin secretion, Insulin-producing cells, Stem cells, Islet ?-cells

title: Use of Respondent-Driven Sampling (RDS) to estimate the prevalence of HIV, syphilis and sexual risk behaviours in Men-who-have-Sex-with-Men (MSM) in Singapore
abs: In recent years, there has been a dramatic increase in HIV diagnoses attributable to transmission amongst men-who-have-sex-with-men (MSM), along with an increase in other sexually transmitted infections (STIs) such as syphilis. However, MSM are a hard-to-reach population in the Singapore context, so that it has been difficult to obtain estimates on the prevalence of HIV, STIs and sexual risk behaviour in this risk group for the purposes of planning and evaluating interventions for reducing transmission. Respondent-driven sampling (RDS) is a relatively new technique which was designed for sampling hard-to-reach populations, using a chain-referral system which relies on respondents to refer other potential respondents, while statistically adjusting for potential biases that might arise through the referral process. We propose to determine the feasibility of using RDS as a sampling methodology for investigating the prevalence of HIV, syphilis and sexual risk behaviours amongst MSM in Singapore. The study will aim to recruit 1000 subjects and obtain blood for HIV and syphilis testing as well as data on sexual behaviour through a self-administered questionnaire. Analysis will be performed with the aid of the Respondent Driven Sampling Analysis Tool (RDSAT) as well as standard statistical packages, and the adjusted and unadjusted results will be compared against estimates of HIV prevalence and risk behaviour obtained from prior surveys using other methodologies (sampling from MSM venues, surveys of sexual health clinic attendees, internet-based surveys). The study will assess the technical feasibility of the methodology, and its potential use as a tool for future surveillance, and as a mechanism for driving peer-led behaviour change interventions for MSM in Singapore. Data and biological specimens collected could also be used for follow-up modelling and molecular epidemiologic studies of HIV transmission in MSM in Singapore.
kw: public health, surveillance, sexual behaviour, HIV, sexually transmitted infections, network

title: Identification, Characterization and Therapeutic Targeting of N-CoR Protein Conformation Defects in Selected Leukemia and Solid Tumor Cells.
abs: We have recently identified N-CoR cleaving aberrant proteases as novel component of cytoprotective UPR (unfolded protein response) which protects acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) cells form ER (endoplasmic reticulum) stress-induced apoptosis. Our preliminary data suggest that activation of cytoprotective UPR is not restricted to APL; rather, several other leukemia and solid tumor cells exhibit cell type specific loss of N-CoR protein, which could result from the activation of cytoprotective UPR due to accumulation of mis-folded N-CoR protein. It is likely that conformational rearrangement resulting from genetic alterations or aberrant post-translational modifications may contribute to the mis-folding and destabilization of N-CoR protein in multiple types of tumor cells. This proposal is conceived with the goal to investigate whether destabilization of N-CoR protein in these tumor cells is due to mis-folding, to characterize the potential genetic alterations or post-translational modifications responsible for mis-folding of N-CoR protein in these tumor cells, and to identify novel N-CoR conformation modifying (NCM) agents that can rescue N-CoR conformation and function. The molecular mechanisms underlying the mis-folding of N-CoR protein will be investigated through analyzing tumor cell specific aberrant post-translational modifications of N-CoR protein and by identifying conformation altering mutations in N-CoR transcripts through specially designed protease sensitivity assay and direct DNA sequencing analysis. To identify novel conformation modifying agents that could rescue N-CoR conformation and promote growth arrest in these tumor cells, a FRET (florescence resonance energy transfer) based high through-put screening of chemical libraries of small molecular inhibitors will be performed using florescence labeled mis-folded N-CoR protein as target. It is likely that mis-folded N-CoR is a common contributing factor in the transformation of some leukemia and solid tumor cells, and therefore, could serve as a common qualitative intra-cellular molecular target for designing a unifying diagnostic and therapeutic approach for certain types of cancer.
kw: N-CoR mis-folding, Post-translational modification, UPR, Moleuclar targeting, Cancer therapeutics, Protein conformation modifier

title: Regulation of stress induced apoptosis and tumorigenesis by Stra13
abs: Regulation of cell death is critical for cellular homeostasis, and defective apoptosis is a hallmark ofcancers. The cellular response to various genotoxic stimuli that cause DNA-damage, as well as tooncogenes, is cell cycle arrest that allows for repair of damaged DNA, or apoptosis that eliminatescells with damaged genomes. A failure of this surveillance response can result in genetic alterationsthat lead to genome instability and development of cancers. The identification and characterization ofgenes that play a role in regulating apoptosis is thus critical to understanding the molecular basis oftumorigenesis.Stra13, a basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) transcription factor is rapidly induced by many genotoxicstimuli, suggesting that it may be a critical regulator of cellular responses to stress signals. Preliminarydata from Stra13-/- mice support this hypothesis. Thymocytes from Stra13-/- mice exhibit defectiveradiation-induced apoptosis, which is dependent on the tumor suppressor p53. Consistently Stra13-/-cells express lower levels of p53 and its transcriptional targets. Nevertheless, unlike p53-/- mice thatare resistant to acute radiation toxicity, Stra13-/- mice, similar to ATM-/- mice, are hypersensitive, andexhibit early lethality compared to wild type mice. Together, these results suggest that Stra13regulates DNA-damage induced apoptosis in both p53-dependent and independent ways. In thisproposal we will genetically examine the extent of functional overlap between Stra13 and p53 inapoptosis and tumorigenesis by generating p53/Stra13 double mutants and examine them fortumor frequency and spectrum. In addition, we will determine whether oncogene-induced p53activation contributes to transformation and tumorigenesis in Stra13-/- cells.Our long-term goal is to understand how Stra13 regulates apoptosis in response to various stresssignaling pathways. We believe that these studies will impact on our understanding of how alteredapoptosis can lead to tumorigenesis, and thus provide insights into the molecular basis ofdevelopment of cancers.
kw: tumour suppressor, apoptosis, Stra13, p53, transformation, tumourigenesis

title: Molecular cues guiding the self-renewal of hematopoietic stem cells
abs: Here we propose to exploit genetic approaches that allow us to decipher the rules of self-renewal of mouse hematopoietic stem cell (HSC).This will hopefully provide us strategies to expand and manipulate physiologically normal HSC in vitro. .Modified transcription factors that are assumed to have a role in hematopoiesis will be ectopically expressed in primitive mouse hematopoietic bone marrow (BM) cells in order to find candidates that can optimally support the expansion of HSC in culture. The best candidates will be then engineered in inducible forms that allow us to perform expression profiling and eventually to identify the potential molecular pathways involved in self-renewal. Importantly inducible approach gives us a tight temporal control over the ectopic expression also in vivo. On long term, we envisage, that rules learnt in the murine system could be transferred into human HSC and experimentally tested in humanized mouse model.
kw: Hematopoietc stem cell, Stem cell self-renewal

title: 5-Substituted Benzimidazoles as Novel Anti-Stroke Drugs
abs: One of the clinical aims to treat stroke patients is to contain the extent of brain injury so as to minimize patients’ cognitive decline. Given time and without treatment, brain tissues surrounding the core of insult (penumbra) can progress to infarction owing to uncontrolled excitotoxicity mediated by tetrameric N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors. Thus, a prime goal towards neuroprotection is to minimize this ischemic penumbra through down-regulating NMDA receptor overactivation. Early NMDA receptor antagonists suffer from undesirable psychomimetic or cardiovascular side effects due to non-subunit selectivity. Recently discovered 5-substituted benzimidazole derivatives exert highly potent NR2B subunit-selective antagonism with reduced hERG-channel activity (psychomimetic) and 1-adrenergic binding (cardiovascular side effects). Selective 5-substituted benzimidazole derivatives showed excellent activity in the carrageenan-induced mechanical hyperalgesia assay in rats and good pharmacokinetic behavior in dogs. However, they have not been tested as anti-stroke agents. In this grant application, we propose to test the hypothesis that ultra high-potent 5-substituted benzimidazole derivatives possess anti-stroke properties. Acute and chronic occlusion of the middle cerebral artery (MCAO) in rat, which model closely to the common clinical cerebral ischemia, would be used as the in vivo animal model to test two prototypic benzimidazoles with reference to the classical anti-stroke compound ifenprodil. We hypothesize that these two NR2B-selective benzimidazoles administered before or after ischemia induction would (a) confer significant reduction in regional cerebral blood flow, cortical water content and the total volume of ischemic brain injury, and (b) drug-treatment before ischemia induction would yield better prognosis owing to the instant availability of drug to exert the dual-inhibition mechanism. The in vivo findings from this application will form the foundation leading to future investigations into the mechanism of NR2-subunit selective antagonism and rational drug designs. The multi-disciplinary collaborations with medicinal chemists will foster strategic research synergy.
kw: Stroke, NR2B selective antagonists, neuroprotection, NMDA receptors, 5-substituted benzimidazoles, ischemia

title: MicroRNA Profiling in Childhood Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia
abs: Despite progress in our understanding of the biology of leukemias with consequent improvement in therapeutics, there is still significant room for improvement. Risk stratified therapy is adopted in acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). However the process and refinement of risk stratification usually occur in a number of steps over a period of time and includes factors such as baseline characteristics (genetics, presenting white cell count and age) as well as post-initial treatment characteristics (Day 8 respond to prednisalone, Day 33 minimal residual disease). The current knowledge state was reached after years of studies based on the DNA-RNA-Protein paradigm including the use of global genomics technology such as gene expression profiling. The recent discovery of non-coding small RNAs (microRNAs), which regulate gene expression and translation by binding to the 3’ untranslated region of coding genes through incomplete complementality, has altered this paradigm by adding an additional layer of control to the relationship between genes and their expression. The unique mechanism of action of microRNAs also means that a small number of microRNAs may control expression of a large number of genes, with a single microRNA predicted to have up to 200 target genes. Due to the pleomorphic nature of pathways and processes critical to cellular physiology and tumorigenesis that are regulated by microRNAs, they have been implicated in cancer biology. In this study, we will use a high-density array platform for microRNA profiling to study global microRNA expression in a large number of samples from patients with ALL entered into a Ma-SPORE clinical trial who have complete associated clinical, gene expression and genetic information from earlier evaluation studies performed in our laboratories. The specific aims of this study are to identify microRNA subsets exhibiting differential expression between malignant and normal blood cells, between the main genetic subtypes of ALL and between patients with different drug responses and clinical outcomes. In the process, novel understanding of disease biology, processes and pathway deregulation that lead to malignant transformation and identification of novel diagnostic markers, therapeutic targets, and predictors of therapeutic response and outcome could be obtained.
kw: microRNA, Prognosis, Leukaemia

title: Effects of hydrogen sulfide on cholesterol biosynthesis and atherogenesis: their possible relationship to reactive oxygen species
abs: Hydrogen sulphide (H2S), a novel gasotransmitter in the vascular system, is involved in the regulation of vascular tone, myocardial contractility and neurotransmission. We have globally profiled the gene expression of H2S-treated vascular smooth muscle cells and identified eight genes associated with cholesterol biosynthesis viz. HMG-CoA synthase, insulin-induced gene1, 7-dehydrocholesterol-reductase 7 and NAD(P)H quinine 1. We hypothesize that H2S could play a critical role in the modulation of cholesterol biosynthesis and thus vascular atherogenesis. Whether its effect is related to reactive oxygen species (ROS) – superoxide, hydrogen peroxide, and hydroxyl ions - is not known.This project proposes to (1) investigate the potential role of H2S on cholesterol biosynthesis and atherogenic development, and (2) identify its relationship to ROS. We will perform studies in New Zealand white rabbits rendered hypercholesterolaemic by feeding on a 1% cholesterol diet for 8 weeks. The rabbits will be treated with different daily doses of NaHS, an H2S donor, or propargylglycine (PAG), an H2S synthase inhibitor, during the 8-week period. In another experiment, hypercholesterolaemic rabbits will be treated with the optimum dose of NaHS identified, together with daily intravenous superoxide dismutase or catalyse over the 8-week period. Serum concentrations of total cholesterol, HDL, LDL, VLDL and triglycerides will be measured in these rabbits and compared with data in controls. ROS levels in blood and liver will also be measured to determine their changes in relation to H2S modulation. Morphological changes in aortic lesions will also be observed under microscopy and analyzed by image software. The expressions of HMG-CoA 1 synthase, insulin-induced gene 1, 7-dehydrocholesterol-reductase 7 and NAD(P)H-quinine 1 will be measured both transcriptionally and translationally. The results of these studies will clarify the functions of H2S and its relationship to ROS in atherogenesis in hypercholesterolaemic rabbits and provide insight into potentially novel pharmacological avenues for treating atherosclerosis.
kw: hydrogen sulfide, HMG CoA synthase, atherosclerosis, reactive oxygen species

title: Carbon nanotube/hydrogel nanobridge to boost neuronal signalling on the neural prosthetic devices
abs: Neural electrodes have been useful tools for neurophysiologists by providing the most feasible way toaccess to the neural signals. The challenges for researchers in this field are to obtain stable neural signalsfor extended periods of time. The goal of this proposal is, therefore to develop and evaluate CarbonNanoTube (CNT) coating schemes to improve the long term performance of neural prosthetic devices.Here, we describe research that will allow us design, synthesize, and characterize new classes of materialssystem with more precise control of structure at the nanometer length scale. These nanobridging schemesinclude networks of CNTs that can be electrophoretically deposited directly on the electrode site (2-D CNTs)and CNTs grown through hydrogel scaffolds (3-D CNTs). The unique electrical properties and high aspectratio of CNTs make them one of the promising candidate materials for modification of the neural electrodes.This proposed study will provide important information that will reveal what combinations of materialschemistry and microstructure are most important in creating chronic performance of the neural prostheticdevices. Moreover, there has been no attempt to utilize CNTs in hydrogel scaffold to coat the neuralelectrodes. In this proposed research, thus, the specific aims are to: (1) design and synthesize CNTnanobridges to link neural electrodes to neurons, (2) characterize the structural, electrical and mechanicalproperties of the CNTs nanobrides, and (3) evaluate cellular response of nerve cells to CNTs coatings.These aims will be achieved by employing an interdisciplinary approach including inorganic chemistry,polymer engineering and cellular biology. The outcome of this proposed research may provide insight intothe design of novel hybrid electrodes that are clinically useful for treatment of various neurodegenerativedisorders.
kw: Neural Electrodes, Hydrogel, Neurodegenerative disorder, Carbon Nanotubes (CNTs), Long-term implantation, Nanobridge

title: Targeting Hepatitis B RNA Splicing as a Novel Approach to Inhibit Viral Replication.
abs: For the 350 million chronic hepatitis B (HBV) patients worldwide, the existing therapies are expensive, and often lead to drug resistance development. HBV RNA splicing, which produce both defective viral particles and express a novel peptide, had been associated with viral persistence. The biological significance is still being investigated.We hypothesize that HBV RNA splicing and the resultant hepatitis B splice-generated peptide (HBSP) acts as an immune decoy to enhance immune tolerance and supports viral replication through increasing the core antigen and X protein expression.The aims of the study are as follows:1.To determine which of the mechanisms are important in causing HBV persistence in a hepatoma co-transfection model. 2.To study the effects of anti-sense RNA inhibition of the HBV RNA splicing and nuclear-cytoplasm export in HBV-producing cells.3.Examine the changes in the proportions of splice variants during the natural history of infected patients to verify if the identified mechanism fits with the clinical picture. Methodology:A splice acceptor mutant (incapable of splicing) 3.2kb HBV genome with its corresponding splice variant DNA will be co-transfected into hepatoma cells in adherent culture at varying proportions, and the influence of the splice products on the cytokine production, expression of viral antigens and viral replication will be studied. Antisense RNA targeting various splice donor and acceptor sites will be transfected into a HBV model cell line to evaluate their effect on viral replication and antigen expression. Finally serum from patients with chronic HBV infection will be analysed for their HBV total and spliced DNA by real-time PCR assay.Approach:This proof-of-concept study will help to delineate the biological roles of HBV RNA splicing and explore its potential to develop into a therapy. The splice/unspliced HBV DNA ratio will be correlated with clinical profiles and value as a prognostic factor.
kw: Hepatitis B, Post-transcriptional regulation, Splice variant, Antisense RNA

title: High Dimensional ROC Analysis: Methods and Applications in Eye and Other Diseases
abs: Statistical methods for disease screening and diagnosis have attracted significant research interests. The Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve, a plot of sensitivity vs 1-specificity of the test, is the standard tool for describing the performance of the screening and diagnostic tests. However, in many situations in biomedical research, the diagnostic decision is not limited to a binary choice (disease vs no disease). Often, clinicians and researchers deal with categorical outcomes such as severity or stages of diseases (e.g., early to late stages of cancer, severity of heart disease etc). New statistical methods are needed for multi-categorical classifications. In this proposal, we will develop theory and methods for high dimensional ROC surface. We will use three population-based studies of eye diseases to test these methods: the Singapore Malay Eye Study (SiMES), a Glaucoma Screening study in the polyclinic and the Blue Mountains Eye Study (BMES) in Australia. SiMES examined 3,280 participants aged 40-80 years to study the prevalence and risk factors for major eye diseases affecting Malay people in Singapore. The Glaucoma Screening study examined 2052 subjects to assess the screening effectiveness of 3 new noncontact devices in identifying angle closure glaucoma and narrow angles. The BMES examined 3,654 persons for eye diseases and followed-up participants over 10 years. We will use these datasets to examine predictive factors for major eye disease outcomes: severity of diabetic retinopathy, severity of cataract, categories of refractive error and severity of age-related macular degeneration in SiMES, severity of narrow angle in the Glaucoma screening study; and 10-year incidence of diabetic retinopathy, cataract, age-related macular degeneration and glaucoma in BMES. Results from this study will allow new statistical methods to determine the utility of tests for categorical outcomes and will be applicable not only to eye diseases, but also cardiovascular disease, cancer and other chronic disorders.
kw: Three way ROC analysis, Multi-category classification, Nonparametric estimation, Volume under ROC surface, Maximum likelihood estimation

title: ROLE OF CD151 IN THE MODULATION OF AIRWAY SMOOTH MUSCLE CONTRACTION
abs: Lung diseases such as asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) are common,debilitating and sometimes fatal; and therefore have immense individual and social costs. Excessiveairway obstruction in response to relatively low concentrations of constricting agents (such asmethacholine or histamine) or indirectly acting stimuli (such as cold air, respiratory infections orallergens, exercise or cigarette smoke) is referred to as airways hyperresponsiveness [AHR,(Thomson, 1983)]. Airway smooth muscle (ASM) contraction is thought to underlie mechanisms ofAHR and in this proposal we aim to investigate the role of CD151 in modulating this process. Thepresent study is novel as it assesses a function for CD151 in the regulation of ASMcontraction – this focus stems from our laboratory’s unique data identifying CD151 as amodulator of intracellular signaling pathways that control contraction. This study will not onlyincrease our understanding of the mechanisms by which AHR occurs but may offer anadditional therapeutic target in the design of more selective agents that control thecontractility of ASM cells for the treatment of obstructive diseases such as asthma and COPD.More specifically, the aims of our study are (a) to investigate the role of CD151 in modulating Gprotein-coupled receptor-mediated ASM contraction in vitro (through assessment of intracellular Ca2+levels in cultured ASM cells) and ex vivo (through assessment of mouse tracheal ring contraction);and (b) to determine the role of CD151 in allergen-induced AHR using genetically modified CD151- mice challenged with inhaled allergen (through assessment of respiratory mechanics - airwayresistance and dynamic compliance). A three-year plan for a multi-disciplinary, translational researchprogram is proposed to complete cell culture-based studies and in vivo analysis of AHR to test thehypothesis that CD151 regulates ASM contraction signaling to influence AHR.
kw: lung disease, airway hyperrespoonsiveness, calcium, airway smooth muscle contraction, tetraspanins

title: Study of exhaled airflows and the transmission of airborne viruses for indoor aerosol infection control
abs: Various infectious agents are known to be transmitted via respiratory aerosols produced either naturally or with oxygen masks. Whilst aerosol transmission can occur between multiple individuals, it is important to assess the two-person transmission scenario, first. A non-invasive, real-time (‘Schlieren’) imaging technique will be used to investigate the interaction of airflows between two individuals: one human volunteer alone, then with a life-like manikin. Otherwise healthy human volunteers, with seasonal cough/cold symptoms will be recruited for the experiments. Their ‘sick’ and ‘well’ airflow patterns will be characterized and compared in a variety of scenarios.The human volunteer will perform various respiratory activities (including coughing, sneezing, breathing and talking) within 1m of the manikin. These experiments are designed to mimic most social interactions:, i.e. conversations across a table, in corridors, on ward rounds and on public transport, etc. It will provide important data on the risk of exposure to infectious aerosols in such everyday situations.Swabs from areas around the “facial mucous membranes” regions of the manikin (i.e. around the eyes, nose and mouth) will be taken for diagnostic testing after each respiratory activity, to determine if any common respiratory virus has passed from the volunteer (whose respiratory virus infection will be laboratory-confirmed) to the manikin.These experiments will be repeated with the volunteers wearing surgical and N95 face masks to determine their effectiveness (i.e. to identify and quantify any air leakage). Finally, the risk of using various types of oxygen masks as sources of potentially infectious aerosols will be assessed. Results from this study will assess the effectiveness of indoor aerosol infection control e.g. effectiveness of various face masks, and identify potential infection risks when using oxygen masks. This data will assist the improvement of infection control guidelines, e.g. optimizing bed-spacing on hospital wards containing potentially infectious patients.
kw: Visualisation, Transmission, Airflow, Control, Aerosol, Infection

title: Engineering human beta defensin 28 for superior salt-resistant properties and antimicrobial potency
abs: The lack of new antibiotics to address growing microbial infections worldwide and the emerging multidrugresistant problems due to widespread misuse of antibiotics, demands alternative antimicrobialstrategies to address this global health crisis. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are a promising class ofmolecules which exhibit rapid and broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity, making them clinically usefulcompounds for development into new antibiotics. However, a barrier to their success as anti-infectiveagents for clinical applications is the instability of most AMPs under physiological salt conditions. Thisstudy seeks to research and address this fundamental problem of salt-intolerance inherent in human betadefensins (HBDs), a potent class of AMPs, and create new salt-tolerant synthetic HBD variants. Themodel peptide to be studied is HBD-28; it has excellent antimicrobial properties and a broad activityspectrum. Wild-type HBD-28 will be subjected to amino acid modification to increase net peptide charge,by substitution of uncharged polar amino acids with dibasic amino acids. Salt-intolerance in HBDs ishypothesized to result from charge-shielding on the microbial membrane, imposed by salt-derived ions,which reduces the electrostatic-driven cell membrane permeabilisation by AMPs. The contributions ofcharge number, proximity and topology on HBD-28 salt-sensitivity will be researched. Computationalmodeling will be used to guide the design of charged HBD-28 mutants to facilitate selection of mutantswith favourable structural energetics and charge distribution for good antimicrobial performance.Consequential peptide structural changes induced by an increase in cationicity, and its effect onantimicrobial spectrum, specificity and cytotoxicity will be thoroughly studied. Resolving the fundamentalproblem of salt-intolerance in beta defensins will widen their therapeutic window and provide a valuabletemplate for the development of salt-resistant antibiotics. A successful research outcome will represent acritical milestone in increasing stability of AMP molecules and expedite their development into successfulantibiotic alternatives.
