title: Dentoalveolar reconstruction using a sugar-coated bone regenerative approach: A pig jaw model
abs: In the dentoalveolar skeleton, an inadequate bone volume often creates problems in the prosthetic and aesthetic reconstruction of partially and completely edentulous situations. The availability of alveolar ridge is critical in determining whether additional ridge augmentation procedure is required prior to dental implant placement. We propose a novel guided bone regeneration (GBR) technique consisting of a slow-degrading, polycaprolactone-tricalcium phosphate (PCL-TCP) sheet for membrane stability, space maintenance and graft protection; and the addition of a porous PCL-TCP scaffold combined with biomolecules as an alternative bone substitute.The biomolecules tested will include the extracellular glycosaminoglycan sugar, heparan sulphate (HS), when used alone or combined with bone morphogenetic protein-2 (BMP-2). The objectives of the study are to:1) Investigate the effects of HS delivered with PCL-TCP scaffolds on host response in dentoalveolar defects. Special attention will be given to the stimulation of endogenous growth factors that play an influential role in bone repair and regeneration.2) Compare the quality and extent of bone formation in dentoalveolar defects between HS alone and HS combined with BMP-2 delivered by PCL-TCP scaffolds.GBR procedures will be performed in the mandibular defects of a pig model. PCL-TCP scaffolds incorporated with HS alone, BMP-2 alone and HS-BMP-2 combined will be contrasted for the amount of bone formation after 3 and 6 months. We hypothesize that this strategy can be used safely and predictably as a barrier membrane for GBR in mandibular defects. The clinical importance of this approach is that the amount of BMP-2 and possibly other growth factors required can be reduced, if co-delivered with HS, which would significantly bring down the cost of treatment. If proven successful, the need for autogenous bone graft (often yielding unpredictable results) in such dentoalveolar reconstructions can be dismissed. An additional benefit is the reduction of patient morbidity and ‘downtime’. Keeping in mind the further anticipated augmentation of wound healing and bone regeneration by HS activity, we present a viable bone regenerative approach that is not only more affordable, but also more effective.

title: Targeting Cancer with Telomerase Interference and Characterization of Progenitor Cancer cells and Cancer Stem cells
abs: New antineoplastic strategies should be directed at targets that are unique to cancer cells andthat are critical to the development of metastases. One such target is the enzyme telomerase,which lengthens and protects the telomeres at the ends of chromosomes. Telomerase is aribonucleoprotein consisting of two core components: a reverse transcriptase protein (TERT, orhTERT in humans) and telomerase RNA (Ter, or hTer in humans). hTer contains a shorttemplate sequence used by hTERT to synthesize telomeric DNA. A growing body of dataindicates that while telomerase activity is lost in most normal, differentiated cells, it is highlyup-regulated in cancer cells and is in fact critical to their continued proliferation. Moreover,telomerase activity plays an important role in stem cell function, and interfering with telomerasemay therefore constitute an effective strategy for controlling so-called cancer stem cells, whichhave recently emerged as important contributors to cancer metastasis and recurrence. We havedeveloped two telomerase-targeting gene constructs: The first encodes a short interfering RNA(siRNA) that knocks down endogenous hTer, and the second encodes an hTer with a mutatedtemplate sequence (MT-hTer). When co-expressed in cancer cell lines, MT-hTer/siRNA causesrapid DNA damage, apoptosis, and cell cycle arrest. We have studied the translationaltherapeutic potential of MT-hTer/siRNA.We have developed new models aimed atdemonstrating whether telomerase-based strategies constitute a viable therapeutic approach tocancer. These pre-clinical models have included tissue cultures of primary cancer cells andcancer stem cells that can be used to test the efficacy of telomerase interference in actual,tumor-derived tissues, thus serving as preclinical proof of principle for this promising newapproach to the treatment of cancer.

title: Signaling Mechanism and Antagonist Design for Treating Human Cancers and OtherDiseases by Targeting Eph Receptors and Ephrins
abs: Eph receptors and ephrins constitute the largest family of receptor tyrosine kinases with 15individual receptors and 9 ligands. Eph-ephrin mediated signaling networks control axon guidance,cell migration, segmentation, tumorogenesis and bone remodeling. A large body of results indicatesthat Eph-ephrin signaling networks play key roles in tumorigenesis, particularly tumor growth,progression and survival. Consequently, the interaction interfaces between Eph and ephrin representattractive targets for drug design to treat human cancers and other diseases.I have been working on Eph-ephrin signaling for more than 10 years and submitted a NMRCproposal in 2006 aiming to understanding signaling mechanism and designing antagonists for theEph-ephrin interaction. However, a concern was raised as whether the active Eph ectodomains couldbe generated, and consequently I was only offered a pilot grant first to test the feasibility. Supportedby this grant, we have now not only demonstrated that the active Eph ectodomains including EphB2,EphA4-EphA8 could be easily expressed in E. coli cells (1-2), but also made a significantbreakthrough in the field. Namely, for the first time we showed that the Eph ectodomain could bespecifically targeted by small molecule antagonists capable of inhibiting retraction and rounding ofPC3 prostate cancer cells (2). This discovery opens up an unprecedented avenue to design andoptimize the small molecule antagonists for treating cancers and other diseases.Therefore, further NMRC funding is urgently needed to continue our exciting research. Thecurrent proposal is thus aimed at deepening our pilot studies on structures, dynamics and interactionsamong Eph receptors and ephrins; as well as their interactions with a diverse spectrum of peptide andsmall molecule antagonists, in an ultimate attempt to design the antagonistic molecules with higheraffinity and specificity which can clinically used to treat human cancers and other diseases.Furthermore, the established platform and methodology in this project will also benefit drug designexcises on other drug targets by the applicant and other scientists.1. title: Phase III, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of post-operative adjuvant concurrent chemo-radiotherapy with or without nimotuzumab for stage III/IV head and neck squamous cell cancer
abs: The aim of the study is to improve the loco-regional control rate and overall survival of locally advanced head and neck squamous carcinoma (HNSCC). We hypothesize that the addition of nimotuzumab (a recombinant humanized murine immune antibody that blocks both epidermal growth factor (EGF) and transforming growth factor (TGF)) to the current gold standard of concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CCRT) (7)(8), an adjuvant setting in patients after resection of their locally advanced HNSCC will confer therapeutic advantage. We have designed a phase III randomized study that includes a placebo arm. We assume a 10% increase in 2 year disease free survival (from 60% to 70%). To achieve statistical significance at 90% power, we calculate the need for 355 patients per arm, assuming also a 10% dropout rate. We aim to accomplish this study with the involvement of a multidisciplinary team of surgical, radiation and medical oncologists actively involved in the management of HNSCC coming from multiple institutions and spanning at least 12 different countries. For quality assurance we will have the involvement of Singapore Clinical Research Institute who will lead the data coordination and ensure fidelity of data collected and statistical analysis; the European Society of Therapeutic Radiation Oncology (EQUAL-ESTRO) for radiation dose and fields and an international independent panel of medical oncologist, radiation oncologist and biostatistician for the Data Monitoring Committee (DMC). This committee will monitor significant events and advise on continuation or termination of trial. Concurrent with the randomized trial, we will be collecting biospecimens including blood, tumour and saliva, pre-treatment and on completion of surgical resections. We hypothesize that there are important biomarkers including clusters of genes, cancer stem cells that will predict prognosis and treatment response. The analyses performed will be very powerful because of the large sample size, the specimens are collected prospectively and because the statistical analyses will be multivariate, incorporating not only treatment but biological and staging data.

title: Retinal Microvascular Changes and Asian Glaucoma Subtypes: Understanding Early Vascular Mechanisms in Asian Glaucoma
abs: Glaucoma is one of the leading causes of irreversible blindness worldwide. Despite extensive research,its etiology is unknown. The main risk factor for the development of glaucoma is raised IOP. However, asignificant proportion of glaucoma patients have IOP within the statistically normal population range.Thus, non-IOP related factors have been implicated in glaucoma pathogenesisThe major non-IOP mechanism hypothesized to contribute to glaucoma development is vasculardisease. Various vascular mechanisms (e.g., abnormal ocular blood flow, hypotension) have beensuggested to lead to ischemia, optic neuropathy and subsequent glaucoma. However, whether vasculardisease is associated with glaucoma, and whether it contributes to a particular subtype of glaucoma,remains unclear. We have developed a precise method to quantify retinal vascular changes fromphotographs, and shown these changes are markers of early vascular diseaseIn the current study, we aim to determine the relationship of a range of novel retinal vascular changes(vessel diameters, tortuosity, branching angle, fractals) with primary glaucoma subtypes (open angle,closed angle, normal tension, high tension) in 600 persons with glaucoma in Singapore. We willcompare the retinal vascular changes between glaucoma subtypes and with 1,200 age-race-gendermatched population controls from studies under the Singapore Epidemiology of Eye Disease (SEED)programme, in which retinal vascular changes have been measured on about 10,000 persons ofChinese, Malays and Indian ethnicity.The identification of early vascular changes in glaucoma will lead to a better understanding of glaucomapathogenesis, and may have implications for treatment, by shifting the focus not only on IOP-loweringmeasures but also targeting arteriolar changes and ischaemic processes that may lead to optic nervedamage.
kw: Pathogenesis, Optic nerve morphology, Intra-ocular pressure

title: Understanding the spread of MRSA within a medical ward at SGH
abs: Methicillin resistant staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) infection has been recognized as a major public health concern in nosocomial environments, locally and internationally. Several interventions have been introduced in an attempt to control or eradicate MRSA from ICUs and general wards but none have been successful since the efforts of Scandinavian countries more than two decades ago. One reason for the failures has been a lack of understanding of the transmission of MRSA at the individual level. We propose an individual-based, spatially-explicit predictive model of movement and interaction patterns at a Medical Ward at the Singapore General Hospital (SGH), in the form of a highly configurable risk assessment software tool so as to model direct and indirect disease transmission among heterogeneous individuals through their role-directed activities within the ward.The vehicle for the software is the customization and extension of an individual-based epidemiological simulation system called PathoSIM that can accurately simulate the dynamics of MRSA spread among staff and patients within the medical ward of SGH. Specifically, the model will predict and explain primary outcome measures (eg morbidities and mortalities) of MRSA based on environmental, social or policy changes impacting:•Type of index individual and quantity•Individual susceptibilities and transmissibility•Individual levels of adherence•Efficacy of intervention controls•Staff Levels•CA-MRSA incidence rateBased on the results, adjustments can then be judiciously and economically applied to improve operations, while also used as a educational tool for increasing awareness and adherence levels among the hospital staff. A unique value of our simulation approach is the use of non-intrusive tracking device during the profiling stage to collect movement patterns of staff at the medical ward. Recent results published at the Keystone Symposium in Bangkok showed that consistent and distinct movement motifs were actually being adopted by staff.Our preliminary from a feasibility study of modeling disease spread at CDC, Tan Tock Seng Hospital has shown useful simulation results that validated contact patterns, and helped determine the yield of contact tracing, as well as cohorting effects.

title: INTRAUTERINE HAEMOPOIETIC STEM CELL GENE THERAPY FOR BETA THALASSAEMIA MAJOR IN A MURINE FETAL MODEL
abs: B-thalassaemia major is a common inherited disease, causing severe morbidity from impaired erythropoiesis and early mortality if untreated. Presently, cure can only be achieved with allogeneic haemopoietic stem cell (HSC) transplantation, but this is hindered by a shortage of haploidentical donors, pre-transplant conditioning-related morbidities, engraftment failure and mortality. Children without donors are subject to life-long transfusions and serious morbidity from iron-overload.Intrauterine gene therapy (IUGT) may be one approach that overcomes these obstacles, where autologous HSC are harvested, transduced with the B-globin transgene and transplanted back into the early-gestation fetus, circumventing the immune system and pre-empting the pathophysiological processes associated with the disease. We seek funding to investigate the hypothesis that b-thalassaemia major can be cured with intrauterine transplantation of transduced HSC using advanced-generation lentiviral vectors in a murine model. Specifically, we aim to determine the effectiveness of HSC transduction in-vitro with a novel lentiviral vector delivering a human mini-beta-globin transgene driven through an erythroid-specific BLCR promoter. Thereafter we will investigate the ability of these transduced HSC to correct anaemia and reduce extra-medullary haemopoiesis in thalassaemic murine fetuses.Briefly, thalassaemic fetal HSC will be transduced in-vitro and assessed for transduction efficiency and erythroid lineage-specific B-globin.expression. Consequently, transduced HSC will be transplanted into mid-gestation fetal mice. Transplanted offspring will be monitored for survival, growth and correction of anaemia and extra-medullary haemopoiesis. Offspring will be harvested serially for vector distribution, transgene expression and iron-loading analyses. With advancements in prenatal diagnosis technology, effecting IUGT can potentially ameliorate severe diseases, rescuing fetuses which may otherwise be stillborn or severely damaged at birth. If successful, it will be applicable to other haematological diseases, including a-thalassaemia, a universally perinatally lethal condition.

title: Improving stem cell-derived insulin-producing cells for type 1 diabetes therapy by enhancement of MafA
abs: A loss of pancreatic islet ß-cell mass plays a critical role in the development of both type 1 and type2 diabetes. Type 1 diabetics need multiple daily insulin injections because their ß-cells are nolonger secreting enough the hormone. Such treatment has some limitations, e.g. hard to manage bythe young children, hypoglycemic risk, and impossible to achieve the physiological insulin releasepattern. An ideal therapy would be the replacement of the lost ß-cells by transplantation. However,the shortage of organ donors has limited the application of such treatment. Derivation of surrogateß-cells from stem cells may solve the problem. We have successfully achieved highly pure insulinproducingcell lines by differentiating mouse embryonic stem and progenitor cells (see 2publications below). These cells can secrete insulin in response to stimulation by glucose in vitroand reverse hyperglycemia in diabetic mice after transplantation. However, further characterizationrevealed that these cells seem immature and less physiologically functional compared to theprimary ß-cells, since they exhibit higher basal insulin release, lower amount of insulin secretionupon glucose stimulation and mitotic growth after transplantation. It is known that MafA is anessential master transcription factor involved in development and differentiation of ß-cells and inmaintenance of normal ß-cell function. The expression of MafA is much lower in our insulinproducingcells compared to that in islets. We hypothesize that such deficiency of MafA mightcontribute to the immaturity and less physiological function of our cells, whereas an enhancement ofMafA could bring the cells to normality. We will use a lentivirus-based system to overexpress MafAin our insulin-producing cells. Subsequently, we will examine insulin production, basal insulinrelease, secretory response to insulin stimulation, proliferation rate, and in vivo function in theMafA-elevated cells. The knowledge from this project will facilitate the derivation of physiologicallyfunctional insulin-producing cells for type 1 diabetes therapy.

title: Genomic analysis and development of a new multilocus variable-number tandem-repeat analysis scheme for molecular epidemiological typing of Acinetobacter baumannii
abs: Introduction and Clinical SignificanceAcinetobacter baumannii is an internationally emerging nosocomial pathogen that is characterized bymultidrug resistance and its propensity to target immunocompromised and intensive-care unit patients.Molecular typing of bacteria is important for understanding their epidemiology and for facilitating infectioncontrol efforts. To date, there is no timely, cost-effective and highly discriminatory typing method for A.baumannii.Specific Aims1. To develop a novel multiple-locus variable-number tandem-repeat analysis (MLVA) scheme formolecular typing of A. baumannii.2. To assemble and annotate whole genome sequences of local epidemic A. baumannii isolates.HypothesisA PCR-based MLVA typing scheme can be developed for Acinetobacter baumanii that is low-cost andrapid while retaining high discriminatory power.Methodology• Two local A. baumannii whole bacterial genomes (previously sequenced commercially) will beassembled and annotated.• Together with three existing published A. baumannii genomes, these will be screened for thepresence of common variable-number tandem-repeat (VNTR) regions.• Primers will be developed for these regions and tested singly and in combination on a largecollection of local A. baumannii isolates to determine the final MLVA scheme that will have themost reproducibility, stability and discriminatory power.• The local isolates will also be typed using pulsed-field gel electrophoresis (PFGE) and multilocussequence typing (MLST) – the current accepted and gold-standard methods for typing of A.baumannii.• Comparisons with regards to concordance and discriminatory power will be made to PFGE andMLST results.

title: Elucidating the DNA damage response pathways in head and neck cancer stem cells.
abs: Head and neck squamous cell cancers (HNSCC) pose an important health problem both locally and worldwide. Despite optimum standard of care, overall survival remains a disappointing 50% at five years, where treatment failure plagues a subset of patients at every stage of disease. Recent data suggest that HNSCCs contain a highly tumorigenic subpopulation of cells termed cancer stem cells (CSC). These have been identified based on expression of cell surface markers and propagated as tumor xenografts in mice. Unfortunately, further experimentation is limited by the complexity of maintaining xenografts and restrictions posed by an in vivo model. In vitro models have been successfully established for a number of solid tumors by identifying the CSC subpopulation in cell lines. Techniques range from using cell-surface markers, enzymatic reactions and the ability for CSCs to be propagated as spheroids in suspension.We have successfully established a CSC model in two well-studied HNSCC cell lines (FadU and H357), grown as spheroids in suspension culture. We intend to use this model to study the DNA damage response pathway in HNSCC. Our aims are fourfold: first to establish the spheroid model in culture using cell lines and primary tumors. Second, to determine cell-cycle, apoptotic and proliferative phenotype in response to radiation. Third, to determine the pathways through which CSCs bypass the usual DNA damage response. This will be done in two parts: to compare the expression profile of using microarray experiments and Western blots focussed on the p53 pathway. Finally, we aim to answer whether targeted therapy, against a number pathways known to be deranged in HNSCC, is able to augment the eradication of CSCs. Preliminary data from our laboratory shows that CSCs fail to activate cell cycle checkpoints in response to x-ray induced damage. We have isolated RNA and cell lysates from these cells at various time points to proceed with microarray and Western blot experiments. We are also in the process of testing different media to establish spheroid cultures from primary tumors.Understanding these pathways will be critical to the paradigm shift required to treat HNSCC and focus the therapeutic endpoint to eradicating CSCs rather than merely reducing tumor bulk alone.

title: Human tear patho-physiology in Dry Eye and Ocular Surface Disease
abs: Multiple population-based studies have highlighted the public health significance of dry eye by its high prevalence among older age groups, and increasing trend with aging population.The irritative symptoms of dry eye are debillitating and result in both psychological and physical effects that impact quality of life, including the limitation and reduced performance of common vision-related daily activities, such as driving. The cost of treatment, lack of cure , and lack of universal standards for diagnosis of dry eye add to the public health impact. Like manay ocular surface diseases, dry eye is caused by dysfunctional tear and not necessarily reduced tear secretion. The human tear film is an important body fliud that protects the ocular structures and serves as medium for transmission of light necessary for vision. We hypothesize that understanding tear proteins and lipids and their variability can help the development of an objective diagnostic test as well as strategies for treatment. Despite its importance, knowlegde about tear components and biochemistry is scanty. The progress of this field is hampered by the inability to rigorously assess the biochemcial characteristics of a minute quantity of tear. Using the infrastructure of Singapore Eye Research Institute,together with the population-based Singapore Indian and Chinese Cohort study, we propose to investigate the epidemiological factors that affect tear proteins and lipids, and their association with dry eye and inflammatory eyelid disease. This monitors intensively, those taking hormonal preparations and those wearing contact lenses. The study uses isobaric tag peptide labeling and mass spectrometry to identify and quantify proteins, state of the art non-invasive imaging for eyelid inflammation, and a system that allows tear osmolarity assessment in a minute amount of human tears.

title: Role of epigenetics in ocular surface wound healing
abs: The wound healing response is a highly orchestrated event that involves many cell types and signaling mechanisms and cell – matrix interactions. A slight deviation from the tightly regulated events will lead to the development of pathological states. Wound healing disorders play a major role in the ocular surface disease, such as pterygium and in post-operative scarring after glaucoma surgery, which increases the risk of surgical failure. Every aspect of wound healing cell function is governed by specific genes expressed. However, the expression of these genes in turn can also be altered through modifications of DNA (methylation) or mRNA (microRNAs) level, which is termed epigenetics. The aims of this study are to evaluate the role of epigenetics in conjunctival wound healing disorders and in turn determine the potential use of miRNA strategies for modulating the wound healing response. It is hypothesised that methylation is present in the promoters of critical genes involved in conjunctival wound healing in addition to the suggestion that miRNAs are centrally involved in the regulation of the cellular events of conjunctival injury, such as that following glaucoma filtration surgery. The role of miRNAs in ocular disease is now emerging as an important field of research, with a wealth of potential as a novel therapeutic and screening strategy. MiRNA expression profiling and DNA methylation analysis on conjunctival tissue samples retrieved from pterygia excised at the time of pterygium surgery and glaucoma patients undergoing filtration surgery will identify the target genes and miRNAs responsible for aberrant wound healing.

title: Prevention of scarring from eye surgeries with small molecule histone deacetylase inhibitors.
abs: The success of ocular surgeries is highly dependent on proper healing at the surgical wound site. In refractive surgery involving penetrating incisions or ablation injury to the cornea, a pathologic healing response may result in an abnormal fibrotic response causing corneal opacity. In glaucoma filtration surgery, excessive postoperative scarring at the subconjunctival wound site significantly reduces surgical success. Anti-scarring agents used to counter this are typically cytotoxic and may result in severe sight-threatening complications. Hence, safer anti-scarring treatments are required. The processes of normal wound healing as well as fibrotic repair are associated with the phenomenon called epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT). EMT describes the process whereby epithelial cells change their phenotype to fibroblastic cells. Fibrotic repair occurs when aberrant EMT produces persistent fibroblasts that secrete excessive amounts of collagen and other extracellular matrix components and causes tissue scarring. Hence, regulating aberrant EMT may alleviate tissue fibrosis. Recent reports revealed that EMT may be subjected to epigenetic regulation by histone deacetylation. Indeed, histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitors comprising of small molecule organic compounds have been demonstrated to suppress EMT in a variety of cell types as well as skin fibrogenesis. In addition, the safety of several HDAC inhibitors such as valproic acid and phenylbutyrate have been well validated as they are already in use clinically for other conditions. This project proposes to employ HDAC inhibitors to regulate the EMT of corneal/subconjunctival cells with a view to blocking scarring in the wounded eye. The efficacy and effects of the HDAC inhibitors will be studied in cultured corneal epithelial cells and Tenon’s fibroblasts. The current proposal is clinically significant since excessive scarring is a major cause of visual morbidity and blindness. Results obtained from this application may lead to novel therapeutic modalities to prevent scarring after ocular surgeries and other ocular fibrotic conditions.
kw: HDAC inhibitors, wound healing, EMT, glaucoma

title: Novel molecular targeted therapeutic development and preclinical drug testing for renal cell carcinoma (RCC) using a RCC-derived murine xenograft model
abs: Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is the most lethal of all urologic malignancies, and its incidence is risingworldwide. With the recent demonstration of efficacy in RCC of molecular targeted therapeutics, it isclear that these new agents are rapidly changing the management of metastatic RCC. However, theexact molecular mechanism accounting for their clinical effect is largely unknown and a significantproportion of patients with metastatic RCC do not respond to these therapeutics. There is clearly a needto explore new molecular treatment targets in RCC, and based on our preliminary work one of thepromising molecular targets is the type 1 insulin-like growth factor receptor (IGF1R). The IGF1R is frequently overexpressed by human tumours, and mediates many aspects of the malignant phenotype. We have recently shown that in clear cell RCC (CC-RCC), the von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) gene product sequesters Sp1 and HuR to suppress IGF1R expression at the level of transcription and mRNA stability. The resultant IGF1R upregulation due to VHL mutations contributes to the survival and chemoresistance of CC-RCC cells. Moreover, IGF1R gene silencing was found to sensitise mutant VHL CC-RCC cells to etoposide, zoledronate and rapamycin. These findings suggest that anti-IGF1R strategies may be of therapeutic benefit in advanced CC-RCC patients. In this project, we aim to employ a RCC-derived murine xenograft model to: (1) test the in vivo efficacy of new molecular targets, including IGF1R, as treatment for advanced RCC, and (2) test the efficacy of combinatory or sequential therapy using currently available and experimental molecular targeted therapeutics in RCC. If IGF1R inhibition proves to have anti-cancer activity in vivo, it will raise the prospects of a novel and more effective treatment strategy for patients with advanced RCC.

title: Evaluation of compounds with electrophilic propensities as potential inhibitors of the thioredoxin system.
abs: In the light of the high prevalence of cancer and refractoriness of malignant tumours to clinical agents, it is necessary to identify novel molecular targets and discover new chemotherapeutics. Accumulating evidence has indicated that the thioredoxin system is a valid therapeutic target. Components of this redox system, thioredoxin and thioredoxin reductase are known to be overexpressed in tumours and associated with cancer drug resistance and poor patient prognosis. In recent years, the selenocysteine-dependent mammalian thioredoxin reductase enzyme has emerged as an important molecular target for anticancer drug development. Numerous natural products and synthetic compounds, including several clinically used chemotherapeutics have been recognized to target thioredoxin reductase. At present, a systematic way for predictive characterization and development of compounds as thioredoxin reductase inhibitors is lacking. Current inhibitors are observed to have in common electrophilic propensities for sulfhydryl groups, for example Michael reaction acceptors containing an alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyl moiety. Our exploratory study aims to evaluate additional classes of structurally diversified compounds containing Michael acceptor moieties for their effects on thioredoxin reductase. Compounds found to possess enzyme inhibitory activity will be further characterized through assessing the target site of action using MALDI mass spectrometry and/or BIAM-labelling assay, determining whether the inhibition is thioredoxin reductase-specific or involves additional antioxidant enzymes such as glutathione reductase, and evaluating their antiproliferative profile and apoptosis inducing potential using the MTT cell viability assay and immunodetection of cleaved caspase 3/PARP respectively. As such, a structure-activity relationship that offers systematic prediction of compounds as thioredoxin reductase inhibitors can be derived. The proposed search for thioredoxin reductase inhibitors from a wealth of biologically relevant natural products and synthetic chemical libraries therefore serves to discover and develop a novel class of thioredoxin reductase-targeted anticancer agents, with their potential of being applied in cancer chemotherapies that may lead to more desirable clinical outcomes.
kw: Thioredoxin reductase, Michael acceptors, Antitumour mechanism of action, Enzyme inhibition, Selenocysteine

title: Targeting Inflammatory Pathways for Prevention and Therapy of Prostate Cancer
abs: Prostate cancer is the fifth commonest cancer in Singapore men with an age-standardized incidence rate of 18.4 per 100,000. Prostate cancer rates have risen quite rapidly in past two decades in Singapore and although some of the increase can be attributed to enhanced detection, much of the increased incidence can be associated with genetic susceptibility, and environmental factors. How prostate cancer cells develop resistance to apoptosis is not fully understood, but transcription factors NF-kB, STAT-3, peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor (PPAR)-a, androgen receptor signaling activation of proteosome, phosphotidylinositol 3’-kinase-AKT, and cyclooxygenase (COX)-2 have all been implicated as survival factors for prostate cancer. In contrast, mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase kinase-1, prostate apoptotic response-4 and a transcription factor, early growth response-1, have been shown to mediate apoptosis in prostate cancer cells. We propose to demonstrate that ursolic acid, a pentacyclic triterpenoid derived from berries, leaves, and fruits of medicinal plants, such as Rosemarinus officinalis, Eriobotrya japonica, Calluna vulgaris, Ocimum sanctum, and Eugenia jumbolana has tremendous potential to treat prostate cancer using prostate cancer cell lines and animal models. To test this hypothesis, we propose the following specific goals:Aim 1: Determine whether ursolic acid inhibits inflammatory network consisting of AKT, NF-kB, STAT3 and associated gene products in prostate cancer cells. Aim 2: Determine whether ursolic acid inhibits the stage-specific development of prostate cancer using transgenic adenocarcinoma of mouse prostate (TRAMP) model.Aim 3: Determine whether ursolic acid can suppress the inflammatory response network consisting of AKT, NF-kB, STAT3 and associated gene products in prostate tissue from TRAMP mice. Ursolic acid lacks toxicity and may also synergize with traditional chemotherapeutics. If experiments proposed here are successful, clinical trials in prostate cancer patients will follow.
kw: Prostate Cancer, Inflammation, AKT

title: The role of the miR-376 cluster genes in inhibiting glioblastoma growth
abs: Altered microRNA (miRNA) expression in human cancers has led to considerable speculation regarding possible roles of these small, non-coding RNAs in regulating cancer growth. Our findings by miRNA microarray screening and qPCR analysis show that the genes in the miR-376 cluster were down-regulated by around 100 folds in human glioblastoma cell lines and tissues samples. Together with other data we have obtained, we hypothesize that: 1.The miR-376 gene cluster is important for negatively regulating the survival and proliferation of glioblastoma cells.2.Ectopic expression of these suppressed miRNA genes through gene transduction could be a novel treatment for glioblastomas. We will test these hypotheses through investigating the mechanisms of the down-regulation of the miR-376 cluster, identifying the putative gene targets of the miR-376 cluster in glioblastoma cells, and determining the effects of ectopic expression of the miR-376 cluster genes on cell survival, and proliferation in vitro and in vivo. Our studies will reveal biological functions of the miR-376 cluster and suggest the feasibility of a novel therapeutic intervention for glioblastoma.
kw: Glioblastoma, MicroRNA, Gene therapy, Gene expression

title: Optical Properties of Novel Nanomaterials and Field Effect Transistor Nanopore Devices for Single Molecular Detection and DNA Sequencing
abs: Semiconductor nanomaterials show great promises as building blocks for nanoelectronics, nanophotonics and biosensors. Researchers have demonstrated a variety of prototypical nanoelectronic circuits, nanophotonic elements and label-free real-time detection of cancer markers or virus. While unique applications of functional nanodevices have been demonstrated, fundamental physical properties of nanomaterials in quantum size regime still remain intriguing to explore. Here, we propose to develop methodology to investigate optical properties of nanowires and nanowire heterostructures in quantum size regime, from which we can address the quantum confinement to phonons and electrons by Raman scattering and photoconductivity, and the interaction between phonons/surface phonons, photons and electrons in field-effect transistor (FET) devices. Secondly, we proposed to use FET nanopore devices (silicon nanowires and graphene) for single molecule analysis and gene sequencing. Among several ultra-low cost sequencing technologies that are being developed, nanopore sequencing is revolutionary according to NIH reports, as it requires minimal specimen treatment, no limit of the DNA fragment length that can be recorded in a single measurement and no enzymatic engineering. The essence is that the sequence can be electrically read out when single DNA molecules translocate through a nanopore. However, the goal has not been achieved after a decade. In our FET nanopore idea, in addition to measuring ionic current as in conventional nanopore, nanopore FET conductance will be locally modulated and gated as charged DNA molecules translocate through the nanopore. Nanowire/graphene nanopore FETs are expected to have higher signal to noise ratio, readily multiplexing capability, thus possess great promise to lead to high throughput, multiplexing and integrated nanosensors for single base resolution nanopore sequencing. The integration of our nanoelectronic devices and novel unprecedented applications in single molecule biosensing and sequencing represents an exciting achievement in the emergent field of nanobiotechnology, which has a tremendous impact in healthcare, medicine and the life sciences.

title: NMDA Receptor-Based Therapeutics for Neurological Disorders
abs: The NMDA receptor (NMDAR) is a glutamate-gated ion channel that plays critical roles in learning and memory, as well as many higher cognitive brain functions. NMDAR hypofunction or over-stimulation results in a range of neurological disorders. Although the NMDAR is an important thera-peutic target, clinical results using antagonists and partial agonists have been disappointing, due to a combination of unacceptable side effects and lack of efficacy.Specific Aims: The goal of the experiments proposed here is to develop a new class of drugs to treat neurological disorders resulting from NMDAR dysfunction.Hypothesis: The hypothesis underlying the proposed experiments is that allosteric modulators of the NMDAR constitute a novel class of safe and effective therapeutics for treatment of several neurologi-cal disorders.Approach: Mutagenesis experiments in our laboratory have identified the binding site for allosteric modulators as the dimer interface formed by two neighboring ligand binding domains. Using the pub-lished high-resolution X-ray structure of this interface, a virtual 3D library of 8,000,000 small mole-cules will be docked into this allosteric binding site, and ranked by their predicted binding affinity. Top ranking compounds will be tested for NMDA receptor efficacy, affinity, selectivity and allosteric mechanism of action. Efficacy of lead compounds will be studied in vitro using cultured hippocampal neurons, and selected compounds will be further evaluated in vivo using rodent behavioral models. This analysis is expected to yield a range of lead compounds, which allosterically attenuate or en-hance NMDA receptor function to a well-defined extent. Because these compounds do not display agonism and are intrinsically dose-limiting, they should be much safer than previously tested drugs.Clinical Significance: The lead compounds produced are expected to enhance current therapeutics for many neurological disorders currently prevalent in South-East Asia, including schizophrenia, chronic depression, ADHD, anxiety, stroke, vascular dementia, Parkinson’s, Huntington’s and Alz-heimer’s disease.
kw: NMDA receptor, drug discovery, schizophrenia, chronic depression, alzhimer's, therapeutics

title: Assessment of coronary plaque characteristics and thrombus detection in patients with acute coronary syndromes using a novel high-resolution intravascular imaging system: an optical coherence tomography study.
abs: Coronary atherosclerotic plaques that contain thin fibroatheroma cap and large necrotic core may be linked to peri-procedural myonecrosis due to fibrous cap rupture and distal embolization of intra-plaque material during percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). Optical coherence tomography (OCT) is a novel high-resolution in vivo intravascular imaging modality capable of identifying coronary plaque characteristics and intra-luminal thrombus. The specific aims of this study are, in patients with acute coronary syndromes undergoing PCI:1.To determine if pre-procedural evaluation of coronary plaque characteristics can predict impaired myocardial perfusion grade and myocardial necrosis after stent deployment.2.To determine if identification of intra-luminal thrombus prior to coronary stent deployment using OCT can predict peri-procedural myocardial necrosis. We hypothesize that (1) compared to fibrous plaques, lipid-laden coronary plaques with thin fibrous caps have higher incidence of rupture during coronary stenting, leading to tissue prolapse and distal embolization of intra-plaque material that cause microcirculation impairment, and (2) identification of intra-luminal thrombus that are not apparent on coronary angiography will predict subsequent myocardial necrosis. We intend to utilize the “frequency domain-OCT” imaging system, which uses the principle of optical frequency domain imaging that allows faster and higher resolution (~10 micro-m) image acquisition compared to previous OCT systems employing time-domain OCT technology. In a prospective, single center study of fifty patients with acute coronary syndromes undergoing PCI, we plan to perform OCT imaging before and after coronary stent deployment. Angiographic results, cardiac biomarker release and 6-month clinical outcomes will be assessed to correlate with OCT-determined plaque characteristics.Our study will explore the potential utility of this novel imaging system in coronary intervention and elucidate the link between plaque characteristics and peri-procedural complications. Our findings may have important implications in developing treatment strategies to reduce this complication and contribute to risk stratification of patients with acute coronary syndromes undergoing PCI.
kw: Coronary plaque, Optical coherence tomography, Acute coronary syndrome, Myocardial necrosis

title: Probing the correlation between oxidative damage and wound healing outcomes
abs: Despite enormous discussion of the topic in literature, the exact role of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in wound healing is unclear. It is known that there is increased ROS in wounds and they could be a potential contribution to slow healing of chronic diabetic wounds. At the same time, it has also been shown that low levels of ROS are needed for normal wound healing. This lack of understanding regarding the role of oxidative stress is partly attributed to the lack of good biomarkers to gauge oxidative damage in wounds and skin. This question is important because it can help answer the question as to whether antioxidants can affect the wound healing process. Thus, we will compare biomarkers of oxidative damage between acute wounds and intact skin and determine the best biomarker/s in wound healing. Antioxidants will then be applied topically to examine their ability to modulate oxidative damage and their effect on wound healing outcome. Lastly, oxidative damage and the effects of topically applied antioxidants on diabetic wounds would be examined. The aims of this project are to answer the following questions:•Is the level of oxidative damage in wounded skin higher than that of intact skin in both healthy and diabetic individuals?•Are biomarkers of oxidative damage good prognostic indicators in wound healing?•Can topical application of antioxidants or pro-oxidants help in wound healing?•Is elevated oxidative stress one of the causes of chronic wounds and impaired vascularization in diabetic individuals?With better biomarkers of wound healing, we hope to understand diabetic wounds as well as provide potential antioxidant-based therapeutic targets in the management of diabetic wounds.
kw: Wound healing, Reactive oxygen species, Antioxidants, Diabetes, Mice, Vascular endothelial growth factor

title: Role of Ribosomal S6 Kinase 2 (RSK2) in neurogenesis: an implication in preventing from neurodegenerative disorder diseases
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Neurodegeneration associated with DNA damage induced p53-mediated apoptosis or the defects in DNA repair. Ataxia-telangiectasia (A-T) is an autosomal recessive disease that associated with DNA repair deficiencies and characterized by neurodegeneration disorder. The gene mutated in A-T, ATM (Ataxia telangiectasia mutated) is an abundant protein in dividing neural progenitor cells, and is required for normal adult neurogenesis and neuronal survival both in vitro and in vivo. RSK2 (Ribosomal S6 Kinase 2) is activated through the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signal pathway, regulates cell survival, proliferation and cell cycle in response to many extracellular stimuli. RSK2 gene mutations are associated with Coffin-Lowry syndrome, a syndromic form of X-linked mental retardation. RSK2-knockout mice display impaired learning and co-ordination skills. Neurodegeneration in the CNS is commonly associated with defects in learning and memory skills. These indicate important functional role of RSK2 in mediating neurogenesis and preventing from neurodegeneration. ATM acts as component of signaling pathways that sense DNA damage at chromatin, initiate DNA repair. In our recent mass-spectrometry analysis, we have identified that RSK2 is chromatin associated during DNA damage. Furthermore our preliminary data also shows ATM activated RSK2 at Ser386 and Thr577 during DNA damage. Interestingly, immunohistochemistry demonstrated that RSK2 co-localized with nestin at SVZ (neurogenic region) from E14 mice. Notably, similar detection for ATM has been found, and they are interacting endogenously. We thus hypothesize that RSK2 is a novel downstream substrate of ATM during DNA damage and mediating neurogenesis. We will study the molecular basis on how ATM activates RSK2 in response to DNA damage. We will generate knockout RSK2 mice to examine its functional role in mediating neural stem cells proliferation, self-renewal and differentiation. Moreover, by identifying other downstream elements that contribute to RSK2 in mediating neurogenesis, we may subsequently provide unique drug target for the treatment of neurodegenerative disorder disease.
kw: Ribosomal S6 Kinase 2, Neural stem cells, ATM, Neurodegeneration, DNA Damage, Neurogenesis

title: To study the tumor tropism of human bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) toward human hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) in vivo and to elucidate the mechanisms underlying the migratory activities exhibited by MSCs.
abs: In recent years, human bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) have emerged as a potential approach for the delivery of therapeutic genes for human cancer therapy due their intrinsic tumor tropism and immunosuppressive properties. However, the kinetic of mobilization of MSCs toward tumor cells and the role of inflammation mediators during this process is not well-studied in vivo. Previously, we have demonstrated that not all MSCs could migrate to tumor cells and highlymigratory MSCs that expressed high levels of matrix metalloproteinase 1 (MMP1) and insulin-like growth factor-II (IGF-II). In the present study, we will further investigate the kinetics of MSC’s tumor tropism in targeting human hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) in vivo and define the functional relationship of MMP1 and IGF-II in mediating the migratory activities of MSCs.HypothesisWe hypothesize that enhanced MSCs will be recruited to inflamed, HCC lesions systemically. Further, MMP1 could potentially act as IGFBP-2 proteinases, resulting in cleavage of the IGFBP2- IGFII complex followed by extracellular release of free IGFII.MethodologyThe kinetic of MSC’s tumor tropism towards HCC will be examined using both DEN-induced and patient-derived orthotopic HCC xenograft mouse models. In addition, we will examine if systemic injection of MSCs isolated from a mouse strain C3H/HeJ which contains a non-functional toll like receptor (TLR-4) could still home to tumor. The functional relationship of MMP1 and IGF-II in the migration of MSCs will also be examined using biochemical analysis and migration assays.Significance of studyThe proposed studies should better our understanding of the kinetics of tumor tropism exhibited by MSCs toward HCC in vivo. This knowledge may assist us in designing improved strategy when employing MSCs as potential carriers of therapeutic genes to human cancer cells.

title: The pathogenesis of anterior uveitis: role of ciliary body and iris epithelium Toll-like receptor and defensin mediated innate immune responses
abs: Anterior uveitis (AU), which involves the inflammation of ciliary body and iris, is the most common form of intraocular inflammation. The clinical manifestations of AU are variable and the pathogenesis of the disease is largely unknown, hindering the development of effective therapy. Recently, cytomegalovirus was identified in the aqueous humour of about 50% of idiopathic AU patients at SNEC. Epithelial cells play important roles in the initiation and prolongation of tissue inflammation. Epithelial cell Toll-like receptors (TLR) are the immediate link between pathogen detection and proinflammatory responses. TLRs are potential therapeutic targets for multiple chronic inflammatory diseases. A second link is defensins of epithelial cell or neutrophil origin. Defensins are natural antimicrobial peptides and potent immunoregulators affecting epithelial cell cytokine secretion and immune cell migration. The association between abnormal levels of defensins and excessive inflammation or susceptibility to infection has been demonstrated in skin, intestine and lung tissues. The proinflammatory role of ciliary body and iris epithelial cells in the development of AU is largely unexplored. We hypothesize that in the partially immune isolated compartment of the anterior chamber, the proinflammatory signals mediated through Toll-like receptors expressed in iris and ciliary body epithelium and defensins play important roles in the pathogenesis of AU. We aim to determine the expression and functions of TLR and defensins in human iris and ciliary body epithelial cells by using primary cultured cells isolated from cadaver tissue. We will also determine changes in TLR mediated cytokine secretion in iris pigmented epithelial cells using iridectomy specimens excised during trabeculectomy surgery of AU patients. We will determine if elevated defensin concentrations are associated with AU by measuring aqueous defensin composition of AU patients in comparison with normals to be obtained from cataract surgery. The study will identify molecular targets for future therapeutic intervention of AU.
kw: Anterior uveitis, Defensin, Ciliary body, Toll-like receptor, Iris, Inflammation

title: Identification of MicroRNAs (miRNA) associated with Leucine rich repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) in the Parkinson’s Disease brain: Effects of LRRK2 Mutations and Relevance to Pathogenesis
abs: BACKGROUNDLeucine rich repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) was identified as a causative gene in Parkinson’s disease (PD). The pathophysiological role of LRRK2 in PD is presently unclear. The G2019S gene variant of LRRK2 has been reported as a common cause of dominant and sporadic PD worldwide. We have also shown that the LRRK2 G2385R variant is a risk factor for PD in Asian populations. There is increasing evidence that Micro-RNAs (miRNAs) play a cardinal role in neuronal development and maintenance by regulating gene expression. However, it is at present unclear which miRNA species interact with LRRK2 under conditions of cellular stress, and how the interaction may be altered by disease relevant-LRRK2 variants. OBJECTIVES1. Using gene expression analyses and miRNA arrays, we will compare the gene expression profile of stably transfected LRRK2 cell lines harboring G2019S and G2385R variants before and after oxidative stress treatment. The differentially expressed genes and miRNAs identified will enable us to further study potential targets or pathways associated with the development of PD. 2. To identify small RNA signatures that are associated with PD, we will utilize Solexa sequencing technologies to characterize dysregulated small RNA in PD and healthy control brain samples.METHODS We will generate LRRK2 G2019S and G2385R stably-transfected neuroblastoma cell lines. Using gene expression and miRNA arrays we will then compare the gene expression and miRNA profile among LRRK2 wild type and variants. We will use Solexa sequencing methods to identify known miRNAs and categorise sequences into potential new miRNAs, as well as other small RNA classes. Furthermore, comparisons of miRNA expression will be made between postmortem PD and control brains. All miRNAs identified will then be correlated with the expression levels of their predicted targets. CONCLUSIONS This exploratory study will investigate the effect of the LRRK2 mutations on gene and miRNA expression. We aim to identify important and key gene and miRNAs that may be dysregulated as a result of LRRK2 mutations and provide further insight into the pathogenetic mechanism of PD.
kw: Gene mutation, in-vitro cell function assay, MicroRNA, Parkinson's Disease, microarray, LRRK2

title: Evolution of hepatitis B quasispecies leads to generation of new CpG motifs that stimulate innate Immunity through Toll Receptor 9
abs: Chronic hepatitis B afflicts over 350 million people and is the main cause of the high burden of chronic liver disease, liver failure and liver cancer in Asia. Chronic hepatitis B damage is characterised by loss of immune tolerance when host immunity against hepatitis B antigens increases for unclear reasons. This is the time when immune damage leading to liver cirrhosis or HBeAg seroconversion leading to partial viral clearance occurs. Previously we have shown that this immune reactive period is associated with increased viral diversity and evolution, particularly during HBeAg seroconversion. We postulate that this increased viral diversity and evolution could be due to a gradual accumulation of mutations (rather than a sudden event) and that these new viral mutations could create new CpG motifs that lead to stimulation of toll receptor 9 (TLR) receptors. To detect when HBV viral diversity increases, 10 HBeAg seroconverters and 10 control patients without HBeAg seroconversion followed long term will be examined yearly with PCR, clonal and sequencing of HBV precore/core gene (>20 clones/sample) followed by alignment using ClustalX, analysis of the viral diversity and evolutionary rate using Pebble 1.0. To study the HBV CpG motifs, 15 HBeAg seroconverters and 15 controls without HBeAg seroconversion will be examined for TLR9 expression in immune cells (baseline, before and after seroconversion) by RT-real time PCR and FACS. PCR and clonal sequencing of full length HBV from baseline and before seroconversion will be performed in order to screen for potential CpG motifs in the HBV genome. Such CpG motifs will be tested for TLR9 simulation activity in HEK 293XL-hTLR9 cell lines with an NFkB reporter system, and confirmed in human PBMCs using RT real time PCR of cytokine genes, FAC scan of intracellular cytokine in B cells and pDCs, and ELISA of secreted cytokines and chemokines. These studies will not only lead to a better understanding of HBV pathogenesis, but also explore a potentially novel approach to treatment of chronic hepatitis B.

title: A randomized phase III study of concurrent cisplatin-radiotherapy with or without induction chemotherapy using gemcitabine, paclitaxel and carboplatin in locally advanced nasopharyngeal cancer
abs: The previously NMRC funded Phase III randomized trial SQNP01 , (NMRC / 0297 / 1998) has confirmed the US Intergroup 00-99 Trial and helped establish concurrent chemo-radiotherapy using the Al-Sarraf regimen as the current gold standard for the treatment of patients with locally advanced Stage 3 and 4 Nasopharyngeal Cancer (NPC) in this part of the world. This trial (SQNP01) has been quoted in the 2006-2008 versions of the NCCN Guidelines for Nasopharyngeal Cancer .The aim of the current NMRC funded Randomized Phase II Trial (NMRC / 1073 / 2006) was to build on the results of SQNP01. While SQNP01 improved overall survival of patients with Stage 3 and 4 NPC from 46% to 65% at 5 years, about 20% of patients still fail distantly. (NMRC / 1073 / 2006) was thus conceived as a pilot study to examine a strategy to reduce distant metastases even further. It made use of induction rather than adjuvant chemotherapy – as adjuvant chemotherapy after chemo-RT was not very well tolerated. Secondly it studied the use of a triplet combination of Gemcitabine, Paclitaxel and Carboplatin (GPC). In the metastatic NPC setting, our center had shown that this GPC triplet combination had achieved an 18.5 month median survival as opposed to 12 months with a standard Cisplatin- 5FU doublet regimen .This Randomized Phase II Trial (NMRC / 1073 / 2006) has served as a pilot, and our current aim is to expand this trial into a Phase III Randomized Trial, after a Data and Safety Monitoring Committee (DSMC) has examined the preliminary results of the trial.Since the current Randomized Phase II Trial (NMRC / 1073 / 2006) began, there have been new therapeutic developments for both Squamous Cell Cancers of the Head and Neck (SCCHN) and for metastatic NPC. In SCCHN, there are currently 4 randomized trials . of Induction triplets versus Induction doublets – and all have shown statistically significant survival benefits for the triplet regimens.In metastatic NPC, trials from Sun-Yet Sen Univeristy, Guangzhou and The Princess Margaret Hospital, Toronto , have both shown impressive overall response rates to Gemcitabine monotherapy when it is given as salvage therapy to patients with metastatic NPC. All these taken with our own initial findings with Gemcitabine , confirms our assertion that Gemcitabine is an important chemotherapeutic drug for the treatment of NPC, and supports its inclusion in our current induction regimen.Similarly, a second trial involving the use of the triplet Gemcitabine, Paclitaxel and Carboplatin (GPC) followed by maintenance 5 Flourouracil showed an improved 24 month median survival compared with 18 months in our original study of GPC alone. The triplets in this second trial were well tolerated, and there was no treatment-associated mortality.All taken together, these findings support our strategy of using an Induction strategy as well as the use of Gemcitabine, Paclitaxel and Carboplatin (GPC) in our regimen. title: Ex vivo hepatocytes for therapy of liver failure
abs: The promise of liver stem cells lies in their potential to provide a continual source of hepatocytes for a wide variety of clinical applications including cellular transplant and inartificial liver device. We hypothesize that amniotic epithelial cells and extra embryonic endodermal cells can be coaxed into hepatocyte-like cells by manipulating the microenvironment. The abundant supply, plasticity as well as their potential of low immunogenicity would make them an ideal source of hepatocyte for clinical transplant. We thus aimed to isolate these cells from placenta, expand them in culture and explore their potential of being converted to functional hepatocytes. The regulatory factors including Sonic Hedgehog, beta catenin, and e cadherin will be explored for their potential as manipulation target in epithelial transition and hepatocyte specification. Scaling up culture protocols will be established. Proof of survival efficacy in small and large animal models in acute liver failure and cirrhosis will be tested by cellular transplant and via extracorporeal assisted liver devices. Amniotic epithelial, extra embryonic endodermal as well as mesenchymal stem cells are cultured in 3D lattice structure and pushed into hepatocytic lineage with FGF4, ITS+ and EGF as well as collagen 3D cell-matrix signaling, augmented with bcatenin and blockage of SHH pathway, and pro-hepatocytic factors. Phenotypic profile will be tested systematically and compared with fetal mature adult hepatocytes. Scaling up will be performed in modular fluidics pump cartridges and in-vivo potential tested via transplantation into galactosamine rat acute liver failure model and retrorsine/CCL4 rat cirrhosis model. Extension is made to pig model of acute liver failure and efficacy of assisted bioartificial liver device with and without transplantation assessed. The successful establishment of functional hepatocytes ex-vivo will pave the way for a liver cell bank for transplantation of patients not suitable for transplant. Hepatocytes will also be invaluable for the pharmaceutical industry.
kw: liver stem cells, liver regeneration, hepatocyte transplant, liver failure

title: Modelling respiratory pathogens in acute-care hospitals: translating lessions from severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) and influenza into plans for outbreak containment
abs: Respiratory pathogens can cause explosive outbreaks in acute-care hospitals, as was the case during the Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS) outbreaks in 2003. Outbreaks of non-pandemic influenza are also frequently reported in hospitals, and severe outbreaks of nosocomial influenza have also been reported during influenza pandemics. Tools are therefore needed to assist policy makers, hospital managers, clinicians, epidemiologists and infection control practitioners in planning for and mitigating the impact of outbreaks of such pathogens. In this study, we aim to develop a simulation model that will help us to translate experiences from historical SARS and influenza outbreaks into appropriate plans for outbreak containment, with a particular emphasis on how to manage epidemics of pandemic and non-pandemic influenza. The study will include: 1. Programming realistic dynamic individual-based and contact network models for simulating disease transmission in an acute-care hospital 2. Conduct of field studies to estimate the movement and contact patterns of healthcare staff, patients and visitors in the hospital environment 3. Collection of data and biological specimens on nosocomial transmission of influenza 4. Modelling of historical data on the outbreaks of Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome, and the prospective data on nosocomial influenza 5. Application of models to answer questions relevant to surveillance and control of nosocomial outbreaks, and the management of hospital resources during epidemics The increasing recognition of the burden of non-pandemic and pandemic influenza in tropical Singapore and the continued outbreaks of H5N1 Avian Influenza in nearby countries gives added impetus to the proposed work. This multi-disciplinary study will bring together experts from clinical, laboratory, computational and statistical sciences, along with world-renowned modelling expertise, to produce a model for answering important questions about managing nosocomial outbreaks. The entire process will also strengthen local capabilities in the field of infectious disease modelling and provide the platform for future collaborations.
kw: infectious disease modelling, influenza, nosocomial infections, severe acute respiratory syndrome, surveillance, epidemics

title: Identification of dengue therapeutics and determination of its neutralization mechanisms using a combination of immunological, biochemical and structural techniques
abs: Project Abstract Dengue virus (DENV) infects approximately 50 to 100 million people worldwide each year, and yet no vaccines or therapeutics are available. In vitro experiments have shown that non-neutralizing antibodies can enhance DENV infection of Fc receptor bearing macrophages, one of the natural host cells for the virus. This suggested that the presence of non-neutralizing epitopes in a vaccine could potentially increase the chances that a person who had received the vaccine would develop the severe form of the disease, dengue hemorrhagic fever. For this reason, a more promising approach for engineering an effective DENV vaccine is to focus on including neutralizing epitopes. Thus, mapping of neutralizing epitopes is a necessary component of DENV vaccine research. Furthermore, understanding the neutralization mechanism of antibodies and the entry of DENV into the host cells also could aid in the design of targeted therapeutics. Thus, the overall goal of this proposal is to understand the mechanism of antibody-mediated neutralization of DENV and the entry of DENV into host cells. To achieve this goal, the following specific aims will be pursued: Specific aim (1): Characterize binding sites and virus neutralization mechanisms of human, mouse, camel antibodies and high affinity pr molecules. Specific aim (2): Identify natural human cells and receptors targeted by DENV. These specific aims will be achieved using a combination of immunological, biochemical and structural techniques (x-ray crystallography and cryoEM image reconstruction). This multi-disciplinary approach will provide a depth of knowledge not possible using a single approach. Significance: The information generated from these studies will contribute to the development of safe and effective vaccine and therapeutics.

title: Genome-wide study of molecular mechanisms that regulate neural stem cell self-renewal and differentiation in Drosophila larval brains
abs: Stem cells must both self-renew, and produce progeny that are committed to differentiation. To do this, stem cells undergo asymmetric cell division. Recently Drosophila larval brain neuroblasts, neural stem cells, have been established as a new model system for the study of stem cell self-renewal and tumorigenesis. Neuroblasts distribute proliferation factors (e.g. aPKC) to the neuroblast daughter and differentiation factors (e.g. Numb) to the Ganglion Mother Cell during asymmetric division. Previously I had identified Aurora-A and Polo as two novel brain tumor suppressors in Drosophila and showed that they regulate Numb asymmetric localization to inhibit neuroblast self-renewal. However, several important questions remain elusive, e.g. how Numb activity and localization are regulated by kinases or phosphatases during asymmetric division? How Polo is regulated during asymmetric division of neuroblasts? I propose to discover novel molecular mechanism of neuroblast asymmetric division to answer the above mentioned questions. I will test if Polo hyperphosphorylates and activates Numb to inhibit neuroblast self-renewal, while PP1 dephosphorylates Numb and modulates its activity or localization. I will also find out the transcription factor that regulates Polo and understand how it may affect neuroblast self-renewal and differentiation. We have identified a novel brain tumor suppressor on the X chromosome and we will continue to characterize its function and reveal its molecular mechanism by which it inhibits neuroblast self-renewal. I also propose to identify and analyze a large number of novel molecules that control neural stem cell self-renewal and differentiation by both forward and reverse genetic screens in a genome-wide manner. This proposed project is original and results from the project will systematically discover a large number of novel molecules that regulate neural stem cells divisions and unravel their mechanisms in regulating this process. It will bring enormous novel insights into the fields of stem cell and cancer biology. This study may also help to develop treatment of related diseases such as brain tumors in human being.

title: Ischemic Stroke with a Focus on Intracranial Stenosis
abs: This proposed research program on intracranial stenosis is divided into clinical and basic science studies that are interconnected synergistically to maximize impact. A target of 1000 stroke patients will be recruited with informed consent in a hospital-based, single centre, prospective study. Patients will be followed up and undergo neuroimaging and neurocognitive studies at baseline and at regular intervals over a period of at least 2 years. Their blood samples will be collected for biomarker and genomic studies. Non-invasive neuroimaging gold-standards for evaluation of intracranial stenosis will be established. Clinical, neuroimaging and neurocognitive outcome measures will be compared between patients with and patients without underlying intracranial stenosis; and high-risk features of intracranial stenosis associated with recurrent stroke or worsened outcome will be identified from detailed epidemiological, neuroimaging, biomarker and genomic studies carried out in this large cohort of patients. Basic science investigations include the establishment of useful animal models, functional genomics, molecular mechanisms and stem cell studies. There is currently no established animal model for intracranial stenosis. We will attempt to create animal models by inducing conditions that are well-established stroke risk factors, e.g. hyperlipidemia, hypertension, and diabetes. Our investigations will also include a thorough functional genomics and RNomics approach to understand the molecular events that take place at different stages of the disease. Underlying molecular mechanisms will be studied to identify novel therapeutic targets. Stem cell therapy for cerebrovascular repair, which could prevent recurrent stroke and enhance neuroregeneration, using adult endothelial progenitor cells (EPC) and mesenchymal stem cells will be investigated. Stem cells will be isolated from peripheral blood and expanded ex vivo with nanostructured scaffold for autologous or allogenic therapeutic transplantation. The efficacy and repair mechanism will be evaluated in animal models. The level of EPC in stroke patients will also be measured potentially for use as a biomarker.
kw: Animal models;Biomarkers;Intracranial stenosis;Molecular mechanisms;Neuroimaging;Stem cell therapy

title: Autologous Cell Therapy for the Aging Heart Using Reprogrammed Cells
abs: The success in obtaining iPS cells from somatic cells is revolutionary and it has brought stem cell therapy to a new era. Researchers are now able to obtain patient-specific iPS cells from dermal fibroblasts. iPS cells, like ‘self-derived’ embryonic stem cells, could be best type of stem cells available. Several leading laboratories across the world are beginning to verify the potency of iPS cells to prepare for good manufacturing practice (GMP) quality iPS cells for regenerative therapy. Aims: 1) To refine methods to generate patient-specific iPS cells and iPS-derived cardiomyocyte (CM) and endothelial cell (EC) capable of translational and clinical applications, 2) To investigate therapeutic function of iPS-CM and iPS-EC in both engineered cardiac tissue graft and single cell preparations for cardiomyogenesis and angiogenesis in pre-clinical myocardial infarction models. 3) To evaluate the long-term engraftment of autologous iPS-derived cardiac tissue graft in a porcine model Methods Unique approaches such as potent molecules from screened chemical libraries to complement known pluripotent plasmid vectors will be adopted to refine techniques to create viral vector-free re-programming of adult somatic cells. With pig model, the contractile and structural contribution of iPS-CM will be first tested by engineering a unique full-thickness cardiac tissue graft in vivo. Next, the cardiac tissue graft will be transplanted to the infarct myocardium via epicardial patching. In a separated approach aiming to enhance the impaired angiogenesis in diabetic patients with myocardial infarction (MI), iPS-ECs from diabetic MI patients will be injected in the infarct myocardium of SCID mice. Finally, an autologous porcine iPS-derived cardiac tissue graft will be grafted onto the myocardium of pig for long-term follow-up (6 months) to study safety and stability of the engrafted tissue in electrophysiology, pharmacology and vascular angiography. Significance: A large and growing number of patients are suffering from chronic heart failure brought about by ischemic heart disease. The debilitating symptoms of most of these elderly patients are comfounded by co-morbidities such as hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, hyperinsulinemia and hyperglycemia which further compromised their self-repairing mechanisms. Autologous iPS-derived cardiomyocytes and endothelial cells may be the most potent source of cells to help them regain a more decent quality of life. Successful execution of this project will pave the ways for clinical studies and practices to improve the lives of a large growing patient population in a society such as Singapore whose citizens are rapidly greying. Catching-up with rapid developments in iPS cell-based research is strategically important for Singapore as a biomedical research hub. This project would firmly solidify Singapore as a global force in pioneering biomedical and translational research.

title: Age-related Neurodegenerative Disease: The Roles of MicroRNAs and Their Targets
abs: Age-related neurodegeneration is a major factor that impairs quality of life in the elderly. Recent studies have implicated microRNAs in neurodegeneration. microRNAs are posttranscriptional regulators of gene expression. The absence of all miRNAs in post-mitotic neurons can lead to progressive neuronal loss and to behavioral defects reminiscent of neurodegenerative disease. While these studies suggest a role for some miRNAs, they leave open the question of which microRNAs play important roles and how they work. This project aims to make use of the sophisticated genetic and neurobiological tools available in Drosophila to systematically study the roles of microRNAs in neurodegeneration.
kw: microRNA;neuron;neurodegeneration;disease model;brain;behavior

title: An Integrated Approach to Overcome Sarcopenia and Frailty in Aging Humans
abs: Aging is associated with a progressive and involuntary loss of muscle mass known as sarcopenia. Between the ages of 50 and 80, muscle mass is reduced by approximately one-third resulting in a significant decrease of muscle strength, consequent frailty, and risk of metabolic syndrome. Sarcopenia has far reaching consequences for the elderly, including impaired physical function, increased risk of falls, fractures, dependency, and in some extreme cases death. In the year 2000 alone, sarcopenia was found to be the 6th leading cause of death and it was estimated that 1.5% of total health care expenditures in the United States, totaling $18.5 billion, was attributable to sarcopenia. Singapore is the third fastest aging nation in the world and the statistics predict that 20% of Singapore’s population will be 65 and above in 2020. Looking forward, sarcopenia will be a tremendous burden on state funded health care system such as Singapore’s. Therefore, the impact on the Singaporean economy of even a modest reduction in sarcopenia would be appreciable. Although sarcopenia is well documented, the etiology and the molecular mechanisms that initiate such a devastating condition still remain poorly understood. Therefore, here we are proposing an integrated program on sarcopenia which excels in science and the potential for IP capture. The proposed R & D program aims to use highly innovative science and cutting edge technologies to (1) identify novel biomarkers for early detection of sarcopenia (2) discover molecular mechanisms behind muscle wasting to prevent sarcopenia, and (3) develop tissue engineering and muscle-stem-cell-based regenerative therapeutics for mitigation of sarcopenia. Academically, this program will help nurture and grow the existing collaborations with our national (NUS) and international collaborators. This program combines engineering sciences, stem cell technologies and molecular cell biology which will lead to capability building in aging research, IP capture and commercialization

title: Understanding how combined temozolomide and radiation can improve clinical outcome of malignant gliomas: Quiescent resistance
abs: Background: Solid tumour cancers, exemplified by malignant glioma (MG) resist therapy, frequently recur and cause death. Despite great advances in science and medicine, improved survival for MG has hardly changed over decades. Recent data showed that combining temozolomide (TMZ) with radiotherapy (RT) significantly improved 2 year survivals of MG compared with radiation alone. However, the underlying mechanism is not clear.Hypothesis: MG contains a large proportion of quiescent cells, which overlap with hypoxic radio-resistant population. We hypothesize that TMZ-induced transcription inhibition suppresses DNA double strand break (DSB) repair in quiescent cells, sensitising them to radiation.Objectives: Using quiescent MG cells, we aim to define 1) TMZ-induced transcription inhibition of non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) gene expression; 2) the role of O6-methylguanine (O6-meG, the major cytotoxic DNA lesion induced by TMZ) in transcription inhibition; 3) enhanced quiescent cell killing by combined TMZ and RT treatment.Methodology: MG cell quiescence will be induced by starvation or multicellular spheroid culture. NHEJ gene expression will be verified by real-time RT-PCR and Western blotting. The role O6-meG in transcription inhibition will be validated in cells pre-treated with or without O6-benzylguane (a non-cytotoxic TMZ analogue which depletes MGMT activity). TMZ and RT cytotoxicity will be determined by DNA damage, viability, colony formation and apoptosis assay. Scientific & clinical significance: Combination of TMZ and RT is now the standard of care in the treatment of MGs and there is a pressing need to understand the mechanism. Cells in hypoxic tumour regions tend to be quiescent and are thought to be one of the major causes of radioresistance. Our proposed study of quiescent cell sensitising to RT by TMZ-induced transcription inhibition will significantly advance understanding of fundamental cellular and molecular mechanisms underpinning a clinical breakthrough. Such understanding will help us to build on what is already working
kw: Quiescent resistance, Radiation, Temozolomide, Gliomas
