title: Exploring the Role of Foxo3a and Pml in the pathogenesis of hepatocellular carcinoma.
abs: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is an aggressive cancer endemic with few effective treatments. Development of the disease is thought to be a multistep process, often initiating as chronic liver disease including chronic hepatitis and cirrhosis, eventually progressing to cancer. Activation of the protein kinase B (Akt) pathway is often implicated in cancer formation, including HCC. We have identified Foxo3a as a potential prognostic marker in HCC. Overstimulation of PI3K/Akt is found in tumours, promoting tumourigenesis via Foxo3a phosphorylation. Trotman et al. (Nature, 2006) has shown in mice, that Pml-PP2A, inactivate phosphorylated Akt and reduced Pml expression leads to inactivation of Foxo3a-mediated effectors. Furthermore, murine Foxo3a knockouts display similar phenotypes as Pml knockouts.Our preliminary data (n=158), show that Foxo3a and Pml, are significant survival prognostic markers in HCC. Combined analysis of Foxo3a and Pml high expressors (2-fold increase) survived 27 versus 95 months for low expressors (2-fold decrease, p=0.034) with strong correlation between both genes (Pearson correlation 0.637, p<0.001). We will study molecular pathways, interaction of Foxo3a and Pml and contribution to HCC oncogenesis. We hypothesize that increased Foxo3a expression in HCC, promotes Pml-Foxo3a association, interfering with Pml-PP2A, causing metastasis and increased mortality; and casein kinase 2 associates with Foxo3a to dysregulate Pml tumor suppressor function. Immunoblotting,immunohistochemistry and real-time PCR will analyze protein levels, localization in human tissues and primary xenografts and quantify mRNA levels. We aim to establish that an association between Foxo3 and Pml exist and determine its role in the pathogenesis of HCC. Our attempts to identify mechanism and function of interaction within Akt/Foxo3a/Pml network will allow potential development of specific-targeted therapy, validating Foxo3a and Pml as prognostic biomarkers, predicting drug sensitivity in HCC.

title: A randomised controlled trial of the efficacy and safety of Alemtuzumab (MABCAMPATH®) for prevention of graft rejection and preservation of renal function in patients receiving kidney transplants
abs: Despite advances in immunosuppression, a combination of agents is necessary to prevent rejection in transplant recipients. However, chronic complications post-transplant include immunosuppressive toxicities such as infection and malignancy, and drug-related non-immunosuppressive side-effects. The search for treatment regimens that allow reprogramming of the recipient immune system thereby permitting the development of allograft tolerance is long awaited. In a pilot randomised, controlled trial assessing the safety and efficacy of alemtuzumab(MABCAMPATH®) with low-dose cyclosporin(CyA) monotherapy in renal transplantation, in comparison to a standard CyA-corticosteroid-azathioprine-based regimen, the incidence of acute rejection(AR) was comparable. While 71% of alemtuzumab-CyA treated patients were corticosteroid-free at 36 months, 100% of control patients received maintenance corticosteroids. This study will examine the safety and efficacy of alemtuzumab with low-dose tacrolimus(FK) monotherapy, versus conventional FK-corticosteroid-azathioprine regimen, in a multicentre randomised trial with National University Hospital(NUH) as one of the participating centres. As FK is more potent than CyA, combination of FK with alemtuzumab may further reduce AR incidence. The use of low-dose FK may further reduce the incidence of chronic allograft dysfunction due to calcineurin-inhibitor toxicity, interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy. 63 patients who demonstrate renal function after transplant surgery will be randomised to CAMPATH or STANDARD in 2:1 ratio. This multi-centre study will involve three other centres in Asia, including the Singapore General Hospital, National Taiwan University Hospital and the National Kidney and Transplant Institute in Manila. Funding for the study has been successfully obtained at these other 3 centres; funding at SGH was obtained through the SingHealth Pivotal Grants Committee. This reapplication for funding is for support for eighteen patients who are anticipated to participate from NUH. In CAMPATH, patients will receive 2 doses of alemtuzumab followed by maintenance low-dose FK. In STANDARD, FK, azathioprine and steroid will be given. Patients will be followed upto three years post-transplant. The primary outcome will be incidence of interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy. Secondary outcome measures include patient and graft survivals, incidence of acute rejection, lymphocyte counts, quality of life, renal function, incidence of steroid-resistant rejection, chronic rejection, delayed graft function, treatment failure, steroid and FK doses after transplantation. Safety parameters include incidence of infections, lymphoproliferative disease and other malignancies and adverse events.
kw: Tacrolimus, Interstitial Fibrosis, Tubular Atrophy, Acute Rejection, Chronic Rejection, Calcineurin Inhibitor Toxicity

title: A study to decipher the pathway(s) involved S-nitrosylation of the tumor suppressor PTEN by an increased intracellular level of superoxide and hydrogen peroxide in normal and malignant cells.
abs: An increase in intracellular superoxide (O2.- ) that does not overwhelm the intracellular anti-oxidant defenses, has been shown to endow tumor cells with a definite and sustained survival advantage over their normal counterpart. However, the events leading to the survival of tumor cells by O2.- are not completely understood. Recently, we demonstrated that oxidative modification of the tumor suppressor PTEN by O2•- is a physiologically relevant mechanism involved in the activation of pathways leading tumor cells formation and maintenance such as activation of the survival kinase Akt. Oxidative modification of PTEN by O2.- was shown to be a S-nitrosylation of the protein. However, the pathway leading to S-nitrosylation of PTEN by O2•- was not elucidated. Hence, the first aim of this proposal will be to decipher the pathway(s) leading to S-nitrosylation PTEN by O2.-. Then because oxidation-mediated inhibition of PTEN activity was first shown to be due to the formation of a disulfide bond rather than S-nitrosylation upon exposure of cells or purified PTEN protein to H2O2, we propose to revisit the nature and the pathway involved in the oxidative modification of PTEN by H2O2. Our hypothesis is that oxidation of PTEN by disulfide bond formation could be a marker of stress while S-nitrosylation of PTEN may represent a post–transcriptional modification more relevant to cell signaling. Finally, in light of the critical role for the inhibition of PTEN activity in the development and maintenance of tumor cells, we propose to evaluate if S-nitrosylation of the tumor suppressor could represent a marker of PTEN inactivation in tumor cell lines as well as in clinical material from patients diagnosed with head and neck cancers. Understanding the pathway(s) and the nature of the oxidative modification induced by O2.- and H2O2 leading to the inactivation of the PTEN protein are critical to design appropriate protocols to reverse this inhibition and potentially establish reduction of PTEN as a new strategy for anticancer drug treatment.
kw: Superoxide, PTEN, Hydrogen peroxide, S-nitrosylation

title: Urinary metabonomic profiling for bladder cancer diagnosis and surveillance
abs: Clinical problem Bladder cancer is the 7th most common cancer worldwide. It is usually superficial at presentation (70%) and usually a transitional cell carcinoma (90%). Though not usually fatal, bladder cancer is characterized by frequent recurrences that can progress to more invasive disease. The recurrence rates for bladder cancer are as high as 50% -70%, therefore, life-long close surveillance is needed which makes this a very expensive cancer to treat. The surveillance generally requires cystoscopy to be carried out frequently. Though many other urinary assays have been analyzed, most do not have the specificity and sensitivity of cystoscopy.AimThe aim of the present study is to validate the potential of urinary metabolites as biomarkers for bladder cancer diagnosis by identifying markers with good discriminative performance for bladder cancer recognition in the urinary metabolite profile. MethodologyUrine samples will be collected from 100 bladder cancer patients and also from an approximately equal number of bladder cancer-free controls. All urine samples will be analyzed by gas chromatography/mass spectrometry and NMR. Cystoscopy and urine cytology data will also be collected on the bladder cancer patients. Urine samples will also be tested for urine cytology, NMP-22 and telomerase. The large data sets will be analyzed by multivariate statistical methods, such as principal component analysis (PCA), to highlight differences between samples based on observed spectral patterns. A new multivariate statistical method orthogonal partial least squares (OPLS) will also be applied to identify subtle changes that can be biased due to large variations within a sample class.OutcomeTo develop a profile that can be used to identify patients with bladder cancer. Urinary profiling is a non-invasive procedure and therefore it is likely to ensure greater patient willingness to comply and participate in screening and will be less costly in the long term.
kw: metabonomics, bladder cancer, urine, NMR, GC/MS

title: Investigating the oncogenic roles of Numb isoforms and isoform-specific expression profiles in brain tumours
abs: Gliomas are a category of central nervous system tumours which are thought to arise from glial cells or their precursors. Glioblastoma multiformes are the most aggressive tumours within this category, and patients typically succumb within a year of diagnosis. Recent gene expression studies suggest that gliomas segregate into two major molecular subclasses, neuronal-like and neural stem cell-like, with implications on clinical survival.Numb is a protein originally studied in neurodevelopment. Its asymmetric segregation during mitosis of a neural stem cell determines whether the daughter cell retains stem-ness or becomes differentiated. Much of the literature suggests that Numb is important in maintaining neural stem cell populations as opposed to neuronal differentiation in mammals. However, Numb isoforms have also been identified to be active at different stages of neurodevelopment to influence both proliferation and differentiation.Although Numb has been studied in the context of cancer biology, little attention has been given to isoform-specific effects thus far. We recently reported that Numb is expressed in astrocytomas, with a trend towards higher Numb expression in higher grade gliomas, suggesting that Numb might function as an oncogene. Although this is contrary to previous studies implicating Numb as a tumour suppressor, we hypothesize that this might be due to isoform-specific effects. We also found that there were differences in the expression of specific Numb isoforms in several high-grade gliomas and glioblastoma cell lines, compared to normal adult brain. This suggests specific Numb isoforms may confer increased malignancy.Our specific aims are to study Numb isoform-specific tumourigenic effects in vitro using established glioblastoma cell lines, and to apply this knowledge in routine histopathological diagnosis of gliomas. This work may be extended in future to correlate the expression of specific Numb isoforms with clinical behaviour, and explore the therapeutic potential of targeted therapy towards the oncogenic isoforms.

title: The response of human NK cells to primary human cells infected with dengue virus.
abs: Dengue virus infections are the most common vector-borne viral illness in Singapore. Anti-dengueimmune responses are protective, but can contribute to the pathology of severe disease. While B celland T cell responses to dengue have been well documented, less is known about the response ofNatural Killer (NK) cells to dengue virus. NK cells are the main lymphocyte subset involved in innateantiviral responses triggered early during viral infections, and may play an important role in determiningsubsequent peak viral loads, which correlate directly with disease severity. NK cells utilize multiplereceptors to recognize virus-infected cells, and respond by secreting cytokines and by activating cytolyticmechanisms. How NK cells recognize and respond to dengue-infected cells is poorly understood.In this proposal, we will 1) Characterize the effector function(s) triggered in primary human NK cells bydengue-infected dendritic cells (DCs). 2) Evaluate the anti-dengue response of primary NK cellsactivated under different conditions. 3) Compare the NK responses triggered by dengue-infected DCsversus dengue-infected human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs). Primary human cells will beused so that our findings can be directly relevant to human biology. In preliminary data, we demonstrateour ability to 1) isolate primary human DCs, 2) infect DCs with dengue virus, and 3) purify primary humanNK cells. By performing co-culture experiments, we have made the novel observation that activatedprimary human CD16- NK cells respond to autologous, dengue-infected DCs by secreting IFNg. We willmine this model system to characterize the response of primary human NK cells to dengue-infectedprimary human cells. The knowledge gained will clarify the role of NK cells in restricting dengue viralreplication, and pave the way for future clinical studies that will address whether anti-dengue NK reactivitycan be correlated with severity of infection.
kw: Natural Killer Cells, Dengue Virus, Innate Immunity, Dendritic Cells

title: Phase I study to investigate genotype-based dose individualization of irinotecan in Asian cancer patients
abs: Irinotecan is a topoisomerase I inhibitor and forms part of an important armamentarium of drugs used in the treatment of lung, colorectal and head and neck cancers. Two main dose limiting toxicities of irinotecan include diarrhoea and neutropenia. The UGT1A1*28 genetic testing was recently approved by FDA to identify cancer patients at risk for irinotecan induced toxicity in Caucasian cancer patients. In Asian cancer patients, the frequency of severe irinotecan-induced diarrhoea is rare and is probably due to the good glucuronidator phenotype of the Asian population, particularly in the Chinese and Malay populations. A probable explanation for this may be due to the low frequency of UGT1A1*28 or UGT1A1*6 in the Asian cancer patients. The frequency of UGT1A1*28 ranges between 2% to 4% in Chinese and Malay populations compared with 13% in the Indians while the allelic frequency of UGT1A1*6 is less that 1% in all three Asian ethnic groups. Severe neutropenia (ANC < 500 cells/) on the other hand, seem to be more common with an incidence of approximately 30% and the risk is higher in cancer patients homozygous for UGT1A128 and/or UGT1A16 alleles.Since homozygosity for UGT1A128 and UGT1A16 alleles are low in Asian cancer patients, particularly Malay and Chinese cancer patients that form the majority of our patient population, and the standard dose of irinotecan of 100mg/m2 is well tolerated, we hypothesize that patients homozygous for the reference UGT1A1 gene or heterozygous for the UGT1A128 or UGT1A16 allele might be able to tolerate higher doses. The aim of this Phase I proposal is to determine the maximum tolerated dose and the dose limiting toxicity of irinotecan based on the UGT1A128 and UGT1A16 genotype status of Asian cancer patients with solid tumours.
kw: Pharmacogenetics, Personalized Medicine, Irinotecan, UGT1A1

title: Systemic Tumor Targeting using Novel Delivery of Chlorin-e6 for Cellular Diagnostic Imaging of Oral Carcinoma
abs: Overexpression of epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) is a key characteristic of human tumors and is frequently linked to more aggressive tumor behaviors including increased proliferation, metastasis, and therapeutic resistance in squamous cell carcinoma of the oral cavity and oropharynx. Over the past years, various strategies ranging from chemotherapy to radiotherapy have been developed to improve treatment outcome. Next to these strategies, antibody therapy has become an additional option and the humanized monoclonal antibody Virosome (Vir), a reconstituted viral envelope provides a broadly applicable delivery system for targeted therapy. Our preliminary in vivo uptake kinetics studies have shown that Vir containing the photosensitizer chlorin e6 (Ce6) has increased rate of cellular uptake and prolonged retention compared to Ce6 alone. Thus, it is reasonable to hypothesize that Vir encapsulated Ce6 is a new and efficient drug delivery system with tumor-specific targeting properties compared to other conventional photosensitizers. Since EGFR is an appropriate cancer target, we believe that tagging Ce6-Vir with anti EGFR and gold nanoparticle (here onwards denoted as Fab'-Ce6-Vir-Au) as cancer-specific probes will provide greater clinical benefits to diagnose oral cancer. This study seeks to develop virosome as a targeted delivery vehicle of a chlorin based photosensitizer using a monoclonal antibody and gold nanoparticle as a molecular-specific contrast agent targeted against EGFR for in vivo assessment of epithelial neoplasia using in-vivo confocal endomicroscopic imaging and optical coherence tomography (OCT). Our approach is to use both in vitro and in vivo strategies to assess molecular and cellular mechanisms involved in Fab'-Ce6-Vir-Au to EGFR positive tumor cells. Our future findings are of immediate clinical relevance and demonstrate the importance of a cellular imaging approach to examine the dynamic process of intra-tumoral photosensitizer distribution. This proposal, to the best of our knowledge, is the first attempt to perform this novel idea of specific targeting using Fab'-Ce6-Vir-Au as a cancer specific probe for diagnostic modalities in oral cancers.

title: The generation of highly osteogenic and vascularised voluminous tissue-engineered constructs with primitive fetal mesenchymal stem cells and endothelial progenitor cells for critical-sized bony defects.
abs: Skeletal disorders resulting from trauma or degenerative conditions results in significant morbidity, with current treatment modalities through the use of autografts, allografts or synthetic grafts being inadequate. Consequently, the field of bone tissue engineering has been under intensive investigations in order to address this un-met need. However, despite the rapid advancements in osteogenic cell sources and scaffold technologies, the inability to rapidly generate neo-vasculature within physiologically complex voluminous scaffolds remains a major limitation hindering its clinical introduction. Endothelial progenitor cells (EPC) are precursor cell types recently identified in the bone marrow, peripheral blood and umbilical cord blood, and have recently been implicated in post-natal vasculogenesis, suggesting their utility for vascularisation of voluminous grafts. We hypothesise that the introduction of primitive EPC to osteogenic mesenchymal stem cell (MSC)-scaffolds will lead to rapid vascularisation and consequential improved cellular survival and osteogenicity, leading to improved bone healing. We aim to investigate the interactions of EPC with primitive MSC within an experimental system capitalising on our expertise in high-porosity bioactive scaffolds, bioreactor systems, stem cell technology and molecular imaging through magnetic resonance technology. We will (1) define co-culture systems for EPC and MSC; (2) investigate the vascularisation and bone repair effect in a rat femoral segmental defect model, and finally; (3) test the performance of EPC / MSC constructs in a clinically relevant critical-sized femoral defect in a mini-pig.Successful rapid vascularisation of physiologically complex tissue-engineered grafts here will be of relevance not only to osteogenic applications, but also to other complex grafts such as hepatic, skeletal and cardiac muscle grafts, and hasten its translation into clinical practice.

title: Projecting Individualized Probabilities of Developing Breast Cancer for Singaporean Women
abs: The best-known model available for predicting an individual women’s chance of developing breast cancer is the Gail model, which has been widely used to counsel women in the United States (US). The model was developed with the following specific standard risk factors: current age, race, age at menarche, age at birth of first live child, number of previous breast biopsy examinations, number of first-degree relatives with breast cancer and presence of atypical hyperplasia and has been validated extensively in the US. However, comparatively few studies have validated it in a non-US population, especially in a predominantly Asian population. Although the Gail model has been shown to be well calibrated with white American women to identify cohorts of high-risk patients who are appropriate participants for chemoprevention trials, further validation of the Gail model’s accuracy in multiethnic populations is desirable. Many other factors that are not currently accounted for by the model, including geographic variation in breast cancer incidence rates, ethnic difference in mammographic densities, diet and lifestyle, etc., may affect its accuracy. Recently, it was shown that the inclusion of breast mammographic density could potentially improve the precision of prediction of the model. Nevertheless, it is not known if the existing breast cancer prediction models are accurate predictors of the disease among Singaporean women.Information on standard risk factors, which were incorporated into the modified Gail model, is available from the Singapore Breast Screening Project (SBSP). The SBSP is a large mammography screening study conducted from 1994 to 1997. Since then, we have also studied mammographic breast density and mammographic parenchymal pattern in several sub-studies within SBSP. The proposed research aims to assess the Gail model and other newly developed models on the inclusion of mammographic breast density and other risk factors, in Singaporean women. We also aim to develop risk prediction models using the SBSP database as a means of providing absolute risk estimates for Singaporean women. The project is expected to contribute to the objective of accurately assessing breast cancer risk for individual Singaporean women in the near future.

title: Selection of Patients Eligible for Potential Revascularization by Multimodality Evaluation of Cerebral Hemodynamics and Vasodilatory Reserve in Presence of Symptomatic Carotid or Middle Cerebral artery Steno-occlusive Disease
abs: Primary specific aim- To assess the cerebral vascular reserve in patients with severe steno-occlusive disease of carotid or middle cerebral arteries (MCA) by transcranial Doppler and Acetazolamide-challenged HMPAO-SPECT.Secondary specific aim- 1.Using the multimodality approach, to select patients who are at higher risk of cerebral ischaemic events and would benefit with revascularization procedures.2.Using vasomotor reactivity as a possible predictor of subsequent cerebral ischaemic events as a result of impaired cerebral hemodynamics.3.Monitoring these patients for the assessment of the risk of subsequent cerebral ischemic events.Hypothesis: Circle of Willis provides collateral pathways to perfuse the affected vascular territories in patients with severe steno-occlusive disease of major arteries. The collateral perfusion may become insufficient in certain physiological circumstances due to failed vasodilatory reserve and intracranial steal phenomenon. We have previously described this phenomenon as ‘Reversed-Robinhood syndrome’ in acute ischaemic stroke patients with persisting arterial occlusions. Intracranial steno-occlusive disease is fairly common in Asian patients, especially of Chinese ethnicity. In a pilot study, we evaluated of cerebral hemodynamics and vasodilatory reserve in our patients with symptomatic, but chronic, internal carotid or MCA severe steno-occlusive disease. We observed intracranial steal phenomenon during bilateral TCD monitoring during breath-holding. This was confirmed in a significant proportion of cases on Acetazolamide-challenged HMPAO-SPECT imaging and presented as ‘cerebral vasodilatory failure’. The information obtained from TCD and SPECT imaging was complementary and extremely useful for therapeutic decisions. Methodology: Symptomatic patients with severe steno-occlusive disease of carotids or middle cerebral artery would undergo diagnostic TCD for assessment of collateral flow and TCD-monitoring for any spontaneous emboli. Bilateral TCD monitoring would be performed during voluntary breath-holding according to a standard scanning protocol to look for the vasomotor reactivity as well as any intracranial steal phenomenon. Patients with impaired vasomotor reactivity and intracranial steal phenomenon would be further evaluated with acetazolamide-challenged HMPAO-SPECT. These subjects would be further followed up during the study period for any subsequent cerebral ischaemic events in the affected arterial territories.Clinical significance- There is no established treatment for patients with chronic carotid or MCA severe steno-occlusive disease. By employing the multimodality approach, we could select few patients for surgical revascularization procedures. With encouraging and satisfactory results after revascularization in selected patients, this novel approach could be applied to larger number of patients to prevent cerebral ischaemic events and reduce the stroke burden.

title: A Phase-Two Study of The Use of Mesenchymal Stem Cells for Enhancing Meniscal Lesions Repair in the Human Knee
abs: Aim: The aim of this translational Phase Two trial is to investigate the safety and efficacy of using autologous mesenchymal stem cell (MSCs) in enhancing the repair of human knee meniscal defects. Hypotheses: We hypothesize that MSCs could enhance the repair of meniscus defects as compared to normal debridement and suture therapy. Methodology: 35 consented patients with meniscus tears or defects will be recruited. Patients will have their bone marrow harvested from their posterior iliac crest and MSC isolated from the bone marrow aspirates. Approximately 3-4 weeks later, MSC will be implanted into the defect area with meniscus repair surgery. All the patients will have to undergo identical post-operation rehabilitation. Post-operation clinical evaluation will also be conducted at 3, 6, 12 and 24 months post-operatively using ICRS, IKDC, Lysholm, VAS and SF-36. While MRI will be perform at 12-months post-operation. All analysis will be perform using STATA version 10 with the statistical significance set at p < 0.05. The improvement of the post-operation scores over the pre-operation scores will be determined using paired-T test when normality assumptions are satisfied. Clinical significance: This project will translate basic science research outcomes of stem cells to the bedside and to our knowledge; our proposed trial is a pioneering trial in using autologous MSC to enhance repair of meniscus defects in the human knee. The use of autologous MSCs also eliminates any potential problems with immunogenicity and rejection.
kw: Meniscus repair, Bone marrow stem cells, Tissue regeneration, Autologous implantation, Clinical trial

title: Strain Engineering for Next-Generation Semiconductor Manufacturing
abs: Transistor miniaturization achieves increased circuit functionality and higher computational speeds together with cost reduction, but immense challenges are faced in developing next-generation technologies. The semiconductor industry urgently needs innovation in materials and device architecture for further improvement in Complementary Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor (CMOS) technology. The proposed research addresses the important challenges in next-generation CMOS transistor technology, including performance enhancement and power consumption reduction. The proposed research will explore new methods in enhancing carrier mobility and transistor drive current, e.g. through strain engineering using novel high-stress materials, stress-memorization techniques, etc. This research will demonstrate new, significant, and manufacturable technologies for boosting carrier mobility and performance in electronic devices. In particular, a new high-stress liner or etch-stop layer with intrinsic stress exceeding 6 GPa will be explored. The proposed research will also address other major bottlenecks encountered by the semiconductor industry, e.g. high series resistance in transistor source/drain regions, through exploration and integration of new metal silicide materials. 20 nm transistors will be realized in this research. The physics of carrier transport in such nanoscale devices will be investigated. By improving the speed of each transistor, the performance of integrated circuits comprising transistors will be improved. Increased speed performance can also be traded-off for reduced power consumption. The proposed research offers immense opportunities for the development of intellectual property and commercialization of new technologies. The candidate will work closely with Chartered Semiconductor on this research effort.
kw: Strained-channel transistors;Transistor strain engineering;Nanoelectronic devices and circuits;Semiconductor process technology;High performance electronic devices;High stress etch-stop layer

title: Generation of Dermatophagoides and Blomia specific CD8 T cell receptor transgenic mice and investigation their role in a mouse asthma model using inhalant allergens
abs: Asthma is an inflammatory lung disease in which CD4 Th2 T cells play an obligatory role. CD8 T cells also respond to allergens and have been shown to inhibit the allergic immune response in studies using ovalbumin (OVA) specific wild type and transgenic T cells. Early in the response, CD8 T cells are able to skew the immune system to a Th1 phenotype. Experimentally polarized Tc2 CD8 T cells can induce a similar inflammatory response to Th2 cells but there is scant evidence that thisoccurs in asthmatic patients. Little is known about the factors that control CD8 T cell priming to allergens in vivo or the difference between CD8 T cells that prevent or promote asthma. The most widely studied model uses OVA, which is not an inhalant allergen, and does not possess the enzymic activity usually found in important allergens. This study seeks to address this question through the generation of CD8 T-cell receptor transgenic mice for real allergens Blomia tropicalisand Dermatophagoides pteronyssinus. These are the main allergens in the equatorial belt that cause asthma. We propose to generate CD8 T cell receptor transgenic mice specific for these allergens. We will use TAP deficient RMAS cells to identify MHC I binding epitopes and an improved process utilizing photocleavable peptides to facilitate the formation of MHC I tetramers. These tetramers will be used to isolate Blot t 5 and Der p 1 specific CD8 T cells and their T cell receptors cloned and used to generate transgenic mice. Blot t 5 and Der p 1 specific transgenicCD8 T cells will be used to determine the capacity of real allergens to activate CD8 T cells in vivo and to influence their capacity to up or down regulate the lung allergic response.
kw: Allergen, CD8, Transgenic, T cell receptor

title: Beyond BRCA1 and BRCA2: Associations between new breast cancer susceptibility alleles and clinico-pathological characteristics in an Asian population, with implications for disease screening and breast cancer management
abs: BackgroundRecently, large genome-wide association studies have identified several loci associated with breast cancer risk. These multi-center studies have involved thousands of breast cancer patients, who were predominantly from Western countries, the majority of whom were unselected for family history. However, there is a lack of information in Asians, in individuals with a family history, and in patients with early onset breast cancer.Aim 1:To determine the frequency of these variants in the following groups of Singapore breast cancer patients:(1)breast cancer patients who have a family history of breast and/or ovarian cancer and are BRCA1/2 mutation negative (n=200);(2) early onset breast cancer patients 40 years) who are BRCA1/2 mutation negative (n=200);(3) unselected breast cancer patients with blood samples reposited at the Tissue Repository of the National Cancer Centre (NCC) and prospective consecutive breast cancer patients presenting at NCC (n=2000). The frequency of these variants will be determined in individuals without cancer (Controls), matched for age and ethnicity (n=2000). The SNPs within the following genes/loci will be analyzed: FGFR2, TNRC9, MAP3K1, LSP1, ERCC4, and loci on 2q35, 5p12, 6q22.33, and 8q24.Aim 2:To determine if there are any associations between the genotypes and clinical parameters (histology; stage; grade; lymph node status; estrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR), HER2/neu status; disease recurrence and disease free survival).Clinical significanceThe determination of associations between these SNPs and clinico-pathological characteristics may have significant impact on disease screening and breast cancer management, and enhance our understanding of the influence of these SNPs on disease progression in an Asian population. In the long term, knowledge gained on the biology of these SNPs and their effect on breast cancer may result in the development of novel treatment strategies for patients stratified according to genotype.
kw: Breast cancer, susceptibility, Single Nucleotide Polymorphism (SNP), Taqman SNP genotyping, Clinical correlations

title: A genome-wide case-control association study for susceptibility loci associated with differential response to environmental insults in sporadic colorectal carcinomas.
abs: Colorectal Cancer (CRC) has emerged as the highest incidence cancer and second leading cause of cancer mortality in Singapore.1 Up to 80% of CRC is sporadic indicating that environmental insults play a greater role than heredity. 2-4 Nevertheless, one study on monozygotic twins has estimated that about 35% of CRC incidence are attributable to genetic predisposition. 4 Hence, other than dominant genes that cause familial CRC, there are other susceptibility loci that can adversely affect response to environmental insults.Several CRC susceptibility loci have recently been identified by genome-wide association studies (GWAS) indicating the feasibility of finding risk loci with this technique. 5-11 The samples genotyped in these studies were heterogeneous, including patients with family history, from different ethnicity and all ages. Thus, these loci are likely to be low penetrant risk alleles for familial CRC but the probability that they could contribute to differential response to environmental insults is low.We aim to perform genome-wide case-control association study on stringently defined disease subgroup and healthy controls to increase the likelihood of identifying loci that are responsive to environmental insults. 1000 sporadic Chinese CRC patients with no family history will be age- (50 or more) and ethnicity-matched to 1000 healthy controls. Genome-wide SNP- and copy number genotyping will be performed with Affymetrix SNP 5 array that covers the whole genome more comprehensively. The data will be analyzed with high-end software. More cases and controls will be recruited as replication panel to validate the results.This study has the potential to uncover novel pathways or insight into environmental risks for a well-defined population that could directly impact on public-health-based disease prevention measures and/or therapeutic strategies. 12 Further, the identification and verification of predictive markers could potentially aid in population screening to identify individuals susceptible to developing sporadic CRC.
kw: Sporadic colorectal cancer risk, Environmental insults, Genome-wide genotyping array, Susceptibility genes, Genome-wide case-control association

title: A Randomized Controlled Trial of an STI/HIV/AIDS Prevention Intervention for Adolescents Attending A Public STI Clinic in Singapore
abs: Background of study Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) among adolescents aged 10 to 19 years in Singapore have increased sharply from 250 cases in 2002 to 775 cases in 2006. The preliminary analysis of unmarried sexually experienced adolescents aged 14 to 19 years attending the Department of STI Control Clinic (DSC) found a high number of sex partners (median:4; range 1-25) and a high prevalence of unprotected sex (90%) and sexually transmitted infections (60%) among them. Specific aimsThis study aims to evaluate the efficacy of behavioral interventions to reduce sexual risk behaviors and sexually transmitted infections among adolescents attending DSC. Design, Setting, and Participants A randomized controlled trial will be conducted on 800 sexually experienced adolescents, with 400 participants assigned to the routine program, and 400 to the new intervention developed from an assessment of their needs. All participants will complete a self-administered questionnaire and an interview on their knowledge of STIs/HIV/AIDS, self-efficacy, skills in negotiating for sexual abstinence or condom use, and sexual behaviors at baseline and at 6- and 12-month post-intervention. All will be tested for STIs.Intervention Participants in the intervention group will receive 6 group or individual counseling sessions on STI/HIV knowledge, life skills, safer sex and healthy relationships over 1 year. They will also be referred to peer educators, counselors and community organizations for proactive social and emotional support delivered through electronic media and other means. The control group will receive the usual 2 counseling sessions - at first and follow-up clinic visit. Outcome Measures The outcome measures will include consistent condom use, secondary abstinence, number of partners, observed condom application skills, incident STI infection and mediators of STI-preventive behaviors such as negotiation skills for sexual abstinence or safer sex. Clinical significance The study will provide pertinent data on effective strategies for STI/HIV/AIDS prevention programs among sexually experienced adolescents in Singapore.
kw: Adolescents, Intervention, Randomized Controlled Trial, Sexual abstinence, Condom use , Sexually transmitted infections

title: Genetic influence of apolipoprotein E on cholesterol metabolism and amyloid pathology in Alzheimer’s disease.
abs: Increasing evidence shows that cholesterol plays a role in the pathogenesis of Alzheimer’s disease (AD). Apolipoprotein E (ApoE) is a key protein in cholesterol metabolism, and inheritance of the ApoE4 allele is a major genetic risk for sporadic AD. ApoE4 is one of three major ApoE alleles in human (E2, E3 and E4). Emerging evidence suggests ApoE role in this association is likely to be complex. One possibility is ApoE isoforms modulating the production, aggregation and clearance of amyloid-ß (Aß) in AD. However, ApoE function in this pathway remains unclear. Interestingly, some cholesterol metabolites could enhance Aß misfolding. But, the triggering factor(s) and underlying mechanisms of this process are unknown. The work proposed in this application will investigate the correlative interaction of these events in AD pathogenesis. Our preliminary data indicates that ApoE isoforms are associated with characteristic profile of neuronal and plasma cholesterol metabolites. We therefore hypothesize that ApoE isoforms differentially modulate the composition of cholesterol metabolites and these metabolites could regulate Aß aggregation. Specific Aim 1: We will examine the genetic and temporal contribution of ApoE isoforms on the cholesterol metabolite contents leading to and during the onset of amyloid pathology in doubly transgenic mice expressing human ApoE and familial-AD mutant human amyloid precursor protein (hAPP[FAD]) using Gas Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry (GC-MS). Specific Aim 2: We will evaluate the influence of ApoE isoforms on the neuronal and plasma cholesterol metabolite profiles of ApoE homozygotes and heterozygotes AD and non-AD patients using GC-MS. Specific Aim 3: We will identify cholesterol metabolites that are able to modulate Aß aggregation using biochemical and immunological methods. This application will provide a deeper insight on the connective role of ApoE isoforms in cholesterol metabolism and amyloid pathology. The information generated may also aid the identification of novel biomarkers and selective therapeutic targets.
kw: Apolipoprotein E, Cholesterol metabolites, Neurodegenerative disease, Alzheimer’s disease, Protein misfolding, Amyloid

title: Ethnicity, reproductive history and the risk of breast cancer.
abs: Background: Singapore breast cancer rates are rising. Low and late parity, which are increasingly common in Singapore, are important risk factors for breast cancer, but the association between reproductive factors and breast cancer has never been well studied in Asian populations. It is therefore impossible to predict how changing reproductive profiles will affect future breast cancer rates. With this study we aim to:I.Define the impact of reproductive factors on the incidence and mortality of premenopausal breast cancer in Singapore and evaluate whether these effects are modified by ethnicity.II. Define ethnic differences in pregnancy characteristics, including placenta weight, weight gain, breast feeding practices and alpha fetoprotein levels, which may modify breast cancer risks later in life and explain ethnic differences in breast cancer risk. Methods: I. In a historical cohort study (Singapore Birth Registry linked with Cancer Registry, including all women who gave birth between 1986-2002) we will quantify associations between reproductive factors (parity, age at first birth, birth weight, gender offspring), ethnicity and breast cancer risk and survival. II. In a cross sectional study, we will compare breast cancer risk factors and pregnancy characteristics (placenta weight, complication rate, weight gain, etc) between 300 Chinese, 200 Malay and 200 Indian pregnant women. For a subgroup of patients we will determine serum levels of alpha fetoprotein and correlate this with placenta weight and ethnicity. Clinical significance: Based on the current epidemiological knowledge it is impossible to infer how changes in reproductive factors in Singapore will affect future breast cancer rates. With this study we will fill knowledge gaps on the relationships between reproductive factors, ethnicity and breast cancer in an Asian population. The results will help us unravel biological mechanisms behind ethnic differences in breast cancer risk, predict future cancer trends and identify future needs for preventive and therapeutic interventions.
kw: Pregnancy hormones, Ethnicity, Parity, Population-based, Reproductive history, Breast cancer

title: Phase I Trial of Intravesical Cytokine Gene Therapy For Bladder Cancer Using Non-viral Vectors in Patients Who are Undergoing Transurethral Resection
abs: Specific aims: We designed this Phase 1 study to determine the safety, feasibility, and biologic activity of an intravesical instillation of a liposome-based transfection system with a plasmid DNA encoding IFN-a.Hypothesis: Intravesical instillation of our vector system is a safe and efficacious method in transfecting bladder cancer in patients. We should be able to achieve transfection of the bladder surfaces in patients with bladder cancer with potential benefits.Methodology: 12 bladder cancer patients will be divided into 3 groups with 4 patients in each group. They will receive 1, 2 or 3 consecutive weekly intravesical administration of the transfection mixture. pUMVC3-IFNa plasmid is constructed by inserting the human IFN-a encoding gene into pUMVC3-a mammalian expression plasmid. The DNA: lipid ratio is determined by our previous in vitro and in vivo studies. The patients will be catheterized to drain the residue urine before the transfection mixture is instilled into the bladder via the catheter. After instillation, the patient will be instructed to turn every 15 min in bed until 2 hours to allow optimal contact. All patients will undergo scheduled transurethral resection of the bladder tumor 2 days after the last instillation. Patients will be closely monitored after study treatment. This includes assessment of clinical symptoms, physical examination, monitoring of vital signs, and recording of adverse events. Patients will be also monitored with complete blood count and renal function, serum electrolytes, liver function, coagulation status, urinalysis and chest xray. Local cellular response will be assessed on hematoxylin and eosin, immunohistochemical staining for infiltrating cell subsets of tumor sections. In addition, urine samples will be checked forcytokine levels.Clinical significance: If successfully conducted, this trial will be the first report of successful gene transfer into the bladder with non-viral vectors in human subjects.
kw: Bladder Cancer, Clinical trial, Gene therapy, Cytokines, Immunotherapy

title: Hydrogen sulfide: a novel neuroprotectant in neurodegenerative disease?
abs: Neurodegenerative disorders represent a major cause of disability and death, with an unmet need for therapies that alter disease progression. Clinical and preclinical studies reveal a previously underappreciated role of excessive glial activation and sustained brain neuroinflammation in the pathophysiology of these progressive neurodegenerative disorders including Parkinson’s disease (PD) and raise the hypothesis that targeting of neuroinflammation might be a therapeutic approach to alter PD progression. Hydrogen sulfide (H2S) has recently been hypothesized to be an important neuromodulator in the brain. Abnormal generation and metabolism of H2S may be actively involved in the pathogenesis of central nervous system (CNS) diseases. We recently reported that both endogenous and exogenous application of H2S produces anti-neuroinflammatory effects in microglial cells. We hypothesize that H2S may have the potentials to produce neuroprotective effects on neurodegenerative disorders (e.g. PD). Rotenone, a naturally derived pesticide, has been used to evoke the behavioral and pathological symptoms of PD in animal models. This project is therefore designed to examine the neuroprotective effects of H2S on rotenone-induced inflammation and pathological processes of neurodegerative diseases. With this model, we will: 1. confirm the anti-neuroinflammatory effects of H2S in microglial cells;2. examine the anti-oxidant effects of H2S in astrocytes;3. investigate the anti-apoptotic effects of H2S in neurons; 4. investigate the beneficial effects of H2S in mixed glia-neuronal co-cultures;5. confirm the neuroprotective effects of H2S in vivo in rats with PD.
kw: Hydrogen sulfide, Neurodegenerative disease, Neuroprotectant, Parkinson’s disease

title: Role of thyroid peroxidase and thyroid peroxidase antibodies in the pathogenesis of extra-thyroidal disease - Depression as a model.
abs: Thyroid peroxidase (TPO) plays an integral role in thyroid hormone synthesis. Like the thyrotropin receptor (TSH-R), another key thyroid protein, TPO has recently been detected at extra-thyroidal sites. We previously reported that TPO is expressed in human orbital tissue and fibroblasts. A recent study suggests that rat cardiomyocytes express multiple thyroidal proteins including TPO. At least in the rat, cardiac tissue appears to be capable of generating low levels of thyroid hormone. Antibodies (Ab) directed against TPO (TPOAb) are the hallmark of autoimmune thyroid disease (AITD) but their expression is also increased in a number of other disease states including depression. We hypothesize that functional TPO is present in brain tissue. TPOAb modulation of brain TPO function may contribute to depression. A more commonly held view is that TPOAb have no physiological effects but are surrogate markers of specific immune responses. This study aims to test both hypotheses by:1) Confirming the presence or absence of TPO in various areas of the human brain2) Determining the prevalence of TPOAb in a cohort of patients with major depressive symptoms and comparing cytokine profiles of TPOAb +ve and TPOAb –ve depressed patients with normal controls.3) Correlating serial biochemical, antibody and cytokine changes with clinical outcome TPO mRNA and protein detection will be carried out using real-time PCR and Western blotting. In the clinical arm, 50 female patients with major depression will be recruited. Thyroid hormone panels (free T4, free T3, TSH), anti-thyroid antibody levels (TPOAb, anti-thyroglobulin antibody/TgAb, anti-thyrotropin antibody/TRAb), serum cortisol and cytokines/chemokines implicated in autoimmune response (IL1B, IL4, IL6, IL10, IL12, IL17A, IFN-gamma, TNF-a, TGF-b-1, MCP-1, MIP-1a, MIP-1b) of these patients will be measured and compared against age-matched controls. Biochemical, Ab and cytokine testing will be repeated at 2 and 6 months and correlated with clinical progress.
kw: Thyroid peroxidase, Depression, Cytokines, Brain, Thyroid peroxidase antibodies

title: Particulate Composite Matrix Delivery System for Enhanced Transmucosal Absorption of Photosensitizer in Oral Carcinoma
abs: Photodynamic therapy and fluorescence diagnosis of advanced malignant tumours that develop in the oral cavity might realize their full clinical potential if the photosensitizers employed could be delivered specifically to the tumour tissue in optimal quantities. Unfortunately, current topical formulations are not able to give adequate penetration of the photosensitizer to deep-seated tumours. A poorly water-soluble photosensitizer, chlorin e6 (Ce6) was shown to be therapeutically useful as a complex, chlorin e6 – polyvinylpyrrolidone, but needed formulation improvements to increase the depth and tumour tissue selectivity of Ce6 penetration. We aim to develop a mucoadhesive topical gel of Ce6 with suitable penetration enhancer to deliver Ce6 deeper to reach tumour targets. The scope of study consists of a preliminary investigation of the influence of various additives on the penetration of Ce6 or its complex into the chick chorioallantoic membrane as a drug transport model. Suitable additives will then be employed in the formulation of mucoadhesive gels to deliver Ce6 or its complex. Microspheres which can be reconstituted into gels will also be explored to preserve the stability of Ce6 during storage. The mechanisms of penetration and distribution of the photosensitizer will be elucidated using confocal laser scanning microscopy and in situ light-induced fluorescence spectroscopy on an orthotopic oral carcinoma model. Potential gels will be further tested in a pilot clinical trial where the depth of penetration and selectivity of Ce6 or its complex in oral malignancy using both in vivo spectrofluorometric tissue measurement and macroscopic fluorescence imaging method coupled with ex vivo confocal fluorescence microscopy. Ultimately, we hope that a novel topical formulation of photosensitizer with enhanced penetration, selectivity and photosensitizing properties towards deep-invasive malignancies will be developed for use in clinical photodynamic therapy of the oral cavity. Potential patent application and commercialisation of the formulation are envisaged.
kw: photosensitizer, chick chlorioallantoic membrane, mucoadhesive gel, chlorin e6, oral carcinoma, drug delivery system

title: Investigation of Transglutaminse-2 function in the development of experimental myopia in mouse
abs: Myopia is a common problem in Singapore and throughout Asia, although the molecular and genetic basis of myopia is not well understood. Myopia is a socio-economic problem; high myopia is sight threatening and increasing in prevalence. At SERI, we have developed a mouse model of experimental myopia, characterized by axial elongation from re-modelling of the sclera or the outer shell of the eye, as in human myopia. Although muscarinic receptor subtypes may be involved in scleral remodelling, we do not know of their exact downstream molecules. From preliminary studies we have found that transglutaminase (TG)-2, a molecule previously implicated in wound healing and migration of cells, was up-regulated in myopic murine sclera compared to control and that atropine, an anti-muscarinic drug down-regulated the gene. Previously TG-2 has also been implicated in the regulation of extracellular matrix molecules such as fibronectin and collagen. We propose to test the hypothesis that TG-2 has a central role in the development of experimental myopia in the mouse, by attempting to induce myopia in TG-2 deleted mice, and mice treated with TG inhibitors. Supporting data in the form of TG-2 associated transcript and proteins in the sclera will be obtained, as well as the growth related changes of these molecules in TG-2 deleted mice. We will also determine the role of TG-2 in muscarinic receptor signalling by using TG inhibitors in muscarinic receptor subtype deleted mice, prior to induction of myopia. If TG-2 or associated molecules play a role in scleral elongation in experimental myopia these may form a basis for a new type of pharmacological intervention in human myopia.
kw: Myopia, Transglutaminase-2, Transglutaminase inhibitors, Treatment, Mouse, Muscarinic receptors

title: Clinical genomics of signature chromosome translocations in cancer: a tissue-based investigation and molecular characterization of breakpoint regions
abs: Molecular cytogenetics of carcinomas is poised for an era of clinically significant discoveries powered by new technological tools for genomic analysis. Molecular and functional characterizations of signature chromosome translocations have proven clinical significance. Fusion genes and transcripts have entered clinical practice as biomarkers for diagnosis, prognosis and patient stratification, and have even led to highly effective therapies transforming fatal malignancies into curable diseases.Although most currently known oncogenic chromosome translocations were discovered in haematological malignancies, there is evidence that carcinomas harbour a comparable range of translocations. We propose a general approach to discovering translocations of pathogenic significance in any carcinoma of interest, using gastric adenocarcinoma as proof of concept. We have identified 5 recurrent breakpoint cytobands (2p22, 4q25, 7q31, 8q22 and 18q21) by spectrally karyotyping 17 human gastric cancer cell lines. To date, our focus on 18q21 shows that cell line translocations are mirrored in 35% of 99 primary gastric adenocarcinomas and are absent in other common carcinomas. Integrating high resolution genome copy number and microRNA expression datasets identifies boundaries of breakpoint regions and reveals an association of dysregulated microRNA expression with translocations. We now propose to (a) verify translocations involving the other 4 cytobands in gastric cancer tissues; (b) molecularly characterize each breakpoint region; and (c) identify genomic aberrations caused by translocations. The project will employ fluorescence in situ hybridization on tissue microarrays, extant datasets of high resolution copy number and exon expression of these cell lines, integrated bioinformatic and statistical data analyses, flow sorting of derivative chromosomes for ultra-high resolution genome tiling arrays, sequencing of breakpoint regions, identification of fusion transcripts by RNA-ligase mediated RACE and validation in clinical biospecimens.Gastric cancer is the second leading cause of global cancer mortality. Defining signature translocations should help to develop targeted measures to prevent, halt and treat gastric cancer.
kw: Tissue microarrays, Chromosome translocations, Chromosome sorting, Tiling and exon arrays, Fusion genes, Fluorescence in situ hybridization

title: Analysing immune cells in the tumour microenvironment and plasma cytokine protein array of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) patients as platforms for prognostic biomarker discovery
abs: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is endemic in Asia due to the high prevalence of hepatitis B viral infection among Asians. Advanced HCC still presents with a poor prognosis with a short median survival, making HCC the third leading cause of cancer death. A recent randomized clinical trial of sorafenib, a small molecule RAF kinase inhibitor, for the treatment of advanced HCC, demonstrated a modest benefit in overall survival compared to placebo. However, longer term disease control of HCC still remains a major therapeutic challenge. The Budhu study showed that a shift away from a pro-inflammatory milieu in the non-cancerous metastatic HCC stroma is related to a more aggressive HCC phenotype and prognosticate for clinical outcome. We are interested in studying whether the newly-identified pro-inflammatory Th17 effector cells might also play a role in determining clinical outcomes in HCC. Th17 is normally inversely related to regulatory T cells differentiation. We therefore hypothesize that a higher expression of Th17 in the HCC microenvironment may represent a better prognosis in HCC as a previous Chinese study showed that higher levels of Treg was associated with a poorer outcome in HCC. We intend to study the expression pattern of ROR, STAT3 and IL-12R mRNA to assess any potential correlations between these three functionally-related molecules and if they may potentially prognosticate at the transcriptome level in HCC.Our preliminary data shows that higher ROR expression in HCC (> 2-fold; n=40) is associated with better survival (median survival 48.07 months) as compared to HCC samples with < 0.5 folds (n=30; median survival 44.80 months) with borderline significance (p=0.073). More significantly, lower expression of IL12R1, a gene related to IL-23, critical to the differentiation towards Th17, (< 0.5-fold; n=63) is associated with poorer survival in HCC (median survival 42.17 months) with p-value of 0.01.Next, we aim to study the protein expression of ROR, STAT3 and IL-12R1 in the tumour microenvironment by performing immunohistochemistry (IHC) on paraffin-embedded HCC tissue sections.Finally, we wish to study if there is a distinct cytokine protein fingerprint in the plasma of patients diagnosed with early stage resected HCC that differentiates (1) better overall survival (OS) in HCC patients from those with a lower OS ; and (2) better relapse-free survival in HCC patients from poorer relapse-free survival in HCC patients. This may enable us to determine a unique HCC protein fingerprint for better patient classification, leading to more careful screening and earlier detection for the high-risk HCC group, and potentially improve HCC patient outcomes.
kw: HCC, Th17, IL-12R?1, ROR?t, prognostic

title: Restoring voice in laryngeal cancer patients. A new device and method for in-office unsedated tracheoesophageal puncture (TEP)
abs: Specific Aims1.Develop a new device for unsedated tracheoesophgeal puncture (TEP) to restore voice in post-laryngectomy patients, which offers superior patient safety and is easier to perform than current methods.2.Test the device using an animal model.3.Develop a prototype suited for human trial.HypothesisThe hypothesis to be tested is that a device can be designed and developed to enable rapid and safe TEP in unsedated post-laryngectomy patients.MethodologyThere are two main phases. The first involves design and development of a prototype device. The second involves testing the prototype in animal experiments.The prototype requires design and development of: 1. An insertion trocar to create a tract between trachea and esophagus. 2. A backstop device to protect the posterior esophageal wall during insertion. A number of different design prototypes are examined using computer modeling to calculate insertion forces required to penetrate the dividing wall between trachea and esophagus without significant tissue deformation and tenting. The prototypes are tested on cadaveric animal tissue. Once the main prototype is created, it is tested on a live pig model.Clinical SignificanceCurrent methods for TEP either require general anesthesia or if performed unsedated are uncomfortable procedures and risk injury to the esophagus.There is a need for a simpler, safer method to perform unsedated TEP. A device for rapid TEP in unsedated patients with minimal risk of complications such as posterior esophgeal wall injury would be a significant advance in voice restoration following total laryngectomy. The purpose of this research proposal is to design and develop such a device. Successful development of the device will improve healthcare by increasing patient safety, reducing hospital stay and costs, and improving quality of life in this patient group. It also provides a unique commercial opportunity to market the device.
kw: Larynx, Voice restoration, Biomedical Engineering, Cancer, Tracheo-esophageal puncture, Medical device

title: Evaluation of the dynamics of TB-specific T-cell response in HIV co-infected patients on treatment for active TB using T-SPOT.TB
abs: In response to Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection, naive T cells proliferate and differentiate into effector cells producing interferon-gamma as well as other T helper type 1 cytokines. The number of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB)-specific T cells can be enumerated in vitro using T-SPOT.TB. This method has proven to be superior to the tuberculosis skin test in diagnosing MTB infection, latent or active. Its performance appears to be unaffected by the degree of immunosuppression therefore making this test especially useful in AIDS patients. Many studies show a lower number of interferon-gamma producing cells measured in treated population than untreated population and a decline in the number when patients complete TB treatment, the test has the potential to be used for treatment response monitoring. However, studies of the dynamics of MTB-specific T cell response have not always been conclusive, especially in the population co-infected with HIV. Because the effect of HIV treatment on MTB-specific T cell proliferation is even less well understood, we propose to use the commercially available T-SPOT.TB to study the dynamics of the MTB-specific T cell response in patients co-infected with HIV. To this end, we plan to enroll and perform T-SPOT.TB test on HIV infected patients when TB treatment is initiated, then follow them with serial T-SPOT.TB tests until completion of TB treatment. As an additional goal, we expect the responses measured by T-SPOT.TB to shed light on the current diagnostic difficulty of differentiating immune reconstitution syndrome from TB progression two conditions for which treatment modalities are completely different but which currently lack a reliable testing method to differentiate between. This study should contribute to an understanding of pathogenesis of TB-related immune reconstitution syndrome in HIV and TB co-infected patients.
kw: HIV, TSPOT TB, Immune Reconstitution Syndrome

title: Designing antibodies for passive immunization of dengue viruses
abs: Dengue is the most significant mosquito-borne viral disease affecting humans and has spread to more than 100 countries in the tropical/subtropical regions of the world thereby placing nearly 2.5 billion at risk of dengue infection. The urban dwelling mosquito species, Aedes aegypti is the principal transmitter of the virus to humans. Infection with dengue virus can result in a spectrum ofclinical manifestations ranging from asymptomatic infection through dengue fever (OF), an acute febrile disease, to dengue hemorrhagic fever (DHF) and dengue shock syndrome (DSS) which are severe, life-threatening complications typified by vascular leakage (reviewed in [1]). Current treatment is limited to the use of analgesics and fluid replacement. Although dengue diseases affect50 -100 million people yearly, with frequent and recurrent epidemics, progress in vaccine development has been slow due in part to the fact that there are four viral 'serotypes', all of which are equally infectious. Even with the development of live attenuated virus (LAV) vaccines, the most advanced amongst all the dengue vaccine initiatives, it remains extremely difficult to select vaccinecandidates that are both highly immunogenic and sufficiently attenuated so as not to cause pathology[2,3]. Hence. alternatives to dengue vaccines. such as passive antibodv therapies and/or anitvirals are needed urgentlv to help control dengue associated diseases in the immediate term. We propose to use structural studies supported bv biophvsical and biosensor technologies in conjunction with classical virological techniques and small animal viremia model studies to develop theraoeuticantibodies that have the potential to be translated rapidlv for use in patients especiallv in countrieslike Singapore where rapid diagnostics is feasible and the possibility of capturing patients in the earlv viremia phase is relativelv high. The antibodies we find and characterize in this studv will also be emploved to address the opposing protective vs pathogenic propertv that is quite unique to dengue.

title: In vitro and in vivo studies of Suprafenacine, a novel microtubule destabilizing anti-cancer drug
abs: Microtubules are polymers of a/ß-tubulin heterodimer and are major components of highly dynamic cytoskeletal fibers and are involved in several cellular functions, including cell division, signaling, and trafficking. The essential role that microtubules play in these cellular processes makes them a suitable target for the development of chemotherapeutic drugs against cancer, because these functions are often dysregulated in many types of cancer. Thus, among anticancer agents, microtubule-targeting drugs are considered as one of the most effective classes of chemotherapeutic agents.Most of these microtubule-targeting drugs are natural products with diverse chemical structures and classified into two groups: those that stabilize microtubules, such as the taxanes (Taxol and Taxotere), epothilones and those that destabilize microtubules such as the Vinca alkaloids. These drugs bind to different sites on the tubulin dimer and exhibit diverse biological effects on microtubule dynamics. One common property of these microtubule-targeting drugs is that they all block mitosis in cell cycle. Microtubule-targeting drugs are shown to be effective chemotherapeutic agents. The taxanes demonstrate effectiveness in the treatment of metastatic breast cancer, non–small-cell lung cancer, refractory ovarian cancer, head and neck, and bladder carcinomas. The Vinca alkaloids are effective in the treatment of leukemia, Hodgkin’s disease, non-Hodgkin’s lymphomas, testicular cancer, Kaposi’s sarcoma, breast cancer, and other malignancies.Although microtubule-targeting drugs have been used successfully in the clinic, efforts are still actively being made to develop novel tubulin-targeting drugs with improved efficacy and toxicity profiles. Our recent structure-based in silico drug screening efforts led us to discover a novel drug named Suprafenacine that exhibits a microtubule-destabilizing property, results in cell cycle arrest, shows selective cytotoxic profile and induce apoptosis. In this proposal we aim to fully characterize the underlying mechanism of SRF and examine the molecular basis of the interaction between SRF and microtubule.
kw: Microtubule, Microtubule-targeting drugs, Bcl-2

title: Statistical estimation of protective efficacy and intervention-attributable reduction in clinical trials of infectious diseases
abs: Vaccination and other preventive medicine are key components of basic health care. Accurate estimates of protective efficacy (PE) and intervention-attributable reduction (IAR) in disease incidence are needed for clinical and policy decision making.Many vaccine trials estimate PE using time to first event only, even if recurrent events are recorded. This under-utilizes data and risks over-estimating PE in the presence of effect waning and under-estimating IAR in the presence of heterogeneity in the population. Furthermore, the effects of preventive medicine may vary from person to person, with some people highly protected, somepartially protected and some unprotected. In practice this heterogeneity is usually ignored. Previous studies have shown that this practice would lead to biased estimates of PE. Some statistical methods that use only time to first events accommodate heterogeneity but have poor identifiability. Moreover, recent works have suggested the importance of taking event dependence into account in the analysis of recurrent events.Using individual-level disease surveillance data and published aggregate data, we will estimate parameters that are useful for methodological studies and planning of future clinical trials, e.g. degree of heterogeneity. Using these results, we will conduct simulation studies of several statistical models. Classical methods based on Poisson distribution for first events and negative binomial (NB) distribution for all events will be compared. It is hypothesized that the NB model gives more precise and less biased estimates. We will generalized a zero-inflated NB model to incorporate variable exposure level for analysis of all events, and evaluate it against a frailty mixing survival model for first events. It is hypothesized that the zero-inflated NB model would have better performance in several aspects. Furthermore, we will explore the presence of event dependence. A new model to simultaneously allow for event dependence, heterogeneity and an unsusceptible fraction will be proposed and evaluated.
kw: Recurrent events, Applied statistics, Vaccine-attributable reduction, Heterogeneity, Infectious diseases, Protective efficacy
