title: Vulnerability, Disease Progression, and Treatment in Schizophrenia and Related Psychoses
abs: Research on schizophrenia, the most disabling of all neuropsychiatric disorders, has advanced recently in three directions: the identification of genetic risk factors, the identification of those at greatest risk for the disorder, and the development of new treatments that may reduce disability. We herein propose a bench-to-bedside research programme of three projects involving several institutions in Singapore, Duke University and the University of Melbourne. The projects and the main hypotheses to be tested: •Project 1: A genome-wide association analysis using the diagnostic phenotype of schizophrenia and cognitive endophenotypes; and a joint genome-wide analysis performed by combining our data with other datasets to increase the power to detect genetic risk factors. •Hypothesis: Risk for schizophrenia is largely controlled by common and rare genetic risk variants that can be identified by genome-wide association and direct re-sequence analyses. The use of neurocognitive-based endophenotypes will enhance the sensitivity of genetic analyses. •Project 2: A prospective study of a large group of individuals who are determined to be at ultra high risk of psychosis.•Hypothesis: The development of psychosis is characterized by certain cognitive abnormalities, progressive alteration of mRNA, lipid, and protein expression patterns, and volume reductions in the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus.•Project 3: A randomized controlled trial to improve neurocognition in patients with schizophrenia. •Hypothesis: Pregnenolone will improve neurocognitive performance compared to placebo. The faculty for this programme include internationally recognized scientists who encompass a broad range of expertise, from basic science (genomics, animal models of cognition and cognitive neuroscience of schizophrenia) to clinical acumen regarding high-risk psychosis studies and treatment of cognitive deficits. We have every expectation that the projects in this program will capture the attention of the world’s leaders in neuroscience research.

title: Genome-wide case-control studies to identify genetic variants and gene-environment interactions involved in the pathogenesis of type 2 diabetes mellitus in Chinese, Malays and Asian Indians living in Singapore
abs: Genetic association studies offer an opportunity to uncover novel genetic loci in the pathogenesis of T2DM. Existing studies have included only individual’s of central European origin. It may not be possible to generalize these findings to populations in Asia due to genetic differences between ethnic groups. Furthermore, existing studies have not utilized methods and designs that are optimal for the examination of copy number variation (CNV) and gene-environment interactions. We will conduct a genome-wide case-control study involving 2128 case-control pairs (incident T2DM) nested in a cohort forming the Singapore Chinese Health Study, 1000 Malay and 1000 Asian Indian case control pairs (prevalent T2DM) derived from the Singapore Consortium of Cohort Studies. These subjects will be genotyped using the Illumina human1.0M beadchip. We will conduct a pooled analysis in all three ethnic groups to identify variants associated with T2DM. These associations will be replicated in an additional 3000 Chinese case-control pairs (prevalent T2DM) from the Singapore Consortium of Cohort Studies. In addition, geneXethnicity interactions will be studied to identify genetic associations that differ between ethnic groups. Finally, we will look for evidence of geneXenvironment interactions considering body mass index, coffee intake, physical activity and dietary patterns as the environmental exposures, using the 2128 case-control pairs from the Singapore Chinese Health Study. These studies leverage on populations already available in Singapore, and may allow us to identify novel genetic loci involved with T2DM that are specifically relevant to Chinese, Malays and Asian Indians. Given that, by 2030, the majority of individuals with T2DM are likely to be of Asian ethnicity, these findings are particularly important. In addition, they may provide an understanding of the pathways through which environmental exposures affect the risk of T2DM. These novel loci may form useful therapeutic targets that will facilitate the development of novel treatments for T2DM.

title: Targeting brain tumor stem cells: DNA double strand break repair following chemoradiation therapy
abs: Targeting brain tumor stem cells: DNA double strand break repair following chemoradiation therapyBackground & Hypothesis: Median survival of malignant glioma patients is less than 12 months in spite of conventional therapies. With enhanced outcome observed from recent clinical trials, the combination of TMZ and RT is now the standard of care in the treatment of gliomas and there is a pressing need to understand the mechanism. Enhanced brain tumor stem cell (BTSC) DNA repair capacity may underpin glioma resistance to radiotherapy (RT). We have characterized BTSCs in glioma patient tissues and TMZ-induced transcriptional regulation of DNA repair in glioma cells. We hypothesize that TMZ-induced transcription inhibition suppresses DNA double strand break (DSB) repair in BTSCs, sensitizing gliomas to radiation.Objectives: We aim to define 1) differential DSB repair capacity in BTSCs; 2) transcription inhibition of DSB repair by O6-methylguanine (O6-meG, TMZ-induced major cytotoxic DNA lesion); 3) BTSC radiosensitization by TMZ.Methodology: BTSCs will be isolated from patient glioma tissues with CD133+ BTSC marker or neurosphere method. DSB repair capacity will be quantified with plasmid substrate harboring DSBs. TMZ-induced down-regulation of DSB repair gene expression will be verified by real-time RT-PCR and Western blotting. The role O6-meG in transcription inhibition will be validated with O6-benzylguanine-induced MGMT depletion. TMZ and RT cytotoxicity will be determined by DNA damage, viability, colony formation and apoptosis assay. The specificity of radiosensitization through TMZ-induced transcription suppression will be verified by siRNAs for key DSB repair genes.Clinical significance: Our novel approach of targeting BTSCs, the glioma tumorigenic population, with RT and TMZ will shed light on the mechanisms of heterogeneity-related tumor relapse. By addressing this important cancer biology/therapy issue, we seek to build and improve on existing glioma therapy.
kw: temozolomide, cancer stem cell, glioma, radiotherapy, DNA repair, chemotherapy

title: Comparison Of Mini-Bypass To Conventional Cardiopulmonary Bypass In Small Asian Patients Undergoing Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting Surgery
abs: Mini-bypass systems have the potential to reduce the problems associated with conventional cardiopulmonary bypass systems by preserving hematocrit, reducing transfusion requirements, and reducing inflammation. Intuitively, this system would be ideal for our smaller Asian patients, who as a result of their body sizes, are prone to severe hemodilution and increased transfusion requirements. However, our initial results based on established Western protocols were not as good as we hoped. Using a modified protocol, we were able to reduce perioperative blood transfusion. Therefore, we intend to prospectively confirm the efficacy of mini-bypass in conjunction with our modified protocol in reducing haemodilution and reducing blood transfusions. We will also establish the safety of this protocol, and investigate if this is associated with reduced inflammation and better cardiovascular, neurological, renal, respiratory and infection outcomes.220 small Asian patients undergoing primary coronary artery bypass grafting with cardiopulmonary bypass will be randomly divided either to utilize the mini-bypass system or the conventional system. Anaesthesia, surgical and perfusion management will be standardized, except for measures specific to the establishment of mini-bypass. The primary outcome measures will be haemodilution during cardiopulmonary bypass, postoperative blood loss, and perioperative blood transfusions. Secondary outcomes include safety profile (air embolization, hypoperfusion), inflammation, clinical outcomes and resource utilization. This project will allow us to confirm our retrospective findings that mini-bypass systems in conjunction with our modified protocol will benefit our smaller patients haematologically and lead to tremendous savings in blood utilization. We will also establish if this protocol is safe, and if there are additional benefits in terms of inflammation, clinical outcomes and resource utilization. Our findings will also be applicable throughout the region, as patients in the region generally lag our Western counterparts in size.
kw: Mini-bypass, Inflammation, CABG, Blood conservation, Clinical outcomes, Small size

title: Development and testing of an image based pathologyslicer with computer aided reconstruction for validation of imaging technologies and ground truth estimation as applied to the patients undergoing radical prostatectomy.
abs: Current techniques to correlate the location prostate cancer between imaging modality and pathology are poor because of imprecise specimen orientation and tissue deformation during pathological slicing. We aim to develop a prostate gland slicing device that has the capability of validating diagnosis made by any imaging modality. It correlates the individual pre-operative image with the corresponding pathological slice. As such, we can determine the efficacy and accuracy of imaging modalities in the diagnosis of prostate cancer.All men with prostate cancer will be offered an imaging modality (MRI/MRS, micro-bubble enhanced contrast ultrasound, tissue parameter imaging) before they undergo radical prostatectomy. These are emerging imaging modalities in the diagnosis and localization of prostate cancer. The images will be read by a radiologist to identify the cancer locations on a 1mm x 1mm grid. After surgery, the prostate specimens will undergo slicing with our device. The pathologist will also identify the locations of the prostate cancer from the specimen slices. The pathologist and radiologist are blinded. An independent assessor correlates their localization of cancer to determine that imaging modality’s accuracy.With the use of multi-directional pins, the image based slicing device supports the prostate gland in the same orientation as the imaging modality employed. It will then cut the specimen into uniform slices corresponding to the images. We will also reconstruct the prostate specimen with the use of laser scanning and reconstruction software before and after slicing process to assess for the presence and degree of resultant deformation. With this study, we will develop a device that correlates current and emerging imaging modalities with pathological data. Its clinical importance lies in the accurate radiological diagnosis of prostate cancer, possibly negating the need for prostate biopsy. Accurate localization will also allows targeted delivery of treatment.

title: Liver progenitor cells in chronic liver injury – a potential source of autologous cells for liver tissue engineering
abs: AIMTo identify the presence of liver progenitor cells in chronically injured livers; to isolate and expand them as cell lines for liver tissue engineering.HYPOTHESESThere has been recent acceptance that a liver stem cell does exist. A subpopulation of small liver progenitor cells have been seen in models of chronic liver injury. These cells are a potential source for regeneration, and have the potential to be used as autologous cell lines for tissue engineering. METHODOLOGYHuman liver tissue will be harvested from portions that accompany pathological portions surgically resected for liver cancers, from explanted livers following liver transplantation, and from cadaveric donor liver grafts harvested but found unsuitable for transplantation. The specimens will be examined histologically to identify the presence of these small oval liver progenitor cells. Special immunohistochemical tests (Cytokeratin immunohistochemical stains) will also be carried out to identify these cells. Liver progenitor cells are then isolated from the diseased livers, and purified by centrifugal elutriation or discontinuous Percoll gradient centrifugation. They are maintained in culture and can be expanded for use in tissue engineering as a source of autologous liver “stem cells”. IMPORTANCE TO MEDICINEEnd-stage liver disease is debilitating and handicaps the patient from normal social activities. To date, liver transplantation remains the only cure but has much operative morbidity and requires life-long immunosuppression. There is also the problem of severe shortage of suitable donors. Much has been done in liver tissue engineering. However the main drawback is in the fact that immunosuppression cannot be avoided if allogenic cells are used. The ability to identify the induction of liver progenitor cells in damaged liver, to isolate and use these autologous cells in creating a liver construct that can potentially be implanted back into the patient, holds great promise in tissue engineering and in the treatment of liver disease.
kw: Liver progenitor cells, Liver tissue engineering, Chronic liver injury, Autologous cell source

title: Assessment of left ventricular hypertrophy and myocardial fibrosis in hypertensive heart disease using cardiovascular magnetic resonance imaging
abs: Background. Left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) occurs in about 20% of hypertensive patients and is a hallmark of hypertensive heart disease (HHD). LVH significantly increases the risk of cardiovascular mortality and morbidity, including heart failure. Increased myocardial fibrosis plays a central role in the transition of LVH to heart failure. Myocardial fibrosis reduces myocardial compliance, thereby resulting in diastolic dysfunction and heart failure, and is associated with arrhythmia and sudden death.Myocardial fibrosis is not easily detected clinically. Endomyocardial biopsy is an invasive procedure with inherent risks. Markers of collagen turnover have been investigated but lack specificity. Ultrasonic backscatter is a potential noninvasive method but has several technical limitations. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) is an emerging noninvasive cardiac imaging modality that is able to provide morphologic, functional and flow information in a single study. It has been used to detect myocardial fibrosis in a variety of conditions such as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy and myocarditis.Hypothesis. Gadolinium-enhanced CMR is able to detect myocardial fibrosis in hypertensive heart disease.Aims. To detect and quantify the amount of myocardial fibrosis in HHD with CMR late gadolinium enhancement technique. This will be correlated to serum levels of collagen turnover, myocardial ultrasonic reflectivity and diastolic function parameters.Method. Forty adult patients with HHD and 20 sex- and age-matched controls will be studied with CMR. The presence of late gadolinium enhancement will be correlated with serum markers of collagen turnover, including procollagen-1 propeptide, matrix metalloproteinase-1, metalloproteinase-9 and tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinase-1 and 2. CMR results will be correlated with alterations in myocardial ultrasonic reflectivity by backscatter analysis and left ventricular diastolic function parameters.Conclusion. We hope to show the utility of CMR in detecting and quantifying the amount of myocardial fibrosis in HHD that may be used to predict prognosis and clinical outcomes in HHD.
kw: Cardiovascular magnetic resonance, Fibrosis, Diastolic function, Myocardium, Gadolinium, Left ventricular hypertrophy

title: Retinal Imaging for Disease Prediction
abs: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) and its major risk factors, diabetes and hypertension, are the leading causes of death, disability, hospitalisation, and morbidity in Singapore and worldwide. However, 50% of CVD cannot be captured by current diagnostics alone. Concurrently, while the pharmaceutical industry has developed a plethora of new therapeutics, it cannot address key questions related to targeted treatment approaches (i.e., who to treat and when to start).The blood vessels in the retina can be observed and monitored non-invasively, and damage to these blood vessels mirror similar damage in the heart, brain, and other organs in the body. Our research has now shown that an assessment of retinal vascular damage using new imaging technology will allow the prediction of diabetes, stroke, heart disease, hypertension and other vascular diseases, independent of conventional risk factors and diagnostic modalities.The programme aims to develop world-leading, bench-to-bedside, translational research in retinal vascular imaging in Singapore. The aims are to design novel software to measure retinal vascular changes, understand the genetics and pathophysiology of different retinal vascular changes, test validity of retinal imaging in population cohorts, determine utility of retinal imaging for risk prediction in clinical settings and increase collaboration between scientists and clinicians. To achieve these objectives, the programme will concentrate on four major vascular diseases: diabetes, stroke, heart disease and hypertension. This will be based on on-going and new research projects in Singapore and internationally that will determine the relationship of retinal vascular imaging as a predictive test for these diseases using >30,000 patients with retinal images. The programme would enable the development of a world-class research team in Singapore. Through earlier identification of CVD via the use of retinal imaging, the long-term outcome is a reduction in the impact of major disease affecting millions of persons in Asia and worldwide.

title: Molecular switch-on and switch-off mechanism of vascular Nox4 by TNF-? induction and PPAR? agonist inhibition
abs: Oxidative stress and reactive oxygen species (ROS) underpin the pathogenesis of cardiovascular diseases including atherosclerosis. NADPH oxidase is a predominant source of ROS and activation of this enzyme leads to intracellular signaling events causing endothelial dysfunction, proliferation of vascular smooth muscle cells and expression of pro-inflammatory genes. Identification of novel signaling and transcription regulatory mechanism of NADPH oxidase components, specifically Nox4, is crucial for improved intervention of atherosclerosis. Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs) are members of the nuclear hormone receptor superfamily of ligand-activated transcription factors. Recent studies have shown that PPAR-y agonists reduce the progression of atherosclerotic lesions by direct anti-atherogenic and anti-inflammatory actions. However, the molecular mechanisms of PPAR-y agonists on NADPH oxidase are undefined. Our published work has shown that TNF- induced oxidative stress in vascular smooth muscle cells is mediated by NADPH oxidase and specifically by upregulation of Nox4. Our preliminary results have shown that JNK signaling pathway mediates TNF induced Nox4 upregulation and oxidative stress in vascular smooth muscle cells. Moreover, both synthetic PPAR-y agonist rosiglitazone (RGZ) and endogenous PPAR-y agonist 15-deoxy 2,14-prostagladin J2 (15d-PGJ2) significantly inhibit TNF-induced Nox4 upregulation and oxidative stress. The inhibitory effect of PPAR-y agonists in our study is revered by selective PPAR-y antagonist GW9962, suggesting that the inhibition is mediated by PPARy dependent mechanism. Furthermore, RGZ shows dose-dependent inhibition of TNF-induced Nox4 upregulation. Based on our published work and preliminary findings, we hypothesize that (1) TNF induced Nox4 upregulation is controlled by JNK signaling mediated transcription regulatory mechanism and (2) Inhibition of RGZ and 15d-PGJ2 on TNF-induced Nox4 upregulation is mediated at JNK signaling mechanism, transcription regulatory mechanism or direct transcription regulation on upstream regulatory region of Nox4 gene. In the current proposal, we aim to investigate the transcription regulatory mechanism of TNF-induced Nox4 upregulation and inhibitory mechanism of RGZ and 15d-PGJ2 on TNF-induced Nox4 upregulation. We will identify the transcription factor(s) that regulates Nox4 and transcription factor binding site by molecular cloning and characterization of Nox4 gene promoter. We will also identify the inhibitory mechanism(s) of RGZ and 15d-PGJ2. Elucidating the novel transcription regulatory mechanism of vascular specific Nox4 holds promise for rational targeted therapy

title: A nutritional and social skills intervention on conduct disorder and hyperactivity
abs: Violence is a world-wide public health problem that has largely defied successful intervention and prevention. The overarching aim of this study is to assess whether a nutritional intervention, when combined with social skills training, is more effective than either approach alone in reducing childhood conduct disorder, the precursor to adult crime and violence. The specific aims are:1. To assess the effectiveness of omega-3 dietary supplementation in reducing both conduct disorder and also comorbid ADHD and conduct disorder.2. To identify factors that moderate the relationship between omega-3 supplementation and antisocial behavior.3. To assess the effectiveness of social skills training in reducing conduct disorder.4. To assess whether omega-3 supplementation interacts with social skills training in reducing conduct disorder5. To uncover mechanisms of action underlying any treatment effect.Hypotheses will be tested in a randomized, placebo-controlled, six-month trial of 600 conduct disordered children aged 9-16 years drawn from the Child Guidance Clinic, a major provider of child and adolescent mental health service in Singapore. Children will be randomly assigned into: (1) standard treatment plus nutritional placebo, (2) omega-3 only, (3) social skills only, (4) both omega-3 and social skills. Diagnostic and behavioral measures of conduct disorder and hyperactivity will be assessed at baseline, half-way through the treatment, end of treatment, and 6 months post-treatment. Before-after measures of putative mechanisms of action (including neuropsychological, cognitive, and emotional functioning) will be taken to assess for changes in these processes. Investing modest resources in early biosocial prevention programs could yield enormous long-term financial benefits in terms of the saved legal, medical, social, and psychological costs resulting from crime. This initial study would be the first to test the efficacy of conjoint omega-3 / social skills treatment program, and the first to identify possible mechanisms by which omega-3 reduces antisocial behavior.
kw: omega-3, conduct disorder, hyperactivity, aggression, social skills, nutrition

title: Targeting the Wnt signaling pathway to inhibit cancer proliferation
abs: Targeting the proliferation of cancer stem cells is a potential new therapeutic approach. The connection between Wnt signaling and cancer is well appreciated, as is the role of Wnt signaling in stem cell proliferation. Some cancers, such as colon cancer and hepatocellular carcinomas, have mutations in components of the Wnt/ß-catenin signaling pathway. In otherr common cancers such as breast cancer and leukemias, cancer proliferation depends on paracrine Wnt signaling, enhanced by increased Wnt secretion and loss of expression of secreted Wnt inhibitors. We postulate that this continued Wnt signaling is required for the proliferation of cancer via multiple mechanisms, including a key role in cancer stem cell maintenance. In this proposal, using several different approaches, we will test the hypothesis;inhibition of Wnt secretion will block proliferation of cancer stem cells and be an effective therapy for cancer.The proposal contains 4 major aims. First, we will pharmacologically target the secretion of Wnt, utilizing a newly developed robust small molecule screen. Second, the site of action and specific targets of these small molecule inhibitors will be determined. Their efficacy in blocking cancer cell progression in cell culture and animal models will be tested. Finally, independently, we will test if genetic inhibition of Wnt signaling at the level of secretion also blocks cancer progression. Successful completion of this proposal will provide new targets for cancer therapyand new small molecules that hit these targets.
kw: Cancer, stem cells, drug screening, signal transduction, development, target validation

title: Neuroergo: A Multimodality Study of The Effects of Cognitive Workload And Sleepy Deprivation On Lapses in Attention and Decision Making
abs: Sleep deprivation (SD) has grown increasingly prevalent in modern society. Ironically, while most persons extend wakefulness seeking to increase productivity, gains from working longer are often undermined by lapses, accidents as well as poor or intemperate decisions that arise from willfully resisting sleep.Despite the adverse consequences of SD, human behavior is difficult to change given the high perceived value of working longer and/or playing harder. The proposed research into the neuralunderpinnings of SD-related cognitive impairment thus seeks to mitigate the growing negative impact of SD on individuals and society through four avenues of inquiry. I seek to:1. Elucidate the neurocognitive mechanisms that contribute to the breakdown of sustained attention during SD by testing the hypothesis that lapses in attention following SD are associated with sensory deficits superposed on the loss of top-down control of attention.2. Evaluate the role of cognitive workload in accelerating cognitive degradation by testing the hypothesis that cognitive workload interacts with SD to exacerbate performance attrition though localc cortical 'use-dependent' effects.3. Evaluate the effect of SD on the risky decision-making by studying the effect of framing, change in relative values of wins $ losses and the effects of negative emotional stimuli.4. Examine the neural correlates of how SD affects reasoning process through causing an individual to shift from analytical to heuristic reasoning.Healthy young adults between 20 to 35 years of age will be studied using a combination of behaviorial, functional neuroimaging and electrophysiological methods. They will be tested following normal sleep and also following 24H SD with cognitive tasks that evaluate (1) sustained attention and vigilance, (2) stimulus discrimination and working memory under varying levels of cognitive load and (3) reasoning and risky decision-making
kw: Sleep Deprivation, Decision making, Functional Neuroimaging, Working Memory, Attention, Cognitive Workload

title: Targeting hematopoietic and leukemic stem cells
abs: The ability to introduce or manipulate expression of genes in hematopoietic stem cells (HSC) through gene therapy methods has been limited. Powerful viral vectors have been developed and utilized in both experimental and human systems, but a number of issues, particularly safety, have demonstrated the need to develop non-viral based vectors for gene therapy. It is important to develop methods to target normal HSC as well as leukemic stem cells (LSC), a subpopulation of cancer cells which confer the self-renewal properties of the malignant leukemic clone. Normal human HSC, and a majority of LSC, express the stem cell antigen CD34. The first part of this proposal will develop human CD34 antibody fusion protein-mediated siRNA delivery to inhibit leukemia oncogenes in human CD34 expressing cells. We will also utilize a novel murine model in which murine HSC express the human CD34 antigen to test human CD34 antibody mediated siRNA in murine leukemia models in vivo. In the second part of this proposal, we will utilize lentiviral siRNA libraries to screen for genes which affect HSC self renewal. Once these genes have been identified, we will investigate whether they are dysregulated in the LSCs of humans with acute leukemia. We will utilize CD34 antibody fusion protein-mediated siRNA delivery to either promote or inhibit self-renewal in both normal HSC and LSC. Finally, by targeting naturally occuring antisense RNAs with siRNAs, we will develop a novel method of increasing gene expression and test its ability to inhibit leukemogenesis. We expect our studies to lead to clinical trials using of this potent, highly specific, and non-toxic means of targeting stem cells.
kw: stem cells, leukaemia, self renewal

title: The effects of altered oxygenation on the molecular biology, structure and function of the retina with particular reference to the role of excitotoxicity in the retinopathy of prematurity.
abs: The retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) is a major cause of blindness in premature infants. A critical role of retinal hypoxia in the genesis of ROP has been established in clinical and experimental studies. This study aims to examine some of the cellular and molecular mechanisms that may be involved in damaging retinal ganglion cells (RGC) in the developing retina and that have not been reported previously. In this context, the role of glutamate excitotoxicity has not been investigated in the retina. The release of excess glutamate under hypoxia in the retina may result in death of RGC by receptor mediated mechanisms involving activation of NMDA receptors or non-receptor mediated mechanisms such as glutamate induced excess production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and inflammatory cytokines. Glutamate may also induce increased production of insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) which may affect the growth of tissues in the neonatal eye resulting in an abnormally increased axial length. One day old rats will be subjected to 75% O2 followed by room air (21%O2). Glutamate concentration, expression of NMDA receptors, ROS, calcium, IGF-1 and cytokines will be measured in the retinas from experimental rats at various time points (24h-28d) and compared to control levels. Cell death will be investigated by electron microscopy and TUNEL. Retinal function will be assessed by electro retinography. Free radical scavenging drugs will be administered in experimental rats to assess their therapeutic potential in ameliorating cell death. The results of the present study will help in better understanding of some of the molecular mechanisms underlying the pathogenesis of ROP. Use of free radical scavengers to mitigate excitotoxic damage would open up a new avenue towards the development of therapeutic intervention in ROP.
kw: Retinopathy of prematurity, Insulin-like growth factor-1, Glutamate, Ganglion cells, NMDA receptors, Myopia

title: Comprehensive analysis and characterization of c-Jun-regulated microRNAs that differentially regulate apoptosis and cellular proliferation/transformation
abs: c-Jun, a member of the AP-1 family of transcription factors, is involved in regulating cellular proliferation and death. The best examples for the role of c-Jun in pathological conditions are seen in neuronal death, especially in disease such as stroke and epilepsy, etc., and in several cancers, where c-Jun is phosphorylated and activated. The essential role of c-Jun in regulating the physiological processes leading to pathological conditions has been established in mouse models. Absence of c-Jun leads to embryonic lethality in mice due to liver and heart development failures owing to elevated apoptosis. Conversely, multiple cell types including neurons lacking c-Jun have been shown to be resistant to a variety of apoptotic stimuli in culture and in vivo. Moreover, absence of c-Jun in adult tissues lead to inhibition of tumour formation in several mouse models and cells lacking c-Jun display a severe proliferation defect. However, how c-Jun activation leads to the seemingly different physiological outcomes is at present unclear. Some transcriptional targets of c-Jun have been identified, including those that regulate proliferation or survival, such as cyclinD1 or FasL, Bim and PTEN, respectively. Nonetheless, how specific sets of target genes are turned-on depending on the cellular context is unclear. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are a class of regulatory RNAs that fine tune the expression of genes in cells, and thereby contribute to the determination of cell fate. Recent interest in this field has resulted in identification of tumour-suppressive or oncogenic miRNAs, many of which are expressed in a tissue-specific manner. We hypothesize here that c-Jun regulate the expression of specific sets of miRNA targets under various cellular context that would eventually lead to the execution of either apoptosis or stimulate survival/proliferation. Therefore, we propose here to comprehensively identify and characterize the miRNA targets of c-Jun, in the context of apoptosis and proliferation, using several models of c-Jun-mediated apoptosis and proliferation, including neuronal cell death, hepatocyte survival and fibroblast proliferation and apoptosis. Once identified, these targets will be validated and characterized through the use of the various cell and mouse models available in our laboratories as well as with the miRNA mimetics and inhibitors available. These studies will not only provide new knowledge in this old field, but will also pave the way for future characterization and the clinical validation of the new identified candidates.
kw: c-Jun, c-Jun, Micro-RNA, Neuronal death, Apoptosis, Proliferation

title: Identification of malaria parasite genes important for virulence and survival in the natural host
abs: Human malaria still remains amongst the most important infectious diseases in the world causing 200¬500 million infections and 1-2 million deaths annually. Rapidly decreasing efficacy of most antimalarial drugs presents a major health concern and thus development of a protective vaccine against this disease is one the most important tasks for the future. Despite extensive efforts a malaria vaccine is still not available. It is becoming increasingly clear that a better understanding of the complex host¬parasite biology is required. To achieve this it is important to complement existing studies performed on cultured parasites with as much in vivo data as possible. Here we propose to conduct genome-wide transcriptome analyses utilizing a range of microarrays recently developed here at SBS, NTU of six malaria parasite species (P. fa/ciparum P. vivax, P. chabaudi, P berghei, P, yoelii and P. know/esl) grown in their natural host in order to identify important molecules that facilitate their interaction with its host and their variable degree of virulence. The main goal is to identify gene that are essential for the parasite survival in its natural conditions and relevant to adaptation of a particular parasite species to its specific host. Moreover, for each species, transcriptome analyses will be extended to various strains with variable levels of virulence. These studies aim to identify new virulence factors of malaria parasites. The candidate genes identified by the proposed global surveys will be further analyzed using targeted gene disruptions taking advantage of the rodent as well as the P. fa/ciparum in vitro cultures. The final goal of these studies is to identify new gene candidates that can be explored by the antimalaria vaccine development community.
kw: malaria, in vivo, host-parasite interaction, microarray, virulance

title: A comparative transcriptional analysis of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus in UK (Caucasian) and Singapore (Chinese) patients.
abs: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a systemic autoimmune disease which is chronic, debilitating and may have life-threatening manifestations, such as renal failure or cerebral involvement. It predominantly affects young women. Compared to Caucasians, it is 4-8 times more common in Chinese, and occurs in younger patients, is more difficult to treat and has distinct clinical features. There is clear evidence that this difference is genetically determined.A lack of clear guidelines on whom to treat with what, when and for how long results in a high treatment-associated morbidity and mortality. We will take blood from SLE patients at presentation with active disease and during different treatment protocols, and will analyze RNA collected from separated cell subsets using oligonucleotide microarrays, correlating expression signatures with extensive clinical data. We will then validate the expression profiles obtained as markers of diagnosis, prognosis, response to treatment and treatment-related toxicity. Comparisons will also be made with data from a group of Caucasian patients with SLE analyzed in parallel by our collaborators in Cambridge. Data obtained from patients with ANCA-associated vasculitis in Cambridge has confirmed the superiority of the cell subset approach (compared to previous work using unseparated cells), demonstrating that it can be used to identify previously undetected patient subsets with distinct prognoses (attracting considerable commercial interest), and also novel pathways involved in disease pathogenesis. The Cambridge component of this collaboration is supported by competitive grant funding from the MRC and Wellcome Trust, and this grant seeks to fund the Singapore component.We therefore expect to identify transcription “signatures” in SLE patients which act as biomarkers, allowing superior targeting of therapy for improved disease response and reduced toxicity in the Singapore population. In addition, comparison between Singaporean and Caucasian patients using this collaborative approach may identify novel immune pathways involved in pathogenesis, perhaps allowing us to explain why SLE in South-East Asians is more common and severe, and providing novel targets for therapeutic intervention in this population.
kw: SLE, Microarray, Transcription, Therapy, Autoimmunity

title: Singapore Eye Research Institute TRIOS Programme (Translational Research Innovations in Ocular Surgery)
abs: This TCR proposal for ophthalmic research aims to develop a 5-year multidisciplinary programme to focus on 2 main causes of global blindness. Corneal disorders and glaucoma are major causes of blindness in the world, particularly in Asia. Corneal disease is the second commonest cause of treatable blindness (12 million cases globally) and glaucoma is a leading cause of irreversible blindness (5 million cases globally).Our programme involves interlinked projects focusing on new translational approaches to resolve challenges facing medical and surgical therapies for these disorders, and assembles collaborative teams of local clinician researchers from both healthcare clusters, and basic scientists and bioengineers from local and international academic research institutions, teamed with industry partners.We aim to investigate the use of novel antifibrotic agents to modulate surgical wound healing and treat ocular inflammatory disease, and develop our new synthetic ocular defensin analogues for antimicrobial therapy, utilizing a new ocular drug delivery system developed by our collaborators. Additional supportive translational projects include development of a novel non-invasive, femtosecond laser confocal imaging device for ultrastructural imaging of ocular tissues, and a new biological tissue glue for ocular surgery.Our corneal surgeons have devised novel forms of femtosecond laser-assisted forms of corneal transplantation, which we will further develop in a series of animal trials, leading to first-in-human clinical trials, and our corneal stem cell group will also initiate studies on ex-vivo corneal endothelial stem cell culture in collaboration with a leading ocular stem cell team in Japan to develop autologous and heterologous forms of cultured corneal endothelial cell transplantation. Our glaucoma group will also focus on further research into Angle Closure Glaucoma, in the form of clinical trials using novel neuroprotective drugs to prevent optic nerve damage in acute glaucoma attacks, and to develop further genetic studies of this primarily Asian form of glaucoma.
kw: Ocular Wound Healing, Ocular Drug Delivery, Ocular imaging, Ocular defensins, Angle closure glaucoma, Femtosecond Laser sugery

title: A Spatio-temporal analysis of Out of Hospital Cardiac Arrests (OHCA) in Singapore, and the relationship with socio-demographic variables.
abs: BackgroundIt has been noticed that acute medical events like cardiac arrests are not random events, but rather have definite time-geographic distribution patterns. This is related to the underlying population demographics and movement patterns. Using Geographic Information Systems (GIS) technology, we are able to depict such time-geographic patterns to aid planning for cardiac arrest interventions, such as Public Access Defibrillation (PAD). DesignThis will be an observational ecological study of pre-hospital cardiac arrests in Singapore aggregated at the development guide plan (DGP) level. Data on cardiac arrests, response times, together with location ID will be collected from the Cardiac Arrest and Resuscitation Epidemiology (CARE) study database. Key covariate data will be obtained from the Singapore Census 2000. ObjectivesThe main objective is to provide an age-standardised, smoothed map of relative risk of pre hospital cardiac arrest in Singapore. This would allow us to assess the potential for the most cost effective community interventions like PAD. The secondary aim is to undertake spatial survival analysis, and determine the factors associated with response time.MethodsUsing GIS technology, we intend to map the cardiac arrest cases in Singapore at the development guide plan (DGP) level. Using population and age data from the census, we will calculate the age-standardised crude relative risk of cardiac arrests for each DGP. Using advanced spatial statistical models, we will calculate the smoothed relative risk of cardiac arrests, after adjustment for key covariates, which helps to identify areas with an elevated risk. Spatial regression models will be used to examine demographics and economic indicators associated with elevated risks. For the secondary aim, we will use spatial survival models to provide hazard ratios of response times for the DGP areas.
kw: Spatial Mapping, Public Access Defibrillation, Geographic Information Systems, Out of hospital, Cardiac arrest

title: Novel Quantum Phases on the Border of Magnetism
abs: One of the most intriguing problems in condensed matter physics is the change of a material from an insulator into a metal or a superconductor. Such a change does not occur as a function of temperature, but rather at absolute zero when some material parameter is tuned, and the subject belongs to the fascinating field of quantum phase transitions. Many interesting and technologically important materials ranging from field-effect transistors and magneto-restrictive films to superconductors find themselves close to the metal-insulator transition. In this regime, competition between several distinct ground states forms electronic heterogeneity, giving rise to coexistence of different ordered phases separated by one or more quantum critical points. This electronic complexity has potential consequences for applications of correlated electronic materials, because in addition to spin and charge the lattice and orbital degrees of freedoms are active, leading to large responses to small perturbations. Moreover, several metallic and insulating phases compete, increasing the potential for novel behaviour. The proposed programme will study the physics of strongly interacting many-body systems with regard to the occurrence and properties of complex macroscopic states. We will demonstrate the implications of electronic heterogeneity in low dimensional systems with rich phase diagrams including insulating, metallic and superconducting ground states. We will investigate methods to discover putative quantum critical points and identify a common physical picture describing the freezing of spin/charge in materials near disorder driven metal-insulator-transitions, and the correlation with the physics of short-range superconducting phase coherence shown to be present up to room temperature. Electronically frustrated correlated electron systems can be then tuned to be exactly at or on the cusp of the transition, where electrons behave most collectively, where with tuning of relevant parameters we alter matter to extreme cases starting from an insulator to a high temperature superconductor.
kw: Quantum tuning;Electronic patterns;Low dimensionality;Frustrated magnetism;Phase transitions;Superconductivity

title: Morphological and molecular characterization of a bi-lobed structure required for organelle biogenesis and cytokinesis in Trypanosoma brucei
abs: Propagation through successive generations requires faithful duplication and segregation of all cellular components during the cell cycle. Many proteins and structures have been found important in this process. Dis-regulation of them often leads to detrimental consequences such as cell death or tumor. In the course of studying centrins, a highly conserved protein involved in cell cycle regulation in the single-celled parasite Trypanosoma brucei, we found it localized to a bi-lobed structure closely associated with the secretory organelles including the Golgi apparatus. Depletion of centrin from the bi-lobed structure inhibited duplication of these secretory organelles and led to cell cycle arrest at cytokinesis. More recently, other conserved proteins important for organelle duplication and cell division were found associated with the bi-lobed structure, suggesting more complex regulation and further attesting its importance. Based on these preliminary studies, we hypothesize that the bi-lobed structure acts as a ‘control centre’, bridging organelle duplication with cell division, and providing precise regulation of cell cycle progress. It is therefore important to further characterize this structure in Trypanosoma brucei, where the bi-lobed structure is best visualized and molecular genetic manipulations are extremely feasible. The specific aims are: 1. Use time-lapse fluorescence microscopy to visualize how the bi-lobed structure duplicates during the cell cycle, understand how this structure helps to define the timing and location and duplication of other organelles. 2. Investigate how bi-lobe mutations affect cell cycle progress, especially mitosis and cytokinesis, in cells fixed and alive. 3. Search for bi-lobe proteins that interact with centrins. Investigate the functions of these proteins in cell cycle regulation, taking advantage of the powerful molecular genetic methods available for T. brucei, such as inducible and inheritable RNA interference, and homologous gene replacement.
kw: Trypanosoma brucei;organelle biogenesis;cytokinesis;cell cycle;basal bodies;centrin

title: Investigating status of tumorigenic barriers in monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance and multiple myeloma
abs: Only a small proportion of patients with monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS), a pre-malignant plasma cell disorder, progresses to malignant multiple myeloma (MM). Yet all the disease-initiating genetic abnormalities are found in MGUS at similar frequencies as MM. Recently, it has been demonstrated that two important tumorigenic barriers, DNA damage response (DDR) and senescence, are activated in pre-malignant tumors, and malignant transformation is accompanied by defects in these barriers. Our hypothesis is that defects in one or both of these barriers also mediate transformation from MGUS to MM. The specific aim of our study is to compare the status of DNA damage checkpoint and senescence between MGUS and MM, using immunohistochemical (IHC) detection of various proteins and phenotypic markers in these pathways. Tissue microarrays (TMA) will be made from bone marrow samples of cases identified as MGUS or MM. IHC will be performed on the TMA. The slides will be stained for markers of the DDR checkpoint (e.g. ATM, CHK, p53), the senescence checkpoint (e.g. p15, p16, p19, p21), apoptosis signaling (BAX, BCL-2, BCL-XL) and phenotypic markers of apoptosis (TUNEL assay, activated caspase-3) and senescence (SA--GAL, H3K9). CD138 positive cells will be scored and the percentage of cells with positive staining for the various markers will be compared between MGUS and MM. It is important to know what mediates the transition from MGUS to MM. Understanding the mechanisms underlying this transition, and whether there is differential involvement of various critical pathways, will provide significant insights into the biology of malignant transformation. More importantly, these insights may inform on chemo-preventive measures.
kw: Multiple myeloma, Monoclonal Gammopathy, Transformation, Senescence, DNA damage checkpoint, Genetics

title: Functional analysis of mutations in Transient Receptor Potential Cation Channel 6 (TRPC6) identified in a Singapore family with autosomal dominant focal segmental glomerulosclerosis by whole-cell patch clamp electrophysiology
abs: Focal and segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) is an important cause of end-stage renal disease (ESRD) worldwide, and accounts for up to 20% of ESRD patients. Mutations in genes encoding for podoycte structural proteins lead to proteinuria and FSGS. More recently, mutations of the transient receptor potential cation channel 6 (TRPC6), a calcium-permeable cation channel at the slit diaphragm, have been found to cause familial FSGS. To date, only 6 missense TRPC6 mutations have been reported.In our preliminary studies, we found a novel missense TRPC6 mutation in 6 members of a Singapore Chinese family with autosomal dominant FSGS. This mutation R68W which resides in exon 2, results in an arginine-to-tryptophan substitution, and occurs in a highly conserved region of the protein. Only the 3 members who manifested with significant proteinuria had a concomitant homozygous 954T>C polymorphism in exon 8 of the podocin gene. We therefore hypothesize that this novel TRPC6 mutation, potentially through interactions with other proteins like podocin, plays an important role in the pathogenesis of FSGS. The primary aim of this proposal is to investigate the functional effect of TRPC6R68W mutation on TRPC6 by recording the ionic currents flowing through the wild-type or mutant TRPC6 channels that are heterologously expressed in human embryonic kidney (HEK293) cells, using the whole-cell patch-clamp technique. The secondary aim is to examine the effect of TRPC6R68W mutation on nephrin, podocin or CD2AP interactions using co-immunoprecipitation studies with myc-tagged mouse nephrin, podocin or CD2AP in human embryonic kidney (HEK293) cells. The heterogenous clinical outcomes of patients with primary FSGS suggests that knowledge of the genetic basis of this disease including TRPC6 status could have clinical utility, not only in identifying those nephrotic patients at risk of ESRD, but also in developing more targeted future therapeutic strategies through a better understanding of the pathogenesis of FSGS.
kw: Focal and segmental glomerulosclerosis(FSGS), Nephrotic syndrome, Transient receptor potential cation channel 6, Whole-cell patch-clamp technique, Mutation, Podocytes

title: Characterization of Slc4a11 Gene Depleted Mice to Study Congenital Hereditary Endothelial Dystrophy (CHED) and Fuchs Endothelial Corneal Dystrophy (FECD).
abs: The endothelial corneal dystrophies, which result from primary endothelial dysfunction, include Fuchs endothelial corneal dystrophy (FECD), posterior polymorphous corneal dystrophy (PPCD) and congenital hereditary endothelial dystrophy (CHED). These dystrophies result in progressive visual loss and blindness due to corneal opacification. FECD is the commonest form of endothelial dystrophy and with its onset in mid adulthood, FECD prevalence is expected to rise sharply in ageing populations such as in Singapore. Last year we identified a putative bicarbonate transporter gene (SLC4A11) as responsible for two endothelial dystrophies, recessive CHED (CHED2) and late onset FECD. Our genetic data and biochemical characterization have indicated that CHED2 and FECD are respectively caused by either complete or partial loss of the plasma membrane transport activity of SLC4A11. To understand the CHED2 and FECD pathobiology we are currently generating a Slc4a11 gene knock out mouse. The specific objectives of this proposal are to first morphologically characterize the homozygous Slc4a11-/- (model for CHED2) and heterozygous Slc4a11+/- (model for FECD) mice in order to see how well these mice model the human diseases. Currently the physiological function(s) of SLC4A11 in the corneal endothelium remains unclear: it may function as a borate transporter or a bicarbonate transporter or both. Differentiating these possibilities is critical as it profoundly impacts on the basic defect in diseases involving SLC4A11. Therefore as the second aim we intend to use the mouse model to explore whether borate is an essential cell survival molecule or whether SLC4A11 functions as a HCO3- transporter important for pH regulation. We also aim to identify the mechanisms of endothelial cell death. The ultimate goal of this research is to identify critical molecules involved in CHED2 and FECD pathology as well as those essential for corneal endothelial cell survival so that we may develop effective long-term therapies for corneal endothelial dystrophies.
kw: CHED, Mouse knock out model, SLC4A11 gene, Corneal endothelial dystrophy, FECD, Cornea

title: Control release of recombinant human bone morphogenetic protein type 2 from heparin conjugated multilayered alginate microbeads to enhance new bone formation in spine fusion
abs: Spine fusion is a common surgical procedure used to treat chronic and debilitating back pain due to degenerative disease. Bone grafts taken from the patient (autogenous grafts) have been shown to be the most reliable way to achieve spinal fusion. However, the use of autogenous bone grafts has been associated with complications of prolonged pain at donor site. In recent years, recombinant human bone morphogenetic protein-2 (rhBMPs) has come to be a revolutionary tool for use as a bone graft substitute in spine fusion. However, the amount of BMP used is unphysiological, being several thousands of times higher than the normal physiological quantity, and as such is associated with great expense such that it is not accessible for most patients. The large quantities of BMP used is the result of poor release kinetics where most of the BMP used is released or lost to the surrounding tissues almost immediately after implantation. Recent studies have shown that optimizing the localized sustained release of rhBMP-2 at smaller doses will be more efficient and cost effective. We hypothesize that a sustained release of rhBMP-2 at nanogram quantities from covalently linked biodegradable polymeric microbeads would provide for a prolonged, site specific delivery of this growth factor and promote spine fusion without the use of autogenous bone grafts. We aim to evaluate a controlled delivery system for rhBMP-2 and to assess fusion induced by the sustained release of rhBMP-2 in an established rat model of spine fusion. 120 male rats divided into ten groups according to the doses (nanogram quantities) of rhBMP-2 will be compared to current, milligram, doses in use. Rate and quality of fusion will be evaluated by X-ray, micro-computed tomography scans, histology and histomorphology. If successful, this research could lead to a novel and cost-effective means of achieving spinal fusion without the use of autografts.
kw: Bone morphogenetic proteins, New bone formation, Alginate microencapsulation, Spine fusion, Control Release

title: Active Targeting of Cancer Cells with Functionalized Superparamagnetic Iron Oxide Nanoparticles
abs: In recent years, increasing efforts have been devoted to the development of superparamagnetic iron oxide (SPIO) nanoparticles for biomedical applications such as magnetic separation of labeled cells, gene delivery, hyperthermia treatment of tumors, and as contrast enhancement agents for magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). SPIO probes for passive tracking or imaging of biological systems via naturally directed physiological processes have been used. For example, the accumulation of intravenously administered colloidal particles in the liver allows malignant tumors in the liver which are typically devoid of Kupffer cells to be differentiated from the healthy tissues through SPIO endowed contrast in MRI1.While passive targeting has a number of potential applications, progress and future developments in the use of SPIO in imaging of cancer tumors can only be realized through active targeting against specific biomolecules to enable early and accurate diagnoses at a stage when the disease would be still treatable. However, a major hurdle for active targeting is accumulating adequate levels of SPIO at the diseased site to allow enhanced contrast and sensitivity for detection. The proposed project intends to address this hurdle via the following strategy: SPIO nanoparticles will be designed to evade capture by the reticuloendothelial system (RES) and concomitantly to possess targeting ligands to increase receptor-mediated endocytosis by the cancer cells. SPIO nanoparticles will first be endowed with a biocompatible shell possessing appropriate surface functional groups, and then surface functionalized with different types of cancer targeting ligands such as antibodies, folic acid and aptamers. The efficacy of such functionalized SPIO nanoparticles will be tested against several cancer cell lines. The relative advantages and limitations of each type of targeting ligands will be established. This research will provide a platform for further development of these “smart” nanoparticles for bioimaging and hyperthermia therapy of cancer tumors.
kw: Magnetic nanoparticles, Targeting ligands, Monoclonal antibodies, Surface functionalization, Aptamers, Cancer

title: Evaluation of the Anti-inflammatory and Beneficial Effects of Recombinant Lactobacilli for Atopic Dermatitis
abs: Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a common pruritic and chronic relapsing inflammatory skin disease of global importance. Current treatment for AD is largely symptomatic, and therefore novel therapy with the prospect of more effective treatment of this chronic disease is much needed. Dust mite allergy plays a major role in the pathogenesis of allergic diseases. Although specific-allergen immunotherapy (SIT) is an effective therapeutic modality for respiratory allergies, its effectiveness in AD is still uncertain. The long term objective of this proposed study is to develop an effective means of SIT via orally administered allergen adjuvanted by probiotics for the treatment of AD. Probiotics, such as lactobacilli, have been shown to have anti-inflammatory and beneficial effects in the prevention and treatment of eczema in humans. These effects could be conferred by the immuno-regulatory properties of probiotics, which may serve as a microbial adjuvant for induction and differentiation of T regulatory cells in an oral mucosal micro-environment. Recent published studies support the notion that antigen delivery through the oral mucosa route is an effective way to induce antigen specific regulatory T cells. Additionally, the majority of the CD4+CD25+Foxp3+ regulatory T cells bear the functional skin-homing receptor. We, therefore rationalize that oral administration of recombinant lactobacilli expressing allergen would be an effective way to induce allergen-specific T-regulatory cells resulting in effective suppression of cellular and neurogenic inflammation seen in atopic dermatitis. The specific aims of this study are: (1) To evaluate the immunological responses in allergen naïve mice fed with recombinant lactobacilli expressing a major dust mite allergen (Blo t 5), and (2) To examine its subsequent effects on dermatitis and histologically on neurogenic inflammation in an experimental atopic dermatitis mouse model. Our proof of concept studies have demonstrated the feasibility of expressing recombinant Blo t 5 in lactobacilli, which when delivered orally could successfully inhibit the production of Blo t 5-specific IgE in a mouse model for AD that has been established in our laboratory. The anticipated results generated from this study will potentially pave the way to develop a new immunotherapeutic strategy for atopic dermatitis.
kw: Atopic dermatitis, Neurogenic inflammation, Immunotherapy, Recombinant probiotics, Allergic inflammation

title: A prospective study of metronomic oral vinorelbine in combination with sorafenib in advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC)
abs: Anti-angiogenesis as a strategy for anti-cancer therapy is now well established. Incorporating this in the treatment of solid tumours such as non-small cell lung cancer(NSCLC) and breast cancer has shown benefit. This study aims to combine two different anti-angiogenic approaches in NSCLC: metronomic chemotherapy with oral vinorelbine and multi-kinase inhibition with sorafenib. Both therapies are orally administered, which is an important step towards making treatment more convenient for cancer patients. Determining the optimal biologic dose(OBD) of anti-angiogenic agents is still a challenge. Biomarkers of antiangiogenesis namely DCE-MR, CEC/CEP, and TSP-1 will be incorporated into this study as an aid towards this aim. This phase I study uses a novel design developed by the investigators that involves intra-patient dose escalation of sorafenib. While the basic design still uses the MTD approach, the inclusion of biomarkers may help us in arriving at the OBD of the combination. This study has been reviewed and discussed extensively with the research division of both Bayer and Pierre Fabre (sponsors of sorafenib and vinorelbine respectively). Both pharmaceuticals have given their approval and will provide the drugs for this study. This is the first time where we have managed to successfully convince 2 pharmaceuticals to sponsor this investigator-initiated study by providing their compounds free of charge.
kw: Phase I, Oral vinorelbine, Anti-angiogenesis, Sorafenib, Biomarkers

title: Identification of the molecular and cellular mechanisms altering dendritic cell motility during atherosclerosis
abs: Atherosclerosis, a chronic inflammation of the arterial wall, represents a major cause of death in Singapore as in industrialized countries and is now recognized as an immunological disorder with an emerging role for dendritic cells (DCs). Normally, activated DCs migrate to the draining lymph nodes (LN) where they interact with lymphocytes to induce an immune response. In atherosclerosis, DCs accumulate in mouse and human lesions, and increasing evidence support the role of DCs in the progression of the disease by stimulating T lymphocytes in situ and by secreting cytokines and chemokines, which in turn favor the recruitment of immune cells into the arterial wall. Thus, elucidating the mechanisms that lead to DC retention within atherosclerotic tissues is now critical and will identify cellular and/or molecular factors that could then serve as targets of new or more potent therapeutic agents.We demonstrated in well characterized-mouse models of atherosclerosis that DCs are trapped because their mobilization to LN is severely compromised despite their activation. Here, we hypothesize that the failure of DCs to emigrate from the tissues may relate to the absence or expression of genes in DCs themselves that are known to govern DC migration. To identify these genes, we propose to compare the gene expression of selected DCs from normal and atherosclerotic aortas by transcriptome array-based analyses (aim 1). Next, we will follow-up on preliminary data suggesting that B cells can modulate DC migration in atherosclerosis, and we will investigate the underlying mechanisms (aim 2). Specifically, we hypothesize that B cells may be atheroprotective by producing antibody and immunoregulatory cytokine but they may, conversely, be detrimental by inducing excessive exacerbation of lymphangiogenesis, which may impair DC emigration, and thus contribute to disease progression. This study will better define the contribution of B cells in atherogenesis that remains unclear so far.
kw: atherosclerosis, Dendritic cell, Dendritic cell migration, B lymphocyte, inflammation, Lymphatic vessel

title: Characterization of the molecular mechanisms involved in the bio-activation of the second line antitubercular drug ethionamide.
abs: Despite tuberculosis (TB) control programs, Mycobacterium tuberculosis remains the most commoncause of infection-related mortality worldwide. Given the overwhelming global impact, the WorldHealth Organization (WHO) declared TB a global public health emergency in 1993. Since then, theincidence of TB and its associated mortality have stabilized. However, these relative successes havebeen hampered by the emergence of drug resistance which now poses a significant worldwide threat.The increasing incidence of circulating multidrug-resistant (MDR) and extensively drug-resistant (XDR)TB strains threatens to return TB treatment to the pre-antibiotic era.Understanding the limitations of the current anti-TB drugs and therapies may help improving them.Ethionamide (ETH) is an anti-TB drug whose hepatotoxicity and gastric intolerability have restrictedthe use to treat MDR-TB infected patients only. ETH is a prodrug that requires activation by amycobacterial enzyme, EthA. The current model for ETH activation involves a repressor, EthR, whichbinds to the promoter region of ethA. In addition a small molecule, hexadecyl octonoate (HexOc) hasbeen recently reported to interact with EthR thereby modulating its repressor activity. The origin ofHexOc has yet to be identified. Moreover, we have observed that the killing efficacy of ETH issignificantly higher during macrophage infection compared to in vitro culture, suggesting a differentialactivation of ETH between in vivo and in vitro culture conditions.In this project, we propose to further study and characterize the molecular mechanisms of ETHactivation. A detailed understanding of these mechanisms would surely help developing strategies toreduce ETH dosage, thereby minimizing ETH-associated side-effects and toxicity and maybe allowingre-considering ETH as a first-line anti-TB drug.
kw: Mycobacterium tuberculosis, ethionamide, TB drug, EthR, EthA

title: A genome-wide search for epigenetic alterations of genes important in development of nasal polyps.
abs: Nasal polyps (NPs) affects 0.2-4.3% of the population worldwide, and is often associated with chronic rhinosinusitis. During the past decade, there have been advances in pharmacologic and surgical therapies, however, the recurrence rate is still unacceptably high. NPs are generally characterized as a benign condition with mucosal inflammation and hyperplastic outgrowth. Our previous study demonstrated that a significant increase of cytotoxic T cells (CD3+/CD8+) is a predominant feature in addition to commonly reported eosinophilia and/or neutrophilia in the literature. In another pilot study, we were able to evidence methylation of some tumor suppressor genes (SHP-1, TSLC1, E-cadherin, and DAP-kinase), but not p16, RASSF1A and SOCS-1, in NPs. Therefore, this study is proposed to investigate whether development of NPs is associated with methylation of some tumor suppress genes or genes which are related to key pathogenic mechanisms of NPs. A genome-wide search for disease-related genes in NP tissue (n=30), chronic sinusitis mucosa (n=30), and a control tissue of inferior turbinate (IT) (n=30) will be performed. This study consist of: (1) Microarray analysis to identify NP specific genes; (2) Gene ontology analysis to choose genes with putative functional links to cancer, inflammation, cell growth/death, cell cycle, cell/tissue morphology; (3) Examination of Promoter CpG islands in down-regulated genes by using website-based software; (4) Validation of expression levels of the selected genes at mRNA level (using real-time RT PCR) and protein levels (using immunohistochemistry or western blot); (5) Validation of gene promoter methylation status by using MSP/BGS techniques. This is a continuation study which will provide in-depth pathogenic mechanisms of disease-related genes in development of hyperplastic outgrowth and epigenetic regulation of inflammatory cells fate and function in chronic sinusitis and NPs. It will help in identifying novel concepts that can be applied in a beneficial way to the clinical treatment and prevention of NPs.
kw: nasal polyps, hyperplastic growth, mucosal inflammation, gene methylation, genome-wide expression profile, Microarray

title: Biomimetic 3D nanofibrous scaffold/MSCs composites for bonegraft applications
abs: There is a great need for artificial bone graft materials for various bone applications. Autograft is the gold standard and has a good clinical track record. However, its supply is limited and there is the issue of donor site morbidity. Allografts and xenografts are usually not preferred owing to the possibility of disease transmission and graft rejection. It is essential to design biomaterials with superior surface characteristics to both facilitate favorable host tissue interactions for their long-term survivability and to enhance tissue regeneration and remodeling. Since bone itself is made of nanocomposite materials (mainly hydroxyapatite (HA) nanocrystallites) in a collagen-rich organic matrix as mineralized nanofibers, the primary objective of this project is to develop a bone-like 3D nanofibrous composite consisting of HA and collagen or other polymers using electrospinning and biomineralization techniques. Currently the electrospinning setup used by most researchers is unable to fabricate 3D scaffolds. Our novel 3D nanofibrous scaffold, named nanoyarn, basically consists of mineralized nanofibrous bundles and is similar to the hierarchical structure of natural bone. This biomimetic scaffold is used to capture bone marrow-derived stem cells (MSCs) directly from marrow, thus eliminating the need for a separate procedure to culture and expand the MSCs. The proposed research is directed at testing the hypothesis that 3D nanofiber incorporating extracellular matrix (ECM) materials and biomolecules are able to capture sufficient numbers of MSCs from the bone marrow aspirate and that the MSCs/nanofibers composite will facilitate bone regeneration. The 3D biomimetic nanofibrous scaffold +/- stem cells will be implanted into a critical sized defect in a rabbit ulnar model to evaluate new bone regeneration. We envisage that the MSCs/3D nanofiber composite has the potential to bring us one step closer to the perfect bone graft substitute.
kw: bone graft, 3D nanofibrous scaffold, tissue engineering, biomimetic, biomineralization, stem cells

title: Magnetic Resonance Elastography for non-invasive assessment of liver fibrosis and characterization offocal liver lesions.
abs: Liver biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosing liver fibrosis, but is subject to sampling error, poor acceptance and procedure related complications. There is a need for safe, non-invasive and accurate investigation for diagnosis of liver fibrosis. Magnetic resonance elastography (MRE) is a unique noninvasiveimaging method that can detect propagating shear waves and measure liver stiffness which represents the effects of fibrosis. The major advantage of MRE is that whole liver can be imaged and is not limited by the body habitus or by the presence of ascites. We aim to establish the usefulness of MRE in Asian patients for non-invasive detection of liver fibrosis and its correlation with histopathology. The second aim is characterization of liver tumors with MRE.Normal volunteers will be sought and recruited for establishing the normal liver stiffness values in Asian population. Patients with biopsy proven liver fibrosis and liver tumors identified by imaging and/or biopsy will be actively recruited for the study. A standard contrast enhanced MRI study of liverwith MR Elastography will be performed. The estimated stiffness of the liver with MRE will be correlated with histological grade of fibrosis and the stiffness of the tumors with histological type/grade of the tumor. Statistical analysis will be performed for accuracy of MRE to distinguish normal fromfibrotic liver and among different grades of fibrosis and also to differentiate benign and malignant tumors.The impact of this technique can be seen in many disease processes including characterization of liver tumors, assessment of treatment response to hepatic fibrosis, and response of the tumors treatment non-invasively. MRE is in clinical use at Mayo Clinic, USA and few other centers have begun the process of clinical implementation. Introducing this non-invasive technique in Singapore, will give us the unique opportunity to be the first center from Asia.
kw: Liver, Tumors, Cirrhosis

title: Genetics of Atopy and Allergic Airway Disease in Singapore
abs: Atopic airway diseases such as asthma and allergic rhinitis represent a global health problem, affecting 10-25% of the world’s population. There are clear evidences to support the concept that allergic diseases are influenced by both genetic and environmental factors. In the past, genome-wide studies have shown linkages between certain phenotypes of allergic diseases and markers on more than 15 human chromosomes. However, variable results were obtained from different studies, possibly due to (1) differences in the susceptibility genes for atopy and allergic diseases in different populations; (2) the lack of sufficient statistical power; (3) insufficient coverage of candidate genes, genetic variations within these genes, and differences in allele frequencies between populations; and (4) developmental and environmental differences influencing variations in our susceptibility to these conditions. The main objectives in this proposal is thus (i) to ascertain large clinically and epidemiologically well-characterized demographic-matched case-control cohorts (of at least 1,000 individuals with allergic disease and 1,000 non-atopic individuals), which will be recruited to provide sufficient statistical power for the identification of major atopic susceptibility genes in our population. Thereafter, (ii) an initial whole genome single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) comparison will be conducted by comparing 500 atopic individuals (with 1st degree family history of disease) with 500 non-atopic controls, in order to detect a menu of significantly associated SNPs. (iii) A follow-up study in another 500 cases and 500 controls will be then performed using the selected list of SNPs to validate the association. This will help identify key genes or haplotypes that are associated with allergic phenotypes and may lead to a better understanding of the mechanisms underlying these diseases, as well as to enable us to subtype atopy and allergic diseases.
kw: Asthma, Allergy, Genome-wide Study, Allergic Rhinitis, Genetic Succeptibility

title: Investigation of anatomical and functional factors affecting voiding dysfunction
abs: The functional basis by which human micturition is achieved and disrupted in bladder outlet obstruction in benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is not fully understood. Although there is a wealth of reported observational data on both normal micturition and obstructed voiding, it is difficult to isolate individual anatomical and functional factors in human subjects, such as bladder neck relaxation, detrusor tension and contraction, prostatic intravesical protrusion, or prostatic elasticity. The present study attempts to overcome this difficulty by building a computer model based on the fundamental physical principles in flow dynamics and fluid structural interaction that can closely mimic the voiding pattern of a real subject, which can then be verified and correlated with clinical studies from actual human subjects who have undergone urological investigations for voiding dysfunction, principally with imaging studies like magnetic resonance imaging, and functional studies like urodynamics and video-urodynamics.. This will allow the investigation of factors that are most important, and their interaction with each other. It is translational in that it synthesizes the disparate factors into one model that may contribute to further understanding of voiding function, and can be used to analyze patients with voiding problems. The clinical significance of this study is that it may further our understanding of voiding function and dysfunction in older males who may have bladder outlet obtruction from benign prostatic hyperplasia, a condition which will increase in prevalence with our aging population. It may identify newer modalities of investigation in such patients, whose assessment is often complicated by other co-morbidities.
kw: Bladder outlet obstruction, Urinary flow, Urodynamics, Diagnostic tool, Flow dynamics, Fluid structural interaction

title: DEVELOPMENT OF NOVEL GENE DELIVERY METHODS FOR CELL THERAPY OF CANCER: COMPARING ELECTROPORATION, NANOPARTICLES, BACULOVIRUS GENE DELIVERY SYSTEMS TO REDIRECT THE SPECIFICITY OF NATURAL KILLER CELLS AND CYTOKINE-INDUCED KILLER CELLS WITH mRNA ENCODING A DUAL SIGNALING ANTI-CD19 RECEPTOR
abs: T lymphocytes, natural killer (NK) cells and cytokine-induced killer (CIK) cells are emerging tools for cell therapy of cancer. To be effective, these immune cells must be harnessed so that they are specifically cytotoxic to cancer cells. This can be achieved by the expression of receptors specific for molecules displayed on cancer cells. In preliminary studies performed by our collaborator Dario Campana at St Jude Children’s Research Hospital, T cells and NK cells were redirected against leukemia and lymphoma cells using a chimeric receptor (anti-CD19-BB-z) that reacts with CD19 (a molecule widely expressed in B cell malignancies) and delivers two stimulatory signals through CD3z and 4-1BB that activate T, NK and CIK cell cytotoxicity. Expression of chimeric receptors is typically achieved using retroviral vectors. However, the translation of this method to clinical use is complex. Electroporation of chimeric receptor-encoding mRNA has recently been shown to produce effective, albeit transient, anti-CD19-BB-z receptor expression. Our overall objective is to widen the options for genetic modification of immune cells for cancer therapy and identify optimal methods for redirecting their specificity. Capitalizing on novel methods for gene delivery developed in Singapore, we propose to pursue the following aims. In Aim 1, we will determine the feasibility of transducing NK cells and CIK cells with anti-CD19-BB-z receptors using biodegradable nanoparticles/reducible polymers for gene delivery. In Aim 2 we will test a baculovirus-mediated transduction. In Aim 3 we will compare the anti-leukemic capacity of NK and CIK cells transduced with nanoparticles/reducible polymers or baculovirus to that of cells transduced with established electroporation and retrovirus transduction methods.
