title: Translational Study Of Autologous Bone Marrow Stem Cell In TGF-beta 1 Loaded Fumarate Based Hydrogel For Chondral Defect Repairing
abs: The ultimate goal of this research proposal is to develop a cell/polymer construct that will aid in the repair of tissue in chondral defects. We hypothesize that the use of bone marrow stem cells (BMSCs) in a construct made from the novel hydrogel material oligo(poly(ethylene glycol) fumarate) (OPF) and including the growth factor TGF-b1 will help repair tissue in such defects by allowing alteration of the local chemical environment experienced by the cells, thus providing a means to enhance the chondral differentiation process to form cartilage tissue.Based on the experiments of this group and our collaborators', a total of 48 minipigs with large chondral defect (9 mm in diameter and 5 mm in depth) will be randomly assigned to four groups defined by different hydrogel fabrication formulae: ?Autologous BMSCs implantation group (control), ?Hydrogel-TGF-?1, ?BMSCs-Hydrogel and ?BMSCs-Hydrogel-TGF-?1. The different hydrogel will be fabricated and filled into the defects. The chondral repair will be evaluated 3 months and 12 months later by the methods of histology/pathology and biomechanics. Excellent results had been achieved in our collaborator's preliminary study using the similar method in small chondral defect (5 mm in diameter and 3 mm in depth in rabbit).If this project succeeds, it will pave the way for a minimally invasive mode of cartilage transplantation because BMSCs-OPF hydrogel can be delivered through arthroscope. It wills optimize the method of the autologous chondrocytes implantation (ACI), which is currently the preferred treatment for the full thickness articular cartilage defects by author and needs a complex open surgical procedure for the chondrocytes delivery. The in-situ gelable property will let the BMSCs-Hydrogel well fit and fast attach to any sharps of the defect to avoid the failure that frequently appeared in ACI due to implants detaching. Numerous patients will benefit from it.

title: Modeling Omi-mediated neurodegeneration in vivo Prospects for drug discovery
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Parkinson’s disease (PD) is the most common neurodegenerative movement disorder that ischaracterized pathologically by the specific loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substania nigra parscompacta. Although a subject of intense research, its etiology is poorly understood and the diseaseremains incurable. A prime suspect implicated in the selective damage to dopaminergic neurons isaugmented cellular oxidative stress arising from mitochondrial dysfunction. Interestingly, mutations ineither one of the 3 distinctive familial PD-linked genes: namely Parkin, PTEN-induced kinase 1(PINK1) and Omi/HtrA2 (high temperature required factor A2), are known to compromisemitochondrial function. Insights into how these PD-linked genes normally interact to maintain optimalmitochondrial function are therefore vital to our understanding of the pathogenesis of PD. However todate, little is known about the PD-linked gene Omi compared to Parkin and PINK1 although a singleheterozygous mutation at amino acid position 399 of Omi converting glycine to serine has beenidentified to be causative of familial PD. A major hurdle is the lack of a good animal model for Omi.Previously, we have successfully recapitulated progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons intransgenic flies overexpressing Parkin mutation R275W. To further our understanding of Omi’s role inPD pathogenesis and the importance of optimal mitochondrial function in the survival of dopaminergicneurons, we aim to (1) generate a Drosophila model for human Omi dysfunction, and (2) use this invivo model to identify modifier genes that promote or suppress Omi mutant-mediatedneurodegeneration. We have taken the initial step to generate these transgenic flies and areproposing to characterize them by examining dopaminergic neuronal survival, locomotive functionand muscular mitochondrial morphology. Given the prospects for using Drosophila as a tool for drugscreening, results obtained from this study will undoubtedly be applicable to therapeutic developmentfor PD.
kw: Parkinson’s disease, Omi, Mitochondria, Neurodegeneration, Drosophila, Parkin

title: Modeling growth plate function with bone marrow derived mesenchymal stem cells to develop improved treatments for growth plate defects in children.
abs: Bone elongation in children occurs at the bone’s extremities in bands of cartilage known as the epiphyseal plate (physis) or growth plate. Physis is a highly organized structure in which chondrocytes progress, in defined zones, from resting chondrocytes, to proliferating then columnar chondrocytes which become hypertrophic, undergo apoptosis and matrix mineralization to culminate in vascular invasion and new bone formation. Physeal defects result in reduced bone length and irregular angularity or shape and are difficult to treat surgically. Cell therapy approaches using physeal tissue or chondrocytes are limited due to insufficient donor cells or tissue, morbidity at the donor tissue harvest site and immune rejection if foreign donor cells are used. These limitations can be overcome by using bone marrow derived mesenchymal stem cells (bMSCs). We have preliminary data to show that differentiation of bMSCs in pellet culture results in a heterogeneous cell population with many of the phenotypic characteristics of normal physeal cells. Differentiation of bMSCs in an agarose scaffold with unidirectional diffusion of media components promotes zonal alignment of the different cell types reminiscent of that found in normal physis. However, columnar chondrocytes are not seen and the cells progress quickly to hypertrophy. We hypothesize that comparison of our physis model tissue with normal physis will identify deficiencies in our model and that application of this data to the development of a multilayer scaffold with different properties in each layer will lead to the generation of a more physiologically accurate model of physis. A physiologically accurate model of physis would provide an invaluable tool with applications from the bench to the bedside. In the laboratory, the physeal model would be invaluable in elucidating the roles and interactions of important factors and signalling pathways in the physis. In the pharmaceutical industry it could be used to study drugs to treat bone disorders or to test drugs that may interfere with physis function if given to children. Clinically, the model could be used to engineer tissue to treat physeal defects in children.
kw: Mesenchymal stem cells, cartilage, physics, signaling pathways

title: Septohippocampal region: role in pain-induced aversion and morphine antinociception
abs: The proposal will test the hypothesis that (a) the nociceptive-aversive drive involves the septohippocampal region of the forebrain, and (b) conversely, the analgesic morphine and NMDA antagonist ifenprodil evoke antinociception by affecting the region. The hypothesis is based on the finding from the laboratory made using the formalin model of persistent inflammatory pain. In this model hind paw injection of formalin induces a spectrum of acute aversive behaviors, and learned behaviors such as avoidance of the context associated with pain. The finding central to the hypothesis is that formalin-induced other sustained moment-to-moment agitation (agitation) and licking of the injured paw was accompanied by relatively robust activation of hippocampus marked by oscillatory theta wave activity in the field CA1. The theta wave is generated as result of activation of the medial septum afferents to the hippocampus. Interestingly, in our experiments the hippocampal activation was not observed during formalin-induced flinching that is organized at the brainstem level. The present proposal will investigate the followings in behaving rat: One, electrophysiological patterns of hippocampal activation and animal agitation with different levels of pain. Two, effects of manipulation of the septohippocampal synaptic transmission with drug microinjection on formalin-induced animal pain. Three, effect of inactivation of the dorsal hippocampus on formalin-induced avoidance behavior. Four, pattern of induction of cellular markers of plasticity in hippocampus with formalin-induced pain. Hippocampal molecular plasticity is associated with avoidance behavior in select paradigms. On successful conclusion, the study will show that the septohippocampal region selectively affect agitation, licking and avoidance behaviors with minimal influence on flinching. This will strengthen the notion that the region is involved in the aversion (unpleasantness) to pain. The unpleasantness is the basis of suffering with dramatic effect on patient lifestyle and understanding the central nervous system basis will open up avenue for exploring novel drug treatment.
kw: inflammatory pain, septohippocampus, drug microinjection, agitation and avoidance, theta and sharp waves, plasticity

title: Identification of Novel Genetic Determinants of Atrial Fibrillation in an Asian Population
abs: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained arrhythmia, reaching epidemic proportions in the aging population, and resulting in significant morbidity, mortality, and socioeconomic burden. In a subset of younger patients (<60 years of age), AF develops in the absence of known risk factors (e.g., congestive heart failure and structural heart disease), a condition classified as lone AF. Genetic polymorphisms have been reported to confer susceptibility to AF. Heritability of AF is further suggested by two population-based studies; the presence of AF in first-degree relatives increases the risk of developing AF. The overall aim of this study is to identify novel genetic determinants of AF in an Asian population. To avoid confounding variables, we will recruit patients with lone AF who lack traditional risk factors. Using this cohort, we aim to:1.Identify disease susceptibility polymorphisms for AF using candidate gene association analysis2.Define interaction of genetic factors with acquired factors in modifying AF risk and phenotypic expression3.Pave the way toward establishing a larger cohort to facilitate genome-wide association analysis in the futureLone AF cases will initially be enrolled from National University Hospital, with eventual enrollment from the National Heart Centre and Tan Tock Seng Hospital reaching a target sample size of 600 cases. This cohort will enable candidate gene association analysis and constitutes the first step toward establishing a larger cohort that may permit genome-wide scanning in the future. Six hundred controls will be obtained from the Singapore Consortium of Cohort Studies. Blood draw for DNA and biomarker analyses, systematic collection of clinical and demographic data, detailed electrocardiographic and echocardiographic evaluation, and applanation tonometry will be performed on all patients at the time of enrollment. Insights into the genetic basis of AF can translate to clinically useful methods for predicting, preventing, and treating AF. In a cohort of Caucasian patients with lone AF, the principal investigator has previously demonstrated an association between a common polymorphism in the human cardiac sodium channel gene and AF. The minor R558 allele of this polymorphism reduces sodium current. Sodium channel blockers, commonly used to treat AF, may be proarrhythmic in patients harbouring the R558 allele by excessively reducing sodium current. If this association is replicated in Asian patients, it may guide our use of Class I antiarrhythmics in treating AF patients in Singapore. The discovery of other functional polymorphisms that not only confer susceptibility to AF, but may also influence prognosis and treatment response, will greatly improve our ability to manage the disease.

title: Four-dimensional Imaging of the Wrist with Dual-Source Computed Tomographic Scanner
abs: Specific Aims : The objective of this project is to advance musculoskeletal imaging by developing four-dimensional (4D) imaging (time-resolved) of the wrist using dual-source computed tomographic (DSCT) scanners. The first specific aim is to determine the morphometric and kinematic accuracy of 4D wrist DSCT imaging. The second specific aim will be to show that 4D DSCT wrist imaging can detect dynamic instabilities of the carpus in-vitro. Hypothesis : The first hypothesis to be tested is that 4D wrist imaging with DSCT scanners will be accurate for morphometric and kinematic measurements of carpal bones.The second hypothesis is that 4D wrist DSCT imaging can be used to detect and quantify carpal bone motion abnormalities in cadaveric wrists with ligamentous injuries. Methodology : Ten cadaveric wrists will be mounted on a custom-made motion jig and will undergo periodic motion while being scanned in a DSCT scanner using retrospective cardiac gated protocol. Approach : This study will involve the development of a motion jig for the hand and wrist to be used during 4D wrist DSCT scanning. This will be done in conjunction with the development of the CT protocol for 4D wrist imaging. Clinical significance : This will be a multi-disciplinary, multi-center, international collaborative project that uses current state-of-the-art CT technology to further develop musculoskeletal imaging. Wrist pain can be the result of static or dynamic carpal instabilities. Static instabilities, with or without arthritis, may be detected on routine static radiographic or CT imaging. However, patients with dynamic instabilities only demonstrate abnormalities during motion, with no apparent abnormality at rest. At the moment, real-time fluoroscopy is the only imaging modality that may be used to detect abnormality in some of these patients. However, fluoroscopy suffers from several important drawbacks which includes low resolution images, and two-dimensional imaging. 4D wrist imaging will be an important tool in the assessment of patients with wrist pain.
kw: Four-dimensional imaging, Dual-source computed tomography, Arthritis of the carpus, Wrist, Carpal instability, Dynamic instability of the carpus

title: Molecular Epidemiology of HIV-1 in Newly-diagnosed Individuals in Singapore.
abs: Background: Human Immunodeficiency Virus type 1 (HIV-1) is a retrovirus and the major etiological agent responsible for the Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (AIDS) global pandemic. HIV-1 is a mutation-prone, therefore genetically ever-changing virus. Molecular epidemiological studies have revealed that HIV-1 is not equally distributed worldwide and characterized by significant genetic diversity. Studies have shown that HIV-1 genetic diversity has a significant impact on (1) the efficacy of molecular methods used in its diagnosis and viral load assays, (2) decision-making in selection of antiretroviral therapy, (3) vaccine development and vaccination strategy. In addition, different HIV-1 variants may differ in transmissibility, infectivity, replicative capacity, and pathogenicity. To date, the molecular epidemiology of HIV-1 in Singapore has not been systematically studies. Aims: In this proposed study, we aim to (1) uncover the genetic diversity of HIV-1 in newly-diagnosed Singaporean patients, (2) study the molecular epidemiology of HIV-1 in these newly-diagnosed patients, (3) assess the utility of the pol gene in HIV-1 transmission analyses.Methodology and approach: Newly-diagnosed HIV-infected individuals in 2008 will be enrolled as study subjects. Blood samples will be obtained from these subjects and HIV-1 genomic RNA will be extracted from plasma. The gag, env, pol genes of HIV-1 will be synthesized by RT-PCR and amplified by nested PCRs and their nucleotide sequences determined using DNA sequencing. Phylogenetic analyses will be performed to determine HIV-1 genotypes and to examine the genetic relationships of the HIV-1 strains found in our local patients so as to infer their epidemiological relationships.Significance: Knowledge of the molecular epidemiology of HIV-1 in Singapore will aid in our understanding of the transmission of the virus and has the potential to influence control and prevention strategies for HIV infection. Information gained from this proposed study may also lead to novel hypotheses for further HIV research.
kw: HIV-1, genetic diversity, Singapore, molecular epidemiology, evolution, phylogenetics

title: Analysis of multivariate failure time data: A semi-competing risks approach
abs: In biomedical studies involving time-to-event outcomes, a subject may experience multiple failures. These failures may be repeated events of the same kind - such as a sequence of myocardial infarctions or infection episodes - or failures of an entirely different nature, such as local or distant recurrences in cancer studies. In the context of competing risks, the failures are usually of different types, and the subject may only fail from one of these distinct causes. We consider a variation of the competing risks problems in which a terminal event (eg. death) censors a non-terminal event (eg. recurrence), but not vice versa. In many instances, it is biologically plausible that the terminal event may be strongly correlated with the non-terminal process. Thus, in clinical trials evaluating therapeutic interventions, inferences on treatment efficacy with respect to disease recurrence for example, may be complicated by dependent censoring from terminating events such as mortality. We develop strategies for analyzing covariate effects on both the terminal and non-terminal events by developing models that incorporate their possible dependence or correlation. The dependence is modeled by including a shared frailty in the hazard function of both the recurrent and terminal events. Regression coefficients and association parameters will be estimated using maximum and profile likelihood methods when assuming parametric and non-parametric baseline hazard functions respectively. The proposed methods will be evaluated, both theoretically and through simulations, and applied to data arising from a randomized clinical trial of patients diagnosed with stage III or IV (non-metastatic) nasopharyngeal cancer.These methods provide a way to estimate the degree of dependence between terminal and non-terminal events and to relate this dependence to covariate effects. In addition, these methods will provide a way to estimate covariate effects on the rates of the non-terminal and terminal events of interest while taking into account the correlation between them. Conventional methods of survival analysis that do not account for such dependence may be invalid, leading to a biased estimate of covariate effects on the events of interest.
kw: Semi-competing, Non-terminal event, Frailty, Terminal event, Dependent censoring

title: Lipidomic analysis of the brain after transcranial magnetic stimulation - potential implication for the role of lipids in epileptogenesis
abs: Lipid mediators play important roles in neuronal signaling. However, little is known about whether changes in these mediators could influence the course and progression of epilepsy. Lipidomics is a novel technique used to study changes in lipids on a systems scale. Our previous study has shown changes in specific ceramdies species, phospholipids, and acetylated phosphatidylethanolamines in the hippocampus of rats after intracerebroventricular injection of the excitotoxin, kainate (Guan et al., 2006). The latter is a glutamate analog, and is widely used in a model of epilepsy in animals. The effects of kainate are however, generalized, causing status epilepticus in most of the rats. The present proposal aims to study the relation between neuronal stimulation and lipid changes in a more “controlled” and graded manner. This is achieved through the use of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). The procedure is non-invasive, utilizing an induced current in the brain after application of an external magnetic pulse, and is a more physiological method of delivering brain stimulations, compared to injection of excitotoxins such as kainate. The brain is subjected to defined number of pulses, and the relation between intensity and frequency of stimulation and lipid changes characterized in a systematic manner. The dependence of any lipid changes on NMDA receptor activation (an indication of postsynaptic lipid changes) and free radicals, could also be examined using intraperitoneal injection of an NMDA receptor antagonist, MK801, and N acetylglutathione, a blood-brain barrier permeable free radical scavenger. Excess TMS is able to cause epilepsy. The relation between excess TMS stimulation, seizures, and the appearance of particular lipid species will also be studied. Subsequent experiments would depend on identification of the precise lipid species that is most linked to appearance of epilepsy. The enzymes that lead to formation fo that species could be studied by immunohistochemistry, and levels of enzyme mRNA, by RT-PCR. Enzyme activity would also be determined by biochemical assay. This would be followed by administration of enzyme inhibitors to attempt to influence the progression of seizures / decrease seizures.It is also conceivable that brain specific lipids could cross the blood brain barrier from the brain into the bloodstream. These could then be used use biomarkers for impending epilepsy, for example in patients with head injury.
kw: Lipidomics, Transcranial magenetic stimulation, Epilepsy, Lipid mediators, Seizures

title: Pre-clinical study of using Nitric Oxide (NO)-donor as potential adjuvant for the development of an effective dendritic cell-based vaccine system.
abs: Dendritic cells (DCs) play crucial role in the induction of antigen-specific T cell responses, and their use for the active immunotherapy of malignancies and other diseases has been studied with considerable interest. DCs are professional antigen presenting cells (APCs) that possess specific and efficient mechanisms to initiate immune responses. MHC class II (MHCII) molecules bind peptides derived from internalised proteins that have entered the endocytic pathway and present them at the cell surface for the activation of CD4+ T cells. After encounter with pathogens, the lowly immunogenic immature DCs go through a maturation process that converts them to highly immunogenic mature DCs. Nitric Oxide (NO) was one of the major molecules produced during DCs maturation. Our preliminary data showed that NO, and overexpression of inducible-Nitric Oxide Synthetase (NOS2) and endothelial Nitric Oxide Synthetase (NOS3) can induce surface expression of MHC II, B7-1 (CD80), and B7-2 (CD86), hallmarks of DCs going through maturation. Consistently, immature DCs treated with NONOate (NO-donor) capable of enhancing T cell proliferation in-vitro in the absence of Lipopolysaccharides (LPS). Based on these findings, we proposed to examine the efficacy of NONOate as adjuvant for the development of an effective dendritic-cell based vaccine system. Mouse bone marrow-derived primary DCs will be loaded with malaria antigen (CSP) and cultured either in the absence or in the presence of various concentrations of NONOate. (1) The amount and types of cytokines produced by untreated and NONOate-treated DCs (CSP-loaded) will be determined by biochemical assays (2)The untreated and NONOate-treated DCs will be injected into syngeneic mice and determined its ability to modulate (i) CSP-specific antibody (ii) cytokines productions, in -vivo.

title: Role of Filamin A association and alternative splicing on Cav1.2 calcium channel expression and function in smooth muscle and neurons: implications in stroke
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: L-type Cav1.2 channels are known to play significant roles in many important cellular processes including muscle contraction, neurotransmission, excitation-transcription coupling and hormone secretion. Alternative splicing of the Cav1.2 ?1-subunit diversifies the electrophysiological and pharmacological properties of these channels. Restricted smooth muscle-selective expression of an alternatively spliced exon 9* provided the basis to screen for muscle-selective interacting proteins. A total of 3.5×106 clones from a human aorta cDNA library were screened. We identified Filamin A (FLNa) as a novel interacting partner of the Cav1.2 L-type channel. The interaction was confirmed with in vitro co-localizatio and co-immunoprecipitation assays.FLNa is a 280 kDa protein belonging to a family of three actin-binding members. Its function is regulated by proteolysis, phosphorylation, the binding of phospholipids and organelle compartmentalization. FLNa regulates cell signaling by the reorganization of the actin cytoskeleton. We hypothesize that FLNa acts as a molecular scaffold bringing Cav1.2 and its interacting partners in close proximity. The interaction of Cav1.2 and FLNa could lead to changes in channel density and voltage-dependent activation. The physiological significance of FLNa will be probed by siRNA technology in tissue cultured cells. We have determined in a rat genetic hypertension model that the combinatorial arrangements of 12 alternatively spliced exons of Cav1.2 changed in hypertensive versus normotensive rat hearts. As such, understanding the dynamic changes in splicing expression profiles of Cav1.2 channels in human Arterial Venous Malformation (AVM) and rat Middle Cerebral Artery Occlusion (MCAO) stroke model would grant insight into the disease and possible explanations to the observed difference in response to drugs like nimodipine.This proposal aims to determine the physiological significance of the organization of Cav1.2 channels in a scaffold with other channels in excitation signalling; as well as the relevance of alternative splicing of Cav1.2 channels in cerebrovascular disorders.

title: Inducible transgenic models for LRRK2-associated parkinsonism
inst: National Neuroscience Institute of Singapore Pte Ltd
abs: Parkinson’s disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder affecting more than 4% of population by age of 85. While a few pathological features have been attributable to the pathogenesis of the disease, the etiology of PD remains elusive. Recently, mutations in the gene encoding leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) have been found to be associated with autosomal dominant parkinsonism [1,2]. The pleomorphic pathology of LRRK2-linked parkinsonism implicates that LRRK2 may act upstream in the signalling pathways that lead to the disease, which makes LRRK2 an extremely attractive target for studying the pathogenesis of PD. At present, about 20 PD-associated LRRK2 mutations have been identified. However, whether and how these mutations contribute to the pathogenesis of PD is unclear. No animal study on LRRK2 has been reported to date.In this study, we would like to develop and use an advanced inducible transgenic mouse approach to investigate how individual LRRK2 mutants participate in the pathogenesis of PD in vivo. Specifically, we would like to address two fundamental questions: 1) whether expression of LRRK2 mutants is sufficient to cause pathologies of PD in vivo? and, 2) whether LRRK2 kinase activity is required for the pathogenesis of PD in vivo? Particularly, we will be focusing our study on two LRRK2 mutations: G2019S (the most prevalent pathogenic mutant identified to date, with elevated kinase activity) and G2385R (a risk variant predominantly, if not exclusively, found in Asian populations, with decreased kinase activity) using G2019S/D2017A (a kinase inactive form of G2019S) and the wild type LRRK2 as controls. We believe that our study proposed here would provide critical insights into the patho-physiological function of LRRK2 in vivo and would facilitate developing novel therapeutic strategy for PD patients.
kw: Parkinson's disease, Animal models, LRRK2, Transgenic mice

title: Adaptation of human influenza A virus in a mouse model for understanding the molecular pathogenesis of influenza pneumonitis
abs: Interspecies transmission of pandemic influenza viruses occurs through adaptation. Evidence suggests that most of these pandemic strains originated from avian strains, which undergo adaptation before acquiring the ability to cause fatal infections in humans. Adaptation results in acquisition of critical determinants of high pathogenicity possibly through sequential changes both in virus and host. The molecular events that occur during adaptation, resulting in enhanced viral replication and high virulence is poorly understood. This proposal aims to explore the molecular and cellular events that occur during mouse adaptation of human influenza A virus (H3N2). The objectives include (i) to evaluate the pathological consequences and tissue tropism during adaptation. Once we determine the pathological basis during adaptation, we will explore this model to identify critical determinants of pathogenicity by comparing low and high virulent variants isolated during adaptation. (ii) to study the changes in the complete viral genome that occur during the virus adaptation in the mouse. We intend to perform homology modeling if we find any noteworthy mutations particularly in hemagglutinin, neuraminidase or polymerase genes to evaluate the impact of those mutations on protein structure and function. (iii) to profile the cytokines in the brochoalveolar lavage fluid and evaluate the cross-talk between the early- and late-stage cytokines, to understand the ontogeny of the inflammatory response in the virus infected lung. Further, we plan to explore the role of interferon regulatory factor-4 (IRF-4) in influenza viral infection using IRF-4 knock-out animals. (iv) to carryout transcriptomic analysis will be carried out with microarray and explore alterations in global gene expression between low and high virulent viral passages. Taken together, these studies will provide insights in understanding the basis of host lung pathogenesis, to identify key alterations in the viral genome and in host genomic response during viral adaptation. The findings will open up avenue for devising novel therapeutic interventions to alleviate influenza pneumonitis, to complement current antivirals and vaccines.
kw: influenza virus, virus adaption, mutation, mouse model, pathogenesis, infectomics

title: M-DCs: A new type of IL-10-producing redulatory dentritic cells of major vaccination and therapeutic potentials.
abs: Dendritic cells (DCs) are key antigen-presenting cells (APCs) essential for the initiation and modulation of adaptive immunity. In humans, monocyte-derived DCs, using GM-CSF and IL-4 ( here named GM-DCs ), have been extensively investigated and also explored for clinical therapies. Having high surface MHC and co-stimulatory molecules, these cells also produce high IL-12 required for the induction of IFN- y or Th1-mediated immunity. In a recent study, DCs were also cultured from cord blood monocytes using M-CSF and IL-4 ( here named M-DCs ). These M-DCs were shown to have similar phenotype as GM-DCs but they produced mainly IL-10 and little IL-12. M-DCs were found to be tolerogenic instead of stimulatory and to induce regulatory T cells. To further understand M-DCs, we cultured these cells from adult blood monocytes. Examining M-DC morphology, phenotype and cytokine profile revealed that they were distinct from GM-DCs and were also distinct from macrophages. On the other hand, they exhibited properties similar to the gut lamina propria mucosal DCs (LP DCs) - dynamic membrane protrusions and producing predominantly IL-10 but little IL-12. We hope to further these studies which are expected to provide important insights into the properties and physiological relevance of M-DCs. In-depth understanding of M-DCs could facilitate clinical applications of these cells, e.g. in vaccination and immunotherapies.As detailed later, work proposed in this project will be focused on the following two aspects of M-DCs: 1 ) basic properties of M-DCs including stability, T cell stimulation and endogenous counterparts and 2 ) mechanisms that suppress M- DC, and promote GM-DC, production of bioactive IL-12.The preliminary expression data on genes associated with M-DCs and GM- DCs will provide further gene targets in achieving these objectives.
kw: dendritic cells, IL-10, macrophages, IL-12, M-CSF, immunohistochemistry

title: The BrkA autotransporter: a novel carrier for the surface display of heterologous antigens in attenuated Bordetella pertussis.
abs: Attenuated Bordetella pertussis, the causative agent of whooping cough, has been proven to be a promising and attractive candidate for vaccine delivery via the nasal route. So far, filamentous hemagglutinin (FHA), the main B. pertussis adhesin has been used as carrier to secrete the foreign antigens. We have investigated the use of the B. pertussis autotransporter BrkA as carrier to expose foreign antigens at the bacterial surface. We have genetically fused three copies of the neutralizing peptide SP70 from the VP1 capsid protein of enterovirus 71 (EV71) within the passenger domain of BrkA and expressed this construct in a highly attenuated B. pertussis strain. A recombinant B. pertussis strain in which three copies of SP70 were fused to full-length FHA was also constructed. Both BrkA-(SP70)3 and FHA-(SP70)3 chimera were successfully surface-exposed and secreted, respectively. Furthermore, we have shown that the nasal administration of the BrkA-(SP70)3 recombinant strain triggered a strong anti-SP70 antibody response in mice with titers significantly higher than those obtained in mice immunized with the FHA-(SP70)3 recombinant strain. These preliminary data clearly indicate that BrkA represents an interesting and promising carrier for the surface-exposition of heterologous antigens in attenuated B. pertussis.In this project, we want to further investigate the protective potential against EV71 of the recombinant B. pertussis strain producing the BrkA-(SP70)3 chimera. Moreover, we propose to fuse a larger sub-fragment of VP1 to BrkA and study whether the chimera is successfully surface-exposed and triggers a protective immune response against EV71.To further explore the potential of BrkA as carrier for heterologous expression in B. pertussis, we propose to fuse to BrkA the extracellular domain of M2 protein (M2e) from influenza A virus. M2e has been described as a universal influenza vaccine candidate due to its highly conserved amino acid sequence among influenza A viruses. (298 words).

title: Lipidomics based diagnostics for ovarian cancer
abs: Epithelial carcinoma of the ovary (ovarian cancer) is a leading cause of death in women withgynecological malignancies. It is amongst the ten most common cancers in Singapore. If diagnosedand treated early, i.e. during confinement to the ovary, the 5-year survival rate is over 90%.Unfortunately, only ~20% of all cases are found at early stages. Thus there is a need for reliablediagnostic tools for early stage tumors.Here we propose to use lipids in a multimarker readout as a novel tool for non-invasive diagnosisfor ovarian cancers. While there has been anecdotal evidence for a correlation of lyso-phospholipidsand ovarian cancers no study so far has used lipidomics, i.e. comprehensive systems-level scaleanalysis of lipids. In a pilot study consisting of ~50 controls and ~100 patients, we have measuredplasma concentrations of nearly 400 lipid species (glycerophospholipids and sphingolipids) byelectrospray ionization mass spectrometry. Using multivariate statistics and supervised machinelearning (based on support vector machines) we are able to classify controls from patients, andbenign from malignant forms, with sensitivities and specificities above those of the existingCA-125 serum marker. We have identified key lipid components which act as markers in thispredictor. In this proposal we plan to1. Extend the list of lipids in order to further increase sensitivity and specificity of our predictor.Oxidized lipids, glycerolipids and sterols will be included.2. Investigate the role of identified lipid pathways in epithelial adenocarcinoma cell lines with cellbiological methods.This project will result in a novel, lipidomics based, biomarker for ovarian cancer. It can beexpected that this method will find applications in multimodal diagnosis and in screens of clinical trialsin the future. The methodology is applicable in principle in other areas of oncology and clinicalresearch and has potential for commercialization.
kw: lipidomics, mass spectrometry, diagnostics, biomarker, machine learning, Ovarian cancer

title: Profiling Molecular Signals Associated With Podocyte Effacement in Minimal Change Nephrotic Syndrome Following Th2 Cytokine Stimulation
abs: Minimal change nephrotic syndrome (MCNS) is the most common childhood glomerulonephritides in Singapore. Studies suggest that MCNS probably results from a primary immune disturbance with a Th2 cytokine bias. We have shown that T-cell interleukin-13 (IL-13) gene was up-regulated during relapses of MCNS. We have recently published an IL-13 overexpression rat model of MCNS with podocyte foot-process effacement, a hallmark of the disease, accompanied by downregulation of podocyte-associated proteins with concurrent upregulation of B7-1 expression via toll-like receptor (TLR) pathways. We hypothesize that downregulation of glomerular expression of nephrin, podocin and dystroglycan in IL-13 transfected rats could either be due to a direct effect of IL-13 signaling on the podocyte, or a consequence of IL-13-induced B7-1 danger signaling via TLR in podocytes.This project aims to investigate the molecular mechanisms by which IL-13 downregulates the expression of podocyte-specific proteins. The specific objectives are:1. To determine the mechanism by which IL-13 induces podocyte B7-1 signaling in the rat IL-13 overexpression model of MCNS, and the role of TLRs in this signaling process. 2. To set up a podocyte cell culture system to study the effect of IL-13 on: a. Expression of podocyte markers, cytoskeletal proteins, integrins and IL-13 receptor subunits, both at the gene transcription (real-time PCR) and protein level (immunoblotting and immunohistochemistry) b. B7-1 and TLR expression, and to further explore this relationship using inhibitory experiments either with siRNA or antibody blocking strategy 3. To study changes in podocyte gene expression profile in the IL-13 overexpression rat model as well as in-vitro podocyte culture system using microarray, so as to map potential IL-13 signaling pathways in the podocyte.Knowledge of the signaling pathways involved in the pathogenesis of this disease may provide us more targeted treatment at the molecular level, allowing us to design new therapeutic strategies.

title: Use of high resolution melting as a screening tool for podocyte mutations in a South-East Asian population
abs: Childhood steroid-resistant or steroid-dependent nephrotic syndrome (SRNS/SDNS) is a potentially debilitating disease because of its poorer prognosis and adverse effects of immunosuppressive therapy. Mutations in podocyte proteins including podocin (NPHS2), nephrin (NPHS1), a-actinin-4 (ACTN4), CD2-adaptor protein (CD2AP), transient-receptor-potential-channel-6 (TRCP6), and more recently wilm’s tumour-1 (WT1), have been identified as important causes. Ethnic differences in genotypes and clinical outcomes have been described in European populations. Our preliminary study has shown a low mutation detection rate of 1.8% in the coding regions of the podocin genes among Singapore patients with sporadic SRNS/SDNS. This concurs with the low mutation rates of 0-4% in Japan and China, in contrast to the higher mutation rates of 8-20% in Caucasian and Middle-Eastern populations. Additionally, we detected polymorphisms 954T>C and 1038A>G in exon 8 in patients and controls, occurring at allelic frequencies similar to those in Taiwan. In Singapore, there appears to be an increased prevalence of SRNS among Malay patients, and a greater tendency towards end-stage renal failure (ESRF). We therefore hypothesize that the pathogenesis of primary glomerulopathies is different in Asian patients, and functional polymorphisms or mutations in podocyte genes may account for the different clinical course. The aim of this study is to screen patients with primary nephrotic syndrome or persistent proteinuria for mutations/polymorphisms in coding and non-coding regions, including the promoter regions of NPHS2, NPHS1, CD2AP, ACTN4, TRPC6 and WT1. Genomic DNA will be subjected to mutational analyses using high resolution melting (HRM) as the initial screen and further validated by direct sequencing. Any genetic variants detected will be checked in healthy controls, and correlated with the clinical course. Further functionality studies will be performed on identified novel mutations. This study may provide a genetic biomarker for SRNS/SDNS, identifying patients at risk of poor response to standard immunosuppressive therapy and progression to ESRF.
kw: Glomerulosclerosis, Proteinuria, Nephrotic syndrome, Mutations, High resolution melting, Podocyte

title: Elucidation of cellular pathways deregulated by HBx through the deregulation of miRNAs.
abs: Majority of the hepatocellular-carcinoma (HCC) patients in Singapore and this part of the world chronically harbour the hepatitis-B virus (HBV). Compelling evidence implicates HBV as a major etiologic factor in HCC. The X protein of HBV, HBx, is a promiscuous transcriptional trans-activator believed to play a role in hepatocarcinogenesis. To develop better strategies in combating HBV-associated HCC, knowledge of the mechanism of HBx’s action in the cell is crucial. In addition to deregulating gene expression by binding to proteins that binds specific genes, we propose that the oncogenic potential of HBx also lies in its ability to deregulate gene expression at post-transcriptional levels via miRNAs. De-regulation of cellular gene expression post-transcriptionally by HBx will be explored through profiling of miRNAs in cells expressing HBx as well as in HBV-positive HCC patients. These profiles will be correlated with the HBx status in these patients as well as their prognosis including their survival, severity/stage of disease and disease progression. miRNA profiling represents a novel way to characterize HBx-associated HCC and complements existing data from microarray studies. The gene targets of the miRNAs will be initially identified using in silico approaches and then validated experimentally. Pathways deregulated by HBx through miRNAs will be delineated through a multi-prong approach. Computational methods will be utilized to integrate data from miRNA expression profiles, prediction of miRNA putative targets, mRNA expression profiles, protein expression profiles and phosphorylation/dephosphorylation profiles so as to identify a few important/significant pathways affected by HBx. The effect of the over-expression / inhibition of these miRNAs in cells on cell growth, cell-cycle and apoptotic profiles, chromosome/genome stability and transformation ability will be examined. The possible identification of significant pathways deregulated by HBx through the deregulation of miRNA expression has potential diagnostic and therapeutic applications and will open up new avenues for future research.
kw: hepatocellular carcinoma, miRNA, Regulation of Gene Expression, HBx, Phosphorylation

title: Molecular Characterisation of the Abnormally Increased but Error Prone non-Homologous End-joining (NHEJ) in Cell Lines Derived from Adult Cancer Patients with Late Radionecrosis
abs: Significance/BackgroundAs many as 5% of individuals undergoing curative conventional radiotherapy experience an unexpected severe late morbidity. In particular, radiation necrosis is irreversible and can be vastly debilitating. To understand the molecular mechanisms underlying radiation necrosis, in our previous proposal, we studied non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) in extracts of cell lines derived from patients with late radio-necrosis. We utilized a cell-free plasmid DNA rejoining system and real-time PCR (qPCR) quantitation. Additionally, since ionizing radiation (IR) produces DNA ends which frequently require processing prior to ligation, we utilized plasmid DNA ends that could be ligated directly and non-compatible ends (which require processing prior to ligation).Paradoxically, we found that the cell extracts (LB0004 and LB0005) display increased rates of in vitro end-joining of non-cohesive termini, as compared to that of normal cell extracts. This increase is seen in the absence of added deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates and is sensitive to inhibition by wortmannin. Sequencing of the joined products reveals that, despite increased rates of end-joining, the process is error-prone with a higher frequency of deletions compared to that observed in normal controls. These findings suggest that a promiscuous, deletion-prone abnormality of NHEJ may underpin the predisposition of certain radiotherapy patients to late radionecrosis.Hypothesis, aim, methodologyWe hypothesize that this is a subclinical defect in NHEJ, which clinically manifests itself upon challenge with high-dose radiation. We aim to further characterise and elucidate the molecular defect(s) underlying the error-prone NHEJ abnormality described. To this end we propose to examine:1.If the defect in each cell line is a gain or a loss of function;2.If the defect is due to genetic alteration (s) in one and the same NHEJ gene;3.The differences in NHEJ protein complexes that are co-immunoprecipitated with antibodies to the known NHEJ proteins or are “pulled down” using a recombinant form of one of the known NHEJ proteins as “bait”; and finally,4.The functional status of the known NHEJ protein complexes in these extracts.

title: Prophylactic laser iridotomy for eyes with narrow drainage angles: A randomized controlled trial.
abs: Glaucoma is the leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide. With ageing of the population, glaucoma morbidity will rise, causing increased health care costs and economic burden for a condition in which visual loss, once established, cannot be reversed. In contrast to western countries, primary angle closure glaucoma (PACG) is a major form of glaucoma in Asia. In a recent population based survey in Singapore, the prevalence of glaucoma was 3.2% in the Chinese population over 40. Glaucoma was the leading cause of blindness, with PACG the most visually destructive form of the disease. It was estimated that 10% of the population have narrow angles (NA), the anatomical trait predisposing to PACG. Laser iridotomy (LI) is a proven treatment for established angle closure. In eyes with NA, LI performed prophylactically can arrest angle-closure, and prevent acute attacks of angle closure from developing. However, as the natural history of NA is not established, data are limited on who should have prophylactic therapy or remain untreated, and it is not known if performing LI for all eyes with NA is cost effective.The proposed study is a randomized controlled trial that aims to compare LI versus no treatment in 544 subjects with NA in order to assess the effectiveness of LI in the prevention of PACG. One eye of each subject will be randomized to undergo LI, and the other eye will be left untreated as an internal control. Subjects will then be followed up once a year for at least 5 years. The outcome criteria will be the development of peripheral anterior synechiae and/or raised intraocular pressure. This study will address the question of whether prophylactic LI can arrest the progressive blinding course for which PACG is renowned. The study findings will have great relevance for the prevention of blindness in the elderly worldwide.
kw: glaucoma, blindness, elderly, angle closure, visual impairment, prevention

title: Identification of genome-wide DNA methylation pattern in Nasopharyngeal carcinoma by the novel MIRA-assisted microarray analysis
abs: Nasopharyngeal cancer (NPC) is a rare tumor arising from the epithelium of nasopharynx and it is one of the most confusing, commonly misdiagnosed and poorly understood diseases. The cancer is an Epstein-Barr virus-associated malignancy with a remarkable racial and geographical distribution. It is more prevalent among Chinese population and more common in men. The etiology of NPC is thought to be associated with a complex interaction of genetic, viral, environmental and dietary factors. NPC is commonly diagnosed late due to its deep location and vague symptoms that appears very late during cancer progression. Hence, studies to understand the molecular characteristics of the malignancy and to discover biomarkers to diagnose, stage and prognosticate the disease are highly warranted for meaningful management of NPC. Methylation of CpG islands in the genomic DNA is one of the epigenetic events that represents an alternative mechanism to deletions or mutations to inactivate tumor suppressor genes. Recent evidence supports the notion that CpG island rmethylation, by silencing key cancer-related genes, plays a major causal role in cancer. Accumulating evidence indicates that CpG island methylation is an early event in cancer development and, in some cases, may precede the neoplastic process. On the other hand, altered DNA methylation can occur at all stages of the cancer progression thus might provide a great value in the classification and staging of cancer. In contrast to the RNA and protein based biomarkers of cancer cells, which are biologically and biochemically unstable, the stable epigenetic inheritance of DNA methylation of informative genes makes them attractive candidates for their utility in cancer detection. Hence, in this exploratory study, genome-wide identification and cataloguing of methylated genes in the nasopharyngneal cancer cell lines in comparison to the normal cells has been proposed. This will be accomplished by selective enrichment of methylated sequences from normal and NPC cell lines by MIRA (methylated-CpG island recovery assay) followed by microarray analysis.
kw: DNA methylation, CpG islands, Microarray, MIRA, NPC, Gene expression

title: Molecular Engineering of Membrane Materials Research and Technology for Energy Development: Hydrogen, Natural Gas and Syngas
abs: Breakthroughs in materials research and engineering for the production of hydrogen, natural gas and syngas require design and synthesis of materials that have specificity and recognition ability at molecular levels to achieve effective purification and separation. Separating H₂ and CO₂ by polymeric membranes is extremely challenging because most polymers show poor H₂/CO₂ selectivity. Even though there is a difference in molecular size (H₂ (2.89 A°) vs. CO₂ (3.30 A°) in kinetic diameter), the solubility of carbon dioxide is much higher than that of hydrogen. Consequently, there is not much permselectivity owing to these competing effects. CO₂-induced plasticization also makes size-based separations difficult. Similarly, current material technologies for natural gas purification and separation are far from perfect - their selectivity is reduced significantly during use because of the CO₂- and H₂S-induced plasticization. Advancements in novel materials as well as physical and chemical modification technologies with the aid of molecular design of materials are needed to stabilize the interstitial chain space and separation performance. Catalytic transformation of methane into syngas can be accomplished with a high conversion by integrating air separation (O₂ + N₂ ---> O₂/N₂) with the catalytic reforming of methane (e.g., 2CH₄ + O₂ ---> 4H₂ + 2CO ). This is the most promising industrial process for syngas production because ceramics containing free electrons and lattice oxygen vacancies make electrochemical separation of O₂ from air with infinite permselectivity possible. Integrating such unique materials with a methane reforming catalyst to form an air separation / methane reforming reactor forms one of our core objectives for building a lab-scale pilot reactor to produce syngas through an energy-saving route. Sophisticated molecular modeling and simulation approaches will be used (i) to analyze experimental data, (ii) to elucidate and model the electrochemical separation and catalytic process, and (iii) to assist the development of tailored functional materials.
kw: Molecular engineering of membrane materials;Hydrogen purification and separation;Natural gas purification and separation;Syngas;Mixed-conducting ceramic materials;Statistical-mechanics modeling and simulation

title: Tri-phasic silk/stem cell-based bone-ligament-bone construct in the repair of medial collateral ligament in rabbits
abs: The exhibition of genomic instability is a major hallmark of all human cancers, particularly solid tumors. These aberrations can range from micro-level DNA instability in mismatch-repair deficient tumors to gross aneuploidy including amplifications, translocations, and deletions of partial or entire chromosomes. Studies have shown that several of these chromosomal aberrations are often recurrently observed across multiple tumor types and are frequently associated with disease prognosis and treatment response, presumably by functionally disrupting key oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes localized within the aberrant genomic region. Over the past few years, the use of microarray-based approaches for studying such chromosomal aberrations (array-based comparative genomic hybridization, array-CGH) has revolutionized our ability to delineate the fine scale structure of these genomic aberrations at unprecedented levels of resolution. However, most array-CGH studies to date have relied on analyzing high-quality genomic DNAs isolated from either fresh or snap-frozen tissues, thereby limiting their applicability to centers where such tissue-banking procedures are commonplace. In contrast, the vast majority of patient materials in standard clinical pathology archives are typically stored as formalin-fixed paraffin embedded (FFPE) tissues. Here, we propose to evaluate the feasibility of performing array-CGH on genomic DNAs isolated from FFPE tissues. Specifically, we aim to I) establish protocols and quality control metrics for extracting FFPE genomic DNA, II) evaluate the robustness of using FFPE extracted gDNA for array-CGH, using three commercial microarray platforms, and III) compare array-CGH profiles from both frozen tissues and FFPE tissues to identify potential systematic patterns of noise or bias associated with FFPE samples. If successful, the ability to perform FFPE-based array-CGH will significantly broaden the utility of this powerful technique, including the ability to analyze retrospective sample banks of FFPE samples, and the interrogation of tumor subcompartments isolated via laser-capture or other microdissection techniques.

title: Roles of mll5 in zebrafish hematopoiesis
abs: MLL5 (Mixed Lineage Leukemia-5) is a candidate tumor suppressor gene, recently identified within the locus of the most common recurring cytogenetic aberrations detected in acute myeloid malignancies. It encodes a novel member of the Trx-G gene family, whose members control the expression of HOX genes in the development through the modulation of chromatin. MLL5 possesses a single PHD zinc finger and a SET domain at its N-terminal region, and is highly conserved throughout evolution. MLL5 protein localized to nuclear speckles and exogenous production of MLL5 protein inhibits cell cycle progression. Depletion of MLL5 resulted in growth arrest both at G1 and G2/M phase and phosphorylation of MLL5 at mitosis is required for cell cycle progression. Silencing of MLL5 homologue, CG9007, in Drosophila embryos was reported to disrupt normal heart development. Given that it might have important roles in cell cycle regulation and development, it is important to establish a suitable animal model to study its biological function. The zebrafish model is chosen because it has been a well-established system for the analysis of vertebrate hematopoiesis. In addition, an efficient morpholino-mediated gene knockdown method has been established. Our pilot study suggested that knockdown of zebrafish mll5 displayed a bloodless phenotype, urging us to further study its roles in hematopoiesis. This research proposal aims to determine the expression patterns of different zebrafish mll5 isoforms during embryogenesis and investigate their functions in hematopoiesis, vasculogenesis and cardiogenesis. The animal model established and the data generated from this study will be important for unraveling the physiological function of MLL5 and potentially contributing to our knowledge of hematopoiesis and hematology
kw: MLL5, morpholino, blood circulation, zebrafish, in situ hybridization, hematopoiesis

title: Lipidomics: Novel Tools and Applications
abs: The critical role of lipids in cell, tissue and organ physiology is demonstrated by a large number of genetic studies and by many human diseases involving the disruption of lipid metabolic enzymes and pathways. Examples of such diseases include cancer, diabetes, neurodegenerative and infectious disorders. So far, the explosion of information in the fields of genomics and proteomics has not been matched by a corresponding advancement of knowledge in the field of lipids. This is largely due to the complexity of lipids and the lack of powerful tools for their analysis. Novel analytical approaches now allow for systems level analysis of lipids and their interacting partners (lipidomics). Here we propose a project on lipidomics which aims to (i) excel in science, research and education of lipid biology, (ii) engineer novel tools for lipid research which go far beyond current trends in biochemical lipidomics, (iii) apply such novel approaches to biomedical and environmental research. We will include two prominent areas of R&D focus in Singapore, namely immunology/infectious diseases and ageing/neurodegeneration. A lipidomics program in such a format does not exist anywhere in the world to our knowledge. The Novartis Institute for Tropical Diseases as well as analytical instrument manufacturer Applied Biosystems are included as industry partners in co-development and application of the above tools. The program will connect nationally and internationally with new initiatives such as the SMART center for Infectious Diseases, SystemsX.ch (ETH Zurich), and the Cellular Neuroscience, Neurodegeneration and Repair (CNNR) program at Yale University (academic partners).
kw: lipidomics;lipid-protein interactions;mass spectrometry;infectious diseases;ageing;systems biology
