title: Toward the development of polyproline type II peptide-based, entropy-driven MHC blocker as novel and general therapeutics and prophylactics for treating autoimmune diseases.
abs: The goal of this project is to explore the development of entropy-driven MHC blocker as ageneral approach for treating autoimmune diseases (ADs), using celiac disease as a model system.Celiac disease is a well-characterized AD in which individuals with class II major histocompatibilitycomplex (MHCII) allele HLA-DQ2 are predisposed to intestinal inflammation upon ingestion of glutenprotein. T-cells are thought to be activated by DQ2 displaying antigenic gluten peptide a-gliadin andattack the intestinal linings. Unlike other ADs that are usually irreversible after onset, celiac disease isremissible if a-gliadin is eliminated from diet, suggesting that the disease is treatable by blockingDQ2-a-gliadin interaction. This unique feature makes celiac disease an ideal model system forestablishing a general approach in developing prophylactic MHCII-blockers for addressing other ADs.Previous crystallographic study showed that, as in most MHCII-peptide complexes, the epitopepeptide, aI-gliadin, adopts a polyproline type II (PPII) conformation when bound to DQ2. Ourhypothesis is that peptides with higher PPII content would bind stronger to MHCII. Peptides thatnaturally assume PPII conformation should have entropic advantage over non-PPII peptides inbinding to MHCII. This entropic advantage would translate into tighter MHCII-peptide interactions. Bycombining the known non-immunogenic a-gliadin motif with the PPII content that permits tighter DQ2-binding than a-gliadin, we anticipate to be able to generate potent natural peptide therapeutics fortreating and preventing ADs. Specifically, we plan to chemically synthesize a library of a-gliadin-likepeptides with varying degrees of PPII content and study the relationships among the PPII content,MHC binding affinity, protease resistivity, cell-penetrating property and antigenicity of the peptidesusing well-established physicochemical, enzymological and cell biological methods. On a long term,our study should help develop a general clinical treatment for alleviating and preventing other ADs forwhich cure or treatment is still sub-optimal or non-existent.
kw: Autoimmune disease, Class II MHC, Polyproline type II, MHC blocker, HLA DQ2, Solid phase peptide synthesis

title: THE ROLE OF HMGB1 PROTEIN IN MEDIATING VASCULAR PERMEABILITY DURING DENGUE VIRUS INFECTION.
abs: Dengue has emerged as the most important arbovirus human disease in the last three decades. Currently, there are no approved anti-viral agents or vaccine for dengue virus. Dengue virus is a member of the Flavivirus genus of the Flaviviridae family that causes dengue fever (DF) and the life-threatening dengue hemorrhagic fever/dengue shock syndrome (DHF/DSS). The pathogenesis of DHF is poorly understood. This project is directed to probe on one of the most important question to be answered with the availability of current technologies. How does the interaction of host factor(s) with dengue virus contribute to the pathogenesis of dengue hemorrhage? Although, some preliminary studies have been carried out to understand mystery of increased vascular permeability during dengue virus infection, the functional role(s) of host protein(s) in mediating increased vascular permeability during dengue virus infection remains largely unknown. In this project, we will examine the role of inflammatory modulating molecules [High Mobility group (HMGB) protein and viral double-stranded RNA] in mediating vascular permeability and their contributions to dengue virus pathogenesis. Both cellular-based and the murine model of vascular permeability will be set up to interrogate the complex interaction of HMGB protein and dengue virus infection. We will also focus on the elucidation of the host genetics\factors and signaling pathway(s) that contribute to dengue virus-induced vascular permeability by using small interfering RNA screen complemented with microarray profiling. Together, these experiments will generate novel insights to the pathogenesis of DHF. Most importantly, the clinical relevant knowledge gained from this study will accelerate the development of anti-dengue virus strategies and better clinical management of this medically important pathogen.
kw: Flavivirus, High Mobility Group Protein, Host factors, Dengue virus, Vascular leak, Anti-viral therapeutics

title: Cryopreserved cadaveric vascular grafts: Studying the long term effects of Cyropreservation
abs: Background and clinical significance of StudyHomografts remain the best grafts for vascular replacement. At present, synthetic grafts are utilized when vascular homografts are not available. However, these synthetic grafts are expensive and are not suitable for certain surgical scenarios. We believe that cryopreservation of cadaveric vascular grafts may potentially address this. Cryopreservation protocols are now well described. Various teams have also studied the effects of cryopreservation on vascular grafts and some preliminary data showed promising results using grafts cryopreserved for short periods. However, very little is known of the effects of cryopreservation over prolonged periods of time. AimWe intend to study the effects of cryopreservation on cadaveric iliac vascular grafts using in vitro models.HypothesisThe duration of cryopreservation does not affect the biomechanical and histopathological properties of vascular homografts.MethodsHarvesting of cadaveric graftsApproximately 12 arterial and 12 vein grafts in 12 months of procurement period will be harvested from cadaveric donors.Treatment of the graftsEach of the harvested grafts will be divided into 2 segments. The first segement will undergo immediate histological and biomechanical assessment immediately and this will serve as control. The second will undergo cryopreservation over several periods. Histological assessement.The morphology of vascular segment will be evaluated by light, scanning and transmission electron microscopy. Biomechanical assessmentEach segment will be tested in a circulation mock, and its pressure and diameter were registered for the assessment of the arterial wall dynamics. Timing of thawing of graft segmentThere will be 12 arterial and venous grafts harvested over a 12 month period. All 12 pairs of segments will be thawed at the same time at the 13th month from the time of first graft harvested thereby giving an average of one-cryopreserved-month interval for all the grafts i.e. the longest cryopreservation time will be 13 months and the shortest will be 1 month.
kw: Cryopreservation, Artery, Biomechanical properties, Homografts, Vein, Histological changes

title: MG11-PEG-modified E1/E3-deleted adenovirus vector for selective gene transfer into Glioma Tumor
abs: AimsTherapeutic gene transfer by recombinant adenovirus (rAdv) offers a potential therapy for the treatment of malignant gliomas. There are, however, two major limitations associated with rAdv for gene delivery. One area is related to the non-tumor selectivity and broad tropism of rAdv and the second area is concerning immune responses directed towards rAdv viral capsid and transgene protein during systemic administration, thereby limiting the length of transgene expression. In this pilot proposal, we would like to test if these 2 limitations of rAdv could be overcome by constructing a chemically modified rAdv with gliomas specificity and reduced vector antigenicity and immunogenicity. Gliomas specificity is achieved by MG11 peptide that had been identified previously in our laboratory. It is a 12-amino acid peptide LWATFPPRPPWL having 64% sequence homology to semaphorin 4B precursor protein. Reduced vector antigenicity and immunogenicity is achieved by using polyethylene glycol (PEG) molecules. PEG modification is a well-established technique for the modification of therapeutic peptides and proteins. In short, the virus capsid of E1/E3 replication-deficient rAdv will be modified with bifunctiotinal PEG and then conjugated with glioma specific, MG11 peptide. HypothesesMG11 on rAdv will target rAdv to human gliomas in vivo. In addition, the surface modification of rAdv capsid with PEGylated-MG11 peptide will ablate the normal tropism and selectively target tumor of glial origin in vivo and thereby reducing potential toxicity to non-targeted normal cells. In addition, PEG-modified rAdv, in contrast to unmodified virus, will be protected from anti-adenoviral neutralizing antibodies presumably due to masking of the antigenic epitopes on the surface of the virus by PEG molecules, thus allowing repeated administrations of rAdv vectors. MethodologyThe E1/E3 replication-defective rAdv vector which expresses firefly luciferase under the control of cytomegalovirus (CMV) promoter will be conjugated with poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) or MG11-PEG. The transduction efficiency of rAdv vectors (PEG-AdLuc and MG11-PEG-AdLuc) into different type of cells will be analyzed. The selective gliomas targeting and infectivity of the rAdv after intravenous injection into U87MG and Hep3B (nonglioma cell control) tumor-bearing athymic nude mice will be assessed by noninvasive imaging. Approach of the research proposal including its importance to science or medicine in particular clinical significanceThe ability to achieve selective targeting of therapeutic genes by MG11-PEG-modified rAdv vector with deletion in the native tropism will improve targeting to gliomas and reduce potential toxicity to non-targeted normal cells. In addition, PEG modification protected the virus from neutralizing antibodies in preimmunised animals, which will allow significant gene expression and repeated administration of rAdv vectors
kw: Replication -deficient Adenovirus vector, Glioma-specific peptide, MG11, Poly(ethylene glycol),PEG, gliomas, Vector antigenicity and immunogenicity, Systemic readministration

title: In vivo and in vitro identifying transcription regulatory mechanism of vascular specific Nox4 in TNF-?-induced oxidative stress.
abs: Oxidative stress and reactive oxygen species (ROS) underpin the pathogenesis of cardiovascular diseases including atherosclerosis. NADPH oxidase is a predominant source of ROS and activation of this enzyme leads to intracellular signaling events causing endothelial dysfunction, proliferation of vascular smooth muscle cells and expression of pro-inflammatory genes. Identification of novel signaling and transcription regulatory mechanism of NADPH oxidase components, specifically Nox4, is crucial for improved intervention of atherosclerosis.Our published work has shown that TNF-a induced oxidative stress in vascular smooth muscle cells is mediated by NADPH oxidase and specifically by upregulation of Nox4. Our preliminary results showed that TNF-a induced oxidative stress in vascular smooth muscle cells through Nox4 up-regulation was mediated by JNK signaling pathway. Moreover, we have shown that Nox4 is the vascular specific isoform that mediates TNF-a induced oxidative stress in vascular smooth muscle cells.In the current proposal, we aim to investigate transcription regulatory mechanism of TNF-a-induced Nox4 upregulation that leads to oxidative stress in vascular smooth muscle cells in vitro and in vivo transgenic TNF1.6 model. We will identify the transcription factor(s) that regulates Nox4 and transcription factor binding site by molecular cloning and characterization of Nox4 gene promoter. Furthermore, we will examine the signaling mechanism and transcription regulation of Nox4 in vascular smooth muscle cells of arterial samples from transgenic TNF1.6 model.Elucidating the novel in vitro transcription regulatory mechanism holds promise for rational targeted therapy. Furthermore, TNF-a-induced oxidative stress through Nox4 upregulation in experimental transgenic model is crucial to understand in vivo inflammatory mechanisms and to develop therapy for atherosclerosis.
kw: TNF, Transcription regulation, Nox4, Oxidative stress, Signaling mechanism

title: The role of epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in colon cancer metastasis: An immunohistochemical analysis of newly identified EMT markers on clinical samples of colon tumors and metastases.
abs: Metastasis is the leading cause of death among colon cancer patients. The current therapeutic regimens remain ineffective in the treatment of advanced stages of colon cancer with metastases. Therefore, an understanding of the molecular mechanisms in the acquisition of the metastatic phenotype is required to provide more effective therapeutic targets and prognostic markers of disease progression. One of the mechanisms implicated in the progression from carcinoma-in-situ to invasive and metastatic cancer is epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT). Molecular markers of EMT, such as E-cadherin and Snail1, have been identified and defines end-points of the EMT process. However, there are numerous examples of advanced carcinoma cells capable of metastasizing, that adopt only a subset of mesenchymal features and retain characteristics of well-differentiated epithelial cells or exhibit an absence of the end-point features of EMT. It appears that the transition from an epithelial to a mesenchymal morphology is a continuum. A deeper understanding of this process is necessary to facilitate the identification of useful targets and markers of metastatic disease. We have derived a metastatic cell line, E1, by in vivo passaging of the poorly metastatic human colon cancer cell line HCT116 in athymic nude mice. The E1 cell line is unique in that it shows stable and partial EMT and hence, would be a useful model to study transitional events underlying this process. Further, it is likely to be a more authentic model since the cell line was derived from an in vivo colony, compared to current models where EMT is induced in vitro by a variety of growth factors. Gene expression array analysis on the E1 cell line in comparison to the parental HCT116 identified the involvement of the Erk signaling pathway and candidate genes including palladin, BMP4, Sox9 and Jag1, in the EMT process. This grant aims to extend the evaluation of 10 candidate genes (palladin, BMP4, Sox 4, Sox9, Jag1, HoxC10, DLG5, TMOD3, ABLIM1, RhoB) to determine their expression and usefulness as markers in human colorectal tumor samples by immunohistochemical analysis
kw: Colon cancer, metastasis, EMT, Invasive front

title: Development and characterization of xeno-/serum-free medium for the enhancement of human bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells ex vivo expansion suitable for efficient clinical cellular therapy.
abs: Bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) are attractive candidates for cell therapy and tissue regeneration due to their relative easy isolation, capacity for ex vivo expansion and multipotency. However, BMSCs are currently expanded in vitro, in the presence of 10–20% fetal calf serum (FCS). This poses a major obstacle for their clinical use due to concern about the biosafety of FCS. In addition, for clinical applications that require vast amounts of MSCs, the time delay caused by current ex vivo expansion protocols might result in senescence of the expanded cells and this may be detrimental to the patient. The objective of this proposal is to identify the available xeno- and serum-free serum replacements that can support BMSC expansion and will be suitable for clinical application. Fibroblast growth factor (FGF) and Wnt signaling activation will be explored for their ability to enhance the proliferation rate of BMSCs in the serum free system. Resulting MSCs will undergo a series of characterization of their phenotype, multipotency, immunogenic properties and senescence status.The resulting outcomes will form the basis for a more comprehensive evaluation of these ex-vivo expanded BMSCs for clinical and therapeutic use.
kw: mesenchymal stem cells, Serum free, senescence, Ex vivo expansion, Xeno-free

title: Evaluation of a combination treatment of traumatic brain injury by neuronal differentiated bone marrow stromal cells and DNA vaccine
abs: Nearly 5.8 million people globally perish from traumatic brain injury (TBI) in 1998 according to the World Health Organization (WHO). Additionally, the number of injury cases requiring prolonged hospitalization is 30-fold greater and the number of cases admitted in intensive care units is 300-fold larger (Holder et al., 2001), In Singapore, trauma remains the 5th leading cause of morbidity and mortality according to the 2005 statistic report from the Ministry of Health and more than half of these have an traumatic brain injury as a primary injury. A large number of TBI victims have long-term disabilities, resulting in a significant economic burden to families, care-givers and society (Marshall et al., 2000), due to the lack of effective therapy.Neural regeneration from endogenous neurons and cell transplantation has shown to be a promising therapy. However, neural regeneration in injury requires anatomical and functional reconstitution of the neuronal pool. After brain injury, death of many neurons and the hostile environment created as a result of the cascades of cell death, as well as the presence of neurite growth inhibitors in the unfavorable metabolic milieu inhibit regeneration in central nervous system (CNS). Therefore, the approach to promote neuronal regeneration by blocking these inhibitors is one of the promising potential therapeutic targets in TBI.On the other hand, cell transplantation has been recently demonstrated as a promising treatment for various neuronal disorders, including TBI. Bone morrow stromal cells (BMSCs) have been used to treat the TBI with optimistic outcomes. However, the efficacy needs to be improved as only a small proportion of bone marrow cells are transformed into neuronal-like cells after transplantation and many BMSCs dies in the hostile conditions of the damaged brain. We assume that neuronal differentiated BMSCs in vitro will enable them more potently participate in the neural regeneration in TBI. Favorable condition created by blocking neurite growth inhibitors with the DNA vaccine will further enhance the neural regeneration. We have previously proven in our studies with regards to the neuroprotective effect of autoantibodies against NGIs induced by DNA vaccine. Moreover, we have also shown that neuronal differentiated BMSCs can effectively participate in the reconstruction of damaged spinal cord. Thus, this proposal is aimed to determine the effects on enhancement regeneration of neuron and recovery of behavior using transplantation neuron differentiated from BMSCs in vitro in combination with DNA vaccine in a rodent TBI model.
kw: Traumatic brain injury, Cell transplatation, DNA vaccine, Bone marrow stromal cell, Neuronal differentiation, Treatment

title: Bionic voice - technology for voice replacement in post-laryngectomised patients.
abs: The speech production process involves lung exhalation vibrating a taught glottis to create a varying pitch signal which resonates through the vocal tract, nasal cavity and out through the mouth. Within the vocal, buccal and nasal cavities, the vellum, tongue, and lip positions play crucial roles in shaping speech sounds ( we refer to this collectively as vocal tract modulation ). Total laryngectomy patients will have lost their glottis and furthermore also to pass lung exhalation through the vocal tract. Partial laryngectomy patients may still retain the power of controlled lung exhalation. Despite the loss of glottis, both classes of patient retain the power of vocal tract modulation - in other words they maintain most of the speech production apparatus. In the 1960s devices such as the electropharynx were developed to resonate the vocal tract, replacing the role of glottal resonance and lung excitation. Resultant speech can be intelligible, but is obviously artificial, and operation of the devices is clumsy. Oesophageal speech is difficult to learn and does not sound like natural speech, but carry risk of infection and are equally clumsy in use. In this project, we will develop portable equipment to ultrasonically map vocal tract shape as a patient 'speaks'. This map plus detected lung exhalation will be applied to an artificial glottal resonance to recreate natural sounding speech within the portable electronics ( in the same way that a handphone works-not using the vocal tract itself to create the sound ). The glottal resonance is to be dynamically and naturally varied based on recordings of the patients' original voice if available, leading to more natural recreated speech. Eventually the 'bionic voice' will return the power of natural-sounding speech to laryngectomy patients, and be useful for temporary voice rest cases.
kw: Laryngectomy, Rehabilitation, Vocal tract, Speech, Glottis, Voice-rest

title: Shoulder biomechanics in massive rotator cuff tears.
abs: Specific aims: To study the disturbance in shoulder biomechanics in patients with massive irreparable rotator cuff tears.Hypothesis: Shoulder abduction and flexion is severely limited in the presence of major cuff tears. We hypothesize that the length tension relationship of the deltoid is disturbed in these patients resulting in its inability to effect abduction or flexion of the shoulder.Methodology: 25 patients with massive irreparable cuff tears that result in loss or weakness of active shoulder abduction will be studied.Both the affected and normal shoulders will be analysed.-Motion analysis of the shoulders will be studied during abduction with radio-opaque markers over bony prominences of the scapulae and the cervical and thoracic spinous processes.-An EMG study using both surface and fine needles on and in the major muscles of the shoulder will be conducted during abduction.-Plain anteroposterior radiography of both shoulders in the neutral and abducted positions will be taken.-Finally still clinical photographs from the back will be taken of both shoulders in the neutral and abducted positions.This study will confirm our hypothesis and help in the design of a subacromial spacer that will restore the normal length tension relationship of the deltoid and which will facilitate shoulder motion. The prosthetic design will be the subject of a subsequent study.
kw: Superior humeral head migration, Premature scapula rotation

title: Glucose-evoked renal cell death and underlying molecular mechanisms: in relevance to the development of diabetic nephropathy
abs: Nephropathy which his one of the microvascular complications in types 1 and 2 diabetes is now the leading cause of end stage renal disease. It casts a great social economic burden on societies. Poor glycemic control, hypertension, dyslipidemia and genetic determinants are amongst the recognized risk factors. Possible interplays between environmental (metabolic and societal) factors and genetic components are also implicated. Despite the consensus on the major risk factors, very little is known about the ideology of diabetic nephropathy. More recently, apoptotic death of renal cells is increasingly recognized in the development of diabetic nephropathy. However, many critical issues remain to be addressed for a better understanding the roles of renal cell apoptosis in pathogenesis of nephropathy in diabetes. In the proposed pilot study, we aim to: 1. establish cell line models of renal cell (mesangial and proximal tubular cells) apoptosis evoked by high concentration of glucose, for investigations of the underlying molecular mechanisms. In this group of experiments, the sensitivity of the two renal cell lines towards glucose toxicity will be determined and compared. These can be achieved by determining cell survival assay rate and percentage of sub-G1 cells, using XTT and flow cytometry assays respectively; 2. investigate whether the polyol pathway (i.e., aldose reductase) and oxidative stress play their roles in the glucose-mediated renal cell apoptosis, aldose reductase inhibition, quantification and modification of reactive oxygen species; and 3. document globally candidate protein signal mediators involving in the glucose-triggered renal cell apoptotic death, through proteomic analysis. All the required techniques are established in my laboratory. Expected outcomes would demonstrate and compare sensitivities of mesangial and proximal tubular cells towards glucose-evoked apoptosis. Molecular analyses would assess roughly possible involvement of redox regulation, and identify some signal transduction proteins in the renal cell apoptosis. Thus, the pilot study would produce a phathophysiology-relevant experimental model for further IRG-based study of renal cell apoptosis and underlying molecular mechanisms, which might identify molecular probes for diagnostic and/or therapeutic development.
kw: Diabetic nephropathy, Glucose toxicity, Apoptosis, Functional proteomics, Cell signal transduction, Redox

title: A Phase One Case-Control Study to Evaluate the Risk Factors for Prostate Cancer
abs: Although the incidence of carcinoma of the prostate (CAP) is increasing rapidly especially in the developed world, the aetiology of this disease remains poorly understood. The rate of CAP in Singapore is rising although not as dramatically. It would be very important at this initial stage (Singapore is one of the few countries in this transitional position with accessible high quality data) to determine what the risk factors are for CAP in Singapore. There are 2 Phases to this study. For this proposal, we are seeking funding for Phase One of the study. The aims of this Phase One are to: 1) Fine-tune the operational aspects for a larger population-based case-control study; 2) Study lifestyle risk factors that may be associated with CP; and 3) Collect blood and tissues samples for Phase Two where we will be studying gene and environment interaction .The Phase Two of the study (once we have successfully carried out Phase One; we will be applying for an IRG) aims to: 1) Evaluate the role of environmental / lifestyle factors as independent risk factors for CAP in Singapore, and the interaction of their effects with dietary and genetic (receptors, inflammatory and metabolic pathway-related) predispositions; and 2) Prospectively examine the effect of clinical features and histological subtypes on prognosis, and to utilize novel molecular markers to identify critical phenotypic characteristics which correlate with treatment outcome and survival. For Phase One of the study, 200 CAP cases and 200 controls, consisting of patients from the Singapore General Hospital (SGH) and community subjects, will be recruited into the study. Each consenting participant will complete an interviewer-administered questionnaire and provide a 20 ml blood sample or a saliva specimen. If Phase Two can be launched within 12 months from the end of Phase 1 recruitment, the 400 subjects will be added to the larger population-based case-control study The study will provide the opportunity to examine unique exposures and gene-environment interactions in CAP aetiology. It will serve as a framework for other clinical and epidemiologic studies. The study will also serve as a springboard for international collaboration.The proposed study is a Phase One, collaborative and multi-disciplinary approach study which will dovetail to a population-based case control study (Phase Two). The budget requested for the two-year project is $173,000, of which 67% is allocated to manpower costs.
kw: incident prostate cancer cases, case-control study, risk factors

title: A Prospective Study of Dietary and Lifestyle Risk Factors of Hip Fractures among the Elderly in the Singapore Chinese Health Study
abs: The general objective of this project is to understand how dietary and lifestyle factors can influence the incidence of osteoporotic hip fractures in the elderly. In particular, we are interested in foods commonly consumed by the Chinese population such as Chinese tea, soy-based products and dark green vegetables, and lifestyle habits such as smoking, alcohol and physical activity. The study usesprospective data from a residential cohort of 63,257 middle-aged and older (45-74 years) Singapore Chinese men and women accrued between 1993 and 1998, known as the Singapore Chinese Health Study (SCHS). At recruitment, each study subject was interviewed in person by a trained interviewer using a structured questionnaire which emphasized current diet assessed via a validated, 165-itemfood frequency questionnaire. The cohort has been passively followed for death through regular record linkage with the population-based Singapore Registry of Births and Deaths. Hip fractures will be identified using the hospital-based discharge summary database. Since this database covers all admissions into public and private hospitals, and virtually all hip fracture patients do get admitted for treatment, we expect the capture of cases to be highly comprehensive, if not complete. We also intend to verify the accuracy of the linkage by manual review of medical records. The proportional hazards (Cox) regression methods will be used to examine the associations between diet/lifestyle factors and risk of hip fractures in multivariate analyses. Although for scientific and resource constraint reasons, the study only involves Chinese, the findings of the study will benefit all Singaporeans,regardless of ethnicity. Eventually, results from this study will help the health professionals know what and how dietary/lifestyle changes can help reduce incidence of osteoporotic hip fractures among elderly and contribute towards the scientific basis for the drawing up of public health programs on prevention of osteoporosis in an Asian population.
kw: Hip fractures, Diet, Chinese, Osteoporosis, Elderly

title: Development of a vocal cord clip and applicator for laryngeal micro-surgery
abs: Specific AimsTo develop a micro-laryngeal vocal cord clip and applicator (MLVCCA) for use in laryngeal microsurgery.(a)Design and build initial prototypes(b)Evaluate effectiveness and efficiency of prototype devices on an animal model(c)Develop a miniature version of the device that could be translated into clinical use.HypothesisPrimary closure of epithelial incisions during laryngeal microsurgery can be achieved by means of a micro-clip developed from a suitable re-absorbable biomaterial, and the clip can be applied using a suitably designed applicator.MethodologyCollaboration will take place between the Department of Otolaryngology, Singapore General Hospital and the Centre for Biomedical Materials Applications & Technology (BIOMAT), Department of Mechanical Engineering, National University of Singapore. The clinician will direct the concept and specifications of the device relevant to its clinical application. The engineers will direct the choice of materials and building processes, and convert the concepts into a working device.Clinical SignificanceAchieving successful closure of epithelial surfaces is important during endoscopic laryngeal microsurgery to prevent granulation and scar tissue formation, which can adversely affect the voice. Successful development of a micro-laryngeal vocal cord clip and applicator has several advantages over current techniques: (1) It will reduce technical complexity in achieving apposition of epithelial flaps compared to current techniques such as micro-suture. This can reduce surgical time and surgeon frustration, and translate into improved surgical results. (2) A micro-clip will provide more secure closure compared to use of tissue glue. Glue is placed beneath the epithelial surface, and may also have detrimental effects on vibration characteristics of the vocal folds. Use of the MLVCCA can also be extended to secure mucosal grafts endoscopically to underlying tissue during laryngeal microsurgery. This can facilitate mucosal resurfacing where more extensive resection is required, for example in endoscopic excision of laryngeal cancer.
kw: Vocla cord, Microlaryngeal surgery, Biomaterial, Mechatronics, Biomedical engineering, Otolaryngology

title: The Role of Visfatin and Adiponectin in Severely Obese Children with Metabolic Complications
abs: IntroductionStill a paucity of information about the role of visfatin and adiponectin in the pathogenesis of obesity and obesity-related co-morbidities such as diabetes, and the relationship of these two adipocytokines with insulin resistance and adiposity in childhood obesity is still not fully resolved.Hypotheses1.Visfatin and total/high molecular weight adiponectin levels are significantly different between obese children with and without obesity-related co-morbidities, namely glucose intolerance, hypertension, dyslipidemia, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and metabolic syndrome2.Visfatin and total/high molecular weight adiponectin levels correlate with insulin resistance, adiposity, lipid levels, liver enzymes levels, severity of metabolic syndrome, feeding behaviour score, and physical activity level.3.Common genetic variants (polymorphisms) of the visfatin gene are associated with obesity-related co-morbidities, insulin resistance, and lipid levels. Aim1.To examine the relationship between two adipocytokines, visfatin and total/high molecular weight adiponectin, and obesity-related traits and co-morbidities.2.To examine the association of three common genetic polymorphisms of the visfatin gene and obesity-related traits and co-morbidities.MethodOver the past four years, we have recruited 245 severely obese local children (mean age 11 years, mean % ideal weight for height 171%) into our obesity gene study (NMRC/0563/2001), where clinical information, feeding habits, physical activity level, body fat, and biochemical profile have been documented. DNA and serum/plasma were collected and stored for nested case control studies. Commercial assay kits will be used to measure the levels of adipocytokines of interest. For genotyping of common polymorphisms, allele-specific PCR will be performed to identify the g.-948 G>T variant, and either of the two variants g.-1001G>T and g.-423 A>G in linkage disequilibrium. In addition, direct sequencing of the visfatin gene (11 exons) and 2000 bp upstream (putative promoter region) of 20 randomly selected subjects for novel variants will be performed, which maybe further genotyped in the study cohort.
kw: obesity, adipokines, hypertension, childhood, diabetes, hyperlipidemia

title: CNP-modified alginate for cell-based cartilage tissue engineering
abs: Cartilage tissue engineering is based on chondrocytes, the only cell type in articular cartilage. Chondrocytes can be either disassociated from host cartilage or differentiated from stem cells, such as bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs). However, cartilage-derived chondrocytes will lose their type-II collagen expressing phenotype during in vitro expansion and chondrocytes differentiated from MSCs are prone to hypertrophy during long-term culture in vitro or after implantation in vivo. As a result, the phenotypic instability of chondrocytes will eventually lead to fibrocartilage formation or even worse, ossification. Thus it remains a big challenge to obtain sufficient number of chondrocytes and maintain their correct phenotype for engineering hyaline cartilage. The key to these issues are to increase the proliferation of the chondrocytes and inhibit the cells from further differentiation to hypertrophy. We hypothesize that C-type Natriauretic Peptide (CNP), a chondrocyte modulator expressed in growth plate that regulates cartilage growth through chondrocyte proliferation and differentiation, may serve to address these issues. This project aims to incorporate CNP into alginate hydrogel scaffold to continuously prolong the proliferation of chondrocytes and postpone the hypertrophy of these cells. CNP will be first introduced into the medium for long-term high-density culture of rabbit cartilage-derived chondrocytes or bone marrow MSCs-differentiated chondrocytes on MillicellTM filters to evaluate effects of CNP on the proliferation and differentiation of these cells and find out a proper concentration to direct its incorporation into alginate hydrogel. Then CNP will be chemically coupled to alginate and the CNP-modified alginate hydrogel loaded with chondrocytes will be further cultured or transplanted to chondral/osteochondral articular defects in rabbits to evaluate the quality and phenotypic stability of the engineered cartilage tissue. The CNP-modified alginate hydrogel developed from this project will potentially generate better quality and highly stable hyaline cartilage and the system may be translated into human applications.

title: Synthesis and development of 18F-ornithine, an analogue of amino acid ornithine, for imaging of hepatoceullar carcinoma (HCC)
abs: Hepatocellular carcinoma is the third most prevalent malignant tumor in Singapore male., The mortality rate within 12month of diagnosis can reach 90%. Early diagnosis is the key to treatment of HCC.There is an important role for PET at the time of initial diagnosis for cancer staging, primarily due to its highersensitivity for detecting extra-hepatic foci of metastases in areas in which CT has sub-optimal sensitivity, such asmetastases in non-enlarged lymph nodes .So far there is no PET radiopharmaceutical suitable for imaging of HCC. We therefore propose a pilot study todevelop a PET radiopharmaceutical in HCCPolyamine is one of the earliest cellular biochemical pathway leading to cell division. Throughout the entire pathwaythe step during which ornithine is converted to putrescine by ornithine decarboxylase (ODC) is the most crucial andrate limiting step. It has been found that the ODC activity is increased in many cancers.18F-ornithine is a novel molecule designed by the principal investigator. The structure of 18F-ornithine is similar toornithine. It is hypothesized that because 18F-ornithine is taken into tumor cells due to similarity in structure.In this proposed study 18F-ornithine will be synthesized and then incubated with Hep2G cells in vitro to determine itsuptake into HCC cells. The in-vitro uptake studies will be repeated in the presence of DMFO, an ODC inhibitor toconfirm that 18F-ornithine uptake is due to increased activity of ODC. The cell uptake study will also be conducted withincreasing concentration of stable ornithine to confirm that the 18F-ornithine are taken into the tumor cells in the sameway as ornithine. Metaboliite study will also be conducted to confirm that the 18F-ornithine is converted to 18Fputrescineby ODC.Finally animal study will be conducted using micro-PET to verify the results of cell culture works

title: Investigation of gain-of-function of the murine p53 mutant, R246S, by functional genomics
abs: p53 is one of the most frequently mutated tumour suppressor genes in human cancers. Mutant p53 often have lost the properties of the wildtype protein (loss-of-function), exert dominant-negative effects towards its wildtype counterpart and is also thought to possess additional oncogenic activities known as 'gain-of-function'. We are interested in studying the function of a particular p53 'hot-spot' mutant, the R249S, which is found predominantly in liver cancers associated with hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection and aflatoxin exposure. In order to understand the physiological and pathological consequences of this mutation, we have generated 'knock-in' mice harbouring the R246S mutant p53, which is the equivalent of R249S in human p53. We propose here to investigate if the R246S mutant confers specific oncogenic 'gain-of-function' phenotypes during carcinogenesis, by analyzing and comparing global transcriptomes of normal and tumour tissues obtained from p53 and R246S 'knock-in' mice. Since p53 has also been suggested to modulate the tumour stroma, we will also analyse the transcriptomes of mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) to explore the possibility of the 'gain-of-function' mediated in stromal cells. Differences in global expression profiles between p53 and the R246S mutant tissues/cells would indicate the presence of 'gain-of-functions' exerted by the R246S mutant and will also enable the identification of novel candidates mediating the R246S dependent 'gain-of-function'. These candidates will be verified if they are direct mutant p53 targets and further studied in future. Scientifically, this study will provide proof for the presence/absence of 'gain-of-function' by R246S mutant, and the mutant p53 targets will be useful to elucidate the physiological consequences of the 'gain-of-function'. Moreover, expression profiles and the mutant p53 targets identified in this study may be used as biomarkers for evaluating the efficacy of mutant p53 re-activating compounds such as PRIMA-1, in both pre-clinical and clinical studies. Finally, these mutant p53 targets may also be novel targets for developing therapeutic strategies.
kw: Knock-in mice, Cancer, Mutant p53, Gain-of-function

title: Randomised Phase II Study of Metronomic Chemotherapy Plus the Same Aromatase Inhibitor Compared to Metronomic Chemotherapy Alone in Women with Hormone Receptor Positive, Her-2 Non-overexpressing Advanced Breast Cancer Whose Disease has Progressed while Receiving an Aromatase Inhibitor, Correlating Response with Circula
abs: Hypotheses and Clinical SignificanceMetastatic breast cancer (MBC) is an increasing health problem. Standard chemotherapy is non-curative with numerous side effects. An alternative is metronomic (ie continuous low dose) chemotherapy, which is active with low toxicity and exerts antiangiogenic rather than cytotoxic effects. However, the optimal agent, dose and schedule of metronomic chemotherapy is unknown and merits further study. Third generation aromatase inhibitors (AI) are standard therapy for hormone receptor positive, postmenopausal women with MBC and have non-overlapping mechanisms of action and toxicities with metronomic chemotherapy, making their combination ideal for study. We hypothesize that metronomic chemotherapy combined with continued AI has better clinical activity compared to metronomic chemotherapy alone in patients with disease progression on an AI. This will have major significance to women with MBC in helping to delay standard systemic chemotherapy.This study also aims to explore the antiangiogenic activity and optimal biological dose of metronomic chemotherapy by assessing changes in blood biomarkers of with serial introduction of each component of metronomic chemotherapy every 2 weeks.Specific AimsPrimaryTo assess clinical benefit in women treated with metronomic chemotherapy plus an aromatase inhibitor compared to metronomic chemotherapy alone.Secondary1. Time to disease progression and overall survival2. Safety and Toxicity3. Correlation between tumour response and markers of angiogenesis (circulating endothelial progenitor cells (CEPs), VEGF, and VEGFR)4. Contribution of methotrexate and prednisolone to metronomic chemotherapy as assessed by change in CEP levels during serial addition of each drugMethodologyStudy Design Randomized phase II design. Seventy women with hormone receptor positive, Her-2 non over-expressing advanced breast cancer whose disease has progressed while receiving an aromatase inhibitor will be recruited over 2 years.

title: Transglutaminase-mitochondria interactions, new opportunities for strategic intervention in ocular surface diseases
abs: Inflammation, especially chronic inflammation, is a debilitating problem in the ocular surface because of irritation, redness and visual loss. Such diseases range from the common pterygium, dry eye and allergic conjunctivitis to the devastating Steven Johnson syndrome. Because inflammation has many components, it is important to delineate a well-defined biological parameter which can be robustly evaluated. One such area is stress-activated apoptosis or programmed cell death. Apoptosis has been shown to be a major process in diseases like dry eye, where hyperosmolarity is the stimulus.Transglutaminase (TGM)-2 is a multi-functional enzyme that plays important roles in apoptosis and inflammation, and has been shown to be a good therapeutic target in animals. Previously we have shown that UVB stimulation induced apoptosis in human corneal epithelial cells, and that inhibition of TGM function protects against such apoptosis. TGM-2 has sequence similarity to a class of pro-apoptotic Bcl-2 proteins, raising the possibility that it may be a sensor of external stress and mediator of mitochondria-mediated apoptosis. We have also shown that TGM-2 binds several mitochondrial proteins and over-expression of TGM-2 activates caspases 9 and caspase 3. In an ocular context, the mechanism of TGM-2 in mitochondria-mediated apoptosis is unknown.We propose to investigate, in cultured human corneal epithelial cells, the interaction of TGM-2 with mitochondrial elements and the consequential activation of apoptosis. Using a variety of imaging, cell, protein and molecular biology techniques, we will identify mitochondrial molecules that interacts with TGM-2 and are sufficient to cause apoptosis. The results of this study will allow us to investigate intervention of TGM-2 action at the mitochondrial level in murine experimentally-induced dry eye as well as in TGM-2 knock out mice. Eventually, we hope to derive clinically useful, topically applied specific modulators of ocular surface inflammation that produce less adverse effects than currently used corticosteroids.
kw: Inflammation, Apoptosis, Human, Ocular diseases, Mitochondria, Laboratory study

title: The retinal pigment epithelium in the development of experimental myopia in normal and muscarinic receptor knock-out mice
abs: Myopia affects approximately 80% of the population of 17-25 years of age in Singapore1, 2. To date, there are only few targets being identified to prevent progression of myopia. Atropine a pan muscarinic antagonist and pirenzipine a M1 specific muscarinic antagonist have been found effective in clinical trials with children in preventing myopia progression. Our goal is to better characterize the effects of muscarinic antagonist therapy at a cellular and molecular level.Eye growth is sensitive to visual experience, and is altered by both form deprivation and optical defocus. Retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), interposed between retina and choroid, is likely to play a critical role in relaying retinal growth signals to the choroid and sclera. Pigment derived growth factor, PEDF, is a novel substrate for MMP-2 and 9. Up-regulation of MMP-2 activity has been reported in scleral thinning of highly myopic eyes in the tree shrew model of myopia. ROP children often experience myopia. Therefore, one goal of this project will be to determine the role of the RPE in myopia development using the mouse model developed here at SERI.Previously, we have shown that both human and mouse sclera and RPE expressed all five muscarinic receptors (mAChRs). However, the cellular and eventually the molecular site of action of the muscarinic antagonists in myopia are not clear. In addition to the fibroblasts of the scleral, the epithelial cells of the RPE would be another possible target for these agents. The strategy would be to use a mAChRs gene deficient mouse for experimental myopia and RPE cultured cells from the background and knock-out animals to uncover RPE response to myopia. Understanding the specific reaction of each receptor subtype to the muscarinic antagonists treatment could enable us to design or develop an effective and specific drug toward the prevention of myopia.

title: Multi-functional Spintronic Materials and Devices
abs: Although metal-based spintronics has seen unparalleled success in both fundamental research and practical applications in data storage, the lack of capability in charge modulation greatly limits its applications in information processing devices. Just like silicon which has served as the basis for pure charge-based electronics, in order for the spintronics to become a true technology, one also needs to establish a right platform on which the spintronics will flourish. That platform must be built on materials and structures that allow both the charge and spin degrees of freedom to be fully explored for desirable functions. The main objectives of this coordinated program are (1) to synthesis and study the physics of a wide range of exotic materials which allow charge-spin interactions in a controllable fashion and (2) to create multifunctional spintronic devices which have potential applications in both information storage and processing. In the proposed program, we will form a strong team consisting of scientists from the two universities (NUS and NTU) and local RI’s (DSI and IMRE). Through international collaborations, we will also invite prominent scientists from overseas to participate in the program. We believe that the formation of a network will enable us carry out coordinated work of high impact and gain an international reputation in the area of spintronics. title: Combined-cycle Solar Energy Self-sustaining Membrane Distillation (MD) and Membrane Distillation Bioreactor (MDBR) Water Production and Recycling System
abs: This proposal aims to achieve a ‘zero-energy’ green water recycling facility using solar energy. The recycling system uses the solar energy to power a patented membrane distillation bioreactor (MDBR) system as well as a MD system for desalination. The bioreactor relies on the thermophilic bacteria to digest organic matters in the sludge. Appropriate heat from the solar harnessing and storage system will be used to keep the micro-organisms active and to provide sufficient temperature difference for the distillation to take place in the membrane. Distillation occurs due to water vapour passing through the membrane and condensing because of the cooler circulating water. Both the photovoltaic and solar thermal energy are to be exploited to maximize the energy per unit area that can be harnessed from the sun so as to optimize the usage of space. Advance thermal energy storage using phase change materials and electric energy conversion and storage system will be researched and applied. Singapore, situated near to the equator has an annual average of 5-6kWhr/m2/day of solar energy. The PV cells efficient are typically 15-18% while solar thermal is 70-80%. With the proper design and sizing of the thermal and electric energy storage system, the challenge is to keep the combined-cycle MD and MDBR systems running continuously 24 hours a day at ‘zero’ running cost.

title: Graphene Related Materials and Devices
abs: The proposed program aims to conduct original and high impact research on graphene-related materials by forming a focus group comprising of materials chemist, physicists and electronic engineers. The program is motivated by rapid breakthroughs in graphene recently, which includes the discovery of room temperature quantum Hall effect, the graphene single electron transistor (SET), and the bipolar superconducting transistor. The continuous miniaturization of silicon chips impose physical limits on device performance which will demand new paradigm shift in materials and circuit design. It is timely for Singapore to establish a focus research team to examine graphene and related materials as an electronic, spintronic and photovoltaic materials. There are challenging problems to be solved before grapheme can be used in logic applications. For mainstream logic applications, the fact that graphene remains metallic even at the neutrality point is a major problem. Our strategies include designing and synthesizing tailored-made graphene with novel structures and composition in order to increase the band gap ΔE, and to impart interesting magnetic properties. For example, for single-layer graphene, ΔE can be induced by spatial confinement or lateral-superlattice potential. Physical methods include the epitaxial growth of single layer graphene on top of crystals with matching lattices such as diamond(111), boron nitride or SiC[1]. Chemical strategies include the synthesis of graphyne and graphdiyne molecules which can form ordered two dimensional crystals at the solid substrate, allowing (sub)molecular scale visualization and electron transporting studies; the ethyne units allow further chemical functionalizations so that complexation with metals will give a series of new materials for wide range of optoelectronic and photovoltaic applications, which will be considered in this project. We will also consider alternative routes to graphene-based electronics by considering graphene not only as a new channel material for field-effect transistors (FET), but also as a conductive sheet, in which various nanometre-size structures can be carved to make (SET) circuitry. Unlike other materials, graphene nanostructures are stable down to true nanometre sizes, allowing the exploration of length scales between SET and molecular electronics. The advantage is that everything including conducting channels, quantum dots, barriers and interconnects can be cut out from a graphene sheet. Using lithographic methods, we will attempt to make and study the operation of spin torque transistor (STT), which operates analogously to a conventional transistor, but with spin bias and spin currents taking the place of charge currents. title: Molecular signature prediction of lymph node metastasis in breast cancer
abs: BackgroundBreast cancer is the most common female malignancy in Singapore. The principle cause of mortality in breast cancer is distant metastasis. Tumor size and lymph node positivity were classically used as prognostic factors for relapse risks. However, up to 30% of lymph node negative patients eventually develop metastasis. Microarray studies in breast cancer have sought to classify patients based on genes expressed in the primary tumor with the prognosis of the patients (metastasis free or overall survival). The treatment received and the genes mediating aggressiveness (earlier manifestation of metastasis) also influenced patient outcomes. Development of metastases is complex and include the ability to migrate from the primary tumor, survival in blood or lymphatic circulation, invasion of distant tissues and establishment of distant metastatic nodules. Aims and MethodsWe propose studying small breast cancers less than 2 cm where metastasis to regional lymph nodes is generally uncommon (about 20% of our patients). Our hypothesis is that these small tumors have acquired the ability to metastasize as an early event in carcinogenesis. Comparison of genes expressed in these small tumors with (n=30) and without (n=30) lymph node metastasis could provide information on previously unknown genes involved in the metastatic process and possibly predict the behavior of tumors detected at an early stage. Clinicopathological data for patients will be collected including immunohistochemical biomarkers. Expression profiling will be performed using the Affymetrix Exon 1.0 ST Array. The gene expression profiles would be subsequently validated on another set of 30 breast cancers. Clinical SignificanceThe potential implications includes identifying breast cancer patients with a small primary tumor but have a high risk of lymph node metastasis in whom a full axillary dissection may be required after sentinel lymph node identification. In addition, this may help to optimise decision making for adjuvant therapy options in patients who are at higher risks
kw: breast cancer, microarray, metastasis, molecular prediction, clinicopathological correlation

title: Development of DNA methylation into a diagnostic tool
abs: Background: Molecular diagnostics involves the application of molecular characteristics found to have diagnostic potential in the laboratory to clinical practice. As such, it is one of the cornerstones of translational medicine. However, the development of candidate molecules from “bench-to-bedside” is not trivial, as shown by their low conversion rate to clinical markers, despite reports on their clinical value. Recently, DNA methylation of tumor suppressor genes has been implicated as one of the earliest molecular alterations in tumorigenesis, suggesting its utility in predicting cancer risk and early cancer detection. However, the supporting evidence often comprises studies of small sample sizes and assays difficult to standardize. General Hypothesis: DNA methylation can be developed into a diagnostic tool, especially in the clinical practice of oncology.Aims: To develop DNA methylation into a diagnostic tool, we aim to:1. Use cervical neoplasia as a disease model, and compare the feasibility, sensitivity and specificity of DNA methylation analysis of >1000 cervical smear samples with conventional cytological assessment and human papilloma virus (HPV) serotyping in predicting the risk for developing cervical cancer.2. Optimize a system for multi-gene methylation detection on custom-designed molecular diagnostic instrumentation.Methodology: Cervical cancer risk prediction has strategically been chosen as the initial application model, due to the ready availability of diagnostic samples (cervical smear samples), recognized diagnostic standards (cytology, HPV serotyping), research evidence and investigator enthusiasm.We have 1) a team of clinicians and scientists with skills and jurisdiction to enable clinical implementation, 2) access to a large series of diagnostic samples (cervical smear samples), 3) assays to maximize accuracy (e.g. pyrosequencing, Methylight)4) an alliance with a leading molecular diagnostic instrument manufacturer. When developed, this diagnostic system may be extended to other non-invasive samples and cancer types, providing significant advances in the fields of cancer risk prediction and early cancer detection.
kw: DNA methylation, molecular diagnostics, translational medicine, Pap smear, multiplex high-throughput, cervical neoplasia as disease model

title: Artificial Mesoscopic Structures for Next Generation Electronic and Photonic Technology
abs: A new era in electronics and photonics is emerging in which naturally occurring materials used to manage electrons or light can be augmented by man-made materials which we refer to here as artificial mesoscopic structures. They are capable of confining, guiding, dispersing and modulating the flow of photons and electrons in radically different ways, thereby providing new opportunities for the control and transfer of information. These structures, with critical dimensions ranging from a few to hundreds of nanometers, are referred to as “mesoscopic” because the dimensions are on the order of the wavelength of electrons or photons, at which scale quantum effects are important and the electron-photon and photon-photon interactions are greatly enhanced. Specifically, plasmonic effects in nanoscale structures and photonic crystal structures which provide stop bands and dramatic dispersive effects, determined primarily by the “crystal” pattern employed, provide a rich source of component and device technology. In addition to the embryonic fields of nanoplasmonics and photonic crystals, new developments in super-resolution imaging using negative index (meta-) materials as well as engineering quantum confinement for improved low threshold sources and lower noise detectors are emerging, lending themselves to integration with plasmonic and photonic crystal components. The exploitation of these structures and effects will impact the industry with the brought major benefits: - A wide range of photonic devices with novel functionalities for an ideal photonic chip that is not only small, but also efficient and capable of high-speed operation and complex electro-optic signal processing. - Artificial materials with new properties due to strong electron-photon interaction, such as meta-materials that has a negative refractive index for electromagnetic waves at certain frequencies, creating the possibility for super-resolution imaging. - Convergence of electronics and photonics that creates potential for order-of-magnitude improvement in device performance and functionality, and provides potential solutions to significant problems, such as optical interconnect for inter- and intra-chip communication bottleneck.

title: Expression of poor prognostic markers in matched primary and metastatic breast tissue
abs: Breast cancer is the commnest cancer in women, with the majority of patients presenting with metastasis in regional lymph nodes eventually succumbing at distant sites. Recent work in gene expression has shown that poor prognostic expression profile is present in the primary tumour at the time of presentation, suggesting its use in selecting patients for adjuvent therapy. The sentinel node biopsy has been validated in breast cancer, the status of the sentinel node accurately reflecting the status of the axillary nodes. As the node is often the only positive node in axilla, these lymph nodes represent the first site of metastasis, and can be reliably obtained. Our hypothesis is that metastasis cancer cells in these nodes have patterns of gene expression that are distinct from their primary origins, and futher changes in gene expression have occurred in non-sentinel node metastasis that have propagated the progressive spread of disease. The aim of our study is to assess the gene expression profile of matched primary tumour, sentinel node metastasis and non node metastasis. This will be carried out by obtaining fresh frozen tissue from primary at diagnostic biopsy , and sentinel and non- sentinel tissue at time of definitive surgery. The identification of genes products associated with metastasis will provide potential targets for therapy; in addition, the changein gene expression profile may also explain the failure in systemic adjuvent therapy, which to date has been based on the predicted sensitivity of the primary tumou.

title: Isolation And Characterization Stem Cells From Human Endometriotic And Endometrial Tissues
abs: Endometriosis is a major cause of debilitating chronic pelvic pain, dyspareunia, and infertility. Theaetiology of this multifactorial disease remains elusive.We have been working on the NMRC research projects, NMRC/0311/1998, and successfully identifed76 differentially expressed genes between autologous endometriotic and endometrial tissues.Notably, the clustering on the expression ratios of 76 genes in the paired samples segregated the 15cases into two major clusters exhibiting a transition from over-expression to under-expression as theseverity of endometriosis progressed from early to late stage. It is possible that some of the genesidentified thus far are exhibits of endometrial stem cells or their progenitor cells.Current evidence indicates that stem cells exist in many adult tissues. We hypothesized thatendometriosis is a disease of ectopic proliferation of endometrial stem cells. Women who have alarger than normal population of endometrial stem cells disseminate a large number of endometrialprogenitor cells to the peritoneum or other anatomical sites. And alterations of endometriotic stemcells gene expression are believed to underpin the pathogenesis of endometriosis.The main purpose of this study is to identify and characterise the population of cells exhibiting adultstem cell activity in tissues obtained from endometrium and endometriosis. Specifically, the studyaims to:1. To isolate and culture the stem cell from human endometrial and endometriotic tissues, anddetermine their stem cell activities in vitro.2. To compare the population size and gene expression profile of endometrial stem cells in theendometrium between women with and without endometriosis.3. To compare the population size and gene expression profile of endometrial stem cells in theendometrium and endometriosis tissues obtained from the same patient.Isolating and characterising human endometrial stem cells would be a breakthrough for future studiesof many endometrial diseases and infertility. More specifically, the findings in this study would providean insight into the causation of endometriosis. It may also provide a basis for innovative therapy ofendometriosis and other endometrial diseases.
